name: Ideal Reconstruction Function for 3D Splatting
head: Optimized 3D splat filter, Tri-cubic reconstruction kernel
body: The Ideal Reconstruction Function for 3D Splatting is a rotationally symmetric, compact-support kernel designed to reconstruct 3D volume data via splatting with minimal visible artifacts. It solves the problem of "Mach bands" and visible individual splat boundaries that occur when approximating smooth volume data with polygon collections or non-optimized kernels. Unlike Gaussian splats, this kernel has a well-defined finite overlap extent and goes to zero in a minimum extent, providing high-quality smooth overlap from any viewing direction at the cost of higher performance penalties for large screen-space splats. It is distinct from its siblings by being mathematically optimized to minimize the relative variance of a constant cube reconstruction in 3D, rather than relying on standard spline continuity constraints alone. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid with intensity values; a viewing direction; a splat center (0,0,0) in local coordinates. Output: A 3D reconstruction kernel function h(x,y,z) and its 2D projected footprint f(x,y) for rasterization. Data Structures: The kernel is defined by two scalar parameters s and t, and two cubic polynomial coefficient sets. t: Support radius (outer boundary). s: Transition radius (inner boundary). g(r): Radial function dependent on r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}. Parameters: Support radius t = 1.556228. Transition radius s = 0.889392. Inner polynomial coefficients (derived from optimization): a=0.557526, b=-1.157743, c=0.671033. Outer polynomial coefficients (derived from optimization): d=0.067599, e=-0.282474. Method Steps: 1. Calculate the radial distance r from the splat center for any point (x,y,z): r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} 2. Evaluate the kernel value h(x,y,z) using the radial function g(r): If 0 < r \le s: g(r) = 0.557526 - 1.157743 r^2 + 0.671033 r^3 If s < r \le t: g(r) = 0.067599 (r - t)^2 - 0.282474 (r - t)^3 If r > t: g(r) = 0 Note: The kernel is C^1 continuous at the origin and at the transition point s. 3. To rasterize, compute the 2D footprint f(x,y) by integrating the 3D kernel along the view direction (z-axis): f(x,y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x,y,z) \, dz This integral has a closed-form solution because h is composed of low-degree polynomials in r^2+z^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def idealreconstructionkernel(x, y, z): """ Computes the value of the ideal 3D reconstruction kernel at (x, y, z). Parameters are fixed constants from the optimization in. """ # Constants t = 1.556228 s = 0.889392 # Calculate radial distance rsq = xx + yy + zz r = rsq 0.5 # Evaluate piecewise polynomial if r > t: return 0.0 elif r <= s: # Inner region: a + br^2 + cr^3 # a = 0.557526, b = -1.157743, c = 0.671033 return 0.557526 - 1.157743 rsq + 0.671033 (rsq r) else: # Outer region: d(r-t)^2 + e(r-t)^3 # d = 0.067599, e = -0.282474 diff = r - t return 0.067599 (diff diff) - 0.282474 (diff diff diff) def computefootprint(x, y): """ Computes the 2D footprint f(x,y) by integrating h(x,y,z) over z. The closed-form integral of the piecewise cubic radial function is required. Not given in the sources. """ pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mach Bands: Using polygon approximations (15-21 triangles) for splats causes visible Mach bands and individual splat visibility because they do not overlap smoothly. This kernel eliminates this by providing smooth, analytic overlap. Precision: The maximum relative deviation from the mean for a constant cube reconstruction is small (0.00534), but intensities may need scaling to maintain accuracy in 8-bit color buffers. Viewing Direction: The kernel is rotationally symmetric, ensuring accuracy from any viewing direction, unlike axis-aligned approximations. Time Complexity: Evaluating the kernel is O(1) per sample. Computing the 2D footprint requires a closed-form integral, which is also O(1) but involves more complex arithmetic than simple polynomial evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) as it is a parametric function. Performance: Higher performance penalty for large screen-space splats compared to Gaussian splats due to the finite support and complex footprint calculation. Quality: Minimizes relative variance of constant cube reconstruction to 0.00119. Maximum projected footprint deviation is approximately 1/256 of the mean, fitting within 8-bit color accuracy. When to use: When high-quality, artifact-free volume rendering is required and polygon-based splatting is insufficient. When not to use: When performance is critical and large screen-space splats are common, or when infinite support (Gaussian) is acceptable for smoother falloff. The method was developed by Laur and Hanrahan, building on Max's 2D ideal reconstruction function [Max92]. While Max's function was designed for 2D image reconstruction, Laur and Hanrahan extended it to 3D signals to replace polygon approximations of splats in volume rendering. The optimization minimizes the relative variance of a constant cube reconstruction, ensuring smooth overlap from any viewing direction. It was implemented using the fast compositing hardware of the SGI VGX. name: SPH Kernel Implementation
head: SPH Kernels
body: The SPH Kernel Implementation provides a polymorphic interface for evaluating Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) kernels, supporting both CPU and GPU execution for density calculation and voxelization. It is distinguished from other splatting kernels by its specific focus on particle-based fluid simulation data structures, utilizing closed-form expressions for kernel values and derivatives in 3D. Unlike general-purpose splatting kernels that may assume isotropic Gaussian or B-spline footprints, this implementation supports specific SPH families (B-splines and Wendland functions) and includes an anisotropic variant for fluid surface rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Particle position \mathbf{x}i, smoothing length h, particle mass m, and kernel type identifier. For anisotropic rendering, the anisotropy matrix \mathbf{H} is also required. Output: Kernel value W(\mathbf{x}) and its spatial derivative \nabla W(\mathbf{x}) at a query point (e.g., voxel center). Data Structures: The implementation uses a polymorphic interface class structure. Concrete implementations store the kernel parameters (e.g., support radius R) and provide methods for evaluation. The voxelization process relies on a kd-tree for neighbor search. Supported Kernels: The module implements the following kernels, each with closed-form 3D expressions for value and derivative: 1. Cubic B-spline 2. Quintic B-spline 3. Wendland C2 4. Wendland C4 5. Wendland C6 6. Wendland C8 Algorithm Steps: 1. Distance Calculation: Compute the Euclidean distance r = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\| or the Mahalanobis distance q = \| \mathbf{H} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i) \| / h for anisotropic cases. 2. Normalization Check: If r > h (or q > 1 for normalized anisotropic forms), return 0. 3. Kernel Evaluation: Evaluate the specific polynomial piecewise function based on the selected kernel type. 4. Derivative Calculation: Compute the gradient \nabla W using the closed-form derivative expression for the selected kernel. 5. Density Bias Correction: Apply density bias correction based on particle mass and smoothing length if computing density. Formulas: For the standard isotropic SPH rendering kernel (commonly used for fluid surfaces), the formulation is: \hat{W}(q) = (1 - q^2)^3+ where q = \frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\|}{h} and (\cdot)+ = \max(\cdot, 0). The normalization constant is C3 = \frac{64}{64\pi} (as cited in source text, though standard normalization for this kernel form typically implies a different constant; the source explicitly states C3 = \frac{64}{64\pi}). For the anisotropic symmetric formulation, the kernel value is computed as: \hat{W}(\|H \cdot x{ij}\|) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \hat{W}(\|Hi \cdot x{ij}\|) + \hat{W}(\|Hj \cdot x{ij}\|) \right) where H is the anisotropy matrix, x{ij} = \mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}j, and |H| is the determinant of H. Parameters: Smoothing Length (h): For isotropic formulation, hi = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3 Nh Vi}{4\pi}} where Vi is the rest volume and Nh = 50 for the cubic spline kernel. Kernel Type: Enumerated type selecting between B-spline and Wendland variants. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatesphkernel(positionquery, particlepos, smoothinglength, kerneltype, anisotropymatrix=None): """ Evaluates the SPH kernel value and derivative. Args: positionquery: Vector3, query point (e.g., voxel center). particlepos: Vector3, particle center. smoothinglength: Float, h. kerneltype: Enum, e.g., 'CUBICBSPLINE', 'WENDLANDC2'. anisotropymatrix: Matrix3x3, optional. If provided, uses anisotropic formulation. Returns: Tuple (value, gradient) """ # 1. Calculate distance metric if anisotropymatrix is not None: # Anisotropic case: Mahalanobis distance diff = positionquery - particlepos # Note: Source uses H xij. Assuming H is applied to the vector. # For symmetric formulation, this is handled at a higher level (see Anisotropic SPH Kernel). # Here we assume a single-particle evaluation with its own H. transformeddiff = anisotropymatrix @ diff q = transformeddiff.norm() / smoothinglength else: # Isotropic case: Euclidean distance diff = positionquery - particlepos r = diff.norm() q = r / smoothinglength # 2. Compact support check if q > 1.0: return (0.0, Vector3(0, 0, 0)) # 3. Evaluate kernel value and derivative based on type # Closed-form expressions are specific to each kernel. # Example for Rendering Kernel (1-q^2)^3+ if kerneltype == 'RENDERINGKERNEL': # Value val = (1.0 - q2)3 # Derivative dW/dr = dW/dq dq/dr # dW/dq = 3(1-q^2)^2 (-2q) = -6q(1-q^2)^2 # dq/dr = 1/h dWdq = -6.0 q (1.0 - q2)2 grad = (dWdq / smoothinglength) (diff / r) if r > 0 else Vector3(0,0,0) return (val, grad) # Other kernels (Cubic B-spline, Wendland C2, etc.) would have their own # closed-form branches here. else: # Placeholder for other closed-form implementations # Implement specific polynomial pieces for Cubic B-spline, Quintic B-spline, # Wendland C2, C4, C6, C8 as defined in. pass An extension of the standard SPH kernel that uses an anisotropy matrix \mathbf{H} to create an ellipsoidal support domain, addressing issues with fluid surface rendering where isotropic support leads to artifacts. It employs a symmetric formulation averaging the kernel evaluation of two interacting particles to ensure consistency. It is used specifically for fluid surface rendering, while the simulation itself may remain isotropic. Time Complexity: O(1) per kernel evaluation. Neighbor search complexity depends on the underlying data structure (kd-tree), typically O(\log N) for search. Memory Complexity: Low, as kernels are stateless functions. The kd-tree requires O(N) space. Strengths: Closed-form derivatives allow for efficient gradient-based operations (e.g., in density calculation or voxelization). Support for multiple kernel types (B-spline, Wendland) provides flexibility for different simulation requirements. Limitations: Anisotropic kernels require non-cubic cells in spatial data structures, complicating neighborhood queries. The source notes a potential ambiguity in the normalization constant for the rendering kernel (C3 = \frac{64}{64\pi}). When to use: When visualizing SPH simulation data, particularly fluid surfaces, where accurate density estimation or smooth voxelization is required. The implementation is based on the C++ module defined in [Bös25], providing a polymorphic interface for SPH kernels. The voxelization algorithm extends the method described in [Pri07] to support 3D voxels. The anisotropic formulation for fluid surface rendering is based on [OVSM98] and [YT13], with symmetric gathering/scattering derived from [HK89]. name: Texture Stretch Weighting
head: wTS Calculation
body: Texture Stretch Weighting (w{TS}) is a weighting term used in point-based neural rendering to compensate for artifacts introduced by weighted average pooling when handling view-dependent effects. It specifically penalizes pixels at grazing angles, thereby increasing the influence of more front-facing views in the final composite. It is distinct from sibling methods like EWA Splatting, which focuses on spatial footprint adaptation, by operating as a scalar weight modifier rather than a geometric projection technique. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The covariance matrix \Sigma of the splat kernel G for a point reprojected into the novel view. Output: A scalar weight w{TS} \in [0, 1] representing the penalty for texture stretch. Data Structures: The method relies on the eigenvalues of the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma derived from the projection of the point's 3D covariance into the image plane. Let \lambda1 and \lambda2 be the eigenvalues of \Sigma, such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge 0. Formula: The weight is calculated as the ratio of the smaller eigenvalue to the larger eigenvalue: w{TS} = \frac{\lambda2}{\lambda1} Where: \lambda1 is the largest eigenvalue of the splat covariance matrix. \lambda2 is the smallest eigenvalue of the splat covariance matrix. Steps: 1. Compute the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma for the splat kernel G at the current pixel location in the novel view. 2. Calculate the eigenvalues \lambda1 and \lambda2 of \Sigma. 3. Compute w{TS} using the ratio \lambda2 / \lambda1. 4. Combine w{TS} with the covariance smoothing weight w{CS} and the probabilistic depth weight w{PD} to form the final weight w: w = w{CS} \cdot w{TS} \cdot w{PD} Parameters: No explicit tuning parameters are defined for w{TS} itself; it is derived directly from the geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Splat: If \lambda1 = 0 (a point with zero extent), the ratio is undefined. In practice, a small epsilon should be added to the denominator to prevent division by zero. Grazing Angles: As the view becomes grazing, the splat stretches, causing \lambda1 \gg \lambda2. This drives w{TS} toward 0, effectively discarding the contribution of that point/view, which is the intended behavior. This is not a separate algorithmic variant but the aggregation step where w{TS} is multiplied with other weights. The final weight w is the product of the covariance smoothing weight w{CS}, the texture stretch weight w{TS}, and the probabilistic depth weight w{PD}. This product is used in the weighted average pooling operation to encode inductive bias for visibility and allow for temporal smoothing. Time and Memory Complexity: The computation of eigenvalues for a 2x2 matrix is O(1) and requires minimal memory overhead. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: It effectively mitigates artifacts in weighted average pooling caused by view-dependent effects by down-weighting stretched (grazing) splats. It improves temporal stability in interactive scenarios. Limitations: It relies on the accuracy of the covariance estimation. It does not handle occlusion directly (that is the role of w{PD}). When to use it: Use this method when performing point-based neural rendering with per-view optimization where view-dependent effects are present and weighted average pooling is used to aggregate features. The method was introduced by Georgios Kopanas, Julien Philip, Tobias Leimkühler, and George Drettakis in the paper "Point-Based Neural Rendering with Per-View Optimization". It addresses the issue that standard weighted average pooling can lead to artifacts when view-dependent effects are present, by introducing a penalty for texture stretch. name: Significant Voxel Extraction
head: Yagel et al. Significant Voxel Extraction
body: Significant Voxel Extraction is a preprocessing technique for volume splatting that accelerates rendering by extracting and storing only the most visually significant voxels, thereby preventing the traversal and processing of the entire volume raster. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Occupancy Voxel Creation by focusing on visual contribution (significance) rather than mere geometric presence, and from Binary Voxel RLE Encoding by selecting a sparse subset for rendering rather than compressing the full grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dense scalar volume dataset V of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Output: A sparse list or structure containing only the indices and values of "significant" voxels. Data Structures: The output is typically a list of tuples or a sparse array format containing: 1. Voxel coordinates (i, j, k). 2. Scalar value v at that coordinate. 3. (Optional) Precomputed significance metric if used for filtering. Steps: 1. Iterate: Traverse the input volume V to access every voxel. 2. Evaluate Significance: For each voxel, determine its visual significance. While the specific metric is not detailed in the provided source, it generally involves evaluating the voxel's contribution to the final image, such as opacity or gradient magnitude. 3. Threshold: Compare the significance metric against a predefined threshold. Voxels below the threshold are considered insignificant and are discarded. 4. Store: If a voxel's significance exceeds the threshold, store its coordinates and value in the output structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractsignificantvoxels(volume, threshold): """ Extracts voxels with significance above a threshold. Args: volume: 3D array of scalar values. threshold: Float value representing the minimum significance required. Returns: list of tuples: [(x, y, z, value),...] """ significantvoxels = [] # Iterate over all voxels in the volume for z in range(volume.shape[2]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[0]): value = volume[z, y, x] # Calculate significance metric # Note: The specific formula for "visual significance" is not # provided in the source. It is assumed to be a function of # the voxel value or its local gradient. significance = computesignificance(volume, x, y, z) # Check if voxel is significant if significance > threshold: significantvoxels.append((x, y, z, value)) return significantvoxels def computesignificance(volume, x, y, z): """ Placeholder for the specific significance metric. Common metrics include opacity transfer function output or gradient magnitude. """ # Implementation detail: This function must be defined by the # specific application's transfer function or gradient calculation. # For example, if using opacity: # return transferfunction(volume[z, y, x]) return volume[z, y, x] # Simplified assumption for structure Parameters: Threshold: The cutoff value for significance. Not given in the sources. Significance Metric: The function used to determine visual importance. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If the significance metric involves floating-point operations, precision errors near the threshold may cause inconsistent culling. Boundaries: Edge voxels may have lower significance due to partial volume effects or lack of neighbors, potentially leading to unintended culling of boundary details. Degenerate Input: Empty regions in the volume will naturally be excluded, which is the desired behavior. Constructs representative sparse voxel subsets using cumulative histograms to threshold scalar quantities like gradient magnitude. It differs from other methods by using histogram-based thresholding for controlled subset selection rather than direct eigenvalue comparison. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of voxels in the input volume, as every voxel must be evaluated to determine significance. Memory Complexity: O(K) where K is the number of significant voxels, where K \le N. Performance: Accelerates rendering by reducing the number of splats processed. The source notes that splatting is inherently faster than ray-casting, and this method further optimizes it by culling non-contributing voxels. Strengths: Reduces rendering cost by avoiding traversal of the entire volume raster. Limitations: Requires a preprocessing step. The quality of the result depends heavily on the definition of "visual significance." When to use: When rendering large volumes where many voxels do not contribute significantly to the final image. When not to use: When the volume is already sparse or when the significance metric is too expensive to compute. The method was introduced by Yagel et al. as a technique to accelerate volume splatting by preprocessing the volume and culling voxels that will not contribute to the final image. It is mentioned in the context of comparing splatting advantages and disadvantages, specifically highlighting the benefit of culling over ray-casting which samples every point along the ray. name: Salient Subset Construction via Cumulative Histograms
head: Representative Subset Construction
body: This method constructs representative sparse voxel subsets (\Gamma and \Lambda) from a dense volume by thresholding scalar quantities (gradient magnitude and negative third eigenvalue) using cumulative histograms. It solves the problem of selecting a controlled percentage of significant voxels for sparse rendering or compression, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like Salient Volume Representation by relying on histogram-based thresholding rather than direct eigenvalue magnitude comparison for subset definition. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset V of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. A target percentage p \in [0, 1] controlling the fraction of voxels to include in the subset. Outputs: Two sparse subsets: \Gamma (selected by gradient magnitude) and \Lambda (selected by negative third eigenvalue). Threshold values T\Gamma and T\Lambda derived from the histograms. Data Structures: Cumulative Histograms: Two arrays, H\Gamma and H\Lambda, storing the cumulative count of voxels up to each bin index. The number of bins is not explicitly specified in the sources [G: Typically determined by the range and resolution of the scalar field, e.g., 256 bins for 8-bit normalized data]. Subset Indices: Lists or bitmasks storing the coordinates of voxels satisfying the threshold condition [G: Standard sparse storage format]. Steps: 1. Compute Scalar Fields: For every voxel v in V, compute: Gradient magnitude: g(v) = ||\nabla V(v)||. Negative third eigenvalue: e(v) = -\lambda3(v), where \lambda3 is the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian matrix of V at v. Note: \lambda3 is typically the most negative eigenvalue for edges/surfaces, so -\lambda3 is positive. 2. Construct Cumulative Histograms: Initialize empty histograms H\Gamma and H\Lambda. Perform one pass through all voxels in V: Bin g(v) into H\Gamma and increment the count. Bin e(v) into H\Lambda and increment the count. Compute cumulative sums for both histograms: H\Gamma[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i} \text{count}\Gamma(j) H\Lambda[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i} \text{count}\Lambda(j) This step runs in linear time O(N) relative to the number of voxels N. 3. Determine Target Voxel Count: Calculate the target number of voxels K for each subset: K = \lceil p \times N \rceil where N = Dx \times Dy \times Dz. 4. Find Threshold via Logarithmic Search: For each histogram (H\Gamma and H\Lambda), perform a binary search (logarithmic time) to find the bin index B such that: H[B-1] < K \le H[B] The bin index B (or the bin boundary value corresponding to B) serves as the threshold T. The sources state "The indices of bins correspond to a threshold," implying the bin index itself or the upper bound of that bin is used as the decision value. 5. Select Voxels: For each voxel v: If g(v) \ge T\Gamma, add v to subset \Gamma. If e(v) \ge T\Lambda, add v to subset \Lambda. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def salientsubsetconstruction(volume, percentagep): """ volume: 3D array of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) percentagep: float between 0 and 1 Returns: subsetgamma, subsetlambda, thresholdgamma, thresholdlambda """ Dx, Dy, Dz = volume.shape N = Dx Dy Dz targetcount = int(percentagep N) # Step 1: Compute scalar fields # Note: Gradient magnitude and Hessian eigenvalues must be computed first. # This is assumed to be done by a helper function not detailed here. gradientmagnitude = computegradientmagnitude(volume) negativeeigenvalue = computenegativethirdeigenvalue(volume) # Step 2: Construct cumulative histograms # Assuming scalar values are normalized to [0, 1] and binned into 256 bins. numbins = 256 histgamma = np.zeros(numbins) histlambda = np.zeros(numbins) for x in range(Dx): for y in range(Dy): for z in range(Dz): gval = gradientmagnitude[x, y, z] eval = negativeeigenvalue[x, y, z] # Bin values (clamp to [0, numbins-1]) bing = int(gval numbins) bine = int(eval numbins) histgamma[bing] += 1 histlambda[bine] += 1 # Cumulative sums cumgamma = np.cumsum(histgamma) cumlambda = np.cumsum(histlambda) # Step 4: Find thresholds via binary search # Find smallest index i such that cum[i] >= targetcount thresholdidxgamma = np.searchsorted(cumgamma, targetcount) thresholdidxlambda = np.searchsorted(cumlambda, targetcount) # The threshold value is the bin index (or corresponding scalar value) # Sources say "indices of bins correspond to a threshold" thresholdgamma = thresholdidxgamma thresholdlambda = thresholdidxlambda # Step 5: Select voxels subsetgamma = [] subsetlambda = [] for x in range(Dx): for y in range(Dy): for z in range(Dz): gval = gradientmagnitude[x, y, z] eval = negativeeigenvalue[x, y, z] bing = int(gval numbins) bine = int(eval numbins) if bing >= thresholdgamma: subsetgamma.append((x, y, z)) if bine >= thresholdlambda: subsetlambda.append((x, y, z)) return subsetgamma, subsetlambda, thresholdgamma, thresholdlambda Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The binning process loses precision. The threshold is discrete, so the actual percentage of voxels included may slightly deviate from p. Degenerate Input: If the volume has constant values, histograms will have a single non-zero bin, potentially leading to all voxels being included or excluded depending on p. Boundary Conditions: Gradient and eigenvalue computations at volume boundaries require careful handling (e.g., zero-padding or reflection). Defines salience via the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian, selecting voxels based on second-order derivatives. Choose this when shape fidelity of boundaries is critical. Differs from this method by not using cumulative histograms for subset selection. Time Complexity: O(N) for histogram construction, where N is the number of voxels. The eigenvalue computation is significantly more expensive than gradient magnitude; sources report eigenvalue computation is on average 2.7 times more expensive than gradient magnitude computation on a Pentium III 800 MHz. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the volume and intermediate scalar fields. Histograms require O(B) space, where B is the number of bins. Performance: Measured on datasets like CT Head (128x128x113) and MRI Head (256x256x109). Gradient magnitude computation took ~50-75 seconds, while eigenvalue computation took ~140-275 seconds on the specified hardware. Strengths: Linear time construction of subsets; control over subset size via p. Limitations: High computational cost of eigenvalue calculation; discrete thresholding may not yield exact percentage p. Originated in the paper "Salient Representation of Volume Data" (2001). The method is part of a broader effort to create efficient sparse representations for volume rendering, leveraging the fact that significant structural information is concentrated in a small subset of voxels. name: Salient Volume Representation
head: Salient Representation, Salient Representation via Smallest Hessian Eigenvalue, Smallest 2nd order directional derivative method
body: Salient Volume Representation is a sparse volume data construction method that identifies significant voxels by computing the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian matrix of the density function. It solves the problem of efficiently representing object boundaries and narrow solid structures (blobs, lines, sheets) by selecting voxels with large negative second derivatives, thereby conveying shape information with fewer voxels than gradient-based methods. Unlike its sibling Salient Subset Construction via Cumulative Histograms which selects subsets based on cumulative thresholds, this method defines the salience metric itself using second-order directional derivatives, specifically the minimal response direction. Inputs: A 3D volume density function I(x, y, z). Outputs: A set of salient voxels \Lambda (and optionally \Gamma) representing the volume structure. Data Structures: Hessian Matrix H(x0): A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix at each voxel x0. Fields: H{xx}, H{yy}, H{zz} (diagonal second partials), H{xy}, H{xz}, H{yz} (off-diagonal mixed partials). Layout: Stored as 9 floating-point values per voxel during computation. Formulas: The method relies on the Taylor expansion of the density function I at point x0 with displacement \Delta x: I(x0 + \Delta x) \approx I(x0) + \Delta x^T \nabla I(x0) + \Delta x^T H(x0) \Delta x \quad (1) The second-order information is expressed by the symmetric Hessian matrix H: H = \begin{pmatrix} I{xx} & I{xy} & I{xz} \\ I{yx} & I{yy} & I{yz} \\ I{zx} & I{zy} & I{zz} \end{pmatrix} \quad (2) where I{ab} = \frac{\partial^2 I}{\partial a \partial b}. For a fixed x0, the term \Delta x^T H \Delta x gives the second derivative of the density in the direction of \Delta x. The eigenvalues \lambdai of H satisfy H vi = \lambdai vi. The salience is determined by the smallest eigenvalue \lambda3 (most negative). Steps: 1. Compute Gradients: Calculate first-order partial derivatives \nabla I at all voxels using standard finite differences or Gaussian derivatives. 2. Compute Hessian: Calculate second-order partial derivatives (I{xx}, I{yy}, I{zz}, I{xy}, I{xz}, I{yz}) at all voxels. This typically involves convolving the gradient components with a Gaussian kernel to handle noise and define a scale. 3. Eigenvalue Decomposition: For each voxel, compute the eigenvalues of the 3 \times 3 Hessian matrix H. Sort them such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3. 4. Salience Calculation: The salience value for a voxel is defined by the smallest eigenvalue \lambda3. Large negative values indicate strong boundaries (inner side) or narrow structures. 5. Subset Construction: Pass the salience values to the parent method Salient Subset Construction via Cumulative Histograms to generate the final sparse subsets \Gamma and \Lambda based on desired voxel percentages. Parameters: Gaussian Scale: The standard deviation \sigma of the Gaussian kernel used for derivative computation. This acts as a structure detector proportional to the scale. Threshold/Percentage: The target percentage of voxels to retain (e.g., 2%, 4%, 0.67%). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Partial Volume Effect: The method suppresses the partial volume effect because it represents object boundaries by their internal parts (large negative second derivatives) rather than the transition zone. Computational Cost: Computing Hessian eigenvalues is approximately 2.7 times more expensive than computing gradient magnitude. Shape Restrictions: Unlike Frangi or Sato methods, this method enforces no shape restrictions (blob, tubular, sheet-like) and detects structures uniformly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehessianeigenvalues(volume): """ Computes the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian matrix for each voxel. Assumes volume is a 3D numpy array or similar. """ # 1. Compute Gaussian derivatives for Hessian components # Hxx, Hyy, Hzz, Hxy, Hxz, Hyz # In practice, these are convolutions of the volume with Gaussian derivatives. # For implementation from text, we assume a function gaussianderivative3d exists. sigma = 1.0 # Typical scale parameter, not given in sources Hxx = gaussianderivative3d(volume, order=(2,0,0), sigma=sigma) Hyy = gaussianderivative3d(volume, order=(0,2,0), sigma=sigma) Hzz = gaussianderivative3d(volume, order=(0,0,2), sigma=sigma) Hxy = gaussianderivative3d(volume, order=(1,1,0), sigma=sigma) Hxz = gaussianderivative3d(volume, order=(1,0,1), sigma=sigma) Hyz = gaussianderivative3d(volume, order=(0,1,1), sigma=sigma) # 2. Initialize output array for smallest eigenvalues saliencemap = np.zeroslike(volume) # 3. Iterate over voxels to compute eigenvalues # Note: For performance, this is usually vectorized, but here shown explicitly. for x in range(volume.shape[0]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for z in range(volume.shape[2]): # Construct Hessian matrix H H = np.array([ [Hxx[x,y,z], Hxy[x,y,z], Hxz[x,y,z]], [Hxy[x,y,z], Hyy[x,y,z], Hyz[x,y,z]], [Hxz[x,y,z], Hyz[x,y,z], Hzz[x,y,z]] ]) # Compute eigenvalues eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H) # Sort eigenvalues: lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3 eigenvalues.sort() eigenvalues = eigenvalues[::-1] # The salience is the smallest eigenvalue (lambda3) saliencemap[x,y,z] = eigenvalues[2] return saliencemap Time Complexity: Higher than gradient-based methods. Computation of Hessian eigenvalues is approximately 2.7 times more expensive than computing gradient magnitude. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the full Hessian matrix (9 values) per voxel during computation, plus the salience map. Performance: Lobster dataset (120x120x34): Uses 2.01% of voxels for subsets. Vertebra1 and Vertebra2 datasets: Uses 4.03% of voxels for subsets. Tooth dataset: Uses 0.67% of voxels for subsets. Strengths: Uniformly identifies object boundaries and narrow structures without shape restrictions; suppresses partial volume effect; reduces necessary voxel count compared to gradient maxima methods by representing objects only by the internal side of boundaries. Limitations: Higher computational cost; requires careful selection of derivation scale. Usage: Evaluated using direct volume rendering provided by the VolumePro architecture. Origin: Introduced in the paper "Salient Representation of Volume Data" (2001). History: The method was developed to address the limitations of edge and line detectors that required special filters for narrow structures. It unifies boundary and structure detection using second-order derivatives. Comparison: It differs from Frangi and Sato methods by enforcing no shape restrictions. It improves upon gradient-based methods by reducing voxel count while maintaining visual quality. name: Particle and Fluid Simulation
body: Particle and Fluid Simulation methods render dynamic fluids and participating media by treating them as collections of discrete particles that are splatted onto the image plane. This approach solves the problem of efficiently visualizing complex, time-evolving fluid dynamics and gaseous volumes without the memory overhead of dense volumetric grids. It sets itself apart from its siblings like Billboards and particles and Screen-Space Fluid Rendering Pipeline by explicitly simulating physical particle properties (position, velocity, density) and projecting them as splats, rather than relying solely on pre-defined textures or screen-space thickness accumulation. The Particle and Fluid Simulation family shares the fundamental mechanism of decomposing a continuous fluid or medium into a set of discrete particles, each carrying physical properties (position, velocity, density) and visual attributes (color, opacity, normal). These particles are transformed into screen space and rasterized using splatting techniques, accumulating their contributions to form the final image. 1. Particle Representation: The fluid or medium is represented by a set of particles Pi. Each particle i is defined by its position \mathbf{p}i, velocity \mathbf{v}i, and visual parameters such as radius ri, color \mathbf{c}i, and opacity \alphai. In Gaussian splatting variants, particles are modeled as 3D Gaussians with a mean position and a covariance matrix \Sigmai. 2. Simulation and Update: Particle positions and properties are updated over time using physics-based simulations, such as Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH), Position-Based Dynamics (PBD), or grid-coupled methods. For example, in PBF, constraints are solved to maintain incompressibility and surface tension. 3. Splatting and Projection: Each particle is projected onto the 2D image plane. For Gaussian particles, the covariance matrix is transformed by the view and projection matrices to determine the 2D footprint (ellipsoid) on the screen. The contribution of each particle to a pixel is calculated based on its kernel function. 4. Compositing: Particle contributions are accumulated to form the final image. Standard alpha blending is used for transparency. However, for specific effects like fluid thickness or foam intensity, additive blending may be employed to accumulate density or intensity values before final compositing. 5. Hybrid Approaches: Some methods combine particle simulations with grid-based velocity projections to improve stability and performance, switching between density volume display and Signed-Distance Field (SDF) raycasting for rendering. Billboards and particles are a method for approximating participating media effects or complex geometry (such as forests) using 2D semi-transparent textures that always face the camera. This approach is primarily chosen for its low computational cost, making it suitable for real-time rendering in industrial simulators and video games where performance is critical. Unlike higher-fidelity volume rendering techniques, it sacrifices geometric accuracy and parallax richness for speed, relying on pre-defined textures or rule-based particle systems. Rendering of spray, foam, and bubble particles advected by fluid, using modified additive splatting with specific kernels and intensities. A post-processing step to enhance fluid realism by synthesizing spray, foam, and bubble particles. Splat particles into foam intensity image using modified additive splatting. Use different kernels for different particle types. Apply a curve to the foam intensity image to scale it into [0, 1] and compose it with rendering. Generate fluid-air mixtures at the crest of the wave. Generate fluid-air mixtures in the impact zone. Foam particle intensity: Larger overall intensity to increase visibility. Spray particle intensity: Smaller intensity to make them less prominent. Bubble particle kernel: Hollow circle structure for convincing underwater appearance. Kernel radius: Typically 2 pixels, scaled based on particle depth in view. Renders dynamic particle-based fluids using ellipsoids splatting, modeling reflection via PBR and refraction via thickness-dependent diffuse color using Beer's Law. Generate spherical fluid Gaussian kernels at each fluid particle. Set initial covariance Ap by particle radius. Set normal np to the surface normal of the nearest surface fluid particle from PBF simulation. Compute fluid thickness τ from modified splatting pipeline using additive blending instead of alpha blending. Shade deformed Gaussian kernels with material {dp, sp, ρp} using Eq. (4) and splat into image cbg. Re-engineer nearly-soft shadows into the system. Combine cbg (solids/background) and cfluid (fluids) to achieve final rendering result. dp = e^(-kτp) cbgp. Where dp is the refraction color, k is absorption coefficient, τp is fluid thickness at pixel p, and cbgp is the background color. sp = 1 (specular material intensity for fluids). ρp = 0.05 (roughness for fluids). A method using particle systems to model gaseous volumes, managing particles and illumination fields via a median k-dtree called a particle map, allowing inhomogeneous anisotropically scattering media and time evolution via fluid dynamics. Use a median k-dtree (particle map) to manage particles and their associated illumination field, storing information for associative searches. When a scattering event occurs, store related information in the particle map instead of a photon map. Distribute incident energy among particles near the point of interaction. Store only the energy that would be scattered into the viewing direction, sacrificing viewpoint independence to avoid the prohibitive cost of storing incident direction for nearby particles. Solve the integral transport equation and source radiance using particle maps via nearest neighbor queries. Combine particle simulation with grid velocity projection. After grid projection and particle step, sort particles by cell index. Create density, velocity, and signed-distance field (SDF) using weighted contribution of adjacent particles. Toggle rendering between density volume display and SDF raycasting display. Displaying movement in time-dependent data using GPU-computed particles emitted from user-placed probe volumes. Advect particles during their lifetime based on the values of the vector field. Render particles as point primitives at their calculated positions (simplest method). Render particles as billboards using a geometry shader to create quads around particle positions. Calculate a sphere based on camera distance and position to perform lighting calculations on the billboards. User-controllable parameters: particle size, color, lifetime, and amount. Per-archetype weather particles spawn in a camera-following box, fall/drift, and wrap. Examples: Mars red dust storm, Titan methane drizzle, Io ash embers (additive), icy-body snow/crystals, faint Earth motes. Airless regolith bodies get none. Count scales with a quality budget. Particle-based fluid simulation and rendering has evolved from simple billboard techniques for smoke and clouds to sophisticated coupled particle-grid systems for realistic water and foam. The particle map technique, introduced by Adabala and Manohar, provides a framework for efficient light transport in participating media using particle-based structures. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) and Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) enabled physically accurate fluid simulations. Recent advancements, such as Gaussian Splashing, integrate these particle simulations with modern neural rendering techniques like 3D Gaussian Splatting to achieve high-fidelity, real-time rendering of dynamic fluids with complex optical effects like refraction and foam. Hybrid approaches, combining particle simulations with grid-based velocity fields, offer a balance between physical accuracy and computational efficiency for large-scale water simulations. GPU-computed particle advection allows interactive visualization of vector fields in scientific data analysis. Camera-following particle systems are utilized in procedural planetary exploration to simulate atmospheric phenomena like dust storms and snow. name: Billboards and particles
head: Billboards, Particles, classical billboards, cross billboards
body: Billboards and particles are a low-cost technique for approximating participating media effects or static geometry (such as forests) by rendering 2D semi-transparent textures that always face the camera. Unlike volume-based splatting methods which compute density integration, this method relies on pre-defined textures placed at static locations or animated particles that move according to rules, making it suitable for real-time industrial simulators where performance is prioritized over physical accuracy. It is distinct from Gaussian splatting or ray-marching as it does not reconstruct a continuous medium but rather composites discrete, camera-facing quads. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of billboards or particles. Each entity i is defined by its position \mathbf{p}i, a 2D texture Ti (color and alpha), and a scale si. For particles, additional state includes velocity \mathbf{v}i and lifecycle parameters (birth/death times). Output: A 2D image where textures are composited using alpha blending. Data Structures: Billboard: Struct containing position (vec3), textureid (index), scale (float), and rotation (float, usually 0 as they face camera). Particle: Struct containing position (vec3), velocity (vec3), textureid (index), scale (float), age (float), maxage (float), and alive (bool). Steps: 1. Initialization: Define the scene with static billboards at artist-specified locations or initialize a pool of particles with positions and velocities. 2. Simulation (Particles Only): For each particle i: Update position: \mathbf{p}i \leftarrow \mathbf{p}i + \mathbf{v}i \cdot \Delta t. Update age: agei \leftarrow agei + \Delta t. Check lifecycle: If agei > max\age, mark particle as dead or reset it. 3. View Transformation: For each visible billboard or particle i: Compute the view vector \mathbf{v}{view} from the camera to \mathbf{p}i. Construct a rotation matrix R such that the billboard's normal aligns with \mathbf{v}{view} (billboarding). For cross billboards, generate 2 to 4 quads with normals distributed around the view direction (e.g., orthogonal axes). 4. Rasterization: Project the transformed quads onto the screen space. For each pixel covered by a quad, sample the texture Ti to get color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha. 5. Compositing: Sort billboards/particles by depth (back-to-front). Apply standard alpha blending: \mathbf{C}{out} = \mathbf{C}{in} \cdot (1 - \alpha) + \mathbf{c} \cdot \alpha. Parameters: Number of Billboards: Determined by scene complexity; dense forests require millions, which is expensive. Cross Billboard Count: Typically 2 to 4 quads per object. Particle Count: High, often thousands, to simulate density. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallax Artifacts: Classical billboards show no parallax when the camera moves, making them acceptable only for axis-symmetrical objects or grazing view angles. Popping: In sparse billboard-based forests, a tree slightly behind another may "pop" in front due to small camera motions, requiring careful sparse placement. Grazing Angle Artifacts: Cross billboards exhibit visible seams or artifacts when any of the constituent quads is viewed at a grazing angle. Lighting Dependency: Billboards are artist-dependent and cannot react to dynamic lighting changes in the environment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(xy for x,y in zip(a,b)) def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) return [x/mag for x in v] if mag > 0 else [0,0,0] def renderbillboards(billboards, camera): # Sort by depth from camera (back-to-front) sortedbillboards = sorted(billboards, key=lambda bb: sum((bb.position[i]-camera.position[i])2 for i in range(3)), reverse=True) # Initialize output image with zeros image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] for bb in sortedbillboards: # Standard billboarding: align normal with view vector viewdir = normalize([camera.position[i]-bb.position[i] for i in range(3)]) # Construct rotation matrix to face camera up = [0, 1, 0] right = normalize(cross(viewdir, up)) up = cross(right, viewdir) # Transform quad vertices to world space quadvertices = [] for v in bb.quadtemplate: rx = dot(right, v)bb.scale + bb.position[0] ry = dot(up, v)bb.scale + bb.position[1] rz = dot(viewdir, v)bb.scale + bb.position[2] quadvertices.append([rx, ry, rz]) # Rasterize and blend for py in range(camera.height): for px in range(camera.width): # Bounding box check for coverage if not (min(v[0] for v in quadvertices) <= px <= max(v[0] for v in quadvertices) and min(v[1] for v in quadvertices) <= py <= max(v[1] for v in quadvertices)): continue # Barycentric interpolation for texture coordinates minx, maxx = min(v[0] for v in quadvertices), max(v[0] for v in quadvertices) miny, maxy = min(v[1] for v in quadvertices), max(v[1] for v in quadvertices) u = (px - minx) / (maxx - minx) if maxx != minx else 0.5 vuv = (py - miny) / (maxy - miny) if maxy != miny else 0.5 # Sample texture color = (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) alpha = 0.5 # Alpha blend existingcolor, existingalpha = image[py][px] newcolor = [existingcolor[j](1-alpha) + color[j]alpha for j in range(3)] newalpha = existingalpha + alpha(1-existingalpha) image[py][px] = (newcolor, newalpha) return image def updateparticles(particles, dt): for p in particles: if p.alive: p.position = [p.position[i] + p.velocity[i]dt for i in range(3)] p.age += dt if p.age > p.maxage: p.alive = False return [p for p in particles if p.alive] Single textured quad facing the camera. Cheapest, but suffers from severe parallax artifacts. Choose for axis-symmetrical objects or distant, sparse geometry. 2-4 crossing quads per object. Reduces parallax but introduces grazing angle artifacts. Choose for slightly more robust static geometry representation where performance is still critical. Dynamic billboards with lifecycle rules. Used for transient effects like smoke, fire, or dust. Choose for animated participating media approximations. Rendering technique using multi-texturing with textures from the two closest cameras, blending billboards back-to-front using the Porter-Duff 'over' operator. Traverse cells back-to-front. For each cell, render the billboard using multi-texturing with weighted textures from the two closest cameras. Blend the RGBA billboard textures using the Porter-Duff 'over' operator. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of billboards/particles. Sorting adds O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing particle/billboard data plus texture memory. Performance: Extremely fast for real-time rendering, making it the preferred choice in industrial simulators despite visual limitations. Strengths: Low computational cost, simple implementation, effective for static or pre-defined effects. Limitations: No parallax (classical), popping artifacts, grazing angle artifacts (cross), artist-dependent, no dynamic lighting interaction. When to Use: Real-time rendering of forests, static volumetric effects (light beams), or simple particle effects where physical accuracy is not required. When Not to Use: Dynamic environments with changing lighting, dense media requiring accurate scattering, or when camera movement is significant and parallax is visible. Billboards have been a common tool for real-time rendering of forests since at least the late 1990s. The technique was reviewed in the context of efficient forest rendering, highlighting its dominance in industrial simulators due to low cost. The application of billboards and particles to participating media (like smoke or light beams) was further detailed in research on real-time light transport, noting their utility in approximating complex scattering effects with simple textures. Volumetric reconstruction and interactive rendering of trees from photographs also utilized these techniques, demonstrating their adaptability to photographic data. name: Screen-Space Fluid Rendering Pipeline
head: Van der Laan et al. pipeline, vtkOpenGLFluidMapper pipeline
body: The Screen-Space Fluid Rendering Pipeline is a real-time rendering technique for visualizing particle-based fluid simulations (such as Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics) by converting discrete particle data into a continuous fluid volume appearance using depth and thickness buffers, thereby avoiding the computational cost of ray tracing. It distinguishes itself from standard particle splatting by accumulating sphere thickness in screen space to derive surface normals and opacity, allowing for the rendering of millions of particles at interactive frame rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of particles Pi provided as vtkPolyData. Each particle is defined by its position \mathbf{p}i, radius ri, and optional scalar color \mathbf{c}i. Output: A final composited image with fluid appearance, including surface normals and opacity derived from screen-space buffers. Data Structures: The pipeline utilizes several render targets (framebuffers) stored in screen space: 1. Depth Buffer: Stores the depth of the nearest particle surface. 2. Thickness Buffer: Accumulates the radial thickness of overlapping particles. 3. Color Buffer (Optional): Accumulates particle colors. 4. Filtered Depth Buffer: Smoothed version of the depth buffer for normal estimation. 5. Filtered Thickness Buffer: Smoothed version of the thickness buffer for opacity/density. Numbered Steps: 1. Depth Pass: Render all particles as spheres into the Depth Buffer with the depth test enabled. This creates a bumpy surface representing the fluid boundary, and automatically discards fluid pixels occluded by static objects. 2. Thickness Pass: Render all particles as spheres into the Thickness Buffer with the depth test disabled and blending enabled. This accumulates the spheres' thickness. 3. Color Pass (Optional): If particle colors are present, repeat the thickness accumulation pass into a Color Buffer using blending to accumulate color intensity. 4. Filtering: Apply filtering to the noisy buffers to produce smooth results. Thickness/Color Filtering: Apply a high-performance, separable Gaussian filter (1-D Gaussian filters in each dimension). Depth Filtering: Apply a depth-specific filter to the Depth Buffer to create the Filtered Depth Buffer. Distinct surfaces close in texture coordinates but with different depths must not be blended, while parts of the same surface with depth differences due to grazing angles must be smoothed. Two modes are available: Bilateral Gaussian Filter (simpler, lower quality) and Narrow-Range Filter (default, higher quality). 5. Composition: Combine the Filtered Depth Buffer (to derive normals), Filtered Thickness Buffer (for opacity/density), and Color Buffer (if used) into the final rendering result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def screenspacefluidrendering(particles, viewportwidth, viewportheight): # Initialize screen-space buffers depthbuffer = np.full((viewportheight, viewportwidth), np.inf, dtype=np.float32) thicknessbuffer = np.zeros((viewportheight, viewportwidth), dtype=np.float32) colorbuffer = np.zeros((viewportheight, viewportwidth, 3), dtype=np.float32) hascolor = any(p.color is not None for p in particles) # Pass 1: Depth Buffer with Depth Test for p in particles: rasterizespheredepth(p, depthbuffer) # Pass 2: Thickness Buffer without Depth Test, Additive Blending for p in particles: rasterizespherethickness(p, thicknessbuffer) # Pass 3: Color Buffer (Optional) if hascolor: for p in particles: if p.color is not None: rasterizespherecolor(p, colorbuffer) # Filtering filteredthickness = separablegaussianfilter(thicknessbuffer) filteredcolor = separablegaussianfilter(colorbuffer) if hascolor else None filtereddepth = narrowrangefilter(depthbuffer) # Default filter # Composition normals = computenormalsfromdepth(filtereddepth) opacity = mapthicknesstoopacity(filteredthickness) return compositebuffers(normals, opacity, filteredcolor) def rasterizespheredepth(p, buffer): # Project sphere to screen, rasterize pixels, write min depth screenpos, radius = projecttoscreen(p.position, p.radius) for y in range(max(0, int(screenpos.y - radius)), min(buffer.shape[0], int(screenpos.y + radius))): for x in range(max(0, int(screenpos.x - radius)), min(buffer.shape[1], int(screenpos.x + radius))): dist = np.sqrt((x - screenpos.x)2 + (y - screenpos.y)2) if dist <= radius: depthval = computespheredepth(screenpos, radius, dist) if depthval < buffer[y, x]: buffer[y, x] = depthval def rasterizespherethickness(p, buffer): # Project sphere to screen, rasterize pixels, add thickness (additive blend) screenpos, radius = projecttoscreen(p.position, p.radius) for y in range(max(0, int(screenpos.y - radius)), min(buffer.shape[0], int(screenpos.y + radius))): for x in range(max(0, int(screenpos.x - radius)), min(buffer.shape[1], int(screenpos.x + radius))): dist = np.sqrt((x - screenpos.x)2 + (y - screenpos.y)2) if dist <= radius: thickness = np.sqrt(radius2 - dist2) buffer[y, x] += thickness def rasterizespherecolor(p, buffer): # Project sphere to screen, rasterize pixels, add color (additive blend) screenpos, radius = projecttoscreen(p.position, p.radius) for y in range(max(0, int(screenpos.y - radius)), min(buffer.shape[0], int(screenpos.y + radius))): for x in range(max(0, int(screenpos.x - radius)), min(buffer.shape[1], int(screenpos.x + radius))): dist = np.sqrt((x - screenpos.x)2 + (y - screenpos.y)2) if dist <= radius: buffer[y, x] += p.color def projecttoscreen(position, radius): # Standard perspective projection to screen coordinates return position.xy, radius def computespheredepth(screenpos, radius, dist): # Depth at distance dist from sphere center on screen return screenpos.z - np.sqrt(radius2 - dist2) def separablegaussianfilter(buffer): # Apply 1-D Gaussian filter in each dimension kernel = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.25], dtype=np.float32) hfiltered = np.convolve(buffer.flatten(), kernel, mode='same').reshape(buffer.shape) return np.convolve(hfiltered.T, kernel, mode='same').T def narrowrangefilter(depthbuffer): # Narrow-Range Filter algorithm not specified in sources return depthbuffer def computenormalsfromdepth(depthbuffer): # Estimate normals from depth buffer gradients return np.gradient(depthbuffer) def mapthicknesstoopacity(thicknessbuffer): # Map accumulated thickness to opacity return np.clip(thicknessbuffer / (thicknessbuffer.max() + 1e-6), 0, 1) def compositebuffers(normals, opacity, color): # Combine buffers into final image return opacity, normals, color Parameters: Depth Filter Mode: 'Bilateral Gaussian Filter' or 'Narrow-Range Filter' (default). Gaussian Kernel Size: For thickness/color filtering, not explicitly sized in sources, but described as separable 1-D. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grazing Angles: At grazing angles, depth differences within the same surface can cause noise. The depth filter must smooth these without blending distinct surfaces. Occlusion: The pipeline correctly handles occlusion by static objects during the depth pass. Artifacts: Discontinuous/noisy surfaces at grazing angles and popping artifacts during camera motion occur due to lack of spatial information in the depth buffer. Performance: The pipeline renders more than 10 million particles in real-time. Hardware: Benchmarked on Intel Core i7-8700K, 32GB RAM, NVIDIA 1080Ti GPU. Resolution: 1920x1080 pixels. Timing: Render time averages over 1000 frames with explicit GPU synchronization (glFinish). Strengths: Real-time performance for large-scale simulations; simple implementation using standard rasterization; automatic occlusion handling. Limitations: Refraction and reflection are non-physical (approximate environment sampling); artifacts at grazing angles and during camera motion; limited to screen-space information. The pipeline is based on the screen-space fluid rendering method introduced by Van der Laan et al.. It was implemented in the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) as the vtkOpenGLFluidMapper class to provide efficient real-time visualization of large-scale particle-based fluid simulations. name: Particle-Based Fire
head: Fuzzy Object Simulation, Primitive Particle Emitter Systems
body: Particle-based fire is a real-time rendering technique that decomposes fire into a set of discrete graphical primitives (particles) regulated by an emitter system. It solves the problem of rendering fuzzy, emissive phenomena efficiently on modern GPU hardware, serving as the standard alternative to prohibitively expensive volumetric rendering. It builds on Particle and Fluid Simulation and is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on discrete particle physics and splatting rather than continuous volume fields or screen-space approximations. Particle-based fire represents the fire medium as a collection of particles Pi, each carrying physical properties (position, velocity) and visual attributes (radius, color, opacity). The simulation updates these particles using physics-based rules, and the rendering projects them onto the 2D image plane for compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Particle emitter parameters, initial particle states (position \mathbf{p}i, velocity \mathbf{v}i, radius ri, color \mathbf{c}i, opacity \alphai), and simulation time step \Delta t. Output: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Each particle i is stored with the following fields: \mathbf{p}i: 3D position vector (x, y, z) \mathbf{v}i: 3D velocity vector (vx, vy, vz) ri: Scalar radius \mathbf{c}i: Color vector (RGB) \alphai: Scalar opacity Steps: 1. Emission: Generate new particles at the emitter source with initial positions and velocities based on turbulence or wind parameters. 2. Simulation: Update particle positions and properties over time \Delta t using physics-based rules such as buoyancy and drag. 3. Projection: Transform particle positions from world space to screen space using the view and projection matrices. 4. Splatting: Project each particle onto the 2D image plane and calculate its screen footprint. 5. Compositing: Accumulate particle contributions to the frame buffer using standard alpha blending for transparency. Parameters: Radius ri: Often enlarged to mitigate atomistic appearance. Particle count: Reduced to improve visual continuity and mitigate atomistic appearance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomistic Appearance: Standard particle fire suffers from appearing "atomistic" and lacking the natural holistic look of fire. Mitigation: Enlarge particle size and reduce particle count to improve visual continuity. A contemporary real-time fire model used in Half-Life 2: Episode 1. It uses a flat view-aligned plane with alpha-blending of colors into a pseudo-random fire pattern to simulate emissive lighting. It achieves fire animation with fewer particles than standard systems by using textured splats based on simple and local dynamics. Wei et al. combined this with the Lattice Boltzmann Model for real-time rendering, displaying around 100 texture splats and rendering the entire image in 15ms. It is chosen for performance-critical scenarios where a holistic look is less critical than speed. Pitfalls include poor scaling of fire size due to the flat geometry, inability to view-align along the y-axis (revealing perspective flaws), and a 5-second repeating texture cycle that limits dynamic change and LOD adjustment. A sophisticated fire model from F.E.A.R. consisting of at least two subsystems: a shader-based flame system and a particle smoke system. External detail helps conceal core flaws. It is chosen for high-quality cinematic effects where multiple layers of complexity are acceptable. Pitfalls include the core fire system being a rigid surface shader that does not evolve in shape over time. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Texture splat variants can render ~100 splats in 15ms. Strengths: Efficient and well-understood for real-time rendering of fuzzy phenomena. Limitations: Can appear atomistic; flat-geometry variants have poor perspective scaling and repetitive animations. When to use: Real-time applications where volumetric rendering is too expensive. When not to use: When a holistic, physically accurate fire appearance is required and performance allows for volumetric methods. Particle-based fire is one of the most efficient and well-understood ways to render fuzzy phenomena in real-time. It emerged as a practical alternative to volumetric rendering, which was considered prohibitively expensive for real-time applications. The technique has been used in numerous games including World of Warcraft, Company of Heroes, Guild Wars, and F.E.A.R.. Research by King et al. and Wei et al. explored textured splats and Lattice Boltzmann models to reduce computational complexity. name: Particle System Renderer
head: PSR
body: The Particle System Renderer (PSR) is a general-purpose, object-order particle rendering system designed for generating visualizations of discrete particle distributions, originally adapted for Radar Cross Section (RCS) data but maintained as a flexible utility. It solves the problem of converting a set of discrete, time-evolving particles with physical properties into a rasterized image by managing particle lifecycles (spawn, move, die) and projecting them onto a defined viewport. Unlike modern GPU-based splatting methods that rely on fragment shaders and depth buffers, PSR is a CPU-based, linked-list-driven system that explicitly manages particle state transitions and supports procedural generation of particle systems from centroids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A data file defining particle systems (centroids, shapes, velocities, lifetimes) and a control file defining the environment (viewport, world limits, camera view, time steps). Output: RLE (Run-Length Encoded) image files, one per frame, generated using the Utah Raster Toolkit. Data Structures: Particles and centroids are stored in a dynamic linked list. Particle Node: Contains position, velocity, color, tail length, time of death, time of spawn, and a flag indicating if the particle is dead. Centroid Node: Defines the origin and shape (spherical or Cartesian) from which particles are generated. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Parse the control file to set the viewport, world limits, camera view (position, center of interest, view plane normal, view up vector), and time increment parameters. Initialize the linked list of particles and centroids. 2. Time Step Loop: For each time step: a. Spawn Check: Iterate through the linked list to identify particles marked for spawning (based on time of spawn attribute). Generate new particle systems at the current position of the spawning particle. The new system's origin is the parent particle's position. b. Update Physics: Update particle positions based on velocity. The system currently supports only linear movement. c. Death Check: Iterate through the list to identify particles whose current time exceeds their time of death. Mark these particles as dead. d. Rendering: Project the active (non-dead) particles onto the 2D image plane defined by the viewport and camera view. e. Cleanup: Remove or mark dead particles so they are no longer displayed in subsequent frames. 3. View Change (Optional): If a view change is specified in the control file, interpolate the View Plane Normal (VPN) and View Up (VUP) vectors from the start values (svpn, svup) to the finish values (fvpn, fvup) over the specified duration or step count. If the freeze token is present, particle growth is halted during this transition. 4. Output: Write the accumulated pixel data to an RLE file, appending the current frame number to the output filename. Formulas and Parameters: Viewport: Defined by two min/max integer pairs (x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}). The range is inclusive. Width W = x{max} - x{min} + 1. World Limits: Defined by min/max integer pairs for clipping, plus front and back clipping planes. View Definition: Requires camera position \mathbf{p}{cam}, center of interest \mathbf{c}{oi}, view plane normal \mathbf{n}{vpn}, and view up vector \mathbf{v}{vup}. Particle Origin (Spherical): Defined by \phi, \theta, r relative to the centroid. Particle Origin (Cartesian): Defined by XYZ coordinates relative to the centroid. Tail Length: A float value specifying the maximum length of the particle's tail. Default is -1, which disables the feature. Time Increment: User-specified step size (seconds) and duration (seconds or number of steps). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Particle: position: Vector3 velocity: Vector3 color: Color taillength: float timeofdeath: float timeofspawn: float spawnsource: str # "generate" or "read" isdead: bool age: float class Centroid: shape: str # "spherical" or "cartesian" origin: Vector3 diameter: float color: Color class Environment: viewport: Tuple[int, int, int, int] # xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax worldlimits: Tuple[int, int, int, int] # xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax clipfront: float clipback: float campos: Vector3 coi: Vector3 vpn: Vector3 vup: Vector3 stepsize: float durationseconds: float durationsteps: int viewchangeactive: bool viewchangestartvpn: Vector3 viewchangestartvup: Vector3 viewchangeendvpn: Vector3 viewchangeendvup: Vector3 freezegrowth: bool def renderparticlesystem(particles: List[Particle], centroids: List[Centroid], env: Environment): currenttime = 0.0 while currenttime < env.durationseconds or env.durationsteps > 0: # 1. Spawn New Particles for p in particles: if not p.isdead and p.timeofspawn > 0 and p.age >= p.timeofspawn: # Generate new system at p's position # Note: Source states only "generate" (random) is currently supported newsystem = generaterandomsystem(p.position, centroids) particles.extend(newsystem) p.timeofspawn = -1 # Prevent re-spawning # 2. Update Physics for p in particles: if not p.isdead: p.position += p.velocity env.stepsize p.age += env.stepsize # 3. Check Death if p.timeofdeath > 0 and p.age >= p.timeofdeath: p.isdead = True # 4. Handle View Change if env.viewchangeactive: # Interpolate VPN and VUP # Note: Exact interpolation formula not given in source, assume linear t = currenttime / env.durationseconds env.vpn = lerp(env.viewchangestartvpn, env.viewchangeendvpn, t) env.vup = lerp(env.viewchangestartvup, env.viewchangeendvup, t) if env.freezegrowth: # Halt particle growth (implementation detail not specified) pass # 5. Render Active Particles image = createimage(env.viewport) for p in particles: if not p.isdead: # Project particle to screen screenpos = project(p.position, env.campos, env.vpn, env.vup, env.viewport) # Check world clipping if iswithinworldlimits(p.position, env.worldlimits, env.clipfront, env.clipback): drawparticle(image, screenpos, p.color, p.taillength) # 6. Output saverle(image, f"outputframe{currenttime}") currenttime += env.stepsize env.durationsteps -= 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fade Time: The feature to fade out particle tails after death is defined as a hook but is not implemented. Direction Attribute: The direction attribute, originally intended to work with velocity, is obsolete. Spawn From: The from token for spawning systems currently only supports the generate token (random generation). The read token (from file) is not supported. Viewport Inclusion: The viewport is inclusive; a range of 0 to 10 is 11 pixels wide, not 10. Tail Length: A negative tail length disables the tail feature; it does not imply an infinite tail. Uses 2D textured quads to represent particles; simpler than PSR's explicit linked-list management but lacks the procedural generation features [9045-billboards-and-particles.md]. A GPU-based approach for fluid rendering using screen-space techniques; PSR is a CPU-based, offline renderer [14414-screen-space-fluid-rendering-pipeline.md]. Specialized for fire effects with specific emission and turbulence models; PSR is a general-purpose system [14658-particle-based-fire.md]. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active particles N per time step, as it iterates through a linked list for spawning, updating, and rendering. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of particles, as each particle is stored in a dynamic linked list node. Performance: Performance is limited by CPU processing speed and the overhead of linked list traversal. The system requires the Utah Raster Toolkit for output, which may add I/O overhead. Strengths: Flexible utility for generating particle systems from centroids; supports procedural generation and explicit lifecycle management (spawn, die). Limitations: No GPU acceleration; limited to linear velocity; no implemented tail fading; spawn from file not supported; obsolete features (direction) remain in the syntax. When to use: For legacy RCS data visualization or when explicit control over particle lifecycle and procedural generation from centroids is required on a CPU-only system. When not to use: For real-time rendering, large-scale particle systems requiring GPU acceleration, or when advanced visual effects like tail fading are needed. The Particle System Renderer (PSR) was developed as part of research into methods for viewing Radar Cross Section (RCS) data in three dimensions. It was designed to be a general-purpose system for generating particle systems, with features added to support RCS data rendering while remaining a flexible utility. The system relies on the Utah Raster Toolkit version 3.0 for generating RLE output files.
