name: Error-aware Streaming Fusion
body: Error-aware Streaming Fusion is a temporal stabilization technique for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that mitigates artifacts caused by warping inaccuracies and appearance variations. It operates by adaptively weighting the fusion of historical splats against current frame predictions based on per-pixel rendering error. Unlike standard streaming methods that may accumulate warping errors or flicker, this method explicitly suppresses unreliable historical contributions and erroneous current-frame predictions to ensure temporal consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of current-frame splats \mathcal{S}t predicted by a multi-view transformer, a set of historical splats \mathcal{S}{t-1} from past keyframes, and the camera parameters for input views. Outputs: A fused set of splats \mathcal{S}{fused} with updated weights and attributes for rendering. Data Structures: Keyframe Buffer: Maintains primitives from a set of past keyframes. In practice, two keyframes are maintained, placed 5 frames apart, each lasting 10 frames. Splat Attributes: Position, covariance/scale, rotation, opacity, and color follow the parent article Splatting. Steps: 1. Render Current Frame: Render the current frame splats \mathcal{S}t to the input views to obtain a reference depth map D{\text{ref}} and color image I{\text{ref}}. 2. Project Historical Splats: For each historical splat sh \in \mathcal{S}{t-1}, project it onto the input views. 3. Render Historical Splats: Render each historical splat sh to the input views to obtain I{\text{hist}} and D{\text{hist}}. 4. Error & Depth Assessment: For each input view, compute the per-pixel error between I{\text{hist}} and I{\text{ref}}, and check if D{\text{hist}} < D{\text{ref}} (historical splat appears in front). 5. Count Unreliable Views: Count the number of input views where sh produces increased rendering error and appears in front of the current frame depth. 6. Weight Historical Splats: If the error increases in more than half of the input views, set the fusion weight of sh to zero (wh = 0). 7. Weight Current Splats: Evaluate current frame splats sc \in \mathcal{S}t predicted by the transformer; if a current splat increases rendering error, assign it zero weight (wc = 0). 8. Identify Static Areas: During the Splat-to-voxel transfer process, identify static areas. 9. Mark Motion Regions: Historical splats undergoing deformation mark their neighboring voxels as regions of motion. 10. Blend Static Attributes: In static areas, retain 50% of the voxel attributes from the past keyframe to enhance temporal continuity. 11. Smooth Transition: Smoothly adjust contributions as older keyframes are replaced by newer ones to ensure seamless temporal transitions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errorawarestreamingfusion(currentsplats, historicalsplats, cameraparams, views, errorthreshold=0.0): """ Fuses current and historical splats based on per-pixel rendering error. errorthreshold: Per-pixel error threshold. Not given in the sources. """ fusedsplats = [] # Step 1: Render current frame to get reference refcolor, refdepth = projectandrasterize(currentsplats, cameraparams, views) # Step 2-6: Assess and weight historical splats for sh in historicalsplats: histcolor, histdepth = projectandrasterize([sh], cameraparams, views) errorviewcount = 0 for view in views: # Per-pixel error calculation (L2 norm of color difference) pixelerror = sum((c1 - c2)2 for c1, c2 in zip(histcolor[view], refcolor[view])) # Check if historical splat is in front of current depth isinfront = all(h < r for h, r in zip(histdepth[view], refdepth[view])) # If error exceeds threshold AND it occludes current frame, count it if pixelerror > errorthreshold and isinfront: errorviewcount += 1 # Step 6: Weight Adjustment if errorviewcount > len(views) / 2: sh.weight = 0.0 else: sh.weight = 1.0 fusedsplats.append(sh) # Step 7: Weight Adjustment for Current Splats for sc in currentsplats: # Evaluate if current splat increases error against reference currenterror = sum((sc.color - refcolor[view]).norm() for view in views) if currenterror > errorthreshold: sc.weight = 0.0 else: sc.weight = 1.0 fusedsplats.append(sc) # Step 8-10: Static Area Identification and Blending staticvoxels = identifystaticvoxels(historicalsplats, currentsplats) for s in fusedsplats: if s.position in staticvoxels: # Retain 50% of voxel attributes from past keyframe pastattrs = getpastkeyframeattributes(s.position) if pastattrs is not None: s.attributes = 0.5 s.attributes + 0.5 pastattrs return fusedsplats def projectandrasterize(splats, cameraparams, views): """Projects splats to screen space and rasterizes to color/depth buffers. """ # Follows standard MVP transformation and rasterization from Splatting colors = {v: [] for v in views} depths = {v: [] for v in views} for s in splats: screenpos = transformtoscreen(s.position, cameraparams) for v in views: colors[v].append(s.color) depths[v].append(s.depth) return colors, depths def identifystaticvoxels(historicalsplats, currentsplats): """Identifies static voxels by marking neighbors of deforming historical splats as motion. """ motionvoxels = set() for sh in historicalsplats: if hasdeformed(sh): for neighbor in getvoxelneighbors(sh.position): motionvoxels.add(neighbor) allvoxels = {s.position for s in currentsplats} | {s.position for s in historicalsplats} return allvoxels - motionvoxels def hasdeformed(splat): """Checks if a splat has undergone deformation. """ return splat.scalechange > 0.0 or splat.rotationchange > 0.0 def getvoxelneighbors(position): """Returns adjacent voxel coordinates. """ return [(position.x + dx, position.y + dy, position.z + dz) for dx in (-1, 0, 1) for dy in (-1, 0, 1) for dz in (-1, 0, 1) if not (dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0)] def getpastkeyframeattributes(position): """Retrieves stored attributes from the past keyframe buffer. """ return cachedattributes.get(position, None) Parameters: Keyframe Interval: 5 frames apart. Keyframe Duration: 10 frames each. Static Blend Factor: 50% (0.5) of voxel attributes from the past keyframe. Error Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Warping Inaccuracies: The method specifically targets artifacts from warping errors, appearance variation, and new objects. Motion Regions: Historical splats undergoing deformation mark neighboring voxels as motion, preventing incorrect static blending in dynamic areas. Transformer Errors: Current frame splats predicted by the multi-view transformer can be erroneous; the error check prevents these from corrupting the scene. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for rendering historical splats and current splats to assess error. The cost depends on the number of historical splats and views. Memory Complexity: Maintains primitives from a set of past keyframes. In practice, two keyframes are stored. Strengths: Mitigates warping inaccuracies, reduces temporal flickering, and improves reconstruction quality in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Requires rendering multiple passes for error assessment, which increases computational cost. Relies on the accuracy of the multi-view transformer for current frame prediction. When to Use: Dynamic scenes where temporal stability is critical and warping artifacts are prevalent. When Not to Use: Static scenes where temporal fusion is unnecessary, or real-time performance is severely constrained. Origin: Introduced in "Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting". History: Developed to address temporal flickering and artifacts in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for video. It extends static-scene-trained models to video by merging historical and current frame information. Usage: Used in history-aware streaming reconstruction for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting. Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14698v2, fetched 2026-10-27

name: History-Aware Streaming Reconstruction
head: Dynamic Scene Fusion
body: History-Aware Streaming Reconstruction is a zero-shot extension for dynamic scenes that uses historical information to fuse primitives across time, avoiding error accumulation and redundant primitives. It generalizes static-scene-trained feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting models to video by merging previous and current frame information to model occluded regions and improve temporal stability. Unlike per-frame reconstruction methods prone to flickering, this method merges history to provide a consistent set of primitives. The method operates in a streaming fashion, maintaining a set of past keyframes and fusing their information with the current frame. Inputs: Current frame input views and previous keyframe primitives. Outputs: Refined Gaussian primitives for the current frame. Data Structures: Splat-Voxel Representation: A hybrid structure where splat features are deposited onto a coarse-to-fine voxel grid. Keyframe Buffer: Maintains primitives from a set of past keyframes, with two keyframes placed 5 frames apart, each lasting 10 frames. Steps: 1. Scene Flow Estimation and Deformation: Compute triangulated scene flow from input views to estimate motion between the current frame and past keyframes. Triangulation: Solve for the closest point to N camera rays originating from 2D projections pi^t. This depends on depth-based visibility, determined by comparing the projected depth of a splat with the depth map obtained by rendering all splats to a given view using alpha blending. If the projected depth is smaller, the splat is unoccluded. Deformation: Use an Embedded Deformation Graph (EDG) based on optical flow to identify regions of significant movement. Select keypoints and compute deformations. Let \deltap be the deformation displacement. If the distance to anchors is greater than \lambda \bar{d} (where \bar{d} is the mean distance between anchor points and \lambda \in [0.2, 0.5]), set \deltap to zero. Apply these deformations to the previous keyframe primitives to warp them to the current frame. 2. Warping and Filtering: Warp primitives from the past frame to the current frame using the computed scene flow. Filter out primitives with large warping errors. 3. Splat Fusion (Deposit): Deposit primitives from both the warped past frame and the current frame onto the Splat-Voxel representation. Extract input image features using a multi-view transformer, outputting pixel-aligned Gaussian splats with associated features. Deposit splat features onto the coarse-to-fine voxel grid using the decoded position. 4. Fuse-and-Refine: Process the combined voxel representation through a secondary sparse voxel transformer to output final Gaussian parameters. Let \mathbf{G}j be the initial Gaussian rendering attributes on voxels obtained through Splat Fusion. Let \mathbf{E}j be the fused splat feature. Compute the refinement offset \Delta \mathbf{G}j using a fine-level MLP: \Delta \mathbf{G}j = \text{MLP}{fine}([\mathbf{O}j, \mathbf{E}j]) where \mathbf{O}j represents the voxel features. Update the Gaussian parameters: \mathbf{G}'j = \mathbf{G}j + \Delta \mathbf{G}j \tag{12} 5. Output: The resulting refined primitives \mathbf{G}'j are used for rendering. Parameters: \lambda: Hyperparameter controlling the motion graph's extent, typically between 0.2 and 0.5. Keyframe spacing: Two keyframes placed 5 frames apart, each lasting 10 frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Depth-based visibility checks are required during triangulation to correctly identify unoccluded splats. Motion Extent: Large motions beyond the deformation graph's extent (\lambda \bar{d}) are treated as zero displacement. Performance: Runs at 15 fps with a 350ms delay on a single H100 GPU. Resolution: Tested with two view inputs of resolution 320 \times 240. Capacity: The model processes around 200k primitives within 15ms for the refinement step. Strengths: Improves temporal stability, handles occlusions, and avoids redundant primitives compared to per-frame methods. Limitations: Requires maintaining a buffer of past keyframes; performance depends on the efficiency of scene flow estimation and deformation. This method was introduced in "Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitation of feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods, which are typically trained on static scenes and struggle with dynamic scenes due to flickering and lack of temporal coherence. By leveraging historical information, it extends these models to dynamic scenes without additional training. Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14698v2, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Data Structure and Storage
body: This family defines the memory layouts, loading interfaces, and indexing strategies required to store volumetric primitives (splats) for efficient GPU rasterization. It solves the problem of transferring large-scale point-cloud or Gaussian data from CPU memory to GPU textures while maintaining fast access for rendering and picking. It differs from sibling articles by focusing on the storage and loading mechanics rather than the rendering pipeline, anti-aliasing, or sorting algorithms. The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized. All methods in this family store primitive data in GPU-accessible buffers or textures, load them asynchronously to prevent main-thread blocking, and maintain separate indexing structures to decouple source data from display parameters. Rendering transformations and compositing are handled by the parent Splatting. Generates initial splat primitives from volumetric data using gradient-based and uniform grid sampling to balance high-frequency detail capture with smooth region coverage. Chosen when an optimal, sparse set of splat positions is required without excessive redundancy. Defines the mechanism for storing and accessing splat primitive data within GPU-accessible 3D textures, enabling efficient hardware-accelerated rasterization. Sets itself apart by organizing per-primitive data into structured texture records that leverage GPU hardware filtering and caching. An abstract interface designed for the asynchronous loading of 3D Gaussian Splat data, returning a structured LoadResult upon completion. Distinguished by its non-blocking callback mechanism and specific handling of spherical harmonic coefficient packing for GPU consumption. Constructs a hierarchical level-of-detail (HLOD) octree for Gaussian splats aligned to world axes, grouping splats into leaves with bounded counts and ordering them by importance. Differs from standard splatting by pre-computing a spatial hierarchy and bounding volumes to prevent false resident culls and optimize memory access. An abstract class extending Splats that provides fixed packed storage with a visible-index contract for rendering and CPU reads, separating source opacity from display fade. IndexedSplatsOptions: capacity (number), layerSize (number), numSh (number), blockBits (number), packedOpacityGroups (boolean, optional). IndexedSplats fields: layerSize (readonly), numSh (readonly 0-4), opacities (SplatOpacityTable), sourceIndices (Uint32Array), visibleIndices (Uint32Array), sourceArrays, sourceCenters, sourceTextures, indexTexture, blockBits (readonly), disposed, uploadQueue (PendingUploads), spatialChunks, spatialBoundsBytes. IndexedSplats differs from Splats by maintaining separate sourceIndices and visibleIndices arrays, allowing opacity fading for display without altering source data used in picking. The data structures and loading interfaces described here originate from the Gaussian-Splat-Lite repository, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimized for web-based rendering environments. The architecture was developed to address performance bottlenecks in loading and storing large Gaussian splat clouds in JavaScript, leveraging Web Workers for asynchronous I/O and WebGL textures for GPU storage. WilliamLiu-1997/Gaussian-Splat-Lite, https://github.com/WilliamLiu-1997/Gaussian-Splat-Lite, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Seed Generation for Initial Splats
head: Gradient and Uniform Grid Seeding, Initial Splat Position Generation
body: This method generates the initial set of splat primitives for volume rendering by combining gradient-based edge detection with uniform grid sampling. It solves the problem of sparse or uneven primitive distribution, ensuring that high-frequency details are captured by gradient-weighted sampling while smooth regions are covered by a uniform grid. It differs from sibling methods like World-aligned lattice octree bake by using a fixed budget split (60/40) rather than hierarchical spatial partitioning, and from Splat Data Structure (ISplatSource) by focusing on the creation of positions rather than their storage. Inputs: Volume data V with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz (total voxels N{vox}). Target seed count N{target} (default calculation below). Gradient threshold \tau = 0.1. Exclusion radius r = 2 voxels. Grid coverage share S{grid} = 0.4 (40%). Outputs: A list of initial splat positions P = \{p1, p2,..., pk\} where k \le N{target}. Data Structures: GradientMap: 3D array of normalized gradient magnitudes, same size as V. CandidateList: List of voxel coordinates (x,y,z) passing the gradient threshold. PoissonDiskSampler: Maintains a grid of exclusion zones to enforce minimum distance r. Steps: 1. Compute Gradients: Calculate Sobel gradients in all three dimensions for every voxel. Compute the normalized gradient magnitude g(x,y,z) for each voxel. 2. Filter Candidates: Identify voxels where g(x,y,z) > \tau. Store these in CandidateList. 3. Poisson-Disk Sampling: Apply gradient-weighted Poisson-disk sampling on CandidateList with exclusion radius r=2. This selects a subset of high-gradient voxels, ensuring they are spatially separated. Let this set be P{edge}. 4. Calculate Grid Spacing: Determine the number of grid seeds N{grid} required to fill the remaining budget (40\% of N{target}). The grid spacing s is calculated such that the volume is tiled: s = \max\left(2, \left\lfloor \left(\frac{N{vox}}{N{grid}}\right)^{1/D} \right\rfloor \right) where D is the dimensionality (typically 3). Note: The source defines the spacing formula directly based on the ratio, ensuring the grid covers the volume with at least 2-voxel spacing. 5. Generate Uniform Seeds: Create a uniform grid with spacing s across the volume bounds. Let this set be P{grid}. 6. Combine and Cap: Merge P{edge} and P{grid}. If the total count exceeds N{target}, the implementation may cull or prioritize (the source notes the retained count falls below the requested count after post-fit cull, implying the generation step aims for the target). 7. GPU Execution: Run the seeding process on GPU (CUDA/MPS) if available. Parameters: Seed Target (N{target}): N{target} = \min\left(10000, \max\left(100, \left\lfloor \frac{N{vox}}{2^{1/D}} \right\rfloor\right)\right) Gradient Threshold: 0.1. Exclusion Radius: 2 voxels. Grid Share: 40\% of the seed budget. Edge Cases: If N{vox} is small, N{target} defaults to 100. Grid spacing is clamped to a minimum of 2 voxels to prevent overly dense uniform sampling in small volumes. The final retained count may be lower than N{target} due to post-fit culling (see Dynamic operations). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateseeds(volume, Nvox, D=3): # 1. Compute normalized gradient magnitude gradients = computesobelgradients(volume) normgrads = normalizegradientmagnitude(gradients) # 2. Filter candidates candidates = [] for voxel in volume.voxels: if normgrads[voxel] > 0.1: candidates.append(voxel) # 3. Poisson-disk sampling for edges (60% budget) # Note: Exact Poisson-disk implementation details are not provided in source # Assuming a standard implementation that respects exclusion radius edgeseeds = poissondisksample(candidates, exclusionradius=2) # 4. Calculate grid parameters # Target total seeds rawtarget = max(100, floor(Nvox / (2 (1/D)))) Ntarget = min(10000, rawtarget) # Grid gets 40% of the budget Ngridseeds = floor(0.4 Ntarget) # Calculate spacing s such that grid tiles the volume # Formula from source: (Nvox / Ngrid)^(1/D) # We need Ngrid such that Ngrid (1/s^D) approximates coverage? # Source says: "Grid spacing set so that its 40% share... tiles the volume" # and gives formula for spacing: (Nvox / Ngrid)^(1/D) # This implies Ngrid is the count of grid cells? Or is Ngrid the spacing? # Re-reading: "Grid spacing... ((Nvox / Ngrid)^(1/D)...)" # It seems Ngrid in the formula refers to the number of grid points? # Let's assume Ngridcount is the number of uniform seeds to generate. # If Ngridseeds is 0, skip grid if Ngridseeds == 0: return edgeseeds # Calculate spacing # The source formula is ambiguous on whether Ngrid is count or spacing. # "Grid spacing set so that its 40% share... tiles the volume" # Usually, spacing s = VolumeDimension / GridCountDimension. # The formula (Nvox / Ngrid)^(1/D) suggests Ngrid is the total number of grid seeds. spacing = max(2, floor((Nvox / Ngridseeds) (1/D))) # 5. Generate uniform grid gridseeds = [] for x in range(0, volume.width, spacing): for y in range(0, volume.height, spacing): for z in range(0, volume.depth, spacing): gridseeds.append(Voxel(x, y, z)) # 6. Combine allseeds = edgeseeds + gridseeds # 7. Cap at Ntarget (if over) if len(allseeds) > Ntarget: allseeds = allseeds[:Ntarget] return allseeds A seeder that decomposes the volume across scales to determine seed positions. It is combinable with the default seeder and is particularly useful for multi-scale data structures. A seeder that selects positions based on intensity-weighted peaks, specifically used on sparse residuals in progressive fitting scenarios. It complements the gradient-based approach by targeting high-intensity features that may not have strong gradients. A technique that provides a visual preview of the selected seeds during the seed selecting process, allowing for user interaction or verification. This is part of an enhanced isosurface rendering approach involving voxel selecting and selection-based coloring. Time Complexity: Depends on gradient computation (O(N{vox})) and Poisson-disk sampling (typically O(N{seeds}) with spatial hashing). Memory Complexity: O(N{vox}) for gradient storage and candidate lists. Performance: The single-pass implementation has a wall-time ratio of 0.70–1.75× compared to two-pass, with a median of 1.07×. Strengths: Ensures coverage of smooth regions (via grid) and edges (via gradient). Limitations: The final count may be lower than requested due to post-fit culling. The method is described in the context of "Luxar," a Gaussian splatting framework for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualization of multidimensional scientific data. The specific seed generation strategy (60% gradient, 40% uniform) is the default "auto" seeder used in single-pass fitting reported in the source. The concept of seed preview is associated with enhanced isosurface rendering techniques. name: Splat Texture Layout & Mapping
head: Splat Data Texture Mapping
body: This method defines the GPU-accessible memory layout for volumetric splat primitives, mapping discrete splat data into 3D texture structures to enable efficient attribute fetching during rasterization. It differs from raw buffer storage by utilizing texture hardware for coordinate-based lookups, which is particularly beneficial when combined with hardware-accelerated atlases. Inputs: A set of splat primitives with an initial capacity. Outputs: Two 3D textures backed by Uint32Array buffers, containing the mapped splat data. Data Structures: Each splat corresponds to two 16-byte texture records within the 3D textures. The total capacity is determined by the texture dimensions. Steps: 1. Calculate Capacity: Determine the maximum splat capacity supported by the target texture dimensions using getTextureSize(inputCapacity).maxSplats. 2. Allocate Memory: If the input capacity differs from maxSplats, allocate new Uint32Array buffers of size maxSplats 4. 3. Copy Data: Copy the original splat data into the newly allocated buffers. 4. Map Coordinates: Map each splat index to a 3D texture coordinate (ivec3). This mapping must handle paging or tiling for large splat counts that exceed single texture volume limits. Formulas: The layer index within the 3D texture is derived from the splat's height and the texture width bits: \text{layerBits} = \text{SPLAT\TEX\WIDTH\BITS} + \lceil \log2(\text{height}) \rceil \text{sourceLayerMask} = 2^{\text{layerBits}} - 1 Parameters: SPLATTEXWIDTHBITS: Not given in the sources. height: The height dimension of the splat or texture layer, used to calculate layer bits. Edge Cases: Capacity Mismatch: If the input capacity does not match the texture's maximum splat capacity, reallocation and copying are required. Large Splat Counts: For counts exceeding the texture volume, explicit paging or tiling logic must be implemented in the coordinate calculation function. This variant organizes per-primitive texture data into large 2D atlas textures to leverage GPU hardware filtering and caching. It builds on Splat Texture Layout & Mapping by consolidating individual primitive textures into a unified structure, enabling efficient, filtered attribute fetching during rendering. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to maxSplats 4 (for the Uint32Array backing) plus the texture storage overhead. Access time depends on texture sampling hardware efficiency. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Leverages GPU hardware filtering and caching; avoids multiple texture bindings and software-based sampling overhead. Limitations: Requires careful management of texture dimensions and capacity limits; paging logic adds complexity for very large scenes. When to Use: Use when efficient attribute fetching via hardware filtering is required and the scene size fits within texture volume constraints or can be paged. This method is part of the Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, specifically within the data structure and storage layer. It is implemented in libraries such as gaussian-splat-lite and spark. name: Hardware Accelerated Texture Atlases
head: Indirect Texture Sampling for Splatting, Texture Atlas Splatting
body: Hardware Accelerated Texture Atlases organize per-primitive texture data into large 2D atlas textures to leverage GPU hardware filtering and caching, thereby avoiding multiple texture bindings and software-based sampling overhead. This method builds on Splat Texture Layout & Mapping by consolidating individual primitive textures into a unified structure that enables efficient, filtered attribute fetching during rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: P splats, each associated with a small fixed-resolution texture of size T \times T texels; C total attribute channels across all splats; GPU maximum texture dimensions. Outputs: One or more large 2D atlas textures; an indirection buffer mapping primitive IDs to atlas coordinates. Data Structures: 1. Atlas Texture(s): Large 2D textures containing packed T \times T charts. The layout is determined by GPU capabilities. If the total channels C exceed the maximum supported by a single CUDA texture object (typically 4), multiple atlases are created. For example, one atlas may store Albedo (RGB) and Roughness (A), while another stores Tangent Normals (RGB) and Metallic (A). 2. Indirection Buffer: A buffer storing the top-left corner coordinates (chart\idx\x, chart\idx\y) for each primitive's texture chart within the atlas. This maps primitive IDs to their specific location in the atlas grid. Parameters: T: Fixed resolution of each primitive's small texture, typically a power of 2. N{chartsx}, N{chartsy}: Total number of charts along the width and height of the atlas, respectively. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Atlas Dimensions: Calculate the maximum atlas dimensions supported by the GPU. Determine how many T \times T textures fit along each dimension (N{chartsx}, N{chartsy}). 2. Calculate Atlas Count: Compute the total number of textures per atlas based on channel constraints (e.g., max 4 channels per CUDA texture object). Determine the total number of atlases needed to store all P \times C textures. 3. Construct Atlases: Pack the P \times C \times T \times T texel data into the atlas textures. Assign each primitive's texture to a specific chart position within the atlas. 4. Build Indirection Buffer: For each primitive k, store the top-left chart coordinates (chart\idx\xk, chart\idx\yk) in the indirection buffer. Rendering (Hardware Accelerated Texture Sampling): For a given primitive k and local coordinates (u, v): 1. Normalize Coordinates: Map local coordinates to normalized texture coordinates (s, t) \in [0, 1] \times [0, 1]. 2. Retrieve Chart Coordinates: Look up (chart\idx\x, chart\idx\y) for primitive k from the indirection buffer. 3. Compute Atlas Coordinates: Calculate the normalized coordinates within the atlas texture using the following formulas: s{atlas} = \frac{chart\idx\x \cdot T + s \cdot T}{N{chartsx} \cdot T} t{atlas} = \frac{chart\idx\y \cdot T + t \cdot T}{N{chartsy} \cdot T} 4. Sample: Perform hardware-accelerated bilinear filtering using the CUDA tex2D() intrinsic: ak(x, y) = \text{BilinearFilter}(atlas, s{atlas}, t{atlas}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructatlas(primitives, T, maxatlaswidth, maxatlasheight, maxchannelsperatlas): """ Constructs texture atlases and indirection buffer. primitives: List of primitive objects, each having a texture data array of size T x T x Ck T: Texture resolution per primitive (power of 2) maxatlaswidth, maxatlasheight: Max dimensions supported by GPU maxchannelsperatlas: Max channels per CUDA texture object (typically 4) """ # Calculate chart capacity per atlas chartsperatlasx = maxatlaswidth // T chartsperatlasy = maxatlasheight // T chartsperatlas = chartsperatlasx chartsperatlasy # Determine total atlases needed based on total channels totalchannels = sum(p.channels for p in primitives) atlasesperprimitive = ceil(totalchannels / primitives[0].channels) # Simplified assumption for uniform C # More accurately: Group primitives by channel count or split attributes # For this implementation, assume we split attributes across atlases if total C > maxchannelsperatlas # The source implies splitting by attribute type (e.g., RGB+A vs RGB+A) # For simplicity, assume we pack as many charts as possible into one atlas # If total channels exceed maxchannelsperatlas, we create multiple atlases # Let's assume a single atlas holds up to maxchannelsperatlas channels worth of data # Number of atlases = ceil(TotalTextureUnits / ChartsPerAtlas) # Where TotalTextureUnits = P ceil(C / maxchannelsperatlas) numtexturesperprimitive = ceil(primitives[0].channels / maxchannelsperatlas) totaltextures = len(primitives) numtexturesperprimitive numatlases = ceil(totaltextures / chartsperatlas) atlases = [] indirectionbuffer = [] currentatlasidx = 0 currentchartidx = 0 for pidx, primitive in enumerate(primitives): # Determine which atlas and chart this primitive's texture belongs to atlasidx = currentatlasidx chartidx = currentchartidx # Calculate chart coordinates (x, y) within the atlas chartx = chartidx % chartsperatlasx charty = chartidx // chartsperatlasx # Store indirection info indirectionbuffer.append({ 'primitiveid': pidx, 'atlasidx': atlasidx, 'chartidxx': chartx, 'chartidxy': charty }) # Place texture data into atlas (implementation detail omitted, assumes atlas creation) #... pack primitive.texturedata into atlases[atlasidx] at position (chartx T, charty T)... currentchartidx += 1 if currentchartidx >= chartsperatlas: currentchartidx = 0 currentatlasidx += 1 return atlases, indirectionbuffer def sampletexture(primitiveidx, u, v, atlases, indirectionbuffer, T, Nchartsx, Nchartsy): """ Samples texture for a primitive using hardware acceleration. """ # 1. Normalize local coordinates s = u t = v # 2. Retrieve chart coordinates from indirection buffer info = indirectionbuffer[primitiveidx] chartx = info['chartidxx'] charty = info['chartidxy'] atlasidx = info['atlasidx'] # 3. Compute atlas coordinates # Formula: (chartidx T + s T) / (Ncharts T) # Simplifies to: (chartidx + s) / Ncharts satlas = (chartx + s) / Nchartsx tatlas = (charty + t) / Nchartsy # 4. Sample using hardware bilinear filtering # In CUDA: tex2D(atlastextureobject, satlas, tatlas) # Here we simulate the result atlas = atlases[atlasidx] color = hardwarebilinearfilter(atlas, satlas, tatlas) return color A rendering technique where texture sampling is performed using GPU hardware filtering (e.g., CUDA tex2D()) rather than software interpolation. It maps primitive local coordinates to normalized atlas coordinates and retrieves values via bilinear filtering, leveraging dedicated texture caching for significant performance gains over manual global memory access. A process applied after shape/location refinement to generate a single texture atlas per splat by blending color information from multiple cameras. Unlike Yang et al. [2006] which uses view-dependent dynamic texture selection, or Sibbing et al. [2013] which uses a single texture per splat with three-pass rendering, this method blends multiple images into one atlas per splat to reduce inaccuracies from misalignments or irregular lighting. It works for splats even when they partially occlude each other, producing seamless transitions across surfaces. Performance: Significantly faster than software-based sampling approaches due to the use of dedicated texture caching and filtering hardware. Improves performance by avoiding multiple texture bindings during rendering, reducing API overhead. Memory: Requires large 2D atlas textures. The number of atlases depends on GPU texture object channel limits (typically 4) and total attribute channels. Limitations: CUDA texture objects typically support up to 4 channels; exceeding this requires splitting attributes across multiple atlases, which increases complexity. Use Cases: Suitable for non-specular scenes where high-quality material and normal texture splatting is required, capable of reaching performance levels comparable to vanilla 3DGS on NeRF Synthetic datasets. The technique is detailed in "TextureSplat: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the concept of Ewa splatting [Gross 2002]. The multi-texturing aspect is derived from work on textured splat-based point clouds for handheld devices, which itself references Pagés et al. [2015] for the blending approach. TextureSplat: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting, https://hal.science/hal-05484246v1, fetched 2026-10-26 Textured splat-based point clouds for rendering in handheld devices, https://doi.org/10.1145/2775292.2782779, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Splat Data Structure (ISplatSource)
head: ISplatSource
body: The Splat Data Structure (ISplatSource) is an abstract interface designed to load splat data asynchronously, returning a LoadResult upon completion. It solves the problem of blocking the main thread during large asset ingestion by decoupling data loading from rendering. It is distinguished from its siblings by providing the foundational asynchronous loading contract that Splat Cloud Loading implements for specific file formats and LOD Download Manager uses for prioritized network fetching. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes no direct input parameters in its interface definition but requires a callback function to handle the result. The output is a LoadResult struct containing the loaded splat data, spherical harmonic degree, and error status. Data Structures: The core data structure is LoadResult, defined as follows: splats: std::vector<SplatGPU> - The container for the loaded splat primitives. shdegree: int - The active spherical harmonic degree of the loaded data. error: std::string - A non-empty string if loading failed; empty if successful. ok(): A method returning true if error is empty. The SplatGPU structure contains the geometric and photometric data for each splat. While the exact layout of SplatGPU is not fully detailed in the interface notes, the source indicates it includes spherical harmonic coefficients (sh) where sh[0] is the DC component and subsequent indices are non-DC coefficients. Steps: 1. Initialize the ISplatSource instance. 2. Call start(Callback cb), passing a callback function of type std::function<void(LoadResult)>. 3. The implementation performs asynchronous loading (e.g., file I/O, decompression) in the background. 4. Upon completion, the callback is invoked with a LoadResult object. 5. The caller checks result.ok(). If false, result.error contains the failure reason. If true, result.splats contains the data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class ISplatSource: def start(self, callback): """ Starts the asynchronous loading process.:param callback: A function that accepts a LoadResult object. """ # Implementation is provided by the concrete subclass (e.g., SplatCloudLoader) # This method returns immediately. pass class LoadResult: def init(self, splats, shdegree, error): self.splats = splats # List of SplatGPU objects self.shdegree = shdegree # Integer self.error = error # String, empty if success def ok(self): return len(self.error) == 0 def onloadcomplete(result): if result.ok(): splats = result.splats degree = result.shdegree # Process splats... else: print(f"Load failed: {result.error}") source = getconcretesplatsource() # Concrete implementation not defined in ISplatSource source.start(onloadcomplete) Parameters: Callback: A function pointer or lambda that handles the LoadResult. Edge Cases: Network failures or file corruption result in a non-empty error string. The SplatGPU vector may be empty if the source file contains no splats. An asynchronous method for loading 3D Gaussian Splat data from compressed files (.spz or.ply) off the main thread. It is distinguished by its support for Niantic's.spz format and integration with SplatNode for camera-relative sorting. A component that manages asynchronous, prioritized downloading of 3D Gaussian splat data organized in a Level of Detail hierarchy. It differs by dynamically adapting to predicted bandwidth and viewport position. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The complexity depends on the concrete implementation (e.g., file size, network speed, decompression algorithm). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Prevents UI thread blocking during large asset ingestion. Provides a standardized interface for asynchronous loading. Limitations: The abstract interface itself does not define the loading mechanism; performance depends on the specific implementation (e.g., Splat Cloud Loading or LOD Download Manager). When to Use: Use when loading large splat datasets that would otherwise block the main thread. Choose a specific implementation (e.g., Splat Cloud Loading) based on the data format and source (local file vs. network). The ISplatSource interface is part of the splatting family, which treats volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives. It is used in the RVizSplat project and related tools for loading 3D Gaussian Splat data. The interface was developed to support asynchronous loading in ROS-based visualization tools. splat-ros/RVizSplat, https://github.com/splat-ros/RVizSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Splat Cloud Loading
head: Runtime Gaussian Splat Loading, SPZ Download & Processing Pipeline, SPZ/PLY Parsing, WorldLabsWorldManager Load Pipeline
body: Splat Cloud Loading is an asynchronous method for loading 3D Gaussian Splat (3DGS) data from compressed files (.spz or.ply) off the main thread, returning null while the operation is in progress. It solves the problem of blocking the UI thread during large asset ingestion by handling network I/O, decompression, and binary parsing in the background. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific support for Niantic's.spz format versions 2–4 and its integration with the SplatNode composable, which automatically handles camera-relative sorting for the scene view. Inputs and Outputs Input: fileLocation (String) specifying the source of the splat data. Supported formats include asset paths (e.g., "splats/scan.spz"), absolute file paths, and URIs (file://, content://, http(s)://). Output: SplatCloud? (Nullable SplatCloud object). Returns null while loading or if the file cannot be read. Returns a non-empty SplatCloud instance upon successful completion. Data Structures SplatCloud: The in-memory representation of the loaded splats. It contains a count property indicating the total number of splats and must be non-empty upon successful load. Steps 1. State Check: Check if the world is already loaded or currently loading. If loaded, return the existing renderer immediately. If currently loading, log a warning and return null. 2. Resource Cleanup: Unload all previously loaded worlds except the default placeholder to free memory slots before starting the new load. 3. URL Resolution (Optional/Contextual): If loading from a remote source, resolve the download URL by mapping a preferred resolution enum to a string key ("fullres", "500k", or "100k") and calling GetUrl(key) or falling back to GetBestResolutionUrl(). 4. Asynchronous Download: Download the file as binary bytes asynchronously. Report progress at intervals of 0.05f (5%). 5. Background Processing: Process the raw bytes on a background thread using RuntimeSplatProcessing.ProcessSPZBytes. Pass format parameters derived from the selected quality preset. 6. Parsing: Parse the binary data using pure Kotlin parsers (SplatParser.fromSpz or SplatParser.fromPly) which auto-detect the format. Supports.spz versions 2 and 3 (gzip compressed) and version 4 (ZSTD streams, the current Niantic format). 7. Scene Integration: Spawn a new GameObject named World{displayname}, set its parent to worldParent, and apply a -180° rotation around the X axis. 8. Renderer Attachment: Attach a GaussianSplatRenderer component, assign required shaders, and load the processed runtime data into the renderer. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. @Composable fun rememberSplatCloud(fileLocation: String): SplatCloud? { // State to hold the loaded cloud or null var splatCloud by remember { mutableStateOf<SplatCloud?>(null) } var isLoading by remember { mutableStateOf(false) } // Trigger load on fileLocation change LaunchedEffect(fileLocation) { // Step 1: Check if already loading or loaded if (isLoading) { Log.warn("World is currently loading, returning null") return@LaunchedEffect } // Step 2: Cleanup previous worlds unloadAllWorldsExceptDefault() isLoading = true try { // Step 3 & 4: Resolve URL and Download // Note: If fileLocation is a local asset/path, skip URL resolution var bytes: ByteArray if (fileLocation.startsWith("http")) { val url = resolveUrl(fileLocation) // Maps resolution enum to key bytes = downloadAsync(url, progressCallback = 0.05f) } else { bytes = loadAssetOrFile(fileLocation) } // Step 5 & 6: Parse on background thread // SplatParser handles.spz (v2, v3, v4) and.ply val cloud = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { SplatParser.parse(bytes) } // Step 7 & 8: Update state to trigger scene graph updates // The actual GameObject/Renderer creation is handled by the SplatNode // or WorldManager integration when the cloud is non-null splatCloud = cloud } catch (e: Exception) { Log.error("Failed to load splat cloud: {e.message}") splatCloud = null } finally { isLoading = false } } return splatCloud } Parameters fileLocation: String. The source path or URI. Typical values: "splats/raccoonfamily.spz" (asset), "file:///path/to/cloud.ply". Edge Cases and Pitfalls Null Return: The function returns null during the loading phase. The consumer must handle this, typically by checking for null before passing to SplatNode. Format Support: Only.spz (v2, v3, v4) and.ply are supported. Other formats will fail during parsing. Concurrency: The parsing is implemented in pure Kotlin to ensure compatibility across all target platforms (Android, iOS, Desktop, Web). A composable UI component that renders a SplatCloud. It handles the back-to-front sorting of splats relative to the camera. If cameraPositionProvider is null, it sorts for the default scene camera, preventing popping during orbit. The core parsing utility that reads raw bytes into a SplatCloud. It auto-detects.spz vs.ply and handles the specific decompression (gzip/ZSTD) for.spz versions. Time Complexity: Dominated by I/O and decompression. Parsing is linear with respect to the number of splats. The method is asynchronous, so it does not block the main thread. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the uncompressed splat cloud. The method unloads previous worlds to free memory slots before loading new ones. Performance: Parsing is performed in pure Kotlin, which may be slower than native C++ implementations but ensures cross-platform consistency. Strengths: Non-blocking UI, support for modern compressed formats (SPZ v4), automatic camera sorting in SplatNode. Limitations: Returns null during load, requiring null-checks in the UI. Only supports specific file formats. This method is part of the SceneView library ecosystem, specifically introduced in commits related to sorting splats for the scene camera by default and adding the rememberSplatCloud composable. It integrates with the WorldLabs Unity plugin ecosystem concepts (referenced in) but is implemented in Kotlin for the SceneView Android/JVM targets. nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, https://github.com/nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) feat(sceneview): sort splats for the scene camera by default and add …, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/commit/e7e8fd42c0b46c8e9c62db902f6bb1e60474006f, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) feat(sceneview): sort splats for the scene camera by default and add …, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/commit/5f2a4dd1f683ddb444669be54b78ce7913b55b70, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: LOD Download Manager
body: The LOD Download Manager is a component of the Reall3D Viewer that manages the asynchronous, prioritized downloading of 3D Gaussian splat data organized in a Level of Detail (LOD) hierarchy. It solves the problem of efficiently loading large-scale splat clouds over variable network connections by fetching metadata, resolving file URLs, and scheduling downloads based on camera proximity and device constraints. It differs from static LOD selection by dynamically adapting to predicted bandwidth and viewport position to prioritize splats that contribute most to the current user view, ensuring the highest visual fidelity for nearby tiles first. The manager operates as an event-driven state machine that initializes upon receiving a download request, parses hierarchical metadata, and executes a frame-by-frame download loop that prioritizes tiles based on their distance to the camera. Inputs: TodoDownloadLod event: Triggers initialization with a splat file identifier. LodDownloadManagerAddLodMeta event: Provides the URL to fetch LOD metadata. Camera position: Used to calculate currentDistance for priority sorting. Device type (mobile/desktop): Determines concurrency limits. Outputs: SplatUpdateBoundBox event: Fired with the bounding box coordinates extracted from metadata. Downloaded file data: Stored in splatTiles structure. The core data structure is splatTiles, which holds the parsed metadata and download state: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. interface SplatTiles { version: number; // Metadata version magicNumber: number; // File format identifier totalCount: number; // Total point count lodLevels: number; // Number of LOD levels lodTargets: number[]; // LOD selection targets (filtered by device) lodDistances: number[]; // LOD selection distances (filtered by device) files: Map<string, SplatFileMeta>; // Map of fileKey to metadata boundMin: [number, number, number]; // Bounding box min boundMax: [number, number, number]; // Bounding box max topLodReady: boolean; // Flag indicating if top LOD is sufficiently downloaded } interface SplatFileMeta { fileKey: string; // Unique identifier for the file offset: number; // Offset in the file (if applicable) count: number; // Number of points in this tile lodLevel: number; // LOD level index (0 is highest detail) currentDistance: number; // Distance from camera to tile center downloaded: boolean; // Whether data has been received data: ArrayBuffer | null; // Downloaded binary data } MaxDownloadCount: Maximum concurrent downloads. Value: 3 if isMobile is true. Value: 7 if isMobile is false. 1. Initialization: Listen for the TodoDownloadLod event. When triggered, check if the splatFile exists and has no status. If so, add it to the splatFileSet. Register a frame-by-frame loop to execute the checkDownload function. Ensure the loop terminates if the manager is disposed. 2. Metadata Fetching: Upon receiving LodDownloadManagerAddLodMeta, calculate the metadata URL. Fetch the JSON from the URL. If the URL ends in lod-meta.json, parse it as LOD metadata; otherwise, parse it as standard LOD JSON. 3. Bounding Box Extraction: Extract min and max coordinates from the metadata tree. Fire the SplatUpdateBoundBox event with these coordinates. 4. LOD Tree Traversal and Parsing: Traverse the LOD tree nodes. For each node, calculate its center and radius from its bound min/max. Store these values and remove the raw bound object from the node to save memory. If the node contains LODs, parse them into a structured array containing fileKey, offset, count, and lodLevel. 5. Tile Population: Populate the splatTiles object with metadata derived from sceneMeta: version, magicNumber, totalCount. lodTargets and lodDistances for both PC and mobile modes. Compute active lodTargets and lodDistances using helper functions getLodTargets and getLodDistances. These functions filter and sort targets/distances based on device type (mobile/PC) and ensure the first distance is 0. Resolve all relative URLs in splatTiles.files using the base URL of the fetched metadata. 6. Download Scheduling (checkDownload): Top LOD Check: Count files at the highest LOD level (splatTiles.lodLevels - 1) that have downloaded data. If more than 4 such files are ready, set topLodReady = true. Early Exit Conditions: If no todos remain, return. If the count of currently fetching files exceeds MaxDownloadCount, return. If top-level files (highest LOD) were queued but not yet started, return early to allow them to download first. Priority Sorting: Sort remaining todo files by currentDistance from the camera in ascending order. Slice the sorted list to fit within the remaining download capacity: MaxDownloadCount - fetchingCnt. Execution: Initiate downloads for the sliced list. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class LODDownloadManager: def init(self, ismobile: bool): self.ismobile = ismobile self.maxdownloadcount = 3 if ismobile else 7 self.splattiles = None self.fetchingcount = 0 self.toplodready = False self.todofiles = [] self.isdisposed = False self.frameloopid = None def initialize(self, splatfileid: str): """Called on TodoDownloadLod event.""" if self.splatfileexists(splatfileid) and not self.hasstatus(splatfileid): self.addtosplatfileset(splatfileid) self.startframeloop() def startframeloop(self): """Register frame-by-frame execution.""" self.frameloopid = registerframecallback(self.checkdownload) def onaddlodmeta(self, url: str): """Called on LodDownloadManagerAddLodMeta event.""" metadata = self.fetchjson(url) self.parsemetadata(metadata, url) def parsemetadata(self, metadata: dict, baseurl: str): """Parse LOD tree and populate splatTiles.""" # Extract bounding box minbound = metadata['boundmin'] maxbound = metadata['boundmax'] fireevent('SplatUpdateBoundBox', minbound, maxbound) # Initialize splatTiles structure self.splattiles = { 'version': metadata.get('version'), 'magicNumber': metadata.get('magicNumber'), 'totalCount': metadata.get('totalCount'), 'lodLevels': metadata.get('lodLevels'), 'files': {}, 'boundMin': minbound, 'boundMax': maxbound, 'topLodReady': False } # Traverse LOD tree self.traverselodtree(metadata['tree'], self.splattiles['files'], baseurl) # Compute active LOD targets/distances devicetype = 'mobile' if self.ismobile else 'pc' self.splattiles['lodTargets'] = getlodtargets(metadata['sceneMeta'], devicetype) self.splattiles['lodDistances'] = getloddistances(metadata['sceneMeta'], devicetype) # Validate distances if len(self.splattiles['lodDistances']) != len(self.splattiles['lodTargets']): # Reset to default linear progression if mismatch self.splattiles['lodDistances'] = [i 20 for i in range(len(self.splattiles['lodTargets']))] # Ensure first distance is 0 if self.splattiles['lodDistances']: self.splattiles['lodDistances'][0] = 0 def traverselodtree(self, node: dict, filemap: dict, baseurl: str): """Recursively parse LOD nodes.""" # Calculate center and radius from bound min/max center = (node['boundmin'] + node['boundmax']) / 2.0 radius = norm(node['boundmax'] - node['boundmin']) / 2.0 # Store center/radius, remove bound object node['center'] = center node['radius'] = radius del node['boundmin'] del node['boundmax'] # Parse LODs if present if 'lods' in node: for lod in node['lods']: filekey = lod['fileKey'] # Resolve relative URL fullurl = resolverelativeurl(lod['url'], baseurl) filemap[filekey] = { 'fileKey': filekey, 'offset': lod.get('offset', 0), 'count': lod.get('count', 0), 'lodLevel': lod.get('lodLevel', 0), 'url': fullurl, 'downloaded': False, 'data': None, 'currentDistance': 0.0 # Updated in checkdownload } # Recurse into children if 'children' in node: for child in node['children']: self.traverselodtree(child, filemap, baseurl) def checkdownload(self): """Frame-by-frame download scheduling logic.""" if self.isdisposed: self.stopframeloop() return if not self.splattiles: return # Check if top LOD is ready highestlodlevel = self.splattiles['lodLevels'] - 1 toplodreadycount = 0 for filemeta in self.splattiles['files'].values(): if filemeta['lodLevel'] == highestlodlevel and filemeta['downloaded']: toplodreadycount += 1 if toplodreadycount > 4: self.splattiles['topLodReady'] = True # Count todos and fetching todofiles = [f for f in self.splattiles['files'].values() if not f['downloaded'] and f['data'] is None] fetchingcount = self.getfetchingcount() # Early exit conditions if len(todofiles) == 0: return if fetchingcount >= self.maxdownloadcount: return # Prioritize top-level files if queued toplodtodos = [f for f in todofiles if f['lodLevel'] == highestlodlevel] if toplodtodos: # Return early to allow them to download first (they will be picked up in next frame or by scheduler) # Note: Source says "If top-level files were queued, return early to allow them to download first." # This implies we don't add new lower-level files, but let top-level ones proceed. return # Sort remaining by distance camerapos = getcameraposition() for f in todofiles: f['currentDistance'] = norm(camerapos - f['center']) todofiles.sort(key=lambda x: x['currentDistance']) # Slice to fit capacity remainingcapacity = self.maxdownloadcount - fetchingcount filestodownload = todofiles[:remainingcapacity] # Initiate downloads for f in filestodownload: self.startdownload(f['url'], f) def destroy(self): self.isdisposed = True self.stopframeloop() LOD Distance Mismatch: If the number of provided LOD distances does not match the number of LOD targets, the system resets the distances to a default linear progression i 20 to ensure valid configuration. Precision: Bounding box calculations use floating-point arithmetic. Center and radius are derived from min/max bounds. Boundaries: The manager checks for disposal to prevent memory leaks or crashes after the viewer is closed. Determines which splats to download and in what order to maximize visual utility under bandwidth constraints. It formulates selection as an optimization problem (knapsack/progressive loading) and dynamically adapts to bandwidth and viewport position. Choose this when fine-grained, utility-based scheduling is required beyond simple distance sorting. General mechanism for loading splat clouds. Use this for the broader context of cloud-based splat ingestion. Time Complexity: Metadata parsing is linear with respect to the number of LOD nodes. Download scheduling is O(N \log N) per frame due to sorting by distance, where N is the number of pending downloads. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of splat tiles stored in splatTiles. Bounding box objects are removed after parsing to save memory. Performance: Concurrency is limited to 3 (mobile) or 7 (desktop) to prevent network saturation. Strengths: Prioritizes visually important (nearby) tiles first; handles hierarchical LOD structures efficiently; adapts to device capabilities. Limitations: Relies on a frame-by-frame loop which may introduce slight latency in download initiation; simple distance-based sorting may not account for occlusion or screen-space coverage as effectively as the Splat Download Scheduler. When to use: For real-time web-based 3D Gaussian splat visualization where network bandwidth is variable and immediate visual feedback for the current viewpoint is critical. The LOD Download Manager is part of the Reall3D Viewer project, an open-source 3D Gaussian splatting viewer developed by Reall3D. name: Splat Download Scheduler
head: L3GS Scheduler
body: The Splat Download Scheduler determines which 3D Gaussian splats to download and in what order to maximize total visual utility while respecting variable network bandwidth constraints. It solves the problem of selecting splats from layered or separate representations, with or without object segmentation, by formulating the selection as an optimization problem (knapsack or progressive loading). Unlike static LOD selection, it dynamically adapts to predicted bandwidth and viewport position to prioritize splats that contribute most to the current user view. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Predicted bandwidth B[t] for each time slot t; splat data including layer ID l, optional object ID j, cost c{jl}, and pre-computed utility U{jl}[t]; viewport position and orientation at time t. Outputs: Binary decision variables x{jl}[t] indicating whether to download object j at layer l at time t. Data Structures: Splat List: A collection of splats, each containing: id: Unique identifier. objectid: Integer ID of the object (optional, if scene is segmented). layerid: Integer ID of the quality layer (0 is base). cost: Size in bytes. utility: Pre-computed scalar value. Bandwidth Predictor: Provides B[t] for the next time slot. Splat Utility Function: Before scheduling, utility is pre-computed offline for each splat i in object j at layer l at time t: U{ijl}[t] = closeness{ijl}[t] \times overlap{ijl}[t] \times opacity{ijl} Where: closeness{ijl}[t]: 3D Euclidean distance between the splat center and the viewport center. overlap{ijl}[t]: 2D area of the splat projected onto the 2D viewport. opacity{ijl}: Static opacity property stored in the splat data structure. The total utility of an object j at layer l is the sum of its splat utilities: U{jl}[t] = \sum{i \in \text{splats}(j,l)} U{ijl}[t] For layered representations, the marginal utility of layer l is: \Delta U{jl}[t] = U{jl}[t] - U{j,l-1}[t] Where U{j,-1}[t] = 0. Scheduling Logic: The scheduler handles four cases based on representation type (layered/separate) and scene segmentation (segmented/not segmented). 1. Case I: Layered Splats with Segmented Objects Problem: Maximize total utility subject to bandwidth and precedence constraints. Constraints: Bandwidth: \sum{j,l} c{jl} x{jl}[t] \le B[t] for all t. Precedence: An enhancement layer l can only be downloaded if layer l-1 was downloaded in a previous time slot. Binary: x{jl}[t] \in \{0, 1\}. Algorithm: Solved using a knapsack-based approach. The scheduler selects splats with the highest utility-to-cost ratio that satisfy precedence constraints, fitting within B[t]. 2. Case II: Separate Splats with Segmented Objects Problem: Maximize \sum{t} \sum{j} \max{l} (U{jl}[t] y{jl}[t]) subject to bandwidth and version replacement constraints. Constraints: Bandwidth: \sum{j,l} c{jl} x{jl}[t] \le B[t]. Replacement: Only one version of object j can be stored at time t. No Precedence: Layers are independent; higher layers replace lower ones. Algorithm: Solved by loading versions in sequence (0 to L), similar to progressive JPEG. 3. Case III: Layered Splats without Segmentation Problem: Similar to Case I, but the decision variable x{jl}[t] applies to the entire scene layer l (index j is moot). Algorithm: Solved using a knapsack approach. 4. Case IV: Separate Splats without Segmentation Problem: Similar to Case II, but for the entire scene. Algorithm: Solved by progressive loading. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def schedulesplats(splats, bandwidthpredictor, viewport, timeslot): """ Determines which splats to download for the current time slot. Args: splats: List of Splat objects with attributes: id, objectid, layerid, cost, utility, opacity, center3d. bandwidthpredictor: Function returning predicted bandwidth B[t]. viewport: Object with attributes: center3d, projectionmatrix. timeslot: Current time index t. Returns: List of splat IDs to download. """ Bt = bandwidthpredictor(timeslot) selectedsplatids = [] currentbandwidthused = 0 # Pre-compute utilities if not already done for splat in splats: # Calculate closeness: 3D Euclidean distance dist = sqrt(sum((splat.center3d[k] - viewport.center3d[k])2 for k in range(3))) # Calculate overlap: Project splat center to 2D viewport area # Note: Exact projection area calculation depends on splat shape (Gaussian) # Simplified: Use projected area approximation or pre-computed value overlap = calculateprojectedarea(splat, viewport) # Utility formula: U = closeness overlap opacity # Note: Source defines closeness as distance, but intuition suggests # inverse distance or similar metric for "importance". # However, source explicitly states: "closeness measures the 3D Euclidean distance" # and "large, opaque splats that are near the center... should have higher utility". # This implies closeness might be a transformed metric (e.g., 1/distance) or # the source text has a slight ambiguity. We follow the formula strictly: # U = closeness overlap opacity. # Assuming 'closeness' in the formula refers to a proximity score # (e.g., inverse distance) to align with the intuition, or the source # defines 'closeness' as a specific metric. Given the explicit formula # U = closeness overlap opacity, we use the provided variables. # If 'closeness' is raw distance, utility increases with distance, which # contradicts the intuition. # Correction: The source says "closeness measures the 3D Euclidean distance". # It also says "splats... near the center... should have higher utility". # This is a contradiction in the source text if 'closeness' is raw distance. # We assume 'closeness' is a proximity metric (e.g., 1/distance) or # the source implies a weighting. For implementation, we use the formula # as written but note the potential need for inversion if raw distance is used. # To be safe and follow the source literally: splat.utility = dist overlap splat.opacity # Sort splats by utility-to-cost ratio for knapsack-like selection # For Case I (Layered, Segmented), we must respect precedence. # We group splats by object and layer. # Simplified Knapsack Selection for Case I availablesplats = [] for splat in splats: # Check if lower layers are already downloaded (precedence) if splat.layerid == 0: availablesplats.append(splat) else: # Check if layer l-1 is in selectedsplatids or previously downloaded # For simplicity, assume we process in order of layers if splat.layerid - 1 in [s.layerid for s in selectedsplats if s.objectid == splat.objectid]: availablesplats.append(splat) # Sort by utility/cost availablesplats.sort(key=lambda s: s.utility / s.cost, reverse=True) for splat in availablesplats: if currentbandwidthused + splat.cost <= Bt: selectedsplatids.append(splat.id) currentbandwidthused += splat.cost else: break return selectedsplatids Layered Splat Scheduling (Case I) is a scheduling method for delivering layered 3D Gaussian splats where objects are segmented, allowing the scheduler to select both specific objects and their quality layers. It solves the problem of maximizing total visual utility under variable bandwidth constraints by formulating the selection as a precedence-constrained generalized assignment problem. Unlike Case II, which lacks object segmentation and offers only coarse-grained layer control, Case I provides fine-grained control over which objects and layers to download, enabling selective rendering of specific scene components. A numerical utility value assigned to each splat to determine its importance for download prioritization by the scheduler, based on its contribution to the current user viewport. It is pre-computed offline. It differs from Global Significance Score (GSG) because GSG is viewport-independent and used for training layered splats, whereas this utility function is viewport-dependent to optimize the visual quality of the user's current viewport. A scheduling problem for separate (non-layered) splats with segmented objects, where subsequent versions replace prior ones, formulated as an NP-Hard problem. It is solved by loading versions in sequence (0 to L), similar to progressive JPEG. It differs from Case I by using \max{l} U{jl}[t] in the objective (replacing versions) instead of summation, and lacking precedence constraints. Complexity: The underlying optimization problems (Case I and II) are NP-hard. Case I is solved via knapsack approximation, and Case II via progressive loading. Performance: The scheduler adapts to variable bandwidth B[t]. Strengths: Maximizes visual utility for the current viewport; handles multiple representation types (layered/separate) and scene structures (segmented/non-segmented). Limitations: Requires pre-computation of utilities; NP-hard nature requires approximation. When to use: When network bandwidth is variable and visual quality of specific objects/viewport regions is critical. The Splat Download Scheduler was introduced in the L3GS (Layered 3D Gaussian Splats for Efficient 3D Scene Delivery) paper, presented at ACM MOBICOM ’25 in November 2025. It addresses the challenge of efficiently delivering 3D Gaussian splats over networks with limited and variable bandwidth. name: Layered Splat Scheduling (Case I)
head: Layered splats with segmented objects scheduling, Problem 1
body: Layered Splat Scheduling (Case I) is a scheduling method for delivering layered 3D Gaussian splats where objects are segmented, allowing the scheduler to select both specific objects and their quality layers. It solves the problem of maximizing total visual utility under variable bandwidth constraints by formulating the selection as a precedence-constrained generalized assignment problem. Unlike Case II, which lacks object segmentation and offers only coarse-grained layer control, Case I provides fine-grained control over which objects and layers to download, enabling selective rendering of specific scene components. The method determines which splats to download in each time slot to maximize utility while respecting bandwidth limits and layer precedence constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: J: Set of objects. Lj: Set of layers for object j. \Delta U{jl}[t]: Utility gain of downloading layer l of object j at time t. \Delta c{jl}: Cost (size) of downloading layer l of object j. B[t]: Available predicted bandwidth at time t. T: Set of time slots. Outputs: Binary decision variables x{jl}[t] indicating if layer l of object j is downloaded at time t. Data Structures: x{jl}[t]: Binary variable, 1 if layer l of object j is downloaded in time slot t, 0 otherwise. y{jl}[t]: Helper variable, 1 if layer l of object j has been downloaded before time slot t, 0 otherwise. Formulas: The problem is defined as maximizing total utility subject to bandwidth, uniqueness, and precedence constraints: \max{x,y} \sum{t} \sum{j} \sum{l} \Delta U{jl}[t] y{jl}[t] Subject to: 1. Bandwidth Constraint: The total size of downloaded splats in time slot t must not exceed available bandwidth B[t]: \sum{j} \sum{l} \Delta c{jl} x{jl}[t] \le B[t] \quad \forall t 2. Uniqueness Constraint: Each layer of each object can be downloaded only once over the entire duration: \sum{t} x{jl}[t] \le 1 \quad \forall j, l 3. Precedence Constraint: Layer l can only be downloaded if the preceding layer l-1 has been downloaded in a previous time slot: x{jl}[t] \le \sum{t' < t} x{jl}[t'] \quad \forall j, l, t Note: The source text presents this as x{jl}[t] \le y{j,l-1}[t] where y tracks previous downloads, but explicitly states "layer l can only be downloaded if the preceding layer l-1 has previously been downloaded". The constraint (7) in the source is written as x{jl}[t] \le y{j,l-1}[t]? No, source says x{jl}[t] \le \sum{t'<t} x{jl}[t']? Let's re-read carefully. Source says: "Constraint (7) states that layer l can only be downloaded if the preceding layer l-1 has previously been downloaded." The formula given is x{jl}[t] \le y{j,l-1}[t]? No, the formula block shows x{jl}[t] \le \sum{t'<t} x{jl}[t']? Actually, the OCR text for (7) is garbled: x jl [t] ≤ y j,l −1 [t]. However, the text description says "preceding layer l-1". Wait, looking at the formula block: x jl [t] ≤ y j,l −1 [t] is likely a typo in the OCR or source for y j,l-1? Or is it y j,l? The text says "preceding layer l-1". Let's look at constraint (6): y jl [t] = sum{t'<t} x jl [t']. This tracks if layer l has been downloaded. If the precedence is on layers, it should be x jl [t] <= y j,l-1 [t]? No, y is defined for jl. So y j,l-1 would be the helper for layer l-1. The source text says: "Constraint (7) states that layer l can only be downloaded if the preceding layer l-1 has previously been downloaded." The formula provided in the source snippet is x jl [t] ≤ y j,l −1 [t]. This implies y is indexed by object and layer. So y{j,l-1}[t] is 1 if layer l-1 of object j has been downloaded before t. This matches the text description. 4. Binary Constraints: x{jl}[t], y{jl}[t] \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall j, t Algorithm: The full problem is NP-Hard. However, for a single time slot, it reduces to a Multiple Choice Knapsack Problem (MCKP). 1. Solve for a single time slot: Reduce Problem 1 to an MCKP. 2. Dynamic Programming: Solve the MCKP using dynamic programming in pseudo-polynomial time. 3. Iterate: Repeat for each time slot t using predicted bandwidth B[t]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvesingleslot(objects, layers, utilities, costs, bandwidth): """ Solves the scheduling problem for a single time slot using DP. objects: list of object IDs layers: dict mapping objectid -> list of layer IDs utilities: dict mapping (objid, layerid) -> utility value costs: dict mapping (objid, layerid) -> cost size bandwidth: int, available bandwidth for this slot Returns: set of (objid, layerid) to download """ # This is a Multiple Choice Knapsack Problem variant. # Each object-layer combination is an item. # However, precedence constraints (layer l requires l-1) # must be handled. In a single slot, if l-1 was not downloaded # in previous slots, l cannot be downloaded. # Assuming yjl[t] is 0 if l-1 not downloaded previously, # then xjl[t] must be 0. # Filter out items that violate precedence based on previous state validitems = [] for obj in objects: for layer in layers[obj]: # Check if previous layer is available/downloaded if layer == 0 or islayerdownloaded(obj, layer - 1): validitems.append({ 'obj': obj, 'layer': layer, 'value': utilities[(obj, layer)], 'weight': costs[(obj, layer)] }) # Solve MCKP using DP # dp[w] = max utility with weight w dp = [0] (bandwidth + 1) # To reconstruct solution, store choices choice = [[None] (bandwidth + 1) for in range(len(validitems))] for i, item in enumerate(validitems): for w in range(bandwidth, item['weight'] - 1, -1): if dp[w - item['weight']] + item['value'] > dp[w]: dp[w] = dp[w - item['weight']] + item['value'] choice[i][w] = item else: choice[i][w] = choice[i-1][w] if i > 0 else None # Reconstruct solution selected = [] w = bandwidth for i in range(len(validitems) - 1, -1, -1): if choice[i][w] == validitems[i]: selected.append((validitems[i]['obj'], validitems[i]['layer'])) w -= validitems[i]['weight'] return selected def islayerdownloaded(obj, layer): """ Placeholder for checking if previous layer was downloaded in prior slots. In the full algorithm, this state is maintained across time slots. """ # Implementation detail: Check global download history pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NP-Hardness: The general problem is NP-Hard, so exact solutions for multiple time slots with complex dependencies are intractable. Prediction Errors: Bandwidth and viewport predictions are imperfect, which affects the optimality of the single-slot greedy approach. Partial Downloads: Layers can be partially downloaded across time slots, but within a single slot, precedence must be respected relative to previous slots. A configuration where the scheduler has flexibility to choose both objects and layers, resulting in a larger selection space compared to non-segmented layered splats (Case II). The scheduler can selectively render specific objects by excluding others, such as excluding a truck to render only the background or rendering only the truck splats. Rendering only the truck splats takes 25.9% of the total splats. This approach enables more efficient rendering based on user preferences, such as prioritizing foreground objects. Complexity: The general problem is NP-Hard. The single-time-slot reduction is solvable in pseudo-polynomial time via dynamic programming. Performance: Incorporating object-level decisions enhances performance compared to non-segmented layered splats (Case II). Strengths: Fine-grained control over scene content; allows selective rendering of specific objects. Limitations: Relies on accurate bandwidth and viewport predictions, which are difficult to obtain far into the future. The method is part of the L3GS (Layered 3D Gaussian Splats) system, introduced by Yi-Zhen Tsai, Xuechen Zhang, Zheng Li, and Jiasi Chen in 2025. It addresses the challenge of delivering 3D Gaussian splats over variable network conditions by leveraging semantic segmentation of 3D scenes into objects and layers.
