name: Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing
head: Alpha Compositing Rendering, accumulate
body: Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing is a method for rendering 2D Gaussian splats by processing individual pixel-Gaussian intersection pairs rather than iterating over pixels or Gaussians in a nested loop. It solves the problem of arbitrary intersection patterns in differentiable rendering by explicitly enumerating all overlaps between pixels and Gaussians, allowing for efficient batched computation and automatic differentiation. Unlike standard rasterization approaches that rely on fixed tile-based sorting or implicit accumulation, this method relies on explicit pairs (gaussianid, pixelid, imageid) to handle complex overlaps and supports the derivation of gradients for the backward pass. Inputs: imageids: Array of shape [M] containing the image index for each intersection. pixelidsx, pixelidsy: Arrays of shape [M] containing the integer pixel coordinates for each intersection. gaussianids: Array of shape [M] containing the index of the Gaussian for each intersection. means2d: Array of shape [N, 2] containing the 2D means of N Gaussians. conics: Array of shape [N, 3] containing the inverse covariance matrix elements (upper triangle) for each Gaussian. Layout: [conic00, conic01, conic22]. opacities: Array of shape [N] containing the opacity \alphai for each Gaussian. colors: Array of shape [N, C] containing the color values for each Gaussian (e.g., C=3 for RGB). imageheight, imagewidth: Dimensions of the output image. MAXALPHA: Scalar clamping value for per-intersection alpha (typically < 1.0 to prevent instability). Outputs: renders: Array of shape [H, W, C] containing the final composited colors. alphasout: Array of shape [H, W, 1] containing the final composited alpha values. Data Structures: deltas: Temporary array of shape [M, 2] storing the vector from the Gaussian mean to the pixel center. sigmas: Temporary array of shape [M] storing the Gaussian exponent values. alphasperisect: Temporary array of shape [M] storing the unclamped or clamped alpha contribution of each intersection. rayindices: Temporary array of shape [M] mapping each intersection to a unique linear pixel index in the flattened image. weights: Temporary array of shape [M] storing the final compositing weight for each intersection. transmittances: Temporary array of shape [M] storing the transmittance at each intersection (used for gradient computation). Steps: 1. Compute Pixel Coordinates: Convert integer pixel IDs to floating-point coordinates by adding 0.5 to center them in the pixel. \text{pixel\coords} = [\text{pixel\ids\x} + 0.5, \text{pixel\ids\y} + 0.5] \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 2} 2. Gather Gaussian Parameters: Using gaussianids, gather the corresponding means2d, conics, opacities, and colors for all M intersections. Let these be means2dselected, conicsselected, opacitiesselected, and colorsselected. 3. Compute Distances (Deltas): Calculate the vector from each Gaussian's 2D mean to the corresponding pixel coordinate. \text{deltas} = \text{pixel\coords} - \text{means2d\selected} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 2} Let \deltax = \text{deltas}[:, 0] and \deltay = \text{deltas}[:, 1]. 4. Compute Gaussian Exponent (Sigma): Compute the exponent \sigmai for the 2D Gaussian function using the conic matrix elements and the deltas. The conic matrix \Sigma'^{-1} is represented by conicsselected as [c{00}, c{01}, c{22}]. \sigmai = 0.5 \left( c{00} \deltax^2 + c{22} \deltay^2 + 2 c{01} \deltax \deltay \right) In code: python sigmas = 0.5 (conicsselected[:, 0] deltas[:, 0]2 + conicsselected[:, 2] deltas[:, 1]2 + 2 conicsselected[:, 1] deltas[:, 0] deltas[:, 1]) Note: The source code uses conicsselected[:, 1] deltas[:, 0] deltas[:, 1] without the factor of 2, implying the input conics might store 2 \times the off-diagonal term or the formula is adapted. We follow the source code exactly. Corrected based on source code: \sigmai = 0.5 \left( c{00} \deltax^2 + c{22} \deltay^2 + c{01} \deltax \deltay \right) 5. Compute Per-Intersection Alpha: Calculate the alpha contribution for each intersection, clamped to MAXALPHA. \alphai^{\text{isect}} = \min(\alphai \cdot e^{-\sigmai}, \text{MAX\ALPHA}) where \alphai is the Gaussian's opacity. 6. Compute Ray Indices: Map each intersection to a unique linear index in the flattened image space to group intersections by pixel. \text{ray\indices} = \text{image\ids} \times (H \times W) + \text{pixel\ids\y} \times W + \text{pixel\ids\x} Note: The source code uses imageids (imageheight imagewidth) + pixelids. Assuming pixelids in the source refers to a flattened pixel index or the code assumes a specific layout. Standard flattening is y \cdot W + x. If pixelids in the source is a single array of flattened indices, the formula is: \text{ray\indices} = \text{image\ids} \times (H \times W) + \text{pixel\ids\flat} 7. Compute Compositing Weights: Sort the intersections for each ray (pixel) by depth (not explicitly detailed in the snippet, but implied by the need for front-to-back or back-to-front accumulation). Then, compute the weights wi using the standard alpha compositing recurrence. wi = \alphai^{\text{isect}} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^{\text{isect}}) This is typically implemented via a cumulative product of transmittances. Let T0 = 1 and Ti = T{i-1} (1 - \alphai^{\text{isect}}). Then wi = T{i-1} \alphai^{\text{isect}}. The function renderweightfromalpha performs this step, returning weights and transmittances. 8. Accumulate Colors: Accumulate the weighted colors for each pixel. C(x) = \sum{i \in \text{pixels}(x)} wi \cdot \text{colors\selected}i This is done using accumulatealongrays(weights, colorsselected, rayindices, totalpixels). 9. Accumulate Alpha: Accumulate the weights to get the final alpha channel (since \sum wi = 1 - TN). A(x) = \sum{i \in \text{pixels}(x)} wi This is done using accumulatealongrays(weights, None, rayindices, totalpixels). 10. Reshape Outputs: Reshape the accumulated arrays to the final image dimensions [H, W, C] and [H, W, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Compute Pixel Coordinates pixelcoords = mx.stack([pixelidsx, pixelidsy], axis=-1).astype(mx.float32) + 0.5 # 2. Gather Gaussian Parameters means2dselected = means2d[gaussianids] conicsselected = conics[gaussianids] opacitiesselected = opacities[gaussianids] colorsselected = colors[gaussianids] # 3. Compute Deltas deltas = pixelcoords - means2dselected # 4. Compute Sigmas # conicsselected: [c00, c01, c22] sigmas = 0.5 ( conicsselected[:, 0] deltas[:, 0]2 + conicsselected[:, 2] deltas[:, 1]2 + conicsselected[:, 1] deltas[:, 0] deltas[:, 1]) # 5. Compute Per-Intersection Alpha alphasperisect = mx.minimum(opacitiesselected mx.exp(-sigmas), MAXALPHA) # 6. Compute Ray Indices # Assuming pixelidsx and pixelidsy are needed for flat index pixelidsflat = pixelidsy imagewidth + pixelidsx rayindices = imageids (imageheight imagewidth) + pixelidsflat # 7. Compute Weights and Transmittances # This step requires sorting intersections per ray by depth (z-order) # and then applying front-to-back compositing. # The source abstracts this into renderweightfromalpha. # We assume a helper function exists that handles the sorting and recurrence. weights, transmittances = renderweightfromalpha( alphasperisect, rayindices, imageheight imagewidth) # 8. Accumulate Colors rendersflat = accumulatealongrays(weights, colorsselected, rayindices, imageheight imagewidth) # 9. Accumulate Alpha alphasflat = accumulatealongrays(weights, None, rayindices, imageheight imagewidth) # 10. Reshape renders = rendersflat.reshape(imageheight, imagewidth, colors.shape[1]) alphasout = alphasflat.reshape(imageheight, imagewidth, 1) return renders, alphasout Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting: The correctness of alpha compositing depends on the correct ordering of Gaussians along the view ray (front-to-back or back-to-front). The source does not detail the sorting mechanism, but it is a critical prerequisite for renderweightfromalpha. Precision: Clamping alpha to MAXALPHA prevents numerical instability when multiple Gaussians overlap significantly, but choosing a value too close to 1.0 can lead to incorrect blending if the sum of alphas exceeds 1.0 locally. Empty Pixels: Pixels with no intersections will have zero values in the accumulated arrays, which is correct for transparent backgrounds. Gamma-Space Alpha Blending performs Gaussian alpha compositing directly in the Gamma color space to match the training conditions of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assets. It solves the quality degradation caused by converting colors to linear space before blending, which is the default behavior in modern linear-rendering pipelines. Unlike its parent method, Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing, which handles arbitrary intersection patterns via explicit pairs, this method assumes a standard front-to-back or back-to-front accumulation where the entire splatting pass occurs within a single Gamma-space context. Capacity Response Modeling is a pruning method that computes individual importance scores and pairwise interaction terms for Gaussian selection by measuring RGB changes when Gaussian opacity varies. It determines which Kb members to retain in each block by accounting for joint rendering effects via the response matrix Rb. It builds on Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing by using its alpha compositing logic to derive gradients for selection, differing from Gamma-Space Alpha Blending which operates in a different color space. Time Complexity: O(M), where M is the number of intersections. The dominant cost is the gathering of parameters and the computation of sigmas and alphas, which are element-wise operations. The sorting and accumulation steps are also linear in M if efficient bucketing or sorting is used. Memory Complexity: O(M) for storing the intersection arrays. The output size is O(H \times W). Performance: This method is highly parallelizable on GPUs due to the explicit intersection list. It avoids the overhead of nested loops and is suitable for differentiable rendering pipelines. Strengths: Handles arbitrary intersection patterns efficiently; supports automatic differentiation; flexible for various Gaussian distributions. Limitations: Requires explicit generation of the intersection list, which can be memory-intensive for scenes with many overlapping Gaussians. Sorting per pixel is required for correct compositing. The method is derived from the 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by using 2D Gaussians for more flexible shape representation. The explicit intersection approach is a key component of differentiable rasterizers for Gaussian splatting, allowing for efficient gradient computation. name: Gamma-Space Alpha Blending
head: Gamma-Space Alpha Blending for 3DGS, Gamma-Space Splat Blending
body: Gamma-Space Alpha Blending performs Gaussian alpha compositing directly in the Gamma color space to match assets trained in Gamma space, avoiding quality loss from post-blend color conversion. It requires the rendering project to be configured in Gamma color space, as converting colors to linear space before blending produces incorrect results and lowers rendering quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D Gaussian splats with associated Gamma-space colors (C) and opacities (\alpha). Output: A composited image buffer in Gamma space. Data Structures: Splat Buffer: Stores position, covariance, opacity, and Gamma-space color per splat. Render Target: A texture buffer configured to store Gamma-space values without intermediate linear-space conversion during accumulation. Steps: 1. Project & Rasterize: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and rasterize them to the render target. 2. Blend in Gamma Space: For each pixel, accumulate splats using standard alpha compositing equations directly on Gamma-space color values: C{out} = C{in} + C{splat} \cdot \alpha{splat} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{splat} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) where C is the Gamma-space color vector and \alpha is opacity. 3. Output: Display the resulting Gamma-space buffer directly. Parameters: GammaToLinear: Boolean flag to attempt color space conversion before blending; disabled by default to prevent quality degradation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Linear Projects: Projects using a linear color space require retraining 3DGS assets with linear-space images, as blending in linear space produces incorrect results. HDRP Limitations: High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP) does not support Gamma mode, making this method incompatible without pipeline changes. GammaToLinear Workaround: Enabling GammaToLinear converts colors to linear space before blending, which leads to incorrect results and lowers rendering quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. colorbuffer = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] alphabuffer = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for splat in splatsforpixel[y][x]: if accalpha >= 1.0: break # Evaluate 2D Gaussian alpha at pixel center (source does not specify) alphasplat = 1.0 # Standard Gaussian evaluation omitted per source effectivealpha = alphasplat splat.opacity if effectivealpha <= 0.0: continue # Gamma-space compositing acccolor = [acccolor[i] + splat.color[i] effectivealpha (1.0 - accalpha) for i in range(3)] accalpha = accalpha + effectivealpha (1.0 - accalpha) colorbuffer[y][x] = acccolor alphabuffer[y][x] = accalpha A vertex and pixel shader pair for the sRGB→linear composite pass using a full-screen triangle. The pixel shader reads the intermediate sRGB-blended splat accumulation texture, converts to linear, and outputs for premultiplied alpha blending onto SceneColor. This variant is used when the initial splatting occurs in Gamma space to match training, but the final composition with the rest of the scene requires Linear space. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves visual fidelity of assets trained in Gamma space without requiring retraining. Limitations: Incompatible with Linear color space projects unless assets are retrained. Incompatible with HDRP. When to use: When rendering standard 3DGS assets (trained in Gamma) in a Gamma-space supported pipeline (Built-in RP, URP). When not to use: In Linear color space projects with existing Gamma-trained assets, or in HDRP. Originating from the practical constraints of integrating 3D Gaussian Splatting into game engines, this method addresses the mismatch between the official 3DGS implementation (which trains in Gamma space) and modern rendering pipelines (which operate in Linear space). It was popularized by community implementations such as gsplat-unity which highlighted that converting color space before blending degrades quality. The approach relies on the fact that standard 3DGS assets are trained using Gamma-corrected images, making Gamma-space blending the only way to maintain quality without retraining. wuyize25/gsplat-unity, https://github.com/wuyize25/gsplat-unity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, https://github.com/YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Capacity Response Modeling
head: Opacity Response Gram Matrix, Quadratic Selection, Quadratic Selection via Opacity Response
body: Capacity Response Modeling is a pruning method that computes individual importance scores and pairwise interaction terms for quadratic selection by measuring RGB changes when Gaussian opacity varies. It determines which Kb members to retain in each block by accounting for joint rendering effects via the response matrix Rb. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians partitioned into blocks. Training views v and their corresponding ground-truth images. For each block b, the set of Gaussians Cb and their parameters (opacity, color, covariance, position). Target retention count Kb for block b (determined by a prior budget allocation step). Outputs: A binary retention vector xb \in \{0, 1\}^{nb} for each block, where x{b,i}=1 indicates the i-th Gaussian is retained. Data Structures: Selected Pixels Set Pb: A set of pairs (v, p) representing view v and pixel coordinate p. Jacobian Matrix Jb: Dimensions 3|Pb| \times nb. Response Matrix Rb: Dimensions nb \times nb, computed as Jb^T Jb. Steps: 1. Pixel Selection: For each block b and camera view v, use projected Gaussian centers as initially selected pixel coordinates. Augment this set with neighboring pixels obtained by offsetting each center. Remove duplicate locations and discard pixels outside the image, collecting selected pixels p for view v as pairs (v, p) into set Pb. 2. Rendered Color Definition: Let L{vp} denote the number of Gaussians covering pixel p in view v, indexed front-to-back as g1, \dots, g{L{vp}}. Let \alpha\ell denote the original alpha of g\ell, given by its activated opacity times its projected Gaussian value. Introduce a continuous multiplier \etai \in [0, 1] for each Gaussian's activated opacity. The modified alpha and incoming transmittance are: \alpha\ell(\eta) = \eta{g\ell} \alpha\ell T\ell(\eta) = \prod{r=1}^{\ell-1} (1 - \alphar(\eta)) Using front-to-back alpha compositing, the rendered RGB channel q \in \{1, 2, 3\} at pixel p in view v is: I{vpq}(\eta) = \sum{\ell=1}^{L{vp}} T\ell(\eta)\alpha\ell(\eta)c\ell^q + T{L{vp}+1}(\eta)c{bg}^q where c\ell is the Gaussian's view-dependent color component, c{bg}^q is the background color component, and T{L{vp}+1} is the transmittance remaining after all contributors. 3. Jacobian Computation: Differentiate each sampled RGB channel with respect to the opacity multiplier of every block member. For i \in Cb, the corresponding entry of Jb \in \mathbb{R}^{3|Pb| \times nb} is: (Jb){(v,p,q),i} = \left. \frac{\partial I{vpq}(\eta)}{\partial \etai} \right|{\eta=1} Rows correspond to sampled view-pixel-channel triples (v, p, q), and columns correspond to the Gaussians in block b. 4. Response Matrix Construction: Compute the opacity-response Gram matrix Rb = Jb^T Jb. The diagonal score Di = (Rb){ii} sums the squared color derivatives for opacity of Gaussian i over all selected pixels, views, and RGB channels. A larger Di indicates that Gaussian i has a greater influence on the rendered image. Each off-diagonal entry is the signed inner product between two response columns; positive entries indicate reinforcing linearized deletion effects, whereas negative entries indicate partial cancellation. 5. Quadratic Selection (QUBO): Solve the following QUBO problem for each block independently: \min{xb \in \{0,1\}^{nb}} Eb(xb) = (1 - xb)^T Rb (1 - xb) + \lambda (1^T xb - Kb)^2 Here x{b,i}=1 if Gaussian is retained, Rb is the response matrix, Kb is the quota, and \lambda is a penalty weight. The first term approximates the rendering change caused by jointly deleting the Gaussians with x{b,i} = 0. The second term penalizes deviations from the allocated quota Kb. 6. Repair and Combine: Repair infeasible solver outputs if necessary, then combine block masks into a model containing exactly K Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computecapacityresponsemodeling(gaussians, views, targetcounts, lambdapenalty=1.0): """ gaussians: List of blocks, where each block is a list of Gaussian objects. Each Gaussian has attributes: alpha (scalar), color (3,), depth (scalar). views: List of view objects. Each view has: gtimage (H, W, 3), backgroundcolor (3,). targetcounts: Dict mapping blockindex -> Kb. lambdapenalty: Scalar lambda for QUBO penalty. Returns: retentionmasks: List of boolean arrays, one per block. """ retentionmasks = [] for bidx, block in enumerate(gaussians): nb = len(block) Kb = targetcounts[bidx] # Step 1: Pixel Selection Pb = set() for view in views: projectedcenters = [(g.pos[0], g.pos[1]) for g in block] selectedpixels = set() for cx, cy in projectedcenters: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: ny, nx = int(cy) + dy, int(cx) + dx if 0 <= ny < view.gtimage.shape[0] and 0 <= nx < view.gtimage.shape[1]: selectedpixels.add((ny, nx)) for p in selectedpixels: Pb.add((view, p)) if not Pb: retentionmasks.append(np.ones(nb, dtype=bool)) continue # Step 2 & 3: Jacobian Computation numpixels = len(Pb) Jb = np.zeros((3 numpixels, nb)) pixellist = list(Pb) for rowidx, (view, p) in enumerate(pixellist): # Assume block is pre-sorted front-to-back coveringgaussians = block Lvp = len(coveringgaussians) alphas = np.array([g.alpha for g in coveringgaussians]) colors = np.array([g.color for g in coveringgaussians]) # Precompute transmittances Tl Ts = np.zeros(Lvp + 1) Ts[0] = 1.0 for l in range(1, Lvp + 1): Ts[l] = Ts[l-1] (1 - alphas[l-1]) cbg = view.backgroundcolor for colidx, gglobal in enumerate(block): # Find position in front-to-back list if gglobal in coveringgaussians: localidx = coveringgaussians.index(gglobal) k = localidx + 1 # 1-based index dI = np.zeros(3) # Term for l == k: Tk alphak ck dI += Ts[k-1] alphas[k-1] colors[k-1] # Terms for l > k: -alphai (Tl / (1 - alphai)) alphal cl denom = 1.0 - alphas[localidx] + 1e-8 for l in range(k + 1, Lvp + 1): dI += (-alphas[localidx] Ts[l-1] / denom) alphas[l-1] colors[l-1] # Background term T{L+1} dI += (-alphas[localidx] Ts[Lvp] / denom) cbg Jb[rowidx 3, colidx] = dI[0] Jb[rowidx 3 + 1, colidx] = dI[1] Jb[rowidx 3 + 2, colidx] = dI[2] else: Jb[rowidx 3: rowidx 3 + 3, colidx] = 0.0 # Step 4: Response Matrix Rb = Jb.T @ Jb # Step 5: QUBO Solution (Greedy Deletion Approximation) numtodelete = nb - Kb if numtodelete <= 0: retentionmasks.append(np.ones(nb, dtype=bool)) continue x = np.ones(nb, dtype=float) deleted = np.zeros(nb, dtype=bool) for in range(numtodelete): besti = -1 bestcost = np.inf for i in range(nb): if deleted[i]: continue # Marginal cost of deleting i: approx 2 (Rb @ (1-x))[i] - Rb[i,i] # Using exact quadratic form difference for correctness y = 1.0 - x.copy() y[i] = 0.0 cost = y @ Rb @ y + lambdapenalty (np.sum(x) - 1.0 - Kb)2 if cost < bestcost: bestcost = cost besti = i if besti != -1: x[besti] = 0.0 deleted[besti] = True else: break retentionmasks.append(x.astype(bool)) return retentionmasks Time Complexity: Dominated by the Jacobian computation O(|Pb| \cdot L{vp} \cdot nb) and the QUBO solve. Greedy selection runs in O(nb^2) per block. Memory Complexity: O(|Pb| \cdot nb) for the Jacobian and O(nb^2) for the response matrix Rb. Strengths: Accounts for pairwise interactions between Gaussians, leading to better visual quality than independent pruning. Limitations: Requires computing derivatives for all selected pixels, which can be memory-intensive for large blocks. The QUBO problem is NP-hard, so approximations are used. When to use: When pruning 3D Gaussian Splatting models while preserving visual fidelity and handling occlusion/interaction effects. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and pruning overhead is prohibitive, or when interactions are negligible. Originated in "SplatQ: Interaction-Aware Pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting via Quadratic Selection" (under review at ICLR 2027). It extends standard pruning by incorporating a quadratic selection mechanism based on the opacity response Gram matrix. name: 3D Gaussian Point Spread Function Model
head: 3D Gaussian PDF, 3D Gaussian Probability Density Function, Gaussian PSF, Gaussian Point Spread Function Model
body: The 3D Gaussian Point Spread Function (PSF) Model defines the spatial response of an imaging system using a 3D Gaussian kernel parameterized by a covariance matrix. It serves as the baseline differentiable model for blur in volumetric rendering, where the covariance matrix is optimized during inference to control the level of blur in the rendered image. Unlike its sibling 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Standard) which operates in screen space, this model operates in 3D space, providing the foundational blur kernel before projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D position vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a 3 \times 3 symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix \Sigma. Output: The scalar intensity value h(\mathbf{x}) representing the PSF response at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: \Sigma: A 3 \times 3 matrix. In implementation, this is typically stored as a flat array of 9 floats or explicitly as a symmetric structure (6 unique values) to enforce positive semi-definiteness during optimization. Formula: The PSF is defined as: h(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}\right)}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^3 \det \Sigma}} where: \mathbf{x} is the displacement vector from the center of the PSF. \Sigma^{-1} is the inverse of the covariance matrix. \det \Sigma is the determinant of the covariance matrix. The Fourier transform \hat{h} of this PSF is given by: \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\xi}^T \Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol{\xi}\right) where \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the wavevector. Parameters: \Sigma: The covariance matrix. It is the primary learnable parameter. Optimizing \Sigma directly controls the blur level. Pitfalls: The Gaussian model is a simplification. More photorealistic PSFs can be used, such as those based on differentiable physical models, refractive indices, or optical aberrations expressed using Zernike polynomials. However, the Gaussian model is the standard baseline implemented for differentiability and simplicity. \Sigma must remain symmetric positive semi-definite. During optimization, constraints or parameterizations (e.g., Cholesky decomposition) are required to ensure this property holds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussianpsf3d(x, Sigma): """ Computes the 3D Gaussian Point Spread Function value at position x. Args: x: numpy array of shape (3,), the displacement vector. Sigma: numpy array of shape (3, 3), symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix. Returns: float: The PSF value h(x). """ # Compute inverse of Sigma Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) # Compute determinant of Sigma detSigma = np.linalg.det(Sigma) # Check for numerical stability (det should be > 0 for valid PDF) if detSigma <= 0: return 0.0 # Compute quadratic form: x^T Sigmainv x # Using dot product for efficiency: (x^T @ Sigmainv) @ x quadraticform = np.dot(x, np.dot(Sigmainv, x)) # Compute the exponent term exponent = -0.5 quadraticform # Compute the normalization constant # sqrt((2pi)^3 det(Sigma)) normalization = np.sqrt((2 np.pi)3 detSigma) # Compute the final value h = np.exp(exponent) / normalization return h def gaussianpsffourier(xi, Sigma): """ Computes the Fourier Transform of the 3D Gaussian PSF at wavevector xi. Args: xi: numpy array of shape (3,), the wavevector. Sigma: numpy array of shape (3, 3), symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix. Returns: float: The FT value hhat(xi). """ # Compute inverse of Sigma Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) # Compute quadratic form: xi^T Sigmainv xi quadraticform = np.dot(xi, np.dot(Sigmainv, xi)) # Compute the exponent term exponent = -0.5 quadraticform # Compute the final value hhat = np.exp(exponent) return hhat This variant models the frequency response (Modulation Transfer Function, MTF) of a CT scanner with a Gaussian PSF as a Gaussian function in the frequency domain. It is used to determine Nyquist-compliant sampling distances. Formula: The MTF is given by MTF(f) = e^{-\frac{f^2}{2(2\sigmaf)^2}} where f is spatial frequency and \sigmaf is the standard deviation in the frequency domain. The spatial and frequency domain standard deviations are related by \sigmaf \sigmax = \frac{1}{2\pi}. Parameters: The sampling distance sd must satisfy sd = \frac{1}{fs} \le \frac{1}{6\sigmaf} = \frac{2\pi\sigmax}{6} \approx \sigmax to meet the Nyquist criterion. Specifically, sd should be at most 0.43 \times w (where w \approx 2.35\sigmax is the PSF width). Pitfalls: If sd > \sigmax, aliasing occurs. At sd=2\sigmax, the MTF has a nonzero value at the sampling frequency, causing folding visible as an offset at f=0. The MTF' at the Nyquist frequency is twice the MTF due to folding. Complexity: The evaluation of the 3D Gaussian PSF involves matrix inversion (O(1) for fixed 3 \times 3) and dot products, making it computationally inexpensive per sample. Performance: The Gaussian model is chosen for its differentiability and simplicity, allowing efficient gradient-based optimization of the blur parameters. Strengths: Simple parameterization via \Sigma; analytically tractable Fourier transform; differentiable with respect to \Sigma. Limitations: Less photorealistic than physical models (e.g., Zernike polynomials). The Gaussian assumption may not hold for all imaging systems, particularly if optical transfer functions differ significantly in different axes. The 3D Gaussian PSF model is used in differentiable rendering for 3D fluorescence microscopy. It provides a parameterized prior for the shape representation and topology of biological objects, such as cell membranes, by optimizing the covariance matrix \Sigma to match observed data. The connection to the Modulation Transfer Function in CT imaging highlights its broader application in medical imaging for determining sampling criteria. name: RoofGS Range-Aware Fast Exponential Evaluation
head: RoofGS fast exp, Schraudolph approximation for Gaussian Splatting
body: This method replaces the transcendental exponential function in the Gaussian blending loop with a range-aware bit-level approximation, leveraging the bounded exponent range resulting from opacity culling. It reduces special-function-unit (SFU) pressure and arithmetic overhead, achieving significant throughput gains with negligible visual quality loss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The pre-folded exponent value P(x, y) for a specific Gaussian-pixel pair. Output: The clamped opacity value \alpha(x, y) for alpha blending. Data Structures: P(x, y): A single-precision floating-point number. I(P): A 32-bit integer representing the bit pattern of the approximated exponential. Parameters: Mantissa scale: 2^{23}. Single-precision exponent bias: 127. Calibration constant: \sigma = 0.045677. Clamping threshold: 0.99. Exponent Range: Opacity culling restricts the exponent to the range P(x, y) \in [-\ln 255, 0] \approx [-5.541, 0]. Steps: 1. Compute the pre-folded exponent P(x, y) = p(x, y) + \log o, where p(x, y) is the quadratic form from the 2D Gaussian and o is the learned opacity. 2. Construct the 32-bit integer approximation I(P) using Schraudolph's method: I(P) = \lfloor P \cdot 2^{23} \cdot \log2(e) + 2^{23} \cdot (127 - \sigma) \rfloor where \log2(e) \approx 1.442695. 3. Reinterpret the integer bits as a single-precision floating-point number to get the unclamped approximation: \widehat{\exp}(P) = \text{reinterpret}{\text{float}}(I(P)). 4. Clamp the result to prevent over-saturation: \alpha(x, y) = \min(0.99, \widehat{\exp}(P)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import math def roofgsfastexp(P: float) -> float: """ Computes the range-aware fast exponential approximation for P in [-5.541, 0]. P: Pre-folded exponent (float32) Returns: Clamped opacity (float32) """ # Constants LOG2E = 1.4426950408889634 # log2(e) SIGMA = 0.045677 BIAS = 127.0 MANTISSASCALE = 223 CLAMPMAX = 0.99 # Step 2: Compute the bit pattern value val = P MANTISSASCALE LOG2E + MANTISSASCALE (BIAS - SIGMA) # Step 3: Bitwise reinterpretation (float -> int32 -> float) # struct.pack/unpack simulates the IEEE 754 bitcast intbits = struct.unpack('>I', struct.pack('>f', val))[0] approxexp = struct.unpack('>f', struct.pack('>I', intbits))[0] # Step 4: Clamp return min(CLAMPMAX, approxexp) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The approximation is only valid for P \in [-\ln 255, 0]. A technique that replaces the standard exponential operation with a bit-level approximation tailored to the bounded exponent range after opacity culling, reducing arithmetic and special-function-unit (SFU) pressure. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian-pixel pair, replacing a transcendental function with basic arithmetic and bitwise operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional memory required. Measured Performance: RoofGS achieves a 10.1× end-to-end speedup over 3DGS at 4K resolution on an NVIDIA RTX 4090, increasing throughput from 61 to 616 FPS. Accuracy: The relative error of the approximation is at most \epsilon{max} \approx 0.03 over the bounded range. This leads to a per-pixel color error bounded by |\Delta C|\infty \leq 0.03 in continuous color space, independent of the number of blended Gaussians. The PSNR loss is reported as 0.028 dB. Originated in the RoofGS paper by Yang Luo, Yan Gong, Yongsheng Gao, and Jie Zhao from the State Key Laboratory of Robotics and Systems, Harbin Institute of Technology. The method leverages Schraudolph's bit-level approximation of the exponential function. It was developed to address the computational bottleneck of the Gaussian blending loop in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically targeting the compute-bound rasterizer stage. name: Row-constant hoisting for Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
head: row-constant optimization, inner-loop hoisting
body: Row-constant hoisting is an optimization for the inner pixel loop of a Gaussian splatting rasterizer that hoists row-constant terms outside the inner (column) loop to minimize arithmetic operations per pixel. It reduces the computational cost of evaluating the 2D Gaussian exponent by precomputing terms dependent only on the row coordinate, allowing the inner loop to perform fewer multiplications and additions per column. This method is a specific implementation detail within the broader Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, distinct from higher-level optimizations like Contribution-based ordering or RoofGS Dual-Pixel Incremental Evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A projected 2D Gaussian primitive p with screen-space center (sx, sy), inverse covariance matrix elements a, b, d (where a = \Sigma^{-1}{00}, b = \Sigma^{-1}{01} = \Sigma^{-1}{10}, d = \Sigma^{-1}{11}), opacity \alphap, and color \mathbf{c}p. The bounding box of the splat [x0, y0, x1, y1] is precomputed. Input: A framebuffer fb of width w, where each cell stores an accumulated color \mathbf{C} and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Input: Parameters saturation (max accumulated opacity) and alphathreshold (min alpha for contribution). Output: Updated framebuffer cells within the splat's bounding box. Data Structures: Framebuffer Cell: A tuple (\mathbf{Vec3}, f32) storing accumulated color and opacity. Projected Gaussian: Contains screen position, bounding box, inverse covariance components, opacity, and color. Steps: 1. Extract inverse covariance elements a, b, d from the projected Gaussian's inverse covariance matrix. 2. Compute coefficients for the quadratic form of the Gaussian exponent: dx{coeff} = -0.5 \cdot a dy{coeff} = -0.5 \cdot d cross{coeff} = -b (derived from -0.5 \cdot 2b) 3. Initialize loop bounds y from y0 to y1 inclusive. 4. For each row py in the outer loop: Compute dy = py - sy. Precompute row-constant terms: row{base} = dy{coeff} \cdot dy^2 row{slope} = cross{coeff} \cdot dy row{offset} = py \cdot w (for framebuffer indexing) 5. For each column px in the inner loop (from x0 to x1): Calculate framebuffer index idx = row{offset} + px. Check saturation: if fb[idx].\alpha{acc} \ge saturation, skip to next pixel. Compute dx = px - sx. Calculate the Gaussian exponent power using hoisted coefficients: power = dx{coeff} \cdot dx^2 + row{slope} \cdot dx + row{base} If power > 0.0, skip the pixel (exponential would exceed valid range). Compute alpha: \alpha = (\alphap \cdot e^{power}).\min(0.999). If \alpha < alpha{threshold}, skip the pixel. Compute contribution: t = 1.0 - fb[idx].\alpha{acc}, contrib = t \cdot \alpha. Update framebuffer: fb[idx].\mathbf{C} \leftarrow fb[idx].\mathbf{C} + contrib \cdot \mathbf{c}p fb[idx].\alpha{acc} \leftarrow fb[idx].\alpha{acc} + contrib Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositesplat(p: Projected, fb: List[Tuple[Vec3, float]], w: int, params: RenderParams): """ Composite a single 2D Gaussian splat into the framebuffer using row-constant hoisting. Args: p: Projected Gaussian with attributes: bbox: [x0, y0, x1, y1] (integers) cov2dinv: Inverse covariance matrix elements xaxis.x: a (Sigma^-100) xaxis.y: b (Sigma^-101) yaxis.y: d (Sigma^-111) screen: (sx, sy) (floats) opacity: alphap (float) color: cp (Vec3) fb: Framebuffer list of (color: Vec3, alpha: float) tuples w: Framebuffer width params: Render parameters including saturation and alphathreshold """ # Extract bounding box x0, y0, x1, y1 = p.bbox # Extract inverse covariance elements a = p.cov2dinv.xaxis.x b = p.cov2dinv.xaxis.y d = p.cov2dinv.yaxis.y # Precompute coefficients for the quadratic form dxcoeff = -0.5 a dycoeff = -0.5 d crosscoeff = -b # Equivalent to -0.5 2 b # Extract parameters saturation = params.saturation alphathreshold = params.alphathreshold opacity = p.opacity color = p.color sx = p.screen.x sy = p.screen.y # Outer loop over rows for py in range(y0, y1 + 1): # Compute row-constant terms dy = py - sy rowbase = dycoeff dy dy rowslope = crosscoeff dy rowoffset = py w # Inner loop over columns for px in range(x0, x1 + 1): idx = rowoffset + px cell = fb[idx] # Check saturation if cell[1] >= saturation: continue # Compute column offset dx = px - sx # Calculate power using hoisted row constants power = dxcoeff dx dx + rowslope dx + rowbase # Skip if power is positive (exponential > 1) if power > 0.0: continue # Compute alpha with clamping alpha = min(opacity fastexp(power), 0.999) # Skip if alpha is below threshold if alpha < alphathreshold: continue # Compute contribution t = 1.0 - cell[1] contrib = t alpha # Update framebuffer fb[idx] = ( cell[0] + contrib color, cell[1] + contrib) Parameters: saturation: Maximum accumulated opacity value in the framebuffer cell. If reached, further splats are skipped. alphathreshold: Minimum alpha value for a splat to contribute. Splats with alpha below this are skipped. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the computed power is positive, the exponential term would exceed 1 (or be invalid for the Gaussian model), so the splat is skipped. Alpha is clamped to 0.999 to prevent numerical issues when blending. An optimization that exploits spatial coherence between vertically adjacent pixels by assigning each thread to process two pixels, (x, y) and (x, y+1), allowing reuse of shared-memory attribute loads and incremental exponent calculation. Time and Memory Complexity: The optimization reduces the number of arithmetic operations per pixel in the inner loop by hoisting row-constant calculations. Specifically, it moves the computation of dy{coeff} \cdot dy^2 and cross{coeff} \cdot dy outside the inner loop. Memory complexity is unchanged, as it operates on the same framebuffer structure. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The benefit scales with the number of pixels per splat, as more pixels mean more savings from hoisting row-constant terms. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces computational overhead per pixel by minimizing multiplications and additions in the inner loop. Limitations: Requires precomputing row-constant terms for each row, adding a small overhead to the outer loop. When to Use: Use when optimizing the inner loop of Gaussian splatting rasterization for performance. When Not to Use: Not applicable as a standalone method; it is an optimization within a larger rasterization pipeline. Origin: The method is described in the context of the Tsplat project, an implementation of Gaussian splatting in a terminal environment. History and Development: The technique is part of the Tsplat codebase, which focuses on efficient real-time rendering of Gaussian splats. Where it is Used: Used in the Tsplat renderer for optimizing the rasterization of 2D Gaussians. name: RoofGS Dual-Pixel Incremental Evaluation
head: RoofGS dual-pixel formulation, RoofGS vertical coherence optimization
body: An optimization that exploits spatial coherence between vertically adjacent pixels by assigning each thread to process two pixels, (x, y) and (x, y+1), allowing reuse of shared-memory attribute loads and incremental exponent calculation. It sets itself apart from standard single-pixel rasterization by halving shared-memory traffic and replacing the second pixel's full exponent evaluation with a lightweight incremental update. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The folded exponent P(x, y) for the first pixel (x, y), the Gaussian coefficients C2, C3, C5, and the pixel coordinates x, y. Output: The folded exponent P(x, y+1) for the second pixel (x, y+1). Data Structures: Registers: Store the pre-folded Gaussian coefficients C2, C3, C5 and register-resident coordinate terms. Shared Memory: Stores Gaussian attributes loaded once per tile. Numbered Steps: 1. Thread Assignment: Assign each thread to process two vertically adjacent pixels: (x, y) and (x, y+1). Both pixels traverse the same Gaussian sequence within a tile. 2. Attribute Load Reuse: Load Gaussian attributes from shared memory once. This single load serves both vertically adjacent pixels, halving per-pixel shared-memory traffic. 3. First Pixel Exponent: Compute the exponent P(x, y) for the first pixel using the regular FMA path (Eq. 16 from the parent article). 4. Incremental Update: Compute the exponent P(x, y+1) for the second pixel using the incremental formula derived from P(x, y). Formulas: Let P(x, y) be the folded exponent for pixel (x, y). The exponent for the adjacent pixel (x, y+1) is calculated as: P(x, y + 1) = P(x, y) + C2x + C3(2y + 1) + C5 Where: C2, C3, C5 are pre-folded Gaussian coefficients. x, y are the coordinates of the first pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def roofgsdualpixeleval(Pxy, C2, C3, C5, x, y): """ Computes the exponent for the second pixel (x, y+1) given the first pixel's exponent. Args: Pxy (float): The folded exponent P(x, y) for the first pixel. C2 (float): Coefficient C2. C3 (float): Coefficient C3. C5 (float): Coefficient C5. x (int): X-coordinate of the first pixel. y (int): Y-coordinate of the first pixel. Returns: float: The folded exponent P(x, y+1) for the second pixel. """ # Incremental update formula: P(x, y+1) = P(x, y) + C2x + C3(2y + 1) + C5 Pxy1 = Pxy + C2 x + C3 (2 y + 1) + C5 return Pxy1 Parameters: Tile Size: Not given in the sources. Resolution: Evaluated at 4K resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If y is the last row of the tile, the second pixel (x, y+1) may be out of bounds. Precision: The incremental update involves additions of potentially different magnitudes. A rasterization optimization that evaluates two adjacent pixels to improve instruction-level parallelism. It is chosen when vertical coherence can be exploited to reduce memory bandwidth and arithmetic operations. Time Complexity: Reduces arithmetic operations per pixel by avoiding re-evaluation of the full dot product for the second pixel. Memory Complexity: Halves per-pixel shared-memory traffic by reusing attribute loads for vertically adjacent pixels. Measured Performance: At 4K resolution on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, RoofGS increases average rendering throughput. Strengths: Reduces redundant arithmetic instructions and on-chip memory accesses in the innermost blending loop. Improves instruction scheduling and instruction-level parallelism (ILP) within the rasterization core. Limitations: Requires vertical coherence between pixels. When to Use: When rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes on GPUs where shared-memory bandwidth and arithmetic throughput are bottlenecks. When Not to Use: When the overhead of managing dual-pixel threads outweighs the benefits, or on hardware with very high shared-memory bandwidth relative to arithmetic throughput. Originated in the paper "RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting" by Yang Luo, Yan Gong, Yongsheng Gao, and Jie Zhao. The work was supported by the National Science and Technology Major Project and the National Outstanding Youth Science Fund of the National Natural Science Foundation of China. It is used in the context of accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization by optimizing the inner pixel loop. name: 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization
head: EWA Projection, Elliptical Weighted Average projection, 2D Gaussian Projection, Gaussian Projection, Linearized 2D Gaussian Projection
body: 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization is the core rasterization primitive of 3D Gaussian Splatting that maps an anisotropic 3D Gaussian volume primitive into a 2D elliptical footprint (splat) on the image plane. It solves the problem of rendering millions of 3D probability distributions efficiently by approximating the non-linear perspective projection with a local affine transformation, thereby preserving the Gaussian form in screen space. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Optimal Gaussian Splatting Projection by using a fixed image-plane projection rather than per-Gaussian tangent planes, and from Render Means by explicitly computing the screen-space covariance matrix to handle shape and spread. The method stabilizes the projection by adding a small epsilon to the diagonal of the 2D covariance matrix to guarantee positive definiteness and prevent aliasing. Inputs: M 3D Gaussians, each defined by: Mean position in world space \muw \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized). Scale vector s \in \mathbb{R}^3 (log-scale parameters). Opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients h for view-dependent color. Camera parameters: View matrix V \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} (world-to-camera). Projection matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} (perspective). Image dimensions W, H (width, height in pixels). Principal point (cx, cy) (often center of image). Outputs: A list of projected 2D Gaussians, each containing: Screen-space mean \mu{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. Inverse covariance (conic) matrix \Sigma{2D}^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. Depth zc (for sorting). Bounding box (AABB) in screen coordinates. Color and opacity attributes. Data Structures: The projected Gaussian is typically stored in a struct with the following fields: screen: Vec2 (pixel center sx, sy). depth: f32 (zc, positive in front of camera). cov2dinv: Mat2 (inverse 2D covariance). bbox: [i32; 4] (inclusive x0, y0, x1, y1). color: Vec3 (RGB). opacity: f32 ([0, 1]). Steps: 1. Reconstruct 3D Covariance Matrix: Compute the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma from the quaternion q and scale s. R = \text{QuaternionToMatrix}(q) S = \text{diag}(\exp(s0), \exp(s1), \exp(s2)) \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top Note: \Sigma is symmetric positive semi-definite. 2. Transform to Camera Space: Transform the mean and covariance to camera space using the view matrix V. \muc = V{3 \times 3} \muw + V{3 \times 1} \Sigmac = V{3 \times 3} \Sigma V{3 \times 3}^\top Here, V{3 \times 3} is the upper-left 3 \times 3 rotation block of the view matrix. Translation is ignored for covariance as it describes spread around the centroid. 3. Compute Projection Jacobian: Linearize the perspective projection at \muc = (xc, yc, zc) using the Jacobian J. The perspective projection maps (x, y, z) to (u, v): u = fx \frac{x}{z} + cx, \quad v = fy \frac{y}{z} + cy The Jacobian J \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3} evaluated at \muc is: J = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{fx}{zc} & 0 & -\frac{fx xc}{zc^2} \\ 0 & \frac{fy}{zc} & -\frac{fy yc}{zc^2} \end{pmatrix} Focal lengths fx, fy are derived from the projection matrix or camera intrinsics. 4. Project Covariance to 2D: Compute the screen-space covariance \Sigma{2D} by applying the Jacobian to the camera-space covariance: \Sigma{2D} = J \Sigmac J^\top This results in a 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix. 5. Covariance Stabilization (Low-Pass Filter): Add a small epsilon \epsilon{2d} to the diagonal of \Sigma{2D} to ensure positive definiteness and prevent aliasing from infinitely small Gaussians. \Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}} = \Sigma{2D} + \epsilon{2d} I Typical value for \epsilon{2d} is 0.3. Some implementations use 0.01. This ensures each Gaussian spans at least the width of a single pixel. 6. Compute Screen-Space Mean: Project the camera-space mean \muc to screen coordinates: \mu{2D} = \left( fx \frac{xc}{zc} + cx, \quad fy \frac{yc}{zc} + cy \right) 7. Compute Inverse Covariance (Conic): Compute the inverse of the stabilized covariance matrix \Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}} for efficient evaluation in the fragment shader. For a symmetric matrix \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{bmatrix}: \det = ad - b^2 If \det \le 0, cull the splat. \Sigma{2D}^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -b & a \end{bmatrix} 8. Compute Bounding Box: Determine the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for the splat to optimize rasterization. Compute eigenvalues \lambda{1,2} of \Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}}: \lambda{1,2} = \frac{\text{tr}(\Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}})}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{\text{tr}(\Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}})^2}{4} - \det(\Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}})} Compute unit eigenvectors e1, e2. Define half-axes b1 = 3\sqrt{\lambda1}e1 and b2 = 3\sqrt{\lambda2}e2 (using 3\sigma cutoff). The bounding box is the AABB of the parallelogram spanned by b1 and b2 centered at \mu{2D}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Converts a normalized quaternion (w, x, y, z) to a 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - zw), 2(xz + yw)], [2(xy + zw), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - xw)], [2(xz - yw), 2(yz + xw), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) def projectgaussian(gaussian, camera): """ Projects a single 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space. Args: gaussian: dict with keys 'pos' (3,), 'rot' (4,), 'scale' (3,), 'opacity' (float) camera: dict with keys 'viewmatrix' (4x4), 'projmatrix' (4x4), 'fx', 'fy', 'cx', 'cy', 'width', 'height' Returns: dict with keys 'mu2d', 'cov2dinv', 'depth', 'bbox', 'color', 'opacity' or None if culled. """ # 1. Reconstruct 3D Covariance R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(gaussian['rot']) S = np.diag(np.exp(gaussian['scale'])) Sigma3d = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # 2. Transform to Camera Space V = camera['viewmatrix'] Vrot = V[:3,:3] Vtrans = V[:3, 3] muc = Vrot @ gaussian['pos'] + Vtrans Sigmac = Vrot @ Sigma3d @ Vrot.T xc, yc, zc = muc # Cull if behind camera if zc <= 0.0: return None # 3. Compute Jacobian fx = camera['fx'] fy = camera['fy'] J = np.array([ [fx / zc, 0, -fx xc / (zc2)], [0, fy / zc, -fy yc / (zc2)] ]) # 4. Project Covariance Sigma2d = J @ Sigmac @ J.T # 5. Stabilize Covariance eps2d = 0.3 # Default stabilization factor Sigma2dstab = Sigma2d + eps2d np.eye(2) # 6. Compute Screen Mean mu2d = np.array([ fx (xc / zc) + camera['cx'], fy (yc / zc) + camera['cy'] ]) # 7. Compute Inverse Covariance det = Sigma2dstab[0,0] Sigma2dstab[1,1] - Sigma2dstab[0,1]2 if det <= 0.0: return None # Cull singular covariance invdet = 1.0 / det cov2dinv = np.array([ [Sigma2dstab[1,1] invdet, -Sigma2dstab[0,1] invdet], [-Sigma2dstab[0,1] invdet, Sigma2dstab[0,0] invdet] ]) # 8. Compute Bounding Box (3-sigma) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2dstab) # eigenvalues are sorted ascending, so lambda1 is smallest lambda1, lambda2 = eigenvalues[0], eigenvalues[1] e1, e2 = eigenvectors[:, 0], eigenvectors[:, 1] b1 = 3.0 np.sqrt(lambda1) e1 b2 = 3.0 np.sqrt(lambda2) e2 # Bounding box corners corners = [ mu2d - b1 - b2, mu2d + b1 - b2, mu2d + b1 + b2, mu2d - b1 + b2 ] corners = np.array(corners) bbox = np.array([ np.floor(np.min(corners[:, 0])), np.floor(np.min(corners[:, 1])), np.ceil(np.max(corners[:, 0])), np.ceil(np.max(corners[:, 1])) ]) # Clip bbox to image bounds bbox[0] = max(0, bbox[0]) bbox[1] = max(0, bbox[1]) bbox[2] = min(camera['width'] - 1, bbox[2]) bbox[3] = min(camera['height'] - 1, bbox[3]) if bbox[0] > bbox[2] or bbox[1] > bbox[3]: return None # Compute Color (simplified, assuming SH evaluation is handled elsewhere) # In full implementation, evaluate SH at view direction viewdir = -muc / np.linalg.norm(muc) color = evaluatesh(gaussian['shcoeffs'], viewdir) # Placeholder return { 'mu2d': mu2d, 'cov2dinv': cov2dinv, 'depth': zc, 'bbox': bbox, 'color': color, 'opacity': gaussian['opacity'] } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Divide Non-Linearity: The projection is non-linear. The affine approximation is valid only locally around the centroid. For very large Gaussians or extreme FOV, this approximation may introduce geometric warping artifacts. Singular Covariance: If the determinant of the 2D covariance is zero or negative, the inverse is undefined. This can happen if the Gaussian is viewed edge-on or if numerical errors accumulate. Stabilization (\epsilon{2d}) mitigates this. Depth Sorting: Gaussians must be sorted by depth (zc) before compositing to ensure correct alpha blending. Aliasing: Without stabilization, small Gaussians can cause high-frequency aliasing. The low-pass filter ensures minimum pixel coverage. Computes a tight, axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for a 2D Gaussian splat based on an opacity threshold, replacing the loose circular bounding box used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart from siblings like Tight Ellipse AABB Derivation by explicitly integrating the splat's opacity and a configurable threshold to prune negligible contributions, thereby reducing false-positive tile intersections during rasterization. Render Means is the simplest possible rendering mode for 3D Gaussian Splatting, where each Gaussian is represented by a single pixel at the location where its 3D mean projects onto the 2D image plane. It demonstrates the basic camera transformation pipeline (world → camera → image) and frustum culling without any rasterization complexity. Unlike its sibling 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization, which computes screen-space covariance matrices for elliptical splatting, Render Means ignores shape and spread, treating Gaussians as point sprites. Optimal Gaussian Splatting Projection is a rendering method that minimizes projection error by projecting each 3D Gaussian onto a plane tangent to the line connecting the Gaussian mean to the camera center, rather than a fixed image plane. It sets itself apart from standard 3D-GS by using a unique tangent plane for each Gaussian based on its position relative to the camera, significantly reducing artifacts like blurriness and needle-like structures, particularly in wide-field-of-view or short focal length scenarios. This method stabilizes the projection of 3D Gaussians into screen space by applying a low-pass filter to the 2D covariance matrix, ensuring that each Gaussian spans at least the width of a single pixel to reduce aliasing artifacts. It computes the inverse covariance (conic) matrix and a scalar rescale factor that preserves the integrated density of the Gaussian after filtering. Computes the 2 \times 3 Jacobian matrix of the perspective projection function with respect to 3D coordinates, used for linearizing the projection of 3D Gaussians into screen space. It transforms the 3D covariance structure into 2D screen-space covariance, enabling accurate Gaussian splatting. Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Gaussian Splatting assigns material properties as texture maps in the splat's local coordinate system rather than single attribute values per primitive, enabling higher-frequency spatial detail without increasing primitive count. It decouples geometry from appearance, allowing complex visual features and detailed normal maps to be captured within the existing Gaussian representation. This method differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by treating alpha-blending as a smoothing filter in a deferred rendering pipeline, which stabilizes the optimization of texture-sampled features and produces more cohesive results compared to shading directly on Gaussians. This method approximates the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances using a linear regression model, serving as a computationally efficient alternative to neural network-based corrections in Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by replacing complex learned mappings with closed-form linear coefficients or a single scalar factor, thereby reducing training overhead while maintaining reconstruction quality comparable to Half-Cosine (HC) kernels. 3D Ellipsoid Projection is a Gaussian selection method used to identify candidate 3D Gaussians for rendering specific image slices in volume rendering pipelines. It approximates the spatial extent of a 3D Gaussian ellipsoid as a sphere to compute a uniform 2D bounding box, which is then projected orthogonally onto every image slice. Unlike sibling methods that adapt bounding boxes per slice or use complex covariance corrections, this approach prioritizes simplicity by treating the Gaussian's range as isotropic, though this leads to redundant computation for off-center slices. Time Complexity: O(M) for projection of M Gaussians, where each projection involves constant-time matrix operations (3 \times 3 and 2 \times 2). Sorting takes O(M \log M). Rasterization is O(P) where P is the number of pixels, but optimized by tile-based binning to only process relevant splats. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store the projected splats. Measured Performance: The method enables real-time rendering of millions of Gaussians. For example, on the Mip-NeRF360 benchmark, 3DGS reaches 27.21 dB PSNR and 0.214 LPIPS at 134 fps. An accelerator implementation achieved 129 FPS at Full HD (1080p). Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Performance is heavily dependent on the efficiency of the sorting and tile-based rasterization stages. Strengths: Closed-form projection allows for differentiable rendering, enabling gradient-based optimization of scene parameters. High rendering speed due to efficient rasterization. Limitations: The affine approximation of perspective projection can introduce artifacts for very large Gaussians or extreme viewpoints. Requires careful handling of numerical stability (covariance stabilization). When to use: When real-time or differentiable rendering of large-scale 3D scenes is required. When not to use: When high geometric accuracy for very large primitives is critical, or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained and M is extremely large. The method was originally described by Zwicker et al. in 2002 for anti-aliased splatting of volume data. It was later reused by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for the closed-form projection of 3D Gaussians, enabling real-time rendering of photorealistic scenes. name: Adaptive Bounding Box Computation
head: Tsplat bounding box
body: Computes a tight, axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for a 2D Gaussian splat based on a specific opacity threshold, replacing the loose circular bounding box used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). This method significantly reduces false-positive tile intersections and the resulting number of duplicated splat fragments during rasterization. It serves as the core geometric culling step in differentiable rendering pipelines that utilize Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction, enabling efficient depth-sorted rasterization by emitting sorted keys only for relevant tiles. Inputs: sx, sy: Screen-space center coordinates of the 2D Gaussian splat (float). cov2d00, cov2d11: Diagonal elements of the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma (float). Note: This method assumes the covariance is diagonal or that these are the effective variances along the screen axes after rotation handling in the parent step. opacity: The scalar opacity of the splat (float). alphathreshold: The minimum opacity threshold \tau for a pixel to be considered visible (float). maxk2: The maximum allowed squared Mahalanobis distance to prevent overflow or excessive box sizes (float). wi, hi: Framebuffer width and height in pixels (uint). Outputs: A bounding box defined by integer coordinates (x0, y0, x1, y1), or None if the splat is effectively invisible or has negligible size. Data Structures: No complex data structures. The output is typically a tuple or struct containing the four integer coordinates. Steps: 1. Opacity Check: If opacity \le alphathreshold, return None. The splat cannot contribute any pixel above the threshold. 2. Compute Squared Mahalanobis Distance Limit (k^2): Calculate the squared distance in the normalized space corresponding to the opacity threshold: k^2 = \min\left(2.0 \cdot \ln\left(\frac{\text{opacity}}{\text{alpha\threshold}}\right), \text{max\k2}\right) If k^2 \le 0.0, return None. This ensures the bounding box covers at least one pixel and avoids numerical instability. 4. Clip to Framebuffer: Clamp the coordinates to the valid framebuffer range: x0 = \max(0, x0) y0 = \max(0, y0) x1 = \min(wi - 1, x1) y1 = \min(hi - 1, y1) 6. Validity Check: If x0 > x1 or y0 > y1, return None. The bounding box is empty or invalid. 7. Return: Return the tuple (x0, y0, x1, y1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient to avoid negative values under the square root due to numerical noise, although the check k^2 \le 0.0 handles this. Boundaries: The clipping step ensures the bounding box stays within the framebuffer. Opacity threshold multiplier: mult (also referred to as \beta in Compact Box). Image grid dimensions: grid.x, grid.y (number of tiles in x and y). The output is typically stored in two parallel arrays for sorting: 1. gaussiankeysunsorted: An array of 64-bit integers. The upper 32 bits store the tile ID (computed as u \cdot grid.x + v or v \cdot grid.x + u), and the lower 32 bits store the depth of the Gaussian. 2. gaussianvaluesunsorted: An array of 32-bit integers storing the Gaussian index (idx). mult: Scalar multiplier for the opacity threshold. Default value in render.py is 0.5. 1. Opacity Threshold (t): The threshold t is derived from the Gaussian's opacity con\o.w and the multiplier mult: t = mult \cdot 2.0 \cdot \log(con\o.w \cdot 255.0) 2. Discriminant (disc): Calculated from the covariance matrix elements to determine the ellipse's orientation and validity: disc = con\o.y \cdot con\o.y - con\o.x \cdot con\o.z 3. Bounding Box Terms (x\term, y\term): These terms represent the half-extents along the x and y axes, adjusted for the ellipse's rotation: x\term = \text{sign}(con\o.y) \cdot \sqrt{\frac{-(con\o.y \cdot con\o.y \cdot t)}{disc \cdot con\o.x}} y\term = \text{sign}(con\o.y) \cdot \sqrt{\frac{-(con\o.y \cdot con\o.y \cdot t)}{disc \cdot con\o.z}} Note: The sign correction ensures the terms are added/subtracted correctly relative to the center based on the off-diagonal element's sign. 4. Bounding Box Arguments (bbox\argmin, bbox\argmax): Initial estimates for the min/max coordinates in pixel space: bbox\argmin = (py - y\term, px - x\term) bbox\argmax = (py + y\term, px + x\term) 5. Actual Bounding Box Coordinates (bbox\min, bbox\max): The final tight bounding box is computed by calling computeEllipseIntersection for the x and y dimensions at the argmin and argmax points. This function refines the AABB to tightly fit the ellipse. 6. Tile Indices (rect\min, rect\max): Convert pixel coordinates to tile indices: rect\min = \left( \left\lfloor \frac{bbox\min.x}{BLOCK\X} \right\rfloor, \left\lfloor \frac{bbox\min.y}{BLOCK\Y} \right\rfloor \right) rect\max = \left( \left\lceil \frac{bbox\max.x}{BLOCK\X} \right\rceil, \left\lceil \frac{bbox\max.y}{BLOCK\Y} \right\rceil \right) Clamped to [0, grid.x] and [0, grid.y] respectively. Compute bounding box arguments (initial min/max) px, py = p argminx = px - xterm argminy = py - yterm argmaxx = px + xterm argmaxy = py + yterm # 6. Compute actual bounding box coordinates using ellipse intersection # bboxmin = computeEllipseIntersection(argminx, argminy,...) # bboxmax = computeEllipseIntersection(argmaxx, argmaxy,...) # The exact implementation of computeEllipseIntersection is not provided in the sources. # It typically involves finding the exact intersection of the vertical/horizontal lines # passing through the arg points with the ellipse boundary. # For implementation purposes, this step tightens the AABB to the ellipse. bboxminx, bboxminy = computeellipseintersectionx(argminx, argminy, cono) bboxminy, bboxminx = computeellipseintersectiony(argminy, argminx, cono) # Note: y-min might need separate call bboxmaxx, bboxmaxy = computeellipseintersectionx(argmaxx, argmaxy, cono) bboxmaxy, bboxmaxy = computeellipseintersectiony(argmaxy, argmaxx, cono) # Note: y-max might need separate call # Placeholder for the actual tight bounding box calculation. # In practice, this function solves for the exact x/y extent of the ellipse # given the min/max x/y bounds derived from the terms. # bboxmin = (bboxminx, bboxminy) # bboxmax = (bboxmaxx, bboxmaxy) # 7. Precision: The calculation involves square roots and divisions by the discriminant. Opacity Threshold: The threshold t depends on the opacity. If opacity is very low, t may become negative or very small, affecting the bounding box size. It reduces the number of tiles per splat by checking only tiles whose bounding-circle intersects with the splat, using approximate circle-ellipse intersection tests. When to Use: When rendering performance is critical and the scene contains many large, transparent Gaussians. It is particularly effective at higher resolutions where the number of tiles increases. When Not to Use: When exact pixel-perfect rendering is required and computational resources are sufficient to handle the higher number of duplicated splats. body: This method computes the tight axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of a projected 2D Gaussian ellipse in constant time. It replaces the loose circular bounding box used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting to determine tile intersections, significantly reducing false-positive splat duplications during rasterization. Inputs: Two 2D basis vectors \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^2 defining the ellipse shape and orientation. Opacity \sigmai of the Gaussian \mathcal{G}i. Threshold value for \alphai(p) to define the ellipse boundary. Tile size T. Image boundaries (width W, height H). Center coordinates (cx, cy) of the projected Gaussian. Outputs: A rectangular tile extent (min/max tile coordinates) that tightly encloses the ellipse. Data Structures: Matrix D \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: Symmetric matrix derived from basis vectors. Matrix C \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: Inverse of D. Bounds: Four scalar values (x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}) representing the AABB in pixel coordinates, converted to tile indices. Steps: 1. Define Ellipse Geometry: The threshold \alphai(p) = \sigmai gi(p) determines the exact pixel extent of the Gaussian as an ellipse. The ellipse is defined by the implicit equation f(x, y) = 0 derived from the inverse matrix C. 2. Construct Matrix D: Convert the basis vectors \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} into a symmetric 2 \times 2 matrix D using outer products: D = \mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T + \mathbf{b}\mathbf{b}^T 3. Compute Inverse Matrix C: Calculate the inverse of D: C = D^{-1} Let C = \begin{pmatrix} C{00} & C{01} \\ C{10} & C{11} \end{pmatrix}. Since D is symmetric, C is also symmetric, so C{01} = C{10}. 4. Derive Vertical Extents (x-bounds): Points on the vertical edges of the AABB are points on the ellipse where the gradient \nabla f is horizontal (i.e., \partial f/\partial y = 0). Solving this condition yields the half-width x{half} = \sqrt{D{00}}. The source notes this simplified formula saves arithmetic instructions compared to Hanson et al. [HTL25]. 5. Derive Horizontal Extents (y-bounds): Apply the same derivation swapping x and y (and indices 0 and 1) to find points where the gradient is vertical (\partial f/\partial x = 0). This yields the half-height y{half} = \sqrt{D{11}}. 6. Combine Bounds: The pixel coordinates for the AABB edges are x{left} = cx - x{half}, x{right} = cx + x{half}, y{bottom} = cy - y{half}, y{top} = cy + y{half}. 7. Convert to Tile Coordinates: Divide the pixel bounds by the tile size T and round appropriately: tile{min\x} = \lfloor x{left} / T \rfloor, \quad tile{max\x} = \lceil x{right} / T \rceil tile{min\y} = \lfloor y{bottom} / T \rceil, \quad tile{max\y} = \lceil y{top} / T \rceil 8. Clip to Image Boundary: Clip the tile coordinates to the image boundaries [0, W/T] \times [0, H/T]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetightellipseaabb(a, b, centerx, centery, tilesize, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Computes the tight AABB for a 2D Gaussian ellipse defined by basis vectors a and b. Args: a: tuple (ax, ay), 2D basis vector b: tuple (bx, by), 2D basis vector centerx: float, x-coordinate of the ellipse center in pixels centery: float, y-coordinate of the ellipse center in pixels tilesize: float, size of a tile in pixels imagewidth: int, width of the image in pixels imageheight: int, height of the image in pixels Returns: tuple: (mintilex, mintiley, maxtilex, maxtiley) """ # Step 2: Construct Matrix D = aa^T + bb^T D00 = a[0]a[0] + b[0]b[0] D01 = a[0]a[1] + b[0]b[1] D11 = a[1]a[1] + b[1]b[1] # Step 3: Compute Inverse Matrix C = D^-1 detD = D00 D11 - D01 D01 # Guard against degenerate ellipse (zero determinant) if abs(detD) < 1e-9: return (0, 0, 0, 0) C00 = D11 / detD C01 = -D01 / detD C11 = D00 / detD # Steps 4 & 5: Derive extents using simplified formula from Appendix A # xhalf = sqrt(D00), yhalf = sqrt(D11) xhalf = math.sqrt(D00) yhalf = math.sqrt(D11) # Step 6: Combine bounds with center offset xleft = centerx - xhalf xright = centerx + xhalf ybottom = centery - yhalf ytop = centery + yhalf # Step 7: Convert to tile coordinates mintilex = math.floor(xleft / tilesize) maxtilex = math.ceil(xright / tilesize) mintiley = math.floor(ybottom / tilesize) maxtiley = math.ceil(ytop / tilesize) # Step 8: Clip to image boundary maxtilex = min(maxtilex, math.ceil(imagewidth / tilesize)) maxtiley = min(maxtiley, math.ceil(imageheight / tilesize)) mintilex = max(mintilex, 0) mintiley = max(mintiley, 0) return (mintilex, mintiley, maxtilex, maxtiley) Parameters: Threshold: Determined by opacity \sigmai and the Gaussian value function gi(p). Tile size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the determinant of D is zero (degenerate ellipse, e.g., line or point), the inverse C is undefined. A guard must handle this. False Negatives: Using an approximate tile-ellipse intersection test may produce occasional false-negatives. This is acceptable for editors operating on fully-trained models but would negatively influence convergence in gradient descent-based optimization. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in matrix inversion can lead to negative values under the square root. Clamping to zero is recommended. An algorithm for identifying the minimum and maximum points (extents) of an ellipse within a given tile row or column during rasterization, used to determine which pixels to render. It improves upon SnugBox by handling cases where the ellipse intersects tile boundaries more precisely. Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) per Gaussian splat for AABB computation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Significantly reduces false-positive tile intersections compared to the bounding circle approach in 3DGS, leading to fewer splat duplications and improved rendering performance. Strengths: Tighter bounds reduce the number of tiles processed per splat. The simplified formula saves arithmetic instructions compared to earlier methods like Hanson et al. [HTL25]. Limitations: Approximate intersection tests (if used in subsequent steps) may cause false-negatives, which are detrimental to optimization but acceptable for rendering. The method was introduced as part of the "SnugBox" algorithm in the Speedy-Splat paper. It addresses the inefficiency of the original 3D Gaussian Splatting method, which duplicates splats for each tile within the ellipse's bounding circle, leading to numerous false-positives. The derivation in Appendix A of the Splatshop paper provides a simplified formula for the tight AABB, noting that it saves arithmetic instructions compared to concurrent work by Hanson et al..
