name: AccuTile
head: Accurate Tile Extent Computation
body: AccuTile is an algorithm for identifying the minimum and maximum points (extents) of a 2D ellipse within a given tile row or column during rasterization, used to determine the exact set of tiles intersected by a Gaussian. It improves upon SnugBox by handling cases where the ellipse intersects tile boundaries more precisely, reducing the number of tiles further than SnugBox. Unlike baseline 3D-GS which allocates tiles based on a square inscribing a circle, or SnugBox which uses a tight bounding box, AccuTile computes the exact Gaussian-to-tile intersections by iterating over the shorter side of the SnugBox tile extent. AccuTile extends the SnugBox method to identify the exact tiles intersected by the Gaussian. It takes as input the tight bounding box produced by SnugBox and its rectangular tile extent. The algorithm iterates over the rows (or columns) of the SnugBox tile extent, processing along the shorter side of the extent. For each row or column, it identifies the exact tile extent by finding the minimum and maximum points of the ellipse inside it. All tiles between these minimum and maximum points are marked as intersecting the ellipse. The algorithm requires only two intersection points per row or column of the SnugBox. Inputs: Ellipse E: Implicitly defined by the projected 2D covariance parameters. SnugBox Bounding Box B: The axis-aligned tight bounding box of the ellipse, with sides denoted by subscripts t (top), b (bottom), l (left), and r (right). SnugBox Tile Extent Rectangle R: The rectangular tile extent of the Gaussian, with sides denoted similarly. Tile size: Implicitly used to convert coordinates to tile indices. Outputs: Tile count C: The total number of tiles intersected by the Gaussian. Processed tiles: The range of tiles for each row/column. Ellipse E: Implicitly defined by the projected 2D covariance parameters. Bounding Box B: Defined by four scalar values: Bt, Bb, Bl, Br representing the top, bottom, left, and right coordinates of the tight bounding box. Tile Extent Rectangle R: Defined by four scalar values: Rt, Rb, Rl, Rr representing the top, bottom, left, and right tile boundaries. Intersection Points: Pairs of (x, y) coordinates representing the intersection of the ellipse with a horizontal or vertical line. 1. Initialize: Set tile count C \leftarrow 0. Set linemin \leftarrow Rb (the bottom line of the rectangle R). 2. Initial Intersection: If linemin \ge Bb (the bottom line of the rectangle is below or at the bottom of the bounding box), compute the initial intersection points imin \leftarrow \text{Intersections}(linemin, E) using Equation 15. If linemin < Bb, no initial intersection is computed for the first row. 3. Loop: For each row r in R (processed from bottom to top): a. Set linemax \leftarrow Rt (the top line of the current row r). b. Upper Intersection: If linemax \le Bt (the top line of the current row is above or at the top of the bounding box), compute the intersection points imax \leftarrow \text{Intersections}(linemax, E) using Equation 15. If linemax > Bt, no intersection is computed for this row. c. Determine Minimum Extent (emin): If the bottom-left corner of the bounding box Bl is within row r, then emin \leftarrow Bl. Otherwise, emin \leftarrow \min(imin, imax). d. Determine Maximum Extent (emax): If the bottom-right corner of the bounding box Br is within row r, then emax \leftarrow Br. Otherwise, emax \leftarrow \max(imin, imax). e. Convert to Tile Indices: Convert emin and emax to tile indices tilemin and tilemax. f. Update Count: C \leftarrow C + (tilemax - tilemin). g. Process Tiles: Call \text{Process}(tilemin, tilemax). h. Update for Next Row: Set imin \leftarrow imax. This reuses the upper boundary intersection of the current row as the lower boundary intersection for the next row, as the boundaries are shared. 4. Return: Return C. Ellipse Equation (Eq. 14): Referenced in sources but not explicitly provided in the text. It defines the 2D ellipse boundary of the projected Gaussian. Intersection Calculation (Eq. 15): Referenced in sources but not explicitly provided in the text. It calculates the intersection points of the ellipse E with a horizontal line y = linemin or y = linemax. Tile Size: Implicitly used to convert coordinates to tile indices. Threshold: The threshold on \alphai(p) = \sigmai gi(p) that defines the ellipse boundary. Not given in the sources. The algorithm handles several cases to ensure correctness: 1. Case 1: Ellipse does not intersect tile row boundary: The entire ellipse lies within the row. The bounding box extrema x{min} and x{max} computed by SnugBox are selected as the furthest extents. 2. Case 2: Ellipse intersects one boundary but not the other: 2.1: Both x{min} and x{max} are in the row. They are assigned as the furthest extent. 2.2: Neither x{min} nor x{max} is in the row, but y{max} (or y{min}) is. The ellipse decreases monotonically from y{max} to the boundary. The row boundary intersections are selected as the furthest extent. 2.3: One critical point (e.g., x{min}) and one extremum (e.g., y{min}) are in the row, but the other extremum (e.g., x{max}) is not. The ellipse increases monotonically from y{min} to the boundary. The ellipse point on the curve that extends to the right of y{min} and intersects the tile row boundary is selected as the maximum extent. 3. Case 3: Ellipse intersects both top and bottom row boundaries: If x{min} or x{max} is in the row, it is assigned as the min/max extent. Otherwise, the ellipse monotonically increases from one boundary to the other. The minimum or maximum boundary point is selected. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def AccuTile(E, B, R, tilesize): """ Computes the exact tile intersection of a Gaussian. Args: E: Ellipse object with attributes xc, yc, a, b (semi-axes). B: SnugBox Bounding Box with attributes t, b, l, r. R: SnugBox Tile Extent Rectangle with attributes t, b, l, r and a list of rows. tilesize: Width/height of a single tile in world/pixel coordinates. Returns: C: Total number of tiles intersected. """ C = 0 linemin = R.b # Initial intersection if the bottom of the tile extent is within or above the bounding box bottom if linemin >= B.b:, imin = Intersections(linemin, E) else: imin = None # Iterate over each row in the tile extent for row in R.rows: linemax = row.t # Compute upper intersection if the top of the row is within or below the bounding box top if linemax <= B.t:, imax = Intersections(linemax, E) else: imax = None # Determine emin if B.l in row: emin = B.l else: if imin is not None and imax is not None: emin = min(imin, imax) elif imin is not None: emin = imin else: emin = imax # Determine emax if B.r in row: emax = B.r else: if imin is not None and imax is not None: emax = max(imin, imax) elif imin is not None: emax = imin else: emax = imax # Convert to tile indices tilemin = int(emin / tilesize) tilemax = int(emax / tilesize) # Update count C += (tilemax - tilemin) # Process tiles Process(tilemin, tilemax) # Update imin for next row imin = imax return C def Intersections(liney, E): """ Computes the intersection points of the ellipse E with the horizontal line y = liney. Returns the left and right x-coordinates, or (None, None) if no intersection. Standard ellipse intersection calculation based on Eq. 15. """ dy = liney - E.yc if abs(dy) > E.b: return None, None delta = 1.0 - (dy dy) / (E.b E.b) if delta < 0: return None, None dx = E.a math.sqrt(delta) return E.xc - dx, E.xc + dx Time Complexity: AccuTile counts tiles in time proportional to the shorter side of the tile extent and processes tiles in time proportional to the tile count. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the Tanks & Temples dataset, AccuTile achieves a 1.67x FPS increase and 1.12x training time decrease compared to baseline 3D-GS, with PSNR 23.73, SSIM 0.849, LPIPS 0.177. On the Deep Blending dataset, AccuTile achieves a 2.32x FPS increase and 1.13x training time decrease compared to baseline 3D-GS, with PSNR 29.12, SSIM 0.885, LPIPS 0.288. AccuTile culminates in an average overall speed-up of 1.99×. Comparison: AccuTile outperforms the StopThePop Tile-Based Culling method in overall runtime. It avoids the overhead of warp-level load balancing and inclusive sums required by the alternative. Strengths: Reduces the number of tiles further than SnugBox, leading to faster downstream functions. Efficiently computes exact Gaussian-to-tile intersections. Limitations: Requires the SnugBox bounding box as input. AccuTile was introduced in the "Speedy-Splat" paper by Hanson et al. in 2025. It is part of the Speedy-Splat method, which aims to provide fast 3D Gaussian Splatting with sparse pixels and sparse primitives. AccuTile extends the SnugBox method, which itself improves upon the baseline 3D-GS tile allocation. The method is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering and training. name: Opacity-aware Non-Square Bounding Box
head: Level-set Bounding Box, Splat Bounding, Tight Bounding Box
body: This method computes a tight, axis-aligned rectangular bounding box for a 2D Gaussian splat based on its projected opacity and covariance, replacing the original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) approach which uses a square bounding box derived from a fixed confidence radius. It reduces false positives in per-tile splat lists by accounting for the Gaussian's actual opacity and the non-square nature of its projected shape. Inputs: \mu{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^2: The projected mean position of the 2D Gaussian. \Sigma{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: The projected 2D covariance matrix. o \in [0, 1]: The opacity of the Gaussian splat. \tau\alpha \in [0, 1]: The opacity threshold below which the splat is skipped (typically \tau\alpha = 1/255). Outputs: b{min} \in \mathbb{R}^2: The minimum corner of the bounding box. b{max} \in \mathbb{R}^2: The maximum corner of the bounding box. Data Structures: The bounding box is represented by two 2D vectors, b{min} and b{max}, defining the axis-aligned rectangle. Steps: 1. Calculate the scaling factor \gamma based on the opacity threshold and the splat's opacity: \gamma = -2 \ln\left(\frac{\tau\alpha}{o}\right) This factor is derived by setting the Gaussian's alpha value equation equal to \tau\alpha and solving for the exponent's numerator. Note: Splats are skipped when their computed \alpha value falls below a threshold \epsilon. 2. Compute the half-extents of the rectangle along the x and y axes using the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix scaled by \gamma: hx = \sqrt{\gamma \cdot \Sigma{2D,1,1}} hy = \sqrt{\gamma \cdot \Sigma{2D,2,2}} Here, \Sigma{2D,1,1} and \Sigma{2D,2,2} are the diagonal elements of \Sigma{2D}. 3. Determine the bounding box corners using the projected mean \mu{2D} = (\mux, \muy): b{min} = (\mux - hx, \muy - hy) b{max} = (\mux + hx, \muy + hy) This follows directly from the rectangle center and half-extents. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeopacityawareboundingbox(mu2d, sigma2d, opacity, taualpha): """ Computes a tight, non-square axis-aligned bounding box for a 2D Gaussian splat. Args: mu2d: Tuple (mux, muy) representing the projected mean. sigma2d: 2x2 matrix (list of lists) representing the projected covariance. opacity: Float representing the splat's opacity o. taualpha: Float representing the opacity threshold (default 1/255). Returns: Tuple (bmin, bmax) where each is a tuple (x, y). """ # Guard against division by zero or log of zero if opacity <= 0.0: return (mu2d, mu2d) # Skip splats below the opacity threshold if opacity < taualpha: return (mu2d, mu2d) gamma = -2.0 math.log(taualpha / opacity) # Extract diagonal covariance elements s11 = sigma2d[0][0] s22 = sigma2d[1][1] # Compute half-extents hx = math.sqrt(gamma s11) hy = math.sqrt(gamma s22) # Compute corners mux, muy = mu2d bmin = (mux - hx, muy - hy) bmax = (mux + hx, muy + hy) return (bmin, bmax) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Zero: If o=0, \ln(\tau\alpha/o) is undefined. Precision: For very small opacities close to \tau\alpha, \gamma approaches 0, resulting in a tight box. For large opacities, \gamma increases, expanding the box. Covariance Degeneracy: If \Sigma{2D} is singular (e.g., a line or point), one half-extent may be zero. Uses an elliptical bound instead of a rectangular one. More accurate but more expensive to test for tile intersection. Choose when precision is critical and performance allows. Computes the AABB of an ellipse. Similar output to this method but derived differently. Choose when using elliptical culling logic. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat. Requires a few arithmetic operations, a logarithm, and square roots. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per splat for the bounding box coordinates. Performance: Reduces false positives in per-tile splat lists compared to the original 3DGS square bounding box. This leads to fewer unnecessary rasterization operations. Strengths: Tighter fit than square boxes; accounts for opacity; simple to implement. Limitations: Still an axis-aligned approximation; may overestimate tile intersections for rotated Gaussians compared to elliptical culling. The original 3DGS method used a square bounding box derived from a 99% confidence ellipse radius (approx. 3\sigma). This approach was criticized for underestimating the size of opaque, axis-aligned splats and overestimating others due to the square constraint. This method was proposed to replace the probabilistic argument with a level-set approach based on the opacity threshold \tau\alpha. It is used in optimized 3DGS renderers to improve culling efficiency. name: Render Means
head: Mean-only rendering, Point projection rendering
body: Render Means is the simplest possible rendering mode for 3D Gaussian Splatting, where each Gaussian is represented by a single pixel at the location where its 3D mean projects onto the 2D image plane. It demonstrates the basic camera transformation pipeline (world → camera → image) and frustum culling without any rasterization complexity. Unlike sibling methods that compute screen-space covariance matrices for elliptical splatting, Render Means ignores shape and spread, treating Gaussians as point sprites. Inputs and Outputs: Input: gs (GaussianSet), camera (Camera), bgcolor (background color). Output: renderedimage (UInt8 Tensor of shape [3, H, W]). Data Structures: The input gs is a GaussianSet containing means (Float32 Tensor, shape [N, 3]), quats (Float32 Tensor, shape [N, 4]), scales (Float32 Tensor, shape [N, 3]), opacities (Float32 Tensor, shape [N]), and shcoefficients (Float32 Tensor, shape [N, S, 3]). Steps: 1. Initialize Image: Create a tensor renderedimage of shape [3, H, W] initialized to bgcolor. 2. Transform Means: Project the 3D means to camera space using the camera's world-to-camera transformation: M{cam} = T{world \to cam} \cdot M{world}. 3. Project to Image: Project the camera-space means to the 2D image plane coordinates (u, v): (u, v) = P(M{cam}). 4. Frustum Culling: Filter out points that are behind the camera or outside the view frustum. 5. Iterate and Render: For each Gaussian i: Check opacity: If opacityi < 0.05, skip the Gaussian. Get integer pixel coordinates: u{int} = \lfloor ui \rfloor, v{int} = \lfloor vi \rfloor. Check bounds: If 0 \le u{int} < W and 0 \le v{int} < H: Retrieve color Ci from precomputed spherical harmonic coefficients. Assign color to pixel: rendered\image[:, v{int}, u{int}] = Ci. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermeans(gsmeans, gsopacities, gsshcolors, camera, bgcolor, H, W): # Initialize rendered image with background color renderedimage = bgcolor[:, None, None].expand(3, H, W).clone() # Project means to image plane meanscam = camera.transformpointsworldtocam(gsmeans) meansimage = camera.projectpointscamtoimageplane(meanscam) # Frustum culling: filter out points behind the camera validindices = [i for i in range(len(gsmeans)) if meanscam[i, 2] > 0] for i in validindices: # Skip low opacity Gaussians if gsopacities[i] < 0.05: continue u, v = meansimage[i] uint, vint = int(u.item()), int(v.item()) # Check image bounds if 0 <= uint < W and 0 <= vint < H: # Assign color to the single pixel renderedimage[:, vint, uint] = gsshcolors[i] return renderedimage Parameters: Opacity Threshold: 0.05. Gaussians with opacity below this value are skipped. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Integer conversion truncates floating-point coordinates, which may cause slight misalignment at high resolutions. Overwriting: Later Gaussians overwrite earlier ones if they project to the same pixel, as no alpha blending is performed. Boundaries: Pixels outside 0, W) \times [0, H) are ignored. [2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization Computes the 2D screen-space covariance matrix and its inverse for a 3D Gaussian splat, ensuring numerical stability by adding a small epsilon to the diagonal to guarantee positive definiteness. It sets itself apart by modeling elliptical shape and spread, unlike the point-based approach of Render Means. Use when shape fidelity is required. Link 2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling Not given in the sources. Link Projection Jacobian Computation Not given in the sources. Link Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Gaussian Splatting Not given in the sources. Link 2D Covariance Correction via Linear Regression Not given in the sources. Link Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians, as each Gaussian is processed once with constant-time projection and assignment. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the output image, with no additional per-Gaussian memory required for covariance matrices or bounding boxes. Strengths: Extremely fast with minimal computational overhead; ideal for debugging, previewing, or visualizing mean locations. Limitations: No shape representation, no alpha blending, artifacts from overwriting, and no smooth edges. When to use: Debugging camera transforms, visualizing point clouds, or when performance is critical and visual fidelity is secondary. When not to use: Final rendering, scenes with overlapping Gaussians requiring blending, or when shape/spread information is important. Render Means is a simplified rendering approach used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting to demonstrate the basic camera transformation pipeline. It serves as a baseline to understand the core concepts of depth sorting and alpha blending by removing the complexity of covariance projection and elliptical splatting. sascha-kirch/splaty, https://github.com/sascha-kirch/splaty, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Optimal Gaussian Splatting Projection
head: Central Radial Projection, Optimal Projection, Optimal Projection Strategy, Tangent Plane Projection
body: Optimal Gaussian Splatting Projection is a rendering method that minimizes projection error by projecting each 3D Gaussian onto a plane tangent to the line connecting the Gaussian mean to the camera center, rather than a fixed image plane. It sets itself apart from standard 3D-GS by using a unique tangent plane for each Gaussian based on its position relative to the camera, significantly reducing artifacts like blurriness and needle-like structures, particularly in wide-field-of-view or short focal length scenarios. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a mean position \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, and other attributes (opacity, color). The camera parameters (center \mathbf{C}, orientation, and projection model) are also required. Output: A 2D screen-space covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} and a 2D mean position \mathbf{m}{2D} for each Gaussian, ready for rasterization. Data Structures: The method requires only minor code modifications to the existing 3D-GS framework and does not introduce complex new data structures. Temporary storage is allocated for tangent plane basis vectors and projected covariances during the transformation pipeline. Steps: 1. Compute Direction Vector: For each Gaussian with mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and camera center \mathbf{C}, compute the direction vector \mathbf{d} from the Gaussian to the camera: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{C} - \boldsymbol{\mu} 2. Define Tangent Plane: Construct a projection plane that is perpendicular to \mathbf{d} and passes through \boldsymbol{\mu}. This plane is tangent to the line connecting \boldsymbol{\mu} and \mathbf{C}. 3. Project to Tangent Plane: Project the 3D Gaussian onto this specific tangent plane instead of the standard z=1 plane. The covariance is rotated into the tangent plane's local orthonormal basis, and the top-left 2 \times 2 block yields the 2D covariance. 4. Transform to Image/Camera Space: Transform the projected Gaussian from the tangent plane back to the standard image or camera coordinate system for rasterization. This requires computing the Jacobian of the perspective projection from the tangent plane to the image plane. 5. Stabilize Covariance: Apply covariance stabilization (e.g., adding a small epsilon \epsilon to the diagonal) to ensure positive definiteness, as described in the parent method [1198-2d-gaussian-projection-with-covariance-stabilization.md]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimalgaussianprojection(gaussianmeans, gaussiancovariances, cameracenter, cameramatrix): """ Projects 3D Gaussians onto tangent planes to minimize projection error. Args: gaussianmeans: List of (N, 3) arrays, positions of N Gaussians in camera space. gaussiancovariances: List of (N, 3, 3) arrays, covariances of N Gaussians. cameracenter: List of (3,) arrays, camera center position C. cameramatrix: List of (3, 3) arrays, intrinsic camera matrix K. Returns: means2d: List of (N, 2) arrays, projected 2D means. covs2d: List of (N, 2, 2) arrays, projected 2D covariances. """ N = len(gaussianmeans) means2d = [[0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] covs2d = [[[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]] for in range(N)] for i in range(N): mu = gaussianmeans[i] Sigma = gaussiancovariances[i] C = cameracenter[i] # Step 1: Direction from Gaussian mean to camera center d = [C[0]-mu[0], C[1]-mu[1], C[2]-mu[2]] normd = (d[0]2 + d[1]2 + d[2]2)0.5 if normd < 1e-8: normd = 1e-8 n = [d[0]/normd, d[1]/normd, d[2]/normd] # Step 2: Construct orthonormal basis (u, v) for tangent plane perpendicular to n ref = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] if abs(n[2]) > 0.9: ref = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Cross product n x ref u = [n[1]ref[2]-n[2]ref[1], n[2]ref[0]-n[0]ref[2], n[0]ref[1]-n[1]ref[0]] normu = (u[0]2 + u[1]2 + u[2]2)0.5 if normu < 1e-8: normu = 1e-8 u = [u[0]/normu, u[1]/normu, u[2]/normu] # Cross product n x u yields v (automatically normalized) v = [n[1]u[2]-n[2]u[1], n[2]u[0]-n[0]u[2], n[0]u[1]-n[1]u[0]] # Step 3: Project covariance to tangent plane # Rotate Sigma into basis [u, v, n] and extract top-left 2x2 block def matvec(M, vec): return [M[0][0]vec[0] + M[0][1]vec[1] + M[0][2]vec[2], M[1][0]vec[0] + M[1][1]vec[1] + M[1][2]vec[2], M[2][0]vec[0] + M[2][1]vec[1] + M[2][2]vec[2]] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] Sigmau = matvec(Sigma, u) Sigmav = matvec(Sigma, v) covtangent = [[dot(u, Sigmau), dot(u, Sigmav)], [dot(v, Sigmau), dot(v, Sigmav)]] # Step 4: Transform from tangent plane to image plane # Project mean mu to image plane (standard perspective projection) z = mu[2] zsafe = max(z, 1e-5) means2d[i][0] = cameramatrix[i][0][0] (mu[0] / zsafe) + cameramatrix[i][0][2] means2d[i][1] = cameramatrix[i][1][1] (mu[1] / zsafe) + cameramatrix[i][1][2] # Jacobian of perspective projection from tangent plane to image plane x, y = mu[0], mu[1] # Jproj is (2,3): [[1/z, 0, -x/z^2], [0, 1/z, -y/z^2]] Jproj = [[1/zsafe, 0, -x/(zsafe2)], [0, 1/zsafe, -y/(zsafe2)]] # Basis vectors u, v form a (3,2) matrix # Jtangent = Jproj @ [u, v] -> (2,2) Jt = [[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]] for r in range(2): for c in range(2): for k in range(3): Jt[r][c] += Jproj[r][k] ([u, v][k][c]) # Final 2D covariance: Sigma2D = Jt @ covtangent @ Jt^T def matmul2x2(A, B): return [[A[0][0]B[0][0] + A[0][1]B[1][0], A[0][0]B[0][1] + A[0][1]B[1][1]], [A[1][0]B[0][0] + A[1][1]B[1][0], A[1][0]B[0][1] + A[1][1]B[1][1]]] def matT2x2(A): return [[A[0][0], A[1][0]], [A[0][1], A[1][1]]] covs2d[i] = matmul2x2(matmul2x2(Jt, covtangent), matT2x2(Jt)) # Step 5: Stabilize covariance (add epsilon to diagonal) covs2d[i][0][0] += 1e-3 covs2d[i][1][1] += 1e-3 return means2d, covs2d Parameters: Focal Length: The method is tested with focal lengths scaled to 0.2 and 0.3 times the original focal length to simulate wide-field-of-view scenarios. Epsilon: A small value added to the diagonal of the 2D covariance for numerical stability (value not specified in sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Time: The method incurs a slight increase in training time due to the additional transformation step from the tangent plane to the image plane. Parallel Normals: When constructing the tangent plane basis, if the direction vector \mathbf{d} is parallel to the reference vector (e.g., z-axis), the cross product becomes zero. The pseudocode handles this by switching the reference vector. Division by Zero: The perspective projection involves division by the z-coordinate. The pseudocode clamps z to a minimum safe value. Time Complexity: The algorithm's time complexity remains unchanged compared to 3D-GS because it avoids dense point sampling. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method significantly reduces blurriness and artifacts compared to the original projection method, particularly in settings with short focal lengths. It outperforms original 3D-GS across various scenes in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics when tested with focal length reduction ratios of \times 0.2 and \times 0.3. Strengths: Reduces projection error, minimizes artifacts like needle-like structures and cloud-like large Gaussians at image edges, and is adaptable to various camera models (pinhole, fisheye, panorama). Limitations: Slight increase in training time due to the additional transformation step. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "On the Error Analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting and an Optimal Projection Strategy". History: It was developed to address the issue of projection errors in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) [17], which tend to escalate with the expansion of the field of view and reduction in focal length. Usage: Implemented in PyTorch based on 3D-GS [17] with custom CUDA kernels for rasterization. Tested on 13 real scenes from the 3D-GS dataset, including Mip-NeRF360 [2], Tanks & Temples [18], and others. Computes the bounding box for each Gaussian splat to optimize rasterization. Adaptive Bounding Box Computation Renders the final image using the projected Gaussians. name: Projection Jacobian Computation
head: perspective projection Jacobian
body: Computes the 2 \times 3 Jacobian matrix of the perspective projection function with respect to 3D coordinates, used for linearizing the projection of 3D Gaussians into screen space. It transforms the 3D covariance structure into 2D screen-space covariance, enabling accurate Gaussian splatting. Inputs: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D Gaussian centers in world space. camera: Camera object providing view transformation and focal lengths. imgsize: Tuple (W, H) representing image width and height. Outputs: J: Tensor of shape (N, 2, 3) containing the Jacobian matrix for each Gaussian. Data Structures: meansviewspace: Tensor of shape (N, 3), view-space coordinates (tx, ty, tz). J: Tensor of shape (N, 2, 3), initialized to zeros. Steps: 1. Validate Camera: Check if the camera is in NDC mode; raise a RuntimeError if camera.inndc() is true. 2. Extract Parameters: Get focal lengths fx, fy = \text{camera.focal\length.flatten()} and image dimensions W, H = \text{img\size}. 3. Transform to View Space: Apply view transformation to 3D means: \text{means\view\space} = \text{view\transform.transform\points}(\text{means\3D}). Extract components: tx = \text{means\view\space}[:, 0], ty = \text{means\view\space}[:, 1], tz = \text{means\view\space}[:, 2]. Compute squared depth: tz^2 = tz \cdot tz. 4. Compute FOV Limits: Calculate half-tangent of field of view: \text{half\tan\fov\x} = 0.5 \cdot W / fx and \text{half\tan\fov\y} = 0.5 \cdot H / fy. Apply safety margin (1.3) to define clamping limits: \text{lim\x} = 1.3 \cdot \text{half\tan\fov\x} and \text{lim\y} = 1.3 \cdot \text{half\tan\fov\y}. 5. Clamp Normalized Coordinates: To prevent division by zero or extreme values near frustum edges, clamp the normalized coordinates (tx/tz, ty/tz) before scaling back: tx = \text{clamp}(tx / tz, -\text{lim\x}, \text{lim\x}) \cdot tz and ty = \text{clamp}(ty / tz, -\text{lim\y}, \text{lim\y}) \cdot tz. 6. Initialize Jacobian: Create tensor J of shape (N, 2, 3) filled with zeros. 7. Fill Jacobian Entries: Assign values using the clamped coordinates: J[:, 0, 0] = fx / tz, J[:, 1, 1] = fy / tz, J[:, 0, 2] = -(fx \cdot tx) / tz^2, and J[:, 1, 2] = -(fy \cdot ty) / tz^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Gaussian Splatting
head: TextureSplat
body: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Gaussian Splatting assigns material properties as texture maps in the splat's local coordinate system rather than single attribute values per primitive, enabling higher-frequency spatial detail without increasing primitive count. It decouples geometry from appearance, allowing complex visual features and detailed normal maps to be captured within the existing Gaussian representation. This method differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by treating alpha-blending as a smoothing filter in a deferred rendering pipeline, which stabilizes the optimization of texture-sampled features and produces more cohesive results compared to shading directly on Gaussians. Inputs: A set of 2D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position, covariance, opacity, and rotation. A target image or set of images for training. A learnable environment map for direct lighting. An extracted mesh for indirect lighting visibility approximation. Outputs: Rendered RGB image. Optimized primitive parameters: positions, covariances, opacities. Optimized texture maps for each primitive: Albedo, Metallic, Roughness, and Tangent Normal. Per-splat indirect lighting Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Each primitive k maintains the following optimized parameters: Splat parameters: Position, covariance (or 2D projection parameters), opacity ok. Local coordinates: t{uk}, t{vk} defining the local space of the Gaussian. Texture coordinates: s{uk}, s{vk} mapping local space to texture space. Material texture maps: T^k\lambda (Albedo, \in [0, 1]^3), T^km (Metallic, \in [0, 1]), T^kr (Roughness, \in [0, 1]), T^kn (Tangent Normal, \in [0, 1]^3). Indirect Lighting: SH coefficients for L^{ind}. Environment Maps: L^{diffuse}{env} and L{env} (specular). Texture Atlas: To leverage hardware-accelerated texture filtering, individual primitive textures are packed into texture atlases, inspired by Ptex and seamless texture atlases. 1. Coordinate Mapping: Map the local splat coordinates (u, v) to texture coordinates (s, t) accounting for the Gaussian kernel's support. The Gaussian kernel effectively drops to zero at approximately S\sigma = 3 standard deviations. The effective support [-S\sigma, S\sigma] \times [-S\sigma, S\sigma] is mapped to texture space [0, 1] \times [0, 1]: s = \frac{u + S\sigma}{2S\sigma}, \quad t = \frac{v + S\sigma}{2S\sigma} where S\sigma = 3. 2. Attribute Splatting (Deferred Rendering): Splat material attributes to screen-space buffers using alpha blending. For each pixel (x, y), the combined buffer X(x, y) aggregates attributes from N primitives: X(x, y) = \sum{i=1}^{N} xi(x, y) \alphai(x, y) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(x, y)) where xi(x, y) is the attribute vector for primitive i: xi(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} \lambdai(x, y) \\ mi(x, y) \\ ri(x, y) \\ Ni(x, y) \\ L^{ind}i(x, y) \end{bmatrix} Here, \lambda is Albedo, m is Metallic, r is Roughness, N is the world-space normal, and L^{ind} is indirect lighting. 3. Texture Sampling: Obtain the attribute value ak(x, y) for primitive k by bilinear filtering from its texture map T^k using the mapped coordinates: ak(x, y) = \text{BilinearFilter}(T^k, s(uk(x, y)), t(vk(x, y))) where T^k is the texture map for primitive k, and uk, vk are the local coordinates. 4. Normal Reconstruction and Transformation: Reconstruction: Tangent normals are encoded using only two components (n{tx}, n{ty}) for memory efficiency. The third component is reconstructed at runtime: n{tz} = \max(0, \sqrt{1 - (n{tx})^2 - (n{ty})^2}) Transformation: Transform the tangent normal nt^k(x, y) to world space using the primitive's rotation matrix Rk: nk(x, y) = Rk \cdot nt^k(x, y) This enables detailed normal variations across the surface of each primitive. 5. Physically-Based Shading: Compute the outgoing radiance Lo(x, y, \omegao) in the direction \omegao using the deferred buffers: Lo(x, y, \omegao) = Ld(x, y, \omegao) + Ls(x, y, \omegao) Diffuse Term: Ld(x, y, \omegao) = \frac{(1 - M(x, y)) L^{diffuse}{env}(N(x, y))}{\pi} where M(x, y) is the aggregated metallic value and L^{diffuse}{env} is the pre-integrated diffuse environment irradiance. Specular Term: Ls(x, y, \omegao) \approx \text{BRDFLUT}(N(x, y) \cdot \omegao, R(x, y)) \cdot (V(x, y)L{dir}(x, y, \omegar, R(x, y)) + (1 - V(x, y))L^{ind}(x, y)) \text{BRDFLUT} is a precomputed 2D lookup texture depending on view angle and roughness. L{dir} is the direct environment lighting queried from a learnable environment map in the reflection direction \omegar, using roughness R(x, y) for mipmap selection. L^{ind} is the indirect lighting, modeled by approximating visibility with ray tracing an extracted mesh and encoding indirect lighting with spherical harmonics. V(x, y) represents visibility. 6. Training Optimization: Use a two-stage optimization process for stability: Stage 1: Train for half the total number of iterations using per-splat single attribute optimization (standard Gaussian Splatting attributes). Stage 2: Optimize material and normal textures initialized from the corresponding attributes from the first stage. Freeze the positions of the primitives. Loss Function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{img} + \lambdan \mathcal{L}n where \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda\mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} with balancing weight \lambda = 0.2. Normal Consistency Loss: \mathcal{L}n = 1 - \tilde{N}(x, y)^T N(x, y) This minimizes the cosine difference between the rendered normal N(x, y) and the surface normal \tilde{N}(x, y) derived from rendered depth. Hardware: Single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU used in experiments. Hardware Acceleration: Individual primitive textures must be packed into texture atlases to leverage hardware-accelerated texture filtering. Use when high-fidelity reflective surfaces and detailed normal maps are required. Use when the primitive count is constrained but high-frequency appearance details are needed. Use if real-time performance is paramount and the overhead of texture atlas management and deferred shading is unacceptable. It adapts techniques from traditional rendering (Gouraud vs. Phong shading) and texture mapping (Ptex) to the Gaussian Splatting framework. name: 3D Ellipsoid Projection
head: Gaussian Selection Method, Sphere Approximation Projection
body: 3D Ellipsoid Projection is a Gaussian selection method used to identify candidate 3D Gaussians for rendering specific image slices in volume rendering pipelines. It approximates the spatial extent of a 3D Gaussian ellipsoid as a sphere to compute a uniform 2D bounding box, which is then projected orthogonally onto every image slice. Unlike sibling methods that adapt bounding boxes per slice or use complex covariance corrections, this approach prioritizes simplicity by treating the Gaussian's range as isotropic, though this leads to redundant computation for off-center slices. Inputs: A 3D Gaussian primitive defined by its mean position \mathbf{\mu} and covariance matrix \Sigma. A set of image slices (depth planes) along the viewing direction. Outputs: A set of candidate Gaussians for each slice, determined by whether the projected bounding box intersects the slice's region of interest. Data Structures: Covariance Matrix \Sigma: A 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix representing the Gaussian's shape and orientation. Eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: The scalar values obtained from the spectral decomposition of \Sigma. Bounding Box: A cube defined by its center \mathbf{\mu} and edge length 2 r{max}. Steps: 1. Compute Eigenvalues: Calculate the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 of the covariance matrix \Sigma. 2. Determine Maximum Axis Length: Identify the largest eigenvalue \lambda{max} = \max(\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3). 3. Calculate Approximation Radius: Compute the radius r{max} of the approximating sphere using the formula: r{max} = 3 \cdot \sqrt{\lambda{max}} The factor of 3 corresponds to the 3\sigma confidence interval, encompassing approximately 99.7% of the Gaussian's probability mass. 4. Define Bounding Cube: Construct a cube centered at the Gaussian's mean \mathbf{\mu} with edge length 2 r{max}. 5. Project to Slices: Orthogonally project this cube onto each image slice. Because the projection is orthogonal and the shape is a cube aligned with the principal axes (or simply treated as a sphere's bounding box), the resulting 2D bounding box is identical for all slices. 6. Selection: Include the Gaussian in the candidate set for a slice if the slice's pixel coordinates fall within the projected 2D bounding box. Pseudocode: Unverified code. In a real implementation, use a standard linear algebra library routine. """ # Placeholder for actual eigenvalue decomposition logic # Standard algorithm: Solve det(A - lambdaI) = 0 # For a 3x3 symmetric matrix, this can be done via Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm # or characteristic polynomial roots. pass Parameters: Confidence Factor: 3 (representing 3\sigma). This is a standard statistical choice for bounding boxes in Gaussian rendering. Epsilon: Not explicitly defined in the source for this specific method, but numerical stability in eigenvalue computation should be considered. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundant Computation: Because the same cubic bounding box is projected onto every slice, slices far from the Gaussian's center may still be processed if they fall within the large projected box, leading to unnecessary rasterization work. Overestimation: The spherical approximation ignores the orientation of the ellipsoid. If the Gaussian is highly anisotropic (e.g., a flat sheet), the sphere will include large volumes of empty space, further exacerbating the redundant computation issue. A Gaussian selection method that uses a factorized Gaussian structure to compute the range of each Gaussian on individual slices, adapting the bounding box for each slice based on depth. Unlike 3D Ellipsoid Projection, which projects a static cubic bounding box onto every slice, Conditional Splatting computes an adapted bounding box for each slice. It models the Gaussian contribution as pi(u, v, t) = pi(u, v|t)pi(t), where pi(u, v|t) is a conditional 2D Gaussian describing the lateral spatial distribution given slice location t, and pi(t) is a 1D Gaussian modeling uncertainty along the depth axis. The conditional mean \mu{u,v|t} shifts with slice depth t, and a distance-dependent scaling factor reduces the extent of the 2D splat as the distance between the 3D Gaussian center and the slice increases. This leads to more efficient sampling by avoiding the processing of overly large, static regions. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of Gaussians and S is the number of slices. Each Gaussian is evaluated against every slice. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only requires storing the bounding box parameters per slice. Performance: The method is computationally simple to implement but inefficient in scenes with many Gaussians or deep volumes, as it processes redundant pixels on slices distant from the Gaussian's center. Strengths: Simple to implement; robust to orientation changes as it relies on the maximum axis length. Limitations: High false-positive rate for candidate selection; significant redundant computation due to identical bounding boxes across all slices. When to use: When implementation simplicity is prioritized over rendering speed, or in shallow volumes where the redundancy is minimal. When not to use: In deep volumetric scenes or with highly anisotropic Gaussians, where adaptive methods like Conditional Splatting offer better efficiency. The 3D Ellipsoid Projection method was introduced in the context of internal scene reconstruction and segmentation using factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting. It serves as a baseline Gaussian selection strategy to identify candidate Gaussians for each pixel/slice before differential rasterization. The method was compared against Conditional Splatting in simulation analyses involving 3D volumes of size 20 \times 20 \times 20. name: Covariance Stabilization and Correction
body: This family addresses the numerical instability and geometric inaccuracies inherent in projecting 3D Gaussian primitives into screen space for differentiable rendering. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts caused by undersampled Gaussians and the discrepancy between analytically projected covariances and the true integrated 2D covariance. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly modifying the covariance matrix—either through low-pass filtering with density preservation or via learned linear corrections—rather than relying solely on geometric projection or bounding box heuristics. All methods in this family operate on the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma^{2D} derived from a 3D Gaussian. The core mechanism involves modifying the entries of this matrix to ensure numerical stability (positive definiteness) or to correct for projection errors. The output is typically a corrected covariance matrix or its inverse (conic matrix) used in the rasterization kernel. The methods assume the input covariance is symmetric and positive semi-definite. This method stabilizes the projection by applying a low-pass filter to the 2D covariance matrix, ensuring each Gaussian spans at least the width of a single pixel to reduce aliasing [3467-2d-gaussian-covariance-stabilization-and-rescaling]. It computes a rescale factor to preserve the integrated density of the Gaussian after filtering. Choose this when aliasing is a primary concern and density preservation is required. See 2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling. This method approximates the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances using a linear regression model, serving as a computationally efficient alternative to neural network-based corrections [9912-2d-covariance-correction-via-linear-regression]. It sets itself apart by replacing complex learned mappings with closed-form linear coefficients or a single scalar factor, reducing training overhead. Choose this when reconstruction quality comparable to Half-Cosine kernels is needed with lower computational cost. See 2D Covariance Correction via Linear Regression. A scalar correction factor applied to the covariance matrix to approximate the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances, replacing a more complex MLP or Simpson's rule integration. Inverse Multiquadric correction factor: 1.38f. Parabolic correction factor: 1.3f. Originating from work on generalizing splatting with decaying anisotropic radial basis functions, these techniques were introduced to improve the fidelity of Gaussian splatting rendering. The stabilization approach addresses the common issue of "sparkles" or aliasing in novel view synthesis, while the correction methods address the geometric mismatch between the projected Gaussian and the true integrated density. name: 2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling
head: Conic Matrix and Rescale Factor, Covariance Rescaling, Gaussian Covariance Pre-filtering, Pixel-spanning Gaussian
body: This method stabilizes the projection of 3D Gaussians into screen space by applying a low-pass filter to the 2D covariance matrix, ensuring that each Gaussian spans at least the width of a single pixel to reduce aliasing artifacts. It computes the inverse covariance (conic) matrix and a scalar rescale factor that preserves the integrated density of the Gaussian after filtering. Inputs: \Sigman^{2D}: The 2D screen-space covariance matrix for the n-th Gaussian. s: The low-pass filter strength hyper-parameter. Default value is 0.3. Outputs: conicandrescale: A 4-component vector containing the upper-triangular elements of the inverse covariance matrix and the rescale factor: [ (\Sigman^{2D} + s\mathbf{I})^{-1}{0,0}, (\Sigman^{2D} + s\mathbf{I})^{-1}{0,1}, (\Sigman^{2D} + s\mathbf{I})^{-1}{1,1}, \text{rescale} ]. Data Structures: \Sigman^{2D}: A 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{00} & \Sigma{01} \\ \Sigma{01} & \Sigma{11} \end{pmatrix}. conicandrescale: A vec4 (or array of 4 floats). Steps: 1. Compute the determinant of the original covariance matrix: \det{\text{pre}} = \det(\Sigman^{2D}) = \Sigma{00}\Sigma{11} - \Sigma{01}^2 2. Apply the low-pass filter by adding the scalar s to the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix: \Sigma{\text{filtered}} = \Sigman^{2D} + s\mathbf{I} = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{00} + s & \Sigma{01} \\ \Sigma{01} & \Sigma{11} + s \end{pmatrix} 3. Compute the determinant of the filtered covariance matrix: \det{\text{post}} = \det(\Sigma{\text{filtered}}) = (\Sigma{00} + s)(\Sigma{11} + s) - \Sigma{01}^2 4. Compute the rescale factor to preserve the integral of the Gaussian density: \text{rescale} = \sqrt{\max(0.0, \frac{\det{\text{pre}}}{\det{\text{post}}})} 5. Compute the inverse of the filtered covariance matrix (the conic matrix) analytically for the 2 \times 2 case: \Sigma{\text{filtered}}^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det{\text{post}}} \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{11} + s & -\Sigma{01} \\ -\Sigma{01} & \Sigma{00} + s \end{pmatrix} 6. Pack the result into the output vector: \text{conic\and\rescale} = [\Sigma{\text{filtered}}^{-1}[0,0], \Sigma{\text{filtered}}^{-1}[0,1], \Sigma{\text{filtered}}^{-1}[1,1], \text{rescale}] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeconicandrescale(cov2d, s=0.3): # cov2d is a 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [b, c]] a, b, c = cov2d[0, 0], cov2d[0, 1], cov2d[1, 1] # Step 1: Pre-filter determinant detpre = a c - b b # Step 2: Filtered covariance afilt = a + s cfilt = c + s # b remains unchanged # Step 3: Post-filter determinant detpost = afilt cfilt - b b # Step 4: Rescale factor # Guard against division by zero or negative ratio inside sqrt ratio = detpre / detpost if detpost != 0 else 0.0 rescale = (max(0.0, ratio)) 0.5 # Step 5: Inverse filtered covariance (Conic matrix) inv00 = cfilt / detpost inv01 = -b / detpost inv11 = afilt / detpost # Step 6: Return vec4 return [inv00, inv01, inv11, rescale] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \det{\text{post}} is zero or negative due to numerical precision, the division in steps 4 and 5 must be guarded. This method approximates the density of a conical frustum segment along a ray as a 3D Gaussian distribution defined by a mean and covariance. It differs from the parent method by operating in 3D space to lift ray-space statistics into a full 3D Gaussian before projection, whereas the parent operates on the already projected 2D covariance. Choose it when differentiable volume rendering with integrated positional encoding is required for conical primitives. A method to define the minimal size of 3D Gaussians based on reconstruction confidence using Variational Bayesian estimation to prevent the 'needle' effect. It calculates the inverse precision matrix for localization and size as \Sigmai^{(XYZ)^{-1}} = \sumc \left( zi^{(c)^2} \sigma^{(w)^2} Wc^T \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} Wc \right)^{-1}, where Wc is the world transformation matrix for camera c and zi^{(c)} is the distance of the Gaussian along the z-axis of camera c. A scaling factor \alpha=2 is used to define confidence intervals \Deltai = \alpha \text{tr}(\Sigmai^{(XYZ)^{-1}})^{-0.5}. Choose it when reconstruction confidence must explicitly bound Gaussian extents to avoid thin artifacts. This approach manipulates overall scene blurriness or sharpness by applying global transformations to per-Gaussian offsets \delta rj and \delta sj predicted by a compact MLP. The offsets control local rotation and scale adjustments alongside the base Gaussian parameters. Choose it when artistic control over depth-of-field or motion-blur effects is required without retraining the base splatting model. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional storage per Gaussian for the rescale factor and conic matrix elements. Strengths: Eliminates high-frequency aliasing artifacts caused by undersampled Gaussians. Preserves the total energy (integral) of the Gaussian density through the rescale factor. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When rendering at resolutions where Gaussians may span less than a pixel, or when training with anti-aliasing enabled. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the need to handle the discrete sampling of continuous Gaussian distributions in rasterization. The specific formulation of the rescale factor to preserve density is detailed in implementations such as Taichi 3D Gaussian Splatting. The anti-aliasing mode in gsplat modifies the 2D Gaussian sizes to ensure they span the width of a single pixel. The BOGausS variant extends the concept of minimal size constraints to a probabilistic precision-based approach. wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) BOGausS: Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.23919/eusipco63237.2025.11226626, fetched 2026-10-26 Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73636-08, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Conical Frustum to Gaussian
head: Conical Frustum to Gaussian Approximation, Frustum Gaussian Approximation, cone ray featurization
body: Approximates a conical frustum (defined by ray origin, direction, start/end distances, and base radius) as a 3D Gaussian distribution (mean and covariance) to enable differentiable volume rendering with integrated positional encoding. It lifts a 1D Gaussian defined along the ray axis and a radial variance into 3D space, aligning the covariance with the ray direction. Inputs: origins: Tensor of shape [B, 3], ray origins. directions: Tensor of shape [B, 3], normalized ray direction vectors. starts: Tensor of shape [B] or [B, nsamples], start distances t0 along the ray. ends: Tensor of shape [B] or [B, nsamples], end distances t1 along the ray. baseradius: Tensor of shape [B] or [B, 1], radius of the frustum at distance t=1 (for cones) or constant radius (for cylinders). rayshape: String, either 'cone' or 'cylinder'. diagonal: Boolean, if True returns diagonal covariance; if False returns full 3 \times 3 covariance. stable: Boolean, if True uses numerically stable formulas for moments; if False uses raw moment formulas (discouraged). Outputs: means: Tensor of shape [B, 3] (or [B, nsamples, 3]), mean positions. covs: Tensor of shape [B, 3, 3] (or [B, nsamples, 3, 3]), covariance matrices. Steps: 1. Calculate Intermediate Parameters: Compute the midpoint \mu and half-width hw of the interval [t0, t1]: \mu = \frac{t0 + t1}{2} hw = \frac{t1 - t0}{2} 2. Compute Denominator (Stable Mode Only): If stable is True, compute a denominator to prevent division by zero when \mu is small: \text{denom} = \max(\epsilon, 3\mu^2 + hw^2) where \epsilon is the machine epsilon for the data type (e.g., torch.finfo(torch.float16).eps). If stable is False, denom is not used in the moment calculations. 3. Compute 1D Longitudinal Moments (t{\text{mean}}, t{\text{var}}): If rayshape is 'cone' and stable is True: t{\text{mean}} = \mu + \frac{2\mu hw^2}{\text{denom}} t{\text{var}} = \frac{hw^2}{3} - \frac{4}{15} \frac{hw^4 (12\mu^2 - hw^2)}{\text{denom}^2} If rayshape is 'cone' and stable is False: t{\text{mean}} = \frac{3(t1^4 - t0^4)}{4(t1^3 - t0^3)} t{\text{mosq}} = \frac{3}{5} \frac{t1^5 - t0^5}{t1^3 - t0^3} t{\text{var}} = t{\text{mosq}} - t{\text{mean}}^2 If rayshape is 'cylinder': The sources do not provide explicit formulas for t{\text{mean}} or t{\text{var}} in cylinder mode, only for r{\text{var}}. 4. Compute Radial Variance (r{\text{var}}): If rayshape is 'cone' and stable is True: r{\text{var}} = \text{base\radius}^2 \left( \frac{\mu^2}{4} + \frac{5}{12}hw^2 - \frac{4}{15} \frac{hw^4}{\text{denom}} \right) If rayshape is 'cone' and stable is False: r{\text{var}} = \text{base\radius}^2 \frac{3}{20} \frac{t1^5 - t0^5}{t1^3 - t0^3} If rayshape is 'cylinder': r{\text{var}} = \text{base\radius}^2 \left( \frac{\mu^2}{4} + \frac{5}{12}hw^2 - \frac{4}{15} \frac{hw^4}{3\mu^2 + hw^2} \right) 5. Lift to 3D (Compute Mean and Covariance): Mean: \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{d} \cdot t{\text{mean}} where \mathbf{d} is the direction vector. Covariance: Compute the squared magnitude of the direction, clamped to a minimum value to avoid division by zero: d{\text{mag\sq}} = \max(\|\mathbf{d}\|^2, 10^{-10}) If diagonal is True: d{\text{outer\diag}} = \mathbf{d}^2 \text{null\outer\diag} = 1 - \frac{d{\text{outer\diag}}}{d{\text{mag\sq}}} t{\text{cov\diag}} = t{\text{var}} \cdot d{\text{outer\diag}} xy{\text{cov\diag}} = r{\text{var}} \cdot \text{null\outer\diag} \text{cov\diag} = t{\text{cov\diag}} + xy{\text{cov\diag}} If diagonal is False: \mathbf{d}{\text{outer}} = \mathbf{d} \mathbf{d}^T \mathbf{I} = \text{Identity}(3) \mathbf{N}{\text{outer}} = \mathbf{I} - \frac{\mathbf{d} \mathbf{d}^T}{d{\text{mag\sq}}} \mathbf{t}{\text{cov}} = t{\text{var}} \cdot \mathbf{d}{\text{outer}} \mathbf{xy}{\text{cov}} = r{\text{var}} \cdot \mathbf{N}{\text{outer}} \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{t}{\text{cov}} + \mathbf{xy}{\text{cov}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def conicalfrustumtogaussian(origins, directions, starts, ends, baseradius, rayshape='cone', diagonal=True, stable=True): """ Approximates a conical frustum as a Gaussian distribution. Args: origins: [B, 3] directions: [B, 3], normalized starts: [B] or [B, nsamples] ends: [B] or [B, nsamples] baseradius: [B] or [B, 1] rayshape: 'cone' or 'cylinder' diagonal: bool stable: bool Returns: means: [B, 3] or [B, nsamples, 3] covs: [B, 3] if diagonal, else [B, 3, 3] """ # Ensure broadcasting compatibility origins = origins.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1, 3] directions = directions.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1, 3] baseradius = baseradius.view(-1, 1, 1) # [B, 1, 1] starts = starts.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1] ends = ends.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1] # 1. Intermediate parameters mu = (starts + ends) / 2.0 hw = (ends - starts) / 2.0 # 2. Denominator if stable: eps = torch.finfo(directions.dtype).eps denom = torch.maximum(eps, 3.0 mu2 + hw2) else: denom = None # 3. Longitudinal moments if rayshape == 'cone': if stable: tmean = mu + (2.0 mu hw2) / denom tvar = (hw2) / 3.0 - (4.0 / 15.0) (hw4 (12.0 mu2 - hw2)) / (denom2) else: denomt = torch.maximum(torch.abs(ends3 - starts3), torch.finfo(directions.dtype).eps) tmean = 3.0 (ends4 - starts4) / (4.0 denomt) tmosq = 3.0 / 5.0 (ends5 - starts5) / denomt tvar = tmosq - tmean2 elif rayshape == 'cylinder': # Sources do not provide explicit tmean or tvar formulas for cylinder mode tmean = mu tvar = hw2 / 3.0 # Standard uniform variance on [-hw, hw] else: raise ValueError("rayshape must be 'cone' or 'cylinder'") # 4. Radial variance if rayshape == 'cone': if stable: rvar = baseradius2 (mu2 / 4.0 + 5.0/12.0 hw2 - 4.0/15.0 hw4 / denom) else: denomt = torch.maximum(torch.abs(ends3 - starts3), torch.finfo(directions.dtype).eps) rvar = baseradius2 3.0/20.0 (ends5 - starts5) / denomt elif rayshape == 'cylinder': rvar = baseradius2 (mu2 / 4.0 + 5.0/12.0 hw2 - 4.0/15.0 hw4 / (3.0 mu2 + hw2)) # 5. Lift to 3D # Mean means = directions tmean.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1, 3] [B, 1, 1] -> [B, 1, 3] # Covariance dmagsq = torch.sum(directions2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # [B, 1, 1] dmagsq = torch.maximum(dmagsq, torch.tensor(1e-10, dtype=directions.dtype)) if diagonal: douterdiag = directions2 # [B, 1, 3] nullouterdiag = 1.0 - douterdiag / dmagsq # [B, 1, 3] tcovdiag = tvar.unsqueeze(1) douterdiag # [B, 1, 3] xycovdiag = rvar.unsqueeze(1) nullouterdiag # [B, 1, 3] covs = tcovdiag + xycovdiag # [B, 1, 3] else: # Full covariance douter = directions.unsqueeze(-1) directions.unsqueeze(-2) # [B, 1, 3, 3] I = torch.eye(3, dtype=directions.dtype, device=directions.device) nullouter = I - douter / dmagsq # [B, 1, 3, 3] tcov = tvar.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) douter # [B, 1, 3, 3] xycov = rvar.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) nullouter # [B, 1, 3, 3] covs = tcov + xycov # [B, 1, 3, 3] return means.squeeze(1), covs.squeeze(1) Parameters: rayshape: 'cone' or 'cylinder'. diagonal: True for diagonal covariance, False for full. stable: True recommended. False causes catastrophic failure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: Setting stable=False causes catastrophic failure due to division by zero or large errors when \mu is small. Always use stable=True. Offsets: The method raises NotImplementedError if frustum offsets are present, as the approximation logic does not support them. Zero Direction: Direction squared magnitude is clamped to at least 10^{-10} to prevent division by zero in covariance calculation. Cylinder Support: Cylinder support is inconsistent across implementations; some raise NotImplementedError while others provide radial variance formulas. A parameterization of an axis-aligned cone used to derive moments for the uniform distribution over a conical frustum, defined as (x, y, z) = \phi(r, t, \theta) = (rt \cos \theta, rt \sin \theta, t) for \theta \in 0, 2\pi), t \ge 0, |r| \le \dot{r}. This derivation underpins the moment calculations for t{\text{mean}}, t{\text{var}}, and r{\text{var}}. Originated in [Mip-NeRF (Barron et al., 2021) to anti-alias neural radiance fields by representing rays as cones rather than lines. Adopted by 3D Gaussian Splatting variants (e.g.,) to project 3D Gaussians onto rays or approximate frustum segments as Gaussians for efficient rendering. The stable formulation was introduced to handle numerical issues near the camera origin. name: Gaussian Preprocessing
head: forward preprocessing, preprocessCUDA
body: Gaussian Preprocessing is a CUDA kernel that transforms 3D Gaussian parameters into voxel-space coordinates, conic matrices, and bounding radii to enable efficient rasterization. It serves as the bridge between the learned Gaussian representation and the tile-based rasterizer, converting world-space attributes into the specific data structures required for the subsequent splatting pass. It is distinct from Conical Frustum to Gaussian by operating on pre-computed covariances and focusing on voxel-space transformation rather than frustum approximation. Inputs and Outputs: The kernel takes as input the 3D means (means3D), scales (scales), rotations (rotations), opacities (opacities), and pre-computed 3D covariances (cov3Dprecomp). It outputs normalized means (means3Dnorm), depths (depths), 2D covariances (cov3Ds), a packed conicopacity array (7 floats per Gaussian: 6 for the upper triangle of the inverse 2D covariance matrix + 1 for opacity), and a bitmask of tilestouched. Data Structures: means3D: float, size P \times 3. scales: glm::vec3, size P \times 3. rotations: glm::vec4, size P \times 4 (quaternions). opacities: float, size P. cov3Dprecomp: float, size P \times 9 (symmetric 3x3 matrix). means3Dnorm: float3, size P \times 3. depths: float, size P. cov3Ds: float, size P \times 6 (upper triangle of 2x2 2D covariance). conicopacity: float, size P \times 7. tilestouched: uint32, size equal to the number of tiles. Parameters: P: Number of Gaussians. BLOCK3DSIZE: 256 (threads per block). NUMCHANNELS: Template parameter for output channels. nVoxelx/y/z: Voxel grid dimensions. sVoxelx/y/z: Voxel sizes (scaling factors). centerx/y/z: Center offset. radiix/y/z: Bounding box radii. Steps: 1. Launch the kernel with one thread per Gaussian. The grid dimension is calculated as \lceil P / 256 \rceil blocks, with a block size of 256 threads. 2. Each thread i processes the i-th Gaussian: a. Transform the 3D mean \mathbf{m} to voxel space using the voxel size and center offset: \mathbf{m}{voxel} = (\mathbf{m} - \mathbf{c}) \odot \mathbf{s}{voxel} where \mathbf{c} = (centerx, centery, centerz) and \mathbf{s}{voxel} = (sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz). b. Store the normalized mean in means3Dnorm[i]. c. Compute the depth z of the transformed mean and store it in depths[i]. d. Retrieve the pre-computed 3D covariance \Sigma{3D} from cov3Dprecomp. e. Compute the 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} by projecting \Sigma{3D} onto the image plane. This involves the view matrix J and the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projection. The resulting 2D covariance is then inverted to form the conic matrix C = \Sigma{2D}^{-1}. f. Pack the upper triangle of C (6 values) and the opacity \alpha into conicopacity[i]. g. Compute the bounding box radii for the Gaussian in voxel space. h. Determine which tiles are intersected by the bounding box and set the corresponding bits in tilestouched. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessgaussian(i, means3D, scales, rotations, opacities, cov3Dprecomp, nVoxel, sVoxel, center, tilestouched, numtiles): # 1. Transform mean to voxel space m = means3D[i] mvoxel = (m - center) sVoxel # 2. Store normalized mean and depth means3Dnorm[i] = mvoxel depths[i] = mvoxel.z # 3. Get pre-computed 3D covariance cov3D = cov3Dprecomp[i] # 9 floats # 4. Compute 2D covariance and conic matrix # Note: The exact projection formula depends on the view matrix and Jacobian, # which are typically passed as additional parameters or computed from camera intrinsics. # Here we assume a helper function exists that performs the projection. cov2D = projectcovariance3dto2d(cov3D) # Returns 6 floats (upper triangle) conic = invert2x2matrix(cov2D) # Returns 6 floats (upper triangle of inverse) # 5. Pack conic and opacity conicopacity[i 7: (i + 1) 7] = conic + [opacities[i]] # 6. Compute bounding box radii # Radii are derived from the eigenvalues of the 2D covariance or pre-computed # based on the 3D scale and rotation. radii = computegaussianradii(cov2D) # 7. Mark tiles touched tilebounds = computetileboundsfromradii(mvoxel.xy, radii) for tile in tilebounds: if 0 <= tile < numtiles: tilestouched[tile] |= (1 << i) # Or use atomic OR if concurrent Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in the inversion of the 2D covariance matrix can lead to instability if the determinant is near zero. A small epsilon should be added to the diagonal before inversion. Boundaries: Ensure that tile indices are clamped to valid ranges to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has zero scale or opacity, the covariance may be singular. Handle this by skipping or setting a default conic matrix. Time Complexity: O(P), where P is the number of Gaussians. Each Gaussian is processed by a single thread. Memory Complexity: O(P) for the output arrays. The tilestouched array size depends on the number of tiles. Performance: The kernel is highly parallel and efficient on GPUs due to the one-thread-per-Gaussian model. Performance scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Fast preprocessing, efficient tile culling, and minimal memory overhead. Limitations: Requires pre-computed 3D covariances. The quality of the rasterization depends on the accuracy of the 2D covariance projection. Gaussian Preprocessing is part of the Gaussian Splatting pipeline, specifically designed for efficient rasterization of 3D Gaussians. It was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering and 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method leverages CUDA for parallel processing to transform 3D Gaussian parameters into a format suitable for tile-based rasterization.
