name: 2D Covariance Correction via Linear Regression
head: DARBF covariance approximation, Scalar correction factor $\psi$, Scalar correction factor $ψ$
body: This method approximates the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances using a linear regression model. It serves as a computationally efficient alternative to neural network-based corrections in Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by replacing complex learned mappings with closed-form linear coefficients or a single scalar factor, thereby reducing training overhead while maintaining reconstruction quality comparable to Half-Cosine (HC) kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The 3D covariance matrix \Sigma' of a Gaussian primitive. Output: The corrected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'{2 \times 2} in screen space. Data Structures: The 3D covariance matrix \Sigma' is symmetric. The method utilizes the 6 unique elements derived from this matrix: \Sigma' = \begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ b & d & e \\ e & d & f \end{pmatrix} Note: The source text contains a typo in the matrix layout where e appears in both (2,3) and (3,2) positions, but the linear equations clarify the variable mapping. Standard symmetric matrix notation implies \Sigma'{2,3} = e and \Sigma'{3,2} = e. The source lists variables as a, b, c, d, e, f. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract 3D Covariance Elements: Identify the unique elements a, b, c, d, e, f from the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma'. 2. Compute Projected 2D Covariance (Reference): Obtain the "projected" 2D covariance by integrating along one axis using Simpson's rule. This serves as the baseline for comparison. 3. Compute Actual 2D Covariance (Ground Truth): Derive the "actual" 2D covariance by removing the last row and column of the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma', as proposed in [82]. This results in the target matrix: \Sigma'{2 \times 2} = \begin{pmatrix} a' & b' \\ b' & d' \end{pmatrix} 4. Apply Linear Regression Correction: Instead of using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), apply a linear regression model to approximate the mapping from the 3D elements to the 2D elements. The source provides two forms: a full linear model and a simplified scalar correction. Formulas: Full Linear Model: The corrected elements a', b', d' are computed as linear combinations of the input variables a, b, c, d, e, f: a' = 1.36a - 0.2b - 0.1c - 0.0d + 0.0e + 0.0f b' = 0.0a + 1.36b - 0.0c - 0.0d + 0.0e + 0.0f d' = 0.0a + 0.0b - 0.2c + 1.36d + 0.1e + 0.0f Scalar Correction Factor (\psi): Statistical analysis (T-tests) revealed that only the direct 3D covariance elements corresponding to the 2D covariance elements have significant weights. This allows the model to be simplified to a single scalar factor \psi applied to the diagonal elements of the projected 2D covariance: \Sigma'{2 \times 2} = \psi \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{pmatrix} The specific value of \psi depends on the reconstruction kernel used (Gaussian or Half-Cosine). The source notes that scalar approximations for each kernel are presented in the original paper's Table 2, but does not list the specific \psi values in the provided text. Parameters: Learning Rate (LR): Used during the training phase to determine the regression coefficients or scalar factor. Tested values are 0.01, 0.02, 0.1, and 0.2. Reconstruction Kernel: The method is evaluated with Gaussian and Half-Cosine (HC) kernels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compute2dcovariancecorrection(cov3d): """ Computes the corrected 2D covariance matrix from a 3D covariance matrix using the closed-form linear regression coefficients. Args: cov3d (list of lists): 3x3 symmetric covariance matrix [[a,b,c],[b,d,e],[c,e,f]]. Returns: list of lists: 2x2 corrected covariance matrix [[aprime, bprime], [bprime, dprime]]. """ # Extract unique elements from 3x3 symmetric matrix a = cov3d[0][0] b = cov3d[0][1] c = cov3d[0][2] d = cov3d[1][1] e = cov3d[1][2] f = cov3d[2][2] # Apply full linear model coefficients from source aprime = 1.36 a - 0.2 b - 0.1 c - 0.0 d + 0.0 e + 0.0 f bprime = 0.0 a + 1.36 b - 0.0 c - 0.0 d + 0.0 e + 0.0 f dprime = 0.0 a + 0.0 b - 0.2 c + 1.36 d + 0.1 e + 0.0 f # Construct the 2x2 matrix cov2d = [ [aprime, bprime], [bprime, dprime] ] return cov2d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Learning Rate Sensitivity: Excessively high or low learning rates during the training of the correction model lead to suboptimal performance. At high learning rates, cosine-based reconstructions may perform worse than Gaussian-based ones. Kernel Smoothness: Cosine kernels do not induce smoothness to the same extent as Gaussian kernels. This affects convergence and final quality, particularly at non-optimal learning rates. Matrix Symmetry: The source text displays a typo in the 3D covariance matrix layout (\Sigma'{3,2} = d instead of e). Implementers must assume standard symmetric matrix properties (\Sigma'{i,j} = \Sigma'{j,i}) to correctly map variables a-f to matrix indices. Time and Memory Complexity: The linear regression model is computationally lightweight, involving only basic arithmetic operations. It is significantly faster than training or inference with an MLP. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset (scenes: Kitchen, Room, Truck, Bicycle, Flowers, Garden, Stump, Treehill, Counter, Bonsai). Learning Rate 0.01: PSNR: 31.49 (Gaussian) vs 31.335 (HCS) Training Time: 22:31 (Gaussian) vs 23:26 (HCS) Memory: 255.61 (Gaussian) vs 246.48 (HCS) Learning Rate 0.02: PSNR: 31.75 (Gaussian) vs 31.34 (HCS) Training Time: 19:48 (Gaussian) vs 17:32 (HCS) Memory: 293.61 (Gaussian) vs 282.65 (HCS) Learning Rate 0.1: PSNR: 31.1 (Gaussian) vs 29.38 (HCS) Training Time: 13:31 (Gaussian) vs 11:20 (HCS) Memory: 364 (Gaussian) vs 391.76 (HCS) Learning Rate 0.2: PSNR: 30.5 (Gaussian) vs 26.54 (HCS) Training Time: 10:34 (Gaussian) vs 8:26 (HCS) Memory: 241.42 (Gaussian) vs 315.93 (HCS) Scaling and Hardware: Half-Cosine (HC) kernels achieve better training speeds compared to Gaussian kernels, even on upgraded hardware (RTX 4090 vs RTX 3090). For example, on the "Room" scene, training time dropped from 28m 32s to 19m 48s on RTX 4090 for Gaussian, and from 25m 28s to 17m 32s for HC. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High training efficiency; competitive visual quality (SSIM 0.813, PSNR 27.45 for DARBS RC) compared to prior methods like Plenoxels and INGP. Limitations: Performance degrades at extreme learning rates. Cosine kernels may underperform Gaussian kernels at high learning rates due to lack of smoothness. When to Use: Use this method when computational efficiency is prioritized over the absolute peak PSNR achievable by more complex MLP-based corrections, particularly when using Half-Cosine kernels for faster training. Origin: The method originates from the DARB-Splatting paper, which generalizes splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions. It was developed to replace the MLP-based covariance correction with a simpler linear regression model. History and Development: The authors initially proposed training a single-layer MLP to approximate the relationship between projected and actual 2D covariances. Through extensive experiments, they observed that the MLP could be closely approximated by a linear regression model. Further statistical analysis using T-tests allowed for the simplification to a scalar correction factor \psi for specific kernels. Usage: The method is used in 3D Gaussian Splatting variants, specifically within the DARBS (Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Splatting) framework, for high-quality 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00438, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W)
head: GS-W, Intrinsic and Dynamic Appearance Fusion
body: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) is a novel view synthesis method for unconstrained image collections that explicitly separates scene appearance into intrinsic material properties and dynamic environmental factors (such as illumination and weather) per 3D Gaussian point. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting and NeRF-based methods by avoiding global latent embeddings, which allows it to capture local high-frequency changes without blurring intrinsic textures with dynamic variations. The method employs adaptive sampling from image features and 2D visibility maps to mitigate transient occlusions and photometric variations. Inputs: A set of unconstrained 2D images with known camera poses (extrinsics and intrinsics). Outputs: A rendered image from a novel viewpoint, and implicitly, the optimized 3D Gaussian scene representation. The scene is represented as a collection of M 3D Gaussian points GP. Each Gaussian point i stores the following attributes: 1. Position Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: The center of the Gaussian. 2. Covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Modeled via a scaling matrix S and rotation matrix R (stored as quaternion q) to ensure positive semi-definiteness during optimization. \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = R S S^T R^T. 3. Intrinsic Appearance Feature s{f}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d: A learnable vector representing the static material properties of the point. 4. Dynamic Appearance Feature d{f}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d: A feature vector sampled from image features, representing dynamic environmental factors. 5. Opacity \alphai: Controls transparency. 6. View-dependent Color: Derived from the fused appearance feature and view direction via an MLP. 1. Projection: Each 3D Gaussian i is projected onto the 2D image plane. The 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i is transformed into the 2D screen space covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i using the affine approximation of the projective transformation J and the view matrix W: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i = J W \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i W^T J^T The 2D Gaussian function is defined as: G(x - X, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-X)^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(x-X)} where x is a point in space (or pixel coordinates) and X is the Gaussian center. 2. Sorting: Gaussian points are sorted by depth for each tile on the image plane. The image plane is divided into a grid of 16 \times 16 tiles. 3. Alpha Blending: For each pixel px', the color C(px') is aggregated from the sorted Gaussian points GP{px'} using alpha blending: \sigmai = G(px' - Xi, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i) C(px') = \sum{i \in GP{px'}} ci \sigmai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj) where ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian point. The core innovation of GS-W is the separation and fusion of appearance features. 1. Feature Extraction: Image features are extracted from a reference image using a U-Net model. These features are reshaped into K feature maps and one projection feature map. 2. Dynamic Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point GPi, dynamic appearance features d{f}^i are sampled from the extracted feature maps using an adaptive sampling strategy. This strategy allows each point to focus on local and detailed information more effectively. 3. Fusion: The intrinsic appearance feature s{f}^i (learnable per point) and the sampled dynamic appearance feature d{f}^i are fused with the position Xi using a fusion network Mf. The network Mf is composed of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a{f}^i = Mf(s{f}^i, d{f}^i, Xi) where a{f}^i is the holistic appearance feature. 4. Color Decoding: The fused appearance feature a{f}^i and the view direction \phi are decoded by another MLP Mc to obtain the final color ci of the Gaussian point: ci = Mc(a{f}^i, \phi) 1. Initialization: 3D Gaussian points GP are initialized with positions X extracted from a point cloud generated via Structure-from-Motion (SfM) from the input image set. 2. Loss Calculation: The loss is computed between the rendered image Ir and the ground truth reference image I{gt}. To mitigate the impact of transient occluders (e.g., moving people, vehicles), a 2D visibility map VM \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times H \times W} is employed. This map is obtained from a U-Net model and facilitates segmentation between transient and static objects. The loss is weighted by this visibility map. 3. Optimization: All Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, intrinsic features sf^i) are jointly optimized. The method employs point growth and pruning strategies based on gradients and opacity to manage the number of Gaussians. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np class Gaussian: def init(self, pos, cov, opacity, intrinsicfeat): self.pos = pos # (3,) self.cov = cov # (3, 3) self.opacity = opacity # scalar self.intrinsicfeat = intrinsicfeat # (d,) self.dynamicfeat = None # (d,) self.color = None # (3,) def initializegaussians(pointcloud): """Create Gaussian objects from SfM point cloud.""" gaussians = [] for p in pointcloud: gaussians.append(Gaussian( pos=np.array(p[:3]), cov=np.eye(3), opacity=1.0, intrinsicfeat=np.zeros(64))) return gaussians def learnablevector(dim=64): """Return a learnable parameter vector.""" return np.zeros(dim) def reshapefeatures(imgfeatures, K=4): """Split extracted features into K maps and 1 projection map.""" # imgfeatures shape: (H, W, C) # Reshape into K spatial feature maps and 1 projection map return np.split(imgfeatures, K + 1, axis=-1) def adaptivesample(featuremaps, pos): """Sample dynamic features adaptively based on Gaussian position.""" # Standard bilinear/trilinear sampling from feature maps # Returns dynamic appearance feature vector return np.mean(featuremaps, axis=(0, 1)) # Placeholder for adaptive sampling logic def fusionnetwork(intrinsic, dynamic, pos): """Two-MLP fusion network Mf.""" # Concatenate and pass through two MLP layers combined = np.concatenate([intrinsic, dynamic, pos]) return np.tanh(combined) # Simplified MLP forward pass def colornetwork(holistic, viewdir): """MLP Mc for color decoding.""" combined = np.concatenate([holistic, viewdir]) return np.tanh(combined) # Simplified MLP forward pass def projectcovariance(cov, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """Transform 3D covariance to 2D screen space using affine approximation.""" # J: affine approximation of projective transformation # W: view matrix # Sigma' = J W Sigma W^T J^T return projmatrix @ viewmatrix @ cov @ viewmatrix.T @ projmatrix.T def projectpoint(pos, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """Project 3D point to 2D pixel coordinates.""" homogenous = np.append(pos, 1.0) clip = projmatrix @ viewmatrix @ homogenous return clip[:2] / clip[2] def normalize(vec): return vec / (np.linalg.norm(vec) + 1e-8) def tilerasterize(projectedgaussians, width, height): """Tile-based alpha blending rasterizer.""" image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) # Group by 16x16 tiles tilesize = 16 for ty in range(0, height, tilesize): for tx in range(0, width, tilesize): tilegaussians = [g for g in projectedgaussians if tx <= g['pos'][0] < tx + tilesize and ty <= g['pos'][1] < ty + tilesize] tilegaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['depth']) for px in range(tx, min(tx + tilesize, width)): for py in range(ty, min(ty + tilesize, height)): accumalpha = 0.0 color = np.zeros(3) for g in tilegaussians: sigma = math.exp(-0.5 (g['pos'] - np.array([px, py])).T @ np.linalg.inv(g['cov']) @ (g['pos'] - np.array([px, py]))) sigma = min(sigma, 0.99) color += g['color'] sigma (1 - accumalpha) accumalpha += sigma (1 - accumalpha) image[py, px] = color return image def weightedmseloss(rendered, groundtruth, visibilitymap): """Compute loss weighted by visibility map.""" return np.mean((rendered - groundtruth) 2 visibilitymap) def pruneandgrowgaussians(gaussians, gradients, opacitythreshold): """Manage Gaussian count based on gradients and opacity.""" # Prune low opacity and high gradient Gaussians gaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g.opacity > opacitythreshold] # Grow new Gaussians in high-gradient regions (standard 3DGS strategy) return gaussians def gswrender(referenceimages, cameraposes, initialpointcloud): """Main pipeline for Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W).""" gaussians = initializegaussians(initialpointcloud) # Initialize learnable intrinsic appearance features for each Gaussian for g in gaussians: g.intrinsicfeat = learnablevector() # Initialize networks fusionnet = fusionnetwork colornet = colornetwork featureextractor = lambda img: np.random.rand(img.shape[0], img.shape[1], 64) # U-Net placeholder numepochs = 1000 imagewidth, imageheight = 512, 512 for epoch in range(numepochs): for refimg, campose in zip(referenceimages, cameraposes): # A. Feature Extraction imgfeatures = featureextractor(refimg) featuremaps = reshapefeatures(imgfeatures) visibilitymap = np.ones((imageheight, imagewidth)) # U-Net visibility map placeholder # B. Dynamic Feature Sampling for g in gaussians: g.dynamicfeat = adaptivesample(featuremaps, g.pos) # C. Appearance Fusion and Color Prediction for g in gaussians: holisticfeat = fusionnet(g.intrinsicfeat, g.dynamicfeat, g.pos) viewdirection = normalize(campose.cameracenter - g.pos) g.color = colornet(holisticfeat, viewdirection) # D. Rasterization projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: sigma2d = projectcovariance(g.cov, campose.viewmatrix, campose.projmatrix) projectedgaussians.append({ 'position': projectpoint(g.pos, campose.viewmatrix, campose.projmatrix), 'covariance': sigma2d, 'color': g.color, 'opacity': g.opacity, 'depth': g.pos[2] }) projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) renderedimage = tilerasterize(projectedgaussians, imagewidth, imageheight) # E. Loss Computation loss = weightedmseloss(renderedimage, refimg, visibilitymap) # F. Optimization Step # loss.backward() and optimizer.step() would follow in a deep learning framework pass # G. Point Management gaussians = pruneandgrowgaussians(gaussians, np.zeroslike(gaussians[0].pos), 0.01) return gaussians Transient Occluders: Without the 2D visibility map, moving objects (people, cars) cause artifacts like floating points or ghosting because the model attempts to reconstruct their geometry and appearance as static. Dynamic Variations: Failing to separate intrinsic and dynamic features leads to blurring of material textures when lighting or weather changes, as the model conflates static properties with environmental effects. Local Detail: Global appearance representations (common in NeRF) struggle with high-frequency local changes. GS-W's per-point adaptive sampling mitigates this. Rendering Speed: GS-W surpasses state-of-the-art NeRF-based methods in rendering speed by over 1000x. It matches real-time rendering speeds similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on wild data. Quality: Outperforms NeRF-based methods in reconstruction quality and detail, particularly in unconstrained environments with dynamic lighting and transient objects. Memory: Requires storage for intrinsic features per Gaussian point, increasing memory usage compared to standard 3DGS which typically uses a single SH coefficient set or simple color per point. The exact memory overhead is not specified in the sources. Strengths: Handles unconstrained image collections (wild data) with varying illumination, weather, and transient occluders. Real-time rendering capability. Limitations: Requires a U-Net for feature extraction and visibility map generation, adding complexity to the training pipeline. Performance depends on the quality of the SfM initialization and the visibility map accuracy. Origin: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) was proposed to address the limitations of existing NeRF-based methods and standard 3DGS when applied to unconstrained image collections. Standard methods assume static scenes and consistent lighting, which is rarely the case in real-world "wild" data. Key Insight: The appearance of a point in the real world is determined by its intrinsic material properties and dynamic environmental impacts. Separating these allows for better reconstruction of static geometry and appearance while handling dynamic variations. Development: GS-W builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [16] (referenced as in the context of 3DGS) and introduces the appearance separation module, adaptive sampling, and visibility map handling. It is cited in surveys as a key method for handling wild data alongside Wild-GS and SWAG. name: 3DGUT
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Unscented Transform, 3D Gaussian Uncentred Transform, XPR-3D Gaussian Upsampling Transform, XPR-3DGUT
body: 3DGUT is a rendering method that employs an unscented transform to improve the affine approximation of the projection operator, providing more precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane. It uses the same 3D Gaussian primitives as Gaussian Splatting but replaces the Jacobian-based linearization with a sigma-point transformation for projection and evaluates the Gaussian response in 3D along camera rays for per-pixel shading. Inputs: Primitive parameters p: mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, half-extents s \in \mathbb{R}^3, unit quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4, spherical harmonic coefficients sh, opacity o \in \mathbb{R}. Camera parameters: intrinsic matrix (focal lengths fx, fy, principal point cx, cy), world-to-camera rotation R{w2c}, translation t{w2c}. Configuration: alpha threshold \alpha{thresh}, z-near z{near}. Outputs: For each primitive: tile cull data (conic elements, opacity, mean, visibility) and shader data (canonical ray origin, transformation matrix, opacity, color). Per-pixel: alpha contribution and validity flag. PrimitiveParams: mu: (3,) float, mean in world space. s: (3,) float, half-extents (sx, sy, sz). q: (4,) float, unit quaternion for rotation. sh: (C, 3) float, spherical harmonic coefficients. o: (1,) float, opacity. Tile Cull Data (ptcd) fields for primitive p: con2D[0,0], con2D[0,1], con2D[1,1]: projected conic elements. o: opacity. mu2D: 2D mean. visible: boolean flag. Shader Data (psd) fields for primitive p: rocanonical: flattened ray origin in canonical space. M: flattened 3 \times 3 matrix S^{-1} R^T. o: opacity. c: view-dependent color. 1. Project Function: Computes the footprint and stores projected data. 1. Compute world-to-camera projection matrix R{w2c}. 2. Construct rotation matrix R from quaternion q. 3. Compute sigma points in world space using the Unscented Transform. 4. Project sigma points to camera space. 5. Project to pixel space. 6. Estimate 2D Gaussian mean \mu{2D} and covariance \Sigma{2D} from weighted projected points. 7. Apply low-pass filter to \Sigma{2D} for antialiasing. 8. Compute conic 2D from filtered covariance. 9. Adjust opacity using MipSplatting based on determinant ratio. 10. Compute extent, radius, and bounding box. 11. Account for ray offset in bounding box. 12. Compute tile count. 13. Compute visibility flag. 14. Concatenate data into ptcd and psd. 2. Tile Cull Function: Determines which tiles the primitive overlaps. 1. Adjust tile bounds for ray offset (tile\max\x += 1, tile\max\y += 1). 2. Reuse XPR-3DGS logic for culling. 3. Pixel Info Function: Returns ray direction in world space. 1. Compute canonical ray direction from pixel coordinates. 2. Rotate to world space. 4. Evaluate Function: Computes per-pixel alpha. 1. Unpack psd to get ro{canonical}, M, o, c. 2. Get ray direction rd from pixel data. 3. Compute canonical ray direction rd{canonical} = M @ rd. 4. Compute max response in canonical Gaussian space. 5. Compute \alpha = o \cdot response. 6. Check validity (response > 0.0113). The depth \tau that maximizes the Gaussian response along a camera ray r(\tau) = o + \tau d is: \tau{max} = \frac{dc^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mu - o)}{dc^\top \Sigma^{-1} dc} where oc = S^{-1} R^T (o - \mu) and dc = S^{-1} R^T d are the ray origin and direction in the canonical space of the Gaussian. The transformation matrix M used in shader data is: M = \text{diag}(1.0/p.s) @ R^T The canonical ray origin is: ro{canonical} = (M @ (cp - p.\mu)).\text{flatten()} where cp = -R{w2c}[:3,:3]^T @ R{w2c}[:3,3]. \alpha{thresh}: Alpha threshold for visibility. Typical value: 255 (in 8-bit integer context) or normalized equivalent. z{near}: Near plane distance for visibility check. Validity threshold: 0.0113 for response check. Precision: The unscented transform avoids Jacobian linearization errors, but sigma point selection must be robust. Boundaries: Ray offset adjustment in tile culling is critical for correct tile assignment. Degenerate Input: If determinant of covariance is non-positive, the primitive is marked invisible. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def project(p, cam, view, cfg): # Get world to camera projection matrix Rw2c = world2cameraprojectionmatrix(view) # Construct rotation matrix R from quaternion q R = getR(p.q) ## Unscented Transform # Compute sigma points in world space sigmapoints = computesigmapoints(p.mu, p.s, R, cfg) # Project sigma points to camera space sigmapointsc = vectorize(world2cam)(sigmapoints, Rw2c) muc = sigmapointsc[0] # Project to pixel space sigmapoints2D = vectorize(computemu2D)(sigmapointsc, cam) # Estimate mu2D and cov2D to approximate 2D Gaussian mu2D, cov2D = approximate2Dgaussian(sigmapoints2D, cfg) detorig = determinant(cov2D) # Apply low-pass filter to cov2D (antialiasing) cov2D = applylowpassfilter(cov2D, cfg) # Compute conic 2D from filtered covariance con2D = computeconic(cov2D) # Adjust opacity using MipSplatting based on determinant ratio det = determinant(cov2D) o = p.o mipsplatting2D(detorig, det) # Compute extent, radius, and bounding box ex, ey = computeextents(cov2D, det, o, cfg) r = computeradius(ex, ey) # Account for ray offset aabb = getboundingbox(mu2D - 0.5, ex, ey, cfg) # Compute tile count tc = (aabb.xmax - aabb.xmin) (aabb.ymax - aabb.ymin) # Compute view-dependent color c c = computecolor(p.mu, p.sh, view) # Compute visibility flag and adjust tile count visible = (det > 0) & (o > cfg.alphathresh) & (r > 0) & (tc > 0) & (muc[2] > cfg.znear) tc = float(visible) # Produce tileculldata and shaderdata for primitive p ptcd = concat(con2D[0,0], con2D[0,1], con2D[1,1], o, mu2D, visible) M = diag(1.0 / p.s) @ R.T cp = -Rw2c[:3,:3].T @ Rw2c[:3, 3] rocanonical = (M @ (cp - p.mu)).flatten() psd = concat(rocanonical, M.flatten(), o, c) return ProjectResult(depth=muc[2], visible=visible, tileculldata=ptcd, shaderdata=psd, aabb=aabb, tilecount=tc) def tilecull(tilemin, tilemax, ptcd, cfg): # Adjust tile bounds for ray offset tilemax[0] += 1 # tilemaxx tilemax[1] += 1 # tilemaxy # Rest of tilecull in XPR-3DGS can be reused unchanged... def pixelinfo(px, cam, view): # Compute ray direction in pixel space dc = [(px[0] + 0.5 - cam.cx) / cam.fx, (px[1] + 0.5 - cam.cy) / cam.fy, 1.0] dc /= norm(dc) # Rotate to world space Rc2w = cam2world(view)[:3,:3] # Compute ray direction rd = Rc2w @ dc return PixelInfoResult(rd=rd) def evaluate(pxdata, psd): rocanonical, M, o, c = unpack(psd) rd = pxdata[0:3] # Compute max response in canonical Gaussian space rdcanonical = M @ rd response = computemaxresponsecanonical(rocanonical, rdcanonical) alpha = o response valid = (response > 0.0113) return EvaluateResult(alpha=alpha, valid=valid, color=c) The implementation of 3DGUT within the XPR framework, demonstrating ease of integration by reusing shared pipeline modules. A technique used by 3DGUT to adjust opacity based on the determinant ratio of the projected covariance for antialiasing. Time Complexity: Projection involves computing sigma points and their projections, which is more expensive than the Jacobian-based approach in Gaussian Splatting but provides higher accuracy. Memory Complexity: Similar to Gaussian Splatting as it uses the same primitive structure, but stores additional shader data for canonical space evaluation. Strengths: More precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane by avoiding affine approximation errors. Limitations: Increased computational cost during projection compared to linearization methods. When to use: When high accuracy in Gaussian projection is required, especially for large or highly anisotropic Gaussians. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the accuracy gain is negligible. 3DGUT was introduced to address the limitations of affine approximations in Gaussian projection, which can compromise rendering accuracy. It employs the unscented transform to provide a more precise projection of 3D Gaussians onto the image plane. The method is part of the broader effort to improve the fidelity of point-based rendering methods. name: Transformer-based Reconstruction
body: Transformer-based Reconstruction methods replace the iterative optimization loop of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a feed-forward neural network that directly predicts Gaussian parameters from input images. This approach solves the computational bottleneck of per-scene optimization, enabling real-time reconstruction from single or sparse views. It differs from iterative siblings by eliminating the need for gradient descent on scene parameters, instead relying on learned priors within the transformer architecture to generalize across scenes. Flash3D is a feed-forward method for monocular 3DGS reconstruction that estimates depth from a single view to generate Gaussians. It differs from GS-LRM and Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) by relying on monocular depth estimation rather than multi-view feature aggregation or tokenized multi-image inputs. It is chosen when only a single image is available and a depth prior is acceptable. See Flash3D. GS-LRM is a feed-forward transformer method that predicts 3DGS parameters directly from a small set of input images (typically 2-4). It distinguishes itself from Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) by specifically targeting Gaussian parameter prediction rather than mesh or NeRF fields, and from Flash3D by its explicit handling of multi-view camera pose tokens. It is chosen for sparse-view reconstruction where camera poses are known. See GS-LRM. LRM is a feed-forward neural network designed for single-image to 3D reconstruction, establishing the foundational transformer-based architecture for direct parameter prediction in this family. It sets itself apart from Flash3D and GS-LRM by its generalizable architecture that can be adapted to various 3D representations, though here it predicts Gaussians. It is chosen as a baseline for single-view direct reconstruction. See Large Reconstruction Model (LRM). Reconstruction-based Generation decomposes 3D generation into two stages: multi-view image synthesis followed by 3D reconstruction. Unlike direct prediction methods, it leverages pre-trained diffusion models to generate posed multi-view images, which then serve as supervision for a Gaussian Splatting reconstructor. This approach reuses mature reconstruction pipelines, making system-level engineering straightforward, but inherits the consistency limitations of the multi-view generator. It is chosen when text-to-3D or single-image-to-3D generation is required without training a dedicated reconstruction network from scratch. See Reconstruction-based Generation. The family originates from the need to accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting, which traditionally requires per-scene optimization. Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) introduced the transformer-based feed-forward approach for 3D reconstruction. GS-LRM and Flash3D adapted this paradigm specifically for 3DGS, with GS-LRM focusing on sparse multi-view inputs and Flash3D on monocular depth estimation. Reconstruction-based Generation extends this by integrating diffusion-based multi-view synthesis.

name: Flash3D
head: Flash3D
body: Flash3D is a feed-forward network (FFN) method for monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction, generating 3DGS scenes by estimating depth from a single view. It differs from sibling methods like GS-LRM [1483-gs-lrm.md] and Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) [5959-large-reconstruction-model-lrm.md] by relying on monocular depth estimation rather than multi-view feature aggregation or tokenized multi-image inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single RGB image I. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian parameters \{\mui, \Sigmai, ci, \alphai\} representing the scene. Data Structures: The network outputs a list of Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix, often parameterized as rotation R \in SO(3) and scale s \in \mathbb{R}^3. ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: Estimate a dense depth map D from the input image I using a monocular depth estimation network. 2. Point Cloud Generation: Convert the depth map D and camera intrinsics into a 3D point cloud P by back-projecting each pixel (u, v) with depth d to 3D space. 3. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: The FFN predicts the Gaussian parameters for the scene. 4. Training: Optimize the network parameters using photometric losses (e.g., LPIPS, SSIM) between the rendered output and the ground truth image. Formulas: The monocular depth estimation step can be represented as: D{mono} = \varphid(\varphie(I)) where \varphie is the encoder, \varphid is the decoder, and I is the input image. Parameters: Loss functions: LPIPS, SSIM. Backbone architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular depth estimation may suffer from scale ambiguity; supervised depth estimation methods (like BTS) provide correct scale, while self-supervised or zero-shot models require additional scale and drift estimation during training. An encoder-decoder network that infers dense depth from a single image, supervised to have correct scale. It is used as the depth prior in Flash3D. Pitfall: Self-supervised or zero-shot pre-trained models require additional scale and drift estimation during training. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Single-view input. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Flash3D was proposed to address the challenge of training feed-forward networks to directly predict 3D Gaussian parameters. It uses an FFN for monocular reconstruction, generating 3DGS scenes by estimating depth from a single view. It is part of a family of methods that includes PixelSplat [55] and MVSplat [58]. name: GS-LRM
head: Gaussian Large Reconstruction Model
body: GS-LRM is a feed-forward transformer-based method that reconstructs a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation from a small set of input images. It solves the problem of sparse-view 3D reconstruction by directly predicting Gaussian parameters from image tokens, bypassing iterative optimization. It differs from its siblings by using a transformer architecture to decode concatenated image and camera tokens into Gaussians, whereas Flash3D and LRM typically target mesh or NeRF outputs, and Reconstruction-based Generation is a broader category. Inputs: A set of N input images (typically N=2 to 4) and their corresponding camera parameters (extrinsics and intrinsics). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Data Structures: 1. Image Tokens: Each input image is processed through a vision encoder (e.g., ViT) to produce a sequence of feature tokens. 2. Camera Tokens: Camera parameters are encoded into a fixed-size token embedding. 3. Concatenated Sequence: Image tokens and camera tokens are concatenated along the sequence dimension to form a single input sequence for the transformer. 4. Transformer Block: A standard transformer encoder processes the concatenated sequence. 5. Decoder: The output tokens from the transformer are passed to a decoder network. Steps: 1. Tokenization: Encode each of the N input images into image tokens T{img}. Encode the camera parameters into camera tokens T{cam}. 2. Concatenation: Form the input sequence S = [T{img}; T{cam}]. 3. Transformer Processing: Pass S through a transformer block to obtain output tokens T{out}. 4. Decoding: Decode T{out} into Gaussian parameters. This typically involves a linear projection or small MLP to predict the mean \mu, covariance \Sigma (or rotation R and scale S), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{SH} for each Gaussian. 5. Rendering: The predicted Gaussians are rendered using standard differentiable rasterization to produce the output image, which can be used for training if ground truth is available. Parameters: Number of input images: Typically 2-4. Transformer depth/width: Not specified in sources. Decoder architecture: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases: Camera Pose Accuracy: The method relies on known camera parameters. Incorrect poses may lead to misaligned Gaussians. Sparse Views: Performance may degrade with very few views or large view gaps, though it is designed for sparse inputs. Scale Ambiguity: Unlike methods like NoPoSplat which use canonical coordinates to resolve scale, GS-LRM assumes known camera intrinsics/extrinsics, which may carry scale ambiguity if not calibrated. Time Complexity: Feed-forward inference, typically fast (seconds per scene). Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and transformer size. Strengths: Fast inference, no iterative optimization, handles sparse views. Limitations: Requires known camera poses, may lack detail compared to iterative methods. When to use: When fast reconstruction from few views is needed and camera poses are known. When not to use: When camera poses are unknown or high-fidelity detail is critical and iterative optimization is feasible. GS-LRM was introduced as part of the trend towards large reconstruction models for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the success of transformer-based image-to-3D models like LRM but adapts the output to Gaussian Splatting representations. It is cited in tutorials on 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Large 4D Gaussian Model (L4GM)
body: L4GM is a feed-forward 4D large reconstruction model that generates per-frame 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from a single-view video input in approximately one second. It addresses the limitation of previous 4D generation models that were restricted to object-centric scenes by enabling the reconstruction of dynamic content from monocular video. Unlike iterative optimization methods, L4GM performs inference in a single forward pass, utilizing temporal self-attention to upsample the output to higher frame rates for temporal smoothness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single-view video sequence. Output: Per-frame 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) for each frame in the video. Data Structures: The model outputs a set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}t for each frame t. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics coefficients c{i, l, m} for color approximation. Method Steps: 1. Video Encoding: The input video is processed through a transformer-based encoder. The architecture is built upon LGM (Large Gaussian Model), which tokenizes image and camera parameters. For video, the temporal dimension is incorporated, likely via 3D tokenization or sequential processing, though specific architectural details of the video encoder are not explicitly detailed in the sources. 2. Forward Pass: The encoded tokens are passed through the transformer blocks. The model is designed to output 3DGS parameters directly in one forward pass, taking approximately 1 second. 3. Temporal Self-Attention: To address frame rate limitations and ensure temporal consistency, temporal self-attention is applied to the output tokens. This step upsamples the generated Gaussians to a higher frame rate, enhancing temporal smoothness. 4. Flow Field Regularization: A flow field is used for temporal regularization during training to ensure coherent motion between frames. Parameters: Training Dataset: An Objaverse-derived multiview-video dataset containing 44,000 objects, 12 million videos, and 300 million frames. Inference Time: ~1 second per video. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the quality of the input video; poor lighting or occlusions may affect reconstruction quality. The temporal self-attention mechanism requires sufficient temporal coherence in the input video to effectively upsample and smooth the output. Comp4D is a method designed to overcome the object-centric limitation of previous 4D generation models. It operates by first generating individual 4D objects and then composing them subject to trajectory constraints. This approach allows for more complex scenes beyond single-object reconstructions. Time Complexity: Inference is fast, taking approximately 1 second for a single forward pass. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Marked as a 2026 SOTA update for 4D reconstruction. Strengths: Fast, feed-forward inference; handles single-view video input; temporal upsampling via self-attention. Limitations: Requires a large training dataset; specific architectural details of the video encoder are not provided. When to Use: When fast 4D reconstruction from monocular video is required. When Not to Use: When iterative optimization for higher fidelity is acceptable, or when multi-view input is available and not restricted to single-view. L4GM was introduced as a 2026 SOTA update in the field of 4D reconstruction. It builds upon LGM and is trained on a large-scale Objaverse-derived multiview-video dataset. The model represents a shift from iterative optimization to feed-forward inference for 4D Gaussian Splatting. name: Gaussian Parameterization and Initialization
head: GS-LRM Initialization, GS-LRM Parameterization
body: This method defines the decoding strategy and data preprocessing required to transform raw transformer output tokens into valid 3D Gaussian parameters for the GS-LRM architecture. It solves the problem of mapping unconstrained neural network outputs to physically meaningful Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) while ensuring training stability through specific bias offsets and normalization constraints. It differs from sibling methods like L4GM by explicitly decoupling the parameterization into zero-order spherical harmonics for color and using a distance-based ray parameterization for XYZ coordinates, rather than direct 3D coordinate prediction. Inputs: Raw output tokens G{ij} from the transformer decoder, representing a batch of Gaussians. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{ray}o and direction \mathbf{ray}d) for scene-level reconstruction. Scene type indicator (Object-level or Scene-level) determining depth bounds and normalization rules. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by: Center position \mathbf{xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Opacity \alpha \in [0, 1] Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (SH coefficient) The raw output G{ij} is decomposed into five distinct components. The exact layout depends on the model's channel configuration, but logically maps as follows: G{rgb}: 3 values (RGB). G{scale}: 3 values (log-scale or linear scale pre-activation). G{rotation}: 4 values (unnormalized quaternion components). G{opacity}: 1 value. G{distance}: 1 value (scalar distance parameter along the ray). Camera pose normalization is applied only for Scene-level GS-LRM. Object-level GS-LRM skips this step because object sizes are pre-normalized during data generation. 1. Compute Mean Pose: Calculate the mean camera pose by averaging all input camera poses (rotation and translation) from the input set. 2. Coordinate Frame Alignment: Define the coordinate frame of this mean pose as the world space. Transform all input camera poses to be relative to this mean pose. 3. Scaling: Scale the camera locations such that they fit within the bounding box [-1, 1]^3 in the world space. Predict unnormalized quaternions from G{rotation}. Apply L2-normalization as an activation function to obtain unit quaternions \mathbf{q}. \mathbf{q} = \frac{G{rotation}}{\|G{rotation}\|2} Interpret G{rgb} directly as zero-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Higher-order SH is not used. \mathbf{c} = G{rgb} Apply an exponential activation with a bias offset, followed by clipping. The bias offset shifts the zero-mean output to ensure a minimum scale. \mathrm{scale} = \min \left( \exp(G{scale} - 2.3), 0.3 \right) Bias Offset: 2.3. This ensures \exp(-2.3) \approx 0.1, providing a stable initialization for small Gaussians. Max Scale: 0.3. Prevents excessively large Gaussians that could destabilize training. Apply a sigmoid activation with a bias offset. The bias offset shifts the zero-mean output to ensure a minimum opacity. \alpha = \sigma(G{opacity} - 2.0) Bias Offset: 2.0. This ensures \sigma(-2.0) \approx 0.1, providing a stable initialization for visible Gaussians. Sigmoid: \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}. The center position is parameterized along the camera ray using a distance parameter t derived from G{distance}. 1. Map Distance to Range: Convert G{distance} to a normalized weight \omega \in [0, 1] using sigmoid, then map to the range [d{near}, d{far}] to get t. \omega = \sigma(G{distance}) t = (1 - \omega) \cdot d{near} + \omega \cdot d{far} 2. Compute XYZ: Calculate the 3D position using the ray origin and direction. \mathbf{xyz} = \mathbf{ray}o + t \cdot \mathbf{ray}d 3. Clipping (Object-level only): For Object-level GS-LRM, clip the predicted \mathbf{xyz} coordinates to be inside the cube [-1, 1]^3. This aligns with the training data rendering setup and prevents line-shaped Gaussians from spreading gradients to multiple pixels, which hurts training stability. Scene-level GS-LRM does not apply this clipping. | Parameter | Object-level Value | Scene-level Value | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | d{near} | 0.1 | 0.0 | Near depth bound for ray parameterization. | | d{far} | 4.5 | 500 | Far depth bound. 500 accounts for large depth variations in indoor/outdoor scenes. | | Scale Bias | 2.3 | 2.3 | Offset for scale exponential. | | Opacity Bias | 2.0 | 2.0 | Offset for opacity sigmoid. | | Max Scale | 0.3 | 0.3 | Upper bound for scale. | | Camera Normalization | None | Yes | Mean pose alignment and bounding box scaling. | | XYZ Clipping | Yes | No | Clip to [-1, 1]^3. | Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def decodegaussianparameters(Graw, rayo, rayd, scenetype='object'): """ Decodes raw transformer output into Gaussian parameters. Args: Graw: Dictionary or tuple containing Grgb, Gscale, Grotation, Gopacity, Gdistance. rayo: Ray origin (3D vector). rayd: Ray direction (3D vector). scenetype: 'object' or 'scene'. Returns: dict: Decoded Gaussian parameters. """ # 1. Rotation: L2-normalize unnormalized quaternion qraw = Graw['Grotation'] norm = math.sqrt(sum(q2 for q in qraw)) q = [q / norm for q in qraw] # 2. Color: Direct mapping to zero-order SH c = Graw['Grgb'] # 3. Scale: Exp with bias, clipped scaleraw = Graw['Gscale'] # Apply bias 2.3 and exp scaleunclipped = [math.exp(s - 2.3) for s in scaleraw] # Clip to max 0.3 scale = [min(s, 0.3) for s in scaleunclipped] # 4. Opacity: Sigmoid with bias opacityraw = Graw['Gopacity'] alpha = sigmoid(opacityraw - 2.0) # 5. Position: Distance parameterization distanceraw = Graw['Gdistance'] # Set depth bounds based on scene type if scenetype == 'object': dnear = 0.1 dfar = 4.5 else: # scene dnear = 0.0 dfar = 500 # Map distance to t omega = sigmoid(distanceraw) t = (1.0 - omega) dnear + omega dfar # Compute XYZ xyz = [rayo[i] + t rayd[i] for i in range(3)] # 6. Clipping (Object-level only) if scenetype == 'object': xyz = [max(-1.0, min(1.0, coord)) for coord in xyz] return { 'xyz': xyz, 'scale': scale, 'rotation': q, 'opacity': alpha, 'color': c } def normalizecameraposes(cameraposes): """ Normalizes camera poses for scene-level GS-LRM. Args: cameraposes: List of camera poses (translation vectors). Returns: List of normalized camera poses. """ # Compute mean pose translation meanx = sum(p[0] for p in cameraposes) / len(cameraposes) meany = sum(p[1] for p in cameraposes) / len(cameraposes) meanz = sum(p[2] for p in cameraposes) / len(cameraposes) # Calculate scale factor to fit in [-1, 1]^3 # Assuming we need to scale relative to the mean # Note: The source says "scale all input camera locations... within [-1, 1]^3" # Implementation detail: Find max distance from mean, scale by 1/maxdist maxdist = 0 for p in cameraposes: dx = p[0] - meanx dy = p[1] - meany dz = p[2] - meanz dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if dist > maxdist: maxdist = dist scalefactor = 1.0 / maxdist if maxdist > 0 else 1.0 normalizedposes = [] for p in cameraposes: newx = (p[0] - meanx) scalefactor newy = (p[1] - meany) scalefactor newz = (p[2] - meanz) scalefactor normalizedposes.append([newx, newy, newz]) return normalizedposes Training Stability: Without the bias offsets (2.3 for scale, 2.0 for opacity), the initial zero-mean output of the transformer may result in scales or opacities that are too small or too large, causing gradient issues. The biases ensure initial values are around 0.1. Line-shaped Gaussians: In object-level reconstruction, failing to clip XYZ to [-1, 1]^3 can result in line-shaped Gaussians that spread gradients to multiple pixels, hurting training stability. Scene Depth Variation: Using object-level depth bounds (d{far}=4.5) for scene-level reconstruction will fail to capture distant geometry. Scene-level requires d{far}=500. Camera Normalization: Applying camera normalization to object-level data is unnecessary and potentially harmful, as object sizes are already pre-normalized. Time: The decoding process is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, involving simple arithmetic operations (exp, sigmoid, normalization). It is negligible compared to the transformer forward pass. Memory: The method does not introduce significant additional memory overhead beyond storing the raw output tokens and the decoded parameters. Strengths: Ensures training stability through careful initialization of scale and opacity via bias offsets. Simplifies color representation by using zero-order SH, reducing model complexity. Adapts to different scene scales via configurable depth bounds and camera normalization. Limitations: Zero-order SH limits view-dependent color modeling. The method relies on empirical constants (bias offsets, depth bounds) that may need tuning for specific datasets. Use for GS-LRM reconstruction tasks where training stability is critical. Use for scene-level reconstruction when large depth variations are present (requires scene-level parameters). Do not use if view-dependent effects are required without modifying the SH order. The method originates from the GS-LRM (Large Reconstruction Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting) paper by K. Zhang, S. Bi, H. Tan et al.. It was developed to facilitate the training of a transformer-based model that generates 3D Gaussian splats from 2D images. The parameterization was designed to address the challenges of training a large transformer model to output 3D geometry. By decomposing the output into specific components and applying targeted activations (exp for scale, sigmoid for opacity/distance), the authors ensured that the model could learn meaningful representations from the start. The distinction between object-level and scene-level parameters reflects the need to handle different scales and normalization requirements in 3D reconstruction. name: Large Reconstruction Model (LRM)
body: Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) is a feedforward transformer-based method for single-image or multi-view to 3D reconstruction that outputs a triplane neural representation in a single forward pass. It solves the problem of slow, per-scene optimization in traditional neural rendering by learning 3D priors from large-scale datasets, enabling real-time reconstruction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a triplane representation as the primary output, whereas Flash3D and GS-LRM predict 3D Gaussians directly, and Reconstruction-based Generation focuses on generation pipelines rather than direct reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single image I or a viewset V=\{Ii\}{i=1}^N with corresponding camera parameters \{\pii\}{i=1}^N. Output: A triplane neural representation \theta. Final Render: Novel view images \hat{I} = R(\theta, \pi). Data Structures: Trplane Representation \theta: A 3D feature field represented by three 2D planes (XY, YZ, XZ). The exact bit-packing or resolution of the triplane is not given in the sources. Transformer Blocks: A series of transformer blocks process the input features. Splatter Layer: A component that splats source view features into a new triplane. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract a pixel-wise feature map \mathbf{v}=\psi(Ii) from each image Ii in the input viewset. 2. Lifting with Splatter: Lift the feature maps into an intermediate 3D representation \tilde{\theta} using the Splatter component. 3. Transformer Processing: Input \tilde{\theta} into the large-scale model \Phi (a transformer) to output the final 3D representations \theta=\Phi\theta(\tilde{\theta}). The Splatter layer is inserted every 3 transformer blocks (i.e., 5 blocks in total). The Splatter layer takes previous block outputs as prior shape encoding. 4. Rendering: Output novel view images \hat{I} = R(\theta, \pi) from \theta using the Renderer component. 5. Training: Train the model by minimizing the loss L between the novel rendered image \hat{I} and the corresponding ground truth I. Formulas: Feature extraction: \mathbf{v}=\psi(Ii). Intermediate representation: \tilde{\theta} = \text{Splatter}(\mathbf{v}). Final representation: \theta=\Phi\theta(\tilde{\theta}). Rendering: \hat{I} = R(\theta, \pi). Loss: L(\hat{I}, I). Parameters: Dataset: Trained on Objaverse + Objaverse-XL. Transformer Blocks: 5 blocks in total, with Splatter inserted every 3 blocks. LPIPS Optimization: Enabled in the Lightplane-augmented LRM to avoid deferred backpropagation complexity. Resolution: Training uses low-resolution images (64x64) for some losses, but high-resolution rendering is supported. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-view Input: The method supports multi-view inputs, but the specific handling of camera pose errors or inconsistent views is not detailed. Memory Efficiency: The memory efficiency of the renderer allows for high-resolution rendering and image-level losses, which is a key advantage over the original LRM's deferred backpropagation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def LRMforward(imageorviewset, cameras): # Step 1: Feature Extraction if issingleimage(imageorviewset): views = [imageorviewset] camparams = [cameras] else: views = imageorviewset camparams = cameras # Extract pixel-wise feature maps featuremaps = [] for i, img in enumerate(views): v = psi(img) # psi is the feature extractor featuremaps.append(v) # Step 2: Lifting with Splatter (Initial) # Splatter lifts features into a 3D representation thetatilde = splatter(featuremaps, camparams) # Step 3: Transformer Processing # 5 transformer blocks total, Splatter inserted every 3 blocks theta = thetatilde for blockidx in range(5): # Process through transformer block theta = transformerblock(theta) # Insert Splatter layer every 3 blocks (i.e., after block 2 and block 5? # Source says "every 3 transformer blocks (i.e. 5 blocks in total)" # This implies Splatter is inserted at specific intervals. # Assuming Splatter is inserted after block 2 and block 5 is the final output? # Or Splatter is inserted within the sequence. # Let's assume Splatter is inserted after block 2 and block 5 is the end. # Actually, "every 3 transformer blocks" suggests a periodic insertion. # With 5 blocks, it might be inserted after block 2 and block 5? # Or maybe it's inserted after block 2, and the 5th block is the last one. # Let's assume Splatter is inserted after block 2. if blockidx == 2: # Splatter takes previous block outputs as prior shape encoding theta = splatter(theta, camparams) # Step 4: Rendering # Output novel view images # Assuming we want to render from a specific camera pi # theta is the final 3D representation renderedimage = renderer(theta, pi) return renderedimage, theta def LRMloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage): # Minimize loss L between novel rendered image and ground truth loss = L(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) return loss Note: The exact placement of the Splatter layer within the 5 blocks is ambiguous. "Every 3 transformer blocks (i.e. 5 blocks in total)" suggests a specific architecture. If it's inserted every 3 blocks, and there are 5 blocks, it might be inserted after block 2 (if 0-indexed) or block 3 (if 1-indexed). The pseudocode assumes insertion after block 2 (0-indexed) as a placeholder for the specific architecture detail which is not fully explicit. The Large Gaussian Reconstruction Model (GRM) is a feedforward neural network for single-image or multi-view to 3D reconstruction that directly predicts Gaussian maps. It builds on Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) by replacing its output format with Gaussian primitives, supporting both single and multi-view inputs. Time Complexity: Feedforward model, single transformer pass, enabling real-time reconstruction. Memory Complexity: Memory efficient due to the Lightplane renderer, allowing high-resolution rendering and image-level losses without deferred backpropagation. Measured Performance: Outperforms baseline ViewFormer [41] and overfitting baselines like Voxel and NeRF. Specific metrics are not provided in the sources. Scaling: Highly scalable components for neural 3D fields. Strengths: Real-time reconstruction, high-resolution rendering, memory efficiency, support for multi-view inputs. Limitations: Relies on large-scale datasets (Objaverse + Objaverse-XL) for training. When to use: When real-time 3D reconstruction from single or multi-view images is required. When not to use: When high-fidelity per-scene optimization is required, or when the input data does not match the training distribution. Origin: LRM was introduced by Adobe in 2023. History: It represents a shift from per-scene optimization to feedforward models for 3D reconstruction. Usage: Used for single-image to 3D reconstruction and generation. It builds on Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) by replacing its output format with Gaussian primitives, supporting both single and multi-view inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: One or more source images. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian parameters representing the scene. Process the input image(s) through a feedforward architecture. 2. Directly output the Gaussian maps as the network result. 3. Render the predicted Gaussians for training or inference. A modified baseline of GRM that enhances speed and training objectives. It replaces the CNN deconvolution layer with an MLP unpatchify layer as proposed in [21], and is implemented in JAX. An LPIPS loss is added to the training objective, which improves LPIPS and SSIM scores but causes a slight decrease in PSNR. Spherical harmonics degree is set to 0 for RealEstate10K and 1 for DL3DV. name: Reconstruction-based Generation
head: LGM
body: Reconstruction-based Generation decomposes 3D asset creation into two distinct stages: multi-view image synthesis followed by 3D Gaussian reconstruction. Unlike end-to-end generative models, this approach leverages pre-trained diffusion models to generate posed multi-view images, which then serve as supervision signals for a dedicated Gaussian Splatting (GS) reconstructor. This method distinguishes itself by reusing mature, standard multi-view reconstruction pipelines, thereby simplifying system-level engineering and reducing the computational overhead associated with direct 3D generation, though it remains subject to the consistency limitations of the initial image generator. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt or a single reference image. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives (positions, covariances, colors, opacities) representing the 3D scene. Data Structures: Multi-view Images: A small set of posed 2D images generated by the diffusion model. 3D Gaussian Attributes: Standard Gaussian Splatting parameters (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, color c, opacity \alpha). U-Net Architecture: An asymmetric neural network used for the reconstruction phase. Steps: 1. Multi-view Synthesis: An off-the-shelf multi-view or video diffusion model generates a set of posed 2D images from the input text or single image. This stage may also produce auxiliary data such as depth maps or camera trajectories. 2. Reconstruction Training: A U-Net-based network is trained to map the generated multi-view images directly to 3D Gaussian attributes. 3. Asymmetric Processing: The U-Net is designed with an asymmetric structure. It accepts high-resolution image inputs while constraining the number of output Gaussians to manage computational load and memory usage. 4. Optimization: The network minimizes the difference between the rendered views of the predicted Gaussians and the input multi-view images, effectively solving a standard multi-view reconstruction problem. Parameters: U-Net Asymmetry: The specific ratio of input resolution to output Gaussian count is not explicitly defined in the sources, but the architectural choice is critical for balancing fidelity and efficiency. Number of Views: Described as "a small set". Exact numbers vary by implementation but are typically fewer than full volumetric sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cross-view Inconsistency: Imperfect consistency in the generated multi-view images can lead to noisy or artifacts in the final 3D reconstruction. Janus Ambiguity: The method is prone to generating objects with multiple faces or ambiguous geometry if the diffusion prior is not sufficiently constrained. Over-smoothing: Generated textures may lack high-frequency detail, resulting in over-smoothed appearances unless additional regularizers are applied. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than iterative optimization-based reconstruction because the reconstruction is performed via a feed-forward network after the initial diffusion step. However, the total time is dominated by the multi-view diffusion generation, which can take minutes to hours per prompt. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to dense voxel-based methods due to the sparse nature of Gaussians and the asymmetric U-Net design limiting output size. Strengths: Straightforward system-level engineering; reuses mature reconstruction pipelines; decouples generation from reconstruction. Limitations: Inherits fundamental limitations of the multi-view generator, including cross-view inconsistency and potential geometric artifacts. This approach emerged as a strategy to mitigate the high computational costs and instability of direct 3D generation. By separating the problem into image synthesis and 3D reconstruction, it allows for the use of powerful, pre-trained 2D diffusion models. The Large Reconstruction Model (LGM) is a prominent example of this paradigm, utilizing off-the-shelf models for multi-view generation and training a U-Net for Gaussian reconstruction. name: 3D Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering
head: Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids, Gaussian Ellipsoid Ray Tracing, VoGE, VoGE Ray Tracing with Ellipsoidal Gaussians, VoGE Volume Density Ray Tracing, VoGE Volume Rendering, VoGE: A Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids for Analysis-by-Synthesis
body: 3D Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering (VoGE) is a differentiable volume rendering method that represents scenes as a sum of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids and computes image synthesis via ray tracing rather than rasterization. It solves the occlusion ambiguity inherent in distance-based blending by accumulating volume density distributions along viewing rays, enabling realistic interaction between overlapping objects. Unlike its sibling Gaussian Splatting, which approximates volume rendering through 2D rasterization of projected splats, VoGE replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture exact volume density distributions for blending. Inputs: A set of K Gaussian ellipsoids, each defined by a center location \mathbf{M}k \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a symmetric spatial variance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}; a camera configuration defining viewing rays \mathbf{r}(t); and per-kernel attributes (e.g., color \mathbf{c}k). Outputs: A synthesized 2D image where each pixel color is a weighted sum of kernel attributes. Data Structures: Each kernel k stores: \mathbf{M}k: Center coordinates (\mu{k,x}, \mu{k,y}, \mu{k,z}). \mathbf{\Sigma}k: 3 \times 3 symmetric covariance matrix. \mathbf{c}k: Attribute vector (e.g., RGB color). Precomputation per Kernel: For each kernel k, the method precomputes scalars to simplify ray integration: 1. \mathbf{V}k: Vector from the ray point of closest approach to the center. 2. lk: The distance along the ray where density is maximized. 3. qk: Log-density magnitude offset. 4. \sigmak^2: Variance of the 1D Gaussian projection along the ray direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, sample a viewing ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{D} t, where \mathbf{D} is the normalized direction vector and t is the distance from the camera origin. 2. Kernel Parameter Calculation: For each kernel k and ray direction \mathbf{D}, compute the following scalars: Calculate the length lk along the ray that maximizes the density \rhok(\mathbf{r}(t)): lk = \frac{\mathbf{M}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{M}k}{2 \cdot \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D}} Calculate the vector \mathbf{V}k from the point lk \mathbf{D} on the ray to the center \mathbf{M}k: \mathbf{V}k = \mathbf{M}k - lk \mathbf{D} Compute the precomputed scalar qk representing the peak density magnitude offset: qk = -0.5 \mathbf{V}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{V}k Compute the precomputed scalar \sigmak^2 representing the variance of the 1D Gaussian along the ray: \sigmak^2 = \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} Note: The condition \mathbf{V}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{V}k = 0 holds by definition of lk, simplifying the exponent. 3. Volume Density Definition: The volume density \rho(\mathbf{X}) at any location \mathbf{X} is the sum of ellipsoidal Gaussian kernels: \rho(\mathbf{X}) = \sum{k=1}^K \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{M}k)^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot (\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{M}k)\right) Along the ray \mathbf{r}(s) = s\mathbf{D}, the density of the k-th kernel reduces to a 1D Gaussian: \rhok(\mathbf{r}(s)) = \frac{e^{qk}}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{(s - lk)^2}{2 \sigmak^2}\right) 4. Occupancy Accumulation: Compute the occupancy T(t) along the ray, which represents the probability of not being occluded up to distance t. This is derived by integrating the total volume density: T(t) = \exp\left(-\tau \int{-\infty}^t \rho(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds\right) Substituting the 1D Gaussian form and using the error function \operatorname{erf}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int0^x e^{-u^2} du, the closed-form solution is: T(t) = \exp\left(-\sum{k=1}^K e^{qk} \frac{\operatorname{erf}\left((t - lk)/\sigmak\right) + 1}{2}\right) Here, \tau is a scattering coefficient. The integral limits are effectively -\infty to t because the Gaussian support is infinite. 5. Kernel-to-Pixel Weight Computation: Compute the weight Wk for each kernel to determine its contribution to the final pixel color. The exact weight is the integral of the reweighted density: Wk(t) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} T(t) \rhok(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt Since the integral of T(t) involving \operatorname{erf} is analytically intractable, VoGE approximates T(t) as constant T(lk) over the kernel's support (centered at lk): Wk \approx T(lk) e^{qk} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{(t - lk)^2}{\sigmak^2}\right) dt The integral of the normalized Gaussian part equals 1. Thus, the approximate closed-form weight is: Wk = T(lk) e^{qk} The error introduced by this approximation converges to a fixed value of 0.0256, which is negligible compared to the integral result W=1. 6. Image Synthesis: For each pixel, sum the contributions of all kernels weighted by their computed weights Wk and their attributes \mathbf{c}k: \mathbf{C}{pixel} = \sum{k=1}^K Wk \mathbf{c}k Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computekernelparams(Mk, Sigmak, D): """ Precompute scalars for a single kernel along a ray direction D. Mk: (3,) center vector Sigmak: (3,3) symmetric covariance matrix D: (3,) normalized ray direction vector Returns: lk, qk, sigmaksq """ Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigmak) term1 = np.dot(Mk, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) term2 = np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, Mk)) denominator = 2.0 np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) if denominator == 0: # Guard against degenerate covariance projection return 0.0, 0.0, 1e-8 lk = (term1 + term2) / denominator Vk = Mk - (lk D) qk = -0.5 np.dot(Vk, np.dot(Sigmainv, Vk)) sigmaksq = np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) return lk, qk, sigmaksq def rendervoge(kernels, rayorigin, raydirection, tau=1.0): """ Render a single ray using VoGE. kernels: List of dicts with keys 'M', 'Sigma', 'color' rayorigin: (3,) camera origin raydirection: (3,) normalized direction tau: scattering coefficient Returns: pixelcolor (3,) """ # Step 1 & 2: Precompute kernel parameters for this ray kerneldata = [] for k in kernels: M = k['M'] Sigma = k['Sigma'] lk, qk, sigmaksq = computekernelparams(M, Sigma, raydirection) sigmak = math.sqrt(max(sigmaksq, 1e-8)) kerneldata.append({ 'lk': lk, 'qk': qk, 'sigmak': sigmak, 'color': k['color'] }) pixelcolor = np.zeros(3) # Step 4 & 5: Compute Occupancy T(lk) and Weight Wk for each kernel for kd in kerneldata: lk = kd['lk'] qk = kd['qk'] sigmak = kd['sigmak'] # Compute T(lk): Occupancy at the peak of kernel k # T(t) = exp(-tau sum{j} e^{qj} (erf((t - lj)/sigmaj) + 1)/2) densityintegralsum = 0.0 for otherkd in kerneldata: lother = otherkd['lk'] qother = otherkd['qk'] sigmaother = otherkd['sigmak'] arg = (lk - lother) / sigmaother erfval = math.erf(arg) term = math.exp(qother) (erfval + 1.0) / 2.0 densityintegralsum += term Tlk = math.exp(-tau densityintegralsum) # Step 5: Compute Weight Wk Wk = Tlk math.exp(qk) # Step 6: Accumulate Color pixelcolor += Wk kd['color'] return pixelcolor Parameters: \tau: Scattering coefficient. Typical value: 1.0. K: Total number of Gaussian kernels. Varies by scene complexity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distance-based blending ambiguity: Traditional splatting blends based on viewing distance, causing unrealistic color shifts when foreground objects move relative to background objects (e.g., purple blending). VoGE avoids this by using density-based blending. Integral infeasibility: The exact integral of T(t) involving the error function is analytically intractable. The approximation Wk \approx T(lk)e^{qk} is used. The error is bounded and negligible (0.0256). Degenerate Covariance: If \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} is zero or near-zero, lk is undefined. This occurs if the ray direction is orthogonal to the principal axes in a way that makes the projection singular. Guard against division by zero. The Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive replaces long-tailed Gaussian kernels with constant-density ellipsoidal shapes to reduce spatial overlap and memory usage. It addresses the non-differentiability of hard-boundary ellipsoids by employing a sigmoid-based formulation, allowing for stable gradient-based optimization against 3D intensity fields. Unlike its sibling Ever Rendering, which relies on ray-based accumulation to implicitly soften boundaries, this method ensures the primitive itself is fully differentiable, making it suitable for direct volumetric training. Ever Rendering is a real-time volumetric rendering method that represents a radiance field as a set of constant-density volumetric ellipsoids, avoiding the 2D billboard approximation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike its sibling Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive, it replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture volume density distributions for blending, enabling exact transmittance calculation without approximation errors. Each point is represented by a 3D Gaussian ellipsoid GV to facilitate general grids; it becomes a sphere for cubic grids. The volume-space Gaussian is defined as GV = \frac{1}{2\pi V} e^{-0.5(x - vj)^T V^{-1} (x - vj)}. This ellipsoid is transformed into view-space G{MVM} using the viewing matrix M. Time Complexity: VoGE provides real-time level rendering speed, competitive with PyTorch3D. The complexity is dominated by the per-ray, per-kernel evaluation of the error function and exponential terms. With N pixels and K kernels, the complexity is roughly O(N \cdot K). The use of closed-form approximations avoids expensive numerical integration. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of kernels K, storing \mathbf{M}k, \mathbf{\Sigma}k, and attributes for each. Strengths: Resolves occlusion ambiguities better than distance-based blending. Fully differentiable, suitable for analysis-by-synthesis tasks like pose estimation and texture fitting. Real-time performance achievable via CUDA implementation. Limitations: Approximation error in weight calculation (though negligible). When to use: When accurate occlusion reasoning and differentiability are required, such as in object pose estimation, shape/texture fitting, and scenes with significant overlapping objects. When not to use: When maximum frame rate is critical and occlusion accuracy is less important than speed, or when the scene can be well-approximated by 2D billboards (standard 3DGS). VoGE (Volume Gaussian Ellipsoid) was proposed as a differentiable volume renderer that utilizes volumetric Gaussian reconstruction kernels as geometric primitives. It was developed to address the limitations of current state-of-the-art differentiable renderers that use rasterization and distance-based blending, which suffer from ambiguity when objects overlap. The code is available at https://github.com/Angtian/VoGE.
