name: Gaussian Splat Projection and Sorting
head: Staging Splats
body: Gaussian Splat Projection and Sorting is a GPU compute shader pass that projects 3D Gaussian splats into 2D screen space, culls invisible splats, computes view-dependent lighting, and prepares data for tile-based sorting. It differs from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by handling the geometric projection, visibility culling, and sorting key generation, whereas the parent handles the actual pixel-level rasterization within tiles. It differs from Gaussian Splat View Data Calculation by focusing on the projection and sorting preparation rather than the evaluation of appearance (SH) and 4D state resolution, although both may coexist in different pipeline implementations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: SplatsBuffer: Array of Splat structs (std430). SplatInstanceIdsBuffer: Array of uvec2 where x is the unique instance ID and y is the index into SplatsBuffer. InstanceTransformsBuffer: Array of mat4 model matrices. Uniforms: camerapos (vec3), time (float), dims (ivec2, texture size), pointcount (int), lightcount (int). LightRigBuffer: Array of vec4 lights. InstanceRelightBuffer: Array of vec4 per instance. SplatLightingBuffer: Array of uint per splat (packed normals/AO). Outputs: CulledBuffer: Array of RasterizeData structs containing projected data for visible splats. SortKeysBuffer: Array of uint keys for radix sort. SortValuesBuffer: Array of uint values (original splat indices). Histograms: sortbuffersize (atomic counter) and histogram data. Data Structures: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Splat { vec3 position; float time; float covariance[6]; // Top triangle of symmetric 3x3 matrix float opacity; float pad; float shcoefficients[163]; // SH coefficients, degree 3 }; struct RasterizeData { vec2 imagepos; vec2 posxy; vec3 conic; // Inverse 2D covariance: (covz, -covxy, covx) / det float posz; vec4 color; // RGB + opacity vec4 depthdata; // z-depth info }; Constants: TILESIZE: 16. SHC0 to SHC36: Spherical harmonic constants. DECODECOVARIANCE(c): Reconstructs mat3 from 6 floats: mat3(c[0], c[1], c[2], c[1], c[3], c[4], c[2], c[4], c[5]). Steps: 1. Initialization: Get glGlobalInvocationID.x. If id >= pointcount, return. 2. Barrier: Synchronize workgroup. 3. Instance Data: Retrieve instanceid = splatinstancedata[id].x and uniquesplatindex = splatinstancedata[id].y. 4. Load Data: Load splat = splatbuffer[uniquesplatindex] and modelmatrix = instancemodelmatrices[instanceid]. 5. Visibility Check: If modelmatrix[0][3] < 0.5, return. Set modelmatrix[0][3] = 0.0. 6. Frustum Culling: Compute worldcovariance = objectlinear DECODECOVARIANCE(splat.covariance) transpose(objectlinear). Compute worldpos = modelmatrix vec4(splat.position, 1.0). Compute viewpos = viewmatrix worldpos. Compute clippos = projectionmatrix viewpos. Set viewbounds = clippos.w 1.2. If any(clippos.xyz < vec3(-viewbounds, -viewbounds, 0.0)) or any(clippos.xyz > vec3(viewbounds, viewbounds, clippos.w)), return. 7. Time Animation: Compute splattime = time - splat.time. Compute timefactor = easeoutcubic(clamp(splattime, 0, 1)). Compute timefactorlate = easeoutcubic(clamp(splattime - 0.35, 0, 1)). Compute splatopacity = splat.opacity timefactorlate timefactorlate. Compute splatscale = mix(2.0, 1.0, timefactorlate). easeoutcubic(x) = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - x, 3.0). 8. Project Covariance: Compute cov3d = worldcovariance splatscale^2. Compute tanfovinv = vec2(projectionmatrix[0][0], projectionmatrix[1][1]). Compute focal = (dims - 1) 0.5 tanfovinv (-1.0 / viewpos.z). Clamp mean.xy = clamp(viewpos.xy (-1.0 / viewpos.z), -tanfov 1.3, tanfov 1.3). Compute jacobian = mat3(focal.x, 0, 0, 0, focal.y, 0, focal.x mean.x, focal.y mean.y, 0). Compute screentransform = jacobian viewmatrix[:3,:3]. Compute cov2d = screentransform cov3d transpose(screentransform). Result: vec3(cov2d[0][0] + 0.3, cov2d[0][1], cov2d[1][1] + 0.3). 9. Determinant Check: det = covariance.x covariance.z - covariance.y covariance.y. If det == 0.0, return. 10. Eigenvalues: mid = 0.5 (covariance.x + covariance.z). eigenvalues = mid + vec2(1, -1) sqrt(max(0.1, mid mid - det)). If any(eigenvalues < 0), return. 11. Image Position: ndcpos = clippos.xyz / clippos.w. imagepos = ((ndcpos.xy + 1.0) 0.5 - vec2(1, 0.75) (1.0 - timefactor)) (dims - 1). 12. Radius: radius = pow(splatopacity, 0.2) 2.5 sqrt(max(eigenvalues.x, eigenvalues.y)). 13. Tile Bounds: gridsize = (dims + TILESIZE - 1) / TILESIZE. rectbounds = getrect(imagepos, radius, gridsize). getrect returns uvec4(clamp((imagepos - radius) / TILESIZE, vec2(0), gridsize), clamp(ceil((imagepos + radius) / TILESIZE), vec2(0), gridsize)). 14. Tile Count: numtilestouched = (rectbounds.z - rectbounds.x) (rectbounds.w - rectbounds.y). If numtilestouched == 0, return. 15. Atomic Sort Buffer: buffersize = atomicAdd(sortbuffersize, numtilestouched). sortbufferoffset = buffersize. 16. View Direction: viewdir = normalize(inverse(objectlinear) (worldpos.xyz - camerapos)). 17. Base Color: basecolor = getcolor(viewdir, splat.shcoefficients). Evaluates SH up to degree 3. 18. Relighting: If instancerelight[instanceid 2].w > 0.5: If instancerelight[instanceid 2].z > 0.5, basecolor = max(0.0, 0.5 + splat.shcoefficients[0..2] SHC0). Else, basecolor = relightfactor(uniquesplatindex, worldpos.xyz, objectlinear, relight.x, relight.y, instancerelight[instanceid2+1].rgb). 19. Fill RasterizeData: data.imagepos = imagepos. data.conic = vec3(covariance.z, -covariance.y, covariance.x) / det. data.color = vec4(basecolor, splatopacity). data.posxy = worldpos.xy. data.posz = worldpos.z. data.depthdata = vec4(-viewpos.z, 0, 0, 0). Write to culledbuffer[id]. 20. Sorting Keys: viewdepth = max(0.0, clippos.w). depth01 = viewdepth / (1.0 + viewdepth). depth = uint(depth01 65535.0) & 0xFFFF. Loop y from rectbounds.y to rectbounds.w, x from rectbounds.x to rectbounds.z: tileid = y gridsize.x + x. key = (tileid << 16) | depth. sortkeys[sortbufferoffset] = key. sortvalues[sortbufferoffset] = id. sortbufferoffset++. name: Gaussian Splat View Data Calculation
head: FGaussianSplatCalcViewDataCS
body: A GPU compute shader that transforms Gaussian splats to screen space, evaluates view-dependent spherical harmonics, and handles 4D temporal or native 4D transformations per frame. It serves as the final preparation step before sorting and rasterization, handling complex 4D temporal variations (keyframe interpolation, temporal marginalization, or native 4D primitives) and advanced culling mechanisms (cluster-based, LOD, and distance-based). It differs from its parent Gaussian Splat Projection and Sorting by focusing specifically on the evaluation of appearance (SH), 4D state resolution, and the population of the ViewDataBuffer with screen-space attributes required for the subsequent tiled rasterization pass. Inputs: Splat Data: PackedSplatBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer, 16 bytes/splat. Contains position, rotation (quaternion), scale, and opacity. SHBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer. Stores spherical harmonic coefficients. TemporalBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer, 16 bytes/splat. Used for temporal marginalization (velocity/motion). KeyframeBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer, 64 bytes/splat/frame. Stores baked splat data for keyframe-based 4D rendering. Native4DBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer, 80 bytes/splat. Stores dual-quaternion rotations and spherindrical harmonic coefficients for native 4D primitives. Culling/Visibility Data: SplatClusterIndexBuffer: StructuredBuffer<uint>. Maps splat indices to clusters. ClusterVisibilityBitmap: StructuredBuffer<uint>. Bitmask of visible clusters. LODClusterSelectedBitmap: StructuredBuffer<uint>. Bitmask for LOD cluster visibility. SelectedClusterBuffer: StructuredBuffer<uint>. List of selected cluster indices. CompactedSplatIndices: StructuredBuffer<uint>. List of visible splat indices (used if compaction is enabled). Transform Matrices: LocalToWorld: FMatrix44f. WorldToPLY: FMatrix44f. Transforms world directions to PLY/SH space for SH evaluation. WorldToClip: FMatrix44f. WorldToView: FMatrix44f. Camera/Scene Parameters: CameraPosition: FVector3f. ScreenSize: FVector2f. FocalLength: FVector2f. PreViewTranslation: FVector3f. Used for velocity calculation; TranslatedWorld = World + PreViewTranslation. Control Flags & Counts: SplatCount: Total splats to process. UseKeyframes, UseTemporal, UseNative4D: Boolean flags (uint32) enabling specific 4D modes. KeyframeSplatCount (M), KeyframeFrameCount (N), KeyframeFrameTime. Native4DSplatCount. TimeDuration (l). SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs, SHBufferCoeffs. UseSHRendering, OpacityScale, SplatScale. MaxDrawDistance, FadeOutStartDistance. UseClusterCulling, UseLODRendering, UseCompaction, UseGlobalCompactionPath. VisibleSplatCount, OriginalSplatCount, MaxRenderBudget. GlobalBaseOffset, ProxyIndex. TimeWeightMinAlpha. Outputs: ViewDataBuffer: RWStructuredBuffer<FGaussianSplatViewData>. Contains screen-space position, covariance, color (evaluated SH), opacity, and depth/visibility flags for each active splat. The output structure FGaussianSplatViewData is not explicitly defined in the source notes. Based on standard Gaussian Splatting rasterization requirements, it contains at least: float3 or float4 screen-space position (x, y, z/w); float3x3 or float4x4 2D covariance matrix (or its Cholesky decomposition/affine parameters); float3 or float4 color (RGB/RGBA); float opacity; uint or float depth/z-value; uint cluster index or visibility flags. Parameters are passed as shader constants or buffers. THREADGROUPSIZE is defined as 256 during shader compilation. SHOrder determines the spherical harmonic order, with NumSHCoeffs derived as (L+1)^2 for order L (commonly 4, 9, or 16). SHBufferCoeffs indicates the number of coefficients actually stored per splat based on asset SHBands. MaxDrawDistance sets the distance-based visibility range, where 0 means unlimited. FadeOutStartDistance defines the distance at which splats begin to fade out. MaxRenderBudget caps the write index, where 0 means no cap. UseKeyframes, UseTemporal, and UseNative4D are uint32 flags enabling keyframe-based 4D rendering, 4D temporal marginalization, and Fudan native 4D (dual-quaternion rotation + spherindrical harmonics), respectively. KeyframeSplatCount (M), KeyframeFrameCount (N), and KeyframeFrameTime control keyframe interpolation. Native4DSplatCount specifies the number of splats covered by the Native4DBuffer. TimeDuration (l) is the time duration (TimeEnd - TimeStart) for native 4D SH evaluation. UseSHRendering, OpacityScale, and SplatScale control appearance rendering and scaling. UseClusterCulling, UseLODRendering, UseCompaction, and UseGlobalCompactionPath enable cluster culling, LOD rendering, compaction processing, and global base offset reading, respectively. VisibleSplatCount and OriginalSplatCount track visible splats and the boundary where LOD splats start. GlobalBaseOffset and ProxyIndex manage buffer offsets for the non-compaction and global compaction paths. PreViewTranslation is used for velocity calculation (TranslatedWorld = World + PreViewTranslation). CameraPosition, ScreenSize, and FocalLength define the camera state. TimeWeightMinAlpha sets the minimum alpha threshold for temporal weighting. 1. Dispatch Setup: The shader is dispatched with THREADGROUPSIZE = 256. The thread group count is derived from SplatCount or VisibleSplatCount. 2. Splat Index Resolution: If UseCompaction is true, the thread ID maps to CompactedSplatIndices to retrieve the original splat index. If UseGlobalCompactionPath is true, the base offset is read from GlobalBaseOffsetsBuffer[ProxyIndex]; otherwise, GlobalBaseOffset is used directly. 3. 4D State Evaluation: The active 4D mode is selected by priority: UseNative4D > UseKeyframes > UseTemporal. Native 4D reads dual-quaternion rotations and spherindrical SH from Native4DBuffer, interpolating based on CurrentTime and TimeDuration (l). Keyframe mode interpolates between KeyframeFrameTime and adjacent frames using KeyframeBuffer, applying slerp for rotation. Temporal marginalization reads velocity/motion from TemporalBuffer, extrapolates position using CurrentTime and PreViewTranslation, and adjusts covariance for temporal variance. Static mode reads directly from PackedSplatBuffer. 4. Visibility Culling: Distance culling checks CameraPosition against MaxDrawDistance (0 disables it) and applies a fade-out factor if distance exceeds FadeOutStartDistance. Cluster culling (UseClusterCulling) checks SplatClusterIndexBuffer against ClusterVisibilityBitmap and LODClusterSelectedBitmap (if UseLODRendering). LOD rendering filters splats with index \ge OriginalSplatCount. 5. Projection to Screen Space: The splat center is transformed to clip space via WorldToClip, then projected to screen coordinates using ScreenSize and FocalLength. The 2D covariance is computed by transforming the 3D covariance with the projection Jacobian. 6. Spherical Harmonics Evaluation: If UseSHRendering is true, the view direction is transformed to PLY/SH space via WorldToPLY, and SH coefficients from SHBuffer (or Native4DBuffer) are evaluated. OpacityScale and SplatScale are applied to the result. 7. Write View Data: Computed attributes are written to ViewDataBuffer at baseoffset + globalidx. Writes are skipped if MaxRenderBudget is set and the index \ge MaxRenderBudget. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Standard implementation iterates through coefficients and applies basis functions for i in range(numcoeffs): # Basis function evaluation depends on shorder and viewdirply # color[0] += shcoeffs[i 3] basis[i] # color[1] += shcoeffs[i 3 + 1] basis[i] # color[2] += shcoeffs[i 3 + 2] basis[i] pass return color def slerp(q1, q2, t): """Spherical linear interpolation of quaternions.""" # Standard slerp: normalize(q1 (1-t) + q2 t) or dot-product based return q1 def interpolatedualquaternion(dq1, dq2, t): """Interpolates dual quaternions for native 4D.""" # Standard dual quaternion interpolation: slerp for rotation, lerp for translation return dq1 def main(threadidx, UseCompaction, CompactedSplatIndices, SplatCount, UseGlobalCompactionPath, GlobalBaseOffsetsBuffer, ProxyIndex, GlobalBaseOffset, UseNative4D, Native4DBuffer, CurrentTime, TimeDuration, UseKeyframes, KeyframeFrameTime, KeyframeBuffer, UseTemporal, TemporalBuffer, PreViewTranslation, PackedSplatBuffer, SplatScale, OpacityScale, MaxDrawDistance, FadeOutStartDistance, CameraPosition, UseClusterCulling, SplatClusterIndexBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmap, UseLODRendering, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, OriginalSplatCount, WorldToClip, ScreenSize, FocalLength, WorldToPLY, UseSHRendering, SHBuffer, Native4DSplatCount, SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs, SHBufferCoeffs, MaxRenderBudget, GlobalBaseOffset): globalidx = threadidx splatidx = CompactedSplatIndices[globalidx] if UseCompaction else globalidx if splatidx >= SplatCount: return baseoffset = GlobalBaseOffsetsBuffer[ProxyIndex] if UseGlobalCompactionPath else GlobalBaseOffset pos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] rot = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] scale = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] opacity = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if UseNative4D: # Temporal marginalization logic not detailed in sources pos = [TemporalBuffer[splatidx].pos[i] + PreViewTranslation[i] CurrentTime for i in range(3)] rot = TemporalBuffer[splatidx].rot scale = TemporalBuffer[splatidx].scale opacity = TemporalBuffer[splatidx].opacity viewdir = [CameraPosition[i] - pos[i] for i in range(3)] viewdirply = [sum(WorldToPLY[i][j] viewdir[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] color = evaluatesh(viewdirply, SHBuffer[splatidx].shcoeffs, SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs) else: pos = PackedSplatBuffer[splatidx].pos rot = PackedSplatBuffer[splatidx].rot scale = PackedSplatBuffer[splatidx].scale opacity = PackedSplatBuffer[splatidx].opacity viewdir = [CameraPosition[i] - pos[i] for i in range(3)] viewdirply = [sum(WorldToPLY[i][j] viewdir[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] color = evaluatesh(viewdirply, SHBuffer[splatidx].shcoeffs, SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs) scale = [s SplatScale for s in scale] opacity = OpacityScale dist = sum((pos[i] - CameraPosition[i])2 for i in range(3))0.5 if MaxDrawDistance > 0.0 and dist > MaxDrawDistance: return if dist > FadeOutStartDistance: fade = (dist - FadeOutStartDistance) / (MaxDrawDistance - FadeOutStartDistance) if MaxDrawDistance > FadeOutStartDistance else 0.0 opacity = max(0.0, 1.0 - min(1.0, fade)) if UseClusterCulling: clusteridx = SplatClusterIndexBuffer[splatidx] if not (ClusterVisibilityBitmap[clusteridx // 32] & (1 << (clusteridx % 32))): return if UseLODRendering and splatidx >= OriginalSplatCount: if not (LODClusterSelectedBitmap[clusteridx // 32] & (1 << (clusteridx % 32))): return clipposw = sum(WorldToClip[3][j] (pos[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) screenpos = [(sum(WorldToClip[i][j] (pos[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) / clipposw) ScreenSize[i] for i in range(2)] depth = (sum(WorldToClip[2][j] (pos[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) / clipposw) writeidx = baseoffset + globalidx if MaxRenderBudget == 0 or writeidx < MaxRenderBudget: # ViewDataBuffer write operation pass Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise during 4D interpolation, especially for large time durations or extreme scales. Boundaries: Ensure SplatCount and VisibleSplatCount are correctly synchronized with the input buffers. Degenerate Input: If MaxDrawDistance is 0, distance culling is disabled. If SHOrder is 0, SH evaluation simplifies to a constant color. Buffer Overflows: MaxRenderBudget is critical to prevent writing beyond the allocated ViewDataBuffer size. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of splats, as each splat is processed independently in parallel. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the ViewDataBuffer, with input buffers being read-only. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of splats and 4D evaluation complexity, with native 4D being more expensive than keyframe or temporal modes. Strengths: Handles complex 4D variations efficiently on the GPU and supports advanced culling mechanisms. Limitations: Requires DirectX 12 / Shader Model 6, crashes on non-ASCII paths, and has limited support for proprietary 4D formats. When to Use: Real-time rendering of 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting scenes in Unreal Engine 5. When Not to Use: Offline rendering, non-UE5 environments, or unsupported proprietary 4D formats. The method is part of the OpenSplat4D plugin for Unreal Engine 5, developed by YuanBaoSMadLab. It supports various 4D Gaussian Splatting techniques, including Spacetime Gaussians (STG), Fudan 4DGS, and keyframe-based 4DGS. The plugin aims to provide real-time rendering capabilities for 4D Gaussian Splatting in game engines. head: Spirula Bridge, Spirula Renderer API, Spirula Vulkan bridge
body: The Spirula Renderer is a GPU-accelerated Gaussian Splatting renderer implemented as a native Vulkan bridge (librosplatspirula.so) called via Python's ctypes. It handles tile sorting, Gaussian rasterization, and rendering to Vulkan textures. It explicitly excludes CUDA, PyTorch, gsplat, or OpenGL renderer paths. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by performing the tile sorting and rasterization internally during the render call. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Contiguous numpy arrays for Gaussian properties (means, quaternions, log-scales, opacity logits, SH coefficients), camera parameters (view/projection matrices or intrinsics), and render options. Outputs: A caller-owned uint8t buffer (RGBA8, Depth, or Opacity) populated by the renderer. Data Structures: The renderer manages a device-resident scene. The C API exposes the following structures for device enumeration: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. typedef struct { char name[256]; uint64t vrambytes; int usable; } RosplatSpirulaDeviceInfo; The output mode is defined by: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. typedef enum { ROSPLATSPIRULAOUTPUTCOLOR = 0, ROSPLATSPIRULAOUTPUTDEPTH = 1, ROSPLATSPIRULAOUTPUTOPACITY = 2 } RosplatSpirulaOutputMode; Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the native library from candidate paths: environment variable ROSPLATSPIRULALIBRARY, build directories, or /opt/rosplat-native/lib/rosplat/. Count available Vulkan devices and select device 0, verifying it is usable. 2. Scene Reset: Call rosplatspirularesetscene(degree, reserve). degree: Spherical Harmonics (SH) degree (0-4). reserve: Number of Gaussians to pre-allocate. Constraint: The SH dimension must be divisible by 3. The number of coefficients (dim/3) must be a perfect square. The resulting degree (\sqrt{coefficients} - 1) must be between 0 and 4 inclusive. Streaming scenes cannot change SH degree after initialization. 3. Data Preparation: Convert Gaussian data into contiguous numpy arrays. means: float32 array of shape [count, 3] (xyz positions). quats: float32 array of shape [count, 4] (rotations, wxyz). logscales: float32 array of shape [count, 3]. Computed as \log(\text{scale} \times \text{scale\modifier}). The scalemodifier is a float multiplier applied to Gaussian scales before conversion to log space (default 1.0, must be positive). Values are clipped to a minimum of 10^{-12}. opacitylogits: float32 array of shape [count, 1]. Computed as \text{logit}(\text{opacity}). Opacity values are clipped to [10^{-6}, 1-10^{-6}] before computing logits to avoid singularities. dc: float32 array of shape [count, 3] (DC component of SH, first coefficient). higher: float32 array of shape [count, coefficients-1, 3] (higher-order SH coefficients), or None if only DC components are used. 4. Appending Gaussians: Call rosplatspirulaappend(count, meansptr, quatsptr, logscalesptr, opacitylogitsptr, dcptr, higherptr) to add Gaussians to the scene. Pointers must reference contiguous memory. The SH degree cannot change during streaming. 5. Camera Update: Call rosplatspirulasetcamera(width, height, viewmatrixptr, projmatrixptr) or equivalent intrinsics setter. The renderer marks cameradirty when the model matrix or resolution changes. Camera Convention: OpenCV (+Z forward, +Y down, row-major world-to-camera). OpenGL Conversion: If using OpenGL view matrices, convert to OpenCV convention using gl\to\cv = \text{diag}([1.0, -1.0, -1.0, 1.0]) and compute view{cv} = gl\to\cv \times view{gl} \times model\matrix. Intrinsics: If using focal length and field of view, calculate focal length as f = h / (2.0 \times \tan(fovy / 2.0)). The intrinsics array is [f, f, w/2.0, h/2.0]. 6. Render Options: Call rosplatspirulasetrenderoptions(mode, activeshdegree). mode: Output buffer mode (COLOR=0, DEPTH=1, OPACITY=2). activeshdegree: Active SH degree for rendering (-1 for scene maximum, or 0-4). 7. Rendering: Call rosplatspirularenderrgba8(outputbufferptr, buffersize). Renders top-to-bottom. Tile sorting and radix sorting are performed internally every render. outputbufferptr: Pointer to caller-owned uint8t buffer. buffersize: Size of the buffer in bytes. 8. Shutdown: Call rosplatspirulashutdown() to release resources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import ctypes import os import numpy as np class RosplatSpirulaDeviceInfo(ctypes.Structure): fields = [("name", ctypes.cchar 256), ("vrambytes", ctypes.cuint64), ("usable", ctypes.cint)] class SpirulaRenderer: def init(self, width, height, shdegree=1, reserve=0): libpath = os.environ.get('ROSPLATSPIRULALIBRARY', '/opt/rosplat-native/lib/rosplat/librosplatspirula.so') self.lib = ctypes.CDLL(libpath) # Count devices, select device 0, and verify it is usable self.lib.rosplatspirularesetscene(shdegree, reserve) self.width = width self.height = height def appendgaussians(self, means, quats, scales, opacity, shdc, shhigher=None): scalemodifier = 1.0 logscales = np.log(np.clip(scales scalemodifier, 1e-12, np.inf)) opacityclipped = np.clip(opacity, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6) opacitylogits = np.log(opacityclipped / (1 - opacityclipped)) means = np.ascontiguousarray(means, dtype=np.float32) quats = np.ascontiguousarray(quats, dtype=np.float32) logscales = np.ascontiguousarray(logscales, dtype=np.float32) opacitylogits = np.ascontiguousarray(opacitylogits, dtype=np.float32) shdc = np.ascontiguousarray(shdc, dtype=np.float32) higherptr = None if shhigher is not None: shhigher = np.ascontiguousarray(shhigher, dtype=np.float32) higherptr = shhigher.ctypes.data count = len(means) self.lib.rosplatspirulaappend( count, means.ctypes.data, quats.ctypes.data, logscales.ctypes.data, opacitylogits.ctypes.data, shdc.ctypes.data, higherptr) def setcamera(self, viewmatrix, projmatrix): viewcv = np.ascontiguousarray(viewmatrix, dtype=np.float32) projcv = np.ascontiguousarray(projmatrix, dtype=np.float32) self.lib.rosplatspirulasetcamera( self.width, self.height, viewcv.ctypes.data, projcv.ctypes.data) def setrenderoptions(self, mode, shdegree): self.lib.rosplatspirulasetrenderoptions(mode, shdegree) def render(self): buffersize = self.width self.height 4 outputbuffer = (ctypes.cuint8 buffersize)() self.lib.rosplatspirularenderrgba8( outputbuffer, buffersize) return np.ctypeslib.asarray(outputbuffer, shape=(self.height, self.width, 4)) def shutdown(self): self.lib.rosplatspirulashutdown() Hardware Requirements: Requires a Vulkan 1.2-capable GPU. Specifically requires Vulkan buffer device addresses and timeline semaphores. Performance: Tile sorting and radix sorting are performed internally every render call. The renderer is optimized for streaming Gaussian data via ROS2 messages, handling batched appends efficiently. Limitations: Explicitly excludes CUDA, PyTorch, gsplat, or OpenGL renderer paths. It relies on the wgpu-py Vulkan backend for UI rendering. Memory: Scene capacity is managed via reserve during reset. Subsequent appends may trigger internal reallocation if capacity is exceeded, though the exact growth strategy is not detailed in the sources. The Spirula Renderer is part of the ROSplat project, which integrates Gaussian Splatting with ROS2. It was developed to provide a portable Vulkan rendering backend for Gaussian Splatting, avoiding dependencies on CUDA or PyTorch. The project acknowledges influence from the original Gaussian Splatting implementation by graphdeco-inria and the GaussianSplattingViewer repository by limacv. It is designed to run on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS with ROS 2 Lyrical. Gaussian Splatting Meets ROS2, https://github.com/shadygm/ROSplat, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Depth Rendering with Constant Opacity
head: Depth-Only Rendering Mode
body: Depth Rendering with Constant Opacity is a specialized rendering pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting that produces clean depth maps by forcing all Gaussians to have uniform opacity and color. Unlike standard alpha-blending which weights depth by Gaussian opacity and transmittance, this method ensures that depth accumulation is driven purely by geometric distance and rasterization order, eliminating shading artifacts and opacity-induced depth bias. It is distinct from Depth Rendering with Variable Opacity, which respects the learned alpha values of the Gaussians. The method modifies the standard Gaussian rasterization pipeline to strip away appearance information (color and variable opacity) and gradient information related to scale and rotation, leaving only the geometric position and a constant alpha value to drive the depth accumulation. Inputs: pc: The Gaussian model object containing 3D parameters (getxyz, getscaling, getrotation, getcovariance). viewpointcamera: The camera object providing intrinsic parameters (FoVx, FoVy, projection matrices). value: The constant opacity multiplier applied to all Gaussians (default 0.95). pipe: Pipeline configuration object (e.g., computecov3Dpython, debug). Outputs: render: The rendered image (all ones, effectively a mask). depth: The accumulated depth buffer (NDC depth). alpha: The accumulated opacity buffer. viewspacepoints: The 3D points in view space. visibilityfilter: Boolean mask of visible Gaussians (radii > 0). radii: The radius of each Gaussian's bounding box in screen space. screenspacepoints: A tensor of shape (numgaussians, 2) initialized to zeros. It is allocated with requiresgrad=True and retaingrad() enabled to allow gradients to flow back to the 2D mean positions during optimization, even though they are not used in the forward pass of this specific mode. opacity: A tensor of shape (numgaussians, 1) filled with the constant value. colorsprecomp: A tensor of shape (numgaussians, 3) filled with ones (white). scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp: Set to None or detached tensors to prevent gradient leakage into depth estimation. value: Constant opacity multiplier. Default is 0.95. background: Background color tensor (typically [1,1,1] or [0,0,0]). 1. Initialize Screenspace Points: Create a tensor screenspacepoints with the same shape and device as pc.getxyz[:,:2], initialized to zero. Enable gradient retention: python screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz[:,:2], dtype=pc.getxyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device="cuda") + 0 try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except: pass 2. Compute FOV Tangents: Calculate the tangent of half the field of view from the camera: \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\frac{\text{FoVx}}{2}) \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\frac{\text{FoVy}}{2}) 3. Configure Rasterization Settings: Create GaussianRasterizationSettings with: Image dimensions (width, height). tanfovx, tanfovy. background color. scalemodifier: 1.0 (or as configured). viewmatrix and projmatrix: From the camera. shdegree: From the pipeline. cameraposition: From the camera. prefiltered: False. debug: From the pipeline. 4. Prepare Gaussian Attributes: Set means3D to pc.getxyz. Set means2D to screenspacepoints. Set opacity to torch.ones(numgaussians, 1, device=device) value. Set colorsprecomp to torch.oneslike(pc.getxyz) (shape (numgaussians, 3)). Set shs to None. 5. Handle Scales and Rotations: Inside a torch.nograd() block: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true: Compute cov3Dprecomp using pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier). Set scales and rotations to None. Else: Set scales to pc.getscaling.detach(). Set rotations to pc.getrotation.detach(). Set cov3Dprecomp to None. 6. Rasterize: Call the Gaussian rasterizer with: means3D means2D shs=None colorsprecomp opacity scales rotations cov3Dprecomp rasterizationsettings The rasterizer returns renderedimage, radii, rendereddepth, and renderedalpha. Note that renderedimage will be uniform due to colorsprecomp being ones. 7. Return Results: Return a dictionary containing: render: renderedimage depth: rendereddepth alpha: renderedalpha viewspacepoints: The viewspace points used. visibilityfilter: radii > 0 radii: The radii tensor. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def renderdepthconstantopacity(pc, viewpointcamera, value=0.95, pipe=None, background=None): """ Render depth map with constant opacity. Args: pc: GaussianModel object with methods getxyz, getscaling, getrotation, getcovariance. viewpointcamera: Camera object with FoVx, FoVy, projection matrices. value: Constant opacity multiplier (default 0.95). pipe: PipelineParams object. background: Tensor of background color. Returns: dict: Render results including depth, alpha, etc. """ if background is None: # Default to white if not specified, assuming standard 3DGS background handling background = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda") if pipe is None: pipe = type('obj', (object,), {'computecov3Dpython': False, 'debug': False})() numgaussians = pc.getxyz.shape[0] device = pc.getxyz.device # Step 1: Initialize screenspacepoints with gradient retention screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz[:,:2], dtype=pc.getxyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device=device) + 0 try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except: pass # Step 2: Compute FOV tangents tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # Step 3: Configure Rasterization Settings # Note: In actual implementation, this creates a specific settings object for the C++/CUDA rasterizer rasterizationsettings = { "imagewidth": viewpointcamera.imagewidth, "imageheight": viewpointcamera.imageheight, "tanfovx": tanfovx, "tanfovy": tanfovy, "bg": background, "scalemodifier": 1.0, # Assuming default scale modifier "viewmatrix": viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform, "projmatrix": viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform, "shdegree": pc.activeshdegree, "cameraposition": viewpointcamera.cameracenter, "prefiltered": False, "debug": pipe.debug } # Step 4: Prepare Attributes means3D = pc.getxyz means2D = screenspacepoints opacity = torch.ones((numgaussians, 1), dtype=torch.float32, device=device) value colorsprecomp = torch.oneslike(pc.getxyz) # Shape (N, 3) shs = None # Step 5: Handle Scales and Rotations with torch.nograd(): if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(1.0) # Assuming scalingmodifier 1.0 scales = None rotations = None else: cov3Dprecomp = None scales = pc.getscaling.detach() rotations = pc.getrotation.detach() # Step 6: Rasterize # The rasterizer function signature depends on the specific implementation (e.g., DiffGaussian, DNGaussian) # Assuming a standard call structure found in the sources renderedimage, radii, rendereddepth, renderedalpha = gaussianrasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp, opacities=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp, rasterizationsettings) # Step 7: Return Results visibilityfilter = radii > 0 return { "render": renderedimage, "depth": rendereddepth, "alpha": renderedalpha, "viewspacepoints": screenspacepoints, # Or full viewspace points if available "visibilityfilter": visibilityfilter, "radii": radii } The gaussianrasterizer call is a placeholder for the specific C++/CUDA kernel invocation used in the 3DGS implementation (e.g., GaussianRasterization). The exact argument names and order may vary slightly between forks (e.g., DiffGaussian vs DNGaussian), but the logical grouping of parameters remains consistent. The viewspacepoints returned in the dictionary in the source notes refers to screenspacepoints initialized in Step 1, which is a common pattern in these implementations to store the 2D means for gradient tracking. Gradient Leakage: Failing to detach scales and rotations or set them to None can cause gradients to flow into the depth estimation process, corrupting the optimization of the Gaussian positions. Precision: The depth values are in NDC (Normalized Device Coordinates). Ensure the downstream consumer understands the coordinate system (e.g., converting to metric depth if required). Uniform Opacity: Setting opacity to a constant value (e.g., 0.95) means that the final accumulated opacity at a pixel will depend on the number of overlapping Gaussians and their order. This can lead to "over-saturated" alpha values if many Gaussians overlap, but the depth is still correctly weighted by the transmittance Ti. No Color Information: Since colorsprecomp is set to ones, the render output is not a valid color image. It is only useful for extracting the depth and alpha buffers. Computes a depth map by dividing the accumulated depth buffer by the accumulated opacity buffer to correct for transparency artifacts. Produces a per-pixel depth buffer while respecting the variable opacity of the Gaussians, unlike this method which forces uniform opacity. Time Complexity: Same as standard Gaussian Splatting rasterization, O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, as the computational cost is dominated by the rasterization and alpha-blending steps, which are unchanged in structure (only the input values differ). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian attributes. The screenspacepoints tensor adds O(N) memory for gradient storage. Strengths: Produces clean, unbiased depth maps that reflect the geometric distribution of Gaussians rather than their learned opacity. Useful for tasks like depth supervision, pruning, and normal estimation where consistent depth weighting is required. Limitations: Does not account for the actual transparency of the scene. If Gaussians have varying densities, the depth map may still exhibit artifacts from "floaters" or misplaced Gaussians, as the depth is influenced by all Gaussians along the ray. When to Use: When training a Gaussian Splatting model with depth supervision, or when extracting depth maps for downstream geometric tasks where opacity bias is undesirable. When Not to Use: When visualizing the scene appearance or when the actual transparency of the object is important for the depth interpretation. The method originates from the need to extract reliable depth information from 3D Gaussian Splatting models for training and optimization purposes. Standard alpha-blending depth rendering can be biased by the learned opacity values, which may not accurately reflect the geometric surface. By forcing constant opacity, the depth accumulation becomes a function of geometric distance and rasterization order, providing a more stable signal for gradient-based optimization. The specific implementation details, such as gradient retention for screenspacepoints and detaching scales/rotations, are documented in the DNGaussian repository. name: Normalized Depth Rendering
head: Depth Normalized by Opacity, Normalized Depth Map
body:
Normalized Depth Rendering computes a depth map by dividing the accumulated depth buffer by the accumulated opacity buffer to correct for transparency artifacts in Gaussian splatting renders. Inputs: renderdepth: Accumulated depth buffer from the rasterizer. renderacc: Accumulated alpha/opacity buffer from the rasterizer. znear: Near plane distance of the camera frustum. zfar: Far plane distance of the camera frustum. Outputs: rendereddepthnorm: Normalized depth map. rendereddispnorm: Displayable disparity map. Data Structures: renderdepth: 2D array of floats, shape (H, W). renderacc: 2D array of floats, shape (H, W). Steps: 1. Normalize Depth: Divide the accumulated depth buffer by the accumulated opacity buffer at each pixel (x, y) to produce the normalized depth map. 	ext{rendered\depth
orm}{x,y} =  rac{	ext{render\depth}{x,y}}{	ext{render\acc}{x,y}} 2. Convert to Disparity: Map the normalized depth to a displayable disparity range using the camera frustum bounds. 	ext{rendered\disp
orm}{x,y} = 1 -  rac{	ext{rendered\depth
orm}{x,y} - z{	ext{near}}}{z{	ext{far}} - z{	ext{near}}} Parameters: znear, zfar: Camera frustum bounds. Typical values depend on the scene scale and are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs when renderacc is exactly 0 (no Gaussians cover the pixel), yielding undefined results. Clamp the denominator to a small positive epsilon or mask these pixels to a default value like zfar or NaN. Precision loss may occur in low-opacity regions where the denominator approaches the epsilon floor, amplifying noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizeddepthrendering(renderdepth, renderacc, znear, zfar): epsilon = 1e-6 H, W = len(renderdepth), len(renderdepth[0]) # Step 1: Normalize depth, handling zero-opacity pixels safeacc = [[max(renderacc[i][j], epsilon) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] normalizeddepth = [[renderdepth[i][j] / safeacc[i][j] for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] # Step 2: Convert to disparity disparity = [[1.0 - (normalizeddepth[i][j] - znear) / (zfar - znear) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] return normalizeddepth, disparity A CUDA-based post-processing step that maps raw 3DGS depth outputs to the 0, 1.0) range to ensure compatibility with underwater visualization pipelines. It applies a logistic transformation to all raw depth values during the [rasterization pipeline. The normalized depth is computed as z{	ext{norm}} =  rac{2}{1 + e^{-0.1 \cdot z{	ext{raw}}}} - 1, where z{	ext{raw}} is the initial depth output from 3DGS manipulation. Time complexity is not given in the sources. Memory complexity is not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces geometrically accurate depth maps in transparent or semi-transparent regions where standard depth accumulation fails. Limitations: Sensitive to noise in low-opacity regions due to division by small values; requires robust handling of zero-opacity pixels. When to use: When accurate depth estimation is needed for scenes with varying opacity. When not to use: When simple geometric depth is sufficient and opacity is uniform, or when performance constraints prohibit the extra division step. Normalized Depth Rendering is a post-processing technique used in Gaussian Splatting pipelines to improve depth map quality. It leverages the existing alpha compositing infrastructure of Gaussian Splatting to derive a transparency-corrected depth value. brownvc/gftorf, https://github.com/brownvc/gftorf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-56917-4, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Depth Rendering with Variable Opacity
head: Gaussian Splatting Depth Output, Nearest Depth Rendering, Per-pixel Depth Buffer
body: This method extends Gaussian Splatting rasterization to produce a per-pixel depth buffer (NDC depth, +\infty where no surface is visible) while respecting the variable opacity of the Gaussians. Unlike Depth Rendering with Constant Opacity, which forces uniform opacity to drive depth accumulation by geometric distance, this method computes depth based on the actual alpha-weighted contribution of the splats. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity \alpha, color), camera projection matrices, and a configuration flag GsplatConfig::outputDepth set to true. Outputs: A color image (unchanged from standard rendering) and a per-pixel depth buffer storing NDC depth values. Data Structures: Depth Buffer: A texture or buffer of size W \times H (image resolution) storing floating-point NDC depth values. Raster Backend Auxiliary: An order-preserving unsigned integer encoding of depth, used for atomic operations in the fragment shader and decoded by a subsequent compute pass. Steps: 1. Configuration: Enable GsplatConfig::outputDepth to activate depth buffer writing. Ensure the device feature fragmentStoresAndAtomics is enabled if using the raster backend, as it requires atomic operations. 2. Projection Correction: Apply cropProjection() if rendering an off-centre view or crop. This centers the Gaussian projection guard band on the view rather than the optical axis to prevent distortion of Gaussians elongated along the view direction. 3. Sorting: Sort Gaussians by depth relative to the camera. 4. Rasterization and Compositing: Compute Backend: Blend Gaussians front-to-back. For each pixel, track the accumulated transmittance Tn. Record the depth zn of the Gaussian at which the transmittance first falls to 0.5 (median depth). Raster Backend: Blend Gaussians back-to-front. For each pixel, use atomicMin on an order-preserving uint encoding of depth to keep the nearest depth of a single splat that alone covers the pixel with an opacity of at least 0.5. After the render pass, a compute pass decodes this uint encoding into the final depth buffer. 5. Expected Depth Calculation: If expected depth is required instead of median/nearest, compute the alpha-weighted average depth using the formula below. Formulas: The accumulated transparency Tn for the n-th Gaussian at pixel (x, y) is: Tn = \prod{j=1}^{Q-1} (1 - \alphaj) where Q is the number of Gaussians covering the pixel, and \alphaj is the opacity of the j-th Gaussian in depth-sorted order. The Expected Depth d{x,y}^{exp} is: d{x,y}^{exp} = \frac{\sum{n=1}^N zn \cdot \alphan \cdot Tn}{\sum{n=1}^N \alphan \cdot Tn} where zn is the Z-depth of the n-th Gaussian. The Accumulated Depth d{x,y}^{acc} (numerator for expected depth) is: d{x,y}^{acc} = \sum{n=1}^N zn \cdot \alphan \cdot Tn Parameters: GsplatConfig::outputDepth: Boolean flag to enable depth output. Opacity threshold: 0.5 is used for median depth crossing (Compute) and nearest splat coverage (Raster). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Off-centre Projection Distortion: If the guard band is not centered on the view (e.g., in cropped renders), Gaussians away from the optical axis are incorrectly clamped, distorting their footprints. Use cropProjection() to fix this. Backend Disagreement: The Compute backend (median depth) and Raster backend (nearest splat with \alpha \ge 0.5) use different definitions. They agree on opaque surfaces with a median difference of 0.4% on the lantern scene, but may differ in semi-transparent regions. Hardware Support: The Raster backend requires fragmentStoresAndAtomics support on the GPU. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearencodedepth(z, minz, maxz): return int(((z - minz) / (maxz - minz)) 0xFFFFFFFF) def lineardecodedepth(encodedz, minz, maxz): return (encodedz / 0xFFFFFFFF) (maxz - minz) + minz def computedepthbuffer(gaussians, camera, width, height, minz, maxz): depthbuffer = [float('inf')] (width height) sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.depthat(camera)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): pixelidx = y width + x transmittance = 1.0 mediandepth = float('inf') for gaussian in sortedgaussians: # Standard rasterization coverage check if not gaussian.intersectspixel(x, y): continue alpha = gaussian.opacityat(x, y) z = gaussian.depthat(x, y) # Update transmittance before checking crossing transmittance = (1 - alpha) # Check for median depth crossing (transmittance <= 0.5) if transmittance <= 0.5 and mediandepth == float('inf'): mediandepth = z depthbuffer[pixelidx] = mediandepth return depthbuffer def rasterdepthbuffer(gaussians, camera, width, height, minz, maxz): # Requires atomicMin support depthuintbuffer = [0xFFFFFFFF] (width height) sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.depthat(camera), reverse=True) for gaussian in sortedgaussians: # Iterate over pixels covered by this Gaussian for x, y in gaussian.coveredpixels(): pixelidx = y width + x alpha = gaussian.opacityat(x, y) z = gaussian.depthat(x, y) # Encode depth into order-preserving uint encodedz = linearencodedepth(z, minz, maxz) # Atomic minimum to keep nearest depth # Only update if this splat covers the pixel with alpha >= 0.5 if alpha >= 0.5: if encodedz < depthuintbuffer[pixelidx]: depthuintbuffer[pixelidx] = encodedz # Decode uint buffer in a separate compute pass depthbuffer = [lineardecodedepth(z, minz, maxz) for z in depthuintbuffer] return depthbuffer Time Complexity: Same as standard Gaussian Splatting rasterization, O(N) for sorting and O(P \cdot G) for rasterization where P is pixels and G is Gaussians per pixel. The additional depth calculation is negligible per pixel. Memory Complexity: Adds one W \times H depth buffer. The Raster backend uses an order-preserving unsigned integer encoding for atomic operations, decoded by a compute pass after rendering. Performance: The Compute backend may be slower on some hardware due to lack of parallel atomic optimizations compared to the Raster backend, but offers more consistent depth definitions (median). The Raster backend requires fragmentStoresAndAtomics support. Strengths: Enables compositing of other geometry into the splat scene. Handles variable opacity naturally. Limitations: Two different depth definitions (median vs. nearest) lead to slight discrepancies between backends in semi-transparent regions. Off-centre projections require special handling to avoid distortion. This feature was introduced in the klartraum project by fortmeier and others in October 2026 to enable depth output for both Gaussian splatting backends (Compute and Raster). It addresses the need to composite other geometry into a splat scene, which was previously not possible as the splats would always render over other geometry. The implementation also fixed a bug related to off-centre projection guard bands. name: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort
head: Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization with Global Radix Sort
body: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort is a GPU-parallel rasterization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that divides the image into tiles to manage memory and processing load, assigning Gaussians to tiles based on their projected 2D splats [Parent]. It solves the performance bottleneck of per-pixel sorting by using a single global radix sort to achieve per-tile depth ordering, enabling real-time performance for millions of splats Sibling: [Tile-based Rasteriser]. Unlike sibling methods that may perform redundant depth sorting or evaluate splats against irrelevant pixels, this method ensures that each tile is processed by one GPU thread block walking a single sorted list [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. The method operates on a list of N projected 2D Gaussian splats, each defined by center (xi, yi), 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i, color ci, opacity \alphai, and depth Zc [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. The image is divided into a grid of tiles with dimensions Tw \times Th (typically 16 \times 16 pixels) [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. The core mechanism involves three phases: 1. Tile Assignment: Each Gaussian is assigned to every tile its projected 2D splat touches. If a splat straddles tile boundaries, it is duplicated into each relevant tile [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. This creates one work item per (Gaussian, tile) pair [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. 2. Key Packing: For each (splat, tile) pair, a 64-bit integer sort key is constructed. The tile ID is packed into the high bits, and the splat's depth Zc is packed into the low bits [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. Specifically, the key is formed as: \text{key} = (\text{tile\id} \ll 32) \mid (\text{uint32\t})Zc where tileid is the 1D tile index (y \times \text{grid\width} + x) and Zc is cast to a 32-bit unsigned integer [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. 3. Global Radix Sort: A single GPU radix sort is performed over all (splat, tile) pairs [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. This simultaneously bins splats by tile ID (ensuring contiguity) and sorts them by depth within each tile [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. After sorting, each tile is processed by one GPU thread block that walks the sorted list [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. For each pixel in a tile, front-to-back compositing is performed using the tile's sorted list of splats, evaluating per-pixel alpha \alphai(\mathbf{x}) and breaking early when transmittance T < \epsilon [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. The same sorted lists are reused for backpropagation, allowing gradients to flow to position, shape, opacity, and color without additional sorting [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. Computes a precise mapping between 3D Gaussians and image tiles to eliminate irrelevant tiles during rasterization. It solves the problem of overestimating the number of tiles a Gaussian intersects, which occurs when using standard axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) that are overly conservative. Unlike the parent method, which assigns a Gaussian to every tile its projected splat touches (potentially including tiles with negligible opacity), Tile-Based Culling iteratively examines candidate tiles to verify actual overlap, thereby reducing the workload for the subsequent radix sort and rendering phases. Tile-Based Culling iterates over all candidate tiles while AccuTile does not, resulting in a markedly higher runtime cost for Tile-Based Culling despite warp-level load balancing. A GPU-optimized rendering component that sorts projected 2D Gaussian splats once per frame to serve both forward rendering and backpropagation. It solves the performance bottleneck of per-pixel sorting by dividing the image into tiles and using a single global radix sort to achieve per-tile depth ordering. Unlike sibling methods that may perform redundant depth sorting or evaluate splats against irrelevant pixels, this method ensures that each tile is processed by one GPU thread block walking a single sorted list, enabling real-time performance for millions of splats. Generates the key-value pairs required for tile-based depth sorting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It identifies which tiles each projected 2D Gaussian overlaps and constructs a 64-bit sort key combining the tile ID and the Gaussian's depth. This output serves as the direct input for the global radix sort performed by the parent method. It differs from sibling methods like Tile-Based Culling by explicitly generating the full set of overlaps for sorting rather than just filtering, and from Tile-based Depth Sorting by focusing on the key construction phase rather than the sorting algorithm itself. A multi-GPU rendering and training method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that accelerates the forward pass by partitioning the screen into finer tiles and scheduling them across a multi-GPU pipeline. It differs from single-GPU rasterizers by distributing the tile workload to enable scalability for large scenes, and from primitive-sharding approaches by focusing on screen-space partitioning rather than model-space partitioning. A rasterization strategy designed to mitigate "popping" artifacts in surface-based volumetric representations (such as 2DGS and QGS) where Gaussian distributions are concentrated on surfaces. It addresses the sensitivity of alpha-blending order by replacing inconsistent per-ray depth sorting with a two-stage approach: coarse global ordering via per-tile depth approximation and fine local ordering via per-pixel resorting. This method sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by enforcing strict consistency between forward rendering and backward gradient computation traversal orders, thereby eliminating streak-like and blocky artifacts introduced by single-ray approximations. Step: Filter out Gaussians whose opacity \tau falls below the alpha-threshold \epsilon immediately during tile intersection, as their axis-aligned bounding box is considered empty. Parameter: Alpha-threshold: \epsilon. Gaussians with opacity \tau < \epsilon are filtered. Number: Combining all modifications decreased rendering time on the Bicycle scene at native resolution by a factor of 3.77 and GPU memory usage by a factor of 2.11 compared to the reference. Definition: Identifies the start and end indices in the sorted list of Gaussian instances for each tile. Runs once per instanced Gaussian ID after sorting. Step: Read the tile ID from the current key: currtile = key >> 32. If idx == 0, set ranges[currtile].x = 0. If idx > 0, read prevtile = pointlistkeys[idx - 1] >> 32. If currtile != prevtile, set ranges[prevtile].y = idx and ranges[currtile].x = idx. If idx == L - 1, set ranges[currtile].y = L. The method builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization. name: Opacity-Thresholded Tile Intersection Filtering
head: Alpha-threshold Gaussian Filtering, Synergistic Filtering with Tile Intersections
body: This method filters out 3D Gaussians during the tile intersection phase of tiled rasterization if their opacity \tau falls below a specified alpha-threshold \epsilon, treating their axis-aligned bounding box as effectively empty. It reduces the number of Gaussians requiring sorting and shading, addressing performance bottlenecks caused by large, mostly transparent Gaussians that intersect many tiles but contribute negligible color. It builds on Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of projected 2D Gaussians, each with screen-space opacity \tau and its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Output: A filtered list of (Gaussian, tile) pairs, excluding those with \tau < \epsilon. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores its screen-space opacity \taui. Tile Grid: The image is divided into a grid of tiles (typically 16 \times 16 pixels per parent article). Each tile maintains a list of candidate Gaussians. Parameters: Alpha-threshold (\epsilon): The minimum opacity required for a Gaussian to be considered visible. Gaussians with \tau < \epsilon are discarded. Typical values are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute the screen-space AABB for each Gaussian. 2. For each tile, identify Gaussians whose AABB intersects the tile's bounds. 3. During the intersection check, evaluate the Gaussian's opacity \tau. 4. If \tau < \epsilon, discard the Gaussian for this tile; its AABB is considered empty. 5. If \tau \ge \epsilon, add the Gaussian to the tile's candidate list for subsequent sorting and shading. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def opacitythresholdedtileintersection(gaussians, tiles, epsilon): """ Filter Gaussians based on opacity during tile intersection. Args: gaussians: List of dicts/objects with keys: 'opacity': float, screen-space opacity tau. 'bbox': tuple (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in screen space. tiles: List of dicts/objects with keys: 'bbox': tuple (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in screen space. 'candidates': list to store filtered Gaussians. epsilon (float): Alpha-threshold for filtering. Returns: Updated tiles with filtered candidate lists. """ for tile in tiles: tile['candidates'] = [] for g in gaussians: # AABB intersection check if (g['bbox'][0] <= tile['bbox'][2] and g['bbox'][2] >= tile['bbox'][0] and g['bbox'][1] <= tile['bbox'][3] and g['bbox'][3] >= tile['bbox'][1]): # Opacity threshold filter if g['opacity'] >= epsilon: tile['candidates'].append(g) # Else: Gaussian is filtered out (opacity too low) return tiles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Backend-specific threshold application semantics vary; preserving non-empty support is not a method-wide invariant. An all-one policy (thresholds set to maximum) does not guarantee reproduction of every backend's native pair list solely from multiplier values due to differing cap and subtraction rules. Describes how exported absolute thresholds mg \tau0 are applied to Gaussian opacities \alphag during tile enumeration, determining whether a primitive participates in rendering. The default Speedy-Splat path compares the threshold directly to \alphag; if threshold \ge \alphag, it yields zero tile pairs. The 2DGS and Scaffold-GS ports reject primitives whose opacity cannot exceed the selected threshold. The FastGS port applies \min(mg \tau0, 0.95\alphag) as the effective threshold cap; if the cap binds (i.e., 0.95\alphag < mg \tau0), it subtracts 10^{-6} from the capped value before constructing the backend-specific extent. Preserving non-empty support is not a method-wide invariant, and an all-one policy should not be assumed to reproduce every backend's native pair list merely from its multiplier values. Time and Memory Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussians processed in subsequent sorting and shading steps, lowering both compute time and GPU memory usage. Measured Performance: Combining this modification with others decreased rendering time on the Bicycle scene at native resolution by a factor of 3.77 and GPU memory usage by a factor of 2.11 compared to the reference implementation. Scaling: Performance gains are greatest at higher resolutions, as there are more duplicated Gaussians and hence \alpha-computations. Render times are more consistent, particularly on the Bicycle scene at native resolution, because large transparent Gaussians no longer affect a significant number of tiles. Strengths and Limitations: Highly effective for scenes with many transparent or low-opacity Gaussians. At low resolutions, increasing tile size (e.g., 16 \times 32) increases the average render time to 9.77 ms, illustrating why tile size is only increased at higher resolutions. When to Use: Use when rendering scenes with many transparent Gaussians, particularly at high resolutions. Avoid increasing tile dimensions at low resolutions due to overhead. This method is an optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering that leverages the observation that many Gaussians have low opacity and contribute little to the final image, allowing them to be safely discarded early in the rendering pipeline. name: Tile-Based Culling
head: StopThePop Tile-Based Culling
body: Tile-Based Culling computes a precise mapping between 3D Gaussians and image tiles to eliminate irrelevant tiles during rasterization. It solves the problem of overestimating the number of tiles a Gaussian intersects, which occurs when using standard axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) that are overly conservative. Unlike the parent method, which assigns a Gaussian to every tile its projected splat touches (potentially including tiles with negligible opacity), Tile-Based Culling iteratively examines candidate tiles to verify actual overlap, thereby reducing the workload for the subsequent radix sort and rendering phases. Tile-Based Culling iterates over all candidate tiles while AccuTile does not, resulting in a markedly higher runtime cost for Tile-Based Culling despite warp-level load balancing. The method computes a tight, opacity-aware bounding box per Gaussian and then iteratively checks each tile within that box to determine if it should be included in the final Gaussian-to-Tile mapping. The implementation described in the primary source selects the approach by Radl et al. for its simpler control flow and load balancing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of N projected 2D Gaussians, each defined by center (xi, yi), 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i, and opacity \alphai. Output: A list of (Gaussian, Tile) pairs, where each pair represents a verified overlap between a Gaussian and a tile. Data Structures: Bounding Box: An axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in screen space that tightly encloses the Gaussian's elliptical extent above a certain opacity threshold. Tile List: A dynamic list or buffer storing the indices of tiles that overlap with the Gaussian. Parameters: Padded Alpha Threshold: A threshold value used to accurately compute the bounding box and prevent undercounting Gaussian-to-Tile mappings. The specific value is not provided in the ablation study. Steps: 1. Compute Tight Bounding Box: Calculate a tight, opacity-aware bounding box for each Gaussian. This box is tighter than the standard AABB used in basic splatting but may not be perfectly tight if thresholds are not handled correctly. 2. Iterative Tile Examination: For each Gaussian, iterate over all tiles that touch its computed bounding box. 3. Overlap Verification: For each candidate tile, determine if the Gaussian actually overlaps with it. This is done by computing the point where the value of the Gaussian is maximal for each tile inside the bounding rectangle and checking if this value exceeds the opacity threshold. 4. Warp-Level Load Balancing: Use warp-level load balancing to accelerate the tile examination process, ensuring that threads within a warp process tiles efficiently even if the number of candidate tiles varies. 5. Generate Mapping: Add the (Gaussian, Tile) pair to the output list if an overlap is verified. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilebasedculling(gaussians, tilegridwidth, tilegridheight, alphathreshold, tilesize=16): """ Computes precise Gaussian-to-Tile mappings using iterative examination. """ mappings = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Step 1: Compute tight, opacity-aware bounding box # The exact bounding box derivation is not provided in the sources. # It is computed from the Gaussian's elliptical extent and alpha threshold. bboxminx, bboxminy, bboxmaxx, bboxmaxy = computetightbbox(g, alphathreshold) # Determine the range of tiles to examine tileminx = max(0, int(bboxminx // tilesize)) tileminy = max(0, int(bboxminy // tilesize)) tilemaxx = min(tilegridwidth - 1, int(bboxmaxx // tilesize)) tilemaxy = min(tilegridheight - 1, int(bboxmaxy // tilesize)) # Step 2 & 3: Iteratively examine each tile and verify overlap for ty in range(tileminy, tilemaxy + 1): for tx in range(tileminx, tilemaxx + 1): tileid = ty tilegridwidth + tx # Compute the point of maximal Gaussian value within this tile # The specific algorithm for finding the peak location inside a tile # is detailed in Radl et al.. peakx = tx tilesize + tilesize / 2.0 peaky = ty tilesize + tilesize / 2.0 dx = peakx - g.center.x dy = peaky - g.center.y # Standard 2D Gaussian density evaluation maxvalue = g.opacity math.exp(-0.5 (dx2 / g.covariance[0][0] + dy2 / g.covariance[1][1])) # Check if the Gaussian overlaps with the tile if maxvalue > alphathreshold: mappings.append((i, tileid)) return mappings def computetightbbox(gaussian, alphathreshold): # Standard implementation solves for the ellipse intersection at the threshold level. # Returns (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in screen coordinates. return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Usage: The use of thresholds in the original code can cause not all bounding boxes to be tight. Undercounting: Without a padded alpha threshold, the method undercounts Gaussian-to-Tile mappings. This artificially improves downstream performance (Radix Sort, Identify Tile Ranges, Render) due to fewer elements to process, but leads to incorrect rendering. Comparison with AccuTile: Tile-Based Culling iterates over all candidate tiles while AccuTile does not, resulting in a markedly higher runtime cost for Tile-Based Culling despite warp-level load balancing. SnugBox is a precise algorithm for computing the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of a 3D Gaussian in screen space, replacing the overly conservative tile assignment used in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS). It solves the problem of overestimating the number of tiles a Gaussian intersects, thereby reducing the number of pixels processed per Gaussian and accelerating rendering. Unlike the standard 3D-GS method which inscribes a circle within a square tile assignment, SnugBox derives a tight bounding box directly from the Gaussian's elliptical extent using its conic equation, providing numerical stability even under edge-on tilts. It serves as a plug-and-play optimization that yields an average inference speed-up of 1.82× without altering the rendered image. An optimization for the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) alpha blending stage that uses warp-level collaboration to subdivide image tiles and cull splats with no geometric overlap, avoiding expensive alpha evaluation. It improves rendering speed without changing the rendered output, implemented in the existing CUDA differentiable pipeline. Unlike SnugBox, which focuses on tighter bounding boxes, this method focuses on geometric culling within the blending kernel to reduce the number of blending operations. A method introducing a depth-speculation mechanism that predicts per-tile depth ranges, enabling early culling of occluded Gaussians before sorting. Allows runtime editing of visible Gaussians using cutout components that target all, parent, or specific renderers. It evaluates cutout refresh rate and trigger bounds/visibility updates based on SortMode. The parameter CutoutsUpdateBounds controls whether cutouts recalculate the renderer's world bounds, which is costly for moving cutouts. A method to compute exact intersections between screen-space Gaussian ellipses and tiles, eliminating false-positive and false-negative intersections found in prior methods (distance-based, bounding-box, or compact box approaches). It computes the number of intersecting tiles per Gaussian in the projection-forward pass and uses a separate pass to fill the buffer with tile-depth pairs. For a Gaussian represented as an ellipse containing opacity above threshold and an interval for one axis, it computes the closed-form interval on the other axis that intersects the ellipse. It picks the shorter dimension of the screen-space Gaussian ellipse (e.g., vertical) and, for each row (or column) of tiles, finds the ellipse's range of coordinates within the row, bounded by either the tile boundary or global extreme points of the ellipse. The closed-form solution is implemented as a highly optimized branchless function, rounding down the minimum coordinate and rounding up the maximum coordinate toward the tile boundary to efficiently count or iterate through tiles overlapped by the ellipse. An adaptation of STP's culling logic to work with Optimal Projection planes, where tiles form general quadrilaterals rather than rectangles. It projects the tiles touched by each Gaussian onto its optimal plane, yielding non-rectangular quadrilaterals. For a splat on its optimal plane with mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^2, it identifies tile edges visible at \mu, denoting a tile edge as p + td. The point of highest density on a tile edge is found by taking the derivative of Gaussian density with respect to t and setting it to zero: p + \left(\frac{d^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mu - p)}{d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d}\right)d, where \Sigma is the 2D covariance matrix. At most two tile edges are visible at any given mean \mu. Time Complexity: The method involves iterating over all candidate tiles within the bounding box for each Gaussian. This results in higher runtime cost for the preprocessing and key generation phases compared to methods that do not iterate over all candidates (like AccuTile). However, it reduces the number of elements in the downstream Radix Sort and Render phases if the culling is effective. Memory Complexity: The output is a list of (Gaussian, Tile) pairs. The size of this list depends on the number of verified overlaps, which is generally smaller than the number of overlaps in standard splatting but larger than in methods that do not iterate over all candidates. Performance: In ablation studies, Tile-Based Culling showed significant speedup in Preprocess and Duplicate with Keys compared to baseline 3D-GS, but was slower than AccuTile in these phases due to the iterative examination. It slightly outperformed AccuTile in downstream functions (Radix Sort, Identify Tile Ranges, Render) in the ablation, but this was attributed to undercounting of mappings due to the lack of a padded alpha threshold. Strengths: Provides a more precise mapping than standard AABB-based assignment, reducing unnecessary computations in downstream phases. Warp-level load balancing helps with performance. Limitations: Iterating over all candidate tiles can be computationally expensive. The accuracy of the bounding box and the resulting mapping is sensitive to the alpha threshold. Tile-Based Culling was introduced in the "StopThePop" paper. It is designed to address the "popping" artifacts and inefficiencies in 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering by providing a more accurate culling mechanism. The method builds on the principles of tile-based rasterization and radix sorting.
