name: CUDA Voxelizer Pipeline
head: CudaVoxelizer Forward/Backward Pass, Tile-based 3D Gaussian Voxelization
body: The CUDA Voxelizer Pipeline is a GPU-accelerated rendering and gradient computation method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that voxelizes 3D Gaussians into a 3D grid, sorts them per tile using radix sort, and renders/backpropagates gradients via tile-based blending. It differs from standard tile-based rasterization by explicitly constructing a 3D voxel grid to manage Gaussian spatial distribution and using a dedicated preprocessing phase to compute norms, depths, and conic opacities before binning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: P: Number of 3D Gaussians. Gaussian parameters: means, scales, rotations, opacities, 3D covariance matrices (\Sigma{3D}). Voxel grid parameters: dimensions (nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz), physical spacing (sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz), and world-space center (centerx, centery, centerz). Flags: scalemodifier (multiplicative factor for scales), prefiltered (skip pre-filtering logic). Outputs: Rendered volume/image. Gradients for 3D mean position, conic matrix, opacity, scale, and rotation. Data Structures: GeometryState: depths[P]: Depth of each Gaussian. internalradiix[P], internalradiiy[P], internalradiiz[P]: Internal radii buffers. means3Dnorm[P]: Normalized 3D means. cov3D[P6]: 3D covariance matrices (6 unique elements per symmetric matrix). conicopacity[P7]: Conic matrix (6 elements) and opacity (1 element). tilestouched[P]: Count of tiles touched by each Gaussian. pointoffsets[P]: Cumulative counts per tile (from prefix sum). scanningspace[dynamic], scansize[dynamic]: Dynamic memory for scanning operations. ImageState: ncontrib[N]: Number of contributing Gaussians per voxel/tile. ranges[N]: Start/end indices per tile, where N = nVoxelx \times nVoxely \times nVoxelz. BinningState: pointlist[P]: Sorted Gaussian indices. pointlistunsorted[P]: Unsorted Gaussian indices. pointlistkeys[P]: Sort keys. pointlistkeysunsorted[P]: Unsorted sort keys. listsortingspace[dynamic], sortingsize[dynamic]: Dynamic memory for sorting. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Allocate geometry buffers. Call FORWARD::preprocess with Gaussian parameters and voxel grid parameters. Compute means3Dnorm, cov3D, conicopacity, and tilestouched. If radiix/y/z pointers are null, fall back to internalradii buffers. 2. Prefix Sum: Compute an inclusive prefix sum over tilestouched to generate pointoffsets. Retrieve total rendered instances: num\rendered = point\offsets[P - 1]. 3. Binning Buffer Allocation: Allocate binning buffers sized for num\rendered. Reconstruct BinningState. 4. Key Generation and Duplication: Launch duplicateWithKeys kernel with \lceil (P + 255) / 256 \rceil blocks of 256 threads. Generate sort keys combining tile ID and depth. Duplicate Gaussian indices based on radii and tile grid. 5. Radix Sort: Calculate radix bits: bit = \text{getHigherMsb}(tile\grid.x \times tile\grid.y \times tile\grid.z). Sort duplicated Gaussian indices by keys using CUB radix sort over range 0, 32 + bit). 6. [Tile Range Identification: Zero-initialize ranges buffer for all tiles. If num\rendered > 0, launch identifyTileRanges kernel with \lceil (num\rendered + 255) / 256 \rceil blocks of 256 threads to compute start/end indices per tile from sorted keys. 7. Forward Rendering: Launch FORWARD::render kernel with tilegrid, block, ranges, pointlist, voxel dimensions, means3Dnorm, conicopacity, ncontrib, and outvolume. Blend Gaussians per tile. 8. Backward Pass: Reconstruct GeometryState, BinningState, and ImageState from provided buffers. Launch BACKWARD::render kernel to compute loss gradients w.r.t. 3D mean position, conic matrix, and opacity. Select cov3D pointer: use cov3Dprecomp if not null, else fall back to geomState.cov3D. Launch BACKWARD::preprocess kernel to compute gradients for mean3D, cov3D, scale, and rotation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cudavoxelizerpipeline(gaussians, voxelparams, imagestate, geometrystate, binningstate): P = gaussians.numgaussians nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz = voxelparams.dimensions sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz = voxelparams.spacing centerx, centery, centerz = voxelparams.center scalemodifier = voxelparams.scalemodifier prefiltered = voxelparams.prefiltered # Step 1: Preprocessing # Allocate GeometryState buffers geometrystate.depths = allocate(P) geometrystate.internalradiix = allocate(P) geometrystate.internalradiiy = allocate(P) geometrystate.internalradiiz = allocate(P) geometrystate.means3Dnorm = allocate(P) geometrystate.cov3D = allocate(P 6) geometrystate.conicopacity = allocate(P 7) geometrystate.tilestouched = allocate(P) # Call FORWARD::preprocess # Inputs: means, scales, rotations, opacities, cov3D, voxelparams # Outputs: means3Dnorm, cov3D, conicopacity, tilestouched, depths, internalradii forwardpreprocess( gaussians.means, gaussians.scales, gaussians.rotations, gaussians.opacities, gaussians.cov3D, nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz, sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz, centerx, centery, centerz, scalemodifier, prefiltered, geometrystate.means3Dnorm, geometrystate.cov3D, geometrystate.conicopacity, geometrystate.tilestouched, geometrystate.depths, geometrystate.internalradiix, geometrystate.internalradiiy, geometrystate.internalradiiz) # Step 2: Prefix Sum # Compute inclusive prefix sum over tilestouched pointoffsets = inclusiveprefixsum(geometrystate.tilestouched) numrendered = pointoffsets[P - 1] # Step 3: Binning Buffer Allocation # Allocate BinningState buffers binningstate.pointlist = allocate(numrendered) binningstate.pointlistunsorted = allocate(numrendered) binningstate.pointlistkeys = allocate(numrendered) binningstate.pointlistkeysunsorted = allocate(numrendered) # Dynamic sorting space allocation binningstate.listsortingspace = allocatedynamic() binningstate.sortingsize = allocatedynamic() # Step 4: Key Generation and Duplication # Launch duplicateWithKeys kernel numblocks = (P + 255) // 256 threadsperblock = 256 duplicatewithkeyskernel( numblocks, threadsperblock, gaussians.indices, geometrystate.internalradiix, geometrystate.internalradiiy, geometrystate.internalradiiz, voxelparams.tilegrid, geometrystate.depths, binningstate.pointlistunsorted, binningstate.pointlistkeysunsorted) # Step 5: Radix Sort tilegridvolume = voxelparams.tilegrid.x voxelparams.tilegrid.y voxelparams.tilegrid.z bit = gethighermsb(tilegridvolume) cubradixsort( binningstate.pointlistkeysunsorted, binningstate.pointlistkeys, binningstate.pointlistunsorted, binningstate.pointlist, numrendered, 32 + bit, binningstate.listsortingspace, binningstate.sortingsize) # Step 6: Tile Range Identification # Zero-initialize ranges imagestate.ranges = zeroallocate(voxelparams.tilegrid.x voxelparams.tilegrid.y voxelparams.tilegrid.z) if numrendered > 0: numblocks = (numrendered + 255) // 256 threadsperblock = 256 identifytilerangeskernel( numblocks, threadsperblock, binningstate.pointlistkeys, voxelparams.tilegrid, imagestate.ranges) # Step 7: Forward Rendering forwardrenderkernel( voxelparams.tilegrid, binningstate.pointlist, geometrystate.means3Dnorm, geometrystate.conicopacity, imagestate.ncontrib, imagestate.ranges, voxelparams.voxeldimensions, imagestate.outvolume) # Step 8: Backward Pass # Reconstruct states from buffers # Launch BACKWARD::render backwardrenderkernel( voxelparams.tilegrid, binningstate.pointlist, geometrystate.means3Dnorm, geometrystate.conicopacity, imagestate.ncontrib, imagestate.ranges, voxelparams.voxeldimensions, imagestate.outvolumegrad, gaussians.gradmeans, gaussians.gradconic, gaussians.gradopacity) # Select cov3D pointer cov3Dptr = gaussians.cov3Dprecomp if gaussians.cov3Dprecomp is not None else geometrystate.cov3D # Launch BACKWARD::preprocess backwardpreprocesskernel( gaussians.gradmeans, cov3Dptr, gaussians.gradscales, gaussians.gradrotations, gaussians.gradopacities) Time Complexity: Dominated by the radix sort, which is O(N \log N) where N is the number of (Gaussian, tile) pairs after duplication. The preprocessing and rendering phases are linear in the number of Gaussians and pixels, respectively. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for GeometryState (O(P)), BinningState (O(N)), and ImageState (O(N)), where N is the number of tiles. Dynamic sorting space adds overhead. Performance: Measured performance depends on hardware, resolution, and scene density. The use of CUB radix sort provides efficient parallel sorting on CUDA GPUs. Strengths: Efficient handling of large numbers of Gaussians through voxelization and tile-based sorting. Reuse of sorted lists for backpropagation. Limitations: Memory overhead for dynamic buffers and duplication. Potential precision issues with depth packing if not handled carefully. When to use: Suitable for real-time or near-real-time rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian scenes on CUDA-capable GPUs. When not to use: Not suitable for non-CUDA hardware or scenes with extremely sparse Gaussians where overhead dominates. The CUDA Voxelizer Pipeline is part of the Gaussian Splatting ecosystem, specifically designed for efficient rendering and training on NVIDIA GPUs. It builds on the principles of tile-based rasterization and differentiable rendering. name: Gaussian Splatting Rendering with Camera Pose Override
head: render function with rel_w2c transform
body: This method modifies the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline to inject a custom world-to-camera transformation matrix (camerapose) during rendering. It transforms the Gaussian 3D means and rotations into the new camera frame while keeping the primitives fixed in their original world-space coordinates. This approach handles the coordinate frame transformation required for novel view synthesis or pose correction, distinct from tile-based memory management methods. The method intercepts the rasterization call, computes a relative world-to-camera matrix from the override pose, transforms the Gaussian attributes (means and rotations) into this new camera frame, and passes them to the rasterizer. Inputs: pc: The GaussianPointCloud object containing 3D means (xyz), rotations (quaternions), scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. viewpointcamera: A camera object containing the intrinsic projection matrix (projectionmatrix) and field of view (FoVx, FoVy). camerapose: A tensor representing the desired world-to-camera transformation. pipe: A pipeline configuration object containing boolean flags computecov3Dpython and convertSHspython. overridecolor: Optional tensor to replace spherical harmonics colors. Outputs: renderimage: The rendered RGB image. viewspacepoints: Screen-space coordinates of the Gaussian centers with gradient tracking enabled. visibilityfilter: A boolean mask indicating which Gaussians were rendered (radii > 0). radii: The screen-space radii of the Gaussians. camerapose: A 4 \times 4 tensor representing the world-to-camera transform. gaussiansxyztrans: Transformed 3D means in the camera frame. gaussiansrottrans: Transformed rotations (quaternions) in the camera frame. projmatrix: The combined projection matrix derived from the viewpoint camera's intrinsics. screenspacepoints: Zero tensor for screen-space points with gradient tracking enabled. 1. Initialize Gradient Tracking: Create a zero tensor for screen-space points to enable backpropagation to 2D means: \text{screenspace\points} = \text{zeros}(\text{shape}(\text{pc.xyz}), \text{dtype}=\text{pc.xyz.dtype}, \text{requires\grad}=\text{True}). Call retaingrad() on this tensor. 2. Compute Field of View Tangents: Calculate the half-field-of-view tangents from the viewpointcamera intrinsics: \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\text{FoVx} \times 0.5) and \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\text{FoVy} \times 0.5). 3. Construct Projection Matrix: Create an identity world-to-camera matrix and combine it with the viewpoint camera's projection matrix: \text{w2c} = \mathbf{I}4 and \text{projmatrix} = \text{w2c} \times \text{viewpoint\camera.projection\matrix}. Extract the camera position from the inverse of the identity matrix: \text{camera\pos} = \text{w2c}^{-1}[3,:3]. 4. Transform Gaussian Attributes: Compute the relative world-to-camera matrix from the camerapose tensor: \text{rel\w2c} = \text{get\camera\from\tensor}(\text{camera\pose}). Transform the 3D means via \text{xyz\homo} = [\text{xyz}, 1] and \text{gaussians\xyz\trans} = (\text{rel\w2c} \times \text{xyz\homo}^T)^T[:,:3]. Transform the rotations using quaternion multiplication: \text{gaussians\rot\trans} = \text{quadmultiply}(\text{camera\pose}[:4], \text{gaussians\rot}). 5. Determine Covariance Representation: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, compute the 3D covariance matrix from the scales and rotations: \text{cov3D\precomp} = \text{pc.get\covariance}(\text{scaling\modifier}). Otherwise, pass scales and the transformed rotations (gaussiansrottrans) separately to the rasterizer. 6. Determine Color Representation: If overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython is true, convert spherical harmonics to RGB in Python: \text{colors\precomp} = \text{clamp}(\text{eval\SH}(\text{active\SH\degree}, \text{shs\view}, \text{dir\pp\normalized}), 0, 1). Otherwise, pass spherical harmonics directly to the rasterizer or use overridecolor. 7. Rasterize: Call the GaussianRasterizer with the transformed means (means3D), transformed means2D, colors/covariances, opacities, and scales/rotations. 8. Return Results: Return the rendered image, viewspace points, visibility filter (radii > 0), and radii. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def renderwithcameraposeoverride(pc, viewpointcamera, camerapose, pipe, overridecolor=None): # Step 1: Initialize screenspace points for gradient tracking screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz, dtype=pc.getxyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device='cuda') + 0 screenspacepoints.retaingrad() # Step 2: Compute half-field-of-view tangents tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # Step 3: Set w2c to identity and compute projection matrix w2c = torch.eye(4).cuda() projmatrix = (w2c.unsqueeze(0).bmm(viewpointcamera.projectionmatrix.unsqueeze(0))).squeeze(0) camerapos = w2c.inverse()[3,:3] # Step 4: Transform Gaussian attributes using the override pose relw2c = camerapose # getcamerafromtensor extracts the 4x4 matrix xyzhomo = torch.cat([pc.getxyz, torch.oneslike(pc.getxyz[...,:1])], dim=-1) gaussiansxyztrans = (relw2c @ xyzhomo.T).T[:,:3] gaussiansrottrans = quadmultiply(camerapose[:4], pc.getrot) # Step 5: Determine covariance representation if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier=1.0) else: cov3Dprecomp = None # Step 6: Determine color representation if overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython: dirpp = gaussiansxyztrans - camerapos.unsqueeze(0) dirppnormalized = torch.nn.functional.normalize(dirpp, dim=-1) # evalsh is a standard spherical harmonics evaluation routine colorsprecomp = evalsh(pc.activeshdegree, pc.getshs, dirppnormalized) colorsprecomp = torch.clamp(colorsprecomp, 0.0, 1.0) else: colorsprecomp = overridecolor if overridecolor is not None else pc.getshs # Step 7: Rasterize # Delegates to the standard tile-based 2D Gaussian rasterization kernel from the parent article renderimage, radii = GaussianRasterizer( means3D=gaussiansxyztrans, means2D=None, shs=colorsprecomp, opacities=pc.getopacity, scales=pc.getscale, rotations=gaussiansrottrans, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp, viewmatrix=None, projmatrix=projmatrix, fullscreen=True, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, campos=None, rendermode='RGB') # Step 8: Return results visibilityfilter = radii > 0 return renderimage, screenspacepoints, visibilityfilter, radii def quadmultiply(q1, q2): """Standard quaternion multiplication q1 q2.""" w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1[..., 0], q1[..., 1], q1[..., 2], q1[..., 3] w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2[..., 0], q2[..., 1], q2[..., 2], q2[..., 3] return torch.stack([ w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2 ], dim=-1) def evalsh(deg, sh, dirs): """Evaluate spherical harmonics at directions.""" # Standard SH basis evaluation omitted for brevity; uses precomputed SH matrices pass def GaussianRasterizer(means3D, means2D, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, fullscreen, shdegree, campos, rendermode): """Standard GPU rasterization kernel for 2D Gaussians.""" # Implementation details are in the parent rasterization article pass camerapose: The specific pose to render from. No default; must be provided. pipe.computecov3Dpython: Boolean. If true, covariances are computed in Python; otherwise, scales and rotations are passed separately. Default is false. pipe.convertSHspython: Boolean. If true, SHs are converted to RGB in Python; otherwise, passed to rasterizer. Default is false. Precision: Ensure camerapose is on the correct device (CUDA) and dtype matches the Gaussian attributes. Boundary Conditions: If camerapose results in Gaussians being behind the camera, the rasterizer handles culling; the visibility filter (radii > 0) identifies valid Gaussians. Degenerate Input: If camerapose is singular or invalid, the transformation will fail; validate camerapose before use. Gradient Flow: The screenspacepoints tensor is initialized to zero and retains gradients, which is crucial for backpropagation if the camera pose is optimized in a training loop. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization step, which is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, assuming tile-based rasterization. The transformation step is also O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing transformed attributes and intermediate tensors. Performance: The overhead of transforming attributes is minimal compared to the rasterization cost. The method is efficient for real-time rendering if the rasterizer is GPU-accelerated. Strengths: Allows flexible camera pose manipulation without retraining the Gaussian model. Useful for novel view synthesis, pose correction, and interactive applications. Limitations: The Gaussian model is fixed in world space; if scene geometry changes, the model must be retrained. The method assumes the Gaussian model was trained with a consistent coordinate system. This method is derived from the implementation details of the InstantSplat repository. It builds upon the foundational 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023) and extends it to support dynamic camera poses without modifying the underlying Gaussian representation. name: Load Balancing for Pixel-parallel Splatting
head: Load balancing algorithm, Load balancing loss
body: A strategy to address uneven computational load across pixel threads in Gaussian rasterization by reducing the number of Gaussians rendered for heavy-load pixels and increasing it for light-load pixels. Uneven load across GPU threads leads to lower rendering efficiency due to thread waiting. Unlike hardware-centric tile/block distribution methods, this approach operates as a software-level loss function and adaptive rendering count adjustment within the pixel-parallel execution model. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of N 3D Gaussians, camera parameters, and the image grid. Output: A modified rendering process where the number of Gaussians processed per pixel is adjusted to minimize load variance, potentially at the cost of slight quality changes in light-load areas. Data Structures: Pixel Load Count (\elli): An integer value representing the number of Gaussians contributing to pixel i. Indicator Function (1{Gj, pi}): A binary value (1 if Gaussian j contributes to pixel i, 0 otherwise). Method Steps: 1. Compute Pixel Loads: Calculate the load \elli for each pixel i by summing the contributions of all Gaussians: \elli = \sum{j \in N} 1{Gj, pi} where N is the total number of Gaussians. 2. Identify Load Imbalance: Determine heavy-load pixels (high \elli) and light-load pixels (low \elli). The rendering efficiency is bottlenecked by the heavy-load threads. 3. Apply Load Balancing Loss: Optimize the Gaussian attributes (such as opacity or radius) using a load balancing loss term. The goal is to reduce \elli for heavy-load pixels and increase \elli for light-load pixels. The loss function utilizes the standard deviation of the pixel loads to quantify imbalance. The weight of the load balancing loss term is denoted as \lambda{load}. 4. Adjust Rendering Count: During rasterization, the actual number of Gaussians rendered is dynamically adjusted based on the learned attributes. Heavy-load pixels render fewer Gaussians, while light-load pixels render more, effectively balancing the thread execution time. Parameters: \lambda{load}: Weight for the load balancing loss term. Typical value: 0.45. \lambda{L1} + \lambda{ssim}: Sum of weights for remaining losses (L1 and SSIM). Typical value: 0.55. Opacity Threshold (\alpha{low}): A threshold for opacity. A typical value is 255, though higher values could further accelerate rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quality Degradation: Reducing the number of Gaussians for heavy-load pixels may cause a decrease in rendering quality. The method attempts to mitigate this by increasing Gaussians for light-load pixels, but this is a trade-off. Thread Waiting: If the load balancing is not effective, GPU thread waiting persists, reducing efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computepixelloads(gaussians, pixels): loads = [0] len(pixels) for i, pixel in enumerate(pixels): for j, gaussian in enumerate(gaussians): # Standard operation: evaluate 2D Gaussian PDF at pixel coordinates # and check if it exceeds the opacity threshold if gaussiancontributestopixel(gaussian, pixel): loads[i] += 1 return loads def gaussiancontributestopixel(gaussian, pixel): # Standard operation: compute Mahalanobis distance using 2D covariance # and return True if the contribution is non-negligible pass def computeloadbalancingloss(loads): meanload = sum(loads) / len(loads) variance = sum((l - meanload) 2 for l in loads) / len(loads) return variance 0.5 def optimizegaussianattributes(gaussians, pixels, lambdaload=0.45, lambdaother=0.55): # The specific gradient update rule for Gaussian attributes is not given in the sources. pass def renderwithloadbalancing(gaussians, pixels, loads): for i, pixel in enumerate(pixels): targetcount = loads[i] if targetcount > threshold: targetcount = max(1, targetcount - reductionfactor) elif targetcount < threshold: targetcount = min(maxgaussians, targetcount + increasefactor) # Standard operation: accumulate color and transmittance for the selected Gaussians renderpixel(pixel, gaussians[:targetcount]) def renderpixel(pixel, selectedgaussians): # Standard operation: evaluate and blend selected Gaussians at pixel coordinates pass A workload distribution strategy to address severe imbalance in tile workloads, using early stopping depth prediction and Morton-order traversal to balance load across rasterization blocks. It differs from the pixel-parallel approach by operating at the tile/block level in hardware. Preprocessing: Discard Gaussians beyond predicted early stopping depth. Remaining Gaussians constitute the tile’s effective workload. Workload Assignment: Compute ideal average workload W. Assign approximately N tiles per block sequentially. If cumulative Gaussian-tile pairs in current block exceed (1 + 1/N)W, defer current tile to next block. Memory Optimization: Employ Morton-order (Z-order) traversal to group spatially adjacent tiles into the same block, reducing memory access overhead. Intra-block Sorting: Sort tiles within each block from light to heavy workload. Reuse Gaussian Sorting Unit (GSU) for this task. Pitfall: Rasterization bubbles occur if high-workload tiles take longer to sort than light tiles take to rasterize. Light-to-heavy ordering ensures sorting finishes before rasterization of heavy tiles begins. A method that reuses image regions and schedules remaining tiles from predicted load. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method is validated on standard datasets and aims to accelerate rendering by improving GPU utilization. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves rendering efficiency by reducing GPU thread waiting caused by uneven loads. Limitations: May cause a decrease in rendering quality for heavy-load pixels due to fewer Gaussians being rendered. Originated in the paper "AdR-Gaussian: Accelerating Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Radius". The method addresses the issue of uneven load distribution in Gaussian Splatting rasterization, which leads to inefficient GPU utilization. name: Half-cosine Squared Splatting
head: 3DHCS, Half Cosine Squared
body: Half-cosine Squared Splatting is a radial basis function technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the standard Gaussian decay with a half-cosine squared function. It solves the problem of slow convergence and high memory usage in standard splatting by providing higher opacity values per primitive, allowing fewer primitives to achieve the same accumulated opacity. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by using a bounded decay profile that accelerates training and reduces memory footprint. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \mu, 3D covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color C); camera projection matrix; image resolution. Outputs: Final pixel color and alpha. Data Structures: cov: 3x3 symmetric 3D covariance matrix. cov2D: 2x2 symmetric 2D covariance matrix (projected). conic: 2x2 symmetric conic matrix (inverse of cov2D), stored as 3 floats (a, b, c) for the upper triangle. muprime: 2D mean in screen space. ellipse: Scalar value representing the squared Mahalanobis distance scaled by the ellipse factor. Parameters: correctionFactor: 1.36. \beta: 2. \xi: 36. ellipseLimit: 9.0. alphaClip: 0.99. Steps: 1. Covariance Correction: Multiply the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma by correctionFactor before projection. \Sigma{corrected} = \Sigma \times 1.36 2. Projection: Project the 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space to obtain the 2D mean \mu' and the 2D covariance \Sigma'{2 \times 2}. 3. Conic Calculation: Compute the inverse of the 2D covariance to get the conic matrix J = (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1}. 4. Ellipse Factor Calculation: For a pixel at screen coordinate x, calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance term dM^2 (referred to as ellipse in code): dM^2 = (x - \mu')^T (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (x - \mu') In the implementation, this is computed using the conic matrix components (a, b, c) where J = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}: dM^2 = a \cdot dx^2 + c \cdot dy^2 + 2 \cdot b \cdot dx \cdot dy where dx = x - \mu'x and dy = y - \mu'y. 5. Boundary Check: If dM^2 < 0 or dM^2 > 9, skip the splat for this pixel. This limits the 2D ellipse to restrict the half-cosine pulse. 6. Weight Calculation: Calculate the half-cosine squared weight w: ellipseFactor = \frac{2 \pi \cdot dM^2}{36} \approx 0.175 \cdot dM^2 w = \cos(ellipseFactor) The validity condition requires the cosine argument to be \leq \pi/2, which corresponds to dM^2 \leq 9. 7. Alpha Computation: Compute the final alpha \alpha: \alpha = \min(0.99, \alpha{primitive} \cdot w) where \alpha{primitive} is the primitive's base opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def halfcosinesquaredsplat(xscreen, muprime, conicmatrix, primitiveopacity): """ xscreen: tuple (x, y) muprime: tuple (mux, muy) conicmatrix: tuple (a, b, c) representing [[a, b], [b, c]] primitiveopacity: float """ dx = xscreen[0] - muprime[0] dy = xscreen[1] - muprime[1] a, b, c = conicmatrix # Calculate squared Mahalanobis distance (ellipse) ellipse = a dx dx + c dy dy + 2.0 b dx dy # Boundary check: skip if outside valid half-cosine pulse range if ellipse < 0.0 or ellipse > 9.0: return 0.0, 0.0 # Calculate ellipse factor using exact 2pi/36 scaling ellipsefactor = 2.0 math.pi ellipse / 36.0 # Calculate cosine weight cosineweight = math.cos(ellipsefactor) # Calculate final alpha with clip alpha = min(0.99, primitiveopacity cosineweight) return alpha, cosineweight Backpropagation Details: The derivatives required for training are: \frac{dw}{d(x - \mu')} = \frac{-2(\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (x - \mu') \sin\left(\frac{(x - \mu')^T (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (x - \mu')}{\xi}\right)}{\xi} \frac{dw}{d((\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1})} = \frac{-(x - \mu') (x - \mu')^T \sin\left(\frac{(x - \mu')^T (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (x - \mu')}{\xi}\right)}{\xi} The gradient w.r.t. the conic matrix entries must account for the correctionFactor if the conic is derived from the corrected covariance. Time Complexity: Similar to standard Gaussian Splatting per primitive, but the cosine calculation is slightly more expensive than the exponential Gaussian decay. However, overall training time is reduced because fewer primitives are needed. Memory Usage: Reduced compared to standard Gaussian Splatting. Half-cosine primitives provide higher opacity values, requiring fewer primitives to achieve the same accumulated opacity coverage. Performance: Demonstrates superior performance in training loss curves and speed compared to Gaussians, despite similar final training loss. Strengths: Faster training, lower memory usage, higher opacity per primitive. Limitations: The bounded nature of the cosine function requires careful boundary checking (ellipse < 9) to avoid invalid values. The computation of trigonometric functions may be slower than simple exponentials on some hardware, though this is offset by the reduced primitive count. Half-cosine Squared Splatting was introduced in the DARB-Splatting paper as a generalization of splatting using decaying anisotropic radial basis functions. It was developed to address the limitations of exponentially decaying functions (like Gaussians) which require many primitives for accurate blending. The method uses \beta=2 and \xi=36 as key parameters for the half-cosine square function. DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00438, fetched 2026-10-30

name: HSPT Cut and Gaussian Loading Optimization
head: GPU Memory Buffer Optimization
body: This method optimizes the HSPT cut and Gaussian loading by storing SPT properties in a continuous GPU buffer and transferring Gaussians via a single copy operation, reorganizing them on the GPU into a Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout. It reduces PCIe bus traffic and kernel launch overhead inherent in hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. Inputs: CPU Gaussian properties stored in a single PyTorch tensor in RAM as an Array of Structures (AoS). SPT properties (\text{min}(i), \text{min}(\text{parent}(i)), \text{scale}(i)) stored in a continuous GPU memory buffer. Current camera pose and view frustum. Outputs: A contiguous GPU buffer containing Gaussian properties in SoA layout, ready for the tiled rasterizer. 1. SPT Properties Buffer (GPU): A single continuous GPU memory buffer storing hierarchical metadata. For each Gaussian i, it stores \text{min}(i), \text{min}(\text{parent}(i)), and \text{scale}(i). 2. Gaussian Properties (CPU): A single PyTorch tensor in RAM in AoS layout, where each Gaussian's properties are stored concurrently. 3. Render Set (GPU): The final SoA layout required by the rasterizer, formed by appending reorganized Gaussians. 1. SPT Cut Execution: The GPU performs the HSPT cut in parallel using optimized CUDA kernels to determine visible Gaussians based on the current view and hierarchical SPT properties. 2. Single Copy Operation: Transfer the properties of all required Gaussians from the CPU AoS tensor to the GPU via a single contiguous memory copy operation. 3. GPU Reorganization: Reorganize the transferred Gaussian properties on the GPU into the SoA layout required by the rasterizer. 4. Append to Render Set: Append the reorganized Gaussians to the current render set. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizegaussianloading(sptbuffer, cpugaussiantensor, cameraparams): # Step 1: Determine visible Gaussians using SPT properties on GPU # The sources state this is performed in parallel using optimized CUDA kernels # on min(i), min(parent(i)), and scale(i) to cull invisible Gaussians. visibleindices = performhsptcut(sptbuffer, cameraparams) # Step 2: Extract required Gaussian properties from CPU AoS tensor requiredgaussians = cpugaussiantensor[visibleindices] # Step 3: Transfer to GPU via single copy operation gpurequiredgaussians = requiredgaussians.to(device='cuda', nonblocking=True) # Step 4: Reorganize from AoS to SoA on GPU # Reshape tensor from (K, D) AoS to (D, K) SoA layout for memory coalescing gpusoAdata = gpurequiredgaussians.t().contiguous() # Step 5: Append to the current render set # Concatenate along the first dimension to form the final render buffer gpurenderset = torch.cat([gpurenderset, gpusoAdata], dim=0) return gpurenderset Cache Flush Interval: When using SPT caching, the entire cache is flushed every 1,000 training iterations to prevent overfitting to persistent cache entries. Memory Thresholds: VRAM usage is bounded by an LRU writeback policy; when the threshold is exceeded, entries are written back to RAM. Precision: Ensure the PyTorch tensor dtype matches the expected GPU kernel input types to avoid implicit conversion overhead. Degenerate Input: If no Gaussians are visible (e.g., camera outside scene bounds), skip the copy and reorganization steps to avoid empty buffer overhead. This variant extends the basic loading optimization by caching SPT cuts in VRAM to avoid redundant RAM-to-GPU transfers for similar views. For each training view, visible Gaussians are assembled from the upper hierarchy, cached SPTs, and skybox Gaussians (which remain in VRAM). If the condition D{\min} \leq \frac{d^j}{\overline{d}^j} \leq D{\max} is met, the cached SPT cut is reused, where d^j is the current distance metric and \overline{d}^j is the average, defining the allowable range for coarser-than-optimal detail. Uncached SPTs are streamed from RAM. Newly loaded SPTs are added to the cache after each iteration. An LRU policy bounds VRAM usage; when the threshold is exceeded, entries are written back to RAM. The entire cache is flushed every 1,000 iterations to prevent overfitting. This stochasticity in Level-of-Detail variability improves training robustness by discouraging overfitting to fixed camera distances and promotes generalization across scales. View selection prioritizes spatial locality by sampling the next training view from the k-nearest neighbours of the current view in a precomputed Euclidean distance graph. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is the RAM-to-GPU transfer, reduced to a single bulk operation per frame. The AoS-to-SoA reorganization is performed on the GPU. Memory Complexity: Requires continuous GPU buffers for SPT properties and the render set. In a 60-million-Gaussian hierarchy on MC-smaller-city+, SPT metadata occupies 680 MB of VRAM and the upper hierarchy occupies 24 MB of VRAM. Performance: On wide-angle aerial views, 2.2 million Gaussians are rendered directly and 2.4 million are retained in the cache, demonstrating effective reuse. The method achieves high reconstruction quality (e.g., 21.71 PSNR) with manageable VRAM usage (15.7 GB training, 17.2 GB inference) compared to competitors like OctreeGS (26.6 GB training). Strengths: Significantly reduces PCIe bandwidth pressure; improves training stability through cache-induced stochasticity. Limitations: Requires careful management of VRAM thresholds; cache misses in large-scale scenes can still incur latency if spatial locality is not maintained via view selection. This method originates from the work on "A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory". It addresses the scalability issues of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in large scenes, where the sheer number of Gaussians makes naive rendering and densification infeasible. The approach builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) by introducing hierarchical memory management and optimized data layout transitions. A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.01110, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Tight Quad Rasterization with Eigenvalue Decomposition
head: Eigenvalue-based Tight Quad Rasterization
body: This method renders 3D Gaussian splats by projecting their anisotropic covariance into screen space and emitting a non-axis-aligned quad per splat to the GPU's fixed-function rasterizer. It solves the problem of overdraw and inefficient clipping inherent in axis-aligned bounding boxes by computing a tight, rotated bounding quad that incorporates the splat's alpha threshold. It differs from software-based CUDA rasterization by leveraging hardware clipping and interpolation, achieving significant speedups on mobile hardware by discarding large, distant Gaussians early. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \mathbf{\mu}, 3D covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color C); camera projection matrix P; clipping thresholds \tau\lambda (max eigenvalue) and \lambda{dist} (distance). Outputs: Rasterized image with blended Gaussians. Data Structures: Gaussian: Struct containing \mathbf{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite), \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, C \in \mathbb{R}^3. Quad Vertices: 4 vertices in screen space (x, y) with associated attributes (color, opacity). Steps: 1. Cull Negative Opacity: If \alpha < 0, discard the Gaussian. 2. Project Covariance: Compute the 2D screen-space covariance \Sigma{2D}. This involves projecting the 3D covariance \Sigma using the camera's Jacobian J and projection matrix P. Let W be the depth scaling factor. The standard EWA splatting approach is used. 3. Eigen Decomposition: Decompose \Sigma{2D} to find eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. These represent the scale and rotation of the Gaussian in screen space. 4. Compute Tight Quad Bounds: Determine the extent of the Gaussian based on \lambda1, \lambda2 and the alpha threshold. Calculate the rotation angle \theta from \mathbf{v}1. Compute the width w and height h of the bounding box aligned with the eigenvectors. The calculation incorporates the splat alpha value to ensure the quad tightly fits the visible portion of the splat. Construct the 4 vertices of the non-axis-aligned quad centered at the projected mean \mathbf{\mu}{2D}, rotated by \theta, with dimensions w \times h. 5. Clipping Check: Check if the maximum eigenvalue \max(\lambda1, \lambda2) > \tau\lambda. If so, discard the Gaussian. (Optional for mobile) Check distance threshold \lambda{dist}. If the Gaussian is too distant, discard it. 6. Rasterization: Emit the quad to the fragment shader. The hardware rasterizer handles clipping against the view frustum and tile boundaries. 7. Blending: In the fragment shader, evaluate the 2D Gaussian density at each fragment inside the quad and blend using the pre-multiplied alpha. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertightquad(gaussian, camera, taulambda): # Step 1: Cull negative opacity if gaussian.alpha < 0: return [] # Step 2: Project covariance to 2D # J is the Jacobian of the projection at gaussian.mean # Sigma2D = J Sigma3D J^T sigma2d = projectcovariance(gaussian.sigma3d, camera) # Step 3: Eigen decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eigendecompose(sigma2d) lambda1, lambda2 = eigenvalues v1, v2 = eigenvectors # Step 4: Compute tight quad # Determine scale factors based on alpha threshold and eigenvalues # This part incorporates alpha into the bound rectangle calculation scale1 = computescale(lambda1, gaussian.alpha) scale2 = computescale(lambda2, gaussian.alpha) # Calculate quad dimensions width = 2 scale1 height = 2 scale2 # Calculate rotation angle from eigenvector angle = atan2(v1.y, v1.x) # Project mean to screen space mean2d = projectpoint(gaussian.mean, camera) # Generate 4 vertices of the rotated quad vertices = generaterotatedquad(mean2d, width, height, angle) # Step 5: Clipping check if max(lambda1, lambda2) > taulambda: return [] # Step 6: Return vertices for rasterization return vertices Parameters: \tau\lambda: Clipping threshold for maximum eigenvalue. Typical value: Not given in the sources. \lambda{dist}: Distance threshold for culling distant Gaussians. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Covariance: If \Sigma{2D} is singular (eigenvalues are zero), the quad collapses. Handle by skipping or using a minimal fallback quad. Large Eigenvalues: Gaussians with large splats but means outside the view frustum are discarded by the \tau\lambda check, preventing unnecessary processing. Time Complexity: O(N) for N Gaussians, with constant-time projection and decomposition per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian for vertex generation. Performance: Achieves 5-10x speedup over original software CUDA rasterizer for high pixel-to-point ratios on mobile hardware. Strengths: Reduces overdraw; leverages fixed-function hardware for clipping and interpolation; efficient culling of large, distant Gaussians. Limitations: Requires GPU support for non-axis-aligned quad rasterization; eigen decomposition can be computationally expensive if not optimized. This method is part of the Shape-Shifting Splats approach for real-time context translation in VR. It builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline but optimizes it for mobile and VR contexts by using tight, rotated quads instead of axis-aligned boxes. It references EWA Splatting [60] for the projection foundation and GSplat [54] for the tight fit concept. Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, https://doi.org/10.1109/vr67842.2026.00046, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Fast Gaussian Rasterization (Covariance Eigen-decomposition and Quad Emission)
head: dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization
body: A GPU-accelerated rasterization method for 3D Gaussian splats that projects the 3D covariance to 2D, computes eigenvalues/vectors to determine basis vectors, and emits a tight quad per splat to the fragment shader for alpha-based blending. It differs from software-based CUDA rasterization by leveraging the fixed-function OpenGL rasterizer via a vertex-geometry-fragment shader pipeline, offloading clipping, interpolation, and blending from software to hardware. This approach reduces CPU/GPU synchronization overhead and explicit sorting stalls, achieving 5-10x speedup over the original software CUDA rasterizer for high pixel-to-point ratios. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a mean position, a 3D covariance matrix (or its decomposition), and color/opacity attributes. Output: A 2D image with alpha-blended colors. Data Structures: The method relies on standard OpenGL shader inputs/outputs. Geometry Shader Inputs: in vec2 basisVector0[]: First basis vector scaled by \sqrt{8} standard deviations. in vec2 basisVector1[]: Second basis vector scaled by \sqrt{8} standard deviations. in vec4 gColor[]: Color and opacity of the splat. in float gDepth[]: Depth of the splat center. Geometry Shader Outputs: out vec2 vPosition: Normalized position within the quad (-1 to 1). flat out vec4 vColor: Interpolated color and opacity. flat out float vDepth: Interpolated depth. Fragment Shader Uniforms: uniform bool useDepth: Flag for depth visualization mode. uniform bool solidMode: Flag for solid opacity mode. uniform bool edgeMode: Flag for edge visualization mode. uniform float eight: Constant value 8.0. uniform float minAlpha: Minimum opacity threshold for discard (Default: 0.004). uniform float maxAlpha: Maximum opacity cap (Default: 0.99). uniform float edgeThreshold: Threshold for edge mode (Default: 0.025). Steps: 1. Project Covariance and Compute Eigenvalues: In the vertex shader (or pre-processing step), extract the 2D covariance components from the projected covariance matrix cov2Dv: a = \text{cov2Dv}.x d = \text{cov2Dv}.z b = \text{cov2Dv}.y Compute the determinant D: D = a \cdot d - b^2 Compute the trace and the term for eigenvalue calculation: \text{trace} = a + d \text{traceOver2} = 0.5 \cdot \text{trace} \text{term2} = \sqrt{\max(0.1, \text{traceOver2}^2 - D)} Compute the eigenvalues \lambda0 and \lambda1 (where \lambda0 \ge \lambda1): \lambda0 = \text{traceOver2} + \text{term2} \lambda1 = \text{traceOver2} - \text{term2} 2. Compute Eigenvectors: Compute the first eigenvector \mathbf{e}0: \mathbf{e}0 = \text{normalize}(\text{vec2}(b, \lambda0 - a)) Derive the orthogonal second eigenvector \mathbf{e}1: \mathbf{e}1 = \text{vec2}(\mathbf{e}0.y, -\mathbf{e}0.x) 3. Compute Basis Vectors: Scale the eigenvectors by \sqrt{8} standard deviations. The factor \sqrt{8} is used instead of the more common 3 standard deviations to eliminate more of the splat with very low opacity. \text{basisVector0} = \mathbf{e}0 \cdot \min(\sqrt{8} \cdot \sqrt{\lambda0}, \text{maxScreenSpaceSplatSize}) \text{basisVector1} = \mathbf{e}1 \cdot \min(\sqrt{8} \cdot \sqrt{\lambda1}, \text{maxScreenSpaceSplatSize}) Note: maxScreenSpaceSplatSize is a hardware-specific cap to prevent excessively large quads. 4. Validate and Prune: Check for illegal covariance matrices or degenerate splats. If any of the following conditions are met, prune the splat by setting gColor.a = 0.0 and returning early: D \le 0.0 a \le 0.0 d \le 0.0 \lambda0 \le 0.01 \lambda1 \le 0.01 \lambda0 < \lambda1 (should not happen with correct ordering) Aspect ratio \frac{\lambda0}{\lambda1} > 10000.0 5. Emit Quad in Geometry Shader: For each of the 4 corners of the quad, defined by vPosition in \{-1, 1\} \times \{-1, 1\}: Discard Check: If gColor[0].a < discardAlpha (0.0001), return without emitting vertices. Compute NDC Offset: \text{ndcOffset} = (\text{vPosition}.x \cdot \text{basisVector0} + \text{vPosition}.y \cdot \text{basisVector1}) \cdot \text{basisViewport} \cdot 2.0 Here, basisViewport scales the basis vectors to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) based on the viewport dimensions. Set Position: \text{gl\Position} = \text{vec4}(\text{ndcCenter}.xy + \text{ndcOffset}, \text{ndcCenter}.z, 1.0) where ndcCenter is the projected center of the Gaussian in NDC space. Pass Attributes: Scale vPosition by \sqrt{8} and pass through vColor (from gColor) and vDepth (from gDepth). 6. Apply Mode-Specific Overrides (Geometry Shader): If solidMode is true, set opacity = 1.0. If useDepth is true, set color = vec3(vDepth). If edgeMode is true and \exp(\text{power}) < \text{edgeThreshold}, set color = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) and opacity = 1.0. 7. Fragment Shader Processing: Alpha Clipping: If the interpolated alpha vColor.a < minAlpha (0.004), discard the fragment. Alpha Capping: If vColor.a > maxAlpha (0.99), cap it to maxAlpha. Blending: Perform standard alpha blending using the fragment's color and alpha against the existing framebuffer content. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeeigenandbasis(cov2Dv, maxScreenSpaceSplatSize): """ cov2Dv: vec4 (x=a, y=b, z=d, w=unused) Returns: basisVector0, basisVector1, eigenValue0, eigenValue1 """ a = cov2Dv.x d = cov2Dv.z b = cov2Dv.y # Determinant D = a d - b b # Eigenvalues trace = a + d traceOver2 = 0.5 trace # Use max(0.1,...) to avoid numerical instability for very small traces term2 = sqrt(max(0.1, traceOver2 traceOver2 - D)) eigenValue0 = traceOver2 + term2 eigenValue1 = traceOver2 - term2 # Eigenvectors # e0 = normalize(vec2(b, eigenValue0 - a)) # Handle potential zero vector if eigenValue0 == a and b == 0 if abs(b) < 1e-6 and abs(eigenValue0 - a) < 1e-6: eigenVector0 = vec2(1.0, 0.0) else: eigenVector0 = normalize(vec2(b, eigenValue0 - a)) # e1 is orthogonal to e0 eigenVector1 = vec2(eigenVector0.y, -eigenVector0.x) # Basis vectors scaled by sqrt(8) sqrt8 = sqrt(8.0) scale0 = min(sqrt8 sqrt(eigenValue0), maxScreenSpaceSplatSize) scale1 = min(sqrt8 sqrt(eigenValue1), maxScreenSpaceSplatSize) basisVector0 = eigenVector0 scale0 basisVector1 = eigenVector1 scale1 return basisVector0, basisVector1, eigenValue0, eigenValue1 def emitquad(basisVector0, basisVector1, gColor, gDepth, ndcCenter, basisViewport, discardAlpha): """ Emits 4 vertices for the quad. Returns list of vertex attributes: (vPosition, vColor, vDepth) """ vertices = [] # Check for early discard if gColor.a < discardAlpha: return vertices # Corners of the quad in local space {-1, 1} x {-1, 1} corners = [(-1, -1), (1, -1), (1, 1), (-1, 1)] for vx, vy in corners: # NDC Offset calculation # ndcOffset = (vx basisVector0 + vy basisVector1) basisViewport 2.0 offsetx = (vx basisVector0.x + vy basisVector1.x) basisViewport 2.0 offsety = (vx basisVector0.y + vy basisVector1.y) basisViewport 2.0 # Final NDC Position finalx = ndcCenter.x + offsetx finaly = ndcCenter.y + offsety finalz = ndcCenter.z finalw = 1.0 # vPosition is scaled by sqrt(8) for fragment shader evaluation vPosition = vec2(vx sqrt(8.0), vy sqrt(8.0)) # Pass through color and depth vColor = gColor vDepth = gDepth vertices.append((vPosition, vColor, vDepth)) return vertices def fragmentshader(vPosition, vColor, vDepth, useDepth, solidMode, edgeMode, edgeThreshold, minAlpha, maxAlpha): """ Returns final color and alpha. """ color = vColor.rgb alpha = vColor.a # Mode overrides if solidMode: alpha = 1.0 elif useDepth: color = vec3(vDepth) elif edgeMode: # Assuming 'power' is computed from vPosition magnitude in the actual shader # For this pseudocode, we assume edge check is done or power is available # If edgeMode and exp(power) < edgeThreshold: # color = vec3(0.0) # alpha = 1.0 pass # Alpha capping if alpha > maxAlpha: alpha = maxAlpha # Alpha clipping if alpha < minAlpha: discardfragment() return color, alpha This method renders 3D Gaussian splats as screen-space quads by leveraging the fixed-function OpenGL rasterizer via a vertex-geometry-fragment shader pipeline, offloading clipping, interpolation, and blending from software to hardware. It differs from CUDA-based software rasterization by reducing CPU/GPU synchronization overhead and explicit sorting stalls, achieving 5-10x speedup over the original software CUDA rasterizer for high pixel-to-point ratios. Time Complexity: O(N) for N splats, dominated by the geometry shader emission and fragment shader blending. The eigen-decomposition is O(1) per splat. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat attributes and intermediate buffers. Measured Performance: Achieves 5-10x speedup over the original software CUDA rasterizer for high pixel-to-point ratios. Strengths: Leverages hardware rasterization, reducing CPU/GPU sync overhead. Tight quad bounding box (\sqrt{8} std devs) reduces overdraw compared to larger bounding boxes. Simple eigen-decomposition avoids iterative solvers. Limitations: Requires OpenGL support for geometry shaders (though widely supported). Pruning conditions (aspect ratio, eigenvalue thresholds) may discard valid splats in edge cases if thresholds are too aggressive. Not directly compatible with Vulkan/Metal without adaptation (geometry shader stage differences). When to Use: Real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian Avatars where performance is critical and OpenGL is available. When Not to Use: When maximum compatibility with non-OpenGL APIs is required, or when the scene has extremely low pixel-to-point ratios where software sorting might be more efficient. This method is part of the "Fast Gaussian Rasterization" implementation by dendenxu, which provides an efficient CUDA/OpenGL hybrid approach for rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the mathematical foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting and optimizes the rasterization step specifically for real-time performance by utilizing the GPU's geometry shader to emit tight bounding quads. dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, https://github.com/dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Rasterization via OpenGL Geometry Shader
head: OpenGL Geometry Shader Rasterization for 3D Gaussians, dsplat pipeline, fast-gauss rasterization
body: This method renders 3D Gaussian splats as screen-space quads by leveraging the fixed-function OpenGL rasterizer via a vertex-geometry-fragment shader pipeline, offloading clipping, interpolation, and blending from software to hardware. It differs from CUDA-based software rasterization by reducing CPU/GPU synchronization overhead and explicit sorting stalls, achieving 5-10x speedup over the original software CUDA rasterizer for high pixel-to-point ratios. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian attributes including position (mean), covariance matrix (or scales/rotations), and opacity/color (RGBA or spherical harmonics). Outputs: A rendered image texture (framebuffer) with alpha blending. Data Structures: Vertex Buffer Object (VBO): Contains attributes per Gaussian point. The layout consists of 4 attributes with sizes [3, 3, 3, 4] floats per vertex, representing: 1. Position (3 floats) 2. Covariance matrix elements (6 floats, packed as two vec3s) 3. Opacity and Color/SH coefficients (4 floats) Attribute Data Type: gl.GLFLOAT or gl.GLHALFFLOAT, determined by the dtype parameter (e.g., torch.float or torch.half). Output Texture Format: gl.GLRGBA16F for half precision, gl.GLRGBA32F for float, or gl.GLRGBA8 for uint8, determined by texdtype. Numbered Steps: 1. Upload Attributes: Upload Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, RGBA) to a vertex buffer object (VBO) on the GPU. 2. Vertex Shader Processing: The vertex shader processes each Gaussian point, passing attributes to the geometry shader. 3. Geometry Shader Emission: The geometry shader emits a quad (4 vertices) per Gaussian. Crucially, it computes the 3D-to-2D covariance projection once per Gaussian rather than per vertex, optimizing performance. 4. Fragment Shader Shading: The fragment shader shades the emitted quad using the interpolated Gaussian alpha and color. 5. Fixed-Function Rasterization: The OpenGL rasterizer handles clipping, interpolation of vertex attributes across the quad, and alpha blending into the framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compileshaders(): # Vertex Shader: Passes position, covariance, and color to geometry shader vertexshadersource = """ #version 430 core layout(location = 0) in vec3 position; layout(location = 1) in vec3 cov1; layout(location = 2) in vec3 cov2; layout(location = 3) in vec4 color; out vec3 vcov1; out vec3 vcov2; out vec4 vcolor; void main() { vcov1 = cov1; vcov2 = cov2; vcolor = color; glPosition = vec4(position, 1.0); // Simplified; actual projection happens in GS } """ # Geometry Shader: Emits quad, computes 2D covariance once geometryshadersource = """ #version 430 core layout(points) in; layout(trianglestrip, maxvertices = 4) out; in vec3 vcov1[]; in vec3 vcov2[]; in vec4 vcolor[]; out vec2 vuv; out vec4 vcolorout; out float vdepth; uniform mat4 projectionmatrix; uniform mat4 viewmatrix; void main() { // 1. Compute 3D-to-2D covariance projection ONCE per Gaussian // This involves projecting the 3D covariance matrix to 2D screen space // using the view and projection matrices. // Let C3D be the 3x3 covariance matrix from vcov1 and vcov2. // Let J be the Jacobian of the projection. // C2D = J C3D J^T // 2. Compute basis vectors (eigenvectors of C2D) and scale factors // to form the quad vertices in screen space. // This step is performed once per input point. // 3. Emit 4 vertices forming a quad // Vertex 0: Center - u - v // Vertex 1: Center + u - v // Vertex 2: Center - u + v // Vertex 3: Center + u + v // where u and v are the scaled eigenvectors. // For each vertex, set glPosition and pass UV coordinates and color glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(center, 1.0); vuv = vec2(0.0); // Placeholder for UV vcolorout = vcolor[0]; EmitVertex(); glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(center + u - v, 1.0); vuv = vec2(0.0, 0.0); EmitVertex(); glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(center + u + v, 1.0); vuv = vec2(1.0, 0.0); EmitVertex(); glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(center - u + v, 1.0); vuv = vec2(0.0, 1.0); EmitVertex(); EndPrimitive(); } """ # Fragment Shader: Shading with Gaussian alpha/color fragmentshadersource = """ #version 430 core in vec2 vuv; in vec4 vcolorout; out vec4 fragcolor; uniform sampler2D gaussiantexture; // If using texture-based approach, otherwise direct void main() { // Evaluate Gaussian PDF at UV coordinates // alpha = exp(-0.5 dot(uv, uv)) opacity // fragcolor = vec4(color alpha, alpha) fragcolor = vcolorout; // Simplified; actual shading requires PDF evaluation } """ return vertexshadersource, geometryshadersource, fragmentshadersource def rendergaussians(gaussians, context): """ Renders 3D Gaussians using the OpenGL Geometry Shader pipeline. """ # 1. Upload Gaussian attributes to VBO vbo = context.createvbo(gaussians.attributes) # 2. Set up shader program vs, gs, fs = compileshaders() shaderprogram = context.createshaderprogram(vs, gs, fs) # 3. Bind VBO and execute draw call context.bindvbo(vbo) context.useshader(shaderprogram) # 4. Draw points which are expanded to quads by GS # glDrawArrays(GLPOINTS, 0, numgaussians) context.drawarrays(GLPOINTS, 0, gaussians.count) # 5. Read back or use framebuffer texture return context.getframebuffertexture() Parameters: dtype: Data type for attributes (torch.float or torch.half). texdtype: Output texture format (gl.GLRGBA16F, gl.GLRGBA32F, or gl.GLRGBA8). initbuffersize: Initial size for buffer allocation. inittexturesize: Initial size for texture allocation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Triangles: Modern graphics hardware rasterization pipelines are not well-optimized for small triangles, which can cause performance drops during high-resolution rendering with large Gaussians. Covariance Computation: The source notes that a fast 3D covariance computation (from scales and rotations) in the shader is not yet implemented; only a PyTorch implementation is available for precomputation. Caching persistent results (e.g., the 6 elements of the covariance matrix) is recommended for best performance. Backward Pass: No backward pass is supported yet. Performance: Can be 5-10x faster than the original software CUDA rasterizer (diff-gaussian-rasterization). Can be 2-3x faster if using offline rendering, though bottlenecked by copying rendered images. Scaling: Speedup is most visible with high pixel-to-point ratio (large Gaussians, small point count, high-res rendering). For extremely dense point clouds (> 1 million points), the CUDA implementation might be faster due to hardware rasterization inefficiencies with small triangles. Strengths: Offloads clipping, interpolation, and blending to the fixed-function OpenGL pipeline, reducing CPU/GPU synchronization overhead and explicit sorting stalls. Uses non-blocking data passing and GPU sorting to minimize stalls. Limitations: No backward pass support. Performance degrades with small triangles in high-resolution rendering. Requires precomputation of covariance in PyTorch as shader-side computation is not yet optimized. When to Use: Real-time and offline 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering where speed is critical and backward pass is not needed. Best for high pixel-to-point ratios. When Not to Use: Extremely dense point clouds (> 1 million points) where CUDA software rasterization may be faster. When backward pass is required. This method is part of the fastgauss library, developed by dendenxu, for real-time and offline 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It builds on the principles of differentiable rendering and Gaussian Splatting, aiming to optimize the rasterization step by leveraging standard graphics APIs instead of custom CUDA kernels. dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, https://github.com/dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: DP-GES Rendering
head: DP-GES depth peeling pass, Depth Peeling for Gaussian-Enhanced Surfels, Depth Peeling for High-Fidelity Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering, Depth Peeling for Surfel Rendering, Ours
body: DP-GES is a sort-free rendering method that combines 2D surfels with semi-transparent boundaries and 3D Gaussians to achieve high-fidelity novel view synthesis, eliminating aliasing and popping artifacts while enabling correct transmittance modulation. It sets itself apart from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization and sibling Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling by introducing a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 uses z-buffer-based depth peeling to extract the nearest three layers of depth, color, and opacity from surfels, and Stage 2 splats 3D Gaussians without sorting, modulating their weights by the transmittance from the peeled surfel layers. Unlike Gaussian-Enhanced Surfels (GES), which uses fully opaque surfels, DP-GES uses semi-transparent boundaries to mitigate aliasing from depth testing and allow differentiable joint optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 2D surfels S, a set of 3D Gaussians G, and camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics). Outputs: Final rendered image color C and weight W (normalized to produce color). Data Structures: Surfel Set S: S = \{pi, ri, si, Bi\}{i=1}^N. pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. si \in \mathbb{R}^2: Anisotropic scaling. Bi: Spherical Beta parameters for view-dependent color. Gaussian Set G: G = \{pi, \sigmai, ri, si, Bi\}{i=1}^M. pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \sigmai: Scale (implied from 3DGS context). ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. si \in \mathbb{R}^2: Scaling. Bi: Spherical Beta parameters. Texture Buffers: A four-channel texture storing peeled depth maps \{Di^s\}{i=1}^2 and transmittance maps \{Ti^s\}{i=1}^2. D3^s and T3^s are not stored because Gaussians beyond the third layer are culled by hardware depth testing. Depth and color/opacity buffers are allocated for the three intermediate peeling layers. Parameters: Number of depth peeling layers: 3. This balances quality and efficiency; 2 layers cause background leakage, and 4 layers drop FPS significantly due to memory bandwidth issues in OpenGL. Opacity modulation parameter w: Fixed constant shared by all surfels. Default value is 30. If w < 1, the surfel is fully translucent; if w = 255, it is completely opaque. Depth margin \epsilons: A tiny depth margin for culling and depth buffer updates. Steps: 1. Stage 1: Surfel Rasterization via Depth Peeling. Initialize depth buffer with far plane. For layer k = 1 to 3: Clear color and opacity buffers for layer k. Rasterize all surfels S. For each surfel fragment at pixel (x,y): Calculate local coordinates (x,y) on the surfel disc. Compute opacity \alphai(x,y) = \min(1, w \cdot G(x,y)), where G(x,y) = \exp(-\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}). Perform depth test against the current depth buffer. If the surfel depth di is greater than the stored depth d{stored} by a small margin, discard. To handle interleaved surfels correctly, surfel IDs are also written to the buffer to identify intersections. Write depth di, color Ci (from Bi), opacity \alphai, and surfel ID to the buffers for layer k. Update the depth buffer with di + \epsilons for subsequent layers. After rasterizing all surfels, the buffers contain the k-th peeled layer's depth Dk^s, color Ck^s, and opacity Ak^s. Post-processing (Surfel Compositing): Alpha-blend the 3 peeled layers using front-to-back compositing (same as 3DGS) to obtain final surfel color CS and transmittance maps \{Ti^s\}{i=0}^3: CS = \sum{i=1}^3 A{si} T{i-1} C{is} + T3^s Cb Ti^s = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i=0 \\ \prod{j=1}^i (1 - A{sj}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where Cb is the background color. Pack D1^s, D2^s, T1^s, T2^s into a four-channel texture. Note: T0^s = 1 is implicit. 2. Stage 2: Sort-Free Gaussian Splatting. Clear final color and weight accumulators. Enable depth testing, disable depth writing. For each pixel \hat{x} (or in parallel via fragment shader): Initialize CG(\hat{x}) = 0, WG(\hat{x}) = 0. For each Gaussian i covering pixel \hat{x}: Calculate Gaussian weight \alphai(\hat{x}) (standard 2D Gaussian projection). Determine Gaussian center depth di. Query transmittance ts(\hat{x}) based on di and peeled depths \{Dj^s\}: ts(\hat{x}) = \begin{cases} T0^s(\hat{x}) & \text{if } di < D1^s(\hat{x}) \\ T1^s(\hat{x}) & \text{if } D1^s(\hat{x}) \le di < D2^s(\hat{x}) \\ T2^s(\hat{x}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Perform depth culling: Calculate indicator 1{dt}(\hat{x}) = 1 if di < ds(\hat{x}) + \epsilons, else 0. ds(\hat{x}) is the depth of the nearest peeled layer i where Ti^s(\hat{x}) = 0. If all Ti^s > 0, ds(\hat{x}) = D3^s(\hat{x}). If 1{dt}(\hat{x}) == 1 and ts(\hat{x}) > 0: Get Gaussian color ci from Bi. Accumulate: CG(\hat{x}) \leftarrow CG(\hat{x}) + 1{dt}(\hat{x}) ci \alphai(\hat{x}) ts(\hat{x}) WG(\hat{x}) \leftarrow WG(\hat{x}) + 1{dt}(\hat{x}) \alphai(\hat{x}) ts(\hat{x}) Final Post-processing: Calculate total weight W{total} = WS + WG, where WS = \sum{i=1}^3 A{si} T{i-1} is the constant sum of surfel color weights. Normalize and output final color: C = \frac{CS + CG}{WS + WG}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderdpges(surfels, gaussians, width, height, farplane, epsilons): # Stage 1: Depth Peeling for Surfels # layerdepths[k][y][x], layercolors[k][y][x], layeropacities[k][y][x] for k=0,1,2 layerdepths = [[[0.0] width for in range(height)] for in range(3)] layercolors = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height) for in range(3)] layeropacities = [[[0.0] width for in range(height)] for in range(3)] currentdepthbuffer = [[farplane] width for in range(height)] for k in range(3): # Clear buffers for layer k for y in range(height): for x in range(width): layerdepths[k][y][x] = 0.0 layercolors[k][y][x] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] layeropacities[k][y][x] = 0.0 for surfel in surfels: for y in range(max(0, surfel.screenymin), min(height, surfel.screenymax)): for x in range(max(0, surfel.screenxmin), min(width, surfel.screenxmax)): localx, localy = surfel.tolocal(x, y) alpha = min(1.0, surfel.w math.exp(-(localx2 + localy2) / 2.0)) if surfel.depth > currentdepthbuffer[y][x] + epsilons: continue layerdepths[k][y][x] = surfel.depth layercolors[k][y][x] = surfel.getcolor() layeropacities[k][y][x] = alpha currentdepthbuffer[y][x] = surfel.depth + epsilons # Post-processing: Alpha blend peeled layers T = [1.0] 4 CS = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for i in range(1, 4): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): A = layeropacities[i-1][y][x] T[i] = T[i-1] (1.0 - A) CS[y][x][0] += A T[i-1] layercolors[i-1][y][x][0] CS[y][x][1] += A T[i-1] layercolors[i-1][y][x][1] CS[y][x][2] += A T[i-1] layercolors[i-1][y][x][2] packedtexture = [[[layerdepths[0][y][x], layerdepths[1][y][x], T[1], T[2]] for x in range(width)] for y in range(height)] # Stage 2: Sort-Free Gaussian Splatting CG = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] WG = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] cullingdepths = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ds = layerdepths[2][y][x] for i in range(3): if T[i+1] < 1e-6: ds = layerdepths[i][y][x] break cullingdepths[y][x] = ds for gaussian in gaussians: for y in range(max(0, gaussian.screenymin), min(height, gaussian.screenymax)): for x in range(max(0, gaussian.screenxmin), min(width, gaussian.screenxmax)): alpha = gaussian.weight(x, y) di = gaussian.depth if di < layerdepths[0][y][x]: ts = T[0] elif di < layerdepths[1][y][x]: ts = T[1] else: ts = T[2] if di < cullingdepths[y][x] + epsilons and ts > 0: c = gaussian.getcolor() CG[y][x][0] += c[0] alpha ts CG[y][x][1] += c[1] alpha ts CG[y][x][2] += c[2] alpha ts WG[y][x] += alpha ts # Final Normalization WS = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): for i in range(1, 4): WS[y][x] += layeropacities[i-1][y][x] T[i-1] TotalW = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] FinalColor = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): TotalW[y][x] = WS[y][x] + WG[y][x] if TotalW[y][x] < 1e-6: TotalW[y][x] = 1e-6 FinalColor[y][x][0] = (CS[y][x][0] + CG[y][x][0]) / TotalW[y][x] FinalColor[y][x][1] = (CS[y][x][1] + CG[y][x][1]) / TotalW[y][x] FinalColor[y][x][2] = (CS[y][x][2] + CG[y][x][2]) / TotalW[y][x] return FinalColor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interleaved Surfels: Two intersecting surfels might be peeled only once along their intersection line if IDs are not tracked. Solution: Write surfel ID into the buffer during rasterization to correctly identify and handle interleaved surfels. Background Color Leakage: If T3 is not zero, background color leaks through. The loss Lt encourages surfels to separate, driving T3 to zero. For pixels covered by fewer than 2 surfel layers, gradients for Lt are masked out. 4-Layer Peeling: Breaks 4-float alignment packing in OpenGL, increasing memory bandwidth usage and dropping FPS. Transparent Objects: Shows artifacts because surfels are mainly opaque. Time Complexity: The surfel rendering is O(Ns \cdot P) across 3 passes, where Ns is the number of surfels and P is pixels. Gaussian rendering is O(Ng \cdot P) but sort-free. Overall, it is faster than sorting-based methods. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for 3 layers of depth/color/opacity during peeling, plus the packed texture for Stage 2. Surfel count is typically <10% of Gaussian count, so peeling cost is negligible. Measured Performance: On RTX 4090 for Mip-NeRF360 dataset: >470 FPS at 1080p. 2.5x faster than vanilla 3DGS and 3x faster than DBS. Ablation FPS (1080p): Full 472, 2 layers 578, 4 layers 278. Strengths: Sort-free, high fidelity, eliminates popping and aliasing, differentiable joint optimization, integrable into existing engines (OpenGL). Limitations: Artifacts on transparent/semi-transparent objects (e.g., glass), slightly higher FLIP error than GES due to view-dependent effects, requires extra initialization and longer training time compared to 2DGS. DP-GES was proposed by Keyang Ye, Hongzhi Wu, and Kun Zhou from Zhejiang University and Hangzhou Research Institute of Holographic and AI Technology. It was published on arXiv in May 2026. It is an improved variant of Gaussian-Enhanced Surfels (GES) [42], addressing GES's limitations of aliasing artifacts and suboptimal reconstruction by introducing semi-transparent surfel boundaries and depth peeling.
