name: Per-fragment Voxel-Cell Mask Injection
head: Fragment SDF Shader Patch, H2′
body: Per-fragment Voxel-Cell Mask Injection is a technique for carving cube-shaped holes in 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by injecting a Signed Distance Field (SDF) evaluation into the fragment shader at runtime. It solves the visual artifacts caused by deleting whole splats (the "H2" baseline) by operating at the fragment level, producing clean, sharp cube edges without forking the underlying renderer. Unlike its sibling Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling which manages opacity globally, this method uses a 3D texture lookup to discard specific fragments, leaving neighboring voxels untouched. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Gaussian Splatting scene rendered via a WebGL renderer (specifically tested with Spark.js/Three.js), a voxel grid defining the carving space, and a set of active carve cells. Output: A rendered image where fragments falling within active carve cells are discarded, creating a hole with the exact shape of the voxel grid cells. Data Structures: The core state is managed by a FragmentSdfShaderPatch class exposing the following uniforms to the shader: 1. uCarveMask: A Data3DTexture (sampler3D) with dimensions matching the voxel grid counts (Nx, Ny, Nz). Data type is Uint8Array, initialized to 0 (not carved). 2. uVoxelOrigin: A vec3 representing the origin of the voxel grid in world space. 3. uVoxelSizeInv: A float equal to 1 / \text{voxelSize}. 4. uVoxelCountsInv: A vec3 equal to 1 / (Nx, Ny, Nz). 5. uCarveBoundsMin / uCarveBoundsMax: vec3 uniforms defining the union Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of all active carve cells for early-out optimization. 6. uCarveCount: An integer uniform tracking the number of active carve cells. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a FragmentSdfShaderPatch instance. Allocate a Data3DTexture sized according to the voxel grid counts. Initialize all texels to 0. 2. Shader Injection: Use the renderer's Material.onBeforeCompile hook to modify the compiled fragment shader source code. 3. Uniform Declaration: Insert the uniform declarations listed above before the out vec4 fragColor; statement. 4. Logic Insertion: Insert the SDF discard logic block immediately before the main body opener void main() { vec4 rgba = vRgba;. 5. Carve Operation: To carve a cell, flip the corresponding byte in the backing Uint8Array to 1. Update uCarveMask.needsUpdate = true to trigger a GPU texture upload. Expand the union AABB to include the new cell. 6. Uncarve Operation: Flip the byte back to 0. Update the texture. Recalculate the union AABB if necessary. Pseudocode: The injected GLSL logic, inserted at the start of the fragment shader's main() function: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. // Uniforms declared before main() uniform sampler3D uCarveMask; uniform vec3 uVoxelOrigin; uniform float uVoxelSizeInv; uniform vec3 uVoxelCountsInv; uniform vec3 uCarveBoundsMin; uniform vec3 uCarveBoundsMax; uniform int uCarveCount; in vec3 vWorldPos; void main() { // Inserted Logic Start if (uCarveCount > 0) { // Early-out AABB check if (vWorldPos.x >= uCarveBoundsMin.x && vWorldPos.x <= uCarveBoundsMax.x && vWorldPos.y >= uCarveBoundsMin.y && vWorldPos.y <= uCarveBoundsMax.y && vWorldPos.z >= uCarveBoundsMin.z && vWorldPos.z <= uCarveBoundsMax.z) { // Map world position to voxel grid coordinates vec3 coord = (vWorldPos - uVoxelOrigin) uVoxelSizeInv; // Normalize to [0, 1] range for texture lookup vec3 texCoord = coord uVoxelCountsInv; // Check if the fragment falls within a carved cell if (texture(uCarveMask, texCoord).r > 0.5) { discard; } } } // Inserted Logic End vec4 rgba = vRgba; //... rest of original shader } Parameters: Voxel Grid Resolution: Determined by the scene scale and desired carving precision. Not given in the sources. Tile Size: Inherits from parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, default 32x32 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on vWorldPos being accurate. If world-space reconstruction is imprecise, the cube edges may appear jagged or misaligned. Boundary Conditions: The AABB early-out is critical for performance. If the union AABB is not updated correctly when adding/removing carves, fragments may be incorrectly discarded or not discarded. Texture Updates: The needsUpdate flag must be set on the Data3DTexture after modifying the Uint8Array to ensure the GPU receives the new data. A variant that renders an axis-aligned box SDF with zero opacity to hide splats inside the box. It avoids thinning artifacts by operating per-sample rather than deleting whole splats. Choose this when you need to hide volumetric regions without affecting neighboring splats. Time Complexity: O(1) per-fragment cost via Data3DTexture lookup. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the voxel grid volume (Nx \times Ny \times Nz) bytes for the Uint8Array backing the Data3DTexture. Measured Performance: p95 latency of 9.6 ms for 256 carves on a scene with 177 K splats (butterfly.spz). Strengths: Produces sharp, clean cube-shaped edges; does not require forking the renderer; scales well with the number of carves (no per-splat sorting or deletion overhead). Limitations: Requires WebGL 2.0+ for Data3DTexture support; carving is limited to axis-aligned cubes defined by the voxel grid; performance depends on the cost of the 3D texture lookup. When to use: When precise, geometrically clean carving is required and the underlying renderer allows shader injection. When not to use: When non-cubic carving shapes are needed, or when the renderer does not support dynamic shader modification or 3D textures. Originating from the splatcarve project by Steve Kwon (2026), this method was developed to demonstrate that browser-based 3D Gaussian Splatting editors could perform complex volumetric edits without forking the rendering engine. It addresses the limitations of the "H2" baseline, which deleted whole splats grouped by voxel, resulting in rough, artifact-prone masks. The "H2′" breakthrough showed that injecting SDF evaluation via THREE.Material.onBeforeCompile could achieve interactive carving latencies with high visual fidelity. stevekwon211/splatcarve, https://github.com/stevekwon211/splatcarve, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF-based Voxel Carving
head: SplatEditCarve
body: SDF-based Voxel Carving removes 3D Gaussian Splatting samples within a volumetric region by rendering an axis-aligned box Signed Distance Field (SDF) with zero opacity. It acts as a visual mask that hides splat samples inside the box while leaving samples outside unchanged, avoiding the thinning artifacts caused by deleting whole splats. Unlike packed-array opacity mutation which deletes whole splats (causing visible thinning in neighboring voxels for anisotropic splats), SDF mutation is per-sample. Inside the box, the sample becomes invisible; outside, it remains untouched, resulting in a hole with the exact shape of the box. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A SplatMesh containing the 3D Gaussian splats, a target voxel defined by localCenter and voxelSize, and a SplatEdit component instance. Output: A visual modification where splats intersecting the voxel volume are masked out (opacity zeroed) without modifying the underlying splat data structure. Data Structures: SplatEdit: A component attached to the SplatMesh that manages SDF masks and maintains a map of active SDFs keyed by voxel identifier. SplatEditSdf: Represents a single carving primitive with fields type (BOX), invert (false), opacity (0), position (local center), and scale (half voxelSize per dimension). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the SplatEdit component with rgbaBlendMode set to MULTIPLY, softEdge set to 0, and sdfSmooth set to 0. 2. Attach the SplatEdit instance as a child of the SplatMesh so that its coordinate system aligns with the mesh's local frame. 3. To carve a voxel at localCenter with voxelSize: create a new SplatEditSdf with type set to BOX, invert set to false, and opacity set to 0. Set the SDF position to the voxel's local center and scale to half the voxelSize in all dimensions. Add the SDF to the SplatEdit instance and store the reference in a map keyed by the voxel identifier. 4. To uncarve: remove the SDF from the SplatEdit instance and delete the reference from the map. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: rgbaBlendMode: Set to MULTIPLY. softEdge: Set to 0. sdfSmooth: Set to 0. voxelSize: The side length of the cubic voxel being carved. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: This method is a visual mask only; the underlying splat data is unmodified. Hard deletes (e.g., for PLY export or multiplayer sync) require baking the SDFs back into packed-array opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class SplatEditSdf: def init(self, sdftype, invert, opacity, position, scale): self.type = sdftype self.invert = invert self.opacity = opacity self.position = position self.scale = scale class SplatEdit: def init(self): self.rgbablendmode = "MULTIPLY" self.softedge = 0 self.sdfsmooth = 0 self.activesdfs = {} # Map: voxelid -> SplatEditSdf def addcarve(self, voxelid, localcenter, voxelsize): sdf = SplatEditSdf( sdftype="BOX", invert=False, opacity=0, position=localcenter, scale=Vec3(voxelsize / 2, voxelsize / 2, voxelsize / 2)) self.activesdfs[voxelid] = sdf def removecarve(self, voxelid): if voxelid in self.activesdfs: del self.activesdfs[voxelid] Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Avoids thinning artifacts in neighboring voxels that occur when deleting whole splats, particularly for anisotropic splats. Provides precise, box-shaped holes. Limitations: Does not remove data, only masks it. Requires additional processing (baking) for permanent removal. When to Use: Use when visual editing of a Gaussian Splatting scene is required without permanently altering the source data or causing visible artifacts from partial splat deletion. When Not to Use: Do not use when permanent data reduction is needed for export or network transmission without a subsequent baking step. Origin: The technique is part of the splatcarve project by stevekwon211. History and Development: The method is described in the context of a stack-based editing system for 3D Gaussian Splatting, where operations are recorded in a history stack. Where it is used: Used in real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting viewers/editors for non-destructive voxel carving. stevekwon211/splatcarve, https://github.com/stevekwon211/splatcarve, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Thread-efficient Partial Rendering
head: Multi-view Tiled Partial Rendering, Subsampled Tile Rendering
body: Thread-efficient partial rendering is a GPU rasterization optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to reduce the computational overhead of multi-view training. It solves the problem of low GPU utilization caused by naive binary masking in tiled rendering, where idle threads wait for active threads to finish. Unlike naive multi-view training which renders all pixels for all views, or naive partial rendering with masks which leaves most threads in a block idle, this method maintains the same number of training pixels as single-view training while maximizing parallelization by assigning multiple GPU blocks to a single tile. The method modifies the standard tiled rasterization loop by decoupling the number of threads per block from the tile size, allowing multiple blocks to cooperatively render a single tile for multiple viewpoints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: K: The number of participating viewpoints. N: The number of pixels (and standard threads) in a tile. DI: A sorted array of Gaussian primitives projected onto the image plane of viewpoint I. PA: An array mapping thread indices to specific pixel coordinates to render. A: An index array defining which pixels are subsampled for each viewpoint. Outputs: Final color and opacity values written to pixel locations PA[k,i]. Data Structures: Shared Memory (Shmemk): An array of size N/K shared across all threads i within block k. Validity Flag (isValid{k,i}): A boolean flag for each thread indicating if its assigned pixel is within image bounds. Intermediate Value (V{k,i}): A temporal variable storing the intermediate result of alpha blending for thread i in block k. Parameters: i: Index of a thread in a tile. k: Index of a GPU block, ranging from 1 to K. N/K: The number of threads per block, which must equal the number of subsampled pixels for the assigned viewpoint. Algorithm Steps: 1. Subsampling: For each viewpoint, subsample the pixels to be rendered within a tile. Pass these subsampled pixel indices as an index array to the rasterizer. 2. Block Assignment: Assign K GPU blocks to a single tile. The number of blocks equals the number of viewpoints K. 3. Thread Configuration: Ensure each block k has exactly N/K threads, matching the number of subsampled pixels for that viewpoint. 4. Viewpoint Allocation: Assign each block k to a specific viewpoint k. 5. Execution: For each block k from 1 to K, execute the following kernel logic: Initialize shared memory Shmemk of size N/K. For each thread i from 1 to N/K in block k: Set isValid{k,i} to true. If the pixel coordinate PA[k,i] is outside the image bounds, set isValid{k,i} to false. While there is unfetched data left in the sorted Gaussian array DI for the assigned viewpoint: Load data from DI at index offset (N/K) + i into Shmemk[i]. If isValid{k,i} is true, update V{k,i} by calling alphaBlending(Shmemk, V{k,i}). Synchronize all threads in block k using synchronize(). Increment offset by 1. Assign the final blended value V{k,i} to pixel PA[k,i]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def threadefficientpartialrenderingblock(k, Nsub, DI, PA): # Shared memory allocation Shmem = [None] Nsub # Thread index within the block (standard execution model intrinsic) i = getthreadindexinblock() # 1. Initialize validity flag isvalid = True # 2. Check image bounds pixelcoord = PA[k, i] if not iswithinimagebounds(pixelcoord): isvalid = False offset = 0 # 3. Process Gaussians while dataexistsinDI(DI, offset, Nsub, i): # Load Gaussian data into shared memory # Index calculation: offset (N/K) + i gaussiandata = getgaussianfromsortedarray(DI, offset Nsub + i) Shmem[i] = gaussiandata # 4. Alpha Blending if valid if isvalid: # Vk,i is stored in thread-local or shared memory depending on implementation # Assuming Vk,i is accumulated across iterations Vki = alphablending(Shmem, Vki) # 5. Synchronize threads in the block synchronizeblock() # 6. Increment offset offset += 1 # 7. Write final result if isvalid: writetopixel(pixelcoord, Vki) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Idle Threads: Naive partial rendering using a binary mask in 3DGS causes idle threads because GPU threads are allocated in blocks. If a tile is masked such that only one pixel is unmasked, all other threads in the block wait, leading to low GPU utilization. This method eliminates that by ensuring every thread in a block has a valid pixel to render. Block Size Alignment: While 3DGS typically aligns tile size with block size, this method requires decreasing the block size to allow multiple blocks to render a single tile. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: The method reduces rasterizer overhead compared to naive multi-view training by rendering only a subset of pixels per view, while maintaining the same total number of training pixels as single-view training. Memory Complexity: Uses shared memory Shmemk of size N/K per block. Performance: Maximizes GPU utilization by eliminating idle threads that occur in naive binary masking approaches. Strengths: Effective parallelization for multi-view training; reduces overhead without sacrificing training pixel count. Limitations: Requires custom kernel implementation to handle multiple blocks per tile and dynamic subsampling indices. When to use: Multi-view training of 3D Gaussian Splatting where GPU utilization is critical. The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient multi-view training for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the inefficiencies of standard tiled rendering when applied to multi-view scenarios, specifically the problem of thread divergence and idle threads caused by binary masking. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (GPU)
head: Gaussian Rasterization (GPU), GaussianRasterizer, RasterizeGaussians, Gaussian Splatting Rasterizer, 3DGS Rasterization
body: A differentiable rasterization method for 3D Gaussians that sorts Gaussians by tile and depth to perform alpha blending in parallel per tile. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of 3D Gaussian splats to a 2D screen while maintaining exact gradients for all Gaussian parameters (means, opacities, scales, rotations, spherical harmonics) via a CUDA backend. It sets itself apart from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by implementing the specific sorting, binning, and tile-based parallel rendering kernels required for the standard 3DGS forward and backward passes, often exposed as a torch.autograd.Function. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes P 3D Gaussians defined by 3D means \mathbf{\mu}{3D}, scales \mathbf{s}, rotations \mathbf{q} (quaternions), opacities \alpha, and color representations (Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{SH} or direct colors \mathbf{c}). Camera parameters include view matrix \mathbf{V}, projection matrix \mathbf{P}, and field of view tangents \tan \thetax, \tan \thetay. Outputs are the rendered RGB image \mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, radii \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{Z}^P, and optionally depth/weight buffers. The backward pass returns gradients for all input parameters. Data Structures: The implementation relies on three main GPU buffers managed by the C++/CUDA backend: 1. GeometryState: Stores per-Gaussian precomputed data. depths: float[P] means2D: float2[P] (screen-space center) cov3D: float[P6] (upper triangle of 3x3 3D covariance) rgb: float[P3] (precomputed color) conicopacity: float4[P] (x,y,z=conic matrix components, w=opacity) internalradii: int[P] tilestouched: uint32t[P] pointoffsets: int[P] (prefix sum of tiles touched) 2. BinningState: Stores sorting keys and values. pointlistkeysunsorted: uint64t[P] (Key: high 32 bits = tile ID, low 32 bits = depth) pointlistunsorted: uint32t[P] (Value: Gaussian index) pointlistkeys: uint64t[P] (Sorted keys) pointlist: uint32t[P] (Sorted indices) 3. ImageState: Stores per-pixel state. accumalpha: float[HW] ncontrib: int[HW] ranges: uint2[HW] (start/end indices in sorted pointlist for each tile/pixel) Parameters: BLOCKX, BLOCKY: Tile dimensions in pixels. Typical value: 16x16. BLOCKSIZE: Threads per block. Typical value: 256. NUMCHANNELS: 3 (RGB). scalemodifier: Multiplier for scale components. Typical value: 1.0. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Projection & Conic Computation): For each Gaussian i: a. Frustum Culling: Check if the Gaussian is within the camera view. If not, skip. b. 3D Covariance: Compute 3D covariance matrix \Sigma{3D} from scale \mathbf{s} and rotation \mathbf{q}. If precomputed, use it. Apply scalemodifier. c. Jacobian: Compute the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. Let \mathbf{W} be the rotation part of the view matrix. The transformation matrix is \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{J}. d. 2D Covariance: Compute screen-space covariance \Sigma{2D} = \mathbf{T} \Sigma{3D} \mathbf{T}^T. e. Low-Pass Filter: Add 0.3 to the diagonal elements of \Sigma{2D} to ensure minimum pixel width/height. f. Conic Matrix: Invert \Sigma{2D} to get the conic matrix \mathbf{C}{2D} = \Sigma{2D}^{-1}. Store as conicopacity where x=C{00}, y=C{01}, z=C{11}, w=\alpha. g. Radius: Compute eigenvalues \lambda{1,2} of \Sigma{2D}: \lambda{1,2} = 0.5 \left( (\Sigma{2D}){00} + (\Sigma{2D}){11} \right) \pm \sqrt{\max(0.1f, 0.25 \left( (\Sigma{2D}){00} - (\Sigma{2D}){11} \right)^2 + (\Sigma{2D}){01}^2)} Calculate radius r = \lceil 3 \sqrt{\max(\lambda1, \lambda2)} \rceil. h. Tile Bounding Box: Determine the tiles touched by the Gaussian's bounding box. i. Key Generation: For each touched tile, generate a 64-bit key: (tileid << 32) | depthpacked. Store Gaussian index as value. If r \le 0, skip. 2. Sorting and Binning: a. Prefix Sum: Compute an inclusive prefix sum over tilestouched to determine offsets for writing to the binning buffer. b. Radix Sort: Sort the generated key/value pairs using CUDA Radix Sort (cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs) to order Gaussians first by tile ID and then by depth. c. Range Calculation: Identify start and end indices in the sorted list for each tile by comparing tile IDs of consecutive keys. Store these ranges in ImageState.ranges. 3. Rasterization (Tile-Parallel Rendering): Each thread block handles one tile. a. Load Range: Load the range of points for the tile from the sorted pointlist. b. Batch Processing: Iterate over Gaussians in batches. Collectively fetch Gaussian data (ID, xy, conicopacity) from global to shared memory. c. Pixel Loop: For each pixel (u,v) in the tile: i. Initialize transmittance T = 1.0 and color C = \text{background}. ii. For each Gaussian j in the tile's range: 1. Compute displacement \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{xy}j - \mathbf{pix}{uv}. 2. Compute power: \text{power} = -0.5 \left( C{00} dx^2 + C{11} dy^2 \right) - C{01} dx dy 3. If \text{power} > 0, continue (outside ellipse). 4. Compute alpha: \alphaj = \min(0.99, \alphaj^{\text{orig}} \cdot e^{\text{power}}). 5. If \alphaj < 1/255, continue. 6. Composite: C \leftarrow C + \alphaj \cdot \mathbf{color}j \cdot T T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphaj) 7. If T < 0.0001, mark done for this pixel. d. Write Output: Write final T, contribution count, and C to output buffers. 4. Backward Pass: The backward pass restores saved tensors from the forward pass (ctx.saveforbackward) and calls the C++ backward kernel C.rasterizegaussiansbackward. It computes gradients for means3D, means2D, dc, sh, opacities, scales, rotations, and cov3Dsprecomp. The exact gradient formulas are implemented in the CUDA kernel, utilizing the saved radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, and imgBuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Actual implementation is in CUDA/C++. """ P = means3D.shape[0] # 1. Precompute 2D properties # In reality, this is done in preprocessCUDA kernel # Compute 3D covariance from scales/rotations # Transform to 2D using Jacobian of projection # Compute conic matrix and radius # Placeholder for CUDA kernel call # geomState = preprocessCUDA(P, means3D, scales, rotations, opacities, shs, dc, # viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg, scalemodifier,...) # 2. Generate Keys and Values # For each Gaussian, determine tiles touched # Create keys: (tileid << 32) | depth # Create values: gaussianindex # Placeholder for CUDA kernel call # binningState = duplicateWithKeys(P, geomState.means2D, geomState.conicopacity, # geomState.depths, geomState.tilestouched,...) # 3. Sort # Sort keys and values using Radix Sort # Placeholder: cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs # 4. Render # Launch tile-parallel kernel # tilegrid = (width + BLOCKX - 1) // BLOCKX, (height + BLOCKY - 1) // BLOCKY # renderCUDA<<<tilegrid, BLOCKSIZE>>>(...) # Return outputs return color, radii, invdepths, accumweights def rasterizegaussiansbackward(gradoutcolor, savedtensors): """ Simplified Python-like representation of the backward pass logic. """ # Restore saved tensors means3D, scales, rotations, opacities, shs, dc, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = savedtensors # Call backward CUDA kernel # Placeholder: C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(...) # Return gradients return gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, graddc, gradsh, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations Multi-scale technique decomposing the image into a Laplacian pyramid of Gaussian splats for independent optimization and rendering at different resolutions. Validation and dispatch layer for MiniGS-specific rasterizer entry points, enabling auxiliary statistics for blur-aware splitting and depth back-sampling during training. Variant accepting camera rotation and translation deltas to render with pose perturbations, returning pixel coverage statistics. Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step O(P \log P) and the rasterization step O(P + H \cdot W \cdot K), where K is the average number of Gaussians per tile. Memory Complexity: O(P) for geometry and binning buffers, O(H \cdot W) for image state. Performance: Highly optimized for GPU parallelism. Tile-based approach ensures memory coalescing and efficient use of shared memory. Typical tile size is 16x16 pixels. Strengths: Differentiable, fast, supports millions of Gaussians, exact gradients. Limitations: Requires significant VRAM for large scenes due to sorting buffers. Depth packing assumes depth fits in 32 bits. When to use: Standard 3DGS rendering and training. When not to use: If VRAM is extremely limited, consider Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling or other memory-efficient variants. Originated from the 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023). The method was developed to enable real-time differentiable rendering of 3D scenes represented as Gaussian splats. It builds on the tile-based rasterization techniques used in traditional graphics pipelines but adapts them for the specific needs of Gaussian splatting, including conic matrix approximation and alpha blending. The implementation is typically provided as a custom PyTorch autograd function wrapping a C++/CUDA backend. name: FastGS Residual Pyramid Rendering
head: Laplacian pyramid accumulation, multi-scale Gaussian rendering
body: FastGS Residual Pyramid Rendering is a multi-scale technique that decomposes the target image into a Laplacian pyramid of Gaussian splats. The coarsest level renders the base image, while subsequent levels render signed residuals (differences) that are upsampled and accumulated to reconstruct the final high-resolution image. It sets itself apart from standard single-scale rasterization by allowing independent optimization and rendering of detail at different resolutions, which facilitates efficient training and high-fidelity reconstruction of complex scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A list of Gaussian models (gaussianslist) organized from coarsest (L0) to finest (L{n-1}); a list of camera views; ground-truth images; a rasterization function (renderfn); and a pyramid processing module (pyramidfunc). Outputs: A rendered image tensor; intermediate buffers for accumulated predictions and ground-truth residuals; and metadata including visibility filters and radii. Data Structures: gaussianslist: A list of gaussians objects, where each object contains 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients). gtgaussianpyrdict: A dictionary mapping camera IDs to lists of ground-truth Gaussian pyramid levels. predaccumulateddict: A dictionary mapping camera IDs to the accumulated prediction tensor at each stage. renderpkg: A dictionary returned by renderfn containing: 'render': torch.Tensor, the rendered image. 'viewspacepoints': torch.Tensor, shape [N, 4], requires gradient. 'visibilityfilter': torch.Tensor, indices where screen-space radii are greater than 0. 'radii': torch.Tensor, screen-space radii of splats. 'accummetriccounts': torch.Tensor, metric accumulation buffer. Parameters: posandneg: Boolean flag. When False, the rasterizer outputs values clamped to [0, 1]. When True, it outputs signed values in [-1.0, 1.0] to represent residuals. mult: Scalar multiplier passed to GaussianRasterizationSettings, likely controlling opacity or scale weighting. rendersize: Target resolution for the current stage, derived from the ground-truth pyramid level shape. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load Gaussian models from subfolders L0 to L{n-1} into gaussianslist. 2. Ground-Truth Pyramid Construction: For each view, compute the ground-truth Gaussian pyramid using pyramidfunc.buildpyrgaussian(gtfull.to('cuda').unsqueeze(0)). Store results in gtgaussianpyrdict. 3. Stage Iteration: Iterate istage from 0 to len(gaussianslist) - 1. 4. Retrieve Data: Retrieve gaussians = gaussianslist[-istage-1] (note: the source code iterates backwards through the list, so index -istage-1 accesses the coarsest level first if the list is ordered finest-to-coarsest, or vice versa depending on construction; the source implies L0 is processed first). Retrieve gtgau = gtgaussianpyrdict[viewpointcam.uid][-istage-1].squeeze(0). 5. Rendering and Accumulation: If istage == 0: Call renderpkg = renderfn(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt.mult, rendersize=gtgau.shape[-2:], posandneg=False). Extract rendering = renderpkg["render"]. Set predaccumulated = rendering. Set gt = gtgau. If istage > 0: Call renderpkg = renderfn(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt.mult, rendersize=gtgau.shape[-2:], posandneg=True). Extract rendering = renderpkg["render"]. Compute upsampled = pyramidfunc.getupsampled([rendering.unsqueeze(0), predaccumulated.unsqueeze(0)]). Squeeze upsampled to remove batch dimension: upsampled = upsampled.squeeze(0). Update predaccumulated = rendering + upsampled. Normalize rendering to [0, 1] via (rendering + 1.0) / 2.0. Compute gt = gtgau - upsampled. Normalize gt to [0, 1] via (gt + 1.0) / 2.0. 6. Training/Update: Use the computed rendering and gt for loss calculation and gradient backpropagation for the current stage's Gaussians. 7. Inheritance/Transition: After each stage (except the last), prepare Gaussians for the next stage. This may involve densification, pruning, or extracting a subset of Gaussians based on pipe.inheritstate (e.g., "keepandadc", "onlyxyz", "withstate"). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def renderfastgsstage(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt, pyramidfunc, gtgau, predaccumulated, istage, renderfn): """ Renders a single stage of the FastGS Residual Pyramid. Args: view: Camera viewpoint object. gaussians: Gaussian model object for the current stage. pipeline: Pipeline configuration. background: Background color tensor. opt: Options object containing 'mult'. pyramidfunc: Module with buildpyrgaussian and getupsampled. gtgau: Ground truth tensor for the current pyramid level. predaccumulated: Accumulated prediction from previous stages. istage: Current stage index (0 for coarsest). renderfn: The rasterization function. Returns: rendering: Rendered image tensor. predaccumulated: Updated accumulated prediction. gt: Normalized ground truth for loss computation. """ rendersize = gtgau.shape[-2:] if istage == 0: # Coarsest level: render base image renderpkg = renderfn( view, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt.mult, rendersize=rendersize, posandneg=False) rendering = renderpkg["render"] predaccumulated = rendering gt = gtgau else: # Subsequent levels: render signed residuals renderpkg = renderfn( view, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt.mult, rendersize=rendersize, posandneg=True) rendering = renderpkg["render"] # Upsample the previous accumulated prediction and the current residual # Note: getupsampled likely performs bilinear or nearest-neighbor upsampling # to match the resolution of the current stage's ground truth. upsampled = pyramidfunc.getupsampled([ rendering.unsqueeze(0), predaccumulated.unsqueeze(0) ]) upsampled = upsampled.squeeze(0) # Update accumulated prediction predaccumulated = rendering + upsampled # Normalize rendering to [0, 1] for loss computation renderingnormalized = (rendering + 1.0) / 2.0 # Compute residual ground truth gt = gtgau - upsampled # Normalize ground truth to [0, 1] gt = (gt + 1.0) / 2.0 rendering = renderingnormalized return rendering, predaccumulated, gt def fastgsrenderloop(gaussianslist, gtfull, viewpointcams, pipeline, background, opt, pyramidfunc, renderfn): """ Main loop for FastGS Residual Pyramid Rendering. """ device = gtfull.device # 1. Build Ground-Truth Pyramid gtgaussianpyrdict = {} for viewpointcam in viewpointcams: gtfullcuda = gtfull.to(device).unsqueeze(0) pyrgpu = pyramidfunc.buildpyrgaussian(gtfullcuda) # Store levels, detaching and moving to device gtgaussianpyrdict[viewpointcam.uid] = [pyrgpu[0]] + [lvl.detach().to(device) for lvl in pyrgpu[1:]] # 2. Initialize Accumulated Predictions predaccumulateddict = {} # 3. Iterate through stages numstages = len(gaussianslist) for istage in range(numstages): # Retrieve Gaussians for this stage # Note: Source code uses gaussianslist[-istage-1], implying list order might be finest-to-coarsest # or the indexing is specific to the implementation. Assuming standard L0..Ln-1 order where L0 is coarsest: gaussians = gaussianslist[istage] for viewpointcam in viewpointcams: gtgau = gtgaussianpyrdict[viewpointcam.uid][istage].squeeze(0) predaccumulated = predaccumulateddict.get(viewpointcam.uid, None) # Render current stage rendering, predaccumulated, gt = renderfastgsstage( viewpointcam, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt, pyramidfunc, gtgau, predaccumulated, istage, renderfn) predaccumulateddict[viewpointcam.uid] = predaccumulated # Perform training step with 'rendering' and 'gt' # (Loss calculation and optimizer step omitted as per source structure) # Prepare Gaussians for next stage (inheritance/densification) if istage < numstages - 1: # Logic for inheritstate, densification, pruning # See source for specific implementation details pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: PyTorch Version Compatibility: The viewspacepoints tensor is initialized with requiresgrad=True, but retaingrad() may fail on older PyTorch versions. The code uses a try-except block to handle this gracefully. Resolution Mismatch: The rendersize must match the shape of the current ground-truth pyramid level gtgau.shape[-2:] to ensure correct upsampling and accumulation. Signed Values: When posandneg=True, the rasterizer outputs values in [-1.0, 1.0]. Failure to normalize these values to [0, 1] before loss computation will lead to incorrect gradients. Time Complexity: The method requires rendering at multiple scales. If there are N stages, the total rendering time is roughly proportional to N times the cost of a single rasterization pass, plus the cost of pyramid construction and upsampling. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases with the number of stages due to the storage of multiple Gaussian models and intermediate pyramid levels. Strengths: Allows for efficient training by starting with coarse details and refining them. Reduces artifacts associated with single-scale rendering at high resolutions. Limitations: Requires careful management of Gaussian inheritance and densification between stages. More complex implementation than single-scale rasterization. When to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of complex scenes is required, and training time/quality trade-offs favor multi-scale optimization. When not to use: For simple scenes or real-time applications where the overhead of multi-scale rendering is prohibitive. FastGS Residual Pyramid Rendering was introduced in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting to improve rendering quality and training efficiency. It builds on the principles of Laplacian pyramids, applying them to the Gaussian splatting framework. The method was developed as part of the "Laplacian-GS" project. name: MiniGS Auxiliary & Depth Rendering Interface
head: MiniGS depth rasterization, MiniGS rasterization auxiliary
body: The MiniGS Auxiliary & Depth Rendering Interface serves as a validation and dispatch layer for MiniGS-specific rasterizer entry points, enabling the return of auxiliary statistics required for blur-aware splitting and depth back-sampling during training. It distinguishes itself from standard rendering by enforcing strict preconditions to ensure the availability of gradient-bearing attributes, thereby supporting the structural optimization phases of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction rather than final inference. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: means3D: 3D Gaussian centers. means2D: Projected 2D Gaussian centers. dc: Diffuse color tensor. shs: Spherical harmonics coefficients tensor. opacities: Gaussian opacity tensor. scales: Gaussian scale tensor. rotations: Gaussian rotation tensor. rastersettings: Configuration object containing inferenceonly (bool) and pixelweights (tensor). Outputs: Returns the result of either minigsrasterizegaussiansaux or minigsrasterizegaussiansdepth, depending on the internal logic of the dispatched function (typically determined by the specific MiniGS variant or settings not fully detailed in the source, but the interface ensures one of these two is called). Data Structures rastersettings: inferenceonly: Boolean flag. Must be False for this interface to function. pixelweights: Tensor. Must be None or empty. Numbered Steps 1. Validate Inference Mode: Check if rastersettings.inferenceonly is True. If so, raise an exception, as this interface does not support inference-only mode. 2. Validate Pixel Weights: Check if rastersettings.pixelweights is not None and has a non-zero number of elements (numel() > 0). If so, raise an exception, as pixel weights are not supported in this path. 3. Validate Attribute Tensors: Ensure that dc, shs, scales, and rotations are not None. These attributes are required for the auxiliary and depth rasterization processes. 4. Dispatch: Call minigsrasterizegaussiansaux with the arguments means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, and rastersettings. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minigsauxiliarydepthinterface( means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings): # Step 1: Check inferenceonly if rastersettings.inferenceonly: raise Exception("MiniGS auxiliary rendering does not support inferenceonly=True.") # Step 2: Check pixelweights if rastersettings.pixelweights is not None and rastersettings.pixelweights.numel() > 0: raise Exception("MiniGS auxiliary rendering does not support pixelweights.") # Step 3 & 4: Validate attributes and dispatch # Note: The source code snippet directly dispatches to minigsrasterizegaussiansaux # without explicit None checks for dc, shs, scales, rotations in the provided snippet, # but the notes state these must not be None. We assume the dispatched function # or a preceding layer handles the None check, or we add it for safety. if dc is None or shs is None or scales is None or rotations is None: raise ValueError("dc, shs, scales, and rotations must not be None.") return minigsrasterizegaussiansaux( means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings) Parameters inferenceonly: bool. Must be False. pixelweights: tensor. Must be None or empty. dc: tensor. Diffuse color. shs: tensor. Spherical harmonics coefficients. scales: tensor. Gaussian scales. rotations: tensor. Gaussian rotations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Inference Mode: The interface explicitly fails if inferenceonly=True. Pixel Weights: The interface explicitly fails if pixelweights are provided and non-empty. Missing Attributes: The method requires all five Gaussian attribute tensors (dc, shs, scales, rotations, opacities) to be present; failure to provide them results in errors. Not given in the sources. The MiniGS Auxiliary & Depth Rendering Interface is part of the MiniGS (Mini Gaussian Splatting) implementation, specifically designed to support training-time operations such as blur-aware splitting and depth back-sampling. It is utilized in the context of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction and is integrated into the training loop of the Improved-GS project. name: GaussianRasterizer_w_pose
body: A variant of the Gaussian rasterizer that accepts camera rotation and translation deltas to render the scene with pose perturbations, returning an additional count of touched pixels (ntouched). It differs from the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (GPU) by exposing pose perturbation inputs and tracking pixel coverage statistics for optimization feedback. Inputs: means3D: 3D Gaussian means, shape (N, 3). means2D: 2D projected means, shape (N, 2), initialized with requiresgrad=True and retaingrad(). shs or colorsprecomp: Spherical Harmonics coefficients or precomputed RGB colors. opacities: Opacity values, shape (N, 1). scales and rotations: Scale and rotation parameters, or cov3Dprecomp if pipe.computecov3Dpython is true. theta, rho: Camera rotation and translation deltas. viewpointcam: Camera object providing FoV and projection matrix. pipe: Configuration object controlling SH evaluation and covariance computation. Outputs: Dictionary with keys: render (image), viewspacepoints (means2D), visibilityfilter (boolean mask), radii, rendereddepth, renderedalpha, ntouched. Steps: 1. Initialize screenspacepoints tensor with requiresgrad=True and call retaingrad() to enable gradients for 2D means. 2. Compute tanfovx and tanfovy from viewpointcam.FoVx and viewpointcam.FoVy. 3. Construct GaussianRasterizationSettingswpose with projmatrixraw, shdegree, campos, and prefiltered=False. 4. Instantiate GaussianRasterizerwpose with the settings. 5. Determine covariance representation: if pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, compute cov3Dprecomp from pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier); otherwise, pass scales and rotations separately. 6. Determine color representation: if overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython is true, convert SHs to RGB in Python using evalsh and clamp; otherwise, pass shs directly. 7. Call the rasterizer with means3D, means2D, shs/colorsprecomp, opacities, scales/rotations/cov3Dprecomp, and pose deltas theta and rho. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderwpose(means3D, means2D, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, viewpointcam, pipe, theta, rho, overridecolor=None): # Step 1: Initialize screenspacepoints for gradient tracking screenspacepoints = means2D.clone().detach() screenspacepoints.requiresgrad = True screenspacepoints.retaingrad() # Step 2: Compute tanfovx and tanfovy tanfovx = torch.tan(viewpointcam.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = torch.tan(viewpointcam.FoVy 0.5) # Step 3: Construct rasterization settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettingswpose( imageheight=int(viewpointcam.imageheight), imagewidth=int(viewpointcam.imagewidth), tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, projmatrixraw=viewpointcam.projectionmatrix @ viewpointcam.worldviewtransform, shdegree=pipe.SHdegree, campos=viewpointcam.cameracenter, prefiltered=False, debug=False) # Step 4: Instantiate rasterizer rasterizer = GaussianRasterizerwpose(rastersettings=rastersettings) # Step 5: Determine covariance representation if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier=1.0) # scalingmodifier assumed 1.0 if not specified else: cov3Dprecomp = None # Step 6: Determine color representation if overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython: colorsprecomp = torch.clamp(evalsh(pipe.SHdegree, shs, means3D), 0.0, 1.0) else: colorsprecomp = shs if overridecolor is None else overridecolor # Step 7: Call rasterizer renderpkg = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=colorsprecomp, opacities=opacities, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp, theta=theta, rho=rho) return renderpkg Not given in the sources.
