name: PyTorch Rasterization Wrapper
head: GaussianRasterizer Wrapper, PyTorch Autograd Rasterizer Wrapper
body: The PyTorch Rasterization Wrapper is a torch.autograd.Function that bridges Python and a C++ rasterization kernel for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It handles the construction of argument tuples for the forward and backward passes, manages buffer persistence, and optionally supports debug mode by copying arguments to the CPU. It serves as the Python-facing interface for the underlying GPU-accelerated rasterizer. Inputs: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D Gaussian means. opacities: Tensor of shape (N, 1), Gaussian opacities. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3), Gaussian scales. rotations: Tensor of shape (N, 4), Gaussian rotations (quaternions). rastersettings: Object containing scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, imageheight, imagewidth, campos, prefiltered, mode, and debug flags. gradoutcolor: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), gradient of the output color image (used in backward pass). Outputs: color: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), rendered color image. radii: Tensor of shape (N), radii of projected Gaussians (used to identify visible Gaussians). Data Structures: geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer: Internal buffers managed by the C++ kernel. These are saved in ctx for the backward pass. Steps: 1. Forward Pass Argument Construction: Construct the args tuple for the C++ forward rasterizer: python args = ( means3D, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.campos, rastersettings.prefiltered, rastersettings.mode, rastersettings.debug) 2. Debug Mode Handling: If rastersettings.debug is true, perform a deep copy of args to CPU tensors for inspection. 3. C++ Forward Rasterization: Call the C++ rasterizer function C.rasterizegaussians(args). python numrendered, color, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = C.rasterizegaussians(args) 4. Save for Backward: Save the necessary tensors and buffers in ctx for the backward pass: python ctx.saveforbackward(means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) Store rastersettings and numrendered in ctx as well (implied by backward usage). 5. Backward Pass Argument Construction: Restore saved tensors from ctx. Construct the args tuple for the C++ backward rasterizer: python argsbackward = ( means3D, radii, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, gradoutcolor, rastersettings.campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rastersettings.mode, rastersettings.debug) 6. C++ Backward Rasterization: Call the C++ backward rasterizer function C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbackward): python (gradmeans2D, gradopacities,, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradscales, gradrotations) = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbackward) 7. Return Gradients: Return the gradients corresponding to the inputs. Note that gradopacities and gradmeans2D are returned, but gradopacities is often not used in standard training pipelines if opacities are not being optimized or if a simplified gradient flow is assumed. The corresponds to an unused gradient (likely related to cov3Dsprecomp or an intermediate buffer depending on the C++ signature). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Debug Mode: Copying arguments to CPU can be slow for large N. Only enable for debugging. Buffer Management: The buffers (geomBuffer, etc.) must be preserved exactly as returned by the forward pass for the backward pass to work correctly. Modifying them or reusing them across different forward calls without proper handling will cause errors. Tensor Types: Ensure all input tensors are on the same device (typically CUDA) as expected by the C++ extension. Time Complexity: Dominated by the C++ rasterization kernel. The wrapper itself adds minimal overhead (tuple construction, function calls). Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate buffers (geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) and saved tensors for the backward pass. Strengths: Provides automatic differentiation for the rasterization process, enabling end-to-end training of 3D Gaussian parameters. Limitations: Relies on a compiled C++ extension. Debug mode can significantly slow down execution. The PyTorch Rasterization Wrapper is part of the r2gaussian project, which implements 3D Gaussian Splatting for medical imaging (CT reconstruction). It adapts the original 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline to work within a PyTorch training loop for gradient-based optimization. Ruyi-Zha/r2gaussian, https://github.com/Ruyi-Zha/r2gaussian, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Rasterization via OpenGL Interop
head: CUDA-GL Interop Rasterization, fast-gaussian-rasterization OpenGL backend
body: This method rasterizes 3D Gaussians by leveraging OpenGL's fixed-function point rendering pipeline via CUDA-OpenGL interop, bypassing the need for custom CUDA kernels for the core rasterization step. It differs from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (GPU) which implement the forward and backward passes entirely in CUDA; instead, this approach offloads the fragment processing to the GPU driver's OpenGL implementation, using CUDA only for data preparation and result retrieval. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: xyz3: Tensor of shape (N, 3), Gaussian centers in world space. cov6: Tensor of shape (N, 6), Upper-triangular covariance matrix elements (or related representation) for each Gaussian. rgb3: Tensor of shape (N, 3), RGB colors. occ1: Tensor of shape (N, 1), Opacity values. rastersettings: A configuration object containing projection matrices, view matrices, image dimensions, and flags. Outputs: outcolor: Tensor of shape (H, W, 4), RGBA image. outdepth: Tensor of shape (H, W), Depth buffer (if enabled). Data Structures: VBO (Vertex Buffer Object): A CUDA-registered OpenGL buffer object. The layout is defined by self.attrsizes and self.glattrdtypes. Attributes are interleaved in a single contiguous tensor data. The vertex buffer is bound with a stride of attrsize elementsize. Attributes are assigned to generic vertex attribute indices 0, 1, 2, \dots based on the order in self.attrsizes. FrameBuffer Object (FBO): Contains attachments for color and depth. Color attachment 0: Renderbuffer rborgba with internal format gltexdtype (e.g., GLRGBA8). Depth attachment: Renderbuffer rboatth with internal format GLDEPTHCOMPONENT. Steps: 1. Concatenation: Concatenate xyz3, cov6, rgb3, and occ1 into a single contiguous tensor data on the GPU. The specific interleaving order is determined by self.attrsizes. 2. View Space Transformation: Transform Gaussian centers xyz3 to view space to compute depth for sorting. Using the view matrix W2C (world-to-camera): \text{view} = \text{xyz3} \cdot W2C{[:3,:3]} + W2C{[:3, 3]} where W2C{[:3,:3]} is the upper-left 3 \times 3 rotation/scaling submatrix and W2C{[:3, 3]} is the translation vector. 3. Sorting: Sort the Gaussian indices by view-space depth (z-component) in descending order (far to near): \text{idx} = \text{argsort}(\text{view}[:, 2], \text{descending}=\text{True}) Reorder the data tensor according to idx and ensure it is contiguous: \text{data} = \text{data}[\text{idx}].\text{ravel}().\text{contiguous}() Note: Sorting is performed even in solid mode, as noted in the source code. 4. CUDA-GL Mapping: Map the CUDA-GL registered VBO resource to obtain its device pointer: (\text{cu\vbo\ptr}, \text{cu\vbo\size}) = \text{cudaGraphicsResourceGetMappedPointer}(\text{self.cu\vbo}) 5. Data Upload: Asynchronously copy the sorted data tensor to the mapped VBO pointer using cudaMemcpyAsync with stream synchronization. 6. Unmap VBO: Unmap the VBO resource to allow OpenGL to access it. 7. Uniform Upload: Upload rasterization settings (projection, view, focal length, principal point) to OpenGL uniforms. Pitfall: If rastersettings contains CUDA tensors, they must be detached and moved to CPU for upload, which may cause synchronization stalls. Coordinate System: If not in offline rendering, flip the Y and Z axes of the camera-to-world matrix (C2W) and adjust the projection matrix K to handle OpenGL's coordinate system differences. 8. Rendering Setup: Bind the Vertex Array Object (VAO) associated with the VBO. If rendering to an offscreen framebuffer (different size or offline mode), bind the FBO, clear buffers, and set viewport/scissor. If rendering to a different viewport, blit the rendered texture to the default framebuffer using glBlitFramebuffer with linear filtering. 9. Draw Call: Draw the Gaussians as points: \text{glDrawArrays}(\text{GL\POINTS}, 0, N) where N is the number of Gaussians. 10. Result Retrieval (Offline/Offscreen): If offline rendering, map the CUDA-GL registered texture resource. Get the mapped array pointer. Copy the RGBA image data back to a PyTorch tensor using cudaMemcpy2DFromArrayAsync. Parameters: rastersettings.imagewidth: Width of the output image in pixels. rastersettings.imageheight: Height of the output image in pixels. rastersettings.tanfovx: Tangent of the horizontal field of view. rastersettings.tanfovy: Tangent of the vertical field of view. rastersettings.viewmatrix: 4x4 view matrix (world to camera). rastersettings.projmatrix: 4x4 projection matrix. rastersettings.usedepth: Boolean flag enabling depth rendering. rastersettings.solidmode: Boolean flag enabling solid mode rendering. rastersettings.edgemode: Boolean flag enabling edge mode rendering. Pitfalls: Synchronization: Moving CUDA tensors to CPU for OpenGL uniform uploads causes stalls. Coordinate Systems: OpenGL uses a different coordinate system than typical computer vision pipelines; Y and Z axes must be flipped, and projection matrices adjusted. Interop Failure: If CUDA-GL interop is unsupported, the method raises a RuntimeError. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np import ctypes import OpenGL.GL as gl import pycuda.driver as cuda import pycuda.gl from pycuda.gl import GraphicsBufferMapping def gaussianrasterizationopengl(xyz3, cov6, rgb3, occ1, rastersettings): """ Rasterize 3D Gaussians using OpenGL via CUDA-GL interop. Args: xyz3: Tensor (N, 3) cov6: Tensor (N, 6) rgb3: Tensor (N, 3) occ1: Tensor (N, 1) rastersettings: Object with attributes: imagewidth, imageheight, tanfovx, tanfovy, viewmatrix, projmatrix, usedepth, solidmode, edgemode. Returns: outcolor: Tensor (H, W, 4) outdepth: Tensor (H, W) or None """ N = xyz3.shape[0] # 1. Concatenate attributes # Assuming attrsizes defines the layout. For simplicity, we assume # the order xyz, cov, rgb, occ as per notes, but actual stride # depends on self.attrsizes and self.glattrdtypes. # data tensor will be (N, totalattrsize) data = torch.cat([xyz3, cov6, rgb3, occ1], dim=1).contiguous() # 2. Transform to view space for sorting # viewmatrix is W2C (World to Camera) w2c = rastersettings.viewmatrix # Extract rotation and translation rot = w2c[:3,:3] trans = w2c[:3, 3] # view = xyz @ rot.T + trans # Note: Matrix multiplication order depends on row/column major. # Source uses: view = xyz3 @ w2cT[:3,:3] + w2cT[:3, 3] # Assuming w2cT is the transpose of the view matrix provided. # If rastersettings.viewmatrix is W2C, then w2cT might be W2C.T # Let's assume standard matrix math: v = M p. If p is column vector. # If xyz3 is (N, 3) rows, then view = xyz3 @ rot.T + trans view = torch.matmul(xyz3, rot.t()) + trans # 3. Sort by depth (z) descending idx = torch.argsort(view[:, 2], descending=True) data = data[idx].contiguous() # 4. Map CUDA-GL VBO # self.cuvbo is the registered resource # cuvboptr, cuvbosize = cudaGraphicsResourceGetMappedPointer(self.cuvbo) # In PyCUDA: with GraphicsBufferMapping(rastersettings.cuvbo) as vboptr: # 5. Copy data to VBO # cudaMemcpyAsync(dst, src, count, kind, stream) # vboptr is the device pointer stream = cuda.Stream() # Assuming data is on GPU vboptr.copyfrom(data, stream=stream) stream.synchronize() # 6. Unmap VBO (handled by context manager above) # 7. Upload Uniforms # Detach and move to CPU if necessary proj = rastersettings.projmatrix.detach().cpu().numpy() view = rastersettings.viewmatrix.detach().cpu().numpy() focalx = rastersettings.tanfovx rastersettings.imagewidth / 2.0 focaly = rastersettings.tanfovy rastersettings.imageheight / 2.0 ppx = rastersettings.imagewidth / 2.0 ppy = rastersettings.imageheight / 2.0 # Set OpenGL uniforms (implementation depends on shader program) gl.glUseProgram(rastersettings.shaderprogram) gl.glUniformMatrix4fv(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "proj"), 1, gl.GLFALSE, proj) gl.glUniformMatrix4fv(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "view"), 1, gl.GLFALSE, view) gl.glUniform1f(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "focalx"), focalx) gl.glUniform1f(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "focaly"), focaly) gl.glUniform1f(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "ppx"), ppx) gl.glUniform1f(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "ppy"), ppy) # 8. Setup Framebuffer if rastersettings.offline or (rastersettings.imagewidth != rastersettings.currentwidth or rastersettings.imageheight != rastersettings.currentheight): gl.glBindFramebuffer(gl.GLFRAMEBUFFER, rastersettings.fbo) gl.glViewport(0, 0, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.imageheight) gl.glClear(gl.GLCOLORBUFFERBIT | gl.GLDEPTHBUFFERBIT) # 9. Bind VAO and Draw gl.glBindVertexArray(rastersettings.vao) gl.glDrawArrays(gl.GLPOINTS, 0, N) # 10. Retrieve Results outcolor = None outdepth = None if rastersettings.offline: # Map texture resource with GraphicsBufferMapping(rastersettings.cutex) as texptr: # Copy RGBA data back # cudaMemcpy2DFromArrayAsync(dst, dstpitch, src, srcpitch, width, height, kind, stream) # This part is complex to represent in pure Python without specific PyCUDA/PyOpenGL bindings # Assuming a helper function exists outcolor = rastersettings.copytexturetotensor(texptr, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.imageheight) else: # Blit if necessary if rastersettings.imagewidth != rastersettings.currentwidth or \ rastersettings.imageheight != rastersettings.currentheight: gl.glBindFramebuffer(gl.GLREADFRAMEBUFFER, rastersettings.fbo) gl.glBindFramebuffer(gl.GLDRAWFRAMEBUFFER, 0) gl.glBlitFramebuffer(0, 0, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.imageheight, 0, 0, rastersettings.currentwidth, rastersettings.currentheight, gl.GLCOLORBUFFERBIT, gl.GLLINEAR) # Read pixels to CPU then to Tensor (slower, but standard for non-offline) # Or use PBOs for async readback pixels = gl.glReadPixels(0, 0, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.imageheight, gl.GLRGBA, gl.GLUNSIGNEDBYTE) outcolor = torch.frombuffer(pixels, dtype=torch.uint8).view(rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, 4).float() / 255.0 # Note: OpenGL reads from bottom-left, so Y might need flipping outcolor = torch.flip(outcolor, [0]) return outcolor, outdepth Uses a residual pyramid structure for multi-scale rendering. Choose when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and multi-resolution details are needed. FastGS Residual Pyramid Rendering Provides interfaces for auxiliary outputs like depth and normals alongside the main color pass. Choose when auxiliary geometry information is required. MiniGS Auxiliary & Depth Rendering Interface Integrates pose estimation directly into the rasterization wrapper. Choose when joint optimization of geometry and camera pose is required. GaussianRasterizerwpose A generic PyTorch wrapper that may abstract over different backends. Choose when backend agnosticism is preferred. PyTorch Rasterization Wrapper Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step O(N \log N) and the OpenGL draw call, which is O(N) in terms of vertex processing but depends on the fragment shader complexity and fill rate. The CUDA-GL interop overhead adds latency for data transfer and synchronization. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the VBO (size proportional to N \times \text{attr\size}) and the FBO attachments (size proportional to H \times W). Performance: Performance is hardware-dependent, relying on the GPU's OpenGL driver efficiency. It may be slower than custom CUDA kernels for very high N due to driver overhead and lack of fine-grained control over tile-based optimization. Strengths: Leverages optimized OpenGL drivers; easier to implement if CUDA kernel development is difficult; supports standard OpenGL features like blending and depth testing. Limitations: Requires CUDA-GL interop support; synchronization stalls when moving data between CUDA and OpenGL contexts; coordinate system conversion overhead; less flexible than custom CUDA for differentiable rendering gradients (often requires approximations or external libraries like diffpointrasterization). When to Use: When CUDA-GL interop is available and a quick implementation is needed; when leveraging existing OpenGL pipelines; when custom CUDA kernel development is not feasible. When Not to Use: When maximum performance is required and custom CUDA kernels can be optimized; when CUDA-GL interop is unsupported; when precise control over differentiable gradients is needed without approximation. This method is part of the "fast-gaussian-rasterization" project, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It was developed to provide an alternative to pure CUDA rasterization by utilizing OpenGL's point sprite capabilities, potentially simplifying the rendering pipeline for certain hardware configurations or software ecosystems. dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, https://github.com/dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: vtkPointGaussianMapper
head: PointGaussianMapper, vtkOpenGLPointGaussianMapper
body: vtkPointGaussianMapper renders point clouds as simple points or anisotropic 3D Gaussian splats without requiring vertex cells, supporting per-point scale, rotation, opacity, and emissive properties. It differs from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by operating in object-order on the CPU-side data structure and projecting Gaussians via a vertex shader rather than GPU-parallel tile-based rasterization, and from Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling by lacking transmittance culling and relying on standard OpenGL blending. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vtkPolyData object containing point positions. If verts cells are present, only points referenced by these cells are drawn; otherwise, all points are drawn. Output: A rendered image of points or Gaussian splats. Data Structures: Position Array: Float positions. If no shift/scale is applied to the VBO, these are uploaded directly. Color Array: RGBA byte colors. Per-Point Attributes: Arrays for scale, rotation, and opacity. These are shared between simple-point and splat modes. Buffers: Per-point buffers are uploaded only when their source data changes. Arrays that do not cover every drawn point are staged. Parameters: scaleFactor: Scalar multiplier for splat size. A value of 0 disables splatting and renders simple points. anisotropic: Boolean flag enabling anisotropic 3D Gaussian splats. rotationArray: Name of the array containing rotation data for anisotropic splats. lowpassMatrix: Matrix used for low-pass filtering in anisotropic splatting calculation. emissive: Boolean flag. When true, splats add their coverage to the alpha channel for correct compositing over transparent backgrounds. scaleArray, scaleArrayComponent, scaleFunction, scaleTableSize: Controls for scale mapping. opacityArray, opacityArrayComponent, scalarOpacityFunction, opacityTableSize: Controls for opacity mapping. splatShaderCode: Custom shader code for splat rendering. boundScale: Bound scale parameter. Steps: 1. Input Validation: Check if polyData contains verts cells. If yes, identify the subset of points referenced by these cells. If no, use all points. 2. Buffer Management: Identify compatible arrays: float positions without shift/scale, RGBA byte colors, and float scale/rotation/opacity arrays. Upload compatible arrays directly to GPU buffers without staging copies. For arrays that do not cover every drawn point or require staging, use staging buffers. Re-upload buffers only if their source data has changed. 3. Rendering Mode Selection: If scaleFactor is 0, render as simple points. If scaleFactor is non-zero, render as Gaussian splats. 4. Simple Point Rendering: Use gl.POINTS primitive type. Submit one vertex per point. 5. Gaussian Splat Rendering: Use a four-vertex triangle strip instance per point. Vertex Shader Projection: The vertex shader projects each 3D Gaussian to a screen-space ellipse using EWA (Elliptical Weighted Average) projection. The shader places the four corners of the triangle strip around the projected Gaussian center. Splat sizes do not apply VBO shift and scale, ensuring data far from the origin retains its splat size. Every splat maintains one consistent winding order to ensure face culling treats rotated splats consistently. Blending: If emissive is true, add splat coverage to the alpha channel. If emissive is false and using default Gaussian falloff, render with translucent geometry so faded corners do not hide objects behind them. Apply opacity array regardless of scalar colors. If opacity is below 1, render translucent. 6. Selection: Hardware selection returns point IDs for simple points and verts cells for splats. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpointgaussianmapper(polydata, scaleFactor, anisotropic, rotationArray, lowpassMatrix, emissive): # 1. Determine points to render if polydata.hasvertscells(): pointstorender = getpointsreferencedbyvertscells(polydata) else: pointstorender = polydata.getallpoints() # 2. Buffer Management # Identify compatible arrays positionarray = polydata.getpositions() colorarray = polydata.getcolors() # RGBA bytes scalearray = polydata.getarray('scale') opacityarray = polydata.getarray('opacity') rotationarray = polydata.getarray(rotationArray) if anisotropic else None # Upload compatible arrays directly if iscompatible(positionarray): uploadbufferdirectly(positionarray) else: uploadbufferstaged(positionarray) if iscompatible(colorarray): uploadbufferdirectly(colorarray) else: uploadbufferstaged(colorarray) if iscompatible(scalearray): uploadbufferdirectly(scalearray) else: uploadbufferstaged(scalearray) if iscompatible(opacityarray): uploadbufferdirectly(opacityarray) else: uploadbufferstaged(opacityarray) if anisotropic and rotationarray is not None: if iscompatible(rotationarray): uploadbufferdirectly(rotationarray) else: uploadbufferstaged(rotationarray) # 3. Render if scaleFactor == 0: # Simple Points setprimitivetype(gl.POINTS) for point in pointstorender: drawvertex(point.position) else: # Gaussian Splats setprimitivetype(gl.TRIANGLESTRIP) # 4 vertices per instance for point in pointstorender: # Get attributes scale = getscale(point, scalearray) opacity = getopacity(point, opacityarray) rotation = getrotation(point, rotationarray) if anisotropic else identitymatrix() # Project to screen space using EWA screencenter, screencovariance = ewaproject(point.position, rotation, scale, cameramatrix) # Generate 4 corners of triangle strip around screencenter corners = generatesplatcorners(screencenter, screencovariance) # Set attributes for the 4 corners for corner in corners: setvertexposition(corner) setcolor(colorarray[point.index]) setopacity(opacity) setemissive(emissive) drawvertex() # 4. Selection Data if hardwareselectionactive(): if scaleFactor == 0: return [point.id for point in pointstorender] else: return [cell.id for cell in polydata.vertscells if cell.referencesany(pointstorender)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Culling: Splats centered outside the view are drawn if their projection reaches into the view. The projection is linearized no further than 30% beyond the view bounds. Winding Order: Every splat maintains one winding order to ensure face culling treats rotated splats consistently. Splat Size Scaling: Splat sizes do not apply VBO shift and scale, ensuring data far from the origin retains its splat size. Opacity Application: The opacity array applies regardless of scalar colors. If opacity is below 1, the property is rendered translucent. Non-emissive Rendering: Non-emissive splats with default Gaussian falloff render with translucent geometry, allowing faded corners to not hide objects behind them. Scalar Colors: Scalar colors are always per-point and never switch to texture coloring, even if interpolateScalarsBeforeMapping is set. Cell Scalars: Cell scalars only color points that are drawn by verts cells. Composite Datasets: Composite datasets are not supported because vtk.js mappers require polydata input. A subclass of vtkPointGaussianMapper designed for dense point clouds, defaulting to opaque simple points. It adds controls for point size multiplier (e.g., for device pixel ratio), round points (which also select as discs), point sizes in model units that follow camera distance, and a draw limit for progressive loading (showing a prefix of points without uploading them again). The OpenGL mapper uses an extension point to determine the number of points each draw submission submits. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Renders point clouds without requiring verts cells; supports anisotropic 3D Gaussian splats; efficient buffer management by sharing buffers between simple-point and splat modes; correct compositing for emissive splats; consistent winding order for face culling. Limitations: Does not support composite datasets; scalar colors are always per-point; non-emissive splats with default Gaussian falloff render with translucent geometry (which may differ from VTK's opaque geometry behavior); splats centered outside the view but projecting into the view are drawn (linearized up to 30% beyond view bounds). When to Use: Use when rendering point clouds as simple points or Gaussian splats in vtk.js without needing complex cell structures, especially for dense point clouds where vtkPointSpriteMapper is preferred. When Not to Use: Do not use for composite datasets or when texture-based scalar coloring is required. vtkPointGaussianMapper was added to vtk.js by PaulHax in a pull request (PR #42) in September 2026, porting VTK's vtkPointGaussianMapper with its API and defaults. It addresses the lack of a counterpart in vtk.js for rendering point clouds as Gaussian splats or showing 3D Gaussian splatting data (scale and rotation per point) without requiring verts cells. vtkPointSpriteMapper was added in the same PR as a subclass for dense point clouds. feat(PointGaussianMapper): add vtkPointGaussianMapper, https://github.com/PaulHax/vtk-js/pull/42, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Feature 3DGS Rendering
head: Differentiable Volumetric Feature Rendering, Joint RGB and Feature Rasterization
body: Feature 3DGS is a method for rendering high-dimensional semantic feature maps alongside RGB images using 3D Gaussians, enabling the distillation of knowledge from 2D foundation models (such as SAM or LSeg) into an explicit 3D scene representation. It sets itself apart from NeRF-based feature field methods by using an explicit representation that avoids interference between the radiance and feature fields, allowing for equal-weighted joint optimization without the sensitivity to hyperparameters required by implicit neural networks. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with optimized parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity, SH coefficients, and feature vectors); camera parameters (view and projection matrices); image resolution H \times W. Outputs: A rendered RGB image \hat{I} and a rendered feature map Fs(\hat{I}) of resolution H \times W \times N (where N is the internal feature dimension, upsampled to M if necessary). Data Structures Each 3D Gaussian i stores the following fields: Center: x \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation: Quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (representing rotation matrix R) Scaling: Factor s \in \mathbb{R}^3 (representing scaling matrix S) Opacity: \alpha \in \mathbb{R} Appearance: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients up to 3rd order (4 bands) Semantic Feature: Vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^N Algorithm Steps 1. Tiling and Culling: Divide the screen into 16 \times 16 tiles. For each tile, cull 3D Gaussians against the view frustum and the tile's axis-aligned bounding box. 2. Projection: For each remaining Gaussian, compute the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma' in camera coordinates to project the 3D Gaussian to 2D space: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^{T} J^{T} where W is the world-to-camera transformation matrix, J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation, and \Sigma is the 3D covariance matrix. Note: To ensure \Sigma remains positive semi-definite during optimization, it is decomposed into rotation R and scaling S such that \Sigma = R S S^{T} R^{T}. 3. Sorting: Sort the Gaussians overlapping each pixel by their depth (distance from camera). 4. Joint Rasterization: For each pixel, perform alpha blending over the sorted overlapping Gaussians i \in \mathcal{N} to compute both the color C and the feature Fs simultaneously: C = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai Ti F{s} = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} fi \alphai Ti where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance, ci is the color derived from SH coefficients, and fi is the semantic feature vector. 5. Upsampling (Speed-up): If the target teacher feature dimension M (e.g., 512 for LSeg) is larger than the initialized Gaussian feature dimension N (N \ll M), apply a lightweight 1 \times 1 convolutional decoder to upsample Fs(\hat{I}) from H \times W \times N to H \times W \times M. 6. Interpolation: Apply bilinear interpolation to resize the rendered feature map Fs(\hat{I}) to match the exact resolution H \times W of the teacher feature map Ft(I). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfeature3dgs(gaussians, camera, imageh, imagew, teacherencoder, decoder): """ Render RGB and Feature maps using Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Distillation. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: center: (3,) q: (4,) quaternion s: (3,) scale alpha: scalar shcoeffs: array for SH evaluation f: (N,) feature vector camera: Object with viewmatrix (W) and projection properties. imageh, imagew: Output resolution. teacherencoder: Function to encode ground truth image I to Ft. decoder: Lightweight 1x1 conv decoder for upsampling features. Returns: renderedrgb: (H, W, 3) renderedfeature: (H, W, M) """ # 1. Initialize output buffers # Note: In a real GPU implementation, this is done in parallel via tiles. # Here we simulate the logic for a single pixel or tile block. # 2. Tile-based processing (Simulated for clarity) tilesize = 16 renderedrgb = np.zeros((imageh, imagew, 3)) renderedfeatureraw = np.zeros((imageh, imagew, N)) # N is internal dim for ty in range(0, imageh, tilesize): for tx in range(0, imagew, tilesize): # Define tile bounds ymin, ymax = ty, min(ty + tilesize, imageh) xmin, xmax = tx, min(tx + tilesize, imagew) # Cull Gaussians against tile AABB and view frustum activegaussians = cullgaussians(gaussians, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, camera) for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): # Project pixel to get ray direction/origin if needed for depth sorting # Sort active gaussians by depth relative to camera sortedgs = sortbydepth(activegaussians, camera) coloracc = 0.0 featureacc = np.zeros(N) transmittance = 1.0 for g in sortedgs: # Evaluate 2D Gaussian at (x, y) # Compute 2D covariance Sigma' from 3D Sigma using J, W sigma2d = projectcovariance(g, camera) # Calculate alpha contribution # alphag = alpha exp(-0.5 (x,y)^T Sigma'^-1 (x,y)) alphag = evaluategaussianalpha(g, x, y, sigma2d) if alphag < epsilon: continue # Evaluate color ci from SH ci = evaluatesh(g.shcoeffs, g.center, camera.viewdirection) # Accumulate weight = alphag transmittance coloracc += ci weight featureacc += g.f weight transmittance = (1.0 - alphag) if transmittance < epsilon: break renderedrgb[y, x] = coloracc renderedfeatureraw[y, x] = featureacc # 3. Upsampling # If N < M, use decoder to upsample if N < M: renderedfeature = decoder(renderedfeatureraw) else: renderedfeature = renderedfeatureraw # 4. Resize to match teacher resolution if necessary (usually HxW is fixed) # Bilinear interpolation is applied if teacher resolution differs renderedfeature = bilinearresize(renderedfeature, teacherencoder.resolution) return renderedrgb, renderedfeature def cullgaussians(gaussians, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, camera): """Filter gaussians that overlap with the tile and are in view.""" active = [] for g in gaussians: # Compute 2D bounding box of Gaussian in screen space bbox = getscreenbbox(g, camera) if intersects(bbox, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) and isinfrustum(g, camera): active.append(g) return active def projectcovariance(gaussian, camera): """Compute 2D covariance Sigma' = J W Sigma W^T J^T""" W = camera.viewmatrix # Sigma is reconstructed from R (from q) and S (from s) R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(gaussian.q) S = np.diag(gaussian.s) Sigma3d = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # Jacobian J depends on camera intrinsics and extrinsics J = computejacobian(camera) Sigma2d = J @ W @ Sigma3d @ W.T @ J.T return Sigma2d Parameters Tile Size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Feature Loss Weight (\gamma): 1.0. D-SSIM Weight (\lambda): 0.2. SH Optimization Schedule: Optimize zeroth-order SH (diffuse color) for the first 1000 iterations. Introduce 1 band every 1000 iterations until all 4 bands are represented. Edge Cases and Pitfalls High-Dimensional Rendering Cost: Rendering high-dimensional feature maps directly (e.g., M=512 for LSeg) is time-consuming. The solution is to initialize Gaussians with a lower-dimensional feature vector N \ll M and use a lightweight 1 \times 1 convolutional decoder to upsample the rendered features to dimension M. Positive Semi-Definite Covariance: The 3D covariance matrix \Sigma must remain positive semi-definite. This is enforced by parameterizing it via rotation R and scaling S rather than optimizing \Sigma directly. Resolution Mismatch: The rendered feature map Fs(\hat{I}) must be resized via bilinear interpolation to match the resolution H \times W of the teacher feature map Ft(I) before calculating the \mathcal{L}1 loss. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization step. The tile-based approach (16 \times 16) manages memory load and allows efficient culling. However, rendering high-dimensional features (N or M) increases computational cost linearly with the feature dimension. The speed-up module (1x1 conv) mitigates this by allowing optimization in lower dimensions. Memory Complexity: Stores N-dimensional feature vectors per Gaussian. Using N \ll M reduces memory footprint during training compared to storing full M-dimensional features. Strengths: Explicit representation avoids the interference between radiance and feature fields common in NeRF-based methods, allowing equal-weighted joint optimization (\gamma=1.0) without adverse effects. It preserves per-pixel accuracy for features by using the same rasterization procedure as RGB. Limitations: Requires a teacher model (e.g., SAM, LSeg) for supervision. High-dimensional feature rendering can be slow without the upsampling decoder. When to use: When distilling semantic features from 2D foundation models into a 3D explicit representation for tasks like promptable segmentation or language-driven 3D understanding. Feature 3DGS was introduced to enable the distillation of 2D foundation models (such as Segment Anything [20] and LSeg [23]) into 3D Gaussian Splatting representations. Unlike NeRF-based approaches where feature and radiance fields share layers, leading to interference and sensitivity to the feature loss weight \gamma, Feature 3DGS uses an explicit representation that decouples these fields. This allows for robust joint optimization of RGB and semantic features, facilitating zero-shot and language-driven 3D computer vision tasks. Feature 3DGS: Supercharging 3D Gaussian Splatting to Enable Distilled Feature Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02048, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting (glTF KHR_gaussian_splatting)
head: 3DGS, Ellipsoid Splatting
body: This method defines the rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian splats stored in glTF assets via the KHRgaussiansplatting extension, treating splats as point primitives with specific geometric and color attributes. It differs from general rasterization implementations by enforcing a strict data layout and transformation constraints defined by the glTF standard, ensuring interoperability and fallback to sparse point cloud rendering if the extension is unsupported. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A glTF scene containing a mesh primitive with mode POINTS (0) and attributes defined by the extension. The scene includes a camera with perspective projection. Output: A 2D image where each pixel is the result of alpha-blending projected Gaussian splats. Data Structures and Layout: The splat data is stored as attributes on a glTF mesh primitive. The primitive mode MUST be POINTS. The glTF material referenced by the primitive MUST be ignored for rendering. 1. POSITION (VEC3): The mean vector \mu in local space. Effective global mean is derived from this attribute and the node's global transformation matrix. 2. ROTATION (VEC4): Unit quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw) in glTF order. Values are guaranteed to be normalized. Supported component types: float32, snorm8, snorm16. 3. SCALE (VEC3): Linear spread (sx, sy, sz) along local principal axes. Values MUST be non-negative. Supported component types: float32, uint8, unorm8, uint16, unorm16. 4. OPACITY (SCALAR): Linear value \alpha \in [0.0, 1.0]. Out-of-range values are invalid. Supported types: float32, unorm8, unorm16. 5. Spherical Harmonics (SH): SHDEGREE0COEF0 (VEC3): Required. Degree 0 coefficients. SHDEGREElCOEFn (VEC3): Required if degree l is used. Degree 1 has 3 coefficients, Degree 2 has 5, Degree 3 has 7. Degrees must be fully defined; partial definitions are invalid. Coefficients are packed from lowest order m to highest. Total 45 coefficients for all 3 degrees. Node Transformation Constraints: The global transformation matrix of the node containing the splat primitive MUST satisfy: Last row is (0, 0, 0, 1). Lengths of the first three columns are finite positive numbers. The determinant of the upper-left 3x3 matrix (formed by dividing each element by its column's length) is close to +1. Non-decomposable matrices or negative scales are undefined. Rendering Steps: 1. Splat Reconstruction (Covariance Construction): Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma in global space. Let \mathbf{M} be the upper-left 3x3 submatrix of the node's global transformation matrix. Construct matrix \mathbf{C} from scale sx, sy, sz and quaternion qx, qy, qz, qw: \mathbf{C} = \begin{pmatrix} sx (1 - 2(qy^2 + qz^2)) & sy (2(qx qy - qw qz)) & sz (2(qx qz + qw qy)) \\ sx (2(qx qy + qw qz)) & sy (1 - 2(qx^2 + qz^2)) & sz (2(qy qz - qw qx)) \\ sx (2(qx qz - qw qy)) & sy (2(qy qz + qw qx)) & sz (1 - 2(qx^2 + qy^2)) \end{pmatrix} Compute \Sigma: \Sigma = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{C}^T \mathbf{M}^T 2. Splat Projection: Mean Vector: Project the global mean vector \mu onto the 2D image plane using standard perspective projection. 2D Covariance: Transform \Sigma to 2D covariance \Sigma' using affine approximation: \Sigma' = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \Sigma \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T Where \mathbf{W} is the 3x3 view-dependent transformation matrix from global to camera space (typically the upper-left 3x3 of the camera view matrix). Where \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian of the perspective projection. 3. Color Computation: Evaluate the spherical harmonics at the viewing direction to determine the RGB color. The color space is specified by the colorSpace property (srgbrec709display or linrec709display). 4. Sorting: Sort splats by distance to the camera origin. The default method is cameraDistance (vector length from splat to camera). 5. Rasterization and Blending: Project each splat onto the 2D plane. Assume a 3\sigma cut-off (Mahalanobis distance of 3 units) for the kernel shape. Alpha-blend the splats in sorted order. Intermediate rendering steps (including alpha blending) MUST be performed before any color gamut or transfer function conversions. Parameters: kernel: String, required. Currently only "ellipse" is defined. colorSpace: String, required. "srgbrec709display" or "linrec709display". projection: String, optional, default "perspective". Specifies projection method. sortingMethod: String, optional, default "cameraDistance". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computecmatrix(scale: np.ndarray, rotation: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Compute the 3x3 matrix C from scale and quaternion. scale: [sx, sy, sz] rotation: [qx, qy, qz, qw] """ sx, sy, sz = scale qx, qy, qz, qw = rotation # Matrix C construction as defined in c00 = sx (1 - 2 (qy2 + qz2)) c01 = sy (2 (qx qy - qw qz)) c02 = sz (2 (qx qz + qw qy)) c10 = sx (2 (qx qy + qw qz)) c11 = sy (1 - 2 (qx2 + qz2)) c12 = sz (2 (qy qz - qw qx)) c20 = sx (2 (qx qz - qw qy)) c21 = sy (2 (qy qz + qw qx)) c22 = sz (1 - 2 (qx2 + qy2)) C = np.array([ [c00, c01, c02], [c10, c11, c12], [c20, c21, c22] ]) return C def rendergaussiansplats(splats: list, cameraviewmatrix: np.ndarray, cameraprojmatrix: np.ndarray, imagewidth: int, imageheight: int): """ Render a list of Gaussian splats. splats: List of dicts with keys: 'position', 'rotation', 'scale', 'opacity', 'shcoeffs', 'nodetransform' """ # Initialize image buffer (assume linear space for blending, convert later if needed) # Using a simple accumulation buffer for alpha blending # Structure: (R, G, B, A) image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 4), dtype=np.float32) # 1. Sort splats by camera distance # Camera position is typically (0,0,0) in view space, but we need global position # For simplicity, assume camera is at origin in world space or transform splats to view space first. # The spec says "vector length from splat to camera origin". # We will transform splat positions to world space first. sortedsplats = [] for splat in splats: # Get global mean # Node transform is 4x4. Last row is (0,0,0,1). nodemat = splat['nodetransform'] poslocal = np.array(splat['position']) poshomogeneous = np.append(poslocal, 1.0) posglobal = nodemat @ poshomogeneous posglobal = posglobal[:3] # Camera distance (assuming camera at world origin for this example, # or use camera position from scene) # Note: In a real glTF viewer, camera position is defined in the scene. # Here we assume standard view projection where camera is at origin in view space. # To get distance, we need world position of camera. # For this implementation, we assume the sorting is done in world space. # If camera is at C, distance is ||posglobal - C||. # Since camera pose is not passed here, we assume standard view matrix implies # we should transform splats to view space and sort by Z or distance in view space? # Spec says "vector length from splat to camera origin". # Let's assume we have cameraworldpos. # For this generic function, we will skip explicit camera position lookup # and assume the caller handles view-space transformation or provides distance. # However, to be self-contained, we need a camera position. # Let's assume camera is at (0,0,0) in world space for this basic example. cameraworldpos = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) dist = np.linalg.norm(posglobal - cameraworldpos) sortedsplats.append((dist, splat, posglobal)) sortedsplats.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) # Back to front # 2. Render for dist, splat, posglobal in sortedsplats: # Extract attributes scale = np.array(splat['scale']) rotation = np.array(splat['rotation']) opacity = splat['opacity'] shcoeffs = splat['shcoeffs'] # Compute Covariance Sigma C = computecmatrix(scale, rotation) M = nodemat[:3,:3] Sigma = M @ C @ C.T @ M.T # Project Mean # Transform global mean to view space # View matrix is inverse of camera-to-world. # We have cameraviewmatrix. poshomogeneousglobal = np.append(posglobal, 1.0) posview = cameraviewmatrix @ poshomogeneousglobal posview = posview[:3] # Perspective projection of mean # Standard perspective division if posview[2] == 0: continue # Behind camera or at infinity # Project to NDC then to screen # Using cameraprojmatrix posndc = cameraprojmatrix @ poshomogeneousglobal # This is incorrect, proj matrix expects view space? # Actually, proj matrix usually takes view space coordinates. # Let's use posview for projection. posviewhomogeneous = np.append(posview, 1.0) posclip = cameraprojmatrix @ posviewhomogeneous if posclip[3] == 0: continue posndc = posclip[:3] / posclip[3] # Screen coordinates screenx = (posndc[0] + 1) 0.5 imagewidth screeny = (1 - posndc[1] - 1) 0.5 imageheight # y is flipped in screen coords usually screeny = (1 - posndc[1]) 0.5 imageheight # Project Covariance to 2D # W is upper-left 3x3 of view matrix W = cameraviewmatrix[:3,:3] # J is Jacobian of perspective projection # Perspective projection: x' = x/z, y' = y/z # J = d(xndc, yndc) / d(xview, yview, zview) # This is complex. The spec says J is the Jacobian. # For a standard perspective projection matrix P, the projection is: # xndc = (P00x + P02z) / (P20x + P22z + P23)... simplified for center projection # Let's assume a standard pinhole camera model for J if P is not decomposed. # However, the spec gives the formula: Sigma' = J W Sigma W^T J^T # We need J. # If we use the standard OpenGL projection matrix, J can be derived. # For simplicity, we assume the projection is perspective and J is computed accordingly. # A common approximation for J in the context of 3DGS is: # J = [ 1/z 0 0; 0 1/z 0; 0 0 0 ] for orthographic? No. # Let's use the standard Jacobian for perspective projection from view space to NDC. # xndc = (f x) / z, yndc = (f y) / z (simplified) # dxndc/dx = f/z, dxndc/dz = -fx/z^2 # This depends on the specific projection matrix. # Since the spec does not define J explicitly, we assume it is the Jacobian of the projection function. # We will compute Sigma' using the provided formula. # Compute J # Assuming standard perspective projection: # xndc = x / z, yndc = y / z (after removing scale/offset for Jacobian) # Actually, the projection matrix P transforms view to clip. # The Jacobian of the perspective divide is needed. # Let's assume the projection is defined by the camera. # We will compute Sigma' in view space first, then project? # No, the formula is Sigma' = J W Sigma W^T J^T. # W transforms global to view. Sigma is global. W Sigma W^T is view covariance. # J transforms view to 2D. # Let's compute the view covariance Sigmaview = W @ Sigma @ W.T # Now project to 2D. # For perspective projection, the 2D covariance is: # Sigma2d = [ 1/z^2 0 0; 0 1/z^2 0; 0 0 0 ] Sigmaview [... ]? # The standard result is: # Sigma2d = [ Sigmaview[0,0]/z^2, Sigmaview[0,1]/z^2,... ] # More precisely: # Sigma2d = J Sigmaview J.T # Where J is the Jacobian of the projection. # For perspective projection x' = x/z, y' = y/z: # J = [ 1/z 0 -x/z^2; 0 1/z -y/z^2; 0 0 0 ] # But we only care about the 2D part. # Sigma2d = [ 1/z 0; 0 1/z ] Sigmaview[0:2, 0:2] [ 1/z 0; 0 1/z ] +... terms involving z? # The full formula is: # Sigma2d = [ 1/z 0 -x/z^2; 0 1/z -y/z^2 ] Sigmaview [ 1/z 0; 0 1/z; -x/z^2 -y/z^2 ] # This is getting complex. We will use the standard 3DGS projection. # Simplified: z = posview[2] if z <= 0: continue # Jacobian for perspective projection (x/z, y/z) # J2x3 = [ 1/z 0 -x/z^2; 0 1/z -y/z^2 ] x = posview[0] y = posview[1] J = np.array([ [1/z, 0, -x/(z2)], [0, 1/z, -y/(z2)] ]) Sigma2d = J @ Sigmaview @ J.T # 3D sigma cut-off # The kernel assumes 3 sigma cut-off. # We need to determine the bounding box of the 2D Gaussian. # Eigenvalues of Sigma2d give the variances along principal axes. eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2d) sigmax = math.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) sigmay = math.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) # Bounding box in pixels # 3 sigma radiusx = 3 sigmax imagewidth / 2 # Approximate scaling radiusy = 3 sigmay imageheight / 2 # Convert to screen coordinates # The screen coordinates are in pixels. # We need to map the 2D covariance from NDC to pixels. # NDC is [-1, 1]. Screen is [0, W]. # Scale factor: W/2. scalex = imagewidth / 2 scaley = imageheight / 2 Sigma2dpixels = np.array([ [Sigma2d[0,0] scalex2, Sigma2d[0,1] scalex scaley], [Sigma2d[1,0] scalex scaley, Sigma2d[1,1] scaley2] ]) eigenvaluespx, eigenvectorspx = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2dpixels) sigmaxpx = math.sqrt(eigenvaluespx[0]) sigmaypx = math.sqrt(eigenvaluespx[1]) minx = int(math.floor(screenx - 3 sigmaxpx)) maxx = int(math.ceil(screenx + 3 sigmaxpx)) miny = int(math.floor(screeny - 3 sigmaypx)) maxy = int(math.ceil(screeny + 3 sigmaypx)) # Clamp to image bounds minx = max(0, minx) maxx = min(imagewidth, maxx) miny = max(0, miny) maxy = min(imageheight, maxy) # 3. Color Computation # Evaluate SH at viewing direction # Viewing direction in world space? Or view space? # SH is usually evaluated in the local space of the splat or world space? # The spec says "computes its color". # We need the direction from splat to camera. camtosplat = posglobal - cameraworldpos camtosplat = camtosplat / np.linalg.norm(camtosplat) # Evaluate SH # SH evaluation is complex. We assume a helper function. color = evaluatesphericalharmonics(shcoeffs, camtosplat) # 4. Alpha Blending # Iterate over pixels in bounding box for py in range(miny, maxy): for px in range(minx, maxx): # Pixel center in NDC ndcx = (px + 0.5) / imagewidth 2 - 1 ndcy = 1 - (py + 0.5) / imageheight 2 # Transform to view space for Gaussian evaluation? # Or use the 2D Gaussian formula directly. # The 2D Gaussian is defined in screen space? # We have Sigma2dpixels. # We need the position of the pixel in the same coordinate system as Sigma2dpixels. # Sigma2dpixels is in pixel coordinates relative to screen center? # No, it's relative to the projected mean in pixel coordinates. # Vector from mean to pixel dx = px - screenx dy = py - screeny # Evaluate 2D Gaussian # G = exp(-0.5 (x-mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x-mu)) posvec = np.array([dx, dy]) try: invsigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2dpixels) exponent = -0.5 posvec @ invsigma @ posvec if exponent > 0: # exp of positive is > 1, but Gaussian is <= 1 exponent = 0 weight = math.exp(exponent) except: weight = 0 if weight < 1e-6: continue # Alpha blending # Cout = Csplat alphasplat weight + Cin (1 - alphasplat weight) # But opacity is per splat. alphasplat = opacity weight if alphasplat > 0: # Pre-multiplied alpha blending # Cout = Csplat alphasplat + Cin (1 - alphasplat) # But we need to handle the existing alpha in the buffer. # Cout = (Csplat alphasplat + Cin alphain (1 - alphasplat)) / alphaout? # Standard over operator: # Cout = Csplat alphasplat + Cin (1 - alphasplat) # alphaout = alphasplat + alphain (1 - alphasplat) currentalpha = image[py, px, 3] currentcolor = image[py, px,:3] newalpha = alphasplat + currentalpha (1 - alphasplat) if newalpha > 0: newcolor = (color alphasplat + currentcolor currentalpha (1 - alphasplat)) / newalpha else: newcolor = currentcolor image[py, px,:3] = newcolor image[py, px, 3] = newalpha # Convert to output color space if colorspace == "srgbrec709display": image = lineartosrgb(image) return image def evaluatesphericalharmonics(coeffs: list, direction: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Evaluate spherical harmonics at a given direction. coeffs: List of VEC3 coefficients. direction: Unit vector. """ # This is a placeholder for the actual SH evaluation. # The spec requires SH evaluation. # Degree 0: 1 coeff. # Degree 1: 3 coeffs. # Degree 2: 5 coeffs. # Degree 3: 7 coeffs. # Total 16 coefficients (45 values). # We assume the coeffs are packed. # Standard SH basis functions # Y0 = 1/sqrt(4pi) # Y1 = sqrt(3/4pi) x, y, z # etc. # For implementation, we use the standard SH evaluation. # This is a complex function. We will assume it is implemented correctly. # Standard SH evaluation routine. # Simplified: Return constant color for degree 0 if len(coeffs) == 1: return coeffs[0] # Full evaluation would require implementing SH basis. # We will return a dummy value for the sake of the example. # In a real implementation, this function must be complete. return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) def lineartosrgb(linear: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Convert linear RGB to sRGB. """ # Standard sRGB transfer function. return np.where(linear <= 0.0031308, 12.92 linear, 1.055 np.power(linear, 1/2.4) - 0.055) Renders 4D Gaussians (3D spatial + 1D temporal) into a 2D image for a specific viewpoint and timestamp. It extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by handling time-dependent opacity, position offsets, and spherical harmonics evaluation in 4D. Unlike static splatting, it accounts for the motion and appearance of primitives over time, enabling the reconstruction of dynamic scenes. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of splats N and the number of pixels P covered by splats. Sorting takes O(N \log N). Rasterization is O(N \cdot k) where k is the average number of pixels per splat. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store splat attributes. O(P) for the image buffer. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable on modern GPUs due to the simplicity of the Gaussian kernel and efficient rasterization. Strengths: High visual quality, real-time rendering, compact representation. Limitations: Large memory footprint for high-resolution scenes. Artifacts can occur with large splats or improper sorting. When to use: Real-time visualization of large scenes, virtual reality, interactive applications. When not to use: Scenes with very high frequency details that require many splats, or when memory is extremely constrained. The KHRgaussiansplatting extension was developed by Khronos Group to standardize the storage of 3D Gaussian splats in glTF assets. It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering paper. The extension aims to establish a solid foundation for integrating 3D Gaussian splatting into glTF assets, enabling future enhancements. https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHRgaussiansplatting/README.md, https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHRgaussiansplatting/README.md, fetched 2026-10-30

name: 4D Gaussian Rasterization
head: 4D Gaussian Splatting Forward Pass, 4DGS Render
body: 4D Gaussian Rasterization renders a scene represented by 4D Gaussians (3D spatial + 1D temporal) into a 2D image for a specific viewpoint and timestamp. It extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting by handling time-dependent opacity, position offsets, and spherical harmonics evaluation in 4D. It differs from sibling methods like SpacetimeGaussians by using a unified 4D Gaussian representation with explicit temporal spherical harmonics, whereas SpacetimeGaussians uses a rendering pipeline with multiple option flags for different rasterization backends. Inputs: viewpointcamera: Object containing FoVx, FoVy, imageheight, imagewidth, worldviewtransform (view matrix), fullprojtransform (projection matrix), cameracenter, and timestamp. pc (GaussianModel): Object containing attributes: getxyz: 3D means tensor. activeshdegree: Spatial SH degree. activeshdegreet: Temporal SH degree. rot4d: Boolean flag for 4D rotation. gaussiandim: Integer dimension (3 or 4). forcesh3d: Boolean flag to force 3D SH evaluation. timeduration: Tuple (tmin, tmax). marginalt: Tensor of marginal time probabilities. envmap: Environment map texture (optional). envmapres: Resolution of environment map (optional). scalest, ts, rotationsr: Time-specific attributes (if gaussiandim == 4). prefiltervar: Prefilter variance threshold (if > 0). pipe: Configuration object with flags: computecov3Dpython: Boolean. convertSHspython: Boolean. envmapres: Integer or None. bgcolor: Background color tensor (3 channels) on GPU. scalingmodifier: Float (default 1.0). Outputs: Dictionary containing: renderedimage: Tensor (C, H, W). viewspacepoints: Tensor of 2D screen-space means with gradients. visibilityfilter: Boolean tensor. radiiall: Tensor of radii. depth: Tensor of depths. alpha: Tensor of alpha values. flow: Tensor of flow vectors. Data Structures: GaussianRasterizationSettings: Struct holding image dimensions, FOV tangents, background color, scaling modifier, view/projection matrices, SH degrees, camera position, timestamp, time duration, 4D rotation flag, Gaussian dimension, and debug flags. GaussianRasterizer: Object initialized with settings, performing the CUDA rasterization. Steps: 1. Initialize Gradients: Create a zero tensor screenspacepoints on CUDA with requiresgrad=True to store gradients of 2D screen-space means. python screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz, dtype=pc.getxyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device="cuda") + 0 try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except: pass 2. Compute FOV Tangents: Calculate tangent of half field of view. python tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) 3. Configure Rasterization Settings: Construct GaussianRasterizationSettings with parameters: imageheight, imagewidth: From viewpointcamera. tanfovx, tanfovy: From step 2. bg: bgcolor if pipe.envmapres is not set, else torch.zeros(3, device="cuda"). scalemodifier: scalingmodifier. viewmatrix: viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform. projmatrix: viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform. shdegree: pc.activeshdegree. shdegreet: pc.activeshdegreet. campos: viewpointcamera.cameracenter. timestamp: viewpointcamera.timestamp. timeduration: pc.timeduration[1] - pc.timeduration[0]. rot4d: pc.rot4d. gaussiandim: pc.gaussiandim. forcesh3d: pc.forcesh3d. Additional flags as needed. 4. Initialize Rasterizer: Create GaussianRasterizer with the configured settings. 5. Retrieve and Preprocess Attributes: Retrieve 3D means, opacity, and other attributes from pc. If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true: Compute pre-computed 3D covariance and mean offset. If pc.rot4d is true, apply the mean offset to means3D. If pc.gaussiandim == 4, multiply opacity by marginal time probability marginalt. If pipe.computecov3Dpython is false: Retrieve raw scales, rotations, and time-specific scales/positions (scalest, ts). If pc.gaussiandim == 4 and pc.rot4d is true, retrieve rotationsr. If pc.gaussiandim == 4, compute temporal direction dirt and use evalshfs4d with spatial direction, temporal direction, and time duration. Clamp result sh2rgb + 0.5 to minimum 0.0. 7. If prefiltered, assign original radii to the positions indicated by mask. name: 4D Gaussian Splatting (DreamGaussian4D)
head: DreamGaussianHD
body: 4D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the DreamGaussian4D method, generates dynamic 4D scenes from a single reference image or video. It differs from sibling methods like AYG by learning motion from a driving video generated by an image-to-video model rather than using a video diffusion prior directly on the scene. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) by extending the static representation to 4D using HexPlane deformations. The method consists of three main phases: static initialization, dynamic generation, and optional refinement/export. Input: A single reference image or video. Output: A dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting representation, optionally exported as an animated mesh. 1. Static 3DGS: Generated via an improved version of DreamGaussian. Contains standard 3D Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). 2. Deformation Field Network: A network added to the static 3DGS to model temporal deformations. 3. HexPlane: Used to model Gaussian deformations for realistic motion. (Note: cites HexPlane [70] as the dynamic representation, while describes a "deformation network" optimized during dynamic generation. The exact internal structure of the HexPlane tensor is not detailed in the provided sources.) 1. Static Initialization: Generate a static 3DGS from the reference image using an improved DreamGaussian pipeline. 2. Driving Video Generation: Use an off-the-shelf Stable Diffusion Video model to generate a driving video from the reference image. 3. Dynamic Generation: Optimize the deformation field network added to the static 3DGS. Use the generated driving video as supervision. Apply a 3D SDS loss based on Zero-1-to-3 XL from sampled views to ensure cross-view consistency. Randomly select some frames to add image-based SDS to ensure generation quality. (Note: states motion is learned from the driving video generated by the image-to-video model, contrasting with AYG.) 4. Refinement (Optional): Perform video-to-video optimization pipeline to improve temporal coherence. 5. Export: Extract a mesh sequence and optimize its texture using an image-to-video diffusion model. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dreamgaussian4d(referenceimage): # Step 1: Static Initialization # Uses improved DreamGaussian static3dgs = dreamgaussianinit(referenceimage) # Step 2: Driving Video Generation # Uses off-the-shelf Stable Diffusion Video drivingvideo = stablediffusionvideogenerate(referenceimage) # Step 3: Dynamic Generation # Initialize deformation field network deformationnet = initializedeformationnetwork() # Optimization loop for epoch in range(numepochs): # Sample frames from driving video videoframes = sampleframes(drivingvideo) # Render dynamic 3DGS using deformation net # Note: Exact 4D rasterization details are in parent [13946-4d-gaussian-rasterization.md] renderedframes = render4dgaussians(static3dgs, deformationnet, videoframes) # Compute 3D SDS loss using Zero-1-to-3 XL # Sampled views are used for this loss views = sampleviews() sdsloss3d = compute3dsdsloss(renderedframes, views, zero1to3xl) # Compute image-based SDS loss for randomly selected frames selectedframes = randomsample(videoframes) sdslossimg = computeimagesdsloss(selectedframes) # Combine losses totalloss = sdsloss3d + sdslossimg # Update deformation network optimize(deformationnet, totalloss) # Step 4: Optional Refinement # Video-to-video optimization for temporal coherence refined3dgs = videotovideorefine(static3dgs, deformationnet) # Step 5: Export # Extract mesh sequence and optimize texture meshsequence = extractmeshsequence(refined3dgs) optimizedmesh = optimizemeshtexture(meshsequence, imagetovideodiffusion) return optimizedmesh Stable Diffusion Video: Off-the-shelf model used for driving video generation. Zero-1-to-3 XL: Used for 3D SDS loss. Temporal Coherence: Addressed via optional video-to-video refinement. Degenerate Input: Not specified in sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Generates dynamic 4D scenes from single image/video. Uses HexPlane for realistic motion. Can export as animated mesh. Limitations: Relies on off-the-shelf diffusion models (Stable Diffusion Video, Zero-1-to-3 XL) which may introduce artifacts. Temporal coherence may require additional refinement. When to use: When 4D generation from a single image is required. When not to use: When video diffusion prior is preferred over driving video. Origin: DreamGaussian4D [15] achieves 4D generation given a reference image. It is based on DreamGaussian [8, 128] for image-to-3D initialization. Development: It utilizes HexPlane [70] to model Gaussian deformations. It contrasts with AYG [48] by learning motion from a driving video generated by an image-to-video model. Usage: Used for dynamic 4D scene generation from single images or videos. name: Softmax-GS Rendering Algorithm
head: Softmax Gaussian Splatting
body: Softmax-GS is a rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that employs a softmax-based competition mechanism to handle overlapping Gaussians, aiming to provide order-invariance and smooth transitions at Gaussian boundaries. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which suffers from popping artifacts due to sorting dependencies, or StopThePop, which exhibits abrupt color changes, Softmax-GS produces flicker-free, smooth transitions by treating overlapping splats as a competitive blending process rather than a strict depth-sorted accumulation. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by replacing the standard alpha blending step with this differentiable, order-invariant softmax competition. Inputs and Outputs: The algorithm takes a set of K Gaussians projected onto a pixel, along with the pixel coordinate x{\text{pixel}}. It outputs the final pixel color c{\text{past}}, depth d{\text{past}}, and transmittance T{\text{past}} after processing all K Gaussians. Data Structures: The method maintains running accumulators for the current pixel: T{\text{past}}: Current transmittance (initialized to 1). c{\text{past}}: Accumulated color (initialized to 0). d{\text{past}}: Moving average of depth (initialized to 0). p{\text{past}}: Moving average of the Gaussian exponent (initialized to 0). Each Gaussian k provides: x[k]: 2D center coordinate. \sigma[k]: 2D conic matrix (inverse covariance). o[k]: Opacity scalar. c[k]: Color vector (RGB). d[k]: Depth scalar. \alpha[k]: Boundary sharpness parameter (Generalized Exponential Function exponent). \beta[k]: Softmax competition temperature parameter. \gamma[k]: Depth decay influence parameter. Steps: 1. Initialize accumulators: T{\text{past}} = 1, c{\text{past}} = 0, d{\text{past}} = 0, p{\text{past}} = 0. 2. Loop for each Gaussian k from 1 to K: a. Compute the vector difference x' = x[k] - x{\text{pixel}}. b. Compute the Mahalanobis distance squared using the conic \sigma[k]. Let p{\text{cur}} be negative half of this distance: p{\text{cur}} = -0.5 \cdot (x')^T \sigma[k] x' c. Compute the raw absorbance a{\text{cur}} using the Generalized Exponential Function (GEF) controlled by \alpha[k]: a{\text{cur}} = o[k] \cdot \exp(-(-p{\text{cur}})^{\alpha[k]}) d. If T{\text{past}} < 1 (i.e., not the first Gaussian or previous Gaussians did not fully block the ray), perform the softmax blending block: i. Record the original transmittance: T{\text{orig}} = T{\text{past}} \cdot (1 - a{\text{cur}}). ii. Compute the past absorbance: a{\text{past}} = 1 - T{\text{past}}. iii. Compute the softmax weight w{\text{cur}} for the current Gaussian based on the competition between the current exponent p{\text{cur}} and the past average exponent p{\text{past}}: w{\text{cur}} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(\beta[k] \cdot (p{\text{past}} - p{\text{cur}}))} iv. Compute the softmax-weighted current absorbance: \hat{a}{\text{cur}} = w{\text{cur}} \cdot a{\text{cur}}. v. Compute the softmax-weighted past absorbance: w{\text{past}} = 1 - w{\text{cur}}, then \hat{a}{\text{past}} = w{\text{past}} \cdot a{\text{past}}. vi. Enforce order invariance and transmittance maintenance by re-normalizing the absorbances to match the original transmittance T{\text{orig}}. The target sum of absorbances is 1 - T{\text{orig}}. The algorithm solves for a scaling factor m such that the new absorbances \bar{a}{\text{past}} and \bar{a}{\text{cur}} satisfy the quadratic constraint derived from T{\text{orig}} = 1 - (\bar{a}{\text{past}} + \bar{a}{\text{cur}}) while preserving their ratio. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm is applied only to the first 128 Gaussians along each ray to maintain linear complexity in the backward pass. This results in incomplete coverage (approx. 85% for indoor, 70% for outdoor scenes). The order-invariance mechanism does not extend to cases with three or more overlapping Gaussians with distinct colors due to bookkeeping complexity under linear-time constraints. Distant semi-transparent Gaussians can bias running estimates of accumulated depth and opacity toward intermediate values, affecting softmax-based competition. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithm maintains linear complexity in the backward pass by limiting the number of Gaussians processed per ray to 128. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 indoor scenes, Softmax-GS accounts for approximately 85% of pixels across test images. On Mip-NeRF360 outdoor scenes, Softmax-GS accounts for around 70% of pixels. In view consistency benchmarks (Table 4 in), Softmax-GS achieves higher PSNR and lower FLIP7 scores compared to 3D GS and StopThePop on scenes like "bicycle", "counter", "kitchen", "train", and "truck". Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Produces smooth, flicker-free transitions at Gaussian crossings, avoiding the popping artifacts of 3D GS and the abrupt color changes of StopThePop. It effectively merges intersecting Gaussians into a single surface. Limitations: Incomplete coverage due to the 128-Gaussian limit; inability to handle >2 overlapping distinct-color Gaussians with order invariance; sensitivity to distant semi-transparent Gaussians biasing depth/opacity estimates.
