head: XPR implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: XPR-3DGS is a point-based differentiable rendering method that implements 3D Gaussian Splatting within the XPR framework. It projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, culls tiles based on conic bounds, and evaluates alpha blending per pixel. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing a high-level, Python-based implementation that requires significantly fewer lines of code than traditional C++/CUDA implementations, while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of 3D Gaussian primitives defined by PrimitiveParams. Output: Rendered image colors and alpha values. Data Structures: The primitive parameters are defined as follows: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class PrimitiveParams: mu: Array # (3,) mean in world space s: Array # (3,) scales q: Array # (4,) unit quaternion for rotation sh: Array # (C, 3) spherical harmonic coefficients o: Array # (1,) opacity Parameters: alphathresh: Threshold for opacity to determine visibility. Default value is 1/255. znear: Near plane distance for camera-space depth check. pixelinfo: Set to None because per-pixel evaluation depends only on the 2D pixel coordinates. Steps: 1. Project: For each primitive p, compute the projection onto the image plane. Compute the world-to-camera projection matrix R{w2c}. Transform the mean \mu to camera space: \muc = R{w2c} \mu. Compute the 2D mean \mu{2D} and the 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} using EWA splatting. Compute the determinant det of \Sigma{2D}. Compute the conic matrix \Sigma{2D}^{-1}, referred to as conic2D. Compute extents ex, ey from \Sigma{2D} and det. Compute radius r from ex, ey. Compute the axis-aligned bounding box aabb using \mu{2D}, ex, ey. Compute tile count tc as the area of aabb in tile units: tc = (aabb.x{max} - aabb.x{min}) \times (aabb.y{max} - aabb.y{min}). Compute visibility flag: visible = (det > 0) \land (o \ge \alpha{thresh}) \land (r > 0) \land (tc > 0) \land (\muc[2] > z{near}). Adjust tile count: tc = tc \times float(visible). Compute view-dependent color c from \mu and spherical harmonics sh. Produce Tile Cull Data (p{tcd}): Concatenate conic2D[0,0], conic2D[0,1], conic2D[1,1], opacity o, \mu{2D}, and visible. Produce Shader Data (p{sd}): Concatenate \mu{2D}[0], \mu{2D}[1], -0.5 \times \text{conic\2D}[0,0], -\text{conic\2D}[0,1], -0.5 \times \text{conic\2D}[1,1], opacity o, and color c. 2. Tile Cull: For each tile in the primitive's bounding box, determine if the tile needs to be processed. Unpack conic, o, \mu{2D}, and visible from p{tcd}. Check if \mu{2D} is outside the tile bounds (tile{min}, tile{max}). Compute the 2D location point{2D} inside the tile that maximizes the Gaussian response. This is either \mu{2D} (if inside the tile) or a point along the edges of the tile facing \mu{2D}. Compute max contribution power: dx = \mu{2D}[0] - point{2D}[0], dy = \mu{2D}[1] - point{2D}[1], power = 0.5 \times (dx^2 \times conic[0] + 2 \times dx \times dy \times conic[1] + dy^2 \times conic[2]). Determine tile visibility: tile\visible = (power \le \log(o / \alpha{thresh})) \land visible. 3. Evaluate: For each pixel px = (x, y) in visible tiles, compute the contribution. Unpack \mu{2D}, conic, o, and c from p{sd}. Compute dx = px[0] - \mu{2D}[0], dy = px[1] - \mu{2D}[1]. Compute power: power = dx^2 \times conic[0] + dx \times dy \times conic[1] + dy^2 \times conic[2]. Compute alpha: \alpha = o \times \exp(power). Validate result: valid = (power \le 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def project(p, cam, view, cfg): # Get world to camera projection matrix Rw2c = world2cameraprojectionmatrix(view) muc = world2cam(p.mu, Rw2c) mu2D = computemu2D(muc, cam) # EWA splatting cov2D, det, = computecov2D(p.s, p.q, muc, Rw2c, cam, cfg) con2D = computeconic2D(cov2D, det) # Compute extent, radius, and bounding box ex, ey = computeextents(cov2D, det, p.o, cfg) r = computeradius(ex, ey) aabb = getboundingbox(mu2D, ex, ey, cfg) # Compute tile count tc = (aabb.xmax - aabb.xmin) (aabb.ymax - aabb.ymin) # Compute visibility flag and adjust tile count visible = (det > 0) and (p.o >= cfg.alphathresh) and (r > 0) and (tc > 0) and (muc[2] > cfg.znear) tc = float(visible) # Compute view-dependent color c c = computecolor(p.mu, p.sh, view) # Produce tile cull data and shader data for primitive p ptcd = concat(con2D[0,0], con2D[0,1], con2D[1,1], p.o, mu2D, visible) psd = concat(mu2D[0], mu2D[1], -0.5con2D[0,0], -con2D[0,1], -0.5con2D[1,1], p.o, c) return ProjectResult(depth=muc[2], visible=visible, tileculldata=ptcd, shaderdata=psd, aabb=aabb, tilecount=tc) def tilecull(tilemin, tilemax, ptcd, cfg): conic, o, mu2D, visible = unpack(ptcd) muoutside = (mu2D[0] < tilemin[0]) or (mu2D[0] > tilemax[0]) or (mu2D[1] < tilemin[1]) or (mu2D[1] > tilemax[1]) # Compute location of the 2D point inside the tile that maximizes the response point2D = computepointwithmaxresponse(tilemin, tilemax, conic, muoutside) # Compute max contribution power of 2D Gaussian dx = mu2D[0] - point2D[0] dy = mu2D[1] - point2D[1] power = 0.5 (dxdxconic[0] + 2dxdyconic[1] + dydyconic[2]) # Keep tile iff max contribution to tile satisfies: o exp(-power) >= cfg.alphathresh tilevisible = (power <= math.log(o / cfg.alphathresh)) and visible return tilevisible def evaluate(pxdata, psd): mu2D, conic, o, c = unpack(psd) dx = pxdata[0] - mu2D[0] dy = pxdata[1] - mu2D[1] power = dx dx conic[0] + dx dy conic[1] + dy dy conic[2] alpha = o math.exp(power) valid = power <= 0. return EvaluateResult(alpha=alpha, valid=valid, color=c) XPR3DGS = MethodSpec(project=project, tilecull=tilecull, pixelinfo=None, evaluate=evaluate) Performance: XPR-3DGS is slower than the Base implementation on Synthetic datasets (0.76x FPS) due to JAX kernel launch overhead being significant at very high frame rates. On 360 and T&T datasets, it achieves 0.95x and 0.96x FPS respectively. Code Size: Requires only 260 to 304 lines of Python, significantly fewer than Base implementations (e.g., 2,153 lines for 3DGS). Strengths: High-level interface enables rapid prototyping; fewer lines of code reduce implementation complexity. Limitations: JAX overhead impacts performance at very high frame rates; pixel evaluation depends only on 2D coordinates, which may be less flexible than methods using per-pixel world-space ray directions. XPR-3DGS is an implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting within the XPR framework, which is an extensible cross-platform point-based differentiable renderer. It utilizes EWA splatting for projection. XPR: An Extensible Cross-Platform Point-Based Differentiable Renderer, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.11529, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering
head: SSVR
body: Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering (SSVR) is a volume rendering technique used as an alternative to vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rasterization to improve geometric fidelity, particularly for depth and surface reconstruction. It produces RGB images nearly identical to standard 3DGS rasterization under suitable conditions but offers geometric advantages by reducing holes and blurred boundaries in depth maps. It is equivalent to 3DGS rasterization when an appropriate vacancy function is applied. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives defined by parameters \theta (position, covariance, opacity, color). Camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, intrinsics). Image resolution and tile configuration (if using tiled rasterization). Outputs: RGB image. Depth map (median depth). Data Structures: Gaussian primitives: Standard 3DGS representation (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients for color). Ray parameters: Origin o, direction d. Core Concept: SSVR reformulates the rendering integral using a "vacancy function" v(x). The density \sigma(x, \omega) is defined as: \sigma(x, \omega) = \omega^\top \nabla \log v(x) where \omega represents the view-dependent color coefficients. Equivalence Condition: To obtain RGB images equivalent to 3DGS rasterization, the vacancy function must be: v(x) = \sqrt{1 - G(x)} where G(x) is the Gaussian density function. Rendering Steps: 1. Ray-Gaussian Intersection: For each pixel, cast a ray. For each Gaussian i intersecting the ray, compute the position t along the ray relative to the Gaussian's maximum t^i along the ray direction. t^i is the sample point where the Gaussian density is maximized along the ray. 2. Transmittance Calculation: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti(t) for each Gaussian i. The transmittance is defined piecewise based on the position t relative to t^i: Ti(t) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{1 - Gi(t)}, & t \le t^i \\ \sqrt{1 - Gi(t^i)}, & t > t^i \end{cases} where Gi(t) is the cumulative opacity (or density integral) of Gaussian i at position t. Note: The source text shows Ti(t) = 1 - Gi(t) in the formula block but explicitly states v(x) = \sqrt{1-G(x)} and T(t) = \exp(-\int \sigma ds) = v(x)/v(tn). The piecewise formula in the source explicitly uses the square root form \sqrt{1-Gi(t)}. We follow the explicit piecewise formula provided in Equation 3 of the source. 3. Color Computation: The final color C is computed by integrating the radiance along the ray: C = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(x(t), \omega) c(x(t), \omega) dt where T(t) is the accumulated transmittance from all Gaussians, \sigma is the density, and c is the color. In practice, this is discretized over the sorted Gaussians. 4. Depth Rendering (Median Depth): For depth rendering, compute the median depth t{med} defined by the point where the accumulated transmittance T(t{med}) = 0.5. Find t{med} using a fixed number of bisection iterations. 5. Backpropagation: During training, differentiate the fixed condition T(t{med}) = 0.5 with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta. Using the chain rule, the gradient is computed as: \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} \frac{\partial t{med}}{\partial \theta} + \frac{\partial T}{\partial \theta} = 0 This allows gradients to flow through the depth definition to optimize the Gaussian parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def stochasticsolidvolumerendering(gaussians, camera, imageshape): """ Renders RGB and Depth using Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. Each has: mean: (3,) covariance: (3,3) opacity: scalar color: (3,) or SH coefficients camera: Camera object with project() and unproject() methods. imageshape: (H, W) Returns: rgb: (H, W, 3) depth: (H, W) """ H, W = imageshape rgb = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) depth = np.zeros((H, W)) # Pre-project Gaussians to 2D to get bounding boxes and screen-space covariance # This step is assumed to be handled by the parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization # which assigns Gaussians to tiles. Here we assume we iterate over visible Gaussians per tile/pixel. for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # Cast ray for pixel (x, y) rayo, rayd = camera.getray(x, y) # Collect intersecting Gaussians for this ray # In a tiled implementation, this would be done per tile visiblegaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Check if Gaussian intersects ray and is within tile bounds if gaussianintersectsray(g, rayo, rayd): # Compute t (position of max density along ray) tstar = computegaussianmaxposition(g, rayo, rayd) visiblegaussians.append((g, tstar)) # Sort Gaussians by tstar (front to back) visiblegaussians.sort(key=lambda item: item[1]) # Initialize accumulated transmittance Tacc = 1.0 coloracc = np.zeros(3) depthsamples = [] # Render loop for g, tstar in visiblegaussians: # Sample points along the ray segment covered by this Gaussian # For simplicity, assume we evaluate at the center or integrate # The source defines Ti(t) piecewise around tstar # Compute Gi(t) at current ray position t # Note: In discrete rasterization, we often evaluate at the center of the splat # or use the precomputed 2D Gaussian. # Let's assume we have a function to get G(t) for a Gaussian at ray position t tcurrent = computerayposition(g, rayo, rayd) # Placeholder for actual intersection Git = computegaussiandensity(g, tcurrent) # Compute Ti(t) according to Eq 3 if tcurrent <= tstar: Ti = np.sqrt(1.0 - Git) else: Gitstar = computegaussiandensity(g, tstar) Ti = np.sqrt(1.0 - Gitstar) # Update accumulated transmittance # Taccnew = Taccold Ti # However, the source defines T(t) as the accumulated transmittance. # In standard volume rendering, T(t) = exp(-int sigma ds). # Here, the vacancy function approach implies a specific integration. # We follow the source's definition: Ti(t) is the transmittance contribution. # Standard alpha blending with vacancy function modification # The source implies T(t) is the product of individual Ti(t) or similar. # Let's assume standard accumulation: Tacc = Ti # Actually, the source says "accumulated transmittance is then computed as shown in Equation 3" # Equation 3 defines Ti(t) for a single Gaussian. # The total T(t) is likely the product of all Ti(t) for Gaussians behind the current point. # For color accumulation: # C = int T(t) sigma c dt # With vacancy function, sigma = omega^T grad log v # This simplifies to color blending with modified weights. # Simplified implementation for 3DGS-like rasterization: # Weight wi = Tacc (1 - Ti) / (1 - Ti) ? No. # Standard 3DGS: wi = alphai prod(Tj) # Here, we use the vacancy function. # Let's use the explicit formula for depth and color from the source context. # The source emphasizes the equivalence to 3DGS when v(x) = sqrt(1-G). # So we can use standard 3DGS rasterization logic but with the vacancy function for depth. # Compute opacity contribution # In 3DGS, alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) # Here, we use the vacancy function directly. # For RGB: # Color contribution from Gaussian i # Ci = Tacc (1 - Ti) ci ? # The source doesn't give the exact color blending formula, only the transmittance. # However, it states equivalence to 3DGS. # So we use standard 3DGS color blending: # alphai = 1 - Ti (if Ti is the transmittance after the Gaussian) # But Ti(t) is defined as the transmittance of the Gaussian. # Let's assume standard alpha blending with the computed Ti # Tacc is the transmittance before this Gaussian. # The transmittance after this Gaussian is Tacc Ti. # The absorbed color is Tacc (1 - Ti) ci. # Wait, Ti(t) in Eq 3 is defined as sqrt(1-G). # If G is the cumulative opacity, then 1-G is the remaining transmittance? # No, G is density. # Let's stick to the source's explicit depth formula and general equivalence. # Update Tacc Tacc = Ti # Accumulate color # Assuming standard 3DGS color blending logic applies due to equivalence # alphacontribution = 1 - Ti (if Ti is the transmittance through the Gaussian) # But Ti is defined as sqrt(1-G). # If G is small, Ti ~ 1. # Let's use the standard 3DGS rasterization for color, as they are equivalent. # The difference is in depth. # For depth, we need to track the transmittance curve. depthsamples.append((tcurrent, Tacc)) # Compute RGB using standard 3DGS blending (due to equivalence) # This is a placeholder for the actual color integration rgb[y, x] = computecolorfromgaussians(visiblegaussians, rayo, rayd) # Compute Depth using Median Transmittance # Find tmed such that T(tmed) = 0.5 # T(t) is the accumulated transmittance. # We have samples (t, Tacc). # Interpolate to find t where Tacc = 0.5 tmed = findmediandepth(depthsamples, targetT=0.5) depth[y, x] = tmed return rgb, depth def computegaussiandensity(g, t): """Compute G(t) for a Gaussian at position t along the ray.""" # Standard 3DGS density computation # G(t) = alpha exp(-0.5 (t - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (t - mu)) # This is a placeholder. The exact implementation depends on the 3DGS density function. pass def computegaussianmaxposition(g, rayo, rayd): """Compute t where Gaussian density is maximized along the ray.""" # This is the projection of the Gaussian mean onto the ray, adjusted for covariance. # For a 3D Gaussian, the maximum along a ray is at the intersection of the ray with the Gaussian's principal axis? # Or simply the point on the ray closest to the mean? # In 3DGS, the 2D projection is used. # For 3D volume rendering, we need the 3D density. # The source mentions t is the location of the Gaussian maximum along the ray. pass def findmediandepth(samples, targetT): """Find t such that T(t) = targetT using bisection.""" # Sort samples by t samples.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Bisection # We need to interpolate between samples to find t where T(t) = targetT # T(t) is piecewise constant or linear? # In volume rendering, T(t) is continuous. # We can interpolate T(t) between samples. # Simple bisection on the ray segment tmin = samples[0][0] tmax = samples[-1][0] for in range(10): # Fixed number of iterations tmid = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 Tmid = interpolateT(tmid, samples) if Tmid > targetT: tmin = tmid else: tmax = tmid return (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 def interpolateT(t, samples): """Interpolate accumulated transmittance T(t) at position t.""" # Find the segment containing t # T(t) is the product of Ti for all Gaussians with ti < t # This requires re-evaluating the product, which is expensive. # In practice, we precompute the T values at sample points. # Here, we assume samples are dense enough or we use linear interpolation. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The square root in the vacancy function v(x) = \sqrt{1 - G(x)} requires G(x) \le 1. If G(x) > 1 due to numerical errors, the result is undefined. Guard against this by clamping G(x) to [0, 1]. Boundaries: The piecewise definition of Ti(t) depends on t^i. Incorrect computation of t^i leads to incorrect transmittance. t^i must be computed accurately as the position of maximum density along the ray. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian is degenerate (e.g., zero covariance), the density is infinite. Handle by capping density or skipping such Gaussians. Time Complexity: Similar to 3DGS rasterization, O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels, assuming efficient sorting and rasterization. The depth computation adds a small constant factor due to bisection. Memory Complexity: Same as 3DGS, O(N) for Gaussian storage. Additional memory for depth samples during bisection is negligible. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable on modern GPUs, similar to 3DGS. Strengths: Improved geometric fidelity for depth and surface reconstruction; reduced holes and blurred boundaries in depth maps. Limitations: Slightly more complex implementation due to the vacancy function and median depth computation. When to use: When geometric accuracy (depth, surface) is more important than raw RGB fidelity, or when 3DGS rasterization produces poor depth maps. When not to use: When RGB fidelity is the only concern and 3DGS rasterization is sufficient, as SSVR offers no RGB advantage. Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering was introduced as an optimization-based method for 3D Gaussian Splatting to improve geometric representation. It builds on the work of Miller et al. (2023), Zhang et al. (2026), and Gomez et al. (2026) who proved the equivalence between SSVR and 3DGS rasterization under suitable conditions. The method is used in contexts requiring accurate camera parameters, often estimated with SfM pipelines, and can be combined with test-time optimization for feed-forward models. name: Mip-Splatting Rasterization Pipeline
head: Gaussian Splatting CUDA Rasterizer, Mip-Splatting Forward/Backward Pass
body: The Mip-Splatting Rasterization Pipeline is a differentiable GPU-based rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates view-dependent scaling (mip-splatting) to handle aliasing and resolution changes. It extends the tiled rasterization approach by using a kernelsize parameter to adjust the Gaussian projection scale, ensuring consistent visual quality across different camera distances and resolutions. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by adding specific preprocessing for mip-levels and a robust binning/sorting mechanism for tile-based rendering. The pipeline consists of a forward pass (rendering) and a backward pass (gradient computation). It relies on three main state structures: GeometryState, ImageState, and BinningState. Inputs: means3D: 3D Gaussian centers, shape (P, 3). scales: Gaussian scales, shape (P, 3). scalemodifier: Scalar multiplier for scales. rotations: Gaussian rotations (quaternions), shape (P, 4). opacities: Gaussian opacities, shape (P). shs: Spherical Harmonics coefficients, shape (P, K, 3) or precomputed colors. colorsprecomp: Precomputed RGB colors, shape (P, 3). If null, SHs are used. viewmatrix: 4 \times 4 view transformation matrix. projmatrix: 4 \times 4 projection matrix. campos: Camera position, shape (3). width, height: Image dimensions. focalx, focaly: Focal lengths in pixels. tanfovx, tanfovy: Tangents of horizontal and vertical field of view. kernelsize: Float controlling the effective Gaussian kernel size for mip-splatting. prefiltered: Boolean flag indicating if SH coefficients are prefiltered. subpixeloffset: Float array of size 2 for subpixel camera offsets. background: Background color, shape (3). Outputs: outcolor: Rendered image, shape (H, W, 3). numrendered: Number of Gaussian instances rendered. Gradients for backward pass: dLdmean3D, dLdcolor, dLdcov3D, dLdsh, dLdscale, dLdrot, dLdopacity, dLdmean2D, dLdconic. GeometryState (allocated for P Gaussians): depths: float, size P. clamped: float, size P \times 3. internalradii: float, size P. means2D: float, size P \times 2 (implied by usage). cov3D: float, size P \times 6. conicopacity: float, size P. rgb: float, size P \times 3. tilestouched: uint32t, size P. scanningspace: void, size varies. pointoffsets: uint32t, size P. ImageState (allocated for N = \text{width} \times \text{height} pixels): accumalpha: float, size N. ncontrib: uint32t, size N. ranges: uint2, size N (stores start/end indices for each tile in the sorted list). BinningState (allocated for P Gaussians): pointlist: uint32t, size P. pointlistunsorted: uint32t, size P. pointlistkeys: uint64t, size P. pointlistkeysunsorted: uint64t, size P. listsortingspace: void, size varies. sortingsize: sizet. 1. Calculate Focal Lengths: If not provided, compute: \text{focal\y} = \frac{\text{height}}{2.0 \times \tan(\text{fov\y})} \text{focal\x} = \frac{\text{width}}{2.0 \times \tan(\text{fov\x})} 2. Initialize GeometryState: Allocate GeometryState buffer of size required<GeometryState>(P) and initialize it. If radii is null, set the radii pointer to geomState.internalradii. 3. Calculate Tile Grid: \text{tile\grid}.x = \lceil \frac{\text{width}}{\text{BLOCK\X}} \rceil \text{tile\grid}.y = \lceil \frac{\text{height}}{\text{BLOCK\Y}} \rceil \text{tile\grid}.z = 1 \text{block}.x = \text{BLOCK\X}, \quad \text{block}.y = \text{BLOCK\Y}, \quad \text{block}.z = 1 Typical values for BLOCKX and BLOCKY are 32. 4. Initialize ImageState: Allocate ImageState buffer of size required<ImageState>(width height) and initialize it. Pitfall: If NUMCHANNELS != 3 and colorsprecomp is null, throw a runtime error. 5. Preprocess (Projection and Mip-Splatting): Launch FORWARD::preprocess kernel with P threads. Inputs: means3D, scales, scalemodifier, rotations, opacities, shs, clamped, cov3Dprecomp, colorsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos, width, height, focalx, focaly, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, radii, means2D, depths, cov3D, rgb, conicopacity, tilegrid, tilestouched, prefiltered. Note: This kernel computes 2D means, covariances, and radii, applying the kernelsize for mip-splatting adjustments. 6. Compute Point Offsets: Compute inclusive prefix sum over tilestouched to get pointoffsets. \text{point\offsets}[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i} \text{tiles\touched}[j] Use cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum. 7. Get Total Rendered Count: Copy the last element of pointoffsets to host variable numrendered. 8. Initialize BinningState: Allocate BinningState buffer of size required<BinningState>(numrendered) and initialize it. 9. Duplicate with Keys (Tile Binning): Launch duplicateWithKeys kernel with (P + 255) / 256 blocks of 256 threads. For each Gaussian, if its bounding box overlaps a tile, emit a key/value pair. Key construction: \text{key} = (\text{tile\y} \times \text{tile\grid}.x + \text{tile\x}) \ll 32 \mid \text{depth} Value: Gaussian index idx. Inputs: means2D, depths, pointoffsets, pointlistkeysunsorted, pointlistunsorted, radii, tilegrid. 10. Radix Sort: Calculate bit depth for radix sort: \text{bit} = \text{getHigherMsb}(\text{tile\grid}.x \times \text{tile\grid}.y) Sort pointlistkeysunsorted and pointlistunsorted using cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs. Inputs: listsortingspace, sortingsize, keysunsorted, keyssorted, valuesunsorted, valuessorted, numrendered, 0, 32 + bit. Result: pointlistkeys (sorted keys) and pointlist (sorted Gaussian indices). 11. Identify Tile Ranges: Zero out imgState.ranges buffer of size tilegrid.x tilegrid.y sizeof(uint2). If numrendered > 0, launch identifyTileRanges kernel with (\text{num\rendered} + 255) / 256 blocks of 256 threads. Logic: If idx == 0, ranges[currtile].x = 0. Else, get prevtile = pointlistkeys[idx - 1] >> 32. If currtile != prevtile, set ranges[prevtile].y = idx and ranges[currtile].x = idx. If idx == L - 1, set ranges[currtile].y = L. Inputs: numrendered, pointlistkeys, imgState.ranges. 12. Determine Feature Pointer: If colorsprecomp is not null, use it; otherwise use geomState.rgb. 13. Render: Launch FORWARD::render kernel. Inputs: tilegrid, block, imgState.ranges, pointlist, width, height, subpixeloffset, means2D, featureptr, conicopacity, accumalpha, ncontrib, background, outcolor. 14. Return: Return numrendered. 1. Initialize States: Initialize GeometryState, BinningState, and ImageState from provided buffers. If radii is null, set radii pointer to geomState.internalradii. 2. Calculate Focal Lengths and Tile Grid: Same as forward pass. 3. Determine Color Pointer: If colorsprecomp is not null, use it; otherwise use geomState.rgb. 4. Render Backward: Launch BACKWARD::render kernel. Inputs: tilegrid, block, imgState.ranges, pointlist, width, height, subpixeloffset, background, means2D, conicopacity, colorptr, accumalpha, ncontrib, dLdpix, dLdmean2D, dLdconic, dLdopacity, dLdcolor. 5. Determine Cov3D Pointer: If cov3Dprecomp is not null, use it; otherwise use geomState.cov3D. 6. Preprocess Backward: Launch BACKWARD::preprocess kernel with P threads. Inputs: P, D, M, means3D, radii, shs, clamped, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, cov3Dptr, viewmatrix, projmatrix, focalx, focaly, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, campos, dLdmean2D, dLdconic, dLdmean3D, dLdcolor, dLdcov3D, dLdsh, dLdscale, dLdrot, conicopacity, dLdopacity. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch import cupy # Assuming CuPy for CUDA kernel launch simulation or similar def mipsplattingforward(means3D, scales, scalemodifier, rotations, opacities, shs, colorsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos, width, height, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, prefiltered, subpixeloffset, background): """ Forward pass for Mip-Splatting Rasterization Pipeline. """ P = means3D.shape[0] # 1. Calculate Focal Lengths focaly = height / (2.0 math.tan(tanfovx)) # Note: tanfovx is usually fovx, but formula uses tan(fov) # Correction: The source says focaly = height / (2.0f tanfovy). # Assuming tanfovx and tanfovy are precomputed tangents. focaly = height / (2.0 tanfovy) focalx = width / (2.0 tanfovx) # 2. Initialize GeometryState geomstate = allocategeometrystate(P) radii = geomstate.internalradii # 3. Calculate Tile Grid BLOCKX = 32 BLOCKY = 32 tilegridx = math.ceil(width / BLOCKX) tilegridy = math.ceil(height / BLOCKY) tilegrid = (tilegridx, tilegridy, 1) block = (BLOCKX, BLOCKY, 1) # 4. Initialize ImageState N = width height imgstate = allocateimagestate(N) if colorsprecomp is None: if NUMCHANNELS != 3: raise RuntimeError("NUMCHANNELS must be 3 if colorsprecomp is null") # 5. Preprocess Kernel # Launch FORWARD::preprocess with P threads # Inputs: means3D, scales, scalemodifier, rotations, opacities, shs, clamped, # cov3Dprecomp, colorsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos, # width, height, focalx, focaly, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, # radii, means2D, depths, cov3D, rgb, conicopacity, tilegrid, # tilestouched, prefiltered launchpreprocesskernel( P, means3D, scales, scalemodifier, rotations, opacities, shs, geomstate.clamped, None, colorsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos, width, height, focalx, focaly, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, radii, geomstate.means2D, geomstate.depths, geomstate.cov3D, geomstate.rgb, geomstate.conicopacity, tilegrid, geomstate.tilestouched, prefiltered) # 6. Compute Point Offsets # cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum geomstate.pointoffsets = cupy.cumsum(geomstate.tilestouched, dtype=cupy.uint32) # 7. Get Total Rendered Count numrendered = geomstate.pointoffsets[-1] # 8. Initialize BinningState binningstate = allocatebinningstate(numrendered) # 9. Duplicate with Keys # Launch duplicateWithKeys kernel launchduplicatewithkeyskernel( (P + 255) // 256, 256, geomstate.means2D, geomstate.depths, geomstate.pointoffsets, binningstate.pointlistkeysunsorted, binningstate.pointlistunsorted, radii, tilegrid) # 10. Radix Sort bit = gethighermsb(tilegridx tilegridy) # cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs binningstate.pointlistkeys, binningstate.pointlist = cupy.radixsortpairs( binningstate.pointlistkeysunsorted, binningstate.pointlistunsorted, numrendered, 0, 32 + bit) # 11. Identify Tile Ranges imgstate.ranges = cupy.zeros((tilegridx tilegridy, 2), dtype=cupy.uint32) if numrendered > 0: launchidentifytilerangeskernel( (numrendered + 255) // 256, 256, numrendered, binningstate.pointlistkeys, imgstate.ranges) # 12. Determine Feature Pointer featureptr = colorsprecomp if colorsprecomp is not None else geomstate.rgb # 13. Render Kernel outcolor = cupy.zeros((height, width, 3), dtype=cupy.float32) launchrenderkernel( tilegrid, block, imgstate.ranges, binningstate.pointlist, width, height, subpixeloffset, geomstate.means2D, featureptr, geomstate.conicopacity, imgstate.accumalpha, imgstate.ncontrib, background, outcolor) return numrendered, outcolor def gethighermsb(n): """Returns the position of the highest set bit.""" if n == 0: return 0 return n.bitlength() - 1 Time Complexity: Dominated by the preprocessing projection (O(P)), the binning and sorting (O(P \log P) or O(P) with radix sort), and the tile-based rendering (O(N + P)). The radix sort is typically efficient on GPU. Memory Complexity: O(P) for geometry and binning states, O(N) for image state. Performance: Highly optimized for GPU execution using CUDA. The tile-based approach reduces memory contention and allows for efficient culling. Mip-splatting adds a small overhead for kernel size adjustment but significantly improves visual quality at varying resolutions. Strengths: Differentiable, handles aliasing via mip-splatting, efficient tile-based rendering, supports SH for view-dependent colors. Limitations: Requires significant GPU memory for large P. Sorting can be a bottleneck if not optimized. The Mip-Splatting Rasterization Pipeline is part of the Mip-Splatting project, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing mip-splatting to handle view-dependent scaling. It was developed by the Autonomous Vision group at ETH Zurich. The method is described in the GitHub repository. autonomousvision/mip-splatting, https://github.com/autonomousvision/mip-splatting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: SimpleRenderer (CPU Gaussian Splatting)
head: Painter's Algorithm Gaussian Rendering, Simplified Gaussian Renderer
body: SimpleRenderer is a CPU-based rendering method for 3D Gaussian point clouds that approximates Gaussian Splatting using a painter's algorithm. It projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen ellipses and composites them to generate an RGB image, suitable for visualization and small-scale point clouds where GPU acceleration is unavailable. Unlike standard 3DD Gaussian Splatting which relies on CUDA-based tile-based rasterization for performance and differentiability, SimpleRenderer uses a simplified 2D ellipse approximation and non-differentiable alpha blending. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (defined by mean position \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color), a camera configuration (intrinsic and extrinsic parameters), and a RenderConfig. Outputs: An RGB image buffer of shape (H, W, 3) with float32 dtype, with values in [0, 1]. Data Structures: RenderConfig: A dataclass containing: backgroundcolor: Tuple of floats, default (0.05, 0.05, 0.08). alphathreshold: Float, default 0.01. nearplane: Float, default 0.1. farplane: Float, default 50.0. PinholeCamera: Defines the projection geometry: width, height: Image dimensions. fx, fy: Focal lengths in pixels. cx, cy: Principal point coordinates. position: Camera position in world coordinates (3,). lookat: Target point in world coordinates (3,). up: Up vector in world coordinates (3,). Steps: 1. Initialize Buffer: Create an output image buffer I of shape (H, W, 3) initialized to backgroundcolor. 2. Iterate Gaussians: Loop through each Gaussian g in the cloud. 3. Project Center: Transform the Gaussian center \mug to camera coordinates: \muc = R^T (\mug - t), where R and t are derived from position, lookat, and up. Project to pixel coordinates: u = \frac{fx \cdot \muc.x}{\muc.z} + cx, v = \frac{fy \cdot \muc.y}{\muc.z} + cy. 4. Culling: Skip the Gaussian if: Its opacity \alphag < \text{alpha\threshold}. Its depth \muc.z is outside [\text{near\plane}, \text{far\plane}]. 5. Project Covariance: Compute the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} by projecting the 3D covariance \Sigmag. This involves the Jacobian J of the perspective projection and the rotation matrix R: \Sigma{2D} = J R \Sigmag R^T J^T The Jacobian J for a point at depth z is: J = \begin{bmatrix} fx/z & 0 & -fx \cdot x/z^2 \\ 0 & fy/z & -fy \cdot y/z^2 \end{bmatrix} (Note: Exact implementation details for the projection of the full 3D covariance to 2D screen space may vary slightly in approximation, but the core principle is the linearization of the projection onto the tangent plane at the Gaussian center). 6. Render Ellipse: For each pixel (x, y) within the bounding box of the projected ellipse: Calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance: D^2 = (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c})^T \Sigma{2D}^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{p} = [x, y]^T and \mathbf{c} = [u, v]^T. Compute the 2D Gaussian weight: w = \exp(-0.5 \cdot D^2). Compute the final opacity contribution: \alpha{final} = \alphag \cdot w. Compute the color Cg from spherical harmonics or stored RGB. Perform alpha blending into the image buffer I at (x, y): I{new} = I{old} \cdot (1 - \alpha{final}) + Cg \cdot \alpha{final} (Note: Standard volume rendering compositing is C = \sum ci \alphai \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj). SimpleRenderer often uses a simpler additive blend or assumes opaque compositing order if not strictly sorting. The source notes imply "accumulating opacity and color" via alpha blending). 7. Finalize: Return the image buffer I. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def simplerenderer(gaussians, camera, config): """ Render 3D Gaussians using a CPU-based painter's algorithm. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mean: np.ndarray (3,) cov: np.ndarray (3, 3) opacity: float color: np.ndarray (3,) or SH coefficients camera: PinholeCamera object with attributes: width, height, fx, fy, cx, cy position, lookat, up config: RenderConfig object with attributes: backgroundcolor, alphathreshold, nearplane, farplane Returns: np.ndarray: Image buffer (H, W, 3) """ H, W = camera.height, camera.width # Initialize output buffer image = np.full((H, W, 3), config.backgroundcolor, dtype=np.float32) # Compute camera rotation matrix R and translation t # z-axis: normalized lookat - position zaxis = camera.lookat - camera.position zaxis /= np.linalg.norm(zaxis) # x-axis: cross(up, z) xaxis = np.cross(camera.up, zaxis) xaxis /= np.linalg.norm(xaxis) # y-axis: cross(z, x) yaxis = np.cross(zaxis, xaxis) R = np.stack([xaxis, yaxis, zaxis], axis=0).T # 3x3 rotation matrix from world to camera t = camera.position for g in gaussians: # 1. Project center to camera coordinates muworld = g.mean mucam = R.T @ (muworld - t) # (3,) depth = mucam[2] # 2. Culling if g.opacity < config.alphathreshold: continue if depth < config.nearplane or depth > config.farplane: continue # 3. Project to pixel coordinates u = (camera.fx mucam[0] / depth) + camera.cx v = (camera.fy mucam[1] / depth) + camera.cy # 4. Project covariance to 2D screen space # Jacobian of perspective projection at mucam # J = d(x,y)/d(X,Y,Z) fx = camera.fx fy = camera.fy J = np.array([ [fx / depth, 0, -fx mucam[0] / (depth2)], [0, fy / depth, -fy mucam[1] / (depth2)] ]) # 2x3 # Sigma2D = J R Sigma3D R.T J.T Sigma2D = J @ R @ g.cov @ R.T @ J.T # 2x2 # 5. Determine bounding box for the ellipse # Eigenvalues of Sigma2D to get axis lengths eigenvalues, = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2D) # Use 3 sigma for bounding box to capture most energy radiusx = 3.0 np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) radiusy = 3.0 np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) minx = int(max(0, u - radiusx)) maxx = int(min(W - 1, u + radiusx)) miny = int(max(0, v - radiusy)) maxy = int(min(H - 1, v + radiusy)) if minx > maxx or miny > maxy: continue # 6. Render ellipse # Precompute inverse covariance for Mahalanobis distance try: Sigma2Dinv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2D) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): p = np.array([x - u, y - v]) D2 = p @ Sigma2Dinv @ p weight = np.exp(-0.5 D2) alphafinal = g.opacity weight if alphafinal < 1e-6: # Optimization: skip negligible contributions continue color = g.color # Assuming pre-computed color for this Gaussian # Alpha blending # Inew = Iold (1 - alpha) + C alpha image[y, x] = image[y, x] (1.0 - alphafinal) + color alphafinal return image Parameters: alphathreshold: Default 0.01. Gaussians below this opacity are skipped. nearplane: Default 0.1. farplane: Default 50.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point precision issues may arise when computing the inverse of \Sigma{2D} if the Gaussian is degenerate (e.g., very thin or flat). A small regularization term may be needed. Boundaries: The bounding box calculation must be clamped to the image dimensions [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1] to avoid out-of-bounds access. Non-differentiable: This method is not differentiable and cannot be used for training. Real 3DGS training requires a CUDA differentiable rasterizer. Uses transmittance culling to skip Gaussians that do not contribute significantly to the final pixel color, improving performance over simple alpha blending. Focuses on the correct projection of 3D Gaussians to 2D and sorting them by depth to ensure correct alpha compositing order, which SimpleRenderer approximates or ignores depending on implementation. A specialized renderer for Gaussian Splatting, likely using different optimization techniques for specific use cases. A variant that assumes constant opacity for depth rendering, simplifying the compositing process. A GPU-optimized method using tiles and radix sort for efficient Gaussian sorting and rendering, contrasting with SimpleRenderer's CPU-based approach. Allows overriding camera poses for rendering, useful for debugging or specific visualization tasks. Techniques for balancing load in parallel rendering implementations. Uses a half-cosine squared kernel for splatting, which may have different visual properties than the standard Gaussian. Optimizes Gaussian loading and culling using HSPT (Hierarchical Spatial Partitioning Tree). A specific rendering algorithm for Gaussian Splatting. Uses voxel-cell masks for per-fragment rendering decisions. Optimizes rendering by processing only relevant parts of the image. The standard GPU-based rasterization method for 3DGS, which SimpleRenderer replaces for CPU-only environments. A VTK-based mapper for Gaussian points. Renders features associated with Gaussians, not just color. Standardized rendering for 3DGS in glTF. Uses softmax for compositing. A specific variant of 3DGS. Uses stochastic methods for volume rendering. Uses mipmaps for anti-aliasing in Gaussian Splatting. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot B), where N is the number of Gaussians and B is the average number of pixels covered by each Gaussian's bounding box. This is significantly slower than GPU-based tile-based rasterization for large N. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the image buffer. No additional large data structures are required for sorting or tiling. Performance: Suitable for small-scale point clouds and visualization. Not suitable for real-time rendering or large scenes due to CPU limitations. Strengths: No GPU required, simple implementation, easy to debug. Limitations: Slow, non-differentiable, limited to small scenes. When to use: Visualization, debugging, environments without GPU support. When not to use: Training, real-time rendering, large-scale scenes. SimpleRenderer is part of the GaussianScan-Recon project, an unofficial implementation of Gaussian Splatting for reconstruction tasks. It was developed to provide a CPU-based alternative to the standard CUDA-based 3DGS renderer, enabling visualization and testing without GPU hardware. The method is explicitly noted as not suitable for training, which requires a differentiable CUDA rasterizer. Laityperfect7/GaussianScan-Recon, https://github.com/Laityperfect7/GaussianScan-Recon, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad)
head: Gaussian Splat Rendering Pipeline, RenderGaussianSplats, Splatv Render Program, VideoRenderProgram, WebGL Instanced Gaussian Splat Rendering
body: Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) is a display-only rendering technique that projects 3D Gaussian distributions into 2D screen-space quads, sorts them by camera-space depth, and renders them using instanced drawing with standard alpha blending. It solves the problem of visualizing large-scale, photorealistic 3D scenes reconstructed via Gaussian Splatting on client-side hardware without requiring neural network inference or server-side ray tracing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by utilizing a CPU-side depth sorting algorithm (often offloaded to a background worker) to resolve the non-commutative nature of alpha blending, whereas the parent 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) describes the general projection and quad-drawing mechanism without specifying the sorting implementation. Unlike Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, this method relies on explicit per-splat sorting rather than tile-based accumulation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A depth-sorted index buffer (Uint32Array) mapping instance IDs to splat indices; view-space projection data (position, axes, color, opacity) stored in textures or buffers; camera matrices (Model-View, Projection); screen resolution parameters. Outputs: A composited color buffer with pre-multiplied alpha blending. Data Structures: Vertex Buffer: Contains 8 floats representing a unit quad: [-2, -2, 2, -2, 2, 2, -2, 2]. Index Buffer (Depth Index): A Uint32Array containing the depth-sorted splat indices, updated via worker messages. Splat Texture: Created with gl.RGBA32UI internal format, gl.RGBAINTEGER format, and gl.UNSIGNEDINT type, sized to the render data width and height. For animated or complex variants, additional textures (e.g., splatRotation as RGBA16F) may be used. View Data: Contains per-splat attributes including position, rotation (quaternion), scale, and color (SH degree 0). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the vertex buffer with quad coordinates and the index buffer for sorted splat indices. Initialize the scene, camera, and render data. 2. Sorting (CPU/Worker): Send initial sort data (positions, dummy transforms, transform indices) to a background worker. On each render frame, update the camera and send the view-projection matrix to the worker. The worker computes the depth-sorted order and returns the depthIndex buffer. 3. Setup Blending: Configure the graphics pipeline for alpha blending: gl.blendFuncSeparate(gl.ONEMINUSDSTALPHA, gl.ONE, gl.ONEMINUSDSTALPHA, gl.ONE). 4. Bind Attributes: Bind the index buffer using gl.vertexAttribIPointer with a divisor of 1 to enable instanced drawing. 5. Vertex Shader Execution: Map the instance ID to the splat index using the order buffer: instID = OrderBuffer[instID]. Load view data for the splat: SplatViewData view = SplatViewData[instID]. Check if the splat is behind the camera (centerClipPos.w <= 0). If so, output a NaN vertex (asfloat(0x7fc00000)) to discard the primitive. Transform the voxel position to view space: vec4 voxelPosViewSpace = MV glin[0].glPosition. Transform to clip space and normalize: vec4 voxelPosClipSpace = P voxelPosViewSpace; voxelPosClipSpace /= voxelPosClipSpace.w. Perform clip-space frustum culling. Calculate the voxel offset: voxelOffset = splatSize \times (scale/gridLength) \times \sqrt{2}. Calculate the half-edge length in clip space: voxelHalfEdgeLengthClipSpace = distance(voxelPosClipSpace, voxelRightEdgeMidPointClipSpace). Define the frustum culling border: voxelFrustumCullingBorder = 1 + voxelHalfEdgeLengthClipSpace. Discard if voxelPosClipSpace.x or y is outside [-voxelFrustumCullingBorder, voxelFrustumCullingBorder]. Calculate the quad position in clip space. For WebGL implementations, map instance ID to quad corners: quadPos = float2(idx&1, (idx>>1)&1) 2.0 - 1.0; quadPos = 2.0. Calculate screen delta: deltaScreenPos = (quadPos.x view.axis1 + quadPos.y view.axis2) 2 / ScreenParams.xy. Final vertex: o.vertex.xy += deltaScreenPos centerClipPos.w. (Optional) Handle selection bits if SplatBitsValid is true, marking selected splats with specific color values. 6. Fragment Shader Execution: Calculate the Gaussian falloff: power = -dot(i.pos, i.pos); alpha = exp(power). If not selected, saturate alpha: alpha = saturate(alpha i.col.a). If selected, apply magenta outline logic: if alpha > 7.0/255.0, set alpha = 1 and i.col.rgb = selectedColor if alpha < 10.0/255.0; otherwise alpha = saturate(alpha + 0.3) and tint i.col.rgb = lerp(i.col.rgb, selectedColor, 0.5). Discard fragment if alpha < 1.0/255.0. Output final color: res = half4(i.col.rgb alpha, alpha). 7. Draw Call: Call gl.drawArraysInstanced(gl.TRIANGLEFAN, 0, 4, vertexCount). Formulas: Voxel Offset: voxelOffset = splatSize \times \frac{scale}{gridLength} \times \sqrt{2}. Frustum Culling Border: voxelFrustumCullingBorder = 1 + distance(voxelPosClipSpace, voxelRightEdgeMidPointClipSpace). Gaussian Falloff: \alpha = e^{-d^T \Sigma2^{-1} d} (evaluated as exp(-dot(i.pos, i.pos)) in simplified implementations). Parameters: ScreenParams.xy: Screen resolution in pixels, used to normalize the screen-space delta of the quad. ufocal: WebGLUniformLocation for camera focal lengths fx, fy. splatCount: The number of splats to render, coerced to the range 0..splatCloud.count. Defaults to the full cloud count. Used for LOD or reveal effects. utime: WebGLUniformLocation for animation time, typically set to Math.sin(Date.now() / 1000) / 2 + 1 / 2. uviewport: WebGLUniformLocation for canvas dimensions [canvas.width, canvas.height]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Behind Camera: Splats with clip-space w \le 0 must be discarded to prevent rendering artifacts. This is handled by outputting a NaN vertex in the vertex shader. Multiple Objects: Multiple Splatv objects are not supported in some implementations (e.g., gsplat.js), triggering a console warning. Worker Initialization: The background worker must be initialized before rendering; checks for renderer.renderProgram.worker === null and returns an error if null. Tone Mapping: The material cancels the View's tone mapping so colors are displayed as stored in the splat data (SH degree 0 only). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(instanceid, quadcornerindex): # 1. Map instance to splat index splatindex = orderbuffer[instanceid] # 2. Load view data viewdata = splatviewdata[splatindex] # 3. Check behind camera centerclipw = viewdata.centerclippos.w if centerclipw <= 0: return NaNVERTEX # Discard primitive # 4. Transform to view/clip space voxelposview = mvmatrix viewdata.position voxelposclip = projectionmatrix voxelposview voxelposclip /= voxelposclip.w # 5. Frustum Culling voxeloffset = splatsize (viewdata.scale / gridlength) sqrt(2) rightedgemid = projectionmatrix (voxelposview.xy + vec2(0.5, 0) voxeloffset) rightedgemid /= rightedgemid.w halfedgelen = distance(voxelposclip, rightedgemid) cullingborder = 1.0 + halfedgelen if abs(voxelposclip.x) > cullingborder or abs(voxelposclip.y) > cullingborder: return NaNVERTEX # Discard primitive # 6. Calculate Quad Position # Map quadcornerindex (0-3) to [-2, -2], [2, -2], [2, 2], [-2, 2] quadx = (quadcornerindex & 1) 2.0 - 1.0 quady = ((quadcornerindex >> 1) & 1) 2.0 - 1.0 quadpos = vec2(quadx, quady) 2.0 # Screen delta calculation screendelta = (quadpos.x viewdata.axis1 + quadpos.y viewdata.axis2) 2.0 / screenparams.xy finalvertex = voxelposclip.xy + screendelta centerclipw return finalvertex def fragmentshader(interpolatedpos, interpolatedcolor): # Calculate Gaussian falloff power = -dot(interpolatedpos, interpolatedpos) alpha = exp(power) # Handle selection if interpolatedcolor.a < 0: # Selected if alpha > 7.0/255.0: if alpha < 10.0/255.0: alpha = 1.0 rgb = selectedcolor # Magenta else: alpha = saturate(alpha + 0.3) rgb = lerp(interpolatedcolor.rgb, selectedcolor, 0.5) else: discardfragment() else: # Not selected alpha = saturate(alpha interpolatedcolor.a) rgb = interpolatedcolor.rgb if alpha < 1.0/255.0: discardfragment() return half4(rgb alpha, alpha) WebGL Gaussian Splatting is a real-time rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) implemented in web browsers using WebGL 1.0, with variants utilizing the Three.js library or running without external dependencies. It solves the problem of displaying large-scale, photorealistic 3D scenes reconstructed via Gaussian Splatting on client-side hardware without requiring neural network inference or server-side ray tracing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by utilizing a CPU-side depth sorting algorithm (often offloaded to a Web Worker) to resolve the non-commutative nature of alpha blending, whereas the parent Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) describes the general projection and quad-drawing mechanism without specifying the sorting implementation. Unlike Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering), this method typically omits spherical harmonics to reduce file size and memory footprint for web delivery. Debug Splat Point Rendering is a diagnostic visualization technique that renders individual 3D Gaussian splats as small screen-space quads centered at their projected positions. Unlike the production rendering path which draws full elliptical splats for opacity blending, this method isolates the center location and basic attributes of each splat, allowing developers to inspect splat distribution, density, and attribute correctness. It serves as a lightweight alternative to full splat rendering for verifying the correctness of the splat data pipeline and camera projection logic. The Gaussian Splat Fragment Shader evaluates the 2D Gaussian probability density function (PDF) at each fragment of a screen-space quad to determine splat coverage and modulate fragment color. It composites the new splat over the existing framebuffer color using pre-multiplied alpha blending. It is distinguished from its parent Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) by performing the per-pixel alpha evaluation and blending logic directly in the fragment shader, handling transparency via alpha cutoffs and discarding fragments behind the camera or with negligible alpha. This method configures the GPU render pass by populating a material property block (or uniform buffer) with splat count, spherical harmonic (SH) degree, brightness, scale, antialiasing settings, transform matrices, and optional skinning or volume lighting data. It solves the problem of efficiently passing per-renderer and global state to the fragment shader without causing state overwrites in multi-camera setups or shader compilation errors when optional features (like skinning) are disabled. It differs from standard mesh rendering by explicitly handling the decoupling of jittered projections and ensuring valid sampled resources even for unused features. Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering) is a GPU-accelerated rendering method for time-varying 3D Gaussian splats that computes time-dependent position, rotation, and scale deltas from packed texture data to enable smooth animation without per-frame CPU updates. It differs from static 3D Gaussian Splatting by evaluating polynomial motion deltas and applying temporal opacity decay in the vertex and fragment shaders, building on the screen-space quad rendering of Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad). A Unity Universal Render Pipeline (URP) ScriptableRendererFeature that renders pre-sorted 3D Gaussian splats into a temporary render target and composites the result onto the camera color buffer. It differs from raw shader implementations by integrating into the URP render graph, handling XR multipass separation, and managing the intermediate render target lifecycle automatically. A rendering method for Gaussian splats that computes anisotropic covariance matrices to handle perspective distortion and view-dependent scaling, improving edge crispness and reducing haze compared to isotropic approximations. In the vertex shader, it computes the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma3 = R \cdot S^2 \cdot R^T, transforms it to view space, computes the perspective Jacobian J, applies a low-pass filter (+0.3 \text{ px}^2) to \Sigma2, and eigen-decomposes it to place quad corners at \text{centre} \pm 3\sqrt{\lambda}v. It requires a third RGBA16F texture (splatRotation) for quaternions. A rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting where each splat is rendered as an isotropic billboard (circle) using the maximum of the three axis scales, ignoring the rotation for the shape geometry. This results in a hazy, over-bright appearance (the 'P1 isotropic artefact'). It fetches per-splat data from two RGBA16F textures, determines billboard size using max axis scale, and renders as hardware-instanced camera-facing quads with batches of at most 65535 instances per draw call. Sorting complexity is O(n \log n) on the CPU. A rendering technique that projects 3D Gaussian ellipses onto the screen space by computing a 2x2 covariance matrix, allowing for accurate anisotropic rendering of splats as ellipses rather than circles. It computes \Sigma = R \cdot S \cdot S^T \cdot R^T, projects it using the view Jacobian, eigen-decomposes to find major/minor axes, and places quad corners on these axes. It differs from isotropic rendering by using the full covariance matrix, reducing overdraw and providing a sharper image. It requires a third RGBA16F texture for rotation/scale data. A vertex shader for rendering Gaussian splats as quads. It takes SplatCount (uint32), DebugMode (uint32: 0=off, 1=cluster colors), and EnableNanite (uint32: 1=Nanite enabled) as parameters. It inputs ViewDataBuffer (StructuredBuffer<FGaussianSplatViewData>) and SortKeysBuffer (StructuredBuffer<uint>). Time Complexity: Sorting is O(n \log n) on the CPU. Rendering is O(n) for the draw call, but fragment processing is proportional to the number of overlapping pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for splat data (positions, rotations, scales, colors) and the sorted index buffer. For 233k splats, sorting involves ~5.6 MB of texture re-upload per frame. Measured Performance: On mid-range phones, fill rate and overdraw dominate performance. Anisotropic ellipses reduce overdraw compared to max-axis discs, offering a performance win. The CPU sort is feasible up to ~300–500k splats; beyond that, LOD/pruning is needed. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard graphics APIs (WebGL, Unity URP); leverages existing instanced drawing capabilities; effective for real-time web and mobile visualization. Limitations: CPU sorting becomes a bottleneck at very high splat counts (>500k); isotropic variants suffer from visual artifacts (haze); multiple Splatv objects are not supported in some WebGL implementations. When to Use: Real-time visualization of Gaussian Splatting scenes in web browsers (WebGL) or Unity URP environments where CPU sorting is acceptable. When Not to Use: Scenes with millions of splats requiring real-time performance without LOD; platforms where CPU sorting is too slow or unavailable (e.g., pure GPU sorting required). Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) is a rendering technique identical in geometry generation to Circle Splat, used for Gaussian Splat visualization, projecting voxels as 2D quads. It is used in gsplat.js for real-time WebGL rendering of Gaussian splats. The method builds on the general 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, adapting it for screen-space quad rendering with CPU-side sorting. It is commonly used in web-based viewers (e.g., gsplat.js) and Unity URP implementations. mmalesadev/svorenderer, https://github.com/mmalesadev/svorenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) aras-p/UnityGaussianSplatting, https://github.com/aras-p/UnityGaussianSplatting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) huggingface/gsplat.js, https://github.com/huggingface/gsplat.js, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) feat(sceneview): sort splats for the scene camera by default and add …, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/commit/5f2a4dd1f683ddb444669be54b78ce7913b55b70, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Explore: Gaussian splatting, OpenUSD, AI world generation, volumetric video — study, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/issues/4023, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, https://github.com/YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: WebGL Gaussian Splatting
head: Gaussian Splat Rendering Pipeline, Gaussian Splatting Web Rendering (Three.js), Gaussian Splatting WebGL, Three.js Gaussian Splatting, Web-based 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering, WebGL 1.0 Gaussian Splatting
body: WebGL Gaussian Splatting is a real-time rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) implemented in web browsers using WebGL 1.0, with variants utilizing the Three.js library or running without external dependencies. It solves the problem of displaying large-scale, photorealistic 3D scenes reconstructed via Gaussian Splatting on client-side hardware without requiring neural network inference or server-side ray tracing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by utilizing a CPU-side depth sorting algorithm (often offloaded to a Web Worker) to resolve the non-commutative nature of alpha blending, whereas the parent Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) describes the general projection and quad-drawing mechanism without specifying the sorting implementation. Unlike Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering), this method typically omits spherical harmonics to reduce file size and memory footprint for web delivery. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary.splat file containing N Gaussian primitives. Each primitive consists of a 3D center, 3D scale, a quaternion stored as 4 bytes (normalized by subtracting 128 and dividing by 128.0, with the z-component negated), and color/alpha data. Output: A 2D screen image rendered via WebGL 1.0 drawElements or drawArrays with instanced rendering, using custom vertex and fragment shaders. Data Structures: The implementation typically uses InstancedBufferGeometry in Three.js. The layout per vertex in the raw.splat file is 32 bytes: 1. center: 3 Float32 (12 bytes, offset 0). 2. scale: 3 Float32 (12 bytes, offset 12). 3. color/alpha: 4 Uint8 (R, G, B, A, offset 24). 4. quaternion: 4 Uint8 (x, y, z, w, offset 28). In the GPU buffers, these are unpacked into: splatColor: Float32Array of size 4N (RGBA, normalized to [0,1]). splatCenterCovariance: Float32Array of size 9N. The covariance matrix \mathbf{V}{rk} is stored as 3 vec3s: [0] is the center, [1] is (M{11}, M{12}, M{13}), [2] is (M{22}, M{23}, M{33}). position: Float32Array of size 18 (6 components for 4 vertices, including duplicates for triangle rendering) defining a quad with corners (2,2,0), (-2,2,0), (-2,-2,0), (2,-2,0). Numbered Steps: 1. Data Parsing and Matrix Construction: Parse the.splat file. For each vertex i: Extract center from fbuffer[8i+0..2], scale from fbuffer[8i+3+0..2], quaternion from ubuffer[32i+28..31] (normalized by subtracting 128 and dividing by 128.0, with z-component negated), and color/alpha from ubuffer[32i+24..27] (divided by 255). Construct a 4 \times 4 instance matrix \mathbf{M}i. Compute rotation matrix \mathbf{R} from q. Scale by scale vector. The matrix is constructed as \mathbf{M}i = \mathbf{R}^T \cdot \text{Scale} \cdot \mathbf{R} \cdot \text{Translate}(\text{center}). Encode color/alpha into matrix elements 3, 7, 11, 15. 2. Depth Sorting (CPU): Calculate depth for each splat using the view vector \mathbf{v}{view} (camera forward direction from camera.matrixWorld elements 2, 6, 10): \text{depth}i = \mathbf{v}{view}[0] \cdot \mathbf{M}i[12] - \mathbf{v}{view}[1] \cdot \mathbf{M}i[13] - \mathbf{v}{view}[2] \cdot \mathbf{M}i[14] Perform a 16-bit single-pass counting sort to reorder indices based on depth. Compute depthInv = (65535)/(maxDepth-minDepth), bin = ((depth-minDepth)depthInv)|0, count bins, compute starts, and place indices in depthIndex array. Reorder the instance matrices and attributes into sortedMatrices and sortedAttributes. This step is often offloaded to a Web Worker to prevent blocking the main thread. 3. Vertex Shader Execution: For each instance (splat) and each vertex of the quad: Frustum Culling: Compute clip-space position \mathbf{pos}{2d} = \text{realProjectionMatrix} \cdot \text{viewMatrix} \cdot \text{vec4}(\text{splatCenter}, 1). Let w = \mathbf{pos}{2d}.w. If \mathbf{pos}{2d}.z < -w or |\mathbf{pos}{2d}.x| > 1.2w or |\mathbf{pos}{2d}.y| > 1.2w, discard the primitive by setting glPosition to (0,0,2,1). Covariance Projection: Compute focal length: focal = \frac{\text{size}.y}{2.0 \cdot \tan(\frac{\text{camera.fov} \cdot \pi}{360.0})}. Compute Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the projection at the splat center \mathbf{c} in camera space \mathbf{c}{cam}: \mathbf{J} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{fx}{cz} & 0 & -\frac{fx cx}{cz^2} \\ 0 & \frac{fy}{cz} & -\frac{fy cy}{cz^2} \end{bmatrix} Compute transformation \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{J}, where \mathbf{W} is the rotation part of the view matrix (transpose of the upper-left 3x3 of viewMatrix). Compute 2D covariance \mathbf{cov}{2D} = \mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{V}{rk} \mathbf{T}. Regularize: \mathbf{cov}{00} \leftarrow \mathbf{cov}{00} + 0.3, \mathbf{cov}{11} \leftarrow \mathbf{cov}{11} + 0.3. Eigenvalue Decomposition: diagonal1 = \mathbf{cov}{00}, diagonal2 = \mathbf{cov}{11}, offDiagonal = \mathbf{cov}{01}. mid = 0.5(diagonal1 + diagonal2). radius = \sqrt{(\frac{diagonal1 - diagonal2}{2})^2 + offDiagonal^2}. \lambda1 = mid + radius. \lambda2 = \max(mid - radius, 0.1). Basis Vectors: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(offDiagonal, \lambda1 - diagonal1). \mathbf{v}1 = \min(\sqrt{2\lambda1}, 1024.0) \cdot \mathbf{d}. \mathbf{v}2 = \min(\sqrt{2\lambda2}, 1024.0) \cdot \text{vec2}(\mathbf{d}.y, -\mathbf{d}.x). Position Output: \mathbf{v}{Center} = \frac{\mathbf{pos}{2d}}{w}. \mathbf{p}{screen} = \mathbf{v}{Center} + \frac{x \cdot \mathbf{v}2 + y \cdot \mathbf{v}1}{\text{viewport}} \cdot 2.0. glPosition = \text{vec4}(\mathbf{p}{screen}, 0.0, 1.0). 4. Fragment Shader Execution: Compute distance from fragment center to splat center in local quad space: A = -\mathbf{v}{Position} \cdot \mathbf{v}{Position}. If A < -4.0, discard fragment. Compute alpha: B = e^A \cdot v{Color}.a. Output color: \text{gl\FragColor} = \text{vec4}(B \cdot v{Color}.rgb, B). 5. Blending: Render with depthTest=false, depthWrite=false. Blending function: blendSrc=OneMinusDstAlphaFactor, blendDst=OneFactor, blendSrcAlpha=OneMinusDstAlphaFactor, blendDstAlpha=OneFactor. Parameters: WebGL Version: 1.0. Culling Bound: 1.2 \cdot w. Covariance Regularization: 0.3 added to diagonal elements. Minimum Eigenvalue: 0.1 for \lambda2. Maximum Axis Length: 1024.0 for \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. Gaussian Cutoff: Discard if squared distance > 4.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting: Incorrect sorting order leads to visual artifacts due to non-commutative alpha blending. The sorting must be updated every frame as the camera moves. A simpler variant using isotropic point sprites with CPU-side back-to-front sorting to correct blending order, lacking anisotropic covariance and spherical harmonics. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N) with counting sort, but dominated by the constant factor of memory access and worker communication. Rendering is O(N) for draw calls. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat data and sorted indices. Performance: Real-time on modern desktop GPUs via WebGL 1.0. Performance scales with the number of splats N and viewport resolution. Strengths: No external dependencies beyond Three.js; works on standard web browsers; efficient on ordinary graphics hardware compared to NeRFs. Limitations: No view-dependent shading (spherical harmonics omitted for file size); limited to WebGL 1.0 features; sorting on CPU can block main thread if not offloaded. When to use: Web-based visualization of static or slowly moving 3DGS scenes. When not to use: High-fidelity view-dependent effects; scenes with extreme depth complexity requiring tile-based rasterization; mobile devices with poor WebGL 1.0 support. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 as a real-time radiance field rendering technique. WebGL implementations, such as the one by antimatter15, adapted this technique for the web using WebGL 1.0 and Three.js, focusing on efficient point-cloud-like rendering without neural network inference. The method was developed to allow interactive viewing of 3DGS models in browsers without heavy dependencies. antimatter15/splat, https://github.com/antimatter15/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, https://github.com/akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Isotropic Gaussian Point-Sprite Rendering
head: Gaussian-opacity point sprites, Soft Gaussian primitives
body: A rendering technique using isotropic 3D point primitives with a Gaussian alpha falloff in screen space, rendered via custom GLSL shaders. It demonstrates soft Gaussian opacity and transparency but does not implement full 3D Gaussian Splatting (no anisotropic covariance, no spherical harmonics, no GPU tile-based rasterization). It sets itself apart from its sibling WebGL Gaussian Splatting by explicitly implementing a CPU-side back-to-front sort to correct the arbitrary alpha blending order inherent in THREE.Points, whereas the parent article describes the general bounding quad approach without detailing the specific sorting mechanism for isotropic sprites. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A THREE.Points object containing attributes: position (vec3), aColor (vec3), and aRadius (float). Uniforms: uScale (float), uPixelRatio (float), uPointMode (float, 0.0 for Gaussian, 1.0 for hard-edged), uOpacity (float). Output: Screen-space pixels with color and alpha, composited using standard source-over blending. Data Structures: THREE.BufferGeometry with Float32Array attributes for positions, colors, and radii. CPU-side index array for sorting. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Execution: For each point primitive: a. Compute the model-view position: mv = modelViewMatrix vec4(position, 1.0). b. Calculate screen-space radius in pixels: \text{radiusPixels} = \text{aRadius} \times \text{uScale} \times 220.0 \times \text{uPixelRatio} / \max(1.0, -\text{mv.z}). c. Set glPointSize by clamping the radius scaled by the point mode factor: \text{gl\PointSize} = \text{clamp}(\text{radiusPixels} \times \text{mix}(1.0, 0.22, \text{uPointMode}), 1.0, 150.0 \times \text{uPixelRatio}). d. Pass color to fragment shader: vColor = aColor. 2. Fragment Shader Execution: For each fragment covered by the point sprite: a. Compute normalized sprite coordinates: p = glPointCoord 2.0 - 1.0. b. Calculate squared distance from center: r2 = dot(p, p). c. Discard fragment if r2 > 1.0. d. Compute alpha: \alpha = \text{mix}(\exp(-4.5 \times r^2), 1.0, \text{uPointMode}) \times \text{uOpacity}. Where r = \sqrt{r2}. e. Discard fragment if \alpha < 0.008. f. Output glFragColor = vec4(vColor, alpha). 3. CPU-Side Back-to-Front Sorting: To ensure correct transparency compositing: a. Trigger sort when camera changes (dirtySort = true). b. Compute camera depth for each point i using the inverse world matrix M: zi = M{2}xi + M{6}yi + M{10}zi + M{14}. Where M is the 16-element array of camera.matrixWorldInverse.elements, and (xi, yi, zi) are the world-space coordinates of point i. c. Sort indices by zi ascending (more negative is farther). d. Reorder position, aColor, and aRadius arrays in the THREE.BufferGeometry attributes according to the sorted indices. e. Set needsUpdate = true on the attributes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def clamp(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(x, hi)) def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def vec4(x, y, z, w): return [x, y, z, w] def vertexshader(position, aColor, aRadius, modelViewMatrix, uScale, uPixelRatio, uPointMode): # position is vec3, aColor is vec3, aRadius is float mv = [sum(modelViewMatrix[r][c] (position[c] if c < 3 else 1.0) for c in range(4)) for r in range(4)] mvz = mv[2] vColor = aColor glPosition = [sum(mv[c] (projectionMatrix[c][r] if False else 0) for c in range(4)) for r in range(4)] radiuspixels = aRadius uScale 220.0 uPixelRatio / max(1.0, -mvz) scalefactor = mix(1.0, 0.22, uPointMode) glPointSize = clamp(radiuspixels scalefactor, 1.0, 150.0 uPixelRatio) return vColor, glPosition, glPointSize def fragmentshader(vColor, uOpacity, uPointMode, pointcoord): # pointcoord is vec2 in [0, 1] p = [pointcoord[0] 2.0 - 1.0, pointcoord[1] 2.0 - 1.0] r2 = dot(p, p) if r2 > 1.0: return None # discard gaussianalpha = math.exp(-4.5 r2) alpha = mix(gaussianalpha, 1.0, uPointMode) uOpacity if alpha < 0.008: return None # discard return [vColor[0], vColor[1], vColor[2], alpha] # glFragColor def sortbackfront(mflat, positions, colors, radii, count): indices = list(range(count)) def getdepth(idx): i3 = idx 3 return mflat[2]positions[i3] + mflat[6]positions[i3+1] + mflat[10]positions[i3+2] + mflat[14] indices.sort(key=getdepth) for attrname, attr in [("position", positions), ("aColor", colors), ("aRadius", radii)]: if attrname in ("position", "aColor"): newdata = [attr[i3 + k] for i in indices for k in range(3)] else: newdata = [attr[i] for i in indices] attr[:] = newdata needsUpdate = True Parameters: uOpacity: Peak opacity multiplier. Typical value: 1.0. uPointMode: Switch between Gaussian (0.0) and hard-edged (1.0). uScale: Global scale factor for point sizes. uPixelRatio: Device pixel ratio (e.g., 1.0 or 2.0). Sorting Cadence: Performed approximately every 150 ms while the camera is moving. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha Blending Order: Three.js does not automatically sort individual points inside a THREE.Points object. Without sorting, alpha blending order is arbitrary, leading to incorrect transparency. Depth Calculation: The depth zi is computed in view space using the inverse world matrix. More negative values indicate points farther from the camera. Precision: The alpha discard threshold is 0.008. Values below this are discarded to optimize rendering. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N \log N) where N is the number of points. This is performed on the CPU, causing overhead. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing positions, colors, radii, and the index array. Measured Performance: The CPU sort introduces latency, especially with large N. The approximate update cadence (150 ms) mitigates this but results in visual jitter if the camera moves rapidly. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard WebGL point sprites; visually demonstrates Gaussian opacity; works in browsers via Three.js. Limitations: No anisotropic covariance (sprites are always circular); no spherical harmonics (view-independent color); no GPU-based tile rasterization; CPU sorting bottleneck. When to use: Educational demos, simple browser-based visualizations where high performance is not critical. When not to use: Production 3DGS rendering, scenes with millions of points, or when anisotropic splats are required. Originating from an interactive browser-based experiment exploring Gaussian point-sprite rendering with Three.js and custom GLSL shaders. Built as an educational graphics demo to understand the basic visual effect of soft Gaussian primitives and transparency, not as a full 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) implementation. It references Kerbl et al. for the underlying 3DGS concept but explicitly states it does not reconstruct scenes from photos or implement production 3DGS.
