name: Splatapult Gaussian Splat Renderer
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (SplatNode pipeline), Gaussian Splatting radiance-field cloud render, SplatNode pipeline, SplatNode render
body: A renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) files that supports VR, camera navigation, and optional spherical harmonic (SH) rendering, using either a C++ radix sort or a GPU-based multi-radix sort for depth sorting. It decodes a 3D Gaussian Splat radiance-field cloud from a PLY file and renders it as hardware-instanced, camera-facing quads on-device. It distinguishes itself from general-purpose GPU-sorted renderers by offloading the depth-sorting of splats to a background CPU thread at a configurable rate, allowing the GPU shader to focus solely on rasterization and alpha-blending. This approach trades off sorting latency for reduced GPU overhead, making it suitable for mobile XR hardware where computational budgets are shared with other system tasks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary PLY file containing 3D Gaussian parameters (positions, covariances, spherical harmonics, opacity). Output: A rendered image with correct alpha blending order (back-to-front). Data Structures: PLY Layout: INRIA binarylittleendian 1.0 format with properties in order: x, y, z, fdc0, fdc1, fdc2, opacity, scale0, scale1, scale2, rot0, rot1, rot2, rot3. Buffers: posBuffer: GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, stores posVec (Gaussian positions x,y,z,1.0). keyBuffer, keyBuffer2: GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, stores depth keys (depthVec). valBuffer, valBuffer2: GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, stores indices (indexVec). histogramBuffer: GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, stores histogram data (histogramVec). atomicCounterBuffer: GLATOMICCOUNTERBUFFER, stores atomicCounterVec. Parameters: NUMBLOCKSPERWORKGROUP: Constant set to 1024. splatCount: Controls the number of splats drawn (0..count), used for LOD or reveal hooks. Defaults to the full cloud count. isFramebufferSRGBEnabled: Boolean flag enabling sRGB framebuffer conversion to reduce color banding; triggers the #define FRAMEBUFFERSRGB in shaders. gaussianCloud->HasFullSH(): Boolean flag indicating if full spherical harmonics are loaded; triggers the #define FULLSH in shaders to enable full SH rendering. useRgcSortOverride: Boolean flag; if true, forces the use of the CPU-based rgc::radixsort instead of the GPU-based multiradixsort even if hardware supports it. cameraPositionProvider: A callback returning the live camera world position, fed to the node's painter's sort each frame. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load vertex, geometry, and fragment shaders (splatvert.glsl, splatgeom.glsl, splatfrag.glsl) with defines for SRGB and Full SH. Load pre-sort compute shader (presortcompute.glsl). If GLEWKHRshadersubgroup is present and useRgcSortOverride is false, load multi-radix sort shaders (multiradixsort.glsl, multiradixsorthistograms.glsl). Reserve posVec and fill it with Gaussian positions (x,y,z,1.0). Build Vertex Array Object (VAO). Resize depthVec. If using multi-radix sort, allocate keyBuffer, keyBuffer2, histogramBuffer, valBuffer, valBuffer2, posBuffer. If not, allocate keyBuffer, valBuffer, posBuffer and create rgc::radixsort::sorter. 2. Decode PLY: Decode the bundled.ply asset off the main thread using SplatParser.fromPly(bytes) to produce a SplatCloud object. Handle null SplatCloud during loading. 3. Pre-sort (Compute Shader): Bind preSortProg. Set uniforms: modelViewProj (projMat modelViewMat), nearFar, keyMax (std::numericlimits<uint32t>::max). Reset atomicCounterBuffer to 0. Bind buffers: slot 0 posBuffer (readonly), slot 1 keyBuffer (writeonly), slot 2 valBuffer (writeonly), slot 4 atomicCounterBuffer. Dispatch compute with LOCALSIZE=256 threads per group: glDispatchCompute(((numPoints + 255) / 256), 1, 1). Barrier: GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT | GLATOMICCOUNTERBARRIERBIT. 4. Get Count: Read atomicCounterBuffer into atomicCounterVec. Set sortCount = atomicCounterVec[0]. Assert sortCount <= numPoints. 5. Sort: Multi-Radix Sort (if enabled): Set NUMELEMENTS = sortCount, NUMWORKGROUPS = (NUMELEMENTS + 1023) / 1024. Loop i from 0 to 3 (NUMBYTES=4): 1. Bind histogramProg, set gshift = 8i. 2. Bind keyBuffer or keyBuffer2 to slot 0, histogramBuffer to slot 1. 3. Dispatch compute NUMWORKGROUPS. 4. Barrier. 5. Bind sortProg, set gshift = 8i. 6. Bind buffers based on parity of i: If even: slot 0=keyBuffer, 1=keyBuffer2, 2=valBuffer, 3=valBuffer2, 4=histogramBuffer. If odd: slot 0=keyBuffer2, 1=keyBuffer, 2=valBuffer2, 3=valBuffer, 4=histogramBuffer. 7. Dispatch compute NUMWORKGROUPS. 8. Barrier. CPU Radix Sort (if multi-radix disabled): Call sorter->sort(keyBuffer->GetObj(), valBuffer->GetObj(), sortCount). 6. Copy Sorted: If using multi-radix sort and NUMBYTES is odd, bind valBuffer2 to GLCOPYREADBUFFER, else bind valBuffer. Bind splatVao->GetElementBuffer() to GLCOPYWRITEBUFFER. Perform glCopyBufferSubData to transfer sorted indices to the VAO element buffer for rendering. 7. Render: On each frame, read the live camera world position and pass it to the node's painter's sort via a cameraPositionProvider callback. The node re-sorts the splats back-to-front based on the camera position so the far side composites correctly behind the near side. Render using hardware-instanced, camera-facing quads. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatapultrender(plybytes, cameraposition, usegpusort=True): # 1. Decode PLY splatcloud = SplatParser.fromPly(plybytes) if splatcloud is None: return None # Handle null case during loading numpoints = splatcloud.count posvec = splatcloud.positions # x,y,z,1.0 # 2. Initialize Buffers if usegpusort: keybuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) keybuffer2 = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) histogrambuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) valbuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) valbuffer2 = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) posbuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) atomiccounterbuffer = allocateatomiccounterbuffer() # Load GPU sort shaders presortprog = loadshader("presortcompute.glsl") histogramprog = loadshader("multiradixsorthistograms.glsl") sortprog = loadshader("multiradixsort.glsl") else: keybuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) valbuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) posbuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) atomiccounterbuffer = allocateatomiccounterbuffer() # Load CPU sort library sorter = rgcradixsort.createsorter() # 3. Pre-sort Compute bindshader(presortprog) setuniform(presortprog, "modelViewProj", projmat modelviewmat) setuniform(presortprog, "nearFar", nearfar) setuniform(presortprog, "keyMax", 0xFFFFFFFF) resetatomiccounter(atomiccounterbuffer) bindbuffer(presortprog, 0, posbuffer, readonly=True) bindbuffer(presortprog, 1, keybuffer, readonly=False) bindbuffer(presortprog, 2, valbuffer, readonly=False) bindbuffer(presortprog, 4, atomiccounterbuffer, readonly=False) dispatchcompute(((numpoints + 255) / 256), 1, 1) barrier(GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT | GLATOMICCOUNTERBARRIERBIT) # 4. Get Count atomiccountervec = readatomiccounter(atomiccounterbuffer) sortcount = atomiccountervec[0] assert sortcount <= numpoints # 5. Sort if usegpusort: numelements = sortcount numworkgroups = (numelements + 1023) / 1024 for i in range(4): # NUMBYTES=4 # Histogram Step bindshader(histogramprog) setuniform(histogramprog, "gshift", 8 i) # Alternate key buffers for histogram keysrc = keybuffer if i % 2 == 0 else keybuffer2 bindbuffer(histogramprog, 0, keysrc, readonly=True) bindbuffer(histogramprog, 1, histogrambuffer, readonly=False) dispatchcompute(numworkgroups, 1, 1) barrier() # Sort Step bindshader(sortprog) setuniform(sortprog, "gshift", 8 i) # Alternate key/val buffers for sort if i % 2 == 0: bindbuffer(sortprog, 0, keybuffer, readonly=True) bindbuffer(sortprog, 1, keybuffer2, readonly=False) bindbuffer(sortprog, 2, valbuffer, readonly=True) bindbuffer(sortprog, 3, valbuffer2, readonly=False) else: bindbuffer(sortprog, 0, keybuffer2, readonly=True) bindbuffer(sortprog, 1, keybuffer, readonly=False) bindbuffer(sortprog, 2, valbuffer2, readonly=True) bindbuffer(sortprog, 3, valbuffer, readonly=False) bindbuffer(sortprog, 4, histogrambuffer, readonly=True) dispatchcompute(numworkgroups, 1, 1) barrier() else: sorter.sort(keybuffer, valbuffer, sortcount) # 6. Copy Sorted if usegpusort: if 4 % 2 != 0: # NUMBYTES is odd (4 is even, so this logic might be flawed in source or implies odd bytes per key? Source says NUMBYTES=4, but check parity. 4 is even. Source says "if NUMBYTES is odd". So this block is skipped for 32-bit sort? Or maybe NUMBYTES refers to something else. Let's follow source literally.) # Source: "If using multi-radix sort and NUMBYTES is odd" # NUMBYTES=4, so this is false. pass else: # Bind valBuffer bindbuffer(GLCOPYREADBUFFER, valbuffer) bindbuffer(GLCOPYWRITEBUFFER, splatvao.elementbuffer) glcopybuffersubdata(GLCOPYREADBUFFER, GLCOPYWRITEBUFFER, 0, 0, sortcount 4) else: # CPU sort result is already in valbuffer bindbuffer(GLCOPYWRITEBUFFER, splatvao.elementbuffer) glcopybuffersubdata(valbuffer, splatvao.elementbuffer, 0, 0, sortcount 4) # 7. Render renderinstancedquads(splatvao, splatcount=numpoints) SplatXR is a Unity-based renderer designed to display 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assets directly on Extended Reality (XR) headsets, supporting both in-editor previews and on-headset execution with automatic camera switching. It distinguishes itself from general-purpose GPU-sorted renderers by offloading the depth-sorting of splats to a background CPU thread at a configurable rate, allowing the GPU shader to focus solely on rasterization and alpha-blending. This approach trades off sorting latency for reduced GPU overhead, making it suitable for mobile XR hardware where computational budgets are shared with other system tasks. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the radix sort implementation (GPU multi-radix or CPU radix). Rendering is O(N) for instanced drawing. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing positions, keys, values, and histograms. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces GPU overhead by offloading sorting to CPU, suitable for mobile XR hardware. Stable within-batch alpha-blend order prevents splat popping during slow camera orbits. Limitations: 24-bit radix sort has artifacts on some datasets, so 32-bit sort is used by default. When to use: Mobile XR hardware, real-time on-device rendering. When not to use: When GPU sorting is preferred or hardware does not support CPU offloading. Origin: Splatapult is a program to display 3D Gaussian Splatting files. History: Developed by Anthony J. Thibault. Usage: Used in Android, Apple, Web, Flutter, and React Native SDKs for real-time on-device Gaussian Splatting rendering. Supports radiance-field captures produced by Scaniverse, Polycam, Luma, and INRIA-style trainers. hyperlogic/splatapult, https://github.com/hyperlogic/splatapult, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) feat(samples): splat-preview demo — first on-device SplatNode render ( #…, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/commit/5682de62179014b063bdff5529bedb8638385f03, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: SplatXR On-Headset 3D Gaussian Splatting Renderer
head: On-Headset Splatting, SplatXR Renderer
body: SplatXR is a Unity-based renderer designed to display 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assets directly on Extended Reality (XR) headsets, supporting both in-editor previews and on-headset execution with automatic camera switching. It distinguishes itself from general-purpose GPU-sorted renderers by offloading the depth-sorting of splats to a background CPU thread at a configurable rate, allowing the GPU shader to focus solely on rasterization and alpha-blending. This approach trades off sorting latency for reduced GPU overhead, making it suitable for mobile XR hardware where computational budgets are shared with other system tasks. Inputs: A standard 3D Gaussian Splatting file in PLY format. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices) for the current rendering context (editor or headset). Outputs: A rasterized image with alpha-blended 3D Gaussian splats. Custom Splat File Format (CSV) At design time, the PLY file is converted into a custom CSV format. This file stores the precomputed attributes required for rendering: Covariance Matrix: Precomputed 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma for each Gaussian. Color: Denormalized color values (RGB). Alpha: Denormalized transparency values. Triangle Arrangement At runtime, the renderer assembles an arrangement of triangles corresponding to the splats. Each Gaussian is represented by a triangle (or set of vertices) in screen space, derived from the covariance and position. These triangles are stored in shader memory. 1. Import and Preprocessing (Design Time): The user specifies a PLY file in the Unity import panel. The plugin computes the covariance matrix for each Gaussian. Color and transparency information are denormalized. The data is saved in the custom CSV format. A game object is added to the scene hierarchy with a predefined splat material and rendering script. 2. Runtime Initialization: The rendering script reads the custom CSV file containing covariance, color, and alpha attributes. The script determines the rendering context (in-editor or on-headset) and switches to the appropriate camera and parameters. 3. Background Sorting: Triangles are sorted from the perspective of the current camera. Sorting occurs in a background CPU thread. The sorting frequency is adjustable, defaulting to 1 Hz. 4. Rendering: The shader receives the sorted triangle arrangement in memory. For each splat-associated triangle, the shader computes the screen-space coverage based on the covariance. The shader performs alpha-blending to produce the final pixel color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class SplatXRRenderer: def init(self, plypath): # Design-time preprocessing self.gaussians = self.convertplytocsv(plypath) # CSV contains: covariancematrix, color, alpha for each Gaussian self.sortingratehz = 1.0 self.lastsorttime = 0.0 self.sortedtriangles = [] def convertplytocsv(self, plypath): """ Reads PLY, computes covariance matrix, denormalizes color/alpha, and saves to CSV. Returns parsed data structure. """ # Implementation details of PLY parsing and CSV writing are omitted. # Core operation: Compute Sigma from PLY parameters. # Denormalize color and alpha. pass def update(self, currenttime, cameraviewmatrix, cameraprojmatrix): """ Called every frame. Handles sorting and rendering coordination. """ # 1. Determine Camera Context if isineditor(): camera = geteditorcamera() else: camera = getheadsetcamera() viewmatrix = camera.getviewmatrix() projmatrix = camera.getprojectionmatrix() # 2. Background Sorting (Throttled) timesincelastsort = currenttime - self.lastsorttime sortinterval = 1.0 / self.sortingratehz if timesincelastsort >= sortinterval: # Sort triangles from camera perspective in background thread self.sortedtriangles = self.sorttrianglescpu( self.gaussians, viewmatrix, projmatrix) self.lastsorttime = currenttime # 3. Render # Pass sortedtriangles to shader self.rendershader(self.sortedtriangles, viewmatrix, projmatrix) def sorttrianglescpu(self, gaussians, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """ Sorts Gaussian splats based on depth from camera. Returns list of triangles sorted back-to-front. """ # Project each Gaussian center to screen space # Compute depth # Sort indices based on depth # Assemble triangle geometry for each Gaussian pass def rendershader(self, triangles, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """ HLSL Shader invocation. Rasterizes triangles and performs alpha blending. """ # Shader logic: # For each triangle: # Compute screen-space coverage from covariance # Sample color # Alpha blend into framebuffer pass Sorting Rate: The frequency at which triangles are re-sorted from the camera's perspective. Default value is 1 Hz. High-Resolution Performance: Splats with 1 million or more Gaussians cause noticeable frame drops and are infeasible on mobile GPUs like the Qualcomm Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 (found in Quest 3) due to shared computational budgets. Passthrough Limitations: On Apple Vision Pro, passthrough shader functionality is limited by Apple’s PolySpatial platform. Level-of-Detail (LoD) Rendering: A technique implemented within SplatXR to mitigate performance issues on high-resolution splats. It displays high-resolution splats only in close proximity to the user while rendering lower-resolution splats at increasing distances. It uses three levels of detail. See Level-of-Detail 3D Gaussian Splatting. Time and Memory Complexity: Sorting complexity is O(N \log N) where N is the number of Gaussians, performed on the CPU at a throttled rate (default 1 Hz). Rendering complexity is O(N) per frame for rasterization and blending, performed on the GPU. Measured Performance: On mobile GPUs such as the Qualcomm Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2, high-resolution splats (1 million+ Gaussians) are infeasible due to computational budget constraints shared with other device tasks. The renderer supports 2 Apple Vision Pro, though passthrough features are limited. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Supports both in-editor and on-headset rendering with automatic camera switching; reduces GPU load by offloading sorting to CPU; supports LoD for high-resolution assets. Limitations: Sorting latency (1 Hz default) may cause visual jitter if the camera moves rapidly between sorts; high-resolution splats are not feasible on current mobile XR hardware without LoD. When to Use: Use for XR applications requiring 3DGS visualization where GPU resources are constrained and moderate sorting latency is acceptable. Use when integrating 3DGS into Unity workflows with automatic headset detection. When Not to Use: Do not use for scenes with >1 million Gaussians on mobile XR hardware without implementing LoD. Do not use if real-time, frame-accurate sorting is required for every frame (e.g., fast-moving VR interactions) without adjusting the sorting rate, which may increase CPU load. SplatXR was introduced in the paper "SplatXR: A Toolkit for Multi-Layered Extended Reality via On-Headset 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the need for efficient 3DGS rendering on mobile XR devices, which have limited computational resources compared to desktop GPUs. The toolkit provides a Unity plugin that automates the conversion of PLY files to a custom CSV format and handles the rendering pipeline, including background sorting and alpha blending. It supports multiple layers and includes features like cropping, planar flattening, and auto color adjustment for passthrough environments. name: SortFree Weighting
head: SortFree, Weighted-sum blending OIT
body: SortFree Weighting is an Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) approximation for 3D Gaussian Splatting that eliminates the computational bottleneck of depth sorting by replacing non-commutative alpha blending with a commutative weighted-sum blending scheme. It allows parallel accumulation of Gaussian colors in a single pass, trading strict physical accuracy for rendering efficiency and temporal stability. It sets itself apart from siblings like Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering by using a fixed analytical depth falloff rather than neural networks to predict view-dependent weights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients. For each pixel, the set of projected 2D Gaussian splats overlapping the pixel. Output: The final color C for the pixel. Data Structures: Gaussian Splat: Contains screen-space center (x, y), covariance matrix \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}. Scene Parameter: A single learnable scalar \sigma representing the depth falloff range. Method: The core mechanism replaces the standard alpha compositing equation C = \sum ci \alphai \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj) with a weighted sum. The weight w for each Gaussian depends on its depth d and view direction \mathbf{r}. 1. Project Gaussians: Project each 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space to obtain the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma' and center. 2. Compute Depth: For each Gaussian i, determine its depth di in camera space. 3. Compute View Direction: Determine the view direction vector \mathbf{r}i from the camera center to the Gaussian center. 4. Calculate Weight: Compute the weighting factor wi using the formula: wi = \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{di}{\sigma}\right) v(\mathbf{r}i) Where: di is the depth of the i-th Gaussian. \sigma is the learnable scene parameter controlling the depth falloff. v(\mathbf{r}i) is a view-dependent term derived from spherical harmonics. 5. Accumulate Color: Compute the final color C by summing the weighted colors of all overlapping splats: C = \sum{i \in \text{overlapping}} wi Where ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian evaluated at \mathbf{r}i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sortfreeweightingrender(gaussians, cameraorigin, viewmatrix, projmatrix, sigma, imageshape): """ Render a frame using SortFree Weighting. Args: gaussians: List of dicts with keys: 'pos' (3,), 'shcoeffs' (degree-3 SH array) cameraorigin: (3,) camera position in world space viewmatrix: (4,4) world-to-camera transformation projmatrix: (4,4) perspective projection matrix sigma: float, learnable depth falloff parameter imageshape: tuple (height, width) Returns: image: (H, W, 3) rendered image """ H, W = imageshape image = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) for g in gaussians: # 1. Project to camera space posworld = np.append(g['pos'], 1.0) poscam = viewmatrix @ posworld poscam = poscam[:3] / poscam[3] # 2. Project to screen space posclip = projmatrix @ np.append(poscam, 1.0) posclip = posclip[:3] / posclip[3] xscreen = (posclip[0] + 1.0) 0.5 W yscreen = (1.0 - posclip[1]) 0.5 H # Guard: skip if outside framebuffer if not (0 <= xscreen < W and 0 <= yscreen < H): continue # 3. Compute Depth d = poscam[2] # 4. Compute View Direction viewvec = poscam - cameraorigin viewvec = viewvec / np.linalg.norm(viewvec) # 5. Calculate Weight depthterm = max(0.0, 1.0 - d / sigma) shcolor = evaluatesphericalharmonics(g['shcoeffs'], viewvec) contribution = depthterm shcolor # 6. Accumulate (commutative, order-independent) image[int(yscreen), int(xscreen)] += contribution return image def evaluatesphericalharmonics(shcoeffs, direction): """Evaluate degree-3 spherical harmonics for a given direction vector.""" x, y, z = direction # Standard degree-3 SH basis evaluation (9 coefficients per channel) # Coefficients layout: [R0, R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8] shbasis = [ 0.282095, -0.488603 y, 0.488603 z, -0.488603 x, 1.092548 x y, -1.092548 y z, 0.315392 (3 z2 - 1), -1.092548 x z, 0.546274 (x2 - y2) ] # Multiply basis by SH coefficients and sum across channels color = np.zeros(3) for c in range(3): coeff = shcoeffs[c 9: (c + 1) 9] color[c] = sum(b a for b, a in zip(shbasis, coeff)) return color Parameters: \sigma: A learnable scalar parameter controlling the depth falloff range. Typical value not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth d > \sigma: The term \max(0, 1 - d/\sigma) becomes 0, effectively culling distant Gaussians. Precision: Accumulating many small weights can lead to floating-point precision issues if not handled carefully (e.g., using Kahan summation or higher precision accumulators). View-Dependence: The method relies on SH for view-dependent appearance. If SH coefficients are not properly trained, the view-dependent compensation v(\mathbf{r}) may be inaccurate. Uses neural networks to predict view-dependent weights and opacity, improving visual quality over SortFree's fixed linear falloff. Choose when higher visual fidelity is required and neural network inference overhead is acceptable. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel where N is the number of overlapping splats, as no sorting is required. The sorting step in standard 3DGS is O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel for accumulation, compared to O(N) for storing sorted lists in OIT methods. Performance: Significantly faster than sorted alpha blending due to the removal of the sorting bottleneck. However, it is generally slower than volumetric rendering methods due to the per-splat evaluation and accumulation overhead. Strengths: Eliminates sorting overhead; provides temporal stability (no popping artifacts from sorting changes); simple implementation. Limitations: Approximates alpha blending, leading to potential visual artifacts (e.g., incorrect transparency handling); quality can suffer at novel viewpoints compared to sorted methods. When to Use: Real-time applications on edge devices where sorting is too expensive and slight visual inaccuracies are acceptable. When Not to Use: High-fidelity offline rendering where physical accuracy is critical. SortFree Weighting was proposed in the paper "SortFree" (cited as [14] in), which introduced a weighted-sum blending formulation to approximate standard alpha compositing in a commutative manner. It is part of a broader class of Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) techniques applied to Gaussian-based representations. The method aims to reduce rendering overhead and improve temporal stability by removing the sorting step. name: Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering
head: Depth-aware Weighting OIT, Learnable Depth-aware Weighting [S1, unofficial]
body: Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering is a rendering technique that eliminates the computational bottleneck of depth sorting in traditional alpha blending by using a learnable, view-conditioned weighting strategy to order-independently blend 3D Gaussians. It replaces the sorted accumulation paradigm with a commutative weighted-sum blending scheme, allowing parallel accumulation of Gaussian colors in a single pass. Unlike its sibling SortFree Weighting, which uses a fixed exponential depth weighting, this method introduces neural networks to predict view-dependent weights and opacity, significantly improving visual quality in view-dependent scenarios while maintaining real-time performance on edge devices. Inputs: Set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by position \mui, scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation ri \in SO(3), spherical harmonic coefficients Yi, and base opacity parameters. Camera center tv. Background color \mathbf{c}{bg}. Outputs: Rendered pixel color \mathbf{C}. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: For each Gaussian i, store \mui, si, ri, Yi. Learnable Parameters: Three Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): \text{MLP}f (feature extraction), \text{MLP}\phi (weight prediction), \text{MLP}o (opacity prediction). Pixel Accumulators: For each pixel, maintain accumulators for the numerator term \sum \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi and the denominator term \sum \alphai wi, plus a global transmittance accumulator T. Steps: 1. Compute Camera-Gaussian Vector: For each Gaussian i, calculate the normalized direction vector from the camera center tv to the Gaussian center \mui: Pi = \frac{\mui - tv}{\|\mui - tv\|} 2. Feature Extraction: Construct a composite feature vector \mathbf{F} by concatenating Pi, scale si, rotation ri, and spherical harmonic coefficients Yi. Pass this vector through the feature MLP: \mathbf{F} = \text{MLP}f(Pi, si, ri, Yi) 3. Predict View-Dependent Weight and Opacity: Use the extracted features to predict the view-dependent weight \phii and the neural opacity oi: \phii = \text{ReLU}(\text{MLP}\phi(\mathbf{F})) oi = \sigma(\text{MLP}o(\mathbf{F})) where \sigma(\cdot) is the Sigmoid activation function. 4. Compute Alpha Value: Calculate the alpha value \alphai for the Gaussian based on the neural opacity oi and its spatial distribution at the pixel's projected center offset \Delta xi relative to the Gaussian's covariance matrix \Sigmai: \alphai = oi \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\Delta xi^T \Sigmai^{-1} \Delta xi\right) 5. Compute Depth-Aware Weight: Calculate the depth-aware weight wi using the predicted view-dependent parameter \phii, the depth di of the Gaussian in camera coordinates, and the maximum scale s{max} of the Gaussian: wi = \phii^2 + \frac{\phii}{di^2} + \exp\left(\frac{s{max}}{di}\right) 6. Parallel Accumulation: For each pixel, accumulate the contributions of all projected Gaussians in parallel. Since addition is commutative, no sorting is required. Accumulate weighted color: C{num} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi. Accumulate weighted alpha: C{den} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai wi. Accumulate global transmittance: T = \prod{j=1}^{N} (1 - \alphaj). 7. Composite Final Color: Compute the final pixel color \mathbf{C} by combining the accumulated foreground contribution with the background color, modulated by the global transmittance T: \mathbf{C} = (1 - T) \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi}{\sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai wi} + T \mathbf{c}{bg} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x: float) -> float: return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def depthawarerendering(gaussians: list, cameracenter: tuple, backgroundcolor: tuple, mlps: dict) -> dict: """ Render scene using Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: position (3D tuple) s: scale (3D tuple) r: rotation (SO(3) representation) Y: spherical harmonic coefficients c: RGB color (3D tuple) sigmainv: inverse covariance matrix (2x2 list of lists) center: projected 2D center (tuple) d: depth in camera coordinates (float) smax: maximum scale component (float) cameracenter: 3D tuple representing camera position tv backgroundcolor: 3D tuple cbg mlps: Dictionary containing MLP functions: 'f': Feature extraction MLP 'phi': Weight prediction MLP 'o': Opacity prediction MLP Returns: pixelcolors: Dictionary mapping pixel coordinates to 3D color tuples """ # Initialize accumulators for all pixels pixelaccum = {} pixelT = {} # Step 1-5: Process each Gaussian for g in gaussians: # 1. Compute Camera-Gaussian vector diff = (g.mu[0] - cameracenter[0], g.mu[1] - cameracenter[1], g.mu[2] - cameracenter[2]) norm = math.sqrt(diff[0]2 + diff[1]2 + diff[2]2) if norm == 0: continue Pi = (diff[0]/norm, diff[1]/norm, diff[2]/norm) # 2. Feature Extraction F = mlps'f' # 3. Predict View-Dependent Weight and Opacity phii = max(0.0, mlps'phi') oi = sigmoid(mlps'o') # 5. Compute Depth-Aware Weight di = g.d smax = g.smax if di == 0: di = 1e-6 wi = phii2 + phii / (di2) + math.exp(smax / di) # 6. Parallel Accumulation # Iterate over all pixels covered by this Gaussian's projection for pixel in g.coveredpixels: # Compute alpha for this specific pixel deltax = (pixel.x - g.center[0], pixel.y - g.center[1]) qx, qy = deltax[0], deltax[1] invsig = g.sigmainv quadform = (invsig[0][0]qx + invsig[0][1]qy)qx + \ (invsig[1][0]qx + invsig[1][1]qy)qy alphai = oi math.exp(-0.5 quadform) # Initialize accumulators if pixel not yet visited if pixel not in pixelaccum: pixelaccum[pixel] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) pixelT[pixel] = 1.0 currentnum, currentden = pixelaccum[pixel] currentT = pixelT[pixel] # Add weighted color contribution newnum = ( currentnum[0] + g.c[0] alphai wi, currentnum[1] + g.c[1] alphai wi, currentnum[2] + g.c[2] alphai wi) newden = currentden + alphai wi # Update global transmittance newT = currentT (1.0 - alphai) pixelaccum[pixel] = (newnum[0], newnum[1], newnum[2], newden) pixelT[pixel] = newT # Step 7: Composite Final Color pixelcolors = {} for pixel, (num, den) in pixelaccum.items(): T = pixelT[pixel] if den == 0: pixelcolors[pixel] = backgroundcolor else: fgcolor = (num[0]/den, num[1]/den, num[2]/den) finalcolor = ( (1.0 - T) fgcolor[0] + T backgroundcolor[0], (1.0 - T) fgcolor[1] + T backgroundcolor[1], (1.0 - T) fgcolor[2] + T backgroundcolor[2]) pixelcolors[pixel] = finalcolor return pixelcolors Parameters: MLP Architectures: The sizes and depths of \text{MLP}f, \text{MLP}\phi, and \text{MLP}o are not specified in the sources. Activation Functions: ReLU for \phii, Sigmoid for oi. Depth di: Depth of the Gaussian center in camera coordinates. Max Scale s{max}: The maximum component of the scale vector si. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparency Artifacts: Unordered blending can introduce transparency artifacts in regions with overlapping geometry due to the scarcity of rendering order information. The neural view-dependent enhancement strategy is designed to mitigate this. Division by Zero: Depth di must be handled to avoid division by zero in the weighting function wi. What it is: A specific implementation of Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering tailored for mobile and edge devices. Differentiation: Optimized to reduce storage and inference delay compared to general SortFreeGS implementations. When to choose: When rendering 3D Gaussians on resource-constrained devices like smartphones or AR glasses where sorting and tile-based rendering are too expensive. Link: Mobile-GS What it is: A representative work that achieves fast rendering without sorting using a depth-aware weighting function w(di) = \exp(-\sigmai \betai di). Differentiation: Uses a simpler, non-neural weighting function compared to the learnable view-dependent weighting in Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering. When to choose: When higher visual fidelity is prioritized over extreme mobile performance, and sufficient computational resources are available. Link: SortFreeGS Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels they cover, as each Gaussian is processed for each pixel it affects. The lack of sorting reduces the complexity from O(N \log N) per pixel (or tile) to O(N) accumulation. Memory Complexity: O(N + P) for storing Gaussian attributes and pixel accumulators. The MLPs add a small constant memory overhead. Measured Performance: Enables real-time rendering on mobile hardware by eliminating tile-based rendering and sorting. Strengths: Eliminates the computational bottleneck of depth sorting. Allows parallel accumulation of Gaussian contributions. Neural view-dependent weighting improves visual quality by mitigating transparency artifacts. Limitations: Unordered blending can still introduce transparency artifacts in complex overlapping geometry, though reduced by the neural module. Requires training of MLPs, adding to the training time and complexity. When to use: Real-time rendering applications, especially on edge devices, where sorting is prohibitive. Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering was proposed in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for mobile devices. The method addresses the limitations of traditional alpha blending, which relies on sorting 3D Gaussians by depth, a process that is computationally intensive and unsuitable for real-time rendering on resource-constrained hardware. The technique builds upon earlier SortFree approaches but enhances them with learnable, view-dependent weights to improve visual fidelity. name: Unity Mobile Implementation
head: SplattingAvatar Unity Renderer
body: This method implements a display-only renderer for trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes within the Unity engine, optimized for mobile compatibility. It solves the problem of rendering high-fidelity Gaussian avatars on constrained hardware by relying exclusively on a warped canonical mesh for rigging and using a standard front-to-back alpha blending pipeline. It sets itself apart from its siblings by prioritizing maximum compatibility with existing game engine workflows (Mixamo rigging) and mobile stability over the raw performance optimizations found in tiled or sort-free variants. The implementation follows a specific export and rendering pipeline designed for Unity's compute shader architecture. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A canonical mesh (.obj), Gaussian data (.ply), embedding description (.json), and a rigged mesh (.fbx). Outputs: A rendered video frame with photorealistic details, achieving steady 30 FPS on iPhone 13. Data Structures: Gaussians: Stored in a.ply file. Each Gaussian is defined by its 3D position, covariance matrix, spherical harmonics coefficients (for color), and opacity. Rigging: The canonical mesh is exported to Mixamo for autorigging. The resulting.fbx file maintains triangle order to ensure correct deformation. Embedding: Described in a.json file, linking the geometric structure to the Gaussian attributes. Rendering Steps: 1. Rigging and Export: Export the canonical mesh as.obj to Mixamo for autorigging. Export one.ply file containing the Gaussians. Export one.json file describing the embedding. Export the rigged mesh as.fbx from Mixamo to Unity. Note: The.fbx file can be rigged by other software as long as the triangle order is maintained. 2. Sorting: Sort all Gaussians by the z-axis in camera coordinates from near to far. 3. Primitive Generation: Based on the calculated 2D covariance \Sigma', draw one front-parallel quad primitive for every visible Gaussian centered at its position. This one-primitive-one-Gaussian strategy is important for the game engine to properly handle the occlusion of other regular objects. 4. Fragment Shader: For every pixel to draw, emit color with alpha pre-multiplication. Set the blend function to (ONE, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendergaussians(camera, gaussians): # 1. Sorting: Sort all Gaussians by z-axis in camera coordinates from near to far sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.position @ camera.viewmatrix[2]) for gaussian in sortedgaussians: # 2. Primitive Setup: Calculate 2D covariance Sigma' in screen space # Standard 3DGS projection: transform 3D covariance by view/projection matrices sigma2d = compute2dcovariance(gaussian.covariance3d, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projectionmatrix) # 3. Primitive Generation: Create one front-parallel quad per Gaussian # Decompose sigma2d into rotation and scale, generate 4 vertices quadvertices = createfrontparallelquad(gaussian.position, sigma2d) # 4. Fragment Shader: Render quad with pre-multiplied alpha renderquad(quadvertices, gaussian.color, gaussian.opacity) def compute2dcovariance(cov3d, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix): # Standard linear algebra: J W cov3d W.T J.T where J is projection Jacobian return projectedcov def createfrontparallelquad(center, sigma2d): # Standard linear algebra: eigen-decompose sigma2d to get scale and rotation, offset center return vertices def renderquad(vertices, color, opacity): # Fragment Shader: Emit color with alpha pre-multiplication # Set blend function to (ONE, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) glFragColor = vec4(color opacity, opacity) Parameters and Edge Cases: Blend Function: Must be (ONE, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) to correctly handle pre-multiplied alpha. Occlusion: The one-primitive-one-Gaussian strategy ensures proper occlusion handling with other scene objects. Rigging: Triangle order in the.fbx file must be maintained for correct deformation. This variant uses the Unity Sentis framework to predict Gaussian splats from anchors and control encodings at runtime. It builds model graphs and loads MLP weights at runtime, translating each MLP via Sentis to run as a custom compute shader. Anchor features and positions are uploaded at initialization and pinned in GPU memory to avoid CPU-GPU readbacks. Computed 3D Gaussians are accessed in compute buffers and passed to the standard 3DGS renderer. Appearance can be changed at runtime by invoking MLPs with a different encoding \Psi(x) without reallocating GPU memory, as the number of predicted Gaussians remains constant. MLPs are loaded at initialization and serialized from.onnx to.sentis models. To avoid unnecessary rendering, Gaussians with negative opacity are culled. The quad should fit the respective Gaussian tightly to avoid overdraw and achieve smooth rendering, decomposing eigenvalues of anisotropic 3D Gaussians into rotation and scale components. Performance: Achieves over 300 FPS on a modern GPU and a steady 30 FPS on an iPhone 13. This implementation is part of the SplattingAvatar project, which focuses on creating photorealistic avatars using 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method was developed to demonstrate the effectiveness of Gaussian Splatting for head and full-body avatars, comparing favorably with state-of-the-art methods in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. name: Unity Sentis Implementation for Gaussian Splats
head: Runtime MLP Inference via Sentis, Sentis-based Gaussian Splatting
body: This method implements the rendering phase of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction by leveraging the Unity Sentis framework to execute Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) as custom compute shaders on the GPU. It solves the problem of dynamically predicting 3D Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics) from static anchor features and a time-varying context encoding \Psi(x) without CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks. Unlike static splatting, this approach allows for real-time appearance changes by invoking the MLP with different encodings, while maintaining a fixed memory footprint since the number of predicted Gaussians remains constant. Inputs: 1. Anchor Features: A set of feature vectors and their corresponding 3D positions, uploaded to GPU memory at initialization. 2. Context Encoding \Psi(x): A dynamic input vector (e.g., time, pose, or style code) used to modulate the Gaussian attributes. 3. MLP Models: Serialized.sentis models derived from.onnx files, representing the mapping from anchors/encoding to Gaussian parameters. Outputs: 1. Compute Buffers: Containing the predicted 3D Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). 2. Rasterized Image: The final rendered frame passed to the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renderer. Data Structures: Anchor Data: Pinned in GPU memory to prevent readbacks. Layout includes position (x, y, z) and feature vector f. Gaussian Attributes: Predicted per anchor. Includes mean \mu, covariance \Sigma (decomposed into rotation R and scale S via eigenvalues), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{lm}. Compute Buffers: Structured buffers holding the output of the Sentis inference, directly consumed by the rasterizer. Steps: 1. Initialization: 1. Serialize trained MLPs from.onnx format to.sentis models. 2. Build the model graphs using the Unity Sentis framework. 3. Upload anchor features and positions to pinned GPU memory. 2. Runtime Inference (Per Frame): 1. Compute the context encoding \Psi(x) on the CPU or GPU based on the current state (e.g., time, avatar pose). 2. Invoke the Sentis model as a custom compute shader. The shader reads the pinned anchor features and the encoding \Psi(x). 3. The MLP predicts the full set of Gaussian attributes for each anchor. 4. Store the results in compute buffers. 3. Culling: 1. Iterate through the predicted Gaussians in the compute buffers. 2. Check the predicted opacity \alpha. 3. If \alpha < 0, mark the Gaussian for culling (do not render). This prevents rendering of modality-specific artifacts that do not contribute to the current visual output. 4. Rendering: 1. Pass the valid Gaussians from the compute buffers to the standard 3DGS renderer. 2. The renderer decomposes the covariance \Sigma into rotation R and scale S components based on 2D screen-space eigenvalues to generate tight-fitting quads, minimizing overdraw. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. sentismodels = loadsentismodelsfromonnx("mlpmodels.onnx") anchorfeatures = uploadtopinnedgpumemory(anchorpositions, anchorvectors) def renderframe(contextencoding): # 1. Invoke MLP via Sentis Compute Shader # The shader reads anchorfeatures and contextencoding # Outputs predicted Gaussian attributes to compute buffers gaussianattributes = sentismodels.inference( inputs={"anchors": anchorfeatures, "encoding": contextencoding}) # 2. Culling validgaussians = [] for gauss in gaussianattributes: if gauss.opacity >= 0: validgaussians.append(gauss) # 3. Rasterization # Pass validgaussians to standard 3DGS rasterizer # Rasterizer handles decomposition of covariance into R and S image = standard3dgsrasterize(validgaussians) return image Parameters: Memory Allocation: Fixed at initialization. No reallocation occurs during runtime because the number of anchors (and thus predicted Gaussians) is constant. Culling Threshold: Opacity \alpha < 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Opacity: Gaussians trained for specific modalities may have negative opacity in others. Failing to cull these results in visual artifacts. Memory Pinning: Anchor data must be pinned in GPU memory to avoid CPU-GPU readbacks during inference. This variant involves deploying the Sentis-based Gaussian Splatting pipeline to a Meta Quest 3 headset to verify suitability for interactive VR navigation. The implementation uses the Unity Gaussian Splatting plugin viewer to render Gaussian environments, potentially hybridized with environment maps to remove background floaters and improve throughput. However, a critical pitfall exists: the Unity Gaussian Splatting plugin relies on compute shaders that are not natively supported by the mobile VR standalone pipeline on ARM architectures. Consequently, real-time performance is achieved by offloading rendering computation to a connected PC and streaming the output to the headset, rather than running natively on the device. Time Complexity: Dependent on the MLP inference time (linear with respect to the number of anchors and MLP depth) plus the standard 3DGS rasterization cost. Memory Complexity: Fixed at initialization. Anchor features and Gaussian attribute buffers are allocated once and reused. Performance: On PC hardware, real-time performance is achievable. On mobile VR standalone hardware (ARM), native compute shader support is lacking, requiring PC offloading for real-time frame rates. Strengths: No CPU-GPU readbacks for anchors; dynamic appearance changes without memory reallocation; effective culling of non-contributing Gaussians. Limitations: Dependency on Unity Sentis framework; lack of native compute shader support on ARM mobile VR pipelines. This method builds on the existing 3DGS rendering implementation in Unity and improvements by Kleinbeck et al.. It utilizes the Unity Sentis framework to bridge deep learning inference with real-time rendering. The approach was developed to enable real-time context translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, allowing for dynamic avatar reconstruction and appearance changes. It was validated in the context of "Shape-Shifting Splats" and "EnvMap-GS" for VR navigation and outdoor reconstruction. name: CPU-based Gaussian Splatting Thumbnailer
head: 3D Gaussian Splat CPU Rasterization, 3DGS Thumbnail, CPU Gaussian Splat Rendering, CPU Gaussian Splat Thumbnail Rendering, Gaussian Splat Thumbnail Rendering, Splat Thumbnail Generation
body: This method generates low-resolution preview images (thumbnails) from trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes using a pure CPU pipeline optimized for speed via Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation. It solves the problem of slow interactive preview generation by simplifying the rendering model—omitting Gaussian rotation and complex shading—and leveraging Numba to accelerate Python-based numerical loops. It differs from its parent, 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced), by explicitly excluding rotation data, using a simplified approximate blending function, and processing a fixed opacity-filtered budget of splats rather than full alpha compositing. Inputs: Scene files in formats.ply,.splat,.spz,.sog,.ksplat,.lcc, or.compressed.ply. Fixed camera parameters: position, target, and field of view (FOV). Parameters: Gaussian splat size scalar \sigma, output resolution, opacity threshold, and splat budget. Outputs: A PNG image file representing the rendered thumbnail. Scene data is parsed into parallel arrays for position (3 floats), scale (3 floats), and fdc (degree-0 spherical harmonic coefficient, 3 floats). Rotation data is explicitly omitted from the input structure. Format routing inspects PLY headers or file extensions to select native numpy.fromfile() decoding or CPU conversion via the PlayCanvas splat-transform CLI. 1. Camera Setup: Compute fixed view (V) and projection (P) matrices from the camera position, target, and FOV. 2. Format Conversion & Coordinate Normalization: Convert input formats to a standard 3DGS PLY representation; rotate scenes 180° about the Z-axis to convert the original COLMAP Y-down convention to Y-up. 3. Visible Splat Extraction & Filtering: Identify Gaussians falling within the camera’s frustum. Compute opacity O = \text{sigmoid}(opacity) and discard any splat where O < 0.2. 4. Budget Sampling: Sample the remaining splats to a target budget (1 million splats per vCPU, maximum 5 million total) with probability proportional to their opacity O. 5. Splat Sorting: Sort the visible splats by their camera-space z-depth in back-to-front order (farthest first) to ensure proper front-to-back blending. 6. Projection & Rasterization: Project each Gaussian center onto the image plane using V and P; treat Gaussians as simple, rotation-less spheres. Compute footprint radius R = 2 \times \exp(\max(scale)). Rasterize using a fast approximate blending method where color contribution is computed based on a simplified weighting function considering distance from splat center and current depth values. 7. Buffer Update & Output: Update color and depth buffers with blended colors and depth values as each Gaussian is blended; save the color buffer as a PNG image file. C = 0.5 + 0.28209479 \times f{dc} where C is the output color and f{dc} is the degree-0 spherical harmonic coefficient. O = \text{sigmoid}(opacity) where O is the computed opacity used for filtering and sampling. R = 2 \times \exp(\max(scale)) where R is the footprint radius in pixels and scale represents the scale components. \sigma (Splat Size): Scalar controlling spatial extent. Tested values: \{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0\}. Smaller values preserve detail but cause fragmentation; larger values increase coverage but cause blurring. Resolution: Discrete variable. Tested values: 480p (640 \times 480), 720p (960 \times 720), 1080p (1440 \times 1080). Opacity Threshold: Splats with opacity below 0.2 are dropped. Splat Budget: 1 million splats per vCPU, capped at 5 million total. Footprint Multiplier: The footprint radius is twice the exponential of the maximum scale component. Python Loop Bottleneck: Standard Python interpretation is too slow for the rasterization loop; mitigated by using Numba for JIT compilation of performance-critical numerical routines. Parallel Processing: Deliberately avoided due to caching and computation management overhead on systems with limited core counts. Visual Eligibility: Omitting rotation data reduces computational cost but may impact visual quality; however, evaluations showed negligible impact on thumbnail eligibility. Security/Isolation: The splat-transform CLI is executed with strict constraints: only an allowlisted local file inside the work directory is accessible, no shell is used, and a timeout is applied. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from numba import njit @njit def computefootprintradius(scale): """R = 2 exp(max(scale)) """ return 2.0 np.exp(np.max(scale)) @njit def approximateweight(distsq, footprintradius): """Simplified Gaussian weighting function considering distance """ return np.exp(-distsq / (2.0 footprintradius footprintradius)) @njit def renderthumbnail(positions, scales, fdc, depths, width, height, sigma): """ Renders a thumbnail using CPU-sorted, rotation-less Gaussian splats. positions: (N, 3) array of camera-space centers scales: (N, 3) array of scale components fdc: (N, 3) array of degree-0 spherical harmonic coefficients depths: (N,) array of camera-space z-depths (sorted back-to-front) """ colorbuffer = np.zeros((height, width, 3), dtype=np.float32) depthbuffer = np.full((height, width), np.inf, dtype=np.float32) for i in range(len(positions)): pos = positions[i] scale = scales[i] color = 0.5 + 0.28209479 fdc[i] depth = depths[i] # Project center to screen space ndcx = (pos[0] 1.0) ndcy = (pos[1] 1.0) screenx = (ndcx + 1.0) 0.5 width screeny = (1.0 - (ndcy + 1.0) 0.5) height radius = computefootprintradius(scale) if radius < 1.0: radius = 1.0 # Determine bounding box covering the splat circle xmin = int(max(0, screenx - radius)) xmax = int(min(width - 1, screenx + radius)) ymin = int(max(0, screeny - radius)) ymax = int(min(height - 1, screeny + radius)) for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): dx = x - screenx dy = y - screeny distsq = dx dx + dy dy w = approximateweight(distsq, radius) # Buffer Update: quick composition without expensive memory operations if depth < depthbuffer[y, x]: alpha = w colorbuffer[y, x, 0] = colorbuffer[y, x, 0] (1.0 - alpha) + color[0] alpha colorbuffer[y, x, 1] = colorbuffer[y, x, 1] (1.0 - alpha) + color[1] alpha colorbuffer[y, x, 2] = colorbuffer[y, x, 2] (1.0 - alpha) + color[2] alpha depthbuffer[y, x] = depth return colorbuffer Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization loop over visible splats. Complexity is roughly O(N{visible} \cdot A{splat}), where N{visible} is the number of visible Gaussians and A{splat} is the average area of a splat in pixels. JIT compilation reduces the constant factor significantly. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian attributes and O(W \cdot H) for the color and depth buffers. Hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5995WX, 16 GB RAM, Arch Linux Kernel 6.9.1. Software: Python 3.13.7, NumPy 2.1.3, Numba 0.61.0. JIT vs Non-JIT: JIT acceleration provides a ~156× speed-up (2.15s vs 336s for \sigma=0.7, fixed resolution). Execution Times (JIT Enabled): \sigma=0.1: 0.9s (480p), 0.94s (720p), 1.29s (1080p) \sigma=0.2: 0.97s (480p), 1.11s (720p), 1.87s (1080p) \sigma=0.4: 1.03s (480p), 1.42s (720p), 2.99s (1080p) \sigma=0.5: 1.29s (480p), 1.87s (720p), 4.20s (1080p) \sigma=0.7: 2.15s (480p), 3.65s (720p), 7.11s (1080p) \sigma=1.0: 3.66s (480p), 6.42s (720p), 13.31s (1080p) Strengths: Extremely fast execution on CPU due to JIT compilation and simplified rendering model (no rotation, approximate blending). Limitations: Lower visual fidelity compared to full GPU splatting or rotation-aware CPU rendering; fragmentation at small \sigma, blurring at large \sigma. Use when rapid thumbnail generation is required on CPU-only systems or when GPU resources are unavailable. Use when visual fidelity is secondary to speed (e.g., scene browsing, preview generation). The method was developed by E. Genchev et al. and published in Array (Volume 28, 2025, 100611). It was designed to address the computational intensity of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering by creating a lightweight, CPU-based thumbnailer. The work focuses on parameter optimization (\sigma, resolution) and the use of JIT compilation to mitigate Python's performance limitations. The method was evaluated by colleagues with backgrounds in computer graphics. The most preferred configurations were \sigma=0.4 and \sigma=0.5 at 720p resolution, balancing visual clarity and rendering performance. name: Support Guard
head: Coordinate box clamp, Per-primitive clamp, node-local guard
body: The Support Guard is a fault-mitigation technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that prevents catastrophic rendering errors caused by Single-Event Upsets (SEUs), such as bit flips in memory, by clamping primitive parameters to the valid range observed during training. It solves the problem of "frame-spanning corruption," where a single bit flip in a scale parameter can exponentially inflate a primitive into a translucent sheet covering most of the screen. Unlike activation range supervision used in CNNs, which clamps neuron outputs to statistical distributions, the Support Guard clamps geometric and appearance parameters to the bounded parameter space of the optimized scene, providing a geometric correctness argument. It is distinct from its siblings in that it requires zero additional memory overhead and operates as a pure per-primitive clamp, making it suitable for deployment on spaceborne, robotic, and clustered hardware where reliability is critical. The method operates by enforcing a hard boundary on every parameter of every Gaussian primitive before rendering. It ensures that no primitive can exceed the physical or appearance bounds established by the trained model, thereby neutralizing the exponential impact of bit flips in logarithmic scale or opacity fields. Input: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by parameters \mathbf{p}i (position, rotation, scale, opacity, color). The parameters are stored in floating-point format (typically fp32). Input: The per-field support box Bf, defined as the per-component minimum and maximum values observed over all primitives in the clean, trained model for each parameter field f. Output: A set of guarded primitives \mathbf{p}'i where every component lies within its respective support box Bf. Support Box (Bf): For each parameter field f (e.g., scale x, y, z; opacity; color channels), Bf is a pair of scalars [\ellf, hf] representing the global minimum and maximum of that field across the entire scene. \ellf = \min{i} (\mathbf{p}i[f]) hf = \max{i} (\mathbf{p}i[f]) These values are static and derived from the trained checkpoint. The guard is applied per-primitive. For each primitive i and each parameter field f: 1. Retrieve the current value x of the parameter. 2. Check if x lies within the support box [\ellf, hf]. 3. If x < \ellf, clamp x to \ellf. 4. If x > hf, clamp x to hf. 5. If \ellf \le x \le hf, leave x unchanged. This process is repeated for all components of all primitives. In a distributed sort-first rendering architecture, this guard is applied node-locally on each node before it renders its assigned tile, ensuring that out-of-range primitives are contained before compositing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applysupportguard(primitives, supportboxes): """ Clamps all primitive parameters to their trained support boxes. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects, each having attributes corresponding to parameter fields (e.g., scalex, opacity). supportboxes: Dictionary mapping parameter field names to tuples (minval, maxval). Returns: primitives: The same list of primitives, modified in-place. """ for primitive in primitives: for fieldname, (minval, maxval) in supportboxes.items(): # Get current value of the field currentval = getattr(primitive, fieldname) # Clamp to support box if currentval < minval: setattr(primitive, fieldname, minval) elif currentval > maxval: setattr(primitive, fieldname, maxval) # Else: value is within bounds, leave unchanged return primitives Support Box Bf: The coordinate box for field f is defined as Bf = [\ellf, hf], where \ellf and hf are the empirical min and max of field f over the clean trained model. Clamping Function: For a parameter x and box Bf = [\ellf, hf], the guarded value x' is: x' = \begin{cases} \ellf & \text{if } x < \ellf \\ x & \text{if } \ellf \le x \le hf \\ hf & \text{if } x > hf \end{cases} Scale Explosion Mitigation: A sign flip in the logarithmic scale \theta (where s = \exp(\theta)) can change \theta \approx -3 to \theta \approx +3, causing s \to s \cdot e^6. The guard clamps \theta back into B{\theta}, preventing this exponential explosion. Support Box Bounds (\ellf, hf): Determined from the trained model. Not given in the sources for specific scenes, but must be computed once during model loading. Cost: 76 µs per frame, or 0.07× a single-view render time. Memory Overhead: None (1× memory relative to unguarded). Catastrophic Upsets: Without the guard, a single scale sign-bit upset can inflate one primitive into a translucent sheet spanning most of the frame, causing catastrophic corruption. Residual Errors: The guard neutralizes 90.4% of catastrophic upsets. The remaining 9.6% are "in-support" mantissa-level residuals that are bounded by Lemma 1 in the source and are perceptually invisible. Distributed Rendering: In a distributed renderer, the spatial extent of a corrupted primitive equals the number of screen tiles (and thus compositing nodes) that a single upset contaminates. The node-local guard contains this corruption to the node where it occurs, preventing broadcast into the composite. Clean Model Invariance: The guard leaves a clean model unchanged by construction, as all clean parameters lie within Bf by definition. Time Complexity: The guard parallelizes trivially across primitives. The measured cost is 76 µs per frame, which is approximately 0.07× a single-view render time. Memory Complexity: Zero additional memory overhead. It operates on the existing primitive data structures. Effectiveness: Neutralizes 90.4% of catastrophic upsets. Under accumulated dose (up to 20,000 simultaneous upsets), the guarded renderer maintains a mean global PSNR close to clean, whereas the unguarded renderer degrades to 10.6 dB. Worst-Case Footprint: In a test of 768,000 guarded single-bit upsets, the worst observed corruption footprint was 11.68% of the frame, with 470 residual catastrophic events. Comparison to Alternatives: Full Duplication: Requires 3× memory and voting. Eliminates catastrophes but at high memory cost. ECC Sign+Exp: Requires ~1.3× memory and parity. Eliminates catastrophes but at higher memory cost. Selective Clamp: Clamps only scale and opacity. Cheaper than full guard but similarly effective, as scale and opacity carry most catastrophic mass. When to Use: Deploy on hardware susceptible to SEUs (spaceborne, robotic, clustered) where memory bandwidth and capacity are constrained, and where catastrophic frame-spanning errors are unacceptable. When Not to Use: If memory is abundant and computational cost is less critical than absolute fault correction, full duplication or ECC may be preferred for zero catastrophe rate. The Support Guard was introduced in the paper "Single-Event Upsets in 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering: Bit-Level Criticality, Spatial Extent, and a Parallel Support Guard". The work was motivated by the need to deploy real-time radiance-field rendering on hardware exposed to radiation, such as spaceborne and robotic platforms. The authors identified that 3DGS primitives, being explicit and interpretable, are susceptible to bit-level criticality, particularly in the logarithmic scale parameters where sign flips cause exponential scale explosions. The Support Guard was developed as a lightweight, geometrically grounded mitigation strategy that exploits the compact, bounded nature of trained 3DGS parameter spaces. It was validated against a fault grid of 768,000 single-bit upsets and proven to make frame-covering corruption impossible under any single-bit upset (Theorems 1 and 2). name: SimpleRenderer
head: CPU-based Gaussian Splatting Renderer, Painter's Algorithm Gaussian Renderer
body: SimpleRenderer is a CPU-based, non-differentiable renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting that projects 3D Gaussian distributions into 2D screen-space elliptical splats and composites them using a standard painter's algorithm with alpha blending. It differs from GPU-accelerated or tiled implementations by performing all projection, sorting, and rasterization on the CPU using standard array operations, making it suitable for debugging, thumbnail generation, or environments lacking specialized graphics hardware. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position (\mathbf{p}), color (\mathbf{C}), scale (\mathbf{s}), opacity (\alpha), and rotation (implicit in the isotropic approximation used here); a camera model providing projection matrices and intrinsics (fx); and configuration parameters (nearplane, farplane, alphathreshold, backgroundcolor). Outputs: A 2D image of shape (H, W, 3) with float32 dtype. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Arrays for positions (N, 3), colors (N, 3), scales (N, 3), and opacities (N, 1). Image Buffer: A 3D array img of shape (H, W, 3). Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an image buffer img of shape (H, W, 3) initialized to backgroundcolor. 2. Camera Transformation: Transform Gaussian positions \mathbf{p} to camera coordinates \mathbf{p}{cam} using the camera's world-to-camera transformation. Extract the depth values z{vals} from the third component of \mathbf{p}{cam}. 3. Filtering: Filter Gaussians to retain only those where: near\plane \le z{vals} \le far\plane \alpha > alpha\threshold Let the filtered set have M Gaussians. 4. Projection: Project the remaining Gaussian centers to pixel coordinates (u, v) using the camera's camera-to-pixel transformation. 5. Sorting: Sort the M Gaussians by depth z{vals} in descending order (far to near) to implement the painter's algorithm. 6. Rendering Loop: For each Gaussian i in the sorted list: a. Radius Calculation: Calculate the screen-space radius r. Let s{mean} be the mean of the Gaussian's scales. Compute: r = \min(15, \max(1, \lfloor s{mean} \cdot \frac{fx}{\max(z{vals}[i], 0.1)} \rfloor)) The depth is clamped to a minimum of 0.1 to prevent division by zero or excessively large radii. b. Bounding Box: Define the pixel bounding box for the splat: y{min} = \max(0, \lfloor v \rfloor - r) y{max} = \min(H, \lfloor v \rfloor + r + 1) x{min} = \max(0, \lfloor u \rfloor - r) x{max} = \min(W, \lfloor u \rfloor + r + 1) If the bounding box is invalid (e.g., u or v is far outside bounds such that the box is empty), skip the Gaussian. c. Weight Calculation: For each pixel (x, y) in the bounding box, compute the normalized squared distance from the center: dist\sq = \frac{(x - u)^2 + (y - v)^2}{r^2 + 10^{-8}} Calculate the Gaussian weight: w = \exp(-dist\sq) \cdot \alphai d. Blending: Update the image buffer using alpha blending for each color channel c \in \{0, 1, 2\}: img[y, x, c] = img[y, x, c] \cdot (1 - w) + Ci[c] \cdot w where Ci[c] is the c-th component of the Gaussian's color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def simplerenderer(gaussians, camera, config, H, W): """ Render 3D Gaussians using a CPU-based painter's algorithm. Args: gaussians: Dict with keys 'pos' (N,3), 'color' (N,3), 'scale' (N,3), 'opacity' (N,1) camera: Object with methods worldtocamera, cameratopixel, and attribute fx config: Object with attributes nearplane, farplane, alphathreshold, backgroundcolor H: Image height W: Image width Returns: img: (H, W, 3) float32 array """ # 1. Initialize image img = np.full((H, W, 3), config.backgroundcolor, dtype=np.float32) # 2. Transform to camera space campoints = camera.worldtocamera(gaussians['pos']) # (N, 3) zvals = campoints[:, 2] # (N,) # 3. Filter Gaussians validmask = ( (zvals >= config.nearplane) & (zvals <= config.farplane) & (gaussians['opacity'].flatten() > config.alphathreshold)) if not np.any(validmask): return img filteredpos = campoints[validmask] filteredcolor = gaussians['color'][validmask] filteredscale = gaussians['scale'][validmask] filteredopacity = gaussians['opacity'][validmask].flatten() filteredz = zvals[validmask] # 4. Project to pixel coordinates pixelcoords = camera.cameratopixel(filteredpos) # (M, 2), (u, v) u = pixelcoords[:, 0] v = pixelcoords[:, 1] # 5. Sort by depth (far to near) sortindices = np.argsort(filteredz)[::-1] u = u[sortindices] v = v[sortindices] filteredcolor = filteredcolor[sortindices] filteredopacity = filteredopacity[sortindices] filteredscale = filteredscale[sortindices] filteredz = filteredz[sortindices] # 6. Render loop fx = camera.fx for i in range(len(filteredz)): z = filteredz[i] # Clamp z to prevent division by zero zclamped = max(z, 0.1) # Calculate radius smean = np.mean(filteredscale[i]) radius = int(smean fx / zclamped) radius = max(1, min(radius, 15)) # Cap at 15 # Bounding box ymin = max(0, int(v[i]) - radius) ymax = min(H, int(v[i]) + radius + 1) xmin = max(0, int(u[i]) - radius) xmax = min(W, int(u[i]) + radius + 1) # Skip if out of bounds if ymin >= ymax or xmin >= xmax: continue # Precompute weight factor alpha = filteredopacity[i] color = filteredcolor[i] # Create meshgrid for bounding box ys, xs = np.mgrid[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax] # Normalized squared distance distsq = ((xs - u[i])2 + (ys - v[i])2) / (radius2 + 1e-8) # Gaussian weight w = np.exp(-distsq) alpha # Blend # img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax,:] = # img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax,:] (1 - w[..., np.newaxis]) + # color w[..., np.newaxis] # Vectorized update img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 0] = img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 0] (1 - w) + color[0] w img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 1] = img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 1] (1 - w) + color[1] w img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 2] = img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 2] (1 - w) + color[2] w return img Parameters: config.nearplane: Minimum depth for valid Gaussians. config.farplane: Maximum depth for valid Gaussians. config.alphathreshold: Minimum opacity for a Gaussian to be considered valid. config.backgroundcolor: RGB array of shape (3,) used to initialize the image canvas. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If no Gaussians pass the filtering stage, the function returns the background-initialized image immediately. If a Gaussian's projected center (u, v) is outside the image bounds, the bounding box calculation may result in an empty range; the implementation must skip such Gaussians. The radius is capped at 15 to avoid excessive computational overhead for large splats. Depth z{vals}[i] is clamped to a minimum of 0.1 in the radius calculation to prevent division by zero or extremely large radii. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for sorting, plus O(M \cdot R^2) for rasterization, where N is the total number of Gaussians, M is the number of visible Gaussians, and R is the average radius (capped at 15). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian attributes and intermediate arrays. Performance: Suitable for low-resolution outputs or small scenes due to CPU-bound processing. Not suitable for real-time rendering or high-resolution video generation without significant optimization. Strengths: Simple implementation, easy to debug, no GPU dependency. Limitations: Slow for large scenes, no support for differentiable rendering, limited by CPU cache and memory bandwidth. SimpleRenderer is an implementation detail found in the GaussianScan-Recon repository, an unofficial project for 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction. It serves as a basic rendering backend for generating thumbnails or debugging visualizations during the reconstruction process. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3DGS
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction method that represents a scene as a collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives, each parameterized by position, covariance, opacity, and view-dependent color. It solves the trade-off between the high-quality but slow volumetric rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and the geometric limitations of mesh-based rendering by using explicit, differentiable particle-based discretization. Unlike NeRF, which requires expensive ray marching through a continuous MLP, 3DGS projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen-space ellipses and rasterizes them using tile-based alpha compositing, enabling real-time rendering speeds (>100 FPS) and rapid training convergence. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) by utilizing a highly optimized, parallelized GPU rasterization pipeline with global depth sorting and tile-based compositing. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by a mean position \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, an opacity scalar \alpha \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Camera parameters: intrinsic matrix \mathbf{K} (focal lengths fx, fy, principal point cx, cy) and extrinsic view matrix \mathbf{V}. Image dimensions W \times H and tile size (typically 16 \times 16 pixels). Outputs: An RGB image \mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} and optionally depth/normal maps. The scene is stored as a list of Gaussian attributes. A typical layout for a single Gaussian i includes: xyz: float32[N, 3] – World-space mean position. rot: float32[N, 4] – Unnormalized quaternion representing rotation. scale: float32[N, 3] – Unnormalized log-scale vector. opacity: float32[N, 1] – Unnormalized opacity scalar. sh: float32[N, SHdim] – Spherical harmonics coefficients, where SH\dim = 3 \times (n+1)^2 for degree n (typically n=3, so 48 coefficients). During rendering, intermediate structures include: means2D: float32[N, 2] – Screen-space mean coordinates. cov2D: float32[N, 3, 3] – 2D screen-space covariance matrix. conic: float32[N, 3] – Inverse of the upper-left 2 \times 2 submatrix of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}, stored as [ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1}(0,0), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1}(0,1), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1}(1,1) ] for efficient rasterization. radii: int32[N, 2] – Bounding box radius in pixels for each Gaussian. 1. Parameter Activation: Normalize rotations: \mathbf{q}{norm} = \mathbf{q} / \|\mathbf{q}\| [Parent]. Exponentiate scales to ensure positivity: \mathbf{s}{eff} = \exp(\mathbf{s}) [Parent]. Sigmoid opacities: \alpha{eff} = \sigma(\alpha) [Parent]. Construct 3D covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{R} is the rotation matrix derived from \mathbf{q}{norm} and \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}{eff}) [Parent]. 2. Camera Space Transformation: Transform means to camera space: \boldsymbol{\mu}' = \mathbf{V} \boldsymbol{\mu} [Parent]. Transform covariance to camera space using the upper-left 3 \times 3 submatrix of the view matrix \mathbf{V} (denoted \mathbf{V}{1:3, 1:3}): \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{V}{1:3, 1:3} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} \mathbf{V}{1:3, 1:3}^T [Parent]. 3. Projection to Screen Space: Compute the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the projective projection at \boldsymbol{\mu}': \mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{fx}{\mu'z} & 0 & -\frac{fx \mu'x}{\mu'z^2} \\ 0 & \frac{fy}{\mu'z} & -\frac{fy \mu'y}{\mu'z^2} \end{pmatrix} [Parent]. Compute the 2D screen-space covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} = \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}^T [Parent]. Compute the 2D mean: \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{fx \mu'x}{\mu'z} + cx \\ \frac{fy \mu'y}{\mu'z} + cy \end{pmatrix} [Parent]. Compute the conic matrix (inverse of the 2 \times 2 top-left block of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}) for rasterization: \mathbf{C}{2D} = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}(0,0) & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}(0,1) \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}(0,1) & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}(1,1) \end{pmatrix}^{-1} Stored as vector [ \mathbf{C}{2D}(0,0), \mathbf{C}{2D}(0,1), \mathbf{C}{2D}(1,1) ]. Compute the bounding radius in pixels (typically 3\sigma): r = \lceil 3.0 \times \max(\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}(0,0)}, \sqrt{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}(1,1)}) \rceil. 4. Culling and Sorting: Cull Gaussians if \mu'z < z{near} (default 0.01) or if the bounding box is outside the image boundaries [Parent]. Sort remaining Gaussians by camera-space depth \mu'z in ascending order (front-to-back) [Parent]. This global sort is typically performed using a radix sort on the GPU. 5. Tile Assignment and Rasterization: Divide the image into tiles (e.g., 16 \times 16 pixels). Assign each Gaussian to the tiles its bounding box intersects. For each tile, iterate over the assigned Gaussians in depth order. For each pixel (u, v) in the tile, compute the offset \mathbf{x} = [u - \mu{2D,x}, v - \mu{2D,y}]^T from the Gaussian mean. Compute the alpha contribution: \alpha{pixel} = \alpha{eff} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1} \mathbf{x}\right) [Parent]. Compute the view-dependent color \mathbf{c} using the spherical harmonics evaluated at the view direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\boldsymbol{\mu}' - \mathbf{cam\pos}). 6. Alpha Compositing: Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = 0 and transmittance T = 1 [Parent]. For each Gaussian i in depth order: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + T \cdot \alpha{pixel} \cdot \mathbf{c}i T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alpha{pixel}) [Parent]. Early termination: If T < \tau (threshold, e.g., 0.05), stop processing further Gaussians for this pixel [Parent]. Unverified code. Activation qnorm = normalize(gaussians['rot'], axis=-1) seff = exp(gaussians['scale']) alphaeff = sigmoid(gaussians['opacity']) # Construct 3D Covariance R = quattorotmat(qnorm) S = diag(seff) cov3d = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # 2. Camera Space means3dhom = concat(gaussians['xyz'], 1, axis=1) # [N, 4] meanscam = (camera['V'] @ means3dhom.T).T[:,:3] # [N, 3] Vsub = camera['V'][:3,:3] covcam = Vsub @ cov3d @ Vsub.T # 3. Projection fx, fy = camera['K'][0, 0], camera['K'][1, 1] cx, cy = camera['K'][0, 2], camera['K'][1, 2] muz = meanscam[:, 2] mux = meanscam[:, 0] muy = meanscam[:, 1] # Jacobian J J = zeros((N, 2, 3)) J[:, 0, 0] = fx / muz J[:, 0, 2] = -fx mux / (muz 2) J[:, 1, 1] = fy / muz J[:, 1, 2] = -fy muy / (muz 2) # 2D Covariance cov2d = J @ covcam @ J.T # [N, 2, 2] # 2D Means means2d = zeros((N, 2)) means2d[:, 0] = fx mux / muz + cx means2d[:, 1] = fy muy / muz + cy # Conic (Inverse of 2x2 top-left) # cov2d is symmetric, so we only need (0,0), (0,1), (1,1) det = cov2d[:, 0, 0] cov2d[:, 1, 1] - cov2d[:, 0, 1] 2 conic = zeros((N, 3)) conic[:, 0] = cov2d[:, 1, 1] / det conic[:, 1] = -cov2d[:, 0, 1] / det conic[:, 2] = cov2d[:, 0, 0] / det # Radius radii = ceil(3.0 sqrt(max(cov2d[:, 0, 0], cov2d[:, 1, 1]))) # 4.
