body: The GSCache DiffRasterizer Interface is a C++ class-based abstraction for managing the differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians. It encapsulates camera state, frame buffer management, and the forward/backward passes required for gradient-based optimization of Gaussian splatting parameters. It distinguishes itself by providing a unified interface that handles not only rendering but also the integration of optimization steps (densification, pruning) and data access for the Gaussian model parameters. The interface is implemented as a C++ class that manages the state of the Gaussian splatting pipeline. It exposes methods for visibility culling, forward rendering, and backward gradient computation. Inputs: Camera parameters (intrinsic and extrinsic), Gaussian model parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), and loss gradients (for backward pass). Outputs: Rendered image (RGB), intermediate buffers (radii, geometry, binning, image), and gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters (d{xyz}, d{cov3D}, d{opacity}, d{color}, etc.). The interface relies on specific structs to manage state and results. Camera Struct Fields: mfovy: float, vertical field of view. mfovx: float, horizontal field of view. maspectratio: float, aspect ratio of the image. mposition: glm::vec3, camera position. mcenter: glm::vec3, camera look-at center. mup: glm::vec3, camera up vector. mviewmatrix: torch::Tensor, view transformation matrix. mprojectionmatrix: torch::Tensor, projection matrix. mpositiontensor: torch::Tensor, camera position as tensor. FrameBuffer Struct Fields: mdirtycpu: bool, flag indicating CPU buffer staleness. mdirtygpu: bool, flag indicating GPU buffer staleness. msize: glm::ivec2, resolution (width, height). mrgb: torch::Tensor, stored RGB image. mrgbrwcpu: torch::Tensor, CPU-accessible read/write RGB buffer. mrgbrwgpu: torch::Tensor, GPU-accessible read/write RGB buffer. DiffRasterizerForwardResult Fields: nrendered: int, number of Gaussians rendered. framebuffer: FrameBuffer, the resulting frame buffer. radii: torch::Tensor, 2D radii of Gaussians. geometrybuffer: torch::Tensor, intermediate geometry data. binningbuffer: torch::Tensor, binning data for sorting. imagebuffer: torch::Tensor, intermediate image data. DiffRasterizerBackwardResult Fields: radii: torch::Tensor, 2D radii. dxyz: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. position. dconic: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. conic matrix. dopacity: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. opacity. dcolor: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. color features. dmean2D: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. 2D mean. dcov3D: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. 3D covariance. dsh: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. spherical harmonics. dscale: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. scale. drotation: torch::Tensor, gradient w.r.t. rotation. 1. Initialization: The rasterizer initializes with Gaussian model parameters (mxyz, mfeatures, mscaling, mrotation, mopacity) and camera settings. It allocates internal buffers for rendering and gradient accumulation (mxyzgradientaccum, mdenom). 2. Visibility Culling: Call markVisible (or setVisible) to determine which Gaussians are within the camera frustum and have non-zero radii. This updates the mvisible tensor. 3. Forward Pass: Call forward with the current camera state. This performs: Projection of 3D Gaussians to 2D. Sorting of Gaussians by depth. Rasterization of Gaussians onto the frame buffer. Returns a DiffRasterizerForwardResult containing the rendered image and intermediate buffers. 4. Backward Pass: Call backward with the loss gradient tensor. This computes gradients for all Gaussian parameters based on the forward pass results and the input loss gradient. It returns a DiffRasterizerBackwardResult containing the gradients. 5. Optimization Step: The gradients are used to update the Gaussian parameters via an optimizer (e.g., Adam). The interface provides optimize() to trigger this. 6. Densification and Pruning: Periodically, densifyAndPrune is called with thresholds (gradientthreshold, opacitythreshold, extent, sizethreshold) to split or clone Gaussians with high gradients or remove those with low opacity or large extent. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class GSCacheDiffRasterizer: def init(self, camera, gaussianmodel, options): self.camera = camera self.model = gaussianmodel self.options = options self.framebuffer = FrameBuffer() self.visible = torch.zeros(gaussianmodel.numgaussians, dtype=torch.bool) self.xyzgradientaccum = torch.zeros(gaussianmodel.numgaussians) self.denom = torch.zeros(gaussianmodel.numgaussians) self.optimizer = Optimizer(gaussianmodel.parameters) def markvisible(self): # Determine visible Gaussians based on camera and radii # Update self.visible pass def forward(self): # Project Gaussians, sort, rasterize # Update framebuffer # Return DiffRasterizerForwardResult pass def backward(self, lossgradient): # Compute gradients w.r.t. Gaussian parameters # Update self.xyzgradientaccum and self.denom # Return DiffRasterizerBackwardResult pass def optimize(self): # Update model parameters using optimizer pass def densifyandprune(self, gradientthreshold, opacitythreshold, extent, sizethreshold): # Split/clone Gaussians with high gradients # Prune Gaussians with low opacity or large extent pass def getxyz(self): return self.model.xyz def getfeatures(self): return self.model.features def getscaling(self): return self.model.scaling def getrotation(self): return self.model.rotation def getopacity(self): return self.model.opacity def getvisible(self): return self.visible def getmaxradii2d(self): return self.maxradii2d def getxyzgradientaccum(self): return self.xyzgradientaccum def getdenom(self): return self.denom def getmaxshdegree(self): return self.maxshdegree def getactiveshdegree(self): return self.activeshdegree def saveply(self, filename): # Save Gaussian model to PLY file pass def loadply(self, filename): # Load Gaussian model from PLY file pass gradientthreshold: Float, threshold for gradient magnitude to trigger densification. Typical value: Not given in the sources. opacitythreshold: Float, threshold for opacity to trigger pruning. Typical value: Not given in the sources. extent: Float, maximum extent for splitting Gaussians. Typical value: Not given in the sources. sizethreshold: Int, minimum size for keeping Gaussians. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Precision: Floating-point precision in GPU computations may affect gradient accuracy. Boundaries: Gaussians near the edge of the frustum may be partially visible, requiring careful culling. Degenerate Input: Zero-opacity Gaussians or zero-radius Gaussians should be handled to avoid division by zero or undefined behavior. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of Gaussians for forward and backward passes, assuming efficient sorting and rasterization. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of Gaussians for storing parameters and intermediate buffers. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of Gaussians and image resolution. Strengths: Unified interface for rendering and optimization, efficient GPU-based computation. Limitations: Memory usage can be high for large scenes. When to use: When differentiable rendering of 3D Gaussians is required for optimization. When not: When real-time rendering without gradients is sufficient. The GSCache DiffRasterizer Interface is part of the GSCache project, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was developed to provide a flexible and efficient interface for differentiable rendering of Gaussian splats. DBauer15/gscache, https://github.com/DBauer15/gscache, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting
head: High Fidelity Point Cloud Rendering via Feature Splatting, PFGS (Point Cloud Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting)
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering pipeline to handle high-dimensional semantic feature tensors alongside RGB color, enabling high-fidelity point cloud rendering where both appearance and semantic information are preserved. It differs from standard 3DGS by modifying the rasterization kernel to accumulate and differentiate multi-channel feature maps in addition to color, allowing for downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation or feature-based reconstruction. It builds on GaussianRasterizationSettings and Gaussian Rasterization (Forward). Inputs: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D Gaussian centers. colorsprecomp: Tensor of shape (N, 3), RGB colors. semanticfeature: Tensor of shape (N, C), C-dimensional semantic features per Gaussian. opacities: Tensor of shape (N, 1), per-Gaussian opacities. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3), Gaussian scales. rotations: Tensor of shape (N, 4), Gaussian rotations (quaternions). cov3Dsprecomp: Tensor of shape (N, 6), precomputed covariances (optional if scales/rotations provided). rastersettings: Configuration object containing camera parameters and image dimensions. Outputs: color: Rendered RGB image tensor of shape (3, H, W). featuremap: Rendered semantic feature tensor of shape (C, H, W). radii: Tensor of shape (N), radius of each Gaussian in pixel space for visibility culling. GaussianRasterizationSettings A named tuple or struct containing: imageheight (int): Height of the output image. imagewidth (int): Width of the output image. tanfovx (float): Tangent of horizontal field of view. tanfovy (float): Tangent of vertical field of view. bg (torch.Tensor): Background color tensor. scalemodifier (float): Global scale modifier for Gaussian sizes. viewmatrix (torch.Tensor): 4 \times 4 view transformation matrix. projmatrix (torch.Tensor): 4 \times 4 projection matrix. shdegree (int): Degree of spherical harmonics (0 for precomputed colors). campos (torch.Tensor): Camera position. prefiltered (bool): Whether SH coefficients are prefiltered. debug (bool): Enable debug mode. CUDA Rasterizer Configuration The underlying CUDA kernel (diff-gaussian-rasterization) requires NUMSEMANTICCHANNELS to be defined in config.h at compile time to determine the dimensionality C of the feature map. 1. Input Validation and Preparation: Check that exactly one of the covariance representations is provided: either (scales, rotations) or cov3Dsprecomp. If scales is None, set to an empty tensor. If rotations is None, set to an empty tensor. If cov3Dsprecomp is None, set to an empty tensor. Ensure semanticfeature is a valid tensor of shape (N, C). 2. Forward Pass Argument Restructuring: Construct the argument tuple for the C++/CUDA rasterizer C.rasterizegaussians in the specific order expected by the kernel: python args = ( rastersettings.bg, means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, # New input for feature splatting opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, rastersettings.prefiltered, rastersettings.debug) 3. Forward Rasterization Execution: Invoke the CUDA kernel: numrendered, color, featuremap, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = C.rasterizegaussians(args). The kernel projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, sorts them by depth, and performs alpha blending. For each pixel, the color is computed as \sumi \alphai ci \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj) and the feature map is computed similarly using the feature vectors fi: F{pixel} = \sumi \alphai fi \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj). Return (color, featuremap, radii). 4. Backward Pass Input: Receive gradients gradoutcolor (shape (3, H, W)) and gradoutfeature (shape (C, H, W)) from the loss function. 5. Backward Pass Argument Restructuring: Construct the argument tuple for C.rasterizegaussiansbackward: python argsbackward = ( rastersettings.bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, # Required for feature gradient computation scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutfeature, # Gradient w.r.t feature map sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rastersettings.debug) 6. Backward Rasterization Execution: Invoke the CUDA kernel: gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbackward). 7. Backward Pass Return: Return gradients in the order corresponding to forward inputs: (gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, gradsh, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, None). The last None corresponds to rastersettings. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class GaussianRasterizer(nn.Module): def init(self, rastersettings): super().init() self.rastersettings = rastersettings # Import the custom CUDA extension # Note: In a real implementation, this would be imported from the compiled module # from diffgaussianrasterization import GaussianRasterizationSettings, GaussianRasterizer as CudaRasterizer # For the purpose of this article, we assume C is the imported module self.C = None def forward(self, means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales=None, rotations=None, cov3Dsprecomp=None): """ Forward pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting. Args: means3D: (N, 3) Tensor of 3D Gaussian centers. colorsprecomp: (N, 3) Tensor of RGB colors. semanticfeature: (N, C) Tensor of semantic features. opacities: (N, 1) Tensor of opacities. scales: (N, 3) Tensor of scales (optional). rotations: (N, 4) Tensor of rotations (quaternions) (optional). cov3Dsprecomp: (N, 6) Tensor of precomputed covariances (optional). Returns: color: (3, H, W) Rendered RGB image. featuremap: (C, H, W) Rendered semantic feature map. radii: (N,) Tensor of radii for visible Gaussians. """ # 1. Validation if scales is None: scales = torch.empty(0) if rotations is None: rotations = torch.empty(0) if cov3Dsprecomp is None: cov3Dsprecomp = torch.empty(0) # Check that exactly one covariance representation is provided hasscalesrot = (len(scales) > 0 and len(rotations) > 0) hascov = len(cov3Dsprecomp) > 0 if not (hasscalesrot ^ hascov): raise ValueError("Exactly one of (scales, rotations) or cov3Dsprecomp must be provided.") # 2. Construct Args for Forward rs = self.rastersettings argsforward = ( rs.bg, means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, rs.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rs.viewmatrix, rs.projmatrix, rs.tanfovx, rs.tanfovy, rs.imageheight, rs.imagewidth, None, # sh (not used if colorsprecomp is provided) rs.shdegree, rs.campos, rs.prefiltered, rs.debug) # 3. Execute Forward Rasterization # C.rasterizegaussians returns: numrendered, color, featuremap, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer numrendered, color, featuremap, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = self.C.rasterizegaussians(argsforward) # 4. Save for Backward # We need to save inputs that are required for the backward pass self.saveforbackward( means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) # Store raster settings in context if needed, or assume they are constant self.rastersettingssaved = rs return color, featuremap, radii def backward(self, gradoutcolor, gradoutfeature): """ Backward pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting. Args: gradoutcolor: (3, H, W) Gradient of loss w.r.t. color. gradoutfeature: (C, H, W) Gradient of loss w.r.t. feature map. Returns: Gradients for all input tensors. """ # Retrieve saved tensors means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = self.savedtensors rs = self.rastersettingssaved # 5. Construct Args for Backward argsbackward = ( rs.bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, scales, rotations, rs.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rs.viewmatrix, rs.projmatrix, rs.tanfovx, rs.tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutfeature, None, # sh rs.shdegree, rs.campos, geomBuffer, None, # numrendered (often passed as 0 or inferred in backward, but source says it's in args) binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rs.debug) # Note: The source notes indicate numrendered is passed in backward args. # In PyTorch custom autograd, we usually don't pass buffers like geomBuffer directly unless the C++ op expects them. # Assuming the C++ op signature matches the forward return buffers for backward input. # 6. Execute Backward Rasterization # Returns: gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations = self.C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbackward) # 7. Return Gradients in Forward Input Order # Forward inputs: means3D, means2D, sh, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings return ( gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, gradsh, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, None # rastersettings does not require gradient) NUMSEMANTICCHANNELS: Must be defined at compile time in submodules/diff-gaussian-rasterization/cudarasterizer/config.h. This determines the channel dimension C of the semanticfeature and featuremap tensors. Visibility Marking: The markVisible method uses C.markvisible(positions, viewmatrix, projmatrix) to return a boolean tensor of points within the camera frustum. Precision: Standard 3DGS precision issues (e.g., depth sorting stability) apply. The addition of feature channels does not change the depth sorting logic but increases memory bandwidth usage during the blending step. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS rasterization, O(N) for projection and sorting, with blending proportional to the number of overlapping Gaussians per pixel. The feature splatting adds a constant factor proportional to the number of feature channels C. Memory Complexity: Increases by O(C \cdot H \cdot W) for the feature map output and intermediate buffers during backward pass, compared to O(3 \cdot H \cdot W) for color only. Performance: Tested on RTX 3090 with PyTorch 1.13.0 and CUDA 11.7. Specific FPS numbers are not provided in the sources, but the method is designed to be efficient enough for real-time or near-real-time rendering of point clouds. Strengths: Enables semantic-aware rendering and reconstruction from point clouds. Limitations: Requires recompilation of the CUDA rasterizer for different feature dimensions. Not given in the sources: specific scalability limits for very large C. Origin: PFGS (Point Cloud Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting) was introduced by Jiaxu Wang, Ziyi Zhang, Junhao He, and Renjing Xu in 2024. Paper: "PFGS: High Fidelity Point Cloud Rendering via Feature Splatting," ECCV 2024. Development: The rasterization kernel is based on Feature-3DGS but with minor differences and bug fixes. It extends the original 3DGS rasterizer to support high-dimensional features. Usage: Used for high-fidelity rendering of point clouds with semantic information, demonstrated on datasets like ScanNet, DTU, and THuman2. Mercerai/PFGS, https://github.com/Mercerai/PFGS, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, Gaussian Splatting Rasterization Pipeline Setup, Gaussian Splatting Rasterization and Rendering Pipeline
body: The Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline orchestrates the differentiable rasterization of a scene represented as a set of 3D Gaussians into a 2D image for a specific camera viewpoint. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of adaptive volumetric primitives by projecting 3D covariances to 2D, evaluating view-dependent colors via Spherical Harmonics (SH), and compositing the results using alpha blending. It sets itself apart from standard polygon rasterization by handling soft, overlapping volumetric primitives with depth-aware sorting, and from NeRFs by utilizing explicit, differentiable geometric primitives that allow for real-time rendering speeds on consumer GPUs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: pc: A GaussianModel object containing: xyz: 3D means, shape [N, 3]. featuresdc, featuresrest: SH coefficients, shape [N, 3] and [N, 45] for degree 3, or combined [N, K, 3]. opacity: Raw opacity values, shape [N]. scaling: Log-scale parameters, shape [N, 3]. rotation: Quaternions (w, x, y, z), shape [N, 4]. activeshdegree: Integer indicating the active SH degree. viewpointcamera: Camera object containing: worldviewtransform: 4 \times 4 view matrix. fullprojtransform: 4 \times 4 projection matrix. cameracenter: Camera position in world space. FoVx, FoVy: Field of view in radians. imagewidth, imageheight: Resolution. pipe: Pipeline configuration object (see parameters). bgcolor: Background color tensor, shape [3]. Outputs: render: Rendered image tensor, shape [3, H, W] (RGB) or extended based on render mode. viewspacepoints: Tensor of 2D screen-space means, shape [N, 2] or [N, 3] (with depth), requiresgrad=True. visibilityfilter: Boolean tensor [N], true if Gaussian radius > 0. radii: Integer tensor [N], screen-space radius of each Gaussian. Data Structures: GaussianRasterizationSettings: Holds camera intrinsics (tanfovx, tanfovy, principal point), extrinsics (viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos), background color, scale modifier, SH degree, and debug flags. GaussianRasterizer: The CUDA/MLX kernel instance initialized with GaussianRasterizationSettings. Steps: 1. Initialize Screenspace Points: Create a zero tensor screenspacepoints on the same device and dtype as pc.getxyz, with requiresgrad=True. Attempt to call retaingrad() on this tensor to ensure gradients are retained for backpropagation. 2. Compute Camera Parameters: Calculate half-field-of-view tangents: \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx} / 2) \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy} / 2). Extract camera position campos from the view matrix V = [R | t; 0, 1] as \text{campos} = -R^T t. 3. Configure Rasterization Settings: Construct GaussianRasterizationSettings with: imageheight, imagewidth from viewpointcamera. tanfovx, tanfovy. bg: Background color. scalemodifier: Default 1.0. viewmatrix: viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform. projmatrix: viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform. shdegree: pc.activeshdegree. campos: viewpointcamera.cameracenter. prefiltered: False. debug: pipe.debug. 4. Select Covariance Representation: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true: Compute cov3Dprecomp by calling pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier). This computes the splat-to-world covariance and transforms it to pixel space using NDC-to-pixel and world-to-pixel matrices. If false: Set cov3Dprecomp to None, and assign scales = pc.getscaling() and rotations = pc.getrotation(). The rasterizer will compute covariances from scales and rotations internally. 5. Select Color Representation: If overridecolor is not None: Set colorsprecomp = overridecolor. Else if pipe.convertSHspython is true: Extract SH coefficients: shsview = pc.getfeatures.transpose(1, 2).view(-1, 3, (pc.maxshdegree+1)2). Compute view directions: dirpp = pc.getxyz - viewpointcamera.cameracenter.repeat(pc.getfeatures.shape[0], 1). Normalize: dirppnormalized = dirpp / dirpp.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True). Evaluate SH: sh2rgb = evalsh(pc.activeshdegree, shsview, dirppnormalized). Clamp: colorsprecomp = torch.clampmin(sh2rgb + 0.5, 0.0). Else: Set shs = pc.getfeatures. 6. Assign Attributes: means3D = pc.getxyz(). means2D = screenspacepoints. opacity = pc.getopacity(). 7. Instantiate Rasterizer: Create GaussianRasterizer using the configured rastersettings. 8. Execute Rasterization: Call the rasterizer with: renderedimage, radii = rasterizer(means3D, means2D, shs, colorsprecomp, opacity, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp). If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, scales and rotations are None. If pipe.convertSHspython is true, shs is None. 9. Construct Return Dictionary: Return: render: renderedimage. viewspacepoints: screenspacepoints. visibilityfilter: radii > 0. radii: radii. Optional Depth Rendering: If returndepth is true: 1. Extract view direction projvect1 (first 3 elements of worldviewtransform[:, 2]) and offset projvect2 (last element). 2. Compute depth means: means3Ddepth = dot(means3D, projvect1) + projvect2. 3. Repeat depth values 3 times to match RGB channel count. 4. Rasterize again with shs=None, colorsprecomp=means3Ddepth, and other attributes same as above. 5. Average the resulting depth image over channels: renderdepth = rendereddepth.mean(dim=0). 6. Add renderdepth to return dict. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math class GaussianRasterizationSettings: def init(self, imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg, scalemodifier, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree, campos, prefiltered, debug): self.imageheight = imageheight self.imagewidth = imagewidth self.tanfovx = tanfovx self.tanfovy = tanfovy self.bg = bg self.scalemodifier = scalemodifier self.viewmatrix = viewmatrix self.projmatrix = projmatrix self.shdegree = shdegree self.campos = campos self.prefiltered = prefiltered self.debug = debug def evalsh(deg, shsview, dirs): """Evaluates spherical harmonics for view-dependent color.""" # Standard SH evaluation: computes basis functions Y(dirs) and dot products with shsview # Returns RGB tensor of shape [N, 3] return torch.zeros(shsview.shape[0], 3, dtype=shsview.dtype, device=shsview.device) class GaussianRasterizer: def init(self, rastersettings): self.settings = rastersettings def call(self, means3D, means2D, shs, colorsprecomp, opacity, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp): """Performs tile intersection, projection, and alpha compositing.""" # Standard rasterization kernel execution renderedimage = torch.zeros(self.settings.imageheight, self.settings.imagewidth, 3, dtype=torch.float32, device=means3D.device) radii = torch.zeros(means3D.shape[0], dtype=torch.int32, device=means3D.device) return renderedimage, radii def render(viewpointcamera, pc, pipe, bgcolor, overridecolor=None): # 1. Initialize screenspace points screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz(), dtype=torch.float32, requiresgrad=True, device="cuda") try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except RuntimeError: pass # 2. Compute camera parameters tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # 3. Configure rasterization settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imageheight=viewpointcamera.imageheight, imagewidth=viewpointcamera.imagewidth, tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bg=bgcolor, scalemodifier=pipe.scalemodifier, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, campos=viewpointcamera.cameracenter, prefiltered=False, debug=pipe.debug) # 4. Select covariance representation if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(pipe.scalemodifier) scales = None rotations = None else: cov3Dprecomp = None scales = pc.getscaling() rotations = pc.getrotation() # 5. Select color representation if overridecolor is not None: colorsprecomp = overridecolor shs = None else: if pipe.convertSHspython: shsview = pc.getfeatures.transpose(1, 2).view(-1, 3, (pc.maxshdegree + 1) 2) dirpp = pc.getxyz - viewpointcamera.cameracenter.repeat(pc.getfeatures.shape[0], 1) dirppnormalized = dirpp / dirpp.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) sh2rgb = evalsh(pc.activeshdegree, shsview, dirppnormalized) colorsprecomp = torch.clampmin(sh2rgb + 0.5, 0.0) shs = None else: colorsprecomp = None shs = pc.getfeatures # 6. Assign attributes means3D = pc.getxyz() opacity = pc.getopacity() # 7. Instantiate rasterizer rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings=rastersettings) # 8. Execute rasterization renderedimage, radii = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=screenspacepoints, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp, opacity=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp) # 9. Construct return dictionary visibilityfilter = radii > 0 result = { "render": renderedimage, "viewspacepoints": screenspacepoints, "visibilityfilter": visibilityfilter, "radii": radii } return result Parameters: pipe.computecov3Dpython: Boolean. If true, compute 3D covariance in Python; otherwise, let rasterizer compute from scales/rotations. pipe.convertSHspython: Boolean. If true, evaluate SH in Python; otherwise, pass SH coefficients to rasterizer. pipe.depthratio: Float. Weight for combining expected and median depth: \text{surf\depth} = \text{render\depth\expected} \times (1 - \text{pipe.depth\ratio}) + \text{pipe.depth\ratio} \times \text{render\depth\median}. scalemodifier: Multiplier for Gaussian scales, default 1.0. nearplane: Near clipping plane, default 0.01. farplane: Far clipping plane, default 10^{10}. eps2d: Regularization added to 2D covariance diagonal, default 0.3. tilesize: Tile side length, default 16. shdegree: SH degree to activate. None means direct color mode. alphamax: Maximum alpha to prevent instability, default 0.99. alphacutoff: Alpha cutoff for early termination, default 1/255. chisquareclip: Chi-square clipping threshold for covariance regularization, default 9.21 (approx 3\sigma). pixguard: Pixel guard band width for culling, default 64. scalefactor: Factor to scale rendering resolution, default 2 (half resolution). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Lower weight precision (e.g., 8-bit) may be required for inference compared to training. Parent Constraints: For mutual exclusivity of representations, None normalization, and device consistency, see Rendering Pipeline and Configuration. Replaces the standard exponential opacity formulation with direct neural network outputs for per-Gaussian opacity and color, retaining the standard 2D Gaussian rasterizer for compositing. It computes view-dependent color and density (\sigma) for each Gaussian center, maps \sigma directly to opacity, and composites using standard alpha blending. Uses an octree structure to manage Gaussians. It initializes GaussianModel with dataset parameters including featdim, noffsets, fork, usefeatbank, appearancedim, addopacitydist, addcovdist, addcolordist, addlevel, visiblethreshold, dist2level, baselayer, progressive, extend. It applies a compatibility patch to gaussianrenderer.generateneuralgaussians to replace apecode[0] with apecode. It sets the anchor mask for the current view using gaussians.setanchormask(view.cameracenter, scene.loadediter, view.resolutionscale). It prefilters voxels to determine visibility using prefiltervoxel(view, gaussians, pipeline, background). It renders the scene using render(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, visiblemask=visible, apecode=args.ape) with apecode defaulting to 10. It clamps the rendered image to [0.0, 1.0] and saves it. It records the number of visible Gaussians per view in perviewcount.json. Integrates 3DGS into the Unity engine. It inserts an additional sorting pass into each camera's command buffer. It inserts draw calls for 3DGS objects into the existing rendering queue for transparent meshes based on their bounding boxes. It differs from separate render texture approaches by avoiding an intermediate texture and color space conversion pass after alpha blending. A technique to resolve popping artifacts (temporal instability) caused by depth-sorting swaps by replacing global sorting with per-pixel depth comparison or ray-tracing. Popping artifacts arise from the depth-sorting step, where overlapping Gaussians may swap their sort order as the camera moves, causing a sudden discontinuity in alpha-blending accumulation. A culling method using axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABB) to check depth and remove Gaussian points behind the camera near-plane. It filters out Gaussian points that lie behind or too close to the near clipping plane before they enter the rendering pipeline. It checks each Gaussian's position relative to the camera near plane, discarding or skipping points that fail the test before projection. The culling condition is z{\max} < z{\text{near}}, where z is the Gaussian center depth in camera coordinates, \Delta z \ge 0 is the half-extent of the AABB along the camera z-axis, z{\min} = z - \Delta z, z{\max} = z + \Delta z, and z{\text{near}} is the camera near-plane depth. Hardware unit design operates with a single MAC unit, latency of 4 cycles, processing inputs (x, y, \text{depth}) and view matrix row [3:0], using D flip-flops (DFF) between operations for timing stability at 800 MHz FP16. It achieves a 56% culling rate on the compressed model, saving 56% of unnecessary Gaussian point computations and memory accesses. It increases throughput from 15.81% to 35.94% (2.27× gain), raising FPS from 20.4 to 46.4 at 1080p. Reconstructs a radiance field representation by rendering RGB, depth, alpha, and normal maps from a set of Gaussian splats for a given set of viewpoints. It initializes background color tensor: background = torch.tensor(bgcolor, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda"). For each viewpoint in the stack, it calls the render function: renderpkg = self.render(viewpointcam, self.gaussians). It extracts RGB from render package: rgb = renderpkg['render']. It extracts alpha from render package: alpha = renderpkg['rendalpha']. It computes surface normal by normalizing the rendered normal: normal = torch.nn.functional.normalize(renderpkg['rendnormal'], dim=0). It extracts depth: depth = renderpkg['depth']. It extracts surface normal from depth: depthnormal = renderpkg['surfnormal']. It appends the CPU tensors of RGB and depth to their respective lists: self.rgbmaps.append(rgb.cpu()) and self.depthmaps.append(depth.cpu()). After processing all viewpoints, it estimates the bounding sphere of the scene: self.estimateboundingsphere(). Time Complexity: The pipeline is dominated by the rasterization step, which is O(N) for N Gaussians, but with a constant factor dependent on tile size and overlap. The projection and covariance computation are also O(N). Memory Complexity: The scene representation requires storage for N Gaussians, each with position, scale, rotation, opacity, and SH coefficients. Optimized scenes can consist of millions of Gaussians and require up to several gigabytes of storage and memory. Measured Performance: On high-end GPUs, the pipeline shows real-time performance. On Apple Silicon with MLX, the full pipeline (forward pass) for 100K Gaussians at 128x128 resolution takes approximately 10-20ms (estimated from 1K/10K timings). Near-plane culling can increase FPS from 20.4 to 46.4 at 1080p. Scaling: The pipeline scales well with resolution and number of Gaussians, but memory usage is a limiting factor on low-end devices. Strengths: Real-time rendering speeds, differentiable, explicit scene representation. Limitations: High memory usage for large scenes, potential for popping artifacts due to depth sorting. When to use: Real-time novel view synthesis on high-end GPUs. When not to use: Low-end devices with limited VRAM, applications requiring strict polygon integration without custom pipelines. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It builds upon EWA volume splatting. The method models a scene as a set of 3D Gaussians with shape and appearance parameters, optimized via differentiable rendering to match a set of recorded images. The optimized scenes usually consist of millions of Gaussians. The pipeline was originally designed for CUDA GPUs. Ports to MLX (gsplat-mlx) have been developed for Apple Silicon. Integrations with Unity and hardware accelerators have also been developed. name: Neural Gaussian Rasterization Pipeline
head: DNGaussian rendering, Neural opacity/color rasterization
body: The Neural Gaussian Rasterization Pipeline replaces the standard exponential opacity formulation of 3D Gaussian Splatting with direct neural network outputs for per-Gaussian opacity and color, while retaining the standard 2D Gaussian rasterizer for compositing. It computes view-dependent color and density (\sigma) for each Gaussian center, maps \sigma directly to opacity, and composites the result using standard alpha blending. The pipeline integrates a neural density network into the Gaussian Splatting rendering loop. Inputs: viewpointcamera: Camera parameters including cameracenter, FoVx, FoVy, projection matrix, and view matrix. pc (GaussianModel): The set of 3D Gaussians containing xyz (3D positions), scalingmodifier, and a neuralrenderer. background: A tensor representing the background color. pipe: A configuration object containing computecov3Dpython, scalemodifier, and other rasterization settings. Outputs: renderedimage: Tensor containing the final RGB image. radii: Tensor indicating which Gaussians are visible (radius > 0). rendereddepth: Tensor containing the accumulated depth. renderedalpha: Tensor containing the accumulated alpha. GaussianModel (pc): xyz: Tensor of 3D positions of N Gaussians. neuralrenderer: A neural network that takes (3,) position and (3,) direction as input and outputs (1,) sigma and (3,) color. getcovariance(scalingmodifier): Method to compute the 3D covariance matrix. getopacity(): Method to retrieve standard learned opacity if neural mode is disabled. GaussianRasterizationSettings: imagewidth, imageheight: Integer dimensions of the output image. tanfovx, tanfovy: Tangent of half horizontal and vertical field of view. background: Background color tensor. scalemodifier: Float multiplier for Gaussian sizes. viewmatrix, projmatrix: Camera transformation matrices. shdegree: Spherical Harmonics degree. cameraposition: Camera center vector. prefiltered: Boolean, typically False for neural variants. 1. Compute Direction Vectors: Calculate the vector from the camera center to each Gaussian center. \mathbf{dir}{pp} = \mathbf{p}c - \mathbf{c}{cam} where \mathbf{p}c is the tensor of Gaussian positions (N, 3) and \mathbf{c}{cam} is the camera center (3,). 2. Normalize Directions: Normalize \mathbf{dir}{pp} along the batch dimension. \mathbf{dir}{pp\normalized} = \frac{\mathbf{dir}{pp}}{\|\mathbf{dir}{pp}\|2} 3. Neural Query: Pass the 3D positions and normalized directions to the neuralrenderer to obtain density (\sigma) and color (\mathbf{c}). \sigma, \mathbf{c} = \text{neural\renderer}(\mathbf{p}c, \mathbf{dir}{pp\normalized}) 4. Opacity Assignment: Assign opacity directly from \sigma without the standard 1 - e^{-\sigma} transformation. \alpha{neural} = \sigma Note: In inference mode, the standard pc.getopacity() may override this. 5. Initialize Screenspace Points: Prepare the 2D mean positions (means2D) for rasterization. These must be initialized with requiresgrad=True to enable gradient flow back to 2D means during rasterization. 6. Configure Rasterization Settings: Compute tangent FOV: \text{tanfovx} = \tan\left(\frac{\text{FoVx}}{2}\right), \quad \text{tanfovy} = \tan\left(\frac{\text{FoVy}}{2}\right) Set scalemodifier (default 1.0). Select covariance computation: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, compute cov3Dprecomp via pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier); otherwise, use precomputed scales and rotations. 7. Rasterize: Execute the rasterizer with means3D, means2D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales/rotations or cov3Dprecomp, returning renderedimage, radii, rendereddepth, renderedalpha. 8. Filter Visibility: Check radii > 0 to exclude frustum-culled or zero-radius Gaussians from further processing (e.g., splitting criteria). Unverified code. Compute direction vectors from camera center to each Gaussian camcenter = viewpointcamera.cameracenter.repeat(pc.getxyz.shape[0], 1) dirpp = pc.getxyz - camcenter # 2. Normalize direction vectors along the batch dimension dirppnormalized = dirpp / dirpp.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) # 3. Query the neural renderer with 3D positions and normalized directions xyzcuda = pc.getxyz.cuda() dircuda = dirppnormalized.cuda() sigma, color = pc.neuralrenderer(xyzcuda, dircuda) # 4. Assign opacity directly from sigma opacity = sigma.view(-1, 1) # 5. Combine opacity (handles inference mode override if needed) finalopacity = pc.combineopacity(opacity) # 6. Compute tangent half-angles tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # 7. Configure rasterization settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imageheight=viewpointcamera.imageheight, imagewidth=viewpointcamera.imagewidth, tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bg=background, scalemodifier=pipe.scalemodifier, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.viewmatrix, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.projmatrix, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, campos=viewpointcamera.cameracenter, prefiltered=False, debug=False) # 8. Select covariance computation mode if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(pipe.scalemodifier) scales = None rotations = None else: cov3Dprecomp = None scales = pc.getscaling rotations = pc.getrotation # 9. Initialize screenspace points (means2D) # Projection logic not given in sources; typically involves perspective projection using viewmatrix and projmatrix. means2D = preparemeans2D(pc.getxyz, rastersettings) # 10. Execute rasterizer rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings) renderedimage, radii, rendereddepth, renderedalpha = rasterizer( means3D=pc.getxyz, means2D=means2D, colorsprecomp=color, opacities=finalopacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp) # 11. Filter visibility (for downstream tasks like splitting) visiblemask = radii > 0 return { 'render': renderedimage, 'radii': radii, 'depth': rendereddepth, 'alpha': renderedalpha, 'visiblemask': visiblemask } def preparemeans2D(means3D, rastersettings): # Projection logic not given in sources; typically involves perspective projection using viewmatrix and projmatrix. raise NotImplementedError(" Projection logic not given in sources.") scalingmodifier: Scales the Gaussian covariance/sizes before rasterization. Default value is 1.0. inference: Boolean flag. When true, overrides neural opacity with pc.getopacity() instead of the neural output. value: Constant opacity multiplier used in depth-only rendering mode. Default value is 0.95. Precision: The neural renderer outputs \sigma directly as opacity. The standard 1 - e^{-\sigma} transformation is omitted, which simplifies the gradient flow but requires careful initialization of the neural network to prevent exploding opacities. Boundaries: Frustum culling is handled by the rasterizer's radii output. Gaussians with radii == 0 are excluded from splitting criteria. Degenerate Input: If dirpp is zero (Gaussian at camera center), normalization fails. A small epsilon should be added to the denominator during normalization to prevent NaN gradients. A rendering pass that isolates opacity computation by using fixed colors and detaching 3D parameters, useful for debugging or training opacity networks. It detaches means3D from the computation graph to freeze 3D positions during the pass, and uses the model's stored opacity values directly instead of neural outputs. Time Complexity: Dominated by the neural network inference for each Gaussian (O(N \cdot D{MLP})) and the rasterization step (O(N \cdot P) where P is pixels). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the neural network weights and the output tensors for \sigma and color for all Gaussians. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of Gaussians N and the complexity of the neural network. Strengths: Allows for view-dependent appearance and complex material representation without explicit spherical harmonics or texture maps. Limitations: Slower rendering due to per-Gaussian neural queries. Requires careful tuning of the neural network architecture and training. When to use: When high-fidelity view-dependent effects are required and rendering speed is secondary to quality. When not to use: For real-time applications requiring high frame rates with large numbers of Gaussians. This pipeline is implemented in the DNGaussian repository. It extends the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by integrating a neural density network to handle opacity and color, aiming to improve reconstruction quality for complex scenes. name: Differentiable Backpropagation Mechanisms
body: This family defines the mathematical and algorithmic mechanisms for computing gradients of the rendering loss with respect to 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) during the training of Gaussian Splatting models. It solves the problem of enabling end-to-end optimization of scene representations by providing differentiable paths from the final pixel color to the underlying 3D attributes. It differs from standard rasterization by explicitly deriving chain-rule gradients for alpha compositing and basis function evaluations, and from non-differentiable methods by supporting arbitrary gradient estimation strategies including per-splat parallelization and stochastic estimation. All mechanisms in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rasterization pipeline defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer. The core principle is the application of the chain rule to the alpha compositing equation: Cj = \sum{s \in \mathcal{O}j} cs \alphas \prod{k \in \mathcal{O}j, k < s} (1 - \alphak) where Cj is the final color of pixel j, cs is the color of splat s, \alphas is its opacity at pixel j, and \mathcal{O}j is the set of splats sorted by depth contributing to pixel j. Gradients flow back through this accumulation. The specific implementation details (parallelization strategy, basis function derivatives, or stochastic approximation) vary by child, but all must correctly propagate \frac{\partial L}{\partial Cj} to \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} where \theta represents the Gaussian parameters. A GPU kernel optimization that eliminates atomic contention by parallelizing the backward pass over 2D splats rather than pixels, using intra-warp shuffling for state exchange. It sets itself apart from pixel-parallel siblings by mapping threads to splats to avoid serialized atomic operations. Choose this for high-performance training on modern GPUs where memory bandwidth and atomic operations are bottlenecks. Computes gradients for Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions (DARBFs) by replacing standard Gaussian derivatives with specific terms derived from the DARBF activation function. It sets itself apart from standard Gaussian backpropagation siblings by handling non-Gaussian basis functions like half-cosine splats. Choose this when using non-Gaussian basis functions that require custom gradient formulas. Estimates gradients on a per-pixel basis using finite differences with random sign vectors, avoiding the need for a differentiable framework. It sets itself apart from exact backpropagation siblings by approximating gradients to bound optimization dimensionality and working with existing non-differentiable rasterizers. Choose this when integrating with non-differentiable rasterizers or when reducing the dimensionality of the optimization problem is critical. Not given in the sources. name: Backpropagation with Per-Splat Parallelization
head: Per-splat backward, Per-splat parallelization, Recursive Per-Splat Parallelization for Backward Propagation, Splat-parallel backprop, Warp-level gradient accumulation
body: This method is a GPU acceleration technique for the backward propagation pass in 3D Gaussian Splatting that eliminates atomic contention and depth-sorting constraints by processing gradients at the splat level within warps, using recursive state circulation. It sets itself apart from the original 3DGS pixel-parallel approach by mapping threads to 2D splats rather than pixels, thereby avoiding serialized atomic operations when multiple threads contend for the same Gaussian's gradient. Unlike Taming-3DGS, which stores pixel states every 32nd splat and enforces strict depth-order traversal causing up to 31 redundant computations per tile, this method imposes no constraint on processing order, avoiding redundant arithmetic. The method replaces the original 3DGS backward pass, where threads map to pixels and iterate over depth-sorted splats, with a scheme where threads maintain per-splat state and exchange smaller per-pixel states (transmittance T and accumulated color C). This approach leverages the differentiability of the forward rasterization defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer. Inputs: Gradient of the loss with respect to pixel colors: \frac{\partial L}{\partial Cj} for all pixels j in a tile. Forward pass checkpoint data: Per-pixel states (transmittance T and accumulated color C) stored at specific intervals during the forward pass. Gaussian parameters: Position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients, and color for all active splats. Tile configuration: A tile of 256 pixels, partitioned into groups matching warp size. Outputs: Gradients with respect to all Gaussian parameters: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} for all splats s in the tile. 1. Per-Pixel State: A tuple (Tj, Cj) representing the transmittance and accumulated color for pixel j. In the forward pass, these are stored for every N-th splat (where N=32). 2. Per-Splat Gradient Accumulator: Global memory location for each splat s storing \frac{\partial L}{\partial \thetas}. 3. Warp Shared Memory/Registers: Used for intra-warp state exchange. Each lane l in a warp of size W=32 holds state for a specific pixel or splat. Warp Size (W): 32 threads. Bucket Size: Splats are divided into buckets of size 32, each scheduled to a CUDA warp. Checkpoint Interval (N): 32 splats. Tile Size: 256 pixels, partitioned into 8 groups of 32 pixels. The backward pass is executed per tile. The tile is processed by warps, where each warp handles a bucket of 32 splats. 1. Initialization: For each pixel j in the tile, retrieve the initial per-pixel state (Tj^{(0)}, Cj^{(0)}) from the forward pass checkpoints. If the pixel has no splats, Tj^{(0)} = 1.0, Cj^{(0)} = 0.0. Each thread in the warp (lane l) is assigned to a specific pixel jl within the warp's group. Lane l fetches the initial state for pixel jl. 2. State Circulation and Gradient Accumulation (Recursive Per-Splat): The warp processes its bucket of 32 splats sequentially. Let the splats in the bucket be s0, s1, \dots, s{31}. For each splat sk in the bucket (where k ranges from 0 to 31): a. State Exchange: Threads exchange per-pixel states (transmittance T and accumulated color C) via intra-warp shuffling. b. Splat Evaluation: The splat sk is evaluated at pixel jl. Compute the splat's opacity \alpha{sk, jl} and color c{sk, jl} at pixel jl using the Gaussian parameters. c. Blending Logic: Apply the alpha compositing equation to update the pixel state for the next splat in the depth order. Specifically, thread l computes the gradient contribution for splat sk at pixel jl. d. Gradient Computation: The gradient for splat sk with respect to pixel jl is computed. Let \frac{\partial L}{\partial C{jl}} be the incoming loss gradient. The contribution to the splat's gradient is derived from the chain rule through the alpha compositing equation. The thread accumulates this gradient into the global gradient accumulator for splat sk. e. State Update for Next Splat: To prepare for the next splat s{k+1} in the bucket, the per-pixel state (T{jl}, C{jl}) is updated to reflect the inclusion of splat sk. This is done by applying the default alpha blending logic: T{new} = T{old} \cdot (1 - \alpha{sk, jl}) C{new} = C{old} + T{old} \cdot \alpha{sk, jl} \cdot c{sk, jl} Threads then exchange pixel states via fast collaborative sharing (intra-warp shuffling). 3. Completion: Repeat the circulation and accumulation for all 8 groups of 32 pixels in the tile (since 256/32 = 8). Atomic updates to the global gradient accumulators are performed for each splat. Since each warp handles a unique bucket of splats, contention is minimized. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backwardpersplatparallelization(tilepixels, splatbuckets, forwardcheckpoints, lossgradients): """ tilepixels: List of 256 pixel indices in the tile. splatbuckets: List of 8 buckets, each containing 32 splat indices. forwardcheckpoints: Dictionary mapping (pixelidx, splatidx) -> (T, C). lossgradients: Array of shape (256,) containing dL/dCj for each pixel. """ W = 32 # Warp size splatgradients = {s: 0.0 for s in set().union(splatbuckets)} # Tile has 8 groups of 32 pixels; each group is processed by one warp pass for groupidx in range(8): pixelgroup = tilepixels[groupidx W: (groupidx + 1) W] # Initialize per-pixel states from forward checkpoints at splat index 0 pixelstates = [forwardcheckpoints[(pixelgroup[l], 0)] for l in range(W)] # Process the bucket of 32 splats sequentially for k in range(W): splats = splatbuckets[groupidx][k] for l in range(W): Tj, Cj = pixelstates[l] # Evaluate splat s at pixel j alphasj = computeopacity(splats, pixelgroup[l]) colorsj = computecolor(splats, pixelgroup[l]) # Compute gradient contribution for splat s at pixel j using chain rule gradcontrib = computegradientcontribution(lossgradients[pixelgroup[l]], Tj, alphasj, colorsj) splatgradients[splats] += gradcontrib # Update state for next splat in the bucket Tnew = Tj (1.0 - alphasj) Cnew = Cj + Tj alphasj colorsj pixelstates[l] = (Tnew, Cnew) # Rotate states to next lane for next splat processing pixelstates = [pixelstates[-1]] + pixelstates[:-1] return splatgradients def computeopacity(splat, pixel): # Standard 2D Gaussian evaluation at pixel coordinates return 1.0 / (1.0 + splat.covariance (pixel - splat.position)2) def computecolor(splat, pixel): # Standard spherical harmonics evaluation at pixel direction return splat.color splat.opacity def computegradientcontribution(lossgrad, T, alpha, color): # Chain rule through alpha compositing: dL/dtheta = dL/dC T alpha dC/dtheta return lossgrad T alpha color Atomic Contention: The original 3DGS method suffers from heavy contention as many threads target the same memory locations for atomic writes. This method mitigates this by parallelizing at the splat level, ensuring each warp handles a unique bucket of splats, thus reducing contention. Depth Sorting: The original 3DGS requires strict depth order traversal, which can lead to redundant computations if the warp size does not align with the number of splats. This method imposes no constraint on processing order, avoiding redundant arithmetic. Occlusion: Iterating the tail of each tile’s depth-sorted list of splats often becomes redundant due to occlusion. The method tracks the last contributor across the tile to skip entire groups of splat-tile pairings in the backward pass, exploiting occlusion observed in the forward pass. Precision: Using tighter culling as proposed by Radl et al. [2024] minimizes redundant splats in both forward and backward passes, which can help maintain numerical stability by reducing the number of operations. This method applies low-level CUDA kernel optimizations to the 3D Gaussian Splatting backward pass to reduce memory access overhead and improve cache utilization. It specifically targets the reduction of redundant global memory transactions and improves warp-level parallelism without altering rendering results or optimization behavior. It differs from structural optimizations like Loss-Accumulation Guided (LAG) densification or pruning by reducing training time independently of the number of Gaussians, providing consistent speedups across all configurations. Time Complexity: The method reduces the time complexity of the backward pass by eliminating atomic contention and redundant computations. The original 3DGS backward pass has a time complexity proportional to the number of splats per pixel times the number of pixels, with a high constant factor due to atomic operations. This method reduces the constant factor by using warp-level parallelism and intra-warp shuffling. Memory Complexity: The method requires storing per-pixel states at checkpoint intervals during the forward pass. The memory overhead is proportional to the number of pixels multiplied by the checkpoint interval N. This is a trade-off for the reduced memory bandwidth usage during the backward pass. Measured Performance: The method provides consistent speedups across all configurations, reducing training time independently of the number of Gaussians. It outperforms the original 3DGS backward pass and other concurrent works like DISTWAR [Durvasula et al. 2023]. Strengths: Eliminates atomic contention, avoids redundant computations, and leverages warp-level parallelism effectively. Limitations: Requires storing checkpoint data during the forward pass, which increases memory usage. The method assumes a warp size of 32, which is standard for CUDA but may need adjustment for other GPU architectures. When to Use: Use this method when training 3D Gaussian Splatting models on CUDA GPUs and performance is a bottleneck. It is particularly effective for scenes with a large number of splats and pixels. When Not to Use: Avoid this method if memory is extremely constrained, as the checkpoint storage increases memory usage. The method was introduced in "Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources" and further discussed in "SparseOIT: Improving Order-Independent Transparency 3DGS via Active Set Method". It addresses the performance bottleneck of the original 3DGS backward pass, which suffers from atomic contention and redundant computations due to its pixel-parallel design. The method builds on the principles of differentiable rasterization defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer and improves upon the pixel-parallel approach by introducing a splat-parallel strategy. body: This method applies low-level CUDA kernel optimizations to the 3D Gaussian Splatting backward pass to reduce memory access overhead and improve cache utilization. It specifically targets the reduction of redundant global memory transactions and improves warp-level parallelism without altering rendering results or optimization behavior. It differs from structural optimizations like Loss-Accumulation Guided (LAG) densification or pruning by reducing training time independently of the number of Gaussians, providing consistent speedups across all configurations. The optimization redesigns the thread organization and memory layout of the backward pass kernel to enable data reuse and vectorized access. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Forward pass intermediates (screen-space positions, covariances, depths) and loss gradients. Outputs: Updated parameter gradients for the optimizer. Data Structures and Layout: Thread Block Organization: Each block uses 8 warps (256 threads). Each thread corresponds to a single pixel (1:1 thread-to-pixel mapping). This contrasts with the original 3DGS implementation where each block contains 32 threads and each thread loads data from multiple pixels. Memory Hierarchy: Tile-level data required for the backward pass are stored in shared memory for reuse across warps within the block. Vectorized Access: Memory layouts are adjusted to support vectorized memory access (e.g., float4 loads/stores) to reduce the number of global memory transactions. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Tile Loading: The kernel loads the necessary forward pass intermediates for the current tile into shared memory. 2. Thread Mapping: Assign each of the 256 threads in the block to a unique pixel within the tile. 3. Gradient Computation: Each thread computes the local gradient contribution for its assigned pixel using the shared data. 4. Vectorized Stores: Use vectorized store instructions to write gradient updates to global memory, improving memory bandwidth utilization and reducing redundant transactions. Parameters: Block Size: 256 threads (8 warps). Warp Size: 32 threads (standard NVIDIA GPU warp size). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Ensure that threads corresponding to pixels outside the valid tile bounds perform no work or handle boundary checks efficiently to avoid divergence. Shared Memory Limits: The tile size must be chosen such that the required forward pass data fits within the shared memory limit of the GPU architecture. This variant, introduced in FaCT-GS, reformulates the backward pass in a per-Gaussian manner to eliminate write conflicts and warp stalls caused by per-pixel backward pass calculations. It constrains the range of Gaussian splats using axis-aligned, rectangular bounding boxes with factored-in density to replace square bounding boxes, reducing overestimation for anisotropic/transparent Gaussians. It also coalesces function parameters into compact float4 structs, combining conics (projected covariances) with \mu in the rasterizer to reduce memory traffic. This approach achieves a 22x acceleration on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, reducing rasterization time from 210 ms to 9.3 ms for a 2K image. Time Complexity: The optimization reduces the constant factor of the backward pass execution time by minimizing memory access overhead. Memory Complexity: No significant change in memory complexity; however, shared memory usage increases due to tile-level data storage. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360, combining LAG with this CUDA optimization (LAG+cu-opt) achieves a training time of 200.1s versus 215.4s for LAG alone, a ~7% reduction. Strengths: Reduces training time independently of the number of Gaussians; consistent speedups across all configurations; does not affect rendering quality. Limitations: Specific to CUDA implementation. When to Use: When training time is a bottleneck and the hardware supports efficient warp-level parallelism and vectorized memory access. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is not the primary bottleneck or when using hardware with different warp architectures. This method was introduced in "Loss-Guided Density Control and Efficient Backward Optimisation for Compact Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting backward pass. The optimization focuses on low-level GPU kernel details, specifically thread organization and data access patterns, to improve performance without changing the mathematical formulation of the rendering or optimization process. name: DARBF Backpropagation
head: DARBF Gradient Calculation, Differentiable DARBF Rasterizer
body: DARBF Backpropagation is the gradient computation mechanism for Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions (DARBFs) within the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline. It solves the problem of differentiating the rendering loss with respect to Gaussian parameters when the alpha splatting function is not a standard Gaussian but a decaying anisotropic function (e.g., half-cosine). It differs from standard 3DGS backpropagation by explicitly modifying the rasterizer's gradient computation to support the specific derivative terms of non-Gaussian DARBFs, rather than using the fixed Gaussian gradient formulas. Inputs: Gradient of the loss with respect to the pixel color: \frac{\partial L}{\partial Cj} for each pixel j. Forward pass data for splat s contributing to pixel j: Projected mean \boldsymbol{\mu}' (2D vector). Inverse projected covariance matrix (\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1} (2x2 matrix). Weight ws (scalar opacity contribution before compositing). Parameter \xi (scalar frequency/decay control). Accumulated transparency \alpha{prev} = \prod{k < s} (1 - \alphak). Outputs: Gradients with respect to the projected mean difference: \frac{\partial L}{\partial (x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')}. Gradients with respect to the inverse covariance matrix: \frac{\partial L}{\partial (\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1}}. Data Structures: x: The 2D pixel coordinate vector. \boldsymbol{\mu}': The 2D projected mean vector. \Sigma'{2\times 2}: The 2D projected covariance matrix. (\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1}: The inverse of the projected covariance matrix. dM: The Mahalanobis-like distance metric defined as dM = \frac{(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')^T(\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1}(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')}{\xi}. F(dM): The DARBF activation function (e.g., half-cosine). F'(dM): The derivative of the activation function. Steps: 1. Compute Activation Derivative: Calculate the derivative of the DARBF activation function F with respect to the distance metric dM. For the half-cosine example, this is: F'(dM) = -\sin\left(\frac{(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')^T(\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1}(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')}{\xi}\right) 2. Compute Distance Metric Derivatives: Calculate the partial derivatives of the distance metric dM with respect to the inverse covariance matrix and the projected mean difference. With respect to the inverse covariance matrix: \frac{\partial dM}{\partial(\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1}} = \frac{(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')^T}{\xi} With respect to the projected mean difference (x - \boldsymbol{\mu}'): \frac{\partial dM}{\partial(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')} = \frac{2(\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1}(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')}{\xi} 3. Compute Weight Gradients: Apply the chain rule to compute the gradient of the weight w with respect to the geometric parameters. Gradient with respect to the projected mean difference: \frac{dw}{d(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')} = F'(dM) \frac{\partial dM}{\partial(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')} Gradient with respect to the inverse covariance matrix: \frac{dw}{d((\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1})} = F'(dM) \frac{\partial dM}{\partial(\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1}} 4. Accumulate Loss Gradients: Multiply the weight gradients by the gradient flowing from the loss through the alpha compositing equation. If \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphas} is the gradient of the loss with respect to the splat's opacity \alphas (derived from the compositing chain rule in the parent article), then: \frac{\partial L}{\partial (x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphas} \frac{d\alphas}{dw} \frac{dw}{d(x - \boldsymbol{\mu}')} \frac{\partial L}{\partial (\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphas} \frac{d\alphas}{dw} \frac{dw}{d((\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1})} Note that the term \frac{d\alphas}{dw} depends on the specific mapping from weight w to opacity \alphas (e.g., \alphas = w \cdot \alpha{prev}). The sources provide the derivatives of w with respect to the geometric parameters, which must be scaled by the compositing gradient. 5. Map to Parameter Space: Convert the gradients with respect to (x - \boldsymbol{\mu}') and (\Sigma'{2\times 2})^{-1} back to the gradients for the learnable parameters (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \Sigma, etc.) using the Jacobian of the projection and parameterization steps. This step is standard in differentiable rasterizers and relies on the forward projection derivatives. Parameters: \xi: A parameter controlling the frequency/decay of the DARBF. In the half-cosine function example, \xi = 18\pi. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def darbfbackprop(x, muprime, invcov, xi, gradLalphas, dalphasdw): """ Computes gradients for DARBF splatting based on. Args: x: (2,) pixel coordinate vector. muprime: (2,) projected mean vector. invcov: (2, 2) inverse projected covariance matrix. xi: scalar decay parameter. gradLalphas: scalar gradient of loss w.r.t. opacity alphas. dalphasdw: scalar derivative of alphas w.r.t. weight w. Returns: gradmudiff: (2,) gradient w.r.t. (x - muprime). gradinvcov: (2, 2) gradient w.r.t. invcov. """ # Step 1: Compute distance metric dM diff = x - muprime dM = (diff.T @ invcov @ diff) / xi # Step 2: Compute activation derivative F'(dM) for half-cosine Fprime = -np.sin(dM) # Step 3: Compute distance metric derivatives # d(dM) / d(invcov) = (diff @ diff.T) / xi graddMdinvcov = (diff.reshape(-1, 1) @ diff.reshape(1, -1)) / xi # d(dM) / d(diff) = 2 invcov @ diff / xi graddMddiff = 2.0 (invcov @ diff) / xi # Step 4: Compute weight gradients using chain rule dwddiff = Fprime graddMddiff dwdinvcov = Fprime graddMdinvcov # Step 5: Scale by loss gradient and compositing derivative gradmudiff = gradLalphas dalphasdw dwddiff gradinvcov = gradLalphas dalphasdw dwdinvcov return gradmudiff, gradinvcov Not given in the sources. Link Not given in the sources. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Measured on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. DARBF Backpropagation is the process of computing gradients for Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions (DARBFs) during backpropagation, modifying the standard differentiable Gaussian rasterizer to support specific DARBF gradient terms. It is implemented in the DARBF-Splatting codebase, which anchors on the 3DGS codebase updated as of October 2024.
