name: Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Differentiable Rasterization
head: Per-Pixel Formulation, Per-Pixel Stochastic Gradient Estimation, Per-Pixel Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Differentiable Rasterization, SGE, Stochastic Gradient Estimation, Stochastic finite difference, transformed rasterizer
body: This method transforms a non-differentiable rasterizer into a differentiable one by estimating gradients on a per-pixel basis rather than on the whole image, bounding the dimensionality of the optimization problem. It computes stochastic gradients for differentiable rasterization by summing per-pixel gradient estimates instead of a full-image error, reducing noise in high-dimensional parameter spaces. Unlike standard Stochastic Gradient Estimation which estimates gradients on the whole image (scaling poorly with dimensionality), this method estimates gradients on a per-pixel basis, bounding the dimensionality to the number of parameters contributing to a single pixel. Unlike backpropagation which requires a differentiable framework (Pytorch/Tensorflow), this method requires no external dependencies and works with existing non-differentiable rasterizers. Inputs: Scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} (e.g., vertex positions, texture values, Gaussian splat parameters), random sign vector \boldsymbol{s}, perturbation magnitude vector \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, number of averaging samples N. Outputs: Gradient estimates \frac{\partial f}{\partial \thetai} for each parameter \thetai. Data Structures: The rasterization pass R is modified to output specific buffers depending on the geometry type: 1. Opaque Geometry: RGB buffer and an ID buffer containing the index of the rasterized triangle for each pixel. 2. Transparent Geometry: RGB buffer and a deep ID buffer containing multiple triangle IDs per pixel, representing an ordered list of triangles seen by the pixel. 3. Textures: RGB buffer, ID buffer, and a UV buffer containing the UV coordinates used to fetch the texture in each pixel. 4. Volumes: RGB buffer and voxel data for ray-marching. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set the current scene parameters to \boldsymbol{\theta} and initialize gradient accumulators for all parameters to zero. 2. Loop for Averaging: Repeat N times with different random sign vectors \mathbf{s}^{(n)}: 1. Perturb Parameters: Generate a random sign vector \boldsymbol{s} where each component si \in \{-1, +1\} with probability 1/2. 2. Forward Pass (+): Perturb the scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} by adding \boldsymbol{s} \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon} to obtain \boldsymbol{\theta}^+ = \boldsymbol{\theta} + \boldsymbol{s} \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon}. Rasterize the scene using \boldsymbol{\theta}^+ to produce image I^+ and auxiliary buffers (ID/UV). 3. Forward Pass (-): Perturb the scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} by subtracting \boldsymbol{s} \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon} to obtain \boldsymbol{\theta}^- = \boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{s} \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon}. Rasterize the scene using \boldsymbol{\theta}^- to produce image I^- and auxiliary buffers (ID/UV). 4. Compute Per-Pixel Gradients: For each parameter \thetai, identify the set of pixels \mathcal{P}i impacted by \thetai using the auxiliary buffers (e.g., ID buffer for triangles, UV buffer for textures). Estimate the gradient for each parameter \thetai using the formula: \frac{\partial f}{\partial \thetai} = \sum{(w,h) \in \mathcal{P}i} \frac{f{w,h}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^+) - f{w,h}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^-)}{2 si \epsiloni} where f{w,h} is the l2 pixel error for pixel (w,h), \mathbf{s} is the random sign vector, \boldsymbol{\epsilon} is the perturbation magnitude vector, and the sum is over pixels impacted by parameter \thetai. 5. Accumulate: Add the estimated gradient to the accumulator for \thetai. 3. Average: Divide the accumulated gradient by N to obtain the final stochastic gradient estimate for each parameter. 4. Update Parameters: Update parameters using the Adam optimizer in a compute shader launched over d threads, using default \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999 and learning rate equal to perturbation amplitude \epsiloni. Note that the division by constants 2, \epsiloni and N in the denominator of Equation (9) can be omitted as Adam is invariant to constant scaling factors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def stochasticgradientestimation(sceneparams, epsilon, N, targetimage, rasterizer, idbuffer, uvbuffer): d = len(sceneparams) H, W = len(targetimage), len(targetimage[0]) gradaccum = [0.0] d for n in range(N): # Generate random sign vector s s = [1.0 if random.random() > 0.5 else -1.0 for in range(d)] # Perturb parameters thetaplus = [sceneparams[i] + s[i] epsilon[i] for i in range(d)] thetaminus = [sceneparams[i] - s[i] epsilon[i] for i in range(d)] # Rasterize and compute per-pixel l2 errors imgplus = rasterizer(thetaplus) imgminus = rasterizer(thetaminus) errplus = [(imgplus[h][w] - targetimage[h][w]) 2 for h in range(H) for w in range(W)] errminus = [(imgminus[h][w] - targetimage[h][w]) 2 for h in range(H) for w in range(W)] # Accumulate gradients per parameter for i in range(d): sumdiff = 0.0 for h in range(H): for w in range(W): # Check if parameter i impacts pixel (w,h) via ID or UV buffers if idbuffer[h][w] == i or uvbuffer[h][w] == i: sumdiff += errplus[h W + w] - errminus[h W + w] if 2 s[i] epsilon[i] != 0: gradaccum[i] += sumdiff / (2 s[i] epsilon[i]) # Average over N samples return [g / N for g in gradaccum] Parameters: N (averaging samples): Number of stochastic gradient estimates averaged to reduce variance. Typical values in experiments are 8 or 32. Another source mentions a typical value of 128. \epsiloni (perturbation magnitude): The learning rate is set equal to \epsiloni in the Adam optimizer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The estimator is stochastic and exhibits variance. The variance increases with the number of dimensions d. This is traded for performance compared to finite differences. Full-image error formulation causes high noise in high-dimensional spaces, making optimization impractical for large scenes (e.g., 100K triangles). Texture gradient estimation approximates the elliptical footprint by only updating the closest texel to the center, which is sufficient if resolution is high enough to avoid sub-pixel scale texels. For subdivision surfaces, the compute shader associates each tessellated triangle to its original triangle and loops over its neighbors in the control mesh using a subdivision data structure. For 3D Gaussian Splats, an additional resampling and splat subdivision compute shader is executed after each gradient descent step. Limits gradient computation to the N nearest Gaussians per pixel. In experiments, N=10 was used. Restricting gradient depth to a small constant (e.g., 10) severely degrades reconstruction quality, proving that full depth complexity is necessary for high-fidelity rendering. On the Average-30K dataset, Full depth achieves PSNR 26.05, while Limited-BW (N=10) drops to 19.19. Limiting gradients to N=10 causes blurry boundaries and loss of detail (e.g., table edges and tree parts become indistinct), whereas unlimited depth complexity preserves sharp boundaries. Time and Memory Complexity: The method executes faster within a rasterization engine but provides noisy gradients, making gradient descent less efficient compared to backpropagation-based methods like nvDiffRast. The total time per step includes Perturbation (P), Rasterization (R), Gradient computation (G), and Descent (D). Measured Performance: Intel Arc 770: Optimization of a control mesh of 2K triangles (50K triangles after subdivision) with 1024^2 PBR textures took 130 seconds. NVIDIA 4090 (1K Triangles): P=12μs, R=28μs, G=13μs, D=21μs, Sum=6.8ms (with N=128). NVIDIA 4090 (10K Triangles): P=14μs, R=38μs, G=14μs, D=21μs, Sum=8.4ms (with N=128). NVIDIA 4090 (100K Triangles): P=54μs, R=126μs, G=35μs, D=105μs, Sum=27ms (with N=128). Comparison with nvDiffRast (1024x1024, 1748 vertices, 1M+ params): nvDiffRast takes 33ms/step with 8 samples; Ours takes 21ms/step with 8 samples. Comparison with nvDiffRast (1024x1024, 1748 vertices, 791K params): nvDiffRast takes 33ms/step with 8 samples; Ours takes 18ms/step with 32 samples. Mesh with Albedo Map (3072 triangles, 1748 vertices, 1024^2 texture): Our method takes 2s, 3s, 8s, 16s, 29s for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 steps shown; nvDiffRast takes 2s, 3s, 9s, 13s, 21s, 27s, 32s. Mesh with Normal Map (3072 triangles, 1748 vertices, 512^2 texture): Our method takes 2s, 3s, 9s, 13s, 21s, 27s; nvDiffRast takes 2s, 3s, 9s, 13s, 21s, 27s. Subdivision Surface (1K control vertices, 24K triangles after 2 levels, 1024^2 textures): Our method takes 3s and 30s. 3D Gaussian Splats (hierarchical, 1K to 128K splats, 128^2 to 512^2 resolution): Our method takes 3s (2K splats), 53s (128K splats). 3D Volume (128^3 RGBA): Our method takes 5s and 32s. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement, no external dependencies (Pytorch/Tensorflow), works with existing non-differentiable rasterizers, scales to 1M+ parameters. Produces qualitatively similar results to nvDiffRast with the same amount of optimization time. Limitations: Noisy gradients require more iterations for convergence compared to deterministic backpropagation. Scope is limited to raster graphics with direct visibility only; it does not cover shadows or multiple-bounce illumination. When to Use: Targeted at game developers and users with existing non-differentiable rasterization engines who cannot use existing differentiable rasterizers due to workflow or platform constraints. Used to optimize 3D assets including meshes, displacement mapping, Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces, semi-transparent geometry, physically based materials, 3D volumetric data, and 3D Gaussian Splats. Origin: Thomas Deliot, Eric Heitz, and Laurent Belcour from Intel Corporation, France. Published in "Transforming a Non-Differentiable Rasterizer into a Differentiable One with Stochastic Gradient Estimation" (arXiv:2404.09758v2, 17 Apr 2024). The method builds on the principle of Stochastic Gradient Estimation, which consists of randomly perturbing the 3D scene parameters such that their gradient can be stochastically estimated and descended. It addresses the scalability issues of full-image SGE by leveraging the bounded dimensionality of per-pixel contributions. name: Multi-view Mini-batch Rasterization
head: Multi-view mini-batch training for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Multi-view mini-batch rasterization is a training strategy that renders multiple viewpoints simultaneously within a single mini-batch to reduce gradient variance and improve convergence speed. It modifies the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rasterizer pipeline by introducing view-specific frustum culling and a composite sorting ID, allowing the rasterizer to process multiple camera views in parallel while significantly reducing memory consumption compared to naive multi-view rendering. Unlike single-view training, this method increases performance metrics (PSNR/SSIM) but introduces higher memory overhead and preprocessing time. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of P 3D Gaussians; a mini-batch of B viewpoints (camera poses and intrinsics); tile resolution and screen dimensions. Outputs: Rendered images for all B viewpoints; gradients for Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) propagated back from the loss function. Data Structures The core data structure is an array of projected Gaussian attributes. To support multi-view processing, the sorting identifier is modified from the standard 3DGS implementation: Standard 3DGS ID: 64-bit integer composed of a 32-bit tile index and a 32-bit depth value. Multi-view ID: 64-bit integer composed of: 16-bit tile index 16-bit viewpoint index (identifying which of the B viewpoints the Gaussian belongs to) 32-bit depth value Numbered Steps 1. Frustum Culling (Per Viewpoint): For each of the B viewpoints in the mini-batch, determine which of the P total Gaussians are visible within the camera frustum. This step identifies the subset of Gaussians participating in rendering for each specific viewpoint before memory allocation. 2. Memory Allocation: Allocate memory only for the Gaussians identified in Step 1. Let N be the total number of Gaussian instances remaining after culling across all viewpoints. Typically, N \ll B \times P because most Gaussians are not visible from every viewpoint. 3. Projection: Compute the projected 2D Gaussian parameters (mean, covariance) for the participating Gaussians in screen space for their respective viewpoints. Note that a single 3D Gaussian may be projected and appear multiple times in the array if it is visible in multiple viewpoints. 4. Duplication and ID Assignment: Duplicate projected Gaussians for each tile they cover. Assign each duplicated Gaussian a unique 64-bit ID using the multi-view format (16-bit tile, 16-bit viewpoint, 32-bit depth). This ensures that projected Gaussians are separated by both tile and viewpoint during sorting. 5. Sorting: Sort the array of projected Gaussians by their 64-bit ID. This groups Gaussians by tile and viewpoint, ensuring that rendering blocks for different viewpoints do not interfere with each other. 6. Rendering: The rasterizer allocates multiple rendering blocks per tile—one block for each viewpoint. Each block renders its designated pixels using only the projected Gaussians corresponding to its assigned viewpoint index. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiviewrasterize(gaussians3d, viewpoints, tilesize, screenwidth, screenheight): """ gaussians3d: List of P 3D Gaussian objects (pos, cov, opacity, color) viewpoints: List of B camera objects (viewmatrix, projmatrix, intrinsics) tilesize: Integer, size of a tile in pixels (e.g., 16) screenwidth, screenheight: Integer, dimensions of the image """ allprojected = [] # Step 1 & 2: Frustum Culling and Memory Allocation for viewpointidx, cam in enumerate(viewpoints): # Standard 3DGS frustum culling logic visible = [g for g in gaussians3d if isinfrustum(g, cam)] # Step 3: Projection for g in visible: # Standard 3DGS projection to screen space proj = projectgaussian2d(g, cam) # Standard 3DGS tile coverage calculation tiles = gettilescovered(proj, tilesize, screenwidth, screenheight) # Step 4: Duplication and ID Assignment for tileidx in tiles: # Construct 64-bit ID: 16-bit tile | 16-bit viewpoint | 32-bit depth idtile = tileidx & 0xFFFF idview = viewpointidx & 0xFFFF iddepth = int(proj.depth) & 0xFFFFFFFF compositeid = (idtile << 48) | (idview << 32) | iddepth allprojected.append({ 'proj': proj, 'id': compositeid, 'viewidx': viewpointidx, 'tileidx': tileidx }) # Step 5: Sorting allprojected.sort(key=lambda x: x['id']) # Step 6: Rendering images = [[0.0] (screenwidth screenheight 3) for in viewpoints] numtilesx = screenwidth // tilesize numtilesy = screenheight // tilesize for ty in range(numtilesy): for tx in range(numtilesx): tileidx = ty numtilesx + tx # Extract Gaussians for this tile (already sorted by composite ID) tilegaussians = [g for g in allprojected if g['tileidx'] == tileidx] # Step 6: Allocate blocks per viewpoint and render for viewpointidx in range(len(viewpoints)): # Filter Gaussians belonging to this specific viewpoint in this tile viewgaussians = [g for g in tilegaussians if g['viewidx'] == viewpointidx] # Standard 3DGS front-to-back alpha compositing per pixel rendertile(images[viewpointidx], tx tilesize, ty tilesize, tilesize, viewgaussians) return images def isinfrustum(g, cam): # Checks if Gaussian bounding sphere intersects camera frustum planes return True def projectgaussian2d(g, cam): # Projects 3D mean and covariance to 2D screen space using camera matrices return {'mean': [0, 0], 'cov': [[1, 0], [0, 1]], 'depth': 1.0} def gettilescovered(proj, tilesize, width, height): # Computes integer tile coordinates covering the 2D Gaussian ellipse return [0] def rendertile(image, tilex, tiley, tilesize, gaussians): # Accumulates pixel colors via front-to-back alpha compositing pass Parameters Pruning Threshold: In standard 3DGS, the threshold for pruning Gaussians is multiplied by the number of images (B) in the mini-batch to account for changed learning patterns. Mean Noise Learning Rate: In 3DGS-MCMC, this rate is divided by the number of images (B) when applying multi-view training. Number of Viewpoints (B): The number of viewpoints rendered per mini-batch. Increasing B improves performance but increases memory and time overhead. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Overfitting: Multi-view mini-batch training can cause overfitting on specific scenes, notably the bicycle/stump scenes in the MipNeRF-360 dataset and scenes in the DeepBlending dataset. Preprocessing Overhead: While rendering overhead is mitigated, the preprocessing steps (culling, sorting, ID assignment) remain. This prevents the method from achieving constant time complexity with respect to the number of images, unlike NeRF-based methods. Gradient Nullification: If viewpoints are positioned symmetrically (e.g., opposite each other facing the origin), gradients from different viewpoints can cancel each other out for positional updates if not handled correctly. Uses vertex shaders for projection, differing in hardware acceleration approach. Gaussian Splat Rasterization (Vertex Shader) Optimizes memory by masking out empty tiles, differing in how it handles sparsity. Masked-Rasterization Focuses on radiative transfer, differing in the physical model used. Differentiable Radiative Rasterization Combines 3D and 2D representations, differing in Gaussian representation. 3D/2D Hybrid Gaussian Rasterization with Fallback Sigma Handles opacity and spherical harmonics differently, differing in color representation. Opacity Rendering with SH Colors Uses unscented transform for uncertainty, differing in probabilistic modeling. 3D Gaussian Unscented Transform (3DGUT) Uses quadratic form expansion, differing in mathematical formulation. RoofGS Quadratic Form Expansion and Coefficient Folding Focuses on transmittance calculation, differing in alpha compositing details. Transmittance of Gaussian Splatting General pipeline setup, differing in configuration scope. Rendering Pipeline and Configuration General backpropagation, differing in gradient flow specifics. Differentiable Backpropagation Mechanisms Time Complexity: Not constant with respect to the number of images due to preprocessing overhead (culling, sorting). Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to naive multi-view rendering (N \ll B \times P), but still higher than single-view training. Performance: On the MipNeRF-360 dataset, using 8 viewpoints in the mini-batch achieved a PSNR of 30.56, SSIM of 0.901, and LPIPS of 0.138 for 3DGS-MCMC + Ours, compared to 29.94 PSNR for the base 3DGS. Strengths: Reduces gradient variance, improves convergence, and lowers memory usage compared to rendering all views independently. Limitations: Preprocessing overhead remains; potential for overfitting on certain scenes; increased memory/time with more viewpoints. When to Use: When training speed and convergence are prioritized, and hardware memory allows for multi-view processing. When Not to Use: When constant time complexity with respect to image count is required, or when dealing with scenes prone to overfitting (e.g., bicycle/stump in MipNeRF-360). The method was introduced in "Efficient multi-view training for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitations of single-view training by leveraging multiple viewpoints per iteration to stabilize gradients. The approach builds on the 3DGS rasterizer [2813-3d-gaussian-splatting-differentiable-rasterizer.md] and modifies its preprocessing and sorting stages to handle multi-view data efficiently. name: Gaussian Normal Estimation
head: Alpha-composited Gaussian normals, Per-pixel Normal Map Estimation from Depth, Per-pixel normal estimation from Gaussians
body: Gaussian Normal Estimation derives per-pixel surface normal maps directly from the geometry of 3D Gaussians during the differentiable rasterization process, providing geometric supervision without requiring additional learnable parameters. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by treating the shortest axis of the Gaussian covariance matrix as the local surface normal, allowing gradients from normal consistency losses to flow back to the Gaussian rotation and scale parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance (scale and rotation), opacity \alpha, and color. For each pixel, the list of contributing Gaussians N sorted by depth (front-to-back). Outputs: A per-pixel estimated normal vector \hat{\boldsymbol{N}} \in \mathbb{R}^3 in camera space. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores a normalized normal vector \hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. This vector represents the direction of the shortest axis of the Gaussian's covariance matrix. In practice, this is derived from the rotation matrix \mathbf{R}i of the Gaussian, typically corresponding to the third column (or the axis associated with the smallest scale eigenvalue). Accumulation State: For each pixel, a running transmittance T (initialized to 1.0) and a running accumulated normal \hat{\boldsymbol{N}} (initialized to \mathbf{0}) are maintained during the rasterization pass. Steps: 1. Normal Extraction: For each Gaussian i, extract the normalized vector \hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i corresponding to the direction of the shortest scaling axis of its covariance matrix. 2. Orientation Correction: At the beginning of training (or per-frame), check the orientation. If the dot product between the current camera viewing direction \boldsymbol{v} and the Gaussian normal \hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i is negative (\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i < 0), flip the direction of the normal (\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i \leftarrow -\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i) to ensure consistent outward-facing orientation. 3. Camera Space Transformation: Transform the extracted normal \hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i from world space to camera space using the current camera rotation matrix \mathbf{R}{cam}. Let the transformed normal be \boldsymbol{n}i. 4. Alpha Compositing: Iterate through the sorted list of Gaussians i \in N contributing to the pixel. For each Gaussian, update the accumulated normal and transmittance: Compute the weight contribution: wi = \alphai Ti, where \alphai is the Gaussian's opacity and Ti is the transmittance accumulated from previous (closer) Gaussians. Update the accumulated normal: \hat{\boldsymbol{N}} \leftarrow \hat{\boldsymbol{N}} + \boldsymbol{n}i wi. Update the transmittance: T{i+1} = Ti (1 - \alphai). 5. Normalization: After iterating through all contributing Gaussians, normalize the resulting vector: \hat{\boldsymbol{N}} \leftarrow \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{N}}}{\|\hat{\boldsymbol{N}}\| + \epsilon}, where \epsilon is a small constant to prevent division by zero. Formulas: The per-pixel normal estimate \hat{\boldsymbol{N}} is computed by alpha-compositing individual Gaussian normals \hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i: \hat{\boldsymbol{N}} = \sum{i \in N} \boldsymbol{n}i \alphai Ti Where: N is the set of Gaussians sorted by depth contributing to the pixel. \boldsymbol{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the normalized vector representing the direction of the shortest axis of the i-th Gaussian, transformed into camera space. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance from previous Gaussians. Parameters: Orientation Flip Threshold: The dot product threshold is 0. If \boldsymbol{v} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{n}}i < 0, flip. Normalization Epsilon: Not given in the sources. A value of 10^{-6} is typical. Pitfalls: Incorrect Normal Orientation: If normals are not consistently oriented relative to the camera, the alpha-composited result will be noisy or incorrect. This is handled by flipping normals based on the dot product with the viewing direction. Degenerate Gaussians: If a Gaussian becomes extremely flat or its scale collapses, the "shortest axis" direction may become unstable. The method assumes Gaussians gradually become flatter and approach a planar shape, making the shortest axis a good normal estimate. Depth Sorting: The accuracy of the normal estimation depends on the correct front-to-back sorting of Gaussians, as in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegaussiannormals(gaussians, cameratransform, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Computes per-pixel normal maps from 3D Gaussians. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: pos: (3,) world position cov: (3,3) covariance matrix or (scale, rotation) alpha: scalar opacity color: (3,) color cameratransform: (4,4) or (3,3) rotation matrix to transform world to camera space. imagewidth, imageheight: int Returns: normals: (H, W, 3) array of estimated normals in camera space. """ # Initialize output normals = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) # Precompute camera rotation matrix for normal transformation Rcam = cameratransform[:3,:3] # For each pixel, we need the list of contributing Gaussians sorted by depth # This is typically handled by the rasterizer's depth sorting step. # Here we assume a function getcontributinggaussians returns sorted list. for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): contributinggaussians = getcontributinggaussians(x, y, gaussians, cameratransform) if not contributinggaussians: continue accumulatednormal = np.zeros(3) transmittance = 1.0 for g in contributinggaussians: # Step 1: Extract normal from Gaussian geometry # The normal is the direction of the shortest axis of the covariance matrix. # If cov is stored as scale and rotation: # scale = g.scale (3,) # rotation = g.rotation (4,) quaternion or (3,3) matrix # The shortest axis corresponds to the minimum scale. # Let's assume we have a function to get the normal vector in world space. nworld = getshortestaxisnormal(g) # Step 2: Orientation Correction # Get camera viewing direction for this pixel (approximate) # In practice, this might be done per-Gaussian or per-pixel. # S1 says "dot product between the current camera viewing direction and the Gaussian normal" # We assume viewing direction is roughly the negative Z axis in camera space, # or we transform the normal to camera space first. # Transform normal to camera space ncam = Rcam @ nworld # Check orientation relative to camera view (assuming camera looks down -Z) # Viewing direction in camera space is (0, 0, -1) # If dot(ncam, (0,0,-1)) < 0, it points away from camera? # S1 says: "flip... if dot product between current camera viewing direction and Gaussian normal is negative" # Let's assume viewing direction v is (0,0,1) in camera space (looking into scene) # or (0,0,-1) depending on convention. Standard OpenGL: camera looks down -Z. # If normal points towards camera, dot(ncam, (0,0,1)) > 0. # Let's follow S1 literally: if dot(v, n) < 0, flip. vcam = np.array([0, 0, 1]) # Assuming camera looks along +Z in some conventions, or adjust. # Actually, standard is camera at origin looking down -Z. # Let's use the dot product with the camera's forward vector. # If the source doesn't specify the exact vector, we assume a consistent convention. # We'll assume vcam is the direction the camera is looking. # If ncam points opposite to vcam, dot < 0. # To be safe and generic, we check if the normal is facing the camera. # If the dot product with the view vector is negative, it's facing away. # We flip it to face the camera. if np.dot(vcam, ncam) < 0: ncam = -ncam # Step 3: Alpha Compositing alpha = g.alpha weight = alpha transmittance accumulatednormal += ncam weight transmittance = (1 - alpha) # Normalize normval = np.linalg.norm(accumulatednormal) if normval > 1e-6: normals[y, x] = accumulatednormal / normval else: normals[y, x] = np.array([0, 0, 1]) # Default normal return normals def getshortestaxisnormal(gaussian): """ Extracts the normalized vector of the shortest axis of the Gaussian's covariance. """ # If covariance is given as scale (s) and rotation (R): # Cov = R diag(s^2) R^T # The axes are the columns of R. # The shortest axis corresponds to the minimum scale. s = gaussian.scale R = gaussian.rotation # (3,3) matrix minidx = np.argmin(s) # The column of R corresponding to the minimum scale nworld = R[:, minidx] return nworld / np.linalg.norm(nworld) Uses the estimated normals \hat{\boldsymbol{N}} to supervise against pseudo-ground truth normals \tilde{\boldsymbol{N}} derived from depth gradients, enforcing local planarity. Uses off-the-shelf monocular depth/normal estimation networks (e.g., ZoeDepth) to provide dense per-pixel normal priors for scenes without ground truth normals. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of contributing Gaussians. This is added to the standard rasterization cost. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W \times 3) for the output normal map. No additional learnable parameters are needed. Strengths: Provides geometric supervision without extra parameters; gradients flow directly to Gaussian rotation and scale, improving geometry alignment. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that Gaussians become planar; noise in depth maps can affect pseudo-normal quality. Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization, where geometric consistency is crucial. DN-Splatter introduced the method to regularize depth and normal estimates. Gaussian Splatting in Mirrors adapted it for reflection-aware rendering, leveraging the planar nature of Gaussians to estimate normals for mirror plane supervision. DN-Splatter: Depth and Normal Priors for Gaussian Splatting and Meshing, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00241, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian Splatting in Mirrors: Reflection-Aware Rendering via Virtual Camera Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.01614, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Rasterization Variant
body: This family defines the specific algorithmic variations of the differentiable rasterization pipeline used to render 3D Gaussians, extending the standard alpha-compositing logic of 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer. It addresses specialized requirements such as dynamic pruning gradients, X-ray physics, hybrid sigma fallbacks, and importance scoring, which the base rasterizer does not natively support. All variants in this family operate on the same fundamental data structures: a set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, and color/features. They share the initial projection step, transforming 3D parameters to 2D screen space using extrinsic/intrinsic matrices and Jacobian transformations to compute 2D covariances. They all utilize a tile-based sorting and accumulation strategy to ensure depth ordering and correct alpha blending. The core divergence lies in how the alpha value \alphai is computed, how the blending loop modifies the transmittance T and color C, and what auxiliary data (masks, counts, or physics parameters) is propagated. Masked-rasterization allows "masked" (probabilistically unused) 3D Gaussians to participate in the rasterization pipeline and receive gradient updates, rather than being strictly culled. It solves the problem of gradient starvation in dynamic pruning scenarios, where Gaussians with zero opacity or scale are filtered out before rasterization and thus cannot update their existence probability. Unlike standard rasterization variants that treat Gaussians as binary present/absent entities based on static attributes, this method applies masks during the blending process to enable dynamic assessment of a Gaussian's contribution. Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR) is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method designed to render novel X-ray projections from radiative 3D Gaussian point clouds. It solves the problem of differentiable volume rendering for X-ray imaging, where the "volume" is represented by a set of Gaussians with associated radiation intensities rather than standard RGB colors. DRR distinguishes itself from sibling methods like 3D/2D Hybrid Gaussian Rasterization with Fallback Sigma by specifically modeling the physics of X-ray attenuation and source-detector geometry, using a specific Jacobian for the X-ray projection and a radiative intensity accumulation model. This method renders 3D Gaussians by combining a screen-space 2D Gaussian approximation with a ray-surfel 3D sigma calculation to determine the tighter bounding sigma for alpha attenuation. It computes a fallback 2D sigma based on pre-computed screen-space means and selects the minimum of the 3D and 2D sigmas to define the effective spread for each Gaussian during accumulation. This variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting extends the standard differentiable rasterizer to output the number of times each Gaussian is activated (rendered) during the forward pass, alongside the standard color and radii tensors. It is primarily used in LightGaussian to compute importance scores for Gaussian pruning and compression. It differs from the standard rasterizer by invoking a specialized C++/CUDA kernel (countgaussians) that tracks per-Gaussian activation counts, whereas siblings like Masked-Rasterization focus on visibility masking or Differentiable Radiative Rasterization focuses on radiative transfer physics. Definition: A rasterization branch (useanalytictau) that computes the per-pixel accumulated analytic line-integral optical thickness \tau along the view ray. Alpha is derived physically as \text{alpha} = 1 - \text{exp}(-\tau) using Beer-Lambert extinction, rather than using heuristic alpha values. The base differentiable rasterizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The variants described here emerge from subsequent research into optimizing training dynamics (Masked-Rasterization, F-Count), extending the representation to non-visible spectra (DRR), and improving numerical stability or approximation accuracy (Hybrid Sigma, Analytic Tau). The codebase structure, particularly the CUDA extensions in diff-gaussian-rasterization, supports these variants through conditional compilation or runtime flags, as seen in the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud repository which integrates analytic-tau and other channels. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Rasterization (Vertex Shader)
head: GSplat Vert, Splat Vertex Shader
body: This method implements the vertex shader stage of a GPU-based rasterizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting, transforming 3D Gaussian primitives into 2D screen-space ellipses for instanced rendering. It differs from fragment-based or compute-shader approaches by performing all geometric projection, covariance transformation, and ellipse basis computation within the vertex shader, passing only the final vertex positions and attributes to the rasterizer. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by handling the specific data unpacking and frustum culling required for efficient vertex-driven splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: utexture: A usampler2D containing packed Gaussian data (position and covariance). projection: A 4 \times 4 projection matrix. view: A 4 \times 4 view matrix. focal: A vec2 containing the focal lengths (fx, fy). viewport: A vec2 containing the viewport dimensions (w, h). position: A vec2 instance attribute representing the local basis of the quad (typically [-2, -2] to [2, 2]). index: A uint instance attribute identifying the Gaussian splat. Outputs: glPosition: The clip-space position of the four vertices of the ellipse quad. Data Structures and Layout: The input texture utexture stores Gaussian data in a 2D grid layout optimized for batched access. Each Gaussian splat i occupies two texels (columns) in the texture. The texture width is fixed at 2048 pixels (1024 Gaussians per row). The row index is calculated as row = i >> 10 (integer division by 1024). The column index for the center data is col = (i & 0x3ff) << 1. The column index for the covariance data is col = ((i & 0x3ff) << 1) | 1. Each texel is a uvec4 (four 32-bit unsigned integers). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Fetch Center Data: Retrieve the packed center position from the texture using the instance index: glsl uvec4 cen = texelFetch(utexture, ivec2((uint(index) & 0x3ffu) << 1, uint(index) >> 10), 0); 2. Transform to Camera Space: Convert the packed integer center to a float vector and transform it into camera space: glsl vec4 cam = view vec4(uintBitsToFloat(cen.xyz), 1.0); 3. Project to Clip Space: Compute the clip-space position: glsl vec4 pos2d = projection cam; 4. Frustum Culling: Perform early-out culling with a 1.2x margin to ensure splats near the edge are not clipped incorrectly by the rasterizer. If the splat is outside the frustum, discard it by setting glPosition to a post-depth value: glsl float clip = 1.2 pos2d.w; if (pos2d.z < -pos2d.w || pos2d.z > pos2d.w || pos2d.x < -clip || pos2d.x > clip || pos2d.y < -clip || pos2d.y > clip) { glPosition = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0); return; } 5. Fetch Covariance Data: Retrieve the packed covariance and color data: glsl uvec4 cov = texelFetch(utexture, ivec2(((uint(index) & 0x3ffu) << 1) | 1u, uint(index) >> 10), 0); 6. Unpack Covariance Components: Unpack the half-precision floating-point components from cov.x, cov.y, and cov.z into vec2 pairs u1, u2, and u3 using unpackHalf2x16. 7. Reconstruct 3D Covariance Matrix: Reconstruct the symmetric 3 \times 3 covariance matrix V{rk} in 3D space from the unpacked components: glsl mat3 Vrk = mat3( u1.x, u1.y, u2.x, u1.y, u2.y, u3.x, u2.x, u3.x, u3.y); 8. Compute Projection Jacobian: Calculate the Jacobian J of the perspective projection transformation: glsl mat3 J = mat3( focal.x / cam.z, 0.0, -(focal.x cam.x) / (cam.z cam.z), 0.0, focal.y / cam.z, -(focal.y cam.y) / (cam.z cam.z), 0.0, 0.0, 0.0); 9. Transform Covariance to Camera Space: Compute the transformation matrix T and the resulting 2D covariance matrix cov{2d}: glsl mat3 T = transpose(mat3(view)) J; mat3 cov2d = transpose(T) Vrk T; 10. Apply Low-Pass Filter: Add a small constant to the diagonal elements to prevent numerical instability and ensure positive definiteness: glsl cov2d[0][0] += 0.1; cov2d[1][1] += 0.1; 11. Compute Eigenvalues: Calculate the eigenvalues \lambda1 and \lambda2 of the upper-left 2 \times 2 submatrix of cov{2d}: glsl float mid = (cov2d[0][0] + cov2d[1][1]) / 2.0; float radius = length(vec2((cov2d[0][0] - cov2d[1][1]) / 2.0, cov2d[0][1])); float lambda1 = mid + radius; float lambda2 = mid - radius; 12. Check Validity: If \lambda2 < 0.0, the covariance is invalid (negative variance). Discard the splat: glsl if (lambda2 < 0.0) { glPosition = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0); return; } 13. Compute Axis Vectors: Determine the major and minor axis directions and magnitudes. The scale factor is 2.5, and the maximum axis length is capped at 1024.0: glsl vec2 diagonalVector = normalize(vec2(cov2d[0][1], lambda1 - cov2d[0][0])); vec2 majorAxis = 2.5 vec2(min(sqrt(2.0 lambda1), 1024.0)) diagonalVector; vec2 minorAxis = 2.5 vec2(min(sqrt(2.0 lambda2), 1024.0)) vec2(diagonalVector.y, -diagonalVector.x); 14. Unpack Color: Extract the RGBA color from the w component of the covariance texel: glsl vec4 color = vec4( float((cov.w) & 0xffu), float((cov.w >> 8) & 0xffu), float((cov.w >> 16) & 0xffu), float((cov.w >> 24) & 0xffu)) / 255.0; 15. Compute Final Vertex Positions: Transform the local quad positions into screen space using the computed axes and viewport dimensions: glsl vec2 vCenter = vec2(pos2d) / pos2d.w; glPosition = vec4( vCenter + (position.x majorAxis + position.y minorAxis) / viewport, pos2d.z / pos2d.w, 1.0); Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def uintbitstofloat(u): import struct return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', u))[0] def unpackhalf2x16(u): lo = u & 0xFFFF hi = (u >> 16) & 0xFFFF def halftofloat(h): sign = (h >> 15) & 0x1 exp = (h >> 10) & 0x1F frac = h & 0x3FF if exp == 0: return (-1)sign (frac / 1024.0) 2-14 elif exp == 31: return (-1)sign float('inf') if frac else (-1)sign float('inf') else: return (-1)sign (1.0 + frac / 1024.0) (2(exp - 15)) return [halftofloat(lo), halftofloat(hi)] def texelfetch(texture, col, row): return texture[row][col] def splatvertexshader(index, position, view, projection, focal, viewport, utexture): # 1. Fetch Center row = index >> 10 colcenter = (index & 0x3ff) << 1 cen = texelfetch(utexture, colcenter, row) # 2. Transform to Camera Space camxyz = [uintbitstofloat(cen[0]), uintbitstofloat(cen[1]), uintbitstofloat(cen[2])] cam = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): cam[i] += view[i][j] (camxyz[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) # 3. Project to Clip Space pos2d = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): pos2d[i] += projection[i][j] cam[j] # 4. Frustum Culling clipmargin = 1.2 pos2d[3] if (pos2d[2] < -pos2d[3] or pos2d[2] > pos2d[3] or pos2d[0] < -clipmargin or pos2d[0] > clipmargin or pos2d[1] < -clipmargin or pos2d[1] > clipmargin): return [0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0] # 5. Fetch Covariance colcov = ((index & 0x3ff) << 1) | 1 cov = texelfetch(utexture, colcov, row) # 6. Unpack Covariance u1 = unpackhalf2x16(cov[0]) u2 = unpackhalf2x16(cov[1]) u3 = unpackhalf2x16(cov[2]) # 7. Reconstruct 3D Covariance Vrk = [[u1[0], u1[1], u2[0]], [u1[1], u2[1], u3[0]], [u2[0], u3[0], u3[1]]] # 8. Compute Jacobian J = [[focal[0] / cam[2], 0.0, -(focal[0] cam[0]) / (cam[2] cam[2])], [0.0, focal[1] / cam[2], -(focal[1] cam[1]) / (cam[2] cam[2])], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]] # 9. Transform Covariance view3x3 = [[view[0][0], view[0][1], view[0][2]], [view[1][0], view[1][1], view[1][2]], [view[2][0], view[2][1], view[2][2]]] T = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): for k in range(3): T[i][j] += view3x3[k][i] J[k][j] cov2d = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): for k in range(3): for m in range(3): cov2d[i][j] += T[k][i] Vrk[k][m] T[m][j] # 10. Low-Pass Filter cov2d[0][0] += 0.1 cov2d[1][1] += 0.1 # 11. Eigenvalues mid = (cov2d[0][0] + cov2d[1][1]) / 2.0 radius = math.sqrt(((cov2d[0][0] - cov2d[1][1]) / 2.0)2 + cov2d[0][1]2) lambda1 = mid + radius lambda2 = mid - radius # 12. Validity Check if lambda2 < 0.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1.0] # 13. Axis Vectors diaglen = math.sqrt(cov2d[0][1]2 + (lambda1 - cov2d[0][0])2) diagonalvector = [cov2d[0][1] / diaglen, (lambda1 - cov2d[0][0]) / diaglen] scale = 2.5 majoraxis = [scale min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda1), 1024.0) diagonalvector[0], scale min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda1), 1024.0) diagonalvector[1]] minoraxis = [scale min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda2), 1024.0) diagonalvector[1], scale min(math.sqrt(2.0 lambda2), 1024.0) -diagonalvector[0]] # 14. Unpack Color color = [ float(cov[3] & 0xff) / 255.0, float((cov[3] >> 8) & 0xff) / 255.0, float((cov[3] >> 16) & 0xff) / 255.0, float((cov[3] >> 24) & 0xff) / 255.0 ] # 15. Final Position vcenter = [pos2d[0] / pos2d[3], pos2d[1] / pos2d[3]] finalx = vcenter[0] + (position[0] majoraxis[0] + position[1] minoraxis[0]) / viewport[0] finaly = vcenter[1] + (position[0] majoraxis[1] + position[1] minoraxis[1]) / viewport[1] return [finalx, finaly, pos2d[2] / pos2d[3], 1.0] Time Complexity: O(1) per splat vertex. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the Gaussian data in the texture, where N is the number of splats, requiring 2 \times N texels. Strengths: Early frustum culling reduces the number of splats processed in later stages. The use of half-precision packing reduces memory bandwidth. Limitations: The fixed texture width of 2048 pixels limits the number of splats per row, potentially requiring multiple rows for large scenes. The method assumes a specific data layout and may require adaptation for different hardware or API constraints. This method is derived from the gsplat-opengl implementation by liaozhangsheng, which provides an unofficial OpenGL-based rasterizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It adapts the differentiable rasterization principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting to a vertex-shader-driven pipeline, optimizing for performance by moving geometric computations to the vertex stage. liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Masked-Rasterization
body: Masked-Rasterization is a differentiable rendering technique that allows "masked" (probabilistically inactive) 3D Gaussians to participate in the rasterization pipeline and receive gradient updates, rather than being permanently filtered out. It solves the problem of outdated Gaussians in dynamic pruning scenarios, where standard alpha-filtering prevents unsampled Gaussians from adjusting their existence probability. It differs from sibling methods like Differentiable Radiative Rasterization by explicitly integrating binary existence masks into the transmittance and color accumulation steps, enabling dynamic assessment of Gaussian contribution without zeroing out their physical attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, color/features \mathbf{c}i, and a learned binary mask mi \in \{0, 1\} representing its probability of existence. Output: The final pixel color C and gradients for Gaussian attributes and masks. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS parameters. Mask: A scalar value mi per Gaussian. Unlike previous methods that multiply mi into opacity or scale, here mi is applied during the blending loop. Numbered Steps: 1. Projection and Splatting: Transform 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space. Compute the 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i using the Jacobian of the projection. Compute the 2D alpha value \alphai for each splat based on its center, scale, and rotation. 2. Alpha Filtering: Filter out splats where \alphai = 0. All remaining splats, along with their associated masks mi, are passed to the masked-rasterization stage. 3. Tile Sorting: Sort the remaining splats by depth within tiles, following the standard shared principles of the parent Rasterization Variant. 4. Masked Blending Loop: For each pixel, iterate through the sorted splats. Update the transmittance T and accumulated color C using the mask mi: Transmittance Attenuation: The transmittance is attenuated by the mask. If mi=0, the transmittance is not reduced (the Gaussian is "invisible" but present for gradient flow). If mi=1, it behaves normally. Color Accumulation: The color contribution is scaled by the mask. If mi=0, no color is added. 5. Gradient Propagation: Gaussians with mi=0 do not receive gradients for their geometric attributes (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \alpha) because they do not affect the final pixel color or transmittance in the forward pass. However, they do receive gradients for their mask mi (and thus their existence probability) based on the loss, allowing them to "learn" when they should become active (mi \to 1). Formulas: Let Ti be the transmittance before splat i, and Ci be the accumulated color. Let \alphai be the Gaussian's opacity and mi be its mask. The standard blending equations are modified as follows: T{i+1} = Ti \cdot (1 - mi \cdot \alphai) C{i+1} = Ci + mi \cdot \alphai \cdot Ti \cdot \mathbf{c}i Where \mathbf{c}i is the color of the Gaussian. Note that \alphai itself is computed from the Gaussian's physical properties (center, scale, rotation) and is not multiplied by mi in its definition, ensuring the Gaussian retains its physical definition even when masked. Parameters: Mask Sampling: Masks are sampled from a probability distribution derived from the Gaussian's current importance/existence probability. Typical pruning ratios reported are 62.4%–75.3%. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Alpha Filtering: If a Gaussian's opacity or scale is set to zero, \alphai becomes zero. This causes the Gaussian to be filtered out before rasterization, preventing it from receiving any gradient updates, including for its mask. This hinders the ability to recover such Gaussians. Unsampled Gaussians: If a Gaussian is not sampled (masked out), it must still be processed in the rasterization loop to receive gradients for its mask. If it is skipped entirely, it remains unchanged, becomes outdated, and risks inaccurate evaluation when eventually sampled in later iterations. Gradient Disconnection: Applying the mask to the geometric attributes (opacity/scale) instead of the blending loop causes the Gaussian to be filtered out, breaking the gradient path for the mask. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskedrasterization(gaussians, masks, imagewidth, imageheight): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: (2,) mean in screen space cov2d: (2,2) 2D covariance alpha: scalar opacity color: (3,) color masks: List of scalar masks mi in {0, 1} """ # 1. Project and compute alpha (Standard 3DGS step) splats = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): alphai = compute2dalpha(g.mu, g.cov2d, g.alpha) if alphai == 0: continue # Filter out zero alpha splats splats.append({ 'index': i, 'alpha': alphai, 'color': g.color, 'mask': masks[i], 'mu': g.mu }) # 2. Sort splats by depth (Standard tile-based sorting) splats = sortbydepth(splats) # 3. Initialize output buffers finalcolor = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) finaltransmittance = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # 4. Rasterize with Masked Blending for pixel in pixels: T = 1.0 C = zeros(3) for splat in splatsintersectingpixel(pixel): m = splat['mask'] a = splat['alpha'] c = splat['color'] # Apply mask to transmittance and color accumulation # If m=0, T remains unchanged, C adds nothing # If m=1, standard blending occurs contribution = m a T C += contribution c T = (1.0 - contribution) finalcolor[pixel] = C finaltransmittance[pixel] = T return finalcolor, finaltransmittance The primary implementation of this method, which uses probabilistic masks to prune Gaussians dynamically. It sets itself apart by allowing masked Gaussians to receive gradients for their existence probability, preventing them from becoming outdated. Choose this when dynamic pruning and efficient memory usage are priorities. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization, as the mask application is a simple scalar multiplication per splat. The overhead is negligible. Memory Complexity: Requires storing an additional mask value per Gaussian. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets, the method achieves pruning ratios of 62.4%, 67.7%, and 75.3% respectively, with rendering speedups of 2.05×, 2.19×, and 3.16×, while sacrificing only 0.02 PSNR on the first two datasets and improving quality on Deep Blending. Strengths: Enables dynamic pruning without losing gradient information for inactive Gaussians; outperforms methods that multiply masks with opacity/scale. Limitations: Requires careful handling of the mask sampling distribution to ensure stable training. When to use: When training 3DGS with aggressive pruning or dynamic scene evolution where Gaussians need to be reactivated. When not to use: For static scenes where a fixed set of Gaussians is sufficient, as the overhead of mask management is unnecessary. Masked-Rasterization was introduced in the paper "MaskGaussian: Adaptive 3D Gaussian Representation from Probabilistic Masks" by. It addresses limitations in previous pruning methods (such as those by [4, 17, 34] cited in) that multiplied masks with Gaussian attributes, leading to zero alpha values and broken gradient paths. The method is part of the broader effort to optimize 3D Gaussian Splatting for efficiency and dynamic scenes. name: Differentiable Radiative Rasterization
body: Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR) is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method designed to render novel X-ray projections from radiative 3D Gaussian point clouds. It solves the problem of differentiable volume rendering for X-ray imaging by adapting the splatting pipeline to model radiation intensity rather than visible light color. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which renders RGB colors, DRR computes scalar intensity values based on the probability density of Gaussians along the X-ray path, enabling end-to-end training of X-ray scanner parameters and Gaussian attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of Np 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi(\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{f}i) \mid i = 1, \dots, Np\}, where \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the mean, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is the covariance, \alphai \in \mathbb{R} is the opacity, and \mathbf{f}i represents learnable inherent point features. Extrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{ext} \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times4}. Intrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{int} \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times3}. X-ray source parameters: distance L{SD} and azimuth angle \phi. Output: Rendered image \mathbf{I}, where each pixel p holds an intensity value I(p) \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian: Stores \boldsymbol{\mu}i (3 floats), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (6 floats, symmetric), \alphai (1 float), and \mathbf{f}i (variable size, used for intensity fitting). Tile: Non-overlapping rectangular regions of the 2D image plane. Gaussians are assigned to tiles based on their 2D bounding boxes. Sorted List: Within each tile, Gaussians are sorted by their depth (distance to the 2D detector). Formulas: 1. Gaussian Probability Density: The probability value of the i-th Gaussian at a 3D point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is: P(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)\right) \quad (6) 2. Projection to Camera Coordinates: Transform the 3D mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i to camera coordinates \mathbf{t}i = (tx, ty, tz)^\top using homogeneous coordinates: \tilde{\mathbf{t}}i = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}{ext} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i = \mathbf{M}{ext} \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad (7) 3. Projection to Image Coordinates: Project \mathbf{t}i to 2D image coordinates \mathbf{u}i \in \mathbb{R}^2: \tilde{\mathbf{u}}i = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{u}i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}{int} \tilde{\mathbf{t}}i = \mathbf{M}{int} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad (7) 4. Covariance Transformation: Compute the covariance in camera coordinates \Sigma'i \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}: \Sigma'i = \mathbf{J}i \mathbf{W}i \Sigmai \mathbf{W}i^\top \mathbf{J}i^\top \quad (8) Where: \mathbf{W}i is the viewing transformation matrix: \mathbf{W}i = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin \phi & \cos \phi & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -\cos \phi & -\sin \phi & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad (9) \mathbf{J}i is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation: \mathbf{J}i = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{L{SD}}{tz} & 0 & -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} \frac{ty}{tz} \\ 0 & \frac{L{SD}}{tz} & -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} \frac{ty}{tz} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad (9) Note: The source text presents a formatting error in the matrix layout for \mathbf{J}i, listing terms as \frac{L{SD}}{tz}, 0, -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} \frac{ty}{tz^2} in the first row. However, standard projective Jacobians and the symmetry with the second row suggest the term is \frac{ty}{tz} or similar scaling. The source explicitly writes \frac{ty}{tz^2} in the text description but the matrix visual is ambiguous. We retain the source's explicit term \frac{ty}{tz^2} as written in the formula block, but note the potential typo. Correction based on standard derivations and source context: The source text says -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} \frac{ty}{tz^2}. This is likely a typo for -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} ty or similar. However, adhering strictly to the provided source text for the formula: \mathbf{J}i = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{L{SD}}{tz} & 0 & -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} \frac{ty}{tz^2} \\ 0 & \frac{L{SD}}{tz} & -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} \frac{ty}{tz^2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} 5. 2D Covariance: Obtain \Sigma''i \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2} by removing the third row and column from \Sigma'i. 6. Radiation Intensity Contribution: For a pixel p, let \mathcal{N} be the set of ordered 3D points (intersections of X-rays with Gaussians) overlapping the pixel. The intensity I(p) is: I(p) = \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbf{i}j \quad (10) Where \mathbf{i}j is the radiation intensity of the j-th intersection point \mathbf{x}j. The contribution is weighted by the probability term: \sigmaj = \alphaj P(\mathbf{x}j | \boldsymbol{\mu}j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j) \quad (10) Note: The source implies \mathbf{i}j is derived from \sigmaj and potentially the learnable features \mathbf{f}j via an inner product with basis weights, though the exact combination function for \mathbf{i}j from \sigmaj and \mathbf{f}j is not explicitly formulaized in the provided text snippets, only that DRR adopts the inner product to fit radiation intensity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian point clouds using the Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) strategy within a cuboid enclosing the object. 2. Projection: For each Gaussian i: a. Compute camera coordinates \mathbf{t}i using \mathbf{M}{ext}. b. Compute image coordinates \mathbf{u}i using \mathbf{M}{int}. c. Compute \mathbf{W}i using azimuth angle \phi. d. Compute \mathbf{J}i using L{SD}, ty, tz. e. Compute \Sigma'i = \mathbf{J}i \mathbf{W}i \Sigmai \mathbf{W}i^\top \mathbf{J}i^\top. f. Extract \Sigma''i by dropping the 3rd row/col of \Sigma'i. 3. Tiling: Partition the image into non-overlapping tiles. 4. Assignment: Assign each Gaussian to tiles whose bounding box overlaps with the Gaussian's 2D projection (\mathbf{u}i, \Sigma''i). 5. Sorting: Sort Gaussians within each tile by their distance to the detector (depth tz). 6. Rasterization: For each pixel p in each tile: a. Identify the ordered set \mathcal{N} of Gaussians overlapping p. b. For each j \in \mathcal{N}, compute \sigmaj = \alphaj P(\mathbf{x}j | \boldsymbol{\mu}j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j). c. Compute radiation intensity \mathbf{i}j based on \sigmaj and learnable features \mathbf{f}j. d. Sum contributions: I(p) = \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbf{i}j. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computejacobian(tz, ty, LSD): """ Computes the Jacobian matrix Ji for the projective transformation. Based on source formula (9). Note: Source contains formatting ambiguity; this implementation follows the explicit text terms. """ # Term A: LSD / tz terma = LSD / tz # Term B: - (LSD / tz^2) (ty / tz^2) # Source text: -\frac{L{SD}}{tz^2} \frac{ty}{tz^2} termb = -(LSD / (tz 2)) (ty / (tz 2)) J = np.array([ [terma, 0.0, termb], [0.0, terma, termb], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] ]) return J def computeviewingmatrix(phi): """ Computes the viewing transformation matrix Wi. Based on source formula (9). """ sinphi = math.sin(phi) cosphi = math.cos(phi) W = np.array([ [-sinphi, cosphi, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0, -1.0], [-cosphi, -sinphi, 0.0] ]) return W def gaussianprobability(x, mu, Sigmainv): """ Computes P(x | mu, Sigma). Based on source formula (6). """ diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diff.T, np.dot(Sigmainv, diff)) return math.exp(exponent) def renderdrr(gaussians, Mext, Mint, LSD, phi, imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize): """ Differentiable Radiative Rasterization. Inputs: gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'mu' (3,), 'Sigma' (3,3), 'alpha' (float), 'f' (features) Mext: (4,4) extrinsic matrix Mint: (4,3) intrinsic matrix LSD: float, source-detector distance phi: float, azimuth angle imagewidth, imageheight: int tilesize: int, size of rasterization tiles Output: image: (H, W) float array """ # Initialize output image image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # 1. Project Gaussians projectedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): mu = g['mu'] Sigma = g['Sigma'] alpha = g['alpha'] f = g['f'] # Homogeneous coordinates muh = np.append(mu, 1.0) # Camera coordinates th = np.dot(Mext, muh) t = th[:3] # tx, ty, tz # Image coordinates uh = np.dot(Mint, th) u = uh[:2] # ux, uy # Covariance transformation W = computeviewingmatrix(phi) J = computejacobian(t[2], t[1], LSD) Sigmaprime = J @ W @ Sigma @ W.T @ J.T # 2D Covariance (skip 3rd row/col) Sigma2d = Sigmaprime[:2,:2] projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu3d': mu, 'mu2d': u, 'Sigma2d': Sigma2d, 'alpha': alpha, 'f': f, 'tz': t[2], 'ty': t[1] }) # 2. Tiling and Sorting # Create tiles numtilesx = (imagewidth + tilesize - 1) // tilesize numtilesy = (imageheight + tilesize - 1) // tilesize # Assign Gaussians to tiles # Simple bounding box check: Gaussian covers tile if its 2D bounding box overlaps # Bounding box can be approximated by mu2d +/- 3sqrt(diag(Sigma2d)) tiles = {} for g in projectedgaussians: mu2d = g['mu2d'] Sigma2d = g['Sigma2d'] # Approximate bounding box radius (e.g., 3 sigma) stdx = 3.0 math.sqrt(Sigma2d[0, 0]) stdy = 3.0 math.sqrt(Sigma2d[1, 1]) minx = mu2d[0] - stdx maxx = mu2d[0] + stdx miny = mu2d[1] - stdy maxy = mu2d[1] + stdy # Determine tile indices tilexstart = int(minx // tilesize) tilexend = int(maxx // tilesize) tileystart = int(miny // tilesize) tileyend = int(maxy // tilesize) for tx in range(tilexstart, tilexend + 1): for ty in range(tileystart, tileyend + 1): if 0 <= tx < numtilesx and 0 <= ty < numtilesy: tilekey = (ty, tx) if tilekey not in tiles: tiles[tilekey] = [] tiles[tilekey].append(g) # Sort Gaussians in each tile by depth (tz) for tilekey in tiles: tiles[tilekey].sort(key=lambda g: g['tz']) # 3. Rasterization for ty in range(numtilesy): for tx in range(numtilesx): tilekey = (ty, tx) if tilekey not in tiles: continue tilegaussians = tiles[tilekey] # Pixel coordinates within the tile for dy in range(tilesize): for dx in range(tilesize): px = tx tilesize + dx py = ty tilesize + dy if px >= imagewidth or py >= imageheight: continue # Check which Gaussians overlap this pixel # This is a simplified check; full implementation requires precise ellipse intersection # For the purpose of this article, we assume the source's "overlapping" implies # a check against the 2D Gaussian PDF or bounding box. # We will iterate all Gaussians in the tile and check if pixel is within bounds. intensitysum = 0.0 for g in tilegaussians: # Check if pixel (px, py) is within the Gaussian's 2D extent # Using a simple bounding box check for implementation completeness mu2d = g['mu2d'] Sigma2d = g['Sigma2d'] stdx = 3.0 math.sqrt(Sigma2d[0, 0]) stdy = 3.0 math.sqrt(Sigma2d[1, 1]) if abs(px - mu2d[0]) <= stdx and abs(py - mu2d[1]) <= stdy: # Compute probability at pixel location (assuming pixel center is the intersection point xj) # Note: In X-ray, xj is the intersection of the ray with the Gaussian. # For rasterization, we approximate xj as the 3D point corresponding to pixel (px, py) # at the depth of the Gaussian? Or simply use the 2D projection probability? # Source says: "ij is the radiation intensity of xj... sigmaj = alphaj P(xj | muj, Sigmaj)" # And "xj is the j-th intersection 3D point". # In standard splatting, we evaluate the 2D Gaussian at the pixel. # Let's assume xj in the formula refers to the 3D point on the ray. # However, DRR renders "projections". The intensity is accumulated. # We approximate P(xj) using the 2D projection probability at the pixel. # Compute 2D Mahalanobis distance diff = np.array([px - mu2d[0], py - mu2d[1]]) try: Sigma2dinv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2d) exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diff.T, np.dot(Sigma2dinv, diff)) prob = math.exp(exponent) except: prob = 0.0 sigmaj = g['alpha'] prob # Compute radiation intensity ij # Source says: "adopts the inner product between a learnable vector... and a set of basis weights" # This part is not fully detailed in the provided text snippets. # We assume ij is proportional to sigmaj or derived from it. # For a complete implementation, the feature fj would be used here. # Since the exact function is not given, we use sigmaj as the base intensity component. ij = sigmaj intensitysum += ij image[py, px] = intensitysum return image Parameters: L{SD}: Distance between X-ray source and detector. \phi: Azimuth angle of the X-ray source. Tile size: Not given in the sources. Number of Gaussians Np: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Jacobian Singularity: If tz = 0, the Jacobian \mathbf{J}i involves division by zero. This occurs when a Gaussian center is on the camera plane. Guard against this by clamping tz to a small epsilon or culling Gaussians with tz \le 0. Covariance Definiteness: \Sigmai must be positive definite. Numerical errors during transformation \Sigma'i = \mathbf{J}i \mathbf{W}i \Sigmai \mathbf{W}i^\top \mathbf{J}i^\top may lead to non-positive definite \Sigma''i. Ensure \Sigma''i is positive definite before inversion or use Cholesky decomposition with fallback. Source Text Ambiguity: The formula for \mathbf{J}i in the source contains a potential typo in the term \frac{ty}{tz^2}. Implementers should verify this against the original paper's derivation or standard projective geometry. Uses masks to handle occlusion or specific regions. Link Combines 3D and 2D Gaussian representations for robustness. Link Uses feature counts to optimize rendering. Link Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians Np and pixels, due to the tile-based sorting and accumulation. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to Np for storing Gaussian attributes and tile lists. Performance: Faster than original 3DGS due to the avoidance of complex Spherical Harmonic (SH) function computations. Strengths: GPU-friendly CUDA implementation; efficient for X-ray novel view synthesis; avoids SfM initialization via ACUI. Limitations: Specific to X-ray imaging (radiative Gaussians); requires accurate L{SD} and \phi parameters. Differentiable Radiative Rasterization was introduced in the paper "Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Efficient X-Ray Novel View Synthesis". It is part of the X-Gaussian framework, which adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for X-ray imaging. The method was developed to enable efficient training of radiative Gaussian point clouds and X-ray scanner parameters without running SfM algorithms, using the Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) strategy. name: 3D/2D Hybrid Gaussian Rasterization with Fallback Sigma
body:
This method renders 3D Gaussians by combining a screen-space 2D Gaussian approximation with a ray-surfel 3D sigma calculation to determine the tighter bounding sigma for alpha attenuation. It computes a fallback 2D sigma based on pre-computed screen-space means and selects the minimum of the 3D and 2D sigmas to define the effective spread for each Gaussian during accumulation. Inputs: means: 3D positions of N Gaussians, shape [N, 3]. opacities: Opacity values of N Gaussians, shape [N]. colors: Rendered colors per Gaussian, shape [N, 3]. normals: Normals per Gaussian, shape [N, 3]. means2dnp: Pre-computed 2D screen-space means for each camera, shape [C, N, 2]. cameras: Camera parameters for C views. backgrounds: Optional background colors per camera, shape [C, 3]. Outputs: rendercolors: Rendered RGB images, shape [C, H, W, 3]. rendernormals: Rendered normal images, shape [C, H, W, 3]. renderalphas: Accumulated alpha images, shape [C, H, W, 1]. Parameters: MAXALPHA: Maximum alpha value per Gaussian. ALPHATHRESHOLD: Minimum alpha to process. TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: Minimum transmittance to continue loop. EPSILON: Depth threshold for skipping, 10^{-10}. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize rendercolors, rendernormals, and renderalphas to zero. Initialize transmittance T = 1.0 for each pixel. 2. Pixel Loop: Iterate over each pixel (py, px) and camera c. 3. Gaussian Loop: Iterate over each Gaussian gi (index gid). a. Coordinate Transformation: Calculate temporary coordinates tmp[0], tmp[1], tmp[2] by projecting the 3D mean of the Gaussian into the camera space. b. Depth Check: If |tmp[2]| < 10^{-10}, skip this Gaussian. c. Screen-Space Coordinates: Calculate screen-space coordinates: us =  rac{tmp[0]}{tmp[2]} vs =  rac{tmp[1]}{tmp[2]} d. 3D Sigma Calculation: Calculate the 3D sigma based on the ray-surfel intersection distance: \sigma{3d} = us^2 + vs^2 e. 2D Fallback Sigma Calculation: Retrieve the pre-computed 2D mean \mu = 	ext{means2d
p}[c, gid]. Calculate differences: dx = px - \mu[0] dy = py - \mu[1] Calculate the 2D fallback sigma: \sigma{2d} = 2.0 	imes (dx^2 + dy^2) f. Hybrid Sigma Selection: Select the tighter bound: \sigma = 0.5 	imes \min(\sigma{3d}, \sigma{2d}) g. Sigma Validation: If \sigma < 0.0, skip the Gaussian. h. Alpha Calculation: Calculate the alpha value: \alpha = \min(	ext{opacities}[gid] 	imes \exp(-\sigma), 	ext{MAX\ALPHA}) i. Alpha Threshold: If \alpha < 	ext{ALPHA\THRESHOLD}, skip the Gaussian. j. Transmittance Check: If current transmittance T < 	ext{TRANSMITTANCE\THRESHOLD}, break the Gaussian loop for this pixel. k. Accumulation: Calculate weight: w = T 	imes \alpha Add to color and normal buffers: 	ext{render\colors}[c, py, px] += w 	imes 	ext{colors}[gid] 	ext{render
ormals}[c, py, px] += w 	imes 	ext{normals}[gid] Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T 	imes (1.0 - \alpha) 4. Alpha Finalization: After the Gaussian loop, set: 	ext{render\alphas}[c, py, px, 0] = 1.0 - T 5. Background Compositing: If backgrounds is not None: a. Convert backgrounds to array bgnp. b. For each camera c, add background contribution: 	ext{render\colors}[c] += (1.0 - 	ext{render\alphas}[c]) 	imes 	ext{bg
p}[c] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hybridgaussianrasterization(means, opacities, colors, normals, means2d, cameras, backgrounds, MAXALPHA=1.0, ALPHATHRESHOLD=1e-4, TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD=1e-4): """ Renders Gaussians using hybrid 3D/2D sigma fallback. Assumes SH degree 0 for simplicity as per source. """ C = len(cameras) N = len(means) H, W = cameras[0].height, cameras[0].width # Initialize output buffers rendercolors = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for in range(C)] rendernormals = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for in range(C)] renderalphas = [[[[0.0]] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for in range(C) for c in range(C): # Initialize transmittance per pixel T = [[1.0 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for py in range(H): for px in range(W): if T[py][px] < TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: break for gid in range(N): # Project 3D mean to camera space tmp = transformpoint(means[gid], cameras[c].viewmat) if abs(tmp[2]) < 1e-10: continue us = tmp[0] / tmp[2] vs = tmp[1] / tmp[2] # 3D Sigma sigma3d = us us + vs vs # 2D Fallback Sigma mu = means2d[c][gid] dx = px - mu[0] dy = py - mu[1] sigma2d = 2.0 (dx dx + dy dy) # Hybrid Sigma sigma = 0.5 min(sigma3d, sigma2d) if sigma < 0.0: continue alpha = min(opacities[gid] math.exp(-sigma), MAXALPHA) if alpha < ALPHATHRESHOLD: continue weight = T[py][px] alpha rendercolors[c][py][px][0] += weight colors[gid][0] rendercolors[c][py][px][1] += weight colors[gid][1] rendercolors[c][py][px][2] += weight colors[gid][2] rendernormals[c][py][px][0] += weight normals[gid][0] rendernormals[c][py][px][1] += weight normals[gid][1] rendernormals[c][py][px][2] += weight normals[gid][2] T[py][px] = (1.0 - alpha) renderalphas[c][py][px][0] = 1.0 - T[py][px] if backgrounds is not None: bg = backgrounds[c] for py in range(H): for px in range(W): alphaval = renderalphas[c][py][px][0] rendercolors[c][py][px][0] += (1.0 - alphaval) bg[0] rendercolors[c][py][px][1] += (1.0 - alphaval) bg[1] rendercolors[c][py][px][2] += (1.0 - alphaval) bg[2] return rendercolors, rendernormals, renderalphas def transformpoint(point, viewmat): """Transform a single 3D point to camera space.""" # Homogeneous coordinates pointhomo = [point[0], point[1], point[2], 1.0] # Matrix-vector multiplication transformed = [ sum(viewmat[i][j] pointhomo[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4) ] return transformed[:3] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by zero in tmp[2] is handled by the 10^{-10} threshold. Boundaries: Screen-space coordinates us, vs can be large for distant Gaussians, leading to large \sigma{3d}. The fallback \sigma{2d} helps mitigate this by using pre-computed means. Degenerate Input: If \sigma < 0.0, the Gaussian is skipped, preventing invalid alpha calculations. Computes gradients for end-to-end training. Augments 3DGS with a neural network for color residuals.
