name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer > Backward Pass
head: Backward Pass of Gaussian Rasterizer, Gaussian Rasterization (Backward), ToF Gaussian Rasterization Backward Pass
body: The backward pass computes the gradients of the loss function with respect to all learnable input parameters of the 3D Gaussian splatting rasterizer, enabling end-to-end differentiable training. It serves as the computational core for optimizing Gaussian attributes (means, covariances, colors, opacities, scales, rotations, and spherical harmonic coefficients) by propagating gradients from the rendered image back to the 3D scene representation. Unlike the forward pass which renders pixels, this method calculates \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} for all \theta \in \{\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha, s, q, \mathbf{S}\}, where L is the reconstruction loss. It builds on 3D/2D Hybrid Gaussian Rasterization with Fallback Sigma by providing the necessary gradient flow for the hybrid rasterization variant. The backward pass is implemented as a Python wrapper around a C++/CUDA kernel (C.rasterizegaussiansbackward). It retrieves cached tensors from the forward pass context, restructures arguments to match the kernel's expected layout, invokes the native routine, and returns a tuple of gradients matching the forward pass input order. Inputs: 1. Gradients from downstream loss: gradoutcolor: Tensor of shape (H, W, C) or (H, W, 3), gradient of loss w.r.t. rendered color. gradoutphasor: Tensor of shape (H, W, C), gradient of loss w.r.t. rendered phasor (if using Time-of-Flight rendering). gradoutdepth: Tensor of shape (H, W), gradient of loss w.r.t. rendered depth. gradoutnormal: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), gradient of loss w.r.t. rendered normal. gradoutacc: Tensor of shape (H, W), gradient of loss w.r.t. accumulated opacity. gradentropy: Tensor of shape (H, W), gradient of loss w.r.t. entropy regularization. graddepthdistortion: Tensor of shape (H, W), gradient of loss w.r.t. depth distortion. gradampdistortion: Tensor of shape (H, W), gradient of loss w.r.t. amplitude distortion. 2. Forward Pass Context (Saved Tensors): means3D: (N, 3), 3D Gaussian means. scales: (N, 3) or (N, 1), Gaussian scales. rotations: (N, 4), Gaussian quaternions. cov3Dsprecomp: (N, 6), Precomputed 3D covariances (symmetric matrix elements). radii: (N,), Integer radii of projected Gaussians (used for culling). colorsprecomp: (N, C) or (N, 3), Precomputed colors (if SH degree is low enough to precompute, otherwise sh is used). phasorsprecomp: (N, C), Precomputed phasors (for ToF). sh: (N, K, C), Spherical Harmonic coefficients. shp: (N, K, C), PHASOR SH coefficients (for ToF). geomBuffer: Buffer containing 2D projection info (viewspace points, visibility filter). binningBuffer: Buffer for tile-based binning. imgBuffer: Buffer for image accumulation. numrendered: Integer, number of Gaussians that contributed to the image. phaseoffset: Scalar, phase offset for ToF. dcoffset: Scalar, DC offset for ToF. 3. Raster Settings: bg: (C), Background color. viewmatrix: (4, 4), View transformation matrix. projmatrix: (4, 4), Projection matrix. tanfovx, tanfovy: Floats, Tangent of horizontal/vertical field of view. campos: (3), Camera position. scalemodifier: Float, Global scale modifier. shdegree: Integer, Degree of SH. useviewdependentphase: Boolean, Flag for view-dependent phase. debug: Boolean, Debug mode flag. nearn, farn: Floats, Near and far clipping planes. depthrange: Float, Depth range for normalization. Outputs: A tuple of gradients corresponding to the forward pass inputs: 1. gradmeans3D: (N, 3) 2. gradmeans2D: (N, 2), Gradient w.r.t. 2D projected means (often unused or None if not optimized). 3. gradsh: (N, K, C) 4. gradshp: (N, K, C), Gradient w.r.t. PHASOR SH coefficients. 5. gradcolorsprecomp: (N, C) 6. gradphasorsprecomp: (N, C) 7. gradopacities: (N,) 8. gradscales: (N, 3) or (N, 1) 9. gradrotations: (N, 4) 10. gradcov3Dsprecomp: (N, 6) 11. gradphaseoffset: Scalar or None 12. graddcoffset: Scalar or None 13. None: For rastersettings (not a tensor). The C++ kernel expects arguments in a specific order. The Python wrapper restructures the inputs into a single tuple args before calling C.rasterizegaussiansbackward. Argument Order for C.rasterizegaussiansbackward: 1. bg 2. means3D 3. radii 4. colorsprecomp 5. phasorsprecomp 6. scales 7. rotations 8. scalemodifier 9. cov3Dsprecomp 10. viewmatrix 11. projmatrix 12. tanfovx 13. tanfovy 14. gradoutcolor 15. gradoutphasor 16. gradoutdepth 17. gradoutnormal 18. gradoutacc 19. gradentropy 20. graddepthdistortion 21. gradampdistortion 22. sh 23. shp 24. shdegree 25. campos 26. geomBuffer 27. numrendered 28. binningBuffer 29. imgBuffer 30. debug 31. nearn 32. farn 33. depthrange 34. useviewdependentphase 35. phaseoffset 36. dcoffset 1. Restore Context: Retrieve all saved tensors and settings from the forward pass context. If debug is true, deep-copy all arguments to CPU to allow snapshotting on exception. 2. Restructure Arguments: Pack the inputs into the tuple order defined above. Handle optional gradients (e.g., if gradoutphasor is not provided, pass a zero tensor or None depending on kernel implementation; typically, unused gradients are zeroed). 3. Invoke Kernel: Call C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(args). 4. Construct Return Tuple: Create a tuple of gradients in the order expected by PyTorch's autograd engine, matching the forward pass input signature. If optimizephaseoffset is False, gradphaseoffset is None. If optimizedcoffset is False, graddcoffset is None. The last element is None for rastersettings. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backward( gradoutcolor, gradoutphasor, gradoutdepth, gradoutnormal, gradoutacc, gradentropy, graddepthdistortion, gradampdistortion, bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, phasorsprecomp, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, sh, shp, shdegree, campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, debug, nearn, farn, depthrange, useviewdependentphase, phaseoffset, dcoffset, optimizephaseoffset, optimizedcoffset): # Step 1: Debug handling if debug: # Deep copy to CPU for snapshotting on exception argscpu = ( bg.cpu().clone(), means3D.cpu().clone(), radii.cpu().clone(), colorsprecomp.cpu().clone(), phasorsprecomp.cpu().clone(), scales.cpu().clone(), rotations.cpu().clone(), scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp.cpu().clone(), viewmatrix.cpu().clone(), projmatrix.cpu().clone(), tanfovx, tanfovy, gradoutcolor.cpu().clone(), gradoutphasor.cpu().clone() if gradoutphasor is not None else None, gradoutdepth.cpu().clone() if gradoutdepth is not None else None, gradoutnormal.cpu().clone() if gradoutnormal is not None else None, gradoutacc.cpu().clone() if gradoutacc is not None else None, gradentropy.cpu().clone() if gradentropy is not None else None, graddepthdistortion.cpu().clone() if graddepthdistortion is not None else None, gradampdistortion.cpu().clone() if gradampdistortion is not None else None, sh.cpu().clone(), shp.cpu().clone(), shdegree, campos.cpu().clone(), geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, debug, nearn, farn, depthrange, useviewdependentphase, phaseoffset, dcoffset) try: # Step 2: Invoke Kernel grads = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argscpu) except Exception as e: # Save snapshot for debugging import pickle with open('snapshotbw.dump', 'wb') as f: pickle.dump(argscpu, f) print(f"Exception in backward pass: {e}") raise e else: # Step 2: Invoke Kernel (GPU) argsgpu = ( bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, phasorsprecomp, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutphasor, gradoutdepth, gradoutnormal, gradoutacc, gradentropy, graddepthdistortion, gradampdistortion, sh, shp, shdegree, campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, debug, nearn, farn, depthrange, useviewdependentphase, phaseoffset, dcoffset) grads = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsgpu) # Step 3: Construct Return Tuple # Order must match forward pass inputs gradmeans3D = grads[0] gradmeans2D = grads[1] gradsh = grads[2] gradshp = grads[3] gradcolorsprecomp = grads[4] gradphasorsprecomp = grads[5] gradopacities = grads[6] gradscales = grads[7] gradrotations = grads[8] gradcov3Dsprecomp = grads[9] # Handle optional phase/dc offsets if optimizephaseoffset: gradphaseoffset = grads[10] else: gradphaseoffset = None if optimizedcoffset: graddcoffset = grads[11] else: graddcoffset = None # rastersettings is not a tensor gradrastersettings = None return ( gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, gradsh, gradshp, gradcolorsprecomp, gradphasorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradphaseoffset, graddcoffset, gradrastersettings) Debug Mode Overhead: If debug is true, all tensors are copied to CPU, which is extremely slow for large scenes. This should only be used for debugging exceptions. Missing Gradients: If certain output gradients (e.g., gradoutphasor) are not required by the loss function, they should be passed as None or zero tensors to the kernel, depending on the kernel's implementation. The kernel must handle these gracefully. Gradient Order Mismatch: The order of gradients returned by the C++ kernel must exactly match the order of inputs in the forward pass. Any mismatch will cause incorrect gradient updates. Non-Optimized Parameters: If phaseoffset or dcoffset are not optimized, their gradients are set to None to prevent PyTorch from trying to update non-trainable parameters. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) in the worst case, where N is the number of Gaussians and H \cdot W is the image resolution. However, due to tile-based rasterization and culling, the effective complexity is closer to O(K \cdot T), where K is the number of Gaussians per tile and T is the number of tiles. Memory Complexity: O(N + H \cdot W) for storing intermediate buffers (geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) and gradients. Performance: The backward pass is typically 1.5x to 2x slower than the forward pass due to the complexity of gradient computation for splatting and blending. Strengths: Fully differentiable, supports arbitrary loss functions, efficient tile-based implementation. Limitations: High memory usage for large scenes, sensitive to numerical precision in gradient computation. When to Use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models with differentiable rendering. When Not to Use: For inference-only applications where gradients are not needed. The backward pass of the 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer was introduced as part of the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper and has been extended in subsequent works such as EGGS and gftorf to support Time-of-Flight (ToF) rendering and other modalities. It is a critical component for optimizing the 3D scene representation from 2D images. name: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting (IBGS)
head: IBGS: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting
body: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting (IBGS) is a novel view synthesis method that augments standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by predicting a color residual from neighboring training images to capture high-frequency details and view-dependent effects that low-degree spherical harmonics cannot represent. Unlike methods that attach per-Gaussian texture maps (high storage) or global texture maps (poor complex scene handling), IBGS uses a lightweight neural network to learn the difference between the base 3DGS rendering and the actual pixel colors observed in source views, maintaining the original storage footprint while significantly improving rendering quality. IBGS decomposes the final pixel color into a base color rendered via standard 3DGS volume rendering and a learned residual derived from multi-view features. The method involves feature extraction from source views, residual prediction via a convolutional decoder, and optional exposure correction. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (centers \mui, covariances \Sigmai, opacities oi, spherical harmonics coefficients hi, and normal vectors ni). Camera poses and intrinsics for the target view and M neighboring source views. Source images C^m{real} for m \in \{1, \dots, M\}. Outputs: Final rendered image C{final} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores center \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, opacity oi \in \mathbb{R}, SH coefficients hi (degree l=2), and normal vector ni \in \mathbb{R}^3. Feature Map: F \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 32}, containing aggregated multi-view features per pixel. Base Image: C \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, the result of standard 3DGS rasterization. Ray Direction Map: D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, containing camera ray directions for each pixel. Residual Map: \Delta C \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, predicted by the decoder. l: Spherical Harmonics degree. Value: 2. K: Number of median intersection points used for feature extraction. Value: 4. M: Number of visible source views used as input. Value: 3. S: Number of candidate source views (closest views) before visibility filtering. Value: 4. \tau: Depth error threshold for visibility check. Value: 0.001. \beta: Weight for L1 vs SSIM in loss. Value: 0.8. \gamma: Weight balancing base image loss vs final image loss. Initial: 1, decreased to 0.5 in last 20,000 iterations. \lambda1, \lambda2: Loss weights for photometric and normal consistency. Value: 0 for first 7,000 iterations, then 0.3 and 0.03 respectively. Opacity prune threshold: 0.05. 1. Base Color Rendering: Compute the base color c(p) for each pixel p using standard 3DGS volume rendering: c(p) = \sum{i} wi ci where wi = \alphai Ti, Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \alphai = oi G{2D}^i(p), and ci = \Psil(hi, vi) is the color of Gaussian i evaluated at ray direction vi using SH degree l. 2. Median Intersection Selection: To filter out floating Gaussians, select K intersection points \{xk(p)\}{k=1}^K where the accumulated transmittance Ti is closest to 0.5. 3. Warping to Source Views: For each selected intersection point xk(p) and each candidate source view m: Project xk(p) to the source view image plane using projection function \pim: \text{coord}{m} = \pim(xk(p)) Bilinearly interpolate the color from the source image C^m{real}: c^{warp}{k,m}(p) = B(\text{coord}{m}, C^m{real}) where B(\cdot) is bilinear interpolation. 4. Visibility Filtering: Select the M visible source views from the S candidates based on depth consistency (threshold \tau). 5. Per-Pixel Feature Extraction: For each visible source view m \in \{1, \dots, M\}: Compute the weighted average warped color: c^{warp}m(p) = \frac{\sum{k=1}^K wk c^{warp}{k,m}(p)}{\sum{k=1}^K wk} Compute the appearance feature deviation: \Delta cm(p) = c^{warp}m(p) - c(p) Define the camera feature \Delta dm(p) \in \mathbb{R}^4 (derived from source view pose/direction). Process features through encoder E (two linear layers, 32 output dim, ReLU): fm(p) = E(\Delta cm(p), \Delta dm(p)) Apply max-pooling across all M views to get aggregated feature \bar{f}(p) \in \mathbb{R}^{32}. Assemble feature map F \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 32}. 6. Exposure Correction (Optional): If applied (e.g., on Tanks and Temples), estimate an affine transformation A^ from the nearest source view and correct the base color: c^{expo}(p) = A^ c(p) If used, replace c(p) with c^{expo}(p) in subsequent steps. 7. Residual Prediction: Feed the base image C (or C^{expo}), ray direction map D, and feature map F into a nine-layer convolutional decoder D(\cdot) with 3 \times 3 kernels to predict the residual map \Delta C: \Delta C = D(C, D, F). 8. Final Rendering: Add the residual to the base image: C{final} = C + \Delta C. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projecttoimageplane(intersections, viewpose, viewintrinsics): """Project 3D intersection points to 2D image coordinates of a source view.""" # Transform to camera space: Xc = R (Xw - t) Xc = viewpose.R @ intersections.T + viewpose.t # Project: u = K Xc / Z coords = viewintrinsics.K @ Xc coords = coords[:2,:] / coords[2,:] return coords.T # Shape: (N, 2) def bilinearinterpolate(image, coords): """Bilinearly sample color from image at given (H, W, 2) coordinates.""" h, w, = image.shape u = np.clip(coords[:, 0], 0, w - 1) v = np.clip(coords[:, 1], 0, h - 1) u0, v0 = np.floor(u).astype(int), np.floor(v).astype(int) u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 wu, wv = u - u0, v - v0 # Interpolate val = (1 - wu) (1 - wv) image[v0, u0] + \ wu (1 - wv) image[v0, u1] + \ (1 - wu) wv image[v1, u0] + \ wu wv image[v1, u1] return val # Shape: (N, 3) def selectmedianindices(transmittance, K): """Select K indices per pixel where transmittance is closest to 0.5.""" # transmittance shape: (H, W, N) diff = np.abs(transmittance - 0.5) # Get indices of K smallest differences indices = np.argpartition(diff, K, axis=-1)[:,:,:K] return indices # Shape: (H, W, K) def filtervisibility(candidateviews, gaussians, camera, tau): """Filter S candidate views to M visible views based on depth threshold tau.""" # Compute depth error for each candidate view against target view geometry # Keep views where max depth error < tau visible = [] for m in candidateviews: deptherr = computedeptherror(gaussians, camera, m) if deptherr.max() < tau: visible.append(m) return visible[:3] # M=3 def computecamerafeature(viewidx, raydirs): """Compute 4D camera feature from view pose and ray directions.""" # Placeholder for view-specific pose encoding; returns dummy 4D feature per evidence return np.zeroslike(raydirs)[:,:,:4] def applyexposure(image, Astar): """Apply affine exposure correction matrix A to image.""" # Astar is 3x3 or 4x4 affine matrix; apply to each pixel return (Astar[:3,:3] @ image.reshape(-1, 3).T + Astar[:3, 3]).T.reshape(image.shape) class IBGS: def init(self, K=4, M=3, S=4, tau=0.001, l=2): self.K = K self.M = M self.S = S self.tau = tau self.l = l # Encoder: 2 linear layers, 32 output dim, ReLU self.encoderW1 = np.random.randn(7, 32) self.encoderb1 = np.zeros(32) self.encoderW2 = np.random.randn(32, 32) self.encoderb2 = np.zeros(32) # Decoder: 9-layer CNN, 3x3 kernels, input channels: 38, output: 3 self.decoderweights = [np.random.randn(32, 38, 3, 3) if i == 0 else np.random.randn(32, 32, 3, 3) for i in range(9)] self.decoderbias = [np.zeros(32) for in range(9)] self.decoderoutW = np.random.randn(3, 32, 3, 3) self.decoderoutb = np.zeros(3) def encoderforward(self, x): # x: (H, W, 7) x = np.tanh(x @ self.encoderW1 + self.encoderb1) x = np.tanh(x @ self.encoderW2 + self.encoderb2) return x # (H, W, 32) def decoderforward(self, x): # x: (H, W, 38) -> (H, 38, W, H) for conv x = np.transpose(x, (0, 2, 1)) for i in range(9): x = np.tanh(np.conv2d(x, self.decoderweights[i], padding=1) + self.decoderbias[i]) x = np.conv2d(x, self.decoderoutW, padding=1) + self.decoderoutb x = np.transpose(x, (0, 2, 3, 1)) return x # (H, W, 3) def render(self, gaussians, camera, sourceviews): # 1. Base render (standard 3DGS rasterization assumed from parent article) C, transmittance, weights, raydirs = standard3dgsrasterize(gaussians, camera, self.l) # 2. Median intersection selection medianindices = selectmedianindices(transmittance, self.K) # 3. Warp to source views candidateviews = selectclosestviews(camera, sourceviews, self.S) visibleviews = filtervisibility(candidateviews, gaussians, camera, self.tau) warpedcolors = [] for m in visibleviews: coords = projecttoimageplane(gaussians[medianindices], sourceviews[m].pose, sourceviews[m].intrinsics) colors = bilinearinterpolate(sourceviews[m].image, coords) warpedcolors.append(colors) warpedcolors = np.stack(warpedcolors, axis=2) # (H, W, M, K, 3) # 4. Feature extraction features = [] for m in range(self.M): avgwarped = np.sum(warpedcolors[:,:, m,:,:] weights[:, medianindices].reshape(weights.shape[0], weights.shape[1], self.K, 1), axis=3) / \ np.sum(weights[:, medianindices], axis=3).reshape(weights.shape[0], weights.shape[1], 1) deltac = avgwarped - C deltad = computecamerafeature(m, raydirs) fm = self.encoderforward(np.concatenate([deltac, deltad], axis=-1)) features.append(fm) F = np.max(np.stack(features, axis=2), axis=2) # (H, W, 32) # 5. Exposure correction (optional) if exposurecorrectionenabled: Astar = estimateexposure(camera, sourceviews) C = applyexposure(C, Astar) # 6. Residual prediction Dmap = raydirs inputtensor = np.concatenate([C, Dmap, F], axis=-1) deltaC = self.decoderforward(inputtensor) # 7. Final rendering Cfinal = C + deltaC return Cfinal, C, deltaC Time Complexity: Dominated by the standard 3DGS rasterization and the lightweight 9-layer CNN decoder. The feature extraction involves projecting K points to M views, which is negligible compared to rasterization for typical K=4, M=3. Memory Complexity: Storage footprint is identical to standard 3DGS (Gaussians + SH coefficients). The neural network weights are small and not stored per-Gaussian. Performance: Significantly outperforms prior Gaussian Splatting approaches in rendering quality (PSNR, SSIM) on benchmarks like Tanks and Temples, Deep Blending, and Mip-NeRF360, without increasing storage. Strengths: Captures high-frequency details and view-dependent effects (specular highlights, reflections) that low-degree SH (l \le 3) misses, without the storage overhead of per-Gaussian textures. Limitations: Requires access to neighboring training images for feature extraction. Performance depends on the quality of multi-view correspondences. Auto-exposure settings in cameras can cause inconsistent brightness across views, introducing noise into Gaussian optimization if uncorrected. When to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required, especially for scenes with complex lighting or fine textures, and storage is constrained. When not to use: If source views are not available or have poor overlap/visibility with the target view. IBGS was proposed by Hoang Chuong Nguyen, Wei Mao, Jose M. Alvarez, and Miaomiao Liu from the Australian National University and NVIDIA. It was published on arXiv in November 2025. The method addresses the limitations of 3DGS, which uses low-degree spherical harmonics to model view-dependent color, limiting its ability to capture spatially varying color and effects like specular highlights. Previous attempts to augment Gaussians with texture maps either struggled with complex scenes (global maps) or introduced high storage overhead (per-Gaussian maps). IBGS leverages image-based rendering principles to "borrow" pixels from source views, modeling the residual color to supplement the base 3DGS rendering. IBGS: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14357v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering with Language Features
head: LangSplat Rendering, Language Feature Rasterization
body: This method extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer to simultaneously render a language feature image alongside the RGB image by passing precomputed per-Gaussian language features to the rasterization backend. It differs from standard 3DGS rendering by adding a parallel feature channel output and normalizing features per Gaussian before rasterization to prevent magnitude bias. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: pc (Gaussian primitive container), opt (configuration with includefeature flag), pipe (pipeline configuration with computecov3Dpython, convertSHspython, and scalingmodifier), bgcolor (background color tensor of shape [3] on GPU). Outputs: renderedimage (RGB tensor), languagefeatureimage (feature tensor), radii (screen-space radii tensor), and a dictionary containing "render", "languagefeatureimage", "viewspacepoints", "visibilityfilter", and "radii". Data Structures: Per-Gaussian Language Features: A tensor retrieved from pc via pc.getlanguagefeature(). The dimensionality depends on the feature level (e.g., 3D or higher), but the rasterization backend expects a feature tensor per Gaussian. GaussianRasterizationSettings: Configuration object passed to the rasterizer backend, specifically setting includefeature=opt.includefeature. Steps: 1. Check the opt.includefeature flag to decide whether to compute and return language features. 2. If opt.includefeature is true, retrieve per-Gaussian language features via pc.getlanguagefeature(). 3. L2-normalize the language features per Gaussian to prevent magnitude bias during blending by dividing by the L2 norm along the last dimension plus a small epsilon. The normalization formula is: \mathbf{f}{norm} = \frac{\mathbf{f}}{\|\mathbf{f}\|2 + \epsilon} where \mathbf{f} is the feature vector, \|\mathbf{f}\|2 is the L2 norm along the last dimension, and \epsilon = 10^{-9}. 4. If opt.includefeature is false, set languagefeatureprecomp to a dummy tensor of shape (1,) matching the dtype and device of opacity. 5. Configure GaussianRasterizationSettings with includefeature=opt.includefeature. 6. Prepare covariance and color data based on pipe settings: if pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, compute 3D covariance in Python via pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier); otherwise, pass scales and rotations to the rasterizer. If pipe.convertSHspython is true, evaluate spherical harmonics in Python using evalsh; otherwise, pass raw SH coefficients (shs) or precomputed colors (colorsprecomp). 7. Call the rasterizer with means3D, means2D, shs/colorsprecomp, languagefeatureprecomp, opacity, and scales/rotations/cov3Dprecomp. 8. The rasterizer returns renderedimage, languagefeatureimage, and radii. Return a dictionary containing "render", "languagefeatureimage", "viewspacepoints", "visibilityfilter" (radii > 0), and "radii". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def renderlanguagefeatures(pc, opt, pipe, bgcolor, imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree): # Step 1-4: Prepare language features if opt.includefeature: languagefeatureprecomp = pc.getlanguagefeature() # L2-normalize to prevent magnitude bias during blending languagefeatureprecomp = languagefeatureprecomp / ( languagefeatureprecomp.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-9) else: # Dummy tensor matching dtype and device of opacity languagefeatureprecomp = torch.zeros(1, dtype=pc.opacity.dtype, device=pc.opacity.device) # Step 6: Prepare covariance and colors if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(pipe.scalingmodifier) scales = None rotations = None else: cov3Dprecomp = None scales = pc.scales rotations = pc.rotations if pipe.convertSHspython: # Evaluate spherical harmonics in Python colorsprecomp = pc.getshcolors() shs = None else: colorsprecomp = None shs = pc.shs # Step 5: Configure rasterization settings rasterizationsettings = { "imageheight": imageheight, "imagewidth": imagewidth, "tanfovx": tanfovx, "tanfovy": tanfovy, "bg": bgcolor, "scalemodifier": pipe.scalingmodifier, "viewmatrix": viewmatrix, "projmatrix": projmatrix, "shdegree": shdegree, "includefeature": opt.includefeature } # Step 7-8: Call rasterizer backend and return results renderedimage, languagefeatureimage, radii = rasterize( means3D=pc.means3D, means2D=pc.means2D, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp, languagefeatureprecomp=languagefeatureprecomp, opacities=pc.opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp, settings=rasterizationsettings) visibilityfilter = radii > 0 return { "render": renderedimage, "languagefeatureimage": languagefeatureimage, "viewspacepoints": pc.means2D, "visibilityfilter": visibilityfilter, "radii": radii } def rasterize(means3D, means2D, shs, colorsprecomp, languagefeatureprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp, settings): # Invokes the CUDA rasterization backend # Returns rendered RGB image, language feature image, and screen-space radii return torch.zeros(1, 3, settings["imageheight"], settings["imagewidth"]), \ torch.zeros(1, 3, settings["imageheight"], settings["imagewidth"]), \ torch.zeros(means3D.shape[0], dtype=torch.int32) Parameters: opt.includefeature (bool): Flag to enable/disable language feature rendering and computation. scalingmodifier (float, default 1.0): Multiplier applied to Gaussian scales during rasterization. pipe.computecov3Dpython (bool): If true, computes 3D covariance in Python; otherwise passes scales and rotations. pipe.convertSHspython (bool): If true, evaluates spherical harmonics in Python; otherwise passes raw SH coefficients. bgcolor (torch.Tensor, shape [3]): Background color tensor on GPU, set to [1,1,1] for white background or [0,0,0] for black. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Magnitude Bias: Failure to L2-normalize language features can lead to magnitude bias during blending, causing incorrect feature interpolation. Feature Dimensionality: The decoder elevates features from 3 dimensions to 512 dimensions for further operations, implying the rasterized language feature image may be low-dimensional (e.g., 3D) and requires post-processing for high-dimensional tasks. Dummy Tensor: When features are disabled, a dummy tensor of shape (1,) must be passed to maintain tensor shape consistency in the rasterizer call. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables simultaneous rendering of semantic/language information alongside geometry and appearance, facilitating tasks like 3D object localization and semantic segmentation. Limitations: Requires precomputed language features and an additional normalization step. The output language feature image is low-dimensional (3D) and requires a decoder for high-dimensional applications. Origin: LangSplat was introduced by Minghan Qin, Wanhua Li, Jiawei Zhou, Haoqian Wang, and Hanspeter Pfister in the paper "LangSplat: 3D Language Gaussian Splatting" (CVPR 2024). History: The method extends the original 3D Gaussian Splatting framework to include language features, allowing for 3D language understanding and interaction. It builds upon the differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians. Usage: Used for 3D object localization on LERF and 3D semantic segmentation on LERF, leveraging preprocessed datasets like 3D-OVS with language features. minghanqin/LangSplat, https://github.com/minghanqin/LangSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

body: Gaussian Rasterization with F-Count is a variant of the 3D Gaussian Splatting differentiable rasterizer that computes an auxiliary output: the number of times each 3D Gaussian is activated (rendered) during the forward pass, alongside the standard color and radii outputs. It sets itself apart from standard rasterization by providing explicit per-Gaussian activation counts (gaussianscount) and an importantscore, which are utilized in downstream tasks such as Gaussian pruning or importance sampling. It builds on Rasterization Variant by modifying the backend dispatch and return signatures to include these counts. Inputs: 1. rastersettings: A GaussianRasterizationSettings NamedTuple containing camera and rendering parameters. 2. means3D: Tensor of 3D Gaussian means. 3. colorsprecomp or sh: Precomputed colors or Spherical Harmonics coefficients (exactly one must be provided). 4. opacities: Tensor of Gaussian opacities. 5. scales and rotations OR cov3Dsprecomp: Either the scale/rotation pair or precomputed 3D covariances (exactly one pair must be provided). 6. fcount: A boolean flag in rastersettings. When True, the F-Count variant is invoked. Outputs: When fcount is True: 1. gaussianscount: Tensor containing the number of times each Gaussian was rendered. 2. importantscore: Tensor containing an importance score (implementation details of calculation not provided in sources). 3. color: The rendered image tensor. 4. radii: The radius of each Gaussian in screen space. When fcount is False: 1. color: The rendered image tensor. 2. radii: The radius of each Gaussian in screen space. Input Validation: Verify that exactly one of shs or colorsprecomp is provided. If both are None or both are not None, raise an exception. Forward Pass Execution: If rastersettings.fcount is True, call C.countgaussians(args). Otherwise, call C.rasterizegaussians(args). Both functions return a tuple of tensors. The standard return is (gaussianscount/numrendered, importantscore/None, numrendered, color, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer). 4. name: Single-Pass Rasterization with Alpha-Blending
head: Single-Pass Anti-Aliased Rasterization, Unified Rasterization
body: This method provides a unified rendering pipeline that rasterizes both 3D Gaussians and triangle meshes in a single pass using alpha-blending, ensuring correct spatial occlusion and color blending without dropping rendering rates. It solves the problem of integrating mesh-based geometry with Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by treating depth-adjacent triangles as a single entity for transmittance calculation, thereby preventing color overflow artifacts that occur when Gaussians are present between overlapping triangles. Unlike standard 3DGS rasterization which handles only Gaussians, or standard rasterization which handles only triangles, this approach combines them in one depth-sorted pass. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position, covariance (scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and RGB color c. A set of triangle meshes, each defined by vertices and faces. Camera parameters (view/projection matrices). Background color C{bg} and background opacity \alpha{bg}. Number of sub-pixels for MSAA, M=4. Outputs: Final pixel color C{pixel} for each pixel in the image. Data Structures: Fragment List: A list of all fragments (Gaussian splats and triangle intersections) overlapping the pixel, sorted by depth (front-to-back). Sub-pixel Grid: For each pixel, a grid of M \times M sub-pixels (typically 4 \times 4) to compute coverage. Algorithm Steps: 1. Depth Sorting: Collect all fragments (Gaussians and triangles) that intersect the pixel's view frustum. Sort them in front-to-back order based on their depth z. Let the sorted list be F1, F2, \dots, FN. 2. Initialize Transmittance: Set the initial transmittance T{in} = 1.0. 3. Process Fragments: Iterate through the sorted fragments i = 1 to N. Determine if fragment Fi is a Gaussian or a Triangle, and apply the corresponding color and transmittance logic. Case A: Fragment is a 3D Gaussian Compute the Gaussian's opacity \alphai and color ci. The transmittance Ti is calculated using the pixel-level transmittance from the previous step: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where T1 = T{in}. Compute the Gaussian's color contribution C{gs, i}: C{gs, i} = Ti \alphai ci Update the pixel-level transmittance for the next fragment: T{i}^{new} = Ti (1 - \alphai) (Note: The sources define Ti in the sum as the transmittance before the current fragment, and update it for subsequent blending). Case B: Fragment is a Triangle Compute the geometric coverage o{ji} \in \{0, 1\} for each sub-pixel j (j=1 \dots M) of fragment i. Compute the sub-pixel transmittance t{ji} for each sub-pixel j, accounting for previous fragments' opacity at the sub-pixel level: t{ji} = \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - o{jk} \alphak) where t{j1} = 1.0. Compute the total coverage Oi for fragment i at the pixel level by averaging the sub-pixel coverages weighted by their respective transmittances: Oi = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} o{ji} t{ji}. Depth-Adjacency Check: Identify if fragment i is depth-adjacent to other triangles. The method treats only depth-adjacent triangles as a single entity for the purpose of calculating the triangle color contribution C{tris} to avoid color overflow. If fragment i is part of a group of depth-adjacent triangles, compute the group's contribution. If it is isolated or part of a Gaussian-dominated region, the logic adapts. However, the core formula for triangle contribution C{tris} is defined as: C{tris} = T{in} \sum{i \in \text{Triangles}} Oi \alphai ci. Crucial Distinction: While C{tris} sums Oi \alphai ci, the transmittance Ti used for the final pixel blending and for updating the state for subsequent fragments (including Gaussians behind triangles) must still be updated correctly. The sources state that Ti is updated by Equation (6) for subsequent blending, even though it is not used in the C{tris} accumulation itself. Update the pixel-level transmittance Ti for the next fragment using the coverage Oi: Ti = \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - Ok \alphak). 4. Final Color Calculation: After processing all N fragments, compute the final pixel color C{pixel} by adding the accumulated triangle contribution C{tris} and the background contribution: C{pixel} = C{tris} + T{bg} C{bg} where T{bg} = TN (1 - \alpha{bg}) and TN is the final transmittance after all fragments. # Or is it the Tin of the whole pixel? # Source says "Tin denotes the transmittance before the ray passes through these fragments". # In the context of a group, Tin is the T at the start of the group. # If we treat each triangle individually (if not adjacent), Tin = Tcurrent. contrib = tuple(Tcurrent Oi alpha c for c in color) Caccum = tuple(a + b for a, b in zip(Caccum, contrib)) # Update Tcurrent for subsequent blending # Source: Ti = prod (1 - Ok alphak) # This is equivalent to Tcurrent (1 - Oi alpha) Tcurrent = Tcurrent (1 - Oi alpha) # Final Color Tbg = Tcurrent (1 - backgroundopacity) Cpixel = tuple(c + Tbg bgc for c, bgc in zip(Caccum, backgroundcolor)) return Cpixel Parameters: M: Number of sub-pixels for MSAA, set to 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Overflow: If all triangles overlapping a pixel are treated as a single entity when Gaussians are present between them, the transmittance for deeper triangles does not account for decay from Gaussians, resulting in white artifacts. The solution is to treat only depth-adjacent triangles as a single entity. Precision: The sub-pixel transmittance calculation t{ji} involves products of many terms, which may suffer from precision issues if many fragments overlap a single sub-pixel. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of fragments N per pixel, O(N), due to the single pass depth sort and accumulation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the fragment list and sub-pixel transmittance states. Performance: The method ensures correct spatial occlusion and color blending without dropping rendering rates compared to separate passes. Strengths: Unified handling of Gaussians and triangles; anti-aliased via MSAA; prevents color overflow artifacts. Limitations: Requires careful handling of depth-adjacency for triangles; sub-pixel transmittance tracking adds complexity. This method was proposed in "UniMGS: Unifying Mesh and 3D Gaussian Splatting with Single-Pass Rasterization and Proxy-Based Deformation". It addresses the limitations of proxy-based 3DGS deformation and the need for unified rendering of mesh and 3DGS in dynamic scenes. name: Camera Pose Gradient Computation
head: Camera pose gradient derivation, Gradient computation for camera pose optimization, Jacobian of Gaussians w.r.t. Camera Poses
body: This method computes the gradient of the rendering loss \mathcal{L} with respect to virtual camera poses \mathbf{T}i to enable the joint optimization of 3D Gaussian parameters and camera trajectories. It differs from standard differentiable rasterization by explicitly deriving the analytical Jacobian of the Gaussian mean transformation with respect to the camera pose, allowing gradients to flow from the image loss back to the pose parameters (rotation and translation). This is distinct from the parent method 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer, which primarily focuses on gradients with respect to Gaussian attributes, by extending the backpropagation path to include the extrinsic camera parameters. The method computes the gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} for a virtual camera pose \mathbf{T}i \in SE(3) associated with the i-th virtual sharp image \mathbf{C}i. The computation relies on the chain rule, decomposing the gradient into terms involving the loss, the rendered image, the Gaussian parameters, and the camera pose. Inputs: \mathcal{L}: The scalar rendering loss (e.g., L1, SSIM) computed between the rendered blurred image and the ground truth. \mathbf{T}i: The virtual camera pose for the i-th view, represented as an element of SE(3). \boldsymbol{\mu}: The 3D mean position of a Gaussian in world coordinates. \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}: The rotation matrix and translation vector components of \mathbf{T}i. \mathbf{C}i: The rendered sharp image for pose \mathbf{T}i. \mathbf{B}k: The blurred image pixels. Outputs: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}: The gradient of the loss with respect to the camera pose parameters. The method operates on standard tensor structures provided by automatic differentiation frameworks (e.g., PyTorch) and linear algebra libraries. Pose \mathbf{T}i: Represented as an SE(3) transformation. In implementation, this is often parameterized by control knots (e.g., \mathbf{T}{start}, \mathbf{T}{end} for linear interpolation, or \mathbf{T}1, \mathbf{T}2, \mathbf{T}3, \mathbf{T}4 for cubic B-spline) which are optimized in the Lie algebra se(3). Gaussian Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}: A 3D vector \in \mathbb{R}^3. Camera Coordinate Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}c: A 3D vector \in \mathbb{R}^3. 1. Compute Loss Gradients: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the blurred image pixels \mathbf{B}k and the sharp images \mathbf{C}i using automatic differentiation. \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{B}k} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}k}{\partial \mathbf{C}i} Note: The term \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}k}{\partial \mathbf{C}i} accounts for the aggregation over n virtual cameras. 2. Decompose Gaussian Parameter Gradients: The gradient with respect to the Gaussian parameters \theta is defined as: \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = \left[ \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}, \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}, \frac{\partial c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}, \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} \right] where \boldsymbol{\mu}' is the transformed mean, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' is the transformed covariance, c is color, and \rho is opacity. 3. Apply Efficiency Approximations: Color c and opacity \rho are independent of the virtual camera pose \mathbf{T}i. Thus, \frac{\partial c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = 0 and \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = 0. For efficiency, the gradient of the transformed covariance \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} is ignored. Consequently, only \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} needs to be computed analytically. 4. Compute Mean Transformation Gradient: Decompose \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} using the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} where \boldsymbol{\mu}c = \mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{t} is the mean transformed into the camera's coordinate space. 5. Evaluate Chain Rule Terms: Rasterization Jacobian: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}}. This is the Jacobian of the rendered image with respect to the Gaussian mean in world coordinates. This term is already computed in the CUDA backend of the differentiable projection and rasterization. Inverse Rotation: \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c} = \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\partial \mathbf{R} \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{t}} = \mathbf{R}^T. Pose Jacobian: \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = \mathbf{I}3 \otimes [\boldsymbol{\mu}^\top \mathbf{I}] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}, where \otimes is the Kronecker operator and \mathbf{I}3 is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix. Note: The source specifies the output dimension as \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}, which implies a specific vectorization or flattening convention for the gradient with respect to the pose parameters. 6. Pose Interpolation Jacobian: The virtual camera pose \mathbf{T}i is interpolated from SE(3) control knots (e.g., \mathbf{T}{start}, \mathbf{T}{end} for linear, or \mathbf{T}1, \mathbf{T}2, \mathbf{T}3, \mathbf{T}4 for cubic B-spline). The Jacobian of \mathbf{T}i with respect to the pose adjustments (e.g., \varepsilon{start}, \varepsilon{end} \in se(3)) is computed using PyPose and PyTorch auto-differentiation. The complete gradient computation is given by: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}:= \left( \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{B}k} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} \left( \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}k}{\partial \mathbf{C}i} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \theta} \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} where: K is the number of pixels. n is the number of virtual cameras. \theta represents the Gaussian parameters. The specific term for the mean transformation is: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}} \mathbf{R}^T \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} Unverified code. name: Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering
head: stochastic solids
body: Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering is a technique that treats Gaussian primitives as continuous stochastic solids, replacing standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rasterization to improve geometric accuracy and depth synthesis quality. It solves the problem of floating-depth artifacts caused by vanilla 3DGS alpha-blending, which blends foreground and background depths, by allowing transmittance to vary continuously along each ray. Unlike sibling methods such as 2DGS which use fixed median-depth selection, this method provides a differentiable, continuous formulation for depth and normal rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d} (or viewing direction \omega), and a set of N 3D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. Outputs: Rendered RGB color \mathbf{I}{pix}, depth map d, and normal map \mathbf{n}. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Defined by 3D position \mu, 3x3 covariance matrix \Sigma (or quaternion scale/rotation), scalar opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Ray: Parametrized as \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where t is the depth along the ray. Formulas: 1. Vacancy Formulation: The per-pixel opacity \alpha is interpreted as the maximum value of the Gaussian primitive along the pixel ray. The vacancy v is defined as: v = \sqrt{1 - G(t^)} where t^ is the location of the maximum Gaussian response along the ray, and G(t^) is the Gaussian response at that location. This converts the 3D Gaussian distribution into a Gaussian primitive suitable for volume rendering. 2. Attenuation Coefficient: For a stochastic solid with vacancy v, the attenuation coefficient \sigma is defined as: \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \omega) = |\omega \cdot \nabla \log(v(\mathbf{x}))| = \frac{|\omega \cdot \nabla v(\mathbf{x})|}{v(\mathbf{x})} where \mathbf{x} is the 3D spatial position and \omega is the viewing direction. 3. Volume Rendering Integral: The rendered color \mathbf{I}{pix} is computed by integrating along the ray from near plane tn to far plane tf: \mathbf{I}{pix} = \int{tn}^{tf} p(t) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}(t), \omega) dt = \mathbf{c} \left( 1 - v(t)^2 \right) where the density p(t) and accumulated transmittance T(t) are: p(t) = T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{x}(t), \omega) T(t) = \exp \left( - \int{tn}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{x}(s), \omega) ds \right) Here, \mathbf{v} denotes the vacancy of the solid. 4. Depth Rendering (Median Depth): The depth map is defined as the median depth, i.e., the location d where accumulated transmittance reaches 0.5. The accumulated transmittance of multiple Gaussian primitives is computed by multiplicative composition. 5. Normal Rendering: Normal maps are rendered directly from Gaussian primitives using the same volume rendering formulation as RGB rendering. For each primitive, the tangent-plane normal of the density surface is computed at the ray intersection under the current viewing direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera origin through the pixel center. 2. Primitive Sorting: Sort all Gaussian primitives intersecting the ray's bounding volume by their distance to the camera (or along the ray parameter t). 3. Vacancy Calculation: For each primitive, determine the maximum Gaussian response G(t^) along the ray segment covered by the primitive. Compute the vacancy v = \sqrt{1 - G(t^)}. 4. Transmittance Integration: Compute the accumulated transmittance T(t) along the ray by integrating the attenuation coefficient \sigma derived from the vacancy v. This is done by multiplicative composition of transmittance contributions from each primitive. 5. Color Computation: Compute the final pixel color \mathbf{I}{pix} using the volume rendering integral, which simplifies to \mathbf{c}(1 - v(t)^2) at the point of maximum response. 6. Depth Solving: Solve for the median depth d where T(d) = 0.5. This is achieved using a fixed number of bisection iterations. 7. Normal Computation: Compute the tangent-plane normal of the density surface at the ray intersection for each primitive. Accumulate these normals using the same volume rendering formulation to produce the final normal map. 8. Backpropagation: Propagate gradients with the closed-form derivative of depth with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta: \frac{\partial d}{\partial \theta} = - \frac{\partial T(d; \theta) / \partial \theta}{\partial T(d; \theta) / \partial d} where d is the median depth location and \theta are the Gaussian parameters. Parameters: Bisection Iterations: A fixed number of iterations is used to solve for the median depth. The exact number is not specified in the sources. Optimizer: AdamW optimizer is used for training. Learning Rate: Initial learning rate 3 \times 10^{-6}, decayed to 1 \times 10^{-8} using cosine annealing. Iterations: 420K iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating-Depth Artifacts: Vanilla 3DGS alpha-blending blends foreground and background depths, producing artifacts. This method avoids this by using continuous transmittance. Discontinuities: Fixed median-depth selection (used in 2DGS) can introduce discontinuities in boundary regions. This method's continuous formulation mitigates this. Gradient Flow: Median-depth rendering affects only a single median Gaussian primitive during backpropagation, which is unfavorable for optimizing generalizable foundation models. This method allows gradients to flow through the continuous volume rendering formulation. Time Complexity: The method requires sorting primitives and integrating transmittance along rays, which is comparable to standard rasterization but involves additional bisection iterations for depth solving. Memory Complexity: Requires storing Gaussian parameters and intermediate transmittance values along the ray. Strengths: Improves geometric accuracy and depth synthesis quality by avoiding floating-depth artifacts. Provides smoother depth maps compared to rasterization-based median depth. Decouples normal supervision from depth rendering, allowing direct normal rendering from primitives. Limitations: More complex than standard rasterization due to the volume rendering formulation and bisection iterations. When to Use: When accurate scene geometry and depth maps are critical, such as in visual geometry grounded transformers or generalizable foundation models. When Not to Use: When computational efficiency is the primary concern and geometric accuracy is less critical, standard 3DGS rasterization may be preferred. Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering was introduced in the paper \text{VG}^2GT: Voxel-Gaussian Splatting Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer. It builds upon the concept of treating Gaussian primitives as continuous stochastic solids, as proposed in [52] (cited in). The method addresses limitations of existing 3DGS variants, such as 2DGS, which use fixed median-depth selection and suffer from discontinuities and limited gradient flow. It is used in the context of feed-forward Gaussian primitives for visual geometry tasks. \text{VG}^2GT: Voxel-Gaussian Splatting Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.01573, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Gaussian Rasterization with Plane/Depth Output
head: GaussianRasterizer, diff-plane-rasterization
body: This method extends the standard differentiable Gaussian rasterizer to simultaneously output color, depth, and geometric auxiliary maps (such as normals or albedo) per pixel. It solves the problem of extracting dense geometric information from 3D Gaussian splats by treating depth and geometric attributes as additional channels in the alpha-compositing accumulation, allowing gradients to flow back to the 3D Gaussian parameters for geometry-aware training. It differs from standard color-only rasterization by maintaining and backpropagating through additional output tensors (outallmap, outplanedepth) alongside the color buffer. The method operates in two phases: a forward pass that projects 3D Gaussians and accumulates color, depth, and geometric maps, and a backward pass that computes gradients for all Gaussian parameters. Forward Inputs: rastersettings.bg: Background color tensor. means3D: 3D mean positions of Gaussians. colorsprecomp: Pre-computed color attributes. opacities: Opacity of Gaussians. scales: Scale factors. rotations: Quaternion rotations. rastersettings.scalemodifier: Scale adjustment factor. cov3Dsprecomp: Pre-computed 3D covariance matrices. allmaps: Auxiliary geometric maps (e.g., normals, depth) associated with Gaussians. rastersettings.viewmatrix: View transformation matrix. rastersettings.projmatrix: Projection matrix. rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy: Tangent of horizontal/vertical field of view. rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth: Output image dimensions. sh: Spherical Harmonics coefficients (if used). rastersettings.shdegree: SH degree. rastersettings.campos: Camera position. rastersettings.prefiltered: Boolean for pre-filtering. rastersettings.rendergeo: Boolean flag to enable geometric output. rastersettings.debug: Boolean for debug mode. Forward Outputs: color: Rendered color image. radii: Radius of each Gaussian in screen space. outobserve: Visibility mask. outallmap: Rendered auxiliary geometric maps. outplanedepth: Rendered depth map. Backward Inputs: All forward inputs plus: allmappixels: Pixel-wise auxiliary map data. radii: From forward pass. gradoutcolor: Gradient of loss w.r.t. color. gradoutallmap: Gradient of loss w.r.t. auxiliary maps. gradoutplanedepth: Gradient of loss w.r.t. depth. geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer: Intermediate buffers from forward pass. Backward Outputs: Gradients for: means3D, means2D, means2Dabs, sh, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, gardallmap. The implementation relies on a C++/CUDA backend (C.rasterizegaussians). The Python interface manages tensor layouts: means3D: Shape (N, 3), float32. colorsprecomp: Shape (N, C), float32, where C is color channels. opacities: Shape (N, 1), float32. scales: Shape (N, 3), float32. rotations: Shape (N, 4), float32 (quaternions). cov3Dsprecomp: Shape (N, 6), float32 (upper triangular covariance). allmaps: Shape (N, M), float32, where M is the number of auxiliary channels. rastersettings: A namespace or dictionary containing camera matrices and image dimensions. 1. Restructure Arguments: Pack all inputs into a single tuple args in the specific order required by the C++ backend: python args = ( rastersettings.bg, means3D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, allmaps, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, rastersettings.prefiltered, rastersettings.rendergeo, rastersettings.debug) 2. Invoke Rasterizer: Call the CUDA kernel C.rasterizegaussians(args). This performs: 3D to 2D projection of Gaussians. Sorting of Gaussians by depth. Alpha compositing for color, depth, and auxiliary maps. 3. Save for Backward: Store all tensors required for gradient computation in the context: python ctx.saveforbackward( outallmap, colorsprecomp, allmaps, means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, sh, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) 4. Return Results: Return color, radii, outobserve, outallmap, and outplanedepth. 1. Restore Tensors: Retrieve saved tensors from the context. 2. Restructure Backward Arguments: Pack inputs including gradients and intermediate buffers: python argsbw = ( rastersettings.bg, allmappixels, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, allmaps, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutallmap, gradoutplanedepth, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rastersettings.rendergeo, rastersettings.debug) 3. Invoke Backward Kernel: Call C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbw). 4. Return Gradients: Return the computed gradients for all Gaussian parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from diffgaussianrasterization import GaussianRasterizationSettings, GaussianRasterizer def forwardgaussianrasterizationwithgeometry( means3D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, allmaps, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, imageheight, imagewidth, sh=None, shdegree=0, campos=None, bgcolor=torch.tensor([0,0,0]), scalemodifier=1.0, prefiltered=False, rendergeo=True, debug=False): """ Forward pass for differentiable Gaussian rasterization with plane/depth output. """ # 1. Setup rasterization settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imageheight=int(imageheight), imagewidth=int(imagewidth), tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bg=bgcolor, scalemodifier=scalemodifier, viewmatrix=viewmatrix, projmatrix=projmatrix, shdegree=shdegree, campos=campos, prefiltered=prefiltered, debug=debug) # 2. Initialize rasterizer rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings=rastersettings) # 3. Perform rasterization # The C++ backend handles the accumulation of color, depth, and allmaps # Returns: colors, radii, viewspacepoints, visibilityfilter, radiiallmap colors, radii, viewspacepoints, visibilityfilter, radiiallmap = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=torch.zeroslike(means3D), # Placeholder if not provided colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp, opacities=opacities, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dsprecomp, allmaps=allmaps # Passed to backend for geometric accumulation) # 4. Extract depth and geometric maps if enabled # Note: The exact extraction of 'outplanedepth' and 'outallmap' depends on the specific # C++ implementation's return structure. In PGSR, these are often part of the output tensors # or derived from the accumulated buffers. outplanedepth = colors[:, 2:3,:,:] # Example: assuming depth is stored in a specific channel or separate output outallmap = radiiallmap # Example: assuming auxiliary maps are returned in radiiallmap or similar return colors, radii, outallmap, outplanedepth def backwardgaussianrasterizationwithgeometry( gradoutcolor, gradoutallmap, gradoutplanedepth, means3D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, allmaps, sh, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, campos, bgcolor, scalemodifier, rendergeo, debug): """ Backward pass for differentiable Gaussian rasterization with plane/depth output. """ # 1. Restructure arguments for C++ backward kernel argsbw = ( bgcolor, allmaps, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, allmaps, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutallmap, gradoutplanedepth, sh, 0, campos, # shdegree assumed 0 for simplicity, adjust as needed geomBuffer, len(radii), binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rendergeo, debug) # 2. Invoke backward kernel # Returns gradients for means2D, means2Dabs, colorsprecomp, opacities, means3D, # cov3Dsprecomp, sh, scales, rotations, gardallmap gradmeans2D, gradmeans2Dabs, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations, gardallmap = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbw) return gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradscales, gradrotations, gradopacities, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsh, gardallmap shdegree: Typically 0 for color-only, higher for SH-based color. voxelsize: Used in post-processing (e.g., 0.002 in PGSR). maxdepth: Culling distance (e.g., 5.0 in PGSR). bgcolor: White [1,1,1] or black [0,0,0]. Debug Mode: If debug=True, tensors are copied to CPU before calling the C++ rasterizer to prevent corruption during exceptions. Snapshots snapshotfw.dump or snapshotbw.dump are saved. Precision: Floating-point precision in depth accumulation can affect gradient stability. Degenerate Input: Gaussians with zero scale or opacity may cause division by zero or invalid gradients.
