name: OmniGS
head: Equirectangular Projection, OmniGS Forward Rendering, OmniGS, Omnidirectional Gaussian Splatting, Omnidirectional Rasterization
body: OmniGS is a method for fast radiance field reconstruction and real-time omnidirectional novel view synthesis using calibrated monocular 360-degree images and sparse SfM point clouds. It replaces the standard perspective camera model with an omnidirectional equirectangular projection model, allowing 3D Gaussians to be splatted directly onto the equirectangular screen space. Unlike sibling methods such as 360-GS, which rely on tangent-plane approximations and two-stage projection, OmniGS uses direct screen-space splatting without requiring scene assumptions or deep networks. Inputs: A set of calibrated monocular 360-degree images. A sparse SfM point cloud. Camera poses and intrinsic parameters (focal lengths fx, fy, principal points cx, cy). Outputs: A reconstructed scene model represented by 3D Gaussians. Rendered omnidirectional images. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian: Defined by a mean position \mathbf{m}, a rotation matrix \mathbf{W}, a scaling vector, and an opacity oi. The covariance in world space is derived from these parameters. Camera Space Point: \mathbf{t} = [tx, ty, tz]^T, obtained by transforming the world position \mathbf{m} using the camera-to-world transformation matrix \mathbf{T}{cw}. Tile Grid: The equirectangular image is partitioned into a grid of tiles. Coordinate Systems: Camera Coordinate System: Follows the SLAM convention: +X is right, +Y is down, and +Z is forward. Latitude-Longitude: Intermediate spherical coordinates. Uniform Screen-Space: Normalized coordinates sx, sy \in -1, 1). Pixel Coordinates: Integer pixel positions px, py on an image of width W and height H. Forward Rendering Steps: 1. Transform to Camera Space: For each 3D Gaussian with world position \mathbf{m}, compute its position in camera space \mathbf{t}: \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{T}{cw} \mathbf{m} where \mathbf{T}{cw} is the 4x4 transformation matrix from world to camera space. 2. Project to Spherical Coordinates: Compute the distance tr and spherical coordinates (longitude lon, latitude lat) from \mathbf{t}: tr = \sqrt{tx^2 + ty^2 + tz^2} \begin{bmatrix} lon \\ lat \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathrm{arctan2}(tx / tz) \\ \arcsin (ty / tr) \end{bmatrix} The ranges are -\pi \le lon < \pi and -\pi/2 \le lat < \pi/2. 3. Map to Uniform Screen-Space: Transform spherical coordinates to uniform screen-space coordinates sx, sy: \begin{bmatrix} sx \\ sy \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} lon / \pi \\ 2lat / \pi \end{bmatrix} This results in -1 \le sx, sy < 1. 4. Map to Pixel Coordinates: Transform uniform screen-space coordinates to pixel positions px, py: \begin{bmatrix} px \\ py \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} (sx + 1) W / 2 \\ (sy + 1) H / 2 \end{bmatrix} where W is the image width and H is the image height. 5. Compute 2D Covariance and Alpha: The 2D covariance matrix in screen space is computed using the Jacobian of the projection and the 3D covariance. The alpha value for the i-th Gaussian at pixel p is: \alphai = oi Gi(\Delta \mathbf{p}i) where Gi is the 2D Gaussian distribution and \Delta \mathbf{p}i is the distance from the pixel to the Gaussian center. 6. Sort Gaussians: Sort the Gaussians contributing to a pixel by their distance from the camera center to the Gaussian kernel center, tr, from nearest to farthest. Note: Perspective cameras sort by tz. 7. [Tile-Based Rasterization: Partition the equirectangular image into tiles. For each tile, identify 2D Gaussians whose radius of influence covers the tile. Render all pixels in the tile simultaneously, assigning one thread per pixel. Threads cooperatively retrieve Gaussian attributes and accumulate alpha-blending results. Stop accumulation when pixel alpha reaches 0.9999 for numerical stability. 8. Alpha Blending: The final color C is computed as: C = \sum{i=1}^N ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) where ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian and N is the number of Gaussians near the pixel. Jacobian for Backpropagation: The derivatives of pixel coordinates with respect to camera-space points are required for optimization: \frac{\partial px}{\partial tx} = +\frac{W}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{tz}{tx^2 + tz^2}, \quad \frac{\partial px}{\partial ty} = 0, \quad \frac{\partial px}{\partial tz} = -\frac{W}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{tx}{tx^2 + tz^2} \frac{\partial py}{\partial tx} = -\frac{H}{\pi} \cdot \frac{tx ty}{tr^2 \sqrt{tx^2 + tz^2}}, \quad \frac{\partial py}{\partial ty} = +\frac{H}{\pi} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{tx^2 + tz^2}}{tr^2}, \quad \frac{\partial py}{\partial tz} = -\frac{H}{\pi} \cdot \frac{tz ty}{tr^2 \sqrt{tx^2 + tz^2}} where tr^2 = tx^2 + ty^2 + tz^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def projectomnidirectional(tx, ty, tz, W, H): """ Projects a 3D point in camera space to equirectangular pixel coordinates. tx, ty, tz: Tensor of shape (N,) W, H: int Returns: px, py tensors of shape (N,) """ # Compute distance tr tr = torch.sqrt(tx2 + ty2 + tz2) # Compute longitude and latitude # arctan2(y, x) in standard math, but here we use arctan2(tx/tz) # Note: The formula in uses arctan2(tx / tz). # Standard arctan2 takes (y, x). Here the "y" component is tx and "x" component is tz. lon = torch.atan2(tx, tz) lat = torch.asin(ty / tr) # Map to uniform screen space [-1, 1) sx = lon / math.pi sy = 2 lat / math.pi # Map to pixel coordinates px = (sx + 1) W / 2 py = (sy + 1) H / 2 return px, py def rendertile(tilegaussians, tilepixels, W, H): """ Renders a single tile. tilegaussians: List of Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, color, opacity) tilepixels: List of pixel coordinates (px, py) in the tile """ # Initialize output buffer # Assuming standard alpha blending accumulation # This is a simplified representation of the thread-cooperative process # Sort Gaussians by tr (distance from camera center) # tr is computed from the Gaussian's camera-space position sortedgaussians = sortbytr(tilegaussians) results = [] for px, py in tilepixels: alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = torch.zeros(3) # Assuming RGB for g in sortedgaussians: # Compute alpha for this Gaussian at this pixel # alphai = oi Gi(deltap) # Gi is the 2D Gaussian PDF evaluated at the offset from center deltap = computeoffset(px, py, g.centerpx, g.centerpy, g.covariance) alphai = g.opacity evaluate2dgaussian(deltap, g.covariance) # Stop if alpha is saturated if alphaacc >= 0.9999: break # Alpha blend weight = alphai (1 - alphaacc) coloracc = coloracc (1 - alphai) + g.color weight alphaacc += weight # If alphaacc is close to 1, we can break early if desired, # but the paper specifies stopping at 0.9999 accumulation or similar logic if alphaacc >= 0.9999: break results.append(coloracc) return results def computejacobian(tx, ty, tz, W, H): """ Computes the Jacobian of pixel coordinates w.r.t camera space points. """ trsq = tx2 + ty2 + tz2 tr = torch.sqrt(trsq) denomxz = tx2 + tz2 sqrtxz = torch.sqrt(tx2 + tz2) dpxdtx = (W / (2 math.pi)) (tz / denomxz) dpxdty = torch.zeroslike(tx) dpxdtz = -(W / (2 math.pi)) (tx / denomxz) dpydtx = -(H / math.pi) (tx ty) / (trsq sqrtxz) dpydty = (H / math.pi) sqrtxz / trsq dpydtz = -(H / math.pi) (tz ty) / (trsq sqrtxz) return { 'dpxdtx': dpxdtx, 'dpxdty': dpxdty, 'dpxdtz': dpxdtz, 'dpydtx': dpydtx, 'dpydty': dpydty, 'dpydtz': dpydtz } Time Complexity: Real-time rendering speed is achieved through GPU acceleration and tile-based rasterization. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of 3D Gaussians and the resolution of the equirectangular image. Strengths: Direct screen-space splatting avoids the suboptimal two-stage projection of tangent-plane methods. It does not rely on scene assumptions or deep networks, enabling application in diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When omnidirectional novel view synthesis is required from monocular 360-degree images. When not: When perspective images are the only input and omnidirectional output is not needed (standard 3DGS is more appropriate). OmniGS was introduced by Longwei Li, Huajian Huang, Sai-Kit Yeung, and Hui Cheng from Sun Yat-sen University and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. The paper was published on arXiv in April 2024 (v5 in November 2024). It addresses the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which only supports perspective images, by extending it to omnidirectional images. name: TR-Gaussians
head: TR-3DGS, TR-Gaussian Splatting, Transmission and Reflection 3D Gaussian Splatting, Transmission-Reflection Gaussians
body: TR-Gaussians is a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based representation designed for the high-fidelity, real-time rendering of planar transmission and reflection effects, such as those found in indoor glass panes. Unlike vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting, which overfits training images by mixing transmission and reflection into low-opacity artifacts, TR-Gaussians explicitly decomposes the scene into real geometry (transmission) and virtual geometry (reflection) using a learnable reflection plane. This separation prevents the entanglement of real scene geometry with virtual reflections, ensuring that reflections remain coherent and artifact-free in novel views where the real scene is occluded or unobserved. TR-Gaussians models a scene containing transparent glass by combining standard 3D Gaussians with a parametric reflection plane. The method separates the rendering process into two passes to compute transmission and reflection components independently, blending them via a view-dependent Fresnel model. Inputs: Camera pose (view and projection matrices). Scene representation: Primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p: Represent the real scene geometry and appearance. Glass Gaussians \mathcal{G}g: Mark the reflective regions on the glass pane. Reflection Plane P: Defined by position, normal, and base reflectance. Training images (for optimization). Outputs: Final rendered image C. Intermediate components: Transmission image Ct, Reflection image Cr, Reflection strength map R. The scene is represented by three distinct components: 1. Primary Gaussians (\mathcal{G}p): Each Gaussian i has: Position \mathbf{u}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}i for view-dependent color ci(\mathbf{d}). 3D Covariance matrix \Sigmai = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^\top \mathbf{R}i^\top, where \mathbf{S}i is the scaling matrix and \mathbf{R}i is the rotation matrix. Note: These are identical to the Gaussians in vanilla 3DGS. 2. Glass Gaussians (\mathcal{G}g): A subset of Gaussians (or a separate set) projected onto the reflection plane to define the shape of the reflective surface. Used to render a binary or soft mask M indicating where the glass pane exists in the screen space. 3. Reflection Plane (P): Defined by a plane equation \mathbf{n}^\top (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}) = 0, where \mathbf{p} is a point on the plane and \mathbf{n} is the unit normal vector. Includes a learnable base reflectance parameter. Initialized during Stage 1 of optimization. The rendering process consists of two passes. Pass 1: Transmission and Mask Computation 1. Transmission Image (Ct): Render the primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p using standard EWA splatting. Project each Gaussian i to screen space: \mathbf{u}'i = \Pi(\mathbf{u}i), \Sigma'i = \Pi(\Sigmai). Evaluate Gaussian value at pixel \mathbf{u}: Gi(\mathbf{u}) = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}'i)^\top (\Sigma'i)^{-1} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}'i)\right) Composite colors and opacities in depth order to produce Ct. 2. Reflection Mask (M): Render the glass Gaussians \mathcal{G}g onto the reflection plane to determine the spatial extent of the glass pane. This produces a mask M(\mathbf{u}) where M(\mathbf{u}) = 1 if the pixel corresponds to the glass, and 0 otherwise. 3. Reflection Strength Map (R): Compute the raw reflection strength R{raw} at each point on the reflection plane using the Fresnel reflectance model. The strength depends on the view direction, surface normal, and base reflectance. Filter the raw strength with the mask: R(\mathbf{u}) = R{raw}(\mathbf{u}) \times M(\mathbf{u}) R(\mathbf{u}) represents the view-dependent ratio of reflected light intensity relative to incident light intensity. Pass 2: Reflection Image Computation 1. Mirrored Gaussians (\hat{\mathcal{G}}p): Generate mirrored Gaussians by reflecting the primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p across the reflection plane P. For each primary Gaussian i with center \mathbf{u}i, compute the mirrored center \hat{\mathbf{u}}i: \hat{\mathbf{u}}i = \mathbf{u}i - 2(\mathbf{n}^\top (\mathbf{u}i - \mathbf{p})) \mathbf{n} Reflect the covariance matrix to account for the coordinate system flip (if necessary for correct orientation, though standard reflection of position and covariance is sufficient for splatting). 2. Raw Reflection Image (C{raw}): Render the mirrored Gaussians \hat{\mathcal{G}}p using standard EWA splatting to produce the raw reflection color C{raw}. 3. Reflection Intensity Map (A): Render the mirrored Gaussians' opacities/depths to compute an intensity map A that weights the reflection based on the visibility and density of the mirrored geometry. 4. Reflection Image (Cr): Combine the raw reflection and intensity: Cr(\mathbf{u}) = C{raw}(\mathbf{u}) \times A(\mathbf{u}) Final Composition Blend the transmission and reflection images using the reflection strength map R: C(\mathbf{u}) = (1 - R(\mathbf{u})) \cdot Ct(\mathbf{u}) + R(\mathbf{u}) \cdot Cr(\mathbf{u}) TR-Gaussians uses a three-stage optimization framework to ensure stable decomposition and prevent local optima. Stage 1: Initialization (3,000 iterations) Goal: Optimize primary Gaussians as vanilla 3DGS and initialize the reflection plane. Loss: L = (1 - \lambda)L1 + \lambda L{D-SSIM} where L1 is the L1 loss, L{D-SSIM} is the D-SSIM loss, and \lambda = 0.5. Output: The final image is set to C = Ct. The reflection plane P is initialized. Stage 2: Reflection Plane Adjustment (3,000 iterations) Goal: Refine the reflection plane and remove "reflection ghosts" from the transmission image. Loss: Enable the full rendering equation (Eq. 1) and additional decomposition losses (depth variance loss Ld and gradient conflict loss Lc, referenced as Eq. 17 in). Gradient Blocking: Gradients from the reflection image Cr are blocked from back-propagating to the primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p. This prevents the optimization from coupling reflection image errors with primary Gaussian placement, which would otherwise lead to incorrectly placed reflection planes. Stage 3: Joint Optimization (24,000 iterations) Goal: Final joint refinement of all parameters. Learning Rate: Reduce the learning rate of the reflection plane's position and normal by a factor of 0.1. Gradients: Allow full gradient propagation between all components. Opacity Perturbation: Enable periodic noise injection to escape local optima. Opacity Perturbation To prevent residual reflection components from remaining in the transmission image, noise is added to the opacities of primary Gaussians behind the reflection plane: 1. Project primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p onto the reflection plane P under all training viewpoints. 2. Select Gaussians whose center projections fall inside the plane boundaries. 3. Add uniformly distributed noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{U}[-0.4, 0.4] to the opacities of selected Gaussians. 4. Clamp opacities to [0, 1] every 1,000 iterations. 5. Interleave perturbation periods with clamping periods to avoid conflict with vanilla 3DGS clamping operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def rendertrgaussians(camera, primarygaussians, glassgaussians, reflectionplane): """ Renders the final image using the TR-Gaussians two-pass pipeline. Args: camera: Camera pose and projection matrices. primarygaussians: List of Gaussian objects (pos, opacity, SH, cov). glassgaussians: List of Gaussian objects defining the glass pane mask. reflectionplane: Object with position p, normal n, and base reflectance. Returns: finalimage: Rendered RGB image. """ # --- Pass 1: Transmission and Mask --- # 1. Render Transmission Image (Ct) # Standard 3DGS splatting for primary Gaussians Ct = render3dgs(camera, primarygaussians) # 2. Render Reflection Mask (M) # Render glass Gaussians to determine the spatial extent of the glass M = rendermask(camera, glassgaussians) # 3. Compute Reflection Strength Map (R) # Calculate Fresnel reflectance for each pixel on the plane Rraw = computefresnelstrength(camera, reflectionplane) # Filter by the mask R = Rraw M # --- Pass 2: Reflection Image --- # 4. Generate Mirrored Gaussians mirroredgaussians = [] for g in primarygaussians: # Reflect position across plane P # d = dot(n, g.pos - p) # gmirrored.pos = g.pos - 2 d n gmirrored = reflectgaussianacrossplane(g, reflectionplane) mirroredgaussians.append(gmirrored) # 5. Render Raw Reflection Image (Craw) Craw = render3dgs(camera, mirroredgaussians) # 6. Render Reflection Intensity Map (A) # Render opacities/depths of mirrored Gaussians to get intensity weighting A = renderintensity(camera, mirroredgaussians) # 7. Compute Reflection Image (Cr) Cr = Craw A # --- Composition --- # Blend Transmission and Reflection finalimage = (1 - R) Ct + R Cr return finalimage def computefresnelstrength(camera, plane): """ Computes the view-dependent Fresnel reflectance for each pixel. """ # Get view direction for each pixel viewdirs = getviewdirections(camera) # Get surface normal for each pixel (constant for planar reflection) normals = plane.normal # Compute Fresnel term (simplified Schlick approximation or exact Fresnel) # Rraw depends on angle between viewdir and normal, and base reflectance Rraw = fresnelmodel(viewdirs, normals, plane.basereflectance) return Rraw def reflectgaussianacrossplane(gaussian, plane): """ Reflects a Gaussian's position and covariance across a plane. """ p = plane.position n = plane.normal # Reflect position # d = dot(n, gaussian.pos - p) # newpos = gaussian.pos - 2 d n d = torch.dot(n, gaussian.pos - p) newpos = gaussian.pos - 2 d n # Reflect covariance (optional depending on implementation, # but position reflection is critical for correct geometry) # For splatting, reflecting position is usually sufficient # if the Gaussian is treated as a point source with spread. return Gaussian(newpos, gaussian.opacity, gaussian.sh, gaussian.cov) def optimizetrgaussians(primarygaussians, glassgaussians, reflectionplane, images, gtimages): """ Multi-stage optimization process. """ # Stage 1: Initialization (3000 iters) for i in range(3000): # Render only Ct Ct = render3dgs(camera, primarygaussians) loss = (1 - 0.5) L1loss(Ct, gtimages) + 0.5 DSSIMloss(Ct, gtimages) loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Initialize reflection plane P here (method specific) # Stage 2: Reflection Plane Adjustment (3000 iters) for i in range(3000): # Render full pipeline finalimage = rendertrgaussians(camera, primarygaussians, glassgaussians, reflectionplane) # Compute loss including decomposition losses (Ld, Lc) loss = computeloss(finalimage, gtimages, primarygaussians, reflectionplane) # Block gradients from reflection component to primary Gaussians # This is implementation-specific: detach reflection image gradients # or mask gradients in the backward pass loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Stage 3: Joint Optimization (24000 iters) for i in range(24000): # Apply opacity perturbation every 1000 iterations if i % 1000 == 0: applyopacityperturbation(primarygaussians, reflectionplane) # Render full pipeline finalimage = rendertrgaussians(camera, primarygaussians, glassgaussians, reflectionplane) # Compute full loss loss = computeloss(finalimage, gtimages, primarygaussians, reflectionplane) # Reduce LR for plane position/normal by 0.1 adjustlearningrates(reflectionplane, factor=0.1) loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Clamp opacities clampopacities(primarygaussians) def applyopacityperturbation(primarygaussians, plane): """ Adds noise to opacities of primary Gaussians behind the reflection plane. """ for g in primarygaussians: # Project center to plane d = torch.dot(plane.normal, g.pos - plane.position) if d < 0: # Behind the plane (assuming normal points out) # Check if projection falls inside plane bounds (simplified) # In practice, check if projected point is within glass mask M noise = torch.rand(1) 0.8 - 0.4 # Uniform [-0.4, 0.4] g.opacity = g.opacity + noise Rendering Speed: Approximately 225 FPS on the RTR dataset, compared to 338 FPS for vanilla 3DGS. This is roughly two-thirds the speed of vanilla 3DGS due to the two-pass rendering and additional computations for the reflection plane and mirrored Gaussians. Training Time: Moderate training time, totaling 30,000 iterations. This is significantly faster than NeRF-based methods which require hours of training. Memory: The representation adds overhead for the reflection plane parameters and the glass Gaussians, but remains comparable to 3DGS in terms of Gaussian count, as it does not rely on excessive low-opacity Gaussians to fit reflections. Strengths: High-fidelity rendering of planar transmission and reflection. Explicit decomposition prevents "reflection ghosts" and noisy artifacts in novel views. Real-time rendering capability. Handles complex view-dependent Fresnel effects. Limitations: Limited to planar reflections (glass panes, mirrors). Performance is lower than vanilla 3DGS. Requires careful initialization and multi-stage optimization to avoid local optima. When to use: Suitable for indoor scenes with transparent glass panes or mirrors where high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required. Not suitable for non-planar reflections or scenes without significant transmission/reflection components. TR-Gaussians was proposed by Yong Liu, Keyang Ye, Tianjia Shao, and Kun Zhou from Zhejiang University. The method was published in the IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG) in 2026 (arXiv preprint 2511.13009v1, Nov 2025). It addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS in handling glass panes, where the standard method fails to distinguish between transmission and reflection, leading to artifacts in novel views. The work builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting and contrasts with methods like MirrorGaussian (which handles only pure reflection) and NeRF-based approaches (which are slower and lack robust decomposition). name: DOF-GS
head: Adjustable Depth-of-Field 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: DOF-GS is a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that incorporates a finite-aperture camera model to explicitly model and render depth-of-field (DOF) effects, enabling post-capture control of aperture and focal distance. Unlike previous NeRF-based techniques that simulate defocus via expensive per-ray blur kernels or recent 3DGS methods that use black-box neural networks for shape offsets, DOF-GS blurs individual Gaussians based on learnable Circle-of-Confusion (CoC) cues before compositing, allowing efficient, differentiable, and intuitive DOF adjustment. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images with moderate defocus blur. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D scene representation \mathcal{S} consisting of anisotropic 3D Gaussian points, and optimized camera parameters (aperture and focal distance) per view. Scene Representation: The scene is represented by a set of K anisotropic 3D Gaussian points \{Gk\}{k=1}^K. Each Gaussian Gk is defined by: Center position uk Covariance matrix \Sigmak, derived from anisotropic scaling sk and quaternion qk Opacity ok Spherical harmonics coefficients hk The 3D Gaussian function is defined as: Gk(p) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(p - uk)^T \Sigmak^{-1} (p - uk)\right) Projection: 3D Gaussian points are projected to 2D screen space. The Jacobian J of the projective transformation is calculated. The 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'k is computed as: \Sigma'k = J W \Sigmak W^T J^T where W is the view matrix transforming points from world space to camera space. The 2D Gaussian in screen space is: G'k(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - u'k)^T \Sigma'^{-1}k (x - u'k)\right) where u'k is the 2D center position post-projection. Standard Rasterization: For each pixel x, a small number Nx of Gaussians within a cutoff radius t are associated with it. The image is rendered using alpha blending: \tilde{I}(x) = \sum{i=1}^{Nx} Ti \alphai ci where \alphai = G'i(x), Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance, and ci is the view-dependent color of the i-th Gaussian. DOF Rendering: A differentiable DOF rendering process is integrated into the rasterizer. Individual Gaussians are blurred based on learnable CoC cues before compositing. This process is fully differentiable, allowing optimization of camera parameters alongside the 3D scene. CoC Calculation: The radius of the Circle-of-Confusion (CoC) R{coc} for an object point at depth zo is determined by the focal length F, aperture diameter A, and focal distance f: R{coc} = \frac{1}{2} F A \frac{|zo - f|}{zo (f - F)} Since F is often much smaller than f and object depths, this is simplified to: R{coc} = \frac{1}{2} Q \left| \frac{1}{zo} - \frac{1}{f} \right| where Q = FA is a simplified aperture parameter. CoC-Guided Detail Enhancement: A lightweight CoC-guided neural network predicts an in-focus mask for each view. These masks are used to enhance details within All-in-Focus (AiF) renderings during optimization, counteracting reduced sharpness due to defocus blur in multi-view inputs. Optimization: The scene representation \mathcal{S} and camera parameters are optimized by minimizing the reconstruction loss L{rec} between rendered views \tilde{I}m and training views Im: \min{\mathcal{S}} \sum{m=1}^M L{rec}(\tilde{I}m, Im) The loss is a weighted combination of MSE and DSSIM: L{rec}(Ia, Ib) = ||Ia - Ib|| + \lambda{dssim} L{dssim}(Ia, Ib) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecocradius(zo, F, A, f): """ Compute Circle-of-Confusion radius. zo: depth of object point F: focal length A: aperture diameter f: focal distance """ # Simplified formula from Q = F A return 0.5 Q abs(1/zo - 1/f) def projectgaussian(Gk, W, J): """ Project 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space. Gk: {uk, Sigmak} W: view matrix J: Jacobian of projective transformation """ uprimek = projectpoint(uk, W, J) # Standard projection Sigmaprimek = J @ W @ Sigmak @ W.T @ J.T return uprimek, Sigmaprimek def rendergaussianwithdof(uprimek, Sigmaprimek, alpha, color, cocradius, pixelx): """ Render a single Gaussian with DOF blur. The Gaussian is blurred based on cocradius before evaluation. """ # In practice, this modifies the effective Sigmaprimek or alpha value # based on the CoC radius derived from the depth of the Gaussian center. # The source states Gaussians are blurred based on learnable CoC cues. # A simple implementation might scale the alpha or sigma by the CoC factor. # Specific implementation of "blurring individual Gaussians" is not detailed # beyond the CoC formula and the claim of differentiability. # We assume the alpha value is modulated or the Gaussian is convolved. # For the purpose of this article, we note the dependency on CoC. effectivealpha = alpha modulationfactor(cocradius) # Placeholder for specific blur kernel application return effectivealpha, color def optimizescene(Gaussians, CameraParams, TrainingImages, Lambdadssim): """ Optimize scene and camera parameters. """ for viewindex, trainingimage in enumerate(TrainingImages): # 1. Get learnable camera params for this view A = CameraParams[viewindex].aperture f = CameraParams[viewindex].focaldistance F = CameraParams[viewindex].focallength # Assumed constant or known # 2. Render scene with DOF renderedimage = renderdofscene(Gaussians, A, f, F) # 3. Compute CoC-guided in-focus mask (via lightweight NN) # The structure of the lightweight NN is not provided. infocusmask = predictinfocusmask(renderedimage, Gaussians) # 4. Enhance details in All-in-Focus rendering using mask # Specific enhancement logic is not detailed. enhancedrenderedimage = enhancedetails(renderedimage, infocusmask) # 5. Compute Loss loss = mseloss(enhancedrenderedimage, trainingimage) + \ Lambdadssim dssimloss(enhancedrenderedimage, trainingimage) # 6. Backpropagate to update Gaussians and CameraParams loss.backward() # Update parameters Gaussians.step() CameraParams.step() Time Complexity: Rendering is efficient, leveraging the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline with additional CoC-based blurring. This is significantly faster than NeRF-based defocus methods which require hours to days of training and yield <1 FPS. Memory Complexity: Stores standard 3DGS attributes plus learnable camera parameters (A, f) per view and a lightweight neural network for CoC-guided detail enhancement. Strengths: Enables post-capture control of aperture and focal distance; differentiable optimization allows learning camera characteristics from defocused images; efficient compared to ray-tracing based defocus methods. Limitations: Requires multi-view defocused images for training; relies on a simplified thin lens model. When to use: When post-capture DOF control and refocusing from multi-view defocused inputs is required. When not to use: For scenes without defocus blur where standard pinhole 3DGS is sufficient, or when real-time performance on extremely low-end hardware is critical without the overhead of the CoC-guided network. DOF-GS was introduced to address the limitations of the pinhole camera model in existing 3DGS methods, which lack effective modeling of defocus effects. It builds on the 3DGS framework [8] and surface-splatting techniques [10], extending them with a finite-aperture camera model. The method was tested on scenes from the multi-view defocus blur dataset [15]. name: Temporal Gaussian Splatting
head: TemporalGS
body: Temporal Gaussian Splatting (TemporalGS) is a training-free, plug-and-play acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that leverages temporal priors from previous frames to reduce computational redundancy in Gaussian preprocessing, sorting, and rasterization. It solves the challenge of high FPS and low latency rendering by culling unnecessary Gaussians and approximating static regions via warped buffers, achieving up to 1.48× acceleration over vanilla 3DGS while maintaining competitive quality. Unlike sibling methods that may require post-training compression or hardware-specific optimizations, TemporalGS operates as a software rasterization plugin that interleaves dynamic culling and selective rendering intervals. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, camera poses Wt (reference) and W{t+i} (target), intrinsic matrix K, and temporal priors from reference frame It (TGB, TAB, Temporal Gaussian Buffer). Outputs: Rendered frame \bar{I}{t+i} for intermediate frames i \in [1, \lambda-1]. Data Structures: 1. Temporal Geometry Buffer (TGB): Stores per-pixel depth Dt(x,y) and depth standard deviation \sigmat(x,y) for the reference frame. Dt(x,y) = \frac{\sum{Gi \in Tk} wi(x,y) di}{\sum{Gi \in Tk} wi(x,y)} \sigmat(x,y) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum{Gi \in Tk} wi(x,y) (di - Dt(x,y))^2}{\sum{Gi \in Tk} wi(x,y)}} Where Tk is the tile containing pixel (x,y), wi is the Gaussian weight, and di is the Gaussian depth. 2. Temporal Appearance Buffer (TAB): The color image of the reference frame It. 3. Temporal Gaussian Buffer (G{rendered}): The subset of Gaussians that contributed to the reference frame. G{rendered} = \{Gi \mid \max{(x,y) \in It} wi(x,y) > 0\} Parameters: \lambda: Interval between reference frames. Accelerates \lambda-1 frames between It and I{t+\lambda}. Typical value: Not given in the sources. \lambda{TDC}: Interval for Temporal Dynamic Culling. Typical value: 50. \lambda{SR}: Interval for Selective Rendering. Typical value: 5. \eta: Threshold percentage of selected tiles triggering a pseudo reference frame. Typical value: 40%. \lambda1, \lambda2: Variance range parameters for surface modeling in TGB. Typical values: \lambda1=3, \lambda2=0. \epsilon: Small constant for depth initialization. Value: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Reference Frame Rendering: Render reference frame It using standard 3DGS. Construct TGB (Dt, \sigmat), TAB (It), and G{rendered}. 2. Initialization: For the target frame t+i, initialize warped depth D'{min} to z{far} + \epsilon and warped standard deviation \sigma'{max} to 0. 3. Forward Warping: Map pixels from It to t+i using camera matrices Wt, W{t+i} and intrinsic K: (x', y') \approx K W{t+i} Wt^{-1} Dt(x,y) K^{-1} [x, y, 1]^T Clip to nearest pixel. If multiple source pixels map to the same destination, preserve the geometry closer to the camera (minimum depth) and maximum standard deviation to obtain high recall. Update D'{min} and \sigma'{max} at the destination pixels. 4. Surface Modeling: Define the visible surface range at t+i as [D'{min} - \lambda1 \sigma'{max}, D'{min} + \lambda2 \sigma'{max}]. 5. Temporal Dynamic Culling (TDC): Performed every \lambda{TDC} frames. Adaptive Frustum Culling (AFC): After near-plane culling, keep only Gaussians Gi where F{min} \leq ndci \leq F{max}. ndci = \text{Pix2NDC}(\mu'i), where \mu'i is the 2D mean of Gi in screen space. F{min} = \min{Gj \in G{rendered}} (ndcj), F{max} = \max{Gj \in G{rendered}} (ndcj). Temporal Occlusion Culling (TOC): Remove Gaussians Gi whose 2D means are in screen space AND whose depth di > D'{min}(\bar{\mu}i) + \lambda2 \sigma'{max}(\bar{\mu}i), where \bar{\mu}i is the nearest screen pixel to Gi's mean. Note: Pixels with no warped geometry retain z{far} + \epsilon depth, allowing new closer surfaces to be included. 6. Selective Rendering (SR): Performed every \lambda{SR} frames. Depth Repair: Identify "no-hit" pixels in warped depth map (where D'{min} == z{far} + \epsilon). If all 3x3 neighbors are valid, fill the pixel with the average of neighbors. Denote repaired depth as D'{min}'. Tile Selection: Perform backward warping (inverse of forward warping) on D'{min}' to query correspondence in reference frame. Mark tile Tk as T{unselected} if any pixel in Tk fails to find correspondence. Combine Selection: T{selected} = T{oc\selected} \cup T{unselected}, where T{oc\selected} are tiles intersecting Gaussians that passed TOC but were not culled by AFC logic (or specifically those requiring re-evaluation). Note: The source defines T{selected} as the union of tiles requiring rendering due to occlusion culling results and unmatched tiles.. 7. Rendering: Sort Gaussians intersecting T{selected} by depth. Render T{selected} tiles using standard alpha blending. For tiles T \setminus T{selected}, use the warped TAB \bar{I}{t \to t+i} obtained via backward warping of It using D'{min}' and bilinear interpolation. Stitch rendered tiles and warped TAB to form \bar{I}{t+i}. 8. Adaptive Reference Frame Insertion: If the number of selected tiles at t+i exceeds \eta\% of total tiles, force t+i+1 to be a pseudo reference frame (rendered with AFC). 9. Loop: Interleave TDC and SR steps for intermediate frames. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalgaussiansplatting(Gaussians, Wref, Wtarget, K, TGB, TAB, Grendered, lambdaval, lambdaTDC, lambdaSR, eta, lambda1, lambda2, zfar, epsilon): """ Render intermediate frame between reference and target using TemporalGS. """ # 1. Forward Warping # Initialize warped buffers warpeddepth = np.fulllike(TGB.depth, zfar + epsilon) warpedsigmamax = np.zeroslike(TGB.depth) # Map reference pixels to target for y, x in pixelsinTGB: depthz = TGB.depth[y, x] # Unproject to 3D p3dref = unproject(x, y, depthz, K, Wref) # Project to target view p2dtarget = project(p3dref, K, Wtarget) tx, ty = cliptopixel(p2dtarget) # Update max sigma and min depth (high recall) sigma = TGB.sigma[y, x] if sigma > warpedsigmamax[ty, tx]: warpedsigmamax[ty, tx] = sigma if depthz < warpeddepth[ty, tx]: warpeddepth[ty, tx] = depthz Dmin = warpeddepth Sigmamax = warpedsigmamax # 2. Temporal Dynamic Culling (if interval matches) if framecount % lambdaTDC == 0: # Adaptive Frustum Culling ndcmin = min([pix2ndc(g.mean) for g in Grendered]) ndcmax = max([pix2ndc(g.mean) for g in Grendered]) filteredGaussians = [] for g in Grendered: # Near-plane culling first if not nearplanecull(g, Wtarget): continue ndc = pix2ndc(g.mean) if ndcmin <= ndc <= ndcmax: # Temporal Occlusion Culling # Find nearest screen pixel to g.mean mubar = nearestscreenpixel(g.mean, Wtarget, K) # Check against warped geometry dminbuf = Dmin[mubar.y, mubar.x] sigmamaxbuf = Sigmamax[mubar.y, mubar.x] # If g is behind the warped surface (considering variance) if g.depth > dminbuf + lambda2 sigmamaxbuf: continue # Cull filteredGaussians.append(g) Gactive = filteredGaussians else: Gactive = Grendered # Use full buffer if not TDC interval, or previous active set? # Source implies TDC filters Grendered. If not TDC, we likely use the result of previous step or full set. # Assuming we maintain the set of Gaussians that contributed to the last valid state. # For simplicity in this plug-in context, we assume Grendered is the base, # but TDC reduces it. If TDC is skipped, we might still use TOC logic if implemented continuously, # but source says TDC is an interval strategy. # Let's assume Gactive is the set passed from previous frame or Grendered if no culling occurred. # To be safe and implementable: if not TDC, we don't do AFC/TOC, so Gactive = Grendered. The remaining Gaussians are rendered. # But SR selects TILES. # Let's assume Tselected contains tiles that need rasterization. # Tumselected are tiles with unmatched pixels. # Tocselected might refer to tiles containing Gaussians that were NOT culled by TOC? # No, TOC removes Gaussians. So Gaussians in non-selected tiles are ignored in rasterization. # So Tselected must contain all tiles that contain ANY surviving Gaussian? # No, that's just standard rendering. # The key is: "render only tiles that cannot be approximated". # So if a tile is NOT selected, we use TAB. This implies Gaussians in non-selected tiles are NOT rendered. # Therefore, Tselected must be the set of tiles containing Gaussians that are NOT approximated by TAB. # Tumselected are tiles with unmatched pixels (geometry changed). # Tocselected: The source says "Tselected = Tocselected U Tumselected". # And "Gaussians intersected with Tselected are sorted". # This implies Tocselected are tiles that contain Gaussians that passed TOC? # If so, we render ALL tiles with surviving Gaussians? # Let's look at "Selective Rendering... leverages a tile selection algorithm to only render a small portion". # This suggests Tselected is a SUBSET of tiles. # If Tocselected is "tiles with surviving Gaussians", that's likely all tiles. # Perhaps Tocselected is empty in the SR context, or refers to tiles where TOC was NOT performed? # Given the text "Tselected = Tocselected U Tumselected", and Toc is part of TDC, # it's possible Tocselected refers to tiles where the culling decision was "keep", # but this is redundant if we just render all kept Gaussians. # Let's stick to the explicit definition: Tumselected are tiles with unmatched pixels. # We will assume Tselected = Tumselected for the purpose of "small portion". # If the source implies Tocselected adds more tiles, it's not defined how. # We will implement Tselected = Tumselected. Tselected = Tumselected else: # If not SR interval, do we render all? # Source: "interleaved every lambdaTDC and lambdaSR intervals". # If not SR, we might just use TAB for everything? Or render all? # "During stream rendering... combined and interleaved". # If SR is skipped, we likely rely on TDC to reduce Gaussians, but render all remaining? # Or use TAB for all? # Standard 3DGS renders all. TemporalGS accelerates. # If SR is off, we probably render all surviving Gaussians (standard 3DGS on filtered set). Tselected = alltiles # 4. Render Image = np.zeroslike(TAB) # Render selected tiles for tile in Tselected: # Get Gaussians intersecting tile Gtile = [g for g in Gactive if intersects(g, tile)] # Sort by depth Gtile.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) # Rasterize Image[tile] = rasterize(Gtile, tile, K) # Warp TAB for non-selected tiles if Tselected != alltiles: # Backward warp TAB using Dminrepaired Iwarped = backwardwarp(TAB, Dminrepaired, K, Wref, Wtarget) for tile in alltiles: if tile not in Tselected: Image[tile] = Iwarped[tile] return Image def hascorrespondence(px, py, Dminrepaired, K, Wref, Wtarget): # Check if (px, py) in target has valid depth if Dminrepaired[py, px] >= zfar + epsilon: return False # Check if backward warp is within bounds # Simplified: if depth is valid, assume correspondence exists return True Time Complexity: Reduces sorting and rasterization cost by culling Gaussians (TDC) and rendering only a subset of tiles (SR). The acceleration factor is up to 1.48× compared to vanilla 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for TGB (depth + sigma), TAB (color), and G{rendered} (Gaussian indices). TGB can be downscaled by factor of 2 on large-scale scenes. Strengths: Training-free, plug-and-play, works with software and hardware rasterization, maintains high quality. Limitations: Performance degrades with significant camera motion or large view changes (triggering pseudo reference frames). Accuracy depends on 3DGS surface representation. When to use: Stream rendering, video playback, or applications requiring high FPS with moderate camera motion. When not to use: Scenes with rapid, large-scale changes where \eta threshold is frequently exceeded, causing frequent reference frame resets. TemporalGS was introduced as the first training-free, plug-and-play algorithmic approach to accelerate 3DGS rendering using temporal priors. It addresses the computational bottleneck of sorting and rasterization in 3DGS by leveraging temporal coherence between consecutive frames. name: Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training
head: Ghost cell techniques adapted for unstructured primitives
body: Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training resolves boundary artifacts in chunked volume training by including ellipsoids from neighboring chunks in the loss computation without updating their parameters, providing boundary context without requiring a global volume or merged model. Unlike chunk-based 3DGS methods that resolve boundary inconsistencies by merging chunks into a global coarse model or through post-training stages, this method requires boundary support during training itself without access to a global volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D ellipsoids partitioned into spatial chunks, each with a defined spatial extent and normalized coordinate space. Output: Updated parameters for the current chunk's ellipsoids, with boundary context provided by ghost ellipsoids from neighbors. Data Structures: Chunk: A spatial subdivision of the volume. Ellipsoid Primitive: Defined by position \mathbf{p}, rotation matrix R, scale matrix S, and covariance \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. Positions are stored with a per-chunk spatial offset mapping them to the shared world coordinate system. Ghost Region: A boundary region around each chunk, defined by the chunk boundary offset, used to identify neighboring ellipsoids that influence the current chunk's loss. Steps: 1. Chunk Partitioning: Divide the volume into chunks. Each chunk is trained in its own normalized coordinate space scaled to its spatial extent (e.g., [-0.5, 0.5]^3 for a volume split into 2 \times 2 \times 2 chunks). 2. Ghost Ellipsoid Identification: For each chunk, identify boundary ellipsoids from all neighboring chunks (face-, edge-, and vertex-adjacent) by selecting those whose centers fall within the ghost region of the current chunk. 3. Voxelization and Loss Computation: Voxelize the ghost ellipsoids together with the current chunk's ellipsoids during the loss computation step. 4. Gradient Update: Ensure that ghost ellipsoids receive no gradient updates. Only the parameters of the ellipsoids belonging to the current chunk are updated. 5. Training Mode Selection: Sequential Mode (Single-GPU): Chunks are trained one at a time using ghost ellipsoids from completed neighbors. Parallel Mode (Multi-GPU): All chunks are trained simultaneously with ghost ellipsoids periodically synchronized across GPUs. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Coordinate Space Rescaling: Training all chunks in a shared [-1, 1]^3 space and applying post-hoc rescaling is computationally impractical. It requires computing \Sigma' = K \Sigma K^T = K R S S^T R^T K^T for each primitive, where K is a chunk-dependent anisotropic scale matrix. Since K and R do not generally commute, this cannot be simplified by scaling S alone. Correctly decomposing \Sigma' back into rotation and scale parameters requires a QR decomposition per primitive. Merging: The per-chunk primitive sets resulting from this method can be merged through simple concatenation without additional alignment, avoiding the need for global model merging. A training scheme for large volumes that partitions the volume into spatially non-overlapping chunks and uses ghost ellipsoids to provide boundary context. Ghost ellipsoids are used to provide boundary context across neighboring chunks during optimization, enabling scalable learning on volumes exceeding GPU memory. Training chunks separately introduces boundary artifacts because ellipsoids near chunk borders lack support from neighboring regions. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates boundary artifacts without requiring a global volume or merged model. Avoids computationally expensive QR decompositions associated with post-hoc rescaling. Limitations: Requires identification of neighboring ellipsoids and synchronization (in parallel mode). When to use: When training large volumes on limited GPU memory by chunking, and boundary consistency is critical. When not to use: When a global model can be afforded or when post-training merging is acceptable. The technique is inspired by ghost cell techniques [45], but adapted for unstructured primitives. Classical ghost cells copy boundary values from adjacent regular grid cells, but this method cannot rely on grid adjacency since the primitives are spatially unstructured. The method addresses the incompatibility of standard 3DGS screenspace rasterization with accurate TF mapping in volumetric settings. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Substitutive LOD with K-wise Moment-Matched Merging
head: Cost-aware merging, Cost-increment relocation, Gaussian Hierarchy, Greedy hierarchical LOD, Joint relaxation LOD, Level of Detail (LOD) via Gaussian Merging, Merged Gaussian LOD
body: Substitutive LOD with K-wise moment-matched merging is a technique for reducing the number of 3D Gaussians in a scene by merging groups of K splats into a single representative Gaussian, thereby boosting rendering performance and managing memory constraints. It addresses the problem of excessive Gaussian counts and associated aliasing artifacts by replacing small or redundant Gaussians with larger, merged ones. Unlike methods that modify Gaussians during reconstruction or prune based on static importance, this method operates on the final set of Gaussians using cost metrics to guide the merging process, allowing for runtime LOD selection. It sets itself apart from siblings like CoR-GS and EffGS by focusing on substitutive merging via moment matching rather than density control or vector quantization. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each Gaussian gi is defined by its mean \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai (or Cholesky factor Ri), and opacity/amplitude \alphai. Outputs: A reduced set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with N' < N Gaussians, where each output Gaussian is a moment-matched merge of K input Gaussians. Data Structures: The implementation relies on a spatial partitioning structure (e.g., grid or octree) to identify candidate groups of K Gaussians for merging. Each Gaussian is stored with its parameters: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (symmetric positive definite). \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity or amplitude. Optional: Color coefficients (not detailed in sources for the merging math). Parameters: K: The number of Gaussians to merge into one. Compression factors of four and above are used in experiments. Cost Metric: One of L2, Cauchy–Schwarz, gKL, W2, MMD, or L∞. Partitioning Algorithm: One of Greedy Hierarchical, Cost-Increment Relocation, or Joint Relaxation. Steps: 1. Spatial Partitioning: Divide the scene into spatial bins or tiles to group nearby Gaussians. 2. Group Selection: Identify groups of K Gaussians within each bin that are candidates for merging. The selection is guided by the chosen cost metric and partitioning algorithm. 3. Merging: For each group of K Gaussians, compute a single merged Gaussian using moment matching. The merged mean \mu' and covariance \Sigma' are computed as the weighted average of the input means and covariances, weighted by their amplitudes \alphai. The merged amplitude \alpha' is optimized to minimize the L2 error between the merged Gaussian and the sum of the original Gaussians. 4. Replacement: Replace the K input Gaussians with the single merged Gaussian in the scene representation. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–4 until the desired compression factor is reached or no further beneficial merges can be found. Formulas: Merged mean: \mu' = \frac{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai \mui}{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai}. Merged covariance: \Sigma' = \frac{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai (\Sigmai + (\mui - \mu')(\mui - \mu')^T)}{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai}. L2-optimal amplitude: \alpha' = \frac{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai \mathcal{N}(\mu'; \mui, \Sigmai + \Sigma')}{\mathcal{N}(\mu'; \mu', 2\Sigma')}, where \mathcal{N}(\mua; \mub, \Sigma{sum}) is the Gaussian PDF evaluated at \mua with mean \mub and covariance \Sigma{sum}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mergegaussians(group): """Merges a group of K Gaussians into one using moment matching.""" totalalpha = sum(g.alpha for g in group) muprime = [sum(g.alpha g.mu[j] for g in group) / totalalpha for j in range(3)] sigmaprime = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for g in group: diff = [g.mu[j] - muprime[j] for j in range(3)] for r in range(3): for c in range(3): sigmaprime[r][c] += g.alpha (g.sigma[r][c] + diff[r] diff[c]) for r in range(3): for c in range(3): sigmaprime[r][c] /= totalalpha numerator = 0.0 for g in group: sumcov = [[g.sigma[r][c] + sigmaprime[r][c] for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] numerator += g.alpha gaussianpdf(muprime, sumcov) denomcov = [[2 sigmaprime[r][c] for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] denominator = gaussianpdf(muprime, denomcov) alphaprime = numerator / denominator return (muprime, sigmaprime, alphaprime) def gaussianpdf(mu, sigma): diff = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] inv = invert3x3(sigma) det = det3x3(sigma) exponent = -0.5 sum(diff[j] sum(inv[j][k] diff[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)) return (1.0 / ((2 3.14159265358979) 1.5 (det 0.5))) (2.718281828459045 exponent) def invert3x3(M): d = det3x3(M) return [[(M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])/d, (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])/d, (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])/d], [(M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])/d, (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])/d, (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])/d], [(M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])/d, (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])/d, (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])/d]] def det3x3(M): return M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0]) def substitutivelod(gaussians, K, metric, algorithm): """Performs substitutive LOD by merging Gaussians.""" bins = {} for g in gaussians: binkey = spatialhash(g.mu) bins.setdefault(binkey, []).append(g) mergedgaussians = [] for binkey, bingaussians in bins.items(): if len(bingaussians) >= K: groups = selectgroupsfrombin(bingaussians, K, metric, algorithm) for group in groups: mergedg = mergegaussians(group) mergedgaussians.append(mergedg) remaining = bingaussians[len(groups)K:] for g in remaining: mergedgaussians.append(g) else: mergedgaussians.extend(bingaussians) return mergedgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spectral lower bounds have explicit limits and counterexamples where they fail to accurately predict merging quality. Precision issues may arise when computing the L2-optimal amplitude, especially for very small or very large Gaussians. Boundary effects in spatial partitioning may lead to suboptimal merging if Gaussians near bin boundaries are not considered. A partitioning algorithm that merges Gaussians hierarchically, similar to the Runnalls algorithm. A partitioning algorithm that relocates Gaussians to minimize the cost increment of merging. It matches greedy merging within 5.5% at compression factors of four and above. A partitioning algorithm that relaxes the merging constraints to find a globally optimal solution. Time Complexity: Depends on the partitioning algorithm and the cost metric. Memory Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussians by a factor of K, thus reducing memory usage by approximately 1/K. Measured Performance: Cost-increment relocation matches greedy merging within 5.5% at compression factors of four and above. Cost-aware merging beats mass-ranked culling with and without amplitude refit on full fits, while culling wins in the median on sparse subsamples. Strengths: Effective at reducing aliasing and managing memory footprint, especially on mobile devices. Limitations: Spectral lower bounds may fail to predict merging quality accurately. When to Use: When memory constraints are tight or rendering performance needs to be boosted without modifying the reconstruction process. When Not to Use: When high fidelity is required and compression artifacts are unacceptable. The method was introduced in the context of Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualization. It builds on earlier work by Yan et al. [24] who combined Gaussians to solve aliasing problems, and Kerbl et al. [18] who introduced a hierarchy of Gaussians. The technique is part of the broader effort to make 3D Gaussian Splatting more efficient and scalable, particularly for mobile and web-based applications. name: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3DGS with temporal constraints, DG-Mesh, Dynamic 3DGS, Li et al
body: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle time-varying scenes by assigning time-varying position and rotation attributes to each Gaussian primitive. It solves the problem of temporal flicker and storage explosion inherent in per-frame baselines by enforcing physical plausibility through local-rigid and As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) or isometry constraints. Unlike 4D Gaussian Splatting which uses implicit neural fields or planes to predict deformation offsets from a canonical space, this method explicitly tracks the motion of each Gaussian particle, offering a more direct representation of dynamic geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of T images \{It\}{t=1}^T with known camera poses \{Ct\}{t=1}^T. Outputs: A set of N dynamic 3D Gaussians, where each Gaussian i is defined by a time-varying position \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t), rotation qi(t), scale \mathbf{s}i (static), opacity \alphai(t), and color representation. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3: Time-varying center position. qi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^4: Time-varying unit quaternion for rotation. \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Static scale vector. \alphai(t) \in \mathbb{R}: Time-varying opacity. Color features: Base color \mathbf{c}{base}, view-related feature \mathbf{f}{view}, time-related feature \mathbf{f}{time}. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a set of 3D Gaussians from the first frame or via structure-from-motion, similar to static 3DGS. 2. Temporal Parameterization: Position and Rotation: Model \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) and qi(t) using explicit functions. Li et al. [81] propose using a polynomial function to model motion and orientation. The final color \mathbf{c}i(t, \mathbf{v}) is computed as: \mathbf{c}i(t, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{c}{base} + \text{MLP}(\mathbf{f}{view}, \mathbf{f}{time}) where \mathbf{c}{base} is the base color, and the MLP outputs a residual color based on view direction \mathbf{v} and time t. 3. Boundaries: Temporal extrapolation outside the training time range may be unstable if the polynomial or RBF functions are not constrained. GaussianFlow is a point-based differentiable rendering approach for dynamic 3D scene reconstruction that models a 4D scene as a set of deformable 3D Gaussian particles advected by an explicit 3D velocity field. It solves the problem of efficient dynamic scene reconstruction by introducing a Dual-Domain Deformation Model (DDDM) that explicitly models attribute deformations (position, rotation, radiance) in both time and frequency domains, eliminating the need for implicit neural fields or per-frame optimization. Unlike Dynamic 3D Gaussians which tracks motion via persistent view synthesis and local constraints, GaussianFlow uses a global flow-based deformation model, achieving 5× faster training than per-frame 3DGS while preserving real-time rendering speeds. Dynamic 3D Gaussians performs tracking by persistent dynamic view synthesis, linking the motion of each Gaussian to the movement of a corresponding 3D point in the scene. It extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle dynamic scenes by explicitly defining a tracking mechanism that differs from its parent Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting and from GaussianFlow by relying on persistent synthesis rather than flow-based deformation fields. SWAGS is a dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting method that addresses the challenge of modeling complex, non-rigid motion in dynamic scenes by partitioning the temporal sequence into distinct windows based on motion intensity. Unlike sibling methods that track a single global deformation field or flow across the entire sequence, SWAGS trains separate dynamic 3DGS models for each window, each with its own canonical space and deformation field, thereby isolating local motion characteristics. This approach improves reconstruction fidelity for highly dynamic segments while maintaining temporal consistency through fine-tuning on overlapping frames. SpeeDe3DGS is a method that accelerates deformable 3DGS by applying temporal pruning. It identifies static and active Gaussians and groups the dynamic parts by motion similarity to reduce the number of deformation queries. This variant constructs an opacity offset table to model changes in digital subtraction angiography. This method leverages a diffusion prior to enhance dynamic scene reconstruction and proposes a neural bone transformation module for reconstructing animatable objects from monocular video. DynMF assumes that each dynamic scene is composed of a finite, fixed number of motion trajectories represented in a learned basis, generated by a small temporal MLP. All motion trajectories in the scene can be linearly represented in this learned basis, with regularization, sparsity, and local rigidity terms introduced during optimization. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to per-frame baselines due to explicit deformation modeling, but depends on the complexity of the temporal functions (polynomial/RBF) and the MLP for color. GaussianFlow claims 5× faster training than per-frame 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Storage is linear in the number of Gaussians N and the size of the temporal parameters (polynomial coefficients, RBF weights, MLP weights). It is more compact than storing a full 3DGS per frame but potentially larger than implicit deformation fields if the number of Gaussians is high. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Large-scale scenes stress the rasterizer through primitive count and memory bandwidth, similar to static 3DGS. Strengths: Real-time rendering of dynamic scenes; explicit representation allows for easy editing and manipulation; avoids overfitting associated with implicit neural fields. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of temporal constraints to avoid artifacts; may struggle with highly complex, non-rigid motions without sufficient Gaussian density. When to use: Real-time dynamic scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. When not to use: Scenes with extremely high-frequency temporal changes that cannot be captured by the chosen temporal functions. Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Luiten et al. in 3DV'24. It emerged as a response to the limitations of per-frame 3DGS training, which suffers from storage explosion and temporal flicker. The method builds on the explicit nature of 3D Gaussian Splatting, extending it to 4D by parameterizing the Gaussian attributes over time. It is part of a broader family of dynamic 3DGS methods, including 4D Gaussian Splatting and Deformable 3DGS, which explore different approaches to modeling temporal dynamics. name: GaussianFlow
head: Dual-Domain Deformation Model (DDDM), Guo et al
body: GaussianFlow is a point-based differentiable rendering approach for dynamic 3D scene reconstruction that models a 4D scene as a set of deformable 3D Gaussian particles advected by an explicit 3D velocity field. It solves the problem of efficient dynamic scene reconstruction by introducing a Dual-Domain Deformation Model (DDDM) that explicitly models attribute deformations (position, rotation, radiance) in both time and frequency domains, eliminating the need for implicit neural fields or per-frame optimization. Unlike Dynamic 3D Gaussians which tracks motion via persistent view synthesis and local constraints, GaussianFlow uses a global flow-based deformation model, achieving 5× faster training than per-frame 3DGS while preserving real-time rendering speeds. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of images (multi-view or monocular video) with known camera poses. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} where each Gaussian i has time-varying attributes: position \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t), rotation qi(t), and radiance/color ci(t). The method outputs a 4D representation that can be rendered at any arbitrary time t. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores base attributes \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, qi \in \mathbb{R}^4, ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^3, \alphai \in \mathbb{R} and DDDM deformation parameters: polynomial coefficients \mathbf{P}{pos}, \mathbf{P}{rot}, \mathbf{P}{color} for time-domain fitting, and Fourier coefficients \mathbf{F}{pos}, \mathbf{F}{rot}, \mathbf{F}{color} for frequency-domain fitting. Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a static 3DGS reconstruction at t0. Initialize DDDM coefficients to zero. 2. Static Optimization: Optimize static Gaussian attributes and DDDM coefficients for a subset of frames or the reference frame to establish a baseline. 3. Dynamic Optimization Loop: a. Forward Pass: For each training image at time tj: i. Compute deformation residuals \Delta \mathbf{A}i(tj) using DDDM. ii. Update Gaussian attributes to \mathbf{A}i(tj). iii. Render the image using differentiable rasterization. b. Loss Computation: i. Image Loss: \mathcal{L}{img} = \lambda{rgb} \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{ssim} \mathcal{L}{SSIM} between rendered and ground truth images. ii. Temporal Smoothness Loss: Encourages smooth deformation over time. iii. KNN Rigid Loss: Regularizes motion trajectory by assuming local neighborhoods of Gaussians move rigidly. iv. Flow Loss: If 2D flow estimation is used, a bidirectional optical flow loss is introduced to align dynamic objects across frames. c. Backward Pass: Compute gradients w.r.t. DDDM coefficients and static attributes. d. Update: Update parameters using an optimizer. 4. Iteration: Repeat step 3 until convergence. Formulas: The Dual-Domain Deformation Model (DDDM) models the time-dependent residual of each attribute using joint polynomial fitting (time domain) and Fourier series fitting (frequency domain). For a Gaussian i and time t, the deformation residual \Delta \mathbf{A}i(t) for attribute \mathbf{A} \in \{\boldsymbol{\mu}, q, c\} is: \Delta \mathbf{A}i(t) = \mathbf{P}i(t) + \mathbf{F}i(t) where: \mathbf{P}i(t) is a polynomial function of t: \mathbf{P}i(t) = \sum{k=0}^{K} \mathbf{a}{k,i} t^k Here, \mathbf{a}{k,i} are learnable polynomial coefficients for Gaussian i, and K is the polynomial degree. \mathbf{F}i(t) is a Fourier series approximation: \mathbf{F}i(t) = \sum{m=1}^{M} \left( \mathbf{b}{m,i} \cos(\omegam t) + \mathbf{c}{m,i} \sin(\omegam t) \right) Here, \mathbf{b}{m,i}, \mathbf{c}{m,i} are learnable Fourier coefficients, \omegam are fixed angular frequencies (e.g., \omegam = \frac{2\pi m}{T} where T is the total duration), and M is the number of harmonics. The final attributes at time t are: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \Delta \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) qi(t) = \text{Normalize}(qi \otimes \Delta qi(t)) ci(t) = ci + \Delta ci(t) where \otimes denotes quaternion multiplication. To prevent optimization problems from uniform time division, adaptive timestep scaling is adopted. The time t is mapped to a scaled time t' where the distribution of t' accounts for the density of keyframes or motion intensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluateddddm(gaussian, t, polycoeffs, fouriercoeffs, omega): # Polynomial part: sum(ak t^k) p = sum(c (t k) for k, c in enumerate(polycoeffs)) # Fourier part: sum(bm cos(omegam t) + cm sin(omegam t)) f = sum(b cos(omegaval t) + c sin(omegaval t) for b, c, omegaval in zip(fouriercoeffs[0], fouriercoeffs[1], omega)) return p + f def optimizegaussianflow(images, poses, initialgaussians, timestamps, numiterations): gaussians = initialgaussians # Initialize DDDM coefficients to zero polycoeffs = {attr: [zeros(dim) for in range(K)] for attr, dim in gaussians.attrs} fouriercoeffs = {attr: [zeros(dim), zeros(dim)] for attr, dim in gaussians.attrs} omega = [2 pi m / T for m in range(1, M + 1)] for iteration in range(numiterations): # Alternate static and dynamic optimization if iteration % 2 == 0: optimizestatic(gaussians, images, poses) else: for img, t in zip(images, timestamps): # Adaptive timestep scaling tscaled = adaptivescale(t) # Compute deformation residuals deltapos = evaluateddddm(gaussians, tscaled, polycoeffs['pos'], fouriercoeffs['pos'], omega) deltarot = evaluateddddm(gaussians, tscaled, polycoeffs['rot'], fouriercoeffs['rot'], omega) deltacol = evaluateddddm(gaussians, tscaled, polycoeffs['color'], fouriercoeffs['color'], omega) # Update attributes gaussians.pos = gaussians.pos + deltapos gaussians.rot = normalize(gaussians.rot deltarot) gaussians.color = gaussians.color + deltacol # Render and compute losses rendered = render(gaussians, poses) loss = lambdargb l1(rendered, img) + lambdassim ssim(rendered, img) loss += lambdasmooth temporalsmoothnessloss(gaussians, t) loss += lambdarigid knnrigidloss(gaussians) # Backward pass loss.backward() # Update parameters updateparameters(gaussians, polycoeffs, fouriercoeffs) return gaussians Parameters: Polynomial degree K: Not given in the sources. Fourier harmonics M: Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Loss weights \lambda{rgb}, \lambda{ssim}, \lambda{smooth}, \lambda{rigid}: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting to Violent Motion: Uniform time division can cause the model to overfit to frames with high motion. Adaptive timestep scaling mitigates this. Precision: Fourier series may require high M for high-frequency motion, increasing memory. Polynomial fitting may struggle with non-smooth motion. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes the scene is captured within the time range [t{min}, t{max}]. A method that directly applies optical flow estimation to the rendered Gaussians, using the flow to align dynamic objects across frames and improve temporal consistency. It contrasts with GaussianFlow, which treats each Gaussian as a dynamic particle advected by a 3D velocity field and models deformation via DDDM. Time Complexity: Training is 5× faster than per-frame 3DGS modeling. Rendering speed is comparable to original 3DGS, enabling real-time performance. Memory Complexity: Higher than static 3DGS due to storage of DDDM coefficients (polynomial and Fourier) for each Gaussian. Lower than implicit neural field methods (like NeRF) which store large networks. Measured Performance: Achieves superior novel view rendering quality compared to previous leading methods on multi-view and monocular datasets (HyperNeRF, Plenoptic). Strengths: Ultra-fast training and rendering; explicit 4D representation; supports both multi-view and monocular videos; no need for neural fields. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of DDDM parameters (K, M); may struggle with highly complex, non-rigid deformations if polynomial/Fourier bases are insufficient; adaptive timestep scaling adds complexity. When to Use: Dynamic scene reconstruction from videos where real-time rendering and fast training are critical, and the motion is not extremely chaotic. When Not to Use: If the scene contains very high-frequency, non-smooth motion that cannot be captured by low-degree polynomials or limited Fourier harmonics, or if per-frame accuracy is more important than global consistency. GaussianFlow was introduced by Guo et al. in 2024. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for static scenes and addresses the limitations of existing dynamic methods, which either suffer from slow training/rendering (NeRF-based) or lack global consistency (per-frame 3DGS). The method was developed to enable fast dynamic scene reconstruction and real-time rendering from both multi-view and monocular videos. It is part of the broader family of dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting methods, which aim to extend the explicit, efficient representation of 3DGS to 4D. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian-Flow: 4D Reconstruction with Dynamic 3D Gaussian Particle, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01997, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade
body: Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade is a method that directly applies optical flow estimation to the rendered Gaussians, using the flow to align dynamic objects across frames and improve temporal consistency. It distinguishes itself from parent method GaussianFlow, which uses an explicit flow field for temporal regularization, by operating directly on the rendered Gaussian primitives rather than an explicit geometric point cloud or a separate flow MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of 2D image frames and a set of 3D Gaussians representing the scene. Output: Temporally consistent 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color) aligned across frames. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: A collection of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by position \mathbf{p}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. Optical Flow Field: A 2D vector field \mathbf{u}(x, y) representing pixel displacement between frames. Steps: 1. Render: Render the current frame using the current set of 3D Gaussians via differentiable rasterization. 2. Estimate Flow: Compute the optical flow \mathbf{u}(x, y) between the rendered frame and the target frame (or previous frame) using a standard Lucas-Kanade optical flow algorithm or a learned equivalent. 3. Align Gaussians: Map the 2D optical flow to 3D space. For each Gaussian, determine its projected 2D center \mathbf{c}i. Apply the flow vector \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{c}i) to update the Gaussian's position or adjust its parameters to minimize the photometric error between the rendered and target frames. 4. Update: Update the Gaussian parameters based on the flow alignment. This may involve translating the Gaussian centers or adjusting their covariances to account for motion blur or deformation. 5. Iterate: Repeat for subsequent frames to maintain temporal consistency. Formulas: Lucas-Kanade Optical Flow: Solves for \mathbf{u} by minimizing: \sum{i \in W} \left( I1(xi + ux, yi + uy) - I0(xi, yi) \right)^2 where I0, I1 are image intensities, W is a window around the pixel, and \mathbf{u} = (ux, uy). Gaussian Update: The position \mathbf{p}i is updated by \Delta \mathbf{p}i derived from the flow. Parameters: Window Size: For Lucas-Kanade, typically 5 \times 5 or 7 \times 7 pixels. Regularization: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases: Occlusions: Flow estimation may fail in occluded regions. Large Motions: Standard Lucas-Kanade assumes small motions; large displacements may require pyramidal approaches. Degenerate Input: Low-texture regions may yield unreliable flow. Scene Flow Prior enhances the temporal consistency of 4D spatio-temporal representations by incorporating a flow Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for motion estimation. It maps spatio-temporal coordinates from \mathbb{R}^4 to motion fields in \mathbb{R}^3, predicting displacement only between adjacent frames to avoid the difficulty of establishing long-term correspondences in deformable scenes. Unlike its parent method, Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade, which applies optical flow to rendered Gaussians, this method operates on explicit geometric point clouds derived from LiDAR data to impose a motion prior and geometric supervision. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and the resolution of the flow estimation. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Direct application to Gaussians; improves temporal consistency. Limitations: Relies on accurate optical flow; may struggle with large motions or occlusions. When to Use: Dynamic scenes requiring temporal consistency in Gaussian Splatting. When Not to Use: Scenes with large, unstructured motions or significant occlusions where flow estimation is unreliable. name: Scene Flow Prior
head: Flow MLP for motion estimation
body: Scene Flow Prior enhances the temporal consistency of 4D spatio-temporal representations by incorporating a flow Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for motion estimation. It maps spatio-temporal coordinates from \mathbb{R}^4 to motion fields in \mathbb{R}^3, predicting displacement only between adjacent frames to avoid the difficulty of establishing long-term correspondences in deformable scenes. Unlike its parent method, Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade, which applies optical flow to rendered Gaussians, this method operates on explicit geometric point clouds derived from LiDAR data to impose a motion prior and geometric supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Spatio-temporal coordinates (\mathbf{x}, t) where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and t is the time index; LiDAR point clouds Si for frame i. Outputs: Predicted scene flow displacement \Delta \mathbf{x}; transformed point cloud \mathbf{x}'. Data Structures: Flow MLP: A standard Multi-Layer Perceptron. The input is processed via positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}, t). Positional Encoding: \gamma(x) = (\sin(2^0 x), \cos(2^0 x),..., \sin(2^{L-1} x), \cos(2^{L-1} x)). Point Clouds: Sets of 3D points S and \hat{S} representing two adjacent frames. Parameters: L: Number of frequency bands in positional encoding. Not given in the sources. K: Number of points in the point cloud sets. Not given in the sources. n: Total number of frames. Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Encode the input coordinate \mathbf{x} and time t using \gamma(\mathbf{x}, t). 2. Flow Prediction: Feed the encoded coordinates into the flow MLP to predict the displacement vector \Delta \mathbf{x}: \Delta \mathbf{x} = \mathrm{MLP}\mathrm{flow}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}, t)) 3. Motion Application: Compute the transformed coordinate \mathbf{x}': \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x} 4. Geometric Loss Calculation: To supervise the motion prediction, calculate the Chamfer Distance (CD) between the predicted transformed point cloud and the ground truth point cloud of the adjacent frame. The flow loss \mathcal{L}\mathrm{flow} is the sum of Chamfer Distances for forward and backward adjacent frames: \mathcal{L}\mathrm{flow} = \sum{j \in \pm 1} \mathrm{CD}(Si + \mathrm{MLP}\mathrm{flow}(Si), S{i+j}) where i \in (0, n-1). 5. Chamfer Distance Definition: The Chamfer Distance between two point cloud sets S and \hat{S} is defined as: \mathrm{CD} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{\hat{p}i \in \hat{S}} \min{pi \in S} \|\hat{p}i - pi\|2^2 + \frac{1}{K} \sum{pi \in S} \min{\hat{p}i \in \hat{S}} \|pi - \hat{p}i\|2^2 where S and \hat{S} are two frames of point clouds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Si: (K, 3) point cloud of frame i Siplus1: (K, 3) point cloud of frame i+1 Siminus1: (K, 3) point cloud of frame i-1 flowmlpweights: weights for the flow MLP Returns: float, Lflow """ # Predict flow for Si # Note: In practice, time t must be encoded.
