If we want to go to i-1, we might need to encode ti and target t{i-1}? # Or the MLP predicts the flow vector at x for the time step. # If we use the same MLP for both directions, it must be symmetric or the loss handles it. # Let's assume for j=-1, we predict displacement to move Si to S{i-1}. # This might require a different input encoding or a separate head. # Without explicit detail, we will assume the MLP can predict the required delta for the target frame. # For the sake of the pseudocode, we will assume a function predictdeltatotarget exists. # Simplified assumption: The MLP predicts the delta to move Si to S{i+1}. # For S{i-1}, we might need to predict delta from S{i-1} to Si and invert? # The formula is explicit: CD(Si + MLP(Si), S{i+j}). # This implies MLP(Si) is the vector to add to Si to match S{i+j}. # This is a "direct displacement" prediction. # We will implement a generic predictdelta that takes source and target info. deltaxbackward = predictdeltatotarget(Si, Siminus1, flowmlpweights) # Sitransformedbackward = Si + deltaxbackward cdbackward = chamferdistance(Sitransformedbackward, Siminus1) return cdforward + cdbackward def predictdeltatotarget(Ssource, Starget, weights): """ Predicts delta to move Ssource to match Starget. This is a placeholder for the specific conditioning of the MLP. In the paper, it seems the MLP takes (x, t). If it predicts delta to S{i+1}, it might take ti. If it predicts delta to S{i-1}, it might take ti and some indication of direction? Or perhaps the MLP is trained to predict the flow field, and we evaluate it. Given the ambiguity, we assume the MLP is conditioned on the source frame's time and the target frame's time. """ tsource = gettimeforframe(i) ttarget = gettimeforframe(i + 1) # For forward # For backward, ttarget would be i-1. # We assume the MLP input includes both times or the relative time. # Since the formula only shows (x, t), we assume t is the source time. # This implies the MLP predicts the flow at time t. # If we want to match S{i-1}, we might need to predict flow at t{i-1} and move S{i-1}? # No, the formula is Si + MLP(Si). # This suggests the MLP predicts the displacement of Si. # If the MLP is time-conditioned, it might predict the velocity or displacement over a fixed step. # We will assume the MLP predicts the displacement for the next frame (j=1). # For j=-1, we might need to predict the displacement from Si to S{i-1}, which is the negative of flow from i-1 to i. # Let's assume we predict flow from i to i+1, and for i-1, we predict flow from i-1 to i and invert? # The formula does not show inversion. # We will stick to the forward case for the main implementation and note the ambiguity for backward. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Long-term Correspondences: The method explicitly avoids long-term correspondences to canonical space because vehicle motion range may span a long distance in autonomous driving scenarios, making such correspondences hard to establish. Precision: The Chamfer Distance involves squared Euclidean norms, which can be sensitive to outliers. The normalization by K helps but large point clouds may require efficient nearest-neighbor search. Boundary Conditions: The index i ranges from 0 to n-1, implying the loss is computed for frames that have at least one adjacent neighbor. The first and last frames might have only one adjacent frame, affecting the sum in \mathcal{L}\mathrm{flow}. Time Complexity: The flow MLP inference is O(N \cdot D \cdot L{mlp}) where N is the number of points, D is input dimension, and L{mlp} is MLP depth. Chamfer Distance computation is O(K^2) naively, but can be optimized to O(K \log K) with spatial indexing. Memory Complexity: Requires storing point clouds for adjacent frames and the MLP weights. Strengths: Enhances temporal consistency by leveraging explicit geometric constraints from LiDAR point clouds. Imposes a motion prior that helps in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Relies on the availability of LiDAR point clouds. Predicting motion only between adjacent frames may accumulate errors over long sequences if not aggregated properly. When to Use: Suitable for dynamic scene reconstruction in autonomous driving scenarios where LiDAR data is available and temporal consistency is critical. It was developed to address the challenges of reconstructing dynamic scenes from LiDAR data, specifically focusing on temporal consistency and geometric accuracy. The method builds on the idea of using flow MLPs for motion estimation, as seen in prior works [20, 46] cited in the source. name: Dynamic 3D Gaussians
body: Dynamic 3D Gaussians performs tracking by persistent dynamic view synthesis, linking the motion of each Gaussian to the movement of a corresponding 3D point in the scene. It extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle dynamic scenes by explicitly defining a tracking mechanism that differs from its parent Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting and from GaussianFlow by relying on persistent synthesis rather than flow-based deformation fields. Inputs: Multi-view video frames \{It\} for t \in [0, T] and camera poses \{Ct\}. Initial static 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}0. Outputs: Time-varying Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}t for all t and rendered dynamic views. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: A struct containing \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (position), q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized quaternion), s \in \mathbb{R}^3 (scale), \alpha \in \mathbb{R} (opacity), c \in \mathbb{R}^K (spherical harmonic coefficients). Anchor Points: A sparse subset of Gaussians selected via farthest point sampling (FPS). Embedded Deformation Graph (EDG): A graph connecting each Gaussian to its K nearest anchor points, with blend weights w{ij} computed based on spatial distances. Numbered Steps: 1. 2D Projection: For a Gaussian at frame t', compute its 2D projections \{pi^{t'} \mid i = 1 \dots N\} across N input views. 2. 2D Tracking: Run a pre-trained 2D point tracking model on \{pi^{t'}\} to obtain corresponding 2D pixel positions \{pi^t\} in frame t. 3. Triangulation: Recover the 3D position \boldsymbol{\mu}i^t by finding the point closest to the N camera rays originating from \{pi^t\}. 4. Motion Propagation: Select anchor points via FPS. Connect each Gaussian to its K nearest anchor points. Compute blend weights w{ij} based on spatial distances. Update \boldsymbol{\mu}i^t by interpolating the motion of the anchor points using the EDG. 5. Keyframe Management: Maintain primitives only from a set of past keyframes. Smoothly adjust contributions as older keyframes are replaced by newer ones to ensure seamless temporal transitions. Formulas: \{pi^{t'} \mid i = 1 \dots N\}: 2D projections at frame t' across N views. \{pi^t\}: 2D pixel positions at frame t. \boldsymbol{\mu}i^t: 3D position at frame t. K: number of nearest anchor points. w{ij}: blend weights based on spatial distance. Parameters: K: Number of nearest anchor points for EDG. N: Number of input views. Tracking Model: Pre-trained 2D point tracking model. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. A method to estimate the 3D position of a Gaussian primitive at a current frame t from its position at a previous frame t' using 2D point tracking and triangulation. It sets itself apart by explicitly using a pre-trained 2D point tracker and EDG for motion propagation, rather than learning deformation fields directly. Choose this when you have multi-view video and want to leverage existing 2D tracking models for robust motion estimation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Real-time 4DGS achieves interactive frame rates by fusing static background Gaussians with a small, fast-updating set of dynamic foreground Gaussians. Strengths: Persistent dynamic view synthesis; leverages 2D tracking and EDG for motion propagation; seamless temporal transitions via keyframe management. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Dynamic 3D Gaussians performs tracking by persistent dynamic view synthesis, linking Gaussian motion to 3D point motion. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting and Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting. The 3D Warping variant uses a pre-trained 2D point tracking model and embedded deformation graph for motion propagation. It is used in applications requiring real-time 4D reconstruction and dynamic view synthesis. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14698v2, fetched 2026-10-27

name: SWAGS
head: SWAGS [S1]
body: SWAGS is a dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting method that addresses the challenge of modeling complex, non-rigid motion in dynamic scenes by partitioning the temporal sequence into distinct windows based on motion intensity. Unlike sibling methods that track a single global deformation field or flow across the entire sequence, SWAGS trains separate dynamic 3DGS models for each window, each with its own canonical space and deformation field, thereby isolating local motion characteristics. This approach improves reconstruction fidelity for highly dynamic segments while maintaining temporal consistency through fine-tuning on overlapping frames. SWAGS extends the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework to 4D by introducing time-varying parameters. Each Gaussian is defined by a position \boldsymbol{\mu}t, rotation qt, scaling St, and opacity \alphat at time t. The scaling matrix in 4D space is formed by adding a scaling factor for the time dimension on the diagonal of the standard 3D scaling matrix. The view-dependent color is represented by a 4D extension of spherical harmonics (SH), expressed as a combination of 3D SH with 1D basis functions over time. The core innovation lies in the window-based decomposition and deformation modeling: 1. Window Partitioning: The dynamic sequence is divided into multiple windows. The partitioning criterion is based on the amount of motion within each segment. 2. Separate Model Training: For each window, a separate dynamic 3DGS model is trained. Each model possesses: A unique canonical space (the reference geometry at a canonical time). A dedicated deformation field. 3. Deformation Field: The deformation field is implemented as a tunable Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). This MLP is designed to focus specifically on modeling the dynamic part of the scene, distinguishing it from static background elements. 4. Fine-Tuning for Consistency: To ensure temporal consistency across window boundaries, the models are fine-tuned using overlapping frames between adjacent windows. During this fine-tuning phase, the MLP parameters are fixed, and only the canonical representation (the 3DGS attributes in the canonical space) is optimized. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def swagstrain(sequenceframes, motionthresholds): """ Trains SWAGS models for a dynamic sequence. Args: sequenceframes: List of image frames with known camera poses and timestamps. motionthresholds: Thresholds or criteria to determine window boundaries based on motion. Returns: A list of trained Dynamic3DGSModel objects, one per window. """ # Step 1: Divide sequence into windows based on motion amount windows = partitionsequencebymotion(sequenceframes, motionthresholds) models = [] for i, window in enumerate(windows): # Step 2: Train separate dynamic 3DGS model for this window # Initialize with canonical space and deformation field model = Dynamic3DGSModel( canonicalspace=initializecanonicalspace(window), deformationfield=TunableMLP() # Focuses on dynamic part) # Train the model for this window model.train(window.frames, window.cameraposes) models.append(model) # Step 4 & 5: Fine-tune for temporal consistency using overlapping frames for i in range(len(models) - 1): # Identify overlapping frames between current window i and next window i+1 overlapframes = findoverlapframes(models[i].window, models[i+1].window) if overlapframes: # Fix the MLP, optimize only canonical representation models[i].freezemlp() models[i+1].freezemlp() # Optimize canonical representations to align across overlap finetunecanonicalrepresentation( models[i], models[i+1], overlapframes) return models class Dynamic3DGSModel: def init(self, canonicalspace, deformationfield): self.canonicalspace = canonicalspace self.deformationfield = deformationfield self.gaussians = [] # List of Gaussian attributes in canonical space def freezemlp(self): """Freeze the deformation field MLP parameters.""" self.deformationfield.requiresgrad = False def train(self, frames, cameraposes): """Standard 3DGS optimization loop for the window.""" for frame, pose in zip(frames, cameraposes): # Render frame using 4D GS (time-varying pos, rot, scale, SH) renderedimage = render4dgaussians( self.gaussians, pose, frame.timestamp, self.deformationfield, self.canonicalspace) # Compute loss and backpropagate loss = computeloss(renderedimage, frame.image) optimize(loss) def render4dgaussians(gaussians, camerapose, timet, deformationfield, canonicalspace): """ Renders a frame at time t using 4D Gaussian Splatting. Transforms canonical Gaussians to world space using deformationfield. Applies time-varying scaling and 4D SH. """ # Get time-varying parameters # Position: mut = canonicalmu + deformationfield(canonicalmu, timet) # Rotation: qt (time-varying) # Scaling: St (diagonal matrix with time scaling factor) # Color: Ct (4D SH: 3D SH combined with 1D time basis) worldgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Apply deformation tmu = g.canonicalmu + deformationfield(g.canonicalmu, timet) # Construct 4D scaling matrix # S4d = diag(S3d, Stime) S4d = construct4dscalingmatrix(g.scale3d, g.scaletime) worldgaussians.append(Gaussian( mu=tmu, q=g.qt, # Time-varying rotation S=S4d, alpha=g.alpha, sh4d=g.sh4d # 4D spherical harmonics)) return rasterize(worldgaussians, camerapose) Complexity: The method introduces overhead due to training multiple models and managing window boundaries. Memory usage scales with the number of windows and the size of each window's Gaussian set. Strengths: By isolating motion into windows, SWAGS can handle scenes with varying motion intensities more effectively than global deformation models. The focus of the MLP on dynamic parts allows for more efficient representation of motion. Limitations: Requires careful selection of window boundaries based on motion. Temporal consistency relies on the fine-tuning step and overlapping frames; poor overlap or insufficient fine-tuning can lead to discontinuities. Performance: Not given in the sources. SWAGS was introduced as a method to improve dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting by addressing the limitations of global deformation fields in handling complex motion. It builds on the parent method Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a window-based approach. The method has been applied in medical fields, such as markerless motion reconstruction for infants and neonates, where additional mask and depth supervisions are used. name: Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is a method that incorporates an epipolar transformer to generalize features between two views, pairing this with a probabilistic prediction of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two or more input images and their camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color coefficients). Data Structures: Gaussian Primitives: A list of objects containing position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4, opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], and color coefficients \mathbf{c}. Feature Tokens: Concatenated sequence of image and camera parameter embeddings processed by the transformer. Steps: 1. Tokenization: Tokenize the input images and camera parameters, then concatenate the tokens from all views. 2. Feature Generalization: Pass the concatenated tokens through a transformer block to generalize features between the views. 3. Probabilistic Prediction: Decode the transformer output tokens into Gaussian parameters, predicting a probabilistic distribution of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. 4. Rendering: Render the predicted Gaussians using differentiable rasterization to produce the output image. 5. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian parameters (and encoder weights if trained end-to-end) by minimizing photometric losses such as LPIPS or SSIM against the input views. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Specific hyperparameters such as transformer depth, heads, and loss weights are not detailed in the source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pose Requirement: Standard implementation requires known camera poses, though variants like NoPoSplat eliminate this need. Depth Ambiguity: Probabilistic prediction along rays may produce multiple Gaussians per ray; standard sorting and alpha blending must handle this correctly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def epipolar3dgs(images, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics): # 1. Tokenization: Embed image patches and concatenate with camera pose embeddings tokens = [] for img, intr, extr in zip(images, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics): # Standard vision transformer patch embedding and positional encoding tokens.append(embedandconcat(img, intr, extr)) combinedtokens = torch.cat(tokens, dim=1) # 2. Feature Generalization: Process tokens through a transformer block # Epipolar transformer generalizes features between views # Exact architectural details (layers, heads, dimensions) are not specified transformeroutput = transformerforward(combinedtokens) # 3. Probabilistic Prediction: Decode tokens into Gaussian parameters # Predicts Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays # MLP decoder outputs position, scale, rotation, opacity, color gaussians = decodetogaussians(transformeroutput) # 4. Rendering: Differentiable rasterization # Project 3D Gaussians to 2D, sort by depth, alpha blend renderedimage = rasterizegaussians(gaussians, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics) return renderedimage, gaussians Pose-Aware Projection (PAP) is a feature aggregation technique used in differentiable volume rendering to extract multi-view contextual information for specific 3D locations (voxels or skeletal Gaussians) by projecting their positions onto 2D feature maps from multiple camera views. It solves the problem of ambiguous feature assignment inherent in global backprojection methods, which ignore actual surface geometry and assume features map reliably to voxel centers via camera rays, leading to errors in occluded or background regions. What sets PAP apart from its parent Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is its focus on aggregating features based on camera distance for selected skeletal primitives rather than generalizing features via an epipolar transformer for all pixels. It differs from its sibling Geometry Aware Feature Extraction by using explicit inverse-distance weighting of projected features rather than cross-view attention guided by geometric constraints. Scaling: Scales with the number of input views and image resolution. Strengths: Leverages epipolar geometry for robust feature generalization; probabilistic prediction allows for flexible Gaussian placement. Limitations: Requires known camera poses in standard formulations, though pose-agnostic variants exist. When to use: When reconstructing 3DGS from limited multi-view inputs with known poses. When not to use: When camera poses are unknown (use NoPoSplat) or when transformer overhead is prohibitive. Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is part of the broader trend of integrating neural rendering techniques with 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds upon methods like PixelSplat, which uses an epipolar transformer for feature generalization between two views. MVSplat extends this to multi-view settings using transformers and cost volumes. GS-LRM tokenizes multiple images and camera parameters for transformer-based decoding. NoPoSplat addresses critical limitations by eliminating the need for known camera poses. The method is supervised by photometric losses such as LPIPS, SSIM, or similar metrics. name: Pose-Aware Projection (PAP)
head: Pose-Aware Projection at selected voxels
body: Pose-Aware Projection (PAP) is a feature aggregation technique used in differentiable volume rendering to extract multi-view contextual information for specific 3D locations (voxels or skeletal Gaussians) by projecting their positions onto 2D feature maps from multiple camera views. It solves the problem of ambiguous feature assignment inherent in global backprojection methods, which ignore actual surface geometry and assume features map reliably to voxel centers via camera rays, leading to errors in occluded or background regions. What sets PAP apart from its parent Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is its focus on aggregating features based on camera distance for selected skeletal primitives rather than generalizing features via an epipolar transformer for all pixels. It differs from its sibling Geometry Aware Feature Extraction by using explicit inverse-distance weighting of projected features rather than cross-view attention guided by geometric constraints. Inputs: 1. A set of selected skeletal Gaussian positions \{\mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d}: (h, w, d) \in \mathcal{I}\}, where \mathcal{I} is the index set of selected voxels/primitives. 2. A set of N pose-aware 2D feature maps \{fn: n = 1, \dots, N\}, obtained from a coarse stage, corresponding to N input camera views. Outputs: 1. A set of PAP-derived feature volumes \{\bar{v}{(h,w,d),n}: (h, w, d) \in \mathcal{I}\} for each view n, containing features sampled at the projected locations. 2. A final aggregated feature volume \hat{v}{h,w,d} for each selected voxel/primitive. Data Structures: \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d}: 3D position vector (x, y, z) of the skeletal Gaussian at voxel indices (h, w, d). fn: 2D feature map for view n, a tensor of shape (Hn, Wn, C), where Hn, Wn are height/width and C is channel depth. \bar{v}{(h,w,d),n}: Feature vector of size C for voxel (h,w,d) from view n. \hat{v}{h,w,d}: Final aggregated feature vector of size C. Steps: 1. Projection & Sampling: For each selected skeletal Gaussian position \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d} and for each view n \in \{1, \dots, N\}: a. Project the 3D position \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d} onto the 2D image plane of view n using standard camera projection. Let the resulting 2D coordinates be (un, vn). b. Sample the feature map fn at coordinates (un, vn) using bilinear interpolation. Let the sampled feature be \bar{v}{(h,w,d),n}. 2. Distance Calculation: For each selected voxel (h,w,d) and each view n, calculate the Euclidean distance z{(h,w,d),n} between the skeletal Gaussian position \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d} and the camera position of view n. 3. Aggregation: For each selected voxel (h,w,d), aggregate the PAP-derived features \bar{v}{(h,w,d),n} from all N views using inverse distance weighting: \hat{v}{h,w,d} = \frac{\sum{n=1}^N z{(h,w,d),n}^{-1} \cdot \bar{v}{(h,w,d),n}}{\sum{n'=1}^N z{(h,w,d),n'}^{-1}} where z{(h,w,d),n} is the distance between \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d} and the n-th view camera position. Parameters: N: Number of input camera views used for projection and aggregation. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-bounds projection: If the projected 2D coordinates (un, vn) fall outside the image boundaries of fn, sampling is undefined. Implementation must handle this, e.g., by clamping or using a default value. Zero distance: If z{(h,w,d),n} = 0 (camera at the same position as the Gaussian), the inverse distance becomes undefined. This is unlikely in practice but should be guarded against. Occlusion: PAP assumes that projecting to the 2D feature map provides relevant context. In occluded regions, the projected feature might come from a different surface, leading to ambiguity. PAP mitigates this by focusing on selected voxels likely to belong to the object, but residual errors may persist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def poseawareprojection(skeletalgaussians, featuremaps, camerapositions, N): """ skeletalgaussians: dict mapping (h, w, d) to 3D position tuple (x, y, z) featuremaps: list of N 2D arrays of shape (Hn, Wn, C) camerapositions: list of N 3D position tuples (cx, cy, cz) N: int Returns: dict mapping (h, w, d) to aggregated feature vector """ C = featuremaps[0].shape[-1] aggregated = {} for (h, w, d), mu in skeletalgaussians.items(): weightedsum = [0.0] C invdistsum = 0.0 for n in range(N): u, v = project2d(mu, featuremaps[n].shape) vbar = sample2d(featuremaps[n], u, v) cam = camerapositions[n] dx, dy, dz = mu[0] - cam[0], mu[1] - cam[1], mu[2] - cam[2] z = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 if z == 0.0: continue invz = 1.0 / z for c in range(C): weightedsum[c] += invz vbar[c] invdistsum += invz if invdistsum > 0.0: for c in range(C): weightedsum[c] /= invdistsum else: weightedsum = [0.0] C aggregated[(h, w, d)] = weightedsum return aggregated def project2d(pos, shape): # Standard pinhole projection assumed return pos[0] / pos[2], pos[1] / pos[2] def sample2d(map2d, u, v): # Bilinear interpolation assumed h, w, c = map2d.shape u = max(0, min(w - 1, u)) v = max(0, min(h - 1, v)) return map2d[int(v), int(u)] Enhances source view features using cross-view attention and geometric constraints (ray projection) to resolve ambiguous feature assignment. It builds on PAP by providing geometrically enhanced features for robust generalization in synthetic-to-real scenarios. Aligns features from neighboring training views with a novel rendered view by explicitly reprojecting 3D coordinates into the novel view and validating via depth-based visibility testing. It differs from PAP by relying on explicit geometric reprojection rather than implicit geometric awareness via distance weighting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Resolves ambiguous feature assignment from global backprojection by aligning selected 3D skeletal primitives with 2D feature maps from different camera views, allowing association with rich, pose-aligned features for accurate fine-grained rendering. Limitations: Still relies on the assumption that 2D features can be reliably mapped to the selected 3D position via projection, which may be inaccurate in highly occluded or textureless regions. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Pose-Aware Projection (PAP) was introduced in the paper "VS-Splat: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse-views". It is part of the fine stage of the VS-Splat method, following the coarse stage and voxel selection. The method was developed to address limitations of global backprojection in voxel-based feature volumes, specifically the discarding of sub-voxel geometric precision and ambiguous feature assignment in occluded regions. VS-Splat: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse-views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.12343, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Geometry Aware Feature Extraction
head: Geometrically Enhanced Feature Aggregation
body: Geometry Aware Feature Extraction is a module that enhances source view features by aggregating information from other source views using geometric constraints (ray projection) and cross-view attention. It resolves the insufficiency of single-point feature extraction for semantic prediction by approximating dense semantic connections in 3D space. It sets itself apart from siblings like 3D Alignment via Reprojection by explicitly modeling the 3D ray structure to guide feature aggregation, rather than relying solely on 2D reprojection alignment. Inputs: Set of N source views \{Ii, Ki, Ei\}{i=1}^N, where Ii is the image, Ki is the camera intrinsic matrix, and Ei = [Ri, ti] contains the rotation matrix Ri and translation vector ti for the i-th view. Number of sample points per ray, Ns. Outputs: Geometrically enhanced features \{F'i\}{i=1}^N. Data Structures: Fi: Feature map extracted from Ii by a shared CNN. Dimensions depend on the CNN architecture. fi: Local feature vector at 2D coordinate ui in Fi. g{js}: Local feature vector at projected coordinate v{js} in Fj. P(s): Position embedding for the s-th sample point along the ray. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each source view i, use a shared Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract feature map Fi from image Ii. 2. Ray Definition: For each 2D coordinate ui = [u, v]^\top on the i-th source view, compute the corresponding ray R in world coordinates parametrized by \delta: R(\delta) = ti + \delta Ri Ki^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} ui \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where Ki is the intrinsic matrix and [Ri, ti] are the extrinsic parameters of the i-th source view. 3. Ray Sampling and Projection: Sample a sequence of points ps = R(\deltas) along the ray R for s = 1, \dots, Ns. Project each point ps to the j-th source view to obtain 2D coordinates v{js} and depth d{sj}: d{sj} \begin{bmatrix} v{js}^\top \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = Kj Rj^{-1} (ps - tj) where v{js} is the 2D coordinate in the j-th source view and d{sj} is the corresponding depth. This yields a collection of projections \{v{js}\}{s=1}^{Ns} for the j-th source view. 4. Stage 1: Intra-View Aggregation: For a target view i and a neighbor view j, let fi be the local feature of Fi at ui, and g{js} be the local feature of Fj at v{js}. Aggregate features from the projection points within the j-th source view using Multi-Head Attention (MHA): gj = \text{MHA}(fi, \{g{js} + P(s)\}{s=1}^{Ns}) Here, fi is the query, \{g{js} + P(s)\}{s=1}^{Ns} serve as the keys and values, and P(s) is the position embedding of the sample index s. 5. Stage 2: Cross-View Aggregation: Aggregate features from other source views. Compute the enhanced feature f'i using MHA: f'i = \text{MHA}(fi, \{gj\}{j=1, j \neq i}^{N}) Here, fi is the query and \{gj\}{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} are the keys and values. 6. Iteration: Apply the above process for all source views to obtain the final geometrically enhanced features \{F'i\}{i=1}^N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryawarefeatureextraction(sourceviews, Ns): """ sourceviews: List of dicts containing 'image', 'K', 'R', 't' for each view i. Ns: Number of sample points along the ray. Returns: List of enhanced feature maps Fprime. """ N = len(sourceviews) F = [] # Step 1: Extract features using shared CNN for view in sourceviews: F.append(sharedcnn(view['image'])) Fprime = [None] N for i in range(N): # Initialize enhanced feature map for view i Fprimei = torch.zeroslike(F[i]) # Iterate over all 2D coordinates ui in the feature map F[i] # In practice, this is done via vectorized operations or grid sampling for ui in allpixelcoordinates(F[i]): fi = getfeatureat(F[i], ui) # Step 2: Define Ray R for ui # R(delta) = ti + delta Ri Ki^-1 [ui, 1]^T # We need to sample delta values. The source does not specify the range. # Assuming a standard depth range [deltamin, deltamax] is provided or inferred. deltas = sampledepths(Ns) rayspoints = [] for delta in deltas: # Compute world point ps homogenousu = torch.tensor([ui[0], ui[1], 1.0]) invKi = torch.linalg.inv(sourceviews[i]['K']) dirvec = sourceviews[i]['R'] @ invKi @ homogenousu ps = sourceviews[i]['t'] + delta dirvec rayspoints.append(ps) viewgjlist = [] # Step 3 & 4: For each other view j, project and aggregate for j in range(N): if i == j: continue # Step 3: Project points to view j gjs = [] for s, ps in enumerate(rayspoints): # dsj [vjs^T, 1]^T = Kj Rj^-1 (ps - tj) invKj = torch.linalg.inv(sourceviews[j]['K']) invRj = torch.linalg.inv(sourceviews[j]['R']) # Compute right hand side rhs = sourceviews[j]['K'] @ invRj @ (ps - sourceviews[j]['t']) # Extract depth and 2D coords dsj = rhs[2] vjs = rhs[:2] / dsj # Get feature at vjs from F[j] # Requires bilinear interpolation or gridsample to handle non-integer coordinates gjs.append(getfeatureat(F[j], vjs)) # Step 4: Stage 1 Aggregation # gj = MHA(fi, {gjs + P(s)}) # Prepare keys/values with position embeddings keysvalues = [gjs[s] + positionembedding(s) for s in range(Ns)] gj = multiheadattention(query=fi, keys=keysvalues, values=keysvalues) viewgjlist.append(gj) # Step 5: Stage 2 Aggregation # f'i = MHA(fi, {gj}{j!=i}) # keysvaluesstage2 = viewgjlist fprimei = multiheadattention(query=fi, keys=viewgjlist, values=viewgjlist) Fprimei[getpixelindex(ui)] = fprimei Fprime[i] = Fprimei return Fprime Parameters: Ns: Number of sample points along the ray. Not given in the sources. Position Embedding P(s): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray projection may fall outside the image boundaries of source views j. The source does not specify handling for out-of-bounds projections. Standard practice is to clamp or ignore such samples. Depth ambiguity: The parametrization \delta requires a range. The source does not specify how \deltas are chosen (e.g., uniform, learned). Implementers must define a depth range [\delta{min}, \delta{max}]. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves N views, Ns samples per ray, and Multi-Head Attention operations, suggesting complexity related to O(N^2 \cdot Ns). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Approximates dense semantic connections in 3D space by reprojecting query rays to source views and aggregating features. Reduces computational cost and GPU memory usage compared to dense multi-view attention while maintaining comparable semantic segmentation performance. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera parameters and geometry. May fail if the geometry prediction is inaccurate, leading to artifacts. When to use: Synthetic-to-real generalization of NeRF where semantic consistency across views is critical. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and Ns or N are large, as the attention mechanism adds overhead. The method was introduced to address the problem where existing NeRF models may fail to accurately predict scene geometry, resulting in serious artifacts in rendered images, particularly in synthetic-to-real generalization scenarios. name: Cross-Reprojection Attention
head: CRA Module, Cross-Reprojection Attention (CRA) Module
body: Cross-Reprojection Attention (CRA) is a two-stage attention mechanism that approximates dense semantic connections in 3D space by reprojecting query rays to source views and aggregating features, solving the insufficiency of single-point feature extraction for semantic prediction. It replaces dense multi-view attention to reduce computational cost and GPU memory usage while maintaining comparable semantic segmentation performance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A query ray r(z) defined by two points pi, pj in the query view; camera poses (R, t) for m source views; camera calibration matrix K; N sample points \{zk\}{k=1}^N along the ray; feature dimension C; number of attention heads H. Outputs: A refined semantic ray feature s and rendered semantic logits \hat{S}(r). Data Structures: 3D Contextual Space (M): A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{m \times N \times C}. It is structured as M = [F1, \dots, Fm]^T, where Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C} contains the features extracted from the i-th source view along the reprojected ray. Attention Projections: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices of shape \mathbb{R}^{N \times dk}, where dk = C/H. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Warping and Feature Extraction: For each source view j \in \{1, \dots, m\} with pose (Rj, tj): a. Define the query ray in the query view coordinate system: r(z) = pi + z \frac{pj - pi}{\|pj - pi\|}, \quad z \in \mathbb{R}. b. Reproject the ray to the source view plane using the warping function w: r^(z) = w(r(z), Rj, tj) = K \pi(Rj \cdot r(z) + tj) where \pi(u) = [ux/uz, uy/uz] is the perspective projection function. c. Extract features Fj(r^(z)) at the N sampled points along r^(z) using a shared U-Net-based CNN. This yields Fj \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}. d. Assemble M = [F1, \dots, Fm]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times N \times C}. 2. Intra-View Radial Attention: Refine the contextual space M to M' by processing each view Fi independently. For each i \in \{1, \dots, m\}: a. Compute projections: QR = Fi Wq, \quad KR = Fi Wk, \quad VR = Fi Wv where Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C} are learnable projection matrices. b. Compute attention heads for h = 1, \dots, H: A^{(h)} = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QR^{(h)} (KR^{(h)})^T}{\sqrt{dk}}\right) VR^{(h)} where dk = C/H. c. Concatenate heads and project: F'i = \text{Concat}(A^{(1)}, \dots, A^{(H)}) Wo. d. Update M' such that M' = [F'1, \dots, F'm]^T. 3. Cross-View Sparse Attention: Decompose M' across views to form semantic rays. For each sample point k \in \{1, \dots, N\}: a. Extract the cross-view feature vector: F'{r^(k)} = [F'1(r^(zk)), \dots, F'm(r^(zk))]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times C}. b. Compute view weights w \in \mathbb{R}^m using a Semantic-aware Weight Network subject to constraints: w \in \mathcal{C}(\tau):= \left\{ w: 0 < wi < \frac{\tau}{m}, \sum{i=1}^m wi = 1 \right\} where \tau > 0 is a hyperparameter bounding deviation from uniform distribution. c. Construct the semantic ray feature s(zk): s(zk) = \sum{i=1}^m wi F'i(r^(zk)). 4. Semantic Field Rendering: Render the final semantic logits \hat{S}(r) using volume rendering along the query ray: \hat{S}(r) = \sum{k=1}^N T(zk) \{1 - \exp(-\sigma(zk)\deltak)\} s(zk) where: \sigma(zk) is the predicted density from a Geometry-aware Network. \deltak = z{k+1} - zk is the interval between sampled points. T(zk) = \exp\left(-\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} \sigma(z{k'})\delta{k'}\right) is the accumulated transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def crossreprojectionattention( querypointsi: torch.Tensor, querypointsj: torch.Tensor, sourceposes: list, K: torch.Tensor, sourceimages: list, numsamples: int = 64, featuredim: int = 256, numheads: int = 8, geometrynetwork: nn.Module = None, cnnextractor: nn.Module = None, tau: float = 1.0) -> torch.Tensor: """ Implements Cross-Reprojection Attention. Returns: semanticlogits (Csemantic,) """ m = len(sourceposes) # 1. Ray Definition direction = (querypointsj - querypointsi) / torch.norm(querypointsj - querypointsi) # Standard NeRF stratified sampling is used in practice. zsamples = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples, device=querypointsi.device) # 2. Build 3D Contextual Space M M = torch.zeros(m, numsamples, featuredim, device=querypointsi.device) for i, (R, t) in enumerate(sourceposes): direxp = direction.unsqueeze(0).expand(numsamples, -1) piexp = querypointsi.unsqueeze(0).expand(numsamples, -1) # r(z) = pi + z direction rz = piexp + zsamples.unsqueeze(1) direxp # (N, 3) # Warping: r(z) = K pi(R r(z) + t) rtransformed = torch.einsum('ij,nj->ni', R, rz) + t # (N, 3) rproj = torch.einsum('ij,nj->ni', K, rtransformed) # (N, 3) rpixel = rproj[:,:2] / (rproj[:, 2:] + 1e-6) # (N, 2) # Extract features using shared U-Net-based CNN Fi = cnnextractor(sourceimages[i], rpixel) # (N, C) M[i] = Fi # 3. Intra-View Radial Attention Mprime = torch.zeroslike(M) Wq = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, featuredim)) Wk = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, featuredim)) Wv = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, featuredim)) Wo = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, featuredim)) for i in range(m): Fi = M[i] # (N, C) Q = torch.einsum('nc,cd->nd', Fi, Wq) Katt = torch.einsum('nc,cd->nd', Fi, Wk) V = torch.einsum('nc,cd->nd', Fi, Wv) dk = featuredim // numheads Qheads = Q.view(numsamples, numheads, dk).transpose(0, 1) Kheads = Katt.view(numsamples, numheads, dk).transpose(0, 1) Vheads = V.view(numsamples, numheads, dk).transpose(0, 1) scores = torch.matmul(Qheads, Kheads.transpose(1, 2)) / (dk 0.5) attnweights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) outheads = torch.matmul(attnweights, Vheads) out = outheads.transpose(0, 1).contiguous().view(numsamples, featuredim) Fiprime = torch.einsum('nc,cd->nd', out, Wo) Mprime[i] = Fiprime # 4. Cross-View Sparse Attention & Semantic Ray Construction # Compute weights w subject to 0 < wi < tau/m and sum(w)=1 # Constraint projection is implemented via clamping and renormalization. rawscores = torch.randn(m, device=Mprime.device) wbase = F.softmax(rawscores, dim=0) w = torch.clamp(wbase, min=1e-6, max=tau / m) w = w / w.sum() # Aggregate features: s(zk) = sumi wi F'i(r(zk)) s = torch.einsum('i,nci->nc', w, Mprime) # (N, C) # 5. Semantic Field Rendering # Predict density sigma from Geometry-aware Network sigma = geometrynetwork(s) # (N,) deltas = torch.diff(zsamples, dim=0) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltas[-1]]) # (N,) alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) # (N,) # T(zk) = exp(- sum{k'=1}^{k-1} sigma(z{k'}) delta{k'}) Tprev = 1.0 - alphas[:-1] T = torch.cat([torch.tensor([1.0], device=sigma.device), torch.cumprod(Tprev, dim=0)]) # Render: Shat(r) = sum T(zk) alphak s(zk) weightsrender = T alphas semanticlogits = torch.einsum('n,nc->c', weightsrender, s) return semanticlogits Parameters: \tau: Hyperparameter for weight distribution deviation bound. Constraint: 0 < wi < \tau/m. Keeps semantic consistency instead of bias across views. \tau=1 corresponds to mean aggregation. dk: Dimension of each attention head. Calculated as dk = C/H, where C is feature dimension and H is number of heads. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The projection function \pi(u) involves division by uz. Ensure uz is not zero (ray parallel to image plane) to avoid division by zero. Add a small epsilon. Boundaries: The reprojection r^(z) may fall outside the image boundaries of source views. The CNN extractor should handle out-of-bounds coordinates (e.g., via padding or clamping). Degenerate Input: The method assumes known camera poses (R, t) and calibration K. Time and Memory Complexity: CRA improves performance by 47.3% in FLOPs and 76.5% in GPU memory compared to dense attention. Measured Performance: On real data (ScanNet), with an input of 1024 \times 64 \times 8 \times 32, the full CRA module achieves 76.30% mIoU and 91.08% Total Accuracy with 5.40 GFLOPs, compared to 10.25 GFLOPs for Dense Attention. Strengths: Captures dense and global contextual information with computational efficiency; avoids heavy computational costs of dense attention. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera poses and calibration; performance depends on the quality of the shared CNN feature extractor. When to use: When generalizable semantic rendering is required with limited computational resources (GPU memory/FLOPs). Origin: Proposed in the S-Ray method. History: Developed to address the insufficiency of single-point feature extraction for semantic prediction in NeRF-based generalization rendering methods. Usage: Used in the S-Ray method for generalizable semantic rendering, compared against MVSNeRF, NeuRay, and Semantic-NeRF. It is designed to work without positional encoding engineering, unlike GPNR. Semantic Ray: Learning a Generalizable Semantic Field with Cross-Reprojection Attention, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01668, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 3D Alignment via Reprojection
head: Feature Reprojection Alignment
body: 3D Alignment via Reprojection is a technique in differentiable volume rendering that aligns features from neighboring training views with a novel rendered view by compensating for pose and geometry discrepancies. It solves the problem of leveraging relevant multi-view contextual information when camera orientations and positions differ significantly. Unlike its parent Pose-Aware Projection (PAP), which aggregates features based on camera distance to resolve ambiguous assignments, this method explicitly reprojects 3D coordinates into the novel view using the pinhole camera model and validates them via depth-based visibility testing. It differs from sibling Geometry Aware Feature Extraction by relying on explicit geometric reprojection rather than implicit geometric awareness. Inputs: Novel view image Ik and its camera pose Ck and intrinsic matrix Kk. Set of n neighboring training images \{Hi\}{i=1}^n with poses Ci and intrinsics Ki. NeRF depth map zi for the novel view, used for visibility checking. Leniency threshold l (typical value: 0.25). Outputs: Reprojected feature map H^f{i \rightarrow k} aligned with the novel view coordinates. Data Structures: Image features I^fk and H^fi: Dense tensors of spatial dimensions matching the input images, with a channel depth of 64. 3D coordinates \bm{x}k: Represented as homogeneous vectors [\bm{x}k, 1] where \bm{x}k = (xk, yk, zk), with (xk, yk) being pixel coordinates and zk the depth. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract 64-dimensional image features from the novel view Ik and each neighboring image Hi using separate small convolutional encoder blocks: I^fk = \text{conv}I(Ik) \{H^fi\}{i=1}^n = \text{conv}H(\{Hi\}{i=1}^n) 2. Coordinate Reprojection: For each pixel in the novel view with 3D coordinate \bm{x}k = (xk, yk, zk), reproject the coordinate into the neighboring camera view i using the pinhole camera model: \bm{x}{k \rightarrow i} = Ki Ci Ck^{-1} Kk^{-1} [\bm{x}k, 1] Here, \bm{x}{k \rightarrow i} = (x{k \rightarrow i}, y{k \rightarrow i}, z{k \rightarrow i}, 1) is the resulting homogeneous coordinate in camera i's space. Ki is the intrinsic matrix of camera i, and Ci is the pose matrix of camera i. 3. Visibility Testing: Calculate a visibility score visi to ensure geometric consistency by comparing the reprojected depth z{k \rightarrow i} with the NeRF-computed depth zi: visi = \mathcal{H}\left(1 - \frac{z{k \rightarrow i}}{zi} + l\right) Where \mathcal{H} is the Heaviside function and l is the leniency threshold (0.25). 4. Feature Copying: Form the reprojected feature map by copying values from the neighbor's feature map H^fi at the projected coordinates \bm{x}{k \rightarrow i} to the original coordinates \bm{x}k, weighted by the visibility score: H^f{i \rightarrow k} \langle \phi(\bm{x}k) \rangle = visi \times H^fi \langle \phi(\bm{x}{k \rightarrow i}) \rangle Where \phi(\bm{x}k) = (xk/zk, yk/zk) represents the 2D normalized coordinates, and \langle \rangle denotes 2D coordinate indexing (sampling). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ConvBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, inch, outch=64): super().init() self.conv = nn.Conv2d(inch, outch, kernelsize=3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): return F.relu(self.conv(x)) def reprojectfeatures(novelimg, neighborimgs, novelpose, neighborposes, novelK, neighborKs, nerfdepth, l=0.25): """ Aligns neighbor features to the novel view via 3D reprojection. Args: novelimg: Tensor (B, 3, H, W) neighborimgs: List of Tensors [(B, 3, H, W)] novelpose: Tensor (4, 4) Camera pose matrix Ck neighborposes: List of Tensors [(4, 4)] Camera pose matrices Ci novelK: Tensor (3, 3) Intrinsic matrix Kk neighborKs: List of Tensors [(3, 3)] Intrinsic matrices Ki nerfdepth: Tensor (B, 1, H, W) Depth map zi from NeRF for novel view leniencythreshold: Float l Returns: reprojectedfeatures: Tensor (B, 64, H, W) Aligned features """ convI = ConvBlock(3) convH = ConvBlock(3) novelfeat = convI(novelimg) neighborfeats = [convH(img) for img in neighborimgs] B,, H, W = novelfeat.shape u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='xy') u = u.float().to(novelimg.device).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) v = v.float().to(novelimg.device).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) z = nerfdepth # Homogeneous coordinate [xk, 1] as defined in source Xkhom = torch.cat([u, v, z, torch.oneslike(z)], dim=1) totalfeat = torch.zeroslike(novelfeat) for feati, posei, Ki in zip(neighborfeats, neighborposes, neighborKs): # Reprojection: x{k->i} = Ki Ci Ck^{-1} Kk^{-1} [xk, 1] Xkflat = Xkhom.permute(0, 1, 3, 2).contiguous().view(B, 4, -1) Xray = torch.matmul(torch.inverse(novelK), Xkflat) Xworld = torch.matmul(torch.inverse(novelpose), torch.cat([Xray, torch.ones(B, 1, Xray.shape[2]).to(novelimg.device)], dim=1)) Xcami = torch.matmul(posei, Xworld) Xproj = torch.matmul(Ki, Xcami[:3,:,:]) Xproj = Xproj.view(B, 3, H, W) xproj, yproj, zproj = Xproj[:, 0], Xproj[:, 1], Xproj[:, 2] # Visibility test vis = (1.0 - zproj / (z + 1e-6) + l) > 0.0 vis = vis.float() # Feature sampling at phi(x{k->i}) = (xproj/zproj, yproj/zproj) # Normalize to [-1, 1] for gridsample xnorm = (xproj / (Ki[0, 0] W) 2 - 1) ynorm = (yproj / (Ki[1, 1] H) 2 - 1) grid = torch.stack([xnorm, ynorm], dim=-1) sampled = F.gridsample(feati, grid, aligncorners=False) totalfeat += vis sampled return totalfeat Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Inconsistency: Errors in camera pose estimation (e.g., from COLMAP) or NeRF geometry lead to imperfect correspondences. Depth Ambiguity: The visibility test relies on the accuracy of the NeRF depth map. Out-of-Bounds: Reprojected coordinates may fall outside the neighbor image boundaries. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of neighbors n. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and neighbors, as features for all neighbors are processed. Performance: Evaluated on LLFF, 360v2, and DTU datasets. Uses 5 neighbors for LLFF/360v2 and 2 for DTU. Strengths: Leverages relevant information from neighbors despite pose differences. Limitations: Dependent on the accuracy of camera poses and NeRF geometry. Originated in RoGUENeRF: A Robust Geometry-Consistent Universal Enhancer for NeRF. It is used to enhance NeRF renderings by aligning features from neighboring training views. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Transformer-based Parameterization
head: GS-LRM
body: This method is a feed-forward neural network approach that reconstructs a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene from a small set of input images by leveraging a Transformer architecture. It solves the problem of sparse-view reconstruction by tokenizing input views and camera parameters, processing them through a Transformer block, and directly decoding the resulting tokens into 3D Gaussian parameters. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md] by replacing iterative optimization with a direct inference pipeline, and from pixel-aligned methods like MVSplat by operating in a global token space rather than per-pixel ray alignment. The method functions as a multi-view feed-forward network. It takes a small set of input images and their corresponding camera parameters as input and outputs a set of 3D Gaussians (position, rotation, scale, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color) that represent the scene. Data Structures: 1. Input Tokens: A sequence of tokens representing the input images and camera poses. 2. Transformer Output: A sequence of latent tokens produced by the Transformer encoder/decoder blocks. 3. Gaussian Parameters: The final output, typically a tensor or list of Gaussian primitives. Steps: 1. Tokenization: The method takes N input images (typically N=2 to 4) and their associated camera parameters. These are converted into a unified token sequence. The images are likely processed through a visual encoder (e.g., ViT) to extract visual features, which are then concatenated with embeddings representing the camera intrinsics and extrinsics. 2. Transformer Processing: The concatenated token sequence is passed through a Transformer block. The Transformer attends to relationships between the different views and camera poses, aggregating multi-view information into the latent tokens. 3. Decoding: The output tokens from the Transformer are decoded into the parameters of the 3D Gaussians. This involves a linear or MLP-based projection from the latent token space to the Gaussian parameter space (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). Formulas: Let I1,..., IN be the input images and C1,..., CN be the camera parameters. The input is tokenized into a sequence T{in}. The Transformer computes T{out} = \text{Transformer}(T{in}). The Gaussian parameters G are decoded as G = \text{Decoder}(T{out}). Parameters: Number of input views: Typically 2 to 4. Transformer depth and width: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Scale Ambiguity: If camera intrinsics are not properly encoded, scale ambiguity may arise. NoPoSplat addresses this by introducing intrinsics token embeddings, but the base GS-LRM method assumes known poses. Sparse Views: Performance may degrade if the number of input views is too small or if overlap is minimal, though the Transformer's attention mechanism helps mitigate this compared to pixel-aligned methods. Replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a voxel-aligned strategy, aggregating multi-view features into a shared 3D voxel grid before regressing Gaussian parameters. Decodes Gaussian attributes (position, rotation, scale, opacity, color) in a fixed sequential order from tri-plane features to reduce degrees of freedom. Maps learned scene tokens into freely placed 3D Gaussians, decoupling placement from fixed camera rays for flexible scene representation. Time Complexity: Inference time is constant with respect to scene complexity once the model is trained, depending primarily on the number of input views and the Transformer size. It is significantly faster than iterative optimization methods like standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the Transformer model weights and the intermediate feature maps. The output Gaussian count is determined by the decoding head and is not explicitly constrained by the input resolution in the same way as pixel-aligned methods. Strengths: Fast inference (feed-forward); handles sparse views better than pixel-aligned methods due to global context aggregation; no need for per-scene optimization. Limitations: Quality may be lower than optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense views; requires training a large neural network; potential for floaters or alignment errors if the Transformer fails to resolve multi-view consistency. When to use: When fast reconstruction from a few images is required, or when iterative optimization is computationally prohibitive. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction from many views is needed and optimization time is acceptable. The method is referred to as GS-LRM in the literature. It builds upon earlier feed-forward networks like MVSplat and PixelSplat. GS-LRM specifically tokenizes images and camera parameters, processes them with a Transformer, and decodes them into Gaussian parameters, representing a shift from pixel-aligned to token-aligned Gaussian prediction. NoPoSplat is a related variant that removes the need for known camera poses. From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting: Theory and Applications, https://doi.org/10.1109/sibgrapi67909.2025.11223276, fetched 2026-10-26

name: VolSplat
head: Rethinking Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Voxel-Aligned Prediction, Voxel-aligned Feed-forward 3DGS
body: VolSplat is a multi-view feed-forward framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that replaces the standard pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction with a voxel-aligned prediction strategy. It solves the problems of view-biased density distributions and alignment errors (such as floaters) inherent in pixel-aligned methods by aggregating multi-view features into a shared 3D voxel grid before regressing Gaussian parameters. Unlike its parent method, which uses a transformer to decode tokens directly into Gaussian parameters, VolSplat explicitly constructs a 3D voxel feature grid via depth unprojection and refines it with a sparse 3D decoder to enable adaptive density control based on volumetric scene complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N input images I = \{Ii\}{i=1}^N where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} and their corresponding camera poses P = \{Pi\}{i=1}^N. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{(\muj, \Sigmaj, \alphaj, cj)\}{j=1}^M, where M is the number of occupied voxels, and novel views rendered from these Gaussians. Data Structures: Voxel Feature Grid: A sparse 3D grid storing features for occupied voxels. Each voxel holds a feature vector f \in \mathbb{R}^C. Gaussian Parameters: For each occupied voxel, the model predicts: Position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or its 6 independent components) Opacity \alpha \in [0, 1] Color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 Steps: 1. 2D Feature Extraction: Extract 2D features for each input image using a Transformer-based network (pretrained image encoder \Phi{image}). Fi^{raw} = \Phi{image}(Ii) 2. Cost Volume Construction: Construct per-view cost volumes using plane sweeping. This involves matching features across views at different depth hypotheses. 3. Depth Prediction: Estimate a depth map Di for each view using a Depth Prediction Module. 4. Unprojection to Voxel Grid: Unproject the 2D features into 3D space using the estimated depth maps Di and camera poses Pi to form an initial voxel feature grid. Features are aggregated into the shared 3D voxel container, decoupling feature fusion from camera view frustums. 5. 3D Feature Refinement: Refine the 3D voxel features using a sparse 3D decoder (implemented as a 3D U-Net). The sparse 3D decoder takes the initial voxel features as input. It predicts residual features \Delta f for each occupied voxel. The refined voxel features f{refined} are obtained by adding the residuals to the original features: f{refined} = f{initial} + \Delta f (See Figure 3 in) 6. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Predict the parameters of a 3D Gaussian for each occupied voxel based on the refined voxel features f{refined}. A prediction head \Psi{pred} maps f{refined} to (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c). 7. Rendering: Render novel views from the predicted 3D Gaussians using standard differentiable Gaussian splatting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volsplatforward(images, cameraposes, voxelgridshape, depthhypotheses): """ images: List of N images, shape (H, W, 3) cameraposes: List of N camera pose matrices (4, 4) voxelgridshape: Tuple (D, Hv, Wv) defining the 3D grid resolution depthhypotheses: List of depth planes for plane sweeping Returns: List of Gaussian parameters for occupied voxels """ N = len(images) # Step 1: Extract 2D features using a pretrained Transformer encoder def transformerencoder(img): # Standard ViT/Transformer forward pass returning feature maps # Internal architecture details not provided in sources return img # Returns feature tensor of shape (Hp, Wp, Cp) rawfeatures = [transformerencoder(img) for img in images] # Step 2: Construct per-view cost volumes with plane sweeping def constructcostvolume(feature, pose, depthplanes): # Projects feature to different depth planes and aggregates multi-view consistency # Standard MVS cost volume construction return feature # Returns cost volume tensor costvolumes = [constructcostvolume(rawfeatures[i], cameraposes[i], depthhypotheses) for i in range(N)] # Step 3: Estimate depth maps def depthpredictionmodule(costvolume): # Predicts depth map from cost volume via regression # Standard depth prediction head return costvolume # Returns depth map tensor depthmaps = [depthpredictionmodule(costvolumes[i]) for i in range(N)] # Step 4: Unproject 2D features to 3D voxel grid def unprojecttovoxelgrid(features, depths, poses, gridshape): # For each view, back-project 2D features to 3D coordinates using depth and pose # Aggregates features into a sparse 3D grid (e.g., max/average pooling) # Exact aggregation function not specified in sources grid = {} for i in range(N): for y in range(features[i].shape[0]): for x in range(features[i].shape[1]): # Compute 3D point from depth, pose, and pixel coords # Map to voxel grid indices # Aggregate feature into grid pass return grid voxelfeaturesinitial = unprojecttovoxelgrid(rawfeatures, depthmaps, cameraposes, voxelgridshape) # Step 5: Refine voxel features using Sparse 3D Decoder (3D U-Net) def sparse3ddecoder(grid): # 3D U-Net forward pass on sparse grid # Returns residual features for each occupied voxel # Architecture details not provided in sources return {k: v 0.1 for k, v in grid.items()} residualfeatures = sparse3ddecoder(voxelfeaturesinitial) # Add residuals to initial features voxelfeaturesrefined = {k: voxelfeaturesinitial[k] + residualfeatures[k] for k in residualfeatures} # Step 6: Predict Gaussian parameters for each occupied voxel def gaussianpredictionhead(feature): # Linear/MLP head mapping feature to (mu, Sigma, alpha, c) # Standard prediction head return feature occupiedvoxels = list(voxelfeaturesrefined.keys()) gaussians = [gaussianpredictionhead(voxelfeaturesrefined[vid]) for vid in occupiedvoxels] return gaussians Parameters: N: Number of input views. H, W: Image height and width. C: Feature dimension. \Phi{image}: Pretrained image encoder (e.g., Transformer-based). h: Function for cross-view feature matching and fusion (used in pixel-aligned baselines, but VolSplat replaces this with volumetric aggregation). U: Feature upsampler (used in pixel-aligned baselines to upsample features to full resolution F{full} = U(F)). VolSplat does not use this upsampling step for the final prediction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions and Low Texture: Pixel-aligned methods suffer from alignment errors in these regions, leading to floaters. VolSplat mitigates this by fusing information from multiple views into a shared 3D container, ensuring robust multi-view consistency. Scene Complexity: Pixel-aligned methods enforce a uniform density distribution (|S| = H \times W \times N), causing redundant primitives in simple regions and failure to capture fine-grained structures. VolSplat enables adaptive density control based on 3D scene complexity, as the distribution of Gaussians is determined by the volumetric structure itself. Discretization Error: Sampling at discrete pixel locations is sensitive to camera calibration and discretization error. Voxel alignment reduces this by operating in a unified 3D space. VS-Splat is a feed-forward framework for 3D object reconstruction from sparse-view 2D images that employs a coarse-to-fine (C2F) strategy to predict 3D Gaussian primitives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like LaRa and GenDen by performing voxel-level selection before generating fine primitives, rather than selecting existing primitives for refinement. This ensures that the coarse representation determines the spatial location for new fine primitives, enabling adaptive density control without auxiliary supervision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on RealEstate10K, ScanNet, and ACID benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Strengths: Robust multi-view consistency due to volumetric aggregation. Cleaner occlusion handling. Adaptive density control based on scene complexity. Eliminates the need for per-query 2D prediction patterns. Limitations: Requires accurate depth estimation for unprojection. Relies on a sparse 3D decoder (3D U-Net), which may have higher computational overhead compared to simple pixel-wise prediction heads. When to use: When multi-view alignment is challenging due to occlusions or low texture, and adaptive density control is required for complex scenes. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and a simpler pixel-aligned method suffices, or when the scene is very simple and uniform density is acceptable. VolSplat was introduced in the paper "VolSplat: Rethinking Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Voxel-Aligned Prediction". It addresses the limitations of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods that rely on pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction paradigms. The method was released with code and checkpoints in September 2025. It is evaluated on large-scale benchmarks such as RealEstate10K, ScanNet, and ACID. name: VS-Splat
head: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting [S1, unofficial]
body: VS-Splat is a feed-forward framework for 3D object reconstruction from sparse-view 2D images that employs a coarse-to-fine (C2F) strategy to predict 3D Gaussian primitives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like LaRa and GenDen by performing voxel-level selection before generating fine primitives, rather than selecting existing primitives for refinement. This ensures that the coarse representation determines the spatial location for new fine primitives, enabling adaptive density control without auxiliary supervision. Inputs: N 2D images \{in: n = 1, \dots, N\} and corresponding camera pose parameters. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gk\} aligned to selected voxels. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Predefined in normalized 3D space [-0.5, 0.5]^3, centered at the origin, using the center-coordinate system. Dimensions are H \times W \times D. All views share this grid. 3D Gaussian Primitive Gk: Parameterized by: Mean vector \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3 (position). Covariance matrix \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, decomposed into scale vector sk \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation quaternion rk \in \mathbb{R}^4. Opacity ok \in [0, 1]. Spherical harmonics coefficients hk \in \mathbb{R}^{3S} (view-dependent color, S basis functions per channel). Algorithm Steps: 1. View-Specific Volumetric Feature Extraction: Extract 2D feature maps from each input image in using a shared feature extractor. Modulate each feature map using Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) with a Plücker embedding map pn derived from camera pose parameters. Backproject the modulated feature maps into the predefined voxel grid to produce view-specific feature volumes vn \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times C} for n=1, \dots, N. 2. Multi-View Feature Aggregation and Compression: Form an initial unified feature volume v0 by concatenating the voxel-wise mean and variance of the view-specific volumes: v0 = \text{Mean}(v1, \dots, vN) \oplus \text{Var}(v1, \dots, vN) where \oplus denotes channel-wise concatenation, and \text{Mean}(\cdot) and \text{Var}(\cdot) are voxel-wise operators across views. Compress v0 using a 3D convolutional compressor \mathcal{C}: v{\text{comp}} = \mathcal{C}(v0), \quad \mathcal{C}: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times 2C} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times \tilde{C}} where \tilde{C} \ll 2C. Transform the compressed volume using a lightweight 3D U-Net variant \mathcal{U}{\text{light}} (with one encoding and one decoding block) to obtain the unified volumetric representation \tilde{v}: \tilde{v} = \mathcal{U}{\text{light}}(v{\text{comp}}) \tilde{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times \tilde{C}}. 3. Coarse Stage (Primitive Prediction): Decode features from \tilde{v} into coarse Gaussian primitives. For each voxel (h, w, d), use a fully-connected decoder \mathcal{D}{\text{crs}} to predict parameters \{\mu{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}, s{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}, r{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}, o{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}, h{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}\}. Position Prediction: Predict a positional offset \Deltak \in [-r, r]^3 for the k-th voxel, where r > 0 is the maximum displacement. Compute the final mean: \muk = \text{voxel\center}k + \Deltak This ensures the primitive remains within its voxel. 4. Voxel Selection Stage: Predict voxel-wise confidence scores \sigma \in [0, 1]^{H \times W \times D} using a fully-connected predictor \mathcal{P}: \mathbb{R}^{\tilde{C}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} and a Gumbel-Sigmoid operator. For each feature vector \tilde{v}{h,w,d}, compute the confidence logit \mathcal{P}(\tilde{v}{h,w,d}). Apply Gumbel-Sigmoid to obtain the score \sigma{h,w,d}: \sigma{h,w,d} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\frac{\mathcal{P}(\tilde{v}{h,w,d}) + g0 - g1}{\tau}\right)} where g0, g1 \sim \text{Gumbel}(0, 1) are i.i.d. samples, and \tau is the temperature. Opacity Refinement: Multiply the coarse opacity by the confidence score to refine it: \tilde{o}{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}} = \sigma{h,w,d} \cdot o{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}. Selection: Define the set of selected indices I where confidence exceeds 0.5: I = \{(h, w, d): \sigma{h,w,d} > 0.5\} The coarse primitives at these indices are termed "skeletal" Gaussian primitives. 5. Fine Stage: Predict multiple fine-grained Gaussian primitives near each "skeletal" primitive at selected voxels (h, w, d) \in I. Use a selective feature refinement module to refine coarse global features by integrating fine local geometric features. Note: The specific architecture of the fine stage decoder is not detailed in the provided sources. 6. Training: Use 2D supervision (rendering loss) on both coarse and fine renderings. The selection module is trained end-to-end solely through the rendering objective, without pseudo-labels or auxiliary supervision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class VSSplat: def init(self, H, W, D, C, Ctilde, rmax, S=3): self.H, self.W, self.D = H, W, D self.C = C self.Ctilde = Ctilde self.rmax = rmax self.S = S # 3D convolutional compressor C: R^{HxWxDx2C} -> R^{HxWxDxCtilde} self.compressor = nn.Conv3d(2 C, Ctilde, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Lightweight 3D U-Net variant Ulight (one encoding, one decoding block) self.unetlight = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(Ctilde, Ctilde, 3, padding=1), nn.Conv3d(Ctilde, Ctilde, 3, padding=1)) # Fully-connected decoder Dcrs: R^{Ctilde} -> R^{3+3+4+1+3S} self.coarsedecoder = nn.Linear(Ctilde, 3 + 3 + 4 + 1 + 3 S) # Fully-connected predictor P: R^{Ctilde} -> R self.confidencepredictor = nn.Linear(Ctilde, 1) def forward(self, images, cameraposes, tau=0.1): N = images.shape[0] viewspecificfeatures = [] # 1. View-Specific Volumetric Feature Extraction # [Comment: Source does not specify the exact 2D feature extractor, AdaLN modulation, or backprojection implementation.] for n in range(N): # [Comment: Placeholder for shared 2D feature extractor, AdaLN with Plücker embedding, and backprojection to voxel grid.] vn = torch.zeros(1, self.C, self.H, self.W, self.D) viewspecificfeatures.append(vn) vstack = torch.stack(viewspecificfeatures, dim=0) # 2. Multi-View Feature Aggregation and Compression # v0 = Mean(v1,..., vN) concat Var(v1,..., vN) meanfeat = torch.mean(vstack, dim=0) varfeat = torch.var(vstack, dim=0, unbiased=False) v0 = torch.cat([meanfeat, varfeat], dim=0) # vcomp = C(v0) vcomp = self.compressor(v0) # vtilde = Ulight(vcomp) vtilde = self.unetlight(vcomp) # 3. Coarse Stage B, Ct, H, W, D = vtilde.shape vflat = vtilde.permute(1, 2, 3, 4, 0).reshape(-1, Ctilde) coarseparams = self.coarsedecoder(vflat) muoffset = coarseparams[:,:3] s = coarseparams[:, 3:6] r = coarseparams[:, 6:10] oraw = coarseparams[:, 10:11] h = coarseparams[:, 11:] voxelcenters = self.getvoxelcenters() # Position Prediction: muk = voxelcenterk + Deltak, Deltak in [-r, r]^3 muoffset = torch.clamp(muoffset, -self.rmax, self.rmax) mu = voxelcenters + muoffset # 4. Voxel Selection conflogits = self.confidencepredictor(vflat).squeeze(-1) # Gumbel-Sigmoid: sigma = 1 / (1 + exp(-(P(v) + g0 - g1)/tau)) g0 = -torch.log(-torch.log(torch.randlike(conflogits) + 1e-10) + 1e-10) g1 = -torch.log(-torch.log(torch.randlike(conflogits) + 1e-10) + 1e-10) sigma = 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-(conflogits + g0 - g1) / tau)) # Opacity Refinement: otilde = sigma ocrs orefined = sigma torch.sigmoid(oraw) # Selection: I = {(h,w,d): sigma > 0.5} threshold = 0.5 selectedmask = sigma > threshold selectedindices = torch.nonzero(selectedmask, astuple=False).squeeze() # 5. Fine Stage # [Comment: The specific architecture of the fine stage decoder is not detailed in the provided sources.] if selectedindices.numel() > 0: vselected = vflat[selectedindices] # [Comment: Fine stage decoder call omitted as architecture is not specified in sources.] fineparams = None return mu, s, r, orefined, h, fineparams else: return mu, s, r, orefined, h, None def getvoxelcenters(self): # Center-coordinate system in [-0.5, 0.5]^3 x = torch.linspace(-0.5 + 1/(2self.H), 0.5 - 1/(2self.H), self.H) y = torch.linspace(-0.5 + 1/(2self.W), 0.5 - 1/(2self.W), self.W) z = torch.linspace(-0.5 + 1/(2self.D), 0.5 - 1/(2self.D), self.D) xx, yy, zz = torch.meshgrid(x, y, z, indexing='ij') return torch.stack([xx, yy, zz], dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3) Parameters: Voxel Grid: [-0.5, 0.5]^3, centered at origin. Temperature \tau: Controls Gumbel-Sigmoid stochasticity. Low \tau pushes scores to 0 or 1. Selection Threshold: 0.5. No tuning required. Max Displacement r: Hyperparameter for positional offset bounds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The Gumbel-Sigmoid approximation requires careful handling of numerical stability in the exponential term, especially with low \tau. Boundaries: Positional offsets are clamped to [-r, r] to ensure primitives stay within voxels. Degenerate Input: If no voxels exceed the 0.5 threshold, the fine stage produces no primitives. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Uses a lightweight 3D U-Net variant and feature compression (\tilde{C} \ll 2C) to reduce memory and computational cost compared to transformer-based approaches. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: End-to-end learnable voxel selection without auxiliary supervision; coarse representation guides fine primitive placement; adaptive density control. Limitations: Relies on a predefined voxel grid; fine stage architecture details are not specified. When to use: Sparse-view 3D object reconstruction where adaptive density and feed-forward efficiency are prioritized. VS-Splat was proposed in the paper "VS-Splat: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse-views". It builds on the background of 3D Gaussian Splatting [7] and voxel-aligned feed-forward models [11, 12], addressing limitations in selection strategies used by prior works like LaRa and GenDen.
