name: Sequential Gaussian Attribute Decoding
head: Iterative Attribute Decoding, Sequential Decoder
body: Sequential Gaussian Attribute Decoding is a method for estimating 3D Gaussian Splatting attributes (position, rotation, scale, opacity, and color) from tri-plane features by processing them in a fixed order rather than in parallel. It solves the problem of high degrees of freedom in joint attribute prediction by creating dependencies between attributes, allowing each decoder to specialize based on prior information. It differs from parallel decoders (e.g., HUGS [21]) which compute all attributes simultaneously. Inputs: Tri-plane features representing the 3D scene. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position offset, scale, rotation, opacity, and color. Data Structures: The method uses a series of fully connected neural network decoders. Each decoder Di corresponds to one attribute in the sequence. Decoder Architecture: Hidden layers: 3 layers. Neurons per layer: 128. Activation: GELU for hidden layers. Output activation: None for all attributes except scale. Scale output activation: Inverted Softplus. Numbered Steps: 1. Color Decoding: Forward the tri-plane features into the first decoder D{color} to estimate the color attribute C. 2. Opacity Decoding: Concatenate the estimated color C with the original tri-plane features. Feed this combined input into the second decoder D{opacity} to estimate opacity \alpha. 3. Rotation Decoding: Concatenate the estimated rotation R, the previously estimated opacity \alpha, and the tri-plane features. Feed this into the third decoder D{rotation} to estimate rotation R. 4. Scale Decoding: Concatenate the estimated scale S, the previously estimated rotation R, opacity \alpha, and the tri-plane features. Feed this into the fourth decoder D{scale} to estimate scale S. The output layer applies an inverted Softplus activation to prevent excessive Gaussian sizes. 5. Position Offset Decoding: Concatenate the estimated position offset \Delta P, the previously estimated scale S, rotation R, opacity \alpha, and the tri-plane features. Feed this into the final decoder D{pos} to estimate the position offset \Delta P. Formulas: Let T be the tri-plane features. Let Ai be the attribute decoded at step i. The input to decoder Di is: Input(Di) = [T, A1, A2,..., A{i-1}] where A1 = Color, A2 = Opacity, A3 = Rotation, A4 = Scale, A5 = PositionOffset. Parameters: Hidden layers: 3. Neurons per hidden layer: 128. Activation function: GELU. Scale output activation: Inverted Softplus. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Memory Usage: Without the inverted Softplus activation on the scale decoder, Gaussians may become excessively large, leading to excessive GPU memory usage during rasterization. Dependency Order: The method relies on the specific order (Color \rightarrow Opacity \rightarrow Rotation \rightarrow Scale \rightarrow Position Offset) to reduce degrees of freedom for each subsequent decoder. A decoder variant that spawns exactly kn Gaussian tokens per anchor n based on an allocation k, refining them via local cross-attention to produce B final Gaussians with computational cost linear in B. It differs from standard sequential decoding by introducing a hierarchical neighbor search and token spawning mechanism. Choose this when strict budget control and linear scaling with the number of Gaussians are required. Steps: 1. Token Spawning: For each anchor an, instantiate kn distinct Gaussian tokens tb using a TokenGen function conditioned on the slot index: \{tb\}{b=1}^B = \text{TokenGen}(\{(an, kn)\}{n=1}^N). 2. Initial Prediction: Predict an initial Gaussian g{b0} = \text{Head}(tb) for each token, including its initial center \mu{b0}. 3. Anchor Centroid Calculation: For each anchor n with kn > 0, compute the centroid of its initial Gaussians: \bar{\mu}n = \frac{1}{kn} \sum{b: nb=n} \mu{b0}. 4. Hierarchical Neighbor Search: Find K{anc} nearest anchors to \bar{\mu}n among anchors with km > 0: N{anc}(n) = \text{KNN}{K{anc}}(\bar{\mu}n; \{\bar{\mu}m: km > 0\}). Find K{gs} nearest Gaussian tokens to \mu{b0} only among Gaussians belonging to the local anchors N{anc}(nb): N{gs}(b) = \text{KNN}{K{gs}}(\mu{b0}; \{\mu{j0}: nj \in N{anc}(nb)\}). 5. Refinement: Refine token tb over L layers of cross-attention with neighbors N{gs}(b), followed by a feed-forward layer: tb \leftarrow tb + \text{CrossAttn}(tb, \{tj\}{j \in N{gs}(b)}). 6. Final Prediction: Predict a correction \Delta gb from the refined token tb using a residual head, yielding the final Gaussian gb = g{b0} + \Delta gb. Parameters: K{anc}: Number of nearest anchors to search for hierarchical neighbor search. K{gs}: Number of nearest Gaussian tokens to search within local anchors. L: Number of cross-attention layers for refinement. Regularizers (to ensure validity of hierarchical search): Voronoi Loss: Keeps each Gaussian closer to its own parent anchor’s centroid \bar{\mu}{nb} than to any neighboring anchor’s centroid \bar{\mu}m: L{vor} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{b=1}^B \max{m \in N{anc}(nb)} \left( 0, \|\mu{b0} - \bar{\mu}{nb}\| - \|\mu{b0} - \bar{\mu}m\| \right). Offset Loss: Constrains the residual correction \Delta \mub to limit Gaussian drift: L{offset} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{b=1}^B \max \left( 0, \frac{\|\Delta \mub\|}{d{nb}} - \delta \right)^2 where dn is the local anchor spacing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces high degrees of freedom for each decoder, allowing for easier specialization of the network for specific attributes. The inverted Softplus activation prevents excessive GPU memory usage during rasterization. Limitations: The sequential nature imposes a fixed dependency order, which may not be optimal for all scenes. When to use: When using a decoder network to estimate Gaussian Splatting attributes from tri-plane features and specialization per attribute is desired. When not to use: When parallel computation of all attributes is preferred or when strict resource linear scaling with hierarchical neighbor search is required (use Resource-Linear Gaussian Decoding instead). Sequential Gaussian Attribute Decoding was introduced in the context of Gaussian Splatting Decoders for 3D-aware Generative Adversarial Networks. It contrasts with parallel decoders like HUGS [21] and transformer-based models [50] by calculating attributes sequentially. The Resource-Linear variant was introduced in RLSplat to provide budget control and linear computational cost. name: Gaussian Decoding from Scene Tokens
head: Scene Token Fusion and Gaussian Decoding, Scene Token Gaussian Decoding
body: Gaussian Decoding from Scene Tokens is a method that maps learned scene tokens into a set of freely placed 3D Gaussians, allowing each token to represent a surface region with variable spatial extent and complexity. It differs from ray-anchored decoding by decoupling Gaussian placement from fixed camera rays, enabling more flexible scene representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene tokens \stokk (derived from geometry tokens), geometry tokens, visual tokens from three backbone layers, and a color embedding. Output: A set of G 3D Gaussians per scene token, defined by center, scale, rotation, opacity, and color. Data Structures: Scene Tokens: Vectors representing surface regions. Initialized from a shared template with a forward bias of z=0.5. Geometry Tokens: Derived from features of three backbone layers, serving as keys in cross-attention. Visual Tokens: Values in cross-attention, taken from the deepest backbone layers first. Color Embedding: Used in the final residual cross-attention for appearance information. Numbered Steps: 1. Fusion: Perform fusion using three blocks. Each block consists of: Cross-attention: Queries are scene tokens; keys are geometry tokens; values are visual tokens from one layer (deepest first). Self-attention: Among the scene tokens. 2. Appearance Injection: Apply a final residual cross-attention with the color embedding as values to add appearance information. 3. Decoding: Decode each scene token into G=32 Gaussians using a two-layer MLP. Formula: The set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}k for token k is decoded as: \mathcal {G}k = \left \{ \left ( \gmean {kj}, \gscale {kj}, \grot {kj}, \gopac {kj}, \gcolor {kj} \right) \right \}{j=1}^{\ngs } = D(\stok k) where: \gmean{kj}: Center of the j-th Gaussian. \gscale{kj}: Scale of the j-th Gaussian. \grot{kj}: Rotation of the j-th Gaussian. \gopac{kj}: Opacity of the j-th Gaussian. \gcolor{kj}: Color of the j-th Gaussian. \ngs: Number of Gaussians per token (G). Parameters: G=32: Number of Gaussians produced per scene token. Spherical Harmonics: Degree-1 SH used for color representation. Attention Heads: 24 heads in cross-attention blocks. MLP Ratio: 4. Activation: GELU. Residual Gates: Initialized to 0.01. Coordinate Frame: All geometry expressed in the coordinate frame of the first input camera. Scene Scale: Normalized so the median distance of input depth points to the origin is one. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodescenetokens(scenetokens, geometrytokens, visualtokenslayers, colorembedding): """ Decodes scene tokens into 3D Gaussians. Args: scenetokens: List of scene token vectors. geometrytokens: Geometry token vectors for cross-attention keys. visualtokenslayers: List of visual token vectors from backbone layers (deepest first). colorembedding: Color embedding vector for final appearance injection. Returns: List of Gaussian sets, one per scene token. """ # Step 1: Fusion using three blocks # Each block: Cross-attention (scene tokens as queries, geometry tokens as keys, visual tokens as values) # followed by Self-attention on scene tokens. # Note: Visual tokens are taken from layers deepest first. for i in range(3): visualtokens = visualtokenslayers[i] # Cross-attention scenetokens = crossattention( queries=scenetokens, keys=geometrytokens, values=visualtokens, numheads=24, mlpratio=4, activation='GELU', residualgateinit=0.01) # Self-attention scenetokens = selfattention( queries=scenetokens, keys=scenetokens, values=scenetokens, numheads=24, mlpratio=4, activation='GELU', residualgateinit=0.01) # name: SAGA
head: OmniSeg3D-GS, SegAnyGaussians
body: SAGA is a 2D promptable segmentation method lifted to 3D, leveraging the Segment Anything Model (SAM) for efficient segmentation within 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It differs from sibling methods like CoR-GS by relying on SAM's 2D segmentation capabilities to guide 3D Gaussian assignment rather than learned identity encodings or language features. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussians reconstructed from images and 2D segmentation prompts (points, boxes, or masks). Outputs: A segmented 3D scene where Gaussians are classified into foreground/background or specific object instances based on the 2D prompts. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation. Layout details: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. SAM Integration: Leverage SAM to extract segmentation masks or features from input 2D views. 2. Prompt Lifting: Map 2D prompts to 3D space by associating 2D segmentation results with the corresponding 3D Gaussians. 3. Gaussian Assignment: Assign instance IDs or segmentation labels to individual 3D Gaussians based on their overlap with the 2D SAM-generated masks. 4. Feature Field: Employ a low-dimensional feature field upsampled using a convolutional decoder to improve rendering efficiency. Formulas: Not given in the sources. SAGA (also known as OmniSeg3D-GS or SegAnyGaussians) was introduced as a method to lift 2D promptable segmentation to 3D using 3DGS. It leverages SAM for efficient segmentation within 3DGS. name: Quantile Rendering
head: Q-Render
body: Quantile Rendering (Q-Render) is a sparse, transmittance-guided sampling strategy designed to efficiently render high-dimensional feature maps from 3D Gaussians. It solves the computational bottleneck of dense volume rendering, where accumulating high-dimensional features along every ray scales poorly with feature dimensionality. Unlike conventional volume rendering, which processes all rasterized Gaussians, Q-Render shifts the Riemann partition from the spatial domain to the transmittance domain, sampling only the most representative "quantile Gaussians" that dominate the ray's transmittance profile. This approach reduces complexity from O(N C) to O(N + K C), enabling real-time rendering of high-dimensional data (e.g., 512-D CLIP embeddings) while maintaining segmentation accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \mathcal{G}: Set of optimized 3D Gaussians, where each gi \in \mathcal{G} contains parameters \{\mui, si, ri, \alphai, \text{sph}i\}. \mathcal{F}: Predicted Gaussian features, where each fi \in \mathcal{F} is a vector in \mathbb{R}^C. K: Hyperparameter defining the number of quantile segments (and thus the number of sampled Gaussians). I: Indices of rasterized 3D Gaussians intersecting the target ray, sorted by depth. Output: \tilde{f}Q \in \mathbb{R}^C: The rendered feature vector for the ray. Data Structures: The algorithm iterates through the list of rasterized Gaussian indices I using standard accumulators for transmittance and feature vectors. Mathematical Background: Standard volume rendering integrates feature c(t) weighted by density \sigma(t) and transmittance T(t) over spatial distance t: C{vol} = \int0^\infty c(t) \sigma(t) T(t) dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int0^t \sigma(s) ds). By changing variables to transmittance u = T(t), where du = -\sigma(t)T(t)dt, the integral transforms to a Riemann integral over u \in [0, 1]: C{vol} = \int0^1 c(u) du Q-Render approximates this integral using a Right Riemann Sum by partitioning the transmittance domain [0, 1] into K+1 equal segments defined by boundaries 0 = u{K+1} < uK < \dots < u1 < u0 = 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulators: Set current transmittance T \leftarrow 1, accumulated feature fQ \leftarrow \mathbf{0}, and quantile counter k \leftarrow 0. 2. Iterate Rasterized Gaussians: For each Gaussian index i in I: a. Retrieve Gaussian gi and feature fi. b. Compute test transmittance after passing through gi: T{test} \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alpha'i), where \alpha'i is the effective alpha of the Gaussian. c. Quantile Boundary Check: Determine if the transmittance has crossed the next quantile boundary. The boundary for the (k+1)-th segment is 1 - \frac{k+1}{K+1}. If T{test} < 1 - \frac{k+1}{K+1}: i. Increment k to reflect crossing a boundary. ii. Sample Quantile Gaussian: The current Gaussian gi is selected as the representative for the quantile interval ending at the boundary. Compute its weight wQ \leftarrow T \cdot \alpha'i (using the incoming transmittance T for correct alpha-blending). iii. Alpha-Blend: Update accumulated feature: fQ \leftarrow fQ + wQ \cdot fi. iv. Handle Multiple Crossings: While T{test} < 1 - \frac{k+1}{K+1}, increment k again to account for cases where a single Gaussian causes the transmittance to drop across multiple quantile boundaries or due to precision issues. d. Termination Check: If T{test} < \frac{1}{K+1}, break the loop, as remaining transmittance is negligible for the quantile approximation. e. Update Transmittance: Set T \leftarrow T{test} for the next iteration. 3. Normalize Feature Vector: Divide the accumulated feature by the remaining transmittance to correct for the unblended portion: \tilde{f}Q \leftarrow fQ / (1 - T). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def QuantileRender(G, F, K, I): """ G: List of Gaussian objects with attribute alpha F: List of feature vectors corresponding to G, each of dimension C K: Number of quantile segments I: List of indices of rasterized Gaussians sorted by depth Returns: Rendered feature vector of dimension C """ T = 1.0 # Current transmittance fQ = [0.0] C # Accumulated feature vector k = 0 # Counter for quantile boundaries crossed for i in I: alpha = G[i].alpha f = F[i] # Transmittance after this Gaussian Ttest = T (1.0 - alpha) # Check if transmittance crossed the next quantile boundary boundary = 1.0 - (k + 1) / (K + 1) if Ttest < boundary: k += 1 # Weight uses current incoming transmittance T for correct blending wQ = T alpha for c in range(C): fQ[c] += wQ f[c] # Handle multiple boundary crossings for the same Gaussian while Ttest < 1.0 - (k + 1) / (K + 1): k += 1 # Termination check for negligible remaining transmittance if Ttest < 1.0 / (K + 1): break # Update transmittance for subsequent Gaussians T = Ttest # Normalize to account for residual transmittance denom = 1.0 - T if denom < 1e-6: return fQ fQnormalized = [val / denom for val in fQ] return fQnormalized Parameters: K: Number of quantile segments. Typical values are 10, 20, 40. K=40 yields best performance, but convergence is achieved at K \ge 10 (~50 mIoU). Using K < 10 causes significant performance drops due to transmittance profile discrepancy. C: Feature dimension (e.g., 512). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fixed K Sensitivity: The optimal K varies with the transmittance distribution of the ray. Using a fixed K=40 is a simplification. Inference with K \neq 40 (when trained with 40) causes significant performance drops, indicating a need for adaptive K selection. Normalization: The final normalization step corrects for residual transmittance T remaining after processing all K quantile Gaussians. Without this, the accumulated feature would be biased because the sum of weights would not equal 1. Precision: The while loop for boundary crossing handles precision issues where multiple boundaries might be crossed by a single Gaussian or due to floating-point errors. An adaptive variant of Q-Render that dynamically selects the number of quantiles K per input ray by predicting feature similarity. Definition: Instead of a fixed K, this method predicts the optimal K based on the ray's transmittance profile. Method: The model is trained with three candidate K values: \{10, 20, 40\}. A similarity-prediction head takes the transmittance profiles \{Tn\} as input and outputs predicted similarity scores for each candidate K. An additional loss computes the difference between predicted similarity scores and actual feature similarity. During inference, the model evaluates these scores and dynamically selects the K that yields the highest predicted similarity. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Reduces complexity from O(N C) in dense volume rendering to O(N + K C), where N is the number of rasterized Gaussians per pixel and C is the feature dimension. This is significantly faster than top-K sampling, which requires sorting and has complexity O(N \log K + K C). Memory: Requires storing the rasterized Gaussian indices and features, similar to standard 3DGS, but reduces the computational load during the accumulation phase. Measured Performance: Speed: On ScanNet scene000600 with 512-D feature maps, Q-Render achieves 28.42 FPS, a ~43.7× speedup over a modified baseline for-loop implementation (0.65 FPS). It is up to 1.5× faster than standard volume rendering (V-Render). Accuracy: On ScanNet, Q-Render with K=10 achieved 50.75 mIoU, comparable to V-Render's 49.02 mIoU, and superior to top-K (e.g., 45.70 mIoU at K=40). At K=40, mIoU reached 50.85. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables real-time rendering of high-dimensional features (e.g., for open-vocabulary segmentation); avoids sorting overhead of top-K; converges quickly with small K. Limitations: Sensitivity to the fixed K hyperparameter; performance drops if inference K differs from training K; theoretical approximation error converges at O(1/K). Quantile Rendering was introduced in the paper "Quantile Rendering: Efficiently Embedding High-dimensional Feature on 3D Gaussian Splatting". It was developed to address the computational cost of rendering high-dimensional features (such as CLIP embeddings) in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which is critical for tasks like open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation. The method builds on the continuous volume rendering integral formulation, shifting the sampling domain from spatial distance to transmittance. It is used in architectures like GS-Mink and GS-PTv3 for generalizable 3D neural networks. name: 4D Gaussian Splatting
head: 4D Gaussian Representation, 4D splats, 4DGS, Dynamic Scene Gaussian Splatting
body: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to model dynamic scenes by treating space and time as a unified four-dimensional continuum, allowing each Gaussian primitive to move, rotate, scale, and change appearance over time. Unlike methods that treat space and time independently or rely on rigid bounding boxes, 4DGS uses a coherent 4D Gaussian model to capture underlying scene motion and appearance changes more effectively, enabling real-time rendering of arbitrary time slices from a single optimized representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of images (video) capturing a dynamic scene, optionally with depth/LiDAR for urban scenes. Camera poses and intrinsics for each frame. Output: A set of 4D Gaussian primitives parameterized by mean, covariance, opacity, and 4D spherical harmonics coefficients, capable of rendering novel views at any time t. Data Structures: Each 4D Gaussian i is defined by the following parameters: Mean: \boldsymbol{\mu}i = (\mu{x}, \mu{y}, \mu{z}, \mu{t}) \in \mathbb{R}^4. Covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, parameterized via rotation \mathbf{R} and scaling \mathbf{S} such that \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T. Scaling: \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz, st). Rotation: \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{L}(ql) \mathbf{R}(qr), constructed from two unit quaternions ql = (a, b, c, d) and qr = (p, q, r, s) representing left and right isoclinic rotations. Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1]. Color: Represented by 4D Spherindrical Harmonics (4DSH) coefficients. The basis function is Z{nl}^m(t, \theta, \phi) = \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{T}t\right) Yl^m(\theta, \phi), where Yl^m are standard 3D spherical harmonics, n is the Fourier order, and l, m are SH degree and order. Rendering Steps: 1. Conditional Gaussian Derivation: For a target time t, compute the conditional 3D Gaussian mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D|t} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D|t} from the 4D parameters using multivariate Gaussian conditioning: \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D|t} = \boldsymbol{\mu}{1:3} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{1:3,4} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4,4}^{-1} (t - \mu4) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D|t} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{1:3,1:3} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{1:3,4} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4,4}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4,1:3} where \boldsymbol{\mu}{1:3} is the spatial mean, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{1:3,4} is the cross-covariance between spatial and temporal dimensions, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4,4} is the temporal variance. 2. Marginal Probability: Compute the marginal probability of the Gaussian existing at time t: pi(t) = \mathcal{N}(t; \mu{4,i}, \Sigma{4,4,i}) This acts as a temporal opacity envelope. 3. Projection: Project the conditional 3D Gaussian onto the image plane to obtain the 2D mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D|t} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D|t} using standard perspective projection and Jacobian approximation as in 3DGS. 4. Rasterization: Render the frame at time t by accumulating colors from all Gaussians sorted by depth. The contribution of each Gaussian is weighted by its marginal temporal probability pi(t): \mathcal{I}(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^N pi(t) pi(u, v|t) \alphai ci(\mathbf{d}, t) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(t) pj(u, v|t) \alphaj) where pi(u, v|t) is the conditional 2D Gaussian probability density, \alphai is opacity, and ci(\mathbf{d}, t) is the view-dependent color evaluated using 4DSH at direction \mathbf{d} and time t. Training: Initialization: For Plenoptic Video datasets, initialize Gaussians using COLMAP point clouds from the first frame, with timestamps uniformly distributed across the scene duration. For D-NeRF, initialize 100,000 random points in [-1.2, 1.2]^3 with mean time set to the scene duration. Optimization: End-to-end optimization using rendering loss (L1 + D-SSIM). Use batch sampling in time to prevent temporal flickering. Densification: Incorporate average gradients of \mut as a density control indicator. Use joint spatial and temporal position sampling during splitting in over-reconstructed regions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def render4dgs(gaussians, camera, timet): """ Render a single frame at timet using 4D Gaussian Splatting. gaussians: List of 4D Gaussian objects. camera: Camera object with projection matrix and intrinsics. timet: Float, the target timestamp. """ # 1. Compute conditional 3D Gaussians for timet projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Extract 4D parameters mu4d = g.mu # (4,) sigma4d = g.sigma # (4,4) # Split into spatial and temporal parts muspatial = mu4d[:3] mutemporal = mu4d[3] sigmaspatialspatial = sigma4d[:3,:3] sigmaspatialtemporal = sigma4d[:3, 3] sigmatemporaltemporal = sigma4d[3, 3] # Compute conditional mean and covariance (Eq 9 in) # mu3d|t = muspatial + Sigmaspatialtemporal Sigmatemporaltemporal^-1 (t - mutemporal) deltat = timet - mutemporal mu3dcond = muspatial + sigmaspatialtemporal (1.0 / sigmatemporaltemporal) deltat # Sigma3d|t = Sigmaspatialspatial - Sigmaspatialtemporal Sigmatemporaltemporal^-1 Sigmatemporalspatial # Note: Sigmatemporalspatial is the transpose of Sigmaspatialtemporal (scalar in this case) sigma3dcond = sigmaspatialspatial - sigmaspatialtemporal (1.0 / sigmatemporaltemporal) sigmaspatialtemporal.T # Compute marginal temporal probability (Eq 10 in) # p(t) = N(t; mutemporal, sigmatemporaltemporal) # Gaussian PDF: 1/sqrt(2pisigma^2) exp(-0.5 (t-mu)^2 / sigma^2) import math pt = (1.0 / math.sqrt(2 math.pi sigmatemporaltemporal)) \ math.exp(-0.5 (deltat 2) / sigmatemporaltemporal) # Project 3D Gaussian to 2D (Standard 3DGS projection) # This involves Jacobian of projection and 3D->2D covariance transformation mu2d, sigma2d = project3dto2d(mu3dcond, sigma3dcond, camera) # Store projected Gaussian with temporal weight projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu2d': mu2d, 'sigma2d': sigma2d, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'pt': pt, 'shcoeffs': g.shcoeffs, 'viewdir': None # To be filled per pixel }) # 2. Rasterize # Sort by depth (z-coordinate of mu3dcond projected) projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['mu2d'][2]) # Assuming z is depth image = zeros(imagewidth, imageheight, 3) for g in projectedgaussians: # Get 2D Gaussian probability at each pixel covered by bounding box # p2d(u,v|t) from sigma2d # Color c(d, t) from 4DSH using viewdir and timet # Accumulate color with opacity and temporal weight pt # Color = pt alpha SHcolor product(1 - prevalpha) accumulatecolor(image, g) return image Spacetime Gaussians (STG) is a 4D Gaussian Splatting method that models dynamic scenes using native 4D primitives, enabling real-time rendering of any arbitrary time slice without per-frame optimization. It distinguishes itself from MLP-based deformation approaches like DGS by explicitly parameterizing temporal opacity envelopes and polynomial trajectories for each Gaussian, allowing for smooth interpolation of geometry and appearance between discrete keyframes. Initial Time Scaling adjusts the temporal variance of initialized 4D Gaussians to match the scene duration, preventing excessive Gaussian proliferation over long videos. It leverages the anisotropic characteristic of Gaussians to maintain tractable Gaussian counts as video length increases, distinguishing it from methods that rely on rigid 3D bounding boxes or dynamic object segmentations. 4D-Rotor Gaussian Splatting is a method for modeling dynamic scenes using 4D rotor-based primitives defined via Clifford algebra. It sets itself apart from siblings like Spacetime Gaussians (STG) by explicitly modeling temporal evolution as a rotation component in spacetime, allowing for rigid body motion representation, whereas STG relies on polynomial trajectories and temporal opacity envelopes. A time-lapse rendering architecture where each timepoint's splats are fitted independently and stored contiguously, with time acting as a hard ordering barrier to prevent LOD rung blending across timepoints. It fits Gaussian splats per timepoint (e.g., 256K per frame) and streams timepoints sequentially, fetching chunks as the timeline advances. Training and rendering modifications for sparse, wide-baseline outdoor scenes to prevent overfitting and model infinite-distance backgrounds. It integrates sparse depth supervision from LiDAR point clouds using an inverse L1 loss, adopts a cube map for the sky, and deactivates the temporal coefficient of 4DSH to reduce overfitting. A variant that disables 4D rotation updates, resulting in less temporal variance and impaired motion fitting. Disabling 4D rotation reduces temporal variance, impairing motion fitting capacity and causing flicker/blur in rendered videos. A method that achieves interactive frame rates by building a specialized renderer that fuses static background Gaussians with a small, fast-updating set of dynamic foreground Gaussians. A method that achieves continuous-time 4D reconstruction by modeling the trajectories with a neural ODE solver, allowing frame rates to be arbitrarily adjusted at test time. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) per pixel, similar to 3DGS, but requires computing conditional Gaussians and marginal probabilities for each Gaussian at the target time t. Training is end-to-end and typically requires 30,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Stores 4D parameters per Gaussian. The number of Gaussians scales with scene complexity but remains stable over video length due to the anisotropic temporal support. Performance: On the D-NeRF dataset (800x800), 4DGS achieves PSNR 31.79, SSIM 0.960, and LPIPS 0.051, with training time reduced to 6m22s (2.8x speedup) and VRAM usage of 1.2GiB compared to the baseline. On the Plenoptic Video dataset, it achieves PSNR 32.01 and 114 FPS. Strengths: Real-time rendering of dynamic scenes, coherent spatiotemporal representation, no need for per-frame optimization at test time. Limitations: Requires synchronized multi-view captures for high-quality results; training is more complex than 3DGS; sensitive to temporal sampling during training to avoid flickering. 4D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Wu et al. in CVPR'24. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting by extending the primitive representation to four dimensions to handle dynamic content. The method addresses the limitations of treating space and time independently, which struggles to capture underlying scene motion. It has been adapted for various applications including urban scenes, timelapses, and real-time rendering. name: Spacetime Gaussians (STG)
body: Spacetime Gaussians (STG) is a 4D Gaussian Splatting method that models dynamic scenes using native 4D primitives, enabling real-time rendering of any arbitrary time slice without per-frame optimization. It distinguishes itself from MLP-based deformation approaches like DGS by explicitly parameterizing temporal opacity envelopes and polynomial trajectories for each Gaussian, allowing for smooth interpolation of geometry and appearance between discrete keyframes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} captured from multiple views at discrete keyframes. Output: A rendered image for any query time t. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores the following fields: 1. Spatial State: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation/scale parameters), and base opacity \alphai. 2. Temporal Envelope: Parameters defining a temporal opacity function ei(t), specifying birth, death, and peak times. 3. Trajectory: Coefficients for a polynomial trajectory pi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3 describing the mean position over time. 4. Appearance: Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients c{i, l, m} for each band l and order m, representing color/intensity. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from keyframe reconstructions, assigning initial spatial parameters \mui, \Sigmai, \alphai and SH coefficients c{i, l, m}. 2. Temporal Parameterization: Learn or assign parameters for the temporal opacity envelope ei(t) and the polynomial trajectory coefficients for pi(t). 3. Query Processing: For a target time t: a. Compute the current mean position: \mui(t) = pi(t). b. Compute the current opacity: \alphai(t) = \alphai \cdot ei(t). c. Retrieve SH coefficients c{i, l, m} (static per Gaussian, as STG emphasizes temporal opacity/position over time-varying SH). d. Project the Gaussian \{\mui(t), \Sigmai(t), \alphai(t), c{i, l, m}\} to 2D screen space using standard differentiable rasterization. 4. Rasterization: Sort Gaussians by depth and composite them using alpha blending to produce the final image. Formulas: Trajectory: pi(t) = \sum{k=0}^{d} a{i,k} t^k, where a{i,k} are polynomial coefficients. Opacity: \alphai(t) = \alphai \cdot ei(t), where ei(t) is the temporal envelope. Parameters: Polynomial degree d: Not given in the sources. Temporal envelope shape: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Out-of-bounds Time: If t is outside the range of the temporal envelope, opacity should be clamped to 0. Precision: Polynomial evaluation can suffer from numerical instability for high degrees or large time ranges; Horner's method is recommended. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderstg(gaussians, timet, camera): projected = [] for g in gaussians: post = evaluatepolynomial(g.polycoeffs, timet) alphat = g.alpha evaluateenvelope(g.envelopeparams, timet) if alphat < 1e-4: continue campos = projectpoint(post, camera) J = computeprojectionjacobian(post, camera) cov2d = J @ g.cov @ J.T projected.append({'pos': campos, 'cov': cov2d, 'alpha': alphat, 'sh': g.sh}) projected.sort(key=lambda x: x['pos'][2]) return rasterize(projected, camera.width, camera.height) def evaluatepolynomial(coeffs, t): pos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for k, c in enumerate(coeffs): pos = [pos[j] + c[j] (t k) for j in range(3)] return pos def evaluateenvelope(params, t): # Envelope shape not specified in sources return 1.0 def projectpoint(p, camera): # Standard perspective projection x, y, z = p fx, fy = camera.fx, camera.fy cx, cy = camera.cx, camera.cy return [fx (x / z) + cx, fy (y / z) + cy, z] def computeprojectionjacobian(p, camera): # Jacobian of perspective projection w.r.t 3D point x, y, z = p fx, fy = camera.fx, camera.fy return [[fx / z, 0, -fx x / (z 2)], [0, fy / z, -fy y / (z 2)]] def rasterize(projected, width, height): image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for g in projected: # Standard 2D Gaussian splatting rasterization pass return image Spacetime is a method that adds a temporal dimension to the feature field, enabling real-time interpolation of both color and geometry between keyframes. It serves as the temporal interpolation mechanism within the Spacetime Gaussians (STG) framework, allowing for smooth rendering of dynamic scenes without requiring per-frame optimization. Unlike methods that treat Gaussians as particles advected by a flow field, Spacetime relies on discrete keyframe queries and interpolation to reconstruct the 4D volume. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved as the temporal query is a simple function evaluation per Gaussian, avoiding expensive MLP inference or per-frame optimization. Memory Complexity: Higher than static 3DGS due to the storage of temporal envelope and trajectory parameters per Gaussian. Strengths: Real-time rendering of arbitrary time slices; no per-frame optimization required; smooth interpolation. Limitations: Relies on polynomial trajectories which may not capture complex non-linear motion as well as flow-based methods; limited to the temporal range of the envelope. When to use: When real-time rendering of dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints is required, and the motion can be approximated by polynomials. When not to use: For highly complex, non-polynomial motion where flow-based methods may provide better temporal regularization. Spacetime Gaussians (STG) was introduced by Li et al. in CVPR'24. It is part of the evolution of 4D Gaussian Splatting, aiming to provide native 4D primitives for dynamic scene representation, contrasting with deformation-based approaches like DGS. name: Spacetime
body: Spacetime is a method that adds a temporal dimension to the feature field, enabling real-time interpolation of both color and geometry between keyframes. It contrasts with flow-based approaches by treating time as an explicit feature dimension that is interpolated during rendering rather than advecting Gaussians via a velocity field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians with spatial parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) and a temporal feature encoding (e.g., positional encoding of time t). The input also includes discrete keyframe data (e.g., deformation deltas or feature grids) associated with specific time steps. Output: Rendered image for an arbitrary continuous time t and view direction. Data Structures: The method relies on storing discrete temporal states. For variants like Temporal Gaussian Interpolation, this includes a gaussians structure containing per-Gaussian attributes, dxyz deformation deltas stored at discrete time intervals (e.g., every 4 frames), and a timestepsdenom scalar defining the granularity of time steps. Steps: 1. Query Temporal Features: For a given view frame ID, determine the relevant time interval. 2. Interpolate Geometry/Features: Calculate the interpolated deformation or feature value based on the distance to the nearest keyframes. 3. Apply Deformation: Adjust the Gaussian positions or feature inputs using the interpolated values. 4. Render: Perform standard 3D Gaussian splatting rasterization using the adjusted parameters. Formulas: For linear interpolation between keyframes (as implemented in Temporal Gaussian Interpolation): d{xyz} = 0.25 \times ((view.frame\id - curr\int\fid) \times d{xyz\next} + (next\int\fid - view.frame\id) \times d{xyz\curr}) Where: curr\int\fid = (view.frame\id // 4) \times 4. next\int\fid = (view.frame\id // 4 + 1) \times 4. d{xyz\curr} and d{xyz\next} are the deformation deltas at the current and next integer time steps. For Attenuating Time Feature: \gamma{time}(t) = \gamma(t) e^{-\frac{\lambda}{2} \frac{L(\gamma(t))}{\Delta x}} Where: \gamma(t) is the original time feature. \Delta x is the norm of the deformation distance. \lambda is the attenuation strength hyperparameter. L(\gamma(t)) is a term related to the feature magnitude. Parameters: \lambda (Attenuation strength): Set to 60. Time step denominator: Typically 4 for the Torf scene type. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: At frame boundaries (multiples of 4), the interpolation weight shifts entirely to the current frame. The implementation must handle view.frameid % 4 == 0 explicitly to use current deltas directly without interpolation. Noisy Reconstructions: If the deformation distance \Delta x is large, the time feature can dominate the coordinate information, leading to noisy novel view synthesis. The attenuation formula mitigates this by reducing the time feature frequency when deformation is large. Zero Deformation: When deformation is close to zero, the full frequency of the time feature is used to avoid division by zero or excessive attenuation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def getinterpolateddeformation(viewframeid, timestepsdenom=4, optimizesynciters=0, iteration=0, querydeformationnetwork=None): """ Calculates interpolated deformation deltas for a given frame. querydeformationnetwork(timeidx) returns a deformation vector. """ # Calculate current and next integer frame IDs currintfid = (viewframeid // timestepsdenom) timestepsdenom nextintfid = (currintfid + 1) timestepsdenom # Query current frame deltas dxyzcurr = querydeformationnetwork(currintfid / timestepsdenom) # If at a keyframe or in early sync phase, use current deltas directly if viewframeid % timestepsdenom == 0 or iteration <= optimizesynciters: return dxyzcurr # Query next frame deltas dxyznext = querydeformationnetwork(nextintfid / timestepsdenom) # Linear interpolation scaled by 1/timestepsdenom weightnext = viewframeid - currintfid weightcurr = nextintfid - viewframeid dxyz = 0.25 (weightnext dxyznext + weightcurr dxyzcurr) return dxyz def attenuatetimefeature(gammat, deltaxnorm, lambdaparam=60): """ Attenuates the time feature based on deformation magnitude. """ # When deformation is close to zero, use full frequency if deltaxnorm < 1e-6: return gammat # L(gamma(t)) is interpreted as the magnitude/norm of the feature itself featurenorm = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in gammat)) # Calculate attenuation factor exponent = -(lambdaparam / 2.0) (featurenorm / deltaxnorm) return gammat math.exp(exponent) A variant that interpolates dynamic Gaussian transformations (d{xyz}) across time steps for specific scene types (e.g., Torf) to ensure smooth motion between discrete keyframes. It sets itself apart by explicitly querying deformation deltas at discrete intervals (every 4 frames) and linearly blending them. Choose this when rendering scenes with known, discrete motion keyframes where smooth interpolation is required without training a continuous flow field. It relies on a deformation network query interface to fetch deformation data. A method to reduce the frequency of the time feature for deforming parts of the scene to prevent the radiance field from relying solely on time features instead of coordinates, which causes noisy novel view synthesis. It sets itself apart by using the norm of the deformation distance (\Delta x) to modulate the time feature's influence. Choose this when dealing with monocular or sparse-view dynamic reconstruction where the network might overfit to time indices rather than learning geometric deformation. It uses an exponential attenuation factor controlled by \lambda=60. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Real-time interpolation is achieved. Strengths: Simple to implement; enables smooth viewing of dynamic scenes without complex flow integration; reduces noise in novel views for deforming objects. Limitations: Interpolation artifacts may occur if keyframes are too sparse; attenuation requires careful tuning of \lambda to balance noise reduction and feature fidelity. When to use: Real-time visualization of dynamic scenes with discrete motion data; dynamic NeRF/Gaussian reconstruction from monocular video. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Spacetime feature extension originated in the context of dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting and Neural Radiance Fields. It builds on the idea that time can be treated as an additional input dimension to the feature field, similar to how spatial coordinates are used. The specific implementations of temporal interpolation and time feature attenuation were developed to address artifacts in dynamic reconstruction, such as those found in the Torf dataset and monocular dynamic scenes. The method is part of the broader evolution of 4D Gaussian Splatting, moving from static rendering to real-time dynamic synthesis. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) brownvc/gftorf, https://github.com/brownvc/gftorf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ced-NeRF: A Compact and Efficient Method for Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v38i4.28138, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Initial Time Scaling
head: Time variance initialization
body: Initial Time Scaling adjusts the temporal variance of initialized 4D Gaussians to match the scene duration, preventing excessive Gaussian proliferation over long videos. It sets the initial time scaling parameter to half of the total scene duration to leverage Gaussian anisotropy, distinguishing it from sibling methods like Spacetime Gaussians (STG) which model spacetime correlations differently, and 4D-Rotor Gaussian Splatting which uses rotation matrices for dynamic deformation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Total scene duration T{total} (in seconds or normalized time units). Output: Initial temporal variance parameter \sigmat for the 4D Gaussian initialization. Data Structures: The 4D Gaussian is defined by a mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^4 (3D space + time) and a covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}. The covariance matrix is typically parameterized by a rotation matrix R \in SO(4) and a scaling matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} (diagonal), such that \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. The temporal variance corresponds to the diagonal element of S associated with the time dimension, denoted as st. Thus, \sigmat = st. Steps: 1. Determine the total duration of the video or dynamic scene, T{total}. 2. Calculate the initial time scaling factor as half of the total duration: \sigmat = \frac{T{total}}{2} 3. Initialize the 4D Gaussian's temporal variance parameter st to \sigmat. 4. Construct the initial covariance matrix \Sigma using this st and appropriate spatial variances and rotations. Parameters: T{total}: Total scene duration. Typical value depends on the video length (e.g., 10 seconds for a short clip). \sigmat: Initial temporal variance. Set to T{total} / 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If T{total} is very large, the resulting \sigmat will be large, leading to wide temporal support. This is intentional to prevent the need for an intractable number of Gaussians to cover the time axis. If the scene duration is not known a priori (e.g., streaming), this method cannot be applied directly without an estimate. Precision issues may arise if T{total} is extremely small or large; ensure floating-point precision is sufficient for the scale of \sigmat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializetemporalvariance(sceneduration): """ Calculate initial temporal variance for 4D Gaussian Splatting. Args: sceneduration (float): Total duration of the scene in time units. Returns: float: Initial temporal variance sigmat. """ # Set initial time scaling to half of the scene's duration sigmat = sceneduration / 2.0 return sigmat Time Complexity: O(1) for initialization. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the parameter. Performance: Reduces the number of Gaussians required to represent dynamic scenes, improving rendering efficiency and reducing memory usage for long videos. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective at controlling Gaussian count, leverages anisotropy. Limitations: Assumes uniform temporal distribution initially; may require further optimization during training to adapt to specific motion patterns. When to use: When rendering long dynamic scenes with 4D Gaussian Splatting to prevent Gaussian proliferation. When not to use: For very short scenes where the overhead is negligible, or if the temporal distribution is highly non-uniform and requires more sophisticated initialization. The method was introduced in "Real-time Photorealistic Dynamic Scene Representation and Rendering with 4D Gaussian Splatting". The authors observed that if 4D Gaussians have only local support in time, the number of Gaussians becomes intractable as video length increases. By leveraging the anisotropic characteristic of Gaussians and setting the initial time scaling to half the scene duration, they avoid this predicament. “Real-time Photorealistic Dynamic Scene Representation and Rendering with 4D Gaussian Splatting”, https://radiancefields.com/papers/real-time-photorealistic-dynamic-scene-representation-and-rendering-with-4d-gaussian-splatting, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Temporal Axis Resolution Adjustment
head: Time Normalization Range Adjustment
body: Temporal Axis Resolution Adjustment reduces the temporal axis resolution of K-Planes feature grids by narrowing the time normalization range to [-0.8, 0.8]. This technique accommodates camera-specific time offsets in unsynchronized video data without degrading rendering performance. It is distinct from Initial Time Scaling, which adjusts Gaussian variance; this method adjusts the feature grid's temporal domain to prevent offset values from deviating outside the learned feature planes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A K-Planes feature grid initialized with a standard temporal normalization range (typically [-1.0, 1.0]). Input: Camera-specific time offsets \deltak for each camera k. Output: A modified K-Planes feature grid with adjusted temporal resolution and normalization range [-0.8, 0.8]. Data Structures: The K-Planes feature grid consists of 2D planes representing spatial and temporal dimensions. The temporal axis resolution is implicitly defined by the normalization range and the grid's depth along the time dimension. No explicit bit-packing or new data structures are introduced; the adjustment is a parameter change in the coordinate normalization function. Steps: 1. Identify the current temporal normalization range of the K-Planes feature grid. The default range is [-1.0, 1.0]. 2. Narrow the temporal normalization range to [-0.8, 0.8]. 3. When sampling coordinates for feature lookup, compute the normalized time coordinate t{norm} for a camera k at time t using the offset \deltak: tk = t + \deltak t{norm} = \text{normalize}(tk, \text{range}=[-0.8, 0.8]) where \text{normalize}(x, [a, b]) = \frac{x - a}{b - a} \times 2 - 1 maps x to [-1, 1] within the specified range. 4. Use t{norm} to index into the temporal axis of the K-Planes feature grid. Parameters: Time normalization range: [-0.8, 0.8]. Original range (for comparison): [-1.0, 1.0]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the time offset \deltak is large, the adjusted range [-0.8, 0.8] ensures that tk remains within the bounds of the feature grid, preventing out-of-bounds access or interpolation errors. Reducing the normalization range effectively reduces the temporal resolution of the feature grid. However, experiments show this does not harm overall performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizetime(t, deltak, rangemin=-0.8, rangemax=0.8): """ Normalize time t with camera-specific offset deltak to the range [-0.8, 0.8] for K-Planes feature grid lookup. """ tk = t + deltak # Map tk from [rangemin, rangemax] to [-1, 1] tnorm = 2.0 (tk - rangemin) / (rangemax - rangemin) - 1.0 return tnorm Sync-K-Planes is a variant of K-Planes adapted for unsynchronized video by incorporating camera-specific time offsets and adjusted time normalization. It is chosen when dealing with imperfectly synchronized video data, such as the Plenoptic Video Dataset, where fast dynamic contents like flames show different visual appearances in the same frame. The training involves two versions: hybrid and explicit. The hybrid version is trained for 90K iterations, and the explicit version for 120K iterations. An ISG sampling strategy is applied for the first 50K iterations with time offset, followed by an IST sampling strategy for both versions. The time offset learning rate is set to 0.1\times the K-Planes backbone learning rate. The time normalization range is set to [-0.8, 0.8] to prevent camera-specific time tk = t + \deltak from deviating from the feature planes. On the flame salmon scene, the hybrid version renders in 15.2 min, trains in 2.0 hrs, and has 27.0 M parameters. The explicit version renders in 22.0 min, trains in 3.8 hrs, and has 50.7 M parameters. Time and Memory Complexity: The method introduces negligible or tolerable differences in rendering and training time compared to the baseline K-Planes. On the flame salmon scene, Sync-K-Planes hybrid has 27.0 M parameters, while the explicit version has 50.7 M parameters. Measured Performance: On the flame salmon scene, reducing the normalization range to [-0.8, 0.8] does not harm overall performance. Sync-K-Planes hybrid PSNR remains ~28.56-28.95. Increasing the temporal-axis resolution back to original settings (by widening the range) shows similar performance, confirming the robustness of the adjustment. Strengths and Limitations: Strength: Handles unsynchronized video data effectively by accommodating camera-specific time offsets. Strength: Maintains high rendering quality (PSNR, SSIM) despite reduced temporal resolution. Limitation: The reduction in temporal resolution may theoretically limit the representation of very high-frequency temporal dynamics, though this was not observed in experiments. When to Use: Use when training K-Planes on unsynchronized video data where camera-specific time offsets are present. Use when computational resources are limited, as the method does not increase complexity. When Not to Use: Not necessary for synchronized video data where time offsets are negligible. Origin: The method was introduced in "Sync-NeRF: Generalizing Dynamic NeRFs to Unsynchronized Videos" by the authors of (2024). History and Development: The technique was developed to address the challenge of imperfect synchronization in video datasets, such as the Plenoptic Video Dataset, where hardware synchronization is not perfect. It builds on the K-Planes architecture and the Sync-NeRF approach to dynamic scene reconstruction. Where it is Used: Used in dynamic NeRF reconstruction for unsynchronized video data. Applied in experiments on the Plenoptic Video Dataset and the flame salmon scene. name: 4D Gaussian Rotation Construction
body: Constructs a 4x4 rotation matrix for 4D Gaussians from two quaternion-like vectors l and r representing temporal and spatial rotations respectively. It explicitly models the temporal dimension as a rotation component alongside the spatial one. Inputs: l: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing temporal rotation quaternions. r: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing spatial rotation quaternions. Outputs: A: Tensor of shape (N, 4, 4) representing the combined 4D rotation matrix. Data Structures: The method operates on batched tensors where N is the number of Gaussians. Intermediate matrices Ml and Mr are of shape (N, 4, 4). Steps: 1. Normalize: Compute the L2 norm of l and r along the last dimension, then divide to obtain normalized quaternions ql and qr. 2. Unpack: Extract components from ql as a, b, c, d and from qr as p, q, rval, s. 3. Construct Ml: Build the temporal rotation matrix Ml using the pattern [a, -b, -c, -d, b, a, -d, c, c, d, a, -b, d, -c, b, a], reshape to (N, 4, 4), and apply the source-specified permutation. 4. Construct Mr: Build the spatial rotation matrix Mr using the pattern [p, q, rval, s, -q, p, -s, rval, -rval, s, p, -q, -s, -rval, q, p], reshape to (N, 4, 4), and apply the source-specified permutation. 5. Combine: Compute the final rotation matrix A as the matrix product Ml @ Mr. 6. Flip Dimensions: Flip the last two dimensions of A to match the rendering pipeline's coordinate convention. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def buildrotation4d(l, r): # Step 1: Normalize lnorm = torch.norm(l, dim=-1, keepdim=True) rnorm = torch.norm(r, dim=-1, keepdim=True) lnorm = torch.clamp(lnorm, min=1e-8) rnorm = torch.clamp(rnorm, min=1e-8) ql = l / lnorm qr = r / rnorm # Step 2: Unpack components a, b, c, d = ql[..., 0], ql[..., 1], ql[..., 2], ql[..., 3] p, q, rval, s = qr[..., 0], qr[..., 1], qr[..., 2], qr[..., 3] # Step 3: Construct Ml # Pattern: [a,-b,-c,-d, b, a,-d, c, c, d, a,-b, d,-c, b, a] # Reshape to (N, 4, 4) and permute as specified by the source Mlflat = torch.stack([ a, -b, -c, -d, b, a, -d, c, c, d, a, -b, d, -c, b, a ], dim=-1).view(-1, 4, 4) # Step 4: Construct Mr # Pattern: [p, q, rval, s, -q, p, -s, rval, -rval, s, p, -q, -s, -rval, q, p] # Reshape to (N, 4, 4) and permute as specified by the source Mrflat = torch.stack([ p, q, rval, s, -q, p, -s, rval, -rval, s, p, -q, -s, -rval, q, p ], dim=-1).view(-1, 4, 4) # Step 5: Combine A = torch.bmm(Mlflat, Mrflat) # Step 6: Flip last two dimensions A = A.transpose(1, 2) return A Parameters: No explicit hyperparameters. Edge Cases: Zero Norms: If l or r has a zero norm, normalization fails. A small epsilon is added to the norm denominator to prevent NaNs. Degenerate Input: If the input quaternions are not unit vectors, the resulting matrix will not be a pure rotation. The normalization step ensures unit length. Constructs a 4x4 transformation matrix for 4D Gaussians by combining 4D scaling and 4D rotation. It initializes a zero matrix L of shape (N, 4, 4), sets the diagonal elements to the scaling factors s[:,0] to s[:,3], computes the rotation matrix R using buildrotation4d(l, r), and returns R @ L. name: Taming 3DGS
head: Budget-constrained 3DGS, Explicit Gaussian Cap, High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources, Taming3DGS
body: Taming 3DGS is a resource-efficiency method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that imposes an explicit cap on the total number of Gaussians to enable high-quality rendering on consumer-grade GPUs. It steers the densification process to spend a fixed budget where it helps most, trading peak quality for faster training and smaller model size. Unlike standard 3DGS which allows unbounded growth, this approach formulates optimization as a mixed-integer problem to maintain a constant Gaussian count. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} with attributes (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients), a target maximum count N{max}, and a training schedule or importance metric. Outputs: A pruned and densified set of Gaussians \{G'i\} where |\{G'i\}| \le N{max}. Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of size N{max} storing each Gaussian's attributes. Global Score: A scalar value per Gaussian, computed from four factors: gradient magnitude, pixel coverage, per-view saliency, and core attributes (opacity, depth, scale). Steps: 1. Initialize: Start with the standard 3DGS initialization. Set current count N = N{init}. 2. Iterative Optimization Loop: a. Perform standard differentiable rasterization and backpropagation to compute gradients. b. Score: Calculate the global score for each Gaussian using the four factors. c. Prune: Identify the least important Gaussians based on the global score. Remove them if N > N{max} or if they fall below a threshold. d. Densify: Identify the Gaussians with the top B scores, where B is the desired number of new Gaussians. Split or clone these Gaussians to increase local density. e. Budget Enforcement: Maintain N \le N{max} by pruning excess Gaussians after densification. 3. Schedule/Policy: Use either a predictable schedule (fixed pruning/densification intervals) or adaptive importance guidance to decide when to apply steps 2b–2e. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def taming3dgsstep(gaussians, Nmax, B): # 1. Compute global score per Gaussian scores = [] for g in gaussians: # Standard differentiable rasterization provides positional gradients grad = computegradientnorm(g) # Projected screen-space area coverage = computescreencoverage(g) # View-dependent saliency metric saliency = computesaliency(g) # Normalized opacity, depth, and scale core = computecoreattributes(g) scores.append(grad + coverage + saliency + core) # 2. Prune least important if over budget if len(gaussians) > Nmax: sortedindices = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: scores[i]) prunecount = len(gaussians) - Nmax removeindices = set(sortedindices[:prunecount]) gaussians = [g for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if i not in removeindices] scores = [s for i, s in enumerate(scores) if i not in removeindices] # 3. Densify top B Gaussians if len(gaussians) < Nmax: sortedindices = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: scores[i], reverse=True) topindices = sortedindices[:B] newprimitives = [] newscores = [] for idx in topindices: g = gaussians[idx] # Standard 3DGS split/clone: generate child with perturbed position/scale child = clonewithperturbation(g, offset=0.01) newprimitives.append(child) newscores.append(0.0) gaussians.extend(newprimitives) scores.extend(newscores) return gaussians, scores Edge Cases: Boundaries: N{max} must be chosen carefully; too low causes quality loss, too high defeats the purpose. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced due to fewer Gaussians to rasterize and backpropagate through. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by O(N{max}), significantly lower than unconstrained 3DGS. Performance: Enables high-quality rendering on consumer-grade GPUs. Strengths: Faster training, smaller model size, predictable resource usage. Limitations: Slight quality loss compared to unconstrained 3DGS. When to use: When hardware resources are limited or training time is a constraint. When not to use: When peak visual fidelity is required regardless of cost. Taming 3DGS was introduced to address the resource intensity of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. It explores a spectrum of trade-offs from predictable schedules to adaptive importance guidance. The method is part of a broader trend of optimizing 3DGS for efficiency, alongside works like LightGaussian and RTGS. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian Splats Part 2: From Photos to a Trained Model, https://alphapixeldev.com/gaussian-splats-part-2-creating-gaussian-splats/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Analytic-Splatting
head: Analytic Integration for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Analytic-Splatting is a rendering method that replaces the point-sampling of 2D Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytical approximation of the integral of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area to reduce aliasing artifacts during zooming or resolution changes. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (Software) which treats pixels as isolated points, or Mip-Splatting which uses a hybrid filtering mechanism that suppresses high-frequency components, Analytic-Splatting preserves high-quality details by analytically integrating the signal using a conditioned logistic function approximation of the Gaussian CDF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by a 3D mean \mathbf{m}, a 3D covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} (or its Cholesky factor), opacity \alpha, and color \mathbf{c}. A camera view (projection matrix) and pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} = [ux, uy]^\top. Output: The final color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) for each pixel. Data Structures: The method operates on the projected 2D Gaussian parameters derived from the 3D input. \hat{\bm{\mu}} \in \mathbb{R}^2: The projected 2D mean. \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2}: The projected 2D covariance matrix. \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}: The inverse covariance matrix, decomposed into coefficients: a = \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{22}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|}, \quad b = -\frac{\hat{\Sigma}{12}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|}, \quad c = \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{11}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|} \{\lambda1, \lambda2\}: Eigenvalues of \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}. \{\mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2\}: Corresponding eigenvectors, forming the matrix V = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}1 & \mathbf{v}2 \end{bmatrix}. \sigma1 = \sqrt{\lambda1}, \sigma2 = \sqrt{\lambda2}: Standard deviations along the principal axes. Numbered Steps: 1. Project 2D Gaussian: Compute the projected 2D mean \hat{\bm{\mu}} and covariance \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} from the 3D Gaussian parameters using the affine approximation of the perspective projection. Compute the inverse \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1} and its coefficients a, b, c. 2. Eigenvalue Decomposition: Perform eigenvalue decomposition on \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} to obtain eigenvalues \{\lambda1, \lambda2\} and eigenvectors \{\mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2\}. 3. Transform Pixel Center: Transform the pixel center \mathbf{u} into the diagonalized coordinate system defined by the eigenvectors. Let \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = [\tilde{u}x, \tilde{u}y]^\top be the transformed coordinates: \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = V^\top (\mathbf{u} - \hat{\bm{\mu}}) Component-wise: \tilde{u}x = v{1x} (ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{1y} (uy - \hat{\mu}y) \tilde{u}y = v{2x} (ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{2y} (uy - \hat{\mu}y) 4. Compute 1D Logistic Approximation: Define the standard logistic approximation function S(x) for the Gaussian CDF: S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-1.6 \cdot x - 0.07 \cdot x^3)} Define the scaled logistic function for standard deviation \sigma: S\sigma(x) = S\left(\frac{x}{\sigma}\right) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-1.6 \cdot \frac{x}{\sigma} - 0.07 \cdot \left(\frac{x}{\sigma}\right)^3\right)} Compute the 1D integral approximations for the x and y axes over the unit pixel window centered at \tilde{u}x and \tilde{u}y: \mathcal{I}{\sigma1} = \sigma1 \left[ S{\sigma1}\left(\tilde{u}x + \frac{1}{2}\right) - S{\sigma1}\left(\tilde{u}x - \frac{1}{2}\right) \right] \mathcal{I}{\sigma2} = \sigma2 \left[ S{\sigma2}\left(\tilde{u}y + \frac{1}{2}\right) - S{\sigma2}\left(\tilde{u}y - \frac{1}{2}\right) \right] 5. Compute 2D Intensity Integral: Calculate the analytically approximated 2D Gaussian integral \mathcal{I}g^\text{2D}(\mathbf{u}) by combining the 1D integrals: \mathcal{I}g^\text{2D}(\mathbf{u}) = 2\pi \mathcal{I}{\sigma1} \mathcal{I}{\sigma2} Note: This replaces the point-sampled Gaussian value g^{2D}(\mathbf{u}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{u}-\hat{\bm{\mu}})^\top \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1}(\mathbf{u}-\hat{\bm{\mu}})\right). 6. Volume Rendering: Compute the final color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) using alpha blending, where the transmittance Ti and the contribution of each Gaussian i use the integral \mathcal{I}{g-i}^\text{2D} instead of the point sample: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) = \sum{i\in N} Ti \mathcal{I}{g-i}^\text{2D}(\mathbf{u} | \hat{\bm{\mu}}i, \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}i) \alphai \mathbf{c}i Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \left(1 - \mathcal{I}{g-j}^\text{2D}(\mathbf{u} | \hat{\bm{\mu}}j, \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}j) \alphaj\right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def logisticcdfapprox(x): """ Approximates the CDF of a standard Gaussian using a logistic function. S(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-1.6x - 0.07x^3)) """ exponent = -1.6 x - 0.07 (x 3) return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(exponent)) def scaledlogisticcdfapprox(x, sigma): """ Approximates the CDF of a Gaussian with standard deviation sigma. Ssigma(x) = S(x / sigma) """ return logisticcdfapprox(x / sigma) def computeanalyticsplatintensity(ux, uy, mux, muy, v1x, v1y, v2x, v2y, lambda1, lambda2): """ Computes the 2D integral approximation Ig^2D for a single Gaussian. Args: ux, uy: Pixel center coordinates. mux, muy: Projected 2D mean of the Gaussian. v1x, v1y: Components of the first eigenvector. v2x, v2y: Components of the second eigenvector. lambda1, lambda2: Eigenvalues of the projected covariance matrix. Returns: The 2D intensity integral value. """ # Step 3: Transform pixel center to diagonalized coordinates # utilde = V^T (u - mu) deltax = ux - mux deltay = uy - muy utildex = v1x deltax + v1y deltay utildey = v2x deltax + v2y deltay # Step 2/4: Standard deviations sigma1 = math.sqrt(lambda1) sigma2 = math.sqrt(lambda2) # Step 4: Compute 1D integral approximations # Isigma = sigma [Ssigma(u + 0.5) - Ssigma(u - 0.5)] # X-axis integral s1plus = scaledlogisticcdfapprox(utildex + 0.5, sigma1) s1minus = scaledlogisticcdfapprox(utildex - 0.5, sigma1) isigma1 = sigma1 (s1plus - s1minus) # Y-axis integral s2plus = scaledlogisticcdfapprox(utildey + 0.5, sigma2) s2minus = scaledlogisticcdfapprox(utildey - 0.5, sigma2) isigma2 = sigma2 (s2plus - s2minus) # Step 5: Compute 2D intensity integral # Ig^2D = 2 pi Isigma1 Isigma2 intensity = 2.0 math.pi isigma1 isigma2 return intensity def renderpixelanalytic(pixels, gaussians): """ Renders a single pixel using Analytic-Splatting. Args: pixels: List of pixel centers (ux, uy) to render. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects. Each object must have: mux, muy (projected 2D mean) v1x, v1y, v2x, v2y (eigenvectors of projected covariance) lambda1, lambda2 (eigenvalues of projected covariance) alpha (opacity) cr, cg, cb (color components) Returns: Dictionary mapping pixel coordinates to final color (r, g, b). """ results = {} for (ux, uy) in pixels: # Sort gaussians by depth (z-order) for correct alpha blending # Note: In a full implementation, depth sorting is required per pixel. # Here we assume 'gaussians' is pre-sorted or we iterate in a fixed order. # For correctness in volume rendering, sorting by depth is critical. sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.zdepth) t = 1.0 # Transmittance colorr = 0.0 colorg = 0.0 colorb = 0.0 for g in sortedgaussians: # Compute analytic intensity intensity = computeanalyticsplatintensity( ux, uy, g.mux, g.muy, g.v1x, g.v1y, g.v2x, g.v2y, g.lambda1, g.lambda2) # Contribution contributionr = t intensity g.alpha g.cr contributiong = t intensity g.alpha g.cg contributionb = t intensity g.alpha g.cb # Accumulate color colorr += contributionr colorg += contributiong colorb += contributionb # Update transmittance t = (1.0 - intensity g.alpha) # Early exit if transmittance is negligible if t < 1e-4: break # Add background color (usually white or black, assumed 0 here for simplicity) results[(ux, uy)] = (colorr, colorg, colorb) return results Parameters: Logistic linear coefficient: 1.6. Logistic cubic coefficient: 0.07. Pixel window size: Assumed to be 1 \times 1 centered at the pixel coordinate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Correlation Term: The 2D integral of a Gaussian with a non-diagonal covariance matrix contains an intractable correlation term b(x-\hat{\mu}x)(y-\hat{\mu}y). Analytic-Splatting resolves this by diagonalizing the covariance matrix and rotating the integration domain to align with the eigenvectors, approximating the 2D integral as a product of two independent 1D integrals. Small Standard Deviation: Unlike Mip-Splatting which convolves with a Gaussian kernel (approximating the integral as g \circledast gw), Analytic-Splatting calculates the integral analytically. This avoids large gaps for high-frequency components (small \sigma) where convolution-based methods might fail. Precision: The logistic approximation is differentiable, allowing for gradient computation. However, extreme values of x/\sigma in the exponential function may lead to overflow or underflow; standard numerical stability techniques (e.g., clamping) should be applied. This method computes the exact gradient of the analytically integrated 2D Gaussian splat intensity with respect to the elements of the 2D covariance matrix (\hat{\Sigma}). It solves the problem of differentiating the analytic approximation used in Analytic-Splatting, which integrates the Gaussian density over the pixel area to reduce aliasing. Unlike point-sampling methods, this gradient accounts for the boundary effects of the pixel window by propagating derivatives through the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix. Time Complexity: The method replaces the exponential function evaluation in standard 3DGS with logistic function evaluations and eigen-decomposition. The logistic function involves exponentials and cubic terms, which are computationally more expensive than a single exponential but cheaper than Monte Carlo super-sampling. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the standard 3DGS parameters, as the integral is computed analytically on the fly. Performance: Analytic-Splatting provides better anti-aliasing capability than standard 3DGS and Mip-Splatting, preserving high-quality details and fidelity, especially during zooming or resolution changes. It avoids the over-smoothing caused by Mip-Splatting's low-pass filtering. Strengths: Analytical solution avoids sampling noise; handles varying resolutions effectively; preserves high-frequency details better than convolution-based methods. Limitations: The eigen-decomposition and logistic function evaluation add computational overhead compared to the simple point-sampling of 3DGS. Analytic-Splatting was introduced by Zhihao Liang et al. in the paper "Analytic-Splatting: Anti-Aliased 3D Gaussian Splatting via Analytic Integration" (arXiv:2403.11056v2, 2024). It addresses the aliasing artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting caused by treating pixels as isolated points, which leads to severe blurring or jaggies when rendering at varying resolutions. The method uses a conditioned logistic function as an analytic approximation of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the Gaussian signal.
