name: GaussianSet Data Structure
head: 3D Gaussian Representation, Gaussian Set
body: The GaussianSet is a class representing a set of 3D Gaussians that stores means, orientations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients, and computes covariance matrices. It solves the problem of efficiently managing high-dimensional geometric and appearance data by organizing them into contiguous tensors suitable for batched processing. Unlike implicit neural fields or hierarchical spatial structures, it maintains a flat list of primitives prioritizing direct tensor access. The GaussianSet serves as the container for primitive parameters and provides methods to compute derived quantities, such as the world-space covariance matrix, required for projection and rendering. Inputs: Raw optimization parameters (quaternions, scales, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) and the number of Gaussians N. Outputs: Normalized quaternions, exponentiated scales, sigmoided opacities, concatenated spherical harmonics coefficients, and computed covariance matrices. The structure consists of the following fields, typically stored as contiguous tensors on the GPU: | Field | Type | Shape | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | means | Float32 | (N, 3) | 3D position of each Gaussian in world coordinates. | | quats | Float32 | (N, 4) | Unit quaternion representing orientation. | | scales | Float32 | (N, 3) | Logarithmic scale parameters (exponentiated at runtime). | | opacities | Float32 | (N,) | Logit opacity values (sigmoided at runtime). | | shcoefficients | Float32 | (N, S, 3) | Spherical harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color. | | covariances | Float32 | (N, 3, 3) | World-space covariance matrices (computed on demand). | Note: S is the number of SH bands per color channel, determined by the SH degree. 1. Normalization of Quaternions: The raw quaternion outputs from the optimizer are normalized to ensure they represent valid rotations. q{normalized} = \frac{q}{\|q\|2} Where q is the raw quaternion tensor of shape (N, 4). 2. Exponentiation of Scales: The scale parameters are stored in log-space to ensure positive values during optimization. They are exponentiated to obtain the actual scale factors. s = \exp(s{raw}) Where s{raw} is the raw scale tensor of shape (N, 3). 3. Sigmoiding of Opacities: Opacity logits are mapped to the range (0, 1) using the sigmoid function. \alpha = \sigma(\alpha{raw}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\alpha{raw}}} Where \alpha{raw} is the raw opacity tensor of shape (N,). 4. Concatenation of SH Coefficients: Spherical harmonics coefficients are often stored in separate tensors for different degrees (e.g., degree 0 and degree N). They are concatenated along the degree dimension. SH = \text{concat}(SH0, SHN, \dots) Resulting in a tensor of shape (N, S, 3). 5. Covariance Matrix Computation: The world-space covariance matrix Cov is computed from the normalized quaternion and exponentiated scale. Cov = R S R^T Where: R is the 3 \times 3 rotation matrix derived from the normalized quaternion q{normalized}. S is the diagonal covariance matrix in local coordinates: S = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) where sx, sy, sz are the components of the exponentiated scale vector s. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def processgaussianset(quatsraw, scalesraw, opacitiesraw, shcoeffsraw): """ Processes raw optimization parameters into the standard GaussianSet format. Args: quatsraw: Tensor of shape (N, 4), raw quaternion outputs. scalesraw: Tensor of shape (N, 3), log-scale outputs. opacitiesraw: Tensor of shape (N,), logit opacity outputs. shcoeffsraw: List of Tensors [sh0, shN], each of shape (N, Si, 3). Returns: A dictionary representing the GaussianSet with processed attributes. """ # 1. Normalize quaternions quatsnorm = torch.nn.functional.normalize(quatsraw, p=2, dim=-1) # 2. Exponentiate scales scalesexp = torch.exp(scalesraw) # 3. Sigmoid opacities opacitiessig = torch.sigmoid(opacitiesraw) # 4. Concatenate SH coefficients shcoefficients = torch.cat(shcoeffsraw, dim=-2) # 5. Compute covariances covariances = computecovariances(quatsnorm, scalesexp) # Means are stored directly; loading procedure not specified in sources. return { "quats": quatsnorm, "scales": scalesexp, "opacities": opacitiessig, "shcoefficients": shcoefficients, "covariances": covariances } def computecovariances(quats, scales): """ Computes the world-space covariance matrix for each Gaussian. Args: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4), normalized quaternions. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3), exponentiated scales. Returns: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 3), covariance matrices. """ # Convert quaternions to rotation matrices w, x, y, z = torch.unbind(quats, dim=-1) xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, xw = xy, xz, xw yz, yw, zw = yz, yw, zw R = torch.stack([ 1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - zw), 2(xz + yw), 2(xy + zw), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - xw), 2(xz - yw), 2(yz + xw), 1 - 2(xx + yy) ], dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3, 3) # Local covariance S = diag(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) scalessq = scales 2 S = torch.zeros(quats.shape[0], 3, 3, device=quats.device, dtype=quats.dtype) S[:, 0, 0] = scalessq[:, 0] S[:, 1, 1] = scalessq[:, 1] S[:, 2, 2] = scalessq[:, 2] # Cov = R S R^T return torch.bmm(torch.bmm(R, S), R.transpose(1, 2)) SH Degree: Determines the number of coefficients S. Time Complexity: Covariance computation is O(N) per Gaussian, involving matrix multiplications. Degenerate Input: If a quaternion is not normalized, the resulting rotation matrix will be invalid, leading to incorrect covariance computation. A scene representation method that compresses Gaussian attributes via neural entropy coding to reduce storage and computational costs. It sets itself apart from standard explicit storage by optimizing anchor attributes and training joint context models to exploit inter-scene redundancy. Choose it when minimizing scene size and transmission bandwidth is critical. A contiguous, column-major flat list variant for efficient batch processing. It differs from hierarchical variants like Octree-GS by simplifying memory management at the cost of adaptive level-of-detail allocation. Choose it when uniform batch processing speed outweighs the need for spatial culling. A parsing routine that decodes raw vertex properties from Polygon File Format (PLY) files into the structured Gaussian representation. It sets itself apart from coordinate conversion and legacy parsing utilities by handling the initial ingestion and decoding of standardized PLY storage. Choose it as the first step in the rendering pipeline when loading pre-trained scenes. A routine that calculates the 3 \times 3 spatial covariance matrix from unconstrained rotation and scale parameters. It sets itself apart from direct covariance optimization by guaranteeing the resulting matrix is always positive semi-definite. Choose it when deriving anisotropic spatial extents for projection is required. Defines the memory organization and mathematical parameterization of a single Gaussian primitive on the GPU. It sets itself apart from low-level binary serialization by focusing on logical attribute types like log-space scales and quaternions. Choose it when designing the internal memory layout for optimization kernels. The foundational scene representation method that replaces implicit neural fields with explicit Gaussian primitives for real-time rendering. It sets itself apart from NeRFs by using a differentiable sort-and-blend rasterizer instead of per-pixel volume integration. Choose it as the baseline architecture for novel view synthesis. A parameterization for joint covariance that uses bounded Cholesky coefficients multiplied by query diagonal scales. It sets itself apart from direct regression methods by implicitly deriving the regression operator from the ambient joint Cholesky factor. Choose it when modeling cross-covariance and spatial extent constraints is necessary. A general mathematical formalism for signal approximation via Gaussian superposition across 2D images, 3D fields, and vector spaces. It sets itself apart from specific rasterization pipelines by providing closed-form operations for high-dimensional applications. Choose it when the problem requires compact, differentiable signal modeling rather than explicit 3D scene rendering. Time Complexity: Covariance computation is O(N) per Gaussian, involving matrix multiplications. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales linearly with N and the number of SH coefficients S. Measured Performance: Computation is performed on the GPU using batched tensor operations. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of primitives and SH degree. Strengths: Supports differentiable optimization and direct tensor access. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Use when batched GPU processing of explicit geometric primitives is required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: ECoNGS Optimization and Coding
head: ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats), Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats
body: ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats) is a scene representation method that transforms time-consuming volume rendering into an efficient process by optimizing neural editable Gaussians and compressing their attributes via neural entropy coding. It solves the problem of large storage and computational costs in volume visualization by extracting multi-view images and point clouds, grouping geometrically similar scenes for joint learning, and compressing anchor attributes to exploit inter-scene redundancy. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which stores all attributes explicitly, ECoNGS uses a two-stage optimization process involving anchor attribute optimization and joint context model training, achieving compression with minimal distortion. ECoNGS operates on a set of basic scenes, each represented by a collection of 3D Gaussian primitives. The method involves data extraction, two-stage optimization, and entropy coding. Inputs: Multi-view images and corresponding point clouds for each basic scene. Hyperparameters: \lambdas = 0.001 (scaling regularization weight), K=10 (number of neural editable Gaussians per anchor), learning rates (0.01 for anchor feature, opacity, scaling, rotation, TF embeddings; 1\times 10^{-4} for palette color), training iterations (10,000 per stage), and \lambdae (trade-off hyperparameter for compression losses). Outputs: A compressed binary bitstream of anchor attributes encoded via arithmetic coding. MLP parameters stored as 32-bit floating-point values. A complete VolVis scene representation formed by compositing trained basic scenes. The method relies on the GaussianSet Data Structure, which stores means, orientations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. ECoNGS introduces: Anchor Points: A subset of Gaussians whose attributes are optimized and compressed. Neural Editable Gaussians: Derived from anchor points; K=10 editable Gaussians are generated per anchor. Context Model: A lightweight MLP used to estimate probabilities for entropy coding. Hash Grids: Used for inter-scene redundancy; M+ and M- denote the total numbers of +1 and -1 values in the hash grids. The 3D Gaussian function is defined as: C(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^s)^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^s)} where \mathbf{x} is an arbitrary 3D position, \mathbf{x}^s is the position attribute of the Gaussian point, and \mathbf{\Sigma} is the covariance matrix. The covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} is parameterized by a scaling factor s and a quaternion rotation vector q to ensure positive semi-definiteness. Rendering uses EWA volume splatting to transform 3D Gaussians G(\mathbf{x}) to 2D Gaussians G'(\mathbf{x}') on the image plane. Pixel color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}') is determined by \alpha-blending: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}') = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \quad \alphai = oi Gi(\mathbf{x}') where c is modeled by spherical harmonics (SH) parameters, oi is opacity, and N is the number of depth-sorted layered 2D Gaussians. Loss Functions: Stage 1 loss: L{\text{stage1}} = L{\text{rec}} + \lambdas \sum{j=1}^{N^s} \text{prod}(\mathbf{s}j) where L{\text{rec}} is the image reconstruction loss (L1 + SSIM), N^s is the number of predicted editable Gaussians, \text{prod}(\cdot) is the vector product of scaling factors, and \lambdas = 0.001. Stage 2 loss: L{\text{stage2}} = L{\text{stage1}} + \lambdae \frac{L{\text{entropy}} + L{\text{hash}}}{N^a \times dA} where N^a is the number of anchors, dA is the sum of all anchor attribute dimensions, and \lambdae is the trade-off hyperparameter. L{\text{entropy}} and L{\text{hash}} encourage distribution of values within anchor attributes and a more concentrated hash grid, reducing bit consumption. 1. Data Extraction: Extract multi-view images and corresponding point clouds from different basic scenes. 2. Scene Grouping: Group geometrically similar scenes for joint learning. 3. Stage 1 Optimization: Optimize only anchor point attributes and lightweight MLPs for 10,000 iterations using L{\text{stage1}}. Turn off uniform noise for the first 3,000 iterations to stabilize optimization. 4. Stage 2 Optimization: Update all parameters, including the context model, for the remaining 10,000 iterations using L{\text{stage2}}. Enable uniform noise after 3,000 iterations. 5. Encoding: Encode the context model first. Then, encode anchor attributes into a binary bitstream using an arithmetic encoder based on probabilities estimated by the context model. 6. Storage: Store MLP parameters as 32-bit floating-point values. 7. Compositing: Composite all trained basic scenes to form a complete VolVis scene representation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def econgsoptimizationandcoding(scenes, groundtruthimages, hyperparams): # Step 1: Data Extraction & Grouping # Sources do not specify the geometric similarity grouping algorithm. groupedscenes = scenes numanchors = len(groupedscenes) # Initialize anchor attributes and lightweight MLPs anchors = [] for in range(numanchors): anchors.append({ 'means': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'quaternions': [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'scales': [1.0, 1.0, 1.0], 'opacities': [1.0], 'shcoeffs': [0.0] 48, 'mlpparams': [0.0] 100 }) # Step 2: Stage 1 Optimization (10,000 iterations) lranchor = hyperparams['learningrates']['anchor'] # 0.01 lambdas = hyperparams['lambdas'] # 0.001 iterations = hyperparams['iterationsperstage'] # 10,000 decayrate = hyperparams.get('decayrate', 0.99) for iteration in range(iterations): # Compute Lstage1 lossstage1 = lossrec + lambdas scalingreg # Backward pass & Parameter update (Adam optimizer) # Sources do not specify the exact gradient computation and Adam state update gradients = computegradients(lossstage1, anchors) for sceneidx in range(numanchors): for key in anchors[sceneidx]: for i in range(len(anchors[sceneidx][key])): anchors[sceneidx][key][i] -= lranchor gradients[sceneidx][key][i] # Exponential decay for anchor feature, opacity, scaling, rotation, and TF embeddings lranchor = decayrate # Step 3: Stage 2 Optimization (10,000 iterations) lranchor = hyperparams['learningrates']['anchor'] lambdae = hyperparams['lambdae'] for iteration in range(iterations): usenoise = True # Enabled after 3,000 iterations # Forward pass with noise renderedimages = rendersceneswithnoise(anchors, usenoise) # Compute Lstage1 components lossrec = computel1loss(renderedimages, groundtruthimages) + computessimloss(renderedimages, groundtruthimages) scalingreg = sum(product(s) for s in [a['scales'] for a in anchors]) lossstage1 = lossrec + lambdas scalingreg # Compute Lentropy and Lhash # Sources do not provide exact formulas for Lentropy and Lhash lossentropy = computeentropyloss(anchors) losshash = computehashloss(anchors) # Compute Lstage2 Na = len(anchors) dA = sum(dim for dim in [len(a['means']) + len(a['quaternions']) + len(a['scales']) + len(a['opacities']) + len(a['shcoeffs']) for a in anchors]) lossstage2 = lossstage1 + lambdae (lossentropy + losshash) / (Na dA) # Backward pass & update gradients = computegradients(lossstage2, anchors) for sceneidx in range(numanchors): for key in anchors[sceneidx]: for i in range(len(anchors[sceneidx][key])): anchors[sceneidx][key][i] -= lranchor gradients[sceneidx][key][i] lranchor = decayrate # Step 4: Encoding # Encode context model first # Sources do not provide exact encoding algorithm contextmodelbitstream = encodecontextmodel(anchors) # Encode anchor attributes using arithmetic encoder based on context model probabilities # Sources do not provide exact encoding algorithm anchorbitstream = encodeanchorattributes(anchors, contextmodelbitstream) # Store MLP parameters as 32-bit floats mlpparameters = [[float(x) for x in row] for row in anchors] return contextmodelbitstream, anchorbitstream, mlpparameters def computecov2d(mean, quat, scale): # Standard 3D to 2D covariance projection via EWA splatting return [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]] def gaussian2deval(cov2d, positions): return [1.0] len(positions) def alphablend(alpha, shcoeffs, viewdirs): return [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]] def computel1loss(rendered, groundtruth): return 0.0 def computessimloss(rendered, groundtruth): return 0.0 def computegradients(loss, params): return {k: [[0.0]len(row) for row in v] for k, v in params.items()} def computeentropyloss(attributes): # Sources do not provide exact formula return 0.0 def computehashloss(hashgrids): # Sources do not provide exact formula return 0.0 def encodecontextmodel(mlpparams): # Sources do not provide exact encoding algorithm return b"" def encodeanchorattributes(attributes, contextmodel): # Sources do not provide exact encoding algorithm return b"" def product(vec): p = 1.0 for x in vec: p = x return p Early Optimization Instability: Uniform noise in quantization can cause instability. This is handled by turning off noise for the first 3,000 iterations. Model Capacity Loss: Too many overlapping primitives can cause model capacity loss. The scaling regularization term \lambdas \sum \text{prod}(\mathbf{s}j) encourages primitives to be small. Precision: MLP parameters are stored as 32-bit floats, which may limit precision compared to higher-precision formats, but is sufficient for the method's goals. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The method involves two stages of optimization, each with 10,000 iterations, and entropy coding. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The method compresses anchor attributes, reducing storage requirements compared to explicit storage of all Gaussian attributes. Measured Performance: Tested on volume datasets such as Argon, Bubble, Combustion, Ionization, and Tangaroa. For example, the Combustion dataset (multivariate) has 41 basic scenes, 1,920 × 2,880 × 480 resolution, and requires 24.3 GB CPU / 12.4 GB GPU memory. Strengths: Efficient rendering via tile-based rasterization, compression of anchor attributes, joint learning of similar scenes. Limitations: Requires multi-view images and point clouds for initialization, may have reconstruction fidelity trade-offs due to compression. When to Use: Suitable for large-scale volume visualization where storage and computational efficiency are critical. ECoNGS was introduced in the paper "ECoNGS: Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats for Volume Visualization". It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Parent] and extends it to volume visualization by incorporating neural entropy coding and joint learning of similar scenes. The method aims to address the limitations of traditional volume rendering, which is computationally intensive, by leveraging the efficiency of Gaussian splatting and the compression capabilities of neural entropy coding. name: GaussianList Data Structure and Initialization
head: GaussianList
body: The GaussianList is a contiguous, column-major data structure that stores the attributes of a set of 3D Gaussians to enable batch processing during differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently managing geometric primitives (positions, scales, rotations, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients) and their derived covariance matrices for rasterization. It differs from hierarchical variants like Octree-GS / Scaffold-GS by using a flat list, which simplifies memory management but lacks adaptive level-of-detail allocation. Inputs: A vector of Gaussian objects containing raw attributes (position, scale, rotation quaternion, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients). Outputs: A GaussianList instance with pre-allocated, normalized, and computed covariance matrices ready for rendering. Data Structures: The GaussianList struct stores attributes in column-major matrices (N columns for N Gaussians): positions: na::Matrix4xX<f32> (4 rows × N columns). The first three rows are the (x, y, z) coordinates; the fourth row is constant 1.0 for homogeneous coordinates. scales: na::Matrix3xX<f32> (3 rows × N columns). Each column i contains the scale factors sx, sy, sz. opacities: na::DVector<f32> (1D vector of size N). Each element i is the opacity \alphai. rotations: na::Matrix4xX<f32> (4 rows × N columns). Each column i contains the quaternion components [w, x, y, z] or [x, y, z, w] depending on implementation, representing orientation. sh: Matrix48xX<f32> (48 rows × N columns). Stores spherical harmonics coefficients. The layout within a column is interleaved by channel: C{0,R}, C{0,B}, C{0,G}, C{1,R}, C{1,B}, C{1,G}, \dots corresponding to RGB channels for each SH degree/order. numgaussians: usize. The count of Gaussians N. cov3d: na::Matrix3xX<f32> (3 rows × N columns). Pre-allocated zeros, filled by computecov3d(). Initialization Steps: 1. Set Count: Set numgaussians to the length of the input Gaussian vector. 2. Center Positions: Initialize avgpos as a zero Vector3. Iterate over all Gaussians, summing their positions into avgpos. Divide avgpos by numgaussians to compute the mean position. Iterate over all Gaussians again, subtracting avgpos from each position to center the cloud at the origin. 3. Construct Matrices: Positions: Iterate over Gaussians, cloning the 3D position components and appending 1.0 to form 4D homogeneous coordinates in positions. Scales: Clone scale components into scales. Opacities: Clone opacity values into opacities. Rotations: Clone quaternion components into rotations. SH: Clone spherical harmonics coefficients into sh. 4. Compute Covariances: Call computecov3d() to calculate the 3D covariance matrices. Covariance Computation (computecov3d): For each Gaussian i from 0 to numgaussians - 1: 1. Extract the rotation quaternion from column i of rotations. 2. Convert the quaternion to a UnitQuaternion, then to a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix R. 3. Create a diagonal scale matrix S where the diagonal elements are the squared scale components: S = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2). 4. Compute the covariance matrix \Sigma = R S R^T. 5. Copy the resulting 3 \times 3 matrix into cov3d at offset i \times 3 (column-major storage). 2D Projection (projectcov3dtoscreen): To project a 3D covariance to screen space for a specific Gaussian and camera: 1. Get the Gaussian position p and the view matrix V. 2. Convert p to a homogeneous vector ph = [x, y, z, 1.0]^T. 3. Transform to camera space: p{cam} = V ph. 4. Get focal lengths fx, fy and the tangent of the FOV \text{htanfovxy}. 5. Compute the tangent of the Gaussian center: t{xz} = p{cam}.x / p{cam}.z, t{yz} = p{cam}.y / p{cam}.z. 6. Clamp tangents to limits: t{clamp} = \min(|t|, 1.3 \times \tan(\text{FOV})) \times p{cam}.z (applied to x and y components respectively). The multiplier 1.3 is the FOV Clamping Limit. 7. Compute the Jacobian J (3 \times 3 matrix) using fx, fy, t.x, t.y, t.z. 8. Compute W as the transpose of the top-left 3 \times 3 submatrix of the view matrix. 9. Compute T = W J. 10. Compute the projected covariance: \Sigma{2D} = T^T \Sigma{3D} T. 11. Extract the top-left 2 \times 2 submatrix as the final 2D covariance. 12. Apply a low-pass filter by adding 0.3 to the diagonal elements \Sigma{2D}[0,0] and \Sigma{2D}[1,1] to ensure the Gaussian is at least one pixel wide/high. The constant 0.3 is the Low-pass filter constant. 13. Return \Sigma{2D}. Color Evaluation: 1. Pass the SH coefficients column for index i, the SH dimension, and the viewing direction to evalsphericalharmonics. 2. Return the resulting color vector and the Gaussian's opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializegaussianlist(gaussians: list) -> dict: """ Initialize a GaussianList from a list of Gaussian objects. gaussians: list of objects with attributes: position (3,), scale (3,), rotation (quat), opacity (float), shcoeffs (48,) """ N = len(gaussians) # 1. Center Positions positions3d = np.array([g.position for g in gaussians]) avgpos = np.mean(positions3d, axis=0) centeredpositions = positions3d - avgpos # 2. Construct Matrices (Column-major: N columns) # positions: 4xN positions = np.zeros((4, N)) positions[:3,:] = centeredpositions.T positions[3,:] = 1.0 # scales: 3xN scales = np.zeros((3, N)) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): scales[:, i] = g.scale # opacities: N opacities = np.array([g.opacity for g in gaussians]) # rotations: 4xN (assuming w,x,y,z or x,y,z,w, adjust as needed) rotations = np.zeros((4, N)) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): rotations[:, i] = g.rotation # Quaternion components # sh: 48xN sh = np.zeros((48, N)) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): sh[:, i] = g.shcoeffs # cov3d: 3xN, initialized to zeros cov3d = np.zeros((3, N)) # 3. Compute Covariances computecov3d(cov3d, scales, rotations, N) return { "positions": positions, "scales": scales, "opacities": opacities, "rotations": rotations, "sh": sh, "numgaussians": N, "cov3d": cov3d } def computecov3d(cov3d: np.ndarray, scales: np.ndarray, rotations: np.ndarray, N: int): """ Compute 3D covariance matrices for all Gaussians. cov3d: 3xN output array scales: 3xN input array rotations: 4xN input array (quaternions) """ for i in range(N): # Extract quaternion quat = rotations[:, i] # Convert quaternion to rotation matrix R (3x3) R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(quat) # Extract scales s = scales[:, i] # Create diagonal scale matrix S = diag(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) S = np.diag(s 2) # Compute covariance: R S R^T cov = R @ S @ R.T # Store in cov3d (column i) cov3d[:, i] = cov.flatten() def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Convert a quaternion [w, x, y, z] or [x, y, z, w] to a 3x3 rotation matrix. Assumes input is normalized. """ # Assuming w,x,y,z layout for standard conversion w, x, y, z = q[0], q[1], q[2], q[3] # Rotation matrix elements xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz wx, wy, wz = wx, wy, wz R = np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) return R def projectcov3dtoscreen(cov3dcol: np.ndarray, position: np.ndarray, viewmatrix: np.ndarray, focalx: float, focaly: float, tanfovx: float, tanfovy: float) -> np.ndarray: """ Project a single 3D covariance matrix to 2D screen space. cov3dcol: 3x3 covariance matrix for one Gaussian position: 3D position vector viewmatrix: 4x4 view matrix """ # 1. Homogeneous position posh = np.array([position[0], position[1], position[2], 1.0]) # 2. Camera space poscam = viewmatrix @ posh # 3. Tangents tz = poscam[2] if tz == 0: tz = 1e-6 # Avoid division by zero tx = poscam[0] / tz ty = poscam[1] / tz # 4. Clamp tangents limitx = 1.3 tanfovx limity = 1.3 tanfovy tx = np.clip(tx, -limitx, limitx) tz ty = np.clip(ty, -limity, limity) tz # 5. Jacobian J (3x3) # Standard projection Jacobian derivation # J = [ fx/z 0 -fxx/z^2 ] # [ 0 fy/z -fyy/z^2 ] # [ 0 0 0 ] # However, source uses a specific formulation involving t.x, t.y # Based on source: J uses focalx, focaly, t.x, t.y, t.z # Let's reconstruct standard projection Jacobian for clarity z = poscam[2] J = np.array([ [focalx / z, 0, -focalx tx / (zz)], [0, focaly / z, -focaly ty / (zz)], [0, 0, 0] ]) # 6. W matrix (transpose of top-left 3x3 of view matrix) W = viewmatrix[:3,:3].T # 7. T = W J T = W @ J # 8. Cov2D = T^T cov3d T cov2dfull = T.T @ cov3dcol @ T # 9. Extract top-left 2x2 cov2d = cov2dfull[:2,:2] # 10. Low-pass filter cov2d[0, 0] += 0.3 cov2d[1, 1] += 0.3 return cov2d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: In projectcov3dtoscreen, if z (depth) is zero, division by zero occurs. A small epsilon should be added to z. Quaternion Normalization: The rotation matrix conversion assumes normalized quaternions. Unnormalized quaternions will produce incorrect scales and orientations. FOV Clamping: The clamping limit 1.3 \times \tan(\text{FOV}) prevents extreme tangents for Gaussians near the frustum edges, but may distort very large Gaussians. Low-Pass Filter: Adding 0.3 ensures minimum pixel coverage but may cause blurring for very small Gaussians. LinPrim Population Control manages the density of linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra) during differentiable volume rendering optimization by pruning, cloning, and splitting primitives to adapt to scene complexity. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by redefining primitive size metrics to accommodate non-spherical kernels and adjusting sampling distributions to respect the anisotropic geometry of linear primitives. Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization establishes the initial state of the 3D Gaussian primitives (\mathcal{G}) from a sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud, providing geometrically accurate starting positions, colors, and covariances. Unlike random initialization, which lacks normal information and accurate geometry, SfM initialization leverages multi-view matching to produce a sparse cloud that serves as a superior prior for the differentiable renderer, significantly improving reconstruction quality and convergence speed. It sets itself apart from dense MVS initialization by avoiding the baking of MVS errors and redundant geometry, relying instead on the optimizer to create detail during training. Octree-GS and Scaffold-GS are hierarchical level-of-detail (LoD) methods that anchor scene content to a sparse voxel grid, using the grid as a scaffold to allocate Gaussians only in occupied regions. This approach naturally adapts to view distance and improves memory efficiency compared to flat Gaussian lists. Scaffold-GS specifically uses anchor points to predict "neural" Gaussians on the fly via a small MLP, achieving approximately 5x less memory usage than vanilla 3DGS at the same quality. Octree-GS builds an explicit octree over the scene, associating each node with a merged Gaussian that summarizes the radiance and opacity of its children, enabling massive scene rendering. GaussianHair is a strand-aware hair rendering method that combines the Marschner Hair Model with Unreal Engine 4’s real-time hair rendering pipeline to create the Gaussian Hair Scattering Model. It uses a hybrid strand + Gaussian Splat (GS) representation to capture complex hair geometry and appearance, enabling fast rasterization and volumetric rendering. It is distinguished from general GS variants by its specific focus on hair topology and physically-based scattering, enabling applications such as editing and relighting. Random Gaussian Generation is the initialization procedure for creating a set of 3D Gaussians from scratch, typically to serve as the starting point for differentiable rendering optimization in methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting. It generates a fixed number of Gaussian primitives with random positions (implicitly at the origin before transformation), scales, orientations, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. It differs from LinPrim Population Control which manages the density of existing Gaussians during training, and from Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization which may use structured or data-driven initialization strategies. This method provides a uniform, uninformative prior over the parameter space. Appearance Modeling uses per-image and per-Gaussian embeddings optimized via an MLP to model view-dependent appearance, illumination, and weather effects. The learning rate for the appearance MLP is 0.0005, for per-image embeddings \mathbf{e}j is 0.001, and for per-Gaussian embeddings \mathbf{z}i is 0.005. Per-image embedding \mathbf{e}j \in \mathbb{R}^{de} has dimension de = 32. Per-Gaussian embedding \mathbf{z}i \in \mathbb{R}^{dz} has dimension dz = 24, initialized using Fourier frequencies with 4 components. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) for copying attributes and O(N) for covariance computation. Projection is O(1) per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing attributes and covariances. The flat list structure has no overhead for hierarchical pointers. Performance: Flat lists are efficient for batch processing on GPUs but may waste memory on empty regions of the scene compared to hierarchical methods. Strengths: Simple implementation, efficient batch processing, easy to integrate with existing renderers. Limitations: No adaptive resolution, high memory usage for large scenes, potential for over-sampling in empty areas. When to Use: Small to medium scenes, real-time applications where simplicity is key, or as a baseline for comparison. When Not to Use: Very large scenes with high dynamic range, or when memory efficiency is critical. The GaussianList data structure is a core component of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) implementations, particularly in open-source projects like thomasantony/splat. It was developed to provide a flexible and efficient way to manage 3D Gaussian primitives for differentiable rendering. The structure has been adopted and adapted in various research projects, including DeSplat, which extends the representation with appearance modeling. thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) DeSplat: Decomposed Gaussian Splatting for Distractor-Free Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.00076, fetched 2026-11-03

name: LinPrim Population Control
head: Adaptive Population Control, LinPrim-MCMC
body: LinPrim Population Control manages the density of linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra) during differentiable volume rendering optimization by pruning, cloning, and splitting primitives to adapt to scene complexity. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by redefining primitive size metrics to accommodate non-spherical kernels and adjusting sampling distributions to respect the anisotropic geometry of linear primitives. Inputs: Current set of primitives \mathcal{P}, each with position \mathbf{p}, color \mathbf{c}, distances to corners \mathbf{d}, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, view-space positional gradient \nabla{\mathbf{p}}, and opacity \alpha. Camera parameters for known views. Scene extent bounds. Outputs: Updated set of primitives \mathcal{P}' with modified count, positions, and sizes. Each primitive stores: position: 3D vector \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. color: 3D vector \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. distances: Array of distances to corner vertices. For octahedra, 3 values (along axes); for tetrahedra, 4 values (to vertices). rotation: Quaternion \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4. gradientmomentum: 3D vector for optimizer state. gradient: 3D view-space positional gradient vector. opacity: Scalar transparency value. type: Enum (OCTAHEDRON, TETRAHEDRON). Remove primitives that fail fidelity or efficiency criteria. Size Definition: For Octahedra: Size S{oct} = 2 \cdot \max(\mathbf{d}), where \mathbf{d} are the distances along the principal axes. For Tetrahedra: Size S{tet} \approx \sqrt{2} \cdot d{max}, where d{max} is the distance to the furthest corner vertex. Criteria: A primitive is pruned if: 1. Opacity is below a threshold. 2. Size exceeds a fraction of the scene extent. 3. Screen-space area exceeds a threshold. (Specific threshold values are not given in the sources.) Initialize primitives from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points: 1. For each SfM point \mathbf{p}i with color \mathbf{c}i: Find distance to closest SfM neighbor d{min}. Set initial distances \mathbf{d} = d{min} for all corners. Set rotation \mathbf{q} to a uniformly random quaternion. Set position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}i. Select primitives with large view-space positional gradients \|\nabla{\mathbf{p}}\|. (Gradient threshold is not given in the sources.) Cloning (for small primitives): 1. Create new primitive with identical features: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{c}{new} = \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d}{new} = \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{q}{new} = \mathbf{q}. 2. Reset gradient momentum to zero. Splitting (for large primitives): 1. Create two new primitives with smaller sizes. 2. Sample positions from a PDF based on the original primitive's geometry. Sampling Logic: Octahedra: Standard deviations \sigmai = di (corresponding distance for each axis). Sample offset \Delta \mathbf{p} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \text{diag}(\sigma^2)). Apply rotation afterwards to spread primitives along longer dimensions. Tetrahedra: Set \sigma = \frac{1}{2} \max(\mathbf{d}) for all dimensions. Sample offset \Delta \mathbf{p} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}). Apply rotation afterwards. Adapt GS-MCMC population control by treating primitives as equivalent Gaussians. 1. Scale octahedron distances: \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{d} / 2.6. 2. Use \mathbf{d}' as Gaussian standard deviations for MCMC sampling. 3. Perform MCMC steps to draw samples from the scene distribution, allowing precise control over final population size. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import copy as stdcopy def quattorotmat(q): """Convert quaternion [w, x, y, z] to 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) def calculatescreenarea(prim, camera): """Estimate screen-space area from camera projection. Not given in the sources. Standard perspective projection used.""" # Placeholder for standard projection logic return 0.0 def cloneprimitive(prim): """Deep copy primitive fields and reset momentum.""" new = stdcopy.deepcopy(prim) new.gradientmomentum = np.zeros(3) return new def pruneprimitives(primitives, camera, sceneextent, opacitythresh, sizefrac, screenthresh): """Remove primitives based on opacity, size, and screen space.""" toremove = [] for i, prim in enumerate(primitives): if prim.opacity < opacitythresh: toremove.append(i) continue if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': size = 2.0 np.max(prim.distances) elif prim.type == 'TETRAHEDRON': size = np.sqrt(2.0) np.max(prim.distances) else: size = 0.0 if size > sizefrac sceneextent: toremove.append(i) continue if calculatescreenarea(prim, camera) > screenthresh: toremove.append(i) for i in reversed(toremove): primitives.pop(i) return primitives def cloneandsplit(primitives, gradthresh, sizethresh): """Clone small primitives with high gradients, split large ones.""" newprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(prim.gradient) if gradnorm > gradthresh: if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': size = 2.0 np.max(prim.distances) else: size = np.sqrt(2.0) np.max(prim.distances) if size < sizethresh: newprimitives.append(cloneprimitive(prim)) else: posa, posb = samplesplitpositions(prim) newa = cloneprimitive(prim) newa.position = posa newa.distances = [d 0.5 for d in prim.distances] newb = cloneprimitive(prim) newb.position = posb newb.distances = [d 0.5 for d in prim.distances] newprimitives.extend([newa, newb]) else: newprimitives.append(prim) return newprimitives def samplesplitpositions(prim): """Sample positions for splitting based on primitive type.""" R = quattorotmat(prim.rotation) if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': sigma = np.array(prim.distances) delta = np.random.normal(0, sigma) posoffset = R @ delta elif prim.type == 'TETRAHEDRON': maxd = np.max(prim.distances) sigma = 0.5 maxd delta = np.random.normal(0, sigma, 3) posoffset = R @ delta else: posoffset = np.zeros(3) posa = prim.position + posoffset posb = prim.position - posoffset return posa, posb def linprimmcmcstep(primitives, scalefactor=2.6): """Apply LinPrim-MCMC adjustments.""" for prim in primitives: if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': prim.distancesscaled = [d / scalefactor for d in prim.distances] # MCMC sampling logic relies on external GS-MCMC implementation Opacity threshold: Not given in the sources. Screen-space area threshold: Not given in the sources. Scene extent fraction: Not given in the sources. Gradient threshold: Not given in the sources. scalefactor (LinPrim-MCMC): 2.6 sceneextent: Bounding box diagonal or max dimension of the scene Tetrahedron Splitting: Non-trivial to sample along principal axes due to lack of symmetry; use isotropic scaling with \sigma = \frac{1}{2} \max(\mathbf{d}). Octahedron Anisotropy: Must sample along local axes before rotating to spread along longer dimensions. Momentum Reset: Cloned primitives must reset gradient momentum to avoid biased updates. Magnitude Mismatch: Direct use of octahedron distances as Gaussian standard deviations is invalid; scaling by 2.6 is required for MCMC compatibility. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficiently adapts to scene detail; prevents over-rendering in uniform regions and under-rendering in complex areas. Strengths: Compatible with 3DGS advancements (e.g., MCMC); handles non-spherical primitives correctly. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of size thresholds. When to Use: When optimizing linear primitives for novel views or high-fidelity reconstruction where fixed initialization is insufficient. LinPrim Population Control originates from the LinPrim paper (2025), which adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques to linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra). It addresses the need for dynamic population management in differentiable volumetric rendering with non-Gaussian kernels. The method incorporates insights from GS-MCMC and Distribution Alignment to handle magnitude differences between linear primitive distances and Gaussian standard deviations. name: Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Initialization, COLMAP Initialization, SfM Initialization, Sparse Point Cloud Initialization, Sparse SfM Initialization, Starter Gaussians, Structure from Motion (SfM) Initialization
body: Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization establishes the initial state of the 3D Gaussian primitives (\mathcal{G}) from a sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud, providing geometrically accurate starting positions, colors, and covariances. Unlike random initialization, which lacks normal information and accurate geometry, SfM initialization leverages multi-view matching to produce a sparse cloud that serves as a superior prior for the differentiable renderer, significantly improving reconstruction quality and convergence speed. It sets itself apart from dense MVS initialization by avoiding the baking of MVS errors and redundant geometry, relying instead on the optimizer to create detail during training. Inputs: A set of 2D images (e.g., from COLMAP). Camera poses (extrinsic: rotation R{cam}, translation T{cam}; intrinsic: focal length f) estimated via SfM. A sparse 3D point cloud \mathcal{P} = \{pi\}{i=1}^N containing 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and RGB colors \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: A set of N learnable 3D Gaussian parameters: Means: \mathbf{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (position) Scales: \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (log-space radii) Rotations: \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Opacities: \alphai \in [0, 1] (stored as logits) Colors: \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics coefficients) The Gaussian parameters are stored as differentiable tensors (e.g., nn.Parameter in PyTorch) on the GPU. Means (\mathbf{\mu}): Tensor of shape (N, 3). Scaling (\mathbf{s}): Tensor of shape (N, 3), storing log-space values. Rotation (\mathbf{q}): Tensor of shape (N, 4), storing quaternions in [w, x, y, z] format. Opacity (\alpha{logit}): Tensor of shape (N, 1), storing logits. Features (\mathbf{f}): Tensor of shape (N, 1, 3) for the DC component (f{dc}) and (N, K, 3) for higher-order SH coefficients (f{rest}), where K depends on the SH degree. 1. SfM Reconstruction: Perform Structure-from-Motion on the input images to estimate camera poses and reconstruct a sparse 3D point cloud with associated colors. Note: Dense MVS clouds are discouraged as they waste time and bake in MVS errors. 2. Position Initialization: Copy the 3D coordinates from the SfM point cloud directly to the Gaussian means tensor. \mathbf{\mu}i = \mathbf{x}i 3. Covariance Initialization (Scale and Rotation): The covariance matrix \Sigma is parameterized by scale \mathbf{s} and rotation \mathbf{q} to ensure positive semi-definiteness. Scale: Compute the distance to the k-nearest neighbors (KNN) for each point. A common implementation uses a fixed base distance or the mean KNN distance. Method A (Fixed Base): Use a base distance d{base} = 0.1. Compute dist2 = \max(0.1, \min(d{base}, 1e-7)). The scale is initialized isotropically: \mathbf{s}i = [\log(\sqrt{dist2}), \log(\sqrt{dist2}), \log(\sqrt{dist2})]^T Method B (KNN-based): Compute the mean distance to the 50 nearest neighbors, apply log, and replicate across dimensions. Or use the mean orientation-aware KNN distance multiplied by a factor s{init} = 1.5. Clamping: During optimization, scales are clamped to a maximum value (e.g., 10.0) to prevent excessively large Gaussians. Rotation: Initialize all quaternions to the identity rotation: \mathbf{q}i = [1, 0, 0, 0]^T Variant (Normal-Aligned): If surface normals are available (e.g., from depth maps), compute the quaternion that aligns the local z-axis with the estimated surface normal. 4. Opacity Initialization: Initialize opacities as logits to ensure valid sigmoid output during training. Method A: Set pre-activation opacity to 8.0. \alpha{logit, i} = 8.0 \implies \sigma(8.0) \approx 0.9997 Method B: Set target opacity to 0.1, compute logit: \alpha{logit, i} = \log\left(\frac{0.1}{1 - 0.1}\right) = \log\left(\frac{0.1}{0.9}\right) Clamping: Clamp initial logit values to a range corresponding to [1e-4, 0.99] to prevent extreme gradients. 5. Color Initialization (Spherical Harmonics): Initialize the zeroth-degree SH coefficient (f{dc}) from the SfM point's RGB color. Higher-order coefficients (f{rest}) are initialized to zero. Normalize RGB to [-0.5, 0.5]. Divide by the SH basis constant C0 = 0.28209479177387814: f{dc, i} = \frac{\mathbf{c}i}{C0} Set f{rest, i} = \mathbf{0}. 6. Covariance Matrix Construction: During rendering, the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma is reconstructed from \mathbf{s} and \mathbf{q}: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T Where R is the rotation matrix derived from \mathbf{q}, and S = \text{diag}(\exp(\mathbf{s})) is the diagonal scaling matrix. Args: sfmpointsxyz: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D coordinates. sfmpointsrgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3), RGB colors in [0, 1]. numneighbors: Number of neighbors for KNN distance calculation. Returns: Dictionary of initialized Gaussian parameters. """ N = sfmpointsxyz.shape[0] # 1. Positions means = sfmpointsxyz.clone().detach() # 2. This is a placeholder for a KD-tree or brute-force KNN implementation. """ # Brute-force distance matrix (for small N) # dists = torch.cdist(points, points) # topkdists, = torch.topk(dists, k+1, largest=False) # +1 to exclude self # meandist = topkdists[:, 1:].mean(dim=1) # Exclude self (index 0) # return meandist # Placeholder: In practice, use a KD-tree library or efficient KNN. # For this example, we return a dummy constant to satisfy syntax. return torch.ones(points.shape[0]) 0.1 Division by Zero: When computing the 2D projection covariance, depth z must be clamped with a small epsilon (e.g., 1e-7) to prevent division by zero in the Jacobian. Numerical Stability: Add a bias of 0.3 to the diagonal elements of the 2D covariance matrix to prevent singular matrices during projection. Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized to unit length before converting to rotation matrices to ensure valid rotations. MVS Bias: Using dense MVS clouds for initialization is discouraged as it wastes time and bakes in MVS errors as starting bias. Random Large-Variance Initialization (RAIN-GS) relaxes the strict Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud assumption required by standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing sparse, large-variance random initialization. Unlike standard methods that rely solely on dense SfM points, this approach allows optimization to proceed even when SfM data is sparse or absent, serving as a fallback or complementary initialization strategy. This method reduces training time for dynamic video scenes by initializing the point cloud of the current frame using the learned model from the previous frame, leveraging temporal correlation between nearby frames. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by explicitly optimizing geometric alignment between consecutive frames via Chamfer distance minimization before refining radiance parameters. Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction is a method for initializing and refining the geometric attributes (position, opacity, and covariance) of 3D Gaussian primitives in a feed-forward or iterative manner, typically leveraging a global volumetric representation rather than per-pixel local volumes. It solves the problem of redundant, inconsistent, and noisy Gaussian initialization found in standard pixel-aligned methods, which often lead to ghosting artifacts and poor global consistency. Unlike siblings that rely on heuristic densification or static point clouds, this method uses a learned neural volume to predict geometry offsets and attributes, enabling efficient reconstruction of large-scale scenes. Background Hemisphere Initialization is a technique for handling unbounded scenes in 3D Gaussian Splatting by modeling the distant background (sky) as a separate, fixed-radius hemisphere of Gaussians. It solves the problem of "cloud-like" artifacts and occlusion errors that occur when foreground Gaussians attempt to model distant sky regions, which degrades novel view synthesis quality. It sets itself apart from standard background models by explicitly disentangling the sky from the foreground geometry, often using a hemisphere to avoid occluding the ground plane. ReSplat Initialization predicts an initial set of 3D Gaussians from a sparse point cloud by aggregating local and global 3D context to compensate for information loss incurred by downsampling the input point cloud by 16x. Unlike naive prediction methods that directly map point features to Gaussian parameters, this method uses a transformer-based encoder to enrich features with neighborhood context before decoding. It sets the stage for the subsequent Recurrent Gaussian Update by providing a structured initial state \mathcal{G}^0. This family of methods initializes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives using pre-existing 3D geometry (point clouds or meshes) rather than relying solely on sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) outputs. It solves the problem of initializing high-quality radiance fields when multi-view images are unavailable or when the user possesses dense, surface-aligned volumetric data (e.g., MPEG plenoptic point clouds or meshes). It differs from Random Large-Variance Initialization by anchoring Gaussians to observed geometry, and from Gaussian Model Initialization by supporting dense mesh inputs and optional fixed-position constraints. A method to initialize the neural point cloud and their features for Point-NeRF using an external point cloud reconstruction (specifically COLMAP). It solves the problem of how to provide initial positions, variances, and feature vectors for the neural points. The variance parameter \gammai for each point pi is initialized to 0.3. To acquire the feature vector fi for a point pi, views where the point is occluded are ruled out, and the view closest to the point is selected. The point is unprojected onto the feature maps extracted by a 2D CNN to obtain fi. The hierarchy is a binary tree. Leaf nodes contain the full set of optimized Gaussian properties (base color, SH coefficients, position, covariance). Internal nodes store merged approximations of their two child nodes. Initializes a single ellipsoid from a set of 3D points using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to determine orientation, center, and radii. The minimum allowed radius r{\min} is typically 0.005 to avoid numerical problems, and a scaling factor \alpha (typically 3) ensures points are mostly covered. Aggregates filtered multiview depth maps from an MVS method into a unified 3D point cloud. An initial optimization phase prunes noisy Gaussians by freezing centers and optimizing other parameters for N{prun} iterations, removing Gaussians with opacity \alphak < \tau. Afterward, all parameters are unfrozen for standard optimization with Adaptive Density Control. Initializes the base feature f{base} and directional feature f{dir} with the RGB color values of the corresponding SfM points. The temporal feature f{time} is initialized as a zero vector. Time Complexity: Initialization time is dominated by the SfM process, which is O(N^2) or O(N \log N) depending on the implementation, where N is the number of images/features. For COLMAP, this can take several minutes for large scenes. Random initialization is significantly faster (seconds) but yields lower quality. Memory Complexity: The initial memory footprint is proportional to the number of SfM points N. Each point requires storage for position (3 floats), color (3 floats), scale (3 floats), rotation (4 floats), and opacity (1 float), totaling approximately 14-16 bytes per point, plus SH coefficients if used. Performance: SfM initialization typically yields higher PSNR (e.g., 26.05 vs 20.42 on Average-30K) and better background quality compared to random initialization. However, it is slower to initialize. Strengths: Provides geometrically accurate starting points, improving convergence and final reconstruction quality. Avoids the "cloud-like" artifacts associated with random initialization in sparse regions. Limitations: Requires high-quality SfM reconstruction. Fails or performs poorly if the input images have insufficient overlap or texture. Dense MVS initialization is discouraged due to bias and computational waste. The method originates from the seminal 3D Gaussian Splatting paper [1], which introduced the use of 3D Gaussians for explicit radiance field representation. The initialization from sparse SfM points was chosen to provide a geometric prior that guides the optimization, as opposed to random initialization which relies entirely on the optimizer to discover the scene geometry. COLMAP is the standard tool used for this purpose. Subsequent work has explored variants such as random initialization for synthetic data, MVS-guided initialization, and neural prediction of geometry. name: Random Large-Variance Initialization
head: RAIN-GS, RAIN-GS Initialization, Sparse-Large-Variance Init
body: Random Large-Variance Initialization (RAIN-GS) relaxes the strict Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud assumption required by standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing sparse, large-variance random initialization. Unlike standard methods that rely solely on dense SfM points, this approach allows optimization to proceed even when SfM data is sparse or absent, serving as a fallback or complementary initialization strategy. Inputs: A set of N 3D points Q = \{q1, \dots, qN\} from a SfM reconstruction, where each qi \in \mathbb{R}^3. A scaling constant k. Outputs: A set of 3D triangles, each defined by three vertices \{v1, v2, v3\}, centered around each SfM point. Data Structures: Each triangle is represented by three 3D vertex positions vi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Additional learnable parameters per triangle include sharpness \sigma, opacity o, and spherical harmonic color coefficients c. Steps: 1. For each SfM point q \in Q: a. Identify the three nearest neighbors of q in the point cloud. b. Calculate d, the average Euclidean distance from q to these three nearest neighbors. c. Sample three vertices \{u1, u2, u3\} uniformly at random from the unit sphere (\|ui\| = 1). d. Scale the sampled vertices by d and translate them by q to create the triangle vertices: vi = q + k \cdot d \cdot ui, \quad i \in \{1, 2, 3\} e. This results in an approximately equilateral, randomly oriented triangle centered at q with size proportional to local point density d. Parameters: k: Scaling constant determining triangle size relative to neighbor distance d. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If d=0 (e.g., duplicate points), the triangle collapses. A guard should handle d \approx 0 by using a minimum distance threshold or skipping the point. Uniform sampling on the unit sphere must be done correctly (e.g., using spherical coordinates with \cos \theta uniform) to avoid clustering at poles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sampleuniformsphere(n): """Sample n points uniformly on the unit sphere.""" phi = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, n) costheta = np.random.uniform(-1, 1, n) sintheta = np.sqrt(1 - costheta2) return np.stack([sintheta np.cos(phi), sintheta np.sin(phi), costheta], axis=-1) def randomlargevarianceinit(points, k=1.0): """ Initialize triangles around SfM points using sparse large-variance random init. Args: points: Array of shape (N, 3) containing SfM 3D points. k: Scaling constant for triangle size. Returns: triangles: Array of shape (N, 3, 3) containing vertices for each triangle. """ N = points.shape[0] triangles = np.zeros((N, 3, 3)) for i, q in enumerate(points): # Compute distances to all other points dists = np.linalg.norm(points - q, axis=1) # Exclude self from nearest neighbor search dists[i] = np.inf # Get indices of the 3 nearest neighbors nnidx = np.argsort(dists)[:3] # Calculate average distance d d = np.mean(dists[nnidx]) # Guard against degenerate triangles when d is near zero if d < 1e-6: triangles[i] = q continue # Sample 3 vertices from unit sphere u = sampleuniformsphere(3) # Scale and translate to form triangle triangles[i] = q + k d u return triangles This variant explicitly uses the SfM point cloud to define the initial geometry. It creates triangles centered at each SfM point, with size proportional to the local point density (average distance to nearest neighbors). It is chosen when SfM data is available but sparse, allowing the model to explore a larger initial volume than point-based initialization. It differs from pure random initialization by anchoring the geometry to known scene structure. Not given in the sources. The method originated in the RAIN-GS approach, which relaxes the SfM-only initialization assumption. The triangle-based initialization variant is detailed in "Triangle Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering". It is part of the broader effort to make Gaussian Splatting more robust to varying input data quality. name: SfM-Based Triangle Initialization
head: Triangle Initialization
body: SfM-Based Triangle Initialization is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian primitives as triangles using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds. It addresses the problem of establishing a geometrically coherent starting state for triangle-based splatting by creating approximately equilateral, randomly oriented triangles centered on SfM points. It differs from Random Large-Variance Initialization by relying strictly on local geometric structure derived from SfM neighbor distances rather than sparse random sampling, ensuring the initial primitives match the scene's local density. Inputs: A set of 3D points Q = \{q1, q2, \dots, qN\} from an SfM reconstruction, where each qi \in \mathbb{R}^3. A scaling constant k. Outputs: A set of 3D triangles, where each triangle is defined by three vertices Vi = \{v{i,1}, v{i,2}, v{i,3}\}. Data Structures: Each triangle primitive stores three 3D vertex positions. Associated parameters (optimized later): sharpness \sigma, opacity o, and spherical harmonic color coefficients c. Steps: 1. For each SfM point q \in Q: a. Identify the three nearest neighbors of q in the SfM point cloud. b. Calculate d, the average Euclidean distance from q to these three nearest neighbors. c. Sample three vertices \{u1, u2, u3\} uniformly at random from the unit sphere. d. Scale the sampled vertices by d and center them at q to compute the triangle vertices vi: vi = q + k \cdot d \cdot ui, \quad i \in \{1, 2, 3\} e. Store the triangle defined by \{v1, v2, v3\}. Parameters: k: A scaling constant determining triangle size relative to neighbor distance d. Typical values are not explicitly given in the source, but it controls the initial scale of the primitives. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse SfM: If the SfM point cloud is sparse, the nearest neighbor distance d may be large, resulting in oversized initial triangles that may not capture fine details. Degenerate Neighbors: If fewer than three neighbors exist for a point, the distance calculation is undefined. This requires a fallback or preprocessing step to ensure sufficient point density. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializetriangles(sfmpoints, k): """ Initialize 3D triangles from SfM points. Args: sfmpoints: Array of shape (N, 3) containing 3D SfM points. k: Scaling constant for triangle size. Returns: triangles: List of arrays, each of shape (3, 3) representing vertices of a triangle. """ from scipy.spatial import KDTree # Build KD-tree for efficient nearest neighbor search tree = KDTree(sfmpoints) triangles = [] for q in sfmpoints: # Find 3 nearest neighbors (excluding the point itself if it's in the tree) # Note: If q is in the tree, the nearest neighbor is q itself (distance 0). # We need the next 3 distinct neighbors. distances, indices = tree.query(q, k=4) # Skip the first neighbor if it is the point itself (distance ~0) # If the point is not in the tree or we want strictly other points, adjust accordingly. # Assuming q is in the tree, indices[0] is q. neighborindices = indices[1:4] neighborpoints = sfmpoints[neighborindices] # Calculate average Euclidean distance to the 3 nearest neighbors dists = np.linalg.norm(neighborpoints - q, axis=1) d = np.mean(dists) # Sample 3 vertices uniformly from the unit sphere # Generate random points and normalize to unit length u = np.random.randn(3, 3) u = u / np.linalg.norm(u, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Scale by d and center at q # vi = q + k d ui vertices = q + k d u triangles.append(vertices) return triangles Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for building the KD-tree and O(N) for querying neighbors, where N is the number of SfM points. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the SfM points and the resulting triangles. Strengths: Provides geometrically meaningful initial primitives that align with the scene's local structure, potentially leading to faster convergence and better reconstruction quality compared to purely random initialization. Limitations: Heavily dependent on the quality and density of the SfM point cloud. Poor SfM results (e.g., missing points, outliers) will lead to poor initialization. This method is described in "Triangle Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering". It was introduced as an alternative to random initialization for triangle-based splatting, leveraging the geometric information available from SfM reconstructions. name: HDR-GS Initialization and Optimization
head: HDR-GS loss, HDR-GS training
body: HDR-GS initialization and optimization is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian primitives and training a Gaussian Splatting model for High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis. It addresses the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which relies on Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images and often lacks accurate Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds for initialization in HDR datasets. Unlike standard 3DGS which initializes from SfM points of LDR inputs, HDR-GS recalibrates camera parameters using SfM on LDR views captured at a single exposure time to generate initial 3D Gaussian positions, then optimizes the scene using a combined pixel-wise loss and a µ-law domain constraint loss. This approach establishes a robust data foundation for 3DGS-based algorithms in 3D HDR imaging. Inputs: A multi-view HDR dataset containing Nv viewpoints. For each viewpoint j, LDR images \hat{I}{lj}(ts) captured at a specific exposure time ts. Ground truth HDR images I{hj} (available for synthetic scenes, not for real scenes). Rendered LDR images \hat{I}{lj}(\Delta tj) and HDR images \hat{I}{hj} generated from the current Gaussian set G. Outputs: Recalibrated camera intrinsics M{int} and extrinsics \{Mj^{ext}\}{j=1}^{Nv}. Initial number of points Np and their 3D positions \{\mui\}{i=1}^{Np}. Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, features, opacity, scaling, rotation) and tone mapper network weights. The method initializes the Gaussian set G as described in GaussianList Data Structure and Initialization. Positions: Initialized from SfM output \{\mui\}. Other Parameters: Randomly initialized. 1. SfM Initialization: Select LDR images \{\hat{I}j(ts)\}{j=1}^{Nv} from the multi-view HDR dataset where all images share the same exposure time ts. This constraint is critical because SfM relies on multi-view feature detection and matching, and exposure changes degrade accuracy. Apply the SfM mapping function F{SfM} to obtain camera parameters and initial point cloud: M{int}, \{Mj^{ext}\}{j=1}^{Nv}, Np, \{\mui\}{i=1}^{Np} = F{SfM}(\{\hat{I}j(ts)\}{j=1}^{Nv}) where Nv is the number of viewpoints, M{int} is the intrinsic matrix (constant across viewpoints), and \{\mui\} are the initial 3D Gaussian positions. 2. Gaussian Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian set G with Np points at positions \{\mui\}. Randomly initialize all other learnable parameters of G (features, opacity, scaling, rotation). 3. Training Loop: For each training iteration (total 3 \times 10^4 iterations): a. Rendering: Render LDR images \hat{I}{lj}(\Delta tj) and HDR images \hat{I}{hj} for a batch of B viewpoints using the current Gaussian set G and camera poses \{Mj^{ext}\}. b. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L = Lp + \gamma \cdot Lc. c. Optimization: Update parameters using the Adam optimizer. Pixel-wise Loss (Lp): Combines L1 loss and D-SSIM loss on LDR images to ensure photometric consistency: Lp = \sum{j=1}^B L1(I{lj}(\Delta tj), \hat{I}{lj}(\Delta tj)) + \lambda \cdot L{D-SSIM}(I{lj}(\Delta tj), \hat{I}{lj}(\Delta tj)) where B is the batch size, I{lj} is the ground truth LDR image, \hat{I}{lj} is the rendered LDR image, and \lambda is a hyperparameter. µ-law Domain Constraint Loss (Lc): Enforces a constraint on the rendered HDR image in the µ-law LDR domain, primarily for synthetic scenes where ground truth HDR is available: Lc = \sum{j=1}^B \left( \frac{\log(1 + \mu \cdot norm(I{hj}))}{\log(1 + \mu)} - \frac{\log(1 + \mu \cdot norm(\hat{I}{hj}))}{\log(1 + \mu)} \right)^2 where I{hj} is the ground truth HDR image, \hat{I}{hj} is the rendered HDR image, \mu is the compression amount, and norm(\cdot) is min-max normalization. Total Loss: L = Lp + \gamma \cdot Lc where \gamma controls the relative importance of Lc. \mu (Compression): The amount of compression in the µ-law normalization. \gamma (Constraint Weight): Synthetic datasets: \gamma = 0.6. Real datasets: \gamma = 0 (since ground truth HDR images are unavailable). \lambda (D-SSIM Weight): Hyperparameter for the D-SSIM term in Lp. Value not explicitly given in the source text, but cited as part of the loss formulation. Optimizer: Adam. \beta1 = 0.9 \beta2 = 0.999 \epsilon = 1 \times 10^{-15} Learning Rates: Point cloud position: Initial 1.6 \times 10^{-4}, exponentially decaying to 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. Point feature: 2.5 \times 10^{-3}. Opacity: 5 \times 10^{-2}. Scaling: 5 \times 10^{-3}. Rotation: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Tone mapper network: Initial 5 \times 10^{-4}, exponentially decaying to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Training Iterations: 3 \times 10^4. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.optim as optim from torch.nn.functional import l1loss def computedssim(img1, img2): # Placeholder for D-SSIM implementation details not provided in source # Assuming a standard D-SSIM function exists pass def minmaxnormalize(img): # norm(·) is min-max normalization minval = img.min() maxval = img.max() return (img - minval) / (maxval - minval + 1e-8) def hdrgsinitializationandoptimization(hdrdataset, sfmalgorithm, mu, gamma, lambdadssim): """ hdrdataset: List of tuples (viewpointid, ldrimagesatexposures, hdrimageifavailable) sfmalgorithm: Function FSfM that takes LDR images and returns intrinsics, extrinsics, points mu: Compression factor for mu-law loss gamma: Weight for mu-law constraint loss (0.6 for synthetic, 0 for real) lambdadssim: Weight for D-SSIM loss """ # Step 1: SfM Initialization # Select LDR images at the same exposure time ts # Note: The source implies selecting views with exposure times t1, t3, t5 for training # and using SfM on LDR images at a single exposure ts. ldrimagesforsfm = [] for view in hdrdataset: # Assuming hdrdataset provides access to LDR images at specific exposures # We select images where exposure == ts if view.exposure == ts: ldrimagesforsfm.append(view.ldrimage) # Apply SfM Mint, Mextlist, Np, mupositions = sfmalgorithm(ldrimagesforsfm) # Step 2: Initialize Gaussian Set G G = GaussianSet() G.positions = mupositions # Shape: (Np, 3) G.features = torch.randn(Np, featuredim) # Random initialization G.opacities = torch.rand(Np) # Random initialization G.scales = torch.rand(Np, 3) # Random initialization G.rotations = torch.rand(Np, 4) # Random initialization # Initialize Tone Mapper Network if used tonemapper = ToneMapperNetwork() # Step 3: Setup Optimizer optimizer = optim.Adam([ {'params': G.positions, 'lr': 1.6e-4}, {'params': G.features, 'lr': 2.5e-3}, {'params': G.opacities, 'lr': 5e-2}, {'params': G.scales, 'lr': 5e-3}, {'params': G.rotations, 'lr': 1e-3}, {'params': tonemapper.parameters(), 'lr': 5e-4} ], betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-15) # Learning rate scheduler for positions and tone mapper # Exponential decay to 1.6e-6 for positions, 5e-5 for tone mapper schedulerpos = optim.lrscheduler.ExponentialLR(optimizer.paramgroups[0], gamma=decayfactor) schedulertm = optim.lrscheduler.ExponentialLR(optimizer.paramgroups[5], gamma=decayfactor) # Step 4: Training Loop numiterations = 30000 batchsize = B for iteration in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Sample batch of viewpoints batchviews = samplebatch(hdrdataset, batchsize) lossp = 0.0 lossc = 0.0 for view in batchviews: # Render LDR and HDR images # Note: Rendering depends on camera pose Mext and intrinsics Mint renderedldr = rendergaussians(G, view.camerapose, view.intrinsics, exposure=view.exposure) renderedhdr = rendergaussianshdr(G, view.camerapose, view.intrinsics) # Get ground truth gtldr = view.ldrimage gthdr = view.hdrimage # May be None for real scenes # Compute Lp l1term = l1loss(renderedldr, gtldr) dssimterm = computedssim(renderedldr, gtldr) lossp += l1term + lambdadssim dssimterm # Compute Lc (only if gthdr is available, i.e., synthetic scenes) if gthdr is not None and gamma > 0: normgthdr = minmaxnormalize(gthdr) normrenderedhdr = minmaxnormalize(renderedhdr) mulawgt = torch.log(1 + mu normgthdr) / torch.log(1 + mu) mulawrendered = torch.log(1 + mu normrenderedhdr) / torch.log(1 + mu) lossc += torch.mean((mulawgt - mulawrendered) 2) # Total Loss totalloss = lossp + gamma lossc # Backpropagate totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # Update learning rates schedulerpos.step() schedulertm.step() return G, tonemapper SfM Input Constraint: Only HDR views under the same exposure time are used as SfM inputs. Using images with different exposure times degrades the accuracy of SfM due to feature detection/matching failures. Real vs. Synthetic Scenes: The µ-law constraint loss Lc is not used for real scenes because ground truth HDR images are not provided. In these cases, \gamma is set to 0. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Training takes 3 \times 10^4 iterations. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Measured Performance: Hardware: Single RTX A5000 GPU. Speed: 126 fps (inference speed on synthetic datasets). PSNR: 41.10 (synthetic), 36.33 (real). SSIM: 0.982 (synthetic), 0.977 (real). LPIPS: 0.011 (synthetic), 0.016 (real). Strengths: Provides a robust initialization for 3DGS in HDR datasets where SfM point clouds are not provided. Achieves high-quality novel view synthesis with fast rendering speeds. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of SfM, which is sensitive to exposure changes. The µ-law constraint loss is only applicable to synthetic scenes with ground truth HDR. HDR-GS was introduced in the paper "HDR-GS: Efficient High Dynamic Range Novel View Synthesis at 1000x Speed via Gaussian Splatting". The method addresses the limitations of voxel-based methods and the original 3DGS, which do not natively support HDR imaging and often lack SfM point clouds for initialization in HDR datasets. It builds on the 3DGS framework [15] and incorporates techniques from HDR-NeRF [14] for handling HDR data. The method was implemented using PyTorch [75] and tested on datasets collected by [14], including real and synthetic scenes from Blender [74].
