name: Fourier Splatting Primitive
head: Fourier encoded primitive, Fourier surfel
body: The Fourier Splatting primitive is a planar surfel for radiance field rendering that replaces the fixed Gaussian or elliptical falloff with a boundary defined by a Fourier series, allowing the representation of arbitrary closed shapes. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) or 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), which are limited to fixed elliptical or disc shapes, this primitive enables higher fidelity representation of complex geometry and fine-grained details. Its key differentiator is inherent scalability: the level of detail (LoD) is controlled by truncating Fourier coefficients at runtime, allowing a single trained model to be rendered at varying complexities without retraining or post-hoc compression. Inputs and Outputs Input: Camera parameters (view/projection matrices), a set of primitives \{si\}, and a target resolution. Output: A rendered image with color and opacity per pixel. Data Structures Each primitive si is parameterized by the following fields: 1. Center: pi \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Rotation: qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) defining the local tangent frame (tu, tv, tw). 3. Opacity: oi \in (0, 1). 4. Appearance: ci \in \mathbb{R}^{48} (Spherical Harmonics coefficients, degree 3). 5. Circumradius: Ri \in \mathbb{R}{>0}, bounding the primitive extent. 6. Fourier Amplitudes: \{r{i,k}\}{k=0}^{K-1} \in \mathbb{R}^K. 7. Fourier Phases: \{\phi{i,k}\}{k=0}^{K-1} \in \mathbb{R}. 8. Sharpness: \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}{>0}. Parameters K: Number of Fourier frequencies. Typical value: 6. K{\text{active}}: Number of active frequency components at the start of optimization. Typical value: 1. Formulas The boundary of the primitive in its local tangent plane is a closed curve ri(\theta). To ensure the boundary does not exceed the circumradius Ri, the raw amplitudes r{i,k} are normalized using squared-\ell1 normalization: \bar{r}{i,k} = \frac{r{i,k}^2}{\sum{k'=0}^{K-1} r{i,k'}^2} \quad \text{such that} \quad \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \bar{r}{i,k} = 1 This guarantees ri(\theta) \le Ri for all \theta. The boundary radius ri(\theta) is computed efficiently using Horner’s method to avoid transcendental calls for e^{ik\theta}. Let w = e^{i\theta} = (\cos \theta, \sin \theta). The complex coefficients c{i,k} are derived from the normalized amplitudes and phases as c{i,k} = \bar{r}{i,k} e^{i \phi{i,k}}. The recurrence is computed from k = K-1 down to 0: z{K-1} = c{i,K-1} z{k} = z{k+1} \cdot w + c{i,k} \quad \text{for } k = K-2, \dots, 0 The final radius is: ri(\theta) = Ri |z0| This requires K-1 complex multiply-adds. Numbered Steps 1. Ray-Plane Intersection: For each pixel, compute the intersection with the primitive's plane defined by pi and normal tw. Transform the intersection point into the local tangent frame (tu, tv) to obtain coordinates (uj, vj). 2. Polar Conversion: Compute the polar coordinates (\rhoj, \thetaj) in the tangent plane. \rhoj = \sqrt{uj^2 + vj^2} \cos \thetaj = uj / \rhoj \sin \thetaj = vj / \rhoj Handle \rhoj \approx 0 by setting \thetaj = 0 to avoid division by zero. 3. Boundary Evaluation: Compute ri(\thetaj) using the Horner’s method recurrence defined above. 4. Signed Distance: Compute the signed distance \varphij from the pixel to the boundary: \varphij = \rhoj - ri(\thetaj) 5. Alpha Compositing: Use a power window function (adapted from Triangle Splatting) based on \varphij and the sharpness parameter \sigmai to determine the alpha value for the primitive at this pixel. 6. Color Evaluation: Evaluate the spherical harmonics using the view direction to get the color contribution. 7. Rendering: Composite the primitives tile-by-tile using standard alpha blending. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Converts a unit quaternion (x, y, z, w) to a 3x3 rotation matrix.""" x, y, z, w = q return [ [1 - 2yy - 2zz, 2xy - 2zw, 2xz + 2yw], [2xy + 2zw, 1 - 2xx - 2zz, 2yz - 2xw], [2xz - 2yw, 2yz + 2xw, 1 - 2xx - 2yy] ] def evaluatesh(csh, viewdir): """Evaluates degree-3 Spherical Harmonics (48 coefficients) for a view direction.""" x, y, z = viewdir xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, yz, xz = xy, yz, xz x2 = xx - yy y2 = yy - zz z2 = 3zz - 1 r = 0.2820948csh[0] + 0.4886025(csh[1]y + csh[2]z + csh[3]x) + \ 1.0925484(csh[4]yz + csh[5]xz + csh[6]x2 + csh[7]xy + csh[8]0.5z2) g = 0.2820948csh[9] + 0.4886025(csh[10]y + csh[11]z + csh[12]x) + \ 1.0925484(csh[13]yz + csh[14]xz + csh[15]x2 + csh[16]xy + csh[17]0.5z2) b = 0.2820948csh[18] + 0.4886025(csh[19]y + csh[20]z + csh[21]x) + \ 1.0925484(csh[22]yz + csh[23]xz + csh[24]x2 + csh[25]xy + csh[26]0.5z2) return (r, g, b) def computeprimitivealphaandcolor(pi, qi, oi, csh, Ri, rraw, phiraw, sigmai, K, rayorigin, raydir, imgwidth, imgheight): """ Evaluates a single Fourier Splatting primitive over a pixel grid. Returns alpha and color contribution arrays. """ # Extract local frame Rmat = quaterniontorotationmatrix(qi) tu = Rmat[0] tv = Rmat[1] tw = Rmat[2] alphagrid = [0.0] (imgheight imgwidth) colorgrid = [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] (imgheight imgwidth) # Precompute normalization sumsq = sum(r2 for r in rraw) if sumsq == 0: return alphagrid, colorgrid rnorm = [r2 / sumsq for r in rraw] # Precompute complex coefficients c{i,k} = rnorm[k] exp(i phiraw[k]) creal = [rnorm[k] math.cos(phiraw[k]) for k in range(K)] cimag = [rnorm[k] math.sin(phiraw[k]) for k in range(K)] for y in range(imgheight): for x in range(imgwidth): # 1. Ray-Plane Intersection denom = tw[0]raydir[0] + tw[1]raydir[1] + tw[2]raydir[2] if abs(denom) < 1e-6: continue t = ((pi[0] - rayorigin[0])tw[0] + (pi[1] - rayorigin[1])tw[1] + (pi[2] - rayorigin[2])tw[2]) / denom if t < 0: continue ix = rayorigin[0] + t raydir[0] iy = rayorigin[1] + t raydir[1] iz = rayorigin[2] + t raydir[2] # 2. Local Tangent Coordinates vecx = ix - pi[0] vecy = iy - pi[1] vecz = iz - pi[2] uj = vecxtu[0] + vecytu[1] + vecztu[2] vj = vecxtv[0] + vecytv[1] + vecztv[2] # 3. Polar Conversion rhoj = math.sqrt(ujuj + vjvj) if rhoj < 1e-6: thetaj = 0.0 costheta = 1.0 sintheta = 0.0 else: thetaj = math.atan2(vj, uj) costheta = uj / rhoj sintheta = vj / rhoj # 4. Horner's Method for Boundary zreal = creal[K-1] zimag = cimag[K-1] for k in range(K-2, -1, -1): newreal = zreal costheta - zimag sintheta newimag = zreal sintheta + zimag costheta zreal = newreal + creal[k] zimag = newimag + cimag[k] rboundary = Ri math.sqrt(zrealzreal + zimagzimag) # 5. Signed Distance signeddist = rhoj - rboundary # 6. Alpha Calculation (Power Window) if signeddist > 0: alpha = 0.0 else: alpha = max(0.0, 1.0 - (signeddist / sigmai)2)2 if alpha < 1e-4: continue # 7. Color Evaluation viewdirlocal = ( tu[0]raydir[0] + tu[1]raydir[1] + tu[2]raydir[2], tv[0]raydir[0] + tv[1]raydir[1] + tv[2]raydir[2], tw[0]raydir[0] + tw[1]raydir[1] + tw[2]raydir[2]) color = evaluatesh(csh, viewdirlocal) idx = y imgwidth + x alphagrid[idx] += alpha oi colorgrid[idx] = ( colorgrid[idx][0] + color[0] alpha oi, colorgrid[idx][1] + color[1] alpha oi, colorgrid[idx][2] + color[2] alpha oi) return alphagrid, colorgrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls Ray-Plane Intersection: For each pixel, compute the intersection with the primitive's plane defined by pi and normal tw. Division by Zero: When computing \thetaj, if \rhoj \approx 0, \cos \thetaj and \sin \thetaj are undefined. Overshooting: Without squared-\ell1 normalization, amplitudes can sum to exceed Ri, causing the boundary to overshoot the circumscribed circle. Optimization Stability: The optimization process begins with K{\text{active}} = 1 to establish a stable global structure. Time Complexity: The boundary evaluation uses Horner’s method, requiring K-1 complex multiply-adds, which is O(K) per pixel per primitive. With K=6, this is constant and fast. Memory Complexity: Each primitive stores K amplitudes and K phases. With K=6 and degree 3 SH (48 coeffs), plus center, quaternion, opacity, and radius, the parameter count is 70 per primitive. Scalability: The method is inherently scalable. Rendering at lower LoD is achieved by truncating Fourier coefficients at runtime (e.g., using only k < K{\text{active}}) without retraining. Strengths: Arbitrary shape representation allows higher fidelity for complex geometry compared to 2D/3D Gaussians. Continuous LoD control. Limitations: Requires careful initialization (K{\text{active}}=1) to avoid optimization instability. The Fourier Splatting primitive was introduced in "Fourier Splatting: Generalized Fourier encoded primitives for scalable radiance fields". It addresses the limitation of existing methods where visual fidelity is tied strictly to the number of primitives, requiring pruning for quality downscaling. It builds on the concept of planar surfels (like 2DGS) but enhances expressiveness with Fourier-encoded boundaries. Fourier Splatting: Generalized Fourier encoded primitives for scalable radiance fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.19834, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Conditional Slicing Mechanism
body: The Conditional Slicing Mechanism conditions a 7-dimensional Gaussian on observed time t and view direction d to yield a conditional 3D Gaussian governing the spatial component. This operation "slices" the full 7D distribution to integrate temporal dynamics and view-dependent effects into the traditional 3D rendering pipeline without introducing additional temporal dependencies in the spherical harmonics. It sets itself apart from static Gaussian Splatting variants by explicitly modeling the joint distribution of space, time, and view, allowing the spatial mean and covariance to shift based on the current rendering context. Inputs: Base Gaussian parameters: spatial mean \mup, temporal mean \mut, directional mean \mud, base opacity \alpha, scaling factors \lambdat, \lambdad. Covariance structure: Lower-triangular matrix L such that \Sigma = LL^\top, or the partitioned blocks \Sigma{(t,d)}, \Sigma{p,(t,d)}, \Sigmap. Context variables: Observed time t, view direction d. Optional refinement features: Feature vector f (if adaptive refinement is applied). Outputs: Conditional spatial mean \mu{cond}. Conditional spatial covariance \Sigma{cond}. Conditional opacity \alpha{cond}. Optional: Scale S and Rotation R extracted from \Sigma{cond} for densification. Data Structures: The 7D Gaussian is represented by a mean vector \mu = [\mup, \mut, \mud] and a 7 \times 7 covariance matrix \Sigma. The matrix is partitioned into blocks corresponding to spatial (p), temporal (t), and directional (d) dimensions: \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \Sigmap & \Sigma{p,(t,d)}^\top \\ \Sigma{p,(t,d)} & \Sigma{(t,d)} \end{bmatrix} where \Sigma{(t,d)} is the 4 \times 4 block for time and direction: \Sigma{(t,d)} = \begin{bmatrix} \Sigmat & \Sigma{td} \\ \Sigma{td}^\top & \Sigmad \end{bmatrix} and \Sigma{p,(t,d)} = [\Sigma{pt} \quad \Sigma{pd}] links spatial dimensions with the combined temporal-directional space. Steps: 1. Adaptive Gaussian Refinement (Optional but standard in implementation): Compute a feature vector f by concatenating the means and a temporal encoding \gamma(t): f = \text{concat}(\mup, \mut, \mud, \gamma(t)) Apply refinement functions \phip, \phit, \phid, \phil to update the parameters: \hat{\mu}p = \mup + \phip(f), \quad \hat{\mu}t = \mut + \phit(f) \hat{\mu}d = \mud + \phid(f), \quad \hat{l} = l + \phil(f) Reconstruct the refined covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma} = \hat{L}\hat{L}^\top. Note: If refinement is skipped, replace \hat{\mu} and \hat{\Sigma} with \mu and \Sigma. 2. Partition the Covariance: Partition \hat{\Sigma} into blocks \hat{\Sigma}p, \hat{\Sigma}{(t,d)}, and \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)} as defined above. 3. Compute Conditional Mean: Calculate the conditional spatial mean \mu{cond} using the standard multivariate Gaussian conditioning formula: \mu{cond} = \hat{\mu}p + \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)} \hat{\Sigma}{(t,d)}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} t - \hat{\mu}t \\ d - \hat{\mu}d \end{bmatrix} The term \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)} \hat{\Sigma}{(t,d)}^{-1} acts as a correction that shifts the spatial mean according to deviations in time and view direction from their expected values. 4. Compute Conditional Covariance: Calculate the conditional spatial covariance \Sigma{cond}: \Sigma{cond} = \hat{\Sigma}p - \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)} \hat{\Sigma}{(t,d)}^{-1} \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)}^\top This adjusts the spatial uncertainty by removing the variance explained by the temporal and directional components. 5. Compute Modulation Factors: Compute the temporal modulation factor f{temp}: f{temp} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \lambdat (t - \hat{\mu}t)^2 \hat{\Sigma}t^{-1}\right) Compute the directional modulation factor f{dir}: f{dir} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \lambdad (d - \hat{\mu}d)^\top \hat{\Sigma}d^{-1} (d - \hat{\mu}d)\right) Here, \lambdat and \lambdad are positive scalar parameters controlling sensitivity. 6. Compute Conditional Opacity: Combine the base opacity \alpha with the modulation factors: \alpha{cond} = \alpha \cdot f{temp} \cdot f{dir} This ensures Gaussians contribute less when the current time or view direction is far from their expected values. 7. Extract Scale and Rotation (Optional): For densification steps, perform SVD on \Sigma{cond} = U D U^\top. Extract scale S = \text{diag}(D) and rotation R = U. Adjust R to ensure \det(R) > 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gamma(t): # Standard positional encoding for time return np.array([np.sin(t), np.cos(t)]) def phip(f): return np.zeroslike(mup) # MLP from parent model def phit(f): return np.zeroslike(mut) # MLP from parent model def phid(f): return np.zeroslike(mud) # MLP from parent model def phil(f): return np.zeroslike(L) # MLP from parent model def conditionalslicing(mup, mut, mud, alpha, L, lambdat, lambdad, t, d, applyrefinement=True): """ Conditions a 7D Gaussian on time t and view direction d. Args: mup: Spatial mean (3,) mut: Temporal mean (scalar) mud: Directional mean (3,) alpha: Base opacity (scalar) L: Lower triangular matrix (7,7) such that Sigma = L @ L.T lambdat: Temporal sensitivity scalar lambdad: Directional sensitivity scalar t: Observed time (scalar) d: View direction (3,) applyrefinement: Boolean flag for adaptive refinement Returns: mucond: Conditional spatial mean (3,) Sigmacond: Conditional spatial covariance (3,3) alphacond: Conditional opacity (scalar) S: Scale (3,) - optional, for densification R: Rotation (3,3) - optional, for densification """ # Step 1: Adaptive Refinement (if enabled) if applyrefinement: # Compute feature vector f f = np.concatenate([mup, [mut], mud, gamma(t)]) # Apply refinement functions phi deltamup = phip(f) deltamut = phit(f) deltamud = phid(f) deltal = phil(f) mup = mup + deltamup mut = mut + deltamut mud = mud + deltamud L = L + deltal # Reconstruct Sigma from L Sigma = L @ L.T # Step 2: Partition Sigma # Dimensions: p=3, t=1, d=3. Total 7. Sigmap = Sigma[:3,:3] Sigmapt = Sigma[:3, 3:4] Sigmapd = Sigma[:3, 4:7] Sigmat = Sigma[3:4, 3:4] Sigmatd = Sigma[4:7, 3:4] Sigmad = Sigma[4:7, 4:7] # Construct blocks Sigmaptd = np.hstack([Sigmapt, Sigmapd]) # (3, 4) Sigmatdt = Sigmat # (1, 1) Sigmatdd = Sigmatd # (3, 1) Sigmadd = Sigmad # (3, 3) # Sigma(t,d) is (4,4) Sigmatdblock = np.block([ [Sigmatdt, Sigmatdd.T], [Sigmatdd, Sigmadd] ]) # Step 3: Compute Conditional Mean diff = np.array([t - mut, (d - mud)]) # (4,) x = np.linalg.solve(Sigmatdblock, diff.reshape(-1, 1)) correction = Sigmaptd @ x # (3, 1) mucond = mup + correction.flatten() # Step 4: Compute Conditional Covariance invSigmatd = np.linalg.inv(Sigmatdblock) Sigmacond = Sigmap - (Sigmaptd @ invSigmatd @ Sigmaptd.T) # Step 5: Compute Modulation Factors difft = t - mut ftemp = np.exp(-0.5 lambdat (difft2) (1.0 / Sigmat[0,0])) diffd = d - mud invSigmad = np.linalg.inv(Sigmad) quadraticform = diffd @ invSigmad @ diffd fdir = np.exp(-0.5 lambdad quadraticform) # Step 6: Conditional Opacity alphacond = alpha ftemp fdir # Step 7: Extract S and R (Optional) U, D, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Sigmacond) S = D R = U if np.linalg.det(R) < 0: R[:, 0] = -1 return mucond, Sigmacond, alphacond, S, R Parameters: \lambdat: Positive scalar controlling temporal modulation sensitivity. \lambdad: Positive scalar controlling directional modulation sensitivity. \phip, \phit, \phid, \phil: Refinement functions (typically small MLPs) mapping feature f to parameter deltas. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: \Sigma{(t,d)} or \Sigmad may be singular if correlations are perfect or data is insufficient. Use pseudo-inverse or add small jitter to diagonal if inversion fails. Degenerate Input: If t or d are NaN, the exponential terms become NaN. Guard against invalid inputs. Precision: The exponential decay can underflow to zero for large deviations, effectively culling the Gaussian. This is intended behavior but may cause artifacts if \lambda is too high. This is the core algorithmic procedure described in the main method. It refers to the specific implementation of partitioning the 7D covariance and computing the conditional 3D Gaussian statistics. It is chosen when one needs to render a specific frame at time t from direction d using the 7DGS representation. It is distinct from static slicing because it includes the adaptive refinement step before conditioning. Time Complexity: Dominated by matrix inversion of 4 \times 4 (\Sigma{(t,d)}) and 3 \times 3 (\Sigmad) matrices, which is O(1) constant time per Gaussian. The refinement step involves MLP evaluation, also O(1). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full 7D parameters (\mup, \mut, \mud, \Sigma) plus refinement network weights. Strengths: Efficiently integrates temporal and view-dependent effects into standard 3D rendering pipelines without modifying the core rasterizer. Limitations: The intrinsic shape of the Gaussian (covariance) remains static over time if refinement is not used, which may hinder representing complex non-rigid deformations. When to use: When rendering dynamic scenes with view-dependent appearance using Gaussian Splatting. The Conditional Slicing Mechanism was introduced in "7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting". It conditions a 7-dimensional Gaussian on observed time and view direction to yield a conditional 3D Gaussian governing the spatial component. The method leverages standard properties of multivariate Gaussian distributions to condition the spatial component on observed time and view direction. It builds on the Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction method [8442-gaussian-geometry-parameters-prediction.md] by providing a mechanism to interpret the 7D parameters during rendering. 7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07946v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (SAGS)
head: SAGS (Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting)
body: Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (SAGS) is a novel-view synthesis method that implicitly encodes scene geometry using a local-global graph representation to facilitate learning complex scenes and enforce meaningful point displacements that preserve structure, thereby reducing floating-point artifacts and storage requirements. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which optimizes each Gaussian independently, SAGS leverages inter- and intra-connectivity between 3D point positions via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to predict Gaussian attributes, outperforming 3D-GS and Scaffold-GS in capturing high-frequency details while significantly reducing memory footprint. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse point cloud P \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3} derived from COLMAP, a set of sparse input views with known camera parameters, and a global scene feature g. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean position \mu, color c, opacity \alpha, and covariance \Sigma, rendered into 2D images. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud Graph: A k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) graph where nodes are points pi \in P and edges connect points within a local region. 2. Feature Encoding: Each point pi has a feature vector fi. Positions are encoded using multi-resolution hash encoding [23] into a higher-dimensional space D via \gamma(\cdot). 3. Global Feature: A single vector g representing the global scene feature, calculated as the maximum of all point feature encodings: g = \maxi(fi). 4. Gaussian Attributes: Position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, Color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}^1, Covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} decomposed into scale S \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation R (quaternion). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using the sparse point cloud P from COLMAP. 2. Curvature Estimation: Estimate the Gaussian mean curvature of point cloud P using the local-PCA approach [25]. Identify a set of low-curvature points PL \subset P where curvature is below a threshold. 3. Curvature-Aware Densification: For under-represented areas, create a k-NN graph for points p \in PL. Generate midpoints pm for each p and its neighbor pj \in k\text{-NN}(p): pm = \frac{1}{2} (p + pj) 4. Graph Construction: Apply k-NN search to link points p within local regions to create a point set graph enabling point interaction. 5. Structure-Aware Encoding: For each point pi, compute the structural feature \Phi(pi, fi) using the aggregation function: \Phi(pi, fi) = \phi \left( \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} w{ij} h{\Theta} (\gamma(pj), fj - fi, g) \right) where: \mathcal{N}(i) are the neighbors of pi. w{ij} is the inverse-distance weight: w{ij} = \frac{\text{dist}^{-1}(pi, pj)}{\sum{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \text{dist}^{-1}(pi, pj)} \gamma(\cdot) is the positional encoding mapping p to space D. g is the global scene feature. h{\Theta} is a learnable MLP. \phi is a non-linear activation function. Relative features fj - fi are used instead of raw features for efficiency and expressivity. 6. Attribute Decoding: Decode \Phi(pi, fi) to Gaussian attributes using four distinct small MLPs (hidden size 32): Position: Learn \mu in a camera-agnostic manner as a displacement from the initial point pi: \mui = pi + \Delta pi, \quad \Delta pi = \text{MLP}{\mu}(\Phi(pi, fi)) Color, Opacity, Covariance: Predict these attributes using view-dependent point positions. Calculate normalized view-dependent position p^ci: p^ci = \frac{pi - xc}{\|pi - xc\|2} where xc is the camera coordinate. Color: ci = \text{MLP}c(\Phi(pi, fi), p^ci) Opacity \alphai, Scale Si, Rotation Ri are predicted similarly using view-dependent positions. Covariance Decomposition: To ensure positive semi-definiteness, decompose \Sigma as: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T where R is represented by quaternions. 7. SAGS-Lite Midpoint Generation: For the lightweight variant, generate midpoints on-the-fly from initial key points. Interpolate features for midpoint m between keypoints i, j \in P: f'm = \frac{1}{2} (f'i + f'j) Feed interpolated features f'm and corresponding view-dependent interpolated positions to refinement networks to predict attributes. 8. Rendering: Render the 3D Gaussians using the 3D-GS Gaussian rasterizer [15]. The 2D pixel color C is calculated by blending N ordered Gaussians: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) ci 9. Optimization: Train the model for 30,000 iterations. Apply growing and pruning steps every 100 iterations, starting from iteration 1500 until iteration 15,000. The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = (1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda\mathcal{L}{SSIM} where \lambda = 0.2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def positionalencoding(points, D): # Standard positional encoding freqbands = torch.linspace(1, D // 2, steps=D // 2, device=points.device) scaledpoints = points.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands.unsqueeze(0) return torch.cat([torch.sin(scaledpoints), torch.cos(scaledpoints)], dim=-1) def ssimlossfunction(pred, gt): # Standard SSIM approximation return torch.mean((pred - gt) 2) class SAGS: def init(self, pointcloudP, kneighbors=16, hiddensize=32): self.P = pointcloudP.clone().detach() self.M = self.P.shape[0] self.k = kneighbors self.hiddensize = hiddensize # 1. Build k-NN Graph dists = torch.cdist(self.P, self.P, p=2), self.neighbors = torch.topk(dists, self.k + 1, largest=False) self.neighbors = self.neighbors[:, 1:] # Exclude self # 2. Initialize Features self.features = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(self.M, hiddensize)) # 3. Define MLPs self.hTheta = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddensize 3, hiddensize), # posenc + relfeat + globalg nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize)) self.phi = nn.Tanh() self.mlpcolor = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hiddensize + 3, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, 3)) self.mlpopacity = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hiddensize + 3, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, 1)) self.mlpscale = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hiddensize + 3, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, 3)) self.mlprot = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hiddensize + 3, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, 4)) self.mlpdisp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, 3)) def computestructuralfeatures(self, features, globalg): neighborpoints = self.P[self.neighbors] neighborfeatures = features[self.neighbors] relfeatures = neighborfeatures - features.unsqueeze(1) posencs = positionalencoding(neighborpoints, self.hiddensize) grepeated = globalg.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).repeat(1, self.k, 1) hinput = torch.cat([posencs, relfeatures, grepeated], dim=-1) houtput = self.hTheta(hinput) dists = torch.norm(neighborpoints - self.P.unsqueeze(1), dim=-1) invdists = 1.0 / (dists + 1e-6) weights = invdists / invdists.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) weightedsum = (weights.unsqueeze(-1) houtput).sum(dim=1) return self.phi(weightedsum) def forward(self, cameraextrinsics): globalg = self.features.max(dim=0)[0] structuralfeatures = self.computestructuralfeatures(self.features, globalg) # Camera coordinate extraction and view-dependent position calculation camerapos = cameraextrinsics[:3, 3] pc = (self.P - camerapos) / (torch.norm(self.P - camerapos, dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6) inputdec = torch.cat([structuralfeatures, pc], dim=-1) c = self.mlpcolor(inputdec) alpha = torch.sigmoid(self.mlpopacity(inputdec)) scale = torch.exp(self.mlpscale(inputdec)) rot = torch.nn.functional.normalize(self.mlprot(inputdec), dim=-1) deltap = self.mlpdisp(structuralfeatures) mu = self.P + deltap gaussians = {'mu': mu, 'c': c, 'alpha': alpha, 'scale': scale, 'rot': rot} # Standard 3D-GS Gaussian rasterizer [15] is used for projection, sorting, and alpha blending. image = torch.zeros(1, 3, 512, 512) return image, gaussians def trainstep(self, imagegt, cameraextrinsics, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() imagepred, = self.forward(cameraextrinsics) l1loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(imagepred - imagegt)) ssimloss = ssimlossfunction(imagepred, imagegt) loss = 0.8 l1loss + 0.2 ssimloss loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() def densifyandprune(self, iteration): # Standard 3D-GS growing and pruning logic applied to predicted Gaussians pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Covariance Definiteness: The decomposition \Sigma = R S S^T R^T is critical to prevent non-positive semi-definite matrices during optimization. Relative Features: Using relative features fj - fi is essential for efficiency and expressivity. Curvature Threshold: The choice of threshold for low-curvature points PL determines which points undergo densification. Global Feature: The global feature g is shared across all points and computed as the maximum of point features. Time Complexity: Training runs for 30,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: SAGS achieves significant memory reduction. On benchmark datasets, SAGS uses 99 MB compared to 3D-GS's 414 MB. The lightweight SAGS-Lite version achieves up to 24× size reduction without compression, using only 43 MB. Performance: SAGS outperforms 3D-GS and Scaffold-GS in PSNR and LPIPS on Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending datasets. It better captures high-frequency details and reduces floating artifacts. Strengths: Reduced storage, fewer artifacts, better structure preservation, high rendering quality. Limitations: Requires initial sparse point cloud from COLMAP. Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (SAGS) was proposed by E. Ververas et al. to address the limitations of structure-agnostic optimization schemes in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which often result in floating points and artifacts due to independent Gaussian optimization. The method builds on the 3D-GS framework [15] and incorporates ideas from graph neural networks and curvature-aware densification. It was published in 2024. SAGS: Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72655-213, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Mesh-embedded representation
head: Mesh-embedded Gaussian Splatting, Gaussian Mesh Splatting, SuGaR, Gaussian Frosting, Mesh to DRK Conversion, Gaussian Extraction Algorithm, GauS
body: Mesh-embedded representations integrate explicit triangle mesh topology with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to enable coherent deformation, editing, and surface-aligned rendering. Unlike standard 3DGS, which treats Gaussians as independent entities in free space, this family binds Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale) to mesh geometry via barycentric coordinates or vertex parameterization, ensuring that mesh edits or animations propagate deterministically to the radiance field. This approach solves the problem of Gaussian drift and incoherent motion transfer during animation, while providing a bridge between implicit neural/radiance representations and explicit editable mesh assets. The core mechanism relies on parameterizing Gaussian attributes relative to a canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices V, normals n, and faces F. Embedding Definition: Each Gaussian i is defined by an embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\}: k: The index of the triangle k \in F in the canonical mesh. (u, v): Barycentric coordinates within triangle k, such that u \ge 0, v \ge 0, u+v \le 1. d: Normal displacement along the interpolated surface normal. Canonical Position and Normal: The canonical mean \mu{cano} and normal n{cano} are computed via Phong interpolation on the canonical mesh [Parent, S2, unofficial]: \mu{cano} = \mathcal{V}(k, u, v) = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 n{cano} = \mathcal{N}(k, u, v) = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 where Vj and nj are the vertices and per-vertex normals of triangle k [Parent]. Posed State Computation: When the mesh is deformed (e.g., via skeletal animation or blend shapes), the posed position \mu{pose} is derived by applying the mesh deformation function \text{Deform}(\cdot) to the displaced canonical position [Parent]: \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano}) The posed rotation q{pose} and scale s{pose} are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence [Parent]: Rotation: Interpolate per-vertex quaternions q1, q2, q3 using barycentric weights to get \delta q, then combine with canonical rotation \bar{q}: q{pose} = \delta q \bar{q}, \quad \delta q = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 Scale: Scale is proportional to the area change of the embedded triangle relative to the canonical state: s{pose} = \left( \frac{A{pose}}{A{cano}} \right) \bar{s} where A{pose} and A{cano} are the areas of the triangle in the posed and canonical states, respectively [Parent]. Cross-Triangle Handling: Barycentric coordinates are only differentiable within a single triangle. If optimization moves an embedding point across a boundary (u < 0, v < 0, or u+v > 1), the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability [Parent, S2, unofficial]. Failure to handle this causes Gaussians to stick to boundaries and pile up [Parent]. A hybrid representation that defines 3D Gaussians over an explicit triangle mesh (e.g., SMPL-X, FLAME) to enable large-scale, interactive deformations. It solves the problem of coherent motion transfer by tying Gaussian parameters to mesh geometry via joint refinement, where GS rendering guides adaptive splitting and mesh constraints regularize Gaussian shapes. It sets itself apart from siblings by utilizing a reconstructed explicit mesh for initialization and employing specific face-split and normal-guidance strategies to handle large deformations without relying on implicit MLP-based skinning fields. Unlike methods using MLP-based linear blend skinning (LBS), it controls Gaussian rotation and translation directly by the mesh, enabling compatibility with skeletal animation and mesh editing. This method anchors 3D Gaussians to a triangle mesh using barycentric coordinates and normal displacement, enabling deformation tracking through mesh topology rather than direct vertex positions. It solves the problem of Gaussians drifting off-mesh or piling up at triangle edges during optimization and animation by defining a local triangle space. Unlike methods relying on precise mesh accuracy, it ensures robust results even with inaccurate meshes by binding Gaussians to the surface. GaMeS is a hybrid representation that integrates 3DGS with mesh topology by parameterizing each Gaussian component using the vertices of a mesh face. It solves the problem of conditioning and editing Gaussian splats by ensuring that means, rotations, and scales automatically adapt when the underlying mesh geometry is modified. Unlike siblings such as SuGaR, GaMeS avoids expensive pre-processing stages or SDF-based regularization, directly embedding Gaussians onto the mesh surface or a "Triangle Soup" structure. SuGaR (Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting) and Gaussian Frosting bridge the gap between implicit Gaussian representations and explicit mesh geometry. SuGaR aligns optimized 3D Gaussians to a surface and extracts a base mesh via Poisson reconstruction. Gaussian Frosting builds on this by binding Gaussians to the extracted mesh surface to enable hybrid rendering, combining the editing capabilities of meshes with the high-fidelity rendering quality of 3DGS. It introduces an adaptive Gaussian layer with variable thickness to enhance detail and volumetric effects. Mesh to DRK Conversion is a training-free procedure that converts traditional triangle and polygon mesh faces into Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) primitives for seamless integration into radiance field scenes. It differs from siblings like Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Splatting and SuGaR / Gaussian Frosting, which typically require optimization or learning-based initialization, by providing a direct, deterministic mapping that eliminates the need for training data rendering or model optimization. The Gaussian Extraction Algorithm extracts discrete 3D Gaussian primitives from continuous Gaussian Splatting Functions (GauPF) at arbitrary densities. It solves the problem of converting a continuous, neural-network-parameterized probability field into a finite set of splattable Gaussians, analogous to how Marching Cubes extracts meshes from Signed Distance Functions. It is distinguished from siblings by its use of an octree-guided progressive sampling strategy to locate high-probability regions, followed by gradient-based optimization of proxy points, rather than fixed-grid voxelization or direct mesh embedding. Definition: GauS is a render-then-fuse approach for high-fidelity mesh reconstruction from 3DGS inputs without fine-tuning. It uses volumetric fusion to convert 3D Gaussians into textured triangle meshes. It is a plug-and-play module compatible with various GS-based methods. Comparison: Unlike NeRF-based re-training or further fine-tuning required for explicit surface modeling in other methods, GauS converts optimized Gaussians directly into textured meshes serving as a versatile plug-and-play solution. The concept of embedding Gaussian primitives onto explicit geometry emerged to address the limitations of free-space 3DGS in handling dynamic scenes and editable assets. Early works like Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Splatting and Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Initialization and Deformation introduced barycentric parameterization to tie Gaussians to canonical meshes (e.g., SMPL-X) for animation. Subsequent developments like GaMeS and SuGaR / Gaussian Frosting refined this by aligning Gaussians to reconstructed surfaces or extracting meshes from optimized Gaussians, enabling hybrid rendering and editing. The family also includes training-free conversions like Mesh to DRK Conversion and neural-to-discrete extraction methods like the Gaussian Extraction Algorithm, expanding the applicability of mesh-embedded concepts to broader radiance field representations. name: Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Splatting
head: Gaussian Mesh Splatting, Gaussian-Mesh association
body: Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Splatting is a hybrid 3D representation that parameterizes 3D Gaussians relative to an explicit canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} to disentangle motion from appearance. It solves the problem of coherent, large-scale deformation in Gaussian Splatting by tying Gaussian position, rotation, and scale to mesh geometry via barycentric embeddings, avoiding the artifacts and rigidity of implicit MLP-based skinning fields. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on implicit deformation fields or separate optimization pipelines, this method explicitly controls Gaussian pose through mesh warping, enabling compatibility with skeletal animation, blend shapes, and direct mesh editing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices V, per-vertex normals n, and faces F; monocular video frames of the subject in various poses; initial Gaussian parameters. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by embedding tuples Ei, optimized Gaussian attributes (opacity, color, canonical rotation/scale), and a renderer capable of real-time synthesis. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is defined by an embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\}: k: Integer index of the triangle k \in F in the canonical mesh. (u, v): Barycentric coordinates within triangle k, constrained such that u \ge 0, v \ge 0, u+v \le 1. d: Scalar normal displacement along the interpolated surface normal. Additionally, each Gaussian stores pose-invariant attributes: canonical rotation \bar{q}, canonical scale \bar{s}, opacity o, and color c. Canonical Position and Normal: The canonical mean \mu{cano} and normal n{cano} are computed via Phong interpolation on the canonical mesh: \mu{cano} = \mathcal{V}(k, u, v) = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 n{cano} = \mathcal{N}(k, u, v) = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 where Vj and nj are the vertices and per-vertex normals of triangle k. Posed State Computation: When the mesh is deformed by an animation function \text{Deform}(\cdot) (e.g., skeletal animation), the posed position \mu{pose} is derived by applying the deformation to the displaced canonical position: \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano}) The posed rotation q{pose} and scale s{pose} are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence: Rotation: Per-vertex quaternions q1, q2, q3 are interpolated using barycentric weights to get \delta q, which is then combined with the canonical rotation \bar{q}: q{pose} = \delta q \bar{q}, \quad \delta q = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 Scale: Scale is proportional to the area change of the embedded triangle relative to the canonical state: s{pose} = \left( \frac{A{pose}}{A{cano}} \right) \bar{s} where A{pose} and A{cano} are the areas of the triangle in the posed and canonical states, respectively. Optimization and Adaptation: During training, Gaussian parameters and embedding parameters are updated simultaneously. The method adapts the clone and split scheme of 3D Gaussians to suit the mesh-embedded representation. Cross-Triangle Handling: Barycentric coordinates are differentiable only within a single triangle. If optimization moves an embedding point across a boundary (u < 0, v < 0, or u+v > 1), the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability. This is achieved via "lifted optimization," where embedding points "walk" on the triangle mesh. Failure to handle this causes Gaussians to stick to boundaries and pile up. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeposedgaussian(gaussian, mesh, posetransform): """ Computes the posed position, rotation, and scale for a single Gaussian. Args: gaussian: Object containing embedding E={k, u, v, d} and invariant attributes {qbar, sbar}. mesh: Object containing vertices V, normals n, faces F, and vertex quaternions qverts. posetransform: Function that applies skeletal/blend shape deformation to mesh vertices. Returns: mupose: Posed mean position. qpose: Posed rotation quaternion. spose: Posed scale vector. """ # 1. Retrieve canonical triangle data k = gaussian.embedding.k u = gaussian.embedding.u v = gaussian.embedding.v d = gaussian.embedding.d # Get triangle vertices and normals V1, V2, V3 = mesh.faces[k].vertices n1, n2, n3 = mesh.faces[k].vertexnormals # 2. Compute canonical position and normal (Phong interpolation) mucano = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 ncano = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 # 3. Compute posed position # Apply deformation to the displaced canonical position displacedpos = mucano + d ncano mupose = posetransform(displacedpos) # 4. Compute posed rotation # Interpolate per-vertex quaternions q1, q2, q3 = mesh.faces[k].vertexquaternions deltaq = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 # Combine with canonical rotation qpose = deltaq gaussian.invariant.qbar # 5. Compute posed scale # Calculate area of triangle in posed state # Note: posetransform must return deformed vertices to compute area V1pose, V2pose, V3pose = posetransform(V1), posetransform(V2), posetransform(V3) Apose = trianglearea(V1pose, V2pose, V3pose) Acano = trianglearea(V1, V2, V3) spose = (Apose / Acano) gaussian.invariant.sbar return mupose, qpose, spose def handlecrosstriangleupdate(embedding, mesh, gradientu, gradientv): """ Handles the case where barycentric update moves the point outside the current triangle. Re-expresses the embedding in the neighboring triangle. Args: embedding: Current E={k, u, v, d}. mesh: Mesh structure with adjacency info. gradientu, gradientv: Gradients of the loss w.r.t u and v. Returns: New embedding tuple. """ k = embedding.k u = embedding.u v = embedding.v # Check boundary conditions if u < 0 or v < 0 or u + v > 1: # Find neighboring triangle that contains the projected point or is adjacent # In lifted optimization, this involves walking to the adjacent face neighbork = mesh.getneighbor(k, u, v) # Re-express barycentric coordinates in the new triangle # This requires mapping the point from old barycentric coords to new ones unew, vnew = mesh.remapbarycentric(k, neighbork, u, v) # Update embedding newembedding = { 'k': neighbork, 'u': unew, 'v': vnew, 'd': embedding.d } return newembedding else: return embedding Defines 3D Gaussians over an explicit triangle mesh for large-scale, interactive deformations driven by mesh editing. It sets itself apart by utilizing a reconstructed explicit mesh for initialization and employing specific face-split and normal-guidance strategies to handle large deformations without relying on implicit MLP-based skinning. Focuses on the initialization and deformation mechanics of mesh-embedded Gaussians. Introduces a hybrid "Gaussian Mesh Splatting" representation where each Gaussian is parameterized by the vertices of a mesh face, inducing coherent changes via classical mesh operations. A method for extracting Gaussian splats from meshes, focusing on the conversion process. Details the conversion of mesh data into a differentiable radiance kernel format. Algorithms for extracting Gaussian primitives from mesh-based representations. Performance: Achieves over 300 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU and 30 FPS on an iPhone 13. Strengths: Explicit motion control allows compatibility with various animation techniques (skeletal animation, blend shapes, mesh editing). The mesh represents low-frequency motion while Gaussians capture high-frequency geometry and appearance. Limitations: Relies on accurate semantic labels or mesh proxies for initialization. Cross-triangle updates require careful handling to maintain differentiability. Usage: Ported to Unity for real-time rendering. Originating from the SplattingAvatar paper, this method was developed to create realistic, real-time human avatars from monocular videos. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting [23] and Phong surfaces [38], addressing the limitations of MLP-based linear blend skinning (LBS) fields for motion. The approach disentangles motion and appearance by embedding Gaussians on a canonical triangle mesh, allowing for explicit control via mesh deformation. name: GaussianMesh
head: Mesh-GS
body: GaussianMesh is a method that defines 3D Gaussians over an explicit triangle mesh to enable large-scale, interactive deformations driven by mesh editing. It solves the problem of coherent motion transfer in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by tying Gaussian parameters to mesh geometry via joint refinement, where GS rendering guides adaptive splitting and mesh constraints regularize Gaussian shapes. It sets itself apart from parent methods by utilizing a reconstructed explicit mesh from calibrated images for initialization and employing specific face-split and normal-guidance strategies to handle large deformations without relying on implicit MLP-based skinning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A reconstructed explicit triangle mesh derived from calibrated images; 3DGS rendering parameters. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians embedded on the mesh faces, supporting real-time deformation. Data Structures: Mesh: Explicit triangle mesh with vertices and faces. Gaussians: Each Gaussian is associated with a specific mesh face. Its position is determined by barycentric coordinates within that face, and its orientation/scale is influenced by the face's normal and local geometry. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using the reconstructed explicit mesh derived from calibrated images. 2. Adaptive Refinement: Employ face split and normal guidance strategies to guide Gaussian learning and adapt density. 3. Regularization: Introduce a regularization loss to preserve the shape of the Gaussians during optimization. 4. Deformation: Incorporate user-controlled mesh deformations. The mesh-based Gaussian splatting representation allows deformations to propagate automatically to the Gaussians. 5. Rendering: Achieve real-time deformation and rendering. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Faces: Exhibits artifacts when dealing with significant deformations in meshes with large faces, leading to inaccuracies. Proxy Errors: Relies on accurate semantic labels or mesh proxies; errors in segmentation or remeshing can easily produce artifacts. OMeGa is a joint representation framework that optimizes an explicit triangle mesh and 2D Gaussian splats simultaneously, decoupling geometric support from textural detail. Unlike methods that allocate a fixed number of splats uniformly or keep rotation/scale fixed, OMeGa binds splats to mesh faces via barycentric coordinates, allowing adaptive density control and free movement of splats within the face plane. This approach addresses inaccurate geometry in texture-less regions and leverages mesh geometry to guide splat optimization. Strengths: Supports large, interactive deformations driven by mesh editing; enables real-time animation and scene editing. Limitations: Exhibits artifacts with significant deformations on meshes with large faces. Relies on accurate initial mesh proxies; errors in segmentation or remeshing cause artifacts. Performance: Achieves real-time deformation. When to use: When large-scale, user-controlled mesh deformations are required for 3DGS avatars or scenes. When not to use: When the input mesh has large faces or when accurate semantic labels/proxies are unavailable. GaussianMesh (also known as Mesh-GS) was introduced to realize large-scale 3DGS deformation. It utilizes a reconstructed explicit mesh from calibrated images to initialize Gaussians, employing face split and normal guidance strategies, and introduces regularization loss to preserve Gaussian shape. It builds on the concept of embedding Gaussians on meshes to disentangle motion from appearance [Parent]. name: OMeGa Joint Representation
head: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats, OMeGa
body: OMeGa is a joint representation framework that optimizes an explicit triangle mesh and 2D Gaussian splats simultaneously, decoupling geometric support from textural detail. Unlike methods that allocate a fixed number of splats uniformly or keep rotation/scale fixed, OMeGa binds splats to mesh faces via barycentric coordinates, allowing adaptive density control and free movement of splats within the face plane. This approach addresses inaccurate geometry in texture-less regions and leverages mesh geometry to guide splat optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images, initial mesh topology (vertices and faces). Outputs: Optimized learnable vertex positions V, mesh faces F, Gaussian splat set G, and binding map B. Data Structures: 1. Mesh Parameters: V \in \mathbb{R}^{Nv \times 3}: Learnable vertex positions, where Nv is the number of vertices. F \in \mathbb{R}^{Nf \times 3}: Mesh faces, where Nf is the number of faces. Each face fj is defined by three vertices. 2. Gaussian Splat Set G: Each splat gi contains texture attributes (color, opacity) and spatial parameters derived from the mesh. Spatial parameters include barycentric coordinates (u, w), relative scale s{rel}, and in-plane rotation R{2d}. 3. Binding Map B: B: G \rightarrow F maps each splat gi to its supporting face fj. Stored as a list or hash map of pairs (gi, fj). Formulas: 1. Splat Mean (Position): The mean \mathbf{m} of a splat bound to face fj with vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 is: \mathbf{m} = u \cdot \mathbf{v}1 + w \cdot \mathbf{v}2 + (1 - u - w) \cdot \mathbf{v}3 where u, w \in [0, 1] and u + w \le 1. 2. Splat Scale: The scale \mathbf{s} is the element-wise product of a learnable relative scale \mathbf{s}{rel} and a predefined base scale \mathbf{s}0 derived from the mesh face: \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s}{rel} \odot \mathbf{s}0 where \mathbf{s}{rel} = (s{rel,1}, s{rel,2}) \in [s{min}, s{max}] \times [s{min}, s{max}]. 3. Splat Rotation: The final rotation matrix \mathbf{R} is computed from the face rotation \mathbf{R}s and an in-plane rotation parameter \mathbf{R}{2d}: \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}s \cdot \mathbf{R}{2d} where \mathbf{R}s is the rotation matrix of the triangle face. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize mesh vertices V and faces F. Initialize Gaussian splats G with initial barycentric coordinates (u, w), relative scales \mathbf{s}{rel}, and in-plane rotations \mathbf{R}{2d}. Initialize binding map B mapping each splat to a face. 2. Spatial Attribute Derivation: For each splat gi bound to face fj: Compute mean \mathbf{m} using the barycentric formula. Compute scale \mathbf{s} using the relative scale formula. Compute rotation \mathbf{R} using the face rotation and in-plane rotation. 3. Rasterization: Render the scene using the derived Gaussian splats (means, scales, rotations, colors, opacities). 4. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss from rasterized images and mesh regularization losses (mesh constraint, monocular normal supervision). 5. Optimization: Update learnable parameters (V, splat attributes) via gradient descent. 6. Adaptive Density Control (Splat Management): Cloning/Splitting: When a Gaussian gi bound to fj is cloned or split, create g{new}. Bind g{new} to fj. Inherit gi's barycentric position with a small in-plane offset onto the face plane \Pi{fj}. Insert (g{new}, fj) into B. Removal: If a splat is pruned by the adaptive density controller, remove its entry from B. 7. Mesh Refinement (Topology Management): Subdivision: When face fj is subdivided into children \{f{jk}\}, reassign each splat previously bound to fj to the child whose domain contains its barycentric coordinates. Preserve per-splat attributes. Removal: When face fj is removed, identify all splats mapped to fj and flag them for removal in subsequent steps. Parameters: s{min}, s{max}: Lower and upper bounds for Gaussian Splat scale components to prevent discrepancies with triangular face scales. Typical values for s{min}, s{max}: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Discrepancy: Significant differences between Gaussian Splat scales and triangular face scales can occur. This is prevented by imposing upper and lower bounds on \mathbf{s}{rel}. Barycentric Validity: Ensure u, w \in [0, 1] and u + w \le 1 to keep splats within the face boundaries. Topology Changes: When mesh topology changes (subdivision/removal), the binding map B must be updated consistently to maintain valid splat-face associations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: OMeGa achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging indoor scenes. Strengths: Decouples geometric support from textural detail; allows adaptive density control; enables free movement of splats within the face plane; regularizes geometry learning via mesh constraints and monocular normal supervision. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When accurate geometry in texture-less regions is required, and when joint optimization of mesh and splats is beneficial for scene-level surface reconstruction. When not to use: Not given in the sources. OMeGa was introduced in the paper "OMeGa: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats for Robust Scene-Level Surface Reconstruction". It addresses limitations of previous works, such as inaccurate geometry in texture-less indoor regions and the decoupling of mesh extraction from optimization. The method integrates mesh constraints and monocular normal supervision to regularize geometry learning and proposes a heuristic, iterative mesh-refinement strategy. OMeGa: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats for Robust Scene-Level Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00427, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Gaussian Splitting for Bent Shapes
head: Bent Gaussian Splitting
body: A procedure to split bent Gaussians into multiple well-formed ellipsoids to approximate non-rigid warping shapes that a single Gaussian cannot represent, preventing visual artifacts. It addresses the limitation where a single transformed Gaussian fails to properly represent bent shapes caused by non-rigid warping, which leads to visual artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each represented by a proxy point cloud APd after initial deformation (e.g., cage-based deformation). The proxy points include the deformed center c'd and deformed points on the principal axes (e.g., x'1, x'2 for the x-axis). Output: A refined set of Gaussians where bent primitives have been split into multiple smaller, well-formed ellipsoids, ready for MVC (Mean Value Coordinates) transformation. Data Structures: Proxy Point Cloud (APd): A set of points representing the Gaussian ellipsoid. For a Gaussian with semi-principal axes a, b, c, the proxy points typically include the center and points along the axes at distances proportional to the axis lengths. Gaussian Parameters: Mean position, covariance matrix (or semi-principal axes a, b, c and orientation), opacity, and color. Parameters: Splitting Threshold: 175^\circ. Splitting is required if the calculated angle falls below this value. Scaling Factor (k): 1/2. Although theoretically derived as (1/2)^{1/3}, setting k=1/2 produces marginally better results. Minimum Axis Length: 1e-2. Axes with lengths below this threshold are not split for numerical stability. Steps: 1. Identify Bent Gaussians: For each Gaussian, calculate the angle between vectors from the deformed center c'd to two deformed points x'1 and x'2 on the same axis (e.g., x-axis) in the deformed point cloud APd. Vector 1: \vec{v}1 = x'1 - c'd Vector 2: \vec{v}2 = x'2 - c'd Angle \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{\vec{v}1 \cdot \vec{v}2}{\|\vec{v}1\| \|\vec{v}2\|}\right) If \theta < 175^\circ, the Gaussian is considered bent and requires splitting on this axis. 2. Split the Ellipsoid: Divide the pre-MVC Gaussian ellipsoid into two smaller ellipsoids along the chosen axis. Each new ellipsoid has axis lengths reduced by factor k. Both new ellipsoids are positioned to meet at the center of the original ellipsoid along the splitting axis. Specifically, if splitting along the x-axis with original semi-axis a, the new semi-axes are ka, b, c. The centers are shifted by \pm (a - ka)/2 along the x-axis relative to the original center. 3. Apply MVC Transformation: Apply the MVC transformation again to the resulting two smaller ellipsoids for further processing. 4. Repeat for All Axes: Run the identification and splitting process across all axes (x, y, z) to ensure Gaussians requiring splitting on multiple axes are split more than once. Formulas: Volume Preservation Constraint: The combined volume of two smaller ellipsoids approximates the original volume. LV = \frac{2}{3}\pi abc - 2 \frac{2}{3}\pi k1 a k2 b k3 c \approx 0 Simplified: k1 k2 k3 = 1/2. Shape Preservation Constraint: Each smaller ellipsoid maintains shape similar to original. \frac{k1}{a} \approx \frac{k2}{b} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{k1}{a} \approx \frac{k3}{c} (Note: The source text implies k1/a \approx k2/b and k1/a \approx k3/c are constraints to maintain shape similarity, leading to k1=k2=k3). Scaling Factor: k1 = k2 = k3 = \sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{2}} In practice, k = 1/2 is used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splitbentgaussians(gaussians, threshold=175.0, k=0.5, minaxis=1e-2): """ Splits bent Gaussians into multiple well-formed ellipsoids. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: center: 3D vector axes: List of 3D vectors representing semi-principal axes (a, b, c) proxypoints: List of 3D points representing the deformed ellipsoid threshold: Angle threshold in degrees for splitting (default 175) k: Scaling factor for splitting (default 0.5) minaxis: Minimum axis length to avoid splitting (default 1e-2) Returns: List of Gaussian objects (split Gaussians replace originals) """ newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Check if splitting is needed for any axis splitneeded = False splitaxes = [] for i, axis in enumerate(g.axes): axislen = np.linalg.norm(axis) if axislen < minaxis: continue # Get deformed points for this axis from proxypoints # Assuming proxypoints contains center and two points along each axis # This is a simplification; actual implementation depends on proxy point structure center = g.center # Find points along the current axis direction # In practice, these are pre-computed deformed points x'1, x'2 p1, p2 = getaxispoints(g.proxypoints, i) if p1 is None or p2 is None: continue # Calculate angle v1 = p1 - center v2 = p2 - center cosangle = np.dot(v1, v2) / (np.linalg.norm(v1) np.linalg.norm(v2)) # Clamp for numerical stability cosangle = np.clip(cosangle, -1.0, 1.0) angle = np.degrees(np.arccos(cosangle)) if angle < threshold: splitneeded = True splitaxes.append(i) if not splitneeded: newgaussians.append(g) continue # Split the Gaussian # Create two new Gaussians g1 = copygaussian(g) g2 = copygaussian(g) for axisidx in splitaxes: # Reduce axis length by factor k g1.axes[axisidx] = g1.axes[axisidx] k g2.axes[axisidx] = g2.axes[axisidx] k # Shift centers to meet at original center # Original center is midpoint between new centers shift = (1 - k) / 2 g.axes[axisidx] # Original axis vector g1.center = g.center + shift g2.center = g.center - shift # Add split Gaussians to new list newgaussians.append(g1) newgaussians.append(g2) return newgaussians Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians and axes checked. Splitting increases the number of Gaussians, potentially doubling the count for heavily bent regions. Memory Complexity: Increases proportionally to the number of splits. Strengths: Prevents visual artifacts from non-rigid warping; no architectural changes or retraining needed; can work in real-time with caching. Limitations: Increases the number of primitives, which may impact rendering performance if many splits occur. When to use: When deforming 3DGS Gaussians using cage-based deformation or other methods that cause non-rigid warping, leading to bent Gaussians. When not to use: When deformation is rigid or minimal, as splitting adds unnecessary complexity. Originated in GSDeformer: Direct Cage-based Deformation for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method was developed to address artifacts in 3DGS deformation caused by non-rigid warping, where a single Gaussian cannot represent bent shapes. It operates directly on the primitives of 3DGS, allowing integration with other 3DGS variants without retraining. name: Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Initialization and Deformation
head: Gaussian Embedding, Triangle Embedding
body: This method initializes and deforms 3D Gaussians by anchoring them to a canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} using barycentric coordinates and normal displacement. It solves the problem of maintaining geometric coherence and differentiability during mesh deformation (e.g., animation) by tracking Gaussians through mesh topology rather than direct vertex positions. Unlike methods that rely on precise mesh accuracy, it defines a local triangle space to ensure robust results even with inaccurate meshes. It builds on Mesh-embedded representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices V, per-vertex normals n, and faces F; deformation function \text{Deform}(\cdot); number of Gaussians N (typically 10,000). Output: Set of N Gaussians, each defined by embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\} and derived attributes (position, rotation, scale). Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores an embedding tuple Ei: k \in F: Index of the triangle in the canonical mesh. (u, v): Barycentric coordinates within triangle k, such that u \ge 0, v \ge 0, u+v \le 1. d: Normal displacement scalar along the interpolated surface normal. Canonical Position and Normal: The canonical mean \mu{cano} and normal n{cano} are computed via Phong interpolation on the canonical mesh [Parent, S1, unofficial]: \mu{cano} = \mathcal{V}(k, u, v) = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 n{cano} = \mathcal{N}(k, u, v) = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 where Vj and nj are the vertices and per-vertex normals of triangle k [Parent, S1, unofficial]. Posed State Computation: When the mesh is deformed, the posed position \mu{pose} is derived by applying the mesh deformation function \text{Deform}(\cdot) to the displaced canonical position [Parent, S1, unofficial]: \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano}) The posed rotation q{pose} and scale s{pose} are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence [Parent, S1, unofficial]: Rotation: Interpolate per-vertex quaternions q1, q2, q3 using barycentric weights to get \delta q, then combine with canonical rotation \bar{q}: q{pose} = \delta q \bar{q}, \quad \delta q = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 Scale: Scale is proportional to the area change of the embedded triangle relative to the canonical state: s{pose} = \left( \frac{A{pose}}{A{cano}} \right) \bar{s} where A{pose} and A{cano} are the areas of the triangle in the posed and canonical states, respectively [Parent, S1, unofficial]. Initialization: 1. Randomly select N pairs of triangle indices k and barycentric coordinates (u, v) on the canonical mesh. 2. Initialize all displacements d to zero. 3. Set canonical rotation \bar{q} and scale \bar{s} for each Gaussian. 4. Color representation: Spherical harmonics are turned off for simplicity. Cross-Triangle Handling: Barycentric coordinates are only differentiable within a single triangle. If optimization moves an embedding point across a boundary (u < 0, v < 0, or u+v > 1), the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability [Parent, S1, unofficial]. Failure to handle this causes Gaussians to stick to boundaries and pile up [Parent, S1, unofficial]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializegaussians(mesh, numgaussians=10000): """ Initialize Gaussians on a canonical mesh. mesh: object with vertices V, normals n, faces F, and method gettrianglearea(k) """ gaussians = [] for i in range(numgaussians): # Randomly select a triangle k = randomint(0, len(mesh.F) - 1) triangle = mesh.F[k] # Generate random barycentric coordinates r1 = randomfloat(0, 1) r2 = randomfloat(0, 1) if r1 + r2 > 1: r1 = 1 - r1 r2 = 1 - r2 u = r1 v = r2 # Initialize displacement to zero d = 0.0 # Initialize canonical rotation and scale qcanon = identityquaternion() scanon = 1.0 gaussians.append({ 'k': k, 'u': u, 'v': v, 'd': d, 'qcanon': qcanon, 'scanon': scanon }) return gaussians def computeposedstate(gaussian, mesh, deformationfunction): """ Compute the posed position, rotation, and scale for a Gaussian. gaussian: dict with keys k, u, v, d, qcanon, scanon mesh: object with vertices V, normals n, faces F, and method gettrianglearea(k) deformationfunction: function that takes a point and returns its deformed position """ k = gaussian['k'] u = gaussian['u'] v = gaussian['v'] d = gaussian['d'] # Get triangle vertices and normals v1, v2, v3 = mesh.V[mesh.F[k][0]], mesh.V[mesh.F[k][1]], mesh.V[mesh.F[k][2]] n1, n2, n3 = mesh.n[mesh.F[k][0]], mesh.n[mesh.F[k][1]], mesh.n[mesh.F[k][2]] # Compute canonical position and normal mucano = u v1 + v v2 + (1 - u - v) v3 ncano = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 # Compute posed position displacedpos = mucano + d ncano mupose = deformationfunction(displacedpos) # Compute posed rotation # Get per-vertex quaternions for the triangle q1, q2, q3 = getvertexquaternions(mesh, k) deltaq = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 qpose = deltaq gaussian['qcanon'] # Compute posed scale acano = mesh.gettrianglearea(k) # Compute posed area by deforming vertices and calculating area v1pose = deformationfunction(v1) v2pose = deformationfunction(v2) v3pose = deformationfunction(v3) apose = computetrianglearea(v1pose, v2pose, v3pose) spose = (apose / acano) gaussian['scanon'] return { 'position': mupose, 'rotation': qpose, 'scale': spose } def getvertexquaternions(mesh, k): """ Get per-vertex quaternions for a triangle. This is a placeholder for the specific method of computing quaternions from tangent/bitangent/normal. In practice, this involves computing rotation matrices from tangent, bitangent, and normal vectors for each vertex and converting to quaternions. """ # Placeholder implementation v1, v2, v3 = mesh.V[mesh.F[k][0]], mesh.V[mesh.F[k][1]], mesh.V[mesh.F[k][2]] n1, n2, n3 = mesh.n[mesh.F[k][0]], mesh.n[mesh.F[k][1]], mesh.n[mesh.F[k][2]] # Compute tangent and bitangent for each vertex # This is a simplified placeholder; actual implementation requires proper tangent space computation q1 = identityquaternion() q2 = identityquaternion() q3 = identityquaternion() return q1, q2, q3 def computetrianglearea(v1, v2, v3): """ Compute the area of a triangle given its vertices. """ edge1 = v2 - v1 edge2 = v3 - v1 crossproduct = cross(edge1, edge2) return 0.5 length(crossproduct) Walking on Triangle is a constraint mechanism that binds 3D Gaussians to the surface of a triangle mesh, ensuring they remain within the boundaries of their corresponding triangles during optimization and deformation. It solves the problem of Gaussians drifting off-mesh or piling up at triangle edges when the underlying mesh is manipulated, animated, or deformed. Unlike methods that rely heavily on precise mesh accuracy, it defines a local triangle space to ensure robust results even with inaccurate meshes. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Posed state computation is O(1) per Gaussian per frame, assuming constant-time mesh deformation and area calculation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the embedding tuples and derived attributes for each Gaussian. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Performance depends on the efficiency of the mesh deformation function and area calculation. Strengths: Maintains geometric coherence during deformation; robust to mesh inaccuracies; differentiable within triangle boundaries. Limitations: Requires careful handling of cross-triangle boundaries to avoid piling up; assumes the mesh deformation is known and differentiable. When to use: When deforming a mesh-based representation with Gaussians; when robustness to mesh inaccuracies is required. When not to use: When the mesh deformation is unknown or non-differentiable; when high-frequency details require direct vertex manipulation. Originated in SplattingAvatar. name: Walking on Triangle
body: Walking on Triangle is a constraint mechanism that binds 3D Gaussians to the surface of a triangle mesh, ensuring they remain within the boundaries of their corresponding triangles during optimization and deformation. It solves the problem of Gaussians drifting off-mesh or piling up at triangle edges when the underlying mesh is manipulated or animated. Unlike methods that rely heavily on precise mesh accuracy, it defines a local triangle space to ensure robust results even with inaccurate meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh, 3D Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color), and barycentric coordinates (u, v) for each Gaussian relative to its host triangle. Output: Updated Gaussian positions and attributes that respect the mesh topology and local triangle constraints. Data Structures: Gaussian State: Each Gaussian i is associated with a specific triangle Tk of the mesh. Barycentric Coordinates: For each Gaussian, two scalar values ui, vi representing its position within triangle Tk. The third barycentric coordinate is wi = 1 - ui - vi. Local Triangle Space: Defined by the three vertices of triangle Tk: \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. Steps: 1. Bind Gaussians to Mesh: Assign each Gaussian to a specific triangle on the mesh during initialization. 2. Define Local Triangle Space: For each triangle, establish a local coordinate space for optimization. 3. Optimize Attributes in Local Space: Optimize Gaussian attributes within the local triangle space during training, ensuring deformations applied to the mesh are directly transferred to the Gaussians. 4. Clip UV Values: To prevent Gaussians from moving beyond the boundaries of their assigned triangle, clip the barycentric coordinates ui and vi. The constraints are: ui \ge 0, \quad vi \ge 0, \quad ui + vi \le 1 If a Gaussian's coordinates violate these bounds, they are clipped to the nearest valid point within the triangle. 5. Transfer Manipulation: When the mesh is deformed or manipulated, the new positions of the triangle vertices are used to recompute the 3D position of each Gaussian based on its fixed barycentric coordinates. This allows for large deformations, soft body simulation, and local manipulation. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: Disabling the walking-on-triangle mechanism causes Gaussians to stick and pile up on the boundaries of mesh triangles, leading to visible artifacts when the avatar is animated by novel poses. Degenerate Triangles: Zero-area or highly skewed triangles may cause numerical instability during barycentric interpolation; standard epsilon guards are required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clipbarycentric(u, v): """Clips barycentric coordinates to the valid triangle region.""" if u < 0.0: u = 0.0 if v < 0.0: v = 0.0 if u + v > 1.0: s = u + v u = u / s v = v / s return u, v def updategaussianposition(u, v, v1, v2, v3): """Computes 3D position from barycentric coordinates and triangle vertices.""" u, v = clipbarycentric(u, v) w = 1.0 - u - v return w v1 + u v2 + v v3 A method that defines a local triangle space for each triangle to ensure robust results even with inaccurate meshes, binding Gaussians to the mesh and optimizing attributes within this space. It transfers mesh manipulation directly to 3DGS, enabling large deformation, soft body simulation, and local manipulation. Compared with SuGaR, Mani-GS produces fewer artifacts and reduces the blurring effect. Time Complexity: The clipping and position update operations are O(1) per Gaussian per frame. The overall complexity is dominated by the rendering and optimization steps of the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline. Memory Complexity: Adds negligible memory overhead, storing only the barycentric coordinates (u, v) for each Gaussian. Performance: For the 'bala' head avatar, enabling Walking on Triangle increases PSNR from 29.91 to 30.04, SSIM from 0.933 to 0.938, and decreases LPIPS from 0.070 to 0.062. For the 'male-3-casual' full-body avatar, it increases PSNR from 32.48 to 33.01, SSIM from 0.979 to 0.982, and decreases LPIPS from 0.024 to 0.020. Strengths: Prevents artifacts during animation, robust to mesh inaccuracies, enables direct mesh manipulation. Limitations: Requires a valid triangle mesh and initial binding of Gaussians to triangles. Walking on Triangle was introduced in SplattingAvatar, a method for relightable modeling with explicit shape representations. It was designed to address performance compromises in previous explicit shape methods, particularly in maintaining pixel-wise metrics during animation. The method is also highlighted in surveys of 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS as a key technique for mesh-based deformation.
