The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeorientedattenuation(x, w, mu, Sigmainv, alpha, n): """ Computes the oriented attenuation coefficient for a single Gaussian. """ # Standard Gaussian density G(x) diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 diff.T @ Sigmainv @ diff G = alpha np.exp(exponent) # Gradient of log(1 - G) # d/dx log(1-G) = (1/(1-G)) (-dG/dx) # dG/dx = G (-Sigmainv @ diff) # So gradlog = (1/(1-G)) G (Sigmainv @ diff) if G >= 1.0: return 0.0 # Avoid division by zero, though G <= alpha <= 1 gradlogterm = (G / (1.0 - G)) (Sigmainv @ diff) # Directional derivative |w. grad| directionalderiv = np.abs(np.dot(w, gradlogterm)) # Half-space indicator if np.dot(n, diff) >= 0: return directionalderiv else: return 0.0 def computevacancyfield(x, gaussians, trainingrays): """ Computes the vacancy field v(x) by iterating over training rays. """ maxtransmittance = 0.0 for o, w in trainingrays: # Find tmax for each Gaussian along this ray # tG = argmaxt G(o + tw) # For a Gaussian with covariance Sigma, the peak is at the projection of mu onto the ray # tG = w. (mu - o) / (w. w) if w is unit, else normalize # However, the source defines tG as argmax. # For a 3D Gaussian G(x) = alpha exp(-0.5 (x-mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x-mu)) # Along ray x(t) = o + tw, the exponent is -0.5 (o + tw - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (o + tw - mu) # This is a quadratic in t. The maximum is at t = - (w^T Sigma^-1 (o-mu)) / (w^T Sigma^-1 w) # Compute product of (1 - Gbar) transmittance = 1.0 for g in gaussians: mu, Sigma, alpha, n = g.mu, g.Sigma, g.alpha, g.n Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) # Find tG A = w.T @ Sigmainv @ w B = w.T @ Sigmainv @ (o - mu) if A == 0: tG = 0 else: tG = -B / A # Evaluate G at min(t, tG) for the point x on the ray # We need t such that o + tw = x => t = w. (x - o) (assuming w unit) tx = np.dot(w, x - o) if tx <= 0: continue # Point is behind camera teval = min(tx, tG) if teval < 0: teval = 0 xeval = o + teval w diff = xeval - mu exponent = -0.5 diff.T @ Sigmainv @ diff Gval = alpha np.exp(exponent) transmittance = (1.0 - Gval) if transmittance > maxtransmittance: maxtransmittance = transmittance return maxtransmittance def computevectorfield(x, gaussians): """ Computes V(x) = sum of gradients for oriented Gaussians. """ V = np.zeros(3) for g in gaussians: mu, Sigmainv, alpha, n = g.mu, np.linalg.inv(g.Sigma), g.alpha, g.n diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 diff.T @ Sigmainv @ diff G = alpha np.exp(exponent) if G >= 1.0: continue # Gradient of log(1-G) gradlog = (G / (1.0 - G)) (Sigmainv @ diff) # Check orientation if np.dot(n, diff) >= 0: V += gradlog return V def extractmeshpivotbased(gaussians, trainingrays): """ Extracts mesh using Pivot-Based Marching Tetrahedra. """ pivots = [] pivotvalues = [] for g in gaussians: mu = g.mu n = g.n # si = || Si Ri^T ni ||2 # Assuming g has S and R attributes S = g.S R = g.R # Scale vector along normal si = np.linalg.norm(S np.linalg.inv(R) @ n) # Note: R is rotation, R^T = R^-1. S is diagonal. # Actually S is usually diagonal scaling matrix. S R^T n. # If S is vector, diag(S) @ R.T @ n Smat = np.diag(S) si = np.linalg.norm(Smat @ (R.T @ n)) p1 = mu p2 = mu + 3 si n pivots.append(p1) pivots.append(p2) v1 = computevacancyfield(p1, gaussians, trainingrays) v2 = computevacancyfield(p2, gaussians, trainingrays) pivotvalues.append(v1) pivotvalues.append(v2) # Apply Marching Tetrahedra on Delaunay triangulation of pivots # This step requires a Delaunay triangulation library # tetrahedra = delaunaytriangulation(pivots) # mesh = marchingtetrahedra(tetrahedra, pivotvalues, threshold=0.5) # Refine vertices to 0.5-isosurface via binary search # for vertex in mesh.vertices: # vertex = binarysearchrefine(vertex, gaussians, trainingrays) return pivots, pivotvalues # Placeholder for actual mesh object def trainorientedgaussians(gaussians, images, cameras, iterations=30000, K=100): """ Main training loop. """ lambdaDN = 0.05 lambdaN = 0.05 lambdapc = 0.6 lambdagc = 0.02 for i in range(iterations): # 1. Render images and normals renderedrgb, rendereddepth, renderednormals = render(gaussians, cameras) # 2. Compute Losses LRGB = photometricloss(renderedrgb, images) LDN = depthnormalconsistency(rendereddepth, images) # Requires ground truth depth or stereo LN = normalalignmentloss(renderednormals, rendereddepth) LMV = multiviewloss(gaussians, images, cameras) Ltotal = LRGB + lambdaDN LDN + lambdaN LN + LMV # 3. Backpropagate and update parameters updateparameters(gaussians, Ltotal) # 4. Densification if i % K == 0: # Compute LN per pixel and propagate to Gaussians errors = computepixelerrors(LN, renderednormals, rendereddepth) propagateerrorstogaussians(gaussians, errors) cloneandfliphigherrorgaussians(gaussians) return gaussians Time Complexity: Rendering is similar to standard 3DGS, O(N) per pixel for splatting. Vacancy field computation for mesh extraction is O(N \cdot R) where R is the number of training rays, which is expensive and typically done offline or sparsely. Memory Complexity: Stores an additional normal vector ni per Gaussian, increasing memory by 3 	imes 4 bytes per Gaussian compared to standard 3DGS. Performance: Produces substantially lighter, fully watertight meshes compared to prior works requiring 9 pivots per Gaussian, without sacrificing surface fidelity. Strengths: Enables explicit geometric field derivation (normals, occupancy) via OaV; restores reciprocity; facilitates high-fidelity mesh extraction. Limitations: Requires Gaussians to properly "wrap" the scene geometry; consistency requirement that the region where transmittance is constant lies inside the object. Hidden Gaussians inside geometry can violate wrapping assumptions and produce artifacts if intersected. When to use: When explicit surface reconstruction (mesh) is required from a radiance field representation, particularly for scenes where standard 3DGS fails to provide clean normals or watertight meshes. When not to use: When only novel view synthesis is needed and mesh extraction is not required, as standard 3DGS is simpler and faster. Oriented Gaussian Splatting was introduced in "From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians". It addresses the lack of reciprocity in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting attenuation, which prevents the direct application of the Objects as Volumes (OaV) framework for deriving explicit geometric fields. The method builds on the OaV theory [39] and integrates with differentiable rasterizers [55, 56, 57]. From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37095-24, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 3D Skew-Normal Splatting
head: Skew-Normal Splatting
body: 3D Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS) is a volume rendering method that replaces the standard symmetric 3D Gaussian kernel with the Azzalini Skew-Normal distribution to model asymmetric structures, such as sharp boundaries and one-sided surfaces, while preserving analytical tractability under affine transformations. It sets apart from its siblings, such as Oriented Gaussian Splatting and Barycentric Splat Parameterization, by introducing a continuous, learnable skewness parameter that allows primitives to interpolate between symmetric Gaussians and half-ellipsoids, enabling the representation of directional asymmetry that symmetric or constrained primitives cannot capture. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Skew-Normal primitives, each defined by location \mui, scale matrix \Omegai, and skew parameter ki; camera parameters (view/projection matrices); and scene geometry. Output: A rendered 2D image where each pixel color C(u) is computed via alpha blending of projected 2D Skew-Normal kernels. Data Structures: Each primitive i stores: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Location parameter. Ri \in SO(3): Rotation matrix. Si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling vector (diagonal of scaling matrix). \Omegai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Scale matrix. ki \in \mathbb{R}^3: Latent skewness variable, factorized into magnitude m{k,i} \in \mathbb{R}+ and direction d{k,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (\|d{k,i}\|2 = 1). ci: Color (typically represented by Spherical Harmonics coefficients). oi \in [-1, 1]: Signed opacity. Parameters: Skew magnitude parameterization: mk = \frac{8}{1 + \exp(-\frac{x}{6})}, where x \in \mathbb{R} is a learnable scalar. Skew direction: dk = \frac{v}{\|v\|2 + \epsilon}, where v \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a learnable vector. Skew vector: k = mk dk. Formulas: The 3D Skew-Normal kernel is defined as: SN(x; \mu, \Omega, k) = G3(x - \mu; \Omega) \Phi \left( \alpha^\top \omega^{-1}(x - \mu) \right) where: G3(x - \mu; \Omega) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2}(x - \mu)^\top \Omega^{-1} (x - \mu) \right) is the unnormalized Gaussian PDF. \Phi(\cdot) is the standard normal CDF. \omega = (\Omega \odot I3)^{1/2} is the diagonal matrix of standard deviations derived from \Omega using the Hadamard product \odot. \alpha = \omega R S^{-1} k is the slant parameter, decoupled from rotation and scale. The spatial mean of the distribution is shifted from the location parameter \mu: \mathbb{E}[X] = \mu + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{R S k}{\sqrt{1+k^\top k}} This offset is used to compute the bounding box center \mu{bbox} for rasterization: \mu{bbox} = \mu^{2D} + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{A R S k}{\sqrt{1+k^\top k}} where \mu^{2D} = A\mu is the projected location. Projection to 2D: The 3D primitive is projected onto the image plane using the affine transformation matrix A = JW \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3} (Jacobian J and world-to-camera W). The resulting 2D Skew-Normal kernel is: SN^{2D}(u; \mu^{2D}, \Omega^{2D}, m^{2D}) = G2(u - \mu^{2D}; \Omega^{2D}) \Phi \left( (m^{2D})^\top (u - \mu^{2D}) \right) with parameters: \mu^{2D} = A\mu, \quad \Omega^{2D} = A\Omega A^\top m^{2D} = \frac{(\Omega^{2D})^{-1} A R S k}{\sqrt{1 + k^\top k} - (A R S k)^\top (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} A R S k} Rendering: Color aggregation uses signed opacity splatting to allow subtractive volumetric density: C(u) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci oi SNi^{2D}(u) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj SNj^{2D}(u)) where \mathcal{N} is the set of depth-sorted intersecting kernels. Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize primitives with standard 3DGS parameters. 2. Phase 1 (Global Structure): Jointly optimize all parameters (R, S, mk, dk) using the Adam optimizer to establish a global scene structure. 3. Phase 2 (Block Coordinate Descent): Use a cyclic alternating schedule to reduce parameter interference: Part 1: Update ellipsoidal base parameters (R, S) while freezing skew parameters (mk, dk). Part 2: Refine skew parameters (mk, dk) while holding (R, S) constant. 4. Positional Update: Update positional parameters \mu using Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC) to escape local minima. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computeskewvector(klatent): """ Factorizes latent k into magnitude and direction. klatent: [2] tensor [x, v] where x is scalar, v is 3-vector. """ x = klatent[0] v = klatent[1:4] # Magnitude parameterization mk = 8.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-x / 6.0)) # Direction parameterization dk = v / (torch.norm(v) + 1e-6) return mk, dk def computeslant(R, S, k): """ Computes decoupled slant parameter alpha. R: [3, 3] rotation matrix S: [3] scaling vector (diagonal elements) k: [3] skew vector (mk dk) """ # Omega = R S S^T R^T # Omegadiag = diag(Omega) # omega = sqrt(diag(Omega)) # Note: omega is diagonal matrix with entries sqrt(Omegaii) Omega = R @ torch.diag(S2) @ R.T omegadiag = torch.sqrt(torch.diag(Omega)) omega = torch.diag(omegadiag) # alpha = omega R S^{-1} k # Sinv is diagonal with 1/Si Sinv = torch.diag(1.0 / S) alpha = omega @ R @ Sinv @ k return alpha, omega def project3dto2dskew(mu3d, Omega3d, R, S, k, A): """ Projects 3D Skew-Normal to 2D. mu3d: [3] Omega3d: [3, 3] R: [3, 3] S: [3] k: [3] A: [2, 3] affine transform matrix (Jacobian WorldToCamera) Returns: mu2d, Omega2d, m2d """ # Project location and covariance mu2d = A @ mu3d Omega2d = A @ Omega3d @ A.T # Compute m2d # Numerator: Omega2d^{-1} A R S k # Denominator: sqrt(1 + k^T k) - (A R S k)^T Omega2d^{-1} (A R S k) ARSk = A @ R @ torch.diag(S) @ k Omega2dinv = torch.inverse(Omega2d) numerator = Omega2dinv @ ARSk term2 = ARSk.T @ Omega2dinv @ ARSk denominator = torch.sqrt(1.0 + torch.dot(k, k)) - term2 m2d = numerator / denominator return mu2d, Omega2d, m2d def renderpixel(u, primitives, Amatrix): """ Renders a single pixel u [2] given a list of primitives. primitives: list of dicts with keys: mu3d, Omega3d, R, S, k, c, o Amatrix: [2, 3] for this pixel's camera view """ # Sort primitives by depth (z) relative to camera # (Assuming depth sorting is handled by the rasterizer pipeline) sortedprimitives = sortprimitivesbydepth(primitives, Amatrix) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 color = torch.zeros(3) for prim in sortedprimitives: mu2d, Omega2d, m2d = project3dto2dskew( prim['mu3d'], prim['Omega3d'], prim['R'], prim['S'], prim['k'], Amatrix) # Compute 2D Skew-Normal value diff = u - mu2d # Gaussian part gaussval = torch.exp(-0.5 diff.T @ torch.inverse(Omega2d) @ diff) # Skew part (CDF) skewarg = m2d.T @ diff skewval = torch.sigmoid(skewarg) # Approximation of Phi if not using special function # Note: Standard Phi is not sigmoid. Implement Phi using erf or library. # Phi(x) = 0.5 (1 + erf(x / sqrt(2))) skewval = 0.5 (1.0 + torch.erf(skewarg / torch.sqrt(2.0))) sn2d = gaussval skewval o = prim['o'] c = prim['c'] # Signed opacity blending contribution = c o sn2d weight = o sn2d (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) color += contribution accumulatedalpha += weight if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Tails: Without bounded skewness, asymmetric tails cause primitives to intersect excessive tiles, degrading tile-based rasterization performance and violating local affine approximation assumptions. The parameterization mk \in \mathbb{R}+ and bounded Mardia's skewness measure prevent this. Parameter Coupling: Strong coupling between scale, rotation, and skewness causes optimization instability. The decoupled parameterization \alpha = \omega R S^{-1} k and factorization of k into mk, dk resolve this. Mean vs Location: The location parameter \mu does not coincide with the spatial mean. Using \mu for bounding box localization leads to inaccurate coverage. The corrected center \mu{bbox} must be used. Computes the parameters of a 2D Skew-Normal distribution (SN2D) resulting from the linear projection of a 3D Skew-Normal kernel (SN3) onto the image plane. It sets apart from standard Gaussian splatting by preserving the asymmetry (skewness) of the 3D primitive during projection, allowing the 2D kernel to model one-sided surfaces and sharp boundaries that symmetric Gaussians cannot. Addresses the discrepancy between the location parameter \mu and the spatial mean \mathbb{E}[X] of the Skew-Normal distribution. It derives a deterministic spatial offset \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{RSk}{\sqrt{1+k^\top k}} to shift the bounding box center to the true spatial mean, ensuring accurate tile culling and rasterization. Time Complexity: Comparable to standard 3DGS and SSS, with overhead from computing the skew term (CDF evaluation) and additional parameter updates. Memory Complexity: Slightly higher than 3DGS due to the storage of skew parameters (k or mk, dk) and the need for more complex gradient computations. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, SNS achieves 30.17 PSNR, 0.895 SSIM, and 0.144 LPIPS, outperforming SSS (29.90 PSNR) and 3DGS (28.69 PSNR). On the drjohnson scene, SNS completes 30,000 iterations in 38m 4s (29.89 dB PSNR), comparable to SSS (38m 7s, 29.66 dB PSNR). Strengths: Continuous interpolation between symmetric and asymmetric shapes; analytical tractability under affine transformations; ability to model sharp boundaries and one-sided surfaces with fewer primitives. Limitations: Optimization instability due to parameter coupling requires complex decoupling strategies and block-wise updates; signed opacity requires careful handling to avoid artifacts. When to use: Scenes with sharp edges, flat surfaces, or one-sided structures where symmetric Gaussians require excessive overlap or fail to capture asymmetry. When not to use: Scenes with purely symmetric, smooth geometry where the added complexity of skewness provides negligible benefit and may hinder convergence. 3D Skew-Normal Splatting was proposed to address the limitations of symmetric Gaussian kernels in representing asymmetric structures. It builds on the Azzalini Skew-Normal distribution, which provides directional asymmetry through a slant parameter. The method was introduced to enable continuous shape interpolation between symmetric Gaussians and half-ellipsoids, allowing for flexible modeling of sharp boundaries and interior regions while maintaining the efficiency of splat-based rendering. It is implemented in PyTorch, extending the 3DGS rasterization engine, and tested on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. 3D Skew-Normal Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.15010, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 2D Skew-Normal Parameter Projection
head: 2D Kernel Parameter Projection, SN2D Projection, Skew-Normal 2D Parameter Computation
body: Computes the parameters of a 2D Skew-Normal distribution (SN2D) resulting from the linear projection of a 3D Skew-Normal kernel (SN3) onto the image plane. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Skew-Normal kernel parameters \mathcal{X} \sim \text{SN3}(\mu, \Omega, \alpha), where \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the mean, \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the covariance, and \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the skewness parameter. Input: Projection matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}. Output: 2D Skew-Normal parameters \mathcal{Y} \sim \text{SN2}(\muY, \OmegaY, \alphaY), where \muY \in \mathbb{R}^2, \OmegaY \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, and \alphaY \in \mathbb{R}^2. Data Structures: The 3D kernel is parameterized using a rotation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, a scale matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (diagonal), and a skewness vector k \in \mathbb{R}^3. The covariance is \Omega = R S S^\top R^\top. The skewness parameter is \alpha = \omega R S^{-1} k, where \omega = (1 + k^\top k)^{-1/2}. Steps: 1. Compute 2D Mean: \muY = A \mu 2. Compute 2D Covariance: \OmegaY = A \Omega A^\top 3. Compute Intermediate Vector v: Calculate the term \omega \delta from the 3D parameters: \omega \delta = \frac{R S k}{\sqrt{1 + k^\top k}} Let v = A (\omega \delta) = \frac{A R S k}{\sqrt{1 + k^\top k}}. 4. Compute 2D Skewness \alphaY: The skewness parameter is derived from the projected intermediate vector and the 2D covariance: \alphaY = \frac{\OmegaY^{-1} v}{\sqrt{1 - v^\top \OmegaY^{-1} v}} (Note: The source derivation includes a normalization factor \omegaY in the numerator, which is absorbed or set to unity during the direct projection step to avoid circular dependency.) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projectskewnormal3dto2d(mu3d: np.ndarray, R: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray, k: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray) -> tuple: """ Projects a 3D Skew-Normal kernel to 2D. Args: mu3d: (3,) array, 3D mean. R: (3, 3) array, rotation matrix. S: (3,) array, scale vector (diagonal elements of S matrix). k: (3,) array, skewness vector. A: (2, 3) array, projection matrix. Returns: mu2d: (2,) array, 2D mean. Omega2d: (2, 2) array, 2D covariance. alpha2d: (2,) array, 2D skewness parameter. """ # 1. Compute 2D Mean mu2d = A @ mu3d # 2. Compute 3D Covariance Omega = R diag(S)^2 R^T Smat = np.diag(S) Omega3d = R @ (Smat @ Smat.T) @ R.T # 3. Compute 2D Covariance Omega2d = A @ Omega3d @ A.T # 4. Compute intermediate vector v = A (R S k / sqrt(1 + k^T k)) knormsq = np.dot(k, k) scalefactor = 1.0 / np.sqrt(1.0 + knormsq) # R @ (S @ k) RSk = R @ (S k) # v = A @ (scalefactor RSk) v = scalefactor (A @ RSk) # 5. Compute alpha2d Omega2dinv = np.linalg.inv(Omega2d) numerator = Omega2dinv @ v denominatorterm = v.T @ Omega2dinv @ v denominator = np.sqrt(1.0 - denominatorterm) alpha2d = numerator / denominator return mu2d, Omega2d, alpha2d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \OmegaY is singular (e.g., the kernel is viewed edge-on and collapses to a line), \OmegaY^{-1} does not exist. Regularization or culling is required. Domain Error: The term 1 - v^\top \OmegaY^{-1} v must be positive to prevent imaginary results in the square root. Evaluating the Skew-Normal distribution requires computing the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF). The implementation uses the erf function for mathematical precision. Using the precise erf function incurs moderate penalties on rendering speed compared to faster analytic approximations. Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "3D Skew-Normal Splatting". The method extends the standard Gaussian Splatting framework by replacing the symmetric 3D Gaussian kernel with the Azzalini Skew-Normal distribution to model asymmetric structures. The 2D projection formula is derived from the properties of the Skew-Normal distribution under linear transformations. 3D Skew-Normal Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.15010, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Barycentric Splat Parameterization
head: GeoSplatting Face-Sampling, Heuristic Gaussian sampling from triangles, Mesh-Gaussian binding via midpoints, Splat center derivation from mesh faces
body: Barycentric Splat Parameterization constrains 2D Gaussian Splat centers to lie on triangular mesh faces using barycentric coordinates, allowing splats to move freely on the face while preserving per-splat attributes. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by deriving geometry directly from mesh topology rather than learning unconstrained centers, and from Oriented Gaussian Splatting by explicitly binding splat scales and orientations to local mesh edge vectors and face area. Inputs: Triangular mesh face Fi with vertices v1, v2, v3. Vertex attributes: Position \mathbf{P}i = (\mathbf{p}{i1}, \mathbf{p}{i2}, \mathbf{p}{i3}), Normal \mathbf{N}i = (\mathbf{n}{i1}, \mathbf{n}{i2}, \mathbf{n}{i3}). Barycentric coordinates u, w for the center, and u, v for midpoints. Hyperparameters: u=0.07, v=0.22, \alpha{jk}, \beta{jk}, \delta{jk}. Outputs: Gaussian parameters: center position \mathbf{c}, normal \mathbf{n}, scaling vector \mathbf{s}, rotation basis vectors \mathbf{r}x, \mathbf{r}y, \mathbf{r}z. Data Structures: Barycentric coordinates are scalars u, w, v \in [0, 1] satisfying u+w \le 1 for centers, and specific values for midpoints. Steps: 1. Define Barycentric Interpolation: For any attribute vector \mathbf{A}i = (\mathbf{a}{i1}, \mathbf{a}{i2}, \mathbf{a}{i3}) defined at triangle vertices and barycentric weights (q1, q2, q3), compute the interpolated value: \mathbf{A}i \odot (q1, q2, q3) = q1 \mathbf{a}{i1} + q2 \mathbf{a}{i2} + q3 \mathbf{a}{i3} 2. Compute Splat Center (Optional/General): If deriving a single center per face using general barycentric coordinates u, w: \mathbf{m} = u \cdot \mathbf{v}1 + w \cdot \mathbf{v}2 + (1 - u - w) \cdot \mathbf{v}3 where \mathbf{v}k are the vertex positions. 3. Compute Midpoints for Heuristic Sampling: Define six midpoints \mathbf{m}{jk} on the edges of the triangle using specific barycentric weights derived from hyperparameters u and v: Edge 1-2: \mathbf{m}{12} = \frac{1-u}{2}\mathbf{v}1 + \frac{1-u}{2}\mathbf{v}2 + u\mathbf{v}3 Edge 2-3: \mathbf{m}{23} = \frac{1-u}{2}\mathbf{v}1 + \frac{1-u}{2}\mathbf{v}2 + u\mathbf{v}3 Edge 3-1: \mathbf{m}{31} = \frac{1-u}{2}\mathbf{v}1 + u\mathbf{v}2 + \frac{1-u}{2}\mathbf{v}3 Edge 4-5 (Edge 1-2 variant): \mathbf{m}{45} = \frac{1-v}{2}\mathbf{v}1 + \frac{1-v}{2}\mathbf{v}2 + v\mathbf{v}3 Edge 5-6 (Edge 2-3 variant): \mathbf{m}{56} = \frac{1-v}{2}\mathbf{v}1 + \frac{1-v}{2}\mathbf{v}2 + v\mathbf{v}3 Edge 6-4 (Edge 3-1 variant): \mathbf{m}{64} = \frac{1-v}{2}\mathbf{v}1 + v\mathbf{v}2 + \frac{1-v}{2}\mathbf{v}3 Note: The source lists identical formulas for (1,2) and (2,3) and for (4,5) and (5,6). This implies the midpoints are defined relative to specific edge orientations or vertex orderings not fully detailed in the excerpt, but the barycentric weights are explicitly given. 4. Sample Gaussian Parameters for Each Midpoint \mathbf{m}{jk}: For each midpoint \mathbf{m}{jk}, calculate the Gaussian parameters: a. Center Position: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot \mathbf{P}i b. Normal: \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot \mathbf{N}i c. Edge Vector: Let \mathbf{b}k be the vertex index of the "end" of the edge corresponding to k (e.g., for edge 1-2, k=2). The vector from the midpoint to the vertex is: \mathbf{e} = (\mathbf{b}k \odot \mathbf{P}i) - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot \mathbf{P}i d. Scaling X: sx = \alpha{jk} \|\mathbf{e}\|2 e. Rotation X: \mathbf{r}x = \frac{\mathbf{e}}{\|\mathbf{e}\|2} f. Scaling Y: sy = \frac{\text{Area}(Fi)}{\beta{jk} \|\mathbf{e}\|2} where \text{Area}(Fi) is the area of the triangular face. g. Rotation Y: \mathbf{r}y = \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{r}x h. Scaling Z: sz = \delta{jk} i. Rotation Z: \mathbf{r}z = \mathbf{n} Parameters: Hyperparameters for generalized geometric alignment: u = 0.07 v = 0.22 \alpha{12}=\alpha{23}=\alpha{31}=0.80 \alpha{45}=\alpha{56}=\alpha{64}=2.08 \beta{12}=\beta{23}=\beta{31}=15.0 \beta{45}=\beta{56}=\beta{64}=13.0 \delta{12}=\delta{23}=\delta{31}=\delta{45}=\delta{56}=\delta{64}=4.5 \times 10^{-5} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: If \|\mathbf{e}\|2 \approx 0 (midpoint coincides with vertex), normalization of \mathbf{r}x fails. Guard against division by zero by clamping \|\mathbf{e}\|2 to a small epsilon or skipping such splats. Face Removal: When a mesh face is removed, all splats mapped to it must be identified and flagged for removal. Not given in the sources. Originating from GeoSplatting and OMeGa, this method addresses the lack of inherent geometry boundaries in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by binding splats to explicit mesh surfaces. It enables physically-based inverse rendering by ensuring shape consistency between the Gaussian representation and the underlying mesh geometry. OMeGa: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats for Robust Scene-Level Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00427, fetched 2026-10-30 GeoSplatting: Towards Geometry Guided Gaussian Splatting for Physically-Based Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51701.2025.02692, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction
head: Direct Multi-Plane Image Gaussian Optimization, DirectMPIGO
body: Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction is a neural rendering method that combines voxel-based density representation with Multi-Plane Image (MPI) depth layers to perform efficient volume rendering. It solves the problem of slow convergence and poor surface quality in implicit neural representations by using explicit grid-based features alongside approximate Signed Distance Function (SDF) supervision. Unlike its sibling Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction, which typically predicts Gaussian parameters or raw densities, DirectMPIGO explicitly predicts an SDF value via a feature grid to enable robust surface extraction and regularization. It is significantly faster than implicit-only methods like NeuralRGB-D but requires larger memory footprints due to the explicit grid storage. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera rays (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), scene bounding box (\mathbf{xyz\min}, \mathbf{xyz\max}), MPI depth planes (mpi\depth), and optional pre-computed mask cache. Outputs: Rendered RGB color and alpha (opacity) for each ray. Data Structures: 1. Density Grid: A DenseGrid (or SparseGrid) storing density values. Shape depends on resolution and mpidepth. 2. Feature Grid (k0): Stores color/feature vectors. Channels = rgbnet\dim (or 3 if rgbnet\dim \le 0). 3. Act Shift Grid: A DenseGrid tensor of shape [1, 1, mpi\depth], requiresgrad=False. Stores logit shifts to equalize initial alpha contributions across MPI depth layers. 4. Mask Cache: A boolean tensor of shape maskcacheworldsize. Tracks occupied voxels to skip empty space during rendering. 5. Color MLP: A multi-layer perceptron mapping features to RGB. Parameters: \mathbf{xyz\min}, \mathbf{xyz\max}: Bounding box of the scene. mpi\depth: Number of depth planes in the MPI representation. fast\color\thres: Threshold for occupancy mask updates; voxels with alpha below this are considered empty. rgbnet\dim: Dimension of the color feature vector. If \le 0, uses raw RGB (dim=3) from k0 grid; otherwise uses MLP output dimension. rgbnet\depth: Depth of the color MLP. rgbnet\width: Width of the color MLP. viewbase\pe: Number of positional encoding frequencies for view direction. voxel\size\ratio: Constant ratio 256.0 / mpi\depth. Initialization Steps: 1. Grid Creation: Initialize density grid using grid.creategrid with densitytype, channels=1, and world size derived from setgridresolution. Initialize k0 grid with k0type and channels determined by rgbnet\dim. 2. World Size Calculation: \begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt{\frac{num\voxels}{mpi\depth \cdot \prod (\mathbf{xyz\max} - \mathbf{xyz\min})[:2]}} \\ world\size[:2] &= (\mathbf{xyz\max} - \mathbf{xyz\min})[:2] \cdot r \\ world\size[2] &= mpi\depth \end{aligned} 3. Act Shift Initialization: Initialize density values g[i] = \frac{1.0}{mpi\depth} - 10^{-6} for all i \in [0, mpi\depth). This ensures uniform initial transmittance. Compute conditional probability: p[i] = \begin{cases} 1 - g[0] & i = 0 \\ \frac{1 - \sum{j=0}^{i+1} g[j]}{1 - \sum{j=0}^{i} g[j]} & i > 0 \end{cases} Compute act shift value at layer i: act\shift[i] = \log \left( \left( p[i] \right)^{-1 / voxel\size\ratio} - 1 \right) 4. Color MLP Initialization: If rgbnet\dim \le 0, set k0 channels to 3 and disable the MLP. If rgbnet\dim > 0, create k0 with rgbnet\dim channels. Initialize MLP: Input dim: dim0 = (3 + 3 \cdot viewbase\pe \cdot 2) + k0\dim. Layers: Linear(dim0, rgbnet\width), ReLU, (rgbnet\depth-2) layers of Linear(rgbnet\width, rgbnet\width) + ReLU, final Linear(rgbnet\width, 3). Initialize final bias to 0. Initialize view direction positional encoding buffer with powers of 2: [2^0, 2^1, \dots, 2^{(viewbase\pe-1)}]. 5. Mask Cache Initialization: If maskcachepath is provided, load it; otherwise, create an all-True boolean tensor of size maskcacheworldsize. Rendering Steps: 1. Ray-Bbox Intersection: For each ray, compute intersection [t{min}, t{max}] with the bounding box defined by \mathbf{xyz\min} and \mathbf{xyz\max}. \begin{aligned} t{min} &= \max(\min(\max(\min(ax, bx), \min(ay, by)), \min(az, bz)), near), far) \\ t{max} &= \max(\min(\min(\max(ax, bx), \max(ay, by)), \max(az, bz)), near), far) \end{aligned} Where ax = (\mathbf{xyz\max}x - ox) / dx, etc., with zero division protection. 2. Sample Points: Calculate number of samples N = \lceil (t{max} - t{min}) \cdot \|d\| / stepdist \rceil. Sample points along the ray within [t{min}, t{max}]. 3. Grid Query: Query density and features from the grids at sampled points. 4. Volume Rendering: Composite color and alpha using the MPI depth layers and the act shift values to balance contributions. Occupancy Cache Updates: 1. Update Occupancy Cache: Query density at cache grid points. Activate voxels where alpha > fast\color\thres. Apply maxpool3d(kernel=3, padding=1) and update mask. 2. Update Occupancy Cache (Low Views): For each ray batch, accumulate gradient counts. Update mask where count \ge maskout\lt\nviews. 3. Scale Volume Grid: If new world size product \le 256^3, recompute mask cache by combining old mask with alpha > fast\color\thres after maxpool3d smoothing. Total Variation Gradient Scaling: \begin{aligned} w{xy} &= weight \cdot \frac{\max(world\size[:2])}{128} \\ wz &= weight \cdot \frac{mpi\depth}{128} \end{aligned} GO-Surf is a differentiable volume rendering method that reconstructs high-fidelity 3D surfaces from RGB-D inputs by optimizing a multi-resolution neural feature grid and a lightweight geometry decoder. It solves the problem of slow convergence and poor surface quality in implicit neural representations by combining explicit grid-based features with approximate Signed Distance Function (SDF) supervision. Unlike its sibling Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction, which typically predicts Gaussian parameters or raw densities, GO-Surf explicitly predicts an SDF value via a feature grid to enable robust surface extraction and regularization. It is significantly faster than implicit-only methods like NeuralRGB-D but requires larger memory footprints due to the explicit grid storage. A voxel transformer that predicts residuals added to initial Gaussian rendering attributes on voxels, rather than generating new attributes directly. The transformer takes fused voxel attributes \mathbf{E}j and offset \mathbf{O}j as input. The residual \Delta \mathbf{G}j is computed as: \Delta \mathbf{G}j = \text{MLP}{fine}([\mathbf{O}j, \mathbf{E}j]) The final splat rendering parameter is: \mathbf{G}'j = \mathbf{G}j + \Delta \mathbf{G}j where \mathbf{G}j is the initial rendering parameter. Predicts a set of learnable Gaussian parameters for each voxel v, including center offset, opacity, covariance, and spherical harmonic color. The output dimension per Gaussian is 38, comprising offset (3), opacity (1), covariance (6), and spherical harmonic color (28). The final 3D Gaussian center \muj is computed by: \muj = r \cdot (\sigma(\bar{\mu}j) - 0.5) + \text{Center}j where \sigma is sigmoid, \bar{\mu}j is the predicted offset, \text{Center}j is the voxel centroid, and r is a scaling factor set to 3 times the voxel size. The sigmoid activation restricts the learnable offset to a localized neighborhood; the -0.5 shift facilitates symmetrical, bi-directional movement from the voxel center. Predicts 3D Gaussians directly from input images, bypassing the triplane intermediate representation. This approach results in faster downstream rendering compared to methods that convert triplanes to Gaussians. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of sampled points per ray and the number of MPI depth layers. Sparse grids reduce computation in empty regions. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the explicit grid storage (density, features, act shift). Memory usage scales with world\size and mpi\depth. Performance: Significantly faster than implicit-only methods like NeuralRGB-D. Supports sparse grids for efficiency. Strengths: Efficient volume rendering with MPI layers; explicit grid features allow for faster convergence; supports sparse grids and occupancy caching. Limitations: Larger memory footprint compared to implicit methods; requires careful tuning of grid resolution and MPI depth. When to Use: When fast convergence and high-fidelity surface reconstruction are needed, and memory is not the primary constraint. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely limited or when implicit representations are sufficient for the application. DirectMPIGO was introduced by Kakao Brain as part of the Nerf-Factory repository. It extends the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) method by incorporating Multi-Plane Image (MPI) depth layers, allowing for more efficient volume rendering and better handling of depth information. Unlike DVGO, which uses dense voxel grids, DirectMPIGO supports sparse grids and MPI depth, improving both speed and quality. kakaobrain/nerf-factory, https://github.com/kakaobrain/nerf-factory, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14698v2, fetched 2026-10-27 VolSplat: Rethinking Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Voxel-Aligned Prediction, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37232-11, fetched 2026-10-26 Neural Rendering — Technologies & Tricks, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-NeuralRenderingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splatting Attribute Prediction
head: Hierarchical Network built on residual correction, Residual Design, Residual Gaussian Prediction, Stage-wise Residual Gaussian Prediction, Voxel Transformer Residual Prediction
body: Gaussian Splatting Attribute Prediction is a method for refining 3D Gaussian primitives by predicting additive residuals to initial rendering attributes, rather than regenerating them from scratch. It solves the problem of high-frequency detail loss in coarse initializations by using a voxel transformer to correct errors on a per-voxel basis. Unlike sibling methods that optimize neural feature grids directly, this approach operates on the Gaussian set's geometric and color parameters via residual correction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial Gaussian rendering parameters \mathbf{G}j and fused voxel attributes \mathbf{E}j for a specific voxel j. Output: Refined Gaussian rendering parameters \mathbf{G}'j. Data Structures: Voxel Attributes (\mathbf{E}j): Fused features deposited from splats into a voxel grid. Offset (\mathbf{O}j): Normalized offset vector for the Gaussian primitive center, scaled to [-1, 1] using grid size h. Gaussian Parameters (\mathbf{G}j): Initial set of rendering parameters (position, scale, rotation, color). Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Fusion: Obtain initial Gaussian rendering parameters \mathbf{G}j and voxel attributes \mathbf{E}j through a Splat Fusion procedure. 2. Residual Prediction: Compute the residual \Delta \mathbf{G}j using a fine-grained Multi-Layer Perceptron (\text{MLP}{fine}) that takes the concatenation of the offset \mathbf{O}j and voxel attributes \mathbf{E}j as input. 3. Attribute Update: Add the predicted residual to the initial parameters to obtain the final splat rendering parameters \mathbf{G}'j. Formulas: The residual is defined as: \Delta \mathbf{G}j = \text{MLP}{fine}([\mathbf{O}j, \mathbf{E}j]) where [\cdot] denotes concatenation. The final parameters are updated as: \mathbf{G}'j = \mathbf{G}j + \Delta \mathbf{G}j Parameters: Kernel Function: A one-dimensional cubic kernel K(x) is used in the underlying voxelization/interpolation process: K(x) = \frac{1}{6}(3|x|^3 - 6x^2 + 4) Color Clamping: Color parameters in the renderer allow signed values with no clamping applied, enabling the additive property required for residual correction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The offset \mathbf{O}j must be normalized to [-1, 1] using the grid size h to ensure stable MLP input. Additivity: The renderer must support additive composition of disjoint Gaussian sets for the residual logic to hold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictgaussianattributes(Ginitial, voxelfeatures, offset, gridsizeh): """ Predicts refined Gaussian attributes by adding residuals to initial attributes. Args: Ginitial: Initial Gaussian rendering parameters (tensor). voxelfeatures: Fused voxel attributes Ej (tensor). offset: Raw offset vector for the primitive center. gridsizeh: Grid size used for normalization. Returns: Gfinal: Refined Gaussian rendering parameters. """ # Normalize offset to [-1, 1] range # Implementation detail: Division by gridsizeh assumes linear scaling. Onormalized = offset / gridsizeh # Concatenate offset and voxel attributes # Assuming standard concatenation along the feature dimension. inputfeatures = concatenate(Onormalized, voxelfeatures) # Predict residual using MLP # MLPfine is assumed to be a defined network module with weights theta. residual = MLPfine(inputfeatures) # Add residual to initial parameters Gfinal = Ginitial + residual return Gfinal A broader framework where the entire Gaussian set is updated incrementally across stages, predicting Gaussians that explain the remaining image error. The specific neural architecture used to process voxelized features and predict residuals. Time Complexity: Depends on the MLP size and voxel grid resolution. The method avoids global optimization per frame, enabling feed-forward inference. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the voxel grid and the MLP weights. Strengths: Reduces the learning burden on individual predictors by focusing on remaining error rather than full image content. Allows for efficient refinement of coarse initializations. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial Gaussian set and voxel fusion. When to use: When high-fidelity details are needed from a coarse initialization, or in feed-forward settings where iterative optimization is too slow. When not to use: When the initial Gaussian set is already high-quality and residuals are negligible. The method originates from research into efficient feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the "Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine" approach. It builds on the concept of residual learning in neural networks, applying it to the geometric and color attributes of Gaussian primitives. The additive property of the renderer, which allows for stage-wise reconstruction, was formalized in the AIR framework. name: GO-Surf Neural Feature Grid Optimization
head: GO-Surf
body: GO-Surf is a differentiable volume rendering method that optimizes a multi-resolution neural feature grid to reconstruct high-fidelity 3D surfaces from RGB-D observations. It solves the problem of fast, dense surface reconstruction by combining explicit grid-based feature storage with implicit SDF decoding, significantly reducing optimization time compared to fully implicit MLP-based methods like NeuralRGB-D. It sets itself apart by using a multi-resolution grid to store geometry and color features, allowing for faster convergence and higher detail capture, albeit at the cost of higher memory usage. Inputs: A set of M images with corresponding depth maps D[u, v] and camera poses (translation t \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation parameterized by Lie Algebra \nu \in \mathfrak{so}(3)). A 3D bounding box defining the scene volume. Outputs: Optimized multi-resolution feature grids (geometry and color). Optimized geometry and color decoder MLPs. Optimized camera poses. Rendered color and depth images. Multi-Resolution Feature Grids: The method uses a set of 3D grids with different voxel sizes. Each grid stores feature vectors. Geometry Grids: 4 levels. Voxel sizes: 3cm, 6cm, 24cm, 96cm. Feature dimension per level (hg): 4. Total geometry feature dimension: 16. Color Grids: 4 levels. Voxel sizes: 3cm, 6cm, 24cm, 96cm. Feature dimension per level (hc): 6. Storage: Trilinear interpolation is used to query features from these grids. A custom CUDA kernel is required to support double back-propagation for computing second-order derivatives (Hessian) of the trilinear interpolation. Decoders: Geometry Decoder: Lightweight MLP with 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons each. Takes the concatenated geometry feature vector (16D) as input and outputs the SDF value \phi(x). Color Decoder: Lightweight MLP with 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons each. Takes the concatenated color feature vector (6D) and viewing direction d as input and outputs the RGB color c. Sampling Points: Points xi along a ray are sampled using importance sampling. Coarse samples: Nc = 96. Fine samples: Nf = 36. Total samples per ray: N = Nc + 3 \times 12 + Nf = 96 + 36 + 36 = 168? No, the text says "starting from Nc=96 coarse samples we iteratively add 12 samples each time [3 times]... and Nf=36 fine samples". So N = 96 + 36 + 36 = 168? Or is Nf the total fine? The text says "Nc=96 coarse samples and Nf=36 fine samples". The importance sampling adds 12 samples each time for 3 steps. So intermediate samples = 3 \times 12 = 36. Total N = 96 + 36 + 36 = 168. Loss Weights: \lambda{rgb} = 10.0, \lambda{depth} = 1.0, \lambda{sdf} = 10.0, \lambda{fs} = 1.0, \lambda{eik} = 1.0, \lambda{smooth} = 1.0. Truncation Threshold (t): 16cm. Free Space Exponential Penalty (\alpha): 5. Smoothness Perturbation Length (\deltas): Between 1mm and 4mm. Sigmoid Smoothness Parameter (s): Learnable parameter controlling the transition smoothness of the SDF to opacity. Optimizer: ADAM. Learning rate for MLP decoders: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Learning rate for feature grids: 1 \times 10^{-2}. Learning rate for camera poses: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: M = 6144 rays per batch. Optimization Iterations: 10,000. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def customgridsample(features, coords): # Forward pass: trilinear interpolation # Backward pass: standard gradient # Second backward pass: custom CUDA kernel for Hessian of trilinear interpolation pass class GeometryDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons self.fc1 = nn.Linear(16, 32) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(32, 32) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(32, 1) # Output SDF def forward(self, x): x = F.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc2(x)) return self.fc3(x).squeeze(-1) class ColorDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons self.fc1 = nn.Linear(6, 32) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(32, 32) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(32, 3) # Output RGB def forward(self, x, d): # x is color feature (6D), d is viewing direction # Concatenate if necessary, but text implies input is feature vector # Assuming feature vector is passed directly x = F.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc2(x)) return self.fc3(x) class GOSurf: def init(self, scenebounds, voxelsizes=[0.03, 0.06, 0.24, 0.96]): self.scenebounds = scenebounds self.voxelsizes = voxelsizes # Initialize Geometry Feature Grids (4 levels) # Dimensions depend on scene bounds and voxel sizes self.geofeatures = [nn.Parameter(torch.rand(dims, 4)) for dims in self.getgriddims(scenebounds, voxelsizes)] # Initialize Color Feature Grids (4 levels) self.colorfeatures = [nn.Parameter(torch.rand(dims, 6)) for dims in self.getgriddims(scenebounds, voxelsizes)] # Initialize Decoders self.geodecoder = GeometryDecoder() self.colordecoder = ColorDecoder() # Initialize Camera Poses (t, nu) self.cameraposes = [nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(3)) for in range(numcameras)] # t self.camerarotations = [nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(3)) for in range(numcameras)] # nu in so(3) # Learnable Sigmoid parameter self.s = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0)) # Hyperparameters self.t = 0.16 # 16cm self.alpha = 5 self.deltas = 0.002 # 2mm average self.Nc = 96 self.Nf = 36 self.M = 6144 self.lambdargb = 10.0 self.lambdadepth = 1.0 self.lambdasdf = 10.0 self.lambdafs = 1.0 self.lambdaeik = 1.0 self.lambdasmooth = 1.0 def getgriddims(self, bounds, voxelsizes): # Calculate grid dimensions based on bounds and voxel sizes # Not given in sources, assume standard calculation: ceil((max-min)/voxelsize) pass def initializesurface(self): # Geometric Initialization: Sphere centered at volume origin # Radius = half the size of the smallest dimension mindim = min(self.scenebounds.max - self.scenebounds.min) radius = mindim / 2.0 # Initialize SDF such that phi(x) = ||x|| - radius # This is done by initializing the grid and decoder to approximate this # Specific initialization details for grid values to match sphere are not given, # but the decoder output should be close to ||x|| - radius for all x. pass def querysdf(self, x): # x: (N, 3) coordinates # Get features from multi-resolution grid features = [] for grid in self.geofeatures: # Normalize coordinates to [-1, 1] for grid sampling coords = self.normalizecoords(x) feat = customgridsample(grid, coords) features.append(feat) geofeat = torch.cat(features, dim=-1) # (N, 16) sdf = self.geodecoder(geofeat) return sdf def querycolor(self, x, d): features = [] for grid in self.colorfeatures: coords = self.normalizecoords(x) feat = customgridsample(grid, coords) features.append(feat) colorfeat = torch.cat(features, dim=-1) # (N, 6) color = self.colordecoder(colorfeat, d) return color def normalizecoords(self, x): # Map x from scene bounds to [-1, 1] # Not given in sources, assume standard normalization pass def samplepoints(self, rayso, raysd): # rayso: (M, 3), raysd: (M, 3) # Importance sampling # 1. Coarse sampling: Nc = 96 points uniformly distributed along ray within bounds # 2. Compute weights from coarse samples # 3. Add 12 samples per step for 3 steps based on weights # 4. Fine sampling: Nf = 36 points # Return all points x, depths d, and weights pass def render(self, rayso, raysd): # Sample points points, depths, weights = self.samplepoints(rayso, raysd) # Query SDF and Color sdf = self.querysdf(points) colors = self.querycolor(points, raysd) # Compute Opacity # alphai = max((sigmas(phi(xi)) - sigmas(phi(x{i+1}))) / sigmas(phi(xi)), 0) # sigmas(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-s x)) sval = torch.sigmoid(-self.s sdf) # sigmas(phi) svalnext = torch.sigmoid(-self.s torch.roll(sdf, -1)) # Handle last point svalnext[-1] = 0 # Or some small value alpha = torch.clamp((sval - svalnext) / sval, min=0) # Compute Transmittance # Ti = product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) T = torch.cumprod(1 - alpha, dim=0) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:1]), T[:-1]], dim=0) # Weights w = T alpha # Render Color and Depth renderedcolor = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) colors, dim=0) rendereddepth = torch.sum(w depths, dim=0) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, points, weights def computelosses(self, rayso, raysd, gtcolor, gtdepth): # Render predcolor, preddepth, points, weights = self.render(rayso, raysd) # RGB Loss lrgb = torch.mean(torch.abs(gtcolor - predcolor)) # Depth Loss (only for valid depth pixels) validmask = gtdepth > 0 ldepth = torch.mean(torch.abs(gtdepth[validmask] - preddepth[validmask])) # SDF Supervision # Approximate SDF bound: b(x) = D[u,v] - d # For each point, find the corresponding depth measurement # This requires mapping points back to image coordinates # Implementation detail: Project points to image plane to get D[u,v] # b = gtdepth - pointsdepthalongray # SDF Loss (near surface) # |D[u,v] - d| <= t nearsurfacemask = torch.abs(gtdepth - points[:, 2]) <= self.t # Assuming z is depth # lsdf(x) = |phi(x) - b(x)| b = gtdepth - points[:, 2] # Simplified, need actual depth value at ray intersection # b(x) is the distance to the observed depth surface along the ray # If point is on ray, b(x) = D[u,v] - draypoint # Let's assume we have bvalues for each point lsdf = torch.mean(torch.abs(pointssdf[nearsurfacemask] - bvalues[nearsurfacemask])) # Free Space Loss (far from surface) # |D[u,v] - d| > t farsurfacemask = ~nearsurfacemask # lfs(x) = max(0, exp(-alpha phi(x)) - 1, phi(x) - b(x)) # Applied when |D[u,v] - d| > t # b(x) is still the bound term1 = torch.exp(-self.alpha pointssdf[farsurfacemask]) - 1 term2 = pointssdf[farsurfacemask] - bvalues[farsurfacemask] lfs = torch.mean(torch.clamp(torch.stack([torch.zeroslike(term1), term1, term2], dim=-1), min=0).sum(dim=-1)) # Eikonal Regularization # leik(x) = (1 - ||grad phi(x)||)^2 # Applied on Sfs (far surface points) # Requires gradient of SDF w.r.t x # Use torch.autograd.grad to compute gradient gradphi = torch.autograd.grad(pointssdf[farsurfacemask], points[farsurfacemask], gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(pointssdf[farsurfacemask]), creategraph=True)[0] leik = torch.mean((1 - torch.norm(gradphi, dim=-1))2) # Smoothness Regularization # lsmooth(x) = ||grad phi(x) - grad phi(x + eps)||^2 # Applied on near-surface points # Sample random perturbation eps eps = torch.randnlike(points[nearsurfacemask]) self.deltas pointsperturbed = points[nearsurfacemask] + eps gradphiperturbed = torch.autograd.grad(self.querysdf(pointsperturbed), pointsperturbed, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(self.querysdf(pointsperturbed)), creategraph=True)[0] gradphinear = torch.autograd.grad(pointssdf[nearsurfacemask], points[nearsurfacemask], gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(pointssdf[nearsurfacemask]), creategraph=True)[0] lsmooth = torch.mean((gradphinear - gradphiperturbed)2) # Total Loss loss = (self.lambdargb lrgb + self.lambdadepth ldepth + self.lambdasdf lsdf + self.lambdafs lfs + self.lambdaeik leik + self.lambdasmooth lsmooth) return loss def optimize(self, images, depths, poses): # Initialize surface self.initializesurface() # Optimizer setup optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([ {'params': self.geodecoder.parameters(), 'lr': 1e-3}, {'params': self.colordecoder.parameters(), 'lr': 1e-3}, {'params': self.geofeatures, 'lr': 1e-2}, {'params': self.colorfeatures, 'lr': 1e-2}, {'params': self.cameraposes, 'lr': 5e-4}, {'params': self.camerarotations, 'lr': 5e-4}, {'params': [self.s], 'lr': 1e-3} ]) for i in range(10000): # Sample batch of rays rayso, raysd, gtcolor, gtdepth = self.samplebatchrays(images, depths, poses) # Compute loss loss = self.computelosses(rayso, raysd, gtcolor, gtdepth) # Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Update camera poses # Camera poses are optimized jointly pass Second-Order Derivatives: Computing the Eikonal and smoothness losses requires the Hessian of the SDF. Standard PyTorch autograd does not support double back-propagation through the standard grid sampler for trilinear interpolation. A custom CUDA kernel must be implemented for the second backward pass. Initialization: Poor initialization can lead to local minima. Initializing the SDF to a sphere centered at the volume origin with radius half the smallest dimension helps convergence. Depth Noise: RGB-D sensors often have noisy depth or missing values (e.g., glass). The SDF regularization and RGB loss help mitigate these artifacts. Time Complexity: Optimization takes 15 to 45 minutes depending on scene size. Significantly faster than NeuralRGB-D (15-25 hours). Memory Complexity: Model size scales with scene resolution. Example: 268 MB for 8.8x9.1x3.4m scene (66.5M params). 41 MB for synthetic scene (10.1M params). Larger memory footprint than implicit MLP methods. Strengths: Fast optimization. High-fidelity surface reconstruction. Good hole-filling ability. Captures thin structures. Limitations: High memory usage. Requires custom CUDA kernel for training. When to Use: When fast reconstruction is required. When high-fidelity surface is needed. When memory is not a constraint. When Not to Use: When memory is very limited. When implicit representation is preferred for scalability. GO-Surf was introduced in the paper "GO-Surf: Neural Feature Grid Optimization for Fast, High-Fidelity RGB-D Surface Reconstruction". It builds on the idea of using neural feature grids for scene representation, combining the speed of explicit grids with the flexibility of implicit decoding. It is an improvement over NeuralRGB-D, which uses a single MLP for the entire scene, resulting in slower optimization. GO-Surf uses a multi-resolution grid to store features, allowing for faster convergence and better detail capture. name: Functional Gaussian Splatting Representation
head: DiffGS Representation, Functional Gaussian Splatting, GauCF, GauPF, GauTF, Gaussian Splatting Functions
body: Functional Gaussian Splatting (DiffGS Representation) solves the problem of representing discrete, unstructured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives as continuous, differentiable functions to enable generative modeling. It disentangles the 3DGS representation into three specific functions: Gaussian Probability Function (GauPF) for geometry, Gaussian Color Function (GauCF) for appearance, and Gaussian Transform Function (GauTF) for structural attributes. Unlike sibling methods that modify the primitive shape or storage structure, this representation maps the discrete set of Gaussians to continuous fields, allowing the use of standard generative frameworks like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs). Inputs and Outputs Input: A fitted set of N discrete 3D Gaussians G = \{gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian gi is defined by its center \sigmai, rotation ri, scale si, opacity oi, and color ci. Output: Three continuous functions: GauPF, GauCF, and GauTF. Data Structures The representation relies on a Feature Triplane t to encode the global latent features of the Gaussian set. Layout: t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C \times 3}. Components: Three orthogonal feature planes \{t{XY}, t{XZ}, t{YZ}\} aligned with the coordinate axes. Feature Extraction: For any 3D query location qj, the corresponding feature vector fj is obtained by projecting qj onto the three orthogonal planes and concatenating the tri-linearly interpolated features from each plane. Mathematical Formulation The geometry of the i-th Gaussian is parameterized by center \sigmai and covariance \Sigmai: gi(x) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (x - \sigmai)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \sigmai) \right) where the covariance matrix \Sigmai is factorized into rotation ri and scale si as: \Sigmai = ri si si^T ri^T Here, ri \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) and si \in \mathbb{R} (scale vector/matrix depending on implementation, typically diagonal). The appearance is controlled by opacity oi \in \mathbb{R} and color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3. The Three Functions 1. Gaussian Probability Function (GauPF): Models the geometry by predicting the probability that a sampled 3D location qj is a Gaussian center. The ground truth probability pj for a query qj is defined based on the distance to the nearest Gaussian center: pj = \text{GauPF}(qj) = \tau \left( \lambda \left( \min{i \in [1,N]} ||qj - \sigmai||^2 \right) \right) where \lambda is a truncation function that filters extremely large distances, and \tau is a continuous function mapping distances to the range [0,1]. 2. Gaussian Color Function (GauCF): Predicts the color attribute ci given the Gaussian center \sigmai: \{ci\} = \text{GauCF}(\sigmai) 3. Gaussian Transform Function (GauTF): Predicts the rotation ri, scale si, and opacity oi given the Gaussian center \sigmai: \{ri, si, oi\} = \text{GauTF}(\sigmai) Prediction via Neural Predictors Given the feature triplane t and a query location qj, the system first extracts features fj = \text{interp}(t, qj). Then, neural predictors \psi{pf}, \psi{cf}, \psi{tf} predict the attributes: \{\hat{p}i\} = \psi{pf}(fj), \quad \{\hat{c}i\} = \psi{cf}(fj), \quad \{\hat{r}i, \hat{s}i, \hat{o}i\} = \psi{tf}(fj) where \hat{p}i, \hat{c}i, \hat{r}i, \hat{s}i, \hat{o}i are the predicted probability, color, rotation, scale, and opacity, respectively. Training Objectives The representation is typically trained within a Gaussian VAE framework. 1. VAE Loss: Combines an L1 reconstruction loss and a KL-divergence regularization term: L{VAE} = ||\{\hat{p}, \hat{c}, \hat{r}, \hat{s}, \hat{o}\} - \{p, c, r, s, o\}||1 + \beta (D{KL}(Q\phi(z|G) || P(z))) where Q\phi(z|G) is the inferred posterior distribution of the latent vector z, and P(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I) is the standard normal prior. 2. LDM Loss: If a Latent Diffusion Model is used for generation, the loss follows the standard denoising objective: L{LDM} = \mathbb{E}{z0, t, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)} ||\epsilon - \epsilon\sigma(zt, \delta(y), t)||^2 where \epsilon\sigma is the noise predictor conditioned on time step t and condition embedding \delta(y) via cross-attention. Pseudocode: Feature Triplane Query and Attribute Prediction Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gettriplanefeature(triplanet, querypointq): """ Extracts features from the triplane for a 3D query point. triplanet: Tensor of shape (3, H, W, C) representing [tXY, tXZ, tYZ] querypointq: Array of shape (3,) representing (x, y, z) Returns: Feature vector fj """ # Project query point onto the three orthogonal planes # tXY: project (x, y, z) -> (x, y) # tXZ: project (x, y, z) -> (x, z) # tYZ: project (x, y, z) -> (y, z) coordsxy = querypointq[:2] # (x, y) coordsxz = [querypointq[0], querypointq[2]] # (x, z) coordsyz = querypointq[1:] # (y, z) # Tri-linear interpolation (or bi-linear for 2D planes) at projected coordinates # Note: Standard triplane implementations use bi-linear interpolation on 2D planes. # Assuming 'interp' handles normalization of coordinates to [0,1] or [-1,1] fxy = interpolatebilinear(triplanet[0], coordsxy) fxz = interpolatebilinear(triplanet[1], coordsxz) fyz = interpolatebilinear(triplanet[2], coordsyz) # Concatenate features from all three planes fj = concatenate([fxy, fxz, fyz]) return fj def predictgaussianattributes(fj): """ Predicts Gaussian attributes from the extracted feature vector. fj: Feature vector from gettriplanefeature Returns: Predicted probability, color, rotation, scale, opacity """ # Apply neural predictors phat = psipf(fj) chat = psicf(fj) rhat, shat, ohat = psitf(fj) return phat, chat, rhat, shat, ohat Edge Cases and Pitfalls Truncation: The GauPF relies on a truncation function \lambda to handle points far from any Gaussian center; failure to truncate can lead to numerical instability or incorrect probability mapping. Discretization: While the representation is continuous, the final output requires extracting discrete Gaussians. The source notes an "octree-guided sampling and optimization" algorithm for this extraction, implying that naive sampling from the continuous functions may not yield optimal discrete primitives without this post-processing step. Complexity: The representation itself is a continuous function evaluation, which is computationally lightweight during inference compared to managing large discrete lists. However, training requires encoding the entire Gaussian set into a latent vector and decoding to a triplane, adding overhead. Strengths: Enables the use of powerful generative models (VAEs, LDMs) on 3DGS data by solving the discreteness and unstructured nature of raw Gaussians. Allows for conditional generation (e.g., from text) and unconditional generation of Gaussians at arbitrary numbers. Limitations: Requires a discretization/extraction algorithm to convert the continuous functions back into renderable 3DGS primitives, which adds complexity to the pipeline. When to use: When the goal is to generate 3D Gaussian Splatting representations using diffusion models or to compress 3DGS into a latent space for efficient storage/transmission. Functional Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the paper "DiffGS: Functional Gaussian Splatting Diffusion". The method addresses the challenge that the discrete and unstructured nature of 3DGS prevents the direct application of well-studied generative frameworks. By disentangling the representation into GauPF, GauCF, and GauTF, the authors enable the training of a Gaussian VAE and a Latent Diffusion Model (based on the DALLE-2 architecture) to generate high-fidelity 3DGS. name: InnerGS Volumetric Rendering
head: Factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inner Scenes
body: InnerGS is a volumetric rendering method that models continuous 3D density using 3D Gaussians to synthesize novel 2D slices at arbitrary depths, avoiding the discrete projection artifacts of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike standard 3DGS which renders pixels via perspective projection of splats onto a camera plane, InnerGS calculates the contribution of each Gaussian directly to a pixel on a 2D slice at a specific depth t along a given axis. This approach enables seamless volumetric interpolation and explicit internal structure reconstruction, making it suitable for applications like medical imaging where internal slices are required. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance (geometry), opacity \alphai, and color ci (derived from Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction). A target slice depth t and pixel coordinates (u, v). Outputs: The final color I(u, v, t) for the pixel on the slice at depth t. Data Structures The method operates on a list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i contains: \mathbf{\mu}i: 3D center position. \mathbf{\Sigma}i: 3D covariance matrix (defining shape/orientation). \alphai: Scalar opacity. ci: Color value (e.g., RGB or SH coefficients). Algorithm Steps 1. Candidate Selection: Identify candidate Gaussians for the target slice. The method sorts Gaussians based on the distance between their centers \mathbf{\mu}i and the slice plane at depth t. Two methods are described for bounding box adaptation: Method 1: Projects a fixed cubic bounding box onto every slice. Method 2: Computes an adapted bounding box for each slice. Method 2 is preferred for efficiency, reducing average bounding box area and false positives, though it introduces a small rate of false negatives. 2. Contribution Calculation: For each pixel (u, v) on the slice at depth t, calculate the scalar contribution pi(u, v, t) of each candidate Gaussian i. This value represents the volumetric density contribution of Gaussian i at that specific 2D location and depth. 3. Volumetric Accumulation: Compute the final color I(u, v, t) using alpha compositing, accounting for the transmittance of preceding Gaussians. Formulas The final color is computed as: I(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^{N} pi(u, v, t)\alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(u, v, t)\alphaj) Where: I(u, v, t): Final color of pixel (u, v) on the slice at depth t. N: Total number of Gaussians. pi(u, v, t): Contribution (density/weight) of Gaussian i at pixel (u, v) and depth t. \alphai: Opacity of Gaussian i. ci: Color of Gaussian i. The product term \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(u, v, t)\alphaj) represents the transmittance, ensuring Gaussians are composited in sorted order (typically by distance to the slice). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderinnerslice(gaussians, slicedeptht, pixelu, pixelv): """ Renders a single pixel on a 2D slice at depth t using InnerGS. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: center: (x, y, z) cov: 3x3 covariance matrix alpha: float opacity color: float3 color slicedeptht: Float, depth along the axis perpendicular to the slice. pixelu, pixelv: Integers, pixel coordinates on the slice. Returns: color: Float3, the accumulated color for the pixel. """ # Step 1: Filter and Sort Candidates # Calculate distance from each Gaussian center to the slice plane. # Note: The exact geometric projection of the Gaussian onto the slice # to compute pi(u,v,t) is implementation-specific to the Gaussian's # covariance and the slice orientation. We assume a helper function exists. candidates = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Calculate distance from Gaussian center to the slice plane at t dist = distancetoslice(g.center, slicedeptht) candidates.append((dist, i)) # Sort by distance (closest first) for correct alpha compositing candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Step 2: Volumetric Accumulation transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for dist, i in candidates: g = gaussians[i] # Calculate contribution pi(u, v, t) # This function computes the Gaussian's density/weight at the specific # pixel (u,v) on the slice at depth t. pi = computegaussiancontribution(g, pixelu, pixelv, slicedeptht) # If contribution is negligible, skip (optimization) if pi < 1e-6: continue # Alpha compositing alphacontribution = pi g.alpha # Update accumulated color # I = Iprev + (1 - Tprev) alpha color accumulatedcolor += transmittance alphacontribution g.color # Update transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - alphacontribution) # Early exit if fully opaque if transmittance < 1e-4: break return accumulatedcolor def computegaussiancontribution(gaussian, u, v, t): """ Computes the scalar contribution pi(u, v, t) of a Gaussian to a pixel on a slice at depth t. Note: The exact mathematical formulation for pi depends on how the 3D Gaussian is projected/intersected with the 2D slice plane. Standard 3DGS uses 2D projection; InnerGS uses volumetric density evaluation at the slice location. """ # Placeholder for the specific density evaluation function. # In a typical implementation, this involves evaluating the 3D Gaussian # PDF at the 3D point corresponding to pixel (u,v) at depth t, # potentially adjusted for the slice's normal vector. # For example, if the slice is the XY plane at Z=t: # point = (u, v, t) # pi = exp(-0.5 (point - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (point - mu)) # This value is then normalized or scaled appropriately. pass Parameters Density Threshold: 0.01. Used during simulation analysis to decide whether a Gaussian is considered "active" at a given pixel. Initial Positions: Uniform 3D grid of 423 points. Used as initialization for Gaussian centers in MRI reconstruction experiments. Training Iterations: Maximum 1,000 iterations or until absolute loss decrease over 100 iterations falls below 1 \times 10^{-4}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls False Negatives: Method 2 (adapted bounding boxes) introduces false negatives (0.126 per pixel) compared to Method 1, meaning some high-density Gaussians might be missed. Precision: The method relies on accurate distance calculations between Gaussian centers and the slice plane to ensure correct sorting and candidate selection. Time Complexity: Rendering time is reduced compared to standard projection methods. In simulation tests on a 20 \times 20 \times 20 volume with 50 Gaussians, Method 2 (InnerGS) took 0.10s per slice compared to 0.69s for Method 1 (3D Ellipsoid Projection). Memory/Processing: Method 2 processes fewer candidate Gaussians per pixel (2.62 vs 16.70) and has a smaller average bounding box area (63.09 vs 209.80). Strengths: Enables synthesis of novel slices at arbitrary depths without relying on projection; provides continuous volumetric interpolation; explicit and explainable representation suitable for medical imaging. Limitations: Introduces a small rate of false negatives in candidate selection; requires careful handling of the contribution function pi(u, v, t) which differs from standard 2D rasterization. Hardware: Experiments conducted on NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. InnerGS was introduced to address the limitation of standard 3DGS, which fails to capture continuous volumetric information between discrete slices, leading to incomplete internal representations. It combines the continuous nature of NeRF-like interpolation with the explicit efficiency of discrete Gaussian representations. The method was specifically designed for internal scene reconstruction and segmentation, with applications in medical imaging such as Brain MRI reconstruction. name: HO-Gaussian
head: Hybrid Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: HO-Gaussian is a point-free representation method for multi-camera urban scenes that combines a grid-based volume with the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipeline to eliminate dependency on Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point initialization. It solves the problem of rendering low-texture, sky, and distant areas in large-scale urban environments where standard 3DGS fails due to sparse or outlier-prone SfM data. Unlike standard 3DGS, which relies on well-initialized point clouds, HO-Gaussian learns Gaussian positions directly from a grid volume, uses Gaussian Directional Encoding to replace spherical harmonics for view-dependent color, and applies neural warping to ensure consistency across multiple camera viewpoints. Inputs: Multi-view RGB images from a multi-camera setup (e.g., autonomous driving rigs); no SfM point cloud or LiDAR data required. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with optimized positions, opacities, and view-dependent colors; rendered novel views. Data Structures: 1. Grid-Based Volume: A 3D voxel grid storing features used for position prediction and directional encoding. The specific resolution and channel dimensions are not given in the sources. 2. Gaussian Set: A collection of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i: Learned from the grid volume, not initialized from points. Opacity \alphai: Standard scalar. Color \mathbf{c}i: Encoded via Gaussian Directional Encoding (GDE) from the grid volume, replacing spherical harmonics coefficients. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the grid-based volume and the Gaussian set without using SfM points or LiDAR, relying solely on supervised information from images. 2. Position Learning: Query the grid-based volume to predict the 3D position \mathbf{p}i for each Gaussian, facilitating the learning of geometric information in sky, distant, and low-texture areas. 3. Gaussian Directional Encoding (GDE): Compute view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i using the grid volume features instead of storing high-order spherical harmonic functions, which reduces disk space requirements from gigabytes to megabytes. 4. Neural Warping: Generate virtual viewpoints and warp features from observed cameras to these viewpoints to enhance consistent appearance and geometry across multiple cameras, reducing overfitting to specific viewpoints. 5. Hybrid Optimization: Iteratively optimize the grid-based volume and the Gaussian parameters (positions, opacities, GDE features) using gradient descent on the rendering loss between rendered images and ground truth RGB images. 6. Point Densification: At regular intervals during training, add new Gaussian positions to regions with high error, low texture, or distant areas, and fine-tune these positions via gradient descent in the Gaussian pipeline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hogaussiantraining(images, cameraposes, numiterations, densificationinterval): def initializegridvolume(): pass # Not given in sources def initializegaussians(): pass # Not given in sources def samplebatch(imgs, poses): return imgs[0], poses[0] # Not given in sources def querygrid(vol, pos): return pos # Not given in sources def querydirectionalencoding(vol, pos, cams): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Not given in sources def generatevirtualviews(cams): return cams # Not given in sources def warpfeatures(vol, cams, views): return [0.0] # Not given in sources def rasterizegaussians(gs, cams): return [0.0] # Not given in sources def computerenderingloss(rendered, gt): return 0.0 # Not given in sources def computewarpingloss(warped, gt): return 0.0 # Not given in sources def gradientdescent(vol, gs, loss): return vol, gs # Not given in sources def densifygaussians(gs, vol, errors): return gs # Not given in sources gridvolume = initializegridvolume() gaussians = initializegaussians() for iteration in range(numiterations): batchimages, batchcameras = samplebatch(images, cameraposes) for g in gaussians: g.position = querygrid(gridvolume, g.initialpos) for g in gaussians: g.color = querydirectionalencoding(gridvolume, g.position, batchcameras) virtualviews = generatevirtualviews(batchcameras) warpedfeatures = warpfeatures(gridvolume, batchcameras, virtualviews) renderedimages = rasterizegaussians(gaussians, batchcameras) loss = computerenderingloss(renderedimages, batchimages) loss += computewarpingloss(warpedfeatures, batchimages) gridvolume, gaussians = gradientdescent(gridvolume, gaussians, loss) if iteration % densificationinterval == 0: gaussians = densifygaussians(gaussians, gridvolume, renderingerrors) return gridvolume, gaussians Parameters: Densification Interval: Not given in the sources. Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. Spherical Harmonics Degree: Replaced by GDE; not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low-Texture Regions: Standard 3DGS treats these as outliers; HO-Gaussian uses grid volume learning and densification to address this. Distant/Sky Areas: SfM points are sparse here; HO-Gaussian learns positions from the grid volume to improve representation. Multi-Camera Consistency: Without neural warping, views from different cameras may conflict; warping ensures mutual learning. Disk Space: Standard 3DGS with spherical harmonics requires gigabytes for large scenes; HO-Gaussian reduces this to ~123MB for the evaluated scene. A technique replacing spherical harmonics with grid-based directional encoding to reduce disk space and model view-dependent color. It sets itself apart by eliminating the need to store high-order coefficients. Choose it when disk space is a constraint in large-scale scenes. Link is a sibling but focuses on textured primitives, not directional encoding. A scheme for multi-camera consistency by warping features to virtual viewpoints. It sets itself apart by enabling mutual learning between camera perspectives. Choose it for multi-camera urban scenes. Link is a sibling but focuses on deformation, not warping for consistency. Time Complexity: Training time is 76 minutes on the evaluated urban scene (Argoverse dataset). Memory Complexity: Model size is 123MB, significantly smaller than baseline 3DGS (557MB) and NeRF-based methods (e.g., LocalRF 3762MB). Measured Performance: On the Argoverse dataset, HO-Gaussian achieves PSNR 30.98, SSIM 0.9043, LPIPS 0.2287 with RGB input only. Rendering Speed: 71 FPS on the evaluated urban scene. Scaling: The method is designed for large-scale urban scenes and multi-camera systems. It scales by using grid-based volume for efficient position and color encoding, avoiding the O(N) storage of spherical harmonics per Gaussian. Strengths: Point-free initialization (no SfM/LiDAR needed), reduced disk space, real-time rendering, good performance in low-texture/distant areas, multi-camera consistency. Limitations: Relies on grid volume learning. When to use: Large-scale urban scene reconstruction from multi-camera RGB data where SfM points are sparse or unreliable. HO-Gaussian was proposed by Li et al. in the paper "HO-Gaussian: Hybrid Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Urban Scenes". It addresses limitations of previous 3DGS-based methods in urban scenes, specifically their reliance on SfM points and difficulties in rendering distant, sky, and low-texture areas. The method was evaluated on the Argoverse and Waymo datasets for autonomous driving scenarios. It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline but introduces hybrid optimization with a grid-based volume, Gaussian Directional Encoding, and neural warping.
