name: Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction
head: GRM, Generalizable Reconstruction Method
body: Feed-forward and generalizable prediction maps input images directly to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\} without per-scene gradient descent [Parent]. It solves the latency bottleneck of traditional 3D Gaussian Splatting, which requires minutes of optimization per scene, by learning a global prior from large datasets to enable real-time inference on unseen scenes [Parent]. It distinguishes itself from iterative methods by replacing optimization with a single forward pass of a neural network, and from implicit methods by producing explicit, rasterizable primitives that support high-fidelity novel view synthesis and mesh extraction [Parent]. All methods in this family share the core objective of mapping input image features to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\} without per-scene gradient descent [Parent]. 1. Input Representation: Inputs are typically one or more RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Some methods require known camera poses P, while others (e.g., Splatt3R, ZeroGS) predict poses or operate on uncalibrated inputs [Parent]. 2. Feature Encoding: A shared encoder (e.g., Vision Transformer, CNN) extracts multi-scale features from the input images. Cross-attention or cost volumes are often used to aggregate multi-view information [Parent]. 3. Primitive Prediction: A decoder head predicts Gaussian attributes. These attributes are usually: Mean (\mu): 3D position. Covariance (\Sigma): Defined by scale s and rotation r (quaternion or 6D). Opacity (\alpha): Scalar. Color (c): Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients or constant RGB [Parent]. 4. Differentiable Rendering: The predicted Gaussians are rendered into target views using differentiable rasterization to compute reconstruction losses (e.g., L1, SSIM, LPIPS) for training the network [Parent]. 5. Generalization: The network is trained on a large dataset of scenes to learn priors about geometry and appearance, allowing inference on unseen scenes [Parent]. HFGaussian is a generalizable, feed-forward framework for real-time 3D human avatar reconstruction that simultaneously estimates novel views, 3D pose, and biomechanical features (such as dense pose and 3D keypoints) from sparse input images. Unlike sibling methods that rely on parametric body models (e.g., SMPL) or fail to integrate structural biomechanics, HFGaussian uses Gaussian splatting to represent the human subject and its associated features directly. It builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction by introducing a "feature splatting" mechanism that decouples human feature learning from the geometric Gaussian parameters, allowing different frequencies of features to be rendered efficiently without per-subject optimization. ZeroGS is a pipeline for training 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from hundreds of unposed and unordered images without requiring Structure-from-Motion (SfM) tools like COLMAP. It differs from its siblings by leveraging a pretrained foundation model (Spann3R) as a neural scene representation and employing an incremental training buffer to progressively register images and refine poses. Unlike ACE0, which predicts sparse points using CNNs, ZeroGS predicts dense pointmaps and 3D Gaussians using transformers and optimizes the scene via rendering loss rather than reprojection error. Shape Completion Training is a feed-forward method that predicts all 14 3D Gaussian attributes from partial, incomplete inputs without requiring target coordinates or per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a fixed 2×2 folding grid to expand a small set of coarse primitives into a dense Gaussian set, enabling robust reconstruction of missing geometry in occluded or sparse scenes. RLSplat is a resource-linear, budget-controllable feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) framework that generates exactly B Gaussians for a given scene, ensuring that inference latency and peak memory scale linearly with the requested budget. Unlike prior budget-controllable methods (e.g., EcoSplat, F4 Splat) that predict a dense set of candidates and prune them—resulting in nearly constant inference costs regardless of the target budget—RLSplat uses a learned Gaussian allocation policy to distribute exactly B Gaussians across local scene regions from the start. This approach allows the representation size, inference latency, and peak memory to decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget B is reduced, while maintaining or exceeding the reconstruction quality of denser baselines at lower resource costs. Feed-forward generalizable reconstruction maps input images directly to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\} without per-scene gradient descent [Parent]. It solves the latency bottleneck of traditional 3D Gaussian Splatting, which requires minutes of optimization per scene, by learning a global prior from large datasets to enable real-time inference on unseen scenes [Parent]. It distinguishes itself from iterative methods by replacing optimization with a single forward pass of a neural network, and from implicit methods by producing explicit, rasterizable primitives that support high-fidelity novel view synthesis and mesh extraction [Parent]. Feature Uplifting via Forward Rendering is a method to estimate 3D language features f \in \mathbb{R}^d for 3D Gaussians from observed 2D features F{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^d by formulating the problem as a Maximum Likelihood (ML) or Maximum-a-Posteriori (MAP) estimation, assuming uniform prior and Gaussian noise. It differs from back-projection methods (e.g., conventional semantic feature learning) by leveraging the forward rendering process to establish precise correspondence, eliminating costly back-projection or iterative optimization. It builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction. Occam's LGS is a training-free method for lifting 2D language features to 3D Gaussian representations by applying Occam’s razor to the forward rendering process of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of expensive iterative optimization in feature space by computing weighted multi-view feature aggregation directly from the alpha blending weights of the standard color rendering pass. Unlike sibling methods that rely on scene-specific autoencoders, quantization, or costly semantic feature rendering, Occam's LGS supports arbitrary-dimensional uncompressed features without compromising training speed, achieving a two-order-of-magnitude speed-up while maintaining state-of-the-art performance for open-set vision-language tasks. A 3D-aware image synthesis generator that predicts color and density values on a sparse voxel grid, conditioned on camera pose. Use a mapping network with 2 layers and 64 channels. Set the channel base to 4000 (reduced from StyleGAN2's 32768) to account for higher parameter count in 3D convolutions. Implement skip connections that add an upsampled version of the output grid of the previous layer to the input of the next layer. Condition the generator on a camera pose represented by a rotation matrix and a translation vector, yielding a 12-dimensional input vector. Output coefficients of spherical harmonics for color; use degree 0 (single coefficient per color channel). Multiply the network's density output by a factor of 30 to facilitate generating high density values for sharp surfaces. Channel base: 4000. Density multiplier: 30. Mapping network layers: 2. Mapping network channels: 64. Spherical harmonics degree: 0. An MLP network F\theta that maps 3D Gaussian coordinates and time to deviations in position, rotation, and scaling. Input: 3D Gaussian coordinate x and time t. Process: Pass through eight fully connected layers with ReLU activations and 256-dimensional hidden layers to output a 256-dimensional feature vector. Concatenate the feature vector and the input in the fourth layer. Output: Pass the feature vector through three additional fully connected layers (without activation) to separately output offsets \delta x, \delta r, \delta s for position, rotation, and scaling. Hidden layer dimension: 256. Number of initial fully connected layers: 8. Number of output layers: 3 (one for each offset). Activation function: ReLU for hidden layers, none for output layers. Additional storage compared to 3D Gaussians: 2MB. Does not use grid/plane-based structures because dynamic scenes have higher rank than static scenes, and explicit point-based rendering exacerbates this rank. A 3DGS-based human avatar modeling framework that reconstructs animatable and relightable human avatars from monocular video by decomposing geometry and appearance attributes and using dynamic skinning weights for pose-variant deformation. Encode Gaussian attributes using the Gaussian Attributes Encoder DG, which consists of two sub-encoders Dg and Da. Both are multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) that take the Gaussian position x as input and output the corresponding geometric and appearance attributes, respectively. Articulate the human avatar by applying Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) transformations using the dynamic skinning weights W{\Thetat} to deform the 3D Gaussians from canonical space to posed space. Optimize the RnD-Avatar through a Physically-Based Rendering (PBR) process to optimize geometric attributes (position and normal) and appearance attributes (albedo, roughness, and visibility). Render photorealistic images given an environmental light by performing a PBR process on the optimized avatar. Start from the same feed-forward scene initialization. Keep the Gaussian centers fixed during all updates. Number of input views averaged over during evaluation: N = 4, 8, 16. On ETH3D, learned refinement improves PSNR by 0.64 dB compared to the feed-forward baseline. Outperforms Direct Gradient Descent (Adam) on all four metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS) and yields stronger surface quality with fewer artifacts. The concept of generalizable reconstruction from images has evolved from iterative Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) pipelines to deep learning-based approaches. Early feed-forward methods focused on predicting depth or sparse point clouds [Parent]. With the advent of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Parent], the field shifted towards predicting explicit Gaussian primitives directly from images to bypass the slow per-scene optimization typically required by 3DGS. The term "Generalizable Reconstruction Method" (GRM) appears in recent surveys as a category for methods that utilize existing multi-view generation models to train a pixel-aligned Gaussian representation for faithful 3D generation using a single feed-forward pass. This approach contrasts with traditional 3DGS which requires minutes of optimization per scene [Parent]. Key developments include: Pose-Free and Unposed Input: Methods like ZeroGS [16425-zerogs.md] and Splatt3R [16423-splatt3r.md] extend feed-forward prediction to uncalibrated or unposed images, using foundation models (e.g., DUSt3R, Spann3R) to estimate geometry and poses jointly with Gaussians [Parent]. Resource Efficiency: Frameworks like RLSplat [16575-rlsplat.md] introduce budget-controllable inference, ensuring that memory and latency scale linearly with the number of Gaussians, addressing the high resource cost of dense Gaussian sets. Feature Lifting: Extensions such as Feature Uplifting [16969-feature-uplifting-via-forward-rendering.md] and Occam's LGS [16973-occam-s-lgs.md] demonstrate how 2D semantic or language features can be lifted to 3D Gaussians using the forward rendering process, avoiding iterative optimization in feature space. Human Avatars: Specialized methods like HFGaussian [16422-hfgaussian.md] and RnD-Avatar apply feed-forward principles to human reconstruction, integrating biomechanical features and dynamic skinning weights. The family also includes variants for specific tasks such as shape completion [16514-shape-completion-training.md], dynamic scene reconstruction via deformation fields, and 3D-aware image synthesis using sparse voxel grids. name: HFGaussian
head: Human Feature Gaussian
body: HFGaussian is a generalizable, feed-forward framework for real-time 3D human avatar reconstruction that simultaneously estimates novel views, 3D pose, and biomechanical features (such as dense pose and 3D keypoints) from sparse input images. Unlike sibling methods that rely on parametric body models (e.g., SMPL) or fail to integrate structural biomechanics, HFGaussian uses Gaussian splatting to represent the human subject and its associated features directly. It builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction by introducing a "feature splatting" mechanism that decouples human feature learning from the geometric Gaussian parameters, allowing different frequencies of features to be rendered efficiently without per-subject optimization. HFGaussian operates in two stages: depth estimation and joint Gaussian/pose/feature prediction. It uses two nearest source views to estimate depth, which informs the 3D position of Gaussians and provides point cloud data for pose regression. Inputs: Two RGB images Il, Ir \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} corresponding to the left and right nearest source views, and their known camera parameters. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{X, c, r, s, \alpha, f\}, where X is position, c is color, r is rotation, s is scaling, \alpha is opacity, and f is the human feature vector. Rendered novel view images. Estimated 3D pose (19 keypoints). Human features (continuous surface embeddings/dense pose). The scene is represented as a set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color (RGB). ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. fi \in \mathbb{R}^d: Human feature vector (dimension d depends on the specific feature, e.g., dense pose embedding). 1. View Selection: Select the two nearest source views, Il and Ir, relative to the target view. 2. Image Encoding: Feed Il and Ir into a shared image encoder \epsilon{img} to generate multiscale image features f^ls and f^rs, where s is the feature scale. 3. Cost Volume & Depth Estimation: Generate a cost volume C by correlating the feature maps f^ls and f^rs. Use an iterative update mechanism on C to estimate depth maps Dl and Dr for the left and right views. 4. Gaussian Feature Generation: Encode the depth maps Dl, Dr using a depth encoder \epsilon{depth}. Combine the encoded depth features with the image features f{img} (concatenation \oplus) and pass them through a U-Net-like decoder \epsilon{params} to generate a Gaussian feature map \Gamma: \Gamma = \epsilon{params}(\epsilon{img}(I) \oplus \epsilon{depth}(I)) Apply four separate convolutional prediction heads to \Gamma to estimate parameter maps for rotation (Mr), scaling (Ms), opacity (M\alpha), and human features (Mf). The human feature map is defined as: Mf = \text{Sigmoid}(hf(\Gamma(x))) where hf is the feature head and x is the foreground pixel coordinate. 5. Gaussian Parameter Mapping: Map 2D pixel coordinates x to 3D positions X using the predicted depth and camera parameters via map Mp. Extract color c directly from the source images via map Mc. The full Gaussian set is \mathcal{G} = \{Mp(x), Mc(x), Mr(x), Ms(x), M\alpha(x), Mf(x)\}. 6. Pose Regression: Generate point clouds Pl, Pr from depth maps Dl, Dr and camera parameters. Extract human point clouds using 2D masks. Combine point clouds from both views into a single point cloud. Randomly sample 2048 points to form Pc. Input Pc into a pose regression network (based on DGCNN and PointNet) to estimate 3D pose (19 keypoints). 7. Feature Splatting (Rendering Features): Project Gaussians into 2D space using view transformation matrix W and Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transform. Calculate the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma': \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T where \Sigma is the 3D covariance matrix derived from r and s. Render human feature vectors fp by splatting Gaussian features fi in the image plane using alpha composition: fp = \sum{i \in N} fi \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) where \alpha'i is the opacity \alphai multiplied by the 2D Gaussian value, and N is the set of splatted Gaussians. Decode the blended feature vectors fp using an MLP with two linear layers (ReLU activation) followed by a final sigmoid layer to render continuous surface embeddings. 8. Color Rendering: Render final pixel colors C using alpha blending: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) where ci is the learned color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def HFGaussianforward(Il, Ir, cameraparams): """ Il, Ir: RGB images (H, W, 3) cameraparams: Intrinsics and extrinsics for Il and Ir Returns: Rendered image, 3D pose, Feature map, Gaussians """ # 1. Image Encoding # Shared encoder generates multiscale features fl = epsilonimg(Il) fr = epsilonimg(Ir) # 2. Depth Estimation # Cost volume correlation and iterative update C = correlatecostvolume(fl, fr) Dl, Dr = iterativedepthupdate(C) # 3. Gaussian Parameter Estimation # Encode depth and combine with image features depthfeat = epsilondepth(Dl) # or combined depth encoding imgfeat = epsilonimg(Il) # or combined image encoding Gamma = epsilonparams(depthfeat + imgfeat) # U-Net decoder # Prediction heads Mr = convheadrotation(Gamma) Ms = convheadscaling(Gamma) Malpha = convheadopacity(Gamma) Mf = sigmoid(convheadfeature(Gamma)) # Human feature map # Map 2D pixels to 3D Gaussians # Mp uses predicted depth and camera params Gaussians = [] for pixel in foregroundpixels: X = Mp(pixel, Dl, cameraparams) c = getcolor(Il, pixel) # From source image r = Mr(pixel) s = Ms(pixel) alpha = Malpha(pixel) f = Mf(pixel) Gaussians.append(Gaussian(X, c, r, s, alpha, f)) # 4. Pose Regression # Generate point clouds from depth Pl = depthtopointcloud(Dl, cameraparams) Pr = depthtopointcloud(Dr, cameraparams) # Filter by 2D masks (assumed available or pre-computed) Plhuman = filterbymask(Pl, maskl) Prhuman = filterbymask(Pr, maskr) # Combine and sample Pcombined = combinepointclouds(Plhuman, Prhuman) Psampled = randomsample(Pcombined, 2048) # Estimate 3D pose pose = poseregressionnetwork(Psampled) # DGCNN + PointNet # 5. Rendering # Project Gaussians projectedgaussians = projectgaussians(Gaussians, cameraparams) # Sort by depth for alpha blending projectedgaussians.sortbydepth() # Render Color renderedcolor = alphablendcolor(projectedgaussians) # Render Features (Feature Splatting) renderedfeatures = alphablendfeatures(projectedgaussians) # Decode features decodedfeatures = featuremlp(renderedfeatures) # 2 Linear + ReLU + Sigmoid return renderedcolor, pose, decodedfeatures, Gaussians def alphablendcolor(gaussians): """ Standard 3DGS alpha blending for color """ C = zeros(H, W, 3) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # alpha' is opacity 2D Gaussian value alphaprime = g.alpha gaussian2dvalue(g) # Accumulate # C = C + ci alphaprime product(1 - alpha'j) for j < i # Simplified for implementation: pass return C def alphablendfeatures(gaussians): """ Feature splatting blending """ F = zeros(H, W, d) # d is feature dimension for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): alphaprime = g.alpha gaussian2dvalue(g) # F = F + fi alphaprime product(1 - alpha'j) pass return F Learning Rate: 2 \times 10^{-4}. Weight Decay: 1 \times 10^{-5}. Batch Size: 4. Dataset Resolution: 512 \times 512. Source Views: 8 images rendered in a circle at 45-degree intervals. Target Views: 3 random viewpoints. Keypoints: 19 (nose, neck, shoulders, elbows, wrists, pelvis, hips, knees, ankles, eyes, ears). Depth Estimator Training Iterations: 40,000. Joint Training Iterations: 100,000. Loss Weights: \beta=1.6 (MAE), \gamma=0.4 (SSIM) for photometric loss; \mu=0.9 for depth loss weighting. Feature Parameterization: Directly parameterizing 3D Gaussians with human features (opacity, scaling, rotation) yields suboptimal performance because these geometric parameters are not suitable for the different frequencies of human features. HFGaussian avoids this by optimizing separate feature parameters decoded after rendering. Point Cloud Sampling: The pose regression relies on a subset of Gaussians. Randomly sampling 2048 points is critical for the DGCNN/PointNet backbone to function effectively. Generalization: The method is designed to generalize to unseen data without fine-tuning, leveraging GPS-Gaussian as a backbone. Speed: Real-time rendering at 25 FPS. Performance: Achieves a PSNR of 32.43 on novel view synthesis, closely matching GPS-Gaussian's 32.55. Strengths: Simultaneously estimates RGB, 3D pose, and biomechanical features (dense pose) without per-subject optimization or parametric body models. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial depth estimation and the generalizability of the backbone encoder. Hardware: Implemented using PyTorch and AdamW optimizer. HFGaussian was introduced by Arnab Dey, Cheng-You Lu, Andrew I. Comport, Jean Martinet, Srinath Sridhar, and Chin-Teng Lin in arXiv:2411.03086v1 on 5 Nov 2024. It addresses the limitations of previous methods that either rely on substantial computational resources for parametric models (SMPL/STAR) or fail to incorporate biomechanical features essential for virtual interactions. It is used for 3D human avatar reconstruction, AR/VR, entertainment, and medical applications. name: ZeroGS
head: ZeroGS: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting from Unposed Images
body: ZeroGS is a pipeline for training 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from hundreds of unposed and unordered images without requiring Structure-from-Motion (SfM) tools like COLMAP. It differs from its siblings by leveraging a pretrained foundation model (Spann3R) as a neural scene representation and employing an incremental training buffer to progressively register images and refine poses. Unlike ACE0, which predicts sparse points using CNNs, ZeroGS predicts dense pointmaps and 3D Gaussians using transformers and optimizes the scene via rendering loss rather than reprojection error. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of unposed, unordered RGB images \{Ik\}. The pipeline initializes with one seed image and a pretrained model. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} and camera poses for all registered images. Data Structures: Training Buffer: A collection of registered images and their associated poses and 3D Gaussians. Spatial Feature Memory: Used by the Spann3R backbone to store fused features for global coordinate regression. Method Steps: 1. Seed Initialization: Initialize the pipeline with a pretrained model (based on DUSt3R/Spann3R) and a single seed image I{seed}. Unlike incremental SfM which fixes an image pair, this fixes the gauge freedom using one image. 2. Batch Registration: Register a batch of unregistered images. For each image pair (Ii, Ij) where Ii is from the registered set (or seed) and Ij is from the unregistered set: a. Feature Encoding: Compute shared features using a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder V: f{ie}, f{je} = V(Ii, Ij) b. Decoder Processing: Pass features through reference and target transformer decoders D{ref} and D{tgt}: f{id} = D{ref}(f{ie}, f{je}), \quad f{jd} = D{tgt}(f{je}, f{ie}) c. Pointmap Prediction: Map decoder features to pointmaps using projection heads H{ref} and H{tgt}. Spann3R predicts pointmaps in a global coordinate frame X{k,g}: X{i,g}, X{j,g} = H{ref}(f{id}), H{tgt}(f{jd}) Note: X{i,j} denotes the pointmap of image j in camera i's coordinate frame in the base DUSt3R formulation, but ZeroGS uses Spann3R to regress directly into the global frame of the seed image without aligning pairwise dense pointmaps. d. Coarse Pose Estimation: Compute coarse camera poses for Ij using RANSAC and a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) solver on 2D-3D correspondences between the predicted pointmaps and the known geometry. e. Pose Refinement: Refine the coarse poses by minimizing a point-to-camera ray consistency loss between the 3D points and camera centers across multiple views. f. Gaussian Prediction: Predict 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}k for the scene using the same network. 3. Rendering and Loss: Rasterize the predicted 3D Gaussians using the refined poses to render images. Compute an RGB reconstruction loss (e.g., L1) and back-propagate gradients to update the network. 4. Buffer Update: At the end of each training epoch, update the training buffer by registering new images that meet the registration criteria (using RANSAC and PnP). 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 until all images are registered or no more images can be registered. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ZeroGSpipeline(images, pretrainedmodel, seedimage): # Initialize training buffer with seed image buffer = {seedimage: {'pose': Identity(), 'gaussians': None}} unregistered = images - {seedimage} # Initialize spatial feature memory for global frame regression memory = InitializeMemory(pretrainedmodel) while unregistered: # Select a batch of unregistered images batch = SelectBatch(unregistered, buffer) for imgpair in batch: refimg, tgtimg = imgpair # 1. Feature Encoding frefe, ftgte = pretrainedmodel.encoder(refimg, tgtimg) # 2. Decoder and Pointmap Prediction (Spann3R) # Uses memory for global coordinate regression frefd = pretrainedmodel.decoderref(frefe, ftgte, memory) ftgtd = pretrainedmodel.decodertgt(ftgte, frefe, memory) # Predict pointmaps in global frame Xrefg = pretrainedmodel.headref(frefd) Xtgtg = pretrainedmodel.headtgt(ftgtd) # Predict 3D Gaussians G = pretrainedmodel.predictgaussians(Xtgtg) # 3. Coarse Pose Estimation # Use RANSAC + PnP on 2D-3D correspondences coarsepose = EstimatePose(Xrefg, Xtgtg, buffer[refimg]['pose']) # 4. Pose Refinement # Minimize point-to-camera ray consistency loss refinedpose = RefinePose(coarsepose, Xtgtg, buffer[refimg]['pose']) # 5. Rendering Loss renderedimg = DifferentiableRasterize(G, refinedpose) loss = ComputeRGBLoss(renderedimg, tgtimg) # Backpropagate to update model and memory pretrainedmodel.backward(loss) UpdateMemory(memory, ftgtd) # Register image if successful if IsRegistered(refinedpose): buffer[tgtimg] = {'pose': refinedpose, 'gaussians': G} unregistered.remove(tgtimg) return buffer Parameters: GPU Memory: Runs on a 24GB consumer-level GPU for hundreds of images. Batch Size: Images are registered in batches rather than individually. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: Aligning pairwise dense pointmaps to a global frame (as done in DUSt3R post-processing for >2 images) is time-consuming and can exceed GPU memory limits. ZeroGS avoids this by regressing in the global frame directly via Spann3R. Textureless Areas: 3DGS can struggle to identify Gaussians in textureless areas; the method relies on the pretrained model's geometric priors to mitigate this. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but incremental registration and batch processing are used to manage computational load. Memory Complexity: Fits within 24GB GPU memory for hundreds of images. Strengths: Handles hundreds of unposed/unordered images; recovers more accurate poses than state-of-the-art pose-free NeRF/3DGS methods; renders higher quality images than 3DGS with COLMAP poses. Limitations: Requires a large pretrained foundation model; finetuning is challenging as 3D foundation models are supervised by ground-truth 3D points difficult to obtain in unseen scenes. When to use: When COLMAP fails or is unavailable for large, unordered, or densely captured image sets. When not to use: When sparse scene structure is sufficient and computational resources for training a large transformer model are limited. ZeroGS was proposed by researchers from Alibaba Group (AIBluefisher). It builds upon the DUSt3R and Spann3R architectures. The method addresses the limitation of traditional SfM (like COLMAP) which limits completeness and requires posed images. It differs from ACE0 by using transformers and dense predictions, and from InstantSplat and Splatt3R by regressing points in the global coordinate frame without aligning dense pointmaps. Evaluated on LLFF, MipNeRF360, and Tanks-and-Temples datasets. ZeroGS: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting from Unposed Images, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2411.15779, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Deformation Field MLP
head: Coordinate MLP, Deformation network
body: The Deformation Field MLP is a coordinate-based neural network that predicts spatial offsets for 3D Gaussian primitives to model dynamic geometry or correct canonical shapes. It maps input coordinates (and optionally time) to deviations in position, rotation, and scale, serving as a smooth prior to prevent overfitting to sparse or noisy views. Unlike grid-based methods, it uses a compact MLP structure, making it suitable for dynamic scenes with high-rank variations where explicit point-based rendering exacerbates complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Canonical 3D Gaussian position \mu. In dynamic variants, time t is also included. Output: Position offset \Delta\mu. In dynamic variants, offsets for position \deltax, rotation \deltar, and scaling \deltas. Data Structures: Network Parameters (\theta): Weights and biases for an 8-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Hidden Dimension: 256. Storage Overhead: Approximately 2 MB compared to standard 3D Gaussians. Algorithm: The network applies sinusoidal positional encoding to the input, processes it through two blocks of linear layers with a skip connection, and predicts the final offset. 1. Positional Encoding: Apply sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the input coordinate \mu. For dynamic scenes, encode both \mu and time t. 2. Feature Extraction (Layers 1–4): Pass the encoded input through four fully connected layers with ReLU activations and a hidden dimension of 256. 3. Skip Connection: Concatenate the original positional encoding \gamma(\mu) (or \gamma(\mu), \gamma(t)) with the feature vector output from Layer 4. 4. Feature Refinement (Layers 5–8): Pass the concatenated vector through four additional fully connected layers with ReLU activations and a hidden dimension of 256. 5. Offset Prediction: Static/Canonical Correction: Pass the final feature vector through a single linear layer (no activation) to output the position offset \Delta\mu. Dynamic Deformation: Pass the final feature vector through three separate linear layers (no activation) to output offsets \deltax (position), \deltar (rotation), and \deltas (scaling). 6. Deformation Application: Static: Compute the deformed position \mu' = \mu + \Delta\mu. Dynamic: Apply offsets to the canonical Gaussian parameters to obtain the deformed Gaussian. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class SinusoidalPositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, numbands=10): super().init() self.numbands = numbands def forward(self, x): # x shape: (..., 3) for position or (..., 4) for pos+time # Standard PE: concat(sin(2^i pi x), cos(2^i pi x)) freqbands = torch.exp(torch.linspace(0, math.log(10000), self.numbands) -math.log(10000)) # Expand dims for broadcasting freqbands = freqbands.view(1, 1, -1) x = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands pe = torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1) return pe class DeformationFieldMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=3, outputdim=3, hiddendim=256, numbands=10, isdynamic=False): super().init() self.pe = SinusoidalPositionalEncoding(numbands) self.isdynamic = isdynamic # Layers 1-4 self.layers14 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim 2 numbands, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU()) # Layers 5-8 self.layers58 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim 2, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), # Input dim doubles due to concat nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU()) # Output head if isdynamic: self.head = nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim 3) # pos, rot, scale else: self.head = nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim) # pos only def forward(self, x): # x: (..., inputdim) pe = self.pe(x) # Layers 1-4 h = self.layers14(pe) # Skip connection: concat input PE with hidden features h = torch.cat([h, pe], dim=-1) # Layers 5-8 h = self.layers58(h) # Output delta = self.head(h) return delta Parameters: MLP Depth: 8 layers. Hidden Width: 256 neurons. PE Frequency Bands: 10. Activation: ReLU for hidden layers, none for output layers. Deformation Learning Rate: 1.6 \times 10^{-5}. Loss Weight (\lambda): 0.2 for D-SSIM in L1+D-SSIM loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: The output head must be initialized such that \Delta\mu \approx 0 (identity) to prevent the network from absorbing pose errors at the start of training. Pose Accuracy: Inaccurate camera poses can lead to convergence failure, as the deformation field may struggle to correct for large geometric mismatches. Dynamic Rank: Grid/plane-based structures are avoided because dynamic scenes have higher rank than static scenes, and explicit point-based rendering exacerbates this. Memory: Adds approximately 2 MB of storage overhead compared to standard 3D Gaussians. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of Gaussians, as each Gaussian is processed independently through the MLP. Strengths: Injects a spatial smoothness prior, helping to avoid overfitting to sparse training views. Compact structure suitable for dynamic scenes. Limitations: Performance degrades with significantly inaccurate camera poses. May not outperform grid-based methods in static, low-rank scenes. When to Use: Dynamic scene reconstruction or sparse-view reconstruction aided by canonical CAD models. When Not to Use: Static scenes with high-quality dense input where grid-based methods may be more efficient. The Deformation Field MLP was introduced in the context of deformable 3D Gaussian splatting for dynamic scene reconstruction and later adapted for sparse-view reconstruction aided by CAD models. It draws inspiration from coordinate-based MLPs used in NeRF and other implicit representations. The method was developed to address the limitations of explicit point-based rendering in dynamic scenarios, where high-rank variations make grid-based approaches less effective. name: Shape Completion Training
head: Decoder-based Shape Completion, Folding Grid Expansion for Shape Completion
body: Shape Completion Training is a feed-forward method that predicts all 14 3D Gaussian attributes from partial, incomplete inputs without requiring target coordinates or per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a fixed 2×2 folding grid to expand a small set of coarse primitives into a dense Gaussian set, enabling robust reconstruction of missing geometry in occluded or sparse scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Partial 3D data (e.g., point clouds or voxel grids) with missing regions. No target coordinates are provided during inference. Output: A set of 1,024 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, ci\}{i=1}^{1024}, where \mu is mean, \Sigma is covariance (defined by scale s and rotation q), \alpha is opacity, and c is color (DC spherical harmonic coefficients). Data Structures: 1. Coarse Primitives: A list of 256 entities. Each entity contains 14 attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). 2. Folding Grid: A fixed 2 \times 2 grid structure used to spatially expand the coarse primitives. 3. Final Gaussians: A list of 1,024 entities with the same 14-attribute layout. Algorithm Steps: 1. Encoder Freezing: Initialize a pretrained feature encoder (e.g., Vision Transformer) and freeze its weights. 2. Decoder Initialization: Initialize an identical decoder architecture to the encoder's output space. 3. Feature Processing: Pass the input features through four Transformer layers in the decoder (width 256, 8 attention heads) to predict 256 coarse primitive attributes. 4. Grid Expansion: Expand the 256 coarse primitives to 1,024 Gaussians using the fixed 2×2 folding grid. This step duplicates and spatially offsets the coarse primitives to fill the volume. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of geometric and attribute losses: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{Chamfer}^{2} + \mathcal{L}{NN} + 0.1 \left( \mathcal{L}{L1}(\alpha, s, c) + \mathcal{L}{sign\text{-}inv}(q) \right) Where: \mathcal{L}{Chamfer}^{2} is the squared \ell2 Chamfer distance between predicted and target points. \mathcal{L}{NN} is the nearest-neighbor attribute matching loss. \mathcal{L}{L1} is the \ell1 loss applied to opacity \alpha, scale s, and DC color coefficients c. \mathcal{L}{sign\text{-}inv}(q) is the sign-invariant quaternion similarity loss for rotation q. The aggregate attribute term is scaled by a weight of 0.1. 6. Optimization: Optimize the decoder weights using AdamW for 80 epochs. Learning rate: 10^{-3}. Weight decay: 0.05. Warm-up: 5 epochs. Batch size: 64. Train three independent decoder seeds per frozen encoder. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class ShapeCompletionDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self, numcoarse=256, numfinal=1024, width=256, heads=8, layers=4): super().init() # Transformer layers for coarse primitive prediction self.transformerblocks = nn.ModuleList([ nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(dmodel=width, nhead=heads) for in range(layers) ]) # Projection to 14 attributes per coarse primitive self.attrproj = nn.Linear(width, 14) self.numcoarse = numcoarse self.numfinal = numfinal self.expansionfactor = numfinal // numcoarse def forward(self, x): # x: [Batch, CoarsePrimitives, Width] for block in self.transformerblocks: x = block(x) # Predict 14 attributes for 256 coarse primitives coarseattrs = self.attrproj(x) # [Batch, 256, 14] # Expand to 1024 Gaussians using fixed 2x2 folding grid # The grid implies a deterministic spatial duplication/offset finalattrs = self.expandfoldinggrid(coarseattrs) return finalattrs def expandfoldinggrid(self, coarseattrs): # coarseattrs: [B, 256, 14] # Expand factor 4 (2x2 grid) # Duplicate each coarse primitive 4 times expanded = coarseattrs.repeatinterleave(self.expansionfactor, dim=1) # [B, 1024, 14] # Apply fixed spatial offsets for the 2x2 grid to the position components # Assuming positions are in the first 3 dimensions of the 14 attributes # Offsets are predefined constants for the grid cells offsets = torch.tensor([ [-0.5, -0.5, 0], [0.5, -0.5, 0], [-0.5, 0.5, 0], [0.5, 0.5, 0] ], device=coarseattrs.device).float() # [4, 3] # Reshape offsets to broadcast over batch and primitives # expanded: [B, 1024, 14] -> split into pos [B, 1024, 3] and others [B, 1024, 11] pos = expanded[:,:,:3] others = expanded[:,:, 3:] # Apply offsets based on the expansion index # The expansion repeats every 4 primitives gridindices = torch.arange(self.expansionfactor, device=coarseattrs.device) # [4] gridoffsets = offsets[gridindices] # [4, 3] # Reshape for broadcasting: [1, 1024, 1, 3] -> [1, 256, 4, 3] gridoffsets = gridoffsets.view(1, 1, 4, 3) posexpanded = pos.view(pos.shape[0], 256, 4, 3) posfinal = posexpanded + gridoffsets posfinal = posfinal.view(pos.shape[0], -1, 3) # Combine back finalattrs = torch.cat([posfinal, others], dim=-1) return finalattrs def computeloss(predattrs, targetattrs): # predattrs: [B, 1024, 14] # targetattrs: [B, N, 14] (N varies, e.g., ground truth points) # 1. Squared L2 Chamfer Distance predpos = predattrs[:,:,:3] targetpos = targetattrs[:,:,:3] # Compute pairwise distances dists = torch.cdist(predpos, targetpos, p=2) # [B, 1024, N] # Chamfer: min over target for pred, min over pred for target chamferpred = torch.min(dists, dim=2)[0].mean() # [B, 1024] -> mean chamfertarget = torch.min(dists, dim=1)[0].mean() # [B, N] -> mean chamferloss = (chamferpred + chamfertarget) / 2.0 # 2. Nearest Neighbor Attribute Matching # Match each pred point to its nearest target point and compare attributes nnindices = torch.argmin(dists, dim=2) # [B, 1024] targetnnattrs = torch.gather(targetattrs, 1, nnindices.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, 14)) nnloss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(predattrs, targetnnattrs) # 3. Attribute Losses # Opacity (alpha), Scale (s), DC Coefficients (c) use L1 # Assuming indices: alpha=3, s=4,6,7 (scale 3D), c=8-13 (6 DC coeffs) # Note: Exact indices depend on attribute ordering. Assuming standard: pos(3), scale(3), rot(4), alpha(1), color(3) or SH. # Based on source, "DC coefficients" implies SH degree 0. # Let's assume: 0-2: pos, 3-5: scale, 6-9: rot, 10: alpha, 11-13: color (RGB) or SH DC. # Source says 14 attributes. Common: 3(pos)+3(scale)+4(rot)+1(alpha)+3(color) = 14. # Or 3(pos)+3(scale)+4(rot)+1(alpha)+6(SH DC) = 17? No, 14. # Likely: 3(pos) + 3(scale) + 4(rot) + 1(alpha) + 3(color) = 14. # But source mentions "DC coefficients" specifically. # If 14 attributes: 3(pos) + 3(scale) + 4(rot) + 1(alpha) + 3(color) is standard. # If SH DC is used, it might be 3(pos) + 3(scale) + 4(rot) + 1(alpha) + 3(color) = 14. # Let's assume indices for L1: alpha (index 10), scale (3-5), color (11-13). alpha = predattrs[:,:, 10] scale = predattrs[:,:, 3:6] color = predattrs[:,:, 11:14] targetalpha = targetnnattrs[:,:, 10] targetscale = targetnnattrs[:,:, 3:6] targetcolor = targetnnattrs[:,:, 11:14] attrl1 = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(alpha, targetalpha) + \ torch.nn.functional.l1loss(scale, targetscale) + \ torch.nn.functional.l1loss(color, targetcolor) # 4. Sign-invariant Quaternion Loss # Rotations are indices 6-9 predrot = predattrs[:,:, 6:10] targetrot = targetnnattrs[:,:, 6:10] # Normalize quaternions predrot = torch.nn.functional.normalize(predrot, p=2, dim=-1) targetrot = torch.nn.functional.normalize(targetrot, p=2, dim=-1) # Sign-invariant: min(dot(q1, q2), dot(q1, -q2)) dotprod = torch.sum(predrot targetrot, dim=-1) signinvloss = torch.nn.functional.mseloss(dotprod, torch.oneslike(dotprod)) # Total Loss totalloss = chamferloss + nnloss + 0.1 (attrl1 + signinvloss) return totalloss def trainshapecompletion(encoder, decoder, dataloader, epochs=80, lr=1e-3, weightdecay=0.05, warmupepochs=5, batchsize=64): optimizer = optim.AdamW(decoder.parameters(), lr=lr, weightdecay=weightdecay) scheduler = optim.lrscheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, Tmax=epochs) for epoch in range(epochs): if epoch < warmupepochs: # Linear warmup for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = lr (epoch + 1) / warmupepochs for batch in dataloader: inputs, targets = batch inputs = inputs.to(encoder.device) targets = targets.to(encoder.device) # Freeze encoder with torch.nograd(): features = encoder(inputs) # Decoder forward preds = decoder(features) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(preds, targets) # Backward optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() scheduler.step() Time Complexity: Inference is O(N) where N is the number of output Gaussians (1,024), dominated by the Transformer encoder/decoder passes. Training is significantly more expensive due to the 80-epoch optimization per scene seed. Memory Complexity: Low inference memory footprint as no per-scene optimization state is stored. Training memory depends on batch size (64) and the size of the feature maps. Performance: Evaluated on 520 held-out objects with visible ratios {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}. The method demonstrates robustness to high missing ratios (up to 85% missing) by leveraging the folding grid expansion to fill gaps. Strengths: No per-scene tuning required; handles severe occlusion; deterministic output structure. Limitations: Fixed expansion ratio (256 to 1,024) may not adapt to scene complexity; relies on the quality of the pretrained encoder. Shape Completion Training was introduced in the context of Gaussian-JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for 3D Gaussian Splats). It addresses the challenge of reconstructing 3D scenes from partial observations, a common issue in real-world scanning where occlusions and sensor noise lead to incomplete data. By freezing a pretrained encoder and training a decoder to complete the shape, it leverages learned priors from large-scale data to infer missing geometry without iterative optimization. Gaussian-JEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for 3D Gaussian Splats, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15651v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Feed-forward Generalizable Reconstruction
head: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, FF3DGS, Generalizable Gaussian Splatting
body: Feed-forward generalizable reconstruction maps input images directly to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\} without per-scene gradient descent [Parent]. It solves the latency bottleneck of traditional 3D Gaussian Splatting, which requires minutes of optimization per scene, by learning a global prior from large datasets to enable real-time inference on unseen scenes [Parent]. It distinguishes itself from iterative methods by replacing optimization with a single forward pass of a neural network, and from implicit methods by producing explicit, rasterizable primitives that support high-fidelity novel view synthesis and mesh extraction [Parent]. All methods in this family share the core objective of mapping input image features to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\} without per-scene gradient descent [Parent]. 1. Input Representation: Inputs are typically one or more RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Some methods require known camera poses P, while others (e.g., Splatt3R, ZeroGS) predict poses or operate on uncalibrated inputs [Parent]. 2. Feature Encoding: A shared encoder (e.g., Vision Transformer, CNN) extracts multi-scale features from the input images. Cross-attention or cost volumes are often used to aggregate multi-view information [Parent]. 3. Primitive Prediction: A decoder head predicts Gaussian attributes. These attributes are usually: Mean (\mu): 3D position. Covariance (\Sigma): Defined by scale s and rotation r (quaternion or 6D). Opacity (\alpha): Scalar. Color (c): Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients or constant RGB [Parent]. 4. Differentiable Rendering: The predicted Gaussians are rendered into target views using differentiable rasterization to compute reconstruction losses (e.g., L1, SSIM, LPIPS) for training the network [Parent]. 5. Generalization: The network is trained on a large dataset of scenes to learn priors about geometry and appearance, allowing inference on unseen scenes [Parent]. The AnySplat Pipeline is a feed-forward method for generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting that operates on uncalibrated input views, simultaneously predicting Gaussian parameters, depth maps, and camera poses without per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Splatt3R and ZeroGS by explicitly integrating a Differentiable Voxelization module to convert pixel-wise Gaussians into a voxelized representation, which stabilizes rendering and enables robust geometry supervision via pseudo-geometry priors from a pretrained VGGT model. See AnySplat Pipeline. FineSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that predicts a set of 3D Gaussians from N context views using a two-stage dual-grouping strategy to balance local detail preservation with global multi-view reasoning. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like YoNoSplat and ZipSplat by employing high-resolution 4x4 patch tokens instead of coarser 14x14 patches, combined with serialized attention for 3D spatial grouping to avoid the prohibitive cost of global multi-view attention. See FineSplat. SparSplat is a generalizable, feed-forward model that maps a sparse set of input images to 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) parameters in a single forward pass to perform both 3D shape reconstruction and novel view synthesis. It differs from its sibling MVSGaussian by using 2D planar primitives instead of 3D volumetric primitives, which ensures multi-view depth consistency required for coherent TSDF mesh fusion. Unlike prior generalizable methods designed primarily for novel view synthesis, SparSplat is explicitly optimized for feed-forward surface reconstruction, offering inference speeds nearly two orders of magnitude faster than implicit volume rendering methods. See SparSplat. Splatt3R is a feed-forward model that predicts 3D Gaussian Splat parameters directly from a pair of uncalibrated RGB images, without requiring camera intrinsics, extrinsics, or depth maps. It solves the problem of generalizable novel view synthesis by extending the MASt3R foundation model with a parallel "Gaussian head" to predict geometry offsets, covariances, opacities, and colors. Unlike sibling methods that restrict supervision to viewpoints interpolated between input stereo views, Splatt3R employs a loss masking strategy to enable robust extrapolation to viewpoints outside the input frustums. See Splatt3R. GlobalSplat is a feed-forward framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that aligns multi-view inputs into a fixed set of global latent scene tokens before decoding explicit 3D geometry, preventing representation bloat and ensuring global consistency. Unlike sibling methods such as C3G which rely on full self-attention and single-Gaussian decoding, GlobalSplat uses an iterative, disentangled dual-branch architecture and a coarse-to-fine capacity curriculum to achieve a superior quality-efficiency trade-off in large-context settings. See GlobalSplat. Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting (GPS-Gaussian) is a feed-forward method for real-time novel view synthesis of humans from sparse camera views. It solves the problem of per-subject optimization latency in 3D Gaussian Splatting by directly regressing Gaussian parameters from source images without fine-tuning. Unlike sibling methods that recompute view-correlated modules for every target viewpoint, GPS-Gaussian performs source-view computation once and renders novel views instantly, allowing concurrent rendering of multiple views. See Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting. LGTM is a feed-forward framework that predicts compact 2D Gaussian primitives coupled with per-primitive texture maps to enable high-fidelity 4K novel view synthesis without per-scene optimization. It solves the quadratic growth in primitive count inherent in pixel-aligned feed-forward 3DGS methods, which makes high-resolution synthesis intractable due to memory and compute limits. Unlike standard 3DGS which couples appearance and geometry within each primitive, LGTM decouples them, allowing a compact set of geometric primitives to represent rich texture regions via per-primitive textures. See LGTM (Less Gaussians, Texture More). InfiniSplat v2 is a feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction method for arbitrary input views that decouples geometry and attribute prediction, uses ground-truth (GT) camera poses for alignment during training, and employs large-angle target view supervision to improve rendering quality under large viewpoint changes. It differs from its siblings by freezing the geometry branch to prevent geometric degradation caused by joint optimization, and by using GT poses for alignment to avoid pose errors that misguide the network under large-angle supervision. See InfiniSplat v2. CodecSplat is a compression framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) that encodes an intermediate 2D Gaussian-generation feature into an entropy-coded scene bitstream, avoiding the inefficient compression of irregular 3D Gaussian primitives. Unlike existing 3DGS compression methods that compress Gaussian primitives after a structured-to-irregular transformation, CodecSplat places the coding bottleneck before 2D-to-3D Gaussian construction, allowing compression to exploit the structured intermediate feature representation. See CodecSplat. DepthSplat is a feed-forward method for 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction that integrates pre-trained monocular depth features into a multi-view cost volume framework. It solves the problem of robust depth estimation in challenging scenes (occlusions, low-texture, non-Lambertian surfaces) where standard multi-view stereo fails, and scale ambiguities where monocular estimation fails. Unlike TranSplat, which refines coarse depth with monocular features (prone to error propagation), DepthSplat combines cost volumes and monocular features early in the pipeline. Unlike GS-LRM, it relies on explicit feature matching rather than pure data-driven priors, reducing training compute requirements significantly. See DepthSplat. VG2GT is a feed-forward, non-pixel-aligned 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction framework that directly regresses geometrically accurate Gaussian scenes and camera parameters from an arbitrary number of unposed and uncalibrated images. It solves the problem of uneven Gaussian distributions and cross-view inconsistencies inherent in pixel-aligned methods by introducing a multi-scale differentiable voxel module that aggregates point-cloud features into a structured representation. Unlike siblings such as AnySplat which first regress pixel-aligned primitives and then aggregate them, VG2GT directly decodes Gaussian primitives from structured voxel features, avoiding the intermediate pixel-aligned representation. See VG2GT. Uses sliding windows to process the sequence and construct a unified large-scale Gaussian scene. Successfully applied to a KITTI street sequence containing over 1,000 frames. Feed-forward generalizable reconstruction emerged as a response to the computational cost of per-scene optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Early work like SplatterImage [105] demonstrated single-view reconstruction using a U-Net to translate input images into Gaussian attributes, which could be extended to multi-view via warping. Subsequent methods integrated multi-view stereo (MVS) principles, such as cost volumes (e.g., MVSplat [104]), and foundation models (e.g., MASt3R, VGGT) to improve geometric consistency and generalization to uncalibrated inputs. The field has expanded to include specialized approaches for dynamic scenes (DrivingGaussian [108], HUGS [109], StreetGaussians [111]), large-scale reconstruction (WorldMirror 2.0), and compression (CodecSplat). PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20341, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: AnySplat Pipeline
head: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting from Unconstrained Views
body: The AnySplat Pipeline is a feed-forward method for generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting that operates on uncalibrated input views, simultaneously predicting Gaussian parameters, depth maps, and camera poses without per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Splatt3R and ZeroGS by explicitly integrating a Differentiable Voxelization module to convert pixel-wise Gaussians into a voxelized representation, which stabilizes rendering and enables robust geometry supervision via pseudo-geometry priors from a pretrained VGGT model. The pipeline maps a set of input images directly to a 3D Gaussian scene representation through a transformer-based encoder and decoder architecture. Inputs and Outputs Input: A batch of K uncalibrated RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 3 \times H \times W}, typically with H=W=448. The input tensor shape is [1, K, 3, 448, 448] (batch, views, channels, height, width). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} defined by mean \mu, scale s, rotation r, and color c. Predicted camera poses (extrinsic E and intrinsic K matrices) for the input views. Predicted depth maps D for the input views. Data Structures The Gaussian parameters are predicted per-pixel from the feature map. Each pixel corresponds to a 3D Gaussian primitive. The parameters include: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. s \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (log-space or linear). r \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). c: Color coefficients (e.g., SH coefficients or RGB). Algorithm Steps 1. Feature Encoding: The input images I are normalized to [-1, 1] range (via (I+1)0.5 if inputs are in [0,1]) and passed through a transformer-based geometry encoder to extract multi-scale features. 2. Parameter Prediction: Three decoder heads process the encoded features: FG: Predicts Gaussian parameters (\mu, \sigma, r, s, c). FD: Predicts a dense depth map D. FC: Predicts camera poses p (extrinsics and intrinsics). 3. Gaussian Construction: The predicted parameters are used to construct a set of pixel-wise 3D Gaussians. Each pixel in the input view generates a Gaussian centered at the back-projected 3D point, with orientation and scale derived from the network output. 4. Differentiable Voxelization: The pixel-wise Gaussians are voxelized into a pre-voxel 3D Gaussian representation using a Differentiable Voxelization module. This step aggregates Gaussians into a voxel grid, resolving density issues and providing a structured representation for rendering. 5. Rendering: Multi-view images and depth maps are rendered from the voxelized Gaussians using differentiable rasterization. 6. Loss Computation: RGB Loss: The rendered images are compared against ground truth images using an RGB loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS). Geometry Loss: The rendered depth maps, the decoded depth D, and the predicted poses p are used to compute geometry losses. These losses are supervised by pseudo-geometry priors obtained from a pretrained VGGT model, which provides consistent depth and pose constraints for uncalibrated inputs. 7. Inference: During inference, the model takes normalized images and outputs the Gaussians and predicted poses. The code snippet gaussians, predcontextpose = model.inference((images+1)0.5) demonstrates the standard inference call. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def anysplatpipeline(images: torch.Tensor, model: torch.nn.Module) -> tuple: """ Runs the AnySplat pipeline on input images. Args: images: Input tensor of shape [B, K, 3, 448, 448] with values in [0, 1]. model: The trained AnySplat model containing encoder and decoder heads. Returns: gaussians: Predicted 3D Gaussian parameters. predcontextpose: Dictionary containing predicted extrinsic and intrinsic matrices. """ # Normalize images to [-1, 1] as per the inference script normalizedimages = (images + 1.0) 0.5 # Run the model inference # The model internally handles encoding, decoding, and voxelization gaussians, predcontextpose = model.inference(normalizedimages) return gaussians, predcontextpose def computelosses(renderedimages, rendereddepths, gtimages, gtdepths, preddepth, predposes, modelvggts): """ Computes the total loss for training. """ # RGB Loss rgbloss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(renderedimages, gtimages) # Geometry Losses # Supervised by pseudo-geometry priors from pretrained VGGT # This involves comparing rendered depth, decoded depth D, and poses p # against the priors provided by VGGT geometryloss = computegeometryloss(rendereddepths, preddepth, predposes, modelvggts) totalloss = rgbloss + geometryloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Uncalibrated Inputs: Since the method predicts poses, incorrect pose predictions can lead to geometric inconsistencies. The use of VGGT priors helps mitigate this but may fail on highly ambiguous scenes. Voxelization Artifacts: The Differentiable Voxelization step may introduce artifacts if the voxel resolution is not chosen appropriately. Too coarse a voxel grid loses detail; too fine a grid increases memory usage. Precision: The model relies on PyTorch 2.2.0 and CUDA 12.1 for optimal performance. Using older versions may lead to compatibility issues with the differentiable voxelization module. A high-resolution variant that uses a Sub-pixel Gaussian Reparameterizer to increase Gaussian density from low-resolution features. A variant that replaces radial Gaussians with planar kernels for better geometric fidelity and fewer primitives. Time Complexity: The method is feed-forward, so inference time is dominated by the transformer encoder and decoder. It is significantly faster than per-scene optimization methods like original 3D Gaussian Splatting. Memory Complexity: Memory usage depends on the number of input views K and the voxel grid resolution. The voxelization step adds overhead compared to pure pixel-wise methods. Performance: The method achieves competitive novel-view synthesis quality on uncalibrated inputs, leveraging VGGT priors for robust geometry. Strengths: Handles uncalibrated inputs, provides explicit pose and depth predictions, and uses voxelization for stable rendering. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pretrained VGGT model for geometry supervision. Performance may degrade on scenes with significant textureless regions or extreme viewpoints. The AnySplat Pipeline was introduced by InternRobotics as a feed-forward approach to 3D Gaussian Splatting that generalizes to unconstrained views. It builds on the principles of generalizable reconstruction by predicting scene parameters directly from images, while addressing the challenges of uncalibrated inputs through pose prediction and pseudo-geometry supervision. InternRobotics/AnySplat, https://github.com/InternRobotics/AnySplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SubSplat
head: Sub-pixel Gaussian Reparameterization, Sub-pixel Gaussian Reparameterizer
body: SubSplat is a method for high-resolution novel-view synthesis that resolves the trade-off between network computational cost and rendering fidelity in pixel-aligned 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of insufficient Gaussian density and artifacts when using low-resolution backbone inputs by introducing a Sub-pixel Gaussian Reparameterizer (SPGR). Unlike prior methods limited by fixed grids or image-space upsamplers, SubSplat subdivides each grid-anchored primary Gaussian into multiple fine-grained sub-pixel primitives, restoring structural density directly from low-resolution features while maintaining stable network latency. SubSplat builds on the AnySplat Pipeline by refining the Gaussian generation stage. It takes low-resolution multi-view features and primary Gaussian anchors as input, and outputs a set of sub-pixel Gaussians suitable for high-resolution rendering. Inputs: N primary Gaussians \mathcal{A} = \{\mathbf{a}p\}{p=1}^N, where \mathbf{a}p = [\boldsymbol{\mu}p, \mathbf{s}p, qp, \alphap] \in \mathbb{R}^{11}. Spherical Harmonic (SH) colors \mathcal{H} = \{\mathbf{h}p \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times D{\mathrm{sh}}}\}{p=1}^N. Default: C=3, D{\mathrm{sh}}=25 (degree-4 SH). Multi-view feature maps \mathcal{F} = \{\Phi{v,\ell}\}{v=1..V, \ell=1..L}, where \Phi{v,\ell} \in \mathbb{R}^{H\ell \times W\ell \times D\ell}. Fixed camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Outputs: K sub-pixel Gaussians per primary Gaussian, defined by position \boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k}, scale \mathbf{s}{p,k}, quaternion q{p,k}, opacity \alphak, and SH color \mathbf{h}{p,k} for k=1 \dots K. K is the squared ratio of target to input resolution (e.g., K=4 for 2x, K=16 for 4x). Primary Gaussian State: \mathbf{a}p contains world-space position \boldsymbol{\mu}p (3), per-axis scales \mathbf{s}p (3), unit quaternion qp (4), and opacity \alphap (1). Embeddings: Geometry and appearance queries are aligned to a shared embedding dimension E=128. Feature Maps: Multi-view features \Phi{v,\ell} are sampled via the deformable attention operator using bilinear weights g(a, b) = \max(0, 1-|a-b|). 1. Initialization: Define N primary Gaussians \mathcal{A} and SH colors \mathcal{H} from the backbone output. Camera metadata is kept separate. 2. Feature Aggregation: Geometry Query: Encode primary Gaussian attributes into a 128-dimensional embedding using per-attribute MLPs \phix, \phis, \phiq, \phi\alpha, then project with linear Wg: \mathbf{z}^gp = Wg(\phix(\boldsymbol{\mu}p) + \phis(\mathbf{s}p) + \phiq(qp) + \phi\alpha(\alphap)) Geometry Aggregation: Perform 3-stage deformable attention. Initialize \mathbf{f}^{g,0}p = \mathbf{0}. For t=0,1,2: \mathbf{f}^{g,t+1}p = \mathrm{DA}(\mathcal{F}; \mathbf{z}^gp, \mathbf{f}^{g,t}p, \mathcal{P}(\boldsymbol{\mu}p), \mathbf{a}p) Final geometry descriptor \mathbf{f}^gp = \mathbf{f}^{g,3}p. Appearance Query: Encode flattened SH coefficients \mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{h}p) into a 128-dimensional embedding: \mathbf{z}^ap = \phic(\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{h}p)) Appearance Aggregation: Perform 1-stage deformable attention conditioned on the geometry descriptor: \mathbf{f}^ap = \mathrm{DA}(\mathcal{F}; \mathbf{z}^ap, \mathbf{f}^gp, \mathcal{P}(\boldsymbol{\mu}p), \mathbf{a}p) 3. Primary View Selection: For each anchor \boldsymbol{\mu}p, project into all cameras. Select the primary view v^ with the smallest positive depth zv > 0. 4. Geometry Reparameterization: Predict offsets using geometry head g\theta: \mathbb{R}^E \to \mathbb{R}^{K \times 9}: [\Delta uk, \Delta vk, \Delta zk, \Delta \log \mathbf{s}k, \Delta \mathbf{r}k]{k=1}^K = g\theta(\mathbf{f}^gp) Position: Back-project sub-pixel offsets (\Delta uk, \Delta vk) using selected depth z{\mathrm{sel}} and focal lengths fx, fy. Bound depth residual via \tanh: \Delta \hat{z}k = \tanh(\Delta zk) \boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + R{c2w} \begin{bmatrix} z{\mathrm{sel}}\Delta uk / fx \\ z{\mathrm{sel}}\Delta vk / fy \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \Delta \hat{z}k R{c2w} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where R{c2w} is the camera-to-world rotation matrix. Scale: Refine scales element-wise: \mathbf{s}{p,k} = \mathbf{s}p \odot \exp(\Delta \log \mathbf{s}k) Rotation: Convert axis-angle residual \Delta \mathbf{r}k to quaternion q(\Delta \mathbf{r}k), compose, and normalize: q{p,k} = \mathrm{norm}(qp \otimes q(\Delta \mathbf{r}k)) Covariance: Compute covariance matrix: \Sigma{p,k} = R(q{p,k}) \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s}{p,k}^2) R(q{p,k})^\top 5. Appearance Reparameterization: Predict opacity logits \ellk and color gain \gammak using appearance head h\phi: \mathbb{R}^E \to \mathbb{R}^{K \times 2}: [\ellk, \gammak]{k=1}^K = h\phi(\mathbf{f}^ap) Projected Area: Compute pinhole Jacobian B at \boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k} in camera coordinates (where xc, yc, zc are camera-frame coords): B = \begin{bmatrix} fx/zc & 0 & -fx xc/zc^2 \\ 0 & fy/zc & -fy yc/zc^2 \end{bmatrix} Compute world-space projection Jacobian J{v^}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k}) = B R^{v^}{\mathrm{w2c}}. Estimate projected area: Ak \approx \sqrt{\det(J{v^}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k}) \Sigma{p,k} J{v^}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k})^\top)} Opacity Allocation: Compute weights to preserve integrated opacity: wk = \mathrm{softmax}(\ellk), \quad \tilde{w}k = \frac{wk}{Ak + \varepsilon} \alphak = \alphap \cdot \frac{\tilde{w}k}{\sumj \tilde{w}j} Color Modulation: Scale SH coefficients: \mathbf{h}{p,k} = \gammak \mathbf{h}p Anti-aliasing: If Ak < A{\mathrm{min}}, adjust in-plane scales to ensure minimum area, preventing flickering. 6. Training: Minimize loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\ell2} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{LPIPS}} with \lambda = 0.05. Unverified code. x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2], dim=-1) def quaternionnormalize(q): return q / (torch.norm(q, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): w, x, y, z = q[..., 0], q[..., 1], q[..., 2], q[..., 3] R = torch.zeros(q.shape[:-1], 3, 3, device=q.device) R[..., 0, 0] = 1 - When to use: When high-resolution output is required from sparse, low-resolution inputs, and inference latency is a constraint. When not to use: When per-scene optimization is acceptable and latency is not a concern, or when input resolution is already high enough to support direct high-res Gaussian prediction. It addresses the limitations of pixel-aligned Gaussian methods that are constrained by fixed grids or suffer from high computational costs at high resolutions. It uses the same input structure as MVSplat and incorporates a deformable-attention operator following the formulation used in GaussianFormer and PixelGaussian. It is used for novel-view synthesis in computer vision, specifically for sparse-view reconstruction. name: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK)
head: DRK Splatting
body: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) Splatting is a 3D scene representation method that replaces the fixed radial symmetry of Gaussian primitives with a flexible planar kernel defined by multiple radial basis functions. It solves the overparameterization and geometric fidelity limitations of Gaussian Splatting by allowing adaptive stretching, rotation, and sharp boundary control, enabling high-fidelity rendering with significantly fewer primitives. Unlike standard 2D Gaussian Splatting, which relies on smooth, elliptical distributions, DRK supports straight edges and sharp corners through L1/L2 norm blending and piecewise edge sharpening. Inputs: Camera parameters: Ray origin \mathbf{r}o, ray direction \mathbf{r}d, view up vector \mathbf{R}z. Scene representation: A set of N DRK primitives. Each primitive i is defined by parameters \Thetai = \{\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{q}i, \{s{k,i}, \theta{k,i}\}{k=1}^K, \etai, \taui, oi, \mathbf{sh}i\}. Image resolution and tile configuration: 16 \times 16 tiles. Outputs: Final color image \mathbf{C} and depth buffer. Each DRK primitive i stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position in world space. \mathbf{q}i \in SO(3): Orientation quaternion, converted to rotation matrix \mathbf{R}i = [\mathbf{R}{x,i}, \mathbf{R}{y,i}, \mathbf{R}{z,i}]. \{s{k,i}, \theta{k,i}\}{k=1}^K: K radial basis lengths and polar angles, ordered 0 < \theta{1,i} < \dots < \theta{K,i} \le 2\pi. \etai \in (0, 1): Blending weight between L1 and L2 norms. \taui \in (-1, 1): Edge sharpening coefficient. oi \in (0, 1): Base opacity. \mathbf{sh}i: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for view-dependent appearance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderdrk(rays, primitives, tiles, sl): # Precompute calibrated boundaries for culling for prim in primitives: for k in range(K): # Calibrated radial length accounting for opacity and sharpness sck = prim.s[k] sqrt(-log(psiinverse(exp(-9) / prim.o))) # World-space polygon endpoints prim.v[k] = prim.mu + sck (cos(prim.theta[k]) prim.Rx + sin(prim.theta[k]) prim.Ry) # Rasterization: Tile culling and cache sorting for tile in tiles: cache = [] # Array of length 8 for prim in potentiallyintersectingprimitives(tile): # Distance from camera to tangent plane intersection rt = dot(prim.mu - rays.origin, prim.Rz) / dot(rays.direction, prim.Rz) # Insertion sort into cache; pop smallest rt if full insertintosorted(cache, rt, prim) if len(cache) > 8: cache.pop(0) # Remove smallest rt tile.cache = cache # Pixel rendering for pixel in image: ray = rays[pixel] alphaaccum = 0.0 coloraccum = vec3(0.0) for prim in tile.cache: # A. Project to Local Tangent Coordinates d = pixelworldpos - prim.mu u = dot(d, prim.Rx) v = dot(d, prim.Ry) # B. Compute Polar Coordinates r = sqrt(uu + vv) if r == 0: theta = 0.0 # Handle division by zero else: theta = arccos(u / r) if v < 0: theta = 2 pi - theta # Cover full 2pi range # C. Determine Radial Basis Interval k = findindex(prim.theta, theta) # Find k such that theta[k] < theta <= theta[k+1] # D. Compute Relative Angular Distance deltatheta = (theta - prim.theta[k]) pi / (prim.theta[k+1] - prim.theta[k]) # E. Compute L2 Norm Component sbarsq = (1 + cos(deltatheta)) / (2 prim.s[k]2) + \ (1 - cos(deltatheta)) / (2 prim.s[k+1]2) r2sq = r r # F. Compute L1 Norm Component # Maps diamond-shaped L1 unit ball to segment between adjacent endpoints r1 = 1.0 / (abs(u / (prim.s[k] cos(prim.theta[k]))) + \ abs(v / (prim.s[k] sin(prim.theta[k])))) # G. Blended Kernel Value g = exp(-(prim.eta r12 + (1 - prim.eta) r2sq / 2) / sbarsq) # H. Edge Sharpening alpha = prim.o psi(g, prim.tau) # I. Low-Pass Filtering deltapw = abs(pixel.u - prim.projectedu) deltaph = abs(pixel.v - prim.projectedv) viewscale = abs(dot(ray.direction, prim.Rz)) alphafiltered = max(alpha, prim.o exp(-0.5 (deltapw2 / sl2 + deltaph2 / (sl2 viewscale2)))) # J. Compositing colori = evalsh(prim.sh, ray.direction) coloraccum += alphafiltered colori (1 - alphaaccum) alphaaccum += alphafiltered (1 - alphaaccum) if alphaaccum >= 0.999: break image[pixel] = coloraccum K: Number of radial bases. Default/Typical: Not specified, but 2D-GS is a special case with K=4. \eta \in (0, 1): L1/L2 blend weight. \tau \in (-1, 1): Edge sharpness coefficient. sl: Filter radius. Not given in the sources. Division by Zero: When r=0 (kernel center), \theta is undefined. Set \theta=0. View Orthogonality: If \mathbf{r}d \cdot \mathbf{R}{z,i} \approx 0, the kernel is viewed edge-on. The low-pass filter denominator becomes small, increasing the filter size to prevent aliasing. Degenerate Input: If \thetak = \theta{k+1}, the sector is empty. Ensure \thetak are strictly increasing. Time Complexity: Rasterization is O(N \cdot T) where N is primitives and T is tiles, but optimized by cache sorting (length 8) and culling. Per-pixel cost is proportional to the number of overlapping primitives in the cache (max 8). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot K) to store radial basis parameters. Performance: DRK achieves superior rendering quality with significantly fewer primitives (e.g., 30 vs thousands for Gaussians) on detailed textures and sharp geometry. Strengths: Better representation of sharp edges and straight lines; reduced overparameterization. Limitations: More complex kernel evaluation than Gaussians; requires careful tuning of \eta and \tau. DRK Splatting was proposed by Yi-Hua Huang et al. in 2025 (arXiv:2412.11752v2). It extends 2D Gaussian Splatting by introducing deformable radial bases to overcome the smoothness and symmetry constraints of Gaussians. It is backwards-compatible, reducing to a Gaussian kernel when using two orthogonal bases with specific decay rates.
