name: Splatt3R
head: Splatt3R: Zero-Shot Gaussian Splatting from Uncalibrated Image Pairs
body: Splatt3R is a feed-forward model that predicts 3D Gaussian Splat parameters directly from a pair of uncalibrated RGB images, without requiring camera intrinsics, extrinsics, or depth maps. It solves the problem of generalizable novel view synthesis by extending the MASt3R foundation model with a parallel "Gaussian head" to predict geometry offsets, covariances, opacities, and colors. Unlike sibling methods that restrict supervision to viewpoints interpolated between input stereo views, Splatt3R employs a loss masking strategy to enable robust extrapolation to viewpoints outside the input frustums. Inputs: Two uncalibrated RGB images I1, I2 \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, where H=W=512. No camera parameters or depth are provided. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}, defined by mean position \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and color c (or spherical harmonics coefficients S). The method predicts per-pixel Gaussian parameters. For each pixel in the input images, the following attributes are predicted: Offset (\Delta): \mathbb{R}^3, representing the displacement from the predicted 3D point. Rotation (q): \mathbb{R}^4, a quaternion representing orientation. Scale (s): \mathbb{R}^3, representing the anisotropic scaling of the Gaussian. Opacity (\alpha): \mathbb{R}, scalar transparency. Color (S): \mathbb{R}^3 (constant view-independent color) or spherical harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color. Splatt3R builds on Feed-forward Generalizable Reconstruction by utilizing a pre-trained "foundation" model for 3D geometry. It is based on MASt3R, a method for stereo reconstruction that predicts 3D point clouds and confidence maps from uncalibrated image pairs. 1. Feature Encoding: Encode the two input images I1, I2 using a shared Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder and cross-attention transformers. These components are frozen during training. 2. Point Cloud Prediction: Use the frozen MASt3R backbone to predict 3D point locations \hat{X}1, \hat{X}2 and confidence maps C1, C2 in the coordinate frame of the first image. 3. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Run a parallel "Gaussian head" (using DPT architecture) to predict offsets \Delta, rotations q, scales s, opacities \alpha, and spherical harmonics S for each pixel. 4. Mean Position Calculation: Calculate the mean position \mu of each Gaussian by adding the predicted offset to the predicted 3D point: \mu = \hat{x} + \Delta where \hat{x} is the 3D point predicted by MASt3R. 5. Covariance Reparameterization: Construct the covariance matrix \Sigma from the rotation quaternion q and scale s to ensure positive semi-definiteness: \Sigma = R(q) S(s) S(s)^T R(q)^T where R(q) is the rotation matrix derived from q, and S(s) is a diagonal matrix with s on the diagonal. 6. Primitive Construction: Construct the final set of Gaussian primitives as the union of primitives predicted from both input images I1 and I2. 7. Rendering: Render the Gaussian set into target views using differentiable rasterization. Activation Functions: Normalization for quaternions, exponential for scales and offsets, and sigmoid for opacities. Color Parameterization: The experiments primarily use constant, view-independent color S \in \mathbb{R}^3, with ablations for view-dependent spherical harmonics. Overlap Thresholds: Hyperparameters \phi and \psi control the selection of context and target images during training. Close: \phi=0.9, \psi=0.9 Medium: \phi=0.7, \psi=0.7 Wide: \phi=0.5, \psi=0.5 Very Wide: \phi=0.3, \psi=0.3 1. Dataset Selection: Select context images such that at least \phi\% of pixels in the second image have correspondences in the first, and target images such that at least \psi\% of pixels are present in at least one context image. 2. Loss Masking: Calculate a loss mask M to prevent supervising pixels that are not feasibly reconstructed. Unproject target image points and reproject them onto context images. Check if the rendered depth matches the ground truth depth. Check if the pixel is inside the frustum of at least one context view. Pixels satisfying these conditions are marked as valid in M. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L as a weighted sum of masked Mean Squared Error (MSE) and LPIPS losses: L = \lambda{MSE} L{MSE}(M \odot \hat{I}, M \odot I) + \lambda{LPIPS} L{LPIPS}(M \odot \hat{I}, M \odot I) where \hat{I} is the rendered image, I is the ground truth target image, and \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. 4. Optimization: Train the Gaussian head using the calculated loss. The MASt3R backbone remains frozen. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def splatt3rforward(I1, I2, mast3rbackbone, gaussianhead): """ Forward pass of Splatt3R. I1, I2: Input images [B, 3, H, W] Returns: Gaussian parameters for novel view synthesis """ # 1. Feature Encoding (Frozen MASt3R Backbone) # The backbone returns 3D points and confidences in the frame of I1 points1, conf1 = mast3rbackbone(I1, I2) # points1: [B, 3, H, W] # Note: MASt3R also predicts points for I2, but Splatt3R primarily # constructs primitives in I1's frame and unions them. # For simplicity, we assume the Gaussian head processes features # derived from the cross-attention output. # 2. Gaussian Parameter Prediction # Gaussian head predicts offsets, rotations, scales, opacities, colors offsets = gaussianhead.predictoffsets(points1) # [B, 3, H, W] rotations = gaussianhead.predictrotations(points1) # [B, 4, H, W] scales = gaussianhead.predictscales(points1) # [B, 3, H, W] opacities = gaussianhead.predictopacities(points1) # [B, 1, H, W] colors = gaussianhead.predictcolors(points1) # [B, 3, H, W] or SH coeffs # 3. Apply Activations # Normalization for quaternions rotations = F.normalize(rotations, dim=1) # Exponential for scales and offsets scales = torch.exp(scales) offsets = torch.exp(offsets) # Or tanh + scale, depending on implementation details not fully specified. # Source says "exponential for scales and offsets". # Sigmoid for opacities opacities = torch.sigmoid(opacities) # 4. Calculate Mean Position # mu = x + delta means = points1 + offsets # 5. Construct Covariance # Sigma = R(q) S(s) S(s)^T R(q)^T # R(q) is rotation matrix from quaternion # S(s) is diagonal scale matrix covariances = quaterniontocovariance(rotations, scales) # 6. Return Gaussian Set # The set is the union of primitives from both images. # In this simplified forward pass, we return parameters for I1's frame. # A full implementation would repeat this for I2 and union the sets. return { 'means': means, 'covariances': covariances, 'opacities': opacities, 'colors': colors } def quaterniontocovariance(quaternions, scales): """ Converts quaternions and scales to covariance matrices. quaternions: [B, 4, H, W] scales: [B, 3, H, W] Returns: [B, 3, 3, H, W] """ # Convert quaternion to rotation matrix # R(q) shape: [B, 3, 3, H, W] R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(quaternions) # Scale matrix S(s) # S(s) is diagonal with scales on diagonal # We need to compute R S S^T R^T # Let D = S S^T (diagonal matrix of squared scales) squaredscales = scales 2 # [B, 3, H, W] # Construct D as a batch of diagonal matrices # D[i,j,k] = squaredscales[i,j,k] if i==j else 0 # Efficiently: R @ D @ R^T # R is [B, 3, 3, H, W] # D is [B, 3, H, W] -> reshape to [B, 3, 1, H, W] for broadcasting? # Actually, standard matrix mult: # Cov = R @ diag(s^2) @ R^T # Reshape for batch matrix multiplication # R: [BHW, 3, 3] # s2: [BHW, 3] B, C, H, W = quaternions.shape Rflat = R.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(-1, 3, 3) # [BHW, 3, 3] s2flat = scales.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(-1, 3) # [BHW, 3] # D = diag(s^2) D = torch.diagembed(s2flat) # [BHW, 3, 3] # Cov = R @ D @ R^T Covflat = torch.bmm(torch.bmm(Rflat, D), Rflat.transpose(1, 2)) # [BHW, 3, 3] # Reshape back Cov = Covflat.reshape(B, H, W, 3, 3).permute(0, 3, 4, 1, 2) # [B, 3, 3, H, W] return Cov def quaterniontorotationmatrix(quaternions): """ Converts quaternions [B, 4, H, W] to rotation matrices [B, 3, 3, H, W]. """ # Standard quaternion to rotation matrix conversion # q = [w, x, y, z] w, x, y, z = torch.unbind(quaternions, dim=1) # Precompute products xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz wx, wy, wz = wx, wy, wz # Construct rotation matrix # Row 1 r11 = 1 - 2(yy + zz) r12 = 2(xy - wz) r13 = 2(xz + wy) # Row 2 r21 = 2(xy + wz) r22 = 1 - 2(xx + zz) r23 = 2(yz - wx) # Row 3 r31 = 2(xz - wy) r32 = 2(yz + wx) r33 = 1 - 2(xx + yy) R = torch.stack([ torch.stack([r11, r12, r13], dim=1), torch.stack([r21, r22, r23], dim=1), torch.stack([r31, r32, r33], dim=1) ], dim=1) # [B, 3, 3, H, W] return R def calculatelossmask(targetpoints, contextpoints, contextdepths, frustums): """ Calculates the loss mask M. targetpoints: [B, 3, H, W] in world space contextpoints: [B, 3, H, W] in world space (from context views) contextdepths: [B, 1, H, W] depth maps of context views frustums: Boolean masks indicating if target points are in context frustums Returns: M [B, 1, H, W] """ # 1. Frustum Culling # Check if target points are inside the frustum of at least one context view infrustum = frustums # [B, 1, H, W] # 2. Covisibility / Depth Matching # Unproject target points to world, reproject to context, compare depth # This requires camera intrinsics and extrinsics which are known during training # but not available at inference. # For each context view: # reprojecteddepth = project(targetworldpoints, contextcam) # gtdepth = contextdepths # depthmatch = |reprojecteddepth - gtdepth| < threshold # Combine with frustum check # M = infrustum AND depthmatch # Placeholder for complex reprojection logic M = infrustum # Simplified for pseudocode completeness return M Time: Splatt3R runs at 4 FPS for 512x512 resolution. This is significantly faster than iterative per-scene optimization methods like standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. Memory: Memory usage is dominated by the ViT encoder and the Gaussian head. The method predicts per-pixel Gaussians, resulting in H \times W primitives per image. On the ScanNet++ test scenes with Close view overlap (\phi=0.9, \psi=0.9): PSNR: 19.66 dB SSIM: 0.757 LPIPS: 0.234 Strengths: Pose-free: Does not require camera intrinsics or extrinsics. Generalizable: Trained on ScanNet++, it generalizes to uncalibrated, in-the-wild images. Extrapolation: Can synthesize views beyond the stereo baseline, unlike many siblings. Limitations: Performance degrades with wider baselines (lower \phi, \psi). Relies on the quality of the MASt3R point cloud prediction; errors in geometry propagate to Gaussian parameters. Constant color parameterization may limit appearance quality compared to view-dependent SH. Use Splatt3R when you have a pair of uncalibrated images and need fast, generalizable novel view synthesis without camera calibration. Use when extrapolation to viewpoints outside the input stereo pair is required. Do not use if high-precision camera poses are available and iterative optimization is acceptable, as standard 3D-GS will likely yield higher quality. Do not use if view-dependent appearance is critical and the constant color ablation is insufficient. Splatt3R was introduced in 2024 by Brandon, Zheng, Iro, and Victor from the University of Oxford. It is based on the MASt3R architecture, which is a foundation model for 3D geometry reconstruction from uncalibrated stereo pairs. The method was trained on the ScanNet++ dataset. It addresses the limitation of existing generalizable 3D-GS methods that only supervise interpolated viewpoints, by introducing a loss masking strategy to enable extrapolation. name: RLSplat
head: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: RLSplat is a resource-linear, budget-controllable feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) framework that generates exactly B Gaussians for a given scene, ensuring that inference latency and peak memory scale linearly with the requested budget. Unlike prior budget-controllable methods (e.g., EcoSplat, F4 Splat) that predict a dense set of candidates and prune them—resulting in nearly constant inference costs regardless of the target budget—RLSplat uses a learned Gaussian allocation policy to distribute exactly B Gaussians across local scene regions from the start. This approach allows the representation size, inference latency, and peak memory to decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget B is reduced, while maintaining or exceeding the reconstruction quality of denser baselines at lower resource costs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of V uncalibrated context images \{Ii\}{i=1}^V and a target integer Gaussian budget B. Outputs: A set of B 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gb\}{b=1}^B and the context camera parameters \{Pi\}{i=1}^V. Each Gaussian gb consists of a 3D center, opacity, scale, rotation, and color coefficients. Data Structures: 1. Anchor Tokens (\{an\}{n=1}^N): A set of N tokens extracted from the geometry backbone, each representing a local 3D region of the scene. 2. Allocation Vector (\mathbf{k}): A discrete vector \mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{Z}{\ge 0}^N where kn is the number of Gaussians assigned to anchor n, such that \sum{n=1}^N kn = B. 3. Gaussian Tokens: A list of B tokens, where anchor n spawns kn tokens. 4. Hierarchical Neighbor Search Structure: Used to efficiently find the K{gs} nearest Gaussian neighbors for each token. Parameters: B: Target Gaussian budget. Typical evaluation values are 2,048 (2K) and 64,000 (64K). On the ACID dataset, B=8,192 is used. K{gs}: Number of nearest Gaussian neighbors each token attends to during refinement. Default ablation value is 16. This can be changed at inference without retraining. K{anc}: Number of anchor neighbors used in the hierarchical neighbor search. Fixed value in ablations is 16. C: Number of rollouts (candidate allocations) drawn per training step for the Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO). Algorithm Steps: 1. Geometry Encoding: The geometry backbone encodes the input images \{Ii\} into N anchor tokens \{an\}{n=1}^N and predicts camera parameters \{Pi\}. 2. Gaussian Allocation: The allocation policy \pi\psi, conditioned on anchor features, predicts a discrete allocation vector \mathbf{k} such that \sum kn = B. This policy is trained using GSPO to maximize reconstruction reward. 3. Token Spawning: Each anchor n spawns kn Gaussian tokens. The total number of Gaussian tokens is exactly B. 4. Resource-Linear Decoding: Initialization: The decoder instantiates initial Gaussian parameters (center, scale, rotation, opacity, color) for each of the B tokens based on their corresponding anchor token. Neighbor Search: For each Gaussian token, the hierarchical neighbor search identifies the K{gs} nearest Gaussian tokens in the current set. Local Refinement: Each Gaussian token refines its parameters via local cross-attention with its K{gs} nearest neighbors. This step ensures consistency among nearby Gaussians. 5. Rendering: The final set of B Gaussians is rendered into target views using differentiable rasterization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch import torch.nn as nn from typing import List, Tuple class RLSplat: def init(self, geometrybackbone, allocationpolicy, decoder, numanchors: int): self.geometrybackbone = geometrybackbone self.allocationpolicy = allocationpolicy self.decoder = decoder self.numanchors = numanchors # Hierarchical neighbor search structure self.neighborsearch = HierarchicalNeighborSearch() def forward(self, images: torch.Tensor, budget: int) -> Tuple[List[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]: """ Args: images: Tensor of shape (V, H, W, 3) or (V, 3, H, W) budget: Integer B, total number of Gaussians to generate Returns: gaussians: List of B tensors, each representing a 3D Gaussian cameras: Predicted camera parameters """ # Step 1: Geometry Encoding # Encodes images into anchor tokens and predicts camera poses anchortokens, cameras = self.geometrybackbone(images) # anchortokens shape: (N, Danchor) # Step 2: Gaussian Allocation # Predict discrete allocation k such that sum(k) == budget # Policy outputs probabilities, sampled to get discrete counts allocation = self.allocationpolicy(anchortokens, budget) # allocation shape: (N,), values in Z>=0, sum == budget # Step 3: Token Spawning # Spawn Gaussian tokens based on allocation gaussiantokens = [] for n in range(self.numanchors): count = allocation[n] # Expand anchor token 'count' times # Add small noise or variation to distinguish spawned tokens if needed # Assuming a learnable embedding or positional encoding is added per spawn tokensforanchor = torch.stack([anchortokens[n] for in range(count)]) gaussiantokens.append(tokensforanchor) gaussiantokens = torch.cat(gaussiantokens, dim=0) # gaussiantokens shape: (B, Dtoken) # Step 4: Resource-Linear Decoding # Initialize Gaussians from tokens initialgaussians = self.decoder.initialize(gaussiantokens) # initialgaussians shape: (B, 14) or similar, containing center, scale, rot, opacity, color # Hierarchical Neighbor Search # Find Kgs nearest neighbors for each Gaussian # Implementation of hierarchical neighbor search depends on specific data structure (e.g., KD-tree or FAISS) # Here we assume a function that returns indices of nearest neighbors neighborindices = self.neighborsearch.findneighbors(initialgaussians, k=self.decoder.Kgs) # Local Refinement via Cross-Attention refinedgaussians = self.decoder.refine(initialgaussians, neighborindices) return refinedgaussians, cameras class HierarchicalNeighborSearch: def init(self): # Placeholder for specific hierarchical search implementation pass def findneighbors(self, gaussians: torch.Tensor, k: int) -> torch.Tensor: """ Finds k nearest neighbors for each Gaussian in the set. Args: gaussians: Tensor of shape (B, 3) representing centers k: Number of neighbors Returns: indices: Tensor of shape (B, k) """ # Standard implementation would use spatial indexing (e.g., FAISS, BallTree) # For the purpose of this article, we assume this function exists and is efficient O(B log B) or similar # The key property is that it is faster than global O(B^2) search pass class Decoder: def init(self, Kgs: int): self.Kgs = Kgs def initialize(self, tokens: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Predicts initial Gaussian parameters from tokens. Args: tokens: Tensor of shape (B, Dtoken) Returns: gaussians: Tensor of shape (B, 14) [center(3), scale(3), rotation(4), opacity(1), color(3)] """ # Linear layers or MLP to predict attributes pass def refine(self, gaussians: torch.Tensor, neighborindices: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Refines Gaussian parameters using local cross-attention. Args: gaussians: Tensor of shape (B, 14) neighborindices: Tensor of shape (B, Kgs) Returns: refinedgaussians: Tensor of shape (B, 14) """ B, = gaussians.shape Kgs = self.Kgs # Gather neighbor features # Assuming neighborindices are valid and within bounds neighborfeatures = gaussians[neighborindices] # Shape: (B, Kgs, 14) # Local Cross-Attention # Standard attention mechanism: Q, K, V derived from gaussians and neighborfeatures # Q from self, K, V from neighbors # This step is O(B Kgs) refined = self.attentionblock(gaussians, neighborfeatures) return refined def attentionblock(self, q: torch.Tensor, kv: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Simplified attention implementation # q: (B, 14), kv: (B, Kgs, 14) # Reshape for attention q = q.unsqueeze(1) # (B, 1, 14) k = kv # (B, Kgs, 14) v = kv # (B, Kgs, 14) # Scaled Dot-Product Attention # scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / sqrt(d) # weights = softmax(scores, dim=1) # out = weights @ v # Actual implementation details omitted for brevity, but must be O(BKgs) pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Allocation Policy Failure: If the allocation policy fails to distribute Gaussians effectively (e.g., assigning zero Gaussians to high-frequency regions), reconstruction quality degrades significantly. The policy is trained with GSPO to mitigate this. Neighbor Search Accuracy: The hierarchical neighbor search must accurately identify true spatial neighbors. Removing the Voronoi loss during training causes Gaussians to leave their anchor's cell, leading to incorrect neighbor retrieval and a 2.51 dB PSNR drop. Projection Loss: Removing the projection loss causes training to fail entirely, as it ties an anchor's Gaussians to the image region it was encoded from. Local Refinement: Removing the local refinement module lowers PSNR by 0.96 dB, as Gaussians cannot be made consistent with their neighbors. Time Complexity: The decoding cost is O(B \cdot K{gs}), scaling linearly with the Gaussian budget B. This contrasts with global self-attention, which costs O(B^2). Memory Complexity: Peak memory usage scales linearly with B. At a budget of 2K Gaussians, RLSplat uses 9.6× less peak memory than F4 Splat. Inference Latency: Latency scales linearly with B. At 2K Gaussians, RLSplat runs 4.1× faster than F4 Splat. Performance: On ACID (B=8,192): PSNR 22.84 dB, SSIM 0.643, LPIPS 0.353. On RE10K (B=8,000): Full-view PSNR 26.51 dB, compared to 23.42 dB for F4 Splat and 21.82 dB for EcoSplat. At 2K Gaussians, RLSplat achieves higher PSNR than F4 Splat. Strengths: True resource-linearity: Cost decreases as budget decreases. High quality at low budgets: Outperforms baselines at every tested budget. Efficient neighbor search: Hierarchical search is 27× faster than exact search (8.1 ms vs. 219.6 ms at 65,536 Gaussians). Limitations: Requires training with GSPO, which involves non-differentiable discrete allocations. Performance depends on the accuracy of the hierarchical neighbor search. When to Use: Applications requiring limited resource budgets, such as AR/VR, robotics, and digital content creation, where inference latency and memory are critical constraints. RLSplat was proposed by Bae, Park, and Kim from KAIST in 2026. It addresses the limitations of prior budget-controllable FF3DGS methods like EcoSplat and F4 Splat, which predict dense sets of Gaussians and prune them, resulting in constant inference costs regardless of the target budget. RLSplat introduces a Gaussian allocation policy trained with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) and a resource-linear decoder with hierarchical neighbor search to achieve true linear scaling of inference cost with the Gaussian budget. RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27712, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LGTM (Less Gaussians, Texture More)
head: Feed-Forward Prediction of Textured Gaussians, Feed-Forward Textured Splatting
body: LGTM is a feed-forward framework that predicts compact 2D Gaussian primitives coupled with per-primitive texture maps to enable high-fidelity 4K novel view synthesis without per-scene optimization. It solves the quadratic growth in primitive count inherent in pixel-aligned feed-forward 3DGS methods, which makes high-resolution synthesis intractable due to memory and compute limits. Unlike standard 3DGS which couples appearance and geometry within each primitive, LGTM decouples them, allowing a compact set of geometric primitives to represent rich texture regions via per-primitive textures. Inputs and Outputs: The network f takes a set of input images \{I^v\}{v=1}^N and their low-resolution counterparts \{I^v{low}\}{v=1}^N as input. It outputs a set of textured 2D Gaussians: f: (I^v, I^v{low}) \rightarrow \{\mui, si, ri, ci, T^ic, T^i\alpha\} where \mui is the mean, si is the scale, ri is the rotation, ci are the spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, T^ic is the color texture map, and T^i\alpha is the alpha texture map for primitive i. Data Structures: Primitive Grid: The primitive network predicts a grid of h \times w 2DGS primitives, where h \times w corresponds to the resolution of the low-resolution input I^v{low}. Per-primitive Texture Maps: Each primitive i has two texture maps: Color texture: T^ic \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times T \times 3} Alpha texture: T^i\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times T} T is the texture resolution, a tunable parameter trading off primitive size and texture size. T^ic is zero-initialized. Architecture: The architecture consists of two submodules: 1. Primitive Network (f{prim}): Processes low-resolution images I^v{low} to predict compact geometric primitives (\mu, s, r, c) and base opacity oi. It uses a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder-decoder to produce a grid of primitives and shared feature maps F^{v}{prim}. 2. Texture Network (f{texture}): Processes high-resolution images I^v and the geometric features F^{v}{prim} to predict per-primitive texture maps T^i\alpha and T^ic. It extracts features via: Patch Features (F^{v}{patch}): Computed from I^v via image patchification and convolutions. Projective Features (F^{v}{proj}): Computed by mapping source image pixels back to primitive local coordinates using the inverse transformation M{i,v}^{-1}. Aggregation: F^{v}{prim}, F^{v}{patch}, and F^{v}{proj} are aggregated to predict the final texture maps. Rendering Formulas: For a ray-splat intersection point u on primitive i, the alpha and color are redefined using textures: ai(u) = oi \cdot T^i\alpha[u] \hat{c}i(u, di) = T^ic[u] + SH(ci, di) where di is the view direction, oi is the base opacity, and T[u] denotes bilinear sampling from the texture map. The alpha texture replaces the standard Gaussian falloff G(u), and the color texture adds high-frequency detail to the SH base color. The final pixel color C is computed by alpha-blending contributions from all primitives sorted by depth: C = \sumi ai(ui) \hat{c}i(di) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - aj(uj)) Projective Feature Computation: To compute projective features, a projective prior texture T^{i, proj}c is computed using the inverse transformation M{i,v}^{-1} which maps primitive local coordinates u to source image pixel coordinates x: T^{i, proj}c[u] = I^v[x] = I^v[M{i,v}^{-1}(u)] Features F^{v}{proj} are then extracted from T^{i, proj}c[u]. Training Strategy: 1. Stage 1 (Primitive Pre-training): Train f{prim} in isolation. Input I^v{low} predicts primitives, but rendering and supervision occur at full resolution H \times W to enforce high-frequency detail learning and anti-aliasing. 2. Stage 2 (Joint Training): Jointly train f{prim} and f{texture}. The learning rate of f{prim} is reduced by 0.1x to maintain geometric stability. 3. Loss: Standard photometric losses (MSE + LPIPS) are used in both stages. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lgtmforward(inputimages, lowresimages, cameraposes): """ Forward pass of LGTM. inputimages: List of RGB images [N, H, W, 3] lowresimages: List of low-res RGB images [N, h, w, 3] cameraposes: Camera poses for each view Returns: List of Gaussian primitives and texture maps """ # Stage 1: Primitive Network # fprim takes low-res images and predicts geometry and base appearance primitives, sharedfeatures = fprim(lowresimages, cameraposes) # primitives contains: mu, s, r, c (SH coeffs), o (base opacity) # sharedfeatures: Fprim from ViT decoder # Stage 2: Texture Network # ftexture takes high-res images and shared features to predict textures texturemaps = ftexture(inputimages, sharedfeatures, primitives) # texturemaps contains: Tc (color texture), Talpha (alpha texture) return primitives, texturemaps def lgtmrender(primitives, texturemaps, cameraposes, imageresolution): """ Render the predicted textured Gaussians. primitives: List of Gaussian parameters texturemaps: List of texture maps per primitive cameraposes: Camera poses imageresolution: (H, W) of the output image Returns: Rendered image """ # Initialize output buffer colorbuffer = zeros(imageresolution) alphabuffer = zeros(imageresolution) # Sort primitives by depth for each pixel sortedprimitives = sortprimitivesbydepth(primitives, cameraposes, imageresolution) for primitive in sortedprimitives: # Find ray-splat intersection points u for each pixel covered by this primitive # u is in local coordinates of the primitive plane u = computeintersection(primitive, cameraposes) # Sample alpha and color from texture maps # Talpha[u] and Tc[u] use bilinear sampling a = primitive.o sampletexture(primitive.Talpha, u) c = sampletexture(primitive.Tc, u) + evaluatesh(primitive.c, primitive.viewdirection) # Alpha blending # Cnew = Cold (1 - a) + c a # Anew = Aold (1 - a) + a # Note: Standard 3DGS blending logic applies here with textured alpha/color updatebuffer(colorbuffer, alphabuffer, u, c, a) return colorbuffer def computeprojectivefeatures(highresimage, primitive, camerapose): """ Compute projective features for a primitive. """ # Compute inverse transformation Minv mapping local u to image pixel x Minv = inversehomography(primitive.M, camerapose) # Map local coordinates u to image coordinates x x = applyhomography(Minv, primitive.localcoordinates) # Sample RGB color from high-res image at x Tproj = sampleimage(highresimage, x) # Extract features from Tproj Fproj = convnetwork(Tproj) return Fproj Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: Standard feed-forward methods fail at 2K+ resolutions due to memory (e.g., NoPoSplat requires >61 GB at 1024x576). LGTM uses <30 GB. Holes in Rendering: Without high-resolution supervision in Stage 1, predicted Gaussians may result in holes as they are not anti-aliased. Geometric Stability: In Stage 2, the primitive network must be trained with a reduced learning rate (0.1x) to prevent destabilizing the geometric foundation. Memory: LGTM trains successfully at 2K and 4K resolutions using under 30 GB of memory. In contrast, NoPoSplat fails to train at 2K or higher due to memory constraints (OOM). Scalability: Scaling from 512 to 4K requires 64× more Gaussians in standard methods, but LGTM scales efficiently at inference with only modest memory and time overhead. Performance: Enables high-fidelity 4K novel view synthesis, a capability previously intractable for feed-forward methods. Strengths: Decouples geometry and appearance; enables high-resolution rendering with significantly fewer primitives; no per-scene optimization required; versatile input support (monocular, posed/unposed two-view, multi-view). Limitations: Requires a dual-network architecture; relies on high-resolution supervision during training to avoid holes. LGTM was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026 by Yixing Lao, Xuyang Bai, Xiaoyang Wu, Nuoyuan Yan, Zixin Luo, Jean-Daniel Nahmias, Yanghai Tsin, Shiwei Li, and Hengshuang Zhao from HKU and Apple. It addresses the limitations of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods which suffer from quadratic primitive growth and the per-scene optimization requirement of textured Gaussian methods. Less Gaussians, Texture More: 4K Feed-Forward Textured Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.25745, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: InfiniSplat v2
head: InfiniSplat
body: InfiniSplat v2 is a feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction method for arbitrary input views that decouples geometry and attribute prediction, uses ground-truth (GT) camera poses for alignment during training, and employs large-angle target view supervision to improve rendering quality under large viewpoint changes. It differs from its siblings by freezing the geometry branch to prevent geometric degradation caused by joint optimization, and by using GT poses for alignment to avoid pose errors that misguide the network under large-angle supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N input RGB images IC = \{Ii\}{i \in C} and optional pose conditions QC (camera intrinsics and poses). In the pose-free setting, QC = \emptyset. Outputs: A set of M 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{(\mum, \xim)\}{m=1}^M, where \mum \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the center and \xim = (\alpham, sm, qm, cm) contains opacity, three-axis scale, rotation (quaternion), and zeroth-order spherical harmonic (SH) color. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: A list of M Gaussians. Each Gaussian stores \mum, \alpham, sm, qm, cm. KNN Graph: A global graph used for Stage II refinement. Nodes are Gaussians. Edges connect each point to its 8 nearest neighbors in feature space. Hidden State: A 16-dimensional vector hm per Gaussian, updated during Stage II. Parameters: Voxel merging side length: 0.004 (in scale-normalized reconstruction frame). Opacity pruning threshold \tau\alpha: 0.01. Mask thresholds: \tau{abs} = 0.03, \tau{rel} = 0.01. Stage I learning rates: 10^{-6} for last 10 attribute-backbone Transformer blocks, 2 \times 10^{-4} for Gaussian head. Stage I training steps: 25,000 steps, 2,000 steps linear warmup, cosine decay to 0.1 times peaks. Stage II learning rate: 2 \times 10^{-4}, cosine decay to 0.1 times initial value, 5,000 steps. AdamW: \beta = (0.9, 0.95), global batch size 16, global L2 gradient clipping at 1.0. Rendering: gsplat with eps2d = 10^{-2}. Steps: 1. Dual-Branch Feature Extraction: Initialize two branches from pretrained DA3 weights. Geometry Branch (\Phi{geo}): Frozen. Predicts depths \hat{C} and cameras \hat{\Pi}C from IC and QC. Attribute Branch (\Phi{attr}): Trainable (last K Transformer blocks fine-tuned). Produces multi-layer patch features FC from IC and QC. 2. Scale Alignment and Point Construction (Stage I): Express predicted and GT poses relative to their respective reference cameras (first input view in sorted order). Normalize predicted depths and translations by s{norm} > 0. Fit an Umeyama similarity transform from the GT trajectory to the normalized predicted trajectory using only input-camera center correspondences. Retain its scale sC. Apply scale alignment to GT translations: t^\starv = sC t^\starv, while rotations remain unchanged: R^\starv = R^\starv. Construct Gaussian centers \mum from normalized predicted z-depth, GT intrinsics, and scale-aligned GT poses. Use a DPT decoder to map FC to per-pixel attributes \xi. Merge Gaussians using voxel merging with side length 0.004. Prune Gaussians with opacity \alpham < \tau\alpha = 0.01. Let the initial scene be \mathcal{G}0 with M Gaussians. 3. Stage I Rendering and Loss: Render \mathcal{G}0 into input views C and target views T: \hat{I}{bv} = \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}0; \Pi^\starv) for v \in V = C \cup T. Construct visibility masks Mv for target views: Retain pixel if GT depth > 10^{-6} and passes validity mask. Retain if at least one input view places it in front of camera and within bounds. Retain if |z{proj} - d{src}| \le \max(\tau{abs}, \tau{rel} d{src}), where z{proj} is point depth in input camera, d{src} is sampled depth. Compute LPIPS spatial distance map dv = \text{LPIPS}{spatial}(Mv \odot \hat{I}v, Mv \odot Iv), zeroing invalid regions before normalization. Compute Stage I loss \mathcal{L}I aggregating L1 error ev and dv over valid pixels Mv(p): \mathcal{L}I = \frac{\sum{v \in V} \sump Mv(p) [ev(p) + dv(p)]}{\max(1, \sum{v \in V} \sump Mv(p))} Update \Phi{attr} and Gaussian head using \mathcal{L}I. 4. Stage II Refinement (Iterative): Feature Projection: Project DPT features to 8 channels via learnable 1 \times 1 conv, merge using Gaussian voxel groups/weights, and reuse. Initialization: Linear projection initializes 16-dim hidden state hm for each Gaussian. Input to Refiner: Concatenate image features, current attributes (\xim), gradient feedback, neighbor distances, and hidden states hm. Project to 64 dims. KNN Transformer Blocks: Process through four blocks. Each block: Single-head attention over 8 neighbors. LayerNorm, MLP, residual connections. Output concatenated with original input, MLP predicts attribute increments \Delta \xim and hidden-state increments \Delta hm. Attribute Updates: Scales: s{new} = s{old} \exp(\Delta \log s) without residual clipping. Opacity-logit, local rotation-vector, RGB-logit increments: a \tanh(\text{raw}) with a = 0.1, 0.25, 1.0 respectively. Hidden-state increments: 0.1 \tanh(\text{raw}). Logit inputs clamped to [10^{-6}, 1-10^{-6}]. Gaussian centers, counts, and correspondence remain fixed. Feedback Loss: Render current scene into input views. Compute \ell{fb} = 0.8 L1 + 0.2 L{DSSIM}, where L{DSSIM} = (1 - \text{SSIM})/2 over valid regions. Gradient Handling: Gradients w.r.t Gaussian attributes are normalized and detached before entering the shared updater. Outer Loss: For each supervised view (input and target, weight 0.5 each), compute \ell{out} = 0.8 L1 + 0.2 L{DSSIM} + 0.5 L{LPIPS}. Multi-step Objective: Sample Kr \in \{1, 2, 3\} updates during training, use 3 at inference. \mathcal{L}{II} = \sum{k=1}^{Kr} 0.9^{Kr-k} \mathcal{L}k^{render} + 0.1 \mathcal{L}{opacity} where \mathcal{L}k^{render} is the grouped outer loss after update k. Opacity Regularization: \mathcal{L}{opacity} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^M [\text{logit}\epsilon(\alpham^{Kr}) - \text{logit}\epsilon(\alpham^0)]^2, \quad \epsilon = 10^{-6} where \text{logit}\epsilon(x) = \log(x / (1-x)) clamped to valid range. First-Order Surrogate Loss: To stabilize training, rendering gradients are computed on independent leaf copies zk = \text{sg}(xk) (where xk collects updated parameters): rk = \text{sg}(\nablaz \mathcal{L}{render}(zk)) \mathcal{L}k^{proxy} = \text{sg}(\mathcal{L}{render}(zk)) + \langle xk - \text{sg}(xk), rk \rangle Gradients flow through \mathcal{L}k^{proxy}. Chunked Execution: Reuse global KNN graph. Stable sort along longest voxel-coordinate axis. Expand core sets of at most 200,000 points with four-hop neighborhoods. Recursively bisect chunks exceeding 300,000 points by point count along core sets' longest axes, recomputing neighborhoods. Retain only core-point outputs. Use gradient checkpointing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def umeyamaalignment(sourcepoints, targetpoints): """ Fits a similarity transform (rotation R, translation t, scale s) from source to target. Returns scale s. """ # Implementation of Umeyama algorithm # 1. Compute centroids mus = sourcepoints.mean(dim=0) mut = targetpoints.mean(dim=0) # 2. Center points X = sourcepoints - mus Y = targetpoints - mut # 3. Compute covariance matrix H = X.T @ Y # 4. SVD U, S, Vt = torch.linalg.svd(H) # 5. Rotation d = (torch.linalg.det(U) torch.linalg.det(Vt.T)) < 0.0 if d: S[-1] = -S[-1] U[:, -1] = -U[:, -1] R = U @ Vt # 6. Scale vars = torch.sum(X2, dim=1).mean() s = torch.sum(S) / vars # 7. Translation (not needed for scale extraction, but for completeness) # t = mut - s R @ mus return s def logit(x, eps=1e-6): x = torch.clamp(x, min=eps, max=1-eps) return torch.log(x / (1 - x)) def tanhsigmoid(x, a): return a torch.tanh(x) class InfiniSplatV2: def init(self): # Placeholder for networks self.phigeo = None # Frozen DA3 geometry branch self.phiattr = None # Trainable DA3 attribute branch self.gaussianhead = None # DPT decoder self.refiner = None # Stage II refiner (KNN Transformer blocks) def stagei(self, images, gtposes=None): """ Stage I: Initial reconstruction. """ # 1. Feature Extraction # Geometry branch (frozen) preddepth, predcameras = self.phigeo(images) # Attribute branch (trainable) features = self.phiattr(images) # 2. Scale Alignment # Normalize predicted depths and translations # Fit Umeyama transform from GT trajectory to normalized predicted trajectory # Use only input-camera center correspondences # Get scale sC sC = umeyamaalignment(gtcamcenters, predcamcenters) # Apply scale to GT translations alignedgtposes = applyscale(gtposes, sC) # 3. Point Construction # Back-project predicted depth using GT intrinsics and aligned GT poses centers = backproject(preddepth, gtintrinsics, alignedgtposes) # 4. Attribute Prediction attributes = self.gaussianhead(features) # 5. Voxel Merging and Pruning gaussians = mergevoxels(centers, attributes, voxelsize=0.004) gaussians = pruneopacity(gaussians, threshold=0.01) return gaussians def stageiloss(self, gaussians, images, gtposes, targetviews): """ Stage I Loss computation. """ # Render into input and target views renderedimages = {} for v in targetviews: renderedimages[v] = render(gaussians, v.pose, v.intrinsics) # Construct masks masks = {} for v in targetviews: masks[v] = constructvisibilitymask(v, gtdepths, tauabs=0.03, taurel=0.01) # Compute LPIPS lpipsmaps = {} for v in targetviews: # Zero invalid regions before normalization maskedrendered = masks[v] renderedimages[v] maskedgt = masks[v] v.gtimage lpipsmaps[v] = lpipsspatial(maskedrendered, maskedgt) # Aggregate Loss totalloss = 0 totalweight = 0 for v in targetviews: mask = masks[v] l1error = torch.abs(renderedimages[v] - v.gtimage) lpips = lpipsmaps[v] # Average over valid pixels validpixels = mask.sum() if validpixels > 0: lossv = (mask (l1error + lpips)).sum() / validpixels totalloss += lossv totalweight += 1 return totalloss / max(1, totalweight) def stageiirefine(self, gaussians, images, gtposes, targetviews, numsteps=3): """ Stage II: Iterative refinement. """ # Initialize hidden states hiddenstates = torch.zeros(gaussians.numgaussians, 16) # Project features projectedfeatures = projectfeatures(self.phiattr(images)) # Build KNN graph knngraph = buildknngraph(gaussians, k=8) for step in range(numsteps): # Prepare input for refiner # Concat: image features, current attributes, gradient feedback, neighbor distances, hidden states inputtensor = preparerefinerinput( projectedfeatures, gaussians.attributes, hiddenstates, knngraph) # Process through KNN Transformer blocks outputtensor = self.refiner(inputtensor) # Predict increments deltaattributes, deltahidden = predictincrements(outputtensor) # Update attributes gaussians.attributes = updateattributes(gaussians.attributes, deltaattributes) # Update hidden states hiddenstates = hiddenstates + deltahidden # Compute Feedback Loss (on input views) renderedinput = render(gaussians, inputviewposes) feedbackloss = computefeedbackloss(renderedinput, inputviewgt, masks) # Compute Outer Loss (on input and target views) renderedall = render(gaussians, allviewposes) outerloss = computeouterloss(renderedall, allviewgt, allmasks) # Compute Opacity Regularization opacityloss = computeopacityregularization(gaussians.attributes) # Multi-step Objective # Note: In training, numsteps is sampled from {1,2,3} # Here we assume we are at the final step for loss calculation if step == numsteps - 1: totalloss = 0.9(numsteps-1-step) outerloss + 0.1 opacityloss else: # For intermediate steps, weight is 0.9^(Kr-k) # But since we are unrolling, we accumulate or use surrogate pass return gaussians def updateattributes(attributes, delta): """ Update Gaussian attributes based on increments. """ # Scales newscales = attributes.scales torch.exp(delta.logscale) # Opacity-logit, local rotation-vector, RGB-logit # a = 0.1 for opacity, 0.25 for rotation, 1.0 for RGB newopacitylogit = attributes.opacitylogit + tanhsigmoid(delta.opacitylogit, 0.1) newrotationvec = attributes.rotationvec + tanhsigmoid(delta.rotationvec, 0.25) newrgblogit = attributes.rgblogit + tanhsigmoid(delta.rgblogit, 1.0) # Clamp logit inputs newopacitylogit = torch.clamp(newopacitylogit, min=1e-6, max=1-1e-6) # Convert logits back to parameters newopacity = sigmoid(newopacitylogit) newrotation = vectoquat(newrotationvec) newrgb = logittorgb(newrgblogit) return Attributes(scales=newscales, opacity=newopacity, rotation=newrotation, rgb=newrgb) Time and Memory Complexity: Stage I is dominated by the forward pass of the DA3 backbone and DPT decoder, which is O(N \cdot H \cdot W) for N input images. Stage II involves iterative refinement with KNN graph operations. The chunked execution limits memory usage by processing core sets of at most 200,000 points and recursively bisecting larger chunks. The global KNN graph is reused, reducing recomputation. Measured Performance: On six datasets (DL3DV, ETH3D, NRGBD, Mip-NeRF 360, RE10K, DTU), InfiniSplat v2 achieves state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. In the pose-conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS decrease by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, compared to the strongest evaluated baselines. Scaling: The method scales to N=4, 8, 16 input views. Training uses 16 H20 GPUs with a global batch size of 16. Stage I takes ~48 hours, Stage II takes ~13 hours. Strengths: Decoupling geometry and attribute prediction prevents geometric degradation. Using GT poses for alignment avoids pose errors under large-angle supervision. Large-angle target view supervision improves rendering quality under large viewpoint changes. Opacity learning suppresses geometrically inconsistent points (outliers). Limitations: Relies on GT camera poses for alignment during training, which may not be available in fully pose-free settings (though it supports pose-free inference by using reference cameras for scale estimation). Joint optimization of geometry and attributes is avoided, which might limit the ability to correct gross geometric errors. When to use: When high-quality novel view rendering under large viewpoint changes is required, and GT camera poses are available for training alignment. When not to use: When computational resources for training are limited (Stage I and II training are non-trivial). When GT poses are not available and pose-free inference quality is critical without the benefit of GT alignment during training (though it supports pose-free inference, the alignment strategy is specific to training). InfiniSplat v2 was introduced by Lin et al. in 2025/2026 as an improvement over DA3-GS and InfiniSplat. It addresses limitations in Gaussian attribute learning, specifically flying-point artifacts and poor performance under large viewpoint changes. The method builds on the Depth Anything 3 (DA3) backbone. InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20341, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: DepthSplat
body: DepthSplat is a feed-forward method for 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction that integrates pre-trained monocular depth features into a multi-view cost volume framework. It solves the problem of robust depth estimation in challenging scenes (occlusions, low-texture, non-Lambertian surfaces) where standard multi-view stereo fails, and scale ambiguities where monocular estimation fails. Unlike TranSplat, which refines coarse depth with monocular features (prone to error propagation), DepthSplat combines cost volumes and monocular features early in the pipeline. Unlike GS-LRM, it relies on explicit feature matching rather than pure data-driven priors, reducing training compute requirements significantly. Inputs: N input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with resolution H \times W, and corresponding camera projection matrices \{Pi\}{i=1}^N (derived from intrinsic and extrinsic parameters). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\muj, \alphaj, \Sigmaj, cj\} for each pixel j in the reference views, where \muj is the mean (3D position), \alphaj is opacity, \Sigmaj is covariance, and cj is color. Data Structures: Monocular Features: Extracted per-view using a Vision Transformer (ViT). Dimensions: N \times C \times \frac{H}{s} \times \frac{W}{s}, where C is feature dimension and s is downsampling factor. Cost Volume: For each view i, a 3D tensor Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{s} \times \frac{W}{s} \times D}, where D is the number of depth candidates. Depth Map: Predicted per-view dense depth Di \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}. Parameters: Downsampling factor (s): Controlled by stride-2 3 \times 3 convolutions. s=4 with two convolutions; s=8 with three. Depth candidates (D): Uniformly sampled from near/far depth ranges. Multi-view Transformer: Contains six stacked self- and cross-attention layers. Neighbor Selection: For N > 2, top-2 nearest neighboring views are selected based on camera distance to the reference view. Steps: 1. Monocular Feature Extraction: For each input image Ii, extract features Fi using a pre-trained monocular depth model (ViT-based). 2. Cost Volume Construction (Multi-View Branch): a. For each reference view i, uniformly sample D depth candidates \{dm\}{m=1}^D from the near/far ranges. b. For each neighbor view j (all views if N \le 2; top-2 nearest if N > 2), warp the features Fj to view i using Pi and each depth candidate dm to obtain warped features F{j \to i}^m. c. Compute feature correlations using the dot-product between Fi and F{j \to i}^m. d. If N > 2, average the correlation values from the two selected neighbor views. e. Stack correlations for all dm to form cost volume Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{s} \times \frac{W}{s} \times D}. 3. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the multi-view cost volumes Ci with the extracted monocular features Fi. 4. Depth Regression: Pass the concatenated features through a 2D U-Net architecture followed by a softmax layer to predict dense per-pixel depth Di. 5. Gaussian Center Unprojection: Unproject the predicted depth maps Di to 3D space using camera parameters Pi to obtain Gaussian centers \muj. 6. Remaining Parameter Prediction: Predict opacity \alphaj, covariance \Sigmaj, and color cj using an additional lightweight network/head operating in parallel with the depth regression. 7. Rendering: Render novel views using the splatting operation with the predicted 3D Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Pre-trained monocular depth encoder (ViT) # Note: In implementation, this is a fixed weight network self.monocularencoder = MonocularDepthEncoder() # Multi-view Transformer for feature alignment self.multiviewtransformer = MultiViewTransformer( numlayers=6, featuredim=featuredim) # alpha, scale(3), color(3) -> simplified for pseudocode) def forward(self, images, projectionmatrices): """:param images: Tensor of shape (N, 3, H, W):param projectionmatrices: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 4):return: List of Gaussian sets for each view """ N,, H, W = images.shape Hds, Wds = H // self.downsamplingfactor, W // self.downsamplingfactor # Step 1: Monocular Feature Extraction # Extract features from pre-trained model monofeatures = self.monocularencoder(images) # Shape: (N, C, Hds, Wds) # Step 2: Cost Volume Construction costvolumes = [] # Determine neighbors for each view # For simplicity, assume projectionmatrices allow distance calculation # In practice, compute pairwise camera distances neighbors = self.selectneighbors(projectionmatrices) for i in range(N): # Reference view features Fi = monofeatures[i] # (C, Hds, Wds) # Select neighbor indices neighborindices = neighbors[i] # Initialize cost volume accumulator # Shape: (Hds, Wds, D) Ci = torch.zeros((Hds, Wds, self.numdepthcandidates), device=images.device) # Sample depth candidates uniformly # Assuming near/far ranges are known or estimated depthcandidates = self.sampledepthcandidates(self.numdepthcandidates) for j in neighborindices: Fj = monofeatures[j] # (C, Hds, Wds) # Warp Fj to view i using Pi and depth candidates # F{j->i}^m shape: (C, Hds, Wds) for each m warpedfeatures = self.warpfeatures(Fj, projectionmatrices[i], depthcandidates) # Compute dot-product correlation # Fi: (C, Hds, Wds) -> (C, HdsWds) # warped: (D, C, Hds, Wds) -> (D, C, HdsWds) Fiflat = Fi.view(Fi.size(0), -1) # (C, HdsWds) warpedflat = warpedfeatures.view(warpedfeatures.size(0), warpedfeatures.size(1), -1) # (D, C, HdsWds) # Correlation: (D, HdsWds) correlations = torch.bmm(warpedflat, Fiflat.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # Reshape to (Hds, Wds, D) correlations = correlations.permute(0, 2, 1).contiguous() # Accumulate (average if multiple neighbors) Ci += correlations # Average if multiple neighbors were used if len(neighborindices) > 1: Ci = Ci / len(neighborindices) costvolumes.append(Ci) # Step 3: Feature Concatenation # Concatenate cost volumes and monocular features # Cost volumes are (N, Hds, Wds, D) # Monocular features are (N, C, Hds, Wds) # Need to align dimensions for U-Net input costvolumestensor = torch.stack(costvolumes, dim=0) # (N, Hds, Wds, D) costvolumestensor = costvolumestensor.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) # (N, D, Hds, Wds) # Expand monofeatures to match batch monofeaturestensor = monofeatures # (N, C, Hds, Wds) # Concatenate along channel dimension combinedfeatures = torch.cat([costvolumestensor, monofeaturestensor], dim=1) # Shape: (N, D + C, Hds, Wds) # Step 4: Depth Regression # 2D U-Net + Softmax depthlogits = self.depthdecoder(combinedfeatures) # Shape: (N, D, Hds, Wds) # Softmax over depth dimension D depthprobs = F.softmax(depthlogits, dim=1) # Weighted sum to get depth map # depthprobs: (N, D, Hds, Wds) # depthcandidates: (D,) depthmapds = torch.sum(depthprobs depthcandidates.view(1, -1, 1, 1), dim=1) # Shape: (N, Hds, Wds) # Upsample depth map to original resolution depthmap = F.interpolate(depthmapds.unsqueeze(1), size=(H, W), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(1) # Shape: (N, H, W) # Step 5: Gaussian Center Unprojection # Unproject depth map using projection matrices gaussiancenters = [] for i in range(N): # Unproject pixel coordinates with depth # This involves back-projecting (x, y, 1) depth using Pi^{-1} centers = self.unprojectdepth(depthmap[i], projectionmatrices[i], H, W) gaussiancenters.append(centers) # Step 6: Remaining Parameter Prediction # Use monofeatures (downsampled) to predict alpha, sigma, color # Note: The source says "parallel" head. We use the same mono features or combined features. # Assuming head takes monofeatures or combined features. # Let's use monofeatures for simplicity as per "additional head" description. gaussianparams = self.gaussianhead(monofeaturestensor) # Shape: (N, Cparams, Hds, Wds) # Step 7: Render (Optional for reconstruction, but part of method) # Render novel views using splatting # This step is typically used for training loss calculation # renderedviews = self.splatrender(gaussiancenters, gaussianparams, novelviewmatrices) return gaussiancenters, gaussianparams def selectneighbors(self, projectionmatrices): """Select top-2 nearest neighbors based on camera distance.""" # Compute pairwise distances between camera centers # Camera centers can be extracted from projection matrices # For pseudocode, assume a helper function N = projectionmatrices.shape[0] neighbors = [] for i in range(N): # depthmap: (H, W) # projectionmatrix: (3, 4) # Returns: (H, W, 3) pass class MonocularDepthEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Pre-trained ViT backbone pass def forward(self, x): return x # name: Gaussian Graph Network
body: Gaussian Graph Network (GGN) is a feed-forward method that generates efficient and generalizable 3D Gaussian representations from multi-view images by modeling relations between Gaussian groups from different views using a Gaussian Graph structure, enabling message passing and aggregation at the Gaussian level. Unlike previous methods that simply combine pixel-aligned Gaussians from multiple views without modeling relations, GGN explicitly models these relations via Gaussian Graphs, allowing each Gaussian to benefit from its connected Gaussian groups through feature fusion. This approach mitigates artifacts and extra memory costs associated with naive combination, enabling the model to benefit from increased input views rather than suffering performance degradation. Inputs: A set of N input images I = \{Ii\} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H \times W \times 3} and their corresponding camera parameters C = \{ci\}. Outputs: Gaussian parameters (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c) representing the 3D scene. Data Structures: Node vi: Represents a group of pixel-aligned Gaussians from view i. It consists of a mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times 3} and a feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times D}. Edge Weight Matrix E{s \to k}: Of size HW \times HW, containing binary values (0 or 1) indicating pixel correspondence between Gaussians in group s and group k. Specifically, e{ij}^{s \to k} = 1 if \psi{proj}(\mu{s,i}, cs) = \psi{proj}(\mu{k,j}, cs), and 0 otherwise, where \mu{s,i} is the center of the i-th Gaussian in group vs and \psi{proj} projects the mean to the image plane of camera cs. Adjacency Matrix A: Of size N \times N, where a{ij} = 1 if i=j, and a{ij} = \psi{overlap}(vi, vj) if i \neq j, with \psi{overlap} computing the overlap ratio between views. Degree Matrix D: Diagonal matrix where d{ii} = \sumj a{ij}. Parameters: N: Number of input images. h: Number of graph layers in the Gaussian Graph Network. n: Number of top edges to preserve during graph pruning. W: Learnable weight matrix of size C \times D used in the linear operation. C: Feature dimension from the 2D backbone. D: Output feature dimension for the graph layers. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract image features F from input images I using a 2D backbone \Phi{image}: F = \Phi{image}(I) where F = \{Fi\} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times C}. 2. Initial Gaussian Prediction: Predict mean positions \mui and features fi for pixel-aligned Gaussians for each view i: \mui = \psi{unproj}(\Phi{depth}(Fi), ci) \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times 3} fi = \Phi{feat}(Fi) \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times D} where \Phi{depth} and \Phi{feat} are neural networks predicting depth maps and Gaussian features, and \psi{unproj} is the unprojection operation. 3. Graph Construction: Construct a Gaussian Graph G with nodes V = \{vi\} = \{(\mui, fi)\} for i=1 to N. Define the adjacency matrix A based on view overlap. 4. Graph Pruning: Prune the graph by preserving edges with the top n weights and ignoring others to limit computational complexity. 5. Normalization: Compute the degree matrix D where d{ii} = \sumj a{ij}, and calculate the scaled adjacency matrix \tilde{A}: \tilde{A} = D^{-1}A \quad \text{or} \quad \tilde{A} = D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}. 6. Message Passing: For each graph layer k from 1 to h, update features fi for each node i=1 to N using the Gaussian-level linear operation: fi \leftarrow \sigma\left( \sum{j=1}^N \tilde{a}{ij} E{j \to i} fj W \right) where \sigma is a non-linearity, E{j \to i} is the edge weight matrix between node j and node i, and W is the learnable weight matrix. 7. Gaussian Pooling: Apply Gaussian pooling to aggregate Gaussians from connected subgraphs Gs: (\mu, f) \leftarrow \sum{s=1}^l \phi{pooling}(Gs) If a subgraph Gs has one node vs, \phi{pooling}(Gs) = vs. Otherwise, aggregation is performed over the connected components. 8. Parameter Prediction: Predict remaining Gaussian parameters from the pooled features f: R, S, \alpha, c \leftarrow \psiR(f), \psiS(f), \psi\alpha(f), \psic(f) Compute covariance \Sigma = RSS^T R^T. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussiangraphnetwork(I, C, h, n): """ I: List of N images, shape (H, W, 3) C: List of N camera parameters h: Number of graph layers n: Number of top edges to preserve """ # Step 1: Feature Extraction # Phiimage is a 2D backbone F = phiimage(I) # F is a list of N tensors, each shape (H/4, W/4, C) # Step 2: Initial Gaussian Prediction mulist = [] flist = [] for i in range(len(I)): # Phidepth predicts depth, psiunproj unprojects to 3D mui = psiunproj(phidepth(F[i]), C[i]) # mui shape: (HW, 3) # Phifeat predicts features fi = phifeat(F[i]) # fi shape: (HW, D) mulist.append(mui) flist.append(fi) # Step 3 & 4: Graph Construction and Pruning # Compute overlap ratios for adjacency matrix A A = computeadjacencymatrix(mulist, C) # A is (N, N) # Prune graph: keep top n edges per node or globally? # Source says "preserving edges with the top n weights". # Assuming global top n or per-node top n. # Implementation detail: Sort edges by weight, keep top n. A = prunegraph(A, n) # Step 5: Normalization D = computedegreematrix(A) # Option 1: Symmetric normalization # Dinvsqrt = matrixinversesqrt(D) # Atilde = Dinvsqrt @ A @ Dinvsqrt # Option 2: Row normalization # Dinv = matrixinverse(D) # Atilde = Dinv @ A # Step 6: Message Passing for k in range(h): newflist = [] for i in range(len(mulist)): sumval = zeroslike(flist[i]) for j in range(len(mulist)): if A[i, j] > 0: # Compute edge weight matrix E{j->i} # E{j->i} is (HW, HW) binary matrix Eji = computeedgematrix(mulist[j], mulist[i], C[j]) # Linear operation: E{j->i} @ fj @ W # fj is (HW, D), W is (D, Dout) # E{j->i} @ fj results in (HW, D) # Then @ W results in (HW, Dout) term = Eji @ flist[j] @ W sumval += Atilde[i, j] term # Apply non-linearity sigma fnew = sigma(sumval) newflist.append(fnew) flist = newflist # Step 7: Gaussian Pooling # Identify connected subgraphs Gs subgraphs = findconnectedcomponents(A) pooledmu = [] pooledf = [] for s in range(len(subgraphs)): Gs = subgraphs[s] # If Gs has one node, return it if len(Gs) == 1: idx = Gs[0] pooledmu.append(mulist[idx]) pooledf.append(flist[idx]) else: # Aggregate Gaussians from connected subgraph # Source implies summation or specific pooling function # Assuming simple summation for demonstration if not specified submu = sum(mulist[idx] for idx in Gs) subf = sum(flist[idx] for idx in Gs) pooledmu.append(submu) pooledf.append(subf) # Step 8: Parameter Prediction # Combine pooled features finalf = concat(pooledf, axis=0) R = psiR(finalf) S = psiS(finalf) alpha = psialpha(finalf) c = psic(finalf) # Compute covariance # Sigma = R @ S @ S^T @ R^T # Note: Source says Sigma = RSS^T R^T. # Assuming R is rotation matrix (3x3) and S is scale matrix (3x3) # Or R is rotation quaternion/axis-angle and S is scale vector. # Standard 3DGS: Sigma = R S S^T R^T Sigma = R @ (S @ S.T) @ R.T return mu, Sigma, alpha, c def computeedgematrix(mus, muk, c): """ mus: (HW, 3) means for group s muk: (HW, 3) means for group k c: camera parameters for projection Returns: (HW, HW) binary matrix """ HW = mus.shape[0] E = zeros((HW, HW)) # Project means to image plane projs = psiproj(mus, c) # (HW, 2) pixel coordinates projk = psiproj(muk, c) # (HW, 2) pixel coordinates for i in range(HW): for j in range(HW): # Check if pixel coordinates match if projs[i] == projk[j]: E[i, j] = 1 else: E[i, j] = 0 return E def computeadjacencymatrix(mulist, C): """ Computes overlap ratio between views. """ N = len(mulist) A = zeros((N, N)) for i in range(N): for j in range(N): if i == j: A[i, j] = 1 else: A[i, j] = psioverlap(mulist[i], mulist[j], C[i], C[j]) return A def computedegreematrix(A): D = zeroslike(A) for i in range(A.shape[0]): D[i, i] = sum(A[i,:]) return D def matrixinversesqrt(M): # Compute inverse square root of diagonal matrix M # M is diagonal, so just invert sqrt of diagonal elements invsqrtdiag = 1.0 / sqrt(diag(M)) return diag(invsqrtdiag) Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the graph construction and message passing. The edge weight matrix computation is O(N^2 \cdot HW^2) if done naively, but pruning reduces the number of active edges. Message passing involves matrix multiplications of size HW \times HW scaled by the number of edges. Memory Complexity: Stores N Gaussian groups, each with HW Gaussians. The adjacency matrix is N \times N, and edge weight matrices are HW \times HW. Pruning reduces memory usage for edges. Performance: Outperforms previous methods under different input settings with higher rendering quality and fewer Gaussian representations. Performance improves as the number of input views increases, unlike previous methods which degrade. Strengths: Efficient and generalizable representations; models relations between Gaussians; benefits from more input views. Limitations: Computational complexity of graph operations; requires careful pruning to limit complexity. Gaussian Graph Network (GGN) was proposed to address the limitations of methods that simply combine pixel-aligned Gaussians from multiple views without modeling relations, which leads to artifacts and extra memory cost. The method was introduced in the paper "Gaussian Graph Network: Learning Efficient and Generalizable Gaussian Representations from Multi-view Images". It builds on the concept of pixelSplat [4] and MVSplat [6] but extends them by introducing Gaussian Graphs for message passing and aggregation. Experiments were conducted on large-scale RealEstate10K and ACID datasets. name: VG2GT
head: VG^2GT, Voxel-Gaussian Splatting Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer
body: VG2GT is a feed-forward, non-pixel-aligned 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction framework that directly regresses geometrically accurate Gaussian scenes and camera parameters from an arbitrary number of unposed and uncalibrated images. It solves the problem of uneven Gaussian distributions and cross-view inconsistencies inherent in pixel-aligned methods by introducing a multi-scale differentiable voxel module that aggregates point-cloud features into a structured representation. Unlike siblings such as AnySplat which first regress pixel-aligned primitives and then aggregate them, VG2GT directly decodes Gaussian primitives from structured voxel features, avoiding the intermediate pixel-aligned representation. Inputs: N unposed and uncalibrated RGB images \{\mathbf{I}i\}{i=1}^N. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} (means \mu, covariances \Sigma, opacities \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c) and camera pose representations \mathbf{C}i. Data Structures: 1. Visual Foundation Model (VFM) Output: Pixel-aligned point maps \mathbf{P}i \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Depth maps \mathbf{D}i \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 1}. Camera pose representations \mathbf{C}i \in \mathbb{R}^9. 2. Voxel Features: Structured 3D grid features resulting from the voxelization of point-cloud features. 3. Gaussian Primitives: Defined by mean \mu, scale s, rotation r (implicit in covariance \Sigma), opacity \alpha, and color c (SH coefficients). Method Steps: 1. Feature Encoding: The framework builds on a frozen pretrained visual foundation model (VGGT). The VFM backbone \mathcal{F} jointly encodes the input images to produce pixel-aligned point maps, depth maps, and camera poses: \mathcal{F}\phi (\{\mathbf{I}i\}{i=1}^N) = \{\mathbf{P}i, \mathbf{D}i, \mathbf{C}i\}{i=1}^N The VFM uses a ViT-based encoder (e.g., DINO) with alternating attention, where patch tokens are downsampled by a factor of 14. 2. Multi-Scale Voxel Module: To improve geometric reasoning and reduce uneven Gaussian distribution, a multi-scale differentiable voxel module is introduced. Coarse Scale: PointTransformer [47] and trilinear interpolation compute complementary geometric features from the point maps. These features are injected into the patch tokens to enhance global scene understanding. Fine Scale: A DPT head [28] extracts global point-cloud features from the enhanced patch tokens. These features are voxelized into a structured 3D representation. 3. Gaussian Primitive Decoding: The resulting voxel features are refined by a PointMLP network. A self-splitting Gaussian head then decodes the refined voxel features to predict the Gaussian primitive parameters (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c). This step directly regresses non-pixel-aligned primitives, avoiding the one-to-one correspondence between 2D pixels and 3D points found in other methods. 4. Training with Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering: During training, standard 3DGS rasterization is replaced with stochastic solid volume rendering to supervise scene geometry. This formulation models Gaussian primitives as continuous stochastic solids and renders them along camera rays, improving the quality of synthesized Gaussian depth maps and strengthening geometric reconstruction accuracy. The rendering equation for the image \mathbf{I}i(\mathbf{p}) at pixel \mathbf{p} remains: \mathbf{I}i(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{g \in \Omega(\mathbf{p})} \left( \prod{j < g} (1 - oj^{(i)}(\mathbf{p})) \right) cg og^{(i)}(\mathbf{p}) where og^{(i)}(\mathbf{p}) is the effective opacity of the g-th Gaussian. 5. Optimization: The original visual foundation model (backbone, depth head, and camera head) is kept fully frozen. Only the multi-scale voxel module and the Gaussian primitive decoding head are optimized. Pitfalls: Pixel-Aligned Artifacts: Using pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives imposes a one-to-one correspondence between 2D pixels and 3D points. In real multi-view observations, the same 3D point is visible from multiple pixels and viewpoints. Pixel-aligned formulations lead to uneven Gaussian distributions and cross-view inconsistencies. VG2GT avoids this by decoding directly from voxel features. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: VG2GT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DTU, Replica, TAT, and ScanNet datasets. Strengths: Directly regresses geometrically accurate and spatially uniform Gaussian scenes. Reduces training cost by keeping the VFM fully frozen. Pluggable into patch-feature-based VFMs. Handles arbitrary numbers of unposed and uncalibrated images. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the underlying frozen VFM (VGGT). Not given in the sources. When to use: When fast, feed-forward 3D reconstruction from unposed images is required with high geometric accuracy and multi-view consistency, and when the computational cost of training a full network is prohibitive. When not to use: When per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher fidelity is needed through fine-tuning, or when the input images have known poses and calibration (simpler methods may suffice). VG2GT was proposed in the paper "VG^2GT: Voxel-Gaussian Splatting Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer". It addresses limitations in existing feed-forward 3DGS methods that commonly use pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives, which lead to artifacts and non-uniform scene representations. The method builds on VGGT [36], a visual foundation model that jointly encodes multi-view images to produce depth, point maps, and camera poses. By introducing a multi-scale differentiable voxel module, VG2GT improves upon the geometric reasoning capabilities of the base VFM. It is designed to be a plug-in module for patch-feature-based VFMs, allowing for efficient training by freezing the backbone.
