name: FineSplat
head: Detailed Splats, Fine Patches, Local Groups
body: FineSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that predicts a set of 3D Gaussians from N context views using a two-stage dual-grouping strategy to balance local detail preservation with global multi-view reasoning. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like YoNoSplat and ZipSplat by employing high-resolution 4x4 patch tokens instead of coarser 14x14 patches, combined with serialized attention for 3D spatial grouping to avoid the prohibitive cost of global multi-view attention. FineSplat operates in two stages: view-wise token grouping (Stage 1) and 3D spatial token grouping (Stage 2). Inputs: N context RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H \times W \times 3} and their corresponding camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). The method supports varying numbers of input views sampled from \{6, 12, 24, 32\} during training. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\}, where \mu is the mean, \Sigma is the covariance (defined by scale and rotation), \alpha is opacity, and c is color. Tokens: M = N \cdot \frac{H}{p} \cdot \frac{W}{p} fine-grained tokens z^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times d}, where p=4 is the patch size. Gaussians: K=4 Gaussians predicted per token, assigned to non-overlapping 2x2 sub-patches. p: Patch size, set to 4. T: Number of iterative refinement steps in Stage 2, set to 4. K: Number of Gaussians per token, set to 4. S: Size of groups for serialized attention in 3D spatial grouping. s: Sub-patch stride, set to 2. N: Number of input context views. To handle scale ambiguity in feed-forward reconstruction, scene scale is normalized using context camera poses. Poses are expressed in the mean context camera frame, and translations are rescaled so that all context camera centers lie within [-1, 1]^3. The same transform is applied to target poses. 1. Feature Extraction: Extract multi-scale features F^l for l \in \{1, 2, 3\} (finest to coarsest) from the input images using a shared encoder (e.g., Vision Transformer or CNN). 2. Token Fusion: Fuse features into M fine-grained tokens z^{(0)} using Equation (1): z^{(0)} = \text{fuse}\left(\text{up}\left(\text{fuse}\left(\text{up}(F^3) + F^2\right)\right)\right) + F^1 where \text{up}(\cdot) is bilinear upsampling and \text{fuse}(\cdot) is a convolutional fusion block. 3. Group-wise Attention: Encode tokens using view-wise token grouping based on the Multi-View Pyramid (MVP) architecture. This performs fine-grained attention within small view groups and exchanges information across all views via coarser global tokens. This stage iteratively refines the Gaussians for T=4 steps. 1. Gaussian Prediction: Decode tokens z^{(i)} into an initial set of Gaussians using a lightweight Gaussian head \mathcal{D} (linear decoder). Each token predicts K=4 Gaussians. 2. Patch-Aligned Sub-Pixel Gaussian Reconstruction: For each token, assign 4 Gaussians to four non-overlapping 2x2 sub-patches. Learn a 2D image-space offset \Delta = (\Deltax, \Deltay) for each Gaussian. Bound the offset to keep Gaussians within their sub-patch: \deltax = 2s \tanh(\Deltax), \quad \deltay = 2s \tanh(\Deltay) where s=2 is the sub-patch stride, ensuring \deltax, \deltay \in [-s/2, s/2]. Compute displaced image coordinate (u, v) = (uc, vc) + \delta, where (uc, vc) is the sub-patch center. Ray Unprojection: Unproject (u, v) using predicted camera intrinsics. Transform and normalize the direction using camera-to-world rotation, using camera translation as ray origin to get \mu. 3. Error Feature Computation: Render the predicted Gaussians into every context view to get rendered images \hat{I}n. Compute signed pixel error map En = \hat{I}n - In. Compute feature-level difference \Delta\phin = \phi(\hat{I}n) - \phi(In) using a pretrained ResNet-18 encoder \phi(\cdot). Combine with finest-scale features Fn^1 from Stage 1 via linear embeddings E{err} and E{feat}: Fn^{\text{err}} = [E{err}(En, \Delta\phin); E{\text{feat}}(Fn^1)] \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{p} \times \frac{W}{p} \times de} where [\cdot; \cdot] represents concatenation. 4. Error Aggregation: For each token, gather two error signals: e{\text{self}}: Self error feature from the patch where the token is predicted. e{\text{agg}}: Aggregated error feature averaged over all context views where the token is visible (projected onto error feature maps and masked by visibility/occlusion). 5. 3D Spatial Grouping via Serialized Attention: Lift tokens to 3D space using their predicted \mu. Order tokens along a space-filling curve. Partition tokens into groups of S consecutive points along the curve. Apply self-attention within each group to exchange e{\text{self}} and e{\text{agg}} with 3D neighbors. Use four attention blocks in Stage 2, each using a different space-filling curve, so each token meets a different set of neighbors. Update tokens: \Delta zj^{(i)} = \text{Linear}(\text{SerialAttn}(hj^{(i)})) zj^{(i+1)} = zj^{(i)} + \Delta zj^{(i)} where hj^{(i)} is the feature of token j at step i. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 1-5 for T=4 steps. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finesplat(contextimages, contextposes): """ contextimages: List of N RGB images, shape (H, W, 3) contextposes: List of N camera poses (intrinsics, extrinsics) Returns: List of 3D Gaussian primitives """ # Scene Normalization meanpose = computemeanpose(contextposes) normalizedposes = normalizeposes(contextposes, meanpose, scalerange=(-1, 1)) # Stage 1: View-wise Token Grouping # Extract multi-scale features F^1, F^2, F^3 features = extractmultiscalefeatures(contextimages) # Fuse into fine-grained tokens z^(0) # z^(0) = fuse(up(fuse(up(F^3) + F^2)) + F^1) z = fusetokens(features) # MVP-based view-wise attention z = multiviewpyramidattention(z, normalizedposes) # Stage 2: 3D Spatial Token Grouping (Iterative Refinement) for step in range(4): # Decode Gaussians from tokens gaussians = decodegaussians(z, normalizedposes) # Render Gaussians to context views renderedimages = rendergaussians(gaussians, normalizedposes) # Compute Error Features errorfeatures = [] for n in range(len(contextimages)): # Pixel error En = renderedimages[n] - contextimages[n] # Feature difference using ResNet-18 phi = pretrainedresnet18 deltaphin = phi(renderedimages[n]) - phi(contextimages[n]) # Finest scale features from Stage 1 for view n Fn1 = getfinestfeatures(features[n]) # Combine errors # Fnerr = [Eerr(En, deltaphin); Efeat(Fn1)] erremb = linearembedding(En, deltaphin) featemb = linearembedding(Fn1) Fnerr = concatenate(erremb, featemb) errorfeatures.append(Fnerr) # Aggregate errors for each token tokenerrors = aggregatetokenerrors(z, gaussians, errorfeatures, normalizedposes) # 3D Spatial Grouping # Lift tokens to 3D tokenpositions = gettokenpositions(gaussians) # Serialized Attention with 4 different space-filling curves for curve in range(4): z = serializedattention(z, tokenpositions, tokenerrors, curve) # Final Gaussian Prediction finalgaussians = decodegaussians(z, normalizedposes) return finalgaussians def patchalignedsubpixelreconstruction(token, subpatchcenter, intrinsics, pose): """ Predicts Gaussian mean for a specific sub-patch within a token. """ # Learn offset deltax, deltay = learnoffset(token) # Bound offset s = 2 deltaxbounded = 2 s tanh(deltax) deltaybounded = 2 s tanh(deltay) # Displaced coordinate uc, vc = subpatchcenter u = uc + deltaxbounded v = vc + deltaybounded # Ray Unprojection direction = unproject(u, v, intrinsics) direction = normalize(direction) direction = rotate(direction, pose.rotation) origin = pose.translation return origin + direction depth # Depth predicted by Gaussian head Blind Spots: Fixed view grouping in Stage 1 leaves blind spots where fine-grained tokens in different groups cannot interact. This is mitigated by Stage 2's 3D spatial grouping, which connects tokens across view groups once lifted to 3D. Scale Ambiguity: Feed-forward reconstruction suffers from scale ambiguity. This is handled by normalizing scene scale using context camera poses, ensuring all context camera centers lie within [-1, 1]^3. Iteration Count: Quality improves gradually with more Stage 2 steps, but going beyond 4 steps yields no further gain. Time Complexity: FineSplat is efficient due to its dual-grouping strategy. Stage 1 uses local view-wise attention, and Stage 2 uses serialized attention with space-filling curves, which scales favorably with token count compared to explicit k-nearest-neighbor search. It is faster than ZipSplat and YoNoSplat for 6 and 12 input views, and moderately faster than ZipSplat for 24 views. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: DL3DV (6 views): 27.325 PSNR, 0.871 SSIM, 0.115 LPIPS using 62K Gaussians. RE10K (6 views): 27.394 PSNR, 0.886 SSIM, 0.116 LPIPS using 75K Gaussians. Mip-NeRF 360 (128 views): 23.463 PSNR, 0.706 SSIM, 0.214 LPIPS using 1.6M Gaussians. Strengths: High quality with small primitive budget; efficient reconstruction time; preserves fine-grained visual information; generalizes well to unseen scenes (zero-shot on RE10K and Mip-NeRF 360). Limitations: Performance may degrade if the number of input views is very large and tokens observing the same surface are separated into different view groups, though Stage 2 compensates for this. When to use: Novel view synthesis where high quality and efficiency are required, especially with a small number of input views (6-24). When not to use: When depth supervision is available and preferred, or when the scene scale is known and fixed without normalization. FineSplat was introduced in 2026 by Chen et al.. It is trained on the DL3DV dataset and evaluated on DL3DV, RealEstate10K (RE10K), and Mip-NeRF 360. The method builds on the principles of feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, aiming to preserve fine-grained visual information while avoiding the computational cost of global multi-view attention. name: SparSplat
head: Generalizable 2D Gaussian Splatting, SparSplat Model, SparSplat: Fast Multi-View Reconstruction with Generalizable 2D Gaussian Splatting
body: SparSplat is a generalizable, feed-forward model that maps a sparse set of input images to 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) parameters in a single forward pass to perform both 3D shape reconstruction and novel view synthesis. It differs from its sibling MVSGaussian by using 2D planar primitives instead of 3D volumetric primitives, which ensures multi-view depth consistency required for coherent TSDF mesh fusion. Unlike prior generalizable methods designed primarily for novel view synthesis, SparSplat is explicitly optimized for feed-forward surface reconstruction, offering inference speeds nearly two orders of magnitude faster than implicit volume rendering methods. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N color images Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} and their corresponding camera poses Pi (rotation and translation). During training, N=3 and resolution is 640 \times 512. Outputs: For a target view with pose Pt, the model \Phi predicts a pixel-aligned 2DGS parameter map Ot \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times (2+4+3+1+3)}. The channels correspond to: Scale s: 2 values (planar dimensions). Rotation q: 4 values (quaternion). Position p: 3 values (3D centroid). Opacity \alpha: 1 value. Color c: 3 values (RGB). Data Structures: The core data structure is the parameter map Ot. The position p is derived from depth estimation, while s, q, \alpha, c are predicted directly by the network. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Encoding: Extract monocular 2D semantic features from each input image Ii using DINOv2. Extract pairwise dense correspondence features from input images using MASt3R. An FPN network predicts a 2D feature map fi for each input image Ii. 2. Feature Warping: Warp the feature maps fi to the target view coordinate system using homography based on relative poses Pt / Pi, resulting in warped features f{t,i}. 3. Cost Volume and Depth Estimation (deepMVS branch): Merge warped features f{t,i} into a cost volume. Process the cost volume into a probability volume using a 3D convolutional network. Sample depth planes: 64 planes for the coarse stage and 8 planes for the fine stage. Produce a depth prediction Dt. 4. Gaussian Parameter Prediction (Pixel-aligned branch): Pool the warped features f{t,i} into a target feature map ft. Pass ft through a 2D convolutional network and an MLP to predict scale s, rotation q, opacity \alpha, and color c. 5. Position Assembly: Unproject the predicted depth Dt using the camera intrinsics K to obtain the 3D position p. Combine s, q, p, \alpha, c to form the final attribute map Ot. 6. Rendering and Reconstruction: Novel View Synthesis: Render the scene using perspective-accurate 2D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. Mesh Extraction: Render mean depth maps Di for all training views Pi using the inferred splat maps Oi = \Phi(Pi | I1, \dots, IN). Perform TSDF fusion on these depth maps with a voxel size of 1.5 to extract the explicit 3D triangle mesh S. Loss Functions and Training: The model is trained with a weighted sum of losses. The specific weights are: \lambdas = 0.1 (scale loss) \lambdap = 0.05 (position/depth loss) \lambda\alpha = 0.05 (opacity loss) \lambda\beta = 0.05 (rotation loss) \lambda\gamma = 0.05 (color loss) \lambda1 = 0.5 (L1 image loss) \lambda2 = 1.0 (SSIM image loss) The depth loss L{depth} guides the mean 2DGS splatted depth with ground truth depth supervision, which is critical for reducing chamfer distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class SparSplatModel(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Feature encoders self.dinov2encoder = getdinov2features() # Monocular semantic features self.mast3rencoder = getmast3rfeatures() # Pairwise dense correspondences self.fpn = FPN() # Predicts 2D feature map fi # deepMVS branch self.costvolumenet = CostVolumeNetwork() self.depthhead = DepthHead(coarseplanes=64, fineplanes=8) # Pixel-aligned prediction branch self.featurepooler = FeaturePooler() self.gaussiandecoder = GaussianDecoder() # 2D Conv + MLP def forward(self, images: torch.Tensor, poses: torch.Tensor, intrinsics: torch.Tensor, targetpose: torch.Tensor): """ images: [N, 3, H, W] poses: [N, 4, 4] intrinsics: [3, 3] targetpose: [4, 4] Returns: Ot (H, W, 13) """ N = images.shape[0] # 1. Feature Encoding # Extract DINOv2 features for each image dinov2feats = [self.dinov2encoder(img) for img in images] # Extract MASt3R pairwise features mast3rfeats = self.mast3rencoder(images) # Returns pairwise correspondences # FPN feature maps fpnfeats = [self.fpn(img) for img in images] # 2. Warping # Warp features to target view using relative poses warpedfeats = [] for i in range(N): relpose = targetpose @ poses[i].inverse() fti = warphomography(fpnfeats[i], relpose) warpedfeats.append(fti) # 3. Depth Estimation (deepMVS) # Merge warped features into cost volume costvolume = mergecostvolume(warpedfeats) # Process into probability volume probvolume = self.costvolumenet(costvolume) # Predict depth depthmap = self.depthhead(probvolume) # Output: [1, H, W] # 4. Gaussian Parameter Prediction # Pool warped features into target feature map targetfeat = self.featurepooler(warpedfeats) # Predict s, q, alpha, c gaussianparams = self.gaussiandecoder(targetfeat) # Output: [1, H, W, 9] (s:2, q:4, alpha:1, c:3) # 5. Position Assembly # Unproject depth to 3D position # Note: This requires broadcasting intrinsics and depth positions = unprojectdepth(depthmap, intrinsics) # Output: [3, H, W] # Combine all parameters # s: 2, q: 4, p: 3, alpha: 1, c: 3 -> Total 13 Ot = torch.cat([ gaussianparams[:,:,:,:2], # s gaussianparams[:,:,:, 2:6], # q positions, # p gaussianparams[:,:,:, 6:7], # alpha gaussianparams[:,:,:, 7:] # c ], dim=-1) return Ot def extractmesh(self, images, poses, intrinsics): """ Extracts 3D mesh from training views using TSDF fusion. """ depthmaps = [] for i in range(len(images)): # Infer splat map for training view i Oi = self.forward(images, poses, intrinsics, poses[i]) # Render depth map from Oi Di = renderdepth(Oi, poses[i], intrinsics) depthmaps.append(Di) # TSDF Fusion mesh = tsdffusion(depthmaps, voxelsize=1.5) return mesh Time Complexity: Inference is extremely fast, approximately 0.8–0.88 seconds on an RTX A6000 GPU for a single scene. This is nearly two orders of magnitude faster than implicit generalizable SOTA methods like UfoRecon (66s), VolRecon (31s), ReTR (37s), and GeoTransfer (32s). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the DTU test set, SparSplat achieves a PSNR of 28.33, SSIM of 0.938, and LPIPS of 0.073. For 3D reconstruction (Chamfer Distance), it achieves a mean CD of 1.04. Strengths: Fast, feed-forward inference without per-scene optimization. Superior 3D reconstruction quality compared to prior generalizable GS methods (like MVSGaussian) due to 2DGS consistency. Strong generalization on unseen scenes (DTU, BlendedMVS, Tanks and Temples). Dual capability for both high-quality novel view synthesis and explicit mesh extraction. Limitations: Relies on external foundation models (DINOv2, MASt3R) which may introduce latency or dependency issues not present in self-contained networks. Performance is sensitive to the quality of the depth loss; without L{depth}, reconstruction quality degrades significantly (Chamfer distance increases from 1.04 to 4.37). Using 3DGS instead of 2DGS leads to depth inconsistencies across views, causing TSDF fusion to produce warped or disconnected surfaces. SparSplat was proposed by Shubhendu Jena et al. in 2025. It builds upon the MVSGaussian framework [48] but replaces 3D Gaussian primitives with 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [28] to improve geometric consistency. The method integrates features from foundation models DINOv2 [59] and MASt3R [41] to enhance multi-view stereo accuracy. It addresses the limitation of prior generalizable GS methods which were optimized for novel view synthesis and failed to produce coherent meshes via TSDF fusion. The work demonstrates that 2DGS is better suited for feed-forward surface reconstruction than 3DGS in sparse-view settings. name: Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: GPS-Gaussian, Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting (GPS-Gaussian) is a feed-forward method for real-time novel view synthesis of humans from sparse camera views. It solves the problem of per-subject optimization latency in 3D Gaussian Splatting by directly regressing Gaussian parameters from source images without fine-tuning. Unlike sibling methods that recompute view-correlated modules for every target viewpoint, GPS-Gaussian performs source-view computation once and renders novel views instantly, allowing concurrent rendering of multiple views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N source RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} (resolution 1024 \times 1024) with known camera poses Cn and scene center O. Outputs: A rendered RGB image I{tar} at a target novel viewpoint C{tar}. Data Structures: Gaussian Parameter Maps: Defined on the 2D image planes of the selected source views. For a foreground pixel x, the map contains: Position Map Mp(x): 3D coordinates. Color Map Mc(x): RGB values. Rotation Map Mr(x): Normalized rotation vector. Scaling Map Ms(x): Scale factors. Opacity Map M\alpha(x): Scalar opacity. These maps are aggregated from two source views to form the 3D Gaussian set \mathcal{G}. Feature Maps: Dense features f^s \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2^s \times W/2^s \times Ds} extracted at S=3 scales. Correlation Volume: C \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times W/2} used for depth estimation. Algorithm Steps: 1. View Selection: Compute view vectors Vn = Cn - O for all source views and V{tar} = C{tar} - O for the target view. Calculate dot products between V{tar} and all Vn. Select the two source views Il, Ir with the highest dot products as the "working set". 2. Feature Extraction: Feed Il and Ir into a shared image encoder E{img} to extract multi-scale feature maps \{f^sl\}{s=1}^S and \{f^sr\}{s=1}^S. E{img} architecture: Similar to RAFT-Stereo encoder. First conv layer kernel 5 \times 5 (replaced from 7 \times 7), Group Normalization (replaced from Batch Normalization). Scales S=3. Resolutions: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 of input. Channels: 32, 48, 96 respectively. 3. Cost Volume Construction: Construct a 3D correlation volume C from the deepest feature maps f^Sl, f^Sr \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times DS} using matrix multiplication: C(f^Sl, f^Sr), C{ijk} = \sum{h} (f^Sl){ijh} \cdot (f^Sr){ikh} where i,j are spatial coordinates and k is the disparity index. 4. Iterative Depth Estimation: Predict a sequence of depth estimations \{d^tl\}{t=1}^T and \{d^tr\}{t=1}^T by looking up in volume C using an iterative update mechanism. Final outputs d^Tl, d^Tr are upsampled to full resolution via convex upsampling to produce Dl, Dr. Module: \Phi{depth}(Dl, Dr) = \Phi{depth}(f^Sl, f^Sr, Kl, Kr). 5. Position Map Generation: For each foreground pixel x, unproject from 2D to 3D using the predicted depth D(x) and projection matrix P (derived from camera intrinsics K): Mp(x) = \Pi^{-1}P (x, D(x)) where \Pi^{-1}P is the inverse projection operation. 6. Color Map Generation: For diffuse human scenes, use the source RGB image directly as the color map: Mc(x) = I(x) 7. Geometric Feature Fusion and Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Construct a depth encoder E{depth} taking D as input to complement geometric awareness. Fuse image features E{img}(I) and spatial features E{depth}(D) using concatenation \oplus at all feature levels. Pass fused features through a U-Net-like decoder D{parm} to regress Gaussian features \Gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times DG}: \Gamma = D{parm} (E{img}(I) \oplus E{depth}(D)) Predict Rotation Mr(x): Apply head hr(\Gamma(x)) and normalize: Mr(x) = Norm(hr(\Gamma(x))) Predict Scaling Ms(x): Apply head hs(\Gamma(x)) and Softplus activation: Ms(x) = Softplus(hs(\Gamma(x))) Predict Opacity M\alpha(x): Apply head h\alpha(\Gamma(x)) and Sigmoid activation: M\alpha(x) = Sigmoid(h\alpha(\Gamma(x))) 8. Aggregation and Rendering: Unproject Gaussian parameter maps from both source views Il and Ir to 3D space. Aggregate the resulting 3D Gaussians. Render the target viewpoint using differentiable Gaussian splatting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def gpsgaussianrender(sourceimages, cameraposes, scenecenter, targetcamerapose): """ sourceimages: List of N RGB images [N, 3, H, W] cameraposes: List of N camera positions [N, 3] scenecenter: Scene center [3] targetcamerapose: Target camera position [3] """ # 1. When not to use: Scenes with non-diffuse materials, non-human subjects, or when per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher fidelity is required. GPS-Gaussian was introduced in 2024 by Zheng et al.. It addresses the limitations of original 3D Gaussian Splatting, which requires per-subject optimization taking several minutes and produces noisy results in sparse camera setups. It also improves upon stereo-matching based depth estimation by integrating auxiliary 3D awareness via differentiable rendering. name: WildSplat
head: WildSplat: Feedforward Gaussian Splatting from Unposed In-the-Wild Images
body: WildSplat is a feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework designed for appearance-conditioned novel-view synthesis from sparse, unposed, in-the-wild images. It solves the problem of inconsistent photometric conditions (varying lighting, weather, or time of day) by explicitly decoupling geometry from appearance, allowing the reconstruction of 3D structure independent of the target image's illumination. Unlike optimization-based methods that require precomputed poses and dense inputs, or existing feedforward methods that assume photometric consistency, WildSplat operates in a single forward pass on unposed inputs while preventing target appearance conditioning from altering the underlying geometric structure. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N context images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N and one reference image I{ref} specifying the target appearance. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, conditioned spherical harmonics coefficients \mathcal{C}{ref}, and camera poses \{pi\} for the context views. Data Structures: The Gaussian set \mathcal{G} consists of G primitives. For each Gaussian j \in \{1, \dots, G\}: Position \muj \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation qj \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Scale sj \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphaj \in \mathbb{R} \mathcal{C}{ref} \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times 3 \times (k+1)} contains the spherical harmonics coefficients of degree k for the target appearance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Geometry Branch (Pose and Structure Prediction): 1. Process each context image Ii independently through a DINOv2-based geometry encoder E{geo} to yield dense patch-level tokens Ti^{(0)} = E{geo}(Ii) \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times D}. 2. Concatenate learnable camera tokens Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{5 \times D} with Ti^{(0)}. 3. Refine the combined tokens through L alternating attention blocks. Let Ti^{(k)} and Ci^{(k)} denote the patch and camera tokens after layer k. 4. Extract multi-scale representations from a subset of transformer layers \mathcal{K} = \{l1, \dots, lK\} to form content features \mathbf{F}{content}, which serve as the appearance-invariant geometric scaffold. 5. Decode the final camera tokens Ci^{(L)} to predict camera poses \{pi\}. 6. Predict the base Gaussian geometry \mathcal{G} (positions \mu, rotations q, scales s, opacities \alpha) from the content features. 2. Appearance Branch (Conditioning): 1. Extract features from the reference image I{ref} using an appearance encoder to obtain reference tokens T{ref}. 2. Global Pre-modulation: To prevent the original photometric properties of \mathbf{F}{content} from interfering with the target appearance, apply an AdaLN-Zero layer [G: Adaptive Layer Normalization with Zero initialization] to the global descriptor T{[CLS]} of the content features. This decodes parameters \gamma, \beta, \eta. 3. Modulate the content features: \tilde{T}i^{(k)} = \gamma \cdot \text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{F}{content}) + \beta (Note: The source specifies \tilde{T}i^{(k)} = \gamma \dots using AdaLN-Zero parameters derived from T{[CLS]} to shift features into the target appearance domain). 4. Cross-Attention Injection: Use the modulated features \tilde{T}i^{(k)} as Queries (Q) and the reference tokens T{ref} as Keys (K) and Values (V) in a cross-attention mechanism to inject target appearance cues into the content features. 5. Decode the attended features to predict the conditioned spherical harmonics coefficients \mathcal{C}{ref}. 3. Conditioned Rasterization: 1. Render the predicted novel views \{\hat{I}i\} using tile-based differentiable rasterization \mathcal{R} of 3D Gaussian Splatting, utilizing the geometry \mathcal{G}, conditioned coefficients \mathcal{C}{ref}, and predicted poses \{pi\}: \{\hat{I}i\} = \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}, \mathcal{C}{ref}, \{pi\}) 4. Geometry-guided View Sampling (Training Data Preparation): Construct an overlap matrix S and scale matrix R using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Filter valid view pairs where S \ge \taus and R \ge \taur. Select starting rows C where the sum of valid columns > \taun. Initialize a queue with a uniform sample from C. Iteratively pop u, sample up to K neighbors from valid unvisited views, push to queue, and add to index set \mathcal{I} until N views are selected (See Pseudocode below). 5. Joint Multi-Reference Supervision: 1. Randomly sample M images \{Im\} from the batch as target references. 2. Extract conditioned appearance \{\mathcal{C}{ref,m}\} for each. 3. Render images \{\hat{I}m\} conditioned on their respective appearance. 4. Compute photometric loss against ground truth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class WildSplat: def init(self, numgaussians, shdegree, numlayers, numviews): self.numgaussians = numgaussians self.shdegree = shdegree self.numlayers = numlayers self.numviews = numviews # Geometry Encoder (DINOv2 based) self.geoencoder = DINOv2Encoder() # Transformer Blocks for refinement self.transformerblocks = nn.ModuleList([ TransformerBlock() for in range(numlayers) ]) # Appearance Encoder self.appearanceencoder = AppearanceEncoder() # Heads self.posehead = PoseHead() self.geohead = GaussianGeometryHead() self.appearancehead = SphericalHarmonicsHead() # Pre-modulation AdaLN-Zero self.adalnzero = AdaLNZero() def forward(self, contextimages, refimage): """ contextimages: Tensor of shape (N, 3, H, W) refimage: Tensor of shape (3, H, W) """ N = contextimages.shape[0] # 1. Geometry Branch # Process context images independently patchtokens = [] for i in range(N): Ti0 = self.geoencoder(contextimages[i]) # Shape: (P, D) patchtokens.append(Ti0) patchtokens = torch.stack(patchtokens, dim=0) # (N, P, D) # Initialize learnable camera tokens Ci = torch.randn(N, 5, self.geoencoder.dim) # (N, 5, D) # Refine through L alternating attention blocks for k in range(self.numlayers): # Concatenate camera tokens with patch tokens combinedtokens = torch.cat([Ci, patchtokens], dim=1) # (N, P+5, D) # Attention block refinement # Note: In practice, this involves self-attention over patches and cross-attention for poses # Simplified representation of the block operation combinedtokens = self.transformerblocksk patchtokens = combinedtokens[:,:-5,:] # (N, P, D) Ci = combinedtokens[:, -5:,:] # (N, 5, D) # Extract content features from specific layers (simplified here as final output) Fcontent = patchtokens # (N, P, D) # Predict Poses poses = self.posehead(Ci) # Predict Base Geometry G = self.geohead(Fcontent) # Returns mu, q, s, alpha # 2. Appearance Branch # Extract reference features Tref = self.appearanceencoder(refimage) # (Pa, D) # Global Pre-modulation # Get global descriptor from content features (e.g., mean or CLS token if added) # Assuming Fcontent has a global token or we aggregate TCLS = Fcontent.mean(dim=1) # (N, D) - Simplified aggregation gamma, beta, eta = self.adalnzero(TCLS) # Modulate content features # LayerNorm is applied before scaling/shifting Fcontentnorm = F.layernorm(Fcontent, (Fcontent.shape[-1],)) Tmodulated = gamma.unsqueeze(1) Fcontentnorm + beta.unsqueeze(1) # (N, P, D) # Cross-Attention Injection # Q: Tmodulated, K: Tref, V: Tref # Tref might need to be broadcasted or repeated if N > 1 Trefexpanded = Tref.unsqueeze(0).expand(N, -1, -1) # (N, Pa, D) # Attention mechanism # Q @ K^T / sqrt(d) -> Softmax -> V attnweights = torch.matmul(Tmodulated, Trefexpanded.transpose(1, 2)) / (Trefexpanded.shape[-1] 0.5) attnweights = F.softmax(attnweights, dim=-1) Fattended = torch.matmul(attnweights, Trefexpanded) # (N, P, D) # Predict Conditioned Appearance (SH Coefficients) Cref = self.appearancehead(Fattended) # (N, G, 3, k+1) # 3. Rendering # Render using differentiable rasterizer # R(G, Cref, poses) renderedimages = rasterize3dgs(G, Cref, poses) return renderedimages, G, Cref, poses def trainstep(self, contextimages, refimages, gtimages): """ contextimages: (B, N, 3, H, W) refimages: (B, M, 3, H, W) - M target references gtimages: (B, M, 3, H, W) - Ground truth for target views """ B, N,,, = contextimages.shape M = refimages.shape[1] # Sample M target references from the batch or external set # In training, we randomly sample M images as targets # For simplicity, assume refimages and gtimages are provided for the M targets renderedimages, G, Cref, poses = self.forward(contextimages[:, 0,:,:,:], refimages[:, 0,:,:,:]) # Loss Calculation # Lrgb lossmse = F.mseloss(renderedimages, gtimages[:, 0,:,:,:]) lossssim = ssimloss(renderedimages, gtimages[:, 0,:,:,:]) losslpips = lpipsloss(renderedimages, gtimages[:, 0,:,:,:]) lossrgb = 1.0 lossmse + 0.05 lossssim + 0.05 losslpips # Lpose (Distillation loss from [11]) losspose = posedistillationloss(poses, gtposes) totalloss = lossrgb + 10.0 losspose return totalloss def geometryguidedviewsampling(S, R, taus, taur, taun, K, N): """ S: Overlap matrix (Nviews, Nviews) R: Scale matrix (Nviews, Nviews) taus: Threshold for overlap taur: Threshold for scale consistency taun: Threshold for number of valid neighbors K: Max neighbors to sample N: Number of views to select """ # Valid mask V = (S >= taus) & (R >= taur) # Valid starting rows validcolsums = V.sum(dim=1) C = [i for i, sumval in enumerate(validcolsums) if sumval > taun] if not C: return [] # Initialize queue import random startnode = random.choice(C) queue = [startnode] visited = {startnode} selectedindices = [startnode] while len(selectedindices) < N and queue: u = queue.pop(0) # Sample up to K neighbors from valid unvisited views neighbors = [v for v in range(len(V)) if V[u, v] and v not in visited] samplesize = min(K, len(neighbors)) if samplesize > 0: samples = random.sample(neighbors, samplesize) for s in samples: queue.append(s) visited.add(s) selectedindices.append(s) return selectedindices[:N] Parameters: \lambda1 = 10 (Pose loss weight) \lambda2 = 1.0 (MSE loss weight) \lambda3 = 0.05 (SSIM loss weight) \lambda4 = 0.05 (LPIPS loss weight) Thresholds \taus, \taur, \taun for view sampling are predefined but exact values are not specified in the provided notes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Varying Focal Lengths: Standard sampling relying on camera extrinsics fails on in-the-wild datasets with varying focal lengths, where minor pose shifts alter captured content. Mitigated by overlap-based sampling using SfM points. Photometric Interference: Content features from the geometry branch retain original photometric properties, potentially interfering with target appearance conditioning. Mitigated by global pre-modulation using AdaLN-Zero to shift features into the target appearance domain. Time Complexity: Single forward pass, making it significantly faster than optimization-based methods (e.g., NeRF-W, GS-W) which require per-scene gradient descent. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians G and the feature dimensions of the encoder/decoder. Not explicitly quantified in the sources. Performance: On MegaScenes (12 views): PSNR 19.20, SSIM 0.683, LPIPS 0.210. On Phototourism (12 views): PSNR 21.47, SSIM 0.788, LPIPS 0.137. Strengths: Handles sparse, unposed, in-the-wild images; decouples geometry and appearance; enables appearance editing. Limitations: Performance is lower than optimization-based methods on dense, consistent inputs (e.g., FSGS achieves higher PSNR on MegaScenes with 12 views: 13.43 vs 19.20? No, WildSplat 19.20 is higher than FSGS 13.43. Wait, Table 1 shows WildSplat 19.20 vs FSGS 13.43. WildSplat is SOTA among feedforward methods and competitive with optimization-based ones in this specific metric, but the source notes it surpasses existing methods). The source states it surpasses existing optimization-based and feedforward methods. WildSplat was introduced by X. Zhang et al. in the paper "WildSplat: Feedforward Gaussian Splatting from Unposed In-the-Wild Images". It addresses the limitations of previous feedforward methods (like pixelSplat, MVSplat) that assume photometric consistency and optimization-based methods (like NeRF-W, GS-W) that require precomputed poses and dense images. It builds on the principles of feedforward 3D reconstruction and 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent, S1]. name: StereoGaussians
body: StereoGaussians is a feed-forward method that predicts a metric 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation from a single calibrated stereo pair, enabling nearby-view extrapolation without per-scene optimization. It differs from its siblings by explicitly transferring frozen stereo features into Gaussian attribute prediction and using a two-layer Gaussian structure with an expanded image canvas to handle disoccluded content and outside-field-of-view regions. Unlike methods that synthesize images directly (e.g., LVSM) or refine inverse depth through a composer (e.g., SHARP), StereoGaussians fixes the front-layer stereo depth and bounds image-plane offsets to provide a structural prior for geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A calibrated rectified stereo pair (left image IL, right image IR), camera intrinsics K (focal lengths fx, fy, principal point cx, cy), and baseline B. Outputs: A set of N Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{(xi, si, qi, \alphai, ci)\}{i=1}^N in the left-camera frame, where xi is position, si is scale, qi is rotation (quaternion), \alphai is opacity, and ci is color (Spherical Harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: The method predicts two layers of Gaussians (front and back) for every pixel on an expanded canvas. Front Layer: Anchored to the stereo-derived depth. Back Layer: Anchored to a local maximum depth in a neighborhood plus a learned offset. Gaussian Attributes per Pixel: Opacity: 1 channel (logit space). Image-plane offset: 2 channels (\deltau, \deltav). Scale: 3 channels (isotropic base scale + multiplicative residual). Rotation: 4 channels (quaternion residual). Color: 27 channels (degree-2 Spherical Harmonics residuals). Total per layer: 37 channels. Back-layer depth offset: 1 scalar channel. Steps: 1. Stereo Feature Extraction: Pass the stereo pair through a frozen pretrained stereo encoder (e.g., FoundationStereo) to obtain a left-reference disparity map d, aligned multiscale features \{Fs\}, and other context features. Compute metric depth z(p) for each pixel p=(u,v): z(p) = \text{clip}\left( \frac{fx B}{d(p)}, z{\min}, z{\max} \right) where fx is the horizontal focal length in pixels, B is the baseline, and z{\min}, z{\max} are clipping bounds. 2. Descriptor Generation: Construct a dense full-resolution descriptor \Phi by concatenating stereo features with resized reference RGB and depth at each scale s: \Phi = D \left[ \{Fs, \downarrows IL, \downarrows z\}s \right] \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W} where D is a DPT-style decoder, [\cdot, \cdot] denotes channel concatenation, and \downarrows resizes inputs to feature scale s (e.g., s=4 implies H/4 \times W/4). Implementation Detail: At each scale, concatenate encoder features with resized RGB (bilinear) and depth (nearest-neighbor). Project to 128 channels via 1\times1 convolution, Group Normalization, and GELU. Use residual convolution units and coarse-to-fine fusion blocks to yield the 128-channel descriptor \Phi at original resolution. 3. Canvas Expansion: Extend the reference RGB IL, processed depth z, and descriptor \Phi by edge-replication padding P (default 16 pixels) on each side to size (H+2P) \times (W+2P). Update canvas intrinsics: Focal lengths remain unchanged. Principal point shifts to \tilde{c}x = cx + P, \tilde{c}y = cy + P. Let the extended inputs be denoted with tildes: \tilde{I}L, \tilde{z}, \tilde{\Phi}. 4. Gaussian Attribute Prediction: Pass extended inputs through a convolutional predictor H to obtain attribute residuals: (\theta{\text{front}}, \theta{\text{back}}, \Delta z) = H([\tilde{I}L, \tilde{z}, \tilde{\Phi}]) Regressor: Two 3\times3 convolutions with intermediate GELU map inputs to a 128-channel tensor h. Output Branches: Each branch processes [h, \tilde{I}L, \tilde{\Phi}] using a 3\times3 convolution, Group Normalization, GELU, and a final 3\times3 convolution. Front/Back Branches: Output 37 channels each (opacity, offset, scale, quaternion, SH). Depth Offset Branch: Outputs a scalar \Delta z. 5. Gaussian Center and Depth Calculation: For each pixel p on the expanded canvas: Front Layer Depth: z{\text{front}}(p) = \tilde{z}(p). Front Layer Center: Compute image-plane offsets (\delta{u,\text{front}}, \delta{v,\text{front}}) = \sigma(o{\text{front}}) - 0.5, bounded to half a canvas pixel. Center is: x{\text{front}}(p) = z{\text{front}}(p) \tilde{K}^{-1} [u + \delta{u,\text{front}}, v + \delta{v,\text{front}}, 1]^\top where \tilde{K} is the expanded canvas intrinsic matrix. Back Layer Depth: Compute local maximum depth in a 9\times9 neighborhood \mathcal{N}9(p) plus a learned positive offset: z{\text{back}}(p) = \max{q \in \mathcal{N}9(p)} \tilde{z}(q) + \text{softplus}(\Delta z(p)). Back Layer Center: Similar to front, using z{\text{back}}(p) and its specific offsets. 6. Gaussian Attribute Composition: Attributes are predicted as residuals around a base defined by the reference image and geometry: Base Scale: Isotropic base scale s{0,\ell} = \kappa \frac{z\ell}{fx fy}, following the metric pixel footprint. Residuals: Scale: Bounded multiplicative updates. Rotation: Additive quaternion updates. Opacity: Updates in logit space. Color: Degree-2 Spherical Harmonic (SH) residuals around a reference-image DC base. 7. Rendering and Training: Concatenate front and back layers. Render target views using differentiable Gaussian rasterization. The back layer is unmasked, allowing learned attributes and visibility to determine contributions. Loss: Minimize \mathcal{L} = \text{MSE}(IT, \hat{I}T) + 0.05 \text{LPIPS}{\text{VGG}}(IT, \hat{I}T), where IT is the target image and \hat{I}T is the rendered prediction. Optimization: AdamW optimizer, LR 4 \times 10^{-4}, weight decay 0.01, momentum (0.9, 0.999). OneCycleLR schedule with 2,700 warm-up steps, initial/final division factors 25/100. Total 30,000 steps. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class StereoGaussiansPredictor(nn.Module): def init(self, encoder, decoderchannels=128, padding=16): super().init() self.encoder = encoder # Frozen stereo encoder self.decoder = DPTDecoder(inchannels=encoder.outchannels, outchannels=decoderchannels) self.padding = padding # Predictor components self.regressor = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(decoderchannels + 3 + 1, 128, 3, padding=1), # +3 for RGB, +1 for depth nn.GELU(), nn.Conv2d(128, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.GELU()) # Output branches self.frontbranch = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(128 + 3 + 1, 128, 3, padding=1), # +3 RGB, +1 depth nn.GroupNorm(8, 128), nn.GELU(), nn.Conv2d(128, 37, 3, padding=1) # 1 op, 2 off, 3 scale, 4 quat, 27 SH) self.backbranch = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(128 + 3 + 1, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.GroupNorm(8, 128), nn.GELU(), nn.Conv2d(128, 37, 3, padding=1)) self.depthoffsetbranch = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(128 + 3 + 1, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.GroupNorm(8, 128), nn.GELU(), nn.Conv2d(128, 1, 3, padding=1)) def forward(self, IL, IR, K, B, zmin, zmax): # 1. Stereo Feature Extraction # encoder returns disparity d and multiscale features {Fs} d, Fs = self.encoder(IL, IR) # Compute metric depth fx = K[0, 0] z = torch.clamp((fx B) / d, zmin, zmax) # 2. Descriptor Generation # Resize RGB and depth for each scale s # DPT decoder fuses features Phi = self.decoder(Fs, IL, z) # Output: [B, C, H, W] # 3. Canvas Expansion P = self.padding ILext = F.pad(IL, (P, P, P, P), mode='replicate') zext = F.pad(z, (P, P, P, P), mode='replicate') Phiext = F.pad(Phi, (P, P, P, P), mode='replicate') # 4. Gaussian Attribute Prediction # Regressor input: Extended RGB, Depth, Descriptor reginput = torch.cat([ILext, zext, Phiext], dim=1) h = self.regressor(reginput) # Branch inputs: h, Extended RGB, Extended Descriptor branchinput = torch.cat([h, ILext, Phiext], dim=1) thetafront = self.frontbranch(branchinput) thetaback = self.backbranch(branchinput) deltaz = self.depthoffsetbranch(branchinput) # 5. Gaussian Center and Depth Calculation # Front Layer zfront = zext # Offsets: sigma(o) - 0.5, bounded to 0.5 offfront = torch.sigmoid(thetafront[:, 1:3,:,:]) - 0.5 offfront = torch.clamp(offfront, -0.5, 0.5) # Back Layer # Local max in 9x9 neighborhood # Note: In practice, use F.maxpool2d with kernel 9 zmaxpool = F.maxpool2d(zext, kernelsize=9, stride=1, padding=4) zback = zmaxpool + F.softplus(deltaz) offback = torch.sigmoid(thetaback[:, 1:3,:,:]) - 0.5 offback = torch.clamp(offback, -0.5, 0.5) # 6. Construct Gaussians # This part typically happens in the rendering step or a separate constructor # returning the parameters needed for the rasterizer return { 'zfront': zfront, 'zback': zback, 'offfront': offfront, 'offback': offback, 'thetafront': thetafront, 'thetaback': thetaback, 'deltaz': deltaz, 'Kext': K # With shifted principal point } Time Complexity: Inference is O(HW) per stereo pair, dominated by the convolutional predictor and encoder. It is significantly faster than per-scene optimization methods which require iterative gradient descent. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with image resolution H \times W due to the dense prediction of Gaussian attributes on the expanded canvas. The expanded canvas increases memory by a factor of (1 + 2P/H)(1 + 2P/W). Performance: On StereoNVS, StereoGaussians achieves 21.261 PSNR, 0.9447 SSIM, and 0.0818 LPIPS. On ReplicaGS, it achieves 30.266 PSNR, 0.9447 SSIM, and 0.0818 LPIPS. Strengths: Handles disoccluded content via the back layer (removing it reduces PSNR by 0.180 dB on StereoNVS and 3.826 dB on ReplicaGS). Handles outside-field-of-view content via canvas padding (removing 16-pixel padding lowers PSNR by 3.168 dB on StereoNVS and 8.732 dB on ReplicaGS). Generalizes to unseen scenes without per-scene tuning. Limitations: Fixed front-layer depth limits stereo-error correction. Teacher artifacts from the training data (SceneSplat-Stereo) can persist. Evaluation is focused on nearby views; larger viewpoint changes are not fully addressed. Composition improves perceptual metrics (LPIPS/SSIM) but lowers PSNR compared to the composer-free variant (0.614 dB higher PSNR for composer-free). StereoGaussians was introduced by to address the need for nearby-view extrapolation in stereo-camera applications, XR headsets, and spatial video. It builds on the principles of feed-forward 3DGS [Parent] and leverages frozen pretrained stereo networks (like FoundationStereo) to transfer geometric priors into Gaussian attribute prediction. The method was trained on a new dataset, SceneSplat-Stereo, constructed from quality-filtered 3DGS teachers, pairing stereo inputs with nearby target views across 803 training scenes. It is used on StereoNVS and ReplicaGS datasets. StereoGaussians: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting from Stereo Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38592, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: GlobalSplat
head: GlobalSplat: Efficient Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting via Global Scene Tokens
body: GlobalSplat is a feed-forward framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that aligns multi-view inputs into a fixed set of global latent scene tokens before decoding explicit 3D geometry, preventing representation bloat and ensuring global consistency. Unlike sibling methods such as C3G which rely on full self-attention and single-Gaussian decoding, GlobalSplat uses an iterative, disentangled dual-branch architecture and a coarse-to-fine capacity curriculum to achieve a superior quality-efficiency trade-off in large-context settings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of C RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} with known camera poses Ti (rotation Ri, translation ti) and intrinsics Ki. Output: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gn\}{n=1}^N, where each Gaussian gn is defined by mean \mun, covariance \Sigman (parameterized by scale sn and rotation rn), opacity \alphan, and spherical harmonics coefficients cn. Data Structures: Latent Tokens: A fixed set of M=2048 learnable latent tokens lj \in \mathbb{R}^{512} and learnable register tokens. Gaussian Candidates: For each latent token, the decoder predicts Ks=16 candidates. Geometry: \mathbf{X}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 3} (means), \mathbf{S}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 3} (log-scales), \mathbf{R}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 6} (6D rotations), \mathbf{O}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 1} (opacity logits), \boldsymbol{\ell}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 1} (importance scores). Appearance: \mathbf{C}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times (3 D{\text{SH}})} (SH coefficients), where D{\text{SH}} = 16. Merged Gaussians: At stage s, candidates are grouped into G=2^s groups of size bs = 16/G. The merged attributes \bar{\mathbf{z}}{p,g} are computed via weighted aggregation. Preprocessing: 1. Scene Normalization: Compute canonical frame origin: \bar{o} = \frac{1}{C} \sum{i=1}^C oi. Compute axes by averaging camera viewing directions and re-orthonormalizing. Let T{\text{avg}} be the resulting average pose. Transform all cameras: \hat{T}i = T{\text{avg}}^{-1} Ti. Compute scene scale: s = \max{a,b} \|\hat{o}a - \hat{o}b\|2. Scale translations: \tilde{o}i = \frac{\hat{o}i}{s}. 2. Image Preprocessing: Resize image to height 256 preserving aspect ratio. Round width to a multiple of patch size 8. Update intrinsics accordingly. Apply centered square crop. Final resize to 256 \times 256. 3. Input Context Construction: Extract patchified RGB tokens u{i,p}^{\text{rgb}} from input view i and patch p. Compute dense Plücker-ray features r{i,p} and patchify. Map rays: \hat{r}{i,p} = W{\text{ray}} r{i,p}. Compute per-view code ei from absolute camera center oi and intrinsics \kappai: ei = W{\text{proj}}\Big ([\text{MLP}{K}(\phi (\kappa i));\ \text{PE}(oi)]\Big) where \phi uses resolution-normalized intrinsics and PE is Fourier positional encoding. Combine: u{i,p}^{\text{cam}} = \hat{r}{i,p} + ei. Concatenate: u{i,p} = [u{i,p}^{\text{cam}}; u{i,p}^{\text{rgb}}]. Algorithm: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GlobalSplat(inputimages, cameraposes, intrinsics): # 1. Preprocessing normalizedposes = normalizescene(cameraposes) processedimages = preprocessimages(inputimages) # 2. Feature Extraction # Extract RGB features and Plücker rays for each view rgbfeatures = extractrgbfeatures(processedimages) # Patchified pluckerrays = computepluckerrays(normalizedposes, intrinsics) # Dense, then patchified # Construct input context tokens # Wray is a learned linear layer rayembeddings = applylinear(pluckerrays, Wray) # Compute per-view camera codes cameracodes = [] for pose, intr in zip(normalizedposes, intrinsics): # Fourier encoding of center, MLP of intrinsics centerpe = fourierencoding(pose.translation) intrmlp = mlp(intr) # Projected combination code = projectlinear(concat(intrmlp, centerpe)) cameracodes.append(code) # Broadcast camera code to all patches and add to ray features inputcontext = [] for i, view in enumerate(processedimages): patches = patchify(view) viewrayemb = rayembeddings[i] # Shape: [numpatches, 256] viewcamcode = cameracodes[i] # Shape: [256] # Add camera code to every patch camtokens = viewrayemb + viewcamcode # Concatenate with RGB features # rgbfeatures[i] shape: [numpatches, 512] contexttokens = concat(camtokens, rgbfeatures[i], dim=-1) inputcontext.append(contexttokens) # 3. Dual-Branch Encoder # Initialize M=2048 latent tokens of dim 512 latenttokens = initializelatenttokens(M=2048, dim=512) # B=4 encoder blocks for b in range(B): # Project latent tokens to geometry and appearance streams fgeo = projectgeo(latenttokens) fapp = projectapp(latenttokens) # Cross-attention with input context # Input context is flattened across views and patches x = flattencontext(inputcontext) fgeo = crossattention(x, fgeo) fapp = crossattention(x, fapp) # Self-attention blocks (L=2) for l in range(L): fgeo = selfattention(fgeo) fapp = selfattention(fapp) # Fuse streams fused = concat(fgeo, fapp, dim=-1) latenttokens = mixermlp(fused) # 4. Dual-Branch Decoder # Project final latent tokens geotokens = projectgeodecoder(latenttokens) apptokens = projectappdecoder(latenttokens) # Predict 16 candidates per latent token # geotokens predicts X, S, R, O, l # apptokens predicts C candidates = predictcandidates(geotokens, apptokens) # 5. Coarse-to-Fine Merging (Stage s=3 for final model) # G = 2^s = 8 groups, bs = 16/8 = 2 candidates per group G = 8 bs = 16 // G gaussians = [] for p in range(M): for g in range(G): # Get candidates for this group groupcandidates = candidates[p, gbs: (g+1)bs] # Compute importance weights using temperature-scaled softmax on logits l logits = groupcandidates['l'] # Shape: [bs] weights = softmax(logits / tau) # Weighted aggregation of attributes mean = weightedsum(groupcandidates['X'], weights) scale = weightedsum(groupcandidates['S'], weights) rotation = weightedsum(groupcandidates['R'], weights) opacity = weightedsum(groupcandidates['O'], weights) color = weightedsum(groupcandidates['C'], weights) # Convert parameters to final Gaussian representation # Mean: offset from 1.5? No, mean is predicted directly or as offset? # Source says "Means initialized with fixed forward offset of 1.5" # and "Scale predicted in log space as offset from -2" # "Opacity predicted in logit space as offset from -5" # "Rotations use continuous 6D parameterization as residual offsets" finalmean = mean + 1.5 # finalscale = exp(scale - 2) # finalopacity = sigmoid(opacity - 5) # finalrotation = residualtorotation(rotation) # gaussians.append(Gaussian(finalmean, finalscale, finalrotation, finalopacity, color)) return gaussians Gaussian Parameterization Details: Means: Predicted values are treated as offsets from a fixed forward offset of 1.5. Scales: Predicted in log space as an offset from -2. Final scale s = \exp(\text{pred} - 2). Opacity: Predicted in logit space as an offset from -5. Final opacity \alpha = \sigma(\text{pred} - 5). Rotations: Continuous 6D parameterization as residual offsets from a static rotation. Training Objectives: The total loss is \mathcal{L} = \lambda{\text{ren}}\mathcal{L}{\text{ren}} + \lambda{\text{con}}\mathcal{L}{\text{con}} + \lambda{\text{reg}}\mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}. Rendering Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{ren}} = \|It - \hat{I}t\|2^2 + \lambda{\text{perc}}\mathcal{L}{\text{perc}}(It, \hat{I}t). Self-Supervised Consistency Loss: Partition views into Ia, Ib. \mathcal{L}{\text{con}} = \|O(Ia) - \text{sg}(O(Ib))\|2^2 + \|D(Ia) - \text{sg}(D(Ib))\|2^2, where O, D are rendered opacity and depth maps. Regularization: \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \lambda{\text{thr}}\mathcal{L}{\text{thr}} + \lambda{\text{fru}}\mathcal{L}{\text{fru}} (soft thresholding and frustum constraint). Coarse-to-Fine Curriculum: Training starts with stage s=0 (G=1, all 16 candidates merged into 1 Gaussian). Capacity increments to G \in \{2, 4, 8\}. The final model uses G=8, resulting in N = 2048 \times 8 = 16,384 Gaussians. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Log-space predictions for scale and opacity require careful handling of numerical stability during exponentiation and sigmoid application. Boundaries: Scene normalization relies on the diameter of the camera constellation; scenes with widely dispersed cameras may require robust outlier handling in the scale computation s. Degenerate Input: If input views have insufficient overlap, the cross-attention mechanism may fail to align features correctly, leading to poor latent token refinement. Time Complexity: Inference is a single forward pass through the encoder-decoder network. On RealEstate10K with 24 input views, inference takes <78 ms. Memory Complexity: Peak GPU memory is 1.79 GB for 24 views on RealEstate10K. Disk size is ~4 MB for the 16K Gaussian representation. Performance: On RealEstate10K with 12 views, GlobalSplat16K achieves PSNR 28.57, SSIM 0.885, LPIPS 0.138. GlobalSplat32K achieves PSNR 29.54, SSIM 0.903, LPIPS 0.121. GlobalSplat2K achieves PSNR 26.83, SSIM 0.838, LPIPS 0.198. Strengths: Compact representation (16K Gaussians) regardless of input view count; fast inference; low memory footprint; global consistency. Limitations: Fixed number of Gaussians may limit detail in very complex scenes compared to dense methods; relies on known camera poses (unlike Splatt3R or ZeroGS). GlobalSplat was introduced by R. Itkin et al. in 2025. It addresses the limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS pipelines that form primitives in dense view-aligned spaces, leading to representation bloat and fragile global consistency as more views are added. By aligning first and decoding later, it provides a more efficient operating point for large-context novel view synthesis. GlobalSplat: Efficient Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting via Global Scene Tokens, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37595-710, fetched 2026-10-29

name: CodecSplat
head: Ultra-compact latent coding framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting
body: CodecSplat is a compression framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) that encodes an intermediate 2D Gaussian-generation feature into an entropy-coded scene bitstream, avoiding the inefficient compression of irregular 3D Gaussian primitives. Unlike existing 3DGS compression methods that compress Gaussian primitives after a structured-to-irregular transformation, CodecSplat places the coding bottleneck before 2D-to-3D Gaussian construction, allowing compression to exploit the structured intermediate feature representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N posed context views C = \{(Ii, Ki, Ti, ni, fi)\}{i=1}^N, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} is a context image, Ki and Ti denote camera intrinsics and extrinsics, and ni, fi are near and far bounds. Output: A self-contained scene bitstream B. Data Structures: Multi-view features (F{mv}): Image and cross-view matching features extracted by the backbone. Encoder-side depth (D{enc}): A tensor in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H \times W} representing depth predictions at the encoder side. Depth matching-probability features (P{depth}): Features containing depth matching probabilities. Gaussian-generation feature (Fg): A dense, regular tensor in \mathbb{R}^{N \times CF \times H \times W} specialized for Gaussian generation. Latent features: The compressed representation of Fg after analysis transform, quantization, and entropy coding. Parameters: Rate control parameter (\lambda): Used in the encoder and decoder to control the trade-off between bitstream size and reconstruction quality. Steps: 1. Multi-view Feature Extraction: The encoder performs multi-view matching and feature extraction on the context views C. This produces multi-view features F{mv}, encoder-side depth D{enc}, and depth matching-probability features P{depth}: (F{mv}, D{enc}, P{depth}) = \text{MVEnc}(C) where \text{MVEnc} denotes the multi-view encoder backbone. 2. Gaussian-Generation Feature Construction: The extracted cues are converted into a dense Gaussian-generation feature Fg: Fg = \text{FeatHead}(I{1:N}, F{mv}, P{depth}) where \text{FeatHead} is a feature head network. 3. Latent Encoding (Encoder Side): Analysis Transform: The feature Fg is transformed into a latent representation. Quantization: The latent representation is quantized using the rate control parameter \lambda. Entropy Coding: The quantized latents are entropy-coded. Bitstream Packing: The encoded latent features and compressed context-view camera parameters are packed into the scene bitstream B. 4. Latent Decoding (Decoder Side): Entropy Decoding: The scene bitstream B is entropy-decoded to recover the quantized latent representation. Synthesis Transform: The latent representation is reconstructed into a feature map using a synthesis transform. Camera Recovery: The compressed context-view camera metadata is recovered. 5. Gaussian Reconstruction: The decoded feature is used for: Depth prediction. Feature refinement. Gaussian parameter prediction (opacity, scale, rotation, color/SH). 2D-to-3D mapping to produce the final 3D Gaussian primitives \hat{\mathcal{G}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def codecsplatencode(contextviews): """ Encodes context views into a scene bitstream. contextviews: List of tuples (I, K, T, n, f) for N views. """ # Step 1: Multi-view feature extraction # MVEnc extracts features and depth from context views Fmv, Denc, Pdepth = MVEnc(contextviews) # Step 2: Construct Gaussian-generation feature # FeatHead combines images, multi-view features, and depth cues Fg = FeatHead(contextviews.images, Fmv, Pdepth) # Step 3: Latent encoding # Analysis transform converts Fg to latent space latent = analysistransform(Fg) # Quantization with rate control lambda # lambda controls the trade-off between size and quality quantizedlatent = quantize(latent, lambda) # Entropy coding bitstreamlatents = entropyencode(quantizedlatent) # Compress camera parameters compressedcameras = compresscameras(contextviews.cameras) # Pack bitstream bitstream = pack(bitstreamlatents, compressedcameras) return bitstream def codecsplatdecode(bitstream): """ Decodes a scene bitstream into 3D Gaussian primitives. bitstream: The encoded scene bitstream. """ # Step 4: Latent decoding # Unpack bitstream bitstreamlatents, compressedcameras = unpack(bitstream) # Entropy decoding quantizedlatent = entropydecode(bitstreamlatents) # Synthesis transform to reconstruct feature Fgdecoded = synthesistransform(quantizedlatent) # Recover camera metadata cameras = decompresscameras(compressedcameras) # Step 5: Gaussian reconstruction # Predict depth and refine features depthpred, refinedfeatures = depthandrefine(Fgdecoded) # Predict Gaussian parameters # Heads predict opacity, scale, rotation, color/SH gaussians = predictgaussians(refinedfeatures, depthpred, cameras) return gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rate-Distortion Trade-off: The choice of \lambda significantly impacts the bitstream size and reconstruction quality. A suboptimal \lambda may lead to excessive compression artifacts or unnecessarily large bitstreams. Structured Feature Assumption: The method relies on the intermediate feature Fg being a regular, structured tensor. If the backbone fails to produce a coherent Fg, the entropy coding efficiency will degrade. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The method produces ultra-compact bitstreams. On the DL3DV dataset, scene sizes range from 20.00–107.77 KiB per scene. On the RealEstate10K dataset, sizes range from 3.37–12.51 KiB per scene. Measured Performance: DL3DV: 23.56–26.36 dB PSNR. RealEstate10K: 24.76–27.05 dB PSNR. Scaling: CodecSplat reduces scene size by roughly one order of magnitude compared with compressing feed-forward generated Gaussian primitives. Strengths: Avoids inefficient compression of irregular 3D Gaussian primitives. Exploits the structured intermediate feature representation for better compression. Preserves controllable rate-distortion behavior. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the feed-forward backbone (e.g., DepthSplat-style) to produce a compressible intermediate feature. Performance is dependent on the rate control parameter \lambda. When to use: When ultra-compact storage or transmission of feed-forward 3D Gaussian scenes is required, and the underlying feed-forward backbone is already trained. When not to use: When per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher fidelity is prioritized over extreme compression ratios, or when the feed-forward backbone does not produce a structured intermediate feature suitable for entropy coding. Origin: CodecSplat was introduced in the paper "CodecSplat: Ultra-Compact Latent Coding for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting". History: It builds upon feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods, specifically those using depth-guided multi-view feature refinement (e.g., DepthSplat). It addresses the limitation of existing 3DGS compression methods that operate on the final irregular 3D representation, which is decoupled from the internal feature-to-Gaussian generation process. Usage: It is used for compressing scenes reconstructed by feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting pipelines, enabling efficient storage and transmission of 3D Gaussian representations. CodecSplat: Ultra-Compact Latent Coding for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.25563, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Feature Plane Compression (CodecGS)
head: Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Optimized Feature Planes and Standard Video Codecs, Tri-plane Architecture
body: Feature Plane Compression (CodecGS) is a method for compressing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by replacing direct storage of unstructured Gaussian primitives with a structured, learnable feature plane representation. It solves the problem of high storage costs and inefficient entropy coding of irregular 3D point clouds by mapping 3D positions to Gaussian attributes via a tri-plane architecture, which is then compressed using standard video codecs. Unlike sibling methods that compress geometry or use anchor-based residual coding, CodecGS leverages the spatial redundancy of natural scenes by organizing parameters in a 2D grid-like structure, allowing the use of mature image/video compression standards. Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene (positions, covariances, colors, opacities) or a feed-forward prediction of Gaussian attributes. Outputs: A compressed bitstream representing the feature planes, decodable into Gaussian attributes for rendering. Data Structures: 1. Tri-Plane Feature Map: A set of three 2D feature planes (Fx, Fy, Fz) corresponding to the xy, yz, and xz projections. Each plane stores a high-dimensional feature vector for each grid cell. 2. Attribute Prediction: For a 3D point \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z), the feature vector \mathbf{f} is obtained by interpolating values from the three planes at the projected coordinates of \mathbf{x}. 3. Encoded Format: Feature planes are normalized and converted to 16-bit integers, conforming to the YUV 16-bit format standard for video codecs. Steps: 1. Tri-Plane Initialization: Initialize three 2D grids (tri-planes) with learnable parameters. The resolution of these planes determines the granularity of the attribute prediction. 2. Two-Phase Training: Phase 1 (Standard 3DGS): Perform standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training to optimize initial Gaussian positions, covariances, and colors. Phase 2 (Feature Plane Optimization): Replace direct Gaussian attribute storage with the tri-plane prediction. The tri-planes are optimized to predict Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity) for any query point \mathbf{x}. 3. Progressive Training Strategy: To address instability caused by sparse 3DGS signals, employ a progressive training strategy. Initially capture coarse geometric information with low-resolution tri-planes, then gradually increase resolution to add finer details. 4. DCT Entropy Modeling: Apply block-wise Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to the feature planes during optimization. This transforms the spatial data to leverage spatial correlations, similar to conventional image signals, improving compressibility. 5. Smoothing Regularization: Add a smoothing regularization term during training to promote locally smooth configurations of Gaussians on the grid, further enhancing compressibility. 6. Quantization and Encoding: Normalize the trained feature planes. Convert the normalized floating-point values to 16-bit integers. Encode the resulting 16-bit integer planes using a standard video codec (e.g., H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def codecgstrainandcompress(gaussianscene, triplaneresolution): """ Trains a tri-plane feature representation for 3DGS and compresses it. """ # Initialize tri-planes: Fx, Fy, Fz of shape (H, W, C) # C is the channel dimension for feature vectors Fx = initializetriplane(triplaneresolution) Fy = initializetriplane(triplaneresolution) Fz = initializetriplane(triplaneresolution) # Phase 1: Standard 3DGS Training # Optimize initial Gaussian primitives (pos, scale, rot, color, opacity) # using standard 3DGS loss (rendering error + regularization) gaussians = standard3dgstraining(gaussianscene) # Phase 2: Feature Plane Training # Replace direct storage with tri-plane prediction # Loss includes rendering error and smoothing regularization for epoch in range(numepochs): # Sample 3D points x from the scene distribution points = sample3dpoints(gaussians) # Predict attributes from tri-planes # Interpolate features from Fx, Fy, Fz at projected coordinates features = predictfeaturesfromtriplanes(points, Fx, Fy, Fz) # Decode attributes from features (pos, scale, rot, color, opacity) predictedgaussians = decodeattributes(features) # Calculate rendering loss loss = calculaterenderingloss(predictedgaussians) # Add smoothing regularization to promote spatial smoothness smoothingloss = calculatesmoothingloss(Fx, Fy, Fz) # Total loss totalloss = loss + lambdasmooth smoothingloss # Update tri-planes using gradient descent updateparameters(Fx, Fy, Fz, totalloss) # Progressive resolution increase if applicable if epoch in progressiveschedule: increasetriplaneresolution(Fx, Fy, Fz) # Post-training: Prepare for video codec # Normalize feature planes to a specific range Fxnorm = normalize(Fx) Fynorm = normalize(Fy) Fznorm = normalize(Fz) # Convert to 16-bit integers (YUV 16-bit format) Fxint = floatto16bitint(Fxnorm) Fyint = floatto16bitint(Fynorm) Fzint = floatto16bitint(Fznorm) # Encode using standard video codec # The codec expects YUV format; map Fx, Fy, Fz to Y, U, V components # or encode each plane separately depending on codec implementation bitstream = videocodecencode(Fxint, Fyint, Fzint) return bitstream def predictfeaturesfromtriplanes(points, Fx, Fy, Fz): """ Interpolate features from tri-planes for given 3D points. """ # Project 3D point x=(x,y,z) to 2D coordinates on each plane # xy-plane: (x, y), yz-plane: (y, z), xz-plane: (x, z) coordsxy = (points.x, points.y) coordsyz = (points.y, points.z) coordsxz = (points.x, points.z) # Sample features from each plane using bilinear interpolation fxy = bilinearsample(Fx, coordsxy) fyz = bilinearsample(Fy, coordsyz) fxz = bilinearsample(Fz, coordsxz) # Combine features (e.g., concatenation or weighted sum) # Note: Exact combination method not specified in sources, # standard tri-plane usage often concatenates or averages. # Assuming concatenation of feature vectors from each plane features = concatenate(fxy, fyz, fxz) return features Parameters: Tri-plane Resolution: Not given in the sources. Determines the spatial granularity. Feature Channel Dimension (C): Not given in the sources. Smoothing Regularization Weight (\lambda{smooth}): Not given in the sources. Quantization: 16-bit integers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Signals: Feature plane training can be unstable due to sparse 3DGS signals. Mitigated by progressive training. Boundary Conditions: Interpolation at the boundaries of the tri-planes requires careful handling (e.g., clamping or padding). Precision: Conversion to 16-bit integers may introduce quantization artifacts. The choice of normalization range is critical. Compression Ratio: Not given in the sources. Rendering Quality: Not given in the sources. Complexity: Encoding complexity depends on the standard video codec used. Decoding involves video decoding followed by tri-plane interpolation. Strengths: Leverages mature video compression standards; exploits spatial redundancy in natural scenes; avoids complex entropy coding of irregular 3D structures. Limitations: Requires training of feature planes; interpolation overhead during rendering; potential loss of high-frequency details due to quantization and video codec compression. When to Use: When high compression ratios are needed and standard video codecs are available; suitable for feed-forward or pre-computed scenes. When Not to Use: When real-time training of feature planes is prohibitive; when exact preservation of unstructured Gaussian data is required without interpolation artifacts. CodecGS was introduced as a method to compress 3D Gaussian Splatting by employing optimized feature planes and standard video codecs. It builds on the observation that 3DGS parameters can be organized in a 2D grid to capitalize on perceptual redundancies found in natural scenes. The method interprets the training process of positioning and optimizing Gaussians as a sampling procedure, drawing inspiration from 3DGS-MCMC approaches. It is implemented in the gsplat library, an open-source library for CUDA-accelerated differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians. 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: latentSplat
head: Autoencoding Variational Gaussians for Fast Generalizable 3D Reconstruction
body: latentSplat is a method for generalizable 3D reconstruction from two reference views that predicts semantic 3D Gaussians in a latent space. It models uncertainty explicitly by storing distributions (mean and variance) of spherical harmonic coefficients for each Gaussian, allowing sampling of specific instances for rendering. Unlike regression-based methods such as pixelSplat which provide a single low-variance solution, latentSplat handles high-ambiguity regions and view extrapolation better, avoiding blurry reconstructions in unobserved areas. Compared to generative diffusion-based methods like GeNVS, it is orders of magnitude faster and scales to high resolutions by using efficient Gaussian splatting for rendering instead of volume rendering or iterative diffusion sampling. Inputs: Two reference views (RGB images) and their corresponding camera poses. Outputs: A synthesized RGB image for an arbitrary novel view. The covariance matrix is \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^\top \mathbf{R}^\top. SH coefficients are computed up to degree 4 for RGB and degree 2 for semantic features (dimensionality 4). Steps: 1. Feature Encoding: Encode the two input views using a DINOv1 ViT-B/8 backbone. Upscale local patch tokens by repeating them to the original patch size. Add a linearly projected global class token to obtain a feature map at the original image resolution. Downscale the input feature maps by a factor of 4 in each dimension for computational feasibility. 2. Epipolar Aggregation: Process 32 samples of each pixel's epipolar line using an Epipolar Transformer. The transformer consists of two blocks with four-head attention. Token dimensionality is 128. Add a skip connection at the original resolution to prevent a bottleneck with low spatial dimensions in the epipolar transformer. 3. Predict \mathbf{h}\mu and \mathbf{h}\sigma for the semantic feature distributions. 4. For each Gaussian i, sample feature coefficients \mathbf{h}i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{h}{\mu,i}, \mathbf{h}{\sigma,i}). 5. Rendering: Render the sampled instance of semantic Gaussians to the target novel view using efficient Gaussian splatting. This produces an auxiliary RGB rendering and feature maps. 6. Decoding: Decode the splatted features into pixel space using a lightweight generative decoder network (VAE-GAN decoder). The decoder is a fully convolutional architecture with four upsample blocks, each containing two residual blocks. Add 1x1 convolutions as skip connections to feed downscaled versions of the intermediate auxiliary RGB renderings and feature maps into each upsample block. Initialize the weights of these additional skip connection layers to zero to avoid noisy gradients. 7.
