name: Feature Uplifting via Forward Rendering
head: Forward Feature Collection, LGS estimator, MAP estimator for LGS, Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation for LGS, Maximum Likelihood Feature Uplifting, Occam's LGS Feature Uplifting
body: Feature Uplifting via Forward Rendering is a method to estimate 3D language features f \in \mathbb{R}^d for 3D Gaussians from observed 2D features F{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^d by formulating the problem as a Maximum Likelihood (ML) or Maximum-a-Posteriori (MAP) estimation, assuming uniform prior and Gaussian noise. It differs from back-projection methods (e.g., conventional semantic feature learning) by leveraging the forward rendering process to establish precise correspondence, eliminating costly back-projection or iterative optimization. It builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction. Inputs: A set of trained 3D Gaussians G = \{G1, \dots, Gm\}, where each Gaussian Gi has mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and color ci. A set of training camera views S = \{s1, \dots, sn\} with known poses. 2D language feature maps F = \{f^{s1}, \dots, f^{sn}\}, where each f^s \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d} is extracted from the input images using a feature extractor (e.g., OpenCLIP ViT-B/16). Outputs: Uplifted 3D language features fi \in \mathbb{R}^d for each Gaussian Gi. A filtered set of semantic Gaussians G^s = \{G^si\}{i=1}^M where M \ll N, representing Gaussians that meaningfully contribute to the scene’s semantic representation. Data Structures: Gaussian: Stores \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or scale si and rotation ri), \alphai \in [0,1], ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, and accumulated feature fi \in \mathbb{R}^d and weight wi \in \mathbb{R}. 2D Feature Map: A tensor of shape H \times W \times d for each view. Formulas: The method assumes a uniform prior p(f) \propto \text{constant}, reducing the MAP estimation to maximizing the likelihood: \arg \maxf p(f | F{2D}) = \arg \maxf p(F{2D} | f) Assuming conditional independence of pixels given the surface representation and 3D features f, the likelihood is: p(F{2D} | f) = \prod{v=1}^V \prod{p \in Pv} p(f{p,v}^{2D} | f) The 2D feature at pixel p in view v is modeled as a weighted sum of 3D Gaussian features plus Gaussian noise: f{p,v}^{2D} = \sum{k=1}^R w{k,p,v} fk + \epsilon{p,v}, \quad \epsilon{p,v} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I) where R is the number of Gaussians along the ray, and w{k,p,v} is the alpha blending weight for Gaussian k at pixel p in view v: w{i,p,v} = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) The log-likelihood to maximize is: \log p(F{2D} | f) = \arg \maxf -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum{v,p} \| f{p,v}^{2D} - \sum{k=1}^R w{k,p,v} fk \|^2 + \text{const} Taking the derivative with respect to the 3D language feature fi of Gaussian i and setting to zero yields: \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum{v,p} w{i,p,v} (f{p,v}^{2D} - \sum{k=1}^R w{k,p,v} fk) = 0 The final closed-form solution for the 3D feature fi of Gaussian i is the weighted average of observed 2D features: fi = \frac{\sum{v=1}^V \sum{p \in Pv} w{i,p,v} f{p,v}^{2D}}{\sum{v=1}^V \sum{p \in Pv} w{i,p,v}} This formula interprets the optimal 3D feature as a weighted average of 2D features observed at pixels where the Gaussian has influence, with weights proportional to the Gaussian’s contribution. Practical Simplification: The method assumes sparse influence: for most views/pixels, one dominant Gaussian has weight close to 1, leading to negligible cross-talk where w{i,p,v} w{k,p,v} \approx 0 for i \neq k. This eliminates cross-Gaussian terms, allowing the closed-form solution above. Parameters: Feature Dimension (d): The dimensionality of the CLIP language features. Evaluated at 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 dimensions. Training Iterations: 30,000 iterations using common Gaussian Splatting parameters. Average Number of Gaussians: ~2,500,000 Gaussians for RGB representation across scenes. LERF Mask Threshold: 0.5 for computing relevancy scores. 3D-OVS Area Thresholds: Reject spurious masks with areas smaller than 0.005% or larger than 0.90% of the image. 3D-OVS Object Stability Threshold: 0.4. Algorithm: 1. Initialize accumulated features fi = 0 and weights wi = 0 for each Gaussian Gi. 2. For each camera view s \in S: a. Iterate through each Gaussian Gi in the view frustum. b. Render Gi to get the alpha blending weight w{i,s} and the projected pixel location \psii = \lfloor x'i \rfloor. c. Extract the 2D feature f{i,s} from the feature map for view s at pixel \psii. d. Update fi \leftarrow fi + w{i,s} f{i,s} and wi \leftarrow wi + w{i,s}. 3. For each Gaussian Gi: a. If wi > 0, normalize fi \leftarrow fi / wi. b. If wi = 0, filter out Gi (no contribution across all views). 4. Return the refined set of semantic Gaussians G^s with uplifted features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def featureuplifting(gaussians, views, featuremaps): """ Uplift 2D language features to 3D Gaussians using forward rendering. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: 3D position alpha: Opacity f: Accumulated feature (initialized to 0) w: Accumulated weight (initialized to 0) views: List of camera view objects with attributes: pose: Camera pose featuremap: 2D feature map tensor (H x W x d) featuremaps: List of 2D feature maps corresponding to views. Returns: gaussians: List of Gaussians with uplifted features f. """ # Step 1: Initialize for g in gaussians: g.f = np.zeros(d) # d is feature dimension g.w = 0.0 # Step 2: Forward Rendering and Aggregation for viewidx, view in enumerate(views): featuremap = view.featuremap # Identify Gaussians in view frustum visiblegaussians = getgaussiansinfrustum(gaussians, view.pose) for g in visiblegaussians: # Project Gaussian center to 2D pixel location # x'i is the projected 2D coordinate xprime = project2d(g.mu, view.pose) psi = floor(xprime) # Integer pixel coordinates # Render Gaussian to get alpha blending weight at this pixel # Note: In a full rasterizer, this is done per-pixel. # Here, we assume we can query the weight contribution of Gaussian i # at pixel psi in view s. wis = computealphablendingweight(g, psi, view) # Sample 2D feature at the projected pixel fis = featuremap[psi.y, psi.x,:] # Accumulate g.f += wis fis g.w += wis # Step 3: Normalization and Filtering semanticgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if g.w > 0: g.f = g.f / g.w semanticgaussians.append(g) # Else: Filter out Gaussian (no contribution) return semanticgaussians def computealphablendingweight(gaussian, pixel, view): """ Computes the alpha blending weight w{i,p,v} for Gaussian i at pixel p in view v. This requires knowing the order of Gaussians along the ray at pixel p. In practice, this is obtained during the forward rendering pass. """ # Get all Gaussians covering pixel p in view v coveringgaussians = getgaussiansatpixel(pixel, view) # Sort by depth (front to back) coveringgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: depth(g.mu, view.pose)) # Find index of current Gaussian try: idx = coveringgaussians.index(gaussian) except ValueError: return 0.0 # Compute weight: alphai product(1 - alphaj) for j < i weight = gaussian.alpha for j in range(idx): weight = (1 - coveringgaussians[j].alpha) return weight Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Dimensionality: High dimensionality (d \gg 3) prevents GPU from fitting all required data in the shader L1 cache, causing color blending issues in Equation 2. Localization Accuracy: Localization accuracy metric is prone to noise because it only measures the closest matching pixel, ignoring feature distribution and object shape. No Contribution: Gaussians with no contributions across all views are filtered out to reduce noise and the number of Gaussians significantly. Dynamic Thresholding: For 3D-OVS, dynamic thresholding is used. For each query, evaluate threshold values with step size 0.01. Create binary mask where relevancy score > threshold. Compute average relevancy score within masked area. Identify stable region: Find region where absolute gradient of average relevancy score (rate of change w.r.t threshold) is below a chosen stability threshold. Select the middle value from the stable range as the final threshold. If multiple stable regions exist, select the highest confidence prediction. Time Complexity: O(N \times V) for feature uplifting, where N is number of Gaussians and V is number of views, but optimized by tile-based rendering and frustum culling. Measured Performance: On LERF dataset, localization accuracy improves to 84.1 when feature dimension reduces to 32D. Feature dimension scalability: 64D features achieve 64.5% mIoU on LERF, outperforming LangSplat baseline by 13.1% mIoU. LERF mIoU improvement: 9.9% improvement over LangSplat under identical experimental settings. 3D-OVS mIoU improvement: 1.6% improvement over LangSplat. Speed: Uplifts features in 16.4 seconds (no setup) or 31.9 seconds (with setup) vs 60-67 minutes for others (LangSplat, GOI, 3DVLM). Hardware: Single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Strengths: Computationally efficient (single forward pass), handles occlusions via frustum culling, establishes precise correspondence, avoids iterative optimization. Limitations: High dimensionality causes cache issues, localization metric is noisy, requires pre-trained Gaussian Splat. When to use: When efficient, accurate 3D language feature lifting is needed from a pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splat model. When not to use: When iterative optimization is acceptable and higher dimensional features are required without compression. Origin: The method is introduced in "Occam's LGS: An Efficient Approach for Language Gaussian Splatting". History: It builds on the principles of 3DGS and probabilistic modeling, formulating feature uplifting as a MAP estimation problem. It differs from conventional semantic feature learning methods that rely on back-projection. Usage: Used for open vocabulary semantic segmentation and 3D scene understanding, evaluated on LERF and 3D-OVS datasets. name: Occam's LGS
head: Language Gaussian Splatting via weighted multi-view feature aggregation, Occam LGS
body: Occam's LGS is a training-free method for lifting 2D language features to 3D Gaussian representations by applying Occam’s razor to the forward rendering process of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of expensive iterative optimization in feature space by computing weighted multi-view feature aggregation directly from the alpha blending weights of the standard color rendering pass. Unlike sibling methods that rely on scene-specific autoencoders, quantization, or costly semantic feature rendering, Occam's LGS supports arbitrary-dimensional uncompressed features without compromising training speed, achieving a two-order-of-magnitude speed-up while maintaining state-of-the-art performance for open-set vision-language tasks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (providing geometry and appearance parameters) and a set of input images with known camera poses. The underlying encoder provides 2D semantic features f \in \mathbb{R}^d for each pixel. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians G = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian Gi is augmented with a high-dimensional semantic feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^d. Data Structures: The primitive Gaussian representation is defined as G = \{x, \Sigma, c, o\}, where: x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the 3D position. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{6} (or \mathbb{R}^{2\times2} when projected) is the covariance matrix. c is the color (or Spherical Harmonics parameters). o \in \mathbb{R} is the opacity. For language splatting, this is augmented to include the semantic feature fi. The rendering process uses a tile-based sorting strategy, partitioning the image into tiles typically spanning 16 \times 16 pixels. Mathematical Formulation: The standard color rendering for a pixel p along a ray with R Gaussians is: C(p) = \sum{i=1}^{R} \alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity contribution of the i-th Gaussian: \alphai = oi \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{2} (p-x'i)^\top \Sigma'^{-1} (p-x'i)} Here, x'i is the projected 2D center and \Sigma' is the projected 2D covariance matrix. The alpha blending weight for Gaussian i is defined as: wi = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) In explicit feature rendering, the semantic feature at pixel p would be: F(p) = \sum{i=1}^{R} wi fi However, explicit rendering is expensive because the high dimensionality d \gg 3 prevents fitting data in the GPU shader L1 cache. Occam's LGS avoids this by aggregating features per Gaussian during the forward pass. Algorithm Steps: For each Gaussian Gi in the scene: 1. Identify the set of views Si where Gi is visible (within the view frustum). 2. For each view s \in Si, determine the Gaussian’s center projected pixel location p{si} = \lfloor x'i \rfloor. 3. During the standard tile-based rendering pass, record the alpha blending weight w{si} and extract the 2D feature f{si} at pixel p{si} from the pre-computed feature map. 4. Compute the weighted average of the multi-view features to assign to Gi: fi = \frac{\sum{s \in Si} w{si} f{si}}{\sum{s \in Si} w{si}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def occamlgslift(gaussians, views, featureextractor): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes x, sigma, c, o. views: List of view objects with attributes camerapose, image, featuremap. featureextractor: Function to extract 2D features from images. """ # Pre-compute 2D features for all views viewfeatures = [] for view in views: # Extract high-dimensional semantic features for the entire image # Shape: (H, W, d) feats = featureextractor(view.image) viewfeatures.append(feats) # Initialize 3D Gaussian features for g in gaussians: g.semanticfeature = None # Process each Gaussian for g in gaussians: visibleviews = [] totalweight = 0.0 weightedfeaturesum = 0.0 # Step 1 & 2: Identify visible views and projected locations for i, view in enumerate(views): # Project 3D center x to 2D pixel coordinates xprime = project3dto2d(g.x, view.camerapose) # Check if within view frustum and bounds if not isinfrustum(xprime, view.resolution): continue # Step 2: Determine pixel location px, py = int(round(xprime.x)), int(round(xprime.y)) # Step 3: Compute alpha blending weight wi # Note: In standard rasterization, this requires sorting and blending. # Occam's LGS leverages the forward pass to get the effective weight. # Here we approximate by computing the Gaussian's contribution to the center pixel. # A more precise implementation would capture the exact wi from the rasterizer. alpha = computealpha(g.o, xprime, g.sigma, view.projectionmatrix) # The weight wi in the context of aggregation is the contribution # of this Gaussian to the pixel. In the absence of occlusion from other # Gaussians at the exact center, wi approximates alpha. # However, the paper implies using the standard alpha blending weight. # For simplicity in this lift, we use the alpha value as the weight # for the feature at the center, assuming the feature map is static. # A rigorous implementation would query the rasterizer's output buffer # for the specific weight wi associated with this Gaussian's contribution. wi = alpha # Extract 2D feature at the projected pixel fi = viewfeatures[i][py, px] visibleviews.append((wi, fi)) # Step 4: Compute weighted average if visibleviews: for w, f in visibleviews: totalweight += w weightedfeaturesum += w f if totalweight > 0: g.semanticfeature = weightedfeaturesum / totalweight else: g.semanticfeature = 0.0 # Or handle as invisible else: g.semanticfeature = 0.0 # Invisible Gaussian return gaussians The pseudocode approximates the extraction of wi. In a real implementation, one would modify the rasterizer to output the specific weight wi contributed by each Gaussian to the pixel, rather than recomputing it from scratch, to ensure consistency with the color rendering pass. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory/Compute: Explicit rendering of semantics is expensive due to high dimensionality d \gg 3, causing cache misses in GPU shaders. Occam's LGS avoids this by aggregating in 3D space. Occlusion: The method relies on the forward rendering pass, which naturally handles occlusion via tile-based sorting. Only visible features are aggregated. Precision: Projecting 3D centers to 2D pixels involves rounding (\lfloor x'i \rfloor). This discretization may introduce minor alignment errors between the feature map and the Gaussian center. Time Complexity: The method is training-free and requires only a single forward pass through the views. It efficiently completes the lifting of 512-dimensional features to 3D in less than one minute. Memory Complexity: It does not require storing large intermediate feature volumes for explicit rendering, reducing memory overhead compared to methods that render features per pixel. Performance: Offers a speed-up of two orders of magnitude compared to existing methods that rely on cumbersome techniques like iterative optimization or quantization. Strengths: Supports arbitrary-dimensional uncompressed features; preserves semantic meaning without preprocessing; enables open-vocabulary generalization; allows for easy scene manipulation and editing. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the underlying 3D Gaussian model and the 2D feature extractor. It does not refine the features through optimization, so errors in the initial geometry or feature extraction are not corrected. Occam's LGS was introduced by Jan-Nico Zaech and Jiahuan Cheng from the INSPIRE Institute. The work is based on the arXiv preprint "Occam's LGS: An Efficient Approach for Language Gaussian Splatting" (arXiv:2412.01807v2), published in March 2025. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and Language Gaussian Splatting, applying Occam’s razor to simplify the pipeline by removing unnecessary optimization steps in feature space. name: Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression
body: Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression (FCGS) is an autoencoder-based compression method that encodes 3D Gaussian attributes into a latent space using hyperpriors and context models, addressing the fidelity drop caused by the non-invertibility of MLPs in geometry attributes. Unlike anchor-based quantization methods that modify Gaussian locations and require finetuning, FCGS creates context grids in a feed-forward manner without altering the original Gaussian positions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, where each Gaussian i has geometry attributes f{geo} \in \mathbb{R}^8 (opacity \alpha, diagonal scaling S, quaternion rotation R) and color attributes f{col} \in \mathbb{R}^{48} (3-degree Spherical Harmonics coefficients). The concatenated attribute vector is f{gau} \in \mathbb{R}^{56}. Output: A compressed bitstream representing the latent variables \hat{y} and hypervariables \hat{z}, which can be decoded back to reconstructed Gaussian attributes \hat{x}. Data Structures: Transform Networks: Analysis transform (ga) and Synthesis transform (gs): Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) with 4 layers each. Hyperprior Analysis (ha) and Synthesis (hs): MLPs with 3 layers each. Context Models: Inter-Gaussian Context: Uses 3D and 2D grids at multiple resolutions to store features f{kv} from previously decoded Gaussians. Intra-Gaussian Context: Processes chunks of the latent vector \hat{y}i sequentially. Probability Model: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) combining parameters from hyperprior, inter-context, and intra-context models. Parameters: Ns: Number of batches for inter-Gaussian context decoding. Typical value: 2. Nc: Number of chunks for intra-Gaussian context. Nc=4 for path m=1 (color via MLP), Nc=3 for path m=0 (color bypass). q: Quantization step size. q=1 if mi=1 (latent space), q is a trainable decimal parameter if mi=0 (bypass). \epsilonm: Hyperparameter threshold for binarizing the mask m. \lambdam: Explicitly NOT used in FCGS to avoid complicating Rate-Distortion (RD) trade-off. Algorithm Steps: 1. Attribute Partitioning: Separate Gaussian attributes into geometry f{geo} and color f{col}. Concatenate to form f{gau}. 2. Mask Generation (MEM): For each Gaussian i, compute a binary mask mi to determine if color attributes pass through the MLPs or bypass them: mi = \text{Sig}(\text{MLP}m(f{gau})) > \epsilonm where \text{Sig} is the Sigmoid function. 3. Latent Encoding: For geometry attributes (f{geo}): Bypass MLPs to ensure exact recovery. Set y = x. For color attributes (f{col}): Apply the Mixture Model (MEM) logic. Compute the latent yi: \hat{y}i = gs(Q(ga(xi))) \times mi + Q(xi) \times (1 - mi) where Q is quantization with step q (1 if mi=1, trainable decimal if mi=0). Compute hyperprior zi = ha(xi). 4. Inter-Gaussian Context Decoding: Split all Gaussians' latents \hat{y} into Ns batches. Decode batches sequentially. For a Gaussian i in the current batch, located at \mu{gi}, identify the set of voxels V{\mui}^g forming its minimum bounding box in the grid. Compute interpolated feature f{i\mu}: f{i\mu} = \sum{k: vk \in V{\mui}^g} wk f{kv} where wk are interpolation weights. Compute inter-context distribution parameters \mu{si}, \sigma{is}, \pi{is}: \mu{si}, \sigma{is}, \pi{is} = \text{MLP}s(\oplus [f{i\mu}, \text{emb}(\mu{gi})]) where \text{emb} is sincos positional embedding and \oplus is channel-wise concatenation. 5. Intra-Gaussian Context Decoding: Split \hat{y}i into Nc chunks. For path m=1, split along channel dimension (Nc=4). For path m=0, split along RGB axis (Nc=3). Compute intra-context parameters for chunk nc: \mu{i,nc}, \sigma{i,nc}, \pi{i,nc} = \text{MLP}c(\hat{y}{i,[0, nc-1]}) Aggregate parameters: \mu{ci}, \sigma{ic}, \pi{ic} = \oplus{nc=1}^{Nc} \{\mu{i,nc}, \sigma{i,nc}, \pi{i,nc}\}. 6. Hyperprior Context: Compute hyperprior parameters \mu{hi}, \sigma{ih}, \pi{ih} from \hat{z}i using hs. 7. Probability Estimation: Combine inter-context, intra-context, and hyperprior parameters using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to estimate the probability of each latent value \hat{y}i. 8. Arithmetic Decoding: Use the estimated probabilities to decode the bitstream into \hat{y} and \hat{z}. 9. Reconstruction: Apply synthesis transform gs to \hat{y} (if mi=1) or use \hat{y} directly (if mi=0) to obtain \hat{x}. The text says: # xhat = gs(Q(ga(x))) m + Q(x) (1-m) # This implies y is the input to gs? No, y is the latent. # Let's follow the formula strictly: # yi = gs(Q(ga(xi))) mi + Q(xi) (1 - mi) # But Q is quantization. In compression, we quantize the latent y. # The text says: "if yi is in the latent space (mi=1), q is 1; otherwise (mi=0), q becomes a trainable decimal parameter." # And "xhat = gs(Q(ga(x))) m + Q(x) (1-m)" # This suggests the quantization happens on the output of the transforms or the input? # Actually, standard AE: x -> ga -> y -> Q -> yhat -> gs -> xhat. # FCGS modifies this: # If m=1: y = Q(ga(x)). Then xhat = gs(y). # If m=0: y = Q(x). Then xhat = y (bypass gs? No, text says "simply bypass the MLPs... setting y=x"). # Wait, if y=x, then xhat = gs(y) = gs(x)? No, "bypass the MLPs... resulting in y=ga(x) or y=x". # If y=x, then we don't use gs? The formula says xhat = gs(...) m + Q(x) (1-m). # This implies if m=0, xhat = Q(x). So gs is not used for m=0. # Re-reading: "xhati = gs(Q(ga(xi))) mi + Q(xi) (1 - mi)" # This means: # If mi=1: xhat = gs(Q(ga(x))) # If mi=0: xhat = Q(x) # So y is not directly xhat. y is the latent to be compressed. # If m=1: y = Q(ga(x)). Compress y. Decode yhat. xhat = gs(yhat). # If m=0: y = Q(x). Compress y. Decode yhat. xhat = yhat. # Let's implement the latent generation for compression y = torch.zeroslike(x) for i in range(self.numgaussians): if mask[i] > 0.5: # Path 1: MLP ylatent = self.ga(x[i]) y[i] = self.quantize(ylatent, q=1.0) else: # Path 0: Bypass y[i] = self.quantize(x[i], q=self.qtrainable) # Hyperprior z = self.ha(x) zquantized = self.quantize(z, q=1.0) return yquantized, zquantized, mask def decode(self, yhat, zhat, gridfeatures, gaussianpositions): """ yhat: [N, 56] (decoded latent) zhat: [N, 64] (decoded hyperprior) gridfeatures: 3D/2D grid structures gaussianpositions: [N, 3] """ xhat = torch.zeroslike(yhat) # Split into batches for Inter-Gaussian Context batchsize = self.numgaussians // self.Ns indices = torch.randperm(self.numgaussians) for ns in range(self.Ns): startidx = ns batchsize endidx = (ns + 1) batchsize currentindices = indices[startidx:endidx] for idx in currentindices: # Inter-Gaussian Context mugi = gaussianpositions[idx] # Get grid features via interpolation fimu = self.interpolategrid(gridfeatures, mugi) posemb = self.sincosposembed(mugi) contextparamsinter = self.mlps(torch.cat([fimu, posemb], dim=-1)) # Intra-Gaussian Context yi = yhat[idx] # Split into chunks if self.Nc == 4: chunks = torch.chunk(yi, 4, dim=-1) else: # Split along RGB (assuming 3 channels for color part? Aggregate intra-context contextparamsintra = torch.cat(contextparamsintra, dim=-1) # Hyperprior Context zi = zhat[idx] contextparamshyper = self.hs(zi) # GMM Probability Estimation (Simplified) # Combine params to get mean/var for quantization error correction # This step is complex and depends on the specific GMM implementation # For the purpose of reconstruction, we assume the decoder uses these params # to refine the probability estimate for arithmetic decoding. # xhat[idx] = self.gs(yhat[idx]) # If MLP path # But we need to know if it was MLP or Bypass. # Let's assume we decode the mask first or it's part of the stream. # For now, just return yhat as a placeholder for xhat # Memory Complexity: Depends on the grid size for inter-Gaussian context. The grids store features for all Gaussians, requiring O(N) space if dense, or less if sparse. Performance: FCGS achieves high compression ratios while maintaining rendering fidelity. It avoids the fidelity drop associated with MLP non-invertibility by bypassing geometry attributes. Strengths: Feed-forward nature allows fast inference without per-scene optimization. Context models improve probability estimation accuracy. Limitations: Requires training on a large dataset. Grid creation and interpolation add computational overhead compared to simple quantization. FCGS was introduced in 2024 by authors associated with the ICLR 2025 conference paper "Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression". It builds upon the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al., 2023] and image compression techniques, specifically autoencoders with hyperpriors and context models. It addresses the limitations of previous compression methods that suffered from fidelity drops due to the non-invertibility of MLPs in geometry attributes. name: SHARE
head: Pose-free 3D Gaussian splatting via shape-ray estimation
body: SHARE is a pose-free framework for generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting that estimates camera poses via predicted rays and uses anchor-aligned coarse-to-fine geometry estimation to predict 3D Gaussian parameters without ground-truth poses. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like PixelSplat and MVSplat by explicitly embedding pose awareness into multi-view cost volumes via Plücker rays, making it robust to pose inaccuracies where generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting methods are highly sensitive. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: M input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^M. For DTU, M=4 (3 context, 1 target); for RealEstate10K, M=5 (2 context, 3 targets). Input resolution is 256 \times 256. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \alpha, \Sigma, c\} and estimated camera poses (implicitly via rays). Data Structures: Cost Volume Ci: For each viewpoint i, a cost volume of shape \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4 \times D}, where D is the number of depth hypotheses. Spatial Weight Volume Wi: Shape \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4}, accounting for view-dependent effects (occlusion, lighting). Canonical Geometry Volume Vg: Shape \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4 \times C}, fusing refined cost volumes. Canonical Feature Volume Vf: Shape \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}, constructed from upsampled multi-view features. Gaussian Primitives: K=3 offsets per anchor. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction and Cost Volume Construction: Extract features from input images. Construct initial cost volumes Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4 \times D} for each viewpoint i using matching Transformer layers. The cost volume is computed as: Ci = \frac{1}{\sqrt{Ci}} \sum{j \neq i} F{j \to i} where F{j \to i} are warped features. 2. Pose-Aware Cost Aggregation: Refine cost volumes Ci through cost aggregation conditioned on predicted Plücker rays. Use patch-wise cross-attention to embed pose awareness into the cost volumes, introducing geometric bias. 3. Spatial Weight Estimation: Estimate a spatial weight volume Wi \in \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4} for each cost volume to account for view-dependent effects such as occlusion and lighting variations. 4. Canonical Volume Construction: Fuse refined cost volumes C'i and weights Wi into a canonical geometry volume Vg \in \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4 \times C}: Vg = \sum{i=1}^M Wi C'i + \phi \oplus C' where C' is the average of all cost volumes, \oplus denotes channel-wise concatenation, and \phi is a CNN layer for channel projection. A mean and variance-based volume is also added following previous MVS techniques. Similarly, construct the canonical feature volume Vf \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} using the same aggregation method with upsampled multi-view features. 5. Coarse Depth Estimation: Compute initial coarse depth z as the expected value over depth hypothesis planes D \in \mathbb{R}^D. The probability of each depth candidate is predicted using Vg through a lightweight MLP depth head fg followed by a softmax function: z = \sumd \text{softmax}(fg(Vg))d \cdot Dd The estimated 3D anchor position pi for pixel i is: pi = o + zi di where o is the ray origin and di is the ray direction. 6. Anchor-Aligned Offset Prediction: Estimate K offset vectors \Delta p{i,k} for each anchor using the canonical feature volume Vf. The offset prediction MLP head fo outputs: \Delta p{i,k} = fo(Vf) where k \in \{1, \dots, K\} and K=3. 7. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Define Gaussian means as \mu{i,k} = pi + \Delta p{i,k}. Predict remaining parameters (opacity \alpha, covariance \Sigma, color c) using an MLP head fp applied to the positional encoding of offsets and the feature volume: \{\alpha, \Sigma, c\}{i,k} = fp(\text{PE}(\Delta p{i,k}), Vf) where \text{PE}(\cdot) denotes positional encoding. 8. Rendering: Rasterize the predicted Gaussians into 2D space to render the target image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shareforward(images, numdepthhypotheses, numoffsets=3): """ Forward pass for SHARE. images: List of M images, shape (M, 3, 256, 256) numdepthhypotheses: D, number of depth planes numoffsets: K, number of Gaussian offsets per anchor """ M = len(images) # 1. Feature Extraction and Cost Volume Construction # Extract features using multi-view fusion backbone (e.g., 6 matching Transformer layers) features = extractfeatures(images) # Shape: (M, Cfeat, H/4, W/4) # Construct initial cost volumes Ci # Ci shape: (M, H/4, W/4, D) costvolumes = [] for i in range(M): # Warp features from other views j to view i warpedfeatures = warpfeatures(features[j] for j in range(M) if j != i, features[i]) # Compute cost volume (simplified aggregation) Ci = aggregatecost(warpedfeatures, features[i]) costvolumes.append(Ci) # 2. Pose-Aware Cost Aggregation # Predict Plücker rays for pose awareness pluckerrays = predictpluckerrays(images) # Shape: (M, H/4, W/4, 6) refinedcostvolumes = [] for i in range(M): # Patch-wise cross-attention conditioned on Plücker rays Crefined = patchcrossattention(costvolumes[i], pluckerrays[i]) refinedcostvolumes.append(Crefined) # 3. Spatial Weight Estimation # Estimate spatial weight volumes Wi weightvolumes = [] for i in range(M): Wi = predictspatialweights(refinedcostvolumes[i]) # Shape: (M, H/4, W/4) weightvolumes.append(Wi) # 4. Canonical Volume Construction # Average cost volumes avgcost = torch.mean(torch.stack(refinedcostvolumes), dim=0) # Fuse into canonical geometry volume Vg # Vg shape: (H/4, W/4, C) Vg = torch.zeros(H/4, W/4, C) for i in range(M): # Weighted sum and concatenation term1 = weightvolumes[i] refinedcostvolumes[i] term2 = convproject(torch.cat([refinedcostvolumes[i], avgcost], dim=-1)) Vg += term1 + term2 # Construct canonical feature volume Vf # Upsample multi-view features and aggregate similarly Vf = constructcanonicalfeaturevolume(images, features) # Shape: (H, W, C) # 5. Coarse Depth Estimation # Lightweight MLP depth head fg depthlogits = depthhead(Vg) # Shape: (H/4, W/4, D) depthprobs = softmax(depthlogits, dim=-1) # Depth hypothesis planes D Dplanes = createdepthplanes(numdepthhypotheses) # Shape: (D,) # Expected depth z z = torch.sum(depthprobs Dplanes, dim=-1) # Shape: (H/4, W/4) # Ray origins and directions (from predicted poses/Plücker rays) rayorigins, raydirections = getrayinfo(pluckerrays) # Shape: (H/4, W/4, 3) # Anchor positions pi anchors = rayorigins + z.unsqueeze(-1) raydirections # Shape: (H/4, W/4, 3) # 6. Anchor-Aligned Offset Prediction # Offset prediction MLP head fo offsets = offsethead(Vf) # Shape: (H, W, K, 3) # 7. Gaussian Parameter Prediction # Upsample anchors to match Vf resolution if necessary, or interpolate anchorsupsampled = interpolate(anchors, targetsize=(H, W)) # Shape: (H, W, 3) # Gaussian means means = anchorsupsampled.unsqueeze(-2) + offsets # Shape: (H, W, K, 3) # Remaining parameters # Positional encoding of offsets peoffsets = positionalencoding(offsets) # MLP head fp alphas, sigmas, colors = gaussianparamshead(peoffsets, Vf) # Shapes: (H, W, K, 1), (H, W, K, 6), (H, W, K, Ccolor) # 8. Rendering renderedimage = rasterizegaussians(means, alphas, sigmas, colors, cameraintrinsics) return renderedimage, means, alphas, sigmas, colors Parameters: Context/Target Images: 3 context + 1 target for DTU; 2 context + 3 targets for RealEstate10K. Input Resolution: 256 \times 256. Number of Gaussian Primitives per Anchor (K): 3. Number of Depth Hypotheses (D): Not given in the sources. Training Iterations: 140K on DTU, 300K on RealEstate10K. Optimizer: Adam. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pose Uncertainty: SHARE is designed to be robust to pose inaccuracies, whereas generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting methods (e.g., PixelSplat, MVSplat) are highly sensitive to pose errors, with even minor Gaussian noise (\sigma = 0.01) causing significant degradation. Depth Discontinuities: Coarse depth estimation may lead to over-smooth geometry in regions with depth discontinuities or complex surfaces. The anchor-aligned coarse-to-fine estimation with offsets mitigates this. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: DTU (Predicted Poses via DUSt3R): PSNR 19.36, SSIM 0.61, LPIPS 0.31. RealEstate10K (Predicted Poses via DUSt3R): PSNR 21.23, SSIM 0.64, LPIPS 0.26. Scaling: Demonstrates scalability to complex, large-scale scenes (RealEstate10K). Strengths: Robust to pose uncertainty; outperforms generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting under noisy pose conditions; achieves LPIPS/SSIM scores comparable to ground-truth poses. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: When ground-truth camera poses are unavailable or unreliable, and robust generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting is required. When Not to Use: When high-precision ground-truth poses are available and pose-free methods are not necessary. SHARE was introduced in the paper "Pose-free 3D Gaussian splatting via shape-ray estimation". It addresses the challenge of generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting without requiring ground-truth camera poses, which are often unavailable or inaccurate in real-world scenarios. The method builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction by incorporating pose estimation directly into the geometry prediction pipeline. name: Feed-Forward Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion
head: HiGDiff, Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion
body: HiGDiff is a feed-forward reconstruction method for computed tomography (CT) that predicts a set of 3D Gaussian primitives from degraded projections without per-scene optimization. It solves the problem of sparse-view, low-dose, or limited-angle CT reconstruction by using two explicit Gaussian banks (structure and detail) initialized from anatomical cues and refined via a sequential structure-to-detail diffusion hierarchy. It differs from single-bank Gaussian reconstruction by maintaining separate banks for global attenuation geometry and residual detail, and from dense voxel diffusion by operating on explicit Gaussian primitives with a sequential hierarchy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Degraded projection data Y \in \mathbb{R}^{Nr}, where Nr is the number of rays. Each ray r has an observed count Yr and a mask Mr \in \{0, 1\} indicating if the ray is observed. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \mathcal{G}s \cup \mathcal{G}d, where \mathcal{G}s is the structure bank and \mathcal{G}d is the detail bank. Each Gaussian i in bank b is defined by mean m{b,i}, covariance \Sigma{b,i} (parameterized by scale and rotation), opacity a{b,i}, and color/attenuation attributes. The final output is the reconstructed attenuation field rendered from these Gaussians. Data Structures: Physics Features (F{phy}): A multi-scale feature pyramid extracted from the initial volume estimate. Anchors (K): A set of landmark-free anatomical anchor points predicted from F{phy}. Foreground Capacity Field (F{fg}): A continuous scalar field predicting the density/capacity for Gaussian placement. Gaussian Bank (\mathcal{G}b): A fixed-cardinality set of Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has attributes \xi{b,i} = [m{b,i}, \Sigma{b,i}, a{b,i}, \dots]. Diffusion State (\delta \xi{b,i}^t): The noise-corrupted Gaussian attributes at diffusion timestep t. Parameters: I0: Incident photon count. \bar{\alpha}{b,t}: Cumulative noise schedule coefficient for bank b at step t. \eta: DDIM inversion parameter (set to 0 for deterministic inversion). \lambda{kp}, \lambda{fg}, \lambdab: Loss weights for anchor consistency, capacity field, and diffusion loss respectively. w(q): Attention weighting function, w(q) = 0.15 + 0.85q. Steps: 1. Initialization: a. Compute estimated photon count for each ray: Ir = I0 \exp(-Yr). b. Compute normalized inverse-noise reliability Wr: Wr = \frac{\frac{\max(Ir, 1)}{Mr}}{\max{l:Ml=1} \max(Il, 1)} where Mr is the observation mask. c. Compute initial volume estimate V0 using filtered back-projection (FBP): V0 = \text{FBP}\theta(Y). d. Compute physics features F{phy} using a physics encoder E{phy} on V0 and the back-projected residual weighted by W: F{phy} = E{phy}(V0, \text{UBP}\theta(W \bullet [Y - \text{Proj}\theta(V0)])) where \text{UBP} is unweighted back-projection and \text{Proj} is forward projection. e. Predict anatomical anchors K and foreground capacity field F{fg}: K = E{kp}(F{phy}) F{fg} = E{fg}(F{phy}, K). f. Initialize the structure bank \mathcal{G}{s,0} and detail bank \mathcal{G}{d,0} using K and F{fg}. Positions are initialized in normalized scanner coordinates [-1, 1]^3. 2. Structure Gaussian Diffusion (Stage I): For each diffusion step t from T down to 1: a. For each structure primitive i: i. Sample physics features at current mean m{s,i}^t: f{s,i}^t = \text{Samp}(F{phy}, m{s,i}^t). ii. Compute context c{s,i}^t by concatenating initial token z{s,i}, sampled features f{s,i}^t, and inverse-standardized initial attributes \phis(g{s,i,0}), then passing through fusion MLP Ms and attention weighting w(q{s,i}^t): c{s,i}^t = w(q{s,i}^t) Ms [z{s,i}, f{s,i}^t, \phis(g{s,i,0})]. iii. Predict noise \hat{\epsilon}{s,i}^t using structure denoiser Ds: \hat{\epsilon}{s,i}^t = Ds(\delta \xi{s,i}^t, c{s,i}^t, t). b. Update state using DDIM inverse step (\eta=0): \delta \xi{s,i}^{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}{s,t}}} \left( \delta \xi{s,i}^t - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}{s,t}} \hat{\epsilon}{s,i}^t \right). c. Apply inverse standardization \phis^{-1} and add correction to \mathcal{G}{s,0}. Apply center clipping and positive numerical floors to ensure valid attributes (e.g., positive scales). 3. Detail Gaussian Diffusion (Stage I): a. Construct stopped conditions for detail diffusion using the refined structure bank. The detail bank is initialized based on the structure bank's output. b. For each diffusion step t from T down to 1: i. For each detail primitive i: Predict noise \hat{\epsilon}{d,i}^t using detail denoiser Dd conditioned on the structure bank and current detail state. ii. Update state using DDIM inverse step: \delta \xi{d,i}^{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}{d,t}}} \left( \delta \xi{d,i}^t - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}{d,t}} \hat{\epsilon}{d,i}^t \right). c. Apply inverse standardization \phid^{-1} and domain validity checks (center clipping, positive floors). 4. Refinement (Stage II): After freezing Stage I modules, a refinement network is trained to correct residual errors after dense voxelization, using stop-gradient to preserve the division between structure and detail. 5. Rendering: Render the attenuation field using the Gaussian renderer: \mathcal{R}G(\mathcal{G}b)(x) = \sum{i=1}^{Nb} a{b,i} \mathcal{G}G(x; m{b,i}, \Sigma{b,i}) where \mathcal{G}G(x; m, \Sigma) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^\top \Sigma^{-1}(x-m)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math def normalizedinversenoisereliability(Y, I0, M): """ Y: (Nr,) observed projections I0: float, incident photon count M: (Nr,) binary mask """ Ir = I0 torch.exp(-Y) maxIr = torch.clamp(Ir, min=1.0) numerator = maxIr / M.clamp(min=1e-9) # Avoid div by zero, M is 0 or 1 # Max over observed rays maxdenom = torch.max(torch.where(M == 1, maxIr, torch.tensor(0.0, device=Y.device))) Wr = numerator / maxdenom return Wr def initializebanks(Fphy, K, Ffg, Ns, Nd): """ Initialize structure and detail Gaussian banks from anchors and capacity field. Returns: Gs0, Gd0 """ # Implementation depends on specific initialization logic from Efg and K # Gs0: (Ns, 3) positions, (Ns, 3) scales, (Ns, 4) quaternions, (Ns, 1) opacities # Gd0: (Nd, 3) positions, (Nd, 3) scales, (Nd, 4) quaternions, (Nd, 1) opacities # Placeholder for specific anchor-to-Gaussian mapping logic Gs0 = initstructurefromanchors(K, Ns) Gd0 = initdetailfromcapacity(Ffg, Nd) return Gs0, Gd0 def structurediffusionstep(Gst, Fphy, Ds, alphabart, phis, phisinv): """ One step of structure diffusion reverse process. """ Ns = Gst.shape[0] ms = Gst[:,:3] # Sample physics features at current means fs = samplefeatures(Fphy, ms) # (Ns, C) # Compute context # zs is initial token, gs0 is initial attributes # This assumes zs and gs0 are available or stored # cs = w(q) Ms([zs, fs, phis(gs0)]) # q is attention weight, computed from current state qs = computeattentionweight(ms) wq = 0.15 + 0.85 qs # Concatenate and pass through MLP context = torch.cat([zs, fs, phis(Gst[:, 3:])], dim=-1) cs = wq.unsqueeze(-1) Ms(context) # Predict noise deltaxit = Gst # Assuming Gst contains the noise-corrupted attributes epshat = Ds(deltaxit, cs, t) # DDIM Inverse Step (eta=0) deltaxitminus1 = (1.0 / math.sqrt(alphabart)) (deltaxit - math.sqrt(1 - alphabart) epshat) # Inverse standardization and validity checks Gstminus1 = phisinv(deltaxitminus1) + Gs0 # Correction added to initialization Gstminus1 = centerclip(Gstminus1) Gstminus1 = positivefloor(Gstminus1) return Gstminus1 def detaildiffusionstep(Gdt, Gs, Fphy, Dd, alphabart, phid, phidinv): """ One step of detail diffusion reverse process. """ Nd = Gdt.shape[0] # Condition on structure bank # Context includes structure bank features and current detail state contextd = computedetailcontext(Gs, Gdt, Fphy) epshat = Dd(Gdt, contextd, t) deltaxitminus1 = (1.0 / math.sqrt(alphabart)) (Gdt - math.sqrt(1 - alphabart) epshat) Gdtminus1 = phidinv(deltaxitminus1) + Gd0 Gdtminus1 = centerclip(Gdtminus1) Gdtminus1 = positivefloor(Gdtminus1) return Gdtminus1 def rendergaussians(Gs, Gd): """ Render attenuation field from structure and detail banks. """ # Sum of Gaussian contributions # RG(Gb)(x) = sum(ai exp(-0.5 (x-mi)^T Sigmai^-1 (x-mi))) # This is typically done via rasterization in a renderer attenuation = renderbank(Gs) + renderbank(Gd) return attenuation def trainstageI(Y, Ns, Nd, Ds, Dd, Ephy, Ekp, Efg, Ms, phis, phid): """ Stage I: Alternating structure and detail updates. """ Wr = normalizedinversenoisereliability(Y, I0, M) V0 = FBP(Y) Fphy = Ephy(V0, UBP(Wr (Y - Proj(V0)))) K = Ekp(Fphy) Ffg = Efg(Fphy, K) Gs0, Gd0 = initializebanks(Fphy, K, Ffg, Ns, Nd) # Diffusion loop for t in T down to 1: # Structure update Gst = addnoise(Gs0, t) Gstminus1 = structurediffusionstep(Gst, Fphy, Ds, alphabarst, phis, phisinv) # Detail update (conditioned on structure) Gdt = addnoise(Gd0, t) Gdtminus1 = detaildiffusionstep(Gdt, Gstminus1, Fphy, Dd, alphabardt, phid, phidinv) # Compute losses lossdiff = computediffusionloss(epshat, epstrue) lossaux = computeauxloss(K, Ffg, Gs, Gd) # Backpropagate lossdiff.backward() lossaux.backward() def trainstageII(Gs, Gd, Y, RefinementNet): """ Stage II: Refinement network training. """ # Freeze Stage I modules # Render Gaussians Attenuation = rendergaussians(Gs, Gd) # Voxelize and refine Voxel = voxelize(Attenuation) RefinedVoxel = RefinementNet(Voxel) # Loss against reference loss = L1(RefinedVoxel, ReferenceCT) loss.backward() Time Complexity: Inference is feed-forward, consisting of a single pass through the physics encoder, anchor/capacity predictors, and two diffusion hierarchies. The complexity is dominated by the diffusion steps (T) and the size of the Gaussian banks (Ns, Nd). Each diffusion step involves sampling features and passing through MLPs/denoisers. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the physics feature pyramid, the two Gaussian banks, and the diffusion states during inference. The fixed-cardinality banks make memory usage predictable. Performance: Designed for extreme CT reconstruction (sparse-view, low-dose, limited-angle). It outperforms single-bank Gaussian reconstruction and dense voxel diffusion in these challenging settings by separating structure and detail. Strengths: Handles degraded projections well; explicit Gaussian representation allows for efficient rendering; hierarchical diffusion improves detail recovery. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of diffusion schedules and loss weights; initialization from anchors may fail if anatomical cues are absent; two-stage training adds complexity. HiGDiff was proposed in "Feed-Forward Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion for Extreme CT Reconstruction" (2026). It builds on the line of work using discretized Gaussian functions for continuous representation. It extends DiffGS, which demonstrated generative modeling of Gaussian attributes, and UltraGS, which adapted Gaussian attributes to medical image formation. HiGDiff integrates explicit Gaussian representation, spatially selective capacity allocation, and a feed-forward structure-to-detail diffusion hierarchy. name: Amortized Image Reconstruction (AIR)
head: Self-Supervised Feed-Forward 2D Gaussian Splatting
body: Amortized Image Reconstruction (AIR) is a self-supervised feed-forward framework that reconstructs a target image into a set of 2D Gaussian primitives in a single network pass, eliminating the costly per-image iterative optimization required by prior methods like GaussianImage. Unlike Instant-GI, which relies on handcrafted priors and pseudo-labels for initialization, AIR uses a stage-wise residual architecture to progressively predict Gaussian primitives from reconstruction residuals, achieving higher quality with encoding times of 160–300 ms. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target RGB image I{gt} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Output: A set of 2D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{\mun, \Sigman, cn\}{n=1}^N, where N is the number of primitives. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive n is defined by: 1. Center: \mun \in \mathbb{R}^2, the 2D coordinates on the image plane. 2. Covariance: \Sigman \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, a symmetric positive-definite matrix. To ensure positive definiteness, it is parameterized by a rotation angle \thetan and scale factors s{n1}, s{n2}: \Sigman = (Rn Sn) (Rn Sn)^T where Rn is a 2D rotation matrix determined by \thetan, and Sn = \text{diag}(s{n1}, s{n2}). 3. Color: cn \in \mathbb{R}^3, the RGB color value. Opacity is absorbed into the color or handled via a scalar \alphan if explicitly modeled, though the source notes cn absorbs opacity in the baseline GaussianImage formulation. Rendering: The rendered image I{render} is computed via differentiable rasterization R(\cdot). For a pixel p, the color Cp is a weighted aggregation of all Gaussians n covering p: Cp = \frac{\sum{n \in \mathcal{N}(p)} cn \alpha{n,p}}{\sum{n \in \mathcal{N}(p)} \alpha{n,p}} where \mathcal{N}(p) is the set of Gaussians covering pixel p, and the weight \alpha{n,p} is: \alpha{n,p} = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} d{n,p}^T \Sigman^{-1} d{n,p} \right) where d{n,p} = p - \mun is the offset vector. Algorithm Steps: AIR operates in two phases: Training (Predict-Optimize-Distill) and Inference (Stage-wise Residual Prediction). 1. Initialization: Start with an empty Gaussian set \mathcal{G}0 = \emptyset and rendered image I0 = 0 (or black). 2. Stage-wise Prediction: For each stage k = 1, \dots, K: a. Compute the current reconstruction residual R{k-1} = I{gt} - I{k-1}, where I{k-1} = R(\mathcal{G}{k-1}). b. The feed-forward predictor network takes I{gt} and/or R{k-1} as input to predict a new set of Gaussian primitives \Delta \mathcal{G}k. c. Stage Control: An explicit mechanism activates new primitives only in under-reconstructed regions (where residual error is high) to ensure compactness. d. Update the accumulated set: \mathcal{G}k = \mathcal{G}{k-1} \cup \Delta \mathcal{G}k. e. Render the current accumulated set to get Ik = R(\mathcal{G}k). 3. Final Output: The final Gaussian set is \mathcal{G}K. Training Strategy (Predict-Optimize-Distill - POD): Direct supervision with rendering loss is unstable due to the under-constrained mapping from image space to Gaussian space. AIR uses a distillation approach: 1. Predict: The predictor outputs \Delta \mathcal{G}k for the current stage. 2. Optimize: A detached copy of the accumulated Gaussian set \mathcal{G}{k-1} \cup \Delta \mathcal{G}k is refined using a few steps of differentiable rendering optimization (gradient descent on Gaussian parameters) to minimize L{render}(R(\mathcal{G}), I{gt}). Let the refined set be \mathcal{G}^{k}. 3. Distill: The refined set \mathcal{G}^{k} serves as a regression target in Gaussian space. The predictor is supervised by the difference between its output \Delta \mathcal{G}k and the increment required to reach \mathcal{G}^{k} from \mathcal{G}{k-1}. 4. Finetuning: After POD stabilizes the predictor, AIR is jointly finetuned across all stages with direct rendering supervision on the whole Gaussian set \mathcal{G}K. Quantization: An image-adaptive quantizer is applied to the predicted Gaussian parameters to enable compact storage without per-image post-optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn from typing import List, Tuple class GaussianPrimitive: """Represents a single 2D Gaussian primitive.""" def init(self, mu: torch.Tensor, theta: torch.Tensor, s: torch.Tensor, c: torch.Tensor): """ mu: (2,) center coordinates theta: (1,) rotation angle s: (2,) scale factors c: (3,) RGB color """ self.mu = mu self.theta = theta self.s = s self.c = c def getcovariance(self) -> torch.Tensor: """Compute Sigma = (RS)(RS)^T.""" # R is 2x2 rotation matrix from theta cost = torch.cos(self.theta) sint = torch.sin(self.theta) R = torch.stack([ [cost, -sint], [sint, cost] ]) S = torch.diag(self.s) RS = torch.matmul(R, S) return torch.matmul(RS, RS.t()) class AIRPredictor(nn.Module): """Feed-forward network predicting Gaussian primitives.""" def init(self): super().init() # Encoder-Decoder architecture details omitted as not specified in source # Placeholder for actual network layers self.encoder = nn.Identity() self.decoder = nn.Identity() def forward(self, image: torch.Tensor, residual: torch.Tensor = None) -> List[GaussianPrimitive]: """ Predicts a list of Gaussian primitives given the input image and optional residual. """ # Implementation specific to the paper's architecture # Inputs: image (H, W, 3), residual (H, W, 3) # Output: List of GaussianPrimitive objects pass def rendergaussians(gaussians: List[GaussianPrimitive], imgh: int, imgw: int) -> torch.Tensor: """ Differentiable rasterization of 2D Gaussians. Returns rendered image (H, W, 3). """ # Initialize output image outimg = torch.zeros((imgh, imgw, 3), device=gaussians[0].mu.device) # For each pixel, aggregate contributions from covering Gaussians # Note: In practice, this is done via spatial hashing or sorting for efficiency for y in range(imgh): for x in range(imgw): pixelpos = torch.tensor([x, y], dtype=torch.float32) numerator = torch.zeros(3) denominator = 0.0 for g in gaussians: # Check if Gaussian covers pixel (simple bounding box or distance check) # Compute alpha mu = g.mu cov = g.getcovariance() try: covinv = torch.inverse(cov) except RuntimeError: continue # Skip if singular d = pixelpos - mu alpha = torch.exp(-0.5 torch.matmul(d.t(), torch.matmul(covinv, d))) # If alpha is negligible, skip if alpha < 1e-6: continue numerator += g.c alpha denominator += alpha if denominator > 0: outimg[y, x] = numerator / denominator return outimg def trainstepaire(imagegt: torch.Tensor, predictor: AIRPredictor, numstages: int = 3): """ Simplified training loop illustrating the POD strategy. """ # 1. Predict initial stage gaussians = [] currentrendered = torch.zeroslike(imagegt) for k in range(numstages): residual = imagegt - currentrendered # Predict new primitives based on residual newprimitives = predictor(imagegt, residual) # 2. Optimize (Distillation Target Generation) # Create a detached copy of the current accumulated set + new primitives tempgaussians = gaussians + newprimitives # Refine tempgaussians using gradient descent on Gaussian params # to minimize rendering loss against imagegt # This is the "Optimize" step refinedgaussians = optimizegaussians(tempgaussians, imagegt, steps=5) # 3. Distill # Compute loss between predicted newprimitives and the increment # required to go from gaussians to refinedgaussians # This updates the predictor parameters distillloss = computegaussianspaceloss(newprimitives, refinedgaussians, gaussians) distillloss.backward() # Update accumulated set gaussians = refinedgaussians # Or gaussians + newprimitives depending on exact distill target definition currentrendered = rendergaussians(gaussians, imagegt.shape[0], imagegt.shape[1]) return gaussians def optimizegaussians(gaussians: List[GaussianPrimitive], target: torch.Tensor, steps: int) -> List[GaussianPrimitive]: """ Performs gradient descent on Gaussian parameters to match target image. Returns optimized list of Gaussians. """ # Convert list to tensors for optimization # This function performs 'steps' iterations of gradient descent # using a differentiable renderer. # Details of the optimizer and loss (L1/SSIM) are standard but not explicitly detailed in source notes. # Standard Adam optimizer with L1 loss is assumed for this step. pass Parameters: Number of Stages (K): Not explicitly fixed in the notes, but described as "stage-wise". Encoding Time: 160–300 ms on Kodak and DIV2K datasets. Optimization Steps (POD): "A few" differentiable rendering optimization steps are used during the distillation phase. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Under-constrained Mapping: Direct supervision with rendering loss leads to unstable optimization. The POD strategy is required to stabilize training. Primitive Allocation: Without Stage Control, predicting primitives uniformly may lead to redundancy. The explicit Stage Control mechanism ensures new primitives are only activated in under-reconstructed regions. Compactness: The goal is to find the smallest Gaussian set G^ satisfying a fidelity target \epsilon: G^ \in \arg \minG |G| \text{ s.t. } L{render}(R(G), I{gt}) \le \epsilon. Time Complexity: Encoding time is 160–300 ms per image on standard datasets (Kodak, DIV2K), significantly faster than iterative methods like GaussianImage which require per-image optimization. Memory Complexity: Uses an image-adaptive quantizer for compact Gaussian storage, reducing memory footprint compared to unquantized representations. Strengths: Fully self-supervised and end-to-end; eliminates per-image test-time optimization; achieves better reconstruction quality than Instant-GI and GaussianImage; no reliance on handcrafted priors (e.g., PPM, dithering). Limitations: Relies on a trained feed-forward network, so it generalizes based on the training data distribution; the POD training strategy adds complexity to the training pipeline compared to direct supervised learning. When to Use: When fast, high-quality image reconstruction into 2D Gaussian splats is required without per-image optimization overhead. When Not to Use: When per-image iterative refinement is acceptable for higher fidelity, or when the input images are significantly out-of-distribution from the training set (Kodak/DIV2K). AIR was introduced by Yuesong Wang in a preprint titled "AIR: Amortized Image Reconstruction Framework for Self-Supervised Feed-Forward 2D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitations of existing 2D Gaussian image reconstruction methods, which either rely on costly per-image iterative optimization (GaussianImage, Image-GS) or handcrafted priors and pseudo-labels (Instant-GI). The method builds on the 2D Gaussian splatting formulation introduced in GaussianImage. name: UniQueR
head: Unified Query-Based Feedforward 3D Reconstruction
body: UniQueR is a feedforward framework for fast 3D reconstruction from unposed images using sparse learnable 3D queries. It predicts camera-to-world transforms and per-view local point maps, then uses queries to spawn Gaussians rendered via differentiable splatting for supervision. It sets itself apart from siblings like HFGaussian and ZeroGS by decoupling the attention mechanism between image tokens and 3D queries to handle high-resolution inputs efficiently, avoiding the quadratic complexity of full self-attention on concatenated tokens. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N of the same scene, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Camera poses are not provided. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} and camera poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^N. Data Structures: Image Tokens: Ti \in \mathbb{R}^{(HW/p^2) \times d}, extracted from each image Ii. Queries: A fixed set of Q learnable queries \mathcal{Q} = \{qi\}{i=1}^Q. Each query qi has a latent embedding and an explicit 3D coordinate pi. Gaussian Set: \mathcal{G} = \bigcup{i=1}^Q \bigcup{k=1}^K (\mu{ik}, \Sigma{ik}, c{ik}, \alpha{ik}), where \mu{ik} is the mean, \Sigma{ik} is the covariance, c{ik} is the color, and \alpha{ik} is the opacity. Parameters: Q = 4096: Number of learnable 3D queries. K = 64: Number of Gaussians spawned per query. p: Patch size of the DINOv2 backbone (typically 14 for ViT-L/14). d: Token dimensionality of the DINOv2 backbone. \lambdad = 0.1: Weight for the scale-invariant rendered-depth loss. \lambdac = 0.2: Weight for the backbone camera loss. Total Gaussians: Q \times K = 262,144. Steps: 1. Image Tokenization: Extract per-frame visual tokens using a DINOv2 Vision Transformer backbone: Ti = \text{DINO}(Ii) \in \mathbb{R}^{(HW/p^2) \times d} where T = HW/p^2 is the number of tokens per image. 2. Cross-View Aggregation: Apply an alternating-attention (AA) transformer to aggregate tokens across N views: \{T^{l+1}i\} = \text{AA-Transformer}(\{T^li\}) where l is the layer index. This alternates between intra-frame and inter-frame attention operations. 3. Geometric Decoding: Decode the aggregated tokens into per-frame geometric annotations: \{Pi, Xi, Ci\} = \text{Decoder}(\{T^li\}) where Pi \in SE(3) is the camera-to-world transform, Xi \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W} is the local point map, and Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} is the confidence map. 4. Query Initialization: Initialize Q queries with hybrid coordinates: Half of the query coordinates are sampled from the predicted non-metric point maps Xi, providing geometric grounding on observed surfaces. The remaining queries are initialized uniformly in the normalized 3D scene range. Note: Random-only initialization is unstable in dense reconstruction because only 2D rendered image losses are available, not ground-truth 3D boxes. 5. Positional Encoding: Convert predicted camera poses Pi into Plücker ray embeddings to serve as positional encodings for the image tokens. Each query qi uses its 3D coordinate pi as its positional embedding. 6. Query Refinement: Update queries using a 12-layer Query Transformer with decoupled attention. In each layer: Q = \text{Cross-Attn}(Q, T) Q = \text{Self-Attn}(Q) This decoupled design reduces complexity from O((Q + NT)^2) to O(QNT + Q^2), enabling scaling to high-resolution images. 7. Gaussian Spawning: For each query qi at location pi: Predict a deformation \delta{qi}. The cluster center becomes pi + \delta{qi}. An MLP decodes K local offsets \delta{g{ik}} for k=1 \dots K. Attribute heads predict opacity \alpha{ik}, scale, rotation, and color c{ik} for each spawned Gaussian. The final Gaussian set is defined as: \mathcal{G} = \bigcup{i=1}^Q \bigcup{k=1}^K (pi + \delta{qi} + \delta{g{ik}}, \Sigma{ik}, c{ik}, \alpha{ik}) 8. Rendering: Render the Gaussian set \mathcal{G} into RGB images \hat{I} and depth maps \hat{D} via differentiable splatting. 9. Supervision: Novel-View Supervision: Supervise renderings of a superset of input views (e.g., 6 renderings for 3 inputs). Held-out target views correct empty holes and discourage reproducing only input-view surfaces. Loss Function: The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}{depth} + \lambdac \mathcal{L}{cam} where \mathcal{L}{rgb} includes L1 and LPIPS in Stage 1, or only L1 in Stage 2. \mathcal{L}{depth} is the scale-invariant rendered-depth loss, and \mathcal{L}{cam} is the backbone camera loss. 10. Staged Training: Stage 1: Train at 224^2 resolution for 100 epochs. \mathcal{L}{rgb} includes L1 and LPIPS. Stage 2: Fine-tune at 448^2 resolution for 20 epochs. \mathcal{L}{rgb} uses only L1 because LPIPS substantially increases training time. The DINOv2 encoder, alternating-attention transformer, and point-map head are frozen. The camera head, Query Transformer, and GS heads are updated. 11. Post Optimization (TTO): Test-time optimization using predicted Gaussians and poses. Render back to input views, compute reconstruction losses, and backpropagate to refine Gaussian parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class UniQueR: def init(self, Q=4096, K=64, patchsize=14, d=1024): self.Q = Q self.K = K self.patchsize = patchsize self.d = d # Backbone components self.dinov2 = DINOv2Backbone() # Frozen self.aatransformer = AlternatingAttentionTransformer() # Frozen self.geometricdecoder = GeometricDecoder() # Frozen # Trainable components self.camerahead = CameraHead() self.querytransformer = QueryTransformer(numlayers=12, Q=Q, d=d) self.gsspawner = GaussianSpawner(Q=Q, K=K, d=d) # Initialize queries self.queries = self.initializequeries() def initializequeries(self): """Hybrid initialization: half from point maps, half uniform.""" # Placeholder for initialization logic; actual coordinates # are set during the first forward pass after geometric decoding. # Latent embeddings are learnable parameters. return nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.Q, self.d)) def forward(self, images): """ images: List of N tensors, each [3, H, W] Returns: Gaussian set G, camera poses P """ N = len(images) # 1. Image Tokenization tokens = [] for i in range(N): # DINOv2 extracts tokens ti = self.dinov2(images[i]) tokens.append(ti) # 2. Cross-View Aggregation aggregatedtokens = self.aatransformer(tokens) # 3. Geometric Decoding poses = [] pointmaps = [] confidences = [] for i in range(N): pi, xi, ci = self.geometricdecoder(aggregatedtokens[i]) poses.append(pi) pointmaps.append(xi) confidences.append(ci) # 4. Query Initialization (Hybrid) # Sample half from point maps, half uniformly # Note: pointmaps are in local camera coordinates; # transforms are needed to bring them to a shared gauge. # The decoder provides Pi (camera-to-world). # We assume a shared gauge is established by applying Pi to Xi. # For implementation, we sample indices and coordinates. # Let's assume we have a function to sample from point maps. querycoords = self.samplequerycoords(pointmaps, poses, self.Q) # Initialize query embeddings (latent) # In the paper, queries have both coordinate and embedding. # The embedding is updated by the transformer. queryembeddings = torch.randn(self.Q, self.d, requiresgrad=True) # 5. Positional Encoding # Image tokens get Plücker ray embeddings from poses # Queries get 3D coordinates as positional embedding # This is handled internally by the attention mechanisms. # 6. Query Refinement # Decoupled attention: Cross-Attn then Self-Attn for layer in self.querytransformer.layers: # Cross-Attn: Queries attend to Image Tokens # PosEnc for queries: 3D coords # PosEnc for tokens: Plücker rays queryembeddings = layer.crossattn(queryembeddings, aggregatedtokens, querypos=querycoords, tokenpos=pluckerrays(poses)) # Self-Attn: Queries attend to Queries queryembeddings = layer.selfattn(queryembeddings, querypos=querycoords) # 7. Gaussian Spawning # Predict deformation for each query deformations = self.gsspawner.predictdeformation(queryembeddings) querycenters = querycoords + deformations # Spawn K Gaussians per query gaussians = self.gsspawner.spawn(querycenters, queryembeddings) # 8. Rendering # Render to input views and held-out views # Assume we have a renderer that takes G and P renderedrgb, rendereddepth = self.render(gaussians, poses) return gaussians, poses def samplequerycoords(self, pointmaps, poses, Q): """Sample Q coordinates from point maps and uniform space.""" # Implementation detail: # 1. Transform point maps to world space using poses. # 2. Sample Q/2 points from the transformed point maps. # 3. Sample Q/2 points uniformly in normalized 3D range. # This is a helper function to be implemented based on # the specific geometry of point maps. pass def render(self, gaussians, poses): """Differentiable splatting renderer.""" # Uses a standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer pass def computeloss(self, renderedrgb, rendereddepth, images, targetdepths): """Compute total loss.""" # Stage 1: L1 + LPIPS # Stage 2: L1 only lrgb = l1loss(renderedrgb, images) # + lpipsloss(...) in Stage 1 ldepth = scaleinvariantdepthloss(rendereddepth, targetdepths) lcam = cameraloss(poses) # From backbone supervision lambdad = 0.1 lambdac = 0.2 return lrgb + lambdad ldepth + lambdac lcam Time Complexity: The decoupled attention design reduces the theoretical attention complexity from O((Q + NT)^2) to O(QNT + Q^2), where T = HW/p^2 is the number of tokens per image. This enables scaling to high-resolution images. Memory Complexity: Substantial memory savings compared to full self-attention, allowing the model to handle larger image sizes and more queries. Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360 with 3 views: PSNR 22.70, SSIM 0.660, LPIPS 0.261, inference time 0.416s on A100. On RealEstate10K with 2 input views: PSNR 20.50, SSIM 0.672, LPIPS 0.196. Model Size: 502.31M trainable parameters; frozen backbone has 890.99M parameters (1.393B total). Strengths: Fast inference (feedforward), handles unposed images, high-fidelity reconstruction with sparse inputs, efficient attention mechanism. Limitations: Requires test-time optimization (TTO) for best results, LPIPS loss increases training time significantly in Stage 2. When to use: When fast, feedforward 3D reconstruction from unposed images is required, and computational resources for per-scene optimization are limited. When not to use: When ground-truth 3D poses are available and per-scene optimization is feasible, or when extremely high resolution is required without the decoupled attention benefit. UniQueR was proposed by C. Peng et al. in the paper "UniQueR: Unified Query-Based Feedforward 3D Reconstruction". It builds on the principles of feedforward reconstruction models like TokenGS but introduces sparse learnable 3D queries to decouple Gaussian prediction from pixels. The method leverages DINOv2 for feature extraction and alternating-attention transformers for cross-view aggregation, similar to VGGT and Pi3. It is trained on datasets including DL3DV-10K, ScanNet++, BlendedMVS, and Co3D. name: Plenoptic Sampling Guided 3DGS Construction
head: White-Box 3DGS Construction, Mesh2GS Construction
body: Plenoptic Sampling Guided 3DGS Construction is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations directly from mesh geometry, using plenoptic sampling theory to theoretically derive the minimum sampling rate for views and the optimal distribution of 3D Gaussians. Unlike heuristic initialization methods that rely on trial-and-error, this approach precisely constrains Gaussian density and camera sampling to achieve Nyquist-level performance for global illumination caching. It sets itself apart by grounding the initialization in signal processing principles, ensuring that the number of Gaussians and sampled views is minimized while maintaining high-fidelity rendering. The method constructs 3D Gaussians from a given scene mesh G by deriving sampling parameters from camera intrinsics and scene depth bounds. The process involves determining the camera sampling interval, computing the world-space Gaussian sampling interval, initializing Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity), and optimizing color attributes using an albedo-shading decomposition strategy. Inputs: Scene geometry: A mesh G representing the scene surfaces. Camera parameters: Focal length f, pixel size \Delta v (or resolution R and field of view \theta), minimum observation distance z{min}, and maximum observation distance z{max}. body: Geometry Guided Gaussian Points Generation (MGadapter) is a method that generates structured 3D Gaussian point attributes from an intermediate triangular mesh, providing explicit geometric guidance to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem of vanilla 3DGS lacking deterministic geometry boundaries and explicit normal directions, which complicates light transport computation and hinders physically-based inverse rendering. Unlike sibling methods that rely on learned approximated normals or real-time optimization to maintain shape consistency, MGadapter uses a predefined heuristic function to map mesh triangles directly to Gaussian points, leveraging well-defined mesh normals for improved accuracy and stable training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangular mesh M derived from a scalar field \zeta via differentiable isosurface extraction (e.g., FlexiCubes). Each triangle face Fi consists of three vertices Pi = (p{i1}, p{i2}, p{i3}) and corresponding vertex normals Ni = (n{i1}, n{i2}, n{i3}). Output: A set of K Gaussian point attributes \{(\mui, Si, Ri, ni) \mid i=1,\dots,K\} for each triangle P. Data Structures: Triangle Face Fi: Defined by vertex positions Pi and vertex normals Ni. Per-vertex Attributes Ai: Stored as tuples Ai = (a{i1}, a{i2}, a{i3}) corresponding to the three vertices of the triangle. Gaussian Point Attributes: Position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Normal ni \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale Si (represented as S{ix}, S{iy}) Rotation Ri (represented as direction vector R{ix}) Opacity: Fixed to 1. Parameters: K: Number of Gaussian points per triangle. Empirically set to K=6. u, v: Scalar parameters defining barycentric coordinates for sampling points. Values are not specified in the sources. \alpha{jk}, \beta{jk}: Scaling factors for the Gaussian dimensions. Values are not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Mesh Generation: Obtain the intermediate triangular mesh M from the scalar field \zeta using a differentiable isosurface extraction technique such as FlexiCubes. 2. Iteration: For each triangle face Fi in mesh M, generate K=6 Gaussian points. 3. Barycentric Coordinate Definition: Define 6 barycentric coordinates \mathbf{b}j for j=1,\dots,6 using parameters u and v: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{b}1 &= (u, u, 1-2u) \\ \mathbf{b}2 &= (u, 1-2u, u) \\ \mathbf{b}3 &= (1-2u, u, u) \\ \mathbf{b}4 &= (v, v, 1-2v) \\ \mathbf{b}5 &= (v, 1-2v, v) \\ \mathbf{b}6 &= (1-2v, v, v) \end{aligned} 4. Midpoint Calculation: Compute 6 midpoints \mathbf{m}{jk} by averaging pairs of barycentric coordinates: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{m}{12} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}1 + \mathbf{b}2}{2} = \left(u, \frac{1-u}{2}, \frac{1-u}{2}\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{23} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}2 + \mathbf{b}3}{2} = \left(\frac{1-u}{2}, \frac{1-u}{2}, u\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{31} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}3 + \mathbf{b}1}{2} = \left(\frac{1-u}{2}, u, \frac{1-u}{2}\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{45} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}4 + \mathbf{b}5}{2} = \left(v, \frac{1-v}{2}, \frac{1-v}{2}\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{56} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}5 + \mathbf{b}6}{2} = \left(\frac{1-v}{2}, \frac{1-v}{2}, v\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{64} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}6 + \mathbf{b}4}{2} = \left(\frac{1-v}{2}, v, \frac{1-v}{2}\right) \end{aligned} 5. Barycentric Interpolation: For any attribute Ai = (a{i1}, a{i2}, a{i3}) defined at the triangle vertices and a barycentric coordinate (q1, q2, q3), compute the interpolated value as: (q1, q2, q3) \odot Ai = q1 a{i1} + q2 a{i2} + q3 a{i3} 6. Gaussian Point Attribute Assignment: For each midpoint \mathbf{m}{jk} (where jk \in \{12, 23, 31, 45, 56, 64\}), assign the Gaussian point attributes: Position: \mu = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi Normal: n = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Ni Scale X: S{ix} = \alpha{jk} \| \mathbf{b}k \odot Pi - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi \|2 Rotation X: R{ix} = \frac{\mathbf{b}k \odot Pi - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi}{\| \mathbf{b}k \odot Pi - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi \|2} Scale Y: S{iy} = \frac{\text{Area}(Fi)}{\beta{jk} \| \dots \|} (Formula incomplete in source) Opacity: Set to 1. name: Optical and Attribute Enhancement
head: Textured-GS, Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement, Defocus Blur Modeling
body: Optical and Attribute Enhancement extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation by allowing spatial variation of color and opacity within individual Gaussian primitives, rather than treating them as uniform ellipsoids with fixed view-dependent color. It solves the limitation of low-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) in capturing high-frequency details and complex surface properties by introducing per-Gaussian texture maps and static attribute-conditioned offsets. It differs from standard 3DGS by evaluating SH basis functions on surface intersection vectors (Textured-GS) or baking MLP-predicted offsets into parameters (Attribute-Conditioned SH), and differs from naive blurring by selectively adjusting Gaussian scales based on defocus depth. The family shares the goal of enhancing the visual fidelity of 3D Gaussians beyond the standard single-color, single-opacity model. All methods operate on the Gaussian primitives defined by position, rotation, scale, and base opacity. They modify the rendering or optimization pipeline to introduce higher-frequency detail or optical effects without necessarily increasing the number of primitives. Textured-GS models spatially defined color and opacity variations across the Gaussian ellipsoidal surface using Spherical Harmonics (SH), evaluated against the surface normal rather than the viewing direction [9436-textured-gs.md]. It allows for deviations from standard ellipsoidal shapes, such as unidirectional opacity, and differs from Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction by using the surface intersection vector for SH evaluation [9436-textured-gs.md]. This module recovers high-frequency visual details lost in low-order SH representations by predicting view-independent offsets via an MLP, which are statically baked into Gaussian parameters before inference [15410-attribute-conditioned-sh-enhancement.md]. It differs from dynamic neural view-dependent enhancement methods by introducing zero additional computational overhead during rendering [15410-attribute-conditioned-sh-enhancement.md]. Models optical defocus by adjusting the scale s of 3D Gaussians based on their distance from the camera's focal plane. During training, larger scale values \hat{s}j are used to rasterize blurred images, while smaller scale values sj are used during testing to render sharp details. Unlike a naive Gaussian kernel that blurs the entire image uniformly, this method selectively enlarges covariances only for Gaussians corresponding to blurred regions. The concept of modeling defocus blur using Gaussian scales originates from the observation that 3D Gaussians with greater dispersion (larger scale s) can represent scene points not located at the focal distance, while smaller scales model points at the focal distance. This approach was formalized in "Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting", which demonstrated that larger scale values are needed to adjust 3D Gaussians to rasterize blurred training images, whereas smaller-sized Gaussians are more suitable for modeling fine details in sharp testing images. The method avoids the limitations of naive Gaussian kernels, which blur the entire image and fail to model spatially varying blurriness.
