name: Sky Dome Initialization
head: Frozen Shell of Gaussians, Sky Dome
body: Sky Dome Initialization handles unbounded scenes in 3D Gaussian Splatting by modeling the distant background as a separate, frozen shell of Gaussians. It solves the problem of cloud-like artifacts that appear when foreground Gaussians attempt to model distant sky regions, which degrades novel view synthesis quality. It sets itself apart from standard background models by explicitly disentangling the sky from the foreground geometry, often using a hemisphere to avoid occluding the ground plane. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images, camera poses, and optionally sky segmentation masks. Outputs: A rendered image where the sky is composited behind the foreground, and a set of frozen Gaussian parameters for the sky dome. Data Structures: The Sky Dome consists of a fixed set of Gaussians. Sphere Variant: Gaussians are distributed on a sphere surface. Hemisphere Variant: Gaussians are distributed on a hemisphere surface, leaving the bottom half empty to render a black background. Mask Data: If using semantic priors, sky masks are stored in a directory structure <dataset-root>/sky/<FILENAME>.png, where FILENAME matches the corresponding dataset image. Steps: 1. Initialize Sky Gaussians: Sample points from a sphere or hemisphere to initialize the sky Gaussian positions. A common method is sampling 100,000 points from a Fibonacci sphere. 2. Freeze Parameters: The position, rotation, and scale of these sky Gaussians are frozen (not optimized) during training. 3. Render Sky Pass: Render the sky dome independently to obtain the sky color C{sky}(p) and opacity O(p) for each pixel. Accumulated transmittance is calculated as: Ti = \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphak) where Ti is the transmittance at step i. Foreground opacity is the sum of sample weights: O(p) = \sumi Ti \alphai. 4. Composite: Combine the foreground and sky colors using compositional rendering. The final pixel color C(p) is: C(p) = \sumi Ti \alphai ci + (1 - O(p)) \cdot C{sky}(p) where ci is the color of the i-th foreground Gaussian. 5. Regularization (Optional): If sky masks are available, apply a loss L{sky} to penalize foreground opacity in sky regions, encouraging O(p) to be close to zero in those areas. L{sky} = \lambda{sky} \sum{p \in \text{sky}} O(p) where \lambda{sky} is a weight (e.g., 10). Parameters: Number of Sky Gaussians: ~32,000 for the dome, which is negligible compared to millions of foreground Gaussians. \lambda{sky}: Set to 10 to remove cloud artifacts in the initial training steps (e.g., first 7,000 steps). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sphere vs. Hemisphere: Using a full sphere can pull geometry onto itself, making the ground less opaque. A hemisphere leaves the bottom half black, preventing interference with foreground geometry. Sparse Free Space: Simply blending sky and foreground colors may not clear artifacts if sparse points exist in free space initially. Convergence Trade-offs: Alternative approaches like sky depth loss or BCE semantic regularization may require longer convergence times and can negatively impact foreground modeling quality. A rendering model that incorporates a spherical environment map composed of Gaussians to model the sky separately from the foreground. It sets itself apart from standard background models by explicitly penalizing foreground opacity in sky regions using semantic masks, rather than relying solely on compositional blending. It is chosen when standard 3DGS produces significant cloud-like artifacts in unbounded scenes. Time and Memory Complexity: The overhead is negligible (~32K Gaussians) compared to the millions of foreground Gaussians. Rendering adds one additional pass for the sky dome. Measured Performance: Effectively disentangles sky from foreground, reducing floaters and improving novel view synthesis quality in unbounded scenes. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of sky Gaussians, which remains constant regardless of scene complexity. Strengths: Simple to implement, low overhead, effective at removing cloud artifacts. Limitations: Requires careful choice between sphere and hemisphere based on scene content (ground visibility). Semantic regularization may slow convergence. When to Use: Unbounded scenes with visible sky where standard 3DGS produces artifacts. When Not to Use: Bounded scenes where the sky is not visible or is fully occluded. Originated as an improvement in Gaussian Splatting implementations to handle unbounded scenes. The "Sky Dome" concept was popularized in unofficial implementations like GaussianSplatting.jl. The "Gaussian Sky Modeling" variant was introduced in GauStudio, a modular framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It is used in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis for outdoor or large-scale scenes. Better Gaussian Splatting in Julia, https://pxl-th.github.io/blog/better-gs-julia/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GauStudio: A Modular Framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting and Beyond, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.19632, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: ReSplat Initialization
head: 3D Context Aggregation, Initial Gaussian Prediction
body: ReSplat Initialization predicts an initial set of 3D Gaussians from a sparse point cloud by aggregating local and global 3D context to compensate for information loss incurred by downsampling the input point cloud by 16x. Unlike naive prediction methods that directly map point features to Gaussian parameters, this method uses a transformer-based encoder to enrich features with neighborhood context before decoding. It sets the stage for the subsequent Recurrent Gaussian Update by providing a structured initial state \mathcal{G}^0. Inputs: N input views with intrinsics Ki, extrinsics Ri, ti, and images Ii. Outputs: M initial 3D Gaussians, where M = N \times H \times W / 16. Each Gaussian j is defined by parameters \mathbf{g}j^0 (concatenated mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, opacity \alpha, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{sh}) and an initial hidden state \mathbf{z}j^0. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud: A set of M points \{\mathbf{p}j\}{j=1}^M with associated feature vectors \{\mathbf{f}j\}{j=1}^M \in \mathbb{R}^{C0}. 2. Gaussian Parameters: \mathbf{g}j^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{C1}, where C1 = 59. This vector concatenates \boldsymbol{\mu}j (3), \alphaj (1), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j (6, using lower-triangular or quaternion representation as per standard GS, though the source specifies the total count), and \mathbf{sh}j (49 for 3rd degree SH, or adjusted based on implementation; the source fixes C1=59). 3. Hidden State: \mathbf{z}j^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{C0}, initialized to the context-aggregated feature \mathbf{f}j^. Parameters: C0: Dimension of the hidden state and context-aggregated features. Values: 256 (small model) or 512 (base model). C1: Total number of parameters per Gaussian. Value: 59. k: Number of neighbors for kNN attention. Value: 16. T: Total number of recurrent iterations (used in subsequent update, not initialization itself, but defines the context of \mathcal{G}^0). Steps: 1. Downsampling: Downsample the input data to M points. The source specifies M = N \times H \times W / 16. This results in a point cloud \{(\mathbf{p}j, \mathbf{f}j)\}{j=1}^M where \mathbf{f}j are features extracted from input images. 2. 3D Context Aggregation: Encode 3D context using six alternating blocks of kNN attention and global attention layers. kNN Attention: For each point, identify k=16 nearest neighbors in 3D space. Compute attention weights based on geometric proximity and feature similarity. Global Attention: Apply self-attention across all M points to capture long-range dependencies. Blocks: Repeat the kNN and global attention blocks six times. Output: Context-aggregated features \{\mathbf{f}j^\}{j=1}^M \in \mathbb{R}^{C0}. 3. Decoding to Gaussians: Use the point cloud \{\mathbf{p}j\}{j=1}^M as the Gaussian centers (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}j = \mathbf{p}j). Decode other Gaussian parameters (\alphaj, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j, \mathbf{sh}j) using a lightweight two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), referred to as the "Gaussian head". Input to MLP: \mathbf{f}j^. Output of MLP: Parameters for \alphaj, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j, \mathbf{sh}j. Form \mathbf{g}j^0 by concatenating all Gaussian parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}j, \alphaj, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j, \mathbf{sh}j). 4. Initialization of Recurrent State: Initialize the hidden state for the recurrent update process: \mathbf{z}j^0 = \mathbf{f}j^. 5. Form Initial Set: Construct the initial Gaussian set: \mathcal{G}^0 = \{(\mathbf{g}j^0, \mathbf{z}j^0)\}{j=1}^M \quad (3) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def resplatinitialization(images, intrinsics, extrinsics, H, W): """ Predicts initial 3D Gaussians from input views. Args: images: List of N images. intrinsics: List of N intrinsic matrices K. extrinsics: List of N extrinsic matrices [R|t]. H, W: Height and width of input images. Returns: G0: List of M initial Gaussians, each tuple (g0, z0). """ N = len(images) M = (N H W) // 16 # Step 1: Downsampling and Feature Extraction # Projects image pixels into 3D space using camera parameters, # samples M points, and extracts initial features. points, features = downsampleandextractfeatures(images, intrinsics, extrinsics, M) # Step 2: 3D Context Aggregation k = 16 C0 = 256 # or 512 depending on model size aggregatedfeatures = features for in range(6): # kNN Attention Block # Standard kNN attention: compute Q, K, V from features, # restrict attention to k neighbors, apply softmax, and aggregate. # Implementation details are not provided in. aggregatedfeatures = knnattention(aggregatedfeatures, points, k) # Global Attention Block # Standard self-attention: compute Q, K, V from all features, # apply softmax to all pairs, and aggregate. # Implementation details are not provided in. aggregatedfeatures = globalattention(aggregatedfeatures) # Step 3: Decoding to Gaussians C1 = 59 gaussianhead = TwoLayerMLP(inputdim=C0, outputdim=C1 - 3) # 3 for mean which is points initialgaussians = [] for j in range(M): pj = points[j] fstarj = aggregatedfeatures[j] # Mean is the point position muj = pj # Decode other parameters from context-aggregated feature decodedparams = gaussianhead(fstarj) # Concatenate to form g0j: mu, alpha, Sigma, sh g0j = np.concatenate([muj, decodedparams]) # Initialize hidden state z0j z0j = fstarj initialgaussians.append((g0j, z0j)) return initialgaussians def downsampleandextractfeatures(images, intrinsics, extrinsics, M): # Standard multi-view geometry projection and sampling to obtain M points and features. # Implementation details are not provided in. pass def knnattention(features, points, k): # Standard kNN attention: compute Q, K, V from features, # restrict attention to k neighbors, apply softmax, and aggregate. # Implementation details are not provided in. pass def globalattention(features): # Standard self-attention: compute Q, K, V from all features, # apply softmax to all pairs, and aggregate. # Implementation details are not provided in. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Downsampling Loss: Naïve prediction from downsampled points leads to considerable performance loss; context aggregation is critical. Precision: The source does not specify floating-point precision requirements, but standard PyTorch implementations typically use FP32 or FP16. Boundary Conditions: The kNN search must handle points near the boundary of the point cloud correctly. Standard kNN implementations handle this by considering only existing points. Time Complexity: Dominated by the six blocks of kNN and global attention. kNN attention is O(M \cdot k \cdot C0) per block, and global attention is O(M^2 \cdot C0) per block. With M being 1/16 of the total pixel count, this is significantly faster than full-resolution attention but still quadratic in M for the global attention component. Memory Complexity: O(M \cdot C0) to store features and hidden states. The Gaussian head is lightweight. Performance: The method compensates for 16x downsampling, allowing for efficient initialization while maintaining high-quality results. Strengths: Efficiently initializes Gaussians from sparse data; leverages 3D context for better feature representation. Limitations: Requires a pre-computed point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP); the global attention component can be memory-intensive for very large scenes. ReSplat Initialization was introduced in "ReSplat: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the challenge of initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting from sparse point clouds, which is common in multi-view stereo pipelines. The method builds on the idea that local and global 3D context can be aggregated to recover information lost during downsampling. It is designed to work with the Recurrent Gaussian Update module of the ReSplat framework. ReSplat: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08575v4, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Point Cloud/Mesh-based Initialization
head: Geometry-based Gaussian Seeding
body: This family of methods initializes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives using pre-existing 3D geometry (point clouds or meshes) rather than relying solely on sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) outputs. It solves the problem of initializing high-quality radiance fields when multi-view images are unavailable or when the user possesses dense, surface-aligned volumetric data (e.g., MPEG plenoptic point clouds or meshes). It differs from Random Large-Variance Initialization by anchoring Gaussians to observed geometry, and from Gaussian Model Initialization by supporting dense mesh inputs and optional fixed-position constraints. All methods in this family map input geometric primitives (vertices or points) to Gaussian centers. The core shared mechanism is the derivation of initial covariance parameters (scale and rotation) and color features from the input geometry or associated rendering data. 1. Position Mapping: Input vertices or points \{pi\} are assigned directly to the xyz tensor of the Gaussian model. 2. Rotation Initialization: The rotation quaternion is initialized to the identity (1, 0, 0, 0) for all Gaussians, implying an initial isotropic orientation unless local normals are available. 3. Color Initialization: The zeroth-order spherical harmonic coefficient (featuresdc) is set to the RGB color of the corresponding point or rendered pixel. Higher-order coefficients (featuresrest) are zero-initialized. 4. Scale Estimation: Scales are derived from local density or depth. Common heuristics include using the median distance to k-nearest neighbors or computing an isometric radius based on focal length and depth. 5. Opacity Initialization: Opacity is initialized to a low value (e.g., raw parameter \approx -2.197 corresponding to 0.1) to prevent early overconfidence and allow gradient propagation. Standard procedure for seeding 3DGS from a sparse SfM point cloud (e.g., COLMAP). It maps each 3D point to a Gaussian, initializing position, SH coefficients, scale, rotation, and opacity. It differs from Random Large-Variance Initialization by anchoring to observed geometry, and from Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction by using heuristic density estimation rather than neural networks. When to choose: When starting with standard SfM sparse points and no dense mesh is available. Key Details: Scale: Estimated via k-nearest neighbor distances (e.g., k=20). A common heuristic sets the scale to a fraction (e.g., 0.1) of the median nearest-neighbor distance. Rotation: Identity quaternion. Opacity: Raw parameter \approx -2.197 (target opacity 0.1). Learning Rates: Position \alpha{xyz} = 0.00016, Color \alpha{color} = 0.0025. Pitfall: Covariance must be symmetric; ensure quaternion normalization. Initializes 3DGS from dense 3D point clouds or meshes, replacing the standard SfM initialization. It solves the problem of creating models from existing volumetric data when original multi-view images are unavailable. Unlike standard 3DGS, it uses dense, surface-aligned points, resulting in cleaner models and faster convergence. When to choose: When starting with a known dense mesh or plenoptic point cloud, and the original camera poses/images are missing or insufficient. Key Details: Input: 3D point cloud or mesh. View-dependent colors are preferred. Process: Renders multi-view images from the geometry to provide training data and camera parameters. Adaptive Density Control: Deactivated if input is dense/clean to preserve geometry; activated if noisy/sparse. Position Learning Rate: Set to 0 to fix splats on the original surface. Other Learning Rates: > 0 for opacity, scale, rotation, color. A variant focusing on isometric spherical initialization based on depth. Rotation: Identity matrix. Scale: Isometric spheres. Radius r is computed as: r = \frac{f \cdot D^{\text{init}}}{H} where f is the vertical focal length, D^{\text{init}} is the initial depth, and H is the image height. Color: SH DC set to pixel color; other coefficients zero. Opacity: Depends on view count N: N=2 \rightarrow 0.6, N=3 \rightarrow 0.5, N=4 \rightarrow 0.35. Opacity decreases with view count to ensure gradient propagation. The standard 3DGS initialization relies on sparse SfM points. Methods using dense point clouds or meshes were developed to leverage existing high-quality geometric representations (e.g., from MPEG or monocular depth estimators) when multi-view data is limited or unavailable. CoherentGS introduced the isometric scale calculation based on depth to handle sparse novel view synthesis. CoherentGS: Sparse Novel View Synthesis with Coherent 3D Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73404-52, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Gaussian Model Initialization
body: Gaussian Model Initialization establishes the initial state of a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene by mapping input geometric primitives—typically a sparse point cloud from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) or LiDAR—into the learnable parameters of the Gaussian set. It solves the problem of defining a valid, differentiable starting configuration for optimization, ensuring that positions, colors, opacities, and covariances are set to values that allow stable gradient propagation without early overconfidence. It differs from its parent method, Point Cloud/Mesh-based Initialization, by providing the specific implementation details of the standard 3DGS initialization pipeline, including the exact tensor layouts and default hyperparameters used in the reference implementation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud \{pi\} where each point i has a 3D position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and an RGB color \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Optional inputs include surface normals (if available) or depth information. Output: A GaussianModel data structure containing tensors for positions (xyz), rotations (quats), scales (scales), opacities (opacity), and spherical harmonic coefficients (featuresdc, featuresrest). Data Structures: The model maintains the following tensors (based on the reference implementation): xyz: Float tensor of shape (N, 3), storing the center coordinates of N Gaussians. quats: Float tensor of shape (N, 4), storing unit quaternions (w, x, y, z) for rotation. scales: Float tensor of shape (N, 3), storing the logarithmic scale parameters (\log sx, \log sy, \log sz). opacity: Float tensor of shape (N, 1), storing the raw opacity parameter \alpha{raw}. featuresdc: Float tensor of shape (N, 1, 3), storing the zeroth-order spherical harmonic coefficients (RGB). featuresrest: Float tensor of shape (N, 15, 3), storing higher-order SH coefficients (zero-initialized). Steps: 1. Position Mapping: Assign the input point cloud coordinates directly to xyz. \mathbf{xyz}i = \mathbf{p}i 2. Rotation Initialization: Initialize all rotation quaternions to the identity quaternion, implying an initial isotropic orientation. \mathbf{quats}i = (1, 0, 0, 0) Note: If local surface normals are available (e.g., from LiDAR or mesh), the rotation can be aligned to the normal frame using local PCA. 3. Color Initialization: Set the zeroth-order SH coefficient to the input RGB color. Higher-order coefficients are zero-initialized. \mathbf{features\dc}i = \mathbf{c}i \mathbf{features\rest}i = \mathbf{0} 4. Scale Estimation: Compute initial scales based on local density. A common heuristic is to use the median distance to the k-nearest neighbors (k{nn}) of each point. si = \text{median}(\{ \|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}j\|2 \mid j \in \text{NN}k(\mathbf{p}i) \}) The scale tensor stores the logarithm: \mathbf{scales}i = \log(si) Alternative: For volumetric data, scales may be derived from depth or focal length. 5. Opacity Initialization: Initialize opacity to a low value to prevent early overconfidence. The raw parameter is typically set to \approx -2.197, which corresponds to an opacity of 0.1 after the sigmoid activation. \alpha{raw, i} = -2.197 \mathbf{opacity}i = \alpha{raw, i} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def initializegaussianmodel(pointsxyz, pointsrgb, knn=20): """ Initialize a Gaussian Model from a point cloud. Args: pointsxyz: numpy array of shape (N, 3) pointsrgb: numpy array of shape (N, 3) with values in [0, 1] knn: Number of nearest neighbors for scale estimation Returns: model: Dictionary-like object with tensors xyz, quats, scales, opacity, featuresdc, featuresrest """ N = pointsxyz.shape[0] # 1. Position Mapping xyz = torch.tensor(pointsxyz, dtype=torch.float32) # 2. Rotation Initialization (Identity) quats = torch.zeros(N, 4, dtype=torch.float32) quats[:, 0] = 1.0 # w=1, x=0, y=0, z=0 # 3. Color Initialization featuresdc = torch.tensor(pointsrgb, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1) # Shape (N, 1, 3) featuresrest = torch.zeros(N, 15, 3, dtype=torch.float32) # 4. Scale Estimation (KNN heuristic) # Compute pairwise distances to find k-nearest neighbors # Note: In practice, use a KDTree for efficiency dists = torch.cdist(xyz, xyz, p=2) # Exclude self (distance 0) by setting diagonal to inf dists[torch.arange(N), torch.arange(N)] = float('inf') # Get knn smallest distances knndists, = torch.topk(dists, knn, dim=1, largest=False) # Median distance (knn is odd for median, or use mean if even) scaleslog = torch.log(knndists[:, knn // 2]) # Shape (N,) scales = scaleslog.unsqueeze(1) # Shape (N, 1) # 5. Opacity Initialization # -2.197 corresponds to sigmoid(-2.197) ≈ 0.1 opacity = torch.full((N, 1), -2.197, dtype=torch.float32) # Construct model model = { 'xyz': xyz, 'quats': quats, 'scales': scales, 'opacity': opacity, 'featuresdc': featuresdc, 'featuresrest': featuresrest } # Validate covariance symmetry (G) # Covariance = R S S^T R^T # With identity rotation and log-scales, S is diagonal. # Check if the resulting covariance matrix is symmetric # This is a sanity check, not part of initialization logic cov = computecovariance(model) assert torch.allclose(cov[0], cov[0].T, atol=1e-6), "Covariance must be symmetric" return model def computecovariance(model): """Helper to compute covariance from quats and scales for validation.""" # Extract rotation matrix from quaternion # Extract scale matrix from log-scales # Cov = R @ diag(exp(scales)) @ diag(exp(scales)) @ R.T # This is a placeholder for the actual matrix math pass Parameters: Learning Rate for xyz: 0.00016. Learning Rate for featuresdc: 0.0025. Initial Opacity Raw Value: -2.197 (Opacity \approx 0.1). K-Nearest Neighbors (k{nn}): 20 is a common default for scale estimation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Covariance Symmetry: The covariance matrix computed from scaling and rotation must be symmetric. Implementation must ensure that the rotation matrix is orthonormal and the scale matrix is diagonal to maintain this property. Boundary Conditions: If the point cloud is sparse, KNN-based scale estimation may yield large initial scales, causing excessive overlap. Conversely, dense clusters may yield tiny scales, leading to under-representation. Missing Normals: Standard SfM point clouds (e.g., from COLMAP) lack surface normals. Rotation must default to identity or be estimated via local PCA. Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) is a deterministic initialization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting in X-ray novel view synthesis that replaces Structure-from-Motion (SfM) by computing camera parameters directly from scanner specifications and uniformly sampling Gaussian centers within a bounding cuboid. It solves the problem of feature detection failure in low-contrast, overlapping X-ray projections, offering a significant reduction in training time compared to SfM-based initialization. DreamGaussian is a text-to-3D generation method that replaces the MipNeRF representation in the DreamFusion framework with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss to optimize 3D Gaussians. It distinguishes itself from its parent method, Gaussian Model Initialization, by providing a complete generative pipeline that not only initializes but fully optimizes a textured 3D asset from text prompts, leveraging the efficient splitting process of 3DGS to accelerate optimization. Unlike standard NeRF-based generation, it extracts a mesh from the generated Gaussians and refines texture details via UV-texture diffusion, enabling high-quality textured mesh generation in approximately 2 minutes. PhysGaussian couples 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with continuum mechanics, specifically the Material Point Method (MPM), to enable the simulation of physical dynamics such as deformation, fracture, and fluid flow. It provides a unified representation for both high-fidelity rendering and physics simulation, supporting materials like cloth, jelly, sand, and snow. Unlike variants that convert Gaussians to meshes for simulation (e.g., GASP), PhysGaussian applies MPM directly over the Gaussian primitives, allowing for differentiable physical interactions within the Gaussian representation. GaussianEditor is a text-driven local editing method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that leverages 2D image-editing models to drive updates of 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of localized appearance and geometry modification by repeatedly rendering GS views, applying 2D edits, and back-propagating the differences to Gaussian parameters. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Spherical Harmonics Initialization or DreamGaussian by its specific use of Hierarchical Gaussian Semantic Tracing (HGS) for adaptive generative guidance and its iterative refinement loop. Gaussian Asset Generation is a deterministic method for creating a reproducible 3D Gaussian Splatting PLY asset, specifically a dense "rainbow sphere" shell, without using randomness or external data. It solves the problem of needing a standardized, visually recognizable test asset for validating parsers and renderers (such as SceneView's PlyParser) by generating a synthetic point cloud with specific color, scale, opacity, and rotation parameters. It differs from other initialization methods like Gaussian Model Initialization or DreamGaussian by being purely synthetic and deterministic, rather than derived from input images or learned optimization. Learning-based and Generative Initialization methods initialize 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters using data-driven priors or learned latent representations rather than heuristic geometric heuristics. This approach solves the problem of poor convergence and structural incoherence in scenes with sparse or ambiguous input data by providing a structured starting point that respects the underlying scene topology. It differs from sibling methods like Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) and Sparse and Efficient Initialization by replacing explicit geometric rules with neural network decoding or optimization-based latent mapping. Sparse and Efficient Initialization establishes a computationally lightweight starting state for 3D Gaussian Splatting by initializing primitives within the visible camera frustum with low opacity and small scales, avoiding the computational overhead of dense scene coverage. It solves the problem of slow convergence and sub-optimal local minima caused by poor initial placement or high initial reflectivity, which leads to interference from closer splats. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing on the initial placement and static pre-training phase rather than iterative refinement (Recurrent Gaussian Update) or uniform density generation (Dense Initialization). It builds on Gaussian Model Initialization. This method creates a denser, more continuous surface representation than single-point ray intersection by pulling randomly sampled queries around 3D anchor points derived from back-projected geometry cues. It solves the problem of sparse geometric supervision by defining an isotropic Gaussian distribution around each anchor to sample a local surface patch, which is significantly more geometry-aware than single-point intersection or simple depth patch back-projection. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly models the local surface neighborhood via statistical sampling rather than uniform grid or mesh-based distribution, enabling patch-level photo consistency which achieves better performance than pixel-level consistency. Parameter and Coordinate Initialization establishes the initial values for learnable attributes of 3D Gaussian primitives, including spherical harmonic coefficients, sampling coordinates, and material parameters, before the optimization process begins. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the specific numerical setup of internal state variables (such as SH coefficients and feature sampling matrices) rather than the geometric placement of the Gaussians themselves. Mesh-based initialization converts a polygonal mesh into a set of 3D Gaussian splats to serve as the starting point for optimization or rendering. It solves the problem of establishing a geometric prior for Gaussian Splatting when a high-quality surface representation is already available, leveraging the explicit nature of Gaussians to support user-guided generation or scene-level inverse rendering. It differs from sibling methods like Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) by deriving positions from continuous surface geometry rather than volumetric bounding boxes, and from Learning-based and Generative Initialization by relying on deterministic geometric sampling rather than neural priors. R2-Gaussian Initialization is a method for initializing 3D Gaussians from volumetric tomography data where SfM is not applicable. It uses a Fast Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm to reconstruct a low-quality volume in under 1 second. Empty spaces are excluded using a density threshold \tau (typically 0.05), and M points (typically 50k) are randomly sampled as kernel positions. Scales are set to the nearest neighbor distances, and rotation is assumed to be identity. Central densities are queried from the FDK volume and scaled down by a factor k (typically 0.15) to compensate for kernel overlay. Persistent Material Descriptors attach samples (m{ik}, b{ik}) with weights based on initial Gaussian support at sampled voxels, keeping identifiers and weights fixed during optimization. The weight w{ik} is computed as: w{ik} \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}{ik} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^\top \Sigmai^{-1}(\mathbf{x}{ik} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)\right), \quad \sumk w{ik} = 1 where (\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \Sigmai) are the initial center and covariance, and \mathbf{x}{ik} is a sampled voxel center. This makes the descriptor scale-aware: sub-voxel primitives concentrate on their own material, while larger primitives integrate over their footprint. Clone and split children inherit descriptors from the nearest pre-existing primitive, and pruning applies one mask to all attributes. Methods to convert other representations (meshes, point clouds) into Fuzzy Metaballs (Gaussian Mixture Models) by fitting a GMM. Two types are described: surface GMM (sGMM) and volumetric GMM (vGMM). To build sGMM, points are sampled from the object surface and fit with EM. To build vGMM, points are sampled from the interior of a watertight mesh and fit with EM. The resulting GMM is optimized using a differentiable renderer, and a mesh can be extracted via marching cubes with an optimized iso-surface level. Experiments show both work well, but vGMM is often preferred. DART Initialization rewrites the SfM cloud P into an augmented cloud P{aug} using a replication multiplier m (default 10). Each augmented point becomes one 3D Gaussian. Covariance is estimated from local point density using a local-PCA neighborhood of size K{nn}=20. Opacity is initialized at 0.1, and color from the SfM color. Tangent-disk radius bounds are \rho{min}=0.008 and \rho{max}=0.04 (fractions of scene radius R). Weiszfeld iterations count Tw=8. A pitfall is that COLMAP point clouds lack usable normals, so surface normals for tangent frames are estimated via local PCA. An initialization strategy designed to support mixed-primitive-based learning, as standard initialization is incompatible with mixed primitives. It initializes the scene using mixed types of primitives (elliptical and non-elliptical). A calibrated photometric stereo method that reconstructs 3D surface normals and albedo by optimizing a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation of the scene using inverse rendering, specifically designed for single-view scenarios where traditional Structure-from-Motion initialization is not possible. It initializes the scene by placing one 3D Gaussian per pixel on a planar grid at z=0. The initial color attribute is set to the maximum intensity observed across all input images with different lighting conditions for that pixel location. The color of a pixel x is computed via alpha blending: c(x) = \frac{\tilde{c}k \tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}k G{\tilde{b}k}(x)}{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}k} \bigoplus{k=1}^K \tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}k G{\tilde{b}k}(x) \bigoplus{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}j G{\tilde{b}j}(x)) where \tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}k is opacity and \tilde{c}k is view-dependent color. SplatFace initializes Gaussians on a template mesh and jointly optimizes Gaussians and the mesh with a splat-to-mesh distance loss. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N \log N) or O(N^2) depending on the KNN implementation, where N is the number of input points. This is negligible compared to the training time. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the Gaussian parameters. Strengths: Provides a robust, differentiable starting point that aligns with the input geometry. The low initial opacity prevents overfitting to noise. Limitations: Relies heavily on the quality of the input point cloud. Sparse or noisy SfM clouds can lead to poor initial coverage or artifacts. When to Use: Standard 3DGS reconstruction from multi-view images or LiDAR scans. When Not to Use: When no geometric prior is available (use uniform or learning-based initialization) or when working with volumetric data requiring specific tomographic initialization (use R2-Gaussian). The standard Gaussian Model Initialization was introduced with the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al.. It has since been adapted for various domains, including SLAM (LIVGaussMap, Gaussian-SLAM), avatar reconstruction (PSAvatar, GaussianAvatars), and medical imaging (FactorSplat, R2-Gaussian). The method mimics the hierarchy of the OpenVDB Grid Tree in some scientific visualization contexts, producing a nested set of overlapping Gaussians. name: Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI)
body: Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) is a deterministic initialization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting in X-ray novel view synthesis that replaces Structure-from-Motion (SfM) by computing camera parameters directly from scanner specifications and uniformly sampling Gaussian centers within a bounding cuboid. It solves the problem of feature detection failure in low-contrast, overlapping X-ray projections, offering a significant reduction in training time compared to SfM-based initialization. Inputs: Scanner parameters: azimuth angle \phi, source-detector distance L{SD}, detector width W, detector height H. Bounding cuboid dimensions: S1, S2, S3 (enclosing the object, centered at world origin). Grid resolution: M1, M2, M3 (number of voxels along each axis). Sampling interval: d. Outputs: Extrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{ext}. Intrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{int}. Set of 3D point positions \mathcal{P}. Number of points Np and initial means \boldsymbol{\mu}i derived from \mathcal{P}. Data Structures: \mathbf{M}{ext}: 3 \times 4 matrix (rotation and translation). \mathbf{M}{int}: 3 \times 4 matrix (intrinsic parameters). \mathcal{P}: Set of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Steps: 1. Compute Extrinsic Matrix: Calculate \mathbf{M}{ext} using the azimuth angle \phi. The elevation angle is fixed at zero. \mathbf{M}{ext} = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin \phi & \cos \phi & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\cos \phi & -\sin \phi & 0 \\ -\cos \phi & -\sin \phi & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} 2. Compute Intrinsic Matrix: Calculate \mathbf{M}{int} using the source-detector distance L{SD} and detector dimensions W, H. \mathbf{M}{int} = \begin{bmatrix} L{SD} & 0 & W/2 & 0 \\ 0 & L{SD} & H/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} 3. Define Bounding Cuboid: Establish a cuboid of size S1 \times S2 \times S3 centered at the world origin (0,0,0) that completely encloses the scanned object. 4. Uniform Sampling: Divide the cuboid into a grid of M1 \times M2 \times M3 voxels. Generate the set of sampled points \mathcal{P} using integer indices ni and sampling interval d: \mathcal{P} = \left\{ \left( \frac{n1 S1}{M1}, \frac{n2 S2}{M2}, \frac{n3 S3}{M3} \right) \mid - \left[ \frac{2}{3} d \right] - 1 \leq ni \leq \left[ \frac{2}{3} d \right] + 1, i = 1, 2, 3 \right\} where ni \in \mathbb{Z} and [\cdot] denotes the floor function or integer part. 5. Initialize Gaussians: Use the size of \mathcal{P} to set the number of points Np and assign the elements of \mathcal{P} as the initial mean positions \boldsymbol{\mu}i for the Gaussian point clouds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeacuiinit(phi, LSD, W, H, S1, S2, S3, M1, M2, M3, d): """ Computes ACUI initialization for X-ray Gaussian Splatting. Args: phi: Azimuth angle in radians. LSD: Source-detector distance. W: Detector width. H: Detector height. S1, S2, S3: Cuboid dimensions along x, y, z axes. M1, M2, M3: Grid resolution (voxel counts) along x, y, z axes. d: Sampling interval. Returns: Mext: 3x4 extrinsic matrix. Mint: 3x4 intrinsic matrix. P: List of 3D points (tuples). Np: Number of points. """ # Step 1: Compute Extrinsic Matrix sinphi = math.sin(phi) cosphi = math.cos(phi) # Mext is 3x4. The source defines a 3x3 rotation part and zeros for translation. Mext = [ [-sinphi, cosphi, 0, 0], [0, -cosphi, -sinphi, 0], [-cosphi, -sinphi, 0, 0] ] # Step 2: Compute Intrinsic Matrix # Mint is 3x4. Source Eq. 12. Mint = [ [LSD, 0, W / 2, 0], [0, LSD, H / 2, 0], [0, 0, 1, 0] ] # Step 3 & 4: Uniform Sampling # Calculate bounds for ni using floor function as denoted by [·] in the source. limit = math.floor((2 / 3) d) nmin = -limit - 1 nmax = limit + 1 P = [] # Iterate over all integer indices within the calculated bounds for n1 in range(nmin, nmax + 1): for n2 in range(nmin, nmax + 1): for n3 in range(nmin, nmax + 1): # Calculate coordinates x = (n1 S1) / M1 y = (n2 S2) / M2 z = (n3 S3) / M3 P.append((x, y, z)) Np = len(P) return Mext, Mint, P, Np Parameters: d: The interval for uniform sampling within the grid. Typical value not given in the sources. \phi: Azimuth angle. L{SD}: Source-detector distance. W, H: Detector dimensions. S1, S2, S3: Cuboid size. M1, M2, M3: Grid voxel counts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard SfM initialization fails for X-ray images because they are grayscale with low contrast and suffer from overlapping layers due to transmission imaging, which degrades feature detection and matching accuracy. ACUI avoids this by bypassing feature detection entirely. The sampling bounds depend on d. If d is not provided, the range of ni cannot be determined. Initializes SH coefficients for view-dependent appearance. ACUI focuses on geometry and camera pose initialization for isotropic radiative models, whereas SH initialization handles appearance. Choose ACUI for X-ray/CT scenarios where camera geometry is known from scanner specs. See Spherical Harmonics Initialization. Time Complexity: The initialization is deterministic and scales with the number of sampled points Np, which is proportional to (2 \lfloor \frac{2}{3} d \rfloor + 3)^3. It avoids the iterative and computationally expensive SfM pipeline. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for Np Gaussian centers and the fixed-size camera matrices. Measured Performance: In X-ray novel view synthesis, ACUI-enabled X-Gaussian achieved 73× inference speed and 7× training speed compared to SOTA methods, with a 6.5 dB PSNR improvement. Strengths: Eliminates the need for feature detection in low-contrast, overlapping X-ray projections; significantly reduces training time; leverages known scanner geometry. Limitations: Assumes a circular cone beam X-ray scanning scenario with equal angular intervals; requires accurate scanner parameters (\phi, L{SD}, W, H); does not account for view-dependent effects (isotropic model). When to use: X-ray novel view synthesis, sparse-view CT reconstruction, scenarios with known scanner geometry and low-contrast grayscale images. When not to use: RGB-based novel view synthesis where SfM is robust; scenarios with unknown or inaccurate camera parameters; view-dependent radiative models. ACUI was proposed in the context of X-Gaussian, a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based framework for X-ray novel view synthesis. It was developed to address the limitations of Structure-from-Motion (SfM) in X-ray imaging, where low contrast and overlapping layers degrade feature matching. The method computes camera parameters and point positions directly from scanner specifications, operating independently of the isotropic radiative model used for rendering. name: DreamGaussian
head: DreamGaussian: Generative 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: DreamGaussian is a text-to-3D generation method that replaces the MipNeRF representation in the DreamFusion framework with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss to optimize 3D Gaussians. It distinguishes itself from its parent method, Gaussian Model Initialization, by providing a complete generative pipeline that not only initializes but fully optimizes a textured 3D asset from text prompts, leveraging the efficient splitting process of 3DGS to accelerate optimization. Unlike standard NeRF-based generation, it extracts a mesh from the generated Gaussians and refines texture details via UV-texture diffusion, enabling high-quality textured mesh generation in approximately 2 minutes. DreamGaussian operates in two distinct stages: (1) SDS-based optimization of 3D Gaussians from a generated image, and (2) mesh extraction and UV-texture refinement. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt describing the desired 3D object. Output: A textured 3D mesh (typically OBJ or similar format) with high-fidelity appearance. Data Structures: The method utilizes the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting data structure, consisting of a list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (parameterized as rotation Ri \in SO(3) and scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics coefficients c{i,lm} for view-dependent color Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a sparse set of 3D Gaussians. The sources note that while DreamGaussian primarily relies on the splitting process of 3DGS, other related methods (like GSGEN or GaussianDreamer) may use Point-E or Shap-E to generate an initial point cloud to mitigate the Janus problem. DreamGaussian itself leverages the inherent splitting mechanism of 3DGS to densify the representation during optimization. 2. SDS Optimization: Render an image from the current 3D Gaussian set using a differentiable rasterizer. Compute the SDS loss by comparing the rendered image against a pretrained 2D diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion). Update the Gaussian parameters (\mu, R, s, \alpha, c) using gradient descent to minimize the SDS loss. Apply the 3DGS splitting process periodically to increase the number of Gaussians in regions of high detail or error, which is described as "very suitable for the optimization progress under the generative settings". 3. Mesh Extraction: Once the Gaussian optimization converges, extract a mesh from the 3D Gaussian representation. This is typically done using surface reconstruction techniques (e.g., Poisson reconstruction or marching cubes on a density field derived from the Gaussians). 4. UV-Texture Refinement: Unwrap the extracted mesh to UV coordinates. Optimize the UV texture map (pixel values) using a pixel-wise Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the rendered texture and the target image generated by the diffusion model. This step refines fine texture details that may be lost during the Gaussian optimization phase. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dreamgaussian(textprompt): # Stage 1: SDS Optimization of 3D Gaussians gaussians = initializegaussians() # Sparse initialization diffusionmodel = loadsdmodel() # Pretrained 2D diffusion model for step in range(numoptimizationsteps): # Render image from current Gaussians renderedimage = render(gaussians, cameraparams) # Compute SDS Loss # Note: Exact SDS implementation details are assumed from standard DreamFusion sdsloss = computesdsloss(renderedimage, textprompt, diffusionmodel) # Backpropagate to update Gaussian parameters gradients = computegradients(sdsloss, gaussians) gaussians = updategaussians(gaussians, gradients) # Apply 3DGS splitting process to densify if step % splitinterval == 0: gaussians = splitgaussians(gaussians, threshold) # Stage 2: Mesh Extraction and Texture Refinement mesh = extractmesh(gaussians) uvmap = unwrapmesh(mesh) # Optimize UV texture texture = initializetexture() for step in range(numtexturesteps): # Render texture from mesh texturedimage = rendertexture(mesh, uvmap, texture, cameraparams) # MSE Loss against target mseloss = meansquarederror(texturedimage, targetimage) # Update texture texture = updatetexture(texture, mseloss) return mesh, texture Parameters: Optimization Steps: Not given in the sources. Split Interval: Not given in the sources. Texture Steps: Not given in the sources. Target Image: Generated from the text prompt using a 2D diffusion model. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Janus Problem: Multi-face artifacts can occur. While DreamGaussian primarily uses 2D SDS, related methods mitigate this with 3D SDS or point-cloud initialization. Optimization Time: The splitting process increases optimization time compared to fixed-resolution NeRFs, but 3DGS remains more efficient than NeRFs for high-resolution rendering. DiffSplat is a method that natively generates 3D Gaussian splats by fine-tuning a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model, exploiting web-scale 2D priors while keeping 3D consistency. It uses a lightweight reconstruction model to bootstrap multi-view Gaussian-splat grids for dataset curation and a 3D rendering loss for cross-view coherence. It achieves inference times of ~1-2 seconds for text- and image-to-3DGS. Marked as a 2026 SOTA update. Generative Gaussian Splatting is a method that generates unbounded 3D cities by progressively extending the Gaussian cloud outward from a given seed region with a diffusion prior. Time Complexity: The method is faster than NeRF-based generation due to the efficiency of 3DGS rendering and splitting. Total generation time is approximately 2 minutes for a textured mesh. Memory Complexity: 3DGS uses little memory compared to NeRFs, allowing for high-resolution rendering. Strengths: High-quality textured mesh generation; efficient optimization due to 3DGS splitting; suitability for generative settings. Limitations: Optimization time is increased by the splitting process compared to static NeRFs. Potential for Janus problem without additional guidance. When to use: When a high-quality textured mesh is required from a text prompt, and speed is a concern relative to NeRF-based methods. When not to use: When unbounded scene generation is required (use Generative Gaussian Splatting) or when native diffusion-based generation without SDS is preferred (use DiffSplat). DreamGaussian was introduced by Tang et al. in ICLR'24. It builds on the DreamFusion framework by replacing MipNeRF with 3DGS, leveraging the efficiency advantages of 3DGS for text-to-3D generation based on SDS loss. The method follows the idea of Magic3D for mesh extraction and UV texture refinement. name: HumanGaussian
body: HumanGaussian is a text-to-3D method specifically designed for generating textured human avatars using 3D Gaussian Splatting Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the oversaturation issue common in diffusion-based 3D generation by employing negative prompt guidance. Unlike general object generators, it leverages a parametric human body model (SMPL-X) to ensure anatomical plausibility during initialization. Inputs: A text prompt describing the desired human appearance. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the human avatar, which can be rendered as RGB and depth images. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Initialized as a point cloud where each point i has position \mathbf{t}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i (parameterized as rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. SMPL-X Template: A parametric human mesh model used as the geometric prior. Steps: 1. Initialization: Randomly sample points on the surface of the SMPL-X template. These points serve as the initial centers \mathbf{t}i for the 3D Gaussians. The initial covariance and opacity are set based on the local surface geometry. 2. Extended Diffusion Model: Extend Stable Diffusion [140] to generate both RGB and depth maps simultaneously from the text prompt. 3. Dual-Branch SDS Construction: Construct a dual-branch Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss to guide the optimization. This involves rendering the current Gaussian set to obtain predicted RGB and depth, and comparing them against the diffusion model's predictions. 4. Negative Prompt Guidance: To address oversaturation, combine the classifier score from the null text prompt with the negative score from the negative prompt. This combined guidance helps prevent the generated colors from becoming overly saturated or unrealistic. 5. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) using the combined SDS loss and negative prompt guidance. 6. Geometry Refinement (Optional): Convert the Gaussian opacity to a signed distance field (SDF) using a NeuS-like method [170, 171] to extract detailed textured meshes and provide additional geometry constraints. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def humangaussianoptimization(textprompt, negativeprompt): # Step 1: Initialize Gaussians from SMPL-X smplmesh = getsmplxtemplate() points = randomsamplesurfacepoints(smplmesh) gaussians = initializegaussiansfrompoints(points) # Step 2: Setup Extended Stable Diffusion # The model outputs both RGB and Depth predictions diffusionmodel = extendstablediffusionforrgbdepth() # Step 3: Optimization Loop for step in range(numsteps): # Render current Gaussians renderedrgb, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(gaussians) # Get diffusion predictions # Note: The exact mechanism for simultaneous RGB/Depth generation # is described as an extension of Stable Diffusion predrgb, preddepth = diffusionmodel.sample( textprompt=textprompt, negativeprompt=negativeprompt, renderedrgb=renderedrgb, rendereddepth=rendereddepth) # Step 4: Compute Dual-Branch SDS Loss # Combines RGB and Depth guidance sdsloss = computedualbranchsdsloss( renderedrgb, rendereddepth, predrgb, preddepth, textprompt, negativeprompt) # Step 5: Compute Negative Prompt Guidance # Combines null text classifier score and negative prompt score # to address oversaturation nullscore = diffusionmodel.getclassifierscore( renderedrgb, nulltextprompt="") negativescore = diffusionmodel.getnegativescore( renderedrgb, negativeprompt) guidanceloss = combinescores(nullscore, negativescore) # Total Loss loss = sdsloss + lambdaneg guidanceloss # Update Gaussians gaussians = optimizegaussians(gaussians, loss) return gaussians def computedualbranchsdsloss(renderedrgb, rendereddepth, predrgb, preddepth, text, negtext): # Placeholder for the specific dual-branch formulation # Sources state it constructs a dual-branch SDS but do not provide the exact mathematical formula # for the combination of RGB and Depth branches. # Typically, this involves computing separate SDS gradients for RGB and Depth and summing them. rgbgrad = computesdsgradient(renderedrgb, predrgb, text, negtext) depthgrad = computesdsgradient(rendereddepth, preddepth, text, negtext) return rgbgrad + depthgrad def combinescores(nullscore, negativescore): # Combines classifier score from null text and negative score from negative prompt # # The exact weighting or combination function (e.g., addition, weighted sum) is not specified in the sources. return nullscore + negativescore Parameters: SMPL-X Template: Used for initialization. Negative Prompt: Used to mitigate oversaturation. NeuS-like Method: Used for geometry refinement and mesh extraction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Oversaturation: A known issue in diffusion-based 3D generation that HumanGaussian specifically addresses via negative prompt guidance. Geometry Accuracy: Relies on the SMPL-X template; deviations from the template may require significant optimization or may result in artifacts if not handled by the NeuS-like refinement. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Generates a textured human avatar from a text prompt. Specific performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) are not provided in the sources. Strengths: Anatomically plausible initialization via SMPL-X; addresses oversaturation via negative prompt guidance; simultaneous RGB and depth generation. Limitations: Relies on the SMPL-X template, which may limit the diversity of human shapes; specific implementation details of the dual-branch SDS and negative prompt combination are not fully detailed in the provided sources. When to use: When generating text-to-3D human avatars with 3D Gaussian Splatting. When not to use: For general object generation or scene generation, where other methods like LucidDreamer or CG3D might be more appropriate. HumanGaussian [263] is part of the recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting for text-to-3D generation. It builds on the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting Gaussian Splatting and extends it to the domain of human avatar generation. It addresses limitations in previous methods by incorporating a parametric human model and advanced guidance techniques from diffusion models. name: PhysGaussian
head: MPM over Gaussians
body: PhysGaussian couples 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with continuum mechanics, specifically the Material Point Method (MPM), to enable the simulation of physical dynamics such as deformation, fracture, and fluid flow. It provides a unified representation for both high-fidelity rendering and physics simulation, supporting materials like cloth, jelly, sand, and snow. Unlike variants that convert Gaussians to meshes for simulation (e.g., GASP), PhysGaussian applies MPM directly over the Gaussian primitives, allowing for differentiable physical interactions within the Gaussian representation. PhysGaussian extends the standard 3DGS parameterization by assigning physical properties to each Gaussian. While the exact mathematical formulation for the coupling between the Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients) and the MPM state variables (mass, velocity, deformation gradient) is not detailed in the provided sources, the method operates by treating each Gaussian as a material point or a collection of points within the MPM grid. 1. Initialization: Start with a standard 3DGS scene initialized via Gaussian Model Initialization. Each Gaussian i is defined by its center \mathbf{p}i, covariance matrix \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i. 2. Physical Property Assignment: Assign physical properties to each Gaussian. In MPM, particles carry mass, velocity, and deformation history. For PhysGaussian, these properties are associated with the Gaussians. 3. Simulation Step: Map Gaussian properties to a background grid (standard MPM procedure). Perform physics simulation (advection, external forces, constitutive model updates) on the grid. Map the updated grid velocities and positions back to the Gaussians. 4. Rendering: Render the updated Gaussians using the standard differentiable rasterization pipeline. Note: The provided sources do not contain the specific equations for the mass assignment, force integration, or the re-parameterization of the Gaussian covariance after deformation. Implementation requires deriving these mappings from standard MPM literature applied to Gaussian primitives. GASP is a pipeline that integrates Gaussian Splatting with physics-based simulations by converting flat Gaussians into triangle faces using the GaMeS reparametrization, simulating the vertices using a standard Material Point Method (MPM) engine, and reassembling the deformed triangles back into Gaussians. It solves the problem of applying physics to Gaussian representations without the artifacts caused by direct vertex processing or the incompatibility of 2DGS with triangle-based simulation. Unlike PhysGaussian, which uses MPM directly over Gaussians, GASP explicitly converts Gaussians to a mesh, simulates the mesh, and converts back, ensuring stable simulations for flat Gaussian components. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a single representation for both rendering and simulation, enabling applications in AR/VFX and robotics simulation where physical plausibility is required. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When physical dynamics (deformation, fracture, fluids) need to be simulated and rendered simultaneously from a 3DGS scan. When not to use: When only static rendering is needed, or when mesh-based simulation is preferred for stability with flat structures. PhysGaussian was introduced in CVPR'24. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which is static and lacks physical properties, by integrating it with the Material Point Method (MPM). This allows for the simulation of various materials including cloth, jelly, sand, and snow. name: GASP
head: GASP (Gaussian Splatting for Physic-Based Simulations), GASP pipeline
body: GASP is a pipeline that integrates 3D Gaussian Splatting with black-box physics engines by converting flat Gaussian components into triangle faces, simulating the vertices using the Material Point Method (MPM), and reconstructing Gaussians from the deformed triangles. It solves the problem of simulating deformable objects in Gaussian representations without requiring modifications to the physics engine or complex mesh extraction strategies like marching cubes. Unlike PhysGaussian, which approximates deformation via first-order linear transformations, GASP operates directly on the geometry of flat Gaussians using the GaMeS parameterization, ensuring stable simulations and avoiding artifacts associated with treating points as discrete entities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A collection of flat Gaussians G = \{(N(mi, Ri, Si), \sigmai, ci)\}{i=1}^p, where mi is the mean, Ri is the rotation matrix, Si = \text{diag}(s{i1}, s{i2}, s{i3}) is the scaling matrix with s{i1} = \epsilon (making the Gaussian effectively 2D), \sigmai is opacity, and ci is color. Output: A time-evolved collection of Gaussians Gt = \{(N(m'i, R'i, S'i), \sigmai, ci)\}{i=1}^p reflecting the physics simulation. Data Structures: Gaussian: Defined by mean m \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, scaling S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (diagonal), opacity \sigma \in \mathbb{R}, and color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Triangle Face (GaMeS): A triplet of vertices V = [v1, v2, v3] representing a flat Gaussian. Triangle Soup: A collection of vertices V and edges E derived from the Gaussians. Parameters: \epsilon: A small constant such that s1 = \epsilon. \alpha: A hyperparameter for the correction algorithm, controlling the threshold for scaling correction. Steps: 1. Initialization (GaMeS Conversion): Convert each flat Gaussian N(m, R, S) into a triangle face V = [v1, v2, v3] using the mapping T(\cdot): v1 = m v2 = m + s2 r2 v3 = m + s3 r3 where r2 and r3 are the second and third columns of the rotation matrix R. This creates a triangle soup (V, E). 2. Physics Simulation: Apply the physics engine (e.g., MPM) to the vertices V individually to obtain deformed vertices Vt: Vt = \{\phi(v, t): v \in V\} where \phi(\cdot, t) is the deformation map provided by the black-box physics engine (such as Genesis, Blender, or Taichi Elements). The edges E are preserved to maintain the triangle structure. 3. Reconstruction (Inverse GaMeS): Recover the Gaussian parameters from the deformed triangle vertices Vt = [v'1, v'2, v'3] using the inverse mapping T^{-1}(\cdot): Mean: \hat{m} = v'1. Rotation Axis 1: \hat{r}1 = \frac{(v'2 - v'1) \times (v'3 - v'1)}{\|(v'2 - v'1) \times (v'3 - v'1)\|} (normalized face normal). Rotation Axis 2: \hat{r}2 = \frac{v'2 - v'1}{\|v'2 - v'1\|} (normalized edge vector). Rotation Axis 3: \hat{r}3 = \text{orth}(v'3 - v'1; \hat{r}1, \hat{r}2) (Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization). Scaling: \hat{s}1 = \epsilon \hat{s}2 = \|v'2 - v'1\| \hat{s}3 = \langle v'3 - v'1, \hat{r}3 \rangle The new rotation matrix is \hat{R} = [\hat{r}1, \hat{r}2, \hat{r}3] and scaling is \hat{S} = \text{diag}(\hat{s}1, \hat{s}2, \hat{s}3). 4. Correction Algorithm: To mitigate artifacts from independent vertex processing, check if the distance between transformed nodes exceeds a threshold relative to original nodes. For each Gaussian face with original vertices V = [v1, v2, v3] and deformed vertices Vt = [v'1, v'2, v'3]: If \|v'1 - v'i\| > \alpha \|v1 - vi\| for i \in \{2, 3\}, then correct the scaling parameter \hat{s}i to \alpha \cdot si (where si is the original scaling parameter before simulation). Note: The source states "si should be identical to that of the original value times α". 5. Hierarchical Simulation (Optional): Use BIRCH clustering to group Gaussians into CoreGaussians and SubGaussians. Simulate only the CoreGaussians using the steps above. Transfer the movement pattern (deformation) from CoreGaussians to their associated SubGaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gasppipeline(gaussians, physicsengine, alpha=1.5): """ gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'm', 'R', 'S', 'sigma', 'c' physicsengine: Object with method 'simulate(points)' returning deformed points alpha: Hyperparameter for correction """ # Step 1: Convert Gaussians to Triangle Soup triangles = [] for g in gaussians: m = g['m'] R = g['R'] S = g['S'] s2 = S[1, 1] s3 = S[2, 2] r2 = R[:, 1] r3 = R[:, 2] v1 = m v2 = m + s2 r2 v3 = m + s3 r3 triangles.append({ 'v1': v1, 'v2': v2, 'v3': v3, 'originals2': s2, 'originals3': s3, 'sigma': g['sigma'], 'c': g['c'] }) # Extract all unique vertices for physics engine # Note: In a real implementation, vertices shared by multiple triangles # must be handled carefully (e.g., by merging indices). # The source describes treating points individually, implying a point cloud approach. # We assume physicsengine takes a list of points and returns deformed points. # To preserve topology, we might need to pass the full set of vertices. allvertices = [] for t in triangles: allvertices.append(t['v1']) allvertices.append(t['v2']) allvertices.append(t['v3']) # Physics simulation deformedvertices = physicsengine.simulate(allvertices) # Step 2 & 3 & 4: Reconstruct Gaussians newgaussians = [] triidx = 0 vertidx = 0 # Re-associate deformed vertices to triangles # Assuming the order of deformedvertices matches the order of allvertices for t in triangles: v1 = deformedvertices[vertidx] v2 = deformedvertices[vertidx + 1] v3 = deformedvertices[vertidx + 2] vertidx += 3 # Inverse GaMeS mhat = v1 # Rotation axes edge1 = v2 - v1 edge2 = v3 - v1 r1hat = np.cross(edge1, edge2) normr1 = np.linalg.norm(r1hat) if normr1 < 1e-8: # Degenerate triangle, fallback or skip r1hat = np.array([0, 0, 1]) else: r1hat = r1hat / normr1 r2hat = edge1 / np.linalg.norm(edge1) # Gram-Schmidt for r3 r3hat = edge2 - np.dot(edge2, r1hat) r1hat - np.dot(edge2, r2hat) r2hat normr3 = np.linalg.norm(r3hat) if normr3 < 1e-8: r3hat = np.cross(r1hat, r2hat) # Fallback else: r3hat = r3hat / normr3 Rhat = np.columnstack((r1hat, r2hat, r3hat)) # Scaling s2hat = np.linalg.norm(edge1) s3hat = np.dot(edge2, r3hat) # Correction Algorithm # Compare deformed distances to original distances origv1 = t['v1'] origv2 = t['v2'] origv3 = t['v3'] origs2 = t['originals2'] origs3 = t['originals3'] distv1v2orig = np.linalg.norm(origv1 - origv2) distv1v3orig = np.linalg.norm(origv1 - origv3) distv1v2deform = np.linalg.norm(v1 - v2) distv1v3deform = np.linalg.norm(v1 - v3) # Correction logic based on source: if deformed dist > alpha original dist # Then scale parameter is corrected to original value alpha # Note: The source says "si should be identical to that of the original value times alpha" # This implies capping the growth. if distv1v2deform > alpha distv1v2orig: s2hat = alpha origs2 if distv1v3deform > alpha distv1v3orig: s3hat = alpha origs3 # s1 is always epsilon s1hat = 1e-6 # epsilon newgaussians.append({ 'm': mhat, 'R': Rhat, 'S': np.diag([s1hat, s2hat, s3hat]), 'sigma': t['sigma'], 'c': t['c'] }) return newgaussians A parameterization of flat Gaussians as triangle faces. It sets one scaling axis to \epsilon, allowing Gaussians to be represented as 2D triangles in 3D space. It is chosen when stable, triangle-based physics simulation is required for Gaussian splats. Link A particle-based physics simulation method used in GASP to compute vertex trajectories. It is chosen for its ability to handle large deformations and complex material behaviors (cloth, sand, etc.) as a black-box engine. Link A method that adapts Newtonian dynamics to 3D Gaussians using first-order approximation of deformation maps. GASP differs by using GaMeS triangles and black-box physics, avoiding the need for engine modifications or linear approximations. Link Time Complexity: The conversion to triangles and back is linear with respect to the number of Gaussians p. The physics simulation cost depends on the engine (e.g., MPM complexity). Hierarchical simulation reduces the number of points simulated, accelerating computation. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of Gaussians, storing vertices and edges for the triangle soup. Performance: The pipeline is described as "notably rapid" and does not increase rendering costs compared to standard GS. Strengths: Compatible with any black-box physics engine (Genesis, Blender, Taichi); avoids artifacts from discrete point processing; avoids complex mesh extraction (marching cubes). Limitations: Relies on the quality of the black-box physics engine; artifacts can still occur if the correction threshold \alpha is not tuned; hierarchical simulation requires clustering overhead. When to use: When simulating deformable objects (cloth, jelly, sand) with Gaussian Splatting and you want to leverage existing physics engines without modifying them. When not to use: When high-fidelity continuous deformation fields are required beyond the triangle approximation, or when the physics engine cannot handle point clouds efficiently. GASP was introduced in the paper "GASP: Gaussian Splatting for Physic-Based Simulations" by Waczja et al. (2024). It builds upon the GaMeS parameterization of flat Gaussians. The method was demonstrated using the Genesis engine, Blender software, and the Taichi Elements library. It addresses limitations in previous methods like PhysGaussian (which requires engine modifications) and mesh-based approaches (which suffer from extraction artifacts).
