name: Recurrent Gaussian Update
head: Feedback Loop Update, ReSplat (Recurrent Gaussian Splatting), Recurrent Gaussian Splating, Recurrent Refinement
body: Recurrent Gaussian Update is a gradient-free, feed-forward refinement method that iteratively corrects initial 3D Gaussian predictions by predicting incremental updates to Gaussian parameters and hidden states based on rendering errors from input views. It solves the problem of inaccurate initial reconstructions in single-step feed-forward models by establishing a feedback loop that progressively refines the Gaussian set without requiring backpropagation or gradient computation. Unlike standard differentiable optimization which relies on iterative gradient descent, this method uses a learned recurrent network to map rendering errors directly to parameter updates, enabling convergence in a fixed number of iterations (typically 4) rather than thousands. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}^0 = \{(\mathbf{g}j^0, zj^0)\}{j=1}^M predicted by a feed-forward initialization network; a set of N input views \{Ii\}{i=1}^N (ground truth images). Outputs: Refined set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}^T = \{(\mathbf{g}j^T, zj^T)\}{j=1}^M after T iterations. Data Structures: Gaussian Parameters (\mathbf{g}j): Vector of dimension C1 containing position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients for Gaussian j. Hidden State (zj): Vector of dimension C0 storing recurrent memory for Gaussian j. Rendering Error (\hat{\mathbf{E}}^t): Tensor of shape N \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times C2, where C2=256. Aggregated Error (\mathbf{E}^t): Tensor of shape M \times C2 (or N \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times C2 before aggregation, mapped to M Gaussians). Numbered Steps: 1. Rendering: Render the input views \{\hat{I}i^t\}{i=1}^N using the current Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}^t at iteration t. 2. Pixel-Space Error Computation: Compute pixel-wise difference: \{\hat{I}i^t - Ii\}{i=1}^N. Perform 4× spatial downsampling on the error using pixel unshuffle to align the spatial resolution with the number of 3D Gaussians. 3. Feature-Space Error Computation: Extract the first three stage features (at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 resolutions) from an ImageNet pre-trained ResNet-18 for both rendered views \{\hat{I}i^t\} and ground-truth views \{Ii\}. Bilinearly resize the three scale features to the 1/4 resolution. Concatenate the resized features. Compute the difference: \{\hat{F}i^t - Fi\}{i=1}^N, where \hat{F}i^t, Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times C2} and C2 = 256. 4. Error Combination: Project the pixel-space error to the feature space using a linear layer followed by Layer Normalization. Add the projected pixel-space error to the feature-space error. Formula: \hat{\mathbf{E}}^t = f \left( \{\hat{I}i^t\}{i=1}^N, \{Ii\}{i=1}^N \right) = \{\hat{F}i^t - Fi\}{i=1}^N + \text{proj}(\{\hat{I}i^t - Ii\}{i=1}^N) where \text{proj} denotes the linear projection and Layer Normalization. The resulting tensor \hat{\mathbf{E}}^t contains N \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} error vectors \hat{\mathbf{e}}j^t \in \mathbb{R}^{C2}. 5. Error Propagation (Global Attention): Apply global attention across all N \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} rendering errors in \hat{\mathbf{E}}^t to aggregate global context. This allows each Gaussian to receive information from all rendering errors, overcoming the limitation of local spatial concatenation. Output: \mathbf{E}^t = \text{global\attention}(\hat{\mathbf{E}}^t) = \{\mathbf{e}j^t\}{j=1}^{M}, where \mathbf{e}j^t is the aggregated error for Gaussian j. 6. Update Module Input: Concatenate the Gaussian parameters \mathbf{g}j^t, hidden state zj^t, and aggregated error \mathbf{e}j^t for each Gaussian j. Input set: \{(\mathbf{g}j^t, zj^t, \mathbf{e}j^t)\}{j=1}^M. 7. Update Prediction: Pass the input set through four kNN attention blocks to model local structural details in 3D space. Decode the incremental updates \Delta \mathbf{g}j^t \in \mathbb{R}^{C1} and \Delta zj^t \in \mathbb{R}^{C0} using a lightweight four-layer MLP head. Formula: \{(\mathbf{g}j^t, zj^t, \mathbf{e}j^t)\}{j=1}^M \rightarrow \{(\Delta \mathbf{g}j^t, \Delta zj^t)\}{j=1}^M. 8. Parameter Update: Update the Gaussian parameters and hidden state: \mathbf{g}j^{t+1} = \mathbf{g}j^t + \Delta \mathbf{g}j^t, \quad zj^{t+1} = zj^t + \Delta zj^t. 9. Iteration: Repeat steps 1–8 for T iterations. During training, T is randomly sampled between 1 and 4. During inference, T is flexible, allowing a speed-accuracy trade-off; convergence is typically observed after 4 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def recurrentgaussianupdate(initialgaussians, inputviews, numiterations): """ Refines initial 3D Gaussians using recurrent error feedback. Args: initialgaussians: List of tuples (gj, zj) for j=1..M. gj is parameter vector (dim C1), zj is hidden state (dim C0). inputviews: List of ground truth images Ii for i=1..N. numiterations: Number of refinement steps T. Returns: Refined list of tuples (gj, zj). """ # Initialize current Gaussians currentgaussians = list(initialgaussians) M = len(currentgaussians) for t in range(numiterations): # 1. Render current Gaussians to get synthetic views renderedviews = render(currentgaussians, inputviews) # Assumes camera poses from inputviews # 2. Compute Pixel-Space Error # Compute pixel-wise difference pixelerrors = [renderedviews[i] - inputviews[i] for i in range(len(inputviews))] # Downsample using pixel unshuffle (4x) downsampledpixelerrors = [pixelunshuffle(err, factor=4) for err in pixelerrors] # 3. Compute Feature-Space Error # Extract features from ResNet-18 (stages 1, 2, 3) renderedfeatures = [extractresnetfeatures(renderedviews[i]) for i in range(len(inputviews))] gtfeatures = [extractresnetfeatures(inputviews[i]) for i in range(len(inputviews))] # Resize to 1/4 resolution and concatenate stages resizedrenderedfeatures = [concatenateresize(feat, targetres='1/4') for feat in renderedfeatures] resizedgtfeatures = [concatenateresize(feat, targetres='1/4') for feat in gtfeatures] # Compute feature difference featureerrors = [resizedrenderedfeatures[i] - resizedgtfeatures[i] for i in range(len(inputviews))] # 4. Combine Errors # Project pixel errors to feature space (dim C2=256) and add to feature errors projectedpixelerrors = [layernorm(linearproj(err)) for err in downsampledpixelerrors] combinederrors = [featureerrors[i] + projectedpixelerrors[i] for i in range(len(inputviews))] # Flatten errors to list of vectors ehatj^t flaterrors = [err.flatten() for err in combinederrors] # Shape: N H/4 W/4 vectors of dim C2 # 5. Global Attention Propagation # Apply global attention to aggregate context for each Gaussian # Note: The paper maps NH/4W/4 errors to M Gaussians via global attention aggregatederrors = globalattention(flaterrors, numgaussians=M) # Returns list of M vectors of dim C2 # 6. Prepare Update Input updateinputs = [] for j in range(M): gj, zj = currentgaussians[j] ej = aggregatederrors[j] updateinputs.append((gj, zj, ej)) # 7. Predict Updates using kNN Attention Blocks and MLP Head # Input: List of (g, z, e) # Output: List of (deltag, deltaz) deltas = updatemoduleknnmlp(updateinputs) # 8. Update Parameters newgaussians = [] for j in range(M): gj, zj = currentgaussians[j] deltag, deltaz = deltas[j] newg = gj + deltag newz = zj + deltaz newgaussians.append((newg, newz)) currentgaussians = newgaussians return currentgaussians def pixelunshuffle(image, factor): """Downsamples image by factor using pixel unshuffle.""" # Reshape H x W x C to H/factor x W/factor x (C factor^2) # Then reshape to H/factor x W/factor x C # Implementation depends on tensor library, but logically rearranges pixels pass def extractresnetfeatures(image): """Extracts features from stages 1, 2, 3 of ResNet-18.""" pass def concatenateresize(featureslist, targetres): """Resizes each feature map in list to targetres and concatenates along channel dim.""" pass def linearproj(tensor): """Applies linear layer to match channel dimension C2.""" pass def layernorm(tensor): """Applies Layer Normalization.""" pass def globalattention(errors, numgaussians): """ Applies global attention across all errors to produce one aggregated error per Gaussian. """ pass def updatemoduleknnmlp(inputs): """ Processes inputs through 4 kNN attention blocks and 4-layer MLP head. Inputs: List of (g, z, e) Outputs: List of (deltag, deltaz) """ pass Parameters: C2: Channel dimension of the feature-space error. Value: 256. T: Total number of iterations. Training: Randomly sampled between 1 and 4. Inference: Flexible, allows speed-accuracy trade-off. Convergence: Observed after 4 iterations. k: Number of neighbors for kNN attention in the recurrent model. Value: 8. (Note: k=16 is used in the initialization model, but 8 in the recurrent model). Spatial subsampling factor: 4× in 3D space for 2-view, 256×256 resolution setups. Gaussians decoded per subsampled 3D point: 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: kNN Bottleneck: The kNN operation during reconstruction is a primary bottleneck for inference speed and requires implementation-level optimization for faster deployment. Global Attention Cost: Performing global attention on N \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} features can be expensive for high-resolution images; efficient implementation is required. Convergence: The model converges after 4 iterations; fewer iterations may result in suboptimal quality, while more iterations yield diminishing returns. The Recurrent Mean-Shift Update is a regularization step applied to the descriptor parameters of 3D Gaussians to enforce holistic separability across the entire scene. It addresses the problem where local segmentation losses only distinguish descriptors within individual image views, failing to ensure that descriptors for the same 3D plane instance remain consistent across different camera viewpoints. By applying a mean-shift operation based on the von Mises-Fisher distribution, it pulls similar descriptors together and pushes dissimilar ones apart globally, improving plane instance segmentation. It differs from standard differentiable updates by operating on the statistical distribution of descriptors rather than individual pixel-wise gradients. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than gradient-based optimization. ReSplat is 100× faster than 3DGS optimization on 8-view DL3DV. Reconstruction time is 1.2–1.7 seconds for 1–2 iterations on 16-view DL3DV. Memory Complexity: Compresses the number of Gaussians by 16× compared to per-pixel feed-forward models (e.g., MVSplat, DepthSplat), resulting in 4× faster rendering speed. Uses 246K Gaussians for 8-view DL3DV and 518K for 16-view DL3DV. Measured Performance: 8-view (512×960) DL3DV: 246K Gaussians, 100× faster than 3DGS optimization, 4× faster rendering than per-pixel models. Outperforms 3DGS by 4.2dB PSNR and DepthSplat by 3.5dB PSNR. 16-view (540×960) DL3DV: 518K Gaussians, reconstruction time 1.2–1.7 sec for 1–2 iterations. Outperforms Long-LRM (518K Gaussians) with 1 iteration (23.23 PSNR vs 22.69 PSNR). 2-view (256×256) RealEstate10K: Outperforms LVSM encoder-decoder by 1.1 dB PSNR, 20× faster rendering than 3DGS-free methods. Scaling: Supports flexible speed-accuracy trade-off at inference by varying the number of iterations T. Strengths: Gradient-free feed-forward architecture eliminates gradient computation, providing a 53× speedup in reconstruction time compared to 3DGS optimization-based refinement. Converges in 4 iterations vs 30,000 for 3DGS. More parameter-efficient than single-step models; ReSplat-Small (77M params) outperforms ReSplat-Large (559M params) and WorldMirror (1263M params) after 4 iterations. Limitations: kNN operation slows down inference speed. Global attention can be computationally expensive for high-resolution images. When to use: When fast, high-quality view synthesis is required from a small number of input views, and gradient-based optimization is too slow. When not to use: When extremely low latency is required and even the feed-forward inference time is prohibitive, or when the scene requires fine-grained optimization that a fixed number of recurrent steps cannot capture. Recurrent Gaussian Update was introduced in the paper "ReSplat: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the concept of feed-forward Gaussian splatting initialization. The method was developed to address the limitations of single-step feed-forward models, which lack the refinement capability of iterative optimization, while avoiding the computational cost of gradient-based methods. It is evaluated on DL3DV, RealEstate10K, and ACID datasets. ReSplat: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08575v4, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Recurrent Mean-Shift Update
head: Holistic separability update, Mean-shift update
body: The Recurrent Mean-Shift Update is a regularization step applied to the descriptor parameters of 3D Gaussians to enforce holistic separability across the entire scene. It addresses the problem where local segmentation losses only distinguish descriptors within individual image views, failing to ensure that descriptors for the same 3D plane instance remain consistent across different camera viewpoints. By applying a mean-shift operation based on the von Mises-Fisher distribution, it pulls similar descriptors together and pushes dissimilar ones apart globally, improving plane instance segmentation. It differs from standard differentiable updates by operating on the statistical distribution of descriptors rather than individual pixel-wise gradients. Inputs and Outputs: Input: \mathbf{Z}, a matrix of shape (N, D) containing the D-dimensional descriptor vectors for N Gaussians. Output: Updated \mathbf{Z} with enhanced separability. Data Structures: \mathbf{Z}: Matrix where each row \mathbf{z}i is the descriptor for the i-th Gaussian. \mathbf{K}: Kernel matrix of shape (N, N). \mathbf{D}: Diagonal matrix of shape (N, N). \mathbf{I}: Identity matrix of shape (N, N). Parameters: \eta (eta): Update rate (learning rate for this step). Typical values are not specified in the sources. \gamma (gamma): Kernel bandwidth controlling the smoothness of the kernel density estimation. Typical values are not specified in the sources. N{steps}: Number of mean-shift steps to perform per update cycle. Not given in the sources. N{iter}: Frequency of applying the update (every N iterations of the main optimization loop). Not given in the sources. Formulas: The update rule is defined as: \mathbf{Z} \leftarrow \mathbf{Z} \cdot (\eta \cdot \mathbf{K} \cdot \mathbf{D}^{-1} + (1-\eta) \cdot \mathbf{I}) Where: 1. \mathbf{K} is the von Mises-Fisher (vMF) kernel matrix: \mathbf{K} = e^{\gamma \cdot \mathbf{Z}^T \cdot \mathbf{Z}} Here, \mathbf{Z}^T \cdot \mathbf{Z} computes the dot products between all pairs of descriptor vectors. The exponential is applied element-wise. 2. \mathbf{D} is a diagonal matrix where the diagonal elements are the row sums of \mathbf{K}: \mathbf{D} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{K}^T \cdot \mathbf{1}) where \mathbf{1} is a column vector of ones. Effectively, D{ii} = \sum{j} K{ji}. Since \mathbf{K} is symmetric (dot product is symmetric), \mathbf{K}^T = \mathbf{K}, so D{ii} = \sum{j} K{ij}. 3. \mathbf{I} is the identity matrix. Steps: 1. Compute the pairwise dot product matrix \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{Z}^T \cdot \mathbf{Z}. 2. Compute the kernel matrix \mathbf{K} = \exp(\gamma \cdot \mathbf{S}) (element-wise exponential). 3. Compute the normalization vector \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{K} \cdot \mathbf{1} (sum of rows of \mathbf{K}). 4. Construct the diagonal matrix \mathbf{D} from \mathbf{v}. 5. Compute the update matrix \mathbf{M} = \eta \cdot \mathbf{K} \cdot \mathbf{D}^{-1} + (1-\eta) \cdot \mathbf{I}. Note: \mathbf{D}^{-1} is simply the reciprocal of the diagonal elements. 6. Update the descriptors: \mathbf{Z}{new} = \mathbf{Z} \cdot \mathbf{M}. 7. Repeat steps 1-6 for a few steps (as specified by implementation details) every N optimization iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def recurrentmeanshiftupdate(Z, eta, gamma, numsteps): """ Applies the recurrent mean-shift update to Gaussian descriptors Z. Args: Z: numpy array of shape (N, D), descriptor matrix. eta: float, update rate. gamma: float, kernel bandwidth. numsteps: int, number of mean-shift iterations to perform. Returns: Z: Updated descriptor matrix. """ N = Z.shape[0] for in range(numsteps): # 1. Compute pairwise dot products: Z^T @ Z is (D, N) @ (N, D) -> (D, D)? # Wait, formula says K = exp(gamma Z^T Z). # If Z is (N, D), Z^T is (D, N). Z^T @ Z is (D, D). # But K is used in Z @ K. Z is (N, D). K must be (D, D) or (N, N)? # Let's re-read carefully: "K = e^(gamma Z^T Z) is vMF distribution of z on sphere" # Usually vMF kernel depends on dot product between samples. # If Z rows are samples, dot products are Z @ Z.T -> (N, N). # The text says: K = e^(gamma Z^T Z). # If Z is (N, D), Z^T is (D, N). Z^T @ Z is (D, D). # Then Z @ K would be (N, D) @ (D, D) = (N, D). This matches dimensions. # However, standard mean shift on descriptors usually implies similarity between Gaussians (N x N). # Let's check D = diag(K^T I). If K is (D, D), D is (D, D). # Then Z @ K @ D^-1 is (N, D) @ (D, D) @ (D, D) = (N, D). # This interpretation (K is DxD) seems mathematically consistent with the matrix multiplication order Z @ K. # BUT, "separability of descriptors for all 3D plane instances" usually implies clustering N items. # Let's look at the source text again: "K = e^(gamma Z^T Z)". # If Z is (N, D), Z^T @ Z is (D, D). This is the Gram matrix of the columns (features). # This computes similarity between features, not between Gaussians. # However, the next line says D = diag(K^T I). # And the update is Z <- Z (eta K D^-1 +...). # If K is (D, D), this updates each feature dimension based on other feature dimensions. # This effectively decorrelates or separates features. # Let's stick to the literal formula provided: K = exp(gamma Z^T @ Z). # Compute S = Z^T @ Z (D, D) S = Z.T @ Z # Compute K = exp(gamma S) (D, D) K = np.exp(gamma S) # Compute Ddiag = sum of rows of K (since K is symmetric, row sum == col sum) # D = diag(K^T I) -> K^T is K. K I is K. diag(K) is diagonal elements? # Wait. "D = diag(K^T I)". # If I is identity, K^T I = K. diag(K) extracts diagonal elements of K. # But earlier I thought D was row sums. # Let's re-read: "D = diag(K^T I)". # In matrix notation, diag(M) usually returns a diagonal matrix with M's diagonal. # Or it returns a vector. The text says "D is the diagonal matrix". # If D is a diagonal matrix, D^-1 is element-wise inverse of diagonal. # If D = diag(K), then Dii = Kii. # Kii = exp(gamma (Z^T @ Z)ii) = exp(gamma ||zi||^2) if Z columns were samples? # No, Z is (N, D). Z^T @ Z is (D, D). (Z^T @ Z)jj = sumi Zij^2 = ||colj||^2. # So Dii = exp(gamma ||featurei||^2). # Let's check the alternative interpretation: K is (N, N). # If K is (N, N), then Z @ K is (N, D) @ (N, N) -> Dimension mismatch. # Unless Z is (D, N). But Z is usually (N, D). # The formula is Z <- Z (eta K D^-1 +...). # If Z is (N, D), K must be (D, D) for Z @ K to work. # Therefore, K is (D, D). # So: # 1. K = exp(gamma Z^T @ Z) [Shape: D x D] # 2. Dmat = diag(diag(K)) [Shape: D x D] # 3. Update = eta K @ Dmat^-1 + (1-eta) ID [Shape: D x D] # 4. Znew = Z @ Update [Shape: N x D] # Extract diagonal of K Ddiag = np.diag(K) # Create diagonal matrix D Dmat = np.diag(Ddiag) # Inverse of D (element-wise inverse of diagonal) Dinvdiag = 1.0 / Ddiag Dinvmat = np.diag(Dinvdiag) # Compute Update Matrix M # Identity matrix of size D ID = np.eye(D) M = eta (K @ Dinvmat) + (1 - eta) ID # Update Z Z = Z @ M return Z Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large N: The number of Gaussians can be very large. While the derived pseudocode computes a D \times D matrix (where D is descriptor dimension, typically small, e.g., 16-64), the source notes that an "efficient way" is used because the number of Gaussians is large. The provided formula operates on the descriptor space (D), not the Gaussian count (N), making it O(N \cdot D^2) per step, which is efficient with respect to N. If the source intended K to be N \times N, the complexity would be O(N^2), which is prohibitive. The literal formula Z^T Z yields D \times D. We follow the literal formula. Precision: Division by zero in D^{-1} if any diagonal element of K is zero. Since K{ii} = \exp(\gamma \cdot ||\mathbf{z}i||^2), it is always positive, so this is safe. Boundaries: The update is applied every N iterations, not every step, to stabilize optimization. This is the specific application of the Recurrent Mean-Shift Update to improve the separability of descriptors for all 3D plane instances across the entire scene. It uses the von Mises-Fisher distribution to model the descriptors on the sphere. It is chosen when plane instance segmentation quality is critical and local view-based losses are insufficient to disambiguate planes seen from different viewpoints. It sets itself apart by enforcing global consistency rather than local discriminative power. Time Complexity: The core update involves computing Z^T Z (O(N D^2)), exponentiation (O(D^2)), and matrix multiplication Z @ M (O(N D^2)). Since D (descriptor dimension) is small and fixed, the complexity is linear with respect to the number of Gaussians N. Memory Complexity: O(N D) to store Z, and O(D^2) for the kernel matrix K. Measured Performance: Ablation studies show that encouraging holistic separability provides effective performance improvement on plane segmentation. Specific metrics (e.g., mIoU) are not provided in the source text for this specific component in isolation, but the full method (Planar Gaussian Splatting) achieves competitive results on ScanNetv2 and Replica. Strengths: Improves segmentation accuracy by resolving ambiguities between planes that are not jointly visible in any single view. Limitations: Requires tuning of \eta and \gamma. Computationally efficient with respect to N due to the descriptor-space formulation, but adds an extra optimization step every N iterations. When to use: When performing 3D plane instance segmentation using Gaussian Splatting and local losses are insufficient for global consistency. When not to use: When computational budget is extremely tight and segmentation accuracy is secondary, or when descriptors are not used for plane segmentation. The method originates from Planar Gaussian Splatting (PGS). It builds on the concept of using 3D Gaussians to represent 3D planes and introduces a recurrent mean-shift update [18] (cited in S1) to maintain holistic separability of descriptors. The approach was developed to address the ambiguity in merging local geometries into 3D planes by learning discriminative descriptors without explicit 2D/3D plane annotations. Planar Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00863, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Structure-Aware Initialization
head: Variance-based Initialization
body:
Structure-Aware Initialization is a strategy that adapts primitive placement and scale to local image complexity using local variance. It solves the problem of inefficient coverage in radiance-field optimization by ensuring dense, fine-grained primitives in complex regions and sparse, coarse coverage in smooth areas. This method accelerates convergence and improves final fidelity, particularly when using high primitive counts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target image I (RGB), canvas dimensions, parameters s{max}, s{min}, \sigmac. Output: Set of initial Gaussian parameters \Theta = \{(xi, yi, si, ci, 
ui, 	hetai)\}. Data Structures: Lattice points: A regular grid of candidate positions (x, y) covering the image canvas. Normalized Local Variance map: NLV: 	ext{canvas} ightarrow [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Compute Local Variance: Calculate the local variance of the target image I across RGB channels using a 7 	imes 7 sliding window. Let V(x, y) be the variance at pixel (x, y). 2. Normalize Variance: Normalize the variance map to [0, 1] to obtain NLV(x, y). NLV(x, y) =  rac{V(x, y) - \min(V)}{\max(V) - \min(V)} [G: Handle case where \max(V) = \min(V) by setting NLV=0 or 0.5 depending on implementation preference, though sources do not specify.] 3. Sample Positions: Sample initial positions (xi, yi) from the lattice points with probability proportional to: P(x, y) \propto 0.1 + 0.9 \cdot NLV(x, y) 4. Initialize Scale: Set the scale si for each sampled point based on its normalized local variance: si = s{max} - (s{max} - s{min}) \cdot NLV(xi, yi) 5. Initialize Color: Sample color ci from a normal distribution centered on the target image color at that position: ci \sim \mathcal{N}(I(xi, yi), \sigmac^2) 6. Initialize Opacity: Fix the opacity parameter 
ui to a constant value to ensure gradient flow: 
ui = -2.0 \quad (\approx 12\% 	ext{ opacity}) 7. Initialize Rotation: Sample rotation angle 	hetai uniformly: 	hetai \sim \mathcal{U}0, 2\pi) Parameters: Sliding window size: 7 	imes 7. Opacity prior 
ui: -2.0. Color noise \sigmac: Not given in the sources. Scale bounds s{max}, s{min}: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Disabling both soft [rasterization and structure-aware initialization often leads to destabilization of the fit and missing fine details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def structureawareinitialization(targetimage, latticepoints, smax, smin, sigmac): """ Initialize Gaussian splats based on local image variance. Args: targetimage: np.array of shape (H, W, 3), RGB image. latticepoints: list of (x, y) tuples covering the canvas. smax: float, maximum initial scale. smin: float, minimum initial scale. sigmac: float, standard deviation for color initialization. Returns: positions: np.array of shape (N, 2) scales: np.array of shape (N,) colors: np.array of shape (N, 3) opacities: np.array of shape (N,) rotations: np.array of shape (N,) """ h, w, = targetimage.shape windowsize = 7 halfwindow = windowsize // 2 # Pad image for boundary handling paddedimage = np.pad(targetimage, ((halfwindow, halfwindow), (halfwindow, halfwindow), (0, 0)), mode='reflect') # Compute variance for each channel in the sliding window # Variance = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 # Use a uniform kernel for the sliding window mean kernel = np.ones((windowsize, windowsize)) / (windowsize 2) def slidingmean(img2d): return np.convolve(img2d.flatten(), kernel.flatten(), mode='valid').reshape(h, w) varr = slidingmean(paddedimage[:,:, 0][halfwindow:-halfwindow, halfwindow:-halfwindow]2) - slidingmean(paddedimage[:,:, 0][halfwindow:-halfwindow, halfwindow:-halfwindow])2 varg = slidingmean(paddedimage[:,:, 1][halfwindow:-halfwindow, halfwindow:-halfwindow]2) - slidingmean(paddedimage[:,:, 1][halfwindow:-halfwindow, halfwindow:-halfwindow])2 varb = slidingmean(paddedimage[:,:, 2][halfwindow:-halfwindow, halfwindow:-halfwindow]2) - slidingmean(paddedimage[:,:, 2][halfwindow:-halfwindow, halfwindow:-halfwindow])2 localvariance = varr + varg + varb # Normalize variance to [0, 1] minvar = np.min(localvariance) maxvar = np.max(localvariance) if maxvar == minvar: nlvmap = np.zeroslike(localvariance) else: nlvmap = (localvariance - minvar) / (maxvar - minvar) # Map lattice points to grid indices # Assuming latticepoints are integer coordinates within [0, H-1] x [0, W-1] latticeindices = [(y w + x) for x, y in latticepoints] probs = 0.1 + 0.9 nlvmap.flatten() probs = probs / np.sum(probs) # Normalize to sum to 1 # Sample N points from latticepoints based on probs numsamples = len(latticepoints) sampledflatindices = np.random.choice(len(probs), size=numsamples, replace=False, p=probs) # Convert flat indices back to (x, y) sampledy = sampledflatindices // w sampledx = sampledflatindices % w positions = np.columnstack((sampledx, sampledy)) # Initialize scale nlvvalues = nlvmap[sampledy, sampledx] scales = smax - (smax - smin) nlvvalues # Initialize color targetcolors = targetimage[sampledy, sampledx] colors = np.random.normal(loc=targetcolors, scale=sigmac, size=(numsamples, 3)) # Initialize opacity opacities = np.full(numsamples, -2.0) # Initialize rotation rotations = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, numsamples) return positions, scales, colors, opacities, rotations This initialization creates an implicit hierarchy where points sampled early are larger and points sampled later are smaller. It uses farthest point sampling to sample positions. For the scale of point i with position x{Ii}, it runs nearest-neighbors across prefixes of the farthest point sampling order so that the initial scale is approximately \min{0 \le j < i} d(x{Ii}, x{Ij}). Unlike standard 3DGS initialization, this method allows larger primitives to potentially replace smaller ones via texture alone during optimization. A pitfall is that using nearest-neighbors initialization from Kerbl et al. [22] leads to small primitives, which is not ideal for this representation. Time and Memory Complexity: The runtime overhead is almost the same as standard initialization. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On 512×512 targets, PSNR improves from 24.4 dB (disabled) to 25.5 dB (enabled). On 1024×1024 targets, PSNR improves from 25.7 dB to 25.9 dB. Using both structure-aware initialization and soft rasterization produces the best results across all targets, with sharper edges, fewer spurious fragments, and reduced seed-to-seed variance. Strengths and Limitations: Accelerates convergence and improves final fidelity, particularly when using high primitive counts. Ensures dense and fine coverage in complex regions while maintaining sparse and coarse coverage in flat areas. Disabling both soft rasterization and structure-aware initialization often leads to destabilization of the fit and missing fine details. When to Use: When using high primitive counts and requiring faster convergence and higher fidelity. When fine detail preservation is critical. Originated in DiffBMP. It is used in differentiable rendering with bitmap primitives to improve the quality of dynamic and spatially constrained rendering. DiffBMP: Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.22625, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Nexels: Neurally-Textured Surfels for Real-Time Novel View Synthesis with Sparse Primitives, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37531-59, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Cluster-level Weighting
head: Adaptive Rendering Weighting, Pyramidal Gaussian Weighting
body: Cluster-level Weighting is a method for adaptively determining the contribution of multi-scale Gaussians in a Pyramidal Gaussian hierarchy during rendering. It solves the problem of balancing detail and performance by assigning unique weight sets to spatial clusters of Gaussians rather than individual splats, thereby incorporating positional context without the computational cost of per-Gaussian weight networks. It differs from sibling methods like Dense Initialization or Structure-Aware Initialization by focusing on the rendering-time adaptive weighting of an existing hierarchical structure, rather than the initialization of the Gaussian parameters themselves. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Pyramidal Gaussians G{py} = \{Gl \mid 1 \le l \le L\}, where Gl contains Gaussians at level l; a subset of the original point cloud P; the number of clusters K; the number of levels L; and the current camera position x{cam}. Output: A weight vector w{k,n} \in \mathbb{R}^L for each cluster k and camera view n, where w{k,n}[l] is the weight for level l of cluster k. Data Structures: 1. Centroids (M): A set of K 3D vectors M = \{mk \mid 1 \le k \le K\}, where mk \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Cluster Indices (k{il}): For each Gaussian i at level l, an integer index k{il} \in \{1, \dots, K\} indicating the assigned cluster. 3. Cluster Embedding (Ec): A learnable tensor of shape K \times D, where D is the feature dimension. Ec[k] is the embedding vector for cluster k. 4. Weighting Network (F\Theta): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with parameters \Theta. Parameters: K: Total number of clusters. Typical value: Not given in the sources. L: Total number of levels in the Pyramidal Gaussian hierarchy. D: Dimension of the cluster embedding feature. P{subset}: A subset of the point cloud P used for clustering to reduce computation time. Steps: 1. Clustering: Run a mini-batched K-means algorithm on P{subset} to compute K centroids M. Note: This step takes approximately 30 seconds. Pitfall: Using the full point cloud significantly increases computation time; a subset is recommended. 2. Assignment: For each Gaussian i at level l with center x{il}, assign it to the nearest centroid: k{il} = \text{NearestNeighbour}(M, x{il}) where \text{NearestNeighbour} returns the index k such that \|x{il} - mk\| is minimized. 3. Weight Computation (Per View): For a given camera view n with center x{cam}: a. Compute the positional encoding of the camera center: PE(x{cam}). b. For each cluster k \in \{1, \dots, K\}: i. Retrieve the cluster embedding Ec[k]. ii. Concatenate the embedding and positional encoding: vk = \text{Concat}(Ec[k], PE(x{cam})). iii. Pass through the weighting network: uk = F\Theta(vk). iv. Apply Softmax to obtain the level weights: w{k,n} = \text{Softmax}(uk) The resulting vector w{k,n} \in \mathbb{R}^L contains the weights for each level l. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeclusterweights(Gpy, Psubset, K, L, D, FTheta, PEfunc): """ Gpy: List of lists, Gpy[l] contains Gaussians at level l. Each Gaussian has a 'center' attribute (3D vector). Psubset: Array of shape (N, 3) representing the point cloud subset. K: Number of clusters. L: Number of levels. D: Dimension of cluster embedding. FTheta: Function representing the MLP FTheta. PEfunc: Function computing positional encoding PE(x). Returns: centroids: Array of shape (K, 3) clusterindices: Dict mapping (level, gaussianindex) -> clusterindex clusterembeddings: Array of shape (K, D) (initialized randomly or loaded) """ # Step 1: Clustering # Use mini-batched K-means on Psubset # Note: Implementation details of mini-batched K-means are external centroids = minibatchedkmeans(Psubset, K) # Step 2: Assignment clusterindices = {} for l in range(L): for i, gaussian in enumerate(Gpy[l]): xil = gaussian.center # Find nearest centroid distances = np.linalg.norm(centroids - xil, axis=1) kil = np.argmin(distances) clusterindices[(l, i)] = kil # Step 3: Initialize Cluster Embeddings # Ec is a learnable tensor of size K x D # In a real implementation, this would be a torch.nn.Parameter or similar Ec = np.random.randn(K, D) return centroids, clusterindices, Ec def getlevelweights(centroids, clusterindices, Ec, FTheta, PEfunc, xcam, L): """ Computes the weight vector for each cluster given a camera position. Returns: weights: Array of shape (K, L) """ K = centroids.shape[0] # Compute positional encoding of camera center pecam = PEfunc(xcam) weights = np.zeros((K, L)) for k in range(K): # Get cluster embedding eck = Ec[k] # Concatenate cluster embedding and camera positional encoding # Concat(·) denotes concatenation operation inputvector = np.concatenate([eck, pecam]) # Pass through MLP FTheta # FTheta is a small MLP logits = FTheta(inputvector) # Apply Softmax # Softmax(u) = exp(u) / sum(exp(u)) explogits = np.exp(logits - np.max(logits)) # Numerical stability softmaxout = explogits / np.sum(explogits) weights[k,:] = softmaxout return weights A small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) F\Theta that computes level-specific weights for each cluster based on the camera position and cluster embedding. It takes the concatenation of the cluster embedding Ec[k] and the positional encoding of the camera center PE(x{cam}) as input and outputs a vector of size L. The architecture is described as "small" in the source, but specific layer sizes or activation functions (other than ReLU mentioned in the figure caption context) are not detailed in the text. The output is normalized via Softmax to ensure the weights sum to one across levels. Time Complexity: The clustering step (K-means) takes approximately 30 seconds for the subset used. The per-frame weight computation is O(K \cdot (D + \text{MLP\cost})), which is negligible compared to the rendering cost of the Gaussians themselves. Memory Complexity: Requires storing K centroids, K cluster embeddings of dimension D, and the MLP parameters. This is minimal compared to the Gaussian data. Strengths: Balances computational cost and adaptability by assigning weights per cluster rather than per Gaussian, avoiding the "substantial computational cost" of per-Gaussian weighting. Captures positional information of Gaussians. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the K-means clustering and the subset selection. The "small" MLP may have limited capacity to model complex view-dependent effects compared to larger networks. When to use: When rendering Pyramidal Gaussians where adaptive multi-scale contribution is needed based on viewpoint and spatial location. When not to use: If per-Gaussian adaptive weighting is required for extreme detail, or if computational resources for the clustering step (30s) are prohibitive during initialization. Cluster-level Weighting is part of the PyGS (Pyramidal 3D Gaussian Splatting) method, introduced by the authors of. It builds on the hierarchical structure of Pyramidal Gaussians, where higher levels have larger scales and lower levels have smaller scales. The method was developed to address challenges in large-scale scene modeling, specifically the need to assess contributions from each level of Gaussians adaptively based on the viewpoint. It references the standard 3DGS sorting and rendering pipeline. PyGS: Large-scale Scene Representation with Pyramidal 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2405.16829, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Supplementing Points for Camera Motion Blur
head: Adding extra points, Point densification via extent-based calculation
body: This method supplements an initial sparse point cloud with additional 3D Gaussian primitives to enable the representation of fine details and tiny objects that are otherwise lost due to sparsity, specifically to handle camera motion blur artifacts. It differs from standard initialization by dynamically calculating the number of required points based on the spatial extent of the existing cloud and ensuring these new points inherit color features from neighbors rather than random initialization, which is critical for high-fidelity deblurring. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An initial sparse point cloud consisting of N 3D Gaussians with positions \mui. Output: An augmented point cloud with N + Np Gaussians, where Np is the number of supplementing points. Data Structures: The method operates on the existing list of Gaussian parameters. For the new points, the covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and rotation Ri are typically initialized using standard sparse initialization principles (e.g., small scale, low opacity) as defined in the parent article. The key differentiator is the calculation of the count Np and the initialization of the color coefficients Ci. Parameters: c: A stability constant, set to 1.1. N{max}: The maximum number of supplementing points allowed, set to 200,000. Algorithm: 1. Calculate Spatial Extent: Determine the bounding box of the current point cloud along the x, y, and z axes. Let Q{max} \in \mathbb{R}^3 be the vector of maximum position coordinates: Q{max} = [\maxi(\mu{i,x}), \maxi(\mu{i,y}), \maxi(\mu{i,z})] Let Q{min} \in \mathbb{R}^3 be the vector of minimum position coordinates: Q{min} = [\mini(\mu{i,x}), \mini(\mu{i,y}), \mini(\mu{i,z})] 2. Calculate Supplementing Point Count (Np): Compute the volume of the bounding box and divide by the cube of the stability constant c. Cap the result at N{max}. Np = \min\left( \frac{\text{prod}(Q{max} - Q{min})}{c^3}, N{max} \right) where \text{prod}(\mathbf{v}) = vx \cdot vy \cdot vz. 3. Generate New Positions: Distribute Np new Gaussian means uniformly within the bounding box defined by Q{min} and Q{max}. Note: The source does not specify the exact sampling distribution (e.g., uniform vs. Poisson disk), but implies uniform distribution within the extent. 4. Initialize Color Features: For each new Gaussian j (where j > N), initialize its color coefficients Cj by interpolating from the nearest neighboring points in the existing cloud. Pitfall: Randomly initializing color features for added points leads to inferior reconstruction quality. 5. Initialize Other Attributes: Initialize covariance \Sigmaj, opacity \alphaj, and rotation Rj for the new points. Standard practice suggests low initial opacity (e.g., 0.01 to 0.1) and small scales to allow optimization to refine them. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def supplementpointsformotionblur(existinggaussians, c=1.1, nmax=200000): """ Supplements the existing point cloud with additional Gaussians to handle camera motion blur. Args: existinggaussians: List or array of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian has a position attribute.mu (shape (3,)). c: Stability constant (default 1.1). nmax: Maximum number of points to add (default 200,000). Returns: augmentedgaussians: List of N + Np Gaussians. """ # 1. Calculate Spatial Extent positions = np.array([g.mu for g in existinggaussians]) if len(positions) == 0: return existinggaussians qmax = np.max(positions, axis=0) qmin = np.min(positions, axis=0) # 2. Calculate Supplementing Point Count # prod(Qmax - Qmin) is the volume of the bounding box extent = qmax - qmin volume = np.prod(extent) np = int(volume / (c 3)) np = min(np, nmax) if np == 0: return existinggaussians # 3. Generate New Positions # Uniformly sample within the bounding box newpositions = np.random.uniform(low=qmin, high=qmax, size=(np, 3)) # 4. Initialize Color Features # Interpolate colors from nearest neighbors # Implementation detail: Use k-NN (e.g., k=3) to find nearest existing points # and average their color coefficients. newcolors = interpolatecolorsfromneighbors(newpositions, existinggaussians) # 5. Initialize Other Attributes # Standard initialization: small scale, low opacity, identity rotation newgaussians = [] for i in range(np): newg = Gaussian() newg.mu = newpositions[i] newg.color = newcolors[i] newg.opacity = 0.01 # Low initial opacity newg.scale = np.array([0.01, 0.01, 0.01]) # Small initial scale newg.rotation = np.array([1, 0, 0, 0]) # Identity quaternion newgaussians.append(newg) # Combine and return augmentedgaussians = list(existinggaussians) + newgaussians return augmentedgaussians def interpolatecolorsfromneighbors(newpositions, existinggaussians): """ Interpolates color features for new points based on nearest neighbors in the existing cloud. """ existingpositions = np.array([g.mu for g in existinggaussians]) existingcolors = np.array([g.color for g in existinggaussians]) # Using simple nearest neighbor for demonstration; in practice, # inverse-distance weighting or k-NN averaging is preferred. # Here we assume a helper function exists to find nearest neighbor indices. # Since we cannot call external libraries, we implement a basic brute-force # nearest neighbor search for completeness. nnew = newpositions.shape[0] nexisting = existingpositions.shape[0] # Calculate distances (Euclidean) # Shape: (nnew, nexisting) dists = np.sqrt(np.sum((newpositions[:, np.newaxis,:] - existingpositions[np.newaxis,:,:]) 2, axis=2)) # Find index of nearest neighbor nearestindices = np.argmin(dists, axis=1) # Retrieve colors of nearest neighbors interpolatedcolors = existingcolors[nearestindices] return interpolatedcolors class Gaussian: def init(self): self.mu = np.zeros(3) self.color = np.zeros(3) # Assuming SH degree 0 for simplicity self.opacity = 0.0 self.scale = np.zeros(3) self.rotation = np.zeros(4) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Clouds: Directly using a sparse point cloud without this densification results in objects being represented by a small number of points or failing to model tiny objects entirely. Color Initialization: Randomly initializing color features for added points yields inferior reconstruction quality (PSNR 23.46, SSIM 0.7411) compared to interpolating colors (PSNR 23.73, SSIM 0.7474) or adding no extra points (PSNR 23.34, SSIM 0.7374). Volume Calculation: If the point cloud is degenerate (e.g., all points on a plane), the volume \text{prod}(Q{max} - Q{min}) may be zero or very small, resulting in Np=0. Time Complexity: The calculation of Np is O(N) to find min/max positions. Generating new points is O(Np). Interpolating colors is O(Np \cdot N) for brute-force nearest neighbor, or O(Np \log N) with spatial indexing. Memory Complexity: Increases by O(Np) Gaussians. Performance: This method improves PSNR and SSIM metrics for scenes with camera motion blur by ensuring dense coverage of the scene volume. Strengths: Prevents failure to model tiny objects; improves deblurring quality by providing valid initial color features. Limitations: Adds computational overhead during initialization; requires careful tuning of c and N{max} to avoid excessive point counts in large scenes. This method was introduced in the context of "Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting" to address the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting when handling camera motion blur. Standard 3D-GS struggles to model camera motion blur, often resulting in fewer Gaussians and poorer reconstruction of dynamic or blurred details. The technique was proposed by B. Lee et al. in the paper "Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting". Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73636-08, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Geometry-aware Gaussian Splatting
body: Geometry-aware Gaussian Splatting (GeoGaussian) is a method that initializes thin Gaussians aligned with surfaces in smoothly connected areas and uses constrained optimization to preserve scene geometry and texture, particularly in low-textured regions. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by explicitly encoding geometric normals into the Gaussian parameterization for smooth surfaces, ensuring that densification (splitting and cloning) occurs within the tangent plane of the surface rather than randomly in 3D space. This approach enhances rendering fidelity in structured regions where traditional methods often suffer from geometric artifacts or texture degradation. Inputs: Input point cloud P (typically generated by SLAM or Structure-fromMotion methods). Camera poses T{cw} for training views. Training images I. Hyperparameters: \lambda1=0.8 (photometric weight), \lambda2=0.3 (geometric weight), \beta1=0.05 (smoothness position weight), \beta2=0.01 (smoothness normal weight), \gamma=0.0002 (gradient threshold), learning rate 0.0002. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, including both standard spherical Gaussians (G{ind}) and thin ellipsoidal Gaussians (G{\theta}), optimized to render novel views. Standard Gaussian (G{ind}): Position: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scale: S \in \mathbb{R}^3 (diagonal scaling matrix Sw = \text{Diag}[s1, s2, s3]). Rotation: R \in SO(3). Opacity: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}. Spherical Harmonics: C \in \mathbb{R}^{(m+1)\times 3}. Thin Gaussian (G{\theta}): Position: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scale: S = [s1, s2, 0.001]^T. The third value s3 is fixed to 0.001 to enforce thinness. Rotation: R = [r1, r2, n]. The third column r3 (denoted as n) is the surface normal vector, decoupled from the covariance optimization. The first two columns r1, r2 are normalized basis vectors perpendicular to r3. Opacity: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}. Spherical Harmonics: C \in \mathbb{R}^{(m+1)\times 3}. Neighbor List: For each thin Gaussian G{\theta}, a list of K=8 nearest neighbors is maintained to compute geometric constraints. This list is updated periodically. 1. Normal Extraction: Extract surface normals for all points in the input point cloud using a standard normal estimation method. 2. Point Classification: Classify points into two groups: S{ind} (Individual points): Points with unreliable normals. A normal is unreliable if: The point has a long distance from its neighbors. Neighbors within a distance threshold have normals with large angle differences relative to the point's normal. S{co} (Smooth surfaces): Points with reliable normals, forming smoothly connected areas. 3. Gaussian Creation: For p \in S{ind}: Initialize a standard Gaussian. Set scale S based on the distance to the nearest neighbor, similar to standard 3DGS. For p \in S{co}: Initialize a thin Gaussian G{\theta}. Set r3 = n (the extracted normal). Compute r1, r2 as orthonormal basis vectors perpendicular to r3. Set S = [s1, s2, 0.001]^T. The values s1, s2 are initialized based on local point density (distance to nearest neighbor). Densification occurs via splitting and cloning. The strategy depends on the Gaussian type. 1. Standard Gaussian Densification (G{ind}): Split: A large Gaussian is split into two smaller Gaussians. The new positions are chosen randomly inside the original ellipsoid. 2. Thin Gaussian Densification (G{\theta}): Cloning (Tangential Cloning): Calculate the accumulated gradient of the position \mu over the last 10 iterations, denoted \delta \mui. If \|\delta \mui\| > \gamma, clone the Gaussian. The new position \mu{i+1} is calculated by projecting the gradient step onto the tangent plane defined by the normal r3: \mu{i+1} = \mui + \delta \mui - (\mathbf{r}3^\top \delta \mui) \mathbf{r}3 (Note: The source notation \mu{i+1} = \mui + \delta \mui - \mathbf{r}3^\top \delta \mui is dimensionally inconsistent for vectors; the corrected vector projection is implemented here to decouple the component perpendicular to the normal as described in the text.) Clone parameters r3, S, C, \alpha to the new Gaussian. Splitting (Tangential Splitting): When splitting a thin Gaussian, the new position \mu{i+1} must lie on the plane established by the original position \mui and normal r3. The condition is: \mu{i+1}^\top \mathbf{r}3 = \mui^\top \mathbf{r}3 And the new Gaussian G{i+1} must remain in S{co}. The optimization minimizes a combined loss function. 1. Photometric Loss: Rendered color ci is compared to ground truth \bar{c}i: E{pho}^i = \| ci - \bar{c}i \| = \| f(\mathcal{G}, T{cw}) - \bar{c}i \| where f rasterizes and blends all Gaussians (standard and thin). 2. Geometric Smoothness Loss: For view-dependent thin Gaussians G{\theta}, compute the loss based on K=8 nearest neighbors m. Outliers with large normal angle differences are filtered out. E{geo} = \beta1 \left\| \mathbf{r}3^\top \mu - \frac{1}{m} \sum{j \in m} \mathbf{r}3^{j\top} \mu^j \right\| + \beta2 \| \mathbf{r}3^j - \mathbf{r}3 \|2 \mathbf{r}3^\top \mu: Distance from world origin to the plane of G{\theta}. \frac{1}{m} \sum \mathbf{r}3^{j\top} \mu^j: Average point-plane distance of the neighborhood. The second term encourages normal alignment with neighbors. 3. Total Loss: L = \lambda1 \sum{\forall k \in H \times W} E{pho}^k + \lambda2 \sum{\mathcal{G}\theta^i} E{geo}^i where \lambda1=0.8, \lambda2=0.3. 1. Iterations 0–2,000: Only photometric constraints (E{pho}) are used. No geometric loss. 2. Iterations 2,000–10,000: Both photometric and geometric losses are used. Densification (split/clone) is active. 3. Iterations 10,000–30,000: Densification ceases. Optimization continues with both losses. 4. Pruning: Gaussians with opacity \alpha < 0.05 are removed throughout training. 5. Neighbor Update: Iterations 0–20,000: Update nearest neighbor list every 100 iterations. Iterations >20,000: Update every 1,000 iterations. 6. Total Iterations: 30,000. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class Gaussian: def init(self, pos, scale, rot, sh, alpha, gtype, normal=None, gradacc=None): self.pos = np.array(pos, dtype=np.float32) self.scale = np.array(scale, dtype=np.float32) self.rot = np.array(rot, dtype=np.float32) self.sh = np.array(sh, dtype=np.float32) self.alpha = float(alpha) self.gtype = gtype # 'ind' or 'theta' self.normal = np.array(normal, dtype=np.float32) if normal is not None else None self.gradacc = np.array(gradacc, dtype=np.float32) if gradacc is not None else np.zeros(3) self.neighbors = [] def initializegeogaussian(pointcloud, normals): gaussians = [] Sind, Sco = [], [] for i, p in enumerate(pointcloud): n = normals[i] if isnormalreliable(p, n, pointcloud, normals): Sco.append(i) else: Sind.append(i) for idx in Sind: p = pointcloud[idx] dist = distancetonearestneighbor(p, pointcloud) scale = np.array([dist, dist, dist], dtype=np.float32) rot = np.eye(3) sh = np.zeros((4, 3), dtype=np.float32) gaussians.append(Gaussian(p, scale, rot, sh, 1.0, 'ind')) for idx in Sco: p = pointcloud[idx] n = normals[idx] dist = distancetonearestneighbor(p, pointcloud) scale = np.array([dist, dist, 0.001], dtype=np.float32) r3 = n / np.linalg.norm(n) r1, r2 = computeorthonormalbasis(r3) rot = np.columnstack((r1, r2, r3)) sh = np.zeros((4, 3), dtype=np.float32) gaussians.append(Gaussian(p, scale, rot, sh, 1.0, 'theta', normal=r3)) return gaussians def isnormalreliable(point, normal, pointcloud, normals, distthresh=0.05, anglethresh=np.pi/4): neighbors = getknearestneighbors(point, pointcloud, k=10) if len(neighbors) == 0: return False for nidx, npoint in neighbors: nnormal = normals[nidx] angle = np.arccos(np.clip(np.dot(normal, nnormal), -1.0, 1.0)) if angle > anglethresh: return False return True def computeorthonormalbasis(r3): if abs(r3[0]) < 0.9: arbitrary = np.array([1, 0, 0], dtype=np.float32) else: arbitrary = np.array([0, 1, 0], dtype=np.float32) r1 = np.cross(arbitrary, r3) r1 = r1 / np.linalg.norm(r1) r2 = np.cross(r3, r1) return r1, r2 def densifygeogaussian(gaussians, gradients, iteration, gamma=0.0002): newgaussians = [] activegaussians = [] for g in gaussians: g.gradacc += gradients.get(g, np.zeros(3)) if g.gtype == 'ind': if islarge(g): g1, g2 = splitstandard(g) newgaussians.extend([g1, g2]) else: activegaussians.append(g) elif g.gtype == 'theta': if np.linalg.norm(g.gradacc) > gamma: deltamu = g.gradacc projonnormal = np.dot(g.normal, deltamu) normalcomponent = projonnormal g.normal tangentstep = deltamu - normalcomponent munew = g.pos + tangentstep gclone = Gaussian(munew, g.scale.copy(), g.rot.copy(), g.sh.copy(), g.alpha, 'theta', normal=g.normal) newgaussians.append(gclone) if islarge(g): munew = splitontangentplane(g) gsplit = Gaussian(munew, g.scale.copy() / 1.6, g.rot.copy(), g.sh.copy(), g.alpha / 2, 'theta', normal=g.normal) newgaussians.append(gsplit) else: activegaussians.append(g) return activegaussians + newgaussians def splitontangentplane(g): offset = np.random.randn(2) tangentoffset = offset[0] g.rot[:, 0] + offset[1] g.rot[:, 1] scalefactor = np.random.uniform(0, 1) np.max(g.scale[:2]) tangentoffset = scalefactor return g.pos + tangentoffset def computeloss(gaussians, images, cameraposes, neighborlists, iteration): photometricloss = 0.0 geometricloss = 0.0 for img, pose in zip(images, cameraposes): rendered = render(gaussians, pose) photometricloss += np.mean((rendered - img) 2) if iteration > 2000: for g in gaussians: if g.gtype == 'theta': neighbors = neighborlists.get(g, []) validneighbors = [n for n in neighbors if np.arccos(np.clip(np.dot(g.normal, n.normal), -1.0, 1.0)) < np.pi/4] if len(validneighbors) > 0: m = len(validneighbors) distself = np.dot(g.normal, g.pos) distavg = np.mean([np.dot(n.normal, n.pos) for n in validneighbors]) term1 = np.abs(distself - distavg) term2 = np.mean([np.linalg.norm(g.normal - n.normal) for n in validneighbors]) geometricloss += 0.05 term1 + 0.01 term2 return 0.8 photometricloss + 0.3 geometricloss def updateneighborlists(gaussians, currentiter): interval = 100 if currentiter < 20000 else 1000 if currentiter % interval == 0: for g in gaussians: if g.gtype == 'theta': g.neighbors = getknearestneighbors(g.pos, gaussians, k=8) def distancetonearestneighbor(p, pointcloud): dists = [np.linalg.norm(p - q) for q in pointcloud if q is not p] return min(dists) if dists else 0.01 def getknearestneighbors(p, targets, k=8): dists = [(np.linalg.norm(p - t.pos), t) for t in targets] dists.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [t for, t in dists[:k]] def islarge(g): return g.alpha > 0.1 and np.max(g.scale) > 0.01 def splitstandard(g): offset = np.random.randn(3) g.scale 0.5 g1 = Gaussian(g.pos + offset, g.scale.copy() / 1.6, g.rot.copy(), g.sh.copy(), g.alpha / 2, g.gtype, normal=g.normal) g2 = Gaussian(g.pos - offset, g.scale.copy() / 1.6, g.rot.copy(), g.sh.copy(), g.alpha / 2, g.gtype, normal=g.normal) return g1, g2 def render(gaussians, pose): # Standard 3DGS rasterization and blending pipeline return np.zeros((100, 100, 3), dtype=np.float32) Time and Memory Complexity: The method requires more GPU resources for training compared to standard 3DGS due to the additional geometric loss computation and neighbor list maintenance. Neighbor lists are updated periodically (every 100 iterations until 20,000, then every 1,000), adding overhead proportional to the number of thin Gaussians. Measured Performance: Evaluated on Replica, TUM RGB-D, and ICL-NUIM datasets. Sparse View Evaluation (R1, 10% data): GeoGaussian: PSNR 31.65, SSIM 0.937, LPIPS 0.041. 3DGS: PSNR 30.49, SSIM 0.932, LPIPS 0.051. LightGS: PSNR 30.54, SSIM 0.932, LPIPS 0.051. Sparse View Evaluation (R1, 100% data): GeoGaussian: PSNR 38.24, SSIM 0.979, LPIPS 0.021. 3DGS: PSNR 37.60, SSIM 0.965, LPIPS 0.028. LightGS: PSNR 38.44, SSIM 0.967, LPIPS 0.025. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Improves rendering quality in novel views, especially in low-textured regions and structured areas (walls, ceilings) where standard 3DGS degrades. Preserves geometry and texture through constrained optimization. Limitations: Requires more training time and GPU resources than standard 3DGS. It functions as a global refinement module and cannot perform real-time optimization, unlike online methods such as Vox-Fusion. When to Use: Use when high-fidelity rendering of structured scenes is required, particularly with sparse input views or in regions with low texture. Use when the input data includes reliable surface normals (e.g., from high-quality SLAM/SfM). When Not to Use: Do not use if real-time optimization is required. Do not use if the input point cloud has poor normal estimation, as the classification of S{co} may be unreliable. Origin: GeoGaussian was proposed by Y. Li et al. in the paper "GeoGaussian: Geometry-Aware Gaussian Splatting for Scene Rendering". History and Development: The method builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting and addresses its limitations in handling smooth surfaces and low-texture regions. It contrasts with voxel-based methods like Vox-Fusion, which integrate implicit neural representations and operate online, whereas GeoGaussian is a global refinement method using differentiable 3D Gaussians. Usage: Evaluated on Replica, TUM RGB-D, and ICL-NUIM datasets. GeoGaussian: Geometry-Aware Gaussian Splatting for Scene Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72761-025, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gaussian Sampling for Surface Patch Anchors
head: Anchor sampling with Gaussian distribution, Pulled Queries, Surface Patch Generation, Surface Patch Sensing via Gaussian Sampling
body: This method creates a denser, more continuous surface representation than single-point ray intersection by pulling randomly sampled queries around 3D anchor points derived from back-projected geometry cues. It solves the problem of sparse geometric supervision by defining an isotropic Gaussian distribution around each anchor to sample a local surface patch, which is significantly more geometry-aware than single-point intersection or simple depth patch back-projection. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly models the local surface neighborhood via statistical sampling rather than uniform grid or mesh-based distribution, enabling patch-level photo consistency which achieves better performance than pixel-level consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D anchor points q obtained by back-projecting geometry cues (predicted monocular depth or dataset-provided sensor cues) to 3D space. Parameters: J: Number of points sampled per surface patch. Typical value: 9. \tau^2: Variance of the isotropic Gaussian distribution controlling patch size. Baseline: distance between two other pixels in the 3D world coordinate. Output: A set of J points s = \{p'j \mid j \in [1, J]\} forming the surface patch around anchor q. Data Structures: Anchor Point q: A 3D vector [x, y, z] in world coordinates. Surface Patch s: A list or array of J 3D vectors p'j, each representing a sampled query point. Steps: 1. Obtain Anchors: For each posed view, back-project geometry cues to obtain 3D anchor points q. 2. Define Distribution: Define an isotropic Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(q, \tau^2) centered at q with variance \tau^2. 3. Sample Points: Sample J points from this distribution to form the surface patch s. 4. Initialize Variance: Set initial \tau^2 to the distance between two other pixels in the 3D world coordinate. 5. Refine (Optional): Apply mask and weight filtering to the sampled points to exclude outliers and prioritize critical surface locations based on gradient alignment to ground truth normals. Formulas: Gaussian Sampling: p'j \sim \mathcal{N}(q, \tau^2) Where p'j is the j-th sampled point, q is the anchor point, and \tau^2 is the variance. Variance Initialization: \tau^2 = \text{distance}(pa, pb) Where pa and pb are two other pixels in the 3D world coordinate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatesurfacepatch(anchorq, variancetau2, numpointsJ): """ Generates a surface patch by sampling points from a Gaussian distribution around a 3D anchor point. Args: anchorq (np.ndarray): 3D anchor point [x, y, z]. variancetau2 (float): Variance of the isotropic Gaussian distribution. numpointsJ (int): Number of points to sample (e.g., 9). Returns: np.ndarray: Array of shape (J, 3) containing the sampled surface patch points. """ # Define the isotropic Gaussian distribution parameters # Mean is the anchor point, covariance is identity scaled by variance mean = anchorq cov = np.eye(3) variancetau2 # Sample J points from the multivariate normal distribution # This covers the local surface patch around the anchor surfacepatch = np.random.multivariatenormal(mean, cov, numpointsJ) return surfacepatch def initializevariance(worldcoords): """ Initializes the variance tau^2 as the distance between two other pixels in the 3D world coordinate. Args: worldcoords (np.ndarray): Array of 3D coordinates of pixels. Returns: float: The squared distance between two arbitrary pixels. """ # Select two arbitrary pixels (e.g., first two) p1 = worldcoords[0] p2 = worldcoords[1] # Calculate Euclidean distance dist = np.linalg.norm(p1 - p2) # Return squared distance as variance return dist 2 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance Too Small: If \tau^2 is too small, the patch does not cover a large enough area, degrading inference performance. Variance Too Large: If \tau^2 is too large, points may be ruled out by masks, decreasing efficiency and performance. Point Count: A small number of points (e.g., J=1) may not adequately represent the surface, while a too large number may not improve performance further but increases time complexity. Refines geometric constraints by filtering outliers and prioritizing critical surface locations using binary masks and scalar weights based on gradient alignment. Time Complexity: Increases with the number of sampled points J. A larger J increases computational cost without necessarily improving performance. Memory Complexity: Proportional to J per anchor, as J points must be stored and processed for loss calculation. Measured Performance: On the Replica dataset, optimal sampling at J=9, \tau^2=\tau^2 yields Acc=0.036, Comp=0.039, CD-L1=0.037, Prec=0.820, Recall=0.777, F-score=0.797. Strengths: Provides a denser and more continuous surface representation than single-point intersection; more geometry-aware; patch-level photo consistency achieves better performance than pixel-level. Limitations: Sensitive to the choice of variance \tau^2; requires back-projected geometry cues (monocular or sensor). When to Use: When a denser surface representation is needed for volume rendering constraints and geometry-aware supervision is beneficial. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited and J cannot be kept small, or when high-quality back-projected geometry cues are unavailable. This method was introduced in the paper "Sensing Surface Patches in Volume Rendering for Inferring Signed Distance Functions". It addresses the limitation of single-point ray intersection in differentiable rendering, where only one point gets supervised on the zero level set. By pulling randomly sampled queries, it leverages the characteristics of Signed Distance Fields (SDF) to move points onto the zero level set using gradients and signed distances. The method was evaluated on datasets such as Replica and ScanNet, demonstrating superiority over previous methods in real-world indoor scenes. Sensing Surface Patches in Volume Rendering for Inferring Signed Distance Functions, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v39i4.32426, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mask and Weight Filtering for Patch Points
head: $w_j$ and $\eta_j$ filtering, $w_j$ and $η_j$ filtering
body:
This method refines the geometric constraints applied to surface patch points during the optimization of a Signed Distance Field (SDF) by filtering outliers and prioritizing critical surface locations. It addresses the problem of noisy or degenerate sampled points on a local surface patch, which can degrade the accuracy of the reconstructed geometry. Unlike the parent method, which samples points around a 3D anchor, this technique specifically modifies the loss calculation by applying a binary mask wj to exclude outliers and a scalar weight \etaj to emphasize points with strong gradient alignment to the ground truth normal. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: q: The 3D anchor point [x, y, z]. J: The number of sampled points on the patch. p'j: The j-th pulled point on the zero level set, derived from q. f	heta: The SDF function parameterized by 	heta. e(q): The eye position or camera pose associated with point q. 
abla f	heta(p'j, e(p'j)): The gradient of the SDF at the pulled point. N^k{GT}(r): The ground truth normal at pixel r corresponding to the view. Outputs: wj: A binary mask value for each point j \in [1, J]. \etaj: A scalar weight value for each point j \in [1, J]. Data Structures The mask w is a vector of size J with binary values \{0, 1\}. The weight \eta is a vector of size J with scalar values in [0, 1] (derived from cosine similarity). Steps 1. Pull Points to Zero Level Set: For each anchor point q, compute the pulled point p'j on the zero level set of the SDF using the signed distance and gradient: p'j = q - f	heta(q, e(q))  rac{
abla f	heta(q, e(q))}{\|
abla f	heta(q, e(q))\|} Note: The calculation of 
abla f	heta(p'j, e(p'j)) involves second-order derivatives due to the dependency of p'j on the previous step, which helps the network find better solutions. 2. Compute Weight \etaj: Calculate the cosine similarity between the SDF gradient at the pulled point and the ground truth normal to determine the importance of the point: \etaj = \cos(
abla f	heta(p'j, e(p'j)), N^k{GT}(r)) This weight focuses the network on points where the gradient is well-aligned with the surface normal. 3. Compute Mask wj: Apply a binary mask to rule out outlier points during the pulling step. The specific thresholding logic for wj is not explicitly defined in the sources, but it is used to filter out points that do not meet geometric consistency criteria. 4. Apply to Loss Function: Use wj and \etaj to modulate the surface fitting loss or other constraints. Points with wj=0 are excluded, and points with higher \etaj contribute more significantly to the optimization. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemaskandweight(q, ftheta, eq, NGT, J): """ Computes the mask wj and weight etaj for J points sampled around anchor q. Args: q: 3D anchor point [x, y, z]. ftheta: SDF function. eq: Eye position/camera pose. NGT: Ground truth normal at the corresponding pixel. J: Number of points in the patch. Returns: w: Binary mask vector of size J. eta: Weight vector of size J. """ # Step 1: Pull points to zero level set # Note: In practice, J points are sampled around q. # For simplicity, we assume p'j is computed for each j. # The source formula uses a single q, but the context implies # J points are sampled and pulled. We compute for each j. w = [] eta = [] for j in range(J): # Sample point pj around q (logic from parent method) pj = samplepointaroundanchor(q) # Compute signed distance and gradient at q distq = ftheta(q, eq) gradq = computegradient(ftheta, q, eq) # Pull to zero level set # p'j = q - ftheta(q, e(q)) gradq / ||gradq|| # Note: The source formula uses grad at q, but the weight uses grad at p'j normgradq = vectornorm(gradq) if normgradq == 0: pprimej = q else: pprimej = q - distq (gradq / normgradq) # Compute gradient at pulled point (involves second-order derivatives) gradpprime = computegradient(ftheta, pprimej, eq) # Step 2: Compute weight etaj # etaj = cos(gradpprime, NGT) cossim = dotproduct(gradpprime, NGT) / (vectornorm(gradpprime) vectornorm(NGT)) etaj = cossim eta.append(etaj) # Step 3: Compute mask wj # The source states wj rules out outliers but does not give the exact threshold. # We mark this as a placeholder for the specific outlier rejection logic. # Typically, this might involve checking if the point is within a certain # distance of the zero level set or if the gradient alignment is above a threshold. # However, to remain faithful to the source which only says "rule out outliers", # we cannot invent the threshold. We assume a binary decision is made. # For implementation, one might use a threshold on etaj or distance. # Since the source does not specify, we leave the logic abstract but functional. # A common heuristic for "outlier" in this context is low alignment or large distance. # We will use a placeholder comment for the exact thresholding rule. # Implementation note: The source does not specify the threshold for wj. # A reasonable implementation might be wj = 1 if etaj > threshold else 0. # But since we must not guess, we will assume the mask is provided or # computed via a separate outlier detection step not detailed here. # To make the code valid, we will assume a simple threshold for etaj as a proxy # for "importance" which correlates with outlier status, but this is a gap fill. # Actually, the source says wj rules out outliers AND etaj focuses on important points. # They are distinct. We cannot implement wj without the rule. # We will set wj to 1 for all points and add a comment that the specific # outlier filtering logic is not provided in the source text. wj = 1.0 # Placeholder: Specific outlier filtering logic not given in source. w.append(wj) return w, eta Parameters J: Number of sampled points. The source indicates performance varies with J (Table 5 in), but the optimal value is not explicitly stated in the notes, only that it affects performance. \lambda1 \dots \lambda6: Weights for the total loss function L = L{RGB} + \lambda1 L{DR} + \lambda2 LN + \lambda3 L{Eik} + \lambda4 L{DC} + \lambda5 L{NCC} + \lambda6 L{Fit}. The mask and weight specifically modulate the surface fitting or normal-related terms. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Removing wj degrades performance due to unfiltered outliers. Removing \etaj degrades performance due to lack of focus on critical surface points. The calculation of 
abla f	heta(p'j, e(p'j)) involves second-order derivatives, which can be computationally expensive or numerically unstable if not handled carefully. This variant refers to the specific geometric operation of moving points from a d-level set to the zero level set of the SDF. It sets itself apart by explicitly using the SDF gradient and signed distance to enforce surface constraints on the pulled points p'j rather than the original anchor q. It should be chosen when explicit surface alignment is required to improve geometry accuracy. The formula is p'j = q - f	heta(q, e(q))  rac{
abla f	heta(q, e(q))}{\|
abla f	heta(q, e(q))\|}. Disabling this mechanism (imposing constraints directly on q) results in lower accuracy (F-score 0.753 vs 0.794 on Replica). Time and Memory Complexity The method adds computational overhead due to the calculation of gradients at pulled points, which involves second-order derivatives. Memory usage increases slightly to store the mask w and weight \eta vectors for each patch. Measured Performance On the Replica dataset, the full method yields Acc=0.037, Comp=0.038, CD-L1=0.037, Prec=0.797, Recall=0.777, F-score=0.794. Removing wj ('No wj') yields Acc=0.039, Comp=0.041, CD-L1=0.038, Prec=0.764, Recall=0.790, F-score=0.772. Removing \etaj ('No \etaj') yields Acc=0.039, Comp=0.042, CD-L1=0.038, Prec=0.733, Recall=0.772, F-score=0.753. Disabling pulling ('No pulling') yields Acc=0.039, Comp=0.042, CD-L1=0.038, Prec=0.733, Recall=0.772, F-score=0.753. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Improves accuracy by filtering outliers and focusing on geometrically consistent points. Enhances the capture of finer geometry details. Limitations: Requires the computation of second-order derivatives, which may be costly. The specific thresholding logic for the mask wj is not provided, making implementation dependent on heuristic choices. When to Use Use when high-fidelity surface reconstruction is required and the SDF is being optimized with multi-view constraints. Use when the sampled points on the patch are prone to outliers or noise. When Not to Use Use with caution if computational resources are limited due to the second-order derivative calculation. Do not use if the ground truth normals are unreliable, as \etaj depends on N^k{GT}(r). This method was proposed in the paper "Sensing Surface Patches in Volume Rendering for Inferring Signed Distance Functions" by Ma et al. (2025). It builds upon the concept of using SDFs to define local patches around ray-surface intersections, enabling explicit surface constraints in volume rendering. The method leverages the gradient and signed distance characteristics of SDFs to pull points onto the zero level set, enhancing accuracy and capturing finer geometry details. It is part of a broader effort to infer SDFs from multi-view images via volume rendering. name: Parameter and Coordinate Initialization
body: Parameter and Coordinate Initialization establishes the initial values for learnable attributes of 3D Gaussian primitives, including spherical harmonic coefficients, sampling coordinates, and material parameters, before the optimization process begins. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the specific numerical setup of internal state variables (such as SH coefficients and feature sampling matrices) rather than the geometric placement of the Gaussians themselves. The family shares the principle of mapping external input data (RGB colors, 3D positions, or reference images) into the specific tensor formats required by the rendering pipeline's forward pass. This involves allocating zero-initialized tensors and applying deterministic transformations (such as normalization constants or linear projections) to set the base state. See Spherical Harmonics Initialization. Initializes K learnable sampling coordinates per Gaussian point to enable adaptive feature sampling on K feature maps. Each Gaussian point i is assigned K sampling coordinates (sc1^i, sc2^i, \dots, scK^i) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 2}. To ensure that points close to each other have similar initial sampling coordinates, linear transformations are used to convert the 3D position Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3 of each Gaussian point into K sampling coordinates. This is achieved by randomly generating K matrices (M^1, M^2, \dots, M^K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 2 \times 3}, constraining each matrix such that the sum of its rows equals 1, and multiplying each matrix M^k with the Gaussian point's position Xi. The initialization formula is: (sc1^1, sc2^2, \dots, sck^K){init} = (M^1 Xi, M^2 Xi, \dots, M^K Xi) \quad (1) The number of feature maps K is typically set to 3 to balance efficiency and effectiveness. Initializes material parameters for rendering. Emission is initialized to 0, roughness to 0.5, and specular to 0.5. Spatially-varying diffuse color is initialized by building a median texture. This involves iterating over all available reference pictures and projecting them in texture space. An online median estimator is employed to avoid memory concerns when handling tens of thousands of views. The median is preferred over the mean filter to suppress view-dependent effects such as specular reflection. A method to calculate point size and transparency for volume rendering based on projected voxel size and Gaussian texture coverage. The point size is calculated as: mPointSize = mGauspara \times m\projectedVoxelSize The transparency is calculated as: mTransParency = 20.2f / \znum Here, mGauspara is the Gaussian texture coverage ratio, with a typical value of 2.0. m\projectedVoxelSize is the calculated projected size of a voxel on screen, dependent on window width and field of view. \znum is the number of depth slices or z-resolution, used to calculate transparency. The initialization of spherical harmonic coefficients for 3D Gaussian Splatting follows the guidelines of the original 3DGS paper, where hyperparameters are set according to established practices. The use of median textures for material initialization originates from differentiable rendering techniques for complex indoor scenes. The specific parameterization for point splatting in cloud rendering is derived from custom implementations.
