name: Spherical Harmonics Initialization
body: Spherical Harmonics Initialization sets the initial view-dependent color coefficients for 3D Gaussian splats by mapping input RGB colors into the zeroth-order (DC) spherical harmonic term. It differs from Spherical Harmonics Evaluation by preparing the parameter tensor for optimization rather than computing colors during rendering, and from Splat Initialization from Normalized Coordinates by relying on external RGB data rather than deriving color from spatial coordinates. Inputs: rgb: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the initial RGB color values for N Gaussians. Values are typically in the range [0, 1]. Outputs: shcoeffs: A tensor of shape (N, 27) containing the initialized spherical harmonic coefficients. The first 3 values correspond to the DC term for R, G, and B respectively; the remaining 24 values are zero. Data Structures: The SH coefficients are stored in a flattened format. For degree L=3, there are 9 coefficients per color channel (R, G, B), totaling 27 coefficients per Gaussian. The layout is [c{0,R}, c{1,R}, \dots, c{8,R}, c{0,G}, \dots, c{8,B}]. Steps: 1. Allocate a zero-initialized tensor shcoeffs of shape (N, 3, 9). 2. Compute the DC coefficient for each color channel by dividing the input RGB value by the normalization constant k0 = 0.28209479177387814. 3. Assign the computed DC coefficients to the index 0 of the last dimension for each color channel. 4. Flatten the tensor from shape (N, 3, 9) to (N, 27) to match the expected parameter layout for the Gaussian Splatting optimizer. Formula: The zeroth-order spherical harmonic coefficient c0 is calculated as: c{0} = \frac{\text{RGB}}{0.28209479177387814} where \text{RGB} is the input color value for a specific channel (R, G, or B), and 0.28209479177387814 is the normalization constant for the zeroth-order spherical harmonic basis function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def initializesh(rgb: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Initialize spherical harmonic coefficients for 3D Gaussian splatting. Args: rgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3) with RGB values in [0, 1]. Returns: Tensor of shape (N, 27) with initialized SH coefficients. """ # N is the number of Gaussians N = rgb.shape[0] # Step 1: Allocate zero tensor of shape (N, 3, 9) # 3 channels (R, G, B), 9 coefficients per channel (degree 3) shcoeffs = torch.zeros(N, 3, 9, dtype=rgb.dtype, device=rgb.device) # Step 2 & 3: Assign scaled RGB values to the DC coefficient index (0) # Normalization constant for zeroth-order SH basis function k0 = 0.28209479177387814 # Extract R, G, B channels. rgb shape is (N, 3). # We need to assign to shcoeffs[:, channel, 0] for channel in range(3): shcoeffs[:, channel, 0] = rgb[:, channel] / k0 # Step 4: Flatten to shape (N, 27) # The standard layout in Gaussian Splatting implementations is (N, 27) shcoeffs = shcoeffs.reshape(N, 27) return shcoeffs Parameters: 0.28209479177387814: The normalization constant for the zeroth-order spherical harmonic basis function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The division by the normalization constant should be performed in floating-point precision (typically float32 or float16) to avoid quantization errors in the initial color values. Input Range: The input RGB values are assumed to be normalized to [0, 1]. If input values are in [0, 255], they must be scaled down before division. Higher Order Coefficients: The initialization sets only the DC term (index 0). All other coefficients (indices 1-8 for each channel) remain zero, which is the standard initialization for view-dependent effects that are learned during training. Initializes a single 3D Gaussian splat with SH degree 3 from normalized coordinates, deriving DC color from position rather than external RGB. Computes view-dependent RGB color by evaluating SH basis functions against viewing direction. Defines a staged training protocol for appearance features, decoupling them from initial geometry optimization. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians. The operation involves a single pass over the input RGB tensor. Memory Complexity: O(N), requiring storage for 27 \times N coefficients. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and computationally inexpensive. Provides a valid starting point for view-dependent color optimization. Limitations: Does not initialize higher-order SH coefficients, which must be learned from data. Relies on the quality of the input RGB colors. When to use: At the start of Gaussian Splatting training when RGB colors are available from a source point cloud or mesh. When not to use: When no RGB data is available, or when using methods that derive color from spatial coordinates. Spherical Harmonics Initialization is a standard step in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines, introduced in the context of learning view-dependent appearance. name: Splat Initialization from Normalized Coordinates
head: UnitShSplats.add
body: This method initializes a single 3D Gaussian splat with spherical harmonic degree 3 from normalized input coordinates in [-0.5, 0.5]^3, scaling them to a physical scene size. It assigns uniform scale, identity rotation, and full opacity, while deriving the zeroth-order spherical harmonic (DC) color directly from the normalized position, with a special case for the corner point (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5). It differs from Spherical Harmonics Initialization by deriving color from spatial coordinates rather than external RGB values, and from Spherical Harmonics Evaluation by being an initialization routine rather than a rendering step. Inputs: npx, npy, npz: Normalized coordinates in [-0.5, 0.5]. size: A scalar constant defining the physical extent of the scene. baseScale: A scalar constant for the initial uniform scale of the Gaussian. alpha: Fixed opacity value (1.0). Outputs: A configured splat object appended to a target list. Data Structures: MutableSplat: An object with fields for position (vec3), scale (vec3), rotation (quat4), opacity (float), and spherical harmonic coefficients (array of floats). GaussianList: A dynamic array of MutableSplat objects. Steps: 1. Create a splat object with spherical harmonic degree 3 using Splats.create(3). 2. Set position coordinates by scaling normalized inputs with size: px = \text{npx} \times \text{size}, py = \text{npy} \times \text{size}, pz = \text{npz} \times \text{size}. 3. Set uniform scale across all axes to baseScale: sx = sy = sz = \text{baseScale}. 4. Set identity rotation quaternion: qx = 0.0, qy = 0.0, qz = 0.0, qw = 1.0. 5. Set opacity by converting a fixed alpha value of 1.0 using alphaToOpacity. 6. Set degree-0 spherical harmonic coefficients based on normalized coordinates, applying a special case for the exact point (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) which uses 0.1 instead of the coordinate offset. 7. Append the configured splat to the target list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializesplat(npx: float, npy: float, npz: float, size: float, basescale: float) -> dict: # 1. Create splat object with SH degree 3 splat = { 'position': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'scale': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'rotation': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0], 'opacity': 0.0, 'sh': [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]] # Degree 3 -> 1 coefficient per RGB channel } # 2. Set position splat['position'][0] = npx size splat['position'][1] = npy size splat['position'][2] = npz size # 3. Set uniform scale splat['scale'][0] = basescale splat['scale'][1] = basescale splat['scale'][2] = basescale # 4. Set identity rotation splat['rotation'] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # 5. Set opacity splat['opacity'] = alphatoopacity(1.0) # 6. Set SH coefficients (DC term) # Special case for the exact corner point (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) iscorner = (npx == -0.5 and npy == -0.5 and npz == -0.5) valx = 0.1 if iscorner else npx + 0.5 valy = 0.1 if iscorner else npy + 0.5 valz = 0.1 if iscorner else npz + 0.5 splat['sh'][0][0] = colortodirectcurrent(valx) splat['sh'][0][1] = colortodirectcurrent(valy) splat['sh'][0][2] = colortodirectcurrent(valz) return splat def alphatoopacity(alpha: float) -> float: # Standard conversion from alpha to opacity for Gaussian Splatting return alpha def colortodirectcurrent(v: float) -> float: # Maps normalized value v in [0, 1] to SH DC coefficient representation return v Parameters: size: Not given in the sources. baseScale: Not given in the sources. alpha: 1.0. Edge Cases: The exact point (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) is handled specially to avoid mapping to a 0.0 color, using 0.1 instead. Floating point equality checks for npx == -0.5 may be sensitive to precision, but the source uses direct equality. Calculates the normal vector of a Gsplat given its scales (vec3) and quaternion (vec4). 1. Find minScale = min(scales.x, min(scales.y, scales.z)). 2. Determine the base normal vector in local space: if scales.z == minScale, normal is vec3(0,0,1); else if scales.y == minScale, normal is vec3(0,1,0); else normal is vec3(1,0,0). 3. Transform the normal to world space using quatVec(quaternion, normal). Not given in the sources. name: Spherical Harmonics Evaluation
head: SH Evaluation, SH2RGB, Splat Lighting
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Evaluation computes the view-dependent RGB color of a 3D Gaussian splat by evaluating real spherical harmonic basis functions against a viewing direction vector and dotting the result with stored SH coefficients. It solves the problem of compactly representing complex lighting effects within the Gaussian representation without requiring explicit light sources or ray tracing. Inputs: shs: Tensor of SH coefficients. Shape is typically (N, 3, (D+1)^2) or flattened as (N, 3 \times (D+1)^2), where N is the number of Gaussians and D is the active SH degree. viewdirs: Tensor of normalized viewing direction vectors (x, y, z) for each Gaussian. Shape (N, 3). activeshdegree: Integer specifying the maximum degree of spherical harmonics to evaluate (typically 0, 1, 2, or 3). Outputs: rgb: Tensor of RGB color values. Shape (N, 3). Data Structures: The SH coefficients are stored per Gaussian, per color channel (R, G, B), and per SH basis function. For degree D, there are (D+1)^2 coefficients per channel. The coefficients are real-valued floats. Constants: The following constants are derived from the normalization of real spherical harmonics (Condon-Shortley phase convention): C0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} \approx 0.28209479177387814 C1 = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}} \approx 0.48860251190291987 C2 = \sqrt{\frac{15}{4\pi}} \approx 1.0925484305920792 C{2,0} = \sqrt{\frac{5}{16\pi}} \approx 0.94617469575755997 C{2,2} = \sqrt{\frac{15}{16\pi}} \approx 0.54627421529603959 C3 = \sqrt{\frac{7}{16\pi}} \approx 0.59004358992664352 C{3,2} = \sqrt{\frac{105}{32\pi}} \approx 2.8906114426405538 C{3,1} = \sqrt{\frac{21}{32\pi}} \approx 0.45704579946446572 C{3,0} = \sqrt{\frac{7}{64\pi}} \approx 0.3731763325901154 Basis Functions: The real spherical harmonic basis functions Yl^m are evaluated based on the direction components x, y, z. Degree 0 (l=0): Y0^0 = C0 Degree 1 (l=1): Y{-1}^1 = -C1 y Y0^1 = C1 z Y1^1 = -C1 x Degree 2 (l=2): Y{-2}^2 = C2 xy Y{-1}^2 = -C2 yz Y0^2 = C{2,0} (3z^2 - 1) Y1^2 = -C2 xz Y2^2 = C{2,2} (x^2 - y^2) Degree 3 (l=3): Y{-3}^3 = C3 y (y^2 - 3x^2) Y{-2}^3 = C{3,2} xyz Y{-1}^3 = C{3,1} y (1 - 5z^2) Y0^3 = C{3,0} z (5z^2 - 3) Y1^3 = C{3,1} x (1 - 5z^2) Y2^3 = \frac{1}{2} C{3,2} z (x^2 - y^2) Y3^3 = C3 x (3y^2 - x^2) Algorithm Steps: 1. Input Validation & Direction: If gradients are required for viewdirs, voxcenters, or campos, raise NotImplementedError. If viewdirs is not provided but voxcenters and campos are, compute viewdirs = normalize(voxcenters - campos). Ensure viewdirs are normalized before evaluation. 2. Reshape: If shs is flattened, reshape to (N, 3, (D+1)^2). 3. Evaluate Bases: Compute SH basis functions for the given activeshdegree and viewdirs. 4. Dot Product: Compute the weighted sum of coefficients and bases: rgbsh = sum(shs bases, dim=-1). 5. Bias & Clamp: Add a 0.5 bias to the resulting color vector to shift the range, then apply ReLU or clamp to [0.0, 1.0] to ensure valid RGB values. \text{rgb} = \text{clamp}(\text{rgb} + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def evalshbases(degree, viewdirs): """ Evaluates real spherical harmonic basis functions for a batch of view directions. Returns tensor of shape (N, (degree+1)^2). """ x = viewdirs[:, 0] y = viewdirs[:, 1] z = viewdirs[:, 2] bases = [] # Degree 0 C0 = 0.28209479177387814 bases.append(C0 torch.oneslike(x)) if degree >= 1: C1 = 0.48860251190291987 bases.append(-C1 y) bases.append(C1 z) bases.append(-C1 x) if degree >= 2: C2 = 1.0925484305920792 C20 = 0.94617469575755997 C22 = 0.54627421529603959 xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, yz, xz = xy, yz, xz bases.append(C2 xy) bases.append(-C2 yz) bases.append(C20 (3zz - 1.0)) bases.append(-C2 xz) bases.append(C22 (xx - yy)) if degree >= 3: C3 = 0.59004358992664352 C32 = 2.8906114426405538 C31 = 0.45704579946446572 C30 = 0.3731763325901154 bases.append(C3 y (yy - 3xx)) bases.append(C32 x y z) bases.append(C31 y (1.0 - 5zz)) bases.append(C30 z (5zz - 3.0)) bases.append(C31 x (1.0 - 5zz)) bases.append(0.5 C32 z (xx - yy)) bases.append(C3 x (3yy - xx)) return torch.stack(bases, dim=1) def sphericalharmonicsevaluation(shs, viewdirs, activeshdegree): """ Computes RGB color from SH coefficients and view directions. Args: shs: Tensor of shape (N, 3, (activeshdegree+1)^2) or (N, 3 (activeshdegree+1)^2) viewdirs: Tensor of shape (N, 3) activeshdegree: Integer, max degree to evaluate Returns: rgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3) """ # Reshape shs to (N, 3, numbases) if flattened if shs.dim() == 2: numbases = (activeshdegree + 1) 2 shs = shs.view(shs.shape[0], 3, numbases) # Note: Sources specify raising NotImplementedError if gradients are required # for viewdirs, voxcenters, or campos. # Note: Sources specify computing viewdirs = normalize(voxcenters - campos) # if viewdirs is not provided. # Note: Sources specify transforming coefficients by the rotation component # of the global transformation matrix using Wigner-D matrices before evaluation. # Evaluate bases shmult = evalshbases(activeshdegree, viewdirs) # Dot product: sum over basis dimension rgbsh = torch.sum(shs shmult[:, None,:], dim=-1) # Add bias and clamp rgb = torch.relu(rgbsh + 0.5) return rgb Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The polynomial terms for higher degrees can suffer from precision loss if z is close to 1 or -1. Boundary Conditions: If viewdirs is not normalized, the SH evaluation will produce incorrect colors. Always normalize viewdirs before evaluation. Coefficient Indexing: Different implementations may store SH coefficients in different orders. The pseudocode assumes the standard ordering Y{-l}^l \dots Yl^l for each l. Performance: Implementations may ignore higher-degree coefficients (e.g., degree 3) for performance reasons. Spherical Harmonics Rotation computes the new SH coefficients of a function after rotating the viewing coordinate system by \pm \pi/2 around the X-axis. It sets itself apart from general rotation methods by using precomputed analytic tables for specific \pm 90^\circ rotations, avoiding expensive matrix multiplications or numerical integration. The Spherical Harmonics Encoder is a neural network module that encodes a 3D direction vector into spherical harmonics coefficients up to a specified degree. It solves the problem of representing directional information (view direction) in a differentiable, basis-function expansion for view-dependent rendering. Spherical Harmonics (SH) Data Extraction parses SH coefficients from a 3D Gaussian Splatting model file (typically a PLY format) into a structured data layout suitable for GPU rendering. It solves the problem of mapping flat, property-based storage in the source file to the hierarchical texture arrays required by the rendering engine. It is distinct from Spherical Harmonics Evaluation, which computes color from these coefficients, and Spherical Harmonics Rotation, which transforms them for view-dependent effects. Spherical Harmonics (SH) Decoding is the process of reconstructing the RGB color of a 3D Gaussian splat from its stored SH coefficients and a specific viewing direction. It serves as the final color computation step in the Gaussian Splatting pipeline, translating directional frequency data into perceptual color. It is distinguished from Spherical Harmonics Evaluation by its specific focus on unpacking and interpreting the raw coefficient storage format (often packed in GPU buffers) rather than just evaluating the basis functions, and from Spherical Harmonics Rotation which handles the transformation of coefficients to camera space. This method computes the RGB color contribution of a 3D Gaussian splat by evaluating real spherical harmonics (SH) against a viewing direction vector. It represents view-dependent lighting effects compactly within the Gaussian representation. It differs from Spherical Harmonics Evaluation by explicitly defining the lighting calculation pipeline, including the Condon–Shortley phase conventions, the mandatory 0.5 bias for numeric stability, and the exact polynomial expansions for degrees 0 through 3. A module that interprets network output as spherical harmonics coefficients to model view-dependent effects and camera-specific parameters, followed by tone mapping. The SH coefficients are the output of the last convolution of the neural network. It applies a tone mapper following Rückert et al. [RFS22] which models exposure time, white balance, sensor response, and vignetting. It uses spherical harmonics degree 2, corresponding to 27 input coefficients (9 coefficients per color channel). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D^2), where N is the number of Gaussians and D is the active SH degree. For fixed degree (e.g., D=2), it is O(N). The evaluation involves a constant number of multiplications and additions per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D^2) to store the SH coefficients. The evaluation itself requires O(N) temporary memory for the basis functions and intermediate color values. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Higher degrees increase the constant factor significantly (degree 3 has 7x more coefficients than degree 1). Strengths: Compact representation of view-dependent effects; differentiable; efficient on GPU. Limitations: High-frequency lighting details may require high degrees, increasing memory and compute cost. When to use: When view-dependent appearance is important and memory/compute budget allows for storing and evaluating SH coefficients. When not to use: For simple, view-independent materials (degree 0 is sufficient), or when extreme high-frequency details are needed and higher degrees are too expensive. Spherical Harmonics have been used in computer graphics for decades to represent lighting and reflectance. In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, they are adopted to provide a compact, differentiable way to model view-dependent appearance without the need for explicit light sources or complex BRDFs. The specific implementation details (polynomial expansions, constants) are derived from standard mathematical definitions of real spherical harmonics. name: Spherical Harmonics Rotation
head: Analytic SH Rotation, Analytic Spherical Harmonics Rotation, SH X-axis rotation tables
body: Spherical Harmonics Rotation computes the new SH coefficients of a function after rotating the viewing coordinate system by \pm \pi/2 around the X-axis. It sets itself apart from general rotation methods by using precomputed analytic tables for specific \pm 90^\circ rotations, avoiding expensive matrix multiplications or numerical integration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of SH coefficients P for a specific band l \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}. Output: A new array of coefficients P' rotated by +\pi/2 or -\pi/2 around the X-axis. Data Structures: The rotation is implemented using precomputed constant arrays (tables) indexed by the band level l. kAnalyticRotatePlusPiHalfAboutXTable: Stores the transformation rules for +\pi/2 rotation. kAnalyticRotateMinusPiHalfAboutXTable: Stores the transformation rules for -\pi/2 rotation. This table is the transpose (inverse) of the plus table. Indexing: The tables are indexed by l-1 (i.e., band 1 is index 0, band 2 is index 1, etc.). Steps: 1. Select the appropriate rotation table based on the desired rotation direction (+\pi/2 or -\pi/2). 2. Index the table using l-1 to retrieve the transformation rules for the target band. 3. Apply the linear combination rules to the input coefficient array P to produce the output array P'. Formulas: Let pi denote the input coefficient at index i (corresponding to m = i - l) and pi' denote the output coefficient. The source provides explicit linear combinations for bands l=1 to l=4 for the +\pi/2 rotation. Band l=1 (3 coefficients): \begin{aligned} p0' &= p1 \\ p1' &= -p0 \\ p2' &= p2 \end{aligned} Band l=2 (5 coefficients): Let si = pi. \begin{aligned} p0' &= s3 \\ p1' &= -s1 \\ p2' &= -0.5 s2 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} s4 \\ p3' &= -s0 \\ p4' &= -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} s2 + 0.5 s4 \end{aligned} Band l=3 (7 coefficients): \begin{aligned} p0' &= \sqrt{5/8}s3 - \sqrt{3/8}s5 \\ p1' &= -s1 \\ p2' &= \sqrt{3/8}s3 + \sqrt{5/8}s5 \\ p3' &= -\sqrt{5/8}s0 - \sqrt{3/8}s2 \\ p4' &= -0.25 s4 - \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4} s6 \\ p5' &= \sqrt{3/8}s0 - \sqrt{5/8}s2 \\ p6' &= -\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4} s4 + 0.25 s6 \end{aligned} Band l=4 (9 coefficients): \begin{aligned} p0' &= -\frac{\sqrt{14}}{4}s5 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}s7 \\ p1' &= -0.75 s1 + \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}s3 \\ p2' &= -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}s5 - \frac{\sqrt{14}}{4}s7 \\ p3' &= \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}s1 + 0.75 s3 \\ p4' &= \frac{3}{8}s4 + \frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}s6 + \frac{\sqrt{35}}{8}s8 \\ p5' &= \frac{\sqrt{14}}{4}s0 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}s2 \\ p6' &= \frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}s4 + 0.5 s6 - \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}s8 \\ p7' &= -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}s0 + \frac{\sqrt{14}}{4}s2 \\ p8' &= \frac{\sqrt{35}}{8}s4 - \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}s6 + 0.125 s8 \end{aligned} Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the +\pi/2 rotation for bands 1-4. The -\pi/2 rotation uses the inverse transformation (transpose of the plus table). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rotateshpluspihalfx(coeffs, bandl): """ Rotates SH coefficients by +pi/2 around the X-axis. Args: coeffs: List of float coefficients for band l, length 2l + 1. Indices correspond to m = -l,..., l. bandl: Integer band level (1, 2, 3, or 4). Returns: List of rotated coefficients. """ if bandl < 1 or bandl > 4: raise ValueError("Only bands 1-4 are supported by analytic tables.") n = 2 bandl + 1 p = coeffs pnew = [0.0] n if bandl == 1: pnew[0] = p[1] pnew[1] = -p[0] pnew[2] = p[2] elif bandl == 2: pnew[0] = p[3] pnew[1] = -p[1] pnew[2] = -0.5 p[2] - (math.sqrt(3) / 2) p[4] pnew[3] = -p[0] pnew[4] = -(math.sqrt(3) / 2) p[2] + 0.5 p[4] elif bandl == 3: pnew[0] = math.sqrt(5/8) p[3] - math.sqrt(3/8) p[5] pnew[1] = -p[1] pnew[2] = math.sqrt(3/8) p[3] + math.sqrt(5/8) p[5] pnew[3] = -math.sqrt(5/8) p[0] - math.sqrt(3/8) p[2] pnew[4] = -0.25 p[4] - (math.sqrt(15) / 4) p[6] pnew[5] = math.sqrt(3/8) p[0] - math.sqrt(5/8) p[2] pnew[6] = -(math.sqrt(15) / 4) p[4] + 0.25 p[6] elif bandl == 4: pnew[0] = -(math.sqrt(14) / 4) p[5] + (math.sqrt(2) / 4) p[7] pnew[1] = -0.75 p[1] + (math.sqrt(7) / 4) p[3] pnew[2] = -(math.sqrt(2) / 4) p[5] - (math.sqrt(14) / 4) p[7] pnew[3] = (math.sqrt(7) / 4) p[1] + 0.75 p[3] pnew[4] = (3/8) p[4] + (math.sqrt(5) / 4) p[6] + (math.sqrt(35) / 8) p[8] pnew[5] = (math.sqrt(14) / 4) p[0] + (math.sqrt(2) / 4) p[2] pnew[6] = (math.sqrt(5) / 4) p[4] + 0.5 p[6] - (math.sqrt(7) / 4) p[8] pnew[7] = -(math.sqrt(2) / 4) p[0] + (math.sqrt(14) / 4) p[2] pnew[8] = (math.sqrt(35) / 8) p[4] - (math.sqrt(7) / 4) p[6] + 0.125 p[8] return pnew def rotateshminuspihalfx(coeffs, bandl): """ Rotates SH coefficients by -pi/2 around the X-axis. Uses the inverse (transpose) of the +pi/2 table. """ # The source states the minus table is the transpose (inverse) of the plus table. # Explicit coefficients for the minus table are not provided in the source. # Implementation requires constructing the plus table matrix, transposing it, and applying it. pass Parameters: bandl: Must be 1, 2, 3, or 4. Higher bands are not covered by the analytic tables. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Band Limit: The analytic tables only cover bands 1-4. For band 0, no rotation is needed (constant). For bands > 4, this method is not applicable. Precision: The coefficients involve square roots and fractions that should be computed in double precision before casting to float to avoid accumulation errors. Boundaries: The method assumes coefficients are ordered by m = -l, \dots, l. It handles the rotation of SH coefficients alongside position and quaternion flips, solving the problem of maintaining visual consistency when the underlying 3D coordinate frame changes. It is distinct from simple affine transforms because it explicitly manages the coupling between geometric flips and SH band rotations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Exact analytic solution for specific rotations; no iterative approximation; very low computational overhead. Limitations: Only supports rotations of \pm \pi/2 around the X-axis. General rotations require different methods. Only supports bands 1-4. name: CoordinateConverter Composition
head: SPZ coordinate conversion pipeline
body: The CoordinateConverter Composition is a composite transformation pipeline in the SPZ format that converts Gaussian splatting parameters between coordinate systems by coupling geometric flips with analytic Spherical Harmonics (SH) rotations. It ensures visual consistency across frame changes by baking \pm\pi/2 X-axis rotations into callable position, quaternion, and per-band SH transformation functions. Inputs: from (source coordinate system identifier), to (target coordinate system identifier), shDegree (maximum SH degree, 0 \le \text{shDegree} \le 4). Output: A CoordinateConverter struct instance containing flip arrays and callable transformation functions. The CoordinateConverter struct layout is as follows: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct CoordinateConverter { std::array<float, 3> flipP; // x, y, z flips for positions std::array<float, 3> flipQ; // x, y, z flips for quaternions (w never flipped) std::array<float, 24> flipSh; // flips for 24 SH coefficients std::array<std::function<void(float)>, SHMAXDEGREE> rotFlipShFuncs; // per-band SH transforms std::function<void(float)> rotFlipPFunc; // position flip + rotation std::function<void(float)> rotFlipQFunc; // quaternion flip + rotation }; 1. Check needRotation by comparing from and to. If identical, return a default converter with identity flips and null functions. 2. Determine backward direction via bit 3 of from. 3. Shift from into the same family as to by adding or subtracting 8 (innerFrom = from ± 8). 4. Recursively call coordinateConverter(innerFrom, to, shDegree) to obtain a base converter with aligned family flips. 5. Bake the inner flip into rotFlipPFunc and rotFlipQFunc, composing it with the appropriate \pm\pi/2 rotation based on the backward flag. 6. Iterate b from 0 to shDegree - 1, select the SH rotation table (minus for backward, plus for forward), retrieve rotFn = shTable[b], and store it in result.rotFlipShFuncs[b]. Position Rotation (Rx): For a position array p = [x, y, z]: Backward (rotated \to standard): Apply flipP, then Rx(-\pi/2) via p[1]=z; p[2]=-y;. Forward (standard \to rotated): Apply Rx(+\pi/2) via p[1]=-z; p[2]=y; then flipP. Quaternion Rotation: Let s = \sqrt{2}/2. The array p holds quaternion components at indices 0–3 (p[0]=x, p[1]=y, p[2]=z, p[3]=w): Backward: Apply flipQ, then quaternion rotation: p[0]=s(-w+x); p[1]=s(y+z); p[2]=s(-y+z); p[3]=s(w+x);. Forward: Apply quaternion rotation: p[0]=s(w+x); p[1]=s(y-z); p[2]=s(y+z); p[3]=s(w-x); then flipQ. SHMAXDEGREE: A constexpr int set to 4, limiting the maximum SH degree handled by rotFlipShFuncs. Precision: The use of \sqrt{2}/2 introduces floating-point approximation. Quaternion W Component: The source explicitly states w is never flipped by flipQ. SH Degree Limit: SHMAXDEGREE is 4, so bands b \ge 4 are not handled by rotFlipShFuncs. Bit 3 Ambiguity: The determination of "backward" relies on bit 3 of from. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Callable SHMAXDEGREE = 4 class CoordinateConverter: def init(self, identity=False): if identity: self.flipP = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] self.flipQ = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] self.flipSh = [1.0] 24 self.rotFlipShFuncs = [lambda x: None] SHMAXDEGREE self.rotFlipPFunc = lambda x: None self.rotFlipQFunc = lambda x: None else: self.flipP = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.flipQ = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.flipSh = [0.0] 24 self.rotFlipShFuncs = [lambda x: None] SHMAXDEGREE self.rotFlipPFunc = None self.rotFlipQFunc = None def coordinateconverter(fromsys: int, tosys: int, shdegree: int) -> CoordinateConverter: # Step 1: Check rotation need if fromsys == tosys: return CoordinateConverter(identity=True) # Step 2: Determine direction via bit 3 isbackward = bool(fromsys & 8) # Step 3: Inner family shift (aligns with tosys) innerfrom = fromsys + 8 if isbackward else fromsys - 8 # Step 4: Recursive call for base flips base = coordinateconverter(innerfrom, tosys, shdegree) result = CoordinateConverter() result.flipP = list(base.flipP) result.flipQ = list(base.flipQ) result.flipSh = list(base.flipSh) s = math.sqrt(2) / 2 # Step 5: Compose rotations into callable functions if isbackward: # Backward: flipP then Rx(-pi/2) def rotflipp(p: List[float]) -> None: p[0] = result.flipP[0] p[1] = result.flipP[1] p[2] = result.flipP[2] y, z = p[1], p[2] p[1] = z p[2] = -y # Backward: flipQ then quaternion rotation def rotflipq(q: List[float]) -> None: q[0] = result.flipQ[0] q[1] = result.flipQ[1] q[2] = result.flipQ[2] # w is never flipped w, x, y, z = q[3], q[0], q[1], q[2] q[0] = s (-w + x) q[1] = s (y + z) q[2] = s (-y + z) q[3] = s (w + x) else: # Forward: Rx(+pi/2) then flipP def rotflipp(p: List[float]) -> None: y, z = p[1], p[2] p[1] = -z p[2] = y p[0] = result.flipP[0] p[1] = result.flipP[1] p[2] = result.flipP[2] # Forward: quaternion rotation then flipQ def rotflipq(q: List[float]) -> None: w, x, y, z = q[3], q[0], q[1], q[2] q[0] = s (w + x) q[1] = s (y - z) q[2] = s (y + z) q[3] = s (w - x) q[0] = result.flipQ[0] q[1] = result.flipQ[1] q[2] = result.flipQ[2] result.rotFlipPFunc = rotflipp result.rotFlipQFunc = rotflipq # Step 6: SH Rotation Assignment # Source does not provide the contents of shminustable or shplustable # table = shminustable if isbackward else shplustable for b in range(shdegree): if b < SHMAXDEGREE: # result.rotFlipShFuncs[b] = table[b] result.rotFlipShFuncs[b] = lambda x: None else: result.rotFlipShFuncs[b] = lambda x: None return result What it is: The composite transformation pipeline described above. What sets it apart: It combines geometric flips with analytic SH rotations in a single callable structure, optimized for the SPZ format's specific coordinate system requirements. When to choose it: Use when loading or saving SPZ files that require coordinate system conversion, or when integrating Gaussian splatting data from different sources with varying coordinate frames. Link: CoordinateConverter Composition Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient, avoids matrix multiplications by using precomputed analytic rotations and flips. Limitations: Limited to SH degree 4 and specific to the SPZ coordinate system encoding. When to use: When working with SPZ files or Gaussian splatting data that requires coordinate system alignment. When not: When using different SH degrees or coordinate systems not covered by the SPZ extensions. The CoordinateConverter Composition is part of the SPZ (Splatting Point Cloud) format developed by Niantic. It is used to handle the conversion of Gaussian splatting parameters between different coordinate systems, ensuring that the visual appearance remains consistent across different viewing contexts. The method is documented in the Niantic Labs SPZ repository. nianticlabs/spz, https://github.com/nianticlabs/spz, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonics Encoder
head: SH Encoding, Spherical Harmonics Basis
body: The Spherical Harmonics Encoder is a neural network module that encodes a 3D direction vector into spherical harmonics coefficients up to a specified degree. It solves the problem of representing directional information (view direction) in a differentiable, basis-function expansion for view-dependent rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A direction vector \mathbf{d} = (x, y, z) of dimension 3. Output: A tensor of SH coefficients with shape (input.shape[:-1], outdim), where outdim is calculated as degree 2. Data Structures and Constants: The encoder uses pre-computed constant values for the SH basis functions. The coefficients are stored in m-order (m=0, then m=-1,1, then m=-2,0,2, etc.). Constants used in the implementation: C0 = 0.28209479177387814 C1 = 0.4886025119029199 C2 = [0.4886025119029199, -0.4886025119029199, 0.7448390646052915, -0.4886025119029199, 0.10925484305920792]. The exact mapping in the source is: index 0 for xy, index 1 for yz, index 2 for 2zz-xx-yy, index 3 for xz, index 4 for xx-yy. C3, C4: Higher degree constants (values not explicitly listed in the provided notes, but structure is implied). Parameters: inputdim: Dimensionality of input vector. Must be 3. degree: Maximum degree of SH to compute. Valid range is 1 to 5. outdim: Output dimensionality, calculated as degree 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodesphericalharmonics(directions: torch.Tensor, degree: int) -> torch.Tensor: # directions shape: (batchdims, 3) assert directions.shape[-1] == 3 # Enforces inputdim == 3 assert 1 <= degree <= 5 # Enforces degree range x, y, z = directions.unbind(dim=-1) outdim = degree 2 result = torch.zeros((directions.shape[:-1], outdim), device=directions.device) # C0 = 0.28209479177387814 C1 = 0.4886025119029199 C2 = [0.4886025119029199, -0.4886025119029199, 0.7448390646052915, -0.4886025119029199, 0.10925484305920792] result[..., 0] = C0 if degree > 1: result[..., 1] = -C1 y result[..., 2] = C1 z result[..., 3] = -C1 x if degree > 2: xx, yy, zz = x x, y y, z z xy, yz, xz = x y, y z, x z result[..., 4] = C2[0] xy result[..., 5] = C2[1] yz result[..., 6] = C2[2] (2.0 zz - xx - yy) result[..., 7] = C2[3] xz result[..., 8] = C2[4] (xx - yy) if degree > 3: # Degree 3 coefficients at indices 9-15 using C3 and cubic terms # Specific formulas not provided in the source notes pass if degree > 4: # Degree 4 coefficients at indices 16-24 using C4 and quartic terms # Specific formulas not provided in the source notes pass return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: For degree 2, index 6, an alternative formula C2[2] (3.0 zz - 1) exists but is commented out in the source because xx + yy + zz == 1 on the unit sphere, yet this alternative leads to different backward gradients. The implementation uses 2.0 zz - xx - yy. Input dimension must be 3. Enforced by assertion assert self.inputdim == 3. Degree must be between 1 and 5. Enforced by assertion assert self.degree >= 1 and self.degree <= 5. SH Feature Encoding is a method for modeling view-dependent effects in neural radiance fields by multiplying each Spherical Harmonics (SH) basis coefficient with a learnable feature vector, rather than using the vanilla scalar SH encoding. It solves the problem of representing directional information (view direction) in a differentiable, basis-function expansion for view-dependent rendering by allowing the magnitude and orientation of the SH response to be modulated by spatially varying features. It differs from vanilla SH encoding Spherical Harmonics Evaluation by introducing learnable per-coefficient feature vectors predicted from the scene's spatial features, and differs from the SPZ Encoder by relying on the explicit SH basis expansion rather than a direct parameterization. The SPZ Encoder serializes Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients into a compact byte array. It handles degree clamping, dimension mapping, and fixed-point quantization for view-dependent color data. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with batch size (number of rays/directions). Strengths: Differentiable, efficient basis expansion for view-dependent effects. Limitations: Limited to low-degree expansions for efficiency; higher degrees require more memory and computation. When to use: When view-dependent color variation is needed in a differentiable rendering pipeline (e.g., NeRF, 3DGS). When not: When view-independent color is sufficient, or when rotation of SH coefficients is required (use Spherical Harmonics Rotation). name: SH Feature Encoding
head: Spherical Harmonics Feature Encoding
body: SH Feature Encoding is a method for modeling view-dependent effects in neural radiance fields by multiplying each Spherical Harmonics (SH) basis coefficient with a learnable feature vector, rather than using the vanilla scalar SH encoding. It solves the problem of representing directional information (view direction) in a differentiable, basis-function expansion for view-dependent rendering by allowing the magnitude and orientation of the SH response to be modulated by spatially varying features. It differs from vanilla SH encoding Spherical Harmonics Evaluation by introducing learnable per-coefficient feature vectors predicted from the scene's spatial features, and differs from the SPZ Encoder by relying on the explicit SH basis expansion rather than a direct parameterization. Inputs: 1. Rendered feature vector F{rendered}: A feature vector output by the Volume Feature Rendering (VFR) or spatial feature representation at the query point. 2. View direction d: A 3D vector representing the camera-to-point direction. 3. SH degree L: The maximum degree of spherical harmonics. Outputs: 1. Final rendered color C: A 3D RGB vector. Data Structures: SH Feature Vector (fl^m): A learnable vector associated with each SH coefficient (l, m), predicted by a spatial MLP from the rendered feature vector. Bottleneck Feature Vector (F{bottleneck}): A view-independent feature vector, also predicted by the spatial MLP. Encoding Vector (E): The concatenation of all SH feature encodings el^m. Numbered Steps: 1. Spatial MLP Prediction: Feed the rendered feature vector F{rendered} into a spatial Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). This MLP outputs two vectors: the SH feature vector F{SH}, which is split into individual feature vectors fl^m for each SH coefficient (l, m) where l \in \{0, \dots, L\} and m \in \{-l, \dots, l\}, and the bottleneck feature vector F{bottleneck}, which is view-independent. 2. SH Feature Encoding: For each SH coefficient (l, m), compute the SH feature encoding el^m by multiplying the learnable feature vector fl^m by the SH basis function value Yl^m(d) for the view direction d. 3. Concatenation: Concatenate all resultant SH encodings el^m to form a comprehensive encoding vector E. 4. Final Concatenation: Concatenate the encoding vector E with the bottleneck feature vector F{bottleneck}. 5. Directional MLP: Feed the concatenated vector into a directional MLP to predict the final rendered color C. Formulas: The core SH feature encoding for coefficient (l, m) is defined as: el^m = fl^m Yl^m(d) Where: el^m is the SH feature encoding vector for degree l and order m. fl^m is the learnable SH feature vector for degree l and order m. Yl^m(d) is the value of the Spherical Harmonics basis function of degree l and order m evaluated at view direction d. d is the view direction vector. l is the degree, m \in \{-l, -(l-1), \dots, 0, \dots, l-1, l\}. The final color is predicted by a directional MLP M{dir} applied to the concatenated features: C = M{dir}(\text{Concat}(E, F{bottleneck})) Where E = \{el^m \mid 0 \le l \le L, -l \le m \le l\}. Parameters: SH Degree (L): The maximum degree of spherical harmonics. Typical values are L=4 for NeRF synthetic datasets and L=7 for Real-world 360 datasets. Number of SH Features: The dimension of the learnable feature vectors fl^m is 4 for NeRF synthetic datasets and 8 for Real-world 360 datasets. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The multiplication of fl^m (learnable vector) and Yl^m(d) (scalar) scales the vector element-wise. Degenerate Input: If the rendered feature vector F{rendered} is zero or undefined, the spatial MLP output may be degenerate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class SHFeatureEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, maxdegree: int, featuredim: int): super().init() self.maxdegree = maxdegree self.featuredim = featuredim # Total coefficients: sum{l=0}^{L} (2l+1) self.numcoeffs = sum(2 l + 1 for l in range(maxdegree + 1)) # Spatial MLP: maps rendered feature to [SH features, bottleneck] # Input/output dimensions are implementation details not specified in sources. self.spatialmlp = nn.Linear(256, self.numcoeffs featuredim + 64) # Directional MLP: maps concatenated features to RGB self.directionalmlp = nn.Linear(self.numcoeffs featuredim + 64, 3) def forward(self, renderedfeature: torch.Tensor, viewdirection: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Step 1: Spatial MLP Prediction mlpout = self.spatialmlp(renderedfeature) shfeaturesflat = mlpout[:,:self.numcoeffs self.featuredim] bottleneckfeature = mlpout[:, self.numcoeffs self.featuredim:] # Reshape to (batch, numcoeffs, featuredim) shfeatures = shfeaturesflat.view(renderedfeature.size(0), self.numcoeffs, self.featuredim) # Step 2: SH Feature Encoding # Compute SH basis values Yl^m(d) for all coefficients in order l=0..L, m=-l..l shbasis = self.computeshbasis(viewdirection) # (batch, numcoeffs) # el^m = fl^m Yl^m(d) shencodings = shfeatures shbasis.unsqueeze(-1) # Step 3 & 4: Concatenation shencodingsflat = shencodings.view(renderedfeature.size(0), -1) combined = torch.cat([shencodingsflat, bottleneckfeature], dim=1) # Step 5: Directional MLP color = self.directionalmlp(combined) return color def computeshbasis(self, d: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: batchsize = d.size(0) shvals = torch.zeros(batchsize, self.numcoeffs, device=d.device) idx = 0 for l in range(self.maxdegree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): shvals[:, idx] = self.shbasisvalue(d, l, m) idx += 1 return shvals def shbasisvalue(self, d: torch.Tensor, l: int, m: int) -> torch.Tensor: x, y, z = d[:, 0], d[:, 1], d[:, 2] r = torch.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) r2 = r r invr = 1.0 / r invr2 = invr invr if l == 0 and m == 0: return torch.fulllike(x, 1.0 / math.sqrt(4 math.pi)) elif l == 1 and m == -1: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) (y invr)) elif l == 1 and m == 0: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) (z invr)) elif l == 1 and m == 1: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) (x invr)) elif l == 2 and m == -2: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) (x y invr2)) elif l == 2 and m == -1: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) (y z invr2)) elif l == 2 and m == 0: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(5 / (4 math.pi)) (3 z z invr2 - 1) 0.5) elif l == 2 and m == 1: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) (x z invr2)) elif l == 2 and m == 2: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) (x x - y y) invr2 0.5) elif l == 3 and m == -3: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(35 / (4 math.pi)) (x y z invr2 invr)) elif l == 3 and m == -2: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(35 / (4 math.pi)) (y (3 x x - y y) invr2 invr)) elif l == 3 and m == -1: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(21 / (4 math.pi)) (y (5 z z - r2) invr2 invr)) elif l == 3 and m == 0: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(7 / (4 math.pi)) (5 z z z invr2 invr - 3 z invr)) elif l == 3 and m == 1: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(21 / (4 math.pi)) (x (5 z z - r2) invr2 invr)) elif l == 3 and m == 2: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(105 / (4 math.pi)) (z (x x - y y) invr2 invr)) elif l == 3 and m == 3: return torch.fulllike(x, math.sqrt(35 / (4 math.pi)) (x x x - 3 x y y) invr2 invr) else: # Higher degrees follow standard normalization conventions return torch.zeroslike(x) Uses scalar SH coefficients directly without learnable feature vectors. Simpler but less flexible for view-dependent effects. Choose when computational resources are limited and view-dependent effects are mild. Spherical Harmonics Evaluation A different method for encoding view direction. Choose when a direct parameterization is preferred over basis expansion. SPZ Encoder Time Complexity: Depends on the number of SH coefficients and the dimension of the feature vectors. The multiplication fl^m Yl^m(d) is O(1) per coefficient if fl^m is a vector of fixed size. The MLPs add linear complexity with respect to their input/output dimensions. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of SH coefficients times the feature vector dimension, plus the MLP parameters. Measured Performance: On NeRF synthetic dataset, VFR with SH feature encoding achieves similar quality to existing methods in significantly less time (0.97 minutes for 6K steps vs hours for NeRF). Scaling: Scales with the number of SH coefficients and the feature vector dimension. Higher SH degrees and feature dimensions increase accuracy but also computational cost. Strengths: Captures complex view-dependent effects by modulating SH coefficients with learnable features. Efficient training compared to some other methods. Limitations: Requires learnable parameters for each SH coefficient, increasing memory usage. Performance depends on the capacity of the spatial and directional MLPs. When to use: When modeling strong view-dependent effects (e.g., specular highlights, reflections) in neural radiance fields. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and view-dependent effects are negligible. SH Feature Encoding was introduced in the context of Volume Feature Rendering (VFR) for fast neural radiance field reconstruction. It is a variant of the rendering equation encoding proposed in [9] (referenced in the sources). The method was developed to improve the modeling of view-dependent effects compared to vanilla SH encoding. The implementation details mention using the NerfAcc library and Multiresolution Hash Grid (MHG) for feature representation. name: SPZ Encoder
body: The SPZ Encoder serializes Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients into a compact byte array. It handles degree clamping, dimension mapping, and fixed-point quantization for view-dependent color data. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes Spherical Harmonics coefficients (floating-point values) and a maximum SH degree as inputs. It outputs a byte array containing the encoded SPZ data. Data Structures: The encoder maintains internal state fields: maxShDegree (clamped degree), fractionalbits (u8), and version (u32, optional). Byte layout details are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Clamp the input SH degree to the specified maximum SH degree. 2. Update the internal maxShDegree field to match the clamped value. 3. Initialize the encoder with the clamped degree, fractionalbits, and optional version. 4. Execute the encoding process to produce the final byte array. Formulas: The unquantized SH coefficient x is calculated from the quantized integer value x{int} as: x = \frac{x{int} - 128.0}{128.0} The inverse operation to quantize a float x to x{int} uses a fixed scaling factor of 128.0. Parameters: fractionalbits (u8) and version (u32, optional). Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unsupported SH degrees log an error and return 0 dimensions. Precision loss occurs during quantization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodespz(shcoefficients: list[float], maxshdegree: int, fractionalbits: int, version: int | None = None) -> bytes: # 1. Clamp SH degree of inner data to specified maximum clampeddegree = maxshdegree # 2. Update internal maxShDegree field maxshdegree = clampeddegree # 3. Map degree to dimensions dimmap = {0: 0, 1: 3, 2: 8, 3: 15} numdims = dimmap.get(clampeddegree, 0) if numdims == 0: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported SH degree: {maxshdegree}") # # 4. Initialize encoder with clamped degree, fractionalbits, and optional version encoderstate = { "maxshdegree": maxshdegree, "fractionalbits": fractionalbits, "version": version } # 5. Execute encoding to produce byte array bytearray = bytearray() bytearray.append(clampeddegree) for coeff in shcoefficients: # Quantize: xint = round(coeff 128.0 + 128.0) xint = round(coeff 128.0 + 128.0) xint = max(0, min(255, xint)) bytearray.append(xint) return bytes(bytearray) Maps SH degree to dimension count: Degree 0 -> 0 dimensions, Degree 1 -> 3 dimensions, Degree 2 -> 8 dimensions, Degree 3 -> 15 dimensions. Unsupported SH degrees log an error and return 0. Reconstructs floating-point coefficients from quantized integers using the formula x = \frac{x{int} - 128.0}{128.0}. Origin and history are not given in the sources. The method is referenced in web-based Gaussian splatting viewers. sparkjsdev/spark, https://github.com/sparkjsdev/spark, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, https://github.com/mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Neural Basis Functions
head: Fourier basis, General basis form, b basis
body: Neural Basis Functions are a set of parameterized mathematical functions used to represent the directional component \tilde{H} in the rendering equation, allowing for the ablation and comparison of different functional forms for view-dependent color prediction. They solve the problem of encoding viewing direction into a differentiable feature vector that a neural network can process. What sets them apart from siblings like Spherical Harmonics Encoder is the explicit use of custom analytic forms (Fourier, Ka,b, Pa,b) tailored to specific viewing constraints (e.g., forward-facing hemispheres) rather than relying on standard orthogonal polynomial bases. The core mechanism involves mapping a viewing direction vector v to a fixed-length feature vector \tilde{H}(v). For forward-facing scenarios, the viewing angle v is constrained to a hemisphere. In this case, the z-component vz is fully determined by the x and y components via the constraint: vz = \sqrt{1 - vx^2 - vy^2} Consequently, the basis functions can be parameterized using only vx and vy. The general form of the neural basis combines real and imaginary parts of complex-valued functions K{a,b} and P{a,b}. A basis similar to the positional encoding used in NeRF [22]. It is defined for forward-facing scenarios using only vx and vy. It is chosen when a simple, high-frequency periodic encoding is sufficient and the viewing domain is hemispherical. See Fourier Basis. A general analytic form using parameters a, b, m. It is chosen for more complex view-dependent effects where the Fourier basis may be insufficient. It is defined for general viewing directions. See Ka,b and Pa,b Basis. The concept was introduced in "NeX: Real-time View Synthesis with Neural Basis Expansion" (CVPR 2021) by Ben Mildenhall, Pratul P. Srinivasan, Rodrigo Ortiz-Cayon, Nima Khademi Kalantari, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Ren Ng, and Abhishek Kar. The work builds upon the neural radiance field (NeRF) framework [22] and aims to provide practical view synthesis with prescriptive sampling guidelines. The ablation study of these basis functions is detailed in the supplementary material of the NeX paper. The Fourier basis \tilde{H}{FS}(v) is designed for forward-facing scenarios where the viewing angle covers a hemisphere. It uses the positional encoding approach similar to NeRF [22]. Given the viewing angle components vx and vy, and a maximum frequency index N, the basis is computed as: \tilde{H}{FS}(v) = [\cos(2^{-1}\pi vx), \sin(2^{-1}\pi vx), \dots, \cos(2^N \pi vx), \sin(2^N \pi vx), \dots, \cos(2^N \pi vy), \sin(2^N \pi vy)] Note: The source text lists the sequence as ending with vy terms, implying interleaved or concatenated frequencies for both axes. The exact ordering in the source is: \cos(2^{-1}\pi vx), \sin(2^{-1}\pi vx), \dots, \cos(2^N \pi vy), \sin(2^N \pi vy). This general form uses complex-valued functions K{a,b}(v) and P{a,b}(v) defined by parameters a, b, m. The components vx, vy, vz are the viewing angle components. The function K{a,b}(v) is defined as: K{a,b}(v) = \left( \frac{vx}{\sqrt{vz - a}} \frac{vz - a}{vz + 1} \right)^m \left( \frac{vy}{\sqrt{vz + 1}} \frac{vz - a}{vz + 1} \right)^m The function P{a,b}(v) is defined as: P{a,b}(v) = vz^{1-a} \frac{vz - 1 + m + 1}{b + 2m + 2} The final neural basis \tilde{H}(v) combines the real and imaginary parts of these functions: \tilde{H}(v) = [ \text{Re}(K{a,b}(v)), \text{Im}(K{a,b}(v)), \text{Re}(P{a,b}(v) \cdot K{a,b}(v)), \text{Re}(K{a,b}(v)), \text{Re}(K{a,b}(v)) ] Note: The source lists \text{Re}(K{a,b}(v)) twice at the end of the vector. The parameters a, b, m are not explicitly defined in the provided notes, but are treated as configurable hyperparameters. name: Spherical Harmonics Data Extraction
head: PLY Harmonics Data Extraction, f_rest extraction
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Data Extraction parses SH coefficients from a 3D Gaussian Splatting model file (typically a PLY format) into a structured data layout suitable for GPU rendering. It solves the problem of mapping flat, property-based storage in the source file to the hierarchical texture arrays required by the rendering engine. It is distinct from Spherical Harmonics Evaluation, which computes color from these coefficients, and Spherical Harmonics Rotation, which transforms them for view-dependent effects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A PLY file containing vertex data for N Gaussians. The data includes standard properties (position, covariance, opacity) and optional SH properties named fresty where y is an integer index. Output: A set of texture data arrays per emitter (Gaussian), organized by SH degree level (L1, L2, L31, L32). Data Structures: The extraction organizes coefficients into four arrays per emitter. Each coefficient is a 3-component vector (RGB). 1. harmonicsL1TextureData: Stores Level 1 harmonics. Contains 9 coefficients (3 degrees \times 3 channels). Layout: 3 pixels per Gaussian, where each pixel holds 3 coefficients. 2. harmonicsL2TextureData: Stores Level 2 harmonics. Contains 15 coefficients. Layout: 5 pixels per Gaussian. 3. harmonicsL31TextureData: Stores the first part of Level 3 harmonics. Contains 12 coefficients. Layout: 4 pixels per Gaussian. 4. harmonicsL32TextureData: Stores the second part of Level 3 harmonics. Contains 9 coefficients. Layout: 3 pixels per Gaussian. Total coefficients per Gaussian: 9 + 15 + 12 + 9 = 45 (15 SH coefficients \times 3 RGB channels). Numbered Steps: 1. Detect Higher Order Harmonics: Iterate y from 0 to 44 with a step of 3. For each y, check if the property key "frest" + y exists in the vertex data. If any key is missing, set higherOrderHarmonicsExists to false and stop. If all are present, set it to true. 2. Extract Level 1 (L1): If higherOrderHarmonicsExists is true, iterate y from 0 to 8 with a step of 3. For each y, read the values for indices "fresty", "fresty+1", and "fresty+2" for the current Gaussian i. Construct an RGB color vector from these three values. Append this vector to harmonicsL1TextureData for the current emitter. 3. Extract Level 2 (L2): If higherOrderHarmonicsExists is true, iterate y from 9 to 23 with a step of 3. For each y, read indices "fresty", "fresty+1", and "fresty+2". Construct the RGB vector and append to harmonicsL2TextureData. 4. Extract Level 3 Part 1 (L31): If higherOrderHarmonicsExists is true, iterate y from 24 to 35 with a step of 3. For each y, read indices "fresty", "fresty+1", and "fresty+2". Construct the RGB vector and append to harmonicsL31TextureData. 5. Extract Level 3 Part 2 (L32): If higherOrderHarmonicsExists is true, iterate y from 36 to 44 with a step of 3. For each y, read indices "fresty", "fresty+1", and "fresty+2". Construct the RGB vector and append to harmonicsL32TextureData. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractshdata(vertexdata: List[Dict[str, float]], numgaussians: int) -> Dict[str, List[List[float]]]: """ Extracts SH coefficients from PLY vertex data. vertexdata: List of dicts, where each dict represents a Gaussian's properties. Keys are strings like 'frest0', 'frest1', etc. Returns: Dictionary with keys 'L1', 'L2', 'L31', 'L32', each containing a list of lists of RGB vectors. """ # Step 1: Check for existence of higher order harmonics higherorderexists = True for y in range(0, 45, 3): key = f"frest{y}" if key not in vertexdata[0]: higherorderexists = False break if not higherorderexists: return {'L1': [], 'L2': [], 'L31': [], 'L32': []} # Initialize storage for one emitter (Gaussian) l1data = [] l2data = [] l31data = [] l32data = [] # Process each Gaussian for i in range(numgaussians): gauss = vertexdata[i] # Step 2: Extract L1 (y=0 to 8, step 3) for y in range(0, 9, 3): r = gauss[f"frest{y}"] g = gauss[f"frest{y+1}"] b = gauss[f"frest{y+2}"] l1data.append([r, g, b]) # Step 3: Extract L2 (y=9 to 23, step 3) for y in range(9, 24, 3): r = gauss[f"frest{y}"] g = gauss[f"frest{y+1}"] b = gauss[f"frest{y+2}"] l2data.append([r, g, b]) # Step 4: Extract L31 (y=24 to 35, step 3) for y in range(24, 36, 3): r = gauss[f"frest{y}"] g = gauss[f"frest{y+1}"] b = gauss[f"frest{y+2}"] l31data.append([r, g, b]) # Step 5: Extract L32 (y=36 to 44, step 3) for y in range(36, 45, 3): r = gauss[f"frest{y}"] g = gauss[f"frest{y+1}"] b = gauss[f"frest{y+2}"] l32data.append([r, g, b]) return { 'L1': l1data, 'L2': l2data, 'L31': l31data, 'L32': l32data } Parameters: higherOrderHarmonicsExists: Boolean flag. Default true. Set to false if any fresty key (for y=0, 3, \dots, 42) is missing from the vertex data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Properties: If the PLY file does not contain higher-order SH coefficients, the extraction must handle the absence gracefully by skipping the respective levels or returning empty arrays. Index Bounds: Ensure that reading fresty+1 and fresty+2 does not exceed the defined range of SH coefficients (up to 44). The loops are structured to prevent out-of-bounds access. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of Gaussians and D is the number of SH coefficients (45 for full SH3). The extraction is a linear scan of the vertex data. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot C), where C is the number of coefficients per Gaussian (45 floats). The data is stored in four separate arrays per emitter. Strengths: Direct mapping from PLY property names to texture data simplifies the pipeline. Separation by level allows for flexible LOD management. Limitations: Requires the PLY file to have specific property naming conventions (fresty). If the file format changes, the extraction logic must be updated. When to Use: When loading a 3D Gaussian Splatting model for rendering in an engine that uses texture-based SH storage. When Not to Use: If the model uses a different SH parameterization or if real-time extraction is not required (e.g., offline processing). The method originates from the implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting in Unreal Engine, specifically the unreal-splat project. It adapts the standard PLY format used by 3DGS to the texture-based SH representation required by the engine's renderer. The separation into L1, L2, L31, and L32 levels reflects the engine's internal organization of SH coefficients for efficient sampling and rotation. name: Spherical Harmonics Decoding
head: RGB SH decoding, SH coefficient unpacking
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Decoding reconstructs the RGB color of a 3D Gaussian splat from its stored SH coefficients. It focuses on unpacking and interpreting the raw coefficient storage format, typically packed in GPU buffers, rather than evaluating the basis functions. It is distinguished from Spherical Harmonics Evaluation which computes the final color from coefficients and direction, and from Spherical Harmonics Rotation which transforms coefficients to camera space. Inputs: coefficientspacked: A flat Uint32Array storing SH coefficients, packed 4 per 32-bit word. degree: The maximum SH degree used (typically 0, 1, 2, or 3). SHKEYS: A lookup table mapping coefficient groups to their corresponding SH basis indices. Outputs: color: A 3-component RGB vector (R, G, B) representing the decoded color. Data Structures: Uint32Array: The storage format where each 32-bit word contains 4 float values, corresponding to one RGB channel component across multiple coefficients. SHKEYS: A mapping array where SHKEYS[coefficient >> 2] determines the base index for the SH basis in the packed buffer. Steps: 1. Compute the coefficient count as degree (degree + 2). 2. Initialize an RGB accumulator to [0, 0, 0] and a result array of the computed length. 3. Iterate through each coefficient index c from 0 to N-1. 4. Determine the source array index using SHKEYS[c >> 2]. 5. Calculate the word offset using base + (c & 3), where base = index 4. 6. Read the 32-bit word from the array, defaulting to 0 if the index is out of bounds or missing. 7. Decode the word to RGB using a helper function decodeShRgbToArray. 8. Store the decoded color in the result array and add it to the RGB accumulator. 9. Return the accumulated RGB color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodeshrgb(coefficientspacked, degree, SHKEYS): # Compute coefficient count as per source numcoeffs = degree (degree + 2) # Initialize RGB accumulator and result array racc, gacc, bacc = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 result = [None] numcoeffs for c in range(numcoeffs): # Determine source array index using SHKEYS lookup index = SHKEYS[c >> 2] base = index 4 offset = c & 3 # Read word, defaulting to 0 if missing word = coefficientspacked[base + offset] if (base + offset) < len(coefficientspacked) else 0 # Decode word to RGB via source-specific function # The exact implementation of decodeShRgbToArray is not provided in the sources. r, g, b = decodeShRgbToArray(word) # Store in result and accumulate result[c] = (r, g, b) racc += r gacc += g bacc += b return [racc, gacc, bacc] Parameters: degree: Integer, typically 0, 1, 2, or 3. SHKEYS: Lookup table mapping coefficient groups to SH basis indices, specific to the implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Reading from Uint32Array requires careful bit-packing interpretation, as the raw bits must be reinterpreted as floats. Missing Data: If a coefficient index is out of bounds, the implementation defaults to 0. Boundary Conditions: Ensure array bounds are checked before accessing coefficientspacked to prevent out-of-bounds errors. Reconstructs the base diffuse color of a 3D Gaussian splat from its stored zeroth-order spherical harmonic coefficient (SH0). It serves as the fallback color mechanism for the COLOR0 attribute in glTF, allowing renderers without 3D Gaussian splatting support to display the point cloud with correct diffuse shading. It is distinguished from higher-degree SH decoding by evaluating only the constant basis function, ignoring directional variation. A decoding strategy that concatenates the accumulated harmonics with ray direction encoding and decodes the final pixel color using a shallow MLP in a single image-space pass. It encodes the ray direction \mathbf{d} using second-degree spherical harmonics \text{SH}2(\mathbf{d}) \in \mathbb{R}^9. The final color \mathbf{c} is computed as: \mathbf{c} = \text{MLP}\theta \left( \sum{i \in \mathcal{G}} \alphai Ti \begin{bmatrix} \sin(\mathbf{f}i) \\ \cos(\mathbf{f}i) \end{bmatrix}, k \cdot \text{SH}2(\mathbf{d}) \right) where \text{MLP}\theta is a shallow MLP with weights \theta, k is a scaling factor, \alphai and Ti are primitive opacity and accumulated transmittance, and \mathbf{f}i are primitive features. The scaling factor k is applied to the spherical harmonics encoding of the ray direction. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of coefficients N, i.e., O(N). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of coefficients N. Strengths: Efficient unpacking from GPU buffers; supports variable degrees; fallback compatibility with glTF. Limitations: Requires specific packing format; SHKEYS lookup is implementation-specific. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussian splats with directional color variation; when compatibility with glTF is required. When not to use: When high-frequency directional detail is not needed (use Degree 0); when real-time performance is critical and degree is high (consider lower degree or neural decoding). Spherical Harmonics Decoding is a core component of 3D Gaussian Splatting, a method for real-time radiance field rendering. The specific packing format described in is from an unofficial implementation (Gaussian-Splat-Lite) aimed at glTF compatibility. Neural Deferred Shading, a variant, was proposed in "Neural Harmonic Textures for High-Quality Primitive Based Neural Reconstruction". name: Spherical Harmonics Degree 0 Color Reconstruction
head: Fallback Color Calculation, SH0 Color Processing, _COEF_0 Decoding
body: Reconstructs the base color of a 3D Gaussian splat from its stored zeroth-order spherical harmonic coefficient (SH0). It serves as the fallback color mechanism for the COLOR0 attribute in glTF, allowing renderers without 3D Gaussian splatting support to color the points in the sparse point cloud. It is distinguished from higher-degree SH decoding by evaluating only the constant basis function, ignoring directional variation. Inputs: coef0: A 3-component vector (RGB) containing the stored SH0 coefficients for the splat. colorspace: A string indicating the color space of the input data (e.g., "srgbrec709display", "linrec709display"). Outputs: color: A 3-component linear RGB vector representing the reconstructed diffuse color. Data Structures: coef0: Typically stored as 3 floats (or packed integers in glTF extensions) representing the RGB coefficients. Steps: 1. For each component C{in} \in \{R, G, B\} of coef0: a. Multiply by the SH0 constant k0 = 0.282095. b. Add the bias b = 0.5. c. Clamp the result to the range [0, 1]. 2. If colorspace is "srgbrec709display", apply the inverse sRGB transfer function to the clamped linear values to decode them into the final linear color space. 3. Return the resulting 3-component vector. Formula: C{out} = \text{clamp}(C{in} \cdot 0.282095 + 0.5, 0, 1) Where C{in} is the stored RGB coefficient and C{out} is the intermediate clamped value. If colorspace is "srgbrec709display", the final color C{final} is obtained by applying the inverse sRGB transfer function to C{out}. Parameters: k0 = 0.282095 (exact value 0.2820947917738781): The multiplicative scaling factor for the degree-0 spherical harmonic basis evaluation. b = 0.5: The bias added to shift the coefficient range to the standard color range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Space Mismatch: The COLOR0 attribute in glTF stores linear values. If the scene uses 'srgbrec709display', the clamped [0, 1] values must be decoded from sRGB to linear before rendering; otherwise, colors will appear washed out or incorrect. Alpha Channel: The alpha channel of the resulting COLOR0 SHOULD contain the opacity of the splat, separate from the RGB reconstruction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructsh0color(coef0: tuple, colorspace: str) -> tuple: """ Reconstructs the base color of a 3D Gaussian splat from SH0 coefficients. Args: coef0: Tuple of 3 floats (R, G, B) representing the stored SH0 coefficients. colorspace: String indicating the color space, e.g., 'srgbrec709display'. Returns: Tuple of 3 floats (R, G, B) in linear color space. """ k0 = 0.282095 bias = 0.5 reconstructed = [] for cin in coef0: cout = cin k0 + bias cout = max(0.0, min(1.0, cout)) if colorspace == "srgbrec709display": # Standard inverse sRGB transfer function if cout <= 0.04045: clinear = cout / 12.92 else: clinear = ((cout + 0.055) / 1.055) 2.4 reconstructed.append(clinear) else: reconstructed.append(cout) return tuple(reconstructed) Time Complexity: O(1) per splat, involving a constant number of arithmetic operations and a conditional branch. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring no additional memory beyond the input coefficients and output color vector. Strengths: Extremely fast execution makes it suitable for fallback rendering where full SH evaluation is not supported. Limitations: Only provides diffuse color and ignores directional lighting effects captured by higher-degree SH coefficients. This method is defined in the KHRgaussiansplatting extension for glTF. It enables interoperability by providing a standardized way to extract the base color from the SH0 coefficient, which is stored in the KHRgaussiansplatting:SHDEGREE0COEF0 attribute. The constant 0.282095 corresponds to the value of the zeroth-order spherical harmonic basis function Y{0,0}. name: Spherical Harmonics Lighting Calculation
head: SH Evaluation with Lighting, SH Lighting
body: This method computes the RGB color contribution of a 3D Gaussian splat by evaluating real spherical harmonics against a viewing direction vector. It represents view-dependent lighting effects compactly within the Gaussian representation. It differs from Spherical Harmonics Evaluation by explicitly defining the lighting calculation pipeline, including the Condon–Shortley phase conventions, the mandatory 0.5 bias for numeric stability, and the exact polynomial expansions for degrees 0 through 3. Inputs: SH{l,m}: The spherical harmonic coefficients for the Gaussian, stored as RGB vectors. For each degree l, there are 2l+1 coefficients (orders m = -l \dots l), each containing values for the red, green, and blue channels. \mathbf{v} = (x, y, z): The normalized viewing direction vector. Outputs: \mathbf{C}{final}: The resulting RGB color vector. Data Structures: The coefficients are stored such that for degree n, the total number of RGB coefficients is SHn \times 3 = SH{total}, where SHn is the count of SH basis functions for that degree. This yields 3 coefficients for Degree 0, 9 for Degree 1, 15 for Degree 2, and 21 for Degree 3. Step-by-Step Calculation: 1. Normalize Direction: Ensure the direction vector \mathbf{v} is a unit vector. In 3D Gaussian Splatting, direction vectors are normalized, so r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} = 1 when evaluating spherical harmonics. 2. Compute Degree 0 (Diffuse): Calculate the zeroth-order contribution. Color{SH0} = SH{0,0} \cdot 0.2820947917738781 Where SH{0,0} is the vector of 3 RGB coefficients for the zeroth-order real spherical harmonic. 3. Compute Degree 1 (First Order): Color{SH1} = SH{1,-1} \cdot y \cdot -0.4886025119029199 + SH{1,0} \cdot z \cdot 0.4886025119029199 + SH{1,1} \cdot x \cdot -0.4886025119029199 Where SH{1,m} are the RGB coefficient vectors for orders -1, 0, 1. 4. Compute Degree 2 (Second Order): Color{SH2} = SH{2,-2} \cdot xy \cdot 1.092548430592079 + SH{2,-1} \cdot yz \cdot -1.092548430592079 + SH{2,0} \cdot (2z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot 0.3153915652525200 + SH{2,1} \cdot xz \cdot -1.092548430592079 + SH{2,2} \cdot (x^2 - y^2) \cdot 0.5462742152960395 5. Compute Degree 3 (Third Order): Color{SH3} = SH{3,-3} \cdot y(3x^2 - y^2) \cdot -0.5900435899266435 + SH{3,-2} \cdot xyz \cdot 2.890611442640554 + SH{3,-1} \cdot y(4z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot -0.4570457994644657 + SH{3,0} \cdot z(2z^2 - 3x^2 - 3y^2) \cdot 0.3731763325901154 + SH{3,1} \cdot x(4z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot -0.4570457994644657 + SH{3,2} \cdot z(x^2 - y^2) \cdot 1.445305721320277 + SH{3,3} \cdot x(x^2 - 3y^2) \cdot -0.5900435899266435 6. Sum and Bias: Sum the contributions from all available degrees and apply the 0.5 bias. Color{final} = Color{SH0} + Color{SH1} + Color{SH2} + Color{SH3} + 0.5 The 0.5 bias is applied to keep the spherical harmonics within the [0, 1] range during training and rendering, ensuring numeric stability and allowing coefficients to remain in a valid range for unsigned normalized color buffers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalharmonicslighting(shcoeffs, directionx, directiony, directionz): """ Computes the RGB color of a Gaussian using Spherical Harmonics. Args: shcoeffs: A dictionary mapping (l, m) tuples to lists of 3 floats [R, G, B]. directionx, directiony, directionz: Components of the normalized viewing direction vector. Returns: List of 3 floats representing the final RGB color. """ # Constants from C0 = 0.2820947917738781 C1 = 0.4886025119029199 C22m2 = 1.092548430592079 C22m1 = -1.092548430592079 C220 = 0.3153915652525200 C221 = -1.092548430592079 C222 = 0.5462742152960395 C33m3 = -0.5900435899266435 C33m2 = 2.890611442640554 C33m1 = -0.4570457994644657 C330 = 0.3731763325901154 C331 = -0.4570457994644657 C332 = 1.445305721320277 C333 = -0.5900435899266435 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Degree 0 if (0, 0) in shcoeffs: coeff = shcoeffs[(0, 0)] color[0] += coeff[0] C0 color[1] += coeff[1] C0 color[2] += coeff[2] C0 # Degree 1 if (1, -1) in shcoeffs and (1, 0) in shcoeffs and (1, 1) in shcoeffs: c1m1 = shcoeffs[(1, -1)] c10 = shcoeffs[(1, 0)] c11 = shcoeffs[(1, 1)] color[0] += c1m1[0] directiony -C1 + c10[0] directionz C1 + c11[0] directionx -C1 color[1] += c1m1[1] directiony -C1 + c10[1] directionz C1 + c11[1] directionx -C1 color[2] += c1m1[2] directiony -C1 + c10[2] directionz C1 + c11[2] directionx -C1 # Degree 2 if all((2, m) in shcoeffs for m in [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]): xy = directionx directiony yz = directiony directionz xz = directionx directionz term20 = 2 directionz2 - directionx2 - directiony2 term22 = directionx2 - directiony2 c2m2 = shcoeffs[(2, -2)] c2m1 = shcoeffs[(2, -1)] c20 = shcoeffs[(2, 0)] c21 = shcoeffs[(2, 1)] c22 = shcoeffs[(2, 2)] color[0] += c2m2[0] xy C22m2 + c2m1[0] yz C22m1 + c20[0] term20 C220 + c21[0] xz C221 + c22[0] term22 C222 color[1] += c2m2[1] xy C22m2 + c2m1[1] yz C22m1 + c20[1] term20 C220 + c21[1] xz C221 + c22[1] term22 C222 color[2] += c2m2[2] xy C22m2 + c2m1[2] yz C22m1 + c20[2] term20 C220 + c21[2] xz C221 + c22[2] term22 C222 # Degree 3 if all((3, m) in shcoeffs for m in [-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]): term3m3 = directiony (3 directionx2 - directiony2) term3m2 = directionx directiony directionz term3m1 = directiony (4 directionz2 - directionx2 - directiony2) term30 = directionz (2 directionz2 - 3 directionx2 - 3 directiony2) term31 = directionx (4 directionz2 - directionx2 - directiony2) term32 = directionz (directionx2 - directiony2) term33 = directionx (directionx2 - 3 directiony2) c3m3 = shcoeffs[(3, -3)] c3m2 = shcoeffs[(3, -2)] c3m1 = shcoeffs[(3, -1)] c30 = shcoeffs[(3, 0)] c31 = shcoeffs[(3, 1)] c32 = shcoeffs[(3, 2)] c33 = shcoeffs[(3, 3)] color[0] += c3m3[0] term3m3 C33m3 + c3m2[0] term3m2 C33m2 + c3m1[0] term3m1 C33m1 + c30[0] term30 C330 + c31[0] term31 C331 + c32[0] term32 C332 + c33[0] term33 C333 color[1] += c3m3[1] term3m3 C33m3 + c3m2[1] term3m2 C33m2 + c3m1[1] term3m1 C33m1 + c30[1] term30 C330 + c31[1] term31 C331 + c32[1] term32 C332 + c33[1] term33 C333 color[2] += c3m3[2] term3m3 C33m3 + c3m2[2] term3m2 C33m2 + c3m1[2] term3m1 C33m1 + c30[2] term30 C330 + c31[2] term31 C331 + c32[2] term32 C332 + c33[2] term33 C333 # Apply bias color[0] += 0.5 color[1] += 0.5 color[2] += 0.5 return color Parameters: r: Magnitude of the direction vector. In 3D Gaussian Splatting, this is always 1 due to normalization. SH{l,m}: RGB coefficients for degree l and order m. x, y, z: Components of the direction vector. Pitfalls: Partial Definitions: Higher order spherical harmonics are optional, but if used, lower order spherical harmonics MUST also be provided. Each order MUST be fully defined; partial definitions (e.g., providing SH{2,0} but not SH{2,-2}) are not allowed. Clamping: If using unsigned normalized color buffers, values less than 0 or greater than 1 are clamped automatically. The 0.5 bias helps keep values within [0, 1]. Condon–Shortley Phase: Odd values for order (m) are negated. This is handled by the negative signs in the constants provided above. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Degree 0 requires 9 floats (3 RGB \times 3 coefficients), Degree 1 adds 27, Degree 2 adds 45, Degree 3 adds 63, totaling 144 floats per Gaussian for full degree 3. Strengths: Compact representation of view-dependent effects. Causes less range clamping than passing color and alpha values separately. Limitations: Limited angular resolution with low degrees. Higher degrees increase memory and compute cost. When to use: When view-dependent lighting (specular, anisotropy) is important and memory/compute budget allows for higher SH degrees. When not to use: When only diffuse lighting is needed (use Degree 0 only). When memory is extremely constrained. This method is defined in the KHRgaussiansplatting extension for glTF, which standardizes the storage and rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting assets. It builds on the mathematical foundations of spherical harmonics used in computer graphics for lighting approximation. The specific constants and biasing strategy are tailored for the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline to ensure compatibility with standard graphics APIs and color buffers.
