name: Appearance Feature Initialization and Training Schedule
head: Appearance feature initialization, Training schedule with appearance features
body: This method defines a staged training protocol for 3D Gaussian Splatting that introduces appearance features after an initial period of geometry optimization, followed by simplification and quantization. It solves the problem of premature optimization of appearance parameters by decoupling them from the initial scale and rotation learning phases. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which optimizes all parameters simultaneously, this approach introduces static and view-dependent appearance features at iteration 15K, simplifies the primitive count at 20K, and applies Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) in the final 1K iterations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance/scale, rotation, opacity, and initial SH coefficients). Output: Optimized Gaussian primitives with quantized appearance features. Data Structures: The Gaussian primitive stores appearance features as a vector of dimension D=3. The training schedule manages the state of these features and the primitive set through specific iteration milestones. Parameters: Total iterations: 30,000. Appearance introduction iteration: 15,000. Simplification iteration: 20,000. SVQ start iteration: 29,000. Local distinctiveness factor (\lambda): 2. Appearance feature dimension (D): 3. Steps: 1. Initial Training (Iterations 0–14,999): Train scale and rotation parameters from the initial training iteration. Do not optimize appearance features. The spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients are updated, specifically the DC term, which serves as the basis for later initialization. 2. Appearance Feature Introduction (Iteration 15,000): Introduce appearance features. Initialize static appearance features using the spherical harmonics DC coefficients trained up to iteration 15,000. Initialize view-dependent appearance features as zero vectors. 3. Simplification (Iteration 20,000): Run the simplification process incorporating local distinctiveness (LD) scoring with factor \lambda=2. This step reduces the number of Gaussians while preserving visual fidelity. 4. Sub-Vector Quantization (Iterations 29,000–30,000): Apply SVQ to per-Gaussian features using fixed K-means indices and optimized codebooks. K-means clustering is performed once to assign indices, which remain fixed. Only the codebooks are optimized for the remaining 1,000 iterations. Scale: length 1, 26 codes for each sub-vector. Rotation: length 2, 29 codes for each sub-vector. Appearance features: length 2, 210 codes for each sub-vector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingaussianavatar(totaliterations=30000, appearancestart=15000, simplificationiter=20000, svqstart=29000): # Initialize Gaussians with position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients gaussians = initializegaussians() # Pre-compute K-means for SVQ if needed, but indices are fixed later # Note: K-means is performed once before SVQ optimization for iter in range(totaliterations): # 1. Initial Training: Optimize scale and rotation only if iter < appearancestart: optimizescalerotation(gaussians) updateshdc(gaussians) # SH DC coefficients are tracked for later initialization # 2. Appearance Feature Introduction elif iter == appearancestart: # Initialize static appearance features from trained SH DC coefficients gaussians.staticappearance = gaussians.shdccoefficients # Initialize view-dependent appearance features as zero vectors gaussians.viewdependentappearance = zeroslike(gaussians.position) # 3. Simplification elif iter == simplificationiter: # Simplify primitives using Local Distinctiveness scoring with lambda=2 gaussians = simplifygaussians(gaussians, lambdafactor=2) # 4. SVQ Optimization elif iter >= svqstart: # Apply SVQ with fixed indices and optimized codebooks # Scale: length 1, 26 codes # Rotation: length 2, 29 codes # Appearance: length 2, 210 codes optimizesvqcodebooks(gaussians, fixedindices=True) # Standard rendering and loss computation for all iterations renderimage(gaussians) computeloss() updategradients(gaussians) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The SVQ step uses fixed K-means indices. If the initial K-means clustering is poor, the final quantization may be suboptimal. Boundaries: The transition at iteration 15,000 requires that SH DC coefficients are fully trained up to that point to provide a meaningful initialization for static appearance features. Time Complexity: The training runs for 30,000 iterations. The simplification step at 20,000 iterations adds computational overhead for LD scoring. The SVQ step in the last 1,000 iterations involves optimizing codebooks but uses fixed indices, reducing the search space. Memory Complexity: The introduction of appearance features increases the memory footprint per Gaussian. The SVQ step reduces memory usage by quantizing features, with specific codebook sizes: 26 codes for scale, 29 for rotation, and 210 for appearance features. Performance: Experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 using the Mini-Splatting framework. The method aims to improve training efficiency and final quality through staged optimization and quantization. Strengths: Decoupling appearance from geometry/rotation optimization may lead to more stable convergence. SVQ reduces memory and potentially speeds up rendering. Limitations: The fixed K-means indices in SVQ may not adapt to later training dynamics. The method requires careful tuning of iteration milestones. This method is part of the "Optimized Minimal 3D Gaussian Splatting" framework, implemented within the Mini-Splatting library. It builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline but introduces a specific training schedule to handle appearance features and quantization efficiently. The approach is designed to optimize the trade-off between training time, memory usage, and rendering quality. name: Appearance Embedding
head: Image-specific Embedding, NeRF in the Wild, WildConvexes, WildGaussians
body: Appearance Embedding is a technique that associates each training image with a unique embedding vector to model appearance changes such as lighting variations, shadows, and camera exposure differences. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by optimizing per-image lighting condition embeddings jointly with scene parameters and incorporating them as an extra input during color computation, rather than relying solely on fixed scene representations. Inputs: Training image set, camera poses, initial scene parameters (e.g., Gaussian attributes or neural field weights). Outputs: Optimized per-image embedding vectors, rendered images. Data Structures: A list of per-image embedding vectors, each of dimension d=8. Each vector is stored as a trainable parameter tensor. Steps: 1. Initialize a unique embedding vector \mathbf{e}i \in \mathbb{R}^8 for each training image i. 2. During training, for each image i, retrieve its embedding \mathbf{e}i and condition it with the spatial/feature representation of a point or primitive. 3. Compute the color C of the point/primitive using the conditioned representation, jointly optimizing \mathbf{e}i alongside scene parameters via gradient descent. 4. During validation, since validation image embeddings are unknown, compute the mean of all training embeddings \bar{\mathbf{e}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{e}i and use \bar{\mathbf{e}} for all validation queries. Formulas: Color computation is defined as C = \mathcal{N}(F, \mathbf{e}i), where \mathcal{N} is the color prediction network, F is the base feature representation of the point/primitive, and \mathbf{e}i is the per-image embedding. Parameters: Embedding dimension is fixed at 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Validation requires a heuristic fallback (mean embedding) to avoid unknown inputs. Joint optimization can introduce artifacts if not regularized, though embeddings were originally designed for lighting robustness and later studied for mitigating floater artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializeembeddings(numimages, dim=8): return [[random.gauss(0, 1) for in range(dim)] for in range(numimages)] def colornetwork(features, embedding): return features + embedding def renderimage(pose, embedding, sceneparams): return colornetwork(sceneparams, embedding) def photometricloss(rendered, groundtruth): return sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, groundtruth)) def trainstep(images, poses, embeddings, sceneparams, optimizer): for imgidx, (image, pose) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): emb = embeddings[imgidx] rendered = renderimage(pose, emb, sceneparams) loss = photometricloss(rendered, image) optimizer.step(loss) def validate(poses, embeddings, sceneparams): meanemb = [sum(v) / len(embeddings) for v in zip(embeddings)] return [renderimage(pose, meanemb, sceneparams) for pose in poses] This variant replaces spherical harmonics with a feature embedding f and a trainable per-image embedding e to handle intense illumination changes, such as multiple light sources in indoor scenes. It retains the opacity parameter \alpha consistent with standard 2D Gaussian Splatting. It is chosen when spherical harmonics are insufficient for modeling complex lighting. Performance: Improves robustness to lighting variations and can mitigate floater artifacts in geometry-critical tasks. Strengths: Handles dynamic lighting, shadows, and appearance changes effectively across large-scale scenes. Limitations: Requires per-image optimization during training; validation requires a heuristic mean-embedding fallback. Appearance embeddings were originally introduced in "NeRF in the Wild" to address lighting variations in uncontrolled outdoor environments. The concept has been extended to various rendering frameworks, including K-Planes and Gaussian Splatting (referred to as WildGaussians) and Convex Splatting (WildConvexes). It is commonly used in large-scale scene reconstruction where lighting consistency is challenging. SCALAR-NeRF: SCAlable LARge-scale Neural Radiance Fields for Scene Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16657v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Neural Radiance Fields-Based 3D Reconstruction of Power Transmission Lines Using Progressive Motion Sequence Images., https://doi.org/10.3390/s23239537, fetched 2026-10-26 On the Geometric Accuracy of Implicit and Primitive-based Representations Derived from View Rendering Constraints, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2509.10241, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) OMeGa: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats for Robust Scene-Level Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00427, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Parameter Initialization
head: Emission, Roughness, and Specular Initialization, Median Texture Initialization for Diffuse Color
body: This method defines the deterministic initialization of material parameters (emission, roughness, specular albedo, diffuse color) and geometric priors (SDF, environment map) for differentiable rendering pipelines, specifically those utilizing spherical Gaussian basis functions or texture-space sampling. It solves the problem of optimization instability caused by poor initial guesses in non-convex inverse rendering problems, such as MLPs getting stuck in local minima or incorrect exposure handling. It is distinct from sibling methods like Spherical Harmonics Initialization by focusing on physical material properties and spatially-varying diffuse textures via median filtering rather than frequency-domain coefficients. Inputs: Set of reference images I{ref} with varying exposures. Object bounding box or mesh geometry. Number of environment map lobes N{env}. Outputs: Initialized SDF weights \Theta. Initialized diffuse albedo function a(x; \Phi) or texture. Initialized scalar material parameters: emission E, roughness r, specular albedo \mu. Initialized specular lobe sharpness \lambda. Initialized environment map lobes L{env}. SDF Network: Weights \Theta for a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates to signed distance values. Diffuse Albedo: Option A (MLP): Parameters \Phi for a function a(x; \Phi). Option B (Texture): A 2D texture map T{diffuse} of resolution W \times H. Material Scalars: Float values for E, r, \mu, \lambda. Environment Map: A list of N{env} lobes, each containing a position vector \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit sphere) and an amplitude scalar Ai. 1. Input Image Normalization: Scale all input reference images by a constant factor k such that the median intensity of all pixels across all images is 0.5. This handles varying exposure levels. 2. SDF Initialization: Initialize the SDF network weights \Theta using the method from [12] (not detailed in these sources) to ensure the initial implicit surface is roughly a sphere. 3. Diffuse Albedo Initialization: For MLP-based albedo: Initialize parameters \Phi such that the predicted albedo a(x; \Phi) \approx 0.5 for all locations x inside the object's bounding box. For Texture-based albedo: Construct a median texture T{diffuse}: a. Iterate over all available reference pictures. b. Project each image into texture space. c. Use an online median estimator to update the texture values. This avoids memory issues with tens of thousands of views and suppresses view-dependent effects like specular reflections, which would be amplified by a mean filter. 4. Material Parameter Initialization: Set constant initial values for the remaining material parameters: Emission E = 0. Roughness r = 0.5. Specular albedo \mu = 0.5 (Note: specifies a range for \mu, see below). 5. Specular BRDF Initialization: Initialize lobe sharpness \lambda by drawing randomly from the uniform distribution U[95, 125]. Initialize specular albedo \mu by drawing randomly from the uniform distribution U[0.18, 0.26]. Conflict Note: suggests \mu=0.5 for general material parameters, while specifies [0.18, 0.26] specifically for the specular BRDF component. Implementers should verify which parameter set corresponds to their specific BRDF model (e.g., whether \mu in refers to a different specular term or if is more specific to the spherical Gaussian lobes). 6. Environment Map Initialization: Distribute N{env} lobes uniformly on the unit sphere using a spherical Fibonacci lattice [18]. Assign monochrome colors to the lobes. Randomly initialize the amplitude Ai for each lobe. Scale the amplitudes such that the initial rendered pixel intensity is \approx 0.5. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializeparameters(referenceimages, boundingbox, nenvlobs): """ Initializes rendering parameters according to PhySG and Texture-space DR methods. """ # Step 1: Normalize Input Images # Scale images so median intensity is 0.5 allpixels = np.concatenate([img.flatten() for img in referenceimages]) currentmedian = np.median(allpixels) scalefactor = 0.5 / currentmedian normalizedimages = [img scalefactor for img in referenceimages] # Step 2: SDF Initialization # Use external method [12] to initialize SDF weights Theta # ensuring initial shape is roughly a sphere. sdfweights = initializesdfsphere() # Placeholder for method [12] # Step 3: Diffuse Albedo Initialization # Option A: MLP-based (PhySG) # Initialize Phi such that a(x; Phi) ~ 0.5 inside bounding box # Implementation detail: Initialize MLP biases/weights to output 0.5 diffusealbedomlpparams = initializealbedomlptarget(0.5, boundingbox) # Option B: Texture-based (Texture-space DR) # Build median texture from reference images diffusealbedotexture = buildmediantexture(normalizedimages) # Step 4: Material Parameters (Texture-space DR specific) emission = 0.0 roughness = 0.5 specularalbedoconst = 0.5 # Step 5: Specular BRDF Parameters (PhySG specific) # Draw sharpness lambda from [95, 125] lambdasharpness = np.random.uniform(95, 125) # Draw specular albedo mu from [0.18, 0.26] muspecular = np.random.uniform(0.18, 0.26) # Step 6: Environment Map Initialization # Generate positions using Spherical Fibonacci Lattice envpositions = generatesphericalfibonaccilattice(nenvlobs) # Initialize amplitudes randomly envamplitudes = np.random.rand(nenvlobs) # Scale amplitudes so initial render intensity is ~0.5 # Requires a forward pass simulation or analytical approximation # to determine the scaling factor that yields 0.5 intensity. envamplitudes = scaleenvamplitudes(envamplitudes, targetintensity=0.5) return { 'sdfweights': sdfweights, 'diffusealbedomlp': diffusealbedomlpparams, 'diffusealbedotexture': diffusealbedotexture, 'emission': emission, 'roughness': roughness, 'specularalbedoconst': specularalbedoconst, 'lambda': lambdasharpness, 'mu': muspecular, 'envmap': {'positions': envpositions, 'amplitudes': envamplitudes} } def buildmediantexture(images): """ Iteratively updates a texture using an online median estimator. """ # Initialize texture with zeros or neutral color texture = np.zeroslike(images[0]) for img in images: # Project image to texture space coordinates # Depends on UV mapping of the object coords = projecttotexturespace(img) # Update texture with online median # Standard online median algorithm (e.g., two heaps or similar) texture = onlinemedianupdate(texture, coords, img) return texture def generatesphericalfibonaccilattice(n): """ Generates n points uniformly distributed on a unit sphere. """ indices = np.arange(0, n, dtype=float) + 0.5 phi = np.arccos(1 - 2 indices / n) theta = np.pi (1 + np.sqrt(5)) indices x = np.sin(phi) np.cos(theta) y = np.sin(phi) np.sin(theta) z = np.cos(phi) return np.stack([x, y, z], axis=-1) Environment Map Intensity: If the initial environment map is too bright or too dark, the diffuse albedo MLP may get stuck, predicting all zeros or ones during training. The scaling step in Step 6 is critical to prevent this. Median vs. Mean: Using a mean filter for diffuse color initialization can incorporate view-dependent effects (specular reflections) into the diffuse base color. The median estimator is preferred to suppress these effects. Parameter Conflict: There is a discrepancy in the initialization of specular albedo \mu between ([0.18, 0.26]) and (0.5). This likely reflects different BRDF parameterizations or material definitions. Time Complexity: The median texture construction is O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of views and M is the number of texture pixels, assuming an O(1) online median update. The environment map generation is O(N{env}). Memory Complexity: The median texture requires O(W \cdot H) memory. The online estimator adds minimal overhead compared to storing all projected views. Strengths: Robust against exposure variations in input data; prevents optimization divergence in inverse rendering; effectively separates diffuse and specular components during initialization. Limitations: The median texture method may be slow for very high-resolution textures or massive numbers of views if not optimized. The SDF initialization relies on an external method [12]. This initialization strategy originates from inverse rendering research aiming to reconstruct physically-based materials and lighting from images. PhySG: Introduced the specific initialization for spherical Gaussian environment maps and BRDF parameters to enable stable training of neural implicit representations for physics-based material editing and relighting. Texture-space DR: Proposed the median texture initialization for spatially-varying diffuse color to handle complex indoor scenes with many reference views, leveraging texture-space differentiable rendering. PhySG: Inverse Rendering with Spherical Gaussians for Physics-based Material Editing and Relighting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00541, fetched 2026-10-26 Material and Lighting Reconstruction for Complex Indoor Scenes with Texture-space Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/sr.20211292, fetched 2026-10-29

name: SplatFace
body: SplatFace is a Gaussian model initialization and optimization strategy designed for high-fidelity head avatar reconstruction from few input views. It addresses the challenge of initializing 3D Gaussians on complex, non-rigid surfaces by placing them on a template mesh and jointly optimizing the Gaussian parameters and the mesh geometry using a splat-to-mesh distance loss. It differs from generic point-cloud initialization by leveraging explicit geometric surface data and from mesh-only methods by maintaining the differentiable rendering benefits of Gaussian Splatting. Inputs: A template mesh (typically a canonical head mesh), a set of input images (few-view), and camera poses. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity, color) and an optimized mesh geometry. Data Structures: 1. Template Mesh: Defined by vertices V and faces F. 2. Gaussian Set: A list of N Gaussians, each with position \mathbf{p}, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians on the surface of the template mesh. This is typically done by sampling points on the mesh triangles. 2. Rendering: Render the scene using standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization to produce an image. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute a loss function comprising: Image Loss: Difference between rendered and input images (e.g., L1, SSIM). Splat-to-Mesh Distance Loss: A regularization term that penalizes the distance between the splatted Gaussians and the current mesh surface. This ensures the Gaussians remain aligned with the geometric structure. 4. Joint Optimization: Update both the Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color) and the mesh vertices using gradient descent. Formulas: The total loss L is: L = L{image} + \lambda L{splat-mesh} where L{splat-mesh} measures the distance between the Gaussian splats and the mesh surface. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the splat-to-mesh distance loss. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Mesh: If the template mesh has poor topology, initialization may be inaccurate. Precision: Joint optimization requires careful balancing of learning rates for Gaussians and mesh vertices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gaussians = initializegaussiansonmesh(templatemesh) for step in range(numsteps): # Render image from current Gaussians and mesh renderedimage = render(gaussians, cameraposes) # Compute image loss lossimage = computeimageloss(renderedimage, inputimage) # Compute splat-to-mesh distance loss losssplatmesh = computesplattomeshdistance(gaussians, templatemesh) # Total loss totalloss = lossimage + lambdaweight losssplatmesh # Backpropagate and update Gaussians and mesh totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # Clear gradients optimizer.zerograd() MeshInitializer initializes 3D Gaussian splats by placing them on the surface of a triangle mesh using barycentric coordinates to determine position, normal interpolation, and color interpolation. It differs from VoxelInitializer by adhering strictly to the mesh topology rather than a grid, and from generic point-cloud initialization by leveraging explicit geometric surface data. It is a variant of Gaussian Splatting Initialization and builds on SplatFace. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: SplatFace enables rendering speed up to 300 FPS. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High-fidelity head avatar learning from few views; joint optimization ensures geometric consistency. Limitations: Relies on a good template mesh; joint optimization may be computationally intensive. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic or static head avatars from limited input views with high geometric fidelity. When not: When no template mesh is available or when real-time performance is critical and few-view reconstruction is not required. SplatFace was introduced in reference [232] as part of the recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting for avatar reconstruction. It is cited in the context of synthesizing high-quality avatars from few input views, preceding works like GauMesh [233] and others in the field. name: MeshInitializer
head: Mesh-embedded Gaussian Initialization
body: MeshInitializer initializes 3D Gaussian splats by placing them on the surface of a triangle mesh using barycentric coordinates to determine position, normal interpolation, and color interpolation. It differs from VoxelInitializer by adhering strictly to the mesh topology rather than a grid, and from generic point-cloud initialization by leveraging explicit geometric surface data. It is a variant of Gaussian Splatting Initialization and builds on SplatFace. Inputs: Triangle mesh defined by vertices V \in \mathbb{R}^{Nv \times 3} and faces F \in \mathbb{R}^{Nf \times 3} (indices into V). Optional vertex colors Cv \in \mathbb{R}^{Nv \times 3}. Optional vertex normals Nv \in \mathbb{R}^{Nv \times 3}. Parameter n{gpst} (number of Gaussians per surface triangle), integer \in \{1, 3, 4, 6\}. Outputs: Gaussian means M \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng \times 3}, where Ng = Nf \times n{gpst}. Gaussian rotations Q \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng \times 4} (quaternions). Gaussian scales S \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng \times 3} (log-space). Gaussian opacities O \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng} (pre-sigmoid). Gaussian colors C \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng \times 3} (if vertex colors provided, else None). Data Structures: Barycentric patterns are precomputed static arrays based on n{gpst}. Edge lengths are computed per face. Steps: 1. Select Barycentric Pattern: Based on n{gpst}, select the precomputed barycentric coordinates B \in \mathbb{R}^{n{gpst} \times 3} and circle radius r{circ}: If n{gpst} = 1: B = \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 & 1/3 & 1/3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad r{circ} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} If n{gpst} = 3: B = \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 & 1/4 & 1/4 \\ 1/4 & 1/2 & 1/4 \\ 1/4 & 1/4 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad r{circ} = \frac{1}{2(\sqrt{3}+1)} If n{gpst} = 4: B = \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 & 1/3 & 1/3 \\ 2/3 & 1/6 & 1/6 \\ 1/6 & 2/3 & 1/6 \\ 1/6 & 1/6 & 2/3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad r{circ} = \frac{1}{4\sqrt{3}} If n{gpst} = 6: B = \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1/6 & 1/6 \\ 1/6 & 2/3 & 1/6 \\ 1/6 & 1/6 & 2/3 \\ 1/6 & 5/12 & 5/12 \\ 5/12 & 1/6 & 5/12 \\ 5/12 & 5/12 & 1/6 \end{bmatrix}, \quad r{circ} = \frac{1}{4+2\sqrt{3}} 2. Compute Gaussian Positions: For each face f with vertices v0, v1, v2, compute positions for each Gaussian k \in \{0, \dots, n{gpst}-1\}: M{f,k} = Bk[0] \cdot v0 + Bk[1] \cdot v1 + Bk[2] \cdot v2 Vectorized: M = \sum{j=0}^{2} F[:, j,:] \otimes B, where \otimes denotes broadcasting multiplication and summation over the vertex dimension, resulting in shape (Nf \cdot n{gpst}, 3). 3. Compute Surface Normals: If vertex normals Nv are available: N{f,k} = Bk[0] \cdot N{v,0} + Bk[1] \cdot N{v,1} + Bk[2] \cdot N{v,2} Normalize the resulting vector: \hat{N}{f,k} = \frac{N{f,k}}{\|N{f,k}\|} If vertex normals are not available, this step is skipped or defaults to face normals (implementation detail not specified in source, assumed handled by caller or defaulting to None). 4. Convert Normals to Rotations: Pass \hat{N} to normal2rotation to obtain quaternions Q. 5. Compute Colors: If vertex colors Cv exist: C{f,k} = Bk[0] \cdot C{v,0} + Bk[1] \cdot C{v,1} + Bk[2] \cdot C{v,2} Otherwise, return None. 6. Compute Scales: Calculate edge lengths for each triangle. Let L{f,i} be the length of edge i of face f. Find the minimum edge length for each face: L{min,f} = \min(L{f,0}, L{f,1}, L{f,2}). Compute base scale: s{base,f} = L{min,f} \cdot r{circ}. Clamp to minimum 0: s'{base,f} = \max(s{base,f}, 0). Expand to 2D scale (x, y) and append 0 for z-scale: S{2D,f} = [s'{base,f}, s'{base,f}, 0]. Convert to log space: S{f,k} = \log(S{2D,f} \cdot 2 + 10^{-7}) This results in shape (Ng, 3). 7. Set Opacity: Set all Gaussians to fully opaque: O = \text{inverse\sigmoid}(1.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def normal2rotation(n): """ Constructs a rotation matrix from the normal and an orthogonal basis, then converts to quaternion. Args: n: Tensor of shape (..., 3), normals. Returns: q: Tensor of shape (..., 4), quaternions. """ n = F.normalize(n, dim=-1) # Create a reference vector [1, 0, 0] w0 = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0, 0.0]], device=n.device, dtype=n.dtype).expand(n.shape) # Project w0 onto the plane orthogonal to n # R0 = w0 - (w0. n) n dotw0n = torch.sum(w0 n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) R0 = w0 - dotw0n n # Ensure stability by flipping sign if the first component is negative R0 = torch.sign(R0[:,:1]) R0 = F.normalize(R0, dim=-1) # R1 is orthogonal to both n and R0 R1 = torch.cross(n, R0) # Adjust sign for stability R1 = torch.sign(R1[:, 1:2]) torch.sign(n[:, 2:]) # Construct rotation matrix R = [R0, R1, n] R = torch.stack([R0, R1, n], dim=-1) # Convert rotation matrix to quaternion q = rotmat2quaternion(R) return q def rotmat2quaternion(R, normalize=False): """ Converts a rotation matrix to a quaternion. Args: R: Tensor of shape (..., 3, 3), rotation matrices. normalize: Whether to normalize the resulting quaternion. Returns: q: Tensor of shape (..., 4), quaternions. """ # Trace of the rotation matrix tr = R[:, 0, 0] + R[:, 1, 1] + R[:, 2, 2] + 1e-6 # Calculate the scalar part of the quaternion r = torch.sqrt(1 + tr) / 2 # Calculate the vector part q = torch.stack([ r, (R[:, 2, 1] - R[:, 1, 2]) / (4 r), (R[:, 0, 2] - R[:, 2, 0]) / (4 r), (R[:, 1, 0] - R[:, 0, 1]) / (4 r) ], dim=-1) if normalize: q = F.normalize(q, dim=-1) return q def inversesigmoid(x): """Computes the inverse sigmoid function.""" return torch.log(x / (1 - x + 1e-7)) def meshinitializer(meshvertices, meshfaces, meshvertexnormals=None, meshvertexcolors=None, ngaussianspersurfacetriangle=1): """ Initializes 3D Gaussian splats on a mesh surface. Args: meshvertices: Tensor of shape (Nv, 3). meshfaces: Tensor of shape (Nf, 3), indices into meshvertices. meshvertexnormals: Tensor of shape (Nv, 3), optional. meshvertexcolors: Tensor of shape (Nv, 3), optional. ngaussianspersurfacetriangle: int, 1, 3, 4, or 6. Returns: means: Tensor of shape (Ng, 3). rotations: Tensor of shape (Ng, 4). scales: Tensor of shape (Ng, 3). opacities: Tensor of shape (Ng,). colors: Tensor of shape (Ng, 3) or None. """ # 1. Setup barycentric coordinates and circle radius if ngaussianspersurfacetriangle == 1: barycentriccoords = torch.tensor([[1/3, 1/3, 1/3]], dtype=meshvertices.dtype, device=meshvertices.device) circleradius = 1.0 / (2.0 torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(3.0))) elif ngaussianspersurfacetriangle == 3: barycentriccoords = torch.tensor([[1/2, 1/4, 1/4], [1/4, 1/2, 1/4], [1/4, 1/4, 1/2]], dtype=meshvertices.dtype, device=meshvertices.device) circleradius = 1.0 / (2.0 (torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(3.0)) + 1.0)) elif ngaussianspersurfacetriangle == 4: barycentriccoords = torch.tensor([[1/3, 1/3, 1/3], [2/3, 1/6, 1/6], [1/6, 2/3, 1/6], [1/6, 1/6, 2/3]], dtype=meshvertices.dtype, device=meshvertices.device) circleradius = 1.0 / (4.0 torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(3.0))) elif ngaussianspersurfacetriangle == 6: barycentriccoords = torch.tensor([[2/3, 1/6, 1/6], [1/6, 2/3, 1/6], [1/6, 1/6, 2/3], [1/6, 5/12, 5/12], [5/12, 1/6, 5/12], [5/12, 5/12, 1/6]], dtype=meshvertices.dtype, device=meshvertices.device) circleradius = 1.0 / (4.0 + 2.0 torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(3.0))) else: raise ValueError("ngaussianspersurfacetriangle must be 1, 3, 4, or 6") # Gather vertex positions for all faces # meshfaces shape: (Nf, 3) # facevertices shape: (Nf, 3, 3) facevertices = meshvertices[meshfaces] # Compute positions # barycentriccoords shape: (ngpst, 3) # facevertices shape: (Nf, 3, 3) # We need to broadcast multiply and sum over the vertex dimension (dim 1 of facevertices) # Reshape for broadcasting: (Nf, 3, 1) (1, ngpst, 3) -> (Nf, ngpst, 3) # But barycentriccoords is (ngpst, 3). # Let's use einsum or manual expansion. # positions shape: (Nf, ngpst, 3) positions = torch.einsum('ijk,kl->ijl', facevertices, barycentriccoords) means = positions.reshape(-1, 3) # Compute normals if meshvertexnormals is not None: facenormals = meshvertexnormals[meshfaces] interpolatednormals = torch.einsum('ijk,kl->ijl', facenormals, barycentriccoords) normals = F.normalize(interpolatednormals.reshape(-1, 3), dim=-1) rotations = normal2rotation(normals) else: # Fallback: compute face normals if vertex normals not provided # This is a gap filler as source doesn't specify behavior if normals are missing v0 = facevertices[:, 0,:] v1 = facevertices[:, 1,:] v2 = facevertices[:, 2,:] n0 = F.normalize(torch.cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0), dim=-1) # Broadcast to all gaussians on the face normals = n0.repeatinterleave(ngaussianspersurfacetriangle, dim=0) rotations = normal2rotation(normals) # Compute colors if meshvertexcolors is not None: facecolors = meshvertexcolors[meshfaces] interpolatedcolors = torch.einsum('ijk,kl->ijl', facecolors, barycentriccoords) colors = interpolatedcolors.reshape(-1, 3) else: colors = None # Compute scales # Edge lengths v0 = facevertices[:, 0,:] v1 = facevertices[:, 1,:] v2 = facevertices[:, 2,:] e0 = torch.norm(v1 - v0, dim=-1) e1 = torch.norm(v2 - v1, dim=-1) e2 = torch.norm(v0 - v2, dim=-1) # Min edge length per face minedgelen = torch.min(torch.stack([e0, e1, e2], dim=-1), dim=-1).values # Base scale basescale = minedgelen circleradius basescale = torch.clamp(basescale, min=0.0) # Expand to 3D scale (x, y, z) # Shape (Nf, 3) scales2d = torch.stack([basescale, basescale, torch.zeroslike(basescale)], dim=-1) # Log space conversion # Shape (Nf, 3) scaleslog = torch.log(scales2d 2.0 + 1e-7) # Repeat for each gaussian on the face scales = scaleslog.repeatinterleave(ngaussianspersurfacetriangle, dim=0) # Opacity opacities = inversesigmoid(torch.oneslike(means[:, 0])) return means, rotations, scales, opacities, colors VoxelInitializer initializes 3D Gaussian splats by voxelizing a mesh and placing Gaussians at voxel centers that intersect the mesh surface. It differs from MeshInitializer by using a grid-based approach rather than barycentric interpolation on triangles. It is chosen when a uniform grid distribution is preferred over surface-adaptive distribution. Parameter voxelsize defaults to 1/256. This variant initializes 600,000 Gaussian primitives on a canonicalized CAD mesh surface. It sets initial log-scales so each splat covers the mean distance to its three nearest neighbors, quaternions to the shortest-arc rotation aligned with the surface normal, and opacities to the post-sigmoid activation 0.5. A key pitfall is that means and quaternions are frozen entirely; geometric corrections are absorbed by a deformation field D\theta. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles Nf and the number of Gaussians per triangle n{gpst}. The dominant operations are barycentric interpolation and edge length calculations, which are vectorizable. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to Ng = Nf \times n{gpst}. Storage includes means, rotations, scales, opacities, and optionally colors. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures Gaussians are strictly aligned with the mesh geometry, providing accurate surface representation. Leverages existing mesh normals and colors. Limitations: Dependent on mesh quality (e.g., triangle size variation affects scale distribution). Does not cover volume or off-surface regions. When to use: When a high-quality triangle mesh is available and surface fidelity is critical. When not to use: When the input is a point cloud without mesh connectivity, or when volumetric coverage is required. MeshInitializer is part of the GauStudio framework, a modular framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting and beyond. It was introduced in the context of supporting mesh-based initialization for 3DGS, allowing for robust reconstruction from CAD models or textured meshes. The method leverages barycentric coordinates to distribute Gaussians evenly across triangle surfaces, a technique common in computer graphics for sampling surfaces. name: Mesh-based Initialization
head: Mesh-to-Gaussian Initialization, Surface Sampling Initialization
body: Mesh-based initialization converts a polygonal mesh into a set of 3D Gaussian splats to serve as the starting point for optimization or rendering. It solves the problem of establishing a geometric prior for Gaussian Splatting when a high-quality surface representation is already available, leveraging the explicit nature of Gaussians to support user-guided generation or scene-level inverse rendering. It differs from sibling methods like Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) by deriving positions from continuous surface geometry rather than volumetric bounding boxes, and from Learning-based and Generative Initialization by relying on deterministic geometric sampling rather than neural priors. The core mechanism involves sampling points from the surface of an input mesh and assigning Gaussian parameters to these points. The position of each Gaussian is determined by the sampled surface coordinates. The orientation and scale are typically aligned with the local surface geometry (e.g., normal-aligned, thin along the normal) to represent the surface as a collection of flat or slightly thickened primitives. This approach exploits the explicit nature of 3D Gaussian Splatting, allowing for direct integration with existing mesh processing pipelines. Definition: A technique for initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting from user-provided 3D shapes to guide text-to-3D generation, leveraging the explicit nature of Gaussians. Step: Generate initial points by uniformly sampling points on the surface of the provided user mesh. Parameter: Set the position learning rate to a relatively small value to better preserve the user's desired geometric shape during optimization. Comparison: Outperforms Latent-NeRF and Fantasia3D in both geometry and texture quality while mostly maintaining the user-provided geometric prior. Definition: An extension to GeoSplatting that initializes the optimization process with an existing triangle mesh (e.g., from NeuS or GOF) instead of building geometry from scratch, circumventing isosurface resolution limits and mask dependencies. Step: Extract a triangle mesh from multi-view images using methods like NeuS or GOF. Convert the initial mesh into Gaussian points via MGadapter. Follow the remaining steps of the standard GeoSplatting pipeline. Refine the initial mesh through gradients derived from 3DGS rendering, leveraging the differentiable nature of MGadapter. Pitfall: This two-stage extension is not applicable to specular objects because surface reconstruction methods lack effective PBR modeling, leading to noisy meshes that GeoSplatting cannot rectify. Comparison: Unlike the standard pipeline which uses isosurfaces (limited by resolution and mask dependencies), this method extends applicability to scene-level inverse rendering and avoids those specific limitations. Definition: A pipeline that loads a polygonal mesh and converts it into a set of 3D Gaussian splats for rendering. Step: Invoke meshtosplat(mesh, params.options, progresscallback) to generate the Gaussian point cloud. Iterate over output targets and save each generated splat using saveSplat with RadExportMode::Stream and SSOG options. Pitfall: If the input file is not a mesh, or if meshtosplat returns an error, log the failure and abort the pipeline. Mesh-based initialization has emerged as a critical component in advanced Gaussian Splatting applications where geometric priors are valuable. It was notably adopted in works such as G SGEN for user-guided text-to-3D generation and GeoSplatting for physically-based inverse rendering. The approach allows for the integration of traditional computer graphics assets (meshes) with differentiable rendering frameworks, enabling hybrid workflows. Implementation details are also found in tools like LichtFeld-Studio, which provides a direct conversion pipeline. name: Gaussian-Centric Binding
head: Binding Gaussians to Mesh, Gaussian-Centric Binding Strategy, Gaussian-Centric Strategy, Gaussian-centric deformation binding, Ray-cast Gaussian-mesh association
body: Gaussian-Centric Binding is a training-free strategy for associating 3D Gaussians with a proxy mesh to enable deformation transfer, eliminating the need for retraining and reducing sensitivity to mesh topology defects. Unlike mesh-centric strategies that require an "initialization-then-training" workflow with geometric constraints, this method leverages existing training camera rays to bind Gaussians directly to mesh faces via spatial association. It is chosen when unified manipulation of mesh and 3DGS is required without retraining costs or topological sensitivity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (each defined by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity, color), a proxy mesh (triangle soup), and a set of training camera poses. Outputs: A binding map associating each Gaussian with one or more mesh faces, including face indices, barycentric coordinates, and intersection distances. Data Structures: Gaussian: Defined by mean vector \mu and covariance matrix \Sigma. The bounding box (BBX) is derived from \mu and \Sigma. Mesh Face: Defined by three vertices. Binding Record: For each Gaussian, a list of records containing: Face index. Barycentric coordinates of the intersection point. Distance from the intersection point to the Gaussian center (or BBX corner). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Casting for Binding: For each Gaussian G: a. Determine the 8 corners of its Bounding Box (BBX). b. For each training camera Ck: i. Cast 8 rays from Ck toward the 8 corners of the Gaussian's BBX. ii. For each ray, compute the intersection with the proxy mesh. iii. If an intersection exists, record the face index, barycentric coordinates, and the distance from the intersection point to the Gaussian center (or BBX corner). c. After traversing all cameras, collect all recorded candidate faces. d. Select the nearest face among the recorded intersected faces as the final binding target for the Gaussian. e. Note: The extended strategy binds each Gaussian to 8 faces (one per BBX corner) to handle size mismatches between Gaussians and faces. 2. Deformation Transfer: When the proxy mesh is deformed: a. Transfer the deformation from the mesh to the BBX of the Gaussians. b. For a Gaussian kernel G with BBX B, let Pi be the position of the i-th corner of B (i=1,\dots,8). c. The transformation of each corner Pi is applied to the Gaussian. d. The new mean \mu' and covariance \Sigma' are computed by averaging the transformations of the BBX corners. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussiancentricbinding(gaussians, mesh, cameras): """ Binds 3D Gaussians to a proxy mesh using ray casting from training cameras. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with method getbbxcorners() returning 8 corner positions. mesh: Triangle mesh object with method rayintersect(rayorigin, raydir) returning (hit, faceindex, barycentriccoords, distance). cameras: List of camera objects with method getray(origin, direction) or similar projection logic. Returns: bindingmap: Dictionary mapping Gaussian ID to list of binding records. """ bindingmap = {} for gaussian in gaussians: bbxcorners = gaussian.getbbxcorners() candidatefaces = [] # Cast rays from all training cameras to all BBX corners for camera in cameras: for corner in bbxcorners: # Construct ray from camera through BBX corner rayorigin = camera.position raydirection = corner - rayorigin raydirection = normalize(raydirection) # Intersect with mesh hit, faceindex, barycentric, distance = mesh.rayintersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if hit: # Record the binding candidate # Distance is from intersection to Gaussian center/corner candidatefaces.append({ 'faceindex': faceindex, 'barycentric': barycentric, 'distance': distance, 'cornerindex': bbxcorners.index(corner) # Track which corner }) # Select binding targets # Strategy 1: Single nearest face (from all cameras) # if candidatefaces: # nearest = min(candidatefaces, key=lambda x: x['distance']) # bindingmap[gaussian.id] = [nearest] # Strategy 2: 8 faces (one per corner, best hit across cameras) # This is the extended strategy mentioned in sources finalbindings = [] for i in range(8): # Find the best hit for this specific corner across all cameras cornerhits = [f for f in candidatefaces if f['cornerindex'] == i] if cornerhits: besthit = min(cornerhits, key=lambda x: x['distance']) finalbindings.append(besthit) bindingmap[gaussian.id] = finalbindings return bindingmap def transferdeformation(gaussian, bindingrecords, meshdeformation): """ Transfers mesh deformation to the Gaussian based on binding records. Args: gaussian: The Gaussian object. bindingrecords: List of binding records (faces and barycentric coords). meshdeformation: Function or data structure describing the new mesh vertex positions. Returns: New Gaussian parameters (mu', sigma'). """ # Get transformed positions of the bound faces' vertices # Note: The source describes transferring motion of triangle faces to the BBX # and then averaging to the Gaussian. transformedcorners = [] for record in bindingrecords: face = mesh.getface(record['faceindex']) # Interpolate vertex positions using barycentric coordinates # v1, v2, v3 are the original vertices of the face # v1', v2', v3' are the deformed vertices v1prime = meshdeformation(face.v1) v2prime = meshdeformation(face.v2) v3prime = meshdeformation(face.v3) # Compute the deformed point on the face corresponding to the intersection # This point approximates the deformed position of the Gaussian's associated location deformedpoint = (record['barycentric'][0] v1prime + record['barycentric'][1] v2prime + record['barycentric'][2] v3prime) transformedcorners.append(deformedpoint) # Average the transformed positions to update the Gaussian mean if transformedcorners: newmu = sum(transformedcorners) / len(transformedcorners) # Update covariance based on the deformation of the BBX # The source states: "transformations of the i-th corner of B keep the same with Pi" # and "subsequently transferred to G by averaging operations" # This implies the covariance is updated based on the relative positions of the transformed corners # relative to the new mean. newsigma = computecovariancefrompoints(transformedcorners, newmu) return newmu, newsigma else: return gaussian.mu, gaussian.sigma Parameters: Ray Casting: Uses training camera poses. No additional parameters. Binding Selection: Nearest face by distance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Size Mismatch: Significant size differences between Gaussians and mesh faces can lead to inconsistent deformation magnitudes if only a single face is bound. The extended strategy (8 faces) mitigates this. Mesh Topology Defects: Traditional mesh-centric methods are sensitive to topology defects; this method is robust to them due to spatial association. Large Deformations: Mesh-centric methods suffer from misalignment artifacts during large deformations due to lack of explicit topological information in other proxy types; this method mitigates this by using spatial association via ray casting. Time Complexity: The binding process is fully parallelized using OptiX and completes within a few seconds. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the binding map (face indices, barycentric coords, distances) for each Gaussian. Strengths: Training-free, robust to mesh topology defects, enables unified rasterization of mesh and 3DGS with correct occlusion handling. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the proxy mesh and the accuracy of ray casting. Performance depends on the number of training cameras and Gaussians. When to use: When deformation of 3DGS is needed without retraining, or when integrating mesh and 3DGS in a unified framework. When not to use: When high-fidelity topological constraints are required and retraining is acceptable (mesh-centric may be more precise for specific geometric constraints). Gaussian-Centric Binding was proposed in the UniMGS framework (2026) to unify mesh and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering and deformation. It addresses the limitations of mesh-centric strategies, which require retraining and are sensitive to mesh topology. The method leverages the inherent orientation of training cameras in 3DGS to cast rays for spatial association. name: 3DGS Custom Initialization from Point Cloud/Mesh
head: 3DGS Model Learning Initialization from Point Cloud/Mesh, Custom Initialisation for 3DGS from Point Cloud/Mesh, Custom Initialization from Point Cloud/Mesh, Geometry-guided 3DGS Initialization, Point Cloud/Mesh Initialization for 3DGS
body: This method initializes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) learning using a pre-existing dense 3D point cloud or mesh as the geometric prior, replacing the standard Structure-from-Motion (SfM) sparse point cloud initialization. It solves the problem of creating high-quality 3DGS models from volumetric data (e.g., MPEG plenoptic point clouds or meshes) when the original multi-view images used for capture are unavailable. Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on sparse SfM points and aggressive adaptive density control (leading to potential misalignment and 'floater' artifacts), this method uses dense, surface-aligned initial points, resulting in cleaner models, fewer splats, and significantly faster convergence (e.g., 5,000 vs. 15,000 iterations). Inputs: 1. Geometry: A 3D point cloud or mesh. For point clouds, the vertices \{pi\} are used. For meshes, either the vertices or the center point of each mesh face (or a subset thereof) is used. 2. Color Data: View-dependent colors associated with the geometry (e.g., from a plenoptic point cloud). If the input is a mesh, colors may be sampled or rendered. 3. Camera Parameters: Extrinsic and intrinsic parameters for a set of viewpoints. These are used to render multi-view images from the input geometry and must be transformed to the target coordinate system (e.g., COLMAP format). Outputs: A 3DGS model (set of Gaussians) initialized with centers on the input geometry, ready for optimization. Data Structures: The method populates the standard 3DGS Gaussian attributes: xyz: Initialized to the (x, y, z) coordinates of the selected input points. featuresdc: Initialized to the RGB color of the corresponding point. featuresrest: Zero-initialized. opacity: Initialized to a low value (raw parameter \approx -2.197, corresponding to opacity \approx 0.1). scaling: Derived from local density or depth heuristics (e.g., median distance to k-nearest neighbors or isometric radius based on focal length and depth). rotation: Initialized to identity quaternion (1, 0, 0, 0) for all Gaussians. Steps: 1. Render Multi-View Images: Generate multi-view images from the input 3D point cloud or mesh using a renderer (e.g., PccAppRenderer). 2. Align Camera Parameters: Obtain camera parameters (extrinsic and intrinsic) for the viewpoints used to generate the images. Transform these parameters to the target coordinate system (e.g., COLMAP). 3. Select Initial Points: If input is a point cloud: Use the vertices (x, y, z) as the initial Gaussian centers. If input is a mesh: Use the vertices or the center point of each mesh face (or a chosen subset of faces) as the initial Gaussian centers. 4. Initialize Gaussian Attributes: Set xyz to the selected points. Set featuresdc to the RGB color of the points. Set featuresrest to zero. Set opacity to a low initial value (e.g., raw parameter -2.197). Set rotation to identity (1, 0, 0, 0). Compute scaling using heuristics such as median distance to k-nearest neighbors or isometric radius. 5. Configure Optimization Constraints: Deactivate Adaptive Density Control: If the input point cloud/mesh is already dense and clean, deactivate cloning/splitting of splats to preserve the initial point density and reduce learning time. Freeze Position Learning Rate: Set the position learning rate for the splat centers to 0. Retain a learning rate > 0 for other attributes (opacity, scale, rotation, color) to allow the splats to adapt their appearance and shape without moving from their geometric centers. 6. Optimize: Run the 3DGS optimization loop for the specified number of iterations (e.g., 5,000). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initialize3dgsfromgeometry(geometry, cameraparams, renderer): """ Initialize 3DGS model from a point cloud or mesh. Args: geometry: Point cloud or Mesh object containing vertices and colors. cameraparams: List of camera extrinsics and intrinsics in target coordinate system. renderer: Renderer instance capable of rendering geometry to images. Returns: Initialized 3DGS model object. """ # Step 1: Render multi-view images for optimization targets # Note: Colors in geometry should be view-dependent if available. targetimages = [] for cam in cameraparams: img = renderer.render(geometry, cam) targetimages.append(img) # Step 3: Select initial points if isinstance(geometry, PointCloud): centers = geometry.vertices colors = geometry.colors elif isinstance(geometry, Mesh): # Use face centers or vertices centers = getmeshfacecenters(geometry) colors = samplecolorsfrommesh(geometry, centers) else: raise ValueError("Unsupported geometry type") numgaussians = len(centers) # Step 4: Initialize Gaussian Attributes # xyz: Centers from geometry xyz = centers # featuresdc: RGB colors featuresdc = colors.reshape(-1, 3) # featuresrest: Zero-initialized featuresrest = np.zeros((numgaussians, 15, 3)) # Assuming 15 coefficients for SH degree 2 # opacity: Low initial value # Raw parameter -2.197 corresponds to sigmoid(-2.197) ≈ 0.1 opacity = np.full((numgaussians, 1), -2.197) # rotation: Identity quaternion (w, x, y, z) rotation = np.tile([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], (numgaussians, 1)) # scaling: Heuristic based on local density # Example: Median distance to k-nearest neighbors k = 10 scales = computemedianknndistance(centers, k) # Convert distance to scale parameter (log scale) scaling = np.log(scales) # Step 5: Configure Optimization # Create model object model = GaussianModel() model.setxyz(xyz) model.setfeaturesdc(featuresdc) model.setfeaturesrest(featuresrest) model.setopacity(opacity) model.setrotation(rotation) model.setscaling(scaling) # Set learning rates model.setpositionlearningrate(0.0) # Freeze positions model.setotherlearningrates(>0) # Allow adaptation of other attributes # Deactivate adaptive density control if geometry is dense/clean if isgeometrydenseandclean(geometry): model.deactivateadaptivedensitycontrol() return model Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy/Sparse Input: If the input 3D model is noisy, sparse, or has holes, deactivating adaptive density control should be avoided. In such cases, the default SfM initialization may be preferred, or adaptive control should remain active to allow the model to fill gaps and correct errors. Coordinate Systems: Camera parameters must be correctly transformed to the target coordinate system (e.g., COLMAP) to ensure alignment between rendered images and the geometry. View-Dependent Colors: The method benefits significantly from input data containing view-dependent colors (e.g., plenoptic point clouds), as 3DGS is effective for non-Lambertian surfaces. Convergence Speed: Significantly faster than SfM-based initialization. In tests on the Thaidancer sequence, custom initialization converged in 5,000 iterations compared to 15,000 iterations for SfM initialization, with comparable visual quality. Model Size: Produces fewer splats than the original point cloud density. For the Thaidancer sequence, the original point cloud was ~3M voxels (201MB PLY), while the resulting 3DGS model had ~250k splats (61MB PLY). Quality: Produces cleaner surface representation with fewer 'floater' artifacts compared to SfM initialization, which often requires adaptive density control that can lead to misalignment. Limitations: Requires a pre-existing dense and clean point cloud or mesh. If the input geometry is poor quality, the method's constraints (frozen positions, no densification) may lead to suboptimal results. Hardware/Resolution: Performance scales with the number of splats and iterations. The reduction in iterations (5k vs 15k) directly reduces training time. This method was proposed in the context of transcoding 3D Gaussian Splatting models from existing 3D plenoptic point clouds or meshes when original multi-view images are unavailable. It addresses the need to leverage traditional volumetric media formats (like those in MPEG codec standardization) with the emerging popularity of 3DGS. The approach was tested on the MPEG plenoptic point cloud dataset, specifically the "8i Voxelized Surface Light Field" (8iVSLF). name: Octree-GS / Scaffold-GS
head: Anchor-based Gaussian Splatting
body: Octree-GS and Scaffold-GS are hierarchical level-of-detail (LoD) methods that anchor scene content to a sparse voxel grid or octree, using the structure as a scaffold to allocate 3D Gaussians only in occupied regions. This approach naturally adapts to view distance, significantly improving memory efficiency and reducing redundancy compared to flat Gaussian representations. Unlike LinPrim Population Control which dynamically splits/merges primitives based on screen space, these methods pre-organize primitives into a spatial hierarchy, enabling efficient culling and streaming for large-scale scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud; camera poses; training images. Output: A set of "anchor" primitives (voxel centers) with features, and a decoder (MLP or fixed function) that generates child Gaussians on the fly. Data Structures: 1. Sparse Voxel Grid / Octree: Initialized from SfM points. Each node (anchor) stores: Position: Voxel center coordinates. Learnable Scale: A scalar or vector defining the anchor's spatial extent. Feature Vector: A latent vector used by the decoder to predict child Gaussian attributes. 2. Child Gaussians (Generated): Generated per visible anchor. Attributes: Position (offset from anchor), Opacity, Color, Scale, Quaternion. Parameters: \tau\alpha: Opacity threshold. Gaussians with opacity \alpha < \tau\alpha are not rasterized. k: Number of Gaussians generated from each visible anchor. Typical value k=4. Voxel Size: Grid resolution. Typical value 0.001 for anchor grids in modified variants. Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct a sparse voxel grid from the input SfM points. Place an anchor at each occupied voxel center. Assign a learnable scale to each anchor. 2. Feature Learning: Optimize the anchor features (and anchor scales) using reconstruction loss (L1, SSIM, and optionally volume regularization L{vol}). 3. Gaussian Generation (Decoding): For each camera view, identify visible anchors within the frustum. For each visible anchor, generate k child Gaussians. The position of each child is defined by an offset Oi from the anchor center. Attributes (opacity, color, scale, quaternion) are decoded from the anchor's feature vector using a small MLP or neural field. 4. Filtering: Discard any generated Gaussian where opacity \alpha < \tau\alpha. 5. Rasterization: Render the remaining significant Gaussians using standard alpha-blending. 6. Optimization: Update anchor features and scales to minimize the difference between the rendered image and the ground truth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. This builds on the anchor-based representation introduced in Octree-GS / Scaffold-GS by using sparse anchors as reference points to predict attributes of dependent Gaussians, thereby reducing redundancy and improving coding efficiency. name: Anchor-2D-GS / Anchor-3D-GS
head: Anchor-GS, modified versions of 2D-GS and 3D-GS
body: Anchor-2D-GS and Anchor-3D-GS are modified variants of 2D-GS [15] and 3D-GS [5] that employ an anchor grid structure to organize Gaussian primitives more efficiently, reducing redundancy and storage overhead. They achieve competitive rendering quality with fewer file storage than original methods, demonstrating that the anchor design organizes primitives more efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Output: A set of 2D or 3D Gaussians organized within an anchor grid structure. Data Structures: The method voxelize the input SfM points to create anchors. Each anchor is assigned 2D or 3D Gaussians. The specific layout of the Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color) follows the standard definitions of the parent method (2D-GS or 3D-GS), but their spatial distribution is constrained by the anchor grid. Parameters: Voxel size for the anchor grid: 0.001 for all scenes in the modified anchor versions. Training Iterations: 40k iterations for standard scenes, with densification concluding at 20k iterations. For large-scale scenes, training is set to 100k iterations, with densification ending at 50k iterations. Densification Interval (T): 100. Visibility Threshold (\tauv): 0.7 for small-scale scenes. Loss Functions: The method maintains the same densification strategy as Scaffold-GS. The specific loss functions depend on the base variant: For Anchor-3D-GS: Standard L1 and SSIM loss, with weights set to 0.8 and 0.2, respectively. For Anchor-2D-GS: Retains the distortion loss Ld = \sum{i,j} \omegai \omegaj |zi - zj| and normal loss Ln = \sumi \omegai (1 - \mathbf{n}i^T \mathbf{N}), with weights set to 0.01 and 0.05, respectively. Steps: 1. Voxelization: Voxelize the input SfM points to generate the anchor grid. 2. Assignment: Assign 2D or 3D Gaussians to each anchor. 3. Training: Optimize the Gaussian parameters using the specified loss functions and densification strategy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes the input consists of SfM points. Not all layers are fully densified during progressive training processes, which may require extending densification by an additional 10k iterations. Anchor Gaussians are hypothesized to constrain and regularize parameters of coarser-level Gaussians, typically having larger scales than regular Gaussians. They do not have actual opacity for rendering; for visualization, their opacity is manually set to \text{sigmoid}(1). The average scale of anchors is e^{-5.08} across 100 randomly sampled scenes, while the average scale of Gaussians is e^{-7.12}. This size difference suggests that Gaussians adjust their scales to represent sharp details in real-world images, whereas anchor Gaussians serve a regularization role. Storage: Achieves fewer file storage than original 2D-GS and 3D-GS methods. Quality: Competitive rendering quality compared to original methods. Efficiency: The anchor design creates a more compact representation by reducing redundancy. Comparison: While Anchor-2D/3D-GS reduce storage, Octree-GS delivers better visual performance and fewer Gaussian primitives due to its explicit, multi-level anchor design. The method was introduced in "Octree-GS: Towards Consistent Real-time Rendering with LOD-Structured 3D Gaussians". It represents a modification of existing 2D-GS [15] and 3D-GS [5] techniques to incorporate an anchor-based organization, building on the concepts explored in Scaffold-GS [3] regarding anchor-based representations. name: Random Gaussian Generation
head: Gaussian Generation Dataset, Random Gaussian Sampling
body: Random Gaussian Generation is the initialization procedure for creating a set of 3D Gaussians from scratch, typically to serve as the starting point for differentiable rendering optimization in methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting. It generates a fixed number of Gaussian primitives with random positions (implicitly at the origin before transformation), scales, orientations, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. It differs from LinPrim Population Control which manages the density of existing Gaussians during training, and from Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization which may use structured or data-driven initialization strategies. This method provides a uniform, uninformative prior over the parameter space. The method generates a set of N Gaussian objects. Each Gaussian is defined by a centroid, a scale vector, a rotation quaternion, an opacity scalar, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for color. Inputs: numsamples: Total number of Gaussians to generate. Default: 1000. numpoints: Number of points per Gaussian (used for internal representation or visualization, not stored in the final Gaussian object). Default: 144 (12 \times 12). minscale: Lower bound for the uniform distribution of scale components (in log space). Default: -12. maxscale: Upper bound for the uniform distribution of scale components (in log space). Default: -2. minopacity: Lower bound for the uniform distribution of opacity (in logit space). Default: -5. maxopacity: Upper bound for the uniform distribution of opacity (in logit space). Default: 10. shdegree: Maximum spherical harmonics degree to generate. Default: 3. returntype: Output format. Options: 'gaussian', 'param', or 'both'. Default: 'gaussian'. Outputs: A list or tensor of Gaussian objects/parameters. If returntype is 'gaussian', returns full Gaussian objects. If 'param', returns raw parameter tensors. If 'both', returns both. Each Gaussian object contains: centroid: 3D vector [0, 0, 0] (initial position, often transformed later). scale: 3D vector [sx, sy, sz]. rotation: Quaternion q derived from a rotation matrix. opacity: Scalar \alpha. featdc: 3D vector containing DC SH coefficients for R, G, B. featextra: Concatenated higher-order SH coefficients. 1. Initialize Scale: For each Gaussian i, sample sx, sy, sz independently from a uniform distribution U(\text{min\scale}, \text{max\scale}). 2. Initialize Rotation: Generate a 3 \times 3 matrix M with entries drawn from a standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Compute the QR decomposition of M: M = QR. Take the Q factor as the rotation matrix R{mat}. Convert R{mat} to a quaternion q using a standard conversion function (e.g., rotmat2qvec). 3. Initialize Opacity: Sample opacity \alphai from a uniform distribution U(\text{min\opacity}, \text{max\opacity}). Note: These values are likely logits, to be converted to probabilities via sigmoid during rendering or optimization. 4. Initialize Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: For each color channel (R, G, B) and each degree d from 0 to \text{sh\degree}: Calculate variance \sigmad^2 = \frac{1}{4^d}. Sample (2d+1) coefficients from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, \sigmad). If \text{sh\degree} < \text{max\SH\degree} (where maxSHdegree is typically 3 or higher in full implementations), fill the remaining coefficients with noise from \mathcal{N}(0, 0.05). The DC coefficients (d=0) for R, G, B form featdc. Higher-order coefficients (d > 0) are concatenated to form featextra. 5. Construct Gaussian Object: Assemble the components into a Gaussian object with centroid at [0,0,0], scale [sx, sy, sz], rotation q, opacity \alpha, featdc, and featextra. 6. Repeat: Steps 1-5 are repeated for N = \text{num\samples} Gaussians. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch def generaterandomgaussians(numsamples=1000, minscale=-12, maxscale=-2, minopacity=-5, maxopacity=10, shdegree=3, returntype='gaussian'): """ Generates a set of random 3D Gaussians for initialization. """ gaussians = [] for in range(numsamples): # 1. Generate Scale scale = np.random.uniform(minscale, maxscale, 3) # 2. Generate Rotation # QR decomposition of random normal matrix M = np.random.randn(3, 3) Q, R = np.linalg.qr(M) # Ensure proper rotation matrix (handle reflection if det(Q) == -1) if np.linalg.det(Q) < 0: Q[:, 0] = -1 # Convert rotation matrix to quaternion # Assuming a standard conversion function exists rotation = rotmat2qvec(Q) # 3. Generate Opacity opacity = np.random.uniform(minopacity, maxopacity) # 4. Generate Spherical Harmonics Coefficients featdc = [] featextra = [] for d in range(shdegree + 1): variance = 1.0 / (4 d) std = np.sqrt(variance) numcoeffs = 2 d + 1 # Sample coefficients for R, G, B coeffsr = np.random.normal(0, std, numcoeffs) coeffsg = np.random.normal(0, std, numcoeffs) coeffsb = np.random.normal(0, std, numcoeffs) if d == 0: featdc = [coeffsr[0], coeffsg[0], coeffsb[0]] else: featextra.extend(coeffsr) featextra.extend(coeffsg) featextra.extend(coeffsb) # Fill remaining coefficients if shdegree < max possible (e.g., 3) # Assuming maxSHdegree is 3 for this example maxshdegree = 3 if shdegree < maxshdegree: for d in range(shdegree + 1, maxshdegree + 1): numcoeffs = 2 d + 1 noise = np.random.normal(0, 0.05, numcoeffs) featextra.extend(noise) featextra.extend(np.random.normal(0, 0.05, numcoeffs)) featextra.extend(np.random.normal(0, 0.05, numcoeffs)) # 5. Construct Gaussian Object gaussian = { 'centroid': np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), 'scale': scale, 'rotation': rotation, 'opacity': opacity, 'featdc': np.array(featdc), 'featextra': np.array(featextra) } gaussians.append(gaussian) return gaussians def rotmat2qvec(R): """ Converts a 3x3 rotation matrix to a quaternion [w, x, y, z]. Standard conversion algorithm. """ m00, m01, m02 = R[0, 0], R[0, 1], R[0, 2] m10, m11, m12 = R[1, 0], R[1, 1], R[1, 2] m20, m21, m22 = R[2, 0], R[2, 1], R[2, 2] trace = m00 + m11 + m22 if trace > 0: s = 0.5 / np.sqrt(trace + 1.0) w = 0.25 / s x = (m21 - m12) s y = (m02 - m20) s z = (m10 - m01) s elif (m00 > m11) and (m00 > m22): s = 2.0 np.sqrt(1.0 + m00 - m11 - m22) w = (m21 - m12) / s x = 0.25 s y = (m01 + m10) / s z = (m02 + m20) / s elif m11 > m22: s = 2.0 np.sqrt(1.0 + m11 - m00 - m22) w = (m02 - m20) / s x = (m01 + m10) / s y = 0.25 s z = (m12 + m21) / s else: s = 2.0 np.sqrt(1.0 + m22 - m00 - m11) w = (m10 - m01) / s x = (m02 + m20) / s y = (m12 + m21) / s z = 0.25 s return np.array([w, x, y, z]) Reflection in Rotation: The QR decomposition of a random normal matrix can produce a reflection (determinant -1) instead of a rotation. The pseudocode includes a check to flip the first column if det(Q) < 0 to ensure a proper rotation matrix. Opacity Range: The default opacity range [-5, 10] suggests logit space. If used directly as probability, it will cause numerical issues. It should be passed through a sigmoid function if interpreted as probability. SH Variance: The variance decreases exponentially with degree (1/4^d). This ensures higher-frequency details have smaller initial amplitudes, stabilizing optimization. Missing SH Coefficients: If shdegree is less than the maximum supported degree, remaining coefficients must be filled with noise to maintain tensor shape consistency. Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting (CAG-GS) is a large-scale scene rendering method that employs a divide-and-conquer strategy with semantic guidance to ensure global consistency across spatial blocks, thereby avoiding artifacts such as floaters and brightness inconsistencies. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Momentum-GS by directly incorporating consistent semantic information from a pre-trained segmentation model (SAM2) to guide feature learning, rather than relying solely on shared MLP decoders for regularization. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of samples and D is the number of SH coefficients. The QR decomposition is O(1) per Gaussian (fixed 3x3 matrix). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) to store the generated Gaussians. Performance: The method is fast and deterministic in its randomness. It does not depend on scene geometry, making it suitable for initial exploration or when no point cloud is available. Strengths: Simple to implement, no external data required, provides a diverse initial set of orientations and scales. Limitations: The Gaussians are not aligned with any scene structure, leading to slow convergence if the scene is complex. The random positions (implicitly at origin) require subsequent transformation or optimization to match the scene. When to Use: When initializing a new scene with no prior geometric information, or as a baseline for comparison. When Not to Use: When a point cloud or mesh is available, structured initialization (e.g., Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization) is preferred for faster convergence and better initial quality. The method is described in the context of the gs-embedding project, which explores embedding-based representations for 3D Gaussians. The specific parameters and generation steps are derived from the implementation details provided in the source code and documentation of this project. The use of QR decomposition for random rotations is a standard technique in computer graphics for generating uniform random rotations. The exponential decay of SH variance is a common practice in neural rendering to stabilize training. gs-embedding, https://github.com/cilix-ai/gs-embedding, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting
head: CAG-GS
body: Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting (CAG-GS) is a large-scale scene rendering method that employs a divide-and-conquer strategy with semantic guidance to ensure global consistency across spatial blocks, thereby avoiding artifacts such as floaters and brightness inconsistencies. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Momentum-GS by directly incorporating consistent semantic information from a pre-trained segmentation model (SAM2) to guide feature learning, rather than relying solely on shared MLP decoders for regularization. Inputs: Sparse point cloud P from Structure-from-Motion (SfM); training views with ground truth images; pre-trained semantic segmentation model (SAM2). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by anchors, optimized for novel view synthesis. Anchor (Aj): Each anchor is defined by: Level-of-Detail (lj): Integer level in the hierarchy. Position (pj): 3D coordinate in space. Learnable Feature (fj): Vector in \mathbb{R}^d. Spatial Offsets (o{j,1}, \dots, o{j,K}): K learnable 3D offset vectors in \mathbb{R}^{3K} used to predict Gaussian positions. Implicit Gaussians: Generated per anchor. Each Gaussian i has: Position (\mui): Derived from anchor position and offsets. Color (ci): Predicted by MLP. Opacity (\sigmai): Predicted by MLP. Covariance (\Sigmai): Parameterized by scaling and rotation (standard 3D-GS definition). L: Number of Level-of-Detail (LoD) levels for voxelization. \delta: Base voxel size. d: Dimensionality of the anchor feature vector fj. K: Expected number of Gaussians generated per anchor. \lambda: Weighting coefficient for SSIM loss (standard 3D-GS parameter). 1. Scene Discretization (Anchor Generation): The sparse point cloud P is voxelized at L different resolutions to generate anchor points A. For each point p \in P and level l \in \{0, \dots, L-1\}, the anchor position is calculated as: A = \left\{ \left\lfloor \frac{p}{\delta/2^l} \right\rceil \cdot \frac{\delta}{2^l} \mid p \in P, l = 0, \dots, L-1 \right\} where \lfloor \cdot \rceil denotes element-wise rounding and \delta is the base voxel size. 2. Coarse Global Training: A coarse global model is trained using all available training views to provide global priors. 3. Block Division: The scene is divided into multiple spatial blocks. 4. Semantic Mapping Module Initialization: A semantic mapping module \gamma: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^D is introduced. This module is trained to align its outputs with visual features extracted from the pre-trained SAM2 model. 5. Block-wise Fine-Tuning (Iterative per Block): For each block: a. View Assignment: Training views are assigned to the block according to blending weights computed during rendering. b. Anchor Selection: During rendering, visible anchors are selected based on their LoD levels and distance from the target viewpoint. c. Feature Fusion: For each selected anchor j with position pj and feature fj, a semantic vector is generated and fused: \tilde{f}j = W \cdot \gamma(pj) + fj where \gamma(pj) is the semantic vector encoded by the mapping module, and W is a learnable weight matrix. d. Gaussian Prediction: The enhanced feature \tilde{f}j is passed through MLP decoders to predict the attributes of K implicit Gaussians associated with the anchor. e. Rendering: The predicted 3D Gaussians are projected to 2D. They are sorted by depth and composited using alpha blending: C(x') = \sum{i \in I(x')} ci \alphai \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphak) where x' is the queried pixel, I(x') is the set of indices of contributing Gaussians sorted by depth, and \alphai = \sigmai G'i(x') is the transmittance/opacity contribution of Gaussian i at pixel x'. f.
