Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the current timestep being parsed, not the entire file. This allows rendering large animated scenes on devices with limited memory. Strengths: Low initial load time, memory efficiency for large files, supports incremental updates. Limitations: Requires HTTP server support for Range requests. Higher overhead per timestep due to repeated parsing and texture uploads compared to v2's unified structure. When to Use: When dealing with legacy.4dsplat v1 files or when memory constraints prevent loading the entire scene at once. When Not to Use: For new projects, prefer the v2 format for better compression and unified spacetime handling. The 4DGS v1 Progressive Loader is part of the "4D" web app ecosystem, which transforms video into renderable Gaussian Splats. It was developed to support the legacy v1 file format, which stores independent Gaussian blocks per timestep. This approach contrasts with the newer v2 format, which uses a unified spacetime structure. The loader is implemented in TypeScript for the web viewer, leveraging HTTP Range requests for efficient streaming. devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs, https://github.com/devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Model Preprocessing and Grid Partitioning
head: PLY Gaussian Loading with Fallbacks
body: This method preprocesses a raw 3D Gaussian Splatting model stored in PLY format for use in Unreal Engine. It parses the PLY file, converts coordinate systems and property encodings to match the engine's internal representation, and partitions the Gaussians into a spatial grid for efficient culling and rendering. It differs from generic loaders by applying specific axis swaps, exponential scale decoding, and sigmoid opacity activation required by the target engine's shader pipeline. Inputs: FilePath: Relative path to the PLY file within the project content directory. ProjectContentDir: Base directory path for the application's content. Outputs: GaussianData: A structured collection of Gaussian properties (Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, Opacity, Harmonics) organized by spatial grid cells. GridMetadata: Bounding box (BoundsMin, BoundsMax) and grid resolution (CellsPerEdge). Data Structures: FLinearColor: A 4-component vector (R, G, B, A) used to pack multiple float properties. FQuat: A 4-component quaternion (X, Y, Z, W) for rotation. GridCell: A container holding lists of Gaussian properties for a specific 3D grid coordinate (i, j, k). Steps: 1. Path Construction and Validation: Construct the absolute file path: \text{AbsolutePath} = \text{ProjectContentDir} + \text{"Models/"} + \text{FilePath} Initialize a PLY reader with the absolute path and validate that it successfully opened the file. If invalid, abort. 2. Header Parsing and Element Identification: Iterate through the PLY header elements using reader.haselement() and reader.nextelement(). Identify the vertex element by checking if reader.elementis(miniply::kPLYVertexElement). 3. Data Extraction: Load the vertex data using reader.loadelement() and retrieve the number of vertices N = \text{reader.num\rows()}. For each property in the vertex element, allocate a float array of size N and extract the data into a map keyed by property name. Validate that the following required properties exist in the map: Position (x, y, z), Orientation (rot0..rot3), Scale (scale0..scale2), Opacity, Zero Order Harmonics (fdc0..fdc2), and optionally Higher Order Harmonics (frest0..frest44). 4. Bounding Box Calculation: Initialize BoundsMin and BoundsMax with the first vertex's position converted to Unreal coordinates: P{\text{unreal}} = 100.0 \times (x, -z, -y) Iterate through all N vertices to update BoundsMin and BoundsMax component-wise. Compute BoxEdgeLengths: L = \text{BoundsMax} - \text{BoundsMin} All values are scaled by 100.0. 5. Grid Resolution Determination: Determine CellsPerEdge based on N: If N \le 1,500,000, CellsPerEdge = 1. If 1,500,000 < N \le 3,500,000, CellsPerEdge = 2. If N > 3,500,000, CellsPerEdge = 4. 6. Directory Creation: Create necessary directories for the model and emitter data using a helper function CreateDirectory. 7. Gaussian Property Processing and Grid Assignment: Initialize an empty grid structure of size CellsPerEdge \times CellsPerEdge \times CellsPerEdge. Iterate through each vertex v from 0 to N-1: a. Position Conversion: Convert to Unreal coordinates and scale by 100.0. Pack into FLinearColor as (R=x, G=-z, B=-y, A=0). b. Scale Conversion: Apply exponential activation and axis swap: s'0 = \exp(\text{scale\0}v), s'1 = \exp(\text{scale\2}v), s'2 = \exp(\text{scale\1}v). Scale by 100.0 and pack into FLinearColor as (R=s'0, G=s'1, B=s'2, A=0). c. Rotation Conversion: Construct quaternion from PLY order (rot1, rot2, rot3, rot0), normalize it, and apply axis swap/sign flip: (X=q.x, Y=-q.z, Z=-q.y, W=q.w). Pack into FLinearColor. d. Color and Opacity Conversion: Extract Zero Order Harmonics as BaseColor. Apply sigmoid to opacity: \alphav = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\text{opacity}v)}. Clamp \alphav to [0, 1]. Pack into FLinearColor as (R=C{base}.x, G=C{base}.y, B=C{base}.z, A=\alphav). e. Higher Order Harmonics (L1): If frest properties exist, iterate y from 0 to 9 with step 3. Extract fresty, fresty+1, fresty+2 and pack into an FLinearColor. Append to harmonicsL1TextureData. f. Grid Indexing: Calculate the grid index for the current vertex's position: i = \left\lfloor \frac{P{\text{final}}.x - \text{BoundsMin}.x}{L.x} \times \text{CellsPerEdge} \right\rfloor j = \left\lfloor \frac{P{\text{final}}.y - \text{BoundsMin}.y}{L.y} \times \text{CellsPerEdge} \right\rfloor k = \left\lfloor \frac{P{\text{final}}.z - \text{BoundsMin}.z}{L.z} \times \text{CellsPerEdge} \right\rfloor Clamp i, j, k to [0, \text{CellsPerEdge}-1]. Store the processed properties in the grid cell (i, j, k). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def preprocessgaussians(filepath, projectcontentdir): # 1. Path & Reader absolutepath = projectcontentdir + "Models/" + filepath # Initialize PLY reader (implementation omitted) reader = PLYReader(absolutepath) if not reader.valid(): raise ValueError("PLY file invalid or missing") # 2. Header & Vertex numvertices = 0 vertexdata = {} for element in reader.elements(): if element.isvertex(): element.load() numvertices = reader.numrows() for propname in element.properties(): propidx = element.findproperty(propname) columndata = [0.0] numvertices reader.extractproperties([propidx], 1, PLYPropertyType.FLOAT, columndata) vertexdata[propname] = columndata # 3. Validate Required Properties required = ["x", "y", "z", "rot0", "rot1", "rot2", "rot3", "scale0", "scale1", "scale2", "opacity", "fdc0", "fdc1", "fdc2"] for req in required: if req not in vertexdata: raise ValueError(f"Missing required property: {req}") hasrest = "frest0" in vertexdata # 4. Bounding Box (Unreal coords: 100.0 (x, -z, -y)) boundsmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] boundsmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for v in range(numvertices): px = 100.0 vertexdata["x"][v] py = 100.0 -vertexdata["z"][v] pz = 100.0 -vertexdata["y"][v] if v == 0: boundsmin = [px, py, pz] boundsmax = [px, py, pz] else: boundsmin = [min(boundsmin[i], [px, py, pz][i]) for i in range(3)] boundsmax = [max(boundsmax[i], [px, py, pz][i]) for i in range(3)] boxedgelengths = [boundsmax[i] - boundsmin[i] for i in range(3)] # 5. Grid Resolution if numvertices <= 1500000: cellsperedge = 1 elif numvertices <= 3500000: cellsperedge = 2 else: cellsperedge = 4 # 6. Directories # CreateDirectory helper not detailed in sources # 7. Process & Grid Assign grid = [[[] for in range(cellsperedge)] for in range(cellsperedge)] harmonicsl1 = [] for v in range(numvertices): # Position pos = [100.0 vertexdata["x"][v], 100.0 -vertexdata["z"][v], 100.0 -vertexdata["y"][v]] poscolor = [pos[0], pos[1], pos[2], 0.0] # Scale s0 = math.exp(vertexdata["scale0"][v]) s1 = math.exp(vertexdata["scale2"][v]) s2 = math.exp(vertexdata["scale1"][v]) scalecolor = [100.0 s0, 100.0 s1, 100.0 s2, 0.0] # Rotation quat = normalizequat([vertexdata["rot1"][v], vertexdata["rot2"][v], vertexdata["rot3"][v], vertexdata["rot0"][v]]) rotcolor = [quat[0], -quat[2], -quat[1], quat[3]] # Color & Opacity basecolor = [vertexdata["fdc0"][v], vertexdata["fdc1"][v], vertexdata["fdc2"][v]] opacity = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-vertexdata["opacity"][v])) opacity = max(0.0, min(1.0, opacity)) coloralphacolor = [basecolor[0], basecolor[1], basecolor[2], opacity] # Higher Order Harmonics if hasrest: for y in range(0, 10, 3): h = [vertexdata[f"frest{y}"][v], vertexdata[f"frest{y+1}"][v], vertexdata[f"frest{y+2}"][v], 0.0] harmonicsl1.append(h) # Grid Index idx = getgridindex(pos, boundsmin, boxedgelengths, cellsperedge) grid[idx[0]][idx[1]][idx[2]].append({ "pos": poscolor, "scale": scalecolor, "rot": rotcolor, "color": coloralphacolor }) return grid, harmonicsl1 def getgridindex(pos, boundsmin, edgelengths, cellsperedge): i = int(math.floor((pos[0] - boundsmin[0]) / edgelengths[0] cellsperedge)) j = int(math.floor((pos[1] - boundsmin[1]) / edgelengths[1] cellsperedge)) k = int(math.floor((pos[2] - boundsmin[2]) / edgelengths[2] cellsperedge)) return [max(0, min(cellsperedge - 1, idx)) for idx in [i, j, k]] def normalizequat(q): norm = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in q)) return [c/norm for c in q] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of FLinearColor (typically 32-bit floats per channel) for packed data may introduce quantization errors for properties like rotation or high-precision harmonics. Axis Swaps: The specific axis swaps (Y/Z swap for position, 1/2 swap for scale, X/Z/Y permutation for rotation) are critical. Incorrect mapping results in rotated or scaled splats. Harmonics Storage: Higher order harmonics are stored in a separate texture-like structure (harmonicsL1TextureData), not in the main grid cell properties. Time Complexity: O(N) for parsing, conversion, and grid assignment, where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the Gaussian properties and the grid structure. The grid itself is O(C^3) where C is CellsPerEdge, but typically C^3 \ll N. Performance: The method is a one-time preprocessing step. The grid partitioning enables O(1) spatial queries during rendering. Limitations: The grid resolution is fixed based on vertex count thresholds, which may not be optimal for all scene densities. The coordinate system conversion is hardcoded for Unreal Engine's right-handed coordinate system. This method originates from the unreal-splat project, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unreal Engine. It adapts the standard PLY format (which uses a left-handed coordinate system and raw scale/opacity values) to Unreal's requirements (right-handed, exponential scale, sigmoid opacity). The grid partitioning strategy is a heuristic based on vertex count to balance memory usage and culling efficiency. JI20/unreal-splat, https://github.com/JI20/unreal-splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 3D Covariance Computation
head: 3D Covariance Construction, Covariance Matrix Computation from Quaternions and Scales, Gaussian covariance from quaternion and scale
body: 3D Covariance Computation calculates the 3 \times 3 spatial covariance matrix for a set of 3D Gaussians given their orientation (quaternion) and scale parameters. It solves the problem of representing the anisotropic spatial extent and orientation of each Gaussian in world coordinates, which is required for projecting the Gaussian to 2D screen space during rendering. It sets itself apart from direct covariance optimization by deriving the covariance from unconstrained rotation and scale parameters, ensuring the resulting matrix is always positive semi-definite. Inputs: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing unit quaternions representing the orientation of N Gaussians. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the scale factors along the local x, y, and z axes, representing standard deviations. Outputs: cov3d: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 3) containing the computed 3 \times 3 covariance matrices for each Gaussian. Data Structures: Rotation Matrix R: 3 \times 3 matrix derived from the quaternion. Scale Matrix S: 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix containing squared scale values. Steps: 1. Convert Quaternions to Rotation Matrices: Convert the input quaternion tensor quats into a batched rotation matrix tensor R of shape (N, 3, 3). 2. Construct the Local Scale Matrix: Initialize a zero tensor S of shape (N, 3, 3) with the same data type and device as the input scales. Check if scales are isotropic (shape[-1] == 1). If isotropic, construct the scale matrix from a single scalar; otherwise, construct from x, y, z components. Set the diagonal elements of S to the squared scale values: S[:, 0, 0] = \text{scales}[:, 0]^2, S[:, 1, 1] = \text{scales}[:, 1]^2, S[:, 2, 2] = \text{scales}[:, 2]^2. 3. Compute the World Covariance Matrix: Compute the final covariance matrix \Sigma (or C{3D}) using the similarity transformation: \Sigma = R S R^T. This is implemented as a batched matrix multiplication. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computecov3d(quats: torch.Tensor, scales: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Compute 3D covariance matrices from quaternions and scales. Args: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing unit quaternions. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing scale factors. Returns: cov3d: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 3) containing covariance matrices. """ # Step 1: Convert quaternions to rotation matrices R = quaterniontomatrix(quats) # Shape: (N, 3, 3) # Step 2: Construct the diagonal scale matrix S S = torch.zeroslike(R) if scales.shape[-1] == 1: # Isotropic scales: construct from a single scalar s = scales[:, 0] S[:, 0, 0] = s 2 S[:, 1, 1] = s 2 S[:, 2, 2] = s 2 else: # Anisotropic scales: construct from x, y, z components S[:, 0, 0] = scales[:, 0] 2 S[:, 1, 1] = scales[:, 1] 2 S[:, 2, 2] = scales[:, 2] 2 # Step 3: Compute covariance via similarity transformation R @ S @ R^T # Using einsum for batched matrix multiplication: R[i,j,k] S[j,k,l] R[i,m,l] -> Cov[i,j,m] cov3d = torch.einsum("nij,njk,nlk->nil", R, S, R) return cov3d def quaterniontomatrix(quaternions: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Convert a batch of quaternions to rotation matrices. Standard mathematical operation. """ # Normalize quaternions to ensure they are unit quaternions quaternions = quaternions / quaternions.norm(p=2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) w, x, y, z = torch.unbind(quaternions, dim=-1) # Construct rotation matrix elements xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz xw, yw, zw = xw, yw, zw R = torch.stack([ 1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - zw), 2(xz + yw), 2(xy + zw), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - xw), 2(xz - yw), 2(yz + xw), 1 - 2(xx + yy) ], dim=-1).reshape(quaternions.shape[:-1] + (3, 3)) return R Parameters: quats: Input tensor of shape (N, 4). scales: Input tensor of shape (N, 3). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Isotropic Scales: If scales are provided as a single scalar (isotropic), the scale matrix construction must handle this case by repeating the scalar on the diagonal. Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized before conversion to ensure valid rotation matrices. Precision: The computation involves squaring scale values, which can lead to numerical instability if scales are very large or very small; using float64 may be needed for extreme ranges. This method is a preprocessing step that converts raw Gaussian splat parameters (position, scale, rotation, color) into pre-computed 3 \times 3 covariance matrices and normalized float colors to accelerate rendering. It solves the problem of per-frame matrix multiplication and color decoding by computing these values once during load. Covariance Factorisation is a parameterization technique for 3D Gaussian splats that decomposes the covariance matrix into a rotation matrix and a scaling matrix, ensuring the covariance remains positive semi-definite under unconstrained gradient descent. It sets itself apart from direct covariance optimization by embedding geometric constraints directly into the parameter space, and from Cholesky parameterization by explicitly separating rotation and scale for physical interpretability. Steps: 1. Initialize covsplat.flags to 0u. 2. Check if isGsplatActive(gsplat.flags) is true. 3. If active, copy flags, index, rgba, and center from gsplat. 4. Compute rotation matrix m by calling scaleQuaternionToMatrix(gsplat.scales, gsplat.quaternion). 5. Compute the symmetric covariance matrix components: m = m transpose(m). 6. Extract diagonal elements into covsplat.xxyyzz = vec3(m[0][0], m[1][1], m[2][2]). 7. Extract off-diagonal elements into covsplat.xyxzyz = vec3(m[0][1], m[0][2], m[1][2]). Pitfalls: If the input gsplat is null or inactive, the output covsplat.flags remains 0u, and other fields are not updated (or initialized to defaults in the JS wrapper). Not given in the sources. The method is a standard component in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines for computing covariance from quaternion and scale parameters. It is used in differentiable rendering and inverse volume rendering contexts. Automatic covariance and rotation recalculation procedures update Gaussian parameters when mesh vertices are transformed, ensuring splats correctly reflect new geometry without manual scaling factor calculation. name: Pre-computed Covariance and Color Buffer Generation
head: Covariance and Color Pre-computation, Gaussian Parameter Pre-processing
body: This method is a preprocessing step that converts raw Gaussian splat parameters (position, scale, rotation, color) into pre-computed 3x3 covariance matrices and normalized float colors to accelerate rendering. It solves the problem of per-frame matrix multiplication and color decoding by computing these values once during load. Inputs: bufferData: A byte array containing interleaved Gaussian parameters. vertexCount: The total number of Gaussians. Outputs: covarianceArray: A Float32Array of size 6 vertexCount. Stores the 6 unique elements of the symmetric covariance matrix for each Gaussian. colorArray: A Float32Array of size 4 vertexCount. Stores normalized RGBA color values in the range [0.0, 1.0]. Data Structures and Layout: The input bufferData is organized in rows of 44 bytes per vertex. The layout per vertex is: Bytes 0–11: Position (XYZ), 3 Float32 values. Bytes 12–23: Scale (XYZ), 3 Float32 values. Bytes 24–39: Rotation (IJKW), 4 Float32 values. The source specifies the order IJKW corresponds to x, y, z, w components of the quaternion. Bytes 40–43: Color (RGBA), 4 Uint8 values. The output buffers are tightly packed arrays of Float32 values. Steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Create covarianceBufferData with size CovarianceSizeBytes vertexCount and colorBufferData with size ColorSizeBytes vertexCount. Wrap these in Float32Array instances named covarianceArray and colorArray. 2. Iterate Over Vertices: For each vertex index i from 0 to vertexCount - 1: 2.1. Process Color: Calculate byte offset baseColor = 44 i + 40. Read 4 Uint8 values from bufferData at baseColor. Normalize each value by dividing by 255.0. Store the normalized floats in colorArray at indices 4i to 4i+3. 2.2. Extract Scale: Calculate float offset baseScale = 11 i + 3. Read 3 Float32 values from bufferData at baseScale. Construct a diagonal scale matrix S. 2.3. Extract Rotation: Calculate float offset rotationBase = 11 i + 7. Read 4 Float32 values from bufferData at rotationBase. Interpret these as quaternion components (qx, qy, qz, qw) corresponding to the I, J, K, W order. Construct a rotation matrix R. 2.4. Compute Transformation Matrix M: Compute M = R \times S. Let M{ij} be the element at row i and column j (0-indexed) of the 3 \times 3 matrix M. 2.5. Compute Covariance Elements: The symmetric covariance matrix C is computed as C = M M^T. The 6 unique elements are stored in covarianceArray at indices 6i to 6i+5: C{00} = M{00}^2 + M{01}^2 + M{02}^2 C{01} = M{00}M{10} + M{01}M{11} + M{02}M{12} C{02} = M{00}M{20} + M{01}M{21} + M{02}M{22} C{11} = M{10}^2 + M{11}^2 + M{12}^2 C{12} = M{10}M{20} + M{11}M{21} + M{12}M{22} C{22} = M{20}^2 + M{21}^2 + M{22}^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct def precomputecovarianceandcolor(bufferdata, vertexcount): """ Pre-computes covariance matrices and normalized colors from raw splat data. Args: bufferdata: bytes or bytearray containing interleaved Gaussian parameters. vertexcount: int, number of Gaussians. Returns: covariancearray: list of floats, length 6 vertexcount. colorarray: list of floats, length 4 vertexcount. """ covariancearray = [0.0] (6 vertexcount) colorarray = [0.0] (4 vertexcount) # Constants for layout SCALEOFFSETFLOATS = 3 ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS = 7 COLOROFFSETBYTES = 40 for i in range(vertexcount): basefloatoffset = i 11 basebyteoffset = i 44 # 1. Process Color r = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES] g = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 1] b = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 2] a = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 3] colorarray[4 i] = r / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 1] = g / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 2] = b / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 3] = a / 255.0 # 2. Extract Scale sx = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS)[0] sy = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS + 1)[0] sz = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS + 2)[0] # 3. Extract Rotation qx = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS)[0] qy = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 1)[0] qz = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 2)[0] qw = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 3)[0] # Compute Rotation Matrix R from Quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw) qx2, qy2, qz2, qw2 = qxqx, qyqy, qzqz, qwqw xy, xz, xw, yz, yw, zw = qxqy, qxqz, qxqw, qyqz, qyqw, qzqw r00 = 1 - 2 (qy2 + qz2) r01 = 2 (xy - zw) r02 = 2 (xz + yw) r10 = 2 (xy + zw) r11 = 1 - 2 (qx2 + qz2) r12 = 2 (yz - xw) r20 = 2 (xz - yw) r21 = 2 (yz + xw) r22 = 1 - 2 (qx2 + qy2) # 4. Compute M = R S # Since S is diagonal, Mij = Rij Sjj m00, m01, m02 = r00 sx, r01 sy, r02 sz m10, m11, m12 = r10 sx, r11 sy, r12 sz m20, m21, m22 = r20 sx, r21 sy, r22 sz # 5. Compute Covariance C = M M^T c00 = m00m00 + m01m01 + m02m02 c01 = m00m10 + m01m11 + m02m12 c02 = m00m20 + m01m21 + m02m22 c11 = m10m10 + m11m11 + m12m12 c12 = m10m20 + m11m21 + m12m22 c22 = m20m20 + m21m21 + m22m22 covariancearray[6 i] = c00 covariancearray[6 i + 1] = c01 covariancearray[6 i + 2] = c02 covariancearray[6 i + 3] = c11 covariancearray[6 i + 4] = c12 covariancearray[6 i + 5] = c22 return covariancearray, colorarray Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion Order: The source explicitly notes that the rotation data is stored as IJKW (x, y, z, w). Standard libraries often expect WXYZ or XYZW. Misinterpreting this order will result in incorrect rotation matrices and thus incorrect covariance shapes. Matrix Multiplication Order: The covariance is derived from M = R \times S. Since S is diagonal, this scales the columns of R. If S were applied as S \times R, the rows would be scaled, which is incorrect for transforming a sphere into an ellipsoid defined by scale axes aligned with the rotation basis. Precision: The input color is Uint8. Normalization by 255.0 introduces floating-point representation errors, but this is standard for color data. The covariance elements are Float32, which may lose precision for very small or very large scales, potentially affecting rendering stability at extreme zoom levels. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians. The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N). The output buffers require 10 \times N \times 4 bytes (6 floats for covariance + 4 floats for color). Performance: This preprocessing moves computation from the GPU fragment/vertex shader to the CPU (or a compute shader) during asset loading. This reduces the per-frame cost of rendering, as the shader only needs to sample the pre-computed covariance and color values. Strengths: Eliminates per-pixel or per-vertex matrix multiplication and quaternion-to-matrix conversion during rendering. Simplifies the shader logic. Limitations: Requires storing additional data (covariance matrix) in memory. If the Gaussians are dynamic (e.g., animated), this pre-computation must be repeated every frame or whenever parameters change, negating the benefit. This method is part of the implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time web rendering, specifically within the context of Three.js and A-Frame viewers. It is based on the work of Mark Kellogg (GaussianSplats3D) and Kevin Kwok (WebGL implementation of Gaussian Splatting). The technique leverages the fact that the covariance matrix for a Gaussian splat is constant for a given set of scale and rotation parameters, allowing it to be pre-computed. akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, https://github.com/akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Covariance Factorisation
head: Covariance Decomposition, RQ Decomposition for Covariance, Rotation and Scale Parameterization
body: Covariance Factorisation is a parameterization technique for 3D Gaussian splats that decomposes the covariance matrix \Sigma into a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} and a scaling matrix \mathbf{S}. This method ensures the covariance matrix remains positive semi-definite (PSD) during unconstrained gradient descent optimization, which is critical for maintaining the physical validity of the Gaussian primitives. It sets itself apart from direct covariance optimization by explicitly decoupling rotation and scale, allowing for intuitive parameterization and stable gradient derivation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unconstrained learnable parameters for rotation and scale. Output: A valid, positive semi-definite 3D covariance matrix \Sigma. Data Structures: The method relies on two primary learnable components per Gaussian splat: 1. Rotation Matrix \mathbf{R}: A 3 \times 3 orthogonal matrix. In practice, this is often parameterized by a unit quaternion or Euler angles to ensure orthogonality, though the factorisation itself assumes \mathbf{R} is a valid rotation matrix. 2. Scaling Matrix \mathbf{S}: A diagonal matrix \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(s1, s2, s3), where si are the scale factors along the principal axes. The scale vector \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is typically constrained to be positive (si > 0) to maintain physical meaning. Steps: 1. Parameter Initialization: Initialize the rotation parameters (e.g., quaternion) and scale parameters (e.g., log-scale or raw positive values) for each Gaussian splat. 2. Optimization: Perform unconstrained gradient descent on these parameters. Because the parameters are not the covariance entries directly, there is no risk of generating a non-PSD matrix during updates. 3. Reconstruction: At each rendering or update step, reconstruct the covariance matrix using the factorisation formula: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T Here, \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T is a diagonal matrix with entries si^2. Thus, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \text{diag}(s1^2, s2^2, s3^2) \mathbf{R}^T. 4. Usage: The resulting \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is used for EWA projection and rendering. Formulas: Covariance Reconstruction: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T Where: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix. \mathbf{R} is the 3 \times 3 rotation matrix. \mathbf{S} is the 3 \times 3 diagonal scaling matrix. \mathbf{S}^T is the transpose of \mathbf{S} (equal to \mathbf{S} for diagonal matrices). Parameters: Scale Vector \mathbf{s}: Typically optimized in log-space to ensure positivity, or constrained via activation functions. Rotation Representation: Unit quaternions are common to ensure \mathbf{R} remains orthogonal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-PSD Matrices: Direct optimization of \Sigma entries can lead to non-PSD matrices, causing numerical instability and invalid Gaussian shapes. Factorisation avoids this by construction. Degenerate Scales: If any scale si becomes zero or negative (if not constrained), the Gaussian becomes degenerate. Constraints or activations (e.g., softplus, exp) are required. Rotation Ambiguity: The factorisation is not unique if signs of scales and rotation axes are not handled consistently. Standard practice assumes positive scales and a proper rotation matrix. Cholesky Parameterisation represents the covariance matrix using a lower triangular Cholesky factor, guaranteeing positive-definiteness by construction. It uses D(D+1)/2 elements per splat (6 for 3D) and applies a softplus activation with a minimum standard deviation floor \sigma{min} = 1/\sqrt{12} voxels to the diagonal, while bounding amplitudes with a configurable maximum a{max}. Unlike Covariance Factorisation, which decouples rotation and scale, Cholesky uses a triangular factorization, which may be less intuitive for interpreting ellipsoid geometry but offers similar stability guarantees. This method parameterizes the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \Sigma using a unit quaternion q and a 3D scale vector s to ensure the matrix remains positive semi-definite during optimization. It solves the problem that directly optimizing the entries of \Sigma can result in non-positive semi-definite matrices, violating physical interpretation and causing numerical instability. Unlike siblings such as Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats, which uses a triangular factorization, this approach explicitly decouples rotation and scale, allowing for efficient gradient derivation and intuitive ellipsoid parameterization. A numerical stability technique for computing the new covariance matrix after recycling, replacing the unsupported \beta() function with \Gamma() and \ln(\Gamma()) to prevent overflow. This variant addresses computational issues in specific update rules for covariance matrices during optimization. A technique to transform a covariance matrix \Sigma into a normalized form \hat{\Sigma} by dividing it by its trace, separating the scaling vector s from the rotation matrix R. The formula is: \hat{\Sigma} = \frac{\Sigma}{\text{Tr}(\Sigma)} = \mathbf{R} \frac{\mathbf{S}^2}{\|s\|2^2} \mathbf{R}^T = \mathbf{R} \hat{\mathbf{S}}^2 \mathbf{R}^T where \|s\|2^2 = \text{Tr}(\Sigma). This normalization ensures the scaling vector has a unit norm, which can be useful for compression or clustering applications. Time Complexity: The reconstruction of \Sigma from \mathbf{R} and \mathbf{S} is O(1) per splat (constant number of multiplications for 3 \times 3 matrices). Memory Complexity: Stores rotation (e.g., 4 floats for quaternion) and scale (3 floats) parameters, totaling 7 floats per splat, compared to 6 floats for the symmetric covariance matrix. However, the overhead is minimal and justified by stability. Strengths: Guarantees positive semi-definiteness, enabling stable unconstrained optimization. Intuitive interpretation of rotation and scale. Limitations: Requires reconstruction step at each iteration. Parameterization of rotation (e.g., quaternion) may introduce singularities or require normalization steps. When to Use: Standard choice for 3D Gaussian Splatting and similar radiance-field optimization methods where stable gradient descent is required. Covariance Factorisation is a core component of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It was developed to address the instability of directly optimizing covariance matrices in differentiable rendering. The method leverages the fact that any positive semi-definite matrix can be decomposed into a rotation and a scaling component, a concept rooted in linear algebra and ellipsoid parameterization. It has since been adopted and adapted in various extensions of 3DGS, such as EVolSplat and compressed variants. name: Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats
head: Cholesky Decomposition for Covariance, Cholesky-based Covariance Parameterization [S1, unofficial]
body: Cholesky Parameterisation is a method for representing the covariance matrix of a Gaussian splat that guarantees positive-definiteness by construction. It parameterizes the covariance using D(D+1)/2 elements per splat (6 for 3D) and applies a softplus activation with a minimum standard deviation floor \sigma{min} = 1/\sqrt{12} voxels to the diagonal, while bounding amplitudes with a configurable maximum a{max}. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unconstrained raw optimization parameters p for the Cholesky factor and amplitude. Output: Lower triangular Cholesky factor L, positive-definite covariance matrix \Sigma, and non-negative amplitude a. Data Structures: The method stores D(D+1)/2 elements per splat. For 3D (D=3), this is 6 elements arranged as the lower triangular part of the Cholesky factor L, where \Sigma = L L^T. Formulas and Parameters: 1. Cholesky Factor Construction: The parameters populate the lower triangular matrix L: L = \begin{bmatrix} l{11} & 0 & 0 \\ l{21} & l{22} & 0 \\ l{31} & l{32} & l{33} \end{bmatrix} Off-diagonal elements l{ij} (i > j) are assigned directly to raw parameters p{ij}. 2. Diagonal Regularization (Minimum Spread): The diagonal elements l{ii} are parameterized using a softplus activation and a minimum standard deviation floor \sigma{min}: l{ii} = \sigma{min} + \text{softplus}(p{ii}) where p{ii} are the raw optimization parameters for the diagonal. \sigma{min} = 1/\sqrt{12} voxels. This value represents the standard deviation of a uniform distribution over a single voxel unit. 3. Amplitude Parameterization: The amplitude a is constrained to be non-negative and bounded above by a configurable maximum a{max}: a = \text{clamp}(\text{softplus}(pa), 0, a{max}) where pa is the raw amplitude parameter. 4. Covariance Reconstruction: The final covariance matrix is computed as: \Sigma = L L^T Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def choleskyparameterization(rawparams, sigmamin=1.0/np.sqrt(12.0), amax=1.0): """ Constructs a valid 3D Gaussian covariance matrix and amplitude from raw parameters. Args: rawparams: Array of 7 floats [p11, p21, p22, p31, p32, p33, pamp] sigmamin: Minimum standard deviation floor (default 1/sqrt(12)) amax: Maximum amplitude bound Returns: L: 3x3 lower triangular Cholesky factor Sigma: 3x3 covariance matrix amplitude: Clamped non-negative amplitude """ # Extract raw parameters p11, p21, p22, p31, p32, p33, pamp = rawparams # Construct lower triangular matrix L # Diagonal elements are regularized to ensure positive definiteness and minimum spread l11 = sigmamin + np.log1p(np.exp(p11)) # numerically stable softplus(p11) l22 = sigmamin + np.log1p(np.exp(p22)) # numerically stable softplus(p22) l33 = sigmamin + np.log1p(np.exp(p33)) # numerically stable softplus(p33) # Off-diagonal elements are unconstrained (can be negative) l21 = p21 l31 = p31 l32 = p32 L = np.array([ [l11, 0.0, 0.0], [l21, l22, 0.0], [l31, l32, l33] ]) # Compute covariance matrix Sigma = L L^T Sigma = L @ L.T # Parameterize amplitude amplitude = np.clip(np.log1p(np.exp(pamp)), 0.0, amax) return L, Sigma, amplitude Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If raw parameters result in extremely small l{ii}, the covariance may become numerically singular. The \sigma{min} floor prevents this but may limit the ability to represent very sharp features smaller than a voxel. Combines Cholesky factorization with skew-symmetric rotation matrices to preserve explicit 3D spatial interpretability while ensuring positive semi-definiteness. Chosen when explicit rotation structure is needed or when generalizing beyond 3D. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat for matrix construction (fixed 3 \times 3 operations). Memory Complexity: Stores D(D+1)/2 elements for covariance and 1 element for amplitude per splat. Strengths: Guarantees positive-definiteness by construction, avoiding the need for projection steps or penalty terms during optimization. Limitations: Loses explicit spatial rotation structure compared to axis-angle or quaternion parameterizations, making it harder to interpret the orientation of the Gaussian directly from the parameters. Cholesky Parameterisation is used in Gaussian splatting for microscopy and multidimensional scientific data visualization. It addresses the challenge of optimizing Gaussian splats where maintaining positive-definite covariance matrices is critical for stable rendering. The method leverages the mathematical property that any positive-definite matrix can be decomposed into a lower triangular matrix and its transpose, allowing unconstrained optimization of the Cholesky factors. name: Spatial-Orthogonal Cholesky Parameterization
head: Hybrid Cholesky-Skew-Symmetric parameterization, UBS covariance parameterization
body: Spatial-Orthogonal Cholesky Parameterization is a method for parameterizing the covariance matrix of N-dimensional Gaussian splats that combines Cholesky factorization with skew-symmetric rotation matrices to ensure positive semi-definiteness while preserving explicit 3D spatial interpretability. It solves the limitation of pure Cholesky parameterization, which loses explicit spatial rotation structure, and the limitation of quaternion parameterization, which does not generalize beyond 3D. It is used in Universal Beta Splatting (UBS) to enable flexible cross-dimensional correlations with non-spatial dimensions (e.g., view, time) while maintaining efficient optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Learnable parameters for a single splat: \boldsymbol{\omega} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Skew-symmetric rotation vector. \mathbf{s}x \in \mathbb{R}^3: Spatial scale vector. \mathbf{s}q \in \mathbb{R}^C: Non-spatial scale vector (for C additional dimensions). \mathbf{L}{qx} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times 3}: Cross-dimensional correlation matrix. \mathbf{L}q \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}: Lower-triangular matrix for non-spatial dimensions (Cholesky factor). Output: The N \times N covariance matrix \Sigma, where N = 3 + C. Data Structures: The covariance matrix \Sigma is constructed as \Sigma = L L^\top, where L is a structured lower-triangular matrix of size N \times N: L = \begin{pmatrix} Rx \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) & \mathbf{0}{3 \times C} \\ \mathbf{L}{qx} & \mathbf{L}q \end{pmatrix} Here, Rx \in SO(3) is the spatial rotation matrix, \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) is a 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix of spatial scales, \mathbf{0}{3 \times C} is a zero matrix, \mathbf{L}{qx} encodes correlations between spatial and non-spatial dimensions, and \mathbf{L}q is a lower-triangular matrix for the non-spatial subspace. Steps: 1. Construct Skew-Symmetric Matrix: Create Ax \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} from \boldsymbol{\omega} = (\omega1, \omega2, \omega3)^\top: Ax = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -\omega3 & \omega2 \\ \omega3 & 0 & -\omega1 \\ -\omega2 & \omega1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} 2. Compute Rotation Matrix: Approximate Rx using the first-order Taylor expansion of the matrix exponential: Rx \approx I + Ax This approximation maintains approximate orthogonality for small \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\| and initializes with identity rotation (\boldsymbol{\omega} = \mathbf{0}). 3. Construct Spatial Block: Compute the spatial part of L: L{xx} = Rx \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) 4. Assemble L: Combine blocks into the full lower-triangular matrix L: L = \begin{pmatrix} L{xx} & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{L}{qx} & \mathbf{L}q \end{pmatrix} 5. Compute Covariance: Calculate \Sigma = L L^\top. The expanded form is: \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} Rx \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x)^2 Rx^\top & Rx \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) \mathbf{L}{qx}^\top \\ \mathbf{L}{qx} \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) Rx^\top & \mathbf{L}{qx} \mathbf{L}{qx}^\top + \mathbf{L}q \mathbf{L}q^\top \end{pmatrix} Parameters: \boldsymbol{\omega}: Initialized to \mathbf{0}. \mathbf{s}x, \mathbf{s}q: Initialized to positive values (e.g., small constants or derived from initial splat size). \mathbf{L}{qx}: Initialized to \mathbf{0}. \mathbf{L}q: Initialized as a lower-triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The first-order Taylor approximation Rx \approx I + Ax is only valid for small \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\|. \mathbf{L}q must remain lower-triangular with positive diagonal entries to ensure \Sigma is positive semi-definite. Time Complexity: Efficient due to the first-order Taylor approximation for rotation, avoiding expensive matrix exponential computations. Memory Complexity: Stores 3 + 3 + C + 3C + C(C+1)/2 parameters per splat. For C=0 (pure 3D), this is 6 parameters, same as standard 3DGS. For C>0, it scales with C^2. Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360 (UBS-3D), achieves 25.54 dB PSNR with 1 hour training time, outperforming Quaternion (25.50 dB, 3h26m), Cholesky (25.28 dB, 1h14m), and Cayley Transform (25.52 dB, 1h16m). Strengths: Generalizes to arbitrary N dimensions, preserves 3D spatial interpretability, enables cross-dimensional correlations, and is computationally efficient. Limitations: The first-order Taylor approximation may not capture large rotations accurately. Pure Cholesky loses spatial structure, and Quaternions do not generalize beyond 3D. When to Use: When rendering N-dimensional radiance fields (e.g., with view or time dimensions) and requiring explicit 3D spatial structure and cross-dimensional correlations. When Not to Use: When only 3D spatial rendering is needed and simplicity is preferred (standard 3DGS or Cholesky may suffice), or when large rotations are expected and higher-order rotation parameterizations are needed. Originated in Universal Beta Splatting (UBS). It addresses the challenge of parameterizing covariance matrices in N-dimensional radiance field rendering, combining the benefits of Cholesky factorization (PSD guarantee, generalization) and skew-symmetric rotation (spatial interpretability). body: This method parameterizes the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \Sigma using a unit quaternion q and a 3D scale vector s to ensure the matrix remains positive semi-definite during optimization. It solves the problem that directly optimizing the entries of \Sigma can result in non-positive semi-definite matrices, violating physical interpretation and causing numerical instability. Unlike siblings such as Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats, which uses a triangular factorization, this approach explicitly decouples rotation and scale, allowing for efficient gradient derivation and intuitive ellipsoid parameterization. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A unit quaternion q = [w, x, y, z]^T representing rotation, and a 3D scale vector s = [sx, sy, sz]^T representing anisotropic scaling. Outputs: The covariance matrix \Sigma or its inverse \Sigma^{-1}, used in the Gaussian density function. Data Structures Quaternion (q): A 4-element vector [w, x, y, z]. Must be normalized to unit length (||q||=1) to represent a valid rotation. Scale Vector (s): A 3-element vector [sx, sy, sz]. These values are typically positive, representing the semi-axis lengths of the ellipsoid. Construction Steps 1. Construct Rotation Matrix (R): Convert the quaternion q into a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix R. The standard conversion from quaternion components w, x, y, z to R is: R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2(y^2 + z^2) & 2(xy - wz) & 2(xz + wy) \\ 2(xy + wz) & 1 - 2(x^2 + z^2) & 2(yz - wx) \\ 2(xz - wy) & 2(yz + wx) & 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2) \end{bmatrix}. Note: Some implementations may use a different convention for quaternion-to-matrix conversion (e.g., row-major vs column-major), but the resulting R must be orthogonal with determinant +1. 2. Construct Scale Matrix (S): Create a 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix from the scale vector s: S = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz) = \begin{bmatrix} sx & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz \end{bmatrix}. 3. Compute Covariance Matrix (\Sigma): The covariance matrix is reconstructed as: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T Since S is diagonal, S S^T = S^2 = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2). Thus: \Sigma = R \begin{bmatrix} sx^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz^2 \end{bmatrix} R^T. This ensures \Sigma is symmetric and positive semi-definite by construction. 4. Compute Inverse Covariance (\Sigma^{-1}): For rendering, the inverse is often required. Using the property (ABC)^{-1} = C^{-1} B^{-1} A^{-1}: \Sigma^{-1} = (R S S^T R^T)^{-1} = R (S S^T)^{-1} R^T = R S^{-2} R^T where S^{-2} = \text{diag}(1/sx^2, 1/sy^2, 1/sz^2). Gradients Instead of relying on automatic differentiation through the complex graph q, s \rightarrow \Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma^{-1} \rightarrow \alpha (where \alpha is opacity/density), gradients for q and s are derived analytically to avoid computational cost and potential numerical errors. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """ Converts a unit quaternion [w, x, y, z] to a 3x3 rotation matrix R. q: array-like of shape (4,) Returns: R, shape (3, 3) """ w, x, y, z = q[0], q[1], q[2], q[3] # Precompute terms to avoid redundant calculations xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz wx, wy, wz = wx, wy, wz R = np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) return R def computecovariance(q, s): """ Computes the covariance matrix Sigma from quaternion q and scale vector s. q: array-like of shape (4,), unit quaternion s: array-like of shape (3,), scale factors Returns: Sigma, shape (3, 3) """ # Ensure q is normalized q = q / np.linalg.norm(q) R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) # S is diagonal matrix of scales S = np.diag(s) # Sigma = R S S^T R^T # Since S is diagonal, S S^T = S^2 Ssquared = np.diag(s2) Sigma = R @ Ssquared @ R.T return Sigma def computeinversecovariance(q, s): """ Computes the inverse covariance matrix Sigmainv from quaternion q and scale vector s. q: array-like of shape (4,), unit quaternion s: array-like of shape (3,), scale factors (must be non-zero) Returns: Sigmainv, shape (3, 3) """ # Ensure q is normalized q = q / np.linalg.norm(q) R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) # Sigmainv = R S^{-2} R^T # S^{-2} is diagonal with 1/si^2 # Guard against division by zero ssqinv = 1.0 / (s2 + 1e-8) Sinvsquared = np.diag(ssqinv) Sigmainv = R @ Sinvsquared @ R.T return Sigmainv Parameters Learning Rate: Applied to q and s during optimization. Typical values are not specified in the sources, but s often requires careful clamping or regularization to prevent collapse or explosion. Clamping: Scale values s are often clamped to a minimum positive value to prevent numerical instability in \Sigma^{-1}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-Positive Semi-Definite Matrix: Directly optimizing \Sigma entries can lead to invalid matrices. This parameterization guarantees validity. Quaternion Normalization: The quaternion must remain unit length. Optimization steps must include renormalization or a projection step. Scale Zero/Negative: If any scale component si is zero, \Sigma^{-1} becomes singular. If negative, the physical interpretation of the ellipsoid axis is ambiguous (though mathematically s^2 is positive). Scales are typically constrained to be positive. Notation Confusion: In probability theory, \Sigma often denotes standard deviation, while \Sigma^2 denotes variance. In this context, \Sigma is the covariance matrix (variance), and s represents the standard deviation-like scale factors. Confusion here leads to errors in constructing S (using s vs s^2). Uses a lower triangular Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix. It guarantees positive definiteness without explicit rotation/scale decomposition. Choose when computational efficiency of matrix inversion is critical and rotation interpretation is less important. See Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats. Time Complexity: Constructing R from q is O(1). Matrix multiplications for \Sigma and \Sigma^{-1} are O(1) for fixed 3 \times 3 size. Analytical gradient derivation is O(1). Memory Complexity: Stores 4 floats for q and 3 floats for s, totaling 7 floats per Gaussian, compared to 6 floats for the upper triangular \Sigma or 9 for full \Sigma. This is slightly more memory than the minimal 6-float representation but provides explicit semantic meaning. Strengths: Guarantees positive semi-definiteness; intuitive interpretation as an ellipsoid; efficient gradient computation via analytical derivatives; avoids complex automatic differentiation graphs. Limitations: Requires careful handling of quaternion normalization; scale parameters may need regularization to prevent degenerate Gaussians. When to Use: Standard for 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization where physical interpretability and stability are prioritized. When Not to Use: If memory is extremely constrained and semantic meaning is irrelevant, Cholesky parameterization might be preferred for its compactness. Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting for novel view synthesis. The method draws from computer graphics traditions of parameterizing ellipsoids with scale and rotation, as well as probability theory's generalization of Gaussian PDFs using covariance matrices. It was introduced to address the instability of direct covariance optimization in differentiable rendering pipelines. name: Automatic covariance and rotation recalculation
head: Automatic parameter update for transformed Gaussians, Covariance update under mesh transformation
body: This method updates the parameters of 3D Gaussians when the underlying mesh vertices are transformed, ensuring that splats correctly reflect the new geometry without requiring manual recalculation of scaling factors. It sets itself apart from vanilla Gaussian Splatting modifications, which often require explicit matrix updates that can introduce holes or blurriness, by moving vertices directly in \mathbb{R}^3 and automatically deriving the new covariance and rotation parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original Gaussian parameters (rotation matrix R, scaling matrix S), and a vertex transformation matrix B \in SO(3) representing the movement or rotation of the mesh vertex in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Updated rotation matrix R' and updated covariance matrix \Sigma'. Data Structures: R: 3 \times 3 rotation matrix. S: 3 \times 3 diagonal scaling matrix. B: 3 \times 3 transformation matrix in SO(3). \Sigma: 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix. Steps: 1. Calculate the new rotation matrix R' by substituting the original rotation R with the transformation B: R' = B R 2. Calculate the new covariance matrix \Sigma' using the new rotation R' and the original scaling S: \Sigma' = R' S S^T R'^T 3. Substitute R' into the covariance equation to express \Sigma' in terms of the original parameters and the transformation B: \Sigma' = (B R) S S^T (B R)^T = B R S S^T R^T B^T Formulas: Original Covariance: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T Updated Covariance: \Sigma' = B R S S^T R^T B^T Parameters: B: The transformation matrix applied to the mesh vertex. Must be in SO(3) (rotation) or include translation if applied to means separately. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Manual Scaling Errors: Manually updating scaling factors via S' = AS (where A is a diagonal scaling matrix) is error-prone because exact scaling factors are not always apparent for intended modifications, especially when scales differ per Gaussian. Shear: If the transformation B introduces non-rigid warping or shear, the resulting covariance matrix may not correspond to a valid rotation and scaling decomposition directly compatible with standard rendering pipelines without further processing (see Covariance Re-fitting). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatecovariance(R, S, B): """ Updates Gaussian covariance and rotation after vertex transformation. Args: R (np.ndarray): Original 3x3 rotation matrix. S (np.ndarray): Original 3x3 diagonal scaling matrix. B (np.ndarray): 3x3 transformation matrix in SO(3). Returns: Rprime (np.ndarray): New rotation matrix. Sigmaprime (np.ndarray): New covariance matrix. """ # Step 1: Calculate new rotation Rprime = B @ R # Step 2: Calculate new covariance # Sigma = R S S^T R^T # Sigmaprime = Rprime S S^T Rprime^T # Equivalent to: B R S S^T R^T B^T # Compute S S^T (since S is diagonal, this is just element-wise square) SST = S @ S.T # Compute original covariance part: R S S^T R^T # This is equivalent to the original Sigma if needed, but we compute directly Sigmaprime = B @ (R @ SST @ R.T) @ B.T return Rprime, Sigmaprime A post-processing step applied to the transformed covariance matrix to recover rotation and scaling parameters compatible with 3DGS rendering, handling potential shear introduced by deformation. It is chosen when the transformation B is non-rigid (e.g., cage-based deformation) and introduces shear, which standard 3DGS rendering cannot handle directly. 1. Perform eigendecomposition on the deformed covariance matrix \Sigmad to obtain the orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors Rd and the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues \Lambdad, such that \Sigmad = Rd \Lambdad Rd^T. 2. Set the new rotation parameter to the orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors Rd. 3. Compute the new scaling parameters from the square roots of the eigenvalues in \Lambdad. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, as it involves fixed-size matrix multiplications (3 \times 3). Memory Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian for storing the updated parameters. Strengths: Eliminates the need for manual scaling factor calculation, reducing user error and visual artifacts like holes or blurriness associated with naive updates. Allows direct manipulation of mesh vertices in \mathbb{R}^3. Limitations: If the transformation is non-rigid, the resulting covariance may require re-fitting (see Covariance Re-fitting) to remain compatible with the rendering pipeline. When to use: When modifying the geometry of a mesh represented by Gaussian splats and automatic parameter updates are desired. When not to use: When the transformation is complex and introduces significant shear, requiring additional re-fitting steps. This method originates from the GaMeS (Mesh-based adapting and modification of Gaussian Splatting) paper, which proposes moving vertices directly in \mathbb{R}^3 to update Gaussian parameters automatically. It addresses limitations in vanilla Gaussian Splatting where explicit matrix updates can lead to visual artifacts. The related Covariance Re-fitting technique is described in GSDeformer, which handles non-rigid cage-based deformations. name: 3D Gaussian Data Layout
head: 3DGS Parameter Storage, Gaussian Struct Definition, GaussianModel, GaussianModel PyTorch Module
body: The 3D Gaussian Data Layout defines the memory organization and parameterization of a single 3D Gaussian primitive within a Gaussian Splatting system. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and accessing heterogeneous geometric attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color) for optimization and rendering. It sets itself apart from its parent GaussianSet Data Structure by defining the atomic unit's internal fields rather than the container's aggregation strategy, and from its sibling Gaussian Data Packing by focusing on the logical attribute types and their mathematical representations (e.g., log-space scales, quaternions) rather than low-level binary serialization. The layout supports two primary implementation paradigms: a C++ struct-based layout for rendering pipelines and a PyTorch tensor-based layout for differentiable optimization. Both store the same logical attributes but differ in activation functions and storage formats. Input: Raw geometric data (e.g., from a point cloud or neural network) or optimized parameters. Output: A structured representation of a single Gaussian primitive ready for covariance computation or rasterization. Defined in, the Gaussian struct uses nalgebra types. It stores precomputed 3D covariance to accelerate projection. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. pub struct Gaussian { pub position: na::Vector3<f32>, // x, y, z pub scale: na::Vector3<f32>, // scale0, scale1, scale2 (linear space) pub opacity: f32, // opacity [0, 1] pub rotation: na::Quaternion<f32>, // w, x, y, z (unit quaternion) pub sh: na::SVector<f32, 48>, // Spherical Harmonics coefficients (DC + 45 rest) pub cov3d: na::Matrix3<f32>, // 3x3 symmetric covariance matrix } shdim: The number of SH coefficients. Common values are 3 (DC only), 12 (degree 1), 27 (degree 2), or 48 (degree 3). cov3d: Precomputed to avoid redundant matrix operations during rasterization. Defined in, GaussianModel stores parameters in log-space or log-odds to ensure positivity during gradient descent, applying activation functions during access. xyz: Tensor(N, 3), float32. Raw positions. featuresdc: Tensor(N, 1, 3), float32. 0th-degree SH coefficients (colors). scaling: Tensor(N, 3), float32. Log-scales. rotation: Tensor(N, 4), float32. Raw quaternions. opacity: Tensor(N, 1), float32. Log-odds. 1. Retrieve Position: Return xyz directly. 2. Retrieve Scale: Compute s = torch.exp(scaling). Clamp to maximum value: s = torch.clamp(s, max=10.0). 3. Retrieve Rotation: Normalize the quaternion: q = torch.nn.functional.normalize(rotation). 4. Retrieve Opacity: Apply sigmoid: o = torch.sigmoid(opacity), mapping log-odds to [0, 1]. 5. Retrieve Color: Extract featdc from featuresdc. If higher degrees are stored, flatten featuresrest into featextra. Combine featdc and featextra for SH evaluation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F class GaussianLayout: def init(self, xyz, featuresdc, scaling, rotation, opacity): self.xyz = xyz self.featuresdc = featuresdc self.scaling = scaling self.rotation = rotation self.opacity = opacity def getposition(self): return self.xyz def getscaling(self): # Convert log-space to linear space with upper bound return torch.clamp(torch.exp(self.scaling), max=10.0) def getrotation(self): # Ensure unit quaternion return F.normalize(self.rotation, dim=-1) def getopacity(self): # Convert log-odds to probability return torch.sigmoid(self.opacity) def getfeatures(self): return self.featuresdc @staticmethod def fromlist(data): """ Reconstruct Gaussian from a flat list/array. Layout: [centroid(3), scale(3), rotation(4), opacity(1), featdc(3), featextra(...)] """ # data is a 1D tensor or array centroid = data[0:3] scale = data[3:6] rotation = data[6:10] opacity = data[10] featdc = data[11:14] featextra = data[14:] # Note: In optimization, scale/opacity are typically stored in log-space. # This constructor assumes raw values if used for initialization, # or log-values if used for loading optimized checkpoints. return GaussianLayout( xyz=centroid, featuresdc=featdc, scaling=scale, # Assuming log-scale if coming from optimizer rotation=rotation, opacity=opacity # Assuming log-odds if coming from optimizer) Quaternion Normalization: Rotations must be unit quaternions. Failure to normalize rotation leads to skewed scaling in the covariance matrix. Scale Clamping: Scales are clamped at 10.0 to prevent numerical instability during rendering. SH Degree Mismatch: The size of featextra depends on maxshdegree. Degree 0 has no extra coefficients; Degree 1 has 9; Degree 2 has 24; Degree 3 has 45. Log-Space Initialization: When initializing from a point cloud, scales and opacities must be converted to log-space before storage in the PyTorch layout. The Gaussian Data Structure (also known as GaussianList) is the primary in-memory container for 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives, organizing per-Gaussian attributes into column-major arrays to facilitate efficient GPU rendering and optimization. It solves the problem of managing a dynamic, large-scale set of heterogeneous geometric primitives by providing a flat, contiguous memory layout that supports batched processing, while explicitly storing precomputed 3D covariance matrices to accelerate the projection step. It sets itself apart from its parent 3D Gaussian Data Layout by defining the specific container type (a list of arrays rather than a struct-of-arrays or array-of-structs) and from its sibling Gaussian Data Packing by focusing on the logical attribute organization rather than low-level bit-packing or serialization. Gaussian Data Packing serializes 3D Gaussian Splat attributes into a fixed-width binary buffer to facilitate efficient GPU-side access during rasterization. It differs from sibling methods like SPZ Packed Format by using an interleaved, texture-friendly layout with a fixed width of 8 uint32t per Gaussian, rather than parallel buffers or image-based compression. GeometryState contains contiguous memory blocks for P Gaussians: depths (float, P), clamped (float, P3), internalradii (float, P), means2D (float, P), cov3D (float, P6), conicopacity (float, P), rgb (float, P3), tilestouched (uint32t, P), scanningspace (variable size from cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum), pointoffsets (uint32t, P). Memory: The C++ struct layout is compact but includes precomputed covariance, increasing per-Gaussian memory usage. The PyTorch layout stores raw parameters, requiring runtime computation of covariance, which trades memory for compute. Performance: Precomputing covariance (C++ layout) accelerates rendering but requires synchronization when Gaussians move. The PyTorch layout defers this cost to the optimization step or requires explicit recomputation. Scalability: The PyTorch layout scales well with batched operations on GPUs due to tensor parallelism. The C++ layout scales with memory bandwidth for rendering. The 3D Gaussian Data Layout originates from the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework. The PyTorch implementation is widely used in optimization pipelines, as seen in and. The C++ struct definition is used in high-performance rendering engines, as seen in. The layout evolved to support differentiable rendering by using log-space parameters for scales and opacities, ensuring gradients flow correctly through positivity constraints. thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cilix-ai/gs-embedding, https://github.com/cilix-ai/gs-embedding, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) metin-yat/mini-splat, https://github.com/metin-yat/mini-splat, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) NorahCadeJS/GAI-GS, https://github.com/NorahCadeJS/GAI-GS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Data Structure
head: GaussianList
body: The Gaussian Data Structure (also known as GaussianList) is the primary in-memory container for 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives, organizing per-Gaussian attributes into column-major arrays to facilitate efficient GPU rendering and optimization. It solves the problem of managing a dynamic, large-scale set of heterogeneous geometric primitives by providing a flat, contiguous memory layout that supports batched processing, while explicitly storing precomputed 3D covariance matrices to accelerate the projection step. It sets itself apart from its parent 3D Gaussian Data Layout by defining the specific container type (a list of arrays rather than a struct-of-arrays or array-of-structs) and from its sibling Gaussian Data Packing by focusing on the logical attribute organization rather than low-level bit-packing or serialization. Input: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. Output: A GaussianList data structure containing column-major matrices for all attributes, enabling efficient iteration during rasterization and gradient computation. The GaussianList struct consists of the following fields: 1. positions: Matrix4xN<f32> Layout: 4 \times N matrix. Rows: x, y, z coordinates in the first three rows; the fourth row is typically padding or homogeneous coordinate (1.0). Memory: Contiguous column-major storage. 2. scales: Matrix3xN<f32> Layout: 3 \times N matrix. Rows: Scale factors along the local x, y, z axes. 3. opacities: DVector<f32> Layout: 1D vector of size N. Values: Scalar opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. 4. rotations: Matrix4xN<f32> Layout: 4 \times N matrix. Rows: Quaternion components (w, x, y, z) for each Gaussian. 5. sh: Matrix48xN<f32> Layout: 48 \times N matrix. Content: Spherical Harmonics coefficients. Detail: Stored in a flat array of size 48 (maximum for degree 3). The layout interleaves channels per degree: C{0,R}, C{0,B}, C{0,G}, C{1,R}, C{1,B}, C{1,G}, \dots. 6. numgaussians: usize The current number of active Gaussians N. 7. cov3d: Matrix3xN<f32> Layout: 3 \times N matrix. Content: Precomputed 3 \times 3 covariance matrices for each Gaussian, flattened into columns. This avoids recomputing the covariance from scale and rotation during every render pass. 1. Initialization: Allocate memory for the GaussianList with a capacity C \ge N. Initialize numgaussians to N. 2. Attribute Population: For each Gaussian i \in [0, N-1]: Extract position \mathbf{p}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, opacity \alphai, and SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigmai using the rotation matrix \mathbf{R}i derived from \mathbf{q}i and the diagonal scale matrix \mathbf{S}i = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}i): \Sigmai = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^T \mathbf{R}i^T Store \mathbf{p}i in positions[:, i]. Store \mathbf{s}i in scales[:, i]. Store \alphai in opacities[i]. Store \mathbf{q}i in rotations[:, i]. Store \mathbf{c}i in sh[:, i]. Store \Sigmai (flattened column-wise) in cov3d[:, i]. 3. Rendering Preparation: The structure is passed to the rasterization pipeline. The cov3d matrix allows the projection step to compute the 2D covariance \tilde{\Sigma}i efficiently using the Jacobian of the projection and the camera rotation. Covariance Construction (Implicit in cov3d generation): \Sigmai = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^T \mathbf{R}i^T Where \mathbf{R}i is the rotation matrix from quaternion \mathbf{q}i, and \mathbf{S}i = \text{diag}(s{i,x}, s{i,y}, s{i,z}). SH Coefficient Layout: For degree L=3, the 48 coefficients are stored as: [C{0,R}, C{0,B}, C{0,G}, C{1,R}, C{1,B}, C{1,G}, \dots, C{3,R}, C{3,B}, C{3,G}] Repeated for each Gaussian column. SH Degree: Typically up to degree 3, resulting in 48 coefficients per Gaussian. Data Type: f32 (32-bit float) for all attributes. Precision: Floating-point errors in quaternion normalization can lead to invalid rotation matrices if not clamped or renormalized before covariance computation. Boundary: If N exceeds the allocated capacity, the buffer must be resized (see Dynamic Buffer Management). Degenerate Input: Scales of zero or near-zero can cause numerical instability in covariance inversion during projection. A small epsilon floor (e.g., 10^{-6}) should be applied to scales before constructing \mathbf{S}i. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def creategaussianlist(gaussians: List[Gaussian]) -> GaussianList: """ Constructs a GaussianList from a list of Gaussian primitives. Assumes Gaussian has fields: pos (Vec3), scale (Vec3), rot (Quat), opacity (f32), shcoeffs (List[f32]). """ n = len(gaussians) if n == 0: return GaussianList(numgaussians=0, positions=None, scales=None, opacities=None, rotations=None, sh=None, cov3d=None) # Initialize matrices with shape (rows, n) positions = Matrix(rows=4, cols=n, data=0.0) scales = Matrix(rows=3, cols=n, data=0.0) opacities = Vector(size=n, data=0.0) rotations = Matrix(rows=4, cols=n, data=0.0) sh = Matrix(rows=48, cols=n, data=0.0) cov3d = Matrix(rows=3, cols=n, data=0.0) for i in range(n): g = gaussians[i] # 1. Store Position positions.setcol(i, [g.pos.x, g.pos.y, g.pos.z, 1.0]) # 2. Store Scale scales.setcol(i, [g.scale.x, g.scale.y, g.scale.z]) # 3. Store Opacity opacities[i] = g.opacity # 4. Store Rotation (Quaternion w, x, y, z) rotations.setcol(i, [g.rot.w, g.rot.x, g.rot.y, g.rot.z]) # 5. Store SH Coefficients (Max 48 for degree 3) # Flatten SH coefficients into the column for c in range(48): if c < len(g.shcoeffs): sh.set(i, c, g.shcoeffs[c]) else: sh.set(i, c, 0.0) # 6. Compute and Store 3D Covariance # Construct Rotation Matrix R from Quaternion R = quattorotationmatrix(g.rot) # Construct Scale Matrix S S = diagmatrix([g.scale.x, g.scale.y, g.scale.z]) # Covariance Sigma = R S S^T R^T # Note: S S^T is diag(s^2) Ssq = diagmatrix([g.scale.x2, g.scale.y2, g.scale.z2]) cov = R @ Ssq @ R.transpose() # Store flattened covariance (column-major) cov3d.setcol(i, [cov[0][0], cov[0][1], cov[0][2], cov[1][0], cov[1][1], cov[1][2], cov[2][0], cov[2][1], cov[2][2]]) # Wait, Matrix3xN means 3 rows, N cols. # So each column is 3 elements. # Correction: cov3d is 3xN. Matrix3xN<f32> is 3xN. # This is a contradiction if it stores the full matrix. # However, if it stores the squared scales in the local frame? No. # Let's assume the source implies the covariance is precomputed and stored. # If it is 3xN, it might store the 3 diagonal elements? # But off-diagonals matter. # Let's stick to the source's explicit field definition: Matrix3xN. # This likely means it stores the 3 eigenvalues?
