Matrix3xN usually means 3 rows, N columns. # If it's 3xN, it's not a 3x3 matrix per Gaussian. # I will assume the source meant Matrix9xN or that it stores a compressed form. # I will write the pseudocode to store the 3 eigenvalues, as that fits 3 rows. eigenvalues = computeeigenvalues(cov) cov3d.setcol(i, [eigenvalues[0], eigenvalues[1], eigenvalues[2]]) return GaussianList( numgaussians=n, positions=positions, scales=scales, opacities=opacities, rotations=rotations, sh=sh, cov3d=cov3d) GSPull is a technique that leverages neural Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or Unsigned Distance Functions (UDFs) to recover detailed mesh structures from 3D Gaussian Splatting representations. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which produces volumetric splats rather than explicit surfaces, by integrating distance-field supervision to refine geometry. Unlike methods that directly pull Gaussians to the zero-level set, GSPull uses dense queries around the zero-level set as strong geometric cues to refine the surface conservatively and gradually, preventing error accumulation from ambiguous pulling directions. A density control mechanism that uses a frequency-aware mask and photometric loss to compute densification and pruning scores for Gaussian primitives, reducing redundancy and improving fidelity compared to vanilla 3DGS. It sets itself apart from its siblings by integrating a frequency-aware mask into the error computation to filter noise, and by weighting pruning scores with image-level photometric loss rather than raw pixel counts, whereas Efficient Pruning Score focuses on second-order sensitivity and Fisher Sensitivity Score uses Hessian approximations. Dynamic Buffer Management handles the resizing of GPU buffers that store 3D Gaussian splat data during training or streaming, ensuring the allocated capacity matches the active Gaussian count. It solves the problem of buffer overflow when densification adds new Gaussians or buffer under-utilization when pruning removes them. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GSPull (which handles data retrieval) and Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring (which determines which Gaussians to add/remove) by focusing on the memory infrastructure required to hold the changing set of active entities. The GS-W Network Architecture is the component of the Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) method responsible for predicting per-Gaussian appearance attributes and visibility from a set of reference images. It solves the problem of adapting 3D Gaussian Splatting to unconstrained image collections by replacing static color attributes with learnable features that are dynamically sampled based on camera viewpoint. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing a U-Net encoder-decoder structure to extract image features and a fusion network to combine these with intrinsic Gaussian attributes, enabling view-dependent appearance modeling without explicit spherical harmonics. VastGaussian is a large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting method that partitions a scene into spatially-disjoint regions to enable independent training and decoupled appearance handling for varying lighting conditions, merging results at render time with feathered overlap. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by solving the scalability and lighting inconsistency problems in city-scale reconstruction through a divide-and-conquer strategy that isolates local geometry and appearance. Data Layout and Storage defines the memory organization, serialization, and runtime management of 3D Gaussian Splat attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics) to enable efficient GPU rendering and optimization. It solves the problem of translating high-level splat representations into contiguous, cache-friendly structures suitable for batched processing, while supporting dynamic scene growth and cross-platform data transfer. It is distinguished from sibling methods by focusing on the raw memory layout and buffer management infrastructure rather than the rendering algorithm itself (GSPull), error-based densification (Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring), or specific network architectures (GS-W Network Architecture). SLAM and Tracking in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables simultaneous localization and mapping by jointly optimizing camera poses and Gaussian parameters from a stream of incoming images. It solves the problem of reconstructing dynamic or large-scale scenes in real-time or near-real-time, where traditional batch optimization is infeasible. What sets it apart from offline 3DGS is the use of a sliding window of keyframes and incremental updates, allowing the system to maintain a consistent map while tracking camera motion without re-optimizing the entire history. Spherical Harmonics (SH) is a mathematical basis used in 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent the view-dependent color of each Gaussian primitive. It solves the problem of modeling directional lighting and material properties that vary with the camera viewing angle, which a single static RGB value cannot capture. Unlike static color representations, SH allows for an analytical Jacobian that propagates gradients from the SH coefficients to camera poses during optimization, enabling joint optimization of geometry and appearance. 7D Gaussian Splatting (7DGS) is a unified framework for the real-time rendering of dynamic scenes with complex view-dependent effects, representing scene elements as seven-dimensional Gaussians spanning spatial position (3D), time (1D), and viewing direction (3D). It solves the problem of simultaneously modeling spatial geometry, temporal dynamics, and view-dependent appearance (such as scattering and anisotropic reflections) in dynamic scenes, a challenge that prior methods like 4DGS and 6DGS addressed in isolation. Unlike its siblings, 7DGS jointly models all three dimensions in a single coherent framework, using a conditional slicing mechanism to transform 7D Gaussians into time- and view-conditioned 3D Gaussians compatible with existing 3DGS rendering pipelines. Deformation and Dynamic Modeling extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent and render time-varying scenes by predicting time-dependent deformation deltas for canonical Gaussian parameters. It solves the problem of reconstructing moving objects (e.g., people, fluids) from multi-view video or casual capture, enabling real-time rendering of dynamic content. It sets itself apart from static methods by introducing a temporal dimension t that modulates the geometry (position, rotation, scale) of the Gaussian set, distinguishing it from sibling methods like Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting which use sparse control points, or Deformable Radial Kernel which modifies the kernel shape. Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) parametrization defines the unconstrained learnable parameters for the attributes of 3D Gaussian kernels, ensuring they remain within valid physical ranges through specific activation functions. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a specialized three-step activation for basis angles \thetak to maintain angular separation and monotonicity, and by providing configurable density control thresholds for sparse training scenarios. Gaussian Grouping is a method that enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by incorporating identity encodings for 3D objects, enabling the system to group splats based on their semantic identity. It solves the problem of precise object-level manipulation in 3D scenes, specifically enabling object removal, inpainting, and recomposition. Compared to sibling methods like DFF, Gaussian Grouping removes objects with greatly reduced artifacts and avoids leaving a blurry background. A technique that introduces a learnable per-Gaussian scalar factor to reparameterize effective Gaussian scales, providing an optimization pathway for adapting primitive extent while retaining existing tile-culling rules. It initializes a learnable scalar \betai \in \mathbb{R} to zero for each Gaussian primitive and optimizes \betai jointly with other Gaussian attributes using the Adam optimizer. The effective covariance is scaled by \gammai^2, where \gammai = \text{sigmoid}(\betai), changing the overall extent while keeping anisotropic axis ratios governed by the base scales. The gradient is computed as \frac{\partial \gammai}{\partial \betai} = 2 \cdot \text{sigmoid}(\betai) \cdot (1 - \text{sigmoid}(\betai)). The projected 2D covariance is \tilde{\Sigma}i^{2D} = \gammai^2 \cdot \Pii \Sigmai \Pii^T. DU replaces V{pq} \text{diag}(\Lambda)V{qq} with a free matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C}, removing spatial normalization and bounded coupling. The matrix learning rate is set to 5 \times 10^{-6}, scaled by the median primitive size. Unrestricted direct coordinates alone do not explain quality gains; structured parameterization performs better. DisC-GS stores control points of Bézier curves directly in 3D spatial coordinates using attribute c{\text{curve}}^{3D} \in \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 3} instead of 2D subspace c{\text{curve}} \in \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 2}. During rendering, the equation used to acquire c{\text{curve}}^{3D} from c{\text{curve}} is omitted, as c{\text{curve}}^{3D} is introduced as a direct attribute. A method tailored for local editing on 3DGS. It extracts the region of interest (RoI) from text instructions, aligns the text RoI with 3D Gaussians through the image space, and delicately edits within the identified 3D Gaussian RoI. Time Complexity: O(N) for initialization and attribute population, where N is the number of Gaussians. Rendering complexity depends on the rasterization algorithm but is linear in the number of splats per tile. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storage. Specifically, 4N floats for positions, 3N for scales, N for opacities, 4N for rotations, 48N for SH coefficients, and 3N (or 9N if full covariance is stored) for cov3d. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Performance is limited by memory bandwidth due to the large SH coefficient storage. Strengths: Efficient GPU access patterns due to column-major layout; precomputed covariance accelerates projection. Limitations: High memory footprint due to SH coefficients; dynamic resizing requires careful buffer management. When to use: Standard 3DGS rendering and optimization. When not to use: Memory-constrained environments where SH degree can be reduced or omitted. The Gaussian Data Structure is the foundational data container for 3D Gaussian Splatting, introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It has been widely adopted in subsequent works for its efficiency in handling large-scale scenes. The structure has evolved to include precomputed covariances and optimized SH storage to improve rendering speed. thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) EffGS: Efficient and High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39553, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) DisC-GS: Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15196v2, fetched 2026-10-26 A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: GSPull
head: GSDF / GSPull
body: GSPull is a technique that leverages neural distance functions (SDFs or UDFs) to recover detailed mesh structures from 3D Gaussian Splatting representations. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which produces volumetric splats rather than explicit surfaces, by integrating distance-field supervision to refine geometry. Unlike methods that directly pull Gaussians to the zero-level set, GSPull uses dense queries around the zero-level set as strong geometric cues to refine the surface conservatively and gradually, preventing error accumulation from ambiguous pulling directions. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color) initialized from standard 3DGS reconstruction. Multi-view images for supervision. A neural network parameterizing the distance field. Outputs: Refined 3D Gaussians with improved geometric alignment. A detailed mesh extracted from the converged distance field zero-level set. Data Structures: The Gaussian set follows the standard 3DGS layout containing position \mathbf{p}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients. The distance field is stored as a neural network mapping 3D coordinates to scalar distance values d(\mathbf{x}). Steps: 1. Initialize Gaussians using standard 3DGS and initialize the distance field network. 2. Jointly optimize the Gaussian parameters and distance field network parameters via gradient descent. 3. Query the distance field at dense points around the current Gaussian positions or surface estimates instead of pulling directly to the zero-level set d(\mathbf{x})=0. 4. Use the dense queries as geometric cues to update Gaussian positions and orientations, applying the refinement gradually. 5. Progressively finetune the Gaussian distribution and distance field representation over time. Formulas: The distance field d(\mathbf{x}) represents the signed or unsigned distance from point \mathbf{x} to the surface. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Ambiguous pulling directions can cause error accumulation if gradients are unclear; GSPull mitigates this by relying on dense queries rather than direct zero-level set pulling. Unlike methods that directly pull Gaussians to the UDF zero-level set, GSPull leverages dense queries around the zero-level set as strong geometric cues. It refines the surface in a conservative and gradual manner, effectively preventing error accumulation caused by ambiguous pulling directions. Time and Memory Complexity: Evaluating the neural distance field network for dense queries adds computational cost during optimization. Memory usage increases due to the storage of the distance field network parameters. Measured performance, hardware specifics, resolution scaling, and scene dependencies are Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: GSPull recovers more detailed mesh structures compared to standard 3DGS. It prevents error accumulation from ambiguous pulling directions. The method requires joint optimization of Gaussians and a neural network. When to Use: Use when explicit, high-quality mesh extraction is required. Use when standard zero-level pulling leads to geometric artifacts. GSPull was introduced as an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting to enable surface reconstruction. It was inspired by similar approaches used in NeRF-based methods. The technique is often cited alongside GSDF as a method that adopts neural distance functions for recovering detailed mesh structures. name: Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring
head: EffGS density control, Frequency-aware mask scoring
body: A density control mechanism that uses a frequency-aware mask and photometric loss to compute densification and pruning scores for Gaussian primitives, reducing redundancy and improving fidelity compared to vanilla 3DGS. It sets itself apart from its siblings by integrating a frequency-aware mask into the error computation to filter noise, and by weighting pruning scores with image-level photometric loss rather than raw pixel counts, whereas Efficient Pruning Score focuses on second-order sensitivity and Fisher Sensitivity Score uses Hessian approximations. Inputs: Set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}t at update step t. K distinct training views sampled uniformly without replacement. Rendered images I{\text{rend}}^j and ground-truth images I{\text{gt}}^j for each sampled view j. Frequency-aware mask M{\text{freq}}^j for each view j. Parameters: \tau \in (0, 1) (error threshold), \taup \in [0, 1) (pruning score threshold), \taud \ge 0 (densification score threshold), \taus > 0 (scale threshold), \rho \in [0, 1] (pruning sampling ratio), \lambda{\text{dssim}} (SSIM weight). Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}{t+1}. Data Structures: \mathcal{V}i: Set of view indices where Gaussian i has a valid projected footprint. \mathcal{A}t: Set of active primitives \{i \in \mathcal{G}t: |\mathcal{V}i| > 0\}. \Omegai^j: Set of pixels where Gaussian i contributes during compositing in view j. M{\text{err}}^j: Composite error mask for view j. Steps: 1. Identify Active Primitives: For each Gaussian i \in \mathcal{G}t and each sampled view j \in \{1, \dots, K\}: Get projected radius ri^j from the rasterizer. Determine visibility: \mathcal{V}i = \{j: ri^j > 0\}. Count visible views: |\mathcal{V}i| = \sum{j=1}^K \mathbb{I}[ri^j > 0]. Define active set: \mathcal{A}t = \{i \in \mathcal{G}t: |\mathcal{V}i| > 0\}. If \mathcal{A}t = \emptyset, skip density control. 2. Compute Composite Error Map: For each sampled view j: Compute raw per-pixel RGB reconstruction error: e^j(\mathbf{u}) = \frac{1}{3} \sum{c=1}^3 \left| I{\text{rend},c}^j(\mathbf{u}) - I{\text{gt},c}^j(\mathbf{u}) \right| Normalize error over pixel grid \mathcal{P}j: \bar{e}^j(\mathbf{u}) = \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{P}j}e^j where \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{P}j} is min-max normalization. If e^j is constant, map to zero. Compute composite error mask M{\text{err}}^j(\mathbf{u}): M{\text{err}}^j(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbb{I} \left[ \bar{e}^j(\mathbf{u}) > \tau \vee \left( M{\text{freq}}^j(\mathbf{u}) = 1 \wedge \bar{e}^j(\mathbf{u}) > 0.5\tau \right) \right] Note: The source text contains a typo M{\text{reeq}} which is corrected to M{\text{freq}} based on context. 3. Compute Densification Scores: For each i \in \mathcal{A}t: Compute weighted pixel count per view: ni^j = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \Omegai^j} M{\text{err}}^j(\mathbf{u}) Compute valid-view average count: Ci = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}i|} \sum{j \in \mathcal{V}i} ni^j Compute densification score: sd^i(t) = \omega(t)Ci where \omega(t) is a positive, nondecreasing clipped-linear schedule over the densification interval. 4. Compute Pruning Scores: For each i \in \mathcal{A}t: Compute image-level photometric loss for view j: E{\text{photo}}^j = (1 - \lambda{\text{dssim}}) \mathcal{L}1^j + \lambda{\text{dssim}} \left( 1 - \text{SSIM}(I{\text{rend}}^j, I{\text{gt}}^j) \right) where \mathcal{L}1^j = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}j|} \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{P}j} e^j(\mathbf{u}). Compute summed, loss-weighted count: Qi = \sum{j \in \mathcal{V}i} ni^j E{\text{photo}}^j Normalize pruning score over active set: sp^i = \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{A}t}Q 5. Execute Pruning: Identify mandatory removals: \mathcal{H}t = \{i \in \mathcal{A}t: oi < 0.1 \vee \gammai < 0.01\} where oi is opacity and \gammai is the learnable scale-modulation factor. Identify candidates: \mathcal{P}t = \{i \in \mathcal{A}t \setminus \mathcal{H}t: sp^i > \taup\} Sample bt = \lfloor \rho |\mathcal{P}t| \rfloor candidates without replacement using weights proportional to sp^i. Removal set: \mathcal{R}t = \mathcal{H}t \cup \text{sampled candidates}. Remove \mathcal{R}t from \mathcal{G}t. 6. Execute Densification: Select surviving active primitives with sd^i(t) > \taud. For each selected primitive i: If largest base-scale component < \taus: Clone and shift along positional gradient. Otherwise: Replace with two smaller Gaussians. New primitives inherit parent's unconstrained modulation parameter \betai \in \mathbb{R}, with \gammai = 2 \text{sigmoid}(\betai) \in (0, 2). Remaining attributes follow clone/split updates. Primitives outside \mathcal{A}t are unaffected. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When pruning and densification coincide, pruning must be applied first. New primitives are scored only at the next density update to avoid using post-update scores for pre-update decisions. Density control is skipped if \mathcal{A}t = \emptyset. A sensitivity-based metric that reparameterizes the Hessian approximation to reduce storage requirements by 36×, enabling soft pruning during training. It sets itself apart from the Composite Error Map by focusing on second-order sensitivity to spatial parameters rather than frequency-aware photometric error. A pruning metric that estimates the impact of each Gaussian on the L2 reconstruction loss using a block-diagonal Hessian approximation. It sets itself apart by evaluating geometric sensitivity through the log-determinant of parameter gradients, avoiding bias toward larger Gaussians. A technique for mapping 2D imagespace photometric errors back to 3D Gaussian primitives by aggregating alpha-weighted error metrics across multiple sampled views. It sets itself apart by ensuring only Gaussians with high visibility and significant contribution to reconstruction error are modified, avoiding overfitting to single-view occlusions. Time Complexity: Dominated by rendering K views and computing error masks. The error map computation is O(K \cdot |\mathcal{P}|) where |\mathcal{P}| is the number of pixels. Scoring is O(|\mathcal{G}t| \cdot K). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the composite error mask M{\text{err}}^j for each sampled view, adding O(K \cdot |\mathcal{P}|) memory overhead. Strengths: Reduces redundancy by focusing on high-error, high-frequency regions. Improves fidelity by weighting pruning with photometric loss. Limitations: Requires rendering K views for scoring, increasing training time. Sensitive to the choice of \tau and \lambda{\text{dssim}}. When to use: When high-fidelity rendering is required and computational budget allows for additional view sampling during training. When not to use: When real-time training is critical or memory is constrained. Originated in EffGS (Efficient and High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting). The method builds on Gaussian Data Structure and integrates frequency-aware masking to improve density control. name: Efficient Pruning Score
head: Pruning (Speedy-Splat), Speedy-Splat Pruning Score
body:
The Efficient Pruning Score is a sensitivity-based metric used to identify and remove redundant 3D Gaussian primitives during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and inefficient gradient flow associated with the original PUP 3D-GS pruning score by reparameterizing the Hessian approximation with respect to the 2D projected Gaussian value gi rather than the 3D spatial parameters. This reparameterization reduces storage requirements by 36×, enabling the score to be computed and applied during training (Soft Pruning) rather than only post-hoc. It sets itself apart from its parent method, the Composite Error Map, by focusing specifically on second-order sensitivity to spatial parameters to reduce Gaussian count, whereas the parent method uses frequency-aware masks and photometric loss for densification control. The method computes a pruning score for each Gaussian primitive to determine its contribution to the reconstruction error. It operates in two phases: Soft Pruning during the initial densification stage and Hard Pruning after densification is complete. Inputs: \mathcal{G}i: The set of N Gaussian primitives. \mathcal{P}{gt}: The set of all training camera poses. I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi): The rendered image for camera pose \phi. gi(\phi, p): The projected scalar value of Gaussian \mathcal{G}i at pixel p for pose \phi.

Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. trainingposes: List of all training camera poses. gradients: 2D array of shape (N, P) containing gradient values dI/dgi for each Gaussian i and each training pose p. Returns: scores: Array of pruning scores for each Gaussian. """ ngaussians = len(gaussians) scores = [0.0] ngaussians for p in range(len(trainingposes)): for i in range(ngaussians): scores[i] += gradients[i][p] 2 return scores def applypruning(gaussians, scores, keepratio=0.1): """ Applies pruning based on the computed scores. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. scores: Array of pruning scores. keepratio: Fraction of Gaussians to retain. Set to 0.1 for ~90% reduction. Returns: prunedgaussians: List of Gaussians remaining after pruning. """ ngaussians = len(gaussians) numtokeep = int(ngaussians keepratio) sortedindices = sorted(range(ngaussians), key=lambda k: scores[k]) keepindices = set(sortedindices[-numtokeep:]) prunedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in keepindices] return prunedgaussians Gradient Availability: The method relies on 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}} being available from the standard backward pass. Precision: Squaring small gradients may lead to underflow or loss of precision if not handled with appropriate data types. Boundary Conditions: The simplification 	ilde{U}i = \sum (
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}})^2 assumes gi is a scalar. A scoring mechanism that selects a subset of Gaussians based solely on intrinsic 3D attributes, decoupling geometry from appearance to prevent high-dimensional spherical harmonics from dominating the selection. It avoids expensive ray-pixel intersections and is chosen when memory efficiency is critical and appearance details are less important than global structure. Time Complexity: The score computation requires iterating over all Gaussians and all training poses. However, since the gradients are already computed during the backward pass, the additional cost is primarily the summation of squared gradients, which is O(N \cdot |\mathcal{P}{gt}|). Memory Complexity: The storage requirement is proportional to N (one score per Gaussian), a 36× reduction compared to the N 	imes 36 storage required by the original PUP 3D-GS score. Measured Performance: The full method (including pruning) achieves 6.51× FPS, 10.6× compression, and 1.45× faster training compared to original 3D-GS. It reduces the total number of Gaussians by approximately 90%. Strengths: Enables training-time pruning, reducing memory footprint and accelerating training and rendering. It maintains high visual quality despite significant compression. Limitations: Requires the standard 3DGS backward pass to expose 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}, which is natively available in the Speedy-Splat implementation. The Efficient Pruning Score was introduced in the Speedy-Splat paper by Zwicker et al. in 2025. It builds upon the PUP 3D-GS method, which demonstrated that post-hoc pruning could reduce Gaussian counts by ~90% but suffered from high memory overhead and inefficient gradient flow. The Speedy-Splat authors identified these drawbacks and proposed the reparameterization to enable efficient, training-time pruning. The method is part of the Speedy-Splat framework, which also includes sparse pixels and sparse primitives techniques. name: Geometry-Driven Pruning Score
body:
A scoring mechanism to select a subset of K Gaussians that preserves global structure and visual appearance using only intrinsic 3D attributes, avoiding expensive ray-pixel intersections. It balances geometric coverage and appearance contribution by weighting normalized opacity and volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by opacity \alphai, scale vector \mathbf{s}i = (s{xi}, s{yi}, s{zi}), and spherical harmonic coefficients. Output: Indices of the top K Gaussians with the highest scores. Data Structures: Gaussian attributes are stored in parallel arrays of size N. Steps: 1. Compute the raw volume Vi for each Gaussian i: Vi =  rac{4}{3} \pi s{xi} s{yi} s{zi} 2. Compute the z-score normalized opacity 
u(\alphai) and volume 
u(Vi) across all N Gaussians: 
u(x) =  rac{x - \mux}{\sigmax} where \mux and \sigmax are the mean and standard deviation of the respective attribute. 3. Compute the pruning score Si for each Gaussian i: Si = \lambda\alpha \cdot 
u(\alphai) + (1 - \lambda\alpha) \cdot 
u(Vi) 4. Select the top K Gaussians with the highest scores Si. Parameters: \lambda\alpha \in [0, 1]: Trade-off parameter controlling the balance between appearance (opacity) and spatial (volume) contribution. Typical value: 0.3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \sigma\alpha or \sigmaV is zero (all Gaussians have identical opacity or volume), z-score normalization is undefined. In this case, the normalized values are set to 0. The source does not specify handling for degenerate inputs or precision limits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def geometrydrivenpruningscore(gaussians, K, lambdaalpha=0.3): """ Select top K Gaussians based on geometry-driven pruning score. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: alpha: float, opacity scale: tuple (sx, sy, sz), scale vector K: int, number of Gaussians to select lambdaalpha: float, trade-off parameter (default 0.3) Returns: List of indices of the top K Gaussians """ N = len(gaussians) if N == 0: return [] # Extract attributes alphas = np.array([g.alpha for g in gaussians]) scales = np.array([g.scale for g in gaussians]) # Compute volumes volumes = (4.0 / 3.0) np.pi scales[:, 0] scales[:, 1] scales[:, 2] # Z-score normalization alphamean = np.mean(alphas) alphastd = np.std(alphas) if alphastd == 0: alphanorm = np.zeros(N) else: alphanorm = (alphas - alphamean) / alphastd volumemean = np.mean(volumes) volumestd = np.std(volumes) if volumestd == 0: volumenorm = np.zeros(N) else: volumenorm = (volumes - volumemean) / volumestd # Compute scores scores = lambdaalpha alphanorm + (1 - lambdaalpha) volumenorm # Select top K topkindices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:K] return topkindices.tolist() PointSplat is a geometry-driven prune-and-refine framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables high-quality reconstruction of compact Gaussian sets without requiring per-scene optimization at deployment. It bridges the gap between Gaussian pruning and transformer refinement by using intrinsic 3D attributes for pruning and a dual-branch encoder for refinement. Unlike image-driven pruning methods that rely on 2D images and per-scene optimization, PointSplat uses only 3D attributes for pruning. Unlike SplatFormer, which concatenates all Gaussian parameters into a single feature vector causing appearance dominance due to high-dimensional spherical harmonics, PointSplat decouples geometry and appearance. FFW computes an importance score for each Gaussian primitive using a combination of position, color, opacity, and transparency to selectively remove less important Gaussians while preserving visual quality. It is chosen when explicit multi-factor weighting is preferred over normalized z-score aggregation. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient as it avoids ray-pixel intersections required by image-driven methods. Strengths: Preserves global structure and visual appearance using only intrinsic 3D attributes. Results remain stable across a range of \lambda\alpha values, demonstrating robustness. Limitations: Relies on z-score normalization, which may be sensitive to outliers in opacity or volume distributions. When to use: When pruning 3D Gaussians for compact representation without per-scene optimization, especially in transformer-based refinement frameworks like PointSplat. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Introduced in the PointSplat framework for efficient geometry-driven pruning and transformer refinement. name: PointSplat
body: PointSplat is a geometry-driven prune-and-refine framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reconstructs compact Gaussian sets without requiring per-scene optimization at deployment. It bridges Gaussian pruning and transformer refinement by ranking Gaussians using only intrinsic 3D attributes and refining them via a dual-branch encoder. Unlike image-driven pruning methods (e.g., LightGaussians, PUP-3DGS, Speedy-Splat) that require 2D images and per-scene optimization, PointSplat operates solely on 3D geometry. Unlike SplatFormer, which concatenates all parameters into a single vector causing appearance dominance from high-dimensional spherical harmonics, PointSplat decouples geometry and appearance to prevent feature imbalance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N from a trained 3DGS model. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonics coefficients \gamma^{(i)}. Output: A refined, compact subset of Gaussians with improved structural integrity and visual quality. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gi retains its standard 3DGS parameters: \mui: Mean position (3 floats). \Sigmai: Covariance matrix, decomposed into rotation Ri (from quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4) and scaling Si (from vector si = [s{xi}, s{yi}, s{zi}]). \alphai: Opacity (1 float). \gamma^{(i)}: Spherical harmonics coefficients. For degree L=3, this results in up to 48 dimensions for appearance coefficients. Method Steps: 1. Geometry-Driven Pruning Score Calculation: Compute a pruning score for each Gaussian Gi based solely on intrinsic 3D attributes (opacity and volume/spatial coverage). The score balances spatial coverage and opacity to select a compact yet informative subset. This avoids complex image-ray interactions. Formula for Gaussian definition: Gi(x) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (x - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)\right) where \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T. Select the top K Gaussians with the highest scores. 2. Dual-Branch Encoder Initialization: Separate the geometric attributes (\mui, Ri, Si) and appearance attributes (\alphai, \gamma^{(i)}) of the retained Gaussians into two distinct branches. This explicit separation prevents feature imbalance where high-dimensional appearance features (e.g., 48D SH coefficients for L=3) dominate lower-dimensional geometric features. 3. Feature Reweighting with Positional Encoding: Reweight the separated geometric and appearance features using positional encoding. This step ensures balanced learning and prevents appearance dominance during transformer refinement. 4. Transformer Refinement: Process the reweighted features through a 3D transformer network (based on PointTransformerV3 architecture) to globally coordinate Gaussian parameters. This captures fine-grained structural details, addressing artifacts such as blurred textures and broken geometric edges that may result from pruning alone. The output is a set of compact, well-aligned ellipsoids. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from typing import List class Gaussian: def init(self, mu: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray, s: np.ndarray, alpha: float, shcoeffs: np.ndarray): self.mu = mu # (3,) mean position self.q = q # (4,) quaternion self.s = s # (3,) scaling vector self.alpha = alpha self.shcoeffs = shcoeffs # (D,) spherical harmonics coefficients def getcovariance(self) -> np.ndarray: R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(self.q) S = np.diag(self.s) return R @ S @ S.T @ R.T def computepruningscore(self) -> float: # Score based on intrinsic 3D attributes: opacity and volume volume = np.prod(self.s) return self.alpha volume def pointsplat(gaussians: List[Gaussian], k: int) -> List[Gaussian]: # Step 1: Geometry-Driven Pruning scores = [g.computepruningscore() for g in gaussians] sortedindices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k] retainedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in sortedindices] # Step 2 & 3: Dual-Branch Encoder and Feature Reweighting geometricfeatures = [] appearancefeatures = [] for g in retainedgaussians: geofeat = np.concatenate([g.mu, g.q, g.s]) geometricfeatures.append(geofeat) appfeat = np.concatenate([[g.alpha], g.shcoeffs]) appearancefeatures.append(appfeat) geometricfeatures = np.array(geometricfeatures) appearancefeatures = np.array(appearancefeatures) # Apply positional encoding and reweighting posencoding = positionalencoding(geometricfeatures[:,:3]) geometricfeatures = geometricfeatures + posencoding # Normalize features to prevent dominance geometricfeatures = geometricfeatures / (np.linalg.norm(geometricfeatures, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) appearancefeatures = appearancefeatures / (np.linalg.norm(appearancefeatures, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) # Step 4: Transformer Refinement # Note: The exact transformer architecture and forward pass are not specified in the sources combinedfeatures = np.concatenate([geometricfeatures, appearancefeatures], axis=1) # refinedfeatures = transformerrefine(combinedfeatures) # Extract refined parameters refinedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(retainedgaussians): # Note: Mapping refined features back to quaternion/scale/etc. is not specified in the sources # Assuming identity mapping for structural completeness refinedg = Gaussian( mu=geometricfeatures[i,:3], q=geometricfeatures[i, 3:7], s=geometricfeatures[i, 7:10], alpha=appearancefeatures[i, 0], shcoeffs=appearancefeatures[i, 1:]) refinedgaussians.append(refinedg) return refinedgaussians def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2yy - 2zz, 2xy - 2zw, 2xz + 2yw], [2xy + 2zw, 1 - 2xx - 2zz, 2yz - 2xw], [2xz - 2yw, 2yz + 2xw, 1 - 2xx - 2yy] ]) def positionalencoding(features: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: # Standard positional encoding using sine/cosine functions scales = np.logspace(-1, 4, features.shape[1]) scaledfeatures = features[:, None,:] scales[None,:, None] return np.sin(scaledfeatures) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Imbalance: If geometry and appearance are not properly separated and reweighted, high-dimensional spherical harmonics coefficients (up to 48D for L=3) can dominate the learning process, leading to suboptimal refinement. Degenerate Input: Pruning based solely on opacity and volume may remove Gaussians critical for fine details if their opacity is low but they cover unique spatial regions. The transformer refinement helps mitigate this by globally coordinating parameters. Deployment Constraints: PointSplat is designed to eliminate reliance on per-scene optimization at deployment, so it trades absolute peak quality for rapid compression and inference efficiency. Time Complexity: Pruning is O(N) to compute scores and select top K. Transformer refinement depends on the transformer architecture but is generally efficient for compact sets. Memory Complexity: Reduced by pruning N to K Gaussians. No additional per-scene optimization memory overhead is incurred. Measured Performance: Experiments on ScanNet++ and Replica datasets demonstrate competitive rendering quality and superior efficiency across varying sparsity levels. Strengths: No reliance on 2D images for pruning. No per-scene optimization required. Avoids feature imbalance through dual-branch encoder. Limitations: May not achieve the same quality as methods with per-scene optimization. Relies on intrinsic attributes which may not capture all visual importance. When to Use: When efficient compression of 3DGS models is needed without per-scene optimization, and when feature imbalance is a concern. PointSplat was introduced in the paper "PointSplat: Efficient Geometry-Driven Pruning and Transformer Refinement for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses limitations in existing 3DGS compression methods, which either rely on image-driven pruning with per-scene optimization or suffer from feature imbalance in transformer-based refinement. The method builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework and integrates concepts from point cloud processing refinements. name: Full Factors Weighted (FFW) Importance Score Pruning
head: MiniGS Pruning, Scorev4
body: Full Factors Weighted (FFW) Importance Score Pruning is a method for selectively removing less important 3D Gaussian primitives during the training of Gaussian Splatting models to reduce memory footprint and rendering latency while preserving visual fidelity. It addresses the limitation of vanilla 3DGS pruning, which relies solely on opacity and transparency, by incorporating position, color similarity, and opacity into a single importance score. Unlike its sibling PointSplat, which focuses on point-based approximations, FFW operates directly on the Gaussian primitives using a comprehensive factor analysis aligned with the alpha-blending rendering equation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, the current camera view (defined by ray r and pixel coordinate Xr), the rendered pixel color cr, and the Gaussian parameters (position Xi, view-dependent color ci, opacity \alphai, transparency Ti). Output: A ranked list of Gaussians and a binary mask indicating which Gaussians to prune (remove) from the scene representation. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian data layout defined in Gaussian Data Structure. Each Gaussian Gi stores: Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: View-dependent color (computed from Spherical Harmonics coefficients). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Intrinsic opacity. Ti \in [0, 1]: Blending transparency, calculated during rasterization as Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), where j iterates over Gaussians sorted by depth. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: 3D covariance matrix. Step-by-Step Procedure: 1. Project Covariance (Optional Context): To determine the 2D extent of the Gaussian for rasterization, the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma is projected to the 2D image plane using the world-to-camera projective transform matrix W and the Jacobian J of the projective transform: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T This step is part of the rendering pipeline that generates the intermediate values (Ti) used in the score. 2. Compute Importance Score: For each Gaussian Gi contributing to the pixel color cr along ray r, calculate the importance score S(Gi, r) using the Scorev4 formula: S(Gi, r) = (1 - \text{mean}(cr - ci)) \cdot \exp(-\|Xr - Xi\|^2) \cdot \alphai \cdot Ti Where: cr is the final rendered color of the pixel. ci is the view-dependent color of the Gaussian Gi. \text{mean}(cr - ci) is the mean absolute difference (or Euclidean distance normalized) between the rendered pixel color and the Gaussian's color. The source uses mean(cr - ci). Xr is the 2D pixel coordinate of the ray. Xi is the 3D center position of the Gaussian. The term \|Xr - Xi\|^2 represents the squared Euclidean distance between the pixel center and the Gaussian center in the projected space (or 3D space if Xr is treated as a 3D point on the ray, but typically implies spatial proximity in the image plane context for weighting). Note: The source formula explicitly writes \exp(-\|Xr - Xi\|^2). \alphai is the blending opacity. Ti is the transparency (accumulated alpha from previous Gaussians). 3. Rank and Prune: Aggregate the scores for each Gaussian across all pixels it contributes to, or use the maximum/average score depending on the specific implementation variant (the source implies a global ranking based on the computed importance). Rank all Gaussians by their importance score in ascending order. Remove the Gaussians with the lowest scores until the target number of primitives K is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeffwscore(gaussian, pixelcolor, pixelcoord, gaussiancolor, gaussiancenter, opacity, transparency): """ Computes the FFW (Scorev4) importance score for a single Gaussian contribution. Args: gaussian: Object containing Gaussian attributes. pixelcolor (vec3): Rendered color of the pixel. pixelcoord (vec2): 2D coordinate of the pixel. gaussiancolor (vec3): View-dependent color of the Gaussian. gaussiancenter (vec3): 3D center of the Gaussian. opacity (float): Blending opacity alphai. transparency (float): Transparency Ti. Returns: float: Importance score. """ # Calculate color similarity factor: (1 - mean(color difference)) # Note: 'mean' typically refers to the mean across RGB channels for the difference vector colordiff = pixelcolor - gaussiancolor colorsimilarity = 1.0 - np.mean(colordiff) # Calculate spatial proximity factor: exp(-squared distance) # Distance between pixel coordinate and Gaussian center. # In practice, Xr is 2D and Xi is 3D. The source formula uses ||Xr - Xi||^2. # This implies projecting Xi to 2D or treating Xr as a 3D point. # Assuming standard implementation where spatial proximity is in image space: # We assume gaussiancenter is projected to 2D or Xr is extended. # For strict adherence to source formula notation: spatialdistsq = np.sum((pixelcoord - gaussiancenter[:2])2) # Assuming projection or 2D match # If 3D distance is intended, use full vector. Source notation ||Xr - Xi||^2 is ambiguous # regarding dimensionality but implies Euclidean distance. # Given Xr is pixel coordinate (2D) and Xi is 3D, we project Xi to 2D for distance. spatialfactor = np.exp(-spatialdistsq) # Combine factors score = colorsimilarity spatialfactor opacity transparency return score def prunegaussians(gaussians, renderdata, targetcount): """ Prunes Gaussians using FFW importance scores. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects. renderdata: Dictionary containing rendered pixel colors, coordinates, and Gaussian contributions. targetcount: Integer, number of Gaussians to keep. Returns: List of Gaussian objects: The pruned set. """ scores = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Aggregate score across all pixels where this Gaussian contributes # Or use a representative score. The source implies a global ranking. # We sum or average the scores from all contributing pixels. pixelscores = [] for pixel in renderdata.contributingpixels[i]: score = computeffwscore( gaussian=g, pixelcolor=pixel.color, pixelcoord=pixel.coord, gaussiancolor=g.color, gaussiancenter=g.center, opacity=g.opacity, transparency=g.transparency) pixelscores.append(score) # Aggregate: Mean score across contributing pixels if pixelscores: avgscore = np.mean(pixelscores) else: avgscore = 0.0 scores.append((i, avgscore)) # Sort by score ascending (lowest importance first) scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) # Determine how many to prune numtoprune = len(gaussians) - targetcount if numtoprune <= 0: return gaussians # Indices to remove indicestoremove = set([idx for idx, in scores[:numtoprune]]) # Return pruned list return [g for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if i not in indicestoremove] Parameters: Target Primitive Count (K): The desired number of Gaussians after pruning. Typical values depend on the scene complexity and hardware constraints. The source reports results for K \approx 400k on Mip-NeRF360, 230k on Tanks&Temples, and 250k on DeepBlending. Color Difference Metric: The source uses mean(cr - ci). This is typically the mean absolute difference across RGB channels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Similarity Negative Values: If mean(cr - ci) exceeds 1, the color similarity factor becomes negative. In standard RGB space with normalized values [0,1], the maximum difference is 1.0, so the factor ranges [0, 1]. Ensure inputs are normalized. Spatial Distance Dimensionality: The formula \|Xr - Xi\|^2 mixes 2D pixel coordinates and 3D Gaussian centers. Implementers must ensure consistent dimensionality, typically by projecting the Gaussian center to the 2D image plane before computing distance. Transparency Zero: If Ti = 0 (fully occluded by previous Gaussians), the score becomes 0. This correctly identifies the Gaussian as having no visual contribution in the current view, but care must be taken not to prune Gaussians that might become visible in other views. Time Complexity: The pruning step requires computing the score for each Gaussian-pixel pair, which is O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels they contribute to. Sorting is O(N \log N). This is significantly cheaper than ray-pixel intersection methods used in Geometry-Driven Pruning Score siblings that require explicit intersection tests. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the scores. No additional large data structures are required beyond the existing Gaussian attributes. Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF360: SSIM 0.798, PSNR 27.10, LPIPS 0.242 with 402.2k primitives. Tanks&Temples: SSIM 0.828, PSNR 23.11, LPIPS 0.207 with 230.7k primitives. DeepBlending: SSIM 0.897, PSNR 25.87, LPIPS 0.316 with 250.7k primitives. Strengths: Incorporates color and position information, preventing the removal of visually important Gaussians that have low opacity. Outperforms vanilla opacity-only pruning (Scorevanilla) and other variants (Scorev1-v3) in quantitative metrics. Limitations: Requires access to rendered pixel colors and intermediate blending values (Ti), which must be stored or recomputed during the pruning phase. The Full Factors Weighted (FFW) Importance Score Pruning, also known as Scorev4, was introduced in the MiniGS method. MiniGS aims to provide an efficient 3D Gaussian splatting pipeline by combining FFW pruning with a Variational Densify Threshold (VDT) module. The method was developed to address the inefficiency of vanilla 3DGS pruning, which fails to account for color and spatial contributions, leading to suboptimal pruning decisions. The approach was evaluated on standard NeRF benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, DeepBlending) using a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. name: Multi-view Alpha-Weighted Error Accumulation
head: Alpha-Weighted Error Accumulation, Alpha-based Importance/Pruning Scoring
body: Multi-view Alpha-Weighted Error Accumulation is a technique for mapping 2D imagespace photometric errors back to 3D Gaussian primitives to compute importance and pruning scores. It solves the problem of excessive or redundant densification caused by relying on single-view gradients by aggregating alpha-weighted error metrics across multiple sampled views. Unlike conventional gradient-based metrics, this method ensures that only Gaussians with high visibility and significant contribution to the reconstruction error are modified, thereby avoiding overfitting to single-view occlusions or transient artifacts. The method computes two scores for each Gaussian primitive i: an importance score Si^+ for densification and a pruning score Si^- for redundancy removal. These scores are derived by aggregating local metrics from a metric map across \mathcal{C} sampled views. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussian primitives, indexed by i. For each Gaussian i: opacity oi, covariance matrix \Sigmai, and position \mathbf{x}i. Number of sampled views \mathcal{C}. Discrete image pixel domain \Omega \subset \mathbb{Z}^2. For each view c \in \{0, \dots, \mathcal{C}\}: Metric map flags M{uv}^{c,+} and M{uv}^{c,-} for each pixel (u,v) \in \Omega. Local photometric loss \mathcal{L}{uv} for each pixel (u,v) \in \Omega. Outputs: Importance score Si^+ for each Gaussian i. Pruning score Si^- for each Gaussian i. Data Structures: The metric map is a binary or categorical flag per pixel per view. M{uv}^{c,+} = 1 indicates a region of high error/importance (poor reconstruction), while M{uv}^{c,-} = 1 indicates a region of low error/artifacts (well-reconstructed, redundant). The local loss \mathcal{L}{uv} is a scalar value representing the photometric difference at pixel (u,v). Formulas: The Gaussian alpha contribution \alphai for a specific pixel projection is defined as: \alphai = oi \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \Delta \mathbf{x}i^T \Sigmai^{-1} \Delta \mathbf{x}i \right) where \Delta \mathbf{x}i is the position offset from the pixel center to the Gaussian center. The importance score Si^+ is computed as: Si^+ = \sum{c=0}^{\mathcal{C}} \sum{(u,v) \in \Omega} \alphai \cdot M{uv}^{c,+} The pruning score Si^- is computed as: Si^- = \sum{c=0}^{\mathcal{C}} \sum{(u,v) \in \Omega} \mathcal{L}{uv} \cdot \alphai \cdot M{uv}^{c,-} Steps: 1. Initialize Si^+ = 0 and Si^- = 0 for all Gaussians i. 2. For each sampled view c from 0 to \mathcal{C}: 3. For each pixel (u,v) in the discrete image domain \Omega: 4. Retrieve metric map flags M{uv}^{c,+}, M{uv}^{c,-} and local loss \mathcal{L}{uv}. 5. For each Gaussian i projecting to (u,v): 6. Compute \alphai using opacity oi, covariance \Sigmai, and position offset \Delta \mathbf{x}i. 7. If M{uv}^{c,+} = 1, add \alphai to the running sum Si^+. 8. If M{uv}^{c,-} = 1, add \mathcal{L}{uv} \cdot \alphai to the running sum Si^-. 9. After iterating all views and pixels, use Si^+ to identify Gaussians for densification and Si^- to identify Gaussians for pruning. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def invertmatrix2x2(M): # Standard 2x2 matrix inversion det = M[0][0] M[1][1] - M[0][1] M[1][0] if det == 0: raise ValueError("Singular covariance matrix") return [[M[1][1] / det, -M[0][1] / det], [-M[1][0] / det, M[0][0] / det]] def computealphaweightedscores(gaussians, views, metricmaps, losses, H, W): """ Compute importance and pruning scores for 3D Gaussians using multi-view alpha-weighted error accumulation. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: opacity, covariance, position, importancescore, pruningscore views: List of view indices c from 0 to C metricmaps: Dictionary mapping (c, u, v) to (Mplus, Mminus) losses: Dictionary mapping (c, u, v) to local loss Luv H, W: Image height and width defining domain Omega Returns: Updated list of Gaussians with computed scores. """ for c in views: for u in range(H): for v in range(W): mplus, mminus = metricmaps.get((c, u, v), (0, 0)) luv = losses.get((c, u, v), 0.0) for g in gaussians: # Compute 2D offset from pixel center to Gaussian center deltax = (g.position[0] - (u + 0.5), g.position[1] - (v + 0.5)) # Compute quadratic form: deltax^T Sigmai^{-1} deltax invsigma = invertmatrix2x2(g.covariance) quadratic = dotproduct(deltax, dotproduct(invsigma, deltax)) alpha = g.opacity math.exp(-0.5 quadratic) # Accumulate importance score if flagged as high error region if mplus == 1: g.importancescore += alpha # Accumulate pruning score if flagged as low error/redundant region if mminus == 1: g.pruningscore += luv alpha return gaussians Parameters: \mathcal{C}: Number of sampled views. Not given in the sources. \Omega: Discrete image pixel domain. Not given in the sources. Thresholds for M{uv}^{c,+} and M{uv}^{c,-}: The sources mention a threshold \tau+ for marking poor reconstruction but do not specify the exact value or how M{uv}^{c,-} is thresholded. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: The covariance matrix \Sigmai must be invertible for the alpha calculation; if singular, a fallback or regularization is required. Single-view Overfitting: Relying on a single view can lead to excessive densification due to occlusions or transient artifacts. Gradient vs. Alpha: Conventional gradient metrics may modify Gaussians with low visibility. A scalar uncertainty feature per Gaussian primitive k capturing how much the primitive contributes to the overall rendering error, weighted by pixel-wise reconstruction error. It is computed as E(k) = \text{mean}{v \in \Omega} \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} e{\bar{x}} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}), where e{\bar{x}} = \|R(\bar{x}) - \hat{R}(\bar{x})\|1 is the per-pixel \ell1 reconstruction error, and \text{agg} \in \{\text{max}, \text{sum}, \text{mean}\} is the aggregation function. To highlight low-opacity Gaussians that still influence reconstruction quality, the opacity term \alphak(\bar{x}) can be omitted from the aggregation. Time Complexity: The complexity is proportional to the number of Gaussians projected onto pixels across all sampled views, with matrix inversion and dot products performed per projection. Memory Complexity: Requires storing metric maps and loss values for all sampled views and pixels, plus the scores for each Gaussian. Strengths: Differentiates important from redundant Gaussians more accurately than gradient-based methods; avoids overfitting to single-view occlusions; reduces redundancy. Limitations: Requires access to multiple views and pre-computed metric maps/losses; more computationally intensive than simple gradient accumulation due to alpha computation and multi-view aggregation. When to use: When densification/pruning based on visibility and multi-view consistency is critical to avoid artifacts and redundancy in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method was introduced in the context of Flux-GS, a variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates multi-view alpha-weighted error accumulation to improve geometry modification and reduce redundancy. It addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS, which uses gradient-based strategies (e.g., positional gradient threshold \|\nabla{\mui} \mathcal{L}\|2 > \tau) that often result in excessive and redundant Gaussian densification. By using alpha-based metrics instead of conventional gradient metrics, the method ensures that only Gaussians with high visibility and contributing to the error are modified. name: Dynamic Buffer Management
head: Capacity Growth
body: Dynamic Buffer Management handles the resizing of GPU buffers that store 3D Gaussian splat data during training or streaming, ensuring the allocated capacity matches the active Gaussian count. It solves the problem of buffer overflow when densification adds new Gaussians or buffer under-utilization when pruning removes them. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GSPull (which handles data retrieval) and Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring (which determines which Gaussians to add/remove) by focusing on the memory infrastructure required to hold the changing set of active entities. The method manages the lifecycle of contiguous memory buffers on the GPU (or CPU, depending on the implementation) that store Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, SH coefficients, opacity). It operates in two modes: explicit capacity growth triggered by overflow, and global buffer lifecycle management for multi-renderer scenarios. Inputs: Current active Gaussian count (numactive), current buffer capacity (capacity), stride size of the Gaussian data structure (stride), and per-renderer splat counts (for global management). Outputs: Updated buffer pointers, new capacity value, and valid memory ranges for the GPU driver/renderer. The primary data structure is a contiguous buffer (e.g., GraphicsBuffer in Unity, Buffer in Vulkan/Metal) with the following layout: Base Buffer: Stores Gaussian attributes. Size = capacity stride sizeof(float). Densification Flags: A boolean or integer array of size capacity, initialized to zero. Scratch Buffers: Temporary buffers used for packing, merging, or sorting. Size scales with capacity. Global State (Multi-Renderer): mbuiltSplatCounts: Array storing the splat count per renderer at the time of the last buffer build. rendererOffsets: Array mapping renderer index to base offset in the global buffer. When the number of active Gaussians exceeds the current buffer capacity, the buffer must be resized. 1. Check Overflow: Compare numactive with capacity. 2. Determine New Capacity: If numactive > capacity, calculate newcapacity = max(capacity 2, numactive). 3. Allocate New Buffers: Allocate a new base buffer of size newcapacity stride sizeof(float). Allocate new densification flags array of size newcapacity, initialized to zero. Allocate new scratch buffers of size proportional to newcapacity. 4. Copy Data: Copy existing Gaussian data from the old buffer to the new buffer. Number of elements to copy: numactive. Bytes to copy: numactive stride sizeof(float). 5. Update Views: Update the GPU buffer view/pointer to point to the new buffer. Update the capacity variable to newcapacity. Discard old buffers. In multi-renderer or streaming scenarios, global buffers must be rebuilt when the set of active renderers or their splat counts change. 1. Detect Change: Check if mbuiltSplatCounts is null or its length differs from activeGsplats.Count. Iterate through activeGsplats and compare each t.SplatCount with mbuiltSplatCounts[k]. If any mismatch is found, mark global buffers as dirty and return true. Note that adding/removing renderers is handled by MarkGlobalBuffersDirty on register/unregister, not by this count check. 2. Rebuild (if dirty): Dispose all global buffers: packed data, SH bands (1-4), order, renderer offsets, renderer transforms, and renderer params. Dispose scratch buffers used for packing/merging to prevent memory leaks. Nullify mbuiltSplatCounts to force recapture of splat counts from scratch on the next build. Re-allocate and populate global buffers based on current activeGsplats counts. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamicbuffermanagement(numactive, capacity, stride, oldbasebuffer, oldflags, oldscratch, activegsplats=None, mbuiltsplatcounts=None): """ Manages buffer resizing and global buffer validity. Args: numactive: Current number of active Gaussians. capacity: Current buffer capacity. stride: Size of one Gaussian in floats. oldbasebuffer: Current base buffer data. oldflags: Current densification flags. oldscratch: Current scratch buffer data. activegsplats: List of objects with 'SplatCount' attribute (for global management). mbuiltsplatcounts: Array of previous splat counts per renderer. Returns: newcapacity: Updated capacity. buffersdirty: Boolean indicating if global buffers need rebuild. """ buffersdirty = False sizeoffloat = 4 # 1. Explicit Capacity Growth if numactive > capacity: newcapacity = max(capacity 2, numactive) # Allocate new buffers newbasebuffer = bytearray(newcapacity stride sizeoffloat) newflags = [0] newcapacity newscratch = bytearray(newcapacity stride sizeoffloat) # Copy existing data bytestocopy = numactive stride sizeoffloat newbasebuffer[:bytestocopy] = oldbasebuffer[:bytestocopy] # Update state capacity = newcapacity oldbasebuffer = newbasebuffer oldflags = newflags oldscratch = newscratch # 2. Global Buffer Lifecycle (if multi-renderer) if activegsplats is not None and mbuiltsplatcounts is not None: if mbuiltsplatcounts is None or len(mbuiltsplatcounts) != len(activegsplats): buffersdirty = True else: for k, gsplat in enumerate(activegsplats): if gsplat.SplatCount != mbuiltsplatcounts[k]: buffersdirty = True break if buffersdirty: # Dispose old global buffers del oldbasebuffer del oldflags del oldscratch mbuiltsplatcounts = None return capacity, buffersdirty Growth Factor: Typically 2 (doubling). Stride: Depends on the Gaussian data structure (e.g., position (3) + covariance (6) + SH (93) + opacity (1) + etc.). Not given in the sources. mbuiltSplatCounts: Array storing splat counts per renderer at last build. Memory Leaks: Failing to dispose scratch buffers when the number of active renderers decreases causes memory leaks. Precision: Copying large buffers may require careful handling of memory alignment and stride to avoid corruption. Asynchronous Changes: Active-set size changes (adding/removing renderers) are not detected by the count check but by explicit dirty flags. Dynamic VBO Range Allocation manages vertex buffer object (VBO) memory ranges for 3D Gaussian splats by dynamically resizing the allocated capacity based on the current number of active splats (quadCount). It addresses frequent reallocation during buffer updates by applying a fixed over-allocation factor. This variant is specific to graphics APIs that use VBOs (like OpenGL/Vulkan) and focuses on minimizing reallocation frequency through over-allocation. This mechanism detects when active renderer splat counts change asynchronously (e.g., in streaming scenarios) and triggers a rebuild of global buffers. It uses a comparison of stored splat counts against current active counts to determine if a rebuild is necessary. Active-set size changes (adding/removing renderers) are handled by MarkGlobalBuffersDirty on register/unregister, not by this count check. This step involves the disposal of all global buffers (packed, SH bands 1-4, order, renderer offsets, renderer transforms, renderer params) and setting references to null. It also disposes scratch buffers used for packing and merging orders/depths to prevent memory leaks when the number of active renderers decreases. Finally, it nullifies mbuiltSplatCounts to force the next EnsureGlobalBuffers call to recapture splat counts from scratch. A buffering mechanism to handle high variability in Gaussian counts per scene, tile, and pixel, reducing latency and improving local memory utilization. It prefetches Gaussian data into a global key-value buffer and serves tile/pixel requests from the buffer to decouple unpredictable Gaussian counts from pipeline stages. A collection strategy storing intersected Gaussian IDs, hit distances, and alpha values in per-pixel linked lists to avoid register spilling and multiple BVH traversals. PPLLs increase FPS from 175 to 248. They are faster than 3DGRT's multiple BVH traversals because they avoid traversal overhead. GRay's PPLL implementation is lighter than EPBRR's, storing only IDs, distances, and alphas, as other attributes can be recomputed. Time Complexity: Buffer resizing is O(N) where N is the number of active Gaussians, due to the memory copy operation. Global buffer rebuild is also O(N) plus overhead for sorting/merging. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales linearly with capacity. Over-allocation (doubling) can lead to up to 2x memory waste before the next resize. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Doubling strategy ensures amortized O(1) cost for insertions, but large jumps in Gaussian count can cause stuttering due to large memory copies. Strengths: Simple to implement; prevents buffer overflow; handles dynamic scene complexity. Limitations: Memory fragmentation if not managed carefully; potential for memory leaks if disposal is not handled correctly in multi-renderer scenarios. When to use: When the number of Gaussians changes significantly during training or runtime. When not to use: When the Gaussian count is static and known in advance. Dynamic Buffer Management is a fundamental component of 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations that support dynamic scenes or training with densification. It originates from the need to manage the variable number of Gaussians in real-time rendering and optimization pipelines. The specific implementations cited here are from unofficial repositories: msplat (Metal-based) and gsplat-unity (Unity-based). Hardware accelerators also employ key-value prefetch buffers to handle Gaussian count variability. Ray tracing implementations use per-pixel linked list replay buffers to manage Gaussian collection efficiently. name: Dynamic VBO Range Allocation
body: Dynamic VBO Range Allocation manages vertex buffer object (VBO) memory ranges for 3D Gaussian splats by dynamically resizing the allocated capacity based on the current number of active splats (quadCount). It addresses frequent reallocation during buffer updates by applying a fixed over-allocation factor. Inputs and Outputs: Input: quadCount (current number of active splats or quad primitives). Output: A VBO range with capacity equal to quadCount OVERCAPACITYINCREASEFACTOR. Data Structures: The VBO range is a contiguous memory block allocated via OpenGL buffer objects. The internal data layout is determined by the parent Gaussian Data Structure; specific byte offsets and strides are not detailed in the sources. Parameters: OVERCAPACITYINCREASEFACTOR: A constant factor of 1.25 used to over-allocate VBO capacity to reduce reallocation frequency. Algorithm: 1. If a VBO range currently exists, delete it. 2. Calculate the new capacity as quadCount OVERCAPACITYINCREASEFACTOR. 3. Allocate a new VBO range with the calculated capacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. OVERCAPACITYINCREASEFACTOR = 1.25 vbohandle = None vbocapacity = 0 def updatevborange(quadcount): global vbohandle, vbocapacity if vbohandle is not None: deletebuffer(vbohandle) vbohandle = None newcapacity = quadcount OVERCAPACITYINCREASEFACTOR vbohandle = createbuffer(newcapacity) vbocapacity = newcapacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision, boundaries, and degenerate input handling are not detailed in the sources. name: Dynamic Buffer Management via CUDA Virtual Memory
head: CUDA VMM, Merging Nodes via Virtual Memory, Virtual Memory Buffering, Virtual Memory Management (VMM) for Dynamic Buffers
body: This method uses CUDA’s virtual memory management (VMM) to manage dynamically sized splat buffers, allowing physical memory to grow or shrink within a single consecutive virtual address range without data copying. It specifically addresses the memory overhead of merging buffers by enabling the expansion of an existing target buffer rather than allocating a new combined buffer. Inputs: A source buffer (capacity A) and a target buffer (capacity B) containing Gaussian splat data; the size of a single splat element S (in bytes). Outputs: A merged target buffer containing all splats from A and B, with no intermediate buffer of size A+B allocated. Data Structures: Virtual Address Range: A reserved contiguous virtual memory region with a modest initial capacity. Physical Memory Map: A tracking structure mapping virtual offsets to committed physical GPU memory pages. Parameters: Physical Granularity (G): The minimum unit of physical memory that can be committed or uncommitted. On an RTX 4090, G = 2 \text{ MB}. Initial Virtual Capacity (V{init}): The size of the initially reserved virtual address range. Typically \ge 100 \text{ MB}. Steps: 1. Initialization: Reserve a virtual address range of size V{init} using VMM APIs. At this stage, no physical GPU memory is allocated. 2. Committing Memory (Add Splats): When splats are added, calculate the required physical memory P{req}. Commit physical memory in chunks of granularity G up to P{req}. 3. Expansion (Out of Virtual Capacity): If P{req} exceeds the currently reserved virtual range, reserve a larger virtual address range. Remap the previously allocated physical memory to the new virtual range. This operation does not copy data. 4. Uncommitting Memory (Delete Splats): To remove splats: a. Sort the splat data such that deleted splats are moved to the end of the buffer. b. De-commit (unmap) the physical memory chunks corresponding to the trailing deleted splats. 5. Merging Buffers (Append A to B): To merge source buffer A into target buffer B without creating a new buffer C of size A+B: a. Increase the virtual capacity of buffer B to accommodate A's data. b. Commit the necessary physical memory in B for A's splats. c. Perform a memcpy of splats from A to the newly committed physical memory in B. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. GRANULARITY = 2 1024 1024 # 2 MB on RTX 4090 def reservevirtualrange(size): """Reserve a virtual address range of the given size.""" return {"virtualsize": size, "physicalpages": {}, "totalsplatcount": 0} def commitphysicalmemory(buffer, offset, size): """Commit physical memory for the given virtual offset and size.""" alignedsize = ((size + GRANULARITY - 1) // GRANULARITY) GRANULARITY buffer["physicalpages"][offset] = alignedsize return alignedsize def remapphysicalmemory(oldbuffer, newbuffer, offset, size): """Remap existing physical pages to a new virtual range without copying data.""" for oldoff, physsize in oldbuffer["physicalpages"].items(): newbuffer["physicalpages"][oldoff] = physsize newbuffer["totalsplatcount"] = oldbuffer["totalsplatcount"] return newbuffer def uncommitphysicalmemory(buffer, offset, size): """De-allocate trailing physical memory chunks.""" alignedsize = ((size + GRANULARITY - 1) // GRANULARITY) GRANULARITY if offset in buffer["physicalpages"]: del buffer["physicalpages"][offset] return alignedsize def copymemory(srcbuffer, srcoffset, dstbuffer, dstoffset, size): """Copy data from source to destination buffer.""" # Standard memory copy operation srcdata = srcbuffer["data"][srcoffset:srcoffset + size] dstbuffer["data"][dstoffset:dstoffset + size] = srcdata def sortdeletedtoend(buffer): """Move deleted splats to the end of the buffer.""" # Data-aware sort or indirect indexing validsplats = [s for s in buffer["data"] if not s.deleted] buffer["data"] = validsplats + [s for s in buffer["data"] if s.deleted] def initbuffer(initialvirtualsize): """Initialize a dynamic buffer with reserved virtual memory.""" buf = reservevirtualrange(initialvirtualsize) buf["data"] = bytearray(initialvirtualsize) return buf def addsplats(buffer, splatdata, splatsize): """Add splats to the buffer. Commits physical memory as needed.""" numsplats = len(splatdata) requiredbytes = numsplats splatsize commitphysicalmemory(buffer, 0, requiredbytes) copymemory(splatdata, 0, buffer, 0, requiredbytes) buffer["totalsplatcount"] += numsplats return buffer def mergebuffers(buffersrc, bufferdst, srcsplatcount, dstsplatcount, splatsize): """Merge source buffer into destination buffer without allocating a new buffer.""" srcbytes = srcsplatcount splatsize currentdstbytes = dstsplatcount splatsize # Expand virtual capacity if needed newvirtualsize = bufferdst["virtualsize"] + srcbytes if newvirtualsize > bufferdst["virtualsize"]: newbuffer = reservevirtualrange(newvirtualsize) bufferdst = remapphysicalmemory(bufferdst, newbuffer, 0, bufferdst["virtualsize"]) # Commit physical memory in destination for source data commitphysicalmemory(bufferdst, currentdstbytes, srcbytes) # Copy data from source to destination copymemory(buffersrc, 0, bufferdst, currentdstbytes, srcbytes) bufferdst["totalsplatcount"] += srcsplatcount return bufferdst def deletesplats(buffer, splatsize, numdeleted): """Remove splats by sorting them to the end and uncommitting memory.""" sortdeletedtoend(buffer) bytestofree = numdeleted splatsize alignedfreebytes = ((bytestofree + GRANULARITY - 1) // GRANULARITY) GRANULARITY validbytes = (buffer["totalsplatcount"] - numdeleted) splatsize uncommitphysicalmemory(buffer, validbytes, alignedfreebytes) buffer["totalsplatcount"] -= numdeleted return buffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Granularity Waste: Physical memory is allocated in 2 MB chunks. For small models, this can leave a sizeable amount of memory unused. This is negligible for models with millions to tens of millions of splats. Sorting Overhead: Deleting splats requires sorting them to the end of the buffer before uncommitting memory. Virtual Expansion Cost: Expanding the virtual range requires reserving a larger range and remapping physical memory, which is fast and avoids data copying. Memory Efficiency: Avoids doubling memory usage during merge operations compared to standard allocation methods. Standard merging creates a new buffer C of size A+B, requiring 2(A+B) memory temporarily. This method reuses buffer B. Performance: As fast as regular buffer allocation for standard operations. Limitations: Large physical granularity (2 MB) can waste memory for small datasets. Optimization Potential: An unimplemented optimization could reduce merge memory overhead to just 2 MB by incrementally committing 2 MB chunks, copying, and freeing source memory. This technique is described in the context of "Splatshop," a system for efficiently editing large Gaussian Splat models. It leverages CUDA's Virtual Memory Management (VMM) API. The approach is particularly relevant for applications requiring frequent dynamic updates, such as selection, deletion, and merging of splat models.
