name: GS-W Network Architecture
head: Gaussian in the Wild model parameters
body: The GS-W Network Architecture is the component of the Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) method responsible for predicting per-Gaussian appearance attributes and visibility from a set of reference images. It solves the problem of adapting 3D Gaussian Splatting to unconstrained image collections by replacing static color attributes with learnable features that are dynamically sampled based on camera viewpoint. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing a U-Net encoder-decoder structure to extract image features and a fusion network to combine these with intrinsic Gaussian attributes, enabling view-dependent appearance modeling without explicit spherical harmonics. Inputs: A set of K reference images (or their extracted feature maps). For each Gaussian point i: Position Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Intrinsic feature s{fi} \in \mathbb{R}^{48}. Dynamic appearance feature d{fi}. Sampling coordinates sc{ki} \in \mathbb{R}^2 for k=1 \dots K. Outputs: Predicted color Ci \in \mathbb{R}^3. Visibility map V (spatial tensor). Data Structures: 1. U-Net Encoder: Uses the first 8 subconvolution modules of a pre-trained ResNet-18. 2. U-Net Decoder 1 (Feature Maps): 4 up-sampling convolution modules. Outputs K+1 feature maps. Each feature map has 16 channels. 3. U-Net Decoder 2 (Visibility): 3 up-sampling convolution modules. Outputs the visibility map. No skip connections from the encoder. 4. Fusion Network (Mf): Two MLP modules. M{f1} has 3 hidden layers with units [128, 96, 64]. M{f2} has 2 hidden layers with units [48, 48]. 5. Color MLP (Mc): 1 hidden layer with 48 units. 6. Sampling Coordinates: K learnable 2D coordinates per Gaussian, initialized via linear transformation of position Xi. Parameters: Positional Encoding: 10 frequencies used for encoding position Xi. Batch Normalization & Activation: Applied in both U-Net decoders. Dropout: 0.1 probability applied to d{fi} during training. Initialization: Xavier initialization for MLP weights. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the reference images through the U-Net encoder (ResNet-18 first 8 modules) to extract image features. 2. Feature Map Generation: Pass encoder features through U-Net Decoder 1 (4 up-sampling convs, batch norm, ReLU, transpose conv, 16 channels) to generate K+1 feature maps. 3. Visibility Prediction: Pass encoder features through U-Net Decoder 2 (3 up-sampling convs, batch norm, ReLU, transpose conv, 16 channels) to generate the visibility map. Skip connections from the encoder to this decoder are omitted to reduce computation. 4. Sampling Coordinate Initialization (Pre-training): For each Gaussian i, initialize K sampling coordinates sc{ki} by applying a linear transformation to its 3D position Xi. 5. Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian i and each of the K feature maps, sample the feature value at the corresponding coordinate sc{ki} from the generated feature maps. This yields K sampled features. 6. Fusion: Concatenate the sampled features, the intrinsic feature s{fi}, the positional encoding of Xi, and the dynamic appearance feature d{fi}. Apply 0.1 dropout to d{fi} during training. Pass this concatenated vector through Fusion Network Mf (MLP 1: [128, 96, 64]; MLP 2: [48, 48]) to produce a fused appearance feature. 7. Color Prediction: Pass the fused appearance feature through Color MLP Mc (1 hidden layer, 48 units) to predict the final color Ci. 8. Training Updates: Update U-Net weights with learning rate decaying from 2 \times 10^{-3} to 2 \times 10^{-5}. Update MLP weights with fixed learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}. Update Gaussian positions with learning rate decaying from 1.6 \times 10^{-4} to 1.6 \times 10^{-7}. Densify Gaussians between iterations 500 and 15,000 with a gradient threshold of 4 \times 10^{-4}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GSWNetwork: def init(self, K, encoderchannels=256, dfidim=64): self.K = K # U-Net Encoder: Pre-trained ResNet-18 first 8 subconvolution modules self.encoder = self.loadpretrainedresnet18encoder() # U-Net Decoder 1: Generate K+1 feature maps # 4 up-sampling convolution modules, batch norm, ReLU, transpose conv, 16 channels self.decoderfeatures = nn.Sequential( nn.ConvTranspose2d(encoderchannels, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 16 (K + 1), kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16 (K + 1)), nn.ReLU()) # U-Net Decoder 2: Generate visibility map # 3 up-sampling convolution modules, NO skip connections from encoder self.decodervisibility = nn.Sequential( nn.ConvTranspose2d(encoderchannels, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 1, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1)) # Fusion Network Mf # Input: K sampled features (16K) + sfi (48) + posenc (20) + dfi (dfidim) fusioninputdim = 16 K + 48 + 20 + dfidim self.mf1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(fusioninputdim, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 96), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(96, 64), nn.ReLU()) self.mf2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 48), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(48, 48)) # Color MLP Mc self.mc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(48, 48), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(48, 3)) # Xavier initialization for MLPs self.initweights() # Sampling coordinates initialization self.sclinear = nn.Linear(3, 2 K) def loadpretrainedresnet18encoder(self): # Returns the first 8 subconvolution modules of a pre-trained ResNet-18 # Implementation depends on the specific framework; here we assume it is loaded externally. pass def initweights(self): for m in [self.mf1, self.mf2, self.mc]: for layer in m: if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear): nn.init.xavieruniform(layer.weight) def forward(self, images, gaussians): N = gaussians['positions'].shape[0] # Step 1: Feature Extraction encoderfeatures = self.encoder(images) # Step 2: Feature Map Generation featuremapstensor = self.decoderfeatures(encoderfeatures) # [B, 16(K+1), H', W'] # Step 3: Visibility Prediction visibilitytensor = self.decodervisibility(encoderfeatures) # [B, 1, H'', W''] # Step 4 & 5: Feature Sampling # Reshape featuremapstensor to [B, K+1, 16, H', W'] featuremapsreshaped = featuremapstensor.view(featuremapstensor.shape[0], -1, 16, featuremapstensor.shape[2], featuremapstensor.shape[3]) sampledfeatures = [] # Normalize sampling coordinates to [-1, 1] for gridsample coords = gaussians['sc'] # [N, K, 2] coordsnorm = 2.0 coords - 1.0 # Assuming coords are in [0, 1] coordsnorm = coordsnorm.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # [N, 1, 1, K, 2] for k in range(self.K): fmapk = featuremapsreshaped[:, k,:,:,:] # [B, 16, H', W'] # Expand to match N gaussians fmapkexpanded = fmapk.unsqueeze(0).expand(N, -1, -1, -1, -1) if fmapk.shape[0] == 1 else fmapk.unsqueeze(0) # gridsample expects grid [B, Hout, Wout, 2] # We sample at single points, so Hout=1, Wout=1 grid = coordsnorm[:,:,:, k,:] # [N, 1, 1, 2] sampled = F.gridsample(fmapkexpanded, grid, aligncorners=True) # [N, 16, 1, 1] sampledfeatures.append(sampled.squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1)) # [N, 16] sampledfeatures = torch.stack(sampledfeatures, dim=1) # [N, K, 16] # Step 6: Fusion posenc = self.positionalencoding(gaussians['positions'], numfrequencies=10) # [N, 20] dfi = gaussians['dfi'] # [N, dfidim] dfidropped = F.dropout(dfi, p=0.1, training=self.training) fusioninput = torch.cat([sampledfeatures.view(N, -1), gaussians['sfi'], posenc, dfidropped], dim=1) fusedfeature = self.mf1(fusioninput) fusedfeature = self.mf2(fusedfeature) # [N, 48] # Step 7: Color Prediction colors = self.mc(fusedfeature) # [N, 3] # Step 8: Visibility visibilitymap = visibilitytensor # [B, 1, H'', W''] return colors, visibilitymap def positionalencoding(self, positions, numfrequencies): # Standard positional encoding # positions: [N, 3] # Output: [N, 2 numfrequencies] freqbands = torch.cat([positions (10000 (2 (i // 2) / 3)) for i in range(numfrequencies)], dim=1) return torch.cat([torch.sin(freqbands), torch.cos(freqbands)], dim=1) The Wave Parameter Estimation Network (WPEN) estimates the constituent wave parameters (amplitude, angular frequency, and propagation direction) of a dynamic ocean from a time sequence of reconstructed geometric data, specifically surface normals and microfacet roughness. It distinguishes itself from direct regression methods by employing a differentiable ocean model as a physics-based loss function, allowing the network to learn by minimizing the geometric discrepancy between predicted and input ocean states. This approach enables self-supervised training where the network iteratively optimizes wave parameters to match real-world geometry reconstructed by preceding stages. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Stores K+1 feature maps (16 channels each) and the visibility map. Gaussian attributes include s{fi} (48 dims), d{fi}, and sc (K \times 2 dims). Performance: On Brandenburg, Sacre, and Trevi scenes, GS-W achieves PSNR of 24.70, SSIM of 0.8655, and LPIPS of 0.1242, with 50.7 FPS and 122.7 MB size. This outperforms global feature (PSNR 22.43) and K-planes-hybrid (PSNR 22.40) methods. Strengths: Captures local highlights and avoids artifacts from transient objects. Adjusts scene appearance in a manner aligned with human perception by weighting features from reference images. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Unconstrained image collections where view-dependent appearance is important and reference images are available. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The GS-W Network Architecture was introduced in the "Gaussian in the Wild" paper, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to unconstrained image collections. It was developed to handle the challenges of dynamic appearance and transient objects in real-world image sets, which standard 3DGS struggles with due to its static color attributes. The method builds on the Gaussian Data Structure and integrates a neural network to predict appearance features dynamically. name: Wave Parameter Estimation Network
head: Geometry-based Wave Parameter Fitting, Iterative Wave Parameter Optimization, UNet/MLP Wave Estimator
body: The Wave Parameter Estimation Network estimates the constituent wave parameters (amplitude, angular frequency, and propagation direction) of a dynamic ocean from a time sequence of reconstructed geometric data, specifically surface normals and microfacet roughness. It distinguishes itself from direct inverse methods by leveraging a differentiable ocean model as a self-supervised loss function, allowing gradients to flow from geometric consistency back to the network parameters. This approach enables iterative optimization where the network matches randomly initialized waves to real geometry. Inputs and Outputs Input: A time sequence of reconstructed ocean geometry, consisting of surface normal maps (Nt) and roughness maps (Rt) for each time step t. Output: A set of 60 constituent wave parameters. Each wave i is defined by three parameters: amplitude hi, angular frequency \omegai, and propagation direction \thetai. Data Structures The network architecture consists of two main components: 1. Feature Extractor: A U-Net [41] that processes the input sequence of normal and roughness maps to extract spatial features. 2. Parameter Decoder: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that maps the extracted features to the final wave parameter vector. Training Procedure The network is trained using a differentiable ocean model implemented in the Taichi framework. The training process involves the following steps: 1. Forward Pass: The U-Net extracts features from the input geometry sequence (Nt, Rt). The MLP decodes these features into a batch of wave parameters \{hi, \omegai, \thetai\}{i=1}^{60}. 2. Differentiable Simulation: The differentiable ocean model uses the predicted wave parameters to generate a synthetic sequence of ocean geometry (\hat{N}t, \hat{R}t). 3. Loss Calculation: The synthetic geometry is compared against the input geometry using a combined loss function L{Geom}. Normal Loss (L{cos}): Measures the cosine similarity between the predicted normal \hat{N}t and the input normal Nt: L{cos} = E{Nt, \hat{N}t} [(1 - \cos(Nt, \hat{N}t))] Roughness Loss (L2): Measures the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the predicted roughness \hat{R}t and the input roughness Rt: L2 = E{Rt, \hat{R}t} [\|Rt - \hat{R}t\|2^2] Total Loss (L{Geom}): A weighted combination of the two losses: L{Geom} = \alpha L2 + \beta L{cos} where \alpha and \beta are hyperparameters balancing the importance of roughness and normal consistency. 4. Optimization: The network weights are updated via backpropagation through the differentiable ocean model to minimize L{Geom}. Pseudocode Unverified code. """ # Initialize network: U-Net for feature extraction, MLP for parameter decoding class WaveParameterEstimationNetwork: def init(self): self.unet = lambda x: x # U-Net forward pass self.mlp = lambda x: x # MLP forward pass def forward(self, Nt, Rt): features = self.unet((Nt, Rt)) return self.mlp(features) network = WaveParameterEstimationNetwork() class Optimizer: def init(self, params): self.params = params def step(self): pass # Update parameters using gradient descent def zerograd(self): pass # Clear gradients optimizer = Optimizer(network.parameters()) for epoch in range(epochs): totalloss = 0.0 for t in range(len(inputgeometrysequence)): Nt, Rt = inputgeometrysequence[t] # 1. Generate synthetic geometry using differentiable ocean model Nhatt, Rhatt = differentiableoceanmodel.simulate(waveparams) # 3. Compute losses # Cosine similarity loss for normals cossim = dot(normalize(Nt), normalize(Nhatt)) Lcos = sum(1.0 - c for c in cossim) / len(cossim) # L2 (MSE) loss for roughness L2 = sum((r - rhat) 2 for r, rhat in zip(Rt, Rhatt)) / len(Rt) # Combined loss Lgeom = alpha L2 + beta Lcos # 4. Backpropagate and update Lgeom.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() totalloss += Lgeom print(f"Epoch {epoch}: Loss = {totalloss / len(inputgeometrysequence)}") return network Edge Cases and Pitfalls Fuzzy Predictions: Raw network predictions may be inaccurate in small areas or lack physical consistency. Spectral Correction: To mitigate fuzzy predictions, post-processing or constraints can be applied to enforce that the frequency fits a known spectral distribution and that frequency and amplitudes are negatively correlated. This correction is based on empirical wave spectrum properties (Eq. 2 in, not explicitly defined in the provided text). Convergence: The iterative optimization process relies on the differentiability of the ocean model; if the model is not fully differentiable or has discontinuities, convergence may fail. Choose this when working with monocular video sequences and needing a self-supervised, differentiable end-to-end pipeline. Time Complexity: Training requires 100 epochs. Each epoch involves forward and backward passes through the U-Net, MLP, and the differentiable ocean model. The complexity is dominated by the differentiable simulation, which scales with the number of waves (60) and the resolution of the geometry maps. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Requires a differentiable ocean model; sensitive to the quality of input geometry (normals/roughness); may produce fuzzy results without spectral correction. name: Differentiable Ocean Inverse Modeling
head: Dynamic ocean inverse modeling, Ocean surface reconstruction via differentable rendering
body: Differentiable Ocean Inverse Modeling is a two-step framework that reconstructs dynamic ocean models from monocular video sequences by first estimating hierarchical surface geometry and then deriving constituent wave parameters. It distinguishes itself from direct inverse methods by leveraging a differentiable ocean renderer and a differentiable ocean model as self-supervised loss functions, allowing gradients to flow from image consistency and physical plausibility back to the neural network parameters. The method operates in two distinct phases: hierarchical geometry reconstruction from images, followed by wave parameter estimation from the resulting geometry sequence. Input: A sequence of monocular images \{It\}{n}, where t denotes the time step and n is the number of frames. Intermediate Output: A sequence of hierarchical ocean geometry \{Gt\}{n}, where each Gt comprises the macrosurface normal Nt and the microfacet roughness Rt. Final Output: A set of constituent wave parameters for each time step, specifically amplitude hi, angular frequency \omegai, and wave direction \thetai for N sampled wave trains. The method processes dense tensor fields and discrete parameter sets. 1. Geometry Maps: Dense fields for normal Nt (3-channel vector per pixel) and roughness Rt (scalar per pixel). 2. Wave Parameters: A discrete set of N tuples \{hi, \omegai, \thetai\} representing the superposed wave trains. 1. Input Processing: For each image It in the sequence, pass it through two separate encoder-decoder neural networks (sub-net1 and sub-net2). 2. Geometry Extraction: Sub-net1 outputs the macrosurface normal map Nt, and sub-net2 outputs the microfacet roughness map Rt. 3. Sequence Assembly: Combine the outputs to form the hierarchical geometry Gt = \{Nt, Rt\} for all t, yielding the sequence \{Gt\}{n}. 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the sequence of geometry maps \{Gt\}{n} through a UNet architecture to extract spatiotemporal features. 2. Parameter Regression: Feed the extracted features into a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) network. 3. Output Generation: The MLP outputs the parameters for N wave trains: amplitude hi, angular frequency \omegai, and direction \thetai. To enable self-supervised training, the method uses a differentiable ocean model to synthesize geometry from the estimated wave parameters. 1. Wave Vector Definition: For each wave i, define the wave vector \mathbf{k}i and wave number ki: \mathbf{k}i = [ki \cos \thetai, ki \sin \thetai] ki = \frac{\omegai^2}{g} where g is the acceleration due to gravity. The parameters are simplified from \{h, \omega, k, \theta\} to \{h, \omega, \theta\}. 2. Nyquist Filtering and Weighting: Apply a Nyquist filter to determine the contribution of each wave to the hierarchical geometry based on wavelength relative to pixel size: Displacement (Long Waves): Waves with wavelength > \text{pixel size} affect macrosurface displacement. Normal (Medium/Long Waves): Waves affecting the macrosurface normal. Roughness (Short/Sub-pixel Waves): Waves with wavelength < \text{pixel size} do not affect height but affect microfacet roughness. 3. Superposition and Geometry Synthesis: Superpose the N filtered wave trains to generate the synthetic geometry sequence \{\hat{G}t\}{n}. The ocean surface is modeled using a triangle mesh deformed by large waves at the grid level, medium-length waves added to the normal at the pixel level, and roughness estimated by measuring the slope variance of small waves at the microfacet level. 1. Rasterization: Render the synthesized geometry \hat{G}t into an image \hat{I}t using the SoftRas method, which provides continuous and differentiable rasterization. 2. Lighting Computation: Compute reflected light from the Sun and sky dome, as well as refracted light from water. 3. Displacement Application: Use the computed displacements to alter geometry, normals, and roughness during the rendering process under given lighting conditions. The networks are trained self-supervised using the following loss functions: 1. Image Consistency Loss: L{\text{Image}} = \mathbb{E}{It, \hat{I}t} [\|It - \hat{I}t\|^2] where It is the input image and \hat{I}t is the re-rendered image. 2. Discriminator Losses: To enforce spatial distribution similarity and temporal coherence, use spatial discriminators Dn (for normal) and Dr (for roughness), and temporal discriminators D{tn} and D{tr}. L{Dn}: Loss from spatial discriminator on normal maps. L{Dr}: Loss from spatial discriminator on roughness maps. L{D{tn}}: Loss from temporal discriminator on normal sequences. L{D{tr}}: Loss from temporal discriminator on roughness sequences. 3. Total Loss: L{\text{Total}} = \alpha L{\text{Image}} + \beta1 L{Dn} + \beta2 L{Dr} + \gamma1 L{D{tn}} + \gamma2 L{D{tr}} where \alpha, \beta1, \beta2, \gamma1, \gamma2 are weighting hyperparameters. 4. Geometry Consistency Loss: The framework measures the consistency between the generated geometry \hat{G}t (from wave estimation) and the input geometry Gt (from image reconstruction) to optimize the wave estimation network, but the exact formula is not explicitly defined in the sources. class EncoderDecoderNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, channels=3): super().init() self.encoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(channels, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()) self.decoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(128, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, channels, 3, padding=1)) def forward(self, x): return self.decoder(self.encoder(x)) class UNet(nn.Module): def init(self, inch=2, outch=256): super().init() self.conv = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(inch, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()) self.pool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1) self.fc = nn.Linear(128, outch) def forward(self, x): return self.fc(self.pool(self.conv(x))) class MLP(nn.Module): def init(self, inch=256, outch=3): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(inch, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, outch)) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) class SpatialDiscriminator(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(32, 1)) def forward(self, x, y): return self.net(x) - self.net(y) class TemporalDiscriminator(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(32, 1)) def forward(self, seqx, seqy): return self.net(seqx) - self.net(seqy) def wavelengthfromk(k): return 2 math.pi / k def applynyquistfilterdisplacement(wavelength, pixelsize=1.0): return torch.where(wavelength > pixelsize, torch.oneslike(wavelength), torch.zeroslike(wavelength)) def applynyquistfilternormal(wavelength, pixelsize=1.0): return torch.where(wavelength > pixelsize 0.5, torch.oneslike(wavelength), torch.zeroslike(wavelength)) def applynyquistfilterroughness(wavelength, pixelsize=1.0): return torch.where(wavelength <= pixelsize, torch.oneslike(wavelength), torch.zeroslike(wavelength)) def differentiableoceanmodelsuperpose(h, kx, ky, wdisp, wnorm, wrough, t, gridres=64): # Simplified superposition: sum of trochoid displacements and normal/roughness contributions # In practice, this computes mesh deformation and pixel-level normal/roughness variance displacement = torch.zeros(gridres, gridres) normal = torch.zeros(gridres, gridres, 3) roughness = torch.zeros(gridres, gridres) for i in range(h.shape[0]): amp = h[i] wdisp[i] phase = kx[i] torch.arange(gridres).unsqueeze(1) + ky[i] torch.arange(gridres).unsqueeze(0) + t disp = amp torch.sin(phase) displacement += disp normal[..., 0] += wnorm[i] amp torch.cos(phase) roughness += wrough[i] amp2 return normal, roughness def softrasrasterize(normal, roughness, extrinsics, lighting): # Placeholder for SoftRas differentiable rasterization # Computes reflected/refracted lighting based on normal, roughness, and camera/lighting return torch.randlike(normal[..., 0]) def computediscriminatorloss(disc, real, fake): return torch.mean(disc(real, fake)2) class DifferentiableOceanInverseModeling: def init(self, numwavetrains, learningrate=1e-4): self.geoencoderdecodernormal = EncoderDecoderNetwork(channels=3) self.geoencoderdecoderroughness = EncoderDecoderNetwork(channels=1) self.wavefeatureextractor = UNet(inch=2) self.waveparametermlp = MLP(inch=256) self.discnormal = SpatialDiscriminator() self.discroughness = SpatialDiscriminator() self.disctemporalnormal = TemporalDiscriminator() self.disctemporalroughness = TemporalDiscriminator() self.alpha = 1.0 self.beta1 = 0.1 self.beta2 = 0.1 self.gamma1 = 0.1 self.gamma2 = 0.1 self.numwavetrains = numwavetrains self.optimizer = optim.Adam( list(self.geoencoderdecodernormal.parameters()) + list(self.geoencoderdecoderroughness.parameters()) + list(self.wavefeatureextractor.parameters()) + list(self.waveparametermlp.parameters()) + list(self.discnormal.parameters()) + list(self.discroughness.parameters()) + list(self.disctemporalnormal.parameters()) + list(self.disctemporalroughness.parameters()), lr=learningrate) def reconstructgeometry(self, image): Nt = self.geoencoderdecodernormal(image) Rt = self.geoencoderdecoderroughness(image) return Nt, Rt def estimatewaveparameters(self, geometrysequence): features = self.wavefeatureextractor(geometrysequence) params = self.waveparametermlp(features) return params def synthesizegeometryfromwaves(self, waveparams, timestep): h = waveparams[:, 0] omega = waveparams[:, 1] theta = waveparams[:, 2] g = 9.81 k = (omega 2) / g kx = k torch.cos(theta) ky = k torch.sin(theta) wl = wavelengthfromk(k) wdisp = applynyquistfilterdisplacement(wl) wnorm = applynyquistfilternormal(wl) wrough = applynyquistfilterroughness(wl) Nhat, Rhat = differentiableoceanmodelsuperpose( h=h, kx=kx, ky=ky, wdisp=wdisp, wnorm=wnorm, wrough=wrough, t=timestep) return Nhat, Rhat def renderimage(self, geometry, extrinsics, lighting): N, R = geometry Ihat = softrasrasterize(N, R, extrinsics, lighting) return Ihat def computeloss(self, It, Ihatt, Nt, Nhatt, Rt, Rhatt, Nseqt, Nhatseqt, Rseqt, Rhatseqt): Limage = torch.mean((It - Ihatt) 2) LDn = computediscriminatorloss(self.discnormal, Nt, Nhatt) LDr = computediscriminatorloss(self.discroughness, Rt, Rhatt) LDtn = computediscriminatorloss(self.disctemporalnormal, Nseqt, Nhatseqt) LDtr = computediscriminatorloss(self.disctemporalroughness, Rseqt, Rhatseqt) Ltotal = (self.alpha Limage + self.beta1 LDn + self.beta2 LDr + self.gamma1 LDtn + self.gamma2 LDtr) return Ltotal def trainstep(self, imagesequence, extrinsics, lighting): self.optimizer.zerograd() batchsize = imagesequence.shape[0] totalloss = 0 for t in range(batchsize): It = imagesequence[t] Nt, Rt = self.reconstructgeometry(It) Gt = torch.cat([Nt, Rt], dim=1) waveparams = self.estimatewaveparameters(Gt) Nhatt, Rhatt = self.synthesizegeometryfromwaves(waveparams, t) Ihatt = self.renderimage((Nhatt, Rhatt), extrinsics, lighting) loss = self.computeloss(It, Ihatt, Nt, Nhatt, Rt, Rhatt, Nt, Nhatt, Rt, Rhatt) totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() self.optimizer.step() Aliasing: Sub-pixel waves (wavelength < \text{pixel size}) cause signal aliasing if not filtered. The Nyquist filter is critical to prevent these waves from affecting surface height, restricting them to microfacet roughness. Viewing Distance: The impact of waves depends on viewing distance. The method assumes a specific relationship between wavelength and pixel size to categorize waves into displacement, normal, and roughness effects. Differentiability: The entire pipeline, including rasterization (SoftRas) and ocean superposition, must be differentiable to propagate gradients from the image loss to the network weights. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Self-supervised; does not require ground-truth wave parameters or geometry for training; leverages physical ocean models for plausibility. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the differentiable ocean model and renderer; sensitive to the quality of the initial geometry reconstruction; requires careful tuning of discriminator weights. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic ocean scenes from monocular video where ground-truth 3D data is unavailable. When not to use: When high-fidelity ground-truth geometry is available and supervised learning is preferred. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "Dynamic ocean inverse modeling based on differentiable rendering". History: It builds upon differentiable rendering techniques (SoftRas) and hierarchical ocean geometry models (displacement, normal, roughness). It addresses the infeasibility of direct wave estimation from images by using a two-step inverse approach. Usage: Used for dynamic ocean reconstruction from monocular video sequences. name: VastGaussian
head: Block-Based Partitioning, Large-Scale 3DGS via Block Partitioning
body: VastGaussian is a large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting method that partitions a scene into spatially-disjoint regions to enable independent training and decoupled appearance handling for varying lighting conditions, merging results at render time with feathered overlap. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by solving the scalability and lighting inconsistency problems in city-scale reconstruction through a divide-and-conquer strategy that isolates local geometry and appearance. Inputs: Input images with known camera poses (SfM reconstruction) and an initial sparse point cloud. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian models, one per partition block, stored in a hierarchical structure. Data Structures: The scene is partitioned into spatially-disjoint regions or overlapping blocks. Each block contains a local set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and metadata defining the block's spatial bounds and overlap region for merging. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the scene into spatially-disjoint blocks based on the camera distribution projected onto the ground. 2. Local Training: Train an independent 3D Gaussian Splatting model for each block. During training, the block is treated as an isolated scene. 3. Appearance Decoupling: Handle varying lighting conditions independently per block by modeling appearance changes with an optimizable appearance embedding for each view. 4. Merging: At render time, combine the contributions from all blocks using feathered overlap to blend adjacent regions. Formulas: No explicit mathematical formulas for partitioning or merging are provided in the sources. Parameters: Block Size: Not explicitly defined in the sources; depends on scene scale and memory limits. Overlap Width: Not explicitly defined; sufficient to allow feathered blending. Max GPUs: Distributed training scales to up to 32 GPUs. Edge Cases: Seams: Poor merging causes visible seams; feathered overlap is required. Lighting Discontinuities: Abrupt lighting changes across block boundaries are mitigated by decoupled appearance embeddings. Memory Limits: Partitioning is necessary when the scene exceeds physical memory. Pseudocode: Pseudocode not provided in the sources. Page Assignment and Merging is a spatial partitioning strategy used in VastGaussian to organize millions of 3D Gaussians into fixed-size memory pages for efficient virtual memory management and rendering. It solves the problem of mapping unstructured Gaussian clusters to a structured, mesh-aligned page hierarchy, ensuring that Gaussians are grouped by spatial locality while respecting hardware page size constraints. Unlike standard grid-based voxelization, this method derives its topology from a proxy triangular mesh, allowing it to handle surface-aligned geometry with varying lighting and appearance. It distinguishes itself by combining mesh-based subdivision with greedy merging and explicit page linking to handle overlapping ellipsoids that cross page boundaries. Similarity Guided Partition is a graph-based clustering algorithm that groups 3D Gaussians into spatially-disjoint blocks of bounded size based on spatial proximity and appearance similarity. It solves the problem of inefficient joint pruning by ensuring that potentially redundant Gaussians are evaluated together within the same optimization block. It sets itself apart from naive spatial partitioning by incorporating a scale-aware affinity metric that accounts for both geometric overlap and appearance consistency, and from sibling methods like Page Assignment and Merging by using a parallel greedy growth strategy on a sparse affinity graph rather than page-based memory management. Progressive Partitioning is a strategy to divide a large scene into multiple cells where training cameras and 3D Gaussians are properly distributed. It distributes training cameras and 3D Gaussians using an airspace-aware visibility criterion. Large Scene Reconstruction via Chunking partitions a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene into manageable chunks to handle physical memory limits and scalability challenges in large scenes. Lin et al. split scenes into chunks based on the distribution of camera positions and the respective Structure from Motion (SfM) reconstruction. Liu et al. split scenes into uniform chunks and prune chunks with low contribution to rendering. Kerbl et al. define a low-resolution skybox on a sphere surrounding each chunk, defining the surrounding scene as background. Zhao et al. distribute Gaussians across multiple GPUs, assigning pixels to be rendered to GPUs in tiles, and transferring the Gaussians between them as needed. The maximum GPU count for distributed training is 32 GPUs. Scalability: Enables reconstruction of city-scale scenes (square kilometers) by breaking them into manageable blocks. Memory: Reduces per-GPU memory footprint by training on chunks. Performance: Distributed training scales to up to 32 GPUs. Quality: Decoupled appearance handling improves visual consistency in scenes with varying lighting. Limitations: Requires careful merging to avoid seams. Complexity increases with the number of blocks. VastGaussian was introduced in CVPR'24. It addresses the lack of large-scale datasets and the scalability challenges of 3D Gaussian Splatting in massive scenes. It builds on the divide-and-conquer approach used in neural radiance fields. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://zenodo.org/records/19690968, fetched 2026-10-26 Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://zenodo.org/records/19690968, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Progressive Partitioning for Large-Scale 3DGS
head: Progressive Data Partitioning
body: Progressive Partitioning is a data distribution strategy for training 3D Gaussian Splatting on large-scale scenes by dividing the environment into spatially-disjoint cells, each containing a subset of training cameras and 3D Gaussians. It solves the memory and time bottlenecks of global optimization by enabling parallel, lower-memory training per cell. It distinguishes itself from naive spatial splitting by using an airspace-aware visibility criterion to ensure sufficient supervision of the volume above the surface, preventing floaters and under-supervision. Inputs: Point cloud P (initially empty or sparse). Set of training views V. Scene dimensions defining the ground plane. Grid dimensions m \times n (number of cells along two axes). Visibility threshold Th. Boundary expansion ratio \alpha (typically 0.2 or 20%). Outputs: A set of m \times n cells. For each cell j: a subset of cameras Vj and a subset of points Pj. Data Structures: Cell j: Defined by a rectangular region on the ground plane with height hj and width wj. Point Cloud Pj: List of 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) associated with cell j. Camera Set Vj: List of camera poses and intrinsics assigned to cell j. Parameters: Th: Visibility threshold. Typical value: 25%. \alpha: Boundary expansion factor. Typical value: 0.2. m, n: Grid dimensions. Example: m=4, n=2 for 8 cells. Steps: 1. Camera-Position-Based Region Division Partition the ground plane into a grid of m \times n cells. Divide the ground plane into m sections along one axis (e.g., X), such that each section contains approximately |V|/m views based on camera positions. Subdivide each section into n segments along the other axis (e.g., Y), such that each segment contains approximately |V|/(m \times n) views. Let the j-th cell be bounded by a rectangle of size hj \times wj. 2. Position-Based Data Selection (Boundary Expansion) Expand the boundaries of each cell to include context from neighboring areas. Calculate expanded dimensions: h'j = hj + \alpha hj w'j = wj + \alpha wj Assign training views V to Vj if the camera position falls within the expanded boundaries of cell j. Assign points P to Pj if the point position falls within the expanded boundaries of cell j. Note: Initially, P may be empty or sparse; this step primarily assigns views. 3. Visibility-Based Camera Selection Refine the camera set Vj for each cell to ensure adequate supervision of the airspace. For each camera Ci not yet selected for cell j: Calculate the projected area of the cell's volume in the image plane of Ci. Airspace-Aware Calculation: Construct an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for the points currently in Pj (or the cell's spatial extent). Project this AABB onto the image plane to get area \Omega{ij}. Calculate visibility: \text{Visibility} = \frac{\Omega{ij}}{\Omegai} where \Omegai is the total pixel area of image Ii. If \text{Visibility} > Th, add Ci to Vj. Pitfall Avoidance: Do not use only the convex hull of surface points (\Omega{surf, ij}) for \Omega{ij}, as this is airspace-agnostic and leads to under-supervision of the volume above the surface and floaters. Use the AABB of the cell's point cloud extent to capture the full volume. 4. Coverage-Based Point Selection Initialize Pj with points that are well-constrained by the selected cameras. Identify points in the global point cloud P that are covered by all views in Vj. Add these points to Pj. This provides better initialization for optimization, reducing depth ambiguity and preventing the creation of floaters for objects outside the cell. 5. Optimization and Cleanup Optimize the 3D Gaussians in Pj using only cameras in Vj. After optimization, remove any 3D Gaussians generated outside the cell's boundaries to prevent artifacts (floaters) in adjacent cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivepartitioning(pointcloud, views, m, n, threshold=0.25, expansion=0.2): """ pointcloud: List of 3D points (initially sparse or empty) views: List of camera objects with position and intrinsics m: Number of sections along axis 1 n: Number of segments along axis 2 threshold: Visibility threshold Th expansion: Boundary expansion ratio alpha """ # Step 1: Camera-Position-Based Region Division # Sort views by position along axis 1 and axis 2 to define grid boundaries # This creates mn cells, each with bounds (hj, wj) cells = creategridcells(views, m, n) # Step 2: Position-Based Data Selection # Initialize Vj and Pj for each cell celldata = {} for j, cell in enumerate(cells): # Expanded boundaries hexp = cell.h (1 + expansion) wexp = cell.w (1 + expansion) # Assign views based on camera position within expanded bounds Vj = [v for v in views if isinexpandedbounds(v.position, cell.bounds, hexp, wexp)] # Assign initial points (if any) based on position Pj = [p for p in pointcloud if isinexpandedbounds(p.position, cell.bounds, hexp, wexp)] celldata[j] = {'V': Vj, 'P': Pj, 'bounds': cell.bounds, 'h': cell.h, 'w': cell.w} # Step 3: Visibility-Based Camera Selection for j, data in celldata.items(): Vj = data['V'] Pj = data['P'] bounds = data['bounds'] h = data['h'] w = data['w'] # Identify cameras not yet in Vj remainingviews = [v for v in views if v not in Vj] for v in remainingviews: # Calculate projected area of the cell's volume in v's image # Use AABB of Pj (or cell bounds if Pj is empty) # Construct AABB from Pj points or cell bounds if Pj: aabb = getaabb(Pj) else: # Fallback to cell bounds if no points yet aabb = getaabbfrombounds(bounds, h, w) projectedarea = projectareatoimage(aabb, v) imagearea = v.imagewidth v.imageheight visibility = projectedarea / imagearea if visibility > threshold: Vj.append(v) data['V'] = Vj # Step 4: Coverage-Based Point Selection for j, data in celldata.items(): Vj = data['V'] Pj = data['P'] # Find points covered by ALL views in Vj # This requires depth consistency or projection checks newpoints = [] for p in pointcloud: if iscoveredbyallviews(p, Vj): newpoints.append(p) # Add to Pj for better initialization data['P'].extend(newpoints) return celldata def iscoveredbyallviews(point, views): """ Check if a 3D point is visible in all provided views. This is a simplified check; in practice, it involves projection and depth testing. """ for v in views: if not isvisibleinview(point, v): return False return True def isvisibleinview(point, view): """ Check if point is within view frustum and not occluded. Placeholder for specific visibility logic. """ # Project point to image plane uv = project3dto2d(point, view) # Check if within image bounds if not (0 <= uv.x < view.imagewidth and 0 <= uv.y < view.imageheight): return False # Check depth (simplified) # In 3DGS, this might involve checking against existing geometry or depth buffer return True Time Complexity: Training time is reduced because each cell is optimized independently and in parallel. The total time is roughly proportional to the time for one cell, rather than the global scene. Memory Complexity: Memory usage per cell is lower, as each cell only stores a subset of Gaussians and cameras. This allows training on hardware with limited VRAM. Performance: In experiments with 8 cells, visibility threshold of 25%, and 60,000 iterations per cell, the method achieved high-fidelity reconstruction on large-scale scenes (e.g., Rubble, etc.). Strengths: Enables large-scale reconstruction on consumer hardware; reduces floaters and airspace artifacts through airspace-aware visibility; provides better initialization via coverage-based point selection. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of grid dimensions (m, n) and visibility threshold (Th); may introduce seams at cell boundaries if not handled by merging techniques (like those in VastGaussian). Progressive Partitioning was introduced by Lin et al. in the VastGaussian paper (CVPR 2024) as a strategy to adapt 3D Gaussian Splatting for large-scale scenes. It addresses the limitations of global optimization, such as high memory consumption and long training times, by partitioning the scene into manageable cells. The method builds on the idea of distributed learning and feature encoding for large scenes. name: Large Scene Reconstruction via Chunking
head: Chunk-based Reconstruction, Scene Partitioning
body: Large Scene Reconstruction via Chunking addresses the physical memory limits and scalability challenges inherent in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when applied to massive environments. By partitioning the scene into spatially disjoint or distributed regions, it enables the reconstruction of datasets that would otherwise exceed GPU memory capacities. Unlike monolithic reconstruction methods, this approach decouples the scene into manageable units, allowing for parallel processing, distributed training across multiple GPUs, or hierarchical memory management. It sets itself apart from siblings like Progressive Partitioning for Large-Scale 3DGS by focusing on static spatial partitioning strategies (uniform, camera-based, or multi-GPU) rather than dynamic progressive refinement, and from Page Assignment and Merging by relying on geometric or camera-distribution logic rather than memory-page optimization. The method involves partitioning the 3D space and/or the training data into chunks, training each chunk independently or in parallel, and handling the boundaries or global consistency through specific techniques. Inputs: A set of input images with known or estimated poses (SfM data), camera intrinsics, and a target scene volume. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the scene, organized by chunk or distributed across devices. The core data structure is the Chunk, which contains a subset of 3D Gaussians. Chunk Definition: A spatial region of the scene. Gaussian Attributes: Position (\mathbf{x}), Covariance (\mathbf{\Sigma}), Opacity (\alpha), Spherical Harmonics coefficients (\mathbf{c}), and Scale (\mathbf{s}). Distribution: Gaussians are assigned to specific chunks based on their spatial location or the camera positions used to observe them. 1. Scene Partitioning: The scene is divided into chunks. Several strategies exist: Camera-Distribution Based: Split the scene based on the distribution of camera positions and the respective Structure from Motion (SfM) reconstruction. This groups cameras and their corresponding scene regions together. Uniform Grid: Split the scene into uniform spatial chunks. Dynamic Hierarchy: Create levels dynamically throughout reconstruction, ranging from 1 level for small scenes to 8 levels for large scenes. 2. Background Handling (Boundary Management): To handle the "surrounding scene" not present in the current chunk: Skybox Method: Define a low-resolution skybox on a sphere surrounding each chunk. The surrounding scene is treated as background. Pruning: In uniform chunking, prune chunks with low contribution to rendering to reduce memory usage. 3. Training: Single-GPU/Chunk: Train each chunk independently. Multi-GPU Distribution: Distribute Gaussians across multiple GPUs. Assign pixels to be rendered to GPUs in tiles. Transfer Gaussians between GPUs as needed for rendering. Dynamic Load Balancing: Implement dynamic load balancing to ensure efficient distributed training. 4. Merging/Integration: If using disjoint chunks, merge the resulting Gaussian sets. If using a hierarchy, manage the levels to maintain memory constraints. Maximum GPU Count: Distributed training can scale to up to 32 GPUs. Hierarchy Levels: Ranges from 1 (small scenes) to 8 (large scenes like CityWalk). Out-of-Memory (OOM): Processing large scenes without a hierarchy or chunking causes OOM errors on standard GPUs (e.g., 24GB) after processing a fraction of frames. For example, in the CityWalk dataset, OOM occurred after 795 out of 4050 frames (<20%) with Gaussian counts exceeding 6.7 million. Boundary Artifacts: Improper handling of chunk boundaries can lead to visible seams or missing geometry. The skybox method mitigates this by providing a consistent background. Pose Quality: In pose-free scenarios, pure rotations prevent triangulation, a limitation shared with COLMAP and ORB-SLAM. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructlargescene(inputimages, sfmdata, maxgpus=32): """ Reconstruct a large scene using chunking strategies. """ # Step 1: Partition Scene # Strategy A: Camera-Distribution Based chunkscamera = partitionbycameradistribution(sfmdata) # Strategy B: Uniform Grid chunksuniform = partitionuniformgrid(sfmdata.scenebounds) # Strategy C: Dynamic Hierarchy (if enabled) if usehierarchy: chunks = createdynamichierarchy(inputimages, maxlevels=8) else: chunks = chunksuniform # or chunkscamera # Step 2: Initialize Background (Skybox) for each chunk for chunk in chunks: chunk.skybox = createlowresskybox(chunk.bounds) # Step 3: Distributed Training if maxgpus > 1: # Distribute Gaussians and Pixels gpuworkers = initializegpuworkers(maxgpus) for chunk in chunks: # Assign pixels to GPUs in tiles tileassignments = assignpixelstogpus(chunk, gpuworkers) # Transfer Gaussians as needed gaussianshards = distributegaussians(chunk.gaussians, gpuworkers) # Train with dynamic load balancing trainchunkdistributed(chunk, gaussianshards, tileassignments, gpuworkers) else: # Single GPU / Sequential Chunk Training for chunk in chunks: # Prune low-contribution chunks if using uniform grid if chunk.contribution < threshold: continue # Train chunk with skybox background trainchunksingle(chunk, chunk.skybox) # Step 4: Merge Results (if disjoint chunks) finalgaussians = mergechunks(chunks) return finalgaussians A variant that applies a lightweight progressive hierarchy to dynamically create levels throughout reconstruction. It ranges from 1 level for small scenes to 8 levels for large scenes like CityWalk. This method maintains peak trained Gaussians below 3.7 million and allocated memory below 12.8 GB, preventing OOM errors that occur without hierarchy (e.g., 6.7 million Gaussians causing OOM on 24GB GPU). It trades a small quality gap versus offline approaches for orders-of-magnitude faster processing and enables scalability to large scenes. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of chunks and the hierarchy depth. Without chunking/hierarchy, memory usage grows linearly with scene size, leading to OOM on standard GPUs (e.g., 24GB) for large scenes. With chunking, memory is bounded by the chunk size and hierarchy limits (e.g., <12.8 GB with hierarchy). Time Complexity: Distributed training across multiple GPUs (up to 32) improves training speed. Dynamic load balancing further optimizes this. Hierarchical approaches offer orders-of-magnitude faster processing compared to offline methods. Strengths: Enables reconstruction of massive scenes (e.g., CityWalk) that exceed single-GPU memory; supports distributed training; handles varying lighting via decoupled appearance handling (as per parent VastGaussian). Limitations: Potential quality gap compared to monolithic offline approaches; boundary artifacts if skybox/pruning is not handled well; pose estimation limitations for pure rotations. When to Use: Large-scale scenes where memory is a constraint; when distributed hardware is available; when processing speed is prioritized over absolute offline optimality. When Not to Use: Small scenes where monolithic reconstruction is sufficient and faster; scenes with pure rotations where pose estimation fails. The challenge of scaling 3D Gaussian Splatting to large scenes was highlighted by Kerbl et al. [18], who noted the lack of huge datasets and the memory limitations of the original method. Lin et al. [19] proposed partitioning scenes based on camera distribution and SfM reconstruction. Liu et al. [20] introduced uniform chunking with pruning. Kerbl et al. [18] also introduced the skybox approach for background handling. Zhao et al. [21] explored multi-GPU distribution with dynamic load balancing. More recently, Meulemann et al. [22] introduced on-the-fly processing for unposed data. The Progressive Hierarchical Memory Management approach was introduced to address OOM issues in immediate reconstruction of unordered input. name: Page Assignment and Merging
head: Gaussian Page Grouping, Mesh-to-Page Mapping
body: Page Assignment and Merging is a spatial partitioning strategy used in VastGaussian to organize millions of 3D Gaussians into fixed-size memory pages for efficient virtual memory management and rendering. It solves the problem of mapping unstructured Gaussian clusters to a structured, mesh-aligned page hierarchy, ensuring that Gaussians are grouped by spatial locality while respecting hardware page size constraints. Unlike standard grid-based voxelization, this method derives its topology from a proxy triangular mesh, allowing it to handle surface-aligned geometry with varying lighting and appearance. It distinguishes itself by combining mesh-based subdivision with greedy merging and explicit page linking to handle overlapping ellipsoids that cross page boundaries. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by mean position \mathbf{p}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{S}, and other properties (color, opacity). A proxy triangular mesh representing the scene geometry, consisting of faces F. A target page size K (maximum number of Gaussians per page). Outputs: A mapping of each Gaussian to a specific page ID. A mapping of each mesh face to a page ID (or null if unassigned). A set of page links indicating spatial overlap between pages. Page: A contiguous block of memory holding up to K Gaussian entries. Fields: Array of K Gaussian structs. Padding: If a page contains fewer than K Gaussians, remaining slots are filled with "zero-property" Gaussians (e.g., zero opacity) to maintain fixed-size alignment. Face Page ID: An integer identifier stored in the mesh face data structure, indicating which page contains the majority of Gaussians associated with that face. Page Link: A bidirectional or unidirectional reference between two page IDs, indicating that Gaussians in one page may occlude or be occluded by Gaussians in the other. 1. Initialization: Create one initial page for each face in the proxy mesh. Assign each Gaussian to the page corresponding to the mesh face whose centroid is nearest to the Gaussian's mean position \mathbf{p}. 2. Subdivision Check: For each page, count the number of assigned Gaussians ni. 3. Subdivision Loop: If ni > K: Select an edge of the triangle associated with the page. Subdivide the triangle by adding a vertex at the midpoint of the selected edge, creating two new triangles. Reassign Gaussians to the new pages based on proximity to the new triangle centroids. Repeat subdivision until ni \le K for all resulting pages. Mitigation: To prevent the creation of thin triangles and T-junctions due to floating-point inaccuracies, the algorithm rotates the vertex order and selects different edges for subsequent subdivisions on adjacent triangles. 1. Neighbor Identification: Identify neighboring pages based on the adjacency of their underlying mesh faces. 2. Merge Process: Iterate through pages. If a page's Gaussian count is below K, attempt to merge it with a neighboring page. Greedy Strategy: Use a breadth-first search to find the best neighbor. Prioritize merging with faces that are geometrically adjacent. Fallback: If no adjacent neighbors remain and the page is still underfilled, select a nearby page (spatially close but not necessarily face-adjacent). Overflow Handling: If merging a neighbor would cause the combined count to exceed K, do not merge directly. Instead, use the current page as a basis for a new merged page, and add the neighbor to this new structure if it fits, or leave it separate. 3. Final Assignment: Gaussians are grouped in memory according to their final page IDs. Unmarked faces (those with no Gaussian mean match) are excluded from rendering. Since 3D Gaussian ellipsoids are volumetric and may extend into neighboring pages, simple spatial partitioning can lead to incorrect visibility culling (marking a page as invisible when it contains visible parts of an ellipsoid). 1. Sampling: Generate M random points uniformly distributed in a unit sphere using spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi), then convert to Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z): \begin{aligned} x &= \sin(\theta) \cos(\phi) \\ y &= \sin(\theta) \sin(\phi) \\ z &= \cos(\theta) \end{aligned} Note: The distribution is non-uniform within the resulting ellipsoid due to the initial uniform sphere sampling. 2. Transformation: Apply the Gaussian's scale \mathbf{S}, rotation \mathbf{R}, and translation \mathbf{p} transforms to each sample point to place them within the Gaussian's ellipsoid volume. 3. Face Proximity Test: For each transformed sample point, find the nearest face on the proxy mesh. 4. Link Establishment: Let P{gauss} be the page ID assigned to the Gaussian. Let P{face} be the page ID of the nearest mesh face for the sample point. If P{gauss} \neq P{face}, establish a link between page P{gauss} and page P{face}. 5. Face Assignment Rule: If a mesh face is not yet assigned to a page, mark it with the page ID that has the highest number of sample points close to it. 6. Overlap Precedence: If multiple pages overlap a single face, the page with the most overlap takes precedence for the face assignment, while other overlapping pages are linked. 7. Rendering Implication: When a page is determined to be visible, all linked pages must also be loaded into GPU memory to ensure correct rendering of overlapping ellipsoids. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def assignpages(gaussians, meshfaces, pagesize): # 1. Initial Assignment pages = {face.id: [] for face in meshfaces} for g in gaussians: nearestface = min(meshfaces, key=lambda f: math.dist(f.centroid, g.mean)) pages[nearestface.id].append(g) # 2. Subdivision for faceid, glist in pages.items(): while len(glist) > pagesize: # Select an edge, split triangle at midpoint, create two new faces newface1, newface2 = splittriangleatmidpoint(faceid, meshfaces) # Reassign gaussians in this region to new faces by distance for i in range(len(glist) - 1, -1, -1): g = glist[i] nearest = min([newface1, newface2], key=lambda f: math.dist(f.centroid, g.mean)) pages[nearest.id].append(g) glist.pop(i) #: Standard triangle splitting logic; re-running nearest-face lookup for affected gaussians. # 3. Merging mergedpages = {} activepages = list(pages.keys()) while activepages: currentid = activepages.pop(0) currentgs = pages[currentid] if len(currentgs) <= pagesize: neighbors = [f.id for f in meshfaces if sharesedge(meshfaces[currentid], f)] merged = False for nid in neighbors: if len(currentgs) + len(pages[nid]) <= pagesize: currentgs.extend(pages[nid]) del pages[nid] merged = True break if not merged and len(currentgs) < pagesize: nearbyid = min(pages.keys(), key=lambda pid: math.dist(meshfaces[currentid].centroid, meshfaces[pid].centroid)) if nearbyid and len(currentgs) + len(pages[nearbyid]) <= pagesize: currentgs.extend(pages[nearbyid]) del pages[nearbyid] mergedpages[currentid] = currentgs else: # Overflow handling: create new merged page basis overflow = currentgs[pagesize:] currentgs = currentgs[:pagesize] mergedpages[currentid] = currentgs activepages.append(currentid) #: Logic assumes subdivision ensures <= pagesize. return mergedpages def establishpagelinks(gaussians, meshfaces, pagemap, numsamples=100): links = set() for g in gaussians: points = [] for in range(numsamples): theta = random.uniform(0, math.pi) phi = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) x = math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) y = math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) z = math.cos(theta) points.append((x, y, z)) transformedpoints = [] for p in points: plocal = (p[0]g.scale.x, p[1]g.scale.y, p[2]g.scale.z) protated = g.rotation plocal #: Matrix-vector multiplication pfinal = (protated[0]+g.mean.x, protated[1]+g.mean.y, protated[2]+g.mean.z) transformedpoints.append(pfinal) pagecounts = {} for p in transformedpoints: nearestface = min(meshfaces, key=lambda f: math.dist(f.centroid, p)) facepageid = pagemap.get(nearestface.id) if facepageid is not None: pagecounts[facepageid] = pagecounts.get(facepageid, 0) + 1 gausspageid = pagemap.get(g.id) if gausspageid is None: continue if pagecounts: bestpage = max(pagecounts, key=pagecounts.get) #: Updates mesh face mapping if unassigned for facepageid, count in pagecounts.items(): if facepageid != gausspageid: links.add((min(gausspageid, facepageid), max(gausspageid, facepageid))) return links def splittriangleatmidpoint(faceid, meshfaces): #: Standard geometric split; returns two new face objects return None, None def sharesedge(facea, faceb): #: Returns True if faces share a vertex pair return False Page Size (K): Determines memory granularity. Not given in the sources. Subdivision Limit: Repeated subdivision can create thin triangles and T-junctions due to floating-point inaccuracies if shared edges create vertices on adjacent triangles. The method mitigates this by rotating vertex order and choosing different edges, though it is not optimal. Unassigned Faces: Faces with no Gaussian mean match are marked as unassigned and excluded from rendering. Zero-Property Padding: Pages are padded with zero-property Gaussians to reach size K. These are easily culled during rendering. Page Linking is a technique to handle overlapping 3D Gaussians that extend into surrounding pages, preventing incorrect invisibility marking by establishing uni- or bi-directional links between pages. It is applied after initial mesh-based assignment to handle overlapping 3D Gaussians that extend into surrounding pages, preventing incorrect invisibility marking. The method uses random sampling within the Gaussian's ellipsoid to identify intersecting pages, achieving O(n) time complexity by testing only the closest face on the proxy mesh for each sample, avoiding the O(n^2) complexity of naive ellipsoid-ellipsoid intersection tests. Time Complexity: Initial Assignment: O(N \cdot F) or O(N \log F) depending on nearest-face search implementation, where N is Gaussians and F is faces. Subdivision: Depends on the number of subdivisions required to fit Gaussians into pages. Merging: Greedy breadth-first approach, generally efficient but depends on mesh connectivity. Page Linking: O(n) where n is the number of Gaussians (or samples processed), as it tests only the closest face on the proxy mesh per sample. Memory Complexity: Storage is proportional to the number of Gaussians plus the overhead of page structures and links. Pages are padded to fixed size K, leading to some memory waste if Gaussians are sparse. Performance: Enables virtual memory management, allowing scene size to exceed system memory limits by mapping Gaussians to memory-mapped files. Parallelizable tasks (e.g., page linking) can be handled in thread pools or compute shaders. Strengths: Efficiently handles large-scale scenes with millions of Gaussians. Mesh-aligned assignment simplifies spatial coherence for surface-based rendering. Page linking effectively handles volumetric overlaps without expensive intersection tests. Limitations: Subdivision can create thin triangles and T-junctions, leading to rendering artifacts. The approximate nature of page linking (using random samples) may miss some overlaps, though it is designed to be sufficient. Non-uniform distribution of sample points within the ellipsoid due to spherical coordinate sampling. Page Assignment and Merging is part of the VastGaussian method, which utilizes virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method was developed to address the scalability issues of 3DGS when dealing with large scenes that exceed GPU memory capacity. By partitioning Gaussians into pages aligned with a proxy mesh, it allows for efficient loading and culling of scene data. The approach builds on earlier virtual texturing concepts, such as those by Mittring et al., but adapts them for volumetric Gaussian representations rather than surface textures. name: Similarity Guided Partition
head: Similarity Guided Partitioning
body: Similarity Guided Partition is a graph-based clustering algorithm that groups 3D Gaussians into spatially-disjoint blocks of bounded size based on spatial proximity and appearance similarity. It solves the problem of inefficient joint pruning by ensuring that potentially redundant Gaussians are evaluated together within the same optimization block. It sets itself apart from naive spatial partitioning by incorporating a scale-aware affinity metric that accounts for both geometric overlap and appearance consistency. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N Gaussians G, a maximum block size M, a neighbor limit k, and a comparison-group size limit. Output: A set of disjoint blocks \{Cb\}{b=1}^B such that |Cb| \le M for all b, covering all Gaussians in G. Data Structures Gaussian: Contains center \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, activated scale vector si \in \mathbb{R}^3, and DC spherical-harmonic descriptor ci \in \mathbb{R}^3. Affinity Graph: A sparse graph where nodes are Gaussians and edges (i, j) have weights a{ij}. Each node stores at most k neighbors with the highest affinity. Block: A set of Gaussian indices. Algorithm Steps The method proceeds in three phases: building the affinity graph, growing blocks in parallel, and filling unused capacity. 1. Build the Graph (Two-Pass Candidate Generation) To efficiently find candidate pairs without quadratic complexity, the algorithm performs two spatial passes with different grid configurations. Pass 1: 1. Assign each Gaussian center \mui to a 3D grid cell. 2. Sort occupied cells by their Morton code to preserve spatial locality. 3. Divide the Morton-ordered Gaussian sequence into the fewest balanced groups such that each group satisfies the comparison-group size limit. 4. For each group, compute pairwise affinities a{ij} for all pairs within the group. 5. For each Gaussian, retain at most the k candidates with the largest affinities. Pass 2: 1. Shift the grid origin and enlarge the grid cell size. 2. Repeat steps 1-5 from Pass 1 using the new grid configuration. Merge: 1. Combine the edges from both passes into a single sparse graph. 2. If an edge (i, j) appears in both passes, keep only one instance, recording its weight only once. 2. Grow Blocks in Parallel Split the Morton-ordered sequence from the first pass into \lceil N/M \rceil balanced intervals. Initialize B = \lceil N/M \rceil blocks. Seed each block Cb with the first Gaussian in its corresponding interval. Mark these Gaussians as assigned. All other Gaussians are unassigned. Iterate for at most 16 iterations: 1. For each unassigned Gaussian i, identify its strongest edge to an assigned neighbor j. Let C(j) be the block containing j. 2. Gaussian i proposes to join C(j). 3. For each block Cb, collect all proposals. 4. Rank proposals by descending edge weight a{ij}, then by ascending Gaussian index i to break ties. 5. Accept the first \min(\text{number of proposals}, M - |Cb|) Gaussians. Mark them as assigned and add them to Cb. 6. If no Gaussian was assigned in this iteration, stop. 3. Fill Unused Capacity Any Gaussians that remain unassigned after the growth phase are assigned to blocks to fill them up to size M. Assignment follows the Morton order from the first pass. Iterate through the Morton-ordered list; if a Gaussian is unassigned, add it to the first block Cb that has remaining capacity (|Cb| < M). Formula The scale-aware affinity a{ij} between Gaussian i and candidate j is defined as: a{ij} = \exp \left( - \sum{d=1}^{3} \frac{(\mu{i,d} - \mu{j,d})^2}{s{i,d}^2 + s{j,d}^2 + \epsilong} \right) - \|ci - cj\|^2 Where: \mu{i,d} is the d-th component of the center of Gaussian i. s{i,d} is the d-th component of the activated scale vector of Gaussian i. ci is the three-channel DC spherical-harmonic descriptor of Gaussian i. \epsilong is a small constant to prevent division by zero. The first term measures spatial proximity normalized by the combined scales of the two Gaussians. The second term penalizes affinity between spatially close Gaussians with dissimilar appearance (high color difference). Parameters M: Maximum allowed block size. Typical value not given in sources. k: Number of nearest neighbors to retain per Gaussian for the sparse graph. Typical value not given in sources. Comparison-group size limit: Maximum size for temporary search windows during candidate generation. Typical value not given in sources. \epsilong: Small constant for numerical stability. Value not given in sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def morton3d(x, y, z): # Standard 3D Morton code (bit interleaving) x, y, z = x & 0x3FFFFFFF, y & 0x3FFFFFFF, z & 0x3FFFFFFF x = (x | (x << 16)) & 0x000000FF000000FF x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x00000000FF0000FF x = (x | (x << 4)) & 0x000000000F000F00 x = (x | (x << 2)) & 0x0000000003000300 x = (x | (x << 1)) & 0x0000000003000300 y = (y | (y << 16)) & 0x000000FF000000FF y = (y | (y << 8)) & 0x00000000FF0000FF y = (y | (y << 4)) & 0x000000000F000F00 y = (y | (y << 2)) & 0x0000000003000300 y = (y | (y << 1)) & 0x0000000003000300 z = (z | (z << 16)) & 0x000000FF000000FF z = (z | (z << 8)) & 0x00000000FF0000FF z = (z | (z << 4)) & 0x000000000F000F00 z = (z | (z << 2)) & 0x0000000003000300 z = (z | (z << 1)) & 0x0000000003000300 return x | (y << 1) | (z << 2) def similarityguidedpartition(Gaussians, M, k, grouplimit, origin1=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), cellsize1=1.0, origin2=(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), cellsize2=2.0, epsilong=1e-6): N = len(Gaussians) indices = list(range(N)) def computeaffinity(i, j): mui, muj = Gaussians[i].mu, Gaussians[j].mu si, sj = Gaussians[i].s, Gaussians[j].s ci, cj = Gaussians[i].c, Gaussians[j].c spatial = sum((mui[d] - muj[d])2 / (si[d]2 + sj[d]2 + epsilong) for d in range(3)) appearance = sum((ci[d] - cj[d])2 for d in range(3)) return math.exp(-spatial) - appearance def runpass(origin, cellsize): cells = {} for idx in indices: mu = Gaussians[idx].mu coord = tuple(int((mu[d] - origin[d]) / cellsize) for d in range(3)) cells.setdefault(coord, []).append(idx) sortedcells = sorted(cells.keys(), key=lambda c: morton3d(c)) sequence = [idx for c in sortedcells for idx in cells[c]] groups = [sequence[i:i+grouplimit] for i in range(0, len(sequence), grouplimit)] localedges = {} for group in groups: for iidx in range(len(group)): for jidx in range(iidx + 1, len(group)): u, v = group[iidx], group[jidx] w = computeaffinity(u, v) if u not in localedges: localedges[u] = [] if v not in localedges: localedges[v] = [] localedges[u].append((v, w)) localedges[v].append((u, w)) topkedges = {} for idx in indices: if idx in localedges: candidates = sorted(localedges[idx], key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0])) topkedges[idx] = candidates[:k] return sequence, topkedges # Pass 1 seq1, edges1 = runpass(origin1, cellsize1) # Pass 2 seq2, edges2 = runpass(origin2, cellsize2) # Merge edges mergededges = {} for idx, neighbors in edges1.items(): for n, w in neighbors: key = (min(idx, n), max(idx, n)) if key not in mergededges: mergededges[key] = w for idx, neighbors in edges2.items(): for n, w in neighbors: key = (min(idx, n), max(idx, n)) if key not in mergededges: mergededges[key] = w # Build adjacency list from merged edges adj = {i: [] for i in indices} for (u, v), w in mergededges.items(): adj[u].append((v, w)) adj[v].append((u, w)) # Grow blocks numblocks = math.ceil(N / M) intervals = [seq1[bM:(b+1)M] for b in range(numblocks)] blocks = [] assigned = [False] N for interval in intervals: if interval: seed = interval[0] blocks.append([seed]) assigned[seed] = True for in range(16): proposals = [] for i in indices: if assigned[i]: continue best = None for n, w in adj[i]: if assigned[n]: if best is None or w > best[1] or (w == best[1] and n < best[0]): best = (n, w) if best: proposals.append((i, best[0], best[1])) if not proposals: break blockproposals = {} for i, n, w in proposals: bidx = next(b for b, blk in enumerate(blocks) if n in blk) blockproposals.setdefault(bidx, []).append((i, w)) for bidx, plist in blockproposals.items(): plist.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0])) cap = M - len(blocks[bidx]) for gidx, in plist[:cap]: blocks[bidx].append(gidx) assigned[gidx] = True # Fill unused capacity for i in seq1: if not assigned[i]: for bidx in range(len(blocks)): if len(blocks[bidx]) < M: blocks[bidx].append(i) assigned[i] = True break return blocks Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The affinity formula involves exponentials and differences of squared terms. Small \epsilong is required to avoid division by zero in the spatial term. Boundaries: The two-pass strategy with shifted grids and enlarged cells is designed to prevent missing pairs that lie on the boundary of a single grid's search window. Degenerate Input: If N < M, a single block is formed. If k=0, no edges are formed, and blocks are filled strictly by Morton order after the growth phase (which will assign no one in the growth phase). Candidate generation is sub-quadratic because grid-based spatial hashing and top-k neighbor selection avoid all-pairs comparisons. Block growth is bounded by 16 parallel iterations. Memory stores the sparse graph with O(N \cdot k) edges and block assignments O(N). Strengths include grouping spatially and appearance-similar Gaussians for effective joint pruning. Limitations include sensitivity to grid parameters and the overhead of the two-pass strategy. Use when joint pruning requires appearance-aware grouping beyond naive spatial partitioning. The method originates from SplatQ, a paper under review for ICLR 2027. It defines local Gaussian sets for response modeling and quadratic selection-based pruning within the SplatQ framework. It builds on the VastGaussian framework, which partitions scenes into spatially-disjoint regions. name: Data Layout and Storage
body: Data Layout and Storage defines the memory organization, serialization, and runtime management of 3D Gaussian Splat attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics) to enable efficient GPU rendering and optimization. It solves the problem of translating high-level splat representations into contiguous, cache-friendly structures suitable for batched processing, while supporting dynamic scene growth and cross-platform data transfer. It is distinguished from sibling methods by focusing on the raw memory layout and buffer management infrastructure rather than the rendering algorithm itself (GSPull), error-based densification (Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring), or specific network architectures (GS-W Network Architecture). Builds on Gaussian Data Structure. The family operates on a Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) paradigm, where each attribute type is stored in a separate contiguous linear buffer [5568-splat-data-buffer-layout.md]. Rotations are stored as N \times 4 floats in scalar-last order (x, y, z, w). Opacities are stored as N floats. Spherical Harmonics coefficients are stored as N \times D \times 3 floats, with indexing idx = ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + c [5570-spherical-harmonics-coefficient-layout.md]. Dynamic scene management supports incremental append operations and dynamic buffer resizing [6907-dynamic-gaussian-splatting-scene-management.md]. Scales are stored in log-space [5568-splat-data-buffer-layout.md]. When writing to buffers, linear values are converted to log-space via \log(). Defines the foundational SoA memory organization for all splat attributes. It serves as the base for other layout methods. Choose when implementing raw buffer population for GPU shaders. Details the specific indexing and flat buffer structure for SH coefficients, ensuring contiguous access for color data. Choose when optimizing SH coefficient retrieval in shaders. Handles the decoding of Gaussian parameters from compressed texture storage into a structured CovSplat representation for rasterization. Choose when working with texture-based splat storage. Manages the runtime lifecycle of splat data structures, including capacity growth and batched updates, enabling real-time scene evolution. Choose for dynamic or streaming scenes. Manages memory allocation and serialization of splat attributes into WebAssembly linear memory for GPU upload or WASM-side processing, handling power-of-2 capacity alignment. Choose for web-based or WASM-targeted renderers. Optimizes large-scale storage and rendering. Choose for massive scene datasets requiring hierarchical or compressed storage. Integrates tracking data into the splat layout. Choose when maintaining spatial consistency across camera poses. Defines the mathematical basis and coefficient ordering for color representation. Choose when implementing or modifying the SH evaluation pipeline. Extends the standard 3D Gaussian parameterization. Choose when requiring additional degrees of freedom for complex geometry or appearance. Handles time-varying attributes within the storage structure. Choose for animating or simulating dynamic scenes. Modifies the radial kernel function for adaptive splat shapes. Choose when standard isotropic or anisotropic kernels are insufficient. Scales are stored internally in log-space. When writing to buffers, linear values are converted to log-space via \log(). When reading for rendering or optimization, log-space values are converted to linear via \exp(). Linear scale is recovered from stored log-scale: s{linear} = \exp(s{log}). Conversion logic is not explicitly detailed in the sources. For each splat i, the quaternion components are written sequentially to indices i \times 4 + 0 through i \times 4 + 3. Rotations are stored as 4-component quaternions in scalar-last order (x, y, z, w) within a FloatBuffer of size N \times 4. A file format for storing HLOD Gaussian splat worlds, extending v1 with HLOD flags, extended headers, and strict bounds validation rules. The header's world AABB must enclose the root node's world AABB. During load, validate header bounds: refuse if non-finite, negative size, or failing to enclose the root's world AABB. Perform bounds validation using double precision to avoid floating-point edge cases. World importer version is 4 (3 handles v1->v2 bake, 4 handles header-bounds rule). PLY/SPZ importer versions remain unchanged from v1. Header contains an 80-byte extension block. Each node/instance record is exactly 128 bytes. Data is organized into bounded, non-overlapping sections. Disjoint noncanonical ordering is permitted in the file layout. Malformed headers containing NaN, infinite position/size, negative size, zero size, half extent, disjoint bounds, one float ULP inside the root's low edge, or widened positive controls must be rejected or handled safely. The Structure-of-Arrays layout for 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the original 3DGS paper. Subsequent implementations, such as JSplat and the gsplat ecosystem, refined the storage for GPU efficiency, introducing log-scale storage for stability and specific quaternion orderings. The GaussianSplatWorld v2 format was developed to support Hierarchical Level of Detail (HLOD) in large-scale scenes, adding strict validation rules to prevent corruption from malformed data. Dynamic scene management techniques evolved to support real-time updates, moving beyond static initialization to support incremental appending and buffer resizing.
