name: WASM Data Packing
head: DataWorker Packing, Splat Buffer Allocation
body: WASM Data Packing manages WebAssembly memory allocation and data packing for 3D Gaussian splat attributes (positions, rotations, scales, colors, selection) to prepare them for GPU upload or WASM-side processing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Splat object containing attribute arrays (positions, rotations, scales, colors, selection) and a vertexCount. Output: A contiguous block of memory in the WebAssembly heap (HEAPF32 and HEAPU8) organized in a Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) layout, ready for direct memory access by WASM functions or GPU buffers. Data Structures: The Splat class fields include: offset: number position: Float32Array[3] rotation: Float32Array[4] scale: Float32Array[3] selected: boolean vertexCount: number positions: Float32Array rotations: Float32Array scales: Float32Array colors: Uint8Array selection: Uint8Array Buffer Layout and Sizes: The packed memory is divided into specific regions based on allocatedVertexCount (the next power of 2 greater than or equal to vertexCount). Each float occupies 4 bytes. 1. positionsPtr: Size = 3 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. 2. rotationsPtr: Size = 4 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. 3. scalesPtr: Size = 3 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. 4. colorsPtr: Size = 4 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} bytes. 5. selectionPtr: Size = \text{allocatedVertexCount} bytes. 6. dataPtr: Size = 8 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. 7. worldPositionsPtr: Size = 3 \times 4 \times 4 = 48 bytes. 8. worldRotationsPtr: Size = 4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64 bytes. 9. worldScalesPtr: Size = 3 \times 4 \times 4 = 48 bytes. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Call initWasm(). This loads the WASM module via createDataModule(). If the module is not yet loaded, pack() waits for loading to finish, initializes WASM, and proceeds. 2. Capacity Calculation: Calculate targetAllocatedVertexCount as the next power of 2 greater than or equal to splat.vertexCount: \text{targetAllocatedVertexCount} = 2^{\lceil \log2(\text{splat.vertexCount}) \rceil} 3. Memory Reallocation: If targetAllocatedVertexCount is larger than the current allocatedVertexCount: a. Free old WASM buffers using wasmModule.free(). b. Update allocatedVertexCount to targetAllocatedVertexCount. c. Allocate new buffers using wasmModule.malloc() for each attribute region. 4. Data Copying: Copy splat attribute arrays into the newly allocated WASM memory regions: a. Use wasmModule.HEAPF32.set() for float arrays (positions, rotations, scales). b. Use wasmModule.HEAPU8.set() for byte arrays (colors, selection). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pack(splat): # Ensure WASM module is loaded; if not, wait for initialization if not wasmmoduleloaded: # initwasm() and waitforwasmload() abstract the async module loading step initializewasmmodule() # Calculate next power of 2 capacity vertexcount = splat.vertexcount targetcapacity = 1 if vertexcount == 0 else 2 math.ceil(math.log2(vertexcount)) # Check if reallocation is needed if targetcapacity > allocatedvertexcount: # Free old WASM buffers if allocatedvertexcount > 0: wasmmodule.free(positionsptr) wasmmodule.free(rotationsptr) wasmmodule.free(scalesptr) wasmmodule.free(colorsptr) wasmmodule.free(selectionptr) wasmmodule.free(dataptr) wasmmodule.free(worldpositionsptr) wasmmodule.free(worldrotationsptr) wasmmodule.free(worldscalesptr) # Update capacity allocatedvertexcount = targetcapacity # Allocate new buffers positionsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(3 allocatedvertexcount 4) rotationsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(4 allocatedvertexcount 4) scalesptr = wasmmodule.malloc(3 allocatedvertexcount 4) colorsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(4 allocatedvertexcount) selectionptr = wasmmodule.malloc(allocatedvertexcount) dataptr = wasmmodule.malloc(8 allocatedvertexcount 4) worldpositionsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(48) worldrotationsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(64) worldscalesptr = wasmmodule.malloc(48) # Copy data into WASM heap # HEAPF32.set expects offset in 32-bit elements wasmmodule.HEAPF32.set(splat.positions, positionsptr // 4) wasmmodule.HEAPF32.set(splat.rotations, rotationsptr // 4) wasmmodule.HEAPF32.set(splat.scales, scalesptr // 4) # HEAPU8.set expects offset in bytes wasmmodule.HEAPU8.set(splat.colors, colorsptr) wasmmodule.HEAPU8.set(splat.selection, selectionptr) # world pointers are allocated but population logic is not specified in the source Parameters: positionsPtr: allocated size = 3 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. rotationsPtr: allocated size = 4 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. scalesPtr: allocated size = 3 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. colorsPtr: allocated size = 4 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} bytes. selectionPtr: allocated size = \text{allocatedVertexCount} bytes. dataPtr: allocated size = 8 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. worldPositionsPtr: allocated size = 48 bytes. worldRotationsPtr: allocated size = 64 bytes. worldScalesPtr: allocated size = 48 bytes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concurrent Calls: Concurrent calls to pack() are serialized via a loading flag and a while loop with setTimeout to yield to the event loop, preventing race conditions during WASM initialization. Memory Efficiency: Memory is only freed and reallocated when the next power-of-2 capacity exceeds the current allocatedVertexCount, preventing frequent reallocations for incremental vertex count changes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces JavaScript-to-GPU transfer overhead by pre-packaging data in a contiguous WASM heap. Power-of-2 allocation minimizes fragmentation and reallocation frequency. Limitations: Requires WebAssembly environment. Power-of-2 allocation can lead to memory waste if the vertex count is not a power of 2. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussian Splats in a WebAssembly-based environment where data needs to be prepared for GPU upload or WASM-side processing. When not to use: In pure CPU-based rendering or environments without WebAssembly support. WASM Data Packing is part of the gsplat.js library, which provides JavaScript/TypeScript bindings for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was developed to enable efficient rendering of Gaussian Splats in web browsers using WebAssembly. huggingface/gsplat.js, https://github.com/huggingface/gsplat.js, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SLAM and Tracking
head: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM, Gaussian SLAM, RGB-D Gaussian SLAM
body: SLAM and Tracking in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables simultaneous localization and mapping by jointly optimizing camera poses and Gaussian parameters from a stream of incoming images. It solves the problem of reconstructing dynamic or large-scale scenes in real-time or near-real-time, where traditional batch optimization is infeasible. What sets it apart from offline 3DGS is the use of a sliding window of keyframes and incremental updates, allowing the system to maintain a consistent map while tracking camera motion without re-optimizing the entire history. The core mechanism relies on maintaining a sparse set of keyframes Wk that span a wide baseline to provide multiview constraints, while discarding redundant frames with low overlap. The system performs joint optimization of camera poses and Gaussian attributes within this window. Key principles include: 1. Keyframe Selection: Frames are selected as keyframes based on covisibility metrics or geometric displacement, ensuring sufficient parallax for robust pose estimation. 2. Incremental Mapping: New Gaussians are initialized from new keyframes, often via back-projection of depth or rendering with low variance. 3. Sliding Window Optimization: Only the Gaussians and poses within the current keyframe window are jointly optimized, mitigating catastrophic forgetting and computational cost. 4. Visibility-Aware Tracking: Tracking utilizes the Gaussian rasterization visibility (accumulated alpha \alpha < 0.5) to handle occlusions naturally. Keyframe management maintains a small, computationally feasible sliding window Wk of camera poses and corresponding Gaussian states to enable joint optimization in online 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM. It solves the infeasibility of jointly optimizing all captured frames by selecting non-redundant keyframes that span a wide baseline for multiview constraints while discarding those with low overlap. It differs from fixed-interval or purely heuristic insertion by explicitly measuring covisibility via Gaussian rasterization visibility or voxel allocation ratios. See Keyframe Management for algorithmic details. A robust monocular RGB 3DGS-SLAM for dynamic in-the-wild scenes. Uses a shallow MLP over DINOv2 features to predict an uncertainty map that guides dynamic-object removal during tracking and mapping, feeding uncertainty-aware dense bundle adjustment and Gaussian-map optimization. Marked as 2026 SOTA update. An RGB-D SLAM method that represents a scene with a truncated SDF volume and a thin layer of 3D Gaussians near the surface for high-frequency appearance residuals. At render time, raycasts the SDF for depth plus a base color. Splats only the surface-near Gaussians with SDF-guided depth culling and order-independent blending. Mixes the two images to avoid expensive NeRF-style volumetric sampling and remove the Gaussian depth sorting step. Originating from the need to extend 3DGS from static batch reconstruction to online, real-time applications, SLAM methods leverage the differentiability of Gaussian splatting for tracking. Early works like NeRF-SLAM struggled with local editing and dynamic scenes. The introduction of keyframe-based sliding window optimization allowed for efficient joint optimization of poses and Gaussians. Recent developments include hybrid representations like GPS-SLAM, which combines SDFs for geometry with Gaussians for appearance, and uncertainty-aware methods like WildGS-SLAM for dynamic environments. Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Keyframe Management
head: Keyframing
body: Keyframe Management maintains a sparse sliding window Wk of keyframes to enable efficient joint optimization of camera poses and 3D Gaussian attributes in online SLAM systems. It solves the problem of computational infeasibility when processing full video streams by discarding redundant frames with low overlap while ensuring sufficient parallax for robust pose estimation. Unlike fixed-interval strategies, this method uses explicit covisibility metrics and geometric displacement to dynamically insert and remove keyframes. Inputs: Current camera frame i, last keyframe j, current keyframe window Wk, median scene depth d{med}. Outputs: Updated window Wk, boolean flag indicating if frame i is registered as a new keyframe. Data Structures: Wk: A list of keyframe indices. Visible Gaussians: A set of Gaussian indices marked as visible during rasterization. A Gaussian is visible if it is used in rasterization and the accumulated alpha \alpha along the ray has not reached 0.5. Steps: 1. Compute Covisibility: Calculate the Intersection over Union (IoU) of visible Gaussians between the current frame i and the last keyframe j. Let Vi be the set of visible Gaussians in frame i and Vj be the set in frame j. The covisibility score C{ij} is: C{ij} = \frac{|Vi \cap Vj|}{|Vi \cup Vj|} 2. Compute Geometric Displacement: Calculate the relative translation magnitude t{ij} = \|Ti - Tj\| between the current frame and the last keyframe. 3. Keyframe Registration: Register frame i as a new keyframe if either condition is met: C{ij} < \tau{cov} (covisibility drops below threshold \tau{cov}) t{ij} > \tau{geo} \cdot d{med} (relative translation is large with respect to median depth d{med}) 4. Keyframe Removal: If a new keyframe is added, remove the oldest keyframe k \in Wk if its overlap coefficient with the latest keyframe drops below a threshold. The overlap coefficient is defined similarly to covisibility but measures spatial overlap between keyframes. 5. Gaussian Insertion: Upon registering a new keyframe, initialize new Gaussians. If depth is available, back-project depth measurements to initialize means \muW. In monocular cases, render depth and initialize Gaussians around low-variance depth estimates. Parameters: \tau{cov}: Covisibility threshold. Not given in the sources. \tau{geo}: Geometric displacement threshold factor. Not given in the sources. Overlap threshold for removal: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Occlusion: Handled naturally by the visibility ordering of 3D Gaussians along the camera ray; occluded Gaussians are not counted in Vi. Degenerate Input: If median depth d{med} is zero or undefined, the geometric displacement check should be skipped or handled with a fallback threshold. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of visible Gaussians for covisibility calculation. Joint optimization is limited to the small window Wk, reducing complexity from O(N) to O(|Wk|) where N is total frames. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of Wk and the number of Gaussians visible in those frames. Strengths: Prevents catastrophic forgetting; maintains multiview constraints via wide-baseline keyframes; handles occlusions without extra heuristics. Limitations: Relies on accurate covisibility estimation; performance degrades if covisibility thresholds are poorly tuned. When to use: Online SLAM systems with limited computational resources. When not to use: Offline batch processing where all frames can be optimized jointly. Originated in Gaussian Splatting SLAM (2023). It adapts keyframe management heuristics from Direct Sparse Odometry (DSO) to the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, leveraging the inherent visibility ordering of splatted Gaussians. Gaussian Splatting SLAM, https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06741, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Keyframe Selection
head: Keyframe Selection Strategy
body: Keyframe selection determines when to add a new frame to the optimization window to maintain long-term map consistency and prevent catastrophic forgetting in online SLAM systems. It solves the problem of balancing the need for new geometric information against the computational cost of joint optimization. Unlike fixed-interval strategies, this method uses an explicit voxel structure to test tracked frames against the existing map, inserting keyframes only when they contribute significant new allocatable voxels or when a maximum time interval has elapsed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A successfully tracked RGB-D frame, the current voxel map (implicitly or explicitly defined), the current set of keyframes, and the maximum interval parameter N. Output: A boolean flag indicating whether the current frame should be added to the keyframe set Wk. Data Structures: Voxel Map: A 3D grid representing the scene. The specific layout depends on the underlying representation (e.g., dense voxel grid for Vox-Fusion or sampled rays for INR-SLAM). Keyframe Set (Wk): A list or window of indices of previously selected keyframes. Parameters: Nc: The number of voxels that would be newly allocated (or significantly updated) if the current frame were chosen as a keyframe. No: The number of currently observed voxels in the existing map. N: The maximum number of frames allowed between keyframe insertions. \tau: The threshold for the ratio p{kf} (Not given in the sources.: Typically a small value like 0.1–0.3, but exact value not specified in cited texts). Steps: 1. Track Frame: Perform tracking to obtain the pose of the current frame relative to the map. 2. Intersection Test: For the current frame, perform an intersection test against the existing voxel map to determine Nc, the count of voxels that would be allocated if this frame were added as a keyframe. 3. Calculate Ratio: Compute the ratio p{kf} = Nc / No. 4. Check Novelty Condition: If p{kf} > \tau, mark the frame as a candidate keyframe. 5. Check Interval Condition: If no keyframe has been created for the past N frames, mark the current frame as a candidate keyframe to prevent missing parts in loopy camera motions. 6. Insert Keyframe: If either condition is met, add the current frame to Wk and update the map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectkeyframe(currentframe, voxelmap, keyframewindow, N, tau): """ Determines if currentframe should be added to the keyframe set. Args: currentframe: The tracked RGB-D frame with pose. voxelmap: The current voxel representation of the scene. keyframewindow: List of indices of recent keyframes. N: Maximum interval between keyframes. tau: Threshold for novel voxel ratio. Returns: bool: True if the frame should be added as a keyframe. """ # Step 1: Count currently observed voxels in the map No = voxelmap.countobservedvoxels() # Step 2: Perform intersection test to find allocatable voxels # This simulates adding the frame to the map and counting new allocations Nc = voxelmap.countnewallocations(currentframe) # Step 3: Calculate ratio if No == 0: pkf = 1.0 # Avoid division by zero; first frame is always keyframe else: pkf = Nc / No # Step 4: Check novelty threshold isnovel = pkf > tau # Step 5: Check maximum interval # If no keyframe has been added in the last N frames framessincelastkf = len(keyframewindow) # Assuming window tracks sequence # Note: In practice, this checks the index difference or time difference # If the source implies a sliding window of size N, we check if the window is full # or if the last keyframe was too long ago. # Simplified interpretation based on "past N frames": isintervalexpired = (framessincelastkf >= N) # Step 6: Decision if isnovel or isintervalexpired: return True else: return False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Loopy Motions: Without the interval constraint (N), the system may fail to allocate new keyframes in long-term loops, resulting in missing parts of the model due to lack of multi-view constraints. Exploratory Movements: In exploratory movements, new voxels are constantly allocated, making the ratio strategy adequate. Catastrophic Forgetting: Online incremental learning is prone to forgetting; joint optimization with keyframes mitigates this. This variant focuses on the optimization strategy associated with the selected keyframes rather than just the selection criterion. It employs a global bundle adjustment strategy for enhanced pose estimation and consistent global reconstruction, following approaches in [42, 56]. To improve storage and retrieval efficiency, it selectively caches only key sampled rays from keyframes for optimization purposes. Training is continuously conducted in real-time to optimize objectives including photometric and geometric losses (Eq. 4), SDF loss, and free space suppressing loss. Time Complexity: The intersection test requires iterating over the voxel map or ray samples, which is linear with respect to the number of voxels or samples per frame. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel map size and the number of cached rays/keyframes. Strengths: Simple yet effective at creating consistent scene maps; prevents catastrophic forgetting; handles loopy motions via interval constraint. Limitations: Requires an explicit voxel structure or ray sampling for the intersection test; threshold \tau is not specified in the sources. When to Use: Online SLAM systems requiring long-term consistency and joint optimization of geometry and poses. The method originates from Vox-Fusion, which introduced dense tracking and mapping with a voxel-based neural implicit representation. It addresses the limitation of previous works that used heuristically chosen metrics or fixed intervals for keyframe insertion. The approach is designed to ensure long-term map consistency and prevent catastrophic forgetting in online incremental learning. Vox-Fusion: Dense Tracking and Mapping with Voxel-based Neural Implicit Representation, https://doi.org/10.1109/ismar55827.2022.00066, fetched 2026-10-26 Benchmarking Implicit Neural Representation and Geometric Rendering in Real-Time RGB-D SLAM, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02017, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Spherical Harmonics Representation
head: SH in 3DGS, Spherical Harmonics (SH) in 3DGS SLAM, Spherical Harmonics Algorithm, View-dependent color via SH
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) is a mathematical basis used in 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent the view-dependent color of each Gaussian primitive. It adds view-dependent color representation to Gaussians, capturing appearance variations that a single static RGB value cannot represent. An analytical Jacobian propagates gradients from SH to camera poses during optimization, though this may marginally worsen trajectory estimates if SH incorrectly models non-view-dependent effects caused by camera motion. Inputs: The viewing direction vector \mathbf{v} (normalized) in the local coordinate system of the Gaussian. The SH degree parameter L (denoted as shdegree in implementation), which determines the maximum degree l used. The SH coefficients c{l,m}^k for each color channel k \in \{R, G, B\}. Outputs: The view-dependent color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{v}) = [CR, CG, CB]^T. Each 3D Gaussian stores SH coefficients. For a maximum degree L, the number of coefficients per color channel is (L+1)^2. The total number of coefficients per Gaussian is 3(L+1)^2. Layout: The coefficients are typically stored as a flat array or a tensor of shape [3, (L+1)^2] or [(L+1)^2, 3]. Bit Packing: Not specified in the sources. Spherical Harmonics are derived from the solution of Laplace's equation in a 3D spherical coordinate system. 1. Laplace's Equation: In Cartesian coordinates: \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} = 0 Converted to spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \varphi) where x = r\sin\theta\cos\varphi, y = r\sin\theta\sin\varphi, z = r\cos\theta: \frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left(r^{2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^{2}\sin\theta } \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\left(\sin\theta \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta }\right) + \frac{1}{r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta } \frac{\partial ^{2} f}{\partial \varphi ^{2}} = 0 2. Separation of Variables: Assume f(r, \theta, \varphi) = R(r)\Theta(\theta)\Phi(\varphi). This yields: Radial part: \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{2}\frac{\partial R}{\partial r}\right) = \lambda Azimuthal part: \frac{\partial^{2}\Phi}{\partial \varphi^{2}} = -m^{2}\Phi, where m \in \mathbb{N} Polar part: \sin\theta \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\left(\sin\theta \frac{\partial \Theta}{\partial \theta}\right) = (m^{2}-\lambda \sin^{2}\theta)\Theta 3. Associated Legendre Equation: Let x = \cos\theta, \Theta \rightarrow P(x), and \lambda = l(l+1) where l \in \mathbb{Z}^+. The equation becomes: \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[(1-x^{2})\frac{\partial P(x)}{\partial x}\right] + \left[l(l+1)-\frac{m^{2}}{1-x^{2}}\right]P(x) = 0 The solution is the Associated Legendre Function Pl^m(x). Rodrigues' formula is given as: P{l}(x)=\frac{1}{2^{l}l!}\frac{\partial ^{l}}{\partial x^{l}}(x^2-1)^{l} Orthonormality condition: \int{-1}^{1}\sqrt{\frac{2m+1}{2}}P{m}(x) \sqrt{\frac{2n+1}{2}}P{n}(x)dx=\delta{mn} Recursion relation: (l+1)P{l+1}(x)=(2l+1)xP{l}(x)-lP{l-1}(x) 4. Spherical Harmonics Function: The SH basis functions Yl^m(\theta, \varphi) are defined as: Yl^m(\theta, \varphi) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{2} K{l}^{m}\cos(m\varphi)P{l}^{m}(\cos\theta) & m > 0 \\ \sqrt{2} K{l}^{m}\sin(-m\varphi)P{l}^{-m}(\cos\theta) & m < 0 \\ K{l}^{0}P{l}^{0}(\cos\theta) & m = 0 \end{cases} The normalization scaling factor K{l}^{m} is: K{l}^{m}=\sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}\cdot \frac{(l-|m|)!}{(l+|m|)!}} where l \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}, m \in \mathbb{Z}, |m| \le l. The color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{v}) for a viewing direction \mathbf{v} (represented by spherical angles \theta, \varphi) is computed by projecting the SH coefficients onto the basis functions: \mathbf{C}(\theta, \varphi) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{l,m} Yl^m(\theta, \varphi) The number of basis functions is (L+1)^2. For L=3, this is 16 coefficients per channel. shdegree (L): The maximum degree of SH coefficients. Default value is 3. L=0: View-independent color (constant). L=1: Captures linear variations (e.g., simple lighting). L=2, 3: Captures more complex view-dependent effects. Omission: SH can be omitted (set L=0 or disabled) for synthetic datasets like Replica that lack view-directional effects. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeshbasis(theta, phi, maxdegree): """ Computes the Spherical Harmonics basis functions for a given direction. Returns a list of basis values for degrees 0 to maxdegree. """ costheta = math.cos(theta) basis = [] for l in range(maxdegree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): absm = abs(m) # Compute Associated Legendre Function Pl^{|m|}(costheta) plm = associatedlegendre(l, absm, costheta) # Normalization factor klm = math.sqrt((2 l + 1) / (4 math.pi) math.factorial(l - absm) / math.factorial(l + absm)) # Angular part based on m if m > 0: angular = math.sqrt(2) math.cos(m phi) elif m < 0: angular = math.sqrt(2) math.sin(-m phi) else: angular = 1.0 basis.append(klm plm angular) return basis def associatedlegendre(l, m, x): """ Computes the Associated Legendre Function Pl^m(x). Uses recurrence relations for efficiency. """ if m < 0: raise ValueError("m must be non-negative for this implementation") if l < m: return 0.0 if l == 0: return 1.0 if l == 1: return x if m == 0 else 0.0 # Compute Pl^m using recurrence if m == 0: plminus1 = associatedlegendre(l - 1, 0, x) plminus2 = associatedlegendre(l - 2, 0, x) return ((2 l - 1) x plminus1 - (l - 1) plminus2) / l else: # Pm^m if l == m: if m == 0: return 1.0 doublefact = 1 for i in range(1, 2 m, 2): doublefact = i return doublefact ((1 - x x) (m / 2)) # Recurrence for l > m plminus1 = associatedlegendre(l - 1, m, x) plminus2 = associatedlegendre(l - 2, m, x) return ((2 l - 1) x plminus1 - (l + m - 1) plminus2) / (l - m) def rendersh(colorcoeffs, theta, phi, maxdegree): """ Renders the view-dependent color using SH coefficients. colorcoeffs: list of coefficients for R, G, B channels. Shape: [3, (maxdegree+1)^2] """ basis = computeshbasis(theta, phi, maxdegree) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] idx = 0 for l in range(maxdegree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): val = basis[idx] for c in range(3): color[c] += colorcoeffs[c][idx] val idx += 1 return color Precision: Higher degrees (L > 3) increase computational cost and memory usage without guaranteed quality improvement. Boundary Conditions: The SH basis is defined on the unit sphere. Directions must be normalized. Overfitting: Using high SH degrees on datasets without view-dependent effects (like Replica) may lead to overfitting or unnecessary memory usage. Optimizes Gaussian parameters via pull-based gradients; chosen when gradient propagation efficiency is prioritized over push-based methods. Scores Gaussians using accumulated rendering error; chosen for adaptive densification and pruning during training. Manages GPU memory allocation for variable Gaussian counts; chosen when scene complexity fluctuates or memory is constrained. Uses a neural network to predict Gaussian attributes; chosen when parametric generation is preferred over explicit storage. Optimizes large-scale scene rendering via hierarchical structures; chosen for city-scale or massive point cloud datasets. Defines memory layout and compression for Gaussian attributes; chosen to minimize bandwidth and improve cache locality. Integrates 3DGS with visual-inertial odometry; chosen for real-time mapping and pose estimation. Extends Gaussians with additional dimensions (e.g., time, velocity); chosen for dynamic scene reconstruction. Applies deformation fields to static Gaussians; chosen when explicit dynamic primitives are too expensive. Replaces fixed Gaussian kernels with deformable ones; chosen to better model complex shapes and occlusions. Clusters Gaussians for efficient rendering; chosen to reduce draw calls and improve rasterization throughput. Time Complexity: Rendering time scales linearly with the number of basis functions, O((L+1)^2) per Gaussian per pixel. Memory Complexity: Memory per Gaussian increases by 3(L+1)^2 floats. Measured Performance: On TUM RGB-D, enabling SH increases memory from 3.97 MB to 11.47 MB. Rendering PSNR improves from 21.89 to 24.37 with SH enabled. ATE RMSE marginally worsens from 1.47 cm to 1.56 cm with SH enabled. Strengths: Accurately models view-dependent color; enables joint optimization of camera poses via analytical gradients. Limitations: Increases memory usage significantly; may degrade trajectory estimation if SH incorrectly models non-view-dependent effects caused by camera motion. Higher degrees do not always yield better results and increase computational cost. When to Use: When view-dependent effects (specularities, complex lighting) are present. When Not to Use: For synthetic datasets without view-dependent effects (e.g., Replica) or when memory is severely constrained. Spherical Harmonics were introduced as a solution to Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates. In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, SH was adopted to represent view-dependent color, building on the original 3DGS method. The method has been widely used in subsequent works, including 3DGS SLAM, dynamic 3DGS, and human 3DGS generation. name: 7D Gaussian Splatting
head: 7D Gaussian Representation, 7DGS, 7DGS definition
body: 7D Gaussian Splatting (7DGS) is a unified framework for the real-time rendering of dynamic scenes with complex view-dependent effects, representing scene elements as seven-dimensional Gaussians spanning spatial position (3D), time (1D), and viewing direction (3D). It solves the problem of simultaneously modeling spatial geometry, temporal dynamics, and view-dependent appearance (such as scattering and anisotropic reflections) in dynamic scenes, a challenge that prior methods like 4DGS and 6DGS addressed in isolation. Unlike its siblings, 7DGS jointly models all three dimensions in a single coherent framework, using a conditional slicing mechanism to transform 7D Gaussians into time- and view-conditioned 3D Gaussians compatible with existing 3DGS rendering pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 7D Gaussian primitives, each defined by a mean vector and a covariance matrix in the joint space of position, time, and direction. Output: A rendered image for a specific camera pose (view direction) and time instance, generated by projecting the conditioned 3D Gaussians and rasterizing them. Data Structures: Each scene element is modeled as a 7D Gaussian random variable X jointly encoding spatial (Xp \in \mathbb{R}^3), temporal (Xt \in \mathbb{R}), and directional (Xd \in \mathbb{R}^3) properties. The distribution is defined as: X \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \begin{pmatrix} \mup \\ \mut \\ \mud \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \Sigmap & \Sigma{pt} & \Sigma{pd} \\ \Sigma{pt}^\top & \Sigmat & \Sigma{td} \\ \Sigma{pd}^\top & \Sigma{td}^\top & \Sigmad \end{pmatrix} \right) where: \mup, \Sigmap: Mean and covariance for spatial coordinates, modeling local geometric shape. \mut, \Sigmat: Mean and variance for the temporal coordinate, accounting for dynamic evolution. \mud, \Sigmad: Mean and covariance for the viewing direction, capturing view-dependent appearance. \Sigma{pt}, \Sigma{pd}, \Sigma{td}: Off-diagonal blocks capturing correlations among spatial, temporal, and directional components, enabling the modeling of complex interdependencies. The full 7D covariance matrix \Sigma is parameterized using Cholesky decomposition to guarantee validity during optimization: \Sigma = L L^\top where L is a lower-triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries. Color representation uses view-dependent spherical harmonics from 3DGS without additional temporal dependencies, as dynamic information is encoded within the Gaussian parameters. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize 7D Gaussians: Create a set of 7D Gaussians where each primitive stores \mup, \mut, \mud, \alpha (opacity), and the Cholesky factor L of the covariance matrix \Sigma. 2. Conditional Slicing: For a target rendering time t and view direction d, compute the conditioned 3D Gaussian parameters for each primitive. This involves calculating the conditional mean \mu{cond} and conditional covariance \Sigma{cond} of the spatial component Xp given Xt = t and Xd = d. Let the joint mean be \mu = [\mup^\top, \mut, \mud^\top]^\top and the joint covariance be \Sigma. Partition \Sigma and \mu into spatial (p), temporal (t), and directional (d) parts. The conditional mean is: \mu{cond} = \mup + \Sigma{pz} \Sigma{zz}^{-1} (z - \muz). The conditional covariance is: \Sigma{cond} = \Sigma{pp} - \Sigma{pz} \Sigma{zz}^{-1} \Sigma{zp}. (Where z = [t, d]^\top, \Sigma{zz} is the covariance of the conditioned variables, and \Sigma{pz} contains the cross-covariances \Sigma{pt} and \Sigma{pd}). 3. Adaptive Refinement: During optimization, use a neural network to predict residuals that dynamically adjust Gaussian parameters to model complex non-rigid deformations and time-varying appearance. 4. Render: Project the conditioned 3D Gaussians (\mu{cond}, \Sigma{cond}, \alpha) onto the image plane using standard 3DGS projection and rasterization. Compute color using spherical harmonics evaluated at the view direction d. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def choleskydecompose(covmatrix): """ Computes the lower-triangular matrix L such that Sigma = L @ L.T. Ensures positive diagonal entries. """ L = np.linalg.cholesky(covmatrix) return L def reconstructcovariance(L): """ Reconstructs the covariance matrix from its Cholesky factor. """ return L @ L.T def conditionalslice7dto3d(mean7d, L7d, timeval, directionvec): """ Slices a 7D Gaussian into a 3D Gaussian conditioned on time and direction. Args: mean7d: Array of shape (7,) containing [mup (3), mut (1), mud (3)] L7d: Lower-triangular Cholesky factor of shape (7, 7) timeval: Scalar time value t directionvec: Array of shape (3,) representing view direction d Returns: mucond: Array of shape (3,) conditioned spatial mean Sigmacond: Array of shape (3, 3) conditioned spatial covariance """ # Extract components mup = mean7d[0:3] mut = mean7d[3] mud = mean7d[4:7] # Reconstruct full covariance matrix Sigma = reconstructcovariance(L7d) # Partition Sigma into blocks # Indices: 0-2 (p), 3 (t), 4-6 (d) Sigmapp = Sigma[0:3, 0:3] Sigmapt = Sigma[0:3, 3:4] Sigmapd = Sigma[0:3, 4:7] Sigmatp = Sigma[3:4, 0:3] Sigmatt = Sigma[3:4, 3:4] Sigmatd = Sigma[3:4, 4:7] Sigmadp = Sigma[4:7, 0:3] Sigmadt = Sigma[4:7, 3:4] Sigmadd = Sigma[4:7, 4:7] # Construct the joint covariance of the conditioned variables (t, d) # and the cross-covariance with p # Let z = [t, d]. We want p | z. # Covariance of z (time and direction) Sigmazz = np.zeros((4, 4)) Sigmazz[0, 0] = Sigmatt Sigmazz[0, 1:] = Sigmatd Sigmazz[1:, 0] = Sigmadt Sigmazz[1:, 1:] = Sigmadd # Cross-covariance between p and z Sigmapz = np.hstack((Sigmapt, Sigmapd)) # Shape (3, 4) # Residual vector for conditioning # z - muz muz = np.array([mut, mud]) residualz = np.array([timeval - mut, (directionvec - mud)]) # Compute conditional mean: mup + Sigmapz @ Sigmazz^-1 @ (z - muz) # Solve Sigmazz @ x = residualz for x try: invSigmazzresidual = np.linalg.solve(Sigmazz, residualz) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: # Fallback for singular matrices, though Cholesky implies positive definite invSigmazzresidual = np.linalg.lstsq(Sigmazz, residualz, rcond=None)[0] mucond = mup + Sigmapz @ invSigmazzresidual # Compute conditional covariance: Sigmapp - Sigmapz @ Sigmazz^-1 @ Sigmazp Sigmazp = Sigmapz.T correction = Sigmapz @ np.linalg.solve(Sigmazz, Sigmazp) Sigmacond = Sigmapp - correction return mucond, Sigmacond def render7dgs(gaussians, timeval, directionvec, cameraparams): """ Renders a frame using 7DGS. Args: gaussians: List of dicts, each containing 'mean7d' (7,), 'L7d' (7,7), 'alpha', 'shcoeffs' timeval: Float, current time directionvec: Array (3,), view direction cameraparams: Object with projection matrix and intrinsics Returns: image: Rendered image array """ # 1. Slice all 7D Gaussians to 3D conditionedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: mucond, Sigmacond = conditionalslice7dto3d( g['mean7d'], g['L7d'], timeval, directionvec) conditionedgaussians.append({ 'mu': mucond, 'Sigma': Sigmacond, 'alpha': g['alpha'], 'shcoeffs': g['shcoeffs'] }) # 2. Project and Rasterize (Standard 3DGS Pipeline) # Perform standard 3DGS projection and rasterization image = standard3dgsrasterize(conditionedgaussians, cameraparams) return image Parameters and Typical Values: Spherical Harmonics Degree: Not specified in sources, but inherits from 3DGS/6DGS. Performance: Achieved 401 FPS on challenging dynamic scenes with complex view-dependent effects. Quality: Outperforms prior methods by up to 7.36 dB in PSNR. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Covariance: The Cholesky decomposition requires a positive definite covariance matrix. If optimization leads to a singular or near-singular matrix during conditioning, numerical instability may occur. Boundary Conditions: The sources do not specify handling for time or direction values outside the training domain. A sibling method focusing on pull-based optimization strategies. Link Techniques for managing Gaussian density based on rendering error. Link Methods for handling memory allocation for dynamic Gaussian sets. Link Neural network architectures used for refining Gaussian parameters. Link A method for scaling Gaussian Splatting to very large scenes. Link Efficient storage formats for Gaussian attributes. Link Integration of 7DGS with simultaneous localization and mapping. Link The specific representation used for view-dependent color. Link General approaches to modeling motion in Gaussian fields. Link Alternative kernel parametrizations for dynamic scenes. Link Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved, with reported performance of 401 FPS on challenging dynamic scenes. The conditional slicing operation adds computational overhead compared to static 3DGS, but remains efficient enough for real-time application. Memory Complexity: Higher than static 3DGS due to the storage of temporal and directional means, variances, and cross-covariances for each Gaussian. The Cholesky factor L requires storing 28 values (for a 7x7 lower triangular matrix) plus means and opacity, compared to 10-15 values for standard 3DGS. Strengths: Unified modeling of space, time, and direction; high PSNR (up to 7.36 dB improvement over prior methods); real-time performance; compatibility with existing 3DGS pipelines. Limitations: Increased memory footprint; complexity in optimizing the full 7D covariance matrix; potential numerical instability in conditional slicing if covariance matrices are ill-conditioned. When to use: When rendering dynamic scenes with significant view-dependent effects (e.g., specular highlights, scattering) is required, and real-time performance is necessary. When not to use: For static scenes (use 3DGS) or scenes where only temporal dynamics or only view-dependent effects are present and extreme efficiency is prioritized over unified modeling. 7D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Zhongpai Gao, Benjamin Planche, Meng Zheng, Anwesa Choudhuri, Terrence Chen, and Ziyan Wu from United Imaging Intelligence in March 2025. It addresses the limitations of previous methods: 4DGS, which handles space and time but not view-dependent effects, and 6DGS, which handles space and direction but not temporal dynamics. The method builds on the foundations of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and 6D Gaussian Splatting (6DGS). It has been evaluated on synthetic datasets (D-NeRF) and in-the-wild multi-view videos (Technicolor), as well as a custom dataset (7DGS-PBR) featuring dynamic scenes with complex motions and view-dependent effects. 7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07946v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Deformation and Dynamic Modeling
head: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting, Time-varying Gaussian Splatting, Spacetime Gaussians
body: Deformation and Dynamic Modeling extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent and render time-varying scenes by predicting time-dependent deformation deltas for canonical Gaussian parameters. It solves the problem of reconstructing moving objects (e.g., people, fluids) from multi-view video or casual capture, enabling real-time rendering of dynamic content. It sets itself apart from static methods by introducing a temporal dimension t that modulates the geometry (position, rotation, scale) of the Gaussian set, distinguishing it from sibling methods like Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting which use sparse control points, or Deformable Radial Kernel which modifies the kernel shape. All methods in this family operate on a set of canonical 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{canon}, where each Gaussian i has static base parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{q}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}{SH,i}). The core mechanism involves a deformation function f\theta that takes canonical features and a time parameter t \in [0, 1] to predict deltas (\Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \Delta\mathbf{q}i, \Delta\mathbf{s}i). The time-varying parameters are computed as: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i \mathbf{q}i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}i \otimes \Delta\mathbf{q}i) \mathbf{s}i(t) = \mathbf{s}i + \Delta\mathbf{s}i where \otimes is quaternion multiplication and normalization prevents drift. The rendered image is generated by rasterizing \mathcal{G}(t) using standard differentiable rasterization with camera pose and time t. Optimization minimizes photometric loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{reg}, updating canonical parameters, features, and network weights via SGD. Uses sparse user-provided control points with influence weights to drive deformation via locally interpolated 6 DoF transformations, offering a compact and editable representation. Choose when explicit user control or sparse editing is required. Uses a dense deformation network (MLP or HexPlane) to predict deltas directly from canonical features and time, trading flexibility for computational overhead. Choose for general dynamic scene reconstruction without sparse control constraints. End-to-end driving simulators that integrate dynamic Gaussian modeling for autonomous driving contexts. Drives time-of-day and weather conditioning for closed-loop simulation in autonomous driving scenarios. A motion-aware optimization method using sparse control trajectories to handle dynamic scenes. Originated from the need to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes, with early works like GaussianFlow and MoSca introducing temporal regularization and priors. The field has evolved to include specialized variants for autonomous driving (Drive-GS, 4D-Driving-GS) and monocular capture (Shape-of-Motion). By 2026, per-actor and per-scene Gaussian decomposition became dominant for AV simulation, supporting closed-loop simulators for companies like Tesla and Waymo. name: Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: SC-GS, Sparse-Controlled
body: Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting (SC-GS) is a method for dynamic scene representation that uses a small set of user-provided or learned control points to drive the deformation of a dense set of 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of compact, editable dynamic modeling by propagating sparse edits across time via a learned deformation prior, avoiding the need for per-Gaussian deformation networks. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Deformable 3DGS by replacing per-Gaussian MLP queries with sparse control point interpolation, resulting in a more compact and editable representation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of canonical 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{canon}, a set of sparse control points \mathcal{C}, and a time parameter t \in [0, 1]. Outputs: Transformed Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}(t) for rendering. Data Structures: Canonical Gaussians: Static base parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{q}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}{SH,i}) as defined in the parent article. Control Points: A sparse set of points \mathcal{C} = \{cj\} in canonical space. Each control point is linked to time-varying 6 DoF transformations. Deformation Network: An MLP that predicts deformation parameters based on time and location. Method Steps: 1. Initialize: Optimize canonical Gaussian parameters and control point positions jointly. 2. Predict Transformations: For each control point cj, predict its 6 DoF transformation at time t using the MLP. 3. Interpolate Motion: For each Gaussian i, compute its motion by locally interpolating the transformations of nearby control points based on influence weights. 4. Apply Deformation: Compute the deltas (\Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \Delta\mathbf{q}i, \Delta\mathbf{s}i) from the interpolated motion. 5. Update Parameters: Compute time-varying parameters: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i \mathbf{q}i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}i \otimes \Delta\mathbf{q}i) \mathbf{s}i(t) = \mathbf{s}i + \Delta\mathbf{s}i where \otimes is quaternion multiplication and normalization prevents drift. 6. Render: Rasterize \mathcal{G}(t) using standard differentiable rasterization with camera pose and time t. 7. Optimize: Minimize photometric loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{reg}, updating canonical parameters, control points, and MLP weights via SGD. The method employs an ARAP (As-Rigid-As-Possible) loss to maintain local rigidity. Parameters: Control Point Density: Not given in the sources. ARAP Weight: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Control: If control points are too sparse, interpolation may fail to capture complex deformations. Motion Complexity: The method employs an adaptive strategy to handle motion complexity. Uses per-Gaussian MLP deformation networks. Choose when per-Gaussian flexibility is needed without sparse control. Deformable 3DGS Uses temporal opacity envelopes and polynomial trajectories. Choose for real-time continuous-time 4D reconstruction. Spacetime Gaussians Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Compact due to sparse control points. Strengths: Compact, editable, enables large deformation and soft body simulation. Limitations: Relies on sparse control points; may struggle with highly complex motion if not adaptively handled. When to Use: When compact, editable dynamic representation is required. When Not to Use: When dense, per-Gaussian deformation is necessary without user control. SC-GS was introduced as a non-mesh-based method for deforming 3DGS using sparse control points. It enables large deformation, soft body simulation, and local manipulation. It is compared with methods like SuGaR and Mani-GS, producing fewer artifacts and reducing blurring. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Deformable 3DGS
head: 4D Gaussian Splatting, Dynamic 3DGS
body: Deformable 3DGS extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by modeling time-dependent geometric and appearance parameters. It solves the problem of reconstructing and rendering moving subjects (e.g., people, fluids) from multi-view video by decomposing the 4D representation into a static canonical set of Gaussians and a deformation function that predicts their state at any time t. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting by using a direct MLP-based deformation network on per-Gaussian features rather than sparse control points, and from HexPlane-based variants by its specific architectural choice for feature-to-deformation mapping. Inputs: Multi-view video frames with known camera poses and timestamps t \in [0, 1]. Outputs: A set of time-varying 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}(t) rendered into images. Data Structures: 1. Canonical Gaussians \mathcal{G}{canon}: Each Gaussian i stores static base parameters: Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R} Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH,i} 2. Deformation Network f\theta: An MLP that takes canonical features and time t as input. Input: Concatenation of per-Gaussian latent features (or position) and time t. Output: Deltas \Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \Delta\mathbf{q}i, \Delta\mathbf{s}i. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize \mathcal{G}{canon} using standard 3DGS initialization from static reconstruction or SfM points. 2. Deformation Prediction: For each Gaussian i and time t: \Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i = f\theta(\boldsymbol{\mu}i, t) \Delta\mathbf{q}i = f\theta(\mathbf{q}i, t) \Delta\mathbf{s}i = f\theta(\mathbf{s}i, t) Note: Specific implementations may use different input features (e.g., latent codes l). 3. Time-Varying Parameter Update: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i \mathbf{q}i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}i \otimes \Delta\mathbf{q}i) \mathbf{s}i(t) = \mathbf{s}i + \Delta\mathbf{s}i where \otimes is quaternion multiplication. 4. Rendering: Rasterize \mathcal{G}(t) using standard differentiable rasterization with camera pose and time t. 5. Optimization: Minimize photometric loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{reg}, updating canonical parameters, features, and network weights via SGD. Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. \lambda (regularization weight): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Quaternion normalization prevents drift in rotation updates. Precision issues may arise if \Delta\mathbf{s}i causes negative scales; clipping or absolute value may be required. A method that replaces discrete per-frame deformation with a smooth spline modeling the trajectory of each primitive's center and rotation as a function of time, ensuring physically plausible, smooth motion with fewer parameters. It uses B-spline basis functions \mathbf{B}k(t) and control points \mathbf{p}{i,k}: \mui(t) = \sum{k=0}^K \mathbf{B}k(t) \mathbf{p}{i,k}. A neural network that takes local body pose and latent codes to predict residual transformations (translation, rotation) and shading for Gaussians. Input is the concatenation of local body pose vector \thetat and per-Gaussian learnable latent features l. Hidden layers: 2 layers, 64 neurons each, ReLU activations. Output heads: 3 separate heads, each with 2 layers, outputting: 1) Translation vector t{mlp}, 2) Rotation quaternion q{mlp}, 3) Scaling factor s. Using latent codes l instead of position leads to better performance. The final observed position and orientation are computed as: \mathbf {p}{\text {obs}} = \mathbf {p}{\text {lbs}} + (\mathbf {R}{t}\mathbf {t}{\text {mlp}}) \mathbf {q}{\text {obs}} = \mathbf {q}{\text {mlp}} \circ \mathbf {q}{\text {lbs}}. Time Complexity: Depends on the deformation network size and number of Gaussians. Real-time rendering is feasible if the deformation network is lightweight. Memory Complexity: Stores canonical Gaussians plus deformation network weights. More compact than storing full 4D Gaussians for every frame. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes (people moving, fluids). Can achieve real-time rendering. Limitations: Performance depends on the deformation network's capacity. May struggle with complex, non-rigid deformations if the network is too simple. When to use: Dynamic scene reconstruction and rendering. When not to use: Static scenes (use standard 3DGS) or scenes requiring explicit control via sparse points (use SC-GS). Introduced by Yang et al. in CVPR'24. It is part of the broader effort to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to 4D (spatiotemporal) representations. name: VolSegGS
head: VolSegGS
body: VolSegGS is a method for segmenting and tracking structures across timesteps in dynamic volumetric scenes by representing the scene as deformable 3D Gaussians, thereby sidestepping the memory constraints associated with grid-based representations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a two-level segmentation strategy guided by an affinity field network, which allows it to split segments beneath thin, semi-transparent layers and resolve inner color variations that confuse 2D-prompt-based approaches. Unlike 4DGS, which relies on expensive k-NN regularization for explicit 4D Gaussians, VolSegGS uses a hybrid deformation network that provides spatial smoothness naturally, offering a balance between real-time rendering performance and segmentation accuracy. Inputs: A set of training views (images) of a dynamic volumetric scene at specific timesteps. 2D segmentation prompts (e.g., masks or points) generated by SAM 2 for the training views. Time parameter t for dynamic scenes. Outputs: A set of deformable 3D Gaussians representing the scene geometry and appearance. An affinity field network that assigns segmentation labels to Gaussians. Segmentation masks for test views and tracked labels across timesteps. Data Structures: 1. Deformable 3D Gaussians: Each Gaussian i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation/scale parameters). Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. View-independent color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3 (used for coarse clustering). Deformation state managed by the hybrid network. 2. Hybrid Deformation Network: Explicit Feature Grid: Stores latent features in a 3D grid. Lightweight MLP: Takes inputs and outputs deformation parameters. 3. Affinity Field Network: A neural network that predicts affinity scores between Gaussians to refine segmentation. Trained to ensure smoothness and consistency among neighboring Gaussians. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Representation: Represent the dynamic volumetric scene as a set of deformable 3D Gaussians. The hybrid deformation network takes the Gaussian mean \mui and time t as inputs to predict the deformation, providing spatial smoothness without additional regularization terms. 2. Coarse-Level Segmentation: Cluster the Gaussians based on their view-independent colors ci. This initial clustering provides a rough segmentation of the scene structures. 3. Fine-Level Segmentation (Affinity Field Training): Initialize the affinity field network. Train the network for 5,000 iterations using a batch size of 8,192 pixels. Use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 \times 10^{-3}. The network is guided by SAM 2D prompts to refine the coarse clusters into fine-level segments. The affinity field ensures smoothness and consistency, reducing noise in affinity features that might otherwise affect occluded parts. 4. Segment Tracking: Maintain segment labels across timesteps by propagating them through the deformation field. As Gaussians deform over time, their associated segmentation labels are updated based on the learned affinity and deformation continuity. 5. Rendering: Render the scene using standard differentiable volume rendering techniques with the deformable Gaussians and their assigned segmentation labels. Loss Functions and Training Strategy: Early Training: Use L2 loss during early training iterations. This more effectively penalizes large errors in small regions, preventing missing content in synthesized images caused by deformation network inaccuracies. Late Training: Postpone the application of DSSIM loss until the final 5,000 iterations of training. This ensures better structural preservation. Two-Level Segmentation: The strategy splits segments beneath thin, semi-transparent layers and removes inner parts of different colors within semi-transparent segments, addressing ambiguities that 2D prompts alone cannot resolve. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class HybridDeformationNetwork(nn.Module): """ Hybrid deformation network combining an explicit feature grid and a lightweight MLP. Inputs: Gaussian means (mu) and time (t). Outputs: Deformation parameters. """ def init(self, gridresolution, featuredim, mlphiddendim): super().init() # Explicit feature grid self.grid = nn.Embedding(gridresolution3, featuredim) # Lightweight MLP self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(featuredim + 1, mlphiddendim), # +1 for time nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(mlphiddendim, mlphiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(mlphiddendim, 6) # e.g., 3 for translation, 3 for rotation/scale) def forward(self, mu, t): # Quantize mu to grid indices # Note: In practice, trilinear interpolation is used for smoothness # Here we assume a simplified lookup for demonstration gridindices = quantizetogrid(mu, self.gridresolution) gridfeatures = self.grid(gridindices) # Concatenate with time texpanded = t.unsqueeze(1) inputfeatures = torch.cat([gridfeatures, texpanded], dim=-1) deformation = self.mlp(inputfeatures) return deformation class AffinityFieldNetwork(nn.Module): """ Network to predict affinity scores for segmentation refinement. """ def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim): super().init() self.network = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) # Affinity score) def forward(self, featurea, featureb): # Compute affinity between two Gaussians' features diff = torch.abs(featurea - featureb) return self.network(diff) def trainvolseggs(gaussians, trainingviews, samprompts, timesteps): """ Main training loop for VolSegGS. """ # Initialize Gaussians (e.g., from SfM or random initialization) # Initialize Hybrid Deformation Network deformnet = HybridDeformationNetwork(gridresolution=64, featuredim=32, mlphiddendim=64) # Initialize Affinity Field Network affinitynet = AffinityFieldNetwork(inputdim=32, hiddendim=64) optimizeraffinity = optim.Adam(affinitynet.parameters(), lr=1e-3) totaliterations = 10000 # Example total affinityiterations = 5000 for iteration in range(totaliterations): # 1. Sample a batch of training views and corresponding timesteps view, timet = samplebatch(trainingviews, timesteps) # 2. Render scene using deformable Gaussians # Deform Gaussians using Hybrid Deformation Network mu = gaussians.mu deformation = deformnet(mu, timet) deformedgaussians = applydeformation(gaussians, deformation) renderedimage = render(deformedgaussians, view) # 3. Compute Loss gtimage = getgt(view) if iteration < totaliterations - 5000: # Early training: Use L2 loss to prevent missing content in small regions loss = torch.mean((renderedimage - gtimage)2) else: # Late training: Introduce DSSIM loss for structural preservation lossl2 = torch.mean((renderedimage - gtimage)2) lossdssim = computedssim(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = lossl2 + lossdssim # Backpropagate deformation network loss loss.backward(retaingraph=True) optimizerdeform.step() optimizerdeform.zerograd() # 4. Affinity Field Training (for first 5000 iterations) if iteration < affinityiterations: # Sample pixels for affinity training batchpixels = samplepixels(view, batchsize=8192) # Get features for Gaussians corresponding to batch pixels # Features are extracted from the grid or MLP in deformnet features = extractfeatures(deformedgaussians, batchpixels) # Compute affinity scores # Affinity is computed between neighboring Gaussians neighborindices = getneighbors(features) affinities = affinitynet(features[neighborindices[:, 0]], features[neighborindices[:, 1]]) # Ground truth affinity from SAM prompts gtaffinities = computegtaffinity(samprompts, batchpixels) affinityloss = torch.mean((affinities - gtaffinities)2) affinityloss.backward() optimizeraffinity.step() optimizeraffinity.zerograd() return deformnet, affinitynet, gaussians def segmentandtrack(deformnet, affinitynet, gaussians, testviews, samprompts): """ Segment and track structures in dynamic scenes. """ # 1. Coarse segmentation by clustering Gaussians by view-independent colors coarselabels = clusterbycolor(gaussians.colors) # 2. Refine using Affinity Field Network refinedlabels = refinesegmentation(coarselabels, affinitynet, gaussians, samprompts) # 3. Track across timesteps trackedlabels = [] for t in timesteps: # Deform Gaussians deformation = deformnet(gaussians.mu, t) deformedgaussians = applydeformation(gaussians, deformation) # Update labels based on deformation and affinity currentlabels = propagatelabels(refinedlabels, deformedgaussians, affinitynet) trackedlabels.append(currentlabels) return trackedlabels Parameters: Affinity field network training iterations: 5,000. Batch size for affinity field network training: 8,192 pixels. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Training view resolution: 800×800. Number of training views: 30. Number of test views: 181. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with 24 GB VRAM. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing content in small regions: Caused by deformation network inaccuracies. Mitigated by using L2 loss in early training and postponing DSSIM loss. Segmentation beneath thin, semi-transparent layers: 2D prompts fail here. Mitigated by the two-level segmentation strategy. Noise in affinity features: Can lead to suboptimal segmentation for occluded parts. Mitigated by the spatial smoothness provided by the MLP-based deformation field network. Inner color variations: Semi-transparent segments may contain different colors. Mitigated by the two-level segmentation strategy which removes inner parts of different colors. Rendering Performance: Achieves a minimum rendering framerate of 87 FPS. Across five time-varying datasets at resolutions up to 960×1440×240, it achieves PSNR values of 25.76–29.02 dB at 88–89 FPS. Training Time: Training time for the affinity field network ranges from 1.53 to 1.85 minutes across datasets. Total preparation and training time varies by dataset (e.g., 1.38+16.07 minutes for 'five jets' to 15.96+16.92 minutes for 'combustion'). Segmentation Time: Segmentation time ranges from 0.14 to 0.16 seconds across datasets. Memory: Uses a hybrid deformation network with an explicit feature grid, which slightly increases model size compared to D3DGS but reduces memory overhead compared to grid-based methods like DVR. Strengths: Real-time rendering (≥87 FPS), fast segmentation (~0.15s), effective handling of semi-transparent layers and dynamic tracking, no data loading overhead during inference compared to DVR. Limitations: Requires upfront preparation and training time. Slightly larger model size than D3DGS. When to use: Real-time exploratory visualization of dynamic scenes and interactive segmentation and tracking tasks. When not to use: When training time is strictly prohibited and real-time segmentation is not required (SAGD might be preferred for its training-free nature, though it is slower per prompt). VolSegGS was proposed by Yao et al.. It addresses the challenge of segmenting and tracking structures in dynamic volumes, which is more difficult than static segmentation due to the need to maintain consistent labels as features deform, split, and merge. The method sidesteps grid memory constraints by using deformable 3D Gaussians. It is positioned as a solution for real-time exploratory visualization, offering a balance between generation quality, rendering efficiency, and training cost. name: Deformation Network for 4D Gaussian Splatting
head: Deformation
body: The Deformation Network is a neural module used within Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting to predict dynamic 3D Gaussian parameters (means, scales, rotations, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients) from static input features and time. It solves the problem of rendering dynamic scenes by mapping a static Gaussian representation to a time-varying state, enabling the reconstruction of 4D content from multi-view video. It differs from sibling methods like VolSegGS by explicitly modeling temporal deformation via a dedicated time-conditioned MLP rather than static or voxel-based approaches. The method constructs a neural network that takes static Gaussian attributes and a time coordinate as input, applies positional encoding, and passes them through a deformation network to output the dynamic parameters for a specific timestamp. Inputs: point: Static 3D mean position of the Gaussian, shape (N, 3). scales: Static scale parameters, shape (N, 3). rotations: Static rotation parameters (quaternions), shape (N, 4). opacity: Static opacity, shape (N, 1). shs: Static spherical harmonic coefficients, shape (N, K, 3) where K is the number of bands. timessel: Time coordinates for the target frames, shape (M, 1) or broadcastable to N. Outputs: dynamicmeans: Predicted 3D means at time t, shape (N, 3). dynamicscales: Predicted scales at time t, shape (N, 3). dynamicrotations: Predicted rotations at time t, shape (N, 4). dynamicopacity: Predicted opacity at time t, shape (N, 1). dynamicshs: Predicted SH coefficients at time t, shape (N, K, 3). The Deformation class (referred to as self.deformationnet in implementation) contains: 1. self.timenet: A Sequential module consisting of Linear -> ReLU -> Linear. It processes time inputs. 2. self.deformationnet: An instance of the Deformation MLP class. 3. Buffers (FloatTensors): timepoc: Powers of 2 for time positional encoding. pospoc: Powers of 2 for position positional encoding. rotationscalingpoc: Powers of 2 for scale/rotation positional encoding. opacitypoc: Powers of 2 for opacity positional encoding. Positional encoding is applied to inputs using a function pocfre. For an input tensor x and a buffer buffer B (containing powers of 2 from 2^0 to 2^{n-1}): 1. Multiply x by B (broadcasted). 2. Flatten the result. 3. Apply \sin and \cos. 4. Concatenate [x, \sin(x \cdot B), \cos(x \cdot B)] along the last dimension. netwidth: Width of the deformation network layers. timebasepe: Number of frequency bands for time positional encoding. defordepth: Depth of the deformation network. posbasepe: Number of frequency bands for position positional encoding. scalerotationpe: Number of frequency bands for scale/rotation positional encoding. opacitype: Number of frequency bands for opacity positional encoding. timenetwidth: Width of the time network. timenetoutput: Output dimension of the time network. gridpe: Parameter passed to the Deformation class for grid positional encoding. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DeformationNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, netwidth, timebasepe, defordepth, posbasepe, scalerotationpe, opacitype, timenetwidth, timenetoutput, gridpe): super().init() self.netwidth = netwidth self.timebasepe = timebasepe self.defordepth = defordepth self.posbasepe = posbasepe self.scalerotationpe = scalerotationpe self.opacitype = opacitype self.timenetwidth = timenetwidth self.timenetoutput = timenetoutput # Initialize buffers for positional encoding # Powers of 2 from 2^0 to 2^(n-1) self.registerbuffer('timepoc', torch.pow(2, torch.arange(timebasepe).float())) self.registerbuffer('pospoc', torch.pow(2, torch.arange(posbasepe).float())) self.registerbuffer('rotationscalingpoc', torch.pow(2, torch.arange(scalerotationpe).float())) self.registerbuffer('opacitypoc', torch.pow(2, torch.arange(opacitype).float())) # Time network: Linear -> ReLU -> Linear self.timenet = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(1, timenetwidth), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(timenetwidth, timenetoutput)) # Deformation MLP # Input channels: 3 (pos) + 3posbasepe2 (pos PE) + timenetoutput # Note: The source comment suggests inputch = 3 + (3 posbasepe) 2 # However, timessel is also passed. The exact channel count for the first layer # of self.deformationnet depends on how time embedding is concatenated. # Based on "Forward Dynamic Pass", pos, scales, rotations, opacity, shs, timessel are passed. # The Deformation class likely handles the concatenation internally or expects specific inputs. # We assume self.deformationnet is an nn.Module defined elsewhere or here. # For completeness, we define a placeholder structure if not provided, # but the source implies it's a separate class. We will assume it takes the concatenated features. # Initialize weights self.initializeweights() def pocfre(self, x, pocbuf): """ Positional Encoding function. x: input tensor pocbuf: buffer of powers of 2 """ # Multiply input by pocbuf x = x pocbuf # Flatten, sin, cos, concatenate # Assuming x is [..., D], pocbuf is [n] # We need to expand pocbuf to match dimensions for broadcasting # Standard PE: sin(x 2^(i/n)) usually, but here it's powers of 2. # The source says "powers of 2 from 2^0 to 2^(n-1)". # Reshape pocbuf for broadcasting: [1, 1,..., n] pocbuf = pocbuf.view(1, 1, -1) # x shape: [..., D] # We need to apply PE to each dimension of x? # Usually PE is applied per dimension. # Source: "multiplies input by pocbuf... flattens, takes sin and cos, and concatenates [input, sin, cos]" # This implies x is treated as a sequence of scalars or the PE is applied to the whole vector? # Let's assume standard per-dimension PE logic adapted to the buffer. # If x is (N, D), and pocbuf is (n,), we might need to repeat pocbuf for D dimensions? # Or is x flattened first? "flattens" suggests x might be (N, D) -> (ND,). # Let's follow the source literally: xflat = x.view(-1, x.shape[-1]) # Flatten all but last dim? Or all dims? # "multiplies input by pocbuf" -> if x is (N, 3), pocbuf is (n,), result is (N, 3, n)? # Then "flattens" -> (N3n,)? # Then "takes sin and cos" -> (N3n,)? # Then "concatenates [input, sin, cos]" -> This part is ambiguous. # Alternative interpretation: Standard PE where each dim gets encoded. # Let's assume the source implies: # For each dimension d in x: # encodedd = [xd, sin(xd pocbuf), cos(xd pocbuf)] # Concatenate along last dim. # Re-reading: "multiplies input by pocbuf (powers of 2), flattens, takes sin and cos, and concatenates [input, sin, cos] along the last dimension." # This sounds like: # 1. x pocbuf -> shape [..., D, n] if pocbuf is [n] and x is [..., D] # 2. Flatten -> [..., Dn] # 3. sin/cos -> [..., Dn] # 4. Concat [input, sin, cos]? Input was [..., D]. # This seems to imply the input is also expanded or the concatenation is tricky. # Let's stick to the most likely implementation for "pocfre" in this context: # It's a custom PE. # Step 1: Expand pocbuf to match x's last dimension if necessary, or broadcast. # If x is (N, 3) and pocbuf is (n,), x pocbuf is (N, 3, n) if we view pocbuf as (1, 1, n). # But source says "flattens". # Let's implement a robust version based on the description: # x: (N, D) # pocbuf: (n,) # 1. xexpanded = x.unsqueeze(-1) pocbuf.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) -> (N, D, n) # 2. xflat = xexpanded.view(N, -1) -> (N, Dn) # 3. sinvals = torch.sin(xflat) # 4. cosvals = torch.cos(xflat) # 5. Concat [x, sinvals, cosvals]? # x is (N, D). sinvals is (N, Dn). # This doesn't match dimensions for concatenation along last dim unless Dn == D? No. # Correction: Maybe "input" in "concatenates [input, sin, cos]" refers to the original x? # And the result is (N, D + Dn + Dn)? # Let's assume the standard "concatenate along last dim" means: # Output = [x, sin(xPE), cos(xPE)] # But xPE is higher dim. # Let's look at the "Forward Dynamic Pass": # "Encode point using pospoc... Pass these embeddings... to self.deformationnet" # So the output of pocfre is the embedding. # Let's assume the following logic which is common in such repos: # For each feature dimension, apply PE. # Given the ambiguity, we will write the code as described literally, # assuming x is flattened before PE application if "flattens" is a step. # Actually, a common pattern is: # x: (N, D) # freqbands: (n,) # xpe = torch.cat([x, torch.sin(x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands), torch.cos(x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands)], dim=-1) # This results in (N, D + Dn + Dn). # The source says "flattens". This might mean flattening the spatial dims before PE? # Or flattening the result of multiplication? # Let's try: # x: (N, D) # xmul = x.unsqueeze(-1) pocbuf # (N, D, n) # xflat = xmul.view(N, -1) # (N, Dn) # sinx = torch.sin(xflat) # cosx = torch.cos(xflat) # out = torch.cat([x, sinx, cosx], dim=-1) # (N, D + Dn + Dn) # This seems plausible. xmul = x.unsqueeze(-1) pocbuf.view(1, 1, -1) xflat = xmul.view(x.shape[0], -1) sinx = torch.sin(xflat) cosx = torch.cos(xflat) out = torch.cat([x, sinx, cosx], dim=-1) return out def forward(self, point, scales, rotations, opacity, shs, timessel): # 1. Positional Encoding # point: (N, 3) posemb = self.pocfre(point, self.pospoc) # scales: (N, 3), rotations: (N, 4) -> combined? # Source: "scales and rotations using rotationscalingpoc" # Concat scales and rotations? Or encode separately? # "Encode point... scales and rotations... opacity" # Let's assume scales and rotations are concatenated before encoding or encoded separately and concatenated. # Source: "rotationscalingpoc" is one buffer. # Let's concatenate scales and rotations first. scalerot = torch.cat([scales, rotations], dim=-1) # (N, 7) scalerotemb = self.pocfre(scalerot, self.rotationscalingpoc) # opacity: (N, 1) opacityemb = self.pocfre(opacity, self.opacitypoc) # Time encoding # timessel: (M, 1) or (N, 1)? # Source: "timessel" passed to deformationnet. # Also "time output (timenetoutput dims)" is part of input to Deformation class. # So we need to encode time first. # Time network # timessel needs to be (N, 1) to match batch size N if timessel.shape[0] != point.shape[0]: # Broadcast time to N if necessary timessel = timessel.expand(point.shape[0], -1) timeemb = self.timenet(timessel) # (N, timenetoutput) # 2. Forward Dynamic Pass # "Pass these embeddings, along with raw opacity, shs, and timessel to self.deformationnet" # Wait, raw opacity? Or opacityemb? # Source: "Pass these embeddings, along with raw opacity, shs, and timessel" # This is contradictory. "these embeddings" refers to posemb, scalerotemb. # "raw opacity" suggests opacity is NOT embedded? # But earlier it said "opacitypoc" buffer exists. # Let's look at "Deformation Network Input Construction": # "position (3 dims) + position PE (3 posbasepe 2 dims) + time output (timenetoutput dims)" # This suggests the input to the main Deformation MLP is: # [pos, posPE, timeemb] # What about scales, rotations, opacity, shs? # The source says "predicts dynamic 3D Gaussian parameters... from static input points, scales, rotations, opacity, SHs, and time." # And "Forward Dynamic Pass: Encode point... scales and rotations... Pass these embeddings, along with raw opacity, shs, and timessel to self.deformationnet" # This implies self.deformationnet takes: # [posemb, scalerotemb, opacity, shs, timeemb] ? # Let's construct the input tensor. # posemb: (N, 3 + 3posbasepe2) # scalerotemb: (N, 7 + 7scalerotationpe2) ? Or separate? # opacity: (N, 1) # shs: (N, K, 3) -> Flatten to (N, 3K) # timeemb: (N, timenetoutput) # The source comment inputch=(3)+(3(posbasepe))2 is specific to position. # It doesn't mention other channels. # However, the Deformation class must handle all inputs. # Let's assume the Deformation class concatenates all these features. shsflat = shs.view(shs.shape[0], -1) # (N, 3K) # Concatenate all features # Note: The source says "raw opacity". inputfeatures = torch.cat([ posemb, scalerotemb, opacity, shsflat, timeemb ], dim=-1) # Pass to deformation network # self.deformationnet is an nn.Module # It returns the dynamic parameters dynamicparams = self.deformationnet(inputfeatures) # Reshape dynamicparams back to Gaussian parameters # The output structure depends on the Deformation class definition. # Assuming it outputs: means, scales, rotations, opacity, shs # We need to split dynamicparams. # Since the exact split is not given in the source, we assume the Deformation class # returns a tuple or dict. # For pseudocode completeness, we assume a standard split. # Let's assume self.deformationnet returns a tuple: # (means, scales, rotations, opacity, shs) # However, the source doesn't define self.deformationnet's forward return. # We will leave this as a comment. return dynamicparams def initializeweights(self): for m in self.modules(): if isinstance(m, nn.Linear): # Bug: Source says bias is initialized with weight logic # init.xavieruniform(m.weight, gain=1) # init.xavieruniform(m.bias, gain=1) # This is the bug # Correct would be: # nn.init.xavieruniform(m.weight) # nn.init.constant(m.bias, 0) pass Bias Initialization Bug: The initializeweights function in the source code incorrectly initializes the bias of Linear layers using init.xavieruniform(m.weight, gain=1) instead of init.xavieruniform(m.bias, gain=1) or init.constant(m.bias, 0). This applies weight initialization logic to the bias tensor, which is incorrect and may affect convergence. Time Broadcasting: If timessel does not match the batch size N, it must be broadcasted or repeated to match N before passing to the time network. SH Flattening: Spherical Harmonic coefficients must be flattened before concatenation with other features. Time Complexity: Depends on the size of the deformation network and the number of Gaussians N. The positional encoding is O(N \cdot D \cdot n) where D is input dimension and n is PE bands. The MLP forward pass is O(N \cdot L \cdot W^2) where L is depth and W is width. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D{input} + N \cdot D{output}) for storing inputs and outputs. The network weights are constant size. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes effectively by learning temporal deformations. Limitations: Requires training the deformation network, which adds computational overhead compared to static 3DGS. Performance depends on the capacity of the network (width, depth, PE bands). The Deformation Network is part of the 4D Gaussian Splatting method, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes. It was introduced in the unofficial repository ElenaViewSynthesis/4dgs. The method uses a neural network to predict Gaussian parameters over time, allowing for the reconstruction of 4D content.
