name: Cage-based Deformation for 3DGS
head: GSDeformer Deformation Algorithm
body: Cage-based deformation for 3DGS (GSDeformer) is a real-time method that transfers geometric deformation from a proxy point cloud to a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene without retraining. It solves the problem of accurately modeling large bending deformations, which standard mean-only optimization fails to capture, by splitting Gaussians and transforming their covariances. Unlike sibling methods such as Deformation Network for 4D Gaussian Splatting or VolSegGS which optimize existing Gaussians, GSDeformer explicitly subdivides ellipsoids to handle complex curvature. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Source 3DGS scene Ss (set of Gaussians), Source Cage Cs, Target Cage Cd, Split threshold angle t. Output: Deformed 3DGS scene Sd. Data Structures: Gaussian: Defined by mean position \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma (or rotation R and scale S), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{lm}. Cage: A polygonal mesh defining the deformation space. Points-represented ellipsoid (AP): A set of points approximating the Gaussian's ellipsoidal shape. Steps: 1. Proxy Construction: For each Gaussian i in the source scene, generate a points-represented ellipsoid set APs. The source notes reference Equation (4) for this conversion, but do not provide the explicit formula. Typically, this involves sampling points on the surface of the ellipsoid defined by \Sigmai and \mui. 2. Cage-based Deformation: Deform the points APs to APd using the source cage Cs and target cage Cd. Convert Euclidean points APs to cage-based coordinates using EulerToMVC(APs, Cs). Interpolate deformation based on the cage topology (standard cage-based deformation logic). Convert back to Euclidean coordinates using MVCToEuler(AP{mvc}, Cd) to get APd. 3. Splitting: Initialize split sets AP{ss} = [APs] and AP{ds} = [APd]. Call the Split function with threshold t to handle large deformations. The Split function iterates over axes a \in \{x, y, z\} and deformed ellipsoids di \in AP{ds}. For each axis, calculate the angle \alpha formed by the endpoints l, r of the axis and the center c of the ellipsoid (\alpha = \angle l-c-r). If \alpha < t, the ellipsoid is too "flat" or bent to be represented by a single Gaussian. It is split into two ellipsoids, dl and dr. dl center is set to \text{mean}(c, l), and the c-l vector becomes its new axis a. dr center is set to \text{mean}(c, r), and the c-r vector becomes its new axis a. The corresponding source ellipsoids in AP{ss} are also split to maintain correspondence. 4. Gaussian Transformation: For each pair of source ellipsoid si \in AP{ss} and deformed ellipsoid di \in AP{ds}: Compute the affine transform T from si to di using Equation (6). This is typically the least-squares affine transform mapping the point set si to di. Compute translation t = \text{center}(di) - \text{center}(si). Transform the original Gaussian i using Equations (7) and (8). Equation (7) likely updates the mean: \mu' = T\mu + t. Equation (8) likely updates the covariance: \Sigma' = T \Sigma T^T (or similar rotation/scaling update). Append the transformed Gaussian to the result set Sd. Note: Spherical harmonics parameters are copied directly without rotation adjustment. Parameters: t: Split threshold angle. Theoretical analysis suggests k (scaling factor related to splitting) should be 3/1 or similar, but the threshold t controls when splitting occurs. A large k (e.g., 1.0) causes spikes; a small k (e.g., 0.1) causes fragmentation. Pitfalls: Mean-only deformation: Optimizing only the position causes significant striping artifacts. No splitting: Disabling splitting causes spiking artifacts in bent regions because a single Gaussian cannot model the deformation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gsdeformerdeform(gsscene, sourcecage, targetcage, splitthreshold): """ Deforms a 3DGS scene using cage-based deformation. Args: gsscene: List of Gaussian objects. Each has.mu,.cov,.opacity,.sh. sourcecage: Cage mesh for source space. targetcage: Cage mesh for target space. splitthreshold: Angle threshold for splitting ellipsoids. Returns: deformedgsscene: List of deformed Gaussian objects. """ deformedgsscene = [] for gaussian in gsscene: # 1. Convert Gaussian to points-represented ellipsoid # Equation (4) from source. Sample points on ellipsoid surface. aps = pointsfromellipsoid(gaussian.mu, gaussian.cov) # 2. Deform points using cage-based deformation # Convert to cage coordinates apmvc = eulertomvc(aps, sourcecage) # Interpolate deformation (implicit in cage-based def) # Convert back to Euclidean apd = mvctoeuler(apmvc, targetcage) # 3. Perform splitting apss = [aps] apds = [apd] apss, apds = splitfunction(gaussian, apss, apds, splitthreshold) # 4. Transform Gaussians for si, di in zip(apss, apds): # Compute affine transform T from si to di # Equation (6) from source. Compute least-squares affine transform. T = computeaffinetransform(si, di) # Compute translation centersi = meanpoint(si) centerdi = meanpoint(di) tvec = centerdi - centersi # Transform Gaussian # Equations (7) and (8) from source. Update mean and covariance. newmu = T @ gaussian.mu + tvec newcov = T @ gaussian.cov @ T.T # Create new Gaussian newgaussian = Gaussian() newgaussian.mu = newmu newgaussian.cov = newcov newgaussian.opacity = gaussian.opacity # Copy SH without rotation adjustment newgaussian.sh = gaussian.sh deformedgsscene.append(newgaussian) return deformedgsscene def splitfunction(gaussian, apss, apds, threshold): """ Splits ellipsoids if the bending angle is too large. """ newapss = [] newapds = [] for si, di in zip(apss, apds): # Check if splitting is needed # The source iterates over axes and checks angle alpha. # If alpha < threshold, split. # For simplicity, we assume a single split decision per ellipsoid here. # In reality, multiple splits might occur. centerdi = meanpoint(di) # Determine principal axis endpoints l, r from di's covariance l, r = getaxisendpoints(di, gaussian.cov) # Calculate angle alpha alpha = anglebetweenvectors(centerdi - l, centerdi - r) if alpha < threshold: # Split into two # Left ellipsoid dl = copyellipsoid(di) dl.center = meanpoint([centerdi, l]) # Shift points shiftpoints(dl.points, centerdi, dl.center) # Update axis dl.axis = dl.center - l # c-l is new axis? Source says "make c-l dl's new a axis" # Right ellipsoid dr = copyellipsoid(di) dr.center = meanpoint([centerdi, r]) shiftpoints(dr.points, centerdi, dr.center) dr.axis = dr.center - r # Corresponding source splits sl = copyellipsoid(si) sl.center = meanpoint([meanpoint(si), l]) # Approximation shiftpoints(sl.points, meanpoint(si), sl.center) sr = copyellipsoid(si) sr.center = meanpoint([meanpoint(si), r]) shiftpoints(sr.points, meanpoint(si), sr.center) newapss.extend([sl, sr]) newapds.extend([dl, dr]) else: newapss.append(si) newapds.append(di) return newapss, newapds def pointsfromellipsoid(mu, cov): """ Sample points on the ellipsoid defined by mu and cov.""" # Eigen decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) # Sample points on unit sphere # Transform by sqrt(eigenvalues) and eigenvectors # Return set of points pass def eulertomvc(points, cage): """ Convert Euclidean points to Cage-based coordinates.""" # Standard cage-based deformation coordinate conversion pass def mvctoeuler(pointsmvc, cage): """ Convert Cage-based coordinates back to Euclidean.""" # Standard cage-based deformation coordinate conversion pass def computeaffinetransform(sourcepoints, targetpoints): """ Compute affine transform T such that T sourcepoints ≈ targetpoints.""" # Least squares solution pass def meanpoint(points): return np.mean(points, axis=0) def getaxisendpoints(ellipsoidpoints, cov): """ Get endpoints of the principal axis.""" eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) maxidx = np.argmax(eigenvalues) axisvec = eigenvectors[:, maxidx] scale = np.sqrt(eigenvalues[maxidx]) center = meanpoint(ellipsoidpoints) l = center - scale axisvec r = center + scale axisvec return l, r def anglebetweenvectors(v1, v2): v1u = v1 / np.linalg.norm(v1) v2u = v2 / np.linalg.norm(v2) return np.arccos(np.clip(np.dot(v1u, v2u), -1.0, 1.0)) def copyellipsoid(ellipsoid): return Ellipsoid(ellipsoid.points.copy(), ellipsoid.center.copy()) def shiftpoints(points, oldcenter, newcenter): points += (newcenter - oldcenter) Time Complexity: Real-time performance is achieved through extensive caching. AP{mvc} and parts of the transform T can be precomputed. The splitting and transformation steps are linear with respect to the number of Gaussians and split ellipsoids. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the proxy point sets and split ellipsoids temporarily. No additional training data or architectural changes are needed. Strengths: Handles large bending deformations accurately via splitting; works on existing trained vanilla 3DGS without retraining; real-time capable. Limitations: Copies spherical harmonics without rotation adjustment, potentially causing color inaccuracies under rotation; point-based deformation (if used instead of cage) is better for small deformations like facial expressions. When to use: When deforming large, complex shapes with significant bending where mean-only optimization fails. When not to use: For small, local deformations (e.g., facial expressions) where point-based methods might be more efficient, or when high-fidelity viewpoint-dependent color rotation is critical. GSDeformer was introduced by the authors of the paper "GSDeformer: Direct Cage-based Deformation for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It adapts traditional cage-based deformation techniques to the specific data structure of 3DGS. The method addresses limitations in prior works like ARAP-GS and VRGS, which only optimize existing Gaussians and fail to model bending accurately. The cage-building process is inspired by the 3DGS marching cube method proposed in SuGaR. name: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) Parametrization
head: DRK attribute modeling
body: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) parametrization defines the unconstrained learnable parameters for the attributes of 3D Gaussian kernels, ensuring they remain within valid physical ranges through specific activation functions. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a specialized three-step activation for basis angles \thetak to maintain angular separation and monotonicity, and by providing configurable density control thresholds for sparse training scenarios. Inputs: Unconstrained learnable parameters for opacity, scale, rotation, sharpness, blending weight, and basis angles, all initialized in (-\infty, \infty). Outputs: Validated Gaussian attributes ready for rendering. Data Structures: The method operates on the scalar learnable variables associated with each Gaussian kernel. No specific bit-packing is defined in the sources; parameters are treated as floating-point values during optimization. Activation Functions: Each attribute is transformed from its unconstrained space to its valid range using the following functions: 1. Opacity (o): Constrained to (0, 1) using a sigmoid function. o = \sigma(\hat{o}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\hat{o}}} where \hat{o} is the unconstrained parameter. 2. Scale (sk): Activated using an exponential function to ensure positive values. sk = \exp(\hat{s}k) where \hat{s}k is the unconstrained parameter. 3. Rotation (q): Constrained to the unit hypersphere using normalization. q = \frac{\hat{q}}{\|\hat{q}\|} where \hat{q} is the unconstrained 4D quaternion vector. 4. Sharpness (\tau): Bounded within (-0.1, 0.99) using a composite function combining sigmoid and linear remapping. The exact linear remapping coefficients are not specified in the sources. 5. L1&L2 Blending Weight (\eta): Activated using a sigmoid function. \eta = \sigma(\hat{\eta}) where \hat{\eta} is the unconstrained parameter. 6. Basis Angles (\thetak): For K basis angles, a three-step activation process is employed to enforce monotonic increase and minimum angular separation: Step 1: Apply sigmoid to unconstrained angles \hat{\theta}k. Step 2: Add a residual term \frac{1}{K-2} to maintain minimum angular separation. Step 3: Apply cumulative summation to enforce monotonic increase. Step 4: Normalize the resulting angles so that the final angle sK = 2\pi. The residual term \frac{1}{K-2} prevents basis polar angles from exceeding \pi, thereby avoiding degradation in representation. Parameters: K (Number of basis angles): Set to 8 to balance flexibility and memory efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def activateopacity(unconstrainedo): """Constrain opacity to (0, 1).""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-unconstrainedo)) def activatescale(unconstraineds): """Constrain scale to positive values.""" return math.exp(unconstraineds) def activaterotation(unconstrainedq): """Normalize quaternion to unit length.""" norm = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in unconstrainedq)) return [x / norm for x in unconstrainedq] def activatesharpness(unconstrainedtau): """ Bound sharpness within (-0.1, 0.99). Note: Exact linear remapping coefficients are not given in sources. Placeholder for composite sigmoid + linear remapping. """ # Generic sigmoid sig = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-unconstrainedtau)) # Linear remapping from (0,1) to (-0.1, 0.99) # Assuming standard linear mapping: y = min + (max - min) x return -0.1 + (0.99 - (-0.1)) sig def activateblendingweight(unconstrainedeta): """Constrain blending weight to (0, 1).""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-unconstrainedeta)) def activatebasisangles(unconstrainedthetas, K=8): """ Activate basis angles with monotonic increase and minimum separation. Args: unconstrainedthetas: List of K unconstrained float values. K: Number of basis angles (default 8). Returns: List of K normalized angles summing to 2pi. """ # Step 1: Apply sigmoid sigmas = [1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-t)) for t in unconstrainedthetas] # Step 2: Add residual term 1/(K-2) residual = 1.0 / (K - 2) adjusted = [s + residual for s in sigmas] # Step 3: Cumulative summation cumulative = [] currentsum = 0.0 for val in adjusted: currentsum += val cumulative.append(currentsum) # Step 4: Normalize to make sK = 2pi finalsum = cumulative[-1] if finalsum == 0: # Avoid division by zero; return uniform distribution if sum is zero return [2 math.pi / K] K normalized = [val / finalsum (2 math.pi) for val in cumulative] return normalized This variant describes the optimization process for DRK parameters. It follows the adaptive training process of 3D-GS, dynamically adjusting kernel density. Learning Rate: DRK-specific parameters (sharpness \tau, blending weight \eta, basis angles \thetak, and scales sk) use a uniform learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-3}. Decay: The learning rate decays gradually to 1 \times 10^{-2} \times (initial rate) at the end of training (35K steps). Note: The source text "1e-2 ×" is ambiguous regarding the multiplier target; it is cited as written. Density Control: Three configurations are defined by pairs of (2D screen gradient densification threshold, opacity pruning threshold): 1. Comparable to 3D-GS: (5 \times 10^{-4}, 5 \times 10^{-2}) 2. Sparse Level 1 (S1): (1 \times 10^{-3}, 5 \times 10^{-2}) 3. Sparse Level 2 (S2): (2 \times 10^{-3}, 1 \times 10^{-1}) Time and Memory Complexity: The sources do not provide explicit Big-O complexity for the activation functions. The choice of K=8 for basis angles is noted to balance flexibility and memory efficiency. Measured Performance: The method demonstrates robustness under noisy conditions, with rendering results shown for noise standard deviations of 0 and 10^{-3}. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: The residual term in basis angle activation prevents polar angles from exceeding \pi, avoiding representation degradation. The configurable density thresholds allow for controlled sparsity (S1, S2). Limitations: The exact linear remapping formula for sharpness is not provided. The learning rate decay target is ambiguously stated as "1e-2 ×". DRK parametrization is part of the Deformable Radial Kernel Splatting method, introduced in a paper published in 2025. It extends the Gaussian Data Structure by providing specialized parameterizations for dynamic and deformable scenes, building on the foundations of 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: GaussianEditor (Local)
body: GaussianEditor is a method tailored for local editing on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It enables 3D inpainting, object removal, and object composition by controlling 3DGS using text prompts and semantic information derived from Gaussian semantic tracing. Unlike global editing approaches, it focuses on delicately editing within a specific region of interest (RoI) identified in the 3D space. Inputs: A pre-trained 3DGS scene representation. Text instructions or prompts defining the desired edit. Semantic information extracted via Gaussian semantic tracing. Outputs: An edited 3DGS scene with modified attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity) within the target RoI. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS data structure defined in Gaussian Data Structure. The editing process modifies the attributes of the Gaussians falling within the identified RoI. Steps: 1. Extract Region of Interest (RoI): Identify the target area for editing based on the provided text instructions. This involves mapping the semantic intent to a spatial region in the 3D scene. 2. Align RoI with 3D Gaussians: Map the identified text-based RoI to the corresponding 3D Gaussians through the image space. This step ensures that the editing operations are applied to the correct set of Gaussians that project to the target area in the rendered views. 3. Delicate Editing: Modify the attributes of the Gaussians within the identified RoI. This may involve updating positions, scales, rotations, or appearance properties to achieve the desired edit (e.g., inpainting, removal, or composition). The editing is performed delicately to maintain consistency with the surrounding scene. Parameters: Text prompt: Defines the edit content. Semantic tracing parameters: Control the accuracy of the RoI identification. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistency across views: Editing in one view may not align with others if the 3D-to-2D mapping is inaccurate. Boundary artifacts: Sharp transitions between edited and unedited regions may occur if the Gaussian attributes are not smoothly interpolated. An independent research variant of GaussianEditor that operates similarly to the appearance editing version but introduces hierarchical Gaussian splatting (HGS) for adaptive generative guidance. This allows for more refined 3D editing tasks such as object inpainting by leveraging a hierarchical structure to guide the editing process. Efficiency: Achieves higher editing efficiency compared to earlier NeRF-based editing methods. Quality: Provides superior rendering quality for edited regions. Capabilities: Supports complex local edits including inpainting, removal, and composition. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of semantic tracing and text alignment; may struggle with ambiguous prompts or complex geometric changes. GaussianEditor was introduced as part of the latest series of work based on 3DGS, aiming to achieve higher editing efficiency and superior rendering quality compared to previous NeRF-based methods. It was developed to address the need for local, text-guided editing in 3D scenes represented by Gaussian splats. The method has been implemented in variants such as GaussianEditor-iN2N and GaussianEditor-DDS, with GaussianEditor-iN2N showing superior results. name: Gaussian Grouping
body: Gaussian Grouping is a method that enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by incorporating identity encodings for 3D objects, enabling the system to group splats based on their semantic identity. It solves the problem of precise object-level manipulation in 3D scenes, specifically enabling object removal, inpainting, and recomposition. Compared to sibling methods like DFF, Gaussian Grouping removes objects with greatly reduced artifacts and avoids leaving a blurry background. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3DGS scene representation (set of Gaussians) and training images. Output: A 3DGS scene where each Gaussian is associated with an object identity, allowing for grouped editing. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) plus an additional Object ID feature. Object ID: An integer or categorical feature added to each splat. Steps: 1. Initialization: Assign initial object IDs to splats using the method from [38]. 2. Training: Refine object IDs throughout the training process. The training process allows the number of splats assigned to each object to be non-uniform, as object IDs are not constrained during training, enabling the training process to allocate splats dynamically for optimal visual quality. 3. Rendering/Editing: Use the object IDs to group splats for specific operations (e.g., removal, inpainting). Parameters: Object ID: An additional feature added to each splat. Pitfalls: The number of splats assigned to each object is non-uniform because object IDs are not constrained during training. A technique to segment a 3DGS scene into semantically meaningful objects by adding an object ID feature to each splat, allowing for object-level scheduling and editing. Initial object IDs are assigned using the method from [38], and these IDs are refined throughout the training process. The number of splats per object is non-uniform as IDs are unconstrained during training. Strengths: Enables object removal, inpainting, and recomposition. Compared to DFF, it removes objects with greatly reduced artifacts without leaving a blurry background. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Gaussian Grouping [56] enhances 3DGS by incorporating identity encodings for 3D objects. It is cited in surveys on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS. name: Gaussian Data Packing
head: GaussianData::pack
body: Gaussian Data Packing serializes 3D Gaussian Splat attributes into a fixed-width binary buffer to facilitate efficient GPU-side access during rasterization. It differs from sibling methods like SPZ Packed Format by using an interleaved, texture-friendly layout with a fixed width of 8 uint32t per Gaussian, rather than parallel buffers or image-based compression. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z), scale \mathbf{s} = (sx, sy, sz), rotation quaternion \mathbf{q} = (w, x, y, z), and color \mathbf{c} = (r, g, b, a). Outputs: packedData: A std::vector<uint32t> of size N \times 8, storing two uvec4 per Gaussian. worldPositions: A std::vector<float> of size N \times 3, storing raw float positions. Data Structures: For the i-th Gaussian (0 \le i < N), packedData stores 8 uint32t values: indices 0–2 hold the bit-reinterpretations of x, y, z; index 3 is a selection flag set to 0; indices 4–6 hold half-precision packed covariance elements; index 7 holds the packed RGBA color. Steps: 1. Initialize packedData with size 8N and worldPositions with size 3N. 2. Loop over each Gaussian i from 0 to N-1: a. Extract \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{c}. b. Store raw floats in worldPositions: worldPositions[3i] = x, worldPositions[3i+1] = y, worldPositions[3i+2] = z. c. Reinterpret x, y, z as uint32t via std::memcpy (or equivalent bit-cast) and store in packedData[i8+0], packedData[i8+1], packedData[i8+2]. d. Set packedData[i8+3] = 0. e. Convert \mathbf{q} to a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix \mathbf{R}. f. Create a diagonal scale matrix \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz). g. Compute \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S}. h. Compute symmetric covariance elements \sigma{jk}: \sigma{xx} = M{00}^2 + M{10}^2 + M{20}^2 \sigma{xy} = M{00}M{01} + M{10}M{11} + M{20}M{21} \sigma{xz} = M{00}M{02} + M{10}M{12} + M{20}M{22} \sigma{yy} = M{01}^2 + M{11}^2 + M{21}^2 \sigma{yz} = M{01}M{02} + M{11}M{12} + M{21}M{22} \sigma{zz} = M{02}^2 + M{12}^2 + M{22}^2. i. Pack \sigma{xx}, \sigma{xy} into packedData[i8+4], \sigma{xz}, \sigma{yy} into packedData[i8+5], and \sigma{yz}, \sigma{zz} into packedData[i8+6] using packHalf2x16. j. Pack color into packedData[i8+7]: packedColor = (r & 0xFF) | ((g & 0xFF) << 8) | ((b & 0xFF) << 16) | ((a & 0xFF) << 24). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct def packhalf2x16(x: float, y: float) -> int: """Pack two IEEE 754 half-precision floats into a 32-bit integer.""" xbytes = struct.pack('e', x) ybytes = struct.pack('e', y) return struct.unpack('<I', xbytes + ybytes)[0] def gaussiandatapacking(gaussians: list) -> tuple: """ Pack Gaussian data into the specified format. Args: gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'pos' (x,y,z), 'scale' (x,y,z), 'rot' (w,x,y,z), 'color' (r,g,b,a). Returns: packeddata: List of uint32t worldpositions: List of float """ n = len(gaussians) packeddata = [0] (n 8) worldpositions = [0.0] (n 3) for i in range(n): g = gaussians[i] x, y, z = g['pos'] sx, sy, sz = g['scale'] w, qx, qy, qz = g['rot'] r, gc, b, a = g['color'] worldpositions[3i] = x worldpositions[3i+1] = y worldpositions[3i+2] = z packeddata[8i] = struct.unpack('I', struct.pack('f', x))[0] packeddata[8i+1] = struct.unpack('I', struct.pack('f', y))[0] packeddata[8i+2] = struct.unpack('I', struct.pack('f', z))[0] packeddata[8i+3] = 0 # Convert quaternion to rotation matrix R norm = (ww + qxqx + qyqy + qzqz) 0.5 w, qx, qy, qz = w/norm, qx/norm, qy/norm, qz/norm R = [ [1 - 2(qyqy + qzqz), 2(qxqy - wqz), 2(qxqz + wqy)], [2(qxqy + wqz), 1 - 2(qxqx + qzqz), 2(qyqz - wqx)], [2(qxqz - wqy), 2(qyqz + wqx), 1 - 2(qxqx + qyqy)] ] # M = R S M = [ [R[0][0]sx, R[0][1]sy, R[0][2]sz], [R[1][0]sx, R[1][1]sy, R[1][2]sz], [R[2][0]sx, R[2][1]sy, R[2][2]sz] ] sigmaxx = M[0][0]2 + M[1][0]2 + M[2][0]2 sigmaxy = M[0][0]M[0][1] + M[1][0]M[1][1] + M[2][0]M[2][1] sigmaxz = M[0][0]M[0][2] + M[1][0]M[1][2] + M[2][0]M[2][2] sigmayy = M[0][1]2 + M[1][1]2 + M[2][1]2 sigmayz = M[0][1]M[0][2] + M[1][1]M[1][2] + M[2][1]M[2][2] sigmazz = M[0][2]2 + M[1][2]2 + M[2][2]2 packeddata[8i+4] = packhalf2x16(sigmaxx, sigmaxy) packeddata[8i+5] = packhalf2x16(sigmaxz, sigmayy) packeddata[8i+6] = packhalf2x16(sigmayz, sigmazz) packedcolor = (int(r) & 0xFF) | ((int(gc) & 0xFF) << 8) | ((int(b) & 0xFF) << 16) | ((int(a) & 0xFF) << 24) packeddata[8i+7] = packedcolor return packeddata, worldpositions Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion Normalization: The input quaternion must be normalized before matrix conversion to ensure valid rotation. Half-Precision Range: Covariance elements stored as half-floats may underflow for very small values or overflow for very large values. Gaussian Splat Texture Packing stores 3D Gaussian Splat attributes in a 2D OpenGL texture to facilitate efficient GPU-side access during rasterization. It solves the problem of transferring large sets of Gaussian parameters from CPU memory to the GPU by packing 8-byte chunks of Gaussian data into a GLRGBA32UI texture. It differs from sibling methods like SPZ Packed Format by using a specific row-major texture layout with a fixed width of 1024 Gaussians per row, whereas PNG-based Gaussian Compression uses lossy image compression. SPZ Packed Format is a binary storage format for 3D Gaussian splats designed for low-precision, non-interleaved memory layouts with ZSTD compression support. It solves the problem of efficient serialization and transmission of large-scale Gaussian datasets by separating attributes into parallel buffers, allowing for optimized entropy coding (e.g., g-zipping) and variable spherical harmonics (SH) degrees up to 4. It is distinguished from interleaved formats by its parallel vector storage and from PNG-based compression by its native binary structure and ZSTD integration. SPZ Packed Gaussian Unpacking decodes compressed Gaussian Splat attributes (positions, scales, rotations, alphas, colors, and spherical harmonics) from the SPZ file format into floating-point arrays, handling coordinate system conversion and quantization inversion. It differs from sibling methods like PNG-based compression by using a binary layout with ZSTD compression (v4) or gzip (v1-3) and specific fixed-point/quantized encodings for each attribute type. A compression technique for trained 3D Gaussian splats that quantizes parameters to 8-bit or 16-bit and stores them as lossless PNG images, optionally using spatial sorting (Morton code) to improve compression ratios. It serves as a port of the PyTorch gsplat compression module to MLX. It achieves approximately 10x compression on standard 3DGS models. Unlike the PyTorch upstream which uses torchpq for k-means clustering of higher-order spherical harmonics, this method falls back to NPZ for higher-order bands due to library availability constraints. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N) for packedData (8N uint32t) and worldPositions (3N float). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear scaling with the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Compact fixed-width layout, direct GPU memory mapping, simple structure. Limitations: Covariance precision limited to half-float, requires CPU-side matrix computation. When to use: Efficient CPU-to-GPU transfer for rasterization pipelines. When not to use: When disk storage compression or variable-length encoding is required. The method is described in, which implements CPU-side packing of Gaussian attributes for transfer to OpenGL textures. liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Texture Packing
head: 2D Texture Array Packing, RGBA32UI Splat Packing
body: Gaussian Splat Texture Packing is a method for storing 3D Gaussian Splat attributes into a 2D texture array to enable efficient GPU-based rendering and reading. It solves the problem of transferring large volumes of Gaussian data (position, scale, rotation, color, SH coefficients) from CPU memory to the GPU by packing multiple attributes into a single GLRGBA32UI texture. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SPZ Packed Format by using a fixed-width 2048-pixel texture with a specific row-major layout, and from PNG-based Gaussian Compression by using uncompressed 32-bit unsigned integer formats for high precision. Inputs: packedData: A flat array of 8-bit or 32-bit integers containing the packed Gaussian attributes. Each Gaussian i occupies 8 consecutive elements (representing 2 uvec4 values, i.e., 32 bytes or 8 uint32s). splatCount: The total number of Gaussians. Outputs: splatTexture: A 2D texture object (GLuint) containing the packed data. Data Structures: Texture Format: GLRGBA32UI (internal format), GLRGBAINTEGER (type), GLUNSIGNEDINT (data type). Texture Dimensions: Width: 2048 pixels. Height: \lceil \text{splatCount} / 1024 \rceil pixels. Layout: Each Gaussian occupies 2 horizontal columns (2 texels). The x-coordinate (column) for Gaussian i is (i \pmod{1024}) \times 2. The y-coordinate (row) for Gaussian i is \lfloor i / 1024 \rfloor. Each texel stores 4 uint32 values. Gaussian i's first 4 attributes are stored in texel (x, y). Gaussian i's next 4 attributes are stored in texel (x+1, y). Parameters: Texture Filters: GLNEAREST for minification and magnification. Wrap Mode: GLCLAMPTOEDGE for both S and T axes. Steps: 1. Calculate texture width W = 2048. 2. Calculate texture height H = \lceil \text{splatCount} / 1024 \rceil. 3. Create a 2D texture with format GLRGBA32UI, dimensions W \times H, and type GLUNSIGNEDINT. 4. For each Gaussian i from 0 to \text{splatCount} - 1: a. Compute row r = \lfloor i / 1024 \rfloor. b. Compute column index c = (i \pmod{1024}) \times 2. c. Calculate the byte offset for the first texel: \text{idx1} = (r \times W + c) \times 4. d. Calculate the byte offset for the second texel: \text{idx2} = (r \times W + c + 1) \times 4. e. Copy packedData[i8 + 0..3] to textureData[idx1..idx1+3]. f. Copy packedData[i8 + 4..7] to textureData[idx2..idx2+3]. 5. Upload textureData to the GPU texture using glTexSubImage2D or glTexImage2D. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packgaussianstotexture(packeddata: list[int], splatcount: int) -> tuple[int, int, list[int]]: """ Packs Gaussian data into a 2D texture layout. Args: packeddata: List of integers representing packed attributes. Each Gaussian has 8 integers (32 bytes). splatcount: Number of Gaussians. Returns: texturewidth: Width of the texture (2048). textureheight: Height of the texture. texturedata: Flattened list of integers representing the texture data. """ texturewidth = 2048 textureheight = (splatcount + 1023) // 1024 # ceil(splatcount / 1024) # Each texel has 4 uint32 values. Total texels = width height. totaltexels = texturewidth textureheight texturedata = [0] (totaltexels 4) for i in range(splatcount): # Calculate row and column row = i // 1024 col = (i % 1024) 2 # Calculate indices in the flattened texture data array # Each texel is 4 integers idx1 = (row texturewidth + col) 4 idx2 = (row texturewidth + col + 1) 4 # Copy first 4 attributes to first texel for k in range(4): texturedata[idx1 + k] = packeddata[i 8 + k] # Copy next 4 attributes to second texel for k in range(4): texturedata[idx2 + k] = packeddata[i 8 + 4 + k] return texturewidth, textureheight, texturedata Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using GLRGBA32UI ensures no quantization loss for integer-packed attributes. If floating-point attributes are used, GLRGBA32F should be used instead, but the packing logic remains similar. Boundaries: The texture height is calculated using ceiling division to ensure all Gaussians fit. Extra texels at the end of the texture are unused and should be ignored during reading. Alignment: The layout assumes 4-byte alignment for uint32. Ensure the packedData array is properly aligned. Packed Splat Reading is a method to read a single 3D Gaussian Splat from a packed texture representation, decoding its geometric and color properties into a Gsplat struct. It distinguishes itself from extended variants by utilizing a single usampler2DArray texture and a standard unpacking routine for the packed data. This method preprocesses parsed 3D Gaussian splat data into eight separate RGBA32F textures, one for each attribute channel (Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, and three Spherical Harmonics levels), to enable efficient on-demand loading by the Unreal Engine Niagara rendering system. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the creation of uncompressed, high-precision floating-point texture assets rather than byte-level compression or Morton-ordering. A method to assign texture dimensions to 2D Gaussian primitives based on their spatial extent, ensuring uniform texel size in world space and adaptive level-of-detail. It computes a uniform texel size T{size} using a hyperparameter T{total} and the sum of scaled areas of all Gaussians. For each Gaussian i, texture width Ui and height Vi are determined by its scaling factors (su)i and (sv)i: Ui = \lceil 6 \times (su)i / T{size} \rceil Vi = \lceil 6 \times (sv)i / T{size} \rceil where T{size} = T{total} / \sum{i \in N} (36 \times (su)i (sv)i). T{total} is a hyperparameter controlling the total number of texels, typically set to 1 \times 10^7. Time Complexity: Packing is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Reading is O(1) per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: The texture size is 2048 \times \lceil N/1024 \rceil \times 16 bytes (for RGBA32UI). This is approximately 32N bytes, which is efficient compared to storing separate arrays for each attribute. Performance: GPU texture sampling is highly optimized. Using GLNEAREST avoids interpolation overhead. Strengths: Simple layout, efficient GPU access, high precision. Limitations: Fixed width limits the number of Gaussians per row. Not suitable for dynamic resizing without reallocation. Originating from implementations like gsplat-opengl, this method is used in real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting renderers to efficiently manage Gaussian data on the GPU. It is a foundational step for rendering pipelines that require fast access to Gaussian attributes. liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) TexGS-VolVis: Expressive Scene Editing for Volume Visualization via Textured Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3634643, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Packed Splat Reading
head: ReadPackedSplat, readPackedArray
body: Packed Splat Reading is a method to read a single 3D Gaussian Splat from a packed texture representation, decoding its geometric and color properties into a Gsplat struct. It distinguishes itself from extended variants by utilizing a single usampler2DArray texture and a standard unpacking routine for the packed data. Inputs: packedSplats: A struct containing: textureArray: usampler2DArray holding the packed splat data. numSplats: int total number of splats. rgbMinMaxLnScaleMinMax: vec4 parameters used during decoding. lodOpacity: bool flag to adjust alpha for level-of-detail rendering. index: int the index of the splat to read. Outputs: gsplat: A Gsplat struct with the following layout: center: vec3 flags: uint scales: vec3 index: int quaternion: vec4 rgba: vec4 Constants: GSPLATFLAGACTIVE: Defined as 1 << 0. Steps: 1. name: Texture-Based Splat Storage Preprocessing
head: Splat Texture Packing, Niagara Splat Texture Generation
body: This method preprocesses parsed 3D Gaussian splat data into eight separate RGBA32F textures, one for each attribute channel (Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, and three Spherical Harmonics levels), to enable efficient on-demand loading by the Unreal Engine Niagara rendering system. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the creation of uncompressed, high-precision floating-point texture assets rather than byte-level compression or Morton-ordering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of parsed Gaussian splat attributes (Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, SH coefficients) typically derived from PLY or SPZ files. Output: Eight UTexture2D assets (Unreal Engine texture objects), each containing an array of FLinearColor values representing the respective attribute channel. Data Structures: The method organizes data using the FGaussianSplattingTextureData structure, which contains eight fields, each being a dynamic array of FLinearColor (4-component float vector): 1. PositionTextureData: Stores 3D coordinates. 2. ScaleTextureData: Stores scale factors. 3. RotationTextureData: Stores rotation quaternions. 4. ColorTextureData: Stores base color. 5. HarmonicsL1TextureData: Stores Level 1 SH coefficients. 6. HarmonicsL2TextureData: Stores Level 2 SH coefficients. 7. HarmonicsL31TextureData: Stores Level 3 SH coefficients (part 1). 8. HarmonicsL32TextureData: Stores Level 3 SH coefficients (part 2). Steps: 1. Parse and Separate: Extract the attribute values for each of the N splats. Separate these values into eight distinct lists corresponding to the fields in FGaussianSplattingTextureData. 2. Texture Creation: For each attribute channel, create a new UTexture2D asset. 3. Texture Configuration: Set the following properties on the created texture: SRGB: false (linear space). MipGenSettings: TMGSNoMipmaps. Compression: CompressionNone. Filter: TFNearest (point sampling). 4. Format Initialization: Initialize the texture source format to ETextureSourceFormat::TSFRGBA32F (32-bit floating point RGBA). 5. Data Copy: Lock the mip level 0 of the texture. Copy the FLinearColor array for the specific attribute into the locked memory using a memory copy operation (e.g., FMemory::Memcpy). Unlock the mip level. 6. Resource Update: Update the texture resources to make them available to the rendering pipeline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocesssplatstotextures(splats: List[Splat], numsplats: int) -> Dict[str, Texture2D]: """ Preprocesses Gaussian splat data into 8 RGBA32F textures. Args: splats: List of Splat objects with attributes: pos (Vec3), scale (Vec3), rot (Quat), color (Vec3), shl1 (Vec3), shl2 (Vec3), shl31 (Vec3), shl32 (Vec3). numsplats: Total number of splats. Returns: Dictionary mapping attribute names to Texture2D objects. """ textures = {} # Define the attribute channels channels = [ "Position", "Scale", "Rotation", "Color", "HarmonicsL1", "HarmonicsL2", "HarmonicsL31", "HarmonicsL32" ] # Helper to extract a specific attribute from all splats def extractattribute(attrname: str) -> List[FLinearColor]: colors = [] for i in range(numsplats): s = splats[i] # Map attribute name to Splat object field val = getattr(s, attrname) # FLinearColor is a 4-component float vector (RGBA) # For 3-component data (pos, scale, color, SH), W is typically unused or set to 1.0 # For 4-component data (rotation/quaternion), all 4 are used. if attrname == "Rotation": colors.append(FLinearColor(val.x, val.y, val.z, val.w)) else: # Assuming 3D vectors for others, pad with 1.0 or 0.0 as per engine convention # Note: FLinearColor usually expects normalized colors, but here it stores raw floats # due to TSFRGBA32F format. colors.append(FLinearColor(val.x, val.y, val.z, 1.0)) return colors for channel in channels: # 1. Extract data for this channel pixeldata = extractattribute(channel) # 2. Create Texture2D tex = createtexture2d() # 3. Configure Texture tex.srgb = False tex.mipgensettings = TMGSNoMipmaps tex.compression = CompressionNone tex.filter = TFNearest # 4. Initialize Source Format tex.sourceformat = TSFRGBA32F # 5. Lock Mip 0 and Copy Data tex.lockmip(0) memoryptr = tex.getmipdata(0) memcpy(memoryptr, pixeldata, len(pixeldata) sizeof(FLinearColor)) tex.unlockmip(0) # 6. Update Resources tex.updateresources() textures[channel] = tex return textures class FLinearColor: def init(self, r, g, b, a): self.r = r self.g = g self.b = b self.a = a class Splat: def init(self, pos, scale, rot, color, shl1, shl2, shl31, shl32): self.pos = pos self.scale = scale self.rot = rot self.color = color self.shl1 = shl1 self.shl2 = shl2 self.shl31 = shl31 self.shl32 = shl32 class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class Quat: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z self.w = w Parameters: Texture Format: TSFRGBA32F (32-bit floating point per channel). Texture Size: N \times 1 or 1 \times N depending on engine implementation, where N is the number of splats. Filtering: TFNearest (Point sampling). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using RGBA32F ensures high precision for SH coefficients and rotations, avoiding quantization errors present in lower-precision formats. Memory Usage: Storing 8 full-precision textures for millions of splats consumes significant VRAM. For example, 2 million splats require 2 \times 10^6 \times 8 \times 16 bytes \approx 256 MB per texture, totaling ~2 GB for all 8 textures. Transformations: Moving, rotating, or scaling the splat actor in the world is not fully supported and may break rendering, as the textures store static world-space attributes. SH Support: Support for Spherical Harmonics may be limited or incomplete in early versions, requiring careful handling of empty or zeroed SH data. Preprocesses splats by dividing them into fixed-size chunks, computing per-chunk bounding boxes, and normalizing data to [0, 1] for efficient storage in 8 separate RGBA32F textures. Converts raw splat data into a compressed, GPU-ready byte buffer layout using Morton ordering and aggressive quantization (Norm11/16/8) for real-time rendering. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of splats, as each attribute is processed once per splat. Memory Complexity: O(N), with a constant factor of 8 for the 8 separate textures. Each texture stores N FLinearColor (16 bytes) values. Measured Performance: Designed for real-time applications, including VR and interactive walkthroughs, supporting models with up to 2 million splats. Strengths: High precision due to 32-bit floating point format; simple integration with Unreal Engine's Niagara system; on-demand loading reduces initial load times. Limitations: High memory footprint compared to compressed formats; lack of support for dynamic transformations of the splat actor; potential instability with large SH datasets. When to Use: When high precision is required for SH coefficients and rotations, and the target platform has sufficient VRAM. Ideal for static scenes or pre-baked splat data in Unreal Engine. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth or VRAM is constrained, or when dynamic transformations of the splat cloud are required. This method originates from the unreal-splat plugin by JI20, which integrates 3D Gaussian Splatting into Unreal Engine's Niagara VFX pipeline. It was developed to address the need for efficient, high-performance rendering of large-scale Gaussian splat models within the Unreal Engine ecosystem, leveraging the engine's texture system for data storage and retrieval. name: Chunked Bounding Box Computation and Normalization
head: ChunkInfo Generation, Gaussian Splat Chunking
body: This method preprocesses a list of 3D Gaussian splats by dividing them into fixed-size chunks, computing per-chunk bounding boxes for position, scale, color, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, and normalizing the data within each chunk to the range [0, 1]. It builds on Texture-Based Splat Storage Preprocessing by preparing the data for efficient storage in 8 separate RGBA32F textures, ensuring that the normalized values fit within the precision limits of the target texture format while preserving relative differences. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of Gaussian splats (splatData), where each splat contains position (float3), scale (float3), rotation (quaternion), color DC0 (float3), opacity (float), and SH coefficients (sh1 through shF). Output: Normalized splat data and a ChunkInfo structure containing the bounding box bounds for each chunk. Data Structures: ChunkInfo: Contains bounds for each chunk. posX, posY, posZ: Each is a float2 storing (min, max) for the respective axis. sclX, sclY, sclZ: Each is a uint packing two 16-bit floats (f16) representing min and max scale. colR, colG, colB, colA: Each is a uint packing two f16 representing min and max color/opacity. shR, shG, shB: Each is a uint packing two f16 representing min and max SH coefficients for the respective color channel. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize min/max accumulators for position (float3), scale (float3), color (float4, combining dc0.xyz and opacity.w), and SH coefficients (float3, accumulating sh1 through shF) to positive/negative infinity respectively. 2. Calculate the start (splatBegin) and end (splatEnd) indices for the current chunk chunkIdx, clamping to the total splatData.Length. 3. Iterate through each splat i from splatBegin to splatEnd. Apply a power transformation to the scale: s.scale = math.pow(s.scale, 1.0f / 8.0f). Apply a square centered 0-1 normalization to the opacity: s.opacity = GaussianUtils.SquareCentered01(s.opacity). Update chunk min/max bounds for position, scale, color (float4 of dc0.xyz and opacity.w), and SH coefficients (sh1 through shF). Note: SH bounds are updated individually for sh1-shF. 4. Enforce a minimum spread of 1.0e-5f on the max bounds to prevent division by zero during normalization: chunkMaxX = math.max(chunkMaxX, chunkMinX + 1.0e-5f) for pos, scl, col, and shs. 5. Store the computed bounds in a ChunkInfo struct. Position bounds are stored as float2 pairs (min, max) for X, Y, Z. Scale, Color, and SH bounds are packed into 32-bit integers using 16-bit float conversion (math.f32tof16) and bitwise OR/shift operations. 6. Normalize the splat data in place for the current chunk. Position, scale, DC0 color, and opacity are normalized using the formula: (value - min) / (max - min). 7. Normalize SH coefficients (sh1 through shF) using the same min/max bounds computed for SHs: (sh - chunkMinshs) / (chunkMaxshs - chunkMinshs). Parameters: kChunkSize: The number of splats per chunk. The specific value is not defined in the sources, but it is used to calculate splatBegin and splatEnd indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computechunkboundsandnormalize(splatdata, chunksize): chunks = [] numsplats = len(splatdata) for chunkidx in range(0, numsplats, chunksize): splatbegin = chunkidx splatend = min(chunkidx + chunksize, numsplats) # Initialize min/max accumulators posmin = [float('inf')] 3 posmax = [float('-inf')] 3 sclmin = [float('inf')] 3 sclmax = [float('-inf')] 3 colmin = [float('inf')] 4 # RGB + Opacity colmax = [float('-inf')] 4 shmin = [float('inf')] 3 # Assuming 3 SH coefficients per channel for simplicity shmax = [float('-inf')] 3 # Process splats in the chunk for i in range(splatbegin, splatend): s = splatdata[i] # Apply power transformation to scale s.scale = [math.pow(val, 1.0/8.0) for val in s.scale] # Apply square centered 0-1 normalization to opacity s.opacity = squarecentered01(s.opacity) # Update position bounds for axis in range(3): posmin[axis] = min(posmin[axis], s.position[axis]) posmax[axis] = max(posmax[axis], s.position[axis]) # Update scale bounds for axis in range(3): sclmin[axis] = min(sclmin[axis], s.scale[axis]) sclmax[axis] = max(sclmax[axis], s.scale[axis]) # Update color bounds (RGB + Opacity) colmin[0] = min(colmin[0], s.color[0]) colmax[0] = max(colmax[0], s.color[0]) colmin[1] = min(colmin[1], s.color[1]) colmax[1] = max(colmax[1], s.color[1]) colmin[2] = min(colmin[2], s.color[2]) colmax[2] = max(colmax[2], s.color[2]) colmin[3] = min(colmin[3], s.opacity) colmax[3] = max(colmax[3], s.opacity) # Update SH bounds (example for 3 coefficients) for axis in range(3): shmin[axis] = min(shmin[axis], s.sh[axis]) shmax[axis] = max(shmax[axis], s.sh[axis]) # Enforce minimum spread minspread = 1.0e-5 for axis in range(3): posmax[axis] = max(posmax[axis], posmin[axis] + minspread) sclmax[axis] = max(sclmax[axis], sclmin[axis] + minspread) colmax[axis] = max(colmax[axis], colmin[axis] + minspread) shmax[axis] = max(shmax[axis], shmin[axis] + minspread) # Handle opacity separately if needed colmax[3] = max(colmax[3], colmin[3] + minspread) # Store bounds in ChunkInfo chunkinfo = ChunkInfo() chunkinfo.posX = (posmin[0], posmax[0]) chunkinfo.posY = (posmin[1], posmax[1]) chunkinfo.posZ = (posmin[2], posmax[2]) chunkinfo.sclX = packf16pair(sclmin[0], sclmax[0]) chunkinfo.sclY = packf16pair(sclmin[1], sclmax[1]) chunkinfo.sclZ = packf16pair(sclmin[2], sclmax[2]) chunkinfo.colR = packf16pair(colmin[0], colmax[0]) chunkinfo.colG = packf16pair(colmin[1], colmax[1]) chunkinfo.colB = packf16pair(colmin[2], colmax[2]) chunkinfo.colA = packf16pair(colmin[3], colmax[3]) chunkinfo.shR = packf16pair(shmin[0], shmax[0]) chunkinfo.shG = packf16pair(shmin[1], shmax[1]) chunkinfo.shB = packf16pair(shmin[2], shmax[2]) chunks.append(chunkinfo) # Normalize splat data in place for i in range(splatbegin, splatend): s = splatdata[i] # Normalize position for axis in range(3): s.position[axis] = (s.position[axis] - posmin[axis]) / (posmax[axis] - posmin[axis]) # Normalize scale for axis in range(3): s.scale[axis] = (s.scale[axis] - sclmin[axis]) / (sclmax[axis] - sclmin[axis]) # Normalize color and opacity s.color[0] = (s.color[0] - colmin[0]) / (colmax[0] - colmin[0]) s.color[1] = (s.color[1] - colmin[1]) / (colmax[1] - colmin[1]) s.color[2] = (s.color[2] - colmin[2]) / (colmax[2] - colmin[2]) s.opacity = (s.opacity - colmin[3]) / (colmax[3] - colmin[3]) # Normalize SH coefficients for axis in range(3): s.sh[axis] = (s.sh[axis] - shmin[axis]) / (shmax[axis] - shmin[axis]) return chunks def squarecentered01(opacity): # Placeholder for GaussianUtils.SquareCentered01 # Assuming it maps opacity to [0, 1] range return max(0.0, min(1.0, opacity)) def packf16pair(minval, maxval): # Convert f32 to f16 and pack into uint minf16 = f32tof16(minval) maxf16 = f32tof16(maxval) return (minf16 << 16) | maxf16 def f32tof16(val): # Placeholder for math.f32tof16 # Convert float32 to float16 representation import struct return struct.unpack('<H', struct.pack('<f', val))[0] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Enforcing a minimum spread of 1.0e-5f prevents division by zero when min and max bounds are equal. Precision Loss: Using 16-bit floats for packing bounds may introduce precision loss, especially for large ranges. Degenerate Input: If a chunk contains only one splat, the min and max bounds will be identical, requiring the minimum spread enforcement. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of splats, as each splat is processed once per chunk. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the normalized splat data and chunk info. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of splats. Strengths: Efficient preprocessing for texture-based storage, ensures data fits within precision limits. Limitations: Precision loss due to 16-bit float packing, potential division by zero if not handled. When to Use: When preparing Gaussian splat data for texture-based rendering pipelines. When Not to Use: When high precision is required for scale or SH coefficients. This method is part of the preprocessing pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically for optimizing data storage and rendering performance in real-time applications. It was developed as part of the World Labs Unity project, which aims to integrate Gaussian Splatting into game engines. nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, https://github.com/nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Data Packing and Compression
head: Gaussian Splat Encoding, Runtime Splat Processing, SPZ Processing
body: This method converts raw Gaussian splat data (typically from SPZ or PLY files) into a compressed, GPU-ready byte buffer layout optimized for real-time rendering. It solves the problem of high memory bandwidth and storage costs associated with storing full-precision floating-point attributes for millions of splats. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by integrating Morton space-filling curve reordering for cache coherence with aggressive per-attribute quantization (Norm11, Norm16, Norm8) and chunk-based storage for spherical harmonics, all implemented in a Burst-compiled, runtime-safe manner. Inputs: Raw splat data array (NativeArray<InputSplatData>), containing position, scale, rotation, color, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Format specifications for each attribute: posFormat, scaleFormat, colorFormat, shFormat. Outputs: Compressed GPU-ready byte buffers stored in RuntimeSplatData. Reordered splat indices based on Morton codes. Data Structures: 1. InputSplatData: The raw input structure. Fields are not explicitly detailed in the source, but implied to contain float3 position, float3 scale, float4 color, and SH coefficients. 2. GaussianSplatAsset.ChunkInfo: Used when SH data is not stored in full float32. Fields are not explicitly detailed, but used to define chunk boundaries for SH data. 3. ReorderMortonJob: A job struct for parallel Morton reordering. const float kScaler = (1<<21)-1 float3 mBoundsMin float3 mInvBoundsSize ReadOnly NativeArray<InputSplatData> mSplatData NativeArray<(ulong, int)> mOrder (stores Morton code and original index) 4. CalcChunkDataJob: A job struct for computing SH chunks. NativeArray<InputSplatData> splatData NativeArray<GaussianSplatAsset.ChunkInfo> chunks Parameters (Defaults): posFormat: GaussianSplatAsset.VectorFormat.Norm11 scaleFormat: GaussianSplatAsset.VectorFormat.Norm11 colorFormat: GaussianSplatAsset.ColorFormat.Norm8x4 shFormat: GaussianSplatAsset.SHFormat.Norm6 Steps: 1. Input Validation: Check if the input splat array is empty. If empty, throw ArgumentException. 2. Scene Bounds Calculation: Iterate through all splats to find the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Initialize bMin to positive infinity and bMax to negative infinity. For each splat position p: bMin = min(bMin, p) bMax = max(bMax, p) 3. Morton Reordering: Calculate inverse bounds size: invSize = 1.0f / (bMax - bMin). For each splat, normalize position to [0, 1]: pos{norm} = (p - bMin) \times invSize Scale to integer range for Morton encoding: ipos = \text{cast\to\uint3}(pos{norm} \times kScaler) where kScaler = (1 \ll 21) - 1. Generate Morton code: code = \text{MortonEncode3}(ipos). Sort splats by code. Reorder the InputSplatData array according to the sorted order. 4. Chunk Data Creation (Conditional): If any format is not full float32 (posFormat != Float32 OR scaleFormat != Float32 OR colorFormat != Float32x4 OR shFormat != Float32), call CreateChunkData. This step likely groups splats into chunks for efficient SH storage, ensuring chunk bounds are clamped to splatData.Length to avoid out-of-bounds access. 5. Position Encoding: Call CreatePositionsData with the reordered splats and posFormat. If posFormat is Norm11: enc = (v.x \times 2047.5f) \mid (v.y \times 1023.5f \ll 11) \mid (v.z \times 2047.5f \ll 21) Stored as 4 bytes (uint). If posFormat is Norm16: enc = (v.x \times 65535.5f) \mid (v.y \times 65535.5f \ll 16) \mid (v.z \times 65535.5f \ll 32) Stored as 4 bytes (uint) + 2 bytes (ushort). 6. Scale and SH Index Encoding: Call CreateOtherData with splats, scaleFormat, and splatSHIndices. Scale encoding follows similar quantization rules as position based on scaleFormat (default Norm11). 7. Color Encoding: Call CreateColorData with splats. Default format Norm8x4 implies 8-bit per channel quantization for RGBA. 8. SH Data Encoding: Call CreateSHData with splats, shFormat, and clusteredSHs. Default format Norm6 implies 6-bit quantization for SH coefficients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packgaussiansplats(splatdata: List[Splat], posformat: str = "Norm11", scaleformat: str = "Norm11", colorformat: str = "Norm8x4", shformat: str = "Norm6") -> RuntimeSplatData: if not splatdata: raise ArgumentException("Input splat array is empty") # Step 2: Calculate bounds bmin = float3(inf, inf, inf) bmax = float3(-inf, -inf, -inf) for splat in splatdata: bmin = min(bmin, splat.position) bmax = max(bmax, splat.position) invboundssize = 1.0 / (bmax - bmin) kscaler = (1 << 21) - 1 # Step 3: Morton Reordering indexedsplats = [] for i, splat in enumerate(splatdata): posnorm = (splat.position - bmin) invboundssize ipos = uint3(posnorm kscaler) mortoncode = mortonencode3(ipos) indexedsplats.append((mortoncode, i)) indexedsplats.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) reorderedsplatdata = [splatdata[idx] for, idx in indexedsplats] # Step 4: Chunk Data (if needed) needschunks = (posformat != "Float32" or scaleformat != "Float32" or colorformat != "Float32x4" or shformat != "Float32") chunks = [] if needschunks: chunks = createchunkdata(reorderedsplatdata) # Ensure chunk bounds are clamped to splatdata.Length for chunk in chunks: chunk.end = min(chunk.end, len(reorderedsplatdata)) # Step 5: Encode Positions posbuffer = bytearray() for splat in reorderedsplatdata: if posformat == "Norm11": enc = (splat.position.x 2047.5) | \ (splat.position.y 1023.5 << 11) | \ (splat.position.z 2047.5 << 21) posbuffer += enc.tobytes(4, byteorder='little') elif posformat == "Norm16": enc = (splat.position.x 65535.5) | \ (splat.position.y 65535.5 << 16) | \ (splat.position.z 65535.5 << 32) # Stored as 4 bytes uint + 2 bytes ushort posbuffer += (enc & 0xFFFFFFFF).tobytes(4, byteorder='little') posbuffer += ((enc >> 32) & 0xFFFF).tobytes(2, byteorder='little') else: # Handle other formats or default to Float32 if not specified pass # Step 6: Encode Scale and SH Indices scalebuffer = bytearray() shindicesbuffer = bytearray() for splat in reorderedsplatdata: # Scale encoding similar to position based on scaleformat if scaleformat == "Norm11": enc = (splat.scale.x 2047.5) | \ (splat.scale.y 1023.5 << 11) | \ (splat.scale.z 2047.5 << 21) scalebuffer += enc.tobytes(4, byteorder='little') # SH indices are stored separately shindicesbuffer += splat.shindex.tobytes(4, byteorder='little') # Step 7: Encode Color colorbuffer = bytearray() for splat in reorderedsplatdata: if colorformat == "Norm8x4": # 8-bit per channel RGBA r = int(splat.color.r 255) g = int(splat.color.g 255) b = int(splat.color.b 255) a = int(splat.color.a 255) colorbuffer += bytes([r, g, b, a]) # Step 8: Encode SH Data shbuffer = bytearray() for splat in reorderedsplatdata: if shformat == "Norm6": # 6-bit quantization for SH coefficients # Implementation details for Norm6 quantization are not fully specified in sources # Assuming standard quantization: coeff (2^5 - 1) for coeff in splat.shcoefficients: q = int(coeff 31.5) shbuffer += q.tobytes(1, byteorder='little') # Simplified, actual packing may vary return RuntimeSplatData(posbuffer, scalebuffer, shindicesbuffer, colorbuffer, shbuffer, chunks) Time Complexity: Dominated by the Morton sort, which is O(N \log N) where N is the number of splats. Bounds calculation is O(N). Encoding is O(N). Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to raw float32 storage. Position and scale drop from 12 bytes each to 4 bytes (Norm11) or 6 bytes (Norm16). Color drops from 16 bytes to 4 bytes (Norm8x4). SH data is heavily compressed via quantization and chunking. Performance: The method is designed for runtime execution using Burst compilation, ensuring zero Editor dependencies and safe usage in builds. Strengths: High compression ratio, cache-friendly ordering via Morton codes, runtime-safe. Limitations: Quantization introduces precision loss. Morton reordering requires sorting, which can be costly for very large datasets if not parallelized effectively. Empty input arrays cause exceptions. This method is part of the WorldLabs Unity integration package, specifically designed for processing SPZ (Splat Zone) files generated by WorldLabs' AI world generation API. It enables efficient runtime rendering of Gaussian Splat scenes in Unity, particularly for VR and mobile platforms. The approach reflects the broader trend in 3D Gaussian Splatting towards optimizing data layouts for real-time rendering engines. nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, https://github.com/nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SPZ Packed Format
head: NGSP, Niantic Gaussian Packed
body: SPZ Packed Format is a binary storage format for 3D Gaussian splats designed for low-precision, non-interleaved memory layouts with ZSTD compression support. It solves the problem of efficient serialization and transmission of large-scale Gaussian datasets by separating attributes into parallel buffers, allowing for optimized entropy coding (e.g., g-zipping) and variable spherical harmonics (SH) degrees up to 4. It is distinguished from interleaved formats by its parallel vector storage and from PNG-based Gaussian Compression by its native binary structure and ZSTD integration. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, scale, rotation (quaternion), opacity (alpha), base color, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Outputs: A binary file stream starting with a header, followed by compressed attribute buffers. Data Structures: The format is identified by the magic number 0x5053474e (ASCII "SPZN"). 1. Header (PackedGaussians): version (uint32t): Format version. Default is LATESTSPZHEADERVERSION (4). numPoints (int32t): Total number of Gaussians. shDegree (int32t): Degree of spherical harmonics. fractionalBits (int32t): Precision bits for fixed-point representations. antialiased (bool): Flag indicating antialiasing usage. usesQuaternionSmallestThree (bool): Default true. Indicates if SmallestThree quaternion encoding is used. hadSkippedExtensions (bool): Flag for extension handling. Note: In implementations supporting extensions, a conditional field std::vector<SpzExtensionBasePtr> extensions may be present, compiled only when SPZBUILDEXTENSIONS is defined. 2. Attribute Buffers: Data is stored in separate std::vector<uint8t> buffers for: positions, scales, rotations, alphas, colors, and sh. 3. Single Gaussian View (PackedGaussian): For indexing, a single Gaussian is viewed as a struct of 92 bytes (for SH degree 4): position: std::array<uint8t, 9> (3 components, 3 bytes each). rotation: std::array<uint8t, 4> (4 components, 1 byte each). scale: std::array<uint8t, 3> (3 components, 1 byte each). color: std::array<uint8t, 3> (RGB, 1 byte each). alpha: uint8t. shR, shG, shB: std::array<uint8t, 24> each (24 coefficients for degree 4). Decoding Steps: 1. Read Header: Parse the first 24+ bytes to determine version, numPoints, shDegree, and flags. 2. Decompress Buffers: If version >= MINZSTDSPZHEADERVERSION (4), decompress the attribute buffers using ZSTD. 3. Decode Attributes: Iterate through each Gaussian index i from 0 to numPoints - 1. 3a. Position, Scale, Color, Alpha: These are stored as quantized uint8 values. The specific quantization depends on fractionalBits and implementation details not fully specified in the core notes. 3b. Rotation (Quaternion): The encoding method depends on usesQuaternionSmallestThree and version. SmallestThree (Default for Version 3+): 1. Pack 4 bytes into uint32t comp. 2. Extract ilargest = comp >> 30. 3. Initialize sumsquares = 0.0f. 4. Loop i from 3 down to 0: If i != ilargest: Extract mag = comp & 0x1FF. Extract negbit = (comp >> 9) & 1. Shift comp right by 10 bits. Calculate rotation[i] = sqrt(0.5f) mag / 511.0f. If negbit is 1, rotation[i] = -rotation[i]. sumsquares += rotation[i] rotation[i]. 5. Calculate rotation[ilargest] = sqrt(max(0.0f, 1.0f - sumsquares)). 6. Apply c.flipQ to the first 3 components of the rotation vector. 7. If c.rotFlipQFunc exists, call it. FirstThree (Legacy): 1. Convert the first 3 uint8s to floats. 2. Scale by 1/127.5. 3. Subtract 1. 4. Multiply by c.flipQ. 5. Copy to rotation[0..2]. 6. Calculate rotation[3] = sqrt(max(0.0f, 1.0f - (rotation[0]^2 + rotation[1]^2 + rotation[2]^2))). 7. If c.rotFlipQFunc exists, call it. 3c. Spherical Harmonics (SH): 1. Read SHMAXCOEFFS (24 for degree 4) uint8 values for each R, G, B channel. 2. Unquantize each coefficient x using: v = \frac{x - 128.0}{128.0} where x is the uint8 value. 3d. Alpha and Color: 1. Alpha is a uint8 representing opacity. 2. Color is unquantized from uint8 to [0, 1] range. 3. Apply base color scale factor: C{base} = C{raw} \times 0.15 (instead of 0.282) to allow out-of-range base colors that higher SH bands can correct. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodegaussian(data, version, usessmallestthree, flipq, rotflipqfunc): # data is a flat byte buffer for one Gaussian # Position, scale, color, alpha quantization depends on fractionalBits (not given in sources) pos = [float(b) for b in data[0:9]] scale = [float(b) for b in data[9:12]] color = [float(b) for b in data[12:15]] alpha = data[15] sh = data[16:16 + 72] # 24 coeffs 3 channels rotation = [0.0] 4 if usessmallestthree and version >= 3: comp = int.frombytes(data[9:13], byteorder='little') ilargest = comp >> 30 sumsquares = 0.0 for i in range(3, -1, -1): if i != ilargest: mag = comp & 0x1FF negbit = (comp >> 9) & 1 comp >>= 10 rotation[i] = (0.5 0.5) mag / 511.0 if negbit: rotation[i] = -rotation[i] sumsquares += rotation[i] 2 rotation[ilargest] = max(0.0, 1.0 - sumsquares) 0.5 else: x, y, z = [float(b) / 127.5 - 1.0 for b in data[9:12]] rotation[0] = x flipq rotation[1] = y flipq rotation[2] = z flipq rotation[3] = max(0.0, 1.0 - (rotation[0]2 + rotation[1]2 + rotation[2]2)) 0.5 rotation[0] = flipq rotation[1] = flipq rotation[2] = flipq if rotflipqfunc: rotflipqfunc(rotation) # SH unquantization shfloats = [(b - 128.0) / 128.0 for b in sh] # Color scaling color = [c 0.15 for c in color] return pos, scale, rotation, alpha, color, shfloats Formulas: SH unquantization: v = \frac{x - 128.0}{128.0} where x is the uint8 value. Inverse sigmoid: v = \ln\left(\frac{x}{1 - x}\right). Color scale factor: C{base} = C{raw} \times 0.15 (instead of 0.282) to allow out-of-range base colors that higher SH bands can correct. Parameters: SHMAXCOEFFS: 24 (for degree 4). DEFAULTSH1BITS: 5 (bits for first SH coefficient). DEFAULTSHRESTBITS: 4 (bits for remaining SH coefficients). LATESTSPZHEADERVERSION: 4. MINZSTDSPZHEADERVERSION: 4. MINSMALLESTTHREEQUATERNIONSVERSION: 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion Reconstruction: If numerical error causes 1 - \sum{i=0}^{2} ri^2 < 0, std::max(0.0f,...) ensures the sqrt argument is non-negative. WASM Memory View: In JavaScript/WebAssembly implementations, the callback must consume the chunk immediately because the typed memory view detaches if any subsequent WASM allocation grows the heap. Version Compatibility: Decoders must check version to determine if ZSTD is used (>=4) and which quaternion encoding is active (>=3 uses SmallestThree). A variant configuration focusing on the packing options for SH coefficients. It uses PackOptions::sh1Bits (defaulting to DEFAULTSH1BITS=5) and PackOptions::shRestBits (defaulting to DEFAULTSHRESTBITS=4) to specify quantization bit depths for SH degree 1 and degree 2+ coefficients respectively. This reduces entropy for g-zipping during the packing phase. Time Complexity: Decompression is linear in the number of bytes, dominated by ZSTD decompression and per-Gaussian decoding. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of Gaussians. Performance: ZSTD compression provides significant size reduction, especially for correlated Gaussian data. SmallestThree quaternion encoding offers better precision for small components compared to FirstThree, at the cost of slightly more complex decoding logic. Strengths: Low precision storage, efficient compression, support for high-degree SH, flexible extension system. Limitations: Requires custom decoder; non-interleaved layout may be less convenient for some rendering pipelines that expect interleaved data; WASM memory management requires careful handling. SPZ Packed Format was developed by Niantic Labs as part of their open-source SPZ library for efficient storage and transmission of 3D Gaussian Splatting data. It evolved to support higher precision requirements (SmallestThree quaternions) and compression (ZSTD) in later versions. The format is used in Niantic's AR/VR applications and open-source 3D Gaussian Splatting toolchains. nianticlabs/spz, https://github.com/nianticlabs/spz, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SPZ v4 Format Parsing
head: SPZ format decoder, SPZ v4, SPZ v4 Reader, ZSTD streams in KMP splat parser, compressed capture reader, parseSplatSpz
body: SPZ v4 format parsing is the method for decoding binary SPZ v4 files containing compressed 3D Gaussian splat data into a usable SplatCloud structure. It solves the problem of loading high-fidelity Gaussian splat captures in environments lacking native system-level decompression libraries, such as web browsers. It is distinguished from earlier SPZ versions (1–3) by using ZSTD compression per attribute instead of a single gzip stream, and from generic PLY parsers by its specific handling of quantized fields and coordinate system transformations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary file with the.spz extension. The file must start with the magic number 0x5053474e (ASCII "SPZN"). Output: A SplatCloud object containing decoded Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, color, spherical harmonics). The output coordinate system is either the file's native "Right-Up-Back" (RUB) or a requested "Right-Down-Front" (RDF) compatible with PLY standards. Data Structures: The SPZ v4 format stores attributes in separate ZSTD-compressed streams. The parser must maintain a buffer for each attribute stream. Quantized fields (e.g., positions, SH coefficients) are stored as integers and require specific scaling constants to be converted to floating-point values. These constants are provided by the reference library. Numbered Steps: 1. Header Validation: Read the first 4 bytes. Verify they equal 0x5053474e. If not, abort. 2. Version Detection: Determine the SPZ version. For v4, proceed to step 3. (For v1–3, use gzip decompression). 3. Stream Initialization: Identify the number of attribute streams defined in the header. Initialize a ZSTD decompressor instance for each stream. The KTX2 ZSTD decoder is recommended for web compatibility. 4. Decompression: For each attribute stream: a. Read the compressed data block. b. Decompress using the ZSTD decoder to obtain raw quantized bytes. 5. Quantization Decoding: For each quantized field: a. Read the quantization parameters (offset, scale, bits) from the reference library constants. b. Convert integer values to float: v{float} = (v{int} - offset) \times scale. 6. Coordinate System Handling: a. By default, return the cloud in the file's native Right-Up-Back (RUB) axes. b. If a PLY coordinate system is requested: i. Transform axes from RUB to Right-Down-Front (RDF). This typically involves flipping the Y and Z axes. ii. Flip the signs of the spherical harmonics coefficients to match the coordinate change. 7. Validation: Compare decoded reference positions against expected values using a relative tolerance to account for precision differences inherent in the quantization process. 8. Extension Check: If the file name includes an extension indicating a coordinate axis move, refuse to parse the file by name rather than rendering it mirrored, to prevent incorrect coordinate mapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parsespzv4(filepath: str, requestplycoords: bool = False) -> SplatCloud: # 1. Header Validation with open(filepath, 'rb') as f: magic = f.read(4) if magic != b'SPZN': raise ValueError("Invalid SPZ magic number") # 2. Version Detection (Assumed v4 based on context) # Read header to determine attribute count and stream sizes header = parsespzheader(f) # 3. Stream Initialization # Initialize ZSTD decoders for each attribute stream # Using KTX2 ZSTD decoder for web compatibility decoders = [ZstdDecoder() for in header.attributestreams] splatcloud = SplatCloud() # 4. Decompression for i, streaminfo in enumerate(header.attributestreams): f.seek(streaminfo.offset) compresseddata = f.read(streaminfo.size) rawbytes = decoders[i].decompress(compresseddata) # 5. Quantization Decoding # Use reference library constants for quantization params quantparams = getquantizationparams(streaminfo.attributename) if streaminfo.attributename == 'position': # Decode positions positions = decodequantizedfield(rawbytes, quantparams) splatcloud.positions = positions elif streaminfo.attributename == 'sh': # Decode Spherical Harmonics shcoeffs = decodequantizedfield(rawbytes, quantparams) splatcloud.shcoeffs = shcoeffs #... handle other attributes (covariance, opacity, etc.) # 6. Coordinate System Handling if requestplycoords: # Transform from Right-Up-Back (RUB) to Right-Down-Front (RDF) # Flip Y and Z axes splatcloud.positions[:, 1] = -1 splatcloud.positions[:, 2] = -1 # Flip signs of spherical harmonics to match coordinate change splatcloud.shcoeffs = flipshsigns(splatcloud.shcoeffs) # 7. Validation # Compare with reference positions using relative tolerance validatepositions(splatcloud.positions, relativetolerance=1e-5) # 8. Extension Check # If file name indicates axis move, refuse if hasaxismoveextension(filepath): raise ValueError("File with axis-move extension refused by name") return splatcloud def decodequantizedfield(rawbytes: bytes, params: QuantParams) -> np.ndarray: # Convert quantized integers to float using reference constants # vfloat = (vint - offset) scale ints = np.frombuffer(rawbytes, dtype=params.dtype) return (ints - params.offset) params.scale Parameters: relativetolerance: Used for position validation. Value not explicitly given, but "relative tolerance" is required. requestplycoords: Boolean flag. Default False (returns RUB). If True, returns RDF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: SPZ v4 reference positions must be compared with a relative tolerance due to quantization precision differences. Coordinate Mapping: Files with extensions indicating axis moves are refused by name, not rendered mirrored, to prevent incorrect mapping. Web Compatibility: Native system decoders are not required; the parser must use web-compatible ZSTD (e.g., KTX2). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of splats and attributes, dominated by ZSTD decompression. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the decompressed SplatCloud. Strengths: Enables web-compatible decoding without native system libraries. Supports high-fidelity data with SH degree 4. Limitations: Requires ZSTD implementation. Coordinate system conversion is non-trivial for SH coefficients. When to use: When loading SPZ v4 files in web environments or when PLY coordinate compatibility is required. When not to use: When native gzip decompression is sufficient (SPZ v1–3) or when coordinate system conversion is not needed and RUB is acceptable. The SPZ format was developed to provide a compressed, efficient storage format for 3D Gaussian splats. SPZ v4 specifically introduces ZSTD compression per attribute, improving compression ratios and enabling web-based parsing. The parser is implemented in the flutter3d package to enable web-compatible SPZ decoding. The format is identified by the magic number 0x5053474e.
