body: SPZ Packed Gaussian Unpacking deserializes compressed Gaussian Splatting data from the SPZ file format into raw floating-point arrays for positions, scales, rotations, alphas, colors, and spherical harmonics. It solves the problem of efficiently loading large-scale 3D Gaussian fields from disk by inverting the quantization, coordinate system conversions, and compression applied during packing. Unlike sibling methods that may use texture atlases or PNG-based storage, this method operates on a contiguous binary stream with a defined header and sequential data sections, supporting both legacy gzip-compressed single-stream formats (v1–v3) and modern ZSTD-compressed multi-stream formats (v4). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A byte buffer containing the SPZ file data. Output: A structured object containing raw float values for positions (numPoints 3), scales (numPoints 3), rotations (numPoints 4), alphas (numPoints), colors (numPoints 3), and spherical harmonics (numPoints shDim 3). Data Structures: The file begins with a header. The layout depends on the version. Legacy Header (v1–v3, 16 bytes, little-endian): magic (Uint32, offset 0): Must equal SPZMAGIC. version (Uint32, offset 4): 1 or 2 (v3 is also handled by this path). numPoints (Uint32, offset 8): Number of Gaussians. shDegree (Uint8, offset 12): Spherical Harmonics degree (0–3). fractionalBits (Uint8, offset 13): Precision for fixed-point positions. flags (Uint8, offset 14): Compression flags. reserved (Uint8, offset 15): Padding. Modern Header (v4, 32 bytes): NgspFileHeader struct containing magic, version, numPoints, shDegree, fractionalBits, flags, numStreams, tocByteOffset, and reserved[12]. If flags & 0x2, Extension ILV records follow the header. A Table of Contents (TOC) follows, consisting of numPoints entries of 16 bytes each (compressed size u64, uncompressed size u64). Attribute streams follow the TOC, each ZSTD-compressed. Parameters: MAXPOINTSTOREAD: 10,000,000. sh1Bits: 5 (default, range 1–8). shRestBits: 4 (default, range 1–8). SHC0: 0.28209479177387814. colorScale: Scaling factor for colors (value not explicitly stated in sources, used in decoding). kMaxCompressionRatio: 1024. kMinBytesPerPoint: 9. Steps: 1. Header Validation: Read the header. Check magic == SPZMAGIC. Check version is 1, 2, 3, or 4. Reject v4 if using a legacy parser. Check numPoints <= MAXPOINTSTOREAD. Check shDegree <= 3. If using v4, read the TOC to locate attribute streams. If using v1–v3, decompress the gzip stream if flags indicate compression. 2. Determine Data Layout: If version == 1, usesFloat16 is true. Positions are stored as 2 bytes per component (Float16). If version >= 2, usesFloat16 is false. Positions are stored as 3 bytes per component (24-bit fixed-point). Calculate shDim = dimForDegree(shDegree). For degree d, shDim = (d+1)^2. 3. Allocate Output Arrays: positions: numPoints 3 floats. scales: numPoints 3 floats. rotations: numPoints 4 floats. alphas: numPoints floats. colors: numPoints 3 floats. sh: numPoints shDim 3 floats. 4. Unpack Positions: Create a CoordinateConverter object c to handle coordinate system flips. If usesFloat16 is true: Cast the packed position buffer to Half. For each component i from 0 to numPoints 3 - 1: val = halfToFloat(packed[i]), out[i] = val c.flipP[i % 3]. If usesFloat16 is false: Calculate scale = 1.0f / (1 << fractionalBits). For each point p from 0 to numPoints - 1: For each component j from 0 to 2: Read 3 bytes from packed at offset corresponding to point p, component j. Reconstruct 24-bit signed integer: fixed32 = src[0] | (src[1] << 8) | (src[2] << 16). Sign-extend if bit 23 is set: if (fixed32 & 0x800000) fixed32 |= 0xff000000. out[p3 + j] = staticcast<float>(fixed32) scale c.flipP[j]. 5. Unpack Alphas: Read 1 byte per point. For each point p: val = src[p] / 255.0f, out[p] = invSigmoid(val). 6. Unpack Colors: Read 3 bytes per point (RGB). For each point p: For each channel c from 0 to 2: val = src[p3 + c] / 255.0f, out[p3 + c] = (val - 0.5f) / colorScale. 7. Unpack Scales: Read 1 byte per component per point. For each point p: For each component j from 0 to 2: out[p3 + j] = src[p3 + j] / 16.0f - 10.0f. 8. Unpack Rotations: Determine if usesQuaternionSmallestThree is true (v3+) or false (v1–v2). If usesQuaternionSmallestThree is false (3 bytes per quaternion): Read 3 bytes per point. Reconstruct 3 signed 8-bit integers. Normalize to [-1, 1] range: q[i] = (src[i] - 127.5f) / 127.5f. Reconstruct w: w = sqrt(1 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2). Apply c.rotFlipPFunc if it exists, otherwise apply c.flipQ. If usesQuaternionSmallestThree is true (4 bytes per quaternion): Read 4 bytes per point. Reconstruct 32-bit integer. Extract largest component index iLargest (2 bits) and 3 components (10 bits each: 1 sign bit, 9 magnitude bits). Magnitude is scaled by sqrt(2) and normalized to 9-bit precision. Reconstruct quaternion, ensuring the largest component is positive (sign flip if needed). Normalize quaternion. Apply c.rotFlipPFunc if it exists, otherwise apply c.flipQ. 9. Unpack Spherical Harmonics (SH): If shDim == 0, return immediately. Read shDim 3 bytes per point. Within-Family Unpacking: For each point p: For each coefficient j from 0 to shDim - 1: For each channel c from 0 to 2: Read 1 byte. Apply sign flip c.flipSh[j] fused with unquantization. out[base + j3 + c] = unquantizeSH(src[base + j3 + c]). Cross-Family Unpacking (Rotation/Flip): If c.rotFlipShFuncs[0] exists: For each band band from 0 to SHMAXDEGREE - 1: If rotFlipShFuncs[band] is null, break. Calculate bandStart = band (band + 2) and bandSize = 2 band + 3. If bandStart + bandSize > shDim, break. For each channel c from 0 to 2: Copy bandSize coefficients to temporary buffer. Apply rotFlipShFuncsband. Copy back to output. 10. Verification: Ensure currentOffset + result.sh.length == buffer.byteLength. Return the structured object. Pitfalls: Version 1 files use legacy float16 encoding for positions, requiring decoding via halfToFloat. Version 2+ uses 24-bit fixed point coordinates. SH Degree 0: If shDim == 0, unpackSh returns immediately without processing, as there is no SH data. Coordinate Conversion: Positions and Rotations use CoordinateConverter which may apply sign flips (c.flipP, c.flipSh) or custom rotation functions (c.rotFlipPFunc, c.rotFlipShFuncs) depending on source and target coordinate systems. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import math import zlib import zstandard as zstd SPZMAGIC = 0x4750535A # MAXPOINTSTOREAD = 10000000 # SHMAXDEGREE = 3 # def dimfordegree(d): return (d + 1) 2 # def halftofloat(h): return struct.unpack('<f', struct.pack('<H', h))[0] # def invsigmoid(x): return math.log(x / (1.0 - x)) # def decompressgzip(data): return zlib.decompress(data, 16 | zlib.MAXWBITS) # def decompresszstdv4(data): return zstd.decompress(data) # class CoordinateConverter: def init(self): self.flipp = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] self.flipq = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] self.flipsh = [1.0] 16 self.rotflippfunc = None self.rotflipshfuncs = [None] SHMAXDEGREE class GaussianCloud: def init(self, positions, scales, rotations, alphas, colors, sh): self.positions = positions self.scales = scales self.rotations = rotations self.alphas = alphas self.colors = colors self.sh = sh def unpackspz(buffer: bytes, colorscale: float = 1.0) -> GaussianCloud: if len(buffer) < 16: raise ValueError("Buffer too small for header") magic = struct.unpackfrom('<I', buffer, 0)[0] if magic != SPZMAGIC: raise ValueError("Invalid magic number") version = struct.unpackfrom('<I', buffer, 4)[0] numpoints = struct.unpackfrom('<I', buffer, 8)[0] shdegree = buffer[12] fractionalbits = buffer[13] flags = buffer[14] if numpoints > MAXPOINTSTOREAD: raise ValueError("Too many points") if shdegree > 3: raise ValueError("Invalid SH degree") # Note: v4 requires parsing the TOC to locate individual ZSTD streams if version >= 4: data = decompresszstdv4(buffer) else: data = decompressgzip(buffer) usesfloat16 = (version == 1) shdim = dimfordegree(shdegree) positions = [0.0] (numpoints 3) scales = [0.0] (numpoints 3) rotations = [0.0] (numpoints 4) alphas = [0.0] numpoints colors = [0.0] (numpoints 3) sh = [0.0] (numpoints shdim 3) coordconverter = CoordinateConverter() posoffset = 0 if usesfloat16: for i in range(numpoints 3): val = halftofloat(struct.unpackfrom('<H', data, posoffset + i2)[0]) positions[i] = val coordconverter.flipp[i % 3] else: scale = 1.0 / (1 << fractionalbits) for p in range(numpoints): for j in range(3): idx = posoffset + p 9 + j 3 b0 = data[idx] b1 = data[idx + 1] b2 = data[idx + 2] fixed32 = b0 | (b1 << 8) | (b2 << 16) if fixed32 & 0x800000: fixed32 |= 0xff000000 positions[p 3 + j] = float(fixed32) scale coordconverter.flipp[j] alphaoffset = posoffset + numpoints 3 (2 if usesfloat16 else 3) for p in range(numpoints): val = data[alphaoffset + p] / 255.0 alphas[p] = invsigmoid(val) coloroffset = alphaoffset + numpoints for p in range(numpoints): for c in range(3): val = data[coloroffset + p 3 + c] / 255.0 colors[p 3 + c] = (val - 0.5) / colorscale scaleoffset = coloroffset + numpoints 3 for p in range(numpoints): for j in range(3): scales[p 3 + j] = data[scaleoffset + p 3 + j] / 16.0 - 10.0 rotoffset = scaleoffset + numpoints 3 usessmallestthree = (version >= 3) for p in range(numpoints): if usessmallestthree: comp = struct.unpackfrom('<I', data, rotoffset + p 4)[0] ilargest = comp & 0x3 q = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] negate = False for i in range(4): if i != ilargest: shift = 10 (i if i < ilargest else i - 1) negbit = ((comp >> (shift + 1)) & 0x1) ^ (1 if negate else 0) mag = (comp >> shift) & 0x1FF q[i] = (mag / 511.0) (1.0 if negbit == 0 else -1.0) q[ilargest] = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - sum(xx for x in q[:3]))) if q[ilargest] < 0: q = [-x for x in q] else: b0 = data[rotoffset + p 3] b1 = data[rotoffset + p 3 + 1] b2 = data[rotoffset + p 3 + 2] x = (b0 - 128) / 127.5 y = (b1 - 128) / 127.5 z = (b2 - 128) / 127.5 w = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - xx - yy - zz)) q = [x, y, z, w] if coordconverter.rotflippfunc: coordconverter.rotflippfunc(q) else: q[0] = coordconverter.flipq[0] q[1] = coordconverter.flipq[1] q[2] = coordconverter.flipq[2] rotations[p 4: p 4 + 4] = q shoffset = rotoffset + numpoints (4 if usessmallestthree else 3) if shdim > 0: for p in range(numpoints): base = shoffset + p shdim 3 for j in range(shdim): for c in range(3): val = data[base + j 3 + c] sh[p shdim 3 + j 3 + c] = unquantizesh(val, coordconverter.flipsh[j]) if coordconverter.rotflipshfuncs[0]: for band in range(SHMAXDEGREE): if coordconverter.rotflipshfuncs[band] is None: break bandstart = band (band + 2) bandsize = 2 band + 3 if bandstart + bandsize > shdim: break for c in range(3): tmp = sh[base + bandstart 3 + c: base + bandstart 3 + c + bandsize] coordconverter.rotflipshfuncsband sh[base + bandstart 3 + c: base + bandstart 3 + c + bandsize] = tmp return GaussianCloud(positions, scales, rotations, alphas, colors, sh) def unquantizesh(val, flip): # Standard 8-bit signed quantization inversion return ((val - 128) / 127.5) flip A parser for SPZ versions 2 and 3, implemented in pure Kotlin as part of the KMP data model. It uses gzip compression and decompresses the data using a pure-Kotlin Inflate implementation. It explicitly rejects SPZ version 4 (which uses ZSTD) with a clear error. File size is approximately 10x smaller than PLY format. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of points and the size of the compressed data. Decompression is the dominant cost for large files. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of points. The output arrays store raw floats, which is significantly larger than the compressed format. Measured Performance: SPZ files are approximately 10x smaller than PLY format. Version 4 (ZSTD) allows for parallel compression of attribute streams, potentially improving load times on multi-core systems. Strengths: Efficient storage, support for high-precision positions (24-bit fixed-point), and flexible SH encoding. Limitations: Legacy versions (v1–v3) use a single gzip stream, which limits parallelism. Version 1 uses Float16 for positions, which may reduce precision compared to v2+. When to Use: When loading pre-trained Gaussian Splatting models from disk. Use v4 for large scenes (>10M points) or when parallel loading is critical. Use v2/v3 for compatibility with older tools. The SPZ format was developed by Niantic. It is used in various renderers and tools, including Spark, PlayCanvas, and Mobile-GS. name: PNG-based Gaussian Compression
head: Compact 3D Scene Representation via Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids, PNG Compression for 3D Gaussians, PNG Compression for Gaussian Splats, gsplat PNG Compression, gsplat_mlx compression
body: PNG-based Gaussian Compression is a lossless compression technique for trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models that quantizes splat parameters into 8-bit and 16-bit PNG images. It serves as a port of the PyTorch gsplat compression module to MLX. By leveraging spatial locality (optionally enhanced via Morton code sorting) and PNG encoding, it achieves approximately 10x compression on standard 3DGS models. It builds on Gaussian Data Packing by mapping scalar and vector fields to image grids, differing from Gaussian Splat Texture Packing which targets GPU texture formats, and SPZ Packed Format which uses a different binary layout. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dictionary of Gaussian splat parameters: means (N, 3), quats (N, 4), scales (N, 3), opacities (N, 1), and sh0 (N, 3). Higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients shN are also supported. Output: A set of PNG image files for each parameter field and a meta.json file containing metadata (shape, dtype, mins, maxs) required for decompression. Data Structures: Metadata (meta.json): Stores shape, dtype, mins, and maxs for each compressed parameter. PNG Images: 8-bit PNGs for scales, quats, opacities, and sh0. 16-bit means are split into two 8-bit PNGs (low byte and high byte). Higher-order SH coefficients shN are stored in NPZ format if K-means clustering is unavailable. Parameters: usesort (bool): Whether to sort splats by Morton code before compression to improve spatial locality. Default: True. verbose (bool): Whether to print progress information. Default: True. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Apply log-transform to means: y = \text{sign}(x) \cdot \log(1 + |x|). Normalize quats to unit length: q{norm} = q / \|q\|. 2. Crop to Square: Calculate side length: n{side} = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor. Calculate number of Gaussians to drop: n{crop} = N - n{side}^2. If n{crop} > 0: Sort opacities in descending order. Keep indices of the top n{side}^2 Gaussians. Apply this mask to all splat parameters. 3. Sorting (Optional): If usesort is True, sort the remaining Gaussians by their Morton code to enhance spatial locality. 4. Quantization and PNG Encoding: 8-bit Parameters (scales, quats, opacities, sh0): Reshape parameter array to (n{side}, n{side}, C) where C is the channel dimension. Compute per-channel minimum (min) and maximum (max). Quantize to 8-bit: img = \text{clip}(\text{round}((arr - \text{mins}) / \text{ranges} \cdot 255), 0, 255) where \text{ranges} = \text{maxs} - \text{mins}. Save as PNG. 16-bit Parameters (means): Perform 16-bit quantization: img16 = \text{round}((arr - \text{mins}) / \text{ranges} \cdot 65535). Split into low byte (img16 \& 0xFF) and high byte ((img16 >> 8) \& 0xFF), stored as two separate 8-bit PNGs. Higher-order SH (shN): If K-means clustering is not available (e.g., in MLX without torchpq), compress using NPZ format. 5. Metadata Storage: Save shape, dtype, mins, and maxs for each parameter in meta.json. Decompression: 1. Load meta.json. 2. Load PNG images and reconstruct quantized arrays. 3. Inverse quantization: 8-bit: arr = \text{normalised} \cdot (\text{maxs} - \text{mins}) + \text{mins}, where \text{normalised} = img / 255.0. 16-bit: Reconstruct 16-bit integer from two PNGs, then arr = \text{normalised} \cdot (\text{maxs} - \text{mins}) + \text{mins}, where \text{normalised} = img16 / 65535.0. 4. Apply inverse log-transform to means: y = \text{sign}(x) \cdot (\exp(|x|) - 1). 5. Normalize quats if necessary (reconstruction should preserve unit length if quantization is precise). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import json import os from PIL import Image def logtransform(x): """Apply log-transform: y = sign(x) log(1 + |x|)""" return np.sign(x) np.log1p(np.abs(x)) def inverselogtransform(x): """Apply inverse log-transform: y = sign(x) (exp(|x|) - 1)""" return np.sign(x) (np.exp(np.abs(x)) - 1) def croptosquare(splats): """Crop splats to nearest perfect square by dropping lowest opacity.""" ngs = splats["means"].shape[0] nside = int(np.sqrt(ngs)) ncrop = ngs - nside nside if ncrop == 0: return splats opacities = splats["opacities"].ravel() keep = np.argsort(opacities)[::-1][:nside nside] keep.sort() cropped = {k: v[keep] for k, v in splats.items()} return cropped def savepng(arr, path): """Save numpy array as PNG.""" Image.fromarray(arr).save(path) def loadpng(path): """Load PNG file to numpy array.""" return np.array(Image.open(path)) def compresspng8bit(arr, mins, maxs): """Compress array to 8-bit PNG using evidence formula.""" ranges = maxs - mins ranges[ranges == 0] = 1.0 # Guard against division by zero img = np.clip(np.round((arr - mins) / ranges 255), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) return img def decompresspng8bit(img, mins, maxs): """Decompress 8-bit PNG to array.""" normalized = img / 255.0 return normalized (maxs - mins) + mins def compresspng16bit(arr, mins, maxs): """Compress array to two 8-bit PNGs (low and high bytes).""" ranges = maxs - mins ranges[ranges == 0] = 1.0 img16 = np.clip(np.round((arr - mins) / ranges 65535), 0, 65535).astype(np.uint16) lowbyte = (img16 & 0xFF).astype(np.uint8) highbyte = ((img16 >> 8) & 0xFF).astype(np.uint8) return lowbyte, highbyte def decompresspng16bit(lowbyte, highbyte, mins, maxs): """Decompress two 8-bit PNGs to array.""" img16 = (highbyte.astype(np.uint16) << 8) | lowbyte.astype(np.uint16) normalized = img16 / 65535.0 return normalized (maxs - mins) + mins def compressgaussianspng(splats, usesort=True, outdir="output"): """Compress Gaussian splats to PNGs.""" os.makedirs(outdir, existok=True) splats["means"] = logtransform(splats["means"]) norms = np.linalg.norm(splats["quats"], axis=-1, keepdims=True) splats["quats"] = splats["quats"] / norms splats = croptosquare(splats) nside = int(np.sqrt(splats["means"].shape[0])) if usesort: # Morton code sorting would be applied here pass meta = {} for param in ["scales", "quats", "opacities", "sh0"]: arr = splats[param] C = arr.shape[-1] arrreshaped = arr.reshape(nside, nside, C) mins = np.min(arrreshaped, axis=(0, 1)) maxs = np.max(arrreshaped, axis=(0, 1)) img = compresspng8bit(arrreshaped, mins, maxs) savepng(img, os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}.png")) meta[param] = {"shape": arr.shape, "dtype": "uint8", "mins": mins.tolist(), "maxs": maxs.tolist()} param = "means" arr = splats[param] C = arr.shape[-1] arrreshaped = arr.reshape(nside, nside, C) mins = np.min(arrreshaped, axis=(0, 1)) maxs = np.max(arrreshaped, axis=(0, 1)) lowbyte, highbyte = compresspng16bit(arrreshaped, mins, maxs) savepng(lowbyte, os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}low.png")) savepng(highbyte, os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}high.png")) meta[param] = {"shape": arr.shape, "dtype": "uint16", "mins": mins.tolist(), "maxs": maxs.tolist()} if "shN" in splats: np.savezcompressed(os.path.join(outdir, "shN.npz"), splats["shN"]) meta["shN"] = {"dtype": "npz"} with open(os.path.join(outdir, "meta.json"), "w") as f: json.dump(meta, f) def decompressgaussianspng(outdir="output"): """Decompress Gaussian splats from PNGs.""" with open(os.path.join(outdir, "meta.json"), "r") as f: meta = json.load(f) splats = {} for param in ["scales", "quats", "opacities", "sh0"]: info = meta[param] img = loadpng(os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}.png")) mins = np.array(info["mins"]) maxs = np.array(info["maxs"]) arr = decompresspng8bit(img, mins, maxs) arr = arr.reshape(info["shape"]) splats[param] = arr param = "means" info = meta[param] lowbyte = loadpng(os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}low.png")) highbyte = loadpng(os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}high.png")) mins = np.array(info["mins"]) maxs = np.array(info["maxs"]) arr = decompresspng16bit(lowbyte, highbyte, mins, maxs) arr = arr.reshape(info["shape"]) splats[param] = inverselogtransform(arr) if "shN" in meta: data = np.load(os.path.join(outdir, "shN.npz")) splats["shN"] = data["arr0"] return splats Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the number of Gaussians is not a perfect square, the lowest opacity Gaussians are removed, potentially losing data. Higher-order SH coefficients (shN) are compressed via NPZ rather than K-means clustering if the upstream dependency torchpq is not available, resulting in less compression. Division by zero in quantization must be handled if max == min for a channel. This method reduces the storage size of trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models by reordering splats into spatially local chunks, normalizing data within each chunk to a 0..1 range, and storing the results in GPU textures using compression formats. It builds on PNG-based Gaussian Compression by introducing spatial locality via Morton ordering to improve the efficiency of block-based texture compression (BCn). Unlike direct compression of raw data arrays, which suffers from poor compression ratios due to spatial discontinuity, this method aligns data with hardware compression block structures. Compression Ratio: Approximately 10x compression on standard 3DGS models. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the original data during preprocessing and the compressed PNGs. Metadata is minimal. Strengths: Lossless compression of quantized data, simple file format (PNG), good compression ratios due to spatial locality. Limitations: Requires cropping to perfect square, higher-order SH compression is less efficient without K-means, PNG is not optimized for GPU texture access. When to Use: When storage size is a concern and random access to individual Gaussians is not required (or can be handled via Morton code indexing). When Not to Use: When GPU texture compression (BCn) is preferred for rendering performance, or when higher-order SH coefficients are significant and K-means is not available. PNG-based Gaussian Compression is a technique for compressing trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models by quantizing parameters into 8-bit and 16-bit PNG images. It was originally developed as part of the gsplat library for PyTorch and later ported to MLX by the gsplat-mlx project. The method leverages the spatial coherence of Gaussian splats to improve compression ratios. nerfstudio-project/gsplat, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/gsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, https://github.com/RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Chunk Compression with Morton Reordering
head: Chunked Gaussian Splat Compression, Morton-Ordered Splat Textures
body: This method reduces the storage size of trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models by reordering splats into spatially local chunks, normalizing data within each chunk to a 0..1 range, and storing the results in GPU textures using compression formats. Unlike direct compression of raw data arrays, which suffers from poor compression ratios due to spatial discontinuity, this method aligns data with hardware compression block structures. Inputs: A list of Gaussian splats, where each splat contains position, scale, rotation, spherical harmonic coefficients, and opacity. Outputs: Compressed GPU textures and chunk metadata (min/max values) for parameter reconstruction. Data Structures: 1. Chunk Metadata: For each chunk, the minimum and maximum values for every data field (position, scale, color, SH) stored in full Float32 precision. 2. Texture Layout: Textures are organized such that one texel represents one splat. Within a chunk of N=256 splats, the data is arranged in a 16 \times 16 square layout. Parameters: Chunk size N: 256 splats. Texture block dimension: 16 \times 16 texels per chunk. Steps: 1. 3D Morton Reordering: Sort the splats in the data array based on their 3D positions using 3D Morton order. The 3D Morton encoding for a vector v = (x, y, z) of 21-bit integers is: MortonEncode3(v) = (MortonPart1By2(v.z) \ll 2) \mid (MortonPart1By2(v.y) \ll 1) \mid MortonPart1By2(v.x) Where MortonPart1By2 interleaves the bits of a 21-bit integer into a 64-bit integer: python def MortonPart1By2(x: int) -> int: x &= 0x1fffff x = (x ^ (x << 32)) & 0x1f00000000ffff x = (x ^ (x << 16)) & 0x1f0000ff0000ff x = (x ^ (x << 8)) & 0x100f00f00f00f00f x = (x ^ (x << 4)) & 0x10c30c30c30c30c3 x = (x ^ (x << 2)) & 0x1249249249249249 return x 2. Chunking: Group the reordered splats into contiguous chunks of size N=256. 3. Chunk Normalization: For each chunk, compute the minimum and maximum values for all data fields across all splats in that chunk using full Float32 precision. Normalize each splat's data values to the range [0, 1] relative to the chunk's computed min/max. Quaternions are encoded using the "smallest three" format, storing the three smallest components and the index of the largest component. 4. 2D Morton Reordering (Texture Layout): Reorder the texture data within each chunk into a 16 \times 16 square layout using 2D Morton order to align with BCn compression block structures. The 2D Morton encoding for a coordinate c = (x, y) within a 16 \times 16 block is: python def EncodeMorton2D16x16(x: int, y: int) -> int: t = ((y & 0xF) << 8) | (x & 0xF) t = (t ^ (t << 2)) & 0x3333 t = (t ^ (t << 1)) & 0x5555 return (t | (t >> 7)) & 0xFF 5. Texture Compression: Encode the normalized splat data into GPU textures using formats such as F32x4 (128-bit), F16x4 (64-bit), Norm102 (32-bit), Norm11 (32-bit), Norm8x4 (32-bit), Norm565 (16-bit), BC7 (8-bit), or BC1 (4-bit). Some formats like Norm102 require engine-specific emulation via Float32 textures and manual shader unpacking (e.g., Unity). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Compression Quality: Storing data in 256 \times 1 stripes causes poor compression quality with BCn formats because the compression is block-based (4 \times 4 texels). Large Chunk Bounds: Morton curve flips can cause large chunk bounds, increasing variance and reducing normalization efficiency; partially filled chunks or Hilbert curves are suggested as mitigations. Precision: Normalization to 0..1 enables lower-precision formats, but format selection significantly impacts PSNR. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Bike Scene: Original 1.42GB. Very Low compression: 74MB (18.7x smaller, PSNR 24.02). Garden Scene: Original 1.35GB. Medium compression: 267MB (5.2x smaller, PSNR 48.63). Comparison: Direct BC7 compression on 256x1 stripe layout yields PSNR 21.71. Reordering into 16x16 blocks improves PSNR to 24.18. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in model size (up to ~19x) with acceptable quality loss at higher compression levels. Leverages existing GPU texture hardware for decompression. Limitations: Requires preprocessing. Lower quality presets (Very Low) may introduce visible artifacts. Some texture formats require engine-specific workarounds. This technique was introduced by Aras Pranckevičius to reduce the storage footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting models, which typically store parameters in full Float32 precision. The method relies on spatial locality via Morton ordering and chunk-wise normalization to make Gaussian data amenable to standard GPU texture compression techniques. name: GeometryState Allocation
head: GeometryState/ImageState sizing, GeometryState::fromChunk, buffer allocation query
body: GeometryState Allocation is the method for determining the memory footprint and initializing the GeometryState structure required for rasterizing P 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of dynamic buffer sizing for per-primitive auxiliary data (such as depths, radii, and conic matrices) that must be allocated before the rasterization kernel executes. It is distinct from Gaussian Data Structure (which defines the primitive's intrinsic attributes) and Gaussian Data Packing (which handles color/feature compression), focusing solely on the transient state needed for the rendering pass. The method computes the required memory for the GeometryState and ImageState buffers based on the number of Gaussians (P) and the image resolution (W \times H). It returns these sizes as scalars to allow the caller to allocate contiguous memory chunks. Inputs: P: Number of 3D Gaussians. W, H: Image width and height. Outputs: geomsize: Integer scalar, total bytes required for GeometryState. imgsize: Integer scalar, total bytes required for ImageState. Data Structures and Layout: The GeometryState is allocated from a memory chunk using an obtain(chunk, field, size, alignment) mechanism. The fields and their sizes for P Gaussians are: 1. depths: float, size P. 2. internalradiix, internalradiiy, internalradiiz: float, size P each. 3. means3Dnorm: float, size P. 4. cov3D: float, size P \times 6. 5. conicopacity: float, size P \times 7 or P. Note: Sources disagree on the multiplier for conicopacity. specifies P \times 7, while specifies P. The implementation must verify the specific kernel requirements.. 6. tilestouched: uint32t, size P. 7. scanningspace: Dynamic size, determined by the output of a device-wide inclusive sum (e.g., cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum) on the number of rendered Gaussians. 8. pointoffsets: uint32t, size P. 9. clamped: float, size P \times 3. 10. means2D: float, size P. 11. rgb: float, size P \times 3. Note: and list slightly different fields. includes internalradii components and means3Dnorm, while includes clamped, means2D, and rgb. A complete implementation likely requires the union of these fields or a specific subset depending on the rasterizer variant. Steps: 1. Allocate two int64 tensors: geomsize and imgsize. 2. Call required<GeometryState>(P) to compute the byte size of the GeometryState buffer. 3. Copy the result to geomsize. 4. Call required<ImageState>(WH) to compute the byte size of the ImageState buffer. 5. Copy the result to imgsize. 6. Return geomsize and imgsize as Python scalars. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocategeometrystate(P: int, W: int, H: int): """ Computes and returns the memory sizes for GeometryState and ImageState. """ # Compute required size for GeometryState based on P Gaussians # The exact formula depends on the union of fields from and # and the alignment requirements of the obtain() function. geomsize = requiredGeometryState(P) # Compute required size for ImageState based on image dimensions imgsize = requiredImageState(W H) return geomsize, imgsize def requiredGeometryState(P: int) -> int: """ Calculates the byte size of GeometryState for P Gaussians. Combines fields from and. """ # Base fields with fixed multipliers # Note: Alignment padding is handled by the obtain() function in practice. # This function estimates the raw data size. # From size = 0 size += P 4 # depths (float) size += P 4 3 # internalradiix, y, z (float) size += P 4 # means3Dnorm (float) size += P 6 4 # cov3D (float) # conicopacity: Disagreement between (P7) and (P). # Using P7 as per which is more specific, but says P. # Implementation should check kernel source. size += P 7 4 # conicopacity (float) size += P 4 # tilestouched (uint32t) size += P 4 # pointoffsets (uint32t) # From size += P 3 4 # clamped (float) size += P 4 # means2D (float) size += P 3 4 # rgb (float) # Dynamic field: scanningspace # Size is not known until the number of rendered Gaussians is determined. # This is typically allocated separately or reserved in the chunk. # Not given in the sources for the initial sizing query. return size def requiredImageState(numpixels: int) -> int: """ Calculates the byte size for ImageState. Not given in the sources. """ # Placeholder for ImageState calculation # Typically involves depth buffers, color accumulation buffers, etc. return 0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Scanning Space: The scanningspace field size is dynamic and depends on the number of rendered (visible) Gaussians, not the total count P. It is allocated later based on the actual output of the scan operation. Field Disagreement: Sources and list different fields for GeometryState. includes internalradii components and means3Dnorm, while includes clamped, means2D, and rgb. The implementer must verify which fields are actually used by the specific rasterizer kernel. Conic Opacity Size: specifies conicopacity as size P \times 7, while specifies P. This discrepancy must be resolved by inspecting the kernel code. Time Complexity: O(1) relative to P for the sizing query, as it involves simple arithmetic on the count. Memory Complexity: The allocated memory scales linearly with P for GeometryState and with W \times H for ImageState. Strengths: Provides a precise, pre-computed buffer size, avoiding dynamic allocation during the critical rendering path. Limitations: Requires accurate knowledge of field layouts and alignment. The dynamic scanningspace field complicates a single static allocation query. GeometryState Allocation is part of the rendering implementation pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It ensures that the GPU kernels have contiguous memory for per-primitive state before rasterization begins. The method is derived from the CUDA/C++ implementations of Gaussian Splatting, specifically the GeometryState and ImageState structures used in the rasterizer. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Preliminaries
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS), 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Representation, 3D-GS, Standard 3DGS representation, Vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a scene representation method that replaces implicit neural fields with an explicit set of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives, enabling real-time rendering via GPU rasterization without ray marching. It solves the trade-off between the high visual quality of neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and the speed of explicit geometry by representing the scene as millions of splats (ellipsoids) that are projected and alpha-composited. Unlike NeRFs, which require per-pixel network queries and volume integration, 3DGS uses a differentiable sort-and-blend rasterizer, allowing for end-to-end optimization of geometric and photometric attributes. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sparse point cloud (typically from Structure-from-Motion, e.g., COLMAP) providing initial positions, and a set of N training images with known camera poses P. Outputs: A rendered image \hat{I} for a novel view, and a set of optimized 3D Gaussian parameters \{\muk, qk, sk, \alphak, \text{SH}k\}{k=1}^K. Data Structures Each Gaussian primitive k stores the following parameters, which are optimized via gradient descent: 1. Mean Position: \boldsymbol{\mu}k \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Rotation: A unit quaternion \mathbf{q}k \in \mathbb{R}^4 (\|\mathbf{q}k\|=1). 3. Scale: A vector \mathbf{s}k \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the scaling factors along the principal axes. These are stored in logarithmic space (\log \mathbf{s}k) to ensure positivity during optimization. 4. Opacity: A scalar raw logit \alphak \in \mathbb{R}. The effective opacity is obtained via a Sigmoid activation: \hat{\alpha}k = \sigma(\alphak). 5. Color: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times (\ell+1)^2}, where \ell is the degree. Vanilla 3DGS uses degree \ell=3, resulting in 16 coefficients per channel (48 floats total). The covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is derived from rotation and scale: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}k = \mathbf{R}k \mathbf{S}k \mathbf{S}k^\top \mathbf{R}k^\top where \mathbf{R}k is the rotation matrix constructed from \mathbf{q}k, and \mathbf{S}k = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}k). Rendering Pipeline 1. Culling: Gaussians outside the view frustum or behind the camera are discarded. 2. Projection: Each 3D Gaussian is projected to the 2D image plane. The 2D mean \boldsymbol{\mu}'k is computed via the projection matrix. The 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'k is approximated using the Jacobian of the projective transformation J and the world-to-camera matrix W: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'k = J W \boldsymbol{\Sigma}k W^\top J^\top. 3. Bounding Box: A 2D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) is computed for each Gaussian based on \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'k (typically expanding the ellipse to cover 3\sigma). 4. Tiling and Sorting: Gaussians are binned into tiles (e.g., 16 \times 16 pixels). Within each tile, Gaussians are sorted front-to-back by their depth (center depth). 5. Rasterization and Compositing: For each pixel, the contributing Gaussians are alpha-composited. The color C(\mathbf{p}) at pixel \mathbf{p} is: C(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{k \in N} \mathbf{c}k(\mathbf{d}k) \, \hat{\alpha}k \, Gk^{2D}(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j < k} \left( 1 - \hat{\alpha}j \, Gj^{2D}(\mathbf{p}) \right) where N is the set of sorted Gaussians covering the pixel, \mathbf{d}k is the view direction, and Gk^{2D}(\mathbf{p}) is the 2D Gaussian kernel value: Gk^{2D}(\mathbf{p}) = \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}'k)^\top (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'k)^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}'k) \right). The term \hat{\alpha}k Gk^{2D}(\mathbf{p}) represents the effective alpha of the k-th splat at the pixel. 6. Loss and Optimization: The rendered image is compared to the ground truth using a combined L1 and SSIM loss: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \|\hat{I} - I\|1 + \lambda (1 - \text{SSIM}(\hat{I}, I)) with \lambda = 0.2. Gradients are backpropagated through the rasterizer to update \boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{s}, \alpha, \text{SH} using the Adam optimizer. Adaptive Density Control (ADC) To handle local minima and varying detail, 3DGS employs periodic densification and pruning every K iterations (typically every 100 iterations within a window of 500–15,000): Gradient Tracking: The magnitude of the 2D position gradient \|\nabla{\boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}} \mathcal{L}\| is tracked for each Gaussian. Clone: If a Gaussian has small scale and high gradient, it is cloned (duplicated with perturbed position) to fill under-reconstructed areas. Split: If a Gaussian has large scale and high gradient, it is replaced by two smaller Gaussians (clones with halved scale) to increase resolution. Prune: Gaussians with opacity below a threshold \epsilon\alpha \approx 0.005 are removed. Opacity Reset: Every 3,000 iterations, all opacities are reset to a low value (e.g., 0.01) to escape local minima where Gaussians are opaque but incorrect. Pseudocode Unverified code. It was developed to address the computational bottleneck of ray marching in NeRFs while maintaining high visual fidelity. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization Parameters
head: 25 Things Every Principal Must Know, 3DGS Training Hyperparameters, Densification and Opacity Reset Settings, Principal Knowledge Points
body: This method defines the hyperparameters and procedural rules for optimizing a set of 3D Gaussians to reconstruct a scene from images. It sets apart from static rendering by introducing adaptive density control (clone, split, prune, opacity reset) and periodic opacity resets, which are critical for converging to a high-fidelity radiance field. Inputs: Initial set of N 3D Gaussians, training images with known camera poses, and optimization hyperparameters. Outputs: Optimized set of Gaussians with updated parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, q, s, \alpha, \mathrm{SH}). Each Gaussian gi stores center \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, orientation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized quaternion), scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathrm{SH}i. The covariance matrix is reconstructed as \Sigmai = Ri \, \mathrm{diag}(si)^2 \, Ri^\top, where Ri is the rotation matrix derived from qi. The training process alternates between rendering, loss computation, and density control. 1. Initialization: Place initial Gaussians using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points and set initial scales based on nearest-neighbor distances. Initialize opacities to a small value. 2. Rendering: Project each Gaussian to 2D using EWA splatting, which linearizes the perspective projection at \boldsymbol{\mu}c to obtain \Sigma{2D}. Render the image via alpha compositing of 2D Gaussian footprints. 3. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) between rendered and ground-truth images. 4. Gradient Accumulation: Accumulate gradients for \boldsymbol{\mu}i and other parameters, tracking the magnitude \|\nabla{\boldsymbol{\mu}i} \mathcal{L}\|. 5. Adaptive Density Control: Performed periodically during training. Clone: For Gaussians with high gradient magnitude and low opacity, clone the Gaussian. Split: For Gaussians with high gradient magnitude and large scale, split the Gaussian into two. Prune: Remove Gaussians with low opacity or small scale. Opacity Reset: Reset opacities of all Gaussians to a small value to prevent saturation and allow further densification. Densification Gradient Threshold (\tau): Approximately 2 \times 10^{-4}. Opacity Reset Interval (K{\text{reset}}): Every 3000 iterations. Clone/Split/Prune Thresholds: Specific scale and opacity thresholds for clone, split, and prune operations are not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizegaussians(gaussians, images, poses, numiterations, gradthreshold=2e-4, opacityresetinterval=3000, cloneopacitythresh=0.01, pruneopacitythresh=0.005): # Standard operations defined inline for self-containment def render(gs, ps): # EWA splatting: linearize perspective at muc to get Sigma2D, then alpha composite footprints return projectedcomposite(gs, ps) def computeloss(rendered, target): # Photometric loss (L1 + SSIM) return l1ssim(rendered, target) def computegradients(loss, gs): # Backpropagate through rendering graph return autograd(loss, gs) def updateparameters(gs, grads): # SGD/Adam step for g in gs: g.mu -= lr grads[g].mu g.alpha -= lr grads[g].alpha g.scale -= lr grads[g].scale g.q -= lr grads[g].q g.SH -= lr grads[g].SH def resetopacities(gs): # Reset all opacities to a small value for g in gs: g.alpha = 0.01 def clonegaussian(g): # Create copy at mu with perturbation, copy q, s, alpha, SH new = copy(g) new.mu += uniformnoise(scale=0.01) gaussians.append(new) def splitgaussian(g): # Create two copies with reduced scale (e.g., /1.6) new1 = copy(g); new2 = copy(g) new1.scale /= 1.6; new2.scale /= 1.6 gaussians.extend([new1, new2]) def prunegaussian(g): # Mark for removal from list g.toremove = True for iter in range(numiterations): renderedimage = render(gaussians, poses) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, images[iter % len(images)]) gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) updateparameters(gaussians, gradients) if iter % 100 == 0: toclone, tosplit, toprune = [], [], [] for g in gaussians: gradmag = norm(gradients[g].mu) if gradmag > gradthreshold and g.alpha < cloneopacitythresh: toclone.append(g) if gradmag > gradthreshold and g.scale > thresholdscale: tosplit.append(g) if g.alpha < pruneopacitythresh: toprune.append(g) for g in toclone: clonegaussian(g) for g in tosplit: splitgaussian(g) for g in toprune: prunegaussian(g) gaussians = [g for g in gaussians if not g.toremove] if iter % opacityresetinterval == 0: resetopacities(gaussians) Precision: Using log-space for scales prevents negative values and improves optimization stability. Boundaries: Low thresholds cause Gaussian explosion; monitor memory usage. Degenerate Input: Low-texture scenes yield small gradients, causing insufficient densification; adjust thresholds or add priors. Popping Artifacts: Arise from per-tile center-depth sort; use StopThePop, GOF, or exact pixel sort to fix them. Fixes scale-aliasing via 3D smoothing + 2D Mip filter. Use when high-frequency details cause aliasing artifacts. Replaces 3D ellipsoids with oriented disks for better surface reconstruction. Use when geometry/mesh extraction is the primary goal. Uses voxel anchors + tiny MLP for compression and far-view extrapolation. Use when model size is a constraint. Provides Level-of-Detail (LoD) from city-scale to centimeter close-ups. Use for large-scale scenes. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Densification adds sparse overhead. Memory Complexity: O(N) per Gaussian. Vanilla 3DGS uses 1–3 M Gaussians for room-scale scenes, occupying 200–800 MB on disk. Performance: Real-time rendering is achievable with tile-based rasterization. Optimization speed scales with N and iteration count. Strengths: High-quality novel view synthesis, real-time rendering, explicit representation. Limitations: Large model size, potential for popping artifacts due to per-tile center-depth sort (mitigated by StopThePop, GOF, exact pixel sort). When to Use: Photorealistic novel view synthesis, room-scale scenes with plenty of views. When Not to Use: When surface mesh quality is critical (use 2DGS), or when model size is extremely constrained (use LightGaussian, SOG, EAGLES, RDO-Gaussian). Benchmarking: Report compression, FPS, and memory alongside quality metrics; numbers without them are misleading. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) replaces NeRF's MLP+ray-march with explicit anisotropic Gaussians and tile rasterization. The optimization parameters described here are based on the original implementation and its refinements. The method has become a standard for radiance-field optimization, with variants addressing compression, dynamic scenes, and geometry extraction. name: N-DGS Bounded Cholesky Parameterization
head: N-DGS
body: N-DGS is a parameterization for the joint covariance of 3D Gaussians that uses bounded Cholesky coefficients multiplied by query diagonal scales to control spatial extent and cross-covariance. It differs from sibling methods like dGS Direct Regression Parameterization by implicitly deriving the regression operator from the ambient joint Cholesky factor, rather than optimizing operational quantities directly. Inputs and Outputs Input: Query diagonal scales \mathbf{s}q \in \mathbb{R}^C, spatial Cholesky factor \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}, bounded cross-covariance coefficients \mathbf{B}e \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times p}, and query Cholesky factor \mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}. Output: Joint covariance blocks \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times C}, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}. Data Structures The parameterization relies on the Cholesky decomposition of the joint covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{(p+C) \times (p+C)}. The lower Cholesky factor \mathbf{L} is partitioned into spatial (p) and query (C) blocks: \mathbf{L} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{D} \end{pmatrix} where \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{D} are lower triangular, and \mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times p} is the cross-covariance Cholesky component. N-DGS parameterizes \mathbf{B} as \mathbf{B} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}q) \mathbf{B}e with |\mathbf{B}{e,jk}| \leq 1 for all entries. Numbered Steps 1. Retrieve query diagonal scales \mathbf{s}q from the Gaussian set. 2. Scale the bounded coefficients: \mathbf{B} \leftarrow \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}q) \mathbf{B}e. 3. Compute spatial covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp} \leftarrow \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^\top. 4. Compute cross-covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \leftarrow \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}^\top. 5. Compute query covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} \leftarrow \mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^\top + \mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\top. 6. Assemble the joint covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq}^\top & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} \end{pmatrix}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ndgsparameterize(A, Be, D, sq): # A: (p, p) lower triangular, Be: (C, p) bounded, D: (C, C) lower triangular, sq: (C,) B = diag(sq) @ Be Sigmapp = A @ A.T Sigmapq = A @ B.T Sigmaqq = B @ B.T + D @ D.T return Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq def ndgsshift(Sigmapq, Sigmaqq, delta): # Sigmapq: (p, C), Sigmaqq: (C, C), delta: (C,) # Solve Sigmaqq @ x = delta for x, then compute shift x = solve(Sigmaqq, delta) return Sigmapq @ x Formulas and Definitions \mathbf{s}q: Diagonal of the query covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}. \mathbf{B}e: Bounded Cholesky coefficient matrix with entries in [-1, 1]. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}: Spatial covariance block. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq}: Cross-covariance block between spatial and query dimensions. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}: Query covariance block. Bounded norm: \|\mathbf{B}\|2 \leq \|\mathbf{B}\|F \leq \sqrt{p} \|\mathbf{s}q\|2. Cross-covariance row bound: \|(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq}){i,:}\|2 \leq \sqrt{p} \|\mathbf{s}q\|2 \sqrt{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}){ii}}. Rendered shift: \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1} \delta = \mathbf{M}{\text{N-DGS}} \delta. Normalized cross-covariance: \mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}^{-1/2} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1/2}. Whitened shift: \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}^{1/2} \mathbf{K} \mathbf{h} where \mathbf{h} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1/2} \delta. Basis-independent bound: \left\| \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}^{-1/2} \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}} \right\|2 \leq \left\| \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1/2} \delta \right\|2. Parameters \mathbf{s}q: Query diagonal scales. \mathbf{B}e: Bounded coefficients constrained to [-1, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls 1. Interpretation of Off-Diagonals: Off-diagonal entries of \mathbf{A} contribute to both \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} and the spatial extent (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}){ii}; they should not be interpreted as producing cross-covariance independently of spatial scale. 2. Ill-Conditioned Query Covariance: A bound on \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} alone does not bound the shift \Delta \mu. The inverse query covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1} and the query deviation \delta also enter the calculation. A narrow or ill-conditioned query covariance can amplify the regression operator. 3. Precision: The inversion of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} during the computation of the shift \Delta \mu can be numerically unstable if \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} is close to singular. dGS is a parameterization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes conditional opacity and position directly from explicit per-primitive parameters, avoiding the query-block inversion and covariance correction required by N-DGS. It replaces the joint covariance-derived conditioning with a Cholesky factor for opacity precision, a spatial coupling factor for position, and a coupling vector to tie them, enabling faster slicing and differentiable optimization of Gaussian positions without local minima. dGS Direct Regression Parameterization Conditional-coordinate parameterization provides a non-redundant, smooth bijection between the space of joint Gaussian covariances and a set of operational quantities: conditional spatial covariance, query-space precision, and a regression operator. It solves the problem of efficiently representing and optimizing the cross-covariance between spatial and query dimensions in differentiable Gaussian splatting by avoiding the computational cost and instability of inverting the query covariance block during rendering. Unlike N-DGS, which derives the regression operator from a joint Cholesky factor, this method directly optimizes the regression operator and precision, treating the coupling as a block shear. Conditional-coordinate parameterization In N-DGS, the off-diagonal entries of \mathbf{A} contribute to both cross-covariance and spatial extent, meaning they cannot be interpreted as producing cross-covariance independently of spatial scale. N-DGS derives the regression operator implicitly from covariance blocks, requiring inversion of the query block to compute the conditional mean. This contrasts with dGS, which directly parameterizes the regression operator \mathbf{M}, avoiding this inversion. The dGS joint covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^ is defined by conditional covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\text{cond}}, regression operator \mathbf{M}, and query precision \boldsymbol{\Pi}. Its blocks are \Sigma{qq}^ = \frac{1}{2\lambdao} \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}, \Sigma{pq}^ = \frac{1}{2\lambdao} \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}), and \Sigma{pp}^ = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\text{cond}} + \frac{1}{2\lambda0} \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{pq}^\top. The opacity exponent corresponds to the query-marginal quadratic form -\lambdao \delta^\top \mathbf{V}{qq} \delta. The coupling strength is controlled by \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \in [0, 1]^C, where \boldsymbol{\Lambda}=0 decouples position from query and \boldsymbol{\Lambda}=1 enables full coupling. The internal factorization of \mathbf{M} into \mathbf{V}{pq} and \boldsymbol{\Lambda} is not claimed to be bijective. Standard Gaussian splatting uses an unnormalized Gaussian kernel, so the normalization factor is omitted from the renderer. Time and Memory Complexity Memory: N-DGS stores the Cholesky factors \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}e, and \mathbf{D}, matching the joint covariance parameter count \frac{p(p+1)}{2} + pC + \frac{C(C+1)}{2}. Time: Rendering requires computing the conditional mean shift \Delta \mu = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1} \delta, which involves inverting \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} (O(C^3)) and matrix-vector multiplication. N-DGS derives the regression operator implicitly from covariance blocks, requiring inversion of the query block, whereas dGS directly parameterizes the regression operator \mathbf{M}, avoiding this inversion. Measured Performance On two trained MCMC scenes with six views each, the opacity-weighted \|\Delta \mu\|/\bar{s} has a median of 0.29–0.30 and a 99th percentile of 4.8–7.0 for N-DGS. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Provides a bounded parameterization for cross-covariance. Limitations: The regression operator is implicit, making it harder to control directly compared to dGS. The shift can be amplified by ill-conditioned query covariance. The bounded Cholesky coefficients do not directly bound the shift, only the cross-covariance norm. When to Use Use N-DGS when the implicit parameterization is acceptable and the query covariance is well-conditioned. When Not to Use Avoid N-DGS if direct control over the regression operator is required or if the query covariance is likely to be ill-conditioned. N-DGS is part of the family of N-Dimensional Gaussian Splatting methods, which extend 3DGS to higher dimensions. It parameterizes the joint covariance using bounded Cholesky coefficients multiplied by query diagonal scales to control spatial extent and cross-covariance.
