name: dGS Direct Regression Parameterization
head: Direct Conditional Parameterization for Gaussian Splatting, dGS
body: dGS is a parameterization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes conditional opacity and position directly from explicit per-primitive parameters, avoiding the query-block inversion and covariance correction required by N-DGS. It replaces the joint covariance-derived conditioning with a Cholesky factor for opacity precision, a spatial coupling factor for position, and a coupling vector to tie them, enabling faster slicing and differentiable optimization of Gaussian positions without local minima. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Base Gaussian parameters (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}p, base opacity \alpha, spatial scales sx, sy, sz), query deviation \boldsymbol{\delta} = \boldsymbol{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}q (where \boldsymbol{q} is the query coordinate in view/time space), and learned conditioning parameters (\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{V}{pq}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}). Outputs: Conditional opacity \alpha{\text{cond}}, conditional mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}}. The conditional covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\text{cond}} remains query-independent and is computed as in standard 3DGS. Data Structures: 1. \mathbf{L} (Cholesky Factor): Lower-triangular matrix in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}, where C is the dimensionality of the query space (e.g., C=3 for view, C=4 for view+time). Diagonal elements use exponential activation to ensure \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top is symmetric positive-definite. For C=4, all 10 lower-triangular entries are learned. 2. \mathbf{V}{pq} (Spatial Coupling Factor): Matrix in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C}. Defined as \mathbf{V}{pq} = \bar{s} \boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq}, where \bar{s} = \text{mean}(sx, sy, sz) is the average spatial scale, and \boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq} is a learnable direction with unit Frobenius norm (\|\boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq}\|F = 1). This enforces \|\mathbf{V}{pq}\|F = \bar{s} and \|\mathbf{V}{pq}^{(i)}\|2 \leq \bar{s}. 3. \boldsymbol{\Lambda} (Coupling Vector): Vector in [0, 1]^C. Weights the precision-transformed query channels in the position update. Channels of the same type (e.g., the three view dimensions) share a logit. Formulas: Opacity Calculation: \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \exp(-\lambdao \|\mathbf{L}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}\|2^2) where \lambdao = 0.35 is a fixed opacity scaling factor inherited from N-DGS. Position Calculation: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta} where \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top is the precision matrix. Expanded Opacity for C=4 (View + Time): \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \exp(-\lambdao (\boldsymbol{\delta}v^\top \mathbf{V}{vv} \boldsymbol{\delta}v + 2\deltat \boldsymbol{\delta}v^\top \mathbf{v}{vt} + \deltat^2 vt)) where \mathbf{V}{vv}, \mathbf{v}{vt}, vt are the view, cross, and time blocks of \mathbf{V}{qq}. Matrix Definitions: \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top \mathbf{M}{\text{dGS}} = \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \mathbf{F}{pq} = \bar{s} \boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq}, \quad \|\boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq}\|F = 1 Parameters: \lambdao: Opacity scaling factor, fixed at 0.35. \bar{s}: Explicit spatial-scale prior on the coupling factor, calculated as the mean of the primitive's spatial scales. Pitfalls: Removing the spatial factor \bar{s} degrades PSNR by 2.65 dB on NeRF Synthetic and 2.97 dB on 6DGS-PBR. \bar{s} is a prior on the coupling factor, not a bound on the effective regression or rendered shift, which also depends on \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\mathbf{V}{qq} and \boldsymbol{\delta}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dgsconditioning(mup, alpha, sx, sy, sz, L, Vpq, Lambda, delta, lambdao=0.35): """ Computes conditional opacity and position for a single Gaussian primitive. Args: mup: Base position (3,) alpha: Base opacity (scalar) sx, sy, sz: Spatial scales (scalars) L: Lower-triangular Cholesky factor (C, C) Vpq: Spatial coupling factor (3, C) Lambda: Coupling vector (C,) with values in [0, 1] delta: Query deviation (C,) lambdao: Opacity scaling factor (scalar) Returns: alphacond: Conditional opacity (scalar) mucond: Conditional mean (3,) """ C = L.shape[0] # 1. Compute L^T delta LTdelta = [0.0] C for i in range(C): s = 0.0 for j in range(i, C): s += L[j, i] delta[j] LTdelta[i] = s # 2. Compute Conditional Opacity: alphacond = alpha exp(-lambdao ||L^T delta||^2) normsq = sum(x x for x in LTdelta) alphacond = alpha math.exp(-lambdao normsq) # 3. Compute Conditional Position: mucond = mup + Vpq @ diag(Lambda) @ Vqq @ delta # Vqq @ delta = L @ (L^T @ delta) Vqqdelta = [0.0] C for i in range(C): s = 0.0 for j in range(i, C): s += L[i, j] LTdelta[j] Vqqdelta[i] = s # Apply diag(Lambda) LambdaVqqdelta = [Lambda[i] Vqqdelta[i] for i in range(C)] # Multiply by Vpq Vpqterm = [0.0] 3 for i in range(3): s = 0.0 for j in range(C): s += Vpq[i, j] LambdaVqqdelta[j] Vpqterm[i] = s # Add to mup mucond = [mup[i] + Vpqterm[i] for i in range(3)] return alphacond, mucond A method for predicting Gaussian parameters from per-pixel features using a discrete probability distribution over depth buckets, solving local minima issues in direct regression. It provides a ~1 dB PSNR boost over direct regression baselines by enabling differentiable optimization of Gaussian positions via a reparameterization trick. Time Complexity: The kernel uses compile-time loop unrolling for C (3 or 4). Each thread processes one primitive. \mathbf{L}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta} uses C(C+1)/2 multiplications followed by a dot product, all in per-thread registers. No intermediate tensors or shared-memory traffic. Memory Complexity: Stores \mathbf{L} (C^2 params), \mathbf{V}{pq} (3C params), and \boldsymbol{\Lambda} (C params). For C=3, dGS uses 22 conditioning parameters; for C=4, it uses 24 parameters. Measured Performance: On an A100 with 1M primitives, slicing time for C=3 is 0.67ms for dGS (7.1x faster than N-DGS at 0.71ms) and 1.34ms for C=4 (7.7x faster than N-DGS at 0.96ms). In a separate harness, dGS is 2.0–2.3× faster than inference-cached N-DGS. Strengths: Avoids query-block inversion, regression construction, and covariance correction. Faster than N-DGS. Preserves compatibility with existing densification strategies as \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\text{cond}} is query-independent. Limitations: Performance gain is most pronounced on Mip-NeRF 360. On 6DGS-PBR, dGS-O (opacity-only) shows modest speedup but quality drop, while dGS recovers quality. When to Use: When faster slicing is required and differentiable position optimization is needed without the complexity of joint covariance parameterization. dGS is introduced in the cited source as a direct alternative to N-DGS. It was developed to address the computational overhead of query-block inversion in N-DGS and UBS, exposing rendered quantities directly through explicit parameters. It is used in UBS implementation experiments and compared against N-DGS under standard 3DGS densification. Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Probabilistic Prediction of Pixel-Aligned Gaussians
head: Discrete Depth Bucketing for Gaussians, Probabilistic Gaussian Prediction
body: This method predicts 3D Gaussian primitive parameters (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics \mathbf{S}) from per-pixel features by modeling the depth distribution as a discrete probability density over depth buckets, rather than regressing a point estimate. It solves the problem of local minima inherent in direct regression of Gaussian centers and enables differentiable training where non-differentiable spawning/pruning heuristics from 3D-GS cannot be applied. It sets itself apart from direct regression methods by predicting a probability distribution \boldsymbol{\phi} over depth bins, which provides an approximate 1dB PSNR performance boost. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Per-pixel feature vector \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] at pixel coordinate \mathbf{u}, camera origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}{\mathbf{u}}, depth range [d{\text{near}}, d{\text{far}}], and number of depth buckets Z. Output: A tuple (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \alpha, \mathbf{S}) representing one Gaussian primitive per pixel (simplified case M=1). Data Structures: Depth Buckets \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^Z: A vector representing discrete depth values in disparity space. The z-th element \mathbf{b}z is defined as: \mathbf{b}z = \left( \left(1 - \frac{z}{Z}\right) \left(\frac{1}{d{\text{near}}} - \frac{1}{d{\text{far}}}\right) + \frac{1}{d{\text{far}}} \right)^{-1} where z \in \{0, \dots, Z-1\} is the bucket index. Probability Vector \boldsymbol{\phi} \in \mathbb{R}^Z: Discrete probabilities predicted by the network, normalized via softmax such that \sumz \phiz = 1. \phiz represents the probability that a surface exists in depth bucket \mathbf{b}z. Offset Vector \boldsymbol{\delta} \in \mathbb{R}^Z: Per-bucket center offsets \deltaz \in [0, 1] that adjust the depth between bucket boundaries. Parameters: Z: Number of depth bins/buckets discretizing the depth range. d{\text{near}}, d{\text{far}}: Near and far planes defining the depth range. M: Number of Gaussian primitives predicted per pixel. The text simplifies to M=1 for the explanation. Steps: 1. Prediction: A neural network f processes the per-pixel feature \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] to predict the depth probability vector \boldsymbol{\phi}, the offset vector \boldsymbol{\delta}, the covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, and the spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{S}: (\boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\delta}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \mathbf{S}) = f(\mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}]) 2. Sampling: Sample a depth bucket index z from the discrete probability distribution parameterized by \boldsymbol{\phi}: z \sim p{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(z) 3. Mean Computation: Compute the Gaussian mean \boldsymbol{\mu} by unprojecting the sampled depth bucket \mathbf{b}z adjusted by the offset \deltaz along the ray direction \mathbf{d}{\mathbf{u}} from the camera origin \mathbf{o}: \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{o} + (\mathbf{b}z + \deltaz)\mathbf{d}{\mathbf{u}} 4. Opacity Assignment: Set the Gaussian opacity \alpha equal to the probability of the sampled bucket: \alpha = \phiz 5. Return: Return the tuple (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \alpha, \mathbf{S}). Backpropagation (Reparameterization Trick): To make sampling differentiable, gradients of the loss \mathcal{L} with respect to the opacity \alpha are assigned to the gradients of the depth probability buckets \boldsymbol{\phi}: \nabla{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \mathcal{L} = \nabla{\alpha} \mathcal{L} This allows gradient descent to increase the opacity of correctly sampled depths (concentrating probability mass) and decrease it for incorrect samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def probabilisticprediction(Fu, b, o, du): """ Predicts a single Gaussian primitive per pixel using probabilistic depth bucketing. Args: Fu: Per-pixel feature vector. b: Depth bucket vector in disparity space, shape (Z,). o: Camera origin vector. du: Ray direction vector. Returns: mu: Gaussian mean vector. Sigma: Gaussian covariance matrix. alpha: Gaussian opacity. S: Spherical harmonics coefficients. """ # f is a neural network predicting parameters phi, delta, Sigma, S = f(Fu) def samplediscrete(p): """Sample an index from a categorical distribution.""" cum = np.cumsum(p) return np.searchsorted(cum, np.random.rand()) # Sample depth bucket index z from discrete distribution phi z = samplediscrete(phi) # Compute mean mu bz = b[z] deltaz = delta[z] mu = o + (bz + deltaz) du # Set opacity alpha to the probability of the sampled bucket alpha = phi[z] return mu, Sigma, alpha, S Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: Directly regressing the Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu} is susceptible to local minima. Non-differentiable Heuristics: The method avoids reliance on spawning and pruning heuristics from 3D-GS, which are not differentiable. Precision: The depth buckets are defined in disparity space to handle non-linear depth distributions, but precision depends on the number of buckets Z. This method predicts the color of a 3D Gaussian primitive by aggregating information from multiple nearby reference frames, using monocular depth priors to filter out occluded regions. It addresses the problem of retrieving inaccurate color information from 2D reference images due to occlusions, which degrades rendering quality in generalizable Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart from direct regression methods by leveraging Inter-View Consistency and explicit visibility estimation to distinguish visible from invisible features, allowing the model to focus on visible views without manual thresholding. Performance: The probabilistic prediction method leads to an approximate 1dB PSNR performance boost compared to the baseline of directly regressing the depth. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Overcomes local minima associated with direct regression; enables differentiable training without non-differentiable heuristics. Limitations: Requires sampling during the forward pass, which introduces stochasticity; relies on the reparameterization trick for gradient flow. When to use: When direct regression of Gaussian centers leads to local minima or when differentiable training is required without relying on 3D-GS heuristics. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "PixelSplat: 3D Gaussian Splats from Image Pairs for Scalable Generalizable 3D Reconstruction". It addresses limitations in predicting Gaussian parameters from reference views, specifically the susceptibility of direct regression to local minima and the inability to use non-differentiable spawning/pruning heuristics. The approach predicts Gaussians from both reference views, with the final set being the union of predicted Gaussians. PixelSplat: 3D Gaussian Splats from Image Pairs for Scalable Generalizable 3D Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01840, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Occlusion-Aware IBR-based Color Prediction
head: IBR Color Prediction, Occlusion-Aware Color Prediction
body: This method predicts the color of a 3D Gaussian primitive by aggregating information from multiple nearby reference frames, using monocular depth priors to filter out occluded regions. It addresses the problem of retrieving inaccurate color information from 2D reference images due to occlusions, which degrades rendering quality in generalizable Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart from direct regression methods by leveraging explicit visibility estimation to distinguish visible from invisible features, allowing the model to focus on visible views without manual thresholding. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitive Gi with center \mui. Set of K nearby reference frames with camera centers tk. Monocular depth maps Dr for the reference frames. Reference frame images. Outputs: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients representing the color ci of the Gaussian. Data Structures: Local color window c{ik} \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times W \times 3}: A 3D tensor of size W \times W \times 3 containing RGB values sampled from the reference frame k. Visibility map v{ik} \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times W}: A 2D tensor of size W \times W containing visibility weights. Distance scalar \delta{ik} \in \mathbb{R}. Relative direction vector \overrightarrow{\mathbf{\theta}}{ik} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: K: Number of nearby reference frames. Not given in the sources. W: Window size for local color sampling. Effective choice is W=3. Steps: 1. Projection: For each reference frame k \in \{1, \dots, K\}, project the 3D Gaussian center \mui to the 2D image plane of the reference frame. 2. Local Color Sampling: Sample a local color window c{ik} of size W \times W \times 3 from the reference frame image k, centered at the 2D projection of \mui. This integrates 2D texture information and enhances robustness against noisy 3D Gaussian locations. 3. Depth Retrieval: Bilinearly retrieve the monocular depth map Dr as pseudo ground truth at the 2D projection location. 4. Distance Calculation: Compute the Euclidean distance \delta{ik} between the Gaussian center \mui and the reference camera center tk: \delta{ik} = \|\mui - tk\|2 5. Visibility Estimation: Estimate the visibility map v{ik} for the window based on the difference between the projected depth and the retrieved monocular depth. The formula is: v{ik} = \frac{\delta{ik} - d{ik}}{\delta{ik}} Here, d{ik} denotes the depth window corresponding to c{ik}. This step eliminates invisibility projections based on depth priors. 6. Relative Direction Calculation: Compute the normalized relative direction vector \overrightarrow{\mathbf{\theta}}{ik} from the camera to the Gaussian: \overrightarrow{\mathbf{\theta}}{ik} = \frac{\mui - tk}{\|\mui - tk\|2} 7. Aggregation: Pass the collected features from all K frames through an aggregation module \mathcal{M} to derive the final Gaussian color ci. The module \mathcal{M} is implemented as a three-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with a width of 64. The input to \mathcal{M} is the set of tuples \{c{ik}, v{ik}, \delta{ik}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{\theta}}{ik}\}{k=1}^{K}. 8. SH Representation: The output of \mathcal{M} is represented as Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients to model view-dependent color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def project2d(point3d, intrinsics, extrinsics): """Projects a 3D point to 2D image coordinates using standard pinhole camera model.""" # Standard graphics operation: p2d = K R [P | t] [point3d; 1] # Returns normalized 2D coordinates (u, v) pass def bilinearsample(tensor, u, v, windowsize): """Samples a windowsize x windowsize region from tensor at (u, v) using bilinear interpolation.""" # Standard graphics operation pass def occlusionawarecolorprediction(mui, refframes, W=3): """ Predicts Gaussian color using occlusion-aware IBR. Args: mui: 3D center of the Gaussian (3,) refframes: List of K reference frame data structures. Each frame contains: 'image': H x Wimg x 3 tensor 'depth': H x Wimg tensor (monocular depth map Dr) 'cameracenter': 3D position tk (3,) 'intrinsics': Camera intrinsic matrix 'extrinsics': Camera extrinsic matrix W: Window size for sampling (default 3). Returns: shcoeffs: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for the Gaussian color. """ features = [] for frame in refframes: tk = frame['cameracenter'] imgk = frame['image'] depthk = frame['depth'] # 1. Project mui to 2D uk, vk = project2d(mui, frame['intrinsics'], frame['extrinsics']) # 2. Sample local color window cik cik = bilinearsample(imgk, uk, vk, W) # Shape: W x W x 3 # 3. Retrieve monocular depth window dik dik = bilinearsample(depthk, uk, vk, W) # Shape: W x W # 4. Calculate distance deltaik deltaik = norm(mui - tk) # 5. Estimate visibility map vik vik = (deltaik - dik) / deltaik # Shape: W x W # 6. Calculate relative direction thetaik thetaik = (mui - tk) / norm(mui - tk) features.append({ 'cik': cik, 'vik': vik, 'deltaik': deltaik, 'thetaik': thetaik }) # 7. Aggregation via MLP M # M is a 3-layer MLP with hidden width 64. # Input: concatenation of features from all K frames. # The exact concatenation strategy is not detailed in the source. # We assume features are flattened and concatenated along the channel dimension. inputtensor = concatenate([f['cik'].flatten() for f in features]) inputtensor = concatenate([inputtensor, f['vik'].flatten() for f in features]) inputtensor = concatenate([inputtensor, [f['deltaik'] for f in features]]) inputtensor = concatenate([inputtensor, f['thetaik'] for f in features]) # 8. SH Representation shcoeffs = aggregationmlp(inputtensor) return shcoeffs def aggregationmlp(x): """ Aggregation module M: 3-layer MLP, width 64. Input x is the concatenated feature vector. Output is SH coefficients. """ # Layer 1: Linear(64) -> ReLU x = relu(linear(x, 64)) # Layer 2: Linear(64) -> ReLU x = relu(linear(x, 64)) # Layer 3: Linear(64) -> SHDIM shcoeffs = linear(x, SHDIM) return shcoeffs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Bilinear retrieval of depth and color requires careful handling of boundary conditions if the projection falls outside the image frame. Occlusion Ambiguity: The visibility formula v{ik} = (\delta{ik} - d{ik})/\delta{ik} assumes that if the monocular depth d{ik} is significantly smaller than the projected depth \delta{ik}, the point is occluded. If d{ik} > \delta{ik}, the visibility might become negative, which should be handled (e.g., clamped to 0) depending on implementation, though the source does not explicitly specify clamping. Noisy Depth: The method relies on monocular depth as pseudo ground truth. Inaccurate depth priors may lead to incorrect visibility estimation. Time Complexity: Depends on K (number of reference frames) and W (window size). For each Gaussian, K projections and window samplings are performed, followed by an MLP inference. Memory Complexity: Stores local color windows and visibility maps for K frames per Gaussian during the forward pass. Strengths: Improves robustness against noisy 3D Gaussian locations by integrating 2D texture information. Effectively distinguishes occlusion-caused features using depth priors, enhancing rendering quality. Limitations: Relies on the quality of monocular depth estimates. Requires access to reference frames and their depth maps. When to use: When generalizable Gaussian Splatting suffers from occlusion artifacts and inaccurate color retrieval from 2D references. When not to use: If monocular depth priors are unavailable or highly unreliable. This method is part of the EVolSplat framework, introduced in "EVolSplat: Efficient Volume-based Gaussian Splatting for Urban View Synthesis". It addresses issues in generalizable Gaussian Splatting where occlusions lead to inaccurate color information. The method extends projection locations into local sample windows and leverages depth priors to eliminate invisibility projections. EVolSplat: Efficient Volume-based Gaussian Splatting for Urban View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.01054, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Conditional-coordinate parameterization
head: Proposition C.1, dGS conditional parameterization
body: Conditional-coordinate parameterization provides a non-redundant, smooth bijection between the space of joint Gaussian covariances and a set of operational quantities: conditional spatial covariance, query-space precision, and a regression operator. It solves the problem of efficiently representing and optimizing the cross-covariance between spatial and query dimensions in differentiable Gaussian splatting by avoiding the computational cost and instability of inverting the query covariance block during rendering. Unlike N-DGS, which derives the regression operator from a joint Cholesky factor, this method directly optimizes the regression operator and precision, treating the coupling as a block shear. Inputs and Outputs Input: A joint covariance matrix \Psi \in \mathbb{R}^{(p+C) \times (p+C)} that is symmetric positive-definite (SPD), where p is the spatial dimension and C is the query dimension. Output: A triplet (\Sigma{\text{cond}}, \mathbf{M}, \mathbf{V}{qq}) where: \Sigma{\text{cond}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p} is the conditional spatial covariance (SPD). \mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times C} is the effective query-to-position regression operator. \mathbf{V}{qq} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C} is the query-space precision matrix (SPD). Data Structures \Sigma{\text{cond}}: Stored as a symmetric matrix. In practice, only the lower triangular part is stored to save memory, requiring p(p+1)/2 parameters. \mathbf{M}: Stored as a dense rectangular matrix, requiring pC parameters. \mathbf{V}{qq}: Stored as a symmetric matrix. In dGS implementations, it is factorized as \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top where \mathbf{L} is lower triangular with strictly positive diagonal entries to ensure positive definiteness, requiring C(C+1)/2 parameters. Numbered Steps 1. Decompose Joint Covariance: Given \Psi, extract the blocks \Sigma{pp} (p \times p), \Sigma{pq} (p \times C), and \Sigma{qq} (C \times C). 2. Compute Query Precision: Invert \Sigma{qq} to obtain \mathbf{V}{qq}. 3. Compute Regression Operator: Multiply \Sigma{pq} by \mathbf{V}{qq} to obtain \mathbf{M}. 4. Compute Conditional Covariance: Subtract the Schur complement term \Sigma{pq} \mathbf{V}{qq} \Sigma{pq}^\top from \Sigma{pp} to obtain \Sigma{\text{cond}}. 5. Validation: Ensure \Sigma{\text{cond}} and \mathbf{V}{qq} are positive definite. If using the Cholesky factorization for \mathbf{V}{qq}, enforce strictly positive diagonal elements in \mathbf{L}. Formulas The joint covariance \Psi is parameterized by the triplet via the following block structure: \Psi = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{pp} & \Sigma{pq} \\ \Sigma{pq}^\top & \Sigma{qq} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{\text{cond}} + \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top & \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} \\ \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top & \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} \end{pmatrix} The blocks are defined as: 1. \Sigma{qq} = \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} 2. \Sigma{pq} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} 3. \Sigma{pp} = \Sigma{\text{cond}} + \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top These relations follow from the block-triangular factorization \Psi = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{I}p & \mathbf{M} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I}C \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{cond}} & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{I}p & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{M}^\top & \mathbf{I}C \end{pmatrix}. The inverse map, recovering the parameters from a given joint covariance \Psi, is: 1. \mathbf{V}{qq} = \Sigma{qq}^{-1} 2. \mathbf{M} = \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} 3. \Sigma{\text{cond}} = \Sigma{pp} - \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} \Sigma{pq}^\top The Schur complement theorem guarantees \Sigma{\text{cond}} \succ \mathbf{0}. The volume-element Jacobian of the coordinate transformation has a closed-form determinant: |\det D\Psi| = (\det \mathbf{V}{qq})^{-(p+C+1)} For spatial dimension p=3, this simplifies to (\det \mathbf{V}{qq})^{-(C+4)}. Parameters p: Spatial dimension (typically 3). C: Query dimension (e.g., number of query features or dimensions). Typical values: For 3D Gaussian Splatting, p=3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Singularity: The map is singular if \mathbf{V}{qq} approaches singularity (\det \mathbf{V}{qq} \to 0) or if \Sigma{\text{cond}} approaches its boundary (becomes singular). The construction \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top with strictly positive Cholesky diagonal keeps the parameterization in the interior of the SPD domain. Precision: Inverting \Sigma{qq} can be numerically unstable if \Sigma{qq} is ill-conditioned. Using the Cholesky factorization of \mathbf{V}{qq} directly avoids explicit inversion in some contexts, but the definition relies on \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def jointtoconditionalparameters(Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq): """ Converts joint covariance blocks to conditional-coordinate parameters. Args: Sigmapp: (p, p) ndarray, symmetric positive-definite. Sigmapq: (p, C) ndarray. Sigmaqq: (C, C) ndarray, symmetric positive-definite. Returns: Sigmacond: (p, p) ndarray, conditional spatial covariance. M: (p, C) ndarray, regression operator. Vqq: (C, C) ndarray, query-space precision. """ # Step 2: Compute Query Precision Vqq = Sigmaqq^-1 Vqq = np.linalg.inv(Sigmaqq) # Step 3: Compute Regression Operator M = Sigmapq Vqq M = Sigmapq @ Vqq # Step 4: Compute Conditional Covariance Sigmacond = Sigmapp - Sigmapq Vqq Sigmapq^T Sigmacond = Sigmapp - Sigmapq @ Vqq @ Sigmapq.T return Sigmacond, M, Vqq def conditionalparameterstojoint(Sigmacond, M, Vqq): """ Reconstructs joint covariance blocks from conditional-coordinate parameters. Args: Sigmacond: (p, p) ndarray, conditional spatial covariance. M: (p, C) ndarray, regression operator. Vqq: (C, C) ndarray, query-space precision. Returns: Sigmapp: (p, p) ndarray. Sigmapq: (p, C) ndarray. Sigmaqq: (C, C) ndarray. """ # Invert Vqq to get Sigmaqq Sigmaqq = np.linalg.inv(Vqq) # Compute Sigmapq = M Vqq^-1 = M Sigmaqq Sigmapq = M @ Sigmaqq # Compute Sigmapp = Sigmacond + M Vqq^-1 M^T Sigmapp = Sigmacond + M @ Sigmaqq @ M.T return Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq Time Complexity: The forward map involves matrix inversion (O(C^3)) and matrix multiplications (O(p^2 C + p C^2)). The inverse map involves similar operations. For fixed p and C, this is constant time per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: The parameter count is \frac{p(p+1)}{2} + pC + \frac{C(C+1)}{2} = \frac{(p+C)(p+C+1)}{2}, which is non-redundant and matches the number of parameters in the full joint covariance matrix. Strengths: Efficiency: Avoids repeated inversion of the query covariance block during rendering by optimizing \mathbf{V}{qq} and \mathbf{M} directly. Stability: The block shear interpretation provides a clear geometric understanding and stable optimization landscape when \mathbf{V}{qq} is kept positive definite. Non-redundancy: The parameterization is a smooth bijection, ensuring no loss of information. Limitations: Singularity Risk: If \mathbf{V}{qq} becomes singular, the parameterization breaks down. Strictly positive Cholesky diagonals are required. Complexity: The inverse map requires matrix inversion, which can be costly for large C. When to Use: Use when optimizing query-dependent Gaussian splats where the query-space precision and regression operator are natural optimization variables. Prefer over N-DGS when avoiding query covariance inversion during rendering is critical. The conditional-coordinate parameterization was introduced in the context of differentiable Gaussian splatting, specifically in the "Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting" paper. It formalizes the relationship between joint Gaussian covariances and their conditional components, providing a theoretical foundation for efficient optimization of query-dependent splats. The method leverages the Schur complement and block-triangular factorization to define a smooth bijection between the joint covariance space and the conditional parameters. name: Gaussian-based Representation
head: Gaussian mixture model
body: Gaussian-based representation encodes signals, data, or geometric structures as an explicit, continuous sum (or mixture) of parameterized Gaussian functions, enabling efficient, closed-form operations for high-dimensional applications. It solves the problem of representing complex, high-frequency signals or 3D scenes with a compact, differentiable primitive set that supports fast rendering and optimization. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Preliminaries, which focuses on specific rasterization pipelines for novel view synthesis, this method provides the general mathematical formalism for signal approximation via Gaussian superposition, applicable to 2D images, 3D fields, and vector spaces. It differs from Gabor Fields by using isotropic or anisotropic Gaussians for direct amplitude modeling rather than decomposing signals into low-pass bases and high-frequency residual kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target signal f{\text{target}}(\mathbf{x}) defined over a domain \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d (e.g., pixel coordinates for images, 3D space for scenes), and a number of primitives N. Output: A set of N Gaussian parameters \{\thetan\}{n=1}^N such that the reconstructed signal f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{n=1}^N Gn(\mathbf{x}) approximates f{\text{target}}(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive n is parameterized by: Location: \boldsymbol\mun \in \mathbb{R}^d. Shape: \boldsymbol\Sigman \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, a symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix. In practice, this is often parameterized via Cholesky decomposition or rotation-scaling decomposition (e.g., quaternion \mathbf{q}n and scale vector \mathbf{s}n) to ensure positive definiteness and reduce parameter count. For 2D image fitting, the covariance uses 3 Cholesky values. Amplitude/Attributes: an. For 2D images, this is typically a color vector (e.g., RGB). For 3D scenes, this may include opacity, view-dependent radiance (via spherical harmonics coefficients), or semantic embeddings. Mathematical Formulation: The canonical Gaussian primitive in d-dimensional Euclidean space is: Gn(\mathbf{x}) = an \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mun)^\top \boldsymbol\Sigman^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mun)\right) The total representation aggregates these as a sum: f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{n=1}^N Gn(\mathbf{x}) where the physical or semantic meaning of f depends on context (image intensity, field value, feature embedding, etc.). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize N Gaussians using vectorized initialization from eigenspaces (EigenGS), mapping principal components to Gaussian space for instant initialization. Recent methods replace per-instance random or iterative optimizations with feedforward network prediction that infers Gaussian parameters or densities in a feedforward pass. 2. Optimization: Minimize a loss function \mathcal{L} between the rendered/evaluated signal f(\mathbf{x}) and the target f{\text{target}}(\mathbf{x}). For 2D images, the primary loss is typically L2 (MSE) or hybrid L2+D-SSIM over all pixels. For 3D scenes, photometric losses over multiple views or ray samples are combined with sparsity, density, or geometric constraints. Gradient descent updates \boldsymbol\mun, \boldsymbol\Sigman, an using the analytic derivatives of the Gaussian function. 3. Adaptive Deployment (Optional): Densification algorithms such as SplitNet or confidence-aware splitting create additional Gaussians where residuals concentrate. Pruning removes Gaussians where coverage is redundant or negligible. Hierarchical and multi-level fitting (Level-of-Gaussian) establishes a coarse, low-frequency backbone, followed by high-frequency or residual Gaussians for detail. 4. Rendering/Aggregation: For 2D images, use permutation-invariant summation; alpha blending or transmittance accumulation is unnecessary as occlusion is irrelevant. For 3D scenes, use rasterized ellipsoid splatting: each Gaussian is projected, depth-sorted, and alpha-blended front-to-back to yield correct occlusion and volumetric effects. 5. Compression (Optional): Apply adaptive quantization, vector quantization, codebook-based compression, and entropy coders (e.g., ANS, Huffman) for compact storage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussianprimitive(x, mu, sigmainv, amplitude): diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diff, sigmainv @ diff) return amplitude np.exp(exponent) def evaluaterepresentation(primitives, xsamples): predictions = np.zeros(len(xsamples)) for i, x in enumerate(xsamples): predictions[i] = sum(gaussianprimitive(x, mu, sigmainv, amp) for mu, sigmainv, amp in primitives) return predictions def traingaussians(targetfn, initialprimitives, xsamples, numiterations, lr): primitives = [list(p) for p in initialprimitives] for in range(numiterations): ypred = evaluaterepresentation(primitives, xsamples) ytrue = np.array([targetfn(x) for x in xsamples]) loss = np.mean((ypred - ytrue) 2) # Compute gradients d(loss)/d(mu), d(loss)/d(sigmainv), d(loss)/d(amp) via automatic differentiation # Update parameters: param -= lr gradient return primitives Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Structures: Very high-frequency structures may require many primitives or specialized learning schedules due to trade-offs between parameter count and signal complexity. Parameter Redundancy: Potential for parameter redundancy or non-uniqueness if the base space is not managed, e.g., ambiguous quaternions or covariances in 3DGS. Positive Definiteness: Covariance matrices must remain symmetric positive-definite during optimization; parameterizing via Cholesky or rotation-scaling decomposition helps. A continuous volumetric representation decomposing signals into a low-pass Gaussian base and anisotropic Gabor kernel residuals, achieving higher PSNR and faster rendering by concentrating spectral energy. A signal representation technique decomposing 1D signals into weighted Gaussian PDFs, offering local representation unlike global Fourier transforms, and approximating signal values rather than data distributions. A compact representation separating coarse structure (Gaussians) from high-frequency residuals (hashed field), preventing aliasing and smoothing artifacts common in single-resolution approaches. Time Complexity: Rendering is highly parallelizable. 2D GaussianImage achieves 1000–2000 FPS, significantly faster than MLP-based Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) or classic codecs (10–150 FPS). 3DGS achieves ~120 FPS on Mip-NeRF 360. Memory Complexity: Depends on N and attribute size. Compact 3DGS uses 29 MB for scene synthesis, compared to 746 MB for standard 3DGS. LIG (9K×9K image) uses 16.7–20.3 GB. Measured Performance: GaussianImage (2D) achieves 44.1 dB PSNR with 0.4 GB memory. 3DGS (Mip-NeRF 360) achieves 27.46 dB PSNR with 746 MB memory. Hybrid mesh–GS achieves 24.28 dB PSNR with 0.74M splats. GARLIC (SIFT1M 128D) achieves Recall@1=0.69 for K-NN classification. Strengths: Orders-of-magnitude faster decoding than INRs; analytic differentiability enables closed-form differential operator evaluation for physics/simulation; adaptable to 2D, 3D, and vector spaces. Limitations: High-frequency structures require many primitives; potential for parameter redundancy; domain-specific rendering optimizations needed. When to Use: When fast rendering, differentiability, and compact representation of complex signals or scenes are required. Ideal for image compression, 3D scene reconstruction, and vector search. When Not to Use: For extremely high-frequency details where the number of required Gaussians becomes prohibitive. Gaussian-based representations leverage the mathematical properties of Gaussian functions, such as closed-form differentiation and convolution, to model signals efficiently. The approach has been applied to image coding (GaussianImage), 3D scene reconstruction (3DGS), and vector search (GARLIC). Recent advancements include feedforward initialization, hierarchical fitting, and hybrid mesh-Gaussian decompositions. The method forms a core modeling primitive in machine learning and graphics, combining analytic structure with empirical efficiency. Gaussian-Based Representation, https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/gaussian-based-representation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gabor Fields
body: Gabor Fields are a continuous volumetric representation that decomposes a signal into a low-pass Gaussian base and a residual of anisotropic Gabor kernels, enabling orientation-selective level-of-detail and accelerated rendering via control variates. Unlike standard Gaussian-based representations, Gabor Fields achieve approximately 2 dB higher PSNR at equal primitive counts and render up to 1.4× faster at equal variance by concentrating spectral energy in specific frequency bands and orientations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target signal or volume to be represented. Output: A set of Gabor primitives \{gi\}, each defined by a Gaussian envelope and a cosine modulation, plus a low-pass Gaussian base. Data Structures: Each Gabor primitive i is defined by the following parameters: Position: \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (center). Covariance: \mathbf{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive-definite matrix defining the Gaussian envelope's shape and orientation). Frequency Vector: \boldsymbol{\omega}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (direction and magnitude of the cosine modulation). Amplitude/Opacity: \alphai \in \mathbb{R} (scalar weight). Color/Value: \mathbf{c}i^{val} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (RGB or scalar value). Sizes and bit packing: Not given in the sources. The decomposition consists of two sets: 1. Gaussian Base: A high-density set of primitives where \boldsymbol{\omega}i = \mathbf{0}. 2. Gabor Residuals: A set of primitives where \boldsymbol{\omega}i \neq \mathbf{0}. Mathematical Definition: The value V(\mathbf{x}) of the Gabor Field at point \mathbf{x} is the sum of the Gaussian base G(\mathbf{x}) and the Gabor residuals R(\mathbf{x}): V(\mathbf{x}) = G(\mathbf{x}) + R(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i \in \text{Base}} \alphai e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}i)^T \mathbf{\Sigma}i^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}i)} + \sum{j \in \text{Residuals}} \alphaj e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}j)^T \mathbf{\Sigma}j^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}j)} \cos(\boldsymbol{\omega}j \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}j)) In the Fourier domain, each Gabor kernel consists of two symmetric lobes at \pm \boldsymbol{\omega}j, concentrating the spectrum in a specific frequency band and orientation, unlike a plain Gaussian which spills across all frequencies. Rendering Algorithm (Control Variate Path Tracing): The rendering leverages the Gaussian base as a control variate to reduce variance and accelerate intersection tests. 1. Preprocessing: Compute the power spectrum for each Gabor kernel analytically. Group residuals by frequency band and orientation. Split frequency bands into oriented, steerable sub-bands to enable ray-space masking. 2. Ray Tracing Loop: For each pixel, cast a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. a. Integrate Gaussian Base (Control Variate): Always trace and analytically integrate the contribution of the Gaussian base primitives along the ray. This accounts for the majority of the density and low-frequency structure. b. Stochastic Selection of Residuals: For each sample point along the ray, stochastically select which Gabor residuals to include in the estimate. Masking: Before intersection, mask kernels that cannot contribute to the ray. This is done by checking if the ray direction aligns with the kernel's wave direction \boldsymbol{\omega}j (where contributions collapse due to cancellation) or if the kernel's frequency is above the current LOD cutoff. Probability: Select residuals based on a power-law probability over frequency. A parameter \beta trades high-frequency error for speed. c. Closed-Form Integration: For each selected Gabor residual, integrate its contribution in closed form along the ray segment. d. Estimator: The final pixel value is the sum of the deterministic Gaussian base integration and the stochastic sum of selected Gabor residuals. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendergaborfield(rayo, rayd, lodcutoff, beta): # 1. Analytically integrate Gaussian base (control variate) basecolor = integrategaussianbase(rayo, rayd) # 2. Stochastically select Gabor residuals residualsum = 0.0 for sample in raysamples: for kernel in gaborresiduals: # Masking: skip kernels that cannot contribute if ismasked(kernel, rayd, lodcutoff): continue # Power-law probability selection if random() < powerlawprobability(kernel.frequency, beta): # Closed-form integration along ray segment residualsum += integrategaborkernel(kernel, rayo, rayd, sample) # 3. Combine deterministic base and stochastic residuals return basecolor + residualsum def ismasked(kernel, rayd, lodcutoff): # Ray alignment: contributions collapse when ray aligns with wave direction if abs(dot(normalize(rayd), normalize(kernel.omega))) > 0.95: return True # LOD cutoff: mask kernels above frequency threshold if kernel.frequency > lodcutoff: return True return False def powerlawprobability(freq, beta): return (1.0 / (1.0 + freq)) beta def integrategaussianbase(rayo, rayd): # Standard volumetric integration of Gaussian base return sum(kernel.alpha kernel.color gaussianrayintersection(kernel, rayo, rayd) for kernel in gaussianbase) def integrategaborkernel(kernel, rayo, rayd, sample): # Standard closed-form integration of Gabor kernel along ray return kernel.alpha kernel.color gaborrayintersection(kernel, rayo, rayd, sample) Parameters: \beta: A parameter for the power-law probability selection of Gabor residuals. Higher \beta prioritizes lower frequencies, trading high-frequency accuracy for speed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Alignment: When a ray aligns with a Gabor kernel's wave direction \boldsymbol{\omega}j, the positive and negative lobes cancel, causing the contribution to collapse. The algorithm must handle this via orientation-selective masking to avoid unnecessary intersection tests. LOD Cutoff: As the frequency cutoff shrinks for LOD, kernels are masked before tracing. This must be done continuously to avoid popping artifacts. Time Complexity: Rendering is accelerated by reducing the number of primitive intersections per ray. The Gaussian base (~2% of total primitives) is always traced, while Gabor residuals are stochastically sampled. Memory Complexity: Maintains two orders of magnitude compression over voxel grids. No extra storage for mipmaps or pyramids is required due to continuous LOD. Performance: In the Disney Cloud scene, unbiased reference rendering took 977 s. Control Variate PLA (Power-Law Accumulating) reduced this to 623 s. Zero NEE (Next-Event Estimation) further reduced it to 522 s, achieving nearly 2× the speed of the Control Variate PLA baseline with close to the same appearance. Gabor Fields achieve ~2 dB higher PSNR at equal primitive count compared to Gaussian-based representations. Gabor Fields render up to ~1.4× faster at equal variance compared to Gaussian-based representations. Strengths: Continuous LOD without re-fitting or extra storage; orientation-selective masking; efficient control variate acceleration; high PSNR. Limitations: Stochastic nature introduces variance (mitigated by control variates); requires careful tuning of \beta for speed/accuracy trade-off. Gabor Fields were introduced by Jorge Condor, Nicolai Hermann, Mehmet Ata Yurtsever, and Piotr Didyk in "Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering," published in ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH 2026). The method builds on Gaussian-based representations by introducing anisotropic Gabor kernels to capture directional high-frequency details, enabling new forms of acceleration and LOD control. name: 1D Gaussian Splatting
head: 1D Gaussian Representation
body: 1D Gaussian Splatting is a signal representation technique that decomposes a one-dimensional signal into a weighted sum of Gaussian probability density functions (kernels). Unlike the Fourier transform, which provides a global frequency decomposition, this method offers a local representation where each kernel decays rapidly with respect to the input variable. It differs fundamentally from Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs): while GMMs use Gaussians to model the distribution of data points, 1D Gaussian Splatting uses them to approximate the value of the signal itself. Inputs: A ground truth signal S(t) sampled at T discrete points t \in \{1, \dots, T\}. The number of Gaussian kernels K. Outputs: A reconstructed signal \hat{S}(t). Optimized parameters for each kernel: mean \mui, standard deviation \sigmai, and weight wi for i=1 \dots K. Data Structures: The representation consists of K Gaussian kernels. Each kernel i is defined by three scalar parameters: 1. \mui: The mean (center) of the Gaussian. 2. \sigmai: The standard deviation (width) of the Gaussian. 3. wi: The weight (opacity) of the Gaussian. To ensure numerical stability during optimization, the variances are initialized and stored as log-variances. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize K Gaussian kernels. Set means \mui and standard deviations \sigmai randomly within reasonable ranges covering the domain of t. Initialize variances as log-variances for numerical stability. Initialize weights wi (Not given in the sources; typically set to 1.0 or small random values). 2. Optimize the parameters \mui, \sigmai, wi using gradient descent to minimize the loss function \mathcal{L}. 3. Compute the reconstructed signal \hat{S}(t) using the optimized parameters. Formulas: The Gaussian kernel function fi(t) is defined as: fi(t \mid \mui, \sigmai) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigmai^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(t-\mui)^2}{2\sigmai^2}\right) The reconstructed signal \hat{S}(t) is the weighted sum of these kernels: \hat{S}(t) = \sum{i=1}^K wi fi(t) The optimization minimizes the Mean Squared Error (L2) loss between the reconstructed signal and the ground truth S(t): \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{T} \sum{t=1}^T (\hat{S}(t) - S(t))^2 Parameters: K: The number of Gaussian kernels used to reconstruct the signal. Learning rate: 0.1. Optimizer: Adam. Iterations: 100,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Smoothing side-effect: A limited number of Gaussians causes the reconstructed signal to be smoother than the ground truth, losing high local variance. This acts as a form of compression. Oscillation: If too many Gaussians are used or hyper-parameters are not tuned, reconstruction quality may oscillate (e.g., between 40 and 45 dB PSNR). Diminishing returns: Reconstruction quality only improves until a certain number of Gaussians is reached; adding more beyond this point may not help or may cause instability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussiankernel(t, mu, sigma): """Computes the value of a 1D Gaussian kernel.""" return (1.0 / np.sqrt(2 np.pi sigma2)) np.exp(-((t - mu)2) / (2 sigma2)) def adamstep(params, grads, m, v, tstep, lr=0.1, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): """Standard Adam optimizer update step.""" m = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) grads v = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) grads2 mhat = m / (1 - beta1tstep) vhat = v / (1 - beta2tstep) return params - lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + eps), m, v def train1dgaussiansplatting(tdata, Sgroundtruth, K, numiterations=100000, lr=0.1): """Trains 1D Gaussian Splatting parameters.""" T = len(tdata) # Initialize parameters mus = np.random.uniform(tdata.min(), tdata.max(), K) logvariances = np.random.randn(K) sigmas = np.exp(logvariances) weights = np.ones(K) # Not given in the sources # Adam state mmus, vmus = np.zeroslike(mus), np.zeroslike(mus) msigmas, vsigmas = np.zeroslike(sigmas), np.zeroslike(sigmas) mweights, vweights = np.zeroslike(weights), np.zeroslike(weights) for step in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Forward pass Shat = np.zeros(T) for i in range(K): fi = gaussiankernel(tdata, mus[i], sigmas[i]) Shat += weights[i] fi # Loss calculation error = Shat - Sgroundtruth loss = np.mean(error2) # Gradients gradmus = np.zeros(K) gradsigmas = np.zeros(K) gradweights = np.zeros(K) for i in range(K): fi = gaussiankernel(tdata, mus[i], sigmas[i]) # dL/dwi gradweights[i] = np.mean(2.0 / T error fi) # dL/dmui dfdmu = fi (tdata - mus[i]) / (sigmas[i]2) gradmus[i] = np.mean(2.0 / T error weights[i] dfdmu) # dL/dsigmai dfdsigma = fi ((tdata - mus[i])2 / (sigmas[i]3) - 1.0/sigmas[i]) gradsigmas[i] = np.mean(2.0 / T error weights[i] dfdsigma) # Update parameters mus, mmus, vmus = adamstep(mus, gradmus, mmus, vmus, step, lr) sigmas, msigmas, vsigmas = adamstep(sigmas, gradsigmas, msigmas, vsigmas, step, lr) weights, mweights, vweights = adamstep(weights, gradweights, mweights, vweights, step, lr) return mus, sigmas, weights Compression: The method compresses data. For a signal with T points, K Gaussians require 2K parameters (mean and sigma) plus K weights. In the Delhi temperature example (113 days), 45 Gaussians (90 parameters) achieved 47 dB PSNR, effectively compressing the data. Performance: In the cited experiment, 45 Gaussians achieved 47 dB PSNR. Quality oscillates between 40-45 dB after K=47. Strengths: Local representation; effective compression for smooth or moderately varying signals; differentiable, allowing gradient-based optimization. Limitations: Limited capacity to represent high local variance without many kernels; potential for oscillation with poor hyper-parameter tuning; smoothing effect may be undesirable for signals with sharp features. When to use: Signal approximation, forecasting (where overall behavior is more interesting than small variations), and compression. 1D Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the paper "Gaussian Splatting: An Introduction". It is presented as an alternative to Fourier decomposition for signal representation, leveraging the local nature of Gaussian kernels. The method is distinct from Gaussian Mixture Models, which model data distributions rather than signal values. name: Gaussian Density Field Representation
head: Gaussian + Hashed Residual Field
body: A compact representation of the density field D as a weighted sum of Gaussians plus a hashed residual field F, allowing efficient modeling of fine density details. It sets itself apart from pure Gaussian splatting methods by explicitly separating coarse structure from high-frequency residuals, enabling precise reconstruction of complex media without requiring a single ultra-high-resolution representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n Gaussian parameters \{wj, cj, rj\}{j=1}^n representing the coarse density field, and optionally a hashed residual field data structure. Output: The total density value D(x) at any spatial point x. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian List: An array of n Gaussians. Each Gaussian j is defined by weight wj (scalar), center cj (3D vector), and radius rj (scalar). 2. Hashed Residual Field: A hash table mapping spatial coordinates to residual values R(x). Hash table size and bucket configuration: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute the sequence of Gaussians and residual fields for the target density distribution. 2. Runtime Evaluation (Direct): For a query point x, compute the Gaussian sum \tilde{D}(x), retrieve R(x) from the hashed residual field, set F(x) = R(x), and return D(x) = \tilde{D}(x) + F(x). 3. Runtime Evaluation (Splatting/Texture-based): To construct the density field for rendering, initialize texture channels. For each Gaussian j, splat its weight wj into Channel 1 to accumulate \tilde{D}(x), with no weight normalization. If a residual field hash table exists, retrieve R(x) for each entry, multiply it by the current \tilde{D}(x) at that location, and store the result in Channel 2. After splatting, for each pixel or voxel, divide the value in Channel 2 by the value in Channel 1 to obtain R(x), then add R(x) to \tilde{D}(x) to yield the final density D(x). Formulas: The density field D(x) is defined as the sum of the Gaussian approximation \tilde{D}(x) and the residual field F(x): D(x) = \tilde{D}(x) + F(x) = \sum{j=1}^n wj \exp\left(-\frac{\|x - cj\|^2}{rj^2}\right) + F(x) Where: x is the query point in 3D space. \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. F(x) is the value retrieved from the hashed residual field. If no residual field is used, F(x) = 0. Parameters: n: Not given in the sources. Hash table size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Preprocessing Limitation: Preprocessing is only for the representation of the density field and does not prevent run-time changes to media properties, lighting, or scene configuration. A texture-based method for constructing the density field per frame by splatting Gaussian weights and residual products into separate color channels, then dividing to recover the residual field. It sets itself apart from direct per-point evaluation by leveraging parallel texture operations for field construction rather than sequential queries. It is chosen when the rendering pipeline supports texture-based splatting and requires fast, frame-by-frame reconstruction of the density field for ray marching or ray tracing. See Gaussian-based Representation. Strengths: Efficient modeling of fine density field details; allows run-time changes to lighting and media properties despite preprocessing. Limitations: Requires preprocessing for the density field representation; accuracy depends on the number of Gaussians and the resolution/coverage of the residual field. When to use: When high-frequency density details are needed and can be captured by a residual field, and when the rendering algorithm can accommodate rapid reconstruction (e.g., via splatting). When not to use: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Originated from the work of Zhou et al. (2007b) and extended in the context of gradient-based interpolation and sampling for real-time rendering of inhomogeneous, single-scattering media. The Gaussian model was chosen for its ability to compactly represent density fields, while the hashed residual field was added to capture details that the Gaussian sum alone could not. The method is used in real-time rendering pipelines for volumetric media, particularly where animated sequences require efficient density field reconstruction per frame. Gradient‐based Interpolation and Sampling for Real‐time Rendering of Inhomogeneous, Single‐scattering Media, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2008.01343.x, fetched 2026-10-27

name: MaskGaussian
head: Masked Gaussian Splatting
body: MaskGaussian is a differentiable pruning method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that models Gaussians as probabilistic entities rather than deterministically removing them based on static importance scores. It solves the problem of sub-optimal reconstruction caused by early pruning by introducing masked-rasterization, which allows gradients to flow to "masked-out" (inactive) Gaussians, enabling them to be re-evaluated and potentially reactivated as the scene evolves. Unlike sibling methods like Compact3DGS which use deterministic pruning or multiply masks with opacity/scale (blocking gradients), MaskGaussian applies masks during the alpha-blending stage, decoupling Gaussian existence from its geometric attributes. MaskGaussian extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline by introducing learnable mask parameters for each Gaussian. The core innovation is a rasterization technique that applies these masks to the blending process, ensuring that even inactive Gaussians participate in the forward pass and receive gradient updates. Inputs: Set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{s}i), color \mathbf{c}i, and opacity \alphai. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Learnable mask scores \mathbf{z}i \in \mathbb{R}^2 for each Gaussian i. Outputs: Rendered image \mathbf{I}. Gradients for all Gaussian attributes and mask scores. Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes (position, scale, rotation, SH coefficients, opacity). Mask Scores: For each Gaussian i, two learnable scalar values \mathbf{z}i = [z{i,0}, z{i,1}]. These are not probabilities but logits for a binary distribution. 1. Mask Sampling: For each Gaussian i, sample a binary mask \mathcal{M}i \in \{0, 1\} from the mask scores \mathbf{z}i using the Gumbel-Softmax trick to ensure differentiability. 2. Standard Splatting (Alpha Computation): Splat all N Gaussians onto the image plane using standard 3DGS rasterization. Compute the splatted density \alphai and transmittance Ti for each Gaussian without applying the mask \mathcal{M}i to the opacity or scale. This ensures that all Gaussians, regardless of their mask value, pass through the alpha-filtering stage and are processed by the rasterizer. \alphai: Splatted density of Gaussian i. Ti: Transmittance reaching Gaussian i, defined as Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) (assuming sorted order). 3. Masked Rasterization (Color and Transmittance Blending): Compute the final pixel color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) and update transmittance using the masks \mathcal{M}i. The mask is applied directly to the color accumulation and transmittance attenuation terms. Color Accumulation: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N \mathcal{M}i \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \cdot Ti Transmittance Update: T{i+1} = \mathcal{M}i \cdot (1 - \alphai) \cdot Ti + (1 - \mathcal{M}i) \cdot Ti If \mathcal{M}i = 1: The Gaussian contributes its color \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \cdot Ti and attenuates transmittance by (1-\alphai). If \mathcal{M}i = 0: The Gaussian contributes no color, and transmittance is unchanged (T{i+1} = Ti). 4. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss L: L = L{render} + \lambdam \cdot Lm Where: L{render} is the standard rendering loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) between the rendered image and the ground truth. Lm is a squared loss on the average number of active Gaussians to constrain the model size: Lm = \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \mathcal{M}i \right)^2 \lambdam is a balancing hyperparameter. 5. Backpropagation: Compute gradients for the mask scores \mathbf{z}i. The gradient of the loss with respect to the mask \mathcal{M}i is derived as: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathcal{M}i} = \alphai \cdot Ti \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})} \cdot (\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{b}{i+1}) Where \mathbf{b}{i+1} is the background color rendered behind the i-th Gaussian: \mathbf{b}{i+1} = \sum{j=i+1}^N \mathcal{M}j \cdot \mathbf{c}j \cdot \alphaj \cdot Tj The gradient flows through the Gumbel-Softmax operation to update \mathbf{z}i. This allows \mathcal{M}i=0 Gaussians to receive meaningful gradients based on their potential contribution (\mathbf{c}i) versus the background (\mathbf{b}{i+1}). 6. Pruning Procedure: Periodically, hard prune Gaussians with near-zero probability of existence. Sample each Gaussian's mask 10 times. If a Gaussian is never sampled (i.e., \mathcal{M}i=0 in all 10 trials), remove it from the scene. This is applied at every densification step and every 1000 iterations after densification. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def gumbelsoftmaxsample(logits, temperature=1.0): """Samples from a Gumbel-Softmax distribution with straight-through estimator.""" gumbels = -torch.emptylike(logits).exponential().log() gumbels = (gumbels + logits) / temperature ysoft = F.softmax(gumbels, dim=-1) index = ysoft.max(1, keepdim=True)[1] yhard = torch.zeroslike(logits, memoryformat=torch.contiguousformat).scatter(1, index, 1.0) return yhard - ysoft.detach() + ysoft def maskedrasterization(gaussians, camera, maskscores, lambdam, iteration, groundtruth): """Forward pass for MaskGaussian.""" N = gaussians.numgaussians # Step 1: Sample masks masksamples = gumbelsoftmaxsample(maskscores) # Shape (N, 2) M = masksamples[:, 1] # Probability of being active # Step 2: Standard Splatting (Alpha computation without mask) # Standard 3DGS projection and alpha computation alpha, depth, indices = projectgaussians(gaussians.pos, gaussians.scales, gaussians.rotations, camera) # Sort by depth (back-to-front) alphasorted, indicessorted = torch.sort(depth, dim=0, descending=True) # Compute Transmittance Ti for all Gaussians (without mask) alphaflat = alphasorted.view(-1, alphasorted.shape[-1]) Tflat = torch.cumprod(1 - alphaflat, dim=1) Tflat = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(Tflat[:,:1]), Tflat[:,:-1]], dim=1) T = Tflat.view(alphasorted.shape) # Step 3: Masked Rasterization Mexpanded = M.view(1, 1, -1).expandas(alphasorted) # Get colors for each Gaussian (Standard SH evaluation) colors = evaluatesh(gaussians.shcoeffs, camera.viewdirs) # Apply Mask to Color Accumulation and Transmittance contribution = Mexpanded colors alphasorted T renderedimage = torch.sum(contribution, dim=2) # Step 4: Loss Computation Lrender = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimage - groundtruth)) # L1 loss # SSIM is a standard differentiable metric added to Lrender avgM = torch.mean(M) Lm = avgM 2 loss = Lrender + lambdam Lm return renderedimage, loss, M def projectgaussians(positions, scales, rotations, camera): """Projects 3D Gaussians to screen space and computes alpha and depth.""" # Standard 3DGS projection logic pass def evaluatesh(shcoeffs, viewdirs): """Evaluates spherical harmonics coefficients for given view directions.""" # Standard 3DGS SH evaluation logic pass \lambdam: Balancing weight for the squared loss Lm. Typical values: 0.1 for iterations 19,000–20,000. 0.0005 or 0.001 for iterations 0–30,000. Pruning Frequency: Every densification step and every 1000 iterations after densification. Sampling Count for Pruning: 10 samples per Gaussian to determine if it should be removed. Gradient Blocking: If masks are applied to opacity or scale (setting them to zero), the Gaussian's density \alpha becomes zero. This causes the Gaussian to be filtered out before rasterization, preventing gradient updates. MaskGaussian avoids this by applying masks during blending. Outdated Gaussians: If masked Gaussians do not receive gradients, they remain static and may become outdated as the scene evolves. MaskGaussian ensures they receive gradients via masked-rasterization. Fine Gaussians: Methods that bind mask gradients to scales/opacity may disadvantage fine Gaussians if they receive negative gradients intended to shrink them. MaskGaussian decouples these. A regularization technique applied to learnable mask parameters in 3D Gaussian Splatting to guide the pruning process and encourage condensed scene representations. It solves the problem of inefficient storage and rendering by promoting both fine-grained sparsity (removing non-essential individual Gaussians) and structural coherence (removing entire anchors). Unlike standard L1-style penalties which may leave anchors with only a few sparsely active Gaussians, hindering compactness, this method uses a group L2 norm to encourage switching off entire anchors cohesively. It builds on MaskGaussian by providing the optimization signal that determines which probabilistic entities should be deactivated. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS rasterization, with minor overhead for mask sampling and blending. The pruning step adds negligible overhead as it is performed periodically. Memory Complexity: Adds 2N learnable parameters (mask scores) for N Gaussians. Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF360: 27.43 PSNR, 1.205M Gaussians, 384.7 FPS (vs. 3DGS: 27.45 PSNR, 3.204M Gaussians, 187.8 FPS). Pruning ratio: 62.4%. Speedup: 2.05x. Tanks & Temples: 23.72 PSNR, 0.590M Gaussians, 558.3 FPS (vs. 3DGS: 23.74 PSNR, 1.825M Gaussians, 254.5 FPS). Pruning ratio: 67.7%. Speedup: 2.19x. Deep Blending: 29.69 PSNR, 0.694M Gaussians, 637.1 FPS (vs. 3DGS: 29.53 PSNR, 2.815M Gaussians, 201.3 FPS). Pruning ratio: 75.3%. Speedup: 3.16x. Strengths: Achieves significant pruning ratios (62-75%) with minimal PSNR loss (0.02 dB). Enables real-time rendering with fewer Gaussians. Allows dynamic re-evaluation of Gaussians, preventing premature pruning. Limitations: Requires modification of the rasterization code to implement masked-rasterization. Hyperparameter \lambdam requires tuning for different scenes and training phases. MaskGaussian was introduced in the paper "MaskGaussian: Adaptive 3D Gaussian Representation from Probabilistic Masks" (CVPR 2025). It builds upon Compact3DGS by extending its pruning approach from deterministic to probabilistic. The method addresses the limitations of previous mask-based pruning methods that multiply masks with Gaussian attributes (opacity/scale), which block gradient flow and lead to sub-optimal reconstruction. By treating pruning as a stochastic sampling process and introducing masked-rasterization, MaskGaussian allows for adaptive pruning that evolves with the scene.
