name: Sparsity Regularization for Pruning
head: Group Sparsity Loss
body: Sparsity Regularization for Pruning is a regularization technique applied to learnable mask parameters to guide the pruning process and encourage condensed scene representations. It solves the problem of inefficient storage and rendering by promoting both fine-grained sparsity (deactivating non-essential individual Gaussians) and structural coherence (removing entire anchors). Unlike standard L1-style penalties that may leave anchors with only a few sparsely active Gaussians, hindering compactness, this method uses a group L2 norm to encourage switching off entire anchors cohesively. It builds on MaskGaussian. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: N: Total number of anchors in the scene. K: Number of Gaussians per anchor. \mathbf{m}j: Vector of K learnable mask parameters for anchor j, where j \in \{1, \dots, N\}. \lambda{\text{mask}}: Hyperparameter balancing the per-Gaussian masking loss. \lambda{\text{group}}: Hyperparameter balancing the group sparsity loss. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}}: Scalar sparsity regularization loss value. Data Structures The method operates on the learnable mask parameters \mathbf{m}j = [m{j,1}, m{j,2}, \dots, m{j,K}]^T for each anchor j. The masks M{j,i} used in the rendering equation are derived from these parameters via the sigmoid function: M{j,i} = \sigma(m{j,i}). Steps 1. Compute Per-Gaussian Mask Activations: For every Gaussian i in every anchor j, compute the sigmoid activation: M{j,i} = \sigma(m{j,i}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-m{j,i}}} 2. Compute Per-Gaussian Masking Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{mask}}): Sum the activations of all N \times K mask entries and normalize by the total count to ensure invariance to scene size: \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} = \frac{1}{NK} \sum{j=1}^{N} \sum{i=1}^{K} M{j,i} This term encourages the deactivation of any single non-essential Gaussian. 3. Compute Group Sparsity Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{group}}): For each anchor j, treat the vector of mask activations \sigma(\mathbf{m}j) as a single group. Compute the L2 norm of this vector. Sum these norms over all N anchors and normalize by N: \mathcal{L}{\text{group}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^{N} \|\sigma(\mathbf{m}j)\|2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^{N} \sqrt{\sum{i=1}^{K} M{j,i}^2} This term is designed to encourage the entire group of Gaussians associated with a single anchor to be "switched off" together. 4. Compute Total Sparsity Loss: Combine the two components using the hyperparameters: \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} = \lambda{\text{mask}} \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} + \lambda{\text{group}} \mathcal{L}{\text{group}} 5. Pruning Decision: An anchor j is considered pruned or inactive for a given Level of Detail (LOD) if all of its associated masks are zero. Formally, if \sum{i=1}^K M{j,i} = 0, the anchor is removed. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List def computesparsityloss(masks: List[List[float]], lambdamask: float, lambdagroup: float) -> float: """ Computes the sparsity regularization loss for 3D Gaussian Splatting pruning. Args: masks: A list of N lists, where each inner list contains K float values representing the learnable mask parameters m{j,i} for anchor j. lambdamask: Weight for the per-Gaussian masking loss. lambdagroup: Weight for the group sparsity loss. Returns: The total sparsity loss scalar. """ N = len(masks) if N == 0: return 0.0 K = len(masks[0]) if K == 0: return 0.0 totalmaskloss = 0.0 totalgrouploss = 0.0 for j in range(N): anchormasks = masks[j] anchorsigmoidsum = 0.0 anchorl2normsq = 0.0 for i in range(K): # Sigmoid activation mval = anchormasks[i] sigmoidval = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-mval)) # Accumulate for Lmask anchorsigmoidsum += sigmoidval # Accumulate for Lgroup (L2 norm squared) anchorl2normsq += sigmoidval sigmoidval # Lmask contribution: sum of all sigmoids totalmaskloss += anchorsigmoidsum # Lgroup contribution: L2 norm of the group anchorl2norm = math.sqrt(anchorl2normsq) totalgrouploss += anchorl2norm # Normalize # Lmask is normalized by NK lmask = totalmaskloss / (N K) # Lgroup is normalized by N lgroup = totalgrouploss / N # Combine loss = lambdamask lmask + lambdagroup lgroup return loss Parameters \lambda{\text{mask}}: Balances the standard per-Gaussian masking loss. Value not given in the sources. \lambda{\text{group}}: Balances the group sparsity loss. Value not given in the sources. Both terms are normalized so that the regularization strength is invariant to scene size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls L1 vs L2: Using an L1-style penalty on the group masks may leave anchors with only a few sparsely active Gaussians, which hinders the compactness of the condensed model. The L2 norm is preferred to encourage cohesive removal of entire anchors. Pruning Condition: An anchor is pruned if \sum{i=1}^K M{j,i} = 0. Initialization: The source does not specify the initialization of m{j,i}. Time Complexity: O(NK) to compute the loss, as it iterates over all N anchors and K Gaussians per anchor. Memory Complexity: O(NK) to store the mask parameters \mathbf{m}j. Strengths: Promotes both fine-grained sparsity and structural coherence, leading to significant storage savings by removing entire anchors. The normalization ensures regularization strength is invariant to scene size. Limitations: Requires tuning of two hyperparameters (\lambda{\text{mask}}, \lambda{\text{group}}). The effectiveness depends on the convergence of the sigmoid activations to 0 or 1. When to use: When using the iterative Gaussian synopsis unfolding scheme and needing to prune anchors to create condensed LODs. When not to use: When structural coherence of anchors is not desired, or when a simpler per-Gaussian pruning strategy is sufficient. The method was introduced in the paper "Unfolding 3D Gaussian Splatting via Iterative Gaussian Synopsis". It is part of a top-down unfolding and pruning scheme where the representation of anchors is optimized for specific levels of detail. The approach addresses the limitations of standard masking losses by explicitly modeling group sparsity to improve the compactness of the 3D Gaussian representation. Unfolding 3D Gaussian Splatting via Iterative Gaussian Synopsis., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2026.3746672, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
head: 2D Gaussian Splatting Surfel Rasterization
body: This method renders a scene represented by 2D Gaussian primitives (surfels) into RGB, alpha, normal, and depth maps using a custom rasterizer. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by operating on surfels projected into screen space, accumulating color and geometric attributes via front-to-back alpha compositing [Parent]. It serves as the Tier-1 NumPy reference implementation for 2D Gaussian Splatting, performing ray-surfel intersection per pixel using the projection matrix. Inputs: means: 3D positions of N surfels, shape [N, 3]. quats: Unit quaternions (w, x, y, z) defining orientation, shape [N, 4]. scales: Local scaling factors, shape [N, 3]. opacities: Per-surfel opacity values, shape [N]. colors: Per-surfel colors, shape [N, D] (where D is color channels, typically 3) or spherical harmonic coefficients if shdegree is provided. viewmats: Camera-to-world transformation matrices, shape [C, 4, 4] (where C is number of cameras). Ks: Camera intrinsic matrices, shape [C, 3, 3]. width, height: Image dimensions. tilesize: Integer, default 16. Side length of tiles for rasterization. nearplane: Float, default 0.01. Near clipping plane distance. farplane: Float, default 1e10. Far clipping plane distance. shdegree: Integer or None. If not None, spherical harmonics are evaluated; otherwise, direct colors are used. backgrounds: Background color for each camera, shape [C, 3]. Outputs: rendercolors: Shape [C, H, W, 3]. renderalphas: Shape [C, H, W, 1]. rendernormals: Shape [C, H, W, 3]. Data Structures: means2d: Projected 2D centers, shape [C, N, 2]. radii: Screen-space radii of surfels, shape [C, N]. depths: Depth of surfel centers, shape [C, N]. raytransforms: Transformation matrices for ray-surfel intersection, shape [C, N, 3, 3] (derived from projection). normals: World-space normals of surfels, shape [C, N, 3]. isectoffsets: Encoded intersection offsets for tile-based processing, shape [C, \text{tile\height}, \text{tile\width}]. flattenids: Flattened indices of surfels intersecting tiles, shape [C, \text{num\intersecting}]. Steps: 1. Projection: Project 2D Gaussian surfels to 2D screen space using fullyfusedprojection2dgs. This function takes means, quats, scales, viewmats, Ks, width, height, nearplane, and farplane. It outputs radii, means2d, depths, raytransforms, and normals. 2. Opacity Broadcasting: Broadcast scalar per-surfel opacities [N] to per-camera [C, N] using mx.broadcastto(mx.expanddims(opacities, axis=0), (C, N)). 3. Color Evaluation: If shdegree is not None: Compute view directions: \text{dirs} = \text{means}[\text{None},:,:] - \text{campos}[:, \text{None},:]. Normalize dirs. Broadcast color coefficients to [C, N, K, 3] (where K is SH coefficient count). Evaluate spherical harmonics: \text{rgb} = \text{spherical\harmonics}(\text{sh\degree}, \text{dirs}, \text{coeffs\broadcast}). Clamp with \text{rgb} = \max(\text{rgb} + 0.5, 0.0). If shdegree is None: Broadcast colors [N, D] to [C, N, D] or use colors [C, N, D] directly as colorsforraster. 4. Tile Intersection: Compute tile dimensions: \text{tile\width} = \lceil \text{width} / \text{tile\size} \rceil, \text{tile\height} = \lceil \text{height} / \text{tile\size} \rceil. Call isecttiles(means2d, radii, depths, tilesize, tilewidth, tileheight, sort=True) to get tilespergauss, isectids, and flattenids. 5. Offset Encoding: Encode intersection offsets using isectoffsetencode(isectids, C, tilewidth, tileheight) to get isectoffsets [C, \text{tile\height}, \text{tile\width}]. 6. Rasterization: Call rasterizetopixels2dgs with means2d, raytransforms, colorsforraster, normals, opacitiescn, width, height, tilesize, isectoffsets, flattenids, and backgrounds. This function performs the per-pixel ray-surfel intersection and accumulation. Per-Pixel Ray-Surfel Intersection (Inside rasterizetopixels2dgs): For each surfel gid in depth order: 1. Compute ray-surfel intersection vectors using the projection matrix Mg (from raytransforms): hu = -Mg[0,:3] + Mg[2,:3] \cdot px hv = -Mg[1,:3] + Mg[2,:3] \cdot py where px, py are pixel coordinates. 2. Compute cross product and guard against degenerate case: tmp = \text{cross}(hu, hv) If |tmp[2]| < 10^{-10}, skip this intersection. 3. Compute intersection coordinates: us = tmp[0] / tmp[2] vs = tmp[1] / tmp[2] 4. Compute 3D sigma from intersection: \sigma{3d} = us^2 + vs^2 5. Compute 2D fallback sigma from distance to center: \sigma{2d} = 2.0 \cdot (dx^2 + dy^2) where dx, dy are distances from pixel to surfel center. 6. Take tighter bound: \sigma = 0.5 \cdot \min(\sigma{3d}, \sigma{2d}) 7. Compute alpha clamped to MAXALPHA: \alpha = \min(\text{opacity} \cdot \exp(-\sigma), \text{MAX\ALPHA}) Negative sigma values are skipped to prevent invalid alpha computation. 8. Accumulate color, alpha, and normal maps via front-to-back alpha compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import math def rasterizetopixels2dgs( means2d: np.ndarray, # [C, N, 2] raytransforms: np.ndarray, # [C, N, 3, 3] colorsforraster: np.ndarray, # [C, N, 3] normals: np.ndarray, # [C, N, 3] opacitiescn: np.ndarray, # [C, N] width: int, height: int, tilesize: int = 16, isectoffsets: np.ndarray, # [C, tileh, tilew] flattenids: np.ndarray, # [C, numintersecting] backgrounds: np.ndarray, # [C, 3]) -> tuple: """ Rasterize 2D Gaussian surfels to pixels. Returns: (rendercolors, renderalphas, rendernormals) """ C = means2d.shape[0] H, W = height, width tileh = math.ceil(H / tilesize) tilew = math.ceil(W / tilesize) rendercolors = np.zeros((C, H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) renderalphas = np.zeros((C, H, W, 1), dtype=np.float32) rendernormals = np.zeros((C, H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) # Initialize compositing buffers accalpha = np.zeros((C, H, W, 1), dtype=np.float32) acccolor = np.zeros((C, H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) accnormal = np.zeros((C, H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) # Process each camera for c in range(C): # Get surfels intersecting this camera's view # flattenids[c] contains indices into the N surfels surfelindices = flattenids[c] numsurfels = len(surfelindices) # Sort surfels by depth for front-to-back rendering # depths are assumed to be available or passed; here we assume means2d depth is implicit or passed separately # For simplicity, we assume surfels are pre-sorted by depth in flattenids or we sort them here # In the reference, isecttiles returns sorted ids for i in range(numsurfels): gid = surfelindices[i] # Get surfel properties m2d = means2d[c, gid] rt = raytransforms[c, gid] color = colorsforraster[c, gid] normal = normals[c, gid] opacity = opacitiescn[c, gid] # Determine which tiles this surfel covers # This is handled by isectoffsets and flattenids structure # In the reference, we iterate over pixels covered by the surfel's tile # For a complete implementation, we would iterate over the bounding box of the surfel in tile space # Simplified: Iterate over all pixels (for reference correctness, though inefficient) # In practice, we only iterate over pixels within the surfel's radius radius = radii[c, gid] # Assume radii is passed or computed minx = max(0, int(m2d[0] - radius)) maxx = min(W, int(m2d[0] + radius)) miny = max(0, int(m2d[1] - radius)) maxy = min(H, int(m2d[1] + radius)) for y in range(miny, maxy): for x in range(minx, maxx): # Compute ray-surfel intersection # hu = -Mg[0,:3] + Mg[2,:3] px # hv = -Mg[1,:3] + Mg[2,:3] py px = float(x) py = float(y) hu = -rt[0,:3] + rt[2,:3] px hv = -rt[1,:3] + rt[2,:3] py tmp = np.cross(hu, hv) if abs(tmp[2]) < 1e-10: continue us = tmp[0] / tmp[2] vs = tmp[1] / tmp[2] sigma3d = us us + vs vs dx = x - m2d[0] dy = y - m2d[1] sigma2d = 2.0 (dx dx + dy dy) sigma = 0.5 min(sigma3d, sigma2d) if sigma < 0: continue alpha = min(opacity np.exp(-sigma), 1.0) # MAXALPHA is typically 1.0 # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = Cin + Csurfel alpha (1 - alphain) # Aout = Ain + alpha (1 - alphain) alphain = accalpha[c, y, x, 0] if alphain >= 1.0: continue weight = alpha (1.0 - alphain) acccolor[c, y, x] += color weight accnormal[c, y, x] += normal weight # Note: Normal compositing is complex, usually weighted by alpha accalpha[c, y, x, 0] += weight if accalpha[c, y, x, 0] >= 1.0: break # Optimization: if fully opaque, stop processing further surfels for this pixel # Apply background for y in range(H): for x in range(W): alphafinal = accalpha[c, y, x, 0] if alphafinal < 1.0: bg = backgrounds[c] rendercolors[c, y, x] = acccolor[c, y, x] + bg (1.0 - alphafinal) else: rendercolors[c, y, x] = acccolor[c, y, x] renderalphas[c, y, x, 0] = alphafinal rendernormals[c, y, x] = accnormal[c, y, x] / (alphafinal + 1e-8) # Normalize normals return rendercolors, renderalphas, rendernormals Enhances 2D Gaussian Splatting by replacing single attribute values per primitive with spatially varying texture maps for material properties and normals. Unlike methods that assign constant attributes to each primitive, this approach decouples geometric representation from appearance, enabling high-frequency specular reconstruction and accurate reflections in reflective scenes without increasing the primitive count. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by leveraging the closed-form ray-splat intersection to map screen pixels to local texture coordinates, allowing hardware-accelerated rendering via texture atlases. This method implements the forward pass of the C++/CUDA rasterizer for Time-of-Flight Gaussian Splatting. It restructures scene and camera parameters into a single tuple, invokes the CUDA kernel, and returns rendered maps including color, phasor, depth, and auxiliary buffers. Renders a scene represented by 2D Gaussian primitives into RGB, alpha, normal, and depth maps using a custom rasterizer. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by operating on surfels (2D Gaussians) projected into screen space, accumulating color and geometric attributes via front-to-back alpha compositing [Parent]. Nexels is a novel view synthesis method that decouples geometry and appearance to achieve a compact representation using a fixed number of primitives per pixel. It uses surfels with a generalized Gaussian kernel for geometry and a shared neural field (Instant-NGP) for view-dependent appearance, rendered via a two-pass process to handle sparse primitives efficiently. Unlike sibling methods that couple appearance to primitives or use slower neural field lookups, Nexels textures only the top-K primitives per pixel, ensuring real-time performance while matching the perceptual quality of 3D Gaussian Splatting with significantly fewer primitives. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) in the naive reference implementation, where N is the number of surfels and H, W are image dimensions. Tile-based optimization reduces this to O(K \cdot H \cdot W) where K is the average number of surfels per tile. Memory Complexity: O(N + H \cdot W) for storing surfel properties and output buffers. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a clear, differentiable (via MLX autodiff in the reference) reference implementation for 2D Gaussian Splatting. Handles multiple camera models (pinhole, fisheye, orthographic). Limitations: The NumPy reference implementation is not differentiable and is slow for large scenes. The CUDA implementation is faster but not detailed in the sources. When to use: For debugging, testing, and educational purposes. For production, use the CUDA implementation. When not to use: When real-time performance is required and the CUDA implementation is not available. The method is part of the 2D Gaussian Splatting framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by using surfels (2D Gaussians) instead of 3D ellipsoids. The reference implementation is provided by the gsplat-mlx library. RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, https://github.com/RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting
head: RefGaussian, TextureSplat
body: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting (TextureSplat) enhances 2D Gaussian Splatting by replacing single attribute values per primitive with spatially varying texture maps for material properties and normals. Unlike methods that assign constant attributes to each primitive, this approach decouples geometric representation from appearance, enabling high-frequency specular reconstruction and accurate reflections in reflective scenes without increasing the primitive count. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by leveraging the closed-form ray-splat intersection to map screen pixels to local texture coordinates, allowing hardware-accelerated rendering via texture atlases. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D Gaussian primitives (surfels), each defined by position pk, tangential vectors t{uk} and t{vk}, scaling factors s{uk} and s{vk}, and learnable opacity ok. Each primitive k has an associated texture map T^k containing material properties (e.g., albedo, roughness, normal maps) in its local coordinate system. Output: A rendered image with accurate specular highlights and reflections. Data Structures: Primitive k: pk: Position in world space. t{uk}, t{vk}: Tangential vectors in world space. s{uk}, s{vk}: Scaling factors along tangential directions. ok: Learnable opacity scalar. T^k: Texture map stored in a unified texture atlas. Texture Atlas: A single large texture containing all primitive textures T^k, packed to leverage GPU hardware-accelerated texture filtering. Numbered Steps: 1. Primitive Definition: Represent the scene using oriented planar disks (2DGS primitives). For each primitive k, define position pk, tangential vectors t{uk} and t{vk}, and scaling factors s{uk}, s{vk}. The primitive's normal is computed as nk = t{uk} \times t{vk}. 2. Ray-Splat Intersection: For each pixel (x, y), determine the intersection with contributing primitives. Using the closed-form ray-splat intersection of 2DGS, map screen-space pixels to local texture coordinates (uk, vk) for each primitive k. The local coordinates correspond to the point on the primitive's tangent plane. 3. Gaussian Evaluation: Evaluate the 2D Gaussian value Gk(u, v) at the local coordinates (uk, vk): Gk(u, v) = \exp \left( - \frac{u^2 + v^2}{2} \right) The effective opacity \alphak(x, y) for primitive k at pixel (x, y) is: \alphak(x, y) = ok Gk(uk(x, y), vk(x, y)) 4. Attribute Retrieval: Retrieve material attributes ak(x, y) from the per-primitive texture map T^k using the local texture coordinates: ak(x, y) = T^k(uk(x, y), vk(x, y)) If the attribute is a normal map, the retrieved normal is in the tangent space of the primitive. 5. Normal Transformation: Transform tangential normal maps to world space. For each primitive, construct a rotation matrix Rk from the tangential vectors t{uk} and t{vk} (and the normal nk). Transform the sampled tangent-space normal n{tangent} to world space: n{world} = Rk \cdot n{tangent} 6. Physically-Based Rendering (PBR): Use the retrieved material attributes (e.g., albedo, roughness, world-space normal) in a physically-based rendering model compatible with deferred shading pipelines to compute the final color contribution, including specular reflections. 7. Alpha Compositing: Accumulate the color contributions of all primitives contributing to pixel (x, y) in front-to-back order. The final pixel color A(x, y) is: A(x, y) = \sum{i=1}^{N} ai \alphai(x, y) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(x, y)) where ai is the color attribute retrieved from T^i (or computed via PBR), and \alphai(x, y) is the effective opacity. name: ToF Gaussian Rasterization Forward Pass
head: ToF Gaussian Rasterization
body: This method implements the forward pass of the C++/CUDA rasterizer for Time-of-Flight Gaussian Splatting. It restructures scene and camera parameters into a single tuple, invokes the CUDA kernel, and returns rendered maps including color, phasor, depth, and auxiliary buffers. Inputs: rastersettings (camera and rendering parameters), gaussians (model attributes), and trainingargs (optimization flags). Data Structures: The method packs all inputs into a single tuple passed to the CUDA kernel. The tuple layout is: 1. rastersettings.bg 2. means3D 3. colorsprecomp 4. phasorsprecomp 5. opacities 6. scales 7. rotations 8. rastersettings.scalemodifier 9. cov3Dsprecomp 10. rastersettings.viewmatrix 11. rastersettings.projmatrix 12. rastersettings.tanfovx 13. rastersettings.tanfovy 14. rastersettings.imageheight 15. rastersettings.imagewidth 16. sh 17. shp 18. rastersettings.shdegree 19. rastersettings.campos 20. rastersettings.prefiltered 21. rastersettings.debug 22. rastersettings.nearn 23. rastersettings.farn 24. rastersettings.depthrange 25. rastersettings.useviewdependentphase 26. phaseoffset 27. dcoffset. Parameters: phaseoffset and dcoffset are scalar values used for offset correction. If rastersettings.optimizephaseoffset (or optimizedcoffset) is true, the raw tensor is used; otherwise, it is detached, converted to a CPU numpy array, and cast to a Python scalar. Steps: 1. Restructure arguments into the tuple defined above, applying the offset handling logic. 2. If rastersettings.debug is true, deep-copy all arguments to CPU before invocation to preserve state for debugging. 3. Invoke the C++/CUDA forward rasterization function C.rasterizegaussians(args). 4. Save relevant tensors for the backward pass: rastersettings, numrendered, colorsprecomp, phasorsprecomp, means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, sh, shp, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, phaseoffset, dcoffset. Restructure arguments phaseoffset = gaussians.getphaseoffset if trainingargs.optimizephaseoffset else gaussians.getphaseoffset.detach().cpu().numpy().item() dcoffset = gaussians.getdcoffset if trainingargs.optimizedcoffset else gaussians.getdcoffset.detach().cpu().numpy().item() args = ( rastersettings.bg, gaussians.means3D, gaussians.colorsprecomp, gaussians.phasorsprecomp, gaussians.opacities, gaussians.scales, gaussians.rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, gaussians.cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, gaussians.sh, gaussians.shp, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, rastersettings.prefiltered, rastersettings.debug, rastersettings.nearn, rastersettings.farn, rastersettings.depthrange, rastersettings.useviewdependentphase, phaseoffset, dcoffset) # 2. Debug handling if rastersettings.debug: argscpu = tuple(x.detach().cpu().clone() if hasattr(x, 'detach') else copy.deepcopy(x) for x in args) # 3. name: Vanilla 2D Gaussian Splatting Rendering
head: 2DGS Renderer, Vanilla2DGSRenderer
body: Renders a scene using 2D Gaussian primitives to compute RGB, alpha, normals, and depth maps via a custom rasterizer. It operates on surfels projected into screen space and accumulates color and geometric attributes via front-to-back alpha compositing [Parent]. Inputs: means3D: 3D mean positions of Gaussians. means2D: 2D screen-space mean positions. shs or colorsprecomp: Spherical Harmonics coefficients or pre-computed colors. opacities: Per-primitive opacity values. scales: Per-primitive scaling factors. rotations: Per-primitive rotations (quaternions). cov3Dprecomp: Pre-computed 3D covariance (optional; if None, computed from scales/rotation). Camera parameters: Intrinsics (FOV, image dimensions), extrinsics (view/projection matrices). backgroundcolor: Background color for alpha compositing. scalingmodifier: Scaling factor for Gaussian sizes. depthratio: Weighting factor for depth estimation (1 for bounded/median, 0 for unbounded/expected). Outputs: renderimage: RGB image. renderalpha: Alpha channel. rendnormal: View-space normals. viewnormal: World-space normals. renddist: Expected depth. surfdepth: Surface depth (weighted combination). surfnormal: Surface normals derived from surface depth. radii: Visibility filter (pixels covered by Gaussians). allmap: Intermediate tensor containing depth, alpha, normals, and distortion. Data Structures: allmap: Tensor with layout: index 0 is expected depth, index 1 is alpha, indices 2-4 are view-space normals, index 5 is median depth, index 6 is depth distortion. Steps: 1. Initialize means2D with requiresgrad=True to capture gradients for 2D means. 2. Compute tanfovx and tanfovy from horizontal and vertical fields of view. 3. Configure rasterization settings with image dimensions, FOV tangents, background color, scaling modifier, view/projection matrices, SH degree, camera position, and prefiltered=False. 4. Instantiate the rasterizer with the configured settings. 5. Set cov3Dprecomp to None to allow the rasterizer to compute covariance from scales and rotation. 6. Call the rasterizer with means3D, means2D, shs/colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, and cov3Dprecomp to obtain renderimage, radii, and allmap. 7. Extract renderalpha from allmap index 1. 8. Extract view-space normals from allmap indices 2-4 and transform to world space by multiplying by the transpose of the camera's world-to-camera rotation matrix. 9. Extract median depth from allmap index 5 and replace NaNs with 0. 10. Extract expected depth from allmap index 0, divide by renderalpha, and replace NaNs with 0. 11. Compute surfdepth as a weighted sum: surfdepth = depthratio mediandepth + (1 - depthratio) expecteddepth. 12. Compute surfnormal from surfdepth using depthtonormal, then multiply by detached renderalpha. 13. Return dictionary containing all outputs. Helper Functions: depthtonormal(depthmap): Reconstruct 3D points from depth map using camera intrinsics and extrinsics, compute spatial derivatives (dx, dy) of the 3D points, compute normal as cross product of derivatives, and normalize. depthstopoints(depthmap): Compute NDC to pixel projection matrix, create meshgrid of pixel coordinates, compute ray directions, and scale by depth to reconstruct 3D points. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def vanilla2dgsrender( means3D, means2D, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, camera, backgroundcolor, scalingmodifier, depthratio, device): # Step 1: Initialize means2D for gradients if not means2D.requiresgrad: means2D = means2D.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) # Step 2: Compute FOV tangents tanfovx = torch.tan(camera.fovx / 2) tanfovy = torch.tan(camera.fovy / 2) # Step 3 & 4: Configure settings and instantiate rasterizer rastersettings = { "imageheight": camera.height, "imagewidth": camera.width, "tanfovx": tanfovx, "tanfovy": tanfovy, "bg": backgroundcolor, "scalemodifier": scalingmodifier, "viewmatrix": camera.viewmatrix, "projmatrix": camera.projmatrix, "shdegree": shs.shape[-1] if shs is not None else 0, "campos": camera.position, "prefiltered": False } # Custom CUDA rasterization kernel handling projection, sorting, and compositing # rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings) # Implementation not provided in sources # Step 5: Set cov3Dprecomp to None cov3Dprecomp = None # Step 6: Rasterize renderimage, radii, allmap = rasterize2dgaussians( means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=None, opacities=opacities, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp) # Step 7: Extract alpha renderalpha = allmap[:, 1,:,:] # Step 8: Extract and transform normals viewnormal = allmap[:, 2:5,:,:] camrotinv = camera.worldtocamrotationmatrix.t() viewnormal = torch.matmul(camrotinv, viewnormal) # Step 9: Extract median depth mediandepth = allmap[:, 5,:,:] mediandepth = torch.nantonum(mediandepth, nan=0.0) # Step 10: Extract and compute expected depth expecteddepth = allmap[:, 0,:,:] expecteddepth = torch.where(renderalpha > 0, expecteddepth / renderalpha, 0.0) # Step 11: Compute surface depth surfdepth = depthratio mediandepth + (1 - depthratio) expecteddepth # Step 12: Compute surface normal surfnormal = depthtonormal(surfdepth, camera) surfnormal = surfnormal renderalpha.detach() # Step 13: Return results return { "renderimage": renderimage, "viewspacepoints": means2D, "visibilityfilter": radii > 0, "radii": radii, "rendalpha": renderalpha, "rendnormal": viewnormal, "viewnormal": viewnormal, "renddist": expecteddepth, "surfdepth": surfdepth, "surfnormal": surfnormal } def depthtonormal(depthmap, camera): # Reconstruct 3D points points3d = depthstopoints(depthmap, camera) # Compute spatial derivatives dx = torch.diff(points3d, dim=-2, prepend=points3d[:,:, -1:,:]) dy = torch.diff(points3d, dim=-1, prepend=points3d[:,:,:, -1:]) # Compute normal via cross product normal = torch.cross(dx, dy, dim=-1) return torch.nn.functional.normalize(normal, dim=-1) def depthstopoints(depthmap, camera): # Compute NDC to pixel projection matrix and meshgrid h, w = depthmap.shape[-2:] y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(h), torch.arange(w), indexing='ij') pixelcoords = torch.stack([x, y], dim=-1).float().to(depthmap.device) # Compute ray directions using camera intrinsics fx, fy = camera.intrinsics[0, 0], camera.intrinsics[1, 1] cx, cy = camera.intrinsics[0, 2], camera.intrinsics[1, 2] raydirs = torch.stack([ (pixelcoords[..., 0] - cx) / fx, (pixelcoords[..., 1] - cy) / fy, torch.oneslike(pixelcoords[..., 0]) ], dim=-1) # Scale by depth points3d = raydirs depthmap.unsqueeze(-1) # Transform to world space using camera extrinsics points3dworld = points3d @ camera.extrinsics[:3,:3].t() + camera.extrinsics[:3, 3] return points3dworld def rasterize2dgaussians(means3D, means2D, shs, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp): # Custom CUDA rasterization kernel # Returns renderimage, radii, allmap pass Not given in the sources. name: Reflective Gaussian Splatting
head: Ref-Gaussian
body: Reflective Gaussian Splatting (Ref-Gaussian) is a framework for the real-time, high-quality rendering of reflective objects with inter-reflection effects. It addresses the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in modeling complex surfaces and multi-view inconsistencies. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by utilizing 2D Gaussian primitives for view-consistent geometry. It employs physically based deferred rendering with split-sum approximation to stabilize optimization and enable efficient inter-reflection modeling without heavy Monte Carlo sampling. Ref-Gaussian extends the Gaussian splatting framework by replacing 3D ellipsoids with 2D oriented planar Gaussian disks and applying deferred shading on pixel-level feature maps. Inputs: Scene representation: A set of N 2D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position \mathbf{p}, tangential vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v, scaling factors su, sv, and material properties. Environment map or light sources for illumination. Outputs: Final pixel radiance L(\omegao). Each 2D Gaussian primitive i stores: Position: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Tangential vectors: \mathbf{t}{u,i}, \mathbf{t}{v,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scaling factors: s{u,i}, s{v,i} \in \mathbb{R}. Material properties: Albedo \lambdai \in [0, 1]^3, metallic mi \in [0, 1], and roughness ri \in [0, 1]. Derived normal: \mathbf{n}i = \mathbf{t}{u,i} \times \mathbf{t}{v,i}. Pixel-level feature maps \mathbf{X} are accumulated during rasterization: \mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{\Lambda}, M, R, N]^T, where \mathbf{\Lambda} is the albedo map, M is the metallic map, R is the roughness map, and N is the normal map. 1. Primitive Definition: Represent the scene using 2D Gaussian primitives to capture detailed geometry and avoid multi-view inconsistencies inherent in 3D Gaussians. The influence of a 2D Gaussian in its local tangent space is defined as: \mathcal{G}(u, v) = \exp\left(-\frac{u^2 + v^2}{2}\right) where (u, v) are coordinates in the local tangent space. 2. Ray-Splat Intersection: Compute the intersection of a ray with a Gaussian splat in homogeneous coordinates. The intersection point \mathbf{x} is calculated as: \mathbf{x} = (xz, yz, z, 1)^T = WH(u, v, 1, 1)^T where H is the 4 \times 4 transformation matrix for the Gaussian: H = \begin{bmatrix} su \mathbf{t}u & sv \mathbf{t}v & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{p} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} Here, \mathbf{p} is the position, \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v are the tangential vectors, and su, sv are the scaling factors. 3. Alpha Blending for Feature Maps: Perform alpha-blending of Gaussian features to create pixel-level feature maps \mathbf{X}, treating alpha-blending as a smoothing filter to stabilize optimization. For each pixel, accumulate the features \mathbf{x}i weighted by opacity \alphai: \mathbf{X} = \sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{x}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{x}i = [\lambdai, mi, ri, \mathbf{n}i]^T and \mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{\Lambda}, M, R, N]^T. The opacity \alphai is calculated by multiplying the Gaussian's intrinsic opacity oi with the Gaussian weight determined by the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i. 4. Deferred Shading with Split-Sum Approximation: Apply the rendering equation on the aggregated feature maps \mathbf{X} rather than shading individual Gaussians before blending. The outgoing radiance L(\omegao) in direction \omegao is given by: L(\omegao) = \int{\Omega} Li(\omegai) f(\omegai, \omegao) (\omegai \cdot \mathbf{N}) \, d\omegai where f(\omegai, \omegao) is the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF), and \mathbf{N} is the normal from the feature map. To model inter-reflection effects efficiently, use the split-sum approximation of the rendering equation, avoiding heavy Monte Carlo sampling. 5. Visibility Computation: Compute visibility for the specular component by performing ray tracing on an extracted mesh. This approach provides accurate visibility for specular terms, unlike methods that trace rays across Gaussians which can be noisy and slow. Unverified code. w) safealpha = [[max(Alpha[y][x], 1e-6) for x in range(W)] for y in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): Lambda[y][x] = (Lambda[y][x][0]/safealpha[y][x], Lambda[y][x][1]/safealpha[y][x], Lambda[y][x][2]/safealpha[y][x]) M[y][x] /= safealpha[y][x] R[y][x] /= safealpha[y][x] N[y][x] = (N[y][x][0]/safealpha[y][x], N[y][x][1]/safealpha[y][x], N[y][x][2]/safealpha[y][x]) image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): image[y][x] = computebrdfradiance(Lambda[y][x], M[y][x], R[y][x], N[y][x], environmentmap) return image def compute2dcovariance(p, tu, tv, su, sv, camera): # Projects 2D Gaussian parameters to screen-space covariance pass def gaussianweight(Sigmaprime): # Returns normalization weight for the 2D covariance return 1.0 def computedistancesq(x, y, Sigmaprime, camera): # Computes squared Mahalanobis distance in screen space pass def getboundingbox(Sigmaprime, camera): # Returns 3-sigma bounding box in screen coordinates pass def computebrdfradiance(albedo, metallic, roughness, normal, environmentmap): # Applies split-sum approximation to the rendering equation pass def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) Albedo (\lambda): Material color property, range [0, 1]^3. Metallic (m): Material metallic property, range [0, 1]. Roughness (r): Material roughness property, range [0, 1]. Multi-view inconsistencies: Standard 3D Gaussians struggle with detailed geometry due to multi-view inconsistencies. Ref-Gaussian uses 2D Gaussians to mitigate this. Optimization stability: Shading directly on Gaussians before alpha-blending can lead to noise in geometry and material. Ref-Gaussian uses deferred shading on pixel-level feature maps to stabilize optimization. Visibility accuracy: Using Monte Carlo sampling across Gaussians for visibility can be slow and noisy. Ref-Gaussian uses ray tracing on an extracted mesh for specular visibility, providing more accurate results. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved by using the split-sum approximation to avoid heavy Monte Carlo sampling and by using efficient rasterization of 2D Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for 2D Gaussian primitives and pixel-level feature maps. The extracted mesh for visibility computation also adds memory overhead. Performance: Ref-Gaussian maintains fast rendering speeds while modeling inter-reflection effects. It is faster than methods using Monte Carlo sampling for visibility. Strengths: High-quality rendering of reflective objects, accurate inter-reflection modeling, stable optimization, real-time performance. Limitations: Requires an extracted mesh for visibility computation, which may add complexity to the pipeline. 2D Gaussians may have limitations in representing complex 3D structures compared to 3D Gaussians in some scenarios. When to use: When rendering reflective objects with complex inter-reflection effects is required, and real-time performance is necessary. When not to use: When the scene does not have significant reflective properties or inter-reflection effects, standard 3D Gaussian Splatting may be sufficient and simpler. Reflective Gaussian Splatting (Ref-Gaussian) was proposed to address the limitations of existing Gaussian splatting methods in rendering reflective objects with inter-reflection effects. It builds on the work of 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) and 2D Gaussian Splatting (Huang et al., 2024). The method was introduced in a paper by Ye et al. (2024). It differs from GShader (Jiang et al., 2024) by using deferred shading and from RelightableGaussian (Gao et al., 2023) by using ray tracing on an extracted mesh for visibility. name: Nexels
head: Neurally-Textured Surfels
body: Nexels is a novel view synthesis method that decouples geometry and appearance to achieve a compact representation using a fixed number of primitives per pixel. It uses surfels with a generalized Gaussian kernel for geometry and a shared neural field (Instant-NGP) for view-dependent appearance, rendered via a two-pass process to handle sparse primitives efficiently. Unlike sibling methods that couple appearance to primitives or use slower neural field lookups, Nexels textures only the top-K primitives per pixel, ensuring real-time performance while matching the perceptual quality of 3D Gaussian Splatting with significantly fewer primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N surfels; camera parameters (origin o, direction d, focal length f); training images for optimization. Outputs: A rendered image I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}; optimized surfel parameters and neural field weights. Data Structures: 1. Surfel: Defined by mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation Ri \in SO^3, scale \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^2, opacity oi \in \mathbb{R}, and gamma parameter \gammai \in \mathbb{R}^2. The surfel normal is derived from the rotation matrix. 2. Non-textured Appearance: Per-primitive view-dependent radiance ci^\odot \in \mathbb{R}^3 parameterized by spherical harmonics coefficients, where S is the number of coefficients (typically S=16 for degree 3). 3. Neural Field: Instant-NGP architecture. Hash-Grid: L levels. Each level \ell has a hash-table H\ell with T entries. Feature dimension is F. Total parameters: L \times T \times F. MLP: G, with 2 hidden layers, width 64, no bias, ReLU activations. Output dimension 48 (for S=16 SH coefficients). 4. Per-Pixel Buffer: Size K. Contains primitive ID, weight, and depth. Total 3K 32-bit registers per pixel. Written into H \times W \times K images I (IDs), D (depths), and W (weights). Parameters: K: Hyperparameter limiting primitives textured per pixel. Typically K=2. P: Hyperparameter controlling max number of primitives. \gammai: Gamma parameter controlling kernel shape. Constrained \gamma \ge 1 for C^\infty continuity. Loss weights: \lambda{alpha}=0.005, \lambda{texture}=0.5, \lambda{opacity}=0.01, \lambda{grid}=0.01, \lambda{D-SSIM}=0.2. Steps: 1. Initialization: Sample point cloud from COLMAP. Use farthest point sampling to reduce to 0.5P points. Initialize scale based on distance to predecessors during sampling. 2. Preprocessing: Sort surfels by the depth of their centers. 3. Collection Pass (First Rendering Pass): For each ray r:= o + td, compute the intersection in primitive space (u, v) differentiably from geometry parameters. Compute the alpha value using the generalized Gaussian kernel: \alphai:= oi \exp \left( - \frac{|u|^{2\gamma{i,1}}}{2} \right) \exp \left( - \frac{|v|^{2\gamma{i,2}}}{2} \right) Compute the blending weight wi:= \alphai Ti, where Ti:= \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Maintain the per-pixel buffer of size K. Update the buffer to store the running primitives with the highest weights. The buffer entries contain primitive ID, weight, and depth t^i(r). Compute the non-textured render Np for pixel p: Np:= \sum{i=0}^{M-1} wi ci^\odot - \sum{i \in Ip} wi ci^\odot where Ip is the set of textured primitives for pixel p (the top K). Write the final ID, depth, and weight buffers into images I, D, W. 4. Texturing Pass (Second Rendering Pass): Compute world-space intersection positions x \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times K \times 3} from the depth buffer D. For each textured primitive j at pixel p, compute the filtered texture radiance ci^\oplus(r): ci^\oplus(r):= G \left( \Deltai(r) \cdot H(xi^(r)) \right) where xi^(r):= o + t^i(r) d is the world-space intersection. The hash-grid feature retrieval H(x) is calculated as: H(x):= [H{0,h0}, \dots, H{L-1,h{L-1}}] \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times F} where hash h\ell is calculated from s\ell \cdot x and indexed into grid level \ell. The down-weighting factor \Delta{i,\ell}(r) for anti-aliasing is: \Delta{i,\ell}(r):= 1 - \exp \left( - \frac{f^2}{2\pi s\ell t^i(r)} \right) where f is focal length, s\ell is scale, and t^i(r) is intersection depth. Compute the final texture T \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times K \times 3} where T{p,j}:= c{I{p,j}}^\oplus(r). Composite the textures with the non-textured render: Ip = Np + \sum{j=0}^{K-1} W{p,j} T{p,j} Pseudocode: Unverified code. surfel['mu']) locald = Rinv @ d # Intersection parameter t in local frame tlocal = -localo[2] / locald[2] u = localo[0] + tlocal locald[0] v = localo[1] + tlocal locald[1] return u, v def updatepixelbuffer(I, Dbuf, Wbuf, weight, surfelid, depth): # For each pixel, insert (weight, surfelid, depth) into top-K list for y in range(I.shape[0]): for x in range(I.shape[1]): pos = 0 while pos < K and Wbuf[y, x, pos] > weight[y, x]: pos += 1 if pos < K: for j in range(K - 2, pos - 1, -1): I[y, x, j+1] = I[y, x, j] Dbuf[y, x, j+1] = Dbuf[y, x, j] Wbuf[y, x, j+1] = Wbuf[y, x, j] I[y, x, pos] = surfelid Dbuf[y, x, pos] = depth Wbuf[y, x, pos] = weight def queryneuralfield(xpositions, f, Dbuf): # xpositions: H x W x K x 3 # Returns: H x W x K x 3 (radiance) L = 16; F = 2; T = 220; s = [2i for i in range(L)] Hgrid = torch.randn(L, T, F) # Placeholder for actual grid G = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(FL, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 48)) radiance = torch.zeroslike(xpositions) for k in range(K): x = xpositions[:,:, k,:] features = [] for l in range(L): h = hashfunction(s[l] x) % T feat = Hgrid[l, h,:] features.append(feat) Hx = torch.cat(features, dim=-1) # LF out = G(Hx) # 48 tstar = Dbuf[:,:, k] delta = 1.0 - The down-weighting factor \Delta{i,\ell}(r) is required to remove noticeable aliasing artifacts. Boundaries: The generalized Gaussian kernel converges to a quad indicator as \gamma \to \infty, providing sharp boundaries. Degenerate Input: Initialization uses farthest point sampling to ensure good coverage. Uses per-primitive textures for reflective scenes. Lindell, et al. in December 2025. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting [20] and Instant-NGP [36]. name: Gaussian Conditional Probability Formulation
head: Conditional Splat, Factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting, Factorized Density, Unnormalized 4D Gaussian probability distribution
body: This method decomposes a 3D Gaussian probability density into a product of a marginal distribution along the depth axis and a conditional distribution over the 2D coordinates given the depth. It treats the unnormalized 4D Gaussian as a special probability distribution over spatial coordinates (u, v) and time t (or depth), enabling factorization into temporal and conditional spatial components. This factorized approach provides a computationally efficient way to model volumetric data for slice-based rendering or tomographic reconstruction compared to processing the full 3D density directly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Gaussian primitive defined by mean vector \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D} and covariance matrix \Sigma{3D}. Output: A factorized representation consisting of a marginal distribution p(t) and a conditional distribution p(u, v | t). Data Structures: The 3D Gaussian is parameterized by: \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D} = [\mux, \muy, \muz]^\top: The mean vector. \Sigma{3D}: The 3 \times 3 symmetric covariance matrix with elements \sigma{xx}, \sigma{xy}, \sigma{xz}, \sigma{yy}, \sigma{yz}, \sigma{zz}. Formulas: The joint density p(u, v, t) is factorized as: p(u, v, t) = p(t) \cdot p(u, v | t) 1. Marginal Distribution p(t): The distribution along the depth axis t is a 1D Gaussian: p(t) \sim \mathcal{N}(\muz, \sigma{zz}) Where \muz and \sigma{zz} are the mean and variance of the Gaussian along the z-axis. Note: defines a more general temporal marginal p(t) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} \det(\Sigmat)^{-1/2} \mathcal{N}(t|\mut, \Sigmat), but for the standard 3DGS depth decomposition, the scalar variance \sigma{zz} is used. 2. Conditional Distribution p(u, v | t): Conditioned on a specific depth t, the distribution over in-plane coordinates (u, v) is a 2D Gaussian: p(u, v | t) \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{uv|t}, \Sigma{uv|t}) Conditional Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{uv|t}: The conditional mean is shifted linearly according to the offset t - \muz: \begin{bmatrix} \muu \\ \muv \end{bmatrix} = \boldsymbol{\mu}{uv|t} = \begin{bmatrix} \mux \\ \muy \end{bmatrix} + \frac{t - \muz}{\sigma{zz}} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{xz} \\ \sigma{yz} \end{bmatrix} This relation reflects how the mean position of the Gaussian footprint in the image plane moves as we slice through different depth levels. Conditional Covariance \Sigma{uv|t}: The conditional covariance matrix is given by the Schur complement: \Sigma{uv|t} = \Sigma{uv} - \Sigma{uv,t} \sigma{zz}^{-1} \Sigma{t,uv} Explicitly, using the elements of \Sigma{3D}: \Sigma{uv|t} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{xx} & \sigma{xy} \\ \sigma{xy} & \sigma{yy} \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sigma{zz}} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{xz} \\ \sigma{yz} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{xz} & \sigma{yz} \end{bmatrix} This matrix accounts for how the uncertainty in u and v directions reduces once the depth t is fixed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianconditionalformulation(mu3d, sigma3d, t): """ Computes the conditional 2D Gaussian parameters for a slice at depth t. Args: mu3d: Array [mux, muy, muz] sigma3d: 3x3 Covariance matrix [[sxx, sxy, sxz], [sxy, syy, syz], [sxz, syz, szz]] t: Depth value (scalar) Returns: muuvcond: Array [muu, muv] sigmauvcond: 2x2 Covariance matrix """ # Extract scalar components mux, muy, muz = mu3d sxx, sxy, sxz = sigma3d[0] syy, syz = sigma3d[1][1], sigma3d[1][2] szz = sigma3d[2][2] # 1. Compute Conditional Mean # muuv|t = [mux, muy] + (t - muz) / sigmazz [sigmaxz, sigmayz] offset = (t - muz) / szz muu = mux + offset sxz muv = muy + offset syz muuvcond = [muu, muv] # 2. Compute Conditional Covariance (Schur Complement) # Sigmauv|t = Sigmauv - (1/sigmazz) Sigmauvt Sigmatuv # Sigmauv is the top-left 2x2 block # Sigmauvt is the column vector [sxz, syz] term1 = sxx - (sxz sxz) / szz term2 = sxy - (sxz syz) / szz term3 = syy - (syz syz) / szz sigmauvcond = [[term1, term2], [term2, term3]] return muuvcond, sigmauvcond Parameters: \mu{3D}: Mean vector. \Sigma{3D}: Covariance matrix. t: Slice depth or time coordinate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by \sigma{zz} occurs in the mean shift and covariance calculation. If \sigma{zz} is near zero, the Gaussian is extremely thin along the depth axis, leading to numerical instability. Guard against division by zero by clamping \sigma{zz} to a small epsilon or handling degenerate Gaussians separately. Boundary: The conditional distribution is valid for any t, but the approximation assumes the Gaussian is well-behaved. For slice-based rendering, this formulation allows processing individual planes efficiently. Extends this formulation to model joint distributions over non-spatial dimensions like viewing direction or time, conditioning on queries to derive view-specific or time-specific 3D Gaussians. It differs from standard 3DGS by explicitly encoding dependencies between geometry and observation parameters. Time Complexity: The factorization allows for efficient slice-based rendering. Instead of integrating the full 3D density, one can process individual planes (slices) using the 2D conditional Gaussian, which is computationally cheaper than processing the full 3D volume directly. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the standard 3D Gaussian parameters, as the conditional parameters are computed on-the-fly from the marginal and covariance. Strengths: Provides a computationally efficient way to model volumetric data, particularly useful in applications like slice-based rendering or tomographic reconstruction. It accurately captures the reduction in uncertainty in u and v directions once depth t is fixed. Limitations: The method relies on the Gaussian assumption. If the underlying density is highly non-Gaussian, the factorization may introduce approximation errors. The accuracy depends on the validity of the Gaussian approximation for the specific primitive. The Gaussian Conditional Probability Formulation is based on the statistical property that a multivariate Gaussian distribution can be factorized into a marginal and a conditional distribution. This property is leveraged in 3D Gaussian Splatting variants (such as 2DGS/1DGS and 4DGS) to enable efficient rendering by decomposing the 3D (or 4D) density into depth/time and spatial components. The method was introduced in the context of factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting for internal scene reconstruction and real-time photorealistic dynamic scene representation. name: N-Dimensional Gaussian (6DGS/7DGS)
head: 6DGS, 7DGS, Gao et al, 2025a, 2025b
body: N-Dimensional Gaussian extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by modeling a joint probability distribution over spatial coordinates and non-spatial dimensions (such as viewing direction or time), then conditioning on the query to derive view-specific or time-specific 3D Gaussians for rendering. Unlike standard 3DGS which treats primitives as static spatial entities, this method explicitly encodes correlations between geometry and appearance/dynamics via cross-covariance terms, allowing for continuous view-dependent effects and temporal coherence without discrete keyframes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N N-dimensional Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i is defined by parameters \{\boldsymbol{\mu}p, \boldsymbol{\mu}d, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd}, \alpha, \lambda\}. Query: A specific non-spatial vector \mathbf{q} (e.g., viewing direction \mathbf{d} or time t). Output: A set of conditional 3D Gaussian primitives \{\boldsymbol{\mu}{cond}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{cond}, \alpha{cond}\} ready for standard 3DGS splatting. Data Structures: Each primitive stores the following fields: \boldsymbol{\mu}p \in \mathbb{R}^3: Spatial mean (position). \boldsymbol{\mu}d \in \mathbb{R}^k: Non-spatial mean (e.g., \mathbb{R}^3 for direction, \mathbb{R}^1 for time). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Spatial covariance block. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}: Non-spatial covariance block. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times k}: Cross-covariance block between spatial and non-spatial dimensions. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity. \lambda \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity modulation scaling factor. Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Joint Distribution: Define the joint vector X = \begin{pmatrix} Xp \\ Xd \end{pmatrix} where Xp represents spatial coordinates and Xd represents non-spatial coordinates. The joint distribution is: X \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}p \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}d \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd} \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd}^\top & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d \end{pmatrix}\right) \quad (5) 2. Condition on Query: Given a query value \mathbf{q} for the non-spatial dimension Xd, compute the conditional mean and covariance for the spatial dimension Xp using standard Gaussian conditioning formulas: \boldsymbol{\mu}{cond} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d^{-1} (\mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}d) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{cond} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd}^\top 3. Modulate Opacity: Calculate the conditional opacity \alpha{cond} based on the likelihood of the query \mathbf{q} under the non-spatial distribution: \alpha{cond} = \alpha \cdot \exp\left(-\lambda (\mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}d)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d^{-1} (\mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}d)\right) 4. Render: Use \boldsymbol{\mu}{cond}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{cond}, and \alpha{cond} as the parameters for the primitive during the standard 3DGS splatting pass. Parameters: \lambda: Controls the sharpness of opacity modulation. Positive values yield sharper peaks, better capturing high-frequency details. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d^{-1}: Requires the non-spatial covariance to be invertible. If singular, pseudo-inverse or regularization is needed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d is not positive definite or invertible, the conditioning step fails. Regularization (e.g., adding \epsilon I) is required. Degenerate Input: If the query \mathbf{q} is far from \boldsymbol{\mu}d, the exponential term in opacity may underflow to zero, effectively culling the primitive. Dimensionality: For 6DGS, k=3 (view direction). For 7DGS, k=4 (view direction + time). Treats the radiance field as a probabilistic mixture of 3D Gaussians, modeling uncertainty and distributional parameters rather than single-point estimates. Choose this when modeling data uncertainty is critical; it differs from N-Dimensional Gaussian by focusing on mixture components rather than conditional distributions over explicit non-spatial dimensions. Time Complexity: Rendering time increases slightly due to the per-primitive conditioning calculation (O(k^3) for matrix inversion if done naively, but k is small: 3 or 4). The splatting pass itself remains O(N) per pixel. Memory Complexity: Each primitive stores additional parameters for the non-spatial mean, covariance, and cross-covariance. For 6DGS, this adds \approx 3 + 6 + 9 = 18 floats per primitive compared to standard 3DGS. For 7DGS, it adds more for the temporal dimension. Strengths: Enables continuous view-dependent appearance and smooth temporal transitions without discrete keyframes or explicit deformation fields. Limitations: Increased memory footprint per primitive. Training requires optimizing cross-covariance terms, which may be more complex than standard 3DGS. When to use: Scenes with strong view-dependent effects (specularities, iridescence) or smooth temporal dynamics where discrete keyframing is insufficient. N-Dimensional Gaussian (6DGS/7DGS) was introduced by Gao et al. in 2025. It extends the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by incorporating conditional probability distributions to handle non-spatial dimensions like viewing direction and time. This approach allows for a more compact and continuous representation of dynamic and view-dependent scenes. name: 3D/4D Gaussian Splatting Mixture Model
head: 3D/4DGS Mixture Model
body: The 3D/4D Gaussian Splatting Mixture Model treats a radiance field as a probabilistic mixture of 3D Gaussian primitives, where each component is defined by location, shape, opacity, and color. It differs from deterministic splatting by framing the rendering process as the evaluation of expected color values conditioned on spatial location, allowing for the modeling of data uncertainty and distributional parameters rather than single-point estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M Gaussian components, each defined by parameters \thetak. For standard 3DGS, these are location \muk, shape \Sigmak, opacity ok, and color sk (via spherical harmonics). For Variational Bayesian GS (VBGS), parameters include distributions over these attributes (e.g., Normal-Inverse-Wishart for color/position, Dirichlet for assignments). Outputs: The expected color C(d) for each pixel d in the rendered image. Data Structures: Standard 3DGS Component: \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean location. \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (shape). ok \in [0, 1]: Opacity. sk: Color coefficients (Spherical Harmonics). VBGS Component (Probabilistic): Represents a distribution over parameters. Requires 29 parameters per component (vs. 14 in gradient baselines) to model the Normal-Inverse-Wishart likelihood for color/position and Dirichlet prior. Stores posterior probabilities p(zn = k|s), representing the probability that data point n belongs to component k given spatial location s. Rendering Formula: The final color C(d) of the d-th pixel is computed by summing contributions from N intersecting Gaussians: C(d) = \sum{i=1}^{N} si oi G{i,2D}(d) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj G{j,2D}(d)) Where: si: Color of the i-th Gaussian. oi: Opacity of the i-th Gaussian. G{i,2D}(d): The value of the 2D Gaussian projected onto the image plane at pixel d. The term \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj G{j,2D}(d)) represents the alpha blending transmittance from previous Gaussians. VBGS Specifics: In VBGS, rendering evaluates the expected color E{p(c|s)}[c]. This is approximated as: E{p(c|s)}[c] \approx \sum{k} p(zn = k|s) ck Where ck is the mean color of component k and p(zn = k|s) is the posterior assignment probability. Note that VBGS sets alpha values to 1 (opaque) for all components, bypassing standard alpha blending as it does not optimize for image reconstruction in the same manner. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian parameters. For VBGS, initialize variational distributions (Normal-Inverse-Wishart, Dirichlet). 2. Projection: Transform 3D Gaussians to 2D Gaussians on the image plane. 3. Assignment (VBGS only): Compute posterior probabilities p(zn = k|s) for each data point n and component k. 4. Rendering: For standard GS: Apply alpha blending formula. For VBGS: Compute weighted sum of expected colors using posterior probabilities. 5. Optimization (VBGS only): Perform Coordinate Ascent Variational Inference (CAVI): Step A: Compute model assignments (Complexity O(nm)). Step B: Compute parameter updates (Complexity O(n)). Parameters: VBGS Memory: Increases by a factor of 2 compared to gradient baselines for the same number of Gaussians due to storing 29 parameters per component. Data Normalization: Data is normalized to zero mean and unit standard deviation before training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VBGS Alpha Blending: Standard alpha blending is not used in VBGS because it does not optimize for image reconstruction; all components are treated as opaque (\alpha=1). Uncertainty: Standard 4DGS does not model asynchronous cameras or multiple types of uncertainty; this requires extensions like GraphiXS. A probabilistic variant that represents a distribution over Gaussian Mixture Model parameters using Normal-Inverse-Wishart likelihoods and Dirichlet priors. It differs from standard GS by optimizing via CAVI rather than gradient descent, allowing for uncertainty modeling. Choose it when modeling data uncertainty or when a probabilistic representation is required, accepting higher memory usage (2x) and computational cost. Link: VBGS. Time Complexity: Standard GS rendering is dominated by sorting and blending N Gaussians. VBGS training involves two steps: assignment O(nm) and parameter updates O(n), where n is data points and m is components. Memory Complexity: VBGS requires 29 parameters per component compared to 14 in standard GS, doubling memory requirements for the same number of Gaussians. Performance: VBGS training can be parallelized on GPU for both components and data. Strengths: Handles data uncertainty; provides probabilistic outputs. Limitations: Higher memory and computational cost for VBGS; standard GS lacks uncertainty modeling. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced as a new paradigm for neural rendering, representing radiance fields with 3D Gaussians. Extensions like GraphiXS address data uncertainty in 4DGS. VBGS applies variational Bayesian methods to Gaussian Splatting, treating it as a Gaussian Mixture Model. name: Primitive Geometry and Distribution
head: Primitive Representation Family
body: This family defines the geometric primitives used to represent 3D scenes in differentiable splatting methods, extending the standard 3D Gaussian ellipsoid to alternative shapes, distributions, and dimensionalities. It solves the limitations of volumetric Gaussian mixtures, such as ambiguous geometry, poor mesh extraction, and inefficient representation of sharp edges or opaque surfaces, by introducing planar disks, fat-tailed distributions, generalized exponential functions, and polyhedral volumes. It differs from sibling methods by varying the fundamental density function or geometric support of the primitive while maintaining the core splatting pipeline of projection and alpha compositing. All child methods share the core requirement of defining a 3D primitive with a position, orientation, scale, and appearance attributes. The standard 3D Gaussian primitive is defined by a mean \boldsymbol{\mu} for position, a covariance \Sigma for shape and orientation, and appearance attributes like Spherical Harmonics coefficients and opacity \alpha. Parameterized as \Sigma^w = R S S^T R^T in world space, where R is rotation and S is scaling. The rendering pipeline projects these 3D primitives to 2D screen space. The covariance transforms via the view matrix W and projection Jacobian J: \Sigma = J W \Sigma^w W^T J^T. The integral of the 3D density along the view direction yields the 2D splat density. Direct Gaussian Splatting (dGS) is a method for N-dimensional splatting that replaces the covariance-derived conditioning step of standard N-DGS with explicit per-primitive parameters, removing the need for per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products during rendering. It solves the computational bottleneck of recovering conditional mean, opacity, and covariance from a joint distribution by directly parameterizing the opacity precision and position regression operator. Unlike N-DGS, which couples position and opacity through shared covariance blocks requiring expensive linear algebra, dGS separates these effects using a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query-to-position regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling. It differs from sibling methods like 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting, Generalized Exponential Splatting, and 2D Gaussian Splatting by explicitly parameterizing the conditioning step rather than deriving it from a joint covariance matrix. See Direct Gaussian Splatting for implementation details. 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting (SSS) is a neural rendering method that replaces the 3D Gaussian primitives of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with flexible Student's t distributions and extends the splatting scheme to include both positive (splatting) and negative (scooping) density components. It solves the expressivity limitations of Gaussian mixtures by utilizing fat-tailed distributions and non-monotonic density modeling, achieving higher parameter efficiency (reducing component counts by up to 82%) while maintaining or improving rendering quality. SSS replaces monotonic Gaussian mixtures with Student's t distributions and employs Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC) to prevent the degree of freedom parameter \nu from collapsing to local minima. See 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting for implementation details. Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) is a 3D scene representation method that replaces the Gaussian basis functions of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Generalized Exponential Functions (GEF). It introduces a learnable shape parameter \beta for each primitive to better model signals with sharp edges and high-frequency content, reducing the number of particles required and thus memory footprint while maintaining competitive rendering quality. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting, which assumes low-pass characteristics, GES allows primitives to adapt their shape to fit high-bandwidth signals like squares and triangles more efficiently. See Generalized Exponential Splatting for implementation details. 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) is a surface reconstruction technique that replaces the volumetric 3D Gaussian ellipsoids of 3D Gaussian Splatting with oriented, zero-thickness 2D disks (surfels). It solves the problem of ambiguous geometry and poor mesh extraction inherent in volumetric representations by aligning primitives with local surface tangent planes, thereby improving multi-view depth consistency and enabling high-resolution normal map recovery. Unlike its sibling Direct Gaussian Splatting, which retains volumetric blobs, 2DGS uses planar primitives to provide unambiguous normals and accurate surface intersection. See 2D Gaussian Splatting for implementation details. Definition: A scene representation using transparent polyhedra (octahedra) bounded by triangular faces with homogeneous density, optimized for differentiable volumetric rendering. Steps: Restrict vertex positions to lie on the coordinate axes relative to the center to prevent degenerate cases and non-triangular faces. Enforce symmetry by choosing a single distance to describe opposing corners, so each pair of opposite vertices shares the same distance from the center. Optimize a rotation quaternion for each primitive to allow arbitrary orientation in space. Parameters: Octahedra memory requirement is 11 floats per primitive (omitting color), comprising center, rotation, corner distances, and opacity. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients are 48 floats per primitive (Degree 2), stored to capture view-dependent appearance. Definition: A modification where regular capped Gaussian primitives are converted to high-opacity Gaussians to boost modeling of opaque surfaces with fewer primitives. Steps: Replace the opacity activation function with abs() and clamp blending weights to 1 from above during rendering. Parameters: Activation switch point is the midpoint of training, specifically 15K iterations. Definition: A method that represents opaque objects with Gaussian density distribution to make the visibility function differentiable, suitable for generative pose estimation. Pitfalls: VSS is hard to handle geometry with high frequency such as sharp corners, and the rendered image is blurry compared with traditional rendering methods. The concept of using explicit geometric primitives for differentiable rendering has evolved from neural radiance fields to explicit point-based representations. The LinPrim method, introduced in "LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering" (2025), proposed transparent polyhedra like octahedra to replace Gaussian blobs, aiming for real-time volumetric rendering with linear primitives. The High-Opacity Gaussian modification, described in "Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources" (2024), optimized the standard 3DGS pipeline by converting primitives to high-opacity states to better model opaque surfaces. The Volumetric Shading System (VSS), referenced in "Jrender: An efficient differentiable rendering library based on Jittor" (2023), was an early approach using Gaussian density for visibility functions, though noted for blurring high-frequency geometry.
