name: Direct Gaussian Splatting
head: dGS, direct conditional parameterization for Gaussian kernel
body: Direct Gaussian Splatting (dGS) is a method for N-dimensional splatting that replaces the covariance-derived conditioning step of standard N-DGS with explicit per-primitive parameters, removing the need for per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products during rendering. It solves the computational bottleneck of recovering conditional mean, opacity, and covariance from a joint distribution by directly parameterizing the opacity precision and position regression operator. Unlike N-DGS, which couples position and opacity through shared covariance blocks requiring expensive linear algebra, dGS separates these effects using a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query-to-position regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling. It differs from sibling methods like 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting, Generalized Exponential Splatting, and 2D Gaussian Splatting by explicitly parameterizing the conditioning step rather than deriving it from a joint covariance matrix. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N primitives. Each primitive i is defined by the base parameters from Primitive Geometry and Distribution (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}p, base opacity \alpha, etc.) plus the conditioning variables: Canonical query mean \boldsymbol{\mu}q (e.g., view direction or time). Cholesky precision factor \mathbf{L} for opacity. Spatial coupling factor \mathbf{V}{pq}. Per-dimension coupling vector \boldsymbol{\Lambda}. Precision matrix block \mathbf{V}{qq} (shared with opacity). Output: Conditional mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}} and conditional opacity \alpha{\text{cond}} for a given query \mathbf{q} (e.g., camera view direction). Data Structures: \mathbf{L}: Lower triangular Cholesky factor of the opacity precision matrix. Size C \times C where C is the dimension of the query space (typically 3 for view direction). \mathbf{V}{pq}: Spatial coupling factor. Size 3 \times C. Constrained such that \|\mathbf{V}{pq}\|F = \bar{s}, where \bar{s} is the mean scale of the primitive. \boldsymbol{\Lambda}: Per-dimension coupling vector. Size C. Controls the interpolation between query-independent position and full covariance coupling. \mathbf{V}{qq}: Precision matrix block for the query space. Size C \times C. Symmetric positive-definite. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Query Deviation: Calculate the deviation of the query from the canonical mean: \boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}q. 2. Compute Opacity: Calculate the conditional opacity using the Cholesky factor \mathbf{L}: \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \exp(-\lambda0 \|\mathbf{L}^T \boldsymbol{\delta}\|2^2). 3. Compute Position Shift: Calculate the shift to the conditional mean using the factorized regression operator: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta}. Note: The term \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta} is computed first, then scaled element-wise by \boldsymbol{\Lambda}, then multiplied by \mathbf{V}{pq}. Formulas: Opacity: \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \exp(-\lambda0 \|\mathbf{L}^T \boldsymbol{\delta}\|2^2) Position: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta} Coupling Interpretation: When \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{0}, the position is query-independent (recovering dGS-O). When \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{1}, position and opacity share the full precision \mathbf{V}{qq}, mirroring N-DGS coupling. Parameters: \lambda0: Scaling factor for the opacity kernel. Default value is 0.35. \mathbf{L}: Learnable Cholesky precision factor per primitive. \mathbf{V}{pq}: Learnable spatial coupling factor per primitive. \boldsymbol{\Lambda}: Learnable per-dimension coupling vector per primitive. \mathbf{V}{qq}: Learnable precision matrix block per primitive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method avoids matrix inversion, improving numerical stability compared to N-DGS. Boundary: The coupling vector \boldsymbol{\Lambda} allows smooth interpolation between decoupled and fully coupled states. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directgaussiansplattingconditioning( q: list, # Query vector (e.g., view direction) muq: list, # Canonical query mean mup: list, # Base position mean alpha: float, # Base opacity L: list, # Cholesky precision factor (C x C) Vpq: list, # Spatial coupling factor (3 x C) Lambda: list, # Per-dimension coupling (C) Vqq: list, # Precision matrix block (C x C) lambda0: float = 0.35 # Scaling factor) -> tuple: """ Computes conditional opacity and mean for a direct Gaussian splatting primitive. Args: q: Query vector (e.g., view direction). muq: Canonical query mean. mup: Base position mean. alpha: Base opacity. L: Cholesky precision factor for opacity. Vpq: Spatial coupling factor. Lambda: Per-dimension coupling vector. Vqq: Precision matrix block. lambda0: Scaling factor for opacity kernel. Returns: mucond: Conditional mean position. alphacond: Conditional opacity. """ # Step 1: Compute query deviation delta = [q[i] - muq[i] for i in range(len(q))] # Step 2: Compute opacity # alphacond = alpha exp(-lambda0 ||L^T delta||^2) LTdelta = [sum(L[j][i] delta[j] for j in range(len(delta))) for i in range(len(delta))] opacityterm = lambda0 sum(x y for x, y in zip(LTdelta, LTdelta)) alphacond = alpha exp(-opacityterm) # Step 3: Compute position shift # mucond = mup + Vpq @ diag(Lambda) @ (Vqq @ delta) # Compute Vqq delta Vqqdelta = [sum(Vqq[i][j] delta[j] for j in range(len(delta))) for i in range(len(Vqq))] # Apply per-dimension coupling: diag(Lambda) (Vqq delta) coupledshift = [Lambda[i] Vqqdelta[i] for i in range(len(Lambda))] # Apply spatial coupling: Vpq coupledshift positionshift = [sum(Vpq[i][j] coupledshift[j] for j in range(len(coupledshift))) for i in range(3)] # Final conditional mean mucond = [mup[i] + positionshift[i] for i in range(3)] return mucond, alphacond Direct Beta Splatting (dBS) is a variant of dGS that swaps the Gaussian opacity decay for a Beta opacity decay, following the UBS implementation. It reuses the direct conditional structure (\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{V}{pq}, \mathbf{V}{qq}) but derives coupling from bandwidth. Unlike dGS, which uses a separate learned coupling \boldsymbol{\Lambda} for position, dBS derives the coupling \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\beta from the opacity bandwidth \boldsymbol{\beta}. It is chosen when a Beta kernel is preferred for its specific decay properties, while retaining the computational benefits of direct conditioning. Definition: A variant of dGS that swaps the Gaussian opacity decay for a Beta opacity decay, following the UBS implementation. Steps: 1. Compute z = \mathbf{L}^T \boldsymbol{\delta}. 2. For each dimension i, compute (1 - \tanh(zi^2))^{\betai}. 3. Multiply these terms together and scale by base opacity \alpha. 4. Compute position: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\beta) \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta}. Formulas: Beta Opacity: \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \prod{i=1}^C (1 - \tanh(zi^2))^{\betai} where z = \mathbf{L}^T \boldsymbol{\delta} and \betai = 4 \exp(\beta{\text{raw}i}). Beta Position: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\beta) \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta} where \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\beta = \min(\boldsymbol{\beta}/4, 1). Parameters: \betai: Bandwidth parameter for Beta kernel, defined as \betai = 4 \exp(\beta{\text{raw}i}). \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\beta: Coupling vector for dBS, derived from bandwidth as \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\beta = \min(\boldsymbol{\beta}/4, 1). Number of Conditioning Parameters: For C=3, UBS and dBS use 19 conditioning parameters; for C=4, they use 27. N-DGS uses 15/16 and dGS uses 22/24 for C=3/4 respectively. Comparison: dGS uses a separate learned coupling \boldsymbol{\Lambda} for position, while dBS derives coupling \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\beta from the opacity bandwidth \boldsymbol{\beta}. Both retain the same direct conditional structure. Time Complexity: Removes per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products required by N-DGS, reducing computational cost per query. Memory Complexity: Stores explicit parameters \mathbf{L}, \mathbf{V}{pq}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}, and \mathbf{V}{qq} per primitive. Measured Performance: Ablation studies show that removing the spatial scale prior \bar{s} degrades PSNR by 2.65 dB on NeRF Synthetic. Strengths: Removes expensive operations, separates position from opacity coupling, and improves numerical stability by avoiding matrix inversion. Limitations: Uses more parameters than N-DGS for C=3 (22 vs 15). When to Use: Chosen when explicit parameterization is preferred to avoid per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and the parameter count of dGS is prohibitive compared to N-DGS. Direct Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the paper "Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting". It builds on the N-DGS framework and the UBS method. The method was developed to address the computational bottleneck of covariance-derived conditioning in N-dimensional splatting. Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: FactorSplat
body: FactorSplat is a per-scene N-dimensional Gaussian splatting (N-DGS) proxy that accepts region-specific intensity-to-RGBA transfer function (TF) curves at inference time, allowing appearance changes without retraining or refitting. It solves the problem of image-trained Gaussian proxies baking one transfer function into their appearance, which prevents supporting new presets without rebuilding the proxy. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting where geometry and appearance are tightly coupled to a single rendering configuration, FactorSplat decouples the geometric primitives from the appearance logic, allowing multiple TFs to share the same underlying Gaussian proxy. It differs from region-aware VEG by using region-specific intensity TFs and cinematic-rendering supervision, combining direct lookup with an image-trained N-DGS proxy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N Gaussian primitives defined by centers \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariances \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, and opacity logits oi. A set of M segmented regions/materials. A target transfer function preset T, defined by region-specific intensity-to-RGBA curves. Output: Rendered image with colors and opacities adjusted for preset T, while maintaining the shared geometry and directional appearance of the base proxy. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitives: For each primitive i: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity logit. \mathbf{C}^{\text{base}}i \in \mathbb{R}^{Qb \times 3}: Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for RGB, where Qb=4 (degree-one SH: 1 DC + 3 directional). Transfer Function Representation: Base preset T0 and target preset T. Common grid of S intensity samples \{hs\}{s=1}^S. Raw TF curves averaged onto B=64 intensity bins: \mathbf{R}^{(B)}T \in [0, 1]^{M \times B \times 4}. Region channel m \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}. Intensity-bin index b \in \{0, \dots, B-1\}. Local Support Data (per primitive i): Ki \le 27: Number of valid samples in the 3 \times 3 \times 3 voxel window around \boldsymbol{\mu}i. \mathbf{m}{ik} \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}: Region channel of the k-th valid sample. \mathbf{b}{ik} \in \{0, \dots, B-1\}: Intensity-bin index of the k-th valid sample. w{ik} \in [0, 1]: Normalized nonnegative weight for the k-th sample, such that \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} = 1. u{ik} = \mathbf{m}{ik} \cdot B + \mathbf{b}{ik}: Encoded integer identifier for the pair (\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik}). Parameters: B = 64: Number of intensity bins for TF discretization. S: Number of intensity samples in the common grid. M: Number of segmented regions/materials. H, r: Hidden and output dimensions of the pointwise MLP \phi\eta. T0: Designated base condition preset. The method is centered on this preset, giving exact identity at T0. h: Calibrated scalar intensity (HU for CT, normalized scalar for MR). Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives with centers \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariances \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, and opacity logits oi. The base opacity is \sigma(oi) where \sigma is the logistic sigmoid. Initialize the pointwise MLP \phi\eta(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{W}2 \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}1 \mathbf{v}) with weights \mathbf{W}1 \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times 4} and \mathbf{W}2 \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times H}. At initialization, for each primitive i, sample the 3 \times 3 \times 3 voxel window around it. Identify valid samples k with region channel \mathbf{m}{ik} and intensity-bin index \mathbf{b}{ik}. Count valid samples Ki \le 27. Compute normalized nonnegative weights w{ik} such that \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} = 1. Define empirical joint mass pi(m, b) = \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} \cdot \mathbb{1}[(\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik}) = (m, b)]. Encode each pair (\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik}) as a single integer u{ik} = \mathbf{m}{ik} \cdot B + \mathbf{b}{ik}. 2. TF Discretization: Export every preset on the common grid of S intensity samples \{hs\} to create the sampled input tensor \mathbf{R}T \in [0, 1]^{M \times S \times 4}. Average raw TF curves onto B=64 intensity bins to get \mathbf{R}^{(B)}T \in [0, 1]^{M \times B \times 4}. 3. Appearance Conditioning (at inference for preset T): Compute the raw, unpremultiplied RGBA change for preset T relative to base T0: \delta \mathbf{r}T(m, b) = \mathbf{R}^{(B)}T(m, b) - \mathbf{R}^{(B)}{T0}(m, b) \in \mathbb{R}^4 where \mathbf{R}T(m, h) = (\mathbf{p}T(m, h), aT(m, h)) \in [0, 1]^3 \times [0, 1]. Physical Lookup: Compute the physical local lookup offset \mathbf{d}i(T) by weighted mean of \delta \mathbf{r}T over the primitive's samples: \mathbf{d}i(T) = \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}T(\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik}) If Ki = 0, set \mathbf{d}i(T) = \mathbf{0}. Learned Residual: Embed each RGBA difference using the bias-free pointwise MLP \phi\eta(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{W}2 \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}1 \mathbf{v}). Pool the local codes for primitive i using weighted sum: \mathbf{z}{i,T} = \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} \cdot \phi\eta(\delta \mathbf{r}T(\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik})) \in \mathbb{R}^r If Ki = 0, set \mathbf{z}{i,T} = \mathbf{0}. Apply Appearance: Both \mathbf{d}i(T) and \mathbf{z}{i,T} modify only the view-independent (DC) color and opacity. Directional SH coefficients remain TF-independent. The backbone opacity passed to the rasterizer is \sigma(oi)s{\text{view}i}(\pi), where s{\text{view}i}(\pi) is the TF-independent opacity attenuation. The final DC color and opacity are adjusted by \mathbf{d}i(T) and \mathbf{z}{i,T}. [G: The exact projection from \mathbb{R}^r to the \mathbb{R}^4 color/opacity space is not specified; typically a small linear layer or bias-free MLP maps \mathbf{z}{i,T} to additive offsets, which are clamped to valid ranges.] 4. Pruning: Prune primitives based on maximum opacity over the training bank of TFs to preserve coverage and protect primitives needed by different training TFs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) def phieta(v, W1, W2): """Bias-free pointwise MLP: phieta(v) = W2 ReLU(W1 v).""" return W2 @ np.maximum(0, W1 @ v) def factorsplatinference( primitives, # List of dicts with keys: mu, Sigma, o, Cbase, mik, bik, wik, Ki tfcurves, # Dict: presetid -> (M, S, 4) array of RGBA values basepresetid, # str: ID of T0 targetpresetid, # str: ID of T M, # int: number of regions B, # int: number of intensity bins (64) S, # int: number of intensity samples W1, W2 # np.arrays for MLP phieta (W1: Hx4, W2: rxH)): """ Computes the appearance-modified DC color and opacity for each primitive for a given target transfer function preset. """ # 1. Discretize TFs # Average raw TF curves onto B bins. # Note: The exact binning algorithm from the sources is not provided. RBbase = np.zeros((M, B, 4)) RBtarget = np.zeros((M, B, 4)) # Implementation of binning from S samples to B bins goes here. # 2. Compute RGBA change deltar # deltarT(m, b) = RT^(B)(m, b) - RT0^(B)(m, b) deltar = RBtarget - RBbase # Shape: (M, B, 4) results = [] for prim in primitives: Ki = prim['Ki'] mik = prim['mik'] # Array of shape (Ki,) bik = prim['bik'] # Array of shape (Ki,) wik = prim['wik'] # Array of shape (Ki,) Cbase = prim['Cbase'] # Shape: (4, 3) -> 1 DC + 3 directional o = prim['o'] sview = prim.get('sview', 1.0) # TF-independent opacity attenuation # Handle edge case: no valid samples if Ki == 0: di = np.zeros(4) # (dci, dalphai) in R^3 x R ziT = np.zeros(W2.shape[0]) else: # 3. Physical Lookup di(T) # deltarT(mik, bik) deltarsamples = deltar[mik, bik,:] # Shape: (Ki, 4) # Weighted mean di = np.sum(wik[:, np.newaxis] deltarsamples, axis=0) # Shape: (4,) # 4. Learned Residual zi,T # phieta(v) = W2 ReLU(W1 v) # Embed each RGBA difference phietasamples = np.array([phieta(v, W1, W2) for v in deltarsamples]) # Shape: (Ki, r) # Weighted sum ziT = np.sum(wik[:, np.newaxis] phietasamples, axis=0) # Shape: (r,) # 5. Apply to DC color and opacity # Cbase[0] is DC color (RGB) # di contains color offset (3) and opacity offset (1) dccoloroffset = di[:3] alphaoffset = di[3] # Projection of ziT to R^4 for color/opacity residual is not specified. # Assuming a linear projection Pz: R^r -> R^4 for demonstration. # In practice, this would be a learned layer or fixed mapping. zproj = np.zeros(4) # Placeholder for [G: projection of ziT] # Final DC Color finaldccolor = Cbase[0] + dccoloroffset + zproj[:3] # Final Opacity # Backbone opacity is sigma(o) sview baseopacity = sigmoid(o) sview finalopacity = np.clip(baseopacity + alphaoffset + zproj[3], 0.0, 1.0) results.append({ 'dccolor': finaldccolor, 'opacity': finalopacity, 'directionalsh': Cbase[1:] # Unchanged }) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If a primitive has no valid samples (Ki = 0), the lookup offset \mathbf{d}i and residual \mathbf{z}{i,T} are set to \mathbf{0}. The region index m only selects the corresponding TF curve; permuting the curve axis and identifiers together leaves the lookup unchanged. Centering the branches on an authored base TF T0 ensures exact identity at T0 (i.e., \mathbf{d}i(T0) = \mathbf{0} and \mathbf{z}{i,T0} = \mathbf{0}). Factorized Appearance Response is the mechanism within FactorSplat that maps a transfer function (TF) T to per-Gaussian color and opacity adjustments using low-rank factorizations. It enables appearance changes without retraining by computing residuals relative to a base appearance, conditioned on the TF. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the geometric primitives from the appearance logic, allowing multiple TFs to share the same underlying Gaussian proxy. Time Complexity: The appearance conditioning is computed once per TF switch. The lookup and residual computation depend on the number of primitives N and the local support size Ki \le 27. The MLP evaluation is constant time per sample. Rasterization remains O(N) per pixel. Memory Complexity: Storage includes the Gaussian primitives (O(N)), the TF curves (O(M \cdot S \cdot 4)), and the MLP weights (O(H \cdot 4 + r \cdot H)). The local support data is stored per primitive (O(N)). Measured Performance: On seven CT and MR scans, FactorSplat improves mean PSNR and changed-region error over region-aware VEG across validation, interpolation, unseen composition, and out-of-distribution (OOD) edits. Strengths: Allows appearance changes without retraining or refitting. Decouples geometry from appearance. Handles region-specific intensity TFs. Limitations: Requires region segmentation. Assumes a common intensity grid. Performance depends on the quality of the base proxy and the TF curves. When to use: When dynamic appearance changes are needed for a fixed geometry, especially in medical volume rendering with region-specific TFs. When not to use: When geometry also needs to change with the TF, or when region segmentation is not available. FactorSplat was introduced in the paper "FactorSplat: Appearance-Controllable Gaussian Proxies for Medical Volume Rendering". It builds on N-DGS and addresses the limitations of image-trained Gaussian proxies that bake one transfer function into their appearance. It is compared to VEG and DeepONet. name: Factorized Appearance Response
head: DC-SH residual factors, Low-rank per-Gaussian factors
body: Factorized Appearance Response is the mechanism within FactorSplat that maps a transfer function (TF) T to per-Gaussian color and opacity adjustments using low-rank factorizations. It enables appearance changes without retraining by computing residuals relative to a base appearance, conditioned on the TF. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the geometric primitives from the appearance logic, allowing multiple TFs to share the same underlying Gaussian proxy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Base Gaussian parameters (opacity oi, base color \mathbf{C}i^{\text{base}}), TF T, region visibility flags vT(m), and learned factors. Outputs: Final color \mathbf{C}i(T) and final opacity \alphai(\pi, T) for each Gaussian i. Data Structures: Color Factors: \mathbf{A}c^i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times r} for each Gaussian i. Opacity Factors: \mathbf{a}\alpha^i \in \mathbb{R}^r for each Gaussian i. Stacked Factors: All color and opacity factors are stacked into a single 4N \times r matrix, where N is the number of Gaussians and r is the latent dimension. Global Gains: \mathbf{g}^c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and g^\alpha \in \mathbb{R}. Constants: \mathbf{e}0 = (1, 0, 0, 0)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{Qb} selects the DC SH row; C0 = 1/(2\sqrt{\pi}) converts RGB offsets to DC-SH coefficients. Parameters: r: Latent dimension, shared across primitives and TFs. \lambdac^R, \lambda\alpha^R > 0: Fixed positive output scales for residual branches. \lambdac^L, \lambda\alpha^L > 0: Fixed positive channel scales for lookup branches. bL, bR \in \{0, 1\}: Enable lookup (L) and residual (R) branches. FactorSplat uses (bL, bR) = (1, 1). \tau = 1/2: Threshold for visibility gate. Steps: 1. Compute Local Code: Determine the local code \mathbf{z}{i,T} for Gaussian i and TF T. 2. Compute Alpha-Change Indicator: Determine if the TF changes the alpha channel relative to the base TF T0: q^\alpha(T) = \mathbf{1} \left[ \left\| \mathbf{R}T^{(B)}[:,:,\alpha] - \mathbf{R}{T0}^{(B)}[:,:,\alpha] \right\|\infty > 0 \right] where \mathbf{R}T^{(B)} is the transfer function response matrix. 3. Compute Residuals: Calculate the color and opacity-logit residuals using the low-rank factors and the local code: \mathbf{r}i^c(T) = \lambdac^R \tanh(\mathbf{A}c^i \mathbf{z}{i,T}) ri^\alpha(T) = q^\alpha(T) \lambda\alpha^R (\mathbf{a}\alpha^i)^\top \mathbf{z}{i,T} The \tanh function acts elementwise. 4. Compute Lookup Responses: Calculate the lookup branch responses using global gains and the local code's lookup components \mathbf{d}i^c(T) and di^\alpha(T): \mathbf{l}i^c(T) = \mathbf{g}^c \odot \mathbf{d}i^c(T) li^\alpha(T) = g^\alpha di^\alpha(T) 5. Combine Branches: Compute the intermediate TF-conditioned opacity \bar{\alpha}i(T) and the DC-SH offset for color: \bar{\alpha}i(T) = \sigma\left(oi + bL \lambda\alpha^L li^\alpha(T) + bR ri^\alpha(T)\right) \mathbf{offset}i(T) = bL \frac{\lambdac^L}{C0} \mathbf{l}i^c(T) + bR \mathbf{r}i^c(T). 6. Compute Final Color: Add the offset to the base color, selecting only the DC component: \mathbf{C}i(T) = \mathbf{C}i^{\text{base}} + \mathbf{e}0 \mathbf{offset}i(T)^T. 7. Apply Visibility Gate: Compute the removed material mass \etai(T) based on region visibility flags vT(m) and base flags v{T0}(m): rT(m) = v{T0}(m)[1 - vT(m)] \etai(T) = \sum{m,b} pi(m,b)rT(m) \gammai(T) = \mathbf{1}[\etai(T) < \tau] where pi(m,b) is the probability mass of Gaussian i in region m and band b. 8. Compute Final Opacity: Apply the visibility gate and view-dependent scaling si^{\text{view}}(\pi): \alphai(\pi, T) = \gammai(T) \bar{\alpha}i(T) si^{\text{view}}(\pi). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: RGB-only edits: If the TF does not change the alpha channel, q^\alpha(T) = 0, which keeps the opacity residual ri^\alpha(T) at zero, preserving the base opacity behavior. Base Appearance Preservation: Both lookup and residual offsets vanish at the base TF T0, ensuring the proxy renders identically to the base appearance when T=T0. Inference Caching: Conditioned SH coefficients and opacity are cached once per TF switch at inference time to avoid recomputation during camera motion. The Factorized Appearance Model is the broader framework that combines the lookup and residual branches with global gains to compute final color and opacity. It defines the variants based on (bL, bR): lookup (1, 0), residual (0, 1), and hybrid (1, 1). FactorSplat uses the hybrid variant (1, 1). The model ensures that both offsets vanish at T0, preserving the shared base appearance. At inference, conditioned SH and opacity are cached once per TF switch, allowing camera motion to use the unchanged N-DGS rasterizer. Time Complexity: Inference time is dominated by the N-DGS rasterizer, which is unchanged from the base method. The appearance response computation is O(N \cdot r) per TF switch, where N is the number of Gaussians and r is the latent dimension. Memory Complexity: Additional memory per Gaussian is O(r) for the color and opacity factors. Strengths: Allows appearance changes without retraining or refitting the Gaussian proxy. Low-rank factorization reduces the parameter count compared to full per-Gaussian per-TF storage. Limitations: The quality of appearance changes is limited by the rank r and the expressiveness of the local codes. When to Use: When dynamic appearance control is required for a fixed geometric proxy, such as in medical volume rendering with multiple tissue segmentations. Factorized Appearance Response was introduced in the FactorSplat paper in 2026. It builds on the N-DGS framework and aims to provide appearance-controllable Gaussian proxies for medical volume rendering. name: Generalized Exponential Splatting
head: GES
body: Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) is a 3D scene representation method that replaces the Gaussian basis functions of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Generalized Exponential Functions (GEF). It introduces a learnable shape parameter \beta for each primitive to better model signals with sharp edges and high-frequency content, reducing the number of particles required and thus memory footprint while maintaining competitive rendering quality. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting, which assumes low-pass characteristics, GES allows primitives to adapt their shape to fit high-bandwidth signals like squares and triangles more efficiently. Inputs: A set of N primitives, each defined by location \boldsymbol{\mu}, scale \alpha, amplitude A, and shape parameter \beta. Target images for optimization. Outputs: Rendered 2D images from novel viewpoints. Optimized primitive parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \alpha, A, \beta). Each primitive i stores: 1. Mean Position (\boldsymbol{\mu}i): 3D vector (x, y, z). 2. Scale/Shape Parameters: \alphai: Scale parameter (analogous to variance/scale in GS). \betai: Shape parameter, constrained to \beta \in (0, \infty). Rotation is handled via the covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i as defined in the parent article. 3. Amplitude (Ai): Positive scalar, analogous to opacity/color intensity scaling. 4. Appearance: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color. The Generalized Exponential Function (GEF) for a 1D signal is defined as: f(x|\mu, \alpha, \beta, A) = A \exp \left( - \left( \frac{|x - \mu|}{\alpha} \right)^\beta \right) where \mu \in \mathbb{R} is the location, \alpha \in \mathbb{R} is the scale, A \in \mathbb{R}^+ is the amplitude, and \beta \in (0, \infty) is the shape parameter. When \beta = 2, the GEF reduces to a scaled Gaussian function. For 3D rendering, the GEF is extended to a multivariate form. Let \mathbf{x} be a point in 3D space, \boldsymbol{\mu} be the mean position, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} be the positive definite covariance matrix. The 3D GEF is defined as: L(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \beta) = \exp \left\{ -\frac{1}{2} \left( (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) \right)^{1/\beta} \right\} The rendering process projects the 3D primitives to 2D screen space. The 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i and mean \boldsymbol{\mu}'i are computed as described in the parent article. The 2D density at pixel u is evaluated as: Ti(u) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (u - \boldsymbol{\mu}'i)^T (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i)^{-1} (u - \boldsymbol{\mu}'i) \right)^{1/\betai} The effective opacity is Ai Ti(u), and colors are composited using alpha blending. Initialization: \beta is initialized to 0, which corresponds to an internal offset; the actual shape parameter used in rendering is \beta{\text{actual}} = \beta{\text{stored}} + 2. Other parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, A) are initialized similarly to 3D Gaussian Splatting. Learning Rates: Position (\boldsymbol{\mu}): Initial 0.00016, Final 0.0000016, Max Steps 30,000, Delay Multiplier 0.01. Feature (SH): 0.0025. Opacity (A): 0.05. Shape (\beta) and Rotation: 0.001. Scaling (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}): 0.005. Densification and Pruning: Densification Start: Iteration 500; End: Iteration 15,000. Gradient Threshold for Densification: 0.0003. Densification Interval: 100 iterations. Opacity Reset Interval: 3000 iterations. Shape Reset Interval: 1000 iterations. Shape Pruning Interval: 100 iterations. Opacity and Shape Pruning Thresholds: 0.005. Percentage of Dense Points: 0.01. Loss Function: SSIM loss with weight \lambda{ssim} = 0.2. Specialized frequency-modulated image loss (Image Laplacian) with weight \lambda\omega = 0.5. For the DoG term in the loss, if \sigma^2 is large, the ground truth image is downsampled by a factor scaleim,freq (0.2) and the mask M\omega is upsampled similarly before calculating the loss. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializeprimitives(N): primitives = [] for in range(N): p = { 'mu': random3dposition(), 'Sigma': randompositivedefinitematrix(), 'A': randompositivescalar(), 'beta': 0.0, 'color': randomcolor() } primitives.append(p) return primitives def render(primitives, camera): screenprimitives = [] for p in primitives: betaeff = p['beta'] + 2.0 mu2d = project3dto2d(p['mu'], camera) Sigma2d = projectcovariance(p['Sigma'], camera) screenprimitives.append({ 'mu': mu2d, 'Sigma': Sigma2d, 'A': p['A'], 'beta': betaeff, 'color': p['color'], 'depth': p['mu'].z }) screenprimitives.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) height, width = camera.resolution image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height)] alphaaccum = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for prim in screenprimitives: bbox = computeboundingbox(prim['mu'], prim['Sigma']) for y in range(max(0, bbox.ymin), min(height, bbox.ymax)): for x in range(max(0, bbox.xmin), min(width, bbox.xmax)): distsq = (vectorsub((x, y), prim['mu'])).T @ inv(prim['Sigma']) @ vectorsub((x, y), prim['mu']) T = math.exp(-0.5 distsq) (1.0 / prim['beta']) alpha = prim['A'] T if alphaaccum[y][x] >= 1.0: continue c = prim['color'] image[y][x] = [ image[y][x][0] + c[0] alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum[y][x]), image[y][x][1] + c[1] alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum[y][x]), image[y][x][2] + c[2] alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum[y][x]) ] alphaaccum[y][x] += alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum[y][x]) return image def optimize(primitives, images, cameras, iterations=40000): for it in range(iterations): cam, gtimage = randomsample(cameras, images) predimage = render(primitives, cam) loss = computeloss(predimage, gtimage) gradients = computegradients(loss, primitives) updateparameters(primitives, gradients, learningrates) if 500 <= it <= 15000 and it % 100 == 0: densifyprimitives(primitives, gradients, threshold=0.0003) if it % 100 == 0: pruneprimitives(primitives, opacitythreshold=0.005, shapethreshold=0.005) if it % 3000 == 0: resetopacity(primitives) if it % 1000 == 0: resetshape(primitives) Numerical Instability: Optimization can fail for certain signal types and component counts due to numerical instability in both Gaussian and GEF mixtures. Analytical Difficulty: The GEF involves complex integrals of exponentials without closed form depending on \beta, making analytical study difficult. Approximation Error: In the worst-case scenario (square larger than circle), the GES approximation results in a 36.34% energy error in the lost energy of all rays passing through all splatting components. The error ratio \eta is bounded by 0.2732 \le \eta \le 0.3634. Memory: GES achieves a reduction of more than 50% in memory requirement compared to Gaussian Splatting. Speed: GES increases rendering speed by up to 39% compared to Gaussian Splatting. Efficiency: GES requires far fewer particles to represent a scene, significantly outperforming Gaussian Splatting in efficiency. Quality: Maintains competitive performance on standard novel view synthesis benchmarks. Limitations: Numerical instability can occur during optimization for specific signals. The approximation error bound (up to 36.34% energy loss in worst-case geometric alignment) is a theoretical limit, though practical error is much smaller due to large component counts and small scales. Origin: GES was introduced in the paper "GES: Generalized Exponential Splatting for Efficient Radiance Field Rendering" (CVPR 2024). Motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) assumes low-pass characteristics, which is suboptimal for 3D scenes with abrupt discontinuities (high-bandwidth signals). This forces GS to use a huge number of very small Gaussians, negatively impacting memory utilization. Development: GES replaces Gaussians with Generalized Exponential Functions (GEF) to better model sharp edges and high-frequency content. It is designed as a plug-and-play replacement for Gaussian-based utilities, including text-to-3D synthesis methods like DreamFusion and DreamGaussian. Usage: Used in modern 3D generation pipelines using score distillation sampling from 2D text-to-image models. name: 2D Gaussian Splatting
head: 2D splats, 2D-GS, 2DGS Scene Representation, Perspective accurate Gaussian Splatting, Surfel Splatting
body: 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) is a surface reconstruction and novel view synthesis technique that replaces the volumetric 3D Gaussian ellipsoids of standard Gaussian Splatting with oriented, zero-thickness 2D disks (surfels). It solves the problem of ambiguous geometry and poor mesh extraction inherent in 3D Gaussian representations by enforcing primitives to align with local surface tangent planes, thereby providing unambiguous surface normals and improving multi-view depth consistency. Unlike its sibling 3D Gaussian Splatting, which models scenes as volumetric blobs, 2DGS models surfaces directly, making it superior for high-resolution normal map recovery and clean mesh extraction. Inputs: A set of N input images \{Ii\} with known camera poses \{Pi\} (rotation and translation). Outputs: A scene representation consisting of a set of M 2D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color. Data Structures: Each primitive j is defined by the tuple Gj = \{\boldsymbol{\mu}j, \mathbf{S}j, \mathbf{R}j, \alphaj, \mathbf{c}j\}: \boldsymbol{\mu}j \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D center position in world space. \mathbf{S}j \in \mathbb{R}^2: Learnable scaling factors (su, sv) defining the extent of the disk along its local tangent axes. \mathbf{R}j \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix derived from a learnable quaternion \mathbf{q}j \in \mathbb{R}^4. The surface normal \mathbf{n}j is determined directly by \mathbf{R}j. \alphaj \in \mathbb{R}^1: Learnable opacity parameter per splat. \mathbf{c}j: Color attributes (e.g., Spherical Harmonics coefficients). Rendering Pipeline: 1. Projection to Screen Space: The 2D primitive is projected from world space to the image plane. Unlike 3D Gaussians which project a 3D covariance, 2DGS constructs a homography matrix \mathbf{H} that maps local UV coordinates to screen space. The homography matrix \mathbf{H} is defined as: \mathbf{H} = \begin{bmatrix} su & tu & 0 & px \\ sv & tv & 0 & py \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where: su, sv are the learnable scaling factors from \mathbf{S}j. tu, tv are tangential vectors derived from the rotation \mathbf{R}j (or quaternion \mathbf{q}j). px, py are the projected center coordinates of the splat in screen space. Note: The sources describe \mathbf{H} as mapping local coordinates to screen space. In implementation, this matrix is used to determine the intersection of a ray with the planar splat. 2. Ray-Splat Intersection and Density Evaluation: For a pixel at screen coordinate \mathbf{x}, the ray-splat intersection is computed. The density contribution is evaluated using a 2D Gaussian function based on the UV coordinates (u(\mathbf{x}), v(\mathbf{x})) of the intersection point on the local tangent plane of the splat: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp \left( - \frac{u(\mathbf{x})^2 + v(\mathbf{x})^2}{2} \right) Here, u(\mathbf{x}) and v(\mathbf{x}) are the coordinates in the local tangent frame. 3. Opacity Adjustment: The adjusted opacity \alpha'i for the splat at pixel \mathbf{x} is calculated by combining the learnable opacity \alphai with the spatial density G(\mathbf{x}): \alpha'i = \alphai G(\mathbf{x}) 4. Alpha Compositing: Primitives are sorted by depth and blended using standard alpha compositing to produce the final color C: C = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} \alpha'i \mathbf{c}i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) where \mathcal{N} is the set of splats contributing to the pixel. Parameters and Edge Cases: Low-Pass Filtering: A low-pass filter is employed during rendering or optimization to avoid degenerated line projections, which can occur when a 2D disk is viewed edge-on. Degeneracy: Because 2D Gaussians have zero thickness, they are prone to aliasing or visibility flickering if not properly filtered. The low-pass filter mitigates artifacts caused by high-frequency variations in the splat density. Normal Consistency: The normal \mathbf{n}j is fixed by the rotation \mathbf{R}j. This provides a consistent normal for the primitive, which is critical for surface reconstruction but requires careful initialization to avoid flipping. Approximates 2D Gaussian ellipses by flattening 3D Gaussians within a differentiable volume rendering framework, enforcing a near-zero determinant covariance for stable surface-like rendering. A differentiable surface splatting renderer for inverse rendering that uses oriented surfels and handles multiple surface layers per pixel through depth-interval merging, replacing binary depth tests with smooth compositing. Enhances 2DGS by defining color and opacity as spatially varying functions of the intersection point on the primitive, allowing a single primitive to fit complex textures. A framework that learns view-dependent 2D splatting kernels implicitly, improving reconstruction quality by allowing kernel profiles to vary with the camera view. A filtering technique for dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting that adaptively adjusts dilation based on primitive scale and visibility to prevent anisotropy distortion and eliminate invisible primitives. Geometry Quality: 2DGS significantly improves multi-view depth consistency and 3D reconstruction quality compared to 3DGS, particularly for hard surfaces and sharp edges. It enables the extraction of clean meshes and high-resolution normal maps. Rendering Performance: The rendering pipeline is similar to 3DGS (rasterization of splats), but the projection step involves computing the homography matrix and ray-splat intersection, which may add slight computational overhead per splat compared to the affine projection of 3D Gaussians. Limitations: For pure image quality on fuzzy or non-surface scenes, 2DGS may perform slightly worse than 3DGS because the zero-thickness assumption does not model volumetric density well. It is less suitable for scenes where the "surface" is ambiguous or volumetric. Use Cases: Best suited for applications requiring accurate geometry, mesh extraction, and normal maps, such as inverse rendering, virtual production, and digital twins. 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) was introduced by Huang et al. in SIGGRAPH 2024. It was developed to address the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting in surface reconstruction, specifically the ambiguity of normals and the difficulty of extracting clean meshes from volumetric ellipsoids. By replacing 3D Gaussians with oriented 2D disks, the method leverages the geometric precision of surfels while maintaining the differentiable rendering efficiency of Gaussian Splatting. It has since become a foundational representation for surface-aware Gaussian splatting variants. name: Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering
head: VoGE
body: Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering (VoGE) approximates 2D Gaussian ellipses by flattening 3D Gaussian ellipsoids to enable stable surface-like rendering. It differs from 2D Gaussian Splatting by operating within a differentiable volume rendering framework that natively supports anisotropic ellipsoidal kernels and enforces a near-zero determinant covariance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Gaussian kernels, each defined by a 3×3 symmetric spatial covariance matrix \Sigmak. Output: A rendered image where surface-like structures are represented by flattened ellipsoids. Data Structures: Covariance Matrix (\Sigmak): A 3×3 symmetric matrix representing the spatial variance of the k-th kernel. \Sigmak = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{k,xx} & \sigma{k,xy} & \sigma{k,xz} \\ \sigma{k,xy} & \sigma{k,yy} & \sigma{k,yz} \\ \sigma{k,xz} & \sigma{k,yz} & \sigma{k,zz} \end{bmatrix} \sigma{k,ii}: Variance along axis i. \sigma{k,ij}: Covariance between axes i and j. Steps: 1. Initialize Kernels: Define each kernel with a 3×3 symmetric covariance matrix \Sigmak. 2. Flatten Ellipsoids: Constrain the determinant of the covariance matrix to approach zero to approximate 2D Gaussian ellipses: \det(\Sigmak) \to 0 This reduces the 3D ellipsoid into a surface-like representation. 3. Render: Project the flattened ellipsoids onto the image plane using the VoGE rendering pipeline, which natively handles the anisotropic nature of the kernels. Parameters: Determinant Threshold: The value to which \det(\Sigmak) is constrained approaches zero (\to 0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hyperbolic Kernels: If spatial covariances (e.g., \sigma{k,xy}) exceed the square root of the product of the corresponding variances (e.g., \sqrt{\sigma{k,xx}\sigma{k,yy}}), the kernel becomes a hyperbola instead of an ellipsoid. For any pair of axes, the condition must hold: \sigma{k,xy} \le \sqrt{\sigma{k,xx}\sigma{k,yy}} Violation of this condition causes the kernel to transition from an ellipsoid to a hyperbola. A rendering mode that natively supports anisotropic ellipsoidal Gaussian kernels where spatial variance is represented by a 3×3 symmetric matrix \Sigmak. It sets itself apart from isotropic splatting by preserving directional variance without forcing spherical symmetry. Link: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows rendering surface-like representations in a stable manner compared to other methods, as demonstrated by flattened ellipsoids. Limitations: The method notes ongoing work on converting triangles into anisotropic Gaussian ellipsoids, indicating incomplete mesh-to-Gaussian conversion at the time of publication. When to use it: Use when stable rendering of surface-like representations is required using Gaussian ellipsoids within a differentiable volume rendering context. When not to use it: Not given in the sources. VoGE (VoGE: A Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids for Analysis-by-Synthesis) was introduced to provide a differentiable volume rendering approach using Gaussian ellipsoids. It builds on the concept of Gaussian splatting but adapts it for surface representation by flattening 3D Gaussians. The method was demonstrated on CAD models from The Stanford 3D Scanning Repository, specifically the Bunny (8171 vertices), Dragon (22998 vertices), and Armadillo (33792 vertices). name: 3D Surface Splatting
head: 3DSS
body: 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS) is a differentiable surface splatting renderer for physically-based inverse rendering that jointly recovers geometry, materials, and illumination from multi-view images by optimizing an unstructured set of oriented surfel primitives. It solves the problem of multi-layer surface separation and visibility discontinuity in surface splatting by formulating surface grouping as an interval-merging algorithm over sorted primitives, replacing binary/ternary depth tests with a smooth, coverage-based compositing model where per-layer opacity arises directly from accumulated Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) reconstruction weights. It sets itself apart from its parent 2D Gaussian Splatting by using a surface rendering model rather than a volumetric one (surfels carry no learnable opacity), and from Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering by explicitly handling multiple surface layers per pixel through depth-interval merging rather than single-layer rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unstructured set of surfel primitives, each defined by center position \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, tangent vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v \in \mathbb{R}^3, and shading attributes (albedo \mathbf{a} \in [0, 1]^3, metallic m \in [0, 1], roughness r \in [0, 1]). Co-optimized HDR environment lighting. Output: A differentiable 2D image (HDR) and gradients for the surfel parameters. Data Structures: Each surfel primitive stores: \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v \in \mathbb{R}^3: Tangent vectors spanning the local tangent plane. These encode orientation and anisotropic scaling. The surface normal is implicitly \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v) / \|\mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v\|. \mathbf{a} \in [0, 1]^3: Albedo. m \in [0, 1]: Metallic. r \in [0, 1]: Roughness. Derived view-space properties: Depth d, symmetric depth extent \delta, and depth interval [d-\delta, d+\delta]. Parameters: \delta{cut}: Kernel support cutoff threshold. The source uses \delta{cut} as a generic parameter for the squared distance threshold \rho^2 \ge \delta{cut}^2. Steps: 1. T-matrix Construction: For each surfel, transform \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v to camera space, yielding \mathbf{c}', \mathbf{t}'u, \mathbf{t}'v. Construct the 4 \times 4 transformation matrix S = [\mathbf{t}'u \ \mathbf{t}'v \ \mathbf{0} \ \mathbf{c}'] mapping local surfel space (unit sphere parameterization) to camera space. Let P be the projection matrix. Compute the T-matrix T = PS. This maps points on the unit sphere in local surfel space to clip space. 2. Bounding Rectangle and Depth Extent: Compute the bounding rectangle of the surfel in screen space using closed-form expressions involving dot products among the rows of T. Compute the symmetric depth extent in view space: \delta = \sqrt{t'{u,z}^2 + t'{v,z}^2} \cdot \delta{cut}, where t'{u,z} and t'{v,z} are the z-components (view-space depth) of the camera-space tangent vectors. The depth interval is [d-\delta, d+\delta] where d is the view-space depth of \mathbf{c}'. 3. Forward Shading (Pre-shading): Shade each surfel before rasterization. Apply forward microfacet shading under the co-optimized HDR environment lighting using split-sum Image-Based Lighting (IBL). This yields a pre-shaded linear radiance \mathbf{c}{pre} for each surfel. This step avoids blending directional quantities (like normals) volumetrically. 4. Tiling and Sorting: Bin surfels into screen-space tiles. Sort the primitives within each tile by their depth interval start d{start} = d - \delta (closest extent to the camera), not by center depth. 5. Per-Pixel Rasterization and Surface Layer Grouping: For each pixel in a tile, iterate through the sorted surfels. Ray-Surfel Intersection: Represent the pixel's viewing ray as the intersection of two clip-space planes: \mathbf{h}u = (-1, 0, 0, u)^T and \mathbf{h}v = (0, -1, 0, v)^T, where (u,v) are the pixel coordinates. Map these planes into the surfel's local coordinate system via T to yield vectors \mathbf{k} and \mathbf{l}. Their intersection with the surfel's plane gives local coordinates (u{local}, v{local}) of the hit point. Distance and Discard: Compute squared distance from surfel center: \rho^2 = u{local}^2 + v{local}^2. If \rho^2 \ge \delta{cut}^2, discard the surfel for this pixel. Weight Evaluation: Compute unnormalized Gaussian reconstruction kernel weight: w = \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \rho^2). Note: The 1/(2\sigma) normalization constant is omitted as weights are used for Shepard normalization later. Interval Merging (Surface Separation): Maintain a list of active surface layers for the pixel. Each layer tracks a running sum of weights and attributes. If the current surfel's depth interval [d-\delta, d+\delta] overlaps with the depth interval of the last surfel added to the current active layer, add the surfel to that layer. If it does not overlap, and since primitives are sorted by d{start}, no future primitive can bridge the gap. Start a new surface layer with the current surfel. This exact gap detection requires no look-ahead or deferred merging. body: This method is the rasterization core of 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS), designed to render an unstructured set of oriented surfel primitives into a 2D image while correctly handling self-occlusion at concavities. It solves the problem where single-layer rasterization approaches fail to distinguish between geometrically distinct surface sheets that project onto the same pixel, resulting in holes or translucent artifacts in high-curvature regions like ears or under chins. It sets itself apart from classical A-buffer approaches by restricting summation to surfels within the same depth-interval layer rather than gathering across all depths, and from single-layer ternary depth tests by detecting gaps in the depth-interval chain to support an arbitrary number of surface layers per pixel. The algorithm processes surfels that have already been shaded via split-sum Image-Based Lighting (IBL) against a co-optimized HDR environment, yielding a pre-shaded linear radiance \mathbf{c}i. The rasterization proceeds in three main phases: tiling and sorting, per-pixel interval grouping, and front-to-back compositing. Inputs: A set of surfels \mathcal{S}, each with position \mathbf{p}i, orientation, size, and pre-shaded color \mathbf{c}i. Camera parameters (view/projection matrices) to compute screen-space positions and depth intervals. Kernel cutoff radius r{\text{cut}}. Half-thickness parameter \varepsilonz^{(i)} for each surfel, defining the depth interval extent. Outputs: A composited HDR image. Gradients flowing back to surfel parameters and the environment map. Screen-space tiles: Surfels are binned into tiles based on their screen-space bounding boxes. Sorted primitive sequence: Within each tile, surfels are radix-sorted by their depth-interval start value z{\text{start}}^{(i)}. Per-pixel accumulators: For each pixel, the algorithm maintains: \mathbf{C}g: Accumulated color for the current surface group g. Wg: Accumulated weight for the current surface group g. z{\text{end}}^{\max}: The farthest depth extent encountered so far in the current group. 1. Tiling and Sorting: Bin surfels into screen-space tiles. Radix-sort the surfels within each tile by z{\text{start}}^{(i)}. 2. Per-Pixel Initialization: For each pixel, initialize group accumulators \mathbf{C}g \leftarrow \mathbf{0}, Wg \leftarrow 0, and z{\text{end}}^{\max} \leftarrow 0. 3. Iterate Surfels: For each surfel i in the sorted sequence: a. Intersection: Compute the ray-surfel intersection to obtain local coordinates (u, v). b. Weight Evaluation: Calculate the MIP-filtered squared distance \rho{\text{mip}}^2 using the precomputed inverse covariance \Sigma{\text{mip}}^{-1}. c. Culling: If \rho{\text{mip}}^2 \geq r{\text{cut}}^2, the surfel does not cover this pixel; skip to the next surfel. d. Weight Calculation: Compute the scalar weight w = nf \cdot \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \rho{\text{mip}}^2). e. Depth Interval: Define the depth interval [z{\text{start}}^{(i)}, z{\text{end}}^{(i)}] where z{\text{start}}^{(i)} = z^{(i)} - \varepsilonz^{(i)} and z{\text{end}}^{(i)} = z^{(i)} + \varepsilonz^{(i)}. f. Gap Detection: If Wg > 0 AND z{\text{start}}^{(i)} > z{\text{end}}^{\max}, a gap is detected between the current surfel and the accumulated group. i. Finalize the current layer by calling FLUSHLAYER(\mathbf{C}g, Wg). ii. Reset accumulators: \mathbf{C}g \leftarrow \mathbf{0}, Wg \leftarrow 0, z{\text{end}}^{\max} \leftarrow 0. g. Update Extent: Update the group's farthest extent: z{\text{end}}^{\max} \leftarrow \max(z{\text{end}}^{\max}, z{\text{end}}^{(i)}). h. Accumulate: Add the surfel's contribution to the current group: \mathbf{C}g \leftarrow \mathbf{C}g + w \cdot \mathbf{c}i and Wg \leftarrow Wg + w. 4. Finalize Last Layer: After processing all surfels for a pixel, if Wg > 0, call FLUSHLAYER(\mathbf{C}g, Wg) to finalize the last accumulated group. 5. Shepard Normalization: For each finalized surface group, normalize the accumulated color by its weight to obtain the layer color: \mathbf{C}{\text{layer}} = \mathbf{C}g / Wg. 6. Coverage Opacity: Compute the coverage opacity \alpha{\text{layer}} for each layer from the accumulated weight Wg using a smooth, monotonically increasing mapping. This replaces threshold-based clamping used in classical A-buffers. 7. Front-to-Back Compositing: Composite the resulting layers front-to-back using the computed coverages and opacities to produce the final pixel color. 8. Post-Processing: Blend the composited HDR image with the background, then apply tone-mapping and gamma correction. Unverified code. Args: sortedsurfels: List of surfels sorted by zstart. camerarayo: Ray origin. camerarayd: Ray direction. rcutsq: Kernel cutoff radius squared. nf: Front-facing normal factor. Returns: finalcolor: The composited HDR color for the pixel. """ # Per-pixel accumulators Cg = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Wg = 0.0 zendmax = 0.0 # List to store finalized layers (color, opacity) layers = [] for surfel in sortedsurfels: # 1. Ray-Surfel Intersection uv = raysurfelhit(camerarayo, camerarayd, surfel) if uv is None: continue u, v = uv # 2. Evaluate MIP-filtered weight rhomipsq = computerhomipsq(u, v, surfel.Sigmamipinv) # 3. Culling if rhomipsq >= rcutsq: continue # 4. Calculate scalar weight w = nf math.exp(-0.5 rhomipsq) # 5. Define depth interval zcenter = surfel.z epsilonz = surfel.epsilonz zstart = zcenter - epsilonz zend = zcenter + epsilonz # 6. Gap Detection if Wg > 0 and zstart > zendmax: # Finalize current group if Wg > 0: layercolor = [Cg[0] / Wg, Cg[1] / Wg, Cg[2] / Wg] layeropacity = mapweighttoopacity(Wg) layers.append((layercolor, layeropacity)) # Reset accumulators Cg = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Wg = 0.0 zendmax = 0.0 # 7. Update extent if zend > zendmax: zendmax = zend # 8. Accumulate Cg[0] += w surfel.color[0] Cg[1] += w surfel.color[1] Cg[2] += w surfel.color[2] Wg += w # Finalize last group if Wg > 0: layercolor = [Cg[0] / Wg, Cg[1] / Wg, Cg[2] / Wg] layeropacity = mapweighttoopacity(Wg) layers.append((layercolor, layeropacity)) # 9. Front-to-Back Compositing finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaacc = 0.0 for layercolor, layeropacity in layers: # Standard front-to-back blending contribr = layercolor[0] layeropacity (1.0 - alphaacc) contribg = layercolor[1] layeropacity (1.0 - alphaacc) contribb = layercolor[2] layeropacity (1.0 - alphaacc) finalcolor[0] += contribr finalcolor[1] += contribg finalcolor[2] += contribb alphaacc += layeropacity (1.0 - alphaacc) return finalcolor \varepsilonz^{(i)}: Half-thickness of surfel i's depth interval. This parameter defines the start and end of the depth interval [z^{(i)} - \varepsilonz^{(i)}, z^{(i)} + \varepsilonz^{(i)}] used for gap detection. Typical values depend on the surfel size and camera distance, but the source does not specify a fixed value. r{\text{cut}}: Kernel cutoff radius. Surfels with \rho{\text{mip}}^2 \geq r{\text{cut}}^2 are skipped. nf: Front-facing normal factor. Used in the weight calculation w = nf \cdot \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \rho{\text{mip}}^2). Self-occlusion at concavities: Without depth-interval grouping, single-layer approaches produce self-occlusion errors at high-curvature concavities (e.g., inside ears or under chins) where surfels from geometrically distinct surface sheets project onto the same pixel. This manifests as holes or translucent patches revealing the background. Silhouette artifacts: Single-layer approaches can produce a "crusty" shell extending beyond the true silhouette, with aliased contours instead of gradual opacity falloff. The multi-layer approach with smooth coverage falloff anti-aliases silhouettes without post-process edge detection. Precision: The gap detection relies on comparing z{\text{start}}^{(i)} with z{\text{end}}^{\max}. Floating-point precision issues could theoretically cause incorrect gap detection if surfels are extremely close in depth, though the source does not specify mitigation strategies. Rasterize-then-splat (RtS) is a method for differentiable rendering of 3D surfaces that supports both explicit and implicit representations, providing derivatives at occlusion boundaries while remaining fast and simple to implement. It differs from alternatives like Soft Rasterizer by avoiding costly closest-point queries or mesh processing, and from Nvdiffrast by requiring no specific GPU hardware or custom derivative code, making its differentiable cost independent of mesh size. Time Complexity: The sorting step is O(N \log N) for N surfels per tile. The per-pixel processing is linear in the number of surfels covering the pixel, with a constant number of operations per surfel (intersection, weight evaluation, accumulation). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the sorted surfel list per tile and per-pixel accumulators. The number of layers per pixel is typically small, so memory overhead is low. Measured Performance: The source does not provide specific performance benchmarks (FPS, memory usage) for the rasterization step alone. It notes that the method is "fast and simple to implement" in the context of RtS comparison, but 3DSS itself is a complex optimization framework. Strengths: Correctly handles self-occlusion at concavities without explicit mesh processing. Anti-aliases silhouettes naturally through smooth coverage falloff. Differentiable gradients flow back through all operations. Limitations: Performance depends on the number of surfels per pixel and the number of layers. The source does not specify how many layers are typical or how this scales with scene complexity. When to use: When rendering unstructured surface representations (surfels) where self-occlusion at concavities is a concern, and differentiability is required. When not to use: For simple opaque meshes where a single layer suffices, or when hardware-specific optimizations (like Nvdiffrast) are available and preferred. 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS) was introduced in the paper "3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering". The method is part of a framework for physically-based inverse rendering that jointly recovers geometry, materials, and illumination from multi-view images. The rasterization algorithm described here is a key component of this framework, enabling the differentiable rendering of surfels. The approach builds on earlier work in splatting and A-buffer techniques but introduces depth-interval grouping to handle multiple surface layers. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Rasterize-then-splat (RtS)
body: Rasterize-then-splat (RtS) is a method for differentiable rendering of 3D surfaces that supports both explicit and implicit representations, providing derivatives at occlusion boundaries while remaining fast and simple to implement. It differs from alternatives like Soft Rasterizer by avoiding costly closest-point queries or mesh processing, and from Nvdiffrast by requiring no specific GPU hardware or custom derivative code, making its differentiable cost independent of mesh size. The method consists of three sequential steps: rasterization of the surface, shading the surface samples, and multi-layer splatting. All derivatives are produced using automatic differentiation on the forward rendering computation. Inputs and Outputs Input: Scene parameters \theta (e.g., camera pose, light parameters, surface definition parameters). Output: Final rendered image S. Data Structures 1. Parameter Buffers (Uk): Per-layer screen-space parameter buffers. For triangle meshes, these consist of per-pixel triangle indices Tk and perspective-correct barycentric coordinates Bk. These are computed via conventional Z-buffer graphics processing using depth peeling to retrieve multiple intersections per pixel. 2. G-buffers (Gk): Interpolated shape attributes (positions, normals) derived from Uk. 3. Splat Colors (Ck): Shaded colors computed via a deferred shading function. 4. Screen-space Positions (Pk): Projected positions of the splats. Steps 1. Sampling (Non-differentiable): Scene parameters \theta are passed through a sampling function U, yielding per-layer screen-space parameter buffers Uk. This step is non-differentiable and computed only in the forward pass. 2. Evaluation (Differentiable): An evaluation function G uses the non-differentiable parameters Uk to interpolate shape attributes (such as positions and normals) into G-buffers Gk. Automatic differentiation is applied to G and downstream functions. 3. Shading and Projection (Differentiable): The evaluated attributes are combined to compute splat colors Ck via a deferred shading function \mathcal{C} and corresponding screen-space positions Pk via a projection function \mathcal{P}. 4. Splatting (Differentiable): Function \mathcal{S} splats the shaded colors Ck at the corresponding pixel locations Pk using a 3x3 kernel to produce the final result S. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizethensplat(sceneparams, camera, surfacedef, imageshape): # Step 1: Non-differentiable sampling # Uk contains per-pixel triangle indices Tk and barycentric coordinates Bk # Computed via conventional Z-buffer with depth peeling Uk = depthpeelingrasterize(surfacedef, camera, imageshape) # Step 2: Differentiable evaluation # Gk contains interpolated positions and normals Gk = evaluateattributes(Uk, surfacedef) # Step 3: Differentiable shading and projection Ck = computeshading(sceneparams, Gk) Pk = projecttoscreen(Gk, camera) # Step 4: Differentiable multi-layer splatting # S is the final image, accumulated using a 3x3 kernel S = zeros(imageshape) for k in range(len(Ck)): for y, x in Pk[k]: for dy in range(-1, 2): for dx in range(-1, 2): ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < imageshape[0] and 0 <= nx < imageshape[1]: weight = 1.0 / 9.0 # 3x3 kernel weight S[ny, nx] += weight Ck[k][y, x] return S def depthpeelingrasterize(surfacedef, camera, imageshape): # Computes Uk using conventional Z-buffer graphics processing with depth peeling # Returns list of layers, each containing Tk and Bk pass # Not given in the sources. def evaluateattributes(Uk, surfacedef): # Interpolates shape attributes (positions, normals) from surfacedef using Tk and Bk Gk = [] for layer in Uk: Tk, Bk = layer['Tk'], layer['Bk'] positions = interpolateattribute(surfacedef.positions, Tk, Bk) normals = interpolateattribute(surfacedef.normals, Tk, Bk) Gk.append({'positions': positions, 'normals': normals}) return Gk def computeshading(sceneparams, Gk): # Deferred shading function C Ck = [] for g in Gk: colors = shade(sceneparams, g['normals'], g['positions']) Ck.append(colors) return Ck def projecttoscreen(Gk, camera): # Projection function P Pk = [] for g in Gk: screenpos = camera.project(g['positions']) Pk.append(screenpos) return Pk Parameters Splatting Kernel Size: 3x3. Depth Peeling: Used to retrieve multiple intersections per pixel for multi-layer splatting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Occlusion Boundaries: RtS provides derivatives at occlusion boundaries, a feature not always present in standard rasterization. Implicit Surfaces: The method supports isosurfaces extracted from implicit surface definitions (e.g., neural radiance fields), avoiding issues with under- or over-sampling of splats by resampling at each frame. Time Complexity: The cost of the differentiable sections is independent of the size of the mesh. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast and simple to implement; requires no differentiable meshing or rasterization steps; efficient for large 3D models; applicable to isosurfaces from implicit definitions; no custom derivative code needed. Limitations: Relies on non-differentiable rasterization for sampling, but provides derivatives at occlusion boundaries. When to use: When rendering large explicit meshes or implicit surfaces (like NeRF isosurfaces) where implementation simplicity and hardware independence are prioritized over specific GPU hardware optimizations. When not to use: Not given in the sources. RtS was introduced by Zhoutong Zhang in the paper "Differentiable Surface Rendering via Non-Differentiable Sampling". It was presented at ICCV 2021. The method was demonstrated for implicit-, mesh-, and parametric-surface-based inverse rendering and neural-network training applications, including the first efficient, differentiable rendering of an isosurface extracted from a neural radiance field (NeRF). It builds on surface splatting techniques [42] and differentiable visibility methods [34], but distinguishes itself by using a true surface representation and resampling splats per frame. name: Spatially Varying Gaussian Splatting (SVGS)
head: SVGS (Spatially Varying Gaussian Splatting)
body: SVGS is a method that utilizes spatially varying colors and opacity within a single Gaussian primitive to improve representation ability, addressing the non-compactness of vanilla Gaussian Splatting where primitives have only a single view-dependent color and opacity. It sets itself apart from baseline Gaussian Splatting methods by defining color and opacity as spatially varying functions of the intersection point p on the Gaussian primitive, rather than constant values per primitive. This allows different rays intersecting the same Gaussian primitive to have different colors if they intersect at different locations, enabling a single primitive to fit complex textures that would otherwise require many primitives in baseline methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin and direction; a set of Gaussian primitives (specifically 2D Gaussian surfels by default). Output: The final color c and opacity \alpha for the ray intersection. Data Structures: The method operates on 2D Gaussian surfels. Each surfel maintains parameters for its geometry (position, orientation, scale) and the parameters for the chosen spatially varying function (e.g., bilinear weights, kernel centers, or MLP weights). The intersection point p is defined in the local 2D coordinate system of the Gaussian surfel, with the Gaussian origin as (0,0) and the ellipse axes as coordinate axes. Formulas: The final color c and opacity \alpha are computed as: c(p, d) = SH(d) + Fc(p) \alpha(p) = F\alpha(p) where: p is the intersection point between the ray and the Gaussian primitive. d is the viewing direction. SH(d) is the view-dependent spherical harmonic color based on d. Fc(p) is the spatially varying color function based on p. F\alpha(p) is the spatially varying opacity function based on p. Parameters: Primitive Type: 2D Gaussian surfels are used as the base primitive representation. Activation: The final color and opacity are normalized to a valid range via a sigmoid activation during training and rendering, allowing intermediate Fc and F\alpha values to be negative. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection Point: Determine the intersection point p between the ray and the Gaussian primitive. For 2DGS-based SVGS, p is defined in the local 2D coordinate system of the Gaussian surfel, with the Gaussian origin as (0,0) and ellipse axes as coordinate axes. 2. Evaluate Spatially Varying Functions: Compute Fc(p) and F\alpha(p) using one of the implemented spatially varying functions (Bilinear Interpolation, Movable Kernels, or Tiny MLPs). 3. Compute View-Dependent Color: Evaluate the spherical harmonic color SH(d) based on the viewing direction d. 4. Combine Color: Calculate the final color c(p, d) by adding the view-dependent color and the spatially varying color component: c(p, d) = SH(d) + Fc(p). 5. Compute Opacity: Set the opacity \alpha(p) to the result of the spatially varying opacity function: \alpha(p) = F\alpha(p). 6. Normalize: Apply sigmoid activation to c(p, d) and \alpha(p) to ensure they are within valid ranges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Compute intersection point p in local 2D coordinates # Intersection calculation not given in the sources p = gaussianprimitive.computelocalintersection(rayorigin, raydirection) # 2. name: SVGS with Movable Kernels
head: Movable Kernels (SVGS Variant), Movable kernels spatially varying function, Ours-MK, SVGS (Movable Kernels), SVGS-MK
body: SVGS with Movable Kernels is a spatially varying function implementation within the SVGS framework that defines k movable exponential kernels located on a Gaussian surfel, weighted by their distance to the intersection point. It enhances scene representation by allowing sub-kernels to adapt their positions during training, providing higher flexibility and stronger expressiveness than fixed-basis methods. It sets itself apart from its sibling Bilinear Interpolation by replacing fixed quadrant weights with learnable, gradient-driven kernel centers, and from Tiny MLPs by using a compact parametric form rather than a neural network. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Gaussian surfel primitive (defined by its mean, covariance, and base opacity/color), camera view, and intersection point p in the local 2D coordinate system (u, v) of the surfel. Output: The final color C and opacity \alpha for the intersection point, computed by blending the contributions of k movable sub-kernels. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive stores the following learnable parameters in addition to the standard 2DGS attributes: k kernel centers: Ki = (K{ix}, K{iy}) for i = 0, \dots, k-1. These are 2D coordinates in the local surfel space. k learnable colors: ci \in \mathbb{R}^3 for i = 0, \dots, k-1. k learnable opacities: \alphai \in \mathbb{R} for i = 0, \dots, k-1. Parameters: k: The number of movable kernels per Gaussian surfel. Default value is k=4. \lambdae: The parameter controlling the changing rate of the kernel function. Default value is \lambdae = 0.1. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: For each Gaussian primitive, initialize k kernel centers Ki, colors ci, and opacities \alphai. 2. Forward Pass (Weight Computation): For a given intersection point p = (u, v) on the surfel: a. Compute the Euclidean distance di between the intersection point p and each kernel center Ki: di = \| p - Ki \|2 b. Compute the weight wi for each kernel using an exponential decay function: wi = \exp(-\lambdae \cdot di) c. Normalize the weights to sum to 1: \hat{w}i = \frac{wi}{\sum{j=0}^{k-1} wj} d. Compute the spatially varying color C(p) and opacity \alpha(p) by blending the learnable attributes using the normalized weights: C(p) = \sum{i=0}^{k-1} \hat{w}i ci \alpha(p) = \sum{i=0}^{k-1} \hat{w}i \alphai 3. Backward Pass (Gradient Calculation): a. Compute the gradients of the loss with respect to C(p) and \alpha(p). b. Propagate these gradients to the learnable parameters ci, \alphai, and Ki. c. Update the kernel centers Ki in the direction of their gradients during optimization. 4. Degeneracy Handling: If a kernel center Ki moves outside the Gaussian support during optimization, the primitive effectively degenerates to standard 2DGS behavior for that primitive. No clamping or projection constraints are applied to keep the kernel inside the support. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computemovablekernelweights(pu, pv, kernelcenters, lambdae): k = len(kernelcenters) weights = [] for i in range(k): ku, kv = kernelcenters[i] distsq = (pu - ku)2 + (pv - kv)2 dist = math.sqrt(distsq) w = math.exp(-lambdae dist) weights.append(w) sumw = sum(weights) if sumw == 0: return [1.0 / k] k normalizedweights = [w / sumw for w in weights] return normalizedweights def evaluatespatiallyvaryingfunction(pu, pv, kernelcenters, colors, opacities, lambdae): k = len(kernelcenters) weights = computemovablekernelweights(pu, pv, kernelcenters, lambdae) r = 0.0 g = 0.0 b = 0.0 alpha = 0.0 for i in range(k): w = weights[i] ri, gi, bi = colors[i] ai = opacities[i] r += w ri g += w gi b += w bi alpha += w ai return (r, g, b), alpha def updatekernelcenters(kernelcenters, gradients, learningrate): k = len(kernelcenters) updatedcenters = [] for i in range(k): ku, kv = kernelcenters[i] dku, dkv = gradients[i] newku = ku - learningrate dku newkv = kv - learningrate dkv updatedcenters.append((newku, newkv)) return updatedcenters Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Kernel Degeneracy: If a kernel center moves outside the Gaussian support, the method degenerates to standard 2DGS behavior for that primitive. The sources state that no special restrictions are imposed to prevent this, as it rarely occurs (probability of remaining inside is >99.5% across datasets). Weight Zero Division: If all exponential weights are effectively zero (e.g., intersection point is very far from all kernels), normalization requires a fallback (e.g., uniform distribution) to avoid division by zero. Uses four fixed kernels located in the four quadrants of the elliptical Gaussian surfel, assigning learnable color and opacity to each quadrant via bilinear interpolation. Simpler but may cause gradient vanishing. Choose when computational simplicity is prioritized over maximum expressiveness. Link Uses a tiny three-layer neural network on each Gaussian surfel to map local coordinates to color and opacity. Strongest representation ability but significantly more parameters. Choose when maximum fidelity is required and parameter budget is less constrained. Link Time Complexity: Training and rendering are slightly slower than 2DGS due to the per-primitive overhead of evaluating k sub-kernels for weight computation, color blending, and gradient calculation. Memory Complexity: Uses approximately 1.4× the parameters of 2DGS. Measured Performance: On the Synthetic Blender dataset, training takes 1083.13s vs 635.25s for 2DGS, with rendering at 133.25 FPS vs 210.73 FPS. Rendering speed still exceeds 30 FPS for real-time use. Strengths: Superior novel view synthesis performance on multiple datasets, particularly excelling at representing complex textures on relatively flat geometries. Maintains superior expressiveness even when 2DGS is forced to use 2× the Gaussians. Compatible with existing acceleration frameworks without architectural changes. Limitations: Slightly slower training and rendering compared to 2DGS. When to Use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of complex textures on simple geometry is required, and real-time rendering (>30 FPS) is still desired. When Not to Use: When maximum training speed is the primary constraint and 2DGS performance is sufficient. SVGS with Movable Kernels was introduced in the paper "SVGS: Enhancing Gaussian Splatting Using Primitives With Spatially Varying Colors". It is part of the SVGS family, which aims to address the non-compactness of vanilla Gaussian Splatting by allowing spatially varying colors and opacity within a single primitive. The method was evaluated on Synthetic Blender, Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, and DTU datasets.
