name: Learning View-Dependent Splatting Kernels
head: Learned Kernels, Learned View-Dependent Splatting Kernels, Neural 2D Splatting Kernels, Ours, View-Dependent 2D Gaussian Splatting
body: Learning View-Dependent Splatting Kernels is a differentiable framework that automatically learns view-dependent 2D splatting kernels as an implicit representation of volumetric primitives, improving reconstruction quality and representation efficiency for novel 3D view synthesis. Unlike 2D Gaussian Splatting and vanilla 3DGS where the kernel shape is a fixed, view-independent function of the Mahalanobis distance, this method introduces learned view-dependency to serve as a form of data-driven consistency, allowing the kernel profile to vary with the camera view. It avoids the computation of line integrals over general 3D primitives by explicitly modeling the integral results via a neural projection and decoder. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of volumetric primitives defined by geometric attributes and a latent vector, along with camera parameters (viewing transformation, projection Jacobian). Output: A view-dependent opacity value for each pixel within the projected bounding ellipse, which is passed to a standard splatting pipeline for coloring and alpha-blending. Data Structures: Each volumetric primitive stores the following attributes: 1. Center: \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D} (3D vector). 2. Scaling factors: \mathbf{s} (3D vector). 3. Rotation: \mathbf{q} (4D quaternion). 4. 3D-Kernel Latent: \mathbf{z}{3D} (5D vector in most experiments). Neural Networks: 1. Projection MLP (\Phi{\text{proj}}): Architecture: 4-layer MLP. Hidden layers: 64 neurons each. Activation: Leaky-ReLU after each layer except the last. Input: \mathbf{z}{3D}, camera-space center \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D}^{\text{cam}}, scaling factors \mathbf{s}, and primitive rotation matrix in camera space \mathbf{R}^{\text{cam}}. Output: \mathbf{z}{2D} (5D vector). 2. Kernel Decoder (\Phi{\text{dec}}): Architecture: 3-layer MLP. Hidden layers: 4 neurons each. Activation: Leaky-ReLU after each layer except the last. Final Layer: Sigmoid function to bound output. Input: Squared Mahalanobis distance r^2 and \mathbf{z}{2D}. Output: Opacity d. Numbered Steps: 1. Project the Bounding Ellipsoid: Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma{3D} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{R} is the rotation matrix derived from \mathbf{q} and \mathbf{S} is the scaling matrix derived from \mathbf{s}. Compute the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} using the EWA splatting approximation: \Sigma{2D} = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \Sigma{3D} \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T where \mathbf{W} is the viewing transformation and \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projection. The projected mean is denoted \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}. 2. Neural Projection: Transform the 3D kernel latent to a 2D kernel latent using the projection MLP: \mathbf{z}{2D} = \Phi{\text{proj}}(\mathbf{z}{3D}, \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D}^{\text{cam}}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{R}^{\text{cam}}) The inputs provide spatial, scale, and view awareness to the MLP. 3. Pre-sample the Kernel Profile: To accelerate rasterization, pre-sample the 1D profile of the kernel decoder. Place N uniform samples of r^2 to cover the range [0,1], denoted \{ri^2\}{1 \le i \le N}. The default value for N is 2. Compute di = \Phi{\text{dec}}(ri^2, \mathbf{z}{2D}) for each sample. Store the results \{di\}. 4. Rasterization (Kernel Evaluation): For a pixel with squared Mahalanobis distance r^2 relative to the projected primitive: Find the closest pre-sampled indices c and c+1 such that rc^2 \le r^2 \le r{c+1}^2. Compute the interpolation factor: \lambda = \frac{r^2 - rc^2}{r{c+1}^2 - rc^2} Compute the final opacity via linear interpolation: d = (1 - \lambda)dc + \lambda d{c+1} The resulting kernel shape is radially symmetric and bounded by the projected 2D ellipse. 5. Joint Optimization: The neural networks (\Phi{\text{proj}} and \Phi{\text{dec}}) and per-primitive attributes (\boldsymbol{\mu}{3D}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{z}{3D}) are jointly optimized with respect to input images. Pre-training Procedure: Initialize \mathbf{z}{3D} to all zeros. Initialize weights in \Phi{\text{proj}} and \Phi{\text{dec}} with He initialization. Randomly sample \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D}^{\text{cam}}, \mathbf{s}, and \mathbf{R}^{\text{cam}}. Randomly sample r^2 to obtain target profile samples. For the volumetric case, the target profile is a 1D cosine function: d = \cos(r^2). For the planar case, 2D Gaussian surfels are used as the target. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def leakyrelu(x, alpha=0.01): return x if x > 0 else alpha x def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) class LinearLayer: def init(self, infeatures, outfeatures): # He initialization for weights self.weights = [[math.sqrt(2.0 / infeatures) (2 random.random() - 1) for in range(infeatures)] for in range(outfeatures)] self.bias = [0.0] outfeatures def forward(self, x): out = [] for i in range(len(self.bias)): val = self.bias[i] for j in range(len(x)): val += self.weights[i][j] x[j] out.append(val) return out class MLP: def init(self, layersizes, activations): self.layers = [] for i in range(len(layersizes) - 1): self.layers.append(LinearLayer(layersizes[i], layersizes[i+1])) self.activations = activations def forward(self, x): h = x for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): h = layer.forward(h) if i < len(self.activations): h = self.activations[i for v in h] return h kerneldecoder = MLP([6, 4, 4, 1], [leakyrelu, leakyrelu, sigmoid]) def precomputekernelsamples(z2d, nsamples=2): """ Pre-samples the kernel decoder for a given 2D latent. Returns lists of squared radii and corresponding opacities. """ # Generate N uniform samples of r^2 in [0, 1] rsquaredsamples = [i / (nsamples - 1) for i in range(nsamples)] # Evaluate decoder at these samples dsamples = [] for rsq in rsquaredsamples: inputvec = [rsq] + list(z2d) opacity = kerneldecoder.forward(inputvec)[0] dsamples.append(opacity) return rsquaredsamples, dsamples def evaluatekernel(rsquared, rsqsamples, dsamples): """ Interpolates the kernel opacity for a given squared Mahalanobis distance. """ # Find the interval [rc^2, r{c+1}^2] containing rsquared c = 0 for i in range(len(rsqsamples) - 1): if rsqsamples[i] <= rsquared <= rsqsamples[i+1]: c = i break else: # Fallback if rsquared is outside range or single sample c = 0 rcsq = rsqsamples[c] rc1sq = rsqsamples[c+1] dc = dsamples[c] dc1 = dsamples[c+1] # Avoid division by zero if samples are identical if rc1sq == rcsq: return dc # Linear interpolation lambdaval = (rsquared - rcsq) / (rc1sq - rcsq) opacity = (1 - lambdaval) dc + lambdaval dc1 return opacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Radial Symmetry: Using a general (non-radially symmetric) 2D kernel causes theoretical discontinuity in mapping arbitrary 3D view conditions to a 2D frame (hairy ball theorem), resulting in rapid rotation of the kernel around certain view directions during animation. Radial symmetry avoids this by eliminating the need for a 2D frame. Parameter \kappa: The parameter \kappa (number of pre-samples N) controls the expressiveness of the learned kernels. Typical values are 2, 4, 8. The memory footprint of the representation does not change with \kappa. Increasing \kappa improves reconstruction quality only when the memory footprint is small. With a large footprint, the trend is not observed, likely because the average screen-space size per primitive becomes too small for higher kernel expressiveness to matter. Precision: The interpolation relies on r^2. Ensure r^2 is computed correctly as the squared Mahalanobis distance (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D})^T \Sigma{2D}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}). Not given in the sources. Link Not given in the sources. Link Not given in the sources. Link Not given in the sources. Link Time Complexity: Rasterization is accelerated by pre-sampling the 1D profile of the kernel decoder with N samples (default 2), storing results, and using linear interpolation during rendering. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint per primitive consists of geometric attributes and the 3D-kernel latent \mathbf{z}{3D}. The memory footprint does not change with the parameter \kappa (number of pre-samples). Measured Performance: On the Tanks & Temples dataset with ~25MB memory footprint, the method (with \kappa=4) achieves 24.08 PSNR with 328K primitives at 102 FPS, outperforming 3DGS (23.12 PSNR, 446K, 295 FPS) and DBS (23.57 PSNR, 417K, 319 FPS). Strengths: Superior representation efficiency and reconstruction quality compared to state-of-the-art techniques on analytical and learned kernels. The learned view-dependency serves as data-driven consistency. Limitations: Rendering speed decreases as \kappa increases or as the number of primitives increases for high-quality results. The method includes a pre-training step to initialize the neural networks and latent codes before joint optimization. When to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required with limited memory budget, and view-dependent appearance variations are significant. When not to use: When real-time performance with very high primitive counts is critical and the overhead of neural network evaluation (even with pre-sampling) is prohibitive, or when the scene is static and view-independent kernels suffice. The method was introduced by Huakeng Ding, Zhanpeng Liu, Fan Pei, Kun Zhou, and Hongzhi Wu in 2026. It builds upon the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting and 2D Gaussian Splatting, addressing the limitation that existing methods use view-independent kernels as a function of Mahalanobis distance. The work extends the idea to learn general 2D kernels for planar primitives in the context of 2D splatting, demonstrating efficiency in representing 2D images as well. name: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting
head: 3D-HGS
body: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting (3D-HGS) is a reconstruction kernel for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the standard full 3D Gaussian with a 3D Half-Gaussian to address shape and color discontinuities (Gibbs phenomenon) at object boundaries and texture-rich areas. It achieves higher rendering quality without compromising speed by allowing each half of the split Gaussian to have different opacity values while sharing geometric parameters. Unlike 2D-GS, which performs surface rendering, 3D-HGS retains volumetric rendering to preserve performance while enabling accurate modeling of discontinuous functions. Inputs: Initial set of 3D Gaussians located at sparse points obtained via Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Camera parameters including the view matrix W and the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation J. Ground-truth images for optimization. Outputs: Rendered 2D images. Optimized parameters for each 3D Half-Gaussian primitive. Each 3D Half-Gaussian primitive extends the standard 3D-GS primitive: Mean (\boldsymbol{\mu}): 3D position vector [\mux, \muy, \muz]^T. Covariance (\Sigma): Defined by scaling matrix S and rotation matrix R in world space: \Sigma^w = R S S^T R^T. Splitting Plane Normal (\mathbf{n}): A 3D vector normal to the plane splitting the Gaussian through its center. Opacities (\alpha1, \alpha2): Two scalar opacity values, one for each half of the split Gaussian. Color: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Half-Gaussians at sparse points from SfM. Set initial opacity to 0.02 for each half. 2. Parameterization: For each kernel, define \boldsymbol{\mu}, S, R, color, \mathbf{n}, and \alpha1, \alpha2. 3. Covariance Transformation (Pre-computation): To approximate the splitting plane, compute a transformed covariance matrix \sigma that represents a smaller circumscribing ellipsoid with a shortened third axis aligned with \mathbf{n}. This is performed every 5000 iterations: Normalize \mathbf{n} \leftarrow \mathbf{n}/\|\mathbf{n}\|. Compute basis vectors v1, v2: If nx = 0 and ny = 0, set v1 = (1, 0, 0) and v2 = (0, 1, 0). Else, v1 \leftarrow (ny, -nx, 0)/\|(ny, -nx, 0)\| and v2 \leftarrow \mathbf{n} \times v1/\|\mathbf{n} \times v1\|. Construct basis matrix basis \leftarrow [v1, v2, \mathbf{n}] (concatenation of column vectors). Transform covariance: cov \leftarrow basis^T \cdot \Sigma \cdot basis. Compute transformed components: a' \leftarrow cov[0, 0] - \frac{cov[0,2]^2}{cov[2,2]}. b' \leftarrow cov[0, 1] - \frac{cov[0, 2] cov[1, 2]}{cov[2, 2]}. c' \leftarrow cov[1, 1] - \frac{cov[1, 2] cov[1, 2]}{cov[2, 2]}. Construct new covariance \sigma in basis frame: \sigma = \begin{bmatrix} a' & b' & 0 \\ b' & c' & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \min(a', c')/100 \end{bmatrix}. Transform back: \sigma \leftarrow basis \cdot \sigma \cdot basis^T. 4. Rasterization: Map 3D Half-Gaussians to 2D images using a GPU-specified tile-based rasterization method. Project covariance to camera space: \Sigma = J W \Sigma^w W^T J^T. Partition \Sigma as: \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma{xx} & \Sigma{xz} \\ \Sigma{zx} & \sigma{zz} \end{bmatrix} where \Sigma{xx} is 2 \times 2, \Sigma{xz} is 2 \times 1, \Sigma{zx} is 1 \times 2, and \sigma{zz} is scalar. Compute conditional mean and variance: \mu{z|xy} = \Sigma{zx} \Sigma{xx}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}. \sigma{zz|xy} = \sigma{zz} - \Sigma{zx} \Sigma{xx}^{-1} \Sigma{xz}. Compute the 2D projected density using the complementary error function (\operatorname{erfc}): \int{\mathbf{n}^T \mathbf{x} \geq 0} HG{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}) dz = \hat{G}{\Sigma}(\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \hat{\mu}) \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{erfc} \left( - \frac{([n1 \ n2] / n3 + \Sigma{zx} \Sigma{xx}^{-1}) \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}}{\sqrt{2 (\sigma{zz} - \Sigma{zx} \Sigma{xx}^{-1} \Sigma{xz})}} \right). where \hat{G}{\Sigma} is the 2D Gaussian component. Use the precomputed \sigma to determine the inner boundary of the Gaussian for splitting, combined with the outer boundary from the original Gaussian, to partition into two halves. 5. Optimization: Optimize parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, S, R, \mathbf{n}, \alpha1, \alpha2) based on a loss function on rendered vs. ground-truth images. Learning rate for \mathbf{n} is 0.003. Learning rates for opacity and \mathbf{n} are reduced by a factor of 1.4 progressively. Perform adaptive kernel density adjustment (pruning and adding) using an opacity threshold of 0.01. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import math def normalize(v): return v / np.linalg.norm(v) def computecovariancetransformation(Sigma, n): """ Computes the transformed covariance matrix sigma for the circumscribing ellipsoid. Sigma: 3x3 covariance matrix of the original Gaussian. n: 3D normal vector of the splitting plane. Returns: 3x3 transformed covariance matrix sigma. """ # Normalize normal vector n = normalize(n) # Compute basis vectors v1, v2 if n[0] == 0 and n[1] == 0: v1 = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) v2 = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) else: v1 = normalize(np.array([n[1], -n[0], 0.0])) v2 = normalize(np.cross(n, v1)) # Construct basis matrix (columns are v1, v2, n) basis = np.columnstack((v1, v2, n)) # Transform covariance to basis frame cov = basis.T @ Sigma @ basis # Compute transformed components aprime = cov[0, 0] - (cov[0, 2]2) / cov[2, 2] bprime = cov[0, 1] - (cov[0, 2] cov[1, 2]) / cov[2, 2] cprime = cov[1, 1] - (cov[1, 2]2) / cov[2, 2] # Construct new covariance in basis frame sigmabasis = np.array([ [aprime, bprime, 0.0], [bprime, cprime, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0, min(aprime, cprime) / 100.0] ]) # Transform back to world/camera frame sigma = basis @ sigmabasis @ basis.T return sigma def projecthalfgaussian(Sigma, n, x, y): """ Computes the 2D projected density of a 3D Half-Gaussian at screen coordinates (x, y). Sigma: 3x3 covariance matrix in camera space. n: 3D normal vector of the splitting plane in camera space. x, y: Screen coordinates. Returns: Projected density value. """ # Partition Sigma Sigmaxx = Sigma[:2,:2] Sigmaxz = Sigma[:2, 2] Sigmazx = Sigma[2,:2] sigmazz = Sigma[2, 2] # Compute conditional mean and variance Sigmaxxinv = np.linalg.inv(Sigmaxx) muzxy = Sigmazx @ Sigmaxxinv @ np.array([x, y]) sigmazzxy = sigmazz - Sigmazx @ Sigmaxxinv @ Sigmaxz # Compute 2D Gaussian component Ghat xyvec = np.array([x, y]) exponent2d = -0.5 xyvec @ Sigmaxxinv @ xyvec Ghat = np.exp(exponent2d) # Compute erfc argument if n[2] == 0: raise ValueError("n3 should not be zero for standard projection") term1 = np.array([n[0], n[1]]) / n[2] term2 = Sigmazx @ Sigmaxxinv argnumerator = (term1 + term2) @ xyvec argdenominator = np.sqrt(2 sigmazzxy) erfcarg = -argnumerator / argdenominator # Compute erfc using standard library erfcval = 0.5 (1.0 - math.erf(erfcarg)) # Final density density = Ghat erfcval return density Normal vector learning rate: 0.003. Opacity threshold for densification/pruning: 0.01. Initial opacity value for half-Gaussians: 0.02. Learning rate reduction factor for opacity and normal vector: 1.4. Covariance transformation frequency: Every 5000 iterations. Division by Zero: In the covariance transformation, division by cov[2,2] occurs if the Gaussian has zero extent along the normal. A standard guard should clamp or perturb cov[2,2] to avoid numerical instability. Normal Vector Orientation: The splitting plane normal \mathbf{n} defines the half-space. The orientation of \mathbf{n} affects which half is active. Boundary Conditions: The approximation of the splitting plane using the circumscribing ellipsoid is valid at the three-sigma boundary. Uses Bézier curves to define the shape of Gaussian primitives, offering a different approach to handling complex geometries compared to the half-gaussian split. Choose when smooth, curved boundaries are needed. Time Complexity: Comparable to standard 3D-GS due to the efficient tile-based rasterization and precomputed splitting plane approximation. Memory Complexity: Slightly higher than 3D-GS due to the additional parameters (\mathbf{n}, \alpha1, \alpha2) per primitive. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art PSNR on MipNeRF-360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending datasets with similar or better rendering speed than 3D-GS. Strengths: Mitigates Gibbs oscillatory effect, better fits vertical discontinuities, higher bandwidth for high-frequency components. Limitations: Requires optimization of additional parameters, which may increase training complexity. 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting was introduced in CVPR 2025 by Haolin Li et al.. It addresses the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting in modeling discontinuous functions, which are common in 3D scenes at edges, corners, and texture-rich areas. The method builds on the principles of 3D-GS but replaces the reconstruction kernel with a 3D Half-Gaussian. 3D-HGS: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01027, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Texture and Appearance Representation
head: Appearance Modeling, View-Dependent Rendering
body: Texture and Appearance Representation defines how the color ci of a 3D Gaussian primitive is determined during rendering, extending the basic geometric parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) and opacity \alphai. It solves the limitation of static color storage by enabling high-frequency details or view-dependent effects (specular highlights, anisotropy) without excessively increasing the number of primitives. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GaussianSet Data Structure by focusing on the semantic definition of color rather than memory layout, and from Primitive Geometry and Distribution by addressing radiance rather than shape. All child methods extend the standard 3D Gaussian primitive i with additional appearance attributes \mathbf{a}i beyond the geometric parameters and opacity \alphai. The rendering pipeline retains the front-to-back alpha-blending equation, but the color contribution ci of each Gaussian is no longer a static vector. Instead, ci is computed by evaluating an appearance function that queries \mathbf{a}i using the viewing direction \mathbf{v}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, or local UV coordinates \mathbf{u}i. The final pixel color is calculated as: C(p) = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} ci(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a}i) \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is the color contribution derived from the specific appearance representation. This approach involves a trade-off between storage bandwidth, computational cost during decoding, and the complexity of the appearance being modeled. Textured Gaussians replace the standard spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients used for view-dependent color in 3D Gaussian Splatting with explicit 2D textures mapped onto each primitive. This method solves the limitation of SH representations in capturing high-frequency appearance details without requiring an increase in the number of primitives. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like View-Dependent Appearance Representations by utilizing spatial UV sampling rather than directional basis functions, enabling high-fidelity texture reconstruction. See Textured Gaussians. This family of methods extends the standard 3D Gaussian primitive with appearance attributes \mathbf{a}i to model view-dependent color ci(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a}i), where \mathbf{v} is the viewing direction. Unlike static color storage, these representations decode color dynamically based on the viewing angle, enabling the modeling of specular highlights, anisotropy, and complex lighting effects. The rendering pipeline retains front-to-back alpha-blending, but the color contribution of each Gaussian is computed via an appearance function that queries \mathbf{a}i using \mathbf{v}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, or local coordinates. This approach trades off storage bandwidth, decoding computational cost, and representation complexity. See View-Dependent Appearance Representations. Models 3DGS to represent 3D shapes and predicts attributes like view-dependent color and opacity using a NeRF-like neural network, replacing the Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients used in original 3DGS. Simplifies the BRDF to a neural shader that predicts specular and diffuse components directly from the view direction and a learnable material feature. Encodes textures as small neural networks evaluated at Gaussian coordinates, which can be deformed to model dynamic appearances and fine geometric displacements. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) method originally used Spherical Harmonics (SH) to represent view-dependent color. However, SH has limitations in capturing high-frequency details and complex lighting effects. Recent advances introduced explicit 2D textures and neural appearance models to overcome these limitations. View-Dependent Gaussian Splatting (VDGS) proposed using NeRF-like networks to predict view-dependent attributes. Neural Texture Splatting extended this by encoding textures as neural networks. These methods aim to improve visual fidelity while maintaining the real-time performance of Gaussian splatting. name: Textured Gaussians
head: Textured 3D Gaussians
body: Textured Gaussians replace the standard spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients used for view-dependent color in 3D Gaussian Splatting with explicit 2D textures mapped onto each primitive. This method solves the limitation of SH representations in capturing high-frequency appearance details without requiring an increase in the number of primitives. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like View-Dependent Appearance Representations by utilizing spatial UV sampling rather than directional basis functions, enabling high-fidelity texture reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians i, where each Gaussian i is defined by its geometric parameters (mean \mathbf{\mu}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i), opacity \alphai, and new appearance attributes: a 2D texture image Ti and local UV coordinates \mathbf{u}i = (ui, vi). Output: A rendered 2D image where each pixel color is computed via alpha-blending. Data Structures: Texture Ti: A 2D image array (e.g., RGB or RGBA) associated with Gaussian i. The resolution is typically small (e.g., 16 \times 16 or 32 \times 32) to balance detail and memory. UV Coordinates \mathbf{u}i: A 2D vector (ui, vi) \in [0, 1]^2 stored per Gaussian, representing the sampling location on Ti. Steps: 1. Rasterization: Project each Gaussian i to 2D screen space using the camera projection matrix and the 3D-to-2D covariance transformation. Sort Gaussians front-to-back based on depth. 2. UV Sampling: For each Gaussian i, retrieve its associated texture Ti and UV coordinates \mathbf{u}i. 3. Color Computation: Sample the color ci from the texture Ti at the location \mathbf{u}i. This is typically done using bilinear interpolation: ci = Ti(\mathbf{u}i) Unlike SH-based methods, ci is static with respect to the viewing direction \mathbf{v} for a given Gaussian, assuming the texture encodes the appearance directly. If view-dependence is required, it must be encoded within the texture itself or via additional parameters. 4. Alpha Blending: Compute the final pixel color C(p) using the standard front-to-back alpha-blending equation, where ci is now the sampled texture color: C(p) = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Parameters: Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Typical values in related literature range from 16 \times 16 to 64 \times 64 pixels. UV Mapping: The method assumes pre-computed or learned UV coordinates \mathbf{u}i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: UV Overlap: If multiple Gaussians map to the same UV coordinates in a shared texture, artifacts may occur. Textured Gaussians typically assign unique textures or UVs per primitive to avoid this. Memory Bandwidth: Storing a texture per Gaussian increases memory usage compared to SH coefficients. The trade-off is between storage bandwidth and computational cost of decoding. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has no associated texture or invalid UV coordinates, the color contribution ci is undefined. A default color (e.g., white or black) should be used as a fallback. A method that disentangles the geometry and appearance of 3DGS. It learns a UV mapping network for points near the underlying surface, enabling manipulation such as texture painting and texture swapping. A method that represents a 3D scene with a proxy mesh with fixed UV mapping where Gaussians are stored on the texture map. This disentangled representation allows animation and texture editing. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by rasterization and texture sampling. Texture sampling is O(1) per Gaussian but involves memory access. Overall complexity is similar to standard 3DGS rasterization, O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Higher than SH-based methods. Each Gaussian requires storing a 2D texture array in addition to geometric parameters. Memory usage scales with N \times H \times W \times C, where H, W are texture dimensions and C is channels. Strengths: Enables high-frequency appearance details without increasing the number of primitives. Allows for explicit texture editing and manipulation. Limitations: Increased memory footprint. Requires UV mapping, which may be non-trivial to compute for complex scenes. When to use: When high-fidelity texture details are required and memory bandwidth is sufficient. When explicit texture editing is needed. When not to use: When memory is constrained or when view-dependent effects are complex and better modeled by SH. Textured Gaussians were introduced as an alternative to spherical harmonics in 3D Gaussian Splatting to address artifacts in scenes with semi-transparent objects and to capture high-frequency details. The approach abandons SH coefficients in favor of explicit 2D textures mapped onto each primitive. This method is part of the broader trend of disentangling geometry and appearance in 3D Gaussian representations. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: View-Dependent Appearance Representations
head: Gaussian Appearance Encoding
body: This family of methods extends the standard 3D Gaussian primitive with appearance attributes \mathbf{a}i to model view-dependent color ci(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a}i), where \mathbf{v} is the viewing direction. Unlike static color storage, these representations decode color dynamically based on the viewing angle, enabling the modeling of specular highlights, anisotropy, and complex lighting effects. The rendering pipeline retains front-to-back alpha-blending, but the color contribution of each Gaussian is computed via an appearance function that queries \mathbf{a}i using \mathbf{v}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, or local coordinates. This approach trades off storage bandwidth, decoding computational cost, and representation complexity. All child methods extend the standard 3D Gaussian primitive i with additional appearance attributes \mathbf{a}i beyond the geometric parameters (\mathbf{\mu}i, \mathbf{\Sigma}i) and opacity \alphai. The rendering pipeline retains the front-to-back alpha-blending equation, but the color contribution ci of each Gaussian is no longer a static vector. Instead, ci is computed by evaluating an appearance function that queries \mathbf{a}i using the viewing direction \mathbf{v}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, or local UV coordinates \mathbf{u}i. The final pixel color is calculated as: C(p) = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} ci(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a}i) \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is the color contribution derived from the specific appearance representation. This approach involves a trade-off between storage bandwidth, computational cost during decoding, and the complexity of the appearance being modeled. Uses Spherical Harmonics (SH) for view-dependent color. Also supports Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) for specular components and Spherical Gaussians (SG) for balancing quality and speed. Supports PBR parameters and indirect illumination. See Fixed Basis Functions. Each point is associated with a compact Neural Feature Vector decoded using a small MLP. See Neural Feature Vectors. Neural features are cached in explicit data structures. Position is projected onto axis-aligned feature planes, and final feature ft is obtained by concatenating three trilinear interpolated features. See Triplane. Features are interpolated from a multi-resolution grid stored using instant-ngp. Supports unbounded scenes via contraction technique. See Hash Grid. A discrete codebook of vector codes is learned during training. Rendering requires only a simple lookup into the codebook using stored indices, exploiting lower bandwidth and computational costs. See Codebook Quantization. The concept of view-dependent appearance in Gaussian splatting was introduced as an enhancement step to boost the representation ability of 3D Gaussians. Traditional Gaussian splatting utilized spherical harmonics (SH) to model view-dependent color. Subsequent work expanded this to include Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) for specular components and Spherical Gaussians (SG) for balancing image quality and rendering speed. To achieve material and lighting decomposition, PBR parameters and indirect illumination were also considered. Alternative approaches moved away from indexing neural feature vectors with point cloud IDs, caching features in explicit data structures like triplanes and hash grids. Codebook quantization was motivated by the balance between compact storage and rendering efficiency, requiring only a simple lookup into the codebook using stored indices at rendering time. GauStudio: A Modular Framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting and Beyond, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.19632, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Bézier Gaussian Triangle
head: BG-Triangle
body: The Bézier Gaussian Triangle (BG-Triangle) is a hybrid 3D primitive representation that combines Bézier triangle surfaces for explicit geometry with 3D Gaussian sub-primitives for appearance, enabling differentiable rendering with sharp boundaries. It solves the problem of blurry or aliased edges common in pure Gaussian splatting by defining the object's silhouette and surface topology via parametric Bézier patches, while using Gaussians only for shading and color. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which relies on the overlap of many opaque Gaussians to form shapes, BG-Triangle maintains distinct, sharp boundaries between primitives, making it particularly suitable for vectorization and compact scene representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Bézier Gaussian Triangle primitives. Each primitive is defined by a degree n, a set of 3D control points \mathbf{p}{i,j,k}, color control points \mathbf{p}{i,j,k}^c, and multi-resolution attribute maps Mh for rotation, scaling, and Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients. Output: A rendered 2D image with photometric accuracy and sharp geometric boundaries. Data Structures: Primitive Index Map (I{id}): \mathbb{Z}^{H \times W}, storing the index of the primitive covering each pixel. Barycentric Coordinate Map (I{uv}): \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, storing the barycentric coordinates (u, v, w) for each pixel relative to its covering primitive. Boundary Point Set (B): A 2D set of pixel coordinates identified as boundary pixels (pixels with neighbors having different I{id} values). Attribute Maps (Mh): 2D textures storing rotation, scaling, and SH coefficients for each primitive, sampled based on barycentric coordinates. Numbered Steps: 1. Tessellation and Rasterization: The non-linear Bézier triangle surface is tessellated into smaller flat triangles to align with the pixel grid. The vertices of these flat triangles inherit the primitive ID and barycentric coordinates. A traditional rasterization pipeline with depth testing is used to render these flat triangles, generating the coordinate map I{uv} and index map I{id}. 2. Boundary Detection: Pixels are marked as boundary pixels if they have neighboring pixels assigned to different primitive IDs. These pixels are stored in the 2D boundary point set B. 3. 3D Coordinate Computation: For each foreground pixel q, the 3D position \mathbf{S}q on the Bézier triangle is computed using the retrieved primitive index I{id}(q) and barycentric coordinates I{uv}(q): \mathbf{S}{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{I}{uv}(\mathbf{q}), \mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{q})) = \sum{i = 0}^{n} \sum{j = 0}^{n - i} B{i, j, k}^{n}(\mathbf{I}{uv}(\mathbf{q})) \mathbf{p}{i, j, k}(\mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{q})) where B{i, j, k}^{n} is the Bernstein polynomial. 4. Sub-Primitive Generation: At each computed 3D coordinate \{\mathbf{S}q\}, a 3D Gaussian sub-primitive is generated on the fly. These Gaussians possess rotation, scaling, and SH coefficients but no opacity, as the geometry is defined by the Bézier triangles. 5. Attribute Interpolation: Diffuse Color: Interpolated using barycentric interpolation of color control points \mathbf{p}{i, j, k}^c: \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{I}{uv}(\mathbf{q}), \mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{q})) = \sum{i = 0}^{n} \sum{j = 0}^{n - i} B{i, j, k}^{n}(\mathbf{I}{uv}(\mathbf{q})) \mathbf{p}{i, j, k}^{c}(\mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{q})) Other Attributes: Rotation, scaling, and SH coefficients are interpolated using a multi-resolution 2D attribute map Mh based on barycentric coordinates via a texture interpolation function \Theta: \mathbf{a}h(\mathbf{q}) = \Theta(\mathbf{M}h(\mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{q})), \mathbf{I}{uv}(\mathbf{q})) where h \in \{\text{rotation, scaling, SH coefficients}\}. 6. Boundary Softening (Discontinuity-Aware Rendering): To handle sharp boundaries without artifacts, the influence of boundary points is softened: Each boundary point bi \in B is treated as an isotropic Gaussian with a fixed scaling factor rb. The projected boundary radius \sigmai is computed for each boundary Gaussian. The blending coefficient w(q) for a pixel q covered by a splatted Gaussian G is determined by its relation to boundary points bi: w(\mathbf{q}) = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } \mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{b}{i}) \neq \mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{q}), \\ \gamma(\|\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{b}{i}\|{2}; \sigmai), & \text{if } \mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{b}{i}) = \mathbf{I}{id}(\mathbf{q}), \\ 1 - \gamma(\|\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{b}{i}\|{2}; \sigmai), & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} where \gamma(d; \sigma) = \min \left( 2^{\frac{d}{\sigma} - 1}, 1 \right). The alpha value \alpha(q) is computed using w(q) and the Gaussian projection, where o is a constant close to 1.0 to aid optimization. 7. Rendering: Point-based alpha blending is applied to obtain the final pixel color. 8. Training (Backward Pass): Derivatives of the control points are computed using the chain rule, leveraging the differentiability of the coordinate interpolation and the blending weight. The photometric loss combines L2 loss and D-SSIM: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}{2} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} where \lambda = 0.2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def bernsteinpolynomial(i, j, k, n, u, v, w): """Computes B{i,j,k}^n(u,v,w) = n!/(i!j!k!) u^i v^j w^k """ coeff = math.factorial(n) / (math.factorial(i) math.factorial(j) math.factorial(k)) return coeff (u i) (v j) (w k) def computebezierpoint(controlpoints, n, u, v, w): """Computes S(u,v,w) on a Bézier triangle """ position = np.zeros(3) for i in range(n + 1): for j in range(n - i + 1): k = n - i - j p = controlpoints[i][j][k] b = bernsteinpolynomial(i, j, k, n, u, v, w) position += b p return position def gammafunction(d, sigma): """Computes gamma(d; sigma) = min(2^(d/sigma - 1), 1) """ if sigma <= 0: return 1.0 return min(2 ((d / sigma) - 1), 1.0) def computeblendingweight(qpos, bipos, qprimid, biprimid, sigmai): """Computes w(q) based on relation to boundary point bi """ dist = np.linalg.norm(qpos - bipos) if biprimid != qprimid: return 0.0 elif biprimid == qprimid: return gammafunction(dist, sigmai) else: return 1.0 - gammafunction(dist, sigmai) def texturelookup(attrmap, u, v): """Standard 2D bilinear texture interpolation """ h, w = attrmap.shape[:2] uidx = min(max(int(u (w - 1)), 0), w - 2) vidx = min(max(int(v (h - 1)), 0), h - 2) ufrac = u (w - 1) - uidx vfrac = v (h - 1) - vidx top = attrmap[vidx, uidx] (1 - ufrac) + attrmap[vidx, uidx + 1] ufrac bottom = attrmap[vidx + 1, uidx] (1 - ufrac) + attrmap[vidx + 1, uidx + 1] ufrac return top (1 - vfrac) + bottom vfrac def projectgaussian2d(mean3d, rotationquat, scalingvec, viewmatrix, projjacobian): """Standard 2D projection of a 3D Gaussian via covariance transform """ # Covariance in world space: Sigmaw = R S S^T R^T # Transformed covariance: Sigma = J W Sigmaw W^T J^T # Returns 2D mean and covariance matrix # Implementation follows standard 3DGS projection pipeline return np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.eye(2) def renderbgtriangle(primitives, Iid, Iuv, B, imageheight, imagewidth, cameraparams): """Main rendering loop for BG-Triangle """ finalcolor = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) o = 1.0 # Constant close to 1.0 for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): q = np.array([x, y]) primid = Iid[y, x] uv = Iuv[y, x] u, v, w = uv[0], uv[1], uv[2] prim = primitives[primid] controlpoints = prim['controlpoints'] colorcontrolpoints = prim['colorcontrolpoints'] attrmaps = prim['attrmaps'] # 1. Compute 3D position Sq = computebezierpoint(controlpoints, prim['degree'], u, v, w) # 2. Interpolate attributes cq = computebezierpoint(colorcontrolpoints, prim['degree'], u, v, w) rotation = texturelookup(attrmaps['rotation'], u, v) scaling = texturelookup(attrmaps['scaling'], u, v) shcoeffs = texturelookup(attrmaps['sh'], u, v) # 3. Project Gaussian to 2D mu2d, sigma2d = projectgaussian2d(Sq, rotation, scaling, cameraparams['view'], cameraparams['jacobian']) # 4. Compute Gaussian contribution diff = q - mu2d invsigma = np.linalg.inv(sigma2d) distsq = diff @ invsigma @ diff gaussianval = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) # 5. Boundary softening wq = 1.0 for bpos, bid, sigmai in B: wq = computeblendingweight(q, bpos, primid, bid, sigmai) # 6. Alpha blending alpha = gaussianval wq o finalcolor[y, x] += cq alpha return finalcolor Parameters: \lambda: Weight for D-SSIM term in loss function, set to 0.2. rb: Fixed scaling factor for isotropic Gaussian treatment of boundary points. o: Constant number close to 1.0 used to help optimization in alpha blending. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tessellation Density: The tessellation of the Bézier triangle must be fine enough to approximate the curved surface without introducing visible artifacts, but coarse enough to maintain performance. Boundary Artifacts: Incorrect handling of boundary pixels can lead to gaps or overlaps between primitives. The discontinuity-aware rendering is crucial for sharp edges. Gradient Computation: The differentiability of the Bézier surface and the blending function is essential for training. A scheme to manage primitive count and quality by splitting under-reconstructed primitives and pruning ineffective ones to improve training efficiency and rendering clarity. Splitting Criteria: Primitives are split if: (1) the average gradient norm of their control points exceeds threshold \taug, indicating under-reconstructed geometry; or (2) the accumulated edge gradients, back-projected from edge detection on training images, exceed threshold \taub. Pruning Criteria: Primitives are pruned based on: (1) visibility (percentage of training views in which the primitive is visible); (2) area; and (3) aspect ratio. Parameters: \taug (threshold for average gradient norm), \taub (threshold for accumulated edge gradients). Time Complexity: Rendering involves tessellation, rasterization, and per-pixel Gaussian splatting. The tessellation step is offline or pre-computed. The rasterization and splatting are similar in complexity to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, but with additional overhead for boundary detection and attribute interpolation from Bézier control points. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of control points, color control points, and multi-resolution attribute maps for each primitive. The approach maintains a compact parameter count compared to purely Gaussian-based models. Strengths: Sharp boundaries, differentiable rendering, compact representation, suitability for vectorization. Limitations: Complexity of implementation due to hybrid nature (Bézier + Gaussian), sensitivity to tessellation density, potential artifacts at boundaries if not handled correctly. When to Use: When sharp geometric boundaries are required, or when a compact representation of complex surfaces is needed. When Not to Use: For scenes with highly complex, non-parametric geometry that cannot be well-approximated by Bézier triangles, or when real-time performance is critical and the overhead of tessellation and boundary handling is unacceptable. The Bézier Gaussian Triangle (BG-Triangle) was introduced in the paper "BG-Triangle: Bézier Gaussian Triangle for 3D Vectorization and Rendering". It builds upon the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and Bézier surfaces, aiming to combine the differentiable rendering capabilities of Gaussians with the explicit geometric control of Bézier patches. The method addresses the limitations of pure Gaussian splatting in representing sharp edges and compact geometry. BG-Triangle: Bézier Gaussian Triangle for 3D Vectorization and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01510, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Shading and Lighting Models
body: Shading and Lighting Models extend the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline to support physically based rendering, self-occlusion, and anti-aliased forward shading. While standard splatting assumes a fixed, uniform lighting environment and simple alpha blending, this family introduces mechanisms for deferred shading pipelines, light-space rasterization for shadows, and analytic integration approximations for multiscale fidelity Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting, Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading, Transparency and Blending Models. It differs from sibling methods like Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading by focusing on material attributes and light interaction rather than just pixel-area integration, and from Transparency and Blending Models by explicitly handling light source geometry and PBR material buffers. All methods in this family operate on 3D Gaussian primitives defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} (or scales and orientation), opacity o, and color \mathbf{c} (or spherical harmonic coefficients). The core challenge is computing the pixel color C and accumulated alpha \alpha given a camera ray. Standard splatting projects 3D Gaussians to 2D ellipses, computes a 2D alpha mask, and blends them in screen space 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization. These models modify the blending or shading stage: some refine the depth metric used for sorting, others integrate the 3D density function directly along the ray, and others use weighted averages to bypass sorting Transparency and Blending Models. All assume the Gaussians are sorted or processed in a manner that approximates front-to-back accumulation to ensure correct occlusion. For relighting, splats must carry physical material attributes: normal, roughness, reflectance (specular strength), and albedo (diffuse color) Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. These are stored in a parallel Material Buffer aligned with the Splat Buffer Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. For self-shadowing, a virtual "sun camera" is constructed to simulate a directional light source Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. This camera is placed at a large distance with a narrow field of view (FOV) to minimize parallax error to below 2% Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. Both relighting (for cache locality) and shadowing (for correct front-to-back accumulation) require sorting Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. Relighting uses spatial locality algorithms like Morton codes Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. Shadowing sorts Gaussians by depth relative to the sun camera Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. During the light pass for shadowing, the projection covariance is not expanded by 0.3I and no amplitude compensation is applied, preserving the main camera pass's sampling expansion Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. In shadowing calculations, sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches are treated as constants to prevent incorrect gradient propagation Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticsplattingforwardshading(pixelu, muhat, sigmahat): """ Computes the 2D Gaussian signal response for a pixel using analytic splatting. Args: pixelu: Tuple (ux, uy) representing the pixel center coordinates. muhat: Tuple (mux, muy) representing the projected 2D mean. sigmahat: Tuple (s11, s12, s22) representing the projected 2D covariance matrix: [[s11, s12], [s12, s22]] Returns: float: The intensity response g^2D(u). """ ux, uy = pixelu mux, muy = muhat s11, s12, s22 = sigmahat # Step 1: Eigendecomposition trace = s11 + s22 det = s11 s22 - s12 s12 # Eigenvalues discriminant = trace trace - 4 det # Guard against negative discriminant due to floating point errors if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) lambda1 = (trace + sqrtdisc) / 2 lambda2 = (trace - sqrtdisc) / 2 # Unnormalized eigenvectors v1hatx = s12 v1haty = lambda1 - s11 v2hatx = lambda2 - s22 v2haty = s12 # Norms normv1 = math.sqrt(v1hatx2 + v1haty2) normv2 = math.sqrt(v2hatx2 + v2haty2) # Guard against division by zero if eigenvalue is zero if normv1 == 0: normv1 = 1e-9 if normv2 == 0: normv2 = 1e-9 # Normalized eigenvectors v1x = v1hatx / normv1 v1y = v1haty / normv1 v2x = v2hatx / normv2 v2y = v2haty / normv2 # Step 2: Coordinate Transformation diffx = ux - mux diffy = uy - muy tildeux = v1x diffx + v1y diffy tildeuy = v2x diffx + v2y diffy # Step 3: Intensity Response # Guard against division by zero for lambda if lambda1 == 0: lambda1 = 1e-9 if lambda2 == 0: lambda2 = 1e-9 term1 = math.exp(-0.5 (tildeux2) / lambda1) term2 = math.exp(-0.5 (tildeuy2) / lambda2) response = term1 term2 # Step 4: Anti-Aliasing via CDF Approximation # The sources indicate scaling x by 1/sigma before applying the logistic approximation, # but the exact formula for Ssigma is truncated in the source text. # response = scaledlogisticcdf(tildeux / math.sqrt(lambda1)) scaledlogisticcdf(tildeuy / math.sqrt(lambda2)) return response Computes the 2D Gaussian signal response for a pixel by performing eigendecomposition on the projected covariance matrix, rotating the coordinate system to decouple axes, and applying a conditioned logistic function to approximate the pixel area integral of the Gaussian CDF. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by replacing the simple Gaussian evaluation at the pixel center with an analytic integration approximation, and from Mip-Splatting by using a logistic function approximation rather than a Mip-NeRF-inspired cone integral, thereby achieving state-of-the-art detail fidelity under multiscale and super-resolution settings at the cost of increased computational operations. Choose this when high-frequency detail preservation is critical and computational budget allows for eigendecomposition per pixel. Define how 3D Gaussian primitives are composited into a 2D image, addressing the limitations of standard front-to-back alpha blending which requires strict depth sorting and assumes non-overlapping primitives. These models range from hybrid approaches that balance performance and accuracy to analytic volumetric integration that eliminates projection artifacts, and order-independent methods that bypass sorting entirely. Choose this when correct occlusion handling is required without the overhead of strict sorting or when dealing with highly overlapping primitives. Extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to support physically based lighting, self-occlusion, and environment reflections. It solves the limitation of standard splatting, which assumes a fixed, uniform lighting environment, by introducing deferred shading pipelines for relighting and dedicated light-space rasterization passes for self-shadowing. Unlike sibling methods that may use simplified shading functions or voxel-based fallbacks, these approaches provide full PBR material attributes and continuous differentiable gradients for shadows without modifying the primary camera's covariance expansion. Choose this when dynamic lighting, shadows, or environment reflections are required. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting method assumes a fixed lighting environment. Extensions to support PBR and shadows emerged to enable interactive relighting and realistic scene synthesis. Deferred shading pipelines for Gaussian Splatting were introduced to handle complex lighting Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting, while light-space rasterization techniques were developed to compute self-occlusion Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting. Analytic approximations for splatting were developed to improve anti-aliasing and super-resolution performance Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading.
