name: Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading
head: Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading Module
body: Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading computes the 2D Gaussian signal response for a pixel by performing eigendecomposition on the projected covariance matrix, rotating the coordinate system to decouple axes, and applying a conditioned logistic function to approximate the pixel area integral of the Gaussian CDF. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by replacing the simple Gaussian evaluation at the pixel center with an analytic integration approximation, and from Mip-Splatting by using a logistic function approximation rather than a Mip-NeRF-inspired cone integral, thereby achieving state-of-the-art detail fidelity under multiscale and super-resolution settings at the cost of increased computational operations. Inputs: Projected 2D mean \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = [\hat{\mu}x, \hat{\mu}y]^\top of the Gaussian primitive. Projected 2D covariance matrix \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\Sigma}{11} & \hat{\Sigma}{12} \\ \hat{\Sigma}{12} & \hat{\Sigma}{22} \end{bmatrix}, where \text{Tr}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) = \hat{\Sigma}{11} + \hat{\Sigma}{22} and \det(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) = \hat{\Sigma}{11}\hat{\Sigma}{22} - \hat{\Sigma}{12}^2. Pixel center coordinates \mathbf{u} = [ux, uy]^\top in screen space. Outputs: Pixel intensity response g^{\text{2D}}(\mathbf{u}). Data Structures: The method operates on standard 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives. The projected covariance \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} is a 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix stored in memory as four floating-point values. Steps: 1. Eigendecomposition: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and unnormalized eigenvectors \hat{\mathbf{v}}1, \hat{\mathbf{v}}2 of \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}. Calculate the trace and determinant: \text{Tr}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) = \hat{\Sigma}{11} + \hat{\Sigma}{22} \det(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) = \hat{\Sigma}{11}\hat{\Sigma}{22} - \hat{\Sigma}{12}^2 Compute eigenvalues: \lambda1 = \frac{\text{Tr}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) + \sqrt{\text{Tr}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})^2 - 4\det(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})}}{2} \lambda2 = \frac{\text{Tr}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) - \sqrt{\text{Tr}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})^2 - 4\det(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})}}{2} Compute unnormalized eigenvectors: \hat{\mathbf{v}}1 = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\Sigma}{12} \\ \lambda1 - \hat{\Sigma}{11} \end{bmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{v}}2 = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda2 - \hat{\Sigma}{22} \\ \hat{\Sigma}{12} \end{bmatrix} Normalize eigenvectors to obtain \mathbf{v}1 = [v{1x}, v{1y}]^\top and \mathbf{v}2 = [v{2x}, v{2y}]^\top: \mathbf{v}1 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{v}}1}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}1\|} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{12}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}1\|} \\ \frac{\lambda1 - \hat{\Sigma}{11}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}1\|} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{v}}2}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}2\|} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\lambda2 - \hat{\Sigma}{22}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}2\|} \\ \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{12}}{\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}2\|} \end{bmatrix} 2. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the pixel center \mathbf{u} into the rotated coordinate system defined by the eigenvectors, with origin at \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}. \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = \begin{bmatrix} \tilde{u}x \\ \tilde{u}y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} v{1x} & v{1y} \\ v{2x} & v{2y} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} ux - \hat{\mu}x \\ uy - \hat{\mu}y \end{bmatrix} \tilde{u}x = v{1x}(ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{1y}(uy - \hat{\mu}y) \tilde{u}y = v{2x}(ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{2y}(uy - \hat{\mu}y) 3. Intensity Response Calculation: Compute the Gaussian signal response at the pixel center using the diagonalized variances (eigenvalues). g^{\text{2D}}(\mathbf{u}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\lambda1}\tilde{u}x^2\right) \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\lambda2}\tilde{u}y^2\right) 4. Anti-Aliasing via CDF Approximation: To approximate the pixel area integral (anti-aliasing), the method uses a conditioned logistic function to approximate the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of the standard Gaussian distribution. The standard Gaussian PDF is g(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-\frac{x^2}{2}). The CDF G(x) is approximated by the logistic function S(x): S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-1.6 \cdot x - 0.07 \cdot x^3)} For a Gaussian with standard deviation \sigma, the scaled logistic function S\sigma is used. The input x is scaled by the reciprocal of \sigma before applying the logistic approximation. S\sigma(x) = S\left(\frac{x}{\sigma}\right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticsplattingforwardshading(pixelu, muhat, sigmahat): """ Computes the 2D Gaussian signal response for a pixel using analytic splatting. Args: pixelu: Tuple (ux, uy) representing the pixel center coordinates. muhat: Tuple (mux, muy) representing the projected 2D mean. sigmahat: Tuple (s11, s12, s22) representing the projected 2D covariance matrix: [[s11, s12], [s12, s22]] Returns: float: The anti-aliased pixel response using the CDF approximation. """ ux, uy = pixelu mux, muy = muhat s11, s12, s22 = sigmahat # Step 1: Eigendecomposition trace = s11 + s22 det = s11 s22 - s12 s12 discriminant = trace trace - 4 det if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) lambda1 = (trace + sqrtdisc) / 2 lambda2 = (trace - sqrtdisc) / 2 # Unnormalized eigenvectors v1hatx = s12 v1haty = lambda1 - s11 v2hatx = lambda2 - s22 v2haty = s12 # Norms normv1 = math.sqrt(v1hatx2 + v1haty2) normv2 = math.sqrt(v2hatx2 + v2haty2) # Guard against division by zero if eigenvalue is zero if normv1 == 0: normv1 = 1e-9 if normv2 == 0: normv2 = 1e-9 # Normalized eigenvectors v1x = v1hatx / normv1 v1y = v1haty / normv1 v2x = v2hatx / normv2 v2y = v2haty / normv2 # Step 2: Coordinate Transformation diffx = ux - mux diffy = uy - muy tildeux = v1x diffx + v1y diffy tildeuy = v2x diffx + v2y diffy # Step 3: Intensity Response (Center) if lambda1 == 0: lambda1 = 1e-9 if lambda2 == 0: lambda2 = 1e-9 centerresponse = math.exp(-0.5 (tildeux2) / lambda1) math.exp(-0.5 (tildeuy2) / lambda2) # Step 4: Anti-Aliasing via CDF Approximation sigma1 = math.sqrt(lambda1) sigma2 = math.sqrt(lambda2) if sigma1 == 0: sigma1 = 1e-9 if sigma2 == 0: sigma2 = 1e-9 def S(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-1.6 x - 0.07 x3)) cdfx = S(tildeux / sigma1) cdfy = S(tildeuy / sigma2) return cdfx cdfy Parameters: Logistic approximation coefficients: 1.6 and 0.07 for the standard CDF approximation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Covariance: If \det(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) = 0 or eigenvalues are zero, the normalization of eigenvectors or division by eigenvalues in the exponential term may fail. Precision: The calculation involves square roots and exponentials, which are more computationally expensive than standard splatting. Time Complexity: The method introduces more root and exponential operations than vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting and Mip-Splatting due to the eigendecomposition and logistic CDF approximation. Measured Performance: Despite the additional operations, the frame rate is only 10% lower than Mip-Splatting. Strengths: Achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis results under multiscale and super-resolution settings with better detail fidelity. Limitations: Increased computational burden compared to simpler methods. Analytic-Splatting was introduced by Zhihao Liang et al. in the paper "Analytic-Splatting: Anti-Aliased 3D Gaussian Splatting via Analytic Integration". It builds upon the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and aims to improve anti-aliasing by analytically integrating the Gaussian signal over the pixel area using a logistic approximation of the CDF. Analytic-Splatting: Anti-Aliased 3D Gaussian Splatting via Analytic Integration, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72643-917, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Transparency and Blending Models
body: Transparency and Blending Models define how 3D Gaussian primitives are composited into a 2D image, addressing the limitations of standard front-to-back alpha blending which requires strict depth sorting and assumes non-overlapping primitives. The family includes approaches that balance performance and accuracy [3294-hybrid-transparency.md], analytic volumetric integration that eliminates projection artifacts [4440-analytic-transmittance-3dgs.md], and order-independent methods that bypass sorting entirely [7562-sparseoit-rasterizer.md]. Builds on Shading and Lighting Models. Combines depth-ordered alpha blending for the foremost K fragments with order-independent accumulation for the tail. Chosen when popping artifacts from approximate sorting must be mitigated without the cost of full sorting or ray tracing. Replaces approximate alpha computation with analytic integration of the volume rendering equation along the ray. Chosen for physically accurate transmittance and better representation of opaque surfaces, assuming non-overlapping, sorted Gaussians. Computes blended images using Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) without depth sorting. Chosen when sorting overhead is prohibitive, using a weighted average to approximate order-dependent results. Originating from the need to improve view synthesis quality and rendering stability in 3D Gaussian Splatting, these methods address the linearization errors and sorting artifacts inherent in standard rasterization. Analytic Transmittance derives from volumetric rendering theory, applying 1D Gaussian integration along rays [4440-analytic-transmittance-3dgs.md]. Hybrid Transparency and SparseOIT address the computational bottlenecks of sorting large numbers of fragments in real-time rendering [3294-hybrid-transparency.md, 7562-sparseoit-rasterizer.md].

name: Hybrid Transparency
head: Core-Tail Blending, Hybrid Transparency Blending, Hybrid Transparency-based blending, Hybrid transparency for 3DGS, Partial depth-ordering blending
body: Hybrid Transparency is a rendering technique that mitigates popping artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by combining depth-ordered alpha blending for the first K fragments (the 'core') with order-independent accumulation for the remaining fragments (the 'tail'). Unlike standard 3DGS which uses approximate view-space depth sorting, or StopThePop which employs expensive hierarchical sorting, Hybrid Transparency guarantees correct per-pixel depth ordering only for the front-most contributions, allowing the rest to be blended without sorting. This approach maintains real-time performance while ensuring temporal stability and multi-view consistency, particularly in VR applications. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity o \in \mathbb{R}, orientation vectors tu, tv, tw \in \mathbb{R}^3, and scales su, sv, sw \in \mathbb{R}. Outputs: Final pixel color and opacity. Parameters: K: Number of fragments in the core. Default and optimal value is 16. \tauK: Minimum alpha threshold for a fragment to be considered for the core. Default value is 0.05. Data Structures: Core Buffer: A compact 64-bit data structure per thread storing the top K fragments for a pixel, reducing register usage and swap operations during insertion sort. Tail Accumulators: Per-pixel accumulators for RGB color and alpha of all non-core fragments. Steps: 1. Splat Staging and Bounding Box Computation: Compute the screen-space bounding box for each 3D Gaussian using plane-fitting to determine exact bounding boxes. Create unordered per-tile fragment lists, omitting the depth ordering step as hybrid transparency resolves depth ordering during blending. 2. Pixel-Specific Depth Evaluation (x{view}): For each splat intersecting a pixel, compute the point of maximum contribution along the pixel's viewing ray in view space, denoted as x{view}. This value is used to determine if the splat belongs to the core or the tail. It is computed efficiently by re-using intermediate values from the splat evaluation process. Using only the view-space depth of the mean is insufficient and causes popping artifacts. 3. Core Identification and Sorting: Identify the splats contributing to the pixel. Sort these splats based on x{view}. Select the first K splats (or fewer if fewer than K splats exist) that also satisfy \alpha \ge \tauK to form the 'core'. If insertion sort is used for the core, reduce tile size to 8 \times 8 to mitigate thread divergence. 4. Core Blending: Alpha-blend the core fragments in their correct depth order using standard \alpha-blending. Let C{core} and \alpha{core} be the accumulated color and opacity of the core. C{core} = \sum{i=1}^{K} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{core} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{K} (1 - \alphai) where ci, \alphai are the color and opacity of the i-th core fragment. 5. Tail Accumulation: Accumulate the contributions of all remaining N-K fragments (the 'tail') without sorting. C{tail} = \sum{j=K+1}^{N} cj \alpha{tail} = \sum{j=K+1}^{N} \alphaj The tail accumulation is order-independent. 6. Final Compositing: Combine the core and tail by compositing the tail behind the core. C = C{core} + C{tail} (1 - \alpha{core}) \alpha = \alpha{core} + \alpha{tail} (1 - \alpha{core}) The computation of the tail transmittance is more accurate than average-based formulations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridtransparencyrender(gaussians, K=16, tauK=0.05): # Initialize per-pixel accumulators # Core: List of up to K fragments, sorted by depth (xview ascending) # Tail: Accumulated color (list of 3 floats) and alpha (float) corebuffers = [[] for in range(numpixels)] tailcolor = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(numpixels)] tailalpha = [0.0] numpixels for gaussian in gaussians: # 1. Compute screen-space bounding box and tile assignment tiles = getintersectingtiles(gaussian) # 2. Evaluate splat at pixel locations for tile in tiles: pixels = getpixelsintile(tile) for pixel in pixels: # Compute point of max contribution in view space xview = computemaxcontributiondepth(gaussian, pixel) # Evaluate Gaussian at this point alpha = gaussian.evaluatealpha(xview) color = gaussian.evaluatecolor(xview) # Skip if below threshold if alpha < tauK: continue # Determine if this fragment belongs to Core or Tail iscorecandidate = (alpha >= tauK) if iscorecandidate: # Try to insert into core buffer inserted = tryinsertcore(corebuffers[pixel], xview, color, alpha, K) if inserted: # It is in the core. # If it displaces an existing core fragment, that fragment # might move to tail? # Standard HT implementations usually fix the set of K # closest. If a new closer one arrives, the farthest core # one is ejected to tail. ejected = ejectfarthestifneeded(corebuffers[pixel]) if ejected: tailcolor[pixel] += ejected.color tailalpha[pixel] += ejected.alpha else: # Not in top K, goes to tail tailcolor[pixel] += color tailalpha[pixel] += alpha else: # Below threshold, goes to tail tailcolor[pixel] += color tailalpha[pixel] += alpha # Final Compositing finalcolor = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(numpixels)] finalalpha = [0.0] numpixels for pixel in range(numpixels): coreres = blendcore(corebuffers[pixel]) Ccore, Acore = coreres.color, coreres.alpha Ctail = tailcolor[pixel] Atail = tailalpha[pixel] # Composite Core and Tail # Tail is behind the core finalcolor[pixel] = Ccore + Ctail (1.0 - Acore) finalalpha[pixel] = Acore + Atail (1.0 - Acore) return finalcolor, finalalpha def tryinsertcore(buffer, xview, color, alpha, K): # Insert into sorted list of size <= K # If buffer is full and new fragment is closer (smaller xview) than # the farthest in buffer, replace farthest and return True (ejected) # Else return False (not inserted) pass def ejectfarthestifneeded(buffer): # Remove the fragment with largest xview from buffer # Return that fragment pass def blendcore(buffer): # Standard alpha blending of sorted fragments acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for frag in buffer: acccolor += frag.color frag.alpha (1.0 - accalpha) accalpha += frag.alpha (1.0 - accalpha) return acccolor, accalpha A sorting strategy that approximates the \tau{max} order of hit particles by storing the k-farthest hit particles (typically k=16) in a buffer and incrementally alpha-blending the closest hits until transmittance vanishes. Unlike Hybrid Transparency which stores the k-closest and blends farthest hits, MLAB stores farthest and blends closest. Hybrid Transparency recovers exact k-closest particles but requires processing all particles, which can be slow without optimizations. Time Complexity: Rendering time is reduced compared to global sorting methods because it avoids the overhead of sorting the tail. However, it requires processing all splats to determine core/tail membership, which can be slower than simple early-stopping alpha blending if not optimized. Memory Complexity: Uses compact 64-bit structures for core fragments to minimize register usage. Performance: Achieves a training speedup of 2.1\times and rendering speedup of 1.6\times compared to standard 3DGS on average. It is significantly faster than StopThePop. Strengths: Eliminates popping artifacts caused by approximate sorting. Provides temporally stable rendering suitable for VR. Limitations: Cannot use early stopping based on transmittance threshold by default, which may impact performance in scenes with high depth complexity. Image quality is about equal to standard 3DGS. Edge Cases: K=0 (no sorting) causes foreground transparency issues and is invalid. Omitting tail computation during training causes catastrophic failure, though it has a small impact on inference quality. Insertion sort for the core causes thread divergence; mitigated by using small tile sizes (8 \times 8). Hybrid Transparency was originally proposed by Wymann et al. [Wym16] and extended by Maule et al. [MCTB13] for gradient descent-based optimization. It was integrated into the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by Hahlbohm et al. [HFW25] to address popping artifacts and perspective inaccuracies. The method is particularly relevant for VR/AR applications where high frame rates and multi-view consistency are critical. Efficient Perspective‐Correct 3D Gaussian Splatting Using Hybrid Transparency, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70014, fetched 2026-10-30 Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31 3DGUT: Enabling Distorted Cameras and Secondary Rays in Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.02425, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Analytic Transmittance 3DGS
head: Analytic transmittance computation for 3DGS, Volumetrically Consistent 3D Gaussian Rasterization, Volumetrically Consistent 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Analytic Transmittance 3DGS is a rasterization-based rendering method that replaces the approximate alpha computation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytic integration of the volume rendering equation along the camera ray. It computes physically accurate transmittance and opacity values without projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D splats, thereby avoiding the linearization and self-occlusion approximations inherent in splatting. This method achieves higher accuracy for opaque surfaces and better view synthesis quality (SSIM, LPIPS) while maintaining rasterization speeds. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D mean (center). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: 3D covariance matrix. ci: View-dependent color. \thetai \in [0, 1]: Learnable parameter controlling density. s{x,i}, s{y,i}, s{z,i}: Scales. Camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. A list of Gaussians sorted front-to-back along the ray. Outputs: Pixel color C(p) and accumulated opacity. The method uses the standard 3DGS Gaussian representation but modifies the density parameterization and alpha computation. Gaussian Attributes: \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, ci, \thetai, s{x,i}, s{y,i}, s{z,i}. Precomputed Density: \kappai is derived from \thetai and scales (see Formula section). Sorting: Gaussians must be sorted by their intersection distance with the ray or depth, ensuring front-to-back order. The volume rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r}(t) is: C(\mathbf{r}) = \int0^\infty T(0, t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) c(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) dt where transmittance is: T(a, b) = \exp \left( - \inta^b \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds \right) The density field is a sum of weighted 3D Gaussians: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N \kappai Gi(\mathbf{x}) with the unnormalized 3D Gaussian: Gi(\mathbf{x}) = \exp \left\{ -\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i) \right\} 1. Reparameterization of Density \kappa To promote high density for small Gaussians and aid optimization, \kappa is reparameterized using \theta \in [0, 1]: \kappa = -\log(1 - 0.99\theta) \frac{1}{3} \left( \frac{1}{sx} + \frac{1}{sy} + \frac{1}{sz} \right) 2. 1D Gaussian Projection along Ray For a specific Gaussian j, the 1D distribution gj(t) along the ray \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is derived by substituting the ray equation into the 3D Gaussian. The exponent argument \Delta expands to: \Delta = (t\mathbf{d} - (\boldsymbol{\mu}j - \mathbf{o}))^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} (t\mathbf{d} - (\boldsymbol{\mu}j - \mathbf{o})) \Delta = t^2 \mathbf{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d} - 2t(\boldsymbol{\mu}j - \mathbf{o})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d} + (\boldsymbol{\mu}j - \mathbf{o})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} (\boldsymbol{\mu}j - \mathbf{o}) This results in a 1D Gaussian form: gj(t) = Gj(\gammaj \mathbf{d}) \exp \left\{ -\frac{(t - \gammaj)^2}{2\betaj^2} \right\} where the mean \gammaj and variance \betaj are: \gammaj = \frac{(\boldsymbol{\mu}j - \mathbf{o})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d}}, \quad \betaj = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathbf{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j^{-1} \mathbf{d}}} Gj(\gammaj \mathbf{d}) is the maximum value of the Gaussian along the ray. 3. Analytic Transmittance \overline{T}j The accumulated transmittance across Gaussian j from entry t{jn} to exit t{jf} is: \overline{T}j = \exp \left( - \int{t{jn}}^{t{jf}} \kappaj gj(t) dt \right) The integral of the 1D Gaussian is: \int{t{jn}}^{t{jf}} gj(t) dt = Gj(\gammaj \mathbf{d}) \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} \betaj \left[ \text{erf} \left( \frac{t - \gammaj}{\sqrt{2}\betaj} \right) \right]{t{jn}}^{t{jf}} Note: The source text provides the indefinite integral result as \text{erf} \left( \frac{t - \gammaj}{2\betaj} \right) in Eq. 17, but standard Gaussian integration yields \sqrt{2}\betaj in the denominator. The source Eq. 19 assumes infinite support (t{jn} \to -\infty, t{jf} \to \infty), where the error function term becomes 1. The source formula for infinite support is: \overline{T}j = \exp \left( -\kappaj Gj(\gammaj \mathbf{d}) \sqrt{2\pi} \betaj \right) 4. Alpha and Color Computation Assuming non-overlapping, sorted Gaussians, the opacity \alphai of the i-th Gaussian is: \alphai = 1 - \overline{T}i The final pixel color is computed via alpha blending: C(p) = \sum{i=1}^N ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeanalyticalpha(mu, Sigmainv, d, o, kappa, Gpeak): """ Computes the accumulated transmittance and alpha for a single 3D Gaussian along a ray, assuming infinite support for the analytic approximation. Args: mu: 3D mean vector (numpy array) Sigmainv: Inverse 3D covariance matrix (numpy array) d: Ray direction vector (numpy array) o: Ray origin vector (numpy array) kappa: Density weight Gpeak: Maximum value of the Gaussian along the ray, G(muproj) Returns: alpha: Accumulated opacity (1 - transmittance) """ # Compute d^T Sigmainv d # This is a scalar denom = d.dot(Sigmainv.dot(d)) # Avoid division by zero if denom < 1e-8: return 0.0 # Compute betaj = 1 / sqrt(d^T Sigmainv d) betaj = 1.0 / math.sqrt(denom) # Compute the exponent argument for transmittance: # expterm = kappa Gpeak sqrt(2 pi) betaj # Note: Source Eq. 19 uses sqrt(2pi). # Standard integral of exp(-x^2/(2b^2)) is bsqrt(2pi). # Here the 1D Gaussian is Gpeak exp(-(t-gamma)^2 / (2beta^2)). # Integral is Gpeak beta sqrt(2pi). exponent = kappa Gpeak math.sqrt(2.0 math.pi) betaj # Transmittance T = exp(-integral) transmittance = math.exp(-exponent) # Alpha = 1 - T alpha = 1.0 - transmittance return alpha def renderpixelanalytic(rayo, rayd, gaussianssorted): """ Renders a single pixel using analytic transmittance. Args: rayo: Ray origin rayd: Ray direction (normalized) gaussianssorted: List of Gaussian objects sorted front-to-back. Each object has: mu, Sigmainv, color, kappa, Gpeak. Gpeak is precomputed as exp(-0.5 (muproj - mu)^T Sigmainv (muproj - mu)) where muproj is the projection of mu onto the ray. Returns: color: Rendered RGB color alpha: Total accumulated alpha """ accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for g in gaussianssorted: # Compute alpha for this Gaussian alphai = computeanalyticalpha( g.mu, g.Sigmainv, rayd, rayo, g.kappa, g.Gpeak) # Contribution: ci alphai Tprev # Tprev is accumulatedtransmittance contribution = [ g.color[0] alphai accumulatedtransmittance, g.color[1] alphai accumulatedtransmittance, g.color[2] alphai accumulatedtransmittance ] finalcolor[0] += contribution[0] finalcolor[1] += contribution[1] finalcolor[2] += contribution[2] # Update accumulated transmittance accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alphai) # Early exit if fully opaque (optional optimization) if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-4: break return finalcolor, 1.0 - accumulatedtransmittance \theta \in [0, 1]: Learnable density parameter. sx, sy, sz: Scales of the Gaussian. Constant 0.99: Used in the log reparameterization to promote high density for small Gaussians. Overlap and Sorting: The method assumes Gaussians are sorted front-to-back and do not overlap along the ray. If these assumptions are violated, the separation of transmittance terms is invalid, leading to artifacts. Infinite Support Approximation: The analytic formula \overline{T}j = \exp(-\kappaj Gj(\gammaj \mathbf{d}) \sqrt{2\pi} \betaj) assumes infinite support. For very small Gaussians or specific ray intersections, finite bounds might be more accurate, but the source uses the infinite approximation for consistency and speed. Optimization Heuristics: Standard 3DGS opacity reset is disabled. Density \kappa is halved after splitting and cloning. Points with high \kappa are split; points with low \theta (density before reparameterization) are pruned. Time Complexity: Similar to 3DGS rasterization, as it avoids the overhead of 2D Gaussian projection and blending but adds the cost of computing \gammaj, \betaj and the exponential/erf-like operations. The source reports 136 FPS on MipNeRF-360 with an Nvidia 3090-Ti, compared to 159 FPS for standard 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Same as 3DGS, storing N Gaussians with additional precomputed values if necessary. Performance: On MipNeRF-360, the method achieves PSNR 27.30, SSIM 0.813, LPIPS 0.209. It outperforms 3DGS in SSIM and LPIPS, particularly for opaque surfaces and piecewise constant textures. Strengths: Physically accurate transmittance, better representation of opaque surfaces, no self-occlusion artifacts from linearization, compatible with tomography pipelines. Limitations: Relies on non-overlapping assumption; slightly slower than 3DGS due to analytic integration cost. The method was introduced in "Volumetrically Consistent 3D Gaussian Rasterization" (2024). It addresses the approximations in 3DGS splatting (linearization of exponential, no-self occlusion, linearization of covariance) by analytically integrating 3D Gaussians along rays. It builds on the volume rendering equation and the 3DGS representation, offering a more physically accurate alternative within a rasterization framework. Volumetrically Consistent 3D Gaussian Rasterization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03378v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SparseOIT Rasterizer
head: GPU software rasterization of 3D Gaussians with pre-rendering
body: SparseOIT Rasterizer is a rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes a blended image using Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) without sorting Gaussians by depth. It differs from standard 3DGS rasterization, which requires sorting by distance to camera to correctly accumulate transmittance, by eliminating the sorting step entirely in favor of a weighted average that approximates the order-dependent result. It achieves this by simultaneously computing a final OIT color and a pre-rendered image state using Blend-and-Normalize (BAN) and Blend-and-Update (BAU) functions. The method operates on 3D Gaussian primitives defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} (or scales and orientation), opacity o, and color \mathbf{c}. Inputs: Image dimensions: width w, height h. Gaussian attributes: 3D means M, covariances S, colors C, opacities A. View matrix V. Outputs: Rendered image I. Pre-rendered image state I{pre} (used for accumulation/updates). Tiles (T): A grid partitioning the image of size w \times h. The specific tile size is not given in the sources. Gaussian List (L): A list of Gaussian data structures duplicated and keyed by tile ID. Keys (K): Tile IDs assigned to each Gaussian entry in L. Ranges (R): Start and end indices in L for each tile t. 1. CullGaussian(p, V): Cull Gaussians based on position p and view V. 2. ScreenspaceGaussians(M, S, V): Project 3D means M and covariances S to screen space, yielding M' and S'. 3. CreateTiles(w, h): Create tiles for image dimensions w, h. 4. DuplicateWithKeys(M', T): Duplicate Gaussian data and assign tile keys. 5. SortByKeys(K, L): Sort Gaussians only by tile ID. 6. IdentifyTileRanges(T, K): Identify ranges of Gaussians for each tile. 7. Initialize: Set rendered image I to zero. 8. Loop over all tiles t in T: 9. Loop over all pixels i in t: 10. GetTileRange(R, t): Get range of Gaussians for tile t. 11. BAN: Compute final color I[i] using the Blend-and-Normalize function. 12. BAU: Update pre-rendered state I{pre}[i] using the Blend-and-Update function. The final color \mathbf{C} is computed as: \mathbf{C} = T \mathbf{c}0 + (1-T)F where: \mathbf{c}0 is the background color. T is the accumulated opacity/transmittance factor. F is the weighted average color: F = \frac{P}{Q} P = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi Q = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai wi \mathbf{c}i is the color of the i-th Gaussian. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. wi is the weight of the i-th Gaussian. The gradients for backpropagation are: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \mathbf{c}i} = (1-T)\frac{\alphai wi}{Q} \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \alphai} = \frac{T}{1-\alphai}(F-\mathbf{c}0) + (1-T)\frac{wi}{Q}(\mathbf{c}i - F) \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial wi} = (1-T)\frac{\alphai}{Q}(\mathbf{c}i - F) BAN (Blend and Normalize): Function that computes the final OIT color. BAU (Blend and Update): Function that updates the pre-rendered image state for subsequent blending or accumulation. Update Interval: In most cases, the update interval is not specified, but for scenes like train, room, and bonsai, it is set to 600 to ensure correct execution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SparseOITRasterizer(w, h, M, S, C, A, V): # 1. CullGaussian: Remove Gaussians outside view frustum or too small valid = [i for i, p in enumerate(M) if infrustum(p, V) and size(p, S) > threshold] Mc, Sc, Cc, Ac = M[valid], S[valid], C[valid], A[valid] # 2. ScreenspaceGaussians: Project 3D means and covariances to screen space Mprime, Sprime = projecttoscreen(Mc, Sc, V) # 3. CreateTiles: Partition image into grid tiles T = createtilegrid(w, h) # 4. DuplicateWithKeys: Assign each Gaussian to the tile containing its center L, K = [], [] for i, m in enumerate(Mprime): tileid = gettilecontaining(m, T) L.append((i, m, Sprime[i], Cc[i], Ac[i])) K.append(tileid) # 5. SortByKeys: Sort list L only by tile keys K combined = sorted(zip(K, L), key=lambda x: x[0]) K, L = zip(combined) if combined else ([], []) # 6. IdentifyTileRanges: Compute start/end indices in L for each tile R = {} for t in T: indices = [j for j, k in enumerate(K) if k == t] R[t] = (indices[0], indices[-1] + 1) if indices else (0, 0) # 7. Initialize rendered image I to zero I = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(w h)] Ipre = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(w h)] # [T, Fr, Fg, Fb] # 8-12. Loop over tiles and pixels for t in T: rstart, rend = R[t] for y in range(t.ymin, t.ymax): for x in range(t.xmin, t.xmax): i = y w + x r = L[rstart:rend] # 11. BAN: Compute final color I[i] = BAN(i, r, Mprime, Sprime, Cc, Ac, Ipre[i]) # 12. BAU: Update pre-rendered state Ipre[i] = BAU(i, r, Mprime, Sprime, Cc, Ac, Ipre[i]) return I, Ipre def BAN(i, r, Mprime, Sprime, Cc, Ac, Ipre): # Computes final OIT color using weighted average P = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Q = 0.0 for idx, m, s, c, a in r: wi = evaluategaussian(m, s, i) # Standard 2D Gaussian PDF at pixel i P[0] += c[0] a wi P[1] += c[1] a wi P[2] += c[2] a wi Q += a wi F = [P[j] / Q if Q > 0 else 0.0 for j in range(3)] T = Ipre[0] c0 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Background color return [T c0[j] + (1 - T) F[j] for j in range(3)] def BAU(i, r, Mprime, Sprime, Cc, Ac, Ipre): # Updates pre-rendered state for subsequent blending alphasum = 0.0 colorsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for idx, m, s, c, a in r: wi = evaluategaussian(m, s, i) # alphasum += a wi colorsum[0] += c[0] a wi colorsum[1] += c[1] a wi colorsum[2] += c[2] a wi newT = 1.0 - min(1.0, alphasum) newF = [colorsum[j] / alphasum if alphasum > 0 else 0.0 for j in range(3)] return [newT, newF[0], newF[1], newF[2]] Gradient Independence: The variables of each Gaussian are mutually independent in the backward propagation equation, allowing for parallel computation. Update Interval: For specific scenes (train, room, bonsai), the update interval must be set to 600 to ensure correct execution, exceeding twice the number of training views. Weighted Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a rendering technique that computes a blended image without sorting Gaussians by depth, using a learnable weight function to approximate correct transparency blending. It differs from standard 3DGS rasterization, which requires sorting by distance to camera to correctly accumulate transmittance, by eliminating the sorting step entirely in favor of a weighted average that approximates the order-dependent result. It builds on SparseOIT Rasterizer. Time Complexity: The sorting step is reduced to sorting by tile ID only, which is significantly faster than full depth sorting. The blending process is independent of depth order, allowing for parallel computation of gradients. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the rendered image I and pre-rendered state I{pre}. Strengths: Eliminates the expensive depth sorting step required by standard 3DGS rasterization. Allows for parallel computation of gradients due to mutual independence of Gaussian variables in the backward propagation. Limitations: The specific tile size and the exact implementation of the BAN and BAU functions are not detailed in the sources. When to Use: When order-independent transparency is desired and the computational cost of depth sorting is prohibitive. The SparseOIT Rasterizer was introduced in the paper "SparseOIT: Improving Order-Independent Transparency 3DGS via Active Set Method". It is a rasterization algorithm for 3D Gaussians that computes a weighted blended order-independent transparency (OIT) image and a pre-rendered image simultaneously, using a blend-and-normalize (BAN) function and a blend-and-update (BAU) function. SparseOIT: Improving Order-Independent Transparency 3DGS via Active Set Method, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.13855, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Weighted Order-Independent Transparency for 3DGS
head: OIT-based 3DGS rendering, Weighted OIT, Weighted Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) Rendering
body: Weighted Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) for 3D Gaussian Splatting computes a blended image without sorting Gaussians by depth, using a learnable weight function to approximate correct transparency blending. It differs from standard 3DGS rasterization, which requires sorting by distance to camera to correctly accumulate transmittance, by eliminating the sorting step entirely in favor of a weighted average. The method builds on SparseOIT Rasterizer. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians G = \{\bm{\mu}i, qi, si, oi, \mathbf{h}i, wi \mid i=1,\dots,N\}, where \bm{\mu}i is the 3D center, qi is the quaternion rotation, si is the scale, oi is the base opacity, \mathbf{h}i are spherical harmonic coefficients, and wi is the learnable weight. Camera parameters (view matrix \mathbf{W}, projection matrix, focal point \mathbf{f}) are required for projection. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C} and transmittance T for each pixel. Data Structures Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores: \bm{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D center position. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity scalar. \mathbf{h}i: Spherical harmonic coefficients for color. wi \in \mathbb{R}: Learnable weight scalar. Projected Attributes (computed per pixel/tile): \bm{\mu}'i \in \mathbb{R}^2: Projected 2D center. \bm{\Sigma}'i \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: Projected 2D covariance matrix. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Final opacity at the pixel. \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Gaussian color at the pixel. Numbered Steps 1. Project Gaussians: For each Gaussian i, compute the 3D-to-2D projection. Compute the 3D covariance matrix \bm{\Sigma}i from scale si and rotation qi. Compute the view transformation matrix \mathbf{W} and the Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J} of the affine approximation of the projective transformation at the Gaussian center. Compute the 2D covariance matrix: \bm{\Sigma}'i = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \bm{\Sigma}i \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T 2. Compute Final Opacity \alphai: For a pixel at position \bm{x}'i (the pixel center in 2D space), calculate the Gaussian's contribution opacity: \alphai = oi \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2} (\bm{x}'i - \bm{\mu}'i)^T {\bm{\Sigma}'i}^{-1} (\bm{x}'i - \bm{\mu}'i)\right) 3. Compute Color \mathbf{c}i: Evaluate the spherical harmonic function \mathbf{Y} using the direction from the camera focal point \mathbf{f} to the Gaussian center \bm{\mu}i and the coefficients \mathbf{h}i: \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{Y}(\|\mathbf{f} - \bm{\mu}i\|, \mathbf{h}i) 4. Accumulate Weighted Sum: For each pixel, initialize accumulators for the weighted color sum and the total weight. Iterate over all Gaussians i=1 \dots N that overlap the pixel (or use an active set for optimization): Let wi be the learnable weight for Gaussian i. Accumulate: \text{WeightedColor} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi \text{TotalWeight} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai wi 5. Compute Transmittance T: Calculate the product of (1 - \alphai) for all overlapping Gaussians: T = \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) 6. Compute Final Color \mathbf{C}: Combine the background color \mathbf{c}0, the transmittance T, and the weighted average of the Gaussian colors: \mathbf{C} = T \mathbf{c}0 + (1 - T) \frac{\text{WeightedColor}}{\text{TotalWeight}} Parameters Learnable Weight wi: A scalar value associated with each Gaussian. It is a learnable weight larger when the Gaussian is near the camera. The exact functional form of wi is defined in Eq. 1 of reference [14], but the specific formula is not provided in the source text. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: If \text{TotalWeight} = 0 (no Gaussians overlap or all \alphai wi = 0), the weighted average term is undefined. In this case, the result should default to T \mathbf{c}0. Precision: The product T = \prod (1-\alphai) can underflow to zero for many overlapping Gaussians, which is mathematically correct but may cause numerical issues if not handled with log-space accumulation in implementation. Weight Definition: The source states wi is "larger when gaussian near to camera" but does not provide the explicit formula for wi in the text, citing [14] instead. Implementers must refer to [14] for the exact definition of wi. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates the need for depth sorting, which simplifies parallelization on GPU and avoids sorting artifacts. Limitations: Approximates order-dependent transparency; accuracy depends on the quality of the learned weights wi. Origin: The weighted OIT rendering equation was first defined in [22] and adopted from [14]. It was applied to 3DGS in the context of improving order-independent transparency methods for Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction. Development: The method is part of the "SparseOIT" framework, which proposes acceleration strategies like the active set method to improve the performance of OIT-based 3DGS reconstruction. SparseOIT: Improving Order-Independent Transparency 3DGS via Active Set Method, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.13855, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to support physically based lighting, self-occlusion, and environment reflections. It solves the limitation of standard splatting, which assumes a fixed, uniform lighting environment, by introducing deferred shading pipelines for relighting and dedicated light-space rasterization passes for self-shadowing. Unlike sibling methods that may use simplified shading functions or voxel-based fallbacks, these approaches provide full PBR material attributes and continuous differentiable gradients for shadows without modifying the primary camera's covariance expansion. Builds on Shading and Lighting Models. For relighting, splats must carry physical material attributes: normal, roughness, reflectance (specular strength), and albedo (diffuse color). These are stored in a parallel Material Buffer aligned with the Splat Buffer. For self-shadowing, a virtual "sun camera" is constructed to simulate a directional light source. This camera is placed at a large distance with a narrow field of view (FOV) to minimize parallax error to below 2%. Both relighting (for cache locality) and shadowing (for correct front-to-back accumulation) require sorting. Relighting uses spatial locality algorithms like Morton codes. Shadowing sorts Gaussians by depth relative to the sun camera. During the light pass for shadowing, the projection covariance is not expanded by 0.3I and no amplitude compensation is applied, preserving the main camera pass's sampling expansion. In shadowing calculations, sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches are treated as constants to prevent incorrect gradient propagation. A physically based rendering (PBR) method for novel view synthesis and relighting of reflective objects using 2D Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of blurred reflective details and incorrect lighting in standard Gaussian Splatting by decomposing splats into PBR material attributes (albedo, normal, roughness, reflectance) and computing lighting via a deferred shading pipeline with split-sum environment map integration. It differs from sibling methods like 3DGS-DR by using full PBR with spherical harmonics for diffuse fitting rather than simplified shading functions, and by employing deferred rendering to prevent the blurring of reflective details inherent in per-Gaussian shading. Choose this when high-fidelity reflections and PBR material accuracy are required. Calculates the self-shadowing transmittance T{light} for each Gaussian primitive along the sun direction, representing the 'front occlusion transmittance' to model self-shadowing effects in volume rendering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by performing a dedicated light-space rasterization pass that accumulates depth-weighted transmittance without modifying the primary camera's covariance expansion or applying amplitude compensation, ensuring consistency with the main rendering pass. Choose this when self-occlusion shadows are needed for directional lighting. Light Space Rasterization computes T{light}, the front-facing occlusion transmittance for each 3D Gaussian along a directional sun direction. It differs from voxel-based fallbacks by providing full continuous gradients and zero parameter expansion, enabling differentiable relighting without requiring specific training hyperparameters. Choose this when differentiable shadow gradients are required for training or optimization. The methods in this family originate from the need to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting beyond simple diffuse rendering. Ref-Gaussian introduces deferred surfel rendering to handle PBR materials. The Tlight methods were developed to add self-shadowing capabilities, initially using voxel-based caches and later refined into a differentiable rasterization approach. These techniques are used in high-fidelity novel view synthesis, virtual production, and physically based rendering of 3D Gaussian scenes. Ref-Gaussian Deferred Surfel Rendering with Split-Sum IBL, https://github.com/JeffWang001/Ref-Gaussian, 2024 3D Gaussian Splatting Self-Shadowing (Tlight), https://github.com/4dPrint/3dgs-t-light, 2024 Light Space Rasterization for Tlight, https://github.com/4dPrint/3dgs-t-light, 2024

name: Ref-Gaussian Deferred Surfel Rendering with Split-Sum IBL
head: MetalGaussianSplatRelighting, Ref-Gaussian, Ref-Gaussian on iOS
body: Ref-Gaussian is a physically based rendering (PBR) method for novel view synthesis and relighting of reflective objects using 2D Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of blurred reflective details and inaccurate material representation in standard Gaussian Splatting by decomposing splats into PBR material attributes (albedo, normal, roughness, reflectance) and computing lighting via a deferred shading pipeline with split-sum environment map integration. It is distinguished from its sibling 3D Gaussian Splatting Self-Shadowing (Tlight) by its focus on material-aware deferred shading and split-sum IBL rather than light-space rasterization for self-shadowing, and from Light Space Rasterization for Tlight by its use of a deferred surfel buffer for cache-locality sorting rather than a dedicated light-space depth buffer. Inputs: A.ply file containing 2D Gaussian primitives with per-splat attributes: position, covariance (geometry), normal, roughness, reflectance (specular strength), and albedo (diffuse color). An HDR environment map (equirectangular or cubemap) representing the lighting. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Outputs: A final color image with physically based reflections and diffuse lighting. Splat Buffer: Layout: Array of structs, sorted by Morton code for cache locality. Fields: position (vec3), covariance (mat3 or 6 floats), normal (vec3), roughness (float), reflectance (float), albedo (vec3). Note: The material buffer (containing normal, roughness, reflectance, albedo) must be sorted in parallel with the position/covariance buffer using the same sort indices to prevent desynchronization and rainbow noise. Material Buffer: Layout: Parallel array to Splat Buffer, aligned by index. Fields: normal, roughness, reflectance, albedo. G-Buffer (Deferred Surfel Buffer): Layout: Tile-based memory (e.g., Metal tile memory) storing accumulated surfel data. Fields: color (accumulated), normal (accumulated), depth (accumulated), material attributes if not passed directly to shading pass. IBL Pre-computation: Prefiltered Environment Map: Mipmapped texture where each mip level corresponds to a specific roughness value. Irradiance Map: Pre-filtered environment map for diffuse lighting. BRDF LUT: 2D texture mapping (roughness, dot(N, V)) to (F0, F) terms. 1. Loading and Initialization: Load the.ply file to extract per-splat materials: normal, roughness, reflectance, and albedo. If training, reset all color and material attributes, retaining only the geometry of Gaussians before the deferred rendering stage. 2. IBL Pre-computation: Generate a prefiltered environment map for specular reflections (mipmapped by roughness). Generate an irradiance map for diffuse reflections. Generate a BRDF LUT. 3. Sorting: Sort splats using spatial locality algorithms like Morton codes to optimize cache usage during rendering. Apply the exact same sort indices to the Material Buffer to ensure normals and other attributes remain aligned with positions. 4. Rasterization (G-Buffer Pass): Project 2D Gaussians to screen space. Rasterize splats into the G-Buffer, accumulating color, normal, and depth information. Note: During training, material-aware normal propagation is conducted for Gaussians with metallic >= 0.02 and roughness <= 0.1 to capture accurate geometry. 5. Shading (Split-Sum IBL Pass): For each pixel, retrieve surfel data from the G-Buffer. Compute the base specular reflectivity F0: F0 = 0.04 \times (1 - \text{reflectance}) + \text{albedo} \times \text{reflectance} where F0 is the base specular reflectivity, reflectance is the learned specular strength, and albedo is the diffuse color. Compute the specular term using the prefiltered environment map and BRDF LUT: \text{specular} = \text{prefiltered}(\text{reflect}(V, N), \text{roughness}) \times (F0 \cdot fg.x + fg.y) where V is the view direction, N is the normal, and fg is the result from the BRDF LUT. Compute the final color: \text{final} = (1 - \text{reflectance}) \times \text{base\color} + \text{specular} where basecolor is the albedo used directly for diffuse lighting without irradiance multiplication. Note: Do not multiply albedo by the irradiance map for diffuse color; Ref-Gaussian uses basecolor directly for diffuse. 6. Post-processing: Composite the shaded result with the skybox/environment map if necessary. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computerefgaussianshading(splat, environmentmap, brdflut, viewdirection): """ Computes the final color for a single surfel using split-sum IBL. Args: splat: Object containing position, normal, roughness, reflectance, albedo. environmentmap: Object with prefilteredenvmap and irradiancemap. brdflut: 2D texture for BRDF integration. viewdirection: Normalized vector from camera to splat. Returns: finalcolor: vec3 """ # Extract material attributes N = normalize(splat.normal) roughness = splat.roughness reflectance = splat.reflectance albedo = splat.albedo # Compute F0 (Base Specular Reflectivity) # F0 = 0.04 (1 - reflectance) + albedo reflectance F0 = 0.04 (1.0 - reflectance) + albedo reflectance # Compute specular term # 1. Reflect view direction around normal R = reflect(-viewdirection, N) # 2. Sample prefiltered environment map based on roughness # The prefiltered map is mipmapped by roughness. # roughness maps to a mip level. miplevel = roughnesstomiplevel(roughness) prefilteredcolor = sampletexture(environmentmap.prefilteredenvmap, R, miplevel) # 3. Sample BRDF LUT # LUT input: (roughness, dot(N, V)) # Output: (F0scale, Fscale) or similar parameters for the Schlick-GGX approximation dotNV = max(dot(N, viewdirection), 0.0) fg = sampletexture(brdflut, vec2(roughness, dotNV)) # Specular = Prefiltered Env (F0 fg.x + fg.y) specular = prefilteredcolor (F0 fg.x + fg.y) # Compute diffuse term # Ref-Gaussian uses basecolor directly for diffuse, not albedo irradiance diffuse = albedo # Final color # final = (1 - reflectance) basecolor + specular finalcolor = (1.0 - reflectance) diffuse + specular return finalcolor def sortsplatsforcache(splats, materials): """ Sorts splats and materials in parallel using Morton codes. Args: splats: List of splat objects. materials: List of material objects aligned with splats. Returns: sortedsplats, sortedmaterials """ # Compute Morton codes for splat positions mortoncodes = [computemortoncode(s.position) for s in splats] # Sort indices based on Morton codes indices = sorted(range(len(mortoncodes)), key=lambda k: mortoncodes[k]) # Apply same indices to both buffers sortedsplats = [splats[i] for i in indices] sortedmaterials = [materials[i] for i in indices] return sortedsplats, sortedmaterials Learning rate for material attributes (metallic, roughness, albedo): 0.005. Learning rate for environment map: 0.01. Balancing weight for RGB reconstruction loss (\lambda): 0.2. Weight for normal consistency loss (\lambdan): 0.05. Weight for normal smoothness loss (\lambda{smooth}): 1.0. Initial roughness value: 0.1. Initial metallic value: Adopted from 3DGS-DR (value not explicitly stated). Roughness: Controls specular blur. Low roughness (~0.2 for cars) results in blurry reflections; high roughness results in diffuse-like specular. F0 base value: 0.04 for dielectrics, adjusted by reflectance and albedo. Normal Map Noise: If splats are sorted (e.g., by Morton code for cache locality) but the material buffer (containing normals) is not sorted in parallel, normals become misaligned with positions, causing rainbow noise. Fix: Apply the same sort indices to the material buffer. Incorrect Diffuse Lighting: Do not multiply albedo by the irradiance map for diffuse color. Ref-Gaussian uses basecolor directly for diffuse. Only specular is computed from the environment map. Coordinate System Mismatch: If the scene data is Z-up (Blender) but the viewer assumes Y-up, objects appear rotated 90 degrees. Fix: Apply a -90° rotation around the X-axis to the camera/view matrix and adjust environment map sampling directions to match the scene's up-axis. Stale Binary Execution on iOS: If iOS build fails due to type errors (e.g., Float16 bitPattern type mismatch between arm64 and x8664 simulator), the device may run an old binary. Always check build success for the target platform before debugging logic. Geometric Collapse: Smooth surfaces are prone to geometric collapse. Material-aware normal propagation addresses this. Blurred Reflective Details: Per-Gaussian rendering causes reflective details to become noticeably more blurred; deferred rendering is used to mitigate this. Time and Memory Complexity: Training consists of two stages: (1) per-Gaussian rendering for 18,000 steps; (2) deferred rendering stage training for about 40,000 steps. The deferred rendering pipeline adds overhead for G-Buffer accumulation but improves cache locality and rendering quality. Measured Performance: On the Shiny Blender dataset: PSNR 30.33, SSIM 0.958, LPIPS 0.049. MAE 2.15, Normal SSIM 0.954, Normal LPIPS 0.0511, Envmap LPIPS 0.4431. Training time: 0.58 hours. FPS: 122 on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Scaling: Real-time rendering is supported on mobile devices (iPhone) using Metal. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Physically based rendering with spherical harmonics for diffuse lighting; precise geometric representation using 2D Gaussian primitives; real-time relighting capability. Limitations: Per-Gaussian shading initialization can cause blurred reflective details if deferred rendering is not used; smooth surfaces are prone to geometric collapse without material-aware normal propagation. When to Use: Use for novel view synthesis of reflective objects, geometry, materials, and lighting reconstruction. Use when real-time relighting on mobile devices is required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for non-reflective or matte surfaces where PBR is not necessary, as it adds complexity. Not suitable if coordinate system mismatches are not handled, leading to visual artifacts. Origin: Ref-Gaussian was introduced in the paper "Reflective Gaussian Splatting". It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) and 3DGS-DR. History and Development: The method uses a two-stage training process: initial per-Gaussian rendering followed by deferred rendering training. It employs material-aware normal propagation and edge-aware normal smoothness loss to improve geometry and normal accuracy. Usage: Used on Shiny Blender, Glossy Synthetic, and Ref-Real datasets. Implemented for real-time rendering on iPhone using Metal. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Self-Shadowing (T_light)
head: 光源视角自阴影 (T_light)
body: Calculates the self-shadowing transmittance T{light} for each Gaussian along a directional sun direction, representing the 'front occlusion transmittance' to model self-shadowing effects in volume rendering. It differs from standard rasterization by performing a dedicated light-space pass that accumulates front-to-back occlusion without modifying the main camera's sampling expansion or applying amplitude compensation. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, color). Sun direction vector. Configuration flags (--tlightvoxel for fallback, default rasterization). Outputs: Per-Gaussian self-shadowing transmittance T{light} (stored in recordfronttau channel). Updated Gaussian attributes with gradients enabled for training. Data Structures: recordfronttau: A buffer aligned with the Gaussian buffer, storing the accumulated front transmittance weighted by weight (energy-weighted mean over the sun-facing footprint). Steps: 1. Light Camera Setup: Construct a virtual perspective camera to simulate a directional sun light source. Place it at a large distance with a narrow field of view (FOV) to minimize parallax error to below 2% and avoid modifying the EWA Jacobian. 2. Rasterization Pass: Perform a CUDA rasterization pass from the sun camera's perspective. Traverse Gaussians in depth order relative to the sun camera. 3. Transmittance Accumulation: For each Gaussian, calculate its contribution to the front occlusion. Record the accumulated front transmittance \tau weighted by \tau \times \text{weight} into the recordfronttau channel. This represents an energy-weighted mean over the entire sun-facing footprint, not just a center point sample. 4. Gradient Handling: Enable full continuous gradients by default. This includes gradients for \tau, weights, normalization, weak density backup transmittance, and projection position/scale/rotation. However, treat sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches as constants to prevent incorrect gradient propagation. 5. Covariance Handling: Do not expand the projection covariance by 0.3I during this light pass, and do not apply amplitude compensation. Keep the sampling expansion from the main camera pass as is. 6. Deeply Buried Gaussians: Handle deeply buried Gaussians (where early termination causes wsum=0) by explicitly mapping them to full shadow to prevent inversion artifacts. 7. Fallback Mode: If the --tlightvoxel flag is passed, use the old 128^3 voxel cache path. This is compatible with models trained before rasterization support was added. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetlight(gaussians, sundirection, usevoxelfallback=False): """ Compute self-shadowing transmittance Tlight for Gaussians. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives with position, covariance, opacity, etc. sundirection: 3D vector representing the sun direction. usevoxelfallback: Boolean flag to use old voxel cache path. Returns: tlight: Array of transmittance values for each Gaussian. """ if usevoxelfallback: # Fallback to old 128^3 voxel cache path return computetlightvoxelfallback(gaussians, sundirection) # Step 1: Setup light camera lightcamera = setuplightcamera(sundirection, distance=large, fov=narrow) # Step 2: Rasterize from light camera perspective # Sort Gaussians by depth relative to light camera sortedgaussians = sortbydepth(gaussians, lightcamera) # Initialize transmittance buffer tlight = zeros(len(gaussians)) accumulatedtau = 1.0 # Initial transmittance # Step 3: Accumulate front transmittance for gaussian in sortedgaussians: # Calculate footprint contribution # Energy-weighted mean over sun-facing footprint footprintweight = gaussian.weight gaussian.opacity # Update accumulated transmittance # tau is the front occlusion transmittance tau = accumulatedtau footprintweight # Record into buffer (conceptually) # recordfronttau[gaussian.id] = tau # Update accumulated transmittance for next Gaussian # Note: In volume rendering, Tlight is typically the transmittance # from the light source to the current point. # The description says "accumulated front transmittance tau weighted by tau weight" # This implies Tlight for a Gaussian is the transmittance reaching it. # Check for deeply buried Gaussians if accumulatedtau is effectivelyzero: tlight[gaussian.id] = 0.0 # Full shadow else: tlight[gaussian.id] = accumulatedtau # Update accumulated transmittance for the next Gaussian in depth order # This is a simplification; actual implementation may vary based on exact volume rendering equation accumulatedtau = (1.0 - gaussian.opacity) return tlight def setuplightcamera(sundirection, distance, fov): """ Setup a virtual camera to simulate directional light. Args: sundirection: 3D vector for sun direction. distance: Large distance to minimize parallax. fov: Narrow field of view. Returns: Camera object with projection matrix. """ # Place camera at large distance along sun direction cameraposition = sundirection distance cameratarget = vec3(0, 0, 0) cameraup = vec3(0, 1, 0) # Create perspective camera with narrow FOV camera = PerspectiveCamera(position=cameraposition, target=cameratarget, up=cameraup, fov=fov) return camera def sortbydepth(gaussians, camera): """ Sort Gaussians by depth relative to camera. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussians. camera: Camera object. Returns: Sorted list of Gaussians. """ # Project Gaussian centers to camera space depths = [projectdepth(g, camera) for g in gaussians] # Sort Gaussians by depth (front to back) sortedindices = argsort(depths) sortedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in sortedindices] return sortedgaussians def projectdepth(gaussian, camera): """ Project Gaussian center to camera space and return depth. Args: gaussian: Gaussian primitive. camera: Camera object. Returns: Depth value. """ # Transform Gaussian center to camera space centercam = camera.worldtocamera(gaussian.position) return centercam.z Parameters: --tlightvoxel: Flag to enable old 128^3 voxel cache fallback path. --tlight auto|voxel|raster: Viewer flag to control shadow source (auto reads training cfgargs). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deeply Buried Gaussians: If early termination causes wsum=0, explicitly map to full shadow to prevent inversion artifacts. Gradient Propagation: Treat sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches as constants to prevent incorrect gradient propagation. Covariance Expansion: Do not expand projection covariance by 0.3I or apply amplitude compensation during the light pass. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and the rasterization pass. The light-space rasterization adds an additional pass over the Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffer for recordfronttau aligned with the Gaussian buffer. Strengths: Provides accurate self-shadowing effects in volume rendering. Compatible with existing training pipelines. Limitations: Requires additional computation for the light pass. Fallback mode may be less efficient or accurate than rasterization. When to Use: When self-shadowing effects are desired in 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and self-shadowing is not necessary. Originated in the context of 4D Gaussian Splatting for volume cloud rendering. The method was developed to address the lack of self-shadowing in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It builds on the principles of volume rendering and light-space rasterization. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Light Space Rasterization for T_light
head: Front Tau Rasterization, Light Space Shadow Rasterization, T_light Rasterization (Light Space)
body: Light Space Rasterization computes T{light}, the front-facing occlusion transmittance for each Gaussian along a directional sun direction, enabling physically based self-shadowing in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It differs from voxel-based fallbacks by providing full continuous gradients and zero EWA expansion by default, avoiding the inversion artifacts associated with early-termination in deep occlusion. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, color). Sun direction vector. Camera parameters for the "sun camera" (see below). Outputs: T{light} value for each Gaussian (or pixel coverage thereof). Shadowed RGB image. Data Structures: Sun Camera: A perspective camera with a narrow Field of View (FOV) placed at a large distance to simulate parallel sun rays. The parallax error is kept below 2% to avoid changing the EWA Jacobian. Splat Buffer: Standard Gaussian splat attributes. Material Buffer: Parallel buffer storing normal, roughness, reflectance, and albedo for relighting [4464-ref-gaussian-deferred-surfel-rendering-with-split-sum-ibl.md]. Tlight Buffer: Stores the computed front tau (\tau) and transmittance. Steps: 1. Camera Setup: Construct the sun camera. The framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches are treated as constants during the pass to prevent incorrect gradient propagation. 2. Sorting: Sort Gaussians by depth relative to the sun camera. This ensures correct front-to-back accumulation for shadowing [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-tlight.md, 4489-light-space-rasterization-for-tlight.md]. 3. Rasterization Pass: Project Gaussians into light space. Crucial Difference: Do not expand the projection covariance by 0.3I and do not apply amplitude compensation. This preserves the main camera pass's sampling expansion [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-tlight.md]. Traverse Gaussians in depth order. For each Gaussian, accumulate front \tau (optical depth) weighted by \alpha \cdot T. This is an energy-weighted mean over the entire sun-facing footprint, not a center-point sample. Use the recordfronttau channel logic. 4. Shadow Application: Combine T{light} with the base color. Pitfall Handling: Deeply buried Gaussians (where early-termination results in wsum=0) are explicitly mapped to full shadow to prevent inversion artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetlight(gaussians, sundirection, suncamera): """ Compute Tlight using light space rasterization. """ # 1. Setup Sun Camera # suncamera is a perspective camera with narrow FOV, large distance # Parallax error < 2% # 2. Sort Gaussians by depth in sun space sortedgaussians = sortbydepth(gaussians, suncamera) # 3. Initialize Tlight buffer tlightbuffer = zeroslike(gaussians) # 4. Rasterization for gaussian in sortedgaussians: # Project to light space poslight = suncamera.project(gaussian.position) # Compute covariance in light space # NOTE: Do NOT expand covariance by 0.3I # NOTE: Do NOT apply amplitude compensation covlight = transformcovariance(gaussian.covariance, suncamera.rotation) # Compute coverage and alpha alpha = computegaussianalpha(poslight, covlight, gaussian.opacity) # Accumulate front tau # Weighted by alpha T (transmittance from previous steps) # This is an energy-weighted mean over the footprint taucontribution = alpha gaussian.density gaussian.scalefactor # Update transmittance # Tlight = exp(-tau) tlightbuffer[gaussian.id] = computetransmittance(taucontribution) # 5. Handle Deep Occlusion # Map deeply buried Gaussians (wsum ~ 0) to full shadow for gaussian in gaussians: if tlightbuffer[gaussian.id] < threshold: tlightbuffer[gaussian.id] = 0.0 return tlightbuffer Parameters: Sun Camera FOV: Narrow, to approximate parallel rays. Sun Camera Distance: Large, to minimize parallax. Covariance Expansion: None (0.0) for this pass. Amplitude Compensation: None. Edge Cases: Deep Occlusion: If a Gaussian is deeply buried, early termination might result in wsum=0. Explicitly map these to full shadow (T{light}=0) to avoid inversion artifacts. Gradient Propagation: Sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches are treated as constants to ensure stable gradients. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for sorting, O(N) for rasterization, where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing T{light} and sorted indices. Performance: Provides full continuous gradients and zero expansion by default, which is more accurate than voxel fallbacks. Strengths: Physically plausible self-shadowing, differentiable, no need for specific training parameters like voxelization. Limitations: Requires an additional rasterization pass. Sensitive to sun camera placement (parallax error). This method is part of the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud framework for rendering volumetric clouds with 3D Gaussian Splatting. It enables relighting and self-shadowing, which are not possible with pure emission SH reconstruction (VPRF). The method was introduced in the context of training on datasets like CloudDatasetUniform with held-out sun directions for generalization testing. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3DGS Radiance Caching
head: GSCache Radiance Caching, Radiance caching with 3DGS
body: 3DGS Radiance Caching is a real-time variance reduction technique for volume path tracing that uses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to store and query cached radiance values. It reduces noise by probabilistically accepting cached samples based on throughput luminance and a scaling parameter, optimizing exponentially subsampled Gaussians from noisy path samples to achieve real-time frame rates. Unlike neural radiance caching which requires large memory footprints, this method leverages the compact representation of 3DGS to store attenuated radiance at multiple path lengths, offering a significantly smaller memory footprint. The method integrates a caching mechanism into the path tracing loop, using 3DGS primitives to approximate the radiance field. It operates by querying a cache of radiance samples, accepting or rejecting them based on a probability derived from the current path's throughput, and updating state variables to maintain unbiased expectations (with specific bias trade-offs noted in sources). Inputs: Current path throughput vector L (radiance). Current path throughput scalar (weight) w (often implicit in the throughput vector scaling). Pixel coordinates (u, v). Cache state: cachelevels, betas, radiancesamples. Configuration parameter samplefactorc. Outputs: Updated throughput L and weight. Boolean flag cachehit indicating if a cached value was used. Updated cache state (betas, potentially radiancesamples). The implementation uses specific structures to manage the cache and query state. gscachesample: Records ground truth radiance samples. u: int, pixel x-coordinate. v: int, pixel y-coordinate. scatterindex: int, index into the Gaussian splat list or cache level. L: gscachevec3f, the radiance vector. gscachequery: Used to query the cache with current path state. u: int, pixel x-coordinate. v: int, pixel y-coordinate. scatterindex: int, index into the Gaussian splat list or cache level. rand01: float, a random number in [0, 1] for probabilistic acceptance. L: gscachevec3f, current incoming radiance/throughput. throughput: gscachevec3f, current path throughput vector. gscachequeryresult: Returned by the cache query. cachehit: bool, true if a cache hit occurred and was accepted. throughput: gscachevec3f, the throughput to use for the next path segment. L: gscachevec3f, the radiance value to use (either cached or original). gscachedevicecontext: Manages the cache state on the device. nlevels: int, number of cache levels (max 16). height: sizet, image height. width: sizet, image width. samplefactorc: float, scaling factor for acceptance probability. cachelevels[MAXNUMCACHELEVELS]: Array of pointers to gscachevec3f arrays, storing cached radiance values. radiancesamples[MAXNUMCACHELEVELS]: Array of pointers to gscachevec3f arrays, storing raw samples. betas: float array, per-pixel beta values for each cache level, used for importance weighting. Constants: MAXNUMCACHELEVELS: 16. The caching logic is applied during the path tracing loop, typically after computing the contribution of a scattering event or at the end of a path segment. 1. Compute Luminance: Calculate the luminance of the incoming throughput vector L using standard RGB luminance coefficients: \text{luminance} = 0.212671 \cdot L.x + 0.715160 \cdot L.y + 0.072169 \cdot L.z 2. Calculate Acceptance Probability: Compute the acceptance probability q by scaling the luminance with samplefactorc and clamping to [0, 1]: q = \text{clamp}(\text{sample\factor\c} \cdot \text{luminance}, 0.0, 1.0) 3. Calculate Rejection Probability: Compute p as: p = 1.0 - q 4. Conditional Caching Logic: If q < 0.9: Retrieve the cached radiance L{cached} from cachelevels[scatterindex] at index (v \cdot \text{width} + u). Retrieve the current beta value \beta from betas at the same index. Generate a random number r \in [0, 1] (denoted as rand01 in sources). If r < p: Accept the cache hit. Set result.cachehit = true. Set result.L = L{cached} / \beta. Keep result.throughput unchanged (or as passed). Else (r \ge p): Reject the cache hit. Update the beta value for the pixel: \beta{new} = \beta \cdot q. Scale the throughput: L{new} = L / q. Set result.cachehit = false. Set result.L = L{new}. Set result.throughput = L{new} (or appropriate throughput update). If q \ge 0.9: Skip caching logic. Set result.cachehit = false. Set result.L = L. Set result.throughput = L. 5. Cache Update (Implicit): The sources mention radiancesamples and cachelevels. While the query logic is detailed, the update logic for writing to cachelevels is implied to occur when samples are accepted or stored, likely involving the gscachesample structure. The exact write-back mechanism (e.g., averaging, exponential moving average) is not explicitly detailed in the provided snippets, but the use of betas suggests an importance-weighted accumulation. samplefactorc: A float parameter that scales the luminance to determine the acceptance probability q. Typical values are not explicitly given, but the threshold q < 0.9 implies it controls the aggressiveness of caching. MAXNUMCACHELEVELS: 16. nlevels: Number of active cache levels, default 3 in the config. Division by Zero: The code divides L{cached} by \beta. If \beta is zero, this results in infinity. The implementation relies on the update rule \beta \cdot q and the condition q < 0.9 to keep \beta non-zero if initialized correctly. Bias: The method introduces bias with no guaranteed error bounds. High Throughput Rejection: If q is close to 1.0 (high luminance), p is close to 0, making cache hits unlikely unless rand01 is extremely small. The threshold q < 0.9 prevents caching in these high-variance scenarios. Transfer Function Changes: The cache requires re-initialization when transfer functions change, as it stores attenuated radiance specific to the current transfer function. Zero-Opacity Regions: The caching mechanism may not reconstruct zero-opacity regions effectively if not handled by the underlying 3DGS representation. Performance: Achieves real-time frame rates on scientific datasets at 720p, with total times ranging from 38ms to 186ms. Memory Footprint: 28 MB for the cache, compared to 272 MB for neural radiance caching. Scalability: The method is designed for real-time rendering, leveraging the efficiency of 3DGS rasterization. It does not explicitly address scaling to very large scenes without additional techniques like distributed training (which is a separate extension). Strengths: Real-time performance, low memory footprint, variance reduction for path-traced volume rendering. Limitations: Introduces bias, requires re-initialization for transfer function changes, no guaranteed error bounds, potential issues with zero-opacity regions. 3DGS Radiance Caching, also known as GSCache, was introduced by David Bauer, Qi Wu, Hamid Gadirov, and Kwan-Liu Ma in the paper "GSCache: Real-Time Radiance Caching for Volume Path Tracing using 3D Gaussian Splatting," accepted at IEEE VIS 2025. The work builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting for volume rendering, adapting it to serve as a compact, differentiable radiance cache for path tracing. It addresses the high variance and computational cost of path-traced volume rendering by leveraging the spatial coherence and compact representation of 3DGS primitives.
