name: Radiative Gaussian Point Cloud Model
head: RIRF, Radiation Intensity Response Function, Radiative Gaussian, X-Gaussian point cloud model
body: The Radiative Gaussian Point Cloud Model is a primitive representation designed for X-ray imaging that replaces the view-dependent Spherical Harmonics (SH) of standard RGB 3DGS with a view-independent Radiation Intensity Response Function (RIRF). It exploits the isotropic nature of X-ray attenuation, where radiation intensity depends on radiodensity rather than view direction, to enable efficient novel view synthesis for transmission imaging. Unlike RGB 3DGS, which models anisotropic surface reflection, this model predicts scalar radiation intensity directly from learnable feature vectors, avoiding the computational complexity of SH functions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of Np Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}x, camera extrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{ext}, and intrinsic matrix \mathbf{M}{int}. Output: A rendered 2D radiation intensity image \mathbf{I}. Data Structures The model defines a set of Gaussian points \mathcal{G}x: \mathcal{G}x = \{Gi(\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{f}i) \mid i = 1, 2, \dots, Np\} \quad (4) Each primitive Gi contains: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^{Nf}: Learnable feature vector representing inherent radiative properties. Radiation Intensity Response Function (RIRF) The core distinction is the RIRF, which predicts the scalar radiation intensity \mathbf{i} of a Gaussian point. It excludes view direction dependence, matching the isotropic nature of X-ray imaging. \mathbf{i}(\mathbf{f}) = \text{RIRF}(\mathbf{f}) = \text{Sigmoid}(\boldsymbol{\lambda} \odot \mathbf{f}) \quad (3) Where: \mathbf{i} \in \mathbb{R}: The predicted radiation intensity. \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nf}: The learnable feature vector for the Gaussian point. \boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nf}: A set of constant weights controlling the importance of each component of \mathbf{f}. \odot: Element-wise multiplication. \text{Sigmoid}(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}. Rendering Pipeline (Differentiable Radiative Rasterization) The rendering process, termed Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR), follows these steps: 1. Projection: Transform 3D Gaussian centers \boldsymbol{\mu}i into camera space using \mathbf{M}{ext}. Project the 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i to 2D screen space \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i using the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projection and the rotation part W of the extrinsic matrix: \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i = J W \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i W^T J^T 2. Intensity Calculation: For each Gaussian i, compute the radiation intensity \mathbf{i}i using the RIRF: \mathbf{i}i = \text{Sigmoid}(\boldsymbol{\lambda} \odot \mathbf{f}i) 3. Rasterization: Render the Gaussians to the image plane. Since the attribute is a scalar intensity \mathbf{i}i (not a vector color), the accumulation is performed over opacity \alphai and intensity \mathbf{i}i. For a pixel p, the final intensity \mathbf{I}(p) is computed by alpha-blending the sorted Gaussians i=1 \dots N contributing to p: \mathbf{I}(p) = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} \mathbf{i}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Parameters Nf: Dimensionality of the feature vector \mathbf{f}. Not given in the sources. \boldsymbol{\lambda}: Constant weights controlling feature component importance. Initialized as fixed constants per the source description. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Isotropy Assumption: The model assumes X-ray attenuation is isotropic. Initialization: Standard Structure-from-Motion (SfM) initialization is unsuitable for X-ray images due to low contrast and overlapping layers. The model relies on custom initialization strategies (e.g., Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization) not detailed in this specific article but referenced in the parent context. What it is: The broader family of methods using Gaussian splatting for radiative (non-optical) imaging. Difference: Focuses on the general adaptation of 3DGS primitives for physical radiative properties (X-ray, thermal, etc.). When to choose: When adapting 3DGS for any non-visible spectrum where view-dependence differs from optical reflection. Link: Radiative Gaussian Splatting What it is: A specific implementation of the Radiative Gaussian Point Cloud Model for X-ray Novel View Synthesis (NVS). Difference: Specifically tailored for X-ray imaging, including custom initialization (ACUI) and Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR). When to choose: For X-ray CT or projection data reconstruction and NVS. Link: X-Gaussian What it is: An alternative radiative primitive representation. Difference: May use different primitive shapes or density representations compared to the Gaussian kernel. When to choose: When Gaussian kernels are insufficient for the specific volumetric structure. Link: Volumetric Primitives Radiance Field Time Complexity: Faster than original 3DGS because RIRF avoids the complex computation of Spherical Harmonics (SH) functions. The forward and backward passes are simplified to element-wise operations and Sigmoid activation. Memory Complexity: Stores a feature vector \mathbf{f}i of size Nf per Gaussian instead of SH coefficients. Memory usage depends on Nf. Strengths: Exploits isotropy of X-ray attenuation; faster training and rendering due to simplified attribute representation; suitable for grayscale, low-contrast X-ray images where SfM fails. Limitations: Assumes isotropic radiation; requires custom initialization for X-ray data; not directly applicable to view-dependent optical phenomena without modification. When to use: X-ray novel view synthesis, transmission imaging reconstruction. When not to use: Optical RGB imaging with strong view-dependent reflections or specularities. The Radiative Gaussian Point Cloud Model was proposed in the context of X-ray Novel View Synthesis (NVS) to address the limitations of standard 3DGS when applied to X-ray imaging. Standard 3DGS uses Spherical Harmonics (SH) to model view-dependent, anisotropic color, which is appropriate for natural light reflection but incorrect for X-ray attenuation, which is isotropic and depends on radiodensity. Additionally, standard SfM initialization is inaccurate for X-ray images due to low contrast and overlapping structures. The model was introduced in "Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Efficient X-Ray Novel View Synthesis". name: Volumetric Primitives Radiance Field
head: VPRF
body: Volumetric Primitives Radiance Field (VPRF) is a rendering integrator variant designed for 3D Gaussian Splatting-like assets, optimized specifically for radiance field optimization and rendering tasks. It shares the core volumetric primitive structure of the Volumetric Primitives Path Tracer (VPPT) but diverges by simplifying the light transport model to consider only primary rays from the camera. Unlike VPPT, which targets general volumetric scattering media, VPRF is tailored for reconstructing and rendering emissive radiance fields. VPRF renders scenes composed of 3D Gaussian kernels by accumulating emission along primary camera rays. It relies on the closed-form integration of spherical harmonics within the segments defined by the intersection of rays and volumetric primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M, where each primitive is defined by position \mathbf{p}i, rotation \mathbf{R}i, and scale \mathbf{S}i Radiative Gaussian Splatting. Each primitive carries view-independent scalar attributes or feature vectors representing emission Radiative Gaussian Splatting. Camera parameters defining primary rays. Output: Pixel colors (radiance) for the image plane. Data Structures: The primitive representation follows the standard 3DGS layout: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix. \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Scale matrix. Covariance: \mathbf{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^\top \mathbf{R}i^\top Radiative Gaussian Splatting. Attributes: View-independent emission coefficients (typically represented via Spherical Harmonics or simple scalars per band/channel) Radiative Gaussian Splatting. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Generate primary rays \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} from the camera center \mathbf{o} through each pixel direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Intersection: For each ray, determine intersections with the 3D Gaussian primitives. The closed-form nature of the Gaussian volume allows for exact calculation of entry and exit points (segments) without probabilistic sampling. 3. Segmentation: Split the ray into segments based on the intersection intervals with the primitives. The order of primitives along the ray is strictly enforced to avoid ordering artifacts. 4. Emission Accumulation: For each segment k within a primitive i, compute the accumulated emission. This is done by integrating the primitive's emission function (modeled via Spherical Harmonics) over the segment length. The integration leverages the analytical properties of the kernel to provide a closed-form solution, eliminating noise associated with stochastic methods. 5. Compositing: Composite the accumulated emissions from all segments along the ray to produce the final pixel color. Since VPRF focuses on primary rays and emission, absorption and scattering between primitives are typically simplified or omitted compared to full path tracing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import math def rendervprf(primitives, camera): """ Render a scene using the VPRF integrator. primitives: List of dicts with keys: p, R, S, emission camera: Object with attributes height, width and method getprimaryray(x, y) """ image = np.zeros((camera.height, camera.width, 3)) for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): rayorigin, raydir = camera.getprimaryray(x, y) totalradiance = np.zeros(3) # 1. Find intersections and sort by distance intersections = [] for prim in primitives: tstart, tend = intersectgaussian(rayorigin, raydir, prim) if tstart is not None: intersections.append((tstart, tend, prim)) # Sort intersections by tstart to ensure correct ordering intersections.sort(key=lambda item: item[0]) # 2. Accumulate emission along segments for tstart, tend, prim in intersections: segmentradiance = integrateemissionsegment(rayorigin, raydir, tstart, tend, prim) totalradiance += segmentradiance image[y, x] = totalradiance return image def intersectgaussian(rayorigin, raydir, prim): """Returns (tstart, tend) or (None, None) if no intersection.""" RT = prim['R'].T Sinv = np.linalg.inv(prim['S']) olocal = Sinv @ RT @ (rayorigin - prim['p']) dlocal = Sinv @ RT @ raydir # Ray-ellipsoid intersection quadratic: at^2 + bt + c = 0 a = np.dot(dlocal, dlocal) if a < 1e-8: return None, None b = 2.0 np.dot(olocal, dlocal) c = np.dot(olocal, olocal) - 1.0 disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return None, None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) return t1, t2 def integrateemissionsegment(rayorigin, raydir, tstart, tend, prim): """ Computes the radiance emitted by a Gaussian primitive along a ray segment. Uses closed-form integration of the 1D Gaussian density weighted by emission. """ RT = prim['R'].T Sinv = np.linalg.inv(prim['S']) olocal = Sinv @ RT @ (rayorigin - prim['p']) dlocal = Sinv @ RT @ raydir # Quadratic coefficients for |olocal + tdlocal|^2 A = np.dot(dlocal, dlocal) B = 2.0 np.dot(olocal, dlocal) C = np.dot(olocal, olocal) if A < 1e-8: return np.zeros(3) # Complete the square: A(t - t0)^2 + D t0 = -B / (2.0 A) D = C - (BB) / (4.0 A) # Closed-form integral of exp(-0.5(At^2 + Bt + C)) using erf integral = math.sqrt(math.pi / (2.0 A)) math.exp(-0.5 D) ( math.erf(math.sqrt(A / 2.0) (tend - t0)) - math.erf(math.sqrt(A / 2.0) (tstart - t0))) emission = prim.get('emission', np.ones(3)) return emission integral Parameters: Spherical Harmonics Degree: Determines the view-independent color fidelity. Ray Depth: Fixed at 1 (primary rays only). Edge Cases: Degenerate Gaussians: If scale matrices result in zero volume, intersection calculations may fail. Guard against zero-scale primitives by clamping scale diagonal elements to a minimum epsilon. Precision: Not given in the sources. A sibling integrator that handles general volumetric scattering media, including multiple scattering and absorption, unlike VPRF's primary-ray-only emission model. Choose VPPT for physically accurate volumetric light transport; choose VPRF for efficient radiance field optimization. The foundational method that replaces RGB opacity/color with view-independent scalar attributes or feature vectors, enabling the emission-based rendering used by VPRF Radiative Gaussian Splatting. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of primitives M and pixels, assuming efficient spatial acceleration structures for intersection testing. The closed-form integration avoids iterative sampling, reducing per-ray cost compared to stochastic volumetric rendering. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to M, storing Gaussian attributes and SH coefficients. Significantly more memory-efficient than voxel grids for complex volumes. Strengths: Zero noise due to analytical integration; fast rendering of emissive media; compatible with radiance field optimization pipelines; avoids ordering artifacts through strict ray ordering. Limitations: Limited to primary rays and emission; does not natively simulate complex scattering or global illumination within the integrator itself, though the closed-form capability can be incorporated into external path tracers. When to use: Radiance field optimization, rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting assets, and scenarios requiring noise-free emissive volume rendering. When not to use: Scenes requiring multiple scattering, complex absorption, or full path-traced global illumination without external integration. VPRF was introduced as part of the "Volumetric Primitives" framework by Facebook Research, designed to render 3D Gaussian Splatting-like assets efficiently. It builds upon the mathematical foundation of representing volumes with compact kernels (Gaussian or Epanechnikov), leveraging their analytical properties for integration. The method is particularly relevant for the reconstruction and rendering of radiance fields from image collections. facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, https://github.com/facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Don’t Splat your Gaussians: Volumetric Ray-Traced Primitives for Modeling and Rendering Scattering and Emissive Media (2025), https://qiita.com/matumu20/items/67b33681dc97ccbcc849, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Domain-Specific Adaptations
body: Domain-Specific Adaptations extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to non-photometric domains by replacing view-dependent RGB color with scalar attributes or specialized geometric intersections. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which optimizes for novel-view synthesis from calibrated RGB images, these methods optimize against 3D volume data, microscopy stacks, or ultrasound probe planes using domain-specific loss functions and rendering primitives. The primitive representation, covariance parameterization, and geometric projection pipeline are inherited from Application-Specific Extensions. The attribute representation and loss functions diverge significantly from the standard RGB opacity/color model. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting uses view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{d}). In radiative and domain-specific variants, this is replaced by view-independent scalar attributes or feature vectors. Adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for medical volume data (CT/MR) by optimizing against a target 3D volume and ROI mask using volumetric losses on rasterized voxel grids, rather than photometric losses on camera views. Decomposes n-dimensional fluorescence microscopy volumes into Gaussian primitives for efficient storage and web visualization, using blind-spot cross-validation to determine splat count and prevent overfitting to noise. Renders 3D ultrasound volumes by treating the probe plane as a 3D intersection target, using 3D Mahalanobis distance to evaluate opacity and avoiding the occlusion modeling required in visual spectrum rendering. Not given in the sources. Volumetric Gaussian Splatting (AVIS) Gaussian Splatting for Microscopy UltraGauss Rendering

name: Volumetric Gaussian Splatting (AVIS)
head: Avis Gaussian Splatting, Volume-supervised 3DGS [S1, unofficial]
body: Volumetric Gaussian Splatting (AVIS) adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for volume-supervised training on 3D medical-style data such as CT or MR volumes. It optimizes a 3D Gaussian representation against a target volume inside a mask region of interest (ROI), using volumetric and mask-aware supervision on rasterized voxel grids instead of photometric losses on rendered camera views. Unlike the original 3DGS which uses calibrated multi-view RGB images for novel-view synthesis, AVIS uses a 3D volume plus aligned ROI mask as input, samples Gaussian initialization from voxels inside the mask (rather than sparse SfM points), and optimizes toward mask density or CT intensity via losses on rasterized voxel grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target 3D volume V (format:.nii,.nii.gz,.npy,.mhd) and an aligned ROI mask M. Output: A set of M 3D Gaussians parameterized by mean \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, and scalar attributes (intensity ai, opacity \alphai). Data Structures: Volume Tensor: Order is [D, H, W] = [Z, Y, X]. Gaussian Coordinates: Normalized [x, y, z] positions in [0, 1]^3. Attributes: Intensity and opacity can be learned, sampled, or sampledmeancovered. Initialization: 1. Load volume V and mask M. 2. Normalize volume intensities to [0, 1] using (intensity - min) / (max - min). Pitfall: If (volume\max - volume\min) \le 10^{-8}, return mid-gray (0.5 if normalized, else volume\min) to avoid division by zero or meaningless gradients. 3. Sample initial Gaussian centers from voxels inside the mask M. The number of points is controlled by --initnpoints. Optimization Steps: 1. Rasterization: Project Gaussians onto a voxel grid. The internal working grid can be downscaled via --volumerenderdownscalefactor. 2. Sampling: Sample the Gaussian field at voxel centers using trilinear interpolation: python import torch def samplevolume(volume, grid, paddingmode='zeros'): # volume: tensor of shape [D, H, W] # grid: tensor of shape [N, 3] containing normalized [x, y, z] coordinates in [0, 1] # paddingmode: string, default 'zeros' volume5d = volume.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) gridexpanded = grid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2) samples = torch.nn.functional.gridsample( volume5d, gridexpanded, mode="bilinear", paddingmode=paddingmode, # Default 'zeros' aligncorners=True) intensities = samples.view(-1, 1) return intensities Footprint Pooling (Optional): If enablefootprintpooling=True and radiusscale > 0, for points where max(scale) >= max(voxelnorm), compute offsets in sigma units using a [-1, 0, 1]^3 meshgrid scaled by 0.5 \times radius\scale (default 2.0). Weights are Gaussian: \exp(-0.5 \times offset^2). Sample volume at pts + scale \times offsets, clamp to [0, 1], and average using weights. 3. Loss Computation: Compute loss between predicted voxel intensities and target volume/mask. Supervision Target (--supervisiontarget): 'mask' optimizes against mask density, 'ct' optimizes against CT intensity, or 'joint' optimizes against both. Loss Types: Mask loss uses mse, dice, tversky, or kl (--volumelosstype). CT loss uses mse, dice, tversky, or kl (--ctlosstype). Weights: --masklossweight and --ctlossweight balance the two losses in joint mode. 4. Densification/Pruning (Optional): If --enabledensification is set, update topology based on --densifyfromiter, --densificationinterval, --densifymaxnewpoints, and --pruneminopacity. (Algorithm details for densification/pruning are not given in the sources.) 5. Update: Update Gaussian parameters using gradients from the loss. Parameters: --supervisiontarget: 'mask', 'ct', or 'joint'. --volumepath: Path to target volume. --maskpath: Path to aligned ROI mask. --initnpoints: Initial Gaussian count. --iterations: Number of optimization steps. --radiusscale: Multiplier for standard deviations in footprint pooling (default 2.0). --paddingmode: Padding mode for interpolation (default 'zeros'). --normalize: Whether to normalize intensity values to [0, 1] (default True). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Nondeterminism: GPU kernels can introduce small nondeterministic differences depending on hardware and library versions, even with seeds set. Near-Constant Volume: If (volume\max - volume\min) \le 10^{-8}, return mid-gray to avoid division by zero. Hounsfield Units: Volumes are normalized to [0, 1] by the loader. Hounsfield Units are not preserved unless the loading path is changed. A volume reconstruction method trained primarily from X-ray projections, using volumetric data only as a regularization signal, optimized to match projection consistency rather than direct volumetric fidelity. It synthesizes X-ray projections from ground-truth volume using TIGRE toolbox, provides both synthetic projections and ground-truth volume to R2-Gaussian during reconstruction, and optimizes the network to match X-ray projections. It achieves higher 2D PSNR than volumetric methods because it is optimized for projection matching, but yields significantly lower 3D PSNR (e.g., 22.92 vs 51.54 on Aneurysm) due to lower 3D spatial fidelity. Training time is notably faster. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient medical data visualization; direct optimization in voxel space; mask-aware supervision. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When visualizing 3D medical data (CT/MR) and supervision from volumetric ground truth is available. When not to use: When novel-view synthesis from multi-view RGB images is required (use original 3DGS). AVIS is a research fork of 3D Gaussian Splatting. The original 3DGS paper, "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering," targets novel-view synthesis from calibrated multi-view images. AVIS retargets this to masked 3D reconstruction from medical volumes. The corresponding paper is expected to be published in CGI conference proceedings. ValentinKraft/vgs, https://github.com/ValentinKraft/vgs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splatting for Microscopy
head: Gaussian Splatting for Microscopy Volumes, nD Gaussian splatting
body: Gaussian Splatting for Microscopy decomposes multidimensional fluorescence microscopy volumes into a mixture of oriented, anisotropic Gaussian primitives, optimizing them against the data to place representational capacity only where signal exists. This approach solves the problem of data transfer and interactive viewing of large n-dimensional datasets by converting voxel grids into compact, GPU-rasterizable geometry, enabling scalable web visualization without intermediate voxel grids. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which uses view-dependent RGB color, this method uses view-independent scalar amplitudes, making it suitable for quantitative scientific data rather than artistic rendering. Input: A preprocessed n-dimensional microscopy volume V: \mathbb{R}^D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}{\ge 0}, typically a fused and deconvolved stack from multi-view light-sheet or confocal microscopy. Output: A set of K Gaussian splats, each defined by position, amplitude, and covariance, stored in a format suitable for streaming (e.g., Zarr archives). Each Gaussian splat k is parameterized by: \boldsymbol{\mu}k \in \mathbb{R}^D: Position (mean) of the Gaussian. ak \in \mathbb{R}{\ge 0}: Amplitude (scalar intensity). \mathbf{L}k \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}: Lower-triangular Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}k, such that \mathbf{\Sigma}k = \mathbf{L}k \mathbf{L}k^\top. The Cholesky parameterization stores D(D+1)/2 elements per splat (6 for 3D), guaranteeing positive-definite covariance by construction. The diagonal of \mathbf{L}k is parameterized as \sigma{\min} + \text{softplus}(\cdot), where \sigma{\min} = 1/\sqrt{12} voxels (the standard deviation of a uniform voxel), ensuring no splat is narrower than a voxel's own spread. Amplitudes are made non-negative by a softplus activation and are upper-bounded by a configurable maximum a{\max}. 1. Registration and Fusion: Multi-view images are registered and fused with intensity equalization. 2. Deconvolution: The fused volume is deconvolved (e.g., ten iterations against the point-spread function) to produce a single fused volume per timepoint. 3. Normalization: Source volumes (stored as 16-bit integers or float32) are normalized to [0, 1] using an affine map of the intensity range. 4. Clipping: Outlier voxels are clipped based on dataset-specific percentiles to prevent noise from dominating the fit: Plain min-max: Kidney, Cells3D, Blastocyst, Tribolium, Mouse heart. 1st–99.5th: OpenCell. 1st–99.999th: C. elegans. 0th–99.999th: Sparse Fly brain. 0th–99.9th: Zebrafish, Drosophila. Neuromast: Background floors (105.99 and 103.89 grey levels) are subtracted, then clipped to 0th–99.9th. 5. Background Floor Handling: For quality benchmarks, no floor suppression is applied. For compression/timing benchmarks, automatic floor suppression subtracts a constant background pedestal before fitting. Initial positions are seeded automatically from the volume using gradient-weighted samples of the volume’s edges, complemented by a coarse uniform grid. The model is optimized using the Adam optimizer. The reconstruction loss is L1 with regularization on splat amplitudes and extents. Fixed-Pool Optimization: Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which grows and prunes the Gaussian set, this method uses a fixed-pool optimizer. Periodically, the least informative splats are relocated to regions of high reconstruction residual. This acts as a fixed-pool analogue to pruning-and-seeding, keeping optimizer tensor shapes constant. Stopping Criterion (Blind-Spot Cross-Validation): The number of splats K is determined by blind-spot cross-validation to prevent overfitting noise: 1. Mask 5% of voxels. 2. Replace masked voxels with donut-median neighborhood values. 3. Score reconstruction on held-out voxels. 4. Stop fitting at the held-out PSNR peak. If the peak is interior or cull-limited, use the peak or the point where cull holds count constant. The volume prediction at voxel \mathbf{x} is: \hat{V}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} ak \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \| \mathbf{L}k^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}k) \|^2 \right) where \boldsymbol{\mu}k is the position, ak is the amplitude, and \mathbf{L}k is the Cholesky factor. Viewer Evaluation: The viewer uses a truncated Gaussian to ensure compact support: \hat{V}{\text{viewer}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} ak \max\left(0, \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \| \mathbf{L}k^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}k) \|^2 \right) - \frac{cT}{1 - cT} \right) where cT = \exp(-T/2) at T = 2.75 standard deviations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def preprocessvolume(volume, datasetname): """Preprocesses a microscopy volume for fitting.""" if datasetname in ['Kidney', 'Cells3D', 'Blastocyst', 'Tribolium', 'Mouse heart']: vmin, vmax = np.min(volume), np.max(volume) elif datasetname == 'OpenCell': vmin, vmax = np.percentile(volume, 1), np.percentile(volume, 99.5) elif datasetname == 'C. elegans': vmin, vmax = np.percentile(volume, 1), np.percentile(volume, 99.999) elif datasetname == 'Fly brain': vmin, vmax = np.percentile(volume, 0), np.percentile(volume, 99.999) elif datasetname in ['Zebrafish', 'Drosophila']: vmin, vmax = np.percentile(volume, 0), np.percentile(volume, 99.9) elif datasetname == 'Neuromast': floor1, floor2 = 105.99, 103.89 volume = volume - floor1 volume = np.clip(volume, 0, None) vmin, vmax = np.percentile(volume, 0), np.percentile(volume, 99.9) else: vmin, vmax = np.min(volume), np.max(volume) return (volume - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) def generateuniformgrid(shape, numpoints): """Generates a coarse uniform grid of positions.""" # Standard grid sampling steps = max(1, int(np.ceil(np.sqrt(numpoints)))) coords = np.meshgrid([np.linspace(0, s-1, steps) for s in shape], indexing='ij') return np.stack(coords, axis=-1).reshape(-1, len(shape)).astype(np.float32) def sampleweighted(shape, weights, numpoints): """Samples positions proportional to a weight map.""" # Standard weighted random sampling flatweights = weights.flatten() flatweights /= flatweights.sum() indices = np.random.choice(len(flatweights), size=numpoints, p=flatweights) positions = np.unravelindex(indices, shape) return np.stack(positions, axis=-1).astype(np.float32) def initializecholesky(numsplats, dim, sigmamin=1.0/np.sqrt(12.0)): """Initializes lower-triangular Cholesky factors with diagonal >= sigmamin.""" # Softplus ensures positivity; initialized to sigmamin for simplicity return np.full((numsplats, dim, dim), sigmamin) def donutmedian(volume, mask, radius=1): """Replaces masked voxels with the median of their neighborhood, excluding the center.""" # Standard morphological operation from scipy.ndimage import genericfilter def medianexcludecenter(window): vals = window.flatten() return np.median(vals[1:]) padded = np.pad(volume, radius, mode='edge') maskpadded = np.pad(mask, radius, mode='constant', constantvalues=False) result = volume.copy() # Apply filter only where mask is True result[mask] = np.median(volume[mask]) return result def reconstructvolume(volumeshape, mu, L, a, T=2.75): """Reconstructs volume from Gaussian splats using truncated Gaussian.""" output = np.zeros(volumeshape) voxelindices = np.indices(volumeshape).reshape(len(volumeshape), -1).T for x in voxelindices: val = 0.0 for k in range(len(mu)): diff = x - mu[k] y = np.linalg.solve(L[k], diff) distsq = np.dot(y, y) cT = np.exp(-T / 2.0) term = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) - cT / (1.0 - cT) val += a[k] max(0.0, term) output[tuple(x)] = val return output def updateadam(param, m, v, grad, t, lr=0.01, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): m[:] = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) grad v[:] = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) grad2 mhat = m / (1 - beta1t) vhat = v / (1 - beta2t) param -= lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + eps) def fitgaussians(volume, maxsplats, maxiterations=20000, patience=500): """Fits Gaussian splats to the volume using fixed-pool optimization.""" K = maxsplats dim = volume.ndim mu = np.vstack([ sampleweighted(volume.shape, np.abs(np.gradient(volume).sum(axis=0)), K // 2), generateuniformgrid(volume.shape, K // 2) ]) L = initializecholesky(K, dim) a = np.ones(K) mmu, vmu = np.zeroslike(mu), np.zeroslike(mu) mL, vL = np.zeroslike(L), np.zeroslike(L) ma, va = np.zeroslike(a), np.zeroslike(a) bestheldoutpsnr = -np.inf optimalK = K patiencecounter = 0 for t in range(1, maxiterations + 1): # 1. Forward pass: compute L1 loss + regularization on a and L # Reconstruction loss is L1 with regularization on amplitudes and extents reconstructed = reconstructvolume(volume.shape, mu, L, a) loss = np.mean(np.abs(volume - reconstructed)) reg = np.mean(a2) + np.mean(L2) loss += reg # 2. Backward pass: compute gradients and update Adam # Optimizer: Adam # Gradients computed via automatic differentiation; standard backprop through the truncated Gaussian sum gradmu, gradL, grada = computegradients(loss, volume, mu, L, a) updateadam(mu, mmu, vmu, gradmu, t) updateadam(L, mL, vL, gradL, t) updateadam(a, ma, va, grada, t) # 3. Fixed-pool relocation (periodically) # Periodically relocate least informative splats to high residual regions if t % 100 == 0: # Identify splats with lowest contribution or highest error, move to high residual pass # 4. Blind-spot cross-validation if t % 500 == 0: heldoutpsnr = evaluatecrossvalidation(volume, mu, L, a) if heldoutpsnr > bestheldoutpsnr: bestheldoutpsnr = heldoutpsnr optimalK = K patiencecounter = 0 else: patiencecounter += 1 if patiencecounter > patience: break return mu, L, a def evaluatecrossvalidation(volume, mu, L, a): """Masks 5% of voxels, replaces with donut-median, scores PSNR on held-out voxels.""" mask = np.random.rand(volume.shape) < 0.05 maskedvol = volume.copy() maskedvol[mask] = donutmedian(volume, mask) reconstructed = reconstructvolume(volume.shape, mu, L, a) mse = np.mean((volume[mask] - reconstructed[mask]) 2) return 10 np.log10(1.0 / mse) Overfitting: Adding more splats beyond the optimal budget causes the model to memorize noise rather than signal, indicated by a growing gap between training PSNR and held-out PSNR. Noise Assumption: Blind-spot cross-validation assumes noise is independent across voxels. On fused or deconvolved volumes, a held-out peak is not guaranteed. If a noise floor is estimable, it caps the budget from above to avoid reproducing noise. Resolution Limits: Structures thinner than the local Gaussian scale (e.g., individual microtubules) blur. Convergence: Convergence is rapid; at 2,000 iterations, training PSNR is within 0.5 dB of the 20,000-iteration value for most volume-capacity cells. Fitting Time: Median 2.4 minutes per volume at a 32K splat budget on an NVIDIA RTX 3070 (8 GiB). Scaling: Adding capacity (splats) outperforms adding iterations. 16K splats × 500 iterations beat 4K splats × 20,000 iterations by an average of +3.03 dB across 17 volumes at 10× fewer splat-iterations. Memory: Fits store volumes 6–340× smaller (median 99.3×) at 26–67 dB PSNR. Tribolium embryo nuclei: 51.4 dB PSNR at 32K splats, 54.9 dB at 512K, 56.0 dB at 2M splats. Kidney nuclei: 34.8 dB PSNR at 32K splats, 45.2 dB at 512K splats. Rendering: On an RTX 3070 at 720p HDR, Gaussian splats maintain 60 FPS (16.7 ms budget) through 10^6 elements. Strengths: Direct GPU rasterization without voxel grids; suitable for streaming where bandwidth and memory are constrained; fast fitting; high compression ratios. Limitations: Structures thinner than the local Gaussian scale blur; not suitable for precise quantification or measurement; fitting is asymmetric (expensive fitting, cheap viewing). Use for interactive web visualization and sharing of large n-dimensional microscopy datasets. Use when bandwidth and client-side memory are constrained. Do not use for precise quantitative analysis, segmentation, or tracking; use source voxels for those tasks. Gaussian Splatting for Microscopy is part of the Luxar framework, an open-source Python system designed for scalable interactive web visualization of multidimensional scientific data. It adapts nD Gaussian splatting for microscopy, validating the approach on 17 volumes from 12 datasets spanning spinning-disk, confocal, light-sheet, and structured-illumination modalities. The method uses blind-spot cross-validation to determine the optimal splat count, balancing PSNR and overfitting. Luxar: Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualisation of multidimensional scientific data, https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.22.753676, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: UltraGauss Rendering
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Ultrasound, Ultrasound Gaussian Splatting
body: UltraGauss is a rendering method for 3D ultrasound volumes that treats the ultrasound probe plane as a 3D intersection target rather than a 2D projection target. It evaluates Gaussian opacity using 3D Mahalanobis distance, thereby avoiding the occlusion modeling inherent in standard RGB Gaussian Splatting. Unlike its siblings which project 3D primitives to 2D image space, UltraGauss lifts 2D pixel coordinates to the probe's 3D coordinate frame to compute intersections. Inputs: Set of M 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Lower-triangular matrix Li \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} parameterizing the inverse covariance (see Covariance Parameterization). Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3 (view-independent). Probe transform matrix W \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (rotation part of extrinsic matrix mapping world to probe frame). Background color c{BG} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and background opacity coefficient \alpha{BG} > 0. Probability density percentage p (typically 0.95). Regularization constant \beta > 0. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{c}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^3 and opacity \hat{\alpha}(x) \in \mathbb{R} for each pixel x in the probe plane. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Stored in contiguous arrays for GPU access. Li is stored as 9 floats (lower triangular). Bounding Box: For each Gaussian, precomputed 3D bounding box [b^{\min}, b^{\max}] based on the ellipsoid encompassing p\% of probability density. Covariance Parameterization: To ensure positive-definiteness and efficient inversion, the inverse covariance \Sigma^{-1} is parameterized using a lower-triangular matrix L: \Sigma^{-1} = LL^T where L is defined as: L = \begin{bmatrix} L{11}^2 + \beta & 0 & 0 \\ L{12} & L{22}^2 + \beta & 0 \\ L{13} & L{12} & L{33}^2 + \beta \end{bmatrix} The diagonal elements are strictly positive due to \beta > 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Transform to Probe Frame: For each Gaussian i, transform mean and covariance to the probe's coordinate frame using W: \mui^{3D} = W^{-1} \mui \Sigmai^{3D} = W \Sigmai W^T The inverse covariance in the probe frame is computed as (\Sigmai^{3D})^{-1} = W^{-T} \Sigmai^{-1} W^{-1} = W^{-T} Li Li^T W^{-1}. 2. Compute Bounding Box: For each Gaussian, compute the 3D bounding box b^{\min/\max} that encloses the ellipsoid containing p\% of the probability mass: b^{\min/\max} = \mu^{3D} \pm \sqrt{\lambda v} where \lambda = \frac{\chi{3,1-p}^2}{\det(\Sigma^{3D})} and v represents the principal axes extents. The value \chi{3,1-p}^2 is 7.815 for p=95\%. 3. Phase 1: Load Balancing / Rejection: Iterate through all Gaussians. Check if the Gaussian's 3D bounding box intersects the probe plane (defined as z=0 in the probe frame). Reject Gaussian i if b^{\min}3 > 0 or b^{\max}3 < 0. Compact the list of accepted Gaussians into a contiguous buffer. 4. Phase 2: Rasterization: For each accepted Gaussian i: Compute the 2D bounding box in the probe plane (z=0) from the 3D bounding box. Iterate over all pixels x = (x1, x2) within this 2D bounding box. Lift pixel x to 3D in the probe frame: x{|0} = [x1, x2, 0]^T. Compute the squared Mahalanobis distance: d^2 = (x{|0} - \mui^{3D})^T (\Sigmai^{3D})^{-1} (x{|0} - \mui^{3D}). Compute opacity contribution: \hat{\alpha}i(x) = \alphai \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} d^2 \right). Atomically add \hat{\alpha}i(x) to the pixel's accumulated opacity \hat{\alpha}(x) and \hat{\alpha}i(x) ci to the color accumulator. 5. Composite: After all Gaussians are processed, compute final color and opacity for each pixel x: \hat{\alpha}(x) = \sumi^n \hat{\alpha}i(x) + \alpha{BG} \hat{c}(x) = \frac{1}{\hat{\alpha}(x)} \left( \sumi^n \hat{\alpha}i(x) ci + \alpha{BG} c{BG} \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def ultragaussrender(gaussians, W, cBG, alphaBG, p=0.95, beta=1e-4, imgh=100, imgw=100): """ gaussians: dict with keys 'mu' (M,3), 'L' (M,3,3), 'alpha' (M,), 'color' (M,3) W: (3,3) rotation matrix from world to probe frame """ M = gaussians['mu'].shape[0] # 1. Transform to Probe Frame Winv = torch.linalg.inv(W) muprobe = torch.matmul(Winv, gaussians['mu'].T).T # (M, 3) Sigmainvworld = torch.bmm(gaussians['L'], gaussians['L'].transpose(1, 2)) # (M, 3, 3) Sigmainvprobe = torch.matmul(torch.matmul(Winv.T, Sigmainvworld), Winv) # (M, 3, 3) Sigmaprobe = torch.linalg.inv(Sigmainvprobe) # (M, 3, 3) # 2. Bounding Box Rejection chi2 = 7.815 if p == 0.95 else torch.distributions.chi2.Chi2(3).icdf(p) zextent = torch.sqrt(Sigmaprobe[:, 2, 2] chi2) zmin = muprobe[:, 2] - zextent zmax = muprobe[:, 2] + zextent mask = (zmin <= 0) & (zmax >= 0) activeindices = torch.where(mask)[0] if len(activeindices) == 0: return cBG, alphaBG muactive = muprobe[activeindices] Sigmainvactive = Sigmainvprobe[activeindices] alphaactive = gaussians['alpha'][activeindices] coloractive = gaussians['color'][activeindices] # 3. Rasterization accalpha = torch.zeros(imgh, imgw) acccolor = torch.zeros(imgh, imgw, 3) for i in range(len(activeindices)): mu = muactive[i] Sigmainv = Sigmainvactive[i] alpha = alphaactive[i] color = coloractive[i] xextent = torch.sqrt(Sigmaprobe[i, 0, 0] chi2) yextent = torch.sqrt(Sigmaprobe[i, 1, 1] chi2) xmin = int(max(0, mu[0] - xextent)) xmax = int(min(imgw-1, mu[0] + xextent)) ymin = int(max(0, mu[1] - yextent)) ymax = int(min(imgh-1, mu[1] + yextent)) if xmin > xmax or ymin > ymax: continue ycoords, xcoords = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(ymin, ymax+1), torch.arange(xmin, xmax+1), indexing='ij') points2d = torch.stack([xcoords.float(), ycoords.float()], dim=-1) points3d = torch.cat([points2d, torch.zeroslike(points2d[...,:1])], dim=-1) diff = points3d - mu.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) left = torch.matmul(diff, Sigmainv) d2 = torch.sum(left diff, dim=-1) alphasplat = alpha torch.exp(-0.5 d2) accalpha[ymin:ymax+1, xmin:xmax+1] += alphasplat acccolor[ymin:ymax+1, xmin:xmax+1] += alphasplat.unsqueeze(-1) color.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # 4. Composite totalalpha = accalpha + alphaBG totalcolor = (acccolor + alphaBG cBG) / totalalpha.unsqueeze(-1) return totalcolor, totalalpha Parameters: \alpha{BG}: Background opacity coefficient. Value not given in the sources, but must be >0 to avoid division by zero. p: Probability density percentage for bounding box. Typical value: 95%. \beta: Regularization constant for covariance parameterization. Value not given in the sources, but must be >0. Initialization of \mui: Uniformly at random within the imaged volume boundaries. Initialization of L{ij}: Uniformly randomly initialized between 0.04 and 0.05, corresponding to a variance between 0.0017 and 0.0043. Learning rate for Gaussian parameters: 0.05. Learning rate for means \mui: Starting value of 0.00016 with exponential decay scheduler. Optimizer: Adam. Initialization of \alphai: 0.731. Initialization of ci: 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: Quaternion normalization for covariance parameterization causes numerical instabilities in this setting. The lower-triangular matrix parameterization with \beta regularization is used instead. Ill-conditioned Inversion: Inverting ill-conditioned \Sigma^{-1} explicitly for resampling is numerically unstable. The lower-triangular factorization L allows efficient inversion via forward substitution. Occlusion: Occlusions do not play as large a role as in the visual spectrum and are not modeled. Time Complexity: The method avoids nested iterations over all pixels and all Gaussians by using bounding box rejection and tile-based distribution. Memory Complexity: Supports up to 2 million Gaussians with respectable reconstruction times on a single NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU. Performance: Measured on NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU. Strengths: Efficient handling of 3D ultrasound volumes; avoids occlusion modeling; stable optimization via triangular covariance parameterization. Limitations: Requires custom CUDA kernels for rasterization and gradients; initialization is random rather than point-cloud derived. UltraGauss was introduced in the paper "UltraGauss: Ultrafast Gaussian Reconstruction of 3D Ultrasound Volumes". It adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for the specific domain of ultrasound imaging, where the probe plane intersects the volume rather than projecting it. The method was implemented in PyTorch with custom CUDA kernels. UltraGauss: Ultrafast Gaussian Reconstruction of 3D Ultrasound Volumes, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2505.05643, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Surface and Mesh Extraction
head: Gaussian Meshing, 3DGS Meshing
body: This family comprises methods to extract explicit triangular meshes from trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. Standard 3DGS represents scenes as implicit volumetric primitives, lacking a native surface representation. These methods solve the problem of obtaining watertight, textured geometry for downstream applications like simulation, AR/VR, or editing. They differ from sibling methods like Radiative and Tomographic Gaussians by focusing on geometric extraction rather than physical property rendering, and from Domain-Specific Adaptations by targeting general mesh generation rather than specific domain constraints like microscopy. All methods in this family operate on the output of a trained 3DGS model \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M. Each primitive Gi is defined by position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and color attributes Radiative Gaussian Splatting. The core challenge is converting these anisotropic, volumetric kernels into a discrete surface representation. This requires either evaluating the implicit density field defined by the Gaussians, leveraging geometric cues (depth/normal) rendered from the splats, or modifying the splat distribution to align with an existing mesh. The rendering pipeline's geometric projection remains consistent: 3D Gaussians are transformed into ray space, and the projected 2D covariance \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i is computed using the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projection and the rotation part W of the extrinsic matrix: \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i = J W \mathbf{\Sigma}i W^T J^T Radiative Gaussian Splatting A method to extract a 3-D triangulated mesh from a trained Gaussian model without retraining, by building a volumetric density field and extracting an isosurface [3692-gaussian-opacity-fields-gof-mesh-extraction.md]. It builds on Surface and Mesh Extraction by treating the Gaussian opacity field as a continuous volumetric density function, distinct from sibling methods that rely on distance fields or direct point-cloud reconstruction. Distance-based Gaussian Splatting is a method that integrates a pre-existing 3D mesh with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to improve rendering quality and geometric consistency in large-scale scenes. It solves the problem of redundant or distorted Gaussian splats in regions where the underlying mesh is inaccurate or overly dense by classifying splats as "tightly-bound" or "loosely-bound" based on their distance to the mesh surface. Unlike standard 3DGS which treats all primitives equally, this method masks occluded splats, prunes those hidden behind the mesh, and aligns tightly-bound splats to the mesh geometry, thereby reducing memory usage and preventing artifacts from mesh reconstruction errors [7411-distance-based-gaussian-splatting.md]. This method segments 3D Gaussian primitives by lifting 2D segmentation masks, generated from a reference view using foundation models like SAM, into 3D space via multi-view label voting [11513-2d-lift-3d-scene-segmentation.md]. It enables partial scene editing (PSE) by decomposing a scene into distinct Gaussian groups, allowing independent manipulation of color, opacity, and lighting [11513-2d-lift-3d-scene-segmentation.md]. Unlike methods that require learnable feature vectors or extensive training for segmentation [11513-2d-lift-3d-scene-segmentation.md], this approach is training-free and relies on geometric projection and voting, though it may require iterative refinement for complex scenes [11513-2d-lift-3d-scene-segmentation.md]. This method extracts a textured triangular mesh from an optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene by converting rendered 2D depth and normal maps into a 3D oriented point cloud, which is then processed by a Poisson surface reconstruction algorithm [12790-mesh-extraction-via-poisson-reconstruction.md][12790-mesh-extraction-via-poisson-reconstruction.md]. It differs from direct meshing approaches like Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF) [3692-gaussian-opacity-fields-gof-mesh-extraction.md] or distance-based methods [7411-distance-based-gaussian-splatting.md] by relying on post-processing rendered geometric cues rather than modifying the core Gaussian representation or optimizing a signed distance field [12790-mesh-extraction-via-poisson-reconstruction.md][12790-mesh-extraction-via-poisson-reconstruction.md]. The extraction of meshes from 3DGS is a necessary step for integrating neural radiance fields and Gaussian splats into traditional computer graphics pipelines. Early 3DGS implementations focused solely on novel view synthesis Radiative Gaussian Splatting. Subsequent research identified the lack of explicit geometry as a limitation for applications requiring collision detection or texture mapping. Methods like GOF [3692-gaussian-opacity-fields-gof-mesh-extraction.md] and Poisson-based extraction [12790-mesh-extraction-via-poisson-reconstruction.md] emerged to bridge this gap, while distance-based approaches [7411-distance-based-gaussian-splatting.md] addressed geometric consistency in large-scale scenes. Gaussian Opacity Fields: Implicit 3D Gaussian Splatting for High-Quality Surface Reconstruction, https://github.com/autonomousvision/gaussian-opacity-fields, 2024 Poisson Surface Reconstruction from 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://github.com/yingfengli/3dgs-mesh, 2024

name: Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF) Mesh Extraction
head: GOF-style 3-D mesh extraction, mesh extraction from standard 3-D Gaussian Splatting
body: A method to extract a 3-D triangulated mesh from a trained 3-D Gaussian Splatting model without retraining, by building a volumetric density field and extracting an isosurface. Inputs: A trained 3-D Gaussian Splatting model \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M where each Gaussian Gi has position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, and opacity \alphai. Outputs: A PLY mesh file containing vertices, faces, and per-vertex colors. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A 3D array of size R \times R \times R storing density values. 2. KD-Tree: Built on the positions \{\mathbf{p}i\} of all Gaussians for nearest-neighbor color lookup. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize a zero-filled 3D array D of size R^3 and determine the bounding box of the scene or the union of all Gaussian extents. 2. Splat each Gaussian with its full anisotropic covariance, truncated at 3\sigma, into the voxel grid. 3. Extract the isosurface from the density field using the marching cubes algorithm (specifically skimage.measure.marchingcubes). 4. Assign per-vertex colours from the DC spherical-harmonics component of the nearest Gaussian, found via KD-tree lookup. 5. Write the mesh to a PLY file named <modelpath>/meshiter{N}res{R}thr{T}.ply. Formulas: The volumetric density field is computed as f(\mathbf{x}) = \sumi \alphai \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{\mu}i)^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}i^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{\mu}i)\right), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D point, \mathbf{\mu}i is the Gaussian mean, \mathbf{\Sigma}i is the covariance matrix, and \alphai is the opacity. Parameters: resolution (R): Voxel grid resolution. Default: 256. densitythreshold (T): Marching cubes isosurface level. Default: 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Truncating at 3\sigma defines the Gaussian extent for splatting. If the density field is entirely below the threshold, no mesh is generated. Floating-point accumulation in the density field may cause overflow if many Gaussians overlap significantly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.spatial import KDTree from skimage import measure def extractmesh(gaussianmodel, resolution=256, densitythreshold=1.0): """ Extract mesh from Gaussian Opacity Fields. """ M = gaussianmodel.positions.shape[0] positions = gaussianmodel.positions # Covariances must be decomposed to 3x3 matrices if stored as quaternions/scales covariances = gaussianmodel.covariances # Shape (M, 3, 3) opacities = gaussianmodel.opacities # Extract DC spherical-harmonics coefficients (M, 3) if stored in full SH format shcoeffs = gaussianmodel.shcoeffs # Compute bounding box from 3σ extents of all Gaussians minbound = np.full(3, np.inf) maxbound = np.full(3, -np.inf) for i in range(M): eigvals = np.linalg.eigvalsh(covariances[i]) extents = 3.0 np.sqrt(eigvals) minbound = np.minimum(minbound, positions[i] - extents) maxbound = np.maximum(maxbound, positions[i] + extents) # Create voxel grid and centers densityfield = np.zeros((resolution, resolution, resolution), dtype=np.float32) voxelcenters = [np.linspace(minbound[d], maxbound[d], resolution) for d in range(3)] X, Y, Z = np.meshgrid(voxelcenters[0], voxelcenters[1], voxelcenters[2], indexing='ij') voxelcoords = np.stack([X, Y, Z], axis=-1).reshape(-1, 3) # Splat Gaussians to voxel grid for i in range(M): mu = positions[i] covinv = np.linalg.inv(covariances[i]) alpha = opacities[i] diff = voxelcoords - mu distsq = np.sum(diff @ covinv diff, axis=1) density = alpha np.exp(-0.5 distsq) densityfield += density.reshape(resolution, resolution, resolution) # Extract isosurface verts, faces,, = measure.marchingcubes(densityfield, level=densitythreshold) # Map voxel indices back to world coordinates voxeltoworld = (maxbound - minbound) / (resolution - 1) vertsworld = verts voxeltoworld + minbound # Build KD-tree for color lookup tree = KDTree(positions), indices = tree.query(vertsworld) colors = shcoeffs[indices] return vertsworld, faces, colors A representation where one flat Gaussian is allocated to each triangle of an extracted mesh, combining mesh geometry with Gaussian splatting. It differs from standard GOF extraction by adding a second training stage to refine the hybrid representation. Stage 1: Train vanilla 3DGS (40k steps: 30k vanilla + 10k SDF regularization). Apply opacity culling. Apply SDF-based regularization to flatten Gaussians. Apply masked opacity regularization. Extract level set from trained 3DGS. Apply Poisson reconstruction to obtain surface mesh. Apply mesh cleanup (duplicate removal). Stage 2: Allocate one flat Gaussian to each triangle of the extracted mesh. Train non-PBR parameters (mesh geometry/location/shape, opacity, radiance SH coefficients, scale). Parameters: Stage 1: 40k steps. Stage 2: 10k steps. Not given in the sources. Originated from the Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF) method by Yu et al., SIGGRAPH Asia 2024. It was added as an extension to the EOGS framework to provide mesh extraction from standard 3DGS without retraining. Add GOF-style 3-D mesh extraction to EOGS, https://github.com/Jay2002-whu/EOGS/pull/1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Phys3DGS: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2409.10335, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Distance-based Gaussian Splatting
head: Mesh-based Gaussian Splatting, Tightly/Loosely-bound Gaussian Splatting
body: Distance-based Gaussian Splatting is a method for integrating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with explicit mesh representations to improve rendering quality and memory efficiency in large-scale scenes. It solves the problem of redundant Gaussian splats occupying GPU memory and degrading rendering fidelity when initialized on high-resolution meshes by classifying splats based on their distance to the mesh surface. Unlike sibling methods that extract meshes from trained Gaussians, this approach builds a connection between a pre-existing mesh and Gaussian splats, masking occluded splats and distinguishing between tightly-bound splats (aligned with the surface) and loosely-bound splats (capturing artifacts or details). Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian splatting model \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M. A 3D mesh M consisting of triangles fj and vertices mj. Training views defined by camera poses Pk. Outputs: A refined set of Gaussian splats \mathcal{G}' classified as tightly-bound (Gt) or loosely-bound (Gl). Rendered images with improved geometric consistency and reduced memory usage. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Gi: Defined by center position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, 3D covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, opacity oi \in [0,1], and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i (represented by spherical harmonics). Covariance Parameterization: \mathbf{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^T \mathbf{R}i^T, where \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a scaling vector and \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is a rotation matrix encoded by a quaternion \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4. 2D Gaussian gi: Defined by 2D center \mathbf{p}'i and 2D covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}'i in ray space. Distance Threshold: d{th} = 0.01. Pruning Interval: Every 500 training iterations. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a 3D Gaussian splat Gi at the center \mathbf{m}j of each triangle fj of the mesh M. 2. Depth Rendering and Occlusion Masking: For each training viewpoint Pk, render a depth map Dk. Add a small offset to the depth: Dk \leftarrow Dk + 0.01. Assume the mesh surface is entirely opaque. Mask out Gaussian splats that are occluded by the mesh surface using the rendered depth map. Specifically, if a Gaussian splat's depth is greater than the mesh depth at that pixel, it is considered occluded and excluded from rendering. 3. Visibility Assessment and Pruning: Assess the visibility of all Gaussian splats across all training views. Identify splats located behind the mesh surface that are never observed by any training view. Remove all redundant Gaussian splats situated behind the mesh surface at specific training iterations (every 500 iterations). 4. Distance Calculation and Classification: Calculate the distance di between each Gaussian splat’s center \mathbf{p}i and the corresponding mesh face fj. Classify Gaussian splats into two categories based on the distance threshold d{th} = 0.01: Tightly-bound splats (Gt): If di < d{th}. Loosely-bound splats (Gl): If di > d{th}. 5. Alignment and Rendering: Flatten and align the tightly-bound splats Gt with the mesh surface. For rendering, transform camera space into ray space using the affine transformation \mathbf{J}i \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times3} defined by the camera position \mathbf{p}{ci}. Compute the 2D covariance in ray space: \mathbf{\Sigma}'i = \mathbf{J}i \mathbf{\Sigma}{ic} \mathbf{J}i^T. Render the image using alpha blending: c = \sum{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1-\alphaj) where \alphai = oi gi(\mathbf{x}), gi(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}'i)^T {\mathbf{\Sigma}'i}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}'i)}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distancebasedgaussiansplatting(mesh, gaussians, trainingviews, dth=0.01, pruneinterval=500): """ Implements Distance-based Gaussian Splatting. Args: mesh: 3D mesh object with triangles fj and vertices mj. gaussians: List of 3D Gaussian splats Gi. trainingviews: List of camera poses Pk. dth: Distance threshold for classification (default 0.01). pruneinterval: Iteration interval for pruning (default 500). Returns: refinedgaussians: List of refined Gaussian splats. """ # Step 1: Initialization # Initialize a 3D Gaussian splat at the center mj of each triangle fj of the mesh M. # Note: This assumes gaussians are initialized based on mesh triangles. # In practice, this step happens before training starts. for triangle in mesh.triangles: center = triangle.center # Create Gaussian Gi at center with initial covariance and opacity gaussians.append(creategaussian(center, mesh)) # Step 2: Depth Rendering and Occlusion Masking for view in trainingviews: # Render depth map Dk from viewpoint Pk depthmap = renderdepth(view, mesh) # Add offset to depth depthmap = depthmap + 0.01 # Mask out Gaussian splats occluded by the surface for gaussian in gaussians: if isoccluded(gaussian, depthmap, view): gaussian.occluded = True else: gaussian.occluded = False # Step 3: Visibility Assessment and Pruning currentiteration = 0 while currentiteration < maxiterations: # Assess visibility across all training views visiblesplats = [] for gaussian in gaussians: isvisible = False for view in trainingviews: if not gaussian.occluded and isobserved(gaussian, view): isvisible = True break if isvisible: visiblesplats.append(gaussian) else: # Identify splats behind mesh never observed pass # Prune redundant splats every 500 iterations if currentiteration % pruneinterval == 0: gaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g in visiblesplats] currentiteration += 1 # Step 4: Distance Calculation and Classification tightlybound = [] looselybound = [] for gaussian in gaussians: # Calculate distance di between Gaussian center pi and mesh face fj distance = calculatedistancetomesh(gaussian.center, mesh) if distance < dth: gaussian.type = "tightlybound" tightlybound.append(gaussian) else: gaussian.type = "looselybound" looselybound.append(gaussian) # Step 5: Alignment and Rendering # Flatten and align tightly-bound splats with mesh surface for gaussian in tightlybound: alignwithmeshsurface(gaussian, mesh) # Rendering is performed using the standard 3DGS pipeline with the refined splats return gaussians def isoccluded(gaussian, depthmap, view): """ Check if a Gaussian is occluded by the mesh surface. """ # Project Gaussian center to 2D p2d = projectto2d(gaussian.center, view) # Get depth of Gaussian depthgaussian = gaussian.center.z # In camera space # Get depth of mesh at p2d depthmesh = depthmap[p2d.y][p2d.x] # If Gaussian depth is greater than mesh depth, it is occluded return depthgaussian > depthmesh def calculatedistancetomesh(point, mesh): """ Calculate the minimum distance from a point to the mesh surface. """ mindist = infinity for triangle in mesh.triangles: dist = pointtotriangledistance(point, triangle) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist return mindist Parameters: d{th} = 0.01: Distance threshold to distinguish tightly-bound and loosely-bound splats. Pruning interval: 500 training iterations. Depth offset: 0.01 added to depth map. Loss weights: \lambda{img} = 0.001, \lambda{nc} = 0.1, \lambda{min} = 0.1, \lambda{max} = 10, \lambda{proj} = 50. Threshold \rho = 0.1. Training iterations: 30,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mesh Artifacts: Tightly binding all splats exclusively to the mesh surface can suffer rendering performance issues when addressing severe mesh artifacts. The loosely-bound splats help capture these inaccuracies. Redundant Splats: Without pruning, initializing splats on every triangle of a high-resolution mesh (e.g., 44 million triangles) leads to a rapid increase in GPU memory usage and undermines rendering quality. Occlusion Assumption: The method assumes the mesh surface is entirely opaque. Memory Efficiency: Significantly reduces GPU memory usage compared to initializing splats on high-resolution meshes by pruning occluded and redundant splats. Rendering Quality: Improves rendering quality by aligning tightly-bound splats with the mesh surface while using loosely-bound splats to capture details and artifacts. Scalability: Suitable for large-scale scenes where meshes have many triangles (e.g., 10^6 units). Limitations: Performance may suffer if the mesh has severe artifacts that are not well-captured by loosely-bound splats. Origin: Proposed in "MeshGS: Adaptive Mesh-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for High-Quality Rendering" by Jaehoon et al.. History: Builds on the original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) method [22] and addresses limitations in methods like LTM and SuGaR which either use minimal triangles (lacking detail) or require significant vertex counts. Usage: Used for high-quality rendering of large-scale scenes with explicit mesh representations. MeshGS: Adaptive Mesh-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for High-Quality Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08941v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 2D-Lift-3D Scene Segmentation
head: 2D-Lift-3D Segmentation for Partial Scene Editing, PSE with 2D-lift-3D segmentation
body: 2D-Lift-3D Scene Segmentation is a training-free method for segmenting 3D Gaussian primitives by lifting 2D segmentation masks from a reference view into 3D space. It solves the problem of partial scene editing (PSE) by decomposing a volumetric scene into distinct Gaussian groups, allowing independent color, opacity, and lighting adjustments per segment. Unlike methods that optimize learnable feature vectors for segmentation, this approach relies on multi-view label voting to assign labels to existing Gaussians without modifying the base scene representation. Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M. A set of training views \mathcal{V}{train} with known camera poses. A reference view V{ref} \in \mathcal{V}{train} (or an arbitrary view rendered from the model). User-specified point prompts on V{ref}. Outputs: A label map L = \{li\}{i=1}^M, where li \in \{0, 1, \dots, K\} assigns each Gaussian Gi to a semantic segment k. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive Gi: Defined by position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and color attributes [Parent]. In TexGS-VolVis, this may also include a textures attribute for stylized scenes. Label Counter: A data structure to store vote counts for each Gaussian across views. Algorithm Steps: 1. Render Reference View: Render an image I{ref} from the reference view V{ref} using the current Gaussian model. 2. Generate 2D Masks: Use the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with user-specified point prompts on I{ref} to generate a 2D segmentation mask M{ref}. 3. Generate Multi-View Masks: For each training view Vj \in \mathcal{V}{train}: a. Render the image Ij from Vj. b. Use SAM with corresponding point prompts (derived from the same semantic part as V{ref}) to generate a 2D mask Mj. 4. Label Propagation (2D): For each Gaussian Gi: a. Project Gi into the 2D image plane of view Vj to determine its screen-space footprint. b. Check if the center (or significant portion) of Gi falls within the foreground region of mask Mj. c. If yes, assign a temporary label l{i,j} corresponding to the segment identified in Mj. 5. Multi-View Label Voting: For each Gaussian Gi: a. Collect all assigned labels \{l{i,j}\} from all views Vj where Gi was visible and segmented. b. Determine the final label li by majority voting among the collected labels. c. If no views provide a valid label, Gi remains unsegmented (background). 6. Decomposition: Group Gaussians by their final label li to form distinct segments for editing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def segmentgaussians(gaussians, trainingviews, referenceview, pointpromptsref, sammodel): """ Segments 3D Gaussians using 2D-lift-3D segmentation with multi-view voting. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives Gi. trainingviews: List of camera poses for all training views. referenceview: Camera pose for the reference view. pointpromptsref: List of 2D points for SAM on the reference view. sammodel: Pre-trained Segment Anything Model. Returns: labels: Array of labels for each Gaussian. """ numgaussians = len(gaussians) # Initialize vote counts for each segment ID. # Assuming K segments based on SAM output or user prompts. # In practice, segment IDs are determined dynamically by SAM. votecounts = {} # Map: (gaussianindex, segmentid) -> count # Step 1 & 2: Reference View Processing refimage = renderscene(gaussians, referenceview) maskref = sammodel.generatemask(refimage, pointpromptsref) # Identify segment IDs present in the reference mask segmentidsref = getuniquesegmentids(maskref) # Initialize votes for these segments for segid in segmentidsref: for i in range(numgaussians): votecounts[(i, segid)] = 0 # Step 3, 4 & 5: Multi-View Processing for view in trainingviews: # Render image for current view viewimage = renderscene(gaussians, view) # Generate mask for current view # Note: Point prompts for other views must be provided or inferred. # The source implies user-specified prompts for "corresponding parts". # Here we assume promptsview are passed or derived. promptsview = getpromptsforview(view, pointpromptsref) maskview = sammodel.generatemask(viewimage, promptsview) viewsegmentids = getuniquesegmentids(maskview) for i in range(numgaussians): Gi = gaussians[i] # Project Gaussian to 2D center2d = projecttoscreen(Gi, view.projectionmatrix, view.extrinsicmatrix) # Check if Gaussian falls within any segment in the mask for segid in viewsegmentids: if ispointinmask(center2d, maskview, segid): # Increment vote for this segment key = (i, segid) if key not in votecounts: votecounts[key] = 0 votecounts[key] += 1 # Step 5: Determine Final Labels via Voting labels = np.zeros(numgaussians, dtype=int) for i in range(numgaussians): maxvotes = -1 bestsegid = -1 # Iterate over all possible segment IDs for this Gaussian for segid in segmentidsref: # Or union of all seen IDs key = (i, segid) votes = votecounts.get(key, 0) if votes > maxvotes: maxvotes = votes bestsegid = segid # If no votes, assign background label (e.g., 0) if maxvotes > 0: labels[i] = bestsegid else: labels[i] = 0 # Background/Unsegmented return labels Parameters: Point Prompts: User-defined 2D coordinates on the reference view. SAM Model: Segment Anything Model, used for mask generation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inefficiency: The method cannot immediately generate a complete 3D segmentation from a single 2D mask created with point prompts. It may require multiple rounds of segmentation for certain scenes, which is inefficient. Visibility: Gaussians not visible in any training view or not covered by SAM masks will not be segmented. Prompt Accuracy: Inaccurate point prompts lead to incorrect 2D masks, propagating errors to the 3D segmentation. SA3D is a method for 3D object segmentation within 3D Gaussian Splatting that leverages the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to generate initial 2D masks from text or point prompts in a single view. It distinguishes itself by alternating between mask inverse rendering and cross-view self-prompting to iteratively refine the 3D mask until complete object segmentation is achieved, avoiding the need for manual multi-view annotation. This variant refines coarse segmentation by learning affinity features from 2D masks generated by SAM, enabling fine-grained structure distinction. It lifts 2D masks to a 3D affinity field, which is then used to subdivide coarse-level color-based segmentation results. The affinity field network is trained using a loss function \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{L2} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{TV} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{DSSIM}, where \mathcal{L}{TV} is total variation loss and \mathcal{L}{DSSIM} is based on the structural similarity index measure (SSIM) between rendered and ground truth images. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians M, the number of training views N, and the cost of SAM inference. For each view, SAM inference and projection checks are performed. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Gaussian primitives and vote counts. No additional large learnable feature vectors are required per Gaussian in the basic voting approach, unlike methods that optimize learnable features. Strengths: Training-free; does not require modifying the base Gaussian representation (e.g., adding learnable features); supports real-time partial scene editing (PSE) after segmentation. Limitations: Inefficient for scenes requiring multiple segmentation rounds; relies on SAM's accuracy; requires point prompts for each segment. When to use: When rapid, training-free segmentation is needed for partial editing of a pre-trained 3DGS scene. When not to use: When high-precision fine-grained segmentation is required without manual prompting (consider affinity-based methods) or when automatic text-driven segmentation without iterative refinement is needed (consider SA3D). The method was introduced in the context of TexGS-VolVis, a framework for expressive scene editing in volume visualization using 2D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on prior work in 2D-lift-3D segmentation [5, 8, 25, 35] and adapts the training-free strategy inspired by SAGD [25] for volumetric data. The approach enables partial scene editing (PSE) and non-photorealistic scene editing (NPSE) by decomposing scenes into editable Gaussian groups. name: SA3D
head: Self-Prompting 3D Segmentation
body: SA3D is a method for 3D object segmentation within 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that leverages the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to generate initial 2D masks from text or point prompts in a single view. It distinguishes itself by alternating between mask inverse rendering and cross-view self-prompting to iteratively refine the 3D mask until complete object segmentation is achieved, avoiding the need for manual multi-view annotation. Inputs: A pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representation. A single reference view image. User prompts (text or points) for the target object. Camera parameters for the reference view and other available views. Outputs: A binary segmentation mask for each 3D Gaussian primitive, resulting in a complete 3D object mask. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation containing position \mathbf{x}, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}, and semantic label s. The label s is initialized to 0 (background) or 1 (foreground) based on the initial SAM mask projection. 2D Masks: Binary masks M{2D} generated by SAM and refined during the process. Steps: 1. Initial Mask Generation: Use SAM [119] on the single reference view with user prompts to generate an initial 2D segmentation mask M{init}. 2. Inverse Rendering: Project the 3D Gaussians to the reference view. Assign the initial 2D mask labels to the Gaussians that contribute to the masked region. Gaussians outside the mask are labeled as background. 3. Cross-View Self-Prompting: Render the current 3D segmentation mask to other available views. Use the rendered masks from other views as "self-prompts" (e.g., points or boxes) for SAM in those views. Generate refined 2D masks for these other views using SAM with the self-prompts. 4. Iterative Refinement: Aggregate the 2D masks from all views (reference and others) to update the 3D Gaussian labels. Re-optimize the 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity) and semantic labels to minimize the discrepancy between the rendered masks and the refined 2D masks. Repeat steps 3 and 4 until the 3D mask converges or a complete object segmentation is achieved. Parameters: Number of iteration steps: Not given in the sources. SAM prompt type: Points or text. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: If the object is heavily occluded in the reference view, the initial SAM mask may be incomplete. The cross-view self-prompting helps recover these regions, but convergence depends on the availability of unoccluded views. Precision: SAM's accuracy is critical for the initial mask. Errors in the initial mask propagate through the self-prompting loop. A method that combines interactive scene object manipulation with exposed region inpainting. It uses a dual-stage self-prompting mask propagation process to transfer given 2D prompt points to 3D mask segmentation, resulting in a user-friendly editing experience. It is chosen when interactive editing and inpainting are required alongside segmentation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Rapid and efficient generation of object labels from text or point prompts. Enables complete object segmentation without manual multi-view annotation. Limitations: Relies on the quality of SAM and the availability of multiple views for cross-view refinement. When to use: When a single-view prompt is available and complete 3D segmentation is needed. When not to use: When no reference view with clear object visibility is available. SA3D was introduced as a method building upon the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [119] to advance 3D segmentation. It is part of a series of works leveraging 3DGS for semantic tasks, following methods like Feature 3DGS [53], SAGA [54], SAGD [55], and Gaussian Grouping [56].
