name: Multi-View Semantic Segmentation Strategy
head: Multi-view segmentation for iVR-GS, SAM 2 based multi-view segmentation
body: This strategy enables open-vocabulary querying and interactive scene editing in Volume Visualization (VolVis) by segmenting multi-view images to train independent, editable 3D Gaussian Splatting (iVR-GS) models for each object. It differs from direct 3DGS segmentation methods by maintaining method-agnostic segmentation and scalability, avoiding modifications to the underlying Gaussian structure. It addresses the view inconsistencies inherent in framewise 2D segmentation by treating multi-view images as a video sequence for tracking. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a scene (typically generated by a Neural Volume Rendering/Synthesis (NVS) model from a continuous circular camera trajectory) and a segmentation method selection. Outputs: Segmented multi-view images/masks for each distinct object, used to train independent iVR-GS models. Data Structures: Multi-view Image Sequence: Treated as a video sequence where frames correspond to viewpoints sampled along a continuous circular camera trajectory. iVR-GS Models: Independent 3DGS models, one per segmented object, assembled to form the final scene. Steps: 1. Select Segmentation Method: Choose a method suitable for the specific dataset from the following categories: pre-segmented, Transfer Function (TF)-based, voxel-based, cross-frame tracking, or direct 3DGS segmentation. 2. Handle Pre-segmented Data: If the dataset (e.g., medical imaging benchmarks like FLARE) provides ground-truth semantic labels, use them directly. 3. Handle TF-based Data: If using TF-based segmentation, rely on voxel intensity and derived attributes. Note that this lacks semantic awareness and is generally not suitable for object-level segmentation. 4. Handle Voxel-based Data: If using voxel-based techniques (e.g., voxel2vec), extract features using voxel coordinates, scalar values, gradients, and neighborhood information. Note that this lacks semantic awareness and is not well-suited for NVS pipelines operating on multi-view images. 5. Perform Cross-Frame Tracking (Recommended for Consistency): Sample multi-view images along a continuous circular camera trajectory to create a video sequence. Use a video object segmentation and tracking model, specifically SAM 2, to segment and track objects across frames. This improves consistency compared to independent framewise segmentation. Pitfall: SAM 2 struggles with transparent and nested objects, which are common in VolVis. 6. Perform Framewise Segmentation (Alternative): Apply 2D foundation models (e.g., SAM) to each rendered viewpoint independently. Pitfall: This results in view inconsistencies due to occlusions, lighting changes, or segmentation artifacts. 7. Train iVR-GS Models: Use the segmented multi-view images as input to train independent iVR-GS models. Specifically, train iVR-GS models using multi-view renderings of objects segmented by methods like LangSplat or SAGD, rather than directly segmenting iVR-Gaussians. Assemble the final scene by combining these component models. Pitfall: This method-agnostic approach may result in some loss of visualization quality compared to direct segmentation. Parameters: Camera Trajectory: Continuous circular trajectory for sampling multi-view images. Segmentation Model: SAM 2 is specified for video object segmentation. Other models like LangSplat or SAGD are cited as sources for segmentation masks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Inconsistencies: Framewise segmentation using 2D foundation models on individual viewpoints leads to inconsistent masks between neighboring frames due to occlusions, lighting changes, or artifacts. Transparent/Nested Objects: SAM 2 struggles with these object types, which are common in VolVis. Semantic Limitations: TF-based and voxel-based techniques lack semantic awareness and fail to segment objects based on semantic meaning. Compatibility: Direct segmentation in 3DGS modifies the underlying Gaussian structure, reducing flexibility and compatibility with other methods. Flexibility: The strategy is method-agnostic, allowing users to select the segmentation technique best suited for their specific dataset (pre-segmented, TF, voxel, tracking, or direct). Consistency: Using SAM 2 for cross-frame tracking improves segmentation consistency across viewpoints compared to independent framewise segmentation. Scalability: By training independent iVR-GS models from segmented multi-view images rather than modifying the 3DGS structure directly, the approach maintains scalability and interoperability. Quality Trade-off: The method-agnostic approach (training iVR-GS from segmented renderings) may result in some loss of visualization quality compared to direct segmentation methods. Limitations: SAM 2 struggles with transparent and nested objects. TF-based and voxel-based methods lack semantic awareness and generalization to complex real-world scenes. This strategy is part of the NLI4VolVis pipeline, which enables natural language interaction for volume visualization via LLM multi-agents and editable 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the need for efficient semantic segmentation across diverse VolVis scenarios to support open-vocabulary querying and interactive scene editing. The approach was developed to overcome the limitations of one-size-fits-all segmentation in VolVis, where datasets vary widely (e.g., medical imaging vs. arbitrary scenes). name: Mesh Extraction via Poisson Reconstruction
head: Poisson Mesh Extraction, Poisson Surface Reconstruction
body: This method extracts a textured triangular mesh from an optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene by converting rendered 2D depth and normal maps into a 3D oriented point cloud, which is then reconstructed into a surface using Poisson surface reconstruction. It differs from implicit field-based siblings like Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF) Mesh Extraction by relying on explicit geometric back-projection rather than density thresholding, and from Distance-based Gaussian Splatting by not requiring distance-field regularization during training. Inputs: An optimized set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M, where each Gi has position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and color attributes. A set of training views with known camera poses and intrinsics. Outputs: A textured triangular mesh. Data Structures: 1. Rendered Depth Map: A 2D array D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} storing the median depth of splats projected to each pixel. 2. Rendered Normal Map: A 2D array N \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} storing the surface normal in camera space for each pixel. 3. Oriented Point Cloud: A list of points P = \{(\mathbf{x}j, \mathbf{n}j, \mathbf{c}j)\}{j=1}^K, where \mathbf{x}j is the 3D position, \mathbf{n}j is the normal, and \mathbf{c}j is the color. Steps: 1. Render Depth: For each training view, project all 3D Gaussians to 2D. The projected 2D covariance is computed as \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i = J W \mathbf{\Sigma}i W^T J^T, where J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projection and W is the rotation part of the extrinsic matrix. Render the depth map D by computing the median depth value of all splats contributing to each pixel. 2. Derive Normals: Convert the rendered depth map D back into 3D space to derive the corresponding normal map N. This is typically done by computing the spatial gradient of the depth map and transforming it to world or camera space. 3. Back-Project to Point Cloud: For each pixel (u, v) in the training views: Retrieve the depth d = D[u, v] and normal \mathbf{n}{cam} = N[u, v]. Unproject the pixel coordinates and depth to obtain the 3D position \mathbf{x} in world space. Transform the normal \mathbf{n}{cam} to world space. Retrieve the color \mathbf{c} from the RGB image at (u, v). Add (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{c}) to the point cloud P. 4. Poisson Reconstruction: Input the oriented colored point cloud P into the Poisson surface reconstruction algorithm. The algorithm solves for an implicit function whose gradient field best matches the normals in P, extracting the mesh as a level set. Parameters: Depth Level: The depth of the octree used in Poisson reconstruction. Typical value: 9. Point Count: The number of points in the input cloud. Typical value: 2 million. Edge Cases: Missing Depth/Normal: Pixels with no splats or invalid depth must be handled (e.g., ignored or filled) before back-projection to avoid artifacts in the point cloud. Normal Consistency: The normals derived from depth gradients must be oriented consistently with the camera view direction to ensure correct surface orientation in the Poisson solver. A framework introduced by Mechrez et al. that effectively preserves structural fidelity while achieving stylization. It modifies the standard Poisson equation to better handle stylization tasks, though its specific application to 3DGS meshing is noted in the context of structural preservation. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rendering of depth/normal maps for all training views and the octree construction in Poisson reconstruction. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of training views and the resolution of the depth/normal maps, plus the memory for the 2 million point cloud and octree. Not given in the sources. Performance: Produces high-quality textured meshes when the Gaussian scene is well-regularized (e.g., using depth and normal priors). Strengths: Simple pipeline; leverages existing Poisson solvers; produces watertight meshes. Limitations: Relies on the quality of rendered depth/normal maps; sensitive to noise in depth gradients; requires sufficient training view coverage. When to use: When a textured mesh is required from a 3DGS model and training data includes depth/normal priors or reliable depth estimation is possible. When not to use: When real-time mesh extraction is needed or when training views are sparse/occluded. Originated from the application of Poisson surface reconstruction [18] to 3DGS scenes, as described in DN-Splatter and AtomGS. The method was adopted to leverage the geometric regularization provided by depth and normal priors during 3DGS optimization, ensuring well-distributed Gaussian positions aligned with the scene surface. name: Rendering Pipelines and Extensions
head: Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipelines, Differentiable Gaussian Rasterization
body: This family defines the computational mechanisms that convert a set of 3D Gaussian primitives (or their variants) into 2D images by projecting them onto the camera plane and compositing them. It solves the problem of efficiently rasterizing soft, view-dependent primitives while supporting inverse rendering tasks such as lighting estimation and physical parameter optimization. What sets these methods apart from standard rasterization is the use of alpha blending or weighted-sum compositing over sorted or spatially hashed primitives, often augmented with volume-based occlusion or explicit geometric intersection for sharp features. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of projecting 3D primitives into 2D screen space and accumulating color based on depth order or spatial locality. 1. Projection: Primitives are transformed from world space to camera space. The 3D covariance matrix \Sigma is transformed using the view matrix W and the Jacobian J of the perspective projection approximation: \Sigmac = J W \Sigma W^T J^T. The 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} is extracted as the upper-left 2\times2 block. 2. Rasterization: Primitives are assigned to screen tiles. Visibility is determined by bounding boxes or projected extents. 3. Compositing: Color is accumulated using front-to-back alpha blending or order-independent techniques. The final intensity for a pixel is If = \sum{i=1}^N ci \tilde{\sigma}i \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \tilde{\sigma}j \tilde{\mathcal{G}}j(\mathbf{p})), where ci is color, \tilde{\sigma}i is opacity or density, and \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) is the 2D Gaussian value at pixel \mathbf{p}. 4. Sorting: Most methods require sorting primitives by depth within tiles to ensure correct front-to-back compositing, although some variants use spatial hashing or cell-level sorting to approximate this or enable order-independent transparency. The standard differentiable rendering technique that synthesizes images by projecting 3D Gaussians and alpha-compositing them. It replaces triangle primitives with Gaussian splats to enable efficient tile-based rasterization and differentiable optimization. Choose this for high-fidelity novel view synthesis where view-dependent color (via spherical harmonics) is required. Defines the general differentiable rendering pipeline for converting 3D Gaussian primitives into 2D images. It serves as the foundational architecture for most 3DGS implementations, handling projection, rasterization, and compositing. Choose this as the base implementation for standard 3DGS rendering. Adapts 3DGS for volume data visualization by removing per-Gaussian color and opacity attributes, training only scalar values. This allows the same underlying scalar field to be visualized with arbitrary transfer functions without retraining. Choose this for scientific visualization of volumetric data (e.g., medical scans, fluids). Augments standard 3DGS by replacing baked view-dependent color with physically based rendering (PBR) parameters (albedo, roughness, normal). This enables dynamic relighting and material decomposition. Choose this when dynamic lighting or material analysis is required. A framework that decouples method-specific logic from the shared rendering pipeline, allowing new methods to be implemented in a few hundred lines of code. It separates core mechanics (parallelization, tiling) from primitive evaluation, enabling portable execution across GPUs, TPUs, and CPUs via the XLA compiler. Choose this for cross-platform compatibility or rapid prototyping of new primitive types. The rendering pipelines for 3D Gaussian Splatting originated from the need to render millions of Gaussian primitives in real-time, a task for which traditional triangle-based rasterizers are inefficient due to the soft, overlapping nature of the primitives. The core algorithm was introduced in the seminal 3D Gaussian Splatting paper [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md], which established the projection and alpha-compositing pipeline. Subsequent extensions have adapted this pipeline for specific domains: volume rendering [6093-volume-encoding-gaussians.md], physical relighting [6227-brdf-and-relighting-extensions.md], and cross-platform deployment [17626-xpr-rendering-pipeline.md]. The pipeline's efficiency relies on the affine approximation of the perspective projection and tile-based sorting, which allows for parallel execution on GPUs. name: Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Rendering, Volume Splatting
body: Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering is a differentiable rendering technique that synthesizes images by projecting 3D Gaussian distributions onto the image plane and alpha-compositing them along viewing rays. It solves the problem of high-fidelity novel view synthesis by replacing traditional triangle primitives with Gaussian splats (probability distributions), allowing for efficient tile-based rasterization and differentiable optimization of scene parameters. Unlike NeRFs which rely on dense volumetric sampling, or traditional rasterizers using triangles, 3DGS projects 3D probability distributions into 2D ellipses, enabling smooth rendering with explicit geometric primitives. The method reconstructs a 3D scene from posed images by optimizing a set of 3D Gaussians. The rendering pipeline consists of loading the scene data, projecting the Gaussians to screen space, sorting them by depth, and performing front-to-back alpha compositing. Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians defined by their parameters, and camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Output: A 2D image (color and optionally depth/opacity) for the given camera pose. The scene is stored as an array of GaussianSplat objects. Each splat contains the following fields: centroid: vec3 (world-space position). opacity: float (scalar transparency). sphericalHarmonics: array<float, 48> (16 coefficients \times 3 RGB channels). scale: array<float, 3> (log-space floats representing the diagonal of the scaling matrix S). rotation: array<float, 4> (quaternion representing the rotation matrix R). SHCOUNT: 16 (number of spherical harmonic coefficients per channel). SHCHANNELCOUNT: 3 (RGB). SHFLOATCOUNT: 48 (total coefficients per splat). Number of Gaussians: Approximately 200,000–500,000 for complex scenes. 1. 3D Gaussian PDF: p(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^d |\Sigma|}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right) where \boldsymbol{\mu} is the centroid and \Sigma is the covariance matrix. 2. Covariance Factorization: To ensure \Sigma remains positive semi-definite (PSD) during optimization, it is parameterized as: \Sigma = R S (R S)^T where R is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion, and S is a diagonal scaling matrix with entries si = \exp(\text{scale}i). 3. Color Computation (Spherical Harmonics): The color \mathbf{c} for a viewing direction \mathbf{d} is computed by evaluating the spherical harmonics basis functions Yi(\mathbf{d}): \mathbf{rgb} = \text{clamp}\left(\mathbf{0.5} + \sum{i=0}^{SH\COUNT-1} \mathbf{shCoeff}i \cdot Yi(\mathbf{d}), 0.0, 1.0\right) A bias of 0.5 is added to center the output around mid-grey before clamping. 4. Rendering Equation (Alpha Compositing): For a pixel p, let the intersecting Gaussians be sorted by depth i=1 \dots N. The final intensity If is: If \approx \sum{i=1}^N ci \tilde{\sigma}i \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \left(1 - \tilde{\sigma}j \tilde{\mathcal{G}}j(\mathbf{p})\right) where ci is the color, \tilde{\sigma}i is the opacity, and \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) is the 2D Gaussian value at pixel p. The product term represents the transmittance from previous Gaussians. 1. Load Scene: Parse the.ply file into an array of GaussianSplat structures. 2. Transform to Camera Space: Transform centroid from world space to camera space using the View matrix. Transform the covariance matrix \Sigma to camera space: \Sigmac = J W \Sigma W^T J^T, where W is the view matrix and J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the perspective projection. 3. Project to 2D: Compute the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} from \Sigmac by taking the upper-left 2\times2 block (affine approximation). Compute the 2D Gaussian value \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) at each pixel covered by the splat's bounding box. 4. Sort: Sort the Gaussians intersecting each pixel (or tile) by their depth (z-coordinate in camera space). 5. Composite: Iterate through the sorted Gaussians for each pixel and accumulate color using the alpha compositing formula. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendergaussiansplats(splats, camera): """ Renders a scene of Gaussian splats for a given camera. splats: list of dicts with keys: centroid, opacity, shcoeffs, scale, rotation camera: dict with keys: viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, width, height, position """ H, W = camera['height'], camera['width'] image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H W)] # 1. Transform Gaussians to camera space camerasplats = [] for s in splats: # Transform centroid centroidcam = applyviewmatrix(s['centroid'], camera['viewmatrix']) # Transform covariance: Sigma = R diag(exp(scale)) diag(exp(scale)) R^T S = diag(s['scale']) R = quaterniontomatrix(s['rotation']) Sigmaworld = R @ S @ S @ R.T # Jacobian of perspective projection approximation at centroid J = perspectivejacobian(centroidcam) Wmat = camera['viewmatrix'] # Sigma in camera space Sigmacam = (J @ Wmat) @ Sigmaworld @ (Wmat.T @ J.T) # Extract 2D covariance (upper left 2x2) Sigma2d = [[Sigmacam[0][0], Sigmacam[0][1]], [Sigmacam[1][0], Sigmacam[1][1]]] camerasplats.append({ 'centroid': centroidcam[:3], 'opacity': s['opacity'], 'shcoeffs': s['shcoeffs'], 'sigma2d': Sigma2d, 'viewdir': normalize(vec3sub(camera['position'], s['centroid'])) }) # 2. Rasterize to pixels for y in range(H): for x in range(W): raydir = unprojectpixel(x, y, camera) candidates = findsplatscoveringpixel(camerasplats, x, y) candidates.sort(key=lambda s: s['centroid'][2]) acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 p = [float(x), float(y)] for s in candidates: # Evaluate 2D Gaussian at pixel diff = vec2sub(p, s['centroid'][:2]) invsigma = inverse2x2(s['sigma2d']) distsq = dot(diff, matvec2x2mul(invsigma, diff)) gval = exp(-0.5 distsq) # Evaluate Color using SH color = evaluatesh(s['shcoeffs'], raydir) # Contribution sigma = s['opacity'] gval weight = sigma (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = [acccolor[k] + color[k] weight for k in range(3)] accalpha += weight if accalpha > 0.99: break image[y W + x] = acccolor return image def evaluatesh(coeffs, direction): """Evaluates spherical harmonics for a given direction.""" rgb = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] for i in range(16): basisval = sphericalharmonicbasis(i, direction) rgb[0] += coeffs[i] basisval rgb[1] += coeffs[16 + i] basisval rgb[2] += coeffs[32 + i] basisval return [max(0.0, min(1.0, c)) for c in rgb] def applyviewmatrix(centroid, viewmat): return [sum(centroid[j]viewmat[j][i] + viewmat[3][i] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] def diag(vals): return [[vals[i] if i==j else 0.0 for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def quaterniontomatrix(q): x, y, z, w = q return [ [1-2(yy+zz), 2(xy-wz), 2(xz+wy)], [2(xy+wz), 1-2(xx+zz), 2(yz-wx)], [2(xz-wy), 2(yz+wx), 1-2(xx+yy)] ] def perspectivejacobian(centroidcam): z = centroidcam[2] return [[1.0/z, 0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0/z, 0.0]] def unprojectpixel(x, y, camera): # Simplified ray direction calculation for orthographic/perspective approximation return normalize(vec3(x - camera['width']/2, y - camera['height']/2, -1.0)) def findsplatscoveringpixel(splats, x, y): # Returns splats whose 2D bounding box covers pixel (x,y) return [s for s in splats if isinsideboundingbox(s, x, y)] def isinsideboundingbox(splat, x, y): # Approximate bounding box check using 2D covariance eigenvalues # In practice, this checks if the pixel falls within the projected ellipse return True # Placeholder for bounding volume hierarchy or tile-based culling def vec3sub(a, b): return [a[i]-b[i] for i in range(3)] def normalize(v): l = (sum(xx for x in v))0.5 return [x/l for x in v] def dot(a, b): return sum(a[i]b[i] for i in range(len(a))) def matvec2x2mul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(2)) for i in range(2)] def inverse2x2(M): det = M[0][0]M[1][1] - M[0][1]M[1][0] return [[M[1][1]/det, -M[0][1]/det], [-M[1][0]/det, M[0][0]/det]] def sphericalharmonicbasis(i, direction): # Standard SH basis evaluation for degree 0-3 # Returns a float based on direction angles (theta, phi) return 1.0 # Simplified for pseudocode completeness Aliasing: High-frequency content can cause aliasing artifacts. 3DGS uses a dilation-based filter to mitigate this, but it may fail with varying focal lengths or camera distances. Covariance Validity: Directly updating the entries of the covariance matrix \Sigma during training does not guarantee it remains positive semi-definite. Using the scale and rotation parameterization ensures \Sigma is always valid. View-Dependent Color: If spherical harmonics are not used (e.g., in some volume rendering adaptations), the scene appears dimmer and less vibrant because it lacks viewpoint-dependent color shifts. Enables rendering of surface normals from 3D Gaussian splats by treating normals as an auxiliary attribute, bypassing the lack of native geometric surface information in volumetric Gaussian ellipsoids. Time Complexity: Rendering scales with the number of pixels and the average number of splats per pixel. Tile-based rasterization reduces the constant factor significantly. Memory Complexity: Memory scales linearly with the number of Gaussians, requiring 200,000–500,000 primitives for complex scenes, resulting in significant memory and storage demands compared to NeRFs. Performance: Uses a tile-based rasterization strategy for parallelization to accelerate volume rendering. Strengths: High visual fidelity, explicit scene representation, differentiable optimization. Limitations: High memory usage, limited ability to handle highly reflective surfaces (due to emission-absorption model baking lighting into SH), and potential aliasing artifacts. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced as a technique to reconstruct 3D scenes from posed images using Gaussian splats instead of triangles. It builds on the principles of volume rendering but adapts them for differentiable optimization of explicit primitives. The method has since been extended for various applications including surface reconstruction and avatar creation. name: Surface Normal Rendering via External Channel
head: External Channel Normal Rendering, PyTorch3D Normal Rendering for Gaussians
body: This method renders surface normals for 3D Gaussian Splatting by treating normals as an extra attribute in an external channel, since Gaussian ellipsoids do not natively contain surface normal information. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Learnable Normals Parameterization by explicitly modifying the Gaussian's internal attribute representation rather than relying on external gradient supervision, and from Normal Field Supervision via Rendering and Depth Derivatives by focusing on the rendering pipeline mechanics rather than the supervision loss formulation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids \{Gi\}, where each Gaussian i is defined by a mean position \mui, a covariance matrix \Sigmai (or rotation Ri and scale Si), and a base color. For normal rendering, an additional attribute ni (the surface normal vector) is associated with each Gaussian. Output: A rendered image containing surface normal vectors (typically encoded as RGB values) and optionally a depth map. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. ni \in \mathbb{R}^3: Surface normal vector (unit length). ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Base color (RGB). \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix defining the ellipsoid shape and orientation. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. Steps: 1. Normal Computation (Pre-processing): If the Gaussians are derived from a mesh (e.g., Stanford 3D Scanning Repository models like Bunny, Dragon, Armadillo), compute the surface normals for the source mesh vertices using a library such as PyTorch3D. These normals are then assigned to the corresponding Gaussians. 2. Attribute Assignment: Assign the computed normal ni to each Gaussian i. This normal is treated as an RGB value for the purpose of rendering. 3. Rendering: Render the Gaussian ellipsoids using standard alpha-blending splatting. During the splatting process, interpolate the normal attribute ni into the image plane, similar to how color ci is interpolated. The result is an image-like map of surface normals. 4. Lighting Integration (Optional): To integrate lighting, first render the surface normals into an image-like map. Then, use a diffuse lighting function (e.g., PyTorch3D.renderer.lighting) to compute the brightness under a point light source based on the rendered normals and the light direction. Formulas: The rendering of the normal field follows the standard alpha-compositing equation, where the normal N at a pixel is the weighted average of the normals of the splatted Gaussians: N = \frac{\sum{i \in \text{sorted}} ni \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj)}{\sum{i \in \text{sorted}} \alphai \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj)} where the Gaussians are sorted back-to-front along the view ray. Parameters: Light Position: Defined by the user for lighting integration. Number of Gaussians: Affects rendering quality. Increasing the number of Gaussians significantly improves rendering quality, though boundaries may be slightly fuzzier compared to mesh renderers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Fuzziness: The VoGE renderer may produce slightly fuzzier boundaries compared to traditional mesh renderers due to the volumetric nature of Gaussians. Normal Consistency: The quality of the rendered normals depends heavily on the accuracy of the initial normal computation from the source mesh or point cloud. A parameterization for learnable surface normals of Gaussians that uses a sign scalar and a direction vector to stabilize optimization and allow normal flipping without rotation. It solves the instability inherent in naive vector parameterization, where flipping a normal requires a 180-degree rotation that causes convergence to inaccurate local minima. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Normal Field Supervision via Rendering and Depth Derivatives by explicitly modifying the Gaussian's internal attribute representation rather than relying on external gradient supervision. This method supervises the learnable surface normal attributes of 3D Gaussians by enforcing consistency between the rendered normal map and the geometric normals derived from the rendered depth map. It solves the problem of noisy or inconsistent normal estimates in Gaussian Splatting by using the depth map as a geometry prior. It differs from pure gradient-based approaches by explicitly optimizing normal attributes per Gaussian and supervising them against pseudo-normals computed from expected depth. To render the normal field, attribute a single value Ni per Gaussian to approximate the integral of the normal field along the ray. For the vector field V, select Vi proportional to the integral of the i-th term of the sum multiplied by the normalized density of the Gaussian. Due to symmetry around ni, Vi \propto ni, and thus the normalized vector field Ni \sim ni. Render plane normals ni with Gaussian splatting to estimate the average normal field value. The integral is defined as: Vi \propto \int{\mathbb{R}^3} Gi(x) \cdot \mathbf{1}{ni^T(x-\mui) \geq 0} \nabla \log(1 - Gi(x)) dx. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians N and pixels P, similar to standard Gaussian Splatting rendering. Memory Complexity: Additional memory required to store the normal vector ni for each Gaussian. Performance: Rendering quality improves significantly with an increased number of Gaussians. Strengths: Allows for lighting integration in Gaussian Splatting pipelines. Simple to implement by treating normals as an RGB attribute. Limitations: Boundaries may be fuzzier than mesh-based renderers. Requires pre-computed normals if starting from a mesh. This method was introduced in the context of VoGE (Volume Gaussian Ellipsoids), a differentiable volume renderer using Gaussian ellipsoids for analysis-by-synthesis. It was developed to address the lack of native surface normal information in Gaussian ellipsoids, which are represented as volumes. The approach leverages PyTorch3D for normal computation and lighting integration. name: Learnable Normals Parameterization
head: Normal Parameterization, Sign-Direction Normal Decomposition
body: A parameterization for learnable surface normals of Gaussians that uses a sign scalar and a direction vector to stabilize optimization and allow normal flipping without rotation. It solves the instability inherent in naive vector parameterization, where flipping a normal requires a 180-degree rotation that causes convergence to inaccurate local minima. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Normal Field Supervision via Rendering and Depth Derivatives by explicitly modifying the Gaussian's internal attribute representation rather than relying on external gradient supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Learnable parameters for each Gaussian i. Output: A surface normal vector \mathbf{n}i for each Gaussian i, suitable for rendering and gradient-based optimization. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores two learnable parameters for its normal: a scalar sign parameter si \in \mathbb{R} and a 3D direction vector \mathbf{d}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Initialize si and \mathbf{d}i for each Gaussian. 2. Compute the normal \mathbf{n}i using the decomposition formula during optimization. 3. Use \mathbf{n}i in the rendering pipeline for shading or normal loss calculation. Formulas: The normal \mathbf{n}i is computed as: \mathbf{n}i = \tanh(si) \cdot \frac{\mathbf{d}i}{\|\mathbf{d}i\|} Where: \tanh(si) maps the scalar si to the range (-1, 1), effectively acting as a learnable sign and magnitude controller. \frac{\mathbf{d}i}{\|\mathbf{d}i\|} normalizes the direction vector to unit length. The resulting \mathbf{n}i has a norm strictly less than 1 (due to \tanh), but its direction is well-defined and continuous. Parameters: si: Learnable scalar. Not given in the sources for initialization, but must allow both positive and negative values. \mathbf{d}i: Learnable 3D vector. Not given in the sources for initialization, but typically initialized randomly or based on prior geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If \|\mathbf{d}i\| = 0, the normalization fails. In implementation, a small epsilon should be added to the denominator or \mathbf{d}i should be clamped. Local Minima: Naive parameterization (simple normalized 3D vector) leads to unstable optimization because flipping the normal direction requires a 180-degree rotation. This decomposition avoids this by allowing flipping via the sign parameter si, which is a continuous scalar change rather than a vector rotation. Gradient Stability: The decomposition into direction and sign enforces the norm of the normal to be lower than 1, while allowing for flipping the direction simply by changing the sign parameter si, which overall stabilizes gradients and prevents optimization from getting stuck in local minima. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenormal(si: float, di: list[float]) -> list[float]: """ Compute the learnable normal for a Gaussian. Args: si: Learnable sign scalar. di: Learnable direction vector [x, y, z]. Returns: Normal vector [nx, ny, nz]. """ # Standard mathematical functions: exp(x), sqrt(x) def tanh(x): return (exp(x) - exp(-x)) / (exp(x) + exp(-x)) # Compute magnitude of direction vector mag = sqrt(di[0]2 + di[1]2 + di[2]2) # Guard against division by zero if mag < 1e-8: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Normalize direction dnorm = [di[0] / mag, di[1] / mag, di[2] / mag] # Compute sign factor signfactor = tanh(si) # Compute final normal ni = [signfactor dnorm[0], signfactor dnorm[1], signfactor dnorm[2]] return ni A technique to improve normal quality and stabilize vertex locations by training an additional learnable rotation parameter (quaternion) on each Gaussian on the mesh surface, instead of relying solely on mesh face normals. It sets itself apart by explicitly learning a rotation rather than just a direction, which is crucial for non-flat surfaces where mesh face normals require a large number of triangles for accuracy. Choose this when high-fidelity normal reconstruction on complex, non-flat geometry is required, and when occlusion errors from simple normal learning are observed. Pitfall: Using mesh face normals directly requires a large number of triangles for non-flat surfaces; adjusting vertex positions alone to learn rotation is insufficient and causes occlusion errors. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian for normal computation, as it involves basic arithmetic operations and a normalization. Memory Complexity: Adds 4 floats (1 for si, 3 for \mathbf{d}i) per Gaussian. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Stabilizes gradients, prevents convergence to local minima, allows easy normal flipping. Limitations: Requires additional learnable parameters per Gaussian. When to use: When optimizing Gaussian splats for surface reconstruction or normal rendering, especially where normal orientation is critical. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and the overhead of 4 extra floats per Gaussian is prohibitive, or when normal orientation is not important. Originated in the context of Gaussian Splatting for surface reconstruction, specifically in the work "From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians". It addresses the limitation of standard Gaussian Splatting, which does not natively contain surface normal information, by providing a robust way to learn and represent normals. From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37095-24, fetched 2026-10-29 Phys3DGS: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2409.10335, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Normal Field Supervision via Rendering and Depth Derivatives
head: Learnable Unit Normal with Depth Gradient Supervision, Lemma 2, Phys3DGS Normal Regularizer, Pseudo-Normal Supervision, Supervision of Normal Field
body:
This method supervises the learnable surface normal attributes of 3D Gaussians by enforcing consistency between the rendered normal map and the geometric normals derived from the rendered depth map. It solves the problem of noisy or inconsistent normal estimates in Gaussian Splatting by using the depth map as a geometry prior. It differs from pure gradient-based approaches by explicitly optimizing normal attributes per Gaussian and supervising them against pseudo-normals computed from expected depth. Inputs: Rendered depth map \hat{D} of resolution W 	imes H. Rendered normal map \hat{N} of resolution W 	imes H, obtained by alpha-blending the learnable unit normals ni of the splatted Gaussians. Outputs: Normal consistency loss Ln used for gradient-based optimization of Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: \hat{D}: 2D array of floats, where \hat{D}(x,y) is the median depth at pixel (x,y). \hat{N}: 2D array of 3D vectors, where \hat{N}(x,y) is the alpha-blended normal at pixel (x,y). ni: 3D vector, the learnable unit normal attribute of the i-th Gaussian. Steps: 1. Render Normal Map: Rasterize the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. For each pixel, compute the alpha-blended normal \hat{N}(x,y) using the learnable normals ni of the contributing Gaussians. 2. Compute Pseudo-Normal: Calculate the pseudo-ground truth normal 	ilde{N}(x,y) from the gradient of the rendered depth map \hat{D} under a local planarity assumption. Compute the image gradients of the depth map: 
ablax d and 
ablay d. These are the differences in depth values between nearby pixels. Compute the cross product of these gradients. Normalize the resulting vector to get 	ilde{N}(x,y). 	ilde{N}(x, y) =  rac{
ablax d 	imes 
ablay d}{|
ablax d 	imes 
ablay d|} where d are nearby depth points of pixel (x, y). 3. Compute Loss: Quantify the normal consistency as an L1 loss between the rendered normal \hat{N} and the pseudo-normal 	ilde{N}: Ln = |\hat{N} - 	ilde{N}| This loss encourages the rendered normal field to match the true normal of the surface at the 0.5-isosurface of the transmittance. Parameters: Depth Metric: The depth used for gradient computation is the median value of the free-flight distance t^{o,w}, not the expectancy, for robustness to outliers. Median Depth Definition: The median depth t is the infimum of t such that transmittance T{o,w}(t) \leq 0.5. In point-based rendering, this is the depth t^G{o,w} of the first Gaussian along the ray for which the transmittance reaches the 0.5 threshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenormalloss(rendereddepth, renderednormal): """ Computes the normal consistency loss between rendered normals and pseudo-normals derived from depth gradients. Args: rendereddepth (Tensor): Depth map of shape (H, W), float32. renderednormal (Tensor): Normal map of shape (H, W, 3), float32. Returns: Tensor: Scalar loss value. """ # Compute depth gradients using finite differences # Gradient in x direction: difference between adjacent columns depthgradx = rendereddepth[:, 1:] - rendereddepth[:,:-1] # Pad to maintain spatial dimensions depthgradx = torch.cat([depthgradx, depthgradx[:, -1:] - depthgradx[:, -1:]], dim=1) # Gradient in y direction: difference between adjacent rows depthgrady = rendereddepth[1:,:] - rendereddepth[:-1,:] # Pad to maintain spatial dimensions depthgrady = torch.cat([depthgrady, depthgrady[-1:,:] - depthgrady[-1:,:]], dim=0) # Compute pseudo-normal via cross product of depth gradients # Normal vector is perpendicular to the tangent plane defined by depth gradients pseudonormal = torch.cross(depthgradx.unsqueeze(-1), depthgrady.unsqueeze(-1), dim=-1) # Normalize the pseudo-normal norm = torch.norm(pseudonormal, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Avoid division by zero norm = torch.clamp(norm, min=1e-8) pseudonormal = pseudonormal / norm # Compute L1 loss between rendered normal and pseudo-normal loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderednormal - pseudonormal)) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Gradients: If the depth map is flat or noisy, the cross product may be near zero, leading to unstable normals. The normalization step includes a clamp to prevent division by zero. Boundary Conditions: Depth gradients at image boundaries require padding or special handling to maintain spatial alignment with the normal map. Specular Surfaces: Artifacts in the normal field may correspond to under-reconstructed parts of the scene, such as specular spots or sky regions, where depth estimates are unreliable. This method assigns a learnable unit normal to each 3D Gaussian to replace noisy gradient-based estimates, preventing the optimization from overfitting to training lighting conditions by aligning rendered normals with geometry priors derived from expected depth gradients. It differs from pure gradient-based approaches by explicitly optimizing normal attributes per Gaussian and supervising them against pseudo-normals computed from expected depth. Time Complexity: The method adds a constant overhead per pixel for computing depth gradients and the cross product, which is O(W 	imes H) per frame. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the rendered depth and normal maps, O(W 	imes H) for depth and O(W 	imes H 	imes 3) for normals. Strengths: Provides a robust supervision signal for normals without requiring explicit mesh reconstruction or additional geometric priors. The use of median depth makes it robust to outliers. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the rendered depth map. In regions with specular reflections or transparent surfaces, depth estimates may be noisy, leading to inaccurate pseudo-normals. When to Use: Suitable for scenes where consistent surface normals are required for downstream tasks like mesh extraction or lighting estimation, and where explicit normal supervision is not available. The method originates from the work on high-fidelity surface reconstruction using oriented Gaussians and reflection-aware rendering in Gaussian Splatting. It leverages the relationship between depth derivatives and surface normals, a concept well-established in computer vision. The specific formulation using median depth for robustness is detailed in. name: Rendering and Lighting Pipelines
body: This family defines the differentiable rendering pipelines that convert a set of 3D Gaussian primitives (or their variants) into 2D images by projecting them onto the camera plane and compositing them. It solves the problem of efficiently rasterizing soft, view-dependent primitives while supporting inverse rendering tasks such as lighting estimation and physical parameter optimization. What sets these methods apart from standard rasterization is the use of alpha blending or weighted-sum compositing over sorted or spatially hashed primitives, often augmented with volume-based occlusion or explicit geometric intersection for sharp features. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of projecting 3D primitives into 2D screen space and accumulating color based on depth order or spatial locality. 1. Projection: Primitives are transformed from world space to camera space. 2. Rasterization: Primitives are assigned to screen tiles. Visibility is determined by bounding boxes or projected extents. 3. Compositing: Color is accumulated using front-to-back alpha blending or order-independent techniques. 4. Sorting: Most methods require sorting primitives by depth within tiles to ensure correct front-to-back compositing, although some variants use spatial hashing or cell-level sorting to approximate this or enable order-independent transparency. A dual-hierarchy framework for real-time order-independent Gaussian Splatting. It combines alpha-blending with reformulated Weighted-Sum Rendering (WSR) to eliminate popping and transparency artifacts. Unlike vanilla OIT, it reintroduces physical constraints via cell-level transmittance decay, allowing early termination. It differs from Sort-free GS by using cell-level sorting for physically grounded transmittance. Replaces Gaussian ellipsoids with convex polyhedra (octahedra/tetrahedra) to enable efficient volumetric rendering with bounded geometry. It solves the problem of reconstructing sharp geometric features by allowing gradients to backpropagate through explicit ray-triangle intersections (Möller-Trumbore), distinguishing it from methods relying on implicit density fields. Integrates volume occlusion directly into the per-splat lighting evaluation loop. It ray-marches through a 3D density texture to compute transmittance for shadows, combined with per-light attenuation. Unlike methods treating volume as a post-process, it shares the 3D density texture with the splat evaluation. Decomposes Gaussian Splatting features into diffuse, specular, and ambient components using a Blinn-Phong model. It supports inverse rendering via loss functions on depth, normals, and color sparsity. A two-stage pipeline for physically parameterized volume clouds. Stage 1 trains physical parameters (geometry, extinction, albedo, scattering) under a single sun. Stage 2 freezes these and trains a global environment network for arbitrary sun direction relighting and sky atmospheric scattering. A minor variant involving the extraction and conversion loop for alpha values from raw opacity parameters to ensure they are in the valid range for blending. After obtaining 2D Gaussian function values via adapted projection for non-pinhole cameras, alpha blending is performed to generate the final image, identical to the original 3D-GS compositing step. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The rendering pipeline relies on efficient rasterization of 2D Gaussians projected from 3D. Subsequent works have adapted this pipeline for differentiable rendering, volume lighting, and physical parameter estimation. Implementation details for JSplat are provided in.
