name: Duplex-GS
head: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting
body: Duplex-GS is a dual-hierarchy framework for real-time order-independent Gaussian Splatting that combines alpha-blending with reformulated Weighted-Sum Rendering (WSR) to eliminate popping and transparency artifacts while reducing sorting overhead. Unlike vanilla OIT-based Gaussian Splatting which lacks physical constraints and causes transparency artifacts, Duplex-GS reintroduces physical constraints via cell-level transmittance decay, eliminating transparency artifacts and enabling early termination. It differs from Sort-free Gaussian Splatting by using cell-level sorting to compute a physically grounded transmittance that decays rapidly upon encountering opaque objects, rather than using linear depth decay. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives organized into ellipsoidal cells (proxies), camera parameters (viewing direction \mathbf{r}n, viewing distance \deltan), and scene latent features. Output: A final rendered color image \mathcal{C}. Data Structures: 1. Cell (Proxy): Position: xn \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scales: Sn \in \mathbb{R}^3 Quaternion: Qn \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized) Calibration Scalar: vn (parameterized by spherical harmonic coefficients for directional variation) Latent Feature Vector: fn 2. Neural Gaussian (emitted by cell n, index k): Center: \mu{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity: \sigma{n,k} \in [0, 1] Color: \mathcal{C}{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale: s{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Quaternion: \mathbf{q}{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized) Learned Offset: \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} \in [-1, 1]^3 Scale Ratio: \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} \in (0, 1) Parameters: K: Predefined number of neural Gaussians emitted per anchor/cell. \epsilon: Predefined threshold for early termination. Cell-level blending halts when Tn^{\text{cell}} < \epsilon. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize cells from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Each cell is centered according to the SfM point. 2. Gaussian Decoding (Layer I): For each cell n and each of its K emitted Gaussians k: Compute Gaussian center: \mu{n,k} = xn + \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} \cdot Sn where \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} is the learned offset and Sn is the cell scaling factor. Decode Opacity: \{\sigma{n,1}, \dots, \sigma{n,K}\} = F\sigma(\mathbf{f}n, \deltan, \mathbf{r}n) where F\sigma is a scene-wise MLP activated by Tanh. Decode Color: \{c^{n,1}, \dots, c^{n,K}\} = Fc(fn, \deltan, dn) where Fc is a scene-wise MLP. Decode Scale State: \{\mathcal{O}{n,1}^{\text{state}}, \dots, \mathcal{O}{n,K}^{\text{state}}\} = Fs(fn, \deltan, dn) where Fs is a scene-wise MLP activated by sigmoid. Decode Quaternion: \{\mathbf{q}{n,1}, \dots, \mathbf{q}{n,K}\} = Fq(fn, \deltan, dn) where Fq is a scene-wise MLP. Compute Gaussian Scale: s{n,k} = \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} Sn where \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} is the output of Fs. Clamp Scale Ratio to ensure Gaussian regions stay inside the cell: \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} = \min \left( \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}}, 1 - \|\mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}}\| \right). Update Cell Quaternion as the normalized weighted average of associated Gaussians' orientations: Qn = \text{norm}\left(\sumk^K q{n,k} \sigma{n,k}\right). 3. Cell Rasterization (Layer I): Assign visible cells to tiles. Apply radix sort to the cell sequence based on depth. This establishes a coarse spatial order for patches of Gaussians. 4. Physical OIT Blending (Layer II): Compute Cell-Level Transmittance: For each sorted cell n, compute the transmittance from preceding cells: Tn^{\text{cell}} = \prod{i=1}^{n-1} \prod{k=1}^{K} (1 - vi \cdot \alpha{i,k}) where vi is the learnable calibration scalar for cell i and \alpha{i,k} is the opacity of the k-th Gaussian in cell i. (Note: The source formula indices for the product upper bound are written as n-1 in the notes, but logically refer to preceding cells i < n and Gaussians k \le K.) Compute Cell Weight: wn = vn \cdot Tn^{\text{cell}}. Early Termination: If Tn^{\text{cell}} < \epsilon, stop processing further cells for this ray/tile. Compute Final Rendered Color: \mathcal{C} = \frac{\sum{n=1}^N wn \sum{k=1}^K \alpha{n,k} \mathcal{C}{n,k}}{\sum{n=1}^N wn \sum{k=1}^K \alpha{n,k}} where \mathcal{C}{n,k} is the color of the k-th Gaussian in cell n. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. K = 4 # Predefined number of neural Gaussians per cell EPSILON = 1e-4 # Early termination threshold class Gaussian: def init(self, center, opacity, color, scale, quaternion): self.center = center self.opacity = opacity self.color = color self.scale = scale self.quaternion = quaternion class Cell: def init(self, position, scales, quaternion, calibrationscalar, latentfeature, offsets, isvisible, depth): self.position = position self.scales = scales self.quaternion = quaternion self.calibrationscalar = calibrationscalar self.latentfeature = latentfeature self.offsets = offsets self.isvisible = isvisible self.depth = depth def vectornorm(v, dim=-1, keepdim=False): return (v 2).sum(dim=dim, keepdim=keepdim) 0.5 def normalize(v): return v / (vectornorm(v, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) def tanh(x): return (2.0 / (1.0 + (-x).exp()) - 1.0) def min(a, b): return a if a < b else b def Fsigma(f, delta, r): return f delta r # Placeholder for learned MLP def Fc(f, delta, d): return f delta d # Placeholder for learned MLP def Fs(f, delta, d): return f delta d # Placeholder for learned MLP def Fq(f, delta, d): return f delta d # Placeholder for learned MLP def decodegaussians(cell, cameraparams): fn = cell.latentfeature deltan = cameraparams.viewingdistance rn = cameraparams.viewingdirection dn = cameraparams.viewingdirection sigmas = tanh(Fsigma(fn, deltan, rn)) colors = Fc(fn, deltan, dn) scaleratiosraw = Fs(fn, deltan, dn) quaternionsraw = Fq(fn, deltan, dn) offsets = cell.offsets centers = cell.position + offsets cell.scales gaussianscales = scaleratiosraw cell.scales offsetnorms = vectornorm(offsets, dim=-1, keepdim=True) scaleratiosclamped = min(scaleratiosraw, 1.0 - offsetnorms) gaussianscales = scaleratiosclamped cell.scales quaternions = normalize(quaternionsraw) gaussians = [] for k in range(K): gaussians.append(Gaussian( center=centers[k], opacity=sigmas[k], color=colors[k], scale=gaussianscales[k], quaternion=quaternions[k])) return gaussians def duplexgsrender(cells, cameraparams): visiblecells = [c for c in cells if c.isvisible] sortedcells = sorted(visiblecells, key=lambda c: c.depth) coloraccumulator = 0.0 weightaccumulator = 0.0 for n, cell in enumerate(sortedcells): transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(n): prevcell = sortedcells[i] prevgaussians = decodegaussians(prevcell, cameraparams) for g in prevgaussians: transmittance = (1.0 - prevcell.calibrationscalar g.opacity) if transmittance < EPSILON: break cellweight = cell.calibrationscalar transmittance currentgaussians = decodegaussians(cell, cameraparams) localcolorsum = 0.0 localweightsum = 0.0 for g in currentgaussians: alpha = g.opacity color = g.color localcolorsum += cellweight alpha color localweightsum += cellweight alpha coloraccumulator += localcolorsum weightaccumulator += localweightsum if weightaccumulator > 0: return coloraccumulator / weightaccumulator return 0.0 Time Complexity: Drastically reduces the overhead of global radix sorting compared to vanilla 3DGS because sorting is performed on the smaller population of cell proxies rather than individual Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory consumption due to the smaller number of cells compared to Gaussians. Performance: Enables real-time performance on diverse real-world datasets. Strengths: Eliminates popping artifacts (locally order-independent) and transparency artifacts (physically grounded transmittance). Allows early termination for acceleration. Limitations: Order confusion caused by overlap among cells is a potential issue, addressed by the calibration scalar vn. When to use: When real-time rendering of Gaussian Splatting is required with high visual fidelity, specifically avoiding transparency and popping artifacts common in sort-free OIT methods. Duplex-GS was introduced in the paper "Duplex-GS: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon Scaffold-GS which introduced anchors as local encoding proxies. Duplex-GS replaces point anchors with ellipsoidal cells to provide explicit geometric structure. It addresses limitations of vanilla OIT-based Gaussian Splatting which lacks physical constraints and causes transparency artifacts. Duplex-GS: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2026.3666188, fetched 2026-10-30

name: LinPrim Differentiable Rendering Pipeline
head: LinPrim Rendering, LinPrim rasterizer, Linear Primitives Rendering, Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering
body: LinPrim is a differentiable rendering pipeline that replaces standard 3D Gaussian ellipsoids with convex polyhedral primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra) to enable explicit geometric optimization via ray-triangle intersections. It solves the problem of reconstructing scenes with sharp, bounded geometry while maintaining real-time performance through a two-stage preprocessing and rasterization architecture. Unlike its sibling Duplex-GS which uses dual representations, or GsplatVolumeLighting which focuses on volumetric lighting, LinPrim relies on explicit convex hulls and differentiable Möller-Trumbore intersections to backpropagate gradients directly onto geometric vertices. The pipeline operates in two distinct stages: per-primitive preprocessing and per-pixel rasterization/compositing. It builds on the Rendering and Lighting Pipelines shared principles of projection, tiling, and front-to-back compositing, but substitutes the Gaussian covariance projection with affine ray space approximation and explicit ray-polyhedron intersection. Inputs: Scene primitives defined by position, rotation, and distance features. Camera pose (view and projection matrices). Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Outputs: Final 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. Gradients with respect to primitive geometric features and SH coefficients. Each primitive stores the following parameters: 1. Geometric Features: Center Position: 3 floats (x, y, z). Rotation: 4 floats (quaternion). Distances: For Octahedra: 3 floats representing the distance from the center to the vertices along the three axes. Symmetry is enforced such that opposite vertices share the same distance, reducing complexity. For Tetrahedra: 12 floats are required due to the lack of symmetry in the general formulation. 2. Color Features: SH Coefficients: 48 floats (Spherical Harmonics up to degree 3, 3 coefficients per channel \times 3 channels \times 4 coefficients per channel). These capture complex reflectance under varying illumination and view angles. This accounts for the majority of memory per primitive. This stage transforms primitives into the camera's coordinate system and prepares them for rasterization. 1. Construction: Construct the primitive geometry from the stored position, distances, and rotation features. For octahedra, enforce symmetry by assigning a single distance to opposing corner pairs. 2. Transformation: Transform the primitive vertices from world space to camera space using the camera pose. 3. Ray Space Approximation: Project the transformed primitives into the 3D affine ray space approximation (EWA Splatting). This approximation is valid because small primitives result in negligible error compared to the performance overhead reduction. 4. Color Calculation: Calculate the view-dependent color for the primitive based on the viewing direction using the stored SH coefficients. 5. Bounding Box Computation: Compute the projected bounding box of the primitive in screen space to determine visibility. 1. Tiling: Tile the screen into regions (tiles). 2. Sorting: Sort primitives within each tile according to an approximate front-to-back order, leveraging techniques from 3DGS. This stage determines visibility and opacity for each pixel. 1. Intersection Test: For each pixel within a primitive's bounding box, cast a ray and determine if it intersects the convex primitive. The primitive is convex, so a ray intersects it either 0 times (not visible) or 2 times (visible). Use the Möller-Trumbore Intersection Algorithm (MTIA) to find the intersection points. This algorithm is fully differentiable, allowing gradients to flow back to the geometric features. 2. Opacity Calculation: If two intersections exist, calculate the opacity based on the distance between the intersection points. Normalization: To handle scale ambiguity (where appearance varies across different scene sizes), normalize the intersection distances. Determine the smallest distance d among all primitives in the scene. Scale all distance measurements relative to d. Density Formula: Given the primitive opacity \alpha, the density \sigma is defined as: \sigma(\alpha) = -\frac{\log(1 - 0.99 \cdot \alpha)}{2 \cdot \min(dx, dy, dz)} where dx, dy, dz are the normalized distances along the axes. 3. Compositing: Aggregate color contributions of all visible primitives in the tile using front-to-back alpha blending. Termination: Stop blending once the cumulative opacity reaches a threshold of 0.999. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def linprimrender(primitives, camerapose, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Renders the scene using the LinPrim pipeline. Args: primitives: List of Primitive objects. camerapose: Camera view and projection matrices. imagewidth: Width of the output image. imageheight: Height of the output image. Returns: renderedimage: 2D array of colors. """ # 1. Preprocessing transformedprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: geometry = constructgeometry(prim) camgeometry = transformtocameraspace(geometry, camerapose) color = evaluatesh(prim.shcoeffs, camerapose.viewdirection) rayspaceprim = projecttorayspace(camgeometry) bbox = computeboundingbox(rayspaceprim, imagewidth, imageheight) transformedprimitives.append({ 'geometry': rayspaceprim, 'color': color, 'bbox': bbox, 'originalprim': prim }) # 2. Global Sorting and Tiling tiles = createtiles(imagewidth, imageheight) for tile in tiles: tileprims = [p for p in transformedprimitives if intersectsbbox(p['bbox'], tile.bbox)] tileprims.sort(key=lambda p: p['geometry'].centerdepth) tile.primitives = tileprims # 3. Rasterization and Compositing renderedimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] minglobald = findminprimitivedistance(transformedprimitives) for tile in tiles: for y in range(tile.ystart, tile.yend): for x in range(tile.xstart, tile.xend): acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for prim in tile.primitives: if not ispixelinbbox(x, y, prim['bbox']): continue ray = createpixelray(x, y, camerapose) intersections = findintersections(ray, prim['geometry']) if len(intersections) != 2: continue dist = distance(intersections[0], intersections[1]) normalizeddist = dist / minglobald # Compute opacity from normalized distance basealpha = prim['originalprim'].opacity minnormdist = min(prim['geometry'].distx, prim['geometry'].disty, prim['geometry'].distz) sigma = -math.log(1 - 0.99 basealpha) / (2 minnormdist) alpha = 1 - math.exp(-sigma normalizeddist) # Alpha blending acccolor[0] = acccolor[0] (1 - alpha) + prim['color'][0] alpha acccolor[1] = acccolor[1] (1 - alpha) + prim['color'][1] alpha acccolor[2] = acccolor[2] (1 - alpha) + prim['color'][2] alpha accalpha += alpha (1 - accalpha) if accalpha >= 0.999: break renderedimage[y][x] = acccolor return renderedimage def constructgeometry(prim): # Extract position, rotation, distances and build octahedron/tetrahedron vertices pass def transformtocameraspace(geometry, camerapose): # Apply view and projection matrices to geometry vertices pass def evaluatesh(shcoeffs, viewdirection): # Evaluate Spherical Harmonics for the given viewing direction pass def projecttorayspace(geometry): # Apply 3D affine ray space approximation (EWA) pass def computeboundingbox(rayspaceprim, width, height): # Compute 2D screen-space bounding box pass def createtiles(width, height): # Divide screen into fixed-size tiles pass def findminprimitivedistance(primitives): mind = float('inf') for p in primitives: d = min(p['geometry'].distx, p['geometry'].disty, p['geometry'].distz) if d < mind: mind = d return mind def findintersections(ray, geometry): # Möller-Trumbore algorithm for ray-triangle intersections # Returns list of intersection points pass def distance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def intersectsbbox(bbox1, bbox2): return not (bbox1.maxx < bbox2.minx or bbox1.minx > bbox2.maxx or bbox1.maxy < bbox2.miny or bbox1.miny > bbox2.maxy) def ispixelinbbox(x, y, bbox): return bbox.minx <= x <= bbox.maxx and bbox.miny <= y <= bbox.maxy def createpixelray(x, y, camerapose): # Construct ray from camera center through pixel (x,y) pass SH Degree: 3 (resulting in 48 coefficients per primitive). Opacity Threshold: 0.999 for stopping compositing. Normalization Factor: The smallest distance d among all primitives in the scene. Scale Ambiguity: Without normalizing intersection distances by the global minimum primitive distance, the appearance of primitives will vary inconsistently across scenes of different sizes. Approximation Error: The 3D affine ray space approximation (EWA) introduces error that grows with distance from the primitive center. This is mitigated by using small primitives, keeping the error negligible. Convexity: The method relies on primitives being convex (octahedra/tetrahedra) to guarantee at most two intersections. Memory: SH coefficients dominate memory usage. Reducing SH degree or primitive count is necessary for large scenes. Time Complexity: Real-time performance is claimed, enabled by the two-stage parallelization (preprocessing and rasterization) and tiling. Sorting is approximate but efficient. Memory Complexity: Dominated by SH coefficients (48 floats per primitive). Geometric parameters are smaller (3 floats for octahedron distances, 12 for tetrahedron). Strengths: Explicit geometric representation allows for differentiable optimization of sharp features and bounded geometry, which Gaussian splatting struggles with. Retains real-time speeds. Limitations: Approximation error in ray space projection; scale ambiguity requires global normalization; memory intensive due to SH storage. When to use: Scenes requiring high-fidelity reconstruction of sharp, bounded geometry with view-dependent lighting, where real-time rendering is required. When not to use: Scenes with highly non-convex geometry that cannot be well-approximated by octahedra/tetrahedra, or where memory is extremely constrained and SH degree must be reduced significantly. LinPrim was introduced in the paper "LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering". It builds on the 3DGS pipeline to accommodate new primitives, using bounded, triangular geometry to expand the applicability of differentiable rendering pipelines. LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16312, fetched 2026-10-26

name: GsplatVolumeLighting
head: Gaussian Splat Volume Ray Marching, Volume Occlusion for 3DGS
body: GsplatVolumeLighting is a volume lighting and occlusion technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that ray-marches through a 3D density texture to compute transmittance for shadow and volume occlusion, combined with per-light attenuation and diffuse shading. It is implemented within the per-splat lighting evaluation loop using a shared 3D density texture. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: GsplatVolumeDensity: A sampler3D texture storing density. The R8 channel encodes \sqrt{\text{normalized optical depth}}. GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams: A float4 packing: x: Optical-depth scale (0 disables occlusion). y: Number of sample steps. z: Start distance. GsplatVolumeBoundsMin / GsplatVolumeBoundsMax: float4 values defining the axis-aligned volume bounds in local space. GsplatVolumeBoundsInvSize: float4 containing the inverse dimensions of the volume bounds. GsplatVolumeEnabled: Boolean flag (0 disables lighting). GsplatVolumeAmbientColor: float4 ambient color. GsplatVolumeLightingParams: float4 packing: y: Ambient intensity multiplier. z: Direct lighting intensity multiplier. GsplatVolumeLightColors: Array of light colors. Light properties: lightType (directional < 0.5, point/spot > 0.5), lightPosition (w > 0.5 for point lights), lightDirection, lightDirection.w (range fade parameter), spotParams (x: min cosine, y: exponent). Splat data: local center, local normal, and world view direction. Outputs: Final lighting value (float), typically added to the splat's base color or used as a multiplier. Data Structures: Volume Texture: sampler3D with R8 format. Values are squared during sampling to recover optical depth contribution. Constants: GSPLATVOLUMEOPAQUEDEPTH = 8.0. Transmittance below \exp(-8) is treated as fully opaque. Steps: 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute directionSign using lerp(-1.0, 1.0, step(0.0, direction)). Clamp the ray direction magnitude to 10^{-5} to prevent division by zero. Compute entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances against boundsMin and boundsMax using directionSign. Return max(0.0, min(farDistance.x, min(farDistance.y, farDistance.z))) as the maximum ray length rayLength. 2. Light Direction Transformation: Transform the light direction to local space using GsplatVolumeWorldToLocal. Normalize the result. If length \le 10^{-6}, return transmittance 1.0. 3. Ray Length Clamping (Point Lights): If lightPosition.w > 0.5 (point light), clamp rayLength to the Euclidean distance from localCenter to lightPosition. 4. Usable Length Check: Calculate usableLength = rayLength - startDistance (where startDistance is GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams.z). If usableLength <= 10^{-5}, return transmittance 1.0. 5. Sample Count and Step Size: Determine sampleCount = clamp((int)round(GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams.y), 1, 24). Compute stepLength = usableLength / sampleCount. 6. Initialization: Initialize UVW coordinates at the midpoint of the first step: uvw = \frac{\text{localCenter} + \text{localDirection} \cdot (\text{startDistance} + 0.5 \cdot \text{stepLength}) - \text{boundsMin}}{\text{boundsSize}} where boundsSize is derived from GsplatVolumeBoundsInvSize (inverse dimensions). Compute step delta: uvwStep = localDirection stepLength invSize. Initialize opticalDepth = 0.0. 7. Ray Marching Loop: Loop sampleIndex from 0 to sampleCount - 1 (max 24). Early Exit: If opticalDepth >= GSPLATVOLUMEOPAQUEDEPTH / strength (where strength is GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams.x), break loop. Boundary Check: If uvw is outside [0, 1] in any dimension, skip sampling for this step. Sampling: Sample the R8 channel of GsplatVolumeDensity. Square the value (di^2) and add to opticalDepth. Advance: uvw += uvwStep. 8. Transmittance Calculation: Compute transmittance T: T = \exp(-\text{strength} \cdot \text{opticalDepth}) where strength is GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams.x and opticalDepth is the accumulated sum of squared samples. 9. Per-Splat Lighting Evaluation: If GsplatVolumeEnabled == 0, return 1.0. Transform splat center to world space. Transform and normalize splat normal. If \text{dot}(\text{worldNormal}, \text{viewDirection}) < 0.0, flip the normal. Compute ambient = GsplatVolumeAmbientColor.rgb GsplatVolumeLightingParams.y. Initialize direct = 0.0. 10. Per-Light Processing (Max 4 Lights): Compute vector toLight and distance. Attenuation: If lightType < 0.5 (directional), attenuation = 1.0. If lightType > 0.5 (point/spot): Compute distanceSquared. Compute normalizedDistanceSquared = distanceSquared lightDirection.w. Compute rangeFade = saturate(1.0 - \text{normalizedDistanceSquared}^2). attenuation = \text{rangeFade}^2 / distanceSquared. Spot Cone Falloff (if lightType > 1.5): Compute spotCosine = dot(lightDirection.xyz, -toLight). Compute spot = saturate((\text{spotCosine} - \text{spotParams.x}) \cdot \text{spotParams.y}). attenuation = \text{spot}^2. Visibility: Compute visibility using the transmittance T calculated in Step 8. Pitfall Mitigation: If irradiance (light intensity before visibility) is \le 0.0, skip transmittance calculation to avoid expensive shadow marches for back-facing or out-of-range lights. Add to direct: direct += GsplatVolumeLightColors[lightIndex].rgb (irradiance visibility). 11. Final Output: Scale direct by GsplatVolumeLightingParams.z. Return max(ambient + direct, 0.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gsplatvolumelighting(splatcenterlocal, splatnormallocal, viewdirection, lightdirectionworld, lightposition, lighttype, lightcolor, lightdirectionw, spotparams, volumedensitysampler, volumeocclusionparams, volumeboundsmin, volumeboundsmax, volumeboundsinvsize, volumeambientcolor, volumelightingparams, volumeenabled): """ Computes volume lighting and occlusion for a single 3D Gaussian Splat. """ if not volumeenabled: return 1.0 # 1. Ray-Box Intersection direction = normalize(lightdirectionworld) dirlen = length(direction) if dirlen < 1e-5: return 1.0 direction = direction / max(dirlen, 1e-5) # directionSign = lerp(-1.0, 1.0, step(0.0, direction)) directionsign = where(direction >= 0.0, 1.0, -1.0) # Compute t0/t1 against boundsMin/BoundsMax t0 = (volumeboundsmin - splatcenterlocal) / direction t1 = (volumeboundsmax - splatcenterlocal) / direction tnear = max(min(t0.x, t1.x), min(t0.y, t1.y), min(t0.z, t1.z)) tfar = min(max(t0.x, t1.x), max(t0.y, t1.y), max(t0.z, t1.z)) # Return max(0.0, min(farDistance.x, min(farDistance.y, farDistance.z))) raylength = max(0.0, min(tfar.x, min(tfar.y, tfar.z))) # 2. Light Direction Transformation # Transform light direction to local space using GsplatVolumeWorldToLocal # (Not given in the sources. Standard inverse rotation matrix multiplication.) locallightdirection = lightdirectionworld locallightdirection = normalize(locallightdirection) if length(locallightdirection) <= 1e-6: return 1.0 # 3. Ray Length Clamping (Point Lights) if lightposition.w > 0.5: disttolight = length(lightposition - splatcenterlocal) raylength = min(raylength, disttolight) # 4. Usable Length Check startdistance = volumeocclusionparams.z usablelength = raylength - startdistance if usablelength <= 1e-5: return 1.0 # 5. Sample Count and Step Size strength = volumeocclusionparams.x if strength == 0: return 1.0 # Occlusion disabled samplecount = clamp(round(volumeocclusionparams.y), 1, 24) steplength = usablelength / samplecount # 6. Initialization # UVW at midpoint of first step uvw = (splatcenterlocal + locallightdirection (startdistance + 0.5 steplength) - volumeboundsmin) volumeboundsinvsize uvwstep = locallightdirection steplength volumeboundsinvsize opticaldepth = 0.0 opaquethreshold = 8.0 / strength # 7. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(samplecount): if opticaldepth >= opaquethreshold: break # Boundary Check if uvw.x < 0.0 or uvw.x > 1.0 or uvw.y < 0.0 or uvw.y > 1.0 or uvw.z < 0.0 or uvw.z > 1.0: uvw += uvwstep continue # Sampling d = texture3D(volumedensitysampler, uvw).r opticaldepth += d d uvw += uvwstep # 8. Transmittance Calculation transmittance = exp(-strength opticaldepth) # 9. Per-Splat Lighting Evaluation # Transform center and normal to world space # (Not given in the sources. Standard transformation matrix multiplication.) centerworld = splatcenterlocal normalworld = normalize(splatnormallocal) # Flip normal if back-facing if dot(normalworld, viewdirection) < 0.0: normalworld = -normalworld ambient = volumeambientcolor.rgb volumelightingparams.y direct = 0.0 # 10. Per-Light Processing # Compute toLight and distance tolight = lightposition - centerworld distancesquared = dot(tolight, tolight) # Irradiance calculation (simplified for single light) irradiance = 1.0 # Placeholder for light intensity/color magnitude # Pitfall Mitigation: Skip if irradiance <= 0.0 if irradiance <= 0.0: visibility = 1.0 else: visibility = transmittance # Attenuation if lighttype < 0.5: attenuation = 1.0 else: normalizeddistancesquared = distancesquared lightdirectionw rangefade = saturate(1.0 - normalizeddistancesquared normalizeddistancesquared) attenuation = (rangefade rangefade) / distancesquared # Spot Cone Falloff if lighttype > 1.5: spotcosine = dot(normalize(lightdirectionworld), -normalize(tolight)) spot = saturate((spotcosine - spotparams.x) spotparams.y) attenuation = spot spot direct += lightcolor.rgb (irradiance visibility attenuation) # 11. Final Output direct = volumelightingparams.z return max(ambient + direct, 0.0) Time Complexity: O(N) per splat per light, where N is the number of samples (max 24). The early exit on opticalDepth >= GSPLATVOLUMEOPAQUEDEPTH / strength can significantly reduce average case performance. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D density texture, where V is the volume resolution. The texture is shared across splats. Performance: The method is designed for real-time rendering in Unity 6, leveraging GPU compute and texture sampling. Strengths: Provides volumetric occlusion and lighting for 3DGS, enhancing realism. Supports Built-in Render Pipeline, URP, and HDRP. Limitations: Limited to 4 lights. Max 24 samples per ray march. Requires a 3D density texture. When to Use: When volumetric occlusion and lighting are required for 3DGS content in Unity 6. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and volumetric effects are not needed, or when more than 4 lights are required. GsplatVolumeLighting is part of the UnitySplats package, a cross-platform Unity 6 package for importing, loading, and rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting content. It is a modified and substantially extended fork of wuyize25/gsplat-unity. The method is used for volume occlusion and lighting of 3DGS content in Unity 6. arloopa/UnitySplats, https://github.com/arloopa/UnitySplats, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NeILF Rendering and Loss Calculation
head: inverse rendering with Blinn-Phong
body:
NeILF Rendering and Loss Calculation is a differentiable rendering pipeline that decomposes Gaussian Splatting features into diffuse, specular, and ambient components using a Blinn-Phong shading model. It enables inverse rendering by optimizing scene parameters against ground-truth images, depth, and normals through a composite loss function. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which renders a single composite color, this method explicitly separates lighting terms to support material editing and physically-based constraints. Inputs: Camera parameters: pose (view matrix), intrinsics (focal length, principal point), resolution (H, W). Gaussian primitives: positions, covariances, opacities, and feature vectors including diffusefactor, specularfactor, ambientfactor, shininess, and offsetcolor. Light parameters: lighttransform (optional transformation for diffuse, shininess, ambient, and specular factors). Optimization weights: lambdarender, lambdaphong, lambdadepth, lambdaopacity, lambdanormalrenderdepth, lambdanormalmvsdepth, lambdaoffsetcolorsparsity, lambdadiffusefactorsmooth, lambdaambientfactorsmooth, lambdanormalsmooth, lambdadssim. Ground truth: gtimage, gtdepth, imagemask, depthmask. Optional MVS normal map. Outputs: render: Final rendered color image. phong: Blinn-Phong rendered color image. normal: Rendered surface normals. pseudonormal: Normals derived from depth. opacity: Rendered opacity mask. depth: Rendered depth map. diffuseterm, specularterm, ambientterm: Individual lighting components. loss: Optimization loss value. Auxiliary data: surfacexyz, viewspacepoints, visibilityfilter, radii, numrendered, numcontrib, hdr, valgamma, tbdict. Data Structures: The rendering results are stored in a dictionary results with the following keys: 'render': Tensor (3, H, W), final color. 'phong': Tensor (3, H, W), Blinn-Phong color. 'normal': Tensor (3, H, W), normal vectors. 'pseudonormal': Tensor (3, H, W), depth-derived normals. 'surfacexyz': Tensor (3, H, W), 3D surface positions. 'opacity': Tensor (1, H, W), opacity mask. 'depth': Tensor (1, H, W), depth values. 'viewspacepoints': Tensor for view-space coordinates. 'visibilityfilter': Boolean mask for active Gaussians. 'radii': Integer mask for visible Gaussians. 'numrendered': Count of rendered Gaussians. 'numcontrib': Count of contributing Gaussians per pixel. 'diffusefactor': Tensor, diffuse material factor. 'offsetcolor': Tensor, color offset for blending. 'shininess': Tensor, specular exponent. 'ambientfactor': Tensor, ambient intensity. 'specularfactor': Tensor, specular intensity. 'diffuseterm': Tensor, computed diffuse color. 'specularterm': Tensor, computed specular color. 'ambientterm': Tensor, computed ambient color. 'hdr': Boolean, HDR flag. 'valgamma': Float, gamma value. 'tbdict': Dictionary for TensorBoard logging. 'loss': Float, optimization loss. Algorithm Steps: 1. Base Rendering: Call renderview to obtain base Gaussian splatting features, including diffusefactor, specularfactor, ambientfactor, shininess, offsetcolor, normals, and opacity. Check istraining; if true, proceed to loss calculation. 2. Light Transform: If lighttransform is not None, apply it to the material factors: 	ext{factor}{new} = 	ext{factor}{old} 	imes 	ext{light	ransform} + 	ext{offset} for diffusefactor, shininess, ambientfactor, and specularfactor. 3. Offset Color Norm: Compute the squared norm of offsetcolor along the last two dimensions: 	ext{offset\color
orm} = \sum{h,w} (	ext{offset\color}{h,w})^2 keeping dimensions for broadcasting. 4. Multi-Gaussian Grouping: If multiple Gaussian groups exist (len(numGSsTFs) > 1): For each group i: Compute diffusecolor for the group's Gaussians: 	ext{diffuse\color} = (	ext{offset\color} + 	ext{palette\color}) \cdot 	ext{clamp}(0, 1) \cdot 	ext{detach}() If opacityfactors[i] exists, multiply the group's opacity by opacityfactors[i]. 5. Diffuse Term Calculation: Compute diffuse intensity: I{diffuse} = 	ext{diffuse actor} \cdot |\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}{inc}| where \mathbf{n} is the surface normal and \mathbf{d}{inc} is the incident light direction. Compute diffuse color: C{diffuse} = (	ext{ambient actor} + I{diffuse}) \cdot 	ext{diffuse\color}. 6. Specular Term Calculation: Compute half-vector: \mathbf{h} =  rac{\mathbf{d}{inc} + \mathbf{d}{view}}{\|\mathbf{d}{inc} + \mathbf{d}{view}\|} where \mathbf{d}{view} is the view direction. name: 4DGS-Volume-Cloud Two-Stage Relighting
head: Frozen Geometry + Environment Network, Stage 1 + Stage 2
body: A two-stage rendering pipeline for physically parameterized volume clouds using 3D Gaussians, designed for real-time rendering and dynamic relighting with arbitrary sun directions. It separates the optimization of static cloud geometry and physical scattering properties (Stage 1) from the learning of global environment lighting (Stage 2), allowing the cloud structure to remain frozen while the environment network adapts to new illumination conditions. Unlike sibling methods that may bake lighting into the primitives or use differentiable volume rendering for both geometry and lighting simultaneously, this method explicitly decouples the geometric occlusion and physical parameters from the environmental inscattering, enabling efficient arbitrary-direction relighting without re-optimizing the cloud itself. The method operates in two distinct phases. Stage 1 optimizes the 3D Gaussian representation of the cloud under a single, fixed sun direction with a black background to learn stable physical parameters. Stage 2 freezes these parameters and trains a global environment network to model sky atmospheric scattering, enabling relighting for any sun direction. Inputs: Stage 1: A dataset of images captured under pure sun illumination with a black background (UE SkyAtmosphere brightness factor = 0). Camera poses and sun directions are provided. Stage 2: The trained Stage 1 model (frozen) and a dataset with the same camera poses and sun directions but with the sky atmosphere enabled (providing ambient sky light). Outputs: Stage 1: A set of 3D Gaussians with optimized physical parameters (position, scale, rotation, extinction, albedo, scattering phase function, and multiple scattering weights). Stage 2: A global environment network (MLP) and precomputed sky visibility transfer vectors, saved as sidecar files alongside the Gaussian point cloud. The 3D Gaussians store physical parameters instead of standard SH colors and opacity: Position: 3 floats (x, y, z). Scale: 3 floats (applied to covariance). Rotation: 4 floats (quaternion w, x, y, z). Extinction Coefficient (\sigmat): 1 float, represented as the volume integral of the extinction coefficient, activated via softplus and clamped to a minimum of 5. Albedo (\omega): 3 floats (RGB), activated via sigmoid to ensure values in [0, 1]. HG g parameter: 1 float, the Henyey-Greenstein phase function anisotropy factor, computed as 0.8 \cdot \tanh(\text{learnable}) to enforce forward scattering. Multiple Scattering Weights (wn): 6 floats, octave energy weights for a 6-order multiple scattering approximation (based on Frostbite/Wrenninge), activated via softplus. Stage 2 Sidecar Files: envnet.pt: PyTorch weights for the global environment network (MLP). skytransfer.npy: NumPy array containing the sky visibility SH transfer vectors V{lm}(x) for each Gaussian. env.json: Configuration file for the environment network. 1. Initialize: Create 3D Gaussians from an initial point cloud. 2. Rasterization Setup: Configure the rasterizer to use analytic optical thickness computation (useanalytictau), which computes the per-pixel accumulated optical thickness \tau along the ray, where opacity is derived physically as \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\tau). 3. Lighting Pass (T{light}): Compute the self-shadowing transmittance T{light} for each Gaussian along the sun direction via a separate "lighting space" rasterization pass. Use a narrow FOV perspective camera to simulate the directional sun. For each Gaussian, record the front-facing accumulated optical thickness \tau using a CUDA kernel (recordfronttau). Compute the weighted mean of \alpha \cdot T over the sun-facing footprint of the Gaussian. 4. Radiance Computation: For each pixel, accumulate radiance from front-to-back sorted Gaussians. The radiance contribution of a Gaussian is: L = \omega \cdot L{light} \cdot \sum{n} wn \cdot T{light}^{b^n} \cdot P(vi, vo; g \cdot c^n) where L{light} is the sun irradiance, P is the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, vi is the incident direction (-vl), and vo is the view direction. 5. Tonemapping: Apply a fixed Narkowicz ACES tonemapping curve to convert linear HDR radiance to LDR for comparison with ground truth images. Optionally, use learnable ACES coefficients if the ground truth uses a different filmic curve. 6. Optimization: Minimize the difference between rendered and ground truth images using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Optimize position, scale, rotation, \sigmat, \omega, g, and wn. 1. Freeze Geometry: Load the Stage 1 model and freeze all Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, \sigmat, \omega, g, wn). 2. Precompute Sky Visibility (V{lm}): For each Gaussian, compute the sky visibility transfer vectors V{lm}(x) in Spherical Harmonics (SH). Scan the hemisphere in N directions using the computeTlightraster function to calculate geometric occlusion from the cloud itself. V{lm} is colorless and purely geometric, computed once on the frozen point set. Default SH order is 2 (9 coefficients), configurable via --envshorder. 3. Train Environment Network: Train a global MLP (the environment network) to predict the sky irradiance field E{lm}(vl) and the sun transmittance parameters. The network takes the sun direction vl as input. Use a learning rate of 1e-3 with an independent optimizer, decaying to 0.1\times. 4. Relighting Rendering: For any new sun direction vl, compute the final radiance L as: L = T{sun}(vl) \odot L{stage1} + \omega \cdot \sum{lm} E{lm}(vl) \cdot V{lm}(x) T{sun}(vl) is the multiplicative sun-atmosphere transmittance (see Formula section). The second term is the additive sky inscattering fill. 5. Save Outputs: Save envnet.pt, skytransfer.npy, and env.json alongside the PLY file. Sun Transmittance (T{sun}): Modeled as a 3-parameter analytic expression: T{sun}(vl) = \exp(-m(\theta) \cdot \tau{rgb}) where: m(\theta) is the Kasten-Young air mass, a fixed geometry function of sun elevation \theta. \tau{rgb} = (\tauR, \tauG, \tauB) are the learnable zenith optical thicknesses for Red, Green, and Blue channels. Note: \tauB > \tauR due to Rayleigh scattering (\propto \lambda^{-4}), causing darkening and reddening at low sun angles. If the sun is below the horizon, a smoothstep gate extinguishes the direct sun term. Final Radiance (L): L = T{sun}(vl) \odot L{stage1} + \omega \cdot \sum{lm} E{lm}(vl) \cdot V{lm}(x) L{stage1}: The radiance computed in Stage 1 (sun term only). E{lm}(vl): Sky irradiance field represented by low-order SH, predicted by the global MLP. V{lm}(x): Precomputed sky visibility transfer vectors for Gaussian at x. \omega: Frozen albedo. SH Order: 2 (9 coefficients) for E{lm} and V{lm} by default. Stage 2 Learning Rate: 1e-3, decaying to 0.1\times. Tonemapping: Fixed Narkowicz ACES by default. Optional learnable ACES coefficients. Tlight Computation: Rasterization-based (useanalytictau) by default. Voxel-based alternative available via --tlightvoxel. Sun Below Horizon: The direct sun term must be multiplicative with T{sun} \le 1 because a purely additive term cannot express the darkening (attenuation) caused by atmospheric path length. A smoothstep gate is used to extinguish the sun term when the sun is below the horizon. Data Bias: The sun direction coverage in the training dataset must be uniform to ensure healthy geometric shadow gradients. Biased direction data can cause vertical extensions to escape supervision. Tonemapping Mismatch: If the ground truth is true linear HDR (no tonemapping), the tonemapping must be disabled (--no-tonemapaces). Using learnable ACES is inappropriate as it cannot represent the identity function. Gradient Continuity: The lighting pass (Tlight) supports full continuous gradients for \tau, weights, normalization, and Gaussian transforms. However, sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches are treated as constants during backpropagation. Unverified code. (2.0 i + 1.0) / N radius = torch.sqrt(1.0 - y2) theta = 2.0 np.pi i / ((1.0 + np.sqrt(5.0)) N) return torch.tensor([radius torch.cos(theta), y, radius torch.sin(theta)]) def projecttosh(order, directions, values): """Project sampled values to SH coefficients of given order.""" # Simplified SH projection for order 2 (9 coeffs) # In practice, this uses standard SH basis evaluation and least-squares fit coeffs = torch.zeros(directions.shape[0], 9) # Placeholder for standard SH basis matrix multiplication return coeffs def rasterizeanalytictau(gaussians, poses): """CUDA rasterizer pass returning per-pixel accumulated optical thickness tau.""" # Returns tensor of shape (H, W) pass def computelightspacetransmittance(gaussians, sundirection): """Lighting pass pass using narrow FOV camera and recordfronttau kernel.""" # Returns tensor of shape (Ngaussians) pass def computeTlightraster(gaussian, direction): """Compute geometric occlusion transmittance for a single Gaussian in a given direction.""" # Returns scalar transmittance value pass class EnvironmentNetwork(nn.Module): """Global MLP for sky irradiance and sun transmittance parameters.""" def init(self): super().init() self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 9)) # Elm self.taurgb = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor([0.1, 0.15, 0.2])) # Learnable zenith optical thicknesses def forward(self, sundirection): Elm = self.mlp(sundirection) return Elm, self.taurgb def stage1train(gaussians, dataset, optimizer): """Stage 1: Train physical parameters under single sun direction.""" for images, poses, sundirections in dataset: tau = rasterizeanalytictau(gaussians, poses) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-tau) Tlight = computelightspacetransmittance(gaussians, sundirections) Lsun = torch.oneslike(images) # Sun irradiance (direction-dependent in practice) phasefunc = heneygreenstein(torch.sum(-sundirections[:, None, None,:] poses.viewdirections[None, None, None,:], dim=-1), gaussians.g) L = torch.zeroslike(images) for n in range(6): L += gaussians.wn[n] (Tlight (2n))[:, None, None, None] phasefunc L = gaussians.omega Lsun L Lldr = applyacestonemap(L) loss = mseloss(Lldr, images) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() def stage2precompute(gaussians, numhemispheresamples=60): """Stage 2 Precomputation: Compute sky visibility SH transfer vectors.""" Vlm = [] for gaussian in gaussians: directions = torch.stack([fibonaccihemispheresample(i, numhemispheresamples) for i in range(numhemispheresamples)]) transmittances = torch.stack([computeTlightraster(gaussian, d) for d in directions]) shcoeffs = projecttosh(2, directions, transmittances) Vlm.append(shcoeffs) return torch.stack(Vlm) def stage2train(gaussians, Vlm, envdataset, envnetwork, optimizer): """Stage 2: Train environment network with frozen geometry.""" for param in gaussians.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False for images, poses, sundirections in envdataset: Elm, taurgb = envnetwork(sundirections) theta = getsunelevation(sundirections) mtheta = kastenyoungairmass(theta) Tsun = torch.exp(-mtheta[:, None] taurgb[None,:]) Lstage1 = renderstage1radiance(gaussians, sundirections) inscattering = torch.zeroslike(images) for idx in range(len(gaussians)): inscattering += gaussians.omega[idx] torch.sum(Elm[idx] Vlm[idx]) L = Tsun Lstage1 + inscattering Lldr = applyacestonemap(L) loss = mseloss(Lldr, images) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() def renderstage1radiance(gaussians, sundirections): """Re-render Stage 1 sun-only radiance for a given sun direction.""" tau = rasterizeanalytictau(gaussians, poses) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-tau) Tlight = computelightspacetransmittance(gaussians, sundirections) Lsun = torch.oneslike(images) phasefunc = heneygreenstein(torch.sum(-sundirections[:, None, None,:] poses.viewdirections[None, None, None,:], dim=-1), gaussians.g) L = torch.zeroslike(images) for n in range(6): L += gaussians.wn[n] (Tlight (2n))[:, None, None, None] phasefunc return gaussians.omega Lsun L Time Complexity: Stage 1 training is comparable to standard 3DGS but with additional overhead for the lighting pass and physical parameter optimization. Stage 2 precomputation is O(N \cdot H) where N is the number of Gaussians and H is the number of hemisphere samples. Stage 2 training is fast as it only optimizes a small MLP. Inference is real-time, dominated by the rasterization of Gaussians and a simple MLP evaluation per pixel. Memory Complexity: Stores physical parameters per Gaussian (extinction, albedo, HG g, 6 scattering weights) plus sidecar files for the environment network and visibility vectors. Strengths: Enables arbitrary-direction relighting without retraining the cloud geometry. Physically based parameters allow for realistic atmospheric effects (reddening at low sun angles). Real-time rendering capability. Limitations: Assumes static cloud geometry (time dimension not implemented in the initial version). Relies on uniform sun direction coverage in the training dataset for robust relighting. The multiplicative sun term requires careful handling of sun below the horizon. When to Use: When dynamic relighting of volume clouds is required in real-time applications, and the cloud geometry is static or can be approximated as such. Suitable for virtual production and interactive visualization. When Not to Use: If the cloud geometry is highly dynamic and cannot be captured by a static Gaussian set. If the training data lacks sufficient sun direction diversity, relighting quality will degrade. The method is based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) and the 3DGS-Volume-Cloud project. It was developed as an independent 4D implementation workspace, with an initial code baseline at commit 69fea2c8d5a13d6c0e41ac12ca45c80b71bd3403. The project aims to replace ray-marching volume clouds in game engines with physically parameterized 3D Gaussians for real-time rendering and dynamic relighting. It is used in the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud project for rendering volume clouds based on the WDAS Cloud dataset. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volume Encoding Gaussians
head: Transfer Function-Agnostic 3D Gaussians for Volume Rendering
body: Volume Encoding Gaussians adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for volume data visualization by removing per-Gaussian color and opacity attributes, training only scalar values to enable interactive transfer function application post-training. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering by decoupling the radiometric representation from the geometric density, allowing the same underlying scalar field to be visualized with arbitrary transfer functions without retraining. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of multi-view images of a volume (e.g., medical scans, fluid simulations) and corresponding camera poses. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean position \mu, covariance \Sigma, and a scalar value s. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (often parameterized by rotation R and scale S). si \in \mathbb{R}: Scalar value (e.g., density, temperature, concentration). Note: Color ci and opacity \alphai are not stored as learnable attributes. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians in 3D space, typically using point cloud data or random initialization within the volume bounds. 2. Rendering: For each pixel \mathbf{p}, project Gaussians to 2D screen space. Compute the 2D Gaussian value \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) using the projected covariance \Sigma{2D}. 3. Compositing: Render the scalar field using front-to-back accumulation. The accumulated scalar Sf at pixel \mathbf{p} is: Sf(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^N si \tilde{\sigma}i \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \tilde{\sigma}j \tilde{\mathcal{G}}j(\mathbf{p})) where \tilde{\sigma}i is a fixed or learned opacity scaling factor (if not removed entirely, but typically opacity is part of the transfer function or fixed for visualization). Clarification: The method focuses on training si. The opacity \alpha might be fixed or derived, but the key is that color is absent. 4. Transfer Function Application: After rendering the scalar field Sf, apply a user-defined transfer function T(s) to map the scalar value to color c and final opacity \alpha: c = Tc(Sf), \quad \alpha = T\alpha(Sf) This step is performed post-rendering, enabling interactive visualization. 5. Optimization: Minimize the difference between the rendered color (after applying a target transfer function) and the ground truth image. The loss is typically: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{RGB} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{depth} where \mathcal{L}{RGB} is computed using the transfer function applied to the rendered scalars. Parameters: Learning rate for \mu, \Sigma, s: Standard Gaussian Splatting rates. Transfer Function: User-defined, e.g., linear, exponential, or custom LUT. Edge Cases: Degenerate Gaussians: Standard Gaussian Splatting safeguards (e.g., resetting scale) apply. Transfer Function Sensitivity: Poor transfer function choice may lead to low contrast or saturation, but does not affect the underlying scalar field quality. GVGEN is a method for 3D generation that operates in 3D space using a 3D Gaussian volume representation. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GaussianCube, which converts a constant number of Gaussians into a voxelized representation via optimal transport, by maintaining a direct 3D Gaussian volume structure. Time Complexity: Similar to 3D Gaussian Splatting, O(N) per pixel for compositing, where N is the number of Gaussians. Transfer function application is O(1) per pixel. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to standard Gaussian Splatting as color and opacity are not stored per Gaussian, only scalar values. Strengths: Interactive transfer function application; no retraining required for different visualizations; efficient storage. Limitations: Requires a suitable transfer function for each dataset; scalar values may not capture complex radiometric properties directly. When to Use: Volume visualization where multiple transfer functions are desired for the same data; interactive exploration. When Not to Use: When color is intrinsically tied to the geometry in a way that cannot be separated by a scalar field. name: BRDF and Relighting Extensions

body: BRDF and Relighting Extensions augment standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by replacing the baked, view-dependent color attribute with physically based rendering (PBR) parameters, enabling dynamic relighting, shadow casting, and material decomposition. Unlike standard 3DGS which captures lighting in spherical harmonics, these methods decouple geometry from material properties, allowing the scene to be illuminated by arbitrary light sources or environment maps. They distinguish themselves from siblings like 3DGS-DR by explicitly storing BRDF parameters (albedo, roughness, normal) per Gaussian, facilitating direct lighting reconstruction via environment maps and indirect lighting via spherical harmonics. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of projecting 3D primitives into 2D screen space and accumulating color based on depth order or spatial locality. 1. Projection: Primitives are transformed from world space to camera space. The 3D covariance matrix \Sigma is transformed using the view matrix W and the Jacobian J of the perspective projection approximation: \Sigmac = J W \Sigma W^T J^T. The 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} is extracted as the upper-left 2\times2 block. 2. Rasterization: Primitives are assigned to screen tiles. Visibility is determined by bounding boxes or projected extents. 3. Compositing: Color is accumulated using front-to-back alpha blending or order-independent techniques. The final intensity for a pixel is If = \sum{i=1}^N ci \tilde{\sigma}i \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \tilde{\sigma}j \tilde{\mathcal{G}}j(\mathbf{p})), where ci is color, \tilde{\sigma}i is opacity or density, and \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) is the 2D Gaussian value at pixel \mathbf{p}. 4. Sorting: Most methods require sorting primitives by depth within tiles to ensure correct front-to-back compositing, although some variants use spatial hashing or cell-level sorting to approximate this or enable order-independent transparency. This method extends standard 3DGS by embedding physically based rendering parameters into each Gaussian primitive, enabling per-point BRDF evaluation and relighting. It distinguishes itself from siblings like 3DGS-DR and Relightable 3D Gaussian by explicitly storing incident lighting and BRDF parameters per Gaussian, facilitating direct lighting reconstruction via environment maps and indirect lighting via spherical harmonics. This method extends standard 3DGS by incorporating classical reflection and shading concepts to address limitations with highly reflective surfaces and enable dynamic relighting. Unlike standard 3DGS, which bakes lighting into spherical harmonics via an emission-absorption model, this approach allows for physically based rendering (PBR) by augmenting Gaussian kernels with environmental information. It leverages the natural normal estimation provided by the shortest axis of the Gaussian kernel to achieve high-quality rendering of reflective objects with training efficiency. Relightable 3D Gaussian extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by assigning per-Gaussian BRDF parameters and precomputed visibility to enable dynamic relighting and shadow casting. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by evaluating material responses to arbitrary light sources rather than relying solely on captured environment maps. Builds on BRDF and Relighting Extensions. Inverse Rendering with Gaussians (GS-IR / GIR) adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting to recover physically accurate material and lighting properties from images by optimizing differentiable shading models. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a split-sum approximation to handle indirect lighting and specular reflections. GaussianShader enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by incorporating trainable material parameters—diffuse color, specular intensity, roughness, and surface normal—along with a global environment map to achieve physically-based rendering (PBR). It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by disentangling geometry from material properties, allowing for accurate specular reflections and relighting capabilities. BRDF Decoder Strategies define how 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives encode and reconstruct material properties (such as albedo, roughness, and metalness) or direct light reflection weights during optimization. While standard 3DGS renders color directly, these strategies decouple geometry and appearance to enable physically-based rendering (PBR) and relighting. They differ from sibling methods by focusing specifically on the decoding mechanism—whether through explicit physical parameter regression or implicit neural mapping—rather than the rasterization or sorting pipeline itself. The extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting to support PBR and relighting emerged as a response to the inability of standard 3DGS to separate geometry from lighting. Standard 3DGS encodes appearance into view-dependent spherical harmonics, making it difficult to relight scenes or recover material properties. Early works such as 3D Gaussian Splatting with BRDF Embedding and GaussianShader introduced per-Gaussian material attributes. Subsequent methods like Inverse Rendering with Gaussians and Relightable 3D Gaussian focused on differentiable optimization of these attributes from multi-view images. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Reflection and Relighting
head: Gaussian-Shader, 3DGS-DR, IRGS, Relightable 3D Gaussians, GS-IR
body: This method extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by incorporating classical physically based rendering (PBR) concepts to address limitations with highly reflective surfaces and enable relighting under novel illumination. Unlike standard 3DGS, which bakes lighting into spherical harmonics coefficients via an emission-absorption model, this approach decomposes geometry, material, and lighting, allowing for dynamic specular shading synthesis. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific integration of secondary ray tracing for interreflections and the derivation of normals from the Gaussian kernel's anisotropy. Inputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, base color/SH). Input images/videos for training. Environment map or lighting parameters for relighting. Outputs: Relit images under novel illumination. Decomposed material maps (albedo, roughness, metallic). Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores additional PBR attributes beyond standard 3DGS: Albedo (\alphai): Per-Gaussian diffuse color. Roughness (\rhoi): Scalar or vector defining surface microfacet distribution. Metallic (mi): Scalar defining the blend between dielectric and conductor. Normal (\mathbf{n}i): Derived from the Gaussian shape or explicitly optimized. Lighting: Scene environment map or learned lighting coefficients. Method Steps: 1. Normal Estimation: The surface normal \mathbf{n}i for each Gaussian is derived from the shortest axis of the Gaussian kernel's covariance matrix \Sigmai. This leverages the anisotropy of the Gaussian to approximate surface orientation without expensive normal estimation networks. Let \Sigmai be the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix. The eigenvector corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue provides the normal direction. 2. Material Decomposition: During training, the model optimizes per-Gaussian albedo, roughness, and metallic values. These parameters define the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) for each primitive. 3. Primary Ray Intersection: For each pixel, a primary ray is cast. The ray intersects Gaussians, and the 2D Gaussian value \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) is computed at the intersection point \mathbf{p} using the projected covariance \Sigma{2D}. 4. BRDF Evaluation: The color contribution is calculated using a PBR shading model (e.g., Cook-Torrance) rather than simple spherical harmonics. The direct lighting is reconstructed using the environment map, while indirect lighting may be modeled via spherical harmonics or baked into the albedo if precomputed. 5. Secondary Ray Tracing (Interreflections): To model interreflections, secondary rays (reflections and refractions) are spawned upon primary ray interactions with Gaussians. Ray tracing techniques are integrated to trace these secondary rays, allowing light to bounce between surfaces. This step distinguishes it from methods that only compute direct lighting. 6. Compositing: Colors are accumulated using front-to-back alpha blending. The final intensity If for a pixel is: If = \sum{i=1}^N ci \tilde{\sigma}i \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \tilde{\sigma}j \tilde{\mathcal{G}}j(\mathbf{p})) where ci is the PBR-computed color (including direct and indirect lighting contributions), \tilde{\sigma}i is the opacity, and \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) is the 2D Gaussian density. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendergaussiansplattingwithreflection(gaussians, camera, envmap): """ Renders a scene using 3D Gaussians with PBR and secondary rays. """ imageheight, imagewidth = camera.resolution outputimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) # Precompute normals from covariance matrices for g in gaussians: # Eigenvector of smallest eigenvalue of covariance matrix Sigma eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eig(g.covariance) g.normal = eigenvectors[:, argmin(eigenvalues)] # Sort gaussians by depth for compositing gaussians = sortbydepth(gaussians, camera) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Cast primary ray ray = camera.getray(x, y) # Collect visible gaussians along ray visiblegaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if intersectsray(g.boundingbox, ray): # Compute 2D Gaussian value at intersection # Project covariance to 2D: Sigma2D = J W Sigma W^T J^T sigma2d = projectcovariance(g.covariance, camera) t = intersectraygaussian(ray, g) if t is not None: p = ray.origin + t ray.direction gval = gaussian2dvalue(p, g.center, sigma2d) if gval > epsilon: visiblegaussians.append((g, gval, t)) # Sort by depth (front-to-back) visiblegaussians.sort(key=lambda item: item[2]) accumulatedcolor = zeros(3) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for g, gval, t in visiblegaussians: # Evaluate BRDF # Direct lighting from env map directlight = evaluatedirectlighting(g.normal, ray.direction, envmap) # Secondary rays for interreflections # Spawn reflection ray reflectionray = reflectray(ray, g.normal) indirectlight = tracesecondaryray(reflectionray, gaussians, envmap) # Combine lighting totallighting = directlight + indirectlight # Compute material color # ci = albedo diffuseterm + specularterm totallighting color = computepbrcolor(g.albedo, g.roughness, g.metallic, g.normal, ray.direction, totallighting) # Alpha blending alpha = g.opacity gval accumulatedcolor += color alpha (1 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedalpha += alpha (1 - accumulatedalpha) if accumulatedalpha > 1.0 - epsilon: break outputimage[y, x] = accumulatedcolor return outputimage def tracesecondaryray(ray, gaussians, envmap): """ Traces a secondary ray (reflection/refraction) to model interreflections. """ # Simple recursive trace or limited depth # Intersect with scene geometry (Gaussians) closesthit = None mint = infinity for g in gaussians: if intersectsray(g.boundingbox, ray): t = intersectraygaussian(ray, g) if t is not None and t < mint: mint = t closesthit = g if closesthit is None: # Hit background, sample environment map return sampleenvmap(ray.direction, envmap) else: # Recursive call or bounce # For simplicity, assume one bounce newray = reflectray(ray, closesthit.normal) return tracesecondaryray(newray, gaussians, envmap) Parameters: Ray Tracing Depth: Not given in the sources. Typically limited to 1-2 bounces for performance. BRDF Model: Cook-Torrance or similar microfacet model. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Estimation Accuracy: The normal derived from the shortest axis of the Gaussian kernel may be inaccurate for highly anisotropic or noisy Gaussians. Training Stability: Optimizing per-Gaussian BRDF parameters can be unstable. Constraints such as anisotropy loss may be needed to prevent excessive stretching. Performance: Secondary ray tracing significantly increases computational cost compared to standard 3DGS. Time Complexity: Higher than standard 3DGS due to BRDF evaluation and secondary ray tracing. Memory Complexity: Increased storage per Gaussian for albedo, roughness, metallic, and normal attributes. Strengths: Enables relighting under novel illumination; handles highly reflective surfaces better than standard 3DGS; leverages 3DGS's natural normal estimation for efficiency. Limitations: Slower rendering speed due to ray tracing; complex training process; potential artifacts from inaccurate normal estimation. When to use: Scenes with significant specular reflections or when relighting is required. When not to use: Real-time applications requiring maximum performance where reflections are not critical; scenes with complex subsurface scattering not modeled by the BRDF. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting uses an emission-absorption model, which bakes lighting into spherical harmonics, limiting its ability to render reflective surfaces or support relighting. Methods like Gaussian-Shader, 3DGS-DR, and IRGS were developed to incorporate classical reflection and shading concepts into the 3DGS framework. These methods estimate per-Gaussian BRDF and lighting decomposition, enabling relighting under novel illumination. The approach leverages the fact that 3DGS naturally offers good normal estimation via the shortest axis of the Gaussian kernel, avoiding the time-consuming training and slow rendering speeds associated with normal estimation in NeRF-based PBR methods. head: GIR, GS-IR, GS-IR / GIR
body: Inverse Rendering with Gaussians (GS-IR / GIR) adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting to recover physically accurate material and lighting properties from images by optimizing differentiable shading models. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a split-sum approximation to handle indirect lighting and specular reflections. GS-IR extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline by replacing the static color attribute with a parameterized shading model. The method optimizes geometry, appearance, and lighting simultaneously. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images \{Ik\}, initial 3D Gaussian points (typically from Structure-from-Motion or a pre-trained 3DGS), and an initial environment light probe. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian attributes (position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, albedo \mathbf{c}d, roughness \rho) and a high-dynamic-range environment map \mathbf{L}e. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (parameterized as rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c}{d,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Diffuse albedo. \rhoi \in [0, 1]: Roughness parameter. \mathbf{L}e: Environment light probe, typically stored as a pre-filtered cubemap or spherical harmonics. Rendering Equation with Split-Sum Approximation: The method uses a split-sum approximation to decouple direct and indirect lighting. The outgoing radiance is approximated as: Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) \approx L{\text{diffuse}} + L{\text{specular}} Where: L{\text{diffuse}} = \frac{\mathbf{c}{d,i}}{\pi} \int{\Omega} Li(\omegai) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai) d\omegai L{\text{specular}} = \int{\Omega} Li(\omegai) fr(\omegai, \omegao) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai) d\omegai The diffuse term integrates against the environment map directly, while the specular term uses a pre-filtered environment map or importance sampling to handle sharp reflections efficiently. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a sparse point cloud. Set initial albedo to mean image color, roughness to a mid-range value (e.g., 0.5), and environment map to a uniform or captured probe. 2. Projection and Rasterization: Project Gaussians to screen space using the camera matrix. Sort primitives by depth within tiles to ensure correct front-to-back compositing. 3. Shading Evaluation: For each pixel covered by a Gaussian, compute the normal \mathbf{n} from the Gaussian's covariance. Accurate normal estimation can be derived from computed depth maps or using the shortest direction axis of Gaussians. Evaluate the BRDF using the current albedo, roughness, and environment map \mathbf{L}e. 4. Compositing: Accumulate colors using front-to-back alpha blending. 5. Loss Computation: Compare rendered images with ground truth using L1 and SSIM losses. 6. Optimization: Update Gaussian attributes and environment map parameters using an Adam optimizer. Regularization terms may be applied to stabilize normals and prevent overfitting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def rendergaussiangir(gaussians, camera, envmap): # 1. Project Gaussians to screen space screengaussians = [] for g in gaussians: campos = camera.worldtocam(g.position) screenpos = camera.projection(campos) screengaussians.append({g, 'screenpos': screenpos}) # 2. Sort by depth within tiles screengaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['screenpos'].z) renderedimage = np.zeros((camera.height, camera.width, 3)) for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): color = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) alpha = 0.0 for g in screengaussians: if not gaussiancoverspixel(g, x, y): continue # Compute normal from Gaussian covariance n = computenormalfromcovariance(g.covariance) # Split-sum shading diffuse = (g.albedo / math.pi) integrateenvmapdiffuse(envmap, n) specular = evaluatespecularbrdf(n, camera.viewdir, g.roughness, envmap) radiance = diffuse + specular # Alpha blending weight = g.opacity gaussianpdf(g, x, y) color = color (1 - weight) + radiance weight alpha = alpha (1 - weight) + weight if alpha > 0.99: break renderedimage[y, x] = color return renderedimage def optimizegsir(images, gaussians, envmap, numepochs=1000): for epoch in range(numepochs): for imagepath, camera in images: gtimage = loadimagefromdisk(imagepath) predimage = rendergaussiangir(gaussians, camera, envmap) loss = l1loss(predimage, gtimage) + ssimloss(predimage, gtimage) loss.backward() gaussians.optimizer.step() envmap.optimizer.step() gaussians.optimizer.zerograd() envmap.optimizer.zerograd() def gaussiancoverspixel(g, x, y): return True def computenormalfromcovariance(cov): return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) def integrateenvmapdiffuse(envmap, normal): return np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) def evaluatespecularbrdf(normal, viewdir, roughness, envmap): return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) def gaussianpdf(g, x, y): return math.exp(-0.5) def l1loss(pred, gt): return np.mean(np.abs(pred - gt)) def ssimloss(pred, gt): return 0.0 def loadimagefromdisk(path): return np.zeros((100, 100, 3)) Methods adapting inverse rendering techniques to 3DGS to handle specular reflections by simplifying the classical rendering equation. These approaches rely on accurate normal estimation, which can be derived from computed depth maps or using the shortest direction axis of Gaussians. The different lighting conditions are then encoded via integrated shading functions. While these 3DGS-based methods achieve rapid convergence, they still introduce substantial noise in geometry, material, and lighting, which remains a limitation for high-fidelity rendering. Time Complexity: Optimization is significantly faster than NeRF-based inverse rendering methods due to the explicit representation and rasterization pipeline, but slower than standard 3DGS due to additional shading computations and environment map updates. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional attributes (albedo, roughness) per Gaussian and the environment map. The environment map size depends on the resolution of the pre-filtered cubemap or SH degree. Strengths: Enables relighting and material editing; faster convergence than implicit methods; handles specular reflections better than standard 3DGS. Limitations: Noise in geometry and material estimation can be substantial. When to use: When relighting or material recovery is required and real-time rendering speed is important. When not to use: When high-fidelity, noise-free material recovery is critical without extensive post-processing or regularization. Inverse rendering with Gaussians emerged as a natural extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23], aiming to add physical properties to the efficient explicit representation. Early attempts to adapt inverse rendering to 3DGS focused on simplifying the classical rendering equation to handle specular reflections. These methods typically derive normals from depth maps or Gaussian axes and encode lighting via integrated shading functions. While they offer rapid convergence compared to NeRF-based approaches, they often suffer from noise in the recovered geometry and materials. name: GaussianShader Material Model
head: GaussianShader
body: GaussianShader enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by incorporating trainable material parameters—diffuse color, specular intensity, roughness, and surface normal—along with a global environment map to achieve physically-based rendering (PBR). It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by disentangling geometry from material properties, allowing for accurate specular reflections and relighting capabilities. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a 3D scene. Outputs: A rendered image and optimized 3D Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: Each Gaussian kernel p stores the following trainable parameters: Position: \mathbf{x}p Opacity: \sigmap Covariance: \mathbf{A}p Diffuse color: \mathbf{d}p Specular intensity: \mathbf{s}p Roughness: \rhop Surface normal: \mathbf{n}p Global Environment Map: \mathcal{E} (pre-filtered into mip maps). Rendering Formula: The color \mathbf{c}p for a kernel is computed as: \mathbf{c}p(\mathbf{r}i) = \mathbf{d}p + \mathbf{s}p \odot \mathcal{L}s(\mathbf{r}i, \mathbf{n}p, \rhop) Where: \mathbf{r}i is the view direction from the camera to pixel i. \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. \mathcal{L}s(\mathbf{r}i, \mathbf{n}p, \rhop) is the specular light contribution for the kernel along \mathbf{r}i, dependent on the normal and roughness. This term is pre-filtered into multiple mip maps. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Separate foreground objects and background from input images. Extract the surface of masked objects. 2. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussian kernels with position, opacity, covariance, and material parameters (\mathbf{d}p, \mathbf{s}p, \rhop, \mathbf{n}p). 3. Shading: For each pixel, determine the view direction \mathbf{r}i. Compute the kernel color \mathbf{c}p using the PBR formula above, utilizing the pre-filtered environment map for \mathcal{L}s. 4. Splatting: Project the 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space. Calculate the 2D Gaussian weight Gk(i) for the k-th kernel at pixel i based on the kernel center's depth and covariance. 5. Compositing: Accumulate colors front-to-back using the standard 3DGS alpha blending process. 6. Optimization: Compare the rendered image with the ground truth training view. Compute a loss function and back-propagate to update \mathbf{x}p, \sigmap, \mathbf{A}p, \mathbf{d}p, \mathbf{s}p, \rhop, \mathbf{n}p. 7. Constraint (Optional): Apply normal orientation constraints to handle challenging reflective scenes, similar to Ref-NeRF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-stretching: Gaussian kernels may over-stretch near solid object surfaces, causing rendering artifacts. An anisotropy loss can be applied to mitigate this. Lighting Overfitting: Geometry attributes (like opacity) may overfit to input lighting conditions, leading to blending artifacts when relit. This method avoids some such issues by explicitly modeling material parameters, though deferred shading techniques (as in DeferredGS) are noted as a separate solution to this specific problem. A method that separately models texture and lighting. It defines additional material parameters on each Gaussian to represent texture and approximates lighting using a learnable environment map. Shares the same disentanglement paradigm as GaussianShader by binding material parameters to 3D Gaussians. It adds normal orientation constraints to Gaussians to deal with more challenging reflective scenes, similar to Ref-NeRF. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides visually accurate representations of specular reflections and simulated interactions between solids and fluids. Allows for independent editing of texture and lighting. Limitations: Requires optimization of additional material parameters per kernel, increasing training complexity compared to standard 3DGS. GaussianShader was introduced to enhance 3DGS with physically-based rendering capabilities. It builds on the 3DGS pipeline and Position-Based Dynamics (PBD). The method is cited in the context of unified particles for motion synthesis and rendering.
