name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Vectors
head: Feature-3DGS, Semantic 3DGS, Open-Vocabulary 3DGS
body: This method extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by attaching a high-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{f}i to each Gaussian primitive, enabling the rendering of semantic, linguistic, or latent feature maps rather than just color. It solves the problem of integrating 2D vision-language models (e.g., CLIP, LSeg) into a 3D representation, allowing for real-time open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and phrase grounding. It differs from sibling methods by serving as the foundational rasterization mechanism for feature accumulation; while siblings like LangSplat or LSeg Feature Encoding apply specific encoders or decoding heads, this article defines the core differentiable alpha-blending accumulation of arbitrary feature vectors \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^d that underpins the entire family. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}, where each gi is defined by position \mathbf{x}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{s}i), opacity \alphai, and a feature vector \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^d. The feature dimension d is typically 512 (CLIP) or 768 (LSeg/CLIP text), but can vary. Output: A 2D feature map \mathbf{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d}, where each pixel p contains the accumulated feature vector \mathbf{F}(p). Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix (or quaternion). \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity (clamped to [0, 1]). \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^d: Feature vector. Rendering Steps: 1. Projection: For each Gaussian i, compute the 2D mean \mathbf{\mu}i and covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}'i in screen space using the camera projection matrix \mathbf{P} and Jacobian \mathbf{J}: \mathbf{\mu}i = \mathbf{P} \mathbf{x}i \mathbf{\Sigma}'i = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^T \mathbf{R}i^T \mathbf{J}^T where \mathbf{S}i is the diagonal scale matrix. 2. Sorting: For each pixel p, identify the set of overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p. Sort \mathcal{O}p front-to-back based on depth zi relative to the camera. 3. Accumulation: Compute the feature vector \mathbf{F}(p) for pixel p using the shared principle of differentiable alpha-blending: \mathbf{F}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{f}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where: \mathbf{f}i is the feature vector of the i-th Gaussian in the sorted order. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance from all preceding Gaussians j < i. If \mathcal{O}p is empty, \mathbf{F}(p) = \mathbf{0}. 4. Post-processing: The resulting feature map \mathbf{F} is passed to a downstream task, such as a segmentation head or a similarity comparison with text embeddings from a vision-language model (e.g., CLIP). Parameters: Feature dimension d: Not given in the sources (varies by encoder, e.g., 512, 768). Opacity \alphai: Optimized during training via photometric loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: High-dimensional feature vectors may require float32 or float16 precision to avoid quantization artifacts during accumulation. Boundaries: Gaussians partially outside the image bounds must be clipped or handled to avoid out-of-bounds memory access during rasterization. Degenerate Input: If all \alphai = 0, \mathbf{F}(p) = \mathbf{0}. If \alphai = 1 for any i, subsequent Gaussians in the stack contribute nothing to \mathbf{F}(p). A mechanism to modulate rendered semantic features based on the scale of the Gaussians, using learned or fixed gate vectors derived from sampled scales. It is chosen when scale-dependent semantic consistency is required, such as in multi-scale segmentation tasks. It differs from standard feature accumulation by introducing a gating factor g that multiplies the accumulated feature. The steps are: 1. Map the distribution of sampled scales to a Gaussian distribution using a transformation function self.qtrans(sampledscales). 2. Compute gates: If scaleawaredim <= 0 or scaleawaredim >= 32, compute gates by passing sampled scales through a learned gate network: gates = self.scalegate(sampledscales.unsqueeze(-1)). Otherwise, discretize scales to integers: intsampledscales = ((1 - sampledscales.squeeze()) scaleawaredim).long(), then lookup pre-computed gates: gates = self.fixedscalegate[intsampledscales].detach(). 3. Repeat rendered features for each sampled scale: featurewithscale = renderedfeatures.unsqueeze(0).repeat([sampledscales.shape[0], 1, 1, 1]). 4. Multiply features by gate vectors: featurewithscale = featurewithscale gates.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) for rasterization, where N is the number of Gaussians and H \times W is the image resolution. The feature accumulation adds a constant factor proportional to the feature dimension d. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot d) to store feature vectors for all Gaussians, plus O(H \cdot W \cdot d) for the output feature map. Measured Performance: Real-time frame rates are achievable on modern GPUs due to the efficiency of the Gaussian rasterizer, similar to standard 3DGS. Strengths: Enables open-vocabulary understanding without retraining the 3D representation; leverages the speed of 3DGS rasterization. Limitations: Feature quality depends on the 2D encoder used during training; high-dimensional features increase memory usage. When to use: When semantic or linguistic understanding is required from a 3D scene, especially for dynamic or real-time applications. When not to use: When only geometric or photometric rendering is needed; when memory is constrained and d is large. Originated from the observation that the speed of the 3DGS rasterizer makes it an ideal platform for distilling 2D vision-model features into a 3D representation. Feature-3DGS and LangSplat pioneered this direction by adding high-dimensional feature vectors to Gaussians. Language Embedded 3D Gaussians expanded this to full scene understanding, encoding object-level embeddings for phrase grounding. Subsequent works like SplatTalk and 3D Vision-Language GS further extended these capabilities. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) yzslab/gaussian-splatting-lightning, https://github.com/yzslab/gaussian-splatting-lightning, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Language Embedded 3D Gaussians
head: LE3DG
body: Language Embedded 3D Gaussians (LE3DG) extends differentiable Gaussian splatting to full scene understanding by encoding object-level embeddings for phrase grounding alongside standard pixel-level features. It enables real-time open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and 3D visual reasoning by allowing rendered feature maps to be queried directly with natural language embeddings from vision-language models. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each defined by position \mathbf{t}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients for color, and a language feature vector \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^d. The input also includes a text query embedding \mathbf{t}{query} from a frozen vision-language model (e.g., CLIP). Output: A 2D feature map \mathbf{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d} representing the scene's semantic structure, which can be compared against \mathbf{t}{query} to produce segmentation masks or localization scores. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: \mathbf{t}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix. \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c}i: Spherical harmonics coefficients for color. \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^d: Language/semantic feature vector. Rendering Pipeline: 1. Projection: Project 3D Gaussian centers \mathbf{t}i to 2D screen space using the camera projection matrix. Compute the 2D covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}'i via Jacobian transformation of the 3D covariance. 2. Sorting: For each pixel p, identify overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p and sort them front-to-back based on depth zi. 3. Feature Blending: Compute the rendered feature vector \mathbf{F}(p) using differentiable alpha blending: \mathbf{F}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{f}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{f}i is the language feature of the i-th Gaussian, \alphai is its opacity, and the product term is the transmittance from preceding Gaussians. If \mathcal{O}p is empty, \mathbf{F}(p) = \mathbf{0}. 4. Querying: Compare the rendered feature map \mathbf{F} against the text query embedding \mathbf{t}{query} (e.g., via cosine similarity) to generate semantic scores. Training: The language features \mathbf{f}i are optimized or initialized to align with the vision-language embedding space. The pipeline is differentiable, allowing gradients to flow from the segmentation loss back to Gaussian attributes and deformation parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: High-dimensional feature vectors (d) may require careful normalization to prevent numerical instability during alpha blending. Ambiguity: Overlapping objects with similar semantic features may result in blended features that do not correspond to any single object, requiring post-processing or specific architectural constraints. A post-processing pipeline for selecting the best semantic-level binary mask by thresholding and evaluating average relevancy within masks. For each class query, three relevancy maps are obtained corresponding to different semantic levels defined by SAM. A threshold of 0.4 is applied to each map: scores below 0.4 become 0, and scores above 0.4 become 1, producing three binary maps. The average relevancy scores within the mask region are calculated for each binary map, and the map with the highest average response is selected as the final predicted binary mask. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the sorting and blending steps, similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, allowing real-time performance. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases by O(N \cdot d) due to the storage of language feature vectors for each of the N Gaussians, where d is the feature dimension. Strengths: Enables open-vocabulary understanding and phrase grounding without retraining the segmentation head for each new vocabulary. Limitations: Requires a vision-language model for query embedding; alignment between geometry and semantics may be imperfect without distillation or specific training. Language Embedded 3D Gaussians builds on the differentiable rendering framework of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It expands feature blending to full scene understanding, encoding object-level embeddings for phrase grounding in addition to pixel-level features. This approach facilitates tasks like 3D visual question answering and zero-shot semantic reasoning by projecting vision-language models into the 3DGS framework. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) LangSplat: 3D Language Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01895, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D Semantic Segmentation Post-processing (3D-OVS)
head: 3D-OVS Semantic Segmentation Pipeline
body: 3D-OVS is a post-processing pipeline for semantic segmentation in 3D Gaussian Splatting systems that resolves ambiguity by selecting the optimal semantic level from multiple candidate relevancy maps. It solves the problem of inconsistent or noisy semantic predictions by thresholding, binarizing, and evaluating average relevancy within masks to choose the best binary mask. It differs from direct thresholding by explicitly comparing multiple semantic levels (derived from different granularities) to mitigate outlier impact. Inputs: Three relevancy maps for a single class query, representing three distinct semantic levels defined by SAM (Segment Anything Model). A threshold value T = 0.4. Outputs: A single binary mask representing the final semantic segmentation for the queried class. Data Structures: Relevancy Map: A 2D image (or 3D volume projected to 2D) where each pixel/voxel contains a float32 score in [0, 1] indicating the relevance of that location to the semantic query. Binary Map: A 2D image where each pixel/voxel is 0 or 1, derived from thresholding the relevancy map. Steps: 1. Thresholding: For each of the three relevancy maps, apply a hard threshold T = 0.4. If score < 0.4, set to 0. If score \ge 0.4, set to 1. This produces three binary maps. 2. Mask Region Calculation: Identify the region of interest (mask) for each binary map. This is typically the set of pixels where the binary value is 1. 3. Average Relevancy Calculation: For each binary map, calculate the average relevancy score of the original (pre-thresholded) relevancy map values within the mask region defined by that binary map. Let Ri be the i-th relevancy map. Let Bi be the corresponding binary map. Let Mi = \{p \mid Bi[p] = 1\} be the mask region. Calculate average relevancy Ai: Ai = \frac{1}{|Mi|} \sum{p \in Mi} Ri[p] If |Mi| = 0, Ai is undefined or treated as 0. 4. Selection: Select the binary map Bk corresponding to the highest average relevancy Ak as the final predicted binary mask. Parameters: Threshold T = 0.4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Mask: If a binary map has no pixels above threshold, the average relevancy cannot be calculated. The implementation must handle this, e.g., by assigning a score of 0 or ignoring that candidate. Ties: If multiple maps have the same highest average relevancy, the selection strategy is not specified in the sources. A deterministic tie-breaker (e.g., lowest index) is recommended. Precision: Relevancy scores are floats; thresholding is a hard cut, which may lead to jagged boundaries if scores are near 0.4. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectbestsemanticmask(relevancymaps, threshold=0.4): """ Selects the best semantic binary mask from three relevancy maps. Args: relevancymaps: List of 3 numpy arrays (H, W), float32, values in [0, 1]. threshold: Float, threshold for binarization. Returns: bestbinarymap: numpy array (H, W), uint8, 0 or 1. """ binarymaps = [] averagerelevancies = [] for rmap in relevancymaps: # Step 1: Thresholding bmap = (rmap >= threshold).astype(np.uint8) binarymaps.append(bmap) # Step 2 & 3: Calculate average relevancy within mask maskregion = bmap == 1 numpixels = np.sum(maskregion) if numpixels == 0: # Edge case: empty mask avgrel = 0.0 else: # Sum of relevancy scores in mask region sumrel = np.sum(rmap[maskregion]) avgrel = sumrel / numpixels averagerelevancies.append(avgrel) # Step 4: Select best bestindex = np.argmax(averagerelevancies) bestbinarymap = binarymaps[bestindex] return bestbinarymap A post-processing or training-time strategy to prune unwanted background elements (e.g., sky) from 3D Gaussian reconstructions by learning a semantic field and using it to mask out non-object regions. It assigns each Gaussian a learnable semantic feature vector, renders pixel-level semantics via alpha blending, and trains these features using cross-entropy loss against pseudo-labels from a pretrained model (e.g., Grounded-SAM). It is chosen when background noise (like sky) degrades reconstruction quality. It differs from direct thresholding by learning semantic features that are robust to noisy pseudo-labels, yielding more accurate semantics than directly using pretrained semantic maps. On the TNT dataset, it increases the F1-score from 0.38 to 0.40. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The post-processing involves thresholding and averaging over pixels, which is linear in the number of pixels N for each of the 3 maps: O(N). Memory Complexity: Requires storing 3 relevancy maps and 3 binary maps temporarily: O(N). Measured Performance: On the 3D-OVS dataset, the method consistently outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in Accuracy and mIoU. On the TNT dataset, semantic trimming (a related post-processing step) increases F1-score by 0.02. Scaling: Performance scales with image resolution; higher resolution means more pixels to process. Strengths: Mitigates outlier impact by selecting the best semantic level; robust to noisy pseudo-labels when combined with semantic trimming. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial relevancy maps; threshold is fixed at 0.4, which may not be optimal for all scenes. When to use: When multiple semantic levels are available and ambiguity exists between them. When not to use: When a single semantic level is sufficient or when real-time performance is critical and the overhead of evaluating multiple maps is prohibitive. Originated in the LangSplat paper (CVPR 2024) by the authors of 3D Language Gaussian Splatting. It is used in 3D-OVS (3D Object Localization and Semantic Segmentation) tasks to improve the accuracy of semantic predictions by leveraging multiple semantic levels. The method builds on the concept of 3D language Gaussians, which encode object-level embeddings for phrase grounding. name: LangSplat
head: Feature 3DGS
body: LangSplat (also known as Feature 3DGS) enables real-time, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation by rendering high-dimensional feature maps from 3D Gaussians that are compared against text embeddings from CLIP. It pioneers the distillation of 2D vision-model features into a 3D representation by attaching a feature vector \mathbf{f}i to each Gaussian, allowing the resulting 2D feature map to be decoded or matched against text queries without retraining the segmentation head. Inputs: 3D Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity \alphai, color) and a high-dimensional semantic feature vector \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^d for each Gaussian. Text labels or category names for querying. Outputs: A 2D feature map \mathbf{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d} and, optionally, semantic segmentation masks or selection scores for 3D Gaussians. Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores \mathbf{f}i. The dimension d is typically 512 (matching CLIP ViT-L/16) or a compressed dimension (e.g., 128) if a speed-up module is used. Text Embeddings: Text features ti \in \mathbb{R}^{512} for C categories, encoded using CLIP’s ViT-B/32 or ViT-L/16 text encoder. The rendering of the feature map follows the standard differentiable alpha-blending accumulation defined in the parent article Semantic and Language Embeddings. For a pixel p, the rendered feature vector \mathbf{F}(p) is: \mathbf{F}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{f}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathcal{O}p is the set of Gaussians sorted front-to-back covering pixel p. To perform semantic segmentation, the rendered feature map is processed as follows: 1. Reshape: The rendered feature map of shape (d, H, W) (e.g., 512 \times 360 \times 480) is reshaped to (H \times W, d) to form the image feature matrix. 2. Text Encoding: Text labels are encoded into features ti \in \mathbb{R}^{512} for C categories using a CLIP text encoder (ViT-B/32 or ViT-L/16). 3. Alignment: Matrix multiplication is applied between the image feature matrix and the text feature matrix to align pixel-level features with text queries. 4. Regularization: LSeg spatial regularization blocks are applied to the aligned features to produce the final semantic segmentation mask. For 3D Gaussian selection (e.g., for editing), semantic scores are calculated per Gaussian: 1. Text Encoding: Encode text labels using CLIP’s ViT-B/32 text encoder to obtain text features ti \in \mathbb{R}^{512} for C categories. 2. Inner Product: Calculate the inner product between the text feature and the 3D Gaussian's semantic feature \mathbf{f}i. 3. Softmax: Apply a softmax function to the inner product results to obtain semantic scores. The scores S \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C} are obtained via: S{i,c} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{f}i \cdot tc) where N is the number of Gaussians and C is the number of categories. Queried by a text label l (or list of labels), selection is performed via: Soft Selection: Based on the category l, select the corresponding column scorel = [s{1l}, s{2l}, \dots, s{Nl}]. Apply binary thresholding: for any i such that s{il} \geq th, set position i to 1 (selected); otherwise 0. Hard Selection: Implicitly defined by choosing a single category column and thresholding. Feature Dimension: 512 for direct rendering with CLIP ViT-L/16; 128 if using a Speed-up Module with upsampling. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 1e-3 for main attributes; 1e-4 for the feature decoder network in the Speed-up Module. Ground Truth Feature Size: 360 \times 480 with dimension 512 for LSeg preparation. Precision: High-dimensional feature vectors (512) increase memory usage. Using a compressed dimension (128) requires a decoder network, which must be optimized separately. Boundary: The number of categories C must match the number of text features encoded. Degenerate Input: If no Gaussians cover a pixel, \mathbf{F}(p) = \mathbf{0}. Preparation of ground-truth features using CLIP ViT-L/16 image encoder (size 360 \times 480, dim 512) and ViT-L/16 text encoder. During inference, the rendered feature (shape 512 \times 360 \times 480) is reshaped to (360 \times 480, 512) for matrix multiplication with text features (shape C, 512) to align pixel-level features with text queries. Chosen when LSeg spatial regularization is required for segmentation. Calculation of semantic scores for each 3D Gaussian by comparing its semantic feature with text features from a CLIP encoder. Text labels are encoded using CLIP’s ViT-B/32 text encoder to obtain ti \in \mathbb{R}^{512} for C categories. Scores S \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C} are obtained via softmax of the inner product. Chosen when 3D Gaussian-level selection (e.g., for editing) is needed rather than pixel-level segmentation. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is enabled by the speed of the 3DGS rasterizer. Feature processing (matrix multiplication) is O(H \cdot W \cdot d \cdot C). Memory Complexity: Proportional to N \cdot d for storing Gaussian features, where d=512 or 128. Strengths: Enables open-vocabulary semantic segmentation in real time; supports 3D Gaussian editing via text queries. Limitations: Performance is limited by the teacher encoder's capability (e.g., CLIP). High-dimensional features increase memory usage. When to use: When real-time, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation or text-guided 3D editing is required. When not to use: When only photometric rendering is needed without semantic understanding. LangSplat (Feature 3DGS) was introduced to pioneer the distillation of 2D vision-model features into a 3D representation. It leverages the speed of the 3DGS rasterizer to render feature maps that are compared against text embeddings from CLIP, enabling open-vocabulary semantic segmentation in real time. The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting by adding a high-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{f}i to each Gaussian. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Feature 3DGS: Supercharging 3D Gaussian Splatting to Enable Distilled Feature Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02048, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Text Embedding Generation with Directional Views
body: This method generates semantic text embeddings conditioned on camera viewing directions to enable view-dependent semantic understanding in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of static semantic representations by appending directional descriptors (e.g., "front view") to text prompts before encoding, allowing the system to distinguish between different viewpoints of the same object. It differs from standard semantic encoding by explicitly coupling the text latent space with spatial orientation, whereas siblings like LangSplat may use more complex cross-attention mechanisms or frozen vision-language models without explicit directional token injection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base text prompt string (e.g., "a chair"), a set of directional descriptors, and a frozen CLIP text encoder. Output: A dictionary of tensors mapping directional keys to embedding vectors. Data Structures: self.embeddings: A dictionary where keys are strings ('pos', 'neg', 'front', 'side', 'back') and values are tensors of shape [1, 77, 768] (batch size 1, sequence length 77, embedding dimension 768). Steps: 1. Tokenization: Tokenize the base prompt using the CLIP tokenizer with padding to the maximum model length. \text{inputs} = \text{tokenizer}(\text{prompt}, \text{padding}=\text{"max\length"}, \text{max\length}=\text{model\max\length}, \text{return\tensors}=\text{"pt"}) 2. Base Encoding: Pass the token IDs through the frozen CLIP text encoder to obtain the base embedding. \text{embeddings} = \text{text\encoder}(\text{inputs.input\ids})[0] 3. Directional Augmentation: For each required direction d \in \{\text{'front'}, \text{'side'}, \text{'back'}\}, append the string ', {d} view' to the original prompt. 4. Directional Encoding: Tokenize and encode the augmented prompts using the same frozen text encoder. Store the resulting tensors in self.embeddings under the corresponding keys. 5. Storage: Store the base positive/negative embeddings under keys 'pos' and 'neg' if required by the downstream segmentation or rendering pipeline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatedirectionalembeddings(self, baseprompt, textencoder, tokenizer, device): """ Generates text embeddings for base prompt and specific directional views. """ # Step 1 & 2: Encode base prompt inputs = tokenizer( baseprompt, padding="maxlength", maxlength=tokenizer.modelmaxlength, returntensors="pt") baseembed = textencoder(inputs.inputids.to(device))[0] # Initialize storage dictionary self.embeddings = { 'pos': baseembed, 'neg': -baseembed # Standard negation for contrastive loss } # Step 3 & 4: Encode directional views directions = ['front', 'side', 'back'] for d in directions: # Append directional descriptor augmentedprompt = f"{baseprompt}, {d} view" # Tokenize and encode dirinputs = tokenizer( augmentedprompt, padding="maxlength", maxlength=tokenizer.modelmaxlength, returntensors="pt") dirembed = textencoder(dirinputs.inputids.to(device))[0] # Store in dictionary self.embeddings[d] = dirembed return self.embeddings Parameters: Direction Set: ['front', 'side', 'back']. For forward-facing scenes (e.g., LLFF dataset), 'top-down view' is excluded. Sequence Length: 77 tokens (standard CLIP limit). Embedding Dimension: 768 (CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder output). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Prompt Syntax: The comma and space before the direction descriptor (, {d} view) are critical for CLIP's tokenization consistency. Omitting them may result in invalid or semantically distinct tokens. Frozen Encoder: The text encoder must remain frozen during the 3D Gaussian optimization process to maintain the stability of the semantic space. A variant where the directional prompt suffix is not pre-computed but dynamically concatenated to the input caption at each training iteration based on the current camera location in the scene. This allows the model to adaptively condition the semantic representation on the instantaneous viewpoint rather than a fixed set of canonical views. It is chosen when dynamic viewpoint-dependent semantic consistency is required during optimization, such as in novel view synthesis with semantic constraints. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L), where N is the number of directional views (typically 3-4) and L is the sequence length (77). This is a one-time cost per prompt during initialization or prompt update. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot L \cdot D), where D is the embedding dimension (768). For 4 directions, this is negligible compared to Gaussian attributes. Performance: Enables view-dependent semantic segmentation and editing. Metrics like CLIP Direction Similarity and CLIP Direction Consistency are used to evaluate the alignment between text changes and image changes. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages robust pre-trained CLIP features; decouples semantic conditioning from geometry optimization. Limitations: Limited to the discrete set of directions defined; does not support arbitrary continuous directional interpolation without additional interpolation steps. Originating from extensions of 3D Gaussian Splatting for semantic and language-aware rendering, this method builds on the principle of differentiable feature accumulation. It was notably detailed in the context of TexGS-VolVis for text-driven non-photorealistic style editing and Blended-NeRF for zero-shot object generation. The approach leverages the CLIP text encoder, which was introduced by Radford et al. (2021), to provide a shared latent space between images and text. dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, https://github.com/dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Blended-NeRF: Zero-Shot Object Generation and Blending in Existing Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.12760v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: TexGS-VolVis Representation and Optimization
head: TexGS-VolVis
body: TexGS-VolVis is a method for representing and editing volume visualization (VolVis) scenes using textured 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). It solves the problem of decoupling geometry from appearance in text-driven non-photorealistic style editing (NPSE), allowing for geometry-consistent stylization without the elliptical artifacts common in coupled representations. Unlike methods that freeze geometry to prevent distortion, TexGS-VolVis uses explicit 2D texture maps to store appearance, preserving geometric fidelity while enabling rich visual expressiveness. Inputs: Multi-view images of a volumetric dataset and text prompts for style transfer or refinement. Outputs: A scene representation consisting of 2D Gaussian primitives with geometry, shading, and texture attributes, along with rendered stylized images. Data Structures: The scene is represented by N 2D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive stores attributes in 32-bit floating-point format. 1. Geometry Attributes: \mu: Center position (3 floats). tu, tv: Orientation vectors, represented as a quaternion (4 floats). su, sv: Scale factors (2 floats). o: Opacity (1 float). 2. Shading Attributes: ka: Ambient coefficient (1 float). kd: Diffuse coefficient (1 float). ks: Specular coefficient (1 float). \beta: Shininess/exponent (1 float). 3. Texture Attribute: Stored separately from individual splats. It is a global texture map shared by the scene. The total number of texels T{total} is fixed per basic scene. Parameter Count: Given N primitives, the total number of parameters for geometry and shading is calculated as: \text{# params} = 3N + 4N + N + N + N + N + N + N + N Where: 3N corresponds to \mu. 4N corresponds to the quaternion for \{tu, tv\}. The remaining N terms correspond to su, sv, o, ka, kd, ks, \beta (1 float each). Optimization Phases: The method proceeds in three sequential phases: 1. 2DGS Initialization: Initialize the geometry and basic appearance using 2DGS. This phase uses explicit ray-splat intersection for perspective-correct splatting and accurate geometry reconstruction. 2. Shading Attributes Optimization: Optimize \{ka, kd, ks, \beta\}. This improves reconstruction accuracy by modeling view-dependent color variations. 3. Texture Attribute Optimization: Optimize the global texture map. This phase introduces a sparsity regularization term that encourages minimal texture values, which may slightly reduce reconstruction accuracy compared to the shading-only phase. Spherical harmonic parameters and view-independent color c{ind} are used only in early phases and are not retrained in the final representation. Scene Editing and Composition: Text Prompt Refinement: Users can iteratively apply new text prompts to an already stylized scene. The previous style pattern is partially preserved while being updated according to the latest prompt. Multi-Scene Composition: The framework accommodates multiple basic scenes (e.g., different transfer functions) in a single visualization. Each basic scene is edited independently and then seamlessly composed. This composition requires no additional optimization, incurring zero extra training costs. Relighting: Lighting direction is adjusted by modifying azimuthal and polar angles, achieving smooth and consistent relighting across the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def texgsvolvisoptimize(multiviewimages, textprompts, numprimitivestarget): N = numprimitivestarget # Phase 1: 2DGS Initialization mu = zeros((N, 3)) # Center positions quatt = randomunitquaternions(N) # Orientation for {tu, tv} su = ones(N) # Scale u sv = ones(N) # Scale v o = ones(N) # Opacity primitives = {'mu': mu, 'quatt': quatt, 'su': su, 'sv': sv, 'o': o} # Phase 2: Shading Attributes Optimization ka = zeros(N); kd = zeros(N); ks = zeros(N); beta = ones(N) shading = {'ka': ka, 'kd': kd, 'ks': ks, 'beta': beta} for in range(shadingiterations): rendered = projectandrasterize(primitives, shading, multiviewimages) loss = meansquarederror(rendered, multiviewimages) shading = gradientdescentstep(shading, loss) # Phase 3: Texture Attribute Optimization Ttotal = 10000000 texturemap = zeros(Ttotal) for in range(textureiterations): rendered = projectandrasterize(primitives, shading, texturemap, multiviewimages) loss = meansquarederror(rendered, multiviewimages) + sparsitylambda sum(texturemap) texturemap = gradientdescentstep(texturemap, loss) return primitives, shading, texturemap def editscene(primitives, shading, texturemap, newtextprompt): updatedtexture = applyip2prefinement(texturemap, newtextprompt) return primitives, shading, updatedtexture def composescenes(scenelist): composed = concatenateattributes(scenelist) return composed def relightscene(primitives, shading, texturemap, azimuth, polar): rendered = projectandrasterize(primitives, shading, texturemap, lightazimuth=azimuth, lightpolar=polar) return rendered Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low-Texture Styles: Flat or low-texture styles cause overly smoothed results, obscuring internal details. Complex Structures: Fragmented or complex structures lack continuous surfaces, preventing coherent style application. Prompt Misinterpretation: Text-driven editing relies on the pretrained IP2P model, which can misinterpret prompts (e.g., associating 'leaf beetle' with green instead of red/yellow/black). Rugged Surfaces: Rugged or highly detailed surfaces (e.g., wood) are harder to fit than smooth ones (e.g., five jets) because they produce complex lighting effects in multi-view images, complicating geometry reconstruction. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The texture attribute dominates memory usage. For a fixed T{total} = 1 \times 10^7 texels, the texture consumes ~114.5 MB per basic scene, regardless of the number of primitives N. Geometry and shading attributes scale linearly with N. On the beetle dataset (47,767 primitives), geometry uses 1.8 MB, shading uses 0.7 MB, texture uses 114.5 MB, and the total is ~117 MB. Texture accounts for >95% of model size. Time: Fitting performance is fast. On the five jets dataset (56,836 primitives), fitting takes 0.8 minutes. Measured Performance: Five Jets Dataset: PSNR is 36.83 dB, SSIM is 0.9889, CPU/GPU memory is 10.0/5.6 GB, and primitives count is 56,836. Other Datasets: PSNR ranges from 24.58 dB (Ionization) to 36.83 dB (Five Jets), and SSIM ranges from 0.8565 to 0.9889. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Decoupling geometry and appearance eliminates elliptical artifacts in text-driven NPSE while preserving visual expressiveness. The method supports iterative text refinement and multi-scene composition with zero extra training cost. It uses 2DGS for accurate geometry reconstruction and perspective-correct splatting. Limitations: Texture memory usage is high and fixed per scene, making compression necessary for large-scale applications. The method struggles with rugged surfaces and low-texture styles. It relies on an external IP2P model for text interpretation, which can be unreliable. When to Use: Use for text-driven non-photorealistic style editing of volume visualizations where geometry consistency is critical. Use when multiple basic scenes (e.g., different transfer functions) need to be composed. Do not use for scenes with highly fragmented structures or when low-texture styles are required, as results may be overly smoothed or incoherent. TexGS-VolVis was introduced in the paper "TexGS-VolVis: Expressive Scene Editing for Volume Visualization via Textured Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), which uses explicit ray-splat intersection for perspective-correct splatting and natively supports 2D texture maps, making it superior for geometry-consistent editing compared to standard 3DGS. The method addresses limitations in previous text-driven NPSE methods that either froze geometry (reducing expressiveness) or coupled geometry and appearance (causing artifacts). TexGS-VolVis: Expressive Scene Editing for Volume Visualization via Textured Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3634643, fetched 2026-10-30

name: LSeg Feature Encoding
head: LSeg
body: LSeg Feature Encoding utilizes the LSeg zero-shot segmentation model as a teacher network to distill semantic features into a 3D neural representation (such as a NeRF or Gaussian field). It solves the problem of generating semantically meaningful feature maps from 3D scenes without requiring per-scene manual annotations by leveraging pretrained vision-language models. It is distinguished from sibling methods like LangSplat by its specific reliance on LSeg’s multi-scale inference pipeline for feature extraction, whereas other methods may use direct CLIP embeddings or different architectural encoders. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D image I of the scene from a specific camera pose, and a set of text query labels T. Output: A 2D feature map \mathbf{F}{img} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d} corresponding to the input image resolution, where d is the feature dimension (typically 512 or 768 depending on the encoder). Data Structures: Image Encoder: Vision Transformer Large with 16x16 patches (ViT-L/16). Text Encoder: CLIP’s Vision Transformer Base with 32x32 patches (ViT-B/32). Feature Map: Resized to the original image dimensions via interpolation after initial computation on reduced-size patches. Steps: 1. Text Encoding: Encode the text query labels T into a text embedding vector \mathbf{t} using the CLIP ViT-B/32 text encoder. 2. Image Encoding: Pass the input image I through the ViT-L/16 image encoder to obtain patch-level visual features. 3. Multi-Scale Inference: To stabilize features and mitigate artifacts from discrete patch processing, perform inference at multiple scales. For the Replica dataset, use scales: [0.75, 0.83, 0.92, 1.0, 1.08, 1.17, 1.25]. For other datasets, use scales: [0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2.0, 2.25]. Note: Large scales involve zooming and cropping the image. While this increases effective resolution, it may lose context information and produce noisy features with incorrect semantic understanding. 4. Feature Aggregation: Combine the features from all scales. The official implementation averages or aggregates these multi-scale predictions to produce a robust feature map. 5. Resizing: Resize the resulting feature map to the original image resolution H \times W using interpolation. 6. Distillation Target: The resulting map \mathbf{F}{img} serves as the target feature map for distilling features into the 3D neural representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lsegfeatureencoding(image: Tensor, textqueries: List[str], datasettype: str) -> Tensor: """ Computes LSeg feature map for a given image and text queries. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Data: LSeg is not robust to OOD data (e.g., "fossils", "T-Rex", "Triceratops") due to overfitting to biases in its training datasets, which are heavily skewed towards traffic scenes. Small Objects: Small objects or parts are often not discriminative by the network. Large Scale Artifacts: Using large inference scales may lose context information and produce noisy features with wrong semantic understanding. This variant refers to the specific application of LSeg as a teacher network to distill features into NeRFs, leveraging pretrained CLIP models as text and image feature encoders. It is chosen for its simplicity of implementation. Other concurrent models or text-unconditional encoders can be used as alternatives, but LSeg is preferred in this context for its direct zero-shot segmentation capability via CLIP. The model is trained on seven datasets: ADE20K, BDD, Cityscapes, COCO-Panoptic, IDD, Mapillary Vistas, and SUN RGBD. Strengths: Provides zero-shot semantic segmentation capabilities for 3D scenes without per-scene annotations. Multi-scale inference stabilizes features and alleviates artifacts caused by discrete patch processing in ViTs. Limitations: Performance degrades significantly on out-of-distribution data due to training dataset bias (traffic scenes). Large inference scales can introduce noise and loss of context. When to use: When zero-shot semantic understanding is required for 3D scene editing or feature distillation, and the scene content is within the distribution of standard segmentation datasets (e.g., indoor scenes, traffic). When not to use: For scenes containing objects outside the training distribution (e.g., dinosaurs, fossils) or when high precision on small objects is critical. These models use pretrained CLIP as both a text encoder and an image feature encoder, training zero-shot image semantic segmentation models in freezing or finetuning manners. name: LSeg Teacher Network for Feature Distillation
head: LSeg Distillation, LSeg Teacher
body: This method uses 2D vision-language models, specifically LSeg, as teacher networks to distill semantic features into 3D representations (such as NeRF or Gaussian Splatting), leveraging pretrained CLIP models for text and image encoding. It differs from global embedding approaches by providing pixel-level or patch-level semantic supervision, allowing for localized semantic editing and segmentation within the 3D scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view input images, text queries (optional, depending on teacher variant), and camera poses. Outputs: Dense, spatially consistent semantic feature maps (pseudo-labels) aligned with the 3D scene geometry. Data Structures: Feature Map: A 2D tensor of shape H \times W \times D, where H, W are image dimensions and D is the feature dimensionality (e.g., 512). Compressed Feature Map: A lower-dimensional tensor resulting from PCA projection, used to reduce memory bandwidth constraints. Steps: 1. Teacher Selection: Select a 2D vision-language model as the teacher. LSeg [44] is commonly used for its simplicity, though other concurrent models or text-unconditional encoders are viable. 2. Feature Extraction: Process each input image through the teacher network. If using a modified Vision Transformer (ViT) for dense prediction, process the image using overlapping patches to extract a high-dimensional feature vector for each spatial patch. Map the extracted internal representations into the targeted text-image contrastive space via a projection layer. 3. Dimensionality Reduction: Apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) localized to the specific dataset to compress the high-dimensional embeddings into a lower-dimensional principal space during intermediate storage. 4. Temporal Smoothing: Apply a temporal smoothing filter across adjacent camera poses to handle multi-view inconsistencies and stabilize the semantic feature maps before optimization. 5. Distillation: Use the resulting dense feature maps as ground truth pseudo-labels for optimizing the 3D representation (e.g., 3D Gaussian primitives). Parameters: Feature Dimension: 512 (typical for the distilled vision-language vectors). Optimization Iterations: 100 iterations (for the distillation phase). Photometric Loss Weight: 0.8. Structural Similarity Color Loss Weighting Factor: 3.2. Pitfalls: Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Data: LSeg is not robust to OOD data (e.g., "fossils", "T-Rex", "Triceratops") due to overfitting to biases in its training datasets (e.g., traffic scenes). Memory Bandwidth: High-dimensional semantic vectors across millions of pixels introduce severe memory bandwidth constraints; compression is necessary. Extracts dense, spatially consistent semantic feature maps from multi-view images to serve as ground truth pseudo-labels for 3D Gaussian optimization, overcoming the lack of localized granularity in global VLM embeddings. It employs a modified Vision Transformer fine-tuned for dense prediction with overlapping patches, PCA-based spatial dimensionality reduction localized to the dataset, and temporal smoothing across adjacent camera poses to handle multi-view inconsistencies. Strengths: Provides localized semantic granularity required for precise scene mapping, which global VLM embeddings lack. Allows for specific ray selection based on text queries (e.g., "apple") for editing. Limitations: Robustness is dependent on the teacher model; LSeg specifically suffers from OOD issues. High computational and memory overhead due to dense feature extraction and storage, mitigated only partially by PCA. When to use: When localized semantic editing or segmentation within a 3D scene is required, and the scene content falls within the teacher model's distribution. When not to use: When the scene contains significant out-of-distribution objects relative to the teacher's training bias (e.g., specific animals or rare objects if using LSeg). The approach leverages 2D vision-language models for feature distillation in 3D representations. LSeg [44] by Li et al. appeared anonymously at OpenReview on September 29th, 2021. Other concurrent studies [52, 99, 103, 72] appeared at arXiv on November or December, 2021, tackling image semantic segmentation with similar approaches using CLIP [69]. The method builds on the premise that freezing or finetuning pretrained CLIP models as text and image encoders enables zero-shot image semantic segmentation, which can then be distilled into 3D fields. name: VLM-Augmented Segmentation
head: Open-Vocabulary Segmentation via InnerGS
body: This method enables open-vocabulary 3D segmentation by augmenting 3D Gaussians with compact language features distilled from a Vision-Language Model (VLM). It solves the problem of high memory consumption associated with explicit high-dimensional semantic modeling by distilling embeddings into compact latent attributes, allowing for volumetric consistency and precise segmentation of Regions of Interest through text queries. It distinguishes itself from siblings like LangSplat by using a scene-specific autoencoder for distillation rather than direct CLIP embedding storage, and from LSeg Feature Encoding by focusing on medical VLM integration and compact latent space projection. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each with position, covariance, opacity \alphai, and a newly assigned compact latent attribute \mathbf{f}i. A pre-trained knowledge-enhanced medical VLM (e.g., Zhao et al., 2025). A scene-specific autoencoder (e.g., Qin et al., 2024) trained to map high-dimensional VLM embeddings to the compact latent space. A lightweight decoder trained to map the rendered latent map back to the semantic space. A text query for open-vocabulary segmentation. Outputs: A rendered latent map \mathbf{F}(v) for a given view v. A segmentation mask derived from the alignment of \mathbf{F}(v) with the text query embedding. Data Structures: Gaussian Attribute \mathbf{f}i: A compact vector in the latent space. The dimension d is determined by the autoencoder's bottleneck size (not explicitly given in sources, but implied to be significantly smaller than the source VLM embedding dimension). Rendered Latent Map \mathbf{F}(v): A 2D map of size H \times W \times d, where H and W are the image dimensions and d is the latent dimension. Steps: 1. Distillation: For each Gaussian i in the scene, extract the high-dimensional embedding from the knowledge-enhanced medical VLM corresponding to the visual features of the Gaussian's location. Pass this embedding through the scene-specific autoencoder to obtain the compact latent attribute \mathbf{f}i. 2. Rendering: For a target view v, identify the set of candidate Gaussians N that project to the image plane. Sort N front-to-back. Compute the rendered latent map \mathbf{F}(v) using the differentiable splatting equation: \mathbf{F}(v) = \sum{i \in N} \mathbf{f}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{f}i is the compact latent attribute of Gaussian i, \alphai is its opacity, and the product term represents the transmittance from preceding Gaussians. 3. Projection: Pass the rendered latent map \mathbf{F}(v) through the lightweight decoder to project it back to the semantic space. 4. Alignment: Compare the projected semantic features with the embedding of the open-vocabulary text query to generate the segmentation mask. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlatentmap(gaussians, viewmatrix, decoder, textqueryembedding): """ Renders a latent map from 3D Gaussians and decodes it for segmentation. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with attributes: position: (3,) opacity: float latentattr: (d,) # Compact language feature viewmatrix: Camera view-projection matrix. decoder: Lightweight neural network to map latent space to semantic space. textqueryembedding: (dsemantic,) # Embedding of the text query. Returns: segmentationmask: (H, W) # Binary or probabilistic mask. """ # 1. Project Gaussians to 2D and sort projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Project 3D position to 2D image coordinates # Calculate 2D covariance and screen-space bounds # If Gaussian intersects image plane, add to list if intersectsimage(g, viewmatrix): projectedgaussians.append(g) # Sort front-to-back based on depth projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) H, W = imagedimensions latentmap = np.zeros((H, W, d)) # d is latent dimension # 2. Differentiable Splatting for g in projectedgaussians: # Get 2D coverage pixels pixels = get2dpixels(g) # Compute alpha contribution # alphai is g.opacity # transmittance is product of (1 - alphaj) for all j before i # Note: In practice, this is often done via a rasterizer that handles # the accumulation efficiently. Here we outline the logic. for p in pixels: # Calculate weight for pixel p from Gaussian g weight = computegaussianweight(g, p) # Accumulate into latent map # F(v)[p] += fi alphai transmittance # The transmittance is handled by the rasterizer's order of operations latentmap[p] += g.latentattr g.opacity weight # 3. Projection to Semantic Space # The decoder maps the latent map back to semantic space semanticmap = decoder(latentmap) # Shape: (H, W, dsemantic) # 4. Open-Vocabulary Alignment # Compute similarity between semanticmap and textqueryembedding # This produces the segmentation mask similarity = cosinesimilarity(semanticmap, textqueryembedding) segmentationmask = (similarity > threshold).astype(float) return segmentationmask Parameters: Latent Dimension d: Not given in the sources. Determined by the autoencoder's bottleneck. Threshold: Not given in the sources. Used in the alignment step. Edge Cases: Empty Gaussians: If N is empty, \mathbf{F}(v) = \mathbf{0}. Precision: The method relies on the accuracy of the autoencoder's reconstruction. Distortion in the latent space may affect segmentation quality. Memory: Significantly reduces memory usage compared to storing high-dimensional VLM embeddings for each Gaussian, as it uses compact latent attributes. Performance: On the CT-ORG subset of SAT-DS, the method achieves a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient (mDSC) of 88.17%, mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) of 83.72%, and Pixel Accuracy (PA) of 98.97%. Liver DSC is consistently above 84.62%. Strengths: Enables open-vocabulary queries without retraining the 3D model; preserves volumetric consistency; computationally efficient due to compact latent space. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of the distilled latent features and the decoder; specific to the domain of the VLM (e.g., medical). The method is part of the InnerGS framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting for medical scene understanding. It builds on the potential for downstream clinical tasks by integrating Vision-Language Models (VLMs). The approach was proposed to circumvent the memory explosion of explicit high-dimensional modeling while preserving volumetric consistency. It references Zhao et al. (2025) for the knowledge-enhanced medical VLM and Qin et al. (2024) for the scene-specific autoencoder. The dataset used for evaluation is CT-ORG, licensed under CC BY 3.0. name: Human and Articulated Avatars
head: Animatable Gaussian Avatars, Dynamic 3DGS Avatars
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct and render animatable human and articulated non-human avatars from multi-view or single-view inputs. It solves the problem of dynamic geometry and appearance modeling by maintaining a canonical space representation where Gaussians are deformed via differentiable functions driven by pose parameters (e.g., skeleton joints, expression coefficients) before rasterization. It sets itself apart from static reconstruction methods by enabling real-time novel view synthesis of dynamic subjects through learned deformation fields or skeletal skinning, and from mesh-based methods by leveraging the explicit, differentiable nature of 3D Gaussians for high-fidelity texture and geometry. All methods in this family rely on the differentiable alpha-blending accumulation of feature vectors or colors during the rasterization step. For a pixel p, the rendered vector \mathbf{V}(p) is computed by sorting overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p front-to-back and applying: \mathbf{V}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{v}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where: \mathbf{v}i is the vector (feature \mathbf{f}i or color \mathbf{c}i) of the i-th Gaussian. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance from all preceding Gaussians j < i. If \mathcal{O}p is empty, \mathbf{V}(p) = \mathbf{0}. For structural extensions, all methods share a canonical space representation where 3D Gaussians are initialized in a reference pose (e.g., T-pose or neutral expression). Deformation is achieved by mapping these canonical Gaussians to a target pose defined by parameters (e.g., skeleton joints, expression coefficients). The rendering pipeline remains differentiable, allowing optimization of Gaussian attributes and deformation parameters via photometric loss. The deformation function D(\cdot) maps a canonical Gaussian i with position \mathbf{p}i^{canonical} to a target position \mathbf{p}i^{target} based on pose parameters \theta: \mathbf{p}i^{target} = D(\mathbf{p}i^{canonical}, \theta) The rotation and scale of the Gaussian may also be transformed by the deformation function to maintain physical consistency. GaussianHead is a method for animatable head reconstruction that uses a tri-plane representation and motion fields to simulate geometrically changing heads in continuous movements. It is designed to render rich textures, including skin and hair. It differs from siblings like GART and D3GA by explicitly leveraging tri-plane features for deformation rather than relying solely on skeleton-based or mesh-based deformation priors. GART is a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based approach designed to animate articulated non-human models, such as animals, by extending the canonical space deformation principles originally developed for human avatars. Unlike sibling methods like GaussianHead or D3GA which focus on specific human facial or body parts, GART generalizes the template-guided parameterization to broader articulated skeletons. It solves the problem of realistic, real-time rendering of complex, non-human articulated figures by mapping canonical 3D Gaussians to target poses via a differentiable deformation function. D3GA is a method for creating animatable human avatars using drivable 3D Gaussians and tetrahedral cages for full-body modeling. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic humans from multi-view videos by providing promising geometry and appearance modeling. It sets itself apart from siblings like SplatArmor and HuGS by utilizing tetrahedral cages as the primary deformation structure for the drivable Gaussians. Push the speed of high-fidelity dynamic human creation to 100 seconds using a fixed-perspective camera. Embed Gaussians onto a canonical human body mesh. Determine the position of a Gaussian by the barycenter and displacement along the normal direction. Attribute the 3DGS with a base of latent features that are weighted by the expression vector from 3DMMs. Allow reconstruction in real-time of animatable heads. Combine hand geometry priors (MANO) with 3DGS. Provide the first real-time hand reconstruction. Apply 3DGS to dynamic head reconstruction using canonical space modeling and deformation prediction. Explore the interaction between hands and objects using 3DGS. The concept of animatable avatars using 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as an extension of static reconstruction methods to handle dynamic subjects. Early works like GaussianAvatar incorporated optimizable tensors with dynamic appearance networks to capture dynamics. Human101 further optimized the training speed for high-fidelity dynamic human creation, achieving 100 seconds using a fixed-perspective camera. Subsequent methods like SplattingAvatar and GoMAvatar embedded Gaussians onto canonical human body meshes, determining positions via barycentric coordinates and normal displacements. For head modeling, MonoGaussianAvatar applied canonical space modeling and deformation prediction, while GaussianHead introduced tri-plane representations and motion fields for continuous movement simulation. HeadGas utilized latent features weighted by 3DMM expression vectors for real-time animatable heads. Extensions to other body parts include 3DPSHR for real-time hand reconstruction using MANO priors and MANUS for hand-object interaction. GART extended these principles to non-human articulated models like animals, and D3GA introduced tetrahedral cages for full-body human modeling. name: GaussianHead
head: GaussianHead [S1]
body: GaussianHead is a method for animatable head reconstruction that uses a tri-plane representation and motion fields to simulate geometrically changing heads in continuous movements. It is designed to render rich textures, including skin and hair. It differs from siblings like GART and D3GA by explicitly leveraging tri-plane features for deformation rather than relying solely on skeleton-based or mesh-based deformation priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians initialized in a canonical space, pose parameters \theta, and expression coefficients. Outputs: A rendered image \mathbf{C}(p) for each pixel p. Data Structures: Tri-plane Representation: A set of three 2D feature planes (XY, YZ, XZ) storing latent features for the head geometry and appearance. Motion Fields: A learned field that predicts the displacement of Gaussians based on pose and expression. Steps: 1. Canonical Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians in a neutral reference pose (e.g., T-pose or neutral expression). 2. Tri-plane Sampling: For each Gaussian, sample latent features from the tri-plane representation based on its canonical position. 3. Deformation Prediction: Use the motion fields to predict the deformation of the Gaussians based on the current pose \theta and expression. This maps canonical positions to target positions: \mathbf{p}i^{target} = D(\mathbf{p}i^{canonical}, \theta, \text{motion\field}) The rotation and scale may also be transformed to maintain physical consistency. 4. Rendering: Render the deformed Gaussians using the standard differentiable splatting pipeline described in Human and Articulated Avatars. Parameters: Tri-plane resolution: Not given in the sources. Motion field network depth: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues in tri-plane sampling may occur if the Gaussian positions fall outside the normalized bounding box of the tri-planes. Degenerate expressions (e.g., extreme mouth openings) may cause self-intersections if the motion field is not sufficiently regularized. FlashAvatar embeds a uniform 3D Gaussian field in a parametric face model and learns additional spatial offsets to capture facial details. It pushes the rendering speed to 300 FPS. It is chosen when high-speed rendering is prioritized over the explicit tri-plane motion field approach of GaussianHead. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: FlashAvatar, a variant, achieves 300 FPS. Strengths: Capable of rendering rich textures including skin and hair. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When reconstructing animatable heads with continuous movements and rich textures. When not: When real-time performance is not critical and simpler deformation models suffice. GaussianHead was introduced in the context of recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting for human and articulated avatars. It builds on the tri-plane representation and motion fields to handle geometric changes in head avatars. name: GART
head: GART, A method that extends the human to more articulated models (e.g, animals) based on the 3DGS representation
body: GART is a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based approach designed to animate articulated non-human models, such as animals, by extending the canonical space deformation principles originally developed for human avatars. Unlike sibling methods like GaussianHead or D3GA which focus on specific human facial or body parts, GART generalizes the template-guided parameterization to broader articulated skeletons. It solves the problem of realistic, real-time rendering of complex, non-human articulated figures by mapping canonical 3D Gaussians to target poses via a differentiable deformation function. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images of an articulated model (e.g., animal) in various poses; a canonical template mesh or skeleton structure defining the reference pose; pose parameters \theta (joint angles/transforms) for the target frame. Outputs: Rendered image \mathbf{C}(p) for each pixel p; optimized Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) and deformation weights. Data Structures: Canonical Gaussians: A set \mathcal{G}{canon} where each Gaussian i has attributes \{\mathbf{p}i^{canonical}, \mathbf{q}i^{canonical}, \mathbf{s}i^{canonical}, \mathbf{c}i, \alphai\} defined in the neutral/reference pose space. Deformation Weights: For each Gaussian, a set of weights w{i,k} corresponding to the influence of skeleton joint k on the Gaussian's position and orientation. Skeleton/Joint Tree: A hierarchical structure defining the parent-child relationships of the articulated model's joints, allowing forward kinematics to compute global joint transforms from local pose parameters \theta. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians in the canonical space, typically using a template mesh or point cloud from the neutral pose. Assign initial deformation weights based on proximity to skeleton joints or mesh skinning. 2. Pose Parameterization: Define the target pose \theta for the current frame. Compute the global transform Tk(\theta) for each joint k in the skeleton using forward kinematics. 3. Deformation: For each Gaussian i, compute its deformed position \mathbf{p}i^{target} and orientation \mathbf{q}i^{target} by blending the transforms of the influencing joints k based on weights w{i,k}: \mathbf{p}i^{target} = \sum{k} w{i,k} \cdot Tk(\theta) \cdot \mathbf{p}i^{canonical} \mathbf{q}i^{target} = \text{Slerp}\left(\mathbf{q}i^{canonical}, \sum{k} w{i,k} \cdot \text{Rot}(Tk(\theta)), \dots\right) \quad \text{} Note: The exact blending formula for rotation and scale is not detailed in the provided sources, but typically involves weighted combination of joint transforms. 4. Rendering: Project the deformed Gaussians to screen space. For each pixel p, sort the overlapping deformed Gaussians \mathcal{O}p front-to-back. Compute the color \mathbf{C}(p) using the standard alpha blending equation provided in the parent article. 5. Optimization: Minimize a photometric loss between the rendered image and the ground truth multi-view images. Optimize Gaussian attributes, deformation weights, and potentially pose parameters if tracking is involved. Parameters: Number of Gaussians: Not given in the sources. Skeleton Complexity: Depends on the target model (e.g., animal rig). Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Poses: Extreme joint angles may cause self-intersection or unnatural deformation if weights are not properly constrained. Precision: Floating-point precision in transform calculations may affect accuracy for very small or distant Gaussians. Boundary Handling: Gaussians near the boundary of the canonical space may have ambiguous joint influences. Uses a canonical mesh or skeleton to define deformation weights, ensuring smooth transitions between poses. Chosen when a template is available. Link to Human and Articulated Avatars. Maps 2D image coordinates to 3D canonical space for initialization or refinement. Chosen when multi-view consistency is critical. Link to Human and Articulated Avatars. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N \log N) due to sorting, where N is the number of Gaussians. Deformation is O(N \cdot K) where K is the number of influencing joints per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N) for Gaussian attributes and weights. Measured Performance: Real-time rendering on consumer-level devices is claimed, similar to standard 3DGS. Strengths: Generalizes to non-human articulated models; real-time performance; differentiable optimization. Limitations: Requires a canonical template; deformation quality depends on weight initialization and optimization; may struggle with complex non-rigid deformations not captured by skeleton. When to Use: When animating articulated non-human models (e.g., animals) with high fidelity and real-time requirements. When Not to Use: For non-articulated objects or when a canonical template is unavailable. GART was introduced in the context of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically extending the human-centric 3DGS animation methods to broader articulated models like animals. It builds upon the foundational work of 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method is part of a growing family of differentiable rendering techniques for avatar reconstruction and animation. name: D3GA
head: D3GA
body: D3GA is a method for creating animatable human avatars using drivable 3D Gaussians and tetrahedral cages for full-body modeling. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic humans from multi-view videos by providing promising geometry and appearance modeling. It sets itself apart from siblings like SplatArmor and HuGS by utilizing tetrahedral cages as the primary deformation structure for the drivable Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view video data of a human subject; pose parameters defining the target animation. Outputs: An animatable 3D Gaussian avatar that can be rendered from arbitrary viewpoints and poses. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Drivable Gaussians initialized in a canonical space. Each Gaussian i has attributes including position \mathbf{p}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. Tetrahedral Cage: A structural mesh composed of tetrahedra that encloses the human body. This cage defines the deformation field. The exact layout of the tetrahedral mesh (vertices, connectivity) is not specified in the sources [G: Standard tetrahedral mesh representation]. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians in a canonical reference pose (e.g., T-pose) [G: Based on Shared principles]. 2. Cage Construction: Construct a tetrahedral cage around the canonical human geometry. This cage serves as the deformation driver. 3. Deformation Mapping: Map the canonical Gaussians to the target pose. The position of each Gaussian is deformed based on its location relative to the tetrahedral cage and the current pose parameters \theta. The deformation function D(\cdot) maps a canonical Gaussian i with position \mathbf{p}i^{canonical} to a target position \mathbf{p}i^{target}: \mathbf{p}i^{target} = D(\mathbf{p}i^{canonical}, \theta) The rotation and scale of the Gaussian are also transformed by the deformation function to maintain physical consistency. 4. Rendering: Render the deformed Gaussians using the standard differentiable rasterization pipeline. For a pixel p, the rendered color \mathbf{C}(p) is computed by sorting overlapping deformed Gaussians \mathcal{O}p front-to-back and applying: \mathbf{C}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{c}i is the color, \alphai is the opacity, and the product term is the transmittance [Shared principles]. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. name: HeadGas
head: Animatable 3D Gaussian Splatting for Heads, HeadGaS, HeadGaS w/ $\nabla(\boldsymbol{u}, \boldsymbol{R})$
body: HeadGaS is a method for real-time animatable 3D head reconstruction and animation that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a base of learnable latent features. It solves the problem of modeling dynamic facial expressions by allowing Gaussians to alter their opacity and color over time, achieving dynamics via over-representation (duplicates of dynamic face areas that become active one at a time) rather than explicit geometric deformation. It sets itself apart from siblings like GaussianHead and GART by blending latent features with 3DMM expression weights to predict appearance, avoiding the complexity of optimizing 3D motion for every Gaussian. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video frames, pre-computed head poses (camera poses Wi), and expression vectors (ei) from a parametric head model (e.g., FLAME or FaceWarehouse). Outputs: Rendered images Ir for given expression and camera parameters. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Ga is defined as a tuple (\Sigma, \mu, F): \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: The 3D covariance matrix. \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: The center position in canonical space. F \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times f{dim}}: The latent feature basis. B is the number of expression weights (e.g., 52 for FLAME), and f{dim} is the feature dimensionality (32). Note: Color c and opacity \alpha are not stored explicitly but are predicted by an MLP. Parameters: f{dim} = 32. B = 52 for FLAME tracking. Spherical Harmonics degree k=3. Rendering resolution: 512^2 pixels. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Acquire head poses and expression weights for each frame. Convert rigid head poses to camera poses to map observations to a canonical head pose. Perform video matting and face parsing to discard background and clothing. 2. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussian centers \mu with 2500 points (subset of 3DMM mesh vertices or random points within near/far bounds). Initialize latent features F with zeros. 3. Feature Blending: For each frame i with expression vector ei \in \mathbb{R}^B, compute the frame-specific feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^{f{dim}} for each Gaussian: fi = F^T ei + f0 where f0 is a bias term. 4. Color and Opacity Prediction: Feed fi and the Gaussian position \mu into an MLP \phi to predict color ci and opacity \alphai: ci, \alphai = \phi(fi, \psi(\mu)) where \psi denotes sinusoidal positional encoding of \mu. The MLP \phi consists of two linear layers with LeakyReLU activations, a hidden layer of 64 channels, and two output branches (color and opacity). The opacity branch ends with a sigmoid activation. 5. Projection: Project Gaussians to image space using camera view Wi. Compute the covariance matrix in camera coordinates \Sigma' using the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transformation: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T. 6. Rendering: Render using a tile-based differentiable rasterizer. For pixel p, sort overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p front-to-back and apply alpha-blending: V(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). 7. Optimization: Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} using Stochastic Gradient Descent with exponential decay scheduling for positions \mu and the MLP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class HeadGaSMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, fdim, bdim): super().init() self.fdim = fdim self.bdim = bdim # MLP architecture: 2 linear layers, hidden 64, LeakyReLU self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(fdim + 3, 64), # fdim features + 3 pos encoding dims? # Note: Source says psi(mu) is input. # Standard 3DGS uses SH for view-dependent color. # HeadGaS predicts ci (RGB) and alphai. # Source says ci in R^{3(k+1)}. # We assume MLP outputs raw RGB and alpha. nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 4) # 3 for color, 1 for opacity) def forward(self, fi, mu): # fi: [N, fdim] # mu: [N, 3] # psi(mu): Sinusoidal positional encoding. # For implementation, we assume a standard 3DGS-style positional encoding # or simply concatenating mu if psi is implicit in the source's "psi(mu)". # Given the source says "psi denotes sinusoidal positional encoding", # we must encode mu. A simple implementation for 3D coords: # We will assume a standard 6-band SH-like encoding or just concat mu # if the source implies psi is a transformation. # However, HeadGaS paper says "psi denotes sinusoidal positional encoding". # To be safe and self-contained, we implement a basic sinusoidal encoding # for the 3 coordinates. # Standard sinusoidal positional encoding for 3D # freqbands = 6 (common in 3DGS) freqbands = 6 scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(freqbands)], dtype=mu.dtype, device=mu.device) # Expand mu to [N, 3, 1] and scales to [1, 1, freqbands] muexp = mu.unsqueeze(-1) # [N, 3, 1] scalesexp = scales.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # [1, 1, 6] # sin(2^i pi mu) posenc = torch.sin(muexp scalesexp torch.pi) # [N, 3, 6] posenc = posenc.view(mu.shape[0], -1) # [N, 18] # Concatenate fi and posenc inputfeat = torch.cat([fi, posenc], dim=-1) # [N, fdim + 18] out = self.net(inputfeat) color = out[:,:3] opacity = torch.sigmoid(out[:, 3:]) # Constrain to [0, 1] return color, opacity def blendfeatures(F, ei, f0): """ F: [N, B, fdim] - Latent basis for N Gaussians ei: [B] - Expression vector for frame i f0: [fdim] - Bias term Returns: fi [N, fdim] """ # F^T ei -> [N, fdim, B] @ [B] -> [N, fdim] # In PyTorch: torch.einsum('nbd,b->nd', F, ei) fi = torch.einsum('nbd,b->nd', F, ei) + f0 return fi def renderheadgas(gaussians, camerapose, expressionvector, mlp, f0): """ gaussians: dict with keys 'mu' [N, 3], 'Sigma' [N, 3, 3], 'F' [N, B, fdim] camerapose: W [4, 4] expressionvector: ei [B] mlp: HeadGaSMLP instance f0: [fdim] """ N = gaussians['mu'].shape[0] B = gaussians['F'].shape[1] fdim = gaussians['F'].shape[2] # 1. Feature Blending fi = blendfeatures(gaussians['F'], expressionvector, f0) # 2. Color and Opacity Prediction ci, alphai = mlp(fi, gaussians['mu']) # 3. Projection (Simplified) # In a real implementation, this involves projecting centers and covariances # using the camera matrix and Jacobian. # Sigma' = J W Sigma W^T J^T # For the purpose of this article, we assume a rasterizer function exists # that takes (mu, Sigma', ci, alphai) and renders. # 4. Rasterization # This step depends on the specific tile-based differentiable rasterizer. # We assume a function rasterize that handles sorting and alpha blending. renderedimage = rasterize( centers=gaussians['mu'], covariances=gaussians['Sigma'], # Will be transformed in rasterizer colors=ci, opacities=alphai, camerapose=camerapose) return renderedimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: Initializing latent features F with zeros leads to the most stable solution. Over-representation: Dynamic areas require multiple Gaussians (duplicates) that become active/inactive based on expression. This increases the number of Gaussians compared to static scenes but is more effective than moving Gaussians. Loss Conflict: Perceptual loss Lp is activated after 10k iterations to avoid conflict with photometric loss at early stages. An ablation variant where Gaussians are transformed using deltas for position (\mu) and rotation (R) predicted by an MLP \phi'. The MLP outputs 3 values of position shift and 4 values of rotation (quaternion). The static Gaussian position is updated as \mu' = \mu + \Delta \mu and rotation as R' = Rt R. A regularization term \lambda\mu L1(\Delta \mu) is added to the loss to encourage small position shifts. This variant requires significantly more Gaussians (234k) than the proposed HeadGaS (28k) because the proposed model's over-representation is more effective and easier to learn. Performance on INSTA dataset: 234k Gaussians, 0.019s rendering time, 29.83 PSNR. Time Complexity: Rendering is real-time, over 100 FPS generally, approximately 250 FPS at 512 \times 512 resolution. Memory Complexity: The method uses over-representation, leading to a higher number of Gaussians than static 3DGS, but fewer than deformation-based variants (28k vs 234k in ablation). Measured Performance: INSTA dataset: PSNR 32.50, SSIM 0.971, LPIPS 0.033, rendering time 0.10s at 512^2 resolution. NBS dataset: PSNR 34.34, SSIM 0.970, LPIPS 0.0311, rendering time 0.10s at 512^2 resolution. PointAvatar dataset: PSNR 36.66, SSIM 0.976, LPIPS 0.0261, rendering time 0.10s at 512^2 resolution. Scaling: Rendering speed accelerated by over 10x compared to interactive NeRF-based baselines. Strengths: Real-time inference, state-of-the-art results (up to 2 dB PSNR improvement over baselines), simple and effective blending in latent space. Limitations: Requires pre-computed head poses and expression weights. Over-representation increases Gaussian count compared to static scenes. HeadGaS was proposed by H. Dhamo et al. in the paper "HeadGaS: Real-Time Animatable Head Avatars via 3D Gaussian Splatting". It extends the explicit 3DGS representation with a base of learnable latent features, inspired by traditional blendshape 3DMMs. The method allows reconstruction in real-time of animatable heads from monocular video. It supports various 3DMM representations, including FLAME and FaceWarehouse.
