name: Optimization and Training
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training, 3DGS Optimization
body: Optimization and Training refers to the iterative procedure that adjusts the parameters of a collection of 3D Gaussian primitives to minimize the perceptual and geometric distortion between rendered views and ground-truth images. It solves the problem of learning a scene representation by using differentiable rendering to backpropagate pixel errors through alpha compositing and projection to update Gaussian geometry, color, and opacity. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific reliance on adaptive densification driven by gradient magnitudes to dynamically modulate the number of Gaussians, ensuring a trade-off between reconstruction quality and representation budget. All methods in this family optimize a set of N 3D Gaussian primitives [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. Each primitive i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Appearance parameters (e.g., spherical harmonic coefficients hi) [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md] The optimization minimizes a loss function \mathcal{L} between rendered images and ground truth views, typically using the Adam optimizer [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. The rendering process involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space, sorting by depth, and alpha blending [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. RadSplat is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes by leveraging a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to generate a dense, topologically correct point cloud, which is then converted into Gaussians. It solves the problem of poor initialization quality and topological artifacts inherent in raw Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds, enabling high-quality rendering with unprecedented speed. Unlike feed-forward methods like MVSplat that regress parameters directly, RadSplat uses a hybrid approach that bypasses the per-scene gradient descent loop for initialization. This family covers the initialization strategies and iterative optimization procedures required to reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D images using 3D Gaussian Splatting [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. It solves the problem of converting sparse or dense image collections into a set of differentiable volumetric primitives that can be rendered in real time [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. It differs from implicit neural field methods by optimizing explicit, static or dynamic ellipsoids via differentiable rasterization, achieving faster convergence and rendering speeds [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization is the training procedure that adjusts the parameters of a collection of 3D Gaussian primitives to minimize the perceptual and geometric distortion between rendered views and ground-truth images. It solves the problem of learning scene representation by using differentiable rendering to backpropagate pixel errors through alpha compositing and projection to update Gaussian geometry, color, and opacity. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific reliance on adaptive densification driven by gradient magnitudes to dynamically modulate the number of Gaussians, ensuring a trade-off between reconstruction quality and representation budget. Applies frequency-domain regularization to the rendered 2D image to encourage high-frequency detail recovery. Optimization process to shape reasonable 3D geometry by integrating a 3D SDS loss with a pre-trained point cloud diffusion model (Point-E) to mitigate the Janus problem. Optimize Gaussian positions using Point-E guidance via 3D SDS loss, avoiding direct alignment to avoid registration/scaling/degeneration challenges. \nabla\theta L{geometry} = E{\epsilonI, t} wI(t)(\epsilon\phi(xt; y, t) - \epsilonI) \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} + \lambda{3D} \cdot E{\epsilonP, t} [wP(t)(\epsilon\psi(pt; y, t) - \epsilonP)] \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}, where pt is noisy Gaussian positions, xt is rendered image, w is weighting function, \epsilon is Gaussian noise. \lambda{3D} = 0.01, loss weight for 3D prior in geometry optimization stage. The optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced alongside the original 3DGS method [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting by providing the differentiable training loop necessary to learn scene parameters from 2D observations. The approach has been extended to address specific challenges such as initialization quality [8059-radsplat.md], frequency detail recovery, and geometry consistency in text-to-3D generation. name: Optical Flow Loss for 3D Gaussian Reconstruction
head: Flow-guided shape reconstruction, L2 flow loss, Optical Flow Weak Supervision, Optical flow regularization
body:
This method improves the 3D shape reconstruction of static objects from video sequences by incorporating an optical flow loss term into the optimization objective. It leverages the temporal prior inherent in video data to resolve concavity/convexity ambiguities that are present when relying solely on silhouette and color loss terms. Unlike standard photometric approaches, this technique uses optical flow as a local estimator of surface correspondence, which is robust to long-term lighting changes and autoexposure variations common in user-captured videos. The method extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization loop by adding a flow consistency term. It assumes that the 3D scene is static and that the camera poses for the input video sequence are known. Inputs: A sequence of video frames, corresponding camera poses (extrinsics), and a single inverse focal length parameter (intrinsics). The method assumes images lack distortion, projection is centered, and pixels are square. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, colors) that minimize the combined loss. The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian Set. For flow computation, it requires: Camera Poses: A list of 4 	imes 4 transformation matrices Ti for each frame i. Inverse Focal Length: A scalar f^{-1}. Image Dimensions: Width W and Height H. 1. Ray Sampling: Select a batch of rays \mathcal{R} from the current frame i. This is identical to the parent method's ray sampling, using the camera intrinsics and extrinsics for frame i. 2. Forward Rendering (Color): Render the color image \hat{C}i for frame i using the current 3D Gaussians. 3. Forward Rendering (Depth/Coordinates): Render the depth image Di and the 3D coordinates of the hit points for each pixel. The 3D coordinate \mathbf{P} for a ray is obtained by back-projecting the depth D from the camera center. Specifically, if \mathbf{r}{dir} is the ray direction in camera space and D is the depth, the point in camera space is \mathbf{P}{cam} = D \cdot \mathbf{r}{dir}. Transform this to world space using the camera pose Ti: \mathbf{P}{world} = Ti \cdot [D \cdot \mathbf{r}{dir}, 1]^T. 4. Compute Rendered Flow (\hat{f}): For each ray in the batch, take the 3D world coordinate \mathbf{P}{world} obtained in Step 3. Transform \mathbf{P}{world} into the coordinate system of the adjacent frame i+1 using T{i+1}^{-1}: \mathbf{P}{cam
ext} = T{i+1}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{P}{world}, 1]^T. Project \mathbf{P}{cam
ext} onto the image plane of frame i+1 using the inverse focal length f^{-1} and image dimensions. Let the projected pixel coordinates be (u{next}, v{next}). Similarly, transform \mathbf{P}{world} into the coordinate system of the previous frame i-1 using T{i-1}^{-1} and project to get (u{prev}, v{prev}). The rendered forward flow estimate for the pixel is \hat{f}{forward} = (u{next} - ui, v{next} - vi). The rendered backward flow estimate is \hat{f}{backward} = (u{prev} - ui, v{prev} - vi). If the Z component of \mathbf{P}{cam
ext} is \le 0, the point is behind the camera and flow is undefined; these rays should be masked out or handled with a large loss penalty. 5. Compute Ground Truth Flow (f): Obtain ground truth optical flow maps between frame i and i+1, and between i and i-1, using an external optical flow estimator (e.g., Unimatch [70] or classic methods like [13]). The ground truth flow f is measured in pixels, scaled to half the shorter image dimension to normalize the loss magnitude. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the accumulated opacity \alpha for each ray from the volume rendering process. Compute Color Loss LC: LC = \alpha \cdot \| c - \hat{c} \|1 where c is the ground truth color and \hat{c} is the rendered color. Colors should be gamma-corrected back to linear intensity before computation. Compute Flow Loss LF: LF = \alpha \cdot \| f - \hat{f} \|1 where f is the ground truth flow and \hat{f} is the rendered flow. Compute Base Loss LM: This is the standard reconstruction loss (e.g., MSE or SSIM) from the parent method. Compute Total Loss L: L = LM + \lambdaC LC + \lambdaF LF where \lambdaC and \lambdaF are the loss weights. 7. Backpropagation: Compute gradients of L with respect to the Gaussian parameters and update them using the Adam optimizer. 8. Scheduling: Apply learning rate decay based on statistical criteria. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeflowloss(gaussians, cameraposes, currentframeidx, gtflowforward, gtflowbackward, invfocallength, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Computes the optical flow loss for a batch of rays. Args: gaussians: 3D Gaussian Set object with methods to render depth and 3D coords. cameraposes: List of 4x4 numpy arrays for all frames. currentframeidx: Index of the current frame being rendered. gtflowforward: Ground truth flow from currentframeidx to currentframeidx + 1. gtflowbackward: Ground truth flow from currentframeidx to currentframeidx - 1. invfocallength: Scalar inverse focal length. imagewidth, imageheight: Image dimensions. Returns: flowloss: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Render depth and 3D coordinates for current frame # Assume renderdepthandcoords returns: # depthmap: (H, W) # hitpointsworld: (H, W, 3) - 3D world coordinates of the hit points # opacities: (H, W) - accumulated opacity per pixel depthmap, hitpointsworld, opacities = gaussians.renderdepthandcoords( cameraposes[currentframeidx], invfocallength, imagewidth, imageheight) # 2. Get adjacent poses posenext = cameraposes[currentframeidx + 1] poseprev = cameraposes[currentframeidx - 1] # 3. Transform hit points to next and previous camera frames # hitpointsworld is (H, W, 3). Convert to homogeneous (H, W, 4) hitpointshom = np.concatenate([hitpointsworld, np.ones((hitpointsworld.shape[0], hitpointsworld.shape[1], 1))], axis=-1) # Transform to next frame hitpointsnextcamhom = np.linalg.inv(posenext) @ hitpointshom.transpose(2, 0, 1) # (4, H, W) hitpointsnextcam = hitpointsnextcamhom[:3,:,:].transpose(1, 2, 0) # (H, W, 3) # Transform to previous frame hitpointsprevcamhom = np.linalg.inv(poseprev) @ hitpointshom.transpose(2, 0, 1) hitpointsprevcam = hitpointsprevcamhom[:3,:,:].transpose(1, 2, 0) # 4. Project to image coordinates # Projection assumes pinhole model with centered principal point and square pixels # u = (xcam / zcam) / invfocallength + width/2 eps = 1e-6 # Project to next frame unext = (hitpointsnextcam[:,:, 0] / (hitpointsnextcam[:,:, 2] + eps)) / invfocallength + imagewidth / 2 vnext = (hitpointsnextcam[:,:, 1] / (hitpointsnextcam[:,:, 2] + eps)) / invfocallength + imageheight / 2 # Project to previous frame uprev = (hitpointsprevcam[:,:, 0] / (hitpointsprevcam[:,:, 2] + eps)) / invfocallength + imagewidth / 2 vprev = (hitpointsprevcam[:,:, 1] / (hitpointsprevcam[:,:, 2] + eps)) / invfocallength + imageheight / 2 # Current frame coordinates (center of pixel) ucurr = np.arange(imagewidth).reshape(1, -1) + 0.5 vcurr = np.arange(imageheight).reshape(-1, 1) + 0.5 ucurr = np.tile(ucurr, (imageheight, 1)) vcurr = np.tile(vcurr, (1, imagewidth)) # 5. Compute rendered flow # Forward flow: change from current to next fhatforwardu = unext - ucurr fhatforwardv = vnext - vcurr # Backward flow: change from current to prev fhatbackwardu = uprev - ucurr fhatbackwardv = vprev - vcurr # 6. Mask invalid points (behind camera) validnext = hitpointsnextcam[:,:, 2] > eps validprev = hitpointsprevcam[:,:, 2] > eps valid = validnext & validprev # 7. Compute L1 loss with opacity weighting # Ground truth flows are pre-scaled to half the shorter image dimension lossforward = np.abs(gtflowforward[:,:, 0] - fhatforwardu) + np.abs(gtflowforward[:,:, 1] - fhatforwardv) lossbackward = np.abs(gtflowbackward[:,:, 0] - fhatbackwardu) + np.abs(gtflowbackward[:,:, 1] - fhatbackwardv) # Apply opacity and validity mask weightedlossforward = opacities lossforward valid weightedlossbackward = opacities lossbackward valid # Mean loss over valid pixels numvalid = np.sum(valid) if numvalid == 0: return 0.0 flowloss = (np.sum(weightedlossforward) + np.sum(weightedlossbackward)) / numvalid return flowloss \lambdaC (Color Loss Weight): 4.5. \lambdaF (Flow Loss Weight): 210. These values are fixed for all experiments in the source. Flow is measured in the scale of half the shorter image dimension. Shape Uncertainty Artifacts: Without flow regularization, rendered flow estimates exhibit artifacts due to shape uncertainty. Color Fidelity: Adding flow loss slightly hurts the color fidelity of the reconstructed models. Camera Intrinsics: The method assumes a single inverse focal length parameter, no distortion, centered projection, and square pixels. Deviations from this may require modification of the projection step. Temporal Consistency: The method requires adjacent frames. For the first and last frames in a sequence, one adjacent flow direction may be unavailable. The source implies using both forward and backward flow for each ray, so boundary frames might need special handling (e.g., only using the available flow direction). Time Complexity: The additional cost is the computation of rendered flow, which involves transforming 3D points and projecting them. This is O(N) where N is the number of rays in the batch. The external optical flow estimation is performed offline or per-frame and is not part of the per-step optimization cost, though it is required for the loss computation. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory beyond storing the ground truth flow maps and intermediate 3D coordinates. Measured Performance: On CO3D sequences, using Color & Learned Flow resulted in a Depth Error of 0.155 and a Runtime of 15 seconds, compared to 0.271 and 17 seconds for No Color or Flow. Strengths: Resolves concavity/convexity ambiguities; robust to lighting changes; produces smoother depth maps; learned flow methods are real-time on GPU. Limitations: Slightly reduces color fidelity; requires known camera poses; assumes static scene. When to Use: When shape accuracy is more important than perfect color fidelity, and when video sequences with known poses are available. When Not to Use: When color fidelity is the primary goal, or when camera poses are unknown. This technique was introduced in "Flexible Techniques for Differentiable Rendering with 3D Gaussians". It builds on the observation that optical flow provides a useful signal for shape estimation, as it is a local estimator robust to long-term lighting changes. The method draws inspiration from classic techniques for shape estimation and sparse particle video trackers. It leverages state-of-the-art learned optical flow methods (e.g., Unimatch [70]) which provide better priors for texture-less areas compared to classic optical flow [13]. name: Density Control and Densification
head: Adaptive Density Control, ADC, Densification
body: Density Control and Densification is a training-time mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that dynamically adjusts the number, position, and scale of Gaussian primitives to match scene complexity [3034-adaptive-densification.md]. It solves the limitation of standard gradient descent, which can only move or scale existing Gaussians but cannot create new ones in empty regions or cleanly remove useless ones. By periodically inspecting view-space positional gradients, it identifies under-reconstructed areas (requiring cloning) and over-reconstructed areas (requiring splitting), ensuring the representation density matches the scene complexity. Unlike standard 3DGS which may allow indefinite growth, variants like OTS+SAtn Densification impose strict caps on the total number of Gaussians to ensure controlled memory usage. All methods in this family operate on the set of N 3D Gaussian primitives defined in Optimization and Training. The core mechanism involves a periodic densification step, typically executed every K=100 iterations starting after a warm-up period (e.g., iteration 100) [3034-adaptive-densification.md][1488-ots-satn-densification.md]. The densification process classifies Gaussians based on their accumulated view-space positional gradient magnitude |\nabla{\mathbf{p}} \mathcal{L}| and their physical size (scale or covariance diagonal) relative to the scene diagonal [3034-adaptive-densification.md][1488-ots-satn-densification.md]. 1. Cloning (Under-reconstructed): Gaussians with high gradients and small sizes are cloned to increase density in under-sampled regions. The clone is placed at the same position with identical scale and rotation, but its opacity is halved (\alpha{new} = \alpha / 2) to preserve the total opacity contribution [3034-adaptive-densification.md][1488-ots-satn-densification.md]. 2. Splitting (Over-reconstructed): Gaussians with high gradients and large sizes are split to capture high-frequency details. The original Gaussian is removed, and two new Gaussians are created. Their positions are sampled from the probability density function (PDF) of the original Gaussian, typically \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{S}) [3034-adaptive-densification.md][1488-ots-satn-densification.md]. The scale is reduced (e.g., by a factor of 1.2^{-1} or \sqrt{3}/2) to maintain volume or fit the detail [3034-adaptive-densification.md][1488-ots-satn-densification.md]. Opacity is also distributed (typically halved) [3034-adaptive-densification.md]. 3. Pruning: Gaussians with low opacity (e.g., \alpha < 0.025) or excessive size are removed to reduce noise and memory usage [3034-adaptive-densification.md][1488-ots-satn-densification.md]. Most implementations enforce a maximum primitive count N{max} (e.g., 500,000 or 1,000,000) to prevent out-of-memory errors [3034-adaptive-densification.md][1488-ots-satn-densification.md]. If the current count N \ge N{max}, densification is skipped or limited [1488-ots-satn-densification.md][15330-primitives-growth-control.md]. OTS+SAtn Densification is a density control strategy adapted from the OTS+SAtn splatting technique to operate within the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework for real-world scene reconstruction. It addresses the problem of unbounded primitive growth and scene-specific overfitting by imposing strict caps on the total number of Gaussians and adapting densification thresholds to match 3DGS conventions. Unlike standard 3DGS which may allow indefinite growth, this method stops densification once a predefined maximum count (e.g., 100k, 500k, 1m, or 5m) is reached, ensuring controlled memory usage while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. Adaptive Densification is the foundational training-time mechanism that dynamically adjusts the number, position, and scale of 3D Gaussian primitives to improve reconstruction quality while managing memory constraints. It solves the limitation of standard gradient descent, which can only move or scale existing Gaussians but cannot create new ones in empty regions or cleanly remove useless ones. By periodically inspecting view-space positional gradients, it identifies under-reconstructed areas (requiring cloning) and over-reconstructed areas (requiring splitting), ensuring the representation density matches the scene complexity. Loss Accumulation Guided (LAG) densification is a density control strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses accumulated reconstruction loss maps to identify under-reconstructed regions, preventing unnecessary Gaussian growth in well-reconstructed areas. Unlike standard adaptive densification which relies solely on view-space positional gradients—often leading to excessive Gaussian proliferation in high-frequency texture regions—LAG introduces a dual-constraint mechanism that inhibits splitting or cloning when the local reconstruction error is already low. This approach reduces the final number of Gaussians and shortens training time at the cost of a slight decrease in rendering metrics. Gaussian Splitting and Pruning is a deterministic density control method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that modifies the primitive count by splitting Gaussians with high reconstruction responsibility and removing those with minimal contribution based on statistical criteria. Unlike heuristic approaches that rely on view-space positional gradients or screen-space size thresholds, this method uses the accumulated per-ray loss and weight statistics to identify under- and over-reconstructed regions. It addresses the problem of fixed primitive counts by iteratively refining the reconstruction after initial convergence, allowing for increased detail in areas with high error while culling noise in areas with low contribution. 3D Gaussian Splatting Adaptive Density Control is a post-densification pruning strategy that removes unstable or low-contribution Gaussian primitives to reduce the final scene representation size (N{GS}) and training time, while maintaining rendering quality. It differs from standard opacity-based pruning by introducing an opacity-gradient metric that combines per-pixel opacity gradients, opacity values, and training loss to identify primitives that are sensitive to optimization or contribute little to the final image. This method complements the geometric densification (cloning/splitting) described in Density Control and Densification by cleaning up redundant primitives after they have stabilized or failed to converge. Steerable Densification with Sampling is a density control method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses image loss and per-Gaussian attributes to rank primitives for resampling, executed at a significantly reduced frequency to prevent over-densification. It differs from standard 3DGS densification by replacing deterministic gradient-based splitting with a probabilistic, score-weighted sampling process, allowing for more interpretable and stable convergence. Soft Pruning is a density control method in 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces the number of Gaussian primitives by removing those with low contribution to the reconstruction loss, specifically to maintain a robust Hessian approximation during optimization. It differs from its sibling Hard Pruning by occurring during the densification stage (immediately before opacity resets) rather than after, allowing the subsequent training iterations to refine the remaining primitives. Primitives Growth Control is a constraint mechanism applied during the densification phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting to prevent unbounded growth of the primitive count, which can lead to out-of-memory errors. It sets itself apart from standard Adaptive Densification (ADC) by enforcing a hard upper bound on the total number of Gaussians and limiting the rate of new primitive creation per step, ensuring stable memory usage even when densification remains active for extended training periods. A variant that integrates specific maintenance loops into the densification phase. Pruning: Uses contribution-based pruning (per-Gaussian Σ(α·T) from CUDA channel) instead of opacity threshold. Resurrection: Uses σt resurrection instead of resetopacity. Since opacity is an analytic quantity under σt parameterization, standard reset is replaced. Densification: Uses adaptive densification threshold based on the top-K% gradient quantile. Maintenance Loop: The cycle of resurrect→prune→reset runs only during the densify phase. The gate closes immediately after densification ends to prevent net destruction during the settle phase. A procedure to decouple existing cells from newly introduced ones during adaptive density control by resetting offsets of significant Gaussians. 1. Grow new cells at Gaussians with high view-space positional gradients. 2. Reset the offsets of the significant Gaussians to zero, reinitializing their positions to the centers of the corresponding cells. A densification strategy that replaces the original threshold-based growth with a pre-determined parabolic schedule to control the peak and final number of Gaussians, avoiding temporary size spikes. Formula: A(x) = \frac{B - S - 2N}{N^2} x^2 + 2x + B, where N is the number of densification steps, B is the final count (budget), S is the number of SfM points at initialization, and x is the current step index. Step: Compute the difference between the current target count (derived from the parabolic schedule) and the accumulated target count, then densify the corresponding number of primitives to account for pruning. The concept of adaptive density control was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023) [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. The method was designed to handle the trade-off between reconstruction quality and memory usage by dynamically adjusting the number of Gaussians during training. Subsequent works have refined this process to address specific issues such as unbounded growth [1488-ots-satn-densification.md], excessive proliferation in high-frequency regions [3298-loss-accumulation-guided-lag-densification.md], and the need for deterministic splitting based on loss statistics [3304-gaussian-splitting-and-pruning.md]. The technique is widely used in real-time radiance field rendering and novel view synthesis applications. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Duplex-GS: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2026.3666188, fetched 2026-10-30 Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources, https://doi.org/10.1145/3680528.3687694, fetched 2026-10-30

name: OTS+SAtn Densification
head: Densification for Real-World Scenes
body:
OTS+SAtn Densification is a density control strategy adapted from the OTS+SAtn splatting technique to operate within the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework for real-world scene reconstruction. It addresses the problem of unbounded primitive growth and scene-specific overfitting by imposing strict caps on the total number of Gaussians and adapting densification thresholds to match 3DGS conventions. Unlike standard 3DGS which may allow indefinite growth, this method stops densification once a predefined maximum count (e.g., 100k, 500k, 1m, or 5m) is reached, ensuring controlled memory usage while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. The method integrates the OTS+SAtn rendering logic with a densification schedule that mirrors the standard 3DGS adaptive control but with specific constraints for real-world datasets like MipNeRF360. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Set of N 3D Gaussians, each with position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{S} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and view-space positional gradient 
abla{\mathbf{p}} \mathcal{L}. Output: Updated set of Gaussians with modified positions, scales, opacities, and potentially new primitives added or removed. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: List of primitives. Each primitive stores \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3} (symmetric positive definite), \alpha \in [0,1], and 
abla{\mathbf{p}} \mathcal{L} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Thresholds: N{max}: Maximum allowed primitives (e.g., 100,000, 500,000, 1,000,000, 5,000,000). 	au{grad}: Gradient threshold for densification candidates. 	au{opac}: Opacity threshold for pruning. 	au{size}: Size threshold for splitting/pruning. Parameters: Densification Interval: Typically every 100 iterations, starting after a warm-up period (e.g., iteration 100), consistent with 3DGS. Gradient Threshold: 	au{grad} = 1.5 	imes 10^{-4}. Opacity Pruning Threshold: 	au{opac} = 0.025. Size Threshold: Primitives larger than 40% of the scene diagonal or 20 pixels in screen space are considered for removal/splitting. Cloning Threshold: Primitives smaller than 1% of the scene diagonal are candidates for cloning. Splitting Scale Factor: New primitives have a relative size of 1.2^{-1} compared to the parent. Steps: 1. Check Limit: If current primitive count N \ge N{max}, skip densification entirely. 2. Evaluate Candidates: Identify Gaussians where |
abla{\mathbf{p}} \mathcal{L}| > 	au{grad}. 3. Classify Candidates: Small: If size (e.g., standard deviation or diagonal of \mathbf{S}) < 1\% of scene diagonal, mark for Cloning. Large: If size > 40\% of scene diagonal or > 20 pixels, mark for Splitting. Prune: If \alpha < 	au{opac}, mark for Removal. 4. Execute Cloning: For each "Small" candidate, create a new Gaussian at \mathbf{p} with identical \mathbf{S} and q. Set new opacity \alpha{new} = \alpha / 2 [3034-adaptive-densification.md]. 5. Execute Splitting: For each "Large" candidate, remove the original Gaussian. Create two new Gaussians. Position Sampling: If using octahedra representation: Sample position from \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{S}) where standard deviations are aligned with and equal to the distances in each dimension. If using tetrahedra representation: Sample position from \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{S}) where standard deviations are equal to half of the largest distance. Scale Adjustment: Set new scale such that the relative size is 1.2^{-1} of the original. Opacity: Distribute opacity (typically halved) [3034-adaptive-densification.md]. 6. Execute Pruning: Remove all Gaussians marked for removal. 7. Gradient Handling: Do not propagate gradients through the density normalization factor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def otssatndensification(gaussians, scenediagonal, maxprimitives, iteration): """ Perform densification for OTS+SAtn adapted to 3DGS. """ if iteration < 100: # Warm-up period return gaussians if len(gaussians) >= maxprimitives: return gaussians # Stop densification if limit reached candidates = [] toremove = [] for g in gaussians: gradnorm = norm(g.gradient) size = getsize(g) # e.g., max diagonal of covariance # Pruning if g.opacity < 0.025: toremove.append(g) continue # Densification Candidates if gradnorm > 1.5e-4: if size < 0.01 scenediagonal: # Small candidates.append(('clone', g)) elif size > 0.40 scenediagonal or size > 20: # Large candidates.append(('split', g)) # Execute Cloning newgaussians = [] for action, g in candidates: if action == 'clone': # Clone at same position, same scale/rotation, halved opacity [3034-adaptive-densification.md] clone = Gaussian( position=g.position, covariance=g.covariance, rotation=g.rotation, opacity=g.opacity / 2.0, gradient=g.gradient) newgaussians.append(clone) elif action == 'split': # Remove original, add two new ones # Position sampling depends on representation if g.representation == 'octahedra': stddevs = getdimensiondistances(g.covariance) pos1 = samplenormal(g.position, stddevs) pos2 = samplenormal(g.position, stddevs) elif g.representation == 'tetrahedra': maxdist = max(getdimensiondistances(g.covariance)) stddevs = [maxdist / 2.0, maxdist / 2.0, maxdist / 2.0] pos1 = samplenormal(g.position, stddevs) pos2 = samplenormal(g.position, stddevs) # Scale reduction by factor 1.2^-1 scalefactor = 1.2 -1 newcov1 = g.covariance (scalefactor 2) # Assuming scale affects covariance quadratically newcov2 = g.covariance (scalefactor 2) newgaussians.append(Gaussian( position=pos1, covariance=newcov1, rotation=g.rotation, opacity=g.opacity / 2.0, gradient=g.gradient)) newgaussians.append(Gaussian( position=pos2, covariance=newcov2, rotation=g.rotation, opacity=g.opacity / 2.0, gradient=g.gradient)) # Remove pruned and add new remaining = [g for g in gaussians if g not in toremove] finalgaussians = remaining + newgaussians return finalgaussians Gradient-based Densification Control is a mechanism for allocating 3D Gaussian primitives to regions with high reconstruction error by using the magnitude of the photometric loss gradient. It ensures efficient spatial allocation by triggering cloning or splitting operations only when primitives exhibit significant gradients, thereby adapting the representation density to the scene's geometric complexity. It differs from fixed-scale splitting methods by relying on gradient magnitude rather than a static fraction of scene extent, allowing for adaptive refinement based on learning progress. Time Complexity: Densification is periodic (e.g., every 100 iterations). The cost is proportional to the number of candidates, which is a subset of N. Memory Complexity: Bounded by N{max}. The method explicitly stops densification at 100k, 500k, 1m, or 5m primitives. Performance: On MipNeRF360, OTS+SAtn with this densification differs from standard 3DGS by at most 4% PSNR across all tested sizes and scenes. Average training times are slightly lower (2%) for OTS+SAtn. Rendering times are balanced. Strengths: Prevents unbounded growth, suitable for large real-world scenes, maintains competitive quality. Limitations: The strict cap N{max} may limit detail in extremely complex scenes if the cap is too low. The specific thresholds (1.5e-4, 0.025) are tuned for real-world scenes and may not be optimal for synthetic data. The method originates from the OTS+SAtn paper, which explores alternative splatting techniques for differentiable rendering. The authors adapted their densification variables to match 3DGS as closely as possible to evaluate performance on real-world datasets like MipNeRF360 and ScanNet++ v2. The specific thresholds and logic are further detailed in the LinPrim paper, which introduces linear primitives and anti-aliasing strategies, noting that gradients are not propagated through the density normalization factor. name: Gradient-based Densification Control
head: Densification and Gradient Threshold, Gradient-based Densification
body: Gradient-based Densification Control is a mechanism for allocating 3D Gaussian primitives to regions with high reconstruction error by using the magnitude of the photometric loss gradient. It ensures efficient spatial allocation by triggering cloning or splitting operations only when primitives exhibit significant gradients, thereby adapting the representation density to the scene's geometric complexity. It differs from fixed-scale splitting methods by relying on gradient magnitude rather than a static fraction of scene extent, allowing for adaptive refinement based on learning progress. Inputs and Outputs Input: The set of 3D Gaussian primitives, each with a position, covariance (or scale/orientation), opacity, and SH coefficients. The current photometric loss gradient with respect to each primitive's parameters. Output: An updated set of primitives where high-gradient primitives are either cloned (if small) or split (if large), and low-gradient/low-opacity primitives may be pruned (in variants). Data Structures Primitive List: A list of Gaussian primitives. Each primitive stores its state (position \mathbf{c}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, SH coefficients). Gradient Magnitude: A scalar value gi for each primitive i, representing the magnitude of the gradient of the rendering loss with respect to the primitive's parameters (typically position or projected center). Parameters Gradient Threshold (thres{grad}): The minimum gradient magnitude required to trigger densification. Typical range: 1 \times 10^{-10} to 6.5 \times 10^{-9}. Tuned per dataset and volume resolution. Percent-Dense Parameter (per{dense}): The threshold for spatial extent (scale) to decide between cloning and splitting. Typical range: 0.001 to 0.01. Represents a fraction of the local or global scale context. Steps 1. Compute Gradient Magnitude: For each primitive i, calculate the gradient magnitude gi of the photometric loss with respect to the primitive's parameters (e.g., projected 2D center or 3D position). 2. Threshold Comparison: Compare gi against thres{grad}. If gi < thres{grad}, the primitive is not selected for densification. 3. Spatial Extent Evaluation: If gi \ge thres{grad}, evaluate the primitive's spatial extent (scale). If the primitive's scale is smaller than the threshold defined by per{dense}, clone the primitive (to add more primitives in under-reconstructed regions). If the primitive's scale is larger than the threshold defined by per{dense}, split the primitive (to reduce over-reconstruction and increase detail). 4. Parameter Adjustment: Jointly adjust thres{grad} and per{dense} during training to control the aggressiveness of densification based on the dataset and volume resolution. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def densificationcontrol(primitives, lossgradients, thresgrad, perdense): """ primitives: List of Gaussian primitives. Each primitive has attributes: scale: float or vector representing spatial extent gradientmagnitude: float, precomputed gradient magnitude lossgradients: Dict mapping primitiveid to gradient tensor (used to compute gradientmagnitude) thresgrad: float, gradient threshold perdense: float, percent-dense threshold for scale comparison Returns: updatedprimitives: List of primitives after cloning/splitting """ updatedprimitives = [] toclone = [] tosplit = [] # Step 1 & 2: Compute gradient magnitude and compare against threshold for prim in primitives: # Compute gradient magnitude from loss gradients # Assuming gradientmagnitude is precomputed or computed here g = prim.gradientmagnitude if g < thresgrad: # Not dense enough, keep as is (or potentially prune in variants) updatedprimitives.append(prim) else: # Step 3: Evaluate spatial extent # Determine if primitive is "small" or "large" relative to perdense # Note: The exact definition of "scale" vs "perdense" depends on implementation. # Typically, perdense is a fraction of scene extent or local density. # Here we assume a simplified comparison based on source description. # Check if scale is below threshold (small -> clone) # The source says "split if large, clone if small" # and perdense determines this boundary. if prim.scale < perdense: toclone.append(prim) else: tosplit.append(prim) # Perform cloning for prim in toclone: # Clone the primitive (copy parameters, potentially perturb position slightly) clone = prim.copy() clone.position += randomsmallnoise() # Standard practice to avoid overlap updatedprimitives.append(clone) # Keep original? Usually original is kept or replaced. # 3DGS typically keeps original and adds new. updatedprimitives.append(prim) # Perform splitting for prim in tosplit: # Split the primitive into two or more smaller primitives # Standard 3DGS split: create 2 children with half scale child1 = prim.split() child2 = prim.split() updatedprimitives.append(child1) updatedprimitives.append(child2) return updatedprimitives Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Gradient values can be extremely small (10^{-10} range), requiring careful handling of floating-point precision. Boundary Conditions: The threshold thres{grad} must be tuned carefully; too high, and no densification occurs; too low, and excessive primitives are created. Degenerate Input: Primitives with zero or near-zero gradients are ignored, which is correct, but primitives with very large gradients might cause instability if not clamped. A densification criterion for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses the mean magnitude of the photometric loss gradient with respect to the primitive's projected 2D screen-space center to identify regions requiring refinement. It differs from 2DGS [Huang et al. 2024] by using an analytical T-matrix backward pass to compute screen-space gradients, avoiding the conflation of depth and lateral motion inherent in projecting 3D center gradients. A splitting/cloning strategy that compares surfel scale against local sampling density (mean neighbor distance) rather than a fixed global scene extent fraction. It maintains a spatial index structure over surfel centers and queries the mean distance \bar{d} to same-orientation nearest neighbors for each surfel to estimate local sampling density. This approach avoids the unsuitability of global scale thresholds, which do not adapt to local density or enforce the spatially varying overlap condition required by the partition-of-unity assumption. A dynamic adjustment process that adds new anchors in high-gradient regions (needing detail) and removes low-opacity anchors (unnecessary) to maintain optimal anchor distribution. It evaluates gradient magnitudes to identify high-gradient regions, adds new anchors where higher detail is needed, identifies low-opacity anchors that contribute little to the final rendering, and prunes them. Key parameters include anchorgrowing (flag to enable adding new anchors) and visiblethreshold (threshold to filter out less important anchor points). Time Complexity: The densification step is O(N) where N is the number of primitives, as it involves iterating through all primitives to check gradients and scales. The spatial index query for density-aware splitting adds a logarithmic factor O(N \log N) or O(N) with efficient spatial hashing. Memory Complexity: Increases with the number of primitives. Cloning and splitting increase the number of primitives, thus increasing memory usage. Pruning reduces it. Measured Performance: The method is tuned for specific datasets (e.g., hemibrain, BigBrain) with gradient thresholds in the range of 10^{-10} to 10^{-9} and percent-dense parameters in 0.001 to 0.01. Strengths: Efficient allocation of primitives to regions with high reconstruction error, adaptive refinement based on learning progress. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of thresholds (thres{grad}, per{dense}) for different datasets and resolutions. Fixed-scale methods (if used) do not adapt to local density. When to Use: When the scene has varying levels of detail and computational resources need to be allocated efficiently. When Not to Use: When the scene is uniform and does not require adaptive refinement, or when computational budget is extremely tight and static resolution is sufficient. Originating from the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting [Kerbl et al. 2023], gradient-based densification control has been adapted for volume rendering and sparse volume representations. It was further refined in methods like 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS) to address local density variations and in Level of Detail systems for Gaussian Splatting to manage anchor points dynamically. The method is used in applications such as connectome analysis (hemibrain, BigBrain datasets) and neural processing for inverse rendering. name: Screen-Space Gradient Densification Criterion
head: Screen-Space Gradient Densification
body: A densification criterion for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses the mean magnitude of the photometric loss gradient with respect to the primitive's projected 2D screen-space center to identify regions requiring refinement. It differs from 2DGS [Huang et al. 2024] by using an analytical T-matrix backward pass to compute screen-space gradients, avoiding the conflation of depth and lateral motion inherent in projecting 3D center gradients. Inputs: Photometric loss \mathcal{L}j for each training view j. Projection matrix T for each view, where T{m,n} is the n-component of the m-th row. Primitive i with projected screen-space center \boldsymbol{\mu}i = (u, v). Outputs: Mean gradient score \bar{g}i for primitive i. Data Structures: Accumulator for gradient scores per primitive. Per-view gradient contributions gx, gy. Steps: 1. For each training view j, compute the projection matrix T. 2. Determine the screen-space center coordinates (u, v) for primitive i using the implicit definition: u = \frac{T{1,z}}{T{4,z}}, \quad v = \frac{T{2,z}}{T{4,z}} where z denotes the specific row index used for projection (typically related to the depth component in the backward pass context). 3. Compute the per-pixel contributions to the screen-space positional gradient using the chain rule through the T-matrix gradients: gx = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial T{1,z}} \cdot T{4,z} gy = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial T{2,z}} \cdot T{4,z} where \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial T{m,z}} are the gradients of the loss with respect to the projection matrix elements. 4. Calculate the gradient norm for the primitive in view j: \left\| \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}j}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}i} \right\|2 = \sqrt{gx^2 + gy^2} 5. Accumulate the gradient norms over all N views where primitive i contributed to the rendered image. 6. Compute the mean gradient score: \bar{g}i = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^N \left\| \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}j}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}i} \right\|2 where N is the number of views in which primitive i contributed. Parameters: Threshold for \bar{g}i to trigger densification: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occluded views: The sum is over views where the primitive contributed. Occluded views where the Gaussian contributes zero are excluded from the count N, preventing artificial depression of the gradient score. Gradient cancellation: The analytical T-matrix backward pass avoids gradient cancellation issues identified in other methods. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computescreenspacegradientscore(primitive, views): """ Compute the mean screen-space gradient score for a primitive. Args: primitive: Object containing properties of the 3D Gaussian. views: List of view objects, each containing projection matrix T and loss L. Returns: float: Mean gradient score bargi. """ totalgradnorm = 0.0 viewcount = 0 for view in views: # Check if primitive contributed to this view if not primitive.contributedto(view): continue viewcount += 1 # Get projection matrix T and loss L for this view T = view.projectionmatrix L = view.loss # Compute screen-space center components # Note: z is the specific row index used for projection in the backward pass # This is implied by the context of T-matrix backward pass T1z = T[0, z] T2z = T[1, z] T4z = T[3, z] # Compute per-pixel contributions to screen-space positional gradient # Using chain rule through T-matrix gradients dLdT1z = view.gradientoflosswrtT[0, z] dLdT2z = view.gradientoflosswrtT[1, z] gx = dLdT1z T4z gy = dLdT2z T4z # Compute gradient norm gradnorm = sqrt(gx2 + gy2) totalgradnorm += gradnorm if viewcount == 0: return 0.0 meangradscore = totalgradnorm / viewcount return meangradscore Normalizes the accumulated photometric gradient by the Gaussian's average rendering contribution across views, rather than the raw number of visible views. It prevents occluded primitives from artificially depressing the gradient score and stalling densification in complex scenes. It builds on Screen-Space Gradient Densification Criterion by refining how the gradient signal is scaled. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of views N for each primitive, as it requires accumulating gradients over all views where the primitive contributes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradient accumulators for each primitive. Strengths: Avoids the discrepancy introduced by projecting 3D center gradients to the image plane, which conflates depth and lateral motion. Prevents gradient cancellation. Limitations: Requires access to the T-matrix backward pass gradients, which may not be available in all rasterizers. When to use: When accurate screen-space gradient estimation is critical for densification, especially in scenes with complex geometry where depth and lateral motion are distinct. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and the approximation used by 2DGS is deemed sufficient. Originated in 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS) [Ye et al. 2024b; Yu et al. 2024b], as an improvement over the densification criterion used in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023] and the approximation used in 2DGS [Huang et al. 2024]. It addresses the issue of over-reconstructed regions being incorrectly identified for refinement by using a principled criterion based on screen-space gradients. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Contribution-Based Normalization
head: Average Contribution Normalization, contribution-weighted densification, mean contribution normalization
body: Contribution-Based Normalization is a densification criterion for 3D Gaussian Splatting that normalizes the accumulated photometric gradient by the Gaussian's average rendering contribution across views, rather than by the raw number of visible views or pixels. It solves the problem of occlusion-induced bias where standard view-count normalization stalls densification for Gaussians that are frequently occluded but still require refinement in visible regions. Unlike its sibling Screen-Space Gradient Densification Criterion which relies on gradient magnitude thresholds, this method scales the gradient signal by the mean blending weight \bar{w}i, ensuring that the densification score reflects the actual influence of the Gaussian on the image rather than its geometric footprint or visibility count. Inputs and Outputs: Input: For each Gaussian i, the accumulated gradient vector \mathbf{g}i over all training views, and the set of per-pixel contribution weights w{i,p} for all pixels p where the Gaussian contributes to the final color. Output: A scalar densification score \gammai. If \gammai exceeds a threshold \tau, the Gaussian is split or cloned. Data Structures: Accumulated Gradient \mathbf{g}i: A 2D vector (g{i,x}, g{i,y}) storing the sum of gradients with respect to the projected screen-space mean \mui across all views. Contribution Weights w{i,p}: A scalar value per pixel p in the view, defined as w{i,p} = \alpha{i,p} T{i,p}, where \alpha{i,p} is the Gaussian's opacity at pixel p and T{i,p} is the transmittance reaching the Gaussian. Formulas: 1. Projected Footprint: The unnormalized Gaussian kernel at pixel p is: G{i,p} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (p - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (p - \mui)\right) where \mui is the projected screen-space mean and \Sigmai is the projected 2D covariance matrix. 2. Per-Pixel Gradient Component: The gradient contribution for the x-component (y is analogous) at pixel p in a specific view is: g{i,x,p} = \frac{\partial Lp}{\partial Cp} \cdot (ci - A{i,p}) \cdot w{i,p} \cdot \frac{\partial \ln(G{i,p})}{\partial \mu{i,x}} where: \frac{\partial Lp}{\partial Cp} is the photometric error gradient at pixel p. ci is the color of Gaussian i. A{i,p} is the accumulated color from Gaussians rendered before i (background/transmittance accumulation). w{i,p} = \alpha{i,p} T{i,p} is the contribution weight. \frac{\partial \ln(G{i,p})}{\partial \mu{i,x}} is the geometric steering term, derived from the Gaussian's shape. 3. Accumulated Gradient: The total gradient for Gaussian i in a view is the sum over all pixels p: \mathbf{g}{i,v} = \sump \mathbf{g}{i,p} The global accumulated gradient \mathbf{g}i is the sum of \mathbf{g}{i,v} over all views v where the Gaussian is rendered. 4. Mean Contribution: The normalizer is the average contribution weight across all pixels p that the Gaussian contributes to in a view: \bar{w}{i,v} = \frac{1}{N{i,v}} \sump w{i,p} where N{i,v} is the number of pixels p where w{i,p} > 0 in view v. Note: The global mean contribution \bar{w}i used in the final score is typically the sum of per-view means or the mean over all pixels across all views, depending on the specific implementation variant. The core definition uses the per-view mean to avoid footprint bias. 5. Densification Score: The final criterion score \gammai is: \gammai = \frac{\|\mathbf{g}i\|}{1 + \sumv \bar{w}{i,v}} The +1 in the denominator prevents division by zero and bounds the score for Gaussians with negligible contribution. Parameters: Threshold \tau: A scalar value triggering densification. Default: 0.002 (improves metrics but increases Gaussian count). Conservative: 0.003 (reduces count while retaining gains). Values > 0.004 lead to under-densification. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecontributionnormalizationscore(gaussian, views): """ Computes the contribution-based normalization score for a single Gaussian. Args: gaussian: Object containing projected mean mui, covariance Sigmai, opacity alpha, and color ci. views: List of view objects, each containing camera projection info and pre-computed transmittance T for the Gaussian. Returns: score: The densification criterion value. """ accumulatedgradient = [0.0, 0.0] # [x, y] components totalmeancontribution = 0.0 for view in views: # 1. Compute projected footprint parameters for this view # Project 3D mean and covariance to 2D screen space mu2d = projectmean(gaussian.mu3d, view.cameramatrix) Sigma2d = projectcovariance(gaussian.Sigma3d, view.cameramatrix, gaussian.mu3d) # 2. Identify contributing pixels and compute weights # In practice, this is done during rasterization. # Here we assume we have access to the list of pixels p where the Gaussian is visible. contributingpixels = getcontributingpixels(gaussian, view) viewgradient = [0.0, 0.0] sumweights = 0.0 countpixels = 0 for p in contributingpixels: # Compute Gaussian kernel value Gi,p diff = p - mu2d exponent = -0.5 diff.dot(Sigma2d.inv() diff) Gip = exp(exponent) # Compute contribution weight wi,p = alpha T # alpha is derived from Gip and the Gaussian's base opacity alphaip = gaussian.opacity Gip Tip = view.transmittanceatpixel(p, gaussian) # Pre-computed or computed via depth wip = alphaip Tip # Compute geometric steering term: d(ln(G))/d(mux) # ln(G) = -0.5 (p-mu)^T Sigma^-1 (p-mu) # d(ln(G))/d(mu) = Sigma^-1 (p - mu) steering = Sigma2d.inv() diff # Compute photometric error and contrast term # Lp is the loss at pixel p, Cp is the final pixel color # dL/dC is the gradient of the loss w.r.t the final pixel color dLdC = view.lossgradient[p] # Ai,p is the accumulated color from previous Gaussians (background) Aip = view.accumulatedcolorbefore[p] contrast = gaussian.color - Aip # Gradient component for this pixel # gi,x = dL/dC (ci - Ai,p) wi,p steeringx pixelgrad = dLdC contrast wip steering viewgradient[0] += pixelgrad[0] viewgradient[1] += pixelgrad[1] sumweights += wip countpixels += 1 # Compute mean contribution for this view if countpixels > 0: meanwview = sumweights / countpixels else: meanwview = 0.0 totalmeancontribution += meanwview accumulatedgradient[0] += viewgradient[0] accumulatedgradient[1] += viewgradient[1] # Compute final score gradnorm = sqrt(accumulatedgradient[0]2 + accumulatedgradient[1]2) score = gradnorm / (1.0 + totalmeancontribution) return score Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cloning Over-densification: The clone operation (creating a new Gaussian at the same position) can cause catastrophic over-densification and inflated counts without quality improvement. Mitigation: Disable cloning by overriding the scene extent or forcing split-only densification. Occlusion Bias: Normalizing by raw view count M (as in standard 3DGS) includes occluded views where the gradient is zero, dragging down the average and stalling densification. This method avoids that by using contribution. Footprint Bias: Using the per-view total weight \sump w{i,p} as the normalizer reintroduces pixel-count dependence, as larger footprints accumulate more weight. The mean contribution \bar{w}i is footprint-free. A variant that scales both the gradient sum and the weight sum by the number of rendered views Ni to compute the densification score. Formula: \gammai^{\text{per-view}} = \frac{\sumv \|\mathbf{g}{i,v}\|/Ni}{1 + \sumv \bar{w}{i,v}/Ni} Comparison: Produces reconstruction quality similar to the baseline normalizer but requires approximately 1.4× more Gaussians to reach the same operating point. A variant that replaces the per-view mean with the per-view total weight W{i,v} = \sump w{i,p} in the denominator. Formula: \gammai^{\text{sum-alloc}} = \frac{\sumv \|\mathbf{g}{i,v}\|}{1 + \sumv W{i,v}} Comparison: This places the denominator on a different scale and reintroduces footprint dependence, leading to instability or divergence on large scenes compared to the mean contribution variant. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P \cdot V), where N is the number of Gaussians, P is the average number of pixels per Gaussian footprint, and V is the number of views. The normalization step is O(V) per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot V) to store accumulated gradients and contribution sums if not computed on the fly. Performance: On occlusion-heavy scenes (e.g., Zip-NeRF), this method outperforms standard baselines (like StopThePop) on all image-quality metrics, reducing LPIPS by up to 12%. It keeps the Gaussian count bounded under long training schedules where other criteria diverge. Scaling: On smaller benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360), it improves metrics at the cost of increased Gaussian count (1.8× on 2DGS, 2.4× on 3DGS at threshold 0.002). Raising the threshold to 0.003 reduces the count closer to baseline levels while retaining gains. Strengths: Robust to occlusion; prevents bias toward large footprints; generalizes to 2DGS and 3DGS renderers. Limitations: Requires careful threshold tuning; prone to over-densification if cloning is not suppressed; higher Gaussian counts than some baseline methods at default thresholds. Originated in the paper "Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting". The method was developed to address the limitations of view-count normalization in the presence of occlusions, which is common in complex scenes. It builds on the observation that the gradient signal is intrinsically contribution-weighted, making the mean contribution a natural normalizer. The method has been ported and validated on 2DGS and 3DGS frameworks, demonstrating its generalizability beyond the original StopThePop baseline. Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27108, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Densification
head: Adaptive Density Control (ADC), Cloning and Splitting, Gaussian Cloning, Splitting, and Pruning, Gradient-based densification, Original Densification
body: Adaptive Densification is a training-time mechanism that dynamically adjusts the number, position, and scale of 3D Gaussian primitives to improve reconstruction quality while managing memory constraints. It solves the limitation of standard gradient descent, which can only move or scale existing Gaussians but cannot create new ones in empty regions or cleanly remove useless ones. By periodically inspecting view-space positional gradients, it identifies under-reconstructed areas (requiring cloning) and over-reconstructed areas (requiring splitting), ensuring the representation density matches the scene complexity. Inputs: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}: Mean positions of n Gaussians. \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}: Standard deviations (scales) of Gaussians. I \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}: Intensities (or opacity/alpha) of Gaussians. \mu.grad: Accumulated view-space positional gradients for each Gaussian. n{max}: Maximum allowed number of Gaussians (default 500,000). \tau: Minimum gradient threshold for densification (default 2 \times 10^{-4}). \theta: Threshold for classifying Gaussians as small or large (default 0.005 of the scene body diagonal). size: Box size parameter for pruning (default 17). Outputs: Updated \mu, \sigma, I arrays reflecting cloned, split, and pruned Gaussians. Data Structures: Arrays for mean, scale, intensity, and gradient accumulation. Boolean masks (maskclone, masksplit, maskprune) to identify candidates. Steps: 1. Iteration Loop: Execute densification every K=100 iterations, starting from iteration 100 up to the maximum training iterations. 2. Gradient Averaging: Calculate the average gradient magnitude for each Gaussian: \text{avg\grad} = \frac{\|\mu.grad\|}{\text{iteration}} 3. Cloning (Under-reconstructed): Identify candidates where \text{avg\grad} \ge \tau AND \sigma \le \theta. Calculate available slots: n{avail} = n{max} - n. Determine number of clones: n{clone} = \min(n{avail}, \text{count}(\text{candidates})). Select top n{clone} candidates based on descending average gradient. Create clones: Duplicate position \mu and scale \sigma. Halve intensity I \leftarrow I/2 to preserve total intensity. Detach gradients of clones (set to zero). Append clones to the set, incrementing n. 4. Splitting (Over-reconstructed): Identify candidates where \text{avg\grad} \ge \tau AND \sigma > \theta. Recalculate available slots: n{avail} = n{max} - n. Determine number of splits: n{split} = \min(n{avail}, \text{count}(\text{candidates})). Select top n{split} candidates based on descending average gradient. Create splits: Sample new positions \mu{new} from the probability density function (PDF) of the original Gaussian. Update scales: Reduce standard deviation by dividing by \sqrt{3}/2 to maintain volume: \sigma{new} = \frac{\sigma{split}}{\sqrt{3}/2} Set intensity I{new} = I{split}. Remove original split Gaussians and append new ones, incrementing n by n{split}. 5. Pruning: Identify Gaussians to remove where \text{avg\grad} \le \tau OR \sigma > 3 \times size. Filter out pruned Gaussians from \mu, \sigma, I. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivedensification(mu, sigma, I, mugrad, iteration, nmax, tau, theta, size): """ Performs adaptive densification (cloning, splitting, pruning) on 3D Gaussians. Args: mu: List of lists, shape (n, d) for Gaussian means. sigma: List of floats, shape (n,) for Gaussian scales. I: List of floats, shape (n,) for Gaussian intensities/opacities. mugrad: List of lists, shape (n, d) for accumulated view-space positional gradients. iteration: Current training iteration number. nmax: Maximum number of Gaussians (default 500,000). tau: Gradient threshold for densification (default 2e-4). theta: Scale threshold for small/large classification (default 0.005 scenediagonal). size: Box size for pruning threshold (default 17). Returns: Updated mu, sigma, I, mugrad arrays. """ import math import random def norm(vec): return math.sqrt(sum(v v for v in vec)) def argsortdesc(arr): return sorted(range(len(arr)), key=lambda i: arr[i], reverse=True) def concatenate(arrays): return [item for arr in arrays for item in arr] def zeros(shape): if len(shape) == 1: return [0.0] shape[0] elif len(shape) == 2: return [[0.0] shape[1] for in range(shape[0])] def samplenormal(mean, std): return random.gauss(mean, std) n = len(mu) # Step 1: Calculate average gradient avggrad = [norm(g) / iteration for g in mugrad] # Step 2: Cloning (Small, High Gradient) clonecandidates = [i for i in range(n) if avggrad[i] >= tau and sigma[i] <= theta] availableslots = nmax - n nclone = min(availableslots, len(clonecandidates)) if nclone > 0: sortedindices = argsortdesc([avggrad[i] for i in clonecandidates])[:nclone] cloneindices = [clonecandidates[i] for i in sortedindices] muclone = [mu[i][:] for i in cloneindices] sigmaclone = [sigma[i] for i in cloneindices] Iclone = [I[i] / 2.0 for i in cloneindices] mugradclone = zeros((nclone, len(mu[0]))) mu = concatenate(mu, muclone) sigma = concatenate(sigma, sigmaclone) I = concatenate(I, Iclone) mugrad = concatenate(mugrad, mugradclone) n += nclone # Step 3: Splitting (Large, High Gradient) splitcandidates = [i for i in range(n) if avggrad[i] >= tau and sigma[i] > theta] availableslots = nmax - n nsplit = min(availableslots, len(splitcandidates)) if nsplit > 0: sortedindices = argsortdesc([avggrad[i] for i in splitcandidates])[:nsplit] splitindices = [splitcandidates[i] for i in sortedindices] munew = [[samplenormal(mu[i][d], sigma[i]) for d in range(len(mu[0]))] for i in splitindices] sigmanew = [sigma[i] / (math.sqrt(3) / 2.0) for i in splitindices] Inew = [I[i] for i in splitindices] keepmask = [i for i in range(n) if i not in splitindices] mu = [mu[i] for i in keepmask] sigma = [sigma[i] for i in keepmask] I = [I[i] for i in keepmask] mugrad = [mugrad[i] for i in keepmask] mugradnew = zeros((nsplit, len(mu[0]))) mu = concatenate(mu, munew) sigma = concatenate(sigma, sigmanew) I = concatenate(I, Inew) mugrad = concatenate(mugrad, mugradnew) n += nsplit # Step 4: Pruning prunemask = [i for i in range(n) if avggrad[i] <= tau or sigma[i] > 3 size] keepmask = [i for i in range(n) if i not in prunemask] mu = [mu[i] for i in keepmask] sigma = [sigma[i] for i in keepmask] I = [I[i] for i in keepmask] mugrad = [mugrad[i] for i in keepmask] return mu, sigma, I, mugrad Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Collisions: Accumulating view-space positional gradients can lead to cancellation if positive and negative gradients occur in different views, resulting in poor densification heuristics. Unbounded Growth: Without the n{max} constraint, the number of Gaussians can grow indefinitely, exhausting memory. Blurry Backgrounds: Disabling splitting leaves over-large Gaussians unbroken, causing blurry backgrounds. Lost Structures: Disabling cloning causes under-covered thin structures (e.g., bicycle spokes) to be lost. Fixed-Pool Relocation redistributes a fixed budget of splats to areas of high reconstruction error without increasing the total component count. It identifies low-importance splats and moves them to local maxima of the positive reconstruction residual, reinitializing them to explore new geometry. Unlike Adaptive Densification, which increases the Gaussian count via cloning and splitting, Fixed-Pool Relocation maintains a constant budget by recycling existing components, making it suitable for memory-constrained environments or scenes where the total number of primitives must remain strictly bounded [3094-fixed-pool-relocation.md]. Blind-Spot Cross-Validation is a model selection procedure that determines the optimal number of Gaussians (splat budget) for a 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction without requiring noise-free ground truth references. It identifies the point of diminishing returns where additional splats begin to memorize noise rather than signal by monitoring the divergence between training and held-out PSNR metrics. Unlike standard cross-validation, it ensures the masked voxel's noise is unpredictable from its neighbors, guaranteeing that fitting the masked data lowers the held-out score if noise is being memorized. Density-Aware Densification is a mechanism for surfel densification that uses a density-aware splitting criterion based on local inter-sample spacing and a screen-space gradient accumulation strategy based on T-matrix backward passes. It maintains the partition-of-unity assumption by adjusting surfel density as geometry evolves during optimization, similar to 3DGS densification. It replaces the ad-hoc projected 3D position gradient used in 2DGS with screen-space gradients from the T-matrix backward pass and replaces the global scale threshold used in 3DGS with a criterion that adapts to spatially varying overlap conditions. Temporal Densification is a strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that detects and resolves reconstruction errors caused by object or camera motion by splitting Gaussians based on the variance of their normalized image error across time segments. It addresses the limitation of static spatial densification, which assumes Gaussians are stationary, by identifying Gaussians whose error fluctuates significantly between keyframes, indicating they fail to track motion. Density-preserving Splitting is a densification strategy that discards cloning operations and relies only on splitting operations to avoid loss function perturbations. Inspired by the observation that original splitting operations cause perturbations in the loss function, this variant modifies the splitting operation so that the resulting density after splitting is similar to the density of the Gaussian being split. Splitting is performed along the longest principal axis, by shifting means by \pm \alpha \sigma, where \alpha is a constant (set to 0.3) and \sigma is the size along the splitting axis. To ensure that the resulting density of the sum of the two children is close to the density of the mother Gaussian, the sizes and opacity of the split Gaussians are adjusted. Time Complexity: Densification is performed periodically (e.g., every 100 iterations), so the overhead is amortized. Memory Complexity: The number of Gaussians N is bounded by n{max} (default 500,000). Performance: Adaptive densification significantly improves reconstruction quality by capturing fine details and thin structures that a fixed initialization cannot represent. Strengths: Automatically adapts to scene complexity; prevents over-smoothing in detailed regions; removes floating artifacts via pruning. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of thresholds (\tau, \theta); prone to gradient collision issues if not handled (e.g., using Absgrad); can lead to unbounded growth if n{max} is not enforced. When to use: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training where high-fidelity reconstruction is required and memory allows for dynamic growth. When not to use: Memory-constrained environments (consider Fixed-Pool Relocation) or scenes with significant motion (consider Temporal Densification). Adaptive Densification was introduced by Kerbl et al. in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper (2023). It was designed to address the sparse initialization problem, where a fixed set of Gaussians cannot adequately represent complex scenes. The method builds on the idea that gradient descent alone is insufficient for creating new primitives, necessitating a discrete densification step. It has since become a standard component of 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines and has inspired numerous variants and improvements. A Survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3807511, fetched 2026-10-27 An Architectural Review of the 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21739653, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Triangle Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/3DV69130.2026.00123, fetched 2026-10-27 Discretized Gaussian Representation for Tomographic Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51701.2025.02325, fetched 2026-10-27 gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 BOGausS: Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.23919/eusipco63237.2025.11226626, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Fixed-Pool Relocation
head: Component Recycling, Dynamic Operations, Relocating low opacity components to high opacity component
body: Fixed-Pool Relocation is a densification strategy that redistributes a fixed budget of splats to areas of high reconstruction error without increasing the total component count. It identifies low-importance splats and moves them to local maxima of the positive reconstruction residual, reinitializing them to explore new geometry. Unlike Adaptive Densification, which increases the Gaussian count via cloning and splitting, Fixed-Pool Relocation maintains a constant budget by recycling existing components, making it suitable for memory-constrained environments or scenes where the total number of primitives must remain strictly bounded. Inputs: Current set of splats (Gaussians) with positions \mu, covariances \Sigma, opacities O, and Adam optimizer states. Current view volume V and reconstructed volume \hat{V}. Residual threshold parameters (e.g., bottom 1%, max 64 splats). Iteration counter. Outputs: Updated set of splats with modified positions, opacities, and covariances. Data Structures: Splat Pool: A list of splats. Each splat contains: mu: 3D position vector. sigma: Isotropic scale parameter (or covariance matrix). opacity: Scalar opacity value. adamm: First moment estimate (vector). adamv: Second moment estimate (vector). lastrelocatediter: Integer iteration index of last relocation (for cooldown). Residual Volume: A 3D grid or sparse structure storing (V - \hat{V})+ values. Steps: 1. Identify Candidates: Calculate an importance score ak for each splat k, defined as amplitude times approximate volume (L{k,ii}). Sort splats by this score. Select the bottom 1% of splats that also sit at low residual. Limit the selection to at most 64 splats per step, ensuring at most one splat is selected per detected residual peak. 2. Find Relocation Targets: Compute the positive reconstruction residual R = (V - \hat{V})+. Find local maxima of R using non-maximum suppression over the volume. 3. Relocate and Reinitialize: For each selected splat k: a. Move its position \muk to the location of a local residual maximum. b. Reinitialize the scale isotropically to \sigma = 0.5 voxels. c. Zero the Adam first- and second-moment estimates (adam\m = 0, adam\v = 0) to allow fresh learning. d. Update lastrelocatediter to the current iteration. 4. Opacity Preservation (Component Recycling): When relocating N new components to the location of an old component (\mu{new} = \mu{old}), preserve the total distribution by adjusting opacity. The new opacity O{new} is calculated from the old opacity O{old} using: (1 - O{new})^N = (1 - O{old}) O{new} = 1 - (1 - O{old})^{1/N} where N is the number of new components created from the old one. Note: In the standard Fixed-Pool Relocation described in, splats are moved rather than split, but the opacity preservation logic is critical when the method is used for densification via relocation (see Subtopics). 5. Cooldown: Prevent the same splat from being relocated again before it adapts. Enforce a cooldown period of at least 1 relocation step (i.e., currentiter - lastrelocatediter >= 1). 6. Cache Reordering (Periodic): Every 1,000 iterations, reorder the splats along a Morton (Z-order) curve to improve GPU cache locality. 7. Conservative Culling (Post-Fitting): After fitting completes, perform a single pass of conservative culling. Remove splats accounting for the lowest fraction of cumulative amplitude. Default retention is 99.9% (removing 0.1%), though 5% removal is used in some Python API defaults. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fixedpoolrelocation(splats, residualvolume, currentiter, config): """ splats: List of Splat objects residualvolume: 3D grid or sparse map of (V - Vhat)+ currentiter: int config: dict with keys 'relocationinterval', 'maxrelocations', 'residualthreshold', 'cooldown' """ if currentiter % config['relocationinterval'] != 0: return splats # Step 1: Identify bottom 1% low-residual splats scores = [s.amplitude s.volume for s in splats] sortedindices = np.argsort(scores) numtorelocate = max(1, int(len(splats) 0.01)) candidates = sortedindices[:numtorelocate] # Limit to maxrelocations (e.g., 64) candidates = candidates[:config['maxrelocations']] # Filter by cooldown candidates = [s for s in candidates if (currentiter - s.lastrelocatediter) >= config['cooldown']] # Step 2: Find local maxima in residual volume # This requires non-maximum suppression on residualvolume peaks = findlocalmaxima(residualvolume) # Assign peaks to candidates (one per peak, up to len(peaks)) assignments = list(zip(candidates, peaks[:len(candidates)])) for splatidx, peakpos in assignments: splat = splats[splatidx] # Step 3: Relocate splat.mu = peakpos # Reinitialize isotropically splat.sigma = 0.5 # voxels # Zero Adam moments splat.adamm = np.zeros(3) splat.adamv = np.zeros(3) # Update cooldown timestamp splat.lastrelocatediter = currentiter # Note: Opacity adjustment depends on variant. # In pure relocation (S1), opacity is kept or re-initialized. # In Component Recycling (S2/S3), opacity is preserved via formula. # If this is a split/relocation hybrid, apply opacity formula: # Onew = 1 - (1 - Oold)^(1/N) # Step 6: Cache Reordering every 1000 iterations if currentiter % 1000 == 0: splats = reordermorton(splats) return splats A variant where relocation is used to densify rather than just redistribute. When a primitive with opacity o, circumradius R, and sharpness \sigma is replaced by N co-located copies, the new opacity is computed as o{\text{new}} = 1 - (1 - o)^{1/N}. For N=2 (standard densification), one child is placed at the sampled position, and the other is offset in the primitive's tangent plane by \eta \epsilon, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and \eta is a noise scale. The scale (circumradius) is corrected to maintain the rendered image using the denominator D = \sum{i=1}^{N}\sum{k=0}^{i-1} \binom{i-1}{k}(-1)^k \frac{o{\text{new}}^{k+1}}{(\sigma(k+1)+1)(\sigma(k+1)+2)} and the formula R{\text{new}} = R \sqrt{\frac{o}{(\sigma+1)(\sigma+2) \cdot D}}. This variant is chosen when the goal is to increase density in under-reconstructed regions while strictly preserving the visual output of the parent primitive before splitting. Time Complexity: O(N) to score and sort splats, where N is the number of splats. Finding residual peaks depends on the resolution of the residual volume. Morton reordering is O(N \log N) or O(N) with efficient encoding. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the splat pool. Requires additional memory for the residual volume if stored explicitly. Performance: Maintains a fixed memory footprint, unlike densification methods that grow N. The 50-iteration interval balances responsiveness with computational overhead. The 1,000-iteration Morton reordering is lightweight but improves rendering throughput. Strengths: Prevents unbounded growth of Gaussian count. Effective for filling holes in sparse reconstructions without adding memory pressure. Limitations: May struggle in highly dynamic scenes if the relocation target (residual peak) moves faster than the splat can adapt. The fixed budget may limit detail in very complex scenes compared to unbounded densification. When to use: Memory-constrained applications, microscopy data (Luxar), or when a strict upper bound on primitive count is required. When not to use: Scenes requiring extremely high detail that exceeds the fixed budget's capacity, or when dynamic objects change structure rapidly. Fixed-Pool Relocation was introduced in the context of scalable Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scientific data visualization, specifically in the Luxar framework. It is also referred to as "Dynamic Operations" in that context. The concept of "Component Recycling" appears in 3D Student Splatting, where it is used to maintain distribution consistency when moving components. The variant involving primitive relocation with scale correction is detailed in Fourier Splatting, which generalizes the approach to non-Gaussian primitives. The method addresses the problem of inefficient coverage in sparse initializations or regions with high reconstruction error, without the memory overhead of traditional densification.
