name: Blind-Spot Cross-Validation
head: Blind-spot cross-validation for Gaussian splat model selection, blind-spot CV, blind-spot validation, luxar gsplat cal
body: Blind-Spot Cross-Validation is a model selection procedure that determines the optimal number of Gaussians (splat budget) for a 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction without requiring noise-free ground truth references. It identifies the point of diminishing returns where additional splats begin to memorize noise rather than signal by monitoring the divergence between training and held-out PSNR metrics. Unlike standard cross-validation, it ensures the masked voxel's noise is unpredictable from its neighbors, guaranteeing that fitting the masked data lowers the held-out score if noise is being memorized. Inputs: Original 3D volume V (normalized to [0, 1]). Gaussian Splatting fitting parameters: conservative culling (99.9% amplitude retention), maximum iterations N{max} = 20,000, early stopping patience P = 500, L1 loss, dynamic operations enabled. Masking seed: 42 (numpy RandomState). Masking fraction: 5% of voxels. Outputs: Optimal splat count K^ where held-out PSNR peaks. Classification of the held-out curve (peak, plateau, or signal-limited). Estimated ensemble noise-floor PSNR ceiling. Data Structures: Volume V: 3D array of voxel intensities. Mask M: Boolean 3D array of same shape as V, with 5% of entries set to True. Filled Volume V{filled}: Copy of V where masked voxels are replaced by the median of their 26 neighbors in a 3x3x3 donut (excluding the center voxel). Steps: 1. Mask Generation: Select 5% of voxels randomly using numpy.RandomState with seed 42 to generate mask M. 2. Volume Filling: Create V{filled} by replacing each voxel v where M[v] is True with the median intensity of its 26 spatial neighbors in the 3x3x3 neighborhood excluding v. Note: A stricter implementation excludes other held-out voxels from the median calculation, but this changes held-out PSNR by at most 0.25 dB and moves no optimum. 3. Splat Sweep: For each splat count K in a geometrically spaced sequence (doubling from 1K to 512K, extended to 1M and 2M): a. Fit Gaussian splats to V{filled} using the specified fitting parameters. b. Compute Training PSNR (PSNR{train}) on unmasked voxels against the original volume V. c. Compute Held-out PSNR (PSNR{held}) on masked voxels against the original volume V (using pre-replacement values). PSNR is computed as 10 \log{10} (1 / \text{MSE}) where MSE is averaged over all voxels including background. 4. Optimum Selection: Identify K^ as the splat count where PSNR{held} peaks. 5. Classification: Classify the held-out curve shape and estimate the noise-floor PSNR ceiling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def blindspotcrossvalidation(volume, seed=42, maskfraction=0.05, maxsplats=2000000, minsplats=1000): # 1. Mask Generation rng = np.random.RandomState(seed) mask = rng.random(volume.shape) < maskfraction # 2. Volume Filling filledvolume = volume.copy() maskedindices = np.where(mask) offsets = [(dx, dy, dz) for dx in [-1, 0, 1] for dy in [-1, 0, 1] for dz in [-1, 0, 1] if not (dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0)] for i, j, k in zip(maskedindices): neighbors = [volume[i+dx, j+dy, k+dz] for dx, dy, dz in offsets if 0 <= i+dx < volume.shape[0] and 0 <= j+dy < volume.shape[1] and 0 <= k+dz < volume.shape[2]] filledvolume[i, j, k] = np.median(neighbors) if neighbors else volume[i, j, k] # 3. Splat Sweep splatcounts = [] k = minsplats while k <= maxsplats: splatcounts.append(k) k = 2 if splatcounts[-1] != maxsplats: splatcounts.append(maxsplats) psnrtraincurve = [] psnrheldcurve = [] for k in splatcounts: # Fit Gaussian splats to filledvolume using conservative culling (99.9% amplitude retention), # 20,000 max iterations, early stopping patience 500, L1 loss, and dynamic operations enabled. splats = fitgaussiansplats(filledvolume, k) # Compute Training PSNR on unmasked voxels against original volume trainmask = ~mask trainvoxelsorig = volume[trainmask] trainvoxelsrendered = rendersplats(splats, trainmask) msetrain = np.mean((trainvoxelsorig - trainvoxelsrendered) 2) psnrtrain = 10 np.log10(1.0 / msetrain) if msetrain > 0 else float('inf') # Compute Held-out PSNR on masked voxels against original volume heldmask = mask heldvoxelsorig = volume[heldmask] heldvoxelsrendered = rendersplats(splats, heldmask) mseheld = np.mean((heldvoxelsorig - heldvoxelsrendered) 2) psnrheld = 10 np.log10(1.0 / mseheld) if mseheld > 0 else float('inf') psnrtraincurve.append((k, psnrtrain)) psnrheldcurve.append((k, psnrheld)) # 4. Optimum Selection bestidx = np.argmax([p for k, p in psnrheldcurve]) optimalk = psnrheldcurve[bestidx][0] # Classify the held-out curve (peak, plateau, or signal-limited) and estimate the ensemble noise-floor PSNR ceiling. return optimalk, psnrtraincurve, psnrheldcurve Parameters: Masking seed: 42. Masking fraction: 5% of voxels. Filling method: Median of 26 neighbors in 3x3x3 donut. Splat sweep range: Geometrically spaced doubling from 1K to 512K, extended to 1M and 2M. Fitting constraints: Conservative culling (99.9% amplitude retention), 20,000 max iterations, early stopping patience 500 iterations, L1 loss, dynamic operations enabled. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If splat count exceeds the optimum, training PSNR continues to rise but held-out PSNR drops, indicating overfitting to noise. Correlated noise from processing (deconvolution, denoising) voids the blind-spot guarantee, allowing models to improve held-out scores by reproducing noise rather than signal. Strict filling (excluding other held-out voxels) changes held-out PSNR by at most 0.25 dB and moves no optimum compared to canonical filling. Time Complexity: The method requires fitting Gaussian splats for multiple splat counts (geometrically spaced doubling from 1K to 512K, extended to 1M and 2M). Each fit takes up to 20,000 iterations with early stopping. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of splats and the volume size. The method stores the original volume, the filled volume, and the splat parameters for each fit during the sweep. Measured Performance: On 17 volumes from 12 datasets and four modalities, the method yields a median 99-fold (6–340-fold) size reduction at 26–67 dB PSNR, in minutes per volume on one GPU. Strengths: Does not require noise-free references; identifies the signal-to-noise boundary; robust to strict filling variations. Limitations: Voided by correlated noise from processing (deconvolution, denoising); requires multiple fits for different splat counts. When to use: When determining the optimal splat budget for Gaussian Splatting without ground truth; when noise characteristics are unknown. When not to use: When the volume has been processed with deconvolution or denoising that correlates noise; when a noise-free reference is available (standard metrics may be more appropriate). Blind-Spot Cross-Validation was introduced in the Luxar paper (2026) for Gaussian splatting in microscopy and scalable interactive web visualization of multidimensional scientific data. It is used to set the splat budget without noise-free references, enabling efficient compression and visualization of large 3D volumes. name: Density-Aware Densification (Splitting Surfels)
head: Adaptive Density Control, Screen-space gradient accumulation, Surfel Densification, Surfel Splitting
body: Density-Aware Densification is a mechanism for surfel densification that uses a density-aware splitting criterion based on local inter-sample spacing and a screen-space gradient accumulation strategy based on T-matrix backward passes. It maintains the partition-of-unity assumption by adjusting surfel density as geometry evolves during optimization, similar to 3DGS densification. It replaces the ad-hoc projected 3D position gradient used in 2DGS with screen-space gradients from the T-matrix backward pass and replaces the global scale threshold used in 3DGS with a criterion that adapts to spatially varying overlap conditions. Inputs: Current set of surfels, each with position \mathbf{c}, tangent scales s1, s2, normalized major tangent axis \hat{\mathbf{t}}{max}, and material attributes. Local mean neighbor distance \bar{d} for each surfel. Densification threshold c{thresh}. Outputs: Updated set of surfels, where selected surfels are replaced by two children. Data Structures: Surfel: Contains position \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, tangent scales s1, s2 \in \mathbb{R}, normalized major tangent axis \hat{\mathbf{t}}{max} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and material attributes (e.g., albedo, normal). Steps: 1. Gradient Accumulation: Compute per-pixel absolute gradient norms directly from the T-matrix backward pass. Accumulate these norms to determine the cumulative screen-space gradient magnitude for each surfel. 2. Criterion Evaluation: For each surfel, calculate the densification criterion \bar{c} (derived from the accumulated screen-space gradients). A surfel is marked for splitting if: \bar{c} \ge c{thresh} \quad \text{AND} \quad \max(s1, s2) > \bar{d} The first condition ensures the surfel is in a region requiring refinement based on image-space error. The second condition targets over-reconstructed primitives whose kernel support is too wide relative to the local point distribution. 3. Splitting: For each marked surfel: Identify the major tangent axis \hat{\mathbf{t}}{max} corresponding to the maximum scale \max(s1, s2). Create two children positioned at: \mathbf{c}{child1} = \mathbf{c} + \frac{s{max}}{2} \hat{\mathbf{t}}{max} \mathbf{c}{child2} = \mathbf{c} - \frac{s{max}}{2} \hat{\mathbf{t}}{max} Set the scale along the split axis (s{max}) for both children to 0.7 \times s{max}. Preserve the orthogonal tangent scale for both children. Inherit all material attributes from the parent surfel. 4. Replacement: Remove the parent surfel and add the two children to the surfel set. Parameters: c{thresh}: Densification threshold. Value not given in the sources. Split scale factor: 0.7. This yields enough mutual overlap between siblings to maintain signal continuity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-splitting in smooth regions: A global scale threshold (as used in 3DGS) over-splits in smooth regions where the local density already satisfies the Nyquist condition. The density-aware criterion avoids this by comparing against local inter-sample spacing. Under-splitting in fine-scale features: A global threshold under-splits at fine-scale features where the local inter-sample spacing is much smaller than the scene-level threshold. The density-aware criterion adapts to this. Zero gradient surfels: Surfels with zero cumulative screen-space gradient magnitude are never reached during the backward pass (occluded, outside frustums, or failed cutoff) and should be pruned. Performance: Full 3DSS configuration with adaptive density control achieves a PSNR-H of 24.32 and Albedo PSNR-L of 41.26, compared to 23.56 PSNR-H and 40.51 Albedo PSNR-L when adaptive density control is disabled. Strengths: Adapts spatially without requiring scene-dependent parameter tuning. Increases model complexity gradually and keeps both children coplanar with the parent, preserving local surface coherence. Limitations: Requires T-matrix backward pass for gradient computation. Without adaptive refinement, under-sampled regions retain coarse coverage that limits both geometric detail and material resolution. Originated in the 3DSS (3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering) paper. It is designed to maintain the partition-of-unity assumption in coverage-based compositing models as geometry evolves during optimization. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Temporal Densification
head: Temporal Splitting
body: Temporal densification is a strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that detects and resolves reconstruction errors caused by object or camera motion by splitting Gaussians based on the variance of their normalized image error across time segments. It addresses the limitation of static spatial densification, which assumes Gaussians are stationary, by identifying Gaussians whose error fluctuates significantly between keyframes, indicating they fail to track motion. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}. A sequence of training images indexed by time t. Hyperparameters: temporal threshold \tau{time}, KNN count K=10, minimum segment length l{seg}. Outputs: An updated set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with new Gaussians added via splitting for those exhibiting high temporal error variation. Data Structures: Keyframe List: For each Gaussian g, a sorted list of keyframe indices [t0^g, t1^g, \dots, tm^g] that partition the frame sequence into segments. Error Buffer: For each Gaussian g and image I, the scalar image error e{g,I} and the number of projected pixels N{g,I}^p. Weights: Precomputed weights w{g,I} for each Gaussian-image pair, derived from the optimization loss weighting scheme. Steps: 1. Segment Definition: Divide the frame sequence for Gaussian g into segments using its keyframes ti^g such that ti^g \le t < t{i+1}^g. If g has only one keyframe t0^g, the segment covers all frames t \ge t0^g. 2. Normalized Error Calculation: For each Gaussian g and image I, compute the normalized image error \bar{e}{g,I} by dividing the raw error e{g,I} by the number of projected pixels N{g,I}^p to normalize for projected area: \bar{e}{g,I} = \frac{e{g,I}}{N{g,I}^p} \quad (24) 3. Weighted Mean and Variance: Compute the weighted mean normalized error \bar{e}g and the standard deviation \sigma{\bar{e}g} for each segment using weights w{g,I}: \bar{e}g = \frac{\sum{I \in \mathcal{I}} \bar{e}{g,I} w{g,I}}{\sum{I \in \mathcal{I}} w{g,I}} \quad (25) \sigma{\bar{e}g} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum{I \in \mathcal{I}} \bar{e}{g,I}^2 w{g,I}}{\sum{I \in \mathcal{I}} w{g,I}} - \bar{e}g^2} \quad (26) 4. Variation Ratio: Calculate the variation ratio \rhog = \sigma{\bar{e}g} / \bar{e}g for each segment. 5. Splitting Criterion: Mark g for splitting if \rhog > \tau{time} for any segment. Also mark g if any of its K=10 nearest neighbors satisfies the criterion, to handle uniformly colored areas where error variation is naturally low. 6. Keyframe Management: For marked Gaussians, add a keyframe at the frame index I{\text{max}} with the maximum error e{g,I} in the relevant segment. If I{\text{max}} coincides with the left keyframe ti^g, insert the segment midpoint instead. Skip insertion if the resulting segments would be shorter than l{seg}. 7. Execution: Perform the split operation on all marked Gaussians. The split direction and plane follow the standard spatial splitting logic from the parent article. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporaldensification(gaussians, frames, keyframesdict, weights, thresholdtau, knn=10, minseglen=10): tosplit = set() newkeyframes = [] for g in gaussians: gid = g['id'] kflist = keyframesdict[gid] if not kflist: continue segments = [] for i in range(len(kflist) - 1): segments.append((kflist[i], kflist[i+1])) if len(kflist) == 1: segments.append((kflist[0], max(frames) + 1)) splitcandidate = False maxeinseg = -1.0 maxframeinseg = None triggersegidx = -1 for segidx, (tstart, tend) in enumerate(segments): segnormerrors = [] segweights = [] for fidx in frames: if tstart <= fidx < tend: e = g['errors'].get(fidx, 0.0) np = g['projectedpixels'].get(fidx, 1) if np == 0: np = 1 normerr = e / np w = weights.get((gid, fidx), 1.0) segnormerrors.append(normerr) segweights.append(w) if not segweights: continue sumw = sum(segweights) if sumw == 0: continue meanerr = sum(e w for e, w in zip(segnormerrors, segweights)) / sumw varerr = sum(e2 w for e, w in zip(segnormerrors, segweights)) / sumw - meanerr2 stderr = (varerr 0.5) if varerr > 0 else 0.0 rho = stderr / meanerr if meanerr != 0 else 0.0 if rho > thresholdtau: splitcandidate = True triggersegidx = segidx for fidx in frames: if tstart <= fidx < tend: e = g['errors'].get(fidx, 0.0) if e > maxeinseg: maxeinseg = e maxframeinseg = fidx break if not splitcandidate: dists = [] for nb in gaussians: if nb['id'] != gid: dx = nb['pos'][0] - g['pos'][0] dy = nb['pos'][1] - g['pos'][1] dz = nb['pos'][2] - g['pos'][2] dists.append((dxdx + dydy + dzdz, nb)) dists.sort() for, nb in dists[:knn]: if nb.get('rho', 0.0) > thresholdtau: splitcandidate = True break if splitcandidate: tosplit.add(gid) if maxframeinseg is not None and triggersegidx != -1: tleft, tright = segments[triggersegidx] newkf = maxframeinseg if maxframeinseg != tleft else (tleft + tright) // 2 if newkf - tleft >= minseglen and tright - newkf >= minseglen: newkeyframes.append((gid, newkf)) for g in gaussians: if g['id'] in tosplit: # Perform standard spatial split operation from parent article pass for gid, kf in newkeyframes: if gid in keyframesdict: keyframesdict[gid].append(kf) keyframesdict[gid].sort() Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing error statistics and weights per Gaussian per frame, increasing memory usage compared to static splatting. Strengths: Effectively reconstructs scenes with oscillatory or complex motion where static Gaussians fail. The method is interleaved with spatial densification every 2 epochs to balance spatial detail and temporal tracking. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to per-frame error aggregation and sensitive to the choice of \tau{time} and l{seg}. When to use: Scenes with significant camera or object motion. Temporal densification was introduced in "Adaptive Spatio-Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scenes with Oscillatory Motion" to address the inability of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle non-rigid or oscillatory motion. It extends the adaptive densification framework by incorporating temporal variance analysis, allowing Gaussians to split not just based on spatial gradient but also on temporal error fluctuation. Adaptive Spatio‐Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scenes with Oscillatory Motion, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70410, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Loss Accumulation Guided (LAG) Densification
head: LAG (Loss-Guided Gaussian generation), LAG strategy, Loss-Guided Density Control, Loss-Guided Gaussian generation (LAG), Loss-guided densification
body: Loss Accumulation Guided (LAG) densification is a density control strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses accumulated reconstruction loss maps to identify under-reconstructed regions, preventing unnecessary Gaussian growth in well-reconstructed areas. Unlike standard adaptive densification which relies solely on view-space positional gradients and often causes excessive Gaussian proliferation in high-frequency texture regions, LAG introduces a dual-constraint mechanism that inhibits splitting or cloning when the local reconstruction error is already low. This approach reduces the final number of Gaussians and shortens training time at the cost of a slight decrease in rendering metrics. LAG operates as a constraint on the densification steps defined in Density Control and Densification. It does not replace the gradient-based classification but adds a loss-based gate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The joint reconstruction loss map from the current backward pass (averaged across RGB channels), the set of Gaussians \{Gi\}, and the accumulated loss mask history. Output: A binary decision (allow/deny) for each candidate Gaussian for splitting or cloning. Data Structures: Loss Map (Lm): A single-channel float32 image of resolution W \times H, where Lm(P) is the mean reconstruction loss at pixel P. Binary Mask (M): A single-channel uint8 image of resolution W \times H, where M(P) \in \{0, 1\}. Densification Score Buffer (DS): A float32 array of size N (number of Gaussians), initialized to 0.0. Parameters: \tau: Loss threshold to distinguish well-reconstructed from under-reconstructed pixels. K: Number of iterations over which the mask is accumulated and the score is averaged. \theta: Size threshold for distinguishing small/large Gaussians. \tau{grad}: Gradient threshold for densification consideration. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Loss Map: During the backward pass, compute the joint reconstruction loss for all pixels. Average the three RGB channels to obtain a single-channel loss map Lm(P) for each pixel P in the image plane. 2. Generate Binary Mask: Apply a threshold \tau to Lm(P) to create a binary mask Mt(P) for the current iteration t: Mt(P) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } Lm(P) > \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Pixels with Mt(P)=1 are considered under-reconstructed; pixels with Mt(P)=0 are well-reconstructed. 3. Accumulate Mask: Store Mt(P) for use in subsequent iterations. The mask is accumulated over K iterations. 4. Compute Densification Score (DS): For each Gaussian Gi, determine the set of pixels \Omegat it covers in the image plane during iteration t. Update the accumulated score. The Densification Score DSi is the average number of high-loss pixels covered by Gi over K iterations: DSi = \frac{1}{K} \sum{t=1}^{K} \sum{P \in \Omegat} Mt(P) where \Omegat is the set of pixels covered by Gaussian Gi in iteration t, and Mt(P) is the mask value for that iteration. 5. Evaluate Densification Criteria: A Gaussian Gi is eligible for splitting or cloning only if both conditions are met: Gradient Condition: The accumulated view-space positional gradient magnitude |\nabla{\mathbf{p}} \mathcal{L}|i exceeds \tau{grad} AND the Gaussian size is appropriate (small for cloning, large for splitting). Loss Condition: The Densification Score DSi is high (indicating the Gaussian consistently covers under-reconstructed regions). The specific threshold for DSi is not given in the sources. 6. Execute Operation: If both conditions are met, perform the standard splitting or cloning operation as defined in Density Control and Densification. If the Loss Condition fails (low DS), skip the operation even if the gradient condition is met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lagdensificationcheck(gaussianid, coveredpixelindices, currentmask, maskhistory, dsbuffer, k, taugrad, accumulatedgradient, sizethreshold): """ Determines if a Gaussian should be densified based on LAG criteria. Args: gaussianid: Integer index of the Gaussian. coveredpixelindices: List of integer indices (flattened) of pixels covered by the Gaussian in the current iteration. currentmask: 2D array (H, W), uint8, binary mask for the current iteration. maskhistory: List of 2D arrays (H, W), uint8, stored masks from previous iterations. dsbuffer: 1D array, float32, accumulated DS values for all Gaussians. k: Integer, number of iterations for averaging. taugrad: Float, gradient threshold. accumulatedgradient: Float, accumulated view-space positional gradient magnitude for this Gaussian. sizethreshold: Float, size threshold for splitting/cloning decision. Returns: bool: True if densification (split/clone) is allowed, False otherwise. """ # Step 3: Accumulate Mask maskhistory.append(currentmask) if len(maskhistory) > k: maskhistory.pop(0) # Step 4: Compute Densification Score (DS) # DS = (1/K) sum{t=1 to K} sum{P in Omegat} Mt(P) totalhighloss = 0 for tmask in maskhistory: for idx in coveredpixelindices: totalhighloss += tmask[idx] ds = totalhighloss / k dsbuffer[gaussianid] = ds # Step 5: Evaluate Criteria # Gradient Condition gradientok = accumulatedgradient > taugrad # Size Condition (from parent article) issmall = gaussian.size < sizethreshold islarge = gaussian.size >= sizethreshold sizeok = issmall or islarge # Loss Condition # DS must be high to indicate under-reconstruction. # Not given in sources dsthreshold = 0.0 lossok = ds > dsthreshold # Dual-Constraint Mechanism return gradientok and sizeok and lossok Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The loss map and mask accumulation must be precise enough to distinguish between well-reconstructed and under-reconstructed regions. Boundaries: The mask M(P) is defined per pixel. Gaussians covering few pixels may have noisy DS estimates. Accumulating over K iterations mitigates this. Degenerate Input: If K is too small, the DS may not be stable. Threshold Selection: The value of \tau and the DS threshold are critical. Incorrect values may either suppress necessary densification or fail to prevent redundancy. A complementary strategy that removes Gaussians with low opacity or high opacity gradients after densification. It targets redundant primitives and works synergistically with LAG to further reduce Gaussian count. See Soft Pruning for related pruning techniques. An optimization technique that reduces the computational cost of the backward pass, often used in conjunction with LAG to further improve training efficiency. Time Complexity: The additional cost of LAG is the computation of the loss map and mask, which is done during the standard backward pass. The DS update requires summing mask values for covered pixels, which is proportional to the number of pixels covered by each Gaussian. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the loss map, mask history (K iterations), and DS buffer. Memory usage is O(W \cdot H \cdot K + N), where W, H are image dimensions, K is the accumulation window, and N is the number of Gaussians. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 bicycle scene, LAG reduced the peak number of Gaussians from 947,136 to 547,083 and training time from unspecified to 190.0 seconds, with SSIM dropping from 0.751 to 0.734 and PSNR from 25.153 to 24.939. Across Mip-NeRF 360, LAG reduces NGS from 0.77M to 0.47M and training time from 245.7s to 215.4s compared to the Base configuration. Scaling: LAG scales with the number of Gaussians and image resolution. The mask accumulation is independent of N, but the DS update depends on coverage. Strengths: Reduces redundant Gaussian growth, shortens training time, and produces more compact scene representations. Limitations: Slight decrease in rendering metrics (SSIM/PSNR) due to suppressed densification in well-reconstructed areas. Requires careful tuning of \tau and K. When to Use: When training time and memory are constrained, and a slight reduction in peak rendering quality is acceptable for a more compact model. Particularly effective when combined with pruning. When Not to Use: When maximum possible rendering quality is required, or when the scene has dynamic regions where reconstruction quality changes rapidly and K cannot adapt quickly enough. Loss Accumulation Guided (LAG) densification was proposed in the paper "Loss-Guided Density Control and Efficient Backward Optimisation for Compact Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the issue of excessive Gaussian proliferation in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, where positional gradients can be large in high-frequency texture regions, leading to unnecessary Gaussian growth and increased computational load. The method leverages the loss maps generated during standard backpropagation to identify persistently under-reconstructed image regions, providing a more stable and reliable measure of reconstruction quality than gradients alone. Loss-Guided Density Control and Efficient Backward Optimisation for Compact Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10572680/v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splitting and Pruning
head: Deterministic splitting, Splitting Gaussians
body: Gaussian Splitting and Pruning is a deterministic density control method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that modifies the primitive count by splitting Gaussians with high reconstruction responsibility and removing those with minimal contribution based on statistical criteria. Unlike heuristic approaches that rely on view-space positional gradients or screen-space size thresholds, this method uses the accumulated per-ray loss and weight statistics to identify under- and over-reconstructed regions. It addresses the problem of fixed primitive counts by iteratively refining the reconstruction after initial convergence, allowing for increased detail in areas with high error while culling noise in areas with low contribution. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} with parameters (position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, color ci, weight \lambdai), a dataset of views, and a loss function L. Outputs: A modified set of Gaussians with updated positions, covariances, opacities, and colors. Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of N objects. Each object stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (or its Cholesky decomposition/eigenvalues/eigenvectors). \lambdai \in \mathbb{R}: Weight (often stored as log-weight for optimization stability). ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color (often stored as inverse-sigmoid for optimization stability). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Ray Batch: A random subset of rays from the dataset (typically 5% of total rays). Statistics: Running means and standard deviations for weights (\mu\lambda, \sigma\lambda) and average losses (\mu{\bar{l}}, \sigma{\bar{l}}). Parameters: z\lambda: Z-score threshold for pruning, typically 2. z{\bar{l}}: Z-score threshold for splitting, typically 1. \epsilonw: Noise scale for weights, typically 0.1. \epsilonc: Noise scale for colors, typically 0.1. Scaling factors derived from half-normal distribution: \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \approx 0.8 and \sqrt{1 - \frac{2}{\pi}} \approx 0.6. Steps: 1. Initial Convergence: Train the initial 3D Gaussian model until it converges. 2. Weight Statistics: Compute the mean \mu\lambda and standard deviation \sigma\lambda of the weights \lambdai assigned to each Gaussian across the dataset. 3. Pruning: Remove Gaussians where the weight is below the threshold: \lambdai \leq \mu\lambda - z\lambda \sigma\lambda. 4. Loss Estimation: Sample a random batch of M rays (e.g., 5% of the dataset). For each ray j in the batch, compute the per-ray loss Lj. For each ray, obtain the set of computed weights w{i,j} for all Gaussians i contributing to that ray. Estimate the average loss associated with each Gaussian i over the batch: \bar{l}i = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^M Lj \cdot w{i,j}. 5. Splitting Criteria Statistics: Compute the mean \mu{\bar{l}} and standard deviation \sigma{\bar{l}} of the average losses \bar{l}i. 6. Splitting: For each Gaussian i where \bar{l}i \geq \mu{\bar{l}} + z{\bar{l}} \sigma{\bar{l}}, perform the following split operation: Eigen-decomposition: Compute the dominant eigenvector \vec{v}1 and dominant eigenvalue \sigma1 of the covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i. New Positions: Generate two new means \mua and \mub by shifting the initial mean \mu in opposite directions along \vec{v}1: \mu{a,b} = \mu \pm \sigma1 \vec{v}1 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}. New Covariances: Create two new Gaussians with identical covariance matrices reconstructed from the initial eigenvalues and eigenvectors, but with the dominant eigenvalue scaled: \sigma{1{a,b}} = \sigma1 \sqrt{1 - \frac{2}{\pi}}. The other eigenvalues remain unchanged. New Weights: Set the log-weights of the new Gaussians by adding Gaussian noise to the initial log-weight: \log(\lambda{a,b}) = \log(\lambda) + \mathcal{N}(0, \epsilonw) where \epsilonw = 0.1. New Colors: Set the inverse-sigmoid colors of the new Gaussians by adding Gaussian noise to the initial inverse-sigmoid color: \sigma^{-1}(c{a,b}) = \sigma^{-1}(c) + \mathcal{N}(0, \epsilonc) where \epsilonc = 0.1. Replacement: Remove the original Gaussian i and add the two new Gaussians a and b to the scene. 7. Optimization: Repeat the optimization process with the modified set of Gaussians. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: p: position (3,) sigma: covariance matrix (3,3) or eigenvalues/vectors lambda: weight (scalar) c: color (3,) alpha: opacity (scalar) raysbatch: List of ray objects, each with: loss: scalar loss value Lj weights: list of weights wi for contributing Gaussians zlambda: Z-score threshold for pruning zl: Z-score threshold for splitting epsilonw: Noise scale for weights epsilonc: Noise scale for colors Returns: Updated list of Gaussians """ # Step 2: Weight Statistics weights = [g.lambdaval for g in gaussians] mulambda = np.mean(weights) sigmalambda = np.std(weights) # Step 3: Pruning # Remove Gaussians where lambdai <= mulambda - zlambda sigmalambda prunedindices = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): if g.lambdaval <= mulambda - zlambda sigmalambda: prunedindices.append(i) # Remove pruned Gaussians (reverse order to maintain indices) for i in reversed(prunedindices): gaussians.pop(i) # Re-index remaining gaussians for loss calculation # Note: In practice, weights wi,j must be recomputed or stored from the forward pass # Here we assume raysbatch contains pre-computed weights for the current Gaussians # If Gaussians were removed, the mapping must be adjusted. # For simplicity, we assume raysbatch is filtered or weights are aligned. # Step 4: Loss Estimation # Estimate average loss for each remaining Gaussian averagelosses = [] M = len(raysbatch) # Initialize sum of losses for each Gaussian losssums = np.zeros(len(gaussians)) for ray in raysbatch: Lj = ray.loss # ray.weights should correspond to the current gaussians list # Assuming ray.weights is a list of weights for the current gaussians for i, wij in enumerate(ray.weights): losssums[i] += Lj wij averagelosses = losssums / M # Step 5: Splitting Criteria Statistics mul = np.mean(averagelosses) sigmal = np.std(averagelosses) # Step 6: Splitting newgaussians = [] splitindices = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): if averagelosses[i] >= mul + zl sigmal: splitindices.append(i) # Process splits # We need to handle the removal of original and addition of new ones carefully # Create a new list for the next iteration nextgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): if i in splitindices: # Perform Split # Eigen-decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(g.sigma) # Sort by eigenvalue descending to get dominant idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx] eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx] sigma1 = eigenvalues[0] v1 = eigenvectors[:, 0] mu = g.p # New means shift = sigma1 v1 np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) mua = mu + shift mub = mu - shift # New covariances # Scale dominant eigenvalue sigma1new = sigma1 np.sqrt(1 - 2 / np.pi) eigenvaluesnew = eigenvalues.copy() eigenvaluesnew[0] = sigma1new # Reconstruct covariance matrix Sigmaa = eigenvectors @ np.diag(eigenvaluesnew) @ eigenvectors.T Sigmab = Sigmaa.copy() # New weights (log-space) loglambdaa = np.log(g.lambdaval) + np.random.normal(0, epsilonw) loglambdab = np.log(g.lambdaval) + np.random.normal(0, epsilonw) lambdaa = np.exp(loglambdaa) lambdab = np.exp(loglambdab) # New colors (inverse-sigmoid space) # Assuming g.c is stored in inverse-sigmoid space for optimization # If g.c is in RGB, convert to inverse-sigmoid first # For this pseudocode, we assume g.c is in the unconstrained parameterization space ca = g.c + np.random.normal(0, epsilonc, 3) cb = g.c + np.random.normal(0, epsilonc, 3) # Create new Gaussian objects ga = Gaussian(p=mua, sigma=Sigmaa, lambdaval=lambdaa, c=ca, alpha=g.alpha) gb = Gaussian(p=mub, sigma=Sigmab, lambdaval=lambdab, c=cb, alpha=g.alpha) nextgaussians.append(ga) nextgaussians.append(gb) else: nextgaussians.append(g) return nextgaussians class Gaussian: def init(self, p, sigma, lambdaval, c, alpha): self.p = p self.sigma = sigma self.lambdaval = lambdaval self.c = c self.alpha = alpha Spatial Splitting with Error Moments is a densification technique that splits Gaussians with error above a threshold \tau{space} by placing a splitting plane through the Gaussian's center, oriented based on the error moments rather than the Gaussian's longest axis. It differs from methods like FCC 24 and DDL 25b, which use a plane perpendicular to the Gaussian's longest axis, by using the error moments to determine orientation to avoid Gaussians becoming too small too quickly. The splitting plane normal n is calculated as the normalized product of the inverse error covariance matrix \mathbf{S}g^c and the first moment vector \mathbf{r}g: n = \frac{(\mathbf{S}g^c)^{-1} \mathbf{r}g}{\left\| (\mathbf{S}g^c)^{-1} \mathbf{r}g \right\|}. Feng et al. Gaussian Splitting is a new Gaussian splitting algorithm proposed by Feng et al. to avoid inhomogeneous 3D Gaussian reconstruction. It makes the boundary of 3D scenes after removal operation sharper. Time Complexity: The method requires an additional forward pass to compute per-ray losses and weights for a batch of rays, followed by statistical computations (O(N) for mean/std) and splitting operations. The splitting itself is O(N) in the worst case if all Gaussians are split. Memory Complexity: Increases the number of Gaussians, potentially up to 2N if all are split, though typically only a subset is split. Requires storage for the ray batch and intermediate loss statistics. Strengths: Deterministic and statistically grounded, avoiding the heuristic nature of gradient-based methods. It allows for iterative refinement after initial convergence, improving detail in high-error regions. Limitations: Requires a full forward pass to compute losses and weights, which can be computationally expensive. The splitting criteria are global (based on batch statistics), which may not adapt as quickly to local variations as gradient-based methods. When to use: When a deterministic, statistically robust method is preferred over heuristic gradient-based densification, or when initial convergence has been reached and further refinement is needed. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and the overhead of the additional forward pass is prohibitive, or when real-time adaptation is required during training. Gaussian Splitting and Pruning was introduced as an alternative to the heuristic techniques for merging and splitting of Gaussians explored in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper. It was developed to provide a deterministic approach to modifying the number of Gaussians in the reconstruction based on statistical criteria. The method is described in "Flexible Techniques for Differentiable Rendering with 3D Gaussians". name: Octree refinement
head: Spatial subdivision refinement
body: Octree refinement is a spatial subdivision technique used to reorder Gaussian splats for progressive rendering, ensuring that sparsely captured areas of a scene are reconstructed earlier than they would be by global contribution metrics alone. It differs from simple global sorting by enforcing a minimum representation per spatial region, thereby improving background quality at the cost of slight foreground degradation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, each with a pre-computed global contribution score Ci derived from rendering error across training views. Output: A refined ordering of Gaussians for progressive loading. Data Structures: Octree: A hierarchical spatial partitioning structure where each node represents a cubic volume. The tree uses a fixed maximum depth. Leaf Node List: For each leaf node, a list of Gaussians whose centers fall within that node's volume. Parameters: Octree Depth: The maximum depth of the octree. A value of 3 consistently yields good results across scenes. Low values have little to no impact on quality. High values (7 or larger) introduce errors such as black blur and cause convergence back to the base global approach. Algorithm Steps: 1. Insertion: Insert all N Gaussians into the octree based on their center positions. Assign each Gaussian to the leaf node corresponding to its spatial location at the specified depth. 2. Selection: For each leaf node in the octree, identify the subset of Gaussians contained within it. From this subset, select the top contributing Gaussians with the highest global contribution scores Ci. Implementation notes suggest using the contribution of the 20 highest contributing Gaussians per pixel as the basis for the initial score, but for the octree step, the selection is strictly per leaf. 3. Aggregation: Collect all selected Gaussians from all leaf nodes. The resulting set forms the refined ordering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def octreerefinement(gaussians, maxdepth=3): """ Refine Gaussian ordering using octree spatial subdivision. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each having: center: (x, y, z) coordinates contribution: float, global contribution score maxdepth: int, maximum depth of the octree (default 3) Returns: orderedgaussians: List of Gaussian objects, sorted by refined priority """ if not gaussians: return [] xs, ys, zs = zip([g.center for g in gaussians]) scenebounds = ((min(xs), min(ys), min(zs)), (max(xs), max(ys), max(zs))) root = OctreeNode(depth=0, bounds=scenebounds) for g in gaussians: leaf = root.insert(g.center, maxdepth) leaf.gaussians.append(g) selectedgaussians = [] for leaf in root.getleaves(): if not leaf.gaussians: continue leaf.gaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.contribution, reverse=True) selectedgaussians.extend(leaf.gaussians) selectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.contribution, reverse=True) return selectedgaussians class OctreeNode: def init(self, depth, bounds): self.depth = depth self.bounds = bounds self.children = [None] 8 self.gaussians = [] def insert(self, center, maxdepth): if self.depth == maxdepth: return self mid = tuple((self.bounds[0][i] + self.bounds[1][i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)) idx = 0 for i, coord in enumerate(center): if coord >= mid[i]: idx |= (1 << i) if self.children[idx] is None: childmin = tuple(self.bounds[0][i] if (idx >> i) & 1 == 0 else mid[i] for i in range(3)) childmax = tuple(mid[i] if (idx >> i) & 1 == 0 else self.bounds[1][i] for i in range(3)) self.children[idx] = OctreeNode(self.depth + 1, (childmin, childmax)) return self.children[idx].insert(center, maxdepth) def getleaves(self): if any(c is not None for c in self.children): for c in self.children: if c is not None: yield from c.getleaves() else: yield self Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Depth Errors: Using an octree depth of 7 or larger introduces rendering errors, specifically "black blur," and causes the method to converge back to the base global contribution approach. Low Depth Impact: Depth values significantly lower than 3 have little to no impact on quality. PSNR Loss: Including the octree refinement results in an average loss in PSNR scores because the foreground (which often contributes more to PSNR) is deprioritized in favor of background coverage. Perceptually, however, background quality improves. An addition to the base contribution metric that uses an octree to force Gaussians to spread out over the scene, ensuring sparsely captured parts are loaded sooner. Parameter: Octree depth parameter. A value of 3 consistently yields good results. Values too low or too high result in insufficient attention to the background. Pitfall: High depth values (e.g., 7 or larger) introduce errors such as black blur and cause convergence to the base approach. Low depth values have little impact. Performance: Including the octree results in an average loss in PSNR scores because the foreground often contributes more to PSNR, but perceptually improves background quality. Strengths: Ensures sparsely captured areas are not under-reconstructed; improves perceptual quality of the background; allows for object-level prioritization if manually segmented. Limitations: Causes a loss in average PSNR scores; high octree depths introduce rendering artifacts; does not account for viewpoint-specific occlusions (frustum culling is a separate step that occurs after global ordering). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the PRoGS (Progressive Rendering of Gaussian Splats) paper, which introduced spatial subdivision techniques to improve the progressive loading of 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions. The method was developed to address the issue where global contribution metrics unfairly under-reconstruct sparsely captured parts of a scene. name: Gaussian Pruning and Sampling
head: GRay pruning, Importance-based pruning, Weight pruning, Weight-Based Pruning
body: Gaussian Pruning and Sampling is a density control strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces the number of primitives by removing those with negligible contribution to the rendered image. It solves the problem of excessive Gaussian count and memory usage by culling Gaussians based on an importance score derived from accumulated blending weights. Unlike Opacity Pruning, which relies solely on opacity values, this method accounts for spatial footprint and occlusion, providing a more accurate measure of a Gaussian's visual impact. It differs from Contribution-based Pruning by using a fixed count or global weight threshold rather than a multi-attribute quantile. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, a set of training views (cameras) \{v\}, and the current state of the Gaussian parameters. Outputs: A reduced set of Gaussians \{Gi'\} with higher average importance scores. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gi stores position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation/scale decomposition), opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and color \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. An importance score Ii \in \mathbb{R} is computed during pruning. Steps: 1. Compute Importance Score: For each Gaussian Gi, calculate its importance score Ii based on the accumulated blending weights across all rays in the training views that intersect the Gaussian. The blending weight w{ij} of Gaussian Gi for ray j is defined as: w{ij} = T{ij} \alpha{ij} where T{ij} is the transmittance accumulated in front of Gi along ray j, and \alpha{ij} is the opacity-weighted 2D footprint of Gi at the intersection point. The importance score Ii is the sum of these weights over all K intersected rays: Ii = \sum{j=1}^{K} w{ij} Alternatively, for a set of N context views, the contribution score si can be computed as the average blending weight over all pixels in all views: si = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^N \sum{u \in \Omegan} T{i,n}(u) \alpha{i,n}(u) where \Omegan is the set of pixels in view n. In practice, si can be obtained efficiently with a single backward pass per view, treating the summed rendering as a function of a unit scalar color assigned to every Gaussian. 2. Thresholding/Selection: Remove Gaussians whose importance score falls below a threshold \gamma{\text{prune}} or keep only the top K Gaussians. The pruning condition is: \left[ \frac{1}{|Vi||v|} \sum{v \in Vi} \sum{r \in v} wi(r) \right] < \gamma{\text{prune}} where Vi is the set of views seeing Gaussian i, v is a view, r is a ray, |v| is the number of rays in view v, and wi(r) is the accumulation weight. Alternatively, keep the K = k \cdot N Gaussians with the highest scores, where k is a target number of Gaussians per view (e.g., k=10,368). 3. Optimization: Optimize the remaining Gaussian representation until convergence, or periodically every 500 iterations. Parameters: \gamma{\text{prune}}: Pruning threshold. Typical value: 10^{-7}. k: Target Gaussians per view. Typical value: 10,368. Pruning Frequency: Every 500 iterations. Pitfalls: Pruning alone does not address inefficient spatial distribution issues like 'overlapping' or 'under-reconstruction'. Opacity-based pruning can cause a noticeable drop in quality if not carefully tuned, as it ignores spatial footprint. Precision issues may arise if the importance scores are very small; ensure numerical stability in the summation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gaussianpruningandsampling(gaussians, views, threshold=1e-7, frequency=500, iteration=0): """ Prune Gaussians based on accumulated blending weights. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: position: list of 3 floats [x, y, z] covariance: list of 2 lists [[c11, c12, c13], [c21, c22, c23], [c31, c32, c33]] opacity: float in [0, 1] color: list of 3 floats [r, g, b] importance: float (initialized to 0.0) views: List of View objects with attributes: cameramatrix: list of 4 lists (4x4 projection/view matrix) imageshape: tuple (H, W) threshold: Float, pruning threshold for importance score. frequency: Int, prune every N iterations. iteration: Int, current training iteration. Returns: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with updated importance scores. """ # Only prune at specified intervals if iteration % frequency != 0: return gaussians # Reset importance scores for g in gaussians: g.importance = 0.0 # Compute importance scores via forward accumulation for view in views: H, W = view.imageshape # Project all Gaussians to 2D for this view projected = [] for g in gaussians: # Project center center3d = g.position cammat = view.cameramatrix # Homogeneous coordinate hcoord = cammat[0][0]center3d[0] + cammat[0][1]center3d[1] + cammat[0][2]center3d[2] + cammat[0][3] cx = (cammat[0][0]center3d[0] + cammat[0][1]center3d[1] + cammat[0][2]center3d[2] + cammat[0][3]) / hcoord cy = (cammat[1][0]center3d[0] + cammat[1][1]center3d[1] + cammat[1][2]center3d[2] + cammat[1][3]) / hcoord # Compute 2D covariance (Jacobian approximation) J00, J01, J02 = cammat[0][0], cammat[0][1], cammat[0][2] J10, J11, J12 = cammat[1][0], cammat[1][1], cammat[1][2] c = g.covariance cov2d = [ [J00c[0][0] + J01c[1][0] + J02c[2][0], J00c[0][1] + J01c[1][1] + J02c[2][1]], [J10c[0][0] + J11c[1][0] + J12c[2][0], J10c[0][1] + J11c[1][1] + J12c[2][1]] ] projected.append({'g': g, 'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cov': cov2d, 'z': center3d[2]}) # Iterate over pixels for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # Sort projected Gaussians by depth along ray sortedproj = sorted(projected, key=lambda p: p['z']) T = 1.0 for p in sortedproj: g = p['g'] cov = p['cov'] cx, cy = p['cx'], p['cy'] # Mahalanobis distance dx, dy = x - cx, y - cy det = cov[0][0]cov[1][1] - cov[0][1]cov[1][0] if det <= 0: continue invdet = 1.0 / det distsq = invdet (cov[1][1]dxdx - 2cov[0][1]dxdy + cov[0][0]dydy) alpha = g.opacity math.exp(-0.5 distsq) if alpha < 1e-4: continue # Blending weight w = T alpha w = T alpha g.importance += w T = (1.0 - alpha) if T < 1e-4: break return gaussians Contribution-based Pruning is a density control strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes redundant primitives by jointly evaluating their opacity and spatial scale attributes. It solves the problem of excessive Gaussian count and memory usage by culling Gaussians that contribute negligibly to the final image, balancing rendering quality with computational efficiency. It differs from its parent, Gaussian Pruning and Sampling, by using a specific multi-attribute quantile threshold rather than a generic accumulated blending weight score. It differs from Opacity Pruning by incorporating scale statistics to prevent the removal of large, transparent primitives that may still occupy significant spatial volume, making it less aggressive than opacity-only baselines. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: With pruning (\gamma{\text{prune}}=10^{-7}): PSNR 26.47, LPIPS 0.236, Opt Time 05:40, FPS 248, Final Gaussians 1.52M. Without pruning: PSNR 26.42, LPIPS 0.234, Opt Time 07:26, FPS 189, Final Gaussians 3.27M. Pruning reduced Gaussians from 6.1 million to 0.6 million, but degraded PSNR from 25.2 dB to 24.9 dB in one experiment. Strengths: Significantly reduces Gaussian count and optimization time while maintaining or slightly improving PSNR. Improves rendering FPS. Limitations: Does not address spatial distribution inefficiencies like overlapping. Aggressive pruning can degrade quality. When to use: When memory or computational resources are limited, and a slight reduction in quality is acceptable for faster training and rendering. When not to use: Not recommended when maximum reconstruction quality is required, as pruning degrades PSNR. Gaussian Pruning and Sampling was introduced as a straightforward approach to reduce the number of Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It is based on the observation that many Gaussians have redundant contributions to the rendered image. The method was further refined and evaluated in subsequent works, such as GRay, which demonstrated its effectiveness in reducing training time and improving rendering speed. It is widely used in variants of 3D Gaussian Splatting to achieve more compact representations. name: Contribution-based Pruning
head: Contribution Pruning, Contribution-Prune
body: Contribution-based Pruning is a density control strategy in 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes redundant Gaussian primitives by jointly evaluating their opacity and spatial scale attributes. It addresses the problem of superfluous or low-impact Gaussians accumulating during densification, which increases computational load and storage costs without improving rendering fidelity. Unlike Opacity Pruning, which relies solely on transparency, or Size-based Pruning, which targets geometric extent alone, this method combines both metrics to identify Gaussians that are simultaneously invisible and geometrically insignificant. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each with attributes including opacity og and scale parameters (from which maximum scale s{\max}(g) is derived). Output: A pruned set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}{\text{new}} with redundant primitives removed. Data Structures: Gaussian Set \mathcal{G}: A collection of Gaussian primitives. Vote Counter Vg: An integer accumulator for each Gaussian g, initialized to 0. Pruning Candidates Sets: \mathcal{C}{\text{opacity}}^{(t)} and \mathcal{C}{\text{scale}}^{(t)}. Parameters: \tau: Pruning threshold (quantile). Determines the cutoff for "low" opacity and scale. Typical value: 0.2. I{\text{prune}}: Pruning interval (number of iterations between pruning checks). v: Vote threshold. A Gaussian is removed if its accumulated votes exceed I{\text{prune}} \cdot v. Steps: 1. Compute Attributes: At iteration t, for each Gaussian g \in \mathcal{G}, retrieve its current opacity og and compute its maximum scale s{\max}(g) across all dimensions. 2. Determine Candidates: Calculate the \tau-quantile for opacity Q\tau(o) and maximum scale Q\tau(s{\max}) across the entire set \mathcal{G}. Identify candidates for pruning based on opacity and scale: \mathcal{C}{\text{opacity}}^{(t)} = \{g \in \mathcal{G} \mid og < Q\tau(o)\} \mathcal{C}{\text{scale}}^{(t)} = \{g \in \mathcal{G} \mid s{\max}(g) < Q\tau(s{\max})\} 3. Intersect Candidates: The set of pruning candidates \mathcal{C}{\text{prune}}^{(t)} is the intersection of opacity and scale candidates: \mathcal{C}{\text{prune}}^{(t)} = \mathcal{C}{\text{opacity}}^{(t)} \cap \mathcal{C}{\text{scale}}^{(t)} 4. Accumulate Votes: For each Gaussian g, update its vote count Vg^{(t)}. If g \in \mathcal{C}{\text{prune}}^{(t)}, increment the vote by 1. Otherwise, the vote remains unchanged (or is not incremented). Vg^{(t+1)} = Vg^{(t)} + \mathbf{1}{\{g \in \mathcal{C}{\text{prune}}^{(t)}\}} where \mathbf{1} is the indicator function. 5. Prune: If the current iteration t is a multiple of I{\text{prune}}, permanently remove all Gaussians g where Vg^{(t)} > I{\text{prune}} \cdot v. The updated set is \mathcal{G}{\text{new}} = \mathcal{G} \setminus \{g \mid Vg^{(t)} > I{\text{prune}} \cdot v\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def contributionbasedpruning(Gaussians, tau, Iprune, v): """ Prunes Gaussians based on joint opacity and scale contribution. Args: Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each having.opacity and.scale (array/vector). tau: Quantile threshold (e.g., 0.2). Iprune: Pruning interval (iterations). v: Vote threshold multiplier. Returns: Pruned list of Gaussians. """ # Initialize vote counters if not present for g in Gaussians: if not hasattr(g, 'votecount'): g.votecount = 0 # Determine if it is time to prune currentiter = getcurrentiteration() # Helper to track iteration if currentiter % Iprune != 0: # Update votes but do not prune yet updatevotes(Gaussians, tau) return Gaussians # Step 1 & 2: Identify candidates opacities = [g.opacity for g in Gaussians] maxscales = [max(g.scale) for g in Gaussians] # max across dimensions # Calculate quantiles qopacity = quantile(opacities, tau) qscale = quantile(maxscales, tau) candidates = [] for g in Gaussians: if g.opacity < qopacity and max(g.scale) < qscale: candidates.append(g) # Step 4: Accumulate votes for g in Gaussians: if g in candidates: g.votecount += 1 # Step 5: Prune thresholdvotes = Iprune v prunedgaussians = [g for g in Gaussians if g.votecount <= thresholdvotes] return prunedgaussians def updatevotes(Gaussians, tau): """Helper to update votes without pruning.""" opacities = [g.opacity for g in Gaussians] maxscales = [max(g.scale) for g in Gaussians] qopacity = quantile(opacities, tau) qscale = quantile(maxscales, tau) for g in Gaussians: if g.opacity < qopacity and max(g.scale) < qscale: g.votecount += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Training Noise: Opacity and scale values can fluctuate significantly during early training. Immediate removal based on a single iteration's metrics may remove valid Gaussians. The voting mechanism mitigates this by requiring consistent low contribution over multiple iterations. Threshold Sensitivity: A larger \tau results in more aggressive pruning (lower quantile cutoff), potentially removing more Gaussians but risking quality degradation if set too high. Single-Criterion Failure: Pruning based solely on opacity or scale leads to substantial performance degradation compared to using both jointly. A variant that explicitly formalizes the vote accumulation mechanism to mitigate noisy fluctuations in opacity or scale during early training. Instead of removing candidates immediately, it accumulates votes Vg^{(t)} for Gaussians selected as pruning candidates \mathcal{C}{\text{prune}}^{(t)} and permanently prunes them only when Vg^{(t)} > I{\text{prune}} \cdot v. This ensures that only Gaussians consistently exhibiting low contribution are removed. A strategy that restricts pruning to the initial 25k iterations to prevent excessive removal during later stages when finer details are critical. It uses specific parameters: I{\text{prune}} = 1000, v = 0.6, and redundancy threshold \tau = 0.2. This allows the model to retain representation capacity while reducing unnecessary primitives in early training. A pruning rule based on theta (coverage) and opacity that localizes sacrifice at city scale, serving as a complementary export to score-based methods. It is designed to remove perceptually redundant mass. At extreme budgets (e.g., 10% primitives), it achieves the best LPIPS scores (0.547 vs 0.557 for score export), keeping street markings and facades legible where other methods blur or collapse. Removes Gaussian points in multiple sequential iterations (e.g., Iter1-3 with rate 0.4, Iter4 with rate 0.2) to reduce model size while maintaining visual quality. This approach allows for fine-tuning between pruning steps, adapting to the remaining point distribution and achieving a better quality-size tradeoff compared to single-pass pruning. It can remove 87% of points with an average PSNR drop of only 0.23 dB. A strategy that prunes Gaussian-tile pairs based on a Gaussian Tile Contribution (GTC) metric, guided by a scaling factor \lambdaG (typical value 0.2). It uses a scene-adaptive threshold \tau determined by the GTC metric, unlike fixed thresholds in other methods. It preserves high-frequency regions (dense, structurally meaningful Gaussians) while removing redundant pairs in low-frequency regions, achieving a 20% FPS improvement with 1% PSNR degradation. A selection algorithm that deletes Gaussians one by one, choosing the one that causes the smallest increase in the unpenalized deletion cost, until the target count is reached. It satisfies the count constraint by construction and does not require a count penalty coefficient. The cost increment for retaining member j is calculated as \Delta{\text{add}}(j) = 2(Rz)j + R{jj}. Analysis of where Gaussians are redistributed by occlusion-aware filters, comparing occlusion-blind count, occlusion-aware count, and average-contribution criterion. The average-contribution criterion concentrates Gaussians on central regions, using more Gaussians (0.97M) than the blind count (0.73M) on the kitchen scene to maintain quality. A combined strategy applying both opacity-based and gradient-based pruning to effectively remove floaters and redundant Gaussians. Used by methods like Trimming the Fat and ELMGS, it can remove 75% of Gaussians while maintaining high visual quality. Time and Memory Complexity: The pruning step involves computing quantiles over the Gaussian set, which is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the quantile algorithm, where N is the number of Gaussians. Vote accumulation is O(N) per iteration. Memory overhead is minimal, requiring only an integer vote counter per Gaussian. Measured Performance: On Mobile-GS (baseline 0.56M Gaussians, 27.22 PSNR, 109 FPS), applying pruning with \tau=0.2 reduces Gaussians to 0.47M, maintains 27.12 PSNR, and increases FPS to 127. Pruning based solely on opacity or scale results in lower PSNR (26.84 and 26.87 respectively) compared to the joint method (27.12). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces storage and computational costs significantly while maintaining high rendering fidelity. The voting mechanism prevents premature removal of valid Gaussians during training fluctuations. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \tau, I{\text{prune}}, and v. Aggressive pruning (high \tau) can lead to visible artifacts in low-frequency regions if not balanced with other strategies like GTC-guided shrinking. When to Use: Use when computational resources are limited (e.g., mobile devices) or when storage size is a constraint. Use in conjunction with other pruning methods (e.g., MaskGaussian, Mini-Splatting) for further reduction. When Not to Use: Avoid if the scene requires very high fidelity in low-frequency regions and the voting threshold is not carefully tuned, as it may remove smooth blending Gaussians. Not recommended to rely on opacity or scale alone, as this degrades performance. Contribution-based Pruning was introduced as part of the Mobile-GS method for real-time Gaussian Splatting on mobile devices. It addresses the need for efficient rendering on hardware with limited computational power and memory. The method builds on the observation that Gaussians with low opacity and small scale contribute minimally to the final image. It differs from earlier pruning methods that might remove Gaussians based on a single attribute or without considering the temporal consistency of their contribution. name: Opacity Pruning
head: Opacity Based Pruning, Opacity and Scale Pruning
body: Opacity Pruning is a density control strategy in 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes Gaussian primitives with low opacity values, under the assumption that they contribute minimally to the final rendered image. It serves as a primary mechanism for eliminating "floaters" (noisy, non-geometric Gaussians) and redundant primitives generated during densification. Unlike gradient-based pruning, which relies on optimization dynamics, Opacity Pruning relies solely on the magnitude of the opacity attribute, making it computationally inexpensive but potentially aggressive if applied without safeguards. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}. Each Gaussian gi has attributes: position \mathbf{x}i, covariance \Sigmai (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{r}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i. A pruning threshold \tau\alpha (typically a small positive value, e.g., 10^{-3} to 10^{-2}, though exact values vary by implementation). Optional: A visibility mask M (binary image) and depth information D. Outputs: A pruned set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' \subset \mathcal{G} containing only those Gaussians deemed significant. Data Structures: The Gaussian set is typically stored in a flat array or a structure-of-arrays (SoA) layout for efficient rasterization. Pruning involves updating this structure, often by compacting the array or marking entries as inactive. Steps: 1. Evaluate Opacity: For each Gaussian gi, retrieve its current opacity value \alphai. 2. Apply Threshold: Compare \alphai against the threshold \tau\alpha. \text{keep}i = (\alphai > \tau\alpha) 3. Optional Visibility Masking: If a visibility mask M is provided (e.g., from a segmentation or depth-based occlusion test), refine the keep condition. A Gaussian is pruned if it is projected onto masked pixels (background/occluded regions). \text{keep}i = \text{keep}i \land \neg \text{projected\onto\mask}(gi, M) 4. Optional Depth/Distance Pruning: Use depth information to prune Gaussians located in free space or beyond a certain distance threshold, controlling density based on scene geometry. 5. Remove Pruned Gaussians: Discard all gi where \text{keep}i is false. This may involve reallocating memory or compacting the Gaussian array to maintain cache coherence for subsequent rasterization steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def opacitypruning(gaussians, threshold, visibilitymask=None, depththreshold=None): """ Prunes Gaussians based on opacity, and optionally visibility and depth. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes.opacity,.position,.scale. threshold: Float, opacity threshold below which Gaussians are pruned. visibilitymask: Optional 2D array, 1 where visible, 0 where masked. depththreshold: Optional float, max depth for valid Gaussians. Returns: List of pruned Gaussians. """ prunedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Step 1 & 2: Opacity check if g.opacity <= threshold: continue # Step 3: Visibility mask check (if provided) if visibilitymask is not None: # Project Gaussian center to 2D image plane u, v = projecttoscreen(g.position, g.covariance, cameraintrinsics) # Check if projection falls within masked (invalid) regions # Assuming mask is 0 for masked, 1 for visible if not iswithinbounds(u, v, visibilitymask.shape): continue if visibilitymask[int(v), int(u)] == 0: continue # Step 4: Depth check (if provided) if depththreshold is not None: depth = projectdepth(g.position, camerapose) if depth > depththreshold: continue prunedgaussians.append(g) return prunedgaussians Parameters: \tau\alpha: Opacity threshold. Not given in the sources. Typical values in related literature range from 10^{-3} to 10^{-2}. Visibility Mask: Binary image indicating valid viewing regions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aggressive Pruning: Removing Gaussians with low opacity may eliminate essential geometry if the Gaussian is occluded or viewed from an angle where its contribution is naturally low, rather than being insignificant. Floaters: Low opacity Gaussians are often "floaters" (noise artifacts), so pruning them is generally beneficial for visual quality. Learnable Masking: Hard thresholding can be suboptimal. Some methods use a learnable binary mask with a straight-through estimator to dynamically determine pruning, combined with a sparsity-inducing loss. Combines opacity thresholds with a multi-view, loss-driven contribution score to prevent the removal of geometrically significant but low-opacity Gaussians. Uses a percentile-based adaptive threshold constrained by an upper limit, rather than a fixed value, to dynamically adjust pruning during training. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians, as it requires a single pass to evaluate opacity. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the Gaussian set; pruning reduces this by removing inactive entries. Strengths: Computationally cheap; effective at removing noise and floaters; simple to implement. Limitations: Can remove valid geometry if the threshold is too high or if Gaussians are occluded; does not account for gradient information or spatial redundancy directly. When to Use: As a baseline pruning step, often in combination with gradient-based pruning to ensure both noise and redundancy are removed. Opacity Pruning originated as a simple heuristic in 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to manage the explosion of Gaussian primitives during densification. It was notably employed in methods like "Trimming the Fat" and ELMGS, often in conjunction with gradient-based pruning to improve compression and visual quality. Variations include learnable opacity masking (CompGS) and volume-based masking (Compact 3D), which integrate pruning into the training loop via differentiable masks. name: Moderate Pruning
head: Contribution Pruning, Contribution-Prune, Multi-view loss-driven pruning
body: Moderate Pruning is a strategy for removing redundant or artifact-inducing 3D Gaussians by combining opacity thresholds with a multi-view, loss-driven contribution score. It solves the problem of aggressive performance degradation caused by standard opacity-only pruning, which often removes essential geometry. Unlike its sibling Adaptive Opacity Pruning, which adjusts opacity thresholds dynamically, Moderate Pruning introduces a secondary metric based on training loss to distinguish between truly non-contributing Gaussians and those that are merely occluded or low-opacity but geometrically significant. Inputs: List of N 3D Gaussians, each with opacity oi and parameters defining its position, scale, rotation, and spherical harmonics. A queue of training views processed during optimization. A current training iteration state. Outputs: A binary pruning mask \mathcal{M}{prune} indicating which Gaussians to remove. Data Structures: Pruning Score (S^-): A scalar value per Gaussian representing its negative contribution to the training loss. A higher S^- indicates the Gaussian contributes more to high-error (low-quality) regions, flagging it as an artifact or redundant point. Quantile Threshold (Q\tau^-(S^-)): The \tau-quantile of the distribution of S^- values across all Gaussians. Steps: 1. Synchronize with Training View Queue: Track the set of training views seen since the last pruning decision. A pruning decision is triggered only after every view in the training set has been seen at least once since the last decision. This ensures Gaussians in rarely observed regions are not pruned due to lack of opportunity. 2. Calculate Pruning Score (S^-): For each Gaussian i, compute S^- based on its impact on low-error pixel regions across multiple views. Implementation note: In practice, this often involves aggregating the gradient magnitude or loss contribution of the Gaussian over the views it has been rendered in, weighted by the error in those regions. The source defines S^- as a "multi-view and loss-driven strategy" where a larger S^- indicates higher impact on low-error regions. 3. Compute Quantile Threshold: Calculate Q\tau^-(S^-), the quantile of the pruning score distribution. The specific quantile \tau is not explicitly defined in the provided notes, but it serves as the cutoff for the "moderate" aspect, allowing some low-opacity Gaussians to survive if their contribution score is low. 4. Generate Pruning Mask: Apply the following logical condition to each Gaussian i: \mathcal{M}{prune} = (oi < o{min}) \land \left( S^- > Q\tau^-(S^-) \right) where: oi is the opacity of Gaussian i. o{min} is the opacity threshold. S^- is the pruning score for Gaussian i. Q\tau^-(S^-) is the quantile threshold. If the condition is true, the Gaussian is marked for pruning. 5. Postpone Pruning to Densification Event: Record the pruning mask \mathcal{M}{prune} when the decision is made. Do not remove Gaussians immediately. Postpone the actual removal to the next densification event (splitting/cloning). This aligns pruning with the densification schedule, avoiding misalignment between the training queue and densification intervals. 6. Execute Pruning: After densification finishes, remove all Gaussians marked in \mathcal{M}{prune}. Contribution pruning continues to remove redundant Gaussians on its own in subsequent cycles. 7. Post-Training Cleanup: After training completes, iterate once through all training views for a final contribution prune to ensure no low-contribution Gaussians remain from the final iterations. Parameters: o{min}: The opacity threshold below which Gaussians are considered for pruning. Typically set to 0.005, conservatively equal to the standard opacity prune threshold. \tau: The quantile parameter for Q\tau^-(S^-). Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rarely Observed Regions: Gaussians in areas rarely seen by the camera may have low S^- simply because they haven't been rendered enough. The synchronization with the full training view queue prevents this. Aggressive Pruning: Using only o{min} leads to a performance slump. Moderate Pruning mitigates this by requiring S^- to exceed the quantile threshold, preserving essential geometry. Misalignment: Running pruning independently of densification can cause misalignment. Integrating the mask recording with the densification event avoids this. Time Complexity: Adds overhead to the training loop for calculating S^- and tracking view visibility. The pruning itself is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, but is deferred to densification events, which are already O(N) operations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing S^- for each Gaussian and tracking view visibility, adding O(N) memory overhead. Performance: Prevents the "performance slump" associated with standard opacity pruning by preserving geometrically significant but low-opacity Gaussians. Improves reconstruction fidelity in occluded regions. Strengths: Handles occlusion better than opacity-only methods; reduces redundant Gaussians without sacrificing quality; integrates seamlessly with existing densification pipelines. Limitations: Requires calculating loss-driven scores, which may be computationally more expensive than simple opacity checks; depends on the synchronization of the training view queue. Moderate Pruning was introduced in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to address the limitations of standard opacity-based pruning. It builds on Opacity Pruning by adding a contribution-based criterion. The method is described in as a way to achieve "moderate pruning" by using a multi-view, loss-driven strategy. It is also referenced in as "Contribution-Prune," noting its use in other works like RadSplat and ReLaGS, and its integration with occlusion-aware densification.
