name: Soft Pruning
head: Hessian-aware pruning, L1 loss pruning
body: Soft Pruning is a density control method in 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces the number of Gaussian primitives by removing those with low contribution to the reconstruction loss, specifically to maintain a robust Hessian approximation during optimization. It differs from its sibling Hard Pruning by occurring during the densification stage (immediately before opacity resets) rather than after, allowing the subsequent training iterations to refine the remaining primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of N 3D Gaussians, each with position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{S} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and accumulated L1 loss \mathcal{L}{L1}. Output: A reduced set of Gaussians with indices of low-loss primitives removed. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i maintains a scalar metric: the accumulated L1 loss \mathcal{L}{L1}^{(i)} over the current training phase. A global counter or flag tracks the current iteration number t. Parameters: Pruning Ratio (r): The fraction of Gaussians to remove. Typical value: 0.8 (80% pruning). Reset Iterations: Specific iteration numbers where pruning is triggered. Typical values: 6000, 9000, 12000. Steps: 1. Check Trigger: At the start of an iteration t, check if t matches a predefined reset iteration (e.g., 6000, 9000, 12000). 2. Compute Score: If triggered, calculate the pruning score for each Gaussian i. The score is based on the accumulated L1 loss \mathcal{L}{L1}^{(i)}. Gaussians with smaller loss are considered less important. 3. Rank and Select: Sort all N Gaussians by their L1 loss in ascending order. Select the bottom r \times N Gaussians for removal. 4. Remove: Delete the selected Gaussians from the scene representation. 5. Proceed: Continue with the standard densification pipeline (cloning/splitting) and then the opacity reset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Timing: Pruning must occur before the opacity reset. If performed after, it becomes "Hard Pruning," which relies on later refinement rather than maintaining the Hessian approximation during the critical densification phase. Loss Convergence: The method relies on the observation that L1 loss converges quickly and remains low except after resets. Pruning when loss is uniformly low is safe. High Pruning Ratios: Unlike standard pruning, high ratios (e.g., 80%) are safe because the subsequent training iterations recover the lost detail. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softpruning(gaussians, currentiteration, resetiterations, pruningratio): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with attribute 'l1loss' currentiteration: int resetiterations: List[int], e.g., [6000, 9000, 12000] pruningratio: float, e.g., 0.8 """ if currentiteration not in resetiterations: return gaussians # Step 1: Sort Gaussians by L1 loss (ascending) # Gaussians with lower loss are less important sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.l1loss) # Step 2: Determine number of Gaussians to prune numtoprune = int(len(sortedgaussians) pruningratio) # Step 3: Keep the top (1 - ratio) Gaussians with highest loss # The bottom 'numtoprune' are discarded gaussians = sortedgaussians[numtoprune:] return gaussians Time Complexity: Sorting the Gaussians by loss takes O(N \log N), where N is the number of primitives. This is performed infrequently (e.g., 3 times in a typical training run). Memory Complexity: Reduces memory footprint by removing primitives. A pruning ratio of 80% can reduce the primitive count significantly, leading to faster rendering and training speeds. Strengths: Maintains Hessian approximation quality by removing only low-contribution primitives before opacity resets. Allows for aggressive pruning (80%) without visual degradation. Limitations: Requires tracking accumulated L1 loss per Gaussian. Timing is critical; incorrect placement in the pipeline degrades performance. Soft Pruning was introduced in the context of "Speedy-Splat," a method for fast 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the issue of Hessian approximation degradation as training progresses and L1 loss becomes small. By pruning before opacity resets, it ensures that the optimization landscape remains well-conditioned for the subsequent densification steps. name: Hard Pruning
body: Hard Pruning is a density control method in 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces model size by a constant ratio at fixed intervals after the densification stage. It differs from Soft Pruning by occurring post-densification rather than during it, relying on subsequent refinement iterations to recover performance. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}. Current training iteration i. Pruning interval \Delta i = 3000. Start iteration i{\text{start}} = 15000. Pruning ratio r = 0.3 (30%). Efficient Pruning Score for each Gaussian. Outputs: Reduced set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}'. Data Structures: Each Gaussian g \in \mathcal{G} has an associated scalar pruningscore derived from the Efficient Pruning Score. Steps: 1. Check if current iteration i satisfies the pruning condition: i \ge i{\text{start}} \quad \text{and} \quad (i - i{\text{start}}) \pmod{\Delta i} = 0 If false, skip pruning. 2. Compute the Efficient Pruning Score for all Gaussians in \mathcal{G}. 3. Sort \mathcal{G} by pruning score. 4. Calculate the number of Gaussians to remove: N{\text{remove}} = \lfloor |\mathcal{G}| \times r \rfloor 5. Remove the N{\text{remove}} Gaussians based on their pruning scores. 6. Continue training to refine the remaining Gaussians. Parameters: \Delta i = 3000 iterations. i{\text{start}} = 15000 iterations. r = 0.3 (30%). Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Increases rendering and training speed by approximately 90% reduction in primitives. Strengths: Simple constant-ratio reduction; effective when combined with post-pruning refinement. Limitations: Requires waiting for densification to complete; performance relies on the quality of the Efficient Pruning Score. When to use: After densification stage to aggressively reduce model size. When not to use: During densification (use Soft Pruning instead). Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Primitives Growth Control
head: Budget control, Growth control
body: Primitives Growth Control is a constraint mechanism applied during the densification phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting to prevent unbounded growth of the primitive count, which can lead to out-of-memory errors. It sets itself apart from standard Adaptive Densification (ADC) by enforcing a hard upper bound on the total number of Gaussians and limiting the rate of new primitive creation per step, ensuring stable memory usage even when densification remains active for extended training periods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of N 3D Gaussian primitives, their associated densification scores (e.g., view-space positional gradients or reconstruction loss metrics), and the target maximum primitive budget N{max}. Output: A filtered list of primitives eligible for cloning/splitting, capped such that the total count does not exceed N{max}. Data Structures: Primitive Set: A list of N objects, each containing position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{S} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and a scalar densification score Ek. Budget Counter: An integer tracking the current number of primitives. Parameters: Growth Fraction (f): The maximum fraction of existing primitives allowed to be added in a single densification step. Typical value: 0.05 (5%). Max Primitives Budget (N{max}): The absolute upper limit on the number of primitives. Typically set to the median number of primitives generated by the baseline 3D Gaussian Splatting method on the same scene, or the peak count reached during unconstrained training. Steps: 1. Identify Candidates: Evaluate all current primitives to determine which ones meet the criteria for densification (e.g., Ek > \tau). Let this set of candidates be C. 2. Calculate Allowance: Compute the maximum number of new primitives allowed in this step: N{allow} = \lfloor f \times N \rfloor where N is the current number of primitives. 3. Check Budget: Determine the remaining budget: N{rem} = N{max} - N The effective limit for new primitives is: N{limit} = \min(N{allow}, N{rem}) If N{limit} \le 0, no new primitives are created. 4. Rank Candidates: Sort the candidate set C in descending order based on their densification score Ek. 5. Select Top-K: Select the top K candidates from C, where K = N{limit}. If |C| \le N{limit}, all candidates are selected. 6. Execute Densification: For each selected candidate, perform the standard cloning or splitting operation as defined in the parent method Density Control and Densification. Primitives not selected are left unchanged. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def primitivesgrowthcontrol(primitives, densificationscores, Nmax, growthfraction=0.05): """ primitives: List of Gaussian primitives. densificationscores: List of float scores corresponding to each primitive. Nmax: Maximum allowed number of primitives. growthfraction: Fraction of current primitives allowed to be added per step. """ N = len(primitives) # Calculate max new primitives allowed by growth rate Nallow = int(growthfraction N) # Calculate remaining budget Nrem = Nmax - N # Effective limit is the minimum of growth allowance and remaining budget Nlimit = min(Nallow, Nrem) # If no budget, return empty list of indices to densify if Nlimit <= 0: return [] # Identify candidates with positive densification score (or threshold > 0) # Assuming densificationscores contains the metric Ek # In standard ADC, candidates are those where Ek > threshold. # Here we assume the caller has already filtered for Ek > threshold, # or we filter here. Let's assume densificationscores are raw metrics # and we need to pick the best ones. # Create list of (index, score) candidates = [(i, score) for i, score in enumerate(densificationscores) if score > 0] # Sort by score descending candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) # Select top Nlimit candidates selectedindices = [idx for idx, in candidates[:Nlimit]] return selectedindices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Budget: If N reaches N{max}, N{rem} becomes 0, and no further densification occurs. This prevents OOM but may halt refinement if the scene still requires higher density. Score Ties: If multiple candidates have identical scores, the selection is arbitrary unless a secondary tie-breaker (e.g., index) is defined. Dynamic N{max}: N{max} is typically static per scene, derived from baseline statistics. Setting it too low may degrade reconstruction quality; setting it too high defeats the purpose of growth control. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) per densification step due to sorting candidates, where N is the number of primitives. This is negligible compared to the rendering cost. Memory Complexity: O(N), as it only stores the primitive list and scores. It prevents memory explosion by capping N. Performance: Ensures stable memory usage during long training runs (e.g., 27k iterations vs. 15k in standard 3DGS) without significant quality loss. Strengths: Prevents out-of-memory errors; allows extended training for better convergence; simple to implement. Limitations: May prematurely stop densification in complex regions if N{max} is set too conservatively; requires tuning N{max} based on baseline runs. Primitives Growth Control was introduced in "Revising Densification in Gaussian Splatting" to address the issue of unpredictable primitive growth in standard Adaptive Densification Control (ADC). The authors observed that while ADC stops after 15k iterations in standard 3DGS, keeping it active for longer (e.g., 27k) leads to memory issues without a cap. The method was developed to enable stable, long-duration training by combining a fixed growth fraction with a global budget limit. name: DashGaussian Primitive Growth Control
head: Double-condition Densification, Primitive Scheduler
body: DashGaussian Primitive Growth Control is a densification scheme that limits the final number of 3D Gaussian primitives (N{GS}) by combining a threshold-based selection with a top-k selection, preventing primitive explosion while maintaining reconstruction quality. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting densification by introducing a primitive budget upper-bound (P{fin}) and a scheduler that dynamically constrains growth in both early low-resolution (LR) and late high-resolution (HR) optimization stages. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussian primitives, densification scores for each primitive, current primitive count N{GS}, target primitive budget upper-bound P{fin}, hyper-parameters \gamma and \eta, and initial resolution factor a. Outputs: A subset of primitives selected for densification (splitting or cloning), constrained such that the final primitive count does not exceed P{fin} significantly, and the optimization continues with Adam optimizer. Primitive List: A collection of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian typically contains position, covariance (or scale/orientation), opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients. The exact layout depends on the backbone (e.g., Taming-3DGS, Mip-Splatting). Densification Scores: A scalar value per primitive indicating its need for densification (e.g., based on gradient magnitude or view-space error). Scheduler State: Tracks the current primitive count N{GS} and the number of primitives added in the current step P{add}. P{fin}: Primitive number upper-bound used in the scheduler. \gamma (gamma): Hyper-parameter controlling the primitive budget convergence. Larger \gamma increases P{fin}, leading to larger N{GS}, higher quality, and longer optimization time. Typical value: 0.98. \eta (eta): Hyper-parameter in the primitive scheduler equation. Combined with \gamma as \eta/(1-\gamma) to determine P{fin} relative to P{add}. a: Hyper-parameter determining initial rendering resolution. Larger a means smaller initial resolution. Typical value: 4. P{add}: The number of primitives added in a specific densification step. The primitive budget upper-bound P{fin} is determined by the scheduler equation (Eq. 5 in). When stable, it converges to: P{fin} = \frac{\eta}{1 - \gamma} P{add} \quad \text{(Eq. 8 in)} This implies that changing \gamma and \eta is equivalent to changing the ratio \frac{\eta}{1-\gamma}. 1. Evaluate Densification: For each primitive, compute its densification score based on the backbone's criteria (e.g., gradient-based). 2. Threshold Selection: Identify primitives that pass a predefined densification threshold. Let this set be S{thresh}. 3. Top-k Selection: From the union of primitives passing the threshold, select the top-k primitives with the highest densification scores. Let this set be S{topk}. 4. Constraint Check (Late HR Stage): In the late high-resolution optimization stage, ensure that the number of primitives passing the threshold is fewer than P{fin} - N{GS}. This ensures that the threshold-based densification and top-k selection mutually constrain densification, preventing explosion. 5. Final Selection: Select primitives from S{topk} for densification. If the number of candidates exceeds the allowed budget (P{fin} - N{GS}), randomly select P{fin} - N{GS} primitives from the top candidates. 6. Densify: Split or clone the selected primitives. 7. Update Count: Update N{GS} and P{add} for the next step. 8. Optimize: Update primitive parameters using the Adam optimizer. Unverified code. Returns: indicestodensify: Indices of primitives selected for densification. """ # Step 1: Threshold Selection # Assume a threshold function exists or is defined by the backbone. # For implementation, we assume a fixed threshold or dynamic one. # The source mentions "densification threshold" but does not give the exact formula. # We assume a standard thresholding operation. threshold = getthreshold(primitives, scores) # Placeholder for backbone-specific threshold logic passingindices = [i for i, s in enumerate(scores) if s > threshold] # Step 2: Top-k Selection # Get scores for passing primitives passingscores = [(scores[i], i) for i in passingindices] # Sort by score descending passingscores.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) # Determine k. The source says "select the top-k primitives that pass the threshold". # It also mentions "randomly select Pi - NGS primitives from them". # This implies k is effectively the number of candidates, and we cap the final selection. # However, the text says "select the top-k... for densification". # And later: "ensure that fewer than Pi - NGS primitives pass the threshold". # Let's assume k is large enough to cover the budget, or k is determined by the budget. # The source says: "randomly select Pi - NGS primitives from them". # This implies we first identify candidates (top-k or all passing), then cap. # Let's interpret "top-k" as selecting the best candidates up to the budget limit. # If we strictly follow "select top-k... then randomly select Pi-NGS", # it implies k >= Pi-NGS. budgetremaining = pfin - ngs # If budget is non-positive, no densification if budgetremaining <= 0: return [] # Select top candidates. The source says "top-k selection". # It doesn't specify k explicitly, but implies it's related to the budget. # "randomly select Pi - NGS primitives from them" suggests we have more candidates than budget. # So we take all passing, or a large top-k, then sample. # Let's take all passing as candidates for simplicity, or top-N where N is large. # The source says "top-k selection to control the growth". # Let's assume k is effectively infinite or large enough, and the cap is the budget. candidates = passingscores # All passing primitives are candidates # Step 3: Constraint and Random Selection # "randomly select Pi - NGS primitives from them" numtoselect = min(len(candidates), budgetremaining) if numtoselect == 0: return [] # Randomly select from the top candidates # Note: The source says "randomly select Pi - NGS primitives from them". # "Them" refers to the primitives selected with the two densification scores as a whole set. # This implies we might have two scores? Limitations: Requires tuning of \gamma and \eta. Removing the scheduler or threshold can lead to undesirable primitive counts or OOM if not careful. name: RadSplat
body: RadSplat is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by leveraging the robust geometric priors of a trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It solves the problem of poor initialization quality and topological inconsistencies inherent in raw Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds. By converting a dense NeRF-derived point cloud into Gaussians, it achieves high-quality rendering with unprecedented speed (900+ FPS) while circumventing the need for extensive per-scene gradient descent loops. RadSplat operates as a hybrid initialization and pruning strategy. It bypasses the standard SfM-based initialization and subsequent long optimization phases by using a pre-trained NeRF to generate a dense, accurate point cloud, which is then converted into 3D Gaussians. Inputs: A trained NeRF model for the target scene. Sparse multi-view images (used to train the initial NeRF, though the NeRF itself is the direct input for Gaussian generation). Outputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N with optimized position, rotation, scale, opacity, and appearance parameters. Data Structures: The output is a standard 3DGS primitive list. Each primitive i contains: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Appearance parameters (e.g., spherical harmonic coefficients) Steps: 1. NeRF Training: Train a standard NeRF on the input sparse multi-view images to learn the scene's implicit radiance field. 2. Dense Point Cloud Generation: Extract a dense point cloud from the trained NeRF. This step leverages the NeRF's ability to resolve geometry robustly, avoiding the sparsity and noise of raw SfM. 3. Gaussian Conversion: Convert the extracted points into 3D Gaussians. The position \mathbf{p}i is set to the point location. Other parameters (scale, rotation, opacity) are initialized based on the local density and geometry inferred from the NeRF or standard heuristics for point-to-Gaussian conversion. 4. Multi-View Pruning: Apply a pruning step using a multi-view importance score to remove redundant or low-contributing Gaussians. This reduces memory usage and training cost while maintaining quality. 5. Optional Fine-tuning: While RadSplat aims to bypass long gradient descent loops, minimal optimization may be applied to refine parameters, though the primary benefit is the high-quality initialization. Parameters: NeRF resolution/depth: Not given in the sources. Pruning threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NeRF Quality Dependency: The quality of the final Gaussian representation is heavily dependent on the quality of the initial NeRF training. Poor NeRF convergence leads to poor initialization. Computational Cost of NeRF: Training the NeRF adds an upfront computational cost, though this is offset by the reduced need for extensive 3DGS optimization. Rendering Speed: Achieves 900+ FPS rendering with high quality. Memory: Reduced memory usage compared to dense SfM-initialized Gaussians due to pruning. Training Time: Drastically shortens or bypasses the per-scene gradient descent loop typically required for 3DGS. Strengths: High-quality initialization, robustness to topological pitfalls of SfM, high rendering speed. Limitations: Requires training a NeRF first, which may be computationally expensive for very large scenes. Not given in the sources for specific memory complexity formulas. RadSplat was introduced as a method to improve the initialization of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitations of raw SfM initialization, which often suffers from noise and topological errors. The method is cited in surveys on 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization and recent advances in the field. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Training Optimization and Initialization
head: 3DGS Initialization Policy, 3D Gaussian Splatting Training, GauFRe
body: This family defines the strategies for seeding the initial set of N 3D Gaussian primitives and the iterative optimization process that adjusts their parameters to minimize the difference between rendered images and ground truth views. It sets itself apart from NeRF-based methods by optimizing explicit geometric and appearance attributes rather than neural network weights, offering significantly faster training and inference speeds [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. Unlike static initialization methods, it employs adaptive density control to dynamically manage the number and distribution of Gaussians during training [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. All methods in this family optimize a set of N 3D Gaussian primitives [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. Each primitive i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Appearance parameters (e.g., spherical harmonic coefficients hi) [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md] The optimization minimizes a loss function \mathcal{L} between rendered images and ground truth views, typically using the Adam optimizer [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. The rendering process involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space, sorting by depth, and alpha blending [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. The 3DGS Initialization Policy defines the strategy for seeding the initial set of N 3D Gaussian primitives before optimization begins. It addresses the problem of sparse or incorrect initial geometry, which can lead to poor convergence or artifacts in the final radiance field. Unlike dynamic densification strategies that spawn primitives during training based on view-space gradients, this policy acts once before optimization using the initial scene geometry or random distribution. It sets apart from standard random initialization by potentially incorporating specific opacity scaling laws derived from order-independent transparency (OTS) formulations [1398-3dgs-initialization-policy.md]. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Training is the iterative optimization process that adjusts the parameters of a set of 3D Gaussian primitives to minimize the difference between rendered images and ground truth views [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. It solves the problem of reconstructing photorealistic 3D scenes from 2D images without relying on neural network weights, instead optimizing explicit geometric and appearance attributes [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. It sets itself apart from NeRF-based methods by offering significantly faster training and inference speeds while achieving comparable image quality [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. Unlike static initialization methods, it employs adaptive density control to dynamically manage the number and distribution of Gaussians [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. GauFRe is a method for real-time dynamic novel view synthesis that represents dynamic scenes using deformable 3D Gaussian primitives [7994-gaufre.md]. It solves the problem of reconstructing non-rigid motion from monocular video by employing a forward-warping deformation field, which explicitly models the temporal evolution of scene geometry [7994-gaufre.md]. Unlike backward-warping approaches common in NeRFs that require querying a canonical space, GauFRe predicts the deformed primitive system at a specific time directly, making it efficient for explicit primitive-based rendering [7994-gaufre.md]. It distinguishes itself by decoupling static and dynamic regions into separate Gaussian sets and applying exponential/normalization constraints to scale and rotation parameters for stable optimization [7994-gaufre.md]. Joint optimization of network weights, feature grids, and latent codes using the total training loss. \Thetas: Learnable parameters of SDF model. \Thetad: Learnable parameters of DDF model. M: SDF and DDF feature grids, M = (Ms, Md). Ms: SDF feature grids, Ms = \{M^si \mid i = xy, yz, zx\}. Md: DDF feature grids, Md = \{M^di \mid i = pxpy, \dots, rzrx\}. Z: Set of latent codes for J training shapes, Z = \{zi \mid i = 1\dots J\}. ws, wd, w\sigma, w{tv}, w{ts}, wl: Weights for respective losses. The foundational 3D Gaussian Splatting method was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023, establishing the explicit primitive-based rendering pipeline [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. The initialization policy utilizing opacity scaling laws was detailed in subsequent analyses of the 3DGS training dynamics [1398-3dgs-initialization-policy.md]. GauFRe extended this framework to dynamic scenes in 2024, introducing forward-warping deformation fields [7994-gaufre.md]. The "Training Optimization" variant referencing SDF/DFD grids originates from the FIRe method for inverse rendering. FIRe: Fast Inverse Rendering Using Directional and Signed Distance Functions, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qj0ymDlRYZs, fetched 2026-10-30

name: 3DGS Initialization Policy
head: Initialization Policy, OTS Initialization
body: The 3DGS Initialization Policy defines the protocol for seeding the initial set of N 3D Gaussian primitives before optimization begins, ensuring a stable starting point for gradient-based training. It distinguishes itself from dynamic densification strategies (like those in 3D Gaussian Splatting Training) by establishing the initial geometric and opacity distribution statically, often using a power-law scaling for opacity to match specific rendering assumptions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry (e.g., SfM point cloud or empty space), target number of Gaussians N. Output: A set of N Gaussians with initialized position \mathbf{p}i, rotation qi, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and appearance parameters. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is stored with: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Unit quaternion for rotation. \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (often initialized isotropically or based on local density). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. hi: Spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Steps: 1. Position Initialization: For synthetic scenes (e.g., Nerf-Synthetic), initialize N Gaussians with random positions uniformly distributed within a unit cube centered at the scene origin. For real-world scenes, positions are typically derived from the Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud. 2. Rotation and Scale Initialization: Rotations qi are typically initialized to identity (random or uniform if specified by the variant). Scales \mathbf{s}i are initialized based on the local point density or a fixed small value. 3. Opacity Initialization (OTS Weight): All Gaussians are initialized to a uniform opacity value \alpha0. This value is derived using a power function of the total number of Gaussians N: \alpha0 = 2 \cdot N^{\gamma} The exponent \gamma depends on the rendering method: \gamma = 0.35 for standard 3DGS. \gamma = 0.55 for OTS-based (Order-Independent Transparency) methods. Note: The result is typically clamped or interpreted as the initial weight for the opacity parameter. 4. Appearance Initialization: Spherical harmonic coefficients are initialized to zero (or a default color). Parameters: N: Total number of Gaussians. Typical values include 4k, 12k, 36k, 100k, 500k, 1M, 5M depending on scene complexity and experiment. \gamma: Exponent for opacity scaling (0.35 for 3DGS, 0.55 for OTS). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incorrect Geometry Initialization: Starting with random positions in real-world scenes without SfM guidance can lead to artifacts like "second ears" or fuzzy surfaces if not corrected early. Opacity Scaling: Using the wrong exponent \gamma can lead to suboptimal convergence or incorrect alpha blending behavior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializegaussians(N, scenetype="synthetic", useots=False): """ Initialize N 3D Gaussians. Args: N (int): Total number of Gaussians. scenetype (str): 'synthetic' or 'realworld'. useots (bool): If True, use OTS opacity scaling (gamma=0.55), else 3DGS (gamma=0.35). Returns: dict: Dictionary containing initialized Gaussian parameters. """ # 1. Initialize Positions if scenetype == "synthetic": # Random positions in unit cube around origin positions = np.random.uniform(-1, 1, size=(N, 3)) else: # Use SfM point cloud (not given in sources, placeholder for external data) # positions = getsfmpoints(N) positions = np.zeros((N, 3)) # Placeholder # 2. Initialize Rotations (Identity) rotations = np.tile([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], (N, 1)) # w, x, y, z # 3. Initialize Scales (Placeholder: typically based on local density) scales = np.ones((N, 3)) 0.1 # Placeholder value # 4. Initialize Opacity if useots: gamma = 0.55 else: gamma = 0.35 # Calculate initial opacity weight # Note: The source says "2 N^0.35" and "2 N^0.55". # This is likely a scaling factor for the opacity parameter, not the raw alpha value # which must be in [0,1]. The exact interpretation of "OTS weight" is not fully detailed # beyond the formula. We assume this value is used to set the initial alpha. opacityweight = 2.0 (N gamma) # Clamp or normalize if necessary (implementation detail) # Typically, opacity is initialized to a small value or the weight itself if it represents # the initial alpha. Given the formula, for N=100k, 2100000^0.35 ≈ 221.5 ≈ 43, # which is > 1. Thus, this is likely a scaling factor for the logit or a specific # parameterization. Without explicit formula for alpha from weight, we store the weight. opacities = np.full(N, opacityweight) # 5. Initialize Appearance (SH Coefficients) # Assuming 3 bands (9 coeffs per channel, 3 channels = 27 coeffs) shcoeffs = np.zeros((N, 27)) return { "positions": positions, "rotations": rotations, "scales": scales, "opacities": opacities, "shcoeffs": shcoeffs } DART is a pre-processing initialization method that enriches a sparse SfM point cloud by generating additional samples on local tangent planes. It addresses sparse seeding in scene peripheries and low-texture regions by assigning disk radii that grow with the point’s distance from a robust scene center. Unlike dynamic densification, DART acts once before optimization using only initial SfM geometry. The Gaussian Allocation Policy (GAP) is a reinforcement learning method that determines how to distribute a fixed budget of 3D Gaussians among learned anchor tokens to maximize rendering fidelity. It differs from heuristic initialization by treating allocation as a discrete optimization problem solved via Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO). A strategy to maximize overlap between cells and emitted neural Gaussians by dynamically aligning cell geometry with Gaussian properties. It involves: 1. Defining the cell's quaternion as a weighted average of the quaternions of its emitted Gaussians. 2. Periodically updating cell centers using \mathbf{x}n = \frac{\sum{k=1}^K \boldsymbol{\mu}{n,k}}{K}, where \mathbf{x}n is the cell center, K is the number of Gaussians in the cell, and \boldsymbol{\mu}{n,k} is the mean of the k-th Gaussian in cell n. 3. Learning 3D covariances and positions of first-layer cells in accordance with updates to second-layer Gaussians. Prunes randomly initialized 3D Gaussians to prevent incorrect initial geometry for other views, enhancing camera tracking performance in monocular SLAM. On TUM RGB-D (Mono), ATE RMSE drops from 46.6 cm (w/o pruning) to 3.96 cm (Ours) on average across f1/desk, f2/xyz, f3/office. An initialization strategy that starts optimization from an inversion result to prevent geometric artifacts. Incorrect geometry initialization at the start of finetuning causes artifacts like a second ear, an unrealistic forehead, and a fuzzy surface. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) for position and opacity assignment. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the initial Gaussian parameters. Performance: The choice of initialization affects convergence speed and final quality. Proper opacity scaling (\gamma) is critical for OTS methods. Strengths: Provides a consistent starting point; OTS-specific scaling improves rendering fidelity for order-independent methods. Limitations: Random initialization in synthetic scenes may not capture scene geometry well without subsequent densification. Incorrect initialization can lead to persistent artifacts. The 3DGS Initialization Policy was introduced in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. The specific opacity scaling formula (2 \cdot N^{0.35} for 3DGS and 2 \cdot N^{0.55} for OTS) was detailed in "Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?". The policy aims to align the initial primitive distribution with the assumptions of the rendering pipeline. Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70032, fetched 2026-10-26 Duplex-GS: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2026.3666188, fetched 2026-10-30 Gaussian Splatting SLAM, https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06741, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Preface: A Data-driven Volumetric Prior for Few-shot Ultra High-resolution Face Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.00315, fetched 2026-10-27

name: DART (Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes)
body: DART is a pre-processing initialization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enriches a sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud by generating additional samples on local tangent planes. It addresses the problem of sparse seeding in scene peripheries and low-texture regions by assigning disk radii that grow with the point’s distance from a robust scene center. Unlike dynamic densification strategies that spawn primitives during training based on view-space gradients, DART acts once before optimization using only the initial SfM geometry, making it independent of the backbone’s densification dynamics. Inputs: Initial SfM point cloud P = \{pi\}{i=1}^N, where each pi has a 3D position and color. Multiplier m: total number of points generated per original SfM point (including the original). Radius bounds \rho{min}, \rho{max}: lower and upper bounds for the sampling disk radius, expressed as fractions of the robust scene radius R. K{nn}: number of nearest neighbors for PCA normal estimation. Tw: number of Weiszfeld iterations for center computation. Outputs: Augmented point cloud P{aug} containing the original points and m-1 new samples per original point. Data Structures: Points are represented as tuples (x, y, z, r, g, b). Vectors are 3D Euclidean vectors. Steps: 1. Compute Robust Scene Center: Calculate the L1-median (geometric median) c of the point cloud P using the Weiszfeld iteration. Initialize c^{(0)} as the arithmetic mean of P. Iterate for Tw steps: c^{(k+1)} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N \frac{pi}{\|pi - c^{(k)}\|}}{\sum{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\|pi - c^{(k)}\|}} 2. Compute Robust Scene Radius: Calculate the robust scene radius R as the 95th-percentile distance from the center c: R = \text{Percentile}{95}\left(\{ \|pi - c\|: pi \in P \}\right) 3. Initialize Augmented Cloud: Set P{aug} \leftarrow P. 4. Process Each Point: For each point pi \in P: a. Distance Calculation: Compute the Euclidean distance di from the center: di = \|pi - c\| Compute the normalized, clipped distance \hat{d}i: \hat{d}i = \text{clip}\left(\frac{di}{R}, 0, 1\right) Normalizing by R prevents distant outliers from collapsing the radius schedule toward \rho{min}. b. Tangent-Plane Estimation: Identify the K{nn} nearest neighbors Ni of pi in P using Euclidean distance. Compute the centroid \bar{p}i of Ni: \bar{p}i = \frac{1}{K{nn}} \sum{j \in Ni} pj Compute the 3 \times 3 sample covariance matrix \text{Cov}(Ni): \text{Cov}(Ni) = \frac{1}{K{nn}} \sum{j \in Ni} (pj - \bar{p}i)(pj - \bar{p}i)^\top Estimate the local normal ni as the unit eigenvector of \text{Cov}(Ni) associated with the smallest eigenvalue: ni = \arg\min{\|u\|2=1} u^\top \text{Cov}(Ni) u Construct an orthonormal tangent basis (ei^{(1)}, ei^{(2)}) by choosing any unit vector ei^{(1)} perpendicular to ni and setting: ei^{(2)} = ni \times ei^{(1)} The normal ni is used only to construct the frame and is not stored on the replicas. c. Radius Assignment: Assign the disk radius \rhoi as a linear function of \hat{d}i: \rhoi = R \cdot \left[ \rho{min} + \hat{d}i (\rho{max} - \rho{min}) \right] A point at the scene center receives \rhoi = \rho{min} R; a point at or beyond the 95th-percentile shell receives \rhoi = \rho{max} R. d. Disk Sampling: For k from 1 to m-1: 1. Draw two independent uniform random variables \xi1, \xi2 \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 1]. 2. Compute polar coordinates: r = \rhoi \xi1 \theta = 2\pi \xi2 Note: The source explicitly defines r = \rhoi \xi1. 3. Compute the new sample position q: q = pi + r \cos(\theta) ei^{(1)} + r \sin(\theta) ei^{(2)} 4. Assign the color of the parent point to q: q.\text{color} \leftarrow pi.\text{color}. 5. Add q to P{aug}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.spatial import KDTree def dart(P, m, rhomin, rhomax, Knn, Tw): """ P: list of points, each point is a dict or object with 'pos' (np.array, shape (3,)) and 'color' (np.array, shape (3,)) m: multiplier rhomin: lower bound fraction rhomax: upper bound fraction Knn: number of neighbors for PCA Tw: Weiszfeld iterations Returns: list of augmented points """ N = len(P) positions = np.array([p['pos'] for p in P]) # Step 1: Compute robust scene center c (L1-median via Weiszfeld) c = np.mean(positions, axis=0) # Initialize at arithmetic mean for in range(Tw): dists = np.linalg.norm(positions - c, axis=1) dists = np.maximum(dists, 1e-8) # Guard against division by zero weights = 1.0 / dists c = np.sum(positions weights[:, np.newaxis], axis=0) / np.sum(weights) # Step 2: Compute robust scene radius R (95th-percentile distance) distsfromc = np.linalg.norm(positions - c, axis=1) R = np.percentile(distsfromc, 95) # # Step 3: Initialize augmented cloud Paug = list(P) # # Precompute KNN tree tree = KDTree(positions) for i, pi in enumerate(P): posi = pi['pos'] # Stage (i): Distance di = np.linalg.norm(posi - c) # dhati = np.clip(di / R, 0, 1) # # Stage (ii): Tangent-plane estimation # Find Knn nearest neighbors, idxknn = tree.query(posi, k=Knn) neighbors = positions[idxknn] # Compute centroid of neighborhood pbari = np.mean(neighbors, axis=0) # # Compute covariance matrix diff = neighbors - pbari CovNi = (diff.T @ diff) / Knn # # Compute normal: eigenvector corresponding to smallest eigenvalue eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(CovNi) ni = eigenvectors[:, 0] ni = ni / np.linalg.norm(ni) # # Construct orthonormal tangent basis # Choose any unit vector e1 perpendicular to n if np.abs(ni[0]) < 0.9: e1 = np.cross(ni, np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])) else: e1 = np.cross(ni, np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0])) e1 = e1 / np.linalg.norm(e1) e2 = np.cross(ni, e1) # # Stage (iii): Radius assignment rhoi = R (rhomin + dhati (rhomax - rhomin)) # # Stage (iv): Disk sampling for k in range(m - 1): # xi1 = np.random.uniform(0, 1) xi2 = np.random.uniform(0, 1) r = rhoi xi1 # theta = 2 np.pi xi2 # qpos = posi + r np.cos(theta) e1 + r np.sin(theta) e2 # qcolor = pi['color'] # Paug.append({'pos': qpos, 'color': qcolor}) # return Paug Parameters: m: Multiplier for the number of additional samples. Total points per original point becomes m. \rho{min}: Lower bound for the disk radius, relative to R. \rho{max}: Upper bound for the disk radius, relative to R. K{nn}: Number of nearest neighbors for PCA. Tw: Number of Weiszfeld iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If a point pi coincides with the center c, the Weiszfeld iteration denominator term \|pi - c\| becomes zero. The pseudocode handles this with a small epsilon. The source explicitly uses r = \rhoi \xi1 for disk sampling, which does not produce a uniform distribution over the disk area (standard uniform sampling uses \sqrt{\xi1}). Implementers should follow the source formula exactly. The normal estimation relies on K{nn} being sufficient to define a plane. In sparse regions, this may be unstable. Initializes point clouds using dense feature matches instead of traditional detector-based matches, balancing training time and rendering quality on textureless surfaces and unbounded backgrounds. It extracts and aggregates dense feature correspondences using hierarchical localization, then forms the point cloud via multi-view 3D triangulation using the Direct Linear Transform (DLT). Time Complexity: The method is a pre-processing step. Computing the center and radius is O(N) or O(N \log N) depending on the median/percentile algorithm. For each of the N points, KNN search is O(K{nn} \log N) or O(K{nn} N), PCA is O(K{nn}), and sampling is O(m). Total complexity is roughly O(N (K{nn} \log N + m)). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot m) to store the augmented cloud. Strengths: It is independent of the backbone's densification dynamics, acting only once before training. It specifically targets sparse periphery regions by increasing disk radius with distance. Limitations: It relies on the quality of the initial SfM point cloud. It does not address over-dense regions (which is handled by the sibling method AGE). When to use: When the initial SfM cloud is sparse in the periphery or low-texture areas, and a static initialization is preferred over dynamic densification for the initial spread. DART was introduced in the paper "DART-3DGS: Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It is designed to work with vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting and anchor-based methods like Scaffold-GS. It is part of a pair of initialization and densification controls, with AGE (Age-Gated Eligibility) handling the opposite problem of uncontrolled cascading splits in dense regions. DART-3DGS: Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13705904, fetched 2026-10-27 GauStudio: A Modular Framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting and Beyond, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.19632, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Allocation Policy
head: GSPO-based allocation
body: The Gaussian Allocation Policy (GAP) is a reinforcement learning method that determines how to distribute a fixed budget of 3D Gaussians among learned anchor tokens to maximize rendering fidelity. It differs from heuristic initialization methods by treating allocation as a discrete optimization problem solved via Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), allowing the policy to learn complex geometric dependencies between anchors and required Gaussian density. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of anchor tokens \{an\}{n=1}^N encoding local 3D regions, and a target Gaussian budget B. Outputs: A discrete allocation vector k = \{kn\}{n=1}^N, where kn is the integer count of Gaussians assigned to anchor n, such that \sum{n=1}^N kn = B. Data Structures: Anchor Tokens: Feature vectors representing geometric primitives. Policy Network \pi\psi: A neural network that takes anchor tokens as input and outputs allocation proportions p = \{pn\}{n=1}^N. Allocation Vector k: Integer array of size N. Algorithm Steps: 1. Proportion Prediction: The policy \pi\psi processes the anchor tokens \{an\} to predict allocation proportions p = \{pn\}{n=1}^N, where pn represents the expected fraction of the budget B assigned to anchor n. 2. Stochastic Sampling (Training): For each training step, draw C candidate allocations (rollouts). For each rollout c \in \{1, \dots, C\}, sample k^{(c)} from a multinomial distribution: k^{(c)} \sim \text{Mult}(B, \text{sg}(p)) where \text{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operator, ensuring gradients do not flow through the sampling process. 3. Representation Generation: For each rollout c, generate the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation G^{(c)} using the allocated counts k^{(c)} and the resource-linear decoder. 4. Rendering and Reward: Render an image \hat{I}^{(c)} from G^{(c)} at novel target views. Compute the reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} between \hat{I}^{(c)} and the ground truth image I. The reward is defined as the negative loss: Rc = -\mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} Gradients are not tracked during this evaluation. 5. Advantage Calculation: Compute the group-relative advantage \hat{A}c by standardizing the rewards within the group of C rollouts: \hat{A}c = \frac{Rc - \text{mean}\{R{c'}\}{c'=1}^C}{\text{std}\{R{c'}\}{c'=1}^C} 6. Importance Ratio: Compute the length-normalized importance ratio sc for each rollout to account for the change in policy probability: sc = \exp \left( \frac{1}{B} \sum{n=1}^N kn^{(c)} \log \frac{pn}{\text{sg}(pn)} \right) 7. Policy Update: Maximize the clipped surrogate objective J{\text{policy}}: J{\text{policy}} = \mathbb{E} \left[ \frac{1}{C} \sum{c=1}^C \min \left( sc \hat{A}c, \text{clip}(sc, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) \hat{A}c \right) \right] where \epsilon is the clipping range. 8. Inference: Bypass stochastic sampling. Convert the expected counts B p into an integer allocation k summing exactly to B using a deterministic rounding procedure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianallocationpolicy(anchortokens, budget, numrollouts, clipepsilon, policynet): """ Implements the Gaussian Allocation Policy optimization step. Args: anchortokens: List of anchor feature vectors. budget: Total number of Gaussians B. numrollouts: Number of candidate allocations C. clipepsilon: Clipping range epsilon. policynet: Neural network returning allocation proportions p. Returns: policynet: Updated network parameters. """ # 1. Predict proportions proportions = policynet(anchortokens) # 2. Sample rollouts using stop-gradient on proportions # ksamples shape: (numrollouts, numanchors) ksamples = samplemultinomial(budget, stopgradient(proportions), numrollouts) rewards = [] importanceratios = [] for c in range(numrollouts): kc = ksamples[c] # 3. Generate 3DGS representation and render # Note: In practice, this involves spawning Gaussians and rasterizing renderedimage = render3dgs(anchortokens, kc) groundtruthimage = getgroundtruthview() # 4. Compute reward loss = computereconstructionloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) reward = -loss rewards.append(reward) # 5. Compute importance ratio # sc = exp( (1/B) sum( kn log(pn / sg(pn)))) logratiosum = 0.0 for n in range(len(anchortokens)): logratiosum += kc[n] log(proportions[n] / stopgradient(proportions[n])) importanceratio = exp(logratiosum / budget) importanceratios.append(importanceratio) # 6. Compute group-relative advantage rewardstensor = tensor(rewards) meanreward = mean(rewardstensor) stdreward = std(rewardstensor) advantages = (rewardstensor - meanreward) / stdreward # 7. Update policy via clipped objective # J = E[ (1/C) sum( min(sc Ac, clip(sc, 1-eps, 1+eps) Ac)) ] ratiostensor = tensor(importanceratios) clippedratios = clip(ratiostensor, 1 - clipepsilon, 1 + clipepsilon) term1 = ratiostensor advantages term2 = clippedratios advantages losses = min(term1, term2) policyloss = mean(losses) # Backpropagate through policynet to update psi updateparameters(policynet, policyloss) return policynet def samplemultinomial(budget, probs, numsamples): """ Samples discrete allocations from a multinomial distribution. Args: budget: Integer B. probs: Tensor of probabilities p. numsamples: Integer C. Returns: Tensor of shape (numsamples, len(probs)) with integer counts summing to budget. """ # Implementation detail: Use a library function or custom C++/CUDA kernel # for efficient multinomial sampling that respects the sum constraint. # Here we assume a standard multinomial sampler exists. return multinomialsample(probs, budget, numsamples) Parameters: C: Number of rollouts (candidate allocations) drawn per training step. \epsilon: Clipping range for the importance ratio in the policy objective. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Probability: If pn = 0 but kn > 0, the log term in the importance ratio becomes undefined. The stop-gradient on the denominator prevents this during training if the policy is well-initialized, but numerical stability requires ensuring pn > 0 or handling the limit. Rounding Errors: At inference, the deterministic rounding of B p must ensure \sum kn = B. Standard rounding may fail this constraint; a specific rounding procedure (e.g., largest remainder method) is required. A heuristic initialization method that replicates Gaussians based on distance to tangent planes, lacking the learned adaptive allocation of GAP. See DART. Time Complexity: The policy optimization step scales linearly with the number of rollouts C and the number of anchors N. Rendering C views per step adds overhead, but 3DGS rasterization is highly efficient, keeping this minimal. Memory Complexity: Requires storing C intermediate 3DGS representations and gradients for the policy network. Memory usage scales with C \times B. Strengths: Enables resource-linear decoding where Gaussian count scales linearly with budget B. Adapts allocation to geometric complexity automatically. Limitations: Requires reinforcement learning training loop, which is more complex to implement than static initialization. Performance depends on the quality of the anchor tokens. The Gaussian Allocation Policy was introduced in the context of resource-linear 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically in the RLSplat framework. It leverages Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) to solve the discrete allocation problem, addressing the need for compact and high-fidelity representations by densely allocating Gaussians to geometrically complex regions. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training
head: 3DGS Learning, G Splats
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Training is the iterative optimization process that adjusts the parameters of a set of 3D Gaussian primitives to minimize the difference between rendered images and ground truth views. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-fidelity, view-dependent 3D scenes from sparse or dense 2D image collections without relying on neural network weights. Unlike NeRFs, which optimize a continuous volumetric field, 3DGS optimizes explicit geometric primitives (means, covariances, opacities, and spherical harmonic coefficients) using differentiable rasterization. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using adaptive density control (splitting, cloning, pruning) to dynamically adjust the number of Gaussians during training, balancing reconstruction fidelity against computational cost. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images (or video frames) with known camera poses (extrinsics R{cw}, t{cw} and intrinsics K). Initial 3D Gaussian parameters derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters: positions \mathbf{p}i, rotations qi, scales \mathbf{s}i, opacities \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients hi. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (initialized from SfM points). Rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion). Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (initialized between 0 and 1). Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] (initialized as a constant). Appearance: Spherical Harmonic coefficients hi (initialized from SfM colors). Rotation Matrix: The unit quaternion q = (qr, qi, qj, qk) is converted to a rotation matrix R(q): R(q) = 2 \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2} - (qj^2 + qk^2) & qi qj - qr qk & qi qk + qr qj \\ qi qj + qr qk & \frac{1}{2} - (qi^2 + qk^2) & qj qk - qr qi \\ qi qk - qr qj & qj qk + qr qi & \frac{1}{2} - (qi^2 + qj^2) \end{bmatrix} The covariance matrix \Sigma is computed from R and \mathbf{s}. Loss Function: The optimization minimizes a composite loss \mathcal{L} between the rendered image \gamma and ground truth \gamma{gt}: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \lambda is the SSIM weight (default 0.2). Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using SfM points. Set \mathbf{p}i from SfM, hi from SfM colors, and qi, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai to constants. 2. View Sampling: Select a training camera V and retrieve the ground truth image \hat{I} at the current resolution. 3. Rendering: Rasterize the Gaussians using camera V to obtain rendered image I. This involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D, sorting by depth, and alpha blending [Parent]. 4. Loss Computation: Compute \mathcal{L} between I and \hat{I}. 5. Backpropagation: Compute gradients \nabla \mathcal{L} for all parameters (\mathbf{p}w, q, \mathbf{s}, h, \alpha) using the chain rule. 6. Parameter Update: Update parameters using the Adam optimizer. 7. Adaptive Density Control: Periodically (every refineEvery steps), apply densification and pruning: Pruning: If \alphai < \epsilon or the Gaussian is too large, remove it. Densification: If positional gradient \nabla{\mathbf{p}} \mathcal{L} > \taup: Over-reconstruction: If covariance norm \|\mathbf{S}\| > \tauS, split the Gaussian. Under-reconstruction: Else, clone the Gaussian. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. M = SfMInitializePositions() # Positions from Structure from Motion S, C, A = InitAttributes() # Covariances, Colors (SH), Opacities i = 0 # Iteration counter while not converged: # 1. Sample View V, Igt = SampleTrainingView() # Camera V and Ground Truth Image # 2. Render I = Rasterize(M, S, C, A, V) # Project and blend Gaussians # 3. Compute Loss L = Loss(I, Igt) # L1 + D-SSIM # 4. Backpropagate and Update Gradients = Backpropagate(L, M, S, C, A, V) M, S, C, A = AdamUpdate(M, S, C, A, Gradients) # 5. Adaptive Density Control (Interleaved) if IsRefinementIteration(i): for each Gaussian g in (M, S, C, A): # Pruning if g.alpha < epsilon or IsTooLarge(g.mu, g.Sigma): Prune(g) # Densification if GradientPosition(g) > taup: if NormCovariance(g.Sigma) > tauS: # Over-reconstruction: Split SplitGaussian(g) else: # Under-reconstruction: Clone CloneGaussian(g) i = i + 1 Parameters: numIters: Total optimization steps. Default: 30,000. shdegree: Spherical harmonic degree. Default: 3. shdegreeinterval: Steps between increasing SH degree. Default: 1,000. resolutionSchedule: Steps between doubling image resolution. Default: 3,000. densifyFrom: Step after which densification begins. Default: 500. densifyUntil: Step after which densification stops. Default: min(15,000, numIters / 2). refineEvery: Frequency of refinement operations. Default: 500. densifygradthresh: Gradient threshold for densification. Default: 0.0002. densifysizethresh: Size threshold for densification. Default: 0.01. splitscreensize: Screen size threshold for splitting. Default: 0.05. maxGaussians: Maximum number of Gaussians. Default: 5,000,000. bgcolor: Background color. Default: [0.613, 0.010, 0.398] (magenta). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Cameras See Points: If all cameras are discarded because they see no sparse points, training fails. Arbitrary Pose Rendering: Requires exactly 16 elements for the camtoworld matrix. Evaluation Mode: Dataset must be loaded with evalmode=True for evaluation. CPU vs GPU: CPU execution is ~100x slower than GPU. Replaces SH color and opacity with physical quantities (extinction, albedo) for real-time relighting. Handles "in-the-wild" scenes with transients and varying illumination using a lightweight MLP and DINO features. Extends training to fisheye and uncentered cameras via differentiable warping. Uses absolute positional gradients to recover fine details and thin structures. Dynamically adjusts Gaussian count via splitting, cloning, and pruning based on gradients and opacity [Parent]. Stabilizes optimization with normal consistency and anisotropy regularization. Initializes geometry with explicit normals for faster convergence of editable Gaussians. Extends loss with normal consistency and anisotropy regularization for solid object simulation. Feed-forward generalizable 3DGS for human subjects. Reduces VRAM and accelerates convergence via data flow restructuring [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. Handles non-rigid motion via temporal deformation fields [13852-deformation-field-modeling]. Reduces memory footprint by compressing primitives [Parent]. Jointly estimates camera poses and Gaussian scene from image sequences [Parent]. Domain-specific modifications for humans or physical plausibility [Parent]. Aligns Gaussians with SDFs or meshes for watertight boundaries [9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment]. Replaces iterative optimization with neural networks [Parent]. Real-time volumetric medical data visualization with dynamic clipping planes. Modifies the Gaussian primitive or kernel function [Parent]. Uses TSP-ordered views for stable large-scale training. Mechanism for calculating derivatives through the rasterizer [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Two-stage inverse rendering with a BVH-accelerated visibility oracle. Reformulates training as MCMC for robust exploration [Parent]. Interprets training as sampling from a target distribution. Minimizes 1D slice color differences for cloning. Integrates global tri-plane and local grid features. Joint optimization of position and appearance via cross-view consistency. Trains 3DGS, renders stereo views, estimates depth, and fuses into a mesh via TSDF. Generates Gaussian-specific pseudo labels from point cloud labels. Reduces redundancy using cross-view consistency loss and adaptive pruning. Samples mini-batches from a single viewpoint to organize data. Trains a 3DGS to render stereo-calibrated novel views, applies stereo depth estimation on the rendered views, and fuses the estimated dense depth maps using a Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) to form a triangular mesh. A labeling pipeline that generates Gaussian-specific pseudo ground truth labels from original point cloud labels, accounting for the densification and pruning processes of 3D-GS optimization. A mechanism comprising a Cross-View Consistency Loss and adaptive pruning to reduce Gaussian redundancy and ensure geometric validity. It selects adjacent view pairs with SSIM > 0.6, computes a Cross-View Consistent Loss (L{CVC}) to penalize residual discrepancies, and prunes Gaussians based on depth/distance consistency conditions (d^ip < 0.01 \land d^jp < 0.5 \lor d^ip > 3\sigma). A training data sampling strategy where data is organized per viewpoint, and a mini-batch consists of data from only a single viewpoint. For each viewpoint i, the dataset Di is collected, and a mini-batch B{3DGS} is sampled from D = \{Di\} with count=1. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly faster than NeRFs, typically completing in minutes to hours depending on scene complexity and resolution. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians N and the number of views P, roughly O(N \cdot P) for differentiable rasterization [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. Performance: Achieves comparable image quality to NeRFs but with much faster training and real-time rendering speeds. Hardware: GPU-accelerated (CUDA/Metal) is standard; CPU execution is ~100x slower. Strengths: Real-time rendering, fast training, high fidelity. Limitations: Can produce "floaters" or artifacts in unconstrained settings; memory intensive for large scenes. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. [9] (cited in). It initializes positions using sparse point clouds from SfM tools like COLMAP [21]. The method falls under the category of radiance fields but differs from NeRFs by using explicit Gaussian primitives. It has been widely adopted for real-time 3D reconstruction and has inspired numerous variants for SLAM, dynamic scenes, and physical parameter optimization.
