name: Physical Parameter Optimization
head: 3DGS Volume Parameters, Participating Medium Parameters, Physical Gaussian Attributes, g Optimization, 物理化的高斯参数
body: Physical Parameter Optimization replaces the standard spherical harmonic (SH) color and empirical opacity attributes of 3D Gaussian Splatting with a set of physical quantities representing a participating medium. This allows for real-time rendering and dynamic relighting (arbitrary sun direction) by solving the radiative transfer equation through the Gaussian primitives rather than approximating lighting with SH coefficients. It is distinct from standard 3DGS training by optimizing extinction, albedo, and scattering asymmetry instead of color and opacity. Inputs: A dataset of images with known camera poses and sun directions (Stage 1: sun-only, black background; Stage 2: environment lighting). Initial 3D Gaussian point cloud (position, scale, rotation, and initial physical parameters). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian attributes: position, scale, rotation, extinction coefficient (\sigmat), scattering albedo (\omega), Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry factor (g), and multiple scattering octave weights (wn). (Stage 2 only) Optimized environment light network parameters. Each Gaussian primitive stores the following physical parameters in addition to standard geometric attributes (position \mathbf{x}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}): 1. Extinction Coefficient (\sigmat): Type: Scalar. Meaning: Extinction cross-section, representing the volume integral of the extinction coefficient. Activation: softplus, clamped at 5.0. 2. Scattering Albedo (\omega): Type: RGB Vector (3 floats). Meaning: Ratio of scattering coefficient to extinction coefficient. Activation: sigmoid. 3. Henyey-Greenstein Asymmetry Factor (g): Type: Scalar. Meaning: Anisotropy factor for the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Activation: 0.8 \times \tanh(g{raw}), favoring forward scattering. 4. Multiple Scattering Octave Weights (wn): Type: Array of 6 learnable scalars. Meaning: Energy weights for the 6th-order multiple scattering octave approximation (based on Frostbite/Wrenninge). Activation: softplus. The training process is divided into two stages: Stage 1: Physical Parameter Training 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians with standard 3DGS geometry and initial physical parameters. 2. Rendering: For each training iteration, render the scene using the physical volume rendering equation. The radiance L is computed by integrating the extinction, albedo, and phase function along the ray. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss L as a weighted sum of L1 and DSSIM: L = 0.8 \cdot L1 + 0.2 \cdot DSSIM where the DSSIM weight \lambda{dssim} = 0.2. 4. Regularization: Apply Soft Anisotropy Regularization if the log-ratio of scales exceeds anisoratiomax: L{aniso} = \lambda{aniso} \cdot (\log(\text{ratio}))^2 with \lambda{aniso} = 0.001. 5. Optimization: Update all parameters using Adam optimizer with specific learning rates (see Parameters). 6. Densification and Pruning: Interval: Iterations 500 to 15,000, every 100 iterations. Densification: Use adaptive densification with densifytopfrac=0.005 and absolute lower bound 5 \times 10^{-5}. Incorporate scale gradients if > 10^{-6}. Pruning: Remove Gaussians with mean contribution \sum (\alpha \cdot T) < 10^{-4}. Post-Densify Pruning: Extra pruning every 1,000 iterations during densification phase. Resurrection: Every 3,000 iterations (during densification phase), reset the lowest contribution 5% of \sigmat Gaussians to 0.1. 7. Tonemapping: Apply fixed ACES tonemapping by default. If tonemaplearnable is enabled, optimize 4 ACES coefficients with a monotonicity penalty \lambda{tonemap\mono} = 10^{-2} to prevent curve inversion in [0, 8]. Stage 2: Environment Light Optimization 1. Freeze: Freeze all Stage 1 geometric and physical parameters. 2. Train: Optimize a global environment light network (MLP for sun direction T{sun} and SH coefficients for sky irradiance E{lm} and visibility V{lm}) using the envlr learning rate. Learning Rates (Initial / Final): Position: 1.6 \times 10^{-4} / 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. \sigmat: 0.025. \omega: 0.0025. g: 0.0025. wn: 0.0025. Scale: 0.005. Rotation: 0.001. Environment Light (Stage 2): 10^{-3}. Decay: Physical parameter learning rates decay exponentially to 1/10 of their initial value over the course of training. Position LR decays over positionlrmaxsteps (default 30,000). Position LR Delay Mult: 0.01. Total Iterations: 30,000. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstage1(gaussians, dataset, iterations=30000): # Initialize optimizers with specific learning rates optpos = Adam(gaussians.position, lr=1.6e-4, delaymult=0.01) optsigmat = Adam(gaussians.sigmat, lr=0.025) optomega = Adam(gaussians.omega, lr=0.0025) optg = Adam(gaussians.g, lr=0.0025) optw = Adam(gaussians.w, lr=0.0025) optscale = Adam(gaussians.scale, lr=0.005) optrot = Adam(gaussians.rotation, lr=0.001) for iter in range(iterations): # 1. Sample camera and sun direction cam, sun = dataset.sample() # 2. Render physical volume # Integrate extinction, albedo, and HG phase function renderedimage = renderphysicalvolume(gaussians, cam, sun) # 3. Compute Loss gtimage = dataset.getgt(cam) l1loss = L1(renderedimage, gtimage) dssimloss = DSSIM(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = 0.8 l1loss + 0.2 dssimloss # 4. Regularization if checkanisotropy(gaussians): loss += 0.001 anisotropypenalty(gaussians) # 5. Backpropagate and Update loss.backward() optpos.step() optsigmat.step() optomega.step() optg.step() optw.step() optscale.step() optrot.step() optpos.zerograd() optsigmat.zerograd() optomega.zerograd() optg.zerograd() optw.zerograd() optscale.zerograd() optrot.zerograd() # 6. Densification and Pruning (Iter 500-15000, step 100) if 500 <= iter <= 15000 and iter % 100 == 0: densifygaussians(gaussians, optpos, optscale, threshold=5e-5, topfrac=0.005) prunegaussians(gaussians, threshold=1e-4) # Resurrection every 3000 iterations if iter % 3000 == 0: resurrectgaussians(gaussians, fraction=0.05, value=0.1) # Post-densify pruning every 1000 iterations if iter % 1000 == 0: prunegaussians(gaussians, threshold=1e-4) # 7. Decay Learning Rates decaylearningrates(optpos, optsigmat, optomega, optg, optw, iter, maxsteps=30000) def trainstage2(gaussians, envnetwork, dataset, iterations=30000): # Freeze Stage 1 parameters gaussians.position.requiresgrad = False gaussians.scale.requiresgrad = False gaussians.rotation.requiresgrad = False gaussians.sigmat.requiresgrad = False gaussians.omega.requiresgrad = False gaussians.g.requiresgrad = False gaussians.w.requiresgrad = False optenv = Adam(envnetwork.parameters(), lr=1e-3) for iter in range(iterations): cam, sun = dataset.sample() renderedimage = renderphysicalvolumewithenv(gaussians, envnetwork, cam, sun) gtimage = dataset.getgt(cam) loss = 0.8 L1(renderedimage, gtimage) + 0.2 DSSIM(renderedimage, gtimage) loss.backward() optenv.step() optenv.zerograd() decaylearningrates(optenv, iter, maxsteps=30000) Anisotropy Control: Position LR must sync with iterations to prevent anisotropy loss of control. Resurrection Loop: Resurrection is only active during the densification period to avoid net destruction loops. Tonemapping: If using learnable tonemapping, ensure monotonicity penalty is applied to prevent curve inversion in [0, 8]. CUDA Compilation: On Windows, ensure MSVC toolset version is compatible with CUDA (e.g., MSVC 14.44 for CUDA 12.8). Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS training, but with additional overhead for physical volume integration and multiple scattering octave calculations. Memory Complexity: Higher than standard 3DGS due to additional physical parameters (\sigmat, \omega, g, wn) per Gaussian. Performance: Enables real-time rendering and dynamic relighting. Strengths: Physically plausible lighting, dynamic sun direction support, stable physical parameters. Limitations: Complex training pipeline (two stages), sensitive to learning rate decay and densification parameters. When to Use: When dynamic relighting and physically accurate volume rendering are required. When Not to Use: When simple static lighting or empirical color representation is sufficient. Physical Parameter Optimization was introduced as part of the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud project, building on the 3DGS-Volume-Cloud repository. It aims to replace ray-marching volume clouds in game engines with 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time rendering and dynamic relighting. The method was developed by hsiang0117 and is documented in the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud GitHub repository. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: WildGaussians
head: Splatting in the Wild images with Appearance-conditioned Gaussians
body: WildGaussians (SWAG) is a 3D Gaussian Splatting method designed for "in-the-wild" 3D reconstruction from unconstrained photo collections characterized by transient objects, occlusions, and varying illumination. It solves the problem of photometric inconsistency and transient artifacts that cause standard 3DGS to produce floaters or color-shifted renders in such settings. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly modeling image-dependent appearance variations via a lightweight MLP and separating static scene geometry from transient occluders using a learnable opacity variation term, enabling the discarding of transient Gaussians to recover a clean static scene. Unlike ClipGS which uses CLIP features, SWAG relies on DINO features and direct color prediction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of uncalibrated or calibrated images \{Ik\} of a scene. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the static scene, and optionally a set of transient Gaussians. The method also produces image-dependent color and opacity adjustments during rendering. Data Structures: 1. 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS parameters: mean \mu, covariance \Sigma (or scale s and rotation q), base opacity \alpha, and base color coefficients (SH) c. 2. Per-Image Embedding: A trainable vector lI \in \mathbb{R}^n for each training image I. 3. Hash Grid Encoding: A hash table encoding for Gaussian centers x, denoted as emb(x). Hash table size T{hash} = 2^{19}. Finest resolution N{max} = 2048. Coarsest resolution N{min} = 16. Number of levels L = 12. 4. MLP F\theta: A 3-layer MLP with 64 hidden units. Inputs: Gaussian base color c, Hash Grid embedding of center emb(x), Per-image embedding lI. Outputs: Image-dependent color c^I and opacity location parameter \Delta \alpha^I. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians from SfM points. Initialize per-image embeddings lI randomly. Initialize Hash Grid and MLP weights. 2. Embedding Computation: For each Gaussian with center x, compute its hash grid embedding emb(x) using the configured Hash Grid parameters. 3. Appearance and Opacity Prediction: For a given training image I and a Gaussian g: Compute the image-dependent color c^I and opacity location parameter \Delta \alpha^I using the MLP: (c^I, \Delta \alpha^I) = F\theta(c, emb(x), lI) where c is the base color derived from SH coefficients. 4. Opacity Variation Sampling: Sample the opacity variation \Delta \tilde{\alpha}^I from a Binary Concrete distribution to allow differentiable masking of transient objects: \Delta \tilde{\alpha}^I = \text{sigmoid} \left[ \frac{1}{T} \left( \log(|\Delta \alpha^I|) + \log(U) - \log(1-U) \right) \right] where U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1) and T is the temperature. 5. Final Opacity Calculation: Compute the final image-dependent opacity \alpha^I: \alpha^I = \max(\alpha - \Delta \tilde{\alpha}^I, 0) where \alpha is the base Gaussian opacity. 6. Rendering: Render the image using standard 3DGS splatting with the modified color c^I and opacity \alpha^I. 7. Loss Computation: Minimize the L1 loss combined with D-SSIM term between the rendered image and the ground truth image I. 8. Optimization: Update 3D Gaussian parameters, MLP weights \theta, Hash Encoder parameters, and per-image embeddings lI via gradient descent. 9. Transient Identification (Post-Training): After training, identify transient Gaussians as those with non-zero variance of their opacity variation \Delta \tilde{\alpha}^I across all training images: \text{Var}(\Delta \tilde{\alpha}^I) \neq 0 Gaussians with \text{Var}(\Delta \tilde{\alpha}^I) = 0 are considered static. 10. Static Scene Extraction: Discard transient Gaussians to keep only the static part of the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class HashGrid: """Minimal self-contained hash grid implementation for pseudocode.""" def init(self, nlevels, nfeaturesperlevel, log2hashmapsize, resolutionmin, resolutionmax): self.nlevels = nlevels self.nfeatures = nfeaturesperlevel self.hashmapsize = 2 log2hashmapsize self.resolutions = [int(resolutionmin (resolutionmax / resolutionmin) (i / (nlevels - 1))) for i in range(nlevels)] self.grids = [torch.randn(self.hashmapsize, self.nfeatures) for in range(nlevels)] def call(self, x): # x shape: (N, 3) embeddings = [] for i, res in enumerate(self.grids): indices = torch.abs(torch.round(x res.shape[0] / 2 + res.shape[0] / 2).long()) % self.hashmapsize idx = indices[:, 0] % self.hashmapsize embeddings.append(self.grids[i][idx]) return torch.cat(embeddings, dim=-1) class WildGaussiansRenderer: def init(self, numimages, hashtablesize=219, nlevels=12, nmin=16, nmax=2048, embeddim=24, temperature=0.1): self.numimages = numimages self.embeddim = embeddim self.T = temperature self.imageembeddings = nn.Embedding(numimages, embeddim) self.hashgrid = HashGrid(nlevels, 2, 19, nmin, nmax) inputdim = 3 + (nlevels 2) + embeddim self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 4)) def forward(self, gaussians, imageidx, basecolorsh): means = gaussians['means'] opacities = gaussians['opacities'] lI = self.imageembeddings(torch.tensor(imageidx)) embx = self.hashgrid(means) lIexpanded = lI.unsqueeze(0).expand(means.shape[0], -1) mlpinput = torch.cat([basecolorsh, embx, lIexpanded], dim=-1) mlpout = self.mlp(mlpinput) cI = mlpout[:,:3] deltaalphaloc = mlpout[:, 3:4] U = torch.randlike(deltaalphaloc) eps = 1e-6 logit = (torch.log(torch.abs(deltaalphaloc) + eps) + torch.log(U + eps) - torch.log(1 - U + eps)) deltaalphatilde = torch.sigmoid(logit / self.T) alphaI = torch.clamp(opacities - deltaalphatilde, min=0.0) return cI, alphaI def identifytransientgaussians(self, alldeltaalphatildes): variance = torch.var(alldeltaalphatildes, dim=0) istransient = variance > 1e-6 return istransient Parameters: Temperature T: Controls the concentration of the Concrete distribution. Set to 0.1 to force a binary distribution from the beginning of training. No annealing is used. Evaluation U: During evaluation, U is fixed at 0.5. Latent embedding size n: Size of per-image embedding vectors. Set to 24. Hash Table Size: 2^{19}. Finest Resolution N{max}: 2048. Number of Levels L: 12. Coarsest Resolution N{min}: 16. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-construction: The method may over-construct static parts of the scene, leading to artifacts such as black spots on roads (e.g., Brandenburg Gate scene) or incorrect rendering of fountain water (e.g., Trevi Fountain scene). Transient Detection: In static scenes, a small percentage of Gaussians (<4%) may be incorrectly detected as transient. Removing them does not significantly affect quality, but care should be taken not to remove valid static geometry. Affine Transformation Limitation: Using affine color transformations instead of the MLP for appearance modeling fails to capture all appearance changes in in-the-wild scenarios. Addresses the limitation of global feature embeddings by extracting dynamic appearance features from a reference image and allowing each Gaussian to sample from multiple feature maps, capturing local details like highlights and shadows. Choose this when local appearance variations are more critical than global scene embeddings. Time Complexity: Training is one order of magnitude faster than previous implicit methods (NeRF-W, Ha-NeRF, CR-NeRF, RefinedFields). Rendering speed matches real-time 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Uses more Gaussians than standard 3DGS due to less frequent densification steps but injection of image-dependent information. The number of transient Gaussians can be significant (e.g., 573,644 in Trevi Fountain vs 109,672 for 3DGS). Performance: Improves 3DGS PSNR by an average margin of 5.01 dB on Phototourism scenes and 5 dB on NeRF-OSR benchmark. Outperforms baselines in SSIM and LPIPS. Strengths: Handles unconstrained photo collections, transient objects, and varying illumination. Enables controllable appearance via latent space interpolation. Limitations: Failure cases include artifacts in specific areas (black spots on roads, fountain water). WildGaussians (SWAG) was introduced to address the limitations of 3DGS in "in-the-wild" settings, which often suffer from artifacts due to transient objects and photometric variations. It builds on the 3DGS framework [8] and incorporates ideas from previous works like Urban Radiance Fields [17] and NeRF-W [14]. The method was evaluated on the Phototourism dataset (Brandenburg Gate, Sacre Coeur, Trevi Fountain) and the NeRF-OSR benchmark. name: Dynamic Appearance Features Modeling
head: Adaptive Sampling with K Feature Maps
body: Dynamic Appearance Features Modeling addresses the limitation of global feature embeddings in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which assume uniform environmental information (lighting, weather) across a scene. By extracting dynamic appearance features from a reference image and allowing each Gaussian point to sample from multiple feature maps, the method captures local details such as highlights and shadows that global embeddings miss. It sets itself apart from methods like NeRF-W and Ha-NeRF, which use global scene embeddings, and CR-NeRF, which integrates features at the 2D level without dynamic 3D environmental information. Inputs: Reference image I{gt} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Known camera pose for the reference image, defining the projection matrix P. Set of N 3D Gaussian points, where each point i has a position coordinate Xi. Outputs: Dynamic appearance feature vector dfi \in \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1)} for each Gaussian point i. Data Structures: Feature Map F: A 2D tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1) \times H \times W}. Projection Feature Map F^P: The first 16 channels of F, shape \mathbb{R}^{16 \times H \times W}. K Feature Maps (F^1, \dots, F^K): The remaining 16K channels of F, evenly divided into K maps, each of shape \mathbb{R}^{16 \times H \times W}. Sampling Coordinates sci: For each Gaussian point i, a set of K learnable 2D coordinates (sci^1, \dots, sci^K), where each sci^k \in [-1, 1]^2. Parameters: K: The number of additional feature maps for adaptive sampling. Typical value: 3. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the reference image I{gt} through a U-Net model with a ResNet backbone to generate the combined feature map F \in \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1) \times H \times W}. 2. Map Division: Split F along the channel dimension into K+1 feature maps: the projection feature map F^P (first 16 channels) and K additional feature maps F^1, \dots, F^K (remaining 16K channels). 3. Projection Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point i: Project its 3D position Xi onto the 2D image plane using the projection matrix P derived from the camera pose, resulting in coordinates \PiP(Xi). Sample the projection feature fi^P \in \mathbb{R}^{16} from F^P at \PiP(Xi) using bilinear interpolation. fi^P = BL(\PiP(Xi), F^P) \quad (6) where BL denotes bilinear interpolation sampling. 4. Adaptive Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point i: Use the learnable sampling coordinates (sci^1, \dots, sci^K) to sample features from the K additional feature maps. Sample features (fi^1, \dots, fi^K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 16} from (F^1, \dots, F^K) using bilinear interpolation at the respective coordinates. (fi^1, fi^2, \dots, fi^K) = BL((sci^1, sci^2, \dots, sci^K), (F^1, F^2, \dots, F^K)) \quad (7) 5. Concatenation: Concatenate the projection feature and the K sampled features to form the dynamic appearance feature dfi. dfi = fi^P \oplus fi^1 \oplus fi^2 \oplus \dots \oplus fi^K \quad (8) where \oplus denotes concatenation. 6. Regularization: Apply a regularization loss L{sc} to prevent sampling coordinates from deviating beyond the effective sampling range [-1, 1]. L{sc} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \max\{0, |sci| - 1\} \quad (9) where N is the total number of Gaussian points and | \cdot | denotes the absolute value applied to each coordinate component. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def extractfeatures(referenceimage: torch.Tensor, unetmodel: torch.nn.Module) -> torch.Tensor: """Extracts the combined feature map F from the reference image using a U-Net with ResNet backbone.""" return unetmodel(referenceimage) def splitfeaturemaps(Fmap: torch.Tensor, K: int): """Splits the combined feature map F into projection feature map F^P and K additional feature maps.""" FP = Fmap[:16,:,:] FK = [Fmap[16 + k 16: 16 + (k + 1) 16,:,:] for k in range(K)] return FP, FK def sampleprojectionfeature(Xi: torch.Tensor, P: torch.Tensor, FP: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Samples the projection feature for a single Gaussian point.""" Xihom = torch.cat([Xi, torch.ones(1, device=Xi.device)]) projected = P @ Xihom u, v = projected[0], projected[1] grid = torch.tensor([[[[u, v]]]], device=Xi.device) FPbatch = FP.unsqueeze(0) return F.gridsample(FPbatch, grid, aligncorners=False).squeeze() def sampleadaptivefeatures(sci: list, FK: list) -> torch.Tensor: """Samples features from K feature maps using learnable sampling coordinates.""" features = [] for k in range(len(FK)): u, v = sci[k][0], sci[k][1] grid = torch.tensor([[[[u, v]]]], device=sci[k][0].device) Fkbatch = FK[k].unsqueeze(0) features.append(F.gridsample(Fkbatch, grid, aligncorners=False).squeeze()) return torch.stack(features, dim=0) def computedynamicappearancefeature(Xi: torch.Tensor, P: torch.Tensor, FP: torch.Tensor, sci: list, FK: list) -> torch.Tensor: """Computes the dynamic appearance feature dfi for a single Gaussian point.""" fiP = sampleprojectionfeature(Xi, P, FP) fiK = sampleadaptivefeatures(sci, FK) return torch.cat([fiP, fiK.flatten()]) def computeregularizationloss(scilist: list, N: int) -> torch.Tensor: """Computes the regularization loss Lsc for all Gaussian points.""" totalloss = torch.tensor(0.0, device=scilist[0][0].device) for sci in scilist: for sc in sci: totalloss += torch.sum(torch.clamp(torch.abs(sc) - 1, min=0)) return totalloss / N Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The projection matrix P must map 3D points to 2D coordinates compatible with the bilinear interpolation function's valid range. Boundaries: The regularization loss L{sc} is designed to keep sampling coordinates within [-1, 1]. If coordinates exceed this range, the loss penalizes them, but sampling outside this range may result in undefined behavior or zero-padding depending on the interpolation implementation. Degenerate Input: If the reference image I{gt} is not available or the camera pose is unknown, the projection feature map F^P cannot be computed, and the method fails. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method was trained on a single Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU for 70k steps, taking approximately 2 hours, with images downsampled twice during training and evaluation. Scaling: Increasing K beyond 3 yields no performance improvement while adding meaningless computational cost, establishing K=3 as optimal. Strengths: Captures local details such as highlights and shadows that global embeddings miss, aligning better with real-world varying environmental influences. Limitations: Limited by the single-view reference image I{gt}, where features sampled from the projection feature map are identical along the same ray, which is unreasonable under uneven lighting. Origin: Introduced in "Gaussian in the Wild: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unconstrained Image Collections". History and Development: Previous methods like NeRF-W and Ha-NeRF used global feature embeddings assuming uniform environmental information, while CR-NeRF integrated features at the 2D level without dynamic 3D environmental information. This method addresses these limitations by allowing each Gaussian point to independently learn its sampling positions. Usage: Used in the WildGaussians framework for 'in-the-wild' settings, integrating robust DINO features and a lightweight appearance modeling module within the 3DGS framework [Parent]. name: Non-Pinhole Camera Training
head: Non-Pinhole Camera Adaptation
body: Non-Pinhole Camera Training extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle camera models that deviate from the standard pinhole assumption, such as fisheye lenses or uncentered projections. It solves the problem of geometric distortion and coordinate misalignment in non-standard imaging systems by integrating differentiable image-space warping and masking into the training loop. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by explicitly supporting uncentered-distorted and uncentered-undistorted camera models, whereas standard 3DGS assumes a centered pinhole model. The method adapts the differentiable rasterizer to accommodate various non-pinhole camera geometries by modifying the projection pipeline. The core requirement is that all coordinate transformations and pixel masking operations must remain differentiable to enable end-to-end gradient backpropagation. Inputs: Training images from non-pinhole cameras (e.g., fisheye, wide-angle), corresponding camera parameters (intrinsics, distortion coefficients, center offsets), and initial 3D Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics). Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian representation and camera parameters that reconstruct the scene under the specific non-pinhole projection. The Gaussian attributes remain standard (position \mathbf{p}, rotation \mathbf{q}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha, SH coefficients). The camera model structure is extended to include: Center Offset: (cx, cy) for uncentered models. Distortion Coefficients: k1, k2, \dots for radial/tangential distortion. Warping Function: A differentiable mapping W: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2 that maps ideal perspective coordinates to distorted image coordinates. 1. Camera Model Selection: Choose the appropriate camera model based on the dataset: Centered-Undistorted: Standard pinhole model (used for Neural 3D Video Dataset). Uncentered-Undistorted: Pinhole model with principal point offset (used for Technicolor Dataset). Uncentered-Distorted: Fisheye or wide-angle model with distortion and offset (used for Google Immersive Dataset). 2. Differentiable Warping: For distorted models, apply a differentiable image-space warping function W to map perspective view coordinates to the distorted image plane. This function must support gradient computation. 3. Masking: Generate a binary mask M to exclude invalid pixels (e.g., black borders resulting from undistortion or out-of-bounds warping). The mask must be differentiable or applied in a way that allows gradients to flow through valid pixels. 4. Rasterization: Render the Gaussians using the adapted projection. The rasterizer computes the contribution of each Gaussian to the image plane, accounting for the warped coordinates and masked regions. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the rendering loss (e.g., L1, SSIM) only over valid pixels where M=1. 6. Optimization: Update Gaussian attributes and camera parameters using gradient descent. The differentiability of W and M ensures gradients propagate correctly from the loss to the Gaussians. Warping: \mathbf{u}{distorted} = W(\mathbf{u}{perspective}), where \mathbf{u} are 2D image coordinates. Masking: \mathbf{I}{rendered} = \mathbf{I}{rendered} \odot M, where \odot is element-wise multiplication. Loss: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i,j} M{i,j} \cdot \|\mathbf{I}{rendered}(i,j) - \mathbf{I}{target}(i,j)\|. Distortion Coefficients: Typically k1, k2 for radial distortion. Values depend on the lens. Center Offset: (cx, cy) determined by camera calibration. Mask Threshold: Pixels with intensity below a threshold (e.g., 0) are masked out. Non-Differentiable Masking: If the mask is not differentiable, gradients may be blocked. Use soft masks or ensure the warping function handles boundaries smoothly. Black Pixels: Undistorted images often have black borders. These must be masked out to prevent loss computation on invalid data. Coordinate System Mismatch: Ensure the warping function aligns with the rasterizer's coordinate system (e.g., origin at center vs. corner). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernonpinhole(gaussians, camera, imagesize): # 1. Project Gaussians to perspective plane perspectivecoords = projecttoperspective(gaussians, camera) # 2. Apply differentiable warping for distorted models if camera.isdistorted: distortedcoords = differentiablewarp(perspectivecoords, camera.distortioncoeffs) else: distortedcoords = perspectivecoords # 3. Rasterize using distorted coordinates renderedimage = rasterize(gaussians, distortedcoords, imagesize) # 4. Apply differentiable mask for invalid pixels mask = generatedifferentiablemask(distortedcoords, imagesize) maskedimage = renderedimage mask # 5. Compute loss against target loss = computeloss(maskedimage, targetimage, mask) return loss A training technique introduced to disentangle defocus-aware and defocus-independent representations in an unsupervised manner by learning to generate images while randomizing the aperture size and latent codes independently. During training, the aperture size is changed randomly, and the latent codes are changed randomly. This technique is similar to techniques commonly used in viewpoint-aware representation learning, which are useful for disentangling the effect of the corresponding factor from latent codes. Adaptation of the 3DGS pipeline to specific non-pinhole datasets. For the Neural 3D Video Dataset, use the original centered-undistorted camera model. For the Technicolor Dataset, implement and use an uncentered-undistorted camera model. For the Google Immersive Dataset, adapt the method to fit an uncentered-distorted camera model using a differentiable image space warping function that maps perspective views to fish-eye distorted views. For real-time demos, retrain models on undistorted videos and apply a differentiable mask to exclude black pixels resulting from undistortion. Image warping and masking must remain differentiable to allow end-to-end training despite the coordinate transformations and pixel masking. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS, but with additional overhead for warping and masking operations. The differentiable warping adds computational cost per pixel. Memory Complexity: No significant increase in memory usage compared to standard 3DGS, as the Gaussian attributes remain the same. Performance: Successfully reconstructs scenes on non-pinhole datasets where standard 3DGS fails entirely, such as the Matterport dataset. Strengths: Handles a wide variety of camera models, including fisheye and uncentered projections. Enables training on real-world data with non-standard lenses. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of differentiable warping and masking. Performance may degrade if the warping function is not smooth or if the mask is not properly handled. When to Use: When training on datasets with non-pinhole cameras (e.g., fisheye, wide-angle, uncentered). When Not to Use: For standard pinhole camera datasets, where standard 3DGS is sufficient and simpler. Non-Pinhole Camera Training was developed to address the limitations of standard 3DGS in handling non-standard camera models. It builds on the differentiable rasterizer of 3DGS, extending it to support various camera geometries. The method has been applied to datasets such as the Neural 3D Video Dataset, Technicolor Dataset, and Google Immersive Dataset. It has also been shown to succeed on the Matterport dataset, where standard 3DGS fails. The technique of Aperture Randomized Training, while related to defocus disentanglement, shares the principle of randomizing camera parameters during training to improve representation learning. name: ToF Scene Rendering Setup
head: ToF Gaussian Splatting Setup, ToF render
body: This method configures the rendering pipeline for Time-of-Flight (ToF) cameras within a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework, enabling the simultaneous optimization of color and ToF data (phasors, depth, amplitude). It differs from standard RGB-only splatting by maintaining separate rasterization settings for color and ToF views, handling multi-modal Gaussian attributes (such as phasor features), and supporting dynamic scene decomposition via motion masks. The setup initializes CUDA tensors for gradient tracking, computes camera projection parameters for both RGB and ToF sensors, and prepares Gaussian attributes for static and dynamic regions before invoking the respective rasterizers. Inputs: pc: GaussianModel instance containing attributes xyz, opacity, scaling, rotation, featurescolor, featuresphasor, and useviewdependentphase. viewpointcamera: Object containing FoVx, FoVy, FoVxtof, FoVytof, worldviewtransform, fullprojtransform, cameracenter, tofimageheight, tofimagewidth, and depthrange. opt: Optimization configuration containing optimizephaseoffset and optimizedcoffset. renderregions: List of strings indicating which parts of the scene to render (e.g., ['static', 'dynamic']). motionmask: Boolean tensor identifying dynamic Gaussians. Outputs: colorimage: Rendered RGB image. tofdata: Rendered ToF data including phasor, depth, pixel indices, and distribution. screenspacepoints: Tensor storing gradients of 2D means. 1. RasterizationSettings: Fields: imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg, scalemodifier, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree, campos, prefiltered, debug, nearn, farn. ToF-specific fields: depthrange, useviewdependentphase, optimizephaseoffset, optimizedcoffset. 2. Gaussian Attributes Tensors (CUDA, requiresgrad=True): means3D: Shape (N, 3). means2D: Shape (N, 2). opacity: Shape (N, 1). scales: Shape (N, 3). rotations: Shape (N, 4) (quaternions). shs: Shape (N, K, 3) (Spherical Harmonics coefficients for color). shsp: Shape (N, K, P) (Spherical Harmonics coefficients for phasor/ToF). screenspacepoints: Shape (N, 2), initialized to zero, with retaingrad() called. 1. Initialize Gradient Tensors: Create screenspacepoints on CUDA with requiresgrad=True and call retaingrad() to preserve gradients for 2D mean updates. 2. Compute Field of View Tangents: Calculate \tan(\text{FoV}x) and \tan(\text{FoV}y) for the RGB camera: \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx}) \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy}) 3. Configure RGB Rasterization Settings: Create RasterizationSettings for color using imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg, scalemodifier, viewmatrix (worldviewtransform), projmatrix (fullprojtransform), shdegree, campos (cameracenter), prefiltered=False, debug=False, nearn (znear), and farn (zfar). 4. Configure ToF Rasterization Settings (if viewpointcamera.FoVxtof is not None): Create RasterizationSettings for ToF using imageheight (tofimageheight), imagewidth (tofimagewidth), tanfovx (\tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx\tof})), tanfovy (\tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy\tof})), bg, scalemodifier, viewmatrix (worldviewtransformtof), projmatrix (fullprojtransformtof), campos (cameracentertof), prefiltered=False, debug=False, nearn (znear), farn (zfar), depthrange (viewpointcamera.depthrange.item()), useviewdependentphase (pc.useviewdependentphase), optimizephaseoffset (opt.optimizephaseoffset), and optimizedcoffset (opt.optimizedcoffset). 5. Initialize Gaussian Attribute Tensors: Create zero tensors on CUDA for means3D, means2D, opacity, scales, rotations, shs, and shsp matching the shapes of the corresponding pc attributes. 6. Populate Static Attributes: If 'static' is in renderregions, copy pc.xyz, pc.opacity, pc.scaling, pc.rotation, pc.featurescolor, and pc.featuresphasor to the zero tensors, excluding Gaussians marked by motionmask. 7. Populate Dynamic Attributes: If 'dynamic' is in renderregions, copy base attributes from pc and apply differentials: means3D adds dxyz, rotations apply rotationactivation to (rotation + drot), shs adds dsh, and shsp adds dshp. 8. Render Color Image: Call the color rasterizer with means3D, means2D, shs, shsp, opacity, scales, rotations, and cov3Dprecomp=None. 9. Render ToF Data: Call the ToF rasterizer with the same Gaussian attributes to produce phasor, depth, pixel, and distribution outputs. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math import dataclasses @dataclasses.dataclass class RasterizationSettings: imageheight: int imagewidth: int tanfovx: float tanfovy: float bg: torch.Tensor scalemodifier: float viewmatrix: torch.Tensor projmatrix: torch.Tensor shdegree: int campos: torch.Tensor prefiltered: bool debug: bool nearn: float farn: float depthrange: float = None useviewdependentphase: bool = False optimizephaseoffset: bool = False optimizedcoffset: bool = False def rotationactivation(q: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Normalize quaternions to unit length.""" return q / torch.norm(q, dim=-1, keepdim=True) def rasterizecolor(settings: RasterizationSettings, means3D, means2D, shs, shsp, opacity, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp): """Performs standard color rasterization using the provided settings and attributes.""" # Standard rasterization step return torch.zeros(settings.imageheight, settings.imagewidth, 3, device='cuda') def rasterizetof(settings: RasterizationSettings, means3D, means2D, shs, shsp, opacity, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp): """Performs standard ToF rasterization using the provided settings and attributes.""" # Standard rasterization step return torch.zeros(settings.imageheight, settings.imagewidth, 4, device='cuda') def setuptofrendering(pc, viewpointcamera, opt, renderregions, motionmask): # Step 1: Initialize gradient tensors screenspacepoints = torch.zeros(pc.xyz.shape[0], 2, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) screenspacepoints.retaingrad() # Step 2: Compute FoV tangents for RGB tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy) # Step 3: Configure RGB Rasterization Settings rgbsettings = RasterizationSettings( imageheight=viewpointcamera.imageheight, imagewidth=viewpointcamera.imagewidth, tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bg=viewpointcamera.bg, scalemodifier=viewpointcamera.scalemodifier, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, campos=viewpointcamera.cameracenter, prefiltered=False, debug=False, nearn=viewpointcamera.znear, farn=viewpointcamera.zfar) # Step 4: Configure ToF Rasterization Settings tofsettings = None if viewpointcamera.FoVxtof is not None: tofsettings = RasterizationSettings( imageheight=viewpointcamera.tofimageheight, imagewidth=viewpointcamera.tofimagewidth, tanfovx=math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVxtof), tanfovy=math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVytof), bg=viewpointcamera.bg, scalemodifier=viewpointcamera.scalemodifier, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.worldviewtransformtof, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.fullprojtransformtof, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, campos=viewpointcamera.cameracentertof, prefiltered=False, debug=False, nearn=viewpointcamera.znear, farn=viewpointcamera.zfar, depthrange=viewpointcamera.depthrange.item(), useviewdependentphase=pc.useviewdependentphase, optimizephaseoffset=opt.optimizephaseoffset, optimizedcoffset=opt.optimizedcoffset) # Step 5: Initialize Gaussian Attribute Tensors N = pc.xyz.shape[0] means3D = torch.zeros(N, 3, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) means2D = torch.zeros(N, 2, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) opacity = torch.zeros(N, 1, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) scales = torch.zeros(N, 3, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) rotations = torch.zeros(N, 4, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) shs = torch.zeros(N, pc.activeshdegree + 1, 3, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) shsp = torch.zeros(N, pc.activeshdegree + 1, pc.phasordim, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) # Step 6: Populate Static Attributes if 'static' in renderregions: staticmask = ~motionmask means3D[staticmask] = pc.xyz[staticmask] opacity[staticmask] = pc.opacity[staticmask] scales[staticmask] = pc.scaling[staticmask] rotations[staticmask] = pc.rotation[staticmask] shs[staticmask] = pc.featurescolor[staticmask] shsp[staticmask] = pc.featuresphasor[staticmask] # Step 7: Populate Dynamic Attributes if 'dynamic' in renderregions: dynamicmask = motionmask # Base copy means3D[dynamicmask] = pc.xyz[dynamicmask] opacity[dynamicmask] = pc.opacity[dynamicmask] scales[dynamicmask] = pc.scaling[dynamicmask] rotations[dynamicmask] = pc.rotation[dynamicmask] shs[dynamicmask] = pc.featurescolor[dynamicmask] shsp[dynamicmask] = pc.featuresphasor[dynamicmask] # Apply differentials means3D[dynamicmask] += pc.dxyz[dynamicmask] rotations[dynamicmask] = rotationactivation(pc.rotation[dynamicmask] + pc.drot[dynamicmask]) shs[dynamicmask] += pc.dsh[dynamicmask] shsp[dynamicmask] += pc.dshp[dynamicmask] # Step 8: Render Color Image colorimage = rasterizecolor( settings=rgbsettings, means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, shsp=shsp, opacity=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=None) # Step 9: Render ToF Data tofdata = rasterizetof( settings=tofsettings, means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, shsp=shsp, opacity=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=None) return colorimage, tofdata, screenspacepoints Parameters: renderregions controls which Gaussians are active, motionmask distinguishes static from dynamic Gaussians, and depthrange limits ToF raycasting. Edge Cases: If viewpointcamera.FoVxtof is None, ToF settings are skipped. If renderregions is empty, no attributes are copied, resulting in empty renders. Precision issues may arise in rotationactivation if quaternions are not normalized after adding differentials. Not given in the sources. This method is part of the Gaussian Splatting framework extended for Time-of-Flight cameras, as implemented in the gftorf project. It builds on Non-Pinhole Camera Training by adding specific support for ToF sensor characteristics. brownvc/gftorf, https://github.com/brownvc/gftorf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: AbsGS
head: Absolute Positional Gradients, Absgrad
body: AbsGS (Absolute Positional Gradients) is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that recovers fine details and thin structures smoothed out during standard optimization. It replaces signed gradient averaging with absolute sums across multiple views to identify "fence-sitting" Gaussians and sharpen edges. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current 3D Gaussian parameters, camera poses for M training views, and ground truth images. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters after densification decisions based on absolute gradient magnitudes. Data Structures: View-space Positional Gradient Accumulator: A per-Gaussian vector storing the accumulated absolute gradient magnitude in the view space. Unlike standard accumulators that sum signed gradients, this stores absolute values to prevent cancellation. Steps: 1. High-Pass Filtering: Compare the rendered image against the ground truth using a high-pass filter to isolate high-frequency residuals. 2. Back-propagation: Back-propagate only the high-frequency residuals to sharpen edges and thin structures. 3. Gradient Accumulation: For each Gaussian n, accumulate the view-space positional gradients across M camera views using absolute sums. 4. Densification Decision: Compare the accumulated absolute gradient magnitude against a threshold to determine if a Gaussian should be split or duplicated. Formula: The accumulated view-space positional gradient for a Gaussian \tilde{\mu}n is computed as: \nabla{\tilde{\mu}n} L = \sum{k=1}^{M} \left( \left| \frac{\delta Lx}{\delta \tilde{\mu}x} \right|, \left| \frac{\delta Ly}{\delta \tilde{\mu}y} \right| \right) Where: M is the number of camera views. \frac{\delta Lx}{\delta \tilde{\mu}x} is the gradient of the loss with respect to the x-component of the Gaussian's position in view space. \frac{\delta Ly}{\delta \tilde{\mu}y} is the gradient of the loss with respect to the y-component of the Gaussian's position in view space. The absolute value operator |\cdot| prevents cancellation between positive and negative view-space gradients from different views. Parameters: absgrad: A boolean API flag to enable absolute gradient accumulation in the rasterization call. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainabsgs(gaussians, cameras, groundtruthimages, numsteps, threshold): for step in range(numsteps): # Render scene and compute high-frequency residuals rgbimage = render(gaussians, cameras[step]) residuals = highpassfilter(rgbimage - groundtruthimages[step]) # Back-propagate residuals loss = computeloss(residuals) loss.backward() # Accumulate absolute view-space positional gradients for g in gaussians: g.gradaccumx += sum(abs(g.dLdxk) for k in range(len(cameras))) g.gradaccumy += sum(abs(g.dLdyk) for k in range(len(cameras))) # Densify based on threshold for g in gaussians: if g.gradaccumx > threshold or g.gradaccumy > threshold: splitorduplicate(g) # Update parameters gaussians.update() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Collisions: Standard signed accumulation causes positive and negative view-space gradients to cancel, producing poor densification heuristics. Fine Detail Smoothing: Without high-frequency emphasis, optimization smooths out thin structures and fine textures. The foundational training loop managing camera sampling and metric evaluation. It differs from AbsGS by using standard signed gradient accumulation for densification. Choose it for baseline training without fine-detail emphasis. The broader category of methods for adding Gaussians during training. It encompasses various heuristics like area-based scaling or normal propagation. Choose it when configuring the overall densification pipeline. The composite loss function combining photometric and perceptual terms. It differs from AbsGS by defining the optimization objective rather than the gradient accumulation method. Choose it to define the training target. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead per rasterization step due to absolute value computation. Reduces total training time by stabilizing convergence. Memory Complexity: No significant overhead beyond storing accumulated gradient vectors per Gaussian. Strengths: Prevents gradient cancellation, improves fine detail recovery, and stabilizes optimization. Limitations: Requires rasterizer modification to support absolute gradient accumulation. When to use: Scenes with fine textures or thin structures where standard densification fails. AbsGS was introduced to address fine detail recovery being smoothed out during 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. It was identified as a solution for "fence-sitting" Gaussians where standard gradient averaging fails. The method is implemented in the gsplat library, providing the absgrad API flag to enable it. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Densification Strategy
head: Adaptive Density Control, Primitive Management, Densification and Splitting
body: Densification strategies dynamically adjust the number and spatial distribution of 3D Gaussian primitives during training to balance reconstruction fidelity against computational cost. They solve the problem of under-representation (blurry or missing details) and over-representation (redundant primitives causing slow rendering) by periodically spawning, splitting, or removing Gaussians based on optimization metrics. This family is distinguished from static initialization methods by its continuous, iterative nature, and from sibling methods like 3DGS-MCMC or Adaptive Gaussian Refinement by its reliance on heuristic thresholds, gradient magnitudes, or multi-view consistency scores rather than complex probabilistic sampling or neural residual prediction. All methods in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by a mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k [Parent]. The core mechanism involves periodic evaluation of a metric per Gaussian to determine if the current representation is insufficient or redundant in a specific region. Common metrics include: 1. Gradient Magnitude: The accumulated 2D positional gradient \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v} \| \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muv^k} \|2. High gradients indicate that the Gaussian's position is not adequately minimizing the loss, suggesting a need for refinement or replacement [13466-densification-and-splitting.md]. 2. Opacity: Low opacity \alphak < \alpha{\min} indicates a primitive contributes negligibly to the rendered image and is a candidate for pruning. 3. Scale: Excessively large scales max(sk) relative to the scene extent e{scene} indicate coarse approximations that may blur details or occlude nearby geometry [13466-densification-and-splitting.md]. Densification operations are typically triggered every N iterations (e.g., refineEvery = 100) to allow the optimizer to stabilize [Parent]. The primary operations are: Splitting: Replacing a parent Gaussian gk with N{children} children. The children's means \mu{child} are sampled from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak) [Parent]. The scale is typically reduced, e.g., s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}}, to increase local density [Parent]. Cloning: Creating an exact copy of gk (same \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) to increase sampling frequency in high-error regions without changing the spatial footprint [Parent]. Pruning: Removing Gaussians that fail to meet opacity or significance thresholds. Buffer management is critical: pruned or split Gaussians require buffer compaction or flag-based marking to maintain contiguous memory access for rasterization [Parent]. GroupFlow is a motion representation technique for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces per-Gaussian neural deformation fields with shared SE(3) transformations for groups of Gaussians. It solves the computational bottleneck of evaluating individual deformation networks for every primitive at every timestep, accelerating rendering and training while maintaining temporal coherence. Unlike methods that retain dense neural fields or use global rigid transforms, GroupFlow captures locally coherent motion by clustering Gaussians based on trajectory similarity and fitting a separate SE(3) trajectory to each cluster. 3DGS-MCMC replaces the standard heuristic-based densification (gradient magnitude thresholds) of 3D Gaussian Splatting with a probabilistic framework based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. It treats the set of 3D Gaussians as samples from an underlying probability distribution, using Metropolis–Hastings steps to guide the spawning and pruning of primitives. This approach allows for precise control over the total number of Gaussians, reduces reliance on high-quality initialization, and yields sharper details and fewer artifacts compared to the original cloning/splitting heuristics. VS-Splat Voxel Selection is a learnable, differentiable mechanism for selecting relevant 3D voxels in feed-forward Gaussian Splatting, replacing static opacity thresholding with a confidence-based selection process. It sets itself apart from siblings like Opacity-Based Thresholding by using a Gumbel-Sigmoid distribution to predict confidence scores, allowing the network to learn which voxels contain object-centric geometry rather than relying on manual hyperparameter tuning. Locality-preserving densification addresses the memory access throttling caused by standard Gaussian densification, where new primitives are appended to the end of parameter buffers, causing spatially close Gaussians to be stored far apart in memory. By reordering the Gaussian parameter buffers based on 3D spatial proximity using Z-ordering (Morton order), this method ensures that neighboring Gaussians in space are also adjacent in memory, thereby improving memory access coalescing. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GroupFlow or 3DGS-MCMC by focusing specifically on the data layout and memory hierarchy optimization rather than changing the geometric splitting logic or sampling distribution. Progressive and Multi-stage Training refers to optimization strategies that decompose the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into sequential phases or stages, rather than optimizing all parameters simultaneously from a static initialization. It solves the problem of optimization instability, error propagation, and insufficient geometric detail that arises when initializing Gaussians randomly or using coarse priors. It sets itself apart from single-stage baselines by decoupling distinct learning objectives (e.g., geometry vs. pose, or coarse vs. fine detail) to stabilize convergence and improve final rendering fidelity. Hyperparameter Settings define the numerical configuration for the optimizer, learning rates, and regularization terms used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. This method solves the problem of stable convergence and high-fidelity reconstruction by tuning the trade-off between fitting training data and maintaining geometric/photometric consistency. It differs from sibling methods like Densification Strategy (which manages primitive count) and Pruning and Sparsification (which removes primitives) by focusing on the gradient descent dynamics and loss weighting rather than structural topology changes. Adaptive Gaussian Refinement is a technique that dynamically adjusts Gaussian parameters using neural network-predicted residuals to improve the modeling of complex non-rigid deformations and time-varying appearance. It addresses the limitation of static covariance matrices in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which cannot adequately represent dynamic behaviors such as motion-induced shape changes. Unlike sibling methods that rely on gradient-based densification metrics (e.g., Adaptive Density Control) or MCMC sampling (e.g., 3DGS-MCMC), this method uses a lightweight neural network to predict continuous corrections to the Gaussian's spatial, temporal, directional, and covariance parameters. This family addresses the generation and initialization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from implicit or single-view inputs, solving the problem of constructing high-fidelity, consistent 3D scenes without iterative per-scene optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Adaptive Density Control by replacing iterative densification heuristics with learned generative priors (diffusion or feed-forward networks) that directly output primitive attributes. The termination entropy criterion is a metric used to calculate information gain in active 3D reconstruction, specifically within the context of Gaussian Splatting training optimization. It serves as a stopping condition or selection heuristic to determine when a region of the scene has been sufficiently modeled or when the agent should move to a new viewpoint. It sets itself apart from gradient-based or opacity-based densification strategies by measuring the uncertainty or disorder in the predicted radiance field distribution rather than the error magnitude or primitive density. Pruning and Sparsification refers to the family of strategies that reduce the cardinality of the 3D Gaussian primitive set \mathcal{G} by removing redundant, insignificant, or high-uncertainty primitives, thereby improving rendering efficiency and reducing memory footprint without degrading visual fidelity. It sets itself apart from densification methods (e.g., Adaptive Density Control) by focusing on removal rather than addition, and from static compression techniques (e.g., LightGaussian) by often employing dynamic, training-aware, or uncertainty-based criteria to preserve structural integrity. Texel Size Adaptation and Primitive Management is a training-time optimization routine that dynamically adjusts the resolution of per-primitive texture maps and the number of 3D Gaussian primitives to balance model capacity and appearance quality. It differs from sibling methods like Adaptive Density Control or GroupFlow by explicitly coupling the geometric density of primitives with the textural detail allocated to them, using quantile-based error thresholds to trigger splitting, upscaling, or downscaling. Densification and Splitting is the core training optimization mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that dynamically adjusts the number and distribution of Gaussian primitives to balance reconstruction fidelity against computational cost. It solves the problem of under-representation (blurry or missing details) and over-representation (redundant primitives causing slow rendering) by periodically spawning, splitting, or removing Gaussians based on optimization metrics. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by being a continuous, iterative process driven by gradient magnitude, opacity, and scale heuristics, distinguishing it from sibling methods that may use score-based budgets [4705-score-based-densification.md], visibility consistency [10074-gaussian-insertion-and-pruning.md], or error-guided sampling [15896-error-guided-guided-sampling.md]. Momentum Consistency-Guided Densification is a strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses kinematic phase-space trajectories (momentum) to guide primitive growth, aiming to overcome floating artifacts in non-manifold regions caused by single-step gradient snapshots. It sets itself apart from standard gradient-based strategies by evaluating the consistency between current gradients and accumulated historical trends, rather than relying solely on instantaneous gradient magnitude. GSGEN Appearance Refinement is an iterative optimization stage in the GSGEN framework designed to improve fine-grained visual details in text-to-3D generation while preserving the fundamental geometry established during the preceding geometry optimization phase. It addresses the limitations of standard gradient-based densification by introducing a compactness-based strategy to "fill holes" in the Gaussian representation and employs specific regularization losses to prevent overfitting and maintain geometric consistency. Unlike sibling methods that rely primarily on positional gradients or opacity thresholds for densification, GSGEN explicitly incorporates a 3D Stable Diffusion Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss and a mean position penalty to ensure 3D consistency and structural integrity. Multi-view Consistency and Scoring is a family of densification strategies for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces or augments single-view gradient-based criteria with multi-view evaluation to constrain Gaussian count and ensure structural consistency. It addresses the overfitting and excessive primitive production inherent in standard single-view densification by leveraging alpha-weighted error accumulation or photometric consistency across multiple viewpoints. Unlike its siblings, this family explicitly integrates importance and pruning scores derived from multi-view photometric loss and alpha contributions into the standard gradient masks, ensuring that densification occurs only where geometry is consistently unresolved across views. This method defines the heuristic-driven densification and pruning strategies used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to dynamically adjust the number and distribution of Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of static representation capacity by allowing the model to increase density in under-reconstructed regions (via cloning/splitting) and remove redundant primitives (via pruning) based on gradient magnitude, opacity, and scale. It is distinguished from sibling methods like 3DGS-MCMC or Adaptive Gaussian Refinement by its reliance on simple, periodic heuristic thresholds rather than complex probabilistic sampling or continuous adaptive learning rates. Multi-view Consistent Densification (VCD) is a strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that identifies primitives for densification based on their contribution to reconstruction errors across multiple camera views, rather than relying solely on image-space gradient magnitude. It reduces Gaussian redundancy by evaluating multi-view consistency, ensuring that new primitives are spawned only in regions where the current representation fails to reconstruct the scene accurately across different viewpoints. A Gaussian Splatting method that combines progressive training with resolution, noise and Gaussian scales, learning to prune and mask primitives and SH bands by their significance, and an accelerated GS training framework to achieve faster run-time, smaller disk size, and faster convergence compared to vanilla GS. 3DGS reconstructs a scene using 3D Gaussian primitives rendered via differentiable volume splatting rasterizer extending EWA volume splatting. Each primitive has 59 parameters: position, covariance (parameterized by scaling matrix S and quaternion rotation q), opacity, diffused color, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients (typically 3 bands). On three datasets, Trick-GS achieves up to 2× faster training, 40× smaller disk size and 2× faster rendering speed compared to vanilla GS, while having comparable accuracy. A process to address noise and missing surface parts in the density space by using perceptual loss to identify problematic geometric aspects and removing outliers. Compute perceptual loss VGG(Sp, Sg) to measure high-level visual similarity between rendered patch Sp and real image patch Sg. Select patches where VGG(Sp, Sg) is lower than half the average value across the training set to prioritize patches with improved visual similarity. Augment the density space by adding a group of points along the pixel ray for selected patches, considering the depth range of neighboring pixels. Remove outliers by examining the number of points within a specified radius around each neural density point; if the count falls below a predefined threshold, the point is removed. Joint optimization of newly added view-dependent Gaussians with pre-existing kernels, refining T, \beta, and opacity orientation using multi-view photometric constraints. During image-space optimization, original Gaussians' rendered outputs are treated as background. After projection, original kernels' opacity is made optimizable while freezing other attributes to mitigate over-occlusion. Apply full parameter optimization to newly added Gaussians. Set number of iterations proportional to training set size to ensure each additional kernel is sampled approximately the same number of times. Optimize parameters with specific learning rates: position (0.000016), diffuse color (0.001), higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients (0.001/20), opacity (0.02), scaling (0.002), rotation (0.0005), opacity lobe orientation d (0.001), opacity lobe width T (0.0002), and sharpness β (0.002). Employ SparseAdam to optimize the opacity of original Gaussian primitives visible in the current viewpoint. A regularizer that penalizes NeRF densities at 3D locations not visible from multiple training views to remove floaters outside the convex hull of training views. Approximate visibility v{ij} of the i-th 3D location in the j-th training view using a frustum check. Implement by defining a single tight sphere around training images. Render batches of rays shooting from a random location on the sphere surface, through the center of the scene, and far into the distance. Render rays using Nerfacto and apply the visibility loss to the sampled points. L{vis} = \sumi V(qi) f\sigma(qi) where f\sigma(qi) = \sigmai is the NeRF density at 3D location qi, and V(qi) = 1{\{\sum{j=1}^n v{ij} < 1\}} indicates if the location is not visible from any training views. Nerfacto uses a proposal sampler [2] to importance sample around surfaces, making the loss effective in quickly culling floating artifacts with high density outside visible regions. The frustum check approximation does not handle occlusions, instead overestimating the number of views a location is visible from. A method to predict the maximum primitive number Pfin for densification, preventing out-of-memory errors and bounding primitive growth. Predict the maximum primitive number Pfin using momentum-based budgeting. Cap primitive growth: if Pfin is extremely large, the primitive number stabilizes to a constant for the scene, preventing OOM. γ, η: hyper-parameters in the momentum-based primitive budgeting method that influence Pfin. Predicted vs actual primitive counts on MipNeRF-360: 3DGS (3.08M vs 2.69M), Mip-Splatting (3.25M vs 3.14M), Taming-3DGS (2.39M vs 2.04M). Uniformly sample depth values from s × d to 7.5 × d, adding small random noise to each sample. d: The maximum depth value present in a training view. s: A scaling factor for the lower bound of the sampling range, typically set to 0.7 for most scenes. Cannot fully eliminate blurring in areas insufficiently covered by the sparse point cloud (e.g., far content outside windows, flames). This occurs because accurate depth is unavailable, forcing Gaussians to spawn across a depth range; Gaussians near correct locations may be pruned later. Potential mitigation: leverage depth priors from learning-based depth estimation methods to constrain the spawning range. Use view-independent colors for Gaussians to avoid duplicate densification. Create a densification mask to determine whether a pixel in a new frame needs densification by considering current Gaussians and the captured depth of the new frame. Has a process to remove outliers in the point cloud. 3DGS optimization has two stages: coarse 3DGS training, and refinement. Has a geometry and texture refinement module to improve generation quality based on hypergraph learning. Each node in the hypergraph is a patch image of a coarse 3DGS. A rule to maintain consistent Gaussian densification behavior when changing the number of interpolated virtual cameras n, by scaling the gradient threshold proportionally. If the number of virtual cameras changes from n to n', the densification gradient threshold must be multiplied by \frac{n}{n'} to match the scaled gradients, because the gradient of every Gaussian during motion-blurred image synthesis is scaled by \frac{1}{n}. n: Number of interpolated virtual images/cameras used for motion blur synthesis. Default value: 10, chosen to balance rendering performance and training efficiency. The concept of adaptive densification originated with the foundational 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023), which introduced the heuristic of cloning and splitting Gaussians based on accumulated positional gradients and opacity thresholds. This approach was designed to automatically adjust the density of primitives to match the complexity of the scene geometry and appearance. Subsequent developments have expanded this core mechanism to address specific challenges such as dynamic scenes, memory efficiency, multi-view consistency [S1, 15793-multi-view-consistency-and-scoring.md], and probabilistic sampling. The method is widely used in novel view synthesis, SLAM, and 3D generation pipelines where high-fidelity reconstruction from sparse or dense image sets is required. name: GroupFlow
head: Groupwise SE(3) Motion Distillation, Temporal Motion Grouping
body: GroupFlow is a motion representation technique for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces per-Gaussian neural deformation fields with shared SE(3) transformations for groups of Gaussians. It solves the computational bottleneck of evaluating individual deformation networks for every primitive at every timestep, accelerating rendering and training while maintaining temporal coherence. Unlike methods that retain dense neural fields or use global rigid transforms, GroupFlow captures locally coherent motion by clustering Gaussians based on trajectory similarity and fitting a separate SE(3) trajectory to each cluster. GroupFlow operates on a dynamic scene represented by a set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each Gaussian gi has a time-varying mean position \mui^t, rotation ri^t, and scale si^t. The method distills the learned deformation field into grouped SE(3) transformations. Inputs: Set of N Gaussians. Number of timesteps F (indices t=0, \dots, F-1). Number of control trajectories (groups) J. Weighting factor \lambdar. Outputs: For each group j \in \{1, \dots, J\}: Initial control point position hj^0 \in \mathbb{R}^3. Time-varying rotation matrices Rj^t \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} for t=0, \dots, F-1. Time-varying translation vectors Tj^t \in \mathbb{R}^3 for t=0, \dots, F-1. Assignment of each Gaussian i to a group j. Data Structures: Gaussian Trajectories: Each Gaussian i is represented as a sequence of mean positions \mathcal{M}i = \{\mui^t\}{t=0}^{F-1}. Control Trajectories: A set of J control points \{hj^t\}{t=0}^{F-1} for j=1, \dots, J. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize J control trajectories \{hj^0\}{j=1}^J at t=0 using farthest point sampling on the initial mean positions \{\mui^0\}{i=1}^N. 2. Trajectory Similarity Calculation: For each Gaussian i and each control trajectory j, compute the similarity score S{i,j} using the temporal mean and standard deviation of the Euclidean distance between the Gaussian's trajectory and the control trajectory's trajectory: S{i,j} = \lambdar \, \mathrm{std}t(\| \mui^t - hj^t \|) + (1-\lambdar) \, \mathrm{mean}t(\| \mui^t - hj^t \|) where: \mui^t is the mean position of Gaussian i at time t. hj^t is the position of control trajectory j at time t. \| \cdot \| denotes the Euclidean norm. \mathrm{mean}t(\cdot) computes the average over t=0, \dots, F-1. \mathrm{std}t(\cdot) computes the standard deviation over t=0, \dots, F-1. \lambdar \in [0, 1] is a weighting factor balancing the importance of trajectory consistency (std) versus average proximity (mean). 3. Group Assignment: Assign each Gaussian i to the group j that minimizes the similarity score S{i,j} (or maximizes similarity, depending on convention; the source implies assignment based on this score). Let \mathcal{M}^j be the set of Gaussians assigned to group j. 4. SE(3) Trajectory Fitting: For each group j, fit a group-wise SE(3) trajectory by optimizing the parameters \{hj^0, Rj^t, Tj^t\} jointly with the scene. The deformation of any Gaussian \mui \in \mathcal{M}^j at timestep t is predicted by applying the learned SE(3) transformation relative to its control point: \mui^t = Rj^t (\mui^0 - hj^0) + hj^0 + Tj^t where: \mui^0 is the initial mean position of Gaussian i. hj^0 is the initial position of control trajectory j. Rj^t is the rotation matrix for group j at time t. Tj^t is the translation vector for group j at time t. 5. Rendering/Training: During rendering or training, instead of querying a neural network for each Gaussian's deformation, apply the corresponding group's SE(3) transformation to the initial mean \mui^0 to obtain \mui^t. Parameters: J: Number of groups/control trajectories. Not given in the sources. \lambdar: Weighting factor for trajectory similarity. Not given in the sources. F: Number of timesteps. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Farthest Point Sampling: The initialization of control points via farthest point sampling at t=0 is critical for covering the scene. Temporal Coherence: The method regularizes the learned motion field by smoothing noisy trajectories, which helps in real-world dynamic scenes. Precision: The SE(3) transformation assumes rigid body motion within each group. If a group contains Gaussians with non-rigid relative motion, the approximation may introduce artifacts. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of transformations per frame from N (per Gaussian) to J (per group), where J \ll N. Memory Complexity: Stores J sets of SE(3) parameters instead of N neural network weights or deformation fields. Performance: On the MonoDyGauBench dataset, integrating GroupFlow into DeformableGS accelerates rendering by 13.71× and shortens training by 2.53× compared to baselines. Strengths: Substantial acceleration in training and rendering; maintains temporally coherent, high-quality motion reconstruction; distills dense deformations into a smaller set of parameters. Limitations: Assumes locally coherent rigid motion within groups; may not capture complex non-rigid deformations if groups are too large or poorly defined. GroupFlow was introduced in the paper "SpeeDe3DGS: Speedy Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting with Temporal Pruning and Motion Grouping". It is part of a pipeline that also includes Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) and Temporal Sensitivity Sampling (TSS) to further optimize dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting.
