name: 3DGS-MCMC
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, MCMC Densification Strategy, MCMC-based Gaussian Lifecycle, Markov Chain Monte Carlo Strategy
body: 3DGS-MCMC replaces the standard heuristic-based densification (gradient magnitude thresholds) of 3D Gaussian Splatting with a probabilistic framework based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. It treats the set of 3D Gaussians as samples from an underlying probability distribution, using Metropolis–Hastings steps to guide the spawning and pruning of primitives. This approach allows for precise control over the total number of Gaussians, reduces reliance on high-quality initialization, and yields sharper details and fewer artifacts compared to the original cloning/splitting heuristics. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current set of N Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk has parameters \muk, \Sigmak, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k; current training iteration t; rendering loss \mathcal{L}; and configuration hyperparameters. Output: Updated set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with modified parameters, potentially different cardinality N'. Data Structures: Gaussian Parameters: Stored in contiguous tensors or arrays. means: [N, 3] float32. scales: [N, 3] float32 (log-space storage is common in implementations). quats: [N, 4] float32 (normalized quaternions). opacities: [N] float32 (logit-space storage is common). shcoeffs: [N, K, 3] or similar, depending on SH degree. Optimizer States: Separate buffers for gradients and optimizer momentum for each parameter group. Binomial Table: A precomputed table binoms of size 51 \times 51 (or similar) where binoms[n, k] = \binom{n}{k}. Parameters: capmax: Maximum number of Gaussians. Default: 1,000,000. refinestartiter: Iteration after which refinement begins. Default: 500. refinestopiter: Iteration after which refinement stops. Default: 25,000. refineevery: Frequency of refinement steps. Default: 100. minopacity: Threshold for considering Gaussians for pruning/relocation. Default: 0.005. noiselr: Learning rate for MCMC sampling noise. Default: 5 \times 10^{-5}. Algorithm Steps: The method is executed periodically every refineevery iterations, starting at refinestartiter and stopping at refinestopiter. 1. Initialization: Ensure optimizer states are synchronized with parameters. Sanity check that each optimizer has one paramgroup and params contain keys 'means', 'scales', 'quats', 'opacities'. 2. Sample Add (Spawn): Calculate current opacities \alpha = \text{sigmoid}(\text{params['opacities']}). Sample n new source indices from the existing population using a multinomial distribution weighted by \alpha. Compute new opacities and scales for these samples using a computerelocation function (see below). Clamp new opacities to [\text{min\opacity}, 1-\epsilon]. Append copies of the sampled Gaussians (with updated opacities/scales) to the parameter arrays. Initialize new optimizer states to zero. 3. Relocation (Prune/Move): Identify "dead" Gaussians (mask=True) and "alive" Gaussians (mask=False). Dead Gaussians are those with low expected contribution or low opacity. Sample new source indices from alive Gaussians using a multinomial distribution weighted by \text{sigmoid}(\text{opacities}). Compute new opacities and scales for the relocated Gaussians using computerelocation with the sampled opacities, \exp(\text{scales}), ratios (bincount of sampled indices + 1), and the binoms table. Clamp new opacities to [\text{min\opacity}, 1-\epsilon]. Update parameters: Set opacities at sampled indices to \text{logit}(\text{new\opacities}), scales to \log(\text{new\scales}), and copy these values to the dead indices. Reset optimizer states at the sampled indices. 4. Inject Noise (Perturbation): Calculate current opacities \alpha and scales s = \exp(\text{params['scales']}). Compute covariance matrices \Sigma from quats and scales. Define a sigmoid function for noise scaling: \text{op\sigmoid}(x, k=100, x0=0.995) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-k(x - x0))}. Generate noise: \text{noise} = \mathcal{N}(0, I) \cdot \text{op\sigmoid}(1 - \alpha) \cdot \text{scaler}. Transform noise by covariance: \text{noise}{\text{cov}} = \Sigma \cdot \text{noise}. Update means: \mu \leftarrow \mu + \text{noise}{\text{cov}}. Formulas: Metropolis-Hastings Spawn Probability: The probability of spawning a new Gaussian at \mu{\text{new}} is determined by the ratio of rendering errors and proposal distributions: \alpha{\text{spawn}} = \min \left( 1, \frac{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{new}})}{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{old}})} \cdot \frac{q(\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{old}}|\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{new}})}{q(\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{new}}|\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{old}})} \right) where \mathcal{L} is the rendering loss and q is the proposal distribution. Relocation Computation: The specific formula for computerelocation is not explicitly detailed in the provided sources, but it utilizes the binomial coefficient table binoms and ratios derived from the multinomial sampling counts to adjust opacities and scales. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def computebinomstable(maxn=50): """Precompute binomial coefficients.""" binoms = torch.zeros(maxn + 1, maxn + 1, dtype=torch.float32) for n in range(maxn + 1): for k in range(n + 1): binoms[n, k] = math.comb(n, k) return binoms def opsigmoid(x, k=100, x0=0.995): """Sigmoid function for noise scaling.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-k (x - x0))) def mcmcdensificationstep( params, optimizers, binoms, capmax, minopacity, refineevery, currentiter, refinestartiter, refinestopiter): """ Perform one MCMC densification step. params: dict with keys 'means', 'scales', 'quats', 'opacities' (tensors of shape [N,...]) optimizers: dict of optimizer states """ # 1. Check if refinement should occur if currentiter < refinestartiter or currentiter > refinestopiter: return if currentiter % refineevery != 0: return # 2. name: Optimization and Training Strategy
head: 3DGS-MCMC Training Strategy, MCMC-based Training with EMA and Regularization
body: This strategy defines the optimization schedule, loss formulation, and regularization techniques for training radiance fields using 3D Gaussian Splatting with MCMC-based densification. It addresses the problem of overfitting to noise and geometric artifacts during the iterative refinement of Gaussian primitives. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by incorporating specific MCMC-derived regularization terms on opacity and scale, using cosine annealing for feature and MLP learning rates, applying Exponential Moving Average (EMA) to MLP weights, and executing a final refinement phase that freezes geometry. Inputs: Initial set of Gaussian primitives (position, scale, rotation, opacity, features). Training images and camera poses. Hyperparameters: \lambda (D-SSIM weight), \lambda\alpha (opacity reg weight), \lambdas (scale reg weight), \gamma (EMA decay), T{refine} (refinement iterations, typically 3000). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian primitives and associated MLP weights. Data Structures: Primitives: Array of size P. Each primitive i has fields: position \mathbf{p}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, opacity \alphai, feature vector \mathbf{f}i. MLP Weights: \theta, filtered version \bar{\theta}. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives and MLP weights. Set EMA weights \bar{\theta}0 = \theta0. 2. Main Training Loop: For each training iteration t: a. Render the scene using the current Gaussian primitives and MLP weights. b. Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using the formula below. c. Perform gradient descent to update primitive parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity) and raw MLP weights \thetat. d. Update the EMA weights \bar{\theta}t using the EMA formula. e. Use a cosine annealing scheduler to determine the learning rates for feature vectors and MLP weights at step t. f. Apply the MCMC-based densification strategy (spawn/prune) to manage the set of primitives P. 3. Refinement Phase: After the main training loop, execute the last T{refine} iterations (typically 3000) with the following modifications: a. Disable all regularization terms (\mathcal{R}\alpha, \mathcal{R}s). b. Freeze all primitive parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity). c. Optimize only the feature vectors and MLP weights \theta. d. Continue using the cosine annealing scheduler for learning rates. Formulas: 1. Opacity Regularization: \mathcal{R}\alpha = \frac{1}{P} \sum{i=1}^P \alphai where P is the number of primitives. 2. Scale Regularization: \mathcal{R}s = \frac{1}{P} \sum{i=1}^P \|\mathbf{s}i\|1 where \mathbf{s}i is the scale vector of primitive i. 3. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} + \lambda\alpha \mathcal{R}\alpha + \lambdas \mathcal{R}s where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the L1 photometric loss, \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} is the differentiable SSIM loss, and \lambda, \lambda\alpha, \lambdas are scalar weights. 4. EMA Update for MLP Weights: \bar{\theta}t \leftarrow \gamma \bar{\theta}{t-1} + (1 - \gamma) \thetat where \bar{\theta}t is the filtered weight at step t, \thetat is the raw updated weight, and \gamma is the decay factor. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for D-SSIM loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda\alpha: Weight for opacity regularization. Not given in the sources. \lambdas: Weight for scale regularization. Not given in the sources. \gamma: EMA decay factor. Not given in the sources. T{refine}: Number of refinement iterations. Typically 3000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Without EMA and regularization, the model may overfit to individual frames or geometric artifacts. Local Minima: In unconditional generation contexts, failing to reset latent representations can cause the model to get stuck in local minima that overfit geometric artifacts. Precision: Half-precision memory fetches on feature vectors are used during rasterization to reduce register pressure, which may introduce precision trade-offs. A training procedure used in unconditional 3D generation (e.g., SSDNeRF) to prevent overfitting to geometric artifacts by periodically resetting latent representations to their mean. It involves resetting triplane codes to their mean value halfway through the training schedule and doubling the total training length to compensate. Without this, the model risks getting stuck in local minima. On the SRN Cars dataset, this approach achieves an FID of 19.04±1.10 and a KID/10⁻³ of 8.28±0.60. Time Complexity: The refinement phase adds a fixed cost of 3000 iterations focused only on features and MLP weights, which is relatively cheap compared to full primitive optimization. Memory Complexity: Uses half-precision memory fetches for feature vectors to reduce register pressure, lowering memory bandwidth requirements during rasterization. Strengths: Enhances robustness to noise and avoids overfitting to individual frames through EMA and regularization. The refinement step slightly improves color fidelity, particularly in large-scale scenes. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization weights and EMA decay. The densification strategy relies on the underlying 3DGS-MCMC method. When to use: Suitable for high-quality radiance-field novel-view synthesis, semantic scene reconstruction, and high-resolution image fitting where noise robustness and color fidelity are critical. When not to use: Not applicable for unconditional 3D generation tasks that require latent resetting (use Latent Resetting variant instead). The optimization strategy is based on the 3DGS-MCMC method. The specific regularization terms and EMA application were introduced in "Neural Harmonic Textures for High-Quality Primitive Based Neural Reconstruction". The latent resetting variant was introduced in "Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF: A Unified Approach to 3D Generation and Reconstruction" for unconditional generation tasks. name: VS-Splat Voxel Selection
head: Ours, VS-Splat selection
body: VS-Splat Voxel Selection is a learnable, differentiable mechanism for selecting relevant 3D voxels in feed-forward Gaussian Splatting, replacing static opacity thresholding with a confidence-based selection process. It sets itself apart from siblings like Opacity-Based Thresholding by using a Gumbel-Sigmoid distribution to predict confidence scores, allowing the network to learn which voxels contain object-centric geometry rather than relying on manual hyperparameter tuning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid (resolution H \times W \times D) and a feature extractor (e.g., DINOv1) producing 2D feature maps from input images. Output: A binary mask of selected voxels and refined opacity values for rendering. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor of resolution H=W=D=48. Confidence Scores: A scalar value per voxel, predicted by a Selective Feature Refinement (SFR) module. Primitives: M=16 fine-grained 3D Gaussians are generated for each selected voxel. Parameters: Gumbel-Sigmoid Temperature (\tau): Linearly annealed from 1.0 to 0.1 over the first 50,000 training iterations, then fixed at 0.1 for the remainder of training and inference. SFR Module Depth (R): Contains R=2 residual convolutional blocks. Channel Compression: The 3D convolutional compressor reduces channel dimension from 2C=1,536 to \tilde{C}=128. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract 2D feature maps from input images using a pre-trained backbone (e.g., DINOv1). 2. Feature Compression: Compress features using a 3D convolutional compressor to reduce channel dimensionality. 3. Confidence Prediction: Pass compressed features through the SFR module to predict confidence scores for each voxel. 4. Voxel Selection: Apply the Gumbel-Sigmoid function to the confidence scores to generate a differentiable binary selection mask. 5. Opacity Refinement: Use the selection mask to refine the opacity values of the Gaussians associated with the selected voxels. 6. Primitive Generation: For each selected voxel, generate M=16 fine-grained 3D Gaussian primitives. 7. Rendering: Render the scene using the selected voxels and their associated primitives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vssplatvoxelselection(voxelgrid, inputimages, temperaturetau): """ Performs voxel selection using VS-Splat method. Args: voxelgrid: 3D tensor of shape (H, W, D) representing the voxel space. inputimages: List of 2D input images. temperaturetau: Float, current Gumbel-Sigmoid temperature. Returns: selectedmask: Binary mask of selected voxels. refinedopacities: Refined opacity values for selected voxels. """ # Step 1: Extract 2D features from input images # Using DINOv1 pre-trained on ImageNet-1K features2d = extractfeaturesdinov1(inputimages) # Step 2: Compress features using 3D convolutional compressor # Reduces channel dimension from 1536 to 128 featurescompressed = compressfeatures3d(features2d, inchannels=1536, outchannels=128) # Step 3: Predict confidence scores using SFR module # SFR module contains R=2 residual convolutional blocks confidencescores = predictconfidencesfr(featurescompressed, numresidualblocks=2) # Step 4: Apply Gumbel-Sigmoid for differentiable selection # temperaturetau is annealed from 1.0 to 0.1 over first 50k iterations selectedmask = gumbelsigmoid(confidencescores, temperature=temperaturetau) # Step 5: Refine opacities based on selection # This step integrates predicted voxel-selection scores into the rendering process refinedopacities = refineopacities(confidencescores, selectedmask) return selectedmask, refinedopacities def gumbelsigmoid(scores, temperature): """ Applies Gumbel-Sigmoid function for differentiable binary selection. Args: scores: Tensor of confidence scores. temperature: Float, temperature parameter for Gumbel-Sigmoid. Returns: Binary mask (soft binary) of selected voxels. """ # Gumbel noise for stochasticity gumbelnoise = samplegumbelnoise(scores.shape) # Gumbel-Sigmoid formula sigmoidinput = (scores + gumbelnoise) / temperature return torch.sigmoid(sigmoidinput) def samplegumbelnoise(shape): """ Samples Gumbel(0, 1) noise. Args: shape: Shape of the output tensor. Returns: Tensor of Gumbel noise. """ # Sample from uniform distribution u = torch.rand(shape) # Gumbel distribution transformation return -torch.log(-torch.log(u + 1e-10) + 1e-10) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temperature Scheduling: Using a fixed high temperature may lead to excessive selection of background voxels, while a fixed low temperature may result in insufficient selection. Deterministic Sigmoid: Replacing Gumbel-Sigmoid with a deterministic Sigmoid function fails to properly select object-centric voxels, leading to significant rendering quality drops. Opacity Thresholding: Simple opacity-based thresholding (OBT) is unreliable for selecting object-centric voxels and requires manual tuning of the threshold value. A variant that replaces the Gumbel-Sigmoid with the deterministic Sigmoid function for voxel selection. It fails to properly select object-centric voxels, leading to significant rendering quality drops. On the CO3D dataset, it yields PSNR 18.01, SSIM 0.835, LPIPS 0.288, and uses 2,223 voxels. Performance: On the CO3D dataset, VS-Splat yields PSNR 21.31, SSIM 0.863, LPIPS 0.213, and uses 19,587 voxels. Comparison: VS-Splat uses approximately 15% fewer voxels than Opacity-Based Thresholding (OBT) while outperforming it across all metrics. OBT yields PSNR 21.21, SSIM 0.859, LPIPS 0.223, and uses 22,867 voxels. Comparison: Simply applying Straight-Through Estimator (STE) to confidence scores results in selecting an extremely limited number of voxels (121 voxels on CO3D), yielding PSNR 14.71, SSIM 0.814, LPIPS 0.317. Scalability: The method uses a voxel grid resolution of H=W=D=48 and generates M=16 primitives per selected voxel. Strengths: Learnable selection allows for better identification of object-centric voxels compared to static thresholds. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the Gumbel-Sigmoid temperature schedule. VS-Splat was proposed in the paper "VS-Splat: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse-views". It addresses the limitations of static opacity thresholding in 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a learnable voxel selection mechanism. The method is particularly effective for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse views. name: Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for Confidence Scores
head: Straight-Through Estimator for Gradient Extension
body: The Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for confidence scores is a gradient approximation technique used in voxel selection schemes to enable backpropagation through discrete selection decisions. It extends gradients beyond the hard selection boundary to prevent optimization stalling. The method is applied within a voxel selection framework where each voxel v is assigned a learned confidence score cv. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Confidence scores \{cv\} for candidate voxels. Output: A binary selection mask mv \in \{0, 1\} and gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial cv} for optimization. Data Structures: Confidence scores: A tensor of floating-point values, typically in [0, 1]. Selection mask: A binary tensor of the same shape as the confidence scores. Steps: 1. Forward Pass (Hard Selection): Compute the binary mask mv using a threshold \tau: mv = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } cv > \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The rendering pipeline uses only voxels where mv = 1. The threshold \tau is a scalar cutoff value. 2. Backward Pass (Straight-Through): Compute gradients by ignoring the discontinuity of the thresholding operation, passing the upstream gradient directly to cv. Parameters: Threshold \tau: A scalar cutoff value. In comparative experiments, it is evaluated alongside opacity-based thresholding (OBT) which uses a predefined threshold of 0.005. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Limited Selection: Simply applying STE to confidence scores results in selecting an extremely limited number of voxels, degrading rendering quality. Optimization Stalling: Without extending gradients beyond the primitive boundary, optimization may stall; STE handles this by allowing gradient flow even where the boundary is hard or truncated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stethresholdforward(confidencescores, threshold): # Forward pass: hard thresholding to binary mask mask = (confidencescores > threshold).float() return mask def stethresholdbackward(gradoutput, confidencescores, threshold): # Backward pass: straight-through estimator # Pass upstream gradient directly, ignoring the non-differentiable threshold return gradoutput Uses a fixed opacity threshold (e.g., 0.005) to select voxels. It is simple but requires manual tuning and can be unreliable for object-centric selection. Uses a stochastic relaxation of the selection process to allow differentiable optimization. It generally yields better voxel selection and rendering quality than STE. Replaces Gumbel-Sigmoid with a standard sigmoid function. This fails to properly select object-centric voxels and leads to significant rendering quality drops. Time Complexity: The forward pass is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. The backward pass is also O(N) as it involves a simple element-wise operation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the confidence scores and the selection mask. Performance: On the CO3D dataset, using STE for voxel selection resulted in a PSNR of 14.71, SSIM of 0.814, and LPIPS of 0.317, with only 121 voxels selected. This is significantly worse than the proposed VS-Splat method (PSNR 21.31, 19,587 voxels). Strengths: Simple to implement; enables gradient flow through hard selection boundaries. Limitations: Can lead to very sparse voxel selection and poor rendering quality if not carefully tuned. The Straight-Through Estimator is a common technique in differentiable programming to handle non-differentiable operations. In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting and voxel selection, it was explored as a variant of the VS-Splat framework to enable gradient flow to confidence scores. It is also used in radiance field methods, such as Fourier Splatting, to extend gradients beyond primitive boundaries and prevent optimization stalling. name: Locality-preserving Densification
head: Z-ordering for Gaussians
body: Locality-preserving densification addresses the memory access throttling caused by standard Gaussian densification, where new primitives are appended to the end of parameter buffers, causing spatially close Gaussians to be stored far apart in memory. By reordering the Gaussian parameter buffers based on 3D spatial proximity using Z-ordering (Morton order), this method ensures that neighboring Gaussians in space are also adjacent in memory, thereby improving memory access coalescing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\} and the current parameter buffer layout. Output: A permuted parameter buffer where the indices of the Gaussians are reordered such that spatial locality is preserved. Data Structures: Gaussian Buffer: An array of structures containing \muk, \Sigmak, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k. The method operates on the indices of this array. Z-order Key: A 64-bit integer derived from the 3D coordinates of \muk. Steps: 1. Trigger Check: Determine if the current training iteration t is a multiple of the Z-ordering frequency T{\text{zorder}}. If not, skip. 2. Coordinate Normalization: Normalize the mean positions \muk of all active Gaussians to a canonical range (e.g., [0, 1]) suitable for Morton coding. Let \mu'k be the normalized position. 3. Z-order Encoding: For each Gaussian gk, compute its Morton code mk from \mu'k. The Morton code interleaves the bits of the x, y, and z coordinates. mk = \text{MortonEncode}(\mu'k.x, \mu'k.y, \mu'k.z) 4. Sorting: Create a list of indices I = [0, 1, \dots, N-1] and sort I based on the ascending order of mk. 5. Buffer Reordering: Rearrange the elements in the Gaussian parameter buffer according to the sorted index list I. This ensures that Gaussians with similar Morton codes (spatially close) are adjacent in memory. 6. Backward Pass Compatibility: Ensure the rendering pipeline uses the per-Gaussian backward pass, as the original backward pass with numerous atomic operations causes high atomic contention when combined with Z-ordering. Parameters: Z-ordering Frequency (T{\text{zorder}}): 5000 iterations. Z-ordering Computational Cost: Approximately 4 ms per million Gaussians. Pitfalls: Atomic Contention: Z-ordering performs effectively only when used with the per-Gaussian backward pass. Using it with the original backward pass heightens atomic contention due to the interaction between the reordered memory layout and the atomic accumulation operations. Small Scene Overhead: Repeated Z-ordering slows down training when the number of Gaussians is small. This is due to a massive increase in atomic contention in the alpha blending backward pass, leading to false sharing. Precision: Normalization range must be consistent across iterations to ensure stable Morton codes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyzordering(gaussians, iteration, tzorder=5000, scenemin=None, scenemax=None): """ Reorders the gaussian buffer based on 3D spatial locality using Z-ordering. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attribute 'mean' (vec3). iteration: Current training iteration number. tzorder: Frequency of Z-ordering application. scenemin, scenemax: Bounding box of the scene for normalization. Returns: None (modifies gaussians in place). """ # Step 1: Trigger Check if iteration % tzorder != 0: return n = len(gaussians) if n == 0: return # Step 2 & 3: Compute Morton Codes mortoncodes = [] for g in gaussians: # Normalize to [0, 1] using scene bounds x = (g.mean.x - scenemin.x) / (scenemax.x - scenemin.x) y = (g.mean.y - scenemin.y) / (scenemax.y - scenemin.y) z = (g.mean.z - scenemin.z) / (scenemax.z - scenemin.z) mortoncodes.append(mortonencode(x, y, z)) # Step 4: Sort Indices indexedcodes = list(enumerate(mortoncodes)) indexedcodes.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) sortedindices = [idx for idx, in indexedcodes] # Step 5: Buffer Reordering gaussians[:] = [gaussians[i] for i in sortedindices] # Step 6: Backward Pass Compatibility # Ensure per-Gaussian backward pass is used to avoid atomic contention. def mortonencode(x, y, z): """ Interleaves bits of x, y, z to form a Morton code. Assumes inputs are scaled to integers in [0, 2^21 - 1]. """ scale = 1 << 21 ix = int(x scale) & ((1 << 21) - 1) iy = int(y scale) & ((1 << 21) - 1) iz = int(z scale) & ((1 << 21) - 1) m = 0 for i in range(21): m |= ((ix >> i) & 1) << (3 i) m |= ((iy >> i) & 1) << (3 i + 1) m |= ((iz >> i) & 1) << (3 i + 2) return m Time Complexity: The Z-ordering step itself is O(N \log N) due to sorting, where N is the number of Gaussians. The computational cost is approximately 4 ms per million Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the Morton codes and sorted indices. No additional memory is required for the Gaussians themselves. Measured Performance: Reduces warp divergence and cache misses, resulting in faster training when scenes contain many Gaussians. It outperforms load-balanced approaches which can cause uncoalesced memory accesses that become a bigger bottleneck as primitives increase. Strengths: Significantly improves memory access patterns during densification, leading to faster training times for large-scale scenes. Limitations: Adds overhead for small scenes (fewer Gaussians) due to false sharing and atomic contention in the backward pass. Requires the per-Gaussian backward pass to be effective. When to Use: Use when training scenes with a large number of Gaussians (e.g., >1M) and densification is active. Do not use if the number of Gaussians is small or if the per-Gaussian backward pass is not implemented. Locality-preserving densification was introduced in the "Faster-GS" paper, which analyzes and improves Gaussian Splatting optimization. The authors observed that memory layout became a throttling factor during densification, as new Gaussians added to the end of buffers caused spatially close primitives to be far apart in memory. By applying Z-ordering every 5000 iterations alongside other optimization passes, the resulting framework achieved up to 5.2× faster training on Deep Blending scenes compared to the original 3DGS implementation. name: Progressive and Multi-stage Training
head: Progressive Training, Multi-stage Optimization, Curriculum Learning for 3DGS
body: Progressive and Multi-stage Training refers to optimization strategies that decompose the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into sequential phases or stages, rather than optimizing all parameters simultaneously from a static initialization. It solves the problem of optimization instability, error propagation, and insufficient geometric detail that arises when initializing Gaussians randomly or using coarse priors. It sets itself apart from single-stage baselines by decoupling distinct learning objectives (e.g., geometry vs. pose, or coarse vs. fine detail) to stabilize convergence and improve final rendering fidelity. All methods in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by a mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k [Parent]. The core mechanism involves periodic evaluation of a metric per Gaussian to determine if the current representation is insufficient or redundant in a specific region. Common metrics include: 1. Gradient Magnitude: The accumulated 2D positional gradient \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v} \| \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muv^k} \|2. High gradients indicate that the Gaussian's position is not adequately minimizing the loss, suggesting a need for refinement or replacement [13466-densification-and-splitting.md]. 2. Opacity: Low opacity \alphak < \alpha{\min} indicates a primitive contributes negligibly to the rendered image and is a candidate for pruning. 3. Scale: Excessively large scales max(sk) relative to the scene extent e{scene} indicate coarse approximations that may blur details or occlude nearby geometry [13466-densification-and-splitting.md]. Densification operations are typically triggered every N iterations (e.g., refineEvery = 100) to allow the optimizer to stabilize [Parent]. The primary operations are: Splitting: Replacing a parent Gaussian gk with N{children} children. The children's means \mu{child} are sampled from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak) [Parent]. The scale is typically reduced, e.g., s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}}, to increase local density [Parent]. Cloning: Creating an exact copy of gk (same \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) to increase sampling frequency in high-error regions without changing the spatial footprint [Parent]. Pruning: Removing Gaussians that fail to meet opacity or significance thresholds. Buffer management is critical: pruned or split Gaussians require buffer compaction or flag-based marking to maintain contiguous memory access for rasterization [Parent]. A training strategy that improves radiance field reconstruction quality by refining the primitive representation (point cloud or mesh) in multiple stages, rather than optimizing a single static configuration. It addresses the problem of insufficient geometric detail in single-stage training, where primitives either fail to capture high-frequency details or become redundant in smooth regions. It sets itself apart from single-stage baselines by dynamically adjusting the density and distribution of primitives based on error metrics during training. This method defines the specific loss function and densification strategy for MeshGS, a variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that aligns primitives with an explicit mesh surface. It solves the problem of standard Gaussian splatting ignoring existing 3D geometry by introducing projection, normal consistency, and scale regularization losses for "tightly-bound" Gaussians. It differs from its siblings by splitting the Gaussian set into tightly-bound (G^t) and loosely-bound (G^l) subsets, applying mesh-aware constraints only to G^t while retaining standard densification for G^l. Fine-tuning in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) refers to the phase of optimization where a pre-initialized or pre-trained set of Gaussian primitives is further refined to improve rendering fidelity, adapt to specific data distributions, or correct initialization artifacts. It serves as a bridge between coarse initialization (e.g., from Structure-from-Motion, feed-forward networks, or grid volumes) and the final high-quality radiance field. Unlike standard training from scratch, fine-tuning leverages existing structural priors, allowing for faster convergence and higher quality results. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy by focusing on the refinement of an already established primitive set rather than the hierarchical construction of the scene representation, and from Training Objective and Densification by often implying a specific phase or strategy applied after initial convergence or during specialized adaptation tasks. This method addresses the instability and incomplete volumetric coverage inherent in optimizing 3D Gaussian representations for shear-warp rendering by enforcing a structured training schedule. It differs from sibling methods like Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy by explicitly decoupling global spatial guidance (via sparse voxels) from local structural continuity (via slices), rather than relying on hierarchical scene decomposition. It outperforms Training Objective and Densification in volumetric consistency by preventing the "unstable global approximation" caused by random voxel sampling alone. Multi-stage training with pose prediction is a progressive optimization strategy for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples geometry learning from pose estimation to stabilize training. It solves the problem of error propagation in end-to-end differentiable rendering, where inaccuracies in predicted camera poses corrupt the learned Gaussian representation. Unlike single-stage approaches, it separates the process into distinct phases: initial pose-aware training, pose-free geometry refinement, and final end-to-end fine-tuning. This method is specifically designed for architectures that predict Gaussians from context views without ground-truth camera supervision during inference. This method defines the iterative optimization step for 3D Gaussian Splatting, combining multiple loss terms (reconstruction, depth, bilateral grid, regularization) to update Gaussian parameters and pose. It differs from standard single-loss training by integrating auxiliary supervisions and post-backward strategy hooks to manage densification and learning rate scheduling. It builds on Progressive and Multi-stage Training by executing the specific loss computations and parameter updates within a single training iteration. Definition: Introduces a progressive propagation strategy to expand the Gaussian cloud, ensuring smooth expansion and better coverage. It computes a local perceptual error map using a lightweight vision-transformer head and densifies only in regions where SSIM falls below a dynamic threshold, significantly improving detail in visually salient areas. Step: Alternate between spatial and temporal densification every 2 epochs to avoid Gaussians failing to reconstruct either motion or appearance detail. Definition: A training strategy that decouples depth network initialization from full model training to improve stability and performance. Step: 1. Construct RGB point clouds for each input view. 2. Project the constructed point clouds to the target view using the differentiable point cloud renderer. 3. Aggregate all point clouds from the various input views to render RGB images at the target view. 4. Optimize the depth network using a photometric loss between the rendered target views and the ground truth target images. 5. Freeze or continue training the initialized depth network and jointly train the entire model (spatial feature network, MLP, renderer, transformer, refinement module). Parameter: Performance improvement: approximately 0.4 dB PSNR gain. Pitfall: Jointly training the depth network and other components from scratch causes instability. Definition: A training strategy that disentangles generalizable 3DGS from a specific number of views, enabling robust view synthesis across broader view ranges regardless of input view count. Step: Train the model on long sequences to disentangle generalizable 3DGS from specific view counts. Progressive and multi-stage training methods have emerged as essential components of 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines to address the sensitivity of the optimization landscape to initialization and hyperparameters. The original 3DGS paper introduced a coarse-to-fine densification schedule, but subsequent research has expanded this into complex multi-stage frameworks for specific challenges such as pose estimation [15018-multi-stage-training-with-pose-prediction.md], mesh alignment [7448-training-objective-and-densification.md], and volumetric data [12921-curriculum-learning-with-slice-and-voxel-supervision.md]. These methods are widely used in novel view synthesis, dynamic scene reconstruction, and feed-forward 3DGS architectures where stability and convergence speed are critical. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Adaptive Spatio‐Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scenes with Oscillatory Motion, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70410, fetched 2026-10-26 FWD: Real-time Novel View Synthesis with Forward Warping and Depth, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01526, fetched 2026-10-29 FreeSplat: Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting Towards Free-View Synthesis of Indoor Scenes, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.17958, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy
head: Hybrid coarse-to-fine densification, multi-stage point cloud refinement
body: A training strategy that improves radiance field reconstruction quality by refining the primitive representation (point cloud or mesh) in multiple stages, rather than optimizing a single static configuration. It addresses the problem of insufficient geometric detail in single-stage training, where primitives either fail to capture high-frequency details or become redundant in smooth regions. It sets itself apart from single-stage baselines by dynamically adjusting the density and distribution of primitives based on error metrics during training. The method operates on a set of primitives (points or mesh vertices) \mathcal{P}. The core mechanism involves periodic densification steps triggered at specific iteration intervals, where primitives are added or modified based on a scoring function derived from rendering error. Inputs: Current primitive set \mathcal{P} (points or mesh vertices). Current iteration I. Rendering loss L (or per-pixel error metrics like DSSIM). Configuration parameters: refinement interval, scoring exponent, max vertex count ratio. Outputs: Updated primitive set \mathcal{P}'. Data Structures: Point Cloud (S1): List of Gaussians. No explicit mesh topology. Densification involves splitting/cloning existing Gaussians. Mesh (S2): List of vertices V and triangles T. Topology is maintained via Delaunay triangulation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Point Cloud (S1): Initialize a sparse set of 3D Gaussians. Mesh (S2): Compute Sobel gradient magnitudes on a downsampled target image. Sample initial vertex positions proportionally to edge strength with a small uniform floor for coverage. Create a Delaunay triangulation of sampled points with boundary vertices ensuring full image coverage. 2. Iteration Loop: For each training iteration I: a. Render the current primitive set to obtain images. b. Compute loss and gradients. c. Update primitive parameters (positions, opacities, colors, etc.) via optimizer. 3. Densification Check: If I satisfies the refinement schedule: Point Cloud (S1): Trigger densification based on gradient magnitude and opacity thresholds (see Parent). Mesh (S2): Proceed to Step 4. 4. Scoring (Mesh Variant S2): For each triangle t \in T: a. Calculate mean DSSIM (\overline{\text{DSSIM}}t) for pixels covered by t. b. Count pixels |\text{pixels}t| covered by t. c. Compute score: \text{score}t = \overline{\text{DSSIM}}t \cdot |\text{pixels}t|^\alpha where \alpha = 0.75. d. Exclude triangles with fewer than 3 pixels. 5. Insertion/Refinement: Mesh (S2): Identify top-scoring triangles. Insert centroid vertices for these triangles. Limit new vertices to 0.35 \times V (where V is current vertex count). Initialize new vertex features by averaging parent triangle vertex features. Re-run Delaunay triangulation on the full vertex set. Check for degeneracy (e.g., colinear vertices) and re-mesh if necessary. Point Cloud (S1): Split or clone Gaussians based on gradient magnitude \tauk and opacity \alphak thresholds [Parent]. Parameters: Refinement Interval: Every 500 iterations for Mesh (S2); periodic for Point Cloud (S1, see Parent). Start/End Iterations (Mesh): Start at 1,500, end at 15,000 (S2). Area-weighting exponent (\alpha): 0.75 (S2). Vertex Growth Ratio: 0.35 (S2). Edge Cases: Degeneracy: Mesh triangles may become degenerate (colinear vertices). Detected and re-meshed. Small Triangles: Triangles with <3 pixels are excluded from scoring to prevent noise-driven splitting. A specific implementation using a sparse mesh that is progressively refined by inserting centroid vertices for high-scoring triangles and re-running Delaunay triangulation. It differs from point-based splitting by maintaining explicit mesh topology and using DSSIM-based scoring with area weighting. Choose this when explicit geometric continuity or mesh-based rendering is required. (https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37032-718) Performance: Significantly improves rendering quality over single-stage training. On the Blender dataset, removing the hybrid strategy reduces PSNR from 30.3 dB to 26.6 dB, SSIM from 0.945 to 0.925, and increases LPIPS from 0.078 to 0.163. Complexity: Adds overhead for periodic densification and re-meshing (S2) or buffer compaction (S1). Mesh re-triangulation is O(V \log V) or similar depending on implementation. Strengths: Captures fine details that single-stage training misses; prevents over-smoothing. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of refinement schedules and thresholds; increased training time due to densification steps. Originated in differentiable point-based radiance field methods to address the limitations of static point cloud initialization. The mesh-based variant was introduced in Neural Harmonic Textures to leverage explicit geometric structures for high-quality reconstruction. It builds on the general principle of progressive refinement in inverse volume rendering [Parent]. name: Coarse-to-Fine Densification
head: Mesh densification, Progressive mesh refinement
body: Coarse-to-Fine Densification is a training strategy for primitive-based neural reconstruction that progressively refines a sparse mesh by inserting new vertices at high-error locations. It solves the challenge of initializing and densifying a mesh representation without manual tuning, ensuring uniform distribution of vertices proportional to their spatial impact on the rendered image. Unlike single-stage training, it decouples initialization from refinement, allowing the mesh topology to adapt to the scene's complexity over time. Inputs: Target image (or batch), initial sparse mesh (vertices and triangles), rendering parameters. Outputs: Refined mesh (vertices, features, topology) after densification steps. Data Structures: Mesh: Set of vertices V and triangles T. Each vertex v \in V has position \mathbf{p}v and feature vector \mathbf{f}v. Triangle Score: Scalar value \text{score}t for each t \in T. Pixel Count: |\text{pixels}t| number of pixels covered by triangle t during rasterization. Steps: 1. Initialization: a. Downsample the target image. b. Compute Sobel gradient magnitudes on the downsampled image. c. Sample initial vertex positions proportionally to edge strength, applying a small uniform floor to ensure coverage. d. Create a Delaunay triangulation of the sampled points. e. Add boundary vertices to ensure full image coverage. f. Initialize vertex features (e.g., color, opacity) based on the target image at the vertex positions. 2. Iterative Densification: For each densification step (every 500 iterations, starting at iteration 1,500 and ending at 15,000): a. Score Triangles: For each triangle t in the current mesh: i. Calculate \overline{\text{DSSIM}}t, the mean DSSIM (structural dissimilarity) of pixels covered by t. ii. Count |\text{pixels}t|, the number of pixels covered by t. iii. If |\text{pixels}t| < 3, exclude t from scoring. iv. Compute score: \text{score}t = \overline{\text{DSSIM}}t \cdot |\text{pixels}t|^\alpha where \alpha = 0.75. b. Select Triangles: Sort triangles by \text{score}t descending. Select the top-scoring triangles such that the total number of new vertices does not exceed 0.35 \times V, where V is the current number of vertices. c. Insert Vertices: For each selected triangle t: i. Compute the centroid position \mathbf{p}{new} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{v \in t} \mathbf{p}v. ii. Initialize new vertex features \mathbf{f}{new} by averaging the features of the parent triangle's vertices: \mathbf{f}{new} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{v \in t} \mathbf{f}v. iii. Add \mathbf{p}{new} and \mathbf{f}{new} to the vertex set. d. Re-triangulate: Re-run Delaunay triangulation on the full updated vertex set. e. Degeneracy Check: Detect if the mesh is degenerate (e.g., colinear vertices). If so, re-mesh. This rarely occurs in practice. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsetofinedensification(mesh, targetimage, iterations, startiter=1500, enditer=15000, step=500): # Initialization downsampledimg = downsample(targetimage) gradients = sobelmagnitude(downsampledimg) vertices = samplevertices(gradients, uniformfloor=0.01) mesh.vertices = vertices mesh.triangles = delaunaytriangulation(vertices) mesh.addboundaryvertices() initializevertexfeatures(mesh, targetimage) for i in range(startiter, enditer + 1, step): # Score triangles scores = {} for t in mesh.triangles: pixels = rasterizetriangle(t, targetimage) if len(pixels) < 3: continue dssim = meandssim(t, pixels) score = dssim (len(pixels) 0.75) scores[t] = score # Select top triangles sortedtriangles = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) maxnewvertices = 0.35 len(mesh.vertices) newvertices = [] trianglestosplit = [] count = 0 for t, score in sortedtriangles: if count >= maxnewvertices: break trianglestosplit.append(t) count += 1 # Insert vertices for t in trianglestosplit: centroidpos = meanposition(t.vertices) centroidfeat = meanfeatures(t.vertices) newv = Vertex(position=centroidpos, features=centroidfeat) newvertices.append(newv) mesh.vertices.extend(newvertices) # Re-triangulate mesh.triangles = delaunaytriangulation(mesh.vertices) # Degeneracy check (simplified) if isdegenerate(mesh): mesh = remesh(mesh) Parameters: \alpha = 0.75: Area-weighting exponent. Densification interval: Every 500 iterations. Start iteration: 1,500. End iteration: 15,000. Max new vertices: 0.35 \times V per step. Minimum pixels for scoring: 3. Edge Cases: Degeneracy: Vertices may become colinear, causing mesh degeneracy. Re-meshing is required, though rare. Small Triangles: Triangles with fewer than 3 pixels are excluded to prevent over-densification of tiny areas. Precision: DSSIM calculation should use standard floating-point precision. Gradient computation on downsampled images reduces memory usage. Time Complexity: Densification occurs every 500 iterations. Each step involves scoring all triangles (O(T)), sorting (O(T \log T)), and Delaunay triangulation (O(V \log V) or O(V^2) depending on implementation). Total overhead is minimal compared to rendering. Memory Complexity: Increases with the number of vertices. Max vertices grow by 35% per step. Performance: Training takes 1-3 minutes on an RTX A6000. Strengths: Automatic initialization, uniform vertex distribution, prevents over-densification of small areas. Limitations: Requires Delaunay triangulation, which can be computationally expensive for very large meshes. Degeneracy handling is necessary but rare. When to Use: When initializing a mesh-based neural reconstruction without manual seed placement. When Not to Use: When real-time densification is required during training (it is periodic). Coarse-to-Fine Densification was introduced in "Neural Harmonic Textures for High-Quality Primitive Based Neural Reconstruction". It addresses the need for robust mesh initialization and refinement in primitive-based neural reconstruction methods. The method uses structural dissimilarity (DSSIM) and area weighting to guide densification, ensuring that vertices are placed where they contribute most to image fidelity. name: Coarse-to-fine Centroidal Voronoi Tesselation (CVT)
head: CVT densification, SDF-aware implicit CVT optimization
body: Coarse-to-fine Centroidal Voronoi Tesselation (CVT) is a method for densifying continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) discretization near a surface by simultaneously optimizing SDF values and their discretization sites. It solves the challenge of generating high-quality 3D reconstructions with millions of sites without the computational prohibitions of explicit Voronoi diagram computation. Unlike its sibling method DMTet, which relies on a known true SDF, this approach adapts locally to the optimized SDF field, ensuring vertices are uniformly distributed to reduce sampling artifacts. Inputs: A 3D region of interest (bounding box). Camera centers for the scene. Initial coarse grid resolution (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16). Outputs: Optimized SDF values and feature values at discretization sites. A refined tetrahedral Delaunay mesh. Optimized color network parameters. Data Structures: Sites: A list of 3D points representing the discretization. KD-Tree: Maintained for each level of discretization to compute K-nearest neighbors (KNN) for gradient propagation and smoothing. Delaunay Tetrahedra: Computed after CVT optimization to define the dual mesh for ray-marching. Parameters: Initial grid resolution: 16 \times 16 \times 16. SDF upsampling threshold: 1.5 \times edge length. KNN re-estimation frequency: Every 100 iterations. Number of neighbors for bisector estimation (N): 24. Number of orthogonal directions per site: 3. Total CVT optimization iterations: 300. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a coarse uniform grid of sites within the bounding box (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16). Add the center of each camera as complementary sites to the CVT to accelerate ray-marching. Initialize SDF values, feature values, and color network parameters. 2. Coarse CVT Optimization: Minimize the CVT energy to move sites to the center of their cells. This establishes the initial uniform distribution. 3. Iterative Densification Loop: Repeat until the expected level of detail is reached: a. Optimization: Optimize color network parameters, SDF values, and feature values within the current CVT configuration. b. Upsampling: i. Identify surface-crossing edges in the dual of the CVT (the associated tetrahedral Delaunay mesh). ii. Add a new point at the center of each identified surface-crossing edge. iii. Identify edges where the SDF value at one endpoint is smaller than 1.5 \times the edge length. iv. Add a new point at the center of these edges as well. c. Implicit CVT Optimization: i. Re-estimate K-nearest neighbors (KNN) for each site every 100 iterations. ii. Minimize the approximate CVT loss (L{CVT}) for 300 iterations using the Adam optimizer. iii. The loss minimization ensures vertices are locally uniformly distributed. d. Mesh Update: i. Compute the Delaunay tetrahedra for the new set of sites. ii. Restart SDF and feature optimization on the new mesh. Implicit CVT Loss Calculation: To avoid explicit Voronoi cell computation, the method uses differences between distances to neighboring bisectors. 1. For each site si: a. Randomly sample two angles (\Theta, \Phi). These angles must be different for each site and change at each iteration. b. Rotate the standard Cartesian basis \{e0, e1, e2\} using (\Theta, \Phi) to obtain \{ej(\Theta, \Phi)\} for j=0,1,2. c. For each of the 3 rotated directions j: i. Find the N=24 nearest neighbors N(si) of si using the KD-tree. ii. Calculate the distance to the closest bisector in direction r: d(si, r) = \min{sj \in N(si)} (\|si - b(si, sj, r)\|^2) where b(si, sj, r) is the distance from si to its bisector with neighbor sj in direction r. iii. Edge Case (Opposite Signs): If the SDF values of si and sj have opposite signs, move the bisector plane to lie on the 0 crossing (aligning with the middle of dual tetrahedra). d. Sum the squared differences between distances to opposite bisectors: L{CVT} = \frac{1}{2} \sum{i} \sum{j=0,1,2} (d(si, ej(\Theta, \Phi)) - d(si, -ej(\Theta, \Phi)))^2 where ej(\Theta, \Phi) is the rotated cartesian basis and d() is the distance to the bisector. Returns a tensor of shape (3, 3) where rows are the new basis vectors. Implementation detail: Standard rotation matrix construction. """ # 1. Initialization sites = generateuniformgrid(boundingbox, initialres) sites = sites + [camera.center for camera in cameras] # Add camera centers sdfvalues = initializesdf(sites) features = initializefeatures(sites) kdtree = buildkdtree(sites) # 2. Coarse CVT Optimization # Minimize CVT energy to move sites to center of cells # (Simplified: assume a standard Lloyd's algorithm step or similar) sites = optimizecvtsites(sites, kdtree) # 3. Iterative Densification for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Optimize network parameters optimizecolornetwork(sites, features, sdfvalues) # Upsampling tetrahedra = computedelaunaytetrahedra(sites) newsites = [] for edge in tetrahedra.edges: s1, s2 = edge.endpoints edgelength = torch.norm(s1 - s2) sdf1 = sdfvalues[s1.index] sdf2 = sdfvalues[s2.index] # Surface crossing edge if (sdf1 > 0 and sdf2 < 0) or (sdf1 < 0 and sdf2 > 0): newsites.append((s1 + s2) / 2.0) # SDF threshold edge if abs(sdf1) < 1.5 edgelength or abs(sdf2) < 1.5 edgelength: newsites.append((s1 + s2) / 2.0) sites = sites + newsites # Rebuild KD-tree occasionally if iteration % 100 == 0: kdtree = buildkdtree(sites) # Implicit CVT Optimization for cvtiter in range(300): # Random angles for each site thetas = torch.rand(len(sites)) 2 np.pi phis = torch.rand(len(sites)) np.pi # Compute Loss lcvtloss = computelcvtloss(sites, sdfvalues, kdtree, thetas, phis) # Backpropagate and update sites lcvtloss.backward() optimizer.step() # Update Mesh tetrahedra = computedelaunaytetrahedra(sites) return sites, sdfvalues, features, tetrahedra Time Complexity: Traditional CVT optimization with millions of sites takes ~5 minutes for Voronoi diagram computation and ~2.5 hours for 30 iterations. The approximated CVT takes ~1 second per iteration, allowing 300 iterations in ~5 minutes. Memory Complexity: Requires maintaining a KD-tree for each level of discretization and storing SDF values, features, and network parameters for all sites. Strengths: Significant computational benefits over explicit Voronoi computation; adapts locally to the optimized SDF field; reduces sampling artifacts by ensuring uniform vertex distribution. Limitations: Does not know the true SDF (unlike DMTet); relies on approximation which may not perfectly match true Voronoi centroids. When to use: When high-quality 3D reconstruction with millions of sites is required, and explicit Voronoi computation is too slow. When not to use: When the true SDF is known and can be used for exact densification (e.g., DMTet scenarios). Origin: Proposed in "VortSDF: 3D Modeling with Centroidal Voronoi Tesselation on Signed Distance Fields" (WACV 2025). History: Inspired by previous work on CVT optimization. The method addresses the limitations of DMTet [28] by handling unknown SDFs. Usage: Used in differentiable rendering strategies for volumetric reconstruction, specifically for efficient sampling of points along pixel viewing lines in non-uniform tetrahedral grids. name: Training Objective and Densification
head: MeshGS Training, Tightly/Loosely-bound Training
body: This method defines the specific loss function and densification strategy for MeshGS, a variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that aligns primitives with an explicit mesh surface. It solves the problem of standard Gaussian splatting ignoring existing 3D geometry by introducing projection, normal consistency, and scale regularization losses for "tightly-bound" Gaussians. It differs from its siblings by splitting the Gaussian set into tightly-bound (G^t) and loosely-bound (G^l) subsets, applying mesh-aware constraints only to G^t while retaining standard densification for G^l. Inputs: Rendered image \hat{I}i and ground truth image Ii. Set of tightly-bound Gaussians G^t and loosely-bound Gaussians G^l. Mesh M consisting of faces fj and vertices vi with face normals nf. Hyperparameters: \lambda{img}=0.001, \lambda{nc}=0.1, \lambda{min}=0.1, \lambda{max}=10, \lambda{proj}=50, \rho=0.1. Training duration: 30,000 iterations. Densification interval: Every 500 iterations. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) and updated set G. Data Structures: Gaussian gi \in G^t: Mean Pi, Scale Si=(s1, s2, s3), Rotation Ri, Opacity \alphai, SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Gaussian gi \in G^l: Same attributes as above. Distance threshold d{th} = 0.01 used to classify Gaussians as tightly or loosely bound. Formulas: 1. Image Loss: L{img} = (1-\lambda{img})L{1}(\hat{I}{i},I{i}) + \lambda{img}SSIM(\hat{I}{i}, I{i}) Where L1 is the L1 loss and SSIM is the Structural Similarity Index. 2. Normal Consistency Loss: L{nc} = \sum{i \in G^{t},f \in F} (1 - n{i} \cdot n{f}) Where ni is the estimated normal of the Gaussian splat and nf is the mesh face normal. 3. Scale Regularization Loss: L{scale} = \sum{i \in G^{t}}(\lambda{min}|\text{min}(s{1}, s{2}, s{3})| + \lambda{max}|\text{max}(s{1}, s{2}, s{3}) - \rho|) Where \rho=0.1 is the threshold for the maximum scale. 4. Projection Loss: s{i} = P{i} + ((P{i} - v{i}) \cdot f{j}) \cdot f{j} L{proj} = \sum{i \in G^{t}}\parallel s{i} - P{i} \parallel {2} Where si is the projection of the Gaussian center Pi onto the mesh face defined by vertex vi and normal fj. 5. Total Loss: L = L{img} + \lambda{nc} L{nc} + L{scale} + \lambda{proj} L{proj} Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians. Classify each Gaussian gi as tightly-bound (G^t) or loosely-bound (G^l) based on its distance to the mesh surface relative to d{th}=0.01. 2. Rendering: Render image \hat{I}i from current Gaussian set. 3. Loss Computation: Compute L{img} using \hat{I}i and Ii. For each gi \in G^t: Estimate normal ni: Identify the axis in Si with the minimum scale value. Apply rotation matrix Ri to this axis to obtain ni in world coordinates. Find the closest mesh face fj (with normal nf) to gi. Compute L{nc} using ni and nf. Compute L{scale} using Si and \rho. Compute projection si of Pi onto face fj and add to L{proj}. Compute Total Loss L. 4. Optimization: Update Gaussian parameters using gradient descent on L. 5. Densification (Every 500 iterations): For G^l: Apply standard 3DGS densification strategy (gradient-based splitting/cloning/pruning). For G^t: Identify Gaussians requiring densification based on standard metrics (implied by "follows original 3DGS" for G^l and distinct strategy for G^t). Cloning: Copy attributes (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) from parent to child. Initialize child position by sampling a point from the corresponding mesh triangle. Splitting: Divide parent scale by a factor of 1.6. Initialize child position by sampling a point from the corresponding mesh triangle. Note: The sources specify sampling from the triangle for both cloning and splitting of G^t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmeshgs(Gt, Gl, mesh, images, iterations=30000, refineevery=500): # Hyperparameters from lambdaimg = 0.001 lambdanc = 0.1 lambdamin = 0.1 lambdamax = 10 lambdaproj = 50 rho = 0.1 dth = 0.01 for iter in range(1, iterations + 1): # 1. Render Ihat = render(Gt + Gl) Igt = images[iter] # 2. Compute Loss Limg = (1 - lambdaimg) L1loss(Ihat, Igt) + lambdaimg SSIMloss(Ihat, Igt) Ltotal = Limg # 3. Tightly-bound losses for g in Gt: # Estimate normal: min scale axis rotated by R minaxisidx = argmin(g.scale) ni = rotateaxis(g.rotation, g.scale, minaxisidx) # Find closest mesh face f with normal nf and vertex v f, v = findclosestmeshface(mesh, g.position) nf = f.normal vi = v.position # Normal Consistency Lnc = sum(1 - dot(ni, nf) for g in Gt for f in mesh.faces) # Simplified aggregation # Scale Regularization smin = min(g.scale) smax = max(g.scale) Lscaleterm = lambdamin abs(smin) + lambdamax abs(smax - rho) Ltotal += Lscaleterm # Projection Loss # Project Pi onto face defined by vi and normal f.normal (assuming f.normal is face normal) # Formula: si = Pi + ((Pi - vi). fj) fj # Note: Source uses fj as normal in projection formula context projectionvec = dot(g.position - vi, nf) nf si = g.position + projectionvec Lprojterm = norm(si - g.position) Ltotal += lambdaproj Lprojterm Ltotal += lambdanc (1 - dot(ni, nf)) # 4. Optimize gradients = computegradients(Ltotal, Gt + Gl) updateparameters(Gt + Gl, gradients) # 5. Densification if iter % refineevery == 0: densifylooselybound(Gl) # Standard 3DGS strategy densifytightlybound(Gt, mesh) # Mesh-aligned strategy def densifytightlybound(Gt, mesh): for g in Gt: if needssplitting(g): # Splitting: scale divided by 1.6, position sampled from triangle newscale = g.scale / 1.6 # Sample point from the closest mesh triangle to g newpos = samplepointfrommeshtriangle(mesh, g) createchildgaussian(g, newpos, newscale, g.opacity, g.shcoeffs) elif needscloning(g): # Cloning: copy attributes, position sampled from triangle newpos = samplepointfrommeshtriangle(mesh, g) createchildgaussian(g, newpos, g.scale, g.opacity, g.shcoeffs) def densifylooselybound(Gl): # Standard 3DGS densification: gradient-based splitting/cloning/pruning # states "follow the method outlined in the original 3DGS" standard3dgsdensification(Gl) Constrains primitive count to a target budget N^ using a redundancy map, eliminating pruning waste. Allocates iterations based on image frequency energy to decouple global coverage from local refinement. Time Complexity: Standard 3DGS optimization complexity, plus overhead for mesh proximity queries and normal estimation for G^t. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for mesh geometry and separate tracking for G^t and G^l. Performance: Evaluated on Mip-NeRF360 and Deep Blending datasets. Strengths: Aligns Gaussians with explicit mesh geometry, preventing expansion into free space. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the input mesh; tightly-bound Gaussians are constrained by mesh topology. When to use: When an explicit mesh is available and high-fidelity alignment with surface geometry is required. When not to use: When no mesh is available or when the scene contains significant non-rigid deformation not captured by the mesh. Originated in MeshGS: Adaptive Mesh-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for High-Quality Rendering. It builds on the original 3DGS densification strategy by introducing mesh-aware constraints. The method distinguishes between tightly-bound and loosely-bound splats to balance mesh alignment and general rendering flexibility. MeshGS: Adaptive Mesh-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for High-Quality Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08941v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Budget-Centered Training
body: Budget-Centered Training (BCT) is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that initializes and constrains the primitive count to the "knee" of the scene's capacity floor curve (N^), ensuring the model is born at the optimal size for a target quality rather than growing large and being pruned later. It differs from standard densification pipelines by replacing gradient-based pruning signals with a redundancy map (\theta) and by treating the primitive budget as a hard constraint during the optimization phase, thereby eliminating wasted computation on primitives that will eventually be removed. Inputs: Scene training views. Measured capacity floor curve for the scene, from which the knee point N^ is identified. Outputs: A 3D Gaussian Splatting model with primitive count capped at N^, optimized for the target quality. Data Structures: Primitive Set: A collection of 3D Gaussians. The total count is maintained \le N^. Redundancy Map (\theta): A spatial map where each region has a value \theta. High local multiplicity (over-covered regions) corresponds to low \theta values. State Variables: N{init}: Initial primitive count. N{stop}: Refine-stop fraction threshold. \theta{waste}: Measured redundancy ratio, defined as N{opt}/N{full}. Numbered Steps: 1. Measure Capacity Floor: Determine the capacity floor curve for the scene. Identify the knee point N^, defined as the budget with the largest steepest-window slope on the error-vs-budget curve. 2. Initialize Model: Set the initial primitive count N{init} to a fixed initial fraction of N^. 3. Compute Redundancy: Calculate the redundancy map \theta per region from the local factoring of the model. Regions with high local multiplicity (low \theta) are identified as over-covered. 4. Optimize with Budget Constraint: Train the model using MCMC densification, but enforce a hard cap on the total primitive count at N^. Densification: Proceed with standard densification logic to add primitives where needed. Pruning: Replace standard pruning signals (positional gradients/opacity) with the \theta redundancy map. Prune primitives inside regions flagged by \theta (specifically those with low \theta) based on their opacity. This removes primitives with the smallest approximation loss. 5. Stop Criterion: Monitor validation improvement. Freeze density control (stop densification/pruning) once the validation improvement falls below \epsilon = 0.5 dB. 6. Refine-Stop: Apply the refine-stop fraction (scaled by \theta{waste}) to determine the final termination of the refinement phase. Formulas: \theta{waste} = N{opt} / N{full}: Measured redundancy ratio used to scale the refine-stop fraction. N^: Knee point of the capacity floor curve, defined as the budget with the largest steepest-window slope on the error-vs-budget curve. \epsilon = 0.5 dB: Rate-based stopping criterion threshold for validation improvement. Parameters: N^: The knee point of the capacity floor curve (minimal primitive count for a given quality target). \epsilon: Rate-based stopping criterion threshold. Typical value: 0.5 dB validation improvement. Initial fraction: A fixed fraction of N^ used to set N{init}. Value: Not specified in the sources. Refine-stop fraction: A second fraction of N^ used to determine when to stop refinement. Scaled by \theta{waste}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The identification of N^ relies on the "steepest-window slope" of the capacity floor curve. Inaccurate measurement of the floor curve leads to suboptimal N^. Degenerate Input: If the scene has very low redundancy (e.g., already compressed models), the capacity floor curve may be flat, making N^ difficult to identify or resulting in minimal gains from BCT. Boundary Conditions: Pruning inside \theta-flagged regions must be careful not to remove primitives that are critical for visibility, even if they are in over-covered regions. The opacity-based pruning within these regions helps mitigate this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def budgetcenteredtraining(scenedata, capacityfloorcurve, Nopt, Nfull): # Step 1: Measure capacity floor curve and identify knee point N # N is the budget with the largest steepest-window slope on the error-vs-budget curve Nstar = maxslopepoint(capacityfloorcurve) # Standard curve knee detection # Step 2: Initialize model at fixed fraction of N thetawaste = Nopt / Nfull # Initial fraction value not specified in sources Ninit = Nstar 0.5 # Placeholder fraction; replace with actual value model = GaussianSet(count=Ninit) # Standard initialization # Step 3: Compute redundancy map theta per region from local factoring # Low theta indicates high local multiplicity (over-covered regions) thetamap = computeredundancymap(model) # Not given in sources; compute local multiplicity per region validationhistory = [] while True: # Step 4: MCMC densification model = densifystep(model, scenedata) # Not given in sources; standard 3DGS densification # Replace standard pruning with theta map; prune inside theta-flagged regions by opacity model = prunebytheta(model, thetamap) # Not given in sources; remove lowest-opacity primitives in low-theta regions # Enforce hard cap at N if model.primitivecount > Nstar: model.prunetocount(Nstar) # Evaluate validation performance valpsnr = evaluatevalidation(model, scenedata) # Not given in sources; standard PSNR computation validationhistory.append(valpsnr) # Step 5: Rate-based stopping criterion # Freeze density control once validation improvement falls below epsilon = 0.5 dB if len(validationhistory) >= 2: improvement = validationhistory[-1] - validationhistory[-2] if improvement < 0.5: break # Step 6: Refine-stop fraction application # Scaled by thetawaste to determine final termination stopthreshold = Nstar getrefinestopfraction(thetawaste) # Not given in sources; apply scaling if model.primitivecount < stopthreshold: model.freezerefinement() return model A two-stage Level-of-Detail (LOD) system where a model is trained at the budget-centered knee (N^) to minimize redundancy, and then a factoring tree is built over this model (and optionally the full model) to allow continuous quality scaling post-hoc. It is chosen when continuous quality scaling across different hardware budgets is required. It sets itself apart by using the BCT-trained model as a root for the factoring tree, ensuring the tree starts with a model that has almost no redundancy to lose. Steps: 1. Train the model at N^ using BCT. 2. Build factoring trees over two roots: the full model and the budget-centered model. 3. Deploy both roots through the same scheduler at a matched budget using an LOD render protocol. Performance: On the 'room' scene, the BCT-born tree renders 34.19 dB, within 0.16 dB of its own root, while the full-born tree collapsed to the same budget renders 22.83 dB. At 50% budget, it beats opacity-ordered pruning by +2.7 to +7.9 dB PSNR, with a cost of only -0.13 and -0.54 dB versus the full model. At 25% budget, the loss is substantial (3.1–13.9 dB) because already-compressed models carry less removable redundancy. Comparison: BCT is the correct front end for factoring tree deployment because a model born at the floor's budget contains almost no redundancy for the tree to lose. Time Complexity: Reduces training time compared to train-then-prune methods because it avoids optimizing and then removing a large number of primitives. The exact speedup is not quantified, but it is described as avoiding "wasted" training time on removed primitives. Memory Complexity: The model memory footprint is capped at N^, which is the minimal primitive count for the target quality. This is significantly smaller than the initial large model used in traditional pipelines. Measured Performance: On the 'room' scene, BCT-trained models achieve high quality (34.19 dB) at matched budgets compared to full models. Scaling: The method scales to city-scale scenes, enabling real-time rendering within consumer GPU memory limits. Strengths: Eliminates redundancy from the start; provides a clear measure of scene capacity; enables efficient LOD via factoring trees. Limitations: Requires accurate measurement of the capacity floor curve; may not provide significant gains on scenes with inherently low redundancy. When to use: When a fixed quality target must be met with minimal primitive count, or when building LOD systems via factoring trees. Budget-Centered Training was proposed in the paper "Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD". It is based on the theory that a measurable capacity floor exists for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes, which defines the minimal achievable rendering error at a given primitive count. The method was developed to address the inefficiency of traditional pipelines that train large models and then compress them, wasting computation on primitives that are eventually removed. It is used in the context of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly for city-scale scenes and real-time rendering applications.
