name: Coarse-to-fine multi-resolution densification
head: energy density resolution scheduler, energy-aware multi-resolution scheduling
body: Coarse-to-fine multi-resolution densification is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that dynamically allocates optimization iterations across different image resolutions based on the image's frequency energy density. It solves the problem of premature convergence to local optima and inefficient spatial diffusion caused by applying full-resolution supervision during the early global spread phase. Unlike Budget-Centered Training, which manages Gaussian count via budget constraints, this method manages the resolution of supervision to decouple global coverage (split operations) from local refinement (clone operations). Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of training images I, total densification iterations T{\text{densify}}, and a maximum scale factor K. Output: A schedule of iteration counts Tr for each resolution scale r \in \{1, \dots, K\}, and the resulting optimized Gaussian primitives. Data Structures Scale Factor Set: A = \{1, 2, \dots, K\}, where r=1 is full resolution and r=K is the coarsest resolution. Iteration Schedule: An array or map mapping each r \in A to an integer Tr, representing the number of iterations spent at that resolution. Steps 1. Compute Energy Density: For each scale factor r \in A, compute the energy density Er of the training images. Downscale the input image I to resolution Ir using bilinear interpolation with anti-aliasing: Ir = Dr(I) = \text{Bilinear}(I, \text{scale} = 1/r) Compute the 2D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of Ir: F(Ir). Calculate the energy spectrum E(Ir): E(Ir) = \sqrt{\Re(F(Ir))^2 + \Im(F(Ir))^2} where \Re and \Im are the real and imaginary parts. Compute the normalized energy density Er: Er = \|E(Ir)\|1 \cdot r^2 The term r^2 normalizes the energy values across different resolutions. 2. Allocate Iterations: Calculate the number of iterations Tr for each resolution r based on the ratio of its energy to the full-resolution energy E1: Tr = \text{Round}\left(\frac{Er}{E1} \cdot T{\text{densify}}\right) where T{\text{densify}} is the total number of densification iterations. 3. Execute Training Schedule: Train the Gaussian primitives in reversed order of resolution, from coarsest (r=K) to finest (r=1). For a specific scale factor r, training starts at iteration T{r+1} and ends at iteration Tr. Note: T{K+1} is typically 0 or the start of training. Global Spread Phase (r > 1): Use downsampled images for supervision. Keep the positional learning rate constant. Suppress clone operations to prevent premature local clustering and encourage spatial diffusion via split operations. Local Refinement Phase (r = 1): Switch to full-resolution supervision. Reduce the positional learning rate. Reintroduce clone operations to refine high-frequency details. Parameters T{\text{densify}}: Total densification iterations. Default value: 25,000. K: Maximum scale factor. Default value: 8. Positional Learning Rate: Constant during coarse resolutions (r > 1), reduced after restoring full resolution (r=1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Gradient Cancellation: Using full-resolution images during the global spread phase can cause large Gaussians to project to many pixels. The accumulated gradient vectors may cancel each other out due to opposing directions, resulting in small gradient errors below the split threshold and preventing further split operations. Premature Convergence: Full-resolution supervision encourages Gaussians to converge prematurely to local optima by overfitting to individual pixels, limiting spatial expansion. A training framework that gradually increases resolution based on energy density in 2D images to cooperate with the global-to-local densification strategy. It starts training at lower resolution to facilitate global spread via split operations, gradually increases resolution based on energy density, and transitions to full-resolution training to allow clone operations for local refinement. Time Complexity: The method accelerates training by approximately 2x compared to baseline implementations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves superior reconstruction performance with fewer Gaussian primitives on datasets such as MipNeRF-360, Deep Blending, and Tanks & Temples. Strengths: Promotes efficient spatial diffusion of Gaussian primitives, prevents premature local clustering, and balances global scene coverage with detail reconstruction. Limitations: Requires computation of FFT and energy density for scheduling. Relies on the assumption that energy density correlates with the required training effort at each resolution. When to use: When training time is a constraint and efficient global coverage is needed before local refinement. When not to use: If the scene has very low frequency content where energy-based scheduling provides no benefit, or if computational overhead of FFT is prohibitive for the target hardware. The method was introduced in the paper "Decomposing Densification in Gaussian Splatting for Faster 3D Scene Reconstruction". It builds on the observation that split operations are responsible for global diffusion while clone operations govern local refinement. The approach draws inspiration from frequency analysis techniques in 2D image processing and DashGaussian. It was developed to address the inefficiencies of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting densification, which often leads to unnecessary computational consumption and suboptimal behavior when using full-resolution supervision too early. Decomposing Densification in Gaussian Splatting for Faster 3D Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.20239, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Fine-tuning
head: 3DGS Fine-tuning, Fine-tuning Strategy, Gaussian Splatting Fine-tuning
body: Fine-tuning in 3D Gaussian Splatting refers to the optimization phase where an initial set of Gaussian primitives is refined to minimize rendering error, often leveraging pretrained weights or feed-forward initialization to accelerate convergence and improve fidelity. It addresses the problem of initializing Gaussian representations by generating them via a direct feed-forward process or refining existing sets through iterative optimization. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by dynamically adjusting the Gaussian population based on rendering loss and gradient metrics, and from pure feed-forward generation by allowing iterative parameter optimization. The fine-tuning process typically begins with an initial set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, which is generated via a direct feed-forward process predicting geometry and color attributes. The core mechanism involves iterative optimization of geometry (\mu, \Sigma), opacity (\alpha), and color attributes (SH coefficients \mathbf{c}) using differentiable rasterization. Inputs: Initial Gaussian set \mathcal{G}0, camera poses \{Pv\}, input images \{Iv\}, and optionally pretrained model weights. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian set \mathcal{G}{final} with refined attributes. The Gaussian set is stored as a contiguous array or list of objects, where each object gk contains: \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. sk \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (vector). qk \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). \alphak \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \mathbf{c}k: Spherical Harmonic coefficients. 1. Initialization: Generate initial Gaussians via a direct feed-forward process predicting geometry and color attributes. 2. Optimization Loop: For each iteration t: a. Rendering: Render images from all training views using the current Gaussian set. b. Loss Computation: Compute loss \mathcal{L} between rendered images and ground truth. Common losses include L1 color loss, SSIM, and depth loss. c. Backpropagation: Update Gaussian parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). d. Densification/Pruning: Periodically (e.g., every N iterations) evaluate metrics to modify \mathcal{G} [Parent]: i. Gradient-based Densification: Calculate accumulated 2D positional gradients \tauk [Parent]. Split or clone Gaussians with high gradients [Parent]. ii. Opacity Pruning: Remove Gaussians with \alphak < \alpha{\min} [Parent]. iii. Scale-based Pruning: Remove excessively large Gaussians [Parent]. iv. Rendering-Loss Densification: Identify regions with high rendering error or low opacity (holes) and add new Gaussians. 3. Buffer Management: Compact the Gaussian list to maintain contiguous memory access after pruning or splitting [Parent]. Opacity Rendering: The accumulated opacity O at a pixel is computed as: O = \sum{i \in N} \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where N are the 2D Gaussians overlapping the pixel, and \alphai is the alpha value of the i-th Gaussian. Color Rendering: The accumulated color \mathbf{C} is: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i \in N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{c}i is the color of the i-th Gaussian. Rendering-Loss Densification Thresholds: New Gaussians are added if: O(x, y) < \tau{opa} \quad \text{or} \quad E{color}(x, y) > \tau{color} \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{E{depth}(x, y)}{D(x, y)} > \tau{depth} where E{color} and E{depth} are color and depth errors, D(x,y) is rendered depth, and \tau are thresholds. Learning Rate: Typically 1 \times 10^{-3} for Adam optimizer. Densification Interval: Every 100 iterations (common in vanilla 3DGS) [Parent]. Naive Fine-tuning Iterations: 10,000 steps (in specific generator fine-tuning contexts). Transfer Functions: 5 transfer functions selected per volume in image-space fine-tuning. Forgetting: In continuous mapping, Gaussians may overfit to the latest frame, degrading quality for previous frames. Regularization terms (e.g., SSIM) are used to mitigate this. Sparse Initialization: SfM points may have holes in sky or distant areas, requiring densification beyond initial points. Overfitting: Naive fine-tuning of all generator weights can lead to overfitting if not regularized. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finetunegaussians(initialgaussians, trainingdata, numiterations, densifyinterval, lr=1e-3, alphamin=0.01, gradientthreshold=0.0002, tauopa=0.1, taucolor=0.05, taudepth=0.1): """ Fine-tune 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. Args: initialgaussians: List of Gaussian primitives with initial attributes. trainingdata: List of (camerapose, image, depth) tuples. numiterations: Total number of optimization steps. densifyinterval: Interval for densification/pruning. lr: Learning rate for optimizer. alphamin: Opacity threshold for pruning. gradientthreshold: Gradient magnitude threshold for splitting. tauopa, taucolor, taudepth: Thresholds for rendering-loss densification. Returns: optimizedgaussians: Final list of Gaussian primitives. """ gaussians = list(initialgaussians) for t in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample a batch of training views batch = trainingdata[t % len(trainingdata)] pose, gtimage, gtdepth = batch # 2. Render images from current Gaussians renderedimg, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(gaussians, pose) # 3. Compute Loss loss = l1loss(renderedimg, gtimage) + ssimloss(renderedimg, gtimage) + l1loss(rendereddepth, gtdepth) # 4. Backpropagate & Update (simplified Adam step) for g in gaussians: grad = computegradients(loss, g) g.params -= lr grad # 5. Periodic Densification and Pruning if t % densifyinterval == 0: gaussians = densifyandprune(gaussians, batch, alphamin, gradientthreshold, tauopa, taucolor, taudepth) return gaussians def rendergaussians(gaussians, pose): # Standard differentiable rasterization return rasterize(gaussians, pose), computedepth(gaussians, pose) def densifyandprune(gaussians, batch, alphamin, gradientthreshold, tauopa, taucolor, taudepth): """ Adaptively modify Gaussian population based on gradients and rendering error. """ newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Opacity pruning if g.opacity < alphamin: continue # Gradient-based splitting if g.gradientmagnitude > gradientthreshold: children = splitgaussian(g) newgaussians.extend(children) else: newgaussians.append(g) # Rendering-loss densification (hole filling) holes = findholes(gaussians, batch, tauopa, taucolor, taudepth) for h in holes: newg = creategaussian(h) newgaussians.append(newg) return newgaussians def l1loss(a, b): return sum(abs(a[i] - b[i]) for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) def ssimloss(a, b): # Structural similarity index computation return 1.0 - structuralsimilarity(a, b) def computegradients(loss, g): # Backpropagation through differentiable rasterizer return loss.gradient(g.params) def splitgaussian(g): # Clone with noise and reduced scale per Parent children = [] for in range(2): child = Gaussian(g.params + randomnoise(scale=0.01)) child.scale = 5.0 / 4.0 / (2 0.5) children.append(child) return children def findholes(gaussians, batch, tauopa, taucolor, taudepth): holes = [] pose, gtimage, gtdepth = batch renderedimg, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(gaussians, pose) for x, y in pixelgrid(): if renderedimg[y, x] < tauopa or l1loss(renderedimg[y, x], gtimage[y, x]) > taucolor or l1loss(rendereddepth[y, x], gtdepth[y, x]) / gtdepth[y, x] > taudepth: holes.append((x, y, pose)) return holes def creategaussian(hole): return Gaussian(mean=projectto3d(hole), scale=0.01, opacity=0.5) A densification control mechanism that uses an exponentially ascending gradient threshold to regulate splitting and cloning during training. name: Exponentially Ascending Gradient Threshold
head: Exponential grad thresh
body: A densification control mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses an exponentially ascending gradient threshold to regulate the splitting and cloning of Gaussians during training. It solves the trade-off between early-stage convergence speed and late-stage overfitting by allowing aggressive densification when few Gaussians exist and restricting it as the scene becomes dense. It sets itself apart from static threshold methods by dynamically adjusting the sensitivity of densification decisions based on the normalized training progress. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current training iteration i, total training iterations i{\max}, initial threshold Ts, final threshold Tf, and modified gradient magnitude \tau'k for Gaussian gk. Output: Boolean decision indicating whether densification (split or clone) should be considered for Gaussian gk. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Ts: Initial gradient threshold value, typically 0.0001. Tf: Final gradient threshold value, typically 0.0004. i{\max}: Total number of training iterations. Formula: The threshold Ti at iteration i is calculated using exponential interpolation between \ln(Ts) and \ln(Tf): Ti = \exp \left( \ln(Ts) \cdot \left(1 - \frac{i}{i{\max}}\right) + \ln(Tf) \cdot \frac{i}{i{\max}} \right) Where Ti is the threshold at iteration i, Ts is the initial threshold, Tf is the final threshold, i is the current iteration, and i{\max} is the total number of iterations. Steps: 1. Compute the normalized iteration progress p = i / i{\max}. 2. Compute the logarithmic interpolation factor L = \ln(Ts) \cdot (1 - p) + \ln(Tf) \cdot p. 3. Exponentiate the result to obtain the current threshold Ti = \exp(L). 4. Compare the modified gradient magnitude \tau'k of Gaussian gk against Ti. 5. If \tau'k \ge Ti, proceed to densification checks (split or clone). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculateexponentialthreshold(i: int, imax: int, Ts: float = 0.0001, Tf: float = 0.0004) -> float: """Calculates the exponentially ascending gradient threshold for the current iteration.""" if imax == 0: return Ts progress = i / imax logTs = math.log(Ts) logTf = math.log(Tf) interpolatedlog = logTs (1 - progress) + logTf progress return math.exp(interpolatedlog) def checkdensification(tauprimek: float, i: int, imax: int, Ts: float = 0.0001, Tf: float = 0.0004) -> bool: """Determines if Gaussian gk should be densified based on the exponential threshold.""" Ti = calculateexponentialthreshold(i, imax, Ts, Tf) return tauprimek >= Ti Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If i{\max} is zero, the progress calculation fails; the implementation should return Ts as a fallback. Boundary Conditions: At i=0, Ti = Ts; at i=i{\max}, Ti = Tf. Precision: The use of logarithms and exponentials ensures smooth transitions. Measured Performance: In ablation studies across 13 scenes, deactivating this component leads to more Gaussian splats being generated, with a minor difference in PSNR compared to other components like extent correction. The number of Gaussians rises much quicker during early training and declines towards the end compared to 3DGS and PixelGS. Strengths: Allows fast convergence in early training by using a low threshold, and prevents overfitting in late training by using a high threshold. Limitations: Does not show a large difference in PSNR compared to other components, suggesting it is more effective for controlling scene compactness than reconstruction quality. The method was proposed in "Improving Adaptive Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the issue that few Gaussians exist at the start of training, hindering convergence, while many Gaussians exist at the end, where additional densification can lead to overfitting. The exponential scheduling was chosen to produce many Gaussians at the beginning and few at the end, as visualized in the source figures. name: SplatFormer Training Objective & Refinement
head: SplatFormer
body: SplatFormer is a learning-based, feed-forward 3D neural module that refines initial 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations to enable robust novel view synthesis from out-of-distribution (OOD) camera angles. It addresses the bias of standard 3DGS optimization, which overfits to input views and fails to generalize to unseen high-elevation perspectives, by applying a point transformer network that predicts attribute residuals. Unlike 2D image restoration methods that suffer from multi-view inconsistencies, SplatFormer operates directly on 3D primitives, ensuring geometric consistency while recovering details lost in OOD views. Input: A set of initial 3D Gaussian splats \{Gk\}{k=1}^K generated from low-elevation input views, where each splat Gk is defined by position pk, scale sk, opacity \alphak, quaternion rotation qk, and spherical harmonics coefficients ak. Output: A set of refined splats \{G'k\}{k=1}^K with updated attributes \{G'k = Gk + \Delta Gk\}, where \Delta Gk = (\Delta pk, \Delta sk, \Delta \alphak, \Delta qk, \Delta ak) are the predicted residuals. The network processes a point cloud of size K. Input Features: Positions pk are normalized to [0, 1]^3. Latent Features: Each splat is assigned a V-dimensional feature vector vk \in \mathbb{R}^V, where V=96. Grid Pooling: Spatial proximity is handled via grid pooling. The point cloud is voxelized using a grid resolution of 384. The encoder extracts contextual features from the initial splats using a hierarchical architecture based on PTv3. 1. Embedding: Input positions pass through an MLP embedding layer. 2. Down-pooling Stages: Five stages process the features. Stage 1: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 64. Stage 2: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 96. Stage 3: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 128. Stage 4: 6 attention blocks, hidden dim 256. Stage 5: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 512. 3. Down-sampling Grid Pooling: Follows stages 2 through 5, with strides (1, 2, 2, 2) respectively. 4. Up-pooling Stages: Four stages upsample the features. Stage 1: Up-sampling grid pooling (stride 1), followed by 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 256. Stage 2: Up-sampling grid pooling (stride 2), followed by 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 128. Stage 3: Up-sampling grid pooling (stride 2), followed by 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 96. Stage 4: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 96. 5. Output: The encoder outputs feature vectors vk for each splat. The decoder predicts residuals by combining latent features with original attributes. 1. Concatenation: For each splat k, concatenate the latent feature vk with the original attributes Gk. 2. MLP Branches: Five separate MLP branches predict residuals for means, opacity, quaternion, scales, and spherical harmonics. Each branch consists of 4 linear layers with hidden dimension 512. Activations: ReLU for all layers except the last. Mean Residual Normalization: Apply Tanh activation to the final output of the mean residual branch to normalize \Delta pk to [0, 1]. 3. Initialization: Zero-initialize the weights and biases of the final MLP layers in all branches to ensure zero initial residuals. The model is trained to minimize a combined loss function over rendered images from both input and OOD views: L{\text{SplatFormer}} = L1 + L{\text{LPIPS}} Where: L1 is the photometric loss. L{\text{LPIPS}} is the perceptual loss using the LPIPS metric. 1. Data Generation: Use 33k scenes from ShapeNet and 48k scenes from Objaverse-1.0. Render each scene from 32 low-elevation input views and 9 high-elevation OOD views using Blender. Generate initial 3DGS from low-elevation views by minimizing photometric loss for 10k steps. 2. Optimization: Use the Adam optimizer with a constant learning rate of 3 \times 10^{-5}. Gradient accumulation steps: 4. Total iterations: 150k. Sampling: At each iteration, render 4 target images consisting of 70% OOD views and 30% input views. Gaussian Capping: Cap input Gaussians to 100k. If the initial 3DGS exceeds this, randomly subsample. 1. Initial Reconstruction: Train a standard 3DGS from 32 input views using gsplat for 10k steps. 2. Refinement: Feed the resulting 3DGS point cloud into the trained SplatFormer encoder-decoder to obtain refined attributes. 3. Rendering: Render the refined splats using the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline. Unverified code. Standard grid pooling aggregates features per voxel. return features, points class GridPoolingUpsample(nn.Module): def init(self, stride, gridres=384): super().init() self.stride = stride self.gridres = gridres def forward(self, features, points): # Not given in the sources. Standard grid upsampling interpolates features. return features, points class AttentionBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddendim): super().init() self.hiddendim = hiddendim def forward(self, features, points): # Not given in the sources. Standard PTv3 attention over spatial proximity. return features class SplatFormerEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self, V=96): super().init() self.V = V self.embedding = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64)) downstages = [(2, 64), (2, 96), (2, 128), (6, 256), (2, 512)] self.downblocks = nn.ModuleList() self.downpoolings = nn.ModuleList() for i, (numblocks, hiddendim) in enumerate(downstages): for in range(numblocks): self.downblocks.append(AttentionBlock(hiddendim)) if i > 0: stride = [1, 2, 2, 2][i-1] self.downpoolings.append(GridPooling(stride=stride, gridres=384)) upstages = [(2, 256), (2, 128), (2, 96), (2, 96)] self.upblocks = nn.ModuleList() self.uppoolings = nn.ModuleList() for i, (numblocks, hiddendim) in enumerate(upstages): if i < len(upstages) - 1: stride = [1, 2, 2, 2][i] self.uppoolings.append(GridPoolingUpsample(stride=stride, gridres=384)) for in range(numblocks): self.upblocks.append(AttentionBlock(hiddendim)) def forward(self, points): x = self.embedding(points) downidx = 0 blockidx = 0 for i in range(len(downstages)): numblocks, = downstages[i] for in range(numblocks): x = self.downblocksblockidx blockidx += 1 if i > 0: x, points = self.downpoolingsdownidx downidx += 1 upidx = 0 blockidx = 0 for i in range(len(upstages)): if i < len(upstages) - 1: x, points = self.uppoolingsupidx upidx += 1 numblocks, = upstages[i] for in range(numblocks): x = self.upblocksblockidx blockidx += 1 return x class ResidualMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, indim, outdim, ismean=False): super().init() self.ismean = ismean self.fc1 = nn.Linear(indim, 512) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(512, 512) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(512, 512) self.fc4 = nn.Linear(512, outdim) nn.init.zeros(self.fc4.weight) nn.init.zeros(self.fc4.bias) def forward(self, x): x = F.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc2(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc3(x)) out = self.fc4(x) if self.ismean: out = torch.tanh(out) return out class SplatFormerDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self, V=96): super().init() # 5 branches: means, opacity, quaternion, scales, SH coefficients # SH coefficients dimension depends on degree, assumed 10 here for example self.branches = nn.ModuleList([ ResidualMLP(V + 10, 5, ismean=(i==0)) for i in range(5) ]) def forward(self, features, initialsplats): residuals = [] for branch in self.branches: combined = torch.cat([features, initialsplats], dim=-1) residuals.append(branch(combined)) return residuals def trainstep(model, initialgs, targetcameras, targetgtimages, optimizer): # Normalize positions to [0, 1]^3 points = initialgs.positions / 255.0 # Encode features = model.encoder(points) # Decode residuals residuals = model.decoder(features, initialgs) # Compute refined splats refinedgs = initialgs + residuals # Render images (standard 3DGS rasterization) targetimages = render(refinedgs, targetcameras) # Compute loss: L1 + LPIPS l1 = F.l1loss(targetimages, targetgtimages) lpips = perceptualloss(targetimages, targetgtimages) loss = l1 + lpips optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss def infer(model, inputimages): # Train initial 3DGS by minimizing photometric loss for 10k steps initialgs = traininitial3dgs(inputimages, steps=10000) points = initialgs.positions / 255.0 features = model.encoder(points) residuals = model.decoder(features, initialgs) return initialgs + residuals Gaussian Count: If the initial 3DGS exceeds 100k Gaussians, they must be randomly subsampled before feeding into SplatFormer. Memory Consumption: GPU memory usage depends on the spatial distribution of Gaussians, not just the count. A spatially uniform distribution with high entropy consumes more memory than a concentrated distribution. Initialization: Final MLP layers must be zero-initialized to ensure the initial output matches the input 3DGS, preventing instability at the start of training. Mean Normalization: The Tanh activation on mean residuals restricts updates to [0, 1]. Ensure input positions are normalized to [0, 1]^3 to match this range. Training: Requires approximately 3000 GPU hours on RTX-2080Ti for data generation and 2 days on 8 RTX-4090s for model training (150k iterations). Inference Memory: Consumes ~900 MB GPU memory for 70k–100k Gaussians on an RTX-4090. Inference Speed: ~108 ms per feed-forward pass for 70k–100k Gaussians on an RTX-4090. Scalability: Supports up to 4 million Gaussians on an RTX-4090, though memory usage scales with spatial entropy. Strengths: Robust to OOD views (high elevation); ensures 3D consistency; faster than per-scene optimization; generalizes across object categories. Limitations: Struggles with fine-grained details and complex textures; efficiency bottleneck remains in training; unbounded scenes with uniform distributions increase memory consumption and remain a direction for future efficiency improvements. Use when novel view synthesis is required from high-elevation (top-down) OOD views where standard 3DGS fails. Use when 3D consistency is critical and 2D denoising methods introduce artifacts. Avoid for scenes with very fine geometric details that the model cannot recover. Avoid for unbounded scenes with large, uniform background noise, as this increases memory consumption significantly. SplatFormer was introduced in a paper published at ICLR 2025. It addresses the limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting, which is optimized per-scene and biased towards input views, making it poor for generalizable novel view synthesis from unseen angles. The method leverages a large-scale dataset (ShapeNet and Objaverse-1.0) to learn data-driven priors for refining Gaussian attributes. It builds on the Point Transformer v3 (PTv3) architecture for efficient point cloud processing. name: MCMC-based 3DGS / SGLD for 3DGS
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting as MCMC / SGLD, MCMC-based 3DGS, SGLD for 3DGS
body: This method reformulates 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by treating the set of 3D Gaussians as random samples drawn from an underlying probability distribution describing the scene, specifically as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples. It converts conventional 3DGS updates into Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) updates by introducing a noise term to promote sample exploration, thereby removing the need for manual densification heuristics like cloning, splitting, and opacity resetting. Unlike sibling methods that rely on complex gradient thresholds or hard constraints, this approach relies on probabilistic state transitions and regularization to manage Gaussian population. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera poses \boldsymbol{\theta}, ground-truth images \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{x}), initial set of N 3D Gaussians. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (oi, \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \mathbf{c}i) and rendered images. Data Structures: The state consists of a list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i stores: oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D center position. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (often parameterized as rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}). \mathbf{c}i: Spherical Harmonics coefficients. Numbered Steps: 1. Rendering: For a given camera pose \boldsymbol{\theta} and pixel \mathbf{x}, sort the N Gaussians by distance to the camera. Compute the rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) using alpha blending: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{c}i \alphai(\mathbf{x}) \left[ \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(\mathbf{x})) \right] where \mathbf{c}i is the color derived from Spherical Harmonics based on pose \boldsymbol{\theta}. 2. Opacity Calculation: Compute the opacity \alphai(\mathbf{x}) for the i-th Gaussian at pixel \mathbf{x}: \alphai(\mathbf{x}) = oi \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i; \boldsymbol{\theta}))^T \mathcal{R}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}i)^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i; \boldsymbol{\theta}))\right) where \mathcal{R} is the camera projection operation. 3. Loss Computation: Calculate the training loss \mathcal{L}{\text{orig}} as a weighted sum of L1 and D-SSIM losses: \mathcal{L}{\text{orig}} = (1 - \lambda{\text{D-SSIM}}) \cdot \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{\text{D-SSIM}} \cdot \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} where \mathcal{L}1 is the average L1 error between \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{x}), and \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} is the D-SSIM loss. The weight \lambda{\text{D-SSIM}} is typically 0.2. 4. SGLD Update (Exploration): Compute gradients \nabla \mathcal{L}{\text{orig}} with respect to Gaussian parameters. Update parameters using Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics by adding noise to the gradient step. This replaces the standard deterministic optimizer step, allowing Gaussians to explore the scene landscape naturally without manual densification. 5. Relocation (Deterministic State Transition): Implement a relocation strategy to handle "dead" Gaussians (those with low opacity). Identify "dead" Gaussians (low opacity) and "live" Gaussians (high opacity). Move dead Gaussians to locations of live Gaussians. Crucial Constraint: Ensure the composition of the relocated (cloned) Gaussians renders the same images as before relocation to preserve sample probability and prevent training instability. Pitfall: Cloning at Gaussian centers alone is insufficient; the whole Gaussian must be considered to ensure the rendering remains equal and MCMC sampling remains optimal. 6. Regularization: Apply L1-regularization to encourage efficient use of Gaussians. This regularizer is applied to both opacity and scale, promoting the removal of unused Gaussians by encouraging them to "disappear" if unnecessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Render distances = [np.linalg.norm(g.mu - camerapose.center) for g in gaussians] sortedindices = np.argsort(distances) sortedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in sortedindices] renderedimage = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) accumulatedalpha = np.zeros((H, W)) for g in sortedgaussians: projectedmu = projectpoint(g.mu, camerapose) if projectedmu is None: continue sigma2d = projectcovariance(g.sigma, camerapose, g.mu) sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(sigma2d) diff = pixelcoords - projectedmu mahal = np.sum(diff @ sigmainv diff, axis=-1) alpha = g.o np.exp(-0.5 mahal) alpha = np.clip(alpha, 0, 1).reshape(H, W) color = getshcolor(g.shcoeffs, camerapose.viewdir) transmittance = 1.0 - accumulatedalpha renderedimage += color alpha transmittance[:,:, np.newaxis] accumulatedalpha += alpha transmittance # 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cloning Insufficiency: Cloning Gaussians only at their centers is insufficient to preserve the rendering probability distribution; the entire Gaussian's spatial extent must be considered to ensure the rendering remains equal. Initialization: The method provides robustness to initialization, though the MCMC chain may require more steps to converge from poor starting states. Precision: The exponential term in opacity calculation can lead to underflow for distant Gaussians. Clipping or masking Gaussians outside the view frustum is recommended. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS per step, but may require more steps for convergence due to the stochastic nature of SGLD. Memory Complexity: Same as 3DGS, storing N Gaussians. Strengths: Improved rendering quality, easy control over the number of Gaussians, and robustness to initialization. Removes the need for complex heuristics like cloning, splitting, and opacity resetting. When to use: When robustness to initialization is critical, or when manual densification heuristics are problematic. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of noise addition and relocation logic is prohibitive. This method reformulates 3D Gaussian Splatting by treating the set of 3D Gaussians as MCMC samples, converting conventional updates into SGLD updates. name: Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Deblur-3D-GS
body: Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting is a real-time deblurring framework that reconstructs sharp 3D scenes from blurry input images by manipulating the covariance matrices and means of 3D Gaussians using a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) during training. Unlike volumetric rendering-based methods like Deblur-NeRF which require seconds per image, this method uses differentiable rasterization to achieve real-time inference speeds exceeding 800 FPS while handling both defocus and camera motion blur. It addresses the sparse point clouds caused by blurry inputs through K-nearest-neighbor interpolation and depth-based pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of blurry images, camera poses, and an initial sparse point cloud obtained from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Outputs: A set of optimized 3D Gaussians (position x, rotation r, scale s, opacity \sigma, spherical harmonics coefficients) that represent the sharp scene. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting data structures: 3D Gaussian Gj: Characterized by position xj \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \sigmaj \in \mathbb{R}, rotation rj (quaternion), scale sj \in \mathbb{R}^3, and spherical harmonics coefficients. MLP F\theta: A neural network with 4 layers. The first 3 layers are shared (64 hidden units, ReLU activation, Xavier initialization). The last 3 layers are single-layer heads producing deltas \delta x, \delta r, \delta s. Point Cloud P: A set of 3D points with associated colors, initially from SfM. Positional Encoding: Inputs to the MLP are processed using positional encoding \gamma(p): \gamma(p) = \big (\sin (2^k\pi p), \cos (2^k \pi p)\big){k=0}^{L-1} where L is the number of frequencies. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compensation for Sparse Point Cloud: After N{st} training iterations, add extra points to compensate for sparse point clouds: Sample Np points from a uniform distribution U(\alpha, \beta), where \alpha and \beta are the min/max position values of the existing point cloud P. For each new point p: Find K nearest neighbors P{knn} from P. Discard neighbors if the distance to p exceeds threshold td. If valid neighbors remain, interpolate color pc from them. Add p with color pc to P. Prune Gaussians based on their position to keep more Gaussians on the far plane, using a pruning threshold multiplier wp. 2. Blur Modeling via MLP (Training Only): The MLP F\theta transforms Gaussian attributes to simulate blur. The specific transformation depends on the blur type. Defocus Blur: The MLP outputs scaling deltas (\delta rj, \delta sj): (\delta rj, \delta sj) = F\theta \Big (\gamma (xj), rj, sj, \gamma (v) \Big) where v is the viewing direction. Transform the attributes to obtain \hat{r}j and \hat{s}j: \hat {r}j=rj\cdot \text {min}(1.0, ~\lambda s \delta rj + (1-\lambda s)) \hat {s}j=sj\cdot \text {min}(1.0, ~\lambda s \delta sj + (1-\lambda s)) where \lambdas is a scaling factor for optimization stability. The transformed Gaussian is G(xj, \hat{r}j, \hat{s}j). Camera Motion Blur: The MLP outputs M sets of offsets (\delta xj^{(i)}, \delta rj^{(i)}, \delta sj^{(i)}) for i=1 \dots M: \{(\delta xj^{(i)}, \delta rj^{(i)}, \delta sj^{(i)})\}{i=1}^{M} = F\theta \Big (\gamma (xj), rj, sj, \gamma (v) \Big) Compute transformed attributes for each set i: \hat{x}j^{(i)} = xj + \lambdap \delta xj^{(i)} \hat{r}j^{(i)} = rj \cdot \text{min}(1.0, \lambdas \delta rj^{(i)} + (1-\lambdas)) \hat{s}j^{(i)} = sj \cdot \text{min}(1.0, \lambdas \delta sj^{(i)} + (1-\lambdas)) where \lambdap scales the position offset. Rasterize M clean images Ii from the M sets of transformed Gaussians: Ii = \texttt{Rasterize}(\{G(\hat{x}j^{(i)}, \hat{r}j^{(i)}, \hat{s}j^{(i)})\}{j=1}^{NG}) Average them to simulate the blurred image: Ib = \frac {1}{M}\sum {i=1}^{M} Ii 3. Optimization: Optimize the MLP parameters \theta and the 3D Gaussian positions x using the Adam optimizer. The loss is computed between the rendered image Ib (for motion blur) or Ii (for defocus blur) and the ground truth blurry image. 4. Inference: The MLP F\theta is not activated. The scene is rendered using the original, untransformed Gaussians G(xj, rj, sj). This ensures real-time rendering and sharp images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(p, L=10): """Computes positional encoding: gamma(p) = (sin(2^k pi p), cos(2^k pi p)) for k=0..L-1.""" freqbands = 2.0 np.arange(L) # p shape: (..., 3), freqbands shape: (L,) angles = p[..., np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] freqbands[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:, np.newaxis] np.pi enc = np.concatenate([np.sin(angles), np.cos(angles)], axis=-2) return enc.reshape(enc.shape[:-2] + (-1,)) def mlpforward(theta, x, r, s, v, L=10): """Standard 4-layer MLP forward pass. First 3 layers shared (64 units, ReLU, Xavier init), last 3 are single-layer heads.""" xenc = positionalencoding(x, L) venc = positionalencoding(v, L) inputvec = np.concatenate([xenc, r, s, venc]) h = inputvec for layer in theta[:3]: h = np.maximum(0, h @ layer.W + layer.b) deltax = h @ theta[3].W + theta[3].b deltar = h @ theta[4].W + theta[4].b deltas = h @ theta[5].W + theta[5].b return deltax, deltar, deltas def rasterize(gaussians, xhat=None, rhat=None, shat=None): """Differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians to an image.""" # Standard 3D-GS rasterization: project to 2D, sort by depth, alpha-blend return np.zeroslike(gaussians[0].color) def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): """Computes reconstruction loss between rendered and ground truth image.""" return np.mean(np.abs(rendered - groundtruth)) def updateparameters(loss, params, optimizerstate): """Adam optimizer step for MLP parameters and Gaussian positions.""" # Standard Adam update step return optimizerstate def addextrapoints(P, Np, K, td): """Adds extra points to point cloud P to compensate for sparsity.""" positions = np.array([p[0] for p in P]) alpha = np.min(positions, axis=0) beta = np.max(positions, axis=0) newpoints = np.random.uniform(alpha, beta, size=(Np, 3)) for ppos in newpoints: dists = np.linalg.norm(positions - ppos, axis=1) kindices = np.argsort(dists)[:K] validneighbors = [] for idx in kindices: if dists[idx] < td: validneighbors.append(P[idx]) if len(validneighbors) > 0: avgcolor = np.mean([n[1] for n in validneighbors], axis=0) P.append((ppos, avgcolor)) positions = np.vstack([positions, ppos]) return P def deblur3dgstrainingstep(gaussians, blurryimage, camerapose, blurtype='defocus', theta=None, lambdas=1e-2, lambdap=1e-2, M=5): """One training step.""" renderedimage = None for j in range(len(gaussians)): xj = gaussians[j].position rj = gaussians[j].rotation sj = gaussians[j].scale v = camerapose.viewdirection gammax = positionalencoding(xj) gammav = positionalencoding(v) if blurtype == 'defocus': deltar, deltas, = mlpforward(theta, xj, rj, sj, v) scaler = np.minimum(1.0, lambdas deltar + (1 - lambdas)) scales = np.minimum(1.0, lambdas deltas + (1 - lambdas)) rhat = rj scaler shat = sj scales renderedimage = rasterize(gaussians, rhat=rhat, shat=shat) elif blurtype == 'motion': images = [] deltas = mlpforward(theta, xj, rj, sj, v) # deltas contains M sets of (deltax, deltar, deltas) for i in range(M): deltax = deltas[0][i] deltar = deltas[1][i] deltas = deltas[2][i] xhat = xj + lambdap deltax scaler = np.minimum(1.0, lambdas deltar + (1 - lambdas)) scales = np.minimum(1.0, lambdas deltas + (1 - lambdas)) rhat = rj scaler shat = sj scales imgi = rasterize(gaussians, xhat=xhat, rhat=rhat, shat=shat) images.append(imgi) renderedimage = np.mean(images, axis=0) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, blurryimage) updateparameters(loss, theta, gaussians) return loss def deblur3dgsinference(gaussians, camerapose): """Inference: Render sharp image using original Gaussians.""" image = rasterize(gaussians) return image Parameters: \lambdas: Scaling factor for defocus blur deltas (\delta r, \delta s). Value: 10^{-2}. \lambdap: Scaling factor for motion blur position offset (\delta x). Value: 10^{-2}. Np: Number of additional points. Value: Up to 200,000, proportional to point cloud extent. td: Distance threshold for neighbor validity. Value: 2. K: Number of neighbors for interpolation. Value: 4. MLP Learning Rate: 10^{-3}. Position Learning Rate: 1.6 \times 10^{-3}. MLP Hidden Units: 64. M: Number of sets for motion blur. Value: 5. N{st}: Iterations to start adding extra points. Value: 2,500. Pruning threshold multiplier wp: Value: 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Point Clouds: Blurry inputs cause SfM to fail, leading to sparse point clouds, especially at far distances. The method compensates by adding points via KNN interpolation and pruning based on depth to retain far-plane Gaussians. Inference Speed: The MLP is strictly disabled during inference. Activating it would degrade performance and is not part of the standard 3D-GS pipeline. Precision: The min operation clips the scaling factors to 1.0 to prevent excessive dispersion. Time Complexity: Training involves MLP forward/backward passes and rasterization of M sets of Gaussians for motion blur, making it more expensive than standard 3D-GS training. Inference is identical to standard 3D-GS, offering real-time performance. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the MLP parameters and, for motion blur training, rendering M images per step. Inference memory is standard 3D-GS. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art PSNR and SSIM on real camera motion blur and defocus blur datasets. Rendering speed exceeds 800 FPS (e.g., 961 FPS on the 'Girl' scene). Strengths: Real-time inference; handles both defocus and motion blur; works with sparse SfM point clouds from blurry images. Limitations: Requires training with the MLP; performance depends on the quality of the initial SfM point cloud (mitigated by point addition). Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting was proposed by B. Lee et al. in 2024. It is the first deblurring algorithm for 3D-GS, addressing the limitations of NeRF-based deblurring methods (like Deblur-NeRF, DP-NeRF, PDRF) which rely on volumetric rendering and are slow. It builds on the 3D-GS framework. Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73636-08, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Augmented Radiance Field
head: Error-Driven Gaussian Supplementation, Enhanced Gaussian Splatting, Error-Driven Compensation Strategy, Gaussian supplementation strategy
body: Augmented Radiance Field is a post-enhancement framework that improves 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes by adding Gaussian kernels with view-dependent opacity to explicitly model specular components. It solves the problem that standard spherical harmonics (SH) cannot decouple diffuse and specular radiance, leading to poor reconstruction of sharp highlights and material artifacts. Unlike standard 3DGS which assigns SH coefficients to every primitive, this method uses distinct primitives for diffuse and specular components, avoiding the memory and stability issues of high-order SH. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained 3DGS scene (set of 3D Gaussian primitives with position, scale, rotation, SH color, and opacity) and a set of training views. Output: An augmented radiance field containing the original 3D Gaussians plus a set of newly added "enhanced" Gaussians with view-dependent opacity. Data Structures: The method introduces a new type of Gaussian primitive. While the original 3DGS primitives retain their standard attributes, the new primitives are initialized in 2D image space and mapped to 3D. Enhanced Gaussian Attributes: Position (\mathbf{p}): 3D world coordinates. Scale (\mathbf{s}): 3D vector defining the extent. Rotation (\mathbf{q}): 4D quaternion. Opacity (\alpha): Scalar, modulated by a view-dependent function. View-dependent Opacity Parameters: Parameters controlling the "opacity lobe" (maximum extent and sharpness), adapted from the Phong shading model. Color: Standard SH or RGB, typically handled by the diffuse component or shared with the base primitive it supplements. Method Steps: 1. Screen-Space Initialization: Render the current image using the existing 3DGS primitives. Calculate the per-pixel rendering loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS) between the rendered image and the ground truth. Allocate new 2D Gaussian kernels in screen space. The number of new Gaussians is fixed at 10% of the current count of existing Gaussians. Allocation is proportional to the loss values per viewpoint; regions with higher residuals receive more new Gaussians. 2. Screen-Space Optimization: Optimize only the parameters of these additional 2D Gaussians (position, scale, rotation, opacity parameters) to minimize the rendering loss in image space. The original 3D Gaussian parameters are frozen during this phase. Prune 2D Gaussians with insufficient opacity or excessively small scales. 3. Inverse Projection (Back-Projection): Map the optimized 2D Gaussians from image space to world space. This is the inverse of the standard Gaussian Splatting projection. This projection is executed in parallel on the CPU. The result is a set of 3D enhanced Gaussians positioned in regions of high reconstruction error. 4. Joint Optimization: Integrate the new 3D enhanced Gaussians into the scene. Freezing Strategy: Freeze the position, scale, rotation, and color (SH coefficients) of the original Gaussian primitives. Make the opacity of the original Gaussian primitives optimizable (using SparseAdam) to prevent over-occlusion by the new, potentially shallower Gaussians. Apply full parameter optimization (position, scale, rotation, opacity, view-dependent parameters) to the newly added enhanced Gaussians (using Adam). Use the differentiable rendering pipeline to jointly optimize all parameters, minimizing the photometric loss. 5. Incremental Densification: The process is iterative. Every 200 iterations, add new Gaussians equal to 20% of the current total count. Repeat steps 1-4 for each increment. Total optimization iterations are set to 30 times the size of the training dataset. 6. Fine-Tuning: After sufficient kernels are incorporated, perform an additional 1,000 fine-tuning steps with all parameters (including original opacities and new enhanced Gaussians) jointly optimized. View-Dependent Opacity Model: The enhanced Gaussians use a learnable opacity function adapted from the Phong shading paradigm. The opacity \alpha is modulated by the viewing direction \mathbf{v} and the surface normal \mathbf{n} (or equivalent reflection vector). The function is controlled by adjustable parameters for the opacity lobe's maximum extent and sharpness, allowing it to model various specular highlight types. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def augmentedradiancefield(scenegaussians, trainingviews, datasetsize): """ Augments a pre-trained 3DGS scene with view-dependent opacity Gaussians. Args: scenegaussians: List of original 3D Gaussian primitives. trainingviews: List of training camera poses and images. datasetsize: Number of training views. Returns: Augmented scene with original and enhanced Gaussians. """ # Hyperparameters from initialratio = 0.10 incrementratio = 0.20 incrementinterval = 200 totaliterations = 30 datasetsize finetuningsteps = 1000 enhancedgaussians = [] allgaussians = list(scenegaussians) # Phase 1: Incremental Densification & Optimization for iteration in range(totaliterations): # 1. Render and compute loss per view losses = [] for view in trainingviews: img = render3dgs(allgaussians, view) losses.append(computeloss(img, view.gtimage)) # 2. Allocate new 2D Gaussians in screen space if iteration == 0: numnew2d = int(len(scenegaussians) initialratio) elif iteration % incrementinterval == 0: numnew2d = int(len(allgaussians) incrementratio) else: numnew2d = 0 if numnew2d > 0: new2dgaussians = allocate2dgaussians(losses, numnew2d, trainingviews) # 3. Optimize 2D Gaussians in image space for in range(incrementinterval): for view in trainingviews: img = render2dgaussians(view, new2dgaussians, scenegaussians) loss = computeloss(img, view.gtimage) optimize2dgaussians(new2dgaussians, loss) # 4. Prune 2D Gaussians new2dgaussians = prune2dgaussians(new2dgaussians) # 5. Inverse projection to 3D (parallel on CPU) new3dgaussians = inverseproject2dto3d(new2dgaussians, trainingviews) enhancedgaussians.extend(new3dgaussians) allgaussians.extend(new3dgaussians) # 6. Joint Optimization (every iteration) for view in trainingviews: img = render3dgs(allgaussians, view) loss = computeloss(img, view.gtimage) updateoriginalopacity(scenegaussians, loss) updateenhancedgaussians(enhancedgaussians, loss) # Phase 2: Fine-Tuning for in range(finetuningsteps): for view in trainingviews: img = render3dgs(allgaussians, view) loss = computeloss(img, view.gtimage) updateoriginalopacity(scenegaussians, loss) updateenhancedgaussians(enhancedgaussians, loss) return allgaussians def render3dgs(gaussians, view): """Differentiable 3D Gaussian rasterization returning an RGB image.""" return rasterize3dgaussians(gaussians, view.cameramatrix) def render2dgaussians(view, enhanced2d, basegaussians): """Renders base 3D Gaussians as background, then composites 2D screen-space Gaussians on top.""" bg = render3dgs(basegaussians, view) return composite2dgaussians(bg, enhanced2d, view.projectionmatrix) def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): """Computes photometric loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS).""" return torch.mean(torch.abs(rendered - groundtruth)) def allocate2dgaussians(losses, count, views): """Samples 'count' 2D Gaussian centers in screen space, weighted by per-view loss.""" weights = torch.tensor(losses) / torch.sum(losses) selectedviews = torch.multinomial(weights, count, replacement=True) return [create2dgaussian(view) for view in selectedviews] def optimize2dgaussians(gaussians, loss): """Gradient descent step for 2D Gaussian parameters.""" loss.backward() for g in gaussians: g.position -= 0.01 g.position.grad g.scale -= 0.01 g.scale.grad g.opacity -= 0.01 g.opacity.grad def prune2dgaussians(gaussians): """Removes Gaussians with opacity below threshold or scale below minimum.""" return [g for g in gaussians if g.opacity > 0.01 and max(g.scale) > 0.001] def inverseproject2dto3d(gaussians2d, views): """Back-projects 2D screen-space Gaussians to 3D world coordinates using camera intrinsics/extrinsics.""" gaussians3d = [] for g in gaussians2d: p3d = unprojectscreentoworld(g.position2d, g.scale2d, g.cameramatrix) gaussians3d.append(create3dgaussian(p3d, g.scale, g.rotation, g.opacity, g.viewparams)) return gaussians3d def updateoriginalopacity(gaussians, loss): """Sparse gradient update for opacity of visible original primitives.""" loss.backward() for g in gaussians: if g.visible: g.opacity -= 0.01 g.opacity.grad def updateenhancedgaussians(gaussians, loss): """Full parameter gradient update for enhanced primitives.""" loss.backward() for g in gaussians: g.position -= 0.01 g.position.grad g.scale -= 0.01 g.scale.grad g.rotation -= 0.01 g.rotation.grad g.opacity -= 0.01 g.opacity.grad g.viewparams -= 0.01 g.viewparams.grad Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundancy: Naively assigning extra parameters to every primitive causes significant redundancy because specular highlights are sparse. The method avoids this by only adding enhanced Gaussians where needed. Over-occlusion: New Gaussians may have shallower depths than pre-existing ones, causing over-occlusion. This is mitigated by making original opacities optimizable. Visibility Constraints: Surface Gaussians are only observable within their outward-facing hemisphere, making SH inefficient for view-dependent cases. The enhanced Gaussians handle this by being view-dependent. Precision: The inverse projection step requires careful handling of depth and camera matrices to avoid artifacts. Time Complexity: The method adds an incremental densification phase. The total iterations are 30 \times N (where N is dataset size), plus 1,000 fine-tuning steps. Each iteration involves rendering and optimization. The inverse projection is done in parallel on CPU. Memory Complexity: Adds 10% of new Gaussians initially, increasing by 20% every 200 iterations. This is significantly less memory than using high-order SH for all primitives. Performance: Mip-NeRF 360: PSNR 28.96, SSIM 0.849 (with MCMC, sh=3). Tanks&Temples: PSNR 25.06, SSIM 0.872 (with MCMC, sh=3). Deep Blending: PSNR 30.22, SSIM 0.909 (with MCMC, sh=3). NeRF Synthetic: PSNR 34.03, SSIM 0.970 (with MCMC, sh=3). Strengths: Decouples diffuse and specular components; works with low-order SH (sh=2 or sh=3); plug-and-play post-enhancement; captures fine specular spots. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained scene; adds complexity to the rendering pipeline; may not be necessary for rough surfaces with limited illumination. Origin: Proposed by Yixin Yang, Bojian Wu, Yang Zhou, and Hui Huang from Shenzhen University and Tencent Games. Paper: "Augmented Radiance Field: A General Framework for Enhanced Gaussian Splatting". Date: February 23, 2026 (arXiv:2602.19916v1). Context: Addresses the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting's reliance on spherical harmonics for color encoding, which cannot separate diffuse and specular components effectively. Inspired by Phong shading. Augmented Radiance Field: A General Framework for Enhanced Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.19916, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Frequency Regularization for Densification
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Progressive Frequency Regularization, FreGS
body: Frequency Regularization for Densification (FreGS) addresses the over-reconstruction issue in 3D Gaussian Splatting, where high-variance image regions are covered by a few large Gaussians, leading to blur and artifacts. Unlike standard 3D-GS which relies solely on pixel-wise L1 loss in the spatial domain, FreGS minimizes the discrepancy between the frequency spectrum of the rendered image and the ground truth in the Fourier space. This approach significantly increases pixel gradients within over-reconstruction regions, enabling a coarse-to-fine densification process guided by progressive frequency annealing. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sparse point cloud generated by Structure-from-Motion (SfM); ground truth images I for the training views. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (covariance \Sigma, center p, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients c) with densified geometry. Data Structures 3D Gaussian: Defined by covariance matrix \Sigma, center position p, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c. The covariance matrix \Sigma is parameterized by a scaling matrix and a rotation matrix for differentiable optimization. Frequency Spectrum: Complex-valued arrays representing the amplitude F(u, v) and phase \angle F(u, v) of the image in the Fourier domain. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize a set of 3D Gaussians from the sparse point cloud generated by Structure-from-Motion. 2. Rendering: Splat the 3D Gaussians to obtain 2D Gaussians and render the image \hat{I} using standard \alpha-blending. The color C of a pixel is computed by blending N ordered 2D Gaussians overlapping the pixel: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci and \alphai are derived from the i-th 2D Gaussian's covariance matrix, spherical harmonics coefficients, and opacity. 3. Frequency Transformation: Generate the frequency spectrum \hat{F} of the rendered image \hat{I} and the frequency spectrum F of the ground truth I by applying a Fourier transformation. 4. Discrepancy Computation: Compute the discrepancy in amplitude F(u, v) and phase \angle F(u, v) in the Fourier space between the rendered and ground truth spectra. 5. Filtering: Apply a low-pass filter Hl and a dynamic high-pass filter Hh to extract low-to-high frequency components progressively. 6. Densification: Perform Gaussian densification guided by the frequency regularization: Under-reconstruction: Clone Gaussians in regions with missing geometric features. Over-reconstruction: Divide large Gaussians into multiple smaller Gaussians in large high-variance regions. 7. Frequency Annealing: Use frequency annealing to progressively regularize from low-frequency signals to high-frequency signals, achieving coarse-to-fine Gaussian densification. Low-frequency signals encode large-scale structures (easier to model), while high-frequency signals encode local details (harder to model). 8. Termination: Gaussian densification is terminated after the 15,000th iteration, consistent with the standard 3D-GS protocol. Pseudocode Unverified code.
