name: Error-Guided Redistribution
body: Error-Guided Redistribution is a family of training optimization strategies for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that addresses reconstruction artifacts and detail loss by dynamically adjusting the spatial distribution of Gaussian primitives based on rendering errors or gradient magnitudes. Unlike standard densification which adds primitives globally or based on simple gradient thresholds, these methods specifically target regions with persistent coarse-scale errors or "hard" gradients, either by reallocating a fixed budget of Gaussians, growing defective primitives, or controlling density via online sparse statistics. All methods in this family operate during the training phase to refine the Gaussian set \{Gi\} without altering the inference-stage alpha-blending rendering pipeline. The core mechanism involves identifying "defective" or "suboptimal" Gaussians based on error metrics (e.g., SSIM, L2 loss) or gradient statistics, and then modifying their parameters or positions to improve reconstruction fidelity. Key shared technical components include: 1. Error/Gradient Identification: Methods compute metrics to identify Gaussians that contribute to high rendering error or possess significant individual view-space gradients. This often involves computing per-pixel or per-Gaussian statistics such as blending weights wi, positional gradients \nabla{\mui} L, or structural similarity indices. 2. Primitive Modification: Identified Gaussians undergo modification. This may involve: Growth: Duplicating and perturbing "hard" Gaussians to recover missing details. Reallocation: Moving low-contribution Gaussians to high-error regions while preserving the total Gaussian count. Density Control: Dynamically splitting or pruning Gaussians based on percentile thresholds of accumulated error statistics. 3. Optimizer Reset: When new Gaussians are created or existing ones are significantly modified (e.g., relocated), their optimizer states (momentum and variance) are reset to allow for rapid convergence in the new configuration. 4. Fixed Budget or Adaptive Count: Some variants (like EGR) strictly maintain a fixed number of Gaussians N during reallocation, while others (like HGS and EDC) allow the count to increase via densification. Hard Gaussian Splatting (HGS) addresses rendering artifacts caused by the smoothing effect of average view-space positional gradients. It identifies "hard Gaussians"—primitives with significant individual view-space gradients or noticeable local rendering errors—and grows them to recover missing details. It differs from siblings like Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation by focusing on growth of defective primitives via multi-view gradient analysis and pixel-level error correlation, rather than reallocation. Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR) redistributes a fixed budget of Gaussian primitives toward regions with persistent coarse-scale reconstruction errors, without increasing the total number of Gaussians. It refines post-densification Gaussian allocation by moving low-contribution (LC) Gaussians to high-error (HE) regions within a fixed Gaussian set, using contribution- and error-aware selection. Unlike methods using explicit rollback, EGR uses adaptive relocation count, parameter reset, and continued optimization. Error-Driven Gaussian Density Control (EDC) dynamically allocates model capacity and removes redundant primitives by accumulating and leveraging per-Gaussian statistics corresponding to sparse pixel errors. It differs from siblings like Hard Gaussian Splatting and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation by relying on online sparse pixel statistics and percentile thresholds rather than post-hoc dense error maps or fixed structural cues, making it significantly more efficient in online sparse training settings. Definition: ACO-EGR is a unified framework that integrates Adaptive-scale Color Offset (ACO) and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR) into a multi-scale 3DGS backbone to jointly address scale-dependent color mismatch and primitive-allocation imbalance. Steps: The framework augments a multi-scale 3DGS backbone with two training-stage modules: ACO adapts per-Gaussian color across rendering scales through scale-specific DC color offsets, while EGR refines post-densification Gaussian allocation by moving low-contribution Gaussians to high-error regions. Comparison: Unlike existing methods that keep fixed color and spatial allocation after densification, ACO-EGR adapts both Gaussian color and primitive allocation together. It improves rendering quality without modifying the inference-stage rendering process itself; it only changes the training/optimization of the Gaussian parameters. The concept of error-guided redistribution in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged from the need to improve multi-scale rendering quality and address artifacts such as blurring and color mismatch that persist after standard densification. The foundational work on Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR) and its integration with Adaptive-scale Color Offset (ACO) was proposed in 2026 by the authors of "Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting". This work demonstrated that adapting Gaussian color and primitive allocation together improves scale-consistent 3DGS rendering on benchmarks like Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending, particularly at coarse scales. Subsequent variants, such as Hard Gaussian Splatting and Error-Driven Gaussian Density Control, have been developed to address specific limitations of gradient averaging and computational efficiency in sparse supervision settings. Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14152713, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Hard Gaussian Splatting
head: REHGS (Rendering Error guided HGS), Rendering Error guided HGS, Rendering Error guided Hard Gaussian Splatting
body: Hard Gaussian Splatting (HGS) is a training-phase densification strategy that addresses artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by growing "hard Gaussians" identified via multi-view significant positional gradients and rendering errors, rather than relying on averaged gradients. It solves the problem where standard 3DGS averaging smooths out individual large gradients and local rendering errors, hindering the growth of defective Gaussians that cause blurring or needle-like artifacts. Unlike its siblings, HGS explicitly decouples the identification of hard Gaussians into two distinct mechanisms: Positional Gradient Driven HGS (PGHGS), which targets cross-view inconsistencies by analyzing the maximum individual view-space gradients, and Rendering Error Guided HGS (REHGS), which targets blurring artifacts by correlating potentially over-large Gaussians with local SSIM errors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The current set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, the current training iteration, the set of training viewpoints \mathcal{V}, and the growth interval M. Outputs: A subset of "hard Gaussians" identified for densification (growth) in the next optimization step. Data Structures: Gaussian Gi: Parameterized by mean vector \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, and opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}. View-space Positional Gradient g{i,j}: The gradient of the rendering loss with respect to the mean \mui of Gaussian Gi under viewpoint j. Contribution Set Si: The set of pixels u in the current image where Gaussian Gi has the maximum contribution. Rendering Model: A 3D Gaussian Gi is splatted to a 2D Gaussian G{i,2D}. The pixel color c(u) is computed via alpha-blending: c(u) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci, \quad wi = \alphai G{i,2D}(u) \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphak G{k,2D}(u)) where wi is the blending weight. Parameters: \tau{grad}: Gradient threshold for Gaussian growing (maintained same as in Scaffold-GS). M: Growing interval for Gaussian growing (maintained same as in Scaffold-GS). k: Index of the largest positional gradient used in PGHGS (set to 3). \lambda: Constant controlling the extent of excavation in PGHGS (set to 1.0). \tau{large}: Threshold to control the extent of potentially large areas for identifying potentially over-large Gaussians (set to 2 \times 10^{-4}). \tau{SSIM}: Threshold to judge rendering quality for identifying hard Gaussians via SSIM (set to 0.7). Algorithm Steps: The method operates during the training phase. For each growth interval of M iterations, the following steps are performed to identify hard Gaussians. 1. Compute View-space Positional Gradients: For each Gaussian Gi and each viewpoint j that observes Gi during the current growth interval M, compute the view-space positional gradient g{i,j} = \nabla{\mui} L. 2. Identify Hard Gaussians via PGHGS (Positional Gradient Driven): For each Gaussian Gi, collect the view-space positional gradients \{g{i,j}\} from all viewpoints j that observed it during the interval M. Sort these gradients by magnitude and select the k largest gradients. Let the set of the k largest magnitudes be \mathcal{G}{i, top-k}. Find the minimum magnitude among these k largest gradients: min\gradi = \min(\mathcal{G}{i, top-k}). If min\gradi \ge \tau{grad}, classify Gi as a hard Gaussian candidate for PGHGS. Note: This strategy exploits cross-view significant positional gradients to uncover hard Gaussians, alleviating rendering inconsistency across views. 3. Identify Hard Gaussians via REHGS (Rendering Error Guided): Step 3.1: Identify Potentially Over-Large Gaussians. For each pixel u in the current rendered image, compute its rendered index idx(u), identifying the Gaussian with maximum contribution: idx(u) = \arg \maxi wi Construct the contribution set Si for each Gaussian Gi: Si = \{ u \mid idx(u) = i, u \in P \} where P is the set of all pixels in the image. Identify Gi as a "potentially over-large" Gaussian if: \|Si\| > \tau{large} \|P\| where \|Si\| is the number of pixels in the set and \|P\| is the total number of pixels. Pitfall: Using only this condition results in false positives because low-textured areas and repetitive textures may also be described by large Gaussians. Step 3.2: Validate with Rendering Errors. For each potentially over-large Gaussian Gi: Project Gi into the current training viewpoint j to obtain the corresponding pixel u{i,j}. Compute the local Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) between the ground truth image Ij and the rendered image \hat{I}j at u{i,j}: SSIM(Ij, \hat{I}j)(u{i,j}). If SSIM(Ij, \hat{I}j)(u{i,j}) < \tau{SSIM}, classify Gi as a hard Gaussian candidate for REHGS. Constraint: Ensure hard Gaussians are seen by at least two views during the M iterations to avoid unstable growth from single-view determination. 4. Densification: Union the sets of hard Gaussians identified by PGHGS and REHGS. Apply the standard 3DGS densification operation (splitting and cloning) to these hard Gaussians. Reset the optimizer states (momentum and variance) for the newly created or modified Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def identifyhardgaussians(gaussians, viewpoints, currentiteration, M, k, taugrad, taularge, taussim): """ Identifies hard Gaussians for densification based on PGHGS and REHGS criteria. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with attributes: mean: R^3 cov: R^3x3 color: R^3 opacity: R gradhistory: List of view-space positional gradients over last M iterations viewhistory: List of viewpoints that observed this Gaussian over last M iterations viewpoints: List of training viewpoints available in current batch/interval currentiteration: Current training iteration M: Growth interval k: Number of largest gradients to consider (default 3) taugrad: Gradient threshold taularge: Threshold for potentially over-large Gaussians (default 2e-4) taussim: SSIM threshold (default 0.7) Returns: setofhardgaussians: Set of Gaussian objects identified as hard """ hardgaussians = set() # --- PGHGS: Positional Gradient Driven --- for G in gaussians: # Collect view-space positional gradients from the last M iterations # Note: In practice, gradients are accumulated or stored per view per iteration viewgradients = [] for v in G.viewhistory: # Retrieve the gradient magnitude for view v during the interval # Assuming gradhistory stores magnitudes or vectors for each view in the interval if v in G.gradhistory: gradmag = norm(G.gradhistory[v]) viewgradients.append(gradmag) if len(viewgradients) == 0: continue # Sort gradients by magnitude and take the k largest sortedgrads = sorted(viewgradients, reverse=True) topkgrads = sortedgrads[:k] # Check if the minimum of the top k gradients exceeds threshold mintopkgrad = min(topkgrads) if mintopkgrad >= taugrad: hardgaussians.add(G) # --- REHGS: Rendering Error Guided --- # Step 1: Render current image and compute contributions renderedimage = renderscene(gaussians, viewpoints) # Returns image and per-pixel max contribution index groundtruthimage = getgroundtruth(viewpoints) # Returns ground truth for current viewpoints # Compute contribution sets for all Gaussians # This requires iterating over all pixels and tracking which Gaussian has max weight contributioncounts = {G: 0 for G in gaussians} pixeltomaxgaussian = {} # Map pixel u to Gaussian G with max wi for u in renderedimage.pixels: # Compute weights wi for all Gaussians covering pixel u # This is typically done during rasterization maxw = -1 maxG = None for G in gaussianscoveringpixel(u): w = computeweight(G, u) if w > maxw: maxw = w maxG = G pixeltomaxgaussian[u] = maxG if maxG is not None: contributioncounts[maxG] += 1 totalpixels = len(renderedimage.pixels) # Identify potentially over-large Gaussians potentiallyoverlarge = [] for G, count in contributioncounts.items(): if count > taularge totalpixels: potentiallyoverlarge.append(G) # Step 2: Validate with SSIM for G in potentiallyoverlarge: # Project G to current viewpoints to find corresponding pixels # We need to check if G causes errors in at least 2 views errorviewscount = 0 for v in G.viewhistory: # Get the pixel uij where G is projected in view v uij = projectgaussiantopixel(G, v) if uij is not None and uij in renderedimage.pixels: # Compute local SSIM # Note: Local SSIM usually requires a window around uij ssimval = computelocalssim(groundtruthimage[v], renderedimage[v], uij) if ssimval < taussim: errorviewscount += 1 # Ensure seen by at least two views to avoid unstable growth if errorviewscount >= 2: hardgaussians.add(G) return hardgaussians def densifyhardgaussians(hardgaussians, gaussians, optimizer): """ Applies densification to hard Gaussians and resets optimizer states. """ newgaussians = [] for G in hardgaussians: # Standard 3DGS split/clone operation # This involves creating child Gaussians with perturbed means and scaled covariances children = splitandclone(G) newgaussians.extend(children) # Remove original G from the active set (or mark for removal) # In 3DGS, splitting replaces the parent with children # Add new Gaussians to the scene gaussians.extend(newgaussians) # Reset optimizer states for new Gaussians for G in newgaussians: optimizer.resetstate(G) return gaussians PGHGS (Positional Gradient driven Hard Gaussian Splatting) is a densification strategy that identifies "hard Gaussians" by analyzing multi-view positional gradients to alleviate cross-view rendering inconsistencies. Unlike standard methods that rely on averaged gradients which may obscure local errors, PGHGS selects Gaussians based on the magnitude of their largest individual view-space gradients, ensuring that regions with significant reconstruction errors are prioritized for growth. REHGS (Rendering Error guided HGS) is a densification strategy that identifies potentially over-large Gaussians causing blurring artifacts, projects them to the image to calculate pixel rendering errors, and considers the Gaussian a hard Gaussian if noticeable errors are detected from multiple viewpoints within the growth interval. It links hard Gaussians with local rendering errors by leveraging Gaussians with maximum contribution to correlate pixel rendering errors. Time Complexity: The identification step requires computing view-space positional gradients for all Gaussians over M iterations, which is O(N \cdot V \cdot M) where N is the number of Gaussians and V is the number of views. The REHGS step requires rendering and computing SSIM for potentially over-large Gaussians, which adds overhead proportional to the number of such Gaussians and the number of views they are observed in. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradient history for each Gaussian over the growth interval M, increasing memory usage by O(N \cdot V) compared to standard 3DGS. Measured Performance: On the Tanks&Temples dataset, HGS achieves superior NVS results compared to standard 3DGS and other baselines. Specifically, for REHGS, varying \tau{SSIM} yields: \tau{SSIM}=0.6 gives PSNR 26.34, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.127; \tau{SSIM}=0.7 gives PSNR 26.36, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126; \tau{SSIM}=0.8 gives PSNR 26.39, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126. Strengths: Effectively resolves blurring and needle-like artifacts by targeting hard Gaussians that standard averaging misses. It can boost both explicit and neural Gaussian methods, showing generalization ability. Limitations: REHGS tends to find noticeable rendering errors but cannot detect some inconspicuous artifacts, which PGHGS probes better. Using only the potentially over-large condition results in false positives in low-textured or repetitive texture areas. When to use: Use when standard 3DGS exhibits strong spurious artifacts, blurring, or needle-like structures in challenging areas due to insufficient Gaussian growth. Hard Gaussian Splatting (HGS) was proposed to address the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in handling challenging areas where the average magnitude of view-space positional gradients fails to drive Gaussian growth. The method was introduced in the paper "Pushing Rendering Boundaries: Hard Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the adaptive density control mechanism of 3DGS and the anchor-based distribution of Scaffold-GS. The code is available at https://github.com/GhiXu/HGS. Pushing Rendering Boundaries: Hard Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04826v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: PGHGS
head: Positional Gradient driven HGS, Positional Gradient driven Hard Gaussian Splatting
body: PGHGS (Positional Gradient driven Hard Gaussian Splatting) is a densification strategy that identifies "hard Gaussians" by analyzing multi-view positional gradients to alleviate cross-view rendering inconsistencies. Unlike standard methods that rely on averaged gradients which may obscure local errors, PGHGS selects Gaussians based on the magnitude of their largest individual view-space gradients, ensuring that regions with significant reconstruction errors are prioritized for growth. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N Gaussians \{Gi\}, their current parameters, and the accumulated view-space positional gradients \{g{i,j}\} for each Gaussian Gi across M training iterations/views. Output: A subset of Gaussians identified as "hard Gaussians" to be densified (cloned/split) in the current growth interval. Data Structures Positional Gradients: For each Gaussian Gi, a list of gradients g{i,j} corresponding to different viewpoints j. The gradient g{i,j} is a vector in view space. Sorted Gradients: A sorted list \{g'{i,1}, \dots, g'{i,n}\} for each Gaussian, ordered by descending norm. Method Steps 1. Compute View-Space Positional Gradients: For each Gaussian Gi and each viewpoint j, compute the view-space positional gradient g{i,j} using the rendering error: g{i,j} = \frac{1}{||P||} \sum{u \in P} eu \frac{\partial Lj}{\partial \mu{i,j}} Where: Lj is the rendering loss under viewpoint j. \mu{i,j} is the pixel-space projection point of Gaussian Gi under viewpoint j. P is the set of total pixel coordinates. eu is the rendering error of pixel u. ||P|| is the number of pixels. The sources define this as the gradient of the average rendering error with respect to the view-space projection point. 2. Sort Gradients: For each Gaussian Gi, sort its n positional gradients across all views in descending order of their norms: \{g'{i,1}, \dots, g'{i,n}\} = \text{sort}{\downarrow}(g{i,1}, \dots, g{i,n}) Where g'{i,k} is the k-th largest positional gradient for Gaussian Gi. 3. Mine Hard Gaussians: A Gaussian Gi is selected as a hard Gaussian if its k-th largest positional gradient satisfies the threshold condition: ||g'{i,k}|| \ge \lambda \tau{grad} Where: k is the number of significant positional gradients considered in the growth interval. \lambda is a weight constant controlling the extent of excavation. \tau{grad} is the base gradient threshold. Parameters k: The rank of the gradient used for selection. Tested values are 1, 2, 3, 4. Lower k relaxes the criterion, producing more growing Gaussians. Higher k degrades metrics because PGHGS cannot mine hard Gaussians sufficiently when k is too large. \lambda: Weight for the threshold. Lower \lambda allows mining more hard Gaussians, improving rendering quality but reducing training efficiency. Higher \lambda degrades PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS while improving training efficiency. \tau{grad}: The gradient threshold. Lowering \tau{grad} to encourage more growth prioritizes well-reconstructed areas, introducing redundant Gaussians and failing to reduce artifacts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Lowering \tau{grad} prioritizes densifying well-reconstructed areas, which introduces redundant Gaussians and fails to reduce artifacts. Reducing k introduces noise that impairs PSNR but improves LPIPS, because LPIPS is evaluated through deep image features which have anti-noise ability. Increasing k degrades almost all rendering metrics. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def selecthardgaussians(gaussians, gradients, k, lambdaval, taugrad): """ Select hard Gaussians based on positional gradients. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with an 'id' attribute. gradients: Dict mapping gaussianid to list of gradient vectors (one per view). k: Integer, rank of gradient to check. lambdaval: Float, threshold weight. taugrad: Float, base gradient threshold. Returns: List of Gaussian objects identified as hard. """ hardgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Get gradients for this Gaussian across all views ggrads = gradients[g.id] # Sort gradients by norm in descending order sortedgrads = sorted(ggrads, key=lambda vec: math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in vec)), reverse=True) # Ensure we have at least k gradients; if not, use the largest available if len(sortedgrads) >= k: kthlargestgrad = sortedgrads[k-1] else: kthlargestgrad = sortedgrads[-1] # Check condition: ||g'i,k|| >= lambda taugrad if math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in kthlargestgrad)) >= lambdaval taugrad: hardgaussians.append(g) return hardgaussians An efficient variant of HGS that adaptively controls the number of hard Gaussians to balance rendering quality and efficiency. It counts the percentage of Gaussians selected by the original growing criterion (Eq. 4) in each growth interval, denoted as Q. During PGHGS, it chooses the top Q Gaussians as hard ones for growing based on the sorted positional gradients \{g'{i,k} | i = 1, \dots, N\}. Time and Memory Complexity Time: Sorting gradients for each Gaussian adds overhead proportional to O(N \cdot M \log M), where N is the number of Gaussians and M is the number of views/iterations. Lower \lambda increases the number of hard Gaussians, which increases training time due to more splatting and optimization. Memory: Requires storing positional gradients for each Gaussian across views. Measured Performance Tanks&Temples Ablation (k variation): k=1: PSNR 26.34, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.123. k=2: PSNR 26.36, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126. k=3: PSNR 26.26, SSIM 0.878, LPIPS 0.131. k=4: PSNR 26.36, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126. Deep Blending Ablation (k variation): k=1: PSNR 30.31, SSIM 0.906, LPIPS 0.211. k=2: PSNR 30.39, SSIM 0.908, LPIPS 0.219. k=3: PSNR 30.40, SSIM 0.908, LPIPS 0.225. k=4: PSNR 30.19, SSIM 0.908, LPIPS 0.230. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Reduces cross-view rendering inconsistency by focusing on local errors rather than averages. Reducing k can improve LPIPS (due to anti-noise ability of deep features) though it may degrade PSNR. Limitations: Lowering \tau{grad} introduces redundant Gaussians in well-reconstructed areas. Increasing k degrades almost all rendering metrics. Higher \lambda improves efficiency but degrades quality. PGHGS was introduced in "Pushing Rendering Boundaries: Hard Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitation of standard positional gradients, which average errors over the entire image and fail to reflect local reconstruction errors, preventing Gaussians from growing in regions with larger local errors. name: Supplementary Point Addition for Sparse Point Clouds
head: Supplementary Point Addition
body: Supplementary Point Addition is a densification technique designed to compensate for the sparsity of 3D Gaussians at the far end of scenes with large depth of field, where Structure-from-Motion (SfM) extraction is poor due to defocus blur. It differs from its siblings by explicitly injecting synthetic points into empty or sparse regions after a fixed number of training iterations, rather than relying on gradient-based densification or geometric replication on tangent planes. This method ensures that distant objects are represented by initial Gaussians, preventing them from being ignored during the adaptive density control phase. Inputs: Existing point cloud P{existing} with positions and colors. Training iteration counter t. Hyperparameters: N{st} (start iteration), Np (number of points), K (KNN neighbors), td (distance threshold). Outputs: Updated point cloud P{new} = P{existing} \cup P{supp}, where P{supp} are the newly added points. Data Structures: P{existing}: List of points, each with position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. P{supp}: List of new points with position \mathbf{x} and interpolated color \mathbf{c}p. Steps: 1. Check Start Condition: If current iteration t < N{st}, terminate. No points are added. 2. Determine Bounds: Calculate the minimum (\alpha) and maximum (\beta) coordinate values across all dimensions of the existing point cloud P{existing}. \alpha = \min{\mathbf{x} \in P{existing}} (\mathbf{x}) \beta = \max{\mathbf{x} \in P{existing}} (\mathbf{x}) Note: The source defines \alpha and \beta as the minimum and maximum values of the position. In implementation, this typically implies finding the bounding box of the existing points. 3. Sample Positions: Generate Np new points P{raw} by sampling uniformly from the distribution U(\alpha, \beta). For each point \mathbf{x}{new} \in P{raw}, sample each coordinate independently from U(\alpha, \beta). 4. Interpolate Colors: For each new point \mathbf{x}{new}: Find the K-Nearest-Neighbors (P{knn}) of \mathbf{x}{new} within P{existing} based on Euclidean distance. Compute the interpolated color \mathbf{c}p from the colors of P{knn}. Implementation Note: The source cites KNN [29] but does not specify the interpolation formula (e.g., inverse distance weighting or simple average). Standard practice for such initialization is inverse distance weighting or uniform averaging. Given the lack of specific formula in, a simple average or uniform weighting is assumed if distances are similar, or inverse distance weighting if specified by the referenced KNN method. For strict adherence to "no guessing," we define the color assignment as an interpolation function f(\mathbf{c}{knn}). 5. Filter by Distance: For each new point \mathbf{x}{new} with nearest neighbor distance d{min}: If d{min} > td, discard \mathbf{x}{new}. Otherwise, add \mathbf{x}{new} with color \mathbf{c}p to P{supp}. 6. Merge: Update the point cloud: P{new} = P{existing} \cup P{supp}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def supplementarypointaddition(existingpoints, currentiteration, Nst, Np, K, td): """ Adds supplementary points to the existing point cloud if the current iteration has reached the start threshold Nst. Args: existingpoints: List of dicts with 'pos' (np.array [3]) and 'color' (np.array [3]). currentiteration: Integer, current training step. Nst: Integer, start iteration for adding points. Np: Integer, number of points to sample. K: Integer, number of neighbors for KNN color interpolation. td: Float, distance threshold to discard points. Returns: Updated list of points. """ if currentiteration < Nst: return existingpoints # Step 2: Determine bounds positions = np.array([p['pos'] for p in existingpoints]) # Find min and max for each dimension mincoords = np.min(positions, axis=0) maxcoords = np.max(positions, axis=0) # Step 3: Sample positions uniformly within the bounding box # U(alpha, beta) implies uniform distribution between min and max per dimension newpositions = np.random.uniform(low=mincoords, high=maxcoords, size=(Np, 3)) newpoints = [] # Precompute KNN structure for efficiency if Np is large, # but for clarity we iterate. for i in range(Np): xnew = newpositions[i] # Step 4: Find K nearest neighbors distances = np.linalg.norm(positions - xnew, axis=1) kindices = np.argsort(distances)[:K] kcolors = np.array([existingpoints[idx]['color'] for idx in kindices]) # Interpolate color. Source does not specify weighting. # Assuming simple average as a baseline for "interpolated color" without distance weighting specified. # If inverse distance weighting is required, it should be implemented here. cp = np.mean(kcolors, axis=0) # Step 5: Check distance threshold mindist = distances[kindices[0]] if mindist <= td: newpoints.append({'pos': xnew, 'color': cp}) # Step 6: Merge updatedpoints = existingpoints + newpoints return updatedpoints Parameters: N{st}: The iteration number at which supplementary point addition begins. Value: 2,500. Np: The number of supplementing points. Value: Proportional to the extent of the point cloud, at most 200,000. K: The number of neighbors for KNN interpolation. Value: 4. td: The minimum distance threshold for discarding points. Value: 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Point Cloud: If P{existing} is empty, bounds \alpha, \beta are undefined. The method assumes a non-empty SfM cloud exists. Precision: The distance threshold td=2 is a fixed value. Its unit (meters, world units) depends on the scene scale. If the scene is scaled differently, this threshold may need adjustment. Color Interpolation: The source does not specify the interpolation kernel. Using simple average may cause color bleeding if neighbors are far apart. Inverse distance weighting is a common alternative but is not explicitly defined in the source. A geometry-only initialization augmentation that replicates points on local tangent planes, targeting sparsely seeded regions peripherally. It is deterministic and relies on geometric relationships rather than uniform sampling. Uses a continuous neural radiance field (MLP) to predict density and position for filling large voids where no initial point cloud exists, differing from the uniform sampling approach. Time Complexity: O(Np \cdot N{existing} \log N{existing}) or O(Np \cdot N{existing}) depending on KNN implementation, where Np is the number of supplementary points and N{existing} is the number of existing points. Memory Complexity: O(Np) for storing the new points. Performance: The method is applied once after N{st}=2,500 iterations. It increases the primitive count by up to 200,000 points. Strengths: Effectively compensates for sparsity in defocus blurry scenes where SfM fails at far distances. Limitations: Adds points uniformly, which may not align perfectly with scene geometry compared to tangent-plane methods. Requires careful tuning of td relative to scene scale. When to Use: Defocus blurry scenes with large depth of field where SfM extraction is poor at the far end. When Not to Use: Scenes with clear SfM initialization or where geometric precision is critical without subsequent densification. The method was introduced in the context of Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting to address the issue of sparse point clouds in defocus blurry scenes. Standard SfM techniques struggle to extract points on the far end of scenes with large depth of field, leading to incomplete 3D Gaussian representations. The technique is part of a broader effort to improve initialization for 3DGS in challenging imaging conditions. name: Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART)
head: DART (Distance-Aware Replication and Training), distance-aware augmentation
body: Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART) is a geometry-only initialization augmentation for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enriches the Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud by replicating points on local tangent planes, specifically targeting sparsely seeded regions in the scene periphery. Unlike depth-based or learned enrichment methods, DART is deterministic and relies solely on the geometric relationship between points and the scene center, adding coverage where SfM extraction is typically poor without modifying the rasterizer or pruning criteria. It serves as a precursor to densification strategies like Age-Gated Densification (AGE), providing a denser initial seed that improves fidelity in sparse areas at the cost of increased primitive count and training time. DART operates as a single, pre-optimization pass over the input SfM point cloud. It does not use depth maps, learned models, or normal estimation. Instead, it constructs a local tangent frame for each point and samples new points on a disk within that plane, where the disk's radius scales with the point's distance from the scene center. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N SfM points P = \{pi\}{i=1}^N, where each pi has a 3D position \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: An augmented set of points P', which includes the original points and newly replicated points. Data Structures: The SfM points are stored as a list or array of 3D coordinates. No persistent data structures are required beyond the temporary storage of the new points during the augmentation phase. Parameters: m: Replication multiplier. Controls the number of extra samples drawn per SfM point. Typical value: m=10 (conservative setting for sparse outdoor scenes). Range swept: \{1, 3, 5, 7, 10\}. \rho{\min}: Minimum density threshold for replication. Value: 0.008. \rho{\max}: Maximum density threshold for replication. Value: 0.04. K{nn}: Number of nearest neighbors used for density estimation. Value: 20. Algorithm Steps: 1. Estimate Scene Center: Compute a robustly estimated scene center \mathbf{c}. The exact method for robust estimation is not specified in the sources. 2. Compute Distances: For each SfM point pi with position \mathbf{x}i, compute its distance from the scene center: di = \|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{c}\|2. 3. Estimate Local Density: For each point pi, estimate its local point cloud density \rhoi using the K{nn} nearest neighbors. The exact formula for \rhoi is not provided in the sources. 4. Determine Replication Radius: Define a radius ri for the tangent disk at pi. The radius grows with distance di. The exact functional form of ri(di) is not provided in the sources. 5. Construct Tangent Frame: For each point pi, construct a local tangent frame. Since DART does not use reliable normals (unlike GeoGaussian), the specific construction method is not detailed in the sources. 6. Replicate Points: For each point pi: If \rho{\min} \le \rhoi \le \rho{\max}, generate m-1 new points on the tangent disk of radius ri centered at \mathbf{x}i. If m=1, no new points are added (DART draws m-1=0 extra samples). The new points are added to the output point set P'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dartaugment(sfmpoints, m=10, rhomin=0.008, rhomax=0.04, knn=20): """ Augments SfM points using Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes. Args: sfmpoints: List of 3D coordinates (N, 3). m: Replication multiplier. rhomin: Minimum density threshold. rhomax: Maximum density threshold. knn: Number of nearest neighbors for density estimation. Returns: augmentedpoints: List of 3D coordinates (N', 3). """ N = len(sfmpoints) points = [list(p) for p in sfmpoints] # Step 1: Estimate Scene Center # Exact robust estimation method not specified in sources. scenecenter = [sum(p[d] for p in points) / N for d in range(3)] # Step 2: Compute Distances distances = [math.sqrt(sum((points[i][d] - scenecenter[d])2 for d in range(3))) for i in range(N)] # Step 3: Estimate Local Density # Exact formula for rhoi not provided in sources. # Standard fallback: inverse of mean distance to KNN neighbors. # Placeholder for KNN search omitted; assume knndistances[i] is computed externally. densities = [1.0 / (sum(knndistances[i]) / knn + 1e-8) for i in range(N)] # Step 4 & 5 & 6: Replicate Points augmentedpoints = [] for i in range(N): pi = points[i] di = distances[i] rhoi = densities[i] # Check density threshold if rhomin <= rhoi <= rhomax: # Step 4: Determine Replication Radius # Exact function ri(di) not provided in sources. # Standard fallback: linear scaling with distance. ri = 0.1 di # Step 5: Construct Tangent Frame # Exact method not provided in sources. # Standard fallback: arbitrary orthonormal basis. ui = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] vi = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Step 6: Replicate Points numnew = m - 1 for j in range(numnew): # Uniform sampling on disk theta = 2.0 math.pi (j / numnew) rsample = ri math.sqrt((j + 1) / numnew) offset = [ rsample (math.cos(theta) ui[d] + math.sin(theta) vi[d]) for d in range(3) ] newpoint = [pi[d] + offset[d] for d in range(3)] augmentedpoints.append(newpoint) # Add original point augmentedpoints.append(pi) return augmentedpoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse SfM: DART is designed for scenes where SfM points are sparse, particularly in the periphery. In densely reconstructed scenes (e.g., Deep Blending's drjohnson), DART has essentially no effect on quality. Density Estimation: The exact formula for local density \rhoi is not provided. Implementers must define a robust density estimator that yields values comparable to the thresholds \rho{\min}=0.008 and \rho{\max}=0.04. Tangent Frame: Since DART does not use normals, the tangent frame construction is ambiguous. Implementers must define a consistent method for generating orthonormal vectors on the tangent plane. Radius Function: The exact relationship between distance di and radius ri is not specified. Implementers must define a scaling function that grows with distance. AGE is a maturity gate for 3D Gaussian Splatting training that prevents densification (splitting and cloning) until a specified training step threshold is reached, thereby pruning unnecessary primitives and controlling memory and time costs. It is designed to work in conjunction with Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART), where DART augments the initial point cloud to improve coverage in sparse regions, and AGE trims the resulting inflated primitive count without degrading reconstruction quality. While competitors like FastGS-Big and Taming-3DGS modify densification criteria or schedules during training, AGE acts as a static maturity gate, deferring eligibility for densification operations. Time and Memory Complexity: DART adds a pre-processing step that scales linearly with the number of SfM points N and the multiplier m. The final Gaussian set is enlarged by 18.6% (from 2.91M to 3.45M points on Mip-NeRF 360 scenes). Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, DART (config 2→4) raises PSNR by 0.22 dB (27.53→27.75), SSIM by 0.013 (0.834→0.847), and LPIPS falls by 0.025 (0.228→0.203). On sparsely seeded Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, LPIPS falls 0.044 on bicycle and 0.024–0.026 on counter and stump. Scaling: The gain is largest on sparsely seeded scenes. On densely reconstructed scenes like Deep Blending's drjohnson, quality is essentially unchanged. Strengths and Limitations: DART is deterministic and does not require depth or external cues. It improves fidelity in sparse regions. However, it increases the final primitive count by 18.6%, raising training time from 24.9 to 31.8 minutes and peak memory from 5.04 to 6.04 GB on Mip-NeRF 360. This increased budget is trimmed by AGE. When to Use: Use DART when the SfM point cloud is sparse, particularly in the scene periphery, and when depth information is unavailable or unreliable. When Not to Use: Avoid DART for densely reconstructed scenes where SfM coverage is already high, as it provides no quality benefit and only increases computational cost. DART was introduced in the paper "DART-3DGS: Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the issue of adaptive density-control rules in 3D Gaussian Splatting that can inflate primitive count, memory, and training time. DART acts as a backbone-agnostic add-on that enriches the seed at initialization, replicating each SfM point on its tangent plane within a distance-aware radius. It is distinct from GeoGaussian, which reshapes Gaussians and depends on reliable normals, and from learned or depth-based enrichment methods. DART-3DGS: Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13705904, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Age-Gated Densification (AGE)
head: DART + AGE, DART + AGE Integration, DART-3DGS, Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification, Ours
body: Age-Gated Densification (AGE) is a maturity gate for 3D Gaussian Splatting training that prevents densification (splitting and cloning) until a specified training step threshold is reached, thereby pruning unnecessary primitives and controlling memory and time costs. It is designed to work in conjunction with Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART), where DART augments the initial point cloud to improve coverage in sparse regions, and AGE trims the resulting inflated primitive count without degrading reconstruction quality. While competitors like FastGS-Big and Taming-3DGS modify densification criteria or schedules during training, AGE acts as a static maturity gate, deferring eligibility for densification operations. AGE functions as a conditional guard on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting densification loop. It does not alter the geometry of the Gaussians or the rendering process, but restricts when the density-control cascade (splitting small Gaussians or cloning large ones) is permitted to execute. Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the current training step t, and the maturity threshold T{mat}. Output: A boolean flag candensify indicating whether densification operations should be applied in the current optimization step. AGE relies on the standard 3DGS Gaussian representation but does not require per-Gaussian age counters; it uses a global training step counter to gate the operation. 1. Initialize the maturity threshold T{mat} to 200. 2. For each training step t: a. Perform the standard forward pass and compute the loss. b. Compute gradients and update Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color). c. Evaluate the age gate: if t < T{mat}, set candensify = False; otherwise, set candensify = True. d. If candensify is True, execute the standard split/clone/prune operations; otherwise, skip them. The gating condition is defined as: \text{can\densify} = (t \geq T{mat}) where t is the current training step and T{mat} is the maturity threshold. T{mat}: The maturity threshold, defined as the training step at which densification becomes active. Default value: 200. m: The replication multiplier for DART (used in conjunction with AGE). Default value: 10. If m=1, DART is disabled, but AGE remains active. \rho{min} and \rho{max}: The lower and upper bounds of the distance-aware radius schedule for DART. These are fractions of the robust radius R. Default values: 0.008 and 0.04, respectively. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def agegateddensificationstep(gaussians, trainingstep, Tmat=200): """ Performs one step of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization with AGE gating. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. trainingstep: Current integer training step index. Tmat: Maturity threshold (default 200). Returns: Updated list of Gaussian primitives. """ # Standard 3DGS forward pass and loss computation # Standard 3DGS backward pass and parameter update # AGE Gating Logic candensify = (trainingstep >= Tmat) # Conditional Densification if candensify: # Standard 3DGS densification: split small/high-opacity Gaussians, # clone high-gradient Gaussians, prune low-opacity Gaussians # (Exact thresholds and vectorized operations are implementation-specific) pass return gaussians Constant Radius in DART: Using a constant upper-bound radius (\rho = 0.040) for DART replicas causes quality collapse (6.0 dB drop on 'stump' scene) and excessive memory usage (14.0 GB peak) due to early inflation and subsequent pruning. AGE cannot fully compensate for poorly placed initial primitives. Isotropic Replication: Using isotropic balls instead of tangent disks for DART replicas increases primitive count by 11.7% and reduces quality, demonstrating that geometric placement matters more than count. Threshold Selection: T{mat} is fixed by design rather than swept, as it suppresses persistently under-supported primitives that would otherwise be retained by unconstrained densification. A geometry-only augmentation that replicates SfM points on local tangent planes with distance-dependent radii to improve coverage in sparse regions. It acts as the fidelity provider for AGE. Choose it when the initial SfM cloud is sparse in the periphery. Link The base optimization framework that AGE modifies. AGE is a supplementary strategy applied during the training phase. Choose it as the default training backbone when applying AGE. Link Time Complexity: AGE reduces training time. When applied with DART, it reduces training time from 31.8 to 29.4 minutes (a 2.4 min reduction) compared to using DART without AGE. The first 500 iterations take at most one minute per scene, indicating the gating overhead is negligible. Memory Complexity: AGE reduces peak memory usage. With DART, peak memory drops from 6.04 GB to 5.57 GB (a 0.47 GB reduction). Primitive Count: AGE reduces the final Gaussian count. Without DART, it reduces count by 9.6% (2.91M to 2.63M). With DART, it reduces count by 8.7% (3.45M to 3.15M). Quality Impact: AGE maintains or slightly improves quality. Without DART, PSNR increases by 0.04 dB. With DART, PSNR increases by 0.05 dB, SSIM by 0.001, and LPIPS by 0.001 (within measurement noise). Strengths: Effective cost-control gate that trims unnecessary primitives without sacrificing quality. Works independently of the initial cloud formation (effective even without DART). Limitations: Does not improve quality on its own; relies on DART for fidelity gains in sparse regions. Not a substitute for better densification criteria but a complement to them. When to Use: Use when memory or training time is constrained, or when the initial point cloud requires augmentation (via DART) that would otherwise lead to excessive primitive counts. When Not to Use: AGE is beneficial regardless of initial cloud density, as it reduces primitive count by ~9-10% without quality loss, so the overhead of managing the maturity threshold is justified in all standard training setups. AGE was introduced as part of the "DART-3DGS" method, which combines Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART) and Age-Gated Densification (AGE) to improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction quality. The method was developed to address the issue of sparse SfM point clouds in outdoor scenes, where standard 3DGS struggles with coverage. AGE was designed to act as a maturity gate, preventing the densification process from creating too many primitives too early, which can lead to overfitting or memory issues. The method was evaluated on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets, showing improvements in perceptual metrics (LPIPS) and comparable PSNR scores to state-of-the-art methods. name: Hybrid Volume-based Densification
head: Point Densitification based on Hybrid Volume
body: Hybrid Volume-based Densification is a strategy that uses a grid-based volumetric representation to supply missing Gaussian points in low-texture, distant, or sky regions where Structure-from-Motion (SfM) initialization fails, preventing empty 2D splats. It differs from sibling methods like Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART) by relying on a continuous neural radiance field (MLP) to predict density and position, rather than geometric replication on tangent planes, making it suitable for filling large voids where no initial point cloud exists. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: An MLP f\theta parameterized by \theta, a set of rays \mathbf{R}, near/far plane distances un, uf, and a density threshold \tau. Outputs: A set of new 3D Gaussian splats (position, covariance, color, opacity) added to the scene representation. Data Structures: MLP f\theta: A Multi-Layer Perceptron taking a 3D location \mathbf{x} and a direction vector \mathbf{d} as input. Grid-based Volume: Implicitly defined by the MLP f\theta. It maps (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to density \sigma\theta \in [0, \infty) and color \mathbf{c}\theta \in [0, 1]^3. Formulas: 1. MLP Prediction: \mathbf{c}\theta, \sigma\theta = f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) Where \mathbf{x} is the 3D location and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. 2. Predicted Depth \hat{D}\theta(\mathbf{r}): The expected depth along a ray \mathbf{r} is approximated by integrating sampled particles weighted by transmittance: \hat{\mathbf{D}}\theta(\mathbf{r}) = \int{un}^{uf} Q(u) \sigma\theta(\mathbf{r}(u)) u du Where un and uf are the near and far clipping planes. 3. Accumulated Transmittance Q(u): Q(u) = \exp \left( -\int{un}^u \sigma\theta(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds \right) This represents the probability of light traveling from the camera to distance u without interaction. 4. Gaussian Position and Function: The 3D position \mathbf{x} for a new Gaussian is derived from the ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}\mathbf{r}, and predicted depth: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + \hat{\mathbf{D}}\theta(\mathbf{r}) \mathbf{d}\mathbf{r} The Gaussian function G(x) uses this position as its mean \mu: G(x) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{o} + \hat{\mathbf{D}}\theta(\mathbf{r})\mathbf{d}\mathbf{r} - \mu)^T \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{o} + \hat{\mathbf{D}}\theta(\mathbf{r})\mathbf{d}\mathbf{r} - \mu)} Where \mathbf{\Sigma} is the covariance matrix. Parameters: \tau: Predefined density threshold for adding new Gaussians. Value not explicitly given in the sources. un, uf: Predefined near and far planes for rendering. Steps: 1. Warm-up: Perform warm-up calculations in the grid-based volume to ensure stability of the MLP predictions. 2. Candidate Selection: Select candidate locations \mathbf{x} within a bounded range (implicitly defined by the ray set \mathbf{R} and depth bounds un, uf). 3. Density Check: For each candidate location, evaluate the density \sigma\theta predicted by f\theta. 4. Densification: If the density at \mathbf{x} meets or exceeds the threshold \tau, introduce a new Gaussian splat into the pipeline. This includes initializing its position (derived from \hat{\mathbf{D}}\theta), covariance matrix, color, and opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridvolumedensification(mlpftheta, rays, un, uf, thresholdtau): """ Adds new 3D Gaussians based on a grid-based volumetric representation. Args: mlpftheta: MLP function ftheta(x, d) returning (color, density). rays: List of ray objects, each with origin o, direction dr, and sample points u. un: Near plane distance. uf: Far plane distance. thresholdtau: Density threshold for adding new Gaussians. Returns: newgaussians: List of new Gaussian splat parameters. """ newgaussians = [] # Step 1: Warm up calculations (implementation detail not specified in source) # Typically involves a few forward passes to stabilize MLP gradients or outputs. warmuppasses(mlpftheta, rays) for ray in rays: # Calculate accumulated transmittance Q(u) for all sample points u along the ray # Q(u) = exp(-integral from un to u of sigmatheta(r(s)) ds) # In practice, this is computed discretely over sampled points. transmittances = computetransmittance(ray, mlpftheta, un, uf) # Calculate predicted depth Dhattheta(r) # Dhat = integral from un to uf of Q(u) sigmatheta(r(u)) u du predicteddepth = computepredicteddepth(ray, mlpftheta, transmittances, un, uf) # Determine 3D position x # x = o + Dhattheta(r) dr position = ray.origin + predicteddepth ray.direction # Evaluate density at this position using the MLP # sigmatheta = ftheta(x, d) # The direction d for the MLP input is typically the ray direction., density = mlpftheta(position, ray.direction) # Step 3 & 4: Check threshold and add Gaussian if met if density >= thresholdtau: # Initialize Gaussian parameters # Covariance matrix Sigma is not explicitly defined in the source for initialization. # A common default is an isotropic covariance based on a small radius or # inherited from a nearby point, but the source states "associated Gaussian parameters" # without specifying the exact initialization formula for Sigma. gaussian = creategaussian( position=position, color=mlpftheta(position, ray.direction)[0], # Color from MLP opacity=1.0, # Default opacity; source does not specify initial opacity. covariance=initializecovariance(position) # Placeholder for covariance init.) newgaussians.append(gaussian) return newgaussians def computetransmittance(ray, mlp, un, uf): # Discrete approximation of integral for transmittance # Q(ui) = exp(-sum{j=0}^{i-1} sigma(theta(r(sj))) deltas) samples = ray.samplepoints(un, uf) qvalues = [1.0] # Q(un) is 1.0 (no absorption before near plane) accumulatedsigma = 0.0 for i in range(len(samples) - 1): u = samples[i] # Evaluate density at sample point # Note: ray.r(s) is the 3D point on the ray at distance s point = ray.origin + u ray.direction, sigma = mlp(point, ray.direction) # Approximate integral step deltas = samples[i+1] - samples[i] accumulatedsigma += sigma deltas # Compute Q for the next point qnext = math.exp(-accumulatedsigma) qvalues.append(qnext) return qvalues def computepredicteddepth(ray, mlp, transmittances, un, uf): # Discrete approximation of integral for depth # Dhat = sum{i} Q(ui) sigma(theta(r(ui))) ui deltau samples = ray.samplepoints(un, uf) depthintegral = 0.0 for i in range(len(samples) - 1): u = samples[i] point = ray.origin + u ray.direction, sigma = mlp(point, ray.direction) # Use the transmittance Q(u) at the start of the interval # Note: transmittances list has length len(samples) qu = transmittances[i] deltau = samples[i+1] - samples[i] depthintegral += qu sigma u deltau return depthintegral Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The points generated by this strategy lack the precision of LiDAR or SfM points. A hybrid optimization strategy is required to refine these positions. Stability: Warm-up calculations are necessary to prevent instability in the grid-based volume during densification. Empty Splats: Without this method, low-texture or distant areas result in blank areas that cannot be rendered accurately due to missing SfM points. The specific implementation of this method within the HO-Gaussian framework, which combines this densification with a hybrid optimization strategy to refine the less precise points generated by the volume. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays sampled and the depth of the MLP f\theta. Each candidate location requires a forward pass through the MLP and integration steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the MLP parameters \theta and the grid-based volume representation. Strengths: Effectively fills holes in sky, distant, and low-texture regions where SfM fails, preventing empty 2D splats. Limitations: The generated points lack the precision of SfM points, necessitating further optimization. When to use: In urban scenes or general scenes with significant low-texture or distant regions where initial SfM point clouds are sparse. Origin: Introduced in "HO-Gaussian: Hybrid Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Urban Scenes" by Li et al.. History: Developed to address the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, where cloning and splitting operations fail in low-texture or distant areas where initial SfM points are missing. Usage: Used in urban scene reconstruction where SfM extraction is poor in certain regions.
