name: Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation
head: EGR
body:
Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR) is a training-stage module that redistributes a fixed budget of Gaussian primitives toward regions with persistent coarse-scale reconstruction errors, without increasing the total number of Gaussians. It refines post-densification Gaussian allocation by moving low-contribution (LC) Gaussians to high-error (HE) regions within a fixed Gaussian set, using contribution- and error-aware selection. Unlike densification methods that increase the primitive count, EGR preserves the total Gaussian count N by relocating existing primitives, serving as a stabilization strategy that redirects allocation toward persistent coarse-scale errors. EGR operates after the densification phase is complete, when the Gaussian count is fixed. It identifies Gaussians that contribute little to rendering or have low gradients (LC candidates) and relocates them to positions occupied by Gaussians that are associated with high reconstruction error (HE candidates). The process involves computing statistics, selecting pairs, relocating parameters, and resetting optimizer states. Inputs: The current set of N Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, their parameters (position \mui, scale Si, rotation Ri, opacity \alphai, SH coefficients ci, ACO offsets \Deltai), the current optimizer states, and the set of training views V. Outputs: The modified set of Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N with updated positions, scales, colors, and opacities for the relocated pairs, and reset optimizer states for those pairs. The Gaussian set is represented as a list or array of structures. Each Gaussian Gi contains: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. Si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (log-space or linear, as per backbone). Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3} or quaternion: Orientation. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. ci: Spherical Harmonics coefficients. \Deltai: ACO (Adaptive-Scale Color Offset) offsets. Optimizer state: Momentum and variance buffers for each parameter. 1. Compute Contribution and Error Statistics: For each Gaussian i, compute three metrics using all scale-1 training cameras. Normalized Blending Weight: For each view v, compute the relative contribution 	ilde{w}i(v): 	ilde{w}i(v) =  rac{wi(v)}{\sum{i'} w{i'}(v) + \epsilon} where wi(v) is the blending weight of Gaussian i in view v, i' indexes projected Gaussians in view v, and \epsilon is a small positive constant (e.g., 10^{-8}). Mean and Max Contribution: Compute the mean contribution Ci^{mean} and maximum contribution Ci^{max} over all views V: Ci^{mean} =  rac{1}{|V|} \sum{v \in V} 	ilde{w}i(v) Ci^{max} = \max{v \in V} 	ilde{w}i(v) where |V| is the number of views. Normalized Gradient Magnitude: Compute the L2 reconstruction loss for view v: L2(v) =  rac{1}{3Hv Wv} \sum{h,w,\ell} (\hat{I}{h,w,\ell}(v) - I{h,w,\ell}(v))^2 where Hv, Wv are image height and width, \hat{I} is rendered color, I is ground truth, and \ell indexes RGB channels. Compute the normalized gradient magnitude Gi^{mean}: Gi^{mean} =  rac{1}{|V|} \sum{v \in V}  rac{\|
abla{	hetai} L2(v)\|}{\sum{i'} \|
abla{	heta{i'}} L2(v)\| + \epsilon} where 
abla{	hetai} L2(v) is the parameter gradient of Gaussian i from this loss. High-Error Metric (Ci^{HE}): Combine reconstruction error with normalized contribution. The source defines Ci^{HE} as an error-weighted contribution metric. While the exact formula for Ci^{HE} is not explicitly expanded in the provided text snippets, it is derived from the reconstruction error and contribution statistics to identify high-error regions. 2. Robust Z-Score Normalization: The measures Ci^{mean}, Ci^{max}, and Gi^{mean} have different numerical ranges. Apply robust z-score normalization to reduce sensitivity to extreme values: z(x) =  rac{x - 	ext{median}(x)}{	ext{median}(|x - 	ext{median}(x)|) + \epsilon} where 	ext{median}(x) is the median of measure x over all N Gaussians. 3. Score Computation: LC Score (si^{LC}): Assign a high score to Gaussians with low normalized mean contribution, max contribution, and gradient magnitude: si^{LC} = \exp(-z(Ci^{mean}) - z(Ci^{max}) - z(Gi^{mean})) HE Score (si^{HE}): Assign a high score to Gaussians with large error-weighted contribution using a percentile score based on rank: si^{HE} =  rac{1}{N-1} \sum{j=1}^N \mathbb{1}[Cj^{HE} < Ci^{HE}] where \mathbb{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function and N is the number of Gaussians. 4. Select Pairs: Select the top M{eff}^{LC} Gaussians with the highest si^{LC} scores as LC candidates. Select the top M{eff}^{HE} Gaussians with the highest si^{HE} scores as HE candidates. The number of relocated pairs M is determined by the smaller effective sample size: M{eff}^q =  rac{1}{\sum{j=1}^N (pj^q)^2} M = \min(M{eff}^{LC}, M{eff}^{HE}) where pj^q are the normalized probabilities derived from the scores for distribution q \in \{LC, HE\}. Round M down to the nearest integer. Pair the M LC Gaussians with the M HE Gaussians. 5. Relocation and Parameter Copying: For each of the M selected pairs (G{LC}, G{HE}): Relocate G{LC} to the position of G{HE}: \mu{LC} \leftarrow \mu{HE}. Copy the scale, orientation, and base color (DC SH coefficient) from G{HE} to G{LC}. Reset the higher-order SH coefficients of G{LC} to zero. Reset the ACO offsets of G{LC} to zero. Clear the optimizer state (momentum and variance) of G{LC}. 6. Opacity Rescaling: After relocation, the paired Gaussians share the same location. Rescale their opacities to preserve the original transmittance according to the opacity split method from 3DGS-MCMC [21]. Let \alpha{LC} and \alpha{HE} be the original opacities. The new opacities \alpha'{LC} and \alpha'{HE} are computed such that the combined transmittance remains consistent with the pre-relocation state. 7. Resume Optimization: Resume standard gradient-based optimization immediately after relocation. The paired Gaussians retain separate parameters and are independently optimized during subsequent training, allowing their appearance parameters to become distinct. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errorguidedreallocation(gaussians, views, optimizer, iteration, config): """ Performs Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu (pos), scale, rot, alpha, shcoeffs, acooffset, optimizerstate views: List of training view objects (camera poses, ground truth images) optimizer: Optimizer object with resetstate(gaussian) method iteration: Current training iteration config: Configuration dict with keys: epsilon (float), reallocationinterval (int), windowstart (int), windowend (int), numrounds (int) Returns: Modified gaussians list """ # Check if reallocation should run if iteration < config['windowstart'] or iteration > config['windowend']: return gaussians if (iteration - config['windowstart']) % config['reallocationinterval'] != 0: return gaussians # Determine round index to limit total rounds roundidx = (iteration - config['windowstart']) // config['reallocationinterval'] if roundidx >= config['numrounds']: return gaussians N = len(gaussians) epsilon = config['epsilon'] # Step 1: Compute Statistics Cmean = np.zeros(N) Cmax = np.zeros(N) Gmean = np.zeros(N) CHE = np.zeros(N) # Placeholder for error-weighted contribution for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): wsumview = [] gradsumview = [] maxw = 0.0 sumw = 0.0 for v in views: # Render and compute blending weights wi(v) # Note: Implementation depends on the specific 3DGS rasterizer wiv = computeblendingweight(g, v) wsumview.append(wiv) # Compute L2 loss and gradient norm # Note: Requires backward pass through the renderer loss, gradnorm = computel2lossandgradnorm(g, v) gradsumview.append(gradnorm) if wiv > maxw: maxw = wiv sumw += wiv # Normalize weights normalizedws = [w / (sumw + epsilon) for w in wsumview] Cmean[i] = np.mean(normalizedws) Cmax[i] = maxw # Normalize gradients normalizedgrads = [gn / (sum(gradsumview) + epsilon) for gn in gradsumview] Gmean[i] = np.mean(normalizedgrads) # Compute CHE (Error-weighted contribution) # Exact formula for CHE is not fully detailed in source, # but it combines reconstruction error and contribution. # Assuming a weighted sum or product based on source description. # For implementation, this must be derived from the specific backbone's error metric. CHE[i] = computehigherrormetric(g, views, epsilon) # Step 2: Robust Z-Score Normalization def robustzscore(values): medianval = np.median(values) mad = np.median(np.abs(values - medianval)) return (values - medianval) / (mad + epsilon) zCmean = robustzscore(Cmean) zCmax = robustzscore(Cmax) zGmean = robustzscore(Gmean) # Step 3: Score Computation # LC Score: High score for low values sLC = np.exp(-zCmean - zCmax - zGmean) # HE Score: Percentile rank # siHE = (1 / (N-1)) sum(1[CjHE < CiHE]) sHE = np.zeros(N) for i in range(N): count = np.sum(CHE < CHE[i]) sHE[i] = count / (N - 1) if N > 1 else 0.0 # Step 4: Select Pairs # Compute effective sample sizes # pj^q are normalized probabilities from scores pLC = sLC / (np.sum(sLC) + epsilon) pHE = sHE / (np.sum(sHE) + epsilon) MeffLC = 1.0 / np.sum(pLC2) MeffHE = 1.0 / np.sum(pHE2) M = min(int(MeffLC), int(MeffHE)) # Get indices of top M LC and HE candidates # Note: Source says "top M", implying highest scores idxLC = np.argsort(sLC)[-M:] idxHE = np.argsort(sHE)[-M:] # Pair them (e.g., sorted order or random pairing) # Source implies pairing selected LC with selected HE pairs = list(zip(idxLC, idxHE)) # Step 5 & 6: Relocation and Opacity Rescaling for idxlc, idxhe in pairs: glc = gaussians[idxlc] ghe = gaussians[idxhe] # Relocate LC to HE position glc.mu = ghe.mu.copy() # Copy scale, orientation, base color (DC SH) glc.scale = ghe.scale.copy() glc.rot = ghe.rot.copy() glc.shcoeffs[0] = ghe.shcoeffs[0].copy() # DC coefficient # Reset higher-order SH and ACO glc.shcoeffs[1:] = 0.0 glc.acooffset = 0.0 # Clear optimizer state optimizer.resetstate(glc) # Opacity Rescaling (3DGS-MCMC split) # Preserve original transmittance alphalc = glc.alpha alphahe = ghe.alpha # Formula from 3DGS-MCMC [21] for splitting opacity # Told = (1-alphalc)(1-alphahe) # New opacities alpha'lc, alpha'he such that (1-alpha'lc)(1-alpha'he) = Told # And typically alpha'lc = alpha'he or based on specific split rule. # Source cites 3DGS-MCMC [21] for the split. # Assuming equal split for simplicity if not specified, # but strictly should follow [21]. # Told = (1 - alphalc) (1 - alphahe) # alphanew = 1 - sqrt(Told) # glc.alpha = alphanew # ghe.alpha = alphanew # Implementing the specific split from 3DGS-MCMC [21] is required here. # Since [21] is not provided in full, we note the operation. # Assuming standard geometric mean split for equal contribution preservation: Told = (1 - alphalc) (1 - alphahe) alphanew = 1 - np.sqrt(Told) glc.alpha = alphanew ghe.alpha = alphanew return gaussians Fixed primitive budget: The total number of Gaussians N remains constant during reallocation. Reallocation interval: 1000 iterations. Reallocation window: Iterations 16,000 to 25,000. Number of reallocation rounds: 10. Epsilon: Small positive constant for numerical stability (value not specified, typically 10^{-8}). Degenerate Input: EGR must not run if densification is still active. It is explicitly disabled during densification (iterations 500-15,000) and only runs after the Gaussian count is fixed. Precision: Robust z-score normalization is used to reduce sensitivity to extreme values in contribution and gradient metrics. Boundary Conditions: If N=1, the HE score calculation involves division by zero; however, EGR operates on a set of Gaussians where N is large. Time Complexity: The method requires computing blending weights, losses, and gradients for all Gaussians and views, which is O(N \cdot |V|). Sorting and scoring are O(N \log N) or O(N). The relocation step is O(M) where M \ll N. Overall, it adds a periodic overhead to the training loop. Memory Complexity: Requires storing statistics (C^{mean}, C^{max}, G^{mean}, C^{HE}) for all Gaussians, which is O(N). Measured Performance: Experiments on MS-GS with three real-scene benchmarks demonstrate improved multi-scale rendering quality, particularly at coarse scales. Strengths: It redirects primitive allocation toward persistent coarse-scale errors without increasing the primitive count. It uses adaptive relocation count, parameter reset, and continued optimization as a stabilization strategy, avoiding explicit rollback or separate re-correction modules. Limitations: It is only applicable after densification is complete. It relies on accurate computation of gradients and blending weights, which can be computationally expensive. When to use: Use when coarse-scale rendering quality is poor and densification has already stabilized the Gaussian count. Use when a fixed budget of primitives is required. When not to use: Do not use during the densification phase (iterations 500-15,000). Origin: EGR was introduced in the paper "Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting" (Mathematics 2026, 14, 2713). History: It is part of the ACO-EGR framework, which jointly addresses scale-dependent color mismatch (via ACO) and primitive-allocation imbalance (via EGR). Usage: It is integrated into multi-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (MS-GS) backbones to improve rendering quality at coarse scales. Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14152713, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Error-Driven Gaussian Density Control
head: Error-Driven Density Control (EDC), Error-based Densification and Pruning, Sparse Error Densification, TurboGS density control
body: Error-Driven Gaussian Density Control (EDC) is a training-phase strategy that dynamically allocates model capacity and removes redundant primitives by accumulating and leveraging per-Gaussian statistics corresponding to sparse pixel errors. It differs from sibling methods like Hard Gaussian Splatting and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation by relying on online sparse pixel statistics and percentile thresholds for adaptive density control, rather than post-hoc dense error maps or fixed reallocation budgets. This approach reduces computational complexity compared to dense error map approaches while improving reconstruction fidelity in challenging regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, current iteration t, hyperparameters \Theta (percentile thresholds), and a set of sampled views Vt with sparse pixel sets P{t,v}. Output: Updated set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} after densification and pruning. Data Structures: Gaussian Properties: Each Gaussian Gi maintains accumulated error e{Gi}, distance metric D{Gi}, and opacity sum \alpha{Gi}. Error Map: A sparse map storing per-pixel errors, used to back-project statistics to Gaussians. Numbered Steps: 1. Back-Projection: During rasterization of the sparse pixel set, back-project pixel errors onto the contributing Gaussians. 2. Aggregation: Aggregate the back-projected error statistics (e{Gi}) for each Gaussian. 3. Thresholding: Compare aggregated error statistics against percentile thresholds defined in \Theta. 4. Densification: For Gaussians with error statistics exceeding the upper percentile threshold, perform densification (splitting or cloning) to recover missing details. 5. Pruning: For Gaussians with error statistics below the lower percentile threshold (or other criteria like screen radius), perform pruning to remove redundant primitives. 6. Optimizer Reset: Reset optimizer states (momentum and variance) for any newly created or significantly modified Gaussians to allow rapid convergence. Formulas: The back-projection accumulates error e, distance D, and opacity \alpha per Gaussian: e{Gi}, D{Gi}, \alpha{Gi} \leftarrow \text{rasterize\forward}(Vt, Pt, L{pix}) where \alphak(p) depends on the projected 2D Gaussian footprint and its opacity. Parameters: Percentile Thresholds: Used to determine cutoff values for Gaussian scores si(t) and error values ei to trigger densification or pruning. Screen Radii: Used in conjunction with error statistics to guide pruning of redundant Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errordrivendensitycontrol(G, Vt, Pt, Lpix, t, Theta): """ G: List of Gaussian primitives Vt: Set of sampled views Pt: Sparse pixel sets for each view Lpix: Per-pixel loss/error map t: Current iteration Theta: Hyperparameters including percentile thresholds """ # Initialize per-Gaussian accumulators eG = {g.id: 0.0 for g in G} DG = {g.id: 0.0 for g in G} alphaG = {g.id: 0.0 for g in G} # Step 1: Back-Projection Pixel Properties to Gaussians # Accumulate (err, dist, alpha) per Gaussian during rasterization for view in Vt: for pixel in Pt[view]: # Identify contributing Gaussians for this pixel contributinggaussians = getcontributinggaussians(pixel, G) error = Lpix[pixel] for g in contributinggaussians: # Accumulate error statistics # Note: Exact weighting function (e.g., by opacity or distance) # is implementation-specific but implied by "back-project" eG[g.id] += error g.opacity DG[g.id] += error g.distance alphaG[g.id] += g.opacity # Step 2: Aggregate and Threshold # Determine which Gaussians to densify or prune based on error statistics densifycandidates = [] prunecandidates = [] # Calculate percentile thresholds from Theta errthresholdhigh = getpercentilethreshold(eG.values(), Theta.upperpercentile) errthresholdlow = getpercentilethreshold(eG.values(), Theta.lowerpercentile) for g in G: if eG[g.id] > errthresholdhigh: densifycandidates.append(g) elif eG[g.id] < errthresholdlow: prunecandidates.append(g) # Step 3: Densify newgaussians = [] for g in densifycandidates: # Split or clone the Gaussian children = splitgaussian(g) newgaussians.extend(children) # Reset optimizer states for new Gaussians resetoptimizerstates(children) # Step 4: Prune Gpruned = [g for g in G if g not in prunecandidates] # Combine remaining and new Gaussians Gupdated = Gpruned + newgaussians return Gupdated Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Replacing EDC with FastGS-style post-hoc full-image error accumulation increases training time and slightly reduces PSNR due to inefficiency in online sparse settings. Sparse supervision may occasionally introduce subtle rippling artifacts in low-frequency regions with weak texture variations (e.g., walls or ceilings), even when the error-map response is already low. Time Complexity: Reduces computational complexity compared to dense error map approaches by using online sparse pixel statistics. Memory Complexity: Reduces final Gaussian count (N{GS}) by removing redundant primitives. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 baseline, adding Err-DP reduces training time to 77 seconds, improves PSNR by +0.02 dB over baseline, and reduces final Gaussian count (N{GS}) to 0.64M. Strengths: Adaptive allocation of capacity to challenging regions; efficient online sparse setting; faster convergence. Limitations: May introduce rippling artifacts in low-frequency regions; performance depends on the quality of sparse pixel sampling. When to Use: When training time is a critical constraint and sparse pixel sampling is employed. When Not to Use: When dense error maps are already available and computational efficiency is not a primary concern. Error-Driven Gaussian Density Control was introduced as part of the TurboGS framework, which accelerates 3D Gaussian Splatting via error-guided sparse pixel sampling and optimization. It was developed to address the inefficiency of post-hoc dense error accumulation methods like FastGS in the context of sparse training. TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.15924, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: CoherentGS
body: CoherentGS is a regularized optimization method for sparse novel view synthesis that introduces structural coherency to explicit 3D Gaussian representations by constraining Gaussian movement in 2D image space. It solves the instability and needle-like artifacts common in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting when trained on extremely sparse input views by enforcing single-view and multi-view consistency, thereby preventing overfitting and allowing for the identification of occluded regions suitable for inpainting. Unlike NeRF-based sparse methods that rely on implicit MLPs and produce blurry occluded regions, CoherentGS maintains an explicit representation that can be cleanly segmented for diffusion-based inpainting. Inputs: N sparse input images with known camera poses. Monocular depth estimates for each input view. Dense flow correspondences between all pairs of input images. Binary segmentation masks derived from thresholding the monocular depth estimates to preserve sharp discontinuities. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position \mathbf{x}, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: The method assigns exactly one Gaussian to every pixel of every input image, creating a structured representation. Let \mathcal{G} be the set of Gaussians. For each input image n \in \{1, \dots, N\} and each pixel \mathbf{p} in that image, there is a corresponding Gaussian g{n,\mathbf{p}} \in \mathcal{G}. The position \mathbf{x}{n,\mathbf{p}} of each Gaussian is constrained to lie on the ray connecting the camera center of view n to pixel \mathbf{p}. Initial positions are determined by the monocular depth estimate D{init}(n, \mathbf{p}). Numbered Steps: 1. Depth-based Initialization: For each input image n and pixel \mathbf{p}, initialize the 3D position \mathbf{x}{n,\mathbf{p}} using the monocular depth estimate D{init}(n, \mathbf{p}). The depth is relative, so the initialization places Gaussians in world space consistent with the camera pose. 2. Implicit Decoder Setup: Initialize an implicit convolutional decoder. This decoder takes the 2D image coordinate \mathbf{p} and the camera pose of the input view n as input. 3. Regularized Optimization Loop: Minimize the optimization objective to update Gaussian parameters \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}. The objective function is: \Sigma^, \alpha^, \mathbf{x}^, \mathbf{c}^ = \arg\min{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}} \mathcal{L}(R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}), R(\mathbf{p})) where \mathcal{P} contains all pixels of every input image, R(\mathbf{p}) is the reference pixel color, and \mathcal{L} is the combination of L1 and SSIM losses. During optimization, the rendering equation for a pixel \mathbf{p} is: R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p})} \mathbf{c}i \gammai \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\gammaj) where \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p}) is the set of ordered Gaussians overlapping pixel \mathbf{p}, and \gammak = f(\Sigmak, \alphak, \mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{p}) computes the effective opacity by evaluating the Gaussian at \mathbf{p} and multiplying by global opacity \alpha. To enforce coherency, the following constraints are applied to the gradients or directly to the parameters: Single-View Coherency: Pass the input view coordinate \mathbf{p} and camera pose to the implicit decoder to predict a residual depth value \Delta D. The updated depth D is D{init} + \Delta D. Gaussians with similar initial depth are forced to move together by the decoder's output, ensuring smooth depth variations within a single view. Binary segmentation masks are applied to the decoder output to preserve sharp discontinuities. Multi-View Coherency: Compute a depth map for all Gaussians for each view. Apply a Total Variation (TV) loss to the rendered depth across all Gaussians to ensure smoothness and consistency across views. Flow-based Loss: Use the pre-computed dense flow correspondences between image pairs. Apply a flow-based loss to constrain optimization by ensuring that corresponding pixels in two images have similar Gaussian positions. This enforces cross-view consistency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coherentgsoptimization(inputimages, cameraposes, monoculardepths, flowcorrespondences, numiterations, lr): N = len(inputimages) H, W = inputimages[0].shape[:2] # Data structure: gaussians[n][p] = {'x': [x,y,z], 'sigma': [[...]], 'alpha': float, 'c': [r,g,b]} gaussians = {} for n in range(N): gaussians[n] = {} for y in range(H): for x in range(W): p = (x, y) rayorigin = cameraposes[n].origin raydir = unprojectray(cameraposes[n], p) depthinit = monoculardepths[n][y, x] gaussians[n][p] = { 'x': [rayorigin[i] + raydir[i] depthinit for i in range(3)], 'sigma': [[1.0 if i==j else 0.0 for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)], 'alpha': 0.5, 'c': list(inputimages[n][y, x]) } def predictresidualdepth(p, cameraidx): # Forward pass of implicit convolutional decoder return 0.0 for iteration in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0.0 # Photometric loss (L1 + SSIM) for n in range(N): renderedcolor = rendercolor(gaussians, cameraposes[n], H, W) totalloss += l1loss(renderedcolor, inputimages[n]) # SSIM loss added per # Single-View Coherency for n in range(N): masks = computesegmentationmasks(monoculardepths[n]) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): p = (x, y) deltad = predictresidualdepth(p, n) # Apply binary masks to preserve sharp discontinuities if masks[y, x] < 0.5: deltad = 0.0 # Loss penalizes deviation from predicted smooth depth field totalloss += abs(deltad) # Multi-View Coherency (TV on rendered depth) for n in range(N): rendereddepth = renderdepth(gaussians, cameraposes[n], H, W) tvloss = computetotalvariation(rendereddepth) totalloss += tvloss # Flow-based Loss for (n1, n2), flowmap in flowcorrespondences.items(): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): p1 = (x, y) dx, dy = flowmap[y, x] p2 = (x + int(dx), y + int(dy)) if 0 <= p2[0] < W and 0 <= p2[1] < H: # Ensure corresponding pixels have similar Gaussian positions totalloss += distance(gaussians[n1][p1]['x'], gaussians[n2][p2]['x']) # Standard automatic differentiation and parameter update grads = computegradients(totalloss, gaussians) updategaussians(gaussians, grads, lr) return gaussians def unprojectray(camera, p): # Convert pixel to normalized coordinates and transform to world ray direction return [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] def rendercolor(gaussians, camera, H, W): # Standard 3DGS alpha compositing per pixel color = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): p = (x, y) # Gather all Gaussians from all views that project to pixel p overlapping = [] for n in range(len(gaussians)): if p in gaussians[n]: overlapping.append(gaussians[n][p]) # Sort Gaussians overlapping p by depth overlapping.sort(key=lambda g: dot(g['x'], camera.viewdir)) accumalpha = 0.0 for g in overlapping: gamma = gaussianopacity(g, camera, p) color[y][x] = [c + g['c'][i] gamma (1 - accumalpha) for i, c in enumerate(color[y][x])] accumalpha += gamma (1 - accumalpha) return color def renderdepth(gaussians, camera, H, W): # Standard depth compositing depth = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): p = (x, y) overlapping = [] for n in range(len(gaussians)): if p in gaussians[n]: overlapping.append(gaussians[n][p]) overlapping.sort(key=lambda g: dot(g['x'], camera.viewdir)) accumalpha = 0.0 for g in overlapping: gamma = gaussianopacity(g, camera, p) depth[y][x] += g['x'][2] gamma (1 - accumalpha) accumalpha += gamma (1 - accumalpha) return depth def gaussianopacity(g, camera, p): # Evaluate Gaussian at pixel p and multiply by global opacity return 0.5 def l1loss(rendered, target): return sum(abs(rendered[i][j][k] - target[i][j][k]) for i in range(len(rendered)) for j in range(len(rendered[0])) for k in range(3)) def computesegmentationmasks(depthmap): threshold = 0.5 return [[1.0 if d > threshold else 0.0 for d in row] for row in depthmap] def computetotalvariation(depthmap): tv = 0.0 for y in range(len(depthmap)): for x in range(len(depthmap[0]) - 1): tv += abs(depthmap[y][x] - depthmap[y][x+1]) return tv def distance(v1, v2): return sum((v1[i] - v2[i])2 for i in range(3))0.5 def computegradients(loss, params): # Standard automatic differentiation or finite difference approximation return params def updategaussians(params, grads, lr): for n in params: for p in params[n]: params[n][p]['x'] = [params[n][p]['x'][i] - lr grads[n][p]['x'][i] for i in range(3)] Parameters: N: Number of sparse input images. Typically 3 or 4. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Number of iterations: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimization Instability: Constraining unstructured Gaussians directly in 3D space causes optimization instability. CoherentGS avoids this by mapping constraints to 2D image space. Occluded Regions: Because the constraints prevent Gaussians from moving freely in 3D space, the method does not reconstruct areas that are occluded in all input images. This is a feature, not a bug, as it allows these regions to be identified and inpainted using diffusion models. Relative Depth: Monocular depth estimates are relative and lack consistency across views. The depth-based initialization positions Gaussians in world space, but the regularized optimization is required to encourage coherent updates. MVGS is a plug-and-play optimization method that improves Novel View Synthesis (NVS) performance for existing Gaussian-based methods by constraining the optimization of 3D Gaussians with multi-view information. It sets itself apart from its parent CoherentGS, which enforces 2D image-space coherency, by explicitly leveraging cross-view consistency through a cross-intrinsic guidance scheme and multi-view cross-ray densification to enhance detail and stability. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: CoherentGS yields high-quality synthesized views compared to state-of-the-art sparse-view NeRF-based approaches (e.g., FreeNeRF, SparseNeRF) on a variety of scenes. Scaling: The method is designed for extremely sparse input views (e.g., 3 images). Strengths: Prevents overfitting to input images; allows identification of fully occluded areas for inpainting; avoids blurry occluded regions common in NeRF-based methods; improves texture and geometry reconstruction. Limitations: Does not reconstruct areas occluded in all input images (requires inpainting); relies on pre-trained monocular depth and flow models. When to use: Sparse novel view synthesis (3-4 input images) in static scenes. When not to use: Scenes where fully automatic reconstruction of all occluded regions without inpainting is required. CoherentGS was proposed by A. Paliwal et al. during an internship at Meta Reality Labs. The work addresses the limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in extremely sparse input settings, where the unstructured representation leads to artifacts. It builds on the explicit representation of 3DGS [23] and integrates concepts from implicit decoders [5, 30, 37] and monocular depth prediction [60] and flow estimation [45] to enforce coherency. name: MVGS (Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting)
head: Multi-view Regulated Learning
body: MVGS is a plug-and-play optimization method that improves Novel View Synthesis (NVS) performance for existing Gaussian-based methods by constraining the optimization of 3D Gaussians with multi-view information. It sets itself apart from standard single-view optimization paradigms by explicitly leveraging cross-view consistency through a cross-intrinsic guidance scheme and multi-view cross-ray densification to enhance detail and stability. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images with known camera poses, an initial set of 3D Gaussians, and a multi-view selection schedule. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a trained scene representation. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian representation. No new complex data structures are introduced, but the optimization loop aggregates gradients across a selected subset of views using a Sum operation instead of an Average operation. Parameters: Ms = \{48, 24, 12, 8\}: The number of views selected for multi-view training at different stages. \tau = 1: A scaling factor used in the proposed method. Other settings follow the baseline implementations (e.g., standard 3DGS hyperparameters). Steps: 1. Multi-view Selection: Select a subset of M views from the available training images for the current optimization iteration, governed by the schedule Ms. 2. Gradient Aggregation: Render the scene from all selected views and compute the loss (e.g., L1 loss between rendered and ground truth images). Compute gradients for the Gaussian parameters with respect to each view's loss. Aggregate the gradients from all selected views using the Sum operation, not the Average operation. This preserves and amplifies the gradient magnitude, enhancing the optimization process for multi-view coherence constraints. 3. Cross-Intrinsic Guidance: Apply the cross-intrinsic guidance scheme to facilitate multi-view training. 4. Multi-view Cross-ray Densification: Apply multi-view cross-ray densification to enhance detail. 5. Update: Update the Gaussian parameters using the aggregated gradients and the densification results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mvgsoptimize(gaussians, images, poses, Ms, tau, iterations): # gaussians: dict of tensors for position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients # images: list of target RGB images # poses: list of camera extrinsics/intrinsics # Ms: list of view counts for training stages, e.g., [48, 24, 12, 8] # tau: learning rate scaling factor, default 1 # iterations: total optimization steps numviews = len(images) for step in range(iterations): # Select number of views based on schedule Ms mindex = step % len(Ms) numviewstouse = Ms[mindex] # Select subset of views (e.g., random or sequential) selectedindices = list(range(numviewstouse)) selectedimages = [images[i] for i in selectedindices] selectedposes = [poses[i] for i in selectedindices] # Initialize gradient accumulators to zero gradacc = {key: zeroslike(param) for key, param in gaussians.items()} # Render and compute loss for each selected view, accumulate gradients for img, pose in zip(selectedimages, selectedposes): renderedimg = differentiablesplatting(gaussians, pose) loss = sum(abs(renderedimg - img)) / 3.0 # L1 loss viewgrads = computeautogradgradients(loss, gaussians) # Aggregate using SUM operation, not Average for key in gradacc: gradacc[key] += viewgrads[key] # Apply cross-intrinsic guidance scheme # [Comment: The exact mathematical formulation for cross-intrinsic guidance is not provided in the sources.] gaussians = applyguidance(gaussians, gradacc, selectedimages, selectedposes) # Apply multi-view cross-ray densification # [Comment: The exact mathematical formulation for multi-view cross-ray densification is not provided in the sources.] gaussians = applydensification(gaussians, selectedimages, selectedposes) # Update Gaussian parameters using aggregated gradients and tau for key, param in gaussians.items(): param.data -= tau gradacc[key] return gaussians def differentiablesplatting(gaussians, pose): # Standard 3D Gaussian splatting rasterization projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D image plane return projectedgaussians def computeautogradgradients(loss, gaussians): # Standard automatic differentiation computing d(loss)/d(param) for each parameter tensor return {key: computegradient(loss, param) for key, param in gaussians.items()} def applyguidance(gaussians, gradacc, images, poses): # [Comment: The exact mathematical formulation for cross-intrinsic guidance is not provided in the sources.] return gaussians def applydensification(gaussians, images, poses): # [Comment: The exact mathematical formulation for multi-view cross-ray densification is not provided in the sources.] return gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Optimizing across multiple views per iteration incurs significantly higher computational cost and longer training time compared to single-view optimization paradigms. Complexity in Simple Scenes: Densification strategies may introduce additional complexity in simpler scenes. Gradient Aggregation: Using Average instead of Sum for gradient aggregation reduces gradient magnitude and leads to inferior results in multi-view training. Time Complexity: Higher than single-view methods due to rendering and gradient computation for M views per iteration. The cost scales linearly with the number of views selected. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art results on standard datasets. On Mip-NeRF 360 'bonsai', PSNR improves from 31.63 to 31.93, SSIM from 0.913 to 0.925, and LPIPS from 0.211 to 0.202. On 'garden', PSNR improves from 32.23 to 32.57, SSIM from 0.813 to 0.856, and LPIPS from 0.170 to 0.123. On Tanks&Temples 'Truck', PSNR improves from 25.18 to 26.14, SSIM from 0.879 to 0.883, and LPIPS from 0.148 to 0.147. Strengths: Plug-and-play integration with existing Gaussian-based methods; improved detail and consistency; robust to complex scenes with dynamic lighting and reflections. Limitations: Longer training time; higher computational cost; densification strategies may introduce additional complexity in simpler scenes. When to Use: When high-fidelity NVS is required for complex scenes and computational resources allow for longer training times. When Not to Use: When training time is a critical constraint or for simple scenes where single-view optimization is sufficient. MVGS (Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting) was proposed by Du et al.. The work is funded by ARC-Discovery grant (DP220100800), ARC-DECRA grant (DE230100477), NVIDIA academic grant program, and Google Research Scholar Program. The method builds upon the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting and aims to address limitations in single-view optimization by incorporating multi-view constraints. name: Pruning and Sparsity Control
body: Pruning and Sparsity Control methods reduce the number of active 3D Gaussians in a radiance field to lower memory and storage costs while preserving rendering quality. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), which relies on fixed opacity thresholds and halts densification mid-training, these techniques actively eliminate redundant primitives throughout optimization using learnable masks, geometric occlusion checks, or quadratic selection. The family shares a four-step mechanism to control sparsity: 1. Selection Criterion: A scalar value or binary flag is computed per Gaussian n based on attributes like scale, opacity, or visibility. 2. Elimination: Gaussians failing the criterion are removed from the scene representation. 3. Integration: Pruning is integrated into the training loop, either periodically at densification intervals or as a post-training refinement step. 4. Loss Regularization: Methods introduce a regularization term to the loss function to encourage sparsity or guide the optimizer to shrink unneeded Gaussians before pruning. Reduces active Gaussians by applying binary masks to scale and opacity attributes based on a learnable parameter. It addresses excessive memory requirements by masking out unessential Gaussians throughout the entire training process, considering both geometric volume and transparency. Unlike standard 3DGS, it does not stop densifying in the middle of training. Choose this method when consistent sparsity control via learnable parameters is desired. Removes occluded 3D Gaussian kernels during optimization to create a compact, "hard" geometry representation by concentrating alpha values into remaining kernels. It distinguishes itself by using explicit geometric occlusion checks (depth sorting) rather than gradient magnitude thresholds. Choose this method when geometric accuracy and removal of truly occluded primitives is prioritized. A post-training refinement technique that combines binary masks from blockwise quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) solvers to retain a specific number of Gaussians. It fine-tunes the retained Gaussians with densification disabled using a weighted loss of L{refine} = 0.8 L1(I, I{gt}) + 0.2 (1 - \text{SSIM}(I, I{gt})). For iterative pruning, the process of partitioning, opacity response computation, budget allocation, and quadratic selection is repeated on the refined model until the target retention ratio is reached. Choose this method when a strict, pre-defined number of Gaussians is required for deployment. Performs exactly 12 iterations of cloning and splitting during training, followed by over 50 iterations of pruning. After densification and guided sampling steps, it gradually prunes Gaussians that exhibit small spatial opacity values to keep the most representative primitives. The proliferation of Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) leads to high memory and storage costs, often including redundant primitives with negligible volume or transparency. Standard 3DGS uses opacity-based pruning which may leave many redundant Gaussians. Recent works like SplatQ and Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting address these inefficiencies. SplatQ evaluates performance on 27 scenes from 5 benchmarks (Mip-NeRF 360, Deep Blending, Tanks and Temples, NeRF Synthetic, Ref-NeRF/Shiny Blender). Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting applies pruning to dynamic view synthesis datasets like Technicolor and Neural 3D Video. name: Gaussian Volume Mask
head: Learnable Opacity Masking, Learnable Volume-based Masking, Learnable volume and transparency masking, Masking Loss for Efficiency Improvement, Masking based on volume and transparency, Volume-based masking
body: Gaussian Volume Mask is a pruning and sparsity control technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces the number of active Gaussian primitives by applying binary masks to their scale (volume) and opacity (transparency) attributes. Unlike the original 3D Gaussian Splatting method, which relies primarily on opacity thresholds to eliminate redundant Gaussians, this method jointly considers geometric volume and transparency, identifying Gaussians that contribute negligibly to the rendered image due to either small size or low visibility. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Visibility-Based Pruning by introducing a learnable parameter for masking that is optimized alongside the scene, allowing for continuous sparsity control throughout the entire training process rather than just at densification intervals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of N Gaussians, each defined by position, rotation, scale sn \in \mathbb{R}^3+, opacity on \in [0, 1], and color. A learnable mask parameter mn \in \mathbb{R} for each Gaussian. Output: A pruned set of Gaussians with modified scale \tilde{s}n and opacity \tilde{o}n, and a binary mask Mn \in \{0, 1\} indicating whether the Gaussian is active. Data Structures: Mask Parameter (m): A vector of size N containing learnable scalar values, one per Gaussian. Initialized to zero or small random values. Binary Mask (M): A vector of size N with values 0 or 1, computed from m during the forward pass. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Binary Mask: For each Gaussian n, compute the binary mask Mn using a straight-through estimator to allow gradient flow through the binarization operation: Mn = \text{sg}(1[\sigma(mn) > \epsilon] - \sigma(mn)) + \sigma(mn) where: \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator. 1[\cdot] is the indicator function (1 if true, 0 if false). \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function. \epsilon is the masking threshold used in the indicator function to determine if a Gaussian is masked. mn is the learnable mask parameter for Gaussian n. 2. Apply Masking to Attributes: Multiply the original scale and opacity by the binary mask to obtain the masked attributes used in rendering: \tilde{s}n = Mn sn \tilde{o}n = Mn on If Mn = 0, the Gaussian's scale and opacity become zero, effectively removing it from the rendering process. 3. Compute Masking Loss: Calculate the masking loss Lm to regularize the number of active Gaussians and encourage sparsity: Lm = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^{N} \sigma(mn) This loss is added to the total training loss. The coefficient \lambdam controls the strength of this regularization. 4. Eliminate Gaussians: At every densification interval, identify Gaussians where Mn = 0 (or \sigma(mn) \le \epsilon) and remove them from the scene representation. This step is performed consistently throughout the entire training process, unlike original 3DGS which stops densifying and pruning in the middle of training. 5. Post-Training Cleanup: After training is complete, permanently remove all Gaussians with Mn = 0 and discard the mask parameter m to save storage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from dataclasses import dataclass import numpy as np from scipy.special import expit @dataclass class GaussianSet: position: np.ndarray # (N, 3) rotation: np.ndarray # (N, 4) scale: np.ndarray # (N, 3) opacity: np.ndarray # (N, 3) color: np.ndarray # (N, 3) def gaussianvolumemaskstep(gaussians: GaussianSet, maskparams: np.ndarray, epsilon: float, lambdam: float): """ Performs one forward pass of Gaussian Volume Masking with straight-through estimator. """ N = gaussians.scale.shape[0] # Step 1: Compute Binary Mask using Straight-Through Estimator sigmam = expit(maskparams) # sigmoid(mn) indicator = (sigmam > epsilon).astype(np.float32) # 1[sigma(mn) > epsilon] # Forward pass returns the binary mask (indicator) # Backward pass (handled by autograd framework) returns gradients through sigmam # Formula: Mn = sg(indicator - sigmam) + sigmam => simplifies to indicator in forward binarymask = indicator # Step 2: Apply Masking to Attributes # Masked scale: stilde = M s maskedscale = binarymask[:, np.newaxis] gaussians.scale # Masked opacity: otilde = M o maskedopacity = binarymask[:, np.newaxis] gaussians.opacity # Step 3: Compute Masking Loss # Lm = (1/N) sum(sigma(mn)) maskingloss = np.mean(sigmam) lambdam # Create a new Gaussian object with masked attributes maskedgaussians = GaussianSet( position=gaussians.position, rotation=gaussians.rotation, scale=maskedscale, opacity=maskedopacity, color=gaussians.color) return maskedgaussians, maskingloss def prunegaussians(gaussians: GaussianSet, maskparams: np.ndarray, epsilon: float) -> GaussianSet: """ Removes Gaussians where the binary mask is 0. """ sigmam = expit(maskparams) binarymask = (sigmam > epsilon).astype(bool) # Filter Gaussians prunedgaussians = GaussianSet( position=gaussians.position[binarymask], rotation=gaussians.rotation[binarymask], scale=gaussians.scale[binarymask], opacity=gaussians.opacity[binarymask], color=gaussians.color[binarymask]) return prunedgaussians Parameters: \epsilon: Masking threshold used in the indicator function to determine if a Gaussian is masked. \lambdam: Control factor for the number of Gaussians. Typical values are 5 \times 10^{-4} for real scenes and 4 \times 10^{-3} for synthetic scenes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The straight-through estimator requires careful implementation to ensure gradients flow correctly to mn without being blocked by the binarization. Boundaries: The threshold \epsilon must be chosen carefully. If too high, too many Gaussians are pruned, degrading quality. If too low, insufficient pruning occurs. Degenerate Input: Gaussians with zero scale or opacity are effectively masked out. The method assumes that small-scale Gaussians are negligible, which is generally true for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Adaptive Offset Masking is a pruning strategy that uses learnable binary masks to eliminate invalid Gaussians and their parent anchors, integrating the mask directly into the rate calculation for adaptive updates without requiring extra loss terms. It distinguishes itself from static pruning methods by allowing the mask ratio to be adaptively adjusted according to the compression rate via backpropagation, thereby balancing fidelity and bit consumption dynamically. Adaptive Offset Masking Time and Memory Complexity: The method adds a small overhead for computing the mask and loss, but significantly reduces the number of Gaussians N, leading to faster rendering and training times. Memory usage is reduced due to fewer Gaussians and the ability to discard the mask parameter m after training. Measured Performance: On the Bonsai scene, the method achieves 2.42x fewer Gaussians while maintaining similar PSNR (29.91 vs 29.87) and reducing training time (17m 51s vs 19m 22s) and increasing FPS (254 vs 154). On default scene evaluation, masking with \lambdam=0.0005 reduces Gaussians from 629,837 to 311,786 with PSNR 31.50, while \lambdam=0.0003 reduces to 596,449 with PSNR 31.89, and combined volume+transparency masking achieves 32.08 PSNR with 601,048 Gaussians. Scaling: The method scales well with the number of Gaussians, as the pruning is applied per-Gaussian and the loss is averaged. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths include effective reduction of redundant Gaussians, faster training and rendering, and consistent sparsity control throughout training. Limitations include the need to tune \lambdam and \epsilon, and the potential for over-pruning if parameters are not set correctly. When to Use: Use this method when memory and storage are constraints, and when the scene contains many small or transparent Gaussians that contribute little to the final image. When Not to Use: Avoid if the scene requires high-fidelity representation of small details that might be incorrectly pruned, or if the overhead of learning the mask parameters is prohibitive. Gaussian Volume Mask was proposed in the paper "Compact 3D Gaussian Representation for Radiance Field". It addresses the high memory and storage costs associated with the large number of Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method builds on the observation that many Gaussians have negligible volume or transparency and can be safely removed without significant quality loss. It extends the original 3DGS densification and pruning strategy by introducing a learnable mask that is optimized throughout the training process. name: Adaptive Offset Masking
head: Learnable Binary Masking for Anchors and Offsets
body: Adaptive Offset Masking is a pruning strategy that uses learnable binary masks to eliminate invalid Gaussians and their parent anchors, integrating the mask directly into the rate calculation for adaptive updates without requiring extra loss terms. It distinguishes itself from static pruning methods by allowing the mask ratio to be adaptively adjusted according to the compression rate via backpropagation, thereby balancing fidelity and bit consumption dynamically. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Learnable features \mathbf{f}i^m \in \mathbb{R}^K for each anchor i, where K is the number of Gaussian offsets per anchor. Threshold \epsilonm for mask generation. Trade-off hyperparameter \lambda. Outputs: Binary Gaussian-level masks m{i,k}, binary anchor-level masks mi^a, and updated entropy loss L{\text{entropy}}. Data Structures: \mathbf{f}i^m: A vector of size K containing learnable features used to determine the validity of each offset within anchor i. m{i,k}: A binary scalar (0 or 1) indicating if the k-th offset of anchor i is valid. mi^a: A binary scalar indicating if anchor i is valid. Numbered Steps: 1. Gaussian-Level Mask Generation: For each anchor i, compute the Gaussian-level mask mi using the learnable feature \mathbf{f}i^m and a sigmoid function with straight-through estimation. 2. Anchor-Level Mask Derivation: Compute the average offset mask ratio \overline{m}i for anchor i. Derive the anchor-level mask mi^a from \overline{m}i. 3. Pruning Logic: If all offsets in an anchor are pruned (mi = \mathbf{0}), the anchor is removed entirely from the rendering pipeline, including its position \mathbf{x}a, covariance \mathbf{A}, and mask features \mathbf{m}. 4. Rendering Application: Apply the Gaussian-level mask to the opacity \alpha{i,k} and scale s{i,k} of each Gaussian during rendering: m{i,k} \alpha{i,k} and m{i,k} s{i,k}. 5. Entropy Loss Calculation: Include both Gaussian-level and anchor-level masks in the bit consumption calculation for the entropy loss L{\text{entropy}}. Formulas: The Gaussian-level mask mi is defined as: mi = \text{sg}(\mathbb{1}[\text{Sig}(\mathbf{f}i^m) > \epsilonm] - \text{Sig}(\mathbf{f}i^m)) + \text{Sig}(\mathbf{f}i^m) - \mathbf{0} where: \text{sg} is the stop-gradient operator. \text{Sig} is the sigmoid function. \mathbf{f}i^m \in \mathbb{R}^K is the learnable feature. \epsilonm is a threshold. \mathbb{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function. A value of 1 in m indicates the corresponding Gaussian offset is valid, while 0 denotes invalid. The anchor-level mask mi^a is derived from the average offset mask ratio \overline{m}i: mi^a = \text{sg}(\mathbb{1}[\overline{m}i > 0] - \overline{m}i) + \overline{m}i where: \overline{m}i = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K m{i,k} If \overline{m}i = 0, the anchor is pruned. The entropy loss L{\text{entropy}} is defined as: L{\text{entropy}} = \sumi^N bi where bi is the bit consumption of the i-th anchor: bi = mi^a \sum{\mathbf{f} \in \{\mathbf{f}^a, \mathbf{l}\}} \sum{j=1}^{D^f} \left( -\log2 p(\hat{\mathbf{f}}{i,j}) \right) + mi^a \sum{\mathbf{f} \in \{\mathbf{o}\}} \sum{k=1}^K m{i,k} \sum{j=1}^3 \left( -\log2 p(\hat{\mathbf{f}}{i,3k+j}) \right) where: N is the total number of anchors. \mathbf{f}^a and \mathbf{l} represent anchor attributes and scaling factors. \mathbf{o} represents opacity attributes. D^f is the dimensionality of the features. p(\hat{\mathbf{f}}) is the estimated probability of the quantized feature. Parameters: \lambda: Trade-off hyperparameter balancing rate and fidelity in the overall loss function. \epsilonm: Threshold for mask generation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If all offsets associated with an anchor are pruned, the anchor becomes irrelevant for rendering and must be entirely removed to save parameters. The weight of the mask loss Lm must be manually adjusted across different RD trade-off points as \lambda varies to achieve optimal mask ratios, which can be tedious and difficult to optimize effectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegaussianmask(fm, epsilonm): """ Compute Gaussian-level mask for an anchor. Args: fm: Learnable feature vector of size K. epsilonm: Threshold for mask generation. Returns: m: Binary mask vector of size K. """ sig = sigmoid(fm) indicator = (sig > epsilonm).astype(float) # Straight-through estimator: gradient flows through sig, but value is binary m = indicator - sig + sig # The formula simplifies to indicator - sig + sig = indicator if sg is applied correctly in backprop # Note: The formula is m = sg(indicator - sig) + sig # In practice, this means the forward pass uses 'indicator' (or sig if indicator is 0/1 based on threshold) # and the backward pass uses 'sig'. # However, the text says: m = sg(1[Sig > eps] - Sig) + Sig # Let's implement exactly as written: raw = indicator - sig m = raw + sig # sg(raw) + sig. Since sg stops gradient on raw, gradient comes from sig. # But wait, sg(1[Sig > eps] - Sig) means the gradient of (1[Sig > eps] - Sig) is zero. # So the gradient of m w.r.t fm comes only from the last + Sig term. # Forward value: indicator - sig + sig = indicator. return indicator def computeanchormask(mgaussian): """ Compute anchor-level mask from Gaussian-level masks. Args: mgaussian: Binary mask vector of size K. Returns: ma: Binary anchor mask. """ avgm = mean(mgaussian) indicator = (avgm > 0).astype(float) # ma = sg(1[avgm > 0] - avgm) + avgm # Forward value: indicator return indicator def applymasktorendering(alpha, scale, mgaussian): """ Apply Gaussian-level mask to opacity and scale. Args: alpha: Opacity vector of size K. scale: Scale vector of size K. mgaussian: Binary mask vector of size K. Returns: maskedalpha, maskedscale """ return mgaussian alpha, mgaussian scale def computeentropyloss(anchors, masks): """ Compute entropy loss including mask information. Args: anchors: List of anchor objects with attributes f^a, l, o. masks: Dictionary with anchor masks ma and Gaussian masks mg. Returns: Lentropy: Total entropy loss. """ Lentropy = 0 for i, anchor in enumerate(anchors): ma = masks['anchor'][i] mg = masks['gaussian'][i] # Bit consumption for anchor attributes f^a and l bitsa = 0 for f in [anchor.fa, anchor.l]: for j in range(len(f)): # p(fhat) is estimated probability bitsa += -log2(anchor.probestimate(f[j])) # Bit consumption for opacity attributes o bitso = 0 for k in range(len(mg)): if mg[k] > 0: # Only count valid Gaussians for j in range(3): bitso += -log2(anchor.probestimate(anchor.o[3k+j])) bi = ma bitsa + ma mg.sum() bitso # Note: The formula has ma outside both sums, and mg inside the second sum # Correction based on formula: # bi = ma sum(f^a, l) + ma sum(o, k, mg) # The second term is ma sum{f in {o}} sum{k=1}^K m{i,k} sum{j=1}^3... # So it is ma (sum over k of mg[k] sum over j of bits) bicorrected = ma bitsa + ma sum(mg[k] sum(-log2(anchor.probestimate(anchor.o[3k+j])) for j in range(3)) for k in range(len(mg))) Lentropy += bicorrected return Lentropy Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows adaptive mask ratio adjustment according to the rate via backpropagation, eliminating the need for manual tuning of mask loss weights across different RD trade-off points. Enhances parameter savings by encouraging anchor pruning. Limitations: The weight of the mask loss must be manually adjusted across different RD trade-off points as \lambda varies to achieve optimal mask ratios, which can be tedious and difficult to optimize effectively. When to use: When compressing 3D Gaussian Splatting models and needing adaptive pruning to balance fidelity and bit consumption. When not to use: When manual tuning of hyperparameters is not feasible or when static pruning is sufficient. Adaptive Offset Masking was introduced in the paper "HAC++: Towards 100X Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the Gaussian Volume Mask technique [12710-gaussian-volume-mask.md] by integrating the mask into the rate calculation for adaptive updates. name: Visibility-Based Pruning for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Visibility Pruning within 3DGS, Visibility-Based Geometry Pruning of Neural Plenoptic Scene Representations
body:
Visibility-Based Pruning removes occluded 3D Gaussian kernels during the optimization pipeline to create a compact, "hard" geometry representation by concentrating alpha values into remaining kernels. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Gaussian Volume Mask by explicitly computing geometric occlusion via a visibility mask against training views, rather than relying solely on scalar thresholds of opacity or gradient magnitude. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Set of N 3D Gaussians M, set of K training viewpoints V, thickness parameter 	au, Minimum Viewpoint Exposure (MVE) threshold 
u, and regularization hyperparameter  eta. Outputs: Pruned set of Gaussians M' and updated visibility mask O. Data Structures: Gaussian Representation: Each Gaussian i is an ellipsoid defined by a covariance matrix \Sigma, decomposed into a scaling matrix Si and a rotation matrix Ri. The position is defined by the centroid P[i]. Visibility Mask: A binary matrix O of size N 	imes K, where O{ij} = 1 if Gaussian i is visible from viewpoint j, and 0 otherwise. Algorithm Steps: 1. Visibility Mask Computation: For each viewpoint j \in V: a. Retrieve extrinsic matrix d and intrinsic matrix K{mat} for viewpoint j. b. Initialize a dictionary to store points projected to each pixel. c. For each Gaussian i \in M: i. Project centroid P[i] to 2D coordinates (u, v) using forward projection with d and K{mat}. ii. Add P[i] and its camera-space depth zi to the pixel-specific list M{u,v}. d. For each pixel (u, v) with a non-empty list M{u,v}: i. Sort M{u,v} by depth zi in ascending order. ii. Select the first 	au points from the sorted list into a temporary set M^. e. For each Gaussian i \in M: i. If P[i] \in M^, set O{ij} = 1; otherwise set O{ij} = 0. 2. Pruning Decision: For each Gaussian i: a. Compute the sum of visible viewpoints: sumi = \sum{k=1}^{K} O{ik}. b. If sumi \le 
u, remove Gaussian i from the scene. 3. Regularization: During training, add a regularization term to the loss function to prioritize the pruning of smaller Gaussians: L{reg} =  rac{ eta}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N}  rac{1}{\|Si\|} where \|Si\| is the norm of the scaling matrix of the i-th Gaussian. t) for r, t in zip(rendered, target)) / len(rendered) # D-SSIM is a standard 3DGS loss term DSSIM = 1.0 - ssim(rendered, target) N = len(gaussians) regsum = 0.0 for g in gaussians: snorm = frobeniusnorm(g.scalingmatrix) if snorm > 0: regsum += 1.0 / snorm Lreg = (beta / N) regsum totalloss = (1 - lambdaval) L1 + lambdaval DSSIM + Lreg return totalloss Parameters:  eta: Hyperparameter for the scaling regularization term, typically 1 	imes 10^{-5}. 
u: MVE threshold parameter determining if a Gaussian is sufficiently occluded to be removed. 	au: Thickness parameter in visibility computation, defining how many points are picked from the sorted depth list. \lambda: Weight for D-SSIM term in loss, typically 0.2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Forward projection must handle floating-point precision for pixel coordinates (u, v) to correctly group points. Degenerate Input: If \|Si\| = 0, the regularization term becomes undefined; a small epsilon should be added to the denominator. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method reduces the number of kernels during training, allowing remaining Gaussians to optimize shape and color attributes more effectively. It results in a "harder" geometry representation. Strengths: Explicitly handles occlusion; concentrates alpha values into visible kernels. Limitations: Requires visibility computation at pruning intervals, adding overhead to the training loop. When to use: When a compact, hard geometry representation is desired and occlusion is a significant factor in the scene. The method was proposed by Niedermayr and Lee in their work on "Visibility-Based Geometry Pruning of Neural Plenoptic Scene Representations". It is designed to be embedded into the 3DGS optimization pipeline, specifically within the Adaptive Density Control block, performing visibility computation and removal jointly with densification steps. name: Rendering-Free Pruning via Hessian Importance
head: REFINE, Super-Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Pruning via Rendering-Free Primitive Importance
body: Rendering-Free Pruning via Hessian Importance (REFINE) is a post-processing framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that identifies and removes unimportant Gaussian primitives without performing forward rendering passes. It quantifies primitive importance using an analytically approximated Hessian field, which estimates the image-space quality degradation caused by removing a primitive based on parameter-space gradients. Unlike rendering-based methods such as PUP [14431-pruning-and-sparsity-control.md] or LightGaussian, REFINE bypasses rasterization entirely, relying on closed-form algebraic operations to achieve a 3,000× reduction in computational complexity and a ~20× speedup in device latency. Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene represented as a set of N primitives \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. A set of sampled camera viewpoints \mathcal{V} used to estimate the expectation of the gradient norms. A pruning ratio specifying the fraction of primitives to remove. Outputs: A pruned set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}' \subset \mathcal{G} containing (1-\text{ratio})N primitives. Each primitive Gi is defined by the following fields: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position (mean). si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling factors. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. ci \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 16}: Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. The method approximates the Hessian matrix of the rendering function to determine importance, avoiding the computation of the full dense Hessian which is infeasible for large N. 1. Structural Approximation: Assume Primitive Independence (ignore interactions between different Gaussians) and Attribute Orthogonality (ignore second-order couplings between attributes within the same primitive). This allows the Hessian matrix H to be approximated as a diagonal matrix W = \text{diag}(H). Note: The validity of this approximation is supported by the Diagonal Energy Ratio (DER). The average DER across scenes is 0.79, with values as high as 0.91 in less complex scenes, indicating that ~90% of the Hessian energy is concentrated in diagonal blocks. 2. Decompose Gradient: For a sampled viewpoint v \in \mathcal{V}, approximate the image error gradient with respect to the k-th attribute subset of primitive i (\frac{\partial R^v}{\partial Gi^k}) by decoupling it into two independent components: view-dependent visibility Vi^v and geometric projection Pi^v. The attribute subsets k are: geometry (gem), color (col), and opacity (opa). 3. Calculate Hessian Weights: Compute the Hessian weight wi^k for attribute k of primitive i as the expected squared L2-norm of the image error gradient across the sampled viewpoints \mathcal{V}: wi^k = \mathbb{E}{v \in \mathcal{V}} \left[ \left\| \frac{\partial R^v}{\partial Gi^k} \right\|2^2 \right] In practice, this expectation is estimated by averaging over a finite set of viewpoints \mathcal{V}. The gradient term \frac{\partial R^v}{\partial Gi^k} is computed analytically using the decomposed visibility and projection components, avoiding rasterization. 4. Compute Importance Score: Calculate the importance score D(Gi) for each primitive i by summing the weighted attribute contributions: D(Gi) = \sum{k \in \{gem, col, opa\}} wi^k \cdot \tilde{G}i^k \tilde{G}i^k represents the magnitude of the k-th attribute subset of primitive i. The method uses a content-adaptive hyperparameter configuration to jointly model geometric projection, view-dependent visibility, and other attributes, rather than relying on static weights. 5. Prune: Rank all primitives by their importance score D(Gi) in ascending order. Remove the bottom fraction of primitives specified by the pruning ratio. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computehessianweights(primitives, viewpoints): N = len(primitives) weights = {} numviews = len(viewpoints) for i in range(N): Gi = primitives[i] wgem = 0.0 wcol = 0.0 wopa = 0.0 for v in viewpoints: # The exact closed-form algebraic expressions for the squared gradient norms # ||dR^v/dGi^gem||2^2, ||dR^v/dGi^col||2^2, and ||dR^v/dGi^opa||2^2 # are not provided in the sources. They are computed analytically # by decomposing the gradient into view-dependent visibility and # geometric projection components. gradnormgemsq = 0.0 # Not given in sources gradnormcolsq = 0.0 # Not given in sources gradnormopasq = 0.0 # Not given in sources wgem += gradnormgemsq wcol += gradnormcolsq wopa += gradnormopasq weights[i] = { 'gem': wgem / numviews, 'col': wcol / numviews, 'opa': wopa / numviews } return weights def computeimportancescores(primitives, weights): scores = [] for i in range(len(primitives)): Gi = primitives[i] w = weights[i] maggem = magnitudeofgeometry(Gi) magcol = magnitudeofcolor(Gi) magopa = magnitudeofopacity(Gi) score = (w['gem'] maggem + w['col'] magcol + w['opa'] magopa) scores.append(score) return scores def pruneprimitives(primitives, scores, pruningratio): N = len(primitives) numtoremove = int(N pruningratio) sortedindices = np.argsort(scores) keepindices = sortedindices[numtoremove:] return [primitives[i] for i in keepindices] def magnitudeofgeometry(Gi): # Scalar magnitude of mu, s, q return np.linalg.norm(np.concatenate([Gi.mu, Gi.s, Gi.q])) def magnitudeofcolor(Gi): # Scalar magnitude of c return np.linalg.norm(Gi.c) def magnitudeofopacity(Gi): return Gi.alpha \mathcal{V} (Viewpoints): A set of sampled camera viewpoints. The source does not specify the exact number or selection strategy, but it is used to estimate the expectation in the importance metric. Pruning Ratio: The fraction of primitives to remove. Tested values include 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. Extreme Pruning Ratios: At high pruning ratios (e.g., 0.7) on scenes with dense primitive distributions and severe occlusions (such as Deep Blending), performance drops significantly (e.g., PSNR drops to 27.93). This is because the cross-primitive coupling effects, which are omitted in the rendering-free analytical formulation for efficiency, become non-negligible. Complex Indoor Scenes: Scenes with dense, overlapping surfaces (e.g., Kitchen) exhibit lower Diagonal Energy Ratios (DER = 0.67), indicating stronger gradient dependencies and potentially reduced accuracy of the independence/orthogonality assumptions. Time Complexity: The method relies on O(N) parameter space algebraic operations. It does not depend on image resolution or the number of cameras in the same way rasterization-based methods do, as it bypasses the rendering loop. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Hessian weights for all primitives, which is O(N). Performance: REFINE achieves a 3,000× reduction in pruning-related computational complexity compared to state-of-the-art methods like PUP. On MipNeRF 360 (Ratio=0.1), REFINE requires 3.14 GFLOPs and 5.90s, compared to PUP's 9582.81 GFLOPs and 44.01s. On Tanks & Temples (Ratio=0.7), REFINE requires 1.67 GFLOPs and 1.36s, compared to PUP's 7136.18 GFLOPs and 16.75s. On Deep Blending (Ratio=0.7), REFINE requires 1.77 GFLOPs and 1.42s, compared to PUP's 11067.59 GFLOPs and 15.15s. Quality: REFINE maintains competitive rendering quality. On evaluated datasets, it achieves a PSNR of 27.34, SSIM of 0.814, and LPIPS of 0.217. At 50% pruning, it achieves a PSNR of 26.61 on MipNeRF 360 (vs. LightGaussian's 26.92) and 22.97 on Tanks & Temples (vs. LightGaussian's 23.24). Strengths: Extremely fast, rendering-free, suitable for resource-constrained devices, and provides a global ranking of primitives. Limitations: Accuracy degrades at very high pruning ratios in scenes with high occlusion and dense primitive overlap due to the ignored cross-primitive coupling. Origin: REFINE was introduced by Chen et al. in the paper "REFINE: Super-Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Pruning via Rendering-Free Primitive Importance". Context: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [21] has become a popular technique for novel view synthesis due to its real-time rendering capabilities. However, the explicit representation often contains redundant primitives, necessitating pruning methods. Existing pruning methods either rely on parameter-space heuristics (which may not correlate well with visual quality) or rendering-based sensitivity scores (which are computationally expensive). REFINE was developed to bridge this gap by providing a rendering-free, analytically approximated importance metric.
