name: GoF-based Dynamic 3DGS Video Construction
head: Group of Frames modeling, Temporal segmentation with deformation fields
body: This method constructs dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) video by temporally segmenting input sequences into Groups of Frames (GoFs) and independently training Gaussian deformation fields within each segment. It solves the problem of motion drift and geometric inconsistencies that occur when modeling long-range temporal dependencies with a single global deformation field. By limiting the motion degree within short segments, it prevents the deformation field from struggling to adapt to complex, long-sequence dynamics. It sets itself apart from global optimization approaches by decoupling static and dynamic components via weighted MLP parameters and separating foreground/background content to reduce training complexity. Inputs: A dynamic video sequence; camera poses and intrinsics for each frame. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives with static attributes (position, base scale, base rotation, base opacity, base color) and dynamic attributes (deformation fields per GoF); a segmentation mask distinguishing foreground from background. Data Structures: 1. Static Scene Model: A global set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}{static} capturing long-sequence static information. 2. GoF Segments: The input sequence is divided into N non-overlapping temporal segments G1, G2,..., GN. 3. Deformation Field MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron f{\theta}(t, \mathbf{x}) for each GoF, parameterized by \theta. 4. Tuning Parameters: A set of scalar weights \alpha applied to MLP parameters to modulate focus on dynamic elements. 5. Foreground/Background Mask: A binary or probabilistic mask M{fg} identifying dynamic regions (e.g., humans, objects) versus static background. Steps: 1. Temporal Segmentation: Divide the input video sequence into multiple GoFs Gi. The duration of each GoF is short enough to limit the degree of motion within the segment. 2. Initial Static Modeling: Construct an initial scene model \mathcal{G}{init} that captures overall information across the entire long sequence. This serves as the baseline for all GoFs. 3. Foreground/Background Separation: Analyze the video content to differentiate between foreground (dynamic elements like human bodies, interacting objects, animals) and background (static environment). This separation reduces the complexity of the deformation field training. 4. GoF-Specific Initialization: For each GoF Gi: Preserve the extensive static regions from \mathcal{G}{init}. Identify dynamic areas within Gi based on the foreground mask. Initialize a GoF-specific model by exclusively fine-tuning the dynamic areas while keeping static regions fixed or lightly regularized. 5. Dynamic MLP Construction: Construct a dynamic Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for each GoF. The MLP takes time t (normalized within the GoF) and spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} as input to predict deformation offsets. 6. Weighted Training: During training, apply tuning parameters (weights) to the MLP parameters. These weights direct the optimization focus toward dynamic elements, effectively decoupling static and dynamic Gaussian components in a smoothly weighted fashion. 7. Deformation Field Derivation: Train the MLP for each GoF to derive the corresponding deformation field. The deformation field maps the static Gaussian positions to their dynamic positions at time t within the GoF. 8. Streaming Optimization (Optional): For transmission, selectively stream only the foreground model (deformation fields and dynamic Gaussians) based on user interaction, while transmitting the static background model once or less frequently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gofbaseddynamic3dgs(videosequence, cameraposes): # Step 1: Temporal Segmentation gofs = segmenttemporalsequence(videosequence, segmentduration=SHORTDURATION) # Step 2: Initial Static Modeling # Construct a global static model capturing long-sequence info staticmodel = initializeglobal3dgs(videosequence, cameraposes) # Step 3: Foreground/Background Separation # Identify dynamic regions (foreground) vs static regions (background) fgbgmasks = computeforegroundbackgroundmasks(videosequence) # Step 4 & 5 & 6 & 7: Per-GoF Processing gofdeformationfields = {} gofgaussianupdates = {} for i, gof in enumerate(gofs): # Extract frames and poses for this GoF gofframes = getframes(gof) gofposes = getposes(gof) # Initialize GoF model from static model gofmodel = copystaticmodel(staticmodel) # Identify dynamic Gaussians in this GoF dynamicgaussians = filtergaussians(gofmodel, fgbgmasks[i], region='foreground') staticgaussians = filtergaussians(gofmodel, fgbgmasks[i], region='background') # Construct Dynamic MLP for this GoF # Input: time t (normalized 0-1 within GoF), spatial coordinate x # Output: deformation offset deltax mlp = DynamicMLP(inputdim=4, hiddendims=[64, 64, 32]) # Define Tuning Parameters for weighted training # These weights modulate MLP parameters to focus on dynamic elements tuningweights = initializetuningweights(mlp) # Training Loop for Deformation Field for epoch in range(MAXEPOCHS): for frameidx, frame in enumerate(gofframes): t = frameidx / len(gofframes) # Normalized time pose = gofposes[frameidx] # Forward pass through MLP for dynamic Gaussians # Get current positions of dynamic Gaussians dynamicpositions = getpositions(dynamicgaussians) # Predict deformation offsets # Input to MLP: [t, t, t, x, y, z] or similar encoding deformationoffsets = mlp.forward(t, dynamicpositions) # Apply deformation deformedpositions = dynamicpositions + deformationoffsets # Render image using deformed positions and static positions renderedimage = render3dgs( staticgaussians, dynamicgaussians, deformedpositions, pose) # Compute loss against ground truth frame loss = computeloss(renderedimage, frame) # Backpropagate with tuning weights # Weights direct focus to dynamic elements loss.backward() applyweights(mlp.parameters(), tuningweights) optimizer.step(mlp) # Store derived deformation field and updates gofdeformationfields[i] = mlp gofgaussianupdates[i] = dynamicgaussians return staticmodel, gofdeformationfields, gofgaussianupdates Parameters: SHORTDURATION: The duration of each GoF. Not given in the sources. MAXEPOCHS: Number of training epochs per GoF. Not given in the sources. tuningweights: Weights for MLP parameters. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Motion Drift: If GoFs are too long, the deformation field may still suffer from long-range temporal dependencies and motion drift. Static Region Corruption: If static regions are not preserved during GoF-specific fine-tuning, geometric inconsistencies may arise across GoF boundaries. Foreground/Background Boundary: Errors in segmentation may lead to incorrect deformation of static background elements or lack of deformation for dynamic foreground elements. Time Complexity: Training time is proportional to the number of GoFs and the complexity of the MLP per GoF. It is generally faster than global optimization for long sequences because each GoF is optimized independently with limited motion. Memory Complexity: Requires storing a static model and multiple deformation fields (MLPs) and dynamic Gaussian updates. Memory usage scales with the number of GoFs and the size of the dynamic foreground. Strengths: Prevents long-range temporal drift; handles complex motion variations better than global fields; reduces training complexity via foreground/background separation; enables efficient streaming by transmitting only dynamic foreground. Limitations: Requires accurate temporal segmentation and foreground/background separation; may introduce discontinuities at GoF boundaries if not handled carefully; not given in the sources for specific performance metrics. When to Use: Dynamic video scenes with significant motion, especially where long-sequence modeling fails; scenarios requiring efficient streaming of dynamic content. When Not to Use: Static scenes; scenes with very short, simple motions where global optimization suffices; scenes where foreground/background separation is ambiguous. This method was proposed to address limitations in capturing long-range temporal dependencies in 3DGS video, which often cause motion drift and geometric inconsistencies. It builds on the idea of using deformation fields to model dynamic scenes but introduces temporal segmentation to limit the motion degree within each segment. The approach is detailed in "Adaptive 3-D Gaussian Splatting Video Streaming". Adaptive 3-D Gaussian Splatting Video Streaming, https://doi.org/10.1109/MNET.2025.3638049, fetched 2026-11-03

name: TIP-Editor
head: Text and Image Prompt-based Editor for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: TIP-Editor is a method for editing existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes using intuitive text and image prompts. It solves the problem of achieving accurate local editing while maintaining multi-view consistency, which is often compromised in text-guided 3D editing. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like GaussCtrl by employing a stepwise 2D personalization strategy with LoRA-based reference image alignment and localization loss, rather than relying on depth-conditioned ControlNet for geometric consistency. Inputs: An existing 3D Gaussian Splatting scene (set of Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients). A text prompt describing the desired edit. An optional reference image for content personalization. Outputs: An edited 3D Gaussian Splatting scene. Data Structures: The 3DGS scene is represented as a collection of Gaussians. Specific internal layouts (e.g., covariance parameterization, SH coefficient storage) are inherited from the base 3DGS representation. A set of "identified Gaussians" is selected for optimization based on the editing region. Steps: 1. Localization: Identify the Gaussians corresponding to the region specified by the prompt. This involves a localization loss for scene adaptation. 2. Content Personalization: Perform a content personalization step based on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to align the generation with a provided reference image, if applicable. 3. Optimization: Optimize the identified Gaussians using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss [89]. 4. Refinement: Apply pixel-level image refinement to the rendered images during optimization to ensure high-quality results. Formulas: SDS Loss: The method utilizes the standard Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss as defined in [89] (referenced in). The exact formula is not provided in the source text. Localization Loss: A localization loss is introduced for scene adaptation, but its mathematical definition is not provided in the source text. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A method for multi-view consistent editing using depth-conditioned ControlNet and attention-based latent code alignment. Choose when geometric consistency via depth guidance is prioritized over LoRA-based reference alignment. Performance: On the Instruct-N2N, DreamEditor, and TIP-Editor comparison, TIP-Editor achieved a CLIPdir score of 15.5, a DINOsim score of 39.5, a Votequality score of 70.8, and a Votealignment score of 81.2. Quality: The editing results exhibit superior quality compared with baselines. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables precise and flexible modifications using text and image prompts. Limitations: Not given in the sources. TIP-Editor is cited in a survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS. It is part of the latest series of methods that employ SDS loss within 3DGS to facilitate creative editing. name: GaussCtrl
body: GaussCtrl is a method for multi-view consistent editing of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes. It solves the inconsistency issues common in text-guided 3D editing by employing a ControlNet conditioned on depth maps to guide the editing of rendered images, ensuring geometric and appearance consistency through attention-based latent code alignment. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like GSEdit [142] and Texture-GS [146] by explicitly using depth-conditioned ControlNet to enforce geometric consistency rather than relying solely on SDS loss or texture mesh disentanglement. Inputs and outputs: Input: An existing 3DGS scene, text prompts, and optionally reference images. Output: An edited 3DGS scene. Data structures: 3DGS representation: Standard 3DGS parameters (position, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients, scale, rotation). ControlNet: A neural network architecture that processes depth maps and text embeddings to guide a diffusion model. Latent codes: Intermediate representations from the diffusion model used for alignment. Steps: 1. Rendering: Render images from the original 3DGS scene from multiple viewpoints. 2. Depth Estimation: Generate depth maps corresponding to the rendered images. 3. ControlNet Conditioning: Use the depth maps as conditional input to the ControlNet. 4. Editing: Perform image editing on the rendered images using the ControlNet guided by text prompts. 5. Latent Code Alignment: Apply attention-based latent code alignment to ensure geometry and appearance consistency between the edited images and the original scene. 6. 3DGS Update: Update the 3DGS parameters based on the edited images, likely using an iterative refinement process integrating 3DGS for fast rendering and InfEdit for rapid processing. name: StylizedGS
head: StylizedGS
body: StylizedGS is a controllable 3D stylization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models that performs color matching with a reference style image while utilizing a 3DGS filter to remove artifacts. It distinguishes itself from other stylization approaches by explicitly optimizing for nearest neighbor feature matching and depth preservation, ensuring the stylized output retains the geometric structure of the original scene while adopting the artistic appearance of the style image. Inputs: A pre-trained 3DGS model (representing the target scene) and a reference style image. Outputs: A stylized 3DGS model with modified colors and features. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS representation: a set of N Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{\mu}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color/view-dependent appearance. StylizedGS modifies the color/feature attributes during optimization. Optimization Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract features from the reference style image using a feature extractor (typically a CNN like VGG, though specific layers are not detailed in the summary). 2. Rendering: Render the current 3DGS model to obtain color and depth maps for each training view. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of the following components: Nearest Neighbor Feature Match Loss (\mathcal{L}{feat}): Measures the discrepancy between the rendered features of the stylized 3DGS and the features of the style image. The method employs a nearest neighbor strategy to match features, ensuring semantic consistency with the style. Depth Preservation Loss (\mathcal{L}{depth}): Ensures that the geometric structure (depth) of the stylized result remains consistent with the original scene, preventing geometric distortion during stylization. 3DGS Filter Loss: A regularization term that utilizes the 3DGS filter to remove artifacts introduced by the stylization process. 4. Optimization: Update the 3DGS parameters (primarily color/feature attributes) to minimize \mathcal{L}. Formulas: The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{feat} \mathcal{L}{feat} + \lambda{depth} \mathcal{L}{depth} + \lambda{filter} \mathcal{L}{filter} Where \lambda{feat}, \lambda{depth}, and \lambda{filter} are weighting hyperparameters. The exact mathematical formulation of \mathcal{L}{feat} using nearest neighbor matching is not provided in the sources. Parameters: Typical values for \lambda weights are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts: Without the 3DGS filter, stylization may introduce visual artifacts; the method specifically addresses this. Geometric Drift: If depth preservation is not enforced, the stylized scene may suffer from geometric inaccuracies. StyleGaussian is a method for real-time 3D style transfer with strict multi-view consistency. It differs from StylizedGS by embedding VGG features directly into 3D Gaussians and using an efficient rendering strategy: it initially renders lower-dimensional features and then maps them to high-dimensional ones. It aligns stylized features with a style image using an AdaIN-like mechanism and decodes features back to RGB using a KNN-based 3D CNN. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: StylizedGS provides controllable 3D stylization with artifact removal. Specific performance metrics or limitations compared to siblings are not detailed in the provided text. StylizedGS is part of the broader effort to apply artistic stylization to 3D Gaussian Splatting models, building on the efficiency of 3DGS while addressing challenges in visual fidelity and computational efficiency common in earlier NeRF-based methods. name: SGD (Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior)
body: SGD is a novel view synthesis method for street scenes that enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by fine-tuning a Stable Diffusion model on driving data and using it to regularize 3DGS training at unseen viewpoints, addressing the sparse-view reconstruction problem. It differs from prior sparse-view NVS methods that rely on object-centric multi-view datasets and relative camera poses; instead, it uses adjacent frames and LiDAR depth for direct fine-tuning on driving data, overcoming the domain gap. SGD consists of two main stages: fine-tuning a Diffusion Model with reference images and LiDAR depth, and integrating this model into the 3DGS pipeline to regularize training via pseudo views. Inputs: A set of training images \{Ii\} and corresponding camera poses \{pi\} captured by a vehicle. 360° LiDAR point clouds to derive depth maps for reference and target views. A fixed text prompt: “A photo a of driving scene.”. Outputs: A fine-tuned Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion 1.5 with injected U-Net features and a trained ControlNet). A 3D Gaussian Splatting model optimized with diffusion-based regularization. The method relies on standard 3DGS data structures (Gaussian positions, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) and Diffusion Model components: U-Net: The backbone of Stable Diffusion, modified to accept concatenated CLIP features. ControlNet: A trainable branch initialized with original Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights, conditioned on depth maps. CLIP Encoder: Used to extract image and text features. This stage prepares the prior by conditioning the diffusion model on adjacent frames and depth. 1. Reference Selection: For a target view, identify the closest preceding and succeeding frames as reference images. 2. Feature Extraction: Extract patchwise CLIP image features from the reference images. Extract CLIP text features from the fixed prompt “A photo a of driving scene.”. Compute depth maps from LiDAR point clouds for both reference and target views. 3. U-Net Injection: Inject the concatenated CLIP image features (from reference images) and CLIP text features into the U-Net during fine-tuning. 4. ControlNet Training: Train a ControlNet branch using the depth map of the target image as the control signal. 5. Training Strategy: Use a two-phase training strategy where the U-Net is fine-tuned and the ControlNet is trained separately. Jointly fine-tuning the U-Net and training the ControlNet simultaneously is avoided because the ControlNet must be initialized with original Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights rather than fine-tuned weights, which produces less authentic outputs. This stage integrates the fine-tuned model into 3DGS to guide synthesis at unseen views. 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussian models from the training views. 2. Pseudo View Generation: Project and rasterize the current 3D Gaussian models to generate pseudo views. Create novel evaluation views by interpolating the position of training/testing views and adding positional perturbations. Adjust rotation of novel views by offsetting angle \pm\delta, \pm2\delta along the z-axis, where \delta is randomly sampled from [15^\circ, 30^\circ]. 3. Regularization Loss: Use the fine-tuned Diffusion Model to provide regularization loss on these pseudo views. 4. Loss Functions: The total loss includes standard 3DGS losses plus regularization losses: L{L1}: L1 loss between pseudo view and diffusion prior. L{LPIPS}: LPIPS loss for perceptual similarity. L{depth}: Depth loss. Note: Applying L{L1} to pseudo views marginally reduces test view PSNR because pixel-level comparison amplifies inherent minor differences between diffusion-generated and real images. 5. Optimization: Update 3D Gaussian parameters using the combined loss. Unverified code. ControlNet(nn.Module): """Trainable ControlNet branch initialized with original SD 1.5 weights.""" def init(self): super().init() # Initialized with original Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights self.encoder = nn.Sequential(...) def forward(self, x, depth): return self.encoder(x, depth) def extractclipfeatures(images, textprompt): """Extract patchwise CLIP image features and text features.""" imagefeatures = clipimageencoder(images) textfeatures = cliptextencoder(textprompt) return imagefeatures, textfeatures def getdepthfromlidar(lidarpoints, camerapose): """Compute depth map from LiDAR point cloud given camera pose.""" projected = projecttoimageplane(lidarpoints, camerapose) depthmap = computezdistance(projected) return depthmap def interpolatepose(poses, t): """Linearly interpolate between camera poses.""" return poses[0] (1 - t) + poses[1] t def perturbposition(pose, magnitude): """Add random positional perturbation to a camera pose.""" offset = torch.randn(3) magnitude pose.position += offset return pose def adjustrotationz(pose, deltadeg): """Offset rotation along the z-axis by deltadeg degrees.""" rad = np.radians(deltadeg) rotz = torch.tensor([[np.cos(rad), -np.sin(rad), 0], [np.sin(rad), np.cos(rad), 0], [0, 0, 1]]) pose.rotation = pose.rotation @ rotz return pose def computestandard3dgsloss(renderedimage, targetimage, targetdepth): """Compute standard 3DGS reconstruction loss (L1 + D-SSIM).""" l1 = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(renderedimage, targetimage) ssim = computedssim(renderedimage, targetimage) return l1 + 0.8 (1 - ssim) def computediffusionregularization(pseudoview, priorview, pseudodepth, priordepth): """Compute L1, LPIPS, and Ldepth losses between pseudo and diffusion prior views.""" l1 = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(pseudoview, priorview) lpips = computelpipsnetwork(pseudoview, priorview) depth = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(pseudodepth, priordepth) return l1, lpips, depth def generatediffusionprior(referenceimages, refdepth, targetdepth, textprompt, sdmodel, controlnet): """Generate a prior view using the fine-tuned Stable Diffusion model.""" imgfeat, txtfeat = extractclipfeatures(referenceimages, textprompt) conditionedinput = torch.cat([imgfeat, txtfeat], dim=-1) priorview = sdmodel.denoise(conditionedinput, targetdepth, controlnet) priordepth = extractdepthfromdiffusionoutput(priorview) return priorview, priordepth def trainstage1unet(sdmodel, dataset, numiterationsunet, textprompt): """Phase 1: Fine-tune U-Net with injected CLIP features.""" for i in range(numiterationsunet): targetview, refimages, refdepth, targetdepth = dataset.sample() imgfeat, txtfeat = extractclipfeatures(refimages, textprompt) conditionedinput = torch.cat([imgfeat, txtfeat], dim=-1) loss = sdmodel.computeloss(conditionedinput, targetdepth, targetview) loss.backward() sdmodel.unet.step() def trainstage2controlnet(sdmodel, dataset, numiterationscontrolnet, textprompt): """Phase 2: Train ControlNet with depth as control signal.""" controlnet = ControlNet() for i in range(numiterationscontrolnet): targetview, refimages, refdepth, targetdepth = dataset.sample() imgfeat, txtfeat = extractclipfeatures(refimages, textprompt) conditionedinput = torch.cat([imgfeat, txtfeat], dim=-1) loss = sdmodel.computeloss(conditionedinput, targetdepth, targetview, controlnet) loss.backward() controlnet.step() return sdmodel, controlnet def trainsgd(gaussianmodel, dataset, sdmodel, controlnet, numiterations, numpseudoviews, textprompt): """Stage 2: Train 3DGS with diffusion regularization on pseudo views.""" for iteration in range(numiterations): targetview, targetpose = dataset.sample() refimages, refdepths = dataset.getadjacentframes(targetview) targetdepth = getdepthfromlidar(dataset.lidar, targetpose) pseudoviews = [] pseudodepths = [] for in range(numpseudoviews): t = np.random.uniform(0, 1) pose = interpolatepose(dataset.trainingposes, t) pose = perturbposition(pose, magnitude=0.5) delta = np.random.uniform(15, 30) multiplier = np.random.choice([-2, -1, 1, 2]) pose = adjustrotationz(pose, multiplier delta) rendered = rasterizegaussians(gaussianmodel, [pose]) pseudoviews.append(rendered) pseudodepths.append(getdepthfromlidar(dataset.lidar, pose)) targetrendered = rasterizegaussians(gaussianmodel, [targetpose]) lossstandard = computestandard3dgsloss(targetrendered, targetview, targetdepth) totall1, totallpips, totaldepth = 0, 0, 0 for pview, pdepth in zip(pseudoviews, pseudodepths): priorview, priordepth = generatediffusionprior(refimages, refdepths, targetdepth, textprompt, sdmodel, controlnet) l1, lpips, depth = computediffusionregularization(pview, priorview, pdepth, priordepth) totall1 += l1 totallpips += lpips totaldepth += depth totalloss = lossstandard + totall1 + totallpips + totaldepth totalloss.backward() gaussianmodel.step() Text Prompt: “A photo a of driving scene.”. Rotation Offset \delta: Randomly sampled from [15^\circ, 30^\circ]. Rotation Adjustment: \pm\delta, \pm2\delta along the z-axis. Depth-only ControlNet: Using only depth ControlNet without reference images causes the text prompt to dominate semantics, yielding high diversity but significant deviation from original scenes. Joint Fine-tuning: Jointly fine-tuning U-Net and training ControlNet simultaneously produces less authentic outputs because ControlNet must be initialized with original Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights rather than fine-tuned weights. L1 Loss on Pseudo Views: Applying L1 loss to pseudo views marginally reduces test view PSNR because pixel-level comparison amplifies inherent minor differences between diffusion-generated and real images. Training Time: Integration of the Diffusion Model increases training time due to the computationally expensive denoising operation. Training Speed: Training speed (iterations/second) drops substantially when introducing pseudo views (from 0 to 1). Rendering Speed: Rendering speed (FPS) remains unaffected by the introduction of pseudo views. Performance (KITTI-75%): PSNR: 23.85, SSIM: 0.837, LPIPS: 0.154. Performance (KITTI-50%): PSNR: 23.62, SSIM: 0.799, LPIPS: 0.158. Performance (KITTI-25%): PSNR: 23.44, SSIM: 0.793, LPIPS: 0.167. Performance (KITTI-360 50%): PSNR: 23.81, SSIM: 0.832, LPIPS: 0.155. Novel View Quality: BRISQUE score: 24.53, FID score: 73.36. Ablation Results: Complete model: PSNR 23.81, SSIM 0.832, LPIPS 0.155. w/o LPIPSpseudo: PSNR 23.11, SSIM 0.818, LPIPS 0.159. w/o L1pseudo: PSNR 23.83, SSIM 0.820, LPIPS 0.163. w/o Ldepthpseudo: PSNR 23.29, SSIM 0.801, LPIPS 0.169. w/o pseudo views (standard 3DGS): PSNR 22.78, SSIM 0.793, LPIPS 0.176. Strengths: Enhances rendering quality from broader views, smoother road surfaces, distinct lane markings, and clearer distant vehicles. Limitations: Longer training time due to diffusion denoising. SGD was proposed to address the challenge of maintaining rendering quality at viewpoints that deviate significantly from training viewpoints in street scenes, a problem stemming from sparse training views captured by a fixed camera on a moving vehicle. It is designed for autonomous driving simulation and street view synthesis, evaluated on KITTI and KITTI-360 datasets. The method leverages prior from a Diffusion Model along with complementary multi-modal data (LiDAR depth) to enhance the capacity of 3DGS. name: Equivalent Distribution Reorganization
head: ReorgGS
body: Equivalent Distribution Reorganization (ReorgGS) is a post-training reorganization method for converged 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models that addresses "parameterization degeneration," a failure mode where high-opacity floaters attenuate gradients to true surfaces and redundant overlapping clusters create strongly coupled parameter blocks. Unlike standard opacity reset, which only rescales opacity on the old overlap graph, ReorgGS rebuilds centers, covariances, and the visibility structure by resampling from the empirical distribution, thereby changing the graph itself. It preserves the original scene support asymptotically while reducing parameter coupling and opacity barriers, delivering up to 0.5 dB higher training PSNR and a 12.8% rendering speedup in representative settings. Inputs and Outputs Input: A converged 3DGS model G = \{gi\}{i=1}^N with parameters \{\mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, Ci\}{i=1}^N that has reached the middle-to-late stage of training, converged, or entered a plateau. Output: A new Gaussian set G' = \{g'j\}{j=1}^M with parameters \{\mu'j, \Sigma'j, \alpha'j, C'j\}{j=1}^M, where M=N. The induced field q(x) = \sum{j=1}^M \alpha'j \mathcal{N}(x | \mu'j, \Sigma'j) approximately preserves the support of the original empirical distribution P(x). Data Structures Original Gaussians: Stored as a list of N primitives. Each primitive i contains: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center coordinates. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (parameterized as Ri Si Si^T Ri^T in standard 3DGS, where Ri is rotation and Si is scale). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Ci: Appearance parameters (e.g., spherical harmonics coefficients). New Gaussians: Same structure as input, but with reorganized parameters. Parameters \alpha0: Initial opacity for all new primitives. Default value: 0.01. k: Number of nearest neighbors used for covariance estimation. Default value: Not explicitly stated as a single integer in the primary text, but the notation implies k is the count. Ablation mentions k=3 as an altered scale, implying k is a tunable parameter. The method uses k nearest neighbors. Steps 1. GMM Modeling: View the current Gaussian set as an empirical Gaussian-mixture field defined as P(x) \approx \sum{i=1}^N \alphai \mathcal{N}(x | \mui, \Sigmai). Define its normalized form as \hat{p}(x) = P(x) / Z, where Z = \int P(x)dx. In implementation, the continuous integral Z does not need to be computed explicitly; sampling only requires the discrete mixture weights. 2. Categorical Sampling: Sample a latent variable zj \in \{1, \dots, N\} from a categorical distribution P(zj = k) = \frac{\alphak}{\sum{l=1}^N \alphal}. Use only opacity \alphak as the categorical weight and do not multiply it by the Gaussian volume. This ignores volume to reduce sampling bias towards abnormally large Gaussians that correspond to blurred regions or artifacts. 3. Gaussian Coordinate Sampling: After choosing category zj = k, sample a new center from the corresponding 3D Gaussian xj \sim \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak). In practice, use the reparameterized form xj = \muk + Lk \epsilon, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and Lk is the Cholesky factor of \Sigmak. Alternatively, since 3DGS parameterizes \Sigmak = Rk Sk Sk^T Rk^T, use Rk Sk as the sampling transform. 4. Anisotropic Initialization: Perform a k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) query for each sampled point xj within the new point set \{xj\}{j=1}^M to obtain its k nearest neighbors \{x{j1}, \dots, x{jk}\}. Estimate the new covariance \Sigma'j using the local second moment: \Sigma'j = \frac{1}{k} \sum{l=1}^k (x{jl} - xj)(x{jl} - xj)^T. 5. Constructing the Reorganized Distribution: Set the new mean \mu'j = xj. Set the new opacity \alpha'j = \alpha0, where \alpha0 is a small opacity value (default 0.01). The spatial scale is determined by \Sigma'j. Inherit the appearance parameter C'j from the nearest old Gaussian: NN(xj) = \arg \mini \|xj - \mui\|^2, C'j = C{NN(xj)}. 6. Recovering Scale and Rotation: Perform eigendecomposition on the estimated covariance: \Sigma'j = Uj \Lambdaj Uj^T. Set the new rotation R'j = Uj and the new scale S'j = \Lambdaj (diagonal matrix of eigenvalues), such that \Sigma'j = R'j S'j (S'j)^T (R'j)^T. Reinitialize the optimizer state for the new parameters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def reorggs(gaussians, alpha0=0.01, k=4): """ Reorganizes a converged 3D Gaussian Splatting model. Args: gaussians: List of dicts or objects with fields: mu: (3,) array, center R: (3,3) array, rotation matrix S: (3,) array, scale alpha: float, opacity C: appearance parameters alpha0: float, initial opacity for new Gaussians k: int, number of nearest neighbors for covariance estimation Returns: newgaussians: List of dicts with reorganized parameters """ N = len(gaussians) newgaussians = [] # Step 1 & 2: Categorical Sampling based on opacity # Normalize opacities to form a probability distribution alphas = np.array([g['alpha'] for g in gaussians]) probs = alphas / np.sum(alphas) # Sample N indices from the categorical distribution # We resample exactly N points to maintain capacity M=N selectedindices = np.random.choice(N, size=N, p=probs) # Step 3: Gaussian Coordinate Sampling sampledcenters = [] for idx in selectedindices: g = gaussians[idx] muk = g['mu'] # Sigmak = Rk @ diag(Sk2) @ Rk.T # For sampling x ~ N(mu, Sigma), we can use Cholesky or RS # Using RS transform as suggested in source # Sk is scale, so standard deviation is Sk. # Sigma = R S^2 R^T. Cholesky of Sigma is R S (if S is diagonal sqrt of variances) # In 3DGS, S is usually the scale factors (std devs). # So L = R @ diag(S) Lk = g['R'] g['S'][np.newaxis,:] # Broadcasting: R Si for each column epsilon = np.random.normal(0, 1, 3) xj = muk + Lk @ epsilon sampledcenters.append(xj) sampledcenters = np.array(sampledcenters) # Shape (N, 3) # Step 4: Anisotropic Initialization (kNN Covariance) # Compute kNN for each sampled point within the NEW point set # Note: This requires a kNN data structure on sampledcenters # Assuming a function getknnindices(points, k) returns indices of k nearest neighbors # for each point in points. knnindices = getknnindices(sampledcenters, k) # Shape (N, k) newcovariances = [] for j in range(N): xj = sampledcenters[j] neighbors = sampledcenters[knnindices[j]] # Shape (k, 3) # Estimate covariance using local second moment # Sigma' = (1/k) sum (xnl - xj)(xnl - xj)^T diffs = neighbors - xj # Shape (k, 3) # Outer product for each neighbor and sum cov = np.zeros((3, 3)) for l in range(k): diff = diffs[l] cov += np.outer(diff, diff) cov /= k newcovariances.append(cov) # Step 5 & 6: Construct new Gaussians for j in range(N): xj = sampledcenters[j] covj = newcovariances[j] # Eigendecomposition to get R' and S' # Sigma = U @ Lambda @ U^T # R' = U, S' = diag(sqrt(Lambda)) ? # Source says: S'j = Lambda (diagonal matrix of eigenvalues) # But standard 3DGS parameterization is Sigma = R S S^T R^T # If S is diagonal matrix of scales, then S S^T = diag(s^2) = Lambda # So S = sqrt(diag(Lambda)) # However, source explicitly says: "set R'j = Uj and S'j = Lambdaj" # This implies S'j in the source context might be the squared scale or # the parameterization is Sigma = R S R^T where S is diagonal of variances. # Standard 3DGS uses S as scale (std dev). # Let's follow the source's explicit instruction: S'j = Lambdaj (diagonal matrix of eigenvalues). # This means the 'S' parameter in the output Gaussian object represents the variance spectrum, # or the source assumes a specific parameterization where S is squared scale. # Given "Sj' = Lambdaj (diagonal matrix of eigenvalues)", we assign eigenvalues to S. eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covj) Uj = eigenvectors Lambdaj = np.diag(eigenvalues) Rprime = Uj # If S is scale, S = sqrt(eigenvalues). If S is variance, S = eigenvalues. # Source: "Sj' = Lambdaj". We will store eigenvalues as S. Sprime = eigenvalues # Inherit appearance from nearest OLD Gaussian # NN(xj) = arg mini ||xj - mui||^2 dists = np.linalg.norm(sampledcenters[:, np.newaxis,:] - np.array([g['mu'] for g in gaussians]), axis=2) nearestoldidx = np.argmin(dists, axis=1)[j] Cprime = gaussians[nearestoldidx]['C'] newgaussians.append({ 'mu': xj, 'R': Rprime, 'S': Sprime, # Storing eigenvalues as per source instruction 'alpha': alpha0, 'C': Cprime }) return newgaussians def getknnindices(points, k): """ Simple O(N^2) kNN for clarity. In practice, use efficient GPU kNN. Returns indices of k nearest neighbors for each point. """ N = points.shape[0] dists = np.linalg.norm(points[:, np.newaxis,:] - points[np.newaxis,:,:], axis=2) # Set diagonal to infinity to exclude self np.filldiagonal(dists, np.inf) # Get indices of k smallest distances indices = np.argpartition(dists, k, axis=1)[:,:k] return indices Edge Cases and Pitfalls Abnormally Large Gaussians: Degenerate 3DGS optimization can produce abnormally large Gaussians corresponding to blurred regions or artifacts. Volume-weighted sampling would amplify these large-scale abnormal structures. This is handled by ignoring volume in the categorical probability calculation, using only opacity \alphak. Opacity Barriers: High-opacity floaters in degenerate distributions can create an opacity barrier where T{gp}(r) \to 0, cutting off optimization paths to surfaces behind them. ReorgGS mitigates this by reducing accumulated foreground opacity A{qd}(r). Precision: The kNN covariance estimation relies on the local density of sampled points. If M is small or k is too small, the covariance estimate may be noisy. The source assumes k \to \infty and k/M \to 0 for asymptotic consistency. Time Complexity: The core algorithmic module (resampling and covariance re-estimation) takes only a few seconds for millions of Gaussians, leveraging efficient GPU kNN implementations. However, as a post-training method, it adds approximately 5 minutes per stage for the LiteGS architecture on an NVIDIA A100 GPU due to subsequent gradient descent steps. Memory Complexity: The method maintains the same number of Gaussians (M=N), so memory usage is comparable to the baseline model. Performance: ReorgGS delivers up to 0.5 dB higher training PSNR and 0.14 dB higher test PSNR over direct continuation. It also provides up to 12.8% rendering speedup (e.g., from 10.75s to 9.37s on LiteGS/A100) due to reduced redundant alpha compositing. Strengths: Improves gradient accessibility, reduces parameter coupling, suppresses persistent floaters, and reduces rendering redundancy without changing the renderer or increasing capacity. Limitations: It is a post-training intervention, requiring a halt in optimization. It does not address the root cause of degeneration during training but mitigates its effects. The improvement is larger under reduced Gaussian budgets where each Gaussian carries more representational pressure. ReorgGS was proposed to address "parameterization degeneration," a late-stage bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting where converged models retain floaters, redundant overlap, and poor gradient accessibility. The method treats distributional equivalence as distinct from optimization equivalence, arguing that reorganizing the parameterization (opacity-density allocation, local overlap, alpha-compositing transmittance, and covariance alignment) is necessary to break fitting ceilings. It is evaluated on vanilla 3DGS, GOF, Taming-3DGS, 3DGS-MCMC, and LiteGS backbones across Mip-NeRF 360, Blender, and Tanks&Temples datasets. ReorgGS: Equivalent Distribution Reorganization for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://github.com/WoojunePark/splatpapers/issues/66, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: S2Gaussian
head: Sparse-View Super-Resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: S2Gaussian is a two-stage framework for reconstructing high-quality 3D scenes from sparse and low-resolution input views, addressing the joint challenge of deficient perspectives and clarity. Unlike methods that treat sparsity and low resolution as isolated problems, S2Gaussian handles this hybrid scenario by initializing high-resolution Gaussians from a densified low-resolution representation and refining them using super-resolved supervision. It sets itself apart from its parent Fine-tuning by introducing a specific "Gaussian Shuffle Split" densification strategy and a "Blur-Free Inconsistency Modeling" scheme to mitigate multi-view artifacts. Inputs: Sparse low-resolution input views (images). Estimated depth information for the scene (used in Stage 1). A pre-trained super-resolution model (used in Stage 2). Outputs: A set of high-resolution 3D Gaussian primitives (positions, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) representing the scene. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Standard 3DGS representation including mean position \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma (or rotation R and scale S), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{lm}. Sub-Gaussians: In the Gaussian Shuffle Split operation, one parent Gaussian is replaced by N sub-Gaussians. The sources specify N=6 as optimal. These sub-Gaussians are symmetrically located along the three principal axes of the original Gaussian. Parameters: Number of sub-Gaussians (N): 6 is the optimal trade-off between detail modeling and complexity/memory overhead. Resolution: The method is designed for super-resolution tasks, e.g., training on low-resolution inputs (e.g., 252 \times 189) and rendering at higher resolutions (e.g., 1008 \times 756). Steps: 1. Stage 1: HR GS Initialization 1. Optimize a low-resolution Gaussian representation using the sparse low-resolution views and the estimated depth information. This provides a reliable base structure and avoids overfitting to specific viewpoints. 2. Densify the optimized low-resolution Gaussians to initialize high-resolution Gaussians using the Gaussian Shuffle Split operation. For each low-resolution Gaussian, generate N sub-Gaussians. The sub-Gaussians are positioned symmetrically along the three principal axes of the parent Gaussian. This creates more compact primitives to facilitate fine-grained detail reconstruction. 2. Stage 2: HR GS Optimization 1. Render pseudo-views from the initialized high-resolution Gaussians (derived from the low-resolution Gaussians). 2. Generate super-resolved images from the original sparse views using the pre-trained super-resolution model. 3. Refine the high-resolution Gaussians by optimizing against both the original sparse views (super-resolved) and the pseudo-views. 4. Apply Blur-Free Inconsistency Modeling to mitigate multi-view inconsistency. Explicitly model the inconsistency between the super-resolved images and the rendered pseudo-views. Learn a blur kernel to reconstruct blur-free results with fine structural details, avoiding the blurring typically introduced by inconsistency modeling. 5. Apply 3D Robust Optimization to eliminate erroneous updates. This strategy prevents Gaussian primitives from simulating corrupted representations when training views are imperfect. Loss Function: The final loss L for high-resolution Gaussian optimization is defined as: L = L{AUX} + L{SR} Where: L{SR} is the super-resolution loss, computed between the rendered high-resolution images and the super-resolved target images. L{AUX} is an auxiliary loss, likely related to the consistency with pseudo-views or depth regularization, though the exact formulation is not detailed in the provided notes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def S2GaussianTrain(sparselrviews, estimateddepth, srmodel): # Stage 1: HR GS Initialization # 1. Optimize low-res Gaussians lrgaussians = InitializeGaussians(sparselrviews) lrgaussians = OptimizeGaussians( gaussians=lrgaussians, views=sparselrviews, depth=estimateddepth, lossfn=DepthRegularizedLoss) # 2. Densify via Gaussian Shuffle Split # N=6 is optimal N = 6 hrgaussians = GaussianShuffleSplit(lrgaussians, N=N) # Stage 2: HR GS Optimization # 3. Render pseudo-views from low-res Gaussians (or initial HR Gaussians) # Note: Pseudo-views are rendered from the low-res representation to provide supervision pseudoviews = RenderGaussians(hrgaussians, cameraposes) # 4. Generate super-resolved targets from sparse views srtargets = srmodel(sparselrviews) # 5. Optimize HR Gaussians hrgaussians = OptimizeGaussians( gaussians=hrgaussians, views=srtargets, pseudoviews=pseudoviews, lossfn=CombinedLoss, blurfreeinconsistency=True, robustoptimization=True) return hrgaussians def GaussianShuffleSplit(gaussians, N=6): """ Densifies each Gaussian into N sub-Gaussians. Sub-Gaussians are symmetrically located along the three principal axes. """ newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Extract principal axes from covariance/rotation axes = GetPrincipalAxes(g.rotation) # Generate N sub-Gaussians # Symmetric placement along axes # Example: 2 along X, 2 along Y, 2 along Z (or similar symmetric distribution) # The exact displacement vector calculation is not fully specified in sources # Assuming symmetric offsets along axes subgaussians = [] for i in range(N): # Placeholder for specific symmetric offset calculation # Based on "symmetrically located along the three principal axes" offset = CalculateSymmetricOffset(i, axes, N) subg = CopyGaussian(g) subg.position += offset # Scale/Opacity might be adjusted to preserve volume/intensity subgaussians.append(subg) newgaussians.extend(subgaussians) return newgaussians def CombinedLoss(rendered, targets, pseudoviews, blurkernel=None): """ L = LAUX + LSR LSR: Super-resolution loss between rendered and super-resolved targets LAUX: Auxiliary loss, potentially involving pseudo-views and blur-free modeling """ # LSR: Loss between high-res render and super-resolved target losssr = ImageLoss(rendered, targets) # LAUX: Involves pseudo-views and blur-free inconsistency modeling # Blur-Free Inconsistency Modeling: Learn blur kernel to handle inconsistency # This part mitigates multi-view inconsistency without blurring the result lossaux = BlurFreeInconsistencyLoss(rendered, pseudoviews, blurkernel) return lossaux + losssr def BlurFreeInconsistencyLoss(rendered, pseudoviews, blurkernel): """ Models inconsistency explicitly via blur kernel learning. """ # If blurkernel is learned, apply it to rendered or pseudo views to match # The goal is to reconstruct blur-free results with fine details # Exact formula not provided in sources # Typically involves minimizing difference between blurred render and pseudo view # or similar consistency term return ConsistencyLoss(rendered, pseudoviews, blurkernel) Time and Memory Complexity: The Gaussian Shuffle Split operation increases the number of Gaussians by a factor of N. With N=6, the storage memory increases significantly (e.g., from 67M to 112M for 4 sub-Gaussians vs 6, on Mip-NeRF 360). More sub-Gaussians increase optimization complexity and memory overhead. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360 \times 4 (24 views), S2Gaussian achieves 22.05 PSNR, 0.687 SSIM, 0.296 LPIPS, and 43.51 FID. It exceeds the top-performing combinatorial method FSGS+SRGS by 2.22 dB PSNR. Strengths: Handles both view sparsity and low resolution simultaneously; produces structure-accurate and detail-faithful 3D scenes; robust to corrupted training views via 3D Robust Optimization. Limitations: Prone to overfitting if high-resolution reconstruction is attempted directly from sparse low-resolution views without the two-stage approach; requires a pre-trained super-resolution model; increased memory usage due to densification. When to use: When reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse and low-resolution input views where both perspective deficiency and clarity are issues. When not to use: When high-resolution input views are available, or when computational resources are severely limited due to the increased number of Gaussians. S2Gaussian was proposed to address the challenging problem of reconstructing high-quality 3D scenes from sparse low-resolution views that simultaneously suffer from deficient perspectives and clarity. Existing methods typically handle either sparse views or low-resolution observations in isolation, failing in hybrid scenarios. The method was introduced in the paper "S2Gaussian: Sparse-View Super-Resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting". name: FreeFix
head: FreeFix: Boosting 3D Gaussian Splatting via Fine-Tuning-Free Diffusion Models
body:
FreeFix is a fine-tuning-free method to improve the rendering quality of extrapolated views in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by leveraging pretrained 2D image diffusion models (IDMs). It solves the problem of artifacts in rendered RGBs and inconsistency across frames that arise when using Video Diffusion Models (VDMs) or naive 2D IDMs, avoiding the computational burden of temporal attention and the loss of per-pixel guidance due to 3D VAE down-sampling. It sets itself apart from siblings like ViewExtrapolator or Difix3D+ by using a 2D–3D interleaved refinement strategy with per-pixel confidence masks derived from Fisher information, rather than relying on rendered opacity or warp masks which fail to identify artifact regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An initial 3DGS model G{init} reconstructed from a sparse or partial training set S{train} = \{(V^tj, I^tj)\}, and a continuous trajectory of m extrapolated viewpoints T{ext} = \{V^e0, V^e1,..., V^e{m-1}\}. Output: A refined 3DGS model G{refined} and a set of refined images for the extrapolated views. Data Structures: 3DGS Model G: Contains N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has position \mui, covariance \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T (where Ri \in SO(3) and Si \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3}), opacity \etai, and color ci. Fixed Image Set F{i-1}: A set of previously refined images \{(V^e0, 	ilde{I}^e{0,f}),..., (V^e{i-1}, 	ilde{I}^e{i-1,f})\}. Affine Matrices: For each generated view, two optimizable matrices Af \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3} and Ab \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 1} are maintained to correct color bias accumulation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with G0 = G{init} and an empty fixed image set F{-1} = \emptyset. 2. Iterate through Extrapolated Views: For each view index i from 0 to m-1: a. 2D Refinement: i. Render the current view V^ei using the current 3DGS model G{i-1} to get the artifact-ridden image 	ilde{I}^ei = \pi(V^ei; G{i-1}) and the opacity map M\alpha = \pi(V^ei; (G{i-1}, \alpha)). ii. Compute the uncertainty map  ar{C}{V^ei; G{i-1}} as the Hessian approximation:  ar{C}{V^ei; G{i-1}} = 
ablaG \pi(V^ei; G{i-1})^T 
ablaG \pi(V^ei; G{i-1}). iii. Compute the certainty map C^{c}{V^ei; G{i-1}} = \exp[-\gammac  ar{C}{V^ei; G{i-1}}] where \gammac is a hyperparameter. iv. Compute the confidence map M^{c}{V^ei; G{i-1}} = \pi(V^ei; (G{i-1}, C^{c}{V^ei; G{i-1}})) \odot M\alpha. v. Encode 	ilde{I}^ei to latent x^r0. Resize M^{c}{V^ei; G{i-1}} to the latent shape to get Mc. vi. Perform diffusion denoising steps. For each step t, calculate the guided prediction x^{t,g}0: If in early stages (overall guidance active): x^{t,g}0 = Mc \odot x^r0 + (1 - Mc) \odot ( eta M\alpha x^r0 + (1 -  eta M\alpha) x^t0). Otherwise: x^{t,g}0 = Mc \odot x^r0 + (1 - Mc) \odot x^t0. Here x^t0 is the standard denoiser prediction xt - \sigmat F	heta(xt, t). vii. Derive the next step input x{t-1} from x^{t,g}0 and xt: x{t-1} =  rac{\sigma{t-1} - \sigmat}{\sigmat} xt -  rac{\sigma{t-1}}{\sigmat} x^{t,g}0. viii. Complete denoising to obtain the fixed image 	ilde{I}^e{i,f}. b. 3D Refinement: i. Update G{i-1} to Gi by optimizing on S{train}, the previous fixed image set F{i-1}, and the current pair (V^ei, 	ilde{I}^e{i,f}). ii. For the current view, apply affine correction to the rendered image \hat{I}^ei before computing loss: \hat{I}'^ei = Af 	imes \hat{I}^ei + Ab. iii. Compute loss L = (1 - \lambdas) ||\hat{I}'^ei - 	ilde{I}^e{i,f}||1 + \lambdas 	ext{SSIM}(\hat{I}'^ei, 	ilde{I}^e{i,f}). Use a smaller weight for generated views compared to S{train} to prevent distortion. iv. Optimize Gi and the affine matrices Af, Ab for this view. c. Update State: Add (V^ei, 	ilde{I}^e{i,f}) to F{i-1} to form Fi. 3. Final Output: Return Gm as G{refined}. Formulas: 3DGS Rendering: \pi(V; G) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphai), where \alphai = \etai \exp[- rac{1}{2} (p - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (p - \mui)]. Uncertainty:  ar{C}{V;G} = 
ablaG \pi(V; G)^T 
ablaG \pi(V; G). Certainty: C^{c}{V;G} = \exp[-\gammac  ar{C}{V;G}]. Confidence Map: M^{c}{V;G} = \pi(V; (G, C^{c}{V;G})) \odot \pi(V; (G, \alpha)). Guided Prediction (Early Stage): x^{t,g}0 = Mc \odot x^r0 + (1 - Mc) \odot ( eta M\alpha x^r0 + (1 -  eta M\alpha) x^t0). Guided Prediction (Later Stage): x^{t,g}0 = Mc \odot x^r0 + (1 - Mc) \odot x^t0. Next Step Input: x{t-1} =  rac{\sigma{t-1} - \sigmat}{\sigmat} xt -  rac{\sigma{t-1}}{\sigmat} x^{t,g}0. Parameters: \gammac: Hyperparameter controlling sensitivity to artifacts in confidence map rendering. Range [0, 1]. Typical values: 0.001, 0.01, 0.1.  eta: Hyperparameter controlling the strength of overall guidance. \lambdas: Weight for SSIM term in the 3D refinement loss. Pitfalls: Using rendered opacity as guidance is ineffective because high-opacity regions can still contain severe artifacts. Using uncertainty maps directly is numerically unstable (0, +\infty)) and can be overwhelmed by low-opacity Gaussians with large uncertainties. Direct application of IDMs without interleaved refinement causes blurriness and inconsistency, especially in low-confidence areas like sky/ground. Color bias accumulation in generated views can lead to a blurry/over-gray effect if not corrected by affine matrices. Time Complexity: Quadratic in sequence length if using VDMs, but FreeFix uses IDMs which are linear per frame, though the interleaved 3D refinement adds optimization cost per view. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the fixed image set F{i-1} and maintaining affine matrices for each generated view. Strengths: Fine-tuning-free, preserves generalization, handles extrapolated views better than naive 2D DMs, avoids VDM computational burden. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial 3DGS, iterative refinement is slower than single-pass methods. When to use: When refining 3DGS from sparse/partial inputs for extrapolated views without access to [fine-tuning resources or VDMs. FreeFix was introduced by Hongyu Zhou et al. from Zhejiang University, University of Maryland, and Huawei. It addresses the trade-off between generalization and fidelity in diffusion-based 3DGS refinement. The method was evaluated on LLFF, Mip-NeRF 360, and Waymo datasets using SDXL and Flux as backbone IDMs. FreeFix: Boosting 3D Gaussian Splatting via Fine-Tuning-Free Diffusion Models, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv69130.2026.00109, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Localized Point Management (LPM)
body: Localized Point Management (LPM) is a training optimization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that identifies error-contributing 3D zones via cross-view feature mapping and performs localized point addition, opacity reset, and pruning to correct under-optimized or ill-conditioned points. Unlike standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) which relies on global gradient thresholds, LPM uses image rendering errors and multiview geometry constraints to target specific regions, improving reconstruction quality without the substantial training overhead of multi-view stereo or additional gradient propagation methods like GaussianPro or PixelGS. LPM operates as a plugin to existing 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines, identifying 3D zones that require densification or geometry calibration based on rendering errors. The method identifies error source zones by projecting 2D error regions from paired views into 3D space using cone intersections, then manipulates points within these zones. Inputs: Current view image I{curr} and ground-truth image I{gt}. Referred (neighboring) view image I{ref}. Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gk\}, where each Gk is defined by mean \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Camera parameters for current and referred views (center o, direction d). Outputs: Updated set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with modified positions, opacities, and counts. Gaussian Point: Defined by \muk (position), \Sigmak (covariance), \alphak (opacity), and appearance features. The covariance \Sigmak is maintained as positive semi-definite during optimization. Error Map: A 2D image of the same resolution as the rendered view, computed pixel-wise against the ground truth. Feature Matches: A set of correspondences M = \{(i, j)\} between local features of the current view A and referred view B, where i, j are indices of matched points. 1. Error Map Generation: Render the current view using the current Gaussian set. Compute the error map E against the ground-truth image I{gt} using an error function (e.g., L1 or L2 loss). 2. Cross-View Region Mapping: Select a neighboring view as the referred image. Extract local features from the current view A and referred view B. Use a feature matcher (e.g., LightGlue) to predict partial assignments M = \{(i, j)\} \subseteq A \times B. Identify paired regions (Re, R'e) based on matched points, where Re is the error region in the current view and R'e is the corresponding region in the referred view. 3. 2D-to-3D Projection (Cone Casting): For the error region Re in the current view, cast a cone of rays C from the camera center o along direction d (pixel center). The apex of the cone is at o. The radius r{Cone} is set to match the radius of the smallest circumscribed circle of the 2D plane error region Re. Similarly, project region R'e to cone C' from the referred camera center. 4. Error Source Zone Identification: Compute the intersection points of rays from cone C and cone C'. Define the error source 3D zone R{zone} as the smallest sphere that contains these intersection points. 5. Point Manipulation within R{zone}: Point Addition (Densification): If points exist in R{zone}: Apply densification at a lower threshold than standard ADC to complement original counterparts. For small Gaussians: Clone them, maintaining size, and reposition along the positional gradient. For large Gaussians in high variance areas: Split them into smaller points. If points are sparse (no points exist): Add new Gaussian points at the center of R{zone}. Point Reset (Geometry Calibration): Identify points at the forefront of R{zone} with the highest opacity. These may occlude valid points and cause incorrect depth estimates. Reset the opacity of these potentially ill-conditioned points to allow correction in subsequent optimization steps. Pruning: To minimize model expansion, adaptively prune points based on opacity values, starting from low to high. The number of points pruned is determined by the density of points in the zone. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localizedpointmanagement(currentview, referredview, gaussians, cameraparams): """ Implements Localized Point Management (LPM) for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: currentview: Image tensor of the current view. referredview: Image tensor of the neighboring view. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: position (3,) sigma: covariance (3,3) alpha: opacity (scalar) features: appearance features cameraparams: Dictionary containing 'o' (center) and 'd' (direction) for current and referred views. Returns: updatedgaussians: List of modified Gaussian objects. """ # Step 1: Error Map Generation # Render current view using current gaussians renderedimage = rendergaussians(gaussians, currentview.camera) # Compute error map against ground truth # Note: Ground truth image is assumed available in currentview context errormap = computeerror(renderedimage, currentview.groundtruth) # Step 2: Cross-View Region Mapping # Extract features featurescurr = extractfeatures(currentview.image) featuresref = extractfeatures(referredview.image) # Match features using LightGlue or similar # M is a list of tuples (idxcurr, idxref) matches = matchfeatures(featurescurr, featuresref) # Identify paired error regions # Re: region in current view with high error # Reprime: corresponding region in referred view errorregions = findhigherrorregions(errormap, threshold=0.5) # threshold example pairedregions = [] for region in errorregions: matchedindices = getmatchedindices(region, matches) if matchedindices: regionref = mapregiontoview(region, matchedindices, referredview) pairedregions.append((region, regionref)) updatedgaussians = list(gaussians) for regioncurr, regionref in pairedregions: # Step 3: 2D-to-3D Projection (Cone Casting) # Get camera parameters ocurr = cameraparams['ocurr'] dcurr = cameraparams['dcurr'] oref = cameraparams['oref'] dref = cameraparams['dref'] # Calculate cone radius from smallest circumscribed circle of 2D region rcurr = radiusofsmallestcircumscribedcircle(regioncurr) rref = radiusofsmallestcircumscribedcircle(regionref) # Define cones conecurr = Cone(center=ocurr, direction=dcurr, radius=rcurr) coneref = Cone(center=oref, direction=dref, radius=rref) # Step 4: Error Source Zone Identification # Compute intersection points of rays from both cones intersectionpoints = intersectcones(conecurr, coneref) if not intersectionpoints: continue # Define 3D zone as smallest sphere containing intersection points zonecenter, zoneradius = smallestspherecontainingpoints(intersectionpoints) Rzone = Sphere(center=zonecenter, radius=zoneradius) # Step 5: Point Manipulation # Identify points within Rzone pointsinzone = [g for g in updatedgaussians if isinsidesphere(g.mu, Rzone)] if not pointsinzone: # Case: Point sparsity - Add new Gaussian points newgaussian = createnewgaussian(center=zonecenter, initialsigma=defaultsigma, initialalpha=0.5) # default values updatedgaussians.append(newgaussian) else: # Case: Points exist - Densification # Apply densification at lower threshold for g in pointsinzone: if issmallgaussian(g): # Clone and reposition along positional gradient newg = clonegaussian(g) newg.mu = newg.mu + learningrate computepositionalgradient(g) updatedgaussians.append(newg) elif islargegaussian(g): # Split into smaller points splitgaussians = splitgaussian(g) updatedgaussians.extend(splitgaussians) # Remove original updatedgaussians.remove(g) # Point Reset (Geometry Calibration) # Find points at forefront with highest opacity # Note: "Forefront" implies closest to camera along viewing direction sortedpoints = sortbydistancetocamera(pointsinzone, ocurr) for g in sortedpoints: if g.alpha > highopacitythreshold: # threshold example # Reset opacity to allow correction g.alpha = initialalpha # e.g., 0.1 or 0.5 # Note: Position and covariance are not reset, only opacity break # Reset only the most occluding point or all high opacity? Source says "points", implying all. # Pruning # Prune points based on opacity, starting from low to high # Number of points pruned determined by density in zone density = len(pointsinzone) / volumeofsphere(Rzone) prunecount = calculateprunecount(density) sortedbyopacity = sortbyopacity(pointsinzone, ascending=True) for i in range(min(prunecount, len(sortedbyopacity))): gtoprune = sortedbyopacity[i] if gtoprune.alpha < pruneopacitythreshold: # threshold example updatedgaussians.remove(gtoprune) return updatedgaussians class Cone: def init(self, center, direction, radius): self.center = center self.direction = direction self.radius = radius def intersectcones(cone1, cone2): # Compute intersection points of rays from cone1 and cone2 # This involves ray-sphere or ray-ray intersection logic # Simplified: return list of 3D points pass def smallestspherecontainingpoints(points): # Welzl's algorithm or similar pass def isinsidesphere(mu, sphere): dist = norm(mu - sphere.center) return dist <= sphere.radius def issmallgaussian(g): # Check determinant or trace of covariance pass def islargegaussian(g): # Check determinant or trace of covariance pass def computepositionalgradient(g): # Return gradient of loss w.r.t mu pass def splitgaussian(g): # Return two new gaussians pass def createnewgaussian(center, initialsigma, initialalpha): # Return new Gaussian object pass def calculateprunecount(density): # Return number of points to prune pass Training Iterations: 30,000 iterations across all scenes. Densification Thresholds: The same thresholds for splitting and cloning points as in the original 3DGS and SpaceTime Gaussian are maintained. Feature Matching: Performed offline to save computational cost. Hardware: Experiments conducted on RTX 3090 GPU with 24GB memory. Standard ADC Limitations: Standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) fails to identify all 3D zones needing densification because local geometry complexity varies beyond single-value thresholding. Ill-Conditioned Points: Standard methods lack mechanisms for ill-conditioned points, such as wrong opacity estimates causing occlusion. LPM addresses this by resetting opacity of high-opacity points in front of error zones. Unnecessary Points: Lowering the threshold in standard 3DGS to catch all points increases Gaussian count, decreases rendering speed, and decreases PSNR due to unnecessary points in dense areas. Time Complexity: LPM adds a slight increase in training time compared to PixelGS and GaussianPro, which have substantially increased training times due to multi-view stereo or extra gradient propagation. Feature matching is performed offline to mitigate cost. Memory Complexity: LPM minimizes model expansion by adaptively pruning points based on opacity and density, keeping the Gaussian count comparable to or lower than methods that simply lower densification thresholds. Performance: On PlayRoom (Deep Blending): PSNR 30.22, LPIPS 0.241, SSIM 0.910 with 232k Gaussians and 22min training time. On Truck (Tanks&Temples): PSNR 25.61, LPIPS 0.154, SSIM 0.883 with 265k Gaussians and 21min training time. Scaling: LPM maintains real-time rendering speed while improving reconstruction quality. Strengths: Versatile plugin with minimal additional cost; improves PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending, and Neural 3D Video datasets. Limitations: May not be optimal for under-optimized points if the densification rules of 3DGS are not sufficient. Origin: Proposed in "Improving Gaussian Splatting with Localized Points Management" (CVPR 2025). History: Developed to address limitations in standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the inability to handle ill-conditioned points and the inefficiency of global thresholding. Usage: Applied to static 3D and dynamic 4D scenes for novel view synthesis. name: ParetoGS
head: ParetoGS: High-Quality Continuous-Budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Adapted Anchors
body: ParetoGS is a continuous-budget 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation that decodes any Gaussian count K from a single asset without separate optimization per budget. It achieves this by constructing a small set of sparse, adapted budget anchors with persistent member identities, encoding their parameter changes relative to a full model in a residual atlas, and interpolating shared parameters while gradually activating entering members at runtime. Unlike prefix-based or hierarchical methods that require fixed orderings or complex transformation modules, ParetoGS explicitly optimizes nested anchors and connects their aligned states, offering superior quality at low budgets compared to FlexGS and NanoGS. Inputs: A fully trained 3DGS model with N Gaussians, optimized using ImprovedGS for 30K iterations. Target anchor budgets Kj and scene data for calibration. Outputs: An ordered full model \ThetaN. A layered residual atlas \Deltaj storing parameter changes for each anchor j relative to the full model. Interval exponents p and q for each anchor interval. Member-order metadata defining the global nested sequence. Gaussian Parameter Vector: Each Gaussian i is defined by \thetai = (xi, si, ri, oi, ci), where: xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Log scale. ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Raw rotation quaternion. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity logit. ci: Spherical-harmonic coefficients. Residual Atlas: For each anchor Kj, the stored residual is \Deltaj = \Theta{Kj} - \ThetaN[1:Kj], where \ThetaN is the full model parameter matrix ordered by the global member sequence. The full model (KM=N) has zero residual and requires no additional state. The atlas uses lossy encoding (quantization) for storage. Interval Metadata: Two scalar exponents p and q are stored per interval between anchors. 1. Full Model Training: Train a 3DGS model for 30K iterations using ImprovedGS densification. 2. Anchor Schedule Definition: Define 11 anchors spanning 0.1% to 100% of the full count N. Target counts are Kj = \text{round}(N \rhoj) for \rhoj \in \{0.001, 0.002, \dots, 0.512, 1\}. 3. Anchor Construction (Contraction): Start from the current anchor (initially the Full model). Contract to the next target budget Kj using GNS (Gaussian Neural Splatting) for 15K–18K iterations. GNS adjusts regularization based on a linear opacity-decay trajectory, advances removal within a selection window, and uses a budget safeguard to retain exactly Kj members. Disable densification during this phase. Hold membership fixed and continue optimizing pixel L1 and SSIM reconstruction losses until 25K iterations total for the stage. Record deletions to determine the entry order \pi{L \to U} for the reverse direction (lower to upper anchor). 4. Member Correspondence: Concatenate the smallest anchor with the entry sequences from subsequent contractions to form a global nested order. This order ensures S(Ka) \subset S(Kb) for Ka < Kb. 5. Residual Encoding: Compute residuals \Deltaj = \Theta{Kj} - \ThetaN[1:Kj] for all non-full anchors. Encode the residuals using quantization rules (details in Appendix A of source). 6. Interval Calibration: For each interval between anchors L and U, calibrate exponents p and q using 10 training views. Minimize reconstruction loss plus penalties for loss regressions and slope deviations at t \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}. Store p and q for the interval. Budget-Conditioned Model: G(K) = \{(zi, \thetai(K)) \mid zi \in S(K)\}, \quad |S(K)| = K where zi is the persistent identity. Membership at Intermediate Budget: For L < K < U: S(K) = S(L) \cup \pi{L \to U}[1: K - L] The first L members are from the lower anchor; the next K-L are the first entries from the upper anchor's entry sequence. Shared Member Interpolation: For shared members i \le L: t = \frac{K - L}{U - L} \thetai(K) = (1 - t^p)\thetai(L) + t^p \thetai(U) where p > 0 controls the trajectory. p=1 is linear; p<1 approaches the upper state earlier; p>1 approaches it later. Entering Member Opacity Gating: For entering members L < i \le K: ai(K) = \text{clip}(tq ai(U), \epsilon, 1 - \epsilon) where ai(U) = \sigma(oi(U)) is the upper-anchor opacity, q > 0 controls activation speed, tq is the normalized progress weight (derived from t), and \epsilon is a clipping epsilon. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def paretogsdecode(K, fullmodel, residualatlas, exponents, memberorder): """ Decode a 3DGS model with exactly K Gaussians. Args: K: Target number of Gaussians. fullmodel: Parameter matrix ThetaN of the full model (N x D). residualatlas: List of encoded residuals Deltaj for each anchor. exponents: List of (p, q) tuples for each interval. memberorder: Global nested order of member indices. Returns: ThetaK: Parameter matrix for K Gaussians. """ # 1. Identify surrounding anchors L and U such that KL <= K <= KU Lidx, Uidx = findanchors(K, anchorbudgets) L = anchorbudgets[Lidx] U = anchorbudgets[Uidx] # 2. Restore endpoint parameters for L and U # ThetaL = ThetaN[1:L] + DeltaLhat # ThetaU = ThetaN[1:U] + DeltaUhat ThetaL = restoreendpoint(L, fullmodel, residualatlas[Lidx]) ThetaU = restoreendpoint(U, fullmodel, residualatlas[Uidx]) # 3. Determine membership S(K) # S(K) consists of first L members from global order, # plus first (K-L) members from the entry sequence pi{L->U} # Note: memberorder provides the global sequence. # The entry sequence pi{L->U} is implicitly defined by the difference # between U's members and L's members in the global order. sharedindices = memberorder[0:L] enteringindices = memberorder[L:K] ThetaK = np.zeros((K, D)) # 4. Interpolate shared members t = (K - L) / (U - L) p = exponents[Lidx][0] # p for interval [L, U] for i, idx in enumerate(sharedindices): # Interpolate parameters in optimization coordinates thetaLi = ThetaL[i] thetaUi = ThetaU[i] thetainterp = (1 - tp) thetaLi + (tp) thetaUi ThetaK[i] = thetainterp # 5. Handle entering members q = exponents[Lidx][1] # q for interval [L, U] epsilon = 1e-4 # Typical clipping epsilon for j, idx in enumerate(enteringindices): # Entering members take upper-anchor geometry and appearance # But opacity is gated thetaUidx = ThetaU[L + j] # Corresponding member in U # Extract opacity logit from upper anchor state oU = thetaUidx[opacitylogitindex] aU = sigmoid(oU) # Gate opacity tq = tq # Assuming tq is t raised to power q based on context aK = clip(tq aU, epsilon, 1 - epsilon) # Convert gated opacity back to logit oK = logit(aK) # Construct final parameter vector thetaKentry = thetaUidx.copy() thetaKentry[opacitylogitindex] = oK ThetaK[L + j] = thetaKentry return ThetaK Anchor Schedule: 11 anchors, \rhoj \in \{0.001, \dots, 1\}. Interpolation Exponent p: Calibrated per interval. Default search grid in Appendix A. Opacity Gating Exponent q: Calibrated per interval. q > 0. Clipping Epsilon \epsilon: Small value, e.g., 10^{-4}. Training Iterations: 30K for Full model; 25K total per anchor stage. Precision: FP16 for calibration residual anchor states; half precision for anchor coefficients and quantization scales. Precision: Quantization of residuals introduces encoding error. Anchor-budget requests incur this error, but interval decoding does not add further estimation error. Boundary Conditions: At K=L, t=0, shared members use \theta(L), and no entering members exist. At K=U, t=1, shared members use \theta(U), and all U-L members are entering with full opacity. Degenerate Input: If K is outside [K{min}, N], the method is undefined. The method assumes N is the count of the fully trained model. ParetoGS builds on On-the-Fly GS Progressive Training by explicitly optimizing nested anchors rather than just adding points dynamically. It differs from Two-stage Optimization by using a continuous budget interpolation rather than distinct stages. ParetoGS uses Pruning and Sparsity Control techniques (specifically GNS) during anchor construction to reduce Gaussian count. It differs from Rendering-Free Pruning via Hessian Importance by using image-supervised optimization for pruning rather than Hessian-based metrics. ParetoGS is a Fine-tuning method that adapts a full model to lower budgets. It differs from Backbone Fine-tuning by focusing on Gaussian count reduction rather than feature backbone adaptation. Time Complexity: Offline Construction: Mean offline time of ~10.3 minutes across 13 scenes, significantly faster than CLOD-3DGS (~35 min) and MGS (~74 min). Runtime: Parameter generation at runtime takes O(K) work for fixed parameter dimension. Memory Complexity: Storage: Encoding reduces mean additional state from 390.0 MB to 85.7 MB across 13 scenes. FlexGS Module: FlexGS-imp uses a fixed ~30 MB budget module. Performance: Quality: ParetoGS attains better average PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS with fewer Gaussians than compared prefix methods at 10% of each method’s own full model across 13 scenes. Low Budgets: At 1% budget, ParetoGS achieves 24.40 dB PSNR vs 18.84 dB for NanoGS-imp. At 0.1%, PSNR is 21.15 dB vs 16.37 dB for NanoGS-imp. Scaling: Quality degrades gracefully with decreasing K, outperforming CLOD-3DGS and MGS at low retention ratios. Strengths: Continuous budget support without per-budget optimization. High quality at very low budgets (0.1%). Compact storage overhead. Limitations: Requires initial full model training. Encoding error from quantization. Calibration required for each interval. Origin: ParetoGS was introduced by Xiaobin et al. in 2026. The paper "ParetoGS: High-Quality Continuous-Budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Adapted Anchors" presents the method as a solution to the inefficiency of pruning and re-optimizing for each budget in 3DGS. History and Development: The method builds on 3DGS (Kerbl et al., 2023) and ImprovedGS (Deng et al., 2026). It addresses limitations of existing scalable methods like FlexGS (Liu et al., 2025a), NanoGS (Xiong et al., 2026), and SCAR-GS (Revilla et al., 2026) by explicitly optimizing nested anchors and connecting their states. Usage: ParetoGS is used for efficient 3DGS representation where multiple resolution levels or budget constraints are required, such as in real-time rendering or streaming applications.
