name: Multi-stage and Progressive Training
body: Multi-stage and Progressive Training refers to strategies that decouple the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters or data streams to improve stability, convergence, or real-time capability. It solves the problem where joint optimization of complex attributes (e.g., materials, codecs) or continuous data ingestion leads to interference, instability, or overfitting. It sets itself apart from single-stage training by separating concerns into distinct phases or temporal streams, and from other methods by specifically targeting parameter decoupling (Two-stage) or incremental field updates (On-the-Fly). The family shares the core mechanism of temporal or parametric decoupling. In multi-stage approaches, the optimization domain is split into sequential phases where base parameters (geometry, appearance) are stabilized before refining specific attributes (materials, latents) while keeping the base fixed. In progressive approaches, the optimization domain is split temporally, allowing the Gaussian field to be updated incrementally as new data arrives, balancing the stability of existing geometry with the plasticity required for new data. Both approaches rely on iterative gradient descent with specific loss functions tailored to the active phase or data subset. Decouples geometric/appearance parameters from material or compression parameters to prevent interference. Choose when optimizing complex attributes like PBR materials or entropy-coded latents that cause instability in joint training. Optimizes 3DGS fields incrementally as new images are acquired, enabling near real-time reconstruction. Choose when processing continuous image streams or large-scale scenes where offline retraining is infeasible. The concept of decoupling optimization stages originates from the need to handle complex attribute sets in 3DGS, such as those required for physically based rendering (GS-IR) or efficient compression (CodecSplat). Progressive training for 3DGS emerged to address the computational cost of retraining on large datasets, enabling incremental updates via On-the-Fly SfM integration. name: Two-stage Optimization
head: GS-IR Training Process
body: Two-stage optimization is a training strategy that decouples the learning of stable geometric/appearance parameters from the optimization of complex attributes (such as material properties or compressed latent codes). It solves the instability caused by simultaneously optimizing high-dimensional generative pipelines and compact, quantized, or physically-based representations. It sets itself apart from single-stage training by preventing the gradient conflicts between generation stability and compression/physical accuracy, and differs from progressive training by using distinct, non-overlapping parameter sets for each stage rather than temporal data splitting. The method consists of two sequential phases. Stage 1 stabilizes the base representation (geometry and appearance) without the constraints of the final target domain (e.g., codec or PBR). Stage 2 fixes these base parameters and optimizes the specific attributes (materials or latent codes) using a rate-distortion or decomposition loss. Inputs: Context views C (images with poses), target view Yt (for supervision), and hyperparameters (\lambda, \gamma, \beta, \lambda{n-TV}, \lambdaM, \lambdaE). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian primitives \hat{G} (or their latent representation) and associated attributes (material M, lighting E, or codec weights). The specific data structures depend on the variant (GS-IR vs. CodecSplat), but generally include: 1. Gaussian Set G: Defined by position p, scale s, rotation q, opacity \alpha, and color/SH coefficients A. In GS-IR, this also includes normal n. In CodecSplat, this includes features F{mv} and depth D{enc}. 2. Material/Lighting Attributes (GS-IR): Albedo a, roughness \rho, metallicity m, and lighting coefficients E. 3. Codec Modules (CodecSplat): Feature encoder, entropy bottleneck, and post-codec refiner. Stage 1: Base Optimization 1. Initialize: Load context views C. Initialize Gaussian parameters T (geometry: p, s, q) and appearance A (color/SH). For GS-IR, also initialize normals n. For CodecSplat, initialize the feed-forward backbone MVEnc and Gaussian heads. 2. Forward Pass (GS-IR): Render the scene to obtain predicted color \hat{I}. 3. Forward Pass (CodecSplat): Extract features: (F{mv}, D{enc}, P{depth}) = MVEnc(C). Generate refined feature: Fg = FeatHead(I{1:N}, F{mv}, P{depth}). Predict codec-free Gaussian set G{cf} from Fg and D{enc}. Render target view: \hat{Y}{tcf} = Render(G{cf}, Kt, Tt). 4. Compute Loss: GS-IR: L{init} = Lc + Ln. Lc: L1 color reconstruction loss. Ln = L{n-p} + \lambda{n-TV} TV{normal}. TV{normal}: Total variation of normals. CodecSplat: L{stage1} = D{render}(\hat{Y}{tcf}, Yt). 5. Update: Minimize L{init} or L{stage1} using Adam optimizer to update T and A (and n for GS-IR) for 30,000 iterations. For CodecSplat, update backbone modules. Stage 2: Attribute/Codec Optimization 1. Freeze: Fix T and A (and n for GS-IR). For CodecSplat, fix the backbone modules trained in Stage 1. 2. Initialize Attributes: GS-IR: Initialize material M=\{a, \rho, m\} and lighting E. CodecSplat: Enable the feature codec and post-codec refiner. 3. Forward Pass (GS-IR): Render with PBR model using M and E. Compute predicted shading \hat{I}{shade}. 4. Forward Pass (CodecSplat): Encode features to latent code. Decode to get Gaussian set \hat{G}. Render target view: \hat{Y}t = Render(\hat{G}, Kt, Tt). Compute codec-side depth loss: Calculate decoder-side normalized inverse-depth S. Calculate encoder-side normalized inverse-depth S{enc}: S{enc,i}(p) = \frac{D{enc,i}(p)^{-1} - fi^{-1}}{ni^{-1} - fi^{-1}} where ni, fi are near/far bounds of context view i. D{codec-depth} = \| S - S{enc} \|1. 5. Compute Loss: GS-IR: Ld = L{shade} + \lambdaM TV{mat} + \lambdaE TV{light}. L{shade} = I - \hat{I}{shade}(M, E, V{illu}). TV{mat}: Total variation of material map \hat{M}. TV{light}: Total variation of lighting \hat{E}. CodecSplat: L{stage2}(\lambda) = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda{max}} \left[ D{render}(\hat{Y}t, Yt) + \gamma D{codec-depth} \right] + \beta R where R is the estimated rate, \gamma=0.1, \lambda{max}=1024. 6. Update: GS-IR: Minimize Ld to optimize M for 10,000 iterations. CodecSplat: Sample \lambda \in [16, 1024] during training. Optimize codec-related modules. GS-IR: Optimizer: Adam. Iterations: 30,000 (Stage 1), 10,000 (Stage 2). \lambda{n-TV}: 5.0. \lambdaM: 1.0. \lambdaE: 0.01. Hardware: Single NVIDIA V100. CodecSplat: Optimizer: AdamW, LR 10^{-4}, weight decay 0.01. \gamma: 0.1. \beta: 10^{-4} (DL3DV), 4 \times 10^{-4} (RE10K). \lambda: Sampled from [16, 1024] during training; fixed at test time. Hardware: Four NVIDIA RTX 5880 48GB GPUs. Instability: Directly training with a quantized bottleneck is unstable; the two-stage approach is required to prevent gradient conflicts. Rate Selection: \lambda must be sampled during training to cover the rate-distortion curve, but fixed at inference for a specific bitrate. Depth Normalization: The codec-side depth loss requires careful normalization using near/far bounds to ensure S and S{enc} are comparable. Optimizes geometry/appearance then material/lighting for inverse rendering. Uses normal gradient-based densification and PBR losses. (implied by S2): Optimizes geometry/appearance then latent codes for compression. Uses rate-distortion loss and codec-side depth supervision. Time Complexity: Stage 1 typically dominates due to longer iteration counts (30k vs 10k) and full backbone training. Memory Complexity: Stage 1 requires storing full backbone gradients. Stage 2 may require additional memory for codec buffers or PBR shading computations. Performance: GS-IR achieves high-fidelity inverse rendering on a single V100. CodecSplat achieves KiB-level compression with minimal quality loss compared to MiB-level baselines. Strengths: Stabilizes training for complex attributes; enables compression without quality collapse. Limitations: Requires two distinct training phases; hyperparameter tuning for loss weights (\lambda, \gamma, \beta) is critical. The concept originates from the need to decouple stable geometric learning from complex attribute optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting. GS-IR introduced the initial stage/decomposition stage split for inverse rendering. CodecSplat adapted this for feed-forward Gaussian compression, separating codec-free generation from codec-aware latent coding. name: Two-stage training procedure for Relightable 3D Gaussians
head: R3DG training, inverse rendering optimization stages
body: This method defines the optimization protocol for Relightable 3D Gaussians (R3DG), a technique that reconstructs relightable scenes from multi-view images by combining standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering with physically based rendering (PBR) and BRDF decomposition. It solves the problem of recovering geometry, material properties (albedo, roughness), and lighting from static multi-view inputs, enabling novel view synthesis and relighting. It sets itself apart from vanilla 3DGS by introducing normal gradient-based densification in the first stage and PBR-specific loss terms in the second stage, while differing from neural relightable methods by maintaining a discrete point-based representation. The training procedure is divided into two distinct stages. Stage 1 establishes the geometric and photometric foundation using 3DGS settings augmented with normal constraints. Stage 2 refines the material and lighting properties by sampling incident rays for PBR evaluation. Inputs: Multi-view images of a static scene. Camera poses for each input view. Initial 3D Gaussian points (typically derived from Structure-from-Motion or similar initialization, though specific initialization details are not provided in the source). Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian attributes: position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients (for view-dependent color), normal vectors, albedo, roughness, and environment map parameters. The method operates on a set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i maintains attributes including: Position \mathbf{p}i Covariance matrix \Sigmai (or rotation/scale representation) Opacity \alphai Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}i Normal vector \mathbf{n}i Albedo \mathbf{a}i Roughness \rhoi Environment map parameters (for lighting) Note: The exact memory layout or bit-packing of these attributes is not specified in the sources. Stage 1: Geometry and Normal Optimization 1. Initialize the 3D Gaussians. 2. Iterate for 30,000 iterations. 3. Densification: Perform normal gradient-based densification. A new Gaussian is split or cloned if the normal gradient magnitude exceeds the threshold Tn = 2 \times 10^{-9}. 4. Rendering: Render the scene from the input camera views using standard 3DGS alpha-blending. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using Equation (16): \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{ssim} \mathcal{L}{ssim} + \lambdan \mathcal{L}n + \lambda{s,n} \mathcal{L}{s,n} + \lambdaO \mathcal{L}O + \lambdau \mathcal{L}u Where: \mathcal{L}1: L1 loss between rendered and ground truth colors. \mathcal{L}{ssim}: SSIM loss. \mathcal{L}n: Normal consistency loss. \mathcal{L}{s,n}: Surface normal smoothness or consistency loss. \mathcal{L}O: Opacity regularization or loss. \mathcal{L}u: Uncertainty or other auxiliary loss. Note: The exact mathematical definitions of \mathcal{L}n, \mathcal{L}{s,n}, \mathcal{L}O, \mathcal{L}u are not provided in the source text. 6. Update: Backpropagate and update Gaussian attributes using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Stage 2: PBR and Material Optimization 1. Iterate for 10,000 iterations. 2. Ray Sampling: For each Gaussian point, sample Ns = 64 incident rays to evaluate the PBR model. 3. Rendering: Render the scene using the PBR model, incorporating the sampled lighting and material properties. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using Equation (17): \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{ssim} \mathcal{L}{ssim} + \lambdal \mathcal{L}l + \lambda{s,b} \mathcal{L}{s,b} + \lambda{s,r} \mathcal{L}{s,r} Where: \mathcal{L}1: L1 loss between rendered and ground truth colors. \mathcal{L}{ssim}: SSIM loss. \mathcal{L}l: Lighting loss (e.g., consistency with estimated environment map). \mathcal{L}{s,b}: BRDF smoothness or consistency loss for base color/albedo. \mathcal{L}{s,r}: BRDF smoothness or consistency loss for roughness. Note: The exact mathematical definitions of \mathcal{L}l, \mathcal{L}{s,b}, \mathcal{L}{s,r} are not provided in the source text. 5. Update: Backpropagate and update Gaussian attributes. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainr3dg(inputimages, cameraposes, initialgaussians, numiterationsstage1=30000, numiterationsstage2=10000): """ Two-stage training procedure for Relightable 3D Gaussians. Args: inputimages: List of input views (H, W, 3) cameraposes: List of camera poses (4, 4) initialgaussians: Initial set of 3D Gaussians numiterationsstage1: Number of iterations for Stage 1 numiterationsstage2: Number of iterations for Stage 2 Returns: Optimized Gaussians with PBR attributes """ gaussians = initialgaussians # Stage 1: Geometry and Normal Optimization for i in range(numiterationsstage1): # Sample a random view from input images viewidx = random.randint(0, len(inputimages) - 1) gtimage = inputimages[viewidx] pose = cameraposes[viewidx] # Normal gradient-based densification # Check normal gradients for each Gaussian for g in gaussians: if g.normalgradientmagnitude > Tn: # Tn = 2e-9 densifygaussian(gaussians, g) # Render scene using standard 3DGS renderedimage = render3dgs(gaussians, pose) # Compute Stage 1 Loss # L = lambda1 L1 + lambdassim Lssim + lambdan Ln + lambdas,n Ls,n + lambdaO LO + lambdau Lu lossl1 = computel1loss(renderedimage, gtimage) lossssim = computessimloss(renderedimage, gtimage) lossn = computenormalloss(gaussians, gtnormals) # Assuming gtnormals available or estimated losssn = computesurfacenormalsmoothness(gaussians) losso = computeopacityloss(gaussians) lossu = computeauxiliaryloss(gaussians) lossstage1 = (lambda1 lossl1 + lambdassim lossssim + lambdan lossn + lambdasn losssn + lambdaO losso + lambdau lossu) # Backpropagate and update lossstage1.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Regular 3DGS densification/pruning steps would occur here # Stage 2: PBR and Material Optimization for i in range(numiterationsstage2): viewidx = random.randint(0, len(inputimages) - 1) gtimage = inputimages[viewidx] pose = cameraposes[viewidx] # Sample incident rays for PBR # Ns = 64 rays per Gaussian point incidentrays = sampleincidentrays(gaussians, Ns=64) # Render scene using PBR model renderedpbrimage = renderpbr(gaussians, pose, incidentrays) # Compute Stage 2 Loss # L = lambda1 L1 + lambdassim Lssim + lambdal Ll + lambdas,b Ls,b + lambdas,r Ls,r lossl1 = computel1loss(renderedpbrimage, gtimage) lossssim = computessimloss(renderedpbrimage, gtimage) lossl = computelightingloss(gaussians, incidentrays) losssb = computebrdfsmoothnessbase(gaussians) losssr = computebrdfsmoothnessroughness(gaussians) lossstage2 = (lambda1 lossl1 + lambdassim lossssim + lambdal lossl + lambdasb losssb + lambdasr losssr) # Backpropagate and update lossstage2.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return gaussians Tn = 2e-9 Ns = 64 lambda1 = 0.8 lambdassim = 0.2 lambdan = 0.01 lambdasn = 0.01 lambdaO = 0.01 lambdau = 0.01 lambdal = 0.0001 lambdasb = 0.01 lambdasr = 0.01 Tn: Normal gradient densification threshold, set to 2 \times 10^{-9}. Ns: Number of incident rays sampled per Gaussian point for PBR in Stage 2, set to 64. \lambda1: L1 loss weight, set to 0.8 for both stages. \lambda{ssim}: SSIM loss weight, set to 0.2 for both stages. \lambdan, \lambda{s,n}, \lambdaO, \lambdau: Stage 1 auxiliary loss weights, each set to 0.01. \lambdal: Stage 2 lighting loss weight, set to 0.0001. \lambda{s,b}, \lambda{s,r}: Stage 2 BRDF loss weights, each set to 0.01. Large-scale scenes: The high density of points in large scenes can slow down optimization significantly because rays are sampled and PBR is performed at each point. This is a limitation of the current pipeline. Static objects only: The method is designed for static objects; dynamic scenes are not supported. Precision: The normal gradient threshold Tn is very small (2 \times 10^{-9}), requiring careful numerical implementation to avoid noise-induced densification or failure to densify. Time Complexity: The method requires 40,000 total iterations (30,000 in Stage 1, 10,000 in Stage 2). Stage 2 is computationally more expensive per iteration due to ray sampling (Ns=64) and PBR evaluation. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians. The high point density required for accurate PBR can lead to high memory consumption, especially in large scenes. Measured Performance: On the Synthetic4Relight dataset, R3DG achieves: Novel View Synthesis (NVS) PSNR: 36.80, SSIM: 0.982, LPIPS: 0.028. Relighting PSNR: 31.00, SSIM: 0.964, LPIPS: 0.050. Albedo PSNR: 28.31, SSIM: 0.951, LPIPS: 0.058. Training time: 0.90 hours. Scaling: Performance degrades or optimization slows down in large-scale scenes due to point density. Strengths: Excels in relighting capability compared to point-based methods. Shows significantly better NVS quality than other relightable methods. Achieves realistic PBR rendering, smooth normal estimation, and accurate visibility on discrete point clouds. Limitations: NVS performance slightly trails vanilla 3DGS. Limited to static objects. High point density slows optimization in large scenes. When to use: For inverse rendering and relighting of static objects from multi-view images where high-quality relighting and material recovery are prioritized over raw NVS PSNR. When not to use: For large-scale dynamic scenes or when vanilla 3DGS NVS performance is the sole metric of interest. The method was introduced in the paper "Relightable 3D Gaussians: Realistic Point Cloud Relighting with BRDF Decomposition and Ray Tracing" by J. Gao et al.. It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [26] and extends it with PBR capabilities. The work was supported by the National Key R&D Program of China and NSFC. name: On-the-Fly GS Progressive Training
head: On-the-Fly Gaussian Splatting
body: On-the-Fly GS Progressive Training is a method for incrementally optimizing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) field as new images are acquired in real-time, enabling near real-time reconstruction without retraining the entire scene from scratch. It differs from offline training by decoupling the optimization domain temporally, appending new Gaussians for newly observed geometry and performing localized, weighted gradient updates for each incoming image. Unlike Two-stage Optimization, which separates geometry and appearance into sequential phases, this method integrates densification and appearance refinement continuously through a hierarchical weighting scheme and adaptive learning rates. The method operates in three distinct phases: Initial Training, Progressive Training, and Final Optimization. Inputs: A sequence of incoming RGB images I{new}, camera poses estimated by On-the-Fly SfM, and the current 3DGS field \mathcal{G} containing N Gaussians. Each Gaussian g is defined by position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color. Outputs: An updated 3DGS field \mathcal{G}' and refined camera poses for the registered images. 3DGS Field: A list of Gaussians. Each Gaussian stores position, rotation, scale, opacity, and SH coefficients. Sparse Point Cloud: A set of 3D points \mathcal{P} generated by On-the-Fly SfM. Search Tree: A spatial index (e.g., KD-tree) built over \mathcal{P} to query nearest neighbors. Image Weights: A map associating each registered image with a scalar weight \omega. Gaussian Count per Pixel: An array Gp storing the number of Gaussians splatting onto pixel p for load balancing. 1. Acquire the first N0 images. 2. Run On-the-Fly SfM to estimate poses and generate the initial sparse point cloud \mathcal{P}0. 3. Initialize the 3DGS field \mathcal{G} using the points in \mathcal{P}0. 4. Perform standard 3DGS optimization for T{init} iterations on these N0 images. 1. Pose and Point Cloud Update: On-the-Fly SfM estimates the pose of the new image n and performs local Bundle Adjustment (BA) to refine poses of neighboring registered images, updating the sparse point cloud \mathcal{P}. 2. Densification: Construct a search tree over the current sparse point cloud \mathcal{P}. For each point p{new} in the new image's point cloud, query the search tree for the nearest neighbor distance d. If d > \tau (predefined distance threshold), classify p{new} as a new point. Initialize new Gaussians for these points and append them to \mathcal{G}. 3. Hierarchical Image Weighting: Calculate weights \omegai for all registered images to determine training priority: Set weight for the new image: \omega{11} = 1. For images i with direct overlap (M{i,n} \neq 0), calculate: \omega{2i} = M{i,n} where M{i,n} is the number of matched feature points between image i and new image n. For images in indirect layers k \ge 3, calculate weights based on the previous layer k-1: \omega{ki} = \frac{\sum{j=1}^{N{k-1}} \omega{j}^{(k-1)} \times M{j,ki}^{(k-1)}}{N{k-1}} where \omega{j}^{(k-1)} is the weight of image j in layer k-1, M{j,ki}^{(k-1)} is the match count between image j and image i, and N{k-1} is the number of images in layer k-1. 4. Training Iteration Allocation: Perform TI total iterations. Split into Local and Semi-Global optimization (each TI/2 iterations): Local Optimization: Select the top Nm images with highest weights as key targets. For each key image i with weight \omegai, allocate iterations T{im}: T{im} = \frac{1 - e^{-\omegai}}{\sum{j=1}^{Nm} (1 - e^{-\omegaj})} \times TI Train the 3DGS field on these images for their allocated iterations. Semi-Global Optimization: Distribute the remaining TI/2 iterations evenly among the other registered images. 5. Adaptive Learning Rate: For each image j trained for Tj iterations, calculate the base learning rate \etaj^c: Calculate progress ti: ti = \begin{cases} 1 & Tj > Ta \\ Tj / Ta & Tj \le Ta \end{cases} Interpolate initial \etaj^0 and final \etaj^f rates: \etaj^c = (\etaj^0)^{1-ti} \times (\etaj^f)^{ti} Adjust for overlapping images I (where M{i,j} > 0): \etaj = \frac{\etaj^c + \sum{i \in I} M{i,j} \times \etai^c}{NI + 1} where NI is the count of overlapping images. 6. Loss Computation and Update: Calculate Load-Balancing-Loss L{load}: L{load} = \text{std}(Gp), \quad p \in \text{image pixels} where Gp is the number of Gaussians associated with pixel p. Compute total loss: L{total} = \lambda1 L1 + \lambda{ssim} L{ssim} + \lambda{load} L{load} Perform gradient descent using Splatting-based parallelism (gradient accumulation per Gaussian). 1. After all images are acquired, perform global Bundle Adjustment on all estimated poses. 2. Apply rapid additional optimization to the final 3DGS field. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def ontheflygstraining(initialimages, newimagestream, params): """ Main loop for On-the-Fly GS Progressive Training. """ # Phase 1: Initialization N0 = params['N0'] Tinit = params['Tinit'] # Assume OnTheFlySfM is a helper class for pose/point cloud estimation sfm = OnTheFlySfM() # Process initial batch poses0, points0 = sfm.process(initialimages[:N0]) gaussians = initializegaussians(points0) # Train initial field trainfield(gaussians, initialimages[:N0], Tinit, params) registeredimages = initialimages[:N0] registeredposes = poses0 sparsepoints = points0 # Phase 2: Progressive Training for newimg in newimagestream: # 1. Update Poses and Points newpose, newpoints = sfm.processsingle(newimg, registeredposes, sparsepoints) # Local BA updates neighboring poses registeredposes = sfm.localbaupdate(registeredposes, newpose, newpoints) sparsepoints = sfm.updatepointcloud(sparsepoints, newpoints) # 2. Densification searchtree = buildsearchtree(sparsepoints) newgaussians = [] for pt in newpoints: dist = searchtree.querynearest(pt) if dist > params['threshold']: newgaussians.append(creategaussian(pt)) gaussians.extend(newgaussians) # 3. Hierarchical Image Weighting weights = calculatehierarchicalweights(registeredimages, newimg, newpose) # 4. name: POD Pretraining
head: POD, Principal Orthogonal Decomposition pretraining, Progressive Optimization Distillation
body: POD Pretraining is a distillation-based amortized optimization procedure that stabilizes the training of feed-forward Gaussian predictors by supervising them with locally refined Gaussian targets instead of unstable image-space gradients. It prevents training collapse in multi-stage residual Gaussian prediction by distilling short-horizon optimized Gaussian increments to provide a more reliable regression target. Unlike direct image-space supervision, which suffers from non-unique inverse mappings and error accumulation, POD mediates the objective through a short local optimization, ensuring one-to-one primitive correspondence and stable gradient directions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Residual image E{i-1} from the previous stage (or initial image for Stage 1), current Gaussian prediction \Delta Gi. Output: Refined Gaussian prediction \Delta Gi (updated via distillation loss). Data Structures: Gaussian Candidate Set (gi): A dense set of Gaussian primitives predicted by the network. Each primitive is defined by standard 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Stage Control Mask: A binary mask determining which stages are active during training. PCA Features: Principal Component Analysis features of the stage outputs, used for analysis but not part of the core training loop. Numbered Steps: 1. Start: Begin with the current Gaussian prediction \Delta Gi for stage i. 2. Local Optimization: Perform a short local optimization (gradient descent) on \Delta Gi using the residual rendering loss \mathcal{L}{render} to arrive at a locally refined solution \Delta G{c,i} within the same parameter neighborhood. This step preserves one-to-one primitive correspondence with the original prediction. 3. Compute Distillation Loss: Calculate the Gaussian-space regression loss between the initial prediction and the refined target: \mathcal{L}{gaussian}(\Delta Gi, \Delta G{c,i}) This loss measures the distance between the predicted parameters and the locally optimized parameters. 4. Accumulate Loss: Compute the total POD pretraining objective by summing the distillation losses across all S stages, weighted by \lambdai: \mathcal{L}{POD} = \sum{i=1}^{S} \lambdai \mathcal{L}{gaussian} where \lambdai balances the contribution of each stage. 5. Update Predictor: Backpropagate \mathcal{L}{POD} to update the feed-forward predictor network. Formulas: Residual Rendering Loss: Used in Step 2 to refine \Delta Gi: \mathcal{L}{render} = 0.7 \mathcal{L}1 + 0.3 (1 - \text{SSIM}) where \mathcal{L}1 is the pixel-wise L1 distortion and SSIM is the structural similarity index. POD Objective: \mathcal{L}{POD} = \sum{i=1}^{S} \lambdai \mathcal{L}{gaussian} The Gaussian-space distillation loss coefficient is multiplied by 100 to match the gradient scale of Gaussian parameter regression. Parameters: \lambdai (Stage Weight): Balances the contribution of each stage. Set uniformly across stages. Distillation Coefficient: Multiplied by 100 during POD pretraining to match gradient scales. Patch Size (p): Controls spatial granularity and maximum number of candidate Gaussians. Evaluated settings: 5, 6, 7, 14. Batch Size: 20 for POD pretraining, 16 for finetuning/quantization, 20 for patch-size adaptation. Iterations: 120k for POD pretraining; 300k for finetuning (100k without quantization, 200k with quantization on final accumulated set GS); 100k for patch-size adaptation. Milestones: Stages progressively activated at iterations [0, 20k, 40k, 60k] during pretraining. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Collapse: Direct image-space supervision alone is under-constrained. The non-unique inverse mapping from residual images to Gaussian parameters leads to ambiguity, amplified by error accumulation and parameter compensation across stages, causing training collapse (e.g., PSNR dropping from 32.13 dB to 16.22 dB at iteration 80k). Feature Dominance: Without POD, the Stage-1 feature can be dominated by a single principal component explaining 98.35% of the variance, leading to a near one-dimensional feature space and collapse. Precision: The local optimization must be short enough to stay within the same parameter neighborhood to ensure valid correspondence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def podpretrainingstep(predictor, residualimage, stageindex, lambdai, numoptsteps): """ Performs one step of POD pretraining for a specific stage. Args: predictor: Feed-forward network predicting Gaussian parameters from residual image. residualimage: Input residual image E{i-1}. stageindex: Current stage index i. lambdai: Weight for the current stage. numoptsteps: Number of local optimization steps to refine the prediction. Returns: loss: The computed POD loss for this stage. """ # Step 1: Get initial prediction # The predictor takes the residual image and outputs a dense candidate set gi # which is then masked to get effective increments Delta Gi deltaGinitial = predictor(residualimage, stageindex) # Step 2: Local Optimization # Clone the initial prediction to optimize locally deltaGopt = deltaGinitial.clone() deltaGopt.requiresgrad = True # Use an optimizer (e.g., SGD or Adam) for the local refinement optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([deltaGopt], lr=0.01) # Learning rate is a placeholder for in range(numoptsteps): optimizer.zerograd() # Render the current optimized Gaussians renderedimage = rendergaussians(deltaGopt) # Compute residual rendering loss # Lrender = 0.7 L1 + 0.3 (1 - SSIM) lossrender = 0.7 l1loss(renderedimage, residualimage) + \ 0.3 (1 - ssimloss(renderedimage, residualimage)) lossrender.backward() optimizer.step() # The result of local optimization is Delta G{c,i} deltaGrefined = deltaGopt.detach() # Step 3: Compute Gaussian-space regression loss # Lgaussian measures the distance between initial and refined parameters lossgaussian = gaussianspaceloss(deltaGinitial, deltaGrefined) # Step 4: Scale and return loss # Multiply by 100 to match gradient scale of Gaussian parameter regression scaledloss = lossgaussian 100 return scaledloss lambdai def trainpodmodel(model, dataloader, numstages, milestones): """ Main training loop for POD pretraining. """ optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=0.001) # Placeholder scheduler = StepLR(optimizer, stepsize=10000, gamma=0.1) # Placeholder for iteration in range(120000): # 120k iterations # Progressive stage activation activestages = [i for i in range(numstages) if iteration >= milestones[i]] for residualimage, in dataloader: totalloss = 0 for stageindex in activestages: # Uniform lambdai lambdai = 1.0 loss = podpretrainingstep(model, residualimage, stageindex, lambdai, numoptsteps=10) # Placeholder totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() scheduler.step() A stage-wise predictor using a DINOv3 ViT-Base encoder and a lightweight convolutional head to predict Gaussian candidates from residual images. It extracts multi-level features from the 5th and 11th transformer layers, projects them to a 1024-dimensional representation, fuses them into a 32-channel spatial feature map, applies patch embedding with patch size p to partition the map into local patches, maps each patch to a 64-dimensional token, and predicts a Gaussian candidate for each token to form the dense candidate set gi. The Stage Control mask is then applied to obtain the effective increments \Delta Gi. The encoder is initialized with pretrained DINOv3 weights, optimized with AdamW with warmup and StepLR decay, and trained for 120k iterations (pretraining), 300k iterations (finetuning), and 100k iterations (patch-size adaptation). Time Complexity: The method adds a local optimization step for each training iteration, increasing per-step time compared to direct feed-forward prediction. However, it amortizes the cost of iterative optimization into a single forward pass during inference. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Gaussian parameters for both the initial prediction and the locally refined target during the backward pass of the distillation loss. Measured Performance: On the DIV2K dataset with 52k Gaussians, Full POD achieves a PSNR of 32.17 dB, MS-SSIM of 0.985, and LPIPS of 0.158, with a rendering time of 162 ms. Direct Supervision collapses to 16.22 dB PSNR. Strengths: Stabilizes training in multi-stage residual Gaussian prediction, prevents training collapse, and provides a more reliable regression target than raw image-space gradients. It produces a more balanced feature distribution (first three PCs explain 28.09%, 22.10%, 14.47% of variance) compared to the collapsed case (98.35% in one PC). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the local optimization steps and distillation coefficient. The initial prediction must be within the same parameter neighborhood for the correspondence to hold. When to Use: When training feed-forward Gaussian splatting models with multiple stages, especially when direct image-space supervision leads to instability or collapse. When Not to Use: For single-stage predictions where the ambiguity is less pronounced, or when computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of local optimization is prohibitive. POD Pretraining was introduced in the AIR (Amortized Image Reconstruction Framework) paper, which proposes a self-supervised feed-forward 2D Gaussian Splatting framework. The method addresses the instability of training multi-stage Gaussian predictors by distilling the results of short-horizon optimizations into the feed-forward network. It builds on the principles of multi-stage and progressive training, specifically addressing the pitfalls of direct image-space supervision in residual Gaussian prediction. name: Finetune Training
head: Cross-stage coordination, Finetuning Phase, Image-space Finetuning, POD + Finetune
body: Finetune Training is a lightweight optimization phase applied after POD (Progressive Optimization Distillation) pretraining to refine the multi-stage Gaussian predictor using direct image-space rendering supervision. It solves the problem of limited cross-stage coordination in distillation-based methods by allowing gradients from the final cumulative rendering to propagate back to earlier stages, thereby redistributing the reconstruction burden and improving the final output quality. Unlike POD, which stabilizes training via local residual targets, finetuning enables joint optimization across all stages, sacrificing intermediate standalone PSNR for superior final-stage reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multi-stage feed-forward predictor P initialized by POD pretraining, which predicts Gaussian increments \Delta Gi at each stage i based on residual features E{i-1}. Output: An optimized predictor P' with parameters adjusted to minimize image-space rendering loss. Data Structures: The predictor maintains a sequence of accumulated Gaussian sets Gi and their corresponding rendered images Ii. Gi = G{i-1} \cup \Delta Gi, where G0 = \emptyset. Ii = \mathcal{R}(Gi), where \mathcal{R} is the differentiable volume rendering operator. The loss is computed for every intermediate stage i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. Parameters: Image-space reconstruction loss coefficient (\lambdai): Set to 1 uniformly across all stages. Rendering Loss (L{render}): A weighted combination of pixel-wise distortion and structural similarity: L{render} = 0.7 L1 + 0.3 (1 - \text{SSIM}) where L1 is the L1 distance between predicted and ground-truth images, and SSIM is the Structural Similarity Index. Steps: 1. Remove Short-Horizon Optimization: Disable the local Gaussian refinement optimizer used during POD pretraining. The model no longer generates pseudo-labels via iterative Gaussian splatting. 2. Forward Pass: For each training batch, pass the input through the multi-stage predictor. At each stage i, compute the accumulated Gaussian set Gi and render the image Ii = \mathcal{R}(Gi). 3. Compute Loss: Calculate the rendering loss L{render}(Ii, I{gt}) for every intermediate stage i. The total loss is the sum of losses across all active stages: L{total} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \lambdai L{render}(Ii, I{gt}) With \lambdai = 1 for all i. 4. Backpropagation: Compute gradients of L{total} with respect to the predictor parameters. Because Ii depends on all preceding increments \Delta G1, \dots, \Delta Gi, gradients propagate back to earlier stages, enabling joint optimization. 5. Update: Update predictor parameters using an optimizer (e.g., AdamW). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finetunestep(predictor, imagegt, optimizer): """ One step of Finetune Training. predictor: Multi-stage Gaussian predictor initialized by POD. imagegt: Ground truth image. optimizer: Optimizer instance (e.g., AdamW). """ optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 accumulatedgaussians = [] # List of Gaussian sets Gi # Stage-wise prediction and rendering currentgaussians = [] for i in range(numstages): # Predict increment from residual features # Note: Residual features E{i-1} are derived from previous stages' outputs deltag = predictor.predictstage(i, currentgaussians) # Accumulate Gaussians currentgaussians = union(currentgaussians, deltag) accumulatedgaussians.append(currentgaussians) # Render intermediate result renderedimage = render(currentgaussians) # Compute loss for this stage # Lrender = 0.7 L1 + 0.3 (1 - SSIM) stageloss = 0.7 l1loss(renderedimage, imagegt) + \ 0.3 (1.0 - ssim(renderedimage, imagegt)) totalloss += stageloss # Backpropagate through all stages jointly totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Scale: In POD, distillation loss is scaled by 100 to match gradient scales. In finetuning, the coefficient is 1, so the learning rate must be adjusted accordingly to avoid instability. Early Stage Degradation: Early stages (Stage 1, 2) may show lower PSNR compared to "Only POD" because they sacrifice standalone accuracy to provide a better basis for later residual correction. This is expected and indicates successful cross-stage coordination. A post-training variant where the costly short-horizon optimization is removed, and the model is trained with direct image-space supervision to refine reconstruction and enable learned quantization. The steps are: 1) Remove POD optimization steps; 2) Train with direct image-space supervision (cross-stage rendering finetuning); 3) Apply learned quantization to compress the Gaussian representation. This allows for compact storage and transmission of the predicted Gaussian parameters. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Per-iteration cost is significantly reduced compared to POD because the short-horizon local optimization loop is removed. However, it requires rendering at every intermediate stage, which adds overhead compared to single-stage methods. Memory: Requires storing intermediate Gaussian sets Gi and rendered images Ii for backpropagation through all stages. Measured Performance: On DIV2K, POD+Finetune lowers cumulative PSNR after Stage 1 (25.58 dB vs 26.58 dB for Only POD) and Stage 2 (27.89 dB vs 28.29 dB), but improves later stages, reaching 30.76 dB at Stage 4 compared to 29.48 dB for Only POD. Finetuning redistributes the reconstruction burden, leading to specialized roles: Stage-1 features show clearer structural patterns, while Stage-4 features contain more high-frequency residual responses. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables joint optimization across stages; improves final reconstruction quality; reduces per-iteration training cost; supports learned quantization. Limitations: Early-stage PSNR may degrade; requires careful tuning of learning rates due to gradient scale changes. When to Use: Use when the goal is to maximize the final accumulated reconstruction quality and enable efficient storage via quantization, and when the computational cost of local refinement in POD is prohibitive. Do not use if strong intermediate-stage standalone accuracy is required. Finetune Training was introduced in the AIR (Amortized Image Reconstruction Framework) paper as a successor to POD pretraining. It addresses the limitation of distillation-based methods where later stages must compensate for upstream errors. The method builds on the observation that supervising cumulative results encourages cross-stage coordination. It is used in self-supervised feed-forward 2D Gaussian Splatting frameworks to achieve high-quality reconstruction with efficient storage. name: Backbone Fine-tuning
head: Tri-plane Feature Adaptation
body: Backbone Fine-tuning adapts the weights of a pre-trained 3D generator (backbone) alongside the decoder to generate Gaussian Splatting attributes, addressing the fact that splats have scale and rotation that influence adjacent regions, unlike NeRF's local color/density. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Exponentially Ascending Gradient Threshold by modifying the generative prior itself rather than just the optimization trajectory, and from Dual-branch Architecture for Attribute Learning by potentially updating geometry if not explicitly frozen. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained 3D generator (backbone) producing tri-plane features or latent representations; input images IC and optional pose conditions QC. Output: Adapted backbone weights and decoder weights that produce Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, color) for splatting. Data Structures: Backbone Copy: A duplicate of the pre-trained 3D generator's weight tensor. Decoder: A network (e.g., sequential decoder) mapping features to Gaussian attributes. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an exact copy of the pre-trained 3D generator's weights. Initialize the decoder network. 2. Joint Optimization: During the training process, optimize the weights of both the backbone copy and the decoder simultaneously. 3. Feature Adaptation: The backbone adapts its tri-plane features to provide a basis suitable for Gaussian attributes, which require spatial extent (scale/rotation) beyond point-wise density/color. Parameters: Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Drift: If the geometry branch is not frozen, fine-tuning can lead to positional updates that compensate for attribute errors, causing local blur and depth distortions. Misalignment: Errors in predicted back-projection poses introduce misalignment with ground truth (GT) supervision cameras. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. backbonecopy = copyweights(pretrained3dgenerator) decoder = initializedecoder() for batch in trainingdata: # Forward pass through backbone copy to get features # Features are adapted via fine-tuned backbone weights features = backbonecopy(batch.inputimages, batch.poseconditions) # Decode features to Gaussian attributes # Attributes include position, scale, rotation, color gaussianattributes = decoder(features) # Render splats using 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer renderedimage = render(gaussianattributes, batch.cameraparams) # Compute loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, batch.gtimage) # Backpropagate to update both backbone copy and decoder loss.backward() optimizer.step(backbonecopy, decoder) optimizer.zerograd() A variant that uses two independently parameterized branches initialized from the same pretrained DA3 weights to preserve depth and camera estimates while adapting Gaussian attributes. It sets itself apart by explicitly freezing the geometry branch to prevent the positional distortions seen in standard backbone fine-tuning. Choose this when preserving the original 3D generator's geometric accuracy is critical. Definition: Two branches (geometry and attribute) initialized from pretrained DA3 weights. Steps: 1. Initialize \Phi{geo} and \Phi{attr} from the same pretrained DA3 weights. 2. Freeze \Phi{geo}, including its depth and camera heads. 3. Fine-tune only the last K Transformer blocks of \Phi{attr}. 4. Map attribute features FC to per-pixel attributes \xi using a DPT Gaussian decoder. 5. Obtain points by back-projection without predicted positional offsets; scales and rotations remain learnable. Formulas: Geometry branch: \hat{D}, \hat{\Pi}C = \Phi{geo}(IC; QC). Attribute branch: FC = \Phi{attr}(IC; QC). Parameters: K: Number of last Transformer blocks in the attribute branch to fine-tune. Typical value: 10. Pitfalls: Fine-tuning the geometry branch (w/o G) or learning positional offsets (w/ O) worsens metrics (LPIPS increases by 16.6% and 23.2% on ETH3D/DTU) because positional updates compensate for attribute errors. Time Complexity: Increases training time due to the optimization of the backbone weights in addition to the decoder and Gaussian parameters. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the backbone weights and their gradients, effectively doubling the memory footprint for the generative model compared to a frozen backbone. Scaling: Allows the generative prior to adapt to the specific statistical distribution of Gaussian attributes, potentially improving generalization to diverse scenes. Strengths: Adapts the tri-plane features to better support the spatial extent of Gaussians, which NeRF-style local features do not inherently provide. Limitations: Risk of geometric distortion if geometry is not frozen; requires careful tuning of the number of fine-tuned blocks (K) in dual-branch variants. When to use: When using a pre-trained 3D generator (like StyleGAN-based or DA3) and standard decoding fails to produce high-quality Gaussian attributes due to mismatched feature semantics. When not to use: When geometric fidelity of the original generator is paramount and cannot be preserved by freezing. Originated in the context of adapting 3D-aware generative models (like StyleGAN or DA3) for Gaussian Splatting. The method was introduced to address the fundamental mismatch between NeRF-style local density/color representations and the extended, oriented nature of 3D Gaussians. It is used in feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction pipelines where a pre-trained 3D generator serves as the backbone.
