name: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy for 3DGS
head: Frequency-staged Training Pipeline, Frequency-staged Training with Archiving, Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies Training Procedure, Laplacian-GS inheritance strategy
body: This method reduces 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training time and memory usage by factorizing the scene representation into a hierarchy of frequency-specific Gaussian fields aligned with a Laplacian pyramid of training images. It optimizes these fields sequentially from coarse to fine, archiving completed fields to free GPU memory, and composes the final image in the image domain. Unlike simultaneous multi-field optimization, this approach reduces the number of active primitives on the GPU at any given stage, offering a speedup with minor quality trade-offs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training views \{v\} with ground truth images \{I^v\} at full resolution; a camera model for each view. Outputs: A set of Gaussian fields \{G^0, \dots, G^{L-1}\} representing the scene across frequency bands. Data Structures: Gaussian Field G^\ell: A set of N\ell anisotropic Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i is parameterized by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \sigmai \in (0, 1) Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, typically decomposed as \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top where Ri is a rotation quaternion and Si is a diagonal scale matrix. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Laplacian Pyramid: A hierarchy of images \{I^{L-1}, \dots, I^0\} where I^0 is the full-resolution ground truth and I^{L-1} is the coarsest low-frequency approximation. Cache: A storage for accumulated rendered predictions \{\hat{I}^v\ell\} used to reconstruct finer levels. Preprocessing: Pyramid Construction 1. For each training view v, construct the resolution pyramid: I^{\ell+1} = \text{Down}(I^\ell) where \text{Down}(\cdot) is Gaussian filtering followed by subsampling. 2. Compute Laplacian residual targets for levels \ell \in \{0, \dots, L-2\}: R^\ell = I^\ell - \text{Up}(I^{\ell+1}) where \text{Up}(\cdot) is the paired upsampling operator. Note: I^{L-1} is the low-frequency target for the coarsest field. Residuals R^\ell are signed and lie in [-1, 1], while base images lie in [0, 1]. Rendering Functions: Renderbase: Standard 3DGS rasterization with post-processing to map SH colors to [0, 1]: ci(d) = \text{clamp}(ci(d) + 0.5, 0, 1) Used for the coarsest level G^{L-1}. Renderres: Modified rasterization that removes the shift and clamp, allowing signed outputs in [-1, 1] to match residual targets. Algorithm: Frequency-staged Training with Archiving Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def laplacianfrequencyhierarchytraining(trainingviews, cameramodels, L=2, iterationsperlevel=[10000, 20000], inheritanceratio=1.0): """ L: Number of pyramid levels. Default 2 (levels 0 and 1). iterationsperlevel: List of iterations for each level, from coarsest (L-1) to finest (0). inheritanceratio: Fraction of Gaussians inherited from previous stage. """ # 1. Precompute Laplacian Pyramids for all training views # Ipyramid[v][l] stores the image at level l for view v Ipyramid = {} for v in trainingviews: Ifull = getgroundtruthimage(v) Ipyramid[v] = [] currentimg = Ifull for l in range(L): Ipyramid[v].append(currentimg) if l < L - 1: currentimg = gaussiandownsample(currentimg) # 2. Initialize cache for accumulated predictions # Cache stores the reconstructed image at level l for view v predictioncache = {} # 3. Iterate from coarsest level (L-1) to finest (0) gaussianfields = {} for l in range(L - 1, -1, -1): # Initialize Gaussian Field G^l if l == L - 1: # Coarsest level: Initialize from COLMAP point cloud Gl = initializefromcolmap(trainingviews) else: # Finer level: Inherit from previous stage G^{l+1} Gprev = gaussianfields[l + 1] Gl = inheritgaussians(Gprev, inheritanceratio) # 4. Training Loop for Level l numiters = iterationsperlevel[L - 1 - l] # Map index to correct iteration count optimizer = Adam(Gl.parameters()) for iteration in range(numiters): # Sample a training view v = sampleview(trainingviews) # Render current field if l == L - 1: # Coarsest level: Render base image Ihatl = renderbase(Gl, v) else: # Finer level: Render residual # Load cached prediction from previous (coarser) level Ihatlplus1 = predictioncache[(v, l + 1)] Iupsampled = upsample(Ihatlplus1) # Render residual field Rhatl = renderres(Gl, v) # Reconstruct full image at this level for loss computation Ihatl = Iupsampled + Rhatl # Compute Photometric Loss # Supervise using the ground truth at the current pyramid level I^vl # This anchors the stage to the correct resolution and reduces error accumulation targetI = Ipyramid[v][l] loss = photometricloss(Ihatl, targetI) # Weighted L1 + SSIM # Backpropagate and update loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Apply densification and pruning specific to 3DGS applydensificationandpruning(Gl, iteration) # 5. Archive and Cache # Cache the accumulated prediction for the next finer stage # Note: In practice, only cache Ihatl in the dataloader; # the Gaussian field Gl is archived (moved off GPU) predictioncache[(v, l)] = Ihatl # Simplified: cache for all views or lazy load # Save and archive Gl (remove from GPU memory) gaussianfields[l] = Gl archivefield(Gl) return gaussianfields def inheritgaussians(Gprev, rho): """ Inherits Gaussians from the previous stage. Strategy: Copy only 3D positions (xyz). Reinitialize scale, opacity, rotation, colors. If rho < 1.0, randomly select a subset of Gaussians. """ Gnew = EmptyGaussianField() # Determine number of Gaussians to inherit Nprev = len(Gprev) Nnew = int(Nprev rho) # Randomly select indices if rho < 1.0, otherwise all if rho < 1.0: indices = random.sample(range(Nprev), Nnew) else: indices = range(Nprev) for i in indices: g = Gprev[i] # Copy only position newg = Gaussian() newg.mu = g.mu # Reinitialize other attributes newg.sigma = randomuniform(0, 1) # Opacity newg.S = randomscale() # Scale newg.R = randomrotation() # Rotation newg.SH = randomshcoefficients() # Colors Gnew.add(newg) return Gnew def gaussiandownsample(img): # Gaussian filtering followed by subsampling (e.g., 2x) filtered = gaussianfilter(img, sigma=1.0) return filtered[::2,::2,:] def upsample(img): # Paired upsampling operator (e.g., nearest neighbor or bilinear) return resize(img, scalefactor=2.0) Parameters: L (Hierarchy Depth): Number of pyramid levels. Default is 2 (levels 0 and 1). Deeper hierarchies make finer residuals harder to represent efficiently, potentially reducing gains. \rho (Inheritance Ratio): Fraction of Gaussians inherited from the previous stage. Default is 1.0. Values < 1.0 accelerate training but cause a clear drop in reconstruction quality. Iterations: Default total 30K iterations split as 10K for the coarsest level and 20K for the finest level in a two-level setup. Optimizer: Adam. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Error Accumulation: Training each field to directly match its Laplacian residual target (R^\ell) can lead to accumulated approximation errors and degraded quality. The method mitigates this by supervising each stage using the reconstructed image \hat{I}^v\ell against the ground truth at that resolution level I^v\ell. Inheritance Ratio: Reducing \rho below 1.0 speeds up training but significantly reduces fidelity because fewer primitives remain to represent fine details. Hierarchy Depth: Using too many levels (deep hierarchies) can degrade quality because high-frequency residuals become difficult for 3DGS to represent efficiently. A broader category of methods that optimize scene representations in stages, often coarse-to-fine. Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy is a specific implementation using frequency decomposition and archiving. Multi-stage and Progressive Training Methods that reduce the number of Gaussians to save memory and speed up training. Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy uses archiving (moving fields off GPU) and optional inheritance ratio reduction to manage active primitives. Pruning and Sparsity Control A backbone framework used to implement Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy. FastGS provides optimized rendering and training routines. FastGS (Note: FastGS is a sibling in the tree, but Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy is implemented on top of it. The link points to the sibling article for context on the backbone). Time Complexity: Reduces training time by optimizing fewer Gaussians per stage and reducing per-iteration cost at coarser levels. On Mip-NeRF 360 1K, it achieves a 1.73x speedup (8.88 to 5.13 minutes) with Taming-3DGS and 1.22x (4.82 to 3.96 minutes) with FastGS. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduces peak VRAM usage by archiving completed Gaussian fields off the GPU. This allows training higher-resolution scenes (2K/4K) that might otherwise OOM. Performance: Slight degradation in reconstruction quality (e.g., 0.34 dB PSNR drop on Mip-NeRF 360 1K) is attributed to approximation errors from hierarchical rendering and composition. Strengths: Efficient training for high-resolution scenes; reduced memory footprint; leverages standard 3DGS densification/pruning. Limitations: Slight quality drop; deeper hierarchies may degrade quality; requires careful tuning of inheritance ratio \rho if speed is prioritized over quality. When to Use: When training time or VRAM is a bottleneck for high-resolution 3DGS scenes. When Not to Use: When maximum reconstruction fidelity is required and training time is not a constraint. The method was introduced in "Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training" (2024/2025). It builds on the observation that low-frequency structures in 3DGS converge earlier than high-frequency details, and that standard 3DGS rasterizers assume non-negative colors, which is incompatible with signed residual learning. The Laplacian pyramid (Burt & Adelson, 1983) provides a framework for decomposing images into frequency bands, allowing separate optimization of coarse and fine details. Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.03334, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Curriculum Learning with Slice and Voxel Supervision
head: Slice and Voxel Supervision Curriculum
body: This method addresses the instability and incomplete volumetric coverage inherent in optimizing 3D Gaussian representations for shear-warp rendering by enforcing a structured training schedule. It differs from sibling methods like Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy by explicitly decoupling global spatial guidance (via sparse voxels) from local structural continuity (via slices), rather than relying on hierarchical scene decomposition. It outperforms Training Objective and Densification in volumetric consistency by preventing the "unstable global approximation" caused by random voxel sampling alone. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of m initial 3D Gaussian kernels \mathcal{G} = \{G1, \dots, Gm\}, where each Gi is centered at a sampled voxel position with learnable mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Output: Optimized Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}^ that minimize rendering loss against target volumetric data (e.g., MRI, Cryosection). Data Structures: Gaussian Set: Contiguous array of m Gaussians. Each Gaussian stores \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or parameterized scale/rotation), \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^K. Voxel Grid: Sparse representation of the volume, mapping 3D coordinates to voxel indices. Algorithm Steps: The training proceeds in two distinct phases to ensure stable convergence: 1. Phase 1: Slice Supervision (Local Structure) Sample a plane with arbitrary orientation \mathbf{n} and offset d. Select sparse pixels on this 2D plane. Map each selected pixel to a 3D voxel coordinate v{3D} using the shear-warp projection geometry. Compute the rendering loss L{slice} between the projected Gaussian slice and the target voxel values at v{3D}. Update Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} using gradient descent on L{slice}. Rationale: This aligns the representation with the shear-warp rendering process, capturing geometric structure and texture continuity. 2. Phase 2: Voxel Supervision (Global Guidance) After Phase 1 stabilizes local structures, introduce voxel supervision. Sample sparse voxels from the volume grid. Compute the rendering loss L{voxel} for these voxels. Update Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} using gradient descent on L{voxel}. Rationale: Sparse voxels provide global coverage, correcting the lack of global spatial guidance present in slice-only training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingaussianvolume(G, targetvolume, numiterations): # Phase 1: Slice Supervision for iter in range(numiterations // 2): # Sample arbitrary plane plane = samplearbitraryplane() # Select sparse pixels on the plane pixels = samplesparsepixels(plane) loss = 0 for pixel in pixels: # Map 2D pixel to 3D voxel coordinate voxelcoord = mappixeltovoxel(pixel, plane) # Render Gaussian contribution at voxelcoord renderedvalue = rendergaussianslice(G, voxelcoord) # Compute loss against target targetvalue = targetvolume[voxelcoord] loss += (renderedvalue - targetvalue) 2 # Update Gaussians gradients = computegradients(loss, G) G = updateparameters(G, gradients) # Phase 2: Voxel Supervision for iter in range(numiterations // 2, numiterations): # Sample sparse voxels voxels = samplesparsevoxels(targetvolume) loss = 0 for voxel in voxels: # Render Gaussian contribution at voxel renderedvalue = rendergaussianvoxel(G, voxel) # Compute loss against target targetvalue = targetvolume[voxel] loss += (renderedvalue - targetvalue) 2 # Update Gaussians gradients = computegradients(loss, G) G = updateparameters(G, gradients) return G Parameters: Sampling Density: Sparse sampling is used for both slices and voxels to ensure efficiency. Exact sparsity ratios are not given in the sources. Phase Split: The sources imply a sequential curriculum (Slice then Voxel) but do not specify the exact iteration count split. A 50/50 split is assumed for pseudocode completeness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Random Voxel Sampling: Using random voxel sampling before or alongside slice supervision leads to unstable global approximation and destabilizes learning. Slice-Only Training: Using only slice supervision limits accurate reconstruction of the full volumetric structure due to lack of global spatial guidance. Voxel-Only Training: Using only voxel supervision (even with MCE importance weighting) lacks structured planar constraints, resulting in lower performance in rendered views. This variant explicitly combines sparse voxel sampling (for global coverage) with slice-based sampling (for spatially correlated regions encoding geometric structure and texture continuity). It aligns with shear-warp volume rendering, which generates images from stacks of 2D slices extracted from a 3D volume. In each iteration, a plane with arbitrary orientation is sampled, sparse pixels are selected, and each pixel is mapped to a 3D voxel coordinate. This strategy ensures the Gaussian representation learns spatial continuity across neighboring regions while maintaining global consistency. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of sampled pixels/voxels per iteration. The two-phase approach may double the training time compared to single-supervision methods, but convergence is more stable. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of Gaussians m and the target volume size for sparse sampling. Strengths: Efficient reconstruction of multimodal volumetric data (MRI, Cryosection); real-time selective visualization support; higher PSNR/SSIM than slice-only or random voxel-only methods. Limitations: Requires careful sequencing of supervision phases; random voxel sampling destabilizes learning if not properly scheduled. When to Use: When reconstructing volumetric medical or scientific data where both global structure and local texture continuity are critical. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is constrained and global volumetric consistency is less important than local surface detail. Originated in the context of Gaussian Volumetric Representation for Efficient Shear-Warp Visualization. The method leverages the alignment between shear-warp rendering (which operates on 2D slice stacks) and slice-based supervision to improve learning efficiency. It was developed to address the limitations of random sampling in Gaussian optimization for volumetric data. Gaussian Volumetric Representation for Efficient Shear-Warp Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37461-535, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-stage Training with Pose Prediction
head: FineSplat training phases
body: Multi-stage training with pose prediction is a progressive optimization strategy for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples geometry learning from pose estimation to stabilize training. It solves the problem of error propagation in end-to-end differentiable rendering, where inaccuracies in predicted camera poses corrupt the learned Gaussian representation. Unlike single-stage approaches, it separates the process into distinct phases: initial pose-aware training, pose-free geometry refinement, and final end-to-end fine-tuning. This method is specifically designed for architectures that predict Gaussians from context views without ground-truth camera supervision during inference. The method consists of three sequential training stages. Each stage uses specific inputs, outputs, and loss functions to progressively refine the model parameters \theta. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of training scenes, each providing V context views (images and poses) and one target view (image only). The number of context views V is sampled from \{6, 12, 24, 32\}. Output: A trained model capable of predicting 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} and camera poses for novel view synthesis from context views alone. Data Structures: The model maintains a set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}. Each Gaussian gk is defined by mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k [Parent]. The model also predicts camera poses P{pred} for context views. Parameters: Optimization: AdamW with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.95, weight decay 0.05 (multi-dimensional params only), gradient clipping max norm 1.0, bfloat16 mixed precision. Perceptual Loss Weight: \lambda = 0.2. Hardware: NVIDIA B200 GPUs. Step-by-Step Procedure: 1. Initialize: Train a pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction decoder for 120,000 iterations. 2. Loss Calculation: Compute the reconstruction loss between rendered target views \hat{I} and ground-truth I, including a camera loss \mathcal{L}{cam} on predicted poses/intrinsics. 3. Update: Optimize all parameters using a learning rate of 2 \times 10^{-5} with no warm-up, decaying to zero via cosine schedule. 4. Decoder Replacement: Replace the pixel-aligned decoder with a patch-aligned Gaussian decoder. 5. Fine-tuning: Continue training for an additional 80,000 iterations on 8 GPUs, maintaining the camera losses. 1. Freeze: Freeze all parameters from Stage 1. 2. Input: Use ground-truth camera poses and intrinsics as input. 3. Iterative Refinement: The model processes the scene through T=4 steps. Let \hat{I}^{(i)} be the rendered target view after step i. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss averaged over all steps i=1 \dots T: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{T} \sum{i=1}^{T} \left( \mathcal{L}2(\hat{I}^{(i)}, I) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{perc}(\hat{I}^{(i)}, I) \right) where \mathcal{L}2 is mean squared error and \mathcal{L}{perc} is VGG-19 perceptual loss. 5. Token Detachment: Detach tokens between steps to prevent gradient flow across steps, ensuring each step learns to improve the state it receives. 6. Update: Optimize Stage 2 parameters using a learning rate of 1 \times 10^{-4} with a 200-iteration linear warm-up, constant until 80% of training, then cosine decay to zero. 7. Duration: Train for 20,000 iterations on 4 GPUs. 1. Unfreeze: Unfreeze all parameters, including the camera pose estimator and Gaussian head. 2. Input: Use fully pose-free setting; both context and target cameras are predicted. 3. Loss Calculation: Supervise Stage-1 Gaussians. Compute the loss averaged over steps i=0 \dots T: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{T+1} \sum{i=0}^{T} \left( \mathcal{L}2(\hat{I}^{(i)}, I) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{perc}(\hat{I}^{(i)}, I) \right) No camera loss is used. 4. Update: Optimize all parameters using a learning rate of 2 \times 10^{-5} with a 200-iteration linear warm-up, followed by cosine decay to zero. 5. Duration: Train for 10,000 iterations on 8 GPUs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scene Scale Normalization: The world frame origin and scale are not fixed by input images. YoNoSplat convention places origin at first context camera and normalizes translations by max pairwise distance between context camera centers. Batch Size: Per-GPU batch sizes vary by view count: \{4, 2, 1, 1\} scenes for \{6, 6, 6, 1\} target views respectively. RLSplat uses a two-stage training process with a Gaussian allocation policy. Stage 1 (Base Training): Train geometry backbone and decoder with random allocations for 40,000 steps. Sample budgets from [2048, 16384V] where V is input views. Stage 2 (Policy Training): Add policy head initialized to uniform probabilities. Fine-tune entire model with policy loss \mathcal{L}{policy} for 5,000 steps. Sample budgets skewed toward lower end. Losses: Total loss combines reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{recon} (MSE + LPIPS), camera loss \mathcal{L}{cam} (translation, rotation, FOV), projection loss \mathcal{L}{proj} (reprojection with cheirality penalty), locality regularizers (\mathcal{L}{vor}, \mathcal{L}{offset}), and policy loss \mathcal{L}{policy} = -J{policy}. Parameters: K{anc} = K{gs} = 16. Time Complexity: The method requires significant training time due to multiple stages. Stage 1 takes 120K + 80K iterations, Stage 2 takes 20K, and Stage 3 takes 10K. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians and the batch size. The use of bfloat16 mixed precision reduces memory footprint. Performance: The multi-stage approach improves stability and final rendering quality compared to end-to-end training from scratch. Strengths: Decouples pose and geometry errors, leading to more robust training. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rates and warm-up schedules for each stage. This method was introduced in the FineSplat paper. It builds upon earlier work in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressing the challenges of training models that predict both geometry and camera poses simultaneously. The approach is inspired by the success of staged training in other neural rendering methods. FineSplat: Fine Patches, Local Groups, Detailed Splats, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25011, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27712, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Free-View Training (FVT)
head: FreeSplat Training
body: Free-View Training (FVT) is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that disentangles model performance from the specific number of input views, enabling robust novel view synthesis across broader view ranges regardless of input view count. It adds geometrical constraints on 3D Gaussian localization by supervising image renderings in broader view interpolations, significantly contributing to depth estimation and adaptation to longer input sequences. Unlike standard 3DGS which often overfits to the specific camera poses provided during training, FVT ensures generalizability by training on long sequences with randomly sampled context views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} (defined by means \mu, covariances \Sigma, opacities \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}), a long sequence of training images with known camera poses, and a hyperparameter T for the number of context views. Output: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} that generalize well to unseen viewpoints. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS representation. No additional complex data structures are required beyond the standard Gaussian attributes and the sequence of training views. Steps: 1. Sequence Selection: Select a long sequence of training views from the dataset. This sequence should contain a variety of viewpoints to encourage generalization. 2. Context View Sampling: For each training iteration, randomly sample T context views from the selected long sequence. These views serve as the supervision signal. 3. Rendering: Render the current 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} from the sampled T context views. This involves projecting the 3D Gaussians to 2D and compositing them to produce rendered images. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the rendering loss (e.g., L1 loss, SSIM) between the rendered images and the ground truth images of the sampled context views. The loss is computed on full resolution to encourage high-resolution renderings, even if intermediate feature extraction uses lower resolution maps. 5. Backpropagation and Optimization: Backpropagate the loss through the rendering process to update the Gaussian parameters (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 for the duration of the training phase. Parameters: T: The number of context views sampled per iteration. Typical values are between 2 and 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Distribution: If the sampled views are too similar, the model may not generalize well. Ensuring the long sequence covers a diverse range of viewpoints is critical. Sequence Length: Training on very short sequences may not provide sufficient geometric constraints. Long sequences are necessary to disentangle generalizability from specific view counts. Computational Cost: Sampling multiple views per iteration increases the computational load per step. However, the efficiency of the feature extraction and aggregation allows for feasible long-sequence training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def freeviewtraining(Gaussians, trainingsequence, T, optimizer, numiterations): """ Perform Free-View Training on 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: Gaussians: Set of 3D Gaussian primitives {g1,..., gN} trainingsequence: List of training views (image, camerapose) T: Number of context views to sample per iteration optimizer: Optimizer for updating Gaussian parameters numiterations: Total number of training iterations Returns: Optimized Gaussians """ for iteration in range(numiterations): # Step 2: Randomly sample T context views from the long sequence sampledviews = randomsample(trainingsequence, T) totalloss = 0.0 # Step 3 & 4: Render and compute loss for each sampled view for view in sampledviews: image, camerapose = view # Render the current Gaussians from the camera pose renderedimage = render(Gaussians, camerapose) # Compute loss between rendered and ground truth image # Loss is computed on full resolution loss = computerenderingloss(renderedimage, image) totalloss += loss # Normalize loss by number of views totalloss = totalloss / T # Step 5: Backpropagate and update Gaussians optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return Gaussians Time Complexity: Increases with the number of sampled views T and the length of the training sequence. Each iteration involves rendering T views, making it more computationally expensive per iteration than single-view training, but the efficient feature extraction allows for feasible long-sequence training. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS, as it operates on the same set of Gaussian primitives. No significant additional memory overhead is introduced by the training strategy itself. Strengths: Disentangles generalizability from specific view counts, enabling robust view synthesis across broader view ranges. Significantly improves depth estimation and adaptation to longer input sequences. Reduces Gaussian redundancy in overlapping regions when combined with feature fusion strategies. Limitations: Requires longer training sequences and potentially more computational resources per iteration due to multi-view sampling. Performance is dependent on the diversity and length of the training sequence. When to use: When the goal is to create a generalizable 3DGS model that performs well on unseen viewpoints, especially in indoor scenes with varying numbers of input views. When not to use: When computational resources are severely limited and single-view or few-view specific reconstruction is sufficient. Free-View Training was introduced in the context of generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically in the FreeSplat and FreeSplat++ papers. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which often overfits to the specific camera poses provided during training, by encouraging the model to learn geometric constraints that are independent of the specific input view count. The method leverages efficient feature extraction and aggregation to make long-sequence training feasible. It has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art novel view synthesis performance in both color and depth maps across different numbers of input views on datasets like ScanNet and Replica. FreeSplat++: Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Indoor Scene Reconstruction., https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2026.3665771, fetched 2026-10-26 FreeSplat: Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting Towards Free-View Synthesis of Indoor Scenes, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.17958, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Training Loop with Mixed Losses and Post-Processing
head: Mixed Loss Training Loop, Post-Processing Training Step
body: This method defines the iterative optimization step for 3D Gaussian Splatting, combining multiple loss terms (reconstruction, depth, bilateral grid, regularization) to update Gaussian parameters and pose. It differs from standard single-loss training by integrating auxiliary supervisions and post-backward strategy hooks to manage densification and learning rate scheduling. It builds on Progressive and Multi-stage Training by executing the specific loss computations and parameter updates within a single training iteration. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} with parameters: means \mu, scales s, rotations q (quaternions), opacities \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}. Camera poses P and intrinsic parameters. Training step index t. Configuration flags: shdegreeinterval, shdegree, depthloss, usebilateralgrid, randombkgd, usel1forrealsamples, ssimlambda, depthlambda, opacityreg, scalereg, visibleadam, packed, appopt, saveply, plysteps, maxsteps. Optimizers for Gaussians, poses, and bilateral grids. Learning rate schedulers. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}'. Updated camera poses P'. Updated bilateral grid parameters (if used). Optional PLY file export. Data Structures: splats: Dictionary or struct containing tensors for means (N \times 3), scales (N \times 3), quats (N \times 4), opacities (N \times 1), sh0 (N \times 3), shN (N \times K). info: Dictionary returned by rasterizer containing radii (N \times N{views}), gaussianids, alphas (H \times W \times N{views}), renders (H \times W \times 3 or H \times W \times 4). bilgrids: Bilateral grid structure if usebilateralgrid is true. Numbered Steps: 1. Spherical Degree Update: Calculate the active spherical harmonic degree for the current step: d{sh} = \min\left(\left\lfloor \frac{t}{\text{sh\degree\interval}} \right\rfloor, d{max}\right) where d{max} is the maximum SH degree configured. 2. Rasterization: Render the current Gaussians from all training views. If depthloss is true, render mode is 'RGB+ED' (RGB + Estimated Depth), producing a 4-channel output. Otherwise, render mode is 'RGB', producing a 3-channel output. Let renders be the output tensor of shape (H, W, C) where C=4 or 3. Let alphas be the accumulated opacity tensor of shape (H, W, N{views}). Let info be the auxiliary data from the rasterizer. 3. Color/Depth Split: If C=4: \text{colors} = \text{renders}[:,:, 0:3] \text{depths} = \text{renders}[:,:, 3:4] Else: \text{colors} = \text{renders} \text{depths} = \text{None} 4. Bilateral Grid Slicing (Optional): If usebilateralgrid is true: Compute grid coordinates gridxy for each pixel. Apply bilateral grid slicing to colors: \text{colors} = \text{slice}(\text{bil\grids}, \text{grid\xy}, \text{colors}, \text{image\ids})["\text{rgb}"] This adjusts colors based on spatial and intensity context. 5. Random Background Composite (Optional): If randombkgd is true: Generate random background color \mathbf{b} \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)^3. Composite: \text{colors} = \text{colors} + \mathbf{b} \cdot (1.0 - \text{alphas}) Note: alphas must be broadcasted appropriately to match colors shape. 6. Pre-Backward Strategy Step: Call strategy.stepprebackward(params, optimizers, state, t, info). This allows strategies (e.g., Default, MCMC) to perform pre-update operations. 7. Reconstruction Loss: Determine if the current sample is a NeRF sample (e.g., from a specific dataset format). Let isnerfsample be a boolean mask. If not isnerfsample.any(): Compute L1 or L2 loss based on usel1forrealsamples. Let this be L{recon}. Compute SSIM loss L{ssim}. Combine: L{recon\total} = L{recon} \cdot (1.0 - \lambda{ssim}) + L{ssim} \cdot \lambda{ssim} Else, use dataset-specific loss. 8. Depth Loss (Optional): If depthloss is true and not isnerfsample.any(): Normalize 3D points to [-1, 1]. Sample depths from the ground truth depth map using bilinear interpolation (F.gridsample). Compute disparity from rendered depth: d{pred} = 1.0 / \text{depths} (where \text{depths} > 0). Compute disparity loss: L{depth} = \text{L1Loss}(d{pred}, d{gt}) \cdot S{scene} where S{scene} is a scene scale factor. Add to total loss: L{total} += \lambda{depth} \cdot L{depth} Else, L{depth} = 0. 9. Bilateral Grid Total Variation (Optional): If usebilateralgrid is true: Compute total variation loss on the bilateral grid parameters: L{tv} = 10 \cdot \text{TotalVariation}(\text{bil\grids.grids}) Add to total loss: L{total} += L{tv} Else, L{tv} = 0. 10. Opacity Regularization (Optional): If \lambda{opacity} > 0: Compute mean of sigmoid-applied opacities: L{opacity} = \lambda{opacity} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\sigma(\alpha)] Add to total loss: L{total} += L{opacity} Else, L{opacity} = 0. 11. Scale Regularization (Optional): If \lambda{scale} > 0: Compute mean of exponential-applied scales: L{scale} = \lambda{scale} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\exp(s)] Add to total loss: L{total} += L{scale} Else, L{scale} = 0. 12. Backward Pass: Compute gradients: \nabla L{total} = \frac{\partial L{total}}{\partial \theta} where \theta includes all trainable parameters (Gaussians, poses, bilateral grids). 13. Visibility Mask Computation (Optional): If visibleadam is true: If packed is true: Create a zero tensor of shape equal to number of opacities. Scatter 1s at indices specified by info["gaussianids"]. Else: Compute mask: M = (\text{info["radii"]} > 0).\text{all}(-1).\text{any}(0) This results in a boolean mask for Gaussians visible in at least one view. 14. Optimizer Step: Step Gaussian optimizer: If visibleadam is true, pass M to optimizer.step(visibilitymask=M). Else, call optimizer.step(). Zero gradients with settonone=True. 15. Pose and Bilateral Grid Optimization: Step poseoptimizers and bilgridoptimizers. Zero their gradients. 16. Scheduler Step: Step all learning rate schedulers. 17. Post-Backward Strategy Step: Call strategy.steppostbackward. If DefaultStrategy, pass packed=cfg.packed. If MCMCStrategy, pass current learning rate lr = schedulers[0].getlastlr()[0]. This handles densification, pruning, and other structural updates. 18. PLY Export (Optional): If t \in \text{cfg.ply\steps} or t = \text{max\steps} - 1 and saveply is true: If appopt is true: Bake appearance by evaluating appmodule at origin (directions \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{0}). Add result to self.splats["colors"]. Apply sigmoid. Convert to SH0 coefficients. Create empty SHN coefficients. Else: Use self.splats["sh0"] and self.splats["shN"] directly. Export Gaussians with means, scales, quats, opacities, sh0, shN. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainingstep(step, splats, optimizers, poseoptimizers, bilgridoptimizers, schedulers, cfg, strategy, scenescale, device): # 1. SH Degree shdegreetouse = min(step // cfg.shdegreeinterval, cfg.shdegree) # 2. Rasterize rendermode = 'RGB+ED' if cfg.depthloss else 'RGB' renders, alphas, info = rasterize(splats, cfg.cameraparams, rendermode) # 3. Split if renders.shape[-1] == 4: colors = renders[..., 0:3] depths = renders[..., 3:4] else: colors = renders depths = None # 4. Bilateral Grid if cfg.usebilateralgrid: gridxy = computegridxy() colors = slicebilateralgrid(cfg.bilgrids, gridxy, colors, cfg.imageids) # 5. Random Background if cfg.randombkgd: bkgd = torch.rand(1, 3, device=device) colors = colors + bkgd (1.0 - alphas) # 6. Pre-Backward strategy.stepprebackward(splats, optimizers, {}, step, info) # 7. Reconstruction Loss isnerfsample = checknerfsample() # Placeholder for dataset-specific logic if not isnerfsample.any(): if cfg.usel1forrealsamples: reconloss = F.l1loss(colors, cfg.gtcolors) else: reconloss = F.mseloss(colors, cfg.gtcolors) ssimloss = computessim(colors, cfg.gtcolors) loss = reconloss (1.0 - cfg.ssimlambda) + ssimloss cfg.ssimlambda else: loss = computedatasetloss(colors, cfg.gtcolors) # Placeholder # 8. Depth Loss if cfg.depthloss and not isnerfsample.any(): # Normalize points and sample depths depthsgt = sampledepthsfromgt() disppred = 1.0 / depths.clamp(min=1e-6) dispgt = 1.0 / depthsgt.clamp(min=1e-6) depthloss = F.l1loss(disppred, dispgt) scenescale loss += cfg.depthlambda depthloss # 9. Bilateral Grid TV if cfg.usebilateralgrid: tvloss = 10 totalvariation(cfg.bilgrids.grids) loss += tvloss # 10. Opacity Reg if cfg.opacityreg > 0.0: opacityloss = cfg.opacityreg torch.sigmoid(splats["opacities"]).mean() loss += opacityloss # 11. Scale Reg if cfg.scalereg > 0.0: scaleloss = cfg.scalereg torch.exp(splats["scales"]).mean() loss += scaleloss # 12. Backward loss.backward() # 13. Visibility Mask visibilitymask = None if cfg.visibleadam: if cfg.packed: visibilitymask = torch.zeroslike(splats["opacities"]) visibilitymask.scatter(0, info["gaussianids"], 1.0) else: visibilitymask = (info["radii"] > 0).all(-1).any(0) # 14. Step Gaussians if cfg.visibleadam: optimizers[0].step(visibilitymask) else: optimizers[0].step() optimizers[0].zerograd(settonone=True) # 15. Step Poses and Bil Grids if poseoptimizers: for opt in poseoptimizers: opt.step() opt.zerograd(settonone=True) if bilgridoptimizers: for opt in bilgridoptimizers: opt.step() opt.zerograd(settonone=True) # 16. Step Schedulers for sched in schedulers: sched.step() # 17. Post-Backward if isinstance(strategy, DefaultStrategy): strategy.steppostbackward(packed=cfg.packed) elif isinstance(strategy, MCMCStrategy): lr = schedulers[0].getlastlr()[0] strategy.steppostbackward(lr=lr) # 18. PLY Export if (step in cfg.plysteps or step == cfg.maxsteps - 1) and cfg.saveply: if cfg.appopt: dirs = torch.zeroslike(splats["means"]) # Placeholder for direction computation bakedcolors = cfg.appmodule(dirs) finalcolors = torch.sigmoid(splats["colors"] + bakedcolors) sh0 = finalcolors shN = torch.zeroslike(splats["shN"]) else: sh0 = splats["sh0"] shN = splats["shN"] exportply(splats["means"], splats["scales"], splats["quats"], splats["opacities"], sh0, shN, step) Parameters: shdegreeinterval: Steps between increasing SH degree. Typical: 1000. shdegree: Maximum SH degree. Typical: 3. depthloss: Boolean flag for depth supervision. Typical: False. usebilateralgrid: Boolean flag for bilateral grid color correction. Typical: False. randombkgd: Boolean flag for random background compositing. Typical: True. usel1forrealsamples: Boolean flag for L1 vs L2 reconstruction loss. Typical: True. ssimlambda: Weight for SSIM loss. Typical: 0.2. depthlambda: Weight for depth loss. Typical: 0.0. opacityreg: Weight for opacity regularization. Typical: 0.0. scalereg: Weight for scale regularization. Typical: 0.0. visibleadam: Boolean flag for visibility-aware Adam updates. Typical: False. packed: Boolean flag for packed Gaussian storage. Typical: False. appopt: Boolean flag for appearance optimization baking. Typical: False. saveply: Boolean flag for PLY export. Typical: True. plysteps: List of steps to export PLY. Typical: [0, 1000, 2000,...]. maxsteps: Total training steps. Typical: 30000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Division by Zero: When computing disparity 1.0/\text{depths}, ensure depths are clamped to a minimum positive value (e.g., 10^{-6}) to avoid NaNs. Visibility Mask Shape: If packed is true, the visibility mask must be created with the correct size corresponding to the packed Gaussian count, not the original count. SH Degree Indexing: Ensure shdegreetouse is correctly mapped to the number of SH coefficients to avoid shape mismatches in rendering. Bilateral Grid Slicing: The slice function must handle out-of-bounds grid coordinates gracefully. Random Background: The alphas tensor must be broadcasted correctly to match the colors tensor shape before compositing. Time Complexity: Dominated by rasterization O(N \cdot V \cdot A) where N is number of Gaussians, V is number of views, and A is image area. Loss computation is O(V \cdot A). Backward pass is similar to forward. Strategy steps are O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for Gaussian parameters. Rasterization requires O(V \cdot A) for intermediate buffers. Bilateral grid adds O(A \cdot C{grid}) memory. Performance: Depends heavily on hardware (GPU memory bandwidth for rasterization). Mixed losses add computational overhead but improve convergence. Strengths: Integrates multiple supervisions for robust training. Handles appearance and geometry jointly. Limitations: Complex configuration. Requires careful tuning of loss weights. Densification strategy integration adds complexity. This method is derived from the AugSplat implementation, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with additional features like bilateral grids and mixed loss training. It builds upon the foundational 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by incorporating these advanced training techniques. AugSplat, https://github.com/llazzaroni/AugSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering, https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/, 2023

name: Hyperparameter Settings
head: Optimizer and Regularization Settings, Optimizer settings, Phys3DGS Hyperparameter Settings, Training Hyperparameters
body: Hyperparameter Settings define the numerical configuration for the optimizer, learning rates, and regularization terms used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. This method solves the problem of stable convergence and high-fidelity reconstruction by tuning the trade-off between fitting training data and maintaining geometric/photometric consistency. It differs from sibling methods like Densification Strategy (which manages primitive count) and Pruning and Sparsification (which removes primitives) by focusing on the gradient descent dynamics and loss weighting rather than structural topology changes. The method configures the optimization loop by setting the optimizer type, learning rates for specific Gaussian attributes, and weights for auxiliary loss terms. Inputs: Model parameters: Position \mu, Color SH coefficients \mathbf{c}, Scale s, Opacity \alpha, and potentially material parameters (Base Color, Metallic, Roughness) or dynamic parameters (MLP weights). Ground truth images and camera poses. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: Optimizer State: Adam optimizer state buffers (first and second moment estimates) for each parameter group. Learning Rate Schedule: A mapping from parameter type to initial learning rate and decay schedule. Parameters and Typical Values: 1. Optimizer: Adam. \beta1 = 0.9 \beta2 = 0.999 \epsilon = 10^{-15}. 2. Learning Rates (LR): Standard 3DGS: Position: 1.6 \times 10^{-4} Color SH: 2.5 \times 10^{-3} Scale: 5 \times 10^{-3} Opacity: 5 \times 10^{-2} Normal Rotation: 1 \times 10^{-3} Phys3DGS (Inverse Rendering): Base Color: 1 \times 10^{-2} Metallic: 1 \times 10^{-2} Roughness: 1 \times 10^{-2} Direct Light SH (deg=0): 2.5 \times 10^{-3} Direct Light SH (deg>0): 1 \times 10^{-4} Indirect Light SH (deg=0): 2.5 \times 10^{-4} Indirect Light SH (deg>0): 1 \times 10^{-3} Visibility SH: 0.1 ToRF (Dynamic/Depth): MLP weights: Initial \gamma{MLP} = 0.0008, decaying exponentially to 1.6 \times 10^{-6} over 60,000 iterations. Reflectivity: Initial value 0.1, LR \gammar = 0.00016. 3. Regularization Strengths (Phys3DGS): Smoothness regularizer for Base Color: \lambda{smooth} = 0.06 Smoothness regularizer for Roughness: \lambda{smooth} = 0.02 Smoothness regularizer for Metallic: \lambda{smooth} = 0.02 Other regularizers (\lambdao, \lambda{sc}, \lambda{sr}): 1.0 4. Loss Weights (ToRF): \alpha = 5 (for real scenes), \alpha = 1 (for synthetic scenes). \beta = 0.0008. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializeoptimizer(params, config): """ Initialize Adam optimizer with specific learning rates per parameter group. params: dict of parameter tensors (position, colorsh, scale, opacity, etc.) config: dict containing lrschedule, beta1, beta2, epsilon """ optimizer = Adam( params=params, lr=config['baselr'], # Not explicitly given as single value, handled by groups betas=(config['beta1'], config['beta2']), eps=config['epsilon']) # Assign learning rates based on parameter type # Example for Phys3DGS/Standard 3DGS hybrid configuration lrmap = { 'position': 1.6e-4, 'colorsh': 2.5e-3, 'scale': 5.0e-3, 'opacity': 5.0e-2, 'basecolor': 1.0e-2, 'metallic': 1.0e-2, 'roughness': 1.0e-2, 'normalrotation': 1.0e-3, 'directlightshdeg0': 2.5e-3, 'directlightshdeggt0': 1.0e-4, 'indirectlightshdeg0': 2.5e-4, 'indirectlightshdeggt0': 1.0e-3, 'visibilitysh': 0.1 } # Group parameters for the optimizer paramgroups = [] for name, tensor in params.items(): lr = lrmap.get(name, 1.0e-3) # Default fallback if not specified paramgroups.append({'params': [tensor], 'lr': lr}) optimizer = Adam(paramgroups, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-15) return optimizer def computeloss(losstype, pred, gt, config): """ Compute loss with specific weights. """ if losstype == 'photometric': # L1 or L2 loss return torch.mean(torch.abs(pred - gt)) elif losstype == 'smoothness': # Smoothness regularizer # lambdasmooth values: 0.06 (base color), 0.02 (roughness/metallic) return config['lambdasmooth'] smoothnessterm(pred) elif losstype == 'otherreg': # Other regularizers (lambdao, lambdasc, lambdasr) return 1.0 otherregularizationterm(pred) return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instability from Erroneous Gaussians: If a single Gaussian behaves abnormally (e.g., driven to the opposite side of the surface, extremely large scale, or extreme opacity), it causes training instability. Mechanism: Erroneous Gaussians interfere with visibility, occluding global illumination. The optimizer compensates by either increasing local illumination intensity (dimming global) or decreasing opacity to extreme values. Result: Global illumination SH coefficients or opacity values receive large gradients, leading to overflow. Mitigation: Use higher weights for other regularizers (\lambdao, \lambda{sc}, \lambda{sr} = 1.0) to constrain this behavior. View Selection Bias: Using training views for optimization focuses on known-view fitting and degrades novel-view performance. Use test views or synthetic views sampled from the estimated camera trajectory instead. Extends 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning Gaussian covariance and opacity on time t and view direction d. It differs from static 3DGS by using a conditional covariance matrix to drive densification and splitting, and from other dynamic variants by integrating these cues directly into the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline with minimal architectural changes. Uses an auxiliary per-pixel error metric to drive densification decisions, rather than relying on positional gradient magnitudes. It solves the limitation of gradient-based methods (sensitive to error changes but blind to absolute error in high-frequency areas) by redistributing per-pixel errors to primitives proportional to their rendering contribution. Distinct from siblings like Conditional 3DGS Optimization and Rendering by explicitly utilizing accumulated L1 error norms as probability weights for splitting. Addresses under-constrained geometry in few-shot neural rendering by integrating precise correspondences from a sparse matching network into 3DGS initialization and optimization. Unlike dense matcher-based methods that introduce blurriness in high-frequency areas, this approach yields precise correspondences that, combined with frequency regularization, enable better reconstruction of fine details. It serves as a densification and initialization strategy enhancing base 3DGS in sparse-view scenarios. A learnable module within the FlexGS framework that adaptively selects a subset of 3D Gaussians during training based on attributes and a desired elastic ratio e, using a differentiable mask. It sets itself apart from non-differentiable thresholding or hard masking by allowing gradients to flow through the selection decision via the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) applied to Gumbel-Softmax outputs, unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed heuristics or non-differentiable hard thresholds. Addresses optimization challenges of large, sparse, unbounded scenes by dividing the environment into independent spatial chunks, each trained separately. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by introducing a skybox for environmental consistency, modifying densification policies to handle sparse gradients, and applying monocular depth regularization for unobserved surfaces. A method simplifying mesh generation by utilizing an initial mesh or estimating it in a single-stage training process, introducing a pseudo-mesh of unconnected triangle faces with Gaussian components positioned on these faces to ensure proper alignment. It realizes deformation by modifying pseudo-mesh positions, with alterations automatically propagating to the Gaussian mesh, enabling real-time animation and scene editing. However, it exhibits artifacts when dealing with significant deformations in meshes with large faces, leading to inaccuracies. Selects specific views for adaptation optimization to prevent overfitting to known training views and maintain novel-view performance. Steps: 1. Avoid using training views (+train) as they focus on known-view fitting. 2. Use test views for optimization. 3. Alternatively, use synthetic views sampled from the estimated camera trajectory (+syn.). Typical number of synthetic views used: 50. On the bicycle scene, PSNR with test views was Zoom-out 30.84, Zoom-in 24.23; with synthetic views: Zoom-out 29.72, Zoom-in 30.05. Time Complexity: Dependent on the optimizer steps and the complexity of the loss function (e.g., inverse rendering with SH coefficients is more expensive than standard photometric loss). The exponential decay of MLP learning rates in ToRF does not change asymptotic complexity but affects convergence speed. Memory Complexity: The Adam optimizer requires storing first and second moment estimates for every parameter, doubling the memory footprint of the learnable parameters. Strengths: Carefully tuned learning rates (e.g., higher LR for opacity and scale) allow for rapid adaptation of primitive properties. Regularization weights prevent instability from outlier Gaussians. Limitations: Improper regularization weights can lead to gradient overflow in SH coefficients or opacity. Using training views for optimization degrades novel view synthesis quality. When to use: Standard 3DGS training requires the base learning rates. Inverse rendering (Phys3DGS) requires specific material and lighting LR settings. Dynamic scenes (ToRF) require MLP decay schedules. Sparse view scenarios may benefit from view selection strategies. The hyperparameter settings for 3D Gaussian Splatting were introduced alongside the original 3DGS paper [Kerbl et al.], establishing the baseline Adam optimizer configuration. Subsequent works have adapted these settings for specific domains: Phys3DGS introduced settings for physically-based inverse rendering, ToRF adapted them for time-of-flight and dynamic scenes, and Mip-Splatting variants explored view selection strategies. The importance of regularization weights to prevent instability was highlighted in Phys3DGS. Time of the Flight of the Gaussians: Optimizing Depth Indirectly in Dynamic Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01958, fetched 2026-10-26 Phys3DGS: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2409.10335, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28 Mipmap-GS: Let Gaussians Deform with Scale-Specific Mipmap for Anti-Aliasing Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00091, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Conditional 3DGS Optimization and Rendering
head: 7DGS to Conditional 3DGS, Optimization and Rendering Pipeline
body: Conditional 3DGS Optimization and Rendering extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle dynamic scenes by incorporating temporal and directional dependencies into the Gaussian parameters. It solves the problem of representing time-varying geometry and appearance by conditioning the Gaussian covariance and opacity on time t and view direction d. It differs from static 3DGS by using a conditional covariance matrix to drive densification and splitting, and from other dynamic variants by integrating these cues directly into the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline with minimal architectural changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of images (video) with known camera poses and timestamps. Output: A set of 7D Gaussians (3D position, 3D covariance, 3D color, opacity) conditioned on time and view direction, rendered as a video sequence. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Gaussian, defined by: Mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. Conditional Covariance \Sigma{cond} \in \mathbb{R}^{7 \times 7}, which encodes spatial, temporal, and angular correlations. Color coefficients c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Conditional Opacity \alpha{cond}, modulated by time and direction. Method Steps: 1. Covariance Decomposition for Densification: To guide splitting and pruning, extract scale and rotation from the conditional covariance \Sigma{cond} using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD): \Sigma{cond} = U D U^T where U is an orthogonal matrix and D is a diagonal matrix of singular values. Define rotation matrix R = U. Define scale vector S = \text{diag}(D). Ensure a right-handed coordinate system by adjusting the last column of R: R{:,3} = R{:,3} \cdot \text{sign}(\det(R)) 2. Conditional Splitting Criteria: Leverage temporal cues for Gaussian splitting in addition to spatial gradients. Quantify spatial-temporal correlation using the magnitude of the off-diagonal block \Sigma{pt} of \Sigma{cond}, which captures interaction between spatial and temporal components. Split a Gaussian if: 1. |\Sigma{pt}| > 0.05 (relative to screen extent). 2. Normalized temporal scale (derived from \Sigmat) > 0.25. This ensures regions with significant motion dynamics are densely represented. 3. Rendering Pipeline: The pipeline remains compatible with standard 3DGS. Convert the 7DGS representation to a 3DGS-compatible format via conditional slicing. Project the resulting conditional 3D Gaussian mean and covariance onto the image plane using standard perspective projection to yield 2D Gaussians. Splat onto the image canvas using a differentiable rasterization routine. Compute final pixel colors by aggregating contributions in a depth-aware, opacity-blended manner. 4. Optimization and Pruning: Use the same loss functions and optimizers as standard 3DGS. Increase the minimum opacity threshold for pruning to \tau{min} = 0.01 to compensate for the modulation of conditional opacity \alpha{cond} by time and view direction. 5. Modulation Parameters: Directional and temporal modulation parameters (\lambdad and \lambdat) are initialized based on dataset characteristics: 0.5 for 7DGS-PBR. 0.05 for D-NeRF. 0.1 for Technicolor. These parameters become trainable after 15,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decomposeconditionalcovariance(Sigmacond): """ Extracts scale and rotation from the conditional covariance matrix. Args: Sigmacond: 7x7 conditional covariance matrix. Returns: R: 3x3 rotation matrix. S: 3D scale vector. """ # SVD decomposition U, D, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Sigmacond) # Define rotation and scale R = U[:,:3] # Extract 3x3 spatial rotation block S = np.diag(D)[:3] # Extract top 3 singular values as scale # Ensure right-handed coordinate system detR = np.linalg.det(R) if detR < 0: R[:, 2] = -R[:, 2] return R, S def checksplittingcriteria(Sigmacond, screenextent): """ Determines if a Gaussian should be split based on temporal cues. Args: Sigmacond: 7x7 conditional covariance matrix. screenextent: Normalization factor for screen size. Returns: bool: True if splitting criteria are met. """ # Extract off-diagonal block Sigmapt (interaction between spatial and temporal) # Assuming layout: [Spatial (3x3), Temporal/Angular (4x4)] # Sigmapt corresponds to the cross-terms between spatial (0-2) and temporal/angular (3-6) Sigmapt = Sigmacond[0:3, 3:7] # Calculate magnitude of spatial-temporal correlation correlationmagnitude = np.linalg.norm(Sigmapt) # Check threshold relative to screen extent if correlationmagnitude <= 0.05 screenextent: return False # Calculate normalized temporal scale from Sigmat (temporal block) Sigmat = Sigmacond[3:7, 3:7] # Assuming temporal scale is derived from the trace or max eigenvalue of Sigmat # Note: Exact derivation of "normalized temporal scale" from Sigmat is not fully specified in beyond "derived from" # We assume it refers to the magnitude of temporal variance components. temporalscale = np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(Sigmat)) if temporalscale > 0.25: return True return False def renderconditionalgaussians(gaussians, cameraparams, timet, viewdird): """ Renders the scene using conditional 3DGS. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with conditional parameters. cameraparams: Camera intrinsic and extrinsic matrices. timet: Current time step. viewdird: Current view direction. Returns: Image tensor. """ # 1. Conditional Slicing: Convert 7DGS to 3DGS-compatible format # This involves evaluating the conditional dependencies for the current t and d projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Get conditional mean and covariance for current t, d mucond = g.getconditionalmean(timet, viewdird) Sigmacond = g.getconditionalcovariance(timet, viewdird) # 2. Project to 2D # Standard perspective projection mu2d, Sigma2d = projecttoimageplane(mucond, Sigmacond, cameraparams) projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu': mu2d, 'Sigma': Sigma2d, 'color': g.color, 'opacity': g.getconditionalopacity(timet, viewdird) }) # 3. Splatting # Differentiable rasterization image = splat2dgaussians(projectedgaussians, imagewidth, imageheight) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: SVD decomposition must handle near-singular covariance matrices carefully to avoid numerical instability in scale extraction. Boundaries: The threshold for splitting (0.05 relative to screen extent) requires accurate calculation of screen extent, which depends on camera FOV and resolution. Degenerate Input: If temporal scale is zero (static scene), splitting criteria based on temporal cues will not trigger, relying solely on spatial gradients. A supervision strategy used during the low-resolution optimization stage to prevent optimization misguidance caused by aliased ground truth images. It differs from standard upsampling by explicitly downscaling target images using an anti-aliasing filter before computing the loss. Time Complexity: Rendering is compatible with standard 3DGS, implying O(N) complexity with respect to the number of Gaussians N per frame. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional covariance blocks for temporal and angular dependencies, increasing memory per Gaussian compared to static 3DGS. Measured Performance: Evaluated on D-NeRF (800x800), Technicolor, and 7DGS-PBR datasets. Experiments conducted on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU (16GB). Strengths: Integrates seamlessly with existing 3DGS training pipeline, leveraging adaptive density control and efficient rasterization with minimal modifications. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of modulation parameters (\lambdad, \lambdat) and thresholds for splitting. When to Use: Dynamic scenes with significant motion and view-dependent appearance changes. When Not to Use: Static scenes where standard 3DGS is sufficient and more efficient. Originated in the paper "7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting". The method builds on the 3DGS framework and extends it to handle 4D scenes (3D space + time) and view-dependent effects by conditioning Gaussian parameters on time and view direction. It was evaluated on synthetic (D-NeRF) and in-the-wild (Technicolor) video datasets. 7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07946v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Ground Truth Downsampling
head: Anti-alias Ground Truth Downsampling
body: Ground Truth Downsampling is a supervision strategy used during the low-resolution (LR) optimization stage of 3D Gaussian Splatting (specifically within the DashGaussian framework) to prevent optimization misguidance caused by aliased ground truth images. It differs from standard upsampling or fixed-resolution training by explicitly downscaling the target images using an anti-aliasing filter before computing the loss against the rendered low-resolution output. This ensures that the Gaussians are optimized to match the frequency content appropriate for the target resolution, rather than attempting to fit high-frequency noise present in the original high-resolution ground truth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: High-resolution ground truth image I{HR}, rendered low-resolution image I{LR} from the current Gaussian scene representation. Output: Downsampled ground truth image I{LR}^{GT} used for loss computation. Data Structures: I{HR}: Tensor of shape (H, W, C), typically 3-channel RGB. I{LR}: Tensor of shape (h, w, C), where h = H/s and w = W/s for some scale factor s. I{LR}^{GT}: Tensor of shape (h, w, C). Steps: 1. Resolution Selection: Determine the target low resolution (h, w) for the current optimization stage. This is often part of a resolution scheduler that gradually increases resolution during training. 2. Anti-Aliased Downsampling: Apply PyTorch's official anti-alias downsampling algorithm to I{HR} to produce I{LR}^{GT}. This step involves a low-pass filter to remove frequencies above the Nyquist limit of the target resolution before subsampling. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 or L2, or SSIM) between the rendered image I{LR} and the downsampled ground truth I{LR}^{GT}. \mathcal{L} = \| I{LR} - I{LR}^{GT} \| 4. Optimization Step: Update the Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) using the gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def groundtruthdownsampling(gthr, renderlr, scalefactor): """ Downsamples high-resolution ground truth to match the resolution of the low-resolution rendering. Args: gthr (torch.Tensor): High-resolution ground truth image, shape (H, W, C) or (B, H, W, C). renderlr (torch.Tensor): Rendered low-resolution image, shape (h, w, C) or (B, h, w, C). scalefactor (int): Integer factor by which to downsample (H/h = W/w = scalefactor). Returns: torch.Tensor: Downsampled ground truth image, shape (h, w, C). """ # Ensure input is in the correct format for PyTorch's anti-alias downsampling # PyTorch's F.interpolate with antialias=True expects channels first (B, C, H, W) # or (C, H, W) if batch dimension is absent. # Check if batch dimension exists if gthr.dim() == 3: gthr = gthr.unsqueeze(0) # Add batch dim needsunsqueeze = True else: needsunsqueeze = False # Apply anti-alias downsampling # Note: PyTorch's F.interpolate with antialias=True uses a Gaussian filter # to low-pass filter the image before downsampling. gtlr = F.interpolate( gthr, size=(renderlr.shape[-2], renderlr.shape[-1]), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False, antialias=True) if needsunsqueeze: gtlr = gtlr.squeeze(0) return gtlr def computeloss(renderlr, gtlr): """ Computes the reconstruction loss between rendered and downsampled ground truth. """ # Example: L1 Loss loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderlr - gtlr)) return loss Parameters: Anti-aliasing Filter: PyTorch's official implementation is used. The specific kernel is not explicitly detailed in the source but is part of the antialias=True flag in F.interpolate. Scale Factor: Determined by the resolution scheduler. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure that the ground truth images are normalized consistently with the rendered images (e.g., [0, 1] or [-1, 1]) before downsampling. Boundary Conditions: The anti-aliasing filter may introduce slight blurring at the edges. This is generally desirable for anti-aliasing but should be noted if edge fidelity is critical. Degenerate Input: If the ground truth image is already at the target low resolution, the downsampling step should be skipped or identity-mapped. Time Complexity: The downsampling operation is O(H \cdot W), which is negligible compared to the rendering and optimization steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the intermediate downsampled ground truth tensor, which is O(h \cdot w \cdot C). Measured Performance: In the DashGaussian framework, this method contributes to a 5dB PSNR improvement over baseline 3DGS on zoom-out tasks. Strengths: Prevents high-frequency aliasing artifacts in the optimization process, leading to more stable convergence at low resolutions. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the anti-aliasing filter provided by the deep learning framework. When to Use: During the low-resolution optimization stages of 3D Gaussian Splatting training, particularly when using a multi-resolution schedule. When Not to Use: When training at a single high resolution where anti-aliasing of the ground truth is not necessary for the target output resolution. Ground Truth Downsampling was introduced as part of the DashGaussian method, which aims to optimize 3D Gaussian Splatting in 200 seconds. The method addresses the issue of aliased supervision hindering optimization when training at low resolutions. It is a key component of the DashGaussian framework, which also includes modifications to learning rate schedules, resolution schedulers, primitive growth schedules, and densification operations. name: Zoom-out Adaptation
head: Downsample-based adaptation, Zoom-out pseudo-GT generation
body: Zoom-out Adaptation is a post-training optimization technique that adapts a pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model to render anti-aliased images at lower resolutions (zoom-out). It solves the problem of geometric dilation and aliasing artifacts (e.g., thick spokes on wheels) that occur when a high-resolution model is viewed at a distance or downsampled. Unlike Mip-Splatting, which uses filters to mitigate dilation, this method generates pseudo-ground truth (pseudo-GT) by downsampling high-resolution renderings and re-optimizes the Gaussians to fit this multi-scale supervision, achieving a 5dB PSNR improvement over baseline 3DGS on zoom-out tasks. Inputs: A pre-trained 3DGS model (positions, covariances, opacities, colors) trained on full-resolution (\times 1) images; camera poses for the target scene. Outputs: An adapted 3DGS model optimized for low-resolution rendering. Data Structures: The 3DGS model retains the standard structure: a list of N Gaussians, each defined by mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or quaternion/scale), opacity \alpha \in [0,1], and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Steps: 1. Baseline Training: Train the initial 3DGS model on full-resolution (\times 1) training images until convergence. 2. High-Resolution Rendering: Render the scene using the trained model at the target lower resolutions (e.g., \times 1/2, \times 1/4, \times 1/8 of the original training resolution). Let I{HR} be the rendered image at the original resolution. 3. Pseudo-GT Generation: Downsample the high-resolution renderings to create the pseudo-ground truth I{pseudo} for the target resolution. This is typically done using standard image downsampling (e.g., average pooling or bilinear filtering). Formula: I{pseudo} = \text{Downsample}(I{HR}, \text{scale}) 4. Adaptation Optimization: Optimize the 3D Gaussian parameters (positions, scales, opacities, colors) by minimizing the reconstruction loss between the rendered image at the target low resolution and the I{pseudo}. Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec}(I{rendered\LR}, I{pseudo}) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{reg} The optimization uses the same camera poses as the original training but renders at the lower resolution. 5. Convergence: Run optimization until convergence. For zoom-out, this typically takes 0.5K iterations. Parameters: Target Resolutions: \times 1/2, \times 1/4, \times 1/8. Optimization Views: Test views or synthetic views sampled from the estimated camera trajectory are preferred over training views to retain novel-view performance. Iterations: 0.5K iterations for zoom-out. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pseudo-GT Quality: The quality of guidance varies by dataset. For the Blender dataset (isolated objects), supervision is intensive and high-quality. For Mip-NeRF 360 (complex backgrounds), the pseudo-GT has limited quality and provides weaker guidance. Needle-like Aliasing: Without adaptation, 3DGS exhibits needle-like aliasing due to intrinsic shrinkage bias when zoomed in, but for zoom-out, the primary artifact is dilation. A technique to adapt a pre-trained 3DGS model for high-resolution rendering (zoom-in) by using a super-resolution network (SwinIR) to generate high-resolution pseudo-GT from low-resolution training data. Unlike zoom-out, which downsamples renderings, this method upscales supervision. It converges in 1K iterations and generates novel views with high fidelity, avoiding the needle-like aliasing of 3DGS and the high-frequency trade-offs of Mip-Splatting. Time Complexity: Convergence is very fast. Zoom-out adaptation converges within 0.5K iterations (on the order of seconds). This is faster than the zoom-in adaptation (1K iterations) and significantly faster than Mip-Splatting's filter update, which is not compatible with all 3DGS variations. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory overhead during rendering, as it reuses the standard 3DGS structure. The optimization phase requires storing the pseudo-GT images. Performance: Improves PSNR by 5dB compared to baseline 3DGS on zoom-out tasks. Visual results show superior handling of dilation artifacts (e.g., wheel spokes) compared to Mip-Splatting. Strengths: Plug-in compatibility with dynamic 3DGS models; no disturbance to deformation networks. Reduces redundancy by allowing up to 25% reduction in splatted primitives without performance loss. Limitations: Effectiveness depends on the quality of pseudo-GT, which is lower for complex scenes like Mip-NeRF 360 compared to synthetic datasets like Blender. Originated in "Mipmap-GS: Let Gaussians Deform with Scale-Specific Mipmap for Anti-Aliasing Rendering" (2025). The method addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which is optimized for a specific resolution and suffers from aliasing when viewed at different scales. It builds on the observation that downsampling high-quality renderings preserves essential scene details, providing a robust supervision signal for scale-specific adaptation.
