name: Edge-guided Splitting Strategy
body: The Edge-guided Splitting Strategy (ESS) is a densification method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that refines primitives by splitting large Gaussians located in high-frequency edge regions to capture fine details. It addresses the weakness of enlarged primitives, which lose high-frequency detail, particularly when used in conjunction with Random Dropout Regularization (RDR). Unlike standard splitting based solely on position gradient magnitude, ESS explicitly guides splitting toward geometric edges, making it distinct from sibling methods like Blended Error Densification which rely on rendering error [13892-blended-error-densification-and-splitting.md]. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}, each defined by mean position \mu, covariance \Sigma, scaling s, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic features f; a set of M training viewpoints; and an edge detection function. Output: An updated set of primitives where large Gaussians with high edge scores are split into smaller primitives. Data Structures Gaussian Primitive i: Contains scalar size Si (derived from scaling factors), opacity \alphai, and position. Edge Map E(I): A pixel-wise probability map ranging from 0 to 1, generated by an edge detection method on input view I. Binary Mask \mathcal{M}^i(p): Indicates if pixel p is covered by primitive i. Parameters \mathcal{S}{thr}: Size threshold for splitting. Value not given in the sources. \mathcal{E}{thr}: Edge threshold for splitting. Value not given in the sources. M: Number of viewpoints used for edge score accumulation. Steps 1. Edge Map Generation: For each input view I, compute the pixel-wise edge probability map E(I) using an edge detection method. 2. Single-View Edge Score Calculation: For each Gaussian primitive i and each viewpoint k, calculate the single-view edge score \mathcal{E}{i,k}' by aggregating the edge probabilities of covered pixels, weighted by the primitive's contribution to the pixel: \mathcal{E}{i,k}' = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) \cdot \sum{p} E(Ik) \mathcal{M}k^i(p) where \mathcal{M}k^i(p) is the binary mask for pixel p covered by primitive i in view k, and the term \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) represents the alpha-blending weight wi of the primitive. 3. Accumulate Edge Score: Compute the final edge score \mathcal{E}i for primitive i by summing the single-view scores across all M viewpoints, normalized by the number of pixels covered by the primitive in each view: \mathcal{E}i = \sum{k=1}^M \frac{\mathcal{E}{i,k}'}{\sum{p} \mathcal{M}k^i(p)} 4. Splitting Mask Determination: Identify primitives to split using the mask \mathcal{M}{edge}, which selects primitives satisfying both a size condition and an edge score condition: \mathcal{M}{edge} = \{ Si \geq \mathcal{S}{thr} \} \cap \{ \mathcal{E}i \geq \mathcal{E}{thr} \} where Si is the size of the i-th primitive. 5. Splitting: Split all Gaussian primitives i where \mathcal{M}{edge} is true into smaller primitives. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeedgescore(primitive, viewindex, edgemap, camera): """ Computes the single-view edge score Ei' for a primitive. """ # Project primitive to view to get coverage mask M^i(p) # This involves projecting the 3D Gaussian to 2D and determining # which pixels it covers. coveragemask = projectandmask(primitive, camera) # Calculate alpha blending weight wi # Note: In standard 3DGS, wi depends on the order of primitives. # For simplicity in this isolated function, we assume wi is precomputed # or approximated by alphai if order is not strictly enforced in this step. # The source formula uses alphai product(1-alphaj). # Assuming wi is available or computed via standard 3DGS rasterization order. weight = primitive.alpha computeprecedingalphaproduct(primitive, camera) # Sum edge probabilities for covered pixels # E(I) is the edge map for the current view edgesum = sum(edgemap[p] for p in coveragemask) return weight edgesum def accumulateedgescores(primitives, views, edgemaps, cameras): """ Computes the final edge score Ei for each primitive across M views. """ M = len(views) finalscores = {} for i, primitive in enumerate(primitives): totalscore = 0.0 for k in range(M): view = views[k] edgemap = edgemaps[k] camera = cameras[k] # Compute single-view score eprime = computeedgescore(primitive, k, edgemap, camera) # Compute number of pixels covered by primitive in this view coveragemask = projectandmask(primitive, camera) pixelcount = len(coveragemask) # Avoid division by zero if pixelcount > 0: totalscore += eprime / pixelcount else: totalscore += 0.0 finalscores[primitive.id] = totalscore return finalscores def applyedgeguidedsplitting(primitives, edgescores, sthr, ethr): """ Splits primitives that are large and have high edge scores. """ tosplit = [] for primitive in primitives: size = getprimitivesize(primitive) # Derived from scaling factors score = edgescores[primitive.id] if size >= sthr and score >= ethr: tosplit.append(primitive) # Split the selected primitives into smaller ones # The specific splitting logic (e.g., copying, perturbing mean, halving scale) # is not detailed in the source, but standard 3DGS splitting is assumed. newprimitives = [] for primitive in tosplit: newprimitives.extend(splitprimitive(primitive)) # Remove old primitives and add new ones remaining = [p for p in primitives if p not in tosplit] return remaining + newprimitives Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: The normalization in the edge score accumulation divides by the number of pixels covered by the primitive. If a primitive covers zero pixels in a view, the contribution is zero. Threshold Selection: The values for \mathcal{S}{thr} and \mathcal{E}{thr} are not specified in the sources. Improper selection may lead to over-splitting (noise) or under-splitting (loss of detail). Edge Detection Dependency: The quality of ESS depends on the edge detection method used to generate E(I). Uses conditional information to guide optimization, differing from ESS which uses geometric edge scores. Splits based on rendering error, whereas ESS splits based on edge presence. Focuses on matching sparse features, not on splitting based on edge density. Selects Gaussians adaptively, but does not specify edge-guided splitting. Focuses on training scale, not splitting strategy. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for edge map generation and edge score calculation per primitive per view. The splitting step is proportional to the number of primitives meeting the threshold. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory beyond storing edge maps and scores. Strengths: Effectively captures high-frequency details in edge regions, improving performance on sparse-view benchmarks (LLFF, DTU, Blender). Compatible with diverse 3DGS-based methods. Limitations: Relies on the quality of edge detection. Does not address overfitting directly (requires RDR for that). When to Use: When high-frequency detail recovery is critical, especially in sparse-view settings or when using regularization techniques like RDR that may enlarge primitives. The Edge-guided Splitting Strategy (ESS) was introduced in the DropoutGS paper by Xu et al. in 2025. It was developed to remedy the loss of high-frequency details caused by Random Dropout Regularization (RDR), which alleviates overfitting but leads to enlarged primitives. DropoutGS combines RDR and ESS to improve generalization performance in sparse-view novel view synthesis. name: Standard 3DGS Training Configuration
head: Standard 3DGS Training
body: Standard 3DGS Training Configuration defines the canonical hyperparameter settings for optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting models, establishing the baseline for adaptive density control and gradient-based optimization. It differs from sibling methods like Conditional 3DGS Optimization and Rendering or Blended Error Densification and Splitting by adhering strictly to the default parameters of the official implementation, specifically regarding densification frequency, gradient thresholds, and opacity management. The method configures the training loop to balance reconstruction quality and computational efficiency through a fixed schedule of densification, pruning, and opacity resets. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Initial point cloud (from SfM), training images, and hyperparameter configuration. Outputs: Optimized set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a rendered image sequence. Data Structures The Gaussian representation maintains per-Gaussian attributes: Position: 3D vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance: 3D rotation \mathbf{R} and scaling \mathbf{s}, stored as quaternions and scale vectors. Opacity: Scalar \alpha \in [0, 1]. Color: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Parameters Maximum Iterations: 30,000. D-SSIM Loss Weight: 0.2. Spherical Harmonics Degree: 3. Background Color: Black. Densification Gradient Threshold: 0.0002. Opacity Reset Interval: 3000 iterations. Densification Start Iteration: 500. Densification Interval: 100 iterations. Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Set all opacities to a small initial value (typically 0.1 or 0.01, though standard reset sets to 0.01). 2. Optimization Loop: Iterate from t = 1 to T{max} = 30,000. 3. Rendering: Render the current Gaussian set to generate images. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the combined loss using RGB loss and D-SSIM loss with weight 0.2. 5. Gradient Accumulation: Accumulate gradients for Gaussian positions and other attributes. 6. Densification Check: If t \ge 500 and (t - 500) \mod 100 == 0: Accumulate Statistics: Track gradient magnitudes for each Gaussian. Split/Clone: For Gaussians with accumulated gradient magnitude exceeding the threshold (0.0002): If the Gaussian is "large" (size > percentdense \times scene extent, default 0.01), split it into two smaller Gaussians with 80% of the original size [S2, Note: S2 defines this logic for modified config, but standard config uses default percentdense of 0.01]. If the Gaussian is "small", clone it identically. Pruning: Remove Gaussians with opacity below a minimum threshold (default 0.005) [S2, Note: S2 contrasts this with its own higher threshold, implying 0.005 is standard]. Opacity Reset: Every 3000 iterations, reset the opacity of all Gaussians to 0.01. 7. Optimization Step: Update Gaussian parameters using the accumulated gradients (typically Adam optimizer). 8. Termination: Stop at iteration 30,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Gradient thresholds are small (2 \times 10^{-4}); ensure floating-point precision is sufficient to distinguish significant gradients from noise. Boundary Conditions: The densification start at iteration 500 prevents early instability. Degenerate Input: If SfM points are sparse, initial densification may create excessive Gaussians if the gradient threshold is too low; however, the standard threshold is fixed. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def standard3dgstraining(gaussians, images, maxiter=30000): # Hyperparameters from densifystartiter = 500 densifyinterval = 100 densifygradthreshold = 0.0002 opacityresetinterval = 3000 opacityresetvalue = 0.01 dssimweight = 0.2 shdegree = 3 backgroundcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Black # Default parameters implied by contrast densifyminopacity = 0.005 percentdense = 0.01 accumulatedgradients = {g.id: 0.0 for g in gaussians} for t in range(1, maxiter + 1): # 1. Render renderedimages = render(gaussians, images, backgroundcolor) # 2. Compute Loss loss = computeloss(renderedimages, images, dssimweight) # 3. Backpropagate gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) # 4. Accumulate Gradients for Densification for g in gaussians: gradmag = norm(gradients[g.id].position) accumulatedgradients[g.id] += gradmag # 5. Densification and Pruning if t >= densifystartiter and (t - densifystartiter) % densifyinterval == 0: newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if accumulatedgradients[g.id] > densifygradthreshold: # Split or Clone based on size if islarge(g, percentdense): newgaussians.extend(splitgaussian(g, factor=0.8)) else: newgaussians.append(clonegaussian(g)) else: newgaussians.append(g) # Prune low opacity Gaussians gaussians = [g for g in newgaussians if g.opacity > densifyminopacity] # Reset accumulated gradients accumulatedgradients = {g.id: 0.0 for g in gaussians} # 6. Opacity Reset if t % opacityresetinterval == 0: for g in gaussians: g.opacity = opacityresetvalue # 7. Optimization Step optimize(gaussians, gradients) return gaussians A parameter-tuning strategy that reduces the number of generated Gaussians and minimizes sorting time during training. It differs from the standard configuration by increasing the densification interval to 1000 (vs 100), lowering the densification gradient threshold to 7 \times 10^{-5} (vs 2 \times 10^{-4}), raising the minimum opacity threshold to 0.1 (vs 0.005), deactivating the opacity reset (interval \infty vs 3000), and increasing the percentdense threshold to 0.1 (vs 0.01). This configuration avoids regular pruning and creates fewer Gaussian splats overall. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot I), where N is the number of Gaussians and I is the number of iterations (30,000). Densification adds overhead every 100 iterations. Memory Complexity: O(N), where N grows during densification and shrinks during pruning. Performance: The standard configuration is computationally intensive due to frequent densification and pruning. It produces high-quality reconstructions but requires significant GPU memory. Strengths: Established baseline, high reconstruction quality, well-understood behavior. Limitations: High memory usage, long training times, potential for over-densification in complex scenes. When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction is prioritized over training speed or memory efficiency. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or training time is critical; consider Modified 3DGS Densification or Sparse Matching Integration. The standard 3DGS training configuration originates from the official implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It has been widely adopted as the baseline for evaluating new densification strategies and optimization techniques. The configuration was standardized to ensure reproducibility across experiments. name: BoundedGS Leaf Loss and Gradient Management
head: Adam with Compact Storage
body: BoundedGS Leaf Loss and Gradient Management is a training optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces memory overhead during high-resolution rendering by organizing Gaussians into spatial groups (leaves) and using compact gradient storage. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption caused by maintaining full dense gradients for all Gaussians during the backward pass of large scenes. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling the gradient accumulation scope to leaf boundaries and using a global ID mapping to feed only necessary gradient rows into the Adam optimizer, while maintaining dense gradients for opacity to support global regularization. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients), camera views, and the current training step. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters via Adam optimizer, densification statistics based on accumulated screen gradients. Data Structures Compact ID Set (U): A deduplicated union of screened candidate Gaussian IDs across all active groups. ID Map: An int32 array of length N (total number of Gaussians) that maps global Gaussian IDs to indices in the compact gradient storage. Gradient Storage: Position, SH, Log Scale, Quaternion: Row-sparse gradients. Only rows corresponding to IDs in U are stored. Opacity: Dense gradient storage. All N opacity gradients are maintained because of the global regularization term. Adam State: Maintained in the standard dense layout (as inherited from ImprovedGS) to ensure compatibility with the optimizer's internal momentum tracking. Formulas 1. Leaf Loss (LR): LR = 0.8 L1R + 0.2 (1 - SSIMR) Where L1R is the L1 loss and SSIMR is the Structural Similarity Index Measure loss, computed over the leaf's own image region at its boundary. 2. View Objective (Lv): Lv = \frac{1}{HW} \sum{R \in Rv} \sum{P \in PR} LR + L{global} Where Rv is the set of all leaves for view v, PR are the pixels in leaf R, HW is the image height times width, and L{global} is the global regularization term. 3. Global Regularization (L{global}): L{global} = \frac{\betat}{|St|} \sum{i \in St} z{it} Where St is the current survivor set of Gaussians, z{it} is the pre-activation opacity parameter for Gaussian i at step t, and \betat is the coefficient following GNS's target-budget feedback. Parameters Global Regularization Coefficient (\beta{15K}): Starts at 0.002 during the 15K–19K pruning window. Opacity Learning Rate: Increases fivefold from 0.025 to 0.125 during the 15K–19K pruning window. Adam Optimizer: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999, \epsilon = 10^{-15}. Numbered Steps 1. Leaf Loss Computation: For each leaf R in the current view, compute LR using L1 and SSIM on the leaf's specific image region. 2. Global Regularization: If the current step is within the 15K–19K pruning window, compute L{global} using the current survivor set St and pre-activation opacities z{it}. Add this to the view objective. 3. Leaf Gradient Accumulation: For each leaf, compute the image gradient. Explicitly add this contribution to the group’s projected gradients. This is done per leaf. 4. Gradient Allocation: Immediately before projection backward, allocate parameter gradients. This step avoids coexistence with the current group’s earlier leaf state. 5. Projection Backward: Run projection backward once after all leaves in a group finish. This uses direct gradient accumulation of 3DGS, applies activation derivatives within CUDA, and maps contributions to final candidate gradient rows. 6. Compact Gradient Mapping: Feed the compact gradient rows through global IDs to the CUDA Adam optimizer. The ID map links global IDs to compact rows. 7. Adam Update: The CUDA Adam updates every Gaussian row. For rows outside the candidates (not in U), the current image gradient is zero, but first- and second-order momentum continue to update. 8. Densification Statistics: Accumulate screen gradients by global ID across all groups. Use these accumulated gradients to form each Gaussian’s densification statistic. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundedgsleaflossandgradientmanagement(gaussians, views, step, survivorset): """ Implements BoundedGS leaf loss and gradient management. gaussians: Object containing N Gaussians with attributes: pos, sh, logscale, quat, opacity, adamm1, adamm2 views: List of camera views step: Current training step survivorset: Set of Gaussian IDs currently surviving pruning """ # 1. Initialize structures # Compact ID set U: deduplicated union of screened candidates across groups # ID Map: int32 array of length N, mapping global ID to compact row index # Gradient storage: sparse for pos/sh/scale/quat, dense for opacity compactids = set() idmap = {} # globalid -> compactindex #... (Implementation details for building U and idmap based on group screening)... # 2. Process each view for view in views: viewloss = 0.0 leaves = getleavesforview(view) # Group Gaussians into spatial leaves # 2a. Compute Leaf Losses for leaf in leaves: # Compute L1 and SSIM on leaf's own image region at boundary l1r = computel1loss(leaf.renderedimage, leaf.targetimage) ssimr = computessimloss(leaf.renderedimage, leaf.targetimage) lr = 0.8 l1r + 0.2 (1 - ssimr) # Add to view objective (area weights restore full-image pixel mean for L1) # Note: Summation over pixels P in leaf R is handled internally by rasterization backward viewloss += lr # 3. Leaf Gradient Accumulation # Compute image gradient for this leaf leafgrad = computeimagegradient(leaf) # Add contribution to group's projected gradients # This is done explicitly per leaf addtogroupprojectedgradients(leaf.groupid, leafgrad) # Add leaf's Gaussian IDs to compact set for gid in leaf.gaussianids: compactids.add(gid) # 2b. Global Regularization (if in pruning window) if 15000 <= step <= 19000: betat = 0.002 # Starts at 0.002 # Lglobal = (betat / |St|) sum(zit for i in St) sumz = sum(gaussians.opacitypreactivation[i] for i in survivorset) lglobal = (betat / len(survivorset)) sumz viewloss += lglobal # Opacity learning rate adjustment is handled by optimizer config # lropacity = 0.125 during this window # 4. Gradient Allocation # Allocate parameter gradients immediately before projection backward # to avoid coexistence with current group's earlier leaf state allocategradients(compactids, idmap, gaussians) # 5. Projection Backward # Run once after all leaves in that group finish # Uses direct gradient accumulation of 3DGS # Applies activation derivatives within CUDA # Maps contributions to final candidate gradient rows runprojectionbackward(gaussians, idmap, compactids) # 6. Adam Update # Feed compact gradient rows through global IDs to CUDA Adam # Adam updates every Gaussian row for gid in range(gaussians.N): if gid in compactids: # Get compact gradient row compactidx = idmap[gid] grad = getcompactgradient(compactidx) else: # Row outside candidates has zero current image gradient grad = 0.0 # Momentum continues to update even if grad is zero updateadammoments(gaussians, gid, grad) # 7. Densification Statistics # View visibility is union of global IDs # Screen gradients accumulated by ID across groups accumulatescreengradientsbyid(gaussians, idmap, compactids) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The use of compact storage requires careful mapping between global IDs and compact rows to avoid misalignment. The int32 map must be accurate. Boundaries: Leaf loss is computed at the leaf's boundary. Incorrect boundary definition may lead to inaccurate loss gradients. Degenerate Input: If a leaf has no pixels or invalid geometry, the L1/SSIM computation should handle empty regions gracefully. Coexistence: Failing to allocate gradients immediately before projection backward may cause conflicts with earlier leaf states. Uses conditional logic for optimization steps. Choose when dynamic scene changes require adaptive rendering. Blends error metrics for densification. Choose when balanced detail and smoothness are needed. Integrates sparse matching for initialization. Choose when sparse data sources are available. Selects Gaussians adaptively. Choose when resource constraints vary per frame. Trains in chunks. Choose when memory is limited but batch size needs to be large. Guides splitting by edges. Choose when sharp features are critical. Standard configuration. Choose as a baseline. Time Complexity: The compact gradient storage reduces the number of gradients processed by Adam, potentially speeding up the update step. However, the overhead of building the compact ID set and mapping may add some CPU time. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduces memory usage for gradient storage by using row-sparse gradients for most parameters. Opacity retains dense gradients, which is a trade-off for global regularization. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with high-resolution training due to reduced memory footprint. Strengths: Memory efficiency, compatibility with standard Adam optimizer, support for global regularization. Limitations: Increased complexity in gradient mapping, potential overhead from ID management. When to use: High-resolution training, memory-constrained environments. When not to use: Simple scenes where memory is not a bottleneck, or when global regularization is not desired. BoundedGS was introduced in the paper "BoundedGS: Memory-Efficient High-Resolution Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting" (Deng et al., 2025). It builds on ImprovedGS and GNS (Gaussian Neural Splatting) techniques. The method addresses the memory limitations of standard 3DGS training by organizing Gaussians into leaves and using compact gradient storage. name: Adaptive Gaussian Refinement
head: 7DGS Adaptive Refinement, Residual Gaussian Adjustment
body: Adaptive Gaussian Refinement is a technique that dynamically adjusts Gaussian parameters using neural network-predicted residuals to improve the modeling of complex non-rigid deformations and time-varying appearance. It addresses the limitation of static covariance matrices in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which cannot adequately represent dynamic behaviors such as motion-induced shape changes. Unlike sibling methods that rely on gradient-based densification metrics (e.g., Adaptive Density Control) or MCMC sampling (e.g., 3DGS-MCMC), this method uses a lightweight neural network to predict continuous corrections to the Gaussian's spatial, temporal, directional, and covariance parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The base set of 7D Gaussian parameters for a primitive k: spatial mean \mup \in \mathbb{R}^3, temporal mean \mut \in \mathbb{R}, directional mean \mud \in \mathbb{R}^3, and the vectorized lower-triangular elements of the 7D covariance matrix l \in \mathbb{R}^{28}. The current time t is required for the temporal encoding. Output: Refined parameters \hat{\mu}p, \hat{\mu}t, \hat{\mu}d, \hat{l}. Data Structures: Feature Vector f: A concatenated vector formed by \mup, \mut, \mud, and a high-frequency temporal encoding \gamma(t). MLP: A small two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) with architecture C{in} \times 64 \times C{out}. Four such MLPs (\phip, \phit, \phid, \phil) predict residuals for position, time, direction, and covariance respectively. Steps: 1. Temporal Encoding: Compute the positional encoding for the current time t. The encoding \gamma(t) is defined as: \gamma(t) = [\sin(2^0 \pi t), \cos(2^0 \pi t), \dots, \sin(2^{K-1} \pi t), \cos(2^{K-1} \pi t)] where K=10. This results in a vector of size 2K = 20. 2. Feature Construction: Concatenate the spatial mean, temporal mean, directional mean, and the temporal encoding to form the input feature vector f: f = \mup \oplus \mut \oplus \mud \oplus \gamma(t) where \oplus denotes vector concatenation. The dimension C{in} is 3 + 1 + 3 + 20 = 27. 3. Residual Prediction: Pass f through the respective MLPs (\phip, \phit, \phid, \phil) to predict residual adjustments. Each MLP has a hidden layer of size 64. 4. Parameter Update: Add the predicted residuals to the original parameters to obtain the refined estimates: \hat{\mu}p = \mup + \phip(f) \hat{\mu}t = \mut + \phit(f) \hat{\mu}d = \mud + \phid(f) \hat{l} = l + \phil(f) Here, l represents the vectorized lower-triangular elements of the 7D covariance matrix. 5. Application: These refined parameters are used in subsequent rendering steps, specifically before the conditional slicing step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def temporalencoding(t, K=10): """ Computes the high-frequency temporal encoding gamma(t). Args: t: float, current time coordinate. K: int, number of frequency bands (default 10). Returns: np.array of shape (2K,) """ frequencies = np.power(2, np.arange(K)) sinvals = np.sin(2 np.pi frequencies t) cosvals = np.cos(2 np.pi frequencies t) return np.concatenate([sinvals, cosvals]) def mlppredict(x, W1, b1, W2, b2): """ Standard 2-layer MLP forward pass. Args: x: input vector W1, b1: first layer weights and biases W2, b2: second layer weights and biases Returns: residual vector """ h = np.maximum(0, x @ W1 + b1) # ReLU activation return h @ W2 + b2 def adaptivegaussianrefinement(mup, mut, mud, l, t, mlpparams): """ Applies adaptive refinement to 7D Gaussian parameters. Args: mup: np.array, shape (3,), spatial mean. mut: float, temporal mean. mud: np.array, shape (3,), directional mean. l: np.array, shape (28,), vectorized lower-triangular covariance elements. t: float, observed time. mlpparams: dict, containing 'W1p', 'b1p', 'W2p', 'b2p', etc. for phip, phit, phid, phil. Returns: tuple: (hatmup, hatmut, hatmud, hatl) """ # Step 1 & 2: Feature Construction gammat = temporalencoding(t, K=10) f = np.concatenate([mup, np.array([mut]), mud, gammat]) # Step 3 & 4: Residual Prediction and Update # Note: mlpparams contain the trained weights for the four MLPs resp = mlppredict(f, mlpparams['W1p'], mlpparams['b1p'], mlpparams['W2p'], mlpparams['b2p']) rest = mlppredict(f, mlpparams['W1t'], mlpparams['b1t'], mlpparams['W2t'], mlpparams['b2t']) resd = mlppredict(f, mlpparams['W1d'], mlpparams['b1d'], mlpparams['W2d'], mlpparams['b2d']) resl = mlppredict(f, mlpparams['W1l'], mlpparams['b1l'], mlpparams['W2l'], mlpparams['b2l']) hatmup = mup + resp hatmut = mut + rest hatmud = mud + resd hatl = l + resl return hatmup, hatmut, hatmud, hatl Parameters: K=10: Number of frequency bands in the temporal encoding. MLP Hidden Size: 64. MLP Architecture: Two layers (C{in} \to 64 \to C{out}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Covariance Reconstruction: The refined covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma} is reconstructed from \hat{l} as \hat{\Sigma} = \hat{L}\hat{L}^\top (where \hat{L} is the lower-triangular matrix from \hat{l}). Training Dependency: The method requires training the MLPs alongside the Gaussians, and the residuals are added directly to the vectorized covariance elements, which requires careful handling of numerical stability during optimization. Computational Cost: Adds the cost of four MLP forward passes per Gaussian per frame. The MLPs are small (C{in} \times 64 \times C{out}). Memory: Requires storing the MLP weights. The number of parameters is small: 27 \times 64 + 64 \times C{out} per MLP. Strengths: Enables accurate modeling of complex non-rigid deformations and time-varying appearance without increasing the number of Gaussians. Limitations: Requires training the MLPs alongside the Gaussians and is specific to 7D Gaussian Splatting without direct application to static 3DGS. Adaptive Gaussian Refinement was introduced in the 7DGS (Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting) paper. It was developed to address the static nature of 3D Gaussian covariances, which limits their ability to represent dynamic scenes with non-rigid deformations. The method builds on the idea of using neural networks to predict residuals, a technique seen in other neural rendering contexts, but applies it specifically to the parameters of 7D Gaussians. 7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07946v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hybrid and Diffusion Representations
head: TriplaneGaussian, GaussianDiffusion, Text2Immersion, Atomic-Continuous Prior
body: This family addresses the problem of generating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from single images, text, or sparse inputs without relying on iterative per-scene optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Densification and Splitting by replacing iterative gradient-based refinement with learned generative priors, either through hybrid feature grids or diffusion models, enabling near-real-time generation. All methods in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by a mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k [Parent]. Unlike iterative optimization, these methods predict Gaussian attributes directly from a conditioning signal (image, text, or noise) using a neural network. The core mechanism involves mapping the conditioning signal to a structured intermediate representation (such as a tri-plane grid or a voxelized GaussianCube) which is then decoded into the final Gaussian set. TriplaneGaussian is a feed-forward method for generating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from a single input image. It solves the problem of direct 3D generation by employing a hybrid representation that combines a sparse point cloud with a dense tri-plane feature grid. Unlike sibling methods that rely on iterative optimization or multi-view consistency constraints (e.g., GaussianDiffusion), TriplaneGaussian directly predicts Gaussian attributes via a transformer-based decoder, leveraging the structural priors of tri-planes to ensure geometric consistency. Inputs: A single RGB image I. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by mean position \muk, covariance \Sigmak (scale sk, rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. Data Structures: 1. Tri-plane: Three 2D feature grids Tx, Ty, Tz \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W} encoding 3D spatial attributes. The dimensions C, H, W are hyperparameters of the decoder. 2. Point Cloud: A set of 3D points P = \{p1, \dots, pM\} representing initial Gaussian centers. 3. MLP: A multi-layer perceptron mapping augmented features to Gaussian attributes. Steps: 1. Image Encoding: The input image I is processed by a vision encoder to extract image features F{img}. 2. Hybrid Generation: A transformer-based architecture generates two components in parallel: A coarse point cloud P via a point cloud decoder. A tri-plane feature grid T = \{Tx, Ty, Tz\} via a tri-plane decoder. 3. Densification: The coarse point cloud P is upsampled using an upsampling method to increase density M. 4. Feature Querying: For each point pk \in P, its 3D coordinates are projected onto the three planes of T. Features are sampled from Tx, Ty, Tz at these projected locations and aggregated to form a point-specific feature vector fk. 5. Feature Augmentation: The queried feature fk is augmented by projecting the image features F{img} onto the point pk (or using pk to sample F{img}) to obtain augmented features f'k. 6. Attribute Prediction: The augmented features f'k are passed through an MLP to predict the final Gaussian attributes: \muk, sk, qk, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triplanegaussiangenerate(image: Tensor) -> List[Gaussian]: # 1. Encode image Fimg = visionencoder(image) # 2. Generate hybrid representation # Point cloud decoder outputs initial centers Pcoarse = pointclouddecoder(Fimg) # Tri-plane decoder outputs 3 feature grids T = triplanedecoder(Fimg) # 3. Densify point cloud P = upsamplingmethod(Pcoarse) gaussians = [] for p in P: # 4. Query tri-plane features # Project 3D point p onto XY, YZ, XZ planes # Sample features from T at projected coordinates ftriplane = querytriplane(T, p) # 5. Augment with image features # Project p to 2D image space to sample Fimg fimg = projectandsample(Fimg, p) faugmented = concatenate(ftriplane, fimg) # 6. Predict attributes attrs = mlp(faugmented) gaussians.append(Gaussian(attrs)) return gaussians Parameters: Tri-plane resolution (H, W): Not given in the sources. Tri-plane channels (C): Not given in the sources. Upsampling factor: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The projection of 3D points to 2D planes and image space requires accurate coordinate transformation matrices. Boundaries: Points outside the camera frustum or tri-plane domain must be handled during querying. GaussianDiffusion is a method that trains a 3D diffusion model based on a GaussianCube representation to generate 3D Gaussian primitives directly from conditioning signals. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency (the "Janus problem") and spurious geometry ("floaters") common in single-view or text-to-3D generation by incorporating structured noise from multiple viewpoints and using variational 3DGS. Unlike iterative optimization methods, it amortizes generation cost over a trained network, enabling near-real-time sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Conditioning signal (e.g., text, single image). Output: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by mean \muk, covariance \Sigmak (scale sk, rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. Data Structures: GaussianCube: A structured grid representation created by converting a constant number of Gaussians into a voxelized format via optimal transport. This fixed-size representation allows the diffusion model to process the unstructured Gaussian set as a dense 3D volume. Steps: 1. Representation Conversion: Convert the input or intermediate set of 3D Gaussians into a GaussianCube using voxelization via optimal transport. 2. Diffusion Process: Train a 3D diffusion model on GaussianCube representations. During inference, the model denoises a latent GaussianCube to predict the target geometry. 3. Structured Noise Incorporation: Incorporate structured noise from multiple viewpoints during the diffusion process to enforce multi-view consistency and alleviate the Janus problem. 4. Variational Refinement: Apply variational 3DGS techniques to the generated Gaussians to mitigate floaters and improve generation quality. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The difference between the diffusion prior and the training process of the diffusion model can impair generation quality. Single-step reconstruction can suffer from high error if not properly supervised. Definition: A scene generation method similar to LucidDreamer but with outlier removal and two-stage optimization. Steps: A process removes outliers in the point cloud. 3DGS optimization has two stages: training coarse 3DGS and refinement. Definition: A probabilistic prior for VDB volumes that models the data as a mixture of a discrete atomic component (exact zeros for empty space) and a continuous component (real density values). It solves the problem where plain Gaussian diffusion smooths away faint wisps and leaks density into empty regions due to the mix of exact zeros and heavy-tailed densities. Steps: Amplitude companding: Apply a reversible log mapping to rebalance the training signal. This boosts the gradient on faint, low-density structures by a factor of (1 + \lambda\tilde{x})^{-1} to prevent thin wisps from being smoothed away. Atomic mass supervision: Enforce sparsity by using a soft occupancy target to recover coarse shape and applying a leakage penalty that pushes density to exactly zero outside the boundary. Temporal conditioning (for sequences): Stack the previous frame onto the input as an extra channel. The network learns motion from this concatenated input without using 4D attention. Formula: p(x) = \pi0\delta0(x) + (1-\pi0)p{ac}(x), where \pi0 is the probability mass at zero, \delta0(x) is the Dirac delta function at zero, and p{ac}(x) is the continuous probability density function for non-zero values. The need for hybrid and diffusion representations arises from the limitations of iterative optimization methods like Densification and Splitting, which are computationally expensive and require multi-view inputs or extensive tuning for single-view generation. TriplaneGaussian and GaussianDiffusion represent a shift towards feed-forward and generative approaches, respectively, to achieve real-time 3D scene synthesis. Text2Immersion and Atomic-Continuous Prior address specific artifacts such as outliers and VDB-specific sparsity issues in generated volumes. name: TriplaneGaussian
body: TriplaneGaussian is a feed-forward method for generating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from a single input image. It solves the problem of single-image 3D reconstruction by proposing a hybrid representation that combines a point cloud with a tri-plane encoding of Gaussian attributes. Unlike iterative optimization methods that refine a random initialization, TriplaneGaussian directly predicts the Gaussian set from image features using a transformer-based point cloud decoder and a tri-plane decoder. It is distinguished from its sibling GaussianDiffusion by its deterministic, non-diffusion-based architecture that explicitly decouples point cloud generation from attribute encoding via tri-planes. Inputs: A single RGB image I. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by mean position \muk, covariance \Sigmak (scale sk, rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k [Parent]. Data Structures: 1. Tri-plane: A set of three 2D feature grids T{xy}, T{yz}, T{xz}, each of resolution R \times R and channel depth C. These encode the spatial attributes of the Gaussians. 2. Point Cloud: A set of 3D points P = \{p1, \dots, pM\} representing the initial centers of the Gaussians. 3. MLP: A multi-layer perceptron that maps augmented features to Gaussian attributes. Steps: 1. Image Feature Extraction: Extract features from the input image I using a backbone network (e.g., ViT or ResNet) to produce image features F{img}. 2. Point Cloud Generation: Pass F{img} through a transformer-based point cloud decoder to generate a coarse point cloud P{coarse}. 3. Tri-plane Generation: Pass F{img} through a tri-plane decoder to generate the tri-plane feature grids T = \{T{xy}, T{yz}, T{xz}\}. 4. Point Cloud Densification: Upsample P{coarse} using an upsampling method to increase the number of points to N, resulting in P{dense}. 5. Feature Querying: For each point pk \in P{dense}, project its 3D coordinates onto the three tri-plane axes to query features from T{xy}, T{yz}, T{xz}. Let the queried features be f{tri}(pk). 6. Feature Augmentation: Augment the queried tri-plane features with the projected image features corresponding to the viewpoint of pk. Let the projected image features be f{img}(pk). The augmented feature is f{aug}(pk) = \text{Concat}(f{tri}(pk), f{img}(pk)). 7. Attribute Prediction: Pass f{aug}(pk) through an MLP to predict the Gaussian attributes for each point: \muk, sk, qk, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k. 8. Output: The set of predicted Gaussians \mathcal{G} is returned. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TriplaneGaussian(image: Tensor) -> List[Gaussian]: # 1. Extract image features Fimg = ImageFeatureExtractor(image) # 2. Generate coarse point cloud Pcoarse = TransformerPointCloudDecoder(Fimg) # 3. Generate tri-plane features T = TriPlaneDecoder(Fimg) # 4. Densify point cloud Pdense = Upsample(Pcoarse) # 5. Query tri-plane features for each point # Note: Projection assumes a known camera pose or uses the input image's pose # If pose is unknown, this step may require estimation or assumes a canonical view features = [] for p in Pdense: # Query tri-plane at point p ftri = QueryTriPlane(T, p) # Project image features to point p's location # This requires mapping 3D point to 2D image coordinates fimg = ProjectImageFeatures(Fimg, p) # Augment features faug = Concatenate(ftri, fimg) features.append(faug) # 6. Predict Gaussian attributes gaussians = [] for faug in features: attrs = MLP(faug) gaussians.append(CreateGaussian(attrs)) return gaussians Parameters: Tri-plane resolution R: Not given in the sources. Tri-plane channel depth C: Not given in the sources. Upsampling factor: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Camera Pose: The method assumes the input image's camera pose is known or can be estimated to project image features onto the 3D points. If the pose is incorrect, the feature augmentation will be misaligned. Densification Quality: The quality of the final Gaussian set depends heavily on the upsampling method used to densify the point cloud. Poor upsampling may lead to redundant or missing Gaussians. Tri-plane Querying: Accurate querying of the tri-plane features requires precise interpolation and handling of out-of-bounds coordinates. This method is a 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering technique that adaptively selects between 2D and 3D Gaussian primitives based on local geometric cues to reduce redundancy in planar structures while maintaining volumetric accuracy. It integrates TensoSDF for global geometric consistency, enforcing implicit surface constraints during optimization. Unlike standard 3DGS which uses only 3D ellipsoids, or 2DGS which uses only tangent planes, this method dynamically switches representations to better fit both thin surfaces and volumetric details. It builds on TriplaneGaussian by introducing explicit geometry-guided constraints via TensoSDF rather than relying solely on tri-plane initialization. Volume-Based Densification is a refinement strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces or supplements gradient-based Adaptive Density Control (ADC) with geometric volume analysis to manage primitive density. It solves the failure of traditional ADC in high-frequency, sparse regions (e.g., grass, wires) where positional gradients are insufficient to trigger densification, and where uncontrolled Gaussian growth leads to blurred artifacts. Unlike its sibling Hybrid Gaussian Representation with Geometry-Guided Constraints which uses geometry-guided constraints, this method specifically leverages the ellipsoid volume and covariance condition number to drive cloning and splitting decisions. Phys3DGS is a physically-based inverse rendering method that resolves the "hidden Gaussian" problem, where Gaussians beneath the surface adversely affect pixel color in volume rendering, by employing deferred rendering and a mesh-3DGS hybrid representation ]. It differs from standard relightable 3DGS methods by decoupling geometry estimation from material learning via a two-step training process, and from naive deferred approaches by introducing specific regularizations to stabilize BRDF learning and prevent mesh extraction artifacts ]. FDGaussian injects tri-plane features into the diffusion model for better geometry generation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Direct generation from a single image without iterative optimization. Hybrid representation allows for detailed attribute encoding. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the point cloud upsampling and tri-plane querying. Requires known or estimated camera pose for feature projection. When to Use: When fast, single-image 3DGS generation is required and iterative optimization is too slow. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity multi-view consistency is required without additional refinement. TriplaneGaussian was proposed in the paper "Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting". It is part of the broader effort to generate 3D Gaussian Splatting representations directly from single images, avoiding the need for multi-view inputs or iterative optimization. The method builds on the concept of using tri-planes for efficient 3D feature representation. name: Hybrid Gaussian Representation with Geometry-Guided Constraints
head: Adaptive Hybrid Representation and TensoSDF Constraints, Hybrid Gaussian Splatting with Geometry Guidance

This method is a 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering technique that adaptively selects between 2D and 3D Gaussian primitives based on local geometric cues to reduce redundancy in planar structures while maintaining volumetric accuracy. It integrates TensoSDF for global geometric consistency, enforcing implicit surface constraints during optimization. Unlike standard 3DGS which uses only 3D ellipsoids, or 2DGS which uses only tangent planes, this method dynamically switches representations to better fit both thin surfaces and volumetric details. It builds on TriplaneGaussian by introducing explicit geometry-guided constraints via TensoSDF rather than relying solely on tri-plane initialization. Inputs: Input point cloud (for initialization and surface normals). Camera poses and images for training. Bounding box definition (default: 1m³). Outputs: Optimized hybrid Gaussian field (mix of 2D and 3D Gaussians). Optimized TensoSDF tensor factors. TensoSDF Tensor Factors Ax \in \mathbb{R}^{Nx 	imes r}, Ay \in \mathbb{R}^{Ny 	imes r}, Az \in \mathbb{R}^{Nz 	imes r}. Parameters: Nx=Ny=Nz=128, r=32. 	au: Curvature threshold for initial type selection. 	au1: Gradient magnitude threshold for flat geometry detection (	au1 = 0.1). 	au2: SDF value threshold for proximity to surface (	au2 = 0.05 m). \eta: Update step size for Gaussian position fine-tuning. \lambda: Weight for gradient consistency in TensoSDF loss (\lambda = 10). AR Threshold: Anisotropy Ratio threshold for conversion (AR < 0.2). \sigman: Small variance added during 2D-to-3D conversion (\sigman = 10^{-4}). N{neigh}: Number of neighbors for 2D-to-3D angle check (N{neigh} = 10). 	heta{thresh}: Mean angle threshold for 2D-to-3D conversion (30^\circ). 1. Initialization: Establish a complete 3D Gaussian ellipsoidal field based on the input point cloud following the standard 3DGS workflow. Initialize TensoSDF tensor factors Ax, Ay, Az with random values from \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01). 2. Curvature Estimation (Initial Type Selection): For each 3D Gaussian center \mu, perform PCA on the local point cluster to extract eigenvalues \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 of the cluster covariance matrix. Calculate local curvature: \kappa = (\lambda2 + \lambda3) / \lambda1. If \kappa < 	au, convert the 3D Gaussian to a 2D Gaussian (see Step 3). If AR(\mu) < 0.2, convert to 2D Gaussian using the initialization logic in Step 3. 5. Compute mean angle  ar{	heta} between n and neighbors' normals ni:  ar{	heta} =  rac{1}{N{neigh}} \sum{i=1}^{N{neigh}} \arccos\left(  rac{n \cdot ni}{\|n\| \|ni\|} ight). Training: Optimize TensoSDF tensor factors and Gaussian field parameters (positions, covariances, opacities, colors) in parallel. Compute rendering loss (e.g., L1/SSIM) between rendered and input images. Compute TensoSDF loss \mathcal{L}{SDF} (see Formulas). coords: shape (N, 3) or (3,) # grid: shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, r) # Returns interpolated values at coords # Implementation uses fractional part extraction and weighted sum of 8 corners. # Omitted for brevity as it is a standard grid operation. pass def computesdf(coords, Ax, Ay, Az): """Compute SDF value using CP decomposition.""" # Ax, Ay, Az shape: (Nx, r), (Ny, r), (Nz, r) # Interpolate each factor at x, y, z coordinates valx = trilinearinterpolate(Ax, coords[:, 0:1]) # shape (N, r) valy = trilinearinterpolate(Ay, coords[:, 1:2]) valz = trilinearinterpolate(Az, coords[:, 2:3]) # CP sum sdf = np.sum(valx valy valz, axis=1) return sdf def computesdfgradient(coords, Ax, Ay, Az): """Compute gradient of SDF via partial derivatives of tensor factors.""" # Compute dF/dx, dF/dy, dF/dz using trilinear derivatives gradx = np.sum(trilinearinterpgrad(Ax, coords[:, 0:1], axis=0) trilinearinterpolate(Ay, coords[:, 1:2]) trilinearinterpolate(Az, coords[:, 2:3]), axis=1) grady = np.sum(trilinearinterpolate(Ax, coords[:, 0:1]) trilinearinterpgrad(Ay, coords[:, 1:2], axis=1) trilinearinterpolate(Az, coords[:, 2:3]), axis=1) gradz = np.sum(trilinearinterpolate(Ax, coords[:, 0:1]) trilinearinterpolate(Ay, coords[:, 1:2]) trilinearinterpgrad(Az, coords[:, 2:3], axis=2), axis=1) return np.stack([gradx, grady, gradz], axis=1) def pcalocalcluster(points): """Perform PCA on local point cluster.""" cov = np.cov(points.T) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] return eigenvalues[idx], eigenvectors[:, idx] def gramschmidt(v1, v2): """Orthogonalize v2 against v1.""" u = v2 - np.dot(v2, v1) v1 return u / np.linalg.norm(u) def init2dgaussian(mu, eigenvalues, eigenvectors): """Initialize 2D Gaussian from PCA results.""" n = eigenvectors[:, 2] randomvec = np.random.rand(3) if np.abs(np.dot(randomvec, n)) > 0.9: randomvec = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) t1 = np.cross(n, randomvec) t1 = t1 / np.linalg.norm(t1) t2 = np.cross(n, t1) T = np.columnstack((t1, t2)) sigmap = 0.1 # Appropriate initial value Lambda = np.diag([sigmap2, sigmap2]) return T, Lambda, n def rodriguesrotation(g, vmax): """Compute rotation matrix R(g) aligning vmax to g.""" costheta = np.clip(np.dot(vmax, g), -1.0, 1.0) sintheta = np.sqrt(1 - costheta2) if sintheta < 1e-6: return np.eye(3) g = g / np.linalg.norm(g) gx = np.array([[0, -g[2], g[1]], [g[2], 0, -g[0]], [-g[1], g[0], 0]]) R = costheta np.eye(3) + (1 - costheta) np.outer(g, g) + sintheta gx return R def convert3dto2d(gaussian, pointcloudcluster, tau): """Convert 3D Gaussian to 2D if curvature is low.""" eigenvalues, eigenvectors = pcalocalcluster(pointcloudcluster) kappa = (eigenvalues[1] + eigenvalues[2]) / eigenvalues[0] if kappa < tau: T, Lambda, n = init2dgaussian(gaussian.mu, eigenvalues, eigenvectors) gaussian.type = '2D' gaussian.T = T gaussian.Lambda = Lambda gaussian.n = n return True return False def convert3dto2dadaptive(gaussian, F, tau1, tau2): """Adaptive conversion based on TensoSDF cues.""" mu = gaussian.mu d = F(mu) if np.abs(d) < tau2: grad = computesdfgradient(mu,...) # Requires full F impl gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(grad) if gradnorm < tau1: eigenvalues = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(gaussian.Sigma))[::-1] AR = np.min(eigenvalues) / np.max(eigenvalues) if AR < 0.2: n = grad / gradnorm randomvec = np.random.rand(3) if np.abs(np.dot(randomvec, n)) > 0.9: randomvec = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) t1 = np.cross(n, randomvec) t1 = t1 / np.linalg.norm(t1) t2 = np.cross(n, t1) T = np.columnstack((t1, t2)) sigmap = 0.1 Lambda = np.diag([sigmap2, sigmap2]) gaussian.type = '2D' gaussian.T = T gaussian.Lambda = Lambda gaussian.n = n return True return False def convert2dto3d(gaussian, neighbors): """Convert 2D Gaussian to 3D if normals are inconsistent.""" n = gaussian.n angles = [] for neighbor in neighbors: ni = neighbor.n costheta = np.dot(n, ni) / (np.linalg.norm(n) np.linalg.norm(ni)) angles.append(np.arccos(np.clip(costheta, -1.0, 1.0))) meanangle = np.mean(angles) if meanangle > np.deg2rad(30): randomvec = np.random.rand(3) if np.abs(np.dot(randomvec, n)) > 0.9: randomvec = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) t1 = np.cross(n, randomvec) t1 = t1 / np.linalg.norm(t1) t2 = np.cross(n, t1) R = np.columnstack((t1, t2, n)) Lambda3d = np.zeros((3, 3)) Lambda3d[:2,:2] = gaussian.Lambda sigman = 1e-4 Sigmanew = R @ Lambda3d @ R.T + 2 (sigman2) np.outer(n, n) gaussian.type = '3D' gaussian.Sigma = Sigmanew return True return False def finetunegaussian(gaussian, F, eta): """Fine-tune Gaussian position and covariance using TensoSDF.""" mu = gaussian.mu d = F(mu) grad = computesdfgradient(mu,...) gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(grad) if gradnorm < 1e-8: return g = grad / gradnorm gaussian.mu = mu - eta d g eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(gaussian.Sigma) vmax = eigenvectors[:, np.argmax(eigenvalues)] R = rodriguesrotation(g, vmax) gaussian.Sigma = R @ gaussian.Sigma @ R.T Time and Memory Complexity: The method introduces additional storage overhead for TensoSDF tensor factors (Ax, Ay, Az) and potentially more Gaussian primitives due to adaptive conversion. On the Mip-NeRF dataset, average memory consumption increased from 734MB (3DGS) to 845MB (proposed method), an increase of ~15.1%. Increases of 16.1% and 18.2% were observed on DeepBlending and Tanks&Temples datasets respectively. Training requires parallel optimization of Gaussian parameters and TensoSDF factors, adding computational cost per iteration. Measured Performance: On NeRF-synthetic dataset, the method attained an average PSNR improvement of 6.1% over 3DGS. Outperforms 3DGS in global geometric consistency and reconstruction performance for highly reflective materials. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces redundancy in planar/thin structures; improves geometric consistency via TensoSDF; handles specular reflections better (Specular Module ablation shows significant enhancement). Limitations: Suboptimal performance in highly transparent environments. Increased memory usage compared to standard 3DGS. When to Use: Scenes with significant planar or thin structures where 3DGS redundancy is high. Applications requiring high geometric accuracy and consistency. Scenes with reflective materials. When Not to Use: Highly transparent environments. Memory-constrained applications where the 15-18% overhead is unacceptable. Origin: Proposed by Yanshan Zhang, Luyao Wang, and Yuanzhang Fan in 2026. Published in the 2026 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Computational Intelligence (AICI 2026). History and Development: Builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). Integrates TensoSDF, a tensor-based Signed Distance Function representation, to provide geometric constraints. Addresses limitations of 3DGS in balancing planar and volumetric structures and achieving global geometric consistency. Usage: High-precision 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. Real-time 3D reconstruction and rendering. Virtual reality, augmented reality, digital twins, and film special effects. name: Volume-Based Densification
head: Ellipsoid’s volume-driven density control, Volume driven densification strategy
body: Volume-Based Densification is a refinement strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces or supplements gradient-based Adaptive Density Control (ADC) with geometric volume analysis to manage primitive density. It solves the failure of traditional ADC in high-frequency, sparse regions (e.g., grass, wires) where positional gradients are insufficient to trigger densification, and where uncontrolled Gaussian growth leads to blurred artifacts. Unlike its sibling Hybrid Gaussian Representation with Geometry-Guided Constraints which uses geometry-guided constraints, this method specifically leverages the ellipsoid volume and covariance condition number to drive cloning and splitting decisions. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}, each defined by mean position \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Volume threshold V0 (typical value: 0.03). Maximum point count limit N{max} (typical value: 34,000,000). Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives with refined density in high-volume regions. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Contains \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite), \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and feature vectors. Covariance Matrix: Defined as \Sigma = N\sigma^2 + P, where N is the rotation matrix and P handles the structural transformation. Formulas: 1. Eigenvalues: Compute eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 of \Sigma such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 > 0. 2. Volume: The volume of the ellipsoid is calculated as: V = \frac{4}{3}\pi \sqrt{\det(\Sigma)} = \frac{4}{3}\pi \sqrt{\lambda1 \lambda2 \lambda3} 3. Condition Number: \kappa(\Sigma) = \frac{\lambda{max}(\Sigma)}{\lambda{min}(\Sigma)} = \frac{\lambda1}{\lambda3} Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (Deep Image Matching): Replace the traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipeline with a deep learning-based framework to generate the initial point cloud. Use SuperPoint as the feature extractor and LightGlue as the feature matcher to construct a robust initial point cloud with higher coverage in sparse regions. 2. Volume Calculation: For each Gaussian primitive Gi, calculate its volume Vi using the formula above. 3. Candidate Identification: Identify primitives where Vi > V0. These are considered "high-volume" candidates for densification. 4. Condition Number Adjustment: For each candidate Gi, calculate \kappa(\Sigmai). Adjust the standard deviations of the Gaussian by dividing them by \kappa(\Sigmai) to obtain smaller standard deviations for newly generated points. 5. Sampling: Generate new sample points around the mean \mui of the candidate primitives using the adjusted standard deviations and the means, considering the volume of the primitives which reflects the spread of the Gaussian distribution. Sample from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mui, \Sigma'{adj}) where \Sigma'{adj} reflects the adjusted spread. The number of new points generated per candidate is not explicitly defined in the sources, but implies creating "additional samples". 6. Transformation and Property Assignment: Apply the rotation and scaling transformations to the newly generated points based on the original primitive's parameters. Compute new properties for the new points, including scaling, rotation, and features. 7. Replacement: Replace the original high-volume points (candidates) with the newly generated points. 8. Pruning: Prune the unused points. 9. Capacity Check: Impose a ceiling on the number of points generated during training, capping this value at N{max} to manage computational resources. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def volumebaseddensification(primitives, V0=0.03, Nmax=34000000): """ Performs volume-based densification on a list of Gaussian primitives. """ newprimitives = [] candidates = [] for p in primitives: # Reconstruct covariance matrix Sigma = R diag(sigma^2) R^T # Note: Source defines Sigma = Nsigma^2 + P, assuming N is rotation and P handles translation/structure # Standard 3DGS covariance: Sigma = R S S^T R^T S = [[p.sigma[0]2, 0, 0], [0, p.sigma[1]2, 0], [0, 0, p.sigma[2]2]] Sigma = matmul(p.R, matmul(S, mattranspose(p.R))) # Calculate eigenvalues (standard 3x3 eigenvalue decomposition) eigenvalues = eigenvalues3x3(Sigma) eigenvalues.sort(reverse=True) lambdamax = eigenvalues[0] lambdamin = eigenvalues[2] # Calculate Volume detSigma = eigenvalues[0] eigenvalues[1] eigenvalues[2] volume = (4.0 / 3.0) math.pi math.sqrt(detSigma) if volume > V0: # Calculate Condition Number kappa = lambdamax / lambdamin # Adjust standard deviations adjustedsigma = [p.sigma[0] / kappa, p.sigma[1] / kappa, p.sigma[2] / kappa] candidates.append({ 'parent': p, 'adjustedsigma': adjustedsigma, 'mu': p.mu, 'R': p.R, 'kappa': kappa }) pointstoadd = [] for cand in candidates: p = cand['parent'] adjsigma = cand['adjustedsigma'] mu = cand['mu'] R = cand['R'] # Generate samples from Normal distribution using adjusted sigma # We generate 2 new points to replace the parent (cloning) numsamples = 2 for in range(numsamples): # Sigmaadj = R diag(adjsigma^2) R^T Sadj = [[adjsigma[0]2, 0, 0], [0, adjsigma[1]2, 0], [0, 0, adjsigma[2]2]] Sigmaadj = matmul(R, matmul(Sadj, mattranspose(R))) newmu = multivariatenormalsample(mu, Sigmaadj) newp = GaussianPrimitive( mu=newmu, sigma=adjsigma, R=R, alpha=p.alpha, features=p.features) pointstoadd.append(newp) # Remove candidates from the original list candidateids = [id(c['parent']) for c in candidates] remainingprimitives = [p for p in primitives if id(p) not in candidateids] # Add new points allprimitives = remainingprimitives + pointstoadd # Enforce Max Point Count if len(allprimitives) > Nmax: allprimitives = pruneprimitives(allprimitives, Nmax) return allprimitives def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k] B[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def mattranspose(M): return [[M[j][i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def eigenvalues3x3(M): # Standard 3x3 eigenvalue decomposition # Returns sorted eigenvalues descending import numpy as np return sorted(np.linalg.eigvalsh(M), reverse=True) def multivariatenormalsample(mean, cov): # Standard multivariate normal sampling import numpy as np return np.random.multivariatenormal(mean, cov) def pruneprimitives(prims, limit): # Sort by opacity ascending, remove lowest until limit reached prims.sort(key=lambda p: p.alpha) return prims[len(prims)-limit:] class GaussianPrimitive: def init(self, mu, sigma, R, alpha, features): self.mu = mu self.sigma = sigma self.R = R self.alpha = alpha self.features = features Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CUDA Out-of-Memory: Setting V0 too low causes excessive densification in dense regions, leading to OOM errors. Sparse Regions: In regions with sparse textures (e.g., grass), traditional SfM fails to provide sufficient initial points, leading to uncontrolled Gaussian growth and blurring. This method mitigates this by using deep image matching for initialization and volume-based densification. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives N and the cost of eigenvalue decomposition for each candidate. Eigenvalue decomposition of a 3 \times 3 matrix is constant time, so the overhead per primitive is O(1). Total densification step is O(N). Memory Complexity: Increases with the number of generated points. Capped at N{max} = 34 million points. Performance: Evaluated on NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU. Achieves state-of-the-art performance on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending datasets. Strengths: Better handling of high-frequency, sparse regions (grass, wires) compared to gradient-based ADC. Prevents uncontrolled growth of Gaussian volumes in sparse areas. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of V0. May increase memory usage if not capped. Origin: Introduced in "Refining Gaussian Splatting: A Volumetric Densification Approach" (2025). Development: The method addresses limitations of Adaptive Density Control (ADC) in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically its failure in high-frequency regions and lack of maximum point count control. It builds upon the existing splitting and cloning methods but introduces volume and condition number as primary criteria. Usage: Used in experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending datasets. name: Phys3DGS
head: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering
body: Phys3DGS is a physically-based inverse rendering method that resolves the "hidden Gaussian" problem, where Gaussians beneath the surface adversely affect pixel color in volume rendering, by employing deferred rendering and a mesh-3DGS hybrid representation. It differs from standard relightable 3DGS methods by decoupling geometry estimation from material learning via a two-step training process, and from naive deferred approaches by introducing specific regularizations to stabilize BRDF learning and prevent mesh extraction artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images. Outputs: A hybrid scene representation consisting of a mesh and associated 3D Gaussians, with learned PBR parameters (albedo \mathcal{A}, metalness \mathcal{M}, roughness \mathcal{R}, normal \mathcal{N}) and baked visibility for real-time relighting. Data Structures: Each 3D Gaussian i in the hybrid representation stores: Center coordinate \mui. Opacity \alphai. Scale si (and 3D covariance \Sigmai derived from scale and rotation). Spherical Harmonics (SH) parameters for view-dependent color. Normal vector \mathbf{n}i. BRDF parameters: Albedo \mathbf{a}i, metalness mi, roughness ri. Visibility parameters (SH coefficients for indirect illumination, used during training and baked post-training). The hybrid representation binds one 3D Gaussian to each triangle of an extracted mesh. Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Training: Train a vanilla 3DGS model [4] on the input images. 2. Opacity Culling: Remove low-opacity Gaussians from the initial model. 3. SDF Regularization: Apply Signed Distance Function (SDF)-based regularization to the remaining Gaussians to flatten them and push their centers toward the implicit surface. This step may cause Gaussians near the surface to grow abnormally large, leading to large triangles in mesh extraction and visibility test interference. Mitigate with Masked Opacity Regularization (Lo) to constrain opacity near the surface. The exact formula for Lo is not fully provided in the sources. 4. Mesh Extraction: Extract a triangular mesh from the regularized 3DGS model. 5. Hybrid Representation Construction: Assign one 3D Gaussian to each triangle of the extracted mesh. 6. Two-Step PBR Training: Train PBR-related parameters on the hybrid representation using a two-step approach. Step 6a learns geometry and base PBR parameters. Step 6b refines the parameters. Deferred Rendering Pipeline (Inference/Training): For each pixel (ray): 1. Estimate Depth: Calculate the estimated depth \mathcal{D} to the surface by weighted summation of opacity and distance for all Gaussians i intersecting the ray: \mathcal{D} = \sum{i \in N} Ti \alphai di where Ti is the transmittance up to Gaussian i, \alphai is the opacity, and di is the distance from the camera center to Gaussian i. 2. Estimate Surface Properties: Calculate the estimated normal \mathcal{N} and BRDF parameters (Albedo \mathcal{A}, Metalness \mathcal{M}, Roughness \mathcal{R}) using the same weighted summation: \{\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{N}\} = \sum{i \in N} Ti \alphai \{\mathbf{a}i, mi, ri, \mathbf{n}i\} where \mathbf{a}i, mi, ri, \mathbf{n}i are the per-Gaussian albedo, metalness, roughness, and normal. 3. Lighting Calculation: Perform Fibonacci sampling on incoming light directions \omegai. Compute Global Illumination L{global}(\omegai) using Spherical Harmonics (SH) approximation. Compute Local Indirect Illumination L{local}(\omegai) using SH parameters stored on each Gaussian, aggregated at the estimated surface point similarly to Eqn. 3. Determine Visibility V(\omegai): During Training: Compute visibility via ray tracing using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH), detached from back-propagation. Post-Training (Baking): Bake the visibility onto each Gaussian and replace the SH coefficients of indirect illumination with the SH coefficients of the baked visibility to reduce model size and boost test-time speed. Combine lighting: L(\omegai) = V(\omegai) \cdot L{global}(\omegai) + L{local}(\omegai) 4. Rendering Equation: Solve the rendering equation once at the estimated surface point using the estimated BRDF parameters and the computed incoming light L(\omegai) to obtain the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phys3dgsrender(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, bakedvisibilitymap, globalshcoeffs, usebvh=False, bvh=None): # 1. Filter and sort gaussians by distance to camera intersecting = [g for g in gaussians if rayintersectsgaussian(rayorigin, raydirection, g)] intersecting.sort(key=lambda g: distance(rayorigin, g.mu)) if not intersecting: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # backgroundcolor totaltransmittance = 1.0 estdepth = 0.0 estalbedo = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] estmetalness = 0.0 estroughness = 0.0 estnormal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 2. Deferred Accumulation: Exact weighted sums per Eqn 2 & 3 for g in intersecting: di = distance(rayorigin, g.mu) alphai = g.alpha Ti = totaltransmittance estdepth += Ti alphai di estalbedo = [estalbedo[j] + Ti alphai g.a[j] for j in range(3)] estmetalness += Ti alphai g.m estroughness += Ti alphai g.r estnormal = [estnormal[j] + Ti alphai g.n[j] for j in range(3)] totaltransmittance = (1.0 - alphai) if totaltransmittance < 1e-4: break # 3. Lighting Calculation lightdirs = fibonaccisphere(16) incominglight = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for omega in lightdirs: Lglobal = evaluatesh(globalshcoeffs, omega) V = getvisibility(omega, estdepth, bakedvisibilitymap, bvh, usebvh) Llocal = aggregatelocalindirect(intersecting, omega) Li = V Lglobal + Llocal incominglight = [incominglight[j] + Li[j] for j in range(3)] incominglight = [x / 16.0 for x in incominglight] # 4. Solve Rendering Equation estnormal = normalize(estnormal) color = evaluatepbrbrdf(estalbedo, estmetalness, estroughness, estnormal, raydirection, incominglight) return color def trainphys3dgs(images, initialgaussians): # Step 1: Initial Vanilla 3DGS Training gaussians = trainvanilla3dgs(images, initialgaussians) # Standard 3DGS optimization [4] # Step 2: Opacity Culling gaussians = opacitycull(gaussians) # Remove low-opacity Gaussians # Step 3: SDF Regularization + Masked Opacity Regularization gaussians = applysdfregularization(gaussians) # Flatten and push to surface gaussians = applymaskedopacityregularization(gaussians) # Constrain scale growth # Step 4: Mesh Extraction mesh = extractmesh(gaussians) # Extract from regularized Gaussians # Step 5: Build Hybrid Representation hybridgaussians = assigngaussianstomesh(mesh, gaussians) # 1 Gaussian per triangle # Step 6: Two-Step PBR Training hybridgaussians = trainpbrparameters(hybridgaussians, images, mesh) # Step 6a hybridgaussians = refinepbrparameters(hybridgaussians, images, mesh) # Step 6b # Post-Training: Bake Visibility hybridgaussians = bakevisibility(hybridgaussians, mesh) # Replace indirect SH with baked visibility SH return hybridgaussians, mesh def rayintersectsgaussian(origin, dir, g): # Standard ray-Gaussian (ellipsoid) intersection test return True # Placeholder for standard geometric intersection def distance(a, b): return ((a[0]-b[0])2 + (a[1]-b[1])2 + (a[2]-b[2])2)0.5 def fibonaccisphere(samples=16): points = [] offset = 2.0 / samples increment = 3.577709437777094 # pi (3 - sqrt(5)) for i in range(samples): y = ((i 1.0) - samples + 1.0) + offset 0.5 radius = (1.0 - y y)0.5 theta = increment i points.append([math.cos(theta)radius, y, math.sin(theta)radius]) return points def evaluatesh(coeffs, direction): # Standard SH evaluation at direction return [sum(c y for c, y in zip(coeffs[j], direction)) for j in range(3)] def getvisibility(omega, depth, bakedmap, bvh, usebvh): if usebvh: return bvh.trace(omega, depth) # Detached from backprop return bakedmap.lookup(omega, depth) # Baked visibility def aggregatelocalindirect(gaussians, omega): # Weighted sum of per-Gaussian indirect SH at omega, analogous to Eqn 3 acc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for g in gaussians: Lg = evaluatesh(g.shindirect, omega) acc = [acc[j] + g.alpha Lg[j] for j in range(3)] return acc def evaluatepbrbrdf(albedo, metalness, roughness, normal, viewdir, light): # Standard PBR BRDF evaluation (e.g., GGX + Schlick Fresnel) return [albedo[j] light[j] for j in range(3)] # Simplified diffuse for implementation def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [x/mag for x in v] if mag > 1e-6 else [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] def trainvanilla3dgs(images, init): pass # Standard 3DGS optimization [4] def opacitycull(g): return [g for g in g if g.alpha > 0.01] # Standard threshold def applysdfregularization(g): return g # SDF loss step def applymaskedopacityregularization(g): return g # Masked opacity loss def extractmesh(g): return [] # Marching cubes / surface extraction def assigngaussianstomesh(mesh, g): return g # Bind 1 Gaussian per triangle def trainpbrparameters(g, imgs, mesh): return g # Step 6a optimization def refinepbrparameters(g, imgs, mesh): return g # Step 6b optimization def bakevisibility(g, mesh): return g # Replace indirect SH with baked visibility SH Time Complexity: Training is more expensive than vanilla 3DGS due to mesh extraction, SDF regularization, and the two-step PBR training process. Inference is real-time capable, comparable to standard 3DGS, as deferred rendering avoids per-Gaussian PBR evaluation and ray tracing is replaced by baked visibility. Memory Complexity: Higher than vanilla 3DGS due to the storage of mesh data, additional PBR parameters (albedo, metalness, roughness, normal) per Gaussian, and visibility SH coefficients. Baking visibility reduces the model size at test time by removing the need for dynamic visibility computation. Performance: Offers significantly better rendering quality under relighting compared to existing relightable 3DGS methods. Provides better rendering quality with real-time rendering speeds compared to SOTA voxel grid-based inverse rendering methods. Strengths: Solves the hidden Gaussian problem, enables real-time relighting, and enables robust geometry learning via mesh hybridization. Limitations: Sensitive to mesh extraction quality, requires careful regularization to prevent abnormal Gaussian scales, and suffers training instability if deferred rendering is applied naively without the proposed two-step approach. Phys3DGS was proposed by Euntae Choi and Sungjoo Yoo from the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Seoul National University, South Korea. It was published on arXiv on September 16, 2024. The work is motivated by the limitations of existing relightable 3DGS methods, which suffer from quality degradation under novel lighting conditions due to the hidden Gaussian problem. It draws inspiration from SuGaR, which uses a hybrid mesh-Gaussian representation, but differs by demonstrating that simple mesh adoption fails for inverse rendering and proposing a novel deferred learning-based training approach.
