name: GaussianDiffusion
head: GaussianDiffusion [S1]
body: GaussianDiffusion is a method that trains a 3D diffusion model based on a GaussianCube representation to generate 3D Gaussian primitives directly from conditioning signals. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency (the "Janus problem") and the generation of spurious artifacts ("floaters") common in single-view 3D generation. Unlike iterative optimization methods, it amortizes the generation cost over a trained network, enabling near-real-time sampling. It is distinguished from its sibling TriplaneGaussian by its use of a voxelized GaussianCube representation converted via optimal transport, rather than tri-plane grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Conditioning signal (e.g., text or image) and noise. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, represented implicitly via a GaussianCube. Data Structures: GaussianCube: A voxelized representation of a constant number of Gaussians. The conversion from the discrete Gaussian set to this structured grid is performed via optimal transport. Diffusion Model: A neural network that predicts noise or scores in the GaussianCube latent space. Steps: 1. Representation Conversion: Convert a constant number of 3D Gaussians into a GaussianCube representation using optimal transport. 2. Diffusion Training: Train a 3D diffusion model on the GaussianCube representations. 3. Structured Noise Incorporation: Incorporate structured noise from multiple viewpoints during the diffusion process to alleviate the Janus problem. 4. Variational 3DGS: Utilize Variational 3DGS principles during generation to mitigate floaters and improve generation results. 5. Generation: Sample from the trained diffusion model to produce the GaussianCube, which is then decoded into the final set of 3D Gaussians. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Janus Problem: Without structured noise from multiple viewpoints, the model may generate inconsistent geometry from different angles. Floaters: Spurious Gaussian primitives may appear; mitigated by using Variational 3DGS. Direct 3D Generation refers to methods that learn a feedforward or diffusion model to output Gaussian fields directly from text or images, without an explicit intermediate image set. It solves the problem of high reconstruction latency and multi-view inconsistency inherent in iterative optimization by amortizing the cost over a trained network. Unlike iterative reconstruction, it naturally promotes multi-view coherence and enables near-real-time sampling at test time. Gaussian Masking is a technique used to prune Gaussians during the training process. It is applied at every densification step and for every 500 iterations after densification stops. Parameters: \lambdam: Loss weight for Gaussian masking loss. Value is 0.05. \epsilonm: Threshold for Gaussian masks. Value is 0.05. Learning rate for Gaussian masks: 0.5. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Alleviates the Janus problem through structured multi-view noise; mitigates floaters via Variational 3DGS; enables near-real-time generation. Limitations: Requires training a diffusion model; relies on optimal transport for representation conversion. When to use: When near-real-time 3D generation from text or images is required, and multi-view consistency is critical. When not to use: When iterative optimization is acceptable and high-fidelity control over individual Gaussians is needed without diffusion artifacts. GaussianDiffusion was proposed in the context of recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting. It addresses limitations in single-view 3D generation, such as the Janus problem and floaters, by integrating diffusion models with a GaussianCube representation. The method builds on the principles of hybrid and diffusion representations, where Gaussian attributes are predicted directly from conditioning signals [Parent]. It is related to other methods like LucidDreamer, which uses interval score matching, and GVGEN, which uses a 3D Gaussian volume representation. name: Direct 3D Generation
head: Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Generation, Amortized 3DGS Synthesis
body: Direct 3D Generation refers to methods that learn a feedforward or diffusion model to output Gaussian fields directly from text or images, without an explicit intermediate image set. It solves the problem of high reconstruction latency and multi-view inconsistency inherent in iterative optimization by amortizing the cost over a trained network. Unlike iterative reconstruction, it naturally promotes multi-view coherence and enables near-real-time sampling at test time. Inputs: Text prompts, input images, or partial 3DGS representations. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives defined by position, covariance (transform), color, and opacity. Data Structures: The method typically disentangles the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation into three distinct functions or latent spaces to handle the high-dimensional output: 1. GauPF (Gaussian Probability Function): Models the 3D locations/geometry of the Gaussians. 2. GauCF (Gaussian Color Function): Models the color attributes. 3. GauTF (Gaussian Transform Function): Models the covariance/transform attributes. In diffusion-based variants (e.g., DiffGS), a Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VAE) maps these functions into a regularized latent space. The latent vector z represents the compressed 3DGS shape. Steps: 1. Training (VAE): Train a Gaussian VAE to map 3DGS functions into a latent vector z. The VAE learns a regularized latent space. 2. Training (Diffusion): Train a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) in the latent space of the Gaussian VAE. The LDM is trained to predict noise or reverse the diffusion process on latent vectors zk. Conditioning inputs (text, image, partial GS) are injected into the LDM. 3. Generation: Start from noise N(0,1). Iteratively denoise from Step K to Step 0 to obtain the clean latent vector z0. Decode z0 using the VAE decoder to recover GauPF, GauCF, and GauTF. 4. Geometry Extraction: Extract 3D Gaussian geometry from GauPF by sampling 3D locations in the 3D space with the highest Gaussian probabilities. 5. Attribute Prediction: Predict the Gaussian attributes (color and transform) using GauCF and GauTF respectively. 6. Discretization (Optional): Apply an octree-guided sampling and optimization algorithm to extract Gaussians at arbitrary numbers. Formulas: Latent Diffusion Process: The model predicts noise for latent vectors zk derived from the VAE. Generation: z0 = \text{Denoise}(zK, \text{Condition}) where zK \sim N(0,1). Parameters: Diffusion Steps K: Not given in the sources. Latent Dimension: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Imperfect Cross-View Consistency: Can lead to noisy surface geometry, duplicated structures, and degraded textures, especially in occluded or textureless regions. High-Dimensional Output: The structured output space (positions, anisotropic covariance, colors, opacity) presents significant modeling challenges. Data Requirements: Requires large, curated 3D training corpora. A diffusion model trained in the latent space of the Gaussian VAE to generate novel 3DGS shapes conditionally or unconditionally. It differs from direct pixel-space diffusion by operating on the compressed latent representation of the Gaussian functions, enabling efficient generation of diverse 3DGS. Training: The LDM is trained to predict noise or reverse the diffusion process on latent vectors zk derived from the VAE. Generation: Starts from noise N(0,1), iteratively denoises to z0 (Step K to Step 0), conditioned on text, image, or partial GS if applicable. Time Complexity: Near-real-time sampling at test time. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the trained feedforward or diffusion model and the VAE. Strengths: Amortizes reconstruction cost; naturally promotes multi-view coherence; enables near-real-time sampling. Limitations: Requires large, curated 3D training corpora; challenges in maintaining controllability (e.g., disentangling geometry from appearance) while scaling; imperfect cross-view consistency can lead to noisy geometry in occluded regions. When to use: When rapid generation from text/images is required and iterative optimization is too slow. When not to use: When exact reconstruction of a specific input is required without generative artifacts. Direct 3D generation methods aim to learn a feedforward or diffusion model that outputs Gaussian fields directly from text or images, without an explicit intermediate image set. Trained on large collections of synthetic or reconstructed data, these models amortize the reconstruction cost. The approach addresses the challenges of the high-dimensional and highly structured output space of 3DGS. DiffGS introduces a Gaussian VAE and LDM framework to generate diverse 3DGS both conditionally and unconditionally. name: Align Your Gaussians (AYG)
body: Align Your Gaussians (AYG) is a text-to-4D synthesis method that generates dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes from text prompts. It solves the problem of creating temporally consistent, deformable 3D content by endowing static 3DGS with dynamics via a deformation network. It is distinguished from static 3D generation methods by its explicit modeling of motion through a text-to-video diffusion prior, and from other 4D methods like DreamGaussian4D by its use of a text-to-video model for motion capture rather than learning motion from a driving video. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt describing the scene and its motion. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians with static attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity) and a deformation field network that maps time to Gaussian attribute updates. Data Structures: Static 3DGS: Standard 3D Gaussian representation. Positions \mathbf{p}, scales \mathbf{s}, rotations \mathbf{q}, colors \mathbf{c}, opacities \alpha. These are fixed after the first stage. Deformation Field Network: A neural network (architecture not specified in sources) that takes Gaussian indices and time t as input, outputting displacement vectors or velocity fields to modulate the static Gaussians. Steps: The method operates in two distinct stages: 1. Static 3DGS Generation: Initialize a static 3DGS representation. Optimize the static Gaussian attributes using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) losses. The SDS losses are derived from a text-to-image diffusion model (Stable Diffusion) and a multi-view consistent prior (MVDream). This stage establishes the base geometry and appearance. 2. Dynamic Generation (Deformation Optimization): Freeze the static Gaussian attributes from Stage 1. Optimize only the parameters of the deformation field network. The optimization uses a Video SDS Loss based on a text-to-video diffusion model to enforce temporal consistency and motion dynamics. To prevent temporal flickering and ensure high visual quality, Image-based SDS losses are applied to randomly selected frames during the dynamic optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gaussians = initialize3dgs() # Positions, scales, rotations, colors, opacity for step in range(staticsteps): loss = computesdsloss(gaussians, textprompt, model=StableDiffusion) loss += computemvdreamloss(gaussians, textprompt) optimize(gaussians, loss) deformationnet = DeformationNetwork() # Parameters to optimize gaussians.requiresgrad = False for step in range(dynamicsteps): t = sampletime() # Apply deformation to get dynamic view dynamicgaussians = applydeformation(gaussians, deformationnet, t) # Video SDS Loss for motion lossvideo = computevideosdsloss(dynamicgaussians, textprompt, model=TextToVideoDiffusion) # Image-based SDS for quality on random frames if randomselection(): lossimage = computeimagesdsloss(dynamicgaussians, textprompt, model=StableDiffusion) loss = lossvideo + lossimage else: loss = lossvideo optimize(deformationnet, loss) Parameters: Text Prompt: Describes the object and motion. Diffusion Models: Stable Diffusion (image), MVDream (multi-view), Text-to-Video Diffusion (motion). Loss Weights: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Inconsistency: Without the image-based SDS on random frames, the video SDS loss alone may lead to flickering or quality degradation. Deformation Field Capacity: The sources do not specify the capacity of the deformation network; insufficient capacity may fail to capture complex motions. Generates 3DGS conditioned on input images or text, focusing on static or single-view consistency, whereas AYG explicitly targets 4D dynamic synthesis. Time Complexity: High, due to the iterative optimization of both static and dynamic components using multiple diffusion models (SDS). Memory Complexity: Moderate, storing static Gaussians and the deformation network parameters. Strengths: Enables text-to-4D generation with explicit dynamic control via text prompts. Limitations: Relies on heavy diffusion-based optimization (SDS), which is computationally expensive compared to feedforward methods. When to use: When text-driven 4D content generation is required and computational resources allow for iterative optimization. When not to use: For real-time applications or when feedforward generation is preferred. AYG was introduced as a method to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to 4D by incorporating deformation fields. It builds on the success of 3D generation using SDS. It is cited in surveys of 3D editing and generation, highlighting its role in enabling text-to-4D synthesis and deformation. name: Conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting Generation
head: Conditional Generation (Text/Image/Partial), DiffGS Conditional
body: Conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting Generation learns a feedforward or diffusion model to output 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations directly from text prompts, input images, or partial 3DGS inputs, bypassing the iterative optimization required by standard reconstruction methods. It differs from sibling methods like Align Your Gaussians (AYG) by focusing on generative completion and synthesis from sparse or semantic conditions rather than aligning existing multi-view images. The method generates 3D Gaussian fields conditioned on external inputs. The core implementation, DiffGS, uses a diffusion framework to denoise Gaussian attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Text prompts, single/multi-view images, or partial 3DGS point clouds/attributes. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: Gaussian Field: A list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has: Position: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale: \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (log-space) Rotation: \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1] Color: \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^k (SH coefficients) Condition Encoder: Text/Image: Frozen CLIP encoder. Partial 3DGS: Modified PointNet. Steps: 1. Condition Encoding: For text: Encode prompt T using frozen CLIP text encoder \gamma{text} to get embedding \mathbf{e}{text} = \gamma{text}(T). For image: Encode input image I using frozen CLIP image encoder \gamma{image} to get embedding \mathbf{e}{image} = \gamma{image}(I). For partial 3DGS: Encode partial Gaussian attributes \mathcal{G}{partial} using modified PointNet \gamma{partial} to get embedding \mathbf{e}{partial} = \gamma{partial}(\mathcal{G}{partial}). 2. Diffusion Process: Initialize noisy Gaussian attributes \mathcal{G}T. Train a neural network \epsilon\theta (or similar diffusion backbone) to predict noise or clean attributes conditioned on \mathbf{e}{cond} (where \mathbf{e}{cond} is \mathbf{e}{text}, \mathbf{e}{image}, or \mathbf{e}{partial}). Optimize the model using the conditional diffusion objective (Eq. 8 in), which typically involves minimizing the difference between predicted and actual noise in the latent space of Gaussian attributes, conditioned on the encoded prompt. 3. Sampling: Iteratively denoise \mathcal{G}t to \mathcal{G}{t-1} using the conditioned model until \mathcal{G}0 is obtained. Parameters: Dataset: ShapeNet chair class with standard splits. CLIP Model: Pretrained CLIP. PointNet: Modified architecture for partial 3DGS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Partial Input Occlusion: The method must handle highly occluded inputs; the PointNet encoder must robustly extract features from sparse partial Gaussians. Semantic Alignment: Text/image conditions must align with the generated geometry; poor alignment results in blurry textures or incorrect shapes. A mechanism for 3D editing (extraction, deletion, appearance modification) in 3D Gaussian Splatting by computing activation scores of 3D Gaussians based on prompts (text, points, boxes) using cosine similarity and softmax. It differs from implicit NeRF feature fields by operating on explicit Gaussian primitives, allowing direct manipulation of color and opacity parameters for specific semantic subsets. Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (AAGS) extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle unconstrained photo collections by explicitly modeling per-image appearance variations and removing transient objects (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles) from the static scene reconstruction. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by integrating a transient object visibility mask and an appearance interpolation mechanism, and from NeRF-based methods like Ha-NeRF by maintaining the efficiency of splatting while achieving competitive or superior perceptual metrics (LPIPS) without requiring test-set images for appearance embedding training. A method operating in two stages for interactive 3D object generation and refinement, optimizing 3D objects through 3DGS and SDS in first stage, then transforming model into InstantNGP structure with interactive hash refinement module in second stage. A reimplementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting adapted for text-to-3D generation, modified to support a learnable MLP background and specific gradient propagation. Gradient back-propagation calculates gradients in the forward rendering order, rather than the inverse order used in the official code. Depth maps are rendered by sampling the view-space depth at the centers of the Gaussians. A z-variance renderer is implemented to compute z-variance for use in a z-var loss term during optimization. Gaussian opacity is clamped to a fixed range during rendering and optimization to stabilize gradients and prevent numerical overflow/underflow. The target number of Gaussians after densification during training is around 10^5 to 10^6. The official implementation propagates gradients in inverse order (last rendered Gaussians receive gradients first), whereas this variant uses rendering order to simplify per-pixel background integration. A technique that pulls Gaussian centers onto the zero-level set of a neural SDF field to prevent floating ellipsoids and achieve accurate geometry estimation. It also pulls query points to Gaussian disks rather than centers to bridge the gap between continuous SDF fields and sparse Gaussian distributions. Steps: 1. Pull Gaussian centers to the zero-level set of the SDF field. 2. Pull neighboring space/query points onto Gaussian disks. 3. Use normalized SDF gradient for the pulling operation. Differs from NeuralPull [45], which pulls query points to Gaussian centers. This method pulls query points to Gaussian disks, better bridging continuous SDF fields and sparse Gaussian distributions. A pruning strategy that removes redundant Gaussians by evaluating their contribution to multi-view reconstruction quality, using photometric loss combined with the densification score. Select Gaussian Gi for pruning if its pruning score s^ip exceeds a predefined threshold \taup. Compute photometric loss E^j{photo} for each view j: E^j{photo} = (1 - \lambda)L^j1 + \lambda(1 - L^j{SSIM}), where L^j1 is mean absolute error and L^j{SSIM} is structural similarity loss. \lambda: Weight for the SSIM term in the photometric loss. Default value is 0.2. \taup: Threshold for the pruning score s^ip. Exploits off-the-shelf models to generate multi-view images from text or a single image. Trains a U-Net-based network to generate 3DGS from multi-view images. The U-Net is asymmetric, which allows for the input of high-resolution images while limiting the number of output Gaussians. A method that takes a texture mesh or pre-trained 3DGS as input. Utilizes Instruct-Pix2Pix and SDS loss to update the input mesh or 3DGS. A method that initializes 3D Gaussians with a visual hull and fine-tunes a pre-trained ControlNet to repair degraded rendered images generated by adding noise to each Gaussian's attributes. Outperforms previous NeRF-based sparse-view reconstruction methods. Time Complexity: Training time depends on the diffusion steps and the complexity of the condition encoder. DiffGS requires training on datasets like ShapeNet. Text-to-3D implementations may take ~40 minutes per prompt for optimization. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians (10^5 to 10^6) and the size of the condition embeddings. Performance: DiffGS produces significantly more visual-appealing and high-fidelity generations in terms of rendering and geometry qualities compared to DiffTF. Strengths: Enables controllable generation from text, images, and partial data; handles occlusions well. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of diffusion parameters; may suffer from blurry textures if not properly conditioned. When to use: When generating 3D assets from text descriptions, single images, or incomplete scans is required. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction from dense multi-view images is available and no generative prior is needed. Originated with DiffGS, which introduced functional Gaussian Splatting Diffusion for conditional generation. The method leverages frozen CLIP encoders for text and image conditioning and modified PointNet for partial 3DGS conditioning. It addresses the limitation of previous diffusion-based 3D generation methods (like DiffTF) which produced blurry results. The approach has been extended to various variants including text-to-3D reimplimentations, interactive generation, and geometry-aware pulling. name: Promptable Explicit Scene Representation
head: Semantic Prompting
body: A mechanism for 3D editing (extraction, deletion, appearance modification) in 3D Gaussian Splatting by computing activation scores of 3D Gaussians based on prompts (text, points, boxes) using cosine similarity and softmax. It differs from implicit NeRF feature fields by operating on explicit Gaussian primitives, allowing direct manipulation of color and opacity parameters for specific semantic subsets. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{xi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian x has a semantic feature vector f(x), color c(x), and opacity \alpha(x). A prompt \tau (text, point, or box). For text prompts: A pre-trained CLIP ViT-B/32 encoder. A set of possible labels \mathcal{T} (e.g., text labels for segmentation or pixel coordinates for point prompts). Outputs: A "Gaussian mask" identifying Gaussians associated with the prompt. An edited radiance field with updated \{ci\} and \{\alphai\} for selected Gaussians, where the count n < N. Data Structures: Gaussian Feature: Each Gaussian x stores a semantic feature vector f(x). The dimensionality is determined by the feature field distillation process (e.g., matching CLIP embedding dimensions). Query Vector: For text, q(\tau) is the CLIP text embedding. For points/boxes, q(\tau) corresponds to the 2D pixel feature projected into 3D via distillation. Steps: 1. Encode Prompt: If \tau is text, compute q(\tau) using the CLIP ViT-B/32 encoder. If \tau is a point or box, retrieve the corresponding 2D feature from the distilled feature field and map it to the 3D Gaussian space. 2. Compute Activation Score: For each Gaussian x, calculate the cosine similarity between its semantic feature f(x) and the query vector q(\tau): s = \frac {f(x) \cdot q(\tau)}{\|f(x)\| \|q(\tau)\|} where s is the activation score. 3. Compute Probability: If a set of labels \mathcal{T} is provided, compute the probability \mathbf {p}(\tau | x) using softmax over all scores sj \in \mathcal{T}: \mathbf {p}(\tau | x) = \text {softmax} (s) = \frac {\exp \left ( s \right)}{\sum {sj \in \mathcal {T}} \exp \left (sj\right)}. 4. Generate Gaussian Mask: Filter Gaussians based on the computed probabilities or scores. Two selection modes are supported: Soft Selection: Threshold the score matrix to include Gaussians with scores above a certain value. Hard Selection: Filter based on the highest score across K categories (where K is the number of object categories). 5. Edit Scene: Update the color c(x) and opacity \alpha(x) of the selected Gaussians. For extraction, set opacity to 0; for deletion, remove or zero out; for appearance modification, change color. 6. Render: Render the edited radiance field using point-based \alpha-blending with the updated set \{ci\}{i=1}^n and \{\alphai\}{i=1}^n, where n < N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def promptableediting(gaussians, prompt, clipencoder, labels=None, threshold=None): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with.feature (f(x)),.color (c),.opacity (alpha) prompt: Text string, or (x, y) point coordinates, or (x1, y1, x2, y2) box coordinates clipencoder: Function to encode text to CLIP embedding labels: Optional list of label strings for softmax normalization threshold: Optional float for soft selection """ # Step 1: Encode Prompt if isinstance(prompt, str): queryvector = clipencoder.encode(prompt) else: # For point/box, retrieve feature from distilled 2D feature field # This assumes a global feature field lookup function exists queryvector = featurefield.lookup(prompt) selectedgaussians = [] scorematrix = [] # Step 2 & 3: Compute Scores and Probabilities for g in gaussians: # Cosine similarity dotproduct = dot(g.feature, queryvector) normf = norm(g.feature) normq = norm(queryvector) if normf == 0 or normq == 0: score = 0.0 else: score = dotproduct / (normf normq) scorematrix.append(score) # If labels are provided, compute softmax probability if labels is not None: # Compute scores for all labels to normalize allscores = [] for label in labels: qlabel = clipencoder.encode(label) slabel = dot(g.feature, qlabel) / (normf norm(qlabel)) allscores.append(slabel) # Softmax expscores = [exp(s) for s in allscores] sumexp = sum(expscores) if sumexp == 0: prob = 0.0 else: # Find index of current prompt's score in allscores to get its probability # Note: In practice, queryvector is derived from one of the labels or a specific prompt # Here we assume we want the probability of the current prompt relative to the set idx = labels.index(prompt) if prompt in labels else -1 if idx != -1: prob = expscores[idx] / sumexp else: prob = 0.0 else: prob = score # Use raw score if no labels for normalization # Step 4: Generate Mask isselected = False if threshold is not None: if prob >= threshold: isselected = True else: # Hard selection: highest score across K categories # Assuming 'labels' defines the K categories if labels is not None and prob > 0: # Simplified logic for hard selection # In hard selection, we typically pick the argmax category # If the prompt matches the argmax category, select maxprob = max(expscores) / sumexp if sumexp > 0 else 0 if prob == maxprob: isselected = True if isselected: selectedgaussians.append(g) # Step 5: Edit Scene # Example: Extraction (set opacity to 0) for g in gaussians: if g in selectedgaussians: g.opacity = 0.0 else: # Optional: Keep others, or remove them from rendering list pass # Step 6: Render # Render using alpha blending with updated gaussians image = renderalphablend(selectedgaussians) return image, selectedgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Norm: If f(x) or q(\tau) has zero norm, the cosine similarity is undefined. Handle by setting score to 0. Implicit vs Explicit: Unlike NeRF-based feature fields where the feature branch shares layers with the radiance field (potentially causing interference), this method uses explicit Gaussian features, avoiding such overlap issues. Distillation Dependency: The quality of f(x) depends on the teacher-student distillation process. Poor distillation leads to inaccurate semantic features. Time Complexity: Computing scores is O(N \cdot D) where N is the number of Gaussians and D is the feature dimension. Softmax is O(N \cdot K) where K is the number of labels. Rendering is O(N) with \alpha-blending. Memory Complexity: Requires storing semantic features f(x) for each Gaussian, increasing memory usage compared to standard 3DGS. Strengths: Enables direct 3D editing (extraction, deletion, modification) using 2D prompts (points, boxes) or text. Leverages pre-trained models (CLIP, SAM) for semantic understanding. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the distilled feature field. Text prompts require CLIP encoding. Hard selection may be less flexible than soft thresholding. Originated in "Feature 3DGS: Supercharging 3D Gaussian Splatting to Enable Distilled Feature Fields" (CVPR 2024). It extends 2D pixel-level promptable editing (from SAM and CLIP) into the 3D realm by distilling 2D features into a 3D feature field associated with 3D Gaussians. name: GSEdit
body: GSEdit is a method for editing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations or texture meshes using text or image instructions. It solves the problem of applying high-fidelity, semantically meaningful edits to existing 3D scenes by leveraging 2D diffusion models. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on geometric consistency constraints like depth maps or intrinsic decomposition, GSEdit primarily utilizes a score distillation sampling (SDS) loss driven by Instruct-Pix2Pix to update the input representation directly. Inputs: A pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting representation or a textured mesh. A text or image instruction defining the desired edit. Outputs: An updated 3D Gaussian Splatting representation or textured mesh reflecting the edit. Data Structures: The input 3DGS consists of a set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}. Each Gaussian gi is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation Ri and scale si) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical harmonics coefficients for color ci Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the input 3DGS or textured mesh. 2. Instruction Processing: Use Instruct-Pix2Pix to generate edited 2D images based on the input instruction and the rendered views of the current 3DGS. Instruct-Pix2Pix takes an input image and a text instruction to produce an edited image. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss. The SDS loss encourages the rendered images from the 3DGS to match the distribution of the edited images generated by Instruct-Pix2Pix. \nabla{x} \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} \left[ w(t) (\epsilon{\theta}(xt, t, c) - \epsilon) \right] Where xt is the noisy version of the rendered image, t is the timestep, \epsilon is the predicted noise, and c is the conditioning (instruction). 4. Optimization: Update the parameters of the 3DGS (positions, covariances, opacities, colors) or the mesh texture using gradient descent to minimize the SDS loss. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for a fixed number of iterations or until convergence. Parameters: Number of optimization iterations: Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Instruct-Pix2Pix model: Used as the source of editing guidance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistency: GSEdit may suffer from multi-view inconsistency issues, as it relies on 2D diffusion without explicit 3D consistency constraints. Precision: The method updates the input representation directly, which may lead to artifacts if the edit is complex or conflicts with the underlying geometry. This variant focuses on editing the albedo (color) of the 3DGS. It initializes new Gaussians on a textured proxy plane and places them in 3D space using proxy depth. Additional albedo Gaussians are spawned by randomly sampling 20% of the pixels covered by the edit in the edited view. The augmented set of albedo Gaussians is then re-optimized to match the edited albedo images rendered from multiple viewpoints. This approach is chosen when the goal is to modify only the appearance (albedo) without altering the geometry. The spawn rate is 20% of pixels covered by the edit. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations and the cost of running Instruct-Pix2Pix and rendering the 3DGS. Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Proportional to the number of Gaussians in the 3DGS representation. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Leverages powerful 2D diffusion models for high-quality edits. Simple to implement if Instruct-Pix2Pix is available. Limitations: May produce multi-view inconsistent results. Relies on the quality of the 2D diffusion model. When to use it and when not: Use when you have a pre-trained 3DGS or texture mesh and want to apply semantic edits using text instructions. Do not use when multi-view consistency is critical and other methods like GaussCtrl are available. GSEdit was introduced in as a method for editing 3D Gaussian Splatting representations. It builds on previous work in NeRF editing, such as InstructNeRF2NeRF, and adapts the approach to 3DGS. The method uses Instruct-Pix2Pix and SDS loss to update the input mesh or 3DGS. It is part of the broader field of 3D editing and generation using diffusion models. name: Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (AAGS)
head: AAGS-A, AAGS-T
body: Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (AAGS) extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle unconstrained photo collections by explicitly modeling per-image appearance variations and removing transient objects (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles) from the static scene reconstruction. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by integrating a transient object visibility mask and an appearance interpolation mechanism, and from NeRF-based methods like Ha-NeRF by maintaining the efficiency of splatting while achieving competitive or superior perceptual metrics (LPIPS) without requiring test-set images for appearance embedding training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of unposed, unconstrained images of a scene. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians with static geometry and appearance features, a transient visibility map, and the ability to render images with specific target appearances. Data Structures: The method builds upon the standard 3D Gaussian representation [G: position \mathbf{p}, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}]. AAGS adds: 1. Appearance Feature Vector (\mathbf{f}{app}): A learnable vector associated with each Gaussian or extracted via a network, used to modulate color based on the target view. 2. Transient Visibility Map (V): A 2D map predicted by a UNet, where V \in [0, 1] indicates the probability of a pixel belonging to a transient object. Network Architectures: 1. Appearance Feature Extractor (E\Phi): Consists of 5 convolutional layers, 1 average pooling layer, and 1 fully connected layer, consistent with Ha-NeRF. It extracts image features to drive appearance. 2. Transient UNet (U\Psi): Consists of 1 downsampling layer and 1 upsampling layer. It predicts the 2D visibility map for transient objects. 3. Color Decoder (F\theta): Consists of 4 fully connected layers, each with a width of 64. It decodes the final color from the Gaussian properties and appearance features. Parameters: \lambda1 = 0.8: Loss weight hyperparameter. na = 48: Image feature length. ng = 24: Image feature length. Spherical Harmonics Degree: 4. Exponential annealing weights: Start at 0.5, decrease to 0.15. Training Procedure: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from the point cloud (standard 3DGS initialization). Initialize E\Phi, U\Psi, and F\theta. 2. Iteration Loop (30,000 total iterations): Densification Phase (Iterations 1–15,000): Perform Gaussian duplication, splitting, and deletion as per standard 3DGS. Static Phase (Iterations 15,001–30,000): Disable duplication, splitting, and deletion to maintain a constant Gaussian count. Forward Pass: Render the scene using differentiable splatting to obtain the rendered image \hat{I}. Pass the input image through E\Phi to extract appearance features. Pass the input image through U\Psi to predict the transient visibility map V. Apply V to mask out transient objects during the loss calculation or rendering. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} (defined in Eq. 10 of, combining photometric loss, transparency loss, and appearance/transient losses). Backpropagation: Update all parameters (E\Phi, U\Psi, F\theta, and Gaussian properties) using Adam optimizer. Appearance Interpolation: To generate novel appearances, AAGS linearly interpolates between the appearance features of two reference images while keeping the 3D structure (Gaussian positions and covariances) fixed. The interpolated features are passed through F\theta to render the new appearance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainaags(images, gtimages, numiterations=30000, densifyuntil=15000): # Initialize Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients) gaussians = initializegaussiansfrompointcloud(images) # Initialize Networks Ephi = AppearanceExtractor() # 5 conv, 1 pool, 1 FC Upsi = TransientUNet() # 1 down, 1 up Ftheta = ColorDecoder() # 4 FC layers, width 64 # Hyperparameters lambda1 = 0.8 na = 48 ng = 24 shdegree = 4 for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Densification control if iteration <= densifyuntil: gaussians.densifyandsplit(images, iteration) gaussians.prune() # Sample a random image from the dataset image = samplerandomimage(images) gt = getgtimage(image) # Extract appearance features appfeatures = Ephi(image) # Predict transient visibility map visibilitymap = Upsi(image) # Render scene # Note: The visibility map is used to mask transient objects. # The exact masking strategy (e.g., multiplying alpha or masking loss) # is implied by "exclude transient objects during rendering". renderedimage, rendereddepth, renderedvisibility = rendergaussians( gaussians, cameraparams, visibilitymap) # Decode color using appearance features # Ftheta takes Gaussian properties and appfeatures decodedcolor = Ftheta(gaussians.properties, appfeatures) # Calculate Loss # Eq. (10) in combines photometric loss, transparency loss, etc. # lambda1 weights specific components. loss = calculateloss( renderedimage=renderedimage, gtimage=gt, visibilitymap=visibilitymap, lambda1=lambda1, shdegree=shdegree) # Backpropagate loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Annealing weights update (start 0.5, end 0.15) def renderwithappearance(gaussians, cameraparams, refimagea, refimageb, alpha=0.5): """ Interpolate appearance between two reference images. """ feata = Ephi(refimagea) featb = Ephi(refimageb) # Linear interpolation of appearance features interpolatedfeat = lerp(feata, featb, alpha) # Render with interpolated features # The rendering process uses Ftheta with the interpolated features image = rendergaussianswithfeatures( gaussians, cameraparams, interpolatedfeat) return image Removes the transient UNet module. Tends to model transient objects as static, causing artifacts, though metrics may appear better on test sets lacking transients. Removes the appearance feature extracting module. Struggles to capture appearance differences between images, leading to low perceptual metrics. Time Complexity: Training runs for 30,000 iterations. On a single RTX 3090, training and rendering are nearly 1000x faster than NeRF-based methods. Memory Complexity: Implemented with PyTorch and CUDA extensions on a single RTX 3090 (24GB memory). Performance: Phototourism Dataset: Brandenburg Gate PSNR 27.20, SSIM 0.9293, LPIPS 0.1341; Sacré-Cœur PSNR 23.23, SSIM 0.8703, LPIPS 0.1729; Trevi Fountain PSNR 23.04, SSIM 0.8037, LPIPS 0.1795. NeRF-OSR Dataset: europa PSNR 21.82, SSIM 0.8069, LPIPS 0.2228; lwt PSNR 23.14, SSIM 0.7972, LPIPS 0.2401; st PSNR 22.31, SSIM 0.6928, LPIPS 0.3421; stjohann PSNR 24.93, SSIM 0.8867, LPIPS 0.1428. Gaussian Count Reduction: Reduces the number of Gaussians compared to baseline 3DGS: Brandenburg Gate (379K vs 521K), Sacré-Cœur (382K vs 461K), Trevi Fountain (896K vs 1070K). Strengths: Handles unconstrained photos, removes transient objects, reduces Gaussian count, faster than NeRFs, better perceptual quality (LPIPS) than SWAG. Limitations: Struggles with highlights and certain objects. Rendering is softer than SWAG (which may be sharper but less perceptually aligned). AAGS was introduced in the paper "AAGS: Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting with Unconstrained Photo Collections". It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS in handling dynamic scenes and appearance variations in unconstrained photo collections, building on the differentiable rendering framework of 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Termination entropy criterion
head: Termination entropy
body: The termination entropy criterion is a metric used to calculate information gain in active 3D reconstruction, specifically within the context of Gaussian Splatting training optimization. It serves as a stopping condition or selection heuristic to determine when a region of the scene has been sufficiently modeled or when the agent should move to a new viewpoint. It sets itself apart from gradient-based or opacity-based densification strategies by measuring the uncertainty or disorder in the predicted radiance field distribution rather than the error magnitude or primitive density. The method evaluates the entropy of the rendered output or the underlying radiance field representation to quantify the amount of information gained from a specific viewpoint or the current state of the model. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, camera poses, and the rendered image or volume representation. Output: A scalar entropy value H representing the uncertainty or information content. Data Structures: The radiance field is represented by the Gaussian primitives. The entropy is computed over the probability distribution of the radiance values or the contribution weights of the Gaussians in the view frustum. Steps: 1. Render: Render the current scene representation from the current camera viewpoint. 2. Compute Distribution: Derive a probability distribution P from the rendered values. In the context of active mapping, this often involves normalizing the radiance or opacity contributions to form a valid probability mass function over the image pixels or volume voxels. 3. Calculate Entropy: Compute the Shannon entropy H of the distribution P: H(P) = - \sum{i} Pi \log Pi where Pi is the probability associated with the i-th element (pixel or voxel). 4. Evaluate Information Gain: Compare the current entropy against a baseline or previous state to determine the information gain. A high entropy indicates high uncertainty or rich information, while low entropy suggests saturation or redundancy. 5. Decision: Use the entropy value to decide whether to terminate the current observation, split Gaussians, or move to a new viewpoint. Parameters: Logarithm base: Typically 2 (bits) or e (nats). Not given in the sources. Thresholds: Specific entropy thresholds for termination are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Probabilities: If Pi = 0, the term Pi \log Pi is defined as 0. Implementation must handle this explicitly to avoid NaNs. Normalization: The distribution must be properly normalized to sum to 1. Incorrect normalization leads to invalid entropy values. Discretization: The choice of discretization (pixels vs. voxels) affects the entropy value. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeterminationentropy(renderedimage): """ Computes the Shannon entropy of the rendered image to assess information content. Args: renderedimage: A 2D array of shape (H, W, C) representing the rendered RGB image. Returns: entropy: A scalar float representing the entropy of the image distribution. """ # Flatten the image to a 1D array of all pixel values pixels = renderedimage.flatten() # Normalize to create a probability distribution # Sum of all pixel values total = np.sum(pixels) # Avoid division by zero if total == 0: return 0.0 probabilities = pixels / total # Filter out zero probabilities to avoid log(0) nonzeroprobs = probabilities[probabilities > 0] # Compute Shannon entropy: H = - sum(p log(p)) # Using natural logarithm, result is in nats. Use np.log2 for bits. entropy = -np.sum(nonzeroprobs np.log(nonzeroprobs)) return entropy Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels or voxels in the rendered output O(N), where N is the number of elements in the distribution. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels or voxels to store the probability distribution. Performance: The method performs consistently better than baselines across all scenes in active 3D reconstruction tasks. It allows the agent to explore more diverse viewpoints and build better 3D models with a limited number of viewpoints. Strengths: Effective for active viewing strategies where the goal is to maximize information gain per viewpoint. It captures the global uncertainty of the scene representation. Limitations: Computationally requires rendering the full scene or a significant portion of it. It may not be as sensitive to local geometric details as gradient-based methods. When to use: Active mapping and planning scenarios where viewpoint selection is critical. When not to use: Static scene reconstruction where viewpoint selection is not a factor, or when computational resources are extremely limited and rendering is too expensive. The termination entropy criterion was introduced in the context of ActiveRMAP (Active Radiance Field for Active Mapping And Planning). It was proposed as a method to guide the camera agent in active 3D reconstruction by selecting viewpoints that maximize the information gain, measured via entropy. The study demonstrated its effectiveness on the NeRF-Synthetic and Tanks & Temple datasets, showing superior performance compared to random and other baseline strategies. name: SAES (Sliding-Window-Averaged Early Stopping)
head: SAES trigger, Structure-Aware Early Stopping, structural saturation detection
body: SAES is an intrinsic training termination criterion for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents over-training and the accumulation of "needle-like" primitives caused by null-space ambiguity in sparse-view reconstruction. Unlike projection-based metrics such as PSNR, which can continue to improve artificially by exploiting geometric ambiguities, SAES monitors the internal dynamics of Gaussian population growth to detect structural saturation, allowing for early stopping without ground-truth volumetric metrics. SAES operates by monitoring the rate at which new Gaussian primitives are added during the densification phase. When this growth rate saturates, it indicates that the Gaussian field has converged structurally, and further densification yields diminishing returns or harmful artifacts. Input: The sequence of active Gaussian counts Nj at specific monitoring steps j. Output: A trigger iteration ts and final training iteration T{final}. The method relies on a sliding window buffer to store recent normalized growth rates. Buffer: A list or queue of size W storing values of \bar{g}j. State Variables: t: Current training iteration. Nt: Number of active Gaussian primitives at iteration t. t{last\monitor}: Iteration of the last monitoring step. \Delta = 100: Monitoring interval in iterations. The growth rate is calculated every \Delta iterations. W = 5: Sliding window size for smoothing the growth rate. \tau = 10^{-3}: Threshold for the sliding-window-averaged growth rate to trigger stopping. t{min} = 2,000: Minimum iteration count before SAES can trigger, preventing premature stopping during early structure formation. \gamma{cool} = 0.2: Learning-rate cooldown factor applied to position and scale learning rates (\eta{xyz}, \eta{scale}) upon triggering. 1. Initialization: Set t{last\monitor} = 0. Initialize an empty sliding window buffer B of capacity W. 2. Monitoring Loop: At each training iteration t: If t > t{last\monitor} + \Delta: Calculate the normalized population growth rate \bar{g}j for the current monitoring step j. Append \bar{g}j to buffer B. If |B| > W, remove the oldest element from B. Update t{last\monitor} = t. Compute the sliding-window-averaged growth rate \bar{g}j (see Formula below). Check SAES trigger condition. 3. Trigger Condition: SAES triggers at iteration ts if: The current iteration t > t{min}. The sliding-window-averaged growth rate \bar{g}j < \tau. 4. Post-Trigger Actions: Set ts = t. Set the final densification iteration T{densify} = ts. No further densification (splitting/cloning) occurs after ts. Set the final training iteration T{final} = 2 \times ts. Training continues until T{final} for refinement. Apply learning-rate cooldown: Multiply current learning rates by \gamma{cool}. Normalized Population Growth Rate (\bar{g}j): The growth rate is normalized to account for the scale of the Gaussian population. Let Nj be the active Gaussian count at monitoring step j, and N{j-1} be the count at the previous monitoring step. The normalized growth rate is: \bar{g}j = \frac{Nj - N{j-1}}{N{j-1}} Note: The sources define \bar{g}j as the "normalized population growth rate" and use it directly in the sliding window average. The formula above represents the standard definition of normalized growth rate consistent with the context of population dynamics. Sliding-Window-Averaged Growth Rate: Let B = [b1, b2, \dots, bk] be the current buffer contents, where k \le W. The averaged rate \bar{g}{avg} is: \bar{g}{avg} = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^{k} bi The trigger condition is \bar{g}{avg} < \tau. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def checksaestrigger(currentiter, activegaussiancount, buffer, params): """ Checks if SAES should trigger based on Gaussian population growth. Args: currentiter (int): Current training iteration t. activegaussiancount (int): Number of active Gaussians Nt. buffer (list): List of recent normalized growth rates. params (dict): Contains delta, windowsize, threshold, tmin, cooldownfactor. Returns: bool: True if SAES triggers, False otherwise. dict: Updated buffer. float: Normalized growth rate calculated (if monitored). """ delta = params['delta'] # 100 windowsize = params['windowsize'] # 5 threshold = params['threshold'] # 1e-3 tmin = params['tmin'] # 2000 # State variables assumed to be maintained in the training loop context # lastmonitoriter: iteration of the last check # prevgaussiancount: N{j-1} if currentiter - lastmonitoriter < delta: return False, buffer, None # Calculate normalized growth rate # Avoid division by zero if population is zero (edge case) if prevgaussiancount == 0: growthrate = 0.0 else: growthrate = (activegaussiancount - prevgaussiancount) / prevgaussiancount # Update buffer buffer.append(growthrate) if len(buffer) > windowsize: buffer.pop(0) # Update state for next step lastmonitoriter = currentiter prevgaussiancount = activegaussiancount # Calculate sliding window average avggrowth = sum(buffer) / len(buffer) # Check trigger conditions if currentiter > tmin and avggrowth < threshold: return True, buffer, avggrowth return False, buffer, avggrowth Division by Zero: If the initial Gaussian population N{j-1} is zero, the normalized growth rate is undefined. The implementation should handle this by setting the growth rate to 0 or skipping the check until a non-zero population exists. Premature Triggering: The parameter t{min} = 2,000 prevents triggering during the early phase where the population is still establishing basic structure. Ignoring this can lead to underfitting. Fluctuations: The sliding window W=5 smooths out iteration-to-iteration noise in densification. A window too small may trigger on transient dips; a window too large may delay stopping. What it is: A method that uses termination entropy to calculate information gain for active 3D reconstruction, serving as the broader criterion framework for SAES. Difference: While SAES specifically monitors population growth rate for early stopping, the Termination Entropy Criterion provides the theoretical basis for determining when information gain is sufficient. When to choose: Use when integrating SAES into a pipeline that already utilizes entropy-based active reconstruction strategies. Link: Termination entropy criterion Time Complexity: SAES adds negligible computational overhead per iteration, as it only requires counting active Gaussians and maintaining a small buffer of 5 floats. The primary benefit is a reduction in total training time. Memory Complexity: Minimal. Requires storing a buffer of size W=5 and a few scalar state variables. Measured Performance: On the FIPS dataset with 25 views, SAES triggers at approximately ts \approx 5,133 iterations (mean across objects), leading to T{final} \approx 10,267. This results in a ~64% reduction in wallclock training time compared to R2-Gaussian, which runs for a fixed 30,000 iterations. SAES is stable across different view counts (10, 20, 25 views) for the same object, with trigger iterations varying by less than 5% for complex objects like Walnut. Strengths: Prevents over-training and the formation of needle-like primitives that exploit null-space ambiguity. Does not require ground-truth volumetric metrics for evaluation. Significantly reduces training time without sacrificing reconstruction quality (PSNR/SSIM). Limitations: Relies on the assumption that population growth saturation correlates with structural convergence, which may not hold for all scene types or initialization strategies. Requires careful tuning of t{min} to avoid early stopping. When to use: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography or reconstruction where training time is a constraint and null-space ambiguity is a concern. When not to use: Dense-view settings where the Gaussian population may continue to refine structure significantly beyond initial saturation, or when ground-truth volumetric metrics are available and preferred. SAES was introduced in the context of diagnosing and controlling optimization drift in sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography, specifically as part of the LADES (Learning and Training Optimization and Initialization for Densification Strategy) framework. The method addresses the "Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence" (PVFD) problem, where projection fidelity (PSNR) continues to improve while volumetric fidelity degrades due to the formation of anisotropic, needle-like primitives. By monitoring intrinsic Gaussian population dynamics rather than external projection metrics, SAES provides a robust, ground-truth-free stopping criterion. name: Pruning and Sparsification
head: Gaussian Sparsification, Primitive Reduction
body: Pruning and Sparsification refers to the family of strategies that reduce the cardinality of the 3D Gaussian primitive set \mathcal{G} by removing redundant, insignificant, or high-uncertainty primitives, thereby improving rendering efficiency and reducing memory footprint without degrading visual fidelity. It sets itself apart from densification methods (e.g., Adaptive Density Control) by focusing on removal rather than addition, and from static compression techniques (e.g., LightGaussian) by often employing dynamic, training-aware, or uncertainty-based criteria to preserve structural integrity. All methods in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by a mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k [Parent]. The core mechanism involves periodic evaluation of a metric per Gaussian to determine if the current representation is insufficient or redundant in a specific region. Common metrics include: 1. Gradient Magnitude: The accumulated 2D positional gradient \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v} \| \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muv^k} \|2. High gradients indicate that the Gaussian's position is not adequately minimizing the loss, suggesting a need for refinement or replacement [13466-densification-and-splitting.md]. 2. Opacity: Low opacity \alphak < \alpha{\min} indicates a primitive contributes negligibly to the rendered image and is a candidate for pruning. 3. Scale: Excessively large scales max(sk) relative to the scene extent e{scene} indicate coarse approximations that may blur details or occlude nearby geometry [13466-densification-and-splitting.md]. Densification operations are typically triggered every N iterations (e.g., refineEvery = 100) to allow the optimizer to stabilize [Parent]. The primary operations are: Splitting: Replacing a parent Gaussian gk with N{children} children. The children's means \mu{child} are sampled from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak) [Parent]. The scale is typically reduced, e.g., s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}}, to increase local density [Parent]. Cloning: Creating an exact copy of gk (same \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) to increase sampling frequency in high-error regions without changing the spatial footprint [Parent]. Pruning: Removing Gaussians that fail to meet opacity or significance thresholds. Buffer management is critical: pruned or split Gaussians require buffer compaction or flag-based marking to maintain contiguous memory access for rasterization [Parent]. Adaptive Density Control dynamically balances addition and removal to maintain an optimal representation budget, rather than simply removing primitives. It sets itself apart from static pruning methods by using gradient magnitude and opacity thresholds to trigger splitting, cloning, or pruning based on local scene complexity. Pruning and Opacity Management focuses on opacity thresholds, transmittance consistency during cloning, and fixed-schedule resets rather than adaptive uncertainty bounds or significance scores derived from view counts. It solves the problem of unbounded Gaussian growth and the persistence of "floaters" or boundary artifacts. Significance-Aware Pruning removes primitives based on their accumulated contribution to the rendered image, rather than solely on opacity or scale. It solves the problem of standard opacity pruning removing large, low-opacity Gaussians that are critical for scene structure and transmittance. Unlike Pruning and Opacity Management which relies on static opacity thresholds, this method spares Gaussians with low opacity but high alpha-blending significance, improving the trade-off between reconstruction quality and scene compactness. Principled Uncertainty Pruning is a post-hoc method for compressing pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) models by removing Gaussians with high uncertainty in their spatial parameters. It solves the problem of visual fidelity degradation at high compression ratios by using a principled sensitivity score derived from the Fisher Information matrix of the reconstruction error. Unlike heuristic methods that rely on opacity or gradient magnitude, PUP quantifies the entropy of the posterior distribution over each Gaussian's position and scale, allowing for aggressive pruning (up to 90%) while preserving fine details and foreground information. TangoGS is a density control strategy that automatically scales the number of Gaussian primitives to match the complexity of the input capture without per-scene tuning. It combines a capture-derived "learning allowance" (model sizing based on track-adjusted pixel count) with training-based quality feedback (PSNR-driven pruning) to determine the final Gaussian population. Unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed thresholds or per-capture calibration, TangoGS uses a shared configuration across diverse scene scales, achieving comparable or better PSNR with significantly fewer Gaussians than baselines like LeGS or 3DGS. Depth-Based Gaussian Pruning varies the opacity pruning threshold based on the relative depth (z-axis value) of 3D Gaussians to preserve points at the far plane in forward-facing scenes. It sets itself apart from standard fixed-threshold pruning by applying a lower threshold (making pruning harder) to distant primitives, thereby compensating for the sparsity of Gaussians that naturally occurs at the back of the scene. Proposes an optimizing-sparsifying loop that interleaves standard training with a sparsification operator. Removes redundant primitives while boosting the influence of the remaining collection. A process to sparsify the generated tree structure to avoid parent-child settings where the parent's size is only marginally larger than the children's, ensuring proper optimization. Mark all leaf nodes (output of 3DGS optimization) as relevant. Find the union of cuts in the tree over all training views for the minimum target granularity \tau{min} = 3 pixels. Find the bottom-most nodes in this union cut. These are the highest-detail relevant nodes. Remove all nodes between them and already marked nodes. Raise the target granularity by 2x and repeat the process until \tau{max} (half the image's resolution) is reached. If a node has K children, the blended weight \alpha' generalizes to: \alpha' = \frac{1}{1 - (1 - \alphap) \frac{1}{K}}. Minimum target granularity \tau{min}: Set to 3 pixels, corresponding to the minimum extent of a primitive 3DGS primitive due to low-pass filtering. The concept of pruning and sparsification in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged alongside the original 3D-GS paper [Parent], which introduced opacity-based pruning as a basic mechanism to remove "floaters" and insignificant primitives during training. Subsequent research has expanded this into a diverse family of techniques. Significance-Aware Pruning addressed the limitations of opacity-only pruning by considering alpha-blending contributions. Principled Uncertainty Pruning introduced a post-hoc compression approach using Fisher Information matrices to quantify geometric uncertainty, enabling high compression ratios. TangoGS and other methods like GaussianSPA and Hierarchy Compaction further refined sparsification by incorporating scene complexity metrics, uncertainty-based scores, and hierarchical tree structures to optimize the trade-off between rendering speed, memory usage, and visual quality. These methods are primarily used in the optimization and training phases of 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines to manage the exponential growth of primitives and ensure efficient real-time rendering. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p-mb2TzVJZk, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Adaptive Density Control
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Adaptive Density Control (ADC), 3DGS ADC, 3DGS density control, Gaussian Culling/Splitting/Duplicating
body: Adaptive Density Control (ADC) is a dynamic optimization strategy used in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to adjust the number and spatial distribution of Gaussian primitives during training. It solves the problem that gradient descent alone cannot change the number of Gaussians or their coarse arrangement, leading to under-reconstructed regions or inefficient memory usage. ADC periodically evaluates metrics such as gradient magnitude, opacity, and scale to trigger densification (cloning or splitting) or pruning. It sets itself apart from static pruning methods (e.g., LightGaussian) by dynamically balancing addition and removal to maintain an optimal representation budget, rather than simply removing primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk has mean \muk, covariance \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. Training images, camera poses, and current iteration step t. Output: Updated set \mathcal{G}' with modified N, where Gaussians are added, removed, or modified based on density control decisions. Data Structures: Gradient Buffer: Accumulates the 2D positional gradient magnitude \tauk for each Gaussian over a collection period (typically one densification interval). Flag Buffers: Used for efficient GPU-based filtering and compaction. Common flags include densifysplitflag, densifydupflag, densifykeepflag, and their prefix sums for compacting the Gaussian array. Random Samples: Pre-generated random samples from \mathcal{N}(0, 1) for splitting perturbations, stored in densifyrandomsamples. Parameters: refineEvery: Interval between densification steps (default: 100 or 1000 depending on implementation). warmupLength: Initial iterations before densification starts [Parent]. stopSplitAt: Iteration after which splitting stops (e.g., maxSteps / 2) [Parent]. T{grad}: Gradient threshold for densification. o{min}: Minimum opacity threshold for pruning. P{dense}: Percent dense hyperparameter to determine split vs. clone based on scale relative to scene extent e{scene}. resetInterval: Interval for opacity reset (e.g., 3000 steps). resetLogit: Opacity reset threshold (logit of 0.25, approx -1.386). Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points or other sources. 2. Gradient Tracking: For each Gaussian gk, track the 2D positional gradient magnitude \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muv^k} for each rendered view v. Compute the average gradient magnitude \tauk over all views in the collection period: \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v=1}^{N{\text{views}}} \left\| \frac{\partial L(Iv, I'v)}{\partial \muv^k} \right\|2 where L is the loss between ground truth Iv and rendered I'v. 3. Densification Trigger: If current step t is within a densification interval (e.g., t \pmod{\text{refineEvery}} == 0) and t < \text{stopSplitAt}, proceed to densification [Parent, S11]. 4. Split/Clone Decision: For each Gaussian gk: If \tauk \ge T{grad}: If \max(sk) > P{dense} \cdot e{scene} (large scale): Split. Replace gk with N{children} (default 2) children. Children means \mu{child} are sampled from \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak) [Parent]. Children scales s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}} [Parent, S11]. Other properties (\alpha, \mathbf{c}, q) are inherited. Else (small scale): Clone. Create an exact copy of gk [Parent, S11]. Correction: If using Opacity Correction after Cloning, set new opacity \hat{\alpha} = 1 - \sqrt{1 - \alpha} to reduce alpha-compositing bias. 5. Pruning: After densification, prune Gaussians: If \alphak < o{min}: Prune. If \max(sk) > 0.1 \cdot e{scene} (excessively large): Prune. 6. Opacity Reset: If t \pmod{\text{resetInterval}} == \text{refineEvery}, reset opacities: For all gk, if \alphak > \text{resetLogit}, set \alphak = \text{resetLogit}. Zero Adam state for opacities. 7. Buffer Compaction: Compact the Gaussian array to remove pruned entries and maintain contiguous memory [Parent, S7]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivedensitycontrol(Gaussians G, step t, params): # 1. Gradient Tracking (accumulated over refineEvery steps) # tau[k] is already computed from previous steps # 2. Densification Trigger if t % params.refineEvery == 0 and t < params.stopSplitAt: newgaussians = [] splitflags = [] cloneflags = [] for k, g in enumerate(G): tauk = g.tau maxscale = max(g.scale) # Split or Clone if tauk >= params.Tgrad: if maxscale > params.Pdense params.escene: # Split children = splitgaussian(g, params.Nchildren) newgaussians.extend(children) splitflags.append(True) cloneflags.append(False) else: # Clone child = clonegaussian(g) # Apply opacity correction if enabled if params.opacitycorrection: child.opacity = 1 - sqrt(1 - g.opacity) newgaussians.append(child) splitflags.append(False) cloneflags.append(True) else: newgaussians.append(g) splitflags.append(False) cloneflags.append(False) G = newgaussians # 3. Pruning prunedG = [] for g in G: if g.opacity < params.omin: continue if max(g.scale) > 0.1 params.escene: continue prunedG.append(g) G = prunedG # 4. Opacity Reset if t % params.resetInterval == params.refineEvery: for g in G: if g.opacity > params.resetLogit: g.opacity = params.resetLogit g.adamopacitystate = 0 # Zero Adam state return G def splitgaussian(g, Nchildren): children = [] for i in range(Nchildren): child = Gaussian() # Sample mean from parent's covariance child.mean = samplefromnormal(g.mean, g.covariance) # Scale down child.scale = g.scale (5.0 / 4.0) / sqrt(Nchildren) # Inherit other properties child.opacity = g.opacity child.shcoeffs = g.shcoeffs child.rotation = g.rotation children.append(child) return children def clonegaussian(g): child = Gaussian() child.mean = g.mean.copy() child.scale = g.scale.copy() child.opacity = g.opacity child.shcoeffs = g.shcoeffs.copy() child.rotation = g.rotation.copy() return child Uses diffusion-based prior loss to guide densification, avoiding SfM bias. Treats Gaussians as MCMC samples, using SGLD updates for densification. Simplifies via stochastic sampling weighted by importance. Defines specific mathematical formulations for importance/error scores. Details geometric mechanics for splitting while preserving integrated density. Removes needle-surgery structural splitting and training calls, keeping standard densification and pruning. Uses log-ratio soft regularization parameters: lambdaaniso (0.001) and anisoratiomax (5). Enforces a strict upper bound on component count. Densification (cloning/splitting) is disabled if count \ge maxsetting and re-enabled only if pruning reduces count below the cap. Corrects bias in alpha-compositing after cloning by setting new opacity \hat{\alpha} = 1 - \sqrt{1 - \alpha}. Time Complexity: Densification and pruning are O(N) per interval, where N is the number of Gaussians. Buffer compaction is also O(N). Memory Complexity: Memory usage grows with N. ADC lacks explicit control over maximum N in its original form, risking out-of-memory errors. Max-Component ADC mitigates this. Performance: Effective for general scenes but can underfit high-frequency regions (e.g., grass) due to low gradient accumulation on large Gaussians. Can overfit simple regions. Strengths: Dynamic adaptation to scene complexity; smooth integration into explicit 3D environments. Limitations: Heuristic thresholds (T{grad}, o{min}) are non-intuitive and sensitive to loss terms. Memory fragmentation can slow optimization. Cloning introduces opacity bias if not corrected. Adaptive Density Control was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023). It was designed to address the static nature of the initial SfM point cloud, allowing the model to grow and refine its representation during optimization. The method has become a standard component of 3DGS training, with numerous variants proposed to address its limitations in memory management, bias, and densification criteria. name: GaussianDreamer
body: GaussianDreamer is a training procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that combines 2D and 3D diffusion model priors to optimize scene representations from text or image prompts. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing a diffusion-based prior loss computed on rendered views, thereby preventing the model from getting stuck in local minima and enhancing the scene's comprehensive observation. Unlike methods relying on Structure from Motion (SfM) point clouds for initialization, this approach exclusively uses LiDAR data or generative models to avoid prior bias. Inputs and outputs: Input: A text or image prompt, a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation (initially sparse), and a pre-trained 2D diffusion model. Output: An optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation with positions, scales, colors, opacities, and rotations. Data structures: 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives: Each primitive i is defined by position \mathbf{\mu}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i (parameterized by scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{R}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. Diffusion Model: A 2D text-to-image or image-to-image model (e.g., Stable Diffusion) used for Score Distillation Sampling (SDS). Numbered steps: 1. Initialization: Use Shap-E to generate an initial point cloud. This point cloud serves as the initial geometry for the 3DGS optimization. 2. Densification: Since the initial point cloud generated by Shap-E is relatively sparse, apply noisy point growth and color perturbation to densify it. This step ensures sufficient coverage for the subsequent optimization. 3. Optimization Loop: Optimize the 3DGS parameters using 2D Score Distillation Sampling (SDS). Sample a random camera pose. Render the current 3DGS representation to obtain a 2D image. Pass the rendered image and the prompt to the 2D diffusion model. Compute the SDS gradient, which approximates the gradient of the diffusion model's log-likelihood with respect to the rendered image pixels. Back-propagate the gradient through the differentiable renderer to update the Gaussian parameters (positions, scales, colors, opacities). 4. Regularization: Optionally, introduce 3D SDS loss to mitigate the Janus problem, although the primary method relies on 2D SDS. Formulas: The SDS loss is computed as: \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} \left[ w(t) \cdot \mathbb{E}{zt \sim pt(z|x)} \left[ \nabla{zt} \log p\theta(zt | x) \cdot \frac{\partial zt}{\partial \mathbf{\theta}{GS}} \right] \right] where zt is the noisy image at timestep t, p\theta is the diffusion model, and \mathbf{\theta}{GS} are the Gaussian parameters. The total loss includes the RGB reconstruction loss and the SDS loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{RGB} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{SDS} where \lambda is a weighting factor. Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. SDS weighting \lambda: Not given in the sources. Number of optimization steps: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: The generated initial point cloud is relatively sparse, which can lead to poor initialization if not densified. The Janus problem (multi-face artifact) may still exist during optimization if the view is sampled one by one, even with 3D SDS loss. Per-scene fitting incurs heavy computational cost (minutes to hours per prompt). Prone to over-smoothing or texture oversaturation unless additional regularizers or multi-view diffusion priors are used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gaussians = shape.generatepointcloud(prompt) gaussians = noisypointgrowth(gaussians) gaussians = colorperturbation(gaussians) for step in range(numsteps): # Sample a random camera pose camera = samplerandomcamera() # Render the current 3DGS representation renderedimage = render3dgs(gaussians, camera) # Compute SDS gradient # Note: The exact implementation of SDS depends on the diffusion model API sdsgradient = computesdsgradient(renderedimage, prompt, diffusionmodel) # Back-propagate to update Gaussian parameters gaussians = updategaussians(gaussians, sdsgradient) # Optional: Add RGB reconstruction loss if ground truth is available if groundtruthimage is not None: rgbloss = computergbloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) gaussians = updategaussians(gaussians, rgbloss) This method is a training procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a fine-tuned Diffusion Model to generate guidance images from randomly sampled "pseudo-views," regularizing the Gaussian model parameters to improve unseen view synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing a diffusion-based prior loss computed on rendered views that do not correspond to ground-truth images, thereby preventing the model from getting stuck in local minima and enhancing the scene's comprehensive observation. Unlike methods relying on Structure from Motion (SfM) point clouds for initialization, this approach exclusively uses LiDAR data to avoid prior bias. A generation paradigm where a powerful 2D or multi-view diffusion model is queried from many camera poses, and its gradients are back-propagated through the differentiable GS renderer to update Gaussian parameters. Early pipelines such as DreamGaussian and GaussianDreamer treat each scene independently and directly optimize positions, scales, colors, and opacities to match diffusion-model guidance while respecting RGB reconstruction losses. Time Complexity: Heavy computational cost, taking minutes to hours per prompt. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Yields high-fidelity geometry and appearance for object- and scene-level content. Can be naturally extended to dynamic or 4D generation with temporal regularization. Limitations: Prone to Janus ambiguity, over-smoothing, or texture oversaturation unless additional regularizers, multi-view diffusion priors, or geometry-aware constraints are applied. The initial point cloud is sparse, requiring densification steps. GaussianDreamer was introduced as an early text- and image-to-3D pipeline that combines the priors of 2D and 3D diffusion models. It utilizes Shap-E to generate the initial point cloud and optimizes 3DGS using 2D SDS. The method is part of the broader category of optimization-based generation methods in GS-based generation.
