name: Diffusion Prior Guidance for Pseudo Views
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Diffusion Prior Regularization, Pseudo-view Regularization, SGD Training
body: This method is a training procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a fine-tuned Diffusion Model to generate guidance images from randomly sampled "pseudo-views," regularizing the Gaussian model parameters to improve unseen view synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing a diffusion-based prior loss computed on rendered views that do not correspond to ground-truth images, thereby preventing the model from getting stuck in local minima and enhancing the scene's comprehensive observation. Unlike methods relying on Structure from Motion (SfM) point clouds for initialization, this approach exclusively uses LiDAR data to avoid prior bias. Inputs: LiDAR point clouds (voxelized-downsampled). Monocular training images (and their poses). A fine-tuned Diffusion Model (specifically a ControlNet variant or image-to-image diffusion model). A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) associated with the Diffusion Model for latent space encoding/decoding. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters \Phi (means \mu, covariances \Sigma, opacities \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color c). The 3D Gaussian Splatting representation consists of a set of Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is parameterized by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (typically parameterized via a rotation matrix and scaling vector). Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics coefficients for view-dependent RGB color ci. The total parameter set is denoted as \Phi = \bigcup \{\Phio, \Phip\}, where \Phio are parameters visible to the current training view vo, and \Phip are parameters visible to the pseudo-views vp. Training Iterations: 50,000. Learning Rate: Decays from 1.6 \times 10^{-4} to 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. Pseudo-view Sampling Interval (k): Every 10 iterations. Number of Pseudo Views (M): 4. Warm-up Period: 500 iterations without pseudo-view sampling. Maximum Noise Level (t{max}): 10. Minimum Noise Level (t{min}): Not explicitly given, but implied to be the start of the denoising process (typically 0 or 1 in diffusion literature, but the text specifies denoising to t{min}). Strength Hyper-parameter Range (s): s{min} = 0.2. s{max} starts at 0.6 and linearly decreases to 0.4 over the training process. Noise Level Formula: t = s \times t{max}, where s is sampled uniformly from [s{min}, s{max}] for each pseudo view. Pseudo-view Orientation Rotation (\delta): The orientation is rotated from training views within range [-\delta, \delta] along the z-axis (yaw angle). The exact value of \delta is not given in the sources. 1. Initialization: Initialize the 3D Gaussian Splatting model using LiDAR point clouds. Voxelize and downsample the LiDAR point clouds with a voxel size of 0.5. Do not use SfM (Structure from Motion) point clouds for initialization. 2. Training Loop (for iteration i = 1 to 50,000): 3. Warm-up Check: If i \le 500, skip pseudo-view sampling. Proceed only to Step 4. 4. Reconstruction Loss Computation (Standard 3DGS): Sample a training view vo. Render the view using differentiable rasterization/splatting to obtain the rendered image Io and rendered depth map \tilde{D}o. Obtain the ground-truth image I{gt} and the completed dense depth map Do (from LiDAR projection) for vo. Compute the reconstruction loss L{recon}: L{recon}(\Phio) = \mathbb{E}{vo} \left[ \| Io - I{gt} \|1 + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM}(Io, I{gt}) + \lambda{depth} \| Do - \tilde{D}o \|1 \right] where \Phio are the Gaussian parameters visible to vo. 5. Pseudo-View Sampling (if i > 500 and i \pmod k == 0): Randomly sample M pseudo views vp = \{vp^j\}{j=0}^{M-1}. Position: Interpolate the position of each pseudo view between the current training view vo and its adjacent views. Orientation: Rotate the orientation of each pseudo view from the training view's orientation within the range [-\delta, \delta] along the z-axis (yaw angle). 6. Pseudo-View Rendering: Render the pseudo views using differentiable splatting with parameters \Phi to obtain rendered pseudo-view images \tilde{I}p(\Phi, vp) \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3 \times H \times W} and depth maps \tilde{D}p. Let \Phip be the union of Gaussian parameters visible to any of the pseudo views vp. 7. Diffusion Guidance Generation: For each rendered pseudo-view image \tilde{I}p^j: Encode \tilde{I}p^j into a latent feature map z using the VAE Encoder. Sample a strength value s uniformly from [s{min}, s{max}]. Calculate the noise level t = s \times t{max}. Add noise to the latent feature map z at level t to obtain the noisy latent zt. Denoise zt using the fine-tuned Diffusion Model from level t down to t{min}. Decode the denoised latent to obtain the guidance image Ig^j. 8. Pseudo Loss Computation: Compute the pseudo loss L{pseudo} for the set of pseudo views: L{pseudo}(\Phip) = \mathbb{E}{vp} \left[ \| Ig - \tilde{I}p \|1 + \lambda{p-lpips} L{lpips}(Ig, \tilde{I}p) + \lambda{p-depth} \| Dp - \tilde{D}p \|1 \right] where Ig and Dp are the guidance images and corresponding depth maps (if available/used) for the pseudo views, and \tilde{I}p, \tilde{D}p are the rendered images and depths. Note: The source defines L{pseudo} using Ig and \tilde{I}p. The depth term \lambda{p-depth} implies a depth loss is also applied, likely against a depth prior or rendered depth, though the specific ground truth for pseudo-view depth is not defined (it uses \tilde{D}p in the rendered term, suggesting the loss might be self-consistency or against a generated depth prior; the source formula explicitly writes \| Dp, \tilde{D}p \|1, implying Dp is the target depth for the pseudo view, possibly derived from the diffusion model or a separate depth estimator, but the text primarily focuses on the image guidance. We retain the formula as given). 9. Total Loss and Optimization: Compute the total loss: L(\Phi) = L{recon}(\Phio) + \lambda{pseudo} L{pseudo}(\Phip) where \Phi = \text{Union}\{\Phio, \Phip\}. Perform gradient descent to update \Phi. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def train3dgswithdiffusionprior( lidarpoints, trainingimages, trainingposes, diffusionmodel, vaeencoder, vaedecoder, numiterations=50000, voxelsize=0.5, k=10, M=4, tmax=10, smin=0.2, smaxinit=0.6, smaxfinal=0.4, lambdassim=0.2, lambdadepth=1.0, lambdapseudo=1.0, lambdaplpips=0.1, lambdapdepth=1.0): # 1. Initialization # Voxelize and downsample LiDAR points voxelizedpoints = voxelizedownsample(lidarpoints, voxelsize) # Initialize 3D Gaussian Splatting model with voxelized points # Do NOT use SfM points gaussians = initialize3dgsfrompoints(voxelizedpoints) # Learning rate schedule parameters lrstart = 1.6e-4 lrend = 1.6e-6 # 2. Training Loop for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Update learning rate (linear decay) currentlr = lrstart - (lrstart - lrend) (iteration / numiterations) # Sample a training view vo, Igto, Dgto = sampletrainingview(trainingimages, trainingposes) # Render training view Io, Dtildeo = render3dgs(gaussians, vo) # Compute Reconstruction Loss lossrecon = computel1(Io, Igto) + \ lambdassim computessim(Io, Igto) + \ lambdadepth computel1(Dgto, Dtildeo) # Initialize total loss totalloss = lossrecon # Pseudo-view regularization (after warm-up) if iteration > 500 and iteration % k == 0: # Sample M pseudo views pseudoviews = samplepseudoviews(vo, trainingposes, M) # Render pseudo views Itildep, Dtildep = render3dgsbatch(gaussians, pseudoviews) # Generate guidance images using Diffusion Model Iglist = [] for i in range(M): # Encode to latent z = vaeencoder(Itildep[i]) # Sample strength s s = random.uniform(smin, smaxcurrent(iteration, smaxinit, smaxfinal, numiterations)) # Compute noise level t t = s tmax # Add noise to latent znoisy = addnoise(z, t) # Denoise using diffusion model zdenoised = diffusionmodel.denoise(znoisy, tstart=t, tend=tmin) # Decode to image Ig = vaedecoder(zdenoised) Iglist.append(Ig) Ig = torch.stack(Iglist) # Compute Pseudo Loss # Note: Dp is assumed to be available or derived; if not, the depth term might be omitted or handled differently. # Based on source formula: Lpseudo = E[ ||Ig - Itildep||1 + lambdaplpips Llpips(Ig, Itildep) + lambdapdepth ||Dp - Dtildep||1 ] losspseudo = computel1(Ig, Itildep) + \ lambdaplpips computelpips(Ig, Itildep) + \ lambdapdepth computel1(Dp, Dtildep) # Dp source not explicitly defined in text, retained from formula totalloss = lossrecon + lambdapseudo losspseudo # Backpropagate and update Gaussians totalloss.backward() optimizer.step(lr=currentlr) optimizer.zerograd() def smaxcurrent(iteration, smaxinit, smaxfinal, numiterations): """Linearly decrease smax from init to final over training.""" progress = iteration / numiterations return smaxinit - (smaxinit - smaxfinal) progress Initialization Bias: Using SfM point clouds is explicitly avoided to prevent prior bias from SfM reconstruction errors or assumptions. Only LiDAR data should be used. Noise Level Control: The strength parameter s controls the deviation from the 3DGS rendering. A small s preserves 3DGS-rendered noise/details, while a large s produces cleaner images but loses details. The decreasing schedule for s{max} ensures that early in training (when 3DGS quality is low), the model relies more on the diffusion prior, and later, it relies more on the 3DGS renderings to preserve details. Pseudo-View Overlap: Pseudo-views are sampled close to training views, leading to considerable overlap in the corresponding Gaussian models. This allows simultaneous multi-view learning and prevents local minima. Time Complexity: The method adds a diffusion model inference step for every k iterations (every 10 iterations in the cited implementation) for M pseudo views (4 views). This significantly increases the per-iteration cost compared to standard 3DGS, which only performs rasterization and loss computation. The diffusion model inference (encoding, noise addition, denoising, decoding) is computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3DGS parameters, the diffusion model weights, and the VAE weights. The latent space operations are memory-efficient compared to pixel-space operations, but the batch processing of pseudo views adds temporary memory overhead. Evaluated on KITTI and KITTI-360 datasets. The method is designed for street view synthesis where LiDAR data is available but SfM might be unreliable or biased. The ablation study on s shows that smaller s preserves details, while larger s cleans up noise but loses detail. The schedule s{max} \in [0.6, 0.4] balances this trade-off. Strengths: Improves unseen view synthesis by regularizing with a diffusion prior. Prevents local minima by leveraging overlapping pseudo-views. Does not rely on SfM point clouds, making it suitable for scenarios with only LiDAR and monocular images. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to diffusion model inference. Requires a fine-tuned diffusion model, which adds a pre-training step (ControlNet training). The quality of the guidance depends on the fine-tuning of the diffusion model. Use when LiDAR data is available but SfM point clouds are not desired or reliable. Use when high-quality novel view synthesis is required, especially for views not seen during training. Use when the scene has complex textures or structures that benefit from diffusion-based regularization. Use standard 3DGS if computational resources are limited and high-quality novel views are not critical. Use if SfM point clouds are available and accurate, as they provide a strong geometric prior without the need for diffusion guidance. The method is described in the paper "SGD: Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior". It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework. The diffusion model is fine-tuned using a ControlNet architecture. The method was evaluated on autonomous driving datasets (KITTI, KITTI-360). The approach was developed to address the limitations of standard 3DGS in synthesizing unseen views, particularly in autonomous driving scenarios where LiDAR data is available but SfM might be insufficient or biased. The authors ablated the impact of the diffusion prior strength s, showing that a decreasing schedule for s{max} yields better results than a fixed value. SGD: Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00375, fetched 2026-10-27

name: MCMC Densification
head: Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamic (SGLD) Densification
body: MCMC Densification is a Bayesian strategy that reformulates the densification of 3D Gaussian primitives as a Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamic (SGLD) update rule. Unlike standard adaptive density control which relies on heuristic thresholds for cloning and pruning based on gradient magnitude, this method treats the set of 3D Gaussians as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples. It adds controlled noise to the center locations of Gaussians during optimization, allowing the representation to explore the parameter space more effectively. This approach reduces reliance on the initial point cloud initialization and allows the target number of Gaussians to be specified prior to optimization. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, where each Gaussian gi is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Learning rate hyperparameter \lambda{lr}. Noise scale hyperparameter \lambda{noise}. Noise term \epsilon sampled from a standard normal distribution. Camera views \mathcal{I} and corresponding ground truth images. Outputs: Updated set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with modified parameters, particularly the center locations \mu. Data Structures: The Gaussian parameters are stored in standard 3DGS format. The key modification is the application of noise to the mean vector \mu after the gradient descent step. Steps: 1. Rasterization and Loss: Render the current Gaussian set \mathcal{G} to obtain RGB images and alpha masks. Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} (e.g., L1 + D-SSIM) against ground truth images. 2. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}. 3. SGLD Update: Update the Gaussian parameters using the SGLD rule. The update rule for the Gaussian set \mathcal{G} is: \mathcal{G} \leftarrow \mathcal{G} - \lambda{\text{lr}} \cdot \nabla{\mathcal{G}} \mathbf{E}{\mathcal{I}} [\mathcal{L}{\text{total}} (\mathcal{G}; \mathcal{I})] + \lambda{\text{noise}} \cdot \epsilon \quad (1) Where: \lambda{lr} is the learning rate. \nabla{\mathcal{G}} \mathbf{E}{\mathcal{I}} [\mathcal{L}{\text{total}} (\mathcal{G}; \mathcal{I})] is the expected gradient of the total loss over the image set. \lambda{noise} controls the magnitude of the injected noise. \epsilon is the noise term. 4. Noise Application: The noise term \lambda{\text{noise}} \cdot \epsilon is specifically applied to the center locations \mu of the Gaussians. This perturbs the positions, encouraging the Gaussians to move towards regions of high probability density in the data distribution, effectively performing densification through re-localization rather than explicit cloning. 5. Regularization: Additional regularization terms may be added to the loss function to stabilize training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mcmcdensificationstep(gaussians, cameras, gtimages, lambdalr, lambdanoise): """ Performs one step of MCMC densification. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes.mu,.cov,.opacity,.sh. cameras: List of camera objects. gtimages: Ground truth RGB images. lambdalr: Learning rate for gradient descent. lambdanoise: Scale factor for the Langevin noise. Returns: Updated gaussians list. """ # 1. Rasterize and compute loss # Render current gaussians to get predicted images predimages = rasterize(gaussians, cameras) # Compute total loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) loss = computeloss(predimages, gtimages) # 2. Compute gradients # Compute gradients with respect to all Gaussian parameters grads = computegradients(loss, gaussians) # 3. Apply SGLD update for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Standard gradient descent step for all parameters g.mu = g.mu - lambdalr grads[i].mu g.cov = g.cov - lambdalr grads[i].cov g.opacity = g.opacity - lambdalr grads[i].opacity g.sh = g.sh - lambdalr grads[i].sh # Add noise to center locations (MCMC step) # epsilon is sampled from standard normal distribution N(0, 1) epsilon = samplenormal(g.mu.shape) g.mu = g.mu + lambdanoise epsilon return gaussians Parameters: \lambda{lr}: Learning rate. Typical values depend on the specific optimizer setup, but standard 3DGS learning rates apply. \lambda{noise}: Noise scale. This hyperparameter controls the exploration capability. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Magnitude: If \lambda{noise} is too large, the Gaussians may diverge or fail to converge to a stable representation. If too small, the method degenerates to standard gradient descent without the benefits of MCMC sampling. Initial Point Cloud: While MCMC densification reduces reliance on the initial point cloud, poor initialization can still lead to suboptimal local minima. Computational Cost: The original implementation involves separate kernels for noise injection, which can be a bottleneck. Dynamic LoD Hierarchy Densification is a strategy for maintaining and evolving a Level-of-Detail (LoD) hierarchy of 3D Gaussians continuously during the optimization phase of Gaussian Splatting training. It solves the problem of post-training hierarchy construction by allowing the hierarchy structure and Gaussian parameters to refine simultaneously as the scene representation evolves. Unlike methods that construct the hierarchy after training is complete, this approach supports stable, progressive refinement and restructuring without requiring a separate post-processing step. It builds on MCMC Densification by applying similar spawning principles to hierarchical nodes. HYDRA is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decomposes complex, multi-lobed primitives into simpler constituents within the MCMC framework. It solves the problem of undersampled regions by subdividing primitives with high positional gradients while preserving the target distribution P(g{\text{new}}) \approx P(g{\text{old}}). It distinguishes itself from standard splitting by using a learned decomposition for large primitives, enabling generalizable planar primitives to operate effectively within MCMC. Fast MCMC Densification is an optimized implementation of the MCMC densification approach from 3DGS-MCMC [39], which treats 3D Gaussians as MCMC samples and uses SGLD updates. It fuses the noise injection step into a single CUDA kernel to reduce the training time bottleneck. On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, the optimized version achieves 28.00 PSNR, 6m17s training time, and 7.2GiB VRAM, compared to the original 27.83 PSNR, 27m22s training time, and 8.9GiB VRAM. The target number of Gaussians for the nine Mip-NeRF360 scenes (alphabetical order) are: 6131954, 1244819, 1222956, 3636448, 5834784, 1852335, 1593376, 4961797, 3783761. The optimized version is significantly faster and uses less VRAM than the original implementation [39], while achieving similar or slightly better quality. Time and Memory Complexity: The original MCMC densification implementation has higher computational overhead due to separate kernels for noise injection, leading to longer training times and higher VRAM usage. The optimized "Fast MCMC Densification" reduces training time significantly (from ~27m to ~6m on Mip-NeRF360) and reduces VRAM usage (from 8.9GiB to 7.2GiB) by fusing operations. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, the optimized MCMC densification achieves a PSNR of 28.00, comparable to or slightly better than the original 27.83 PSNR. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces reliance on the initial point cloud; allows specifying the number of Gaussians prior to optimization; leads to improved rendering quality. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the noise scale hyperparameter \lambda{noise}; original implementation is computationally expensive. When to Use: Use when the initial point cloud is sparse or inaccurate, or when a specific target number of Gaussians is desired. Use when rendering quality is prioritized over training speed, or when using the optimized implementation. When Not to Use: Use standard adaptive density control if training speed is critical and the initial point cloud is high quality. MCMC Densification was proposed by Kheradmand et al. (2024) in the context of 3DGS-MCMC. It adopts a Bayesian perspective to reformulate the densification strategy in Gaussian Splatting as a Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamic (SGLD) update rule. This approach replaces the splitting, cloning, and pruning steps of adaptive density control with a re-localization scheme that preserves sample probability. gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic LoD Hierarchy Densification
head: Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchy Densification
body: Dynamic LoD Hierarchy Densification is a strategy for maintaining and evolving a Level-of-Detail (LoD) hierarchy of 3D Gaussians continuously during the optimization phase of Gaussian Splatting training. It solves the problem of post-training hierarchy construction by allowing the hierarchy structure and Gaussian parameters to refine simultaneously as the scene representation evolves. Unlike methods that construct the hierarchy after training is complete, this approach supports stable, progressive refinement and restructuring without requiring a separate post-processing step. It builds on MCMC Densification by applying similar spawning principles to hierarchical nodes. The method maintains a hierarchical structure of 3D Gaussians throughout the entire training process. As Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) and their spatial distribution change during optimization, the hierarchy is updated to reflect these changes. This requires efficient view-dependent selection from the hierarchy, which is challenging when the structure changes dynamically. Data Structures: Hierarchical Sequential Point Trees (HSPT): A hybrid data structure adapted from Sequential Point Trees (SPTs) [Dachsbacher et al. 2003] to support Gaussian Splatting. It enables efficient, parallelizable LoD selection while remaining robust to hierarchy updates during training. Hierarchy Nodes: Each node in the hierarchy represents a 3D Gaussian primitive. Intermediate nodes aggregate geometric primitives from their children. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians (leaves and intermediate nodes). Camera views and parameters. Target granularity range [\tau{min}, \tau{max}). Outputs: Updated hierarchy structure and Gaussian parameters. Optimized intermediate nodes. Steps: 1. Hierarchy Maintenance: Continuously update the hierarchy as Gaussian parameters evolve. This involves restructuring the tree to maintain valid LoD cuts based on the current spatial distribution of Gaussians. 2. LoD Selection: For each training view, compute the appropriate LoD cut efficiently using the HSPT. This avoids full tree traversal, which is expensive for large, dynamically changing models. 3. Densification: Apply densification strategies (inspired by MCMC-style spawning) to add new Gaussians or refine existing ones within the hierarchy. This supports stable and progressive refinement. 4. Hierarchy Optimization (Optional Variant): Optimize intermediate nodes to improve visual quality by propagating gradients through them. Load the generated hierarchy. Randomly select one training view and a target granularity \tau\epsilon from the range [\tau{min}, \tau{max}). Perform cut selection and interpolation for the selected granularity. Propagate gradients through interpolation weights and the expression of \alpha' to optimize child and parent nodes simultaneously. Use EWA filtering for correct anti-aliasing, as hierarchies operate at different scales. 5. Caching: Implement a lightweight caching system to track recently accessed data and reduce CPU-GPU data transfer overhead during training and rendering. Formulas: Target Granularity Sampling: Sample target granularities \tau\epsilon using a canonical random variable \xi \in [0, 1): \tau\epsilon = \tau{max} \tau{min}^{\frac{1-\xi}{\xi}} Interpolation: Gradients propagate through interpolation weights and the expression of \alpha' (Eq. 12 in) to enable smooth switching between hierarchy levels. Parameters: \tau{min}: Minimum target granularity. Not given in the sources. \tau{max}: Maximum target granularity. Not given in the sources. \xi: Canonical random variable in [0, 1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Node Degradation: Optimizing higher LOD levels may degrade the quality of leaves due to interpolation. To avoid this, leaf nodes are not changed during optimization. Hierarchy Updates: The hierarchy structure changes during optimization, making efficient selection challenging. The HSPT is designed to handle this. Anti-Aliasing: Hierarchies operate at different scales, requiring correct anti-aliasing. The EWA filtering solution of Yu et al. [2023] is used. CPU-GPU Transfer: Large models require significant data transfer. A caching system is introduced to mitigate this. Optimizing intermediate nodes of the hierarchy to improve visual quality by propagating gradients through them, treating them as 3D Gaussian primitives. This involves randomly selecting a training view and a target granularity \tau\epsilon from [\tau{min}, \tau{max}), performing cut selection and interpolation, and propagating gradients through interpolation weights and \alpha' to optimize child and parent nodes simultaneously. Leaf nodes are not changed during optimization to prevent degradation. EWA filtering is used for anti-aliasing. Time Complexity: Efficient LoD selection is achieved using HSPT, avoiding full tree traversal. However, maintaining the hierarchy during training adds overhead. Memory Complexity: The hierarchy adds some memory overhead compared to a flat list of Gaussians. A caching system is used to reduce CPU-GPU transfer overhead. Performance: Enables real-time rendering of very large datasets by streaming detail proportional to view distance. Strengths: Continuous refinement during training, no post-training hierarchy construction, efficient view-dependent selection, reduced CPU-GPU transfer. Limitations: Complexity of maintaining and updating the hierarchy during training, potential for leaf node degradation if not handled correctly. When to Use: Large-scale reconstruction where post-training hierarchy construction is impractical or where continuous refinement is beneficial. When Not to Use: Small-scale scenes where the overhead of hierarchy maintenance is not justified. The method was proposed in "A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory". It builds on the concept of hierarchical Level-of-Detail models inspired by Kerbl et al. [2024] and MCMC-style spawning [Kheradmand et al. 2024]. The Hierarchical Sequential Point Trees (HSPT) are adapted from SPTs [Dachsbacher et al. 2003]. The hierarchy optimization variant is described in "A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets". name: HYDRA Densification
head: HYDRA, HYDRA: Hybrid Decomposition for Rendering-Aware Preservation
body: HYDRA is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decomposes complex, multi-lobed primitives into simpler constituents within the MCMC framework. It solves the problem of undersampled regions by subdividing primitives with high positional gradients while preserving the target distribution P(g{\text{new}}) \approx P(g{\text{old}}). It distinguishes itself from standard splitting by using a learned decomposition for large primitives, enabling generalizable planar primitives to operate effectively within MCMC. Inputs: Current set of Gaussian primitives g. Absolute gradient accumulation for each primitive (used to identify high-gradient regions). Pre-trained MLP f\psi. Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives with increased density in high-gradient areas. Data Structures: Primitive parameters: center o, covariance (encoded via scale/rotation or Fourier coefficients \sigma, \{\phik\}, \{rk\}), color, orientation. Boundary representation for large primitives: radial function ri(\theta) sampled at M angles. Steps: 1. Identify High-Gradient Primitives: Compute absolute gradient accumulation for all primitives. Select those with high gradient accumulation for densification. 2. Classify Primitive Size: Determine if the primitive is "small" or "large" based on its circumradius or boundary complexity. 3. Apply Splitting Strategy: Case (i) Scale-preserving split: For smaller primitives, reduce the circumradius and place two children symmetrically offset in the parent's tangent plane. Apply the mass-preserving relocation formulas with N=2. Case (ii) Learned lobe decomposition: For large primitives with complex, multi-lobed boundaries: a. Identify the S deepest valleys along the boundary ri(\theta) sampled at M angles. b. Partition the boundary into S angular segments. c. For each segment, compute the center of mass (rM, \thetaM) and angular bounds (\theta{\min}, \theta{\max}). d. Use the pre-trained MLP f\psi to generate child primitive parameters: f\psi: \left (\sigma,\, \{\phi k\},\, \{rk\},\, rM,\, \theta M,\, \theta {\min },\, \theta {\max }\right) \mapsto \left (\sigma ',\, \{\phi 'k\},\, \{r'k\},\, \Delta r,\, \Delta \theta,\, o',\, R'\right) where (\Delta r, \Delta \theta) is the polar offset used to compute the child center in the parent’s tangent plane. e. Children inherit color and orientation from the parent. f. Remove the parent primitive. 4. Update Count: The net increase in primitives is S-1 for each decomposed large primitive. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Primitive: def init(self, id, sigma, phik, rk, center, color, orientation, R): self.id = id self.sigma = sigma self.phik = phik self.rk = rk self.center = center self.color = color self.orientation = orientation self.R = R def hydradensification(primitives, gradients, mlpfpsi, sizethreshold): """ Densify primitives using HYDRA strategy. primitives: List of Primitive objects. gradients: Dict mapping primitive.id -> absolute gradient accumulation. mlpfpsi: Pre-trained MLP function for learned decomposition. sizethreshold: Threshold to classify primitives as small or large. """ newprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: # Step 1: Identify High-Gradient Primitives via absolute gradient accumulation if gradients[prim.id] < sizethreshold: newprimitives.append(prim) continue # Step 2: Classify Primitive Size based on circumradius or boundary complexity issmall = prim.R < sizethreshold # Exact classification logic not given in sources. if issmall: # Step 3(i): Scale-preserving split # Sources do not specify the exact relocation formulas (Eqs. 9 & 10 in source). # Symmetric offset in parent's tangent plane with reduced circumradius: offset = math.sqrt(prim.R / 2) child1 = Primitive(f"{prim.id}c1", prim.sigma, prim.phik, prim.rk, (prim.center[0] - offset, prim.center[1]), prim.color, prim.orientation, prim.R / 2) child2 = Primitive(f"{prim.id}c2", prim.sigma, prim.phik, prim.rk, (prim.center[0] + offset, prim.center[1]), prim.color, prim.orientation, prim.R / 2) newprimitives.extend([child1, child2]) else: # Step 3(ii): Learned lobe decomposition # Sources do not specify the valley detection algorithm. # We assume boundary sampling at M angles returns S segments. segments = [] # Sources do not specify the valley detection algorithm. S = len(segments) for i, segment in enumerate(segments): # Compute segment properties rM, thetaM = 0.0, 0.0 # Exact computation not given in sources. thetamin, thetamax = 0.0, 0.0 # Exact computation not given in sources. # Step 3(ii)d: Use pre-trained MLP fpsi to generate child parameters childparams = mlpfpsi( prim.sigma, prim.phik, prim.rk, rM, thetaM, thetamin, thetamax) # Unpack MLP output sigmaprime, phikprime, rkprime, deltar, deltatheta, oprime, Rprime = childparams # Compute child center in parent's tangent plane using polar offset dx = deltar math.cos(deltatheta) dy = deltar math.sin(deltatheta) childcenter = (oprime[0] + dx, oprime[1] + dy) # Step 3(ii)e: Children inherit color and orientation from the parent child = Primitive( id=f"{prim.id}child{i}", center=childcenter, sigma=sigmaprime, phik=phikprime, rk=rkprime, color=prim.color, orientation=prim.orientation, R=Rprime) newprimitives.append(child) # Step 4: Parent is removed, net increase is S-1 primitives return newprimitives Parameters: M: Number of angles sampled for boundary representation. Not given in the sources. S: Number of segments/lobes. Not given in the sources. \lambda: Weight for D-SSIM loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{\text{dist}}: Weight for depth distortion loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{\text{normal}}: Weight for normal consistency loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues in computing valleys and centers of mass for complex boundaries. Ensuring the MLP f\psi is properly trained and generalized. Handling degenerate primitives with no clear valleys. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives, the complexity of boundary sampling (M), and the MLP inference cost. Memory Complexity: Increases by S-1 primitives per large primitive decomposed. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality among planar-primitive frameworks and comparable perceptual metrics to leading volumetric representations on standard benchmarks. Strengths: Enables generalizable planar primitives within MCMC; handles complex, multi-lobed boundaries effectively. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained MLP; potentially higher computational cost for large primitives compared to simple splits. When to use: When rendering complex scenes with multi-lobed structures using planar primitives within an MCMC framework. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Importance-Weighted Stochastic Sampling for Gaussian Simplification
head: Importance Sampling Simplification, Stochastic Pruning
body: This method simplifies a set of 3D Gaussians by replacing deterministic pruning with stochastic sampling weighted by Gaussian importance, thereby preserving local geometric structure. Unlike deterministic pruning, which removes neighbors with similar importance simultaneously and disrupts geometry, this approach maintains the overall scene structure while reducing the Gaussian count. It serves as a core simplification step within the Optimization and Densification Strategy pipeline. Inputs: A set of N Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}N\}. An importance value Ii for each Gaussian i. A target number of Gaussians to keep, N{target} (where N{target} < N). Outputs: A subset of N{target} Gaussians selected via stochastic sampling. Data Structures: Importance Array: A 1D array of size N containing float values Ii. Probability Array: A 1D array of size N containing float values Pi. Selection Mask: A boolean array of size N indicating which Gaussians are kept. Steps: 1. Calculate Importance: Compute the importance metric Ii for each Gaussian. The source indicates that blending weight-based importance yields better performance than other metrics (e.g., scale or rendered index alone). Specific combinations of blending weight, scale, and rendered index may vary by scene type (indoor vs. outdoor). 2. Normalize Importance: Compute the sum of all importance values: S = \sum{j=1}^{N} Ij 3. Compute Sampling Probabilities: Calculate the sampling probability Pi for each Gaussian: Pi = \frac{Ii}{S} 4. Stochastic Sampling: Sample N{target} indices from the set \{1, \dots, N\} according to the probability distribution \{P1, \dots, PN\}. The selected Gaussians form the simplified set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def importanceweightedstochasticsampling(gaussians, importancevalues, targetcount): """ Simplifies a set of Gaussians using importance-weighted stochastic sampling. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects. importancevalues: List of float importance scores Ii for each Gaussian. targetcount: Integer, the desired number of Gaussians to keep. Returns: List of selected Gaussian objects. """ n = len(gaussians) if targetcount >= n: return gaussians # Step 1 & 2: Compute sum of importance totalimportance = sum(importancevalues) # Guard against division by zero if totalimportance == 0: # If all importances are zero, sample uniformly or randomly probabilities = [1.0 / n] n else: # Step 3: Compute sampling probabilities probabilities = [ival / totalimportance for ival in importancevalues] # Step 4: Sample indices based on probabilities selectedindices = weightedsamplewithoutreplacement(range(n), probabilities, targetcount) # Return the selected Gaussians return [gaussians[i] for i in selectedindices] def weightedsamplewithoutreplacement(population, weights, k): """ Samples k unique indices from population with given weights without replacement. Uses cumulative weights and linear scan for selection. """ n = len(population) if k > n: raise ValueError("k cannot exceed population size") selected = [] currentweights = list(weights) currentpopulation = list(population) for in range(k): totalw = sum(currentweights) r = random.uniform(0, totalw) cumsum = 0.0 idx = 0 for i, w in enumerate(currentweights): cumsum += w if cumsum >= r: idx = i break selected.append(currentpopulation[idx]) currentweights.pop(idx) currentpopulation.pop(idx) return selected Parameters: Importance Metric (Ii): The value used to weight sampling. Blending weight-based importance is recommended for best performance. Target Count (N{target}): The number of Gaussians to retain. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deterministic Pruning Failure: Direct pruning disrupts local geometry because neighboring Gaussians often have similar importance, causing them to be removed or preserved simultaneously. This leads to significant chamfer distance between centers of pruned and non-simplified Gaussians, especially at low preserving ratios. Zero Importance: If all Ii are zero, the probability distribution is undefined. A uniform distribution or random sampling should be used as a fallback. A sampling approach that considers the geometric structure of the scene to enhance rendering quality while maintaining a sparse set of Gaussians. It addresses the limitations of direct pruning by assigning each Gaussian a pre-defined importance value Ii and sampling based on this distribution. However, specific implementation details of the weighting/sampling distribution are not fully detailed in the source text beyond the general stochastic formulation. It is chosen when preserving local geometry is critical and deterministic pruning leads to suboptimal simplification results due to the removal of neighboring Gaussians with similar importance. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) to compute importance and normalize probabilities. Sampling is O(N{target} \log N) or O(N{target}) depending on the sampling algorithm used. Memory: O(N) to store importance and probability arrays. Measured Performance: Mini-Splatting (using this method) outperforms VQ (pruning from [21]) and LightGaussian (prune/recovery from [11]) at similar Gaussian counts. Stochastic sampling maintains overall geometry better than deterministic pruning, as evidenced by lower chamfer distance. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Preserves local geometric structure better than deterministic pruning; robust to large pruning ratios where deterministic methods fail. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the importance metric (blending weight vs. scale vs. rendered index) for different scene types (indoor vs. outdoor). When to Use: Use when simplifying 3D Gaussian representations for resource-efficient training and rendering, and when preserving geometric fidelity is more important than strict deterministic removal of low-importance elements. The concept of pruning in neural representation was initially introduced for grid-based neural radiance fields [21, 41] and extended to Gaussian representations. This specific importance-weighted stochastic sampling method was introduced in the Mini-Splatting paper. It was developed to address the collapse in rendering quality observed when using direct pruning at large ratios, by leveraging the observation that stochastic sampling better maintains overall geometry. name: Splitting Criteria and Prioritization
head: Densification scoring, Gradient-based splitting metrics
body: Splitting Criteria and Prioritization determines which 3D Gaussians should be subdivided (split or cloned) during the training of Gaussian Splatting models to adapt their density to scene complexity. It solves the problem of static primitive distribution by dynamically adding primitives in high-error regions while removing redundant ones. It differs from its siblings by offering specific mathematical formulations for computing the "importance" or "error" score of a Gaussian, such as using squared gradient norms for multi-view consistency, complexity-aware sampling for LoD, or average contribution for occlusion handling. The core mechanism involves computing a scalar score S(G) for each Gaussian G based on training gradients, opacity, or reconstruction error. This score is compared against a threshold \tau. If S(G) > \tau, the Gaussian is marked for densification. The specific definition of S(G) varies by child method. Common inputs include the loss gradient \nabla L, the Gaussian's opacity \alpha, and its screen-space footprint. The decision is typically made periodically during training steps. A densification strategy for multi-view training that replaces the summation of 2D positional gradient vectors with a sum of squared norms. It resolves invalid vector arithmetic across different image planes by ensuring error metrics remain valid. It yields higher reconstruction quality with fewer primitives compared to standard positional-gradient rules. Replaces opacity-only heuristics with a composite importance score incorporating image complexity, opacity, and scale. It solves inefficient primitive distribution by biasing densification toward high-complexity regions. It differs from standard 3DGS by using a complexity field as a surrogate for reconstruction error and from siblings by explicitly modeling the exponential relationship between particle count and visual complexity. Determines split/clone decisions based on the mean blending weight per view rather than a binary view count. It solves occlusion bias where fully occluded views inflate the denominator and dilute the gradient signal. It intrinsically weights views by their actual contribution, preventing occluded views from biasing the average downward. A criterion for prioritizing which Gaussians to split, based on rate-distortion optimization to maximize PSNR gain. It associates a reconstruction Squared Error SE{c,i} to each Gaussian i in camera view c, defined as: SE{c,i} = \sum{p \in Ic} wi^{(c)} (R^{(c)}(p) - I^{(c)}(p))^2 where I^{(c)} is the ground-truth image, R^{(c)}(p) is the rendered pixel value, and wi^{(c)} is the blending weight. This formulation spreads the error metric across Gaussians, allowing the selection of Gaussians that will induce the highest gain in PSNR quality when split. The concept of adaptive density control in Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper. The specific splitting criteria discussed here, such as the Multi-View Density Control Criterion and Average Contribution Criterion, are refinements proposed in subsequent research to address limitations in multi-view consistency and occlusion handling. The distortion-based prioritization is described in BOGausS. BOGausS: Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.23919/eusipco63237.2025.11226626, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-View Density Control Criterion
head: Absolute-gradient split proxy, FastGS criterion, Multi-view Adaptive Density Control (ADC)
body:
The Multi-View Density Control Criterion is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting designed to resolve invalid vector arithmetic that occurs when applying standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) to multi-view training. Standard ADC sums 2D positional gradients from pixels covering a Gaussian; however, in multi-view training, a single Gaussian is projected onto multiple image planes, and adding 2D gradient vectors from different view spaces is mathematically invalid, potentially resulting in zero vectors even if the underlying 3D gradients are significant. This method replaces vector addition with the summation of squared norms, ensuring that error metrics remain valid across viewpoints. It yields higher reconstruction quality with fewer primitives compared to standard positional-gradient rules. The method computes a scalar error score E1(G) for each Gaussian G by aggregating the squared magnitudes of gradients from all pixels that project onto G across all viewpoints. Inputs: N: Total number of viewpoints (images) used in the training batch. G: A specific 3D Gaussian primitive. \mathcal{P}k: The set of pixels in viewpoint k that are covered by the projection of G. 
abla{\pi} L: The 2D positional gradient of the loss L with respect to the pixel coordinates (u, v) for pixel \pi. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard gradient buffers. The criterion operates on the scalar values derived from the gradient tensors. Algorithm: 1. Initialize the error score for Gaussian G to zero: E1(G) \leftarrow 0. 2. Iterate over each viewpoint k from 1 to N. 3. For each pixel \pi in the set \mathcal{P}k (pixels covered by G in viewpoint k): a. Retrieve the 2D positional gradient 
abla{\pi} L. b. Compute the squared Euclidean norm of this gradient: \|
abla{\pi} L\|^2. c. Add this squared norm to the error score: E1(G) \leftarrow E1(G) + \|
abla{\pi} L\|^2. 4. Compare E1(G) against a threshold 	au (typically derived from the parent splitting criteria logic). If E1(G) > 	au, mark G for densification (splitting or cloning). Formula: E1(G) = \sum{k=1}^{N} \sum{\pi \in \mathcal{P}k} \|
abla{\pi} L\|^2 Where: N is the number of viewpoints. \mathcal{P}k is the set of pixels in viewpoint k covered by G. 
abla{\pi} L is the 2D positional gradient at pixel \pi. \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. Parameters: The threshold 	au is not defined by this specific criterion in isolation but is passed from the parent Splitting Criteria and Prioritization. The specific hyperparameter controlling the constraint strength in related implementations is the DS Threshold (DSTH), with a default value of 30. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Vector Addition: The primary pitfall avoided by this method is the direct summation of 2D gradient vectors \sum 
abla{\pi} L from different viewpoints. As shown in, adding 2D gradients from different image planes (different coordinate spaces) can result in cancellation (e.g., two identical 3D gradients producing 2D gradients that sum to zero), leading to incorrect densification decisions. Precision: Squared norms are always non-negative, preventing cancellation errors. However, large gradients may cause overflow if not handled with appropriate data types (e.g., float32 vs float64). Boundary Conditions: Pixels on the boundary of the Gaussian's support must be correctly identified to ensure \mathcal{P}k is accurate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemultiviewerror(G, viewpoints, gradients): """ Computes the Multi-View Density Control error score for a Gaussian. Args: G: The Gaussian primitive object. viewpoints: List of viewpoint indices [0,..., N-1]. gradients: A dictionary or array where gradients[k][pi] is the 2D positional gradient vector for pixel pi in viewpoint k. Returns: E1: Scalar error score. """ E1 = 0.0 for k in viewpoints: # Get pixels covered by G in viewpoint k # Implementation detail: This requires the projection logic from the # rendering pipeline to determine which pixels are covered by G. coveredpixels = getcoveredpixels(G, k) for pi in coveredpixels: # Retrieve 2D gradient vector for pixel pi in viewpoint k gradvec = gradients[k][pi] # Compute squared Euclidean norm # gradvec is typically a 2D vector [du, dv] squarednorm = gradvec[0]2 + gradvec[1]2 # Accumulate E1 += squarednorm return E1 A hyperparameter threshold that controls the densification constraints of Gaussians in the context of the Multi-View Density Control Criterion. Increasing DSTH imposes stricter constraints, reducing the number of Gaussians (NGS), rendering quality, and training time. The default value is 30. For the playroom scene in the DeepBlending dataset, it is set to 60, while other scenes use 30. Time Complexity: The computation involves iterating over all pixels covering each Gaussian across all viewpoints. The cost is proportional to the number of covered pixels and viewpoints. It is generally faster than methods requiring complex vector operations or covariance updates during the scoring phase. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory is required as it operates on existing gradient buffers. Performance: The multi-view criterion yields an average improvement of 0.67 dB in PSNR and 0.028 in LPIPS compared to standard methods, while using 28% fewer primitives at the same rendering time. Comparison: In the "garden" scene, the standard positional-gradient rule produces 240,075 primitives with a PSNR of 26.83 and LPIPS of 0.1303. The multi-view criterion produces 148,658 primitives with a PSNR of 27.06 and LPIPS of 0.1247. Strengths: Resolves the invalid arithmetic issue in multi-view training; reduces primitive count without sacrificing quality. Limitations: Requires access to per-pixel gradients for all viewpoints in the batch. Usage: Applied during the teacher training phase to control primitive count and distribution. The method was proposed to address a fundamental incompatibility between standard 3D Gaussian Splatting's densification strategy and multi-view training pipelines. Standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) relies on summing 2D positional gradients, which is valid for single-view or independent-view updates but fails when gradients from different view spaces are summed directly. The Multi-View Density Control Criterion was introduced in "Efficient multi-view training for 3D Gaussian Splatting" as a space-independent error metric. It is also referenced in the context of ultrafast spatial texture-atlas splatting and loss-guided density control. name: Complexity-Aware Adaptive Density Control
head: Complexity-Aware Density Control, Complexity-Aware Level of Details, Complexity-Guided Relocation
body: Complexity-Aware Adaptive Density Control is a training optimization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces opacity-only heuristics with a composite importance score incorporating image complexity, scale, and opacity. It solves the problem where standard densification concentrates primitives in already-resolved high-opacity regions while neglecting unresolved complex areas, and where low-complexity regions degrade prematurely under budget constraints. It sets itself apart from siblings like Multi-View Density Control Criterion by explicitly modeling spatial complexity as a surrogate for reconstruction error to guide relocation and pruning, rather than relying solely on gradient magnitude or multi-view consistency. The method operates by maintaining a per-Gaussian complexity field, updating it online during training, and using it to bias both the relocation of new primitives and the retention of existing ones under varying capacity budgets. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians G = \{gj\}. Training view i with image Ii. Rendered image E(Ii^\tau) at capacity factor \tau \in (0, 1]. Rendered image E(Ii^{full}) at full capacity \tau=1. Complexity map Ci^{2D} for view i, computed via delentropy. Outputs: Updated complexity values Cj for each Gaussian. Relocation probabilities p(gj) for densification. Importance scores S(gj) for pruning/retention. Gaussian gj: \muj \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \alphaj \in [0, 1]: Opacity. s(gj) \in [0, 1]: Max-normalized scale (derived from covariance eigenvalues). Cj \in \mathbb{R}: Raw complexity value (exponential moving average). \tilde{C}j \in [0, 1]: Min-max normalized complexity. 1. Complexity Map Computation: For the current training view i, compute the 2D complexity map Ci^{2D}(u) using delentropy. 2. Complexity Update: For each Gaussian gj whose mean \muj projects into the current view's frustum: Project \muj to image plane coordinates uj = \pii(\muj). Retrieve complexity Ci^{2D}(uj). Update Cj using exponential moving average with learning rate \eta \in (0, 1]: Cj \leftarrow (1 - \eta) Cj + \eta Ci^{2D}(uj) Initialize Cj = 0 for new Gaussians. 3. Normalization: Compute \tilde{C}j by min-max normalizing Cj across the current batch or training history to the range [0, 1]. 4. Relocation Sampling (Densification): When densifying, sample a source Gaussian gj to split/relocate with probability: p(gj) = \alphaj \cdot \exp(\tilde{C}j) Apply complexity dropout: with probability \delta = 0.2, set \tilde{C}j = 0 before computing p(gj). This prevents collapse onto fixed complex regions by allowing opacity-only scoring for a fraction of candidates. 5. Importance Scoring (Pruning/LoD): For a given capacity budget \tau, compute the importance score S(gj) to determine retention: S(gj) = \alphaj + \lambda \cdot \frac{s(gj)}{\exp(\tilde{C}j)} \lambda = 2 is a fixed scalar weight. Gaussians with the highest S(gj) are retained up to the budget limit. 6. Variance Loss Minimization: To ensure uniform degradation across levels of detail, minimize the spatial variance of the reconstruction error residual: \Deltai(u) = E(Ii^{full})(u) - E(Ii^{\tau})(u) L{var} = \text{Var}{u \in \Omega} \Deltai(u) The total training loss combines L1+D-SSIM on full and budgeted renders with this variance term: \mathcal{L}{total} = \text{Average}(\mathcal{L}{L1+D-SSIM}) + \lambda{var} L{var} \lambda{var} is a hyperparameter balancing the variance term. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def updatecomplexity(gaussians, viewi, eta): """ Update complexity field for Gaussians visible in viewi. """ # Compute 2D complexity map for the view (delentropy) complexitymap = computedelentropycomplexity(viewi.image) for g in gaussians: # Project mean to image plane u = projecttoimage(g.mean, viewi.cameraparams) # Check if within frustum if isinfrustum(u, viewi): # Get complexity at pixel c2d = complexitymap[u.y, u.x] # Exponential moving average update g.complexityraw = (1 - eta) g.complexityraw + eta c2d def normalizecomplexity(gaussians): """ Min-max normalize complexity to [0, 1]. """ if not gaussians: return minc = min(g.complexityraw for g in gaussians) maxc = max(g.complexityraw for g in gaussians) rangec = maxc - minc if rangec == 0: for g in gaussians: g.complexitynorm = 0.0 else: for g in gaussians: g.complexitynorm = (g.complexityraw - minc) / rangec def samplerelocation(gaussians, dropoutprob=0.2): """ Sample a Gaussian for relocation/densification based on complexity-aware probability. """ if not gaussians: return None # Apply dropout: set complexity to 0 with probability dropoutprob weights = [] for g in gaussians: cnorm = g.complexitynorm if np.random.rand() < dropoutprob: cnorm = 0.0 # p(g) = alpha exp(Ctilde) w = g.opacity np.exp(cnorm) weights.append(w) # Normalize weights to sum to 1 totalw = sum(weights) if totalw == 0: return gaussians[np.random.randint(len(gaussians))] probs = [w / totalw for w in weights] idx = np.random.choice(len(gaussians), p=probs) return gaussians[idx] def computeimportancescore(gaussian, lambdaweight=2.0): """ Compute importance score for pruning/LoD selection. S(g) = alpha + lambda scale / exp(Ctilde) """ cnorm = gaussian.complexitynorm # Avoid division by zero or extreme values if exp is too large/small # Note: exp(Ctilde) is in [1, e] since Ctilde in [0, 1] score = gaussian.opacity + lambdaweight (gaussian.scalenormalized / np.exp(cnorm)) return score def selectprimitivesforbudget(gaussians, budgetratio): """ Select Gaussians to retain based on importance score and budget. """ if not gaussians: return [] # Compute scores scoredgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: s = computeimportancescore(g) scoredgaussians.append((s, g)) # Sort by score descending scoredgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) # Select top K k = int(len(gaussians) budgetratio) selected = [g for s, g in scoredgaussians[:k]] return selected def computevarianceloss(renderfull, renderbudgeted): """ Compute spatial variance of reconstruction error residual. Lvar = Var(E(Ifull) - E(Ibudgeted)) """ residual = renderfull - renderbudgeted # Variance over all pixels u in Omega varloss = np.var(residual) return varloss \eta \in (0, 1]: Learning rate for complexity exponential moving average. \lambda = 2: Fixed scalar weight for the scale term in importance score. \delta = 0.2: Complexity dropout probability. \lambda{var}: Weight for the variance loss term (Not given in the sources). Complexity Collapse: Without dropout (\delta=0), Gaussians may collapse onto fixed complex regions. Dropout \delta=0.2 mitigates this. Normalization Range: \tilde{C}j must be normalized to [0, 1] for the exponential term to behave as intended (mimicking exponential growth of particle count). Budget Variation: The scoring function assumes the optimizer varies \tau during training. At \tau=1, all primitives are available; at \tau<1, only top-scoring primitives are used, which may shift optimization support. Scale Normalization: s(gj) must be max-normalized to ensure consistent weighting across different scenes or training stages. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for computing delentropy complexity maps and updating per-Gaussian complexity fields. Complexity update is O(N) per view where N is the number of Gaussians. Relocation and pruning remain O(N) due to sorting/scoring. Memory Complexity: Requires storing Cj and \tilde{C}j per Gaussian, adding minimal memory overhead. Performance: Outperforms baselines like OctreeGS, FlexGS, 3DGS-MCMC, LightGaussian, and MGS at lower capacity budgets (e.g., 10%, 1%, 0.1%) while maintaining comparable quality at full capacity. Strengths: Prevents premature degradation of low-complexity regions; ensures uniform degradation across LoDs; avoids over-concentration in complex areas. Limitations: Requires computing delentropy complexity maps; sensitive to normalization of complexity and scale; requires varying \tau during training for optimal LoD-awareness. When to Use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models with variable capacity budgets or when uniform quality degradation across different levels of detail is required. When Not to Use: If computational resources are extremely limited and delentropy computation is prohibitive; if fixed capacity is used without LoD variation. Complexity-Aware Adaptive Density Control was introduced in the paper "KoalaGS: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting". It addresses limitations in standard 3DGS variants that rely on opacity as a proxy for reconstruction error, which leads to under-served unresolved regions and poor degradation at low budgets. The method builds on the idea that complexity is a surrogate for reconstruction error and integrates it into the density control mechanism for both densification and pruning. name: Average Contribution Criterion
head: Ours
body: The Average Contribution Criterion is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that determines whether a Gaussian should be split or cloned based on its mean blending weight per view rather than a binary view count. It solves the problem of occlusion bias inherent in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting criterion, where fully occluded views inflate the denominator and dilute the average gradient signal. By weighting views by their actual contribution, it prevents occluded views from biasing the average downward and produces fewer Gaussians at matched quality compared to pixel-count-based methods. The method computes a scalar densification score \gammai^{\text{Ours}} for each Gaussian i by aggregating positional gradients across all views in which the Gaussian contributes, normalized by the sum of its mean blending weights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: For a Gaussian i, the set of views Vi where it contributes to at least one pixel. For each view v \in Vi, the per-pixel blending weights w{i,p} and the gradient of the training loss with respect to the Gaussian's projected screen-space mean \mui. Output: A scalar score \gammai^{\text{Ours}}. If \gammai^{\text{Ours}} > \tau, the Gaussian is marked for densification (split or clone). Data Structures: N{i,v}: Integer count of pixels in view v where Gaussian i contributes (w{i,p} > 0). w{i,p}: Scalar blending weight for pixel p in view v, defined as w{i,p} = \alpha{i,p} T{i,p}, where \alpha{i,p} is opacity and T{i,p} is transmittance. g{i,v}: 2D vector gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mui} accumulated over pixels in view v. Formulas: 1. Per-pixel gradient factorization: The per-view gradient is the sum of weight-independent vectors s{i,p} scaled by blending weights: g{i,v} = \sum{p \in \text{pixels in } v} w{i,p} s{i,p} where s{i,p} combines photometric residual, geometric steering, and local contrast. 2. Mean blending weight: The average contribution of Gaussian i in view v: \bar{w}{i,v} = \frac{1}{N{i,v}} \sum{p \in \text{pixels in } v} w{i,p} Note: \bar{w}{i,v} \in 0, 1). 3. Densification Score: \gammai^{\text{Ours}} = \frac{1}{1 + \sum{v \in Vi} \bar{w}{i,v}} \sum{v \in Vi} \|g{i,v}\| The denominator includes a floor constant of 1 to prevent unbounded scores for rarely observed Gaussians. Parameters: Densification Threshold (\tau): 0.002. This value was calibrated on the Mip-NeRF360 sweep subset (bicycle, bonsai, counter, garden) and kept fixed for all experiments. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeaveragecontributionscore(gaussiani, views): """ Computes the densification score for a Gaussian based on average contribution. Args: gaussiani: Object containing properties of the Gaussian. views: List of view indices where gaussiani contributes to at least one pixel. Returns: float: The densification score gammaiOurs. """ sumgradientmagnitudes = 0.0 summeanblendingweights = 0.0 for v in views: # 1. Compute per-view gradient g{i,v} # g{i,v} is accumulated over pixels p where w{i,p} > 0 # g{i,v} = sump (w{i,p} s{i,p}) # s{i,p} is the weight-independent vector (photometric residual, geometric steering, local contrast) # Implementation note: This is typically available from the backward pass of the rasterizer. giv = computeperviewgradient(gaussiani, v) # 2. Calculate mean blending weight wbar{i,v} # Identify pixels p in view v where gaussiani contributes contributingpixels = getcontributingpixels(gaussiani, v) Niv = len(contributingpixels) if Niv == 0: continue # Should not happen if v is in 'views' sumw = 0.0 for p in contributingpixels: # w{i,p} = alpha{i,p} T{i,p} wip = getblendingweight(gaussiani, p) sumw += wip wbariv = sumw / Niv # 3. Accumulate for the final score sumgradientmagnitudes += norm(giv) summeanblendingweights += wbariv # 4. Compute final score with denominator floor of 1 denominator = 1.0 + summeanblendingweights score = sumgradientmagnitudes / denominator return score Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Denominator Floor: Without the constant 1 in the denominator, rarely observed Gaussians (where \sumv \bar{w}{i,v} \to 0) would receive unbounded scores, causing training divergence. Occlusion Awareness: The criterion is intrinsically occlusion-aware because \bar{w}{i,v} contains transmittance T{i,p}. Partially occluded views have lower \bar{w}{i,v}, reducing their influence on the denominator and preventing the dilution effect seen in view-count methods. Independence from Footprint: Using mean blending weight \bar{w}{i,v} instead of total weight or pixel count ensures the criterion is independent of screen-space footprint area. This avoids suppressing large Gaussians that require densification. Uses a different metric for view contribution. Choose when multi-view consistency is prioritized over per-view blending weight averaging. Incorporates scene complexity metrics. Choose when adaptive thresholds based on local geometry complexity are needed. Time Complexity: The criterion requires iterating over all views where the Gaussian contributes and summing per-pixel blending weights. This is O(N{pixels}) per Gaussian per densification step, similar to the [original 3DGS criterion but with slightly more overhead due to weight averaging. Memory Complexity: No additional significant memory overhead beyond storing per-view gradient accumulations and blending weight sums. Performance: On Zip-NeRF scenes (30k iterations), it achieves 25.81 PSNR, 0.830 SSIM, 0.330 LPIPS, 0.106 GMSD using 1.133 million Gaussians in 29.9 minutes. On 210k iterations, it achieves 26.60 PSNR, 0.852 SSIM, 0.282 LPIPS, 0.087 GMSD using 2.495 million Gaussians in 262.9 minutes. Scalability: The method is self-limiting and does not require distance scaling guard rails. It stays bounded even at 300k iterations (2.75M Gaussians) while continuing to improve LPIPS and GMSD. Strengths: Produces the fewest Gaussians (roughly 55–75% of other criteria's counts) at matched quality. Avoids the instability and over-densification of raw pixel-count criteria. Independent of scene extent, making it robust for large scenes. Limitations: Requires calibration of the threshold (0.002) on a subset. The score scale is different from the original 3DGS criterion, necessitating threshold recalibration. When to use: When occlusion is significant, when training stability is a concern (avoiding divergence), and when compactness (fewer Gaussians) is desired without sacrificing quality. When not to use: If strict compatibility with the original 3DGS threshold is required without recalibration. The Average Contribution Criterion was introduced in "Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses limitations in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting densification criterion, which weights every view equally regardless of visibility, and pixel-count-based criteria (like PixelGS) which entangle view visibility with screen-space footprint. The method was developed to provide a more faithful measure of observation by using mean blending weights, which are independent of coverage and occlusion-aware. name: Frequency-Aware Adaptive Splat Spawning

body: Frequency-Aware Adaptive Splat Spawning is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that spawns new splats in regions of high-frequency content or low opacity (holes) by scoring pixels based on frequency gaps and alpha gaps, then sampling new splats from the nearest existing cloud points. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly incorporating image frequency analysis into the splitting decision, targeting detail loss rather than just gradient magnitude or opacity thresholds. Inputs: Rendered color image I{pred} and alpha map \alpha{pred} for the current training step. Current set of 3D Gaussians (splats) with attributes: means \mu, scales s, rotations q, colors c, opacities \alpha. Camera extrinsics W2C (rotation R, translation t) and intrinsics K (fx, fy, cx, cy). Current training step t{step} and total iterations T{total}. Target splat count N{target} (default 500,000 if \le 0). Outputs: Updated set of 3D Gaussians with new splats added via splitting existing ones. Data Structures: Splats: List of objects or tensors containing \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, s \in \mathbb{R}^3, q \in \mathbb{R}^4, c \in \mathbb{R}^3, \alpha \in \mathbb{R}. Score Map: 2D tensor of size H \times W storing spawn scores per pixel. Steps: 1. Check Spawning Conditions: Proceed only if: t{step} > 100 t{step} \pmod{50} == 0 Current splat count N{curr} < N{target} t{step} < 0.85 \times T{total} 2. Compute Spawn Scores: Initialize splatscores tensor of zeros, size matching the number of splats. Project all splat centers to 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) in camera space: \mu{cam} = R \mu + t z = \mu{cam, z} u = \left\lfloor \frac{\mu{cam, x}}{z} fx + cx \right\rfloor v = \left\lfloor \frac{\mu{cam, y}}{z} fy + cy \right\rfloor Clamp z \ge 0.1. Filter valid splats where u, v are within image bounds and z > 0.1. Compute Frequency Gap: \text{freq\gap} = \text{ComputeFrequencyGap}(I{pred}, I{gt}) Note: The exact formula for ComputeFrequencyGap is not provided in the source, but it measures high-frequency discrepancies between predicted and ground truth images. Compute Alpha Gap: \text{alpha\gap} = \max(0, 0.5 - \alpha{pred}) Note: \alpha{pred} is the rendered alpha map. Assign scores to valid splats based on their projected pixel coordinates: \text{splat\scores}[i] = \text{freq\gap}[ui, vi] + 2.0 \times \text{alpha\gap}[ui, vi] 3. Select Splats to Split: Calculate number of splats to split: N{split} = \min\left(\left\lfloor \frac{N{curr}}{10} \right\rfloor, N{target} - N{curr}, 5000\right) Select top N{split} splats with highest scores using torch.topk. Let these indices be I{split}. 4. Split Selected Splats: For each parent splat p \in I{split}: Find the longest axis of the Gaussian: a{long} = \arg\maxj(sp[j]) Compute the world-space direction of the longest axis: d{world} = Rp[:, a{long}] where Rp is the rotation matrix derived from quaternion qp. Compute offset distance: d{offset} = \exp(sp[a{long}]) \times 0.5 Compute offset vector: \Delta = d{world} \times d{offset} Create two child splats (parent and child): Means: \mu{parent} = \mup + \Delta \mu{child} = \mup - \Delta Scales: Halve the longest axis in log space: s'{parent}[j] = s'{child}[j] = sp[j] \quad \text{for } j \neq a{long} s'{parent}[a{long}] = s'{child}[a{long}] = sp[a{long}] - \ln(2) Note: The source subtracts 0.693 (\ln 2) from the scale value, implying scales are stored in log space or the operation is applied to log-scales. If scales are linear, this operation is invalid. Given the context of "subtracting 0.693", it is assumed scales are in log space or the source implies log-scale representation. Other Attributes: Copy q, c, \alpha from parent to both children. Replace the parent splat with the two children in the splat list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: splats: Dict of tensors for splat attributes (means, scales, quats, colors, opacities). imagespred: Rendered color images (B, H, W, 3). imagesgt: Ground truth color images (B, H, W, 3). alphaspred: Rendered alpha maps (B, H, W, 1). w2c: World-to-camera transformation (B, 3, 4) [R|t]. intrinsic: Camera intrinsic matrix (B, 3, 3). step: Current training step. totaliters: Total training iterations. targetsplats: Target number of splats. Returns: Updated splats dict. """ # 1. Check conditions if step <= 100 or step % 50 != 0 or step >= 0.85 totaliters: return splats ncurr = splats['means'].shape[0] if ncurr >= targetsplats: return splats # 2. Compute scores # Project splat centers to 2D means = splats['means'] # (N, 3) Rcam = w2c[:,:3,:3] # (B, 3, 3) tcam = w2c[:,:3, 3] # (B, 3) # Assuming single camera for simplicity, or batched. # The source implies a single view or per-view processing. # We'll assume batch dimension B=1 for the main logic, or loop over B. # For clarity, we assume single camera parameters for the spawn logic # as the source code snippet uses single extrinsic/intrinsic. # Transform means to camera space meanscam = means @ Rcam[0].T + tcam[0] # (N, 3) z = meanscam[:, 2] # Clamp z z = torch.clamp(z, min=0.1) # Project to 2D fx, fy = intrinsic[0, 0, 0], intrinsic[0, 1, 1] cx, cy = intrinsic[0, 0, 2], intrinsic[0, 1, 2] u = ((meanscam[:, 0] / z) fx + cx).long() v = ((meanscam[:, 1] / z) fy + cy).long() # Filter valid splats H, W = imagespred.shape[1:3] validmask = (u >= 0) & (u < W) & (v >= 0) & (v < H) & (z > 0.1) if not torch.any(validmask): return splats # Compute frequency gap and alpha gap # Note: ComputeFrequencyGap is not defined in source. # We assume it returns a tensor of same shape as imagespred[...0] freqgap = computefrequencygap(imagespred, imagesgt) # Placeholder for undefined function alphagap = torch.relu(0.5 - alphaspred.squeeze(-1)) # (B, H, W) # Initialize scores splatscores = torch.zeros(ncurr, device=means.device) # Assign scores to valid splats # Flatten indices for indexing validu = u[validmask] validv = v[validmask] # Accumulate scores (if multiple splats project to same pixel, sum? Source says "set score") # Source: "set score to freqgap at projected pixel coordinates" # This implies a map-based accumulation or direct assignment. # We'll use scatteradd to handle overlaps if any, or direct assignment if unique. # Given the source uses "set", we assume direct assignment or max. # Let's use scatteradd for robustness. freqgapval = freqgap[0, validv, validu] # (Nvalid,) alphagapval = alphagap[0, validv, validu] # (Nvalid,) scores = freqgapval + 2.0 alphagapval # Scatter scores to splatscores splatscores[validmask] = scores # 3. Select splats to split nsplit = min(ncurr // 10, targetsplats - ncurr, 5000) if nsplit <= 0: return splats, topkidx = torch.topk(splatscores, nsplit) splitidx = topkidx[splatscores[topkidx] > 0] # Ensure positive scores if splitidx.numel() == 0: return splats # 4. Split splats parentmeans = means[splitidx] parentscales = splats['scales'][splitidx] parentquats = splats['quats'][splitidx] parentcolors = splats['colors'][splitidx] parentopacities = splats['opacities'][splitidx] # Find longest axis longestax = torch.argmax(parentscales, dim=-1) # (Nsplit,) # Get rotation matrices Rsplat = quattorotmat(parentquats) # (Nsplit, 3, 3) # Direction of longest axis axdir = Rsplat[torch.arange(len(splitidx)),:, longestax] # (Nsplit, 3) # Offset distance offsetdist = torch.exp(parentscales[torch.arange(len(splitidx)), longestax]) 0.5 # Offset vector offset = axdir offsetdist.unsqueeze(-1) # (Nsplit, 3) # New means newmeansparent = parentmeans + offset newmeanschild = parentmeans - offset # New scales (halve longest axis in log space) # Assuming scales are in log space as per source subtraction of ln(2) newscales = parentscales.clone() newscales[torch.arange(len(splitidx)), longestax] -= np.log(2) # Concatenate newmeans = torch.cat([newmeansparent, newmeanschild], dim=0) newscales = torch.cat([newscales, newscales], dim=0) newquats = torch.cat([parentquats, parentquats], dim=0) newcolors = torch.cat([parentcolors, parentcolors], dim=0) newopacities = torch.cat([parentopacities, parentopacities], dim=0) # Remove old splats and add new ones mask = torch.ones(ncurr, dtype=torch.bool) mask[splitidx] = False remainingmeans = means[mask] remainingscales = splats['scales'][mask] remainingquats = splats['quats'][mask] remainingcolors = splats['colors'][mask] remainingopacities = splats['opacities'][mask] finalmeans = torch.cat([remainingmeans, newmeans], dim=0) finalscales = torch.cat([remainingscales, newscales], dim=0) finalquats = torch.cat([remainingquats, newquats], dim=0) finalcolors = torch.cat([remainingcolors, newcolors], dim=0) finalopacities = torch.cat([remainingopacities, newopacities], dim=0) splats['means'] = finalmeans splats['scales'] = finalscales splats['quats'] = finalquats splats['colors'] = finalcolors splats['opacities'] = finalopacities return splats def computefrequencygap(pred, gt): """Placeholder for undefined frequency gap computation.""" # Source does not define this function. # It likely involves FFT or Laplacian pyramid differences. return torch.abs(pred - gt) # Dummy implementation Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Frequency Gap Undefined: The source does not provide the implementation for ComputeFrequencyGap. Implementers must define this, e.g., using high-pass filtering or Laplacian differences. Scale Representation: The source subtracts \ln(2) from scales. This implies scales are stored in log space. If scales are linear, this operation is incorrect. Implementers must ensure consistency. Pixel Overlap: Multiple splats may project to the same pixel. The source uses "set score", which may imply overwriting. Using scatteradd or scattermax is safer to accumulate scores. Boundary Conditions: Splats projecting outside image bounds or with z \le 0.1 are ignored. Time Complexity: O(N) for projection and score computation, where N is the number of splats. Splitting is O(N{split}). Overall per-step cost is linear in N. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat attributes and score maps. Strengths: Targets both geometric detail (frequency) and coverage (alpha holes). Limitations: Depends on the quality of the frequency gap metric. May over-split in noisy regions if frequency gap is not robust.
