name: Splitting Mechanics and Density Preservation
head: Gaussian Splitting, Density-Preserving Split
body: This article defines the geometric and parametric mechanics for splitting a parent 3D Gaussian into two children and the strategies for preserving integrated density during this operation. It solves the problem of introducing high-frequency detail by replacing a single large primitive with two smaller, adjacent primitives without causing artifacts from opacity or density mismatches. It is distinguished from cloning (exact duplication) and naive splitting (which may cause loss perturbations) by explicitly adjusting child parameters to match the parent's integrated density. All splitting variants in this family share the following mechanism: 1. Axis Selection: The split occurs along the principal axis with the largest scale value \sigma{max} of the parent Gaussian [Parent]. 2. Mean Shift: The means of the two children are shifted along this axis by a distance \Delta = \alpha \cdot \sigma{max}, where \alpha is a constant [Parent]. 3. Inheritance: Rotation and Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients are copied from the parent to both children [Parent]. 4. Density Preservation: The scales and opacities of the children are adapted such that the sum of their densities approximates the parent's density, preventing artifacts. Uses standard split-and-clone. Splits "large" Gaussians by shifting means and resetting opacity/scale, clones "small" ones. Focuses on preserving integrated density during the split operation using an adaptation function that accounts for opacity variations. Discards cloning. Dual-mode approach. Splits over-reconstructed Gaussians and clones under-reconstructed ones. Uses standard density preservation approximations. Originating from the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework, splitting mechanics were introduced to densify sparse initializations. The density-preserving variant was later proposed to mitigate loss perturbations and cluster formation caused by naive splitting. name: 3DGS Adaptive Density Control
head: Dynamic Gaussian Densification, Pruning and Splitting, cloning, splitting, and pruning
body: Adaptive Density Control (ADC) is a training-time optimization mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that dynamically adjusts the number of Gaussian primitives to balance reconstruction fidelity against computational cost. It solves the problem of sparse initialization by densifying under-represented regions (via splitting and cloning) and pruning over-represented or erroneous regions (via opacity-based removal). Unlike static initialization methods, ADC continuously monitors view-space positional gradients to guide these operations, ensuring the primitive count adapts to scene complexity. It builds on Splitting Mechanics and Density Preservation for the geometric transformation of primitives. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians G. Training images and camera poses. Current iteration number t. Hyperparameters: warm-up period T{warm}, densification interval T{int}, gradient threshold T{grad}, opacity threshold T{op}, final densification iteration T{final}, opacity reset interval T{reset}, opacity reset clip C{op}. Outputs: Updated set of 3D Gaussians G' with modified count, positions, scales, opacities, and SH coefficients. Data Structures: Gaussian: A struct containing: mean: 3D position vector \mathbf{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3. scale: 3D scale vector \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (log-space or linear, typically log-space for optimization stability, but ADC decisions use linear scale magnitudes). opacity: scalar \alpha \in [0, 1]. rotation: quaternion or 3x3 rotation matrix. shcoeffs: Spherical Harmonic coefficients. accumulatedgradient: scalar, sum of view-space positional gradient magnitudes since the last densification step. visiblecount: integer, count of iterations where the Gaussian was visible (inside viewing frustum) since the last densification step. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Set accumulatedgradient and visiblecount to 0 for all Gaussians. Set current iteration t = 0. 2. Gradient Accumulation (Per Iteration): For each training iteration t: a. Render the scene and compute the loss (weighted combination of L1 and D-SSIM, weights 0.8 and 0.2 respectively). b. Compute gradients of the loss with respect to the Gaussian means \mathbf{\mu} in view space. c. For each Gaussian gi that was visible in this iteration: i. Compute the magnitude of the positional gradient: |\nabla{\mathbf{\mu}} L|. ii. Add this magnitude to gi.accumulatedgradient. iii. Increment gi.visiblecount. 3. Densification Check (Periodic): If t > T{warm} and (t - T{warm}) \pmod{T{int}} == 0 and t < T{final}: a. Selection: Identify Gaussians gi where the average gradient magnitude exceeds the threshold T{grad}: \frac{gi.\text{accumulated\gradient}}{gi.\text{visible\count}} \ge T{grad}. b. Densification Action: For each selected Gaussian gi: i. Determine if it is "large" or "small" based on its maximum scale \max(\mathbf{s}i) relative to the scene extent e{scene} (Note: Original ADC uses a fixed threshold or implicit comparison; states "large ones are split... small ones are duplicated". The specific threshold for "large" vs "small" in the original paper is not explicitly defined as a formula in, but provides a revised version using P{dense} \cdot e'{scene}. For the original ADC, we follow 's description: split if large, clone if small. The exact boundary is implementation-dependent but typically involves comparing scale to a fraction of the scene bounding box or a fixed pixel threshold in screen space. Given the lack of a precise formula in for the original, we note this as a pitfall. However, explicitly says "large ones are each split... small ones are simply duplicated". We will assume a heuristic threshold T{split} exists, often derived from scene size or fixed value. Correction: does not give a formula for the split threshold in the original ADC, only that it exists. We will describe the action based on the size classification.) If gi is classified as large: Split gi into two children using the mechanics defined in Splitting Mechanics and Density Preservation. Reset gi.accumulatedgradient and gi.visiblecount to 0. If gi is classified as small: Clone gi (duplicate in place). Reset gi.accumulatedgradient and gi.visiblecount to 0. c. Pruning: i. Identify Gaussians gi where gi.\text{opacity} < T{op}. ii. Remove these Gaussians from G. d. Reset Accumulators: For all remaining Gaussians, reset accumulatedgradient and visiblecount to 0. 4. Opacity Reset (Periodic): If t > T{warm} and t < T{final} and (t - T{warm}) \pmod{T{reset}} == 0: a. For all Gaussians gi: i. Set gi.\text{opacity} = \min(gi.\text{opacity}, C{op}). This encourages the removal of "floaters" (Gaussians with low opacity that persist) by capping their opacity, making them candidates for pruning in the next densification step. 5. Termination: Stop densification and pruning after iteration T{final}. Parameters (Typical Values from): T{warm}: 600 iterations. T{int}: 100 iterations. T{grad}: 2 \times 10^{-4}. T{op}: 0.05. T{final}: 14900 iterations. T{reset}: 3000 iterations. C{op}: 0.01. Loss weights: L1 = 0.8, D-SSIM = 0.2. Optimizer: Adam, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, \epsilon=10^{-15}. Learning Rates: Scale = 0.005, Rotation = 0.001, Opacity = 0.025 (halved from 0.05 in official codebase). Mean learning rate decays exponentially from 1.6 \times 10^{-4} to 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. SH 0th degree = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}, remaining SH = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}. SH Degree Progression: Only 0th degree at start; next higher degree enabled every 1000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Split Threshold Ambiguity: The original paper describes splitting "large" and cloning "small" Gaussians but does not provide a precise mathematical formula for the threshold distinguishing "large" from "small" in the initial release. Implementers must infer this from code or later revisions (e.g., uses P{dense} \cdot e'{scene}). This is a critical implementation gap in the textual description. Gradient Noise: View-space positional gradients can be noisy. The accumulation over T{int} iterations helps smooth this, but very small visiblecount values (e.g., 1) can lead to unstable average gradient calculations. Guard against division by zero or use a minimum count threshold. Opacity Reset Timing: Opacity resets occur every 3000 iterations. If a Gaussian's opacity is capped at 0.01, it must survive until the next pruning step (every 100 iterations) to be removed. If the pruning threshold is not met, it remains. This can lead to temporary accumulation of low-opacity Gaussians. Color Clipping: Original implementation clips colors to [0,1] during training; some variants (e.g., Faster-GS) clip only during inference to avoid zeroing gradients for pixels marginally above one. name: Age-Gated Eligibility (AGE)
head: AGE (Age-Gated Densification), cost-control gate, maturity window
body:
Age-Gated Eligibility (AGE) is a densification control mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents newly created primitives from undergoing split or clone operations immediately after birth. It solves the problem of uncontrolled cascading growth, where a Gaussian born at iteration k splits at k+1, its child splits at k+2, and so on, which inflates the primitive count, peak memory usage, and training time in dense regions. Unlike standard adaptive density control which re-evaluates all primitives regardless of age, AGE defers the first split-or-clone decision until a Gaussian has survived a fixed maturity window, thereby damping the densification cascade and bounding the final primitive budget without degrading image quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each tagged with a birth iteration bi; the current optimization iteration t; the densification cadence \Deltad; the maturity threshold T{mat}; and the gradient threshold 	aug. Output: A subset of Gaussians eligible for densification (split or clone) in the current cycle. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i in the set \mathcal{G} maintains a scalar field bi, representing the iteration index at which the Gaussian was created (for initial points) or last split/clone. Parameters: T{mat}: Maturity threshold in iterations. Default value: 200. This is fixed by design as 2\Deltad. \Deltad: Densification cadence (interval between densification steps). Default value: 100. 	aug: Threshold for accumulated 2D-projected positional gradient magnitude. Standard 3DGS value. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: At the start of training (iteration 0), tag every initial Gaussian i with its birth iteration bi = 0. 2. Iteration Loop: During optimization, every \Deltad iterations, execute the densification cycle. 3. Age Calculation: For each Gaussian i, calculate its current age 
ui(t) at iteration t using the formula: 
ui(t) = t - bi 4. Eligibility Check: Determine the mature set M(t) containing all Gaussians that have reached the maturity threshold: M(t) = \{ i: 
ui(t) \ge T{mat} \} 5. Densification: For each Gaussian i \in M(t), evaluate the standard 3DGS split-or-clone criteria: Check if the accumulated 2D-projected positional gradient magnitude exceeds 	aug. If the gradient condition is met: If the Gaussian is "large" (scale above a certain threshold), perform a split operation. If the Gaussian is "small" (scale below the threshold), perform a clone operation. For split operations, the new child Gaussians are tagged with the current iteration t as their birth iteration b{new} = t. For clone operations, the clone retains the birth iteration of the parent or is tagged with t (standard 3DGS behavior applies, but AGE only gates the eligibility to perform the operation). 6. Skip Immature: Gaussians i where 
ui(t) < T{mat} are skipped in this cycle. They are re-evaluated in the next densification opportunity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def agegateddensification(gaussians, currentiteration, Tmat, deltad, taug): """ Perform age-gated densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each having attributes: bi: birth iteration (int) accumulatedgrad: accumulated 2D-projected positional gradient magnitude (float) scale: scale metric to determine large vs small (float) opacity: opacity value (float) currentiteration: The current optimization iteration number (int) Tmat: Maturity threshold in iterations (int, default 200) deltad: Densification cadence (int, default 100) taug: Gradient threshold for densification (float) Returns: Updated list of Gaussians (with new children added if split/clone occurred) """ if currentiteration % deltad != 0: return gaussians finalgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: age = currentiteration - g.bi if age < Tmat: finalgaussians.append(g) continue if g.accumulatedgrad > taug: if islarge(g.scale): children = splitgaussian(g, currentiteration) finalgaussians.extend(children) else: clone = clonegaussian(g, currentiteration) finalgaussians.append(clone) else: finalgaussians.append(g) return finalgaussians def islarge(scale): # Standard 3DGS scale threshold check return scale > 0.01 def splitgaussian(g, t): # Standard 3DGS split: creates two children with bi = t return [Gaussian(bi=t, scale=g.scale / 1.6, opacity=g.opacity / 2.0), Gaussian(bi=t, scale=g.scale / 1.6, opacity=g.opacity / 2.0)] def clonegaussian(g, t): # Standard 3DGS clone: creates one child with bi = t return Gaussian(bi=t, scale=g.scale, opacity=g.opacity) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initial Primitives: Under the standard 3DGS schedule, densification begins at iteration 500. Since T{mat}=200, initial primitives (tagged bi=0) have an age of 500, which is \ge T{mat}. Thus, initial primitives are already mature at the first densification cycle. Early Densification Schedules: If a training schedule densifies earlier than iteration 500 (e.g., at iteration 100), initial primitives would be immature (100 - 0 < 200). The tag bi is retained so AGE remains well-defined for such schedules. Cascade Prevention: Without AGE, a Gaussian born at step k can split at k+1, its child at k+2, causing an uncontrolled cascade. AGE ensures that with T{mat}=200 and \Deltad=100, a Gaussian can split or clone at most once every two densification cycles, converting an unbounded cascade into controlled refinement. The Spawn Gate is a mechanism that predicts the survival probability of a Gaussian spawn candidate at birth time to veto low-survival candidates, thereby controlling the peak population size during training. It sets itself apart from heuristic densification rules by using a learned predictor to rank candidates, ensuring a deterministic peak-memory reduction without degrading final image quality. Time and Memory Complexity: AGE adds no architectural change and no per-iteration overhead beyond a single age comparison (
ui(t) \ge T{mat}) per Gaussian. The added cost is not an early-training overhead: the first 500 iterations take at most one minute in every scene. Measured Performance: On standard benchmarks, enabling AGE reduces the final Gaussian count from 3.45 M to 3.15 M (an 8.7% reduction). Training time is lowered by 2.4 minutes (from 31.8 to 29.4 minutes). Peak memory is reduced by 0.47 GB (from 6.04 to 5.57 GB). Image quality remains unchanged within measurement noise (PSNR +0.05 dB, SSIM +0.001, LPIPS +0.001). AGE lowers the Gaussian count during densification by 16–23% relative to DART alone at iteration 5k on scenes like bicycle, stump, and drjohnson. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Bounding the primitive budget, reducing memory and training time, preventing cascading splits in dense regions, and acting as a general control independent of how the initial cloud was formed (works with or without DART augmentation). Limitations: Requires tuning of T{mat} and \Deltad (though fixed by design in the source). It does not improve quality directly but preserves it while reducing cost. When to Use: Use AGE when training 3D Gaussian Splatting models to control memory usage and training time, especially when using denser initialization strategies like DART that might otherwise inflate the primitive count. Age-Gated Eligibility (AGE) was introduced in the paper "DART-3DGS: Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It is designed to work in conjunction with Distance-Aware Replication Training (DART) to bound the primitive budget that DART's denser initialization might otherwise inflate. AGE acts as a cost-control gate, distinct from relocation [9] and gradient-criterion reweighting [4]. DART-3DGS: Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13705904, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Spawn Gate
head: Gaussian spawn gate, Learned gate, Leave-one-scene-out gate, Rank veto, Survival prediction gate
body: The Spawn Gate is a mechanism that predicts the survival probability of a Gaussian spawn candidate at birth time to veto low-survival candidates, thereby controlling the peak population size during training. It sets itself apart from heuristic densification rules by using a learned predictor to rank candidates, ensuring a deterministic peak-memory reduction without degrading final image quality. The method operates during the densification window, specifically monitoring spawn events to veto candidates before they are instantiated. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of spawn candidates Ct generated at densification step t. Each candidate j is associated with a parent Gaussian j. Output: A subset of instantiated candidates C't = Ct \setminus Vt, where Vt is the set of vetoed candidates. Data Structures For each candidate j spawned from parent j at step t, a feature vector x{j,t} is assembled. The layout is: x{j,t} = [\bar{g}j, \alphaj, \bar{s}j, \tauj, dj, \ellj, t, 1{[split]}] Where: \bar{g}j: View-space positional gradient magnitude averaged over dj views that observed the parent. \alphaj: Parent opacity. \bar{s}j: Mean of the parent’s three scale axes. \tauj: Parent’s age in iterations since its own birth. dj: Densification denominator, the number of views that accumulated gradient onto the parent. \ellj: Child’s LOD level (parent’s level for a clone, one level finer for a split). t: Current training iteration. 1{[split]}: Binary indicator, 1 if the candidate is a split, 0 if it is a clone. Parameters \rho: Veto fraction. Typical value: 0.6. This value is chosen as the largest reclaim inside the quality-neutral flat region; \rho \le 0.6 matches ungated quality, while decline appears at \rho \ge 0.75. Onset iteration: The iteration at which the gate activates. Typical value: 24k. This is fixed by the sharp drop in survival rates observed after iteration 24k. Gate window: The gate is active during the interval [24k, 32k). Algorithm 1. Monitor Spawns: During the gate window [24k, 32k), collect all new spawn candidates Ct at each densification step t. 2. Feature Extraction: For each candidate j \in Ct, extract the features \bar{g}j, \alphaj, \bar{s}j, \tauj, dj, \ellj from the parent Gaussian and the current iteration t. Determine if the candidate is a split or clone to set 1{[split]}. 3. Prediction: Query a pre-trained gradient-boosted tree predictor f with the feature vector x{j,t} to obtain a survival score pj: pj = f(x{j,t}) \in [0, 1] The predictor f is trained on lineage data from other scenes (leave-one-scene-out) to ensure transferability. 4. Ranking: Rank all candidates in Ct by their predicted survival score pj in ascending order. 5. Veto Selection: Select the top \lceil \rho |Ct| \rceil candidates with the lowest predicted survival scores to form the veto set Vt: Vt = \arg \min{S \subseteq Ct, |S|=\lceil \rho |Ct| \rceil} \sum{j \in S} pj Vetoing by rank ensures the gate depends only on the ordering of f, allowing a single predictor to transfer across scenes with different candidate volumes and score calibrations. 6. Instantiation: Instantiate only the remaining candidates: C't = Ct \setminus Vt Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spawngate(candidates, predictor, rho, currentiteration): """ Veto low-survival spawn candidates based on a learned predictor. Args: candidates: List of spawn candidate objects. Each object has attributes: parent: The parent Gaussian object. issplit: Boolean, True if split, False if clone. predictor: A gradient-boosted tree model with a predict() method. rho: Float, fraction of candidates to veto (e.g., 0.6). currentiteration: Integer, current training step. Returns: List of instantiated candidates. """ scoredcandidates = [] for cand in candidates: parent = cand.parent # Extract features gbar = parent.avgviewspacegradientmagnitude alpha = parent.opacity sbar = (parent.scalex + parent.scaley + parent.scalez) / 3.0 tau = currentiteration - parent.birthiteration d = parent.densificationdenominator l = parent.lodlevel + 1 if cand.issplit else parent.lodlevel # Assemble feature vector issplitval = 1.0 if cand.issplit else 0.0 x = [gbar, alpha, sbar, tau, d, l, currentiteration, issplitval] # Predict survival probability p = predictor.predict(x) scoredcandidates.append({ 'candidate': cand, 'score': p }) # Sort by predicted survival score ascending (lowest first) scoredcandidates.sort(key=lambda item: item['score']) # Determine number of candidates to veto: ceil(rho |Ct|) numtoveto = math.ceil(rho len(scoredcandidates)) numtoveto = max(0, min(numtoveto, len(scoredcandidates))) # Veto the bottom candidates vetoedindices = set(range(numtoveto)) instantiated = [] for i, item in enumerate(scoredcandidates): if i not in vetoedindices: instantiated.append(item['candidate']) return instantiated Edge Cases and Pitfalls Threshold vs. Rank: Using a fixed probability threshold instead of rank-based vetoing causes the actual veto rate to vary per scene because base survival rates differ across scenes. Rank vetoing ensures a deterministic peak-population cut. Timing: Delaying the veto decision beyond spawn time forfeits the peak-memory benefit because non-surviving spawns are allocated for the delay duration \Delta. Waiting until simplification recovers no peak. Predictor Transfer: The predictor must be trained on scenes other than the evaluation scene (leave-one-scene-out) to ensure it generalizes. Transfer is harder across domain gaps (e.g., synthetic scenes like MatrixCity). Memory Reduction: On the Building scene with \rho=0.6 and onset 24k, peak memory is reduced from 10.89M (ungated) to 9.23M Gaussians, with PSAR remaining flat at 23.46 dB. On Rubble, the learned gate captures 98% of the peak-population cut achievable by a perfect-foresight oracle, while matching the oracle's quality. Quality Impact: All veto rates \rho \le 0.6 match the ungated quality, so vetoing up to 60% of late candidates is quality-neutral; a measurable decline appears only at \rho \ge 0.75. Performance: The predictor achieves a held-out AUC of 0.748–0.787 when trained and tested on the same scene's lineage. Leave-one-scene-out predictors achieve an AUC of 0.750–0.770 on unseen scenes, dropping to 0.702 on the synthetic MatrixCity scene. Comparison: The learned gate (AUC 0.750–0.770) significantly outperforms random vetoing. Random vetoing discards true survivors at the 21.2% base rate, while the learned gate discards them at 11.1%, preserving quality. Strengths: Deterministic peak-population control; transferable across scenes; quality-neutral at optimal settings. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained predictor; performance degrades on out-of-distribution scenes (e.g., synthetic vs. real); sensitive to the onset iteration choice. The Spawn Gate was introduced in the BlitzGS paper. It addresses the issue of transient peak population sizes during 3D Gaussian Splatting training, which dictate per-GPU memory limits. The method leverages the observation that survival to the final model is predictable from spawn-time features, particularly in the late densification window where survival rates drop sharply. name: Density-preserving Gaussian splitting
head: BOGausS splitting, SplitAdaptation
body: Density-preserving Gaussian splitting is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that modifies child parameters to ensure the sum of their densities approximates the parent's density, thereby preventing loss function perturbations and Gaussian clustering. Unlike standard 3DGS splitting which may cause instability, this method discards cloning operations entirely and relies solely on splitting with learned opacity and size adaptations. Inputs: Parent Gaussian parameters: mean \mu{p}, scale \sigma{p} (vector), rotation R{p}, opacity o{p}, and spherical harmonic coefficients C{p}. Splitting constant \alpha = 0.3. Learned adaptation function SplitAdaptation. Outputs: Two child Gaussians with updated means, scales, opacities, and inherited rotation/SH coefficients. Data Structures: Gaussian parameters are stored as standard 3DGS attributes: 3D mean, 3D scale (log-space or linear), 4D quaternion rotation, scalar opacity, and SH coefficients. Steps: 1. Axis Selection: Identify the principal axis with the largest scale value \sigma{max} of the parent Gaussian [Parent]. 2. Mean Shift: Calculate the shift distance \Delta = \alpha \cdot \sigma{max}. Create two new means \mu{c1} and \mu{c2} by shifting the parent mean \mu{p} along the selected axis by +\Delta and -\Delta respectively. 3. Parameter Adaptation: Compute the child scale \sigma{c} and opacity o{c} using the learned offline function: (\sigma{c}, o{c}) = SplitAdaptation(\sigma{p}, o{p}) This function ensures the resulting density of the sum of the two children is close to the density of the mother Gaussian. 4. Inheritance: Copy the parent's rotation R{p} and spherical harmonic coefficients C{p} to both children [Parent]. 5. Cloning Discard: Do not perform cloning operations; rely exclusively on splitting for densification. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def densitypreservingsplit(parentgaussian, alpha=0.3): """ Performs density-preserving splitting on a parent Gaussian. Args: parentgaussian: Object containing mean (mu), scale (sigma), rotation (R), opacity (o), and SH coefficients (C). alpha: Constant for mean shift magnitude (default 0.3). Returns: List of two child Gaussian objects. """ # 1. Axis Selection: Find axis with largest scale # sigma is typically a vector [sx, sy, sz] maxscaleidx = argmax(parentgaussian.sigma) sigmamax = parentgaussian.sigma[maxscaleidx] # 2. Mean Shift # Create basis vector for the selected axis axisvector = [0, 0, 0] axisvector[maxscaleidx] = 1.0 shiftdistance = alpha sigmamax # Shift means by +shift and -shift along the axis muc1 = parentgaussian.mu + (axisvector shiftdistance) muc2 = parentgaussian.mu - (axisvector shiftdistance) # 3. Parameter Adaptation # Apply learned offline adaptation function # Note: SplitAdaptation is a learned function, not a simple formula sigmac, oc = SplitAdaptation(parentgaussian.sigma, parentgaussian.o) # 4. Inheritance # Rotation and SH coefficients are copied directly Rc = parentgaussian.R Cc = parentgaussian.C # 5. Construct Children child1 = Gaussian( mu=muc1, sigma=sigmac, R=Rc, o=oc, C=Cc) child2 = Gaussian( mu=muc2, sigma=sigmac, R=Rc, o=oc, C=Cc) return [child1, child2] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Loss Perturbation: Original splitting operations cause perturbations in the loss function. This method mitigates this by adapting parameters. Clustering: The method prevents clusters of Gaussians, a problem observed in other splitting strategies. Opacity Variation: Unlike some similar mechanisms, this method explicitly accounts for opacity variations during adaptation. Complexity: The splitting operation itself is O(1) per Gaussian. The adaptation function SplitAdaptation is learned offline, so its runtime cost during training is negligible (typically a lookup or simple neural network inference). Performance: By discarding cloning operations, the method simplifies the densification process and reduces the risk of inconsistent results in indoor and outdoor scenes. It replaces opacity reset with pruning based on an opacity threshold (e.g., 1% of total Gaussians). Strengths: Prevents loss perturbations and Gaussian clustering; handles opacity variations. Limitations: Requires offline learning of the adaptation function; discards cloning which may limit some forms of densification flexibility. This method is part of the BOGausS (Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting) framework. It addresses issues identified in original 3DGS splitting, such as loss perturbations and clustering, by modifying the splitting operation to preserve density. It builds on ideas from [16] and contrasts with [17] by incorporating opacity variations. The approach is inspired by rate-distortion optimization principles for prioritizing splits. name: Adaptive Density Control (Split & Clone)
head: Clone, Split, ADC
body: Adaptive Density Control (ADC) is a densification strategy used during the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting to adjust the local density of Gaussians to match scene complexity. It solves the problem of insufficient representation in complex regions (under-densification) by either duplicating or subdividing Gaussians based on their coverage relative to the target reconstruction region. It is distinguished from its siblings by its dual-mode approach: it explicitly clones Gaussians that are too small to cover a region and splits those that are too large, whereas variants like Density-preserving Gaussian splitting or 3DGS Adaptive Density Control may drop the clone operation or use different sampling strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, each defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai (or scale \sigmai and rotation Ri), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients ci. A binary mask indicating which Gaussians are marked for densification. Output: An updated set of Gaussians where marked Gaussians are replaced by either two children (Split) or two identical copies (Clone). Data Structures: Each Gaussian G stores: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector (diagonal of covariance). q \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. c \in \mathbb{R}^k: SH coefficients. Steps: 1. Evaluate Coverage: For each Gaussian marked for densification, compare its spatial extent (coverage) against the target reconstruction region or scene extent. 2. Classify: If the Gaussian is too small (Under-Reconstruction), mark it for Clone. If the Gaussian is too large (Over-Reconstruction), mark it for Split. 3. Execute Clone: Create two new Gaussians G{c1}, G{c2} identical to the parent Gp in all attributes (\mu, \sigma, q, \alpha, c). In some implementations, slight perturbations may be added to means to prevent exact overlap, but the core definition is duplication. 4. Execute Split: Follow the Splitting Mechanics and Density Preservation [Parent] protocol: Identify the principal axis with the largest scale \sigma{max}. Shift the means of the two children along this axis by \Delta = \alpha{shift} \cdot \sigma{max} (where \alpha{shift} is a constant, typically 0.5 or similar, though exact value not given in sources [Parent]). Copy rotation and SH coefficients from parent to children [Parent]. Adapt scales and opacities to preserve density [Parent]. Note: Some variants sample child positions from the parent's distribution rather than deterministic shifts, but the standard ADC definition relies on the split mechanics described in the parent article. Parameters: Thresholds: The criteria for "too small" vs "too large" are relative to the scene extent or local detail size. Exact numerical thresholds are not given in the sources. Opacity Reset: To clear floaters, opacities may be reset to near zero (e.g., 0.01) every 3000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Bias: Cloning introduces an opacity bias because two identical Gaussians with opacity \alpha effectively contribute more density than one, potentially leading to over-reconstruction. Floater Clusters: Excessive cloning on scenes where the scene extent is not well-matched to the size of detail can cause large clusters of floating artifacts. Thin Structures: Removing cloning breaks thin structures (e.g., bicycle spokes), causing them to appear fragmented. A variant that drops the clone operation entirely, using only splitting. If a Gaussian is marked for densification and is large, it is split into two downscaled children sampled from the parent's distribution. If it is small, it applies a geometrically more meaningful split procedure (e.g., from Deng et al.) rather than cloning. This approach avoids the opacity bias and floater clusters associated with cloning but requires careful handling of small Gaussians. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of marked Gaussians. Cloning is O(1) per Gaussian; Splitting is O(1) but involves more arithmetic for scale/rotation adaptation. Memory Complexity: Increases the total number of Gaussians, doubling the count for cloned/split items. Performance: On the Average-30K dataset, the full method achieves a PSNR of 26.05. Removing Split drops PSNR to 23.90, while removing Clone drops it to 25.91. This indicates Split has a larger impact on overall image quality, particularly background coherence, while Clone is critical for thin structures. Strengths: Effectively handles both under-densified (small detail) and over-densified (blurry) regions. Limitations: Cloning can introduce opacity bias and floaters if scene extent estimation is poor. The method was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper (Kerbl et al., 2023) as "Adaptive Density Control". It is a core component of the training optimization loop, allowing the static set of initial Gaussians to adapt to the geometric and textural complexity of the scene during differentiable rendering optimization. name: Pruning and Opacity Management
head: Opacity Management, Component Recycling
body: Pruning and Opacity Management is a family of training-time strategies for 3D Gaussian Splatting that controls the population of primitives \mathcal{G} to balance representation density against overfitting and computational cost. It solves the problem of unbounded Gaussian growth and the persistence of "floaters" or boundary artifacts by periodically evaluating metrics (opacity, gradient, scale) to remove redundant primitives or reinitialize them. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Significance-Aware Pruning and Principled Uncertainty Pruning by focusing on opacity thresholds, transmittance consistency during cloning, and fixed-schedule resets rather than adaptive uncertainty bounds or significance scores derived from view counts. All pruning and sparsification strategies in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by a mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. The core mechanism involves periodic evaluation of a metric per Gaussian to determine if the current representation is insufficient or redundant in a specific region. Common metrics include: 1. Gradient Magnitude: The accumulated 2D positional gradient \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v} \| \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muv^k} \|2. High gradients indicate that the Gaussian's position is not adequately minimizing the loss, suggesting a need for refinement or replacement. 2. Opacity: Low opacity \alphak < \alpha{\min} indicates a primitive contributes negligibly to the rendered image and is a candidate for pruning. 3. Scale: Excessively large scales max(sk) relative to the scene extent e{scene} indicate coarse approximations that may blur details or occlude nearby geometry. Densification operations are typically triggered every N iterations (e.g., refineEvery = 100) to allow the optimizer to stabilize. The primary operations are: Splitting: Replacing a parent Gaussian gk with N{children} children. The children's means \mu{child} are sampled from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak). The scale is typically reduced, e.g., s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}}, to increase local density. Cloning: Creating an exact copy of gk (same \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) to increase sampling frequency in high-error regions without changing the spatial footprint. Pruning: Removing Gaussians that fail to meet opacity or significance thresholds. Buffer management is critical: pruned or split Gaussians require buffer compaction or flag-based marking to maintain contiguous memory access for rasterization [Parent]. The GES Optimization Strategy is a training protocol for Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) that controls shape density by selectively pruning splats based on shape attributes, thereby eliminating the need for a variable density mechanism. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by optimizing a specific shape parameter \beta alongside position, opacity, and covariance, using a frequency-modulated loss to enhance edge fidelity. Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) is a pruning method for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes low-impact Gaussians by calculating a temporal sensitivity score approximating the second-order sensitivity to the L2 loss across all training views. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Spatially Constrained Optimization which focuses on static spatial density, by explicitly aggregating gradient information over time to identify primitives that are redundant across the temporal sequence of a dynamic scene. Opacity Split for Cloning is a method to initialize the opacity of cloned 3D Gaussian primitives to maintain transmittance consistency, preventing the cloned child from having less impact than the parent alone. It solves the problem where standard cloning in 3D Gaussian Splatting causes the parent and child to jointly attenuate the background transmittance more than the parent did alone, biasing the alpha blending process. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing specifically on the algebraic decomposition of opacity \alpha during the cloning step, rather than adjusting gradients or scales. GRay Optimization Settings define the hyperparameter configurations for training 3D Gaussian Splatting using the GRay ray-tracing renderer. Unlike standard 3DGS or 3DGRT, these settings explicitly disable opacity resets and size-based pruning. The method offers two distinct presets: GRayLQ for high-speed, low-quality training, and GRayHQ for high-quality, slower training. Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger is the standard strategy for managing the population of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of balancing scene representation density against overfitting by periodically duplicating small Gaussians with high gradients, splitting large Gaussians with high gradients, pruning low-opacity Gaussians, and resetting opacities to prevent stagnation. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a fixed iteration schedule and specific scalar thresholds for gradient magnitude and scale, rather than adaptive per-Gaussian thresholds or view-count-based criteria. It builds on Pruning and Opacity Management. Spatially Constrained Optimization is a post-processing constraint workflow applied to differentiable bitmap or Gaussian primitives to enforce full opacity rendering of target objects and clean up boundary artifacts. It solves the problem where applying an opacity loss alone forces primitives to render fully opaque but leaves low-opacity "ghost" primitives lingering on object boundaries, which degrade visual quality. It sets itself apart from standard pruning strategies by re-initializing transparent primitives rather than removing them, thereby maintaining primitive count and coverage in complex regions. Definition: A training-time component management strategy that replaces vanilla 3DGS densification/pruning by resampling low-opacity components into high-opacity ones to maintain efficiency without unbounded growth. Step: Every n training iterations: 1) Compute opacity values for all active components. 2) Construct a Multinomial distribution from these opacity values. 3) Sample components with relatively high probability to replace low-opacity ones. Parameter: n: iteration interval for recycling. Value not specified in this section; detailed recycling formulae are deferred to Sec. 5. Pitfall: Recycling must not significantly alter the rendered image. The operation is only valid when the change to the current state (rendering result) after recycling is minimal. Definition: A routine to reduce floaters and overfitting by removing triangles that explain small amounts of data within a single view. Step: During rasterization, calculate the maximum volume rendering blending weight T \cdot o (transmittance times opacity) for each triangle across all training views. Prune triangles if their maximum weight is less than threshold \tau{prune}. Additionally, prune triangles not rendered at least twice with more than one pixel of coverage. Parameter: \tau{prune}: A user-defined threshold for the maximum volume rendering blending weight below which a triangle is pruned. The concept of managing Gaussian density through pruning and densification was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper. Subsequent works have adapted these mechanisms for specific rendering primitives (e.g., triangles in) or optimization constraints (e.g., GRay, GES). The "Scooping" or recycling mechanism was proposed to address the unbounded growth of components in standard 3DGS. 3D Student Splatting and Scooping, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01960, fetched 2026-10-29 Triangle Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/3DV69130.2026.00123, fetched 2026-10-27

name: GES Optimization Strategy
head: GES Training, Generalized Exponential Splatting Optimization
body: The GES Optimization Strategy is a training protocol for Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) that controls shape density by selectively pruning splats based on shape attributes, thereby eliminating the need for a variable density mechanism. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by optimizing a specific shape parameter \beta alongside position, opacity, and covariance, using a frequency-modulated loss to enhance edge fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\} as input, where each primitive gk is defined by mean position xk \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, opacity \kappak \in \mathbb{R}, shape parameter \betak \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. Initial estimates for \Sigmak and xk are derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, while all \betak values are initialized to 2 to represent pure Gaussian splats. The output is the optimized set of parameters \{x, \Sigma, \kappa, \beta, \mathbf{c}\} for the scene representation. Data Structures: Each Gaussian gk stores the following fields in contiguous memory for rasterization: xk \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix. \kappak \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \betak \in \mathbb{R}: Shape parameter. \mathbf{c}k: Spherical harmonic coefficients. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set \betak = 2 for all k, and initialize xk, \Sigmak from SfM data. 2. Iteration Loop: For t = 1 to T{\text{total}}: a. Forward Pass: Render the image using the current \mathcal{G} and compute \mathcal{L}1, \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}}, and \mathcal{L}{\omega} using the mask M\omega derived from \omega = t/T{\text{total}}. b. Backward Pass: Compute gradients for x, \Sigma, \kappa, \beta, \mathbf{c} using stochastic gradient descent (SGD). c. Update: Apply gradient updates, using a learning rate of 0.0015 specifically for \beta. d. Periodic Operations: i. Shape Reset: If t \pmod{1000} == 0, reset shape parameters. ii. Shape Pruning: If t \pmod{100} == 0, evaluate shape attributes and prune splats whose shape metric exceeds 0.5 or whose density gradient exceeds 0.0003. iii. Other Densification: Apply opacity splitting and pruning shared with Gaussian Splitting. Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} combines an L1 metric, a Structural Similarity (SSIM) loss, and a frequency-modulated loss \mathcal{L}{\omega}: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{L1}\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{\text{ssim}}\mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} + \lambda{\omega}\mathcal{L}{\omega} where \lambda{L1}, \lambda{\text{ssim}}, and \lambda{\omega} are scalar weighting coefficients. The frequency-modulated loss uses masks M\omega to focus on specific frequency bands. A linear schedule determines the target normalized frequency \omega during optimization: \omega = \frac{t}{T{\text{total}}} where t is the current iteration and T{\text{total}} is the total number of iterations. This schedule ensures that all parts of the image are covered by the masks, progressively focusing on high frequencies (details) as optimization advances. Parameters: Total iterations T{\text{total}}: 40,000. Density gradient threshold: 0.0003. Learning rate for \beta: 0.0015. Shape reset interval: 1,000 iterations. Shape pruning interval: 100 iterations. Pruning threshold (shape-based): 0.5. Shape strength parameter: 0.1. Image Laplacian scale factor: 0.2. \lambda{\omega} coefficient: 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Sensitivity: The Difference of Gaussians (DoG) filter used in the frequency loss may be sensitive to high frequencies, requiring careful mask design. Precision & Acceleration: The optimization relies on GPU-powered computation and specialized CUDA kernels to handle memory requirements and accelerate gradient updates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizeges(G, targetimages, Ttotal=40000): # G: list of Gaussians with fields x, Sigma, kappa, beta, c for t in range(1, Ttotal + 1): # 1. Forward pass & loss computation renderedimg = render(G) omega = t / Ttotal L1 = computeL1(renderedimg, targetimages[t]) Lssim = computessim(renderedimg, targetimages[t]) Lw = computefrequencyloss(renderedimg, targetimages[t], Momega(omega)) L = lambdaL1 L1 + lambdassim Lssim + lambdaw Lw # 2. Backward pass & parameter update grads = computegradients(L, G) updateparameters(G, grads, lrbeta=0.0015) # 3. Periodic densification & pruning if t % 1000 == 0: resetshapeparameters(G) # Standard SGD reset or re-normalization; exact mechanism not specified in sources. if t % 100 == 0: prunebyshape(G, shapethreshold=0.5, gradthreshold=0.0003) applyopacitysplitting(G) # [Parent] Time Complexity: Not explicitly stated, but optimized for GPU acceleration. Memory Complexity: Optimized parameter memory requirements are mentioned but not quantified. Performance: Evaluated on an A6000 GPU. Achieves a balance between high fidelity and efficiency in novel view synthesis tasks. Strengths: Eliminates the need for a variable density mechanism and enhances edge fidelity via frequency-modulated loss. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of frequency masks and shape parameters. Origin: Introduced in "GES: Generalized Exponential Splatting for Efficient Radiance Field Rendering" (CVPR 2024). Development: Builds on Gaussian Splatting principles but introduces the shape parameter \beta and frequency-modulated loss for better detail reconstruction. Usage: Novel view synthesis tasks. name: Temporal Sensitivity Pruning
body:
Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) is a sparsification method for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes low-impact primitives by aggregating gradient-based sensitivity scores across multiple training views and timesteps. It differs from standard opacity-based pruning by explicitly accounting for the temporal consistency and deformation dynamics of the scene, ensuring that Gaussians contributing to stable, high-fidelity reconstruction over time are retained while those causing redundant neural inference load are eliminated. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}N\}, where each \mathcal{G}i has parameters \{\mui, ri, si, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i\} and a deformation field \mathcal{D} mapping static parameters to time-dependent states. A set of training poses and timesteps \mathcal{P}{gt}. Output: A binary mask or updated set of Gaussians indicating which primitives are pruned. Data Structures: 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i}: A scalar score per Gaussian, initialized to 0. \mathcal{P}{gt}: A list or set of tuples (\phi, t), where \phi is a camera pose and t is a timestep. Steps: 1. Initialize Scores: For each Gaussian \mathcal{G}i, initialize the temporal sensitivity score 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} = 0. 2. Iterate Training Data: For each training configuration (\phi, t) \in \mathcal{P}{gt}: a. Deform: Compute the time-dependent parameters for \mathcal{G}i using the deformation field: (\mu'i, r'i, s'i) = \mathcal{D}(\mui, ri, si, t). b. Render Gradient: Calculate the gradient of the rendered image I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) with respect to the projected value gi of the Gaussian \mathcal{G}i in image space. Let this be 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi). c. Accumulate: Add the squared gradient to the score: 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} \leftarrow 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} + \left( 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) ight)^2 3. Prune: Periodically during training, compare 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} against a threshold (or rank order). Prune Gaussians with low cumulative scores to reduce the number of primitives and neural inference load. Formula: The TSP score 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} approximates the second-order sensitivity to the L2 loss: 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} \approx 
abla{gi}^2 L2 \approx \sum{(\phi, t) \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} \left( 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) ight)^2 Where: 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} is the temporal sensitivity score for Gaussian \mathcal{G}i. gi is the value of \mathcal{G}i projected onto the image space. \mathcal{P}{gt} is the set of training poses \phi and timesteps t. I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) is the rendered image at pose \phi and timestep t. Parameters: \mathcal{P}{gt}: The set of training poses and timesteps used for sensitivity aggregation. The choice of this set determines the temporal coverage of the sensitivity analysis. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Noise: Since gradients are computed from discrete training frames, they may be noisy. This can lead to the retention of "floaters" (unstable Gaussians) that appear static in observed views but drift at unseen timestamps. This is often addressed by combining TSP with Temporal Sensitivity Sampling (TSS). Deformation Variability: Gradients are inherently time-dependent due to deformation updates. Incorrectly handling the deformation field \mathcal{D} during gradient computation can lead to inaccurate sensitivity scores. Uses first-order gradients of total image energy. Simpler but less robust to temporal dynamics than TSP. Perturbs timestamps during sensitivity estimation to suppress floaters. Used in conjunction with TSP. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot |\mathcal{P}{gt}|), where N is the number of Gaussians and |\mathcal{P}{gt}| is the number of training poses/timesteps. Requires rendering and gradient computation for each Gaussian across all training views. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sensitivity scores 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i}. Performance: In dynamic scenes, integrating TSP into DeformableGS accelerated rendering by 6.78× on average while maintaining neural-field fidelity and using 10× fewer primitives. Strengths: Reduces neural inference load by removing low-impact Gaussians. Stabilizes temporal pruning by considering temporal consistency. Limitations: Computationally expensive to calculate sensitivity scores for all Gaussians across all timesteps. May require complementary methods (like TSS) to handle floaters. TSP was introduced in the context of Speedy Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting (SpeeDe3DGS) to address the computational expense of neural inference in dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting models. It builds on DeformableGS and aims to bridge the efficiency-fidelity gap by removing redundant primitives through temporally aggregated sensitivity analysis. SpeeDe3DGS: Speedy Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting with Temporal Pruning and Motion Grouping, https://speede3dgs.github.io/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Sensitivity Calculation and Pruning
head: Gradient-based Sensitivity Pruning
body: Sensitivity Calculation and Pruning is a method to eliminate 3D Gaussians that have no impact on training images by calculating sensitivity using the gradient of total image energy with respect to parameters. It differs from its parent, Temporal Sensitivity Pruning, by using a first-order gradient of total image energy rather than a second-order approximation of the L2 loss, and from Gradient-based Pruning by specifically targeting the elimination of splats with zero sensitivity in color parameters to remove structural redundancy. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, where each Gaussian i has parameters including position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color. Training images and their corresponding camera poses. Pruning threshold \tau (value not given in the sources). Outputs: Pruned set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' containing only Gaussians with non-zero sensitivity. Data Structures: Gaussian parameters are stored in standard 3DGS format. Sensitivity score Si for each Gaussian i. Steps: 1. Render Training Images: Render the current set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} to generate images for all training views. 2. Calculate Total Image Energy: Compute the total image energy E across all training views. The specific formula for energy is not explicitly defined in the sources, but it is derived from the rendered pixel values. 3. Compute Sensitivity: For each Gaussian i, calculate its sensitivity Si using the gradient of the total image energy E with respect to the Gaussian's parameters (specifically the color parameters). Critical Implementation Detail: When calculating the gradient, do not clamp negative direction-dependent colors to zero. The standard 3DGS rendering pipeline clamps negative SH coefficients to zero during forward rendering. However, for sensitivity calculation, these clamped values must be treated as continuous to avoid setting partial derivatives to zero in the backward pass. If clamping is applied, SH coefficients that contribute to training images will incorrectly yield zero sensitivity. 4. Identify Zero-Sensitivity Gaussians: Identify Gaussians where the sensitivity in the color parameters is exactly zero. The sources observe that up to 15% of Gaussians may exhibit this property. 5. Prune: Eliminate all Gaussians with zero sensitivity from the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatesensitivityandprune(gaussians, trainingviews): """ Prunes Gaussians with zero sensitivity to total image energy. """ # Step 1: Render images without clamping negative colors for gradient calculation # Note: Standard rendering might clamp, but sensitivity calc requires unclamped gradients renderedimages = renderunclamped(gaussians, trainingviews) # Step 2: Calculate total image energy # Formula for E is not explicitly given, assumed to be sum of squared pixel values or similar totalenergy = calculatetotalimageenergy(renderedimages) # Step 3: Calculate gradients of total energy w.r.t. Gaussian parameters # Specifically focus on color parameters (SH coefficients) gradients = computegradients(totalenergy, gaussians, trainingviews) # Step 4: Identify Gaussians with zero sensitivity in color parameters zerosensitivityindices = [] for i, gaussian in enumerate(gaussians): # Check if gradient magnitude for color parameters is zero colorgradient = gradients[i].colorparams if iszero(colorgradient): zerosensitivityindices.append(i) # Step 5: Remove zero-sensitivity Gaussians prunedgaussians = [g for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if i not in zerosensitivityindices] return prunedgaussians def renderunclamped(gaussians, views): """ Renders images but ensures gradients flow through negative color values. In standard 3DGS, negative SH outputs are clamped to 0. Here, we must avoid this clamping for the backward pass. """ # Implementation detail: This requires modifying the rasterizer's backward pass # to not apply max(0, x) to the color contribution before gradient computation. return standardrasterize(gaussians, views, clampcolors=False) def iszero(vector, epsilon=1e-6): """ Check if a vector is effectively zero. """ return np.linalg.norm(vector) < epsilon Parameters: Pruning threshold: Not given in the sources. The method primarily targets zero sensitivity, but higher thresholds can be used to remove more Gaussians. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clamping Artifacts: If negative direction-dependent colors are clamped to zero during the backward pass, the partial derivatives become zero, resulting in zero sensitivity for SH coefficients that may still contribute to training images. This must be avoided. Loss of Fine Details: Using higher pruning thresholds (beyond zero) can remove fine details, such as small leaves, from the reconstruction. Defines sensitivity as the expected gradient magnitude of the global photometric loss over a fixed accumulation window, performing sparsification online to avoid prohibitive time costs. Evaluates the magnitude of gradients associated with each Gaussian during training to remove structurally redundant or poorly aligned Gaussians, rather than just transparent ones. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The sources note that a notable number of Gaussians (up to 15%) may have no impact on training images and can be safely eliminated. Strengths: Removes Gaussians that have no impact on training images, potentially reducing model size without significant loss in PSNR if thresholds are low. Limitations: Higher pruning thresholds can lead to the removal of fine details (e.g., small leaves). When to use: When aiming to reduce model size by removing structurally redundant Gaussians that do not contribute to the rendered output. When not to use: When preserving fine geometric details is critical, as aggressive pruning may remove them. This method is described in "Compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting for Accelerated Novel View Synthesis". It addresses the issue of redundant Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting by identifying those with zero sensitivity to the total image energy. Compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting for Accelerated Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00985, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification
body: Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification is a method for maintaining model compactness in 3D Gaussian Splatting by evaluating the actual contribution of each primitive within the optimization loop. It solves the problem of prohibitive time costs associated with offline pruning by performing sparsification online, ensuring the model remains refined throughout training. It differs from its parent, Sensitivity Calculation and Pruning, by specifically defining sensitivity as the expected gradient magnitude of the global photometric loss over a fixed accumulation window, rather than a general gradient of total image energy. Inputs and Outputs Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians with opacity \alphai, the global photometric loss \mathcal{L}, the sparsification lower-bound threshold \tau{\text{low}}, and a fixed accumulation window. Output: A binary survival state \mathcal{S}i for each primitive i. Data Structures Primitive State: Each Gaussian primitive i maintains a statistical sensitivity score Si. Accumulation Window: A fixed window of optimization iterations used to compute the expected value of the gradient magnitude. The exact size of the accumulation window is not given in the sources. Parameters \tau{\text{low}}: The sparsification lower-bound threshold (also referred to as \tauC in implementation details). It controls the compactness of the model. Set to 0.01. Steps 1. Compute Gradient: For each primitive i, compute the partial derivative of the loss function \mathcal{L} with respect to its opacity \alphai, denoted as \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alphai}. 2. Calculate Sensitivity: Compute the statistical sensitivity Si as the expected value of the absolute gradient magnitude over the fixed accumulation window: Si = \mathbb{E} \left[ \left| \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alphai} \right| \right] where \mathbb{E} denotes the expectation over the accumulation window. 3. Determine Survival State: Compare Si against \tau{\text{low}} to determine the survival state \mathcal{S}i: \mathcal{S}i = \begin{cases} \text{keep} & \text{if } Si \geq \tau{\text{low}} \\ \text{prune} & \text{if } Si < \tau{\text{low}} \end{cases} 4. Prune: Remove primitives where \mathcal{S}i = \text{prune} from the scene representation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def statisticalsensitivitysparsification(primitives, gradients, windowsize, taulow): """ Computes statistical sensitivity and prunes primitives based on the threshold. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects, each with an 'id' and 'alpha'. gradients: List of floats, the absolute gradient magnitudes |dL/dalphai| for each primitive in the current iteration. windowsize: Integer, the number of recent iterations to average over. taulow: Float, the sparsification lower-bound threshold (default 0.01). Returns: keptprimitives: List of primitive objects to keep. history: Dictionary mapping primitive id to a list of recent gradient magnitudes. """ # Initialize history buffers for each primitive history = {p.id: [] for p in primitives} sensitivities = {} # Update history with current iteration gradients for p, gradmag in zip(primitives, gradients): history[p.id].append(gradmag) # Keep only the last 'windowsize' entries if len(history[p.id]) > windowsize: history[p.id].pop(0) # Compute expected value (mean) over the window for p in primitives: if len(history[p.id]) > 0: sensitivities[p.id] = sum(history[p.id]) / len(history[p.id]) else: sensitivities[p.id] = 0.0 # Apply pruning threshold keptprimitives = [] for p in primitives: if sensitivities[p.id] >= taulow: keptprimitives.append(p) return keptprimitives, history Edge Cases and Pitfalls Window Size: The exact size of the accumulation window is not given in the sources. Precision: The computation requires accurate gradient tracking. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Online sparsification is performed within the optimization loop, avoiding the prohibitive time cost of offline pruning. The exact cost per iteration is not specified. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the history of gradient magnitudes for each primitive over the accumulation window. Measured Performance: In the ACE-GS framework, this method significantly reduces training duration compared to existing baselines while maintaining superior rendering quality. Strengths: Maintains model compactness without significant overhead; ensures the model remains refined throughout training. Limitations: The choice of \tau{\text{low}} and the accumulation window size can impact performance. When to Use: Use when training time is a constraint and model compactness is desired. When Not to Use: Use when offline pruning is feasible and computational resources are abundant, or when the accumulation window cannot be effectively defined. Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification was introduced in the ACE-GS paper, which aims to balance accuracy, compactness, and efficiency in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It is part of the ACE-GS framework, which also includes a Cross-Dimensional Residual Frequency Compensation module. name: Gradient-based Pruning
head: Gradient Magnitude Pruning
body:
Gradient-based Pruning is a training-time sparsification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes Gaussians contributing minimally to the optimization process by evaluating the magnitude of their associated gradients. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods, such as Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification, by directly measuring the gradient signal intensity rather than statistical variance or opacity thresholds, allowing for efficient GPU implementation while effectively eliminating visual artifacts like floaters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} currently active in the scene, their parameters (position \mathbf{t}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}), and the accumulated gradient magnitudes \mathbf{g} for each Gaussian during the current training phase. Output: A pruned set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' \subset \mathcal{G} with redundant entries removed. Data Structures: Gradient Accumulator: A vector or array of size |\mathcal{G}| storing the cumulative gradient magnitude for each Gaussian. For EfficientGS, this is a cumulative sum. For Kim et al., it may include separate components for position and SH coefficients. Threshold: A scalar value 	au determining the minimum gradient magnitude required to retain a Gaussian. Steps: 1. Gradient Accumulation: During each training iteration, after the backward pass, compute the gradient magnitude for each Gaussian. For position-based pruning, calculate the Euclidean norm of the positional gradient 
abla{\mathbf{t}i} L for Gaussian i. For SH-based pruning (Kim et al.), calculate the norm of the gradient with respect to spherical harmonics coefficients 
abla{\mathbf{c}i} L. Accumulate these magnitudes over time. EfficientGS uses a cumulative sum: Gi^{(t)} = Gi^{(t-1)} + \|
abla{\mathbf{p}i} L\| where \mathbf{p}i represents the parameters of interest (position or SH). 2. Thresholding: Compare the accumulated gradient magnitude Gi against a threshold 	au. If Gi < 	au, the Gaussian is marked for removal. The threshold 	au can be static or adaptive based on the distribution of gradient magnitudes in the current batch. 3. Pruning: Remove all marked Gaussians from the scene representation. Trimming the Fat and ELMGS apply this to remove up to 75% of Gaussians. 4. Optional: Opacity Reset: When a Gaussian is pruned, its opacity may be reset or redistributed to neighboring Gaussians to alleviate interference with residual distribution tracking. Parameters: Threshold 	au: Not given in the sources. Typically determined empirically or via percentile-based selection (e.g., remove bottom 10-25% of Gaussians by gradient magnitude). Accumulation Window: The number of iterations over which gradients are summed. EfficientGS uses cumulative sums, implying a long-term or epoch-spanning window. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Gradient magnitudes can vary significantly across scenes. Normalization or adaptive thresholds are necessary to avoid removing too many or too few Gaussians. Degenerate Input: Gaussians with zero gradient (e.g., occluded or static background) may be pruned prematurely if the threshold is too low. SH Gradients: Incorporating SH gradients (Kim et al.) adds complexity but refines pruning by considering color/appearance contribution, not just geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientbasedpruning(gaussians, accumulatedgradients, threshold): """ Prunes Gaussians with accumulated gradient magnitude below threshold. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: id: Unique identifier accumulatedgrad: Current cumulative gradient magnitude accumulatedgradients: List of floats, same length as gaussians, representing the accumulated gradient magnitude for each Gaussian. threshold: Float, the minimum accumulated gradient magnitude to keep a Gaussian. Returns: prunedgaussians: List of Gaussian objects that survived pruning. """ prunedgaussians = [] for i, gaussian in enumerate(gaussians): gradmag = accumulatedgradients[i] if gradmag >= threshold: prunedgaussians.append(gaussian) else: # Gaussian is pruned. # Optional: Reset opacity or redistribute weight pass return prunedgaussians Utilization-Based Pruning (UBP) is a training-time sparsification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes Gaussians with negligible contribution to the rendered image gradient, replacing opacity reset to alleviate interference with residual distribution tracking and compress scene representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by evaluating the gradient of the rendered image with respect to Gaussian positions rather than the loss gradient, allowing for efficient GPU implementation while effectively eliminating visual artifacts like floaters. Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration for gradient accumulation and pruning, where N is the number of Gaussians. Cumulative sum updates are O(1) per Gaussian per iteration. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store accumulated gradients. Measured Performance: Trimming the Fat and ELMGS remove 75% of Gaussians while maintaining high visual quality. Strengths: Effective at removing redundant Gaussians and floaters. Efficient on GPU due to simple magnitude comparisons. Limitations: Requires careful threshold selection. May remove Gaussians that are temporarily occluded but important for later views. When to Use: When computational efficiency is critical and visual quality must be maintained with fewer Gaussians. When Not to Use: When the scene has dynamic elements where temporary occlusion is common, or when SH details are critical and position-only pruning is insufficient. Gradient-based Pruning originated as a method to improve the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting training by removing Gaussians that contribute minimally to the optimization process. It has been adopted and extended by several methods, including EfficientGS, GDGS, Trimming the Fat, ELMGS, and Kim et al.. Kim et al. extended the approach by incorporating SH gradients alongside positional gradients. Compression in 3D Gaussian Splatting: A Survey of Methods, Trends, and Future Directions, https://doi.org/10.1109/TCSVT.2026.3676048, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Utilization-Based Pruning
head: utilization pruning
body: Utilization-Based Pruning (UBP) is a training-time sparsification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes Gaussians with negligible contribution to the rendered image gradient, replacing opacity reset to alleviate interference with residual distribution tracking and compress scene representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by evaluating the gradient of the rendered image with respect to Gaussian positions rather than the loss gradient, allowing for efficient GPU implementation while effectively eliminating visual artifacts like floaters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of active 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the current training step t, and a history of rendered images. Output: A pruned set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with low utilization removed. Data Structures: Gaussian g: Contains position xg, opacity, scale, rotation, and spherical harmonic coefficients. Rendered Image \hat{I}^{(t)}: A 2D array of pixel values at step t. Accumulator: A buffer storing the squared gradient magnitudes for each Gaussian over a window of steps. Parameters: \kappa = 10^{-8}: The threshold for pruning. If ug < \kappa, the Gaussian is removed. T = 100: The interval (in steps) at which the utilization metric is computed and pruning is considered. |NT(t)| = 100: The number of previous images accumulated in the window for averaging. Pruning Schedule: UBP is executed every 100 steps, specifically from step 500 to step 15,000. Formula: The utilization ug of a Gaussian g is defined as the average squared gradient of the rendered pixel values with respect to the Gaussian's position, accumulated over a window of images: ug = \frac{\sum{t} \sum{(w,h) \in NT(t)} \left( \frac{\partial \hat{I}{h,w}^{(t)}}{\partial xg} \right)^2}{2} Where: ug is the utilization metric for Gaussian g. \hat{I}{h,w}^{(t)} is the rendered pixel value at pixel coordinates (h,w) for view t. xg is the 3D position of Gaussian g. NT(t) is the set of |NT(t)|=100 images accumulated over the previous T=100 steps. The division by 2 arises from the derivative of the squared term in the accumulation. Note: This metric uses the gradient of the rendered image with respect to Gaussian positions, not the gradient of the loss function. Computing the derivative with respect to projected positions (2D) rather than 3D positions allows for a less memory-intensive GPU implementation while providing a similar metric to prior work. Numbered Steps: 1. Accumulation: For each Gaussian g, accumulate the squared gradient of the rendered image with respect to its position over the current step t. This is done for all pixels (h,w) covered by the Gaussian. 2. Windowing: Maintain a rolling window of the last |NT(t)|=100 images. Every T=100 steps, compute the average utilization ug across this window. 3. Evaluation: Compare ug against the threshold \kappa = 10^{-8}. 4. Pruning: If ug < \kappa, remove Gaussian g from the scene representation. 5. Frequency: Repeat steps 1-4 every 100 steps, starting from step 500 and ending at step 15,000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def utilizationbasedpruning(gaussians, renderedimageswindow, step, threshold=1e-8): """ Prunes Gaussians with low utilization based on image gradient. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with a 'position' attribute. renderedimageswindow: List of the last 100 rendered images (tensors). step: Current training step. threshold: Pruning threshold kappa. Returns: prunedgaussians: List of Gaussians remaining after pruning. """ # Pruning is only active between step 500 and 15000, every 100 steps if step < 500 or step > 15000 or step % 100 != 0: return gaussians prunedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: utilizationsum = 0.0 numimages = len(renderedimageswindow) # Accumulate squared gradient over the window of images for img in renderedimageswindow: # Compute gradient of rendered image w.r.t Gaussian position # Note: In practice, this is often computed w.r.t projected positions # for memory efficiency, but the formula defines it w.r.t xg. # We assume a function 'computeimagegradient' that returns # the gradient vector dI/dxg for the given Gaussian and image. grad = computeimagegradient(g.position, img) # Square the gradient magnitude gradsq = sum(val2 for val in grad) # Accumulate utilizationsum += gradsq # Average over the window and divide by 2 as per formula # Formula: ug = (sum(sum(grad^2))) / 2 # The sources state averaging across the image and accumulating over images. # The denominator 2 is explicit in the source formula (11). utilization = utilizationsum / 2.0 # Prune if below threshold if utilization >= threshold: prunedgaussians.append(g) return prunedgaussians def computeimagegradient(position, image): """ Computes the gradient of the rendered image with respect to the Gaussian position. This is a placeholder for the specific differentiable rasterization logic. In the source, this is computed w.r.t projected positions for efficiency. """ # Implementation detail: # The source notes that computing w.r.t projected positions is used for # memory efficiency. The gradient is backpropagated from the pixel values # through the splatting function to the Gaussian position. # This function would return a vector of the same dimension as position (3). pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Metric Degradation: UBP may slightly degrade quantitative metrics such as PSNR and LPIPS, but produces cleaner renderings with fewer floaters, as these metrics do not fully reflect the presence of floaters. Floater Removal: The method is particularly effective at removing "floaters" (erroneous Gaussians) in cluttered scenes. The parent method that evaluates the magnitude of gradients associated with each Gaussian during training. UBP is a specific instantiation that uses image gradient magnitude rather than loss gradient magnitude [17720-gradient-based-pruning.md]. Compression: On clean MipNeRF360 datasets, UBP reduces the number of Gaussians by 2× to 4.5× while preserving rendering quality. In distractor-filled scenes, it decreases the number of Gaussians by 4× to 6×. Performance: Enabling UBP translates to at least a 2× reduction in training time and a 3× reduction in inference time. Strengths: Effective compression, removal of floaters, and alleviation of interference with residual distribution tracking compared to opacity reset. Limitations: Slight potential degradation in quantitative metrics (PSNR/LPIPS). When to Use: Recommended for both cluttered and clean datasets to compress scene representation and improve rendering cleanliness. Utilization-Based Pruning was introduced in the paper "SpotLessSplats: Ignoring Distractors in 3D Gaussian Splatting" by Sabour and Goli et al.. It was developed as an improvement over opacity reset, which can interfere with residual distribution tracking. The method leverages the observation that Gaussians contributing minimally to the image gradient are likely artifacts or redundant primitives.
