name: Opacity Split for Cloning
head: Cloning Strategy for Gaussian Splatting, Revising Densification Opacity Initialization
body: Opacity Split for Cloning is a method to initialize the opacity of cloned 3D Gaussian primitives to maintain transmittance consistency, preventing the cloned child from having less impact than the parent alone. It solves the problem where standard cloning in 3D Gaussian Splatting causes the parent and child to jointly attenuate the background transmittance more than the parent did alone, biasing the alpha blending process. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A parent Gaussian g{parent} with opacity \alpha{old} selected for cloning. Output: N Gaussians (the parent and N-1 clones, or N clones replacing the parent) with updated opacity \alpha{new}. Data Structures: Gaussian definition follows the parent's shared principles Pruning and Opacity Management. Steps: 1. Select Parent: Identify a Gaussian g{parent} with opacity \alpha{old} to be cloned. 2. Calculate New Opacity: Compute the target opacity \alpha{new} for all resulting Gaussians using the transmittance preservation formula. For the specific case of cloning into two entities (parent + 1 clone) as described in: \alpha{new} = 1 - \sqrt{1 - \alpha{old}} For the general case of cloning into N identical copies as described in, where the total transmittance must be preserved: (1 - \alpha{new})^N = 1 - \alpha{old} \implies \alpha{new} = 1 - (1 - \alpha{old})^{1/N} 3. Assign Opacity: Set \alpha{parent} = \alpha{new} and \alpha{clone} = \alpha{new} for all N-1 clones. 4. Handle Covariance: states that opacity adjustment alone is insufficient because Gaussians are not point sources, so the covariance \Sigma must also be altered. proposes minimizing the error of integrated 1D slices passing through the Gaussian centers: \text{minimize } \left\| \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathbf{C}^{new}(x) dx - \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathbf{C}^{old}(x) dx \right\|2^2, \quad \forall \mathcal{S} where \mathcal{S} represents arbitrary slices and x denotes points along the slice. This ensures the integral of the color/radiance along any slice through the center is preserved. The exact analytical update equation for \Sigma is not provided in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Gaussian: def init(self, mu, sigma, alpha, c): self.mu = mu self.sigma = sigma self.alpha = alpha self.c = c def copy(self): return Gaussian(self.mu.copy(), self.sigma.copy(), self.alpha, self.c.copy()) def opacitysplitforcloning(gaussian, numtotal): """ Computes the split opacity for a cloned Gaussian. Args: gaussian: Gaussian object with attribute 'alpha' (float in [0, 1]). numtotal: Integer N, the total number of resulting Gaussians. Returns: newalpha: The opacity value to assign to all resulting Gaussians. """ alphaold = gaussian.alpha if numtotal <= 0: raise ValueError("numtotal must be at least 1") # Guard for numerical stability when alphaold is very close to 1 if alphaold >= 1.0: return 1.0 # General formula from: (1 - alphanew)^N = 1 - alphaold newalpha = 1.0 - (1.0 - alphaold) (1.0 / numtotal) return newalpha def clonegaussianwithopacitysplit(gaussian, numtotal): """ Clones a Gaussian and splits its opacity according to. Args: gaussian: The parent Gaussian to clone. numtotal: The total number of Gaussians after cloning. Returns: List of new Gaussian objects. """ newalpha = opacitysplitforcloning(gaussian, numtotal) newgaussians = [] for in range(numtotal): newg = gaussian.copy() newg.alpha = newalpha # Covariance Σ must also be altered to minimize slice integral error. # The exact update formula for Σ is not provided in the sources. newgaussians.append(newg) return newgaussians Parameters: N (numtotal): The number of resulting Gaussians. Typically N=2 (parent + 1 clone) in standard densification steps, but the formula generalizes to any N. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Point Source Assumption: Equation (1 - \alpha{new})^N = 1 - \alpha{old} is derived assuming point sources or identical spatial overlap. Since Gaussians have extent (\Sigma), this opacity split alone is insufficient to perfectly preserve rasterization if \Sigma is not also adjusted. Transmittance Bias: If standard cloning is used (copying \alpha{old} to both parent and child), the combined transmittance becomes (1-\alpha{old})^2, which is lower than (1-\alpha{old}), causing excessive darkening/occlusion of background elements. Numerical Stability: When \alpha{old} is very close to 1, (1-\alpha{old}) approaches 0. Care must be taken in floating-point arithmetic to avoid NaN or Inf results when taking roots or logs. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian cloned. The opacity calculation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per clone. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively mitigates the transmittance bias introduced by naive cloning; preserves the visual appearance of the scene during densification. Limitations: Does not address the spatial extent mismatch (covariance) unless combined with covariance adjustment. Relies on the assumption that cloned Gaussians are perfectly co-located. When to use: When performing densification via cloning in 3D Gaussian Splatting to prevent artifacts caused by incorrect opacity accumulation. Origin: The specific formula \alpha{new} = 1 - \sqrt{1 - \alpha{old}} for N=2 is attributed to Bulo et al. (2024). The generalization to N copies and the discussion of covariance adjustment are discussed in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo. History: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting clones Gaussians by copying all attributes, including opacity, which causes issues with alpha blending transmittance. Subsequent works like Bulo et al. (2024) and PixelGS (Zhang et al., 2024) proposed modifications to densification criteria and opacity initialization to correct this. Usage: Used in advanced implementations of 3D Gaussian Splatting training pipelines, particularly those focusing on adaptive density control and high-fidelity reconstruction. 3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, https://ubc-vision.github.io/3dgs-mcmc/, fetched 2026-10-26 Improving Adaptive Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.5220/0013308500003912, fetched 2026-10-30

name: GRay Optimization Settings
head: GRayLQ, GRayHQ
body: GRay Optimization Settings define the hyperparameter configurations for training 3D Gaussian Splatting using the GRay ray-tracing renderer. Unlike standard 3DGS or 3DGRT, these settings explicitly disable opacity resets and size-based pruning. The method offers two distinct presets: GRayLQ for high-speed, low-quality training, and GRayHQ for high-quality, slower training. The optimization process manages the set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} by adjusting opacity thresholds, pruning criteria, and spherical harmonic (SH) update frequencies based on the selected preset. Inputs: Training iterations N{iter} (default 7500 for LQ, unspecified for HQ). Resolution (experiments conducted at half resolution). Outputs: Optimized set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}{final} with updated positions, covariances, opacities, and SH coefficients. Parameters and Logic: The core logic differs between the two presets. 1. GRayLQ (Low Quality/High Speed): Opacity Threshold: \alpha{\min} = 0.02. Generalized Exponent: \alpha{\expo} = 3. Pruning Threshold: \mu{\prune} = 5 \times 10^{-7}. Scale Decay: \eta{\decay} = 0.9998. SH Stepping Laziness: Enabled at \alpha{\lazy} = 12. Iterations: N{iter} = 7500. Initialization Binning: Enabled with threshold \alpha{\bin} = 0.04. This removes over 15% of initial Gaussians, reducing count from 3.97M to 3.27M with minimal quality loss (PSNR 26.49 \to 26.47, LPIPS 0.234 \to 0.236). 2. GRayHQ (High Quality): Opacity Threshold: \alpha{\min} = 0.001. Generalized Exponent: \alpha{\expo} = 1 (matching 3DGS). Gradient Threshold: \tau{\min} = 0.001 (matching 3DGRT). Pruning Threshold: \mu{\prune} = 10^{-9}. Scale Decay: Disabled entirely. Initialization Binning: Disabled. Implementation Details: No Opacity Resets: The method does not perform periodic opacity resets, a common practice in 3DGS. No Size Pruning: Gaussians are not pruned based on their scale/size, unlike 3DGS. DHT (Dynamic Hash Table): Disabling DHT leads to rapid quality deterioration if \tau{\min} is high (e.g., PSNR 24.54 at \tau{\min}=0.03). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configuregraysettings(preset: str) -> dict: config = { "disableopacityresets": True, "disablesizepruning": True } if preset == "GRayLQ": config.update({ "alphamin": 0.02, "alphaexpo": 3, "muprune": 5e-7, "etadecay": 0.9998, "alphalazy": 12, "niterations": 7500, "enableshlaziness": True, "enableinitbinning": True, "alphabin": 0.04, "disablescaledecay": False, "taumin": None }) elif preset == "GRayHQ": config.update({ "alphamin": 0.001, "alphaexpo": 1, "muprune": 1e-9, "niterations": None, "enableshlaziness": False, "enableinitbinning": False, "disablescaledecay": True, "taumin": 0.001 }) else: raise ValueError("Unknown preset") return config A configuration optimized for speed. It uses aggressive pruning (\alpha{\min}=0.02, \mu{\prune}=5\times10^{-7}) and SH laziness to achieve training times under a minute and high FPS, at the cost of lower PSNR/SSIM. A configuration optimized for quality. It uses strict thresholds (\alpha{\min}=0.001, \mu{\prune}=10^{-9}), disables scale decay and binning, and matches 3DGS/3DGRT exponents. It yields higher quality metrics but requires significantly longer training time (36+ minutes) and retains more Gaussians. GRayLQ: Performance: Trains in under a minute (Opt Time 00:46). Metrics (Half Resolution): PSNR 26.23, SSIM 0.839, LPIPS 0.191. Gaussian Count: Starts at 3.27M, ends at 0.48M. FPS: 1051 FPS. Scaling: More than doubles 3DGS's frame rate. GRayHQ: Performance: Opt Time 36:11. Metrics (Half Resolution): PSNR 27.41, SSIM 0.847, LPIPS 0.154. Gaussian Count: Starts at 3.97M, ends at 3.79M. FPS: 55 FPS. Scaling: Improves quality over GRayLQ and approaches 3DGS-DI without reaching it. Comparison: GRayLQ sacrifices quality for speed, while GRayHQ sacrifices speed for quality. GRayHQ retains significantly more Gaussians (3.79M vs 0.48M) due to lower pruning thresholds and disabled scale decay. GRay is a ray-tracing based 3D Gaussian Splatting renderer. The optimization settings were introduced to balance the trade-off between training speed and reconstruction quality, leveraging specific ray-tracing properties that allow for different pruning and opacity management strategies compared to splatting-based renderers. GRay: Ray Tracing 3D Gaussians Near the Speed of Splats, https://doi.org/10.1145/3804496, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger
head: 3DGS Densification, AbsGS Densification, Default Densification Strategy, densify_from_iter trigger
body: Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger is the standard strategy for managing the population of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of balancing scene representation density against overfitting by periodically duplicating small Gaussians with high gradients, splitting large Gaussians with high gradients, pruning low-opacity Gaussians, and resetting opacities to prevent stagnation. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a fixed iteration schedule and specific scalar thresholds for gradient magnitude and scale, rather than adaptive per-Gaussian thresholds or view-count-based criteria. It builds on Pruning and Opacity Management. The method operates on the set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\} defined in Pruning and Sparsification. It maintains running accumulators for 2D positional gradients and visibility counts to make densification decisions. Inputs: Current training iteration t. Set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} with parameters: mean \muk, scale sk (3D), opacity \alphak, rotation qk, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. Gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muk} from the backward pass. Configuration parameters (see Parameters). Outputs: Updated set \mathcal{G}' with modified counts, positions, scales, and opacities. grad2d: A tensor of shape (N, 2) storing the running accumulation of image plane gradient norms for each Gaussian. count: A tensor of shape (N,) storing the running accumulation of visibility counts (number of views in which the Gaussian contributed to the rendered image). activemask: A boolean tensor of shape (N,) indicating which Gaussians are currently active (not pruned). pruneopa: Opacity threshold below which Gaussians are pruned. Default: 0.005. growgrad2d: Image plane gradient threshold for splitting/duplicating. Default: 0.0002. growscale3d: 3D scale threshold (normalized by scene scale) below which Gaussians are duplicated. Default: 0.01. growscale2d: 2D scale threshold (normalized by image resolution) above which Gaussians are split. Default: 0.05. prunescale3d: 3D scale threshold (normalized by scene scale) above which Gaussians are pruned. Default: 0.1. prunescale2d: 2D scale threshold (normalized by image resolution) above which Gaussians are pruned. Default: 0.15. refinestartiter: Iteration after which refinement begins. Default: 500. refinestopiter: Iteration after which refinement stops. Default: 15,000. refineevery: Number of steps between refinement operations. Default: 100. resetevery: Number of steps between opacity resets. Default: 3000. pauserefineafterreset: Number of steps to pause refinement after an opacity reset. Default: 0. absgrad: Boolean flag to use absolute gradients instead of average gradients for densification. Default: False. densifyfromiter: Iteration threshold that triggers densification specifically for white-background datasets. If the dataset uses a white background, densification starts at this iteration regardless of refinestartiter. opacityresetinterval: Iteration interval at which Gaussian opacities are reset. If resetevery is not specified, this may be used. 1. Initialization: Create grad2d and count tensors initialized to zero for each Gaussian in \mathcal{G}. 2. Pre-backward Accumulation: For each Gaussian gk that contributes to the rendered image for the current view: Compute the 2D positional gradient norm \tauk = \| \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muk} \|2. If absgrad is True, accumulate the absolute gradient value; otherwise, accumulate the norm. Update grad2d[k] += \tauk and count[k] += 1. 3. Opacity Reset Check: Determine if an opacity reset is required. A reset occurs if: The current iteration t is a multiple of opacityresetinterval (or resetevery), OR The dataset uses a white background AND t == densifyfromiter. If a reset is triggered, call resetopacity(). 4. Refinement Check: Determine if densification/pruning should occur. This happens if: t \ge refinestartiter t < refinestopiter t \pmod{\text{refine\every}} == 0 The system is not paused after a reset (i.e., t > last reset time + pauserefineafterreset). 5. Densification and Pruning Operations: If the refinement check passes, iterate through all active Gaussians gk: Normalize Gradient: Compute the average gradient \bar{\tau}k = \frac{\text{grad2d}[k]}{\text{count}[k]}. If count[k] == 0, skip. Pruning: If \alphak < pruneopa, mark gk for pruning. If max(sk) > prunescale3d (normalized) OR max(\text{scale2d}k) > prunescale2d (normalized), mark gk for pruning. Densification (Split/Clone): If \bar{\tau}k > growgrad2d: If max(sk) < growscale3d (normalized): Clone gk. Create a copy with the same \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}. If max(\text{scale2d}k) > growscale2d (normalized): Split gk. Replace gk with N{children} children (typically 2 or 4). Sample child means \mu{child} \sim \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak). Set child scale s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}}. Copy other attributes (\alpha, \mathbf{c}, q) to children. Remove parent gk. Reset Accumulators: Clear grad2d and count for the next interval. 6. Buffer Compaction: Remove pruned Gaussians from \mathcal{G} and compact the memory buffers to maintain contiguous access for rasterization [Parent]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def opacityresetanddensification( gaussians, iteration, grad2dbuffer, countbuffer, config): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes.mu,.scale,.opacity,.rotation,.shcoeffs iteration: Current training step integer grad2dbuffer: Tensor of shape (N, 2) or (N,) depending on absgrad countbuffer: Tensor of shape (N,) config: Dictionary containing all threshold parameters """ # Step 2: Accumulate gradients (called during backward pass) # This function is invoked by the training loop's backward hook def accumulategradients(gaussianidx, gradnorm): if config.get('absgrad', False): grad2dbuffer[gaussianidx] += abs(gradnorm) else: grad2dbuffer[gaussianidx] += gradnorm countbuffer[gaussianidx] += 1 # Step 3: Opacity Reset resetinterval = config.get('opacityresetinterval', config.get('resetevery', 3000)) iswhitebg = config.get('iswhitebackground', False) densifyfromiter = config.get('densifyfromiter', 0) shouldreset = False if iteration % resetinterval == 0: shouldreset = True if iswhitebg and iteration == densifyfromiter: shouldreset = True if shouldreset: resetopacity(gaussians) # Reset accumulators to avoid immediate densification based on pre-reset gradients grad2dbuffer.zero() countbuffer.zero() return # Step 4: Refinement Check refinestart = config.get('refinestartiter', 500) refinestop = config.get('refinestopiter', 15000) refineevery = config.get('refineevery', 100) pauseafterreset = config.get('pauserefineafterreset', 0) # Check if paused after reset (simplified logic: assume reset happened recently if count is low or explicit flag) # In practice, a 'lastresetiter' variable is tracked. # Here we assume if we just reset, we skip refinement for pauseafterreset steps. # For this implementation, we assume the caller handles the pause flag or we check iteration delta. # Simplified: if iteration < lastresetiter + pauseafterreset, skip. # We will assume 'paused' is passed or derived. For this standalone function, we assume not paused unless specified. ispaused = False # Placeholder for external state if (iteration >= refinestart and iteration < refinestop and iteration % refineevery == 0 and not ispaused): # Step 5: Densification and Pruning newgaussians = [] prunedindices = set() for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): if countbuffer[i] == 0: continue avggrad = grad2dbuffer[i] / countbuffer[i] # Pruning Conditions ispruned = False if g.opacity < config.get('pruneopa', 0.005): ispruned = True # Scale pruning requires normalized scales. # Assuming g.scale is 3D scale vector. # maxscale3dnorm = max(g.scale) / scenescale # maxscale2dnorm = max(projectedscale) / imageresolution # For pseudocode, we assume helper functions exist or values are pre-normalized. if max(g.scale) > config.get('prunescale3d', 0.1): # Assuming normalized ispruned = True if max(g.scale2d) > config.get('prunescale2d', 0.15): # Assuming normalized ispruned = True if ispruned: prunedindices.add(i) continue # Densification Conditions if avggrad > config.get('growgrad2d', 0.0002): # Clone if small if max(g.scale) < config.get('growscale3d', 0.01): # Assuming normalized clone = Gaussian.copy(g) newgaussians.append(clone) # Parent is effectively replaced by clone if we remove it, # but standard 3DGS clones in addition or replaces? # Note: S8 says "Cloning: Creating an exact copy... to increase sampling frequency". # Usually, cloning adds a new Gaussian. The parent remains? # In standard 3DGS code, cloning adds a new Gaussian to the list. newgaussians.append(g) # Keep parent # Split if large elif max(g.scale2d) > config.get('growscale2d', 0.05): # Assuming normalized children = splitgaussian(g) newgaussians.extend(children) # Parent is removed else: newgaussians.append(g) else: newgaussians.append(g) gaussians = newgaussians # Step 6: Buffer Compaction # Remove pruned gaussians from the list (already handled by filtering in loop above) # Reset buffers grad2dbuffer.zero() countbuffer.zero() def resetopacity(gaussians): """ Resets opacity of all Gaussians to a low value or initial value. Standard 3DGS resets to a small value (e.g., 0.01) or re-initializes. """ for g in gaussians: g.opacity = 0.01 # Typical reset value def splitgaussian(g): """ Splits a Gaussian into children. """ Nchildren = 2 # Typical value children = [] for in range(Nchildren): child = Gaussian.copy(g) # Sample new mean child.mu = samplefromnormal(g.mu, g.covariance) # Adjust scale child.scale = g.scale (5.0 / 4.0) / (Nchildren 0.5) children.append(child) return children Precision: Gradient accumulation in grad2d can suffer from precision loss if not normalized properly. Use absgrad if gradients are sparse or large. Boundaries: The refinestopiter prevents infinite densification. Ensure refinestartiter is set after initial convergence to avoid premature splitting. Degenerate Input: If count[k] == 0, the average gradient is undefined. Skip densification for such Gaussians. White Background: Standard densification may fail on white-background datasets because the background absorbs error. The densifyfromiter trigger is specifically for this case. Densification Threshold Calibration determines the scalar value that triggers the splitting of 3D Gaussians during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of balancing scene representation density against overfitting and computational instability. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a single global scalar threshold applied to a normalized gradient score, rather than adaptive per-Gaussian thresholds or view-count-based criteria. It builds on Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger. Joint Deletion Cost Approximation is a method for pruning that approximates the cost of deleting multiple Gaussians simultaneously using a quadratic form. It solves the problem of inaccurate pruning decisions when Gaussians are deleted in bulk. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its use of a Hessian approximation Rb to model interactions between deleted Gaussians. It builds on Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger. Formula: The approximate deletion cost is E{del}(zb) = zb^T Rb zb = \sumi (Rb){ii} z{b,i} + 2 \sum{i<j} (Rb){ij} z{b,i} z{b,j}, where zb = 1 - xb are binary deletion variables. Pitfall: The approximation may become less accurate when many Gaussians are deleted together. Responses are recomputed after model refinement in each subsequent pruning round. Smooth Opacity Decay is a smoother pruning mechanism that decreases opacity gradually instead of hard resets, avoiding training shocks and misleading error statistics. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its continuous opacity reduction and residual transmittance regularization. It builds on Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger. Parameters: Opacity decay amount: 0.001 per densification run. Residual transmittance regularization weight: 0.1. Pitfall: Constant opacity lowering invites the model to use the background more, potentially creating holes visible from novel views. Opacity Lobe Modulation is a technique applying generalized Phong shading to opacity modulation rather than radiance modeling, allowing the opacity lobe to decouple each Gaussian kernel's contribution to final exitant radiance, providing stability against depth sorting permutations. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its use of view-dependent opacity with fixed color magnitudes, unlike DBS which uses spherical beta functions for color. It builds on Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger. Parameters: Opacity lobe orientation d learning rate: 0.001. Opacity lobe width T learning rate: 0.0002. Sharpness β learning rate: 0.002. Complexity: Minimal overhead, requiring only 5 parameters per instance, with ~10% of primitives storing these additional parameters. 3D Gaussian Editing Operations are procedures to modify 3D Gaussians (opacity and color) based on selected regions for extraction, deletion, or appearance modification. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit support for semantic feature-based editing. It builds on Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger. Steps: Extraction: Keep opacity \alphai for selected, set to 0 for unselected. Deletion: Set opacity to 0 for selected, keep \alphai for unselected. Appearance Modification: Update color ci using an appearance function. Representation: xi = (fi, \alphai, ci) where fi \in \mathbb{R}^{512} is semantic feature. Time Complexity: O(N) per refinement step, where N is the number of Gaussians. The cost is dominated by gradient accumulation and the split/clone operations, which are proportional to the number of active Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian parameters and the grad2d/count buffers. Buffer compaction may cause temporary memory spikes [Parent]. Measured Performance: In standard 3DGS training, refinement occurs every 100 iterations between steps 500 and 15,000. This results in approximately 140 refinement steps per scene. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. However, frequent splitting can lead to exponential growth in N if thresholds are too low, causing memory exhaustion. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective at capturing fine details, widely adopted as the default strategy. Limitations: Hard resets can cause training instability. Fixed thresholds may not adapt well to scenes with varying complexity. White-background datasets require special handling. When to use: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training on diverse scenes. When not to use: Scenes with white backgrounds (use densifyfromiter variant), or when smooth training dynamics are critical (use Smooth Opacity Decay). The Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger strategy originates from the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023). It was designed to dynamically adjust the density of Gaussian primitives to match the complexity of the scene being reconstructed. The method has become the de facto standard for 3DGS training and is the foundation for many subsequent optimization strategies. carlinds/splatad, https://github.com/carlinds/splatad, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Yang-SyZng/AVM-GS, https://github.com/Yang-SyZng/AVM-GS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) SplatQ: Interaction-Aware Pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting via Quadratic Selection, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13503, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Revising Densification in Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73036-820, fetched 2026-10-26 Augmented Radiance Field: A General Framework for Enhanced Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.19916, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Feature 3DGS: Supercharging 3D Gaussian Splatting to Enable Distilled Feature Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02048, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Smooth Opacity Decay
head: Alternative to Opacity Reset
body: Smooth Opacity Decay is a regularization technique used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting to manage primitive sparsity without the instability of hard opacity resets. It solves the problem of training shocks and misleading error statistics that occur when primitives are abruptly pruned, which can trigger incorrect densification decisions. Unlike hard resets, this method gradually reduces opacity, though it introduces a tendency for the model to over-rely on the background, potentially creating visible holes in novel views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of 3D Gaussians (splats) with current opacity parameters, the current learning rate, and the densification schedule. Output: Updated opacity parameters for the splats. Data Structures: splats['opacities']: A tensor of shape (N, 1) or (N) containing the logit or raw opacity values for N Gaussians. The exact representation (logit vs. sigmoid output) depends on the implementation variant. Steps: The method applies a decay to the opacity of each primitive after every densification run. There are two primary variants described in the sources: the standard fixed-amount decay and the strategy-dependent decay. 1. Standard Fixed-Amount Decay: After each densification run, decrease the opacity of each primitive by a fixed amount \Delta. Formula: \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} - \Delta Where \Delta = 0.001. This gradual reduction moves opacities toward the pruning range without sudden changes in the densification metric. 2. Strategy-Dependent Decay: If the strategy name is 'mrnf': Compute sigmoid opacity: \alpha{sig} = \sigma(\text{splats}['\text{opacities}']) Multiply by decay factor: \alpha{sig}' = \alpha{sig} \times \text{decay\factor} Convert back to logit: \text{splats}['\text{opacities}'] = \log\left(\frac{\alpha{sig}'}{1.0 - \alpha{sig}' + \epsilon}\right) Where \epsilon = 10^{-8}. Else if opacitydecay > 0: Subtract the decay term scaled by the learning rate: \text{splats}['\text{opacities}'] = \text{splats}['\text{opacities}'] - \text{opacity\decay} \times \text{lr} Where opacitydecay is the decay factor multiplier. 3. Residual Transmittance Regularization: To counteract the tendency of the model to use the background (which causes holes), minimize the average value of the residual transmittance (residual probabilities of alpha-compositing) for every pixel. Loss term: L{residual} = \lambda{res} \times \text{mean}(\text{residual\transmittance}) Where \lambda{res} = 0.1 is the regularization weight. Parameters: Opacity decay amount: 0.001 per densification run. Residual transmittance regularization weight: 0.1. Opacity decay multiplier: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Holes in Novel Views: The constant push towards lowering opacity invites the model to make more use of the background. This can generate holes in the scene that are visible from novel views. Misleading Error Statistics: While smooth decay avoids the immediate shock of hard resets, improper tuning can still lead to suboptimal densification if the decay rate is too aggressive relative to the densification frequency. A regularization step that reduces Gaussian opacity to prevent over-saturation. It is applied either via sigmoid scaling for the 'mrnf' strategy or direct subtraction for others. It uses a decay factor multiplier to control the rate of reduction. Time Complexity: O(N) per densification step, where N is the number of Gaussians, as it iterates over all primitives to update opacity. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it updates the opacity tensor in place. Strengths: Avoids training shocks and misleading error statistics associated with hard opacity resets. Provides smoother training dynamics. Limitations: Can lead to background over-reliance and visible holes if not counteracted by residual transmittance regularization. When to use: When using error-based densification methods where hard resets would trigger incorrect densification decisions. Applicable to both standard 3DGS and Mip-Splatting extensions. Smooth Opacity Decay was proposed as an improvement to the Adaptive Density Control (ADC) mechanism in Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitations of the original opacity reset strategy, which was found to be harmful for error-based densification methods. The method is designed to favor primitive pruning in a smoother way, preserving sparsification properties while avoiding sudden changes in the densification metric. It has been shown to benefit both standard 3DGS and its Mip-Splatting extension. name: Densification Threshold Calibration
head: Threshold sweep
body: Densification Threshold Calibration determines the scalar value that triggers the splitting of 3D Gaussians during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of balancing scene representation density against overfitting and computational instability. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a single global scalar threshold applied to a normalized gradient score, rather than adaptive per-Gaussian thresholds or view-count-based criteria. It builds on Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger. Inputs and Outputs Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians, their accumulated gradient sums, and their accumulated contributions per view. Output: A scalar threshold value \tau used to decide if a Gaussian should be split. Data Structures Gaussian: gradientsum: Float. Sum of gradient magnitudes over recent iterations. accumulatedcontribution: Float. Sum of rendering contributions (opacity \times depth weight) across views. count: Integer. Number of Gaussians in the scene. Formula The densification score Si for a Gaussian i is calculated as: Si = \frac{\text{gradient\sum}i}{\text{floor} + \text{accumulated\contribution}i} A Gaussian is split if Si > \tau. Parameters \tau (threshold): Default value is 0.002. Swept values include 0.001, 0.004, and 0.03. floor: Constant added to the denominator. Default value is 1. Swept values include 0, 0.5, 2, and 4. Steps 1. Initialize floor to 1. 2. For each Gaussian i in the scene: a. Retrieve gradientsumi and accumulatedcontributioni. b. Calculate Si = \frac{\text{gradient\sum}i}{\text{floor} + \text{accumulated\contribution}i}. c. If Si > \tau, mark Gaussian i for splitting. 3. Split all marked Gaussians. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Divergence with Floor=0: If floor is 0 and accumulatedcontribution is between 0 and 1, the denominator is less than 1, inflating the score unboundedly as the sum approaches zero. This causes training divergence. Over-densification: A threshold too low (e.g., 0.001) creates excessive Gaussians (4.90M on calibration subset), lowering PSNR. Under-densification: A threshold too high (e.g., 0.004) creates too few Gaussians (0.66M on calibration subset), raising LPIPS. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def densifygaussians(gaussians, threshold=0.002, floor=1.0): """ Determines which Gaussians to split based on the densification threshold. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes 'gradientsum' and 'accumulatedcontribution'. threshold: Scalar threshold for splitting (default 0.002). floor: Constant added to denominator to prevent score inflation (default 1.0). Returns: List of Gaussian objects marked for splitting. """ tosplit = [] for g in gaussians: # Calculate normalized score # Note: accumulatedcontribution is a float, gradientsum is a float score = g.gradientsum / (floor + g.accumulatedcontribution) # Check against threshold if score > threshold: tosplit.append(g) return tosplit A constant floor added to the accumulated contribution in the denominator of the densification criterion to prevent score inflation when accumulated contribution is between 0 and 1. It is chosen as the minimal value (1) guaranteeing the denominator does not fall below 1. Other floors act as a reparameterization of the threshold rather than a quality parameter, as matched counts yield similar quality. Without a floor (floor=0), training diverges on Zip-NeRF scenes within ~1,800 iterations, exceeding the 16.8M trainable limit. Swept values include 0, 0.5, 2, and 4. Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration, where N is the number of Gaussians, as each Gaussian's score is computed independently. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store gradient sums and accumulated contributions. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 calibration subset (bicycle, bonsai, counter, garden), threshold 0.002 yields 1.79M Gaussians with the best PSNR, SSIM, and GMSD. Scaling: The calibrated threshold of 0.002 is used unchanged on every other scene and dataset. Strengths: Simple to implement; robust when combined with a denominator floor. Limitations: Requires careful selection of the floor value to avoid divergence; sensitive to threshold choice (over/under-densification). When to use: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training with occlusion-aware densification. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and a lower-fidelity representation is acceptable (use higher threshold). Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization, specifically in the "Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting" paper. The method was developed to address the instability of gradient-based densification when accumulated contributions are low, leading to the introduction of the denominator floor and the calibration of the threshold via sweep on a representative subset of scenes. name: Spatially Constrained Optimization
head: Opacity Loss with Re-initialization
body:
Spatially Constrained Optimization is a post-processing constraint workflow applied to differentiable bitmap or Gaussian primitives to enforce full opacity rendering of target objects and clean up boundary artifacts. It solves the problem where applying an opacity loss alone forces primitives to render fully opaque but leaves low-opacity "ghost" primitives lingering on object boundaries, which degrade visual quality. It sets itself apart from standard pruning strategies by re-initializing transparent primitives rather than removing them, thereby maintaining primitive count and coverage in complex regions. It builds on Pruning and Opacity Management and differs from siblings such as GES Optimization Strategy, Temporal Sensitivity Pruning, Opacity Split for Cloning, GRay Optimization Settings, and Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of primitives \mathcal{G} with current parameters \Theta, target image I^{	ext{target}}, and target alpha mask I\alpha^{	ext{target}}. Output: Updated primitive parameters \Theta' with re-initialized boundary primitives. Data Structures: Primitive i defined by position 
ui, opacity \sigma(
ui), and other rendering parameters. Buffers for opacity values and re-initialization flags. Parameters: Prune threshold: Opacity threshold below which primitives are marked for re-initialization. Typical value: 0.3. Prune iterations: Frequency of re-initialization steps. Typical value: every 50 iterations. \lambda\alpha: Weight for the opacity matching term in the loss function. Steps: 1. Compute Loss: Calculate the spatially constrained loss \mathcal{L} to optimize primitive parameters \Theta. The loss consists of an image reconstruction term (masked by the target alpha) and an opacity matching term: \mathcal{L} = \| (I\alpha^{	ext{target}} > 0) \odot (I - I^{	ext{target}}) \|2^2 + \lambda\alpha \| I\alpha - I\alpha^{	ext{target}} \|2^2 where I is the rendered image, I\alpha = 1 - TN is the rendered alpha (from Eq. 4 in), and \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. 2. Gradient Update: Perform a gradient descent step on \Theta using \mathcal{L}. 3. Identify Boundary Primitives: For each primitive i, check its opacity \sigma(
ui). If \sigma(
ui) < 	ext{prune threshold} (typically 0.3), mark the primitive for re-initialization. 4. Re-initialize: Instead of pruning (removing) the marked primitives, re-initialize them randomly using the Structure-aware initialization method. This involves sampling new positions and parameters to ensure coverage. 5. Iterate: Repeat steps 1-4 every prune iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Destabilization: Re-initialization is excluded during an initial warmup period and final iterations to prevent destabilizing the optimization. Boundary Artifacts: Using opacity loss alone without re-initialization leaves low-opacity primitives on boundaries, producing inferior qualitative results compared to the combined approach. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def spatiallyconstrainedoptimization(primitives, targetimage, targetalpha, prunethreshold=0.3, pruneiterations=50, warmupiters=100, totaliters=1000, lambdaalpha=1.0, learningrate=0.01): """Spatially constrained optimization workflow.""" H = len(targetimage) W = len(targetimage[0]) for i in range(totaliters): # 1. Render forward pass renderedimage, renderedalpha = forwardrender(primitives, H, W) # 2. Compute loss imageloss = 0.0 alphaloss = 0.0 for r in range(H): for c in range(W): mask = 1.0 if targetalpha[r][c] > 0 else 0.0 for k in range(3): imageloss += mask (renderedimage[r][c][k] - targetimage[r][c][k])2 alphaloss += (renderedalpha[r][c] - targetalpha[r][c])2 totalloss = imageloss + lambdaalpha alphaloss # 3. Gradient update grads = computegradients(totalloss, primitives) for p in primitives: p.pos = [p.pos[d] - learningrate grads[d] for d in range(3)] p.opacity = max(0.0, min(1.0, p.opacity - learningrate grads['opacity'])) # 4. Re-initialization step if i > warmupiters and i % pruneiterations == 0: for p in primitives: if p.opacity < prunethreshold: reinitializeprimitive(p) return primitives def forwardrender(primitives, H, W): """Differentiable rasterization logic.""" return [[[0.0]3 for in range(W)] for in range(H)], [[0.0]W for in range(H)] def computegradients(loss, primitives): """Gradient computation via autodiff or chain rule.""" return {'pos': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'opacity': 0.0} def reinitializeprimitive(p): """Structure-aware random re-initialization.""" p.pos = [random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for in range(3)] p.opacity = 0.5 p.scale = [0.1, 0.1, 0.1] p.rotation = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] p.sh = [0.0] 48 A mechanism to handle transparent primitives in spatially constrained rendering by re-initializing them randomly instead of pruning them, to prevent destabilization and ensure coverage. It differs from standard pruning (e.g., [34]) by maintaining the primitive count and potentially aiding coverage in complex regions. Definition: Check opacity \sigma(
ui). If \sigma(
ui) < 	ext{prune threshold} (typically 0.3), mark for re-initialization. Re-initialize using Structure-aware initialization method. Parameters: Prune threshold: 0.3; Prune iterations: every 50 iterations. Pitfall: Re-initialization is excluded during an initial warmup period and final iterations to prevent destabilization. A method to render only foreground by optimizing primitive opacity to match target alpha, enabling applications like appearance editing. Definition: Optimize \Theta using loss \mathcal{L} = \| (I\alpha^{	ext{target}} > 0) \odot (I - I^{	ext{target}}) \|2^2 + \lambda\alpha \| I\alpha - I\alpha^{	ext{target}} \|2^2. Re-initialize transparent primitives instead of pruning them for further applications. Time Complexity: Adds a periodic re-initialization step every prune iterations (e.g., 50 iterations). The re-initialization cost depends on the complexity of the Structure-aware initialization method. Memory Complexity: Maintains the same number of primitives as the initial setup, as transparent primitives are re-initialized rather than pruned. Performance: On RTX 3090, 512x512 resolution, forward/backward runtime is approximately 1360ms/2337ms with 6.4 GB VRAM (for the base DiffBMP implementation, which includes these features). Strengths: Produces the best qualitative results by combining opacity loss with re-initialization, effectively cleaning up boundary artifacts. Enables foreground-only rendering and appearance editing. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of warmup and final iteration exclusions to avoid destabilization. When to use: When full opacity rendering of target objects is required and boundary artifacts are a concern. Particularly useful for downstream applications like appearance editing. Introduced in the DiffBMP paper as a modification of triangle mesh rendering work [52]. It was developed to support foreground-only rendering and appearance editing. The method combines opacity loss with a re-initialization mechanism to address the issue of low-opacity primitives remaining on object boundaries. name: Significance-Aware Pruning
head: Pruning based on accumulated alpha blending coefficients, Significance Pruning, Significance-based Pruning
body: Significance-Aware Pruning is a pruning strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes primitives based on their accumulated contribution to the rendered image, rather than solely on opacity or scale. It solves the problem of standard opacity pruning removing large, low-opacity Gaussians that are critical for scene structure and transmittance. Unlike Pruning and Opacity Management which relies on static opacity thresholds, this method spares Gaussians with low opacity but high alpha-blending significance, improving the trade-off between reconstruction quality and scene compactness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gn\}, where each gk has opacity ok, and the accumulated alpha blending coefficients wk^p for each pixel p across all views rendered between the current densification step and the previous one. Output: A subset of \mathcal{G} with Gaussians marked for removal. Data Structures: \sigmak: A scalar value representing the accumulated significance of Gaussian k. \Sigma: A list or array of all \sigmak values for k \in \{1, \dots, n\}, i.e., \Sigma = \{\sigma1, \dots, \sigman\}. Parameters: o{min}: The minimum opacity threshold. Gaussians with ok < o{min} are candidates for pruning. N{prune}: The number of Gaussians to prune in the current step. In practice, the pruning rate or count may decay over iterations (e.g., using a decay factor of 0.7) to gradually reduce the number of pruned Gaussians as training progresses. N{\text{pixel}}: The total number of pixels across all views rendered between densification steps. Steps: 1. Accumulate Significance: For each Gaussian gk, compute its accumulated significance \sigmak by summing its alpha blending coefficients wk^p over all pixels p in all views rendered since the last densification step: \sigmak = \sum{p=1}^{N{\text{pixel}}} wk^p Here, wk^p is the alpha blending coefficient of Gaussian k at pixel p. 2. Build Significance Set: Construct the set \Sigma containing \sigmak for all n Gaussians: \Sigma = \{\sigma1, \dots, \sigman\} 3. Identify Candidates: Select the subset of Gaussians \mathcal{C} where the opacity is below the threshold: \mathcal{C} = \{ gk \mid ok < o{min} \} 4. Select Pruning Targets: From the candidate set \mathcal{C}, identify the N{prune} Gaussians with the lowest accumulated significance values in \Sigma. Let this subset be \mathcal{P}: \mathcal{P} = \text{argmin}{gk \in \mathcal{C}} (\sigmak, N{prune}) If |\mathcal{C}| < N{prune}, prune all candidates in \mathcal{C}. 5. Prune: Remove all Gaussians in \mathcal{P} from \mathcal{G}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def significanceawarepruning(gaussians, alphablendingcoeffs, omin, nprune): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with attributes 'opacity' and 'id'. alphablendingcoeffs: Dict mapping gaussianid to a list/array of wk^p for all pixels. omin: Float, minimum opacity threshold. nprune: Int, number of Gaussians to prune. Returns: Set of gaussianids to prune. """ # Step 1 & 2: Compute significance sigmak and build set Sigma sigmas = {} for g in gaussians: gid = g.id # Sum alpha blending coefficients over all pixels wlist = alphablendingcoeffs[gid] sigmak = sum(wlist) sigmas[gid] = sigmak # Step 3: Identify candidates with low opacity candidates = [] for g in gaussians: if g.opacity < omin: candidates.append(g) if not candidates: return set() # Step 4: Select nprune Gaussians with lowest sigma among candidates # Sort candidates by their sigma value (ascending) candidatessorted = sorted(candidates, key=lambda g: sigmas[g.id]) # Take the bottom nprune prunecount = min(nprune, len(candidatessorted)) topruneids = set() for i in range(prunecount): topruneids.add(candidatessorted[i].id) # Step 5: Return IDs to prune return topruneids Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Low-Opacity Gaussians: Standard opacity pruning removes large Gaussians with low opacity, which can damage scene structure because these Gaussians contribute significantly to transmittance and alpha blending. Significance-aware pruning avoids this by checking \sigmak. Size Pruning Interference: Standard size pruning (removing large Gaussians) can cause an increase in total Gaussian count as multiple small Gaussians replace one large one, harming compactness. This method focuses on opacity and significance, avoiding the adverse effects of size-based removal. Accumulation Window: The accumulation of wk^p must occur between densification steps. Decay of Pruning Rate: In practice, N{prune} or the pruning rate may decay over iterations (e.g., using a decay factor of 0.7) to gradually reduce the number of pruned Gaussians as training progresses. A dynamic variant that adjusts the final Gaussian count and pruning aggressiveness based on training PSNR, replacing fixed hyperparameters with a dynamic keep ratio. Time Complexity: Computing \sigmak requires iterating over all pixels for all Gaussians between densification steps. This adds overhead to the rendering pass or requires maintaining a buffer of wk^p. Memory Complexity: Requires storing wk^p for all Gaussians and pixels between densification steps, or accumulating \sigmak incrementally. Performance: Improves scene compactness by reducing the total number of Gaussians needed for high-quality reconstruction, as it avoids retaining insignificant low-opacity Gaussians while preserving significant ones. It can reduce storage and potentially improve rendering FPS by reducing the primitive count. Strengths: More accurately reflects a Gaussian's contribution to the scene by considering both opacity and spatial extent (via alpha blending). Prevents the removal of large, structurally important Gaussians with low opacity. Limitations: Requires additional computation to accumulate and sum alpha blending coefficients. Originated as an improvement to the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting densification algorithm, specifically addressing the limitations of opacity and size pruning. It was introduced in the context of improving Adaptive Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method integrates the Gaussian's opacity ok and its alpha blending coefficient wk into the pruning decision to better evaluate contribution to scene reconstruction. name: Quality Feedback Count Adaptation
head: Adaptive Keep Ratio, Keep ratio adaptation, PSNR-Dependent Retention, Sensitivity-Based Pruning
body: Quality Feedback Count Adaptation is a dynamic pruning mechanism that adjusts the final Gaussian count based on the training PSNR, using a keep ratio function to compress or expand the population relative to the learning allowance. It replaces the fixed keep ratio hyperparameter with a dynamic value computed from training progress, controlling the fraction of Gaussians retained during pruning and final selection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current training PSNR, current Gaussian population size N, two linear map constants calibrated from standard scenes, and a boolean flag indicating whether the step is the final selection. Output: A dynamic keep ratio \rho \in [0, 1] and the target number of Gaussians for the next densification step or final selection. Data Structures: Gaussian Population: A list or array of Gaussian primitives supporting indexing for pruning. Keep Ratio (\rho): A single floating-point value computed per growth/pruning event. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Keep Ratio: At each growth/pruning event, compute the keep ratio \rho from the preceding epoch's training PSNR using a linear map. 2. Apply to Densification: Apply the computed \rho to set the densification target at the growth event. 3. Apply to Soft Prune: Apply the computed \rho to set the fraction of Gaussians kept during the soft prune step. 4. Final Selection: At the end of training, apply the terminal \rho value to determine the fraction of Gaussians retained from the training population. Formulas: The keep ratio is a fixed function of training PSNR: \rho = a \cdot \text{PSNR} + b, where a and b are linear map constants. A ratio of \rho = 0.5 corresponds to 31.8 dB PSNR. The final selection removes nothing below a 20 dB floor. Parameters: Linear Map Constants: Two constants used to map training PSNR to \rho. They are calibrated once on standard scenes and applied unchanged to large captures, but exact numerical values are not provided in the sources. PSNR Floor: 20 dB. Below this threshold, the final selection removes nothing. Initial Keep Ratio: \rho \approx 0.61 at the first growth events when training PSNR is below 20 dB. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Terminal Reading Bias: The terminal keep ratio reading is taken after the last opacity decay, which briefly lowers training PSNR, causing the terminal reading to sit above the last learning reading. This means the final retention rate might be slightly higher than expected based on the final PSNR snapshot. Low PSNR Scenes: For scenes ending below 27 dB, the keep ratio is high (0.54–0.58), retaining 82–97\% of the population. On some large captures (Sci-Art, Residence), the retained fraction s\rho reaches 0.98, meaning the terminal step removes almost nothing and the growth target alone sets the final size. High PSNR Scenes: For scenes ending above 33 dB, the keep ratio is low (0.46–0.49), retaining 56–64\% of the population. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computekeepratio(psnr: float, a: float, b: float, isfinalselection: bool) -> float: """ Computes the dynamic keep ratio rho from training PSNR. a and b are linear map constants calibrated on standard scenes. """ # Final selection removes nothing below the 20 dB floor if isfinalselection and psnr < 20.0: return 1.0 # Linear map: rho = a psnr + b rho = a psnr + b return rho Selective Pruning with Sensitivity Ranking is a post-growth pruning mechanism that selects the final Gaussian population in a single event, matching the cumulative effect of periodic pruning throughout training. It differs from its parent, Quality Feedback Count Adaptation, by executing the reduction as a one-time "final selection" rather than a dynamic adjustment based on current learning allowance, and by explicitly ranking Gaussians by sensitivity to determine retention. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Standard Captures: On scenes ending >33 dB (Kitchen, Bonsai, Room, Dr Johnson, Playroom), \rho ranges from 0.46 to 0.49, retaining 56–64\% of the population. Medium Captures: On scenes ending 27–31 dB, \rho ranges from 0.51 to 0.53, retaining 70–82\% of the population. Complex/Large Captures: On scenes ending <27 dB (including 5 of 8 large captures), \rho ranges from 0.54 to 0.58, retaining 82–97\% of the population. Adaptive vs. Fixed: A fixed keep ratio of 0.5 approximates the adaptive rule for high-PSNR captures (max 4\% count change, 0.08 dB difference) but selects smaller, lower-quality models for lower-PSNR captures. On the Garden scene, the adaptive ratio of 0.54 retains 1.29\times the Gaussians for 0.15 dB higher PSNR and 0.014 lower LPIPS compared to a fixed 0.5. On complex scenes (Garden, Building, Rubble, Sci-Art), adaptive \rho (0.54–0.58) retains 1.29\times–1.66\times more Gaussians, yielding 0.13–0.16 dB higher PSNR and 0.006–0.019 lower LPIPS. Training Progress: During a single run, \rho falls by 0.04 to 0.09 on standard captures and by 0.02 to 0.07 on large captures. Terminal \rho values range from 0.50 to 0.58 across captures. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Quality Feedback Count Adaptation is part of the TangoGS method, introduced in "Gauss What You Need: Compact Gaussian Splatting Across Scene Scales". It is designed to work in conjunction with Significance-Aware Pruning and capture-derived learning allowances to achieve compact yet high-quality Gaussian Splatting models across standard and large-scale captures. The method was implemented in TangoGS for densification control and final model selection. name: Selective Pruning with Sensitivity Ranking
head: Final Selection, Single Prune
body: Selective Pruning with Sensitivity Ranking is a post-growth pruning step that selects the final Gaussian population in a single event, matching the cumulative effect of periodic pruning throughout training. It ranks Gaussians by sensitivity and retains a calculated count. Inputs: Current Gaussian population P with count N{\text{pre}}. Current training PSNR \rho. Current iteration T{\text{curr}} and total training iterations T{\text{total}}. Sensitivity scores for each Gaussian in P. Outputs: Pruned Gaussian population P' with count NG. Data Structures: Each Gaussian gi \in P has a scalar sensitivity score si. si is defined as the accumulated, opacity-weighted effect on training views. Steps: 1. Calculate the number of remaining events h in a reference pruning schedule. 2. Compute the keep fraction f based on \rho and a multiplier s > 1. 3. Calculate the retained count NG using N{\text{pre}}, f, and h. 4. Rank all Gaussians in P by si in descending order and select the top NG to form P'. 5. Optimize P' for the remainder of training iterations. Formulas: Reference schedule spacing: events are spaced 8\% of T{\text{total}} apart. Remaining events: h = \max\left(0, \left\lfloor \frac{T{\text{total}} - T{\text{curr}}}{0.08 \cdot T{\text{total}}} \right\rfloor\right). Keep fraction: f = \min(1, s \cdot \rho). Retained count: NG = N{\text{pre}} \cdot f^h. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectivepruningwithsensitivityranking(P, rho, Tcurr, Ttotal, s, Pstar): # 1. Calculate remaining reference events h interval = 0.08 Ttotal h = max(0, int((Ttotal - Tcurr) // interval)) # 2. Calculate keep fraction f f = min(1.0, s rho) if rho <= Pstar: f = 1.0 # 3. Calculate retained count NG Npre = len(P) NG = max(1, int(round(Npre (f h)))) # 4. Rank and select Psorted = sorted(P, key=lambda g: g.sensitivityscore, reverse=True) Pprime = Psorted[:NG] # 5. Optimize retained population for the remainder of training iterations # (External optimizer call omitted; implementation not given in sources) return Pprime Parameters: s: Multiplier for the keep fraction. s > 1. Not given in the sources. \rho: Current training PSNR. P^: PSNR threshold below which no removal occurs. T{\text{total}}, T{\text{curr}}: Total and current training iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Removal at Low PSNR: If \rho \le P^, f=1, so the final selection removes nothing. Irreversibility: Gaussians removed during this final selection stage cannot be regrown. Therefore, s > 1 retains a larger fraction than a standard soft prune at the same PSNR level. Precision: NG must be an integer. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a deterministic final population size that accounts for the cumulative effect of pruning. Limitations: The final selection is irreversible. The choice of s and P^ is critical and not specified in the sources. When to use: At the end of the growth phase, before the final optimization stage. When not to use: If regrowth is still desired after pruning. Selective Pruning with Sensitivity Ranking is implemented in LiteGS (Liao et al., 2025). It is part of a densification strategy that includes growth and periodic pruning. The method aims to compactify the Gaussian representation by selecting the most significant Gaussians in a single event, mimicking the effect of continued periodic pruning. name: Principled Uncertainty Pruning
head: Fisher Information-based pruning score, PUP 3D-GS, PUP 3D-GS Pruning Score & Pipeline, Principled Uncertainty Pruning for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body:
Principled Uncertainty Pruning (PUP) is a post-hoc method for compressing pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) models by removing Gaussians with high uncertainty in their spatial parameters. It solves the problem of visual fidelity degradation at high compression ratios by using a principled sensitivity score derived from the Fisher Information matrix of the reconstruction error. Unlike heuristic methods that rely on opacity or gradient magnitude, PUP quantifies the entropy of the posterior distribution over each Gaussian's position and scale, allowing for aggressive pruning (up to 90%) while preserving fine details and foreground information. PUP operates as a multi-round prune-refine pipeline applied to a converged 3D-GS model. It does not modify the training pipeline but instead evaluates a sensitivity score for each Gaussian to determine which ones to remove. Input: A converged 3D-GS model \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each Gaussian gk has mean \muk, scale sk, rotation qk, opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. A set of ground truth training images \mathcal{I} with corresponding camera poses \Phi. Output: A pruned set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with reduced cardinality. The method computes a 6 	imes 6 Fisher Information matrix block for each Gaussian, corresponding to its 3D mean position (\mux, \muy, \muz) and 3D scale parameters (sx, sy, sz). Fisher Matrix (Fk): A 6 	imes 6 symmetric positive semi-definite matrix for Gaussian gk. Pruning Score (Sk): A scalar value derived from Fk. Patch Size: The sensitivity score is computed over image patches. Default is 4 	imes 4 pixels. Alternatives 2 	imes 2 and 8 	imes 8 are also supported. Pruning Percentages: Round 1 prunes 80% of Gaussians. Round 2 prunes 50% of the remaining Gaussians. Total pruning is ~90%. Fine-tuning Iterations: 5,000 iterations per round, totaling 10,000 iterations. 1. Compute L2 Loss: Calculate the L2 reconstruction error over the training views: L2 =  rac{1}{2} \sum{\phi \in \Phi} \|I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) - I{gt}(\phi)\|2^2 where I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) is the rendered image for pose \phi using Gaussians \mathcal{G}, and I{gt}(\phi) is the ground truth image. 2. Approximate Hessian via Fisher Information: The exact Hessian of the L2 loss with respect to Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} is: 
abla{\mathcal{G}}^2 L2 = \sum{\phi \in \Phi} 
abla{\mathcal{G}} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) 
abla{\mathcal{G}} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi)^T + (I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) - I{gt}(\phi)) 
abla{\mathcal{G}}^2 I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) Since the model is converged, the residual term (I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) - I{gt}(\phi)) approaches zero, causing the second-order term to vanish. The Hessian is approximated by the Fisher Information matrix: F \approx \sum{\phi \in \Phi} 
abla{\mathcal{G}} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) 
abla{\mathcal{G}} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi)^T. 3. Compute Block-wise Fisher Matrix: To reduce memory usage and focus on geometric uncertainty, restrict the Fisher matrix to the spatial mean and scale parameters only (6 parameters per Gaussian). Exclude rotation and RGB color parameters. For each Gaussian gk, compute the 6 	imes 6 block Fk of the global Fisher matrix. The memory requirement scales linearly with the number of Gaussians N, specifically N 	imes 36 elements. 4. Calculate Pruning Score: The pruning score Sk for Gaussian gk is the log determinant of its Fisher block: Sk = \log \det(Fk) This score represents the entropy of the second-order Laplace approximation of the posterior distribution for that Gaussian. Higher entropy indicates higher uncertainty, making it a candidate for pruning. 5. Multi-Round Prune-Refine Pipeline: Round 1: 1. Sort all Gaussians by Sk in descending order. 2. Remove the top 80% of Gaussians (highest uncertainty). 3. Fine-tune the remaining Gaussians for 5,000 iterations using standard 3D-GS optimization to recover quality. Round 2: 1. Recompute the Fisher matrices and pruning scores for the remaining Gaussians. 2. Remove the top 50% of the remaining Gaussians. 3. Fine-tune for another 5,000 iterations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def principleduncertaintypruning(gaussians, trainingimages, trainingposes, patchsize=4, round1prunepct=0.8, round2prunepct=0.5, finetuneiters=5000): """ Performs Principled Uncertainty Pruning on a 3D-GS model. """ def extractpatches(tensor, patchsize): # tensor shape: (H, W, C, P) where P=6 params # Returns shape: (numpatches, patchsizepatchsizeC, P) H, W, C, P = tensor.shape patches = tensor.reshape(H // patchsize, patchsize, W // patchsize, patchsize, C, P) patches = patches.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5).reshape(-1, patchsize patchsize C, P) return patches def computefisherblock(g, poses, images, patchsize): nparams = 6 fisherblock = np.zeros((nparams, nparams)) for pose, gtimg in zip(poses, images): # Requires differentiable rasterizer backward pass to compute dIG/dparams gradimgparams = computegradientofrenderedimagewrtspatialparams(g, pose) gradpatches = extractpatches(gradimgparams, patchsize) for patchgrad in gradpatches: fisherblock += patchgrad.T @ patchgrad return fisherblock scores = [] for g in gaussians: Fk = computefisherblock(g, trainingposes, trainingimages, patchsize) epsilon = 1e-6 Fkreg = Fk + epsilon np.eye(6) try: logdet = np.log(np.linalg.det(Fkreg)) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: logdet = -np.inf scores.append(logdet) scores = np.array(scores) # Round 1 ngaussians = len(gaussians) npruneround1 = int(ngaussians round1prunepct) indicestopruneround1 = np.argsort(scores)[-npruneround1:] activemask = np.ones(ngaussians, dtype=bool) activemask[indicestopruneround1] = False activegaussians = [g for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if activemask[i]] # Standard optimizer loop (e.g., Adam) on remaining Gaussians for finetuneiters steps activegaussians = finetunegaussians(activegaussians, trainingposes, trainingimages, finetuneiters) # Round 2 activescores = [] for g in activegaussians: Fk = computefisherblock(g, trainingposes, trainingimages, patchsize) Fkreg = Fk + epsilon np.eye(6) try: logdet = np.log(np.linalg.det(Fkreg)) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: logdet = -np.inf activescores.append(logdet) activescores = np.array(activescores) nactive = len(activegaussians) npruneround2 = int(nactive round2prunepct) indicestopruneround2 = np.argsort(activescores)[-npruneround2:] activemaskround2 = np.ones(nactive, dtype=bool) activemaskround2[indicestopruneround2] = False finalgaussians = [g for i, g in enumerate(activegaussians) if activemaskround2[i]] finalgaussians = finetunegaussians(finalgaussians, trainingposes, trainingimages, finetuneiters) return finalgaussians def computegradientofrenderedimagewrtspatialparams(g, pose): # Requires differentiable rasterizer backward pass to compute dIG/dparams # Returns array of shape (H, W, 3, 6) pass def finetunegaussians(gaussians, poses, images, iterations): # Standard optimizer loop (e.g., Adam) on remaining Gaussians for iterations steps pass Convergence Requirement: The method assumes the scene is fully converged. The Fisher approximation relies on the residual (IG - I{gt}) being small. Pruning before convergence degrades the approximation and final quality. Memory Constraints: Including rotation parameters expands the Fisher matrix to 10 	imes 10, increasing memory usage by 2.78×. This can cause out-of-memory errors on 16GB GPUs (e.g., RTX A4000). Excluding rotations is critical for standard hardware. RGB Parameters: Using RGB color parameters for the sensitivity score degrades image quality. The RGB score correlates with visibility rather than reconstruction error sensitivity. Patch Size: While 4 	imes 4 is the default, 2 	imes 2 and 8 	imes 8 patches produce similar results, though 4 	imes 4 yields slightly better metrics. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is computing the Fisher matrices, which scales linearly with the number of Gaussians N and the number of training views. The fine-tuning steps add additional time proportional to the number of iterations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage for Fisher matrices is proportional to N 	imes 36 elements (for the 6 	imes 6 block). This fits within 16GB GPUs for typical scene sizes. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, PUP achieves an average PSNR of 26.67, SSIM of 0.7862, and LPIPS of 0.2719 after 90% pruning, with an average FPS of 204.81 on an RTX A4000. On the Deep Blending playroom scene, it accelerates rendering from 76.65 FPS to 318.06 FPS (4.15× speed-up). Strengths: Preserves fine details and foreground information better than heuristic methods like LightGaussian. Achieves higher compression ratios (up to 90%) with less quality degradation. Limitations: Requires a converged model. Not suitable for online or incremental training scenarios where the model is not yet stable. Principled Uncertainty Pruning (PUP) was introduced by Alex Hanson, Allen Tu, Vasu Singla, Mayuka Jayawardhana, Matthias Zwicker, and Tom Goldstein from the University of Maryland, College Park. The method addresses the limitations of previous pruning techniques that relied on heuristics, which often failed to preserve visual fidelity at high compression ratios. PUP builds on the concept of Fisher Information as a measure of parameter sensitivity, adapting it to the specific structure of 3D Gaussian Splatting. PUP 3D-GS: Principled Uncertainty Pruning for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.00558, fetched 2026-10-29

name: TangoGS
head: Gauss What You Need
body: TangoGS is a density control strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that automatically scales the number of Gaussian primitives to match the complexity of the input capture without per-scene tuning. It combines a capture-derived "learning allowance" (model sizing based on track-adjusted pixel count) with training-based quality feedback (PSNR-driven pruning) to determine the final Gaussian population. Unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed thresholds or per-capture calibration, TangoGS uses a shared configuration across diverse scene scales, achieving comparable or better PSNR with significantly fewer Gaussians than baselines like LeGS or 3DGS. TangoGS operates on the set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} defined by the parent [Parent]. The method manages the population size through three phases: allowance calculation, budgeted densification with soft pruning, and final selection. Inputs: Capture metadata: number of images N{\text{img}} (including held-out), mean track length, sparse model point count. Training metrics: mean per-image PSNR P from the preceding epoch. Hyperparameters: T{\text{ref}}, g, s, c, P^, h. Outputs: A pruned subset of Gaussians \mathcal{G}{final} with size NG. Gaussian Parameters: Unclustered, then filtered, then reclustered into Morton-ordered groups of 128 elements to align with batch removal operations. Sensitivity Scores: Accumulated per-Gaussian scores from the LiteGS kernel, mapped back to original indices via a culling map. Adam Buffers: Reclustered alongside parameters to maintain contiguous memory access. T{\text{ref}} = 2,462,476: Reference count, rounded geometric mean of linear allowances over 13 standard scenes. g \approx 0.063362106: Effective scaling factor from track-adjusted pixels to Gaussians, implemented via nested rounding. s = 1.7: Scaling factor for the final selection keep fraction. c = 0.0075: Coefficient for PSNR-based threshold adjustment. P^ = 20 \text{ dB}: Threshold PSNR above which no removal occurs. h: Number of remaining events in a reference pruning schedule spaced 8% of total training iterations apart. Split/Clone Threshold: 0.001 (maximum gradient magnitude). Opacity Decay: Factor 0.5 per step, floor 1/128. SH Learning Rate Divisor: 20. 1. Calculate Learning Allowance (T{\text{cap}}): Compute the linear allowance T{\text{lin}} based on the capture's track-adjusted pixel count \mathcal{A} (derived from N{\text{img}} and track data): T{\text{lin}} = \text{round} \left[ 0.90 \cdot \text{round}(0.07040234 \cdot \mathcal{A}) \right] Compute the capped allowance: T{\text{cap}} = \text{round} \left[ T{\text{ref}} \cdot \left( \frac{T{\text{lin}}}{T{\text{ref}}} \right)^{0.5} \right] 2. Initialize Training Schedule: Densification starts at 2% of total training iterations. Soft pruning begins at ~9% of total training iterations. Densification ends at 80% of total training iterations. Growth events are spaced 5 epochs apart for runs \ge 150 epochs; for shorter runs, spacing is reduced proportionally to a minimum of 1 epoch. 3. Budgeted Densification (at each growth event): Calculate the adaptation target T{\text{adapt}} using the mean per-image PSNR P from the preceding epoch: \rho = 0.7382 - 0.0075 \cdot P T{\text{adapt}} = \rho \cdot T{\text{cap}} Note: The intercept 0.7382 results from rounding the main paper's formula \rho = \frac{1}{s} - c(P - P^) with s=1.7, c=0.0075, P^=20. Ramp the Gaussian count linearly from the initial point count to T{\text{adapt}} over the growth window using standard splitting/cloning based on gradient magnitude > 0.001 [Parent]. Newly created Gaussians are exempt from pruning until they have trained. 4. Soft Pruning (at each growth event, if applicable): Rank Gaussians present before the growth phase using sensitivity scores (accumulated over the epoch via LiteGS kernel). Keep the top fraction \rho of Gaussians. Remove the rest. Removal counts are rounded down to the nearest multiple of 128. Guard: If removal would exceed 90% of the population, abort the prune. 5. Final Selection (at 80% of training iterations): Let N{\text{pre}} be the population entering this event. Calculate the final keep fraction: f = \min(1, s \cdot \rho) where \rho is recalibrated from the preceding epoch's PSNR. The retained count is: NG = N{\text{pre}} \cdot f^h Rank all N{\text{pre}} Gaussians by sensitivity score. Keep the top NG Gaussians. Optimize this final population for the remainder of training. """ # Constants TREF = 2462476 G = 0.063362106 S = 1.7 C = 0.0075 PSTAR = 20.0 INTERCEPT = 0.7382 # Rounded from 1/1.7 - 0.0075(20-20) # 1. Calculate Allowance # A is track-adjusted pixel count derived from capturemetadata A = calculatetrackadjustedpixels(capturemetadata) Tlin = round(0.90 round(0.07040234 A)) Tcap = round(TREF (Tlin / TREF)0.5) # Schedule parameters densifystart = 0.02 totaliterations prunestart = 0.09 totaliterations densifyend = 0.80 totaliterations # Epoch spacing logic (simplified) epochspacing = 5 if totalepochs < 150: epochspacing = max(1, 5 (totalepochs / 150)) currentgaussiancount = len(gaussians) initialcount = currentgaussiancount # 2. Training Loop for iter in range(totaliterations): # Standard 3DGS training step (forward, loss, backward) loss = renderandcomputeloss(gaussians) optimizer.step() # Quality Feedback: Calculate mean per-image PSNR P P = computemeanperimagepsnr(gaussians) # 3. Growth Events if iter >= densifystart and iter <= densifyend: if isgrowthevent(iter, epochspacing): # Calculate adaptation target rho = INTERCEPT - C P Tadapt = rho Tcap # Budgeted densification: ramp up to Tadapt # This involves splitting/cloning existing Gaussians # based on gradient magnitude > 0.001 targetcount = interpolatecount(initialcount, Tadapt, iter, densifystart, densifyend) densifygaussians(gaussians, targetcount, threshold=0.001) # Soft Pruning (if after prunestart) if iter >= prunestart: # Rank Gaussians present BEFORE growth by sensitivity score scores = computesensitivityscores(gaussians) keepfraction = rho keepcount = round(len(gaussians) keepfraction) # Guard against catastrophic collapse if keepcount < 0.1 len(gaussians): abortprune() else: # Remove bottom (1-rho) Gaussians # Round removal count to multiple of 128 removecount = len(gaussians) - keepcount removecount = (removecount // 128) 128 prunegaussians(gaussians, removecount, scores) # 4. Final Selection if iter == densifyend: Npre = len(gaussians) # Recalibrate rho from preceding epoch rhofinal = INTERCEPT - C P f = min(1.0, S rhofinal) # Calculate retained count # h is number of remaining events in reference schedule (8% spacing) # For implementation, h is a constant derived from totaliterations NG = round(Npre (f h)) # Rank and keep top NG scores = computesensitivityscores(gaussians) finalgaussians = selecttopk(gaussians, scores, NG) # Optimize final population gaussians = finalgaussians break return gaussians Determines the target Gaussian population size based on capture characteristics (track-adjusted pixels) to replace fixed defaults. It ensures model budget invariance to redundant views, unlike sibling methods that scale with view count or SfM density. Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to standard 3DGS, with minor overhead for sensitivity score accumulation and periodic pruning. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower than standard 3DGS and baselines like LeGS. On 13 standard benchmark scenes, TangoGS uses 48% fewer Gaussians while matching mean PSNR. Performance: Matches or exceeds baseline PSNR on 21 captures (13 standard, 8 large) with a single shared configuration. Strengths: Automatic scaling across scene sizes; no per-capture tuning required; robust to redundant views. Limitations: Requires accurate track data and sparse models for allowance calculation; sensitivity scoring adds minor computational overhead. When to use: When deploying 3DGS on diverse captures without manual hyperparameter tuning. When not to use: When strict real-time training constraints prohibit the sensitivity score accumulation or when capture metadata is unavailable. TangoGS was introduced in the paper "Gauss What You Need: Compact Gaussian Splatting Across Scene Scales". It builds on LiteGS for sensitivity scoring and integrates with standard 3DGS optimization. The method addresses the limitation of fixed Gaussian counts or per-scene tuning in previous density control strategies.
