name: Capture-Conditioned Learning Allowance
head: Learning Allowance, Track-Adjusted Pixel Allowance
body: A method to determine the target Gaussian population size for 3D Gaussian Splatting based on capture characteristics, specifically using track-adjusted pixels normalized against standard scenes, to replace fixed defaults. It differs from sibling methods by ensuring the model budget is invariant to redundant views, whereas alternatives like total pixel count scale with view count and SfM point counts scale with matched-observation density rather than capture scale. Inputs and outputs: Input: The set of training images (views) for a capture. Output: A scalar multiplier or target count for the Gaussian population, derived from the track-adjusted pixel statistic. Data structures: Not specified in the sources. The method relies on a statistical summary of the capture. Steps: 1. Compute Track-Adjusted Pixels: Calculate a metric based on the unique visual information in the capture, normalized against a reference set of standard scenes. (Exact formula not given in the sources.) 2. Normalize: Compare the capture's statistic against the baseline of 13 standard captures. 3. Determine Allowance: Use the normalized statistic to set the Gaussian budget. A fixed 0.5 rule approximates the adaptive rule on captures with the highest training PSNR but selects smaller, lower-quality models on others. Parameters: Reference set: 13 standard captures. Fixed rule approximation: 0.5. Edge cases and pitfalls: Size Invariance vs. Rendering Invariance: Even with track-adjusted pixels, duplicating views and halving training epochs causes a loss in large-capture PSNR. Comparison with Total Pixels: Total pixels are sensitive to redundant views; duplicating every image multiplies the total-pixel allowance by \sqrt{2} and increases the mean final count by 36% to 38%. Comparison with SfM Points: SfM point allowances follow matched-observation density per image pixel rather than the capture itself, spending 4% more Gaussians on standard scenes and 12% more on large captures for the same quality. A baseline method for candidate subset selection in dynamic resampling, used to isolate the effect of dynamic versus static restriction. It samples a candidate subset once per stage and keeps it fixed for all acquisition steps within that stage. It uses the same subset size determined by \epsilon as LiTe-GS for fair comparison. A fixed subset can occasionally be favorable, allowing SSG to outperform LiTe-GS on specific settings, but remains permanently restricted to that realization. On Blender (Ship) with K=4, \epsilon=0.1: PSNR 25.40, SSIM 0.829, LPIPS 0.158. On MipNeRF 360 (Garden) with K=3, \epsilon=0.40: PSNR 20.17, SSIM 0.541, LPIPS 0.436. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On standard scenes, track-adjusted pixels use 4% fewer Gaussians than SfM points and reach the same mean quality (within 0.04 dB and 0.003 LPIPS). On large captures, they use 12% fewer Gaussians than SfM points. Scaling: Track-adjusted pixels remain stable (within 10% of original count) when views are duplicated, whereas total pixels increase by 36% to 38%. Strengths and Limitations: The primary strength is invariance to redundant views. A limitation is that it does not prevent quality loss if the number of training epochs is reduced due to duplicated views. When to use: When the capture may contain redundant or duplicated views and a stable model budget is required. When not to use: When rendering invariance is critical despite changes in training data volume, as size invariance does not guarantee rendering invariance. Originated in the work on "Gauss What You Need: Compact Gaussian Splatting Across Scene Scales". It is part of the TangoGS framework, which automates density controller decisions including Gaussian budget selection. The method was developed to address the sensitivity of fixed defaults and alternative statistics (total pixels, SfM points) to capture scale and redundancy. Gauss What You Need: Compact Gaussian Splatting Across Scene Scales, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31248, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) LiTe-GS: Oracle-Efficient Next Best View Selection for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30393, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Depth-Based Gaussian Pruning
head: Depth-adaptive pruning, relative depth pruning
body: Depth-Based Gaussian Pruning is a strategy that varies the opacity pruning threshold based on the relative depth (z-axis value) of 3D Gaussians to preserve points at the far plane in forward-facing scenes. It sets itself apart from standard fixed-threshold pruning by applying a lower threshold (making pruning harder) to distant primitives, thereby compensating for the sparsity of Gaussians that naturally occurs at the back of the scene. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk has mean position \muk = (xk, yk, zk), opacity \alphak, and other attributes. Parameters: tp: Base pruning threshold. Typical values: 5 \times 10^{-3} for real defocus blur datasets, 1 \times 10^{-2} for real camera motion blur datasets. wp: Pruning threshold multiplier based on depth. Typical value: 3. Output: A subset of Gaussians retained after pruning. Data Structures: The method operates on the existing Gaussian buffer. No new complex structures are required beyond the standard Gaussian attributes. The relative depth is derived directly from the zk coordinate. Steps: 1. Determine Relative Depth: For each Gaussian gk, identify its zk coordinate. In forward-facing scenes, zk serves as a proxy for relative depth from the viewpoint. 2. Calculate Depth Multiplier: Determine the multiplier wk for each Gaussian based on its zk. The source specifies that the multiplier is determined by relative depth, with the lowest threshold applied to the farthest point. While the exact interpolation function is not explicitly defined in the provided text, the logic implies a mapping where wk scales with depth. Let z{min} and z{max} be the minimum and maximum z values in the scene (or a relevant subset). A linear interpolation is implied by "determined depending on the relative depth": wk = 1 + (wp - 1) \cdot \frac{zk - z{min}}{z{max} - z{min}} Note: The source states the lowest threshold is applied to the farthest point. Since the effective threshold is tp \cdot wk (or similar scaling), and we want to preserve far points, the threshold for far points must be lower? Or does the multiplier apply to the opacity? The text says "pruning threshold tp is scaled by wp... lowest threshold is applied to the farthest point." If the threshold is the minimum opacity required to survive, a "low threshold" means it is easier to survive. Thus, for far points, the required opacity is lower. This implies the multiplier reduces the threshold. However, wp=3 is >1. If tp is scaled by wp, the threshold becomes higher, making pruning harder (more points survive). This aligns with "preserve more points located at the far plane". So, the farthest point gets the highest multiplier? The text says "lowest threshold is applied to the farthest point". This is contradictory if "threshold" means the value tp \cdot w. If wp=3, and we want the lowest threshold value, we should multiply by a small number. Let's re-read carefully: "pruning threshold tp is scaled by wp where wp is determined depending on the relative depth, and the lowest threshold is applied to the farthest point." If wp is the multiplier, and the result is the threshold, then the farthest point has the smallest multiplier. But wp is given as a single value 3. This suggests wp is the range or the max multiplier. Let's assume the multiplier mk ranges from 1 (near) to wp (far). Then the threshold is tp \cdot mk. A higher threshold means stricter pruning (higher opacity required). This would prune more far points. This contradicts "preserve more points". Alternative Interpretation: The "threshold" refers to the allowance for low opacity. Or, the multiplier is applied inversely. Let's look at the standard 3D-GS pruning: remove if \alpha < tp. If we want to preserve far points, we want to remove fewer far points. So we need a higher opacity requirement? No, if we raise the requirement, we remove more. We need a lower opacity requirement. So the threshold t{eff} should be lower for far points. Re-reading S1: "prune 3D Gaussians depending on their positions... prune out less 3D Gaussians placed on the far edge... relying on the relative depth. Specifically, the pruning threshold tp is scaled by wp... and the lowest threshold is applied to the farthest point." If the threshold is T, and we prune if \alpha < T, then a "low threshold" means we prune less (easier to survive). So T{far} < T{near}. The text says tp is scaled by wp. If wp=3, and it's a multiplier, does it mean T = tp / w(z)? Or T = tp \cdot (1/w(z))? Given wp=3 is a single parameter, it likely defines the ratio between near and far thresholds. Let T{near} = tp. Let T{far} = tp / wp. Then Tk = tp \cdot \left( 1 + ( \frac{1}{wp} - 1) \frac{zk - z{min}}{z{max} - z{min}} \right). This ensures T{far} is the lowest threshold. 3. Apply Pruning: For each Gaussian gk, calculate its effective threshold Tk. If \alphak < Tk, remove gk from the set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthbasedpruning(gaussians, tp, wp): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes.alpha,.z tp: Base pruning threshold (float) wp: Depth multiplier (float, e.g., 3) """ # Find depth range zvalues = [g.z for g in gaussians] if not zvalues: return [] zmin = min(zvalues) zmax = max(zvalues) # Handle degenerate case where all z are same if zmax == zmin: threshold = tp return [g for g in gaussians if g.alpha >= threshold] retainedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Calculate relative depth factor # Interpolate multiplier from 1 (near) to 1/wp (far) # This ensures the threshold is lowest at the far plane relativedepth = (g.z - zmin) / (zmax - zmin) # Multiplier for the threshold: starts at 1.0 for near, goes to 1/wp for far # This makes the threshold smaller (easier to survive) for far points depthfactor = 1.0 + ( (1.0 / wp) - 1.0) relativedepth effectivethreshold = tp depthfactor if g.alpha >= effectivethreshold: retainedgaussians.append(g) return retainedgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-forward-facing scenes: The method relies on zk as relative depth. It is explicitly designed for forward-facing scenes (e.g., DeblurNeRF dataset). For general 360-degree scenes, z is not a consistent depth metric across viewpoints, and this method may fail or require viewpoint-dependent depth calculation. Depth Range Calculation: z{min} and z{max} should likely be computed over the entire scene or a sliding window if the scene geometry changes significantly during training. Using global bounds is standard for static scenes. Precision: Ensure floating-point comparisons for \alphak < Tk are stable. Time Complexity: O(N) per pruning step, where N is the number of Gaussians. The depth range calculation is one pass, and the filtering is another. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory (storing min/max z). Performance: Improves reconstruction quality in forward-facing scenes by preventing the loss of distant geometry, which is often under-represented due to lower pixel coverage and gradient magnitude. Limitations: Not applicable to non-forward-facing or general 3D scenes without modification. Requires the scene to have a well-defined "far" plane relative to the camera orientation. Originating from work on Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting, this method addresses the issue of Gaussian sparsity at the far end of forward-facing scenes. It builds on the standard 3D-GS adaptive density control but introduces depth-awareness to the pruning phase. The approach was validated on datasets with camera motion blur and defocus blur, such as those from the DeblurNeRF benchmark. Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73636-08, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Advance Floater Pruning
head: Advanced Floater Pruning, Advanced Floater Removal, Floater Pruning, Pruning, Pruning heuristic
body: Advance Floater Pruning is an explicit and adaptive operator designed to identify and eliminate undesired floating artifacts (misplaced Gaussians) in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations, particularly in sparse-view synthesis settings. It distinguishes itself from standard pruning by analyzing the relative difference between mode-selected depth and alpha-blended depth to detect "floaters"—low-opacity Gaussians positioned close to the camera center that cause misalignment between depth metrics. Unlike Depth-Based Gaussian Pruning, which adjusts thresholds based on scene depth to preserve far-plane points, this method targets geometric inconsistencies caused by transmittance budget depletion near the camera. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained 3DGS representation G, a set of training cameras I, and curve parameters a and b. Output: The 3DGS representation G with identified floater Gaussians removed. Data Structures: 3DGS Representation G: Contains Gaussian primitives with attributes including position, covariance, opacity, and color. Depth Maps: Rendered per training view i: d^{alpha}i: Alpha-blending depth map. d^{mode}i: Mode-selection depth map. Relative Difference Map \Deltai: Per-pixel relative difference between d^{mode}i and d^{alpha}i. Floater Mask Fi: Binary mask indicating pixels with relative difference exceeding the threshold. Definitions: Alpha-blending depth (d^{alpha}): Calculated as the weighted sum of depths along a ray, influenced by all Gaussians: d^{alpha}{x,y} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai di where Ti is the accumulated transmittance for the i-th Gaussian, \alphai is the alpha-compositing weight, and di is the depth of the Gaussian. Mode-selection depth (d^{mode}): The depth value corresponding to the Gaussian with the maximum alpha-compositing weight (or softmax-weighted depth) along the ray. Relative Difference (\Deltai): For each training view i, the per-pixel relative difference is computed as: \Deltai = \frac{d^{mode}i - d^{alpha}i}{d^{alpha}i} Dip Statistic: A measure of uni-modality applied to the distribution of \Deltai values. Parameters: a = 0.97: Exponential curve parameter for threshold conversion. b = -7.5: Exponential curve parameter for threshold conversion. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the average dip statistic \bar{D} = 0.0. 2. For each training view i \in I: a. Render the alpha-blending depth map d^{alpha}i from G using view i. b. Render the mode-selection depth map d^{mode}i from G using view i. c. Compute the relative difference map \Deltai = (d^{mode}i - d^{alpha}i) / d^{alpha}i. d. Compute the dip statistic for the distribution of \Deltai values. e. Add this dip statistic to \bar{D}. 3. Compute the average dip statistic: \bar{D} = \bar{D} / |I|, where |I| is the number of training views. This score represents the scene-wide presence of floaters. 4. For each training view i \in I: a. Calculate the threshold \taui using the percentile function with an exponential curve based on the average dip statistic: \taui = \text{percentile}(\Deltai, a e^{b \bar{D}}) The percentile function selects the value below which a given percentage of \Deltai values fall. The argument a e^{b \bar{D}} maps the dip statistic to a percentile value. b. Generate the floater mask Fi where Fi = 1 if \Deltai > \taui, and 0 otherwise. c. Identify the indices of all Gaussians contributing to pixels where Fi = 1. This includes the mode Gaussian and other Gaussians along those rays. d. Remove these identified Gaussians from G. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def advancefloaterpruning(G, trainingcameras, a=0.97, b=-7.5): """ Prunes floaters from 3D Gaussian Splatting representation G. Args: G: 3DGS representation containing Gaussians. trainingcameras: List of camera parameters for training views. a: Curve parameter for threshold conversion. b: Curve parameter for threshold conversion. Returns: G: Pruned 3DGS representation. """ totaldipstatistic = 0.0 numviews = len(trainingcameras) # Step 1: Compute average dip statistic across all views for i in range(numviews): cam = trainingcameras[i] # Render depth maps # Note: Implementation of alphablendingdepth and modeselectiondepth # depends on the specific 3DGS rasterizer. dalpha = alphablendingdepth(G, cam) dmode = modeselectiondepth(G, cam) # Compute relative difference # Avoid division by zero; handle background pixels if necessary # Assuming dalpha is valid for foreground pixels deltai = (dmode - dalpha) / dalpha # Compute dip statistic for the distribution of deltai # The dip statistic measures the maximum difference between the # empirical distribution function and the best-fitting unimodal distribution. dipstat = computedipstatistic(deltai.flatten()) totaldipstatistic += dipstat averagedipstatistic = totaldipstatistic / numviews # Step 2: Apply pruning for each view for i in range(numviews): cam = trainingcameras[i] # Re-render or use cached depth maps dalpha = alphablendingdepth(G, cam) dmode = modeselectiondepth(G, cam) deltai = (dmode - dalpha) / dalpha # Calculate threshold # The percentile argument is a value between 0 and 100. # a exp(b Dbar) maps the dip statistic to this percentile. percentilevalue = a math.exp(b averagedipstatistic) # Ensure percentilevalue is within valid range [0, 100] percentilevalue = max(0.0, min(100.0, percentilevalue)) threshold = percentile(deltai.flatten(), percentilevalue) # Generate floater mask floatermask = deltai > threshold # Identify Gaussians to remove # This requires mapping pixel coordinates in floatermask back to # the Gaussians that contributed to those pixels during rendering. gaussianstoremove = masktogaussianindices(G, cam, floatermask) # Remove Gaussians G.removegaussians(gaussianstoremove) return G Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If d^{alpha}i is zero (e.g., background pixels), the relative difference \Deltai is undefined. Implementation must handle background pixels, typically by excluding them from the dip statistic calculation and mask generation. Transmittance Threshold: Floaters arise because 3DGS halts rasterization once a transmittance threshold is reached. Near-camera floaters deplete this budget early, preventing convergence at the correct depth. Bimodal Distribution: The method relies on the observation that floaters cause a bimodal distribution in \Deltai. If the scene does not exhibit this characteristic (e.g., no floaters), the dip statistic will be low, resulting in a high percentile threshold and minimal pruning. Timing: Pruning is applied once after training completes, not during training iterations. Time Complexity: The method requires rendering depth maps for all training views twice (once for dip statistic calculation, once for pruning) and computing dip statistics. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of training views and pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth maps and relative difference maps for all training views. Performance: Effectively removes "background collapse" and floating artifacts in sparse-input settings. Strengths: Explicitly targets geometric inconsistencies (floaters) that are not addressed by opacity-based pruning. Adaptive thresholding based on scene-wide dip statistic allows it to handle varying levels of floater presence. Limitations: Only applicable after training. Relies on the assumption that floaters cause bimodal depth difference distributions. Origin: Introduced in the paper "SparseGS: Sparse View Synthesis Using 3D Gaussian Splatting". Context: Developed to address artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting when trained on sparse input views. The method complements other regularization techniques like Unseen Viewpoint Regularization and Score Distillation Sampling. History: The concept of "floaters" in 3DGS refers to low-opacity Gaussians near the camera that cause misalignment between mode-selection and alpha-blending depths. This pruning heuristic was empirically derived by examining \Deltai distributions across various scenes. Sparsegs: Sparse View Synthesis Using 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00100, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Weighted Floater Removal
body: Weighted Floater Removal (WFR) is an explicit post-processing method to eliminate 3D Gaussian floaters in whole-scene reconstruction by verifying multi-view depth consistency. Unlike TSDF Fusion, which incurs high computational costs by building voxel volumes and extracting meshes, WFR directly adjusts Gaussian opacities based on accumulated weights, avoiding rendering holes while maintaining geometric accuracy. It specifically addresses floaters introduced after the current view's processing in the incremental PTF module, which the parent Advance Floater Pruning fails to remove. Inputs and Outputs Input: Global 3D Gaussian primitives \{\mug, \alphag, \omegag\} obtained after unprojecting and fusing whole-scene input views via the PTF module; predicted depth maps dt for each input view; rendered depth maps dg for the global Gaussians. Output: Adjusted global Gaussian opacities \alphag with floaters suppressed. Data Structures Global Gaussians: A list or array of primitives, each containing: \mug: 3D center coordinates (x, y, z). \alphag: Opacity scalar. \omegag: Weight scalar (accumulated during PTF). Depth Maps: 2D arrays for each input view, indexed by pixel (u, v), containing predicted depth dt(u,v) and rendered depth dg(u,v). Parameters \delta: Pre-defined threshold to determine if predicted depth is significantly larger than the rendered depth of the nearest global Gaussian. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Retrieve the global set of 3D Gaussian primitives \{\mug, \alphag, \omegag\} resulting from the PTF module. 2. Traversal: Iterate through each input view t in the scene. 3. Projection: For the current view t, project all global Gaussian centers \mug onto the 2D image plane. 4. Pixel-wise Processing: For each pixel i in the current view: a. Define S'i as the set of 3D Gaussian primitives that project onto pixel i. b. Calculate the rendered depth of the nearest global Gaussian primitive in S'i: d{g, \min}(i) = \min{j \in S'i} dg(j) where dg(j) is the depth of Gaussian j. c. Identify potential floaters m'i using the threshold \delta and the predicted depth dt(i): m'i = \begin{cases} \arg \min{j \in S'i} dg(j), & \text{if } dt(i) - \min{j \in S'i} dg(j) > \delta \\ \emptyset, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} If m'i is not empty, the Gaussian at m'i is a potential floater because the predicted depth indicates a surface further away than the nearest rendered Gaussian, suggesting noise-induced misalignment. d. Calculate the accumulated neighbor weight \tilde{\omega}g(m'i) for the identified floater. This involves summing the weights \omegag of neighboring Gaussians to adaptively assign higher weights to correct primitives. e. Reduce the opacity \alphag of the floater m'i based on \tilde{\omega}g(m'i) to eliminate its influence without creating holes. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def weightedfloaterremoval(globalgaussians, inputviews, delta): """ globalgaussians: List of dicts with keys 'mu' (3D vector), 'alpha' (float), 'omega' (float) inputviews: List of dicts with keys 'predicteddepth' (2D array), 'rendereddepth' (2D array), 'projectionmatrix' delta: Float threshold """ # Step 1: Global Gaussians are already provided from PTF # Step 2: Traverse input views for view in inputviews: predicteddepth = view['predicteddepth'] rendereddepth = view['rendereddepth'] projmatrix = view['projectionmatrix'] # Step 3: Project global Gaussians to current view # For each Gaussian, compute 2D projection and depth projectedgaussians = [] for g in globalgaussians: # Project 3D center mu to 2D pixel coordinates and depth # This requires standard perspective projection logic u, v, depthg = project3dto2d(g['mu'], projmatrix) projectedgaussians.append({ 'index': globalgaussians.index(g), 'u': u, 'v': v, 'depth': depthg, 'omega': g['omega'], 'alpha': g['alpha'] }) # Group Gaussians by pixel pixeltogaussians = {} for pg in projectedgaussians: key = (pg['u'], pg['v']) if key not in pixeltogaussians: pixeltogaussians[key] = [] pixeltogaussians[key].append(pg) # Step 4: Pixel-wise processing h, w = predicteddepth.shape for u in range(w): for v in range(h): # Get predicted and rendered depth for pixel i dt = predicteddepth[v, u] dgmin = float('inf') candidategaussian = None # Find nearest global Gaussian in S'i if (u, v) in pixeltogaussians: neighbors = pixeltogaussians[(u, v)] # Find min depth minneighbor = min(neighbors, key=lambda x: x['depth']) dgmin = minneighbor['depth'] # Check floater condition if dt - dgmin > delta: candidategaussian = minneighbor # If floater identified, adjust opacity if candidategaussian is not None: # Calculate accumulated neighbor weight # Note: Exact formula for neighbor weight accumulation is not fully specified in sources # Assuming neighbor weight is sum of omegas of nearby Gaussians in 3D space or image space # For implementation, one might query a spatial index for neighbors of candidategaussian['mu'] neighborweights = getneighborweights(candidategaussian, globalgaussians) accumulatedweight = sum(neighborweights) # Reduce opacity based on accumulated weight # The source mentions "weighted opacity reduction method" but does not give the exact formula # for updating alpha. A common approach is scaling alpha by a factor related to accumulated weight. # Since the exact formula is missing, we mark this step. # candidategaussian['alpha'] = updateopacity(candidategaussian['alpha'], accumulatedweight) pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Depth comparison dt(i) - dg(j) is sensitive to noise in predicted depth maps. Boundaries: The method relies on the existence of projected Gaussians in S'i; empty pixels are ignored. Degenerate Input: If no Gaussians project to a pixel, S'i is empty, and no floater is detected. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians and pixels, as it involves a single pass over input views and pixel-wise checks. Memory Complexity: Requires storing global Gaussian attributes and depth maps; significantly lower than TSDF Fusion which requires voxel volumes. Strengths: Explicitly removes floaters without high computational cost; avoids holes in renderings; seamlessly integrates with feed-forward 3DGS frameworks. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of predicted depth maps; sensitive to the threshold \delta. When to use: When reconstructing generalizable 3D scenes with feed-forward models where floaters are caused by depth prediction noise. When not to use: When high-precision mesh extraction is required, as this method only adjusts opacities. Weighted Floater Removal was introduced in FreeSplat++ as part of a generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for efficient indoor scene reconstruction. It addresses the limitation of the PTF module, which only removes floaters added before the current view, by explicitly checking multi-view depth consistency. The method is inspired by TSDF Fusion but avoids its computational overhead by operating directly on Gaussian primitives. FreeSplat++: Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Indoor Scene Reconstruction., https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2026.3665771, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Pruning
head: Triangle Pruning based on Volume Rendering Weight
body: Adaptive Pruning is a sparsification technique used in triangle-based splatting methods to reduce floaters and prevent overfitting by removing primitives that contribute negligibly to the rendered image. Unlike Gaussian Splatting methods that rely on opacity thresholds or gradient magnitudes, this method operates on the volume rendering blending weight (T \cdot o) of individual triangles. It is specifically designed to eliminate triangles that explain only small amounts of data within a single view, thereby improving the generalization of the radiance field representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D triangle primitives \mathcal{T} = \{t1, \dots, M\}, each with position, orientation, scale, opacity o, and color. A set of training views with known camera poses. Output: A filtered subset of triangles \mathcal{T}' \subset \mathcal{T} with updated buffers. Data Structures: Triangle Buffers: Arrays storing vertex positions, normals, opacities, and colors for all active triangles. Weight Accumulator: A buffer of size M storing the maximum volume rendering weight observed for each triangle across all training views. Render Count: A buffer of size M storing the number of views in which a triangle was rendered with significant coverage. Parameters: \tau{\text{prune}}: User-defined threshold for the maximum volume rendering blending weight. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but it serves as the primary cutoff for significance. step: Current training iteration counter. pruneinterval: Frequency of pruning execution (e.g., 200 steps). minviews: Minimum number of views a triangle must be rendered in (typically 2). minpixels: Minimum pixel coverage required per view (typically > 1 pixel). Steps: 1. Weight Accumulation: During rasterization for each training view, calculate the volume rendering blending weight for each triangle. The weight is defined as W = T \cdot o, where T is the transmittance and o is the opacity. 2. Update Max Weight: For each triangle ti, update its maximum observed weight: W{\max}(ti) = \max(W{\max}(ti), W(ti)) 3. Update Render Count: Increment a counter for each triangle that is rendered with more than one pixel of coverage in the current view. 4. Pruning Execution: If the current step satisfies the pruning interval condition (e.g., step > 0 and step % 200 == 0) and prunethreshold > 0, proceed to filter. 5. Filtering Criteria: A triangle ti is pruned if it meets any of the following conditions: W{\max}(ti) < \tau{\text{prune}}. The number of views in which it was rendered with >1 pixel coverage is less than minviews (typically 2). 6. Buffer Compaction: Create a boolean mask alive where alive[i] is true if ti is not pruned. Filter all triangle buffers (positions, opacities, colors, etc.) using this mask to maintain contiguous memory. 7. Optimizer Reset: Re-initialize the optimizers and learning rate scheduler to account for the change in the number of parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivepruning(triangles, views, tauprune, step, pruneinterval, minviews=2, minpixels=1): """ Prunes triangles based on volume rendering weight and view coverage. """ # Step 1-3: Accumulate weights and counts during rasterization (assumed done per view) # Wmax is maintained across steps # viewcounts is maintained across steps # Step 4: Check pruning condition if step <= 0 or step % pruneinterval != 0 or tauprune <= 0: return triangles # Step 5: Determine alive mask alivemask = torch.zeros(len(triangles), dtype=torch.bool) for i in range(len(triangles)): # Condition 1: Max weight threshold weightok = triangles.Wmax[i] >= tauprune # Condition 2: View coverage threshold # Note: viewcounts[i] stores how many views rendered this triangle with > minpixels coverage coverageok = viewcounts[i] >= minviews # Triangle is alive if it meets BOTH criteria (pruned if it fails ANY) # The source says "prune all triangles whose max weight < tau... Additionally, prune all triangles not rendered at least twice..." # This implies logical OR for pruning conditions. ispruned = (not weightok) or (not coverageok) alivemask[i] = not ispruned # Step 6: Filter buffers # Assuming triangles is a dictionary or object with tensor attributes for key in triangles.attributes: triangles[key] = triangles[key][alivemask] # Update Wmax and viewcounts to match new size triangles.Wmax = triangles.Wmax[alivemask] viewcounts = viewcounts[alivemask] # Step 7: Reset optimizers resetoptimizers(triangles) return triangles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The transmittance T calculation must be numerically stable, especially when opacity is very low or high. Boundary Conditions: Triangles on the boundary of the scene may have lower weights due to partial visibility; ensure \tau{\text{prune}} is set low enough to avoid removing valid geometry. Degenerate Input: If no triangles survive pruning, the method should handle empty sets gracefully to avoid crashes during rasterization. Time Complexity: Pruning itself is O(M) where M is the number of triangles, dominated by the buffer filtering and optimizer reset. The weight accumulation is part of the rasterization cost, which is already O(M \cdot N{\text{views}}). Memory Complexity: O(M) for storing W{\max} and viewcounts buffers. Strengths: Effectively removes "floaters" (artifacts that appear in only one view) and reduces overfitting to training data. It is simpler than gradient-based densification as it relies on direct rendering contribution. Limitations: Requires tracking per-triangle statistics across all views, which adds memory overhead. The threshold \tau{\text{prune}} is user-defined and may require tuning. When to use: When using triangle-based splatting (e.g., Convex Splatting) and observing artifacts from overfitted primitives. When not to use: In Gaussian Splatting, where opacity-based pruning is more common and integrated with densification heuristics [13466-densification-and-splitting.md]. Adaptive Pruning was introduced in the context of Triangle Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering. It draws inspiration from the densification and pruning routines used in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) but adapts them to the triangle primitive representation. The method addresses the issue where the support of the window function can be significantly larger than the triangle, leading to potential overfitting if not managed. name: Texel Size Adaptation and Primitive Management
head: Adaptive Texture Allocation, Primitive Management via Quantile Error
body: Texel Size Adaptation and Primitive Management is a training-time optimization routine that dynamically adjusts the resolution of per-primitive texture maps and the number of 3D Gaussian primitives to balance model capacity and appearance quality. It differs from sibling methods like Adaptive Density Control or GroupFlow by explicitly coupling the geometric density of primitives with the textural detail allocated to them, using quantile-based error thresholds to trigger splitting, upscaling, or downscaling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}, where each primitive k has an associated texture grid (texel map) and a computed error metric Ei. Output: Updated primitive set \mathcal{G}' with modified counts, scales, and texture resolutions. Data Structures: Primitive: Contains mean position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics, and a texture grid. Texture Grid: A 2D array of values (channels) representing local appearance details. The resolution is defined by t2pr (texels per primitive axis). Error Metric Ei: A scalar value representing the reconstruction error for primitive i. The specific formula for Ei is not detailed in the source, but it is used to rank primitives. Parameters: \tau{tr}: Texture resolution threshold. Controls splitting aggressiveness. Starts at 64, reduced to 32 by iteration 7000. \tau{ds}: Downscale threshold. Controls downscaling ease. Higher values make downscaling easier. \lambda{texture}: Controls texture variance. Higher values yield smoother results; lower values reduce texel count per primitive. t2pr: Texture size per primitive (texels per axis). Initialized at iteration 500 to the closest power of two such that the smallest axis is 8 texels wide. Quantile: Top 90% of errors are considered for splitting/upscaling. Interval: Routine runs every 250 iterations until 25,000 iterations. Steps: 1. Initialization: At iteration 500, initialize texture grids to 0. Set t2pr for each primitive to the closest power of two such that the smallest axis is 8 texels wide. 2. Periodic Check: If iter mod 250 == 0 and iter <= 25000: a. Compute error Ei for all primitives. b. Identify the set of primitives in the top 90% of errors. c. For each primitive k: i. Splitting: If texture resolution > \tau{tr} AND Ek is in the top 90%: Split the primitive along overflowing axes. (Note: The exact splitting geometry follows the parent Densification Strategy principles, typically replacing one parent with children sampled from \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak)). ii. Upscaling: If t2pr > 1 AND Ek is in the top 90%: Decrease texel size (Upscale). This is implemented using PyTorch's interpolate function with a scale factor of 2. iii. Downscaling: Else if Ed < \tau{ds}: Increase texel size (Downscale). Implemented using PyTorch's interpolate with a scale factor of 2. Note: The source uses Ed in the condition but does not explicitly define Ed other than implying it relates to the error or texture state. Given the context of "Downscale threshold", it likely refers to the current error metric or a derived texture quality metric. We assume Ed is the error metric Ek or a related local error measure. The method was introduced by Panagiotis Papantonakis, Georgios Kopanas, Frédo Durand, and George Drettakis in "Content-Aware Texturing for Gaussian Splatting". name: Densification and Splitting
head: Adaptive Density Control, Densification Strategy
body: Densification and Splitting is the core training optimization mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that dynamically adjusts the number and distribution of Gaussian primitives to balance reconstruction fidelity against computational cost. It solves the problem of under-representation (blurry or missing details) and over-representation (redundant primitives causing slow rendering) by periodically spawning, splitting, or removing Gaussians based on optimization metrics. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by being a continuous, iterative process driven by gradient magnitude, opacity, and scale heuristics, distinguishing it from sibling methods that may use score-based budgets [4705-score-based-densification.md], visibility consistency [10074-gaussian-insertion-and-pruning.md], or error-guided sampling [15896-error-guided-guided-sampling.md]. All methods in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by a mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. The core mechanism involves periodic evaluation of a metric per Gaussian to determine if the current representation is insufficient or redundant in a specific region. Common metrics include: 1. Gradient Magnitude: The accumulated 2D positional gradient \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v} \| \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muv^k} \|2. High gradients indicate that the Gaussian's position is not adequately minimizing the loss, suggesting a need for refinement or replacement. 2. Opacity: Low opacity \alphak < \alpha{\min} indicates a primitive contributes negligibly to the rendered image and is a candidate for pruning. 3. Scale: Excessively large scales max(sk) relative to the scene extent e{scene} indicate coarse approximations that may blur details or occlude nearby geometry. Densification operations are typically triggered every N iterations (e.g., refineEvery = 100) to allow the optimizer to stabilize. The primary operations are: Splitting: Replacing a parent Gaussian gk with N{children} children. The children's means \mu{child} are sampled from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak). The scale is typically reduced, e.g., s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}}, to increase local density. Cloning: Creating an exact copy of gk (same \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) to increase sampling frequency in high-error regions without changing the spatial footprint. Pruning: Removing Gaussians that fail to meet opacity or significance thresholds. Buffer management is critical: pruned or split Gaussians require buffer compaction or flag-based marking to maintain contiguous memory access for rasterization [Parent]. Score-based Densification is a constructive training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that controls model size by adding new primitives only to those Gaussians that maximize a specific quality score, ensuring the final model adheres to a user-defined budget without requiring pruning [4705-score-based-densification.md]. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which relies on heuristic thresholds and subsequent culling, this method uses a purely constructive schedule that steers densification toward Gaussians contributing most to reconstruction quality, avoiding optimization instability caused by aggressive removal [4705-score-based-densification.md]. Gaussian Insertion and Pruning is a dynamic management strategy for 3D Gaussian primitives used primarily in monocular and RGB-D SLAM systems [10074-gaussian-insertion-and-pruning.md]. It solves the problem of maintaining a coherent 3D structure in real-time by inserting new Gaussians to capture newly visible scene elements and pruning those that are geometrically unstable or contribute negligibly to the render [10074-gaussian-insertion-and-pruning.md]. Unlike static densification strategies that rely on gradient magnitude thresholds, this method relies on visibility consistency across a sliding window of keyframes and opacity thresholds to manage the primitive set [10074-gaussian-insertion-and-pruning.md]. Error-guided Guided Sampling (EMS) is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that targets regions of high perceptual error rather than relying solely on gradient magnitude or opacity thresholds. It identifies low-SSIM training views, computes a pixel-wise error mask, and spawns new Gaussians specifically in high-error areas while using depth information and spatial masks to prevent overlapping placements and edge artifacts [15896-error-guided-guided-sampling.md]. Unlike standard densification which refines existing primitives based on local gradients, EMS performs a global view-based error analysis to insert new primitives where the current representation fails to reconstruct the image structure [15896-error-guided-guided-sampling.md]. AdpSplit is an error-driven adaptive split operator for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces fixed-cardinality random child placement with view-loss-aware child generation [16061-adpsplit.md]. It determines the number of split children and initializes their parameters from L1-pixel-error region statistics, enabling fewer densification iterations and reduced training time while preserving rendering quality [16061-adpsplit.md]. Unlike vanilla 3DGS which uses a fixed N=2 binary split, AdpSplit adaptively determines the number of children based on the observed error structure, avoiding the bottleneck where binary splits require \log2 G rounds to expose a structure requiring G Gaussians [16061-adpsplit.md]. Child Gaussian Initialization is the specific procedure for generating the geometric and photometric properties of new 3D Gaussian primitives during the splitting phase of adaptive densification [16063-child-gaussian-initialization.md]. It solves the problem of how to accurately map a parent Gaussian's error region—identified in camera space—into a valid 3D Gaussian in world space, ensuring the child is positioned on the scene geometry and oriented correctly relative to the viewing direction [16063-child-gaussian-initialization.md]. It sets itself apart from generic splitting methods by explicitly unprojecting image-space covariance ellipses into world-space scales and orientations using Mahalanobis distance minimization and perspective-aware clamping, rather than simple isotropic scaling or random sampling [16063-child-gaussian-initialization.md]. A densification step added to the 3DGS baseline that improves rendering quality and LPIPS metrics. Adding Blur Split to 3DGS baseline increases Gaussians from 3.35M to 3.74M, SSIM from 0.815 to 0.819, and LPIPS from 0.216 to 0.195. A densification strategy where respawn and densify operations are performed in parallel, requiring specific edge case handling to prevent hierarchy degeneration. If two sibling nodes both need to be respawned, only respawn the right node. This causes the left node to become a new dead leaf, which will be respawned in the next densification iteration. If a node needs to be respawned whose sibling is not a leaf node, replace the entire parent node with the subtree of the node being respawned. Apply a pruning strategy: zero the opacity of Gaussians that have not contributed for a number of iterations equal to twice the size of the training set. These will be respawned in the next densification iteration. Adjusting and removing the densifyandsplit operation within the densifyandprune process to improve speed without impacting rendering quality. When a Gaussian triangle is cloned or split into two new Gaussian triangles, assign µ1 to each new triangle in the same manner as standard Gaussian Splatting assigns µ to new ellipses. Assign both new cloned/split Gaussian triangles the same parameters µ2 and µ3 as the original Gaussian triangle. When a Gaussian line is cloned or split, assign µ1 and µ2 to each new Gaussian line in the same way as µ1 and µ2 are assigned to new Gaussian triangles. A densification strategy that improves the quality of re-observed parts of the environment and allows the map to be extended by densifying regions based on color and depth rendering errors. On the Replica dataset (Room0), adding densification improved PSNR from 25.58 to 25.96 dB and SSIM from 0.85 to 0.89. Unlike methods that use separate neural networks for color and depth (e.g., Point-SLAM), this method optimizes the same Gaussian parameters for both, which can impact depth estimation but allows for unified densification. A two-phase densification strategy that separates global spatial distribution from local refinement to reduce computational redundancy in early optimization stages. Phase 1 (Global Spread): Apply only the split operation to achieve fast and effective spatial distribution, leveraging minimal Gaussian counts to minimize redundant computation on localized details. Phase 2 (Local Refinement): Employ both split and clone operations. Since satisfactory spatial distribution is established, clone operations enable efficient local refinement. Tdensify: Total densification iteration count. Default value is 25K. The concept of adaptive densification was introduced with the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023). The original method established the heuristic-based split, clone, and prune cycle driven by gradient magnitude and opacity. Subsequent works have refined this process: Mini-Splatting introduced blur splitting to improve LPIPS; HSPT introduced parallel respawning with edge case handling for large-scale reconstruction; I3DGS explored removing split operations to speed up training; Mixed-Primitive methods extended densification to triangles and lines; SLAM-based methods like the one in introduced rendering-guided densification for RGB-D consistency; and Global-to-Local frameworks separated global spread from local refinement to reduce computational redundancy. name: Score-based Densification
head: Budget-constrained Optimization, Guided Densification
body: Score-based Densification is a constructive training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that controls model size by adding new primitives only to those Gaussians that maximize a specific quality score, ensuring the final model adheres to a user-defined budget without requiring pruning. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which relies on heuristic thresholds and subsequent culling, this method uses a purely constructive schedule that steers densification toward Gaussians contributing most to reconstruction quality, avoiding optimization instability caused by aggressive removal. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, a set of training views, a target model size budget B, and a growth curve function N(t). Outputs: A refined set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with size |\mathcal{G}'| \approx B. Data Structures: Gaussian: Inherits standard 3DGS fields: mean \muk, covariance \Sigmak, opacity \alphak, spherical harmonics \mathbf{c}k. Score Buffer: A scalar value Sg stored per Gaussian, initialized to zero. Saliency Map: A 2D tensor per view representing pixel-wise importance. Steps: 1. Sample Views: Select a batch of training views for the current iteration. 2. Compute Saliency: Render the current Gaussians and compute per-pixel saliency to identify important regions. 3. Compute Per-Gaussian Score (Sg): For each Gaussian gk, aggregate metrics into a scoring function F. The score combines: Gradient magnitude: Accumulated 2D positional gradients \tauk. Saliency: The sum of saliency values projected onto the Gaussian's footprint. Primitive properties: Current scale and opacity. Sg(gk) = F(\tauk, \text{saliency}k, \text{properties}k) The exact weighting of F is implementation-dependent but must prioritize gradients in high-saliency regions. 4. Select Top Gaussians: Rank all Gaussians by Sg in descending order. Select the top Gaussians such that the total number of Gaussians after splitting matches the target count N(t) defined by the growth curve. 5. Densify: For each selected Gaussian gk: Clone: Create a copy of gk with identical parameters \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}. Split: Replace gk with children sampled from \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak). The number of children per split is determined by the remaining budget and the current count. Typically, one clone and one split (or similar) are performed to double the local density. 6. Update Growth Curve: Increment the iteration counter. The target size N(t) follows a curve mimicking standard 3DGS behavior but is fitted to reach exactly B at the end of training. Parameters: Budget B: The final number of Gaussians. Growth Curve: A function N(t) mapping iteration t to target count. Edge Cases: Budget Exhaustion: If the current count exceeds B before the end of training, no further densification occurs. Degenerate Gaussians: Gaussians with near-zero opacity or extremely small scales should be excluded from scoring to prevent noise amplification. Pixel-GS is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that modifies the gradient-based splitting signal to account for the spatial footprint of each Gaussian primitive. It addresses the baseline's tendency to under-densify regions by scaling the positional gradient by the number of pixels a Gaussian influences and applying a depth-dependent scaling factor to suppress floaters. It yields state-of-the-art rendering quality compared to standard 3DGS, though it typically results in a higher number of Gaussian primitives. Perceptual-GS replaces the simple gradient threshold densification heuristic with a scene-adaptive perceptual signal to improve detail in visually salient areas. It computes a local perceptual error map using a lightweight vision-transformer head and densifies only in regions where Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) falls below a dynamic threshold. Late Densification is a temporal strategy that enables densification back between iterations 20K to 20.5K for every 100 iterations to help the model recover loss from pruning of false-positive Gaussians. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method addresses training speed obstacles by proposing faster, numerically equivalent solutions for gradient computation and attribute updates. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method ensures predictable memory usage bounded by B. Performance: Eliminates the need for pruning/culling passes, reducing training time variability and avoiding optimization peaks. Strengths: Controlled model size, no post-training culling required, stable optimization. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Score-based Densification was introduced to address the unpredictable storage demands and fluctuating training times of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was proposed in "Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources" (2024) as a guided, purely constructive alternative to heuristic-based densification. The method builds on the observation that redundancy in 3DGS can be managed by steering additions toward high-quality-contributing primitives rather than removing low-quality ones. name: Perceptual-GS
head: Perceptual Gaussian Splatting
body: Perceptual-GS replaces the simple gradient-threshold densification heuristic of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting with a scene-adaptive perceptual signal to improve detail in visually salient areas. It computes a local perceptual error map using a lightweight vision-transformer head and densifies Gaussians only in regions where the Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) falls below a dynamic threshold. This approach addresses the limitation of gradient-based methods that may miss high-frequency details not strongly represented in parameter gradients. Inputs: Current 3D Gaussian cloud parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Input image views and corresponding camera poses. A pre-trained lightweight vision-transformer head for perceptual error estimation. A dynamic SSIM threshold \tau{SSIM}. Outputs: Updated 3D Gaussian cloud with densified primitives in perceptually significant regions. Data Structures: Perceptual Error Map: A 2D tensor of the same resolution as the rendered image, storing local perceptual error values computed by the vision-transformer head. SSIM Map: A 2D tensor storing local SSIM values between the rendered image and the ground truth image. Steps: 1. Render: Render the current Gaussian cloud to obtain the predicted image I{pred} for each input view. 2. Compute SSIM: Calculate the local SSIM map M{SSIM} between I{pred} and the ground truth image I{gt}. The SSIM is computed over local windows. 3. Compute Perceptual Error: Pass I{pred} and I{gt} through the lightweight vision-transformer head to generate a local perceptual error map M{perceptual}. The specific architecture of the head is not detailed in the sources. 4. Densification Decision: For each pixel or region, check if M{SSIM} < \tau{SSIM}. If true, mark the region for densification. The threshold \tau{SSIM} is dynamic, adapting during training. 5. Spawn Gaussians: In regions marked for densification, spawn new Gaussians. The exact initialization strategy (e.g., cloning, splitting) is not specified in the sources, but it builds on the standard densification mechanisms of 3D Gaussian Splatting. 6. Optimize: Update all Gaussian parameters using gradient descent, minimizing the perceptual loss and/or photometric loss. Parameters: Dynamic SSIM Threshold \tau{SSIM}: Not given in the sources. Vision-Transformer Head: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The perceptual error map computation may introduce numerical instability if not properly normalized. Boundaries: Regions with low gradient magnitude but high perceptual error may be densified, potentially leading to overfitting if not regularized. Degenerate Input: If the ground truth image is unavailable or corrupted, the SSIM and perceptual error maps cannot be computed. Color-cued GS leverages the view-independent (0th) spherical harmonics (SH) coefficient gradient to better assess color cues for densification, while using the 2D position gradient more coarsely to refine areas where structure-from-motion (SfM) struggles to capture fine structures. This method modifies the densification process to prioritize color accuracy and structural refinement in challenging regions. Time Complexity: Increased due to the additional computation of the perceptual error map and SSIM map. The vision-transformer head adds inference time per iteration. Memory Complexity: Increased due to the storage of the perceptual error map and SSIM map. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves detail in visually salient areas; scene-adaptive; reduces artifacts in complex regions. Limitations: Computationally expensive; requires a pre-trained vision-transformer head; dynamic thresholding may be difficult to tune. When to Use: When high-fidelity detail in visually salient areas is critical and computational resources are available. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is required or computational resources are limited. Perceptual-GS was introduced as an improvement over the simple gradient threshold densification heuristic in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It aims to address the limitation of gradient-based methods in capturing high-frequency details. Pixel-GS is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that modifies the gradient-based splitting signal to account for the spatial footprint of each Gaussian primitive. It addresses the baseline's tendency to under-densify regions by scaling the positional gradient by the number of pixels a Gaussian influences and applying a depth-dependent scaling factor to suppress floaters. It yields state-of-the-art rendering quality compared to standard 3DGS, though it typically results in a higher number of Gaussian primitives. Pixel-GS operates within the densification loop of 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It replaces the standard densification trigger (average magnitude of positional gradient) with a pixel-weighted, depth-aware metric. abla{\mathbf{p}j^{(v)}}| is the magnitude of the positional gradient for Gaussian j in view v. Note: Pixel-GS sums absolute gradients across views rather than averaging. N{pix, j} is the total number of pixels influenced by gj across all views. dj is the depth (distance to camera) of Gaussian j. f(dj) is a depth-dependent scaling factor. While the exact function is not specified in the sources, it is designed to suppress densification in distant regions to prevent floaters. A common implementation uses an inverse depth or exponential decay, e.g., f(dj) = 1/dj or e^{-dj}, to reduce the score for far-away Gaussians. 4. Select for Splitting: Compare Sj against a threshold or select the top-k Gaussians with the highest scores. These Gaussians are candidates for splitting. 5. Split: For each selected Gaussian gj: Clone gj to create two new Gaussians. Perturb the position of the clone slightly (e.g., along the normal or random direction). Adjust the scale and opacity of the parent and child to maintain coverage (standard 3DGS splitting procedure). Parameters: Threshold for splitting: Not given in the sources. Typically a percentile-based threshold (e.g., top 10% of gradients) or a fixed count. Depth scaling factor f(dj): Not given in the sources. Inverse depth is a common heuristic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Summing gradients across views can lead to large values for Gaussians visible in many views. Normalization may be required if scores are compared across different training steps. Boundaries: Gaussians at the edge of the scene may have lower N{pix, j} due to partial visibility, potentially leading to under-densification at boundaries. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has zero gradient, it will not be split, which is correct behavior. Modifies the gradient-based densification strategy to account for the spatial footprint of each Gaussian primitive. It scales the positional gradient by the number of pixels a Gaussian influences and applies a depth-dependent scaling factor to encourage densification in background regions while suppressing it in the foreground. This approach yields state-of-the-art rendering quality compared to standard 3DGS, though it typically results in a higher number of Gaussian primitives. Time Complexity: The additional cost is proportional to the number of Gaussians and views, as pixel coverage must be tracked and gradients summed. This is negligible compared to the rendering and backpropagation steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N{pix, j} and accumulated gradients for each Gaussian. This is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Measured Performance: Yields state-of-the-art rendering quality compared to standard 3DGS. However, it typically results in a higher number of Gaussian primitives. Strengths: Recovers detail that the baseline misses by weighting gradients by pixel coverage. Suppresses floaters via depth scaling. Limitations: Higher number of Gaussians increases memory usage and potentially rendering time if not optimized. When to use: When high reconstruction quality is prioritized over model size and rendering speed. When not to use: When memory or rendering speed is constrained, or when the scene is simple and the baseline is sufficient. Pixel-GS was introduced as part of the evolution of 3D Gaussian Splatting densification strategies. It differs from the original baseline by changing the densification signal from the average magnitude of the positional gradient to a sum of absolute gradients weighted by pixel coverage. It is related to AbsGS, which also uses absolute gradients but without the pixel coverage weighting. The method is cited in recent surveys of 3D Gaussian Splatting advancements. head: Pixel-aware and Depth-scaled Gradient Densification
body:

It scales the positional gradient by the pixel count and applies a depth-dependent scaling factor to encourage densification in background regions while reducing it in foreground regions. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each having an id 'k'. views: List of view objects, each having an id 'nu'. pixelcounts: Dict mapping (k, nu) to count(gk^nu). rendereddepths: Dict mapping (k, nu) to depth(gk^nu). gradnorms: Dict mapping (k, nu) to ||dL/dmuk^nu||2. gamma: Depth scaling hyperparameter. sceneextent: The extent of the scene. Returns: dict: Mapping of Gaussian id 'k' to refined gradient tau'k. """ weightedgradientsum = {g.id: 0.0 for g in gaussians} pixelcountsum = {g.id: 0.0 for g in gaussians} for g in gaussians: k = g.id for nu in views: nuid = nu.id count = pixelcounts[(k, nuid)] depth = rendereddepths[(k, nuid)] gradnorm = gradnorms[(k, nuid)] if sceneextent is None: raise ValueError("sceneextent must be provided to compute depth scaling.") depthscale = depth / (gamma sceneextent) fknu = max(0.0, min(1.0, depthscale)) weightedgradientsum[k] += fknu count gradnorm pixelcountsum[k] += count results = {} for k in weightedgradientsum: totalcount = pixelcountsum[k] if totalcount == 0: results[k] = 0.0 else: results[k] = weightedgradientsum[k] / totalcount return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Visibility: If a Gaussian is not visible in any view, 	ext{count}(gk^

name: Gaussian Insertion and Pruning
head: Monocular Gaussian Initialization
body: Gaussian Insertion and Pruning is a dynamic management strategy for 3D Gaussian primitives used primarily in monocular and RGB-D SLAM systems. It solves the problem of maintaining a coherent 3D structure in real-time by inserting new Gaussians to capture newly visible scene elements and pruning those that are geometrically unstable or contribute negligibly to the render. Unlike static densification strategies that rely on gradient magnitude thresholds, this method relies on visibility consistency across a sliding window of keyframes and opacity thresholds to manage the primitive set. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}. Current camera pose and intrinsics. Rendered depth map D for the current frame. Keyframe window Wk containing recent keyframes. Opacity threshold \alpha{\text{prune}} = 0.7. Keyframe window size |Wk| (e.g., 10 for Replica, 8 for TUM). Outputs: Updated set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with new insertions and pruned elements. Data Structures: Keyframe Window (Wk): A fixed-size buffer storing recent keyframes. Visibility Counter: For each newly inserted Gaussian, a counter tracks how many frames in Wk have observed it. A Gaussian is marked as "visible" from a view if it was used in rasterization and the ray's accumulated \alpha has not yet reached 0.5. Steps: 1. Initialization of New Gaussians: When a new keyframe is added to Wk, new Gaussians are inserted to capture newly visible regions. The mean position \muW is initialized based on the rendered depth D. For pixels p with valid depth Dp, sample the depth from a normal distribution: z \sim \mathcal{N}(Dp, 0.2\sigmaD). For pixels without depth estimates (unobserved regions), sample from a normal distribution centered at the median depth \hat{D} of the rendered image: z \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat{D}, 0.5\sigmaD). This accounts for incorrect depth estimates by introducing higher variance. The 2D position (u, v) is taken directly from the pixel coordinates. The 3D mean \muW is computed by back-projecting (u, v, z) using camera intrinsics. 2. Visibility-Based Pruning (Geometric Stability): This step ensures that inserted Gaussians are consistent with the scene geometry across multiple views. Condition: Only perform this pruning once the keyframe window Wk is full. Check: For each Gaussian inserted within the last 3 keyframes, count the number of other frames in Wk where it was observed. Action: If a Gaussian is unobserved by at least 3 other frames in Wk, it is considered geometrically unstable and is pruned. 3. Opacity-Based Pruning: Action: Iterate through all Gaussians in \mathcal{G}. Condition: If opacity \alphak < 0.7, remove the Gaussian. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def gaussianinsertionandpruning(G, currentframe, Wk, sigmaD, Wkthreshold): """ G: List of active 3D Gaussians (each is a dict/object with keys: mean, opacity, insertionkeyframeindex, visibilitycount) currentframe: Object with attributes: isnewkeyframe (bool), rendereddepth (2D array), intrinsics (fx, fy, cx, cy) Wk: List of keyframes sigmaD: Standard deviation of depth noise Wkthreshold: Maximum size of the keyframe window """ # Step 1: Insert new Gaussians if a new keyframe is added if currentframe.isnewkeyframe: D = currentframe.rendereddepth # Compute median depth of the rendered image flatdepth = [d for row in D for d in row if d > 0] mediandepth = sorted(flatdepth)[len(flatdepth) // 2] if flatdepth else 0.0 height, width = D.shape for y in range(height): for x in range(width): Dp = D[y, x] # Initialize mean position based on depth if Dp > 0: # valid depth z = random.gauss(Dp, 0.2 sigmaD) else: z = random.gauss(mediandepth, 0.5 sigmaD) # Back-project to 3D using pinhole camera model fx, fy, cx, cy = currentframe.intrinsics X = (x - cx) z / fx Y = (y - cy) z / fy muW = (X, Y, z) # Create new Gaussian with default properties newg = { 'mean': muW, 'opacity': 0.1, 'scale': 0.01, 'rotation': [1, 0, 0, 0], 'insertionkeyframeindex': len(Wk) - 1, 'visibilitycount': 0 } G.append(newg) # Step 2: Visibility-Based Pruning # Only perform once the window is full if len(Wk) >= Wkthreshold: # Identify Gaussians inserted in the last 3 keyframes recentgaussians = [g for g in G if len(Wk) - g['insertionkeyframeindex'] <= 3] toremove = [] for g in recentgaussians: # Count observations in Wk # Note: Visibility is determined during rasterization of each keyframe in Wk # If g was used and accumulated alpha < 0.5, it is "observed" if g['visibilitycount'] < 3: toremove.append(g) G = [g for g in G if g not in toremove] # Step 3: Opacity-Based Pruning G = [g for g in G if g['opacity'] >= 0.7] return G Parameters: \alpha{\text{prune}} = 0.7: Opacity threshold for pruning. |Wk|: Keyframe window size (10 for Replica, 8 for TUM). Depth variance factors: 0.2\sigmaD for observed pixels, 0.5\sigmaD for unobserved. Edge Cases: Incorrect Depth: In monocular settings, rendered depth may be incorrect. The high variance initialization (0.5\sigmaD) for unobserved regions helps mitigate this, but many inserted Gaussians may be geometrically invalid and will be pruned by the visibility check. Window Not Full: Visibility-based pruning is skipped until Wk is full, preventing premature removal of valid Gaussians that simply haven't been seen by enough frames yet. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. Gaussian Insertion and Pruning was introduced in "Gaussian Splatting SLAM". It adapts the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation for simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). The method addresses the challenge of maintaining a consistent 3D map in real-time by dynamically managing the Gaussian primitives based on visibility and opacity, rather than relying solely on gradient-based densification used in static reconstruction.
