name: Error-guided Guided Sampling
head: Error-guided multi-scale sampling, Guided sampling step
body: Error-guided Guided Sampling (EMS) is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that targets regions of high perceptual error rather than relying solely on gradient magnitude or opacity thresholds. It identifies low-SSIM training views, computes a pixel-wise error mask, and spawns new Gaussians specifically in high-error areas while using depth information and spatial masks to prevent overlapping placements and edge artifacts. Unlike standard densification which refines existing primitives based on local gradients, EMS performs a global view-based error analysis to insert new primitives where the current representation fails to reconstruct the image structure. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}. Current training iteration I. Current camera view V with image I{img}, ground truth I{gt}, and depth map D. Parameters: emsstartfromiterations, selectedlength, opt.emsthr, opt.farray, opt.rayends, opt.shuffleems. Outputs: Updated Gaussian set \mathcal{G}' with new primitives added. Updated buffers: visibilityfilter, radii, viewspacepointtensor. Data Structures: visibilityfilter: Boolean tensor of shape (N), where N is the number of Gaussians. Extended by concatenating zeros for new points. radii: Float tensor of shape (N), storing the 2D radius of each Gaussian. Extended by concatenating zeros. viewspacepointtensor: Float tensor of shape (N, 3), storing the 3D position of each Gaussian in viewspace. Extended by concatenating zeros. Steps: 1. Trigger Check: EMS is triggered if all conditions are met: I > \text{emsstartfromiterations} A specific flag flagems == 2 is set. \text{emscnt} < \text{selectedlength} (count of EMS iterations performed). V.\text{image\name} \in \text{selectviews} (a pre-selected list of views to process). I - \text{lasterems} > 100 (minimum 100 iterations since last EMS run). If triggered: Remove V.\text{image\name} from selectviews. Increment emscnt. Update lasterems = I. Compute current SSIM of the rendered view. 2. Error Mask Generation: If current SSIM < 0.88: Normalize images: I{adj} = \frac{I{img}}{\text{mean}(I{img}) + 0.01} GT{adj} = \frac{I{gt}}{\text{mean}(I{gt}) + 0.01} Compute absolute difference per channel, sum over channels (dim=0), and flatten. Sort the flattened differences. Find the threshold value at percentile opt.emsthr. Create binary error mask M{err}: M{err}(p) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \text{diff}(p) > \text{threshold} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 3. Patch Processing: Pad M{err} to multiples of 16 \times 16 using constant padding (value=0). Extract 16 \times 16 patches with stride 16 \times 16. Filter patches: Calculate sum of each patch. Keep patch if sum > 16 \times 16 \times 0.85. Broadcast the kept patch mask back to 16 \times 16 size to create M{patch}. 4. Depth Estimation: Extract depth map D for the current view. Pad D to multiples of 16 \times 16. Unfold into 16 \times 16 patches. Reshape patches to (B, P, 256). Compute median depth per patch along the spatial dimension (dim=2). Broadcast median depth back to patch size, reshape, and permute to match image dimensions. Crop to original depth size. 5. Center Masking (Spacing Control): Initialize a mask M{center} of ones with image dimensions. Set every other pixel in a 16 \times 16 grid to 0: M{center}(i, j) = 0 \quad \text{if } i \in \{0, 2, \dots, 14\} \text{ and } j \in \{0, 2, \dots, 14\} Multiply M{patch} by M{center} (element-wise). Unfold, permute, and reshape back to image size. Crop to image dimensions. Remove a 10% border from M{center} (top/bottom: H/10, left/right: W/10) to prevent edge artifacts. 6. Invalid Depth Handling: Create invalid depth mask where D == 15.0 (treated as invalid/occluded). Find non-zero indices in the processed center mask (M{final}). These are badindices. Compute median depth of valid depth map at the 70th percentile (D{med}). Clamp depth values: D{clamped}(p) = \begin{cases} D{med} & \text{if } D(p) > D{med} \\ D(p) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 7. Gaussian Spawning: Call gaussians.addgaussians(badindices, V, D{clamped}, I{gt}, numperay=\text{opt.farray}, ratioend=\text{opt.rayends}, depthmax=D{max}, shuffle=\text{opt.shuffleems}). This function spawns new Gaussians at the badindices locations, using the depth map for placement and the error mask to guide density. 8. Buffer Update: Let N{new} be the number of spawned Gaussians. Extend visibilityfilter by concatenating torch.zeros(Nnew) along dim=0. Extend radii by concatenating torch.zeros(Nnew) along dim=0. Extend viewspacepointtensor by concatenating torch.zeros(Nnew, 3) along dim=0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errorguidedguidedsampling(gaussians, iteration, viewpointcam, opt, emscnt, lasterems, selectviews): # 1. Trigger Check if iteration <= opt.emsstartfromiterations: return emscnt, lasterems, selectviews if opt.flagems != 2: return emscnt, lasterems, selectviews if emscnt >= opt.selectedlength: return emscnt, lasterems, selectviews if viewpointcam.imagename not in selectviews: return emscnt, lasterems, selectviews if iteration - lasterems <= 100: return emscnt, lasterems, selectviews # Triggered selectviews.remove(viewpointcam.imagename) emscnt += 1 lasterems = iteration # Render current view to get image and depth renderresult = renderviewpoint(gaussians, viewpointcam) Iimg = renderresult['image'] D = renderresult['depth'] Igt = viewpointcam.gtimage # Compute SSIM currentssim = computessim(Iimg, Igt) if currentssim >= 0.88: return emscnt, lasterems, selectviews # 2. Error Mask Generation Iadj = Iimg / (torch.mean(Iimg) + 0.01) GTadj = Igt / (torch.mean(Igt) + 0.01) diff = torch.abs(Iadj - GTadj) diffsum = diff.sum(dim=0) # Sum over channels diffflat = diffsum.flatten() diffflatsorted, = torch.sort(diffflat) threshold = diffflatsorted[int(len(diffflatsorted) opt.emsthr / 100.0)] outmask = (diffsum > threshold).float() # 3. Patch Processing H, W = outmask.shape kh, kw = 16, 16 dh, dw = 16, 16 # Pad to multiples of 16 padh = (kh - H % kh) % kh padw = (kw - W % kw) % kw outmaskpadded = torch.nn.functional.pad(outmask, (0, padw, 0, padh), mode='constant', value=0) # Unfold into patches patches = outmaskpadded.unfold(0, kh, dh).unfold(1, kw, dw) patchessum = patches.sum(dim=(2, 3)) patchesmusk = (patchessum > kh kw 0.85).float() # Broadcast mask back # Note: In PyTorch, unfolding creates a view. We need to reconstruct or use scatter. # Simplified logic: create a zero tensor of padded size, then fill in the kept patches. Mpatch = torch.zeroslike(outmaskpadded) # This step requires careful indexing to map patch indices back to pixel coordinates. # For implementation clarity, we assume a helper broadcastpatches exists or implement via scatter. # Here we describe the logical operation: # Mpatch = patchesmusk 1.0, reshaped and permuted back to (H+padh, W+padw) Mpatch = broadcastpatches(patchesmusk, H+padh, W+padw, kh, kw, dh, dw) # 4. Depth Estimation Dpadded = torch.nn.functional.pad(D, (0, padw, 0, padh), mode='constant', value=0) Dpatches = Dpadded.unfold(0, kh, dh).unfold(1, kw, dw) Dpatchesreshaped = Dpatches.reshape(-1, kh kw) Dmedian = torch.median(Dpatchesreshaped, dim=1) # Broadcast median depth back to patch size Dmedianpatches = broadcastpatches(Dmedian.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1), H+padh, W+padw, kh, kw, dh, dw) Dmedianimg = Dmedianpatches[:,:H,:W] # 5. Center Masking Mcenter = torch.ones((H, W)) for i in range(0, kh, 2): for j in range(0, kw, 2): # This logic applies to the 16x16 grid pattern repeated # In practice, this is a checkerboard pattern with period 2 in the 16x16 block # But the source says "every other pixel in 16x16 grid", implying a sparse grid. # The source code snippet: "set every other pixel in 16x16 grid to 0 (i, j in range(0, kh, 2), range(0, kw, 2))" # This creates a mask where only (0,0), (0,2)... are 1? No, it sets them to 0. # So (1,1), (1,3)... are 1? # Let's re-read: "initialize midpatch of ones, set every other pixel... to 0" # This implies a sparse sampling grid. pass # Correct interpretation of source: # Mcenter is initialized to ones. # Pixels at (i, j) where i is even and j is even (within the 16x16 block) are set to 0. # This creates a grid of available positions. Mcentersparse = torch.ones((H, W)) for i in range(0, H, 2): # Assuming the pattern repeats or applies globally? # The source says "in 16x16 grid". This likely means the pattern is applied per 16x16 block. # However, the code snippet range(0, kh, 2) suggests it's defining the pattern within the block. # Let's assume a global checkerboard with stride 2 for simplicity, or block-wise. # Given "center mask to prevent overlapping", a global stride-2 grid is standard. for j in range(0, W, 2): Mcentersparse[i, j] = 0 # Apply to patches Mfinal = Mpatch Mcentersparse # Remove 10% border offsetH = H // 10 offsetW = W // 10 Mfinal = Mfinal[offsetH:-offsetH, offsetW:-offsetW] # 6. Invalid Depth Handling invaliddepthmask = (D == 15.0) # Find non-zero indices in Mfinal (relative to cropped image) # Map back to original image coordinates badindicesglobal = torch.nonzero(Mfinal, astuple=False) + torch.tensor([[offsetH, offsetW]]) badindicesflat = badindicesglobal[:, 0] W + badindicesglobal[:, 1] # Clamp depth validdepth = D[~invaliddepthmask] Dmed = torch.median(validdepth) Dclamped = torch.where(D > Dmed, Dmed, D) # 7. Spawn Gaussians newgaussians = gaussians.addgaussians( badindicesflat, viewpointcam, Dclamped, Igt, numperay=opt.farray, ratioend=opt.rayends, depthmax=gaussians.depthdict[viewpointcam.imagename], shuffle=(opt.shuffleems != 0)) # 8. Buffer Update Nnew = newgaussians.shape[0] gaussians.visibilityfilter = torch.cat([gaussians.visibilityfilter, torch.zeros(Nnew, device="cuda")]) gaussians.radii = torch.cat([gaussians.radii, torch.zeros(Nnew, device="cuda")]) gaussians.viewspacepointtensor = torch.cat([gaussians.viewspacepointtensor, torch.zeros(Nnew, 3, device="cuda")]) return emscnt, lasterems, selectviews Parameters: opt.emsthr: Percentile threshold for error mask generation. Controls sensitivity. Value not specified in sources. kh, kw: Patch kernel size, fixed at 16. dh, dw: Patch stride, fixed at 16. opt.farray: Number of points to spawn per error region/ray. opt.rayends: Ray end parameter for Gaussian placement. emsstartfromiterations: Iteration index after which EMS begins. selectedlength: Maximum number of EMS iterations allowed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Depth: Depth values exactly equal to 15.0 are treated as invalid and masked out to prevent spawning in occluded regions. Edge Artifacts: A 10% border is stripped from the center mask to prevent overlapping Gaussians at image boundaries. Clustering: The center mask uses a checkerboard-like pattern (every other pixel set to 0) to enforce minimum spacing between newly spawned Gaussians. Precision: Normalization uses +0.01 to avoid division by zero. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of views processed and the resolution. The patch-based processing is O(H \times W) per view. The sorting and percentile calculation is O(H \times W \log(H \times W)). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the error mask, depth map, and intermediate patch tensors. Buffer extension is O(N{new}). Strengths: Targets perceptual errors (SSIM) rather than just gradient magnitude, which can be noisy or misleading in complex scenes. The depth-aware spawning helps in reconstructing geometry in high-error areas. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to per-view error analysis and patch processing. Requires careful tuning of thresholds (emsthr, emsstartfromiterations). When to use: In dynamic or 4D scenes (e.g., SpacetimeGaussians) where standard densification fails to capture temporal consistency or complex structures. When not to use: In static scenes with simple geometry where gradient-based densification is sufficient and faster. It was developed by researchers at OPPO US Research. The method addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS densification, which relies on gradient magnitude and 2D radius thresholds, by incorporating SSIM-based view selection and pixel-wise error thresholding. oppo-us-research/SpacetimeGaussians, https://github.com/oppo-us-research/SpacetimeGaussians, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: AdpSplit
head: Adaptive Split, Error-Driven Adaptive Splitting
body: AdpSplit is an error-driven adaptive split operator for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces fixed-cardinality random child placement with view-loss-aware child generation. It determines the number of split children and initializes their parameters from L1-pixel-error region statistics, enabling fewer densification iterations and reduced training time while preserving rendering quality. Unlike vanilla 3DGS which uses a fixed N=2 binary split, AdpSplit adaptively determines the number of children based on the observed error structure, avoiding the bottleneck where binary splits require \log2 G rounds to expose a structure requiring G Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of split candidates \mathcal{S} identified by the standard 3DGS gradient-and-size rule; the current Gaussian set \mathcal{G}; a set of V sampled training views. Output: A refined Gaussian set \mathcal{G}' with split candidates replaced by their children and a preserved parent copy. Data Structures: Gaussian gi: Defined by mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (parameterized by scale si and rotation qi), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Dominant Gaussian Map Dv: For each pixel u in view v, stores the index of the Gaussian with the largest alpha-weighted contribution. Error Region R{qv}: A set of 2D pixel coordinates \{u\} sharing the same error band, dominated by candidate i, and connected via 8-neighbor chains. Parameters: \tau{l1}: Normalized L1-error threshold. Default: 0.1. r{erode}: Erosion filter length. Default: 2. L: Number of error-level bands. Default: 3. m{min}: Minimum error-region area threshold. Default: 5. \gammad: Distance threshold for merging. Default: 2.0. \gammac: Color threshold for merging. Default: 0.15. N{max}: Maximum children per parent. Default: 19 (9 for outdoor MipNeRF360/Deep-Blending playroom). V: Number of sampled views. Default: 20 (10 for outdoor MipNeRF360/Deep-Blending playroom). \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability in Mahalanobis distance. Value not specified. Steps: 1. Candidate Selection: Identify split candidates \mathcal{S} using the standard 3DGS rule: i \in \mathcal{S} \iff gi \ge \taug \land \max(si) > \taus, where gi is the average gradient statistic and \taug, \taus are densification thresholds. 2. Error Region Partitioning: For each candidate i \in \mathcal{S}: a. Render V sampled training views. Collect the dominant Gaussian map Dv for each view v: Dv(u) = \arg \max{k \in \mathcal{O}v(u)} T{k,v}(u) \alpha{k,v}(u) where \mathcal{O}v(u) is the set of Gaussians contributing to pixel u, and T{k,v}(u) is the transmittance. b. Compute the min-max-normalized per-pixel L1 error map Ev(u): Ev(u) = \frac{|\hat{I}v(u) - I{gt,v}(u)|1 - E{min}}{E{max} - E{min}} where E{min} and E{max} are the minimum and maximum L1 errors over all pixels in view v. c. Create a binary metric map Mv(u) = \mathbb{I}[Ev(u) > \tau{l1}] marking high-error pixels. d. Apply an erosion filter with length r{erode} to Mv to remove isolated noisy pixels. e. Stratify normalized error values into L error-level bands over [\tau{l1}, 1], denoting the band index by Bv(u). f. Identify distinct error regions R{qv} for candidate i in view v as maximal groups of neighboring high-error pixels dominated by i and sharing the same error band: R{qv} = \{ u \mid Mv(u) = 1, Dv(u) = i, u \sim8 uq, Bv(u) = Bv(uq) \} where u \sim8 uq means u is reachable from seed uq via an 8-neighbor chain satisfying the same conditions. g. Discard regions with area A{qv} < m{min}. h. For each retained region R{qv}, compute statistics: centroid (\bar{x}{qv}, \bar{y}{qv}), area A{qv}, dominant PCA direction e{q1,v}, orthogonal direction e{q2,v}, standard deviations (\sigma{1,v}, \sigma{2,v}) from pixel covariance, and ground-truth RGB value r{qv} at the centroid. 3. Child Initialization: For each retained region R{qv} of candidate i: a. Define the camera ray \ell{qv}(t) = ov + t \hat{d}{qv}, where ov is the camera center and \hat{d}{qv} is the unit ray direction. b. Compute the optimal depth t^{qv} by minimizing the Mahalanobis distance to the parent center \mui: t^{qv} = \arg \mint (\ell{qv}(t) - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (\ell{qv}(t) - \mui) = \frac{(\mui - ov)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} \hat{d}{qv}}{\hat{d}{qv}^\top \Sigmai^{-1} \hat{d}{qv} + \epsilon} c. Initialize the child parameters: \mu{qv} = \ell{qv}(t^{qv}) R{qv} = [\hat{u}1 \mid \hat{u}2 \mid zv] s{qv} = (\|\mathbf{a}{q1,v}\|, \|\mathbf{a}{q2,v}\|, \|\mathbf{a}{q2,v}\|) c{qv} = r{qv}, \quad \alpha{qv} = \alphai where \hat{u}1, \hat{u}2 are orthonormal in-plane axes from unprojected PCA axes \mathbf{a}{q1,v}, \mathbf{a}{q2,v}, and zv is the camera forward direction. 4. Cross-View Child Merging: For each parent i, merge redundant children generated from different views: a. Connect two child proposals G^{(j)} and G^{(k)} if their symmetric Mahalanobis distance is below \gammad and their maximum RGB-channel difference is below \gammac: \delta^\top \Sigmaj^{-1} \delta + \delta^\top \Sigmak^{-1} \delta \le \gammad \quad \text{and} \quad \|c^{(j)} - c^{(k)}\|\infty \le \gammac where \delta = \mu^{(k)} - \mu^{(j)}. b. Group connected proposals in the merge graph (transitive closure). For a merged group \mathcal{M} with M = |\mathcal{M}| proposals: \mu{\mathcal{M}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m \in \mathcal{M}} \mu^{(m)}, \quad c{\mathcal{M}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m \in \mathcal{M}} c^{(m)} \bar{\Sigma}{\mathcal{M}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m \in \mathcal{M}} \Sigma^{(m)} = E \Lambda E^\top \lambda{\mathcal{M},r} = \max{m \in \mathcal{M}} \left( |er^\top (\mu^{(m)} - \mu{\mathcal{M}})| + \sigma{m,r} \right)^2, \quad r \in \{1, 2, 3\} \Sigma{\mathcal{M}} = E \text{diag}(\lambda{\mathcal{M}}) E^\top where er are eigenvectors of \bar{\Sigma}{\mathcal{M}} and \sigma{m,r} is the 1\sigma extent of member m along er. c. Sort children by covariance extent and keep the largest N{max} proposals. 5. Insertion: a. Append the merged children to the Gaussian set. b. Include a parent copy with opacity reduced by a factor of Ni + 1 (where Ni is the number of children) and scale unchanged to cover error-perfect regions and keep total opacity unchanged. c. Remove the original parent candidate from the set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def adpsplit(candidates, gaussians, views, params): """ candidates: List of Gaussian indices to split. gaussians: Current set of Gaussians. views: List of view indices to sample. params: Dictionary of hyperparameters. Returns: Updated list of Gaussians. """ newgaussians = [] for i in candidates: parent = gaussians[i] children = [] # 1. Error Region Partitioning regions = [] for v in views[:params['V']]: # Render view v and get dominant map Dv and error map Ev Dv, Ev = renderview(v, gaussians) # Normalize error Emin = Ev.min() Emax = Ev.max() if Emax == Emin: continue Enorm = (Ev - Emin) / (Emax - Emin) # Binary mask and erosion Mv = (Enorm > params['taul1']).float() Mv = erosionfilter(Mv, params['rerode']) # Stratify into bands # Assuming L bands over [taul1, 1] in normalized space # This step requires binning Enorm values > taul1 bands = stratifyerror(Enorm, Mv, params['L']) # Find regions dominated by parent i # Dv contains Gaussian indices parentmask = (Dv == i) activemask = Mv parentmask (bands > 0) # bands=0 if not high error # Group connected components (8-neighbor) with same band # This is typically done via connected components or flood fill regionindices = findconnectedregions(activemask, bands) for q, regionidx in enumerate(regionindices): regionpixels = getregionpixels(regionidx, activemask) if len(regionpixels) < params['mmin']: continue # Compute statistics centroid = computecentroid(regionpixels) area = len(regionpixels) pcaaxes, stds = computepca(regionpixels) gtcolor = computegtcolor(centroid, v) regions.append({ 'centroid': centroid, 'area': area, 'pcaaxes': pcaaxes, 'stds': stds, 'gtcolor': gtcolor, 'view': v }) # 2. Child Initialization childproposals = [] for reg in regions: # Back-project centroid ov, dhat = getcameraray(reg['view'], reg['centroid']) # Mahalanobis distance minimization # t = ((mui - ov)^T Sigmai^-1 dhat) / (dhat^T Sigmai^-1 dhat + eps) diff = parent['mu'] - ov invSigma = torch.linalg.inv(parent['Sigma']) numerator = torch.dot(diff, torch.matmul(invSigma, dhat)) denominator = torch.dot(dhat, torch.matmul(invSigma, dhat)) + 1e-6 tstar = numerator / denominator muchild = ov + tstar dhat # Initialize rotation and scale # u1, u2 from unprojected PCA axes # zv is camera forward direction u1, u2 = unprojectpcaaxes(reg['pcaaxes'], reg['view']) zv = getcameraforward(reg['view']) Rchild = torch.stack([u1, u2, zv], dim=1) schild = torch.tensor([ torch.norm(reg['pcaaxes'][0]), torch.norm(reg['pcaaxes'][1]), torch.norm(reg['pcaaxes'][1]) # Thickness along camera forward ]) childproposals.append({ 'mu': muchild, 'R': Rchild, 's': schild, 'c': reg['gtcolor'], 'alpha': parent['alpha'], 'Sigma': computecovariance(Rchild, schild) }) # Fallback if no regions found if not childproposals: # Vanilla split with N=2 children = vanillasplit(parent) else: # 3. Cross-View Child Merging mergedchildren = mergechildren(childproposals, params['gammad'], params['gammac']) # Sort by covariance extent and keep Nmax mergedchildren.sort(key=lambda c: torch.trace(c['Sigma']), reverse=True) children = mergedchildren[:params['Nmax']] # 4. Insertion # Add parent copy with reduced opacity parentcopy = parent.copy() parentcopy['alpha'] = parent['alpha'] / (len(children) + 1) newgaussians.append(parentcopy) newgaussians.extend(children) return newgaussians def mergechildren(proposals, gammad, gammac): if not proposals: return [] # Build adjacency graph n = len(proposals) adj = [[False] n for in range(n)] for j in range(n): for k in range(j + 1, n): dj = proposals[j] dk = proposals[k] delta = dk['mu'] - dj['mu'] # Symmetric Mahalanobis distance distsq = (delta.T @ dj['Sigma'].inverse() @ delta + delta.T @ dk['Sigma'].inverse() @ delta) # Color difference colordiff = torch.max(torch.abs(dj['c'] - dk['c'])) if distsq <= gammad and colordiff <= gammac: adj[j][k] = True adj[k][j] = True # Connected components visited = [False] n groups = [] for j in range(n): if not visited[j]: group = [] stack = [j] while stack: curr = stack.pop() if visited[curr]: continue visited[curr] = True group.append(curr) for k in range(n): if adj[curr][k] and not visited[k]: stack.append(k) groups.append(group) merged = [] for group in groups: M = len(group) mus = torch.stack([proposals[j]['mu'] for j in group]) colors = torch.stack([proposals[j]['c'] for j in group]) sigmas = torch.stack([proposals[j]['Sigma'] for j in group]) muM = mus.mean(dim=0) cM = colors.mean(dim=0) # Covariance merging Sigmabar = sigmas.mean(dim=0) eigvals, eigvecs = torch.linalg.eigh(Sigmabar) # Compute merged variance along each axis lambdaM = [] for r in range(3): er = eigvecs[:, r] maxextent = 0 for j in group: # 1-sigma extent of member j along er sigmaj = sigmas[j] # sigmam,r is sqrt(er^T Sigmam er) ? # Source says: sigmam,r is 1-sigma extent. # Usually 1-sigma extent along axis e is sqrt(e^T Sigma e). # But formula uses max(|e^T (mu - muM)| + sigmam,r)^2 # Let's assume sigmam,r is the standard deviation along that axis. sigmamr = torch.sqrt(er.T @ sigmas[j] @ er) dist = torch.abs(er.T @ (proposals[j]['mu'] - muM)) extent = dist + sigmamr if extent > maxextent: maxextent = extent lambdaM.append(maxextent2) SigmaM = eigvecs @ torch.diag(torch.tensor(lambdaM)) @ eigvecs.T merged.append({ 'mu': muM, 'c': cM, 'Sigma': SigmaM, 'alpha': proposals[group[0]]['alpha'], # Inherited 'R': computerotationfromcov(SigmaM) # Approximation or store R }) return merged Time Complexity: The method adds overhead per densification step due to rendering V views, computing error maps, and merging children. However, it reduces the total number of densification iterations required to achieve target quality, leading to net training time reductions of 9.2%–22.3% across benchmarks. Memory Complexity: The number of Gaussians may increase slightly compared to shortened schedules but remains below full densification baselines in most cases. The cross-view merging graph can become overly deep during low-resolution early training, increasing training time despite comparable Gaussian counts. Performance: On MipNeRF360, 3DGS-AdpSplit achieves 27.54 PSNR, 0.810 SSIM, 0.225 LPIPS, 1391s training time, 2.55M Gaussians, and 105.13 FPS. FastGS-AdpSplit matches full FastGS PSNR, improves LPIPS from 0.261 to 0.260, and trains in 143s (16.4% reduction). On Deep-Blending, FastGS-AdpSplit trains a scene in 83 seconds. Strengths: Recovers lost quality from shortened training schedules; prioritizes small details; drop-in replacement for existing accelerators. Limitations: Effective when densification is limited to 9k iterations; overly large early Gaussians can generate floating children from unreliable error regions; naive increase in random children amplifies noise. AdpSplit was introduced in the preprint "AdpSplit: Error-Driven Adaptive Splitting for Faster Geometry Discovery in 3D Gaussian Splatting" (2026). It addresses the bottleneck in vanilla 3DGS where binary splitting requires many densification rounds to expose fine details, which is inefficient for accelerated training schedules. It is integrated as a drop-in replacement for the split operator in pipelines such as 3DGS, MiniSplatting, DashGaussian, SpeedySplat, and FastGS. name: Child Gaussian Initialization
head: AdpSplit child initialization, Error-driven child creation
body: Child Gaussian Initialization is the specific procedure for generating the geometric and photometric properties of new 3D Gaussian primitives during the splitting phase of adaptive densification. It solves the problem of how to accurately map a parent Gaussian's error region—identified in camera space—into a valid 3D Gaussian in world space, ensuring the child is positioned on the scene geometry and oriented correctly relative to the viewing direction. It sets itself apart from generic splitting methods by explicitly unprojecting image-space covariance ellipses into world-space scales and orientations using Mahalanobis distance minimization and perspective-aware clamping, rather than simple isotropic scaling or random sampling. Inputs: Parent Gaussian gi with mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, and opacity \alphai. Camera intrinsics (fx, fy, px, py) and extrinsics (camera center ov in world coordinates, camera-to-world rotation R{c2w}). Image-space error region centroid (\bar{x}{qv}, \bar{y}{qv}) and covariance matrix in image space (defined by PCA directions e{1}, e{2} and standard deviations \sigma1, \sigma2). Ground-truth RGB value r{qv} at the region centroid. Parent maximum scale s{pmax} = \maxk(sk) for clamping limits. Outputs: Child Gaussian g{qv} defined by mean \mu{qv}, covariance \Sigma{qv}, opacity \alpha{qv}, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{qv}. Data Structures: The covariance \Sigma is stored as a 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix, or equivalently parameterized by scale vector s \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (or rotation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}). In this method, the output is explicitly constructed as R{qv} \text{diag}(s{qv}^2) R{qv}^T. Steps: 1. Compute Camera-Space Ray Direction: Calculate the unnormalized ray direction in camera space from the image centroid: d{cam,v} = \begin{bmatrix} (\bar{x}{qv} - px)/fx \\ (\bar{y}{qv} - py)/fy \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} 2. Transform to World-Space Ray: Convert the ray direction to world coordinates and normalize it: \hat{d}{qv} = \frac{R{c2w} d{cam,v}}{\| R{c2w} d{cam,v} \|} 3. Define Back-Projected Ray: Define the ray \ell{qv}(t) originating from the camera center ov: \ell{qv}(t) = ov + t \hat{d}{qv} 4. Find Optimal Depth (t^): Find the point on the ray that minimizes the Mahalanobis distance to the parent center \mui. Let A = \Sigmai^{-1} and b = \mui - ov. The distance squared is f(t) = (t \hat{d}{qv} - b)^T A (t \hat{d}{qv} - b). Minimizing f(t) yields: t^ = \frac{b^T A \hat{d}{qv}}{\hat{d}{qv}^T A \hat{d}{qv} + \epsilon} where \epsilon is a small constant (e.g., 10^{-8}) added to the denominator for numerical stability. 5. Set Child Mean: The child's 3D position is the point on the ray at depth t^: \mu{qv} = \ell{qv}(t^) 6. Compute Camera-Space Depth: Calculate the depth in camera space units: t^{z,v} = \frac{t^}{\| d{cam,v} \|} 7. Unproject Image-Space Covariance to World-Space Axes: Let uv and wv be the camera right and down directions in world coordinates (derived from R{c2w}). The image-space PCA directions e{1}, e{2} and scales \sigma1, \sigma2 define the error ellipse. We compute intermediate components w{1x,v}, w{1y,v}, w{2x,v}, w{2y,v} using a clamping function \text{clip}(x, a) = \text{sign}(x) \min(|x|, a) to prevent excessively large scales: w{1x,v} = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t^{z,v}}{fx} e{1,x} \sigma1, s{pmax} |e{1,x}| \right) w{1y,v} = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t^{z,v}}{fy} e{1,y} \sigma1, s{pmax} |e{1,y}| \right) w{2x,v} = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t^{z,v}}{fx} e{2,x} \sigma2, s{pmax} |e{2,x}| \right) w{2y,v} = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t^{z,v}}{fy} e{2,y} \sigma2, s{pmax} |e{2,y}| \right) Unproject these components into world-space vectors a{q1,v} and a{q2,v}: a{q1,v} = w{1x,v} uv + w{1y,v} wv a{q2,v} = w{2x,v} uv + w{2y,v} wv 8. Determine Child Scales: The scales are the lengths of the unprojected vectors. The third scale (depth) is set equal to the second scale (transverse): s{q1,v} = \| a{q1,v} \|, \quad s{q2,v} = \| a{q2,v} \|, \quad s{q3,v} = s{q2,v} 9. Enforce Orthonormality: Due to perspective projection and clamping, a{q1,v} and a{q2,v} may not be orthogonal. Apply Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to obtain orthonormal in-plane axes \hat{u}1, \hat{u}2: \hat{u}1 = \frac{a{q1,v}}{\| a{q1,v} \|} \hat{u}2 = \frac{a{q2,v} - (a{q2,v}^T \hat{u}1)\hat{u}1}{\| a{q2,v} - (a{q2,v}^T \hat{u}1)\hat{u}1 \|} 10. Construct Child Covariance: Let zv be the camera forward direction in world coordinates. Form the rotation matrix R{qv} = [\hat{u}1 \mid \hat{u}2 \mid zv]. The child covariance is: \Sigma{qv} = R{qv} \text{diag}(s{q1,v}^2, s{q2,v}^2, s{q3,v}^2) R{qv}^T 11. Initialize Color and Opacity: Color: Set the DC spherical harmonic coefficient to the ground-truth RGB value r{qv} at the centroid. Set all higher-order SH coefficients to zero. Opacity: Set \alpha{qv} = \alphai (inherit parent opacity). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializechildgaussian(parentgaussian, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, imageregion, groundtruthrgb, parentmaxscale): """ Initialize a child Gaussian from an error region in a specific view. Args: parentgaussian: dict with 'mu' (3,), 'Sigma' (3,3), 'alpha' (float) cameraintrinsics: dict with 'fx', 'fy', 'px', 'py' cameraextrinsics: dict with 'ov' (3,), 'Rc2w' (3,3) imageregion: dict with 'centroid' (2,), 'e1' (2,), 'e2' (2,), 'sigma1', 'sigma2' groundtruthrgb: (3,) array parentmaxscale: float Returns: childgaussian: dict with 'mu', 'Sigma', 'alpha', 'SHdc' """ # 1. Camera-space ray direction cx, cy = imageregion['centroid'] fx, fy, px, py = cameraintrinsics['fx'], cameraintrinsics['fy'], \ cameraintrinsics['px'], cameraintrinsics['py'] dcam = np.array([(cx - px) / fx, (cy - py) / fy, 1.0]) # 2. World-space unit ray direction Rc2w = cameraextrinsics['Rc2w'] dworldunnorm = Rc2w @ dcam dhat = dworldunnorm / np.linalg.norm(dworldunnorm) # 3. Ray parameters ov = cameraextrinsics['ov'] mui = parentgaussian['mu'] Sigmaiinv = np.linalg.inv(parentgaussian['Sigma']) # 4. Optimal depth t A = Sigmaiinv b = mui - ov numerator = b @ A @ dhat denominator = dhat @ A @ dhat + 1e-8 # epsilon for stability tstar = numerator / denominator # 5. Child mean muchild = ov + tstar dhat # 6. Camera-space depth tz = tstar / np.linalg.norm(dcam) # 7. Unproject covariance # Camera axes in world space uv = Rc2w @ np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Right wv = Rc2w @ np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Down e1 = imageregion['e1'] e2 = imageregion['e2'] s1 = imageregion['sigma1'] s2 = imageregion['sigma2'] def clip(x, a): return np.sign(x) np.minimum(np.abs(x), a) # Compute components w1x = clip((tz / fx) e1[0] s1, parentmaxscale np.abs(e1[0])) w1y = clip((tz / fy) e1[1] s1, parentmaxscale np.abs(e1[1])) w2x = clip((tz / fx) e2[0] s2, parentmaxscale np.abs(e2[0])) w2y = clip((tz / fy) e2[1] s2, parentmaxscale np.abs(e2[1])) # Unproject to world vectors a1 = w1x uv + w1y wv a2 = w2x uv + w2y wv # 8. Child scales s1child = np.linalg.norm(a1) s2child = np.linalg.norm(a2) s3child = s2child # 9. Orthonormalization (Gram-Schmidt) u1hat = a1 / s1child u2hat = a2 - np.dot(a2, u1hat) u1hat u2hat = u2hat / np.linalg.norm(u2hat) # 10. Construct Covariance zv = Rc2w @ np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # Forward Rchild = np.columnstack((u1hat, u2hat, zv)) scalessq = np.array([s1child2, s2child2, s3child2]) Sigmachild = Rchild @ np.diag(scalessq) @ Rchild.T # 11. Color and Opacity alphachild = parentgaussian['alpha'] SHdc = groundtruthrgb # Assuming SHdc is just RGB for DC term return { 'mu': muchild, 'Sigma': Sigmachild, 'alpha': alphachild, 'SHdc': SHdc } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: The denominator in t^ calculation can approach zero if the ray is nearly orthogonal to the principal axis of the parent covariance. Adding \epsilon is required. Orthogonality Loss: Perspective projection and clamping can break the orthogonality of the unprojected axes. Gram-Schmidt is mandatory to ensure a valid rotation matrix. Scale Explosion: Without clamping using s{pmax}, unprojected scales can become arbitrarily large in the distance, leading to rendering artifacts. The clamping function limits the scale relative to the parent's maximum extent. Time Complexity: O(1) per child Gaussian, involving matrix inversions (3 \times 3) and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per child. Strengths: Produces geometrically accurate child positions on the scene surface (via Mahalanobis minimization) and correctly oriented scales that respect perspective distortion. This leads to faster convergence and better detail preservation compared to isotropic splitting. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than simple random sampling or isotropic scaling. Requires access to camera intrinsics/extrinsics and image-space error regions. When to use: When high-fidelity geometry reconstruction is required and the parent Gaussian has identified a significant error region in a specific view. This method was introduced in the AdpSplit paper, which proposes error-driven adaptive splitting for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitations of standard densification strategies that do not account for the specific geometry of the error region or the perspective projection effects when creating new primitives. The method is part of the broader effort to optimize the initialization of new Gaussians during the training process to accelerate convergence and improve final rendering quality. name: Momentum Consistency-Guided Densification
head: Inherent Momentum Consistency-Guided Densification
body:
Momentum Consistency-Guided Densification is a training optimization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses kinematic phase-space trajectories (momentum) to guide primitive growth, aiming to overcome floating artifacts in non-manifold regions caused by single-step gradient snapshots. It sets itself apart from standard gradient-based strategies by evaluating the cosine consistency between current gradients and accumulated historical trends, rather than relying solely on instantaneous gradient magnitude. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the accumulated momentum buffer mt for each primitive, the current loss gradient 
ablap \mathcal{L}t with respect to primitive attributes p = \{x, \alpha, s, r, c\}, and hyperparameters \gamma (momentum decay), 	au{grad} (gradient threshold), kE (densification interval), and \epsilon (stability constant). Output: A binary mask \mathbb{I}{densify} indicating which Gaussians should be densified (split or cloned) at the current step. Data Structures: Momentum Buffer (mt): A tensor matching the shape of 
ablap \mathcal{L}t, storing the exponential moving average of gradients. Initialized to zero at the start of training. Gradient Tensor (
ablap \mathcal{L}t): A tensor of shape (N, D) where N is the number of primitives and D is the attribute dimensionality. Parameters: \gamma (momentum decay factor): Balances historical trends and current observations in the momentum calculation. Value not explicitly given in sources. 	au{grad} (gradient magnitude threshold): Predefined threshold for gradient magnitude. Value not explicitly given in sources. kE (densification interval): Fixed at 100 iterations. \epsilon: Numerical stability constant to prevent division by zero. Value not explicitly given in sources. Steps: 1. Momentum Update: At every iteration t, update the momentum buffer for each Gaussian i using the exponential moving average of the current loss gradient: mt^{(i)} = \gamma \cdot m{t-1}^{(i)} + (1 - \gamma) \cdot 
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)} where 
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)} is the gradient of the loss with respect to the primitive attribute set p for Gaussian i at iteration t. 2. Consistency Score Calculation: Compute the momentum consistency score \Psii for each Gaussian i. This score measures the cosine similarity between the current gradient vector and the accumulated momentum: \Psii =  rac{mt^{(i)} \cdot 
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)}}{\|mt^{(i)}\| \cdot \|
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)}\| + \epsilon} where \cdot denotes the dot product, \|\cdot\| denotes the L2 norm, and \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. 3. Population Average Calculation: Calculate the mean consistency level  ar{\Psi} of the current primitive population:  ar{\Psi} =  rac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \Psii where N is the total number of Gaussians. 4. Densification Trigger: Determine if a Gaussian should be densified using the dynamic trigger function \mathbb{I}{densify}: \mathbb{I}{densify}^{(i)} = (\|
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)}\| > 	au{grad}) \land (\Psii >  ar{\Psi}) Densification is triggered only if the gradient magnitude exceeds 	au{grad} AND the consistency score is higher than the population average. 5. Execution: If \mathbb{I}{densify}^{(i)} is true, perform densification operations (splitting or cloning) as defined in the parent Densification Strategy. This check is performed every kE = 100 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. momentumbuffer: 2D list of shape (N, D) storing momentum for all attributes. lossgradients: 2D list of shape (N, D) storing gradients for all attributes. gamma: Momentum decay factor. taugrad: Gradient magnitude threshold. epsilon: Numerical stability constant. kE: Densification interval. currentiter: Current training iteration. Returns: densifymask: Boolean list of length N indicating which Gaussians to densify. newmomentumbuffer: Updated 2D list of shape (N, D). """ N = len(gaussians) D = len(lossgradients[0]) newmomentum = [[0.0] D for in range(N)] # 1. Momentum Update for i in range(N): for d in range(D): newmomentum[i][d] = gamma momentumbuffer[i][d] + (1 - gamma) lossgradients[i][d] # Only evaluate densification at interval kE if currentiter % kE != 0: return [False] N, newmomentum # 2. Consistency Score Calculation consistencyscores = [] gradmagnitudes = [] for i in range(N): dotprod = sum(newmomentum[i][d] lossgradients[i][d] for d in range(D)) normm = sum(newmomentum[i][d] 2 for d in range(D)) 0.5 normg = sum(lossgradients[i][d] 2 for d in range(D)) 0.5 consistencyscores.append(dotprod / (normm normg + epsilon)) gradmagnitudes.append(normg) # 3. Population Average meanconsistency = sum(consistencyscores) / N # 4. Densification Trigger densifymask = [] for i in range(N): highgrad = gradmagnitudes[i] > taugrad highconsistency = consistencyscores[i] > meanconsistency densifymask.append(highgrad and highconsistency) return densifymask, newmomentum Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating Artifacts: Standard gradient-based strategies can create floating artifacts in non-manifold regions due to reliance on single-step gradient snapshots. This method mitigates this by using momentum, which represents more deterministic historical motion trends. Numerical Stability: The denominator in the consistency score calculation includes \epsilon to prevent division by zero when norms are near zero. Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The choice of \gamma and 	au{grad} is critical. The source does not provide specific values, implying they may require tuning or follow default 3DGS configurations. Time Complexity: The additional cost per iteration is the momentum update and consistency score calculation, which are O(N \cdot D) operations where N is the number of Gaussians and D is the attribute dimensionality. The densification check itself is O(N). This is lightweight compared to the rendering and gradient computation steps. Memory Complexity: Requires an additional momentum buffer of size O(N \cdot D). Strengths: Reduces floating artifacts in complex/non-manifold regions by leveraging historical gradient information. Scene-adaptive without manual hyperparameter search for the consistency threshold (uses population mean). Limitations: Requires maintaining an additional buffer. Performance depends on the choice of \gamma and 	au{grad}. When to use: When standard densification leads to floating artifacts or noisy geometry in non-manifold regions. When not to use: If memory is extremely constrained (due to the momentum buffer) or if the scene is simple and standard densification suffices. Origin: Proposed in the ACE-GS paper. History: Developed to address limitations of standard gradient-based densification in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the issue of floating artifacts in non-manifold regions. name: GSGEN Appearance Refinement
head: GSGEN refinement stage, compactness-based densification
body:
GSGEN Appearance Refinement is an iterative optimization stage in the GSGEN framework designed to improve fine-grained visual details in text-to-3D generation while preserving the fundamental geometry established during the preceding geometry optimization phase. It addresses the limitations of standard gradient-based densification by introducing a compactness-based strategy to "fill holes" in the Gaussian representation and employs specific regularization losses to prevent overfitting and maintain geometric consistency. Unlike sibling methods that rely primarily on positional gradients or opacity thresholds for densification, GSGEN explicitly incorporates a 3D Stable Diffusion Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss and a mean position penalty to ensure 3D consistency and structural integrity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} initialized from the geometry optimization stage, where each Gaussian gi has position pi, opacity oi, and other attributes (scale, rotation, SH coefficients). A pre-trained 2D diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion). Output: Refined set of 3D Gaussians with improved appearance and denser, more complete geometry. Data Structures: KD-Tree: Used to store Gaussian positions for efficient nearest-neighbor queries. Gaussian Attributes: Position pi \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity oi \in \mathbb{R}, Scale, Rotation, SH Coefficients. Parameters: \lambda{SDS} = 0.1: Weight for the 3D SDS loss. \lambda{mean} = 1.0: Weight for the mean position regularization loss. \lambda{opacity} = 100.0: Weight for the opacity regularization loss. \alpha{min}: Threshold for pruning Gaussians with low opacity (value not explicitly given in sources, but referenced as a threshold). K: Number of nearest neighbors considered for compactness-based densification (value not explicitly given in sources). N{views}: Number of views sampled per iteration (stratified sampling on azimuth is used). Steps: 1. Loss Computation: For each iteration, compute the total refinement loss L{refine} for each Gaussian parameter 	heta (including positions, opacities, and appearance attributes): 
abla	heta L{refine} = \lambda{SDS} \mathbb{E}{\epsilonI, t} \left[ wI(t) (\epsilon\phi(xt; y, t) - \epsilonI)  rac{\partial x}{\partial 	heta} ight] + \lambda{mean} \sumi 
abla	heta ||pi|| + \lambda{opacity} \sumi 
abla	heta 	ext{sg}(||pi||) \cdot oi Where: \epsilon\phi(xt; y, t) is the noise prediction from the diffusion model \phi given noisy image xt, text prompt y, and timestep t. \epsilonI is the ground truth noise (sampled from standard normal). wI(t) is the weighting function for the SDS loss.  rac{\partial x}{\partial 	heta} is the gradient of the rendered image x with respect to the Gaussian parameters 	heta. ||pi|| is the Euclidean norm of the position of the i-th Gaussian. 	ext{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operation. oi is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. 2. Compactness-Based Densification: For each Gaussian gi, query its K nearest neighbors using the KD-Tree. For each neighbor gj, if the distance d(pi, pj) between the centers is smaller than the sum of their radii (ri + rj), perform densification: Add a new Gaussian between gi and gj. The radius of the new Gaussian is equal to the residual distance (implied: the gap between the overlapping spheres). This step aims to "fill the holes" and create a more complete geometry structure. 3. Opacity Regularization and Pruning: Add an extra loss term to regularize opacity, proportional to the distance of the Gaussian to the center of the scene (implied by "distance to the center" in, though the formula uses ||pi|| which is distance from origin). Periodically (every N iterations, consistent with parent [Parent]), remove Gaussians with opacity oi < \alpha{min}. 4. Geometric Consistency Penalty: The term \lambda{mean} \sumi 
abla	heta ||pi|| penalizes Gaussians that deviate significantly from their positions obtained during the preceding geometry optimization stage. This ensures that the refinement process does not distort the fundamental 3D structure. 5. Optimization Step: Update Gaussian parameters 	heta using the computed gradients 
abla	heta L{refine}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gsgenappearancerefinement(Gaussians, diffusionmodel, textprompt, numiterations, K, alphamin, lambdasds, lambdamean, lambdaopacity): """ GSGEN Appearance Refinement stage. Args: Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: pos, opacity, radius, etc. diffusionmodel: Pre-trained Stable Diffusion model. textprompt: Text prompt for generation. numiterations: Number of refinement iterations. K: Number of nearest neighbors for compactness-based densification. alphamin: Opacity threshold for pruning. lambdasds: Weight for SDS loss. lambdamean: Weight for mean position regularization. lambdaopacity: Weight for opacity regularization. Returns: Refined Gaussians. """ # Build KD-Tree for nearest neighbor queries kdtree = buildkdtree([g.pos for g in Gaussians]) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample views (stratified sampling on azimuth) views = sampleviewsstratifiedazimuth() # 2. Compute gradients for all Gaussians gradients = {g: torch.zeroslike(g.getallparams()) for g in Gaussians} for g in Gaussians: # Render image for current view # Note: In practice, this involves differentiable rasterization # For simplicity, we assume a function renderimage(gaussians, view) # and compute gradients w.r.t g's parameters # 2a. 3D SDS Loss # Sample noise epsilonI and timestep t epsilonI = torch.randnlike(renderedimage) t = sampletimestep() # Get noisy image xt xt = addnoise(renderedimage, t) # Predict noise from diffusion model epsilonpred = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(xt, textprompt, t) # Compute SDS gradient # wI(t) is the weighting function wt = computesdsweight(t) # Gradient of rendered image w.r.t Gaussian parameters # This requires backprop through the renderer gradsds = computesdsgradient(epsilonpred, epsilonI, wt, renderedimage, g) gradients[g] += lambdasds gradsds # 2b. Mean Position Regularization # Penalize deviation from original position (||pi||) # Note: The formula in uses ||pi||, which is distance from origin. # This acts as a regularizer to keep Gaussians near the origin or prevent drift. gradmean = lambdamean computegradientofnorm(g.pos) gradients[g] += gradmean # 2c. Opacity Regularization # Regularize opacity with weight proportional to distance to center # Formula: lambdaopacity gradtheta (sg(||pi||) oi) # sg(||pi||) stops gradient through the position norm opacityregterm = torch.stopgradient(torch.norm(g.pos)) g.opacity gradopacity = lambdaopacity computegradientofopacityreg(opacityregterm, g) gradients[g] += gradopacity # 3. Update Gaussian parameters for g in Gaussians: g.updateparameters(gradients[g]) # 4. Compactness-Based Densification # Rebuild KD-Tree if necessary (or update incrementally) # For simplicity, rebuild here kdtree = buildkdtree([g.pos for g in Gaussians]) newgaussians = [] for g in Gaussians: # Find K nearest neighbors neighbors = kdtree.query(g.pos, k=K) for neighbor in neighbors: dist = torch.norm(g.pos - neighbor.pos) sumradii = g.radius + neighbor.radius if dist < sumradii: # Add new Gaussian between them # Radius equal to residual residualradius = sumradii - dist newg = creategaussianbetween(g, neighbor, residualradius) newgaussians.append(newg) Gaussians.extend(newgaussians) # 5. Pruning # Periodically prune Gaussians with low opacity if iteration % pruneinterval == 0: Gaussians = [g for g in Gaussians if g.opacity >= alphamin] return Gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-densification: If the threshold for compactness-based densification is too low, it may lead to excessive Gaussian proliferation and memory issues. Geometry Distortion: Without the mean position regularization, the SDS loss might cause the geometry to drift or distort, leading to the "Janus problem". Opacity Instability: Low opacity Gaussians can cause noise in the rendering; pruning them is essential for stability. Joint optimization of material properties M = {(aj, rj, mj)} and environment lighting L over 7000 additional iterations, using re-rendering loss Lcolor augmented with segmentation, IID, and diffusion priors to resolve ill-posedness and overfitting. Time Complexity: The compactness-based densification step requires O(N \log N) for KD-Tree construction and O(N \cdot K) for neighbor queries per iteration, where N is the number of Gaussians and K is the number of neighbors. The SDS loss computation involves rendering and backpropagation through the diffusion model, which is computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians, which can increase significantly due to compactness-based densification. Performance: GSGEN produces more complete geometry structures and finer details compared to methods relying solely on gradient-based densification. It effectively mitigates the Janus problem. Strengths: Preserves geometry while improving appearance; fills holes in the Gaussian representation; reduces overfitting to specific views. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the diffusion model guidance and densification steps; requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (\lambda{SDS}, \lambda{mean}, \lambda{opacity}). When to use: When generating 3D assets from text prompts where geometric consistency and fine detail are critical, and the initial geometry optimization has produced a sparse or incomplete representation. When not to use: When computational resources are limited, or when the initial geometry is already dense and well-formed, as the densification step may add unnecessary complexity. GSGEN (Gaussian Splatting for Generation) was introduced in the paper "Text-to-3D using Gaussian Splatting". The appearance refinement stage was developed to address the challenges of overfitting and geometric inconsistency in text-to-3D generation methods that use 3D Gaussian Splatting as the underlying representation. The method builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent] and integrates 2D image priors from pre-trained diffusion models. name: GAINS Stage II: Material Properties
head: GAINS Material Optimization, Joint Material and Lighting Optimization
body: This method jointly optimizes material properties and environment lighting to resolve the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering from sparse views, preventing overfitting and enabling robust relighting. It distinguishes itself from its parent GSGEN Appearance Refinement by introducing segmentation-based intra-class consistency, intrinsic image decomposition priors, and multi-illuminated score distillation to regularize material estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Gaussian primitives G (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients) from Stage I; material parameters M = \{aj, rj, mj\} (albedo, roughness, metallicity) for each Gaussian j; environment lighting L; input images Ii with known intrinsics. Outputs: Optimized material parameters M, environment lighting L, and updated Gaussian class membership vectors Ej. Data Structures: Gaussian Class Membership: Each Gaussian j is extended with a one-hot vector Ej \in \{0, 1\}^K, where K is the number of semantic classes. Ej encodes the Gaussian's class membership for segmentation guidance. Material Parameters: Stored per Gaussian. aj (albedo), rj (roughness), mj (metallicity). Numbered Steps: 1. Segmentation Mask Lifting: Sample V=100 novel viewpoints orbiting the scenery. Render SH-colored images \{\hat{I}v\}{v=1}^V from these viewpoints. Generate segmentation masks for each \hat{I}v using SAM. Extract features f{v,s} = [g{v,s}, h{v,s}] for each mask region s in view v, where g{v,s} are CLIP features and h{v,s} are DINOv2 features. For each view, lift the mask and features to the Gaussian that contributes most to the pixel color (based on \alpha-blending weights). Merge collected Gaussian objects from previous lifting operations using geometric and feature similarity scores to assign class labels Ej. 2. Intra-Class Consistency (ICC) Loss Calculation: For each captured viewpoint i, identify the set of masks Si rendered from that view. Compute the ICC loss \mathcal{L}{ICC} using the formula below, where si \in Si is a mask region, A{si} is the rendered masked albedo, R{si} is the rendered masked roughness, M{si} is the rendered masked metallicity, and E{si} is the masked re-render loss. Apply the scaling function \gamma(|si|) = \exp(25 \cdot |I| / ||si||^2), where |I| is the total image area and ||si||^2 is the number of pixels in the mask. 3. Intrinsic Image Decomposition (IID) Loss Calculation: Obtain the IID diffuse albedo \hat{A}i for each captured image Ii using Teamwork [24] (or RGB2X [43] for outdoor data). Compute the IID loss \mathcal{L}{IID} = \beta(\tau) \cdot ||Ai - \hat{A}i||2^2, where Ai is the rendered diffuse albedo. Apply the linearly decreasing weight \beta(\tau) based on the current iteration step \tau to mitigate view-inconsistency in IID estimates. Note: IID supervision is not applied to roughness and metallicity due to their lower robustness and higher view-inconsistency. 4. Multi-Illuminated Score Distillation Sampling (MI-SDS) Loss Calculation: Start diffusion guidance after 3000 optimization steps. Render relit images R{mat}(Cj, G, M, El) from a novel view Cj under randomly selected lighting El from a predetermined set \{El\}{l=1}^{|E|}. Compute the noisy latent Z{jl} = \alphat R{mat}(Cj, G, M, El) + \sigmat \epsilon, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) and \alphat, \sigmat are diffusion schedule parameters. Calculate the MI-SDS loss \mathcal{L}{MI-SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} w(t) ||\epsilon\phi(Z{jl}; t) - \epsilon||2^2, where \epsilon\phi is the pretrained diffusion model. Use a guidance scale of 100. 5. Final Loss Combination and Optimization: Combine all losses: \mathcal{L}{mat} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda{ICC} \mathcal{L}{ICC} + \lambda{IID} \mathcal{L}{IID} + \lambda{MI-SDS} \mathcal{L}{MI-SDS} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV}. \mathcal{L}{TV} is a total variation loss on the reconstructed lighting for smoothing. Optimize M and L for 7000 additional iterations. Formulas: The Intra-Class Consistency loss \mathcal{L}{ICC} is defined as: \mathcal{L}{ICC} = \frac{1}{|Si|} \sum{si \in Si} \gamma(|si|) \cdot \left( \mathcal{L}{r,m} + \mathcal{L}a + \mathcal{L}e \right) Where the components are: \mathcal{L}{r,m} = \text{Var}(R{si}) + \text{Var}(M{si}) \mathcal{L}a = \left( (1-R{si}) + M{si} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{3} \sum{c=1}^3 \text{Var}(A{si}^{(c)}) \mathcal{L}e = \left( (1-M{si}) + R{si} \right) \cdot E{si} The scaling function is: \gamma(|si|) = \exp\left(25 \cdot \frac{|I|}{||si||^2}\right) The IID loss is: \mathcal{L}{IID} = \beta(\tau) \cdot ||Ai - \hat{A}i||2^2 The MI-SDS loss is: \mathcal{L}{MI-SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} w(t) ||\epsilon\phi(Z{jl}; t) - \epsilon||2^2 Parameters: \lambda{ICC} = 0.1 \lambda{IID} = 2 \lambda{MI-SDS} = 0.0001 \lambda{TV} = 0.1 V = 100 (number of sampled novel viewpoints) MI-SDS guidance scale: 100 MI-SDS start step: 3000 Optimization iterations: 7000 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posedness: Multiple combinations of material M and lighting L produce similar appearances, leading to ambiguous estimates, especially with sparse views. Mitigated by segmentation, IID, and diffusion priors. IID View-Inconsistency: IID diffuse albedo estimates may be view-inconsistent. Mitigated by weighting the loss with \beta(\tau), which linearly decreases over iterations. Specular/Metallicity IID: IID supervision is avoided for specular roughness and metallicity as these parameters are less robust and exhibit more inconsistencies across views. Time Complexity: The method adds significant overhead due to the lifting process (rendering 100 views, running SAM/CLIP/DINOv2) and the MI-SDS loss (diffusion model inference). The optimization runs for 7000 additional iterations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the one-hot class vectors Ej for all Gaussians and caching features/masks during the lifting phase. Strengths: Produces robust, relightable material properties even from sparse inputs by regularizing against overfitting. Limitations: Relies on external models (SAM, CLIP, DINOv2, Teamwork/RGB2X, Diffusion) which may introduce errors or inconsistencies. The lifting process assumes accurate segmentation and feature matching. GAINS (Gaussian-Based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures) was introduced by P. Noras et al. in 2024. Stage II specifically addresses the material estimation phase, building on the geometry reconstruction from Stage I. The method is designed for inverse rendering from sparse multi-view captures, aiming to produce intrinsic images (albedo, roughness, metallicity) and environment lighting suitable for relighting. GAINS: Gaussian-Based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37602-218, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Multi-view Consistency and Scoring
head: Multi-view regulated densification, MVGS densification
body: Multi-view Consistency and Scoring is a family of densification strategies for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces or augments single-view gradient-based criteria with multi-view evaluation to constrain Gaussian count and ensure structural consistency. It addresses the overfitting and excessive primitive production inherent in standard single-view densification by leveraging alpha-weighted error accumulation or photometric consistency across multiple viewpoints. Unlike its siblings, this family explicitly integrates importance and pruning scores derived from multi-view photometric loss and alpha contributions into the standard gradient masks, ensuring that densification occurs only where geometry is consistently unresolved across views [S1, 15406-multi-view-alpha-based-densification.md, 15464-multi-view-consistency-scoring-for-densification.md]. All methods in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk is defined by a mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \Sigmak (parameterized by scale sk and rotation qk), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. The core mechanism involves periodic evaluation of a metric per Gaussian to determine if the current representation is insufficient or redundant in a specific region. Common metrics include: 1. Gradient Magnitude: The accumulated 2D positional gradient \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v} \| \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muv^k} \|2. High gradients indicate that the Gaussian's position is not adequately minimizing the loss, suggesting a need for refinement or replacement. 2. Opacity: Low opacity \alphak < \alpha{\min} indicates a primitive contributes negligibly to the rendered image and is a candidate for pruning. 3. Scale: Excessively large scales max(sk) relative to the scene extent e{scene} indicate coarse approximations that may blur details or occlude nearby geometry. Densification operations are typically triggered every N iterations (e.g., refineEvery = 100) to allow the optimizer to stabilize. The primary operations are: Splitting: Replacing a parent Gaussian gk with N{children} children. The children's means \mu{child} are sampled from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak). The scale is typically reduced, e.g., s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}}, to increase local density. Cloning: Creating an exact copy of gk (same \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) to increase sampling frequency in high-error regions without changing the spatial footprint. Pruning: Removing Gaussians that fail to meet opacity or significance thresholds. Buffer management is critical: pruned or split Gaussians require buffer compaction or flag-based marking to maintain contiguous memory access for rasterization [Parent]. Replaces single-view gradient-based criteria with multi-view evaluation to constrain Gaussian count and ensure structural consistency. It explicitly integrates importance and pruning scores derived from photometric loss and alpha contributions into the standard gradient masks. Computes per-Gaussian scores based on multi-view photometric consistency to guide both densification (importance) and pruning. It differs from standard gradient-based densification by aggregating L1 reconstruction errors across multiple camera views, identifying Gaussians that consistently fail to reconstruct the scene geometry or appearance. A densification module that adjusts the densification threshold based on multi-view discrepancies to help 3D Gaussians fit each view better and capture finer scene details. When the measured discrepancies between views become large, it increases the densification effect by adding half of the original densification threshold (\beta/2) to the active threshold. The method relies on a Heaviside step function H(\cdot) to gate the discrepancy calculation, returning 1 if the input is \ge 0, which prevents negative discrepancy values from triggering densification. The adjusted threshold is defined as \hat{\beta} = \beta - \frac{\beta}{2} H(r\tau^i - 1), where \tau is a predefined hyperparameter adjusting the extent of the discrepancy between each camera, and \beta is the original baseline threshold for standard Gaussian densification. The concept of multi-view consistency in Gaussian Splatting was introduced in MVGS (Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting for Novel View Synthesis). The method was developed to address the limitations of standard 3DGS densification, which often leads to overfitting and redundant primitives due to reliance on single-view gradients. By regulating densification through multi-view constraints, the method facilitates better multi-view training and captures finer scene details. MVGS: Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting for Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2410.02103, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning
head: Multi-view Consistency-Guided Densification, Stratified Camera Sampling
body: Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning is a training optimization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces single-view gradient-based criteria with multi-view consistency metrics to constrain Gaussian count and prevent overfitting. Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on positional gradients from a single view—prone to excessive primitive production and redundancy—this method leverages alpha-weighted error accumulation across multiple sampled viewpoints to accurately identify regions requiring densification and primitives eligible for pruning. It builds on Multi-view Consistency and Scoring by operationalizing consistency checks into specific clone, split, and prune masks. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk has mean \muk, covariance \Sigmak, opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. Training camera set \mathcal{C}. Ground truth images C{gt}. Hyperparameters: \tau^+: Loss threshold for poor reconstruction (default: 0.1). \tau^-: Loss threshold for well-reconstructed regions (default: 0.01). Q\tau^+: Quantile for densification importance (default: 0.6). Q\tau^-: Quantile for pruning (default: 0.1). N{cam}: Number of cameras to sample (default: 6). \lambda: Weight for DSSIM in loss function (standard 3DGS value, typically 0.2). Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}' after cloning, splitting, and pruning operations. Binary masks \mathcal{M}{clone} and \mathcal{M}{split} identifying Gaussians to modify. Pruning mask identifying Gaussians to remove. Metric Map (M): A binary map M \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W} per view, where H, W are image dimensions. M{u,v}^{+, c} = 1 if pixel (u,v) in view c has high error. M{u,v}^{-, c} = 1 if pixel (u,v) in view c has low error. Importance/Pruning Scores (S^+, S^-): Arrays of size N (number of Gaussians). Si^+: Accumulated alpha-weighted error for Gaussian i. Si^-: Accumulated loss-weighted alpha for Gaussian i. Base Masks (\mathcal{M}{clone}^{base}, \mathcal{M}{split}^{base}): Binary masks derived from standard positional gradient thresholds \|\nabla{\mui} \mathcal{L}\|2 > \tau{grad}. 1. Stratified Camera Sampling: To ensure comprehensive geometric coverage and alleviate view redundancy, partition the training camera set \mathcal{C} into angular bins defined with respect to the scene center x^. Select N{cam} representative views that maximize angular dispersion. Let the sampled camera set be \mathcal{C}{sample} \subset \mathcal{C} with |\mathcal{C}{sample}| = N{cam}. 2. Render and Compute Loss: For each camera c \in \mathcal{C}{sample}, render the current Gaussian primitives to obtain image C^c. Compute the pixel-wise photometric loss \mathcal{L}{u,v}^c using the hybrid objective: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}1(C, C{gt}) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{DSSIM}(C, C{gt}) where \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 distance and \mathcal{L}{DSSIM} is the difference in Structural Similarity. 3. name: Multi-View Consistency Scoring for Densification
head: gaussian pruning and densification score
body: This method computes per-Gaussian scores based on multi-view photometric consistency to guide both densification (importance) and pruning operations during 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. It differs from standard gradient-based densification by explicitly aggregating binary error flags across multiple camera views to identify regions with persistent reconstruction errors, and normalizes the accumulated loss to prioritize primitives for refinement. It builds on Multi-view Consistency and Scoring. Inputs: camlist: List of viewpoint camera objects. gaussians: Current Gaussian representation (means, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients). pipe: Rendering pipeline configuration. bg: Background color/tensor. args: Configuration object containing lossthresh (threshold for high-error classification) and mult (scaling factor for rendering). DENSIFY: Boolean flag. If True, computes importance score for densification; if False, computes only pruning score. Outputs: importancescore: Per-Gaussian integer counts of views marking the Gaussian as high-error, floor-averaged across views. Only returned if DENSIFY is True. pruningscore: Normalized (0..1) per-Gaussian score used to prioritize densification or pruning. Higher scores indicate worse reconstruction consistency. Data Structures: fullmetriccounts: Tensor of shape (N,) storing the accumulated count of high-error views per Gaussian. Initialized to None. fullmetricscore: Tensor of shape (N,) storing the accumulated weighted photometric loss per Gaussian. Initialized to None. metricmap: Binary tensor of shape (H, W) indicating which pixels have high loss. Steps: 1. Initialize fullmetriccounts and fullmetricscore to None. 2. Loop over each view index v in camlist: a. Retrieve myviewpointcam = camlist[v]. b. Render the image using the current Gaussians: I{render} = \text{render\fastgs}(my\viewpoint\cam, \text{gaussians}, \text{pipe}, \text{bg}, \text{args.mult}) c. Compute the photometric loss Lv for this view: Lv = \text{compute\photometric\loss}(my\viewpoint\cam, I{render}) d. Retrieve the ground truth image I{gt} = my\viewpoint\cam.\text{original\image}.\text{cuda}(). e. Compute the normalized L1 loss map: L{norm} = \text{get\loss}(I{render}, I{gt}) f. Create a binary metric map where pixels with loss exceeding the threshold are marked as 1: M = (L{norm} > \text{args.loss\thresh}).\text{int}() g. Render again with metric collection enabled to accumulate per-Gaussian contributions: \text{render\pkg} = \text{render\fastgs}(my\viewpoint\cam, \text{gaussians}, \text{pipe}, \text{bg}, \text{args.mult}, \text{get\flag}=\text{True}, \text{metric\map}=M) h. Extract the accumulated loss counts for this view: Cv = \text{render\pkg}["\text{accum\metric\counts}"] i. Update global accumulators: If fullmetriccounts is None, set fullmetriccounts = Cv. Else, fullmetriccounts += Cv. If fullmetricscore is None, set fullmetricscore = Lv \cdot Cv. Else, fullmetricscore += Lv \cdot Cv. 3. Compute the pruning score by normalizing fullmetricscore to the range [0, 1]: \text{pruning\score} = \frac{\text{full\metric\score} - \min(\text{full\metric\score})}{\max(\text{full\metric\score}) - \min(\text{full\metric\score})} 4. If DENSIFY is True, compute the importance score by floor-dividing the total counts by the number of views: \text{importance\score} = \lfloor \text{full\metric\counts} / |\text{camlist}| \rfloor Else, set importancescore to None. 5. Return importancescore and pruningscore. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ fullmetriccounts = None fullmetricscore = None numviews = len(camlist) for viewidx in range(numviews): myviewpointcam = camlist[viewidx] # Render image renderimage = renderfastgs(myviewpointcam, gaussians, pipe, bg, args.mult)["render"] # Compute photometric loss photometricloss = computephotometricloss(myviewpointcam, renderimage) # Get ground truth gtimage = myviewpointcam.originalimage.cuda() # Compute normalized loss and threshold l1lossnorm = getloss(renderimage, gtimage) metricmap = (l1lossnorm > args.lossthresh).int() # Render with metric accumulation renderpkg = renderfastgs( myviewpointcam, gaussians, pipe, bg, args.mult, getflag=True, metricmap=metricmap) accumlosscounts = renderpkg["accummetriccounts"] # Update accumulators if fullmetriccounts is None: fullmetriccounts = accumlosscounts.clone() else: fullmetriccounts = fullmetriccounts + accumlosscounts if fullmetricscore is None: fullmetricscore = photometricloss accumlosscounts.clone() else: fullmetricscore = fullmetricscore + (photometricloss accumlosscounts) # Compute pruning score (normalized) minscore = torch.min(fullmetricscore) maxscore = torch.max(fullmetricscore) denom = maxscore - minscore # Handle division by zero if all scores are identical if denom == 0: pruningscore = torch.zeroslike(fullmetricscore) else: pruningscore = (fullmetricscore - minscore) / denom # Compute importance score if densifying importancescore = None if DENSIFY: importancescore = torch.floordivide(fullmetriccounts, numviews) return importancescore, pruningscore Parameters: lossthresh: Threshold for classifying a pixel as high-error. Typical value: Not given in the sources. mult: Scaling modifier for rendering. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If max(fullmetricscore) == min(fullmetricscore), the denominator in the pruning score calculation becomes zero. The implementation must handle this, e.g., by setting the score to 0 or 1 depending on convention. Initialization: fullmetriccounts and fullmetricscore must be initialized to None or zero tensors of the correct shape before the loop to avoid type errors or incorrect accumulation. Device Placement: Ground truth images and intermediate tensors must be on the same device (typically CUDA) to avoid runtime errors. Uses ray tracing and multi-view photometric loss to target complex, texture-dense areas consistently observed across perspectives, adapting thresholds based on camera geometry. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot R), where V is the number of views in camlist and R is the cost of rendering a single view. The method requires two renders per view (one for loss, one for metric accumulation). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing fullmetriccounts and fullmetricscore, where N is the number of Gaussians. Additional memory for intermediate render buffers per view. Strengths: Explicitly targets regions with persistent multi-view inconsistency, which are often indicative of missing geometry or artifacts. The binary thresholding reduces sensitivity to absolute loss magnitude variations across views. Limitations: Requires multiple renders per optimization step, increasing computational overhead. Sensitive to the choice of lossthresh. When to use: When standard gradient-based densification fails to resolve multi-view inconsistencies or artifacts in texture-dense regions. When not to use: When computational resources are severely constrained, or when the scene is static and well-reconstructed with standard methods. This method is part of the FastGS (Fast Gaussian Splatting) optimization pipeline, which aims to accelerate and improve the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It leverages multi-view consistency as a more robust signal for densification than single-view gradients, addressing the issue of overfitting to specific viewpoints or noise. fastgs/FastGS, https://github.com/fastgs/FastGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

body: Cross-ray Densification is a strategy that selectively increases 3D Gaussian density in multi-view overlapped regions to enhance multi-view consistency during optimization. It is divided into Multi-view Augmented Densification (MVAD), which adapts the densification threshold based on camera geometry, and Cross-ray Densification, which uses ray tracing to identify 3D regions contributing significantly to multiple views. Unlike standard densification which relies solely on 2D gradient magnitude, this method leverages multi-view photometric loss and ray intersection geometry to target complex, texture-dense areas that are consistently observed across different camera perspectives. The method consists of two coupled components: Multi-view Augmented Densification (MVAD) and Cross-ray Densification. MVAD adjusts the global densification threshold based on the geometric diversity of the training views, while Cross-ray Densification identifies specific 3D volumes for densification using 2D loss maps and ray casting. Inputs: M: Number of training views. L: Set of multi-view loss maps, where Lm is the loss map for view m. \beta: Original densification threshold. \tau: Predefined hyperparameter for discrepancy adjustment. (h, w): Dimensions of the sliding window for region localization. nr: Number of rays cast per window vertex (fixed at 4). Outputs: A set of densified 3D Gaussians located in identified multi-view overlapped regions. Loss Map (Lm): A 2D array of photometric loss values (e.g., L1 or L2 loss) for each pixel in view m. Camera Poses: For each view m, the translation vector tm and rotation matrix Rm. Regions (R): A list of 2D bounding box coordinates identified in the loss maps. Cuboids: 3D volumes defined by the intersection of ray planes from multiple views. MVAD determines whether to enhance densification based on the geometric distinctness of the training views. 1. Normalize Camera Translations: Normalize the translation vectors of all sampled views into a unit sphere to make the strategy scene-adaptive. 2. Compute Discrepancies: Calculate the multi-view consistency discrepancies \{ri\} for all unique pairs of cameras. The number of pairs is n = (M^2 - M)/2. ri is computed using the relative translation distance and the similarity of the rotation matrices between each camera pair. 3. Adjust Threshold: Modify the densification threshold \hat{\beta} using the Heaviside function H(\cdot): \hat{\beta} = \beta - \frac{\beta}{2} H\left(\tau - ri\right) Where: H(x) = 1 if x \ge 0, else 0. If discrepancies ri are large (specifically ri < \tau), the term H(\tau - ri) becomes 1, reducing the threshold by half (\hat{\beta} = \beta/2). This enhances densification in complex areas. If discrepancies are small (ri \ge \tau), H(\tau - ri) = 0, and \hat{\beta} = \beta, preventing over-densification in simple regions. This step locates 3D regions containing Gaussians that contribute to multiple views by intersecting rays cast from high-loss 2D regions. 1. Loss Map Analysis: For each view m \in [1, M], calculate the loss map Lm. 2. Region Localization: For each loss map Lm, compute the average loss within a sliding window of size (h, w). Identify regions R containing the largest average loss values. These regions correspond to texture-dense or high-error areas. 3. Ray Casting and Intersection: For each identified 2D region r \in R, cast nr = 4 rays from each vertex of the region into the scene. Compute the intersection planes formed by rays originating from different camera perspectives. Treat the cuboids formed by these intersecting planes as the multi-view overlapped regions. These cuboids contain critical 3D Gaussians that significantly influence rendering from multiple views. 4. Densification: Identify all 3D Gaussians located inside these identified cuboids and apply densification operations exclusively to them. Unverified code.
