name: Soft Rasterization
head: Blurring Primitives, SAR Feature Rasterizer, Soft Rasterization for Gradient Enrichment
body: Soft rasterization is a differentiable rendering technique that mitigates the discontinuities inherent in standard rasterization by blending facet contributions for pixels near primitive edges. It solves the problem of sparse and vanishing gradients caused by the non-uniformity of bilinear interpolation operands, which typically have similar values except at object boundaries. Unlike standard hard rasterization, it yields slightly distorted images but allows backpropagating more useful gradients, thereby stabilizing optimization and preventing gradient vanishing at edges. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D primitive geometry, camera parameters, and a blending radius parameter \sigma. Outputs: A rendered image or feature map with softened edges and enriched gradients suitable for backpropagation. Data Structures: The pipeline transforms coordinates through specific spaces depending on the application. For SAR, the sequence is World Space \rightarrow View Space \rightarrow Range Space \rightarrow Ground Space \rightarrow NDC Space. For standard rendering, World Space \rightarrow View Space \rightarrow NDC Space is typical. A fragment buffer stores per-pixel attributes (color, alpha, normals) derived from the rasterized primitives. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Transform primitive vertices from World Space to View Space, then to NDC Space. In SAR-specific implementations, intermediate steps include a Range Transform (z-coordinates become y-coordinates) and Ground-plane Projection (stretches perceived y-dimension so each pixel maps to a consistent-sized cell on ground). 2. Soft Rasterization: For each pixel, determine the contribution of all overlapping primitives. Instead of a binary inside/outside test, compute a soft coverage value based on the distance from the pixel to the primitive edge. The blending is controlled by a radius parameter \sigma. Pixels near the edge receive blended contributions from both the primitive and the background or adjacent primitives. 3. Shading: Compute per-pixel features based on the rasterized fragments. Silhouette: Create a mask from fragments that have no corresponding facets. Surface Normals: Compute per-pixel surface normals \hat{n} relative to the illumination direction \hat{q}. For monostatic SAR, the normal feature d is calculated as d = -\hat{q} \cdot \hat{n}, where \cdot denotes the inner product. Alpha Channel: Determine visibility. In SAR contexts, this involves rasterizing a reference view from the radar perspective to mask out self-shadowed facets before calculating the alpha channel for the main view. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss between the rendered image and the ground truth. The gradients flow through the soft rasterization stage, providing non-zero gradients for primitive parameters even when the primitive is not strictly inside the pixel in a hard-rasterization sense. Parameters: Blending Radius (\sigma): Controls the level of soft rasterization distortion. Typical values used in training are 0, 10^{-5}, 10^{-4}, and 10^{-3}. Gaussian Blur Kernel: In some implementations, Gaussian blur is applied to each primitive before optimization to enrich gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softrasterize(primitives, camera, sigma): """ Renders primitives using soft rasterization with blending radius sigma. Implements: Coordinate Transformations, Rasterization, Shading. """ H, W = camera.resolution renderedimage = zeros((H, W, 3)) # 1. Coordinate Transformations for prim in primitives: # Standard: World -> View -> NDC # SAR adds Range Transform and Ground-plane Projection viewverts = prim.vertices @ camera.viewmatrix.T ndcverts = viewverts @ camera.projectionmatrix.T prim.ndcverts = ndcverts # 2. Soft Rasterization & 3. Shading for y in range(H): for x in range(W): totalcolor = zeros(3) totalalpha = 0.0 # Sort primitives by depth for correct blending sortedprims = sorted(primitives, key=lambda p: depthatpixel(p, (x, y))) for prim in sortedprims: # Compute soft coverage based on distance to edge disttoedge = signeddistancetotriangleedge(prim.ndcverts, (x, y)) if sigma > 0: coverage = exp(-0.5 (disttoedge / sigma)2) else: coverage = 1.0 if disttoedge < 0 else 0.0 if coverage > 0: # Interpolate attributes using barycentric coordinates bary = barycentriccoords(prim.ndcverts, (x, y)) color = interpolate(prim.colors, bary) alpha = prim.alpha # Over operator blending blendedalpha = coverage alpha totalcolor = totalcolor (1 - blendedalpha) + color blendedalpha totalalpha += blendedalpha (1 - totalalpha) # Compute shading features if needed if prim.requiresnormals: normal = interpolate(prim.normals, bary) # d = -qhat. nhat (monostatic SAR) pass renderedimage[y, x] = totalcolor # 4. Loss Computation # Compute loss between renderedimage and groundtruth # loss.backward() propagates gradients through soft coverage return renderedimage def zeros(shape): return [0.0] prod(shape) def depthatpixel(prim, pixel): return mean(prim.ndcverts[:, 2]) def signeddistancetotriangleedge(verts, pixel): # Returns signed distance from pixel to triangle edge in NDC space return 0.0 # Standard barycentric edge function evaluation def barycentriccoords(verts, pixel): # Returns barycentric weights summing to 1.0 return [1.0/3, 1.0/3, 1.0/3] # Placeholder for actual barycentric calculation def interpolate(values, bary): return sum(v b for v, b in zip(values, bary)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts: Soft rasterization yields slightly distorted images, particularly near edges, due to the blending. Gradient Sparsity: Vanilla rasterization produces sparse gradients because bilinear interpolation operands have similar values except at boundaries. Soft rasterization mitigates this by smoothing edges. Precision: The choice of \sigma controls distortion levels; values range from 0 (hard rasterization) to 10^{-3}. Time Complexity: The soft rasterization step adds minimal computational overhead compared to standard rasterization, as it primarily modifies the edge evaluation logic. The overhead is reported to be almost the same as standard rendering in ablation studies. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory is required beyond standard frame buffers and primitive attributes. Performance: Soft rasterization yields consistent PSNR gains. In ablation studies, enabling soft rasterization improved PSNR from 24.4 to 24.7 on 512×512 targets and from 25.5 to 25.7 on 1024×1024 targets. Strengths: Stabilizes optimization, prevents gradient vanishing at edges, and enriches gradients for better convergence. Limitations: Introduces slight image distortion/artifacts. Not suitable for applications requiring pixel-perfect geometric accuracy without post-processing. Soft rasterization was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering to address the non-differentiability of standard rasterization operators. It is based on the soft rasterizer described in prior literature. The technique has been adapted for various domains, including Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery and bitmap primitive rendering (DiffBMP). In SAR, it is part of the SAR Feature Rasterizer pipeline. In DiffBMP, it is used as an optimization helper to align sparse gradients. name: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting Covariance Transformation and Regularization
head: 3D-HGS
body: This method modifies the covariance structure of 3D Gaussians to enforce half-ellipsoid geometry, allowing them to model sharp surface boundaries and occlusions more effectively than full ellipsoids. It solves the problem of "bloated" or "double-sided" Gaussian artifacts that occur when full ellipsoids intersect object surfaces, by projecting the covariance into a local basis aligned with a surface normal and regularizing the depth component. Unlike Frequency Regularization which operates in the spectral domain, or Hard and Soft Depth Regularization which uses external depth priors, this method intrinsically alters the Gaussian shape during training to match surface geometry. The method transforms the standard 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \Sigma into a "half-Gaussian" form by aligning it with a local surface normal and suppressing the variance along the normal direction. This transformation is applied periodically during training. Input: The original 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, which is symmetric and positive definite. The surface normal vector n \in \mathbb{R}^3 at the Gaussian's position \mu. Output: The regularized covariance matrix \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, representing a half-Gaussian oriented along n. The covariance matrix is stored as a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. In implementation, this is often derived from scale s and rotation q parameters as \Sigma = R S S^T R^T, where R is the rotation matrix from quaternion q and S is the diagonal scale matrix. The transformation operates directly on the 3 \times 3 matrix representation. The transformation is performed every 5000 training iterations. 1. Normalize Normal: Ensure the surface normal is unit length: n \leftarrow \frac{n}{\|n\|} 2. Construct Local Basis: Create an orthonormal basis matrix B where the third column is the normal n, and the first two columns v1, v2 span the tangent plane. If nx = 0 and ny = 0 (i.e., n is parallel to the z-axis): v1 = (1, 0, 0)^T, \quad v2 = (0, 1, 0)^T Otherwise: v1 = \frac{(ny, -nx, 0)^T}{\|(ny, -nx, 0)\|} v2 = \frac{n \times v1}{\|n \times v1\|} Concatenate to form the basis matrix: B = [v1, v2, n] 3. Project to Local Basis: Transform the covariance matrix into the local coordinate system defined by B: \text{cov} = B^T \Sigma B Let \text{cov}{ij} denote the element at row i, column j of this matrix. 4. Compute Regularized Diagonal/Off-Diagonal Terms: Calculate the modified terms a', b', c' which effectively marginalize out the normal direction variance from the tangent plane components: a' = \text{cov}{0,0} - \frac{\text{cov}{0,2}^2}{\text{cov}{2,2}} b' = \text{cov}{0,1} - \frac{\text{cov}{0,2} \cdot \text{cov}{1,2}}{\text{cov}{2,2}} c' = \text{cov}{1,1} - \frac{\text{cov}{1,2}^2}{\text{cov}{2,2}} Note: This step assumes \text{cov}{2,2} > 0. If \text{cov}{2,2} is near zero, numerical stability measures are required. 5. Construct Regularized Local Covariance: Build the new covariance matrix \sigma{\text{local}} in the basis space. The tangent plane components (0,0; 0,1; 1,1) are updated to a', b', c'. The cross-terms with the normal (0,2; 1,2) are set to 0. The normal variance (2,2) is set to a small fraction of the tangent variances to enforce flatness: \sigma{\text{local}} = \begin{pmatrix} a' & b' & 0 \\ b' & c' & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \min(a', c') / 100 \end{pmatrix} The matrix is symmetric, so \sigma{\text{local}, 1,0} = b' and \sigma{\text{local}, 2,0} = \sigma{\text{local}, 0,2} = 0, etc. 6. Transform Back to World Space: \sigma = B \sigma{\text{local}} B^T Regularization Interval: The transformation is applied every 5000 iterations. Opacity Thresholds: To support the half-Gaussian representation and reduce noise, the opacity threshold for densification and pruning is increased to 0.01, and the initial opacity for half-Gaussians is reset to 0.02. Flatness Factor: The normal variance is scaled by 1/100 relative to the minimum tangent variance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def transformcovariancetohalfgaussian(covmatrix: np.ndarray, normal: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Transforms a 3x3 covariance matrix into a half-Gaussian form aligned with a surface normal. Args: covmatrix: 3x3 symmetric covariance matrix Sigma. normal: 3D unit normal vector n. Returns: Regularized 3x3 covariance matrix sigma. """ # 1. Normalize normal n = normal / np.linalg.norm(normal) # 2. Construct basis # Check if normal is parallel to Z axis if abs(n[0]) < 1e-6 and abs(n[1]) < 1e-6: v1 = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) v2 = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) else: # v1 is perpendicular to n and lies in XY plane projection v1 = np.array([n[1], -n[0], 0.0]) v1 = v1 / np.linalg.norm(v1) # v2 is orthogonal to both n and v1 v2 = np.cross(n, v1) v2 = v2 / np.linalg.norm(v2) # Basis matrix B = [v1, v2, n] B = np.columnstack((v1, v2, n)) # 3. Project to local basis covlocal = B.T @ covmatrix @ B # 4. Compute modified terms # Guard against division by zero or near-zero cov[2,2] cov22 = covlocal[2, 2] if cov22 < 1e-8: cov22 = 1e-8 aprime = covlocal[0, 0] - (covlocal[0, 2]2) / cov22 bprime = covlocal[0, 1] - (covlocal[0, 2] covlocal[1, 2]) / cov22 cprime = covlocal[1, 1] - (covlocal[1, 2]2) / cov22 # 5. Construct regularized local covariance # The normal variance is minimized to enforce half-Gaussian (flat) geometry mintangentvar = min(aprime, cprime) normalvar = mintangentvar / 100.0 sigmalocal = np.array([ [aprime, bprime, 0.0], [bprime, cprime, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0, normalvar] ]) # 6. Transform back to world space sigma = B @ sigmalocal @ B.T return sigma Degenerate Normal: If the normal vector is zero or undefined, the basis construction fails. A fallback basis (e.g., identity) or skipping the regularization for that iteration is required. Positive Definiteness: The transformation may result in a covariance matrix that is not strictly positive definite if a' or c' become negative due to numerical errors or ill-conditioned input \Sigma. Clamping negative eigenvalues to a small positive value is recommended. Frequency: Applying this transformation too frequently may destabilize training. The source specifies every 5000 iterations. Time Complexity: The transformation involves matrix multiplications (3 \times 3) and vector operations, which is O(1) per Gaussian. However, it is only applied every 5000 iterations, so the per-frame overhead during rendering is negligible. The densification/pruning adjustments (opacity thresholds) may slightly increase the number of Gaussians, impacting rasterization time. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond the standard Gaussian parameters. The method modifies existing covariance data. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, 3D-HGS with an efficient rasterizer achieves 125 FPS and 29.66 PSNR using 3.8M kernels, compared to 3DGS which uses 3.2M kernels. On Tank & Dengin, it achieves 160 FPS and 24.45 PSNR with 1.8M kernels. On Tank & Blending, it achieves 126 FPS and 29.76 PSNR with 2.6M kernels. Strengths: Effectively models sharp surface boundaries and occlusions, reducing "ghosting" artifacts common in full-Gaussian splatting. Consistently outperforms original 3DGS in PSNR. Limitations: Requires accurate surface normals for the transformation. If normals are noisy or incorrect, the half-Gaussian orientation will be wrong, potentially degrading quality. The method increases the number of kernels required to achieve comparable detail to 3DGS in some scenes (e.g., 3.8M vs 3.2M on Mip-NeRF 360). The method was introduced in the paper "3D-HGS: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework Parent by addressing the limitation of full ellipsoids in representing sharp geometric features. The concept of half-Gaussians is inspired by the need to model one-sided surfaces, similar to techniques used in implicit surface representations. The method is evaluated against Scaffold, mip-splatting, and MCMC architectures. 3D-HGS: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01027, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Hard and Soft Depth Regularization
body: Hard and Soft Depth Regularization is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents detail loss and blurred appearance by constraining geometry updates to spatial reshaping (movement of centers) rather than deforming Gaussian shapes. It solves the conflict where forcing anisotropic Gaussians to fit smooth monocular depth estimates causes the primitive geometry to conform to the depth rather than the complex color appearance. It sets itself apart from standard depth regularization by freezing scale and rotation parameters and rendering two distinct depth maps to independently update center positions and opacities. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each defined by position \mu, scale s, rotation quaternion q, and opacity \alpha. A monocular depth estimate D{mono} for the current view. Camera parameters for the current view. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters (specifically \mu and \alpha) after one regularization step. Data Structures: Gaussian State: A list or array of Gaussian objects. Each object stores: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. s \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (log-space or linear, depending on implementation). q \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. \alpha \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Depth Maps: Two rendered depth maps, D{hard} and D{soft}, generated from the current Gaussian state. Method Steps: 1. Freeze Shape Parameters: During the depth regularization step, the scale parameters s and rotation quaternions q of all Gaussians are frozen. They are not updated by the gradients computed in this step. 2. Render Hard Depth Map (D{hard}): Render a depth map using the standard alpha-blending accumulation, but weighted by opacity to represent the "hard" surface closest to the camera. This map is used to compute gradients for position updates. Note: The exact definition of "hard" vs "soft" in the source is implied by the gradient targets: D{hard} targets position \mu, D{soft} targets opacity \alpha. In standard differentiable rendering, D{hard} is often the expected depth or the depth of the first hit, while D{soft} might be the alpha-weighted average depth. The source states: "Use the first depth map to compute gradients that update only the center positions \mu. Use the second depth map to compute gradients that update only the opacities \alpha". 3. Render Soft Depth Map (D{soft}): Render a second depth map. This map is used to compute gradients for opacity updates. The source implies this map helps balance coarse depth fitting with fine color appearance. 4. Compute Position Loss (\mathcal{L}{pos}): Compare D{hard} with the monocular depth estimate D{mono}. Compute a loss (e.g., L1 or L2) between the rendered hard depth and the monocular depth. \mathcal{L}{pos} = \text{Loss}(D{hard}, D{mono}) 5. Compute Opacity Loss (\mathcal{L}{alpha}): Compare D{soft} with the monocular depth estimate D{mono}. Compute a loss between the rendered soft depth and the monocular depth. \mathcal{L}{alpha} = \text{Loss}(D{soft}, D{mono}) 6. Compute Gradients: Compute gradients of \mathcal{L}{pos} with respect to the Gaussian positions \mu. Compute gradients of \mathcal{L}{alpha} with respect to the Gaussian opacities \alpha. Gradients for s and q are explicitly ignored or zeroed out. 7. Update Parameters: Update \mu using the gradients from \mathcal{L}{pos}. Update \alpha using the gradients from \mathcal{L}{alpha}. Do not update s or q. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardandsoftdepthregularization(gaussians, camera, monoculardepth, lrpos, lralpha): """ Performs one step of Hard and Soft Depth Regularization. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes mu, s, q, alpha. camera: Camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics). monoculardepth: 2D array representing the monocular depth estimate. lrpos: Learning rate for position updates. lralpha: Learning rate for opacity updates. Returns: Updated gaussians list. """ # Step 1: Freeze shape parameters (s, q) by not including them in the computation graph # or by zeroing their gradients after backward pass. # Step 2: Render Hard Depth Map # Dhard is typically the expected depth or depth of the first hit. # Implementation detail: Render depth weighted by opacity, but prioritizing closer Gaussians. Dhard = renderharddepth(gaussians, camera) # Step 3: Render Soft Depth Map # Dsoft is typically the alpha-weighted average depth. Dsoft = rendersoftdepth(gaussians, camera) # Step 4: Compute Position Loss # Example: L1 loss between rendered hard depth and monocular depth losspos = torch.mean(torch.abs(Dhard - monoculardepth)) # Step 5: Compute Opacity Loss # Example: L1 loss between rendered soft depth and monocular depth lossalpha = torch.mean(torch.abs(Dsoft - monoculardepth)) # Step 6: Compute Gradients # Gradients for mu and alpha gradmu = torch.autograd.grad(losspos, [g.mu for g in gaussians], retaingraph=True) gradalpha = torch.autograd.grad(lossalpha, [g.alpha for g in gaussians]) # Step 7: Update Parameters for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Update position g.mu = g.mu - lrpos gradmu[i] # Update opacity g.alpha = g.alpha - lralpha gradalpha[i] # Do NOT update s and q # g.s = g.s # g.q = g.q return gaussians def renderharddepth(gaussians, camera): """ Renders a depth map where depth is determined by the closest Gaussian hit. This approximates the 'hard' surface. """ # Standard differentiable rasterization, but depth is stored as the z-coordinate # of the hit point, weighted by opacity. # To make it 'hard', we might use the depth of the first Gaussian in the sorted list # or a specific weighting. The source does not specify the exact rendering equation # for Dhard vs Dsoft, only that they are two distinct maps. # A common implementation for 'hard' depth in 3DGS is the expected depth # or the depth of the first hit. # For this pseudocode, we assume a standard differentiable renderer that outputs # depth. We distinguish 'hard' by using the depth of the first hit (closest). pass def rendersoftdepth(gaussians, camera): """ Renders a depth map using alpha-weighted average depth. """ pass Parameters: Learning Rates: Separate learning rates for position (\mu) and opacity (\alpha) updates. Typical values are not given in the sources. Loss Function: The source does not specify the exact loss function (e.g., L1, L2, Charbonnier) used for \mathcal{L}{pos} and \mathcal{L}{alpha}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Detail Loss: Applying depth regularization directly to NeRF-style MLPs or un-frozen Gaussian shapes forces the primitive geometry to conform to smooth monocular depth estimates, which conflicts with complex color appearance and causes detail loss. Noise: Gaussian radiance fields are more sensitive to small depth errors than NeRFs, which may result in a noisy distribution of primitives and failures in regions with complex textures. Scale Invariance: Existing scale-invariant depth losses often align depth maps to a fixed scale, which can overlook minor depth variations. This method addresses this by separating position and opacity updates, but the source notes that scale-invariant losses are a general issue in the field. Global-Local Depth Normalization is a depth regularization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents scale-invariant losses from overlooking minor depth variations, thereby improving detailed geometry reshaping in texture-rich regions. It sets itself apart from standard scale-invariant losses by combining global scale preservation with local scale amplification, addressing the issue where existing methods align depth maps to a fixed global scale and ignore small local errors. Depth Reinitialization is a regularization strategy that alleviates 'overlapping' and 'under-reconstruction' artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging dense depth information to reorganize the spatial distribution of Gaussians. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by rejecting standard alpha-blended depth maps in favor of geometric mid-point depths to generate clean, artifact-free point clouds for reinitialization. Position Regularization prevents floating artifacts and dramatic geometry shifts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by constraining Gaussian centers to remain close to their initial mesh positions or a reference surface. It differs from sibling methods like Global-Local Depth Normalization, which focuses on depth consistency, and Depth Reinitialization, which resets positions based on depth errors, by directly penalizing displacement from a known geometric prior (SMPL mesh or initial mesh bounds) rather than enforcing consistency with rendered depth maps [9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md]. Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization is a regularization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enforces spatial coherence in Gaussian positions and opacities during training, specifically addressing artifacts in sparse-view novel view synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by replacing independent per-pixel residual updates with a learned implicit decoder that produces smooth, coherent residual fields for depth and opacity, supplemented by multiview total variation and optical flow constraints. This prevents the "semi-transparent" artifacts and detail loss common when optimizing Gaussians against sparse input views. Geometric Regularization via Bilateral Filter is a regularization loss that enforces coherent motion by grouping Gaussians in image space using a bilateral filter approach, avoiding the dampening of independent motion caused by spatial KNN. It is used in scenes with oscillatory motion to prevent the grouping of spatially close but independently moving objects (e.g., leaves of a tree). Steps: 1. For a training image I at time tI, sample another time t'. 2. Compute the 6D screw-axis representation of the transformation between tI and t' for each Gaussian. 3. Blend these vectors to form an image the same way color is blended. 4. For each pixel p, compute a weighted sum of the squared distances of the splatted screw-axis representations between p and neighboring pixels p'. Formula: The geometric loss is: \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}} = \sum{p' \in \mathcal{N}(p)} k{c,c'} k{d,d'} k{p,p'} \|sp - s{p'}\|^2 where k{c,c'} is color similarity, k{d,d'} is depth similarity, k{p,p'} is spatial distance weight, and sp, s{p'} are screw-axis representations. Pitfall: Unlike standard bilateral filters, the loss is not divided by the sum of the weights because the goal is comparison, not energy conservation. Isotropic Regularization maintains coherent 3D structure and optimizes newly inserted Gaussians using current and random past keyframes to prevent forgetting. It is used in continuous SLAM to prevent Gaussians from becoming highly elongated along the viewing direction, which creates artifacts. Steps: 1. Use keyframes in current window Wk and two random past keyframes Wr per iteration. 2. Compute the isotropic regularization loss based on scaling parameters. Formula: E{iso} = \sum{i=1}^{|\mathcal{G}|} \|\mathbf{s}i - \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i \cdot \mathbf{1}\|1 where \mathbf{s}i are scaling parameters, \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i is their mean, and \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Prevents detail loss and blurred appearance caused by forcing anisotropic Gaussians to fit smooth monocular depth. Balances coarse depth fitting with fine color appearance. Limitations: Gaussian radiance fields are more sensitive to small depth errors than NeRFs, which may result in a noisy distribution of primitives. Existing scale-invariant depth losses may overlook minor depth variations. When to Use: When using monocular depth estimates for regularization in 3D Gaussian Splatting, especially in scenes with complex color appearance where shape deformation would cause detail loss. When Not to Use: When the scene geometry is simple and monocular depth is accurate, or when computational resources are limited and the overhead of rendering two depth maps is prohibitive. Hard and Soft Depth Regularization was proposed in the context of optimizing sparse-view 3D Gaussian Radiance Fields. It addresses the limitations of existing depth regularization strategies for NeRFs, which commonly employ depth to regularize the entire model, creating a potential geometry conflict in the Gaussian fields. The method is based on the observation that the basis of scene geometry lies in the position of the Gaussian primitives rather than their shape. name: Global-Local Depth Normalization
body: Global-Local Depth Normalization is a depth regularization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents scale-invariant losses from overlooking minor depth variations, thereby improving detailed geometry reshaping in texture-rich regions. It sets itself apart from standard scale-invariant losses by combining global scale preservation with local scale amplification, addressing the issue where existing methods align depth maps to a fixed global scale and ignore small local errors. It builds on Hard and Soft Depth Regularization and differs from siblings Depth Reinitialization, Position Regularization, and Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization by explicitly decoupling absolute scale maintenance from local error amplification during gradient computation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered depth map \hat{D}, ground truth depth map D{gt} (if available) or reference depth, and optimization hyperparameters. Outputs: Gradient updates for 3D Gaussian parameters (centers, scales, opacities) guided by a combined global-local depth loss. Data Structures: Depth maps are treated as 2D tensors of floating-point values representing distance from the camera plane. Patches are extracted from these maps for local normalization. Method Steps: 1. Compute Global Normalized Depth Loss: Calculate the depth error using a scale-invariant loss function that aligns the predicted depth \hat{D} with the ground truth D{gt} (or a reference) to preserve absolute scene scale knowledge. Let this be \mathcal{L}{global}. 2. Compute Local Normalized Depth Loss: Extract local depth patches from \hat{D} and D{gt}. Apply local scale normalization to these patches to amplify and refocus the loss on small local depth errors. Let this be \mathcal{L}{local}. 3. Combine Losses: Sum the global and local normalized losses to form the total depth regularization loss \mathcal{L}{depth}: \mathcal{L}{depth} = \mathcal{L}{global} + \mathcal{L}{local} 4. Optimize: Use \mathcal{L}{depth} to guide gradient updates during the optimization of 3D Gaussians, encouraging the learning of small local depth changes in a scale-invariant way. Formulas: While the specific mathematical formulation of the global and local normalization functions is not explicitly detailed in the provided excerpts, the concept relies on: Global Scale: Ensuring the overall magnitude of \hat{D} matches the scene scale. Local Scale: Normalizing depth values within local patches to highlight variations. Parameters: Weighting between \mathcal{L}{global} and \mathcal{L}{local}: Not given in the sources. Patch size for local normalization: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Standard scale-invariant depth losses align all depth maps to a fixed global scale, which ignores minor local depth changes. This leads to noisy primitive distributions and reconstruction failures in regions with intricate textures. Gaussian radiance fields are more sensitive to small depth errors compared to NeRF, exacerbating these issues. A strategy to optimize Gaussian normals by guiding them with pseudo-normals derived from depth gradients, while smoothing them using Total Variation (TV) regularization to address noise and lack of multi-view consistency. Definition: This variant uses the depth gradient to derive pseudo-normals \hat{n}{\hat{D}} which guide the optimization of normals \hat{n} within the 3D Gaussians. It addresses the challenge of generating reasonable normals within the 3DGS-based framework. Steps: 1. Calculate Pseudo-Normals: Compute the depth gradient normal \hat{n}{\hat{D}} from the generated depth map \hat{D}. 2. Compute Normal Penalty Loss: Calculate the penalty loss \mathcal{L}{n-p} between the Gaussian normal \hat{n} and the pseudo-normal \hat{n}{\hat{D}}. 3. Compute TV Regularization: Compute the TV normal regularization term \text{TV}{\text{normal}} to smooth \hat{n}. 4. Optimize: Optimize the 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} (including normals \hat{n}) by minimizing the combined loss \mathcal{L}c + \mathcal{L}n. Formulas: Pseudo-normal calculation: \hat{n}{\hat{D}} = \nabla{uv} \hat{D} where \nabla{uv} is the spatial gradient operator on the depth map. Normal penalty loss: \mathcal{L}{n-p} = \| \hat{n} - \hat{n}{\hat{D}} \| This term aligns the Gaussian normal \hat{n} with the depth gradient normal \hat{n}{\hat{D}}. Total normal loss: \mathcal{L}n = \mathcal{L}{n-p} + \lambda{n-TV} \text{TV}{\text{normal}} This combines the penalty and TV smoothness regularization. Depth Generation Context: The depth map \hat{D} is computed via volumetric accumulation: \hat{D} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \hat{w}i di where di is the distance from the i-th 3D Gaussian to the image plane, and \hat{w}i = \frac{Ti \alphai}{\sum{j=1}^N Tj \alphaj} are weights derived from transmittance Ti and opacity \alphai. To avoid disc aliasing from peak selection, depth is treated as a linear interpolation of distances. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: DNGaussian (using this method) demonstrates competitive quality and superior details compared to state-of-the-art methods in sparse-view settings on LLFF, Blender, and DTU datasets. It achieves a 25× reduction in training time and over 3000× faster rendering speed compared to some baselines. Strengths: Prevents noisy primitive distributions in texture-rich regions; enhances detailed geometry reshaping; maintains absolute scale knowledge. Limitations: Standard scale-invariant losses fail to capture small local errors, leading to reconstruction failures in complex textures. When to Use: When optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for scenes with intricate textures and when standard scale-invariant depth losses result in noisy geometry. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Introduced in DNGaussian (2024) to address the sensitivity of Gaussian radiance fields to small depth errors. History: Developed as an improvement over existing scale-invariant depth losses that overlook small losses. Usage: Used in sparse-view 3D Gaussian radiance field optimization. name: Depth Reinitialization
head: Depth-based densification
body: Depth Reinitialization is a regularization strategy that alleviates 'overlapping' and 'under-reconstruction' artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging dense depth information to reorganize the spatial distribution of Gaussians. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by rejecting standard alpha-blended depth maps in favor of geometric mid-point depths to generate clean, artifact-free point clouds for reinitialization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, camera parameters, and ground truth color images. Output: A reorganized set of Gaussian positions and colors, initialized from a dense point cloud derived from rendered mid-point depth. Data Structures: Gaussian Gi: Defined by center \mathbf{c}i, scale si = (s{x,i}, s{y,i}, s{z,i}), rotation matrix Ri, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Ray r(t): Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, transformed into the local coordinate system of the Gaussian ellipsoid. Formulas: The Gaussian is modeled as an ellipsoid in 3D space: g(x, y, z) = \frac{x^2}{sx} + \frac{y^2}{sy^2} + \frac{z^2}{sz} = 1 where s = (sx, sy, sz) is the scale. The depth of the mid-point for Gaussian Gi, denoted d{mid}^i, is calculated by finding the intersection of the transformed ray with this ellipsoid surface. For multiple Gaussians contributing to a pixel, the method selects the Gaussian with the maximum contribution weight to avoid alpha blending artifacts: i{max} = \arg \maxi wi d{mid} = d{mid}^{i{max}} where wi is the contribution weight of Gaussian i to the pixel. Parameters: Total number of sampled points: Empirically set at around 3.5 million for each scene. Numbered Steps: 1. Render Depth Map: For each pixel, identify the Gaussian G{i{max}} with the maximum contribution wi. Calculate the mid-point depth d{mid} of this Gaussian using the ellipsoid intersection method. Store this as the depth value for the pixel. Pitfall: Do not use standard blending depth d{blend} = \sum{i=1}^N wi \cdot di (where di is center depth), as it produces misleading depth maps with artifacts like depth collapse, object misalignment, and blending boundaries. 2. Reproject to World Space: Convert the 2D depth map values d{mid} back into 3D world coordinates using the camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. This generates a dense set of 3D points. 3. Sample Initial Points: Randomly select a subset of these reprojected points. The total number of sampled points is approximately 3.5 million per scene. 4. Assign Colors: Assign the ground truth color from the corresponding pixel in the input image to each sampled point. 5. Reinitialize: During optimization, repeatedly reinitialize the Gaussian representation (positions and colors) with these sampled points to reorganize the spatial distribution of Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def rotatevector(vec, rotmat): return [sum(rotmat[i][j] vec[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] def generateray(u, v, camKinv, camcenter): dirworld = rotatevector([u, v, 1.0], camKinv) norm = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in dirworld)) dirworld = [c/norm for c in dirworld] return list(camcenter), dirworld def reprojecttoworld(u, v, depth, camKinv, camcenter): dirworld = rotatevector([u, v, 1.0], camKinv) norm = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in dirworld)) dirworld = [c/norm for c in dirworld] depthvec = [depth c for c in dirworld] return [camcenter[i] + depthvec[i] for i in range(3)] def computecontribution(g, u, v): # Simplified weight proxy for the Gaussian's contribution to the pixel return g.alpha def calculatemidpointdepth(rayo, rayd, g): localo = rotatevector([rayo[i] - g.center[i] for i in range(3)], g.rotmat) locald = rotatevector(rayd, g.rotmat) invs = [1.0/g.scale[0], 1.0/(g.scale[1]2), 1.0/g.scale[2]] a = sum(locald[i]2 invs[i] for i in range(3)) b = 2.0 sum(locald[i] localo[i] invs[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(localo[i]2 invs[i] for i in range(3)) - 1.0 disc = b2 - 4ac if disc < 0: return None t1 = (-b - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2a) t2 = (-b + math.sqrt(disc)) / (2a) return (t1 + t2) / 2.0 def depthreinitializationstep(gaussians, cameras, gtimages, numsamples=3500000): worldpoints = [] worldcolors = [] for cam in cameras: for u, v in cam.pixelcoords: rayo, rayd = generateray(u, v, cam.Kinv, cam.center) maxw = -1.0 bestdepth = None for G in gaussians: tmid = calculatemidpointdepth(rayo, rayd, G) if tmid is not None: w = computecontribution(G, u, v) if w > maxw: maxw = w bestdepth = tmid if bestdepth is not None: pworld = reprojecttoworld(u, v, bestdepth, cam.Kinv, cam.center) worldpoints.append(pworld) worldcolors.append(gtimages[cam.id][u, v]) indices = list(range(len(worldpoints))) random.shuffle(indices) selected = indices[:numsamples] sampledpts = [worldpoints[i] for i in selected] sampledcols = [worldcolors[i] for i in selected] for i, G in enumerate(gaussians): G.center = sampledpts[i % len(sampledpts)] G.color = sampledcols[i % len(sampledcols)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blending Depth Artifacts: Using standard blending depth d{blend} = \sum wi di introduces noise from depth artifacts (depth collapse, object misalignment) which degrades reinitialization quality. Center vs. Mid-point: While depth from Gaussian centers yields comparable rendering metrics (SSIM/PSNR) to mid-point, mid-point yields superior dense point cloud reconstruction. Mid-point is preferred for reinitialization. Precision: The discriminant check in ellipsoid intersection is crucial to handle non-intersecting rays. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead during the optimization loop for rendering depth maps and reprojecting points. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the depth map and the sampled point cloud (3.5M points). Measured Performance: Adding Depth Reinitialization to Blur Split increases the number of Gaussians from 3.74M to 4.32M, SSIM from 0.819 to 0.832, and LPIPS from 0.195 to 0.175. Strengths: Alleviates overlapping and under-reconstruction; produces dense and uniform point distributions; improves LPIPS (human perception). Limitations: Increases Gaussian count; relies on accurate depth rendering; sensitive to the choice of depth metric (mid-point vs center vs blend). When to use: When high-quality dense point cloud reconstruction is desired alongside rendering, or when facing severe overlapping/under-reconstruction issues. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and Gaussian count must be kept low, or if depth accuracy is poor. Depth Reinitialization was introduced in the context of "Mini-Splatting," a method to represent scenes with a constrained number of Gaussians. It builds on the observation that utilizing depth to enhance neural rendering is effective, as seen in NeRF-based algorithms. The specific formulation using mid-point depths for 3D Gaussian Splatting was proposed to address the limitations of alpha-blended depth maps in Gaussian-based representations. Mini-Splatting: Representing Scenes with a Constrained Number of Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72980-510, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Isotropic Regularization
head: Mapping with Isotropic Regularization
body: Isotropic Regularization is a geometric constraint used in continuous SLAM-based Gaussian Splatting to prevent the formation of highly elongated Gaussian primitives along the viewing ray direction. While standard differentiable rendering imposes no constraint on Gaussian scaling along the viewing ray, this lack of constraint causes artifacts and tracking instability in continuous SLAM scenarios where viewpoints are not carefully selected. It sets itself apart from its parent Hard and Soft Depth Regularization by explicitly penalizing anisotropy (stretching) rather than just enforcing depth consistency, and from Global-Local Depth Normalization by operating on the scale parameters directly rather than depth values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, where each Gaussian i has scaling parameters \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A scalar regularization loss E{iso} added to the total optimization objective. Data Structures: \mathcal{G}: Set of active Gaussians. \mathbf{s}i: Scaling vector for Gaussian i. \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i: Mean scale of Gaussian i across its three dimensions. \mathbf{1}: Vector of ones with length 3. Steps: 1. For each Gaussian i in the set \mathcal{G}: a. Calculate the mean scale \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i = \frac{1}{3} \sum{j=1}^{3} \mathbf{s}i[j]. b. Compute the L1 norm of the difference between the scale vector \mathbf{s}i and the mean scale vector \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i \cdot \mathbf{1}. 2. Sum these differences over all Gaussians to obtain E{iso}. Formula: E{iso} = \sum{i=1}^{|\mathcal{G}|} \|\mathbf{s}i - \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i \cdot \mathbf{1}\|1 Where: |\mathcal{G}| is the number of Gaussians. \|\cdot\|1 is the L1 norm. \mathbf{s}i is the scaling parameter vector for Gaussian i. \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i is the mean of the components of \mathbf{s}i. \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. Parameters: No explicit hyperparameters are defined for the basic isotropic regularization term itself. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The L1 norm is used to penalize elongation, encouraging sphericality (isotropy). Context: This regularization is applied during the "Mapping" phase of the SLAM pipeline, which uses keyframes in the current window Wk and two random past keyframes Wr to avoid forgetting the global map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeisotropicregularization(gaussians): """ Computes the isotropic regularization loss for a set of Gaussians. Args: gaussians: A list or array of Gaussian objects, each having a 'scales' attribute. 'scales' is a vector of 3 floats [sx, sy, sz]. Returns: A scalar float representing the total isotropic regularization loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 for gaussian in gaussians: # Get the scaling vector si si = gaussian.scales # Calculate the mean scale stildei meanscale = sum(si) / 3.0 # Create a vector of ones scaled by the mean # In numpy: meanscale np.ones(3) meanvector = [meanscale, meanscale, meanscale] # Compute the L1 norm of the difference: ||si - meanvector||1 # In numpy: np.sum(np.abs(si - meanvector)) diff = [si[j] - meanvector[j] for j in range(3)] l1norm = sum(abs(d) for d in diff) totalloss += l1norm return totalloss A variant applied specifically to key Gaussian primitives initialized from 2D keypoints. It prevents center drift by freezing the positions of these key primitives during optimization and enforces isotropy via a soft scale regularization. The loss is defined as L{reg} = \sum{s,m \in Pk} |s - \delta \cdot (1 - m)|, where Pk is the set of key primitives, s is the 3D scale vector, m is the 2D keypoint score from SuperPoint, and \delta is a scale threshold. This serves to control the 3D scale based on 2D confidence and enforce uniform scale across axes. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians |\mathcal{G}|, as it requires a single pass to compute mean scales and L1 norms. Memory Complexity: Minimal, requiring only temporary storage for mean scales and differences. Strengths: Prevents artifacts caused by highly elongated Gaussians along the viewing direction, which is critical for continuous SLAM stability. Encourages sphericality, leading to more coherent 3D structure. Limitations: Does not directly constrain depth or position, only shape (scale anisotropy). May need to be combined with other constraints (like depth or position regularization) for full geometric stability. When to use: In continuous SLAM pipelines where viewpoint diversity is limited and tracking stability is paramount. When not to use: In novel view synthesis with carefully selected, diverse viewpoints where anisotropic Gaussians might naturally form to represent thin structures, and where other constraints are sufficient. Isotropic Regularization was introduced in the context of Gaussian Splatting SLAM to address the instability of 3D Gaussian Splatting in continuous mapping scenarios. The method was proposed by the authors of "Gaussian Splatting SLAM" (2023). It is part of the "Mapping" stage of the SLAM pipeline, which optimizes the global map using current and past keyframes. Gaussian Splatting SLAM, https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06741, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) SplatLoc: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based Visual Localization for Augmented Reality., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3549563, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Position Regularization
head: Position Constraint Loss, Surface Regularization Loss
body: Position Regularization prevents floating artifacts and dramatic geometry shifts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by constraining Gaussian centers to remain close to their initial mesh positions or a reference surface. It differs from sibling methods like Global-Local Depth Normalization, which focuses on depth consistency, and Depth Reinitialization, which resets positions based on depth errors, by directly penalizing displacement from a known geometric prior (SMPL mesh or initial mesh bounds) rather than enforcing consistency with rendered depth maps [9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current Gaussian positions (\mu or pi), initial Gaussian positions (\mu{init} or stored initial positions), reference mesh vertices (vi), and hyperparameters (\tau{pos}, \lambda{sr}). Outputs: A scalar loss value used for gradient-based optimization. Data Structures: Gaussian positions: Vector of 3D coordinates. Mesh vertices: Array of 3D coordinates from the reference mesh (e.g., SMPL). Initial positions: Stored copy of Gaussian positions at initialization. Formulas: Two primary formulations exist in the literature: 1. Mesh-Proximity Loss (Human Gaussian Splatting): L{mesh} = \sumi \text{ReLU}(\|vi - pi\|2^2 - \tau{pos}) Where: pi: Canonical position of the i-th Gaussian. vi: Nearest vertex on the SMPL mesh to pi. \tau{pos}: Threshold representing the maximum expected distance between skin and clothes. \text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x). 2. Surface Regularization Loss (Phys3DGS): L{sr} = \|\mu - \mu{init}\|2^2 Where: \mu: Current position of a Gaussian bound to the extracted mesh. \mu{init}: Initial position of that Gaussian, stored separately at the start of training. Parameters: \tau{pos}: Threshold for max distance between skin and clothes. Value not explicitly given in sources. \lambda{sr}: Weight for the surface regularization loss in the total loss function. Value not explicitly given in sources. Steps: 1. Identify the reference geometry: either the SMPL mesh vertices or the initial Gaussian positions. 2. For each Gaussian, find the nearest reference point (vi or \mu{init}). 3. Compute the squared Euclidean distance between the current Gaussian position and the reference point. 4. Apply the specific loss function: If using Mesh-Proximity: Apply ReLU to the difference between squared distance and \tau{pos}. Sum over all Gaussians. If using Surface Regularization: Compute the squared L2 norm of the difference between current and initial positions. 5. Multiply by the respective weight (\lambda{sr} if applicable) and add to the total loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nearest Vertex Search: Finding vi requires efficient nearest-neighbor search. In, this is done per Gaussian. Gradient Flow: In, the gradient of the distance \|vi - pi\|2 is not backpropagated through the loss to avoid instability in skinning weight supervision, though it is used in the ReLU threshold calculation. Storage: requires storing \mu{init} separately for every Gaussian, increasing memory usage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def positionregularizationloss(gaussians, meshvertices=None, initialpositions=None, taupos=0.0, lambdasr=1.0): """ Computes position regularization loss. Args: gaussians: Object with attribute 'positions' (N, 3) meshvertices: Optional, (M, 3) array of SMPL mesh vertices initialpositions: Optional, (N, 3) array of initial Gaussian positions taupos: Threshold for mesh proximity loss lambdasr: Weight for surface regularization loss Returns: Scalar loss value """ loss = 0.0 if meshvertices is not None: # Mesh-Proximity Loss (Human Gaussian Splatting) # Find nearest vertex for each Gaussian # Note: Efficient nearest neighbor search required nearestvertices = findnearestvertices(gaussians.positions, meshvertices) # Compute squared distances distsq = np.sum((gaussians.positions - nearestvertices) 2, axis=1) # Apply ReLU threshold # ReLU(distsq - taupos) meshloss = np.sum(np.maximum(0, distsq - taupos)) loss += meshloss elif initialpositions is not None: # Surface Regularization Loss (Phys3DGS) # Compute L2 norm squared between current and initial positions diff = gaussians.positions - initialpositions srloss = np.sum(diff 2) loss += lambdasr srloss else: raise ValueError("Either meshvertices or initialpositions must be provided") return loss This variant specifically encourages Gaussian positions to stay close to the SMPL mesh to avoid floating artifacts in animatable avatars. It is chosen when rendering clothed bodies where the distance between skin and clothes is bounded by \tau{pos}. It differs from general surface regularization by using a mesh-proximity threshold rather than a fixed initial position constraint. Time Complexity: Depends on the nearest-neighbor search for mesh vertices. If brute-force, O(N \cdot M) where N is Gaussians and M is mesh vertices. With spatial indexing (e.g., KD-tree), it approaches O(N \log M). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing initial positions if using Phys3DGS variant. No extra memory for SMPL variant if mesh is loaded separately. Strengths: Prevents floating artifacts and dramatic position shifts during training. Effective for inverse rendering and animatable avatars. Limitations: Requires a reference mesh or initial positions. May restrict the model's ability to learn complex geometry if the prior is inaccurate. When to use: When training on animatable avatars with SMPL priors or when inverse rendering requires stable geometry near the initial mesh. When not to use: When no mesh prior is available and initial positions are not reliable. Originated in Human Gaussian Splatting (2024) for real-time rendering of animatable avatars, where it prevents floating artifacts by constraining Gaussians to the SMPL mesh. Also used in Phys3DGS (2024) for physically-based inverse rendering to prevent dramatic position shifts of vertices caused by large gradients in HDR space. Human Gaussian Splatting: Real-Time Rendering of Animatable Avatars, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00081, fetched 2026-10-26 Phys3DGS: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2409.10335, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization
body: Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization is a regularization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enforces spatial coherence in Gaussian positions and opacities during training, specifically addressing artifacts in sparse-view novel view synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by replacing independent per-pixel residual updates with a learned implicit decoder that produces smooth, coherent residual fields for depth and opacity, supplemented by multiview total variation and optical flow constraints. This prevents the "semi-transparent" artifacts and detail loss common when optimizing Gaussians against sparse input views. The method optimizes the Gaussian parameters (\Sigma, \mathbf{c}) indirectly by optimizing the parameters of an implicit convolutional decoder (\phi) that generates residual corrections for initial depth and opacity estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Set of input views V. Initial depth maps D^{\text{init}}n for each view n, obtained via monocular depth estimation (Yang et al. [60]). Initial Gaussian parameters \Sigma, \mathbf{c}. Camera poses for each view. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters \Sigma^, \mathbf{c}^. Optimized decoder parameters \phi^. Data Structures: Implicit Decoder f\phi: A convolutional neural network taking the normalized view index n as input. Segmentation Mask S: A binary mask of shape (C, H, W), where C=5 is the number of regions. Optical Flow Correspondences: Pairs of pixels (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) between views i and j computed via optical flow (Shi et al. [45]). Forward-Backward Consistency Mask M{i \rightarrow j}: A binary mask indicating reliable pixel correspondences between views i and j. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute initial depth maps D^{\text{init}}n for all input views using a monocular depth estimator. Initialize Gaussian parameters \Sigma, \mathbf{c} using standard 3DGS initialization. Initialize decoder parameters \phi randomly. Initialize segmentation masks Sn for each view by dividing the image into C=5 regions based on D^{\text{init}}n. 2. Residual Depth Estimation (Single-View Constraint): For each view n, pass the normalized view index n to the decoder f\phi(n). The decoder outputs a C-channel residual depth tensor. Compute the final residual depth \Delta Dn by applying channelwise summation (chsum) of the element-wise product of the segmentation mask Sn and the decoder output: \Delta Dn = \text{chsum}(Sn \odot f\phi(n)) This ensures smooth deformation within regions while allowing discontinuities between regions. 3. Residual Opacity Estimation: Similarly, estimate residual opacity using a decoder (or shared architecture) producing C-channel residual opacity. Combine with initial opacity to obtain final opacity at each pixel. 4. Gaussian Position Update: For each pixel \mathbf{p} in view n, compute the updated 3D position \mathbf{x} by projecting the residual depth into 3D space: \mathbf{x} = g(D^{\text{init}}n [\mathbf{p}] + \Delta Dn [\mathbf{p}], \mathbf{p}) Here, g(d, \mathbf{p}) is the function that projects pixel \mathbf{p} into 3D space according to depth d. The Gaussian centers are updated to these positions \mathbf{x}. 5. Multiview Total Variation Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{multi}}): Render the depth map R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, d} for each view using the current Gaussian parameters and updated positions. Compute the rendered disparity as 1 / (1 + R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, d}). Compute the global TV loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} = \left\| \nabla \left( \frac{1}{1 + R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, d}} \right) \right\|1 Compute the masked TV loss using the segmentation mask S: \mathcal{L}{\text{MTV}} = \left\| \nabla \left( S \odot \left( \frac{1}{1 + R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, d}} \right) \right) \right\|1 Combine them with a schedule parameter \lambdas: \mathcal{L}{\text{multi}} = (1 - \lambdas)\mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} + \lambdas\mathcal{L}{\text{MTV}} \lambdas is initialized to 0 and gradually increased to 1 by the end of optimization. 6. Flow Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{flow}}): For each pair of views (i, j) with corresponding pixels (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) identified by optical flow: Compute the 3D positions for both pixels using their respective residual depths: Di [\mathbf{p}] = D^{\text{init}}i [\mathbf{p}] + \Delta Di [\mathbf{p}] Dj [\mathbf{q}] = D^{\text{init}}j [\mathbf{q}] + \Delta Dj [\mathbf{q}] \mathbf{x}i = g(Di [\mathbf{p}], \mathbf{p}), \quad \mathbf{x}j = g(Dj [\mathbf{q}], \mathbf{q}) Compute the flow loss using the consistency mask M{i \rightarrow j}: \mathcal{L}{\text{flow}} = \sum{(i, j)} \sum{\mathbf{p}} \left\| M{i \rightarrow j} \odot \left( \mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}j \right) \right\|1 p and q are corresponding pixels calculated using an existing optical flow method. 7. Multisampling: During rendering for color loss calculation, evaluate multiple samples within each pixel and average them to obtain the pixel color. This ensures Gaussians properly cover the pixel area, preventing semi-transparency in novel views. 8. Optimization Step: Minimize the total objective function with respect to \Sigma, \phi, \mathbf{c}: \Sigma^, \phi^, \mathbf{c}^ = \arg \min{\Sigma, \phi, \mathbf{c}} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}} \mathcal{L}(R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}), R(\mathbf{p})) + \betam \mathcal{L}{\text{multi}} + \betaf \mathcal{L}{\text{flow}} Typical weights: \betam = 5, \betaf = 0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def coherent3dgsoptimization(inputviews, initialdepths, initialgaussians, decoder, numregions=5, numepochs=1000): """ Optimizes 3D Gaussians using coherent regularization. """ phi = decoder.parameters() Sigma = initialgaussians.Sigma c = initialgaussians.c alpha = initialgaussians.alpha H, W = initialdepths[inputviews[0]].shape cameraposes = {v: getcamerapose(v) for v in inputviews} # referencecolors = {v: getreferenceimage(v) for v in inputviews} # optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(phi) + [Sigma, c], lr=1e-3) # segmentationmasks = {} for viewidx in inputviews: segmentationmasks[viewidx] = computesegmentationmask(initialdepths[viewidx], numregions) # flowcorrespondences = {} consistencymasks = {} for i, viewi in enumerate(inputviews): for j, viewj in enumerate(inputviews): if i >= j: continue flowcorrespondences[(viewi, viewj)] = computeopticalflow(viewi, viewj) # consistencymasks[(viewi, viewj)] = computeconsistencymask(flowcorrespondences[(viewi, viewj)]) # lambdas = 0.0 for epoch in range(numepochs): lambdas = min(1.0, epoch / numepochs) residualdepthsmap = {} for viewidx in inputviews: normalizedviewidx = viewidx / len(inputviews) residualdepthtensor = decoder(normalizedviewidx) S = segmentationmasks[viewidx] residualdepth = np.sum(S residualdepthtensor, axis=0) residualdepthsmap[viewidx] = residualdepth Dinit = initialdepths[viewidx] updateddepth = Dinit + residualdepth positions = [projectpixelto3d(p, updateddepth[p], cameraposes[viewidx]) for p in range(H W)] Rd = renderdepth(Sigma, alpha, positions, cameraposes[viewidx]) Rc = rendercolor(Sigma, alpha, positions, c, cameraposes[viewidx], multisample=True) disparity = 1.0 / (1.0 + Rd) graddisparity = np.gradient(disparity) LTV = np.sum(np.abs(graddisparity)) maskeddisparity = S disparity gradmaskeddisparity = np.gradient(maskeddisparity) LMTV = np.sum(np.abs(gradmaskeddisparity)) Lmulti = (1 - lambdas) LTV + lambdas LMTV Lflow = 0.0 for (viewi, viewj), flow in flowcorrespondences.items(): if viewi == viewidx or viewj == viewidx: for p, q in enumerate(flow): Di = initialdepths[viewi][p] + residualdepthsmap[viewi][p] Dj = initialdepths[viewj][q] + residualdepthsmap[viewj][q] xi = projectpixelto3d(p, Di, cameraposes[viewi]) xj = projectpixelto3d(q, Dj, cameraposes[viewj]) M = consistencymasks[(viewi, viewj)][p] Lflow += M np.linalg.norm(xi - xj, ord=1) Lcolor = np.mean(np.abs(Rc - referencecolors[viewidx])) totalloss = Lcolor + 5.0 Lmulti + 0.1 Lflow totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return Sigma, c, phi def computesegmentationmask(Dinit, numregions): # Divide image into C regions based on Dinit [G: Wang et al. strategy] pass # Not given in the sources. def computeopticalflow(viewi, viewj): # Compute optical flow between viewi and viewj [G: Shi et al.] pass # Not given in the sources. def computeconsistencymask(flow): # Compute forward-backward consistency mask pass # Not given in the sources. def projectpixelto3d(p, depth, camerapose): # Standard pinhole projection inverse pass # Not given in the sources. def renderdepth(Sigma, alpha, positions, camerapose): # Standard 3DGS depth rendering pass # Not given in the sources. def rendercolor(Sigma, alpha, positions, c, camerapose, multisample): # Standard 3DGS color rendering with multisampling pass # Not given in the sources. Parameters: C=5: Number of segmentation regions. \betam = 5: Weight for multiview TV loss. \betaf = 0.1: Weight for flow loss. \lambdas: Schedule parameter for TV loss, starting at 0 and ending at 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: Standard center-sampling leads to semi-transparency. Sharp Discontinuities: Smooth decoder alone fails. Optical Flow Errors: Unreliable correspondences must be masked out using forward-backward consistency. Time Complexity: Higher than standard 3DGS due to the additional decoder forward pass, segmentation mask computation, and flow loss calculation. The decoder parameters \phi are optimized alongside Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires storing segmentation masks and optical flow correspondences. Performance: Improves novel view synthesis quality in sparse-view settings by reducing artifacts and improving geometry coherence. Strengths: Handles sparse inputs better than standard 3DGS; enforces smooth geometry; prevents semi-transparency. Limitations: Requires monocular depth estimation for initialization; relies on optical flow which can be noisy; computationally more expensive. When to use: Sparse-view novel view synthesis where standard 3DGS produces blurry or transparent artifacts. When not to use: Dense-view settings where standard 3DGS performs well; real-time applications where the additional computational cost is prohibitive. Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization was introduced in "CoherentGS: Sparse Novel View Synthesis with Coherent 3D Gaussians" by A. Paliwal et al.. It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework and addresses its limitations in sparse-view scenarios. name: FreGS
head: Frequency-aware regularization for 3DGS, Progressive frequency regularization
body: FreGS is a training optimization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents overfitting and high-frequency artifacts by applying progressive frequency regularization to the primitives. It addresses the problem of over-reconstruction, where the model captures noise or fine details that do not generalize, by constraining the spectral content of the rendered images to match the ground truth in the frequency domain. Unlike sibling methods that focus on geometric shape constraints or depth supervision, FreGS operates exclusively on the frequency discrepancy between rendered and target images. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, color), camera parameters, ground truth images, and a frequency regularization weight \lambda. Output: Updated Gaussian parameters after one training step. Data Structures: Gaussian Cloud: Standard 3DGS structure. Frequency Domain Representation: 2D Fourier Transform of the rendered and ground truth images. Method Steps: 1. Render: Render the current Gaussian cloud to obtain image I{render}. 2. Transform: Compute the 2D Fourier Transform of I{render} to get F{render} and of the ground truth I{gt} to get F{gt}. 3. Compute Discrepancy: Calculate the frequency discrepancy \mathcal{L}{freq} between F{render} and F{gt}. 4. Regularize: Add \lambda \mathcal{L}{freq} to the total loss. 5. Backpropagate: Compute gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters and update them. Formulas: The total loss is: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{photometric} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{freq} where \mathcal{L}{freq} measures the difference in the frequency domain. The specific formulation of \mathcal{L}{freq} is not detailed in the provided sources, but it is described as regularizing frequency discrepancies. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for frequency regularization. Typical value not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-smoothing: Excessive regularization may remove valid high-frequency details. Precision: Fourier transforms require careful handling of numerical precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fregsstep(gaussians, camera, gtimage, lambdafreq): # Render current state renderedimage = render(gaussians, camera) # Compute Fourier transforms Frendered = fft2(renderedimage) Fgt = fft2(gtimage) # Compute frequency loss # Specific formula for Lfreq not provided in sources Lfreq = computefrequencydiscrepancy(Frendered, Fgt) # Total loss Ltotal = Lphotometric(renderedimage, gtimage) + lambdafreq Lfreq # Backpropagate and update gradients = computegradients(Ltotal, gaussians) update(gaussians, gradients) General approach to frequency domain constraints. Frequency Regularization Blurs target supervision for gradient stability. Smoothed 2D Supervision Enforces surface-like properties via covariance. 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting Covariance Transformation and Regularization Uses depth estimates for geometric constraints. Hard and Soft Depth Regularization Adapts geometry across scales. Cross-scale geometric adaptation General geometric constraints. Geometry Regularization Time Complexity: Additional cost of Fourier transforms per step. Not given in sources. Memory Complexity: Storage for frequency domain representations. Not given in sources. Performance: Prevents overfitting and high-frequency artifacts. Improves visual quality by addressing over-reconstruction. Strengths: Effective at reducing noise and artifacts. Limitations: May remove valid details if \lambda is too high. Specific performance metrics not given in sources. When to use: When over-reconstruction or high-frequency artifacts are observed. When not to use: When fine detail recovery is critical and not smoothed out. FreGS was introduced to address over-reconstruction in 3D Gaussian Splatting by regularizing frequency discrepancies. It applies progressive frequency regularization to primitives to prevent overfitting and high-frequency artifacts during training. The method is cited in surveys on 3DGS rasterization and compression. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Cross-scale geometric adaptation
head: Lgeo, Reprojection error supervision, Reprojection-based cross-scale geometric adaptation
body: Cross-scale geometric adaptation is a self-adaptive regularization method that uses reprojection errors across multiple voxel scales to guide geometry learning without requiring explicit depth ground truth. It selects render depths with minimal reprojection error across different scales as pseudo labels, ensuring geometric integrity and reducing floaters more robustly than single-scale depth priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training views i and j (where j is a neighboring or novel view), camera intrinsics Ki, Kj, camera poses (Ri, ti), (Rj, tj), RGB maps Ci, Cj, and a multi-scale voxel representation with render depths D{il}(pi) at scale l for pixel pi. Outputs: Geometric adaptation loss \mathcal{L}{geo} and the selected pseudo-ground truth depth D'(r{train}) for each training ray r{train}. Data Structures: Multi-scale Voxels: A hierarchy of voxel grids at low, medium, and high resolutions. The method assumes a shared or weight-sharing voxel structure across scales to capture varying scene frequencies. Ray Data: For each training ray r{train}, the system stores the 2D pixel coordinate pi in frame i. Numbered Steps: 1. Reprojection to 3D (Frame i): For a pixel pi in frame i, compute its homogeneous coordinate \tilde{p}i. Calculate the 3D point in the camera coordinate system of frame i (x{li}) using the depth D{il}(pi) at scale l and camera intrinsics Ki: x{li} = D{il}(pi) Ki^{-1} \tilde{p}i Alternatively, the 3D point can be determined directly from the ray origin oi(pi) and direction vi(pi): xl = oi(pi) + D{il}(pi) vi(pi) 2. Transform to World Coordinates: Transform x{li} to world coordinates xl using frame i's rotation Ri and translation ti: xl = Ri x{li} + ti 3. Reproject to Frame j: Transform the world coordinate point xl to the camera coordinate system of frame j using frame j's rotation Rj and translation tj: x{li \to j} = Rj^T (xl - tj) 4. Project to 2D (Frame j): Project x{li \to j} back to the 2D pixel coordinate system of frame j using intrinsics Kj and the projection function \pi([x, y, z]^T) = [x/z, y/z]^T: \tilde{p}{li \to j} = \pi(Kj x{li \to j}) 5. Compute Reprojection Error: Calculate the error el(pi) for scale l as the difference between the original RGB pixel Ci(pi) and the warped RGB pixel Cj(\tilde{p}{li \to j}) from frame j: el(pi) = Ci(pi) - Cj(\tilde{p}{li \to j}) 6. Select Pseudo-Ground Truth: Identify the scale l that minimizes the reprojection error for the given ray. This scale's depth is selected as the pseudo-ground truth depth D'(r{train}): D'(r{train}) = \arg \minl (el(r{train})) 7. Compute Loss: Calculate the geometric adaptation loss \mathcal{L}{geo} as the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered depth Dl(r{train}) and the selected pseudo-ground truth depth D'(r{train}) across all training rays R{train}: \mathcal{L}{geo}(r{train}) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \| \hat{D}l(r{train}) - D'(r{train}) \|^2 (Note: The source formula sums over scales l and rays r{train}. The exact aggregation over rays is implied by the summation notation.) Parameters: Scales: Typically includes Low, Medium, and High resolution voxels. Weighting Factor \lambda: Part of the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{photometric} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{geo} (implied by parent structure). Value not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: The method relies on accurate camera poses. In scenarios with significant viewpoint changes or sparse training views (e.g., 360° datasets), generalization may be challenging. Local Minima: Omitting novel view rays risks local minima, causing incorrect geometry. Scale Mismatch: Using a single scale depth prior (\mathcal{L}d) alone can suffer from higher error later in training due to scale mismatches, whereas \mathcal{L}{geo} refines depth progressively. Returns: loss: Scalar geometric adaptation loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 for ray in rays: pi = ray.pixelcoordinate framei = ray.sourceframe framej = ray.targetframe # Neighbor or novel view Ki = intrinsics[framei.id] Kj = intrinsics[framej.id] Ri, ti = poses[framei.id] Rj, tj = poses[framej.id] Ci = framei.rgbmap Cj = framej.rgbmap minerror = infinity bestscaledepth = None bestscaleidx = -1 # Iterate over all voxel scales for l, voxelgrid in enumerate(voxelgrids): # 1. Transform to World Coordinates # xl = Ri xli + ti xl = Ri @ xli + ti # 4. Transform to Camera Coordinates of frame j # xlij = Rj^T (xl - tj) xlij = Rj.T @ (xl - tj) # 5. Project to 2D in frame j # pi([x,y,z]) = [x/z, y/z] if xlij[2] == 0: continue # Avoid division by zero pj = [xlij[0] / xlij[2], xlij[1] / xlij[2]] # 6. Compute Reprojection Error # el(pi) = Ci(pi) - Cj(pj) # Assuming Cj is sampled at pj (with interpolation if needed) Cjval = samplergb(Cj, pj) error = np.linalg.norm(Ci[pi] - Cjval) if error < minerror: minerror = error bestscaledepth = Dil bestscaleidx = l # 7. Compute Loss against best scale depth # Lgeo = sum || Dl - D' ||^2 # Here D' is bestscaledepth. # The source sums over scales l, comparing rendered depth Dl to D'. # We assume Dl is the depth rendered at scale l for this ray. for l, voxelgrid in enumerate(voxelgrids): Dl = voxelgrid.renderdepth(pi, framei.cameraorigin, framei.cameradirection) diff = Dl - bestscaledepth totalloss += diff 2 return totalloss Time Complexity: Increases with the number of scales and the cost of reprojection for each scale per ray. Requires rendering depth at multiple scales and performing coordinate transformations for each. Memory Complexity: Requires storing multi-scale voxel grids and RGB maps for training views. Performance: Significantly reduces floaters and improves convergence quality across scales compared to training without geometric adaptation. Achieves lower final depth error than single-scale depth priors (\mathcal{L}d). Strengths: Self-adaptive; does not require complex scheduling or external depth priors. Robust to geometric noise compared to feature-warping methods like GeCoNeRF. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera poses. Performance may degrade in few-shot scenarios with sparse views or large viewpoint changes. Origin: Proposed in FrugalNeRF. History: Developed to accelerate and regularize training in extreme few-shot novel view synthesis without learned priors. It addresses the issue of floaters and sub-optimal convergence in multi-scale voxel-based NeRFs. Usage: Used in FrugalNeRF for few-shot NeRF training, often combined with novel view regularization and weight-sharing voxels.
