name: Geometry Regularization
head: Gaussian Flattening, Normal Consistency and Flattening
body: Geometry regularization improves the structural integrity and smoothness of reconstructed surfaces in 3D Gaussian Splatting by constraining the geometric shape of the Gaussians, distinct from depth supervision which primarily constrains positional accuracy. It addresses the issue of "floaters" and noisy geometry by enforcing two specific constraints: aligning the orientation of rendered depth normals with per-Gaussian normals, and flattening each Gaussian along its smallest axis to better approximate surface surfels. This method is particularly useful for reducing artifacts in complex geometries where standard photometric loss alone leads to ambiguous depth estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Per-Gaussian parameters (position \mu, scale s \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation q, opacity \alpha); rendered depth map D; rendered normal map N{rendered}; per-Gaussian normal estimates N{gauss}. Outputs: Gradient updates for Gaussian parameters to minimize geometric inconsistency. Data Structures: OptimizationParams: A configuration struct containing the boolean flag usenormalloss. Scaling Factor: Vector s \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the anisotropic scale of each Gaussian. Steps: 1. Enable Regularization: Set usenormalloss = true in the optimization configuration. 2. Compute Rendered Normals: Differentiably render the scene to obtain a normal map N{rendered} from the depth buffer. This involves computing surface normals from the depth map D using finite differences or analytical derivatives of the projection. 3. Normal Consistency Loss: Calculate the alignment between the rendered normal N{rendered} at each pixel and the corresponding per-Gaussian normal N{gauss} derived from the Gaussian's rotation matrix. The loss penalizes misalignment, effectively pinning the surface orientation. 4. Flattening Loss: For each Gaussian, identify the smallest component of the scaling vector s. Minimize this component towards zero during optimization. This forces the Gaussian to become a flat disk (surflet) aligned with the surface, reducing volume artifacts. Formulas: Let si \in \mathbb{R}^3 be the scaling vector for Gaussian i. The flattening loss \mathcal{L}{flat} for a single Gaussian is: \mathcal{L}{flat} = \min(s{i,1}, s{i,2}, s{i,3}) The total regularization loss combines normal consistency and flattening: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} + \lambda{flat} \mathcal{L}{flat} where \mathcal{L}{norm} measures the dot product or angular difference between N{rendered} and N{gauss}, and \lambda are weighting factors. Parameters: usenormalloss: Boolean flag to enable the feature. \lambda{norm}, \lambda{flat}: Weights for normal consistency and flattening terms. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Refitting: Depth maps must be refitted against a prior point cloud to the correct scale before use. Depth maps that fail this refitting process are discarded and not used for supervision. Precision: The minimization of the smallest scale component requires careful handling to prevent numerical instability when scales approach zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryregularizationloss(gaussians, rendereddepth, renderednormals, params): """ Computes geometry regularization loss for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: scale: s (R3 vector) rotation: q (quaternion) position: mu (R3 vector) rendereddepth: Depth map D (H x W) renderednormals: Normal map Nrendered (H x W x 3) params: OptimizationParams with usenormalloss (bool) Returns: loss: Scalar tensor representing the regularization loss """ if not params.usenormalloss: return 0.0 loss = 0.0 # Step 1: Flattening Loss # Minimize the smallest component of the scaling factor towards zero for g in gaussians: s = g.scale # s is R3 minscale = min(s[0], s[1], s[2]) loss += minscale # Step 2: Normal Consistency Loss # Align rendered normals with per-Gaussian normals # Note: Exact mapping of pixels to Gaussians and normal derivation # from rotation matrix is assumed to be handled by the differentiable renderer. # Here we assume renderednormals and gaussiansnormals are aligned. # Calculate per-Gaussian normals from rotation # Ngauss = R(q) [0, 0, 1] (assuming local Z is normal) # This step requires differentiable access to the Gaussian parameters # and the rendering pipeline to compute gradients w.r.t mu, s, q, alpha. # Compute loss between rendered normal and Gaussian normal # Lnorm = 1 - dot(Nrendered, Ngauss) # Sum over all visible pixels/Gaussians # Placeholder for specific normal alignment implementation details # as the exact derivation of Ngauss from q and the pixel-to-Gaussian # correspondence is renderer-specific. # loss += lambdanorm normalconsistencyterm return loss A specific variant of geometry regularization that focuses exclusively on flattening Gaussian kernels into 3D surfels aligned with the surface. It minimizes the smallest component of the scaling factor s \in \mathbb{R}^3 towards zero. This aids in determining Gaussian normals by selecting the shortest scaled edge, effectively defining the surface orientation based on the thinnest dimension of the Gaussian. It is chosen when the primary goal is to enforce planar surface approximations without necessarily enforcing strict normal consistency with rendered depth maps. Time Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of Gaussians for computing scale minima and normal alignment. The depth refitting step adds preprocessing cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for rendered depth and normal maps, and potentially intermediate buffers for normal consistency calculations. Strengths: Significantly reduces "floaters" and improves surface smoothness and geometric coherence. Limitations: May reduce the number of remaining points if combined with pruning, potentially compromising detail if not balanced with entropy loss. Requires accurate depth refitting; failed refits are discarded, which may reduce supervision signal in sparse regions. When to use: When high-quality surface geometry is required, and floaters are a persistent issue. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited, or when the scene contains significant non-planar, volumetric details that should not be flattened. Originating from improvements to 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations, this technique was popularized in community-driven optimizations such as those in GaussianSplatting.jl and frameworks like GauStudio. It addresses the limitation of standard photometric loss, which often results in ambiguous geometry, by introducing explicit geometric constraints. The concept of flattening Gaussians into surfels is inspired by earlier work on surface reconstruction using Gaussian kernels. name: Base 3DGS Optimization
head: Base 3DGS Optimization with Normal Attribute
body:
Base 3DGS Optimization initializes the geometric attributes of 3D Gaussian primitives to provide a robust geometric baseline for subsequent shading attribute optimization, such as in iVR-GS Training. It differs from standard 3DGS by incorporating an explicit normal attribute n for each Gaussian and optimizing it via a normal consistency loss, despite the normal not affecting the final rendered color or alpha in the base stage. This initialization accelerates the convergence of editable Gaussian optimization by ensuring accurate surface geometry representation before decomposing color and lighting. The method takes multi-view input images, camera poses, and initial Gaussian parameters as inputs, and outputs optimized Gaussian primitives with geometry and auxiliary normal attributes. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is parameterized by the tuple \{\mui, qi, si, oi, ni, ci\}: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. ni \in \mathbb{R}^3: Normal attribute (unit vector). ci: View-dependent color, represented by Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians with standard 3DGS parameters \{\mui, qi, si, oi, ci\} and assign initial normal attributes ni. 2. Rendering: For a given viewpoint, render the depth map D and normal map N using the current Gaussian parameters. The rendering follows the alpha compositing equation: \{D, N\} = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} Ti \alphai \{di, ni\} where \mathcal{N} is the set of Gaussians sorted by depth, Ti = \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance, \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian, di is the depth of the i-th Gaussian, and ni is the normal attribute of the i-th Gaussian rotated to camera space. 3. Pseudo-Normal Computation: Compute a pseudo-normal map 	ilde{N} from the rendered depth map D under the local planarity assumption. This involves estimating the surface normal from the depth gradient at each pixel. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss as a combination of L1 and SSIM losses for the base 3DGS output color and alpha channels, along with the normal consistency loss. The normal consistency loss is defined as \mathcal{L}n = ||N - 	ilde{N}||2. 5. Optimization: Update all parameters \{\mui, qi, si, oi, ni, ci\} using gradient descent. Adjusting n does not affect the rendering results of base 3DGS; it is optimized only to accelerate convergence of editable Gaussian optimization. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–6 for the specified number of iterations or until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def base3dgsoptimization(gaussians, images, cameras, numiterations): optimizer = Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=1e-3) # Not given in the sources for in range(numiterations): idx = random.randint(0, len(images) - 1) gtrgb = images[idx] camera = cameras[idx] D, N = renderdepthnormal(gaussians, camera) C, alphamap = renderrgbalpha(gaussians, camera) Ntilde = computepseudonormal(D) loss = computel1(C, gtrgb) + computessim(C, gtrgb) + computel2(N, Ntilde) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return gaussians def renderdepthnormal(gaussians, camera): sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: np.dot(g.mu, camera.viewdir) + camera.origin.dot(camera.viewdir)) H, W = camera.imageshape D = np.zeros((H, W)) N = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) T = np.ones((H, W)) for g in sortedgaussians: di = np.dot(g.mu, camera.viewdir) + camera.origin.dot(camera.viewdir) ni = rotatequaternion(g.n, g.q) ni = rotatevector(ni, camera.rotation) alphai = computegaussianalpha(g, camera) weight = T alphai D += weight di N += weight ni T = (1 - alphai) if np.max(T) < 1e-4: break return D, N def renderrgbalpha(gaussians, camera): sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: np.dot(g.mu, camera.viewdir) + camera.origin.dot(camera.viewdir)) H, W = camera.imageshape C = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) alphamap = np.zeros((H, W)) T = np.ones((H, W)) for g in sortedgaussians: alphai = computegaussianalpha(g, camera) ci = evaluatesh(g.c, camera.viewdir) weight = T alphai C += weight ci alphamap += weight T = (1 - alphai) return C, alphamap def computepseudonormal(depthmap): dx, dy = np.gradient(depthmap) normal = np.stack([-dx, -dy, np.oneslike(depthmap)], axis=-1) return normal / np.linalg.norm(normal, axis=-1, keepdims=True) def computel1(a, b): return np.mean(np.abs(a - b)) def computel2(a, b): return np.mean((a - b) 2) def computessim(a, b): return 1.0 # Standard SSIM implementation Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Irrelevance in Base Stage: Adjusting the normal attribute n does not affect the rendering results (color/alpha) of the base 3DGS. It is optimized solely to accelerate the convergence of subsequent editable Gaussian optimization. Alpha Channel Optimization: Unlike IBR methods that only synthesize RGB, 3DGS reconstructs per-pixel alpha. Optimizing the alpha channel can enhance reconstruction quality. Pseudo-Normal Accuracy: The pseudo-normal 	ilde{N} relies on the local planarity assumption. In regions with high curvature or noise, this approximation may be inaccurate, potentially leading to suboptimal normal initialization. iVR-GS Training is a two-stage optimization procedure for Inverse Volume Rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (iVR-GS) that separates the initialization of scene geometry from the optimization of editable shading attributes. It builds on Base 3DGS Optimization by first establishing a robust geometric baseline and then refining Gaussian primitives for visual exploration. It differs from one-stage training by accelerating convergence and reducing the number of required primitives while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality. The 3D smoothing filter prevents 3D Gaussian primitives from becoming smaller than the maximal sampling frequency induced by the training images, thereby mitigating aliasing artifacts when rendering at different sampling rates (e.g., varying focal length or camera distance). It sets a lower bound on Gaussian scale based on the highest spatial frequency captured during training. Unlike the 2D Mip filter which addresses projection aliasing, this filter operates in 3D space to constrain the intrinsic size of the Gaussians. Editable Gaussian Optimization decomposes color and lighting from the scene using the Blinn-Phong model instead of SH coefficients, enabling scene editing. It assigns additional shading attributes to each Gaussian primitive optimized in base 3DGS: an offset color \Delta c \in \mathbb{R}^3, ambient/diffuse/specular coefficients \{ka, kd, ks\}, and a shininess term  eta. The voxel color cv is expressed as cp + \Delta c, where cp \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a palette color parameter shared by all Gaussians within a basic scene. cp is fixed as the mean color value of input multi-view images during training and can be adjusted during inference. To reduce model size, low-opacity Gaussians are removed periodically, and an L1 regularization term encourages low opacity to neutralize the tendency to use more Gaussians for compact surfaces due to normal-dependent color. Sparsity regularization (L1 loss of rendered offset color map) is added to \Delta c to avoid significant palette color shiftings. Geometry-Guided Optimization is an optimization phase using Edge-Aware Normal Loss and Multi-Scale SSIM loss to ensure geometric accuracy without affecting RGB fidelity. It computes a normal map N from an unprojected depth map D using the cross product of gradients: N = (
ablax D 	imes 
ablay D) / ||

ablay D||. It derives a curvature map |

abla I| from the ground truth RGB image, then applies a weight function \omega(x) = (x - 1)^q (where q is a positive even integer) to balance edge influence on curvature. The Edge-Aware Normal Loss is calculated as L{normal} =  rac{1}{HW} \sum |

abla I|). It replaces standard SSIM with Multi-Scale SSIM (MS-SSIM) and computes the composite loss as L = (1 - \lambda{ms-ssim})L1 + \lambda{ms-ssim}L{ms-ssim} + \lambda{normal}L{normal}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The base 3DGS optimization provides a geometric baseline that accelerates the convergence of editable Gaussian optimization. Strengths: Provides accurate geometry initialization for subsequent shading decomposition; leverages normal consistency to improve geometric fidelity. Limitations: The normal attribute does not affect rendering in the base stage, so its optimization is purely for initialization purposes. Relies on local planarity assumption for pseudo-normal computation. Base 3DGS Optimization was introduced in the iVR-GS paper as a preliminary step for inverse volume rendering with editable 3D Gaussian Splatting. It adapts the original 3DGS framework by adding a normal attribute and optimizing it via a consistency loss, drawing inspiration from prior work on normal consistency. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26 AtomGS: Atomizing Gaussian Splatting for High-Fidelity Radiance Field, https://core.ac.uk/works/391753628, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: iVR-GS Training
body: iVR-GS Training is a two-stage optimization procedure for Inverse Volume Rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (iVR-GS) that separates the initialization of scene geometry from the optimization of editable shading attributes. It builds on Base 3DGS Optimization by first establishing a robust geometric baseline and then refining Gaussian primitives for visual exploration. It differs from one-stage training by accelerating convergence and reducing the number of required primitives while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality. The method optimizes a set of 3D Gaussians to match input volume data and target visualizations through a sequential two-stage process. Inputs: Target volume data (scalar field). Transfer function (TF) parameters defining the desired visualization. Camera poses for training views. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}, each defined by: Position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation Ri \in SO(3) (represented as a quaternion or rotation matrix) Scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Normal ni \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit vector) Shading attributes (e.g., color or density coefficients) Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Stored in contiguous arrays or structures of arrays (SoA) for efficient GPU access. Base 3DGS Model: A subset of Gaussians fixed or heavily constrained during the second stage, representing the underlying geometry. Editable Gaussians: The primary set of Gaussians optimized in the second stage, allowing for interactive editing. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Base 3DGS Optimization (30,000 iterations) Initialize a set of 3D Gaussians from the volume data. Optimize position, rotation, scale, and opacity to capture the basic scene geometry and density distribution. Use the loss function defined below. Note: This stage corresponds to the "Base 3DGS Optimization" phase, ensuring the geometric foundation is solid before introducing shading-specific edits. 2. Stage 2: Editable Gaussian Optimization (10,000 iterations) Initialize editable Gaussian primitives on the geometry established in Stage 1. Optimize normal attributes ni and shading attributes. Keep base geometry attributes (position, scale, rotation) relatively stable or allow limited adjustment to fit shading details. Apply specific regularization terms to maintain normal consistency and prevent overfitting. Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted combination of reconstruction loss and regularization terms: \mathcal{L} = 0.8 \mathcal{L}{L1} + 0.2 \mathcal{L}{SSIM} + 0.1 \mathcal{L}{reg} + 0.01 \mathcal{L}{normal} Where: \mathcal{L}{L1} is the L1 loss between rendered and target images. \mathcal{L}{SSIM} is the Structural Similarity Index loss. \mathcal{L}{reg} is the L1 regularization term for Gaussian attributes (e.g., scale, opacity). \mathcal{L}{normal} is the normal consistency loss. Parameters: Loss Coefficients: \lambda{L1} = 0.8, \lambda{SSIM} = 0.2. Regularization Scaling: \lambda{reg} = 0.1 for the L1 regularization term in editable Gaussian training. Normal Consistency Scaling: \lambda{normal} = 0.01 for all other regularization terms and normal consistency loss. Learning Rate: 0.01 for normal and shading attributes. Other attributes (e.g., opacity) use the same learning rates as the original 3DGS optimization. Iterations: 30,000 for Stage 1, 10,000 for Stage 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ivrgstraining(volumedata, tfparams, cameraposes, gtimages): # Stage 1: Base 3DGS Optimization (30,000 iterations) gaussians = initializefromvolume(volumedata) # Standard 3DGS initialization optimizer = Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=original3dgslr) # Adam optimizer for iteration in range(30000): renderedimage = differentiablerasterize(gaussians, cameraposes) # Standard differentiable rasterization targetimage = gtimages[iteration % len(gtimages)] lossl1 = sum(abs(renderedimage - targetimage)) / len(renderedimage) lossssim = computessim(renderedimage, targetimage) # Standard SSIM computation lossreg = sum(abs(gaussians.scale)) / len(gaussians.scale) + sum(abs(gaussians.opacity)) / len(gaussians.opacity) totalloss = 0.8 lossl1 + 0.2 lossssim + 0.1 lossreg optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # Stage 2: Editable Gaussian Optimization (10,000 iterations) editablegaussians = initeditableonbase(gaussians) # Initialize editable primitives on Stage 1 geometry optimizer = Adam(editablegaussians.parameters(), lr=0.01) # Mixed learning rates: 0.01 for normal/shading, original for others for iteration in range(10000): renderedimage = differentiablerasterize(editablegaussians, cameraposes) targetimage = gtimages[iteration % len(gtimages)] lossl1 = sum(abs(renderedimage - targetimage)) / len(renderedimage) lossssim = computessim(renderedimage, targetimage) lossreg = sum(abs(editablegaussians.scale)) / len(editablegaussians.scale) + sum(abs(editablegaussians.opacity)) / len(editablegaussians.opacity) lossnormal = computenormalconsistency(editablegaussians) # Normal consistency loss totalloss = 0.8 lossl1 + 0.2 lossssim + 0.1 lossreg + 0.01 lossnormal optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return editablegaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure normal vectors are normalized after updates to maintain unit length. Boundaries: Handle edge pixels in rendering to avoid artifacts during loss calculation. Degenerate Input: If volume data is sparse, Stage 1 may require more iterations to capture geometry accurately. It explicitly separates the training into a 30,000-iteration base 3DGS phase and a 10,000-iteration editable Gaussian phase. It is chosen when computational efficiency and reduced model size are priorities. Compared to one-stage training (40,000 iterations from scratch), it accelerates optimization, uses fewer primitives, and reduces training time by over 2× while maintaining similar reconstruction quality. Time Complexity: The two-stage approach reduces total training time by over 2× compared to one-stage training. Memory Complexity: Uses fewer primitives than one-stage training, resulting in smaller file sizes (e.g., 8.8 MB vs 16.7 MB for one basic scene in Table 2 of). Performance: Maintains similar PSNR and LPIPS metrics to one-stage training. Strengths: Faster convergence, smaller model size, efficient use of primitives. Limitations: Requires careful initialization of editable Gaussians on the base geometry. When to Use: When training time and model size are critical constraints. When Not to Use: If maximum possible reconstruction quality is required regardless of resource cost, one-stage training might be considered, though iVR-GS claims comparable quality. iVR-GS was introduced in the paper "iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting". The method leverages the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting for volume rendering and introduces a two-stage training strategy to enable interactive editing of volume visualizations. It builds upon the base 3DGS optimization framework to provide a robust geometric foundation before refining shading attributes. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26

name: iVR-GS Two-Stage Training
head: Base 3DGS + Editable Gaussian Optimization, Two-Stage Training for 3DGS
body: iVR-GS Two-Stage Training is a training strategy for Inverse Volume Rendering with Gaussian Splatting (iVR-GS) that decouples the reconstruction of static scene geometry from the optimization of editable primitives. It solves the problem of slow convergence and excessive memory usage when optimizing editable Gaussian primitives from scratch. By first establishing a base 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model, it accelerates optimization and reduces the number of required primitives compared to one-stage training, while maintaining similar reconstruction quality. The method consists of two sequential optimization phases. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of multi-view images of the target scene. Output: A composed model consisting of a base 3DGS representation and a set of editable Gaussian primitives. Data Structures: 1. Base 3DGS Model: Standard 3D Gaussian primitives defined by position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color. 2. Editable Gaussian Primitives: Additional Gaussian primitives optimized to enable scene editing capabilities. Steps: 1. Base 3DGS Training: Initialize a standard 3DGS model. Optimize the base 3DGS parameters to capture the basic scene geometry. Run for 30,000 iterations. Note: This step establishes the foundational radiance field and geometry without the complexity of editability constraints. 2. Editable Gaussian Optimization: Initialize editable Gaussian primitives on top of the converged base 3DGS geometry. Optimize the parameters of these editable primitives to enable scene editing. Run for 10,000 iterations. Note: This step fine-tunes the representation specifically for editability, leveraging the stable geometry from Stage I. Parameters: Base 3DGS iterations: 30,000. Editable Gaussian iterations: 10,000. Total iterations: 40,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: The editable primitives must be initialized on the base 3DGS geometry. Initializing from scratch (one-stage) leads to slower convergence. Precision: Standard 3DGS optimization precision applies to Stage I. Stage II focuses on the delta required for editability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ivrgstwostagetraining(images): # Stage I: Train base 3DGS basegaussians = initialize3dgs(images) for iteration in range(30000): # Standard 3DGS optimization step basegaussians = optimize3dgsstep(basegaussians, images, iteration) # Stage II: Optimize editable primitives editablegaussians = initializeeditableprimitives(basegaussians) for iteration in range(10000): # Optimization step for editability editablegaussians = optimizeeditablestep(editablegaussians, basegaussians, images, iteration) return composedmodel(basegaussians, editablegaussians) Time Complexity: Two-stage training takes 40,000 iterations total (30,000 + 10,000). One-stage training takes 40,000 iterations from scratch. However, two-stage training is over 2× faster in wall-clock time than one-stage training. Memory Complexity: Two-stage training uses fewer primitives and results in smaller file sizes compared to one-stage training. For example, on the VolVis scene, two-stage training used 375,352 primitives (8.8 MB) versus 711,169 primitives (16.7 MB) for one-stage. Quality: Both methods achieve similar reconstruction quality (PSNR and LPIPS). Strengths: Faster optimization, smaller model size, fewer primitives. Limitations: Requires two distinct phases; initial base model must be sufficiently converged before Stage II. The method was introduced in the iVR-GS paper. It addresses the inefficiencies of optimizing editable Gaussian primitives directly from scratch, which was found to be slow and resource-intensive. The two-stage approach was validated on datasets like five-jet and supernova. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stage II: Align 3DGS with Radiance Field
head: Field-wise Feature Error Minimization, Radial Feature Optimization
body: This method is the second stage of the iVR-GS training pipeline, designed to minimize the discrepancy between the rendering of deformed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and the rendering of the deformed radiance field defined by radial features. While Stage I establishes the initial deformation, Stage II finetunes the Gaussian configuration (position, rotation, scaling, spherical harmonics, and opacity) to ensure the deformed Gaussians faithfully capture the field-wise deformation. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS optimization by explicitly aligning the Gaussian splats with a ground-truth radiance field derived from an embedded deformation graph, rather than just matching pixel colors. Inputs: A set of n Gaussians \{Gi\} with parameters \{pi, ri, si, Hi, \alphai\} at rest shape. A deformation graph defined by control points (selected via Furthest Point Sampling from Gaussian centers) and KNN edge connections. A rest-shape radiance field representation. Hyperparameters: \lambda{lpf} (low-pass filter bandwidth), n{dim} (sample points per axis), \lambda1, \lambda2 (error weights). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters \{pi, ri, si, Hi, \alphai\} that minimize the total error E{total}. Gaussian i: pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling. Hi: Spherical Harmonics coefficients. \alphai: Opacity (raw scalar). \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix, computed from ri, si. Sample Points: Set \{xj\} uniformly distributed within the Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABB) of Gaussians at rest shape. Adjacency list mapping each sample point to its nearest control points on the deformation graph (computed via KNN). Spatial Hash: Used to map Gaussians to grid cells for fast updates of spatial relations between Gaussians and sample points during optimization. The radiance field is characterized by two radial features: Feature F (encoding rotated harmonics color) and Opacity O (indicating transparency): F(p) = \sum{i=1}^n \alphai Gi(p - pi) \cdot Hi \quad (7) O(p) = \sum{i=1}^n \alphai Gi(p - pi) \quad (8) where Gi(x) is the Gaussian kernel: Gi(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} x^\top \Sigmai^{-1} x\right) \quad (8) The ground truth radial features F^ and O^ are computed at sample points xj after applying embedded deformation. The deformation of a point vi to \tilde{v}i is given by: \tilde{v}i = \sumj wj(vi) \left( Aj (vi - gj) + gj \right) + tj \quad (5) where wj(vi) is the weight from the j-th control node, gj is the control point position, Aj is the affine transformation, and tj is translation. The deformation gradient tensor is used to compute F^ and O^ at the new positions. The total error to minimize is: E{total} = E{feature} + \lambda1 E{opacity} + \lambda2 E{boundary} \quad (14) Where: E{feature} \approx \sum{j=1}^m |F^(xj) - F(xj)| (9, 11) E{opacity} \approx \sum{j=1}^m |O^(xj) - O(xj)| (10, 12) E{boundary} = \sum{xj \in \mathcal{O}} |O^(xj) - O(xj)| (13) \mathcal{O} = \{ \forall xj: O^(xj) = 0 \} denotes sample points in unoccupied space. The adaptive anisotropic low-pass filter adjusts the covariance matrix \Sigmai to handle aliasing during deformation: \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top + \frac{\lambda{lpf}}{n{dim}^2} Ak Ak^\top \quad (15) where Ak is a 3 \times 3 matrix estimating the first-order approximation of the deformation field near the grid cell center k, and n{dim} is the number of sample points per axis. \lambda{lpf}: Controls the passing bandwidth of the low-pass filter. Typical value: 0.2. n{dim}: Number of sample points per axis in each grid cell. \lambda1, \lambda2: Weights for opacity and boundary errors. Not given in the sources. w{rot}, w{reg}, w{con}: Weights for the deformation graph optimization (Stage I). Values: 1, 10, 100 respectively. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stage2align3dgswithradiancefield(gaussians, deformationgraph, hyperparams): """ Finetunes Gaussian configuration to align with deformed radiance field. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes p, r, s, H, alpha. deformationgraph: Object containing control points and KNN adjacency. hyperparams: Dict with keys lambdalpf, ndim, lambda1, lambda2. Returns: Optimized gaussians. """ # 1. Initialization and Sampling # Extract AABB for each Gaussian at rest shape aabbs = [extractaabb(g) for g in gaussians] # Uniformly place sample points within bounding boxes samplepoints = [] for aabb in aabbs: points = uniformsampleinaabb(aabb, countperaxis=hyperparams['ndim']) samplepoints.extend(points) # Construct adjacency to control points on deformation graph for sample points using KNN # Note: KNN is performed against the control points of the deformation graph samplepointadjacency = knn(samplepoints, deformationgraph.controlpoints, k=4) # k is typical for deformation weights # Use spatial hashing to fast update spatial relations spatialhash = SpatialHash(gaussians, cellsize=hyperparams['ndim']) # Pre-compute harmonic features and opacity features at sample points for rest-shape # This establishes the baseline O and F before deformation is applied to the field # However, the method describes computing F and O AFTER deformation # So we store rest-shape samples for reference if needed, but primary targets are deformed # 2. Optimization Loop optimizer = Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=0.001) # Standard 3DGS learning rate for iteration in range(maxiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # A. Compute Ground Truth Radial Features (F, O) # Apply embedded deformation to sample points to get new positions in the warped field deformedsamplepoints = [] for xj in samplepoints: # Find influence weights wj from control points weights = computedeformationweights(xj, samplepointadjacency) # Compute deformed position using Eq. 5 deformedpos = computeembeddeddeformation(xj, weights, deformationgraph) deformedsamplepoints.append(deformedpos) # Compute ground truth radial features F and O at deformed sample points # This requires the deformation gradient tensor at sample points # F and O are derived from the deformed radiance field definition Fstar, Ostar = computegroundtruthradialfeatures(deformedsamplepoints, deformationgraph) # B. Compute Deformed Gaussian Radial Features (F, O) # Update Gaussian positions based on current optimization variables # Note: In this stage, we optimize the Gaussians themselves to match the field # The Gaussians are deformed according to their current parameters deformedgaussians = applydeformationtogaussians(gaussians, deformationgraph) # Compute radial features F and O from deformed Gaussians using standard equations (7, 8) Fgauss, Ogauss = computegaussianradialfeatures(deformedgaussians, deformedsamplepoints) # C. Compute Errors # Efeature: Difference in harmonic features Efeature = sum(abs(Fstar[j] - Fgauss[j]) for j in range(len(samplepoints))) # Eopacity: Difference in opacity Eopacity = sum(abs(Ostar[j] - Ogauss[j]) for j in range(len(samplepoints))) # Eboundary: Restrict optimization to unoccupied space sample points # O = {∀xj: O(xj) = 0} denotes sample points in unoccupied space unoccupiedindices = [j for j, ostar in enumerate(Ostar) if ostar == 0] Eboundary = sum(abs(Ostar[j] - Ogauss[j]) for j in unoccupiedindices) # Total Error Etotal = Efeature + hyperparams['lambda1'] Eopacity + hyperparams['lambda2'] Eboundary # D. Apply Adaptive Anisotropic Low-Pass Filter # Estimate post-deformation sampling intervals by calculating 3x3 matrix Ak # Ak offers first-order approximation of deformation field near grid cell center for g in gaussians: gridcell = spatialhash.getcell(g.p) Ak = computedeformationgradientmatrix(gridcell, deformationgraph) ndim = hyperparams['ndim'] lambdalpf = hyperparams['lambdalpf'] # Compute covariance with low-pass filter R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(g.r) S = scalematrix(g.s) Sigmabase = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # Add low-pass filter term Sigmafiltered = Sigmabase + (lambdalpf / (ndim 2)) (Ak @ Ak.T) # Update Gaussian covariance g.Sigma = Sigmafiltered # E. Backpropagation and Update Etotal.backward() # Apply sigmoid activation to opacity and exponential activation to scaling for stability for g in gaussians: g.alpha = sigmoid(g.alpharaw) g.s = exp(g.sraw) optimizer.step() return gaussians Boundary Deformation: The deformation graph is agnostic to model boundaries, potentially deforming unoccupied space. This is handled by the E{boundary} term, which restricts optimization influence to sample points where O^(xj) = 0. Aliasing: Undersampling high-frequency Gaussians during deformation causes aliasing. This is mitigated by the adaptive anisotropic low-pass filter, which adjusts the Gaussian size based on the deformation gradient. Filter Sensitivity: An over-conservative \lambda{lpf} (e.g., 0.02) leads to under-sampling, while an over-aggressive value (e.g., 2.0) causes blurriness. A value of 0.2 is empirically found to be robust. Time: The method requires computing KNN for sample points and updating spatial hashes at each optimization iteration. The computation of radial features F and O scales with the number of Gaussians n and sample points m. The use of spatial hashing accelerates the update of spatial relations. Memory: Requires storing sample points, their adjacency to control points, and the spatial hash structure. The number of sample points is proportional to the number of Gaussians. Implemented on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 24GB GPU using C++ and CUDA. The method is validated on synthetic and real-world data (e.g., Stripes, Glove, Pinocchio, Bunny, Shoe, Cup). The results are not sensitive to \lambda{lpf} within a reasonable range. Strengths: Faithfully captures field-wise deformation; handles aliasing adaptively; prevents deformation of unoccupied space. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of features and KNN adjacency; adds computational overhead to the training process. The method originates from the paper "As-Rigid-As-Possible Deformation of Gaussian Radiance Fields". It was developed to address the issue where rasterizing deformed 3DGS does not always align with the rendering obtained from the deformed radiance field. The method builds upon previous work in 3DGS [9], EWA-Splatting [42], and Mip-Splatting [20], adapting their filtering strategies to the dynamic deformation context. It utilizes embedded deformation techniques similar to those in [16] and [36]. name: Adaptive Anisotropic Spatial Low-Pass Filter
head: Adaptive Anisotropic 3D Low-Pass Filter
body: This filter prevents artifacts such as holes caused by undersampling of high-frequency features in Gaussian radiance fields during deformation. It differs from fixed isotropic low-pass filters by adapting to varying spatial sampling intervals, thereby reducing blurring and preserving high-frequency signals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} representing the radiance field, where each Gaussian Gi is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Output: The same set of Gaussians, potentially with modified parameters or used as a regularization term during optimization. Data Structures: Gaussian: Standard 3D Gaussian representation. Covariance: \Sigmai is a 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix. Method: The filter is applied to handle high-frequency signals and varying sampling intervals during deformation. The core mechanism involves an adaptive anisotropic low-pass filter. 1. Calculate Sampling Interval: Determine the local spatial sampling interval for each Gaussian based on its covariance or neighborhood density. This accounts for changes in sampling intervals during deformation. 2. Adaptive Anisotropic Filtering: Apply a low-pass filter that is adaptive (scales with the sampling interval) and anisotropic (respects the orientation of the Gaussian). Unlike a fixed isotropic filter, this approach adjusts to the deformation-induced changes in sample spacing. The filter captures high-frequency features in the spatial radiance field. Parameters: \lambda{lpf}: The weight for the adaptive anisotropic 3D low-pass filter. Typical value: 0.2. This value is identical to the parameter used in Mip-Splatting. Pitfalls: Undersampling Artifacts: Without this filter, optimization results exhibit artifacts such as holes due to undersampling of the original radiance field’s spatial signals. Blurring: Using a fixed isotropic low-pass filter causes blurring in regions where sampling intervals change due to deformation. Performance: In some regions, results without the low-pass filter are worse than the baseline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with mean, covariance, opacity, etc. lambdalpf: Weight for the filter (default 0.2). Returns: Modified list of Gaussians. """ for gaussian in gaussians: # 1. Determine local sampling interval # This step adapts to deformation-induced changes in sampling intervals # Implementation detail: Calculate based on Gaussian covariance or KNN neighbors samplinginterval = computesamplinginterval(gaussian) # 2. Apply adaptive anisotropic low-pass filter # The filter is anisotropic to preserve orientation and adaptive to scale # Implementation detail: Convolve or regularize based on lambdalpf and samplinginterval # The exact kernel or regularization term is not specified in the sources gaussian = applyfilter(gaussian, lambdalpf, samplinginterval) return gaussians def computesamplinginterval(gaussian): # Placeholder for the specific method to compute sampling interval # The sources mention handling "variations in sampling intervals" # but do not provide the exact formula. # Typically, this might be derived from the trace of the covariance matrix # or the distance to nearest neighbors in the KNN step (k=8 or 10). pass def applyfilter(gaussian, lambdalpf, samplinginterval): # Placeholder for the adaptive anisotropic filter application # The sources state this reduces artifacts and preserves high-frequency signals # but do not provide the explicit mathematical operation. # This likely involves scaling the covariance or applying a directional blur # based on the anisotropy of the Gaussian and the computed sampling interval. pass Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method allows experiments to be executed on a single GPU with 8GB of VRAM. Strengths: Reduces the occurrence of artifacts (holes) and better preserves original spatial signals compared to no filter or fixed isotropic filters. Limitations: Requires careful parameter tuning (\lambda{lpf}) and computation of sampling intervals during deformation. When to use: When dealing with deforming Gaussian radiance fields that contain high-frequency features and varying sampling intervals. When not to use: When the scene is static and sampling intervals do not change, a fixed isotropic filter might suffice, though the adaptive version is more robust. Origin: The method is described in "As-Rigid-As-Possible Deformation of Gaussian Radiance Fields". History: It was designed to address artifacts in Gaussian radiance fields during deformation, specifically holes caused by undersampling. Usage: Used in the optimization process of Gaussian radiance fields, particularly in conjunction with KNN (k=8 or 10) for deformation. name: GSP Training Loss
head: GSP Loss
body: The GSP Training Loss is the objective function used to optimize the parameters of 3D Gaussian kernels, including position, opacity, covariance, and material properties, within the Gaussian Splashing method. It extends the standard color reconstruction loss with normal consistency and anisotropy regularization to prevent artifacts caused by excessive kernel elongation during solid object simulation. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which focuses on static geometry, this loss is designed to maintain geometric stability and physical plausibility in physically-based rendering contexts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image, ground truth training image, Gaussian kernel parameters (position \mathbf{x}p, opacity \sigmap, covariance \mathbf{A}p, material properties \{dp, sp, \rhop, \mathbf{n}p\}), and camera parameters. Outputs: Scalar loss value used for back-propagation to update kernel parameters. Data Structures: Gaussian Kernel p: Defined by position \mathbf{x}p, opacity \sigmap, covariance matrix \mathbf{A}p, and material properties. Scaling Vector \mathbf{S}p: Derived from the covariance matrix, containing scalings S{p1}, S{p2}, S{p3} such that S{p1} \ge S{p2} \ge S{p3}. Formula: The total loss \mathcal{L} is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambdan \mathcal{L}{normal} + \lambdaa \mathcal{L}{aniso} Where: \mathcal{L}{color} is the color loss between the rendered image and the training image. \mathcal{L}{normal} is the normal consistency regularization, adopted from GaussianShader. \mathcal{L}{aniso} is the anisotropy loss. \lambdan and \lambdaa are weighting coefficients. The anisotropy loss \mathcal{L}{aniso} is calculated as: \mathcal{L}{aniso} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|} \sum{p \in \mathcal{P}} \max\left( \frac{S{p1}}{S{p2}} - a, 0 \right) Where: \mathcal{P} is the set of all Gaussian kernels. S{p1} is the largest scaling of kernel p. S{p2} is the second largest scaling of kernel p. a is a ratio threshold. Parameters: \lambdan = 0.2. \lambdaa = 10. a = 1.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Ambiguity: The minimal axis scaling S{p3} is explicitly excluded from the anisotropy loss constraint. Constraining S{p3} would cause normal ambiguity for spherical Gaussian kernels, as the shading normal is based on the minimal axis. Over-stretching: The anisotropy loss specifically mitigates rendering artifacts near solid objects by preventing Gaussian kernels from becoming excessively elongated or compressed under large deformations. A loss term used in adaptive spatio-temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting to ensure that Gaussians splatted to the same pixels have consistent velocities. It is inspired by depth distortion loss. For a single pixel p, the loss is defined as: \sum{g} \sum{g'} w{g,p} w{g',p} \| \mathbf{v}g - \mathbf{v}{g'} \|^2 where w{g,p} are the splatting weights of Gaussian g to pixel p, and \mathbf{v}g is the velocity of Gaussian g. This term is applied in addition to the geometric and color losses. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method enables high-frequency detail reconstruction and handles solid simulation dynamics effectively. Strengths: Prevents artifacts from over-stretched kernels in solid object rendering. Ensures temporal consistency in dynamic scenes via velocity distortion. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \lambdan and \lambdaa. The velocity distortion loss involves pairwise Gaussian comparisons per pixel. The GSP Training Loss originates from the Gaussian Splashing method, which unifies particles for versatile motion synthesis and rendering. It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting method by incorporating physically-based rendering concepts and a position-based tension model. The normal consistency term is adapted from GaussianShader. The velocity distortion loss is introduced in the context of adaptive spatio-temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting for scenes with oscillatory motion. name: Wolf et al. Stereo Method
head: Stereo 3DGS, Stereo-calibrated 3DGS
body: The Wolf et al. Stereo Method is a post-processing pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that converts the discrete, volumetric representation into a continuous, watertight triangular mesh. It solves the problem of poor geometric reconstruction quality inherent in standard 3DGS by leveraging novel view synthesis to generate stereo-calibrated image pairs, extracting dense depth maps via stereo matching, and fusing them into a mesh using Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) integration. Unlike methods that modify the Gaussian representation itself (e.g., 2D-GS) or rely on implicit neural fields, this approach remains agnostic to the underlying 3DGS structure, treating it merely as a high-fidelity renderer for stereo pairs. The method operates in three sequential stages: stereo view generation, stereo depth estimation, and TSDF fusion. Inputs: A trained 3DGS model (Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients), a set of training images covering the region of interest, and the scene radius/diameter. Outputs: A triangular mesh representing the scene surface. The 3DGS model is assumed to be fully optimized and stored in a format compatible with the standard 3DGS rasterizer. No additional data structures are introduced by the method itself; it relies on external stereo matching algorithms and TSDF volume implementations. 1. Stereo View Generation Select a training image pose (RL, TL) as the left camera. Compute the right camera pose (RR, TR) using a horizontal baseline b. Render the left and right images using the trained 3DGS model. 2. Stereo Depth Estimation Input the rendered left and right image pairs into a stereo matching algorithm. The method cites DLNR as the preferred algorithm, but any state-of-the-art neural stereo matching model is applicable. Output dense depth maps for each view. 3. TSDF Fusion Aggregate all extracted depth maps into a 3D volume. Perform Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) integration to fuse the depths. Extract the zero-level set from the TSDF volume to generate the triangular mesh. Stereo Camera Pose The right camera pose is derived from the left camera pose (RL, TL) and a horizontal baseline b: RR = RL TR = TL + (RL \times [b, 0, 0]) Where: RL, RR \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} are the rotation matrices for the left and right cameras. TL, TR \in \mathbb{R}^3 are the translation vectors for the left and right cameras. b is the horizontal baseline distance. [b, 0, 0] is the baseline vector in the local coordinate system of the left camera, rotated by RL to the world frame. Baseline Parameter The baseline b is set to 7% of the scene radius (or 3.5% of the scene diameter). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def wolfstereomethod(trained3dgs, trainingimages, sceneradius): """ Generates a triangular mesh from a trained 3DGS model using stereo depth fusion. Args: trained3dgs: Optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting model. trainingimages: List of training image poses and data. sceneradius: Radius of the scene bounding volume. Returns: mesh: Triangular mesh object. """ # Step 1: Generate Stereo Views # Select a training image pose as the left camera leftpose = trainingimages[0].pose # (RL, TL) # Calculate baseline baseline = 0.07 sceneradius # Calculate right camera pose # RR = RL # TR = TL + (RL [baseline, 0, 0]) rightpose = computestereopose(leftpose, baseline) # Render left and right images leftimage = trained3dgs.render(leftpose) rightimage = trained3dgs.render(rightpose) # Step 2: Stereo Depth Estimation # Use a stereo matching algorithm (e.g., DLNR) # Note: The specific implementation of the stereo matcher is external depthmapleft, depthmapright = stereomatch(leftimage, rightimage) # Step 3: TSDF Fusion # Initialize TSDF volume tsdfvolume = initializetsdfvolume(sceneradius) # Fuse depth maps into TSDF volume # This step typically involves projecting depth maps into 3D and updating the volume fusedepthintotsdf(tsdfvolume, depthmapleft, leftpose) fusedepthintotsdf(tsdfvolume, depthmapright, rightpose) # Extract mesh from TSDF volume mesh = extractmeshfromtsdf(tsdfvolume) return mesh def computestereopose(leftpose, baseline): """ Computes the right camera pose given the left pose and baseline. """ RL, TL = leftpose # Rotate the baseline vector [b, 0, 0] by RL baselinevector = RL @ np.array([baseline, 0, 0]) TR = TL + baselinevector RR = RL return (RR, TR) Baseline (b): Set to 7% of the scene radius. This provides a "sweet spot" in the range of 14% to 70% of the scene diameter, balancing disparity visibility and occlusion. Coverage: A sufficient amount of images covering the region of interest must be used to ensure sufficient coverage and avoid noisy artifacts. Pose Selection: The left image of the stereo pair should be at the same pose as a training image to stay close to training data, resulting in cleaner renders. Stereo Matching Algorithm: DLNR with pre-trained Middlebury weights is cited as providing the best qualitative and quantitative results. This variant focuses on the specific strategy for generating stereo-calibrated views from a single-camera 3DGS reconstruction. It sets the left camera pose to match a training image pose (RL, TL) and computes the right pose with a horizontal baseline b as RR = RL and TR = TL + (RL \times [b, 0, 0]). The baseline b is set to 7% of the scene radius to optimize the disparity range. This approach leverages the novel view synthesis capabilities of 3DGS to effectively convert a monocular capture into a stereo capture. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rendering of stereo views and the stereo matching process. The TSDF fusion is generally linear in the number of depth pixels and volume voxels. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the TSDF volume, which scales with the volume of the scene and the chosen resolution. Strengths: Produces watertight, smooth triangular meshes; leverages state-of-the-art stereo matching algorithms; agnostic to the 3DGS representation details. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 3DGS renderings; noisy or incomplete 3DGS reconstructions can lead to poor depth estimates; the discrete nature of 3DGS may limit geometric accuracy compared to implicit methods. When to use: When a high-quality triangular mesh is required from a 3DGS reconstruction, and the scene is well-covered by training images. When not to use: When the scene has large unobserved regions or when the 3DGS reconstruction is noisy due to insufficient training data. The method was introduced by Wolf et al. in the paper "GS2Mesh: Surface Reconstruction from Gaussian Splatting via Novel Stereo Views". It addresses the limitation of 3DGS in producing explicit geometry, which is often noisy or incomplete due to the discrete nature of the Gaussian representation. By using 3DGS as a renderer for stereo pairs, the method bypasses the need for explicit geometry optimization during training, instead relying on post-processing for surface extraction. This approach has been cited as a significant advancement in geometry reconstruction for 3DGS. name: GPS-Gaussian
head: Generalizable Point-based Gaussian Splatting
body: GPS-Gaussian is a generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting technique that estimates instant novel views from sparse source views without requiring per-scene fine-tuning or optimization. It solves the problem of slow, iterative optimization in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by directly regressing Gaussian parameters from 2D image features. It is distinguished from its sibling Base 3DGS Optimization by its feed-forward nature, and from WildGaussians by its specific focus on human subjects trained on large-scale human data. Inputs: Sparse source views (images) and their corresponding camera parameters (intrinsics K, extrinsics). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position \mu, color c, opacity \alpha, and covariance \Sigma, which can be rendered to novel views. Data Structures: The method operates on 2D Gaussian parameter maps defined on the sparse source view image plane. Feature maps: fs \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times Ds}, where H, W are image dimensions and Ds is the feature dimension. Gaussian Maps: Pixel-wise maps for position Mp, color Mc, rotation Mr, scaling Ms, and opacity M\alpha. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass each source view I through an image encoder \epsilon{img} to extract dense feature maps fs \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times Ds}. 2. Correlation Volume Generation: For a target view I{tar}, select two neighboring source views Ir and Il. Generate a 3D correlation volume C using the feature maps from these source views (f{r}, f{l}). 3. Depth Estimation: Iteratively estimate depth maps \langle Dl, Dr \rangle using the correlation volume C and camera parameters (Kr, Kl) via a depth estimation module \phi{depth}: \langle Dl, Dr \rangle = \phi{depth}(f{l}, f{r}, Kl, Kr) 4. 3D Position Unprojection: Use the estimated depth and camera projection matrix to unproject pixel coordinates x from the image plane to 3D coordinates Mp(x). 5. Color Assignment: Set the color map Mc(x) directly from the source image color I(x). 6. Gaussian Feature Generation: Generate depth features using a depth encoder. Combine these with the image feature fs using concatenation (\oplus) and pass through a U-Net-like decoder to generate pixel-wise Gaussian features \Gamma: \Gamma = D{parm}(\epsilon{img}(I) \oplus \epsilon{depth}(I)) 7. Parameter Prediction: Use three prediction heads to generate the remaining Gaussian feature maps: Mr (rotation), Ms (scaling), and M\alpha (opacity). 8. Rendering: Render the scene using the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline. Formulas: 3D Gaussian Representation: G(x) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)} where \mu is the 3D position and \Sigma is the 3D covariance matrix. 2D Covariance Projection: The 3D covariance \Sigma is decomposed into a rotation matrix R and a scaling matrix S. The 2D covariance \Sigma' is projected using the view transformation matrix W and the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transform: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T Alpha Blending: The final pixel color C is computed via alpha blending: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) where ci is the learned color and \alpha'i is the re-scaled opacity. Parameters: Feature map dimensions: H/2 \times W/2 \times Ds. Loss functions: Photometric loss and depth loss are used to optimize the method end-to-end. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the accuracy of the depth estimation module \phi{depth}; errors in depth directly propagate to 3D position errors. The method is designed for human subjects; performance on non-human scenes is not guaranteed as it is trained on large amounts of human data. No fine-tuning or optimization is performed at inference time, so the quality is limited by the generalization capability of the trained network. FaCT-GS is a framework for fast and flexible Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction that optimizes the voxelization and rasterization pipelines of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of slow convergence and high computational cost in Gaussian-based tomographic reconstruction by removing view-dependent occlusion logic, coalescing data structures, and enabling rapid fitting to pre-existing volumes for warm-starting. It is distinguished from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by its removal of depth-sorting overhead and from GPS-Gaussian by its specific focus on CT geometry and voxelization-based initialization. SegAnySplatting Feature Optimization is a method for optimizing semantic features for 3D Gaussians, incorporating scale-awareness via a learned gate and feature smoothing. It builds on GPS-Gaussian by adding a mechanism to distill semantic information (e.g., from CLIP or LSeg) into the Gaussian attributes while handling the multi-scale nature of 3D Gaussians. It differs from FaCT-GS by focusing on semantic feature distillation with scale-adaptive gating rather than compact factorized color representations. Joint Fine-tuning is a training strategy within the GPS-Gaussian framework that progressively co-optimizes a 3D Gaussian Splatting model and an Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) model to refine scene geometry. It addresses the ambiguity in pulling Gaussians to a surface by using dense queries around the UDF zero-level set as geometric cues, preventing error accumulation. Unlike methods that regress Gaussian parameters directly from sparse views without optimization, this approach iteratively improves both representations. Conditional Slicing is a mechanism that projects high-dimensional (7D) Gaussians into 3D counterparts conditioned on specific time and view direction, preserving computational efficiency of 3DGS. It conditions the 6D Gaussian on the viewing direction d (where Xd = d) to yield a conditional 3D Gaussian for the spatial component, using the conditional distribution formulas from 6DGS. The conditional mean is calculated as \mu{cond} = \mup + \Sigma{pd} \Sigmad^{-1} (d - \mud), where \mup is the spatial mean, \Sigma{pd} is the cross-covariance between position and direction, \Sigmad is the directional covariance, d is the viewing direction, and \mud is the directional mean. The conditional covariance is calculated as \Sigma{cond} = \Sigmap - \Sigma{pd} \Sigmad^{-1} \Sigma{pd}^\top, where \Sigmap is the spatial covariance. The opacity of each Gaussian is modulated to reflect the alignment between the current view direction and the Gaussian’s preferred direction: f{cond} = \exp(-\lambda (d - \mud)^\top \Sigmad^{-1} (d - \mud)), \alpha{cond} = \alpha \cdot f{cond}, where \lambda is a positive scaling parameter controlling the sensitivity of the opacity modulation to view direction alignment. Time Complexity: The method is feed-forward, allowing for instant novel view estimation without iterative optimization. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature maps and the correlation volume during inference, but avoids storing large per-scene optimization states. Performance: Enables real-time rendering speeds. Strengths: Eliminates the need for per-scene optimization, making it suitable for applications requiring immediate novel view synthesis from sparse inputs. Limitations: Limited to human subjects due to training data bias. Accuracy depends on the depth estimation module. GPS-Gaussian was introduced as a generalizable approach for 3D human representation that takes advantage of 2D Gaussian parameter maps to estimate human features and 3D pose in real-time. It is cited as reference [73] in the source document. It builds on the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting to overcome the performance constraints of using the same set of Gaussians for various human features which may have different frequencies. name: FaCT-GS
body: FaCT-GS is a framework for fast and flexible Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction that optimizes the voxelization and rasterization pipelines of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of slow convergence and high computational cost in Gaussian-based tomographic reconstruction by removing view-dependent occlusion logic, coalescing data structures, and enabling rapid fitting to pre-existing volumes for warm-starting. It is distinguished from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by its removal of depth-sorting overhead and its specific adaptation to CT geometry. Inputs: A set of N X-ray projection images (views). Camera parameters for each view (pinhole or cone-beam geometry). Optional: A pre-existing volumetric prior (e.g., from FDK reconstruction) for initialization. Outputs: A set of M 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^M representing the 3D volume. Each Gaussian i is defined by a center \mathbf{p}i, a covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, an opacity/weight Gi, and other attributes. To reduce memory traffic, parameters are coalesced into compact float4 structs: 1. Voxelizer Struct: Combines position and radius. 2. Rasterizer Struct: Combines the projected conic (inverse covariance) \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i^{-1} and the integration factor \mui. The projection of a 3D Gaussian onto the 2D detector plane yields a 2D Gaussian. The intensity I(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) at a pixel coordinate \hat{\mathbf{x}} on the detector plane is computed as: I(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \sum{i=1}^M Gi^2 \left( \hat{\mathbf{x}} \mid \mui \rhoi, \hat{\mathbf{p}}i, \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i \right) Where: M is the number of Gaussians. Gi is the Gaussian weight. \mui is an integration factor. \rhoi is a scaling factor. \hat{\mathbf{p}}i is the projected center of the i-th Gaussian. \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i is the projected covariance matrix of the i-th Gaussian. The term Gi^2 (\dots) represents the 2D Gaussian function evaluated at \hat{\mathbf{x}} with the specified parameters. 1. Initialization: Initialize the set of 3D Gaussians via gradient-based initialization from an FDK reconstruction or by fitting Gaussians to a pre-existing volumetric prior. 2. Voxelization: Discretize the 3D space into a regular grid and accumulate Gaussian contributions within each voxel to produce a dense volumetric representation. This avoids mapping Gaussians to a 2D plane but incurs cubic growth in grid elements. 3. Projection: For each view, project the 3D Gaussians onto the 2D detector plane, transforming the 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i into \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i and the center \mathbf{p}i into \hat{\mathbf{p}}i. 4. Culling: For each pixel, identify contributing Gaussians by accumulating contributions only for Gaussians satisfying |\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}i| < 3\lambda{\text{MAX}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i), where \lambda{\text{MAX}} is the largest eigenvalue of the projected covariance \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i. 5. Rasterization: Compute the intensity contribution of each culling-passed Gaussian using the rendering formula. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, do not sort Gaussians by depth or accumulate in a specific order, as the integration order along the ray does not affect the measured signal in CT. Use the coalesced float4 structs for memory-efficient access to conics and \mu values. 6. Optimization Loop: Compare the rendered projections with the acquired X-ray images, compute the loss, and update the Gaussian parameters (centers, covariances, weights, etc.) via gradient descent. M[0][1] M[1][0] return [[M[1][1] / det, -M[0][1] / det], [-M[1][0] / det, M[0][0] / det]] def matdet2x2(M): return M[0][0] M[1][1] - M[0][1] M[1][0] def project3dto2d(center3d, cov3d, R, t, fx, fy, cx, cy): pcam = [R[0][0]center3d[0] + R[0][1]center3d[1] + R[0][2]center3d[2] + t[0], R[1][0]center3d[0] + R[1][1]center3d[1] + R[1][2]center3d[2] + t[1], R[2][0]center3d[0] + R[2][1]center3d[1] + R[2][2]center3d[2] + t[2]] if pcam[2] <= 0: return None, None p2d = [(pcam[0] fx / pcam[2]) + cx, (pcam[1] fy / pcam[2]) + cy] J = [[fx / pcam[2], 0, -(pcam[0] fx) / (pcam[2]2)], [0, fy / pcam[2], -(pcam[1] fy) / (pcam[2]2)]] cov3d2 = [row[:2] for row in cov3d] cov2d = matmul2x2(J, matmul2x2(cov3d2, [[row[0] for row in J] for in range(2)])) return p2d, cov2d def evaluate2dgaussian(x, y, mu, rho, p2d, cov2d): diffx = x - p2d[0] diffy = y - p2d[1] invcov = matinv2x2(cov2d) exponent = -0.5 (diffx invcov[0][0] diffx + diffx invcov[0][1] diffy + diffy invcov[1][0] diffx + diffy invcov[1][1] diffy) normconst = 1.0 / (2.0 math.pi math.sqrt(matdet2x2(cov2d))) return (mu rho) normconst math.exp(exponent) def renderfactgs(projections, gaussians, cameraparams): renderedimages = [] for viewidx, target in enumerate(projections): h, w = target.shape image = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] R, t, fx, fy, cx, cy = cameraparams[viewidx] for g in gaussians: p2d, cov2d = project3dto2d(g.center, g.cov, R, t, fx, fy, cx, cy) if p2d is None: continue tr = cov2d[0][0] + cov2d[1][1] det = matdet2x2(cov2d) disc = math.sqrt(max(0, tr2 - 4 det)) lambdamax = (tr + disc) / 2.0 radius = 3.0 lambdamax minx = max(0, int(p2d[0] - radius)) maxx = min(w, int(p2d[0] + radius) + 1) miny = max(0, int(p2d[1] - radius)) maxy = min(h, int(p2d[1] + radius) + 1) for y in range(miny, maxy): for x in range(minx, maxx): dist = math.sqrt((x - p2d[0])2 + (y - p2d[1])2) if dist < radius: pdf = evaluate2dgaussian(x, y, g.mu, g.rho, p2d, cov2d) image[y][x] += (g.weight 2) pdf renderedimages.append(image) return renderedimages Culling Threshold: 3\lambda{\text{MAX}}. Execution Time: Approximately 2 minutes per scan on 75 projections of 512^2 size; competitive results after 45 seconds. Scalability: Generates high-quality reconstructions in about 1 minute for 1k projections and 4 minutes for 2k projections. Occlusion Logic: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting accumulates splat contributions in a specific order to model view-dependent occlusion. In CT, integration order along the ray has no effect on the measured signal. Removing this ordering logic is critical to avoid unnecessary overhead. Memory Traffic: Failure to coalesce function parameters into compact float4 structs (combining position/radius in voxelizer, conics/\mu in rasterizer) leads to higher memory traffic and reduced performance. Voxelization Cost: Voxelization is computationally expensive due to the cubic growth in the number of grid elements. Care must be taken with grid resolution. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than State of the Art GS CT reconstruction. Over 4x faster on standard 512^2 projections and over 13x faster on 2k projections. Memory Complexity: Reduced by coalescing parameters into float4 structs. Voxelization incurs cubic growth in grid elements. Scalability: Scales well with projection and output volume size. Strengths: Fast execution, flexible initialization (including warm-starting from pre-existing volumes), and compression properties comparable to 2D JPEG stacks. Limitations: Voxelization can be computationally expensive for high-resolution grids. When to use: Sparse-view tomography, fast CT reconstruction, scenarios requiring warm-starting from prior volumes. When not to use: Standard 3D rendering with view-dependent occlusion is required. FaCT-GS was introduced to address the limitations of Gaussian Splatting-based CT reconstruction, specifically the slow convergence and high computational cost. It builds on the observation that projecting a 3D Gaussian yields a 2D Gaussian, allowing for simplified rendering equations. The method was developed to enable rapid fitting of Gaussians to pre-existing volumes, serving as a prior for warm-starting or as a compressed representation. It is related to R2-Gaussian, which also highlighted the irrelevance of integration order in CT, but FaCT-GS fully removes the ordering logic from the pipeline.
