name: SegAnySplatting Feature Optimization
head: Scale-Aware Semantic Features, SegAnyGS
body: SegAnySplatting Feature Optimization optimizes semantic features for 3D Gaussians by incorporating scale-awareness through a learned gate and feature smoothing. It differs from FaCT-GS by focusing on distilling semantic information (e.g., from CLIP or LSeg) into Gaussian attributes with scale-adaptive gating, rather than compact factorized color representations. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a frozen pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model and a training dataset containing semantic masks or features as input, and outputs an optimized semantic feature tensor attached to each Gaussian. Data Structures: The semantic features are stored as a torch.nn.Parameter of shape (ngaussians, nfeaturedims) and initialized with torch.randn(...) 1e-2. The scale gate is implemented as an nn.Sequential module containing nn.Linear(1, nfeaturedims) followed by nn.Sigmoid(). The background color is stored as a torch.nn.Parameter of shape (nfeaturedims,), initialized to zeros, and marked as non-trainable. Parameters: The method uses nfeaturedims (int, default 32) for the number of semantic feature dimensions per Gaussian. It uses scaleawaredim (int) to control scale awareness, where values <=0 or >=32 trigger the adaptive scale gate. It uses smoothK (int, default 16) for the feature smoothing kernel size. It uses smoothdropout (float, default 0.5) for the feature smoothing dropout rate. It uses rfn (float, default 1.0) as the feature normalization factor. It uses downsamplefactor (int) to reduce the resolution of the rendered feature map and accelerate distillation. Steps: 1. Load the pre-trained Gaussian model and freeze its geometric and color parameters. 2. Gather all scale values from the training dataset to compute upperboundscale. 3. If scaleawaredim is not in the range [1, 31], initialize a quantile transformer (qtrans) with a uniform output distribution to normalize the scale values. 4. If scaleawaredim is in the range [1, 31], initialize a fixed scale gate tensor fixedscalegate of shape (scaleawaredim + 1, 32) where row i contains 1s in the first 32 - \text{scale\aware\dim} + i positions and 0s elsewhere. 5. Preprocess masks by sorting them by scale in descending order and sampling indices for the largest, smallest, and random intermediate scales. 6. Render semantic features from the Gaussians, downsample the feature map using downsamplefactor, compute the distillation loss against ground-truth semantic features, apply feature smoothing with kernel size smoothK and dropout smoothdropout, and update Semantic Features and Scale Gate via gradient descent. 7. After distillation, visualize the rendered feature map using the provided viewer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SegAnySplattingFeatureOptimization: def init(self, ngaussians, nfeaturedims=32, scaleawaredim=0, smoothK=16, smoothdropout=0.5, rfn=1.0): self.ngaussians = ngaussians self.nfeaturedims = nfeaturedims self.scaleawaredim = scaleawaredim self.smoothK = smoothK self.smoothdropout = smoothdropout self.rfn = rfn # Semantic Features: (ngaussians, nfeaturedims) self.semanticfeatures = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(ngaussians, nfeaturedims) 1e-2) # Background Color: (nfeaturedims,), not trainable self.backgroundcolor = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(nfeaturedims), requiresgrad=False) # Scale Gate initialization if not (1 <= scaleawaredim <= 31): self.scalegate = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, nfeaturedims), nn.Sigmoid()) self.fixedscalegate = None else: self.fixedscalegate = torch.zeros(scaleawaredim + 1, 32) for i in range(scaleawaredim + 1): self.fixedscalegate[i,:32 - scaleawaredim + i] = 1.0 self.scalegate = None self.qtrans = None def quantilenormalize(self, scales): # Standard quantile normalization mapping to uniform distribution sortedscales, = torch.sort(scales) ranks = torch.searchsorted(sortedscales, scales) return ranks / len(scales) def preprocessscales(self, scales): upperboundscale = torch.max(scales) if self.scalegate is not None: self.qtrans = self.quantilenormalize(scales) return upperboundscale def preprocessmasks(self, masks, scales): sortedindices = torch.argsort(scales, descending=True) sortedmasks = [masks[i] for i in sortedindices] n = len(sortedmasks) indices = [0, n - 1] if n > 2: midindices = torch.randint(1, n - 1, (max(1, n // 4),)) indices.extend(midindices.tolist()) return [sortedmasks[i] for i in indices] def smoothfeatures(self, features): # Apply spatial smoothing via average pooling and dropout if self.smoothdropout > 0: features = F.dropout(features, p=self.smoothdropout, training=True) k = self.smoothK if features.dim() == 2: features = F.avgpool2d(features.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), kernelsize=k, stride=1).squeeze() return features def renderandoptimize(self, gaussians, semantictargets, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() # Standard 3DGS rasterization accumulating semantic features renderedfeatures = self.renderfeatures(gaussians) # Downsample for speed renderedfeatures = F.avgpool2d(renderedfeatures, kernelsize=2, stride=2) # Loss loss = F.mseloss(renderedfeatures, semantictargets) # Smoothing smoothed = self.smoothfeatures(renderedfeatures) # Loss typically computed on smoothed or original features; here on original per standard distillation loss.backward() optimizer.step() def renderfeatures(self, gaussians): # Standard 3DGS projection and accumulation scales = gaussians.scales # (ngaussians, 3) scalarscales = torch.max(scales, dim=1).values if self.scalegate is not None: gate = self.scalegate(scalarscales.unsqueeze(1)) features = self.semanticfeatures gate else: # Map scalar scale to fixed gate row index scalenorm = scalarscales / (torch.max(scalarscales) + 1e-8) rowidx = torch.clamp((scalenorm self.scaleawaredim).long(), 0, self.scaleawaredim) gate = self.fixedscalegate[rowidx] features = self.semanticfeatures gate # Rasterize features to image space return features # Simplified return for pseudocode structure Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If scaleawaredim falls outside [1, 31], the adaptive gate is automatically selected. The downsamplefactor must be \ge 1 to prevent invalid tensor shapes during distillation. Degenerate scale values (e.g., all zeros) should be handled by the quantile transformer or clamped to a minimum positive value. Precision issues with the random initialization are mitigated by the 10^{-2} scaling factor. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method uses downsamplefactor to reduce the resolution of the rendered feature map and accelerate distillation. Strengths, limitations, and usage recommendations: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the gaussian-splatting-lightning repository. It extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to support semantic feature optimization, building on appearance modeling and visibility map concepts from earlier sections. yzslab/gaussian-splatting-lightning, https://github.com/yzslab/gaussian-splatting-lightning, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Joint Fine-tuning
head: Progressive Joint Optimization
body: Joint Fine-tuning is a training strategy within the GPS-Gaussian framework that progressively co-optimizes a 3D Gaussian Splatting model and an Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) model to refine scene geometry. It addresses the ambiguity in pulling Gaussians to a surface by using dense queries around the UDF zero-level set as geometric cues, preventing error accumulation. Unlike methods that regress Gaussian parameters directly from sparse views without optimization, this approach iteratively improves both representations. Inputs: Sparse source views (images). Initial 3D Gaussian distribution (positions, scales, rotations, opacities, colors). Initial UDF field (parameterized by a neural network). Camera poses for source views. Outputs: Refined 3D Gaussian parameters. Refined UDF field. Gaussian Model: Set of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian k has position \mathbf{p}k, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}k, opacity \alphak, and color \mathbf{c}k. UDF Model: Neural network f{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) predicting unsigned distance at point \mathbf{x}. Ray Vk: Ray passing through Gaussian k's center. 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian model and UDF model. The UDF is not perfectly accurate initially. 2. Progressive Joint Optimization Loop: a. Ray Casting: For each Gaussian k, define a ray Vk passing through its center. b. Depth Projection: Calculate dt, the depth of the projection point from Gaussian k onto Vk. c. UDF Query: Query the UDF at the Gaussian's position to get dn, the depth of the surface point \{qn\} along the ray direction. d. Loss Calculation: Compute a geometric consistency loss. The source mentions a stop-gradient operation sg(\cdot) applied to the UDF prediction to stabilize training. The loss pulls the Gaussian towards the UDF surface using dense queries around the zero-level set rather than a direct pull to the zero-level set itself. e. Gradient Update: Update both the Gaussian parameters and the UDF network parameters \theta using the combined loss. The stop-gradient sg(\cdot) is applied to the UDF term to prevent conflicting gradients. f. Iteration: Repeat steps 2a-2e for multiple epochs. The process is "progressive," meaning the refinement happens over time, continuously improving each model. The geometric loss leverages the depth difference between the Gaussian projection and the UDF surface. Let dt be the depth of the Gaussian's projection onto the ray Vk and dn be the depth of the surface point \{qn\} predicted by the UDF. The update involves a stop-gradient operation sg(\cdot) on the UDF term: \mathcal{L}{geo} = \| dt - sg(dn) \|^2 (Note: The exact loss function formula is not fully provided in the source text, but the components dt, dn, and sg(\cdot) are explicitly defined.) Progressive Schedule: Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Ambiguous Pulling Directions: Directly pulling Gaussians to the UDF zero-level set can cause error accumulation due to ambiguous directions. This method avoids this by using dense queries around the zero-level set. UDF Accuracy: The UDF is not perfectly accurate, but provides reliable optimization directions. Poor initial UDF quality may slow convergence. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jointfinetuning(gaussians, udfnet, sourceviews, cameras, epochs): for epoch in range(epochs): for gaussian in gaussians: # Step 1: Define ray Vk through Gaussian center ray = getraythroughgaussiancenter(gaussian, cameras) # Step 2: Get depth of Gaussian projection dt dt = gaussian.depthalongray(ray) # Step 3: Query UDF for surface depth dn # The UDF predicts unsigned distance. We assume dn is derived from # the UDF zero-level set intersection along the ray. dn = udfnet.getsurfacedepth(ray) # Step 4: Compute geometric loss with stop-gradient on UDF term # sg() denotes stop-gradient operation loss = (dt - stopgradient(dn)) 2 # Step 5: Backpropagate to update both Gaussian and UDF loss.backward() # Step 6: Optimizer step for both models optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return gaussians, udfnet def stopgradient(tensor): # Returns tensor detached from computation graph return tensor.detach() A method for compressing 3D Gaussian Splatting models. It focuses on reducing memory footprint through factorization, unlike Joint Fine-tuning which focuses on geometric refinement via UDFs. Optimizes features for segmentation-aware Gaussian Splatting. It targets semantic feature learning rather than geometric refinement through joint UDF optimization. Time Complexity: Higher than non-optimizing methods like the initial GPS-Gaussian regression because it involves iterative joint optimization of Gaussians and a UDF network. Memory Complexity: Requires storing both the Gaussian parameters and the UDF network parameters. Strengths: Prevents error accumulation from ambiguous pulling directions by using dense queries around the zero-level set. Continuously improves geometry over time. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to joint optimization. Relies on the UDF providing reliable directions despite not being perfectly accurate. When to Use: When high-fidelity geometry is required and sparse views are available, and computational resources allow for iterative optimization. When Not to Use: When real-time inference without fine-tuning is required, as this method is a training-time optimization. Joint Fine-tuning, also known as Progressive Joint Optimization, was introduced in the VRP-UDF paper. It builds on the GPS-Gaussian framework, which initially introduced Gaussian parameter maps on sparse source views to regress parameters jointly with a depth estimation module without fine-tuning. The Joint Fine-tuning method extends this by adding a progressive joint optimization step to refine the geometry further. It addresses limitations in existing methods that directly pull Gaussians to the UDF zero-level set. name: Optimization and Training Efficiency
body: This family addresses computational bottlenecks in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training, such as high VRAM consumption and slow convergence. It distinguishes itself from standard training [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md] by restructuring data flow, fusing optimizer kernels, or modifying learning rate schedules to accelerate convergence and reduce memory usage. The methods in this family share the following foundational mechanisms: 1. Differentiable Rasterization Core: All methods rely on the differentiable alpha-blending rasterizer. The forward pass computes pixel color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) via depth-sorted alpha blending, and the backward pass computes gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta. 2. Gradient Accumulation: Gradients are accumulated over multiple training steps or views before an optimizer update. In distributed settings, gradients or intermediate rendering states are synchronized across devices. 3. Adaptive Representation: Many optimization variants modify the Gaussian representation or its distribution to improve efficiency or fidelity, requiring corresponding adjustments to the gradient computation or data flow. 4. Hardware Acceleration: Methods leverage GPU parallelism, often using CUDA kernels, Tensor Cores (via GEMM reformulation), or half-precision arithmetic to accelerate the rasterization and gradient computation. Parameter-Specific Learning Rates configures the Adam optimizer with distinct learning rates for each Gaussian attribute group (means, opacities, scales, colors) to stabilize training and prevent rapid divergence. Unlike a uniform learning rate, this method assigns higher rates to attributes requiring aggressive adaptation (e.g., colors) and lower rates to stable geometric parameters (e.g., means), addressing the varying sensitivity of different Gaussian properties during differentiable rasterization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like CLM or FastGS by focusing exclusively on the optimizer's parameter grouping strategy rather than modifying the rasterization core or representation density. This family encompasses methods that accelerate the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by optimizing the computational efficiency of the backward pass, managing memory across multiple devices, and handling specialized gradient flows such as those for probabilistic masks. It solves the bottleneck where the O(N \cdot P) complexity of differentiable rasterization (where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels) limits scalability to large scenes or complex representations. It is distinguished from standard 3DGS training [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md] by explicitly restructuring data flow (per-splat vs. per-pixel), distributing state across GPU clusters [7349-grendel-gs.md], or computing gradients for auxiliary latent variables like masks [4254-maskgaussian-gradient-computation.md]. CLM is a training optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes the GPU memory barrier by offloading Gaussian states to CPU memory and overlapping CPU-side optimizer updates with GPU rendering. It solves the problem of VRAM exhaustion and communication stalls in large-scale scenes by implementing a smart caching policy that keeps frequently updated Gaussians on the GPU while streaming others. Unlike baseline offloading which incurs significant latency, CLM uses pipelining and early Adam updates to hide communication overhead, enabling training of scenes that exceed GPU memory on a single device. FastGS is a general acceleration framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that significantly reduces training time by regulating the number of Gaussians based on multi-view consistency, dispensing with explicit budgeting mechanisms. It re-engineers the training loop using dynamic sparse rasterization and fast gradient checkpointing to skip negligible computations. Unlike sibling methods that rely on Gaussian-associated properties (Taming-3DGS) or indirect gradient approximations (Speedy-Splat), FastGS directly evaluates each Gaussian's contribution to multi-view reconstruction quality to guide densification and pruning. Fused Backward and Optimizer is a training optimization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates the Adam optimizer step directly into the backward pass of the differentiable rasterizer. It solves the bottleneck where parameter updates consume 40–60% of training time by eliminating separate optimizer kernels and reducing VRAM usage through the avoidance of intermediate parameter buffers. It differs from sibling methods like FastGS by prioritizing memory efficiency and correctness over maximum speed, whereas FastGS and CLM focus on skipping computations for invisible Gaussians to achieve higher speedups at the cost of potential quality degradation or inconsistency. Definition: Addresses oscillation in gradient updates for scaling and rotation parameters caused by a poorly conditioned learning rate ratio. Step: Rescales the scaling gradient with the inverse of the current scale to stabilize convergence. Impact: Cuts training time by nearly half compared to standard 3DGS. Step: Reduce training iterations from the original 30,000 to 1,000 for the Neural3DVideo dataset and to 1,500 for the LongVolumetricVideo dataset. Keep all other parameters identical to the original 3DGS implementation. Pitfall: Using the original 30,000 iterations on sparse input data causes overfitting. Impact: Reduces training time and improves novel view synthesis by approximately 4 PSNR. Definition: Loading ground truth images from disk every iteration instead of storing them in VRAM, to enable training on consumer hardware with limited VRAM for ultra-large-scale datasets. Comparison: Standard 3DGS stores the entire training dataset in VRAM for speed. This method loads images from disk every iteration, saving VRAM but reducing training performance. Definition: Controlling the sampling rate by adjusting the sampling gap value to influence training speed and rendering quality. Step: Increase the sampling gap value to decrease the sampling rate, which is inversely proportional to the sampling rate. Pitfall: Increasing the sampling gap increases pc time and makes the rendering result blurrier. Impact: On the truck dataset with 3000 training steps, increasing the sampling gap from 2 to 500 increases pc time from 0.17739 to 0.20525. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training > Parameter-Specific Learning Rates
head: Per-parameter group learning rates, Adam parameter learning rates, Gaussian Optimizer Configuration
body: Parameter-Specific Learning Rates configures the Adam optimizer with distinct learning rates for each Gaussian attribute group (means, opacities, scales, colors, rotations) to stabilize training and prevent rapid divergence. Unlike a uniform learning rate, this method assigns higher rates to attributes requiring aggressive adaptation (e.g., colors) and lower rates to stable geometric parameters (e.g., means), addressing the varying sensitivity of different Gaussian properties during differentiable rasterization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like CLM or FastGS by focusing exclusively on the optimizer's parameter grouping strategy rather than modifying the rasterization core or representation density [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. Inputs: Gaussian parameters \theta: means \mathbf{p}, opacities \alpha, scales \mathbf{s}, colors \mathbf{c} (and optionally rotations \mathbf{q} or spherical harmonics coefficients). Optimizer hyperparameters: base Adam settings (\beta1, \beta2, \epsilon). Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \theta' after an optimization step. Data Structures: The optimizer maintains separate state buffers (first and second moment estimates) for each parameter group. The parameter groups are defined as lists of tensors, where each tensor corresponds to a specific attribute of all active Gaussians. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Adam optimizer with a base learning rate of 0.0 (since rates are handled per group) and \epsilon = 1\times10^{-15}. Set \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.999. 2. Parameter Group Definition: Define parameter groups with specific learning rates. The standard configuration for 3D Gaussian Splatting assigns rates as follows: Opacities: lr{\alpha} = 0.00085 Scales: lr{\mathbf{s}} = 0.001 Colours: lr{\mathbf{c}} = 0.02 Means: lr{\mathbf{p}} = 0.00015 Note: Some implementations use pre-activation values for opacities and scales with a higher learning rate of 0.05. 3. Trainability Check: Verify that all required parameters are marked as trainable. In isotropic mode, quaternions are excluded from optimization; attempting to optimize them raises a RuntimeError. 4. Optimizer Step: For each training iteration: Compute gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} via the backward pass of the differentiable rasterizer. Execute optimizer.step(), which applies the Adam update rule using the group-specific learning rates. Execute optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) to free memory. 5. Cache Management: Immediately after the optimizer step, call torch.cuda.emptycache() to release unused GPU memory. Formulas: The Adam update for a parameter group g with learning rate lrg is: \mathbf{m}t = \beta1 \mathbf{m}{t-1} + (1 - \beta1) \mathbf{g}t \mathbf{v}t = \beta2 \mathbf{v}{t-1} + (1 - \beta2) \mathbf{g}t^2 \hat{\mathbf{m}}t = \frac{\mathbf{m}t}{1 - \beta1^t}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{v}}t = \frac{\mathbf{v}t}{1 - \beta2^t} \theta{t+1} = \thetat - lrg \cdot \frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}t}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}t} + \epsilon} Where \mathbf{g}t is the gradient for the group, and \thetat represents the parameters in that group (e.g., all means, all colors). Parameters with Typical Values: Standard 3DGS: lr{\alpha}=0.00085, lr{\mathbf{s}}=0.001, lr{\mathbf{c}}=0.02, lr{\mathbf{p}}=0.00015. X-Gaussian Variant: Position lr starts at 1.9\times10^{-4} and decays exponentially to 1.9\times10^{-6}. Point feature lr = 2\times10^{-3}. Opacity lr = 8\times10^{-3}. Scaling lr = 5\times10^{-3}. Rotation lr = 1\times10^{-3}. Gaussian-Flow Variant: Position lr = 4\times10^{-4} with exponential decay of 8\times10^{-7}. Rotation lr = 0.002. DDDM parameters lr = 4\times10^{-4}. Weight decay 8\times10^{-7} applied to all parameters. 2D Gaussian Variant: Image-space coordinates lr = 0.001 \times \text{mean}(\text{width}, \text{height}). Color lr = 0.01. Opacity lr = 0.02. Scale lr = 0.001. Rotation angle lr = 0.02. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Isotropic Mode: If the Gaussian representation is isotropic, rotation parameters (quaternions) are not optimized. The training code must check checkiftrainable() to avoid runtime errors. Precision: The epsilon value is set to 1\times10^{-15} to prevent division by zero in the Adam update, which is critical for small gradients in opacity or scale. Memory: Frequent optimizer steps without cache management can lead to OOM errors; torch.cuda.emptycache() is recommended after each step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.optim as optim def setupoptimizer(gaussians, config): """ Setup parameter-specific Adam optimizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: gaussians: Object containing trainable parameters (means, opacities, scales, colors, rotations). config: Dictionary containing hyperparameters. Returns: optimizer: Adam optimizer instance. """ # Extract parameters based on trainability flags # Note: In isotropic mode, rotations are excluded means = gaussians.getmeans() opacities = gaussians.getopacities() scales = gaussians.getscales() colors = gaussians.getcolors() # Check if rotations should be included if gaussians.isisotropic(): rotations = None else: rotations = gaussians.getrotations() # Define parameter groups with specific learning rates # Standard 3DGS rates lrmeans = 0.00015 lropacities = 0.00085 lrscales = 0.001 lrcolors = 0.02 lrrotations = 0.001 # Default, varies by variant paramgroups = [ {'params': means, 'lr': lrmeans}, {'params': opacities, 'lr': lropacities}, {'params': scales, 'lr': lrscales}, {'params': colors, 'lr': lrcolors}, ] if rotations is not None: paramgroups.append({'params': rotations, 'lr': lrrotations}) # Initialize Adam with base lr=0.0 (rates are per group) and eps=1e-15 optimizer = optim.Adam(paramgroups, lr=0.0, eps=1e-15, betas=(0.9, 0.999)) return optimizer def trainingstep(gaussians, optimizer, loss): """ Perform one optimization step. """ # Zero gradients optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) # Compute loss (forward pass + backward pass handled by autograd) # loss = computerenderingloss(gaussians, cameras, gtimages) # Backward pass loss.backward() # Optimizer step optimizer.step() # Release GPU cache torch.cuda.emptycache() return loss BOGausS (Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting) is a modified Stochastic Gradient Descent optimizer designed to ensure unbiased state estimation for sparsely-viewed and split Gaussians. It addresses performance degradation caused by biased moment estimates in standard Adam when Gaussians are occluded or rarely updated. It sets itself apart by using Gaussian-dependent time steps and precision-aware scaling factors derived from reconstruction confidence intervals, rather than global iteration counts and uniform learning rates. This variant emphasizes the operational sequence of the optimizer step and memory management. It specifies that gaussians.optimizer.step() must be followed immediately by gaussians.optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) and torch.cuda.emptycache() to release unused GPU memory back to the system. This variant optimizes 2D Gaussian primitives in image space using the Adam optimizer. It adds 20% of new Gaussian primitives every 200 iterations and prunes those with opacity below 0.005 or covering fewer than 25 pixels. Learning rates are scaled by image dimensions: coordinates lr = 0.001 \times \text{mean}(\text{width}, \text{height}), color lr = 0.01, opacity lr = 0.02, scale lr = 0.001, and rotation angle lr = 0.02. A specific implementation of 2D Gaussian optimization that includes clustering of sampling pixels to remove foreground/background before projection. It calculates the initial value of parameter T for supplementary Gaussians as T = \frac{7\bar{\theta}i}{\pi}, constrained to [0.01, 1.0]. Time Complexity: The optimization step is O(N) with respect to the number of Gaussians N, as Adam updates are element-wise operations on the parameter tensors. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the parameters and their first/second moment estimates. The use of settonone=True in zerograd helps mitigate memory fragmentation. Performance: Using distinct learning rates stabilizes training, preventing the rapid divergence often seen with uniform high learning rates on sensitive parameters like colors or scales. Strengths: Improves convergence stability; allows fine-tuning of geometric vs. photometric attributes independently. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of per-group rates; different variants (e.g., X-Gaussian vs. Standard 3DGS) use significantly different values, making transfer of settings non-trivial. When to use: Standard 3DGS training where stability is prioritized over speed; scenes with high dynamic range or complex lighting where color convergence is slow. When not to use: When using variants like BOGausS that require adaptive, Gaussian-dependent learning rates. The concept of parameter-specific learning rates in 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the original 3DGS paper and subsequent implementations to handle the disparate convergence speeds of different Gaussian attributes. The Adam optimizer with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, \epsilon=10^{-15} is the standard baseline. Variants like X-Gaussian and Gaussian-Flow have adapted these rates for specific domains (X-ray, 4D reconstruction), while 2D Gaussian methods extend the concept to image-space primitives. name: BOGausS Optimizer
head: Unbiased Sparse Adam Optimizer
body:
BOGausS (Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting) is a modified Stochastic Gradient Descent optimizer designed to ensure unbiased state estimation for sparsely-viewed and split Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It addresses the performance degradation caused by biased moment estimates in standard Adam when Gaussians are occluded or rarely updated. It sets itself apart by using Gaussian-dependent time steps and precision-aware scaling factors derived from reconstruction confidence intervals, rather than global iteration counts and uniform learning rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gradient 
abla	heta \mathcal{L}t for parameter 	heta at update step t; current state variables \widehat{g}{t-1}, \widehat{g}{t-1}^2, t{prev}; learning rate \eta	heta; Adam parameters  eta1,  eta2 (denoted  etas^\star); scaling factor \Delta	heta. Output: Updated parameter 	heta{t+1}; updated state variables \widehat{g}t, \widehat{g}t^2, t. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive maintains optimizer state variables independent of the global iteration counter: t: Scalar integer, representing the Gaussian's specific lifespan (number of times it has been updated). Initialized to 0. \widehat{g}: First moment estimate (mean of gradients). Vector of same shape as 	heta. Initialized to 0. \widehat{g}^2: Second moment estimate (mean of squared gradients). Vector of same shape as 	heta. Initialized to 0. Parameters: \eta	heta: Learning rate for parameter 	heta.  eta1,  eta2: Exponential decay rates for moment estimates (standard Adam values, e.g., 0.9, 0.999). \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability (standard Adam value, e.g., 10^{-8}). \Delta	heta: Scaling factor. For localization and size parameters, \Delta	heta is the confidence interval \Deltai derived from reconstruction confidence metrics. For all other parameters (e.g., opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), \Delta	heta = 1. \alphat: Inheritance factor for time during splitting. \alphag: Inheritance factor for gradient states during splitting. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Adaptive Coefficients: Calculate the time-dependent coefficients \alpha{1,t} and \alpha{2,t} based on the Gaussian's updated lifespan t \ge 1: \alpha{s,t} = \max(1/t, 1 -  etas^\star) where s \in \{1, 2\}. The coefficient uses the step count including the current update to avoid division by zero when t=0. 2. Update First Moment: \widehat{g}t = \widehat{g}{t-1} + \alpha{1,t}(
abla	heta \mathcal{L}t - \widehat{g}{t-1}) This is an exponential moving average update where the step size adapts to the Gaussian's age. (Note: The source contains a typographical error \widehat{g}{-1}; it is corrected here to \widehat{g}{t-1} to match the recursive definition.) 3. Update Second Moment: \widehat{g}t^2 = \widehat{g}{t-1}^2 + \alpha{2,t}((
abla	heta \mathcal{L}t)^2 - \widehat{g}{t-1}^2) Similarly, this maintains an unbiased estimate of the second moment. 4. Parameter Update: 	heta{t+1} = 	hetat + \eta	heta \Delta	heta  rac{\widehat{g}t}{\widehat{g}t^2 + \epsilon} The update is scaled by \Delta	heta to account for the sensitivity of the parameter to changes. 5. Increment Lifespan: t \leftarrow t + 1 The Gaussian's specific time counter is incremented only if it was updated in this pass. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: \widehat{g}0 and \widehat{g}0^2 must be exactly 0. t must be 0 for new Gaussians. Splitting: When a Gaussian splits, the child Gaussians inherit state. The time t and gradient states are scaled by inheritance factors \alphat and \alphag to maintain unbiasedness across the split. Parameterization: Size parameters \sigmaa must be linearly parameterized (	heta\sigma = \sigma). Using logarithmic parameterization (	heta\sigma = \log \sigma) is incompatible with the precision-aware update \Delta	heta and leads to instability (exploding sizes) in outdoor scenes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bogaussupdate(param, grad, state, config): """ param: current parameter value (tensor) grad: gradient of loss w.r.t param (tensor) state: dict containing 't', 'g', 'g2' for this specific Gaussian/param group config: dict containing 'eta', 'beta1', 'beta2', 'eps', 'delta' """ t = state['t'] g = state['g'] g2 = state['g2'] # Increment t for the current update step (k = t + 1) k = t + 1 # Calculate adaptive coefficients using updated lifespan to avoid 1/0 # alphast = max(1/k, 1 - betas) alpha1 = max(1.0 / k, 1.0 - config['beta1']) alpha2 = max(1.0 / k, 1.0 - config['beta2']) # Update first moment estimate # gt = g{t-1} + alpha1 (grad - g{t-1}) g = g + alpha1 (grad - g) # Update second moment estimate # g2t = g2{t-1} + alpha2 (grad^2 - g2{t-1}) g2 = g2 + alpha2 (grad grad - g2) # Parameter update # theta{t+1} = thetat + eta delta gt / (g2t + eps) update = config['eta'] config['delta'] g / (g2 + config['eps']) param = param + update # Update state state['t'] = k state['g'] = g state['g2'] = g2 return param, state SparseGaussianAdam is a sparse variant of the Adam optimizer designed specifically for 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It addresses the computational and memory inefficiency of standard Adam by applying parameter updates only to Gaussians that are visible in the current rendering pass, thereby skipping updates for occluded or out-of-view primitives. It builds on BOGausS Optimizer by integrating visibility-aware state management into the Adam update logic. Time Complexity: Per-update complexity is O(1) per active Gaussian parameter, similar to Adam. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) where N is the number of Gaussians and D is the dimensionality of the parameters being optimized. BOGausS requires maintaining per-Gaussian state variables (t, \widehat{g}, \widehat{g}^2), increasing memory overhead compared to a global optimizer state. Strengths: Prevents performance decrease and improves convergence for sparsely viewed Gaussians by ensuring unbiased state estimation. Adapts to scene content and camera setup via confidence intervals. Reduces artifacts like exploding sizes in outdoor scenes by using linear parameterization and precision-aware updates. Limitations: Higher memory footprint due to per-Gaussian state tracking. Requires careful handling of state inheritance during Gaussian splitting. Not given in the sources: specific scaling with resolution or number of Gaussians beyond the linear memory cost. BOGausS was proposed in the paper "BOGausS: Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the observation that standard Adam's biased moment estimates degrade performance when Gaussians are occluded or rarely updated (sparse viewing). The method draws inspiration from Variational Bayesian Inference to define confidence metrics on geometry reconstruction, which are then used to adapt the optimizer. It also introduces a density-preserving Gaussian splitting mechanism that allows smooth loss transition. name: SparseGaussianAdam
head: Sparse Adam for Gaussian Splatting, Sparse Gaussian Adam Optimizer
body: SparseGaussianAdam is a variant of the Adam optimizer designed for 3D Gaussian Splatting that restricts parameter updates to only those Gaussians currently visible in the rendered image. It solves the problem of biased state estimation and inefficient computation caused by sparse visibility in differentiable rendering, where most Gaussians do not contribute to the loss in any given frame. It differs from standard Adam by explicitly compensating for the learning rate bias correction based on the ratio of active parameters to total parameters, and from its parent BOGausS Optimizer by relying on a custom CUDA kernel for visibility-aware updates rather than unbiased stochastic gradient estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Parameter tensor P (shape [N, M]), gradient tensor G (shape [N, M]), visibility mask V (boolean tensor of length N, where Vi = \text{True} if Gaussian i is visible), base learning rate \eta, epsilon \epsilon, momentum coefficients \beta1, \beta2. Output: Updated parameter tensor P. Data Structures: The optimizer maintains state per parameter group. Each state entry contains: step: A scalar float32 representing the current optimization step count. expavg: A tensor of the same shape as the parameter, initialized to zeros, storing the first moment estimate. expavgsq: A tensor of the same shape as the parameter, initialized to zeros, storing the second moment estimate. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: If the state for the parameter is empty, initialize step to 0.0 (float32), expavg to a zero tensor with the same shape and memory format as the parameter, and expavgsq to a zero tensor with the same shape and memory format. 2. Increment Step: Increment the step counter: step \leftarrow step + 1. 3. Retrieve State: Retrieve expavg and expavgsq from the optimizer state. 4. Calculate Dimensions: Determine N, the number of visible Gaussians (active parameters), and M, the number of elements per Gaussian, calculated as M = \text{param.numel()} // N. Note: N is derived from the number of True values in the visibility mask. 5. Compute Effective Learning Rate: Calculate the bias-corrected effective learning rate \eta{eff}: \eta{eff} = \eta \frac{\sqrt{1 - \beta2^{step}}}{1 - \beta1^{step}} where \eta is the base learning rate, \beta1 = 0.9, and \beta2 = 0.999. 6. Apply Update: Invoke the custom CUDA kernel C.adamUpdate with the following arguments: param: The parameter tensor P. param.grad: The gradient tensor G. expavg: The first moment estimate. expavgsq: The second moment estimate. visibilitymask: The boolean mask V. lr: The effective learning rate \eta{eff}. beta1: 0.9. beta2: 0.999. eps: The epsilon value \epsilon. N: The number of visible Gaussians. M: The number of elements per Gaussian. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsegaussianadamstep(param, grad, visibilitymask, lr, eps, beta1, beta2): """ Performs one step of the SparseGaussianAdam optimizer. Args: param (torch.Tensor): The parameter tensor of shape (Ntotal, M). grad (torch.Tensor): The gradient tensor of shape (Ntotal, M). visibilitymask (torch.Tensor): Boolean tensor of shape (Ntotal,) indicating visible Gaussians. lr (float): Base learning rate. eps (float): Epsilon for numerical stability. beta1 (float): Exponential decay rate for the first moment estimates. beta2 (float): Exponential decay rate for the second moment estimates. Returns: torch.Tensor: Updated parameter tensor. """ # 1. Initialize state if empty if not hasattr(sparsegaussianadamstep, 'state'): sparsegaussianadamstep.state = {} state = sparsegaussianadamstep.state.get(id(param)) if state is None: state = { 'step': 0.0, 'expavg': torch.zeroslike(param, memoryformat=torch.preserveformat), 'expavgsq': torch.zeroslike(param, memoryformat=torch.preserveformat) } sparsegaussianadamstep.state[id(param)] = state # 2. Increment step state['step'] += 1 step = state['step'] # 3. Retrieve state expavg = state['expavg'] expavgsq = state['expavgsq'] # 4. Calculate dimensions # N is the number of visible Gaussians N = visibilitymask.sum().item() # M is the number of elements per Gaussian M = param.numel() // N # 5. Compute effective learning rate # Bias correction for Adam biascorrection1 = 1 - beta1 step biascorrection2 = 1 - beta2 step lreff = lr (biascorrection2 0.5) / biascorrection1 # 6. Apply update via CUDA kernel # The kernel handles the sparse update logic internally using the visibility mask # C.adamUpdate(param, grad, expavg, expavgsq, visibilitymask, lreff, beta1, beta2, eps, N, M) # Since we cannot call the actual C++ kernel in pure Python pseudocode, # we describe the logical update for visible elements only. # For elements where visibilitymask is False, expavg and expavgsq are NOT updated. # For elements where visibilitymask is True, standard Adam update is applied. if N > 0: # Select visible parameters and gradients visibleparam = param[visibilitymask] visiblegrad = grad[visibilitymask] visibleexpavg = expavg[visibilitymask] visibleexpavgsq = expavgsq[visibilitymask] # Standard Adam update for visible parameters # expavg = beta1 expavg + (1 - beta1) grad visibleexpavg.mul(beta1).add(visiblegrad, alpha=1 - beta1) # expavgsq = beta2 expavgsq + (1 - beta2) grad^2 visibleexpavgsq.mul(beta2).addcmul(visiblegrad, visiblegrad, value=1 - beta2) # Bias-corrected moment estimates denom = (visibleexpavgsq.sqrt() / (biascorrection2 0.5)).add(eps / biascorrection1) # Update parameters stepsize = lreff / denom visibleparam.addcdiv(visibleexpavg, denom, value=-stepsize) # Write back to full tensors param[visibilitymask] = visibleparam expavg[visibilitymask] = visibleexpavg expavgsq[visibilitymask] = visibleexpavgsq else: # No visible Gaussians, skip update pass return param Parameters: lr: Base learning rate. Typical values depend on the specific Gaussian attribute (e.g., position, rotation). eps: Epsilon for numerical stability. Passed to the update function. N: Number of visible Gaussians. Used to scale the learning rate compensation and passed to the C++ update function. M: Number of parameter elements per Gaussian (e.g., 3 for means, 4 for rotations). beta1: First moment decay rate, typically 0.9. beta2: Second moment decay rate, typically 0.999. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the parameter gradient is None or has zero elements, the step is skipped to avoid errors in state initialization or update. Precision issues may arise if N is very small, leading to unstable bias correction. The sources do not specify a minimum N threshold. The calculation of M assumes that the parameter tensor is evenly divisible by N. If N=0, division by zero occurs. The pseudocode handles this by skipping the update. GaussianAdam is a custom variant of the Adam optimizer designed specifically for 3D Gaussian Splatting that tracks per-Gaussian visibility via a last-seen step counter and maintains a learning rate history buffer for adaptive scheduling. It differs from standard Adam by explicitly managing per-Gaussian visibility and a dedicated learning rate history buffer, enabling step-dependent learning rate scheduling per Gaussian rather than a global schedule. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) per step, where N is the number of visible Gaussians and M is the number of elements per Gaussian. This is significantly faster than standard Adam (O(N{total} \cdot M)) when visibility is sparse. Memory Complexity: O(N{total} \cdot M) for storing expavg and expavgsq for all Gaussians, even if only N are visible. The sources do not specify if sparse tensors are used for the state. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of visible Gaussians. Performance improves as visibility becomes sparser. Strengths: Reduces computation by a factor of N (number of Gaussians) by only updating visible Gaussians. Compensates for learning rate bias correction in sparse updates. Limitations: Requires a custom CUDA kernel (C.adamUpdate) for efficient implementation. Not suitable for scenarios where all Gaussians are visible, as the overhead of the custom kernel may outweigh the benefits. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models with sparse visibility, such as in large scenes or early training stages. When not to use: When visibility is dense, or when a standard Adam implementation is preferred for simplicity. SparseGaussianAdam originates from the 3D Gaussian Splatting literature, specifically in implementations that optimize for training efficiency and memory usage. It is a variant of the Adam optimizer tailored to the sparse nature of Gaussian visibility in differentiable rendering. The method is used in various Gaussian Splatting training pipelines to accelerate convergence and reduce computational overhead. name: GaussianAdam Optimizer
body: GaussianAdam is a custom variant of the Adam optimizer designed specifically for 3D Gaussian Splatting that tracks per-Gaussian visibility via a last-seen step counter and maintains a learning rate history buffer for adaptive scheduling. It differs from standard Adam by explicitly managing per-Gaussian visibility and a dedicated learning rate history buffer, enabling step-dependent learning rate scheduling per Gaussian rather than a global schedule. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Parameter tensor param, gradient tensor param.grad, hyperparameters lr (base learning rate), eps (numerical stability epsilon), featurewidth (number of contiguous scalar values per Gaussian), maxsteps (buffer size), currentstep (optimization iteration). Output: Updated param tensor and updated state dictionary. Data Structures: The state dictionary contains the following fields with exact layouts: step: int64 scalar, tracking the current optimization step. expavg: float32 tensor, shape matches param, storing the first moment estimate. expavgsq: float32 tensor, shape matches param, storing the second moment estimate. lastseenstep: int32 tensor, shape (N,), where N is the number of Gaussians, storing the last step each Gaussian was visible. lrhistory: float32 tensor, shape (maxsteps,), storing the learning rate history for adaptive scheduling. Parameters: maxsteps: int, maximum optimization steps for lrhistory buffer size. lr: float, base learning rate. eps: float, epsilon for numerical stability in denominator. featurewidth: int, number of contiguous scalar values per Gaussian in the parameter group. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize state with step (int64), expavg (float32, same shape as param), expavgsq (float32, same shape as param), lastseenstep (int32, size N), and lrhistory (float32, size maxsteps). 2. Compute currentstep. 3. Ensure lrhistory has sufficient capacity for currentstep. 4. Record lr into lrhistory at index currentstep. 5. Compute visible mask based on Gaussian visibility (e.g., radii or rendering contribution). 6. Resolve featurewidth. 7. Apply the Adam update using hyperparameters 0.9, 0.999, and eps, masking updates to visible Gaussians and using lastseenstep for visibility tracking. 8. Update state['step'].fill(currentstep). name: Optimization and Parallelization
head: Distributed Training, Parallel Backpropagation, Multi-GPU 3DGS
body: This family encompasses methods that accelerate the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by parallelizing the differentiable rasterization and gradient computation across multiple processing units or optimizing the data flow for single-device efficiency. It solves the computational bottleneck of the O(N \cdot P) complexity inherent in standard alpha-blending backpropagation, where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels. It is distinguished from its siblings by its focus on architectural parallelism (multi-GPU distribution) and algorithmic restructuring (per-splat vs. per-pixel gradients) rather than just hyperparameter tuning or specific loss formulations. The methods in this family share the following foundational mechanisms: 1. Differentiable Rasterization Core: All methods rely on the differentiable alpha-blending rasterizer. The forward pass computes pixel color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) via depth-sorted alpha blending, and the backward pass computes gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. 2. Gradient Accumulation: Gradients are accumulated over multiple training steps or views before an optimizer update. In distributed settings, gradients or intermediate rendering states are synchronized across devices [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. 3. Adaptive Representation: Many optimization variants modify the Gaussian representation or its distribution to improve efficiency or fidelity, requiring corresponding adjustments to the gradient computation or data flow [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. 4. Hardware Acceleration: Methods leverage GPU parallelism, often using CUDA kernels, Tensor Cores (via GEMM reformulation), or half-precision arithmetic to accelerate the rasterization and gradient computation [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. Computes gradients for probabilistic masks \mathcal{M}i applied to Gaussians. It distinguishes itself by explicitly backpropagating through the mask modulation of both the foreground color accumulation and the background transmittance path, handling the singularity when \mathcal{M}i \alphai \to 1. The core iterative loop that initializes Gaussians and optimizes them via gradient descent. It is distinguished by its nested axis/slice loop structure and periodic refinement phases (pruning, cloning, splitting) that dynamically adapt the Gaussian count based on gradient norms and opacity thresholds. Replaces the standard per-pixel backward pass with a per-splat (per-Gaussian) approach. It partitions Gaussians into warp-sized buckets (32) to minimize atomic contention and warp stalls, yielding a 4–5× speedup while maintaining numerical equivalence. A distributed framework that partitions the Gaussian primitive list across multiple GPUs to overcome single-device memory limits. Unlike single-machine streaming solutions, it distributes the parameter table across a cluster, requiring inter-GPU communication to aggregate partial render results for correct alpha blending. Provides concrete hyperparameters and kernel-level details, including half-precision rasterization, adaptive density control thresholds (e.g., opacity < 0.05 for pruning), and scene extent calculation methods to stabilize training. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The initial implementation focused on single-GPU efficiency. Subsequent work addressed scalability: MaskGaussian introduced mask-based gradient computation for specific applications; Parallelization for Backpropagation optimized the backward kernel for single-GPU speed; Grendel-GS extended the method to multi-GPU clusters for billion-primitive scenes; and various implementation details (half-precision, adaptive density) were standardized to enable practical training. Scene Extent Calculation notes. Covariance decomposition notes.

name: MaskGaussian Gradient Computation
head: Gradient of Masks, Mask Gradient Backpropagation
body: MaskGaussian Gradient Computation is a method for computing the gradient of the loss with respect to probabilistic masks \mathcal{M}i applied to 3D Gaussians during differentiable rasterization. It solves the problem of backpropagating gradients through a masked alpha-blending process where the mask modulates the opacity of each Gaussian. It is distinguished from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting backpropagation by explicitly accounting for the gradient contribution of the mask on both the foreground Gaussian color accumulation and the background transmittance path. The method computes \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathcal{M}i} for a pixel \mathbf{x} by decomposing the pixel color into a Gaussian-contributed part and a background-contributed part, then applying the chain rule through the alpha-blending recurrence. Inputs: \mathcal{L}: The scalar loss value. \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})}: The gradient of the loss with respect to the final pixel color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) (a 3D vector). N: The number of Gaussians sorted by depth for the current pixel. For each Gaussian i \in \{1, \dots, N\}: \alphai: Opacity scalar. \mathbf{c}i: Color vector (RGB). \mathcal{M}i: Mask scalar for the i-th Gaussian. \mathbf{c}{bg}: Background color vector (RGB). T{N+1}: The final transmittance after all N Gaussians. Outputs: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathcal{M}i}: The gradient of the loss with respect to the mask \mathcal{M}i for each Gaussian i. The computation requires storing intermediate rendering states during the forward pass to be used in the backward pass. Intermediate Colors \mathbf{b}i: An array of size N+2. \mathbf{b}{N+1} = \mathbf{c}{bg} (Background color). \mathbf{b}i stores the accumulated color from Gaussian i to the last Gaussian N. \mathbf{b}1 is the final Gaussian color contribution \mathbf{c}g(\mathbf{x}). Transmittances Ti: An array of size N+1. Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \mathcal{M}j \alphaj). T1 = 1. T{N+1} is the final transmittance. 1. Forward Pass (Accumulation): Compute the intermediate colors \mathbf{b}i and transmittances Ti for i = N down to 1: \mathbf{b}i = \mathcal{M}i \alphai \mathbf{c}i + (1 - \mathcal{M}i \alphai) \mathbf{b}{i+1} Ti = T{i+1} (1 - \mathcal{M}i \alphai) \quad \text{with } T{N+1} \text{ computed as } \prod{j=1}^N (1 - \mathcal{M}j \alphaj) Note: The final transmittance T{N+1} is also used in the background gradient term. 2. Compute Gradient for Gaussian Path: For each Gaussian i from 1 to N: The gradient contribution from the Gaussian color path is derived from \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}i} = Ti \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})} and \frac{\partial \mathbf{b}i}{\partial \mathcal{M}i} = \alphai (\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{b}{i+1}). \text{Term}1 = \alphai Ti \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})} (\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{b}{i+1}) 3. Compute Gradient for Background Path: The background color is \mathbf{c}b(\mathbf{x}) = T{N+1} \mathbf{c}{bg}. The gradient of the background color with respect to the mask \mathcal{M}i is: \frac{\partial \mathbf{c}b(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \mathcal{M}i} = \frac{-\alphai T{N+1}}{1 - \mathcal{M}i \alphai} \mathbf{c}{bg} The contribution to the loss gradient is: \text{Term}2 = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})} \cdot \left( \frac{-\alphai T{N+1}}{1 - \mathcal{M}i \alphai} \mathbf{c}{bg} \right) Note: This term represents the change in the amount of background visible due to the masking of the i-th Gaussian. 4. Combine Gradients: The total gradient for mask \mathcal{M}i is the sum of the two terms: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathcal{M}i} = \text{Term}1 + \text{Term}2 \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathcal{M}i} = \alphai Ti \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})} (\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{b}{i+1}) - \frac{\alphai T{N+1}}{1 - \mathcal{M}i \alphai} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})} \mathbf{c}{bg} \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}): Final pixel color. \mathbf{c}g(\mathbf{x}): Color contributed by Gaussians, equal to \mathbf{b}1. \mathbf{c}b(\mathbf{x}): Color contributed by background, equal to T{N+1} \mathbf{c}{bg}. \mathbf{b}i: Intermediate color from Gaussian i to N. \mathbf{b}{N+1}: Background color \mathbf{c}{bg}. Ti: Transmittance up to (but not including) Gaussian i. T1 = 1. T{N+1}: Final transmittance after all Gaussians. \mathcal{M}i: Mask value for Gaussian i. \alphai: Opacity of Gaussian i. \mathbf{c}i: Color of Gaussian i. \mathbf{c}{bg}: Background color. \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})}: Gradient of loss w.r.t. pixel color. \lambdam: A weighting parameter for the mask gradient loss term. Value: 0.1. Used during training iterations 19,000 to 20,000. Division by Zero: The term \frac{1}{1 - \mathcal{M}i \alphai} in the background gradient path becomes undefined if \mathcal{M}i \alphai = 1. In practice, \alphai is often clamped or \mathcal{M}i is constrained to prevent this singularity. If \mathcal{M}i \alphai \to 1, the transmittance T{i+1} goes to 0, and the background contribution vanishes, but the derivative requires careful handling or epsilon addition. Precision: The product of transmittances Ti can underflow to zero for deep scenes with many opaque Gaussians. Standard epsilon guards for transmittance should be applied. Ordering: Gaussians must be sorted by depth for the alpha-blending recurrence to be valid. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemaskgradients( dLdc: Vector3, # Gradient of loss w.r.t. pixel color alphas: List[float], # Opacities alphai colors: List[Vector3], # Colors ci masks: List[float], # Masks Mi cbg: Vector3, # Background color N: int # Number of Gaussians) -> List[float]: """ Computes dL/dMi for all i in 1..N. Assumes Gaussians are sorted by depth. """ # Initialize arrays b = [Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] (N + 2) T = [0.0] (N + 2) # Forward pass: Compute intermediate colors bi and transmittances Ti # b[N+1] is background b[N + 1] = cbg # Compute T[N+1] first for the background gradient term # T[N+1] = product{j=1 to N} (1 - Mj alphaj) T[N + 1] = 1.0 for j in range(N): T[N + 1] = (1.0 - masks[j] alphas[j]) # Compute b[i] and T[i] from N down to 1 # T[i] is transmittance BEFORE Gaussian i # b[i] is color accumulated FROM Gaussian i onwards for i in range(N - 1, -1, -1): # T[i] = T[i+1] (1 - Mi alphai) # Note: T array index i corresponds to Gaussian i+1 in 0-indexed list # Let's align indices: Gaussian i (1-based) is index i-1 in lists # T[i] in formula is transmittance before Gaussian i # T[N+1] is after Gaussian N # Formula: Ti = prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - Mj alphaj) # We can compute T[i] (transmittance before Gaussian i) from T[i+1] # T[i] = T[i+1] / (1 - Mi alphai) ? No, T[i+1] = T[i] (1 - Mi alphai) # So T[i] = T[i+1] / (1 - Mi alphai) is risky if denominator is 0. # Better: Compute T[i] iteratively from T[1]=1 or T[N+1] backwards? # The formula for gradient uses Ti (transmittance before Gaussian i). # Let's compute T[i] for i=1..N+1. pass # Re-do forward pass carefully with indices # T[k] stores transmittance before Gaussian k (1-based) # T[1] = 1.0 # T[k+1] = T[k] (1 - Mk alphak) Tarr = [0.0] (N + 2) Tarr[1] = 1.0 for i in range(1, N + 1): idx = i - 1 # 0-based index for masks/alphas/colors Tarr[i + 1] = Tarr[i] (1.0 - masks[idx] alphas[idx]) # b[k] stores color from Gaussian k to N # b[N+1] = cbg # b[k] = Mk alphak ck + (1 - Mk alphak) b[k+1] barr = [Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] (N + 2) barr[N + 1] = cbg for i in range(N, 0, -1): idx = i - 1 alpha = alphas[idx] c = colors[idx] m = masks[idx] barr[i] = m alpha c + (1.0 - m alpha) barr[i + 1] # Backward pass: Compute gradients dLdM = [0.0] N for i in range(1, N + 1): idx = i - 1 alpha = alphas[idx] c = colors[idx] m = masks[idx] Ti = Tarr[i] TNplus1 = Tarr[N + 1] biplus1 = barr[i + 1] # Term 1: Gradient from Gaussian color path # dL/dMigauss = alphai Ti dL/dc (ci - b{i+1}) term1 = alpha Ti dLdc (c - biplus1) # Term 2: Gradient from Background path # dL/dMibg = dL/dc ( - alphai T{N+1} / (1 - Mi alphai) cbg) # Guard against division by zero denom = 1.0 - m alpha if abs(denom) < 1e-8: # If denom is 0, the mask fully blocks the Gaussian. # The background term derivative is singular. # In practice, this case implies T{i+1} = 0, so background is 0. # The gradient w.r.t mask for background is 0 if background is 0? # Actually, if Mi alphai = 1, then T{i+1} = 0. # The term is -alpha T{N+1} / 0. # If T{N+1} is also 0, it's 0/0. # We assume epsilon guard denom = 1e-8 term2 = dLdc (-alpha TNplus1 / denom cbg) dLdM[idx] = term1 + term2 return dLdM The overall training loop that utilizes these gradients. Training Pipeline Methods for distributing the gradient computation across multiple GPUs or pixels. Parallelization for Backpropagation A sibling method that also modifies the Gaussian representation for efficiency, but uses a different pruning strategy. Grendel-GS The base rasterization and parameterization details that MaskGaussian builds upon. 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of Gaussians covering the pixel. This is the same complexity as standard 3D Gaussian Splatting backpropagation, as it involves a single pass forward and a single pass backward. Memory Complexity: O(N) per pixel to store intermediate colors \mathbf{b}i and transmittances Ti for the backward pass. This requires storing these values during the forward rasterization step. Performance: The method adds minimal computational overhead compared to standard 3DGS backpropagation, primarily due to the additional arithmetic in the background gradient term. Strengths: Allows for differentiable mask optimization, enabling adaptive Gaussian pruning and representation refinement during training. Limitations: Requires careful handling of the singularity when \mathcal{M}i \alphai \approx 1. The background gradient term can be numerically unstable if not guarded. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models with adaptive mask-based pruning or representation learning, specifically when the mask values are trainable parameters. When not to use: For standard 3DGS training without mask optimization, or when the background is not explicitly modeled as a separate color component. MaskGaussian was introduced in the paper "MaskGaussian: Adaptive 3D Gaussian Representation from Probabilistic Masks". The method extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by introducing probabilistic masks that modulate Gaussian opacity. The gradient computation for these masks was omitted from the main manuscript for brevity but is detailed in the supplementary material. The method is compared against LightGaussian, which compresses trained models, whereas MaskGaussian applies pruning during training from scratch, specifically using the mask gradient optimization between iterations 19,000 and 20,000 with a weight \lambdam = 0.1. name: Training Pipeline
head: 3DGS Learning, Full Training Procedure, G Splats, Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization, Inner 3D Gaussian Splatting Training, Iterative optimization loop, Main Training Loop
body:
The Training Pipeline is the iterative optimization loop for 3D Gaussian Splatting that initializes a set of 3D Gaussians and optimizes their parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color) via gradient descent. It solves the problem of reconstructing a 3D scene from 2D observations by dynamically adapting the Gaussian representation through pruning, cloning, and splitting. It is distinguished from its siblings by its core structure: a nested loop over spatial axes and slices that accumulates gradients across multiple views before a single optimizer step, coupled with periodic refinement phases that modify the Gaussian count. The pipeline operates as a standard differentiable rendering training loop, but with specific data organization (axis-aligned slices) and dynamic topology management. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of training slices D = \{(Ii^{	ext{axis}}, \pii^{	ext{axis}})\}, where 	ext{axis} \in \{x, y, z\}, I is a 2D slice image, and \pi is the slice position. Input: Initial Gaussian parameters 	heta, typically initialized on a regular 3D grid of resolution g{	ext{res}} or from SfM points. Input: Hyperparameters: opacity threshold 	au\alpha, gradient threshold 	aup, scale threshold 	aus, and maximum iterations T{	ext{max}}. Output: Optimized set of Gaussians G = \{( oldsymbol{\mu},  oldsymbol{\Sigma}, \mathbf{c}, \alpha)\}. Data Structures: Gaussian State (G): Each Gaussian n is defined by mean  oldsymbol{\mu}n, covariance  oldsymbol{\Sigma}n, color \mathbf{c}n, and opacity \alphan. The covariance is decomposed into rotation Rn and scale Sn such that  oldsymbol{\Sigma}n = Rn Sn Sn^	op Rn^	op. Optimizer State: Adam optimizer state for parameters 	heta. Loss Accumulators: Scalar L{	ext{total}} and gradient tensor 
abla	heta. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Build a regular grid P of size g{	ext{res}} (or use SfM points). Initialize each Gaussian with mean  oldsymbol{\mu} around grid points and default values for scale s, color c, opacity \alpha, and quaternion q. 2. Optimizer Setup: Initialize the Adam optimizer with parameters 	heta and learning rate \eta. 3. Outer Loop: Iterate from step t = 1 to T{	ext{max}}. 4. Reset Accumulators: Set total loss L{	ext{total}} \leftarrow 0 and zero gradients 
abla	heta \leftarrow 0. 5. Axis Loop: Iterate over axes 	ext{axis} \in \{x, y, z\}. 6. Slice Loop: For each slice (Ii^{	ext{axis}}, \pii^{	ext{axis}}) in the dataset D{	ext{axis}}: a. Covariance Computation: Compute 3D covariance  oldsymbol{\Sigma}n \leftarrow Rn Sn Sn^	op Rn^	op. b. Rendering: Rasterize the Gaussian parameters to predict the image I{	ext{pred}} \leftarrow 	ext{Rasterize}( oldsymbol{\mu}n,  oldsymbol{\Sigma}n, \alphan, \mathbf{c}n). c. Loss Computation: Compute loss L between predicted image I{	ext{pred}} and ground truth slice Ii^{	ext{axis}}. d. Accumulate Loss: L{	ext{total}} \leftarrow L{	ext{total}} + L. 7. Backpropagation: Perform backward pass on L{	ext{total}} to compute gradients 
abla	heta. 8. Parameter Update: Update parameters 	heta using the Adam optimizer step. 9. Refinement Check: If the current step is a refinement iteration (determined by schedule IsRefinementIteration(t)): a. Gaussian Iteration: Iterate over all Gaussians ( oldsymbol{\mu},  oldsymbol{\Sigma}, \mathbf{c}, \alpha) \in G. b. Pruning Condition: If opacity \alpha < 	au\alpha or the Gaussian is too large (IsTooLarge( oldsymbol{\mu},  oldsymbol{\Sigma})), remove the Gaussian. c. Densification Condition: Else if the L2 norm of the gradient of  oldsymbol{\mu} with respect to loss is greater than 	aup (\|
abla{ oldsymbol{\mu}} L\|2 > 	aup): i. Over-reconstruction Check: If the Frobenius norm of  oldsymbol{\Sigma} is greater than 	aus (\| oldsymbol{\Sigma}\|F > 	aus), split the Gaussian. ii. Under-reconstruction Action: Else, clone the Gaussian. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Initialization # Build regular grid P of size gridresolution # Initialize Gaussians G with mean mu around grid points # Default values for scale s, color c, opacity alpha, quaternion q G = [] for point in buildregulargrid(gridresolution): G.append(Gaussian(mu=point, s=defaultscale, c=defaultcolor, alpha=defaultopacity, q=defaultquaternion)) # 2. Optimizer Setup # Initialize Adam optimizer with parameters theta and learning rate eta optimizer = Adam(parameters=G, lr=initiallr) # 3. Outer Loop for step in range(1, maxiterations + 1): # Resolution schedule if step < 5000: resolution = (540, 960) else: resolution = (1080, 1920) # 4. Reset Accumulators Ltotal = 0.0 optimizer.zerograd() # 5. Axis Loop for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: # 6. Slice Loop axisslices = [s for s in trainingslices if s.axis == axis] for sliceimage, slicepos in axisslices: # 6a. Covariance Computation for g in G: g.Sigma = g.R @ (g.S @ g.S.T) @ g.R.T # Rn Sn Sn^T Rn^T # 6b. Rendering # Ipred = Rasterize(mu, Sigma, alpha, c) # Rasterize projects Gaussians to 2D slice view Ipred = rasterize(G, slicepos, axis, resolution) # 6c. Loss Computation # L = lambda1L1 + lambda2(1-SSIM) + lambda3VGG + lambda4LPIPS L = computeloss(Ipred, sliceimage) # 6d. Accumulate Loss Ltotal += L # 7. Backpropagation Ltotal.backward() # 8. Parameter Update optimizer.step() # 9. Refinement Check if isrefinementiteration(step): gaussianstoremove = [] gaussianstosplit = [] gaussianstoclone = [] # 9a. Gaussian Iteration for g in G: # 9b. Pruning Condition if g.alpha < alphathreshold or istoolarge(g.mu, g.Sigma): gaussianstoremove.append(g) # 9c. Densification Condition elif norm(g.gradmu) > gradientthreshold: # 9c-i. Over-reconstruction Check if frobeniusnorm(g.Sigma) > scalethreshold: gaussianstosplit.append(g) # 9c-ii. Under-reconstruction Action else: gaussianstoclone.append(g) # 9b. Pruning Action for g in gaussianstoremove: G.remove(g) # 9c-i. Split Action for g in gaussianstosplit: splitgaussian(G, g) # 9c-ii. Clone Action for g in gaussianstoclone: clonegaussian(G, g) return G def buildregulargrid(res):... # Not given in the sources. def rasterize(G, pos, axis, res):... # Calls differentiable alpha-blending rasterizer def computeloss(Ipred, Igt): return L1 + SSIM # Standard loss def istoolarge(mu, Sigma): return frobeniusnorm(Sigma) > somethreshold # def norm(v): return sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) def frobeniusnorm(M): return sqrt(sum(M[i][j]2 for i in range(3) for j in range(3))) def splitgaussian(G, g):... # Not given in the sources. def clonegaussian(G, g):... # Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The covariance decomposition  oldsymbol{\Sigma} = R S S^	op R^	op requires stable rotation representations (quaternions) to avoid singularities. Boundaries: The axis-loop structure assumes the scene can be adequately covered by orthogonal slices. If the scene has strong depth-dependent structures not aligned with axes, coverage may be uneven. Degenerate Input: If the initial grid resolution g{	ext{res}} is too low, the model may fail to capture fine details; if too high, training becomes computationally expensive and prone to overfitting. The Mini-Splatting Pipeline is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that explicitly manages the total number of Gaussians through periodic densification, simplification, and depth-based reinitialization phases. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by enforcing a constrained Gaussian count via a manually controlled sampling ratio. This method computes quantitative validation metrics (primarily PSNR) and saves visual examples by rendering novel views from the optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting model and comparing them against ground truth images. It is distinct from the training loop as it operates in evaluation mode (istrain=False) with gradient tracking disabled, ensuring that the optimization state is not updated during metric calculation. The FaCT-GS optimization loop extends the standard pipeline by adding a 3D total variation (TV) regularization term. It rasterizes Gaussians into a 2D image \mathbf{I}r and compares it to projection data \mathbf{I}{gt} using L1 and SSIM losses. Additionally, it voxelize a small, randomly sampled section of the volume \mathbf{V}{px3} and calculates 3D total variation \mathcal{L}{TV} as a homogeneity regularization prior. The total loss is \mathcal{C}{	ext{total}} = \mathcal{L}1 (\mathbf{I}1, \mathbf{I}{	ext{tet}}) + \alpha{	ext{SSIM}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{SSIM}} (\mathbf{I}1, \mathbf{I}{	ext{tet}}) + \alpha{	ext{TV}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{TV}} (\mathbf{V}{32^3}), where \alpha{	ext{SSIM}} and \alpha{	ext{TV}} are SSIM and TV loss weights respectively. In the backward pass, the loss is used to prune, clone, or split Gaussians (Adaptive Control) and adjust parameters based on propagated gradients. The sampling size for voxelization is increased from 8^3 to 32^3. The Cut-Set Gradient Update method modifies the standard gradient accumulation by identifying the "cut set" of Gaussians intersecting the current training view and updating only their parameters. Gradients propagate to Gaussians in the middle of the hierarchy, diffusing across the entire structure over many iterations with diverse views. This approach is used to fulfill tight memory requirements in large-scale reconstruction. This variant initializes the model using LiDAR point clouds and pseudo-view guidance. It projects LiDAR frames to corresponding image frames to assign color to each LiDAR point, then re-projects colored points into 3D space. It accumulates all frames of point clouds and voxel-downsamples with a voxel size of 5. The training schedule includes a warm-up phase of 500 iterations without sampling pseudo views, followed by a guided phase where 4 pseudo views are sampled for every 10 iterations. Total training iterations are 50,000. This strategy adapts the training pipeline for functional MRI (fMRI) data by freezing geometry parameters (Gaussian positions and covariances) and allowing only color and opacity to vary over time. It uses a two-stage strategy: Stage 1 builds a static anatomical structure over 1000 warm-up iterations using initial frames; Stage 2 runs 3000 iterations where only color and opacity evolve temporally. It processes datasets like OpenfMRI (160 temporal frames, 33 axial brain slices at 64x64 resolution) with 140 frames for training and every 8th frame (20 total) for testing. A custom data loader ensures all slices from a given timestamp are processed synchronously to preserve inter-slice consistency. This strategy includes background Gaussians in rendering computation but keeps them fixed during optimization. It initializes foreground Gaussians using the filtered point cloud generated during segmentation. It confines foreground Gaussians to the spherical volume defined by inner radius Ri. It optimizes foreground Gaussians using standard 3D Gaussian Splatting loss on original unmasked images. It performs spatial pruning: deletes any foreground Gaussian that moves beyond the inner radius Ri. Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the rasterization and backpropagation steps, which are linear in the number of Gaussians N and pixels P per slice. The nested loop over axes and slices multiplies this by the number of slices S, resulting in O(S \cdot N \cdot P) per iteration. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of Gaussians N and their parameters (position, covariance, color, opacity). The cut-set variant reduces memory by only storing gradients for the cut set. Measured Performance: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training typically runs for 30,000 iterations. fMRI adaptation uses 4,000 total iterations (1,000 warm-up + 3,000 temporal). Strengths: Dynamic adaptation allows the model to start with a coarse representation and refine it, balancing efficiency and fidelity. Limitations: The axis-slice structure may not be optimal for all scene geometries. The refinement steps (pruning/splitting) add overhead and require careful tuning of thresholds 	au\alpha, 	aup, 	aus. When to use: Use for general 3D scene reconstruction from multi-view images or slices. Use FaCT-GS for CT reconstruction where homogeneity is desired. Use fMRI adaptation for temporal medical imaging. The Training Pipeline originates from the 3D Gaussian Splatting method by Kerbl et al. [2023], which introduced differentiable rasterization for 3D Gaussians. The specific inner loop structure with axis-aligned slices and dynamic densification/pruning was detailed in subsequent works such as InnerGS and FaCT-GS. The method has been adapted for various domains including fMRI, CT, and large-scale reconstruction.
