name: Mini-Splatting Pipeline
body: The Mini-Splatting Pipeline is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that explicitly manages the total number of Gaussians through periodic densification, simplification, and depth-based reinitialization phases. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by enforcing a constrained Gaussian count via a manually controlled sampling ratio. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, camera poses, and multi-view images. Output: A set of optimized 3D Gaussians and, for the compression variant, a compressed model representation. Data Structures: The pipeline maintains a dynamic list of Gaussians. Each Gaussian g is defined by standard 3D Gaussian Splatting attributes: center \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or rotation quaternion \mathbf{q} and scale vector), opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}. Parameters: DensificationIteration: 15,000. SimplificationIteration1: 15,000. SimplificationIteration2: 20,000. Depth Reinitialization Interval: Every 5,000 iterations. Sampling Ratio: Manually controlled parameter affecting the final Gaussian count; high ratios may cause background distortion. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the set of Gaussians from SfM points. Set iteration counter i = 0. 2. Loop: While not converged: a. Render and Loss: Render the current Gaussian set and compute loss against ground truth images. b. Densification: If i is a multiple of DensificationIteration (15K), perform densification. The design of importance metrics for this step is case-dependent and hand-crafted, presented as an experimental trick in the appendix. c. Depth Reinitialization: If i is a multiple of 5,000, perform depth-based reinitialization. d. Simplification: If i = \text{SimplificationIteration1} (15K), perform simplification. If i = \text{SimplificationIteration2} (20K), perform simplification again. e. Increment: i \leftarrow i + 1. Variants: Mini-Splatting-D: Disables the simplification process entirely. Mini-Splatting-C: Applies compression to the trained model. Gaussian centers are stored as float32. Other attributes (scales, SH coefficients) are processed using Region-adaptive Hierarchical Transform (RHT) [6] with a depth level of 16 and a quantization step of 0.02. The transformed coefficients are then losslessly compressed using numpy.savezcompressed(). Pitfalls: Sky Areas: The depth-based reinitialization strategy fails in areas without reliable depth values, such as the sky. Background Distortion: A high sampling ratio leads to distortion in the background. Manual Tuning: The number of Gaussians is manually controlled by the sampling ratio, and finding the minimal number for high-quality rendering remains a challenge. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minisplattingpipeline(sfmpoints, images, cameraposes): # Initialize Gaussians from SfM points gaussians = initializefromsfm(sfmpoints) i = 0 densificationinterval = 15000 simplificationiter1 = 15000 simplificationiter2 = 20000 reinitinterval = 5000 while not converged(): # Standard 3DGS differentiable rasterization and loss computation # renderedimages = rasterize(gaussians, cameraposes) # loss = computeloss(renderedimages, images) # loss.backward() if i % densificationinterval == 0: # Importance metrics are case-dependent and hand-crafted # gaussians = densifygaussians(gaussians) if i % reinitinterval == 0: # Fails in sky regions without reliable depth values # gaussians = depthreinitializegaussians(gaussians) if i == simplificationiter1: # gaussians = simplifygaussians(gaussians) if i == simplificationiter2: # gaussians = simplifygaussians(gaussians) i += 1 return gaussians Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, Mini-Splatting achieves the following metrics: SSIM: bicycle 0.772, flowers 0.626, garden 0.847, stump 0.806, treehill 0.654, room 0.921, counter 0.904, kitchen 0.926, bonsai 0.940, truck 0.874, train 0.796, johnson 0.912, playroom 0.912. PSNR: bicycle 25.15, flowers 21.58, garden 26.84, stump 27.26, treehill 22.72, room 31.39, counter 28.41, kitchen 31.17, bonsai 31.57, truck 25.09, train 21.28, johnson 29.47, playroom 30.49. LPIPS: bicycle 0.225, flowers 0.327, garden 0.150, stump 0.199, treehill 0.312, room 0.211, counter 0.199, kitchen 0.130, bonsai 0.199, truck 0.159, train 0.245, johnson 0.257, playroom 0.250. Comparison: Mini-Splatting demonstrates consistent improvement compared to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in most scans and surpasses Zip-NeRF in SSIM and LPIPS metrics on certain datasets. Strengths: Reduced Gaussian count leads to lower memory usage. The compression variant (Mini-Splatting-C) further reduces storage size. Limitations: Manual tuning of the sampling ratio is required. Depth-based reinitialization fails in sky regions. High sampling ratios can distort backgrounds. Mini-Splatting was introduced in the paper "Mini-Splatting: Representing Scenes with a Constrained Number of Gaussians". It builds on the foundational 3D Gaussian Splatting framework Parent. name: Validation Metric Computation & Logging
head: Testing Loop Evaluation, Validation Metric Computation, Validation Metrics
body: This method computes quantitative validation metrics (primarily PSNR) between rendered novel views and ground truth images, and saves example outputs for visual inspection. It operates in evaluation mode with gradient tracking disabled, distinguishing it from the training optimization loop. Inputs: Model parameters and scene data containing training and testing camera poses. testingiterations: List of iterations at which validation metrics are computed and logged. Outputs: Mean PSNR score for test and training subsets. Saved JPEG images of rendered novel views. Data Structures: psnrlist: List of floating-point PSNR values collected during the validation pass. validationconfigs: Dictionary mapping configuration names ('test', 'train') to camera lists. Steps: 1. Setup: Clear the CUDA cache. Initialize psnrlist as empty. Select one random index showidx for visualization. 2. Trigger: Check if the current training iteration exists in testingiterations. If not, skip validation. 3. Configuration: Define validationconfigs with two entries: 'test' using all cameras from scene.getTestCameras(), and 'train' using 5 evenly spaced cameras from scene.getTrainCameras() at indices 5 to 30 with a step of 5. 4. Iteration Loop: For each camera index in the selected configuration: a. Fetch data for the view. Move all tensors to the GPU. b. Run the model forward pass with istrain=False inside a gradient-disabled context. c. Render the novel view. Apply background color compositing if applicable. d. Metric Computation: Clamp the rendered image and ground truth to [0.0, 1.0]. Compute the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) between the rendered image I{render} and ground truth I{gt}: \text{PSNR} = 10 \cdot \log{10} \left( \frac{1}{\text{MSE}(I{render}, I{gt})} \right) where \text{MSE}(I{render}, I{gt}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (I{render,i} - I{gt,i})^2 and N is the number of pixels. Accumulate PSNR (and L1 loss if required) across cameras. Append the PSNR value to psnrlist. e. Visualization: If the current index equals showidx: detach the tensor from the computation graph, multiply pixel values by 255, permute dimensions from CHW to HWC, convert to a NumPy array, and save as a JPEG file. 5. Aggregation: Compute the mean of psnrlist. Round the result to 4 decimal places. If the mean PSNR is less than 10, print an error message and exit. Log the final PSNR to the logger. gtclamped) 2) # if mse == 0: psnrval = 100.0 # else: psnrval = 10 math.log10(1.0 / mse) # currentpsnrlist.append(psnrval) # # 4d: Visualization if idx == showidx: # imgtensor = renderedimg.detach() 255 # imgtensor = imgtensor.permute(1, 2, 0).cpu().numpy() # cv2.imwrite(f"validation{configname}{idx}.jpg", imgtensor[:,:,::-1].astype(np.uint8)) # # Step 5: Aggregation meanpsnr = sum(currentpsnrlist) / len(currentpsnrlist) # meanpsnr = round(meanpsnr, 4) # if meanpsnr < 10: # logger.error(f"Validation PSNR too low: {meanpsnr}") exit() logger.info(f"{configname} PSNR: {meanpsnr}") # Parameters: testingiterations: List of integers specifying training iterations to run validation. bgcolor: Background color used for compositing transparent renders (default 0.0). Edge Cases: MSE = 0: If the rendered image is identical to the ground truth, PSNR is undefined due to \log(0). Assign a high constant (e.g., 100.0). Empty Camera Lists: If a configuration returns zero cameras, skip the loop or raise an error. Index Out of Bounds: When selecting training camera indices, ensure they do not exceed the list length. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Validation runs only at specified iterations, not every step. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The CUDA cache is cleared before execution to manage memory. Strengths: Provides objective quantitative feedback (PSNR) and visual sanity checks (saved JPEGs). Limitations: Computationally expensive if validation iterations are frequent. This procedure is part of the training loop for differentiable rendering implementations, specifically noted in repositories handling stereo matching and novel view synthesis. It builds on the general rasterization and optimization loop defined in Training Pipeline. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Initialization & Training Schedule
head: LiDAR-guided 3DGS Training, Pseudo-view Guided 3DGS Training
body: This method defines the initialization and iterative training schedule for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models, specifically addressing robust initialization via LiDAR data and regularization via pseudo-view guidance. It solves the problem of poor initialization and training instability in sparse or unstructured scenes by combining geometric priors with diffusion-based regularization. It differs from standard 3DGS pipelines by explicitly integrating LiDAR point cloud processing for initialization and a staged pseudo-view sampling schedule for training stability. The method consists of two distinct phases: Initialization and Training Schedule. The specific implementation details vary between the LiDAR-guided approach and the improved optimization pipeline. The initialization process converts sparse LiDAR data into a dense set of 3D Gaussians. 1. Color Assignment: Project each LiDAR point from the frame to the corresponding image frame to retrieve its color. 2. Re-projection: Re-project the colored LiDAR points back into 3D space to create a colored 3D point cloud. 3. Accumulation: Accumulate point clouds from all available frames. 4. Voxel Downsampling: Apply voxel downsampling to the accumulated points with a voxel size of 5 to reduce density and remove outliers. 5. Gaussian Initialization: Initialize the 3D Gaussian model parameters (positions \mu, covariances \Sigma, colors, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients) from the downsampled point cloud. Covariances are typically initialized based on the local point density or a fixed small value, and opacity is set to a low initial value (e.g., 0.1) to allow for densification during training. The training is performed using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for a total of 50,000 iterations. The schedule is divided into two phases: 1. Warm-up Phase: Train for the first 500 iterations without sampling pseudo views. This allows the model to stabilize based on the real input images. 2. Guided Phase: For every 10 iterations, sample 4 pseudo views. These pseudo views are rendered from the current 3DGS model and used to generate guidance images via a fine-tuned Diffusion Model. Pseudo-view Generation: Render random views not present in the training set. Diffusion Guidance: The rendered pseudo-view is encoded into a latent feature map by a VAE Encoder. Noise at level t \sim [t{min}, t{max}] is added. The Diffusion Model denoises the latent feature from level t to t{min}, and the result is decoded to generate a guidance image. Classifier-Free Guidance: To enable classifier-free guidance, text prompts and reference images are set to empty with a 10% probability during training. Parameters: Set t{max} = 10. An alternative schedule uses Adam optimization with a Cosine Annealing Learning Rate schedule. 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians G with positions \mu, covariances \Sigma, colors C, opacity \alpha, and SH coefficients. Set initial learning rate LR{initial} and CosineAnnealingLR schedule. 2. Iterative Loop: Run for 30,000 iterations. 3. Resolution Switching: If iteration t < 5,000: Render at low resolution Rt = (540, 960). If iteration t \ge 5,000: Render at high resolution Rt = (1080, 1920). 4. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss L as a weighted sum of components: L = \lambda1 L1 + \lambda2 (1 - SSIM) + \lambda3 VGG + \lambda4 LPIPS where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3, \lambda4 are the weights for L1, SSIM, VGG, and LPIPS losses respectively. 5. Gradient Update: Compute gradients \nabla L with respect to Gaussian parameters and update parameters using Adam and the current learning rate from the CosineAnnealingLR schedule. 6. Adaptive Pruning: For each Gaussian Gi: If opacity \alphai < 0.005 or the size of covariance \Sigmai exceeds a threshold, remove Gi from G. 7. Improved Densification: For each Gaussian Gi: If gradient magnitude \nabla L(Gi) > \tau: If size of \Sigmai > \tauS: Split Gi into G{new} with \Sigma{new} = 0.8 \Sigmai. Else: Clone G{new} at \mui + \text{noise}(\sigma). Add G{new} to G. 8. Optimized Spherical Harmonics: Compute SH-to-RGB conversion outside the rasterizer for each Gi to improve performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def train3dgslidarguided(LiDARframes, Imageframes, DiffusionModel, VAE, numiterations=50000): # 1. Initialization coloredpoints = [] for frame in LiDARframes: # Project LiDAR to image to get color pointswithcolor = projectlidartoimage(frame.LiDARpoints, frame.Image) # Re-project to 3D points3d = reprojectto3d(pointswithcolor) coloredpoints.extend(points3d) # Voxel downsampling with voxel size 5 initialpoints = voxeldownsample(coloredpoints, voxelsize=5) # Initialize Gaussians from points gaussians = initializegaussians(initialpoints) # 2. Training Schedule for t in range(1, numiterations + 1): if t <= 500: # Warm-up phase: no pseudo views loss = computeloss(gaussians, Imageframes) else: # Guided phase: sample 4 pseudo views every 10 iterations if t % 10 == 0: pseudoviews = samplepseudoviews(gaussians, numviews=4) guidanceimages = [] for view in pseudoviews: # Render pseudo view renderedlatent = VAE.encode(render(view)) # Add noise noisylatent = addnoise(renderedlatent, tnoise=random.uniform(tmin, 10)) # Denoise and decode denoisedlatent = DiffusionModel.denoise(noisylatent, tnoise) guidanceimage = VAE.decode(denoisedlatent) guidanceimages.append(guidanceimage) loss = computelosswithguidance(gaussians, Imageframes, guidanceimages) else: loss = computeloss(gaussians, Imageframes) # Update parameters updategaussians(gaussians, loss) return gaussians A variant that replaces SGD with Adam and introduces a resolution switch and adaptive densification/pruning. It uses a total of 30,000 iterations, switching from low resolution (540x960) to high resolution (1080x1920) at iteration 5,000. It employs a composite loss function with L1, SSIM, VGG, and LPIPS components, and optimizes spherical harmonics computation outside the rasterizer. Time Complexity: The LiDAR-guided method adds an initialization cost proportional to the number of LiDAR points and frames. The training cost is dominated by the rasterization and diffusion guidance. Sampling pseudo views every 10 iterations adds a constant overhead. The improved pipeline reduces training time by using lower resolution for the first 5,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians. Voxel downsampling reduces initial memory usage. Adaptive pruning removes low-opacity Gaussians, reducing memory over time. Strengths: LiDAR initialization provides robust geometric priors, reducing artifacts in sparse regions. Pseudo-view guidance regularizes training, improving generalization to unseen views. Resolution switching accelerates early training. Limitations: Requires LiDAR data for initialization in the LiDAR-guided variant. Diffusion guidance adds significant computational overhead during training. The schedule parameters (e.g., 500 warm-up, 10 iteration interval) are specific to the cited implementations and may need tuning for other datasets. The LiDAR-guided initialization and pseudo-view training schedule was introduced in "SGD: Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior". The improved optimization pipeline with Adam and resolution switching was proposed in "Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Accurate Image Reconstruction". These methods build upon the original 3D Gaussian Splatting framework Parent to address initialization quality and training efficiency. name: Parallelization for Backpropagation
head: Per-splat Backpropagation
body: Parallelization for Backpropagation is a training optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the standard per-pixel backward pass with a per-splat (per-Gaussian) approach to accelerate gradient computation. While the standard method computes gradients by iterating over pixels and accumulating contributions from visible Gaussians using atomic operations, this method iterates over Gaussians and updates the gradients of the pixels they cover. This shift addresses the performance bottleneck of atomic contention in the per-pixel approach, where splats contributing to arbitrary numbers of pixels require frequent global memory synchronization. It yields a 4–5× reduction in training time while maintaining numerical equivalence to the original backpropagation. The method restructures the backward pass to operate on fixed-size buckets of Gaussians, typically aligned with GPU warp sizes (e.g., 32 Gaussians), to minimize warp stalls and false sharing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the camera parameters for the current view, and the gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered pixel colors \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}}. Output: The accumulated gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} for all Gaussian parameters \theta (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: Gaussian Bucket: A contiguous block of 32 Gaussians (one warp) processed in parallel. Gradient Buffer: A pre-allocated buffer for \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} for the current bucket, initialized to zero. Pixel Gradient Cache: Temporary storage for \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}} values, accessed via the rasterization order. Steps: 1. Sort and Rasterize: Perform the forward pass to determine the depth-sorted order of Gaussians for each pixel. Store the list of visible Gaussians per pixel or, more efficiently for the backward pass, the list of pixels covered by each Gaussian (or use a tile-based approach where Gaussians are projected to screen space). 2. Bucket Assignment: Partition the N Gaussians into buckets of size W=32 (warp size). 3. Parallel Gradient Accumulation: For each bucket: a. Initialize local gradient accumulators for the parameters of the Gaussians in the bucket. b. For each Gaussian gi in the bucket: i. Compute the Jacobian of the rendering equation with respect to gi's parameters. This involves the derivative of the alpha-blending function. ii. Identify the set of pixels Pi covered by gi. iii. For each pixel p \in Pi, retrieve the pre-computed pixel loss gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}p}. iv. Compute the contribution to the gradient of gi using the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta{gi}} += \frac{\partial \mathbf{c}p}{\partial \theta{gi}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}p}. c. Write the accumulated gradients for the bucket to global memory. 4. Optimization: Use numerically equivalent but faster formulations for the Jacobian computations, avoiding redundant operations. Formulas: The core update for a Gaussian g with parameters \thetag is: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \thetag} = \sum{p \in \text{covered}(g)} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}p} \frac{\partial \mathbf{c}p}{\partial \thetag} Where \frac{\partial \mathbf{c}p}{\partial \thetag} is the derivative of the alpha-blended color at pixel p with respect to the Gaussian's parameters. The per-splat approach computes this sum by iterating over g and then p, whereas the per-pixel approach iterates over p and then g, requiring atomic adds for \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \thetag} when multiple Gaussians contribute to the same pixel. Parameters: Bucket size: 32 (warp size). Edge Cases: Empty Buckets: If N is not a multiple of 32, the last bucket may contain fewer Gaussians; handle gracefully. Precision: The method claims numerical equivalence, so standard float32 precision is maintained. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def persplatbackward(Gaussians, pixelgradients, cameraparams): """ Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with parameters theta. pixelgradients: Array of shape (H, W, 3) containing dL/dc. cameraparams: Camera intrinsics and extrinsics. """ # Pre-compute which pixels each Gaussian covers (or use tile-based rasterization) # This is typically done during the forward pass or a lightweight projection step gaussianpixelmap = computegaussianpixelcoverage(Gaussians, cameraparams) # Initialize global gradient buffer globalgradients = zerolike(Gaussians) # Process in warps of 32 numwarps = (len(Gaussians) + 31) // 32 for w in range(numwarps): startidx = w 32 endidx = min(startidx + 32, len(Gaussians)) bucket = Gaussians[startidx:endidx] # Local accumulators for this warp localgrads = zerolike(bucket) # Parallel execution over the warp (conceptually) for i, g in enumerate(bucket): # Get pixels covered by this Gaussian coveredpixels = gaussianpixelmap[g.id] # Compute Jacobian dC/dTheta for this Gaussian # This involves the derivative of the alpha blending equation jacobian = computejacobian(g, cameraparams) # Accumulate gradients from all covered pixels for p in coveredpixels: # dL/dThetag += dL/dCp dCp/dThetag # Note: dCp/dThetag is a vector/matrix depending on parameter type localgrads[i] += jacobian pixelgradients[p] # Write back to global memory for i, g in enumerate(bucket): globalgradients[startidx + i] = localgrads[i] return globalgradients The Per-Gaussian Backward Pass is a backward pass optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that parallelizes gradient computation over Gaussians rather than pixels to reduce atomic contention. It addresses the performance bottleneck of standard pixel-parallel backpropagation, where splats contributing to arbitrary numbers of pixels require frequent atomic operations for accumulation. By operating on fixed-size buckets of 32 Gaussians (one GPU warp), it significantly reduces warp stalls and false sharing associated with global memory synchronization. Time Complexity: The method reduces training time by 4–5× compared to the standard per-pixel backpropagation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the mapping of Gaussians to pixels or vice versa, which may increase memory usage slightly compared to the standard approach, but the reduction in atomic operations reduces memory bandwidth pressure. Strengths: Eliminates atomic contention, reduces warp stalls, and improves GPU utilization by aligning computation with warp boundaries. Limitations: Requires careful management of the Gaussian-to-pixel mapping, which may be complex to implement efficiently. When to use: When training speed is a critical bottleneck and the hardware supports efficient warp-level parallelism. The method was introduced in "Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources" (2024) as part of a broader effort to optimize the 3D Gaussian Splatting training pipeline. It addresses the scalability issues of the original 3DGS method, which suffered from slow training times due to the inefficiencies of the per-pixel backward pass. name: Per-Gaussian Backward Pass
head: Tile-based backward pass
body: The Per-Gaussian Backward Pass is a backward pass optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that parallelizes gradient computation over Gaussians rather than pixels to reduce atomic contention. It addresses the performance bottleneck of standard pixel-parallel backpropagation, where splats contributing to arbitrary numbers of pixels require frequent atomic operations for accumulation. By operating on fixed-size buckets of 32 Gaussians (one GPU warp), it significantly reduces warp stalls and false sharing associated with global memory synchronization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gradients of the loss with respect to the rendered image pixels (\frac{\partial L}{\partial I}), the forward pass state (Gaussian parameters, tile assignments, and stored alpha blending states). Output: Gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: Alpha Blending State Buffer: A buffer storing the intermediate alpha blending state (accumulated opacity and color) at each non-empty pixel. This state is recorded after every 32nd splat in the respective tile list during the forward pass. Gaussian Buckets: Gaussians are grouped into buckets of size 32, corresponding to one GPU warp. Steps: 1. Forward Pass Recording: During the forward rasterization pass, for each tile, store the alpha blending state at each non-empty pixel after processing every 32nd Gaussian (splat) in the tile's sorted list. 2. Bucket Assignment: Group the Gaussians into buckets of 32. Each warp is assigned to process one bucket. 3. Gradient Replay: For each bucket, threads collaboratively replay the alpha blending process using warp-level primitives. Instead of writing gradients to global memory and accumulating via atomics, threads compute gradients locally based on the stored alpha states and the final pixel gradients. 4. Parameter Update: Accumulate the computed gradients for the Gaussians in the current bucket. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pergaussianbackward(tilegaussians, alphastates, pixelgradients): """ tilegaussians: List of Gaussians assigned to this tile, sorted by z-order. alphastates: 3D array [numtiles][numpixelsintile][numsteps] storing alpha blending state after every 32nd splat. pixelgradients: Gradient of loss w.r.t. final pixel colors [numtiles][numpixelsintile][3] """ numgaussians = len(tilegaussians) # Initialize gradients for all Gaussians in this tile gradients = [ZeroGradient() for in tilegaussians] # Process Gaussians in buckets of 32 (one warp) for bucketstart in range(0, numgaussians, 32): bucketend = min(bucketstart + 32, numgaussians) bucket = tilegaussians[bucketstart:bucketend] # For each pixel in the tile for pixelidx in range(numpixelsintile): if pixelidx is empty or not covered by any gaussian in bucket: continue # Get final pixel gradient gradfinal = pixelgradients[tileidx][pixelidx] # Retrieve stored alpha states for this pixel # We need states at steps: 32, 64,..., up to the last multiple of 32 <= bucketend # And potentially the final state if bucketend is not a multiple of 32 # Replay blending for the bucket # This involves iterating through the bucket's Gaussians and # computing their contribution to the pixel gradient using the # stored alpha states to avoid recomputing the forward pass entirely. # Simplified logic for one pixel in one bucket: # 1. Start with final gradient gradfinal. # 2. Iterate backwards through the bucket's Gaussians. # 3. Use stored alpha states to determine the "background" color/alpha # seen by each Gaussian in the bucket. # 4. Compute local gradient for each Gaussian based on its opacity, # color, and the gradient of the background. # Note: Exact implementation details of the replay loop depend on # the specific alpha blending formula used in the forward pass. # The key is that atomic operations are avoided by computing # gradients locally within the warp. for i in range(len(bucket) - 1, -1, -1): gaussian = bucket[i] # Retrieve alpha state before this gaussian was processed # This requires mapping the global index to the stored step index stepidx = getalphastatestepindex(bucketstart + i) alphastatebefore = alphastates[tileidx][pixelidx][stepidx] # Compute gradient for this gaussian # gradg = gradfinal d(I)/d(gaussian) # d(I)/d(gaussian) depends on gaussian's opacity, color, and # the accumulated alpha from previous gaussians (alphastatebefore) gradg = computegaussiangradient(gaussian, alphastatebefore, gradfinal) gradients[bucketstart + i] += gradg # Update gradfinal for the next (previous in z-order) gaussian # This is effectively reversing the blending step gradfinal = reverseblendgradient(gradfinal, gaussian, alphastatebefore) return gradients Parameters: Bucket Size: 32 Gaussians (one warp). Tile Size: Typically 16x16 pixels (256 pixels). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VRAM Usage: This approach increases VRAM usage due to the storage of alpha blending states. This is mitigated by exploiting shared memory to reduce memory costs and overall VRAM allocations. Precision: Storing intermediate alpha states may introduce precision issues if not handled carefully, though the sources do not specify exact precision requirements. Empty Pixels: Pixels not covered by any Gaussian in a bucket should be skipped to avoid unnecessary computation. Optimizes the backward pass by dynamically selecting between parallelization strategies to minimize atomic contention. The core method of parallelizing gradient computation over Gaussians in fixed-size buckets to reduce atomic contention. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of required atomic operations by a factor equal to the number of pixels in each tile (256 for 16x16 tiles). Memory Complexity: Increases VRAM usage. On Mip-NeRF360 outdoor scenes (RTX 4090), VRAM increases from 6.33GiB to 7.69GiB (1.20x increase). Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 outdoor scenes (RTX 4090), training time decreases from 16m56s to 14m14s (1.20x speedup over base). On RTX 5090, training takes 163 seconds on average, a 5x improvement over the original implementation. Strengths: Significantly reduces warp stalls and false sharing during z-order sorting. Limitations: Increased VRAM usage. The Per-Gaussian Backward Pass was introduced by Mallick et al. [56] (cited in) to address the computational suboptimality of atomic operations in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting backpropagation. It is part of the broader effort to optimize training efficiency in differentiable volume rendering. name: Adaptive Scheduling for Backward Pass Implementations
head: Rasterization backward with adaptive scheduling, Thompson sampling scheduler for backward pass
body: This method minimizes atomic contention and maximizes thread utilization during the 3D Gaussian Splatting backward pass by dynamically switching between two distinct rasterization implementations. It sets itself apart from static backward strategies by using a Thompson sampling scheduler to select the fastest implementation based on measured latency, addressing the performance variance across different scenes and hardware configurations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of projected Gaussians binned to tiles, training configuration (scene, hardware), and current latency beliefs. Output: Accumulated gradients for Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: Latency Beliefs: Two probability distributions (e.g., Beta distributions) storing the estimated latency performance for Implementation 1 and Implementation 2. Shared Memory: Used in Implementation 2 to store pre-computed transmittance and derivatives. Parameters: Batch Size (S): Chosen by rounding up \sqrt{NP} to a multiple of subgroup size, capped at 128, where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels in the tile. Gaussian Parameterization: Follows [LDC 25] to simplify opacity computation into matrix multiplication. Steps: 1. Initialize Latency Beliefs: Initialize probability distributions for the latency of Implementation 1 and Implementation 2. 2. Select Implementation: Use Thompson sampling to randomly select an implementation based on the current latency beliefs, favoring implementations with higher probabilities of being faster. 3. Execute Selected Implementation: If Implementation 1 is selected: 1. Launch one thread block per tile. 2. Calculate dynamic Gaussian batch size S = \min(128, \text{round\up}(\sqrt{NP}, \text{subgroup\size})). 3. Process Gaussians in batches of size S for each tile. If Implementation 2 is selected: 1. For a Gaussian batch, run a forward pass parallelized over pixels. 2. Compute transmittance and its derivative with respect to Gaussian parameters for each Gaussian-pixel pair. 3. Store these values in shared memory. 4. Run a backward pass parallelized over Gaussians. 5. Fetch pre-computed transmittance and derivatives from shared memory. 6. Compute accumulated gradients. 4. Update Latency Beliefs: Measure the actual latency of the selected implementation. Update the corresponding probability distribution based on the measured latency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def selectimplementation(latencybeliefs): """ Select implementation using Thompson sampling. latencybeliefs: List of [alpha, beta] for each implementation. Returns: Index of selected implementation (0 or 1). """ samples = [] for alpha, beta in latencybeliefs: # Sample from Beta distribution sample = random.betavariate(alpha, beta) samples.append(sample) # Select implementation with highest sample return samples.index(max(samples)) def updatebelief(latencybeliefs, selectedimpl, latency): """ Update latency belief based on measured latency. latencybeliefs: List of [alpha, beta] for each implementation. selectedimpl: Index of selected implementation. latency: Measured latency (lower is better, so we might invert or use as reward). """ # Note: The source says "updates belief based on measured latency". # Standard Thompson sampling for minimization often uses inverse latency or # treats latency as a cost. Here we assume a simple update where lower latency # increases the "success" parameter (alpha) or decreases "failure" (beta). # A common approach for minimization is to treat 1/latency as reward. # However, without specific update rule, we mark as for implementation detail. # Placeholder for specific update rule not detailed in source. # Typically: alpha += 1 / latency or similar. # We will assume a simple exponential moving average or Bayesian update # is handled by the scheduler library, but here we note the action. # For the sake of self-contained pseudocode, we assume a simple update: # If latency is low, increase alpha (confidence in speed). # This is a implementation detail as the exact update function is not specified. alpha, beta = latencybeliefs[selectedimpl] # Example update: increase alpha inversely proportional to latency # This is a guess as the source does not specify the exact Bayesian update. newalpha = alpha + 1.0 / latency latencybeliefs[selectedimpl] = [newalpha, beta] def implementation1(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize): """ Implementation 1: One thread block per tile, dynamic batch size. tilegaussians: List of Gaussians in the tile. P: Number of pixels in the tile. """ N = len(tilegaussians) if N == 0: return # Calculate batch size S sqrtnp = math.sqrt(N P) # Round up to multiple of subgroupsize S = math.ceil(sqrtnp / subgroupsize) subgroupsize # Cap to maxbatchsize S = min(S, maxbatchsize) # Process in batches for i in range(0, N, S): batch = tilegaussians[i:i+S] # Process batch (details of gradient accumulation omitted as per source focus on scheduling) pass def implementation2(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize): """ Implementation 2: Forward pass over pixels, backward pass over Gaussians, shared memory. tilegaussians: List of Gaussians in the tile. P: Number of pixels in the tile. """ N = len(tilegaussians) if N == 0: return # Calculate batch size S (same logic as Impl 1 for consistency, though source doesn't explicitly link S to Impl 2) sqrtnp = math.sqrt(N P) S = math.ceil(sqrtnp / subgroupsize) subgroupsize S = min(S, maxbatchsize) # Forward pass parallelized over pixels # Compute transmittance and derivatives for each Gaussian-pixel pair # Store in shared memory sharedmemorydata = [] for i in range(0, N, S): batch = tilegaussians[i:i+S] # For each pixel in tile, compute contribution from batch # This part is complex and depends on specific rasterization logic # Source says: "compute transmittance and its derivative... store in shared memory" # We assume a function exists for this computeforwardandstore(batch, P, sharedmemorydata) # Backward pass parallelized over Gaussians # Fetch from shared memory and compute accumulated gradient computebackwardfromshared(sharedmemorydata, tilegaussians) def computeforwardandstore(batch, P, sharedmemorydata): """ Placeholder for forward pass logic. Computes transmittance and derivatives for Gaussian-pixel pairs. """ pass def computebackwardfromshared(sharedmemorydata, tilegaussians): """ Placeholder for backward pass logic. Fetches from shared memory and computes gradients. """ pass def runadaptivebackward(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize, latencybeliefs): """ Main function to run adaptive backward pass. """ selectedimpl = selectimplementation(latencybeliefs) starttime = time.time() if selectedimpl == 0: implementation1(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize) else: implementation2(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize) endtime = time.time() latency = endtime - starttime updatebelief(latencybeliefs, selectedimpl, latency) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The source mentions handling tile boundaries efficiently using branchless functions for ellipse range, but this is part of the projection step, not the backward scheduling. Degenerate Input: If a tile has no Gaussians, both implementations should handle this gracefully (e.g., return immediately). A scheduling mechanism that jointly adjusts the tile-wise pixel sampling rate (r{tile}) and the number of sampled views (K) over training iterations to allocate more computation during difficult stages and reduce it as optimization converges. It sets itself apart from static sampling strategies by dynamically scaling the view budget and pixel density based on reconstruction error and training progress, achieving a trade-off between training speed and reconstruction quality. Time Complexity: The latency of Implementation 1 is approximately proportional to the product of the number of batches (P+S)/P and the number of Gaussians traversed per batch (N+S)/S. Implementation 2's complexity is not explicitly given, but it aims to improve thread utilization and minimize divergence. Memory Complexity: Implementation 2 uses shared memory to store transmittance and derivatives, which may limit the batch size or tile size based on available shared memory. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA RTX 3090, Implementation 2 is 20%-30% faster than Implementation 1 on the Mip-NeRF 360 bicycle scene, but Implementation 1 is faster on the garden scene. Scaling: The method adapts to different scenes and hardware configurations automatically via the Thompson sampling scheduler. Strengths: Reduces atomic contention, maximizes thread utilization, and automatically selects the fastest implementation for a given context. Limitations: The overhead of Thompson sampling is minimal but non-zero. The performance gain depends on the availability of a faster implementation for the specific scene. When to Use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models and performance varies significantly across scenes or hardware. When Not to Use: When a single implementation is consistently faster across all scenarios, or when the overhead of scheduling is not justified by the performance gain. This method was introduced in "VkSplat: High-Performance 3DGS Training in Vulkan Compute". It addresses the high atomic contention and subgroup reduction issues present in existing 3DGS training implementations. The approach is inspired by [MGK 24] for the first implementation and aims to improve upon [KKLD23] and [YLK 25] by dynamically selecting the best backward pass strategy. VkSplat: High-Performance 3DGS Training in Vulkan Compute, https://doi.org/10.2312/egs.20261024, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive View and Pixel Sampling Scheduling
head: Adaptive Scheduling of View Budget and Pixel Sampling, Sampled view number scheduling, Tile-wise pixel sampling rate scheduling, query sampling schedule
body: A scheduling mechanism that jointly adjusts the tile-wise pixel sampling rate (r{tile}) and the number of sampled views (K) over training iterations to allocate more computation during difficult stages and reduce it as optimization converges. It sets itself apart from static sampling strategies by dynamically scaling the view budget and pixel density based on reconstruction error and training progress, achieving a trade-off between training speed and reconstruction quality. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: Current iteration t, initial mean view error \bar{E}{init}, current mean view error \bar{E}t, densification/pruning cutoff iteration \tau{until}, tile sampling scale \lambda, minimum/maximum view budgets K{min}, K{max}, transition speed \alpha, and minimum/maximum sampling rates r{min}, r{max}. Outputs: Tile-wise pixel sampling rate r{tile}^{(t)} and sampled view number Kt for the current iteration. Data structures: No persistent data structures are required beyond scalar values for error tracking and iteration counters. The scheduler computes values on-the-fly. Parameters: \lambda: Tile sampling scale. Typical value not given in the sources. K{min}, K{max}: Minimum and maximum number of sampled views. The source uses a range of 10 \to 3 (i.e., K{max}=10, K{min}=3). \alpha: Controls the transition speed of the view budget scheduling. Value not given in the sources. \tau{until}: The last iteration for densification and pruning. Value not given in the sources. \bar{E}{init}: Initial mean view error. Computed at the start of training. \bar{E}t: Current mean view error at iteration t. Steps: 1. Compute Error Ratio (rt): Calculate the normalized error ratio by clipping the square root of the ratio of current error to initial error. rt = \text{clip}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\bar{E}t}{\bar{E}{init} + \epsilon}}, 0, 1\right) where \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. 2. Compute Sinusoidal Modulation (\phi(rt)): Apply a sinusoidal function to amplify sampling variation in the low-error regime. \phi(rt) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} rt\right) This modulation is chosen because reconstruction error drops rapidly in early training and remains in a narrow range later, making sinusoidal modulation more sensitive to subtle differences than linear or exponential variants. 3. Compute Progress Coefficient (\rhot): Determine the annealing factor based on training progress relative to the densification phase. \rhot = 1 - \text{clip}\left(\frac{t}{\tau{until}}, 0, 1\right) This coefficient gradually reduces sampling intensity after the densification and pruning phase is complete. 4. Compute Tile-wise Pixel Sampling Rate (r{tile}^{(t)}): r{tile}^{(t)} = r{min} + (r{max} - r{min}) \left(1 - \rhot \phi(rt)\right) where r{min} = \lambda / K{max} and r{max} = \lambda / K{min}. 5. Compute Sampled View Number (Kt): Kt = \text{round}\left(K{min} + (K{max} - K{min}) e^{-\alpha(1 - \rhot \phi(rt))}\right) This formula exponentially decays the view budget as the term (1 - \rhot \phi(rt)) increases, shifting from global multi-view consistency to local refinement. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeschedulingparams( t: int, tauuntil: int, Et: float, Einit: float, lambdascale: float, Kmin: int, Kmax: int, alpha: float, epsilon: float = 1e-6) -> tuple[float, int]: """ Computes the tile-wise pixel sampling rate and sampled view number for the current training iteration. Args: t: Current training iteration. tauuntil: Iteration after which densification/pruning stops. Et: Current mean view error. Einit: Initial mean view error. lambdascale: Tile sampling scale. Kmin: Minimum number of sampled views. Kmax: Maximum number of sampled views. alpha: Transition speed control for view budget. epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability. Returns: (rtile, Kt): Tile-wise pixel sampling rate and sampled view number. """ # Step 1: Compute Error Ratio # Clip the square root of the error ratio to [0, 1] errorratioraw = math.sqrt(Et / (Einit + epsilon)) rt = max(0.0, min(1.0, errorratioraw)) # Step 2: Compute Sinusoidal Modulation phirt = math.sin(math.pi / 2 rt) # Step 3: Compute Progress Coefficient # Clip t / tauuntil to [0, 1], then subtract from 1 progressratio = max(0.0, min(1.0, t / tauuntil)) rhot = 1.0 - progressratio # Step 4: Compute Sampling Rate Bounds rmin = lambdascale / Kmax rmax = lambdascale / Kmin # Step 5: Compute Tile-wise Pixel Sampling Rate # rtile = rmin + (rmax - rmin) (1 - rhot phi(rt)) modulationfactor = 1.0 - rhot phirt rtile = rmin + (rmax - rmin) modulationfactor # Step 6: Compute Sampled View Number # Kt = round(Kmin + (Kmax - Kmin) exp(-alpha modulationfactor)) viewbudget = Kmin + (Kmax - Kmin) math.exp(-alpha modulationfactor) Kt = round(viewbudget) return rtile, Kt Edge cases and pitfalls: Very small view budget: Setting K=1 degrades performance due to insufficient multi-view constraints. Large fixed budget: Using a large fixed budget (e.g., K=10) increases training time without quality gains. Division by zero: Ensure \bar{E}{init} + \epsilon > 0 to prevent division by zero in the error ratio calculation. Negative sampling rate: The clipping in rt and \rhot ensures the modulation factor stays within bounds, but implementation should verify r{tile} \ge 0. Time Complexity: The scheduling computation itself is O(1) per iteration. However, the method reduces the total training time by reducing the number of sampled views and pixels in later stages. The source reports a reduction in training time from 81s (linear schedule) to 77s (sinusoidal schedule) while improving PSNR. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead compared to static sampling, as it only computes scalar values. Measured Performance: On the tested scenes, the sinusoidal schedule achieved a PSNR of 27.57, SSIM of 0.794, and LPIPS of 0.256, outperforming linear (PSNR 27.35) and exponential (PSNR 27.27) schedules. Scaling: The method scales by reducing computation as the model converges, making it more efficient for long training runs. Strengths: Improves sensitivity to subtle reconstruction differences in the low-error regime; achieves best trade-off between speed and quality by gradually shifting from global multi-view consistency to local refinement. Limitations: Requires tracking initial and current mean view errors; sensitive to the choice of \alpha and \tau{until}. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models and seeking to accelerate convergence without sacrificing quality, particularly when reconstruction error dynamics are non-linear. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited in the early stages and multi-view consistency is critical (avoid K=1). The method was introduced in the paper "TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization". It addresses the inefficiency of fixed sampling rates in 3D Gaussian Splatting training, where early iterations require dense sampling for global consistency and later iterations benefit from sparse sampling for local refinement. The sinusoidal modulation was found to outperform linear and exponential variants based on ablation studies. TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.15924, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Cooperative Scheduling and Synchronization
head: Cooperative Scheduling, Synchronization for Backward Pass
body: Cooperative Scheduling and Synchronization addresses idle resources and gradient contention caused by uneven tile lists, variable pixel traversal, and backward propagation accumulation. It sets itself apart from static mapping strategies by dynamically redistributing work and organizing computation to minimize global atomic updates, replacing them with local reductions or cache-cooperative operations. The core mechanism relies on two primary optimizations to handle the irregularity of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization: 1. Dynamic Work Redistribution: Static mappings of Gaussians to tiles or pixels are prone to warp divergence due to footprint coverage and early termination. Cooperative scheduling dynamically assigns tiles or Gaussians to threads/warps to balance the load, ensuring that resources remain active even when the number of pairs (N{pair}) and evaluations (N{eval}) is unchanged. 2. Local Gradient Reduction: Backward propagation requires accumulating gradients from many pixels into each Gaussian. Instead of performing frequent global atomic updates, these methods organize computation to combine gradients locally (within a warp, tile, or Gaussian-centric block) before writing the final result back to global memory. This reduces global atomic contention and improves memory coherency. Redistributes work through dynamic tile assignment and enables Gaussian parallel rendering inside a warp. See Balanced 3DGS. Uses parameter hoisting, warp culling, and coherent blending to reuse data and coordinate pixel processing within tiles. See Local-GS. Combines warp reduction with cache cooperation to reduce global atomic updates and contention during backward propagation. See DISTWAR. Organizes backward computation around Gaussians, combining gradients before writing them back, replacing some global updates with local reduction. See Taming 3DGS. Combines a refined Gaussian-centric backward pass with a parameter layout that keeps spatially nearby Gaussians close in memory, reducing global updates and enabling more regular reads. See Faster-GS. The concept emerged as a response to the inefficiencies of static rasterization schedules in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Uneven tile lists and variable pixel traversal leave GPU resources idle. The approach was developed by multiple independent research groups to optimize both forward and backward passes: Balanced 3DGS [15] introduced dynamic tile assignment. Local-GS [62] focused on warp-level coordination. DISTWAR [17] targeted backward propagation contention. Taming 3DGS [63] reorganized backward computation around Gaussians. Faster-GS [64] optimized parameter layout for spatial locality. These methods are cited in the broader survey "From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS". From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06157, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Per-Gaussian Backward
head: Bucket-based backward, Mallick et al. backward
body: Per-Gaussian Backward is a backward pass optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that parallelizes gradient computation over Gaussians rather than pixels to reduce atomic contention. It differs from standard pixel-parallel backpropagation by operating on fixed-size buckets of 32 Gaussians (one GPU warp), allowing threads to collaboratively replay the alpha blending process using warp-level primitives. This approach significantly reduces warp stalls that occur when threads synchronize while loading alpha blending states from global memory. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Forward pass buffers storing intermediate color and transmittance after every 32nd Gaussian, the final number of contributing Gaussians per pixel, Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color), and tile definitions. Outputs: Gradients for Gaussian attributes written to global memory. Data Structures: 1. Intermediate Buffers: Allocated during the forward pass to store per-pixel state. intermediatecolor[tileid][pixel]: Accumulated color after every 32nd Gaussian. intermediatetransmittance[tileid][pixel]: Accumulated transmittance after every 32nd Gaussian. contributingcount[tileid][pixel]: Final number of contributing Gaussians per pixel. Size: Determined by the known lengths of the per-tile Gaussian lists. 2. Bucket: A group of 32 Gaussians associated with a single tile. 3. Shared Memory Buffer: Used by a warp (32 threads) to store alpha blending states (color/transmittance pairs) for the current bucket's pixels before they are needed. Numbered Steps: 1. Forward Pass Buffer Population: During the forward rendering pass, after processing every 32nd Gaussian in a tile's list, write the current accumulated color and transmittance for all pixels in that tile into the intermediate buffers. Also, write the final count of contributing Gaussians per pixel. 2. Bucket Launch: For each tile, launch a kernel block where each thread block (warp) handles one bucket of 32 Gaussians. 3. Thread Assignment: In a warp of 32 threads, thread i (where i \in [0, 31]) is responsible for computing the gradient contribution of the i-th Gaussian in the bucket across all pixels in the associated tile. 4. Shared Memory Pre-loading: All 32 threads in the warp collaboratively load a batch of alpha blending states into shared memory (one per thread) before they are needed. From that point on, the first thread in each warp reads the next state directly from shared memory instead of global memory. 5. Gradient Replay: Starting from the initial color and transmittance values stored in the buffers (or loaded into shared memory), the warp replays the blending process using warp-level primitives to efficiently compute the necessary gradients. 6. Atomic Accumulation: Each thread writes the accumulated gradients to global memory using atomics, as Gaussians can be inside multiple buckets across tiles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def PerGaussianBackward(bucketgaussians, tileid, intermediatecolor, intermediatetransmittance, sharedmem, gradientsglobal): threadid = getthreadid() # standard CUDA/OpenCL primitive gauss = bucketgaussians[threadid] pixelindices = getpixelindicesforgaussian(gauss, tileid) # standard rasterization query # 1. Collaborative shared memory load for p in pixelindices: sharedmem[threadid][p] = (intermediatecolor[tileid][p], intermediatetransmittance[tileid][p]) syncthreads() # warp barrier to ensure all loads complete # 2. Gradient replay using warp-level primitives colorgrad = 0.0 transgrad = 0.0 for p in pixelindices: c, t = sharedmem[threadid][p] # Replay blending process to compute gradients # The sources do not specify the exact chain-rule implementation for alpha blending gradients. dc = computealphablendinggradient(gauss, p, c, t) # standard chain-rule computation colorgrad += dc # 3. Atomic accumulation to global memory gradientsglobal[gauss.id].position += gauss.positiongrad gradientsglobal[gauss.id].covariance += gauss.covariancegrad gradientsglobal[gauss.id].opacity += gauss.opacitygrad gradientsglobal[gauss.id].color += colorgrad Parameters: Bucket Size: 32 Gaussians (one warp). Tile Size: Typically 16x16 pixels (256 pixels per tile). Shared Memory Usage: 32 entries per warp, each entry containing color and transmittance for the relevant pixel range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Warp Stalls: If threads are synchronized while the first thread loads alpha blending state from global memory, the entire warp stalls. This is mitigated by collaborative loading into shared memory. Multiple Tile Membership: A single Gaussian may contribute to multiple tiles. Therefore, gradient accumulation must use atomic operations in global memory. Buffer Size: The intermediate buffers must be sized according to the maximum number of 32-Gaussian buckets in any tile. This is determined by the per-tile Gaussian list lengths. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, but with a significantly reduced constant factor due to warp-level parallelism and reduced global memory traffic. Memory Complexity: Additional memory for intermediate buffers: O(T \cdot B \cdot P) where T is the number of tiles, B is the average number of buckets per tile, and P is the number of pixels per tile. Performance: The shared memory optimization improves kernel runtime by up to 2x compared to the original Mallick et al. implementation. Strengths: Reduces atomic contention by parallelizing over Gaussians; minimizes global memory latency through shared memory usage; efficient use of warp-level primitives. Limitations: Requires additional memory for intermediate buffers; complex implementation due to warp-level synchronization and shared memory management; Gaussians spanning multiple tiles still require atomic writes. Per-Gaussian Backward was proposed by Mallick et al. [56] as a key optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It was later analyzed and improved by the Faster-GS team, who introduced the shared memory optimization to reduce warp stalls. The method is part of the broader effort to make differentiable volume rendering and radiance field optimization computationally efficient.
