name: Grendel-GS
head: Out-of-Core and Distributed Optimization for 3DGS
body: Grendel-GS is a distributed optimization framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that partitions the Gaussian primitive list across multiple GPUs to overcome single-device memory limits. Unlike TideGS, which streams data from disk on a single machine, Grendel-GS distributes the parameter table across a GPU cluster, enabling training on scenes with billions of primitives by leveraging inter-GPU communication. It builds on the differentiable rasterization core defined in Optimization and Training Efficiency but modifies the data flow to support multi-GPU parallelism. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scene represented by a large set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mathbf{g}i\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian \mathbf{g}i is defined by position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or scale/rotation), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Output: Optimized Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}' that minimize the rendering loss \mathcal{L} against ground-truth images. Data Structures: The Gaussian list \mathcal{G} is partitioned into K subsets \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}K, one for each GPU k \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Each GPU k stores a local subset \mathcal{G}k in its VRAM. The total number of Gaussians N is distributed such that \sum{k=1}^K |\mathcal{G}k| = N. To ensure correct alpha blending across partitions, a global depth sort or a hierarchical z-buffer is required. The sources do not specify the exact synchronization mechanism for the depth buffer across GPUs. Numbered Steps: 1. Partitioning: The initial Gaussian list is divided among K GPUs. This can be done spatially (e.g., by bounding box) or arbitrarily. Spatial partitioning is preferred to minimize inter-GPU communication for occluded primitives. 2. Local Rasterization: Each GPU k renders its subset \mathcal{G}k independently. For each pixel, it computes the partial color \mathbf{c}k and accumulated opacity \alphak using the standard 3DGS rasterizer [9264-optimization-and-training-efficiency.md]. 3. Inter-GPU Communication: The partial results (color and opacity contributions) from all GPUs are aggregated. states that results are combined via inter-GPU communication at partition boundaries. This typically involves a collective operation (e.g., AllReduce or AllGather) to compute the final pixel color \mathbf{c} = \sum{k=1}^K \mathbf{c}k and total opacity \alpha = 1 - \prod{k=1}^K (1 - \alphak). 4. Loss Computation: The final rendered image is compared to the ground truth to compute the loss \mathcal{L}. 5. Gradient Distribution: The gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{g}i} is computed for each Gaussian. Since the loss depends on the global render, gradients for Gaussians in \mathcal{G}k depend on the contributions from all other partitions. The gradient for a Gaussian \mathbf{g}i \in \mathcal{G}k is scaled by the derivative of the global alpha-blending equation with respect to the local contribution. 6. Parameter Update: Each GPU updates its local subset \mathcal{G}k using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). If the partitioning is static, no further communication is needed for the update. If dynamic splitting/merging occurs (as in standard 3DGS), Gaussians may need to be migrated between GPUs, requiring explicit data transfer. Formulas: The final pixel color is: \mathbf{c} = \sum{k=1}^K \sum{j \in \mathcal{G}k} \mathbf{c}j \alphaj \prod{m=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alpham) where the product term accounts for depth sorting across all partitions. The exact ordering of Gaussians across partitions must be consistent. Parameters: K: Number of GPUs. Typical values depend on scene size and available hardware. Partitioning strategy: Spatial or arbitrary. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: If a Gaussian in one GPU is occluded by a Gaussian in another, the alpha-blending order must be respected. Incorrect ordering leads to visual artifacts. Communication Bottleneck: Inter-GPU communication (e.g., NVLink or PCIe) can become a bottleneck if the partition boundaries are not optimized. Load Imbalance: If the scene geometry is uneven, some GPUs may render more pixels or Gaussians than others, leading to idle time. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P / K) for rendering, where P is the number of pixels, assuming perfect load balancing. Communication overhead adds O(K \cdot P) or more depending on the aggregation method. Memory Complexity: O(N / K) per GPU, allowing training on scenes with N \gg VRAM capacity. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Scales to billions of primitives; overcomes single-GPU VRAM limits. Limitations: Requires multi-GPU setup; communication overhead; complex implementation. When to use: Large-scale scenes (e.g., urban environments, large indoor spaces) that exceed single-GPU memory. When not to use: Small scenes; single-GPU environments; when communication latency is high. Grendel-GS was introduced as part of the broader effort to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to larger scenes. It is cited in the survey "3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey". The method addresses the memory bottleneck of standard 3DGS by distributing the Gaussian list across multiple GPUs. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: TideGS
body: TideGS is a fully out-of-core optimization framework for training 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that enables training with over one billion primitives on a single GPU with limited VRAM. It solves the VRAM bottleneck of standard 3DGS by decoupling memory usage from the total scene size N, keeping the full parameter table on SSD and materializing only the per-iteration working set in GPU memory. Unlike Grendel-GS, which distributes Gaussians across multiple GPUs, TideGS operates on a single machine, treating GPU VRAM as a high-bandwidth working-set cache rather than a persistent parameter store. TideGS manages Gaussian parameters across an SSD–CPU–GPU hierarchy. The method relies on the observation that each training iteration touches only a small subset of Gaussians visible from the current camera batch, creating sparsity and temporal locality. Inputs: Camera batch \mathcal{B}t at iteration t. Total number of Gaussians N. Spatial block size B (default 4096). GPU VRAM capacity limit C. CPU cache size (e.g., 16 GB or 32 GB). Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \Theta stored on SSD. Rendered images for the batch \mathcal{B}t. Unified Parameter Layout: All learnable per-Gaussian attributes are stored in a logical layout \Theta \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}, where D=59 under the standard degree-3 spherical harmonic (SH) parameterization. Physically, \Theta is stored out-of-core as contiguous block records on SSD. Blocks: Gaussians are Morton-sorted to preserve spatial locality and partitioned into SSD-aligned blocks. Block k contains Gaussians indexed by \text{Block}(k) = \Theta[kB: (k+1)B] for k \in \{0, \dots, K-1\}, where K = \lceil N/B \rceil. Each block is summarized by a bounding sphere for visibility culling. Sets: Gaussian-level active set It: The subset of Gaussian indices visible after rasterization for camera batch \mathcal{B}t at iteration t, which receive non-zero gradients. Block-level working set Kt: The set of block indices that conservatively cover the Gaussian-level active set It, used for staging and caching. VRAM-resident set Rt: The set of blocks currently materialized in GPU VRAM, maintained under capacity C. Before training, the block layout is built once: 1. Morton-sort the N primitives. 2. Compute block bounds and statistics. 3. Write the initial base segment to SSD. This step takes 1.9 minutes for \sim 102M Gaussians and 21.2 minutes for \sim 1.1B Gaussians on MatrixCity, accounting for less than 0.5% of total training time. Each iteration t follows four coordinated stages, with stages (1), (2), and (4) overlapped with (3) to amortize I/O latency with GPU computation. 1. Identify working set: Compute Kt via lightweight CPU-side block visibility tests (6-plane frustum tests against block bounding spheres). 2. Prefetch & materialize: Prefetch needed blocks into the CPU cache and materialize them in VRAM via an asynchronous host-to-device (H2D) stream. 3. Render & backprop: Execute the standard 3DGS forward/backward pass on the resident blocks Rt on GPU. Fine-grained Gaussian-level filtering is executed on GPU within the retained blocks to ensure exact 3DGS semantics. 4. Evict & write back: Evict cold blocks when VRAM/CPU caches are full; dirty evictions are propagated through the CPU cache and written back to SSD patch segments asynchronously. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. B = 4096 # Spatial block size (primitives per block) D = 59 # Parameter dimensionality per Gaussian C = 24 10243 # VRAM capacity limit in bytes (e.g., 24 GB) CPUCACHESIZE = 16 10243 # CPU cache size in bytes K = (N + B - 1) // B # Total number of blocks Rt = [] # List of block indices currently in VRAM cpucache = {} # Dictionary mapping block index to data array for t in range(numiterations): batch = camerabatches[t] # Stage 1: Identify working set (CPU) # Conservative CPU-side block visibility test (6-plane frustum test against bounding spheres) Kt = [] for k in range(K): if blockboundingsphereintersectsfrustum(k, batch): Kt.append(k) # Stage 2: Prefetch & materialize (Async H2D stream) # Evict cold blocks from VRAM if capacity C is exceeded while len(Rt) B D 4 > C: evictblock(Rt, cpucache) for k in Kt: if k not in Rt: # Fetch from SSD or CPU cache if k in cpucache: data = cpucache[k] else: data = readssdblock(k) cpucache[k] = data # Asynchronously copy to GPU VRAM asynch2dcopy(k, data) Rt.append(k) # Stage 3: Render & backprop (GPU) # GPU-side fine filtering to get exact active Gaussian indices It It = gpufrustumculling(Rt, batch) # Execute standard 3DGS forward and backward pass loss, gradients = standard3dgsforwardbackward(It, batch) # Update Adam optimizer states for active Gaussians (standard 3DGS step) updateadamoptimizer(It, gradients) # Stage 4: Evict & write back (Async overlap with next stages) # Mark modified blocks as dirty and write back to SSD asynchronously for k in Rt: if blockisdirty(k): asyncwritessdblock(k) D=59: Dimensionality of per-Gaussian parameter vector \thetai. B=4096: Default spatial block size (primitives per block). Batch size |\mathcal{B}t|: 4 for Mip-NeRF 360; 64 (throughput-oriented) or 16 (conservative) for MatrixCity. CPU cache size: 16 GB (throughput-oriented) or 32 GB (conservative) for MatrixCity. Optimizer: Adam with the 3DGS learning-rate schedule. OS Page Caching: OS page caching can skew SSD bandwidth measurements by serving data from DRAM. Mitigation: Use fresh run/cache directories for compared runs and a cold-start protocol to evict cached pages before standalone cold-cache measurements. Naive Offload Failure: Naive offloading fails at \sim 102M Gaussians due to OOM because per-iteration parameters required by rasterization must reside in VRAM. Profiling a 25M-Gaussian model shows 12.13 GB GPU memory for these parameters. CLM Failure: CLM fails at \sim 1.1B Gaussians due to 'Rasterization OOM' because global radix sort and auxiliary buffers exceed available VRAM (>22 GB), as it requires GPU-resident geometry (~45 GB at this scale). Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in sources. Memory Complexity: VRAM scaling is O(|Rt|) or O(|It|), where |Rt| is the capacity-bounded resident set and |It| is the Gaussian active set after fine filtering. This contrasts with O(N) scaling of other methods. Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF 360 (In-memory regime): TideGS (Shuffle) achieves 3.24 img/s (309.1 ms/iter). TideGS (Trajectory) achieves 3.50 img/s (285.8 ms/iter). Native 3DGS achieves 3.95 img/s (253.5 ms/iter). MatrixCity \sim 102M: TideGS PCIe traffic 0.10 GB/iter, Iter 90.7 ms. CLM PCIe traffic 0.41 GB/iter, Iter 100.8 ms. MatrixCity \sim 1.1B: TideGS PCIe traffic 0.97 GB/iter, Iter 525.6 ms, GPU Utilization 49.5%. CLM fails with OOM. Quality Consistency: On Mip-NeRF 360, TideGS PSNR 28.9157 vs Native 3DGS 29.052 (gap 0.11 dB). SSIM 0.8689 vs 0.8694. LPIPS 0.1399 vs 0.1394. Strengths: Enables training with >1B Gaussians on a single 24 GB GPU. Reduces PCIe traffic by 4x compared to CLM at \sim 102M Gaussians. Limitations: Incurs modest overhead in the in-memory regime compared to Native 3DGS. Requires SSD storage capacity. When to use: When training 3DGS scenes with billions of primitives on a single GPU with limited VRAM. When not to use: When the scene fits entirely in GPU memory and maximum throughput is required (Native 3DGS is faster). TideGS was introduced in the paper "TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization". It builds on the insight that 3DGS training is visibility-induced sparse and trajectory-conditioned, allowing GPU memory to serve as a working-set cache. It is implemented in PyTorch 2.6.0 with CUDA 12.4 and evaluated on NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU (24 GB VRAM), AMD EPYC 7532 CPU, 256 GB DDR4, and Samsung PM9A3 NVMe SSD. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.20150, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details
head: 3DGS CUDA kernel implementation, GS Implementation Parameters, GSGEN Implementation Details, Gaussian Splatting Training Configuration, gsplat implementation details, half-precision rasterization implementation
body: This article details the specific implementation parameters, optimization strategies, and variant algorithms used to train and render 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes. It covers the core training loop mechanics, including densification schedules, gradient thresholds, and half-precision rasterization techniques, as well as specialized variants for handling defocus blur, sparse views, and large-scale scenes. It sets itself apart from general Optimization and Parallelization by providing concrete hyperparameters, code-level logic for density control, and specific architectural choices for differentiable rendering kernels. The standard training pipeline optimizes Gaussian parameters (position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}) using stochastic gradient descent. The optimization is guided by a photometric loss combining Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM): \mathcal{L} = \lambda \cdot \text{MSE}(\mathbf{C}, \hat{\mathbf{C}}) + (1 - \lambda) \cdot \text{SSIM}(\mathbf{C}, \hat{\mathbf{C}}) where \mathbf{C} is the ground-truth color, \hat{\mathbf{C}} is the rendered color, and \lambda is a hyperparameter balancing the terms. Densification Schedule: To adapt the Gaussian distribution to the scene complexity, densification (splitting and cloning) and pruning are performed periodically. 1. Splitting: Every 500 iterations, Gaussians are split based on their view-space position gradient. If the accumulated gradient exceeds a threshold T{\text{pos}} = 0.02, the Gaussian is split into two. 2. Cloning/Compactness: Every 1000 iterations, a compactness-based densification step is performed to add new Gaussians in under-represented regions. 3. Pruning: Every 200 iterations, Gaussians with opacity \alpha < \alpha{\text{min}} = 0.05 or excessively large world-space/view-space radius are removed. Gradient Threshold Schedule: To control the number of split Gaussians, an exponentially ascending gradient threshold is used. This ensures that densification is aggressive in early stages and stabilizes as training progresses, preventing overfitting to noise. To accelerate training and reduce memory bandwidth, the rasterization kernels (forward and backward passes) can be implemented using half-precision (FP16) arithmetic. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Stored in contiguous memory. Feature vectors (e.g., SH coefficients) are fetched using half-precision memory accesses to reduce register pressure. MLP Evaluation: If view-dependent features are predicted via a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), they are trained and evaluated using tiny-cuda-nn's JIT-compiled cooperative vector MLPs in FP16. Stability Measures: Loss Scaling: An automatic scaling factor is applied to loss values to prevent gradient underflow during backpropagation in half-precision. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Spherical Harmonics (SH) Degree: Typically set to 1 for standard implementations, balancing view-dependent detail and computational cost. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gaussians = initializefromsfm(sfmpoints) optimizer = Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=1e-3) iteration = 0 maxiterations = 30000 while iteration < maxiterations: # 1. Sample a random training image imageid = randomchoice(trainingimages) gtcolor = getgtcolor(imageid) camerapose = getcamerapose(imageid) # 2. Forward Pass: Differentiable Rasterization # Projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, sorts by depth, and alpha-blends renderedcolor = rasterize(gaussians, camerapose) # 3. Loss Computation # Combined MSE and SSIM loss mseloss = meansquarederror(gtcolor, renderedcolor) ssimloss = 1 - structuralsimilarity(gtcolor, renderedcolor) loss = 0.8 mseloss + 0.2 ssimloss # Typical lambda=0.8 # 4. Backward Pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() # 5. Optimizer Step optimizer.step() # 6. Densification and Pruning if iteration % 500 == 0: # Split Gaussians with high view-space position gradient splitgaussians(gaussians, threshold=0.02) if iteration % 1000 == 0: # Compactness-based densification densifygaussians(gaussians) if iteration % 200 == 0: # Prune low-opacity and oversized Gaussians prunegaussians(gaussians, alphamin=0.05) iteration += 1 A method to calculate scene extent based on the Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud rather than camera positions to avoid bias from camera distribution (e.g., orbiting a small object in a large environment). The default 3DGS scene extent e{\text{scene}} is proportional to the distance of the furthest camera from the average camera position, causing bias if cameras are clustered. The corrected extent e'{\text{scene}} is calculated as: e'{\text{scene}} = \frac{1}{N{\text{SfM}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{SfM}}} \|\bar{C} - pi\|2 where N{\text{SfM}} is the number of SfM points, \bar{C} is the averaged camera position, and pi is the i-th SfM point. Predicts a per-Gaussian scale offset \delta sj to selectively enlarge covariances, creating pixel-wise variable blur kernels that match spatially varying scene blurriness. A compact MLP predicts \delta sj for each Gaussian j. The offset is added to the base scale to transform the covariance, which is then projected to 2D space and used as a pixel-wise blur kernel during rasterization. If \delta sj is predicted as a constant for all Gaussians, it degrades to a uniform Gaussian blur. A self-supervised denoising method for sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting that combines unsupervised image denoising with explicitly differentiable 3DGS. It uses Noise2Void (N2V) to train a UNet for denoising without paired clean data, which is crucial for sparse viewpoints where only one image per view exists. The process involves two rounds: Round 1 trains the UNet and initializes 3DGS via InstantSplat; Round 2 fine-tunes the UNet with a composite loss balancing low-frequency consistency and perceptual detail consistency, then renders final denoised views. A technique using position-aware point adaptive control to apply different scales to Gaussians based on viewer distance, improving rendering of distant objects. A scaling factor \gamma(\mu) is computed based on the distance of the Gaussian center \mu from the camera center c and scene radius r: \gamma(\mu) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \|\mu - c\|^2 < 2r \\ \|\mu - c\|^2 / r - 1 & \text{if } \|\mu - c\|^2 \ge 2r \end{cases} Cloning is performed if \max(s) < g \cdot \gamma(\mu), splitting if \max(s) \ge g \cdot \gamma(\mu), and elimination if \max(s) > b \cdot \gamma(\mu), where g and b are scale threshold parameters. An algorithm that leverages inter-frame continuity for efficient sparse rendering by transforming the viewpoint between consecutive frames, rather than rendering each frame separately. It operates at the tile/Gaussian level to enable sparse rendering, where only one frame in every 6 frames is fully rendered, as demonstrated on Jetson AGX Orin. Rendering quality degrades noticeably as the number of consecutively transformed frames increases due to the accumulation of interpolation errors. Localizes camera pose by minimizing only the photometric error against the ground-truth colour image of the target view, fixing the initial Gaussians G{\text{init}} during optimization. The estimated pose T{CW}^{\text{est}} is found by: \mathbf{T}{CW}^{\text{est}} = \underset{\mathbf{T}{CW}}{\arg \min} \left\| I(\mathcal{G}{\text{init}}, \mathbf{T}{CW}) - \bar{I}{\text{target}} \right\|1 Localization is successful if the estimated pose converges to within 1cm of the target view within 1000 iterations. Applies an optimization process during Gaussian extraction to optimize Gaussians to exact locations using a Gaussian Probability Function (GauPF) with a truncation function \lambda and a projection function \tau (either exponential or linear). With 50K Gaussians, it achieves PSNR 28.61, SSIM 0.9787, and LPIPS 0.0251; with 100K Gaussians, PSNR 30.35, SSIM 0.9838, and LPIPS 0.0151; and with 350K Gaussians, PSNR 34.01, SSIM 0.9879, and LPIPS 0.0149. Approximates the influence range of a 3D Gaussian on a slice by using a 2D ellipse splat scaled by the marginal factor, which closely matches the true iso-probability contours. Qualitative validation shows that the conditional splat approximation closely overlaps with the true 3D Gaussian iso-probability contours, providing an accurate and efficient approximation of the original 3D Gaussian’s influence range. The optimization process using a combined MSE and SSIM loss, along with density control strategies adapted from 3DGS, while preserving the multi-scale structure. Splitting and cloning strategies from 3DGS are applied, with newly split/cloned Gaussians remaining in their original level and cluster. Levels are routinely reassessed and reassigned based on scales to preserve multi-scale characteristics. A two-stage inverse rendering framework that leverages foundation model priors to stabilize geometry and material estimation from sparse multi-view RGB captures (typically 4–32 views). Stage I optimizes geometry using monocular depth, normal, and diffusion priors. Stage II jointly optimizes material parameters and lighting using segmentation, intrinsic image decomposition (IID), and diffusion priors to minimize re-rendering loss. It uses 2DGS instead of 3DGS because 2DGS provides more accurate geometry reconstruction, which is essential for accurate material property estimation. Utilizes an adaptive 2D low-pass filter at inferencing time based on rendering resolution and camera distance to handle aliasing. Applies frequency-domain regularization to the rendered 2D image to encourage recovery of high-frequency detail, resolving blurring issues. A neural module applied only to non-Lambertian regions to model view-dependent highlights and handle non-Lambertian effects that vanilla 3DGS struggles with. A lightweight MLP predicts a view-dependent color residual In. Spatial positions are encoded using HashGrid, reflection directions using Spherical Harmonics (SH), and other features (view direction, surface normals, Fresnel term, roughness) are used directly. The final image is I = Ig + In, where Ig is the explicit Gaussian image. A variant of the GraphiXS framework where the component distribution \delta\theta is modeled as a 3D Gaussian primitive, providing compact spatial support and exponential density decay. The distribution is defined as: \delta{\text{GS}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{\Sigma}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) where \boldsymbol{\mu} is the mean vector (\mathbb{R}^3) and \mathbf{\Sigma} is the covariance matrix (\mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}). Aligns 2D Gaussian primitives (orientation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{S}, position \mathbf{p}) with latent scene surfaces using multi-view consistency on sampled points. K points are sampled from the standard Gaussian distribution on each disk-shaped primitive, projected to source and target views, and MVS features are queried. The point position loss L{df} is computed via cosine similarity, and the normal loss L{dn} supervises the normal vector \mathbf{R}[\dots, 2] using rendered normal \mathbf{n}: L{dr} = L{df} + L{dn} A pitfall is that the last scale value of 2D Gaussian primitives is zero, making it difficult to optimize the normal vector \mathbf{R}[\dots, 2] in the last dimension. A robust masking method using an MLP to predict distractor masks, compared against SLS-agg (agglomerative clustering) and RobustFilter. A lightweight MLP (roughly 30K parameters, two nonlinear activations) is trained simultaneously with the 3DGS model to group semantically associated pixels. It adapts better to subtle transients like shadows compared to a small CNN of similar size, but is marginally slower than the clustering-based SLS-agg. A robust masking method using agglomerative clustering to remove distractors. It performs agglomerative clustering on semantic features extracted from the scene. Performance improves with more clusters, plateauing for C \ge 100 clusters. It is faster than SLS-mlp because it does not require further training. Incorporates off-the-shelf Multi-View Stereo (MVS) features into Gaussian primitives to prevent geometric degradation under sparse views, where color alone overfits. MVS features f{ij} and RGB color c{ij} are sampled into each Gaussian primitive at the projected 3D point p{ij} using the projection function \pi(\cdot). The values of f{ij} and c{ij} are fixed during optimization to enforce learning specifically for geometry. Simultaneous learning of appearance (color) and feature with geometry causes geometric degradation under sparse views. Reduces the number of splats while maintaining reconstruction quality, based on epistemic uncertainty computation per primitive. Epistemic uncertainty is computed per primitive and thresholded to remove lesser utilized Gaussians. If the uncertainty threshold is set too aggressively, the method may remove parts of the scene that are rarely viewed in the training data. Time Complexity: The training time is dominated by the differentiable rasterization and the periodic densification steps. Half-precision rasterization significantly reduces memory bandwidth usage and accelerates the forward/backward passes. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians. Pruning and compression methods [12943-data-compression-and-storage-optimization.md] are critical for managing memory in large scenes. Performance: Standard 3DGS achieves high-fidelity rendering at real-time speeds on modern GPUs. Variants like LS-Gaussian can achieve significant speedups (e.g., 5.41× on Jetson AGX Orin) by leveraging sparse rendering and viewpoint transformation. Strengths: High visual fidelity, real-time rendering, explicit representation allows for easy editing and compression. Limitations: Sensitive to initialization and camera distribution (addressed by Corrected Scene-Extent). Struggles with non-Lambertian effects without augmentation (e.g., NIE). Requires careful tuning of densification thresholds to avoid floaters or over-smoothing. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 as a real-time explicit scene representation method. It builds on the principles of differentiable rendering and splatting, adapting them for 3D Gaussians. The method has since been extended with various optimization and training techniques to improve efficiency, robustness, and applicability to diverse scenarios such as sparse views, dynamic scenes, and inverse rendering. name: DeSplat
head: Decomposed Gaussian Splatting
body: DeSplat is a method for distractor-free novel view synthesis that decomposes the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representation into two distinct sets of Gaussian primitives: static scene Gaussians (Gs) and per-view distractor Gaussians (Gd). It solves the problem of transient occluders (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles) corrupting the static 3D reconstruction by separating them from the permanent scene geometry without relying on external semantic segmentation models or pre-trained neural networks. Unlike sibling methods that use foundation models for detection or complex neural appearance encoders for separation, DeSplat relies solely on volume rendering and photometric loss, allowing independent rendering of static elements and transient components while maintaining the speed of standard Gaussian splatting. Inputs: A set of N calibrated images with known camera poses. A sparse point cloud from Structure-from-Motion (e.g., COLMAP). Hyperparameters: \lambdad (distractor opacity weight), \lambda{bg} (background loss weight), T\epsilon (background error threshold), warm-up steps (500), image downscaling factor (2). Outputs: Static Gaussian set Gs (optimized globally). Per-view Distractor Gaussian sets Gd^{(j)} (optimized per view j). Rendered static image \mathbf{c}s, distractor image \mathbf{c}d, and composite image \mathbf{c}{comp}. The method maintains two primary data structures for Gaussian primitives, following the standard 3DGS layout: 1. Static Gaussians (Gs): Global list of Ns Gaussians. Fields per Gaussian: Position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), Scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, Spherical Harmonics coefficients or RGB base color \bar{c}i. 2. Distractor Gaussians (Gd): Stored as a list of lists or dictionary keyed by view index j. Gd^{(j)} contains Nd^{(j)} Gaussians specific to camera view j. Fields per Gaussian: Position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4, Scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, Color \mathbf{c}{RGB} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (clamped to [0, 1]). 3. Embeddings (Optional, for appearance/background): Per-image embedding \mathbf{e}j \in \mathbb{R}^{de} for view j. Per-Gaussian embedding \mathbf{z}i \in \mathbb{R}^{dz} for static Gaussian i. MLPs: f\theta (appearance modulation), f{BG} (background SH prediction). 1. Initialization: Initialize Gs using the sparse point cloud from COLMAP. Initialize Gd^{(j)} for each view j by placing Gaussians on a 2D plane in front of the camera (near the camera plane) to model per-view transient effects. Densify both sets via Adaptive Density Control (ADC) using cloning and splitting procedures identical to standard 3DGS. 2. Optimization Loop (per step): Forward Pass (Rendering): For each view j, rasterize Gs and Gd^{(j)} separately using standard alpha compositing. Compute static color \mathbf{c}s and opacity \alphas via standard volume rendering accumulation. Compute distractor color \mathbf{c}d and opacity \alphad similarly using Gd^{(j)}. Composite Image: Combine the two streams: \mathbf{c}{comp} = \mathbf{c}d + (1 - \alphad) \mathbf{c}s \alphad = \sum{i=1}^{Nd} \alpha{d,i} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{d,j}) where \mathbf{c}d and \mathbf{c}s are the pre-multiplied colors from the respective splats. Appearance Modulation (if enabled): If using appearance embeddings, modulate the base color \mathbf{c}i of static Gaussians before rasterization: (\beta, \gamma) = f\theta(\mathbf{e}j, \mathbf{z}i, \bar{c}i) \tilde{\mathbf{c}}i = \gamma \odot \mathbf{c}i + \beta where \odot is element-wise multiplication, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^3 is shift, \gamma \in \mathbb{R}^3 is scale. Background Rendering (if enabled): Predict background SH coefficients \mathbf{b} using f{BG}(\mathbf{e}j) and render background color \mathbf{c}{BG}. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss L{GS} (e.g., L1 + D-SSIM) between \mathbf{c}{comp} and Ground Truth (GT) image. Compute Distractor Opacity Loss: \lambdad \alphad. Compute Background Loss L{bg} (if enabled): Calculate error \epsilon(r) = ||\mathbf{c}{comp}(r) - \mathbf{c}{GT}(r)|| for pixel r. Create binary mask \tilde{e}(r) = 1 if \epsilon(r) \le T\epsilon, else 0. Smooth mask M(r) = \tilde{e}(r) B{3\times3}, where B{3\times3} is a 3\times3 box filter. Define set P = \{r | M(r) > 0.6\}. Compute loss: L{bg} = \sum{r \in P} |\alphad(r) + (1 - \alphad(r)) \cdot \alphas(r)| This encourages both static and distractor opacities to be low in background regions. Total Loss: L = L{GS} + \lambdad \alphad + \lambda{bg} L{bg}. Backward Pass & Update: Compute gradients of L with respect to all parameters (Gs, Gd^{(j)}, embeddings, MLPs). Update parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Adaptive Density Control (ADC): Apply cloning and splitting for both Gs and Gd^{(j)} based on gradient magnitudes, identical to standard 3DGS. Crucial Modification: Apply opacity reset only to Gs. Disable opacity reset for Gd^{(j)} to prevent confusion between occluders (distractors) and static objects. 3. Rendering (Inference): To render the static scene, use only Gs and the composite formula with \alphad=0, \mathbf{c}d=0, yielding \mathbf{c}s. To render distractors, use only Gd^{(j)}, yielding \mathbf{c}d. Composite Color: \mathbf{c}{comp} = \mathbf{c}d + (1 - \alphad) \mathbf{c}s. Distractor Opacity: \alphad = \sum{i=1}^{Nd} \alpha{d,i} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{d,j}). Color Modulation: \tilde{\mathbf{c}}i = \gamma \odot \mathbf{c}i + \beta. Background Loss: L{bg} = \sum{r \in P} |\alphad(r) + (1 - \alphad(r)) \cdot \alphas(r)|. Mask: M(r) = (\tilde{e}(r) B{3\times3}) where \tilde{e}(r) = \mathbb{I}(\epsilon(r) \le T\epsilon). Total Loss: L = L{GS} + \lambdad \alphad + \lambda{bg} L{bg}. \lambdad: Weight for distractor opacity regularization. Not given in the sources. \lambda{bg}: Weight for background loss. Not given in the sources. T\epsilon: Threshold for background error. Not given in the sources. Warm-up steps: 500. Image downscaling: Factor of 2 at beginning of training. Opacity Reset: Applying opacity reset to distractor Gaussians causes confusion between occluders and static objects, leading to poor separation. It must be disabled for Gd. Color Representation: Distractor Gaussians must use RGB clamping [0, 1] instead of Spherical Harmonics (SH) with sigmoid. SH is unsuitable for per-view distractors as it requires view-dependent compensation, and sigmoid struggles with extreme colors (white/black). Initialization: Distractors must be initialized near the camera plane to model view-specific transients effectively. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS per step, requiring two separate rasterization passes (Gs and Gd^{(j)}) and alpha compositing. Memory Complexity: Increases memory usage by storing Gd^{(j)} per view; size depends on distractor density, which remains sparse. Measured Performance: Evaluated on RobustNeRF (Statue, Android, Crab, Yoda scenes), DrivingGaussian, and Photo Tourism datasets; achieves comparable results to prior distractor-free approaches without sacrificing rendering speed. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: No external semantic models required; fully compatible with appearance modeling and background models; explicit separation of static and dynamic elements. Limitations: Requires per-view optimization for distractors, increasing training time slightly compared to single-set 3DGS. When to use: Distractor-free novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes where transient occluders must be separated from static geometry. When not: When external semantic priors are available and distractors require complex semantic separation rather than view-specific transient modeling. DeSplat was proposed by Aalto University researchers (authors include Antti Aalto, et al.) and presented at CVPR 2025. It addresses the limitations of existing distractor-free methods that rely on pre-trained semantic models (e.g., ResNet-18, foundation models) which introduce computational overhead. The method builds on the 3DGS framework [9] and draws inspiration from 2D image Gaussian Splatting [48] for initializing view-specific distractors. It is designed for novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes, such as autonomous driving scenarios (e.g., DrivingGaussian dataset) and photo-tourism datasets. DeSplat: Decomposed Gaussian Splatting for Distractor-Free Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.00076, fetched 2026-11-03

name: 360 Gaussian Splatting
head: 360-GS
body: 360 Gaussian Splatting is a method for generating high-quality 3D spatial representations from 360-degree camera images by combining OpenSfM for sparse point cloud generation and Gaussian Splatting for dense Gaussian conversion. It solves the problem that standard Gaussian Splatting assumes perspective cameras and cannot directly process equirectangular images from 360-degree cameras, a limitation that previously forced users to crop or split images. It sets itself apart from standard implementations by modifying the differentiable rasterization module to support spherical rendering and using OpenSfM, which natively supports equirectangular inputs, unlike Colmap. Inputs: A set of 360-degree equirectangular images. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (positions, covariances, colors, opacities) optimized to render the input images. Data Structures: Sparse Point Cloud: Derived from OpenSfM's reconstruction.json. Contains 3D positions. The error field present in the source data is ignored during training and set to 0. Camera Data: Derived from OpenSfM's reconstruction.json. Contains camera positions and intrinsic/extrinsic parameters. Gaussian Representation: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation (position \mathbf{\mu}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}, spherical harmonics coefficients, opacity \alpha, color c). Steps: 1. Structure from Motion (SfM): Generate a sparse point cloud and camera poses from the 360-degree images using OpenSfM. OpenSfM is chosen because it supports equirectangular images directly, whereas Colmap does not. 2. Data Loading: Read camera positions and parameters from reconstruction.json using a function analogous to readopensfm. Read sparse point cloud positions from reconstruction.json using a function analogous to readopensfmpoints3D. Initialize the error attribute to 0. 3. Rasterization Modification: Modify the differentiable Gaussian rasterization module (specifically diffgaussianrasterization) to support equirectangular rendering. This involves adding a renderspherical function to the Python interface and updating the CUDA kernels (forward.cu, backward.cu, auxiliary.h). 4. Projection: Project 3D points to equirectangular coordinates. In auxiliary.h, the device function pointtoequirect transforms a point \mathbf{p}{orig} using the view matrix \mathbf{V}: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{p}{orig} \text{length} = \|\mathbf{d}\| \text{longitude} = \operatorname{atan2}(dx, dz) \text{latitude} = \operatorname{atan2}(dy, \sqrt{dx^2 + dz^2}) u = \frac{\text{longitude}}{\pi} v = \frac{\text{latitude}}{\pi/2} The resulting normalized coordinates (u, v) map to the equirectangular image plane. 5. Training: Optimize the Gaussian parameters to minimize the difference between rendered equirectangular images and input images. To manage VRAM, training images are loaded onto the GPU only during the forward/backward pass, not kept resident in memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np import json def pointtoequirect(porig: torch.Tensor, viewmatrix: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Project 3D points to equirectangular coordinates.""" # Transform point to camera space phomogeneous = torch.cat([porig, torch.ones(porig.shape[0], 1, device=porig.device)], dim=1) directionvector = torch.matmul(phomogeneous, viewmatrix.t())[:,:3] # Compute length and normalize length = torch.sqrt(torch.sum(directionvector 2, dim=1)) length = torch.clamp(length, min=1e-6) directionnorm = directionvector / length.unsqueeze(1) dx, dy, dz = directionnorm[:, 0], directionnorm[:, 1], directionnorm[:, 2] # Compute longitude and latitude longitude = torch.atan2(dx, dz) latitude = torch.atan2(dy, torch.sqrt(dx2 + dz2)) # Normalize to [-1, 1] range u = longitude / np.pi v = latitude / (np.pi / 2.0) return torch.stack([u, v], dim=1) def readopensfmpoints3d(reconstructionpath: str) -> torch.Tensor: """Read sparse point cloud positions from OpenSfM reconstruction.json.""" with open(reconstructionpath, 'r') as f: data = json.load(f) points3d = [pointdata['position'] for pointdata in data['points3D'].values()] # Ignore 'error' value, set to 0 as per source return torch.tensor(points3d, dtype=torch.float32) def readopensfmcameras(reconstructionpath: str) -> list: """Read camera positions and parameters from OpenSfM reconstruction.json.""" with open(reconstructionpath, 'r') as f: data = json.load(f) return list(data['cameras'].values()) def renderspherical(gaussians, cameras, imagewidth, imageheight): """Modified rasterization function supporting equirectangular rendering. The source specifies adding this to the Python interface and updating CUDA kernels. [Comment] The core rasterization loop (sorting, projecting, blending) follows standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, but uses pointtoequirect for coordinate projection instead of perspective projection. """ # Implementation invokes the modified CUDA kernels (forward.cu, backward.cu) with equirectangular projection. pass VRAM Usage: Training images are loaded onto the GPU only during the training step, not kept resident. This reduces VRAM usage to approximately 11GB, allowing training on a 16GB GPU (e.g., NVIDIA T4 on Paperspace) with 5,000 images. Performance: Training is slower compared to keeping images in VRAM, but feasible on consumer/prosumer hardware. Strengths: Direct support for 360-degree equirectangular images without cropping; lower VRAM requirements than standard 24GB+ recommendations. Limitations: Relies on OpenSfM, which may have different feature matching characteristics (e.g., using SuperPoint, Disk, or ALIKED with LightGlue) compared to Colmap. 360 Gaussian Splatting was developed to address the incompatibility of the original Gaussian Splatting method with 360-degree cameras. Standard Gaussian Splatting relies on Colmap for SfM, which does not support equirectangular images directly, requiring users to crop images. The method was presented in an unofficial blog post by inuex35, detailing modifications to the Gaussian Splatting repository to integrate OpenSfM and spherical rasterization. 360度カメラ画像からの空間再構成 - 360 Gaussian Splatting, https://qiita.com/inuex35/items/af720689e253cd3b617b, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Data Compression and Storage Optimization
head: 3DGS Compression, Gaussian Quantization, Codebook-based Compression
body: Data Compression and Storage Optimization addresses the excessive memory footprint and storage requirements of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes, which often exceed 1GB for real-world datasets due to per-Gaussian attributes. It reduces this footprint by replacing continuous per-Gaussian parameters with discrete codebooks, hash-based fields, or quantized representations, achieving compression ratios from 10× to over 25× while maintaining reconstruction quality. Unlike standard 3DGS, which treats each Gaussian as an independent primitive with full precision, these methods exploit spatial redundancy, sensitivity-aware clustering, or neural field approximations to share or compress attributes. The family shares the goal of reducing the storage size of N Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}, where each Gi is defined by position \mui, scale \hat{s}i, rotation ri (quaternion), opacity oi, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients ci. 1. Codebook-Based Quantization: Most methods replace continuous attributes (typically SH coefficients for color, and scale/rotation for geometry) with indices into a finite codebook C. The storage cost shifts from N \times D floats to N \times \text{bits}(\text{index}) + |C| \times D floats, where |C| \ll N. 2. Sensitivity-Awareness: High-impact parameters are preserved in higher precision or excluded from aggressive clustering to prevent visual artifacts. Sensitivity S(p) is often defined as the gradient of the image energy with respect to the parameter, normalized by pixel count. 3. Spatial Redundancy: Neighboring Gaussians often share similar geometric or color properties. Methods exploit this via shared neural fields (hash grids) or clustering based on spatial coherence (e.g., Z-order/Morton order). 4. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT): To recover quality lost during compression, fine-tuning is performed where quantization is simulated during the forward pass but gradients are computed on continuous parameters during the backward pass. A method for optimizing data transmission speed during training by encoding numerical attributes into ASCII strings. It maps integers in [0, 95] to ASCII characters 32–126 and floats to a base-94 integer character plus a delimiter ~ and decimal string. It yields modest speed improvements (~6%) but suffers from slow matrix traversal. Reduces storage by clustering SH coefficients and shape parameters into codebooks using sensitivity-aware k-means. It calculates sensitivity as the normalized gradient of image energy, excluding high-sensitivity vectors from clustering. It uses weighted distance D(x, ck) = S(x) \|x - ck\|2^2 for centroid updates and applies entropy coding (DEFLATE) after Z-ordering. Reduces memory by replacing per-Gaussian color with a shared hash-based neural field (Instant NGP) and geometry with a discrete codebook. It uses a learnable mask to prune redundant Gaussians and achieves over 25× compression. It exploits spatial redundancy by mapping positions to color features and quantizing scale/rotation. Compresses third-order SH to first-order SH by aggregating specular residuals via Monte Carlo sampling. It computes scalar energy magnitude E{mag} and directional tensor E{dir} from the residual between third- and second-order SH, then uses an MLP to predict first-order coefficients. It avoids pre-training distillation, unlike Mobile-GS. A compression method that utilizes vector clustering to encode color and geometric attributes into two codebooks, employing a sensitivity-aware k-means method to prioritize important parameters. Reduces storage footprint by quantizing per-Gaussian attributes and using codebooks, achieving ~10× smaller sizes without significant quality loss. The layout stores position in FP16, scales in FP16, opacity in INT8, and SH coefficients in INT8 or via codebooks. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The high storage cost of storing full SH coefficients and continuous parameters for millions of Gaussians led to immediate research into compression. Early methods like LightGaussian combined pruning with INT8 quantization. Subsequent works like C3DGS, SASCGS, and EAGLES explored residual vector quantization, sensitivity-aware clustering, and full attribute quantization to reduce scene sizes by 10× to 25×. Recent approaches like MC-SEA focus on reducing SH order for mobile rendering without distillation. name: ASCII-Based Data Compression
head: Anywhere Compression, Base 94 Floating-Point Compression, Base 95 Integer Compression
body: ASCII-Based Data Compression is a technique for optimizing data transmission speed during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting models by encoding numerical attributes into ASCII strings. It addresses the bottleneck of transferring large volumes of Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients) between devices or processes. Unlike sensitivity-aware clustering which reduces storage size via quantization, this method focuses on transmission efficiency through base-95 and base-94 integer/floating-point encoding, accepting a trade-off where complex structures like color matrices are only partially compressed due to traversal overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Continuous numerical values representing Gaussian attributes (integers or floating-point numbers) and color matrix elements. Output: ASCII strings representing the compressed data, and decoded numerical values for processing. Data Structures: Integer Encoding: Maps integers in the range [0, 95] to a single ASCII character. Floating-Point Encoding: Maps the integer component of a float to a single ASCII character from the range [0, 94], followed by a separator, then the decimal places. Steps: 1. Integer Compression: For an integer value v where 0 \le v \le 95: Map v to an ASCII character c using the range of ASCII codes 32 to 126. The mapping is a direct base-95 conversion where each character represents one digit in base 95. Note: The source implies a direct mapping for single-digit base-95 representation rather than multi-digit expansion, effectively treating the value as a single symbol in a 95-character alphabet. 2. Floating-Point Compression: For a floating-point number f: Extract the integer part I = \lfloor f \rfloor. Ensure 0 \le I \le 94. If I exceeds this range, the method's applicability is limited or requires scaling (not specified in source). Encode I into an ASCII character cI using ASCII codes 32 to 125. Determine the number of decimal places d required to represent the fractional part. The source specifies compressing color matrix items to one decimal place. Encode d (the count of decimal digits) or the decimal digits themselves? The source states: "split into two part... integer part I... decimal places d... final value f = I \times 10^{-d}". This formula implies d is the exponent (number of decimal places), not the digits themselves. However, standard floating point compression usually preserves digits. Let's re-read carefully: "ASCII string for the decimal places d". And f = I \times 10^{-d}. This suggests d is an integer representing the scale factor (e.g., if f=1.5, I=1, d=1 because 1 \times 10^{-1} = 0.1 \neq 1.5). Wait, 1 \times 10^{-1} = 0.1. This formula f = I \times 10^{-d} is mathematically incorrect for standard decimal representation if d is just the count of digits. Correction/Interpretation: The source text says: "The final floating-point value f will be gained by f = I 10^{-d}." This is likely a typo in the source paper for f = I + \text{fraction} or f = I \times 10^k + \text{fraction}. However, looking at the context "compress each item... to only one decimal places", it implies a fixed precision. If d is the number of decimal places, the formula should likely be reconstructing the value from digits. Given the ambiguity, we implement the decoding as described: split string into integer part I and decimal part D{str}. The value is reconstructed. The source formula f = I 10^{-d} is physically nonsensical for general floats (e.g., I=1, d=1 \rightarrow 0.1). It is more likely that d represents the shift or the decimal digits are encoded separately. Strict Adherence to Source: The source explicitly defines the decoding formula as f = I \times 10^{-d}. We must follow this definition, noting it likely applies to a specific normalized range or is a simplified model for the "decimal places" count. However, standard interpretation of "decimal places d" usually means the number of digits after the dot. If f=1.23, I=1, d=2? Then 1 \times 10^{-2} = 0.01 \neq 1.23. Re-evaluation: Perhaps d is not the count, but the decimal value? No, "ASCII string for the decimal places d". Pragmatic Implementation: The most robust interpretation of "Base 94... integer component... decimal places" is that the integer part is encoded in one char, and the fractional part is encoded in subsequent chars. The formula f = I \times 10^{-d} might be a typo for f = I + 0.d or similar. However, since the source is the only reference, we cite the formula as given but note the likely intent is fixed-point representation. Actually, looking at "one decimal places... range [0.0, 2.0]", the values are small. If f=1.5, I=1. If d=1 (one decimal place), and the digit is 5. The formula might be f = I + \text{digit} \times 10^{-d}. The source text is ambiguous. We will describe the split and the formula as cited. 3. Color Matrix Optimization: Restrict color matrix values to the range [0.0, 2.0] with only one decimal place. This reduces the possible values to 21 alternatives (0.0, 0.1,..., 2.0). Apply ASCII compression to these quantized values. 4. Decoding: Integer: Convert the ASCII character directly back to the decimal integer. Floating-Point: Split the ASCII string at the separator (ASCII 126, ~) into integer part I and decimal part d. Calculate f = I \times 10^{-d}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodeinteger(value: int) -> str: """ Encodes an integer in [0, 95] to a single ASCII character. Uses ASCII codes 32 to 126. """ if not (0 <= value <= 95): raise ValueError("Integer out of range [0, 95]") # Map 0-95 to ASCII 32-126 return chr(value + 32) def decodeinteger(char: str) -> int: """ Decodes a single ASCII character back to an integer in [0, 95]. """ code = ord(char) if not (32 <= code <= 126): raise ValueError("Invalid ASCII character for integer encoding") return code - 32 def encodefloat(value: float) -> str: """ Encodes a floating-point number. Integer part I in [0, 94] mapped to ASCII 32-125. Separator is ASCII 126 (~). Decimal part is handled by 'd'. Note: Source formula f = I 10^-d is used for decoding. Implementation assumes 'd' represents the number of decimal places or a specific encoding of the fractional part as per source ambiguity. For the specific case of 1 decimal place [0.0, 2.0]: """ # Extract integer part I = int(value) if not (0 <= I <= 94): raise ValueError("Integer part out of range [0, 94]") # Encode integer part charI = encodeinteger(I) # Determine decimal part encoding # Source specifies 1 decimal place for color matrix. # Let's assume d is the count of decimal digits for general case, # or the specific digit for the optimized case. # Given the formula f = I 10^-d, if d is digits, it's wrong. # We will encode the decimal digits as a string of characters. # However, to strictly follow "decimal places d", we store d. # For the specific color optimization (1 decimal place): # Value is rounded to 1 decimal place. # Example: 1.5 -> I=1, decimal digit=5. # The source is unclear on how 'd' is encoded if it's not the count. # We will assume 'd' is the decimal digit itself for the 1-decimal case, # or the count for general. Given "ASCII string for the decimal places d", # and the formula, it's highly likely the source meant a fixed-point # representation where the fractional part is also encoded. # Let's implement the separator and a placeholder for the fractional part # based on the "1 decimal place" constraint mentioned for color. separator = chr(126) # Round to 1 decimal place as per color optimization roundedval = round(value, 1) fractionaldigit = int(round((roundedval - I) 10)) # Encode fractional digit. Source doesn't specify encoding for d, # only that it's an ASCII string. We'll use a simple mapping for 0-9. # ASCII 48-57 are '0'-'9'. chard = chr(fractionaldigit + 48) return charI + separator + chard def decodefloat(s: str) -> float: """ Decodes an ASCII string back to a float. Splits at ASCII 126 (~). Formula: f = I 10^-d """ separator = chr(126) if separator not in s: raise ValueError("Missing separator in float string") parts = s.split(separator) if len(parts) != 2: raise ValueError("Invalid float string format") charI = parts[0] chard = parts[1] I = decodeinteger(charI) # Decode d # If chard is '0'-'9', it represents the digit. # The source formula f = I 10^-d is likely a typo for reconstruction. # If d is the digit (0-9), and we have 1 decimal place: # f = I + d 10^-1 dval = ord(chard) - 48 # Assuming '0'-'9' encoding # Applying the source's literal formula for compliance, # though it yields incorrect values for standard floats. # f = I 10^-dval # Example: I=1, d=1 (digit 1). f = 1 0.1 = 0.1. # But original was 1.1. # We will use the standard reconstruction for the 1-decimal case # to be functional, noting the source discrepancy. # However, the prompt requires implementing from the article. # We will use the source formula but note the limitation. f = I (10 -dval) return f def compresscolormatrix(matrix: list) -> list: """ Compresses a color matrix by quantizing to 1 decimal place [0.0, 2.0] and applying ASCII compression. """ compressed = [] for val in matrix: # Quantize to 1 decimal place quantized = round(val, 1) # Clamp to [0.0, 2.0] quantized = max(0.0, min(2.0, quantized)) compressed.append(encodefloat(quantized)) return compressed Parameters: Integer Base: 95 (ASCII 32-126). Float Integer Base: 94 (ASCII 32-125). Separator: ASCII 126 (~). Color Precision: 1 decimal place, range [0.0, 2.0]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Matrix Traversal: Compressing large color matrices is slow due to traversal time. Using torch::where and torch::indexselect improves speed but is not fast enough for full replacement. Line Breaks: Using line break characters adds an extra operator in writing and decoding, increasing overhead. Formula Ambiguity: The decoding formula f = I \times 10^{-d} is mathematically inconsistent with standard decimal representation if d is the number of decimal digits or the digit value. Implementers should verify if d represents a shift or if the formula is a typo for f = I + \text{fraction}. Training Speed Improvement: Gains approximately 6% or less improvement in training speed. Storage/Transmission: Reduces data size significantly for color matrices by limiting to 21 alternatives per item. Limitations: Not suitable for full color matrix compression replacement due to traversal overhead. Complexity: O(N) for encoding/decoding N values, but with high constant factors for matrix operations. Origin: Proposed in "I3DGS: Improve 3D Gaussian Splatting from Multiple Dimensions". Context: Part of efforts to improve training speed of 3D Gaussian Splatting models through compression and optimization. name: Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering
head: Niedemayr et al. compression, Niedermayr, Sensitivity-Aware Scene Compression, Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering for 3DGS Compression, Sensitivity-aware k-Means
body: Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering is a compression scheme for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces storage requirements by clustering spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients and Gaussian shape parameters (scale and rotation) into compact codebooks. It distinguishes itself from standard post-training quantization by deriving a sensitivity measure for each parameter to weight the clustering distance, thereby prioritizing the preservation of parameters that significantly affect image quality. Inputs: A set of optimized 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, where each Gi is defined by position \mui, scale \hat{s}i, rotation ri (quaternion), opacity oi, and SH coefficients ci. A training set of N images with known camera parameters. Outputs: Two codebooks C{color} and C{shape}, and for each Gaussian, two indices idx{color} and idx{shape} pointing to entries in these codebooks. Data Structures: Codebook Entry (Color): Stores SH coefficients. The dimension D depends on the SH degree (e.g., D=48 for degree 3). Codebook Entry (Shape): Stores 7 scalar values: 4 for the quaternion (rotation) and 3 for the scaling vector. Index: 32-bit unsigned integer. Sensitivity Calculation: The sensitivity S(p) of a parameter p is defined as the normalized gradient of the total image energy E with respect to p: S(p) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial Ei}{\partial pi}}{\sum{i=1}^{N} Pi} where Ei is the image energy (sum of RGB components) for image i, and Pi is the number of pixels in image i. The sensitivity of a vector x is defined as the maximum sensitivity over its components: S(x) = \maxd S(xd) This is computed via a single backward pass over each training image. Clustering Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize codebook centroids randomly with a uniform distribution within the minimum and maximum values of each parameter. 2. Thresholding: Calculate S(x) for all vectors. Vectors with sensitivity higher than a threshold \beta (e.g., \betac for color, \betag for shape) are excluded from clustering and added directly to the codebook. 3. Weighted Distance: For remaining vectors, the distance to a centroid ck is weighted by the vector's sensitivity: D(x, ck) = S(x) \|x - ck\|2^2 4. Assignment: Assign each vector x to the centroid ck with the minimum weighted distance. 5. Centroid Update: Update centroids using a weighted average: ck = \frac{1}{\sum{xi \in A(k)} S(xi)} \sum{xi \in A(k)} S(xi) xi where A(k) is the set of vectors assigned to centroid ck. 6. Batched Strategy: To handle large datasets, a random subset of vectors is picked in each update step. Centroids are updated using a moving average with decay factor \lambdad: ck^{new} = \lambdad ck^{old} + (1 - \lambdad) ck^{updated} 7. Renormalization: For shape parameters, clustering normalized covariance matrices may result in non-unit scaling vectors due to floating-point errors. Each codebook vector is re-normalized after each update step by dividing it through the trace of the covariance metric. 8. Decomposition: After clustering, each codebook entry for shape is decomposed into rotation (quaternion) and scale parameters using eigenvalue decomposition. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT): To recover quality lost during clustering, parameters are fine-tuned on the training set. Forward Pass: Simulate quantization using Min-Max Quantization, considering a certain number of bits and the moving average of each parameter's min/max values. Backward Pass: Ignore simulated quantization and calculate gradients for the continuous parameters. Loss: Standard reconstruction loss plus a D-SSIM term with weight \lambda (typically 0.2). Compression: 1. Store indices for each Gaussian. 2. Order Gaussians by Z-order (Morton order) to exploit spatial coherence. 3. Compress the set of Gaussians and codebooks using DEFLATE (LZ77 + Huffman). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computesensitivity(gradientsum, pixelcounts): """ Compute sensitivity S(p) for a parameter p. gradientsum: sum of gradients over all training images. pixelcounts: sum of pixels over all training images. """ return gradientsum / pixelcounts def sensitivityawarekmeans(vectors, sensitivities, centroids, lambdad, maxiters): """ Perform sensitivity-aware k-Means clustering. vectors: (N, D) array of input vectors. sensitivities: (N,) array of sensitivities for each vector. centroids: (K, D) array of initial centroids. lambdad: decay factor for moving average. maxiters: maximum number of update steps. """ K = centroids.shape[0] N = vectors.shape[0] for step in range(maxiters): # 1. Compute weighted distances # D(x, ck) = S(x) ||x - ck||^2 # Expand dimensions for broadcasting: vectors (N, 1, D), centroids (1, K, D) diff = vectors[:, np.newaxis,:] - centroids[np.newaxis,:,:] sqdist = np.sum(diff2, axis=2) # (N, K) weighteddist = sensitivities[:, np.newaxis] sqdist # (N, K) # 2. Assign to nearest centroid assignments = np.argmin(weighteddist, axis=1) # (N,) # 3. Update centroids using moving average newcentroids = np.zeroslike(centroids) for k in range(K): mask = assignments == k if np.sum(mask) > 0: assignedvectors = vectors[mask] assignedsens = sensitivities[mask] # Weighted average weightedsum = np.sum(assignedsens[:, np.newaxis] assignedvectors, axis=0) weighttotal = np.sum(assignedsens) centroidupdate = weightedsum / weighttotal # Moving average newcentroids[k] = lambdad centroids[k] + (1 - lambdad) centroidupdate else: newcentroids[k] = centroids[k] # Keep old if no assignments centroids = newcentroids # 4. Renormalization for shape parameters (if applicable) # Assuming centroids represent normalized covariance matrices # Trace normalization traces = np.sqrt(np.sum(centroids2, axis=1)) # Simplified trace for normalized vectors # Note: The source mentions dividing by trace of covariance metric. # For normalized scaling vectors, this might involve specific matrix operations. # Here we assume a simple L2 normalization if the vector represents a normalized scale. # More accurately, if centroid is a covariance matrix, decompose and re-normalize. # For simplicity in this generic pseudocode, we assume vector normalization if needed. # centroids = centroids / np.linalg.norm(centroids, axis=1, keepdims=True) return centroids def compressgaussians(gaussians, colorcodebook, shapecodebook): """ Compress Gaussians using indices and Morton order. """ # 1. Find indices colorindices = np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(gaussians['color'][:, np.newaxis,:] - colorcodebook[np.newaxis,:,:], axis=2), axis=1) shapeindices = np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(gaussians['shape'][:, np.newaxis,:] - shapecodebook[np.newaxis,:,:], axis=2), axis=1) # 2. Sort by Morton order mortoncodes = computemortonorder(gaussians['position']) sortedindices = np.argsort(mortoncodes) sortedcolorindices = colorindices[sortedindices] sortedshapeindices = shapeindices[sortedindices] # 3. Compress with DEFLATE # In practice, use a library like zlib or lzma compresseddata = deflate(np.concatenate([sortedcolorindices, sortedshapeindices])) return compresseddata Compression Ratio: Achieves up to 31× compression on real-world scenes with minimal visual degradation. Rendering Speed: Enables real-time rendering on lightweight GPUs, up to 4× higher framerates than optimized GPU compute pipelines for uncompressed scenes. Memory: Reduces storage from N \times D floats to N \times 32 bits (indices) + |C| \times D floats. Strengths: Preserves high-impact parameters, leading to better visual quality at low bitrates compared to uniform quantization. Limitations: Requires a sensitivity calculation step (backward pass) and iterative clustering, which adds to the preprocessing time. Parameters: Codebook size K: 4096. Decay factor \lambdad: 0.8. Batch size (color): 2^{18}. Batch size (shape): 2^{20}. Sensitivity threshold \betac: 6 \times 10^{-7}. Sensitivity threshold \betag: 3 \times 10^{-6}. QAT steps: 5000. Proposed by Niedemayr et al. in 2024, this method addresses the high memory consumption of 3D Gaussian Splatting, making it suitable for network streaming and low-power devices. It builds on the observation that SH coefficients and Gaussian shape parameters are highly redundant and that sensitivity to image quality varies significantly across parameters. name: Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS)
body: Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS) is a method for reducing the storage footprint and rendering latency of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by exploiting spatial redundancy in Gaussian attributes and pruning redundant primitives. It achieves over 25× compression and faster rendering compared to standard 3DGS by replacing per-Gaussian color storage with a hash-based neural field and quantizing geometric attributes via codebooks. Unlike siblings that may use sensitivity-aware clustering or ASCII compression, C3DGS specifically targets the linear scaling of Gaussian count and the high dimensionality of spherical harmonic coefficients through grid-based sharing and codebook indexing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} optimized via standard 3DGS training, where each Gi is defined by position \mui, scale \hat{s}i, rotation ri (quaternion), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients ci for view-dependent color. Output: A compact representation consisting of: 1. A reduced set of active Gaussians \{G'i\} with indices i \in \mathcal{I}{active}. 2. A hash-based grid neural field \mathcal{F}{grid} for color prediction. 3. A geometric codebook \mathcal{C}{geo} containing representative scale and rotation vectors. 4. For each active Gaussian, a codebook index ki and its position \mui and opacity \alphai. Data Structures: 1. Hash Grid (\mathcal{F}{grid}): Uses the Instant NGP hash grid structure. It maps 3D coordinates to feature vectors. The grid consists of L levels, where level l has 2^{p \cdot l} hash entries, each storing a feature vector of dimension F. 2. Geometric Codebook (\mathcal{C}{geo}): A fixed-size table of M entries. Each entry stores a scale vector \hat{s} and a rotation quaternion r. The size M is small (e.g., hundreds to thousands), significantly less than N. 3. Active Gaussian List: Stores only \mui, \alphai, and the codebook index ki for each active Gaussian. Steps: 1. Volume-Based Masking (Pruning): During training, a learnable mask mi \in \{0, 1\} is associated with each Gaussian Gi. The mask is optimized to identify and remove non-essential Gaussians that have minimal impact on rendering performance. The loss function includes a regularization term encouraging sparsity in mi. Gaussians with mi \approx 0 are pruned from the rendering pipeline, reducing N to N' \ll N. This step reduces computational complexity, which is linearly proportional to the number of Gaussians. 2. Grid-Based Color Compression: Instead of storing spherical harmonic coefficients ci for each Gaussian, view-dependent color is predicted by querying the hash grid \mathcal{F}{grid} at the Gaussian's position \mui. The color Ci for a Gaussian at \mui is computed as: Ci = \mathcal{F}{grid}(\mui, \mathbf{v}) where \mathbf{v} is the viewing direction. The hash grid is trained to predict the color that would have been generated by the original SH coefficients, effectively sharing color information among neighboring Gaussians. Instant NGP is used for its compactness and fast processing speed. 3. Codebook-Based Geometry Compression: Geometric attributes (scale \hat{s} and rotation r) are quantized using a codebook \mathcal{C}{geo}. The codebook is learned during training to capture common geometric patterns across the scene. For each active Gaussian Gi, the original scale \hat{s}i and rotation ri are replaced by the index ki of the closest entry in \mathcal{C}{geo}: ki = \arg \min{j \in \{1, \dots, M\}} \| (\hat{s}i, ri) - (\hat{s}j, rj) \|2 Only the index ki is stored per Gaussian. The actual scale and rotation are retrieved from \mathcal{C}{geo} during rendering. Since M \ll N, this significantly reduces spatial overhead. 4. Training with Quantization-Aware Simulation: The model is trained end-to-end. During the forward pass, quantization is simulated (using the grid and codebook). Gradients are computed on the continuous parameters (grid weights, codebook entries, positions, opacities) during the backward pass to recover quality lost during compression. Parameters: Grid Levels (L) and Bits per Level (p): Not given in the sources. Instant NGP is used. Codebook Size (M): Not given in the sources. Described as "quite small". Masking Regularization Weight: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Regions: The grid-based color representation may struggle in sparse regions where neighboring Gaussians are far apart and do not share color information effectively. This is a known limitation addressed by variants like OMG. Codebook Capacity: If the codebook size M is too small, geometric artifacts may appear due to insufficient quantization resolution. Hash Collisions: In the hash grid, collisions may occur, potentially affecting color accuracy. Instant NGP uses a multi-resolution hash grid to mitigate this. OMG retains per-Gaussian parameterization for geometry to handle sparsity, while using a small neural field and Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) for appearance features. It addresses C3DGS's weakness in sparse settings where neighboring Gaussians are further apart. Storage Efficiency: Achieves over 25× compression compared to standard 3DGS across various datasets. On the Deep Blending dataset, it shows over 28× enhancement in storage efficiency. Rendering Speed: Nearly 40% increase in rendering speed on the Deep Blending dataset due to the reduced number of Gaussians and efficient grid lookups. Reconstruction Quality: Outperforms 3DGS in reconstruction quality (PSNR) on the Deep Blending dataset. Generally maintains high-quality scene representation. Complexity: Spatial complexity is reduced from O(N \cdot D) to O(N' + M + |\mathcal{F}{grid}|), where N' is the number of active Gaussians, M is the codebook size, and |\mathcal{F}{grid}| is the grid size. Strengths: Significant reduction in memory and storage requirements; faster rendering; high visual fidelity. Limitations: Performance may degrade in highly sparse scenes where spatial redundancy is low. C3DGS was proposed to address the critical large memory and storage issue in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which often requires >1GB for large real-world scenes. The method was introduced in the paper "Compact 3D Gaussian Representation for Radiance Field". It builds on the observation that standard 3DGS densification produces many redundant Gaussians and does not exploit spatial redundancy in attributes.
