name: Optimized Minimal 3D Gaussian Splatting (OMG)
body: Optimized Minimal 3D Gaussian Splatting (OMG) is a method for compact 3D Gaussian representation that retains per-Gaussian parameterization for geometry (scale and rotation) to handle sparsity, while using a small neural field and Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) for appearance features to exploit local continuity. It achieves state-of-the-art storage compression (e.g., >300× relative to 3DGS in the bicycle scene) while maintaining high visual fidelity, building on Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS) by addressing the weakness of neural fields in sparse settings where neighboring Gaussians are further apart. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians initialized from training data. Output: A compressed representation consisting of quantized geometric attributes, quantized appearance features, and a set of pruned Gaussians, stored in a single file. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Attributes: Center position: p \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Opacity: o \in [0, 1]^N. 3D Scale: s \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Rotation (Quaternion): r \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 4}. SH Coefficients (0-degree, static color): h^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. SH Coefficients (1-3 degrees, view-dependent color): h^{(1,2,3)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 45}. 2. Learned Features: Static feature: T \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}. View-dependent feature: V \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}. D is the feature dimensionality. 3. SVQ Codebooks: For each sub-vector partition m \in \{1, \dots, M\}, a codebook C^{(m)} of size B \times L. M is the number of sub-vectors, L is the sub-vector length, B is the codebook size. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian set using K-means clustering. 2. Feature Learning: Learn per-Gaussian static feature T and view-dependent feature V. 3. Space Feature Computation: For each Gaussian n, compute the space feature Fn based on its center position pn: Fn = \text{MLP}s(\gamma(pn)) where \gamma(\cdot) is positional encoding and \text{MLP}s(\cdot) is a neural network. 4. Appearance Generation: Compute static color, opacity, and view-dependent color using the learned features and space feature: h^{(0)}n = \text{MLP}t(\text{cat}(Tn, Fn)) on = \text{MLP}o(\text{cat}(Tn, Fn)) h^{(1,2,3)}n = \text{MLP}v(\text{cat}(Vn, Fn)) where \text{cat}(\cdot, \cdot) denotes concatenation, and \text{MLP}t, \text{MLP}o, \text{MLP}v are MLPs for static color, opacity, and view-dependent color, respectively. 5. Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) Application: Geometry: Apply SVQ to geometric attributes sn and rn to get quantized vectors \hat{s}n and \hat{r}n for rendering. Appearance: Concatenate appearance features Tn and Vn. Apply SVQ to the concatenated vector. Split the result back into quantized components \hat{T}n and \hat{V}n to replace Tn and Vn in Equations (3) and (4). SVQ Formulation: For a vector z \in \mathbb{R}^{ML}, split into M sub-vectors zm \in \mathbb{R}^L. The quantized vector \hat{z} is: \hat{z} = q(z; M) = \text{cat}(C^{(1)}[i1], \dots, C^{(M)}[iM]) where the index for sub-vector m is selected as: im = \arg \minj \|zm - C^{(m)}[j]\|2^2, \quad m \in \{1, \dots, M\}. 6. Training Strategy: Train using rendering loss. In the final 1,000 iterations, freeze the selected codebook indices and fine-tune only the codebook using the rendering loss. 7. Importance Scoring and Pruning: Base Importance Score (\bar{I}i): Determine if Gaussian i is the dominant contributor for at least one ray \rho. Let w{i,\rho} be the blending weight for ray \rho and NR be the total number of training rays: \bar{I}i = \begin{cases} \sum{\rho=1}^{NR} w{i,\rho} & \text{if } \exists \rho \in \{1, \dots, NR\} \text{ s.t. } w{i,\rho} = \maxj w{j,\rho} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Local Distinctiveness: Approximate neighbor selection by sorting Gaussians in Morton order and selecting adjacent indices as local neighbors. Compute the mean L1 distance to K-nearest neighbors Ni^K: \text{Distinctiveness}i = \frac{1}{D} \sum{j \in Ni^K} \|Ti - Tj\|1. Final Importance Score (Ii): Ii = \bar{I}i \left( \frac{1}{D} \sum{j \in Ni^K} \|Ti - Tj\|1 \right)^\lambda where \lambda is a scaling factor. Thresholding: Remove low-importance Gaussians using CDF-based thresholding with threshold \tau. 8. Post-processing and Storage: 1. Apply 16-bit quantization to position p and compress with G-PCC. 2. Huffman encode SVQ indices. 3. Store all components in a single file with LZMA compression. Rendering Equation: To render an image, Gaussians are depth-sorted. For a pixel coordinate x: C(x) = \sum{k=1}^{N(x)} ck \alphak(x) \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(x)) where ck is color, \alphak(x) is 2D opacity, and N(x) is the number of Gaussians around x. The 2D opacity for Gaussian n is: \alphan(x) = on \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (x - p'n)^T \Sigma'n (x - p'n)\right) where p'n and \Sigma'n are the projected center and covariance. Parameters: Threshold \tau values for OMG variants: XS=0.96, X=0.98, M=0.99, L=0.999, XL=0.9999. K: Number of nearest neighbors for distinctiveness calculation. Not given in the sources. \lambda: Scaling factor for distinctiveness. Not given in the sources. D: Feature dimensionality. Not given in the sources. M, L, B: SVQ parameters (sub-vectors, length, codebook size). Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity: Neural fields assume local continuity, which weakens as Gaussians become sparser. OMG mitigates this by retaining per-Gaussian attributes for geometry and using SVQ for appearance. Redundancy: Naive thresholding based on blending weights can remove all similar Gaussians simultaneously or retain redundant ones. The local distinctiveness metric addresses this. Training Overhead: Updating indices and codes at every iteration increases training time. Freezing indices in the final 1K iterations reduces this overhead. Storage: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, OMG-XS achieves nearly 50% reduction in storage compared to LocoGS-S while retaining PSNR and SSIM. In the bicycle scene, OMG-XS achieves over 300× compression relative to 3DGS. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, OMG consistently shows the smallest storage requirements while maintaining high performance. Strengths: Effective in extreme compression scenarios; retains high visual fidelity despite reducing the number of Gaussians by an additional 20% compared to Mini-Splatting. Limitations: Requires post-processing steps (G-PCC, Huffman, LZMA) for final storage. OMG was proposed to address the challenges of representing minimal Gaussian primitives efficiently. It builds on the observation that existing neural field approaches weaken in sparse settings, while disregarding continuity leads to inefficient representation. The method was evaluated on real-world datasets including Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending. name: Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator
head: Monte Carlo directional moments, Specular Energy Aggregator
body: The Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator (MC-SEA) is a compression technique that maps high-order (third-order) Spherical Harmonics (SH) radiance energy into a compact lower-order (first-order) subspace without pre-training or distillation, preserving specular features. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and inference cost associated with third-order SH in mobile rendering by extracting directional moments of the specular residual via Monte Carlo projection. Unlike Mobile-GS, which uses distillation from a high-order teacher model, MC-SEA compresses energy directly, replacing teacher-student distillation to improve training efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Third-order SH coefficients ci \in \mathbb{R}^{(Lo+1)^2 \times 3} for each Gaussian primitive i, where Lo=3. Output: First-order SH coefficients c'i \in \mathbb{R}^{(Lt+1)^2 \times 3} for each primitive i, where Lt=1, and aggregated latent variables E{mag} and E{dir}. Data Structures: Spherical Samples: A set of K unit direction vectors D = \{dk\}{k=1}^K \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 3}. Latents: E{mag} \in \mathbb{R}: Scalar specular energy magnitude. E{dir} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Directional moment matrix (outer product aggregation). MLP \Psi: A neural network mapping latents to first-order SH. It has one hidden layer with 64 neurons. MLP \Phi: Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module. It has 4 layers with ReLU activation and hidden neurons (128, 64, 32, 12). Parameters: K: Number of spherical sample points. Default is 2048. Sensitivity analysis shows PSNR improves monotonically from K=64 to K=2048, then plateaus at K=4096. Steps: 1. Spherical Sampling: Generate K directional vectors D = \{dk\}{k=1}^K by sampling \phik \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 2\pi) and \thetak = \arccos (1 - 2\xik) where \xik \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1), then converting to Cartesian dk = [\sin \thetak \cos \phik, \sin \thetak \sin \phik, \cos \thetak]^T. 2. Energy Aggregation: Evaluate the photometric residual c{res}(dk) = ci(dk) - c^2i(dk) between third-order SH radiance ci and second-order SH radiance c^2i. Compute magnitude E{mag} and direction E{dir}: E{mag} = \frac {1}{K} \sum {k=1}^{K} \max (0, c{res}(\mathbf {d}k)) E{dir} = \frac {1}{K} \sum {k=1}^{K} \mathbf {d}k \otimes \max (0, c{res}(\mathbf {d}k)) where \otimes represents the outer product. 3. Neural Network Mapping: Predict first-order SH coefficients c' using MLP \Psi conditioned on aggregated latents E{mag}, E{dir} and normalized Gaussian position f(\hat {\mu }): c' = \Psi (E{mag},E{dir}, f(\hat {\mu })) where f(\hat {\mu }) = \hat {\mu } if \|\hat {\mu }\|2 \leq 1, else \left ( 2 - \frac {1}{\|\hat {\mu }\|2} \right) \frac {\hat {\mu }}{\|\hat {\mu }\|2}. 4. Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement: Predict residual offset \Delta ci = \Phi ([\mui, \hat{s}i, ri, oi, \hat{c}'i]) using MLP \Phi concatenating normalized position \mu, normalized scale \hat{s}, rotation quaternion r, opacity o, and normalized SH \hat{c}'. Final coefficients c^{out}i = c'i + \Delta ci. The final layer of \Phi is zero-initialized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def montecarlospecularenergyaggregator(cithirdorder, mu, shat, r, o, cifirstorderapprox, K=2048): """ Compress third-order SH coefficients to first-order using MC aggregation. Args: cithirdorder: Array of shape (16, 3) representing 3rd-order SH coefficients. mu: Position vector (3,). shat: Scale vector (3,). r: Rotation quaternion (4,). o: Opacity scalar. cifirstorderapprox: Approximate first-order SH coefficients (4, 3) for normalization. K: Number of Monte Carlo samples. Returns: cout: Enhanced first-order SH coefficients (4, 3). """ # Step 1: Uniform Spherical Sampling # Generate K random directions phi = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, K) xi = np.random.uniform(0, 1, K) theta = np.arccos(1 - 2 xi) # Convert to Cartesian coordinates sintheta = np.sin(theta) costheta = np.cos(theta) cosphi = np.cos(phi) sinphi = np.sin(phi) D = np.stack([ sintheta cosphi, sintheta sinphi, costheta ], axis=1) # Shape (K, 3) # Step 2: Energy Aggregation # Evaluate third-order SH radiance at directions D # Note: cithirdorder is (16, 3). We need a function to evaluate SH at direction d. # Assuming SH evaluation function sheval(coeffs, direction) exists or is implemented. # For implementation completeness, we assume a helper evaluatesh is available. cid = evaluatesh(cithirdorder, D) # Shape (K, 3) # Evaluate second-order SH radiance at directions D # Second-order SH has 9 coefficients. We assume cisecondorder is derived or available. # The source defines residual as ci(dk) - c^2i(dk). # We need c^2i. Typically, this is the projection of ci onto 2nd order basis. # For the purpose of this pseudocode, we assume getsecondorderradiance computes c^2i(d). c2id = getsecondorderradiance(cithirdorder, D) # Shape (K, 3) # Photometric residual cres = cid - c2id # Shape (K, 3) # Clamp negative residuals to 0 (specular energy is positive) crespos = np.maximum(0, cres) # Shape (K, 3) # Compute Magnitude Emag = np.mean(crespos) # Scalar # Compute Direction (Outer Product Aggregation) # Edir = (1/K) sum(dk outer cresposk) # dk is (3,), cresposk is (3,). Outer product is (3, 3). # We sum these matrices. Edir = np.zeros((3, 3)) for k in range(K): dk = D[k] # (3,) resk = crespos[k] # (3,) Edir += np.outer(dk, resk) Edir = Edir / K # Step 3: Neural Network Mapping # Normalize position munorm = normalizeposition(mu) # Predict first-order SH coefficients using MLP Psi # Psi takes [Emag, Edirflat, munorm] # Emag is scalar, Edir is (3,3) -> flatten to 9, munorm is (3,) inputtopsi = np.concatenate([ [Emag], Edir.flatten(), munorm ]) cprime = mlppsi(inputtopsi) # Shape (4, 3) # Step 4: Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement # Normalize SH coefficients for input to Phi cprimenorm = normalizesh(cprime) # Concatenate attributes # mu is normalized in f(mu), but Phi input uses mu. Source says "normalized position mu". # Let's assume mu passed to Phi is already normalized or handled by f(mu) logic if needed. # Source: "concatenating normalized position mu...". We use munorm. inputtophi = np.concatenate([ munorm, shat, r, [o], cprimenorm.flatten() ]) deltac = mlpphi(inputtophi) # Shape (4, 3) # Final coefficients cout = cprime + deltac return cout def evaluatesh(coeffs, directions): """ Evaluate Spherical Harmonics at given directions. coeffs: (Lmax+1)^2, 3 directions: (K, 3) Returns: (K, 3) """ # Implementation of SH basis evaluation # This is a standard graphics operation. # For L=3, there are 16 coefficients per channel. # We compute Ylm(d) for each d and sum coeffs Ylm. K = directions.shape[0] Lmax = 3 numcoeffs = (Lmax + 1)2 # Precompute SH basis values for all directions # Ylm values for L=0..3 # This function would contain the explicit SH polynomial formulas. # Since the prompt requires self-contained code, we outline the logic. # In practice, one would use a precomputed table or explicit polynomial evaluation. # Placeholder for actual SH evaluation logic # Y = computeshbasis(directions, Lmax) # Shape (K, numcoeffs, 3) # radiance = np.einsum('kc,kc->kc', Y, coeffs) # Shape (K, 3) # return radiance pass def getsecondorderradiance(cthirdorder, directions): """ Project third-order coefficients to second-order and evaluate. """ # Project cthirdorder to csecondorder (first 9 coeffs) csecondorder = cthirdorder[:9,:] return evaluatesh(csecondorder, directions) def normalizeposition(mu): """ Normalize position using the function f(mu) from the source. """ norm = np.linalg.norm(mu) if norm <= 1.0: return mu else: return (2 - 1.0/norm) (mu / norm) def normalizesh(c): """ Normalize SH coefficients. """ # Simple normalization for demonstration. # Source mentions normalized SH chat'. # Typically involves dividing by max coefficient or L2 norm. # We assume a standard normalization. return c / (np.linalg.norm(c) + 1e-8) def mlppsi(x): """ MLP Psi: One hidden layer with 64 neurons. Input: [Emag, Edir(9), mu(3)] -> 13 dims Output: cprime (4, 3) -> 12 dims """ # Weights and biases would be initialized. # Source: "initialized with one hidden layer containing 64 neurons". # No specific initialization weights given, so we assume standard initialization. # This is a placeholder for the neural network forward pass. pass def mlpphi(x): """ MLP Phi: 4 layers with ReLU, hidden neurons (128, 64, 32, 12). Input: [mu(3), s(3), r(4), o(1), chat'(12)] -> 23 dims Output: deltac (4, 3) -> 12 dims Final layer zero-initialized. """ pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Orthogonality: Naive aggregation of raw SH polynomials is futile because the integral of any purely high-order SH polynomial (l \ge 1) over the sphere evaluates to strictly zero due to orthogonality. The method uses the residual between orders to avoid this. Optimization Stability: The final linear layer of the enhancement MLP \Phi is strictly zero-initialized, allowing the model to fall back to standard 3DGS at the start of training. High-Order Inefficiency: High-order SH polynomials are inefficient for sharp specular lobes due to their dense and global nature, requiring many coefficients to cancel out background to fit a sparse peak. Time Complexity: The aggregation step is O(K) per Gaussian, where K is the number of samples. The neural network mapping is constant time per Gaussian. The compression is executed only once during training. Memory Complexity: Reduces storage from third-order SH (16 coefficients per channel) to first-order SH (4 coefficients per channel) plus the latent variables E{mag} and E{dir}, and the MLP parameters. Performance: On mobile hardware (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 GPU), Flux-GS achieves 151 FPS compared to 11 FPS for Mobile-GS and 137 FPS for 3DGS, while maintaining competitive PSNR (30.14 vs 30.21 and 30.31). Strengths: Eliminates the need for costly distillation, significantly reducing overhead while maintaining high-fidelity rendering. Zero-cost SH enhancement at inference time. Limitations: Requires a training curriculum (3k iterations of third-order SH before aggregation). The Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator was proposed by Xiaobiao Du, YuAn Wang, Hao Li, Bosheng Wang, Xun Sun, and Xin Yu in the paper "Monte Carlo Energy Aggregation for Mobile 3D Gaussian Splatting" (Flux-GS). It was presented in 2026. The method addresses the limitations of Mobile-GS, which uses distillation, by providing a direct compression method. name: SOGS (Second-Order Anchor for Advanced 3D Gaussian Splatting)
head: Second-Order Anchor
body: SOGS is an anchor-based 3D Gaussian Splatting technique that introduces second-order statistics to achieve superior rendering quality while simultaneously reducing anchor feature dimensions and overall model size. It distinguishes itself from standard anchor methods like Scaffold-GS by using covariance-based feature augmentation to capture co-variation patterns across feature dimensions, allowing for smaller feature vectors without sacrificing detail. Inputs: A sparse point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP) representing the scene geometry; ground truth images for training. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by anchor features, optimized for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: Anchors: A set of N anchor points initialized from the input point cloud. Anchor Feature Vector (f^a): For each anchor, a vector f^a \in \mathbb{R}^D, where D is the feature dimension. Scaling Factor (l^a): A scalar associated with each anchor. Offsets (o^a): A vector o^a \in \mathbb{R}^{3K} containing K 3D offsets for each anchor. Covariance Matrix (\Sigma): A D \times D matrix computed from the anchor features. Eigenvectors (P): The top M eigenvectors of \Sigma, forming a D \times M matrix. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize N anchors from the input point cloud. For each anchor i, store the feature vector f^ai \in \mathbb{R}^D, scaling factor l^ai, and offsets o^ai \in \mathbb{R}^{3K}. 2. Compute Second-Order Statistics: Treat the D feature dimensions as variables and the N anchors as observed samples. Compute the covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D} across the D dimensions using the anchor feature set. Select the top M eigenvectors P \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times M} from \Sigma to capture the top-M co-variation patterns across feature dimensions. 3. Feature Augmentation and Gaussian Prediction: Combine the eigenvectors P with the original anchor feature f^a to perform anchor feature augmentation. Use the augmented features to construct second-order anchors and predict 3D Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity). 4. Rendering: Project the 3D Gaussians to 2D. Render the image using alpha-blending of projected 2D Gaussians: C = \sum{n \in N} cn \alphan \prod{z=1}^{n-1} (1 - \alphaz) where cn and \alphan are the color and opacity of the n-th 2D Gaussian, and the sum is over all N Gaussians sorted by depth. 5. Selective Gradient Loss: Extract gradient maps from the rendered image and the corresponding ground truth image using the Sobel operator. Compute the difference between these gradient maps. Use this difference to compute a selective gradient loss that adaptively focuses optimization on image regions where texture and geometry are hard to render, enabling dynamic region selection during training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.ndimage import convolve def computecovariancematrix(anchorfeatures): # anchorfeatures: numpy array of shape (N, D) mean = np.mean(anchorfeatures, axis=0) centered = anchorfeatures - mean return np.dot(centered.T, centered) / (anchorfeatures.shape[0] - 1) def selecttopeigenvectors(covmatrix, M): # covmatrix: numpy array of shape (D, D) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covmatrix) sortedindices = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] return eigenvectors[:, sortedindices[:M]] def sobelgradient(image): # image: numpy array of shape (H, W, C) or (H, W) gray = np.mean(image, axis=2) if len(image.shape) == 3 else image sobelx = np.array([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]) sobely = np.array([[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]]) gradx = convolve(gray, sobelx, mode='constant') grady = convolve(gray, sobely, mode='constant') return np.sqrt(gradx2 + grady2) def trainsogs(pointcloud, groundtruthimages, D, M, learningrate, lambdagrad, numepochs): # Initialize N anchors from point cloud, store f^a, l^a, o^a anchors = initializeanchorsfrompointcloud(pointcloud, D) # Not given in the sources. for epoch in range(numepochs): for gtimage in groundtruthimages: covmatrix = computecovariancematrix(anchors.features) P = selecttopeigenvectors(covmatrix, M) # Combine P with f^a for feature augmentation augmentedfeatures = anchors.features @ P # Not given in the sources. # Predict 3D Gaussian attributes from augmented features gaussians = predictgaussianattributes(augmentedfeatures, anchors) # Not given in the sources. renderedimage = rendergaussians(gaussians) # Not given in the sources. colorloss = np.mean((renderedimage - gtimage)2) gradloss = np.mean(np.abs(sobelgradient(renderedimage) - sobelgradient(gtimage))) totalloss = colorloss + lambdagrad gradloss # Backpropagate to update anchors updateanchorswithgradient(anchors, totalloss, learningrate) # Not given in the sources. Parameters: D: Anchor feature dimension. Typical values are reduced compared to standard methods to leverage the second-order statistics. M: Number of top eigenvectors selected from the covariance matrix. Not given in the sources. K: Number of offsets per anchor. Not given in the sources. \lambda{grad}: Weight for the selective gradient loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Computing the covariance matrix and eigendecomposition requires numerical stability, especially if D is large or N is small. An anchor-based method that uses MLPs to predict Gaussian attributes from anchor features. SOGS improves upon this by using second-order statistics to reduce feature size while maintaining quality. Scaffold-GS Introduces grid-based context modeling and entropy encoding to reduce model size. SOGS achieves similar size reduction through second-order anchor statistics without explicit entropy coding. HAC Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: SOGS achieves superior rendering quality with reduced model sizes compared to Scaffold-GS and other anchor-based methods. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. SOGS was proposed by Jiahui Zhang, Fangneng Zhan, Ling Shao, and Shijian Lu from Nanyang Technological University, Harvard University, MIT, and UCAS-Terminus AI Lab. It was published in CVPR 2025. The method addresses the trade-off between rendering quality and model size in anchor-based 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically improving upon Scaffold-GS. name: Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints
body: This family of methods modifies the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation to improve geometric fidelity, enforce surface constraints, or extract explicit geometry, addressing the limitation that base 3DGS produces volumetric, soft primitives that lack precise surface alignment and watertight mesh compatibility [S1, 14095-mesh-extraction-and-representation.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DeSplat and 360 Gaussian Splatting by focusing on the structural definition of the primitives (e.g., planar alignment, SDF coupling, or discontinuity boundaries) rather than just rendering efficiency or compression. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. This family modifies the standard 3DGS representation to improve geometric fidelity, rendering efficiency, or physical accuracy. It sets itself apart by addressing specific limitations of the base method: Inverse Multiquadric Splatting changes the radial basis function for better tail behavior; Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation decouples visibility from opacity to allow aggressive culling; Content-Aware Texturing adds dynamic textures to capture high-frequency details; Directed Distance Field provides a neural oracle for secondary rays; and Atomized Proliferation constrains Gaussian sizes for precise geometry. Choose this when you need to refine the primitive shape or density function itself. Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting (DisC-GS) enables 3DGS to represent and render sharp boundaries and discontinuities, addressing the limitation of standard 3DGS which tends to blur such features. It differs from sibling methods like Planar Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling boundaries as cubic Bézier curves within the Gaussian's local subspace and applying a "pre-scissoring" operation during rendering, rather than relying solely on geometric constraints or mesh extraction. Choose this when rendering scenes with sharp occlusion boundaries or thin structures. This family converts the volumetric, implicit representation of 3DGS into explicit geometric structures, primarily triangular meshes or dense point clouds, to enable compatibility with standard 3D graphics pipelines, mesh editing tools, and physics simulations. Unlike standard 3DGS, which renders via alpha-blended splats, these methods extract a discrete surface or point set that approximates the radiance field, allowing for operations such as texture mapping, rigging, and collision detection. The key distinction lies in whether the extraction is driven by surface-alignment regularization during training (e.g., SuGaR) or by post-hoc probabilistic sampling of the trained density field (e.g., Point Cloud Conversion). Choose this when you need a watertight mesh for downstream applications. Appearance and Physical Modeling extends the standard 3DGS representation to support physically based rendering (PBR), relighting, and volumetric light transport, solving the limitations of base 3DGS which relies on fixed Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients that cannot accurately represent complex specularities, dynamic lighting, or non-vacuum media. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Gaussian Representation and Truncation by focusing on the radiance and material representation rather than geometric simplification, and distinguishes itself from Physics and Optical Modeling by prioritizing surface material decomposition and relighting over volumetric attenuation equations, although both families modify the core Gaussian properties beyond simple color. Choose this for PBR or volumetric effects. Neural SDF Inference via Gaussian Pulling is a method for reconstructing continuous 3D surfaces from multi-view RGB images by jointly optimizing a set of 3D Gaussians and a neural Signed Distance Function (SDF). It solves the problem of inferring accurate geometry from 3DGS, which typically suffers from discreteness, sparseness, and off-surface drift, making direct SDF inference difficult. Unlike standard 3DGS which renders appearance without explicit surface constraints, this method dynamically aligns Gaussians to the SDF's zero-level set and constrains them to be thin disks tangent to the surface, enabling robust surface reconstruction. It differs from Gaussian Representation and Truncation by explicitly coupling the Gaussian positions to a continuous implicit field via differentiable pulling, and from Mesh Extraction and Representation by learning the SDF directly rather than extracting meshes from static Gaussian clusters. Choose this for high-fidelity surface reconstruction from RGB inputs. Planar Gaussian Splatting (PGS) is an unsupervised neural rendering framework that reconstructs 3D geometry and explicitly parses 3D planar surfaces from multiple RGB images without requiring 3D labels or depth supervision. It extends the standard 3DGS representation by introducing discriminative 3D plane descriptors and enforcing local planar alignment constraints. Unlike sibling methods that focus on high-fidelity rendering or generic mesh extraction, PGS is designed to identify distinct 3D plane instances through a hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Tree (GMT). It sets itself apart by using 2D segmentation priors from foundation models (like SAM) to guide the learning of these descriptors, enabling robust planar reconstruction across different scenes. Choose this for scenes dominated by planar structures like indoor environments. 3D Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction (3DGSR) is an implicit surface reconstruction method that integrates a neural Signed Distance Field (SDF) with the explicit 3DGS representation. It solves the problem of extracting high-quality, watertight meshes from 3DGS, which traditionally yields unstructured point clouds that are difficult to process with standard post-processing techniques like Poisson reconstruction. Unlike sibling methods that rely on post-processing or separate optimization stages, 3DGSR unifies the optimization of the Gaussian appearance and the implicit surface geometry end-to-end. It achieves this by coupling the SDF with the Gaussians via alignment constraints and regularizing the SDF using volumetric rendering consistency, enabling reconstruction quality superior to Gaussian-based methods like 2DGS while maintaining the rendering speed of 3DGS. Choose this for end-to-end surface reconstruction with high geometric accuracy. Sparse2DGS is a Gaussian Splatting method designed for surface reconstruction from sparse input views, addressing the ill-posed nature of geometric optimization when dense Structure-from-Motion points are unavailable. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS and its sibling 2DGS by initializing primitives with unsupervised Multi-View Stereo (MVS) points and employing geometric-prioritized enhancements—such as fixed feature splatting and selective updates—to prevent appearance overfitting and improve geometric learning. Choose this when training data is sparse. Step: During optimization, use Eq. (6) to extract depth values z from the current scene estimate. These depth values are then used to update the medium-parameter estimates (B\infty, Bb). Formula: Depth extraction from 3DGS: z = \frac{\sum{i=1}^M di \alphai Ti}{\sum{i=1}^M \alphai Ti}. Here di is the depth of Gaussian i. This is computed at each pixel during rendering. Definition: A constraint to prevent discrepancies between Gaussian Splat scales and the scales of corresponding triangular mesh faces by bounding the relative scale coefficients. Formula: s = s{rel} \odot s0, where s is the final scale, s{rel} = (s{rel,1}, s{rel,2}) \in [s{min}, s{max}] \times [s{min}, s{max}] is the coefficient vector, s0 is the predefined scale derived from the mesh faces, and \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. Parameter: s{min}, s{max}: The lower and upper bounds for the relative scale coefficients s{rel}. Definition: A method to solve for the normal attribute n for each 3D Gaussian by optimizing it from an initial random vector via back-propagation, perceiving the depth of all Gaussians along a ray as a distribution. Step: Determine the normal for each pixel by estimating the expectation of the depth distribution along the ray. Formula: Normal consistency loss: \mathcal {L}{n}=\|\mathcal {N}-\tilde {\mathcal {N}}\|2. Definition: An extension of 3DGS where Gaussians are constrained to a 2D tangent plane to resolve the conflict between volumetric Gaussians and surface representation, enabling accurate normal map estimation. Step: Normal Rendering: Perform splatting of normals in the same manner as color splatting to generate a normal map, leveraging the tangent plane constraint. Formula: A point P on the 2D Gaussian plane with coordinates (u, v) is defined as: P(u, v) = pk + su tu u + sv tv v = H(u, v, 1, 1)^T, where H = [pk, tu, tv, tw] is the transformation matrix. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 as a real-time explicit scene representation. Subsequent work focused on extracting explicit geometry from these soft primitives, leading to families like Mesh Extraction and SDF-based reconstruction. Methods like DisC-GS and Planar GS address specific geometric artifacts (blurring, lack of planarity) inherent in the original formulation. The integration of SDFs (e.g., Neural SDF Inference, 3DGSR) represents a shift towards hybrid explicit-implicit representations for higher geometric fidelity. name: Gaussian Representation and Truncation
body: This family of methods modifies the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to improve geometric fidelity, rendering efficiency, or physical accuracy. While the parent article Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints establishes the base Gaussian primitives, these methods alter the density function, truncation logic, texture mapping, or proliferation strategy. They set themselves apart by addressing specific limitations of the base method: Inverse Multiquadric Splatting changes the radial basis function for better tail behavior; Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation decouples visibility from opacity to allow aggressive culling; Content-Aware Texturing adds dynamic textures to capture high-frequency details; Directed Distance Field provides a neural oracle for secondary rays; and Atomized Proliferation constrains Gaussian sizes for precise geometry. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. Replaces the standard Gaussian density function with an inverse multiquadric radial basis function to modify alpha blending behavior. It uses a function with heavier tails, which can improve the representation of certain geometric structures or reduce artifacts in specific optimization scenarios. Choose this when standard Gaussians fail to capture long-range dependencies or exhibit artifacts in dense regions. Modifies the fragment culling logic to decouple the visibility threshold from the Gaussian's opacity parameter. It solves the problem where the original implementation's opacity-dependent truncation prevents consistent optimization of low-opacity Gaussians and limits the aggressiveness of spatial truncation. Choose this when you need to aggressively prune distant fragments without affecting the learned opacity of near-field Gaussians. Augments 2D Gaussian primitives with spatially varying texture maps to capture high-frequency appearance details that fixed spherical harmonics cannot represent. It distinguishes itself by dynamically allocating texture resolution based on local image content and error, avoiding the convergence issues associated with cloning-based densification. Choose this for scenes with high-frequency textures (e.g., fabric, foliage) where SH coefficients are insufficient. A neural implicit representation that serves as a constant-time, constant-memory ray oracle for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. It maps a ray origin and direction to the distance to the first surface and a visibility probability, enabling efficient secondary ray queries for shadows, ambient occlusion, and global illumination without requiring a mesh or traversing a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH). Choose this when you need fast, differentiable secondary ray queries (shadows/Occlusion) that scale independently of the number of Gaussians. A training optimization strategy that enhances geometric precision by constraining Gaussians representing fine details into "Atom Gaussians" (isotropic spheroids with uniform size) and prioritizing their proliferation to align with scene geometry, followed by pruning to merge large smooth surfaces. Choose this when you need precise geometric reconstruction and reduced Gaussian count for complex scenes with fine details. Removes redundant or low-impact 3D Gaussians from a trained or training model to reduce memory footprint and rendering latency while preserving visual fidelity. Unlike sibling methods that focus on geometric simplification of primitives or opacity-independent truncation, this family focuses on the selection and elimination of entire Gaussian entities based on their contribution to the rendered image or their geometric degeneracy. It is distinct from Gaussian Representation and Truncation by actively modifying the set of Gaussians \{Gi\} rather than just their rendering parameters. POG (Eq. 8) improves LPIPS slightly but degrades PSNR significantly compared to Hard Gaussians (HG, Eq. 9). POG overgrows already learned areas, making them susceptible to redundant Gaussians, which causes PSNR degradation. AtomGS uses Atomized Proliferation to constrain ellipsoid Gaussians of various sizes into uniformly-sized Atom Gaussians, applying a progressive split schedule to emphasize densification in accordance with scene details. It retains larger anisotropic Gaussians for the background and uses Geometry-Guided Optimization with an Edge-Aware Normal Loss to impose stricter constraints on flat surfaces. During pruning, it merges Gaussians covering large, less detailed surfaces, resulting in a similar or reduced number of Gaussians compared to original 3DGS while retaining competitive quality. Unlike standard 3DGS which freely drifts and splits, AtomGS provides precise guidance on where to focus Gaussians for better 3D geometry optimization. A transparent Gaussian kernel where opacity is view-dependent, modeled by a half-period cosine function to approximate specular reflectance lobes. It adds 5 learnable parameters to the standard 3DGS configuration. The opacity is defined as: \hat{\alpha}(\theta, \beta, T, \alpha) = \alpha \cdot \frac{\cos(\max(0, \min(\frac{2\theta}{T}, \pi)))+1}{2}\exp(\beta) where \alpha is the base opacity, \theta is the angle between view direction and lobe central orientation, T controls angular span, and \beta modulates sharpness. T is initialized as c\bar{\theta}i/\pi based on viewpoint density, and \beta is initialized to zero. If \theta increases, transparency diminishes to zero, ensuring minimal impact on viewpoints outside the lobe's influence and preventing artifacts. GS-IR extends the vanilla 3D Gaussian representation by adding a normal vector and material properties to the geometric and appearance parameters. Geometric properties T are defined as a set containing position vector p, scaling vector s, unit quaternion q for rotation, and normal vector n. Material properties M are defined as a set containing albedo a, roughness \rho, and metallicity m. Vanilla 3D Gaussian appearance parameters A consist of opacity \alpha and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients fc for view-dependent color. The base 3D Gaussian Splatting method was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. Subsequent works have explored various optimizations: Hard Gaussian Splatting (HGS) introduced Potentially Over-large Gaussians and Hard Gaussians to address blurring and needle-like artifacts; AtomGS introduced Atomized Proliferation and Geometry-Guided Optimization for high-fidelity radiance fields; Augmented Radiance Field introduced View-Dependent Opacity Kernels for specular reflectance; and GS-IR extended the representation for inverse rendering with material properties. name: Inverse Multiquadric Splatting
head: 3DIQS, Inverse Multiquadric
body: Inverse Multiquadric Splatting replaces the standard Gaussian density function with an inverse multiquadric radial basis function to modify the alpha blending behavior during rendering. It sets itself apart from the base Gaussian Splatting method by using a function with heavier tails, which can improve the representation of certain geometric structures or reduce artifacts in specific optimization scenarios. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha{base}, and color. For each pixel/ray intersection, the 2D projected mean \boldsymbol{\mu}' and 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'{2 \times 2} are computed. Output: The final alpha value \alpha for the splat, and gradients for the mean and covariance matrices during backpropagation. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS conic matrix representation for the 2D projection. The conic matrix \mathbf{C} is the inverse of the 2D covariance matrix, often stored in a compact symmetric format. Let \mathbf{C} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}, where the entries correspond to the inverse covariance elements. The 2D distance vector is \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}' = (d.x, d.y). Parameters: correctionFactor: A scalar multiplier applied to the covariance matrices. Value: 1.38. ellipsemax: The upper bound for the ellipse term to skip distant splats. Value: 9.0. alphamax: The maximum clamped alpha value. Value: 0.99. Formulas: The 3D inverse multiquadric function is defined as: f(dM) = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\xi} (dM)^2 + 1} where dM \geq 0. In the implementation, the parameter \xi is absorbed into the correction factor or set such that the term simplifies to the form used in the code. The 2D splat weight w is calculated as: w = \frac{1}{\left[ \frac{1}{\xi} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}')^T (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}') + 1 \right]} In the CUDA implementation, the term \frac{1}{\xi} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}')^T (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}') is computed as ellipse. The final alpha is: \alpha = \min(0.99, w \cdot \alpha{base}) where w = \frac{1}{ellipse + 1}. Steps: 1. Covariance Scaling: Multiply the 3D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} and the projected 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'{2 \times 2} by correctionFactor (1.38). 2. Ellipse Calculation: Compute the quadratic form ellipse using the conic matrix entries (a, b, c) and the 2D distance vector \mathbf{d} = (d.x, d.y): ellipse = a \cdot d.x^2 + c \cdot d.y^2 + 2b \cdot d.x \cdot d.y 3. Boundary Checks: If ellipse \leq 0, skip the splat. If ellipse \geq 9.0, skip the splat. 4. Alpha Computation: Calculate the weight G (or w) and the final alpha: G = \frac{1}{ellipse + 1} \alpha = \min(0.99, \alpha{base} \cdot G) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inversemultiquadricforward(cono, d, alphabase, correctionfactor=1.38): """ cono: Conic matrix entries (a, b, c, w) where a, b, c form the symmetric 2x2 inverse covariance. d: 2D distance vector (dx, dy) from pixel center to gaussian mean. alphabase: The base opacity of the gaussian. """ # 1. Scale covariance (conceptually, affects cono if derived from cov, # but in the provided code, cono is already the conic. # The code scales cov2D before inversion to conic. # Here we assume cono represents the scaled conic.) # 2. Calculate ellipse term a, b, c = cono.a, cono.b, cono.c dx, dy = d.dx, d.dy ellipse = a dx dx + c dy dy + 2.0 b dx dy # 3. Boundary checks if ellipse <= 0.0 or ellipse >= 9.0: return None, None # Skip splat # 4. Calculate weight and alpha G = 1.0 / (ellipse + 1.0) alpha = min(0.99, alphabase G) return alpha, G def inversemultiquadricbackward(alpha, G, dLdalpha, cono, d, correctionfactor=1.38): """ alpha: The computed alpha. G: The weight 1/(ellipse+1). dLdalpha: Gradient of loss w.r.t alpha. cono: Conic matrix entries. d: 2D distance vector. """ # Gradient w.r.t G dLdG = alphabase dLdalpha # Note: alphabase is needed here. # In the source code: dLdG = cono.w dLdalpha. # Assuming cono.w stores alphabase or it is passed separately. # Let's assume alphabase is available as 'basealpha'. # From source: const float dLdG = cono.w dLdalpha; # We need basealpha. Let's assume it's passed or stored. # For the sake of self-contained pseudocode, we assume basealpha is known. # Gradient of G w.r.t ellipse components # dLdG is gradient of loss w.r.t G. # G = 1 / (ellipse + 1) # dG/d(ellipse) = -1 / (ellipse + 1)^2 ellipse = cono.a d.dx d.dx + cono.c d.dy d.dy + 2.0 cono.b d.dx d.dy # dLdellipse = dLdG dG/d(ellipse) # dG/d(ellipse) = -1 / (ellipse + 1)^2 # Source uses: ellipsepow = - dLdG 2.f / pow(ellipse + 1.f, 2.f) # Wait, source calculates dGddelx directly. # dG/d(dx) = dG/d(ellipse) d(ellipse)/d(dx) # d(ellipse)/d(dx) = 2 (adx + bdy) # Source code logic: # const float dLdG = cono.w dLdalpha; # const float ellipsepow = - dLdG 2.f / pow(ellipse + 1.f, 2.f); # const float dGddelx = ellipsepow (d.x cono.x + d.y cono.y); # Note: cono.x is 'a', cono.y is 'b', cono.z is 'c' in the source snippet? # Source: cono.x d.x d.x + cono.z d.y d.y + 2.f cono.y d.x d.y # So cono.x=a, cono.y=b, cono.z=c. # dG/d(dx) = (-1/(ellipse+1)^2) 2 (adx + bdy) # dG/d(dy) = (-1/(ellipse+1)^2) 2 (cdy + bdx) # Source: dGddelx = ellipsepow (d.x cono.x + d.y cono.y) # ellipsepow = - dLdG 2 / (ellipse+1)^2 # So dGddelx = dLdG dG/d(dx) denomsq = (ellipse + 1.0) 2 factor = -2.0 dLdG / denomsq # Gradient w.r.t mean (dx, dy) # dLdmeanx = dLdG dG/d(dx) # dLdmeany = dLdG dG/d(dy) dLdmeanx = factor (cono.a d.dx + cono.b d.dy) dLdmeany = factor (cono.b d.dx + cono.c d.dy) # Gradient w.r.t conic matrix (a, b, c) # d(ellipse)/da = dx^2 # d(ellipse)/db = 2dxdy # d(ellipse)/dc = dy^2 # dLda = dLdG dG/d(ellipse) d(ellipse)/da # dLda = (-1/(ellipse+1)^2) dLdG dx^2 # Source: halfellipsepow = 0.5 ellipsepow # dLda = halfellipsepow d.x d.x # halfellipsepow = - dLdG / (ellipse+1)^2 # So dLda = - dLdG / (ellipse+1)^2 dx^2 halffactor = -dLdG / denomsq dLda = halffactor d.dx d.dx dLdc = halffactor d.dy d.dy dLdb = halffactor 2.0 d.dx d.dy return dLdmeanx, dLdmeany, dLda, dLdb, dLdc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Splats with ellipse \leq 0 or ellipse \geq 9.0 are skipped. This prevents numerical instability and unnecessary computation for very distant or degenerate projections. Covariance Scaling: The correction factor 1.38 must be applied to the covariance matrices before projection/inversion to ensure the correct shape of the inverse multiquadric function. Time Complexity: Similar to standard Gaussian Splatting, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations per pixel per Gaussian. The boundary checks may reduce the number of active splats slightly. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead compared to standard 3DGS, as it uses the same data structures. Strengths: Can provide better fitting for certain types of geometry or reduce artifacts compared to Gaussian splatting in specific contexts. Limitations: The choice of correction factor and boundary limits is heuristic. It may not generalize as well as Gaussian splatting for all scenes. When to use: When standard Gaussian Splatting exhibits artifacts or fails to represent certain features, and when the specific benefits of the inverse multiquadric function are desired. Inverse Multiquadric Splatting was introduced in the paper "DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions". It is part of a family of methods that generalize the radial basis functions used in splatting beyond the standard Gaussian. name: Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation
head: Modified truncation
body: Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation is a modification to the fragment culling logic in 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples the visibility threshold from the Gaussian's opacity parameter. It solves the problem where the original implementation's opacity-dependent truncation prevents consistent optimization of low-opacity Gaussians and limits the aggressiveness of spatial truncation. It sets itself apart from siblings like Pruning and Reduction by modifying the runtime rendering loop's culling condition rather than post-processing the Gaussian set, and from Inverse Multiquadric Splatting by retaining the Gaussian density function while altering its evaluation threshold. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian Gi has mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and color \mathbf{c}i. A camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega. Output: A rendered pixel color, with gradients computed for \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i. Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of Gaussians. Each Gaussian stores \alphai separately from the spatial density value. Threshold: A scalar \tau\alpha (typically 1/255) representing the minimum transparency value for a fragment to be considered visible. Method Steps: 1. Project Gaussian: For a given ray, compute the 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} and mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D} of the Gaussian in screen space. 2. Compute Density: Evaluate the unnormalized Gaussian density response D at the pixel center (or ray intersection point) using the standard Gaussian function: D = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D})\right) 3. Check Truncation (Opacity-Independent): Compare the density response D directly against the threshold \tau\alpha. If D < \tau\alpha, skip this fragment (do not contribute to color or gradients). If D \ge \tau\alpha, proceed to step 4. 4. Compute Transparency: Calculate the final transparency \alpha{frag} by multiplying the density response by the Gaussian's learned opacity parameter: \alpha{frag} = D \cdot \alphai 5. Blend: Use \alpha{frag} in the standard alpha-blending equation to accumulate color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendergaussianopacityindependent(gaussian, rayorigin, raydirection, taualpha=1/255): # 1. Project Gaussian to 2D # Compute 2D covariance Sigma2D and mean mu2D based on camera projection sigma2d, mu2d = project2d(gaussian.sigma, gaussian.mu, gaussian.rotation, cameramatrix) # 2. Compute Density Response D # Calculate distance squared from pixel center to Gaussian mean in 2D distsq = dot(gaussian.pixelcenter - mu2d, inverse(sigma2d) (gaussian.pixelcenter - mu2d)) densityresponse = exp(-0.5 distsq) # 3. Check Truncation BEFORE multiplying by opacity if densityresponse < taualpha: return None # Skip fragment, no gradient contribution # 4. Compute final transparency alphafrag alphafrag = densityresponse gaussian.opacity # 5. Return contribution for blending return { 'alpha': alphafrag, 'color': gaussian.color, 'densityresponse': densityresponse, # Needed for gradient computation 'opacity': gaussian.opacity } Parameters: \tau\alpha: The transparency threshold. Default in original 3DGS is 1/255. Truncation Radius (k\sigma): The number of standard deviations at which D drops below \tau\alpha. In the original method, this is effectively capped at \approx 3.03\sigma for high-opacity Gaussians due to the opacity reset clip. This method allows k to be set lower (e.g., 1\sigma, 2\sigma). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Reset Interaction: The original 3DGS implementation clips opacity to a maximum of 1/100 during resets. In the original method, this clip enforces an upper bound on \tau\alpha, preventing truncation at fewer than 3.03\sigma for high-opacity Gaussians. This modification bypasses that limitation by checking D before opacity multiplication. Low Opacity Gradients: The original implementation ignores gradients for opacity when opacity is zero, interpreting opacity as part of the response. This modification allows gradients to flow even when the final \alpha{frag} is small, as long as D \ge \tau\alpha. Aggressive Truncation: Truncating at 1\sigma results in a minimum contributing fragment opacity of \approx 0.61, meaning Gaussians are effectively treated as nearly opaque. This can lead to visual artifacts if the scene contains transparent objects. Time Complexity: Training time increases compared to the default truncation. For example, on Mip-NeRF360, 3.33\sigma truncation with modification takes 5m07s vs 4m31s for default. 1\sigma truncation takes 2m26s. Memory Complexity: VRAM usage decreases with more aggressive truncation. 1\sigma uses 4.5\text{GiB}, 2\sigma uses 5.5\text{GiB}, and 3.33\sigma uses 6.4\text{GiB} (with modification) vs 6.1\text{GiB} for default. Gaussian Count: The number of Gaussians created during densification is reduced with more aggressive truncation. 1\sigma results in 1.39\text{M} Gaussians, 2\sigma in 2.22\text{M}, and 3.33\sigma in 2.79\text{M} (with modification) vs 2.70\text{M} for default. Quality: PSNR decreases with more aggressive truncation. 1\sigma yields 25.86 PSNR, 2\sigma yields 27.23 PSNR, and 3.33\sigma yields 27.57 PSNR (with modification) vs 27.54 PSNR for default. Strengths: Allows for consistent truncation at fewer standard deviations; enables gradient flow for low-opacity Gaussians that would otherwise be ignored; reduces memory footprint and Gaussian count. Limitations: Increased training time for equivalent truncation levels; aggressive truncation (1\sigma) significantly reduces image quality; minimum fragment opacity is high (\approx 0.61 at 1\sigma), limiting transparency modeling. This method was proposed in "Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization". It addresses limitations in the original 3DGS implementation regarding opacity-dependent truncation and gradient computation for low-opacity Gaussians. Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Content-Aware Texturing for Gaussian Splatting
head: Content-Aware Texturing, Ours
body: This method augments 2D Gaussian primitives with spatially varying texture maps to capture high-frequency appearance details that fixed spherical harmonics cannot represent. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by dynamically allocating texture resolution based on local image content and error, avoiding the convergence issues associated with cloning-based densification. Unlike GSTex which uses a fixed texel budget on pretrained primitives, this approach optimizes primitives and textures from scratch, and unlike BBSplat which uses a fixed texel-to-primitive ratio, it adapts texel size to scene frequency. Inputs: A set of 2D Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}, each defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, scale \boldsymbol{\sigma}i, rotation \mathbf{R}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}{SH}. Input views \Pi with ground truth images. Outputs: Optimized primitives with dynamic texture maps Ti and parameters. Data Structures: Primitive Parameters: 59 floats per primitive. 2DGS base: 3 (pos) + 2 (scale) + 4 (rot) + 1 (opacity) + 48 (SH color) = 58 params. Additional: 1 float for texel size ratio t2pri. Texture Map Ti: Stored in a custom "jagged" tensor structure to handle varying resolutions. Format: RGB offsets. 3 floats per texel. Values constrained to [-1, 1] via sigmoid activation on unactivated features c'{Ti}: c{Ti} = 2\sigma(c'{Ti}) - 1. Coordinate Systems: pw: Intersection point in world space. p{w0} = pw - \boldsymbol{\mu}i: World space centered on primitive. pl = \mathbf{R}i^{-1} p{w0}: Local axis-aligned space (pl \in \mathbb{R}^2). pc = \mathbf{S}i^{-1} pl: Local normalized/canonical space, where \mathbf{S}i = \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}i). Rendering: The color of a ray \mathbf{r} is computed by alpha blending: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sumi wi(pi) ci(\mathbf{d}) = \sumi Ti oi Gi(pi) ci(\mathbf{d}) where Ti = \prod{j<i} (1 - oj Gj(pj)) is the transmittance, Gi(pi) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2} pi^\top pi) is the Gaussian density in canonical space, and ci(\mathbf{d}) is the primitive color. The primitive color combines spherical harmonics and texture offset: ci = \text{SH}(\mathbf{d}) + \text{bilerp}(Ti, u) where u is the UV coordinate in texture space. To prevent texture stretching during optimization, u is defined in world space units rather than canonical space: u = \frac{pl}{ki} + T{\text{offset}} Here, ki is the texel size in world space units (same units as scale \boldsymbol{\sigma}), and T{\text{offset}} centers the texture map. The texel size ki is derived from the minimum pixel size k{\min} and the primitive's texel-to-pixel ratio t2pri: ki = k{\min} \cdot t2pri t2pri takes values that are powers of two, with a lower bound of 1. Training Loss: The total loss L is the sum of RGB, texture sparsity, and opacity regularization terms: L = L{\text{RGB}} + L{\text{texture}} + L{\text{opacity}} 1. RGB Loss: Weighted L1 and SSIM: L{\text{RGB}} = (1 - \lambda{\text{SSIM}}) L1 + \lambda{\text{SSIM}} L{\text{SSIM}} Typical \lambda{\text{SSIM}} = 0.2. 2. Texture Sparsity Loss: Pushes texel values toward zero to allow downsampling: L{\text{texture}} = \lambda{\text{texture}} \sumi |c{Ti}| 3. Opacity Regularization: Incentivizes low-contribution primitives to disappear: L{\text{opacity}} = \lambda{\text{opacity}} \frac{1}{N} \sumi oi Primitive Management and Densification: Cloning is avoided because superimposing multiple textured primitives causes convergence difficulties. Instead, splitting is used for geometric error, and texture resolution is adjusted for appearance error. 1. Error Calculation: For each primitive i and view \pi, compute per-pixel error E^\pii weighted by primitive contribution w^\pii(r): E^\pii = \sum{r \in Pi} E^\pi(r) w^\pii(r) where Pi is the set of pixels covered by primitive i. The total error Ei is the weighted sum across all views \Pi: Ei = \frac{\sum{\pi \in \Pi} E^\pii w^\pii}{\sum{\pi \in \Pi} w^\pii}, \quad w^\pii = \sum{r \in Pi} w^\pii(r) This differs from [RPK24] by using a weighted sum instead of maximum error. 2. Upscaling (Appearance Error): Select the top 10% of primitives with highest Ei. Condition: Only upscale if t2pri \ge 2. Action: Halve t2pri (increasing texture resolution by factor of 4). 3. Downscaling (Low Frequency): Compute appearance error Ed by comparing original texture T{\text{orig}} to a low-pass filtered version T{\text{lowpass}}, weighted by Gaussian falloff: Ed = \frac{\sump G(p)(T{\text{orig}}(p) - T{\text{lowpass}}(p))}{\sump G(p)} If Ed < \tau{ds}, double t2pri (reducing texel count by 4). 4. Splitting (Geometric Error): If a primitive in the top 10% error list has texture resolution exceeding threshold \tau{tr}, it is split. Action: Replace primitive with two new primitives. Displacement: Each displaced by \pm 1 standard deviation along the axis. Properties: New primitives have half the scale in the corresponding axis, half the texture resolution, and G(1) times the opacity. Texture Init: New texture maps are created by sampling the original point at the respective locations. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Texture Stretching: Naive mapping using canonical space causes stretching and local minima. The world-space mapping u prevents this. Primitive Growth: If a primitive grows outside its allocated texture grid (due to lack of allocation or hitting the 256 limit), zero-padding is used. Since texels are offsets, this reduces to the DC color. Memory Limit: Hard limit of 256 texture resolution to avoid excessive memory usage. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, primitives, t2prthreshold=2.0): """ Renders a single ray using content-aware textured 2D Gaussians. """ # 1. Sort primitives by depth along ray sortedprims = sortprimitivesbydepth(primitives, rayorigin, raydirection) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for prim in sortedprims: # 2. Compute intersection in camera space # Note: Implementation uses Eq 1 directly in camera space, not R2->R2 transform intersection = computeintersection2dgaussian(prim, rayorigin, raydirection) if intersection is None: continue pw = intersection.point pl = transformtolocalspace(pw, prim.mu, prim.R) # 3. Compute Gaussian weight pc = transformtocanonicalspace(pl, prim.sigma) gaussianweight = exp(-0.5 dot(pc, pc)) # 4. Compute color # SH color shcolor = evaluatesphericalharmonics(prim.shcoeffs, raydirection) # Texture offset # ki is texel size in world space units ki = prim.kmin prim.t2pr u = (pl / ki) + prim.toffset texeloffset = bilerp(prim.texturemap, u) ci = shcolor + texeloffset # 5. Alpha blend opacity = prim.opacity gaussianweight contribution = accumulatedtransmittance opacity ci accumulatedcolor += contribution accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - opacity) if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-4: break return accumulatedcolor def manageprimitives(primitives, errorimages, views, tauds=0.01, tautr=128): """ Adjusts texture resolution and splits primitives based on error. """ # 1. Compute per-primitive error errors = [] for prim in primitives: primerror = 0.0 totalweight = 0.0 for view in views: # Compute weighted error for this view viewerror = 0.0 viewweight = 0.0 for pixel in prim.coveredpixels[view]: w = prim.contributiontopixel(pixel) e = errorimages[view][pixel] viewerror += e w viewweight += w primerror += viewerror totalweight += viewweight if totalweight > 0: avgerror = primerror / totalweight else: avgerror = 0.0 errors.append((prim, avgerror)) # 2. Sort by error errors.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) top10percent = errors[:len(errors)//10] # 3. Upscale high error primitives for prim, err in top10percent: if prim.t2pr >= t2prthreshold: prim.t2pr /= 2.0 # 4. Downscale low error primitives for prim in primitives: # Compute Ed (appearance error) Ed = computeappearanceerror(prim) if Ed < tauds: prim.t2pr = 2.0 # 5. Split primitives with high error and high texture resolution for prim, err in top10percent: if prim.t2pr > tautr: splitprimitive(prim) Complexity: Training is 1.5-2x slower and rendering is 25% slower compared to 2DGS due to per-ray texture querying overhead. Memory: Uses a "jagged" tensor structure for textures. Total parameters depend on dynamic texel allocation. Performance (DeepBlending): SSIM 0.907, PSNR 30.03, LPIPS 0.303, 222K points, 21.6M texels, 78.1M params, 70 FPS. Performance (Mip-Nerf-360): SSIM 0.795, PSNR 27.00, LPIPS 0.263, 218K points, 46.6M texels, 152.6M params, 67 FPS. Performance (Tanks&Temples): SSIM 0.835, PSNR 23.43, LPIPS 0.225, 164K points, 10.4M texels, 41.1M params, 121 FPS. Strengths: Significantly fewer parameters than GSTex and BBSplat while achieving competitive or superior quality. Adapts to scene content frequency. Limitations: Slower training and rendering than base 2DGS. Cloning-based densification is incompatible. The method was introduced by Papantonakis, Kopanas, Durand, and Drettakis in 2025. It builds on the 2D Gaussian Splatting representation. It addresses the limitation of fixed spherical harmonics in capturing high-frequency details and the inefficiency of fixed texel budgets in methods like GSTex. name: Directed Distance Field (DDF) for Gaussian Splatting
head: Directed Distance Function, ray-query oracle
body: The Directed Distance Field (DDF) is a neural implicit representation that serves as a constant-time, constant-memory ray oracle for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes. It maps a ray origin and direction to the distance to the first surface and a visibility probability, enabling efficient secondary ray queries for shadows, ambient occlusion, and global illumination without requiring a mesh or traversing a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH). Unlike sibling methods that scale with the number of Gaussians, the DDF’s query cost and memory footprint remain fixed regardless of scene size. The DDF is trained to approximate the distance to the nearest surface along a given direction, supervised by clean distance data derived from the Gaussian scene or a neural surface fit. Input: Ray origin \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and unit direction \mathbf{d} \in S^2. Output: Scalar distance t to the first surface and scalar visibility \xi \in [0, 1] representing the probability that the ray hits the scene. The hit point is \mathbf{x} + t\mathbf{d} when \xi is high. The field consists of a multiresolution hash grid encoding for the position and a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). 1. Multiresolution Hash Grid (Position Encoding): Levels: 16. Features per level: 2. Entries per level: 2^{19} (524,288). Base resolution: 16. Growth factor: 1.5. Bounding Box: A box bounding the normalized object. Total Parameters: \approx 13 million. 2. Sinusoidal Encoding (Direction Encoding): Bands: 4 sinusoidal bands. 3. MLP: Layers: 2. Width: 64. Total Parameters: \approx 8,000. 4. Total Memory: ~52 MB. The network is trained using the Adam optimizer for 30,000 steps with a batch size of 16,384 rays. The learning rate starts at 3 \times 10^{-3} and is decayed by a cosine schedule to 5% of its initial value. Loss Function: The loss combines a clamped L1 error on the distance and a Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) on the visibility: L = \text{ClampedL1}(t{pred}, t{target}) + 0.3 \times \text{BCE}(\xi{pred}, \xi{target}) The L1 term is clamped to a maximum value (the box scale) to prevent far-away surfaces from dominating the gradient. Supervision Sources: 1. GS-Rendered Depth: Provides primary ray targets from the camera frustum. Note: This supervision is insufficient for thin features. 2. Clean Distance (Sphere Tracing): A neural surface (e.g., NeuS) is fit to the images, and rays are sphere-traced to generate clean distance targets. This is critical for recovering thin geometry like mug handles or animal legs. 3. Ground Truth Mesh (Optional): For evaluation, rays are ray-casted against ground-truth meshes. Self-Consistency Regularization: To sharpen thin features and ensure consistency along rays, 30% of the training batch is replaced with shifted points. For a ray hitting at distance t, a point shifted forward by distance s along the ray is sampled. The DDF evaluated at this shifted point must predict distance t-s. Unverified code. Quality: Reproduces reference ray-traced shadows at 30.3 dB and ambient occlusion at 21.3 dB across 142 objects and real captured scenes. The Directed Distance Field for Gaussian Splatting was introduced to address the limitation of 3DGS rasterization, which only supports primary camera rays and cannot efficiently trace secondary rays for global illumination. The method builds on the multiresolution hash grid encoding technique from tinycudann. It enables a mesh-free pipeline for global illumination in Gaussian Splatting scenes by distilling the scene geometry into a compact neural field. name: Pruning and Reduction
head: Gaussian pruning, 3DGS pruning, vertex pruning, SplatQ
body: Pruning and reduction methods remove redundant or low-impact 3D Gaussians from a trained or training model to reduce memory footprint and rendering latency while preserving visual fidelity. Unlike sibling methods that focus on geometric simplification of primitives or opacity-independent truncation, this family focuses on the selection and elimination of entire Gaussian entities based on their contribution to the rendered image or their geometric degeneracy. It is distinct from Gaussian Representation and Truncation by actively modifying the set of Gaussians \{Gi\} rather than just their rendering parameters. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. Vertex-level pruning is a geometric simplification mechanism applied to mixed-primitive splats (Gaussian triangles and lines) during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It removes redundant vertices from primitives that have collapsed or degenerated into lower-dimensional shapes, converting them into simpler primitives (ellipses or lines) to refine the surface representation. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting, which only performs primitive-level opacity pruning, this method operates on the vertex level within the mixed-primitive framework. SplatQ is a post-training pruning framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that addresses the spatial quality imbalance and loss of joint rendering effects inherent in global Top-K selection methods. Unlike sibling methods that rank Gaussians independently, SplatQ partitions primitives into size-limited blocks based on spatial and appearance similarity, allocates retention quotas to balance regional quality, and solves a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem within each block to jointly select Gaussians under a fixed global budget. Definition A pruning mechanism designed to support mixed-primitive-based learning, as standard pruning is incompatible with mixed primitives. Step Prune vertices of the mixed primitives to optimize the representation. Definition A method to reduce the number of Gaussians using a learnable mask during optimization, targeting small-sized kernels for removal. Step Apply binary masks M to the opacities and scale attributes of the kernels at every densification step. Use residual vector quantization with L stages of vector quantization for geometric attributes like scale and rotation. Represent view-dependent colors via a grid-based neural field using hash grids for input positions, features, and view direction, fed into an MLP. Formula The end-to-end loss is: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{ren} + \lambdam \mathcal{L}m + \mathcal{L}r + \mathcal{L}s where \mathcal{L}{ren} is L1+SSIM loss, \mathcal{L}m is masking loss (\frac{1}{N} \sum \sigma(mn)), and \mathcal{L}r, \mathcal{L}s are rotation and scale objective functions. Parameter \epsilon: Masking threshold for the sigmoid function in the learnable mask. \lambdam: Weight for the masking loss term, typically 5 \times 10^{-4}. Definition Application of visibility-based pruning to 3D Gaussian Splatting, using Gaussian centroids as reference points for visibility calculation. Step Represent each Gaussian kernel by its centroid position, scaling matrix S, and rotation matrix R defining the covariance \Sigma. Use the Gaussian centroids as the 3D points pi in the visibility mask computation algorithm. Pruning in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a solution to the high memory consumption and computational cost associated with the large number of Gaussians required for high-fidelity reconstruction. Early methods relied on simple opacity thresholds, but later approaches introduced geometric constraints (vertex pruning for mixed primitives) and optimization-based selection (SplatQ, learnable masks) to maintain quality at lower densities. Visibility-based pruning leverages the fact that occluded Gaussians contribute little to the final image, allowing for aggressive reduction in complex scenes.
