name: Vertex-level Pruning in Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting
head: Mixed-Primitive Vertex Pruning
body: Vertex-level pruning is a geometric simplification mechanism applied during the training of Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting (MP-GS) to remove redundant vertices from Gaussian triangles and lines, converting them into lower-order primitives (ellipses or lines). It addresses the issue of "messy" representations where high-order primitives persist in regions that can be adequately modeled by simpler shapes, thereby refining the surface representation and reducing storage overhead. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which only performs primitive-level opacity pruning, this method operates on the vertex level within mixed-primitive frameworks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of mixed-primitive Gaussians \{Gi\}, where each primitive is defined by a set of vertices \{\boldsymbol{\mu}j\}, covariance parameters, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. Output: A refined set of primitives with reduced vertex counts where geometric redundancy is detected. Data Structures: Each mixed primitive stores its vertices explicitly. For a Gaussian triangle, three vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}1, \boldsymbol{\mu}2, \boldsymbol{\mu}3 are stored. For a Gaussian line, two vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}1, \boldsymbol{\mu}2 are stored. The primitive type (triangle, line, ellipse) is tracked. Parameters: \omega{dist}: The threshold for determining if vertices are "close". Default value: 0.5. \omega{pear}: The threshold for determining if Gaussian triangle vertices are collinear. Default value: 0.9. Algorithm Steps: Vertex-level pruning is triggered whenever primitive-level pruning is performed during the learning procedure. The process evaluates the geometric configuration of each primitive: 1. Check for Gaussian Triangle Collapse to Ellipse: For a Gaussian triangle primitive with vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}1, \boldsymbol{\mu}2, \boldsymbol{\mu}3: Calculate the maximum pairwise L2 distance among the three vertices: d{max} = \max(\|\boldsymbol{\mu}1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}2\|2, \|\boldsymbol{\mu}2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}3\|2, \|\boldsymbol{\mu}3 - \boldsymbol{\mu}1\|2) If d{max} < \omega{dist}, the vertices are considered close. Prune vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}2 and \boldsymbol{\mu}3. Convert the primitive into a Gaussian ellipse centered at \boldsymbol{\mu}1. 2. Check for Gaussian Triangle Degeneration to Line: For a Gaussian triangle primitive where the condition in Step 1 is not met (vertices are not close): Compute the Pearson correlation coefficient from the coordinates of the three vertices. Let the vertices be represented as a matrix V where rows are vertices. The correlation is computed across the dimensions. If the absolute value of the Pearson correlation coefficient exceeds \omega{pear}, the vertices are considered nearly collinear. Convert the primitive from a Gaussian triangle to a Gaussian line. 3. Check for Gaussian Line Collapse to Ellipse: For a Gaussian line primitive with vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}1, \boldsymbol{\mu}2: Calculate the L2 distance: d = \|\boldsymbol{\mu}1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}2\|2 If d < \omega{dist}, the vertices are considered close. Prune vertex \boldsymbol{\mu}2. Reduce the primitive to a Gaussian ellipse centered at \boldsymbol{\mu}1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexlevelpruning(primitive, omegadist=0.5, omegapear=0.9): """ Prunes vertices from a mixed-primitive Gaussian based on geometric redundancy. Args: primitive: An object containing: type: 'triangle', 'line', or 'ellipse' vertices: List of numpy arrays [mu1, mu2,...] covariance: Covariance matrix or parameters opacity: Scalar alpha color: Color vector omegadist: Threshold for vertex proximity (default 0.5) omegapear: Threshold for collinearity (default 0.9) Returns: Updated primitive object """ if primitive.type == 'triangle': mu1, mu2, mu3 = primitive.vertices[0], primitive.vertices[1], primitive.vertices[2] # Step 1: Check if vertices are close d12 = np.linalg.norm(mu1 - mu2) d23 = np.linalg.norm(mu2 - mu3) d31 = np.linalg.norm(mu3 - mu1) maxdist = max(d12, d23, d31) if maxdist < omegadist: # Prune mu2 and mu3, convert to ellipse at mu1 primitive.type = 'ellipse' primitive.vertices = [mu1] # Note: Covariance must be preserved or recomputed for the ellipse return primitive # Step 2: Check if vertices are collinear # Form matrix V with vertices as rows V = np.vstack([mu1, mu2, mu3]) # Compute Pearson correlation coefficient # Using numpy corrcoef which returns a matrix; take the off-diagonal element corrmatrix = np.corrcoef(V.T) # Handle potential NaNs if variance is zero if np.isnan(corrmatrix[0, 1]): pearsonval = 0.0 else: pearsonval = abs(corrmatrix[0, 1]) if pearsonval > omegapear: # Convert triangle to line primitive.type = 'line' # Keep mu1 and mu2 as the line endpoints primitive.vertices = [mu1, mu2] # Note: Covariance must be adjusted for line representation return primitive elif primitive.type == 'line': mu1, mu2 = primitive.vertices[0], primitive.vertices[1] # Step 3: Check if line vertices are close dist = np.linalg.norm(mu1 - mu2) if dist < omegadist: # Prune mu2, reduce to ellipse at mu1 primitive.type = 'ellipse' primitive.vertices = [mu1] return primitive return primitive Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Covariance Preservation: When converting a triangle to a line or ellipse, or a line to an ellipse, the covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} must be appropriately transformed or re-initialized to maintain the visual appearance of the primitive. The source notes do not specify the exact mathematical transformation for \boldsymbol{\Sigma} during these conversions. Collinearity Calculation: The Pearson correlation coefficient calculation assumes the vertices are treated as variables. If vertices are identical or degenerate in a way that causes zero variance, the correlation is undefined (NaN). The pseudocode above handles this by defaulting to 0.0. Interaction with Densification: Vertex pruning does not reduce the representation to only point-centered ellipses because the original densification mechanism (cloning and splitting) continues to operate alongside pruning. Storage Reduction: The vertex pruning mechanism reduces the average storage size required to store vertex coordinates by 24% compared to the variant without pruning. Performance: The method adds a lightweight geometric check during the pruning phase. It does not significantly increase rendering time as it only modifies the data structure during training updates. Quality: Ablation studies show that the framework with vertex pruning performs better in surface reconstruction metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance) compared to the variant without it. Vertex-level pruning was introduced in the context of Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting (MP-GS), a method that extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by using Gaussian triangles and lines in addition to point-centered Gaussians. The method was proposed to handle the increased complexity of mixed primitives, where standard opacity-based pruning is insufficient to remove geometrically redundant vertices. A Mixed-Primitive-based Gaussian Splatting Method for Surface Reconstruction, https://core.ac.uk/works/308836756, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: SplatQ
head: SplatQ: Post-training Gaussian pruning via QUBO
body: SplatQ is a post-training pruning framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that addresses the spatial quality imbalance and ignored joint deletion effects of global Top-K methods. It partitions Gaussians into size-limited blocks based on spatial and appearance similarity, allocates retention quotas to balance regional budget, and uses a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model to jointly select Gaussians within each block, thereby accounting for pairwise interactions and overlapping contributions. Inputs: A pretrained 3DGS model with N Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian Gi is defined by center \boldsymbol{\mu}i, scale si, rotation quaternion \mathbf{r}i, zeroth-order (DC) color coefficients \mathbf{c}i, higher-order spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients \mathbf{h}i, and opacity \alphai. A target retention count K and a maximum block size M. Outputs: A pruned set of K Gaussians and their optimized attributes. Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of N Gaussian objects. Blocks: A partition of the Gaussian indices into sets \mathcal{C}b, where |\mathcal{C}b| \le M. Response Matrix \mathbf{R}b: For each block \mathcal{C}b, a matrix storing individual deletion responses and pairwise interaction coefficients derived from sampled pixel renderings. Quotas: A vector \mathbf{K} = [Kb] where \sumb Kb = K. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the N Gaussians into blocks \{\mathcal{C}b\} of size at most M. This is done using spatial proximity and appearance similarity to group potentially redundant Gaussians together, avoiding the quadratic cost of all-pairs comparison by using a 3D grid and Morton ordering. 2. Opacity Response Modeling: For each block \mathcal{C}b, compute the response matrix \mathbf{R}b. This involves sampling pixels from multiple views and estimating the change in rendered color when individual Gaussians are deleted and when pairs of Gaussians are deleted jointly. 3. Budget Allocation: Assign a retention quota Kb to each block \mathcal{C}b such that \sumb Kb = K. Initial quotas are derived from importance estimates, then smoothed to prevent the budget from concentrating in regions with consistently high scores, which causes spatial quality imbalance. 4. Quadratic Selection: For each block \mathcal{C}b, formulate a QUBO objective to select exactly Kb Gaussians to retain. The objective incorporates individual responses, pairwise interaction terms from \mathbf{R}b, and a penalty for deviating from Kb. Solve the QUBO using Simulated Annealing (SA) or a Coherent Ising Machine (CIM). 5. Fine-tuning: Fine-tune the attributes (\boldsymbol{\mu}i, si, \mathbf{r}i, \mathbf{c}i, \mathbf{h}i, \alphai) of the retained Gaussians without changing the count K to recover rendering quality. Formulas: The Gaussian representation is: Gi = (\boldsymbol{\mu}i, si, \mathbf{r}i, \mathbf{c}i, \mathbf{h}i, \alphai) where \boldsymbol{\mu}i is the center, si is the scale, \mathbf{r}i is the rotation quaternion, \mathbf{c}i and \mathbf{h}i are the zeroth-order and higher-order spherical-harmonic coefficients, and \alphai is the opacity. The QUBO objective for a block \mathcal{C}b with binary retention variables xi \in \{0, 1\} (1 if retained, 0 if deleted) is: \min{\mathbf{x}} \left( \sum{i \in \mathcal{C}b} wi xi + \sum{i, j \in \mathcal{C}b, i < j} w{ij} xi xj + \lambda \left( \sum{i \in \mathcal{C}b} xi - Kb \right)^2 \right) where wi represents the individual deletion response (cost of removing Gi), w{ij} represents the pairwise interaction effect, and \lambda is a penalty weight enforcing the quota Kb. Parameters: N: Total number of Gaussians in the pretrained model. K: Exact number of Gaussians to retain. M: Maximum size of each block \mathcal{C}b. Kb: Retention quota for block b. \mathbf{R}b: Response matrix for block b. Pitfalls: Spatial Quality Imbalance: Global ranking methods concentrate the budget in regions with high scores, leaving other regions with insufficient capacity. Non-Additive Degradation: Independent scoring fails to capture joint effects because overlapping Gaussians may jointly support a pixel; removing multiple Gaussians is not strictly additive. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatqprune(gaussians, targetcount K, maxblocksize M): """ Prune 3D Gaussians using SplatQ. Args: gaussians: List of N Gaussian objects with attributes (mu, s, r, c, h, alpha). K: Target number of Gaussians to retain. M: Maximum size of each block. Returns: prunedgaussians: List of K Gaussian objects with optimized attributes. """ N = len(gaussians) # Stage 1: Partitioning # Use 3D grid and Morton ordering to group by spatial proximity and appearance similarity # to avoid O(N^2) pairwise comparisons. blocks = partitionbysimilarity(gaussians, maxsize=M) # Stage 2: Opacity Response Modeling # For each block, compute response matrix Rb using sampled pixels from multiple views. # Rb stores individual deletion effects and pairwise interactions. responsematrices = {} for block in blocks: responsematrices[block.id] = computeresponsematrix(block, gaussians) # Stage 3: Budget Allocation # Assign retention quota Kb to each block such that sum(Kb) = K. # Smooth importance-based quotas to prevent concentration in high-score regions. quotas = allocatebudget(blocks, responsematrices, K) # Stage 4: Quadratic Selection # For each block, solve QUBO to select Kb Gaussians. retainedgaussians = [] for block in blocks: Kb = quotas[block.id] Rb = responsematrices[block.id] # Formulate QUBO: min sum(wixi) + sum(wijxixj) + lambda(sum(xi) - Kb)^2 # Solve using Simulated Annealing (SA) or Coherent Ising Machine (CIM) selectedindices = solvequbo(Rb, Kb) # Add selected Gaussians to the retained list for idx in selectedindices: retainedgaussians.append(block.gaussians[idx]) # Stage 5: Fine-tuning # Fine-tune attributes of retained Gaussians without changing count K. prunedgaussians = finetune(retainedgaussians, gaussians) return prunedgaussians def partitionbysimilarity(gaussians, maxsize M): """ Partition Gaussians into blocks based on spatial proximity and appearance similarity. Uses 3D grid and Morton ordering for efficiency. """ # Implementation detail: Map Gaussians to 3D grid cells. # Sort cells using Morton order to preserve spatial locality. # Group Gaussians into blocks of size <= M from the sorted list. # Note: Exact implementation of Morton ordering and grid mapping is not specified in sources. pass def computeresponsematrix(block, allgaussians): """ Compute the response matrix Rb for a block. Samples pixels from multiple views. Estimates individual deletion effects (wi) and pairwise interactions (wij). """ # Implementation detail: Render scene with and without specific Gaussians/pairs. # Measure change in pixel color. # Note: Exact sampling strategy and error metric are not specified in sources. pass def allocatebudget(blocks, responsematrices, K): """ Assign retention quotas Kb to blocks such that sum(Kb) = K. Smooths initial importance-based quotas to prevent spatial imbalance. """ # Implementation detail: Calculate initial importance from Rb. # Apply smoothing function to distribute K more evenly. # Note: Exact smoothing algorithm is not specified in sources. pass def solvequbo(Rb, Kb): """ Solve the QUBO problem for a block. Objective: min sum(wixi) + sum(wijxixj) + lambda(sum(xi) - Kb)^2 """ # Implementation detail: Use Simulated Annealing (SA) or Coherent Ising Machine (CIM). # Note: Specific SA parameters or CIM hardware details are not specified in sources. pass def finetune(retainedgaussians, originalgaussians): """ Fine-tune attributes of retained Gaussians. """ # Implementation detail: Run 3DGS training steps on retained Gaussians only. # Optimize mu, s, r, c, h, alpha. # Note: Specific learning rate and duration are not specified in sources. pass Complexity: The partitioning step avoids O(N^2) pairwise comparisons by using a 3D grid and Morton ordering. The QUBO solving is performed per block, with block size limited to M, making it scalable to millions of Gaussians where a global N \times N matrix would be impractical. Performance: SplatQ ensures balanced reconstruction quality across scene regions, unlike global Top-K methods which may leave distant or low-score regions with insufficient capacity. Strengths: Accounts for joint deletion effects and pairwise interactions, which independent scoring methods ignore. Guarantees exact global retention count K. Limitations: Requires multiple rendering passes for response matrix estimation. Relies on heuristic smoothing for budget allocation. SplatQ was proposed by Hongbin Ye et al. and presented at ICLR 2027 (preprint arXiv:2610.13503, October 2026). It addresses limitations in existing 3DGS pruning methods that rely on global Top-K selection based on independent importance scores, which fail to ensure balanced reconstruction quality and ignore joint deletion effects. name: Attribute Pruning
head: SH Degree Adjustment, Spherical Harmonics Pruning
body: Attribute pruning selectively reduces the storage and computational burden of per-Gaussian attributes, primarily spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, to optimize memory usage and rendering efficiency in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Unlike sibling methods that focus on geometric redundancy or quantization, this method dynamically tailors the precision of view-dependent color representation to local scene complexity, allowing high-fidelity detail where needed while using minimal attributes in simpler regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian has associated SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i representing view-dependent color. Output: A pruned set of Gaussians with reduced attribute storage, maintaining visual fidelity while lowering memory footprint. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gi stores SH coefficients. In standard 3DGS, SH up to degree 3 is used for RGB data, resulting in 48 coefficients (16 per channel). This consumes 81% (48 out of 59 attributes) of the storage size for a single Gaussian. Steps: 1. Evaluate Scene Complexity: Analyze the local complexity of the scene or the importance of view-dependent effects for each Gaussian. 2. Determine SH Degree: Assign a SH degree to each Gaussian based on the evaluation: For less complex regions, assign a single degree (basic RGB color, typically degree 0). For complex regions requiring detailed representation, assign higher degrees (e.g., degree 1, 2, or 3). 3. Adjust Coefficients: Reduce the number of stored SH coefficients for Gaussians assigned lower degrees. This involves truncating higher-order coefficients that are not needed for the assigned precision. 4. Render: Use the adjusted SH coefficients during the splatting process to compute view-dependent colors. Formulas: The number of SH coefficients C for degree L and color channels K is given by: C = (L+1)^2 \times K For RGB (K=3) and degree 3 (L=3): C = (3+1)^2 \times 3 = 16 \times 3 = 48 This results in 48 coefficients per Gaussian. Parameters: SH Degree: Typically ranges from 0 (basic RGB) to 3 (high detail). Storage Reduction: Degree 3 SH consumes 81% of Gaussian storage attributes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: Aggressively reducing SH degree in complex regions may lead to visible artifacts or loss of fine detail. Uniform vs. Adaptive: Applying uniform SH degree across the entire scene is inefficient; adaptive pruning is required for optimal balance. Alternative Representations: Completely forgoing SH in favor of NeRF-like MLPs or classical shading can reduce attributes further but requires custom, potentially slower rendering pipelines. Reduced3DGS is a specific implementation of attribute pruning that addresses large storage sizes by reducing primitive count, adjusting SH bands, and quantizing attributes. It introduces a scale- and resolution-aware redundant primitive removal method that extends opacity-based pruning by incorporating a redundancy score to identify regions with many low-impact primitives. For SH adjustment, it evaluates color consistency across views and reduces higher-order SH bands when view-dependent effects are minimal. Additionally, it uses K-means clustering to develop a codebook and applies 16-bit half-float quantization to remaining uncompressed floating-point values. Memory Efficiency: Significantly reduces storage size by lowering the number of SH coefficients per Gaussian. Degree 3 SH accounts for 81% of Gaussian attributes; reducing this degree yields substantial savings. Computational Efficiency: Fewer coefficients to evaluate during rendering can improve computational efficiency, especially on memory-constrained devices. Visual Fidelity: Maintains high visual fidelity in complex regions while accepting lower precision in simpler areas. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of SH degree assignment to avoid artifacts. Replacing SH entirely with other methods (e.g., MLPs) may introduce rendering overhead. Use Cases: Ideal for applications where memory and computational resources are limited, such as VR headsets or mobile devices, and for scenes with varying levels of geometric and photometric complexity. Attribute pruning emerged as a response to the high memory footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly due to the storage requirements of high-degree spherical harmonics. The method builds on the observation that not all parts of a scene require high-fidelity view-dependent color representation. It is part of a broader effort to compress and optimize 3DGS for real-time applications and constrained hardware. 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting
head: DisC-GS
body: Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting (DisC-GS) is a framework that enables 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent and render sharp boundaries and discontinuities, addressing the limitation of standard Gaussian Splatting which tends to blur such features. It differs from sibling methods like Planar Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling boundaries as cubic Bézier curves within the Gaussian's local subspace and applying a "pre-scissoring" operation during rendering, rather than relying solely on geometric constraints or mesh extraction [S1, 14095-mesh-extraction-and-representation.md]. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian Gi is defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, rotation \mathbf{R}i, scale \mathbf{S}i, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. For 2D Gaussian Splatting, the last column of \mathbf{S}i is fixed to zero. The input also includes the camera projection matrix \mathbf{P} and viewing transformation matrix \mathbf{W}, and a user-defined hyperparameter M (number of Bézier curves per Gaussian). Outputs: A rendered image C(p) for each pixel p, where discontinuities are preserved. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gi is augmented with an additional attribute \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}} \in \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 2}. Layout: \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}} stores 4M points in the 2D coordinate system defined by the Gaussian's center \boldsymbol{\mu}i (origin), rotation matrix column \mathbf{r}{1,i} (x-axis), and rotation matrix column \mathbf{r}{2,i} (y-axis). Interpretation: These points serve as control points for M cubic Bézier curves representing the boundaries of the Gaussian's projection. Numbered Steps: 1. Local to World Transformation: For each Gaussian Gi, transform the control points from its local 2D subspace to the 3D world space. Let \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}}[i,:] denote the i-th point in the local attribute (for i \in \{0, \dots, 4M-1\}). The 3D control points \mathbf{c}{\text{3D\curve}}[i] are computed as: \mathbf{c}{\text{3D\curve}}[i] = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}}[i, 0] \times \mathbf{r}{1,i} + \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}}[i, 1] \times \mathbf{r}{2,i} Note: \mathbf{r}{1,i} and \mathbf{r}{2,i} are unit vectors, so normalization is omitted. 2. Projection to Image Plane: Project the 3D control points onto the image plane to obtain the 2D control points \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[i]: \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[i] = \mathbf{P} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{c}{\text{3D\curve}}[i] where \mathbf{P} is the projective transformation matrix and \mathbf{W} is the viewing transformation matrix. 3. Implicit Curve Representation: For each of the M cubic Bézier curves defined by four ordered control points \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \boldsymbol{\omega}1, \boldsymbol{\omega}2, \boldsymbol{\omega}3 (where \boldsymbol{\omega}k = \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j+k] for curve index j), compute the implicit representation B{\text{imp}}(x, y): B{\text{imp}}(x, y) = \gamma{xxx} x^3 + \gamma{xxy} x^2 y + \gamma{xyy} x y^2 + \gamma{yyy} y^3 + \gamma{xx} x^2 + \gamma{xy} xy + \gamma{yy} y^2 + \gammax x + \gammay y + \gamma0 = 0 The coefficients \gamma are obtained via O(1) arithmetic operations on the control point coordinates. 4. Indicator Function Construction: Define the single-curve indicator function g{\text{sc}} for a pixel p=(xp, yp): g{\text{sc}}(\boldsymbol{\omega}0, \boldsymbol{\omega}1, \boldsymbol{\omega}2, \boldsymbol{\omega}3; p) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } B{\text{imp}}(xp, yp) > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} For M > 1 curves, the combined indicator function g(p) is the product of individual indicators: g(p) = \prod{j=0}^{M-1} g{\text{sc}}(\mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j], \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j+1], \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j+2], \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j+3]; p) A pixel is "scissored out" (g(p)=0) if it is outside at least one of the M curves. 5. Discontinuity-Aware Rendering: Compute the color C(p) using a modified \alpha-blending function: C(p) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \betai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \betaj) where the effective opacity \betai for the i-th Gaussian is: \betai = \alphai gi(p) \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,2D})^\top (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{i,2D})^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,2D})\right) Here, \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,2D} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{i,2D} are the projected mean and covariance of the i-th Gaussian, and gi(p) is the indicator function for the i-th Gaussian. 6. Gradient Approximation: During backpropagation, use a Bézier-boundary gradient approximation strategy to enable gradients to pass through the discontinuous indicator function g(p), maintaining differentiability for learning \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def cubicbezierimplicitcoeffs(w0, w1, w2, w3): """ Computes the coefficients gamma for the implicit representation of a cubic Bezier curve. w0, w1, w2, w3: numpy arrays of shape (2,) representing control points. Returns: dict of gamma coefficients. Note: Implementation details for O(1) arithmetic operations are omitted as per source which refers to supplementary material for exact derivation. """ # Placeholder for the specific algebraic derivation provided in supplementary # This function must return gammaxxx, gammaxxy, etc. raise NotImplementedError("See supplementary for exact O(1) arithmetic derivation") def bezierindicator(p, coeffs): """ Evaluates the implicit function Bimp(x, y) for a pixel p. p: numpy array of shape (2,) [x, y] coeffs: dict of gamma coefficients Returns: float value of Bimp(x, y) """ x, y = p gamma = coeffs val = (gamma['gammaxxx'] x3 + gamma['gammaxxy'] x2 y + gamma['gammaxyy'] x y2 + gamma['gammayyy'] y3 + gamma['gammaxx'] x2 + gamma['gammaxy'] x y + gamma['gammayy'] y2 + gamma['gammax'] x + gamma['gammay'] y + gamma['gamma0']) return val def prescissorrender(gaussians, cameramatrixP, cameramatrixW, M): """ Renders an image using Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting. gaussians: list of N Gaussian objects. Each has: mu: (3,) mean R: (3,3) rotation matrix alpha: scalar opacity color: (3,) color ccurve: (4M, 2) control points in local 2D space cameramatrixP: (4,4) projection matrix cameramatrixW: (4,4) viewing matrix M: int, number of Bezier curves per Gaussian Returns: renderedimage (H, W, 3) """ # Assume image dimensions H, W are known or derived from camera frustum # For simplicity, we iterate pixels. In practice, rasterization is used. # Precompute projected Gaussians projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Project mean mu2d = cameramatrixP @ cameramatrixW @ np.append(g.mu, 1) mu2d = mu2d[:2] / mu2d[2] # Perspective divide # Project covariance (simplified Jacobian J omitted for brevity, assume standard 3DGS projection) # Sigma2D = J @ W @ Sigma3D @ W.T @ J.T # This step relies on standard 3DGS projection logic projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu2d': mu2d, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'color': g.color, 'ccurve': g.ccurve }) # Initialize image # Note: Full rasterization loop is complex; this pseudocode outlines the core DisC-GS logic # for a single pixel p. def renderpixel(p): colorsum = np.zeros(3) alphasum = 0.0 # Sort Gaussians by depth (standard 3DGS step) #... sorting logic... for pg in projectedgaussians: # 1. Transform local control points to 3D # r1, r2 are first two columns of R r1 = pg['R'][:, 0] r2 = pg['R'][:, 1] c3dcurve = np.zeros((4M, 3)) for i in range(4M): c3dcurve[i] = pg['mu'] + pg['ccurve'][i, 0] r1 + pg['ccurve'][i, 1] r2 # 2. Project control points to 2D c2dcurve = np.zeros((4M, 2)) for i in range(4M): pt3dhom = np.append(c3dcurve[i], 1) pt2dhom = cameramatrixP @ cameramatrixW @ pt3dhom c2dcurve[i] = pt2dhom[:2] / pt2dhom[2] # 3. Compute Indicator Function g(p) gval = 1.0 for j in range(M): w0 = c2dcurve[4j] w1 = c2dcurve[4j+1] w2 = c2dcurve[4j+2] w3 = c2dcurve[4j+3] coeffs = cubicbezierimplicitcoeffs(w0, w1, w2, w3) bimp = bezierindicator(p, coeffs) if bimp <= 0: gval = 0.0 break if gval == 0: continue # 4. Compute Beta # Sigma2D calculation omitted, assume standard 3DGS projection # distsq = (p - mu2d).T @ inv(Sigma2D) @ (p - mu2d) # beta = alpha gval exp(-0.5 distsq) # Simplified beta for pseudocode structure beta = pg['alpha'] gval 1.0 # Placeholder for Gaussian term # 5. Alpha Blending colorsum += pg['color'] beta (1 - alphasum) alphasum += beta (1 - alphasum) return colorsum # Iterate over all pixels # renderedimage = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) # for y in range(H): # for x in range(W): # p = np.array([x, y]) # renderedimage[y, x] = renderpixel(p) return None # Placeholder Parameters: M: User-defined hyperparameter representing the number of Bézier curves per Gaussian distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiability: The indicator function g(p) is piecewise constant, making the forward rendering process non-differentiable. Naive integration breaks backpropagation. Zero Gradients: Even in differentiable segments, the gradient of g(\cdot) with respect to its inputs is zero, which fails to guide the learning of \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}} without the Bézier-boundary gradient approximation strategy. Viewpoint Inconsistency: Using 3D Gaussians can result in viewpoint inconsistency. DisC-GS fixes the last column of the scale matrix \mathbf{S} to be a zero vector for 2D Gaussians to mitigate this. Time Complexity: The implicitization of cubic Bézier curves and evaluation of the indicator function is O(1) per curve per pixel. With M curves per Gaussian and N Gaussians, the overhead per pixel is proportional to N \times M. Memory Complexity: Each Gaussian stores an additional attribute \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}} \in \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 2}, increasing memory usage by 8M floats per Gaussian. Strengths: Enables accurate rendering of sharp boundaries and discontinuities, which standard Gaussian Splatting blurs. Limitations: Requires careful handling of differentiability via the gradient approximation strategy. Performance depends on the choice of M. Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting (DisC-GS) was proposed to address the key intrinsic limitation of Gaussian Splatting: its inability to render discontinuities and boundaries accurately. It is the first effort to enable Gaussian Splatting to represent and render boundaries properly in its image rendering pipeline. The method builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation and incorporates insights from cubic Bézier curves. name: Mesh Extraction and Representation
head: Surface Extraction from Gaussians, Gaussian-to-Mesh Conversion
body: This family of methods converts the volumetric, implicit representation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into explicit geometric structures, primarily triangular meshes or dense point clouds, to enable compatibility with standard 3D graphics pipelines, mesh editing tools, and physics simulations. Unlike standard 3DGS, which renders via alpha-blended splats, these methods extract a discrete surface or point set that approximates the radiance field, allowing for operations such as texture mapping, rigging, and collision detection. The key distinction lies in whether the extraction is driven by surface-alignment regularization during training (e.g., SuGaR) or by post-hoc probabilistic sampling of the trained density field (e.g., Point Cloud Conversion). All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. SuGaR (Surface-aligned Gaussian Splatting) extracts a high-quality triangular mesh from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by regularizing the Gaussians to align with the true scene surface during optimization. Unlike standard 3DGS, which produces a volumetric representation, SuGaR enables the extraction of an editable surface mesh and facilitates scene editing using traditional mesh-editing tools. It distinguishes itself by jointly optimizing the Gaussians and the mesh, and by introducing a "Frosting" layer to handle fuzzy materials where surface alignment is insufficient. This method converts a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representation into a dense, standard point cloud (PLY format) that visually approximates the original radiance field, enabling compatibility with general 3D software that does not support Gaussian primitives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SuGaR Mesh Extraction by focusing on direct probabilistic sampling from the Gaussian distributions rather than optimizing a separate mesh or point set via differentiable rendering losses, although it optionally uses rendering to refine colors and visibility. A representation that connects Gaussian splats to a mesh structure, enabling real-time editing and animation by directly manipulating mesh vertices. Train GS with flat Gaussians. Construct an initial Triangle Soup. Adjust the Triangle Soup during training. For mesh-based input, fit a pre-existing mesh (e.g., FLAME) to the data. Number of Gaussians per face: 100 (used in facial reconstruction experiments). GPU hardware: Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB (used for NeRF-Synthetic dataset experiments). Artifacts appear with significant changes on meshes with large faces. Handled by dividing large faces into smaller ones using subdivision. How to change Gaussian components when mesh faces are split is not apparent. Differs from vanilla GS by automatically recalculating Gaussian parameters (covariance, rotation) when vertices are moved, avoiding holes and blurriness. Used in the GaMeS model for 3D face reconstruction, object editing, and animation. The need for mesh extraction from 3DGS arises from the limitations of the native Gaussian representation for applications requiring explicit geometry, such as physics simulation, texture baking, and integration with standard CAD or game engine pipelines. SuGaR was introduced by Guedon and Lepetit (2023) to address the lack of surface continuity in standard 3DGS by introducing surface-alignment regularization. The Triangle Soup concept, utilized in models like GaMeS, extends this by explicitly linking Gaussian parameters to mesh topology for editable animations. Point cloud conversion methods provide a simpler, post-hoc alternative for visualization and compatibility with legacy software that cannot handle Gaussian primitives. GaMeS: Mesh-based adapting and modification of Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2026.114561, fetched 2026-10-29 SuGaR: Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for Efficient 3D Mesh Reconstruction and High-Quality Mesh Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12775, fetched 2024-05-20

name: SuGaR Mesh Extraction
head: Gaussian Frosting (as a precursor component), Surface-aligned Gaussian Splatting
body: SuGaR Mesh Extraction is a method for converting the volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting representation into a editable triangular mesh by regularizing the Gaussians to align with the true scene surface during optimization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting to Point Cloud by enforcing surface alignment constraints rather than simple density sampling, enabling the use of traditional mesh-editing tools. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N optimized via standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Output: A triangular mesh \mathcal{M} and a set of Gaussians bound to this mesh. Data Structures: Gaussians: Defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. Mesh: A triangular mesh \mathcal{M} extracted via Poisson reconstruction. Frosting Layer: A secondary set of Gaussians sampled around the mesh to handle fuzzy materials. Method Steps: 1. Surface-Aligning Regularization: During the 3DGS optimization process, a regularization term is applied to encourage the Gaussians to align with the true surface of the scene. This minimizes the distance between the Gaussian mass and the underlying geometry. 2. Point Sampling: Points are sampled from the visible level set of the Gaussian splatting density function. The density function for a Gaussian Gi is: Gi(\mathbf{x}) = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)\right) Points are selected where the accumulated density along viewing rays exceeds a threshold. 3. Poisson Reconstruction: The sampled points are used to reconstruct a triangular mesh \mathcal{M} using Poisson surface reconstruction. Octree Depth (D): A critical hyperparameter for Poisson reconstruction. The sources note that D should be tuned based on scene complexity to reduce surface artifacts such as holes and ellipsoidal bumps. An automatic estimation technique for D is described in the Gaussian Frosting paper. 4. Gaussian Bounding: The original Gaussians are bounded to the extracted mesh \mathcal{M}. This involves associating each Gaussian with the nearest surface element or constraining their means to lie near the mesh. 5. Joint Optimization: The mesh \mathcal{M} and the bounded Gaussians are jointly optimized. This refines the geometry and appearance simultaneously. 6. Frosting Layer Creation (Optional/Extended): For fuzzy materials (e.g., hair, grass), a "Frosting" layer is created. The discrepancy between the regularized Gaussians and the extracted mesh is used as a cue for thickness. A novel, densified set of Gaussians is sampled inside a layer around the mesh vertices. The density function of unconstrained Gaussians is used to refine the intervals of this layer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sugarmeshextraction(gaussians, images, cameraintrinsics): """ Extracts a mesh from 3D Gaussians using surface alignment regularization. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with properties (mu, sigma, alpha, color). images: List of training images. cameraintrinsics: Camera parameters for the training views. Returns: mesh: Triangular mesh object. boundedgaussians: Gaussians bound to the mesh. frostinggaussians: Optional Gaussians for fuzzy regions. """ # Step 1: Regularized Optimization # Initialize Gaussians with standard 3DGS parameters currentgaussians = initializegaussians(gaussians) # Define regularization term Lreg that penalizes distance from surface # Note: The exact mathematical form of Lreg is not provided in sources # It encourages alignment of Gaussians with the true scene surface for iteration in range(numiterations): # Render images from current Gaussians renderedimages = rendergaussians(currentgaussians, images, cameraintrinsics) # Compute loss # Ltotal = Lrender + lambda Lreg # Lrender is standard photometric loss # Lreg is the surface alignment regularization loss = computeloss(renderedimages, images) + lambdareg computesurfacealignmentloss(currentgaussians) # Backpropagate and update Gaussians currentgaussians = optimizegaussians(currentgaussians, loss) # Step 2: Sample points from visible level set # Accumulate density along rays for each pixel densityfield = accumulatedensity(currentgaussians, images, cameraintrinsics) # Sample points where density exceeds threshold # The specific threshold value is not given in sources sampledpoints = samplelevelset(densityfield, threshold=0.5) # Step 3: Poisson Reconstruction # Determine Octree Depth D based on scene complexity # Automatic estimation method described in octreedepth = estimateoctreedepth(sampledpoints) mesh = poissonreconstruction(sampledpoints, octreedepth=octreedepth) # Step 4: Bound Gaussians to Mesh # Associate each Gaussian with the mesh surface boundedgaussians = bindgaussianstomesh(currentgaussians, mesh) # Step 5: Joint Optimization # Optimize mesh vertices and Gaussian parameters jointly # Note: Specific joint optimization algorithm details are not provided for jointiter in range(numjointiterations): # Render using bounded Gaussians and current mesh jointrendered = renderboundedgaussians(boundedgaussians, mesh, images, cameraintrinsics) jointloss = computeloss(jointrendered, images) # Update mesh and Gaussians mesh = optimizemesh(mesh, jointloss) boundedgaussians = optimizegaussians(boundedgaussians, jointloss) # Step 6: Create Frosting Layer for fuzzy materials # Calculate discrepancy between regularized Gaussians and mesh # Large discrepancy indicates fuzzy materials discrepancy = computegaussianmeshdiscrepancy(boundedgaussians, mesh) # Sample additional Gaussians in regions with high discrepancy frostinggaussians = samplefrostinglayer(boundedgaussians, mesh, discrepancy) return mesh, boundedgaussians, frostinggaussians Parameters: Octree Depth (D): Critical hyperparameter for Poisson reconstruction. Typical values are not explicitly stated, but the source emphasizes that selecting the right D drastically improves quality and reduces artifacts like holes and bumps. An automatic tuning method is proposed. Regularization Weight (\lambda{reg}): Weight for the surface alignment term. Not given in the sources. Density Threshold: Threshold for sampling points from the level set. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fuzzy Materials: A large discrepancy between regularized Gaussians and the extracted mesh indicates fuzzy materials or surfaces that require volumetric rendering (e.g., hair, grass). In these cases, the mesh extraction alone is insufficient, and the Frosting layer is necessary. Surface Artifacts: Incorrect Octree Depth D leads to holes and ellipsoidal bumps on the surface. Vanilla 3DGS Limitation: Vanilla 3DGS lacks regularization for surface alignment, leading to poor mesh extraction without the SuGaR regularization step. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method enables efficient mesh extraction and scene editing using traditional mesh-editing tools. The automatic tuning of Octree Depth D reduces surface artifacts, improving rendering performance. Strengths: Produces editable triangular meshes; handles fuzzy materials via Frosting layer; reduces surface artifacts with proper D tuning. Limitations: Requires regularization during optimization; may struggle with inherently volumetric/fuzzy scenes if Frosting layer is not used. SuGaR (Surface-aligned Gaussian Splatting) was introduced to address the lack of explicit surface representation in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was later extended by the Gaussian Frosting method to handle complex radiance fields with volumetric effects. The method is used for scene editing, shape deformation, and morphing tasks. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting to Point Cloud
head: 3DGS to Point Cloud Conversion, 3DGS-to-PC, Gaussian Splatting Point Cloud Generation, Gaussian Splatting to Dense Point Clouds
body: This method converts a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representation into a dense, standard point cloud format (e.g., PLY) that approximates the original geometry and appearance, enabling compatibility with general 3D software that does not support Gaussian splats. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SuGaR Mesh Extraction by focusing on generating a high-fidelity point cloud (and optionally a mesh via Poisson reconstruction) directly from the Gaussian distributions, rather than extracting a watertight mesh through explicit surface optimization. The process involves filtering Gaussians by visibility and opacity, sampling points from the Gaussian probability distributions, and optionally re-rendering colors from camera views to ensure photorealistic appearance in the final point cloud. Inputs: A 3DGS scene file (PLY or splat) containing N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from scale \mathbf{S}i and rotation \mathbf{R}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color. Camera parameters (transforms, intrinsics) if color rendering is enabled. Configuration settings (see Parameters). Outputs: A point cloud file (PLY) containing points \mathbf{p}j, colors \mathbf{c}j, and optionally normals \mathbf{n}j. Optionally, a mesh file (PLY) generated from the point cloud. Data Structures: GaussPointCloudSettings: NamedTuple containing: renderertype: str ('cuda' or 'python') numpoints: int (default 10,000,000) prioritisevisiblegaussians: bool (default True) mahalanobisdistancestd: float (default 2.0) cameraskiprate: int (default 0) rendercolours: bool (default True) minopacity: float (default 0.0) boundingboxmin: list of 3 floats (default None) boundingboxmax: list of 3 floats (default None) calculatenormals: bool (default True) culllargepercentage: float (default 0.0) removeunrenderedgaussians: bool (default True) colourresolution: int (mapped from colourquality) maxshdegree: int (default 3) exactnumpoints: bool (default False) visibilitythreshold: float (default 0.05) surfacedistancestd: float (default None) generatemesh: bool (default False) quiet: bool (default False) device: str (default 'cuda') PointCloudData: NamedTuple containing: points: torch.Tensor of shape (M, 3) colours: torch.Tensor of shape (M, 3) normals: torch.Tensor of shape (M, 3) Parameters: numpoints: Total target points. Default: 10,000,000. exactnumpoints: If True, forces the output to match numpoints closely (slower). Default: False. noprioritisevisiblegaussians: If True, ignores visibility contributions when distributing points. Default: False. visibilitythreshold: Minimum Gaussian contribution to be included. Default: 0.05. surfacedistancestd: Cull Gaussians further than X standard deviations from predicted surfaces. Default: Disabled. cleanpointcloud: Remove outliers using Open3D. Default: False. generatemesh: Generate mesh via Poisson reconstruction. Default: False. poissondepth: Depth for Poisson reconstruction. Default: 10. laplacianiterations: Laplacian smoothing iterations for mesh. Default: 10. cameraskiprate: Cameras to skip during rendering. Default: 0. norendercolours: Skip color rendering. Default: False. colourquality: Quality level ('tiny', 'low', 'medium', 'high', 'ultra', 'original'). Default: 'high'. boundingboxmin/max: Spatial bounds for inclusion. Default: Disabled. nocalculatenormals: Skip normal calculation. Default: False. mahalanobisdistancestd: Max Mahalanobis distance for sampling. Default: 2.0. minopacity: Minimum opacity threshold. Default: 0.0. cullgaussiansizes: Percentage of largest Gaussians to remove. Default: 0.0. maxshdegrees: SH degree of input. Default: 3. numsampleattempts: Attempts per Gaussian (5 if exactnumpoints is False, else 100). renderertype: 'cuda' or 'python'. Default: 'cuda'. Steps: 1. Load and Validate Gaussians: Load Gaussian parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i) from the input file. Validate covariance matrices \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i to ensure they are positive semidefinite. If any are not, clamp them or remove the corresponding Gaussians. 2. Filter Gaussians: Apply culling criteria to the set of N Gaussians: Opacity: Remove Gaussians where \alphai < \text{min\opacity}. Bounding Box: Remove Gaussians where \boldsymbol{\mu}i is outside [\text{bounding\box\min}, \text{bounding\box\max}]. Size: Remove the top \text{cull\gaussian\sizes} \times 100\% of Gaussians ranked by size (approximated by surface area). Visibility: If prioritisevisiblegaussians is True, render the scene from all camera views (or a subset based on cameraskiprate) to compute the total contribution of each Gaussian. Remove Gaussians with total contribution < \text{visibility\threshold}. Surface Distance: If surfacedistancestd is set, cull Gaussians that are further than this threshold from predicted surfaces. 3. Calculate Point Allocation: Determine the number of points to sample from each remaining Gaussian. Compute the surface area Ai of each Gaussian ellipsoid using its eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 from \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i: a = \sqrt{\lambda1}, \quad b = \sqrt{\lambda2}, \quad c = \sqrt{\lambda3} Ai \approx 4\pi \left( \frac{a^p b^p + a^p c^p + b^p c^p}{3} \right)^{1/p}, \quad p = 1.6075 If prioritisevisiblegaussians is True, use the visibility contribution vi as the weight; otherwise, use opacity \alphai. Calculate magnitude mi: mi = \sqrt{Ai} \times vi Distribute the total numpoints among Gaussians proportional to mi. If exactnumpoints is False, use a fixed number of sample attempts per Gaussian (5); otherwise, use 100 attempts. 4. Sample Points: For each Gaussian i: Sample points \mathbf{p} from the multivariate normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i). Reject samples where the Mahalanobis distance dM exceeds \text{mahalanobis\distance\std}: dM = \sqrt{(\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}i)} Add valid points to the point cloud. If exactnumpoints is False, stop sampling for this Gaussian once the allocated count is reached or attempts are exhausted. 5. Render Colors (Optional): If rendercolours is True: Initialize a Gaussian renderer with the loaded Gaussians and camera parameters. For each camera (skipping based on cameraskiprate), render the scene to obtain per-pixel colors and depths. Map the generated points to the rendered images. Update the point colors with the rendered values, weighted by the Gaussian contributions. Color resolution is determined by colourquality: tiny=180, low=360, medium=720, high=1280, ultra=1920, original=None. 6. Calculate Normals (Optional): If calculatenormals is True: Compute normals for each point. For points sampled directly from the Gaussian mean, use the normal derived from the Gaussian's covariance matrix (principal axis). For other points, estimate normals from local neighborhood or use the Gaussian's orientation. 7. Post-Processing: If cleanpointcloud is True, remove outliers using Open3D's statistical outlier removal. If generatemesh is True: Identify surface Gaussians using surfacedistancestd or other heuristics. Cull non-surface Gaussians. Generate a separate point cloud with a fixed average of 25 points per surface Gaussian, capped at half the total requested points. Perform Poisson surface reconstruction with poissondepth and apply laplacianiterations of smoothing. 8. Save Output: Save the final points, colors, and normals to a PLY file. Returns xyz, scales, rots, opacities, shcoeffs.""" # Implementation details omitted; assume standard PLY loader for 3DGS pass def validatecovariances(xyz, scales, rots): """Ensure covariances are positive semidefinite.""" # Construct covariance from scale and rotation # R = quattorotmatrix(rots) # S = diag(scales) # Sigma = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # Check eigenvalues. Clamp or remove invalid Gaussians. pass def getgaussianmagnitudes(gaussians, contributions=None): """Calculate magnitude for point allocation based on surface area and contribution.""" # Compute eigenvalues of covariance eigvals = torch.linalg.eigvals(gaussians.covariances).real a = torch.sqrt(eigvals[:, 0]) b = torch.sqrt(eigvals[:, 1]) c = torch.sqrt(eigvals[:, 2]) p = 1.6075 radicand = (torch.pow(ab, p) + torch.pow(ac, p) + torch.pow(bc, p)) / 3.0 surfacearea = 4.0 torch.pi torch.pow(radicand, 1.0/p) surfacearea = torch.sqrt(surfacearea) if contributions is None: contributions = gaussians.opacities magnitudes = surfacearea contributions return magnitudes def samplepointsfromgaussians(gaussians, numpointspergaussian, mahalanobisstd): """Sample points from Gaussian distributions, rejecting those outside Mahalanobis distance.""" points = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): mean = g.xyz cov = g.covariance numsamples = numpointspergaussian[i] # Sample from MultivariateNormal samples = torch.distributions.multivariatenormal.MultivariateNormal(mean, cov).sample((numsamples,)) # Calculate Mahalanobis distance diff = samples - mean # Solve Sigma @ x = diff for x, then x.T @ diff # Or use cholesky decomposition L = torch.linalg.cholesky(cov) y = torch.linalg.solve(L, diff.T) mahalanobisdist = torch.norm(y, dim=0) validmask = mahalanobisdist <= mahalanobisstd validsamples = samples[validmask] points.append(validsamples) if len(points[-1]) == 0: # Fallback: add mean if no samples valid points[-1] = mean.unsqueeze(0) return torch.cat(points, dim=0) def rendercolors(points, gaussians, cameras, renderertype, colourresolution): """Render colors for points using Gaussian splatting.""" # Initialize renderer # For each camera: # Render image # Project points to image plane # Assign color from rendered image pass def convert3dgstopointcloud(inputpath, outputpath, settings): # 1. Load gaussians = loadgaussians(inputpath) # 2. Validate gaussians.validatecovariances() # 3. Filter if settings.minopacity > 0: gaussians.applyminopacity(settings.minopacity) if settings.boundingboxmin is not None: gaussians.applyboundingbox(settings.boundingboxmin, settings.boundingboxmax) if settings.cullgaussiansizes > 0: gaussians.culllargegaussians(settings.cullgaussiansizes) contributions = None if settings.prioritisevisiblegaussians: # Render to get contributions contributions = getvisibilitycontributions(gaussians, settings) gaussians.applyvisibilitythreshold(settings.visibilitythreshold, contributions) # 4. Allocate Points magnitudes = getgaussianmagnitudes(gaussians, contributions) totalmag = magnitudes.sum() if totalmag == 0: raise Exception("No Gaussians remain after culling.") if settings.exactnumpoints: numattempts = 100 else: numattempts = 5 # Distribute points proportionally to magnitude pointspergaussian = (magnitudes / totalmag settings.numpoints).long() # 5. Sample points = samplepointsfromgaussians(gaussians, pointspergaussian, settings.mahalanobisdistancestd) # 6. Colors if settings.rendercolours: colors = rendercolors(points, gaussians, settings.cameras, settings.renderertype, settings.colourresolution) else: colors = gaussians.getinitialcolors(points) # Fallback color # 7. Normals if settings.calculatenormals: normals = calculatenormals(points, gaussians) else: normals = None # 8. Save saveply(outputpath, points, colors, normals) Time Complexity: Dominated by the visibility rendering step if prioritisevisiblegaussians is True, which is O(N \cdot C \cdot R) where N is Gaussians, C is cameras, and R is resolution. Sampling is O(M) where M is the number of generated points. Memory Complexity: O(N + M) to store Gaussians and the resulting point cloud. Performance: Generating 10 million points typically takes several minutes on a modern GPU, depending on the number of cameras and resolution. Using cuda renderer is significantly faster than python. Strengths: Produces high-quality, dense point clouds that closely mimic the original 3DGS appearance. Flexible filtering options allow for noise reduction and scene simplification. Limitations: The point cloud is not watertight. Color accuracy depends on the number of cameras used for rendering; sparse views may result in inconsistent colors. exactnumpoints is computationally expensive. When to use: When a standard point cloud format is required for downstream applications (e.g., meshing, visualization in non-Gaussian software). When not to use: When a watertight mesh is needed directly (use SuGaR Mesh Extraction or other meshing methods) or when real-time rendering is required (use the original 3DGS representation). 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 as a real-time radiance field representation. While 3DGS offers high-quality rendering, it is not compatible with many standard 3D processing tools. The "3DGS to Point Cloud" conversion method, as implemented in the repository by Lewis-Stuart, addresses this interoperability gap by sampling points from the Gaussian distributions. This approach leverages the fact that a Gaussian distribution can be approximated by a set of points, allowing the scene to be represented as a traditional point cloud. name: Appearance and Physical Modeling
head: Relightable Gaussians, Inverse Rendering Gaussians, Physically-Based Gaussian Splatting
body: Appearance and Physical Modeling extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation to support physically based rendering (PBR), relighting, and volumetric light transport, solving the limitations of base 3DGS which relies on fixed Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients that cannot accurately represent complex specularities, dynamic lighting, or non-vacuum media. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Gaussian Representation and Truncation by focusing on the radiance and material representation rather than geometric simplification, and distinguishes itself from Physics and Optical Modeling by prioritizing surface material decomposition and relighting over volumetric attenuation equations, although both families modify the core Gaussian properties beyond simple color. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. Color and Appearance Modeling extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation by replacing or augmenting the fixed Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients with more flexible mechanisms to represent view-dependent color, lighting, and material properties. It solves the limitations of base 3DGS, which struggles with complex specularities, dynamic lighting variations, and transient objects in unstructured datasets. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Physics and Optical Modeling by focusing on the radiance and material representation rather than volumetric light transport equations. Physics and Optical Modeling extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation to handle non-vacuum media and physically consistent surface extraction by modifying the rendering equation or the underlying density field. It solves the problem of light transport in scattering media (e.g., underwater fog) and the geometric inconsistency of discrete alpha-blending for surface reconstruction. Unlike Color and Appearance Modeling, which focuses on view-dependent shading and material properties in clear space, this family explicitly models volumetric attenuation and backscatter or reformulates the Gaussian primitive as a continuous attenuation field. Definition Relightable 3D Gaussians is a differentiable point-based rendering framework that enhances vanilla 3D Gaussians by associating extra properties (normal vectors, BRDF parameters, and incident lighting) to achieve photo-realistic relighting and BRDF decomposition from multi-view images. Implementation Steps 1. Assign a normal vector \mathbf{n}, BRDF values, and incident light information to each 3D Gaussian point to model per-point light reflectance. 2. Apply physically based rendering (PBR) to get a PBR color for each 3D Gaussian point, which is then alpha-composited to obtain the rendered color for the corresponding image pixel. 3. Split the incident light into a global environment map and an indirect incident light field for robust material and lighting estimation. 4. Introduce proper regularizations to enhance geometry and mitigate material-lighting ambiguity, including constraints on depth distribution, smoothness priors, and a lighting regularization. Definition GeoSplatting Loss Function is a composite loss function for end-to-end training of GeoSplatting, combining photometric loss, entropy loss, smoothness regularization, and light regularization. Implementation Steps 1. Compute L1 loss and SSIM loss between rendered image and ground truth. 2. Compute object mask loss L{mask} (MSE between rendered alpha map and ground truth object mask). 3. Add entropy loss L{entropy} to constrain the shape, following DMTet and FlexiCubes. 4. Apply smoothness regularization on kd and ks, and light regularization, following NVdiffrecmc and R3DG. Formula The photometric loss is computed as: L{img} = L1 + \lambda{ssim} L{SSIM} + \lambda{mask} L{mask} where L{mask} is MSE between rendered alpha map and ground truth object mask. Comparison Unlike vanilla 3DGS or other methods requiring dist loss or pseudo depth normal loss for geometric constraints, GeoSplatting does not require these regularization terms due to explicit geometry guidance. Definition Split-Sum Warm-up is a training initialization technique that uses the split-sum approximation to pre-compute lighting integrals during early training stages to mitigate optimization instability caused by noisy geometry. Implementation Steps 1. During early training, use the split-sum approximation (Eq. 6) which enables fast pre-computation and enhances evaluation speed. 2. After the warm-up stage, transition to Monte Carlo sampling of the full rendering equation (Eq. 2) to incorporate shadow effects and inter-reflection. Formula The split-sum approximation assumes no self-occlusion and is defined as: Lo(\omegao) \approx \left[ \int{\mathcal{H}} fr(\omegai, \omegao) |\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai| \, d\omegai \right] \cdot \left[ \int{\mathcal{H}} L{dir}(\omegai) D |\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai| \, d\omegai \right] Pitfall Directly evaluating the full integral in Eq. 2 is inefficient and may lead to optimization instability during initial training when geometry is noisy. Split-sum avoids this but lacks self-occlusion modeling, potentially baking shadows into albedo. Relightable 3D Gaussians was introduced by Gao et al. in 2024, presenting a framework for photo-realistic relighting using BRDF decomposition and ray tracing. GeoSplatting was introduced by its authors in 2025, focusing on geometry-guided physically-based inverse rendering. These methods address the need for editable, physically plausible scene representations in computer graphics and vision applications, moving beyond static appearance capture. name: Color and Appearance Modeling
head: Appearance Modeling, View-Dependent Color Modeling
body: Color and Appearance Modeling extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation by replacing or augmenting the fixed Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients with more flexible mechanisms to represent view-dependent color, lighting, and material properties. It solves the limitations of base 3DGS, which struggles with complex specularities, dynamic lighting variations, and transient objects in unstructured datasets. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Physics and Optical Modeling by focusing on the radiance and material representation rather than volumetric light transport equations. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. DAVIGS is a plug-and-post appearance modeling method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that mitigates floaters and color distortions caused by appearance variations (e.g., daylight changes, ISP processing, local lighting) by transforming rendered images at the image level using 3D consistent features. Unlike coupled methods that manipulate Gaussian properties and slow rendering, or decoupled methods that only handle mild global variations, DAVIGS decouples global view-dependent appearance from local spatial changes, ensuring 3D consistency while maintaining real-time rendering speeds by discarding the appearance module after optimization. See DAVIGS. Compact View-dependent Color replaces the per-Gaussian Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients with a shared grid-based neural field to represent view-dependent color, significantly reducing the parameter count from 48 coefficients per Gaussian to a compact neural representation. Unlike sibling methods that use post-processing transformations DAVIGS, factorized illumination 3iGS, or image-conditioned modulation SWAG, this method substitutes the directional encoding entirely with a spatial-hash-based MLP, addressing the disk space explosion caused by high-order SH storage. See Compact View-dependent Color. 3iGS enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by modeling outgoing radiance as a function of a continuous local illumination field and individual Gaussian BRDF attributes, rather than optimizing outgoing radiance in isolation. It solves the problem of inaccurate specular view-dependent effects in reflective scenes by separating scene lighting from material properties, enabling physically plausible shading while maintaining the rapid rendering speeds of rasterization. Unlike vanilla 3DGS, which uses spherical harmonics for view-dependent color without physical interpretability, 3iGS explicitly models diffuse color and specular highlights via a neural renderer and a factorized tensor illumination grid. See 3iGS (Factorised Tensorial Illumination for 3D Gaussian Splatting). Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization refers to the family of methods that determine, compress, or regularize the view-dependent color coefficients \mathbf{c}i(\omega) stored per 3D Gaussian primitive in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem of efficiently representing complex lighting and specular effects while managing memory bandwidth, training stability, and computational cost. It differs from its siblings by focusing specifically on the SH coefficient representation itself (storage, degree, or estimation) rather than the camera pose optimization [10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md] or the multi-view training loop structure [13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. See Spherical Harmonics Optimization. SWAG is an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to handle unstructured, in-the-wild image collections by modeling appearance variations and handling transient objects (occluders) without supervision. It sets itself apart from base 3DGS and siblings like DAVIGS and 3iGS by using a per-image embedding vector and an MLP to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling the disentangling of static scene geometry from dynamic occluders and lighting conditions. See SWAG (Splatting in the Wild images with Appearance-conditioned Gaussians). Definition: Uses multi-resolution hash grids with MLP headers to model PBR attributes (albedo, roughness, metallic) as continuous fields, avoiding learnable parameters for varying numbers of Gaussian points. Layout: Ed HashEnc: 16 levels, 2^{19} max entries per level, 2 feature dimensions per entry, coarsest resolution 32, finest resolution 4096. Ed MLP: 32x32x32x6 layers, Kaiming-uniform init, Sigmoid activation. Es MLP: 32x32x3 layers, Kaiming-uniform init, None activation. Code: diffAlbedo = Ed(centerPos), (roughness, metalness) = Es(centerPos). Originating from the limitations of base 3DGS in handling complex lighting and dynamic scenes, these methods evolved to incorporate neural fields, factorized illumination, and image-conditioned modulation. They are primarily used in novel view synthesis, inverse rendering, and augmented reality applications where high-fidelity appearance and physical plausibility are required.
