name: Spherical Harmonics Optimization
head: SH Optimization, SH Coefficient Optimization, View-Dependent Color Optimization
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization refers to the family of methods that determine, compress, or regularize the view-dependent color coefficients \mathbf{c}i(\omega) stored per 3D Gaussian primitive in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem of efficiently representing complex lighting and specular effects while managing memory bandwidth, training stability, and computational cost. It differs from its siblings by focusing specifically on the SH coefficient representation itself (storage, degree, or estimation) rather than the camera pose optimization [10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md] or the multi-view training loop structure [13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation reduces the spherical harmonics (SH) degree of 3D Gaussian elements from third-order to first-order to decrease parameter count and computation cost, enabling real-time rendering on mobile devices. It differs from standard SH degree reduction by employing a distillation strategy where a student model with first-order SH approximates the directional radiance of a pretrained third-order teacher model, rather than simply truncating coefficients. This approach minimizes the quality loss associated with aggressive compression, achieving a 61% reduction in parameters and 52% reduction in computation with only a 0.48 dB PSNR drop. See First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation. This method derives analytical Jacobians of the SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to enable efficient gradient-based camera tracking. It solves the problem of high computational overhead and redundant parameterization inherent in automatic differentiation when optimizing camera poses in SLAM systems. Unlike prior ray-intersection methods that assume fewer Gaussians, this approach provides the first analytical Jacobians for EWA splatting and 3DGS, ensuring the Jacobian dimensionality matches the six degrees of freedom of the Lie algebra. See Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation. This method enables stable optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by training on multiple images per iteration, addressing the high variance of gradients inherent in the standard single-view approach. While standard 3DGS renders one image per iteration due to rasterization overhead, this method uses thread-efficient partial rendering to gather pixels from multiple views without idle thread waste, reducing mini-batch gradient variance and improving convergence stability compared to Spherical Harmonics Optimization and First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation. See Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization (SH VQ) is a compression technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces per-splat SH coefficients with indices pointing to a shared palette of distinct SH vectors, reducing memory footprint at the cost of minor lighting artifacts. It differs from First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation by retaining full SH basis functions (rather than reducing to first-order) and from Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation by focusing on storage compression rather than gradient computation. It is chosen when memory bandwidth or storage size is the primary bottleneck and view-dependent specular effects must be preserved better than simple color quantization allows. See Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization. This method estimates spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for mesh vertices by solving a global weighted least-squares problem that jointly fits RGB observations from all calibrated views. It distinguishes itself from iterative optimization approaches by providing an analytical closed-form solution, utilizing adaptive regularization to constrain SH bands based on the directional support available at each vertex. See Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation. Adaptive SH Regularization is a technique for stabilizing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficient estimation in sparse or unevenly observed scenes by suppressing higher-order SH components that lack sufficient directional support. It prevents overfitting to input views and improves generalization to unseen viewpoints, distinguishing itself from methods that rely on iterative optimization or fixed SH complexity. See Adaptive SH Regularization. Definition: Setting the maximum degree of Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients to 0 to remove superfluous operations and improve training speed, as higher-degree SH coefficients for color remain unchanged during training. Step: Modify the model code to delete operations relative to the max degree in the model and set the max degree parameter to 0. Pitfall: In the original 3D Gaussian Splatting model, features represented by SH coefficients with degree > 0 are unchanged during all training, making them useless. Number: Directly changing the max degree to 0 yields a 16.25% improvement compared to the default. With specific changing code, it yields a 16.57% improvement but increases CPU-GPU process time. The use of Spherical Harmonics for view-dependent appearance in 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the original 3DGS paper [12] (cited in). Subsequent work has focused on optimizing the efficiency and stability of these coefficients, including distillation for mobile deployment, vector quantization for memory reduction, and regularization for sparse view scenarios. I3DGS: Improve 3D Gaussian Splatting from Multiple Dimensions, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06408v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation
head: Mobile-GS SH Distillation, SH Knowledge Distillation, SH Order Reduction via Distillation, SH degree reduction, Spherical Harmonics degree reduction
body: First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation reduces the spherical harmonics (SH) degree of 3D Gaussian elements from third-order to first-order to decrease parameter count and computation cost, enabling real-time rendering on mobile devices. It differs from standard SH degree reduction by employing a distillation strategy where a student model with first-order SH approximates the directional radiance of a pretrained third-order teacher model, rather than simply truncating coefficients. This approach minimizes the quality loss associated with aggressive compression, achieving a 61% reduction in parameters and 52% reduction in computation with only a 0.48 dB PSNR drop. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pretrained teacher 3D Gaussian Splatting model using third-order SH (16 coefficients per color channel, 3 \times 16 total) and a set of training images with corresponding camera poses. Output: A student 3D Gaussian Splatting model using first-order SH (4 coefficients per color channel, 3 \times 4 total) with optimized parameters. Data Structures: The student model maintains the standard 3DGS Gaussian attributes: \boldsymbol{\mu}: 3D mean position (float32, 3 values). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}: Covariance matrix (float32, 6 values due to symmetry). \alpha: Opacity (float32, 1 value). \mathbf{c}: SH coefficients for first-order (float32, 12 values: 4 per RGB channel). \mathbf{s}: Scale (float32, 3 values). Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the student model with the same Gaussian primitives (means, covariances, scales, opacities) as the teacher model. Initialize the student's first-order SH coefficients \mathbf{c} to approximate the teacher's third-order SH coefficients \mathbf{c}^{tea} via a linear projection or random initialization. 2. Rendering: Render the scene using the student model to obtain pixel colors \mathbf{C}p and depths \hat{\mathbf{D}}p for each pixel p in the training set P. The rendering follows the standard 3DGS equation [Parent]. 3. Teacher Rendering: Render the scene using the frozen teacher model to obtain teacher pixel colors \mathbf{C}p^{tea} and depths \hat{\mathbf{D}}p^{tea}. 4. Distillation Loss Calculation: Compute the distillation loss \mathcal{L}{\text{dstill}} and scale-invariant depth distillation loss \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}. 5. Optimization: Update the student model parameters (primarily \mathbf{c}, and potentially \alpha and \boldsymbol{\mu} if joint optimization is used) by minimizing the combined loss. Formulas: The color distillation loss is calculated as: \mathcal{L}{\text{dstill}} = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{p \in P} \|\mathbf{C}p^{tea} - \mathbf{C}p\| where P is the set of pixels, \mathbf{C}p^{tea} is the rendered pixel color from the teacher, and \mathbf{C}p is the rendered pixel color from the student. The scale-invariant depth distillation loss is: \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}(\mathbf{D}, \mathbf{D}^{tea}) = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{p \in P} \left( \log(\hat{\mathbf{D}}p) - \log(\hat{\mathbf{D}}p^{tea}) \right)^2 - \frac{1}{|P|^2} \left( \sum{p \in P} \left( \log(\hat{\mathbf{D}}p) - \log(\hat{\mathbf{D}}p^{tea}) \right) \right)^2 where \hat{\mathbf{D}}p^{tea} = \mathbf{D}^{tea} + \epsilon and \epsilon = 1e-8 is added for training stability. Parameters: Target SH degree: 1. Epsilon \epsilon: 1e-8. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def firstordershdistillation(teachermodel, studentmodel, trainingdata, numiterations): """ Distill third-order SH from teacher to first-order SH in student. """ # Initialize student SH coefficients to first-order approximation of teacher # This can be done by projecting teacher's 16 coefficients to 4 coefficients # or initializing with zeros and letting optimization handle it. # For implementation, we assume studentmodel.shcoeffs is initialized. optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(studentmodel.parameters(), lr=1e-3) for iteration in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Get a batch of training images and camera poses images, cameras = trainingdata.getbatch() # Render student scene studentoutputs = studentmodel.render(cameras) studentcolors = studentoutputs['colors'] # Shape: (H, W, 3) studentdepths = studentoutputs['depths'] # Shape: (H, W, 1) # Render teacher scene (frozen) with torch.nograd(): teacheroutputs = teachermodel.render(cameras) teachercolors = teacheroutputs['colors'] teacherdepths = teacheroutputs['depths'] # Calculate Color Distillation Loss # Ldstill = mean(||Ctea - Cstu||) colorloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(teachercolors - studentcolors)) # Calculate Depth Distillation Loss # Ldepth = scale-invariant log loss epsilon = 1e-8 teacherdepthssafe = teacherdepths + epsilon studentdepthssafe = studentdepths + epsilon logdiff = torch.log(studentdepthssafe) - torch.log(teacherdepthssafe) # Mean of log differences meanlogdiff = torch.mean(logdiff) # Variance-like term: mean of squared diff - squared mean diff depthloss = torch.mean(logdiff 2) - (meanlogdiff 2) # Total Loss totalloss = colorloss + depthloss # Backpropagate totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return studentmodel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Reliability: The teacher's depth may not always be reliable, so strict L1/L2 depth losses are avoided in favor of scale-invariant loss. Initialization: Poor initialization of first-order SH coefficients may lead to slow convergence or suboptimal local minima. Projecting teacher coefficients to first-order is a common initialization strategy. Precision: The epsilon value (1e-8) is critical for numerical stability in the log-depth loss. Reduces SH degree from 3 to 2, 2 to 1, or 3 to 1 without distillation. Less effective than distillation for maintaining quality at low degrees. Further compresses the distilled SH features using neural vector quantization, reducing storage further. Removes Gaussian points based on their contribution to the image, often used in conjunction with SH distillation for higher compression. Time Complexity: Rendering is faster due to fewer SH coefficients (4 vs 16 per channel). The distillation training time is comparable to standard 3DGS training but requires rendering from the teacher model at each step, increasing training time. Memory Complexity: Reduces SH storage by 61% (from 16 to 4 coefficients per channel). Performance: On Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending datasets, SH distillation from degree 3 to 1 results in a 0.48 dB PSNR drop compared to the original 3DGS. Strengths: Significant reduction in model size and rendering time, suitable for mobile devices. Limitations: Quality loss compared to full third-order SH. First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation was introduced in Mobile-GS (2026) as part of a suite of techniques to enable real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting on mobile devices. It builds on the observation that third-order SH introduces a significant storage burden. The method is related to LightGaussian, which uses distillation to project third-order SH to second-order. name: Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation
head: Analytical Jacobians for 3DGS, Camera Pose Jacobian Derivation (Lie Group), Lie Algebra Jacobian for 3DGS
body: This method derives analytical Jacobians of the SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to enable efficient gradient-based camera tracking. It solves the problem of high computational overhead and redundant parameterization inherent in automatic differentiation when optimizing camera poses in SLAM systems. Unlike prior ray-intersection methods that assume fewer Gaussians, this approach provides the first analytical Jacobians for EWA splatting and 3DGS, ensuring the Jacobian dimensionality matches the six degrees of freedom of the Lie algebra. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera pose T{CW} \in SE(3), 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \muW, covariance \SigmaW, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}). Output: Jacobians \frac{\partial \muI}{\partial T{CW}} and \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial T{CW}} required for gradient descent optimization of the camera pose. Data Structures: T{CW}: 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix representing the camera-to-world pose. \muC: 3 \times 1 vector representing the Gaussian mean in camera coordinates. W: 3 \times 3 rotation matrix component of T{CW}. \tau: 6 \times 1 vector in Lie algebra se(3), composed of rotation vector \theta and translation vector \rho. \times: Skew-symmetric matrix operator mapping a 3D vector to a 3 \times 3 matrix. Mathematical Definitions: The derivative on the manifold is defined using the Lie algebra exponential and logarithmic maps: \frac{\mathcal{D}(f(\mathbf{T}))}{\mathcal{D}\mathbf{T}} \triangleq \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{\text{Log}(f(\text{Exp}(\tau) \circ \mathbf{T}) \circ f(\mathbf{T})^{-1})}{\tau} where \mathbf{T} \in SE(3), \tau \in se(3), and \circ is group composition. The chain rule decomposes the Jacobians for the projected mean \muI and covariance \SigmaI: \frac{\partial \muI}{\partial T{CW}} = \frac{\partial \muI}{\partial \muC} \frac{\mathcal{D}\muC}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial T{CW}} = \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial J} \frac{\partial J}{\partial \muC} \frac{D\muC}{DT{CW}} + \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial W} \frac{DW}{DT{CW}} where J is the Jacobian of the perspective projection. Step-by-Step Derivation: 1. Derive \frac{\mathcal{D}\muC}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}}: The Gaussian mean in camera coordinates is \muC = R{CW} \muW + t{CW}. Let \mathbf{T} = T{CW} and perturb it by \text{Exp}(\tau) where \tau = [\theta, \rho]^T. \frac{\mathcal{D}\muC}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} = \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{\text{Exp}(\tau) \cdot \muC - \muC}{\tau} Using the approximation \text{Exp}(\tau) \approx I + \tau^\wedge: = \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{(I + \tau^\wedge) \muC - \muC}{\tau} = \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{\tau^\wedge \muC}{\tau} Expanding \tau^\wedge \muC = \theta^\times \muC + \rho = -\muC^\times \theta + \rho: = \begin{bmatrix} I & -\muC^\times \end{bmatrix} where I is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix and \muC^\times is the skew-symmetric matrix of \muC. 2. Derive \frac{DW}{DT{CW}}: Let W be the rotation component of T{CW}. Perturb the rotation part of the Lie algebra by \theta. \frac{DW}{DT{CW}} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial W}{\partial \thetax} & \frac{\partial W}{\partial \thetay} & \frac{\partial W}{\partial \thetaz} & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} The derivative of the rotation matrix W with respect to the rotation vector components is derived from \frac{\partial W}{\partial \thetai} = ei^\times W, where ei are basis vectors. \frac{\partial W}{\partial \thetax} = e1^\times W = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} W = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -W{3,1} & -W{3,2} & -W{3,3} \\ W{2,1} & W{2,2} & W{2,3} \end{bmatrix} Generalizing for all columns W{:,i}: \frac{DW}{DT{CW}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -W{,1}^\times \\ 0 & -W{,2}^\times \\ 0 & -W{,3}^\times \end{bmatrix} where W{:,i} is the i-th column of W and the block structure reflects the 3 \times 6 output dimension relative to the 6 DOF input. 3. Compute Final Jacobians: Substitute the manifold derivatives into the chain rule equations. The term \frac{\partial \muI}{\partial \muC} and \frac{\partial J}{\partial \muC} are standard differentiable projection operations. The term \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial W} accounts for the rotation of the 3D covariance into the camera frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def skewsymmetric(v): """Converts a 3D vector to a 3x3 skew-symmetric matrix.""" return np.array([ [0, -v[2], v[1]], [v[2], 0, -v[0]], [-v[1], v[0], 0] ]) def computecamerajacobians(muC, W): """ Computes the analytical Jacobians of camera pose TCW (SE(3)) with respect to the Gaussian mean in camera coordinates muC and the rotation component W. Args: muC: numpy array, shape (3,), Gaussian mean in camera coordinates. W: numpy array, shape (3,3), Rotation matrix component of TCW. Returns: dmuCdT: numpy array, shape (3, 6), Jacobian of muC w.r.t TCW. dWdT: numpy array, shape (3, 6), Jacobian of W w.r.t TCW. """ # 1. Jacobian of muC w.r.t TCW # Formula: [I, -muC^x] I3 = np.eye(3) muCskew = skewsymmetric(muC) dmuCdT = np.hstack([I3, -muCskew]) # 2. Jacobian of W w.r.t TCW # Formula: Block matrix involving skew-symmetric of columns of W # dW/dT = [0, -W{:,1}^x; 0, -W{:,2}^x; 0, -W{:,3}^x] # This results in a 3x6 matrix. # The first 3 columns (translation part) are zero. # The last 3 columns (rotation part) are derived from columns of W. Wcol1 = W[:, 0] Wcol2 = W[:, 1] Wcol3 = W[:, 2] # Skew symmetric matrices of the columns Wcol1skew = skewsymmetric(Wcol1) Wcol2skew = skewsymmetric(Wcol2) Wcol3skew = skewsymmetric(Wcol3) # Construct the 3x6 matrix # Rows correspond to the 3 rows of W, columns correspond to 6 DOF of TCW # The structure in the source is: # [ 0 -W{:,1}^x ] # [ 0 -W{:,2}^x ] # [ 0 -W{:,3}^x ] # Note: The source notation implies a block arrangement where each row block # corresponds to a row of the derivative matrix. Let's reconstruct carefully. # The derivative dW/dT is 3x6. # Row 0 of dW/dT: [0, 0, 0, -W{0,1}^x, -W{0,2}^x, -W{0,3}^x]? # No, the source shows: # [ 0 -W{,1}^x ] # [ 0 -W{,2}^x ] # [ 0 -W{,3}^x ] # This notation usually means: # The top-left 3x3 block is 0. # The top-right 3x3 block is composed of skew-symmetric matrices of W's columns? # Let's look at Eq 6: # dW/dTCW = [ 0 -W{,1}^x; 0 -W{,2}^x; 0 -W{,3}^x ] # This is a 3x6 matrix. # Column 0-2 are 0. # Column 3 is -W{:,1}^x? No, W{,1}^x is a 3x3 matrix. # The source likely means: # The derivative is a 3x6 matrix. # The rotation part (cols 3-5) is constructed such that: # dW/dtheta = [e1^x W, e2^x W, e3^x W] # e1^x W = [0,0,0; 0,0,-1; 0,1,0] W = [0,0,0; -W31,-W32,-W33; W21,W22,W23] # This is a 3x3 matrix. # So dW/dT is 3x6. # Cols 0-2 are 0. # Cols 3-5 are the columns of the matrix [e1^x W, e2^x W, e3^x W]? # No, [e1^x W, e2^x W, e3^x W] is 3x9. # The derivative dW/dtheta is a 3x3 matrix for each thetai? # dW/dthetax is 3x3. # So dW/dT is 3x6. # The j-th column of dW/dT corresponds to the derivative w.r.t the j-th element of tau. # tau = [thetax, thetay, thetaz, rhox, rhoy, rhoz] # dW/drho = 0 (3x3 zero matrix? No, W doesn't depend on translation). # So cols 3-5 (translation) are 0. # Cols 0-2 (rotation) are dW/dtheta. # dW/dtheta is a 3x3 matrix? No, W is 3x3. dW/dtheta is a tensor 3x3x3. # Vectorized: dW/dtheta is 3x9? # The source Eq 6 shows a 3x6 matrix. # Let's re-read Eq 6 carefully. # dW/dTCW = [ 0 -W{,1}^x; 0 -W{,2}^x; 0 -W{,3}^x ] # This notation is ambiguous. Let's look at the derivation of dW/dthetax. # dW/dthetax = e1^x W. This is a 3x3 matrix. # If we vectorize W into a 9-vector, the Jacobian is 9x6. # But the source presents a 3x6 matrix. # This implies the derivative is taken with respect to the rows or columns? # Actually, looking at Eq 31: dW/dthetax = [0; -W3,:; W2,:]. This is 3x3. # The source likely flattens W or applies the Jacobian to a specific vector. # However, for the purpose of implementing the gradient update, we need the full Jacobian. # Given the constraint "no figures", we must rely on the explicit matrix form in Eq 6. # If Eq 6 is 3x6, it might be representing the derivative of a specific component or a simplified view. # But Eq 31 shows a 3x3 matrix. # Let's assume the standard vectorization: Wvec = vec(W). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of Lie algebra ensures minimal parameterization, avoiding redundant computations and singularities associated with Euler angles. Boundaries: The method assumes the Gaussian is visible and differentiable. Occlusions or depth discontinuities may require robust loss functions (e.g., penalizing low-opacity pixels). This variant optimizes only the current camera pose without updating the map representation. It minimizes photometric residuals E{pho} = \| I(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{T}{CW}) - \bar{I} \|1 and/or geometric residuals E{geo} = \| D(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{T}{CW}) - \bar{D} \|1, where I is the rendered image and D is the depth rasterization. It optimizes affine brightness parameters for exposure variation and penalizes non-edge or low-opacity pixels. The depth rasterization is computed via alpha-blending: \mathcal{D}p = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} zi \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), where zi is the distance to the Gaussian mean along the camera ray. This approach is chosen for real-time SLAM tracking where map updates are decoupled from pose estimation. Time Complexity: The analytical derivation eliminates the overhead of automatic differentiation, making view synthesis and gradient computation computationally efficient. This is crucial for SLAM systems requiring at least 50 iterations per frame. Memory Complexity: Minimal parameterization using Lie algebra reduces memory overhead compared to redundant representations. Performance: The system operates at 3.2 FPS with monocular input and 2.5 FPS with depth on the Replica dataset. Strengths: Enables accurate tracking in SLAM systems using 3DGS as the sole representation. Unifies tracking, mapping, and novel view synthesis. Limitations: Requires careful keyframe management to avoid infeasible joint optimization of all poses and Gaussians. Performance may degrade with large baselines if keyframes are not selected based on covisibility. This method originates from the Gaussian Splatting SLAM paper, which introduced the first analytical Jacobians of SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussians used in EWA splatting and 3DGS. Prior methods assumed fewer Gaussians and relied on ray-intersection, making them inapplicable to 3DGS. This derivation enables new applications of 3DGS beyond SLAM, such as dynamic tracking and 4D scene representation, by providing efficient gradient computation for camera pose optimization. name: Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Multi-View Mini-Batch Training for 3DGS, Thread-Efficient Partial Rendering for Multi-View 3DGS
body:
This method enables stable optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by training on multiple images per iteration, addressing the high variance of gradients inherent in the standard single-view approach. While standard 3DGS renders one image per iteration due to rasterization overhead, this method uses thread-efficient partial rendering to gather pixels from multiple views without idle thread waste, reducing mini-batch gradient variance and improving convergence stability. The method modifies the training loop to sample a mini-batch containing pixels from N different images, rather than a single image. This requires two key adaptations: a rendering strategy that avoids the overhead of full multi-view rasterization, and a densification strategy compatible with multi-view gradient accumulation. Inputs: A set of N training images with corresponding camera poses; the current 3D Gaussian parameters (means \mu, covariances \Sigma, opacities \alpha, colors c). Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters and rendered images for loss computation. The rasterizer uses a tile-based architecture. Tile: A subdivision of the image plane. Block: A group of threads allocated to a single tile. Thread: A processing unit within a block. Layout: A single block is allocated to a single tile. A thread is freed only when all peer threads in the same block have completed their work. The color \hat{C}(p) for a pixel p is computed via alpha-blending of M sorted 2D projected Gaussians \{Gj\}{j=1}^M: \hat{C}(p) = \sum{i=1}^{M} ci Ti oi Gi(p) where: Ti = \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - ok Gk(p)) is the transmittance. Gi(p) = \exp(- rac{1}{2}(p - \mu'i)^T (\Sigma'i)^{-1} (p - \mu'i)) is the 2D projected Gaussian density. \mu' and \Sigma' are the projected 2D mean and covariance derived from the 3D mean \mu, scale S, rotation R, color c, and opacity o. The effectiveness of multi-view training is justified by the variance of mini-batch gradients. The variance of vectors x is defined as: V(x):= E[\|x - \mu\|2^2] \quad 	ext{where} \quad E[x] = \mu The variance of the mini-batch gradient 
abla  ar{\phi}k is estimated using Monte Carlo sampling over K sampled mini-batches S: V{Bk \in S} (
abla  ar{\phi}k) = E[\|
abla  ar{\phi}k - P(wt)\|2^2] where P(wt) is the true gradient at weights wt. Experiments show multi-view mini-batches yield smaller variance than single-view, leading to more stable optimization. 1. Mini-batch Sampling: Randomly sample a set of pixels from N different training images to form a mini-batch Bk. Unlike NeRF, which randomly samples data from the entire training dataset to form a mini-batch, standard 3DGS typically uses a single-view image per iteration due to rasterization constraints. 2. Thread-Efficient Partial Rendering: Instead of rendering all pixels of all N images (which causes idle threads in naive implementations), the rasterizer processes only the required pixels for the sampled mini-batch. The rasterizer splits the image into tiles. A single block is allocated to a single tile. Threads cooperate to preprocess Gaussians and render pixels in their assigned tiles. Crucially, the implementation ensures that threads are not freed until all peer threads in the same block complete, preventing the idle thread overhead seen in naive multi-view attempts. 3. Forward Pass: Compute \hat{C}(p) for all sampled pixels p \in Bk using the rendering equation. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss \phii(w) = L(w, ri, ci) for each pixel, where L penalizes deviation from the label. The total loss for the mini-batch is:  ar{\phi}k(w) =  rac{1}{|Bk|} \sum{i \in Bk} \phii(w) 5. Backward Pass: Compute gradients 
abla  ar{\phi}k(wt) with respect to the Gaussian parameters. 6. Weight Update: Update weights using the learning rate \etat: w{t+1} = wt - \etat 
abla  ar{\phi}k (wt) 7. Adaptive Density Control (ADC) Adaptation: Standard ADC assumes single-view training, where all 2D positional gradients reside within a single plane. Multi-view training risks arithmetic between vectors in different image spaces. The method introduces a 3D-space D-SSIM loss to replace the standard 2D version, ensuring valid vector arithmetic across different view planes during densification. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def trainstep(gaussians, images, cameras, learningrate, numviews): # 1. Mini-batch Sampling: Randomly sample pixels from N different images batchpixels = [] batchgtcolors = [] batchcameras = [] for in range(numviews): idx = random.randint(0, len(images) - 1) img = images[idx] cam = cameras[idx] # Sample a subset of pixels from the image pixels, gtcolors = samplepixels(img) batchpixels.append(pixels) batchgtcolors.append(gtcolors) batchcameras.append(cam) # 2. Thread-Efficient Partial Rendering renderedcolors = [] for pixels, camera in zip(batchpixels, batchcameras): # Preprocess Gaussians: project 3D Gaussians to 2D for this camera projectedgaussians = preprocessgaussians(gaussians, camera) # Render only the required pixels using tile-based rasterization colors = renderpartial(projectedgaussians, pixels) renderedcolors.append(colors) # 3. Loss Computation totalloss = 0.0 for rendered, gt in zip(renderedcolors, batchgtcolors): totalloss += meansquarederror(rendered, gt) avgloss = totalloss / len(batchpixels) # 4. Backward Pass gradients = computegradients(avgloss, gaussians) # 5. Update Parameters updatedgaussians = updateparameters(gaussians, gradients, learningrate) # 6. Adaptive Density Control (Modified for Multi-View) updatedgaussians = adaptivedensitycontrolmultiview(updatedgaussians, gradients, batchcameras) return updatedgaussians def samplepixels(image): # Returns a subset of pixel coordinates and their ground truth colors H, W = image.shape[:2] indices = random.sample(range(H W), min(H W, H W // 2)) pixels = [(idx // W, idx % W) for idx in indices] gtcolors = [image[y][x] for x, y in pixels] return pixels, gtcolors def preprocessgaussians(gaussians, camera): # Projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space projected = [] for g in gaussians: mu2d = camera.project2d(g.mean) Sigma2d = camera.projectcovariance(g.covariance) projected.append({'mean': mu2d, 'cov': Sigma2d, 'color': g.color, 'opacity': g.opacity}) return projected def renderpartial(projectedgaussians, pixels): # Alpha-blends projected Gaussians for each pixel rendered = [] for p in pixels: x, y = p transmittance = 1.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Sort Gaussians by depth for correct alpha blending sortedgaussians = sorted(projectedgaussians, key=lambda g: g['depth']) for g in sortedgaussians: dist = (x - g['mean'][0])2 + (y - g['mean'][1])2 invcov = inversematrix(g['cov']) density = math.exp(-0.5 dist @ invcov) alpha = g['opacity'] density color = [color[c] + g['color'][c] alpha transmittance for c in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break rendered.append(color) return rendered def computegradients(loss, parameters): # Standard automatic differentiation return torch.autograd.grad(loss, parameters, retaingraph=True) def updateparameters(parameters, gradients, learningrate): return [p - learningrate g for p, g in zip(parameters, gradients)] def adaptivedensitycontrolmultiview(gaussians, gradients, cameras): # Uses 3D-space metrics to avoid cross-plane vector arithmetic for g, grad in zip(gaussians, gradients): gradnorm = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in grad)) if gradnorm > 0.01: densify(g) return gaussians def densify(gaussian): # Standard 3DGS densification: clone and split based on gradient magnitude pass def meansquarederror(rendered, gt): return sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, gt)) / len(rendered) def inversematrix(matrix): # Standard 2x2 matrix inverse a, b = matrix[0][0], matrix[0][1] c, d = matrix[1][0], matrix[1][1] det = a d - b c return [[d/det, -b/det], [-c/det, a/det]] Learning Rate (\etat): Used in weight update w{t+1} = wt - \etat 
abla  ar{\phi}k (wt). Number of Sampled Mini-batches (K): Used for Monte Carlo variance estimation. Number of Views (N): The number of images included in a single mini-batch. Idle Threads: Naive multi-view training causes significant overhead because the tile-based rasterizer allocates a single block to a single tile. Rendering multiple images creates idle threads when peer threads in the same block complete work. ADC Incompatibility: Standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) assumes single-view training, assuming all 2D positional gradients reside within a single plane. Multi-view training risks performing arithmetic between vectors in different spaces (different image planes), resulting in a suboptimal densification process. Gradient Variance: Single-view training has higher gradient variance, leading to less stable optimization compared to multi-view. Time Complexity: Higher per-iteration cost than single-view due to rendering multiple images, but mitigated by thread-efficient partial rendering which avoids idle threads. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for storing gradients and parameters for multiple views simultaneously. Performance: Multi-view mini-batch training results in smaller variance of mini-batch gradients than single-view, leading to more stable and effective optimization. Strengths: More stable optimization; reduced gradient variance. Limitations: Requires modified densification logic to handle multi-view gradient arithmetic; higher computational overhead per iteration if not implemented with thread-efficient partial rendering. When to use: When training stability is prioritized over per-iteration speed, and when the hardware supports efficient multi-threaded tile-based rasterization. When not to use: When strict single-view ADC compatibility is required without modification, or when hardware lacks efficient multi-threading support. Origin: Proposed by Minhyuk Choi, Injae Kim, and Hyunwoo J. Kim from Korea University and KAIST. History: Standard 3DGS uses single-view mini-batch training because its rasterization pipeline makes gathering individual pixels from multiple images difficult. NeRF, in contrast, uses multi-view mini-batches. This method bridges the gap by adapting 3DGS to multi-view training efficiently. Usage: Used in inverse rendering tasks where stable optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting is required. Efficient multi-view training for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2506.12727, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization
head: SH clustering, SH palette
body: Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization (SH VQ) is a compression technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces per-splat SH coefficients with indices pointing to a shared palette of distinct SH vectors, reducing memory footprint at the cost of minor lighting artifacts. It differs from First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation by retaining full SH basis functions (rather than reducing to first-order) and from Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation by focusing on storage compression rather than gradient computation. It is chosen when memory bandwidth or storage size is the primary bottleneck and view-dependent specular effects must be preserved better than simple color quantization allows. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N Gaussian splats, each with a view-dependent color defined by SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^{45} (excluding the zeroth-order term, which is treated as base color). Output: A palette \mathcal{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 45} of K distinct SH vectors, and an index array \mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{Z}^{N} where \mathbf{I}[i] is the index into \mathcal{P} for splat i. Data Structures: 1. Palette (\mathcal{P}): A list of K vectors. Each vector contains 45 floating-point numbers (15 per RGB channel). Stored as FP16. 2. Indices (\mathbf{I}): An array of N integers. Each integer is 16 bits wide, capable of addressing up to 65,536 palette entries. Parameters: K (Palette Size): Typically 4,000 to 16,000 items. N (Number of Splats): Scene-dependent (e.g., 6.1 million for the 'bike' scene). Dimensionality D: 45 (excluding the 0th-order SH coefficient). Steps: 1. Extract SH Data: Collect the 45-dimensional SH coefficient vector for every splat in the scene, excluding the 0th-order coefficient. 2. Cluster: Perform vector quantization (clustering) on the N data points in \mathbb{R}^{45} to find K cluster centers. This forms the palette \mathcal{P}. Note: Standard k-means is too slow for millions of splats in 45 dimensions. A mini-batch k-means variant is used. 3. Assign Indices: For each splat i, find the palette index k such that the Euclidean distance between the splat's SH vector \mathbf{c}i and the palette entry \mathcal{P}[k] is minimized: \mathbf{I}[i] = \arg \min{k \in \{0, \dots, K-1\}} \| \mathbf{c}i - \mathcal{P}[k] \|2^2 4. Store: Save \mathcal{P} and \mathbf{I}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sphericalharmonicsvectorquantization(shdata: np.ndarray, k: int) -> tuple: """ Compress SH coefficients using vector quantization. Args: shdata: Array of shape (N, 45) containing SH coefficients for N splats. Excludes the 0th-order coefficient. k: Number of palette entries (cluster centers). Returns: palette: Array of shape (k, 45) containing the cluster centers. indices: Array of shape (N,) containing the index of the closest palette entry for each splat. """ nsplats = shdata.shape[0] # Step 1: Initialize centroids randomly from the data # Standard k-means initialization; random subset of data points rng = np.random.defaultrng() initialindices = rng.choice(nsplats, k, replace=False) centroids = shdata[initialindices].copy() # Step 2: Mini-batch K-Means Clustering # Using a fixed number of iterations for determinism; # in practice, convergence criteria or max iterations are used. maxiterations = 100 batchsize = 256 for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Sample a mini-batch of indices batchindices = rng.choice(nsplats, batchsize, replace=False) batchdata = shdata[batchindices] # Assign each point in the batch to the nearest centroid # Calculate distances: (batchsize, k) # dist = ||x - c||^2 = ||x||^2 + ||c||^2 - 2 x.c # Efficient distance calculation without explicit loop sqnormsdata = np.sum(batchdata 2, axis=1, keepdims=True) sqnormscentroids = np.sum(centroids 2, axis=1, keepdims=True).T distances = sqnormsdata + sqnormscentroids - 2 np.dot(batchdata, centroids.T) assignments = np.argmin(distances, axis=1) # Update centroids based on the batch for j in range(k): mask = assignments == j if np.any(mask): batchpoints = batchdata[mask] centroids[j] = np.mean(batchpoints, axis=0) # Step 3: Final Assignment for all splats # Calculate distances for all splats to all centroids sqnormsall = np.sum(shdata 2, axis=1, keepdims=True) sqnormscentroidsfinal = np.sum(centroids 2, axis=1, keepdims=True).T finaldistances = sqnormsall + sqnormscentroidsfinal - 2 np.dot(shdata, centroids.T) indices = np.argmin(finaldistances, axis=1) # Convert to FP16 for storage as per source palettefp16 = centroids.astype(np.float16) return palettefp16, indices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Curse of Dimensionality: Clustering millions of splats in 45 dimensions is computationally expensive and slow. Lighting Artifacts: Quantization introduces minor lighting artifacts, particularly in specular highlights, though shininess effects are generally retained. Index Size: Indices are stored as 16 bits regardless of whether K < 65,536, wasting some bits if K is small. Memory Footprint: Palette: K \times 45 \times 2 bytes (FP16). For K=16,000, this is ~1.44 MB. Indices: N \times 2 bytes. For N=6.1 million, this is ~12 MB. Total SH storage: ~13.44 MB for the 'bike' scene with K=16,000. Compression Ratio: Achieves ~14.9x compression for the 'Low' preset (SH clustered into 16k) compared to uncompressed PLY, reducing total scene data from 1.4 GB to ~98-93 MB depending on other components. Quality: 'Low' preset (K=16,000): PSNR ~35.17-35.32. 'Very Low' preset (K=4,000): PSNR ~30.19-32.27. Retains "shininess" effects better than lower-dimensional approximations. Performance: Clustering time: Custom mini-batch k-means is ~3x faster than Faiss and significantly faster than scikit-learn. Rendering: No change in rendering complexity; index lookup is O(1) per splat. Strengths: Significant memory reduction; preserves view-dependent effects; simple to implement. Limitations: Introduces quantization artifacts; clustering is slow for very large scenes; requires pre-processing. Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization was introduced by Aras Pranckevičius in a blog post titled "Making Gaussian Splats more smaller". It was developed as part of a toy "Gaussian Splatting for Unity" implementation to enable efficient real-time rendering of large scenes on constrained hardware. The method draws inspiration from traditional computer graphics palette-based rendering and vector quantization techniques. Making Gaussian Splats more smaller, https://aras-p.info/blog/2023/09/27/Making-Gaussian-Splats-more-smaller/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation
head: Global LLS System, Normal System Solution
body: This method estimates spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for mesh vertices by solving a global weighted least-squares problem that jointly fits RGB observations from all calibrated views. It distinguishes itself from iterative optimization approaches by providing an analytical closed-form solution, utilizing adaptive regularization to constrain SH bands based on the directional support available at each vertex. Inputs: A mesh M with Nv vertices. K calibrated RGB images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K. SH degree L (typically up to order 2, i.e., s=0,1,2). Regularization strengths \gammas (supported) and \gammau (under-supported). Minimum confidence weight threshold \epsilonw. Outputs: Estimated SH coefficients X^ for each vertex. Data Structures: Rasterization Records (R): Stores per-pixel data including vertex indices i{s,k,r}, SH basis features \phi{s,k,r}, and confidence weights w{k,r}. Global Matrices: A \in \mathbb{R}^{(KHW) \times (qNv)}: The design matrix mapping vertex SH coefficients to pixel observations. B \in \mathbb{R}^{(KHW) \times 3}: The observation matrix containing pixel RGB values. W \in \mathbb{R}^{(KHW) \times (KHW)}: A diagonal matrix of confidence weights. \Lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{(qNv) \times (qNv)}: Block-diagonal regularization matrix. H \in \mathbb{R}^{(qNv) \times (qNv)}: The normal matrix (A^\top W A + \Lambda). G \in \mathbb{R}^{(qNv) \times 3}: The right-hand side (A^\top W B). View Counts (n^vi): Integer count of views contributing to vertex i. Parameters: \gammas: Supported SH regularization strength. Typical value: 0 < \gammas \ll \gammau. \gammau: Under-supported SH regularization strength. Typical value: \gammau \gg \gammas. \delta: PCG convergence tolerance. T{max}: Maximum PCG iterations. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Gradient-Guided Densification): For each triangle j and view k, identify pixels \Omega{k,j} covered by the triangle. Compute multiview image-space variation: Sj \triangleq \sum{k=1}^K \sum{p \in \Omega{k,j}} \|\nabla Ik(p)\|^2. Select triangles with large Sj for subdivision. Place new vertices at the mean of surface samples mapped from covered pixels using barycentric weights. Replace parent triangles with three child triangles. Re-rasterize after densification rounds. 2. Initialization: Initialize rasterization records R and view counts \{n^vi\}{i=1}^{Nv} to zero. 3. Per-View Rasterization and Matrix Assembly: For each view k = 1 \dots K: Rasterize mesh M to initialize per-view matrix Ak. For each valid pixel p{k,r}: Retrieve vertex indices i{s,k,r} and scaling factors \lambda{s,k,r} for SH orders s=0,1,2. Compute SH basis features: \phi{s,k,r} \leftarrow \lambda{s,k,r} Y(dk), where Y(dk) is the SH basis evaluated at view direction dk. Set row r of Ak at column i{s,k,r} to (\phi{s,k,r})^\top. Compute confidence weight w{k,r} using the method's specific weighting equation (Eq. 19 in source). Store \{i{s,k,r}, \phi{s,k,r}\}{s=0}^2 and w{k,r} in R. Construct observation vector Bk \leftarrow [Ik(p{k,1}) \dots Ik(p{k,HW})]^\top. Construct weight matrix Wk \leftarrow \text{diag}(w{k,1}, \dots, w{k,HW}). Update view counts \{n^vi\} based on rasterized pixels. 4. Global Matrix Assembly: Assemble global matrices: A \leftarrow [A1^\top \dots AK^\top]^\top. B \leftarrow [B1^\top \dots BK^\top]^\top. W \leftarrow \text{blkdiag}(W1, \dots, WK). 5. Regularization Construction: For each vertex i = 1 \dots Nv: Construct regularization block \Lambdai using n^vi, \gammas, and \gammau according to Eq. (26) in the source. Assign \gammas if the vertex has sufficient directional support, otherwise \gammau. Assemble global regularization matrix: \Lambda \leftarrow \text{blkdiag}(\Lambda1, \dots, \Lambda{Nv}). 6. Normal System Formation: Compute H \leftarrow A^\top W A + \Lambda. Compute G \leftarrow A^\top W B. Here, H \in \mathbb{R}^{qNv \times qNv} is the shared normal matrix for three color channels, and G \in \mathbb{R}^{qNv \times 3} contains weighted observation terms for R, G, B channels. 7. Solution: Solve for X^ using the Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG) method. Explicit inversion of H is avoided due to computational cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def closedformsceneappearanceestimation(mesh, images, gammas, gammau, delta, tmax): """ Estimates SH coefficients for mesh vertices via global LLS. """ Nv = mesh.numvertices K = len(images) # Step 1: Gradient-Guided Densification (Preprocessing) # Compute Sj for all triangles, subdivide high-variation triangles, re-rasterize # This modifies 'mesh' in place or returns a refined mesh refinedmesh = gradientguideddensification(mesh, images) # Step 2: Initialization rasterizationrecords = {} viewcounts = [0] Nv # Step 3 & 4: Per-View Rasterization and Global Assembly Alist = [] Blist = [] Wlist = [] for k in range(K): Ik = images[k] Ak = [] Bk = [] Wk = [] # Rasterize refinedmesh in view k # Get pixel-to-triangle/vertex correspondence pixels = rasterize(refinedmesh, view=k) for p in pixels: if not p.isvalid: continue # Retrieve SH features # is: vertex indices for SH orders s=0,1,2 # lambdas: scaling factors is, lambdas = getshfeatures(p, viewdirection=p.viewdir) # Compute phis = lambdas Y(dk) phis = [lambdas[s] sphericalharmonicbasis(p.viewdir, s) for s in range(3)] # Construct row for Ak # Ak maps vertex SH coeffs to pixel observation rowA = [] for s in range(3): vertexidx = is[s] # Append phis[s] to appropriate column block for this vertex # Assuming q coefficients per vertex (e.g., 9 for order 2) # This logic assumes a flattened structure where vertex i's coeffs are at offset iq rowA.append(phis[s]) # Simplified: actual implementation requires sparse row construction Ak.append(rowA) # Observation Bk.append(Ik[p.pixelcoords]) # Confidence weight wk,r (Eq 19 in source) w = computeconfidenceweight(p, Ik) Wk.append(w) # Update view counts for s in range(3): viewcounts[is[s]] += 1 # Store in records for PCG setup rasterizationrecords[p.id] = { 'vertexindices': is, 'phi': phis, 'weight': w } Alist.append(np.array(Ak)) Blist.append(np.array(Bk)) Wlist.append(np.diag(Wk)) # Assemble Global Matrices A = np.vstack(Alist) B = np.vstack(Blist) W = scipy.linalg.blockdiag(Wlist) # Step 5: Regularization Construction Lambdablocks = [] for i in range(Nv): nv = viewcounts[i] # Construct Lambdai based on nv, gammas, gammau (Eq 26 in source) Lambdai = constructregularizationblock(nv, gammas, gammau) Lambdablocks.append(Lambdai) Lambda = scipy.linalg.blockdiag(Lambdablocks) # Step 6: Normal System # H = A^T W A + Lambda # G = A^T W B # Note: For large scenes, explicit formation of H is avoided in PCG setup. # However, for clarity of the closed-form definition: H = A.T @ W @ A + Lambda G = A.T @ W @ B # Step 7: Solve using PCG Xstar = trianglepcgsolver(G, rasterizationrecords, Lambda, delta, tmax) return Xstar def trianglepcgsolver(G, records, Lambda, delta, tmax): """ Solves H X = G using matrix-free PCG with triangle structure. """ X = np.zeroslike(G) for channel in range(3): # R, G, B g = G[:, channel] r = g.copy() eta = np.dot(g, g) # Preconditioner solve Pz = r # P is typically diagonal or block-diagonal approximation of H # Here, we use the diagonal of Lambda or H as preconditioner z = preconditionersolve(r, Lambda) p = z.copy() sigma = np.dot(r, z) for t in range(tmax): # h = H p # Matrix-vector product using triangle structure h = trianglenormalproduct(p, records) alpha = sigma / np.dot(p, h) X[:, channel] += alpha p r -= alpha h if np.dot(r, r) <= delta delta eta: break z = preconditionersolve(r, Lambda) sigmanew = np.dot(r, z) beta = sigmanew / sigma p = z + beta p sigma = sigmanew return X def trianglenormalproduct(p, records): """ Computes H p without forming H explicitly. H = A^T W A + Lambda """ # This requires iterating through pixels and accumulating contributions # to the vertex blocks. result = np.zeroslike(p) # Add Lambda p # Lambda is block diagonal, so apply block-wise # Implementation detail: apply Lambda blocks to corresponding vertex segments of p # Add A^T W A p # 1. Compute v = A p v = np.zeros(len(records)) for pid, rec in records.items(): # p has shape (Nv, q) # rec['vertexindices'] gives indices # rec['phi'] gives features # This is complex sparse multiplication. # Simplified: v[r] = sums phis p[vertexidx] pass # 2. Compute w = W v w = np.zeroslike(v) for pid, rec in records.items(): w[pid] = rec['weight'] v[pid] # 3. Compute result += A^T w for pid, rec in records.items(): wval = w[pid] for s in range(3): idx = rec['vertexindices'][s] # Accumulate wval phis into result block for idx pass return result Complexity: The global LLS solve complexity is dominated by PCG iterations. Setup is O(KHWq^2 + Nv q^3). Each PCG iteration is O(KHWq + Nv q^2). Total solve time T{solve} = O(KHWq^2 + Nv q^3) + O(T{pcg}(KHWq + Nv q^2)) + O(KHWq + Nv q). Strengths: Provides an analytical solution, avoiding iterative gradient descent. Adaptive regularization ensures the normal matrix is strictly positive definite, guaranteeing a unique global minimizer. Limitations: Requires a mesh prior. Explicit formation of H^{-1} is avoided, but assembling A and B can be memory-intensive for high-resolution scenes. The method assumes calibrated views. This method originates from "CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors". It addresses the limitation of coarse triangles in mesh-based appearance representation by introducing gradient-guided densification and a global least-squares formulation with adaptive SH regularization. name: Adaptive SH Regularization
head: Directional support-aware SH regularization
body: Adaptive SH Regularization is a technique for stabilizing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficient estimation in sparse or unevenly observed scenes by suppressing higher-order SH components that lack sufficient directional support. It prevents overfitting to input views and improves generalization to unseen viewpoints, distinguishing itself from methods that rely on iterative optimization or fixed SH complexity. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N Gaussians, each with mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and initial SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i. A set of K observed camera views with poses \{\mathbf{P}k\}{k=1}^K. Output: Regularized SH coefficients \hat{\mathbf{c}}i for each Gaussian. Data Structures SH Coefficients: Stored as a vector of size (L+1)^2 for degree L. Directional Support Metric: A scalar value per Gaussian per SH band, derived from the viewing directions relative to the Gaussian's orientation. Steps 1. Evaluate Directional Support: For each Gaussian i and each SH band l, calculate a support metric based on the distribution of viewing directions from the K input cameras relative to the Gaussian's local frame. 2. Apply Support Criterion: Compare the support metric against a threshold (implicitly defined in the source's equation 25). If the support is insufficient (weakly supported), apply strong regularization to the non-DC components (l > 0) of that band. If the support is sufficient (well-supported), apply weak regularization or none, preserving the directional detail. 3. Preserve DC Component: The zeroth-order (DC, l=0) component is always preserved regardless of support, as it represents the average color. 4. Solve Regularized System: Incorporate the adaptive regularization weights into the linear least squares (LLS) system used to estimate or refine the SH coefficients. This improves the conditioning of the system, allowing faster convergence. Formulas Regularization Weight: The regularization strength \lambda{i,l} for Gaussian i and band l is determined by the support criterion. If support < \text{threshold}: \lambda{i,l} is large for l > 0. If support \ge \text{threshold}: \lambda{i,l} is small for l > 0. For l=0: \lambda{i,0} \approx 0. LLS System: The system solved is of the form (\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{\Lambda}) \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{b}, where \mathbf{\Lambda} is a diagonal matrix containing the adaptive regularization weights \lambda{i,l}. Parameters Support Threshold: Implicitly defined in equation (25) of the source. Not given in the sources. SH Degree (L): Typically 3 or higher, depending on scene complexity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Overfitting: Without regularization, unconstrained SH coefficients lacking sufficient directional constraints overfit input views and generalize poorly to unseen viewpoints, producing noisy colors. Convergence Failure: Unregularized systems may fail to converge within a reasonable iteration count (e.g., T{max}=300) due to poor conditioning. Degenerate Input: In scenes with very few views (K small), many Gaussians will have insufficient support, leading to heavy suppression of non-DC components and potentially oversmoothed appearance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveshregularization(gaussians, cameraposes, shdegree, supportthreshold): """ Applies adaptive SH regularization based on directional support. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: mean position cov: covariance matrix shcoeffs: array of shape (numbands,) viewdirs: list of viewing directions from input cameras cameraposes: List of camera pose matrices shdegree: Integer, degree of spherical harmonics supportthreshold: Float, threshold for directional support metric Returns: Regularized SH coefficients for each Gaussian """ numbands = (shdegree + 1) 2 regularizedcoeffs = [] for g in gaussians: coeffs = g.shcoeffs.copy() regularizationweights = np.zeros(numbands) # Calculate directional support for each band for l in range(shdegree + 1): # Determine number of bands for this degree numlbands = 2 l + 1 startidx = l l endidx = startidx + numlbands # Evaluate support metric for this band group # Note: Exact formula for support metric is implicit in source eq (25) # Assuming a metric based on the spread of viewing directions # relative to the Gaussian's orientation. supportmetric = evaluatedirectionalsupport(g, cameraposes, l) # Apply regularization based on support if supportmetric < supportthreshold: # Weakly supported: strong regularization for non-DC if l > 0: regularizationweights[startidx:endidx] = 1.0 # Strong weight else: # DC component preserved regularizationweights[startidx:endidx] = 0.0 else: # Well-supported: weak or no regularization regularizationweights[startidx:endidx] = 0.0 # Weak weight # Solve regularized LLS system # Assuming a function that solves (A^T A + Lambda) c = A^T b # where Lambda is diagonal with regularizationweights regularizedcoeffs.append(solveregularizedlls(g, regularizationweights)) return regularizedcoeffs def evaluatedirectionalsupport(gaussian, cameraposes, l): """ Evaluates the directional support for a specific SH degree l. Placeholder for the implicit support metric from source eq (25). Typically involves projecting camera directions onto the Gaussian's local coordinate system and measuring the angular coverage. """ # Simplified implementation: measure the variance of viewing directions # projected onto the Gaussian's principal axes. # This is a heuristic; the exact metric is not provided in the sources. viewdirs = getviewingdirections(gaussian, cameraposes) if len(viewdirs) == 0: return 0.0 # Project directions onto the Gaussian's local frame localdirs = projecttolocalframe(viewdirs, gaussian.cov) # Calculate support metric (e.g., angular spread) # Using standard deviation of angles as a proxy for support angles = np.arccos(np.clip(np.dot(localdirs, localdirs[0]), -1.0, 1.0)) support = np.std(angles) return support Uses only the first-order SH terms to reduce computational cost while maintaining basic view-dependent effects. Choose when real-time performance is critical and high-frequency view dependence is not required. [9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md] Provides analytical derivatives for the rendering process with respect to camera parameters, enabling more efficient optimization. Choose when optimizing camera poses jointly with scene parameters. [10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md] Optimizes training efficiency by leveraging multiple views simultaneously. Choose when training on large datasets with many input views. [13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md] Reduces memory usage by quantizing SH coefficients. Choose when memory is a constraint and slight quality loss is acceptable. [14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md] Estimates appearance using a closed-form solution, avoiding iterative optimization. Choose when fast, non-iterative appearance estimation is needed. [16750-closed-form-scene-appearance-estimation.md] Time Complexity: Solving the global LLS system scales with the number of observations, but remains more efficient than iterative optimization of large parameter sets. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory overhead compared to standard SH storage, as regularization weights are computed on-the-fly or stored per-band. Measured Performance: On the C3VD c t1 b scene with K=7 views and L=3, adaptive regularization improves test-view PSNR from 33.66 to 34.69. Convergence: With regularization, the PCG residual decreases rapidly; without it, the system fails to converge within T{max}=300 iterations. Strengths: Improves conditioning of the appearance estimation problem, reduces unstable view-dependent appearance, and yields more stable fidelity gains as the number of views increases. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the support threshold; may oversmooth appearance in regions with very sparse observations. When to Use: Sparse or unevenly observed scenes, scenes with limited input views, or when stable generalization to unseen viewpoints is critical. When Not to Use: Dense, uniformly observed scenes where standard SH optimization converges well and high-frequency detail is preserved. Adaptive SH Regularization was introduced in the context of CF-Splat (Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors). It addresses the challenge of overfitting in SH-based appearance modeling when directional support is insufficient. The method builds on the principle that SH coefficients should be constrained based on the available viewing directions, rather than being optimized unconstrained. name: SWAG (Splatting in the Wild images with Appearance-conditioned Gaussians)
body: SWAG is an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to handle unstructured, in-the-wild image collections by modeling appearance variations and handling transient objects (occluders) without supervision. It sets itself apart from base 3DGS and siblings like DAVIGS and 3iGS by using a per-image embedding vector and an MLP to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling the disentangling of static scene geometry from dynamic occluders and lighting conditions. SWAG operates on the standard 3DGS rendering equation but modifies the color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai terms to be image-dependent. Inputs: A set of unstructured images \{Ij\} with known camera poses; initial 3D Gaussian parameters derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (centroid, scale, rotation, base opacity, base color), a Hash Grid encoding, per-image embeddings, and an MLP. At inference, it renders novel views and can separate static/transient components. For each Gaussian i, the model optimizes the following parameters: 1. Centroid: \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 2. Scale: \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 3. Rotation: \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) 4. Base Opacity: \alphai \in \mathbb{R} 5. Base Color: \mathbf{c}i encoded as spherical harmonic coefficients. Additionally, the model optimizes: 1. Hash Grid Encoding: A hash table mapping 3D positions to feature vectors. Hash Table Size (T): 2^{19}. Coarsest Resolution (N{min}): 16. Finest Resolution (N{max}): 2048. Number of Levels (L): 12. Encoding: \text{emb}(\mathbf{x}i) is the output of the Hash Grid for center \mathbf{x}i. 2. Per-Image Embedding: A latent vector \mathbf{l}{Ij} \in \mathbb{R}^{24} for each training image j. 3. MLP (F\theta): A multi-layer perceptron with 8 layers, input dimension 3 (concatenated features), hidden layer size 51, and output dimension 64. 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using SfM points. Initialize Hash Grid, per-image embeddings \mathbf{l}{Ij}, and MLP weights \theta randomly. 2. Feature Encoding: For each Gaussian i and training image j: Compute the spatial encoding: \mathbf{e}x = \text{HashGrid}(\mathbf{x}i). Retrieve the image embedding: \mathbf{l}{Ij}. Retrieve the base color: \mathbf{c}i. 3. Appearance and Opacity Modulation: Concatenate inputs for the MLP: \mathbf{z} = [\mathbf{c}i; \mathbf{l}{Ij}; \mathbf{e}x]. Pass \mathbf{z} through the MLP F\theta to get an output vector \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{64}. The output \mathbf{y} is split to produce: Image-dependent color modulation \mathbf{c}{Ij} (derived from part of \mathbf{y}). Image-dependent opacity variation parameter \Delta \alpha{Ij} (derived from part of \mathbf{y}). Concrete Distribution Sampling: To handle transient objects, \Delta \alpha{Ij} serves as the location variable for a concrete distribution (Gumbel-Softmax or similar reparameterization trick). Sample \Delta \tilde{\alpha}{Ij} from this distribution. Final Opacity: The effective opacity for Gaussian i in image j is modulated by \Delta \tilde{\alpha}{Ij}. The method ensures Gaussians do not vary opacity to compensate for appearance variation, allowing transient Gaussians to be identified by high variance in \Delta \tilde{\alpha}{Ij} across images. 4. Rendering: Render the image using the modified color \mathbf{c}{Ij} and modulated opacity. 5. Optimization: Minimize the reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) against the ground truth image Ij. Learning Rates: Image embeddings: 0.0025. Hash Grid: 0.0025. MLP F\theta: 0.0025. Densification: Standard 3DGS densification (splitting/cloning) occurs every 2000 iterations, ending at iteration 30,000. Total iterations: 60,000. 6. Transient Object Removal (Inference/Post-processing): Identify transient Gaussians as those with high variance in \Delta \tilde{\alpha}{Ij} across training images. Pitfall Handling: Simply removing all transient Gaussians can leave holes (black spots) in areas with frequent transients (e.g., clouds, tourists). Adaptive Threshold: To mitigate holes, remove Gaussians based on an adaptive threshold \lambda rather than zero variance: remove if \text{Var}(\Delta \tilde{\alpha}{Ij}) < \lambda. This requires manual tuning of \lambda. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SWAG: def init(self, numimages, hashtablesize=219, nlevels=12, nmin=16, nmax=2048): # Hash Grid Encoder (simplified representation of the actual implementation) self.hashgrid = HashGrid( nlevels=nlevels, nmin=nmin, nmax=nmax, hashtablesize=hashtablesize) # MLP for appearance and opacity modulation # Input: Base Color (3) + Image Embedding (24) + Hash Grid Output (3) -> 30? # Note: Source says Input dimension 3, Hidden 51, Layers 8. # This likely refers to the MLP processing the concatenated features # or a specific subset. Based on "Input dimension: 3" and "Hidden layers size: 51", # and "Output dimension: 64", we assume the MLP takes a 3D input vector # derived from the context, or the source implies a specific 3-channel feature. # However, the text says "MLP takes as inputs the Gaussians’ colors c, # the associated image embedding lI, and their encoded centers emb(x)". # Concatenation of c (3), lI (24), emb(x) (3) = 30 dims. # The source table says "Input dimension: 3". This is contradictory. # Given "Hidden layers size: 51" and "Number of layer: 8", # and standard MLP structures, we assume the input is the concatenated vector. # We will define the MLP to accept the concatenated input. layers = [] indim = 3 + 24 + 3 # c + lI + emb(x) hiddendim = 51 outdim = 64 for in range(7): # 8 layers total, 7 hidden + 1 output layers.append(nn.Linear(indim if == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, outdim)) self.mlp = nn.Sequential(layers) # Per-image embeddings self.imageembeddings = nn.Embedding(numimages, 24) # Hyperparameters self.lrimageemb = 0.0025 self.lrhash = 0.0025 self.lrmlp = 0.0025 def forward(self, gaussians, imageidx): """ gaussians: dict with keys 'c' (N, 3), 'x' (N, 3), etc. imageidx: tensor of shape (N,) or scalar index for the current image """ # 1. Get features c = gaussians['c'] # (N, 3) x = gaussians['x'] # (N, 3) # Hash Grid Encoding embx = self.hashgrid(x) # (N, 3) assuming 3D output per level/level sum? # Standard HashGrid outputs a vector. Let's assume it outputs 3D features # to match the "Input dimension 3" note if it refers to the final concat dim # before MLP, but the text says MLP takes c, lI, emb(x). # If emb(x) is 3D, c is 3D, lI is 24D. # Image Embedding # Assuming imageidx is broadcastable or scalar for the whole batch # (since all Gaussians in a batch belong to one image during training) lI = self.imageembeddings(imageidx).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 24) -> (N, 24) via broadcast # Concatenate # c: (N, 3), lI: (N, 24), embx: (N, 3) # Total input dim: 30 inputvec = torch.cat([c, lI, embx], dim=-1) # (N, 30) # 2. MLP Forward y = self.mlp(inputvec) # (N, 64) # 3. Extract Color and Opacity Variation # The source says output is cI and DeltaalphaI. # We assume a split of the 64-dim vector. # Let's assume first 3 dims are color modulation and one dim is opacity param. # Note: The exact split is not specified in the source notes. # We will assume a standard split for demonstration. cI = y[:,:3] # (N, 3) deltaalphaI = y[:, 3] # (N,) # 4. Concrete Distribution Sampling for Opacity # Sample from Concrete distribution with location deltaalphaI # This allows differentiable sampling of binary-like variables # For implementation, we use the Gumbel-Softmax trick or similar. # Here we assume a simple sampling function. deltaalphatilde = sampleconcrete(deltaalphaI, temperature=1.0) # 5. Modulate Opacity # Base opacity alpha is in gaussians['alpha'] alphamodulated = gaussians['alpha'] (1 + deltaalphatilde) # Example modulation # 6. Render # Use alphamodulated and cI in the standard 3DGS renderer # This part is handled by the parent method [Color and Appearance Modeling] return cI, alphamodulated def sampleconcrete(loc, temperature=1.0): """ Simplified sampling from a concrete distribution. In practice, this involves Gumbel noise. """ # Gumbel noise u = torch.randlike(loc) g = -torch.log(-torch.log(u + 1e-10) + 1e-10) # Concrete sample y = (g + loc) / temperature # Sigmoid to bound between 0 and 1 if needed, or tanh for symmetric # The source uses it as a variation parameter, likely bounded or unbounded. # We return the raw sample for flexibility. return y class HashGrid(nn.Module): def init(self, nlevels, nmin, nmax, hashtablesize): super().init() self.nlevels = nlevels self.nmin = nmin self.nmax = nmax self.hashtablesize = hashtablesize # Implementation details of HashGrid are complex and usually library-specific. # For the purpose of this article, we assume it maps 3D coords to features. pass SWAG-A (No Transient Detection): Uses appearance modeling but no transient handling. Results in closer colors to ground truth than 3DGS but still suffers from floaters caused by transient objects. SWAG-T (No Appearance): Uses transient detection but no appearance conditioning. Eliminates floaters and produces occluder-free scenes but suffers from color alterations (averaging) like base 3DGS. Time Complexity: Training time almost doubles compared to base 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Increased due to Hash Grid, MLP, and per-image embeddings. Hash Grid size is 2^{19} entries. Inference Time: Inference time per frame is 10 times longer than 3DGS due to the MLP evaluation and Hash Grid lookups. Strengths: Handles unstructured in-the-wild data; disentangles static and dynamic Gaussians; enables controllable appearance via embedding interpolation; removes transient objects without supervision. Limitations: Slower training and inference than 3DGS; requires manual tuning of threshold \lambda for transient removal to avoid holes; less than 20% of Gaussians capture transient objects on average. When to use: When reconstructing scenes from unstructured internet photo collections with significant lighting variations and transient occluders (e.g., tourists, clouds). When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the scene is static/controlled; when manual tuning of transient removal thresholds is undesirable. SWAG was proposed by H. Dahmani et al. in the paper "SWAG: Splatting in the Wild images with Appearance-conditioned Gaussians". It addresses the poor performance of standard 3DGS on unstructured in-the-wild data by incorporating appearance modeling and transient object handling. The method was evaluated on the Phototourism Dataset (Brandenburg Gate, Sacré Cœur, Trevi Fountain) and the NeRF-OSR Dataset.
