name: Physics and Optical Modeling
body: Physics and Optical Modeling extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to handle non-vacuum media and physically consistent surface extraction by modifying the rendering equation or the underlying density field. It solves the problem of light transport in scattering media and the geometric inconsistency of discrete alpha-blending for surface reconstruction. Unlike Color and Appearance Modeling, which focuses on view-dependent shading in clear space, this family explicitly models volumetric attenuation and backscatter or reformulates the Gaussian primitive as a continuous attenuation field. This family inherits the standard 3DGS representation and rendering pipeline from Appearance and Physical Modeling. What it is: A method that reformulates rasterization-based 3DGS into a volumetric ray-marching framework by mapping discrete Gaussians to a continuous attenuation field \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) [9624-continuous-attenuation-model-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Distinction: Unlike standard alpha-blending which assumes negligible 3D overlap, this model explicitly defines a view-dependent density that preserves ellipsoidal geometry, enabling unbiased surface extraction [9624-continuous-attenuation-model-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. When to choose: When multi-view consistent depth maps and surface extraction are required, avoiding the surface erosion caused by standard alpha-blending approximations [9624-continuous-attenuation-model-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Link: Continuous Attenuation Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting What it is: An adaptation of 3DGS for underwater environments that learns direct attenuation (Bd), infinite backscatter color (B\infty), and backscatter coefficient (Bb) [13980-underwater-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-backscatter-loss.md]. Distinction: It explicitly models the physical interaction of light with water (color cast and visibility loss), which vanilla 3DGS fails to handle, while remaining significantly faster than NeRF-based underwater alternatives [13980-underwater-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-backscatter-loss.md]. When to choose: For 3D reconstruction in aquatic scenes where color distortion and attenuation are dominant [13980-underwater-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-backscatter-loss.md]. Link: Underwater 3D Gaussian Splatting with Backscatter Loss Step: 1. Divide the depth map (from the current scene estimate) into 10 evenly-spaced clusters covering the range from \min(z) to \max(z). 2. Within each cluster, identify pixels in the ground-truth image whose RGB triplets are below the bottom 1st percentile. 3. These triplets serve as an overestimate of the backscatter signal Bs. 4. Use nonlinear least squares fitting on pairs (Bs, z) to estimate parameters B\infty and Bb. 5. Re-estimate backscatter parameters B\infty and Bb every 500 optimization steps to guide convergence toward the medium coefficients. Formula: The base loss function is: L = \sum{k=1}^K (1 - \lambda1) \| Ik^{gt} - Ik^r(\Theta) \|{\ell1} + \lambda1 L{D-SSIM}(Ik^{gt}, Ik^r(\Theta)) where K is the number of images and \lambda1 \in [0,1] is user-defined. Parameter: Backscatter parameter bounds are B\infty \in [0, 1] and Bb \in [0, 5]. Pitfall: The camera sensor must have a linear response to light. In-camera processed.jpg images or gamma-corrected images cannot be used unless non-linearities can be reversed. The continuous attenuation model was introduced to address the geometric inconsistencies of discrete Gaussian splatting for surface extraction, leveraging theoretical results from Orienting Attenuation (OaV) [9624-continuous-attenuation-model-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Underwater 3D Gaussian Splatting (Gaussian Splashing) was developed to extend 3DGS to aquatic environments by incorporating ocean optics models, specifically addressing the limitations of vanilla 3DGS in handling distance-dependent attenuation and color casts [13980-underwater-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-backscatter-loss.md]. Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-56917-4, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Continuous Attenuation Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Attenuation-based 3DGS, Equivalent Ray-Marching Formulation
body: The Continuous Attenuation Model reformulates the discrete, rasterization-based alpha-blending image formation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into a continuous volumetric ray-marching framework. This equivalence allows the application of theoretical results from Optimal Alpha Blending (OaV) and other volume rendering techniques to 3DGS, specifically enhancing surface extraction by ensuring unbiased, ellipsoidal isosurfaces. Unlike the standard rasterization approach which assumes negligible 3D overlap, this model explicitly defines a view-dependent attenuation coefficient \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) that preserves the geometric fidelity of the Gaussian primitives during ray integration. The method maps a set of N 3D Gaussians to a continuous attenuation field. It relies on two key assumptions: (a) statistical independence of Gaussians (following RayGauss [7]), and (b) non-overlapping Gaussian primitives. While assumption (b) is an approximation similar to front-to-back alpha blending, it is effective in practice for novel view synthesis. Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gi is defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{w}). A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{w}. Output: The continuous attenuation coefficient field \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) and the equivalent transmittance function T{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}(t). The model does not introduce new storage structures but reinterprets the existing Gaussian parameters. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) 1. Flight Distance to Maximum Contribution For a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{w}, the flight distance t{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}^G to the point of maximum Gaussian contribution is the value t \geq 0 that maximizes the Gaussian density along the ray: t{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}^G:= \arg \max{t \geq 0} \{G(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{w})\} For a single Gaussian, this occurs at the point on the ray closest to the mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, projected onto the ray direction. 2. Continuous Transmittance Function The transmittance for a single Gaussian along the ray is defined as: T{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}(t) = 1 - G(\mathbf{o} + \min(t, t{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}^G)\mathbf{w}) This formulation ensures that the transmittance reaches its maximum value (minimum density contribution) at the point of maximum Gaussian contribution. 3. View-Dependent Attenuation Coefficient The attenuation coefficient \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) is derived from the transmittance to ensure consistency with alpha blending and geometric constraints: \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \max(0, -\mathbf{w} \cdot \nabla \log(1 - G(\mathbf{x}))) This specific definition ensures that the transmittance reaches its maximum at the point of maximum contribution and maintains ellipsoidal isosurfaces. 4. Rendering Equivalence The rendered color C{\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}} using the density-based model is: C{\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}} = \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{w}) \int0^{+\infty} -\frac{d}{dt} T{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}(s) ds = \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{w}) G(\mathbf{o} + t{\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}}^G \mathbf{w}) This matches the alpha-blending expression for a single Gaussian, assuming the ray origin \mathbf{o} is in empty space (G(\mathbf{o}) \approx 0). The following Python-like pseudocode computes the attenuation coefficient for a single Gaussian at a point \mathbf{x} along a ray direction \mathbf{w}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussiandensity(x, mu, Sigmainv): """ Computes the value of the Gaussian density function G(x). """ diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diff, np.dot(Sigmainv, diff)) return np.exp(exponent) def gradientlogtransmittance(x, mu, Sigmainv, w): """ Computes -w. grad(log(1 - G(x))). This is the attenuation coefficient sigma(x, w). """ # Compute G(x) Gx = gaussiandensity(x, mu, Sigmainv) # Avoid log(0) if G(x) is 1 (unlikely in empty space, but guard against it) if Gx >= 1.0: return 0.0 log1minusG = np.log(1.0 - Gx) # Gradient of log(1 - G(x)) with respect to x # d/dx log(1 - G) = (1 / (1 - G)) (-dG/dx) # dG/dx = G(x) (-Sigmainv (x - mu)) diff = x - mu gradG = Gx (-np.dot(Sigmainv, diff)) gradlog1minusG = -gradG / (1.0 - Gx) # Dot product with ray direction w # sigma = max(0, -w. gradlog1minusG) # Note: The formula is -w. grad(log(1-G)). # grad(log(1-G)) is a vector. We take the dot product with w. # Then negate. dotproduct = np.dot(w, gradlog1minusG) sigma = -dotproduct return max(0.0, sigma) def computeflightdistance(mu, Sigmainv, o, w): """ Computes t{o,w}^G = argmax{t>=0} G(o + tw). For a single Gaussian, this is the projection of (mu - o) onto w, clamped to t >= 0. """ # Vector from origin to mean v = mu - o # Project v onto w # t = (v. w) / (w. w) # Assuming w is normalized, w.w = 1 t = np.dot(v, w) # Clamp to t >= 0 return max(0.0, t) Non-Spherical Isosurfaces: Using a simpler attenuation formulation \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2} |\mathbf{w} \cdot \nabla \log(1 - G(\mathbf{x}))| (as in GGGS [57]) produces non-spherical surfaces for a single Gaussian. This leads to non-multi-view consistent depth maps and surface erosion. Geometric Constraint: The proposed model enforces ellipsoidal isosurfaces for transmittance, ensuring unbiased, spherical isosurfaces aligned with the visible part of the Gaussian. Overlap Assumption: The equivalence relies on the non-overlapping assumption. Discrepancies occur when this condition is not met, such as in poorly supervised background regions. Complexity: The computational complexity is comparable to standard 3DGS rasterization for rendering, as it evaluates the same Gaussian primitives. However, ray-marching implementations may incur higher overhead due to the iterative evaluation of the attenuation field along the ray. Performance: The model is designed to be equivalent to the rasterization-based model, so it does not inherently degrade novel view synthesis quality. Strengths: Enables high-fidelity surface reconstruction by providing unbiased, multi-view consistent depth maps and normals. It allows the use of volume rendering techniques for surface extraction. Limitations: Relies on the approximation of non-overlapping Gaussians, which may fail in complex scenes with significant occlusion or poor supervision. The Continuous Attenuation Model was introduced in "From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians". It builds on the observation that while 3DGS rasterization is efficient, it lacks the theoretical grounding for surface extraction provided by volumetric rendering. The work connects 3DGS to Optimal Alpha Blending (OaV) and addresses the limitations of previous attenuation models like GGGS [57], which failed to preserve geometric consistency. name: Underwater 3D Gaussian Splatting with Backscatter Loss
head: 3DGS adapted to aquatic environments
body: This method adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for underwater environments by integrating ocean optics models, specifically learning direct attenuation (Bd), infinite backscatter (B\infty), and backscatter coefficient (Bb). It solves the problem of color distortion and visibility loss in aquatic scenes by modifying the rendering equation to account for light transport in a scattering medium. Unlike vanilla 3DGS, which fails to handle the predominant bluish palette and distance-dependent degradation, this method maintains real-time inference speeds while significantly improving reconstruction quality at unbounded camera-to-scene distances. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N initialized from a sparse point cloud (e.g., via COLMAP); a set of K input images \{Ik^{gt}\}{k=1}^K with known camera poses; ground-truth depth estimates or a mechanism to derive them from the Gaussian representation. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters \Theta (means, covariances, opacities, colors) and medium parameters Bd, B\infty, Bb; rendered novel-view images. Data Structures The scene is represented by the standard 3DGS structure: \boldsymbol{\mu}i: Mean position (3 floats). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i: Covariance matrix, derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i (6 floats for rotation quaternion, 3 for scale) [Parent]. \alphai: Opacity (1 float). \mathbf{c}i: View-dependent color, typically stored as spherical harmonic coefficients [Parent]. Bd: Direct attenuation parameter (1 float per Gaussian or global, modulating RGB values). B\infty: Infinite backscatter parameter (1 float, bounded [0, 1]). Bb: Backscatter coefficient parameter (1 float, bounded [0, 5]). Rendering Equation The rendering process evaluates Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The specific underwater rendering equation incorporating attenuation and backscatter is referenced as Eq. (5) in the source. The depth map z is extracted from the 3DGS representation using a customized CUDA implementation, mapping the initial output via a shifted and scaled logistic function: z = \frac{2}{1 + e^{-0.1 \cdot z}} - 1. Optimization Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using COLMAP sparse point cloud. Initialize medium parameters Bd, B\infty, Bb. 2. Initial Parameter Estimation (Backscatter Guidance): Identify pixels in the ground-truth image whose RGB triplets fall below the bottom 1st percentile of all pixel values. These pixels serve as an overestimate of the backscatter. Model the backscatter color Bs at a pixel with depth z as: Bs = B\infty (1 - e^{-Bb z}) where Bs is the color value and z is the depth estimate at such a pixel. Use nonlinear least squares fitting on the pairs of (Bs, z) values to estimate initial parameters \hat{B}\infty and \hat{B}b, ensuring they remain within bounds [0, 1] and [0, 5] respectively. 3. Alternating Optimization: Minimize the total loss L(\Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb) using the Adam optimizer. The rendered images Ik^r are functions of \Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb. Every 500 iterations, re-compute the initial estimates \hat{B}\infty and \hat{B}b using the current depth map estimates and the nonlinear least squares procedure. This refines the guidance for the medium parameters as depth improves. 4. Loss Function: The total loss is defined as: L(\Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb) = \sum{k=1}^K (1 - \lambda1) \|Ik^{gt} - Ik^r(\Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb)\|{\ell1} + \lambda1 L{D-SSIM}(Ik^{gt}, Ik^r(\Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb)) + \lambda2 L{bs}(B\infty, Bb) where: \| \cdot \|{\ell1} is the L1 norm. L{D-SSIM} is the D-SSIM loss. L{bs} is the backscatter guidance loss: L{bs}(B\infty, Bb) = \|B\infty - \hat{B}\infty\|{\ell1} + \|Bb - \hat{B}b\|{\ell1} where \hat{B}\infty and \hat{B}b are the initial estimates. Parameters \lambda1: Weight for the D-SSIM loss term. Value: 0.3 (inherited from original 3DGS). \lambda2: Weight for the backscatter loss term. Value: 0.1 (fixed across all scenes). Learning Rate: Identical for Bd, B\infty, Bb and the Gaussian color parameters ci. Optimization Bounds: B\infty \in [0, 1], Bb \in [0, 5]. Bd follows the normalized RGB image range and physically non-negative attenuation assumption. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def underwater3dgstraining(Gaussians, images, cameraposes, K, lambda1=0.3, lambda2=0.1, steps=30000): """ Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with parameters mu, Sigma, alpha, ci images: List of ground truth images Igt cameraposes: List of camera poses K: Number of images """ # Initialize medium parameters Bd = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1)) # Direct attenuation Binf = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1)) # Infinite backscatter Bb = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1)) # Backscatter coefficient # Optimization bounds handling (clipping or projection) # Binf in [0, 1], Bb in [0, 5] optimizer = optim.Adam(list(Gaussians.parameters()) + [Bd, Binf, Bb], lr=0.001) # LR inherited from 3DGS for step in range(steps): # 1. Render # Ir and z are outputs of the underwater-aware rendering pipeline Ir, z = rendergaussians(Gaussians, Bd, Binf, Bb, cameraposes) # 2. Compute Photometric and Structural Losses lossl1 = 0 lossdssim = 0 for k in range(K): Igt = images[k] lossl1 += torch.norm(Igt - Ir[k], p=1) lossdssim += computedssim(Igt, Ir[k]) lossphoto = (1 - lambda1) lossl1 + lambda1 lossdssim # 3. Compute Backscatter Guidance Loss # Estimate Binfhat and Bbhat from current depth z and dark pixels Binfhat, Bbhat = estimatebackscatterguidance(z, images) lossbs = torch.norm(Binf - Binfhat, p=1) + torch.norm(Bb - Bbhat, p=1) # 4. Total Loss loss = lossphoto + lambda2 lossbs # 5. Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() # 6. Clip parameters to bounds with torch.nograd(): Bd.clamp(min=0) # Non-negative attenuation Binf.clamp(min=0, max=1) Bb.clamp(min=0, max=5) optimizer.step() # 7. Alternating Update: Re-estimate guidance every 500 steps if step % 500 == 0: # Re-compute Binfhat and Bbhat using current depth map # This involves identifying dark pixels and fitting Bs = Binf (1 - exp(-Bb z)) Binfhat, Bbhat = estimatebackscatterguidance(z, images) # The loss function will use these new hats in the next iteration def estimatebackscatterguidance(z, images): """ Identifies pixels with RGB < 1st percentile. Fits Bs = Binf (1 - exp(-Bb z)) to these pixels. Returns Binfhat, Bbhat. """ # Flatten images and z # Find indices where RGB values are in bottom 1% # Extract corresponding z values and Bs (RGB values) # Perform nonlinear least squares fit # Return fitted Binf and Bb pass # Implementation details in Supplementary Information Time Complexity: Training takes only several minutes. Memory Complexity: Average memory consumption is ~500 MB per scene over 30,000 steps on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. Performance: Inference speed is ~140 FPS average across multiple datasets, enabling real-time novel-view synthesis. Strengths: Significantly improves reconstruction quality in underwater scenes compared to vanilla 3DGS, particularly at larger distances and unbounded camera-to-scene distances. Much faster than NeRF-based methods (STNeRF, STNeRFacto) in both training and inference. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth estimation for the backscatter guidance; performance may degrade if depth maps are poor. Traditional metrics like PSNR can be misleading in underwater scenarios due to the predominant bluish color palette. When to use: Underwater 3D reconstruction, novel view synthesis, and color-reconstruction applications where real-time rendering is required. When not to use: Scenes with extreme turbidity where the backscatter model assumptions break down, or when high-fidelity color accuracy is required without considering the physical medium (vanilla 3DGS might be preferred for speed if quality is not critical). Origin: The method was introduced in "Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater". History: It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [Parent] and adapts it to aquatic environments by incorporating ocean optics models. It addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS in handling underwater light transport. Usage: Evaluated on the TableDB dataset (172 images, 1384×918 resolution, unbounded camera-to-scene distances) and public underwater datasets (Red Sea, Curaçao, Panama). Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-56917-4, fetched 2026-10-27

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction

body:
3D Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction (3DGSR) is an implicit surface reconstruction method that integrates a neural Signed Distance Field (SDF) with the explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation. It solves the problem of extracting high-quality, watertight meshes from 3DGS, which traditionally yields unstructured point clouds that are difficult to process with standard post-processing techniques like Poisson reconstruction. Unlike sibling methods that rely on post-processing or separate optimization stages, 3DGSR unifies the optimization of the Gaussian appearance and the implicit surface geometry end-to-end. It achieves this by coupling the SDF with the Gaussians via alignment constraints and regularizing the SDF using volumetric rendering consistency, enabling reconstruction quality superior to Gaussian-based methods like 2DGS while maintaining the rendering speed of 3DGS. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, initialized from SfM points (mean  oldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance  oldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, color coefficients). A set of training images with known camera poses. Hyperparameters:  eta (SDF-to-opacity shape, learnable), \lambda (SSIM weight in photometric loss), learning rates for Gaussians and SDF. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}. Optimized SDF field f: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R}. A triangular mesh extracted from the zero-level set of f using Marching Cubes. 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation. Each Gaussian i stores:  oldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3}: Rotation matrix (derived from quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4). \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale factors.  oldsymbol{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^	op \mathbf{R}i^	op: Covariance matrix. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c}i: Color coefficients (e.g., SH coefficients). SDF Field: Implemented using multiresolution hash grids [Müller et al. 2022] combined with a single-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The MLP takes hashed grid features as input and outputs the scalar SDF value f(\mathbf{x}) and its gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) for any query point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 1. Gaussians: Initialize using standard 3DGS SfM initialization. 2. SDF Field: Initialize the neural SDF field using either random initialization or sphere initialization. The method aligns the SDF with the Gaussians to enforce surface constraints. Two strategies are defined; the loose coupling strategy is used by default. This strategy uses the SDF to constrain the distribution and orientation of Gaussians without directly dictating their opacity. Distance Regularization: Forces Gaussians to be near the surface defined by f(\mathbf{x}) = 0. For each Gaussian i, the loss encourages f( oldsymbol{\mu}i) \approx 0. Direction Alignment: Aligns the orientation of the Gaussian (specifically the direction of its shortest axis) with the surface normal \mathbf{n}i = 
abla f( oldsymbol{\mu}i). This prevents the generation of redundant Gaussian points far from the surface and reduces the Gaussian count by ~20%. This strategy uses the SDF to directly control Gaussian opacity via a differentiable transformation. SDF-to-Opacity Transformation: The opacity \alphai of a Gaussian at  oldsymbol{\mu}i is derived from the SDF value f( oldsymbol{\mu}i) using a bell-shaped function \Phi eta: \Phi eta(f(\mathbf{x})) =  rac{e^{- eta \cdot f(\mathbf{x})}}{(1 + e^{- eta \cdot f(\mathbf{x})})^2} where  eta is a learnable parameter controlling the shape. Photometric Loss: The opacity is optimized to match rendering contributions. The loss is: Lc = \lambda{LD-SSIM} + (1 - \lambda)L1 This encourages Gaussians contributing to the image to have high opacity, pushing f(\mathbf{x}) closer to 0. Pitfall: Tight coupling can disrupt surface reconstruction in low-frequency flat areas if high-frequency textures cause non-uniform Gaussian distribution, leading to noisy surfaces. Because Gaussians provide sparse supervision (only at occupied locations), the SDF field requires dense regularization to prevent artifacts in free space. This is achieved by aligning geometric attributes rendered from the SDF with those derived from 3DGS. 1. Ray Sampling: During each training iteration, sample a subset of rays \mathbf{r}. 2. SDF Volumetric Rendering: Render depth 	ilde{D}(\mathbf{r}) and normal 	ilde{\mathbf{N}}(\mathbf{r}) from the SDF field using ray-casting. For a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, sample points xi along the ray. Compute transmittance Ti^r and alpha \alphai for each sample: Ti^r = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alphai = \max \left(  rac{\phis(f(xi)) - \phis(f(x{i+1}))}{\phis(f(xi))}, 0 ight) where \phis is the Sigmoid function. Accumulate depth and normal: 	ilde{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ti^r \alphai ti 	ilde{\mathbf{N}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ti^r \alphai 	ilde{\mathbf{n}}i where 	ilde{\mathbf{n}}i = 
abla f(xi) is the normal from the SDF gradient. 3. Consistency Loss: Align the SDF-rendered geometry with the geometry derived from 3DGS (pseudo-depth D and normal \mathbf{N}). Depth Loss: L{vd} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| D(\mathbf{r}) - 	ilde{D}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 Normal Loss: L{vn} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) - 	ilde{\mathbf{N}}(\mathbf{r}) \|1 + \| 1 - \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot 	ilde{\mathbf{N}}(\mathbf{r}) \|1 where \mathcal{R} is the set of sampled rays. 1. Forward Pass: Render images from current Gaussians. Compute photometric loss (L1, SSIM) against ground truth images. 2. Geometry Extraction: Compute Gaussian-derived depth D and normal \mathbf{N} (pseudo-geometry). 3. SDF Regularization: Sample rays, render SDF depth 	ilde{D} and normal 	ilde{\mathbf{N}}, compute L{vd} and L{vn}. 4. Coupling Loss: If Loose: Compute distance and orientation regularization losses for Gaussians based on f( oldsymbol{\mu}i) and

Backward Pass: Update Gaussians (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) and SDF field parameters using the combined loss. 6. Returns Dgs, Ngs. """ # Placeholder for 3DGS rasterization logic that outputs depth/normal # In practice, this involves sorting Gaussians and alpha blending # Dgs: (H, W), Ngs: (H, W, 3) pass def rendersdfvolumetric(self, raydirs, origins, numsamples=64): """ Render depth and normal from SDF using volumetric rendering. """ # Sample points along rays # t values linearly spaced or stratified t = torch.linspace(0.1, 10.0, numsamples).to(raydirs.device) points = origins.unsqueeze(1) + t.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) raydirs.unsqueeze(1) # (B, numsamples, 3) fvals, gradvals = self.sdfnet(points.reshape(-1, 3)) fvals = fvals.reshape(points.shape[:2]) gradvals = gradvals.reshape(points.shape[:2], 3) # Compute alpha using Sigmoid phis = torch.sigmoid(fvals) # Alpha formula: max((phis(xi) - phis(x{i+1})) / phis(xi), 0) # Handle boundary: phis(x{M+1}) = 0 phinext = torch.cat([phivals[:, 1:], torch.zeroslike(phivals[:,:1])], dim=1) alpha = torch.clamp((phivals - phinext) / (phivals + 1e-6), min=0.0) # Transmittance T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) # Accumulate Depth and Normal # Depth: sum(T alpha t) depthsdf = torch.sum(T alpha t, dim=1) # Normal: sum(T alpha grad) # gradvals are normals from SDF gradient normalsdf = torch.sum(T.unsqueeze(-1) alpha.unsqueeze(-1) gradvals, dim=1) normalsdf = normalsdf / (torch.norm(normalsdf, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6) return depthsdf, normalsdf def computelosses(self, gtimage, renderedimage, Dgs, Ngs, Dsdf, Nsdf): losses = {} # 1. Photometric Loss (for Gaussians) losses['photometric'] = (1 - self.lambdass) torch.abs(renderedimage - gtimage).mean() + \ self.lambdass (1 - ssim(renderedimage, gtimage)) # 2. """ # Create grid x = torch.linspace(bounds.min, bounds.max, resolution) y = torch.linspace(bounds.min, bounds.max, resolution) z = torch.linspace(bounds.min, bounds.max, resolution) xx, yy, zz = torch.meshgrid(x, y, z, indexing='ij') points = torch.stack([xx, yy, zz], dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3) # Query SDF with torch.nograd(): fvals, = self.sdfnet(points) fgrid = fvals.reshape(resolution, resolution, resolution) # Marching Cubes vertices, faces = marchingcubes(fgrid.numpy(), level=0.0) return vertices, faces Sparse Supervision: Optimizing Gaussians only provides supervision at Gaussian locations. Without volumetric rendering regularization, the SDF may develop artifacts in unoccupied free space (floating artifacts). Tight Coupling Artifacts: In low-frequency flat areas, high-frequency textures can cause non-uniform Gaussian distribution. Tight coupling forces SDF values to zero in these dense regions, leading to noisy surface structures and visible artifacts. Rendering Quality: Tight coupling may compromise rendering quality if Gaussian locations are inaccurate, as it enforces geometric constraints that conflict with appearance optimization. Initialization: Poor SDF initialization can lead to convergence issues. Sphere or random initialization is recommended. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: Significantly faster than neural implicit methods. Training time is reduced from ~12 hours to ~30 minutes, a speedup of more than 20 times. This is achieved by avoiding time-consuming color prediction branches and volumetric rendering losses for optimization, relying instead on 3DGS for supervision. Memory: Uses multiresolution hash grids for the SDF, which are memory-efficient compared to dense voxel grids. The number of Gaussians can be reduced by 20% using loose coupling, further saving memory. Measured Performance: Accuracy: Achieves a Chamfer-L1 error of 0.72 on benchmark datasets, compared to 1.40 for 2DGS (a state-of-the-art Gaussian-based method). Rendering Quality: Maintains the high rendering quality and efficiency of 3DGS. Strengths: End-to-end optimization of geometry and appearance. Eliminates post-processing steps like depth fusion or Poisson reconstruction. High-quality surface reconstruction with intricate details. Fast training speed. Limitations: Tight coupling is sensitive to texture frequency and can produce noisy surfaces. Requires careful balancing of consistency losses to prevent SDF artifacts. When to Use: When high-quality mesh extraction is required from 3DGS data. When training speed is a priority compared to neural implicit methods. When post-processing pipelines are undesirable. When Not to Use: If the scene has very high-frequency textures on flat surfaces and tight coupling is preferred (loose coupling is safer). If the primary goal is only novel view synthesis without mesh extraction (standard 3DGS is sufficient). Origin: 3DGSR was introduced by Xiaoyang Lyu, Yang-Tian Sun, Yi-Hua Huang, et al. from The University of Hong Kong and Shanghai AI Lab. The paper was published in ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024). History and Development: The method addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS, which optimizes for photorealistic rendering but lacks explicit geometric structure, making mesh extraction difficult. Previous Gaussian-based methods like 2DGS [Huang et al. 2024] suffered from oversmoothed reconstructions and higher Chamfer-L1 errors. Neural implicit methods [Wang et al. 2021; Yariv et al. 2021] provided good geometry but were slow to train and render. 3DGSR bridges this gap by coupling an implicit SDF with explicit Gaussians, leveraging the strengths of both. Usage: Used for implicit surface reconstruction in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines. 3DGSR: Implicit Surface Reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3687952, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Sparse2DGS
head: Geometry-Prioritized Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views
body: Sparse2DGS is a Gaussian Splatting method designed for surface reconstruction from sparse input views, addressing the ill-posed nature of geometric optimization when dense Structure-from-Motion points are unavailable. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting and its sibling 2DGS by initializing primitives with unsupervised Multi-View Stereo (MVS) points and employing geometric-prioritized enhancements—such as fixed feature splatting and selective updates—to prevent appearance overfitting and improve geometric learning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N sparse input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Outputs: A set of 2D Gaussian primitives representing the 3D surface, optimized to minimize reconstruction error. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a set of 2D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive G is defined by: Central position \mathbf{p}. Two principal tangential vectors \mathbf{t}u and \mathbf{t}v. Scaling vector (su, sv). The rotation matrix is \mathbf{R} = (\mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v, \mathbf{t}z), where \mathbf{t}z = \mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v. The scale matrix is \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(su, sv, 0). The local tangent plane in world space is parameterized as: P(u, v) = \mathbf{p} + su \mathbf{t}u u + sv \mathbf{t}v v \quad (1) The Gaussian value for a point \mathbf{u} = (u, v) in the local uv space is: G(\mathbf{u}) = \exp\left(-\frac{u^2 + v^2}{2}\right) \quad (2) MVS-derived feature maps \{Di\}{i=1}^N (dense depth maps) are used for initialization and supervision. Numbered Steps: 1. MVS Initialization: Run an unsupervised MVS network (specifically CLMVSNet) on the input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N to estimate dense depth maps \{Di\}{i=1}^N. Back-project the depth maps Di into 3D space and fuse them to create a point cloud \{\mathbf{p}{ij} \mid 1 \le i \le N, 1 \le j \le HW\}. Initialize the 2D Gaussian primitives' central positions \mathbf{p} using this MVS point cloud. 2. Geometrically Enhanced Supervision (Feature Splatting): Sample the MVS-derived feature maps (depth/geometry) into the Gaussian splatting process. Crucial Constraint: Keep the feature values and RGB color values fixed during optimization. This provides geometrically expressive supervision and prevents the model from overfitting to appearance in sparse views, which would otherwise compromise geometry. 3. Gaussian Primitive Regularization: Apply a reparameterization-based disk sampling strategy to regularize the geometric properties (position, orientation, scale) of the primitives. Reformulate the Gaussian properties into point representations. Optimize these properties using a unified point-based, cross-view consistency loss. This ensures that the 2D disk-like primitives maintain coherent geometry across views. 4. Selective Gaussian Update: Instead of using standard densification (splitting/copying) which can fail under ill-posed sparse-view conditions, selectively update the existing MVS-initialized Gaussian primitives. Use rendered geometric cues to guide these updates, allowing for self-guided geometric corrections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparse2dgs(inputimages, numviews): """ inputimages: List of N images [H, W, 3] numviews: N """ # Step 1: MVS Initialization # Run unsupervised MVS (e.g., CLMVSNet) to get depth maps depthmaps = runmvsnetwork(inputimages) # Back-project and fuse depth maps to point cloud # i: image index, j: pixel index mvspointcloud = [] for i in range(numviews): for j in range(H W): pij = backproject(depthmaps[i], j) mvspointcloud.append(pij) # Initialize 2D Gaussians with MVS points # Each Gaussian G has: p, tu, tv, su, sv gaussians = [] for p in mvspointcloud: # Initialize tangential vectors and scales arbitrarily or via normal estimation tu, tv = initializetangents(p) su, sv = 1.0, 1.0 # Initial scale g = Gaussian(p=p, tu=tu, tv=tv, su=su, sv=sv) gaussians.append(g) # Step 2: Optimization Loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): losses = [] for viewidx in range(numviews): image = inputimages[viewidx] # Render current view using 2D Gaussian Splatting # Note: Feature and Color values are FIXED from MVS/Initialization renderedimage, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(gaussians, viewidx) # Compute loss against ground truth image # Since color is fixed, this loss primarily drives geometric consistency # and prevents appearance overfitting colorloss = computecolorloss(renderedimage, image) losses.append(colorloss) # Compute geometric consistency loss using MVS depth # Compare rendered depth with MVS depth map mvsdepth = depthmaps[viewidx] geoloss = computedepthconsistency(rendereddepth, mvsdepth) losses.append(geoloss) # Step 3: Regularization # Apply disk sampling regularization to reformulate properties # into point-based supervision regloss = applydisksamplingregularization(gaussians) losses.append(regloss) # Backpropagate and update gradients # Only update geometric parameters (p, tu, tv, su, sv) # Do NOT update color or feature attributes optimize(gaussians, losses) # Step 4: Selective Update # Instead of densification, selectively update primitives # based on geometric cues gaussians = selectiveupdate(gaussians, rendereddepth, mvsdepth) return gaussians Parameters: N: Number of sparse input views. H, W: Height and width of input images. Di: Dense depth maps estimated by the MVS network for view i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Appearance Overfitting: In sparse views, optimizing color and geometry simultaneously leads to severe degradation where color overfits the sparse inputs, compromising geometry. Sparse2DGS mitigates this by fixing feature and color values during optimization. Ill-posed Geometry: Standard densification strategies fail under sparse-view conditions. Sparse2DGS uses selective updates instead. Textureless Regions: Challenges in textureless areas are amplified with sparse views; the geometric-prioritized supervision helps address this. Performance: Achieves a Chamfer Distance (CD) error of 1.13 on the DTU dataset with 3 views. This is significantly lower than 2DGS (2.81), GOF (2.82), and PGSR (2.08). Efficiency: Training time is 10 minutes, which is 2x faster than the NeRF-based fine-tuning approach SparseNeus (25 minutes). Strengths: Robust geometric learning under ill-posed conditions; complete and accurate reconstruction from sparse images; faster than NeRF-based methods. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the unsupervised MVS initialization (CLMVSNet); performance is specific to sparse-view scenarios. Sparse2DGS was proposed to address the limitations of previous Gaussian Splatting methods that rely on dense views for initialization, which struggle with extremely sparse Structure-from-Motion points. It combines the strengths of Gaussian Splatting and Multi-view Stereo (MVS) through geometric-prioritized enhancement schemes. The method was introduced in the paper "Sparse2DGS: Geometry-Prioritized Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views". Sparse2DGS: Geometry-Prioritized Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.01056, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Planar Gaussian Splatting
head: PGSR, Planar GS
body: Planar Gaussian Splatting (PGS) is an unsupervised neural rendering framework that reconstructs 3D geometry and explicitly parses 3D planar surfaces from multiple RGB images without requiring 3D labels or depth supervision. It extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation by introducing discriminative 3D plane descriptors and enforcing local planar alignment constraints. Unlike sibling methods that focus on high-fidelity rendering or generic mesh extraction, PGS is designed to identify distinct 3D plane instances through a hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Tree (GMT). It sets itself apart by using 2D segmentation priors from foundation models (like SAM) to guide the learning of these descriptors, enabling robust planar reconstruction across different scenes. PGS operates on a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi retains the standard parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). Additionally, each Gaussian carries two new parameters: a surface normal vector \mathbf{n}i and a learnable plane descriptor vector \mathbf{z}i. The descriptor \mathbf{z}i is constrained to unit norm (\|\mathbf{z}i\|2 = 1) and serves to identify distinct 3D planes. Gaussian Field: A list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix. \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \mathbf{c}i: Spherical Harmonics coefficients (Degree 2). \mathbf{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Surface normal (unit vector). \mathbf{z}i \in \mathbb{R}^d: Plane descriptor (unit vector, d=3 in experiments). KNN Structure: For each Gaussian, a list of K nearest neighbor indices is maintained to compute local covariance and smoothing. Region Adjacency Graph (RAG): A graph where nodes are 2D segments and edges represent adjacency, used to merge segments belonging to the same plane. 1. Gaussian Placement: Initialize Gaussian locations and colors using a sparse point cloud obtained by running Structure-from-Motion (SfM) on the training images. 2. Leaf Node Generation (Optional/Alternative): Instead of initializing all Gaussians randomly, leaf nodes of the Gaussian Mixture Tree can be generated by: Prompting SAM with a 32 \times 32 grid on input images to get masks. Ignoring segments with high normal vector variance. Lifting boundary points of valid SAM masks into 3D space using rendered depth maps and camera parameters. Computing the mean and covariance of these 3D boundary points to form initial Gaussian distributions. The training runs for 15,000 iterations on a single GPU. The core loop involves standard 3DGS densification (cloning, splitting, culling) and the following specialized steps: 1. Rendering: Render the scene to obtain photometric loss. Use Spherical Harmonics of degree 2. 2. Plane Descriptor Learning (Linear Regression): Render a 2D descriptor image where each pixel is the blended 3D descriptor \mathbf{z} of the Gaussians visible at that pixel. Let \mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times d} be the matrix of rendered descriptors for P pixels, augmented with a column of 1s. Let \mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times m} be the one-hot label matrix for the m segments in the current view (derived from SAM). Solve for weights \hat{\mathbf{W}} using the closed-form solution: \hat{\mathbf{W}} = (\mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Z})^{-1} \mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Y} Compute the prediction \hat{\mathbf{y}}i = [\mathbf{z}i | 1] \hat{\mathbf{W}} for each pixel. Compute segmentation loss: \mathcal{L}{seg} = \sum{i} \| \mathbf{y}i - \hat{\mathbf{y}}i \|1 Backpropagate \mathcal{L}{seg} to update \mathbf{z}i. Note: This regression is recomputed for each camera view. The number of segments m varies per image. 3. Segment Merging (RAG): Construct a RAG from the 2D segments. Cut edges in the RAG if the planar distance between segments exceeds 10 cm or the surface normal cosine distance exceeds 20 degrees. Merge remaining connected components to form consistent 2D plane labels for the current view. 4. Local Planar Alignment: Applied every 500 iterations. For each Gaussian, find its K=30 nearest neighbors (KNN). Compute the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix of the KNN Gaussian centers. Perform Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the covariance matrix. Identify the local tangent plane using the two eigenvectors corresponding to the two largest eigenvalues. Project the Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu}i onto this local tangent plane. Apply Laplacian smoothing to \mathbf{n}i and \mathbf{z}i by averaging over the features of the KNN neighbors. 5. Holistic Separability (Mean-Shift): Applied once after 2,000 iterations, then every 100 iterations. Goal: Enhance separability of descriptors \mathbf{z} for distinct planes. Update rule for the descriptor matrix \mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}: \mathbf{Z} \leftarrow \mathbf{Z} \cdot (\eta \cdot \mathbf{K} \cdot \mathbf{D}^{-1} + (1-\eta) \cdot \mathbf{I}) Where: \mathbf{K} is the pairwise distance kernel using the von Mises-Fisher distribution. \mathbf{D} is the diagonal matrix of row sums of \mathbf{K}. \mathbf{I} is the identity matrix. \eta is a mixing parameter. \gamma = 60 is the kernel parameter (used in von Mises-Fisher). Efficient Implementation: Computing \mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} is infeasible for large N. Instead: 1. Estimate \mathbf{K} on a random subset of M points (M \ll N) without replacement. 2. Propagate and share the estimated kernel and update vectors across all KNN samples within the chosen set. 3. Repeat sampling until an update vector is computed for all samples or their neighbors. 4. Perform 10 update steps per run. 5. This process takes approximately 1 second on GPU. 6. KNN Recomputation: Recompute KNN indices after any refinement to the Gaussian field (cloning, splitting, culling). Training Iterations: 15,000. Hardware: Single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti. Gradient Densification Threshold: 0.001 (increased to limit cloning/splitting). Spherical Harmonics Degree: 2. RAG Thresholds: Planar distance 10 cm, Normal cosine distance 20 degrees. Mean-Shift Frequency: Once after 2k iterations, then every 100 iterations. Mean-Shift Steps: 10 per run. Mean-Shift Gamma (\gamma): 60. KNN Neighbors (K): 30. Local Planar Alignment Frequency: Every 500 iterations. Kernel Computation: Computing the full kernel \mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} is quadratic in memory and infeasible for millions of points. The sampling strategy is required. SAM Ambiguity: SAM may return subparts, parts, or entire objects for a single point. High-variance normal segments are ignored as invalid. Multi-view Association: SAM masks lack semantic information, making 2D-3D lifting difficult due to unknown mask associations and variable numbers of segments. The linear regression approach handles this by solving for weights per view. This subtopic details the mechanism for learning 3D plane descriptors \mathbf{z} by lifting 2D segmentation masks from SAM. It involves rendering 3D descriptors to 2D and solving a linear regression problem to map them to 2D segment labels. It sets itself apart by avoiding explicit 3D plane labels, using 2D priors instead. Choose this when you need to incorporate semantic segmentation priors into 3D Gaussian optimization without 3D ground truth. Link: Plane Descriptor Learning via 2D SAM Lifting (Note: Placeholder link as specific article doesn't exist, linking to parent context). This subtopic describes enforcing Gaussian centers to lie on object surfaces by projecting them onto local tangent planes computed from KNN covariance matrices. It sets itself apart by providing a geometric constraint that aligns Gaussians with surfaces, improving mesh quality. Choose this when you need to extract cleaner meshes from 3DGS. Link: Local Planar Alignment. This subtopic describes the probabilistic bottom-up modeling of scene geometry. It sets itself apart by hierarchically grouping Gaussians to identify distinct 3D plane instances. Choose this when you need to parse the scene into explicit planar components. Link: Gaussian Mixture Tree. Time Complexity: The mean-shift update is optimized to take approximately 1 second on GPU despite N being in the millions, due to the sampling strategy. The linear regression is recomputed per view but is fast. Memory Complexity: Avoids O(N^2) memory for the kernel matrix by using random sampling. Performance: On ScanNet, PGS achieves an Accuracy of 0.137 and Completeness of 0.118, outperforming PlanarRecon (0.154 Accuracy, 0.187 Completeness). Strengths: Unsupervised, no depth/3D labels required, fast optimization compared to other optimization-based planar methods, robust across datasets. Limitations: Relies on SAM quality, Spherical Harmonics degree 2 limits high-frequency color detail, densification threshold is higher to limit Gaussian count. When to use: When 3D planar reconstruction is needed from RGB images without depth supervision. When not to use: When high-fidelity rendering is the primary goal (SH degree 2 is used) or when 3D ground truth is available and supervised methods are preferred. Planar Gaussian Splatting (PGS) was introduced by Farhad G. Zanjani, Hong Cai, Hanno Ackermann, Leila Mirvakhabova, and Fatih Porikli from Qualcomm AI Research. The paper was published on arXiv on December 2, 2024, and later in WACV 2025. It addresses the challenge of identifying 3D planar surfaces in images, which is difficult for standard 3DGS due to its floating ellipsoid nature. PGS builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [16] and leverages foundation models like SAM [17] to provide 2D priors. name: CADSplat
head: Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting Aided by CAD Models
body: CADSplat reconstructs photorealistic, geometrically accurate digital twins from sparse (< 15 views), wide-baseline posed images by regularizing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an explicit Computer-Aided Design (CAD) shape prior. It differs from generative priors (e.g., pixelSplat, MVSplat) and learned priors (e.g., InstantSplat) by imposing a strict, explicit prior from the object's specific CAD model rather than a learned generative prior that may hallucinate content. This approach provides geometric disambiguation under occlusion and scarcity, enabling applications such as markerless augmented reality registration, per-image object pose estimation, and the transfer of part labels from design to reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N posed images (N < 15), segmented object silhouettes for each image, and a library of CAD models (or a specific candidate CAD model). Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients), camera-to-object poses, and a non-rigid deformation field mapping the CAD mesh to the physical object. Data Structures: 1. CAD Mesh: A triangular mesh representing the canonical object shape. 2. Gaussian Primitives: Anchored to the CAD mesh surface. Each primitive is defined by position \mathbf{p}, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}. 3. Deformation Network D\theta: A neural network that outputs a displacement vector for any point on the CAD mesh. 4. Pose Parameters: A global Sim(3) transformation (scale, rotation, translation) or per-camera corrections. Numbered Steps: 1. CAD Model Retrieval and Initial Registration: Render silhouettes from candidate CAD models in the library. Match segmented object silhouettes from input images against rendered CAD silhouettes. Select the best-matching CAD model and its associated camera-to-object poses. Note: This silhouette-based consensus registration is coarsely accurate (median rotation error ~6.2°, position error ~18.6% on SCO-CAD). 2. Scene Initialization: Position the selected CAD mesh at the intersection of the cameras' viewing directions. Rescale the mesh to cover the same surface area as the ground-truth masks. Anchor 3D Gaussian primitives to the surface of the retrieved CAD model. 3. Geometric Warmup (Mask Alignment): Optimize pose and deformation against silhouette signals before appearance optimization begins. Purpose: Prevents texture fitting to misregistered surfaces. Without this, reconstruction collapses (PSNR 18.88, IoU 0.784). 4. Joint Optimization: Simultaneously optimize three components: 1. 3DGS Parameters: Standard 3DGS optimization (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). 2. Camera-to-Object Registration: Refine the initial poses using a global Sim(3) transformation (or per-camera corrections for datasets with inaccurate calibration like MVMC). 3. Non-Rigid Deformation Field D\theta: A network that "wraps" the CAD mesh onto the physical observation, accounting for shape differences due to machining tolerances, wear, or design variations. 5. Regularization: SH Neighbor Smoothness: Pull each splat’s SH coefficients toward those of its 20 canonical-neighbor splats to remove high-frequency color changes in unobserved views. Splat Dropout: Ensure splats occluded in training views but visible in held-out views still receive an optimization signal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cadsplattraining(images, silhouettes, cadlibrary, numviews): # Step 1: Retrieve CAD model and initial poses bestcadmodel, initialposes = matchsilhouettes(images, silhouettes, cadlibrary) # Step 2: Initialize Scene # Position mesh at intersection of viewing directions, rescale to match mask area cadmesh = initcadmesh(bestcadmodel, images) gaussians = anchorgaussianstomesh(cadmesh) # Initialize deformation network and pose parameters deformationnet = initdeformationnetwork() poseparams = initposeparams(initialposes) # Step 3: Geometric Warmup # Optimize pose and deformation using only silhouette loss for warmupstep in range(WARMUPITERATIONS): deformedmesh = applydeformation(cadmesh, deformationnet) renderedsilhouettes = rendersilhouettes(deformedmesh, poseparams) lossmask = computesilhouetteloss(renderedsilhouettes, silhouettes) optimize(deformationnet, poseparams, lossmask) # Step 4: Joint Optimization for step in range(TOTALITERATIONS): deformedmesh = applydeformation(cadmesh, deformationnet) # Render Gaussians renderedimages, rendereddepths = rendergaussians(gaussians, deformedmesh, poseparams) # Photometric Loss lossphoto = computephotometricloss(renderedimages, images) # Regularization: SH Neighbor Smoothness # For each gaussian, find 20 canonical neighbors and pull SH coefficients lossshsmooth = computeshsmoothnessloss(gaussians, numneighbors=20) # Regularization: Splat Dropout # Randomly drop splats to ensure visibility in held-out views lossdropout = computedropoutloss(gaussians, renderedimages, images) # Total Loss loss = lossphoto + lambdash lossshsmooth + lambdadropout lossdropout # Update all parameters optimize(gaussians, deformationnet, poseparams, loss) return gaussians, poseparams, deformationnet def applydeformation(mesh, net): # For each vertex v in mesh, compute displacement d = net(v) # Return new mesh with vertices v + d pass def anchorgaussianstomesh(mesh): # Sample points on mesh surface # Initialize Gaussian positions at these points # Initialize covariances based on local surface geometry pass Parameters: Input View Count: Fewer than 15 views. Performance degrades gracefully to as few as 3 views. SH Neighbors: 20 canonical neighbors for smoothness regularization. Camera Calibration: Wide-baseline, posed images. Poses are not necessarily pre-calibrated perfectly; they are refined during optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CAD Mismatch: The matched CAD model rarely matches the physical object perfectly. Without the deformation field, the system treats the CAD model as rigid, causing ghosting. Misregistration: Silhouette-based registration is only coarsely accurate. Without the geometric warmup phase, texture is fitted to a misregistered surface, and geometry never recovers. View Count Sensitivity: CAD initialization is superior to generic sphere initialization in sparse regimes (e.g., 3 views). However, with 9-13 views, sphere initialization becomes competitive or slightly superior, as photometric signals are rich enough for the deformation field to carve the object. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On SCO-CAD with 3 views, CAD initialization yields PSNR 20.710 vs 19.312 for sphere, and IoU 0.929 vs 0.879. On SCO-CAD full budget, sphere initialization yields PSNR 23.535 vs 23.239 for CAD, and IoU 0.946 vs 0.942. Deformation alone (no pose opt) achieves PSNR 22.92 and IoU 0.941, within 0.3 dB of the full method. Pose optimization alone (no deformation) achieves PSNR 22.67. Without mask alignment, reconstruction collapses to PSNR 18.88 and IoU 0.784. SH neighbor smoothness increases PSNR from 22.93 to 23.13 and reduces mLPIPS from 0.039 to 0.032. On NeRS MVMC dataset, CADSplat achieves PSNR 18.7, SSIM 0.767, LPIPS 0.157, outperforming NeRS (PSNR 16.5) and CADSim (PSNR 17.7). Scaling: The method is designed for sparse views. The CAD prior becomes more meaningful as views become scarcer. Strengths: Provides geometric disambiguation under occlusion and scarcity. Enables applications beyond novel-view synthesis, such as markerless AR registration and part label transfer. Limitations: Requires a CAD model library or a specific CAD model. Performance degrades if the CAD model is a poor match for the physical object (though deformation helps). When to use: Sparse-view reconstruction of objects with available CAD models. When not to use: Dense-view reconstruction where generic initialization is competitive. Objects without CAD models. CADSplat was introduced in 2026 by researchers from the Digital Future Lab, Flanders Make, Hasselt University, Belgium. The method addresses the challenge of reconstructing digital twins from sparse, wide-baseline images by leveraging explicit CAD priors, contrasting with learned generative priors. CADSplat: Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting Aided by CAD Models for Robust, Photorealistic Digital-Twin Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18473, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Perceptual Wrapper
head: Perceptual Wrapper for 3DGS, Perceptual Wrapper with Common Randomness
body: The Perceptual Wrapper (PW) is a plug-and-play 2D module that enhances the rendered outputs of existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by synthesizing high-frequency texture details in a content- and view-dependent manner. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS in rendering sharp textures, particularly under memory-constrained or rate-distortion-optimized (RDO) pipelines where blurriness is exacerbated. Unlike methods that modify the 3D primitive densification or loss functions directly (e.g., Perceptual-GS), PW operates as a post-processing synthesis network in the image domain, conditioned on pseudo-random Gaussian noise and Plücker embeddings, and is trained using Wasserstein Distortion (WD) loss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base rendered image I{base}^{vj} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W} from view vj, a multi-scale pseudo-random Gaussian noise pyramid C, and per-pixel 6D Plücker embeddings P^{vj} \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times H \times W}. Output: A residual texture detail map R^{vj} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}, which is added to the base image to produce the final output I{final}^{vj}. Data Structures: 1. Base Rendered Image (I{base}^{vj}): The standard 3DGS rendering result for view vj. 2. Noise Pyramid (C): An 8-level spatial pyramid C = \{Ci\}{i=0}^7. Level Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{2^i} \times \frac{W}{2^i}}. C0 has dimensions H \times W. Values are sampled independently from a standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1). The same fixed random seed is used for all views and between training/decoding (common randomness). 3. Plücker Embeddings (P^{vj}): A 6-channel tensor where each pixel (x,y) contains the vector P(x,y) = (d, o \times d). Synthesis Network Architecture: The network f\theta is lightweight, similar to the COOL-CHIC family: 1. Concatenate inputs: I{base}^{vj}, C (upsampled to H \times W via bilinear interpolation), and P^{vj}. 2. Two 1 \times 1 convolutional layers. 3. Two 3 \times 3 residual convolutional layers. 4. Output: R^{vj}. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Plücker Embeddings: For each pixel (x,y) in the target view vj, calculate the normalized viewing direction d and the moment vector o \times d: d = \frac{R K^{-1}[x,y,1]^T}{\|R K^{-1}[x,y, 1]^T\|} \in \mathbb{R}^3 where K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the camera intrinsic matrix, R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the camera-to-world rotation matrix, and o \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the camera center in world coordinates. 2. Generate Noise Pyramid: Using a fixed random seed, generate the 8-level noise pyramid C. Values are drawn from \mathcal{N}(0, 1). This noise is view-consistent and shared across encoding/decoding. 3. Render Base Image: Render the scene using the current 3DGS representation to obtain I{base}^{vj}. 4. Upsample Noise: Bilinearly upsample each level Ci of the noise pyramid to the resolution H \times W. 5. Synthesis Forward Pass: Process the concatenated inputs through the synthesis network f\theta to generate the residual: R^{vj} = f\theta(\{I{base}^{vj}, C, P^{vj}\}) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. 6. Reconstruct Final Image: Add the residual to the base image: I{final}^{vj} = I{base}^{vj} + R^{vj}. Training Procedure: The training is a two-stage, per-scene optimization process: 1. Stage 1 (Warm-up, Iterations 0–14,999): Optimize the underlying 3DGS representation only. Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{3DGS-D} + \mathcal{L}{Reg} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{rate} (if applicable). The synthesis network is inactive. Duration: 15,000 iterations. This ensures stable densification and pruning of Gaussian primitives before introducing the wrapper. 2. Stage 2 (Joint Optimization, Iteration 15,000+): Activate the synthesis network. Replace \mathcal{L}{3DGS-D} with Wasserstein Distortion \mathcal{L}{WD}. Jointly optimize the synthesis network parameters \theta and the 3DGS representation. Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{WD}(I{final}^{vj}, I{gt}^{vj}) + \mathcal{L}{Reg} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{rate} \mathcal{L}{WD} is evaluated between the reconstructed image I{final}^{vj} and ground truth I{gt}^{vj} across training views. Parameters: Stage 1 Iterations: 15,000. Noise Distribution: Standard Normal \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Pyramid Levels: 8 (i=0 to 7). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimization Instability: Directly optimizing the full pipeline with WD loss from the start can destabilize 3DGS training, especially if Gaussian densification/pruning are still evolving. The two-stage approach mitigates this. View Consistency: The noise must be view-consistent (fixed across views) to ensure coherent texture synthesis for novel views. Time Complexity: The synthesis network is lightweight (two 1\times1 and two 3\times3 conv layers), incurring negligible overhead to rendering speed. Memory Complexity: Adds minimal memory overhead for the synthesis network weights and the noise pyramid (which is generated on-the-fly from a seed, requiring no storage of noise parameters). Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, the lowest-rate point achieved by PW attained an Elo score on par with the highest-rate point of baseline methods (CAT-3DGS Pro and HAC++), corresponding to a 6x reduction in bit-rate at equivalent perceptual quality. Strengths: Plug-and-play compatibility with any existing 3DGS representation; effective at mitigating blurriness in highly textured regions under bandwidth constraints; view-dependent texture synthesis. Limitations: Requires a two-stage training process; relies on a fixed random seed for noise generation. When to use: When perceptual quality is prioritized over strict pixel-wise fidelity, or when operating under strict storage/transmission bandwidth constraints. When not to use: When strict photometric accuracy (e.g., PSNR) is the primary metric, as WD loss optimizes for perceptual similarity rather than pixel-wise error. The Perceptual Wrapper was introduced by H.-B. Yang et al. in the paper "Seeing What Matters: Perceptual Wrapper with Common Randomness for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitations of previous perceptual methods like Perceptual-GS, which used sensitivity-guided densification and conventional L1/SSIM losses. PW leverages insights from image and video compression communities regarding objective quality metrics that correlate with human perception, specifically using Wasserstein Distortion. It was implemented in PyTorch and tested on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs, evaluated on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets. name: Inverse and Internal Rendering
head: GS-IR, Inner 3D Gaussian Splatting, Internal View Synthesis, Volumetric Plane-Based Gaussian Selection
body: Inverse and Internal Rendering extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to solve problems where standard surface-based supervision is insufficient: estimating physical properties from unknown lighting (Inverse Rendering) and reconstructing occluded internal structures from sparse, pose-free data (Internal Rendering). Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes for camera-visible surfaces, this family enables photorealistic relighting via baked occlusion caches and volumetric inference via conditional 2D splatting or plane-based Gaussian selection. The methods share the core 3D Gaussian representation defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details, where each primitive i is defined by mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, opacity \alphai, and color ci. The rendering equation for a pixel remains the standard alpha-compositing formula: I(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^{N} pi(u, v, t)\alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(u, v, t)\alphaj) where pi is the screen-space density contribution. However, the optimization targets and geometric constraints diverge significantly from standard surface reconstruction. GS-IR is a plane-based internal rendering framework that replaces exterior-view supervision with cross-sectional supervision sampled from a volume to reconstruct internal volumetric structure. It is applied to 3DGS, 2DGS, and Mip-Splatting without modifying their rasterizers. Definition and Steps: 1. Virtual cameras define slicing planes within the volume. 2. A binary mask selects the Gaussian subset whose centers lie within the plane thickness. 3. The selected Gaussian subset is rendered using the original Gaussian rasterizer. 4. Optimization is performed against ground-truth cross-sections generated through trilinear resampling. 5. Distance-aware soft weighting is applied to continuously attenuate Gaussian opacity as the distance from the Gaussian to the plane increases. Parameters: Plane thickness: The spatial extent within which Gaussian centers are selected by the binary mask. Performance: Improves PSNR by up to 21.52 dB and SSIM by up to 0.54 on KiTS23 CT and IXI MRI datasets. Comparison: Unlike conventional 3DGS which constrains camera-visible surfaces, GS-IR focuses optimization gradients on interior Gaussians to supervise occluded internal regions. This procedure efficiently captures global illumination by updating 3D Gaussians using path-traced renderings, combined with albedo-shading decomposition. Steps: 1. Utilize path-traced renderings to efficiently update 3DGS and capture global illumination effects. 2. Apply albedo-shading decomposition strategy to separate intrinsic scene properties for efficient global illumination capture. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents scenes with anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized from multi-view images and rendered through differentiable rasterization and alpha compositing. Conventional 3DGS training primarily constrains camera-visible surfaces, whereas occluded interior regions remain insufficiently supervised. In medical imaging, internal view synthesis requires cross-sectional images from volumetric CT and MRI datasets at arbitrary plane orientations and spatial positions. GS-IR investigates whether Gaussian primitives can reconstruct internal volumetric structure under cross-sectional supervision. For inverse rendering, NeRF-based methods use implicit neural representations and ray tracing (backward mapping), which suffer from low expressive power and high computational complexity. GS-IR addresses the specific challenges of applying 3DGS to inverse rendering: the lack of native plausible normal generation and the inability of forward mapping to trace occlusion for indirect lighting. It estimates scene geometry, surface material, and environment illumination from multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. Inner 3D Gaussian Splatting (InnerGS) solves the problem of reconstructing internal volumes from slice-based inputs (e.g., medical imaging or material scans) where camera poses and projection matrices are unavailable. Unlike standard 3DGS, which relies on camera projection and tends to concentrate Gaussians on object surfaces leaving interiors empty, InnerGS uses Conditional Splatting to adaptively determine Gaussian influence per depth slice. It explicitly factorizes the 3D density into conditional 2D splats and a marginal 1D depth Gaussian, enabling tile-based rasterization without external camera parameters. name: GS-IR
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, Inverse Rendering with Gaussians
body: GS-IR is an inverse rendering approach based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that leverages forward mapping volume rendering to achieve photorealistic novel view synthesis and relighting results. It estimates scene geometry, surface material, and environment illumination from multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. Unlike NeRF-based inverse rendering methods that use implicit neural representations and ray tracing (backward mapping), which suffer from low expressive power and high computational complexity, GS-IR uses 3D Gaussians and forward mapping splatting for real-time rendering efficiency. It addresses the specific limitations of 3DGS in inverse rendering: the lack of native plausible normals and the inability of forward mapping to trace occlusion for indirect lighting. The GS-IR framework consists of three stages: an initial stage for geometry reconstruction, a second stage for occlusion precomputation, and a final stage for material and illumination optimization. Inputs: Multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians representing geometry, material (albedo, metallic, roughness), and an environment map for illumination. The method builds on the 3D Gaussian representation defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details. Each primitive i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} Opacity \alphai Color ci Additionally, GS-IR defines additional material parameters on each Gaussian to represent texture. These include Albedo, Metallic, and Roughness. Lighting is approximated by a learnable environment map. The initial stage optimizes 3D Gaussians for geometry reconstruction using differentiable splatting. A key challenge is that 3DGS does not support producing plausible normals natively, and its adaptive control of Gaussian density may lead to loose geometry, making accurate scene normal estimation difficult. To address this, GS-IR introduces a depth-derivation-based regularization strategy. 1. Render the depth map \hat{D} using differentiable splatting. 2. Compute pseudo-normals \hat{n}{\hat{D}} from the depth gradient: \hat{n}{\hat{D}} = \nabla{uv} \hat{D} where \nabla{uv} denotes the gradient in the image plane. 3. Use these pseudo-normals to supervise the optimization of normals stored within the 3D Gaussians. Forward mapping (e.g., rasterization and splatting) cannot trace occlusion like backward mapping (e.g., ray tracing), making it difficult to calculate occlusion for indirect lighting. To address this, GS-IR uses a baking-based method embedded in the pipeline to cache occlusions into volumes. 1. Precompute occlusion based on the learned geometric information (depth and normal) from Stage 1. 2. Store the occlusion data in a spherical harmonics-based architecture to model indirect illumination. This approach is inspired by the "Indirect Lighting Cache" used in real-time rendering. The final stage combines differentiable splatting with a physically-based rendering (PBR) pipeline. 1. Optimize illumination (environment map) and material-aware 3D Gaussians. 2. The rendering equation for a pixel remains the standard alpha-compositing formula: I(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^{N} pi(u, v, t)\alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(u, v, t)\alphaj) where pi is the screen-space density contribution. 3. The color ci is now derived from the PBR pipeline using the material parameters (albedo, metallic, roughness) and the estimated environment illumination. Normal Estimation: 3DGS does not natively produce plausible normals. The depth-derivation regularization is required to mitigate this. Occlusion: Forward mapping cannot trace occlusion. The baking-based method is a necessary workaround. Geometry Looseness: Adaptive control of Gaussian density may lead to loose geometry, complicating normal estimation. Efficiency: GS-IR achieves real-time rendering efficiency by using 3D Gaussians and forward mapping splatting, contrasting with the high computational complexity of NeRF-based methods. Scene Scope: Unlike TensoIR, which leverages ray tracing of NeRF to directly model occlusion and indirect illumination but is limited to object-level scenes, GS-IR handles occlusion via baking and is available for both objects and unbounded scenes. Expressiveness: The flexible and expressive 3DGS representation allows for fast and compact geometry reconstruction. GS-IR is the first work to introduce the 3DGS technique for inverse rendering, simultaneously estimating scene geometry, materials, and illumination from multi-view images. It was proposed by researchers from the School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Tencent. The source code is available at https://github.com/lzhnb/GSIR.
