name: 3D Difference-of-Gaussians (3D-DoG)
head: 3D Difference-of-Gaussians (3D-DoG) primitive, 3D-DoG
body: 3D Difference-of-Gaussians (3D-DoG) is a volumetric primitive variant designed to enhance the representation of fine geometric details and edges in compact 3D Gaussian Splatting models. It solves the limitation of standard smooth Gaussian kernels, which struggle to capture high-frequency details when the number of primitives is aggressively reduced. Unlike standard 3D Gaussians that only contribute positive density, the 3D-DoG models both positive and negative spatial responses, allowing it to implement color subtraction in \alpha-blending to sharpen boundaries. It is distinct from sibling optimization techniques like DeSplat or TurboGS by introducing a specific mathematical primitive structure rather than altering the rendering pipeline or training schedule directly. The 3D-DoG primitive is defined as the difference between a primary Gaussian G(\mathbf{x}) and a pseudo-Gaussian Gp(\mathbf{x}). The primary Gaussian retains standard parameters, while the pseudo-Gaussian shares the same center coordinates but has modified opacity and scale parameters. Input: The parameters of the primary 3D Gaussian \mathbf{G} (center \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}{color}) and the new learnable parameters for the pseudo-Gaussian. Output: A composite primitive that renders with a positive-density lobe and a negative-density ring, effectively subtracting color from overlapping regions to enhance contrast. The 3D-DoG primitive extends the standard 3D Gaussian parameter set with four additional learnable parameters per primitive: 1. Opacity factor: f\alpha 2. Scaling factors: f{xs}, f{ys}, f{zs} These parameters are typically initialized to values less than 1.0. The 3D-DoG primitive \text{DoG}(\mathbf{x}) is calculated as: \text{DoG}(\mathbf{x}) = G(\mathbf{x}) - Gp(\mathbf{x}) Where G(\mathbf{x}) is the primary Gaussian and Gp(\mathbf{x}) is the pseudo-Gaussian. The pseudo-Gaussian Gp(\mathbf{x}) shares the same center and rotation as G(\mathbf{x}) but uses a different scaling matrix \mathbf{S}p and opacity \alphap. The scaling matrix \mathbf{S}p is calculated by element-wise multiplication of the primary Gaussian's scaling matrix and the transpose of the pseudo-Gaussian's scaling factors matrix: \mathbf{S}p = \begin{bmatrix} sx & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} f{xs} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & f{ys} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & f{zs} \end{bmatrix}^T Note: Since the scaling factors matrix is diagonal, the transpose operation does not change the matrix structure, but the formula explicitly denotes the element-wise product of the primary scales and the factors. The opacity \alphap of the pseudo-Gaussian is calculated as: \alphap = f\alpha \cdot \alpha Where \alpha is the opacity of the primary Gaussian. f\alpha: Opacity factor for the pseudo-Gaussian. Set to values less than 1.0. f{xs}, f{ys}, f{zs}: Scaling factors for the pseudo-Gaussian. Set to values less than 1.0. These four parameters are learnable during optimization. 1. Pruning Phase: Perform standard 3D Gaussian densification and pruning. The 3D-DoG is not introduced during initial densification. 2. Activation: After the pruning process finishes, activate 3D-DoG primitives in the compact model. This is done by enabling the parameters [f{xs}, f{ys}, f{zs}] and \alphap for all primitives. 3. Optimization: Continue training with the same loss functions. The primary Gaussian and pseudo-Gaussian parameters are jointly optimized. 4. Density Control: Evaluate \alphap across all primitives to identify those with the lowest values, which indicate marginal impact of the pseudo-Gaussian representation. 5. Degeneration: If \alphap falls below a predefined threshold (or reaches 0), the 3D-DoG degenerates into a standard 3D Gaussian, as the negative component vanishes. 6. Proportion Optimization: Optimize the overall proportion of 3D-DoG primitives in the point cloud after pruning. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Gaussian3DDoG: def init(self, primarygaussian, falpha, fxs, fys, fzs): """ Initialize a 3D-DoG primitive. Args: primarygaussian: Object containing standard 3D Gaussian params (center, rotation, scale, opacity, color) falpha: Opacity factor for pseudo-Gaussian (< 1.0) fxs, fys, fzs: Scaling factors for pseudo-Gaussian (< 1.0) """ self.primary = primarygaussian self.falpha = falpha self.fxs = fxs self.fys = fys self.fzs = fzs # Calculate pseudo-Gaussian parameters # Sp = diag(sx, sy, sz) diag(fxs, fys, fzs)^T # Since diagonal, this is element-wise multiplication self.pseudoscalex = primarygaussian.scalex fxs self.pseudoscaley = primarygaussian.scaley fys self.pseudoscalez = primarygaussian.scalez fzs # alphap = falpha alpha self.pseudoopacity = falpha primarygaussian.opacity # Pseudo-Gaussian shares center and rotation with primary self.pseudocenter = primarygaussian.center self.pseudorotation = primarygaussian.rotation def evaluate(self, x): """ Evaluate the 3D-DoG primitive at point x. DoG(x) = G(x) - Gp(x) """ # Evaluate primary Gaussian G(x) gprimary = self.primary.evaluate(x) # Evaluate pseudo-Gaussian Gp(x) # Gp uses same center/rotation but different scale and opacity gpseudo = Gaussian3D( center=self.pseudocenter, rotation=self.pseudorotation, scale=(self.pseudoscalex, self.pseudoscaley, self.pseudoscalez), opacity=self.pseudoopacity, color=self.primary.color # Color is typically shared or derived).evaluate(x) return gprimary - gpseudo def isstandardgaussian(self): """ Check if the 3D-DoG has degenerated to a standard Gaussian. This occurs when alphap is effectively 0. """ return self.pseudoopacity <= 0.0 Degeneration: When \alphap = 0, the 3D-DoG becomes equivalent to a standard 3D Gaussian. This is a valid state and should be handled by the renderer to avoid unnecessary computation of the negative component. Negative Density: The negative-density component implements color subtraction in \alpha-blending. Implementers must ensure the rendering pipeline supports negative opacity contributions or subtracts colors appropriately during compositing. Activation Timing: 3D-DoG is only introduced after the pruning phase, not during initial densification. Activating it too early may destabilize training or lead to suboptimal primitive distribution. Computational Overhead: 3D-DoG introduces additional computational overhead compared to standard Gaussians. It is recommended for compact models where the benefit of sharper details outweighs the cost. Time Complexity: Increases per-primitive rendering cost due to the evaluation of two Gaussians (primary and pseudo) and their subtraction. Memory Complexity: Adds 4 learnable parameters (f\alpha, f{xs}, f{ys}, f{zs}) per primitive. Performance: Improves reconstruction quality for fine details and edges in compact models. It allows sharper structures to be preserved under aggressive pruning. Strengths: Enhances boundary and texture representation; more responsive to fine geometric details than standard Gaussians. Limitations: Higher computational cost; not beneficial for smooth regions where standard Gaussians suffice; requires careful tuning of the pruning schedule to activate at the right time. When to use: In compact 3D Gaussian Splatting models where memory is constrained but high-frequency detail preservation is critical. When not to use: In initial training phases or when the model is not being aggressively pruned, as the overhead may not be justified. The 3D Difference-of-Gaussians (3D-DoG) primitive was introduced in the paper "Prune Wisely, Reconstruct Sharply: Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting via Adaptive Pruning and Difference-of-Gaussian Primitives". It addresses the limitations of compact 3D Gaussian Splatting, where standard smooth Gaussian kernels fail to capture fine details after aggressive pruning. The method is part of a broader framework that includes a Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler (RPS) and Spatio-spectral Pruning Score (SPS). name: Hardware and Computational Acceleration
head: 3DGS Acceleration, 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization
body: This family addresses the computational bottlenecks in the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering and training pipelines, specifically targeting the memory-bound front-end (projection and sorting) and the compute-bound rasterization stage [12180]. It sets itself apart from generic optimization by employing hardware-aware strategies, such as leveraging Tensor Cores via GEMM transformation, and algorithmic innovations like comparison-free sorting [12180], index-parity sharding [15108], and cache-based lazy memory management [17592] to overcome single-GPU memory and compute limits. The 3DGS rendering pipeline consists of two primary stages, each with distinct optimization goals [12180]: 1. Front-End (Memory-Bound): Projection and Sorting: 3D Gaussians are projected to 2D, generating a depth key for each. To ensure correct alpha compositing, Gaussians must be sorted front-to-back (increasing depth) within each image tile. Attribute Fetching: For each Gaussian-pixel pair, attributes (opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients) are fetched from global memory. Optimization Goal: Reduce global memory traffic and bandwidth usage. This is achieved by compressing data (quantization, key compression) and fusing kernels to avoid intermediate writes [12180]. 2. Rasterization (Compute-Bound): Alpha Compositing: The final pixel color C is computed via alpha blending: C = \sum{i=1}^N ci \alphai Ti, \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is the color, \alphai is the opacity, and Ti is the transmittance [12180]. Gaussian Evaluation: The opacity \alphai for a pixel at (x,y) relative to a Gaussian center (u,v) is computed as [12180]: \alphai = o \exp(p(x, y)) where o is the base opacity and p(x, y) is the Gaussian power: p(x, y) = -\frac{1}{2} \left( a(x - w)^2 + b(x - u)(y - v) + c(y - v)^2 \right) Here, a, b, c are derived from the projected 2D covariance matrix, and (w, v) are the center coordinates [12180]. Optimization Goal: Increase instruction-level parallelism (ILP) and reduce expensive operations (like exp) within the per-pixel loop [12180]. For distributed training, the global set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} is partitioned across M GPUs. Each GPU maintains a local shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)} and its optimizer state. The training loop involves local projection of the shard, communication (e.g., all-to-all exchange) to route Gaussians to responsible GPUs, filtering via importance scoring or pruning, and local rasterization with gradient updates [15108]. Addresses the computational bottlenecks in the 3DGS rendering pipeline, specifically targeting the memory-bound front-end (projection and sorting) and the compute-bound rasterization stage [12180]. It sets itself apart from generic optimization by employing hardware-aware strategies, such as the Roofline model to identify resource constraints, and algorithmic innovations like comparison-free sorting to reduce synchronization overhead. Distributed training and sharding partition the global set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} and optimizer states across M GPUs to enable city-scale optimization that exceeds single-GPU memory and compute limits. Unlike spatial block partitioning, which suffers from cross-block visibility waste, imbalanced shards, and expensive merge steps, BlitzGS uses index-parity sharding combined with all-to-all communication to route Gaussians to responsible tiles, ensuring balanced loads without final merging. Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting is a multi-GPU extension of the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) pipeline designed for scientific visualization, enabling the scalable processing of large datasets that exceed the memory capacity of a single GPU. Unlike standard 3D-GS which operates on a single device, this method distributes the optimization of Gaussian primitives across multiple GPUs using a data-parallel approach adapted from Grendel-GS, allowing for high-resolution reconstruction of complex scientific isosurfaces. It sets itself apart by bypassing image-based reconstruction in favor of direct initialization from volume data, specifically targeting the memory bottlenecks encountered when handling millions of Gaussians in HPC environments. Cache-based Lazy Memory Management (CLM) is a memory offloading system that enables the training of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes on a single consumer-grade GPU by exploiting the inherent sparsity of memory access patterns. Unlike naive offloading strategies that load the entire scene representation to the GPU, CLM keeps Gaussians in CPU memory and loads only the subset accessed by the current view, overlapping communication with computation to hide latency. This approach allows training scenes with over 100 million Gaussians on hardware with limited VRAM, such as the NVIDIA RTX 4090, without requiring multi-GPU setups or compromising rendering quality. Cache-Less Memory (CLM) is a system design that enables the training and rendering of large or highly detailed 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes on a single consumer-grade GPU by offloading non-critical Gaussian parameters and optimizer state to the CPU. It solves the GPU memory bottleneck inherent in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging attribute-wise offloading, microbatch pipelining, and spatial locality to minimize GPU-CPU communication overhead. Unlike sibling methods that focus on compression or hierarchical structures, CLM retains full precision by keeping selection-critical attributes (position, rotation, scale) in GPU memory for frustum culling while moving color and opacity to CPU memory. Definition An acceleration approach for 3D Gaussian Splatting that utilizes Tensor Cores on GPUs by reformulating the blending process into a GEMM-compatible form. Step Transform the conventional 3DGS blending process into a GEMM-style formulation equivalently to leverage Tensor Cores. Develop a CUDA kernel implementing the transformed blending process, designed as a three-stage double-buffered pipeline with asynchronous memory copy to overlap computation and memory access. Parameter Tile size: The 2D screen is divided into tiles, with 16x16 pixels mentioned as an example. Thread block size: Rendering a 16x16 tile is assigned to a thread block of 256 threads. Layout Gaussian features computed in preprocessing include depth d and RGB color c. Number GEMM-GS achieves an average 1.42× speedup over vanilla 3DGS implementation. GEMM-GS provides an additional 1.47× speedup when combined with existing acceleration approaches. Comparison GEMM-GS is orthogonal to existing acceleration methods (compression-based or preprocessing-based), allowing it to provide additional speedup when combined with them. Origin: GEMM-GS was introduced in 2026 to address the lack of General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) operations in the standard 3DGS pipeline, which overlooks the evolving Tensor Cores of modern GPUs. Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting targets scientific visualization, adapting data-parallel approaches from Grendel-GS to handle large datasets [16979]. Cache-based Lazy Memory Management addresses the VRAM limitations of consumer-grade GPUs for large-scale scenes [17592]. RoofGS is an end-to-end acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that optimizes the rendering pipeline by aligning software strategies with hardware bottlenecks identified via the Roofline model. It solves the problem of uncoordinated optimization in 3DGS, where different stages are constrained by different resources (memory bandwidth vs. compute throughput). It sets itself apart from generic optimization by explicitly using the Roofline model to identify the "knee" point and applying memory-centric optimizations to stages below it and compute-centric optimizations to stages near it. See RoofGS. Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting restricts depth sorting operations to individual tiles to avoid global synchronization, reduce hardware complexity, and achieve fixed latency per output. Unlike global radix sort, which incurs high memory traffic and variable latency due to histograms and prefix sums, this method provides deterministic O(N) cycles suitable for low-power hardware accelerators. It serves as the sorting mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting, ensuring Gaussians are ordered front-to-back for correct alpha compositing within each tile. See Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting. Optimize static Gaussians for the initial 3000 iterations as a warm-up phase. Jointly optimize both the Gaussians and the deformation field after the warm-up phase. Total loss L = Lcolor + λ1 Lscales, where Lcolor is the color loss and λ1 is a weighting factor. λ1: Weight for the scale loss, set to 0.1. λv: Weight for another loss term (value 0.2), though its specific definition is not detailed in this excerpt. Changing the default white background (RGB 1.0) to a gray value to improve training speed while maintaining rendering quality. Background value bg: The three same values for RGB background channels. Optimal range is 0.3 ≤ bg ≤ 0.5. Changing the background must be balanced; while it improves speed, extreme values may negatively impact learning rate, training loss, and PSNR states. On the truck dataset with 500 training steps, setting bg=0.4 reduces pc time by approximately 21.85% compared to the default white background. A sorting-free rendering method that uses a transmittance proxy enriched with view-dependent modulation. Pixel color C = (1 - T) \sum{i=1}^N \frac{ci \alphai + T ci bg}{\sum{i=1}^N \alphai wi} + T ci bg. Weight wi = \phii^2 + \frac{\phii}{di^2} + \exp \left( \frac{x{max}}{di} \right). T is transmittance, ci is color, \alphai is opacity, bg is background color, di is depth, \phii is auxiliary feature from MLP, x{max} is a constant. Unlike SortFreeGS which uses Gaussian depth but not scale, Mobile-GS exploits both depth and scale attributes to compute importance weight, reflecting that farther Gaussians have lower contribution and larger Gaussians provide more meaningful evidence. Unlike GES which uses a two-stage rendering pipeline (depth image then filtering), Mobile-GS is single-stage and better suited for mobile deployment. The optimization of the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline has evolved to address the high memory bandwidth requirements of sorting and the computational cost of per-pixel Gaussian evaluation. Early implementations relied on standard radix sorts, which were later refined by hardware-specific approaches like RoofGS and comparison-free sorting. Concurrently, training efficiency improvements, such as background color tuning and specific loss weighting, have been integrated into the pipeline. Mobile-oriented variants like Mobile-GS have further explored sorting-free alternatives to enable real-time rendering on resource-constrained devices. name: RoofGS
head: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: RoofGS is an end-to-end acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that optimizes the rendering pipeline by aligning software strategies with hardware bottlenecks identified via the Roofline model. It solves the problem of uncoordinated optimization by applying memory-centric reductions to bandwidth-limited front-end stages and compute-centric instruction-level parallelism (ILP) to compute-bound rasterization stages. It sets itself apart from generic optimization by explicitly using the Roofline "knee" to dictate whether a stage should prioritize memory traffic reduction or arithmetic throughput. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each defined by center \mathbf{t}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity o, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH}. Camera parameters (view/projection matrices). Output: Rasterized 2D image pixels. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Compressed to reduce memory footprint. For third-degree SHs (D{SH}=3), the baseline requires 192 bytes per Gaussian (48 coefficients \times 4 bytes). RoofGS uses low-bit quantization with a single shared scale for all SH coefficients. Depth Keys: Compressed dynamic keys for sorting. Tile Data: Intermediate buffers for front-end fusion. Numbered Steps: 1. Front-End Fusion (Memory-Bound Optimization): Compact Attribute Storage: Quantize SH coefficients to reduce global memory traffic. Instead of storing full-precision coefficients, store quantized values with a shared scale factor. Dynamic Depth-Key Compression: Compress the depth keys used for sorting to reduce memory bandwidth usage during the projection and sorting phase. Cross-Stage Kernel Fusion: Fuse the projection, sorting, and attribute fetching kernels to avoid writing intermediate data to global memory. This reduces the dominant global memory traffic in bandwidth-bound stages. 2. Rasterization Reorganization (Compute-Bound Optimization): Dual-Pixel ILP: Reformulate the per-pixel Gaussian evaluation to increase instruction-level parallelism inside the blending loop. Fast Exponential Evaluation: Optimize the computation of the Gaussian power and opacity to reduce arithmetic overhead. Formulas: The Gaussian power p(x, y) for a pixel at (x, y) relative to a Gaussian center (u, v) is computed as: p(x, y) = -\frac{1}{2} \left( a(x - w)^2 + b(x - u)(y - v) + c(y - v)^2 \right) where a, b, c are derived from the projected 2D covariance matrix, and (w, v) are the center coordinates. Note: The source uses (u, v) for center and (w, v) in the formula; standard notation typically aligns center as (u, v) and uses (x-u, y-v). The unclamped opacity contribution is then computed as: \tilde{\alpha}(x, y) = o \exp(p(x, y)) where o is the base opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def roofgsrender(gaussians, camera): # 1. Front-End: Memory-Bound Optimization # Project Gaussians to 2D and compute depth keys projected = [] for g in gaussians: # Project center and covariance center2d, cov2d = project2d(g.center, g.cov, camera) depth = g.center.z # Or projected depth projected.append({ 'center': center2d, 'cov': cov2d, 'depth': depth, 'opacity': g.opacity, 'shcoeffs': quantizesh(g.shcoeffs) # Low-bit compression }) # Sort Gaussians front-to-back using compressed keys # Cross-stage fusion: combine sorting with attribute fetching sortedgaussians = sortfronttoback(projected, key='depth') # 2. Rasterization: Compute-Bound Optimization # Initialize output image image = zeroslike(targetresolution) # Process each tile for tile in tiles: # Fetch Gaussians relevant to the tile tilegaussians = gettilegaussians(sortedgaussians, tile) # Process pixels in the tile with Dual-Pixel ILP for y, x in tile.pixels: # Accumulate color and alpha color = vec3(0) alpha = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for g in tilegaussians: # Compute Gaussian power dx = x - g.center.x dy = y - g.center.y # a, b, c derived from g.cov p = -0.5 (a dx2 + b dx dy + c dy2) # Fast exponential evaluation alphag = g.opacity fastexp(p) # Alpha compositing color += g.color alphag transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - alphag) alpha += alphag transmittance # Early exit if transmittance is negligible if transmittance < epsilon: break image[tile.y, tile.x] = color return image Parameters: SH Degree (D{SH}): Typically 3, requiring 48 coefficients per Gaussian. Quantization Scale: Single shared scale for all SH coefficients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: Quantizing SH coefficients may introduce color artifacts if the scale is not chosen carefully. Depth Key Compression: Aggressive compression may lead to sorting errors if depth precision is insufficient. A methodology that uses stage-wise performance characterization to match optimization strategies to the dominant hardware constraints of the baseline pipeline, by reducing intermediate data movement in the front end and reducing arithmetic overhead in rasterization. It solves the problem of uncoordinated software optimization in volume rendering contexts, where different stages of the rendering pipeline are bottlenecked by different hardware resources (memory bandwidth vs. compute throughput). It sets itself apart from generic optimization by explicitly using the Roofline model to identify the "knee" point and applying memory-centric optimizations to stages below it and compute-centric optimizations to stages near it. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Reduced due to low-bit Gaussian-attribute compression and dynamic depth-key compression. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces dominant global memory traffic in bandwidth-bound stages and increases ILP in compute-bound stages. Limitations: Relies on accurate Roofline characterization; quantization may affect visual quality. When to use: When rendering 3DGS on hardware where memory bandwidth and compute throughput are distinct bottlenecks. When not to use: When hardware bottlenecks are not aligned with the Roofline model's assumptions. RoofGS was introduced in the paper "RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds on prior roofline analyses [13, 43, 44] which showed that the rasterization stage of 3DGS is compute-bound. The method organizes the rendering pipeline according to a stage-specific optimization principle: bandwidth-limited stages prioritize reductions in global memory traffic, whereas compute-intensive stages prioritize lower instruction cost and increased instruction-level parallelism (ILP). name: Roofline-guided stage-wise optimization
body: Roofline-guided stage-wise optimization is a methodology that uses stage-wise performance characterization to match optimization strategies to the dominant hardware constraints of the baseline pipeline, by reducing intermediate data movement in the front end and reducing arithmetic overhead in rasterization. It solves the problem of uncoordinated software optimization in volume rendering contexts, where different stages of the rendering pipeline are bottlenecked by different hardware resources (memory bandwidth vs. compute throughput). It sets itself apart from generic optimization by explicitly using the Roofline model to identify the "knee" point and applying memory-centric optimizations to stages below it and compute-centric optimizations to stages near it. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Baseline 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipeline stages, hardware specifications (peak compute throughput P{\text{peak}}, memory bandwidth BW), and kernel execution traces. Output: An optimized pipeline where specific stages are modified to address their identified bottlenecks. Data Structures: Sorting Key: A dynamic 32-bit integer packing the tile index and quantized depth. Attributes: Compressed spherical harmonics (SH) and geometric attributes. Method Steps: 1. Roofline Characterization: For each stage in the rendering pipeline, calculate the arithmetic intensity I and the achievable performance P using the Roofline model. P = \min(P{\text{peak}}, BW \cdot I) \quad (1) Where: P{\text{peak}} is the peak compute throughput of the hardware. BW is the memory bandwidth of the hardware. I is the arithmetic intensity, defined as operations divided by data movement (I = F/B). 2. Identify Bottleneck Regime: Compare the stage's arithmetic intensity I to the hardware's balance point (knee) I{\text{knee}}. I{\text{knee}} = \frac{P{\text{peak}}}{BW} \quad (2) If I \ll I{\text{knee}}, the stage is bandwidth-bound (memory traffic sensitive). If I \approx I{\text{knee}}, the stage is compute-bound (arithmetic overhead sensitive). 3. Apply Front-End Optimizations (Bandwidth-Limited Stages): For stages identified as bandwidth-bound (typically preprocessing and sorting): Compress SH and geometric attributes to reduce memory footprint. Pack tile index and quantized depth into a single dynamic 32-bit sorting key to reduce intermediate data movement. Fuse preprocessing, tile duplication, and key generation into a single kernel to minimize global memory traffic. 4. Apply Rasterization Optimizations (Compute-Limited Stages): For stages identified as compute-bound (typically rasterization): Evaluate two adjacent pixels simultaneously to increase instruction-level parallelism (ILP). Replace standard exponential operations with a bit-level approximation tailored to alpha-thresholded blending to reduce arithmetic overhead. Parameters: Hardware Balance Point (I{\text{knee}}): On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, P{\text{peak}} = 82.6 \text{ TFLOPS} and BW = 1008 \text{ GB/s}, resulting in I{\text{knee}} \approx 81.9 \text{ FLOPS/Byte}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The bit-level approximation in rasterization must be carefully calibrated to maintain visual fidelity while reducing arithmetic cost. Kernel Fusion: Fusing too many stages may exceed register limits or warp occupancy thresholds, potentially degrading performance. Workload Scaling: Optimizations tuned for a specific Gaussian count may not scale linearly; the total-frame speedup can be non-monotonic due to auxiliary overheads not eliminated by the primary optimization path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rooflineguidedoptimization(stages, Ppeak, BW): """ Applies Roofline-guided optimizations to a rendering pipeline. Args: stages: List of stage objects with 'name', 'flops', 'bytes' attributes. Ppeak: Peak compute throughput (TFLOPS). BW: Memory bandwidth (GB/s). Returns: optimizedstages: List of optimized stage configurations. """ Iknee = Ppeak / BW optimizedstages = [] for stage in stages: # Calculate arithmetic intensity Istage = stage.flops / stage.bytes if Istage < Iknee: # Bandwidth-bound: Optimize for memory traffic reduction stage.attrs = compressshandgeometry(stage.attrs) stage.sortkey = packtileindexanddepth(stage.tileidx, stage.quantdepth) stage.kernel = fusepreprocesstiledupkey(stage) else: # Compute-bound: Optimize for arithmetic intensity/ILP stage.pixelproc = evaltwoadjacentpixels(stage.pixelproc) stage.blendop = bitlevelalphaapprox(stage.blendop) optimizedstages.append(stage) return optimizedstages def compressshandgeometry(attrs): """Compress spherical harmonics and geometric attributes to reduce memory footprint.""" return quantizeandpack(attrs, bits=16) def packtileindexanddepth(tileidx, quantdepth): """Pack tile index and quantized depth into a single dynamic 32-bit sorting key.""" return (tileidx << 16) | (quantdepth & 0xFFFF) def fusepreprocesstiledupkey(stage): """Fuse preprocessing, tile duplication, and key generation into a single kernel.""" return stage.mergekernels(['preprocess', 'tiledup', 'keygen']) def evaltwoadjacentpixels(proc): """Evaluate two adjacent pixels simultaneously to increase instruction-level parallelism.""" return proc.processwarppair() def bitlevelalphaapprox(blend): """Replace standard exponential operation with a bit-level approximation tailored to alpha-thresholded blending.""" return blend.replaceexpwithbitwiseapprox() A diagnostic method to isolate how sort/reordering and raster stages behave as Gaussian workload increases, using a fixed high-workload view from the bicycle scene. It synthetically scales the workload from 5M to 30M Gaussians and measures median-of-5 timings under a locked RTX 4090 timing-only protocol. At 30M emitted entries, the sort stage improves by 1.71x and the raster stage by 1.42x compared to the baseline. At 5M points, Base Sort is 1.051ms, TileGS Sort is 0.387ms (2.72x speedup); Base Raster is 2.277ms, TileGS Raster is 1.554ms (1.46x speedup). At 30M points, Base Sort is 5.709ms, TileGS Sort is 3.340ms (1.71x speedup); Base Raster is 7.980ms, TileGS Raster is 5.603ms (1.42x speedup). The total-frame speedup is smaller and not monotonic because the diagnostic includes non-raster and auxiliary overheads not eliminated by the binned raster path. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory usage is reduced in the front end due to attribute compression and key packing. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, the FP32-DRAM balance point is approximately 81.9 FLOPS/Byte. In the Synthetic Scale-Up Stress Diagnostic, TileGS showed consistent improvements in sort and raster stages as workload increased. Scaling: The absolute timing gaps between optimized and baseline stages widen with scale. The total-frame speedup is not monotonic and is smaller than individual stage speedups due to auxiliary overheads. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Tailors optimizations to specific hardware bottlenecks, leading to significant speedups in critical stages. Limitations: The total-frame speedup may be limited by non-optimized auxiliary overheads. The method requires detailed hardware-specific knowledge (e.g., P{\text{peak}}, BW). When to use it: When optimizing a rendering pipeline for a specific hardware target where different stages have distinct bottlenecks. When memory bandwidth is a significant constraint in the front end. When not to use it: When the pipeline is uniformly compute-bound or memory-bound across all stages, as the stage-wise differentiation offers less benefit. When hardware specifications are unknown or highly variable. Roofline-guided stage-wise optimization is part of the RoofGS framework, presented in "RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the Roofline model to identify dominant bottlenecks in the 3DGS rendering pipeline. The method addresses the limited attention to coordinated software optimization across the whole rendering pipeline in prior work. It is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering acceleration. name: Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting
head: Comparison-Free Depth Sorting, Tile-Local Sorting
body: Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting restricts depth sorting operations to individual image tiles to avoid global synchronization, reduce hardware complexity, and achieve fixed latency per output. Unlike full-scene sorting methods that incur high memory overhead and variable latency due to global scans and prefix sums, this method processes Gaussians locally within tiles using a deterministic, comparator-free algorithm. It is specifically designed for hardware accelerators where predictable scheduling and low power consumption are critical, such as in AR/VR rendering pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians projected into 2D, each associated with a tile identifier and a depth value. The depth values are non-negative (near-plane culling excludes points with depth < 0). Output: The Gaussians sorted front-to-back (increasing depth) within each tile, ready for alpha compositing. Data Structures: Sorting Key: A tuple \langle \text{tile-id}, \text{depth} \rangle. Element Vector Table (EVT): A binary vector of size N used to track the status of elements. Initialized to all 1s, indicating all elements are unsorted. An element is marked as sorted (removed from consideration) by setting its corresponding bit to 0. Bit Width (n): The number of bits used to represent the depth value. Algorithm Steps: The sorting process identifies the Largest Element (LE) iteratively N times. For each iteration, the LE is removed from the unsorted set, and the process repeats until the EVT is all 0s. 1. Initialization: Initialize the EVT of size N with all bits set to 1. 2. Concurrent Phase (Bitwise Filtering): Process the N elements in k parallel clusters. Iterate through the bits of the depth value from the Most Significant Bit (MSB) to the Least Significant Bit (LSB). Sign Bit Handling: Skip the sign bit operation because near-plane culling ensures depth is always non-negative (sign bit is always 0). For each bit position, filter out elements that are smaller than the current candidate maximum using bitwise AND operations and multiplexer-based selection within cascaded blocks. 3. Sequential Phase (Refinement): Pass the outputs from the concurrent phase clusters to a linear array of k cascaded blocks. Further refine the selection to identify the single Largest Element (LE) among the currently unsorted elements (those with EVT bit = 1). 4. Data Conflict Resolution (Duplicate Handling): If multiple elements have the same maximum depth value, the EVT might return multiple "1"s, leading to ambiguity. Resolve conflicts using bitwise inverter, bitwise AND, and an adder to uniquely identify one instance. Compute the new flag FO{NEW} to update the EVT: FO{NEW} = Fo \ \& \ (\sim Fo + 1'b1) where Fo is the current flag vector. This operation isolates the least significant bit of the conflict set, ensuring deterministic selection of one element among duplicates. 5. Update and Iterate: Set the bit corresponding to the identified LE in the EVT to 0. Repeat steps 2–4 until the EVT contains all 0s, indicating all N elements are sorted. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilebasedcomparisonfreesort(gaussians, nbits): """ Sorts Gaussians within a tile using comparison-free sorting. gaussians: List of objects with attributes.depth (n-bit integer) and.id. nbits: Number of bits in the depth representation. Returns: List of Gaussians sorted by depth (front-to-back). """ N = len(gaussians) if N == 0: return [] # EVT tracks unsorted elements: 1 means unsorted, 0 means sorted evt = [1] N sortedgaussians = [] # Iterate N times to extract one element per cycle for in range(N): leindex = -1 ledepth = -1 # Concurrent Phase: Find candidate Largest Element (LE) # We simulate the hardware logic: filter by bits from MSB to LSB # Note: Sign bit is skipped as depth >= 0 # Initialize candidates as all unsorted elements candidates = [i for i in range(N) if evt[i] == 1] if not candidates: break # Iterate from MSB (nbits-1) down to 0 for bitpos in range(nbits - 1, -1, -1): if not candidates: break # Filter candidates based on the current bit # We want to keep candidates that have the '1' bit if possible, # or if no '1' bits exist, keep those with '0'. # In hardware, this is done via bitwise AND and MUX selection. hasone = False for idx in candidates: if (gaussians[idx].depth >> bitpos) & 1: hasone = True break if hasone: # Keep only those with bit set to 1 candidates = [idx for idx in candidates if (gaussians[idx].depth >> bitpos) & 1] else: # Keep only those with bit set to 0 candidates = [idx for idx in candidates if not ((gaussians[idx].depth >> bitpos) & 1)] # Sequential Phase: Resolve conflicts if multiple candidates remain # Hardware uses FONEW = Fo & (~Fo + 1) to pick the LSB of the conflict set # Here, we pick the first candidate (deterministic) to match the logic of # isolating a single element. if candidates: # In hardware, the conflict resolution logic ensures a unique LE is picked # even if depths are identical. We pick the first one for simulation. leindex = candidates[0] ledepth = gaussians[leindex].depth # Update EVT: Mark this element as sorted evt[leindex] = 0 # Add to sorted list sortedgaussians.append(gaussians[leindex]) return sortedgaussians Parameters: N: Number of Gaussians in the tile. n: Bit width of the depth value. k: Number of parallel clusters (hardware-dependent). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Depths: The algorithm must handle duplicate depth values. The conflict resolution logic (FO{NEW}) is critical to ensure deterministic selection and avoid errors in the final result. Sign Bit: The sign bit is always 0 due to near-plane culling. Ignoring it reduces computational complexity. Variable N: The number of Gaussians per tile varies significantly. The algorithm must handle arbitrary N without fixed-size buffers that assume a maximum scene complexity. A tile-based, comparison-free sorting algorithm that uses an Element Vector Table (EVT) to identify the largest element in O(N) deterministic cycles, avoiding the high memory overhead of radix sort. It employs concurrent and sequential phases with bitwise operations to filter elements, making it suitable for hardware implementation where low gate count and predictable latency are required. Time Complexity: O(N) deterministic cycles for sorting N elements. Hardware Complexity: Low gate count compared to radix sort, which requires parallel scans and prefix sums. Latency: Fixed per-output latency, avoiding the latency spikes associated with global synchronization in full-scene sorting. Performance: Achieves full-HD rendering at 129 FPS, offering 3× higher throughput and 5.98× smaller area compared to prior 3DGS accelerators like GSCore. Strengths: Predictable scheduling, low power consumption, suitability for AR/VR hardware, and efficient handling of variable Gaussian counts per tile. Limitations: Requires hardware-specific implementation for optimal performance; software simulation may not reflect the true parallel efficiency. The method originates from research into hardware accelerators for 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically addressing the bottleneck of depth sorting in real-time rendering. Traditional sorting methods like radix sort are resource-intensive and suffer from variable latency, making them unsuitable for low-power AR/VR hardware. The tile-based comparison-free approach builds on parallel comparison-free algorithms [21, 22] (cited in) but adds optimizations such as sign bit skipping and conflict resolution for duplicate values. It was implemented in a hardware accelerator that demonstrated significant improvements in throughput and area efficiency over previous designs like GSCore [10]. name: Distributed Training and Sharding
head: Distributed 3DGS, Multi-GPU Sharding
body: Distributed training and sharding partition the global set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} and optimizer states across M GPUs to enable city-scale optimization that exceeds single-GPU memory and compute limits. Unlike spatial block partitioning, which suffers from cross-block visibility waste, imbalanced shards, and expensive merge steps, BlitzGS uses index-parity sharding combined with all-to-all communication to route Gaussians to responsible tiles, ensuring balanced loads without final merging. The rendering pipeline of 3DGS consists of two primary stages, each with distinct optimization goals [12180]: 1. Front-End (Memory-Bound): Projection and Sorting: 3D Gaussians are projected to 2D, generating a depth key for each. To ensure correct alpha compositing, Gaussians must be sorted front-to-back (increasing depth) within each image tile. Attribute Fetching: For each Gaussian-pixel pair, attributes (opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients) are fetched from global memory. Optimization Goal: Reduce global memory traffic and bandwidth usage. This is achieved by compressing data (quantization, key compression) and fusing kernels to avoid intermediate writes [12180]. 2. Rasterization (Compute-Bound): Alpha Compositing: The final pixel color C is computed via alpha blending: C = \sum{i=1}^N ci \alphai Ti, \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is the color, \alphai is the opacity, and Ti is the transmittance [12180]. Gaussian Evaluation: The opacity \alphai for a pixel at (x,y) relative to a Gaussian center (u,v) is computed as [12180]: \alphai = o \exp(p(x, y)) where o is the base opacity and p(x, y) is the Gaussian power: p(x, y) = -\frac{1}{2} \left( a(x - w)^2 + b(x - u)(y - v) + c(y - v)^2 \right) Here, a, b, c are derived from the projected 2D covariance matrix, and (w, v) are the center coordinates [12180]. Optimization Goal: Increase instruction-level parallelism (ILP) and reduce expensive operations (like exp) within the per-pixel loop [12180]. For distributed training, the global set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} is partitioned across M GPUs. Each GPU maintains a local shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)} and its optimizer state. The training loop involves local projection of the shard, communication (e.g., all-to-all exchange) to route Gaussians to responsible GPUs, filtering via importance scoring or pruning, and local rasterization with gradient updates [15108]. BlitzGS is a distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework designed to accelerate city-scale training by reducing the active Gaussian workload at three coupled levels: system-level sharding, model-level population control, and view-level filtering. Unlike spatial block partitioning which suffers from cross-block visibility waste and imbalanced shards, BlitzGS shards Gaussians by index parity and uses a single all-to-all communication step to distribute rendering tiles, ensuring balanced loads without a final merge step. It achieves nearly an order-of-magnitude speedup over baselines like Momen.GS and CityGS-X while maintaining high reconstruction quality. GS-Cache is a holistic rendering framework designed to support real-time rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models at the city level, achieving >72 FPS at binocular 2K resolution. It addresses the computational bottleneck of the "Gaussian Derivation Stage" in structured Gaussian methods (e.g., Scaffold-GS, Octree-GS) by employing a cache-centric de-redundancy pipeline. Unlike native 3DGS or unstructured methods, GS-Cache specifically targets structured representations where anchors derive neural Gaussians, optimizing inter-frame redundancy in parameter decoding while maintaining rasterization quality. Definition: A hardware architecture co-designed with the LS-Gaussian algorithm to support workload-aware mapping, featuring a streaming pipeline that allows continuous processing across hardware modules without requiring global synchronization. Step: The accelerator predicts the workload for each tile based on viewpoint transformation to enable more balanced parallel computation. Comparison: Unlike naive assignment of tiles to rendering blocks which fails to achieve balanced load distribution, this architecture uses workload prediction to mitigate inter-block idling and intra-block bubbles. Definition: Divides the scene into fixed world-space spatial blocks (e.g., uniform grid). Each GPU is bound to a specific block and trains its Gaussians independently. Step: Construct a uniform grid (e.g., 4×5 or 5×6). Assign each block a boundary halo of neighboring Gaussians for cross-block consistency. Train blocks independently across GPUs. During rendering, cameras near block boundaries trigger cross-block visibility overlap and boundary reassignment. Perform a final single-GPU merge to assemble the full scene. Pitfall: Overlapping blocks re-optimize the same surfaces, wasting computation. In a 20-block split, 23.5M Gaussians are optimized but only 5.37M survive merge (77% discarded). Finer partitions increase redundancy and training time with negligible quality gain (<0.2 dB). Number: On Building (1,920 cameras, 4 GPUs), 86.8% of cameras fall in ≥2 blocks for 20-block partition, and 95.5% for 30-block partition. Wall-clock time for split/make-span/merge reaches 115.6–169.8 min vs 39 min for sharding. Definition: Distributes a single global Gaussian model across multiple GPUs by assigning Gaussians to ranks based on index parity. Each GPU holds a balanced, scene-wide slice of the model. Step: Assign each Gaussian primitive to a GPU rank using index parity. During rendering, distribute each step through balanced tile allocation across GPUs. Route projected Gaussians to tile owners via all-to-all communication. Train using a single global camera stream. Each camera enters training once per iteration with no cross-block duplication. Only distributed cost is the all-to-all exchange inside each render step. Number: On a 4-GPU setup (Building scene, 1,920 cameras), communication cost for routing projected Gaussians to tile owners is 3–5 ms per iteration, staying under 7% of total iteration time. Comparison: Unlike spatial block partitioning, it eliminates boundary reassignment, cross-block visibility overlap, and the final single-GPU merge step. Storage and per-step rendering remain evenly distributed as GPU count grows. Originating from the need to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to city-scale scenes, distributed training methods evolved from naive spatial partitioning to sophisticated index-parity sharding. Spatial block partitioning was found to be inefficient due to boundary overlaps and merge costs. BlitzGS introduced index-parity sharding to eliminate these issues, achieving significant speedups. Concurrently, LS-Gaussian focused on hardware-aware streaming and workload prediction to reduce stalls in real-time rendering. name: BlitzGS
head: BlitzGS: City-Scale Gaussian Splatting at Lightning Speed
body: BlitzGS is a distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework designed to accelerate city-scale training by reducing the active Gaussian workload at system, model, and view levels. Unlike spatial block partitioning which suffers from cross-block redundancy and imbalance, BlitzGS shards Gaussians by index parity and couples this with importance-based pruning and distance-based Level-of-Detail (LOD) filtering. It achieves nearly an order-of-magnitude speedup over baselines like Momen.GS and CityGS-X while maintaining high reconstruction quality. Inputs: A set of calibrated images, an initial set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, and M GPUs. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients) and a rendered novel view. Data Structures: Global Gaussian Set \mathcal{G}: Partitioned into shards \mathcal{G}^{(m)} for each GPU m \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}. Sharding Strategy: Gaussians are assigned to GPU m based on index parity: even indices to one subset of GPUs, odd indices to the other, ensuring balanced distribution without spatial locality constraints. Tile Ownership: The image plane is divided into tiles. Each tile is assigned to a specific GPU. Algorithm Steps: 1. System-Level Sharding and Distribution: Partition \mathcal{G} into shards \mathcal{G}^{(m)} such that GPU m stores approximately |\mathcal{G}|/M Gaussians based on index parity. Each GPU m projects its local shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)} to 2D screen space. Perform a single all-to-all communication step to route projected Gaussians to the GPUs responsible for the tiles they cover. 2. Model-Level Population Control: Importance Scoring: Compute an importance score for each Gaussian based on its contribution to the loss or gradient magnitude. Pruning: Remove Gaussians with low importance scores to reduce redundant primitives. Spawn Gating: Before spawning new Gaussians (e.g., via densification), evaluate a lightweight gate. If the candidate is predicted not to survive (low importance), withhold it from spawning. Gradient Reweighting: Use the importance signal to reweight density control gradients during optimization. 3. View-Level Filtering: Distance-Based LOD Gate: For each camera, drop Gaussians that are too fine (small scale) relative to the camera distance, as they contribute negligible detail. Importance-Based Mask: Skip Gaussians with negligible cross-view contribution during rasterization. 4. Rasterization and Optimization: Each GPU composites pixels for its assigned tiles using the received Gaussians. Compute loss and backpropagate gradients. Update Gaussian parameters using the optimizer state maintained locally on each GPU. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blitzgstraining(images, initialgaussians, numgpus, numiterations): # 1. Initialization # Shard Gaussians by index parity shards = partitionbyparity(initialgaussians, numgpus) optimizerstates = [createoptimizerstate(shard) for shard in shards] for iteration in range(numiterations): # 2. System-Level: Projection and Communication projectedgaussians = [] for m in range(numgpus): # Project local shard proj = project2d(shards[m], images[iteration].camera) projectedgaussians.append(proj) # All-to-all exchange: route Gaussians to tile owners # Each GPU receives Gaussians covering its assigned tiles receivedgaussians = alltoallexchange(projectedgaussians) # 3. Model-Level: Population Control # Compute importance scores for all active Gaussians importancescores = computeimportance(receivedgaussians, optimizerstates) # Prune low-importance Gaussians activegaussians = prunebyimportance(receivedgaussians, importancescores) # Spawn gating: evaluate new candidates before adding candidates = densificationcandidates(activegaussians) survivingcandidates = spawngate(candidates, importancescores) activegaussians = merge(activegaussians, survivingcandidates) # 4. View-Level: Filtering # Distance-based LOD: drop too-fine Gaussians filteredgaussians = applylodgate(activegaussians, images[iteration].camera) # Importance mask: skip negligible contributors finalgaussians = applyimportancemask(filteredgaussians, importancescores) # 5. Rasterization # Each GPU renders its tiles renderedimages = [] for m in range(numgpus): # Render tiles owned by GPU m tileimages = rasterizetiles(finalgaussians, images[iteration].camera, m) renderedimages.append(tileimages) # 6. Optimization # Compute loss and update loss = computeloss(renderedimages, images[iteration].groundtruth) gradients = backward(loss) # Reweight gradients by importance reweightedgradients = reweightgradients(gradients, importancescores) # Update optimizer states for m in range(numgpus): updateoptimizer(optimizerstates[m], reweightedgradients[m]) shards[m] = optimizerstates[m].getparameters() return shards Parameters: Hardware: 4x NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Sharding: Index parity (even/odd). LOD Threshold: Not given in the sources. Importance Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Imbalanced Shards: Spatial block partitioning can lead to imbalanced shards due to varying scene density. Index parity sharding avoids this. Cross-Block Visibility: Spatial partitioning causes visibility waste at block boundaries. Index parity sharding eliminates this need for a final merge step. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced. On the Rubble scene, BlitzGS takes 39 minutes compared to 5 hours 3 minutes for Momen.GS and 4 hours 45 minutes for CityGS-X. Memory Complexity: By pruning redundant Gaussians and gating spawns, the peak population of Gaussians is limited, reducing memory usage per GPU. Performance: Achieves scene-average PSNR of 24.66 dB on Residence and 33.79 dB on Rubble. Strengths: Near order-of-magnitude speedup on city-scale scenes; avoids cross-block redundancy; balanced load distribution. Limitations: Requires all-to-all communication; effectiveness depends on the accuracy of the importance scoring and spawn gating. When to use: Large-scale, city-scale 3DGS training where speed is critical and high-quality reconstruction is required. When not to use: Small-scale scenes where the overhead of distributed communication and complex filtering may not be justified. BlitzGS was introduced by Zhongtao Wang, Huishan Au, Yisong Chen, Meng Gai, Yilong Li, Fei Zhu, Mai Su, Haojie Jin, and Guoping Wang in the paper "BlitzGS: City-Scale Gaussian Splatting at Lightning Speed". The work addresses the high computational cost of city-scale 3DGS training, which involves preprocessing, communication, and rasterization of overly dense primitive sets. It builds on insights from prior work on distributed 3DGS. BlitzGS: City-Scale Gaussian Splatting at Lightning Speed, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.13794, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: GS-Cache Inference Framework
head: GS-Cache
body: GS-Cache is a holistic rendering framework designed to support real-time rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models at the city level, achieving >72 FPS at binocular 2K resolution by using a cache-centric de-redundancy pipeline and elastic parallel scheduling. It specifically targets 'Structured Gaussian derivation methods' (like Scaffold-GS and Octree-GS) which use anchors to derive neural Gaussians, addressing the bottleneck of the 'Gaussian Derivation Stage' (decoding anchor features) which dominates computation time. Unlike native 3DGS or unstructured methods, GS-Cache optimizes the derivation stage by caching decoded parameters, while leaving the rasterization stage uncached to preserve visual quality against occlusion changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera pose (view/projection matrices), structured 3DGS model (anchors, MLP weights, anchor features), previous frame's cache state. Output: Rendered image (binocular 2K), updated cache state. Data Structures: Cache: Stores decoded Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients) indexed by anchor ID. The layout is not explicitly defined in the sources, but it maps anchor indices to Gaussian parameters. Anchor Set (X): The set of anchors required for decoding in the current frame. Newly Decoded Anchors (Xk'): The subset of anchors from X that were not found in the cache or required re-decoding from the previous k frames. Steps: 1. Binocular De-redundancy: Process camera inputs to identify unique view frustums, reducing redundant anchor queries for binocular rendering. 2. Anchor Filtering: Compute anchor indices from the camera input. Filter the global anchor set to identify X, the anchors necessary for the current frame. 3. Index Mapping: Translate anchor indices to cache indices to locate existing Gaussian parameters in the cache. 4. Cache Scheduling: The cache scheduler loads necessary model parameters (MLP weights) for anchors not in the cache. It determines which anchors need decoding based on the cache hit/miss status. 5. Dynamic Cache Depth Scheduling: Calculate the expected reuse depth using the heuristic function H and the update rate: \text{depth} = H\left(\frac{|Xk'|}{|X|}\right) where |Xk'| is the number of newly decoded anchors from the previous k frames, and |X| is the total anchor set for decoding in the current frame. The function H adjusts the depth of reuse and cached parameters according to the intensity of decoding calculations. 6. Anchor Decoding (Derivation Stage): For anchors in the cache: Retrieve cached Gaussian parameters. For anchors not in the cache: Decode anchor features into neural Gaussian parameters using the MLP (weights \theta). Update the cache with newly decoded parameters. Flush cache entries that have exceeded the dynamic reuse depth to prevent significant rendering errors due to viewpoint changes. 7. Gaussian Rasterization (Rasterization Stage): Project the decoded 3D Gaussians to 2D. Perform alpha compositing to generate the final image. This stage is not accelerated by caching because slight perspective changes significantly affect occlusion, and caching here would degrade visual quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gscacherender(camerapose, model, prevcache, k, Hfunc): # 1. Binocular De-redundancy and Anchor Filtering uniqueviewfrustums = binocularderedundancy(camerapose) anchorindices = computeanchorindices(uniqueviewfrustums, model) X = filteranchors(anchorindices, model) # Anchors needed for current frame # 2. Index Mapping and Cache Lookup cacheindices = maptocacheindices(anchorindices) cachedparams = prevcache.get(cacheindices) # 3. Identify Newly Decoded Anchors (from previous k frames logic) # Note: Xk' is defined as newly decoded anchors from previous k frames. # In implementation, this likely tracks anchors that were decoded recently. # For the current frame's update rate calculation, we need the count of # anchors that will be newly decoded or were recently decoded. # The source defines |Xk'| as "newly decoded anchors from the previous k frames". # We assume a tracking mechanism exists for this count. numrecentlydecoded = getrecentlydecodedcount(k) # 4. Dynamic Cache Depth Scheduling updaterate = numrecentlydecoded / len(X) expectedreusedepth = Hfunc(updaterate) # 5. Cache Scheduling and Decoding # Load MLP weights if not already loaded mlpweights = model.getmlpweights() newgaussians = {} for anchorid in X: if anchorid in cachedparams: # Hit: Use cached parameters gaussian = cachedparams[anchorid] else: # Miss: Decode anchor features anchorfeature = model.getanchorfeature(anchorid) gaussian = anchordecoder(anchorfeature, mlpweights) newgaussians[anchorid] = gaussian # 6. Update Cache # Flush old entries based on expectedreusedepth prevcache.flush(expectedreusedepth) # Insert new/updated entries prevcache.update(newgaussians) # 7. Rasterization (Uncached) # Project all Gaussians (cached + new) projectedgaussians = projectgaussians(gaussians, camerapose) # Sort and Rasterize image = rasterize(projectedgaussians) return image, prevcache Parameters: k: The number of previous frames from which newly decoded anchors (Xk') are considered for the update rate calculation. H: The guiding function of the heuristic cache reuse depth scheduling strategy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewpoint Correlation: Neural Gaussian appearance has viewpoint correlation. Reusing cached results without restraint can cause rendering errors (e.g., around centered targets). The dynamic cache depth scheduling suppresses rapid appearance changes caused by cache flushing. Occlusion Sensitivity: The rasterization stage cannot be cached because occlusion changes significantly with slight perspective shifts. Caching rasterization results would degrade visual quality. Performance: Achieves an average frame rate exceeding 72 FPS at binocular 2K resolution for large-scale city-level scenes. Complexity: The framework reduces inter-frame redundancy in the derivation stage, which is the dominant computation time for structured Gaussian derivation methods. Strengths: Enables real-time photo-realistic rendering of large-scale 3DGS models, particularly for VR applications requiring binocular stereo. It is model-agnostic regarding the specific pipeline structure, relying on a heuristic strategy. Limitations: Specifically targets structured Gaussian derivation methods (Scaffold-GS, Octree-GS). name: Distributed Batched Rendering Loop
head: Distributed 3DGS Rendering Loop
body: The Distributed Batched Rendering Loop is a parallelized training and inference pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that processes multiple camera views simultaneously across a cluster of GPUs. It solves the memory and compute bottlenecks of single-GPU training by partitioning the global set of 3D Gaussians and distributing the rendering workload, enabling high-resolution and large-scale scene reconstruction. Unlike standard single-view rendering, this method employs dynamic load balancing and sparse all-to-all communication to ensure efficient data distribution and aggregation across distributed ranks. The method iterates over a dataset of camera poses in fixed-size batches, coordinating data movement and computation across multiple GPU devices. Inputs: dataset: A collection of camera poses and associated ground-truth images. gaussians: The global set of 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonic coefficients) partitioned across GPUs. args.bsz: The batch size, defining the number of camera views processed per iteration. args.samplefreq: Frequency for saving rendered images (if not -1). args.generatenum: Maximum number of images to generate. Outputs: Rendered images for the batched cameras, aggregated and saved to disk. batchedcameras: A list or tensor containing the camera parameters (extrinsics, intrinsics) for the current batch. batchedstrategies: A data structure defining the workload division, specifying which GPU handles which part of the rendering task for the current batch. gpuid2tasks: A mapping from GPU ID to the specific rendering tasks assigned to that GPU. batchedscreenspacepkg: A preprocessed data structure holding the 3DGS data and screenspace packages required for the distributed rendering kernel, generated after the all-to-all communication step. 1. Batch Initialization: Iterate through the cameras in steps of args.bsz. Calculate the number of cameras to load for the current iteration, ensuring the last batch does not exceed the dataset size. 2. Camera Fetching: Retrieve the batch of camera parameters from the dataset. 3. Strategy Calculation: Compute the workload division and map rendering tasks to specific GPUs based on the current batch and historical strategy data. 4. Camera Data Transfer: Transfer the camera parameters from CPU memory to the global memory of all participating GPUs according to the calculated strategy. 5. Preprocessing and Communication: Preprocess the 3DGS data for the current batch. Execute a sparse all-to-all communication operation across all GPUs. This step routes the relevant 3D Gaussians to the GPUs responsible for rendering the pixels they affect, based on the dynamic load balancing strategy. The output is batchedscreenspacepkg. 6. Rendering: Execute the distributed rendering kernel using batchedscreenspacepkg and batchedstrategies to generate the batched images. 7. Aggregation: If multiple GPUs are involved (utils.DEFAULTGROUP.size() > 1), perform a sum reduction (torch.distributed.allreduce) to aggregate the rendered images across all ranks. 8. Post-processing and Saving: Clamp the pixel values to the valid range [0.0, 1.0] and save the images to disk, respecting the args.samplefreq and args.generatenum constraints. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.distributed as dist import torchvision.utils numcameras = len(dataset) idx = 1 while idx <= numcameras: # Step 1: Calculate batch size numcameratoload = min(args.bsz, numcameras - idx + 1) # Step 2: Fetch cameras batchedcameras = dataset.getbatchedcameras(numcameratoload) # Step 3: Compute workload division batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks = startstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory) # Step 4: Transfer camera data to GPUs loadcamerafromcputoallgpuforeval(batchedcameras, batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks) # Step 5: Preprocess and All-to-All Communication batchedscreenspacepkg = distributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal( batchedcameras, gaussians, pipeline, background, batchedstrategies=batchedstrategies, mode="test") # Step 6: Render batchedimage, = renderfinal(batchedscreenspacepkg, batchedstrategies) # Step 7: Aggregate results if utils.DEFAULTGROUP.size() > 1: # Sum reduction across all ranks dist.allreduce(batchedimage, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, group=utils.DEFAULTGROUP) # Step 8: Clamp and Save image = torch.clamp(batchedimage, 0.0, 1.0) # Check if we should save based on frequency and limit if args.samplefreq != -1 and (idx % args.samplefreq == 0): if args.generatenum is None or (idx // args.samplefreq) <= args.generatenum: torchvision.utils.saveimage(image, f"render{idx}.png") idx += args.bsz args.bsz: Batch size for camera processing. Controls how many views are processed per iteration. args.samplefreq: Sampling frequency for saving renders. If not -1, only saves every args.samplefreq-th image. args.generatenum: Maximum number of images to generate before breaking the loop. Last Batch Size: The loop must handle the case where the total number of cameras is not divisible by args.bsz. The calculation min(args.bsz, numcameras - idx + 1) ensures the final batch is processed correctly without index out-of-bounds errors. Distributed Group Check: The aggregation step explicitly checks utils.DEFAULTGROUP.size() > 1 to avoid unnecessary communication overhead when running on a single GPU. Precision: Pixel values are clamped to [0.0, 1.0] after aggregation to handle potential floating-point inaccuracies or overflow during the sum reduction. Time Complexity: The rendering time is dominated by the all-to-all communication and the rasterization step. The batched approach allows for better GPU utilization by keeping the compute units busy while communication occurs or by overlapping them, reducing the per-image latency compared to sequential single-view rendering. Memory Complexity: By partitioning the 3D Gaussians across M GPUs, the memory requirement per GPU is reduced by approximately a factor of M, allowing for the training of scenes with tens of millions of Gaussians (e.g., 40.4 million Gaussians on 16 GPUs) that would not fit on a single GPU. Performance: On the "Rubble" dataset, distributing 40.4 million Gaussians across 16 GPUs achieved a test PSNR of 27.28, compared to 26.28 PSNR with 11.2 million Gaussians on a single GPU. This demonstrates that scaling up the number of Gaussians via distributed rendering improves visual quality. Strengths: Enables high-resolution and large-scale 3D reconstruction; supports batched training for improved learning rate scaling (sqrt(batch size) rule). Limitations: Requires complex communication overhead (all-to-all); dependent on the efficiency of the sparse communication implementation. It was developed to address the limitations of single-GPU training, which cannot handle high-resolution and large-scale 3D reconstruction tasks due to GPU memory capacity limits. The system relies on sparse all-to-all communication and dynamic load balancing to parallelize computation across multiple GPUs. name: Online Image Rendering Placement
head: Image patch placement, Online placement of image rendering
body: Online Image Rendering Placement is a per-iteration optimization step in distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting training that assigns image patches to GPUs to minimize inter-node communication and balance computational load. It differs from static graph partitioning by dynamically solving for the optimal data placement for each small training batch using a fast heuristic solver, rather than relying on offline pre-computed assignments. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The current batch of B image patches (derived from B training images), the global set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} partitioned across N GPUs, and the local shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)} on each GPU m. Outputs: A placement vector W, where Wj is the GPU ID assigned to render image patch j. Data Structures: Patch-GPU Access Pattern Matrix (A): A B \times N integer matrix where A{j,k} represents the number of 3D Gaussians required from GPU k to render image patch j. This is determined via frustum culling. Placement Vector (W): An array of length B storing GPU indices. Parameters: B: Batch size of training images. Typical value: 16–64. N: Number of GPUs. p: Granularity factor. Each H \times W image is divided into p^2 patches of size Hp \times Wp. Typical p: 2–8. \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta: Configurable coefficients for the objective function. Steps: 1. Frustum Culling: Each GPU k performs frustum culling on its local shard \mathcal{G}^{(k)} for every image patch j in the batch. It counts the number of visible Gaussians A{j,k} needed from its own memory. 2. Exchange Access Pattern: All GPUs exchange their local A{j,k} values to construct the global matrix A. 3. Initial Placement (LSA): Solve a Linear Sum Assignment (LSA) problem to minimize total communication volume. This provides an initial placement W{init}. 4. Local Search Refinement: Iteratively refine W{init} to balance load (send, receive, compute) using a greedy steepest-ascent strategy. Swaps are performed until convergence or a time budget is reached. 5. Hierarchical Assignment (Optional): For multi-node setups, first assign patches across machines, then assign patches within a machine to local GPUs. For intra-node assignment, set \alpha=0 to de-prioritize communication. Formulas: The optimization aims to minimize a relaxed objective function. The loads for GPU k are defined as: \text{send}k = \sum{j=1}^{B} [Wj \neq k] \cdot A{j,k} \text{recv}k = \sum{j=1}^{B} [Wj = k] \cdot \left( \sum{i=1}^{N} A{j,i} - A{j,k} \right) \text{comp}k = \sum{j=1}^{B} [Wj = k] \cdot \sum{i=1}^{N} A{j,i} Where [P] is the indicator function, returning 1 if predicate P is true, 0 otherwise. The relaxed objective for local search is: \beta \cdot \|\text{send}\|p + \gamma \cdot \|\text{recv}\|p + \delta \cdot \|\text{comp}\|p Where \|\text{send}\|p = \left( \sum{k=1}^{N} \text{send}k^p \right)^{1/p}, and similarly for recv and comp. The parameter p in the norm is distinct from the patch granularity p; typically p=2 or p=\infty is used for norms to smooth the non-smooth max terms. The original ILP formulation (solved heuristically) is: \text{minimize } \alpha \cdot \sum{j=1}^{B} \left( \sum{i=1}^{N} A{j,i} - A{j,Wj} \right) + \beta \cdot \maxk (\text{send}k) + \gamma \cdot \maxk (\text{recv}k) + \delta \cdot \maxk (\text{comp}k) Subject to: \sum{j=1}^{B} [Wj = k] = \frac{B}{N}, \quad \forall k \in \{1, \dots, N\} This constraint ensures each GPU renders exactly B/N patches, simplifying MPI-based system development. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def onlineimagerenderingplacement(batchpatches, globalgaussians, gpushards, numgpus, patchgranularity, alpha, beta, gamma, delta): """ batchpatches: List of B image patches. globalgaussians: Full set of 3D Gaussians (for reference, though shards are used). gpushards: Dict mapping GPU ID to local Gaussian shard. numgpus: N. patchgranularity: p (integer). alpha, beta, gamma, delta: Objective coefficients. Returns: W: List of GPU IDs for each patch, length B. """ B = len(batchpatches) # Step 1 & 2: Frustum Culling and Exchange # Each GPU computes its local Ajk and exchanges to form global A A = exchangeaccesspattern(batchpatches, gpushards, numgpus) # Step 3: Linear Sum Assignment for initial placement # Minimize total communication: sum(Aji - Aj,Wj) # This is equivalent to maximizing sum(Aj,Wj) # Construct cost matrix C where C[j, k] = -A[j, k] costmatrix = -A.T # Shape (N, B) or (B, N) depending on solver convention # Solve LSA (e.g., using Hungarian algorithm) # Result is a mapping from patches to GPUs Winit = solvelsa(costmatrix, B, numgpus) # Step 4: Local Search Refinement W = refineloadbalance(Winit, A, B, numgpus, beta, gamma, delta) return W def exchangeaccesspattern(patches, shards, numgpus): """ Performs frustum culling on each GPU and gathers the access matrix A. A[j, k] = number of gaussians from GPU k needed for patch j. """ B = len(patches) A = zeros((B, numgpus), dtype=int) # Parallel execution on each GPU for k in range(numgpus): shard = shards[k] for j, patch in enumerate(patches): # Frustum culling logic # 1. Transform patch bounding box to world space or gaussians to clip space. # 2. Count gaussians in shard that intersect the patch frustum. count = frustumcullcount(shard, patch) A[j, k] = count # All-gather A across all GPUs Aglobal = allgather(A) return Aglobal def solvelsa(costmatrix, B, N): """ Solves the Linear Sum Assignment problem. costmatrix[j, k] is the cost of assigning patch j to GPU k. Returns W where W[j] is the assigned GPU. """ # Hungarian algorithm implementation # Standard library or custom implementation of O(B^3) Hungarian method rowind, colind = hungarianalgorithm(costmatrix) # rowind contains indices 0..B-1, colind contains assigned GPU indices 0..N-1 W = zeros(B, dtype=int) for j, k in zip(rowind, colind): W[j] = k return W def refineloadbalance(W, A, B, N, beta, gamma, delta): """ Greedy local search to balance send, recv, and comp loads. """ # Define p-norm helper def pnorm(vec, p=2): return sum(vp for v in vec)(1/p) currentW = W.copy() # Time budget or convergence check maxiterations = 1000 for iteration in range(maxiterations): bestswap = None bestcost = infinity # Calculate current loads loads = calculateloads(currentW, A, B, N) currentcost = beta pnorm(loads['send']) + gamma pnorm(loads['recv']) + delta pnorm(loads['comp']) # Try all pairwise swaps for i in range(B): for j in range(i + 1, B): # Swap assignments tempW = currentW.copy() tempW[i], tempW[j] = currentW[j], currentW[i] # Calculate new loads newloads = calculateloads(tempW, A, B, N) newcost = beta pnorm(newloads['send']) + gamma pnorm(newloads['recv']) + delta pnorm(newloads['comp']) if newcost < currentcost: if newcost < bestcost: bestcost = newcost bestswap = (i, j) if bestswap is None: break # Convergence i, j = bestswap currentW[i], currentW[j] = currentW[j], currentW[i] return currentW def calculateloads(W, A, B, N): """ Computes send, recv, and comp loads for each GPU. """ send = zeros(N) recv = zeros(N) comp = zeros(N) for k in range(N): for j in range(B): assignedgpu = W[j] # Total points needed for patch j totalpointsj = sum(A[j,:]) if assignedgpu != k: # GPU k sends points to the assigned GPU send[k] += A[j, k] else: # GPU k renders patch j # It receives points from other GPUs recv[k] += (totalpointsj - A[j, k]) # It computes for all points in patch j comp[k] += totalpointsj return {'send': send, 'recv': recv, 'comp': comp} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: ILP Solver Speed: Standard ILP solvers (e.g., Gurobi) are too slow and unpredictable for online optimization per iteration. The LSA+Local Search heuristic is required. Granularity: Using whole images limits flexibility when scaling to many GPUs. Patching (p=2–8) allows finer-grained placement. Intra-node Communication: For multi-node setups, intra-node bandwidth is high. Setting \alpha=0 during intra-node assignment de-prioritizes communication volume in favor of load balancing. Time Complexity: The LSA step using the Hungarian method has time complexity O(B^3). The local search step depends on the number of swaps and the cost of load recalculation, but is generally fast enough for online use. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the B \times N access pattern matrix A. Strengths: Reduces inter-node communication volume and balances GPU load dynamically, which is critical for large-scale distributed training where static partitioning may become suboptimal due to random batch sampling. Limitations: Adds computational overhead per iteration due to frustum culling and the placement solver. The heuristic does not guarantee a global optimum. Online Image Rendering Placement is part of the Gaian system for scaling point-based differentiable rendering for large-scale reconstruction. It addresses the limitations of offline graph partitioning, which clusters points and images for the entire dataset but cannot adapt to the random small batches used in training. By performing placement online, the system can optimize for the specific data access patterns of each training iteration.
