name: Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scientific Visualization, Distributed 3D-GS, Multi-GPU 3D-GS
body: Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting is a multi-GPU extension of the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) pipeline designed for scientific visualization, enabling the scalable processing of large datasets that exceed the memory capacity of a single GPU. It differs from standard 3D-GS by partitioning the global set of Gaussian primitives and training data across multiple GPUs, utilizing a fused all-reduce scheme for gradient synchronization to maintain high-fidelity isosurface reconstruction at scales previously infeasible. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scientific volume data (e.g., CFD simulation outputs), number of GPUs M, image resolution R \times R. Output: Optimized set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} and rendered images matching synthetic camera views. Data Structures: The global set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} is partitioned into M shards \mathcal{G}^{(m)}, where each GPU m \in \{0, \dots, M-1\} holds a local shard. Each Gaussian primitive retains the standard 3D-GS attributes: center position \mathbf{x}, covariance matrix \Sigma (or rotation/scale parameters), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for view-dependent color. The optimizer state (momentum, variance) is also sharded locally [15108]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Extract an isosurface point cloud directly from the scientific volume data using ParaView. This point cloud serves as the initialization for the Gaussian primitives, bypassing image-based reconstruction methods. 2. Data Partitioning: Distribute the global point cloud and corresponding Gaussian parameters across the M GPUs such that each GPU holds a shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)}. Distribute the training data (synthetic camera views) across the workers. 3. Synthetic View Generation: Generate a set of synthetic camera views in a structured orbit. The number of views is increased to 448 (compared to 250 in prior work [4]) to better support the complexity of scientific data. 4. Distributed Training Loop: a. Local Forward Pass: Each GPU performs local projection and rasterization of its shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)} to render images for its assigned subset of camera views [15108]. b. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss (e.g., L1, SSIM) between rendered images and ground truth views. c. Gradient Synchronization: Synchronize gradients across all GPUs via a fused all-reduce scheme. This ensures that the global optimization step accounts for gradients from all shards. d. Local Update: Each GPU updates its local shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)} and optimizer state using the synchronized gradients [15108]. 5. Rendering: For inference, the distributed shards can be aggregated or accessed via all-to-all communication to render high-resolution images [15108]. Parameters: Number of Synthetic Camera Views: 448. Image Resolutions: 512x512, 1024x1024, 2048x2048. Hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Pitfalls: Memory Limits: A single NVIDIA A100 GPU supports up to approximately 11.2M Gaussians. Datasets exceeding this limit (e.g., Miranda with ~18M Gaussians) are infeasible on a single GPU and require distributed training. Communication Overhead: While not explicitly quantified, the reliance on fused all-reduce implies that network bandwidth and latency between GPUs are critical factors for performance. Scalability: The method achieves significant speedups with increased GPU counts. For the Kingsnake dataset (4M Gaussians) at 2048x2048 resolution, using 4 GPUs provides a 5.6x speedup compared to a single GPU (8.50 min vs 48.00 min). Memory Efficiency: Enables training on datasets with >11.2M Gaussians, which exceed single A100 memory capacity. Performance: On the Miranda dataset (18M Gaussians) at 2048x2048 resolution with 4 GPUs, training time is 16.84 minutes. Quality: Maintains high reconstruction quality. Kingsnake (4 GPUs): PSNR 29.32, SSIM 0.97, LPIPS 0.03. Miranda (4 GPUs): PSNR 36.37, SSIM 0.99, LPIPS 0.011. Limitations: Requires access to multi-GPU hardware (e.g., HPC nodes) and efficient interconnects for all-reduce operations. This method was presented in 2025 by Mateevitsi, Papka, Petruzza, and Sizzi from the University of Illinois Chicago, Argonne National Laboratory, and Utah State University. It builds on previous work by Sewell et al. [4] which demonstrated high-fidelity isosurface reconstruction using Gaussian primitives, and incorporates the distributed training design from Grendel-GS [6] to enable scalable processing of large scientific datasets. The work aims to integrate 3D-GS into HPC-based scientific workflows for real-time post hoc and in situ visualization. name: Cache-based Lazy Memory Management
head: CLM (Cache-based Lazy Memory management)
body: Cache-based Lazy Memory Management (CLM) is a memory offloading technique that enables the training of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes on a single consumer-grade GPU by keeping the majority of Gaussians in CPU memory and loading them only when necessary. It exploits the inherent sparsity of 3DGS memory access patterns, where each training iteration accesses only a small subset of the scene's Gaussians, to minimize GPU memory usage while hiding CPU-GPU communication overhead through pipelining. Unlike naive offloading strategies that load all Gaussians to the GPU, CLM reduces the memory footprint to the active subset and overlaps communication with computation to maintain performance. CLM operates by partitioning the 3D Gaussian dataset between GPU and CPU memory, dynamically managing the transfer of Gaussians based on the specific view being rendered in each training iteration. The method relies on four key observations regarding the 3DGS training pipeline: (1) the set of Gaussians accessed by a view can be computed ahead-of-time; (2) there is substantial overlap in Gaussian access between different views; (3) training exhibits spatial locality, meaning views in the same region access similar Gaussians; and (4) gradient computation and parameter updates can be overlapped with communication. Inputs: \mathcal{G}{total}: The complete set of N 3D Gaussians stored in CPU memory. \mathcal{V}: The set of training views (images with poses). GPU{mem}: The available memory on the consumer-grade GPU (e.g., 24 GB on RTX 4090). Outputs: \mathcal{G}{GPU}: The subset of Gaussians currently resident in GPU memory. Updated parameters for \mathcal{G}{GPU} after the training iteration. Each 3D Gaussian consists of 59 learnable parameters. These parameters are stored in a format that includes the parameter value, its gradient, and two additional versions for the Adam optimizer state. Gaussian Parameter Layout: 3D Position: 3 parameters. Covariance (Scale + Rotation): 3 + 4 = 7 parameters. Spherical Harmonics: 48 parameters. Opacity: 1 parameter. Total Parameters per Gaussian: 59. Memory Layout per Parameter: Each parameter requires 4 bytes for the value, 4 bytes for the gradient, and 2 additional 4-byte versions for optimizer state. Total memory per parameter: 4 \times 4 = 16 bytes. Total Memory per Gaussian: 59 \text{ params} \times 16 \text{ bytes/param} = 944 bytes. Total Model State Memory: For N Gaussians, the memory required is N \times 59 \times 4 \times 4 bytes. 1. Pre-compute Access Sets: For each training view v \in \mathcal{V}, compute the set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}v that will be accessed during the rasterization and back-propagation of that view. This is done ahead-of-time. 2. Identify Overlaps: Analyze the access sets \mathcal{G}v to identify Gaussians that are accessed by multiple views. These overlapping Gaussians are candidates for caching in GPU memory to reduce repeated communication. 3. Schedule Iterations: Order the training iterations (views) to exploit spatial locality. Views that are spatially close and likely to access the same Gaussians are scheduled consecutively to maximize the reuse of cached Gaussians in GPU memory. 4. Pipeline Execution: For each training iteration i corresponding to view vi: a. Overlap Communication: Initiate the transfer of required Gaussians from CPU to GPU for the next iteration v{i+1} while the GPU is computing the current iteration vi. This overlaps GPU computation with CPU-GPU communication. b. Rasterize: Perform the 3DGS rasterization on the currently loaded Gaussians \mathcal{G}{GPU} for view vi. c. Back-propagate: Compute gradients for the loaded Gaussians. d. Overlap Updates: Overlap the gradient computation and a substantial portion of the Gaussian parameter update (Adam optimizer step) with the ongoing communication for the next iteration. 5. Update Memory: After the iteration, update the GPU memory cache with the newly accessed Gaussians for the next step, evicting those no longer needed based on the schedule. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. GPUcache = set() accesssets = {v: computeaccessset(v) for v in views} scheduledviews = scheduleviews(views, accesssets) for i in range(len(scheduledviews)): currentview = scheduledviews[i] nextview = scheduledviews[i+1] if i+1 < len(scheduledviews) else None # Step 1: Overlap communication for next view with current computation if nextview is not None: requirednext = accesssets[nextview] # Identify Gaussians in next view not currently in GPU cache toload = requirednext - GPUcache # Initiate asynchronous transfer of toload from CPU to GPU asynctransfercputogpu(toload) # Step 2: Rasterize current view using currently loaded Gaussians # Ensure all required Gaussians for currentview are in GPUcache # (This may involve blocking if previous async transfer is not complete, # but ideally pipelined) ensureincache(accesssets[currentview]) # Perform forward pass (rasterization) and backward pass (gradient computation) renderedimage = rasterize(currentview, GPUcache) gradients = computegradients(renderedimage, groundtruth[currentview]) # Step 3: Overlap parameter update with communication # Update parameters for Gaussians in currentview updateparameters(GPUcache, gradients) # Update GPU cache state GPUcache = accesssets[currentview] Gaussian Parameter Count: 59 per Gaussian. Memory per Parameter: 16 bytes (4 bytes for parameter, 4 bytes for gradient, 8 bytes for optimizer state). Typical Hardware: Consumer-grade GPU with 24 GB memory (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 4090). Naive Offloading Overhead: Naively offloading all Gaussians to the CPU and loading them per iteration incurs significant performance overhead due to CPU-GPU communication latency and the time required to run the Adam optimizer on the CPU. Memory Proportionality: Naive offloading fails to scale because it still requires loading all Gaussians to the GPU at some point, keeping GPU memory requirements proportional to the total number of Gaussians. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The system must handle cases where the number of Gaussians exceeds the GPU memory capacity (e.g., 102 million Gaussians on an RTX 4090) by strictly limiting the GPU cache to the active subset. Time Complexity: The method aims to hide communication overhead by overlapping it with GPU computation and CPU-based parameter updates. The performance overhead is described as "modest" compared to a baseline without offloading for small scenes. Memory Complexity: GPU memory usage is proportional to the number of Gaussians accessed by a single view (or a small batch of views), rather than the total number of Gaussians N. This allows scaling to scenes with 100-102 million Gaussians on a 24 GB GPU. Measured Performance: CLM successfully trains a scene with 102 million Gaussians on a single RTX 4090. It achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality. Strengths: Enables training of large scenes on single consumer GPUs; reduces GPU memory requirements; maintains rendering quality. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling and pre-computation of access sets; performance may degrade if spatial locality is poor or if the active subset is too large for the GPU. When to Use: When training large-scale 3DGS scenes on hardware with limited GPU memory (e.g., consumer-grade GPUs). When Not to Use: When sufficient GPU memory is available to hold all Gaussians, as naive in-GPU training may be simpler and potentially faster due to lower latency. CLM was introduced in the paper "CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting," accepted to ASPLOS ’26. The work addresses the memory barrier that prevents scaling 3DGS to large scenes on single consumer-grade GPUs, which typically have 24 GB of memory. Prior to CLM, scaling 3DGS required either multiple GPUs (adding significant cost) or reducing scene fidelity through pruning. The core insight is that 3DGS computation is inherently sparse, allowing for effective memory offloading. name: Cache-Less Memory (CLM)
body: Cache-Less Memory (CLM) is a training and rendering system for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that enables large or highly detailed scenes to be processed on a single consumer-grade GPU by offloading Gaussian parameters and optimizer computation to the CPU. It solves the GPU memory capacity bottleneck inherent in standard 3DGS by leveraging attribute-wise offloading, microbatch pipelining, and spatial locality to minimize GPU-CPU communication overhead. Unlike Cache-based Lazy Memory Management, which relies on caching strategies for memory reuse, CLM explicitly partitions attributes between CPU and GPU memory and uses precise caching of intersecting Gaussians across microbatches to hide communication latency. Input: A set of training images/views, a scene representation consisting of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, and a batch of images to process. Output: Updated Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale, color, opacity) and the rendered image. CLM splits Gaussian attributes into two sets based on their necessity for frustum culling: 1. Selection-Critical Attributes: Stored in GPU memory for all Gaussians. These include position, rotation, and scale. They constitute less than 20% (10 out of 59 floats) of a Gaussian's memory footprint. These are never swapped to CPU memory to avoid communication overhead during culling. 2. Non-Critical Attributes: Stored in CPU memory. These include color (spherical harmonic coefficients) and opacity. These are loaded into GPU memory only when required for rasterization. The CLM training loop processes a batch of images by dividing it into microbatches, where each microbatch consists of a single image. 1. Attribute-Wise Offload: Initialize GPU memory with selection-critical attributes (position, rotation, scale) for all Gaussians. Store non-critical attributes (color, opacity) in CPU memory. 2. Microbatch Pipelining: Divide the batch into microbatches i = 1 \dots K. Start the forward pass for microbatch i+1 as soon as the backward pass for microbatch i completes. Use double-buffering to overlap communication and computation. 3. Precise Gaussian Caching (Forward): For microbatch i, perform frustum culling using the selection-critical attributes in GPU memory to identify the set of in-frustum Gaussians Si. When loading Gaussians for microbatch i+1, identify the intersection Si \cap S{i+1}. Copy the parameters for Gaussians in Si \cap S{i+1} from microbatch i's GPU tensors (already in GPU memory). Load only the Gaussians in S{i+1} \setminus Si from CPU memory into GPU memory. 4. Rasterization and Backpropagation: Perform forward and backward passes for the current microbatch. 5. Gradient Caching (Backward): After microbatch i finishes, compute gradients for all Gaussians in Si. Transfer gradients only for Gaussians in Si \setminus S{i+1} to CPU memory. Copy gradients for Gaussians in Si \cap S{i+1} into microbatch i+1's gradient buffer to be accumulated. 6. CPU Adam Update: Perform Adam optimizer updates on the CPU for the gradients accumulated in the previous step. This overlaps with the forward/backward computation of subsequent microbatches. 7. Pipeline Order Optimization: Schedule microbatches to maximize spatial locality (overlap) between consecutive microbatches. Formulate as a Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) where nodes are microbatches and the distance between microbatches i and j is the symmetric difference |Si \oplus Sj|. Use stochastic local search with a greedy heuristic to find the schedule. Frustum Culling Threshold: Gaussians are culled if they are outside 3 standard deviations (3\sigma) of the Gaussian's distribution. This is standard practice in existing 3DGS implementations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clmtrainingloop(images, gaussians, batchsize): # 1. Attribute-Wise Offload # Selection-critical attributes (pos, rot, scale) in GPU memory gpuselection = gaussians.selectioncriticalattributes # Non-critical attributes (color, opacity) in CPU memory cpunoncritical = gaussians.noncriticalattributes # 2. Pipeline Order Optimization # Schedule microbatches to maximize overlap schedule = optimizeschedule(images) # Initialize double buffers for communication gpubufferprev = None gpubuffernext = None for i, image in enumerate(schedule): # Microbatch i # 3. Precise Gaussian Caching (Forward) if i == 0: # Load all non-critical attributes for the first microbatch gpunoncritical = loadfromcpu(cpunoncritical, getinfrustumindices(image, gpuselection)) else: # Identify intersection with previous microbatch previndices = gpubufferprev.indices currindices = getinfrustumindices(image, gpuselection) intersection = set(previndices) & set(currindices) newindices = set(currindices) - set(previndices) # Copy intersecting Gaussians from previous buffer gpunoncritical = copyfrombuffer(gpubufferprev, intersection) # Load new Gaussians from CPU gpunoncritical = loadfromcpu(cpunoncritical, newindices, gpunoncritical) # Rasterization and Backpropagation gradients = forwardbackward(image, gpuselection, gpunoncritical) # 4. Gradient Caching (Backward) if i < len(schedule) - 1: nextindices = getinfrustumindices(schedule[i+1], gpuselection) nextintersection = set(currindices) & set(nextindices) # Transfer gradients for non-overlapping Gaussians to CPU transfergradientstocpu(gradients, set(currindices) - set(nextintersection)) # Copy overlapping gradients to next buffer gpubuffernext = copygradients(gradients, nextintersection) else: # Final microbatch: transfer all remaining gradients to CPU transfergradientstocpu(gradients, currindices) # 5. CPU Adam Update # Update parameters on CPU using accumulated gradients updategaussiansoncpu(gaussians, gradients) # Swap buffers for next iteration gpubufferprev = gpubuffernext GPU Memory Limit: The system assumes that selection-critical attributes fit in GPU memory. If the number of Gaussians is extremely large, even this subset may not fit, requiring further optimization not covered by CLM. Communication Overhead: The effectiveness of CLM depends on the overlap between consecutive microbatches. If the schedule is poor, communication overhead may not be hidden effectively. Precision: Standard 3DGS implementations use 3\sigma for frustum culling. Deviating from this may affect accuracy or performance. Memory Complexity: The memory overhead of double-buffering for pipelining is independent of scene and batch size. The total GPU memory usage is dominated by the selection-critical attributes, which are less than 20% of the total Gaussian memory footprint. Time Complexity: Microbatch pipelining overlaps communication with computation, hiding communication overhead. The scheduling problem is NP-hard (TSP), but a greedy heuristic is used for efficient approximation. Strengths: Enables training/rendering of large scenes on consumer-grade GPUs. Reduces GPU memory requirements. Overlaps communication with computation. Limitations: Requires CPU computation for optimizer updates. Performance depends on the quality of the microbatch schedule. When to use: When GPU memory is insufficient to store all Gaussian attributes for a scene. When not to use: When GPU memory is sufficient for the scene, as the overhead of CPU-GPU communication and CPU computation may not be justified. CLM was introduced in the paper "CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS training, which requires significant GPU memory for Gaussian parameters and optimizer states. CLM extends effective GPU memory capacity by offloading Gaussian parameters and optimizer computation to the CPU, while leveraging sparsity and spatial locality to reduce overhead. The design is built on CUDA but is agnostic to the rendering backend and can be ported to Vulkan. name: Grendel
head: distributed 3DGS training system
body: Grendel is a distributed training system for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that partitions parameters and parallelizes computation across multiple GPUs to overcome single-GPU memory constraints in high-resolution and large-scale reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from single-GPU baselines and divide-and-conquer approaches like CityGS by supporting batched training with multiple views and exploiting mixed parallelism (Gaussian-wise and pixel-wise) with sparse all-to-all communication to handle dynamic workload imbalances. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images (batched), initial 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), and optimizer states. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters and rendered images. Data Structures: Gaussian Parameters: Distributed uniformly across G GPUs. Each GPU stores a subset of Gaussians, including their parameters and optimizer states (Adam moments). Pixel Blocks: Images are partitioned into 16 \times 16-pixel blocks. Runtime Estimates: A history of rendering times per pixel block is maintained to estimate computational load. Numbered Steps: 1. Gaussian-wise Distribution (Forward): Partition the 3D Gaussians (parameters and optimizer states) uniformly across G GPUs. Each GPU independently computes the Gaussian transformation for its assigned subset of Gaussians. Note: Computation load per Gaussian is assumed uniform, so uniform distribution is sufficient for this step. 2. Sparse All-to-All Communication (Forward): Each GPU determines the set of Gaussians that intersect with its assigned pixel partition. Perform sparse all-to-all communication to transfer only the intersecting Gaussians to the GPUs responsible for rendering those pixels. Optimization: Assign contiguous image areas to GPUs during pixel-wise distribution to exploit spatial locality and minimize the number of Gaussians transferred. 3. Pixel-wise Distribution (Rendering & Loss): Partition each image in the batch into 16 \times 16-pixel blocks. Distribute consecutive subsequences of blocks to different GPUs using an adaptive strategy based on estimated runtime. Each GPU renders its assigned blocks and computes the loss. Note: A GPU may be assigned blocks from different images in the batch. 4. Sparse All-to-All Communication (Backward): Perform a reversed all-to-all communication to transfer gradients back to the GPUs holding the corresponding Gaussian parameters. 5. Optimizer Update: Each GPU updates the parameters and optimizer states for the Gaussians it owns. 6. Dynamic Load Balancing (Pixel-wise): After the first few epochs, record the rendering time (including loss and backward computation) for each pixel block. Compute the average per-pixel computation time for each GPU based on its assigned blocks. Re-split images in subsequent iterations so that the sum of computation times for pixels assigned to all GPUs is equal, using 16 \times 16 blocks as the split granularity. Use Algorithm 1 to calculate division points for rebalancing. 7. Dynamic Load Balancing (Gaussian-wise): Redistribute 3D Gaussians uniformly after every few densification steps (cloning and splitting) to restore uniformity, as new Gaussians are added at varying rates depending on local scene details. Pseudocode: Algorithm 1 Calculation of Division Points Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatedivisionpoints(estimatedruntimes: list, numgpus: int) -> list: """ Calculate division points to split pixel blocks among GPUs for load balancing. Args: estimatedruntimes: List of estimated runtimes for each pixel block (ET). numgpus: Number of GPUs (G). Returns: DP: List of division points (indices) to split the blocks. """ import torch # 1: CT <- TORCH.CUMSUM(ET) cumulativetimes = torch.cumsum(torch.tensor(estimatedruntimes), dim=0) # 2: ETgpu <- CT[B-1]/G totaltime = cumulativetimes[-1] targettimepergpu = totaltime / numgpus # 3: TH <- TORCH.ARANGE(0, G) ETgpu thresholds = torch.arange(0, numgpus) targettimepergpu # 4: DP <- TORCH.SEARCHSORTED(CT, TH) # Searchsorted returns indices where thresholds would be inserted to maintain order. # These indices represent the division points between GPU assignments. divisionpoints = torch.searchsorted(cumulativetimes, thresholds) # 5: return DP return divisionpoints.tolist() Formulas: Learning Rate Scaling: \lambda' = \lambda \times \sqrt{\text{batch\size}} Where \lambda is the original learning rate and \lambda' is the adjusted learning rate. Momentum Scaling (Adam): \beta1' = \beta1^{\text{batch\size}}, \quad \beta2' = \beta2^{\text{batch\size}} Where \beta1, \beta2 are the original first and second moment estimates, and \beta1', \beta2' are the adjusted parameters. Parameters: Block Size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Maximum Tested Batch Size: 32. Learning Rate Scaling Rule: \sqrt{\text{batch\size}}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hyperparameter Stability: Increasing batch size without adjusting hyperparameters leads to unstable and inefficient training. The Independent Gradients Hypothesis assumes gradients from different views are independent, but cameras with similar poses offer similar gradients, causing correlation and sparsity changes as batch size increases. Workload Imbalance: Static workload partitioning is suboptimal due to dynamic and unbalanced workloads caused by varying Gaussian densities and scene complexity (e.g., sky vs. detailed foreground). A method for differentiable rendering that complements distributed training by optimizing the splatting process itself. DeSplat Focuses on spherical scene representation, which may interact with distributed partitioning strategies. 360 Gaussian Splatting Reduces memory footprint, potentially easing the burden on distributed GPU memory. Data Compression and Storage Optimization Time Complexity: Training time scales with the number of Gaussians and images. Grendel achieves near-linear speedup in rendering speed with added GPUs. Memory Complexity: Memory usage per GPU is reduced by distributing Gaussians and pixel blocks. Measured Performance: Rubble (3436x4591, 40.4M Gaussians): 21.7 img/s on 4 GPUs vs. 8.8 img/s on 1 GPU. Training time on 4 A100s: 51 minutes vs. CityGS Official's 2 hours 3 minutes. Test PSNR: 27.28 (16 GPUs) vs. 26.28 (1 GPU, 11.2M Gaussians). Matrixcity Block-all (1080x1920, 24M Gaussians): 76.8 img/s on 4 GPUs vs. 29.2 img/s on 1 GPU. Training time on 4 A100s: 54 minutes vs. CityGS Official's 3 hours 31 minutes. Bicycle (1275x1920): 80.3 img/s on 4 GPUs vs. 42.6 img/s on 1 GPU. Training time on 4 A100s: 1 hour 13 minutes vs. CityGS Official's 1 hour 20 minutes. Strengths: Handles high-resolution and large-scale scenes; supports batched training for better GPU utilization; dynamic load balancing handles scene complexity variations. Limitations: Communication overhead from sparse all-to-all operations; requires careful hyperparameter scaling for large batches. When to Use: Large-scale, high-resolution 3D reconstruction tasks that exceed single-GPU memory limits. When Not to Use: Small-scale scenes where single-GPU training is sufficient and simpler to implement. Grendel was introduced in the paper "On Scaling Up 3D Gaussian Splatting Training" (ICLR 2025) by researchers from NYU Systems. It addresses the limitation of 3DGS training being confined to a single GPU, which restricts the resolution and scale of reconstructible scenes. The system is open-source and available at https://github.com/nyu-systems/Grendel-GS. On Scaling Up 3D Gaussian Splatting Training, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91989-32, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Pruning and Density Control
head: Gaussian Pruning, Density Control, Adaptive Pruning
body: Pruning and Density Control refers to the family of techniques used to manage the number and distribution of 3D Gaussian primitives during the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem of balancing reconstruction fidelity against computational cost and memory usage by dynamically removing redundant or low-importance Gaussians and controlling the growth of new ones. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by employing dynamic, often concave-up, growth curves that synchronize primitive count with increasing resolution to fit high-frequency details only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3DGS primitive representation: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Color coefficients \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics) The core mechanism involves calculating an importance score for each Gaussian and removing those below a threshold or ranking. Methods typically employ a "concave-up" growth curve for primitives, where growth accelerates over time, synchronized with increasing rendering resolution to fit high-frequency details only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. This family defines the temporal scheduling of primitive creation (densification), removal (pruning), and resource allocation (resolution) during the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem of balancing reconstruction fidelity against computational cost by controlling when and how new Gaussians are introduced relative to the rendering resolution and optimization progress. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by employing dynamic, often concave-up, growth curves that synchronize primitive count with increasing resolution to fit high-frequency details only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. See Optimization Schedule and Densification. The Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler (RPS) is a dynamic pruning strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that adaptively determines pruning timing and refining intervals based on reconstruction quality, addressing the instability of fixed-schedule pruning. Unlike heuristic methods that prune at fixed iterations with preset ratios, RPS analyzes reconstruction loss to automatically identify optimal pruning times and progressively reduces the number of pruned primitives to adapt to scene complexity and redundancy levels. See Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler. DropGaussian is a structural regularization technique designed to mitigate overfitting in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when trained on a sparse set of input views. It operates by randomly excluding a subset of Gaussians from the rendering and gradient computation during training, while simultaneously scaling the opacity of the remaining Gaussians to preserve the total color contribution. Unlike prior-based methods that rely on external depth signals or 2D generative models, DropGaussian is prior-free and introduces no additional computational complexity or external data requirements. See DropGaussian. A pruning technique that identifies and removes redundant Gaussians by gauging their impact on deformation, distinguishing between stable and deformed Gaussians. An importance ranking mechanism that incorporates spectral information into the importance ranking of Gaussian primitives to enable stable pruning. It measures the importance of a Gaussian primitive in both spatial and spectral domains. A criterion for evaluating the importance of each Gaussian by measuring its contribution from both spatial and spectral (frequency) perspectives to prevent pruning of primitives essential for sharp structures. Step Iteratively remove low-score points that are relatively unimportant across both spatial and spectral domains. Combine the normalized spatial score and spectral score using weighting coefficients \lambdas and \lambdaf to obtain the final Spatio-spectral Pruning Score \tilde{U}i^. Formula \tilde{U}i^ = \lambdas \frac{(\nabla{gi} IG)^2}{\|\tilde{U}s\|^2} + \lambdaf \frac{(\nabla{gi} \text{FFT}(IG))^2}{\|\tilde{U}f\|^2} where \tilde{U}i^ is the Spatio-spectral Pruning Score, \lambdas and \lambdaf are weighting coefficients balancing spatial and frequency contributions, and \|\tilde{U}s\| and \|\tilde{U}f\| are normalization terms for spatial and frequency scores respectively. Parameter \lambdas: Weighting coefficient for the spatial-domain gradient term. \lambdaf: Weighting coefficient for the frequency-domain gradient term. The concept of pruning in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a response to the high memory and computational costs associated with the dense primitive representations required for high-fidelity rendering. Early implementations relied on fixed schedules for densification and pruning, which often led to instability or suboptimal final models. The introduction of adaptive strategies, such as the Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler, aimed to stabilize training by linking pruning actions to measurable improvements in reconstruction loss. Concurrently, techniques like DropGaussian were developed to address specific failure modes in sparse-view scenarios, where overfitting to visible structures left distant or occluded primitives under-optimized. The Spatio-spectral Pruning Score further refined the importance metric by incorporating frequency-domain information, allowing for more robust removal of primitives that do not contribute to fine details. These methods collectively form the foundation for efficient and stable 3DGS optimization. name: Optimization Schedule and Densification
body:
This family defines the temporal scheduling of primitive creation, removal, and parameter updates during 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training. It solves the problem of balancing reconstruction fidelity against optimization complexity by synchronizing the growth of Gaussian primitives with rendering resolution and error metrics. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by employing dynamic, often concave-up, growth curves that accelerate primitive count as high-frequency details are fitted, distinct from sibling methods like Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler which focus on pruning thresholds, or DropGaussian which focuses on specific dropout mechanisms. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3DGS primitive representation: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Color coefficients \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics) The core mechanism involves calculating an importance score for each Gaussian and removing those below a threshold or ranking. Methods typically employ a "concave-up" growth curve for primitives, where growth accelerates over time, synchronized with increasing rendering resolution to fit high-frequency details only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. Error-Driven 2D Gaussian Training is a densification strategy that samples and optimizes 2D Gaussian kernels in image space using a differentiable rasterizer, then back-projects them to 3D to initialize new 3D primitives. It solves the problem of initializing view-dependent Gaussian kernels for complex specular radiance reconstruction, where proper initialization is critical. It sets itself apart from standard 3D densification by optimizing in 2D image space with the pre-rendered image as a fixed background, allowing for precise error-driven placement before 3D projection. See Error-Driven 2D Gaussian Training. DashGaussian is a scheduling scheme for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that accelerates optimization by reformulating the process as a frequency component fitting task. It cooperatively allocates rendering resolution and primitive count to strip redundant complexity, distinguishing itself from vanilla 3DGS and other backbones by producing a concave-up primitive growth curve that spans the entire optimization process. Unlike methods that peak in primitive count at half-iteration or use concave-down curves, DashGaussian synchronizes primitive growth with increasing resolution to fit high-frequency details only after low-frequency structures are established. See DashGaussian. This article defines the specific hyperparameters, optimization schedules, and training protocols required to converge 3D Gaussian Splatting models, particularly in generative and downstream transfer contexts. It addresses the configuration of learning rates, iteration counts, and loss weights necessary to stabilize training, while also detailing standardized protocols for downstream tasks like classification and segmentation. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the configuration of the training loop itself rather than the geometric densification logic or rendering primitives. See Training Configuration and Hyperparameters. Definition An optimization framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses learned networks for initialization, densification, and parameter updates to accelerate surface reconstruction. Steps 1. Initialize Gaussians G0 from SfM points P using an initializer network fI: G0 \leftarrow fI(P). 2. Iterate for t = 0 to T - 1. 3. Reset gradient accumulator 
abla Gt \leftarrow 0. 4. For all images, compute rendering loss L, compute gradient \delta Gt, and accumulate: 
abla Gt \leftarrow 
abla Gt + \delta Gt. 5. Generate new Gaussians \hat{G}t using a densifier network fD on current Gaussians Gt, accumulated gradients 
abla Gt, and time step t: \hat{G}t \leftarrow fD(Gt, 
abla Gt, t). 6. Concatenate new Gaussians:  ar{G}t \leftarrow Gt \cup \hat{G}t. 7. Compute update \Delta  ar{G}t using an optimizer network fO: \Delta  ar{G}t \leftarrow fO( ar{G}t, 
abla  ar{G}t, t). 8. Update Gaussians: G{t+1} \leftarrow  ar{G}t + \Delta  ar{G}t. Steps 1. Disable the Level-of-Detail (LOD) gate during the density-control window (iterations 2,000–32,000). 2. Engage the LOD gate after the first importance-scoring pass (T1). 3. After the importance-scoring pass, reweight density-control gradients using the per-Gaussian visibility factor \phii for the remainder of the density-control window. Parameters Density control interval: Runs every 1,000 steps from iteration 2,000 up to 32,000 (last event at 31,000). Comparison Extending training iterations (e.g., 500k–1000k) does not significantly improve quality on aerial scenes (e.g., Building 19.27→19.50 dB), indicating deficits stem from representation structure rather than insufficient budget. Definition A densification criterion to improve normal recovery in thin regions by introducing an additional densification criterion on the gradient of normals, beyond the vanilla 3DGS gradient of view space points. It densifies Gaussians whose normal gradient exceeds a threshold Tn. Steps 1. Calculate the normal gradient for each Gaussian. 2. Densify Gaussians whose normal gradient exceeds a threshold Tn. Parameters Tn: The threshold for normal gradient magnitude used to trigger densification. Typical value: 2 	imes 10^{-9}. Definition A densification strategy that decouples split and clone operations across densification phases to accelerate optimization. It uses split for global spread at low resolution and suppresses clone, then reintroduces clone for local refinement at full resolution. Steps 1. Calculate the norm of the average position gradient of each Gaussian primitive every 100 iterations. 2. If the gradient norm exceeds a predefined threshold, check the maximum scale of the Gaussian primitive. 3. If the maximum scale exceeds a given scale threshold, split the Gaussian into smaller components. 4. Otherwise, clone the Gaussian with the same parameters. 5. During low-resolution training, promote Gaussian primitives' global spread with the split operation and suppress clone operations to prevent premature local clustering. 6. When transitioning to full-resolution training, reintroduce clone operations to refine high-frequency details. Parameters Gradient calculation frequency: 100 iterations. Comparison Unlike standard 3DGS which applies split and clone simultaneously, this method decouples them across phases (global vs local) to address inefficient spatial spread and redundant primitives. Formula The final primitive count P{fin}^{(i)} at step i is calculated as: P{fin}^{(i)} = \max(P{fin}^{(i-1)}, \gamma \cdot P{fin}^{(i-1)} + \eta \cdot P{add}) where P{add} is the number of primitives densified in step i. P{fin}^{(0)} is initialized as 5 \cdot P{init}. Parameters Power factor in primitive growth: Starts at 2 and gradually decreases to 1 along the optimization process to suppress early growth and encourage mid-stage growth. Hyperparameter \gamma: Momentum decay factor for primitive budget. Default value: 0.98. Hyperparameter \eta: Force scaling factor for primitive budget. Default value: 1. Resolution modulation: The continuous scalar r(i) is modulated to \lfloor r(i) floor in practice to encourage faster primitive growth. Pitfall Too much primitive growth at the end of optimization results in poor convergence. Mitigated by the concave-up scheduling function and momentum-based budgeting. Definition A staged sampling schedule for supervising 3D refinement that balances fitting the current refined view with preserving rendering ability in original and previously refined views. Steps 1. Divide the total 3D refinement steps into three equal phases (first third, subsequent third, final third). 2. In the first third, designate every 3 steps as 'current-refine steps' to optimize using the current refined image \hat{I}^{i,e,f}{ie}. 3. In the subsequent third, designate every 5 steps as 'current-refine steps'. 4. In the final third, designate every 8 steps as 'current-refine steps'. 5. For all non-current-refine steps, randomly sample views from the training set S{train} and the previous refined set F{i-1}. Parameters Selection weight for F{i-1} is lower than for S{train} to prioritize original training data over previously refined views. The concept of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting involves balancing the number of primitives against rendering quality and training time. Early works like vanilla 3DGS used fixed schedules for densification and pruning [Parent]. Subsequent research introduced dynamic scheduling, such as DashGaussian, which reformulates optimization as frequency fitting to accelerate convergence. Other approaches, like QuickSplat, utilize learned networks for densification, while BlitzGS focuses on system-level workload reduction through LOD gating. Normal gradient-based densification was introduced to improve geometric fidelity in thin regions. Global-to-local strategies decouple split and clone operations to improve efficiency. Finally, 3D refinement strategies employ staged view sampling to preserve rendering ability during fine-tuning. name: Error-Driven 2D Gaussian Training
head: 2D Gaussian Initialization, Image Space Optimization
body: Error-Driven 2D Gaussian Training is a densification strategy that samples and optimizes 2D Gaussian kernels in image space using a differentiable rasterizer, then back-projects them to 3D to initialize new 3D primitives. It solves the problem of initializing view-dependent Gaussian kernels for complex specular radiance reconstruction, where proper initialization is critical. It sets itself apart from standard 3D densification by optimizing in 2D image space with the pre-rendered image as a fixed background, allowing for precise error-driven placement before 3D projection. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered images I = \{Ii\}{i=1}^M and depth maps D = \{Di\}{i=1}^M from standard 3DGS training for all M training views. Outputs: A set of supplementary 2D Gaussian primitives \{x, \alpha, c, d, r, s\}{2D} optimized per view, which are subsequently back-projected to 3D. Data Structures: Each 2D Gaussian primitive is defined by the following parameters: x: Image-space coordinates (u, v). \alpha: Opacity. c: Color. d: Depth, used for rendering-order sorting. r: Rotation angle between the primary axis and the image y-axis. s: Scale along the two principal axes. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-rendering: Obtain rendered images I and depth maps D from the standard 3DGS training pipeline. 2. Depth Map Rendering: Render depth maps for each training image to ensure correct rendering order. Compute depth values at points where transmittance first drops below 0.5 during rasterization. This represents positions where 3D Gaussians attain maximal response along camera rays. 3. Initialization: Predefine the total number of supplementary Gaussians for the scene. Allocate them across views proportional to their respective rendering loss values. Initialize new Gaussians with minimal opacity and color sampled from the current rendered image at their mean positions. 4. Spatial Distribution: Determine the spatial distribution of new kernels through multinomial sampling across pixel coordinates. The selection probability for each pixel (u, v) follows: p(u, v) \propto [(1 - \lambda{SSIM}) L1(u, v) + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM}(u, v)]^2 where L1 and L{SSIM} are the loss metrics, and weights match the original 3DGS paper. 5. Optimization: Overlay supplementary 2D Gaussians on each rendered image. Optimize their parameters using a differentiable rasterizer that emulates 3DGS’s differentiable rendering. Use the pre-rendered image Ii as a fixed background. 6. Depth Update: During optimization, update each primitive’s depth d via nearest-neighbor sampling on the depth map Di using its current image-space coordinates. 7. Augmentation and Pruning: Periodically augment the kernel set by introducing 20% new primitives at fixed intervals. Prune primitives that exhibit excessive transparency or occupy insufficient pixels. 8. Back-projection: After optimization, back-project the 2D primitives into world space to serve as high-quality initializations for new 3D Gaussians. This involves foreground-background separation through point cloud clustering, determination of 3D Gaussian rotations and scales via Weighted Principal Component Analysis (WPCA), and final calibration of the scales. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errordriven2dtraining(renderedimages, depthmaps, numsupplementarygaussians, lambdassim): """ Optimizes 2D Gaussian kernels in image space and prepares for back-projection. name: Training Configuration and Hyperparameters
head: Decoder Training Setup, Hyperparameter Tuning, Training Configuration for Gaussian Splatting Decoder
body: This article defines the specific hyperparameters, optimization schedules, and training protocols required to converge 3D Gaussian Splatting models, particularly in generative and downstream transfer contexts. It addresses the configuration of learning rates, iteration counts, and loss weights necessary to stabilize training, while also detailing standardized protocols for downstream tasks like classification and segmentation. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the configuration of the training loop itself rather than the geometric densification logic or rendering primitives. The training process involves optimizing the Gaussian parameters (\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{s}i, \mathbf{q}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i) using gradient descent. The specific configuration depends on the target application (e.g., generative decoding vs. downstream classification). Inputs: Input images (and optionally depth/normal maps), camera poses, and initial Gaussian initialization (often from SfM points or a latent code). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian attributes and, in generative contexts, a trained decoder mapping latent codes to Gaussian parameters. The training state maintains the standard 3DGS primitive attributes: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Color coefficients \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics) The general training loop follows these steps, with specific hyperparameters detailed below: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from SfM point clouds or a generative prior. 2. Camera Sampling: Sample camera poses based on the target domain. 3. Rendering: Render the scene using differentiable splatting. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L based on the task (photometric, depth, or classification). 5. Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to Gaussian attributes. 6. Update: Apply optimizer step (typically Adam or AdamW). 7. Densification/Pruning: Periodically adjust Gaussian count based on density control criteria (see Parent). The total loss L is a weighted sum of task-specific terms. Photometric Stereo Loss: For methods utilizing inverse rendering with lighting, the loss is defined as: L = Lc + \lambda Ln Where: Lc is the L1 photometric loss between the rendered image and the observed image. Ln is a normal regularization term ensuring Gaussians align with the true object surface, calculated via the gradient of the depth map. \lambda is a weighting factor. Lambertian Reflectance Model: The rendering intensity I(x,y) is modeled as: I(x,y) \propto l^T \cdot n(x,y) Where l is the light direction and n(x,y) is the surface normal. This model is used to calculate self-occlusions (shadows) by analyzing surface alignment with the light direction. Generative/Decoder Loss: For generative decoders, loss weights are typically set as (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3, \lambda4, \lambda5) = (0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0, 0.2) unless stated otherwise. General Training Parameters: Optimizer: Adam or AdamW. Learning Rate: Generative Decoder (PanoHead/EG3D): 0.0009. ModelNet10/40 (Downstream): 10^{-3}. ShapeNet-Part (Downstream): 10^{-4}. Weight Decay: 0.05 (for AdamW in downstream tasks). Warm-up: 5 epochs (for downstream tasks). Batch Size: Generative Decoder: Not explicitly specified, but standard batch training is implied. ModelNet10/40: 256. ShapeNet-Part: 16. Iterations/Epochs: Generative Decoder: 500,000 iterations. Downstream Tasks: 300 epochs. VoxelTTO Specific Parameters: Voxel Size: 0.002 meters (optimal balance of performance and computation). Splits per Voxel: 2 (optimal; 4 splits show no substantial improvement). TTO Iterations: 20 (balances accuracy and efficiency). Depth Loss: Used by default; removing it slightly reduces geometric accuracy. Camera Sampling Strategies: PanoHead: Random cameras sampled all around the head (360°). EG3D: Mainly frontal views with small vertical and horizontal rotations. Initialization Sensitivity: 3DGS is sensitive to initialization. RAIN-GS addresses this by initializing Gaussians sparsely with large variance and progressively applying low-pass filtering to avoid 2D projections smaller than a pixel. Occlusion Artifacts: Standard densification can create "popping" artifacts in occluded regions. StopThePop integration uses occlusion-aware densification to restrict statistics to views where Gaussians actually contribute, reducing popping and keeping occlusion boundaries intact. Run-to-Run Variation: Downstream fine-tuning (e.g., ModelNet) can exhibit appreciable run-to-run variation. Results should be interpreted with caution regarding small cross-environment differences. The Adaptive Gaussian Refinement Strategy is a densification and pruning mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that dynamically adjusts the number and size of Gaussians during training based on 2D gradient magnitude and screen-space size. It solves the problem of fixed Gaussian counts by growing Gaussians in regions with high reconstruction error and pruning those that are redundant or overly large. It differs from standard densification by explicitly tracking screen-space radii to enable screen-aware splitting and pruning, and by using a reset-based accumulation of gradient statistics to avoid bias from early training steps. A standardized training and evaluation pipeline for classification and part segmentation tasks using Gaussian inputs. It defines specific protocols for ModelNet10/40 and ShapeNet-Part datasets to ensure reproducibility and fair comparison. ModelNet10/40: Uses 1,024 Gaussians, 64 groups of 32, and all 14 attributes. Full fine-tuning, linear probing, and three-layer MLP probing run for 300 epochs with AdamW, learning rate 10^{-3}, weight decay 0.05, 5 warm-up epochs, and total batch size 256. Frozen probing updates only the classifier. ShapeNet-Part: Uses 2,048 Gaussians, 128 groups of 32, batch size 16, learning rate 10^{-4}, and 300 epochs. A framework that integrates occlusion-aware densification with StopThePop's per-pixel depth ordering to remove popping artifacts and keep occlusion boundaries intact. It replaces the visibility filter with an occlusion-aware filter that updates Gaussian statistics only from views in which the Gaussian is actually rendered. It also introduces a contribution-based densification criterion, replacing the raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. This reduces the Gaussian count by up to 63% while improving image quality metrics (up to 6% lower LPIPS) on occlusion-heavy scenes. A method that initializes Gaussians sparsely with large variance from the SfM point cloud and progressively applies low-pass filtering to avoid 2D Gaussian projections smaller than a pixel, addressing sensitivity to initialization. A method that uses pixel-level error as a densification criterion and revises the opacity setting during the cloning process, leading to a more stable training process. A calibrated photometric stereo method that reconstructs 3D normal maps from multiple images with different lighting by optimizing Gaussian Splatting parameters using inverse rendering and a Lambertian reflectance model. It calculates self-occlusions (shadows) by analyzing if surfaces are aligned with the light direction, enabling view-dependent rendering despite a fixed camera. The loss function minimizes the L1 photometric loss and a normal regularization term. Time Complexity: Training time is dominated by the number of iterations and the number of Gaussians. Generative decoding requires 500,000 iterations, while downstream tasks require 300 epochs. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians. Occlusion-aware methods (StopThePop) can reduce the required Gaussian count by up to 63% compared to view-count normalizers, reducing memory footprint. Performance: VoxelTTO adds negligible overhead (2.304s vs 2.293s for 10 images) when retaining frozen attention computations in BF16. Strengths: Standardized protocols ensure reproducibility. Occlusion-aware methods improve quality in complex scenes. Limitations: Run-to-run variation in downstream tasks can obscure small performance gains. 3D Gaussian Splatting has become a dominant representation for explicit 3D scene representation. Training configurations have evolved from basic novel view synthesis to complex generative decoding and downstream transfer tasks. Key developments include the integration of occlusion-aware densification, standardized downstream protocols, and specialized methods for photometric stereo and initialization sensitivity. name: Adaptive Gaussian Refinement Strategy
head: GS Adaptation, SplatAdapt
body: The Adaptive Gaussian Refinement Strategy is a densification and pruning mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that dynamically adjusts the number and size of Gaussians during training based on 2D gradient magnitude and screen-space size. It solves the problem of fixed Gaussian counts by growing Gaussians in regions with high reconstruction error and pruning those that are redundant or overly large. It differs from standard densification by explicitly tracking screen-space radii to enable screen-aware splitting and pruning, and by using a reset-based accumulation of gradient statistics to avoid bias from early training steps. The method operates as a callback attached to the training loop, executing at specific intervals to modify the Gaussian set. It relies on accumulated 2D gradients and screen-space radii to make decisions. Inputs: Current training step step. Gaussian parameters: means, quaternions, scales, opacities, colors. Gradient information: 2D mean gradients (or absolute gradients) for visible Gaussians. Screen-space radii: maximum radius in pixels for each visible Gaussian. Configuration parameters (see below). scenescale: A normalization factor for 3D scale thresholds. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters (means, quaternions, scales, opacities, colors) after growth, splitting, and pruning operations. The strategy maintains a state dictionary state per refinement cycle: grad2d: Tensor of shape [N], accumulating the squared L2 norm of 2D gradients for each Gaussian. count: Tensor of shape [N], accumulating the number of times each Gaussian has been visible/updated. radii: Tensor of shape [N], accumulating the maximum screen-space radius observed for each Gaussian. scenescale: Float, the normalization factor for 3D scales. These tensors are initialized to None and created on the fly if not present, matching the device and size of the current Gaussian set. refinestopiter: Integer. Refinement stops when step >= refinestopiter. refinestartiter: Integer. Refinement begins only when step > refinestartiter. refineevery: Integer. Refinement steps occur every refineevery iterations. resetevery: Integer. Running statistics (grad2d, count, radii) are reset every resetevery iterations. pauserefineafterreset: Integer. If step % resetevery >= pauserefineafterreset, refinement is paused immediately after a reset to allow statistics to accumulate. refinescale2dstopiter: Integer. If > 0, screen-space radius tracking is enabled. If 0, screen-space refinement is disabled. absgrad: Boolean. If True, uses absolute gradients (absgrad); if False, uses raw gradients. keyforgradient: String. Key in the info dict storing 2D gradients, typically 'means2d' or 'gradient2dgs'. growgrad2d: Float. Threshold for mean normalized gradient magnitude. Gaussians exceeding this are candidates for growth/splitting. growscale3d: Float. Threshold for 3D scale. Gaussians with max(exp(scales)) <= growscale3d scenescale are candidates for duplication. growscale2d: Float. Threshold for screen radius. If refinescale2dstopiter > 0, Gaussians with radii > growscale2d are candidates for splitting. pruneopa: Float. Threshold for opacity. Gaussians with sigmoid(opacity) < pruneopa are pruned. prunescale3d: Float. Threshold for 3D scale. If step > resetevery, Gaussians with max(exp(scales)) > prunescale3d scenescale are pruned. prunescale2d: Float. Threshold for screen radius. If refinescale2dstopiter > 0, Gaussians with radii > prunescale2d are pruned. revisedopacity: Boolean. Passed to split/duplicate functions to determine opacity handling. 1. Initialize State: Create state dict with grad2d, count, radii (if refinescale2dstopiter > 0), and scenescale. Initialize tensors to None. 2. Pre-backward Callback: Assert keyforgradient exists in info. Retain gradient on the tensor. 3. Post-backward Check: If step >= refinestopiter, return immediately. 4. Update State: Accumulate gradient norms and counts per Gaussian. Normalize gradients: Multiply gradient x by width/2 ncameras, y by height/2 ncameras. Initialize state tensors: If grad2d/count/radii are None, create zero tensors of size ngaussian on the same device. Handle unpacked mode: If packed=False, select visible Gaussians where radii[..., 0] > 0.0, extract gsids and filter grads/radii. Accumulate gradient norm: Add norm(grads, dim=-1) to state['grad2d'] at indices gsids. Accumulate count: Add 1.0 to state['count'] at indices gsids. Compute mean gradient: Divide state['grad2d'] by state['count'] clamped to min 1. 5. Refinement Trigger: If step > refinestartiter AND step % refineevery == 0 AND step % resetevery >= pauserefineafterreset, proceed to grow/prune. 6. Grow Gaussians: Call growgs to duplicate small/high-gradient Gaussians and split large/high-gradient Gaussians. Identify small Gaussians: max(exp(scales)) <= growscale3d scenescale. Identify high gradient: grads > growgrad2d. Identify duplication candidates: isgradhigh AND issmall. Identify large Gaussians: NOT issmall. Identify split candidates: islarge. If refinescale2dstopiter > 0 and step < refinescale2dstopiter, also include if radii > growscale2d. Final split mask: isgradhigh AND issplit. Duplicate: If ndupli > 0, call duplicate() with mask isdupli. Adjust split mask: Append zeros of length ndupli to issplit so newly duplicated Gaussians are not split in the same step. Split: If nsplit > 0, call split() with mask issplit and revisedopacity. 7. Prune Gaussians: Call prunegs to remove low-opacity or oversized Gaussians. Prune condition: sigmoid(opacity) < pruneopa. Prune size condition: If step > resetevery, add Gaussians with max(exp(scales)) > prunescale3d scenescale. Prune screen size condition: If step < refinescale2dstopiter, add Gaussians with radii > prunescale2d. Final prune mask: isprune OR istoobig. Remove Gaussians: If nprune > 0, call remove() with mask isprune. 8. Reset Stats: Zero out grad2d, count, and radii tensors. Empty CUDA cache. 9. Reset Opacity: If step % resetevery == 0, call resetopa with value pruneopa 2.0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiverefinementstep(step, gaussians, info, config): """ Performs one step of adaptive refinement for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: step: Current training iteration. gaussians: Object containing Gaussian parameters (means, quats, scales, opacities, colors). info: Dictionary containing gradient information and metadata. config: Configuration object with refinement parameters. """ # 1. Initialize State if not hasattr(adaptiverefinementstep, 'state'): adaptiverefinementstep.state = { 'grad2d': None, 'count': None, 'radii': None, 'scenescale': 1.0 # Placeholder, should be derived from scene } state = adaptiverefinementstep.state # 2. Pre-backward Callback (Handled by framework, ensure gradient retention) # Assert config.keyforgradient in info # info[config.keyforgradient].retaingrad() # 3. Post-backward Check if step >= config.refinestopiter: return # 4. Update State # Normalize gradients grads = info[config.keyforgradient] if config.absgrad: grads = grads.abs() # Normalize by image dimensions and number of cameras # Note: width, height, ncameras should be available from context width = info.get('width', 1) height = info.get('height', 1) ncameras = info.get('ncameras', 1) # Assuming grads shape is [N, 2] for 2D means grads[:, 0] = width / 2 ncameras grads[:, 1] = height / 2 ncameras # Initialize state tensors if None ngaussians = gaussians.numgaussians if state['grad2d'] is None: state['grad2d'] = torch.zeros(ngaussians, device=grads.device) state['count'] = torch.zeros(ngaussians, device=grads.device) if config.refinescale2dstopiter > 0: state['radii'] = torch.zeros(ngaussians, device=grads.device) # Handle unpacked mode if not info.get('packed', True): # Select visible Gaussians visiblemask = info['radii'][:, 0] > 0.0 gsids = info['gsids'][visiblemask] visiblegrads = grads[visiblemask] visibleradii = info['radii'][visiblemask] else: gsids = torch.arange(ngaussians, device=grads.device) visiblegrads = grads visibleradii = info.get('radii', torch.zeros(ngaussians, device=grads.device)) # Accumulate gradient norm gradnorms = torch.norm(visiblegrads, dim=-1) state['grad2d'][gsids] += gradnorms # Accumulate count state['count'][gsids] += 1.0 # Accumulate radii if enabled if config.refinescale2dstopiter > 0: state['radii'][gsids] = torch.maximum(state['radii'][gsids], visibleradii) # Compute mean gradient meangrad = state['grad2d'] / torch.clamp(state['count'], min=1) # 5. Refinement Trigger if (step > config.refinestartiter and step % config.refineevery == 0 and step % config.resetevery >= config.pauserefineafterreset): # 6. Grow Gaussians issmall = torch.max(torch.exp(gaussians.scales), dim=1)[0] <= config.growscale3d state['scenescale'] isgradhigh = meangrad > config.growgrad2d isdupli = issmall & isgradhigh islarge = ~issmall issplit = islarge.clone() if config.refinescale2dstopiter > 0 and step < config.refinescale2dstopiter: issplit = issplit | (state['radii'] > config.growscale2d) finalsplitmask = isgradhigh & issplit # Duplicate ndupli = isdupli.sum().item() if ndupli > 0: gaussians.duplicate(isdupli) # Adjust split mask to exclude new Gaussians newzeros = torch.zeros(ndupli, dtype=torch.bool, device=finalsplitmask.device) finalsplitmask = torch.cat([finalsplitmask, newzeros], dim=0) # Split nsplit = finalsplitmask.sum().item() if nsplit > 0: gaussians.split(finalsplitmask, config.revisedopacity) # 7. Prune Gaussians isprune = torch.sigmoid(gaussians.opacities) < config.pruneopa istoobig = torch.zeroslike(isprune, dtype=torch.bool) if step > config.resetevery: istoobig = istoobig | (torch.max(torch.exp(gaussians.scales), dim=1)[0] > config.prunescale3d state['scenescale']) if config.refinescale2dstopiter > 0: istoobig = istoobig | (state['radii'] > config.prunescale2d) finalprunemask = isprune | istoobig nprune = finalprunemask.sum().item() if nprune > 0: gaussians.remove(finalprunemask) # 8. Reset Stats state['grad2d'].zero() state['count'].zero() if config.refinescale2dstopiter > 0: state['radii'].zero() torch.cuda.emptycache() # 9. Reset Opacity if step % config.resetevery == 0: gaussians.resetopacity(config.pruneopa 2.0) Screen-size pruning bug: The official code implements screen-size pruning but it is disabled by default (refinescale2dstopiter=0) due to a bug referenced in GitHub issue #123. Newly duplicated Gaussians: Must not be split in the same iteration. The split mask is extended with zeros corresponding to the number of duplicated Gaussians. Gradient normalization: Gradients are normalized by image dimensions and number of cameras to ensure consistent thresholds across resolutions and views. Time Complexity: O(N) per refinement step, where N is the number of Gaussians. The cost is dominated by gradient accumulation and the duplicate/split/remove operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for state tensors (grad2d, count, radii). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. The use of packed/unpacked modes allows for memory-speed trade-offs. Strengths: Dynamic adaptation to scene complexity, reduces over-smoothing in high-detail areas, and prevents excessive Gaussian count in simple areas. Limitations: Dependent on gradient quality, sensitive to parameter tuning, and screen-space pruning may be buggy. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting on complex scenes with varying levels of detail. When not to use: When screen-space refinement is disabled due to bugs, or when fixed Gaussian counts are sufficient. The Adaptive Gaussian Refinement Strategy is an implementation detail from the gsplat library, specifically the SplatAdapt module. It is based on the densification strategies proposed in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper but enhanced with screen-space awareness. The method is part of the training optimization pipeline, aiming to improve reconstruction quality by dynamically adjusting the Gaussian representation. carlinds/splatad, https://github.com/carlinds/splatad, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Pruning
head: Dominant Gaussian Retention, TopK Pruning
body: Gaussian Pruning is a post-densification strategy in 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes redundant "auxiliary" Gaussians by retaining only the "dominant" Gaussians that contribute most significantly to the final pixel color for each ray. It solves the problem of excessive Gaussian count and storage overhead caused by densification, which generates many redundant points with low geometric meaning. Unlike controlling split positions during densification, which is computationally intensive and limits freedom, this method is applied after densification and is simpler. It guarantees real-time rendering for large-scale scenes with nearly identical rendering quality while significantly reducing Gaussian count and storage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of all 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} after the densification phase, and the set of training images/views. Output: A reduced set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' containing only those identified as dominant. Data Structures: Each Gaussian gi is defined by its mean \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai (decomposed into rotation R and scaling S such that \Sigma = RSS^T R^T), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color represented by spherical harmonics (SH). During rendering, Gaussians are projected to 2D using the projective transform matrix P and Jacobian J, resulting in \Sigma' = JP\Sigma P^T J^T. The algorithm requires tracking a global boolean flag or set for each Gaussian to determine if it has been marked as dominant at least once across all pixels and views. Numbered Steps: 1. Iterate over all training images and pixels: For each pixel p in each training image, identify the set of overlapping Gaussians Np sorted by depth (front-to-back). 2. Calculate Contribution Weights: For each Gaussian gi \in Np, calculate its contribution weight weighti^p to the pixel color using the alpha-blending formula: weighti^p = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity of gi, and the product is over all Gaussians j preceding gi in depth order within Np. 3. Identify Dominant Gaussians per Pixel: Sort the weights of all Gaussians in Np in ascending order. Identify the top-K Gaussians with the highest weights as dominant for pixel p. A Gaussian g is considered dominant for pixel p if: weightg^p \ge \text{sort}(\{-weightj^p, gj \in Np\})[K] where \text{sort} returns the K-th largest weight (equivalent to the K-th element in the ascending sorted list of negative weights). 4. Global Retention Check: Mark Gaussian g as retained globally if it is identified as dominant for at least one pixel across all training images. 5. Deletion: Delete all Gaussians that were not marked as retained. These are considered "auxiliary" Gaussians that lack real geometric meaning and merely take on color rendering work belonging to dominant Gaussians. 6. Post-Pruning Optimization: Continue optimizing the colors (and potentially other attributes) of the retained dominant Gaussians, allowing them to gradually absorb the rendering work previously handled by the deleted auxiliaries. Parameters: K: The number of top-weight Gaussians to retain per pixel as dominant. Typical Value: 1. Effect: Smaller K enforces stricter filtering (more removal, potential quality degradation); larger K retains more Gaussians (higher quality, higher storage/compute). The default/final value used in the source is 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The weight calculation involves products of (1-\alphaj). If \alphaj is very close to 1, the product can underflow or become numerically unstable if not handled carefully, though standard alpha blending usually mitigates this. Boundary Conditions: If a pixel has fewer than K overlapping Gaussians, all overlapping Gaussians are retained as dominant. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has zero opacity, its weight is zero, and it will likely be pruned unless K is larger than the number of non-zero weight Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianpruning(gaussians, trainingviews, K=1): """ Prunes redundant Gaussians based on their contribution weight to pixels. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects. Each has attributes: id: unique identifier alpha: opacity depth: depth value for sorting (pre-computed or computed on fly) isretained: boolean flag, initialized to False trainingviews: List of view objects. Each has: pixels: list of pixel coordinates cameraparams: for projection K: int, number of dominant Gaussians to keep per pixel. Returns: List of retained Gaussian objects. """ # Step 1: Mark all as not retained initially for g in gaussians: g.isretained = False # Step 2: Iterate over all views and pixels for view in trainingviews: # Get all pixels in this view pixels = view.getallpixels() for p in pixels: # Get overlapping Gaussians for this pixel, sorted by depth # This requires a spatial structure (e.g., BVH or grid) or brute force # For implementation completeness, we assume a function exists overlappinggaussians = getoverlappinggaussians(p, gaussians) if not overlappinggaussians: continue # Sort by depth (front to back) # Note: In standard 3DGS, depth sorting is part of the rendering pass overlappinggaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) # Step 3: Calculate weights weights = [] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for g in overlappinggaussians: # weighti^p = alphai product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) weight = g.alpha accumulatedtransmittance weights.append((g, weight)) # Update transmittance for next Gaussian accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - g.alpha) # Step 4: Identify top-K dominant Gaussians # Sort weights in ascending order to find the K-th largest # We need the K-th largest value. # If len(weights) < K, all are dominant. if len(weights) <= K: dominantindices = range(len(weights)) else: # Sort by weight ascending weightssorted = sorted(weights, key=lambda x: x[1]) # The K-th largest is at index len(weights) - K # Example: K=1, len=5. Sorted: [w0, w1, w2, w3, w4]. # Largest is w4 (index 4). 5-1 = 4. thresholdindex = len(weights) - K thresholdweight = weightssorted[thresholdindex][1] # Identify Gaussians with weight >= threshold dominantindices = [i for i, (g, w) in enumerate(weights) if w >= thresholdweight] # Step 5: Mark retained for idx in dominantindices: g, w = weights[idx] g.isretained = True # Step 6: Filter Gaussians retainedgaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g.isretained] return retainedgaussians A sibling method that adjusts Gaussian properties based on error metrics. It differs by focusing on refinement rather than removal. Choose when fine-tuning geometry is needed. Link A sibling method that adds new Gaussians only where necessary. It differs by increasing density rather than decreasing it. Choose when the scene is under-represented. Link Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The pruning step requires iterating over all pixels and their overlapping Gaussians. Sorting weights per pixel adds a logarithmic factor relative to the number of overlapping Gaussians. The overall complexity is proportional to the total number of ray-Gaussian intersections across all training views. Memory: Significantly reduces memory usage by deleting Gaussians. Storage is reduced from 734MB (vanilla 3DGS) to 98MB (with pruning, K=1) on Mip-NeRF360. Peak GPU memory also decreases (e.g., from 12.8GB to 8.8GB in ablation studies). Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 with K=1: SSIM 0.817, PSNR 27.38, LPIPS 0.216, Training Time 19m41s, FPS 218, Storage 98MB. On Mip-NeRF360 with K=2: SSIM 0.818, PSNR 27.43, LPIPS 0.210, Training Time 20m44s, FPS 185, Storage 123MB. On Mip-NeRF360 with K=3: SSIM 0.818, PSNR 27.45, LPIPS 0.209, Training Time 21m07s, FPS 174, Storage 137MB. Compared to vanilla 3DGS (SSIM 0.815, PSNR 27.21, FPS 134, Storage 734MB), Gaussian Pruning improves FPS and drastically reduces storage with negligible quality loss. Scaling: The method scales well to large-scale high-resolution scenes by reducing the number of Gaussians, which directly impacts rendering speed and storage. Smaller K leads to faster rendering and less storage but may degrade quality slightly. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Dramatically reduces Gaussian count and storage; improves rendering speed; simple to implement; guarantees real-time rendering for large-scale scenes. Limitations: May remove Gaussians that have low weight in training views but are important for novel views if not carefully tuned; quality degradation if K is too small. When to Use: Use when training large-scale scenes with high Gaussian counts to reduce storage and improve rendering speed. Use when computational resources are limited. When Not to Use: Use with caution if the scene has complex, thin structures where many Gaussians might have low individual weights but collectively contribute to appearance. Do not use if maximum possible quality is required regardless of storage/speed. Gaussian Pruning was introduced in the paper "EfficientGS: Streamlining Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale High-Resolution Scene Representation". The method is inspired by NeRF importance sampling strategies. It addresses the redundancy generated by the densification process in 3D Gaussian Splatting, where many auxiliary Gaussians are created that lack real geometric meaning. The authors observed that each ray passes through many Gaussians, but only a few dominate the color contribution. By retaining only these dominant Gaussians, the method streamlines the scene representation.
