name: Hierarchical, Graph-Based, and Adaptive Structures
head: Adaptive Spatial Partitioning, Dynamic Gaussian Selection, Scale-Adaptive Splatting, Cross-Level Feature Coupling
body: This family addresses the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) regarding memory efficiency, rendering quality at varying scales, and structural coherence in large or complex scenes. While standard 3DGS uses a flat list of Gaussians, these methods introduce hierarchy, graph connectivity, or dynamic adaptation to optimize training, reduce memory footprint, and eliminate artifacts like aliasing or boundary discontinuities. They differ from siblings like TurboGS (which focuses on rasterization speed) and Data Compression (which focuses on storage) by modifying the geometric representation or optimization graph itself. All methods in this family modify the standard 3DGS primitive set or its optimization/rendering pipeline to introduce structure or adaptivity. Primitive Representation: Gaussians are defined by mean \mathbf{\mu}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (derived from scale \mathbf{s} and rotation \mathbf{q}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}. Rendering Equation: The color C for a pixel is computed via alpha-blending of overlapping Gaussians sorted by depth: C = \sum{i \in N{active}} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where N{active} are the Gaussians overlapping the pixel. Adaptivity: Methods either partition the scene (graph/tree), select a subset of primitives (dynamic), or deform primitives based on view scale (adaptive). TraGraph-GS handles large-scale scenes by decoupling training into local regions using a camera connectivity graph. It constructs a graph G=(V, E, w) where vertices are images and edge weights are feature match counts. It segments this graph into k regions using BFS. Local Gaussians are trained per region with multi-view (NCC) and multi-scale constraints. A global coarse representation is trained on downsampled data. Novel views are rendered by combining local and global Gaussians using a progressive weighting strategy based on a matching score S and overlap threshold \beta to eliminate boundary artifacts. FlexGS enables dynamic inference-time adaptation to memory constraints without retraining. It uses a learnable Gaussian selector (trained with Gumbel-Softmax relaxation) to choose a subset of K=eN Gaussians based on a target ratio e. A ratio-dependent transformation field then adjusts the parameters (position, scale, opacity) of the selected Gaussians to compensate for the visual loss of the pruned ones. This allows a single model to serve varying hardware constraints (e.g., mobile vs. desktop). Mipmap-GS eliminates aliasing artifacts (zoom-in spikes, zoom-out thickness) by deforming pre-trained Gaussians at test time. It optimizes the Gaussians against scale-specific "pseudo ground-truth" images generated by resizing the base rendering: super-resolution (SwinIR) for zoom-in and bilinear interpolation for zoom-out. The optimization minimizes the L2 loss between the rendered image at the target scale and the pseudo-GT, updating Gaussians via gradient descent for 1,000 iterations. Hierarchical Anchor Coupling (HAC) solves feature isolation in octree-based 3DGS. It aggregates context from adjacent octree levels (coarser and finer) to compute a per-level feature adjustment \delta^l. This adjustment is broadcast as a residual to all visible anchors at that level: \hat{f}i = fi + \delta^{li}. The context is computed using Structure-Aware Containment Aggregation (SACA) operators. If a level lacks an adjacent neighbor (boundary case), the self-context is used. This injects shared structural information while preserving per-anchor variation. Not given in the sources. 3D Gaussian Splatting introduced a fast, differentiable rendering technique using explicit Gaussian primitives. However, standard 3DGS suffers from high memory usage, boundary artifacts in large scenes, and aliasing at varying zoom levels. Recent research has focused on hierarchical structures (octrees, graphs) and adaptive mechanisms to improve scalability and quality. TraGraph-GS addresses large-scale scene partitioning. FlexGS addresses dynamic memory constraints. Mipmap-GS addresses scale-dependent aliasing. Hierarchical Anchor Coupling addresses feature propagation in hierarchical representations. Source notes provided in the prompt for the family and child articles.

name: TraGraph-GS
head: Trajectory Graph-based Gaussian Splatting
body: TraGraph-GS is a high-quality rendering method for arbitrary large-scale scenes that employs graph-based adaptive spatial partitioning, regularization constraints, and adaptive region selection to maintain real-time performance and visual fidelity across vastly different scales. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and its siblings by decoupling the scene into connected subgraphs based on camera feature matching, enabling independent local training and a progressive rendering strategy for novel viewpoints that avoids boundary artifacts. Unlike FlexGS which focuses on dynamic adaptivity, or Mipmap-GS which handles scale via mipmaps, TraGraph-GS explicitly models the structural connectivity of input images to partition the scene and uses a coarse global representation combined with sorted local contributions for novel view synthesis. Inputs: A set of disordered scene photographs (images) and their associated camera poses. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (local and global) and a rendering pipeline capable of generating novel views. Data Structures: 1. Camera Connectivity Graph: G = (V, E, w), where V = \{v1,..., vn\} are image vertices, E are edges, and w: E \rightarrow \mathbb{R} are weights representing feature matching counts (covisibility). 2. Local Gaussians: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} trained independently for each segmented region Pi. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by mean \mathbf{\mu}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (from scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}i. 3. Global Gaussians: A coarse set of 3D Gaussians trained on downsampled data to capture overall scene structure. Algorithm Steps: 1. Graph Construction: Construct the camera connectivity graph G. For every pair of images, count the number of matched features. Assign this count as the edge weight w{ij}. 2. BFS-Based Graph Segmentation: Divide G into k regions \{Pi\}{i=1}^k ensuring connectivity and balanced node distribution: Initialize unassigned nodes U = V. Identify the node n with the highest degree in U as a seed node. Perform Breadth-First Search (BFS) from the seed, adding nodes to the current region until it contains |V|/k nodes. For remaining unassigned nodes, calculate a score si relative to existing regions and assign them to maintain balance. 3. Local Training with Regularization: Train local 3D Gaussians independently for each region Pi using the following loss function: L = (1 - \lambda)L1 + \lambda L{SSIM} + L{mv} where L1 and L{SSIM} are standard reconstruction losses. Multi-View Constraint (L{mv}): For textureless regions, render depth and normal maps. For a pixel p in a reference view, establish a spatial plane (d, \mathbf{n}). Use homography warping to project p to a corresponding pixel p' in a neighborhood view. Minimize the difference using Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC): L{mv} = \sum{p \in Pi} (1 - \text{NCC}(p, p')) Multi-Scale Constraint: Apply position-aware point adaptive control to adjust Gaussian scales based on viewer distance. Define a scale factor \gamma(\mathbf{\mu}) where r is the scene radius and \mathbf{c} is the camera center: \gamma(\mathbf{\mu}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \|\mathbf{\mu} - \mathbf{c}\|2 < 2r \\ \|\mathbf{\mu} - \mathbf{c}\|2 / r - 1 & \text{if } \|\mathbf{\mu} - \mathbf{c}\|2 \ge 2r \end{cases} If the directional gradient exceeds a threshold: Clone if \max(\mathbf{s}) < g \cdot \gamma(\mathbf{\mu}). Split if the condition is not met. Prune Gaussians with low opacity. 4. Global Representation Training: For novel viewpoints, train a coarse global Gaussian representation by downsampling point clouds and images. Avoid the densification process to prevent excessive memory consumption. 5. Adaptive Region Selection (Novel View Rendering): Render the novel viewpoint using local and global Gaussians separately. Calculate a matching score S for each local-global Gaussian pair: S = (1 - \lambda)L1 + \lambda L{SSIM} Higher scores indicate higher visibility likelihood. Sort local Gaussians in descending order of S: G1, G2,..., Gk. Compute projection opacity oi(p) for each pixel p: oi(p) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Compute final pixel color c(p) using a progressive rendering strategy with weights wi based on an overlapped opacity threshold \beta: wi = \begin{cases} oi(p) & \text{if } \sum{j=1}^{i-1} oj(p) < \beta \\ 0 & \text{if } \sum{j=1}^{i-1} oj(p) \ge \beta \end{cases} c(p) = \sum{i=1}^{k} wi ci(p) where ci(p) is the color rendered by local Gaussian Gi. Parameters: k: Number of segmented regions (Not given in the sources). \lambda: Weight for SSIM loss (Not given in the sources). r: Scene radius (Not given in the sources). \beta: Overlapped opacity threshold for progressive rendering (Not given in the sources). g: Scaling factor for cloning criterion (Not given in the sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overflow: Unbalanced node distribution in segmentation can lead to memory overflow. The BFS method is chosen specifically to prevent this. Boundary Artifacts: Naively combining local Gaussians can cause floating artifacts or holes at region boundaries. The progressive rendering strategy with matching scores mitigates this. Textureless Regions: Standard 3DGS struggles with geometry in textureless areas; the multi-view constraint is required to address this. Time Complexity: Training is parallelized across regions, reducing per-region memory and potentially time. Novel view rendering involves sorting local Gaussians and progressive blending, adding overhead compared to standard alpha-blending. Memory Complexity: By partitioning the scene and using a coarse global representation for novel views, memory usage is controlled. Global training avoids densification to prevent excessive consumption. Performance: Evaluated on large-scale aerial (up to 3,019 images) and ground datasets (e.g., SmallCity, Campus). Maintains real-time performance across vastly different scales. Strengths: Handles arbitrary large-scale scenes; improves texture details and geometry in textureless regions; avoids boundary artifacts in novel views. Limitations: Requires feature matching for graph construction; performance depends on the quality of the graph segmentation. TraGraph-GS was proposed to address the limitations of existing methods in rendering large-scale scenes, such as memory overflow and boundary artifacts. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting [11] and extends them with graph-based partitioning and regularization constraints. The method was introduced in a paper published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence in 2026. name: FlexGS
head: Flexible 3D Gaussian Splatting, Elastic 3DGS
body: FlexGS is an elastic inference method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that enables a single trained model to adapt to varying computational constraints at inference time by selecting and transforming a subset of Gaussians based on a desired model size ratio, without requiring additional fine-tuning. It solves the problem that standard 3DGS models are too memory-intensive for devices with restricted resources (e.g., smartphones, VR headsets) and that previous compression methods require costly separate fine-tuning runs for each target compression ratio. Unlike post-hoc pruning methods that use fixed heuristics to retain Top-K Gaussians, FlexGS jointly trains a learnable selector and a transformation field to dynamically adjust the primitive set. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained 3DGS model consisting of N Gaussians, each characterized by position \mathbf{X}, scaling vector \mathbf{s}, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{SH}. A target ratio e \in (0, 1] specifying the fraction of Gaussians to retain. Output: A subset of K = eN Gaussians, with modified parameters, ready for rendering. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i is defined by: Position \mathbf{X}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scaling vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or \mathbb{R}^4 for normalized quaternion). Opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}. Color \mathbf{c}i defined by spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{SH}i \in \mathbb{R}^{(d+1)^2} where d is the SH degree. Selector Output: A binary scaler \lambdai \in \{0, 1\} for each Gaussian, where \lambdai = 1 indicates selection. Core Formulas: 1. Gaussian Definition: The spatial distribution is defined by mean \mathbf{X} and covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}: G(\mathbf{X}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{X}} The covariance is decomposed into scaling matrix \mathbf{S} and rotation matrix \mathbf{R}: \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^\top \mathbf{R}^\top where \mathbf{S} is derived from \mathbf{s} and \mathbf{R} from \mathbf{q}. 2. Rendering Equation: Color C for a pixel is computed via alpha-blending of overlapping Gaussians sorted by depth: C = \sum{i \in N{active}} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where N{active} are the selected Gaussians overlapping the pixel. 3. Selection Constraint: The sum of selected Gaussians must equal the target count: \sum{i=1}^{N} \lambdai = eN. Steps: 1. Training Phase (Joint Optimization): Initialize a standard 3DGS model with N Gaussians. Introduce a Learnable Gaussian Selector: A module that takes Gaussian attributes (\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{q}, \alpha, \mathbf{SH}) and the target ratio e as input, and outputs a probability distribution over \lambdai. To handle the discrete nature of \lambdai, the method uses Gumbel-Softmax relaxation during training to allow gradient backpropagation. Introduce a Ratio-Dependent Gaussian Transformation Field: A module that takes the selected Gaussians and the ratio e as input, and outputs displacement/adjustment parameters to modify the attributes of the selected Gaussians. This compensates for missing details caused by pruning. Optimize the 3DGS parameters, selector weights, and transformation field weights jointly using standard rendering loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM). The selector learns to identify important Gaussians dynamically as attributes evolve, avoiding the need for frequent re-computation of static importance scores. 2. Inference Phase (Elastic Deployment): Given a target ratio e (e.g., 0.1 for 10% of Gaussians): Select: Pass the pre-trained Gaussians and e through the learned selector to obtain binary mask \lambdai. Filter the Gaussian set to keep only those with \lambdai = 1. The number of kept Gaussians is K = eN. Transform: Pass the selected Gaussians and e through the learned transformation field. Apply the predicted adjustments to the position, scale, or other attributes of the selected Gaussians to restore visual fidelity lost by pruning. Render: Render the transformed subset using the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline. Parameters: Target Ratio (e): A float between 0 and 1. Typical values depend on hardware constraints (e.g., 0.1 for mobile, 0.5 for VR). Not given in the sources for specific training hyperparameters (e.g., learning rates, number of iterations). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Extreme Compression: Fixed heuristic selection may fail when selecting very small percentages (e.g., 1%) because importance scores must be frequently re-computed as Gaussian attributes evolve during training. FlexGS addresses this by learning the selection dynamically. Discrete Optimization: Direct optimization over discrete binary choices \lambdai is ineffective for gradient descent. The method must use relaxation techniques (like Gumbel-Softmax) during training, which may introduce approximation errors. Pseudocode: import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class FlexGS: def init(self, gaussians, selectornet, transformnet): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes X, s, q, alpha, SH selectornet: nn.Module that outputs selection probabilities given attributes and ratio transformnet: nn.Module that outputs transformation deltas given attributes and ratio """ self.gaussians = gaussians self.selector = selectornet self.transform = transformnet def trainstep(self, images, cameras, targetratio, optimizer): """ Jointly optimize 3DGS, selector, and transform network. """ optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Get selection probabilities using Gumbel-Softmax relaxation # selectornet takes batch of Gaussian attributes and targetratio selectionprobs = self.selector(self.gaussians, targetratio) # Relax binary selection to continuous for backprop # lambdarelaxed is the soft selection mask lambdarelaxed = self.gumbelsoftmax(selectionprobs, hard=False) # 2. Apply selection mask to Gaussians (soft selection) # In practice, this might involve masking attributes or weights selectedgaussians = self.applyselection(self.gaussians, lambdarelaxed) # 3. Apply transformation to compensate for pruning # transformnet takes selected Gaussians and targetratio transformdeltas = self.transform(selectedgaussians, targetratio) transformedgaussians = self.applytransform(selectedgaussians, transformdeltas) # 4. Render images using transformed Gaussians renderedimages = render3dgs(transformedgaussians, cameras) # 5. Compute loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, images) # 6. Backpropagate loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss def infer(self, targetratio): """ Deploy the model with a specific compression ratio. """ # 1. Hard selection based on learned probabilities selectionprobs = self.selector(self.gaussians, targetratio) # Use argmax or threshold to get binary mask lambdahard = (selectionprobs > 0.5).float() # Simplified thresholding # 2. Filter Gaussians selectedindices = torch.where(lambdahard == 1)[0] selectedgaussians = [self.gaussians[i] for i in selectedindices] # 3. Transform selected Gaussians transformdeltas = self.transform(selectedgaussians, targetratio) transformedgaussians = self.applytransform(selectedgaussians, transformdeltas) return transformedgaussians def gumbelsoftmax(self, logits, tau=1.0, hard=False): """Standard Gumbel-Softmax relaxation.""" gumbels = -torch.emptylike(logits).exponential().log() gumbels = (logits + gumbels) / tau ysoft = F.softmax(gumbels, dim=-1) if hard: index = ysoft.max(1, keepdim=True)[1] yhard = torch.zeroslike(logits).scatter(1, index, 1.0) ret = yhard - ysoft.detach() + ysoft else: ret = ysoft return ret def applyselection(self, gaussians, mask): """Apply soft selection mask to Gaussian attributes.""" # Implementation depends on specific attribute masking strategy # Placeholder for specific implementation details not provided in source return gaussians def applytransform(self, gaussians, deltas): """Apply transformation deltas to Gaussian attributes.""" # Implementation depends on specific transformation strategy # Placeholder for specific implementation details not provided in source return gaussians def render3dgs(self, gaussians, cameras): """Standard 3DGS rendering pipeline.""" # Placeholder for standard 3DGS rasterization return None def computeloss(self, rendered, target): """Compute L1 and SSIM loss.""" # Placeholder for standard loss computation return None Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to standard 3DGS but requires joint optimization of the selector and transformation networks, potentially increasing per-step cost. Inference time is reduced proportionally to the target ratio e, as fewer Gaussians are rendered. Memory Complexity: Training memory is higher than standard 3DGS due to the additional networks (selector and transformer). Inference memory scales with the target ratio e, allowing deployment on devices with limited VRAM. Measured Performance: Experiments on ZipNeRF, MipNeRF, and Tanks&Temples scenes demonstrate effectiveness in balancing rendering speed and visual quality. Specific PSNR/SSIM metrics or FPS numbers are not provided in the sources. Strengths: Single model supports arbitrary compression ratios without retraining. Adapts to diverse hardware constraints (smartphones, VR). Avoids the need for separate fine-tuning runs for each ratio. Limitations: Requires joint training of additional modules, increasing training complexity. Performance at extreme compression ratios (e.g., 1%) may be challenging due to the difficulty of learning robust selection and transformation policies. When to use: When deploying 3DGS on multiple devices with varying computational capabilities and avoiding the cost of maintaining multiple pruned models. When not to use: When maximum possible quality is required for a single fixed hardware configuration (standard 3DGS or post-hoc pruning with fine-tuning might yield better results for that specific ratio). FlexGS was introduced by Hengyu Liu, Yuehao Wang, Chenxin Li, Ruisi Cai, Kevin Wang, Wuyang Li, Pavlo Molchanov, Peihao Wang, and Zhangyang Wang from The Chinese University of Hong Kong, University of Texas at Austin, and Nvidia. The paper "FlexGS: Train Once, Deploy Everywhere with Many-in-One Flexible 3D Gaussian Splatting" was published in CVPR 2025 (arXiv:2506.04174v1, June 4, 2025). It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS in terms of memory overhead and the rigidity of previous compression methods that require separate fine-tuning for each target compression ratio. name: Gaussian Mixture Tree Construction
head: Hierarchically Merging Gaussians
body: Gaussian Mixture Tree (GMT) Construction is a post-processing method that organizes 3D Gaussian primitives into a hierarchical tree structure to identify distinct 3D plane instances in a scene. It solves the problem of spatially scattered Gaussian centers by grouping them into coherent planar surfaces, enabling higher-level semantic or geometric understanding. Unlike sibling methods that focus on rendering efficiency or compression, GMT explicitly models the scene as a composition of 3D planes using Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) to join nodes recursively from leaves to root. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of Ns leaf nodes, where each leaf node Gi represents a local cluster of Gaussian primitives. Each node Gi is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, normal vector ni \in \mathbb{R}^3, and plane descriptor zi \in \mathbb{R}^k (typically k=3). Output: A set of parent nodes Gs representing merged plane instances, and the root of the Gaussian Mixture Tree. Data Structures Each node in the GMT stores: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix. n \in \mathbb{R}^3: Surface normal vector. z \in \mathbb{R}^k: Plane descriptor vector (learnable or derived from 2D segmentation). Algorithm Steps The construction follows a greedy hierarchical merging strategy: 1. Initialize counter L = 0 and output set Gs = \emptyset. 2. Iterate through each leaf node i from 1 to Ns: a. Check if node i is already a descendant of any existing node in Gs. If yes, skip to the next i. b. If node i is not yet merged, initialize it as a candidate for a new parent node. c. Iterate through each subsequent leaf node j from i+1 to Ns: i. Check if node j is already a descendant of any existing node in Gs. If yes, skip to the next j. ii. Calculate the Bhattacharya distance DB(Gi, Gj) and the cosine similarity difference between descriptors zi and zj. iii. If DB(Gi, Gj) \leq \epsilonB AND 1 - \langle zi \cdot zj \rangle \leq \epsilonz: 1. Merge Gi and Gj into a parent node G{ij}^p with parameters (\mup, \Sigmap) using the GMM merging formulas. 2. Update Gi \leftarrow G{ij}^p. 3. Break the inner loop (stop checking further j for this i). d. Insert the resulting node Gi into Gs. e. Increment L \leftarrow L + 1. Formulas The merging of two Gaussian distributions Gi(\mui, \Sigmai) and Gj(\muj, \Sigmaj) into a parent Gp(\mup, \Sigmap) uses the following equations: \mathbf{\Sigma}p = \mathbf{\Sigma}j \cdot (\mathbf{\Sigma}i + \mathbf{\Sigma}j)^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}i \mathbf{\mu}p = \mathbf{\Sigma}j \cdot (\mathbf{\Sigma}i + \mathbf{\Sigma}j)^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{\mu}i + \mathbf{\Sigma}i \cdot (\mathbf{\Sigma}i + \mathbf{\Sigma}j)^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{\mu}j The merging criterion relies on the Bhattacharya distance DB: DB(Gi, Gj) = \frac{1}{8}(\mathbf{\mu}i-\mathbf{\mu}j)^{T}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{\mu}i-\mathbf{\mu}j) + \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(\frac {\det \mathbf{\Sigma }}{\sqrt {\det \mathbf{\Sigma }i \det \mathbf{\Sigma }j}}\right) where \mathbf{\Sigma} = (\mathbf{\Sigma}i + \mathbf{\Sigma}j)/2. Parameters \epsilonB: Threshold for the Bhattacharya distance. Not given in the sources. \epsilonz: Threshold for the cosine similarity difference between plane descriptors zi and zj. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructgaussianmixturetree(leafnodes, epsilonb, epsilonz): """ Constructs a Gaussian Mixture Tree by hierarchically merging leaf nodes. Args: leafnodes: List of Node objects, each with attributes: mu: numpy array (3,) Sigma: numpy array (3, 3) z: numpy array (k,) ismerged: boolean (initially False) epsilonb: float, Bhattacharya distance threshold. epsilonz: float, cosine similarity difference threshold. Returns: parentnodes: List of merged Node objects representing plane instances. """ parentnodes = [] n = len(leafnodes) for i in range(n): nodei = leafnodes[i] # Skip if already merged into a previous parent if nodei.ismerged: continue # Start a new potential parent node with nodei currentnode = nodei for j in range(i + 1, n): nodej = leafnodes[j] # Skip if already merged into a previous parent if nodej.ismerged: continue # Calculate Bhattacharya distance # Sigmaavg = (Sigmai + Sigmaj) / 2 sigmaavg = (currentnode.Sigma + nodej.Sigma) / 2.0 # Term 1: Mahalanobis distance part diffmu = currentnode.mu - nodej.mu try: invsigmaavg = np.linalg.inv(sigmaavg) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: # Handle singular matrix if necessary continue term1 = 0.25 diffmu.T @ invsigmaavg @ diffmu # Term 2: Determinant part detsigmaavg = np.linalg.det(sigmaavg) detsigmai = np.linalg.det(currentnode.Sigma) detsigmaj = np.linalg.det(nodej.Sigma) # Avoid log of non-positive numbers if detsigmaavg <= 0 or detsigmai <= 0 or detsigmaj <= 0: continue term2 = 0.5 np.log(detsigmaavg / np.sqrt(detsigmai detsigmaj)) dbdist = term1 + term2 # Calculate cosine similarity difference # Normalize descriptors if not already normalized zinorm = currentnode.z / (np.linalg.norm(currentnode.z) + 1e-8) zjnorm = nodej.z / (np.linalg.norm(nodej.z) + 1e-8) cosinesim = np.dot(zinorm, zjnorm) cosinediff = 1.0 - cosinesim # Check merging criteria if dbdist <= epsilonb and cosinediff <= epsilonz: # Merge nodej into currentnode # Sigmap = Sigmaj (Sigmai + Sigmaj)^-1 Sigmai sumsigma = currentnode.Sigma + nodej.Sigma try: invsumsigma = np.linalg.inv(sumsigma) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue currentnode.Sigma = nodej.Sigma @ invsumsigma @ currentnode.Sigma # Mup = Sigmaj (Sigmai + Sigmaj)^-1 Mui + Sigmai (Sigmai + Sigmaj)^-1 Muj termmu1 = nodej.Sigma @ invsumsigma @ currentnode.mu termmu2 = currentnode.Sigma @ invsumsigma @ nodej.mu currentnode.mu = termmu1 + termmu2 # Update descriptors? The source does not specify how zp is calculated. # Assuming z is inherited or updated by a separate learning process # For this implementation, we keep currentnode.z as is or average it? # Source says "plane descriptor z" is introduced for each primitive. # Merging logic for z is not explicitly defined in the provided text. # We will assume z is not updated in the merge step itself, # or handled by the "Learning Plane Descriptors" section separately. # Mark nodej as merged nodej.ismerged = True # Break inner loop as nodei has found a partner and merged break # Add the resulting node to parent nodes parentnodes.append(currentnode) return parentnodes Complexity: The algorithm involves nested loops over Ns leaf nodes, resulting in O(Ns^2) comparisons in the worst case. Each comparison requires matrix inversion and determinant calculation, which is O(1) for fixed 3 \times 3 matrices but adds constant overhead. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a hierarchical representation of 3D planes, facilitating semantic understanding and compact scene representation. Limitations: Computationally expensive if the number of leaf nodes is large, as raw Gaussian primitives are first clustered into leaves. The quality depends on the accuracy of the plane descriptors z and the thresholds \epsilonB, \epsilonz. The method was introduced in "Planar Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the issue that optimizing 3D Gaussian parameters leads to centers moving close to object surfaces, making it difficult to identify distinct planar structures. The approach uses a probabilistic model (Gaussian Mixture Tree) to recursively join nodes from leaves to root, identifying 3D plane instances. Plane descriptors are learned by lifting 2D information (normals from Omnidata, masks from SAM) to 3D. Planar Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00863, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mipmap-GS
head: Mipmap-Gaussian Splatting
body: Mipmap-GS is a test-time adaptation method that deforms pre-trained 3D Gaussians into scale-adaptive primitives to eliminate aliasing artifacts (zoom-in spikes and zoom-out thickness) caused by fixed Gaussian distributions at varying zoom factors. Unlike methods that apply post-processing filters or hierarchical level-of-detail selection, Mipmap-GS self-adjusts primitive properties and distribution by optimizing against scale-specific mipmap-like pseudo ground-truth, effectively informing the Gaussians of the new sampling rate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of single-scale trained base Gaussians G = \{Gk\}{k=1}^K, where each Gaussian Gk is defined by mean \mathbf{\mu}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (derived from scale \mathbf{s} and rotation \mathbf{q}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}. A set of viewpoints V = \{vj\} and a target zoom factor N. Output: Optimized Gaussians G{opt} = \{G^{opt}k\}{k=1}^K adapted to the scale defined by N. Data Structures: The Gaussian representation follows the standard 3DGS layout [Parent]: \mathbf{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. \alpha \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c}: Spherical harmonics coefficients. No additional data structures are introduced; the method modifies the parameters of the existing Gaussian primitives. Parameters: N: The zoom factor. For zoom-in, N > 1 (upsampling); for zoom-out, N < 1 (downsampling). S: Number of adaptation iterations. Typically 1,000 (1K) iterations are sufficient for convergence. \beta: Learning rate for the optimization step. r(x): The mipmap resizing function. For zoom-in, super-resolution methods like SwinIR are used. For zoom-out, bilinear interpolation is used. Algorithm Steps: 1. Base Rendering: Render the base Gaussians G at the basic scale (\times 1) for a randomly selected viewpoint vj to obtain the base image \hat{x}j. 2. Pseudo-GT Construction: Apply the resizing function r(\cdot) to \hat{x}j to generate the scale-specific pseudo ground-truth \hat{y}j = r(\hat{x}j). If zoom-in (N > 1), upsample \hat{x}j by factor N using super-resolution. If zoom-out (N < 1), downsample \hat{x}j by factor 1/N using bilinear interpolation. 3. Adaptive Rendering: Render the current optimized Gaussians G^{(i)} (initially G^{(0)} = G) at the target scale to produce the rendered image xj. Note: The rendering equation remains the standard alpha-blending, but the Gaussians G^{(i)} have been deformed. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the scale-aware guidance loss L between the rendered image xj and the pseudo-GT \hat{y}j: L(xj, \hat{y}j) = \| xj - \hat{y}j \|2^2 where \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm. 5. Optimization Step: Update the Gaussians using gradient descent: G^{(i+1)} = G^{(i)} - \beta \nabla{G^{(i)}} L(xj, \hat{y}j) 6. Pruning/Densification: If the iteration count i is a multiple of 100, perform densification or pruning operations to maintain a compact representation. 7. Repeat: Iterate steps 1-6 for S iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mipmapgsoptimize(basegaussians, viewpoints, zoomfactor, numiterations, learningrate): """ Deforms base Gaussians to adapt to a specific zoom scale. Args: basegaussians: List of Gaussian primitives {Gk}. viewpoints: List of camera viewpoints {vj}. zoomfactor: Float N. >1 for zoom-in, <1 for zoom-out. numiterations: Integer S (typically 1000). learningrate: Float beta. Returns: optimizedgaussians: List of deformed Gaussian primitives. """ # Initialize current Gaussians as a copy of base Gaussians currentgaussians = copy(basegaussians) for i in range(numiterations): # 1. Select a random viewpoint vj = randomchoice(viewpoints) # 2. Render base Gaussians at basic scale (x1) to get base image # This uses the original, undeformed basegaussians baseimage = render(basegaussians, vj, scale=1.0) # 3. Construct pseudo-GT using mipmap resizing function r(x) # For zoom-in: super-resolution (e.g., SwinIR) # For zoom-out: bilinear downsampling pseudogt = resizemipmap(baseimage, zoomfactor) # 4. Render current (deformed) Gaussians at the target scale # The rendering process implicitly handles the scale change via # the deformed Gaussian parameters or explicit scale factor in rasterizer renderedimage = render(currentgaussians, vj, scale=zoomfactor) # 5. Compute L2 loss between rendered image and pseudo-GT loss = l2loss(renderedimage, pseudogt) # 6. Compute gradients and update Gaussians gradients = computegradients(loss, currentgaussians) currentgaussians = updategaussians(currentgaussians, gradients, learningrate) # 7. Active pruning/densification every 100 iterations if i % 100 == 0: currentgaussians = densifyorprune(currentgaussians) return currentgaussians def resizemipmap(image, zoomfactor): """ Applies mipmap-like resizing. """ if zoomfactor > 1.0: # Zoom-in: Upsample using super-resolution # Note: SwinIR is referenced in sources, but for implementation # a generic super-resolution model or high-quality interpolation is used. return superresolutionupsample(image, zoomfactor) else: # Zoom-out: Downsample using bilinear interpolation targetheight = int(image.height zoomfactor) targetwidth = int(image.width zoomfactor) return bilinearresize(image, targetwidth, targetheight) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zoom-in Spikes: Caused by varying shrinkage bias leading to confusion during accumulation when sampling rates change. The method addresses this by deforming Gaussians rather than relying on constant dilation. Zoom-out Thickness: Caused by constant dilation leading to excessively wide coverage and thick structures. The method addresses this by adapting Gaussian size and opacity to the lower resolution. High-Frequency Loss: Unlike Mip-Splatting which uses smoothing filters that suppress high-frequency components, Mipmap-GS preserves finer details by using pseudo-GT derived from the base rendering. Pruning Strategy: Unlike standard 3DGS which stops pruning halfway, Mipmap-GS performs active pruning throughout the entire optimization process to ensure a compact representation, especially important for zoom-out where fewer Gaussians are needed. Uses a graph-based structure to manage Gaussian connectivity and optimization. Link Introduces flexible primitives to handle complex geometry. Link Uses a hierarchical structure with anchors to couple Gaussians for multi-scale rendering. Link Time Complexity: The method requires O(S \cdot J) rendering and optimization steps, where S is the number of iterations (1K) and J is the number of viewpoints sampled per iteration. It is significantly faster than training from scratch, requiring only 3% of the iterations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is comparable to standard 3DGS, potentially reduced due to active pruning during optimization. Measured Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, Mipmap-GS outperforms standard 3DGS by an average of 9.25 dB PSNR for zoom-in and 10.40 dB for zoom-out. At \times 1/2 zoom-out on NeRF Synthetic, it achieves SSIM 0.971, PSNR 32.71, LPIPS 0.026, compared to 3DGS SSIM 0.951, PSNR 27.14, LPIPS 0.031. On Mip-NeRF 360 at \times 1/2 zoom-out, it achieves SSIM 0.854, PSNR 28.57, compared to 3DGS SSIM 0.774, PSNR 26.66. Strengths: Plug-in module compatible with any 3DGS model; test-time adaptation without retraining; preserves high-frequency details better than filtering-based methods. Limitations: Requires test-time optimization for each new scale; performance depends on the quality of the super-resolution/downsampling function. Mipmap-GS was proposed to address the aliasing and blurriness issues in 3D Gaussian Splatting when zooming in or out. Traditional methods like Mip-Splatting use heuristic 2D/3D filters that suppress high frequencies, while hierarchical methods like Octree-GS use level-of-detail selection which can be sensitive to hyperparameters. Mipmap-GS introduces a scale-aware guidance loss that deforms Gaussians to match the target scale, inspired by the mipmap technique but applied dynamically at test time. name: Hierarchical Anchor Coupling
head: Per-level hierarchical anchor coupling
body: Hierarchical Anchor Coupling (HAC) is a module that establishes cross-level gradient pathways in structured 3D Gaussian splatting by aggregating context from adjacent octree levels and broadcasting a residual feature adjustment to all visible anchors at a specific level. It solves the problem of feature isolation, where backpropagation graphs in anchor-based octree pipelines lack connections between features at level li and adjacent levels li \pm 1. Unlike sibling methods that may modify primitive geometry or rendering equations, HAC operates exclusively on the feature aggregation stage, introducing a shared residual component that preserves intra-level variation while enabling cross-level information flow. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of visible anchors V for a training camera, where each anchor i has a base feature vector fi and an octree level li. Output: Enhanced feature vectors \hat{f}i for each visible anchor, which replace fi as input to the downstream Neural Gaussian decoding MLPs. Data Structures: Visible Anchor Set (V): The collection of anchors overlapping the current view frustum. Level Set (LV): The set of unique octree levels present in V, defined as LV = \{li: i \in V\}. Level-Specific Visible Anchors (Vl): The subset of visible anchors at level l, defined as Vl = \{i \in V: li = l\}. Context Vector (tl): A concatenated vector of shape \mathbb{R}^{3d}, where d is the feature dimension. Adjustment Vector (\deltal): A residual vector of shape \mathbb{R}^d computed for each level. MLP (g\theta): A two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron with ReLU activation, mapping \mathbb{R}^{3d} \to \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d. The hidden dimension is d=32. Parameters: Granularity: The method defaults to per-level granularity, computing a single shared adjustment \deltal for all anchors at level l. A per-anchor alternative exists but is not the default. Aggregation Operators: A{par} (coarser-level) and A{chi} (finer-level) incorporate octree topology. These are specified by the Structure-Aware Containment Aggregation (SACA) module, which is external to HAC but required for context computation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify the set of visible levels LV and the visible anchors Vl for each level l \in LV. 2. For each level l \in LV, compute three context vectors: Self-context (c{self}^l): The uniform mean of features at level l: c{self}^l = \frac{1}{|Vl|} \sum{i \in Vl} fi Coarser-level context (c{par}^l): Aggregated from the adjacent coarser level (l-1) using operator A{par}: c{par}^l = A{par}(\{fi\}{i \in V{l-1}}) Finer-level context (c{chi}^l): Aggregated from the adjacent finer level (l+1) using operator A{chi}: c{chi}^l = A{chi}(\{fi\}{i \in V{l+1}}) 3. Boundary Handling: If level l lacks an adjacent coarser level (e.g., root level) or finer level (e.g., leaf level), the corresponding context vector defaults to the self-context c{self}^l. 4. Concatenate the three context vectors into a per-level triplet tl: tl = [c{par}^l; c{self}^l; c{chi}^l] \in \mathbb{R}^{3d} 5. Pass the triplet through the MLP to compute the level-wise adjustment: \deltal = g\theta(tl) 6. Broadcast the adjustment \deltal as a residual to all visible anchors at level l to produce enhanced features: \hat{f}i = fi + \deltal, \quad \forall i \in Vl 7. Replace original features fi with enhanced features \hat{f}i for downstream rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalanchorcoupling(visibleanchors, levelset, aggregationops, mlp): """ visibleanchors: List of objects with attributes.id,.level,.feature levelset: Set of unique levels present in visibleanchors aggregationops: Dictionary containing 'par' (coarser) and 'chi' (finer) functions mlp: Two-layer MLP function gtheta Returns: enhancedfeatures: Dictionary mapping anchorid to enhanced feature vector """ # Group anchors by level anchorsbylevel = {} for anchor in visibleanchors: l = anchor.level if l not in anchorsbylevel: anchorsbylevel[l] = [] anchorsbylevel[l].append(anchor) enhancedfeatures = {} # Process each visible level for l in levelset: currentanchors = anchorsbylevel[l] if not currentanchors: continue # 1. Compute Self-Context # Uniform mean of features at current level featurescurrent = [a.feature for a in currentanchors] cself = sum(featurescurrent) / len(featurescurrent) # 2. Compute Coarser-Level Context (l-1) levelcoarser = l - 1 if levelcoarser in anchorsbylevel and anchorsbylevel[levelcoarser]: featurescoarser = [a.feature for a in anchorsbylevel[levelcoarser]] cpar = aggregationops'par' else: # Boundary case: default to self-context cpar = cself # 3. Compute Finer-Level Context (l+1) levelfiner = l + 1 if levelfiner in anchorsbylevel and anchorsbylevel[levelfiner]: featuresfiner = [a.feature for a in anchorsbylevel[levelfiner]] cchi = aggregationops'chi' else: # Boundary case: default to self-context cchi = cself # 4. Concatenate into Triplet # Assuming feature dimension is d, triplet is 3d triplet = concatenate([cpar, cself, cchi]) # 5. Compute Adjustment via MLP deltal = mlp(triplet) # 6. Broadcast Residual to all anchors at this level for anchor in currentanchors: enhancedfeatures[anchor.id] = anchor.feature + deltal return enhancedfeatures Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Levels: Levels at the top (root) or bottom (leaf) of the octree may lack adjacent coarser or finer levels. The algorithm must detect this and substitute the missing context with the self-context c{self}^l. Empty Levels: If a level has no visible anchors, it is skipped in the loop, but its context may still be required by adjacent levels. The aggregation operators A{par} and A{chi} must handle empty input sets gracefully, likely returning zero vectors or defaulting to self-context if the level is absent from LV. Feature Dimension Consistency: The MLP expects an input of size 3d. If the base feature dimension d varies, the concatenation and MLP weights must be adjusted accordingly. Time Complexity: The MLP g\theta is invoked once per visible level, not once per visible anchor. The cost of MLP evaluation scales with the number of visible levels |LV|. Computing level-wise means and broadcasting residuals scales linearly with the number of visible anchors |V|. Memory Complexity: HAC adds 4,160 parameters via the shared two-layer MLP (hidden dimension d=32). The total parameter increment is below 0.1% of the model size. Performance: On the Mill19-Building scene, HAC yields a PSNR improvement of +1.91 dB over the baseline. Training time increases slightly (e.g., from 2h15m to 2h22m in ablation studies) due to per-view aggregation, but the net rendering speed improves because HAC reduces the number of decoded and rasterized Neural Gaussians by roughly 35%. Granularity Trade-offs: Per-Level (Default): Faster (~20% faster in training) and better for dense repetitive structures (e.g., +1.06 dB on Building). Acts as an implicit regularizer against over-parameterization. Per-Anchor: Computes a distinct \deltai for every anchor via spatial lookup. Cost grows linearly with |V|. Slightly better for simpler geometry (e.g., +0.21 dB on Rubble) but slower. Strengths: Alleviates feature isolation; low parameter overhead; compatible with various backbones (CityGS-X, Octree-GS, Proxy-GS). Limitations: Relies on the underlying octree structure; performance gain depends on scene topology (less effective on simple geometry compared to complex structures). Hierarchical Anchor Coupling was introduced in the paper "TopoGS: Topology-Aware Anchor Feature Aggregation for Large-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting". It was developed to address the lack of cross-level gradient pathways in existing anchor-based octree pipelines. The method is integrated into the TopoGS framework and has been shown to transfer effectively to other structured 3DGS backbones like Octree-GS and Proxy-GS. name: Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids
head: Self-Organizing Gaussians
body: Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids is a compact 3D scene representation that reorganizes the high-dimensional parameters of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into a 2D grid with local homogeneity to drastically reduce storage size without compromising visual quality. It differs from fixed-ordering methods like Z-order curves or tri-planes by using an unsupervised learning model to determine the grid layout per scene, thereby preserving topological relationships and exploiting perceptual redundancies in natural scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of optimized 3DGS primitives (means \mathbf{\mu}, covariances \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacities \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}) for a specific scene. Output: A 2D grid representation where Gaussian parameters are arranged to maximize local similarity, enabling efficient compression. The uncompressed Gaussians retain the standard 3DGS structure for seamless renderer integration. Data Structures: The method organizes attributes into multiple data layers that share a consistent 2D layout. Each layer corresponds to a specific attribute type (e.g., position, scale, rotation, color). The grid dimensions are not fixed by a spatial partitioning rule but are determined by the optimization process to fit the number of Gaussians N. The layout preserves neighborhood structure such that Gaussians with similar high-dimensional parameter vectors are placed adjacent to each other in the 2D grid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a 2D grid of size H \times W (where H \times W \ge N) with random or uniform vectors representing the high-dimensional Gaussian parameters. 2. Self-Organization (Competitive Learning): For each Gaussian i in the scene with parameter vector \mathbf{x}i: Find the Best Matching Unit (BMU) in the grid, i.e., the grid node k with the closest distance to \mathbf{x}i (typically Euclidean distance in the parameter space). Update the BMU and its neighbors in the grid to move closer to \mathbf{x}i. The update rule follows the Self-Organizing Map (SOM) principle: \mathbf{w}k(t+1) = \mathbf{w}k(t) + \eta(t) \cdot h{ck}(t) \cdot (\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{w}k(t)) where \mathbf{w}k is the weight vector of node k, \eta(t) is the learning rate, and h{ck}(t) is the neighborhood function (e.g., Gaussian) centered at the BMU c. Repeat until convergence or a fixed number of epochs. This step maps the high-dimensional data to the 2D grid while preserving topological relationships. 3. Assignment: Assign each Gaussian to its corresponding grid cell based on the final BMU positions. If multiple Gaussians map to the same cell, they are stored in a list or the grid size is adjusted. 4. Training with Smoothness Loss: During the subsequent 3DGS training phase, enforce local smoothness between neighboring parameters in the grid. Add a smoothness loss term \mathcal{L}{smooth} to the standard 3DGS loss \mathcal{L}{render}: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{render} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{smooth} \mathcal{L}{smooth} penalizes large differences between the parameters of Gaussians that are adjacent in the 2D grid, encouraging local homogeneity. 5. Compression: Apply standard image compression techniques (e.g., JPEG, WebP, or neural codecs) to each data layer of the 2D grid. The consistent 2D layout allows these codecs to exploit spatial redundancies effectively. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the smoothness loss. Not given in the sources. Grid Dimensions (H, W): Determined by the number of Gaussians and the optimization. Not given in the sources. Learning Rate (\eta): For the SOM initialization. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Encoding Complexity: The self-organization step requires a computationally expensive optimization process to determine the element order, which is a significant overhead compared to fixed-ordering methods. Precision: The mapping relies on the high-dimensional parameter space. If the parameter space is not normalized, distance metrics may be skewed. Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: If the scene has low redundancy (e.g., random noise), the grid may not achieve significant compression. The method assumes perceptual redundancies present in natural scenes. Time Complexity: Encoding is computationally expensive due to the self-organization optimization step. Rendering time is comparable to standard 3DGS as the uncompressed Gaussians use the same structure. Memory Complexity: Storage size is reduced by a factor of 17x to 42x for complex scenes. Strengths: Maintains fast rendering and high visual quality while drastically reducing storage. It adapts to the specific scene, unlike fixed-ordering methods. Limitations: High encoding complexity. Requires per-scene optimization. When to use: When storage size is a critical constraint (e.g., resource-constrained devices) and encoding time is not a bottleneck. When not to use: When real-time encoding is required or for scenes with low perceptual redundancy. Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids was introduced by Wieland Morgenstern, Florian Barthel, Anna Hilsmann, and Peter Eisert from Fraunhofer Heinrich Hertz Institute and Humboldt University of Berlin. The method was published in arXiv:2312.13299v2 on May 2, 2024. It is based on the concept of Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), an unsupervised learning model that projects high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional grid, preserving topological relationships through competitive learning. The method addresses the high storage requirements of 3DGS, which hinders practical deployment on resource-constrained devices, by exploiting perceptual redundancies in natural scenes. Compact 3D Scene Representation via Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73013-92, fetched 2026-10-26 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Variable Basis Mapping (VBM)
body: Variable Basis Mapping (VBM) is a framework that transforms volumetric fields into 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations through wavelet-domain analysis, enabling real-time volumetric visualization by avoiding the prohibitively high computational costs of direct volume rendering. Unlike iVR-GS, which uses randomly initialized Gaussians, or VEG, which uses heuristic density-based spheres, VBM establishes a direct, mathematical bridge using wavelet analysis to exploit structural and statistical information. Inputs and Outputs Input: A physical volumetric field F discretized into a uniform grid of resolution G^3, where G is the volumetric data resolution. Intermediate: A radiance field RF \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times G \times G \times 4} obtained by applying a transfer function TF: \mathbb{R}^r \to \mathbb{R}^4 to F, producing RGBA vectors (color c, opacity \alpha). Output: A set of N anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by center \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, color ci, and opacity \alphai. Data Structures 1. Wavelet-to-Gaussian Transition Bank: A precomputed lookup structure mapping canonical wavelet atoms to optimal Gaussian surrogates. It stores the parameters (\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha) for the canonical kernel \psi{j,k=(0,0,0)} at each decomposition level j. 2. Gaussian Primitive: Defined by the tuple (\mui, \Sigmai, ci, \alphai). The radiance field is approximated by: RF(x) \approx \sum{i=1}^{N} ci \frac{\alphai}{\sqrt{\det(\Sigmai)}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)\right) where \mui is the center, \Sigmai is the covariance matrix, ci is the color, and \alphai is the opacity. Steps 1. Precompute Transition Bank: Compute optimal Gaussian surrogates for canonical wavelet atoms across multiple scales. To avoid cubic complexity (J \times G^3 fittings), only the canonical kernel \psi{j,k=(0,0,0)} is computed for each level j. Remaining kernels are derived analytically via translation and scaling, guaranteed by the group representation theorem. 2. Wavelet Decomposition: Express the radiance field RF in a compact multi-scale form using the 3D Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). The field is decomposed into low-frequency coefficients c{0,k} and high-frequency coefficients d{j,k}: RF(x) \approx \sum{k} c{0,k} \phi(x - k) + \sum{j=0}^{J-1} \sum{k} d{j,k} \psi{j,k}(x) where J is the number of decomposition levels, \phi is the scaling function, and \psi{j,k} are dyadic wavelet atoms defined as \psi{j,k}(x) = 2^{3j/2} \psi(2^j x - k). 3. Analytical Gaussian Construction: Map the discrete wavelet coefficients directly to 3DGS parameters using the precomputed Transition Bank. Each wavelet basis \psi{j,k} is mapped to a Gaussian basis, and the associated coefficients c{j,k} (color) and \alpha{j,k} (opacity) are translated into the corresponding 3DGS parameters (\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha). 4. Image-Space Fine-Tuning: Apply a lightweight optimization stage in image space to refine the representation and improve rendering fidelity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def variablebasismapping(physicalfieldF, resolutionG, numlevelsJ, transferfunction): """ Transforms a volumetric field into 3DGS using VBM. Args: physicalfieldF: ndarray of shape (G, G, G, r) resolutionG: int, dimension of the cubic grid numlevelsJ: int, number of wavelet decomposition levels transferfunction: callable, maps physical values to RGBA Returns: gaussians: list of Gaussian primitives (mu, Sigma, c, alpha) """ # Step 1: Convert physical field to radiance field # RF shape: (G, G, G, 4) RF = transferfunction(physicalfieldF) # Step 2: Precompute Wavelet-to-Gaussian Transition Bank # Only compute for canonical kernel at k=(0,0,0) for each scale j transitionbank = {} for j in range(numlevelsJ): # Compute optimal Gaussian surrogate for canonical wavelet atom psij,0 # This involves statistical estimation of the best-fit Gaussian parameters # for the shape defined by psij,0(x) = 2^(3j/2) psi(2^j x) canonicalgaussian = computecanonicalgaussiansurrogate(j) transitionbank[j] = canonicalgaussian # Step 3: Perform 3D Wavelet Decomposition on RF # Decompose each channel (R, G, B, A) separately lowfreqcoeffs = {} # c0,k highfreqcoeffs = {} # dj,k for channelidx in range(4): channeldata = RF[:,:,:, channelidx] # Perform DWT coeffs = performdwt3d(channeldata, numlevelsJ) lowfreqcoeffs[channelidx] = coeffs['low'] highfreqcoeffs[channelidx] = coeffs['high'] # Step 4: Map Wavelet Coefficients to Gaussian Primitives gaussians = [] # Map low-frequency scaling function coefficients # phi(x-k) maps to a Gaussian centered at k with parameters derived from transition bank # Note: Scaling function phi is not in the wavelet bank, so a separate mapping or # approximation is required. [G: Assume a standard Gaussian approximation for phi or # treat low-freq as a single large Gaussian or set of Gaussians based on grid spacing] for k in gridindices(resolutionG): # Extract coefficients for all channels at position k clow = [lowfreqcoeffs[ch][k] for ch in range(4)] # Map to Gaussian parameters. # Since phi is not in the wavelet bank, we approximate or use a default mapping. # [G: Use a fixed Gaussian shape for the scaling function component, # centered at k, with width related to grid resolution] mu = k Sigma = computescalingfunctioncovariance(resolutionG) c = clow[:3] alpha = clow[3] gaussians.append((mu, Sigma, c, alpha)) # Map high-frequency wavelet coefficients for j in range(numlevelsJ): for k in gridindicesatscale(j, resolutionG): # Get canonical Gaussian parameters for this scale j basegaussian = transitionbank[j] # Apply translation and scaling to basegaussian to match psij,k # Due to translation covariance, mu and Sigma are transformed based on k and j mu = transformtranslation(basegaussian.mu, k, j) Sigma = transformscaling(basegaussian.Sigma, j) # Extract wavelet coefficients for this atom chigh = [highfreqcoeffs[ch][j][k] for ch in range(4)] # Scale the color and opacity by the wavelet coefficient magnitude # The wavelet coefficient acts as a weight for the basis function # [G: The paper states coefficients are "systematically translated". # Typically, ci = chigh weight, alphai = alphahigh weight or similar] # Assuming linear mapping for simplicity as exact formula not provided: color = chigh[:3] opacity = chigh[3] gaussians.append((mu, Sigma, color, opacity)) # Step 5: Image-Space Fine-Tuning # Optimize the parameters of gaussians to minimize rendering error gaussians = finetunegaussians(gaussians, RF) return gaussians def computecanonicalgaussiansurrogate(j): """ Computes the optimal Gaussian (mu, Sigma, c, alpha) that best approximates the canonical wavelet atom psij,0(x) = 2^(3j/2) psi(2^j x). This is done via statistical estimation (e.g., moment matching or least squares). """ # [G: Implementation detail omitted. Requires numerical optimization # to fit a Gaussian to the wavelet shape.] pass def performdwt3d(data, levels): """ Performs 3D Discrete Wavelet Transform. Returns low-frequency and high-frequency coefficient arrays. """ # [G: Standard DWT implementation. Returns nested arrays or flattened indices] pass def transformtranslation(mu, k, j): """ Translates the Gaussian center based on wavelet index k and scale j. """ # [G: k is the spatial translation index. The wavelet atom is shifted by k/2^j in physical space] return mu + k / (2j) def transformscaling(Sigma, j): """ Scales the Gaussian covariance based on wavelet scale j. """ # [G: The wavelet atom is scaled by 2^j. Covariance scales by (2^j)^2] return Sigma (2j)2 def computescalingfunctioncovariance(resolutionG): """ Computes covariance for the scaling function phi approximation. """ # [G: Approximation of the scaling function's spatial extent] pass def finetunegaussians(gaussians, targetRF): """ Refines Gaussian parameters using image-space optimization. """ # [G: Standard 3DGS optimization loop (e.g., Adam) minimizing L1/L2 loss # between rendered images and target RF slices] pass Parameters G: Volumetric data resolution. The dataset is discretized into a uniform grid of resolution G^3. J: Number of decomposition levels in the wavelet transform. N: Number of Gaussian primitives in the 3DGS representation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Representational Gap: There is a substantial representational gap between wavelet and Gaussian bases, making direct conversion nontrivial. Computational Complexity: A naïve implementation of Wavelet-to-Gaussian transitions incurs cubic computational complexity (J \times G^3 fittings), resulting in prohibitive computational cost. The VBM method avoids this by computing only canonical kernels and deriving others analytically. A method for dynamic scene representation. Extends 3DGS to 360-degree panoramic scenes. Techniques to reduce the storage footprint of Gaussian primitives. Approximates gradients at Gaussian boundaries using Bézier curves. Uses second-order optimization for better convergence. The standard iterative training process for 3DGS. Incorporates geometric priors into the representation. Uses perceptual loss functions to improve visual quality. Optimizes training speed for 3DGS. Samples pixels based on rendering error to focus optimization. Adapts rendering resolution based on frequency content. Renders from internal viewpoints or inverts the rendering process. Infers Signed Distance Fields from Gaussians. Uses multi-view consistency constraints. Adds a lightweight neural network on top of Gaussians for detail. Uses Fisher Information for efficient optimization. Integrates semantic labels or language queries. Uses DoG primitives for sharper edges. GPU/ASIC optimizations for rendering. Removes redundant Gaussians during training. Explores quantum computing for Gaussian optimization. Specialized for human avatars. Extends 3DGS to 4D dynamic scenes. Hierarchical structure for Gaussians. Uses triangles instead of Gaussians. Generalizes to unseen scenes with semantics. Uses softmax blending for opacity. Scales rendering across multiple machines. Uses t-distributions for heavier tails. Advanced data structures for Gaussians. Adds reflection models. Time Complexity: The precomputation step is reduced from O(J \times G^3) to O(J) by leveraging translation covariance and computing only canonical kernels. The mapping step is O(N) where N is the number of coefficients. Fine-tuning is comparable to standard 3DGS optimization. Memory Complexity: Stores N Gaussian primitives. The Transition Bank is small (O(J)). Performance: Significantly accelerates convergence and enhances rendering quality compared to heuristic initialization methods like iVR-GS and VEG. Enables real-time volumetric visualization. Strengths: Principled mathematical bridge between volumetric analysis and 3DGS; exploits structural and statistical information; efficient precomputation. Limitations: Representational gap between wavelet and Gaussian bases requires careful approximation; relies on the quality of the wavelet transform and transfer function. When to use: Real-time visualization of large-scale volumetric data where direct volume rendering is too slow. When not to use: Scenes where the volumetric data does not have strong structural regularities exploitable by wavelets, or when extremely high-fidelity direct volume rendering is required without approximation. Variable Basis Mapping (VBM) was proposed in 2026 by Cai Yucheng et al. from USTC. It addresses the challenge of real-time visualization of large-scale volumetric data, which suffers from prohibitively high computational costs with direct volume rendering and voxel-based methods. The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and integrates concepts from wavelet analysis. It is the first framework to establish a direct, mathematical bridge between volumetric analysis and 3DGS.
