name: Human Gaussian Splatting
head: HUGS, Human Gaussian Splats
body: Human Gaussian Splats (HUGS) is a neural rendering framework that represents an animatable human avatar and a static scene using 3D Gaussians, trained on 50–100 frames of monocular video to enable novel view and novel pose synthesis at 60 FPS. It sets itself apart from implicit neural field methods by allowing test-time rendering without evaluating triplane/MLPs for new poses, and from static 3DGS by disentangling the human and scene to allow human transfer to other scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A monocular video sequence of 50–100 frames containing a moving human and a static scene. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the static scene and a set of 3D Gaussians representing the human. The human Gaussians are parameterized by mean locations in a canonical space, features from a triplane, and properties predicted by MLPs. The system outputs rendered images for novel views and novel poses. Data Structures: Scene Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation (center \mu, opacity, color, scale, rotation) initialized from COLMAP point cloud. Human Gaussians: Canonical Center (\mui): 3D location in the canonical (T-pose) space. Feature Vector (fi): Concatenation of feature vectors f{xi}, f{yi}, f{zi} retrieved from a triplane F \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times h \times w \times d} at location \mui. Appearance Properties: RGB color, opacity oi. Geometry Properties: Offset \Delta \mui, Rotation matrix Ri (parameterized by first two columns), Scale Si (three axes). Deformation Properties: LBS weights Wi \in \mathbb{R}^{nk}, where nk is the number of joints. Base Scale (si): A scalar multiplier for the MLP-predicted scale. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: 1. Estimate SMPL pose parameters \thetat for each image t and shared body shape parameters \beta using a pretrained SMPL regressor. 2. Initialize Human Gaussian centers \mu at the vertices of the canonical-posed SMPL mesh (T-pose). The number of human Gaussians equals the number of SMPL vertices (nv = 110,210). 3. Initialize Scene Gaussians from the COLMAP structure-from-motion point cloud. 4. Pretrain the feature triplane and three MLPs (Appearance DA, Geometry DG, Deformation DD) for 5,000 iterations to output: RGB: [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] Opacity: 0.1 Offset \Delta \mu: 0 Rotation R: Aligning the z-axis with the corresponding SMPL vertex normal. Scale S: Average incoming edge lengths of the SMPL mesh. LBS Weights W: Weights from the SMPL model. 5. Initialize base scale si = 1 for each human Gaussian. 2. Optimization Loop (12,000 iterations): 1. Forward Pass (Rendering): 1. Given a joint configuration G (pose), for each Human Gaussian i: Interpolate the triplane at \mui to get f{xi}, f{yi}, f{zi}. Concatenate to form fi. Input fi to DA to output RGB and opacity. Input fi to DG to output \Delta \mui, Ri, Si. Input fi to DD to output LBS weights Wi. 2. Deformation: Transform Human Gaussians using Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) with Wi and joint transformations Gk \in SE(3). 3. Splatting: Combine transformed Human Gaussians and Scene Gaussians. Splat onto the image plane using alpha blending. 2. Loss Calculation: Compute total loss \mathcal{L} (see Formulas). 3. Backpropagation: Update \mu, triplane, and MLP parameters using Adam optimizer (lr=10^{-3}, cosine schedule). 4. Density Control (Every 600 iterations): 1. Clone: Repeat existing centers in \mu. 2. Split: Randomly sample new centers within existing Gaussians' shapes (R, S). 3. Prune: Remove Gaussians based on loss gradient and opacity. 4. Scale Adjustment: When splitting, divide the base scale s by 1.6. The actual scale is s \times S{MLP}. 3. Test-Time Rendering: 1. Construct the 3D Gaussians explicitly from the optimized parameters. 2. For a new pose G, apply LBS to the Human Gaussians using the learned Wi and G. 3. Splat and render. No MLP evaluation is required for pose changes. Formulas: SMPL Posed Vertex (for initialization/regularization only): vi = \left( \sum{k=1}^{nk} W{k,i} Gk \right) pi Where vi is the posed vertex, W{k,i} is the LBS weight for joint k and vertex i, Gk is the joint transformation in SE(3), and pi is the resting vertex location. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\lambda1 \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{vgg}}}{\text{scene + human}} + \underbrace{\lambda1 \mathcal{L}^h1 + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}^h{\text{ssim}} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}^h{\text{vgg}}}{\text{human}} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{\text{LBS}} Where \mathcal{L}1, \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}}, \mathcal{L}{\text{vgg}} are L1, SSIM, and Perceptual losses. Human losses are computed on human-only renderings against ground truth human regions (from segmentation). LBS Regularization Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{LBS}} = \| W - \hat{W} \|2^F Where \hat{W} is the distance-weighted average of LBS weights of the k=6 nearest SMPL vertices. Parameters: \lambda1 = 0.8 \lambda2 = 0.2 \lambda3 = 1.0 \lambda4 = 1000 Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 10^{-3}, cosine schedule. SMPL Mesh: Upsampled version with nv = 110,210 vertices and nt = 220,416 faces. Used only for initialization and regularization. Split Scale Divisor: 1.6. Pitfalls: Artifacts: Holes or pop-outs can occur during articulation if Gaussians are not coordinated to retain surface integrity. This is mitigated by learning LBS weights. Pose Errors: Off-the-shelf SMPL regressors may produce inaccurate pose parameters \theta. This is mitigated by adjusting \theta per image during optimization. Training Time: Approximately 30 minutes on a GeForce 3090Ti GPU. Rendering Speed: 60 FPS at HD resolution. Memory: Final human representation consists of ~200K Gaussians on average. Strengths: ~100x faster to train than previous works (e.g., NeuMan, Vid2Avatar); state-of-the-art rendering quality; disentangled representation allows human transfer to other scenes; test-time animation without MLP evaluation. Limitations: Requires monocular video input; relies on SMPL prior for initialization (though Gaussians can deviate); potential artifacts if LBS coordination fails. When to use: When animatable human avatars from monocular video are needed with high rendering speed and novel pose synthesis. When not to use: When multi-view capture is available and higher geometric fidelity without parametric priors is required, or when real-time training is not feasible. HUGS was introduced by Jen-Hao Rick Chang et al. in 2023 (published at CVPR 2024). It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [15] and the SMPL body model [4] to address the challenge of animating humans in neural rendering. Previous methods relied on implicit neural fields or multi-view capture setups. HUGS enables novel-pose synthesis and novel-view synthesis from short, in-the-wild monocular videos. HUGS: Human Gaussian Splats, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00055, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Uncertainty and Probabilistic Modeling
head: Probabilistic Gaussian Splatting, Uncertainty Quantification in 3DGS
body: This family of methods addresses the lack of confidence metrics in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing probabilistic frameworks, uncertainty quantification, and active view selection. Unlike deterministic rendering, these approaches model the scene representation or data acquisition process as stochastic, enabling the estimation of model confidence, robust handling of missing or asynchronous data, and optimization of training view selection. What sets this family apart from siblings like Pruning and Density Control or Data Compression and Storage Optimization is the explicit modeling of epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty to guide training, visualization, or active learning, rather than merely optimizing geometric fidelity or storage efficiency. The core mechanism across these methods is the introduction of stochasticity into the Gaussian Splatting pipeline, either by treating parameters as random variables, quantifying information gain via second-order derivatives, or aggregating visibility metrics as uncertainty proxies. 1. Probabilistic Parameterization: In frameworks like GraphiXS and latentSplat, learnable parameters (e.g., Gaussian means, covariances, opacities) are treated as latent variables. Camera poses and frame times may also be modeled as random variables rather than fixed observations. Inference is performed via Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation, incorporating prior distributions to regulate component behavior. 2. Fisher Information as Uncertainty Proxy: Methods like FisherRF and FreeFix utilize the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) to quantify uncertainty. The FIM is approximated by the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood with respect to the model parameters. For 3DGS, the uncertainty attribute \bar{C}{V;G} for a Gaussian G under view V is derived from the negative log-likelihood of the rendered pixel \pi: \bar{C}{V;G} = -\log pf(\pi|V; G) This is equivalent to the expected value of the second derivative of the log-likelihood (the Hessian H[\pi|V; G]), provided regularity conditions are met: the partial derivative of the probability density function pf with respect to G exists almost everywhere, the integral of pf can be differentiated under the integral sign, and the support of pf does not depend on G. 3. Expected Information Gain (EIG) for View Selection: Active view selection leverages the sparsity of the Hessian. The EIG for a candidate view is approximated by the trace of the product of the Hessian of the candidate view (H{cand}) and the Hessian of previous views (H{prev}): \text{EIG} \approx \text{Tr}(H{cand} \cdot H{prev}) This computation is efficient due to the sparsity of the Hessian in 3DGS, allowing real-time evaluation. 4. Visibility-Based Uncertainty Aggregation: Post-training uncertainty representations, such as in PRIMU, aggregate contribution factors \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}) over visible pixels. The training-view coverage V(k) for a Gaussian k is defined as: V(k) = \max{v \in \Omega} \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}) where \Omega is the set of training views, v^{(k)} are pixels where opacity exceeds a threshold, and \text{agg} is an aggregation function (max, sum, or mean). FisherRF is a method for active view selection and uncertainty quantification in Radiance Fields. It sets itself apart by focusing on the selection of new training views to maximize Expected Information Gain (EIG), rather than just optimizing existing parameters. It leverages the sparsity of the Hessian to achieve real-time evaluation speeds (70 fps). GraphiXS is a probabilistic framework that incorporates data uncertainty (view sparsity, missing frames, camera asynchronization) into Gaussian Splatting. It treats learnable parameters as latent variables and camera poses/times as random variables, inferred via Maximum a Posteriori (MAP). The 'X' allows instantiation with different primitives (e.g., Gaussians, Student’s-t). It is a general framework that can upgrade existing methods to handle multiple types of data uncertainty. PRIMU provides uncertainty estimation via primitive-based representations of error and coverage. It computes scalar uncertainty features per Gaussian primitive, such as the number of training views observing the primitive (F(k)) or the aggregated contribution factors (V(k)). These representations are computed in a post-processing step without modifying the rendering or optimization. latentSplat uses variational Gaussians to model uncertainty. It renders the standard deviation \sigma of variational Gaussian features to visualize model uncertainty. Background regions outside reference camera frustums are explicitly handled by setting the background standard deviation to one, matching the feature map sampling strategy. This results in darker regions (higher uncertainty) for invisible or partially visible backgrounds. This variant defines the uncertainty attribute of 3DGS based on the negative log-likelihood of the rendered pixel value, interpreted as Fisher information. Definition: Computes an uncertainty attribute for 3D Gaussians based on the negative log-likelihood of the rendered pixel value, interpreted as Fisher information. Step: Compute the dot product of the gradient with itself to obtain the uncertainty value \bar{C}{V;G}. Formula: \bar{C}{V;G} = -\log pf(\pi|V; G) where pf is the probability density function of the rendered pixel \pi given view V and Gaussian parameters G. Pitfall: The derivation assumes volume rendering of 3D Gaussians meets regularity conditions: partial derivative exists almost everywhere, integral differentiability, and support independence from G. This variant represents uncertainty by aggregating visibility metrics. Definition: A scalar uncertainty feature per Gaussian primitive k representing the number of training views that observe the primitive, or capturing how strongly the primitive is covered in at least one training view, based on its contribution factors. Formula: F(k) = |\Omegak|, where \Omegak is the set of training views where the k-th Gaussian primitive lies within the viewing cone. V(k) = \max{v \in \Omega} \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}), where v^{(k)} denotes the pixels of view v in which the opacity of the k-th Gaussian exceeds a small threshold, and agg is an aggregation function. Parameter: Aggregation function agg: Can be 'max', 'sum', or 'mean'. Opacity threshold: Gaussians are considered visible if \alphak(\bar{x}) \ge 1/255 and Tk(\bar{x}) \ge 10^{-3}. Pitfall: To highlight low-opacity Gaussians that still influence reconstruction quality, the opacity term \alphak(\bar{x}) can be omitted from the aggregation. This variant focuses on rendering uncertainty maps. Definition: Renders the standard deviation \sigma of variational Gaussian features to visualize model uncertainty, with background regions explicitly handled. Step: Sets the background standard deviation to one for empty regions outside reference camera frustums, matching the feature map sampling strategy. Renders darker regions as higher uncertainty; main objects show lower uncertainty than background, with higher uncertainty at edges/fur compared to uniform surfaces. The concept of uncertainty in neural rendering has evolved from error estimation in NeRFs to probabilistic modeling in Gaussian Splatting. Early works focused on post-hoc error estimation. The integration of Fisher Information for active learning in 3DGS was introduced in [FreeFix]. The general probabilistic framework for 4DGS, GraphiXS, was proposed to handle data uncertainty holistically. Variational approaches like latentSplat introduced Bayesian inference to Gaussian Splatting. FreeFix: Boosting 3D Gaussian Splatting via Fine-Tuning-Free Diffusion Models, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv69130.2026.00109, fetched 2026-10-30 Graphical X Splatting (GraphiXS): A Graphical Model for 4D Gaussian Splatting under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1145/3799902.3811085, fetched 2026-11-05 PRIMU: Uncertainty Estimation for Novel Views in Gaussian Splatting from Primitive-Based Representations of Error and Coverage, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02443v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) latentSplat, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16292, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: FisherRF
head: Active View Selection and Mapping with Radiance Fields Using Fisher Information
body: FisherRF is a method for active view selection and uncertainty quantification in Radiance Fields that directly quantifies observed information on model parameters using Fisher Information, selecting candidate views by maximizing Expected Information Gain (EIG). It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SOGS or Gaussian Frosting by focusing on the selection of new training views rather than just optimizing existing parameters, leveraging the sparsity of the Hessian to achieve real-time evaluation speeds (70 fps). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained or partially trained Radiance Field model (specifically 3D Gaussian Splatting or Plenoxels), a pool of candidate camera viewpoints, and the current set of training views. Output: A ranked list of candidate views based on their Expected Information Gain (EIG), or a selected subset of views for active mapping. Data Structures: Hessian Matrix (H): Represents the second-order derivatives of the loss function with respect to the model parameters. In 3D Gaussian Splatting, this is computed per Gaussian. Fisher Information Matrix (FIM): Approximated by the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood. Method Steps: 1. Compute Hessian: For the current model state, compute the Hessian matrix of the parameters with respect to the negative log-likelihood for each 3D Gaussian. The Hessian of the objective function in volumetric rendering is independent of ground truth data or actual image measurements, depending only on the camera parameters of the views used for training. 2. Approximate Information Gain: To make computation tractable, approximate the decrease in entropy (Information Gain) by its upper bound. This bound is defined as the trace of the product of the Hessian of the candidate view (H{cand}) and the Hessian with respect to all previous views (H{prev}): \text{EIG} \approx \text{Tr}(H{cand} \cdot H{prev}) 3. Leverage Sparsity: The matrices are highly sparse due to the disentangling of scene parameters with respect to disparate rays. This sparsity allows for a cost-effective computation of the matrix trace, with complexity comparable to back-propagation. 4. Rank and Select: Evaluate all candidate views using the approximation. Select the view(s) with the highest EIG for the next iteration of training or mapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefisherinformationgain(model, candidateviews, trainingviews): """ Computes the Expected Information Gain for a set of candidate views based on the Fisher Information (Hessian) of the current model. Args: model: A 3D Gaussian Splatting or Plenoxels model instance. candidateviews: List of camera poses to evaluate. trainingviews: List of camera poses already used for training. Returns: List of tuples (view, score) sorted by score descending. """ # Step 1: Compute Hessian for current training views # The Hessian is independent of ground truth, relying only on camera params. # In 3DGS, this is computed per Gaussian. Hprev = model.computehessian(trainingviews) scores = [] for view in candidateviews: # Step 2: Compute Hessian for the candidate view Hcand = model.computehessian([view]) # Step 3: Approximate EIG as Trace(Hcand Hprev) # Due to sparsity, this trace computation is efficient (~back-prop cost) # Assuming Hprev and Hcand are sparse matrices or diagonal approximations # where the trace of the product can be computed element-wise or via sparse dot products. eig = traceproduct(Hcand, Hprev) scores.append((view, eig)) # Step 4: Sort by EIG scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) return scores def traceproduct(H1, H2): """ Computes the trace of the product of two sparse matrices. Tr(A B) = sumi sumj Aij Bji For sparse matrices, this is optimized by iterating over non-zero elements. """ # Implementation detail: Iterate over non-zero entries of H1. # If H1 and H2 are diagonal (common approximation in 3DGS for efficiency), # Tr(H1 H2) = sum(H1diag H2diag). # The source notes mention "diagonal Hessian computation" in comparison to Goli et al. return sum(h1 h2 for h1, h2 in zip(H1.diagonal(), H2.diagonal())) Parameters: Performance Metric: The method evaluates views at 70 fps when using 3D Gaussian Splatting. Hessian Computation Time: 11.3 ms ± 33.3 µs for the diagonal Hessian computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity Assumption: The efficiency relies on the high sparsity of the Hessian due to the disentangling of scene parameters. If the scene representation is dense or parameters are highly coupled, the trace computation may become expensive. Approximation Error: The use of the trace of the product as an upper bound for entropy decrease is an approximation. It may not perfectly capture the true Information Gain in all scenarios, though it is stated to be effective. Time Complexity: The computation of the trace is as cost-effective as back-propagation due to matrix sparsity. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluates views at 70 fps with 3D Gaussian Splatting. The Hessian computation takes 11.3 ms ± 33.3 µs, compared to 1.1 s ± 2.5 ms for alternative methods like Goli et al.. Strengths: Direct quantification of uncertainty on model parameters; efficient CUDA implementation for diagonal Hessian computation; state-of-the-art results in view selection and active mapping. Limitations: Relies on the sparsity of the Hessian; uses an approximation for Information Gain. When to use: When active view selection or active mapping is required for Radiance Fields, particularly 3D Gaussian Splatting or Plenoxels. When not to use: When the scene representation is dense and sparsity cannot be exploited, or when exact Information Gain is required over computational speed. FisherRF was introduced by W. Jiang et al. in the paper "FisherRF: Active View Selection and Mapping with Radiance Fields Using Fisher Information". It addresses the problem of active "training" view selection for volumetric rendering, a problem that was extensively studied before radiance fields but lacked literature specific to them. The method builds on the framework of 3D Gaussian Splatting and Plenoxels, leveraging their differentiable nature and parameter structure. It improves upon previous methods like Goli et al. by computing the Hessian directly rather than relying on hypothetical perturbation fields and multiple backward passes. FisherRF: Active View Selection and Mapping with Radiance Fields Using Fisher Information, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72624-824, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting
body:
Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting (VBGS) is a training method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that frames optimization as variational inference over the parameters of a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), rather than using gradient descent through a differentiable renderer. By leveraging the conjugacy of multivariate Gaussians, VBGS derives closed-form update rules that enable continual learning from sequential data without catastrophic forgetting or the need for replay buffers. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting which optimizes maximum likelihood estimates via backpropagation, VBGS maintains a distribution over parameters, making it distinct from sibling methods like DeSplat and SOGS that rely on gradient-based or second-order optimization techniques. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of observed data points D = \{(sn, cn)\}{n=1}^N, where sn is the spatial coordinate (2D for images, 3D for point clouds) and cn is the color (RGB). For 3D rendering, camera parameters are required to project Gaussians to the image plane. Outputs: The variational posterior parameters q(\mus, \Sigmas, \muc, \Sigmac, \pi) for K Gaussian components, which define the scene representation. Data Structures: Each of the K components stores 29 parameters representing the Natural-Inverse-Wishart (NIW) likelihood for color and position, and the Dirichlet prior for component assignments. Spatial Parameters (q(\mu{k,s}, \Sigma{k,s})): NIW distribution defined by natural parameters \eta{0,s} and 
u{0,s}. \eta{0,s} = (\kappa{0,s} \cdot m{0,s}, V{0,s} + \kappa{0,s} \cdot m{0,s} \cdot m{0,s}^T) 
u{0,s} = (\kappa{0,s}, n{0,s} + Ds + 1) Where m{0,s} is the mean, \kappa{0,s} is the concentration, n{0,s} is degrees of freedom, V{0,s} is the inverse scale matrix, and Ds is dimensionality (2 or 3). Color Parameters (q(\mu{k,c}, \Sigma{k,c})): Mean q(\mu{k,c}) is Normal with parameters derived from NIW natural parameters \eta{0,c} = (\kappa{0,c} \cdot m{0,c}, V{0,c} + \kappa{0,c} \cdot m{0,c} \cdot m{0,c}^T) and 
u{0,c} = (\kappa{0,c}, n{0,c} + Dc + 1). Covariance q(\Sigma{k,c}) is a Delta distribution \delta(\epsilon I), where \epsilon is a fixed hyperparameter ensuring components commit to a specific color. Consequently, n{k,c} and V{k,c} are kept fixed. Assignment Parameters (q(\pi)): Dirichlet distribution with natural parameter \eta{0,z} = \alpha0. Assignments (q(zn)): Categorical distribution with parameters \gamman. Algorithm Steps: The training uses Coordinate Ascent Variational Inference (CAVI) to maximize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). 1. Initialization: Initialize prior natural parameters \eta0, 
u0 for all K components. If using "Data Init", initialize means based on sampled data points; otherwise, use random initialization. Set \Sigma{k,c} covariance to \epsilon I. 2. E-Step (Compute Assignments): For each data point n and component k, compute the unnormalized log-assignment \hat{\gamma}{n,k}: \log \hat{\gamma}{n,k} = \mathbb{E}{q(\mu{k,s}, \Sigma{k,s})}[\log p(sn | \mu{k,s}, \Sigma{k,s})] + \mathbb{E}{q(\mu{k,c}, \Sigma{k,c})}[\log p(cn | \mu{k,c}, \Sigma{k,c})] + \mathbb{E}{q(\pi)}[\log p(zn=k)] Normalize to obtain probabilities: \gamma{n,k} =  rac{\hat{\gamma}{n,k}}{\sum{j=1}^K \hat{\gamma}{n,j}} Note: The expectations for the MVN log-likelihoods under NIW posteriors are computed using standard variational inference identities. 3. M-Step (Parameter Updates): Update the natural parameters of the posteriors using the sufficient statistics of the data weighted by assignments \gamma{n,k}: \eta{k} = \eta{0,k} + \sum{n=1}^N \gamma{n,k} T(xn) 
u{k} = 
u{0,k} + \sum{n=1}^N \gamma{n,k} Where T(xn) is the sufficient statistic for the data point (e.g., sn and sn sn^T for spatial, cn and cn cn^T for color). For spatial: \eta{k,s} \leftarrow \eta{0,s} + \sumn \gamma{n,k} (sn, sn sn^T) For color: \eta{k,c} \leftarrow \eta{0,c} + \sumn \gamma{n,k} (cn, cn cn^T) For assignments: \alphak \leftarrow \alpha{0,k} + \sumn \gamma{n,k} 4. Continual Learning / Reassignment (Optional): In streaming settings, unused components (where \alphak equals prior \alpha0) may be reassigned to improve coverage. Identify unused components. Sample n components (e.g., 5% of unused) proportional to negative ELBO (poor fit). Replace their means \mu{k,s} and \mu{k,c} with the location and color of sampled data points. Reset their natural parameters to priors and run CAVI. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def vbgsupdate(datapoints, K, priors, epsilon): """ datapoints: list of (s, c) tuples, where s is (Ds,) and c is (3,) K: number of components priors: dict containing initial natural parameters for spatial, color, and assignment epsilon: fixed covariance scale for color """ N = len(datapoints) # Initialize variational parameters from priors # etas, nus for spatial NIW # etac, nuc for color NIW (covariance fixed) # alpha for Dirichlet assignment etas = np.copy(priors['etas']) # Shape (K, 2Ds) or similar packed form nus = np.copy(priors['nus']) # Shape (K, 2) etac = np.copy(priors['etac']) nuc = np.copy(priors['nuc']) alpha = np.copy(priors['alpha']) # Shape (K,) # E-Step: Compute assignments # gamma[n, k] gamma = np.zeros((N, K)) for n in range(N): sn, cn = datapoints[n] loggamma = np.zeros(K) for k in range(K): # Compute expected log likelihood for spatial # E[log N(sn | mu, Sigma)] under NIW(q(mu, Sigma)) # This involves terms with trace(V^{-1} (sn - m)(sn - m)^T) etc. # Simplified representation: logps = expectedlogmvnspatial(sn, etas[k], nus[k]) # Compute expected log likelihood for color # Covariance is fixed Delta(epsilon I), so it's a standard MVN log prob # with fixed covariance epsilonI and mean derived from etac, nuc muck = getmeanfromniw(etac[k], nuc[k]) logpc = logmvn(cn, muck, epsilon np.eye(3)) # Expected log prior for assignment logpz = np.log(alpha[k] + 1e-10) # Approximation or exact Dirichlet expectation loggamma[k] = logps + logpc + logpz # Normalize loggamma -= np.log(np.sum(np.exp(loggamma))) gamma[n,:] = np.exp(loggamma) # M-Step: Update parameters # Sufficient statistics # Ts = [sn, sn @ sn.T] # Tc = [cn, cn @ cn.T] for k in range(K): # Spatial Update sumgammas = np.sum(gamma[:, k]) sumgammass = np.zeros((Ds, Ds)) sumgammasvec = np.zeros(Ds) for n in range(N): w = gamma[n, k] sn = datapoints[n][0] sumgammasvec += w sn sumgammass += w np.outer(sn, sn) # Update natural parameters # etas = (kappam, V + kappamm^T) # nus = (kappa, n + D + 1) # We accumulate sums to prior # Note: Direct update of natural parameters requires careful inversion to get m, V if needed for next step expectations # However, CAVI updates natural parameters directly. # Prior natural params etas0k = priors['etas'][k] nus0k = priors['nus'][k] # Add sufficient stats weighted by gamma # etas has two parts: kappam and V + kappamm^T # nus has two parts: kappa and n + D + 1 # Update kappa and n (from nus) # nus[0] is kappa, nus[1] is n + D + 1 newkappas = etas0k[0] / getmfrometa(etas0k) # This is complex, usually we track m, kappa, V, n directly # Simplified: The source says etak = eta0 + sum gamma T(x) # We must implement the exact vector addition for the natural parameter space. # For implementation, it is easier to maintain m, kappa, V, n and convert to eta for storage if needed, # but the source specifies natural parameter updates. # Let's assume we maintain the sufficient statistics sums directly in the natural parameter space # etask = etas0k + [sumgammasvec, sumgammass] # nusk = nus0k + [sumgammas, sumgammas] # nus[1] is n+D+1, so we add sumgamma to n part? # nus = (kappa, n + D + 1). The sum of 1s is sumgamma. So nus[1] += sumgamma. # Correct update for nus: nus[k, 0] = nus0k[0] # kappa is part of eta usually? No, nus = (kappa, n+D+1) in source notation? # Source: nu0,s = (kappa0,s, n0,s + Ds + 1). eta0,s = (kappa0,s m0,s, V0,s + kappa0,s m0,s m0,s^T) # So kappa is in BOTH eta and nu? Yes, for NIW. # Update nus nus[k, 0] += np.sum(gamma[:, k]) # Add to kappa? No, nus[0] is kappa. # Wait, source eq 22: nuk = nu0 + sum gamma. # So nus[k, 0] += sumgammas # nus[k, 1] += sumgammas # Update etas # etas[0] is kappam. New kappa is nus[k,0]. New m is sumgammasvec / sumgammas. # So new etas[0] = nus[k,0] (sumgammasvec / sumgammas) # etas[1] is V + kappamm^T. # This requires converting back and forth or maintaining sufficient stats. # To avoid ambiguity, we store the accumulated sufficient statistics in the natural parameter form # as defined by the source: etas[k, 0] = etas0k[0] + sumgammasvec etas[k, 1] = etas0k[1] + sumgammass # Color Update # Similar to spatial, but covariance is fixed. sumgammac = np.sum(gamma[:, k]) sumgammacc = np.zeros((3, 3)) sumgammacvec = np.zeros(3) for n in range(N): w = gamma[n, k] cn = datapoints[n][1] sumgammacvec += w cn sumgammacc += w np.outer(cn, cn) etac[k, 0] = priors['etac'][k, 0] + sumgammacvec etac[k, 1] = priors['etac'][k, 1] + sumgammacc # Assignment Update alpha[k] = priors['alpha'][k] + sumgammac # sumgamma is same for all k per n, but summed over n return etas, nus, etac, nuc, alpha def expectedlogmvnspatial(s, eta, nu): """ Computes E{q(mu, Sigma)}[log N(s | mu, Sigma)] for NIW posterior. q(mu, Sigma) ~ NIW(m, kappa, V, n) """ # Extract parameters from natural params # eta = (kappam, V + kappamm^T) # nu = (kappa, n + D + 1) kappa = nu[0] nplusDplus1 = nu[1] n = nplusDplus1 - s.shape[0] - 1 m = eta[0] / kappa Vpluskmm = eta[1] V = Vpluskmm - np.outer(m, m) kappa D = s.shape[0] # Log prob expectation for NIW: # E[log p] = -D/2 log(2pi) - 1/2 log|Sigma| - 1/2 (s-m)^T Sigma^{-1} (s-m) # Expectations: # E[log|Sigma|] = const + sum psi((n+1-i)/2) # E[Sigma^{-1}] = n V^{-1} # This is a complex formula. For implementation, use standard NIW log-likelihood expectation. # Not provided in closed form in source, but implied by "Eq[log p]". # Placeholder for standard NIW expectation calculation. pass Parameters: \epsilon: Hyperparameter for fixed color covariance (Delta distribution). Ensures color commitment. K: Number of mixture components (e.g., 10K, 100K). Reassign fraction: Fraction of unused components to reassign (e.g., 0.01 for Replica, 0.05 for Habitat). Learning rate: Not used in VBGS (closed-form), but used for gradient baseline comparison (0.1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intractable Posterior: Exact inference is intractable due to component interactions; mean-field approximation is required. Color Blending: Without fixing color covariance, components may blend colors. Solved by using a Delta distribution for q(\Sigma{k,c}). Alpha Blending: VBGS does not optimize for image reconstruction loss, so standard alpha blending is not sensible. All Gaussians are set to opaque (alpha=1). Memory: Memory usage is 2x the gradient baseline due to storing distribution parameters (29 vs 14 per component). Large Scale Data: If data does not fit in memory, batched processing is required, which reduces the speed advantage over gradient methods. Time Complexity: Model assignment (E-step) is O(nm) where n is data points and m is components. Parameter update (M-step) is O(n). Memory Complexity: Increases by a factor of 2 compared to the gradient baseline (3DGS) for the same number of Gaussians. Performance: On Tiny ImageNet, VBGS wall-clock time is 0.03 \pm 0.03 s vs Gradient 0.05 \pm 0.02 s (RTX 4090). In 3D continual learning (Blender), VBGS (Random Init) achieves 11.19 \pm 3.53 dB error vs Gradient 21.26 \pm 1.76 dB. Strengths: Enables continual learning without catastrophic forgetting; no replay buffers needed; single update step is faster than accumulated gradient steps when data fits in memory. Limitations: Requires RGBD data (not just RGB); memory intensive; speed advantage lost with batched processing for large datasets. VBGS was proposed to address the limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which relies on backpropagation and struggles with catastrophic forgetting in continual learning scenarios. It frames Gaussian splatting training as variational inference, leveraging the conjugacy of multivariate Gaussians to derive closed-form updates. The method is benchmarked on TinyImageNet, Blender 3D models, and Habitat scenes. Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03592v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: PRIMU
head: Primitive-based Representations of Uncertainty
body: PRIMU is a post-hoc uncertainty estimation (UE) framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) that constructs primitive-level representations of error and visibility/coverage from training views to estimate uncertainties for novel views. Unlike methods that estimate per-primitive uncertainty during training or rely on parameter variances, PRIMU operates entirely as post-processing without requiring GS retraining. It extracts 13 optionally direction-dependent features from training-view coverage and reconstruction error, rendering them as uncertainty feature maps which are aggregated via pixel-wise regression on holdout data. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (parameters: positions, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonic coefficients); a set of training views with known ground truth; a set of holdout views with known ground truth (for regression training); a set of novel views (for inference). Outputs: Per-pixel uncertainty maps (color and depth) for novel views; optionally, active view selection recommendations. Data Structures The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive k is defined by: Mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation/scale representation). Opacity scalar gk. Color coefficients for spherical harmonics. The method computes a feature vector fk \in \mathbb{R}^{13} for each primitive k. These features are derived from training view statistics. Numbered Steps 1. Project Training Errors and Coverage to Primitives: For each training view v \in \Omega (where \Omega is the set of training views): a. Render the scene using the trained GS model to obtain the rendered color Cv(\bar{x}) and depth Dv(\bar{x}) for each pixel \bar{x}. b. Compute the per-pixel reconstruction error e{\bar{x}} (e.g., \ell1 error between rendered and ground truth). c. For each Gaussian primitive k, identify the set of pixels v^{(k)} in view v where the primitive's opacity \alphak(\bar{x}) exceeds a small threshold. d. Compute the contribution factor for primitive k at pixel \bar{x}: c{k, \bar{x}} = \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}), where Tk(\bar{x}) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(\bar{x})) is the accumulated transparency. e. Aggregate these contributions to form primitive-level representations. The paper defines three specific representations, which can be combined or selected: i. Field-of-View (FoV) Count: F(k) = |\Omegak|, where \Omegak is the set of training views in which primitive k lies within the viewing cone. ii. Training-View Coverage: V(k) = \max{v \in \Omega} \left( \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} (\alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x})) \right), where \text{agg} \in \{\text{max, sum, mean}\}. iii. Rendering Error: E(k) = \text{mean}{v \in \Omega} \left( \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} (e{\bar{x}} \cdot \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x})) \right). f. Construct the 13-dimensional feature vector fk for each primitive. The exact composition of the 13 features is not fully detailed in the provided text, but it includes the above representations and is optionally direction-dependent. 2. Render Uncertainty Feature Maps: For a novel view v{novel}: a. Project all Gaussian primitives onto the image plane of v{novel} to obtain 2D Gaussians with mean \bar{\mu}k and covariance \bar{\Sigma}k. b. The opacity of primitive k at pixel \bar{x} is \alphak(\bar{x}) = gk \Phi(\bar{x}; \bar{\mu}k, \bar{\Sigma}k), where \Phi is the 2D Gaussian density. c. Render the scene using the standard alpha-blending equation to get the final color C(\bar{x}) and depth D(\bar{x}): C(\bar{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}) ck(\vec{d}) where ck(\vec{d}) is the color of the k-th Gaussian dependent on view direction \vec{d}, and Tk(\bar{x}) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(\bar{x})). d. Simultaneously, render the primitive-level feature maps. For each feature fk, compute its contribution to each pixel \bar{x} using the same opacity and transparency weights: Uf(\bar{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}) fk This produces an uncertainty feature map Uf for each of the 13 features. 3. Aggregate via Pixel-wise Regression: a. Collect the rendered uncertainty feature maps U{f1}, \dots, U{f{13}} for the novel view. b. Train a gradient boosting regression model on holdout data. The input to the model is the vector of feature map values at each pixel [U{f1}(\bar{x}), \dots, U{f{13}}(\bar{x})]. The target is the true error (e.g., \ell1 error between rendered and ground truth) for those pixels in the holdout views. c. Apply the trained regression model to the feature maps of the novel view to predict the final uncertainty estimate U(\bar{x}) for each pixel. 4. Active View Selection (Optional): a. Use the uncertainty feature maps directly to guide active view selection (AVS). b. Prioritize viewpoints with high uncertainty indicators (e.g., high mean or max values in the feature maps) to select new training views, without requiring the regression model. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor def computeprimitivefeatures(primitives, trainingviews, groundtruths): """ Computes 13-dimensional feature vectors for each Gaussian primitive based on training view coverage and error. primitives: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mean: (3,) cov: (3,3) or (scale, rot) opacity: scalar shcoeffs: for color trainingviews: List of view parameters (cameras) groundtruths: Dict mapping viewid to (colorimg, depthimg) Returns: features: (Nprimitives, 13) array """ N = len(primitives) features = np.zeros((N, 13)) # Placeholder for the exact 13 features. # Based on the text, these include FoV count, coverage, error, # and potentially direction-dependent variants. for k, prim in enumerate(primitives): # 1. Field-of-View Count fovcount = 0 for vid, cam in enumerate(trainingviews): # Check if primitive is within viewing cone of cam if isinfov(prim, cam): fovcount += 1 features[k, 0] = fovcount # 2. Training-View Coverage (V) # Aggregate contribution factors alpha T over visible pixels maxaggcoverage = -np.inf for vid, cam in enumerate(trainingviews): # Render primitive contributions for this view # Get pixels where alpha > threshold visiblepixels = getvisiblepixels(prim, cam, threshold=1e-4) if len(visiblepixels) == 0: continue # Compute contribution factors for these pixels # alphak(x) = g Phi(x; mu, Sigma) # Tk(x) = product(1 - alphaj) for j < k # Note: In practice, Tk is computed during standard rendering contributions = [] for px in visiblepixels: alpha = computealpha(prim, px, cam) # Tk requires sorting and previous alphas. # Assuming standard GS rendering provides this or we approximate # by using the primitive's own alpha as a proxy if T is not stored per-pixel per-primitive # The paper uses alphak Tk. # For simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume we can access # the contribution factor ck = alphak Tk from the rendering pass. ck = getcontributionfactor(prim, px, cam) contributions.append(ck) if contributions: aggval = np.max(contributions) # agg in {max, sum, mean} if aggval > maxaggcoverage: maxaggcoverage = aggval features[k, 1] = maxaggcoverage if maxaggcoverage > -np.inf else 0 # 3. Rendering Error (E) meanerror = 0.0 errorsum = 0.0 count = 0 for vid, cam in enumerate(trainingviews): visiblepixels = getvisiblepixels(prim, cam, threshold=1e-4) if len(visiblepixels) == 0: continue gtcolor, gtdepth = groundtruths[vid] renderedcolor, rendereddepth = renderview(cam, primitives) # Full scene render for px in visiblepixels: ck = getcontributionfactor(prim, px, cam) # Per-pixel L1 error err = np.mean(np.abs(renderedcolor[px] - gtcolor[px])) errorsum += err ck count += ck if count > 0: meanerror = errorsum / count features[k, 2] = meanerror # 4-13. Other features (direction-dependent, etc.) # The paper mentions 13 features, optionally direction-dependent. # Specific definitions for features 3-12 are not provided in the excerpt. # Assuming these might include directional coverage, error variance, # or SH coefficient magnitudes. We leave them as zeros for now. return features def renderuncertaintymaps(primitives, novelview): """ Renders the uncertainty feature maps for a novel view. primitives: List of Gaussian objects novelview: Camera parameters Returns: featuremaps: (13, H, W) array colormap: (3, H, W) depthmap: (1, H, W) """ H, W = novelview.resolution featuremaps = np.zeros((13, H, W)) # Standard GS rendering for color and depth colormap, depthmap = rendergs(primitives, novelview) # Get primitive features (precomputed) # In a real implementation, features are computed once and stored # Here we assume we have access to them # features = computeprimitivefeatures(...) # Project primitives to 2D projectedprims = projectto2d(primitives, novelview) # Sort front-to-back projectedprims.sort(key=lambda p: p.depth) # Render feature maps using alpha blending accumulatedtransparency = np.ones((H, W)) for prim in projectedprims: k = prim.index alpha = prim.alpha # Computed from 2D Gaussian density # Create alpha mask for this primitive alphamask = np.zeros((H, W)) # Fill alphamask with alpha values at relevant pixels # Efficient rasterization of 2D Gaussian is required here. # For pseudocode, we assume a function that returns the alpha field. alphafield = rasterize2dgaussian(prim) # Contribution weight contribution = alphafield accumulatedtransparency # Add to feature maps # features[k] is the 13-dim vector for this primitive for fidx in range(13): featuremaps[fidx] += contribution prim.features[fidx] # Update transparency accumulatedtransparency = (1 - alphafield) return featuremaps, colormap, depthmap def trainandpredictuncertainty(trainingfeaturemaps, trainingerrors, novelfeaturemaps): """ Trains a gradient boosting regressor and predicts uncertainty for a novel view. trainingfeaturemaps: List of (13, H, W) arrays for holdout views trainingerrors: List of (H, W) arrays of true errors for holdout views novelfeaturemaps: (13, H, W) array for the novel view Returns: uncertaintymap: (H, W) array """ # Flatten feature maps and errors nviews = len(trainingfeaturemaps) H, W = trainingfeaturemaps[0].shape Xtrain = [] ytrain = [] for i in range(nviews): # Flatten (13, H, W) to (HW, 13) fmaps = trainingfeaturemaps[i].transpose(1, 2, 0) # (H, W, 13) errors = trainingerrors[i] # (H, W) # Reshape to (Npixels, 13) Xtrain.append(fmaps.reshape(-1, 13)) ytrain.append(errors.flatten()) Xtrain = np.vstack(Xtrain) ytrain = np.concatenate(ytrain) # Train Gradient Boosting Regressor model = GradientBoostingRegressor(nestimators=100, maxdepth=5) model.fit(Xtrain, ytrain) # Predict for novel view fmapsnovel = novelfeaturemaps.transpose(1, 2, 0) # (H, W, 13) Xnovel = fmapsnovel.reshape(-1, 13) ypred = model.predict(Xnovel) uncertaintymap = ypred.reshape(H, W) return uncertaintymap Parameters Number of features: 13. Regression model: Gradient boosting regression. Aggregation functions: max, sum, or mean for contribution factors. Opacity threshold: A small threshold to determine visible pixels (value not specified). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Geometry Misalignment: Gaussian splats may misalign with scene geometry even when rendered appearance is correct, leading to depth error between true geometry and splat distribution. PRIMU aims to capture this via error-based features. Undefined Depth Error: Undefined depth error is represented as light gray in visualizations, implying handling of missing or invalid depth values is necessary. Generalization: The regression model shows generalization capabilities to unseen scenes, but performance may vary. Time Complexity: The method adds a post-processing step. Computing primitive features requires iterating over training views and primitives, which is O(N{views} \cdot N{primitives} \cdot N{pixels}) in a naive implementation, but optimized via rasterization. Rendering feature maps is O(N{primitives} \cdot N{pixels}). Regression training is O(N{holdout\pixels} \cdot N{trees} \cdot \text{depth}). Inference is O(N{novel\pixels}). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 13-dimensional feature vector per primitive (O(N{primitives})) and the rendered feature maps for holdout views during training (O(N{holdout\views} \cdot H \cdot W \cdot 13)). Strengths: Post-hoc (no retraining); interpretable features; strong correlation with true errors, especially for depth and foreground objects; generalizes to unseen scenes; enables active view selection. Limitations: Requires holdout data for regression training (unless generalizing to unseen scenes); 13 features may be complex to interpret fully; performance depends on the quality of the initial GS model. When to use: Safety-critical domains like robotics and medical imaging where reliable uncertainty estimates are essential. When not to use: When computational resources for post-processing are extremely limited and approximate variance-based methods are sufficient; when no holdout data is available and generalization to unseen scenes is not acceptable. PRIMU was introduced by Stehr et al. from the University of Wuppertal, Queensland University of Technology, and University of Osnabrück. It addresses the challenge of uncertainty estimation in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which is critical for deploying GS in safety-critical domains. Existing methods often estimate per-primitive uncertainty during training or rely on parameter variances, whereas PRIMU operates as a post-processing framework. PRIMU: Uncertainty Estimation for Novel Views in Gaussian Splatting from Primitive-Based Representations of Error and Coverage, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02443v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: SCION
head: Scene Composition with Instanced Neural Primitives
body: SCION is a hierarchical compositional scene representation that replaces the millions of independent Gaussians used in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a compact vocabulary of reusable local primitives and lightweight world-space instances. It solves the redundancy and lack of structural manipulation handles in standard 3DGS by discovering and encoding repetitive structures end-to-end from multi-view captures. Unlike prior codebook methods that share parameters across distinct splats or require manual instance selection, SCION builds shared primitives and recovers structure automatically, enabling compact storage (e.g., 1.2 MB) and instance-level editing without retraining. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of posed RGB images \{Iv\} with calibrated cameras \{\piv\} and a sparse COLMAP point cloud. Output: A scene representation consisting of a primitive vocabulary \mathcal{C} and a set of instances \Phi, optimized to render novel views with high fidelity. Data Structures The representation consists of two main components: 1. Primitive Vocabulary \mathcal{C} = \{ck\}{k=1}^K: A library of K reusable primitives. Each primitive ck is a bundle of Sk local-frame Gaussians (splats). The j-th splat in primitive k has parameters \theta{kj}^L = (\mu{kj}^L \in \mathbb{R}^3, q{kj}^L \in S^3, s{kj}^L \in \mathbb{R}^3, o{kj}^L \in \mathbb{R}, c{kj}^L \in \mathbb{R}^3). \mu^L: Position, q^L: Unit quaternion rotation, s^L: Anisotropic log-scale, o^L: Opacity logit, c^L: RGB color (zeroth-order spherical harmonic). Total parameters per primitive: P{splat} \times Sk, where P{splat} = 14. 2. Instances \Phi = \{\phii\}{i=1}^N: N lightweight world-space placements. The i-th instance has parameters \phii^W = (\mui^W \in \mathbb{R}^3, qi^W \in S^3, si^W \in \mathbb{R}, oi^W \in \mathbb{R}, ai \in \{1, \dots, K\}). \mu^W: World position, q^W: World rotation, s^W: Scalar log-scale, o^W: Opacity logit, ai: Discrete index selecting the primitive c{ai}. Total parameters per instance: P{instance} = 10 (excluding the integer assignment). Rendering Assembly Rendering materializes transient Gaussians by combining local splats with instance transforms. For each instance i and each local splat j in its assigned primitive k=ai, the world-frame Gaussian parameters \tilde{\theta}{ij}^W are computed as: \tilde{\mu}{ij}^W = \mui^W + qi^W \text{rotate}(s{ij}^L, \mu{ai j}^L) \tilde{s}{ij}^W = s{ai j}^L + si^W \mathbf{1} \tilde{q}{ij}^W = qi^W \otimes q{ai j}^L \tilde{o}{ij}^W = o{ai j}^L + oi^W \tilde{c}{ij}^W = c{ai j}^L where q(\cdot) denotes rotation of a vector by a quaternion, \otimes is quaternion composition, and \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. The total number of assembled Gaussians is T = \sum{i=1}^N S{ai} = \sum{k=1}^K nk Sk, where nk is the number of instances assigned to primitive k. Optimization Procedure The representation is fitted via joint optimization over discrete (assignment) and continuous parameters. The assignment ai is fixed after initialization using frozen DINOv3 features. Optimization proceeds in two alternating phases per iteration to decouple gradients: 1. Splat Pass: Render view with detached instance parameters: \hat{I}\theta = \mathcal{R}(\theta, \text{sg}(\phi)). 2. Instance Pass: Render view with detached primitive parameters: \hat{I}\phi = \mathcal{R}(\text{sg}(\theta), \phi). Here \mathcal{R} is the Gaussian rasterizer and \text{sg} stops gradients. Loss Functions The total loss combines photometric, regularization, and adversarial terms: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{recon}^{(t)}(\hat{I}\theta, I) + \mathcal{L}{reg} + \mathcal{L}{recon}^{(t)}(\hat{I}\phi, I) + \mathcal{L}{reg} + \mathbb{1}{t \ge tD} \lambda{adv} \mathcal{L}{adv}(\hat{I}\theta, I) Reconstruction Loss: \mathcal{L}{recon}^{(t)}(I, \hat{I}) = (1 - \lambda{ssim}) \|I - \hat{I}\|1 + \lambda{ssim}(1 - \text{SSIM}(I, \hat{I})) + \mathbb{1}{lpips}(t) \lambda{lpips} \text{LPIPS}{vgg}(I, \hat{I}) Regularization Loss: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \mathcal{L}{scale} + \mathcal{L}{opac} + \lambda{anch} \sumi |si^W| + \lambda{cap} \sumi [\max(0, si^W - \tau{cap})] + \lambdac \sum{k \in \mathcal{C}{\ge 2}} \frac{1}{|Ak|} \sum{j \in Ak} \|\mu{kj}^L - \bar{\mu}k\|2^2 \mathcal{L}{scale}: Penalizes anisotropic local-frame splat scales. \mathcal{L}{opac}: Caps large local opacity logits. \lambda{anch}: Anchors instance log-scale near initialization. \lambda{cap}: Caps positive instance log-scales to prevent runaway growth. \lambdac: Keeps primitive active splats close to their local-frame mean \bar{\mu}k. \mathcal{C}{\ge 2}: Set of primitives with at least two active splats. Ak is the active subset of primitive k. Adversarial Loss: Added after warmup step tD to preserve per-instance sharpness against averaged reconstruction losses. It uses a discriminator on randomly cropped real and rendered patches. Densification (Density Optimization) SCION uses two-level densification scoped to primitives and instances. Splat Density Optimization: Uses the MH-3DGS birth rule scoped to one primitive. A dead row in ck is filled with an opacity-weighted alive donor from ck, and new children are written back into ck. 1. Z-scoring: Parent importance score is z-scored within each primitive to respond to local under-fitting. 2. Density Normalization: Acceptance is divided by same-primitive voxel density to prevent births piling up. 3. Mass Correction: When a row is copied into \nu overlapping instances, opacity and scale are corrected to preserve alpha-compositing mass. Instance Density Optimization: 1. Pruning: Remove instances with opacity below threshold or non-finite parameters. 2. Ranking: Rank remaining instances by accumulated gradient magnitude \bar{h}i: \bar{h}i = \frac{\sum{v \in W} \sum{j=1}^{S{ai}} \|\nabla{\piv} (\tilde{\mu}{ij}^W)\|2^2}{\sum{v \in W} S{ai}} 3. Cloning (Small Instances): If linear scale e^{si^W} is below threshold: \mu{i'}^W = \mui^W + \eta{clone} e^{si^W} \xi, \quad \xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) q{i'}^W = qi^W, \quad s{i'}^W = si^W, \quad o{i'}^W = oi^W, \quad a{i'} = ai 4. Subdivision (Large Instances): Split into M children. Children inherit rotation, assignment, and opacity. \mu{i,m}^{W'} = \mui^W + \eta{sub} e^{si^W} \epsilonm, \quad \epsilonm \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) s{i,m}^{W'} = si^W - \frac{1}{3} \log M o{i,m}^{W'} = oi^W Pitfall: Instance children occupy different world positions, so they do not use the alpha-compositing opacity correction applied to splat copying. Reducing opacity here would remove rendered mass. Parameters P{splat} = 14: Parameters per local splat. P{instance} = 10: Parameters per instance. \lambda{anch}, \lambda{cap}, \lambdac: Regularization weights. tD: Warmup step for adversarial loss. M: Number of children when subdividing a large instance. Complexity: Representation space complexity is O(K \bar{S} + N), where \bar{S} is the average number of local splats per primitive, K is the number of primitives, and N is the number of instances. This is significantly smaller than the O(\sum Si) complexity of unshared 3DGS. Storage: SCION maintains high quality even at 1.2 MB storage size. Compression Ratio: Relative to an unshared representation with the same assembled Gaussians: CR = \frac{B{ours}}{P{splat} \sum{k=1}^K nk Sk} where B{ours} = P{splat} \sum{k=1}^K Sk + P{instance} N. Strengths: Compact representation, direct editing/animation handles, end-to-end structure discovery, rate-distortion favorable to existing compression methods. Limitations: Trade-off of per-pixel fidelity for reusable structures; optimization is more complex due to two-level densification and adversarial loss. SCION was introduced to address the redundancy in neural scene representations that model elements independently. Traditional methods treat each Gaussian as unique, storing millions of parameters. SCION leverages the fact that natural and built worlds are full of repetition (e.g., grass blades, bricks, leaves). It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [Kerbl et al., 2023] and addresses limitations of prior codebook-style methods like Splat and Replace, which require manual instance selection or start from already trained scenes. SCION recovers structure end-to-end from multi-view captures, enabling instance-level scene editing and animation without retraining. SCION: Scene Composition with Instanced Neural Primitives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.02322, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: On-the-Fly GS
head: Gaussian on-the-fly Splatting
body: On-the-Fly GS is a progressive framework for near real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) field optimization that enables robust online training during discrete image acquisition. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which requires offline training after full Structure-from-Motion (SfM) processing. Unlike SLAM-based methods such as GS-SLAM or RTG-SLAM that require spatial and temporal continuity and often depth priors, On-the-Fly GS handles discrete images captured in an arbitrary manner without spatiotemporal continuity, relying only on a certain degree of overlap with previously registered images. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A stream of discrete RGB images captured in arbitrary order; an On-the-Fly SfM module that estimates camera poses and generates sparse point clouds. Outputs: An optimized 3D Gaussian field that renders the scene with high fidelity as new images arrive. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Field: A collection of 3D Gaussians representing the scene. Each Gaussian is defined by position, covariance (scale and rotation), opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Image Queue: A buffer of acquired images waiting for processing. Training State: Per-image counters tracking the number of training iterations each image has undergone to manage learning rates. Parameters: N0: The number of initial images used to train the initial 3DGS field before progressive optimization begins. Iteration Limit: A stricter limit on the number of training iterations in Phase 1 to prevent overfitting to the initial few images. Steps: 1. Phase 1: Initial 3DGS Training. The On-the-Fly SfM module estimates poses and generates a sparse point cloud for the first N0 images. An initial 3DGS field is trained using the original 3DGS training method. A stricter limit is imposed on the number of training iterations to prevent overfitting to these initial images. 2. Phase 2: Progressive Optimization (per new image). As a new image arrives, the On-the-Fly SfM module updates the camera poses of both the newly acquired and previously registered images, while refining the sparse point cloud. Based on the updated sparse point cloud, newly optimized Gaussians are appended to the existing 3DGS field. Local & Semi-Global Optimization: Based on overlapping relationships, each local connected image is assigned a weight. This weight determines the number of training iterations each image undergoes, prioritizing the newly added image and its local overlapping images. Adaptive Learning Rate: The learning rate for each image is calculated based on the number of iterations it has undergone. Images with fewer training iterations are assigned higher learning rates, while images with more iterations receive lower learning rates. Load-Balancing Strategy: A load-balancing strategy, inspired by Adr-Gaussian, is incorporated to mitigate the over-accumulation of 3D Gaussians and ensure fast training of newly added regions. Splatting-based Parallel Computation: Back-propagation is re-implemented by transitioning from pixel-based parallelism to splatting-based parallel computation, drawing from Taming-3DGS, to enhance training efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. N0 = 3 # Example value for initial images scene = Empty3DGaussianField() imagequeue = Queue() imageiterationcounts = {} # Maps imageid -> int (iterations) def onimagearrived(imageid, imagedata): imagequeue.enqueue((imageid, imagedata)) processqueue() def processqueue(): while not imagequeue.empty(): imageid, imagedata = imagequeue.dequeue() # 1. Update SfM and Geometry # On-the-Fly SfM updates poses and sparse points poses, sparsepoints = ontheflysfm.update(imageid, imagedata, scene) # 2. Initialize Gaussians for new image # Append new Gaussians based on sparse points newgaussians = initializegaussians(sparsepoints) scene.append(newgaussians) # 3. Determine Training Strategy # Calculate weight based on overlap with existing images overlapweight = calculateoverlapweight(imageid, scene) # Determine number of iterations for this image # Prioritize new image and its neighbors numiterations = determineiterations(overlapweight, imageid) # 4. Adaptive Learning Rate # Get current iteration count for this image currentiters = imageiterationcounts.get(imageid, 0) # Calculate learning rate based on iterations # Fewer iterations -> Higher LR lr = calculateadaptivelr(currentiters) # 5. Optimization Loop for i in range(numiterations): # Splatting-based parallel computation # Render image from current scene state renderedimage = scene.render(imageid, poses[imageid]) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(renderedimage, imagedata) # Back-propagate using splatting-based parallelism # (Transition from pixel-based to splatting-based) gradients = backpropsplatting(loss, scene, imageid, poses[imageid]) # Update Gaussians scene.update(gradients, lr) # Update iteration count imageiterationcounts[imageid] = currentiters + 1 # 6. Load Balancing # Mitigate over-accumulation of Gaussians scene.applyloadbalancing() def calculateadaptivelr(iterations): # Higher LR for fewer iterations # Lower LR for more iterations # Specific formula not given in sources return baselr / (1 + decayrate iterations) def determineiterations(overlapweight, imageid): # Prioritize new image and overlapping neighbors # Specific formula not given in sources return baseiterations overlapweight Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Training the initial field with too few images risks overfitting to the initial few images (e.g., 2 or 3 images). Mitigated by a stricter iteration limit in Phase 1. Learning Rate Decay: The standard learning rate decay strategy of original 3DGS, based on complete field quality, is not applicable because acquired images with fewer iterations exhibit lower rendering quality. Discrete Images: The method must handle images without spatiotemporal continuity, requiring only a certain degree of overlap with previously registered images. Time Complexity: Near real-time optimization per new image. The method reduces training time significantly, optimizing each new image in seconds. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Reduces training time significantly compared to offline training. Strengths: Enables robust online training during image acquisition; handles discrete images captured in an arbitrary manner; does not rely on depth priors. Limitations: Requires a certain degree of overlap with previously registered images. When to use: When near real-time 3DGS optimization is needed during image capture, especially for discrete images without spatiotemporal continuity. When not to use: When offline training after full SfM processing is acceptable and real-time updates are not required. On-the-Fly GS was introduced by Cheng and Xin Wang in a paper published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (LRA) in 2025. It addresses the limitations of existing SLAM-based 3DGS methods (e.g., GS-SLAM, RTG-SLAM) which require spatial and temporal continuity and often depth priors. The method builds on the original 3DGS training method and incorporates strategies from Adr-Gaussian (load-balancing) and Taming-3DGS (splatting-based parallel computation). name: View-Dependent and Appearance Modeling
head: View-Dependent Appearance, Anisotropic Reflective Modeling
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to model complex, view-dependent lighting effects such as specular highlights and anisotropic reflections, which standard isotropic spherical Gaussians cannot capture accurately. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by replacing or augmenting the static spherical harmonic color representation with physically based rendering (PBR) models or directional anisotropic functions, enabling faithful reproduction of shiny and metallic surfaces. All methods in this family share the goal of decomposing appearance into geometric and directional components to support view-dependent shading. 1. Primitive Representation: Gaussians are augmented with parameters beyond position, covariance, and opacity. These include material properties (roughness, metallic, albedo) or directional spread parameters (sharpness, bandwidths). 2. Directional Evaluation: The contribution of a Gaussian to a pixel is modulated by the viewing direction relative to the primitive's orientation. This is achieved either through Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) or neural networks predicting view-dependent attributes. 3. Physical or Approximate Shading: Colors are computed using PBR models (diffuse + specular) or directional basis functions, rather than simple SH evaluation. 4. Differentiable Optimization: All parameters are optimized via gradient descent using a photometric loss, requiring differentiable rendering of the directional components. ARS-GS embeds Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) within a Physically Based Rendering (PBR) pipeline, aligning them with GGX microfacet models to model environmental illumination and enable accurate mesh reconstruction via light-transport simulation. Unlike Spec-Gaussian, which uses ASG primarily for appearance fitting, ARS-GS strictly embeds ASG within a PBR pipeline by aligning it with GGX microfacet models. It solves the problem of vanishing gradients in highly reflective regions by introducing a shortcut connection mechanism that links spatial coordinates directly to ASG color attributes, enabling rapid updates of specular reflections when primitives undergo positional changes. See Anisotropic Reflective Spherical 3D Gaussian Splatting. Spec-Gaussian is a method that utilizes anisotropic spherical Gaussians to approximate 3D scene appearance, specifically designed to handle complex shading such as specular and anisotropic components. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by replacing isotropic spherical Gaussians with anisotropic variants to better model directional reflectance properties. See Spec-Gaussian. VDGS produces more faithful view-dependent effects by modeling 3DGS to represent 3D shapes and predicting attributes like view-dependent color and opacity with a NeRF-like neural network instead of spherical harmonic coefficients. On the MipNeRF 360 dataset, it achieves a PSNR of 27.66, SSIM of 0.809, and LPIPS of 0.223. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting uses spherical harmonics to encode view-dependent color, which struggles with high-frequency specularities and anisotropic reflections. Recent advances introduced anisotropic representations and PBR integration to address these limitations. ARS-GS and Spec-Gaussian leverage Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) to model directional reflectance, with ARS-GS specifically integrating GGX microfacet models for physical accuracy. VDGS employs a neural network to predict view-dependent attributes, offering an alternative to explicit directional basis functions. These methods are used in high-fidelity 3D reconstruction, digital twins, and virtual production where realistic lighting interactions are critical.
