name: Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling
head: Err-SPS, Tile-Wise Pixel Sampling (EPS), Tile-wise Sparse Pixel Sampling, sparse pixel training
body: Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling (Err-SPS) is a training optimization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces dense, per-pixel rasterization and supervision with a sparse, error-guided sampling strategy. It dynamically reallocates computation from "easy" (low-error) regions to "challenging" (high-error) regions, significantly reducing training time and Gaussian count while preserving high-frequency details when combined with structure-aware losses. It differs from sibling methods like TurboGS by specifically defining the tile-wise sampling logic and the associated EMA update rules for the error and age maps, which serve as the foundation for the broader TurboGS framework. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians G, camera views Vt for tile t, ground truth images I, current Error Map E, current Age Map A, training progress \rhot \in 0, 1), and sampling schedule parameters K{max}, K{min}. Outputs: A subset of sampled pixels P{t,v} per view v in tile t, updated Error Map E, updated Age Map A, and gradients for the sampled pixels. Data Structures: Error Map (E): A 2D array storing the per-pixel reconstruction error ([L1 loss) from previous iterations. Stored in half-precision (float16) on the GPU. Age Map (A): A 2D array storing the number of consecutive iterations a pixel has not been sampled. Stored in uint16 precision. Sampling Schedule: Parameters K{max} (max pixels to sample) and K{min} (min pixels to sample) control the sparsity level based on training progress \rhot. Algorithm Steps: 1. Query Sampling Rate: Determine the number of pixels to sample Kt for the current tile based on the schedule using K{max}, K{min}, E{init}, \Theta, t. 2. View Selection: Select views Vt for the tile. While Err-SPS focuses on pixel sampling, TurboGS employs Geometry-Aware View Sampling (GVS) to anchor by error and sample by pose/distance. 3. Tile-Wise Pixel Sampling: Select Kt pixels P{t,v} for each view v \in Vt within the tile. Pixels are prioritized based on: Error (E): Higher error pixels are prioritized to focus optimization on difficult areas. Age (A): Higher age pixels (longer time since last sampled) are prioritized to ensure periodic revisiting and prevent stagnation. The selection is ordered by tile indices. 4. Gather Ground Truth and Error: Retrieve ground truth colors c^ and compute current errors e^ for the sampled pixels P{t,v}. 5. Sparse Forward Rendering: Perform rasterization restricted to the sampled pixel set \{(v, p) | v \in Vt, p \in P{t,v}\}, preserving tile-parallel forward execution. 6. Sparse Loss and Gradients: Compute loss L only over sampled pixels. The loss formulation is: L = \sum{v \in Vt, p \in P{t,v}} \ell1(p) + \sum{v \in Vt, \tau} \lambda\tau^{ncc} L\tau^{S-NCC} where \ell1 is the L1 loss, \lambda\tau^{ncc} is a weighting coefficient, and L\tau^{S-NCC} is the sparse normalized cross-correlation term computed over sampled pixels within a tile. 7. EMA Error-Map Update: Update the Error Map using Exponential Moving Average (EMA) only for the sampled pixels: Ev(p) \leftarrow (1-\beta)Ev(p) + \beta e{t,v}(p) \quad \text{for } p \in P{t,v} where \beta is the EMA decay factor. 8. Age Map Update: Increment the Age Map A globally for all pixels, but reset A(p) = 0 for all sampled pixels p \in P{t,v}. 9. Gaussian Backward: Compute gradients for Gaussian properties using a per-Gaussian backward mechanism (splat-parallel computation) restricted to the sampled pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errorguidedsparsepixelsampling(G, Vt, I, E, A, rhot, Kmax, Kmin, beta): # 1. Query sampling rate Kt = querysamplingschedule(Kmax, Kmin, E, G, rhot) # 2. View Selection (Optional in pure Err-SPS, but part of TurboGS context) # Vt = geometryawareviewsampling(Kt, rhot) Pt = [] # List of sampled pixels per view # 3. Tile-Wise Pixel Sampling for v in Vt: # Prioritize by Error E and Age A # Select top Kt pixels based on combined score # Note: Exact weighting of E and A is not specified in sources indices = gettopkindices(E, A, Kt) Pv = [pixelatindex(i) for i in indices] Pt.append((v, Pv)) # 4. Gather GT Color & Error cstar = [] estar = [] for v, Pv in Pt: gtcolors = getgtcolors(v, Pv, I) renderedcolors = rasterizeforward(G, v, Pv) currenterrors = computel1loss(renderedcolors, gtcolors) cstar.append(gtcolors) estar.append(currenterrors) # 5. Sparse Forward Rendering (Implicit in step 4 for error calc) # 6. Sparse Loss & Grads # L = sum(L1) + sum(S-NCC) # Gradients are computed for sampled pixels only grads = computesparsegradients(cstar, estar, G, Pt) # 7. EMA Error-Map Update for v, Pv in Pt: for p in Pv: E[v][p] = (1 - beta) E[v][p] + beta estar[v][p] # 8. Age Map Update A = A + 1 # Increment all for v, Pv in Pt: for p in Pv: A[v][p] = 0 # Reset sampled pixels # 9. Gaussian Backward G = applygradients(G, grads) return G, E, A Parameters: \beta (EMA decay): Not given in the sources. \lambda\tau^{ncc}: Weighting coefficient for S-NCC. Not given in the sources. K{max}, K{min}: Max/min pixels to sample. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Relying solely on sparse-pixel L1 supervision degrades reconstruction quality, particularly high-frequency details. Sparse supervision may introduce subtle rippling artifacts in low-frequency regions with weak texture variations (e.g., walls or ceilings). Replacing Err-SPS with random pixel sampling (RPS) causes failure to preserve high-frequency details and drops in PSNR. A broader training framework that incorporates Err-SPS as its core sampling component, along with geometry-aware view sampling, error-driven density control, and a hybrid optimizer. Choose TurboGS when you need the full acceleration pipeline including density control and optimized solver. TurboGS Time Complexity: Significantly reduces training time. On Mip-NeRF 360, Err-SPS reduces training time from 891s to 85s compared to vanilla 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussians (NGS) from 2.73M to 0.76M on Mip-NeRF 360, indicating lower memory footprint for the scene representation. Scaling: The method scales with the number of tiles and views, but the sparsity factor Kt controls the computational load per iteration. Strengths: Accelerates training by avoiding redundant gradient computation on well-reconstructed pixels; preserves high-frequency details when combined with S-NCC. Limitations: May introduce artifacts in low-texture regions; requires complementary structure-aware losses to maintain quality. When to use: When training time is a bottleneck and the scene has sufficient texture for error-guided sampling to be effective. When not to use: For scenes with large uniform regions where error maps may not accurately reflect reconstruction difficulty without additional regularization. Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling was introduced as part of the TurboGS framework by Hanson et al. in 2026. It is motivated by the observation that as training progresses, only a small subset of pixels remains difficult to reconstruct, while most become well-explained and yield marginal gradients. The method builds on the principles of sparse pixel training and per-Gaussian backward mechanisms. name: Truncated Gradient Updates for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: TruncGradGS, Truncated Gradient Method
body: Truncated Gradient Updates is a training optimization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses vanishing gradients in "dead" Gaussians (those with low opacity) to enable long-range movement and convergence. It solves the problem where poorly initialized or distant Gaussians fail to receive gradient signals because they are filtered out by the rasterizer's alpha-blending cutoff, preventing them from moving to their correct positions. Unlike standard backpropagation which only updates Gaussians contributing to the final pixel color, this method computes a surrogate gradient for non-contributing Gaussians based on their Mahalanobis distance, allowing them to "pull" toward visible pixels. It is distinct from sibling methods like Bézier-boundary gradient approximation by using a linear surrogate model for the truncated gradient rather than boundary approximations, and from Sparse SH Order Increment by focusing on spatial movement rather than frequency domain updates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The current set of 3D Gaussians (means \mu, covariances, opacities \sigma, colors, SH coefficients), camera parameters, ground-truth image I{gt}, and rendered image \hat{I}. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters after the optimization step. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS Gaussian primitive structure. Key fields involved are: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D mean position. \sigma \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity scalar. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Alpha value after density scaling (often \alpha = \sigma \cdot \alpha{density}, but the source uses \sigma \alpha to denote the effective contribution threshold). p \in \mathbb{R}^2: 2D pixel center coordinate. a, b, c: Coefficients derived from the Gaussian covariance matrix for Mahalanobis distance calculation (from Eq. 8 of). Parameters: \tau{pruning}: The opacity threshold below which a Gaussian is considered "dead" and eligible for truncated gradients. m: Slope parameter influencing the range of action of the truncated gradient. Lower m yields a near-constant long-range gradient; higher m yields sharp decay. \tau: The cut-off threshold for the squared Mahalanobis distance. \lambda: Loss weight for SSIM (typically 0.2, inherited from parent). Numbered Steps: 1. Render and Compute Loss: Render the image \hat{I} using the differentiable rasterizer. Compute the photometric loss \mathcal{L} using the standard weighted sum: \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is L1 loss and \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} is differentiable SSIM. 2. Identify Dead Gaussians: For each Gaussian i, check if its opacity \sigmai is below the pruning threshold \tau{pruning}. Only Gaussians satisfying \sigmai < \tau{pruning} are candidates for truncated gradient updates. 3. Compute Mahalanobis Distance: For each pixel p and candidate Gaussian i with mean \mui, calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance rs: rs = \|\mui - p\|2^2 The threshold condition involves the quadratic form: K = a(\mu{ix} - px)^2 + 2b(\mu{ix} - px)(\mu{iy} - py) + c(\mu{iy} - py)^2 where a, b, c are coefficients from the Gaussian's covariance matrix. 4. Determine Gradient Path: For each pixel-Gaussian pair, determine the update path based on the effective contribution \sigmai \alphai and the Mahalanobis distance relative to the threshold \tau: Normal Path: If \sigmai \alphai \ge 1/255, the Gaussian contributes to the pixel. Use standard backpropagation gradients \nabla \mathcal{L}. Truncated Path: If \sigmai \alphai < 1/255 (low density or low opacity) AND the Mahalanobis distance is above the threshold (specifically, the distance d(p) > \tau), apply the truncated gradient. Condition Check: Only apply if \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alphai} < 0. If positive, the gradient would cause repulsion. Calculation: Compute the truncated gradient surrogate. The cut-off gradient is defined as G'(x), where x is the solution to G(x) = \tau. The solution for the displacement is: rs = \|\mu - p\|2^2 \left( 1 \pm \sqrt{\frac{-2 \log \tau}{K}} \right) (Note: The source provides the solution for rs in the context of the cut-off point. The gradient direction is towards the pixel p). Special Case: If the low contribution is due to low opacity \sigma (but distance is high), compute the gradient only for opacity \sigma. Skip Path: If \sigmai \alphai < 1/255 AND the Mahalanobis distance is below the threshold, the Gaussian receives no gradients. 5. Expand Tile Coverage (Implementation Detail): For dead Gaussians whose radius is below a threshold, expand their tile-coverage radius in the rasterizer. This ensures they are not culled during the tile-based rasterization pass, allowing them to receive the truncated gradient contributions from distant pixels. 6. Interleaved Optimization: Alternate between: Optimization steps using truncated gradients for dead Gaussians. Normal optimization steps with Adaptive Density Control (ADC) turned on. This prevents perturbations from accumulated truncated gradients from interfering with ADC decisions. 7. Delay Pruning: Do not prune Gaussians during the main training loop. Delay pruning until the end of training to allow dead Gaussians to converge to distant pixels via truncated gradients before removal. 8. Dynamic Scene Handling (Optional): For dynamic scenes, create viewpoint-dependent motion masks via frame-difference and image processing. Ignore contributions of static pixels to reduce computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetruncatedgradients(gaussians, pixels, loss, params): """ Computes gradients for 3D Gaussian Splatting using truncated gradient updates. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives with attributes: mu: (3,) mean position sigma: scalar opacity alpha: scalar alpha (density scaled) cov: covariance matrix (for a, b, c) pixels: List of pixel centers p (2,) and ground truth colors loss: Scalar loss value L params: Configuration parameters taupruning: Opacity threshold for dead Gaussians m: Slope parameter for truncated gradient decay tau: Mahalanobis distance threshold lambda: SSIM weight (0.2) Returns: gradients: Dictionary of gradients for each Gaussian parameter """ gradients = {g.id: {'mu': np.zeros(3), 'sigma': 0.0, 'alpha': 0.0} for g in gaussians} # Standard backpropagation for contributing Gaussians standardgrads = computestandardgradients(gaussians, pixels, loss, params) for g in gaussians: # Step 2: Identify Dead Gaussians if g.sigma >= params.taupruning: # Use standard gradients only gradients[g.id]['mu'] = standardgrads[g.id]['mu'] gradients[g.id]['sigma'] = standardgrads[g.id]['sigma'] continue # Step 3 & 4: Process Dead Gaussians # Check alpha gradient sign to prevent repulsion dLdalpha = standardgrads[g.id]['alpha'] # If alpha gradient is positive, do not apply truncated gradient # to avoid long-range push/repulsion if dLdalpha >= 0: gradients[g.id]['mu'] = standardgrads[g.id]['mu'] gradients[g.id]['sigma'] = standardgrads[g.id]['sigma'] continue # Calculate Mahalanobis distance components # a, b, c from covariance matrix (Eq. 8 in) a, b, c = getmahalanobiscoeffs(g.cov) truncatedmugrad = np.zeros(3) truncatedsigmagrad = 0.0 for p in pixels: # Compute squared Mahalanobis distance metric K dx = g.mu[0] - p.x dy = g.mu[1] - p.y K = a dx2 + 2 b dx dy + c dy2 # Check if distance is above threshold # The source defines the cut-off condition via the solution to G(x) = tau # We approximate the condition d(p) > tau using the derived rs formula # If K is very small, avoid division by zero if K < 1e-8: continue # Determine if truncated gradient should be applied # Condition: sigma alpha < 1/255 AND distance > threshold if g.sigma g.alpha < 1.0/255.0: # Check if distance is sufficiently large to warrant truncated gradient # The source implies a threshold on the Mahalanobis distance # We use the cut-off point logic: if the Gaussian is "far" enough # that it doesn't contribute, but is within the "pull" range. # Calculate the cut-off distance parameter # rs solution from source: rs = ||mu - p||^2 (1 +/- sqrt(-2 log tau / K)) # This defines the boundary. If the actual distance is beyond the # contribution threshold but within the truncated gradient range, apply it. # Simplified logic based on source: Apply if distance > tau # Since exact tau mapping to pixel space depends on projection, # we use the Mahalanobis distance metric directly. # Note: The source states "d(p) > tau" for truncated gradient. # We assume tau is pre-computed or derived from the rasterizer's cutoff. if isdistanceabovethreshold(g.mu, p, K, params.tau): # Compute truncated gradient direction # Direction is towards the pixel p direction = p - g.mu[:2] # 2D projection difference norm = np.linalg.norm(direction) if norm > 0: direction = direction / norm # Magnitude depends on slope m and distance # Lower m -> near-constant gradient; Higher m -> sharp decay # The source defines cut-off gradient as G'(x) where G(x)=tau # We approximate the magnitude as a function of distance decay distsq = dx2 + dy2 # Linear surrogate approximation for truncated gradient # The exact formula for G'(x) is in supplementary material # We use a simplified decay model consistent with the description gradientmagnitude = computetruncatedmagnitude(distsq, K, params.m, params.tau) truncatedmugrad += direction gradientmagnitude # If low opacity is the cause, also compute gradient for sigma if g.alpha > 0.5: # Heuristic: if alpha is high, low sigma is the cause truncatedsigmagrad += gradientmagnitude g.alpha # Simplified chain rule # Accumulate gradients # Note: Standard gradients for dead Gaussians are typically zero or negligible # because they don't contribute to the pixel color. gradients[g.id]['mu'] = standardgrads[g.id]['mu'] + truncatedmugrad gradients[g.id]['sigma'] = standardgrads[g.id]['sigma'] + truncatedsigmagrad return gradients def isdistanceabovethreshold(mu, p, K, tau): """ Checks if the Mahalanobis distance is above the threshold tau. The source uses a threshold on the squared Mahalanobis distance. """ # The source defines the cut-off via the solution to G(x) = tau. # We approximate this by checking if the distance metric exceeds a scaled tau. # Exact implementation depends on the specific rasterizer's cutoff definition. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a pre-computed threshold. return K > tau def computetruncatedmagnitude(distsq, K, m, tau): """ Computes the magnitude of the truncated gradient. Lower m -> near-constant; Higher m -> sharp decay. """ # Simplified model: G'(x) decays with distance. # The source mentions a linear surrogate function. # We use a simple exponential decay controlled by m. # This is a placeholder for the exact supplementary formula if K == 0: return 0.0 # Normalize distance by K to get a dimensionless metric normalizeddist = distsq / K # Decay function magnitude = np.exp(-m normalizeddist) return magnitude Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Model Divergence: Accumulated truncated gradients can surpass true gradients, causing divergence for "very bad fits" (no normal gradients) or "good fits" (true gradient near zero). Mitigated by applying truncated gradients ONLY to dead Gaussians (\sigmai < \tau{pruning}). Repulsion: Applying truncated gradients when \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alphai} > 0 causes Gaussians to repel each other. Always check the sign of the alpha gradient. Tile Culling: Dead Gaussians may be culled by the rasterizer's tile-based culling, preventing them from receiving gradients. Mitigated by expanding their tile-coverage radius if below a threshold. Performance Overhead: The method can be 1–10× slower to train than the baseline due to additional gradient computations. Mitigated by restricting computations to dead Gaussians and using motion masks for dynamic scenes. Time Complexity: Training time is 1–10× slower than the baseline 3DGS, depending on the scene and primitive count. Inference speed is unaffected. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory overhead compared to standard 3DGS, as it modifies the optimization loop rather than the data structure. Measured Performance: Static Scenes (Mip-NeRF360, Random Init): PSNR 25.16 (vs 24.74), SSIM 0.8511 (vs 0.8351), LPIPS 0.1974 (vs 0.2106), #GS 0.799M (vs 1.126M). Dynamic Scenes (Neural 3D Video): PSNR 31.70 (vs 30.22), SSIM 0.9493 (vs 0.9443), LPIPS 0.1339 (vs 0.1360), #GS 1.733M (vs 2.806M). Scaling: The method scales with the number of Gaussians and pixels. Performance overhead is mitigated by only processing dead Gaussians and using motion masks for dynamic scenes. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality for poorly initialized scenes and dynamic scenes with large spatio-temporal divergence. Reduces the number of Gaussians needed for high-quality reconstruction. Limitations: Slower training time. Requires careful tuning of the slope parameter m and pruning threshold \tau{pruning}. When to Use: Use for static or dynamic scene reconstruction where initialization is poor or there is significant motion. It is a plug-and-play module for 3DGS, 2DGS, 4DGS, CEM-4DGS, and 4DScaffold. When Not to Use: Avoid if training time is a critical constraint and the scene is well-initialized. Do not apply to all Gaussians, as it degrades performance. The method was introduced by T. Morales, N.-Q. Le-Pham, R. Atkins & B.-S. Hua in the paper "TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates". It addresses the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in handling "dead" Gaussians that fail to converge due to vanishing gradients. The method is designed to be a generalizable improvement for both static and dynamic scene reconstruction. name: Sparse SH Order Increment
head: SOI, Sparse Order Increment of SH
body: Sparse SH Order Increment (SOI) is a training optimization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces GPU memory consumption and storage overhead by initializing all Gaussians with Spherical Harmonic (SH) order 0 and selectively promoting them to higher orders based on view-dependent color error. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which assigns full 3rd-order SH coefficients to every Gaussian, SOI exploits the redundancy in SH representations by only assigning higher-order coefficients to Gaussians that exhibit significant color deviation from ground truth across training views. This approach guarantees better rendering quality for a given sparse rate compared to random selection of Gaussians for order increment. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each defined by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and SH coefficients c{k,l,m} for order l and degree m. Training dataset consisting of N images with dimensions H \times W. Sparse rate parameter rs (fraction of Gaussians to promote). Iteration schedule for SOI execution. Outputs: Updated set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with potentially increased SH orders for a subset of Gaussians. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian gk stores its current SH order Lk (integer, typically 0 \le Lk \le 3). Color Difference Metric: A scalar value dk computed for each Gaussian k to rank them. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: At the start of training, set the SH order Lk = 0 for all Gaussians k \in \mathcal{G}. This minimizes initial GPU memory usage. 2. Pruning (Pre-condition): Before the first SOI execution, perform Gaussian pruning to remove low-opacity or redundant Gaussians. This step is critical to minimize GPU memory overhead before allocating higher-order SH coefficients. 3. Compute Color Difference: For each Gaussian k, calculate the view-based color difference dk across all training views. The formula is: dk = \frac{1}{N \cdot H \cdot W} \sum{p=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}(k \in \mathcal{N}p) \cdot wk^p \cdot |Cp - Cp^{gt}| Where: N is the number of training images. H, W are the image height and width. p iterates over all training images (or pixels, depending on interpretation of the summation index in the source; the source formula sums over p=1 to N, implying image-level or aggregated pixel-level error, but the denominator N \cdot H \cdot W suggests normalization by total pixel count. The source text says "sum{p=1}^{N}" but defines p as pixels in the variable list. However, the denominator N \cdot H \cdot W implies the sum is over all pixels in all images. Let's look closely at the source formula: dk = \frac{1}{N \cdot H \cdot W} \sum{p=1}^{N}.... The source text says "p iterates over all pixels" but the sum limit is N. This is a contradiction in the source notation. However, the denominator N \cdot H \cdot W strongly implies the sum is over all pixels in the dataset. The indicator \mathbb{1}(k \in \mathcal{N}p) checks if Gaussian k contributes to pixel p. wk^p is the contribution weight. Cp is rendered color, Cp^{gt} is ground truth. We will assume the sum is over all pixels p in the training set, normalized by total pixel count N \cdot H \cdot W. \mathbb{1}(k \in \mathcal{N}p) is an indicator function equal to 1 if Gaussian k overlaps pixel p (i.e., contributes to its color), and 0 otherwise. wk^p is the contribution weight of Gaussian k to pixel p during alpha blending. Cp is the rendered color at pixel p. Cp^{gt} is the ground truth color at pixel p. | \cdot | denotes the absolute difference (or L1 norm per channel). 4. Ranking: Sort all Gaussians in \mathcal{G} in descending order based on their computed difference dk. 5. Selection: Select the top rs \cdot |\mathcal{G}| Gaussians from the sorted list. These are the Gaussians with the highest color deviation, indicating a higher demand for complex color representation. 6. Increment: For each selected Gaussian, increment its SH order by one (Lk \leftarrow Lk + 1). This involves allocating memory for the new SH coefficients and initializing them (typically to zero or inheriting from a lower-order approximation if applicable, though the source does not specify initialization of new coefficients, standard practice implies zero-initialization or copying lower-order terms). 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-6 every several iterations. For small scenes (30,000 total iterations), SOI is executed at iterations 16,000, 17,000, and 18,000. For large scenes (60,000 total iterations), the steps are modified proportionately (e.g., 32,000, 34,000, 36,000). The total number of SOI executions is 3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparseshorderincrement(gaussians, trainingdata, rs, currentiteration, totaliterations): """ Perform Sparse SH Order Increment if the current iteration matches the schedule. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with attribute 'shorder' and 'id'. trainingdata: Dataset containing N images of size H x W. rs: Sparse rate (fraction of Gaussians to promote). currentiteration: Current training step. totaliterations: Total number of training steps. Returns: Updated list of Gaussians. """ # Determine if SOI should be executed # For small scenes (30k), steps are 16000, 17000, 18000 # For large scenes (60k), steps are proportional (approx 32000, 34000, 36000) # The source states SOI is performed 3 times. if currentiteration not in getsoIschedule(totaliterations): return gaussians # Step 2: Pruning is performed before SOI. # This is handled by the parent training loop's densification/pruning step. # We assume gaussians are already pruned. # Step 3: Compute color difference dk for each Gaussian differences = [] for g in gaussians: dk = 0.0 totalpixels = 0 for imageidx in range(len(trainingdata)): image = trainingdata[imageidx] # Render the image using current Gaussians to get Cp # This requires the differentiable rasterizer from the parent loop renderedimage = renderimage(gaussians, image.camerapose) # Calculate contribution of Gaussian g to each pixel # Note: In practice, this might be accumulated during rendering # Here we assume we can access per-pixel contributions for y in range(image.height): for x in range(image.width): # Check if Gaussian g contributes to pixel (x,y) # weightk^p is the alpha weight of g at pixel (x,y) weight = getcontributionweight(g, x, y, renderedimage) if weight > 0: # Indicator function 1(k in Np) is 1 if weight > 0 indicator = 1 colordiff = abs(renderedimage[y, x] - image.gt[y, x]) dk += indicator weight colordiff totalpixels += 1 # Normalize by total pixel count N H W # Note: The source formula divides by NHW. # If totalpixels is not equal to NHW (due to empty pixels), # we still divide by the global total to match the source definition. globaltotalpixels = len(trainingdata) image.height image.width dk /= globaltotalpixels differences.append((g.id, dk)) # Step 4: Sort by difference descending differences.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) # Step 5: Select top rs percentage numtopromote = int(rs len(gaussians)) selectedids = [diff[0] for diff in differences[:numtopromote]] # Step 6: Increment SH order for selected Gaussians for g in gaussians: if g.id in selectedids: if g.shorder < 3: # Max order is typically 3 g.shorder += 1 # Initialize new SH coefficients to zero or appropriate values initializeshcoefficients(g, g.shorder) return gaussians def getsoIschedule(totaliterations): """ Returns the iteration steps for SOI execution. Based on source: 3 times total. Small scenes (30k): 16000, 17000, 18000. Large scenes (60k): Proportional. """ if totaliterations <= 30000: return [16000, 17000, 18000] else: # Proportional scaling # 16000/30000 = 0.5333 # 17000/30000 = 0.5666 # 18000/30000 = 0.6000 scale = totaliterations / 30000.0 return [int(16000 scale), int(17000 scale), int(18000 scale)] def initializeshcoefficients(gaussian, neworder): """ Initialize SH coefficients for the new order. Source does not specify, but standard practice is zero-initialization. """ # Allocate memory for SH coefficients of order neworder # Number of coefficients for order L is (L+1)^2 numcoeffs = (neworder + 1) 2 gaussian.shcoeffs = [0.0] numcoeffs Parameters: rs (Sparse Rate): The fraction of Gaussians selected to receive increased SH order. Typical value: 0.2 (20%). Higher rs slightly improves quality; rs=0.5 yields quality similar to full SH, proving SH redundancy. Iteration Steps: For small scenes (30,000 iterations), SOI is executed at iterations 16,000, 17,000, and 18,000. For large scenes (60,000 iterations), steps are modified proportionately. Total Executions: 3 times during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overflow: If rs is too high or pruning is insufficient, GPU memory may exceed limits during the allocation of higher-order SH coefficients. Pruning must be performed before SOI. Precision: The color difference calculation involves summing over all pixels, which may require double precision to avoid numerical instability if the number of pixels is very large. Boundary Conditions: If the number of Gaussians is small, rs \cdot |\mathcal{G}| may be zero. Ensure at least one Gaussian is promoted if rs > 0 and |\mathcal{G}| > 0. Max Order: SH order cannot exceed 3 (standard for 3DGS). Ensure increments do not exceed this limit. A baseline method where Gaussians are selected randomly to increment SH order. SOI outperforms this method in rendering quality for the same rs value. The standard 3DGS approach where all Gaussians use 3rd-order SH. SOI achieves comparable quality with significantly reduced storage and memory. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: SOI significantly reduces peak GPU memory consumption and final storage size compared to full SH. For example, on Mip-NeRF360, SOI with rs=0.2 reduces storage to 98MB compared to higher values for larger rs or full SH (implied by "significantly reduce storage overhead"). Peak GPU memory is reduced from 12.8GB (baseline) to 8.8GB with SOI (rs=0.2). Time: Training time is slightly reduced or comparable. On Mip-NeRF360, SOI (rs=0.2) training time is 19m41s, compared to 25m57s for the baseline with selective densification only. Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF360 (rs=0.1): SSIM 0.815, PSNR 27.27, LPIPS 0.218, FPS 215, Storage 78MB. Mip-NeRF360 (rs=0.2): SSIM 0.817, PSNR 27.38, LPIPS 0.216, FPS 218, Storage 98MB. Mip-NeRF360 (rs=0.5): SSIM 0.819, PSNR 27.46, LPIPS 0.213, FPS 220, Storage 158MB. Comparison: SOI with rs=0.2 achieves similar quality to full SH but with much lower storage and memory. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces GPU memory overhead, allowing training of larger scenes. Reduces storage size. Maintains high rendering quality. Faster training due to reduced memory pressure and potentially fewer operations per Gaussian in early stages. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of rs and iteration steps. Performance may degrade if the wrong module execution time is chosen for different scene scales. When to Use: Use when GPU memory is limited or storage size is a concern. Use for large-scale scenes where full SH is prohibitive. Use when training time needs to be reduced. When Not to Use: Use when maximum possible rendering quality is required regardless of memory/storage (use full SH). Use when scene complexity is very low and SH order 0 is sufficient (no need for SOI). Origin: Sparse SH Order Increment was proposed in the paper "EfficientGS: Streamlining Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale High-Resolution Scene Representation". The paper was published in 2025 (based on the DOI date) and presented by authors from the EfficientGS project. History and Development: The method builds upon the original 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [Kerbl et al., 2023] and addresses the limitations of high memory consumption and storage size associated with full 3rd-order SH coefficients. It was developed to enable efficient training and rendering of large-scale, high-resolution scenes. Where it is used: Used in the EfficientGS framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. Validated on datasets including Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending. name: Regression-based FisherRF
head: FisherRF with meta-regression, Modified FisherRF
body: Regression-based FisherRF is a variant of the FisherRF uncertainty estimation method that replaces direct variance-to-pixel mapping with a meta-regression model. It solves the problem of estimating pixel-wise rendering uncertainty by using grouped Gaussian parameter variances as input feature maps to predict uncertainty, rather than summing color parameter variances directly. It differs from the original FisherRF by aligning its pipeline with PRIMU's feature map regression approach, allowing for fair comparison of uncertainty estimation quality. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by mean position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. Camera parameters for the target view. Outputs: A set of six uncertainty feature maps, one for each parameter group. A pixel-wise uncertainty map predicted by the regression model. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting primitive structure [14, cited in S1, unofficial]. The parameters are grouped into six categories based on the original GS implementation: 1. Mean (position) 2. Scale 3. Rotation 4. Opacity factor 5. Spherical harmonics color parameters of degree zero (c0) 6. Higher degree spherical harmonics color parameters (c{k>0}) Note: The scale and rotation groups correspond to the primitive's covariance matrix. Steps: 1. Compute Parameter Variances: For each Gaussian primitive, compute the variance of its parameters. In the context of FisherRF, these variances are derived from the diagonal entries of the Fisher Information Matrix of the Gaussian primitive with respect to the gradient of the rendering function. 2. Group Variances: Aggregate the computed variances per primitive into the six predefined categories. 3. Form Feature Maps: Aggregate the grouped variances across all primitives to form six distinct uncertainty feature maps, one for each category. 4. Regression: Feed the six feature maps into a meta-regression model. 5. Predict Uncertainty: The regression model outputs a pixel-wise uncertainty map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. Each primitive has: mean: (3,) scale: (3,) rotation: (4,) (quaternion) opacity: (1,) shcoeffs: (K, 3) where K is number of SH bands camera: Camera parameters for projection. Returns: uncertaintymap: (H, W) predicted uncertainty. featuremaps: List of 6 tensors, each (H, W). """ # Step 1: Compute variances for each primitive # In FisherRF, variance is derived from the Fisher Information Matrix diagonal. # This requires computing the gradient of the rendering function w.r.t. parameters. # For implementation, we assume a function computefishervariances exists # that returns the variance for each parameter group per primitive. variances = computefishervariances(gaussians, camera) # Step 2 & 3: Group variances and form feature maps # Group 1: Mean meanvariance = variances['mean'] featuremapmean = aggregatetoimage(meanvariance, gaussians, camera) # Group 2: Scale scalevariance = variances['scale'] featuremapscale = aggregatetoimage(scalevariance, gaussians, camera) # Group 3: Rotation rotationvariance = variances['rotation'] featuremaprotation = aggregatetoimage(rotationvariance, gaussians, camera) # Group 4: Opacity opacityvariance = variances['opacity'] featuremapopacity = aggregatetoimage(opacityvariance, gaussians, camera) # Group 5: SH Degree 0 sh0variance = variances['shdegree0'] featuremapsh0 = aggregatetoimage(sh0variance, gaussians, camera) # Group 6: SH Degree > 0 shhighvariance = variances['shhigher'] featuremapshhigh = aggregatetoimage(shhighvariance, gaussians, camera) featuremaps = [ featuremapmean, featuremapscale, featuremaprotation, featuremapopacity, featuremapsh0, featuremapshhigh ] # Step 4 & 5: Regression # The regression model is not specified in the source. # It is assumed to be a neural network that takes the 6 feature maps as input. # Standard practice would be a CNN or MLP. uncertaintymap = regressionmodel(featuremaps) return uncertaintymap, featuremaps def computefishervariances(gaussians, camera): """ Compute variances based on Fisher Information Matrix. This is a placeholder for the specific FisherRF variance computation. The source states that diagonal entries of the Fisher Information Matrix correspond to variances of the Gaussian primitive parameters. """ # Implementation details for Fisher Information Matrix computation are not provided # in the source text. This function would compute the Hessian or gradient # statistics to estimate parameter variances. raise NotImplementedError("Fisher Information Matrix computation details not provided in source.") def aggregatetoimage(variances, gaussians, camera): """ Aggregate per-primitive variances into a 2D image feature map. Standard alpha-blending or accumulation based on rasterization order. """ # Implementation details for aggregation are not provided in the source text. # This function would project primitives to 2D and accumulate variances # at each pixel, likely using the same rasterization pipeline as rendering. raise NotImplementedError("Aggregation details not provided in source.") Parameters: Parameter Grouping: The six groups are fixed as defined in the original GS implementation [14, cited in S1, unofficial]. The original method that uses the sum of color parameter variances for direction-dependent uncertainty. Regression-based FisherRF is a modification of this. The primary method that uses a meta-regression model for uncertainty estimation. Regression-based FisherRF is designed to be comparable to PRIMU. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Gaussian Primitive Training Schedule
head: Reduced Iteration Schedule, Two-Phase Training Schedule
body: This method reduces the training iteration count of 3D Gaussian Splatting from the conventional ~300,000 steps to approximately 6,000 steps by leveraging dense initial point cloud initialization. It achieves satisfactory reconstruction quality significantly faster than standard baselines by splitting the optimization into two short phases separated by pseudo-view depth refinement. Inputs: A dense initial point cloud (e.g., from DUSt3R or similar dense reconstruction). A set of input training views with known camera poses. Hyperparameters: totaliterations = 6000, phase1iterations = 3000, phase2iterations = 3000, densifyinterval = 500, densifyskip = 1500. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: Gaussians: List of primitive objects. Each primitive stores: position: 3D vector (x, y, z) scale: 3D vector (sx, sy, sz) rotation: Quaternion (qw, qx, qy, qz) opacity: Scalar \alpha \in [0, 1] shcoeffs: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for color. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian primitives using the dense point cloud. Set the current iteration counter t = 0. 2. Phase 1 Training: For t from 0 to 2999: Sample a random training image and camera pose. Render the image \hat{I} using the differentiable rasterizer. Compute loss \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} with \lambda = 0.2. Backpropagate gradients and update parameters using Adam (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99). If t > 1500 and t \pmod{500} == 0: Apply densification strategy (splitting high-gradient Gaussians, pruning low-opacity ones) as defined in AbsGS. 3. Pseudo-View Depth Optimization: Render RGB images for "pseudo views" (synthetic views generated from the current Gaussian representation). Perform depth optimization specifically for these pseudo views to refine geometric consistency. 4. Phase 2 Training: For t from 3000 to 5999: Sample a random training image and camera pose. Render the image \hat{I}. Compute loss \mathcal{L}. Backpropagate and update parameters. If t \pmod{500} == 0: Apply densification strategy. 5. Completion: Return the optimized Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingaussianschedule(gaussians, trainingviews, denseinitpoints): # Initialize Gaussians from dense point cloud gaussians = initializefrompoints(denseinitpoints) totaliterations = 6000 phase1end = 3000 densifyskip = 1500 densifyinterval = 500 for t in range(totaliterations): # 1. Sampling viewidx = randomchoice(trainingviews) camerapose = trainingviews[viewidx].pose gtimage = trainingviews[viewidx].image # 2. Rendering renderedimage = render(gaussians, camerapose) # 3. Loss Computation # Standard 3DGS loss: Limg = (1 - lambda) L1 + lambda D-SSIM lambdaweight = 0.2 loss = computeloss(renderedimage, gtimage, lambdaweight) # 4. Backpropagation & Update gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) updateparameters(gaussians, gradients, optimizer="Adam", beta1=0.9, beta2=0.99) # 5. Densification/Pruning # Skip first 1500 iterations, then every 500 iterations if t > densifyskip and (t - densifyskip) % densifyinterval == 0: applydensification(gaussians, gradients) # Special Step: Pseudo-View Depth Optimization after Phase 1 if t == phase1end: pseudoviews = generatepseudoviews(gaussians) for pview in pseudoviews: pgtimage = render(pview.camerapose, gaussians) # Depth optimization loop for pseudo views optimizedepthforpseudoview(gaussians, pview) return gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization Density: The method relies on "sufficiently dense point clouds" for initialization. Sparse initialization may not converge within 6,000 iterations. Densification Timing: Applying densification too early (before iteration 1500) is explicitly avoided to prevent instability during the initial convergence phase. Pseudo-View Generation: The quality of the "pseudo views" and the subsequent depth optimization step is critical for the second phase's success. Time Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to standard 3DGS. Requires ~6,000 iterations versus ~300,000 for conventional methods. This represents a ~50x reduction in training time. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS, as the number of Gaussians is determined by the initialization density and densification strategy, not the iteration count. Performance: Achieves "satisfactory results" in the first 3,000 iterations. Hardware: Experiments conducted on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Strengths: Drastic reduction in training time; suitable for applications requiring rapid reconstruction from dense inputs. Limitations: Dependent on high-quality dense initialization; may not generalize well to sparse input scenarios where standard 300,000 iterations are needed for convergence. This training schedule is associated with methods like GBR (Generative Bundle Refinement) which combine dense reconstruction backbones (e.g., DUSt3R) with Gaussian Splatting. The approach exploits the fact that dense initialization reduces the search space, allowing convergence in far fewer steps. name: CompGS Training Loop
head: CompGS Training
body: The CompGS training loop is the optimization procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting that incorporates auxiliary parameters and adaptive control mechanisms to refine Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of static Gaussian initialization by iteratively updating positions, scales, opacities, colors, and auxiliary features through a differentiable rendering pipeline. It is distinguished from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by the explicit management of auxiliary parameters (updated via a separate optimizer) and a specific adaptive control schedule for pruning and growing primitives based on view-dependent error metrics. Inputs: Dataset of training views, where each sample contains: image tensor, image dimensions (H, W), tangent half-FOV (\tan(\text{fov}x), \tan(\text{fov}y)), camera center, camera index, world-to-view matrix, and world-to-image projection matrix. Initial Gaussian model initialized from sparse point clouds (Structure-from-Motion). Configuration parameters: maxiterations, ssimweight, stopiteration, controlbaseinterval, numtrainingviews, auxupdateenable, controlstartbaseinterval. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian model parameters (means, covariances/scales, opacities, colors, auxiliary features). Evaluation metrics (PSNR, SSIM) on validation views. GaussianModel: Stores parameters for N Gaussians. Fields include means (\mathbb{R}^3), scales (\mathbb{R}^3), opacities (\mathbb{R}), colors (\mathbb{R}^3 or spherical harmonics coefficients), and auxiliary parameters (dimensions defined in config). RenderSettings: Struct containing camidx, imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, campos, viewmatrix, projmatrix. RenderResults: Struct containing renderedimg (tensor), predicttime, rendertime. Optimizers: WarpedAdam instances for main Gaussian parameters and auxiliary parameters. 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian model from sparse SfM point clouds. Initialize gaussianoptimizer and auxoptimizer using WarpedAdam. Configure learning rate schedulers for means and network parameters. 2. Training Loop (for iteration i from 0 to maxiterations): Sample Selection: Select a random training view sample. Learning Rate Update: Update learning rates for Gaussian means using the scheduler. Rendering: Construct RenderSettings from the sample. Set retaingrad = (i < stopiteration). Call gaussianmodel.render(rendersettings, retaingrad) to obtain renderresults. Loss Computation: Compute L1 loss: L{L1} = \frac{1}{N} \sum |I{rendered} - I{target}|. Compute SSIM loss: L{SSIM} = 1 - \text{SSIM}(I{rendered}, I{target}). Compute rendering loss: L{render} = (1 - \text{ssim\weight}) L{L1} + \text{ssim\weight} L{SSIM}. Compute regularization loss: L{reg} = 0.01 \times \text{mean}(\text{scales}). (Note: Source describes this as "mean of the product of scales (volume proxy)", but explicitly states "0.01 times the mean of the product of scales". Implementation usually implies a volume regularization term. We follow the text: "0.01 times the mean of the product of scales"). Total loss: L{total} = L{render} + L{reg}. Backward Pass: If auxupdateenable is true and iteration is within the auxiliary update range (defined by controlstartbaseinterval and stopiteration): Compute gradients for auxiliary parameters. Step auxoptimizer. Zero gradients for auxiliary parameters. Compute gradients for main Gaussian parameters. Step gaussianoptimizer. Zero gradients for main Gaussian parameters. Adaptive Control: If enabled and i is within the control range and i \pmod{(\text{control\base\interval} \times \text{num\training\views})} == 0: Perform pruning (remove low-opacity Gaussians) and growing (duplicate high-error Gaussians). 3. Evaluation: Render all validation views. Save original and rendered images. Calculate PSNR per view using MSE: \text{PSNR} = 10 \log{10}(1 / \text{MSE}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traincompgs(dataset, gaussianmodel, config): # 1. Initialization gaussianoptimizer = WarpedAdam(gaussianmodel.mainparams) auxoptimizer = WarpedAdam(gaussianmodel.auxparams) if config.auxupdateenable else None lrscheduler = partial(updatelrmeans, optimizer=gaussianoptimizer, lrupdateconfigs=gaussianmodel.getlrconfigs(config), maxiterations=config.maxiterations) stopiteration = config.adaptivecontrol.stopiteration ssimweight = config.training.ssimweight for iteration in range(config.maxiterations): # 2. Sample and LR Update sample = dataset.getrandomsample() lrscheduler(iteration=iteration) # 3. Rendering rendersettings = RenderSettings( camidx=sample.camidx, imageheight=sample.imageheight, imagewidth=sample.imagewidth, tanfovx=sample.tanhalffovx, tanfovy=sample.tanhalffovy, campos=sample.cameracenter, viewmatrix=sample.worldtoviewprojmat, projmatrix=sample.worldtoimageprojmat) retaingrad = iteration < stopiteration renderresults = gaussianmodel.render(rendersettings, retaingrad=retaingrad) # 4. Loss Computation l1loss = F.l1loss(renderresults.renderedimg, sample.img) ssimloss = 1 - ssim(renderresults.renderedimg.unsqueeze(0), sample.img.unsqueeze(0), datarange=1.0) renderingloss = (1 - ssimweight) l1loss + ssimweight ssimloss # Regularization: 0.01 mean of product of scales # Note: 'product of scales' implies volume. If scales are (sx, sy, sz), product is sxsysz. # The source says "mean of the product of scales". scales = gaussianmodel.scales volumeproxy = torch.prod(scales, dim=-1) # Product across dimensions regloss = 0.01 torch.mean(volumeproxy) totalloss = renderingloss + regloss # 5. Backward and Optimization if auxoptimizer is not None: # Check if aux update is enabled for this iteration range # Source: "Update auxiliary parameters if auxupdateenable is true (iteration range defined by controlstartbaseinterval and stopiteration)" # Assuming controlstartbaseinterval is a start iteration index if config.auxupdateenable and iteration >= config.controlstartbaseinterval and iteration < stopiteration: totalloss.backward(retaingraph=True) # Retain graph for aux if needed, or separate backward # Specific implementation detail: Aux params might be updated separately auxoptimizer.step() auxoptimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() gaussianoptimizer.step() gaussianoptimizer.zerograd() # 6. Adaptive Control if config.adaptivecontrol.enabled: interval = config.controlbaseinterval dataset.numtrainingviews if iteration < stopiteration and iteration % interval == 0: adaptivecontrolstep(gaussianmodel, iteration) # 7. Evaluation evaluateandsave(dataset, gaussianmodel, config) Gradient Retention: Gradients must not be retained after stopiteration to save memory, but must be retained during the adaptive control phase if it occurs after the main optimization loop's gradient-free phase. Auxiliary Parameter Timing: Auxiliary parameters are only updated within a specific iteration range. Outside this range, they remain static or are removed. Precision: PSNR calculation involves log10(1/MSE). If MSE is zero (perfect reconstruction), this results in infinity. A small epsilon should be added to MSE in practice, though not explicitly stated in the source. Time Complexity: Dominated by the differentiable rendering step per iteration. Adaptive control adds overhead proportional to the number of primitives. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of Gaussians and auxiliary parameter dimensions. Performance: Uses WarpedAdam optimizer. Performance metrics (PSNR/SSIM) are calculated post-training. Strengths: Adaptive control allows dynamic refinement of the Gaussian set. Auxiliary parameters enable more complex feature representations. Limitations: Complexity of managing two optimizers and specific iteration schedules. The CompGS training loop is part of the CompGS (Compressed Gaussian Splatting) framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with compression and auxiliary parameter handling. name: Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) Loss
head: MAC loss, MAC-Splat loss
body: The Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) loss is a regularization objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enforces geometric and photometric agreement between matched Gaussians across different views. It solves the ambiguity problem in sparse-view reconstruction by using high-confidence 2D pixel correspondences as anchors to jointly regularize Gaussian position, shape, and appearance in a common world coordinate frame. Unlike standard photometric losses that only compare rendered pixels, MAC loss directly constrains the underlying 3D Gaussian parameters, providing robustness to outliers and preventing geometric degeneracy. Inputs: A set of matched pixel pairs M = \{ (p1^k, p2^k) \}{k=1}^K between two training images I1 and I2, where each pair has an associated joint confidence weight wk. Camera-to-world transformation matrices T{wc}^v = [\mathbf{R}^v | \mathbf{t}^v] for each view v \in \{1, 2\}. Predicted dense parameter maps for each view, aligned with the descriptor grid, containing for each pixel (u,v): Centroid in camera space: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cam}}^{v}(u,v) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix in camera space: \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{cam}}^{v}(u,v) \in \text{Sym}^+(3). Opacity: \alpha^v(u,v) \in \mathbb{R}. Spherical Harmonic coefficients: \mathbf{c}^v(u,v). Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{MAC}}. Data Structures: The parameter maps are dense grids. Sampling is performed via differentiable bilinear interpolation at coordinates p1^k and p2^k. Covariance matrices are symmetric positive definite (Sym^+(3)). Steps: 1. Gaussian Extraction: For each matched pixel pair k, bilinearly sample the predicted parameter maps at coordinates p1^k (view 1) and p2^k (view 2) to obtain two Gaussians G1^k and G2^k: Gk^v = \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cam}}^{v,k}, \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{cam}}^{v,k}, \alpha^{v,k}, \mathbf{c}^{v,k} \right), \quad v \in \{1, 2\} where the superscript k denotes sampling at pv^k. 2. World-Space Transformation: Transform the centroids and covariance matrices from camera space to world space using the camera-to-world rotation \mathbf{R}^v and translation \mathbf{t}^v: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{world}}^{v,k} = \mathbf{R}^v \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cam}}^{v,k} + \mathbf{t}^v \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{world}}^{v,k} = \mathbf{R}^v \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{cam}}^{v,k} (\mathbf{R}^v)^\top 3. Positional Consistency: Compute the L1 distance between world-space centroids. Apply Huber loss \mathcal{H}(\cdot) only if both centroids are in front of their respective cameras (z{\text{cam}} > 0): \mathcal{L}{\text{pos}}^{(k)} = \mathcal{H}\left( \|\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{world}}^{1,k} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{world}}^{2,k}\|1 \right) 4. Shape Consistency: Compute the loss based on the log-eigenvalues of the world-space covariance matrices. Let \lambda^{v,k}i be the eigenvalues of \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{world}}^{v,k} for i=1,2,3. The loss is the Huber distance between the sorted log-eigenvalues: \mathcal{L}{\text{shape}}^{(k)} = \mathcal{H}\left( \sum{i=1}^3 | \log \lambda^{1,k}i - \log \lambda^{2,k}i | \right) Note: The sources specify using log-eigenvalues to respect the geometry of Sym^+(3) and ensure invariance to rotation and uniform scaling, avoiding Euclidean distance which lacks these properties. 5. Appearance Consistency: Compute the L1 distance between opacity and spherical harmonic coefficients: \mathcal{L}{\text{app}}^{(k)} = \| \alpha^{1,k} - \alpha^{2,k} \|1 + \| \mathbf{c}^{1,k} - \mathbf{c}^{2,k} \|1 6. Aggregation: Combine the terms weighted by the match confidence wk and scalar hyperparameters \lambdap, \lambdas, \lambdaa: \mathcal{L}{\text{MAC}} = \frac{\sum{k=1}^K wk \left( \lambdap \mathcal{L}{\text{pos}}^{(k)} + \lambdas \mathcal{L}{\text{shape}}^{(k)} + \lambdaa \mathcal{L}{\text{app}}^{(k)} \right)}{\sum{k=1}^K wk + \epsilon} where \epsilon is a small constant to prevent division by zero. Parameters: \lambdap, \lambdas, \lambdaa: Scalar weights for positional, shape, and appearance consistency. Values not given in the sources. \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability. Value not given in the sources. wk: Joint confidence of the k-th match. Computed by the semantic fusion module (e.g., MASt3R/DINOv3 backbone). Value not given in the sources. \tau{\text{conf}}: Confidence threshold for filtering matches. If no match survives (wk > \tau{\text{conf}}), the loss for that region falls back to zero. Value not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Geometric Degeneracy: As a Gaussian's smallest eigenvalue \lambda{\min} approaches zero, the gradient of the log-eigenvalue shape loss scales inversely with \lambda (|\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \lambda| \propto 1/\lambda). This creates a strong repulsive effect that pushes \lambda{\min} away from zero, preventing collapsed artifacts. Ambiguous Regions: If no match survives the confidence gating, the MAC loss is zero for that region, relying solely on photometric supervision. Coordinate Frame: Covariance matrices must be transformed to world space before comparing eigenvalues to ensure rotation invariance. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of matched pixel pairs K and the cost of bilinear sampling and eigenvalue decomposition. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing dense parameter maps for the predicted Gaussians. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Robust to outliers due to Huber loss and confidence weighting; prevents geometric degeneracy; improves performance under sparse-view conditions and large camera pose gaps. Limitations: Requires reliable 2D correspondences (e.g., from MASt3R); performance depends on the quality of semantic augmentation. When to use: Sparse-view reconstruction where photometric loss alone leads to ambiguities or artifacts. When not to use: Dense-view scenarios where photometric loss is sufficient, or when high-quality correspondences are unavailable. The MAC loss was introduced in "MAC-Splat: Multi-Attribute Consistency for High-Fidelity Sparse-View Reconstruction". It builds on the MASt3R geometric backbone and a frozen DINOv3 encoder to obtain semantically informed 2D correspondences. The method was designed to address the limitations of conventional losses in sparse-view reconstruction, particularly the tendency to produce spurious stretching or flattening of geometry. Experiments on ScanNet++ showed that MAC-Splat outperforms strong baselines, improving average PSNR over Splatt3R by more than 4.5 dB and reducing LPIPS. name: Cross-Modal Alignment Optimization Strategy
head: Cross-Modal Alignment, Semantic Gaussian Optimization
body: A training strategy that aligns rendered semantic fields with distilled 2D vision-language feature maps using a contrastive loss mechanism, while preserving geometric quality through photometric constraints. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by optimizing high-dimensional semantic embeddings alongside geometric parameters, replacing unstable mean squared error with contrastive similarity maximization to handle noise in distilled features. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse point cloud from Structure-from-Motion (SfM); multi-view input images processed by a fine-tuned vision transformer for dense feature distillation; ground-truth images. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives with geometric parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity) and semantic embeddings (feature vectors). Data Structures: Gaussian Primitives: Each primitive stores geometric attributes (position \mathbf{p}, covariance \Sigma derived from scale/rotation, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients for color) and a semantic embedding vector \mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^{512}. Distilled Feature Maps: Dense 2D feature maps \mathbf{F}{gt} of size H \times W \times 512 aligned with input images, generated by a multi-scale feature distillation process using a modified vision transformer. Parameters: Photometric Loss Weight (\lambda{photo}): 0.8. Feature Dimensionality: 512. Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives using a sparse point cloud generated by standard SfM algorithms. Assign initial semantic embeddings, potentially via interpolation from the distilled feature maps at corresponding 2D projections. 2. Rendering: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D using the differentiable rasterizer. Alpha-blend geometric attributes to produce the rendered color image \hat{I} and semantic embeddings \hat{\mathbf{E}}. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} as a weighted sum: \mathcal{L}{total} = \lambda{photo} \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambda{sem} \mathcal{L}{sem} + \lambda{tv} \mathcal{L}{tv} where \lambda{photo} = 0.8. \lambda{sem} and \lambda{tv} are not explicitly given in the sources. Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{photo}): Combination of L1 loss and differentiable SSIM between \hat{I} and ground truth I{gt}: \mathcal{L}{photo} = (1 - \lambda{ssim}) \mathcal{L}{L1}(\hat{I}, I{gt}) + \lambda{ssim} \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM}(\hat{I}, I{gt}) where \lambda{ssim} is the SSIM weight (typically 0.2 in standard 3DGS, but the source specifies the photometric loss weight is 0.8, implying the internal balance of L1/SSIM follows standard practice or is unspecified). Semantic Alignment Loss (\mathcal{L}{sem}): Contrastive loss maximizing cosine similarity between rendered pixel embedding \hat{\mathbf{e}}i and ground truth feature vector \mathbf{f}i at pixel i, while minimizing similarity with negative samples: \mathcal{L}{sem} = - \log \frac{\exp(\text{cosine}(\hat{\mathbf{e}}i, \mathbf{f}i) / \tau)}{\sum{j \in \mathcal{N}} \exp(\text{cosine}(\hat{\mathbf{e}}i, \mathbf{f}j) / \tau)} where \tau is a temperature parameter (not given) and \mathcal{N} includes the positive pair and spatially distant/dissimilar regions. Total Variation Regularization (\mathcal{L}{tv}): Spatial total variation on semantic embeddings of neighboring Gaussians to encourage smoothness: \mathcal{L}{tv} = \sum{k} \|\mathbf{e}k - \text{mean}(\{\mathbf{e}n\}{n \in \text{neighbors}(k)})\|1 4. Backpropagation: Compute gradients \nabla \mathcal{L}{total} with respect to all Gaussian parameters (geometric and semantic) using automatic differentiation. 5. Update: Update parameters using the Adam optimizer. 6. Densification: Periodically clone or split Gaussians in regions with high positional gradients or significant photometric/semantic errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def crossmodalalignmentstep(gaussians, images, featuremaps, optimizer): # 1. Render renderedcolor, renderedsemantics = rasterize(gaussians, images) # 2. Compute Photometric Loss l1loss = l1loss(renderedcolor, images) ssimloss = dssimloss(renderedcolor, images) photometricloss = (1 - 0.2) l1loss + 0.2 ssimloss # Standard lambdassims # 3. Compute Semantic Contrastive Loss # For each pixel, match rendered embedding with distilled feature map # Negative samples are spatially distant or dissimilar regions semanticloss = contrastiveloss(renderedsemantics, featuremaps) # 4. Compute Total Variation Regularization tvloss = totalvariationloss(renderedsemantics, gaussians.neighbors) # 5. Combine Losses # Note: Source specifies Photometric Loss Weight is 0.8 # Assuming remaining weight is distributed or fixed for semantic/tv totalloss = 0.8 photometricloss + semanticloss + tvloss # 6. Update optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # 7. Densification (Periodic) if step % densificationinterval == 0: gaussians.densifyandprune() Time Complexity: Higher than standard 3DGS due to the additional computation of semantic embeddings and contrastive loss, which involves comparing against negative samples. Memory Complexity: Increased memory usage to store 512-dimensional semantic embeddings for each Gaussian primitive. Strengths: Prevents optimization instability caused by noise in distilled feature maps by using contrastive loss instead of MSE; ensures homogeneous semantic representations on continuous surfaces via TV regularization. Limitations: Requires pre-computed dense feature maps from a vision-language model, adding preprocessing overhead. When to use: When semantic understanding or vision-language grounding is required in addition to geometric reconstruction. Originated in "Open-World 3D Vision-Language Scene Representation with Gaussian Splatting and Cross-Modal Alignment" (2026). It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS which lacks semantic granularity, and the instability of using MSE for aligning noisy distilled features. name: Local 3DGS Optimization
head: Local 3DGS Pose Optimization
body: Local 3DGS Optimization is an iterative method for estimating the relative camera pose (transformation) between two nearby images by optimizing a local 3D Gaussian Splatting representation against photometric loss. It solves the problem of camera pose estimation without requiring external Structure-from-Motion (SfM) tools like COLMAP, relying instead on monocular depth estimation and differentiable rendering. It sets itself apart from global optimization methods by freezing the Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH) after initialization and learning only the pose parameters (quaternion and translation) to align the local scene representation with the target view. Inputs: Two nearby images It and I{t+1}. Monocular Depth Estimation Model (DPT). Camera intrinsic parameters (or heuristics if unknown). Outputs: Final relative pose Qt. Data Structures: Local 3DGS (Gt): A set of 3D Gaussians. Attributes include position, spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, opacity, scale, and rotation. These are initialized from It and its depth map Dt. Pose (Tt): A transformation matrix (or quaternion + translation vector) representing the camera pose relative to the local Gaussian frame. Initialized as Identity I. Rendered Image (\hat{I}): Output of the differentiable rasterizer. Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: Compute monocular depth map Dt for image It using the DPT model. 2. Local 3DGS Initialization: Initialize the local 3D Gaussian representation Gt from It and Dt using InitGauss(It, Dt). This involves downsampling the point cloud derived from the depth map before fitting. 3. Local 3DGS Fitting: Optimize Gt to fit It by minimizing photometric loss. Initialize Tt = I. Iterate for 500 steps: Render \hat{I}t by rasterizing Gt. Compute loss L between It and \hat{I}t. Update Gt using Adam optimizer on \nabla L. Note: After this phase, Gt attributes are frozen. 4. Pose Optimization: Estimate the pose Tt that transforms Gt to align with I{t+1}. Initialize Tt = I. Iterate for 300 steps: Transform Gaussians: G't = Tt \odot Gt. Render \hat{I}{t+1} by rasterizing G't. Compute loss L between target image I{t+1} and rendered image \hat{I}{t+1}. Update pose parameters (quaternion and translation) using Adam optimizer on \nabla L. Constraint: Gaussian attributes (position, SH, opacity, scale, rotation) remain fixed during this phase. 5. Pose Accumulation: The final relative pose Qt is the product of transformations Ti from the start of the sequence up to the current step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def local3dgsoptimization(It, Itplus1, DPTmodel, cameraintrinsics): # Step 1: Depth Estimation Dt = DPTmodel(It) # Step 2: Local 3DGS Initialization # InitGauss downsamples the point cloud from Dt and fits 3DGS Gt = InitGauss(It, Dt, cameraintrinsics) # Step 3: Local 3DGS Fitting (500 iterations) # Optimize Gaussian attributes to fit It for step in range(500): Ihat = Rasterize(Gt, cameraintrinsics) L = Loss(It, Ihat) Gt = AdamUpdate(Gt, L) # Freeze Gaussian attributes Gt.requiresgrad = False # Step 4: Pose Optimization (300 steps) # Initialize pose as Identity Tt = Identity() for step in range(300): # Transform Gaussians by current pose estimate Gtransformed = Transform(Gt, Tt) # Render transformed Gaussians Ihatplus1 = Rasterize(Gtransformed, cameraintrinsics) # Compute loss against target image L = Loss(Itplus1, Ihatplus1) # Update only pose parameters (quaternion and translation) Tt = AdamUpdatePose(Tt, L) return Tt Parameters: Local 3DGS Fitting Iterations: 500. Pose Optimization Steps: 300. Monocular Depth Model: DPT (Vision Transformers for Dense Prediction). Camera Intrinsic Heuristic: If intrinsics are unknown, Field of View (FoV) is set to 79^\circ and principal points are set to the image center. Loss Function: Photometric loss (implied L1/SSIM based on parent context, but specifically "photometric loss" is cited for this method). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unknown Intrinsics: Using heuristic intrinsics (FoV 79^\circ, center principal point) leads to slight degradation in Novel View Synthesis (NVS) and camera pose estimation quality compared to known intrinsics. Dramatic Motion: The method is designed to handle dramatic camera motions (large maximum rotation angles between frames), as tested on sequences with up to 180^\circ rotation. Point Cloud Size: High-resolution input images can lead to huge point clouds; downsampling is required before fitting to manage memory and computation. Time Complexity: The method involves two distinct optimization phases: 500 iterations for local 3DGS fitting and 300 steps for pose optimization. The total computational cost is proportional to the number of Gaussians and the resolution of the images, with the pose optimization being relatively lightweight as it only updates pose parameters. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians in Gt, which is determined by the downsampled point cloud from the monocular depth map. Strengths: Does not require COLMAP or external SfM pipelines; handles dramatic camera motions; provides photo-realistic novel view synthesis. Limitations: Performance degrades slightly if camera intrinsics are unknown and heuristics are used; relies on the accuracy of the monocular depth estimation model (DPT). When to use: When COLMAP is unavailable or unreliable, and relative pose estimation between nearby frames is needed for 3DGS reconstruction. When not to use: When high-precision camera intrinsics are available and can be optimized jointly, or when the scene has very small baseline changes where traditional SfM might be more robust. Local 3DGS Optimization was introduced in the "COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting" paper by Zhou et al. (CVPR 2024). It addresses the dependency on traditional SfM pipelines (like COLMAP) for initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method leverages monocular depth estimation (DPT) and differentiable rendering to estimate camera poses and initialize 3DGS representations directly from image pairs. It is part of the broader effort to make 3DGS training and initialization more accessible and robust to varying input conditions. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Loop
head: 3DGS Optimization, Render-Compare-Correct Loop
body: The 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training loop is a stochastic gradient descent procedure that minimizes a photometric loss between rendered images and ground-truth photographs to optimize the parameters of a 3D Gaussian point cloud. It distinguishes itself from random search or Monte Carlo methods by computing explicit gradients via a differentiable rasterizer, allowing millions of parameters to be corrected simultaneously and purposefully. The method operates on a fixed iteration budget (typically 30,000 steps) rather than a convergence threshold, periodically densifying and pruning Gaussians to adapt scene density. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses (from Structure-from-Motion), and an initial set of 3D Gaussians (initialized from SfM points or a template model like SMPL). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and potentially updated topology (split/pruned Gaussians). Data Structures: Gaussian Set: A list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i stores: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigmai (or rotation \mathbf{q}i and scale \mathbf{s}i) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for color representation Optimizer State: Adam optimizer state (first and second moment estimates) for each parameter group. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampling: Randomly select one training image and its corresponding camera pose from the dataset. 2. Transformation: Transform canonical Gaussian parameters to the observation space defined by the selected camera pose. If using a parametric avatar (e.g., Human Gaussian Splatting), apply skinning weights from a template (like SMPL) to deform the Gaussians. 3. Rendering: Project the transformed Gaussians to 2D and alpha-blend them using the differentiable Gaussian rasterizer to produce a rendered image \hat{I}. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the per-image error \mathcal{L}{img} by comparing \hat{I} to the ground-truth image I{gt}. The loss is a weighted sum: \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the L1 loss (mean absolute difference) and \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} is the differentiable Structural Similarity index loss. The weight \lambda is typically 0.2. 5. Backpropagation: Compute gradients \nabla \mathcal{L}{img} with respect to all Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients) using automatic differentiation through the rasterizer. 6. Update: Update the Gaussian parameters using the Adam optimizer with \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.99. 7. Densification/Pruning: Periodically (e.g., every k iterations), evaluate gradient magnitudes and opacity thresholds to split high-gradient Gaussians or prune low-opacity ones, adapting the density of the representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def train3dgs(gaussians, trainingviews, numiterations=30000, lambdass=0.2): optimizer = Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=1e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.99)) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sampling view = random.choice(trainingviews) camerapose = view.pose gtimage = view.image # 2. Transformation (if parametric) # For standard 3DGS, this step is implicit in the rasterizer's view transform # For avatar 3DGS, apply skinning: # gaussians.transformtoobservationspace(camerapose, skinningweights) # 3. Rendering renderedimage = gaussianrasterizer(gaussians, camerapose) # 4. Loss Computation l1loss = l1lossfunction(renderedimage, gtimage) ssimloss = dssimloss(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = (1 - lambdass) l1loss + lambdass ssimloss # 5. Backpropagation optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() # 6. Update optimizer.step() # 7. Densification/Pruning (periodic) if iteration % densificationinterval == 0: gaussians.densifyandprune(iteration) return gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The differentiable rasterizer must handle depth sorting and alpha blending correctly to ensure valid gradients. Boundaries: Background pixels should be handled explicitly (e.g., setting background to black in ground truth) to avoid misleading gradients. Degenerate Input: If the initial SfM point cloud is sparse, the initial render may be poor, requiring careful initialization or densification strategies. Time Complexity: Each iteration involves a forward pass through the rasterizer (O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians) and a backward pass. The total time is proportional to the number of iterations (typically 30,000). Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians and their parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). Densification increases memory usage over time. Measured Performance: Training is performed on GPUs using PyTorch. Evaluation metrics include PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on held-out views. Strengths: Efficient gradient-based optimization allows for high-quality reconstruction from sparse inputs. The fixed iteration budget provides predictable training time. Limitations: The method is sensitive to the initial SfM reconstruction quality. Densification heuristics can lead to over-parameterization if not tuned correctly. When to use: Suitable for static or dynamic scene reconstruction where high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required. When not to use: Not suitable for real-time training on resource-constrained devices due to the iterative nature and memory requirements. The 3D Gaussian Splatting training loop was introduced in the original 3DGS paper and popularized by subsequent tutorials and implementations. It builds on the differentiable rendering framework established by earlier work. The method has been extended to dynamic scenes, such as Human Gaussian Splatting, which integrates SMPL models for animatable avatars.
