name: Mip-Splatting Training Loop & Evaluation Pipeline
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Schedule, Mip-3DGS Training Loop
body: This method defines the complete training iteration and evaluation procedure for Mip-Splatting, a variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses aliasing by rendering at multiple resolutions. It handles camera sampling, subpixel-aware rendering, hybrid loss computation, adaptive densification/pruning, and quantitative metric reporting. It distinguishes itself from the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Loop by introducing subpixel jittering for both the rendered image and the ground truth, and by dynamically adjusting the spherical harmonics (SH) degree during training to prevent high-frequency artifacts. Inputs: gaussians: The set of 3D Gaussians with parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). viewpointstack: A list of available training cameras. trainCameras: The full list of training cameras, indexed by resolution level. gtimage: The ground truth image for the sampled view. opt: Optimization hyperparameters (learning rates, densification thresholds, intervals). dataset: Dataset configuration flags (rayjitter, resamplegtimage, samplemorehighres, kernelsize). Outputs: Updated gaussians parameters. Quantitative metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) during evaluation phases. Data Structures: gaussians.maxradii2D: A tensor tracking the maximum image-space radius for each Gaussian, used for pruning. gaussians.viewspacepointtensor: Stores the 2D screen-space positions of Gaussians for gradient-based densification. Parameters: opt.iterations: Total training iterations (Default: 30,000). opt.densifyfromiter: Iteration after which densification begins (Default: 500). opt.densifyuntiliter: Iteration after which densification stops (Default: 15,000). opt.densificationinterval: Frequency of densification steps (Default: 100). opt.opacityresetinterval: Frequency of opacity resets (Default: 3,000). opt.densifygradthreshold: Gradient threshold for splitting (Default: 0.0002). opt.lambdadssim: Weight for the D-SSIM loss term (Default: 0.2). dataset.kernelsize: Kernel size for rendering (Default: 0.1). dataset.rayjitter: Boolean flag to enable subpixel offset generation. dataset.resamplegtimage: Boolean flag to resample ground truth images. dataset.samplemorehighres: Boolean flag to increase high-resolution sampling probability. Steps: 1. Learning Rate Update: Update the learning rates for all Gaussian parameters using gaussians.updatelearningrate(iteration). 2. SH Degree Increase: Every 1,000 iterations, increment the active spherical harmonics degree using gaussians.oneupSHdegree(). 3. Camera Sampling: Pop a random camera from viewpointstack. If dataset.samplemorehighres is true and a random float is less than 0.3, override the selection with a high-resolution camera from trainCameras[highresolutionindex]. 4. Subpixel Offset Generation: If dataset.rayjitter is enabled, generate a subpixel offset tensor of shape (H, W, 2) with values uniformly distributed in [-0.5, 0.5] on CUDA. Otherwise, set subpixeloffset = None. 5. Rendering: Render the scene by calling render(viewpointcam, gaussians, pipe, background, kernelsize=dataset.kernelsize, subpixeloffset=subpixeloffset). Extract the rendered image, viewspacepointtensor, visibilityfilter, and radii from the returned dictionary. 6. Ground Truth Resampling: If dataset.resamplegtimage is true, resample the ground truth image using the subpixeloffset via createoffsetgt(gtimage, subpixeloffset). 7. Statistics Tracking: Update max image-space radii for pruning: gaussians.maxradii2D[visibilityfilter] = torch.max(gaussians.maxradii2D[visibilityfilter], radii[visibilityfilter]). Add densification statistics: gaussians.adddensificationstats(viewspacepointtensor, visibilityfilter). 8. Densification and Pruning: If iteration > opt.densifyfromiter and iteration % opt.densificationinterval == 0: Determine sizethreshold: Set to 20 if iteration > opt.opacityresetinterval, else None. Call gaussians.densifyandprune(opt.densifygradthreshold, 0.005, scene.camerasextent, sizethreshold). Call gaussians.compute3Dfilter(cameras=trainCameras). 9. Opacity Reset: If iteration % opt.opacityresetinterval == 0 or if dataset.whitebackground is true and iteration == opt.densifyfromiter, reset the opacities of the Gaussians. 10. 3D Filter Update (Post-Densification): If iteration > opt.densifyuntiliter, if iteration % 100 == 0, and if iteration < opt.iterations - 100, update the 3D filter via gaussians.compute3Dfilter(cameras=trainCameras). 11. Optimizer Step: Perform the optimizer step using gaussians.optimizer.step() followed by gaussians.optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True). Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is computed as: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda{\text{dssim}}) \mathcal{L}{\text{L1}} + \lambda{\text{dssim}} (1 - \text{SSIM}(I{\text{render}}, I{\text{gt}})) where \mathcal{L}{\text{L1}} is the L1 loss between the rendered image I{\text{render}} and the (potentially resampled) ground truth image I{\text{gt}}, and \lambda{\text{dssim}} is the D-SSIM weight. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mipsplattingtrainingloop(iteration, gaussians, viewpointstack, trainCameras, gtimage, opt, dataset, scene): # 1. Update Learning Rates gaussians.updatelearningrate(iteration) # 2. Increase SH Degree every 1000 iterations if iteration % 1000 == 0: gaussians.oneupSHdegree() # 3. Sample Camera viewpointcam = viewpointstack.pop() if dataset.samplemorehighres and random.random() < 0.3: viewpointcam = trainCameras[highresolutionindex] # 4. Generate Subpixel Offset if dataset.rayjitter: subpixeloffset = torch.rand((viewpointcam.imageheight, viewpointcam.imagewidth, 2), device='cuda') - 0.5 else: subpixeloffset = None # 5. Render Scene renderdict = render( viewpointcam, gaussians, pipe, background, kernelsize=dataset.kernelsize, subpixeloffset=subpixeloffset) image = renderdict["render"] viewspacepointtensor = renderdict["viewspacepoints"] visibilityfilter = renderdict["visibilityfilter"] radii = renderdict["radii"] # 6. Resample Ground Truth if enabled if dataset.resamplegtimage: gtimageresampled = createoffsetgt(gtimage, subpixeloffset) else: gtimageresampled = gtimage # 7. Track Statistics gaussians.maxradii2D[visibilityfilter] = torch.max( gaussians.maxradii2D[visibilityfilter], radii[visibilityfilter]) gaussians.adddensificationstats(viewspacepointtensor, visibilityfilter) # 8. Densification and Pruning if iteration > opt.densifyfromiter and iteration % opt.densificationinterval == 0: sizethreshold = 20 if iteration > opt.opacityresetinterval else None gaussians.densifyandprune( opt.densifygradthreshold, 0.005, scene.camerasextent, sizethreshold) gaussians.compute3Dfilter(cameras=trainCameras) # 9. Opacity Reset if iteration % opt.opacityresetinterval == 0: gaussians.resetopacities() elif dataset.whitebackground and iteration == opt.densifyfromiter: gaussians.resetopacities() # 10. Post-Densification 3D Filter Update if iteration > opt.densifyuntiliter: if iteration % 100 == 0 and iteration < opt.iterations - 100: gaussians.compute3Dfilter(cameras=trainCameras) # 11. Optimizer Step gaussians.optimizer.step() gaussians.optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) return image, gtimageresampled Evaluation Pipeline: During evaluation phases (triggered by --testiterations): 1. Load rendered images from testpreds{scale} and ground truth images from gt{scale} directories. 2. Compute per-image SSIM, PSNR, and LPIPS (using a VGG network). 3. Average metrics across all images in the view set. 4. Log metrics to TensorBoard and save to results.json and perview.json. Time Complexity: The training loop adds overhead for subpixel offset generation and ground truth resampling, but the core rasterization complexity remains similar to standard 3DGS. The periodic compute3Dfilter calls add computational cost, particularly after densification stops. Memory Complexity: Requires storing maxradii2D and viewspacepointtensor for each Gaussian. The subpixel offset tensor requires O(H \times W \times 2) memory per iteration. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts through subpixel jittering and multi-resolution rendering. The adaptive SH degree increase prevents high-frequency noise in early training stages. Limitations: The subpixel jittering and resampling require careful implementation to maintain differentiability. The periodic 3D filter updates can slow down the latter stages of training if not optimized. When to use: When rendering scenes with high-frequency details or when aliasing artifacts are prominent in standard 3DGS. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of subpixel operations is prohibitive. Mip-Splatting was introduced by the autonomousvision group as an extension to 3D Gaussian Splatting to address aliasing issues. It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by incorporating techniques from mip-mapping and subpixel rendering. The method is implemented in the mip-splatting repository. autonomousvision/mip-splatting, https://github.com/autonomousvision/mip-splatting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Distributed 3DGS Training Loop with Adaptive Workload Division
head: Batched Distributed 3DGS Training, Grendel-GS Training Pipeline
body: This method implements a distributed training workflow for 3D Gaussian Splatting that batches camera selection, divides rendering workloads across multiple GPUs using an adaptive strategy history, synchronizes losses, and schedules densification and spherical harmonics (SH) degree updates. It differs from standard gradient accumulation by optionally scaling gradients by batch size to avoid explicit accumulation buffers and by dynamically balancing the computational load of rendering different camera views across the GPU cluster. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training dataset, initial 3D Gaussian scene parameters, distributed environment configuration (number of GPUs, backend), and hyperparameters (args.bsz, args.lambdadssim, args.lrscalemode, args.localsampling, args.saveiterations, args.checkpointiterations, testingiterations). Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters, strategy history log, and periodic checkpoints. Data Structures: batchedscreenspacepkg: Dictionary containing at least "batchedcudaargs", a list of CUDA argument structures. Each structure contains a "statscollector" field. batchedlosses: Tensor of shape (N, 2) where N is the batch size. Index 0 holds the first loss component (L1), index 1 holds the second loss component (used in DSSIM calculation). strategyhistory: List of previous workload division strategies and their associated statistics, used to adapt future divisions. gpuid2tasks: Mapping of GPU IDs to the specific camera tasks assigned to each GPU for the current batch. Parameters: args.bsz: Batch size per iteration step. Controls the loop range and serves as the divisor for gradient scaling. args.lambdadssim: Weight for the DSSIM loss component. Default value not specified in the sources. args.lrscalemode: String controlling gradient scaling. If not equal to "accumu", gradients are explicitly divided by args.bsz before the optimizer step. args.localsampling: Boolean flag. If true, enables distributed camera index gathering across GPUs using torch.distributed.allgatherintotensor. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the training loop from startfromthisiteration to optargs.iterations with a step size of args.bsz. Set up progress bar updates every args.bsz iterations. 2. Logging Setup: Log the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) loss to the progress bar every 30 batches (checked via iteration // args.bsz % 30 == 0). 3. State Update: Update the learning rate and increment the trained batch counter. Clear timing variables. Start NVTX profiling range if enabled. 4. SH Degree Update: Upscale the spherical harmonics degree by one level every 1000 iterations. This is determined by utils.checkupdateatthisiter(iteration, args.bsz, 1000, 0). 5. Camera Selection: If args.localsampling is true: Assert that args.bsz is divisible by utils.WORLDSIZE. Gather local camera indices across all GPUs using torch.distributed.allgatherintotensor, convert to numpy, and fetch the corresponding camera objects. Otherwise: Fetch camera objects directly via traindataset.getbatchedcameras(args.bsz). 6. Workload Division Strategy: Initialize the workload division strategy by calling startstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory). This returns batchedstrategies and gpuid2tasks. 7. Data Loading: Load camera data from CPU to all GPUs using loadcamerafromcputoallgpu(batchedcameras, batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks). 8. Preprocessing: Preprocess the 3D Gaussian Splatting data and perform all-to-all communication. If args.backend == "gsplat", call gsplatdistributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal. Otherwise, call distributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal. 9. Rendering: Render images and extract compute locations by calling gsplatrenderfinal or renderfinal with batchedscreenspacepkg and batchedstrategies. Extract batchstatisticcollector from batchedscreenspacepkg["batchedcudaargs"]. 10. Loss Computation: Compute the loss by calling batchedlosscomputation with the rendered images, cameras, compute locations, strategies, and statistic collectors. 11. Backpropagation: Execute the backward pass using losssum.backward(). 12. Strategy Update: Update the workload division strategy by calling finishstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory, batchedstrategies, batchstatisticcollector). 13. Loss Synchronization: Synchronize losses across all GPUs using dist.allreduce(batchedlosses, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, group=utils.DEFAULTGROUP). 14. EMA Logging: Update the EMA loss for logging. If emalossforlog is None, set it to the mean of batchedlosscpu. Otherwise, update using: EMA = 0.6 \cdot EMA + 0.4 \cdot \text{mean}(batched\loss\cpu). 15. Evaluation: Trigger evaluation if the current iteration matches testingiterations. Log validation configurations for both test and train sets. 16. Densification: Perform densification by calling gsplatdensification or densification with the current iteration, scene, gaussians, and screenspace package. 17. Saving: Save Gaussians if the current iteration falls within args.saveiterations. Write the strategy history to a JSON file if args.savestrategyhistory is true. Save checkpoints if the current iteration falls within args.checkpointiterations. Create the directory (Rank 0), synchronize ranks via torch.distributed.barrier, and save gaussians.capture() and the iteration number to a.pth file. Formulas: The combined batch loss is calculated as: L{batch} = (1 - \lambda{dssim}) \cdot L{0} + \lambda{dssim} \cdot (1 - L{1}) where L{0} is the first loss component (typically L1), L{1} is the second loss component (typically SSIM-related), and \lambda{dssim} is args.lambdadssim. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.distributed as dist import numpy as np def distributed3dgstrainingloop( traindataset, gaussians, optargs, args, utils, startfromthisiteration=0): """ Distributed training loop for 3D Gaussian Splatting with adaptive workload division. """ iteration = startfromthisiteration emalossforlog = None strategyhistory = [] # Assume these are defined in the surrounding context or passed in # backend = args.backend # WORLDSIZE = utils.WORLDSIZE # DEFAULTGROUP = utils.DEFAULTGROUP while iteration < optargs.iterations: # Step 2: Log EMA loss every 30 batches if iteration // args.bsz % 30 == 0: if emalossforlog is not None: print(f"[ITER {iteration}] EMA Loss: {emalossforlog}") # Step 3: Update LR, clear timers, start profiling utils.updatelearningrate(iteration) utils.cleartimers() if args.profile: torch.cuda.nvtx.rangepush(f"iter{iteration}") # Step 4: SH Degree Update if utils.checkupdateatthisiter(iteration, args.bsz, 1000, 0): utils.upscaleshdegree(gaussians) # Step 5: Camera Selection if args.localsampling: assert args.bsz % WORLDSIZE == 0 # Gather local indices localindices = traindataset.getlocalindices(args.bsz // WORLDSIZE) gatheredindices = [torch.zeroslike(localindices) for in range(WORLDSIZE)] dist.allgather(gatheredindices, localindices) allindices = torch.cat(gatheredindices).numpy() batchedcameras = [traindataset.getcamera(idx) for idx in allindices] else: batchedcameras = traindataset.getbatchedcameras(args.bsz) # Step 6: Workload Division Strategy batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks = startstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory) # Step 7: Load Camera Data loadcamerafromcputoallgpu(batchedcameras, batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks) # Step 8: Preprocessing and All-to-All if args.backend == "gsplat": batchedscreenspacepkg = gsplatdistributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal(gaussians, batchedstrategies) else: batchedscreenspacepkg = distributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal(gaussians, batchedstrategies) # Step 9: Rendering if args.backend == "gsplat": gsplatrenderfinal(batchedscreenspacepkg, batchedstrategies) else: renderfinal(batchedscreenspacepkg, batchedstrategies) batchstatisticcollector = batchedscreenspacepkg["batchedcudaargs"][0]["statscollector"] # Step 10: Loss Computation batchedlosses = batchedlosscomputation( renderedimages=batchedscreenspacepkg["renderedimages"], cameras=batchedcameras, computelocations=batchedscreenspacepkg["computelocations"], strategies=batchedstrategies, statisticcollectors=batchedscreenspacepkg["batchedcudaargs"]) # Step 11: Backpropagation # Combine losses according to formula # Lbatch = (1 - lambdadssim) L0 + lambdadssim (1 - L1) # Note: batchedlosses shape is (N, 2). Index 0 is L0, Index 1 is L1. lambdadssim = args.lambdadssim L0 = batchedlosses[:, 0] L1 = batchedlosses[:, 1] losssum = torch.mean((1 - lambdadssim) L0 + lambdadssim (1 - L1)) losssum.backward() # Step 12: Update Strategy finishstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory, batchedstrategies, batchstatisticcollector) # Step 13: Synchronize Losses batchedlossessum = batchedlosses.clone() dist.allreduce(batchedlossessum, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, group=DEFAULTGROUP) # Step 14: EMA Logging batchedlosscpu = batchedlossessum.cpu().mean(dim=0) # Mean across batch and components? # Source says "mean(batchedlosscpu)". Assuming mean over the batch dimension of the tensor. # The tensor is (N, 2). Mean over dim 0 gives (2,). Then mean of that? # Let's follow the text: "mean(batchedlosscpu)". If batchedlosscpu is the result of allreduce, it's still (N, 2) on each rank? # No, allreduce sums. So it's (N, 2) summed across ranks? # Actually, allreduce with SUM sums the tensor across all ranks. # If each rank has (N, 2), the result is (N, 2) where each element is sum over ranks. # Then mean(batchedlosscpu) likely means mean over the batch dimension N. meanloss = batchedlosscpu.mean() if emalossforlog is None: emalossforlog = meanloss else: emalossforlog = 0.6 emalossforlog + 0.4 meanloss # Step 15: Evaluation if iteration in args.testingiterations: utils.evaluate(gaussians, traindataset, iteration) # Step 16: Densification if utils.shoulddensify(iteration): if args.backend == "gsplat": gsplatdensification(iteration, gaussians, batchedscreenspacepkg) else: densification(iteration, gaussians, batchedscreenspacepkg) # Step 17: Saving if iteration in args.saveiterations: utils.savegaussians(gaussians, iteration) if args.savestrategyhistory: with open(f"strategyhistory{iteration}.json", "w") as f: json.dump(strategyhistory, f) if iteration in args.checkpointiterations: if utils.getrank() == 0: os.makedirs(f"checkpoints/iter{iteration}", existok=True) dist.barrier(group=DEFAULTGROUP) if utils.getrank() == 0: torch.save({ 'gaussians': gaussians.capture(), 'iteration': iteration }, f"checkpoints/iter{iteration}/checkpoint.pth") # Gradient Scaling if args.lrscalemode != "accumu": for param in gaussians.parameters(): if param.grad is not None: param.grad /= args.bsz # Optimizer Step utils.optimizerstep(gaussians) iteration += args.bsz if args.profile: torch.cuda.nvtx.rangepop() Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the rendering and all-to-all communication steps. The adaptive workload division aims to balance the rendering time across GPUs, reducing idle time compared to static partitioning. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians and the batch size. The distributed approach allows larger effective batch sizes by distributing the memory load across multiple GPUs. Measured Performance: The source provides performance metrics (throughput, PSNR, running time) for various scenes (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360 scenes) and configurations (1 GPU vs 4 GPUs, batch size 1 vs 4). Specific numbers are not extracted in the notes, but the method is designed to improve throughput on multi-GPU setups. Strengths: Adaptive workload division handles heterogeneous rendering costs for different camera views. Distributed processing enables training on larger scenes or with larger batch sizes. Limitations: Requires careful synchronization and communication overhead management. The args.localsampling constraint requires batch size to be divisible by the number of GPUs. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting on large datasets or scenes that require multiple GPUs for feasible training times, and when camera views have varying computational costs. This method originates from the Grendel-GS project, an unofficial implementation or extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting training techniques. It addresses the scalability issues of standard 3DGS training by introducing distributed rendering and adaptive workload balancing. nyu-systems/Grendel-GS, https://github.com/nyu-systems/Grendel-GS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction
head: Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction Pipeline, Incremental 3D Gaussian Splatting Reconstruction, Incremental 3DGS with Loop Closure, Main Pipeline for Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction, Real-time 3DGS Reconstruction, Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting Pipeline, Two-Level Matching 3DGS
body: Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction is a streaming pipeline that processes an unordered sequence of RGB images to produce a real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. It solves the problem of incremental reconstruction from unordered inputs by maintaining global consistency through loop closure and a covisibility graph, while optimizing Gaussian primitives in real-time. Unlike batch methods, it interleaves feature matching, pose estimation, and Gaussian optimization to keep the delay between capture and processing start below 0.8 seconds. It distinguishes itself from other training optimizations by focusing on the pipeline structure for incremental input rather than just the loss function or densification schedule. The method operates as a streaming loop. It takes an unordered stream of images and outputs a 3DGS model consisting of optimized Gaussian primitives and camera poses. Registered Keyframes (M): A set of keyframes that have been successfully registered to the global map. Covisibility Graph (G{graph}): Structured as a triple (M, E, W), representing the set of registered keyframes, edges E between them, and edge weights W. Note: The source pseudocode uses G for both the graph and primitives; this implementation distinguishes them as G{graph} and G{prims}. Active Gaussian Primitives (G{prims}): The set of 3D Gaussians currently in the scene. Gaussian Hierarchy (H): A structure managing the hierarchy of Gaussians, updated based on the graph and image. Shelf (Shelf): A buffer for unmatched frames that cannot be processed immediately. N=20: The fixed number of keyframes selected for local bundle adjustment. \tau{lc} = 5: The threshold for the minimum graph distance (hops) between clusters to trigger loop closure. \tauv: The threshold for the minimum number of valid matching pairs required to trigger loop closure. Welding Window (W): Defined as the union of the top N/2 keyframes from cluster C1 and the top N/2 keyframes from cluster C2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mainpipeline(imagestream): # 1. Initialize data structures M = set() # Registered keyframes Ggraph = (set(), set(), dict()) # Covisibility graph: (nodes, edges, weights) Gprims = set() # Active Gaussian primitives H = set() # Gaussian hierarchy Shelf = [] # Shelved unmatched frames # 2. Bootstrap: Process first 8 well-connected keyframes # This step initializes the map with a stable base. bootstrapkeyframes = getfirst8wellconnectedimages(imagestream) for img in bootstrapkeyframes: processimage(img, M, Ggraph, Gprims, H, Shelf) # 3. Stream processing loop for Iq in imagestream: processimage(Iq, M, Ggraph, Gprims, H, Shelf) # 4. Post-processing: Retry shelved frames processshelvedframes(Shelf, M, Ggraph) def processimage(Iq, M, Ggraph, Gprims, H, Shelf): # Two-Level Matching V, Kprime = TwoLevelMatching(Iq, M) # If no matches, shelve if not V: Shelf.append(Iq) return # Update Covisibility Graph UpdateGraph(Ggraph, Iq, V) # Loop Detection loop, C1, C2 = LoopDetection(Iq, Kprime, Ggraph) # Select Keyframes for Local BA S = SelectKeyframes({Iq}, Ggraph, N=20) # Local Bundle Adjustment LocalBA(S, Gprims) # Handle Loop Closure if loop: WeldingBA(C1, C2, Ggraph) BackbonePropagation(Ggraph, C1, C2, Gprims) # Place New Gaussians PlaceGaussians(Iq, Ggraph, Gprims) # Update State M.add(Iq) UpdateHierarchy(Ggraph, H, Iq) OptimizeGaussians(M, Ggraph, Gprims) # Retry Shelved Frames RetryShelved(Shelf, M, Ggraph) def TwoLevelMatching(Iq, M): # Extract features for 4 rotations (0, 90, 180, 270 degrees) # Use MixVPR to detect orientation # Use XFeat for keypoints/features based on detected orientation # Return matches V and candidate keyframe indices K' pass def LoopDetection(Iq, Kprime, Ggraph): # Identify disjoint clusters C1, C2 in the visual neighborhood # Check if dG(C1, C2) > 5 and min(|C1|, |C2|) > tauv # Return loop flag and clusters pass def SelectKeyframes(query, Ggraph, N=20): # Select N=20 keyframes from the neighborhood for optimization pass def LocalBA(S, Gprims): # Fast Bundle Adjustment # Allow each landmark to be observed by a fixed subset of keyframes # selected based on covisibility, rather than all keyframes in S pass def WeldingBA(C1, C2, Ggraph): # Select anchor keyframes Ia1, Ia2 from C1, C2 based on connectivity # Compute rigid transform Tdelta between optimized and initial poses # Estimate scale change sdelta from landmark depth variations # Compute similarity transform Sdelta = Sim3(Tdelta, sdelta) pass def BackbonePropagation(Ggraph, C1, C2, Gprims): # Build backbone path B using Dijkstra on Ggraph between Ia1 and Ia2 # Calculate interpolation weight alpha(Ib) for each node Ib in B # Interpolate rotation (6D) and scale (linear) to get Sdelta,b # Propagate corrections to keyframes not in welding window # Tinew = Sdelta,b o Tiold pass def PlaceGaussians(Iq, Ggraph, Gprims): # Instantiate new Gaussian primitives for Iq based on graph G pass def UpdateHierarchy(Ggraph, H, Iq): # Update Gaussian hierarchy H with new image Iq pass def OptimizeGaussians(M, Ggraph, Gprims): # Optimize Gaussians in registered set M using graph G # Uses standard 3DGS optimization steps (densification/pruning) pass def RetryShelved(Shelf, M, Ggraph): # Continuously compute best MixVPR match between shelved frames and M # If best match cosine similarity > last registered image's similarity, # attempt to add shelved frame to M pass 1. Rotation Invariant Matching Standard CNN descriptors are not rotation invariant. To handle strong rotations, the pipeline extracts MixVPR and XFeat features for four rotations of the image (0^\circ, 90^\circ, 180^\circ, 270^\circ). For XFeat, keypoints are extracted only from the upright image, but features are sampled in all four rotated images. MixVPR is used first to detect the orientation, allowing the system to select the corresponding XFeat features for matching efficiently. 2. Fast Bundle Adjustment To scale to N=20 keyframes, the method uses a custom Fast BA. Previous fast BA solutions scale quadratically because every landmark is observed by all keyframes. This method scales linearly by allowing each landmark to be observed by a fixed subset of keyframes in the local window, selected based on covisibility. This reduces the number of observations significantly. 3. Loop Closure and Drift Correction Accumulated drift causes Gaussians to be optimized incorrectly, leading to spiky artifacts and superimposition. Loop closure is detected when disjoint clusters C1 and C2 are found in the visual neighborhood. A loop closure occurs if the graph distance dG(C1, C2) > \tau{lc}=5 and the size of the smaller cluster > \tauv. Anchor Selection: The most connected keyframes I{a1} and I{a2} are selected from C1 and C2 based on their connection count c(I, W) to the welding window W. Transformation: A rigid transform T\Delta is computed between the optimized and initial poses of the anchor. A scale change s\Delta is estimated from landmark depth variations. The similarity transform is S\Delta = \text{Sim3}(T\Delta, s\Delta). Propagation: A backbone path B is built between I{a1} and I{a2} using Dijkstra's algorithm on the covisibility graph (loop edges are not yet added). The transformation is interpolated along the backbone: \alpha(Ib) = \frac{dG(Ib, I{a2})}{dG(I{a1}, I{a2})} S{\Delta, b} = \text{interpSim3}(I, S\Delta, \alpha(Ib)) Rotations are interpolated using 6D representation, and scale is interpolated linearly: s{\Delta, b} = s\Delta^{\alpha(Ib)}. Application: For keyframes Ii not in the welding window, the closest backbone node Ib^ is found, and the pose is updated: Ti^{\text{new}} = S{\Delta, b^} \circ Ti^{\text{old}}. 4. Shelving Frames that cannot be matched or fail pose initialization are added to the Shelf. The system continuously computes the best MixVPR match between shelved frames and the registered set M. If the best match cosine similarity is above the last registered image's similarity, the shelved frame is processed. After capture ends, remaining shelved frames are processed starting from the best VPR match. Variable Name Collision: The source pseudocode assigns both the covisibility graph and active Gaussian primitives to the variable G. Implementers must distinguish them (e.g., G{graph} vs G{prims}) to avoid overwriting. Memory Constraints: While efficient, the method can still face VRAM limitations on very large scenes or high-resolution inputs if not managed carefully (e.g., AnySplat runs out of memory on H100 for StaticHikes due to image size constraints). Drift Artifacts: Without loop closure, accumulated drift introduces spiky artifacts and superimposition in the Gaussian model. Time Complexity: The local bundle adjustment scales linearly with the number of keyframes in the window due to the covisibility-based landmark observation subset. The overall pipeline keeps the delay between capture and processing start below 0.8 seconds (time to handle two keyframes). Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of active Gaussians and the size of the covisibility graph. It is more memory-efficient than feed-forward methods like AnySplat which require large vision model backbones and are limited to 448x448 images. Performance: MipNeRF360: PSNR 26.29, SSIM 0.839, LPIPS 0.241 in 0:01:17. TUM: PSNR 24.51, SSIM 0.861, LPIPS 0.174 in 0:01:36. StaticHikes: PSNR 23.78, SSIM 0.760, LPIPS 0.242 in 0:01:49. Strengths: Real-time incremental reconstruction, robust to rotation, handles loop closures to prevent drift, scalable to larger local windows (N=20) compared to previous fast BA methods. Limitations: Requires unordered input to be processed sequentially; performance depends on the quality of feature matching; may require post-capture fine-tuning for optimal quality (e.g., +10-30 epochs improves metrics). The method is described in "Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction of Unordered Input with Global Consistency" by Andreas Meuleman, Linus Franke, Boris Zhestiankin, Camille Montemagni, and George Drettakis, published in SIGGRAPH Conference Papers 2026. It addresses the limitations of previous fast BA solutions which did not scale well beyond N=5 keyframes. Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction of Unordered Input with Global Consistency, https://doi.org/10.1145/3799902.3811167, fetched 2026-10-26

name: BAD-Gaussians
head: Bundle Adjusted Deblur Gaussian Splatting
body: BAD-Gaussians recovers a sharp 3D scene representation by jointly learning camera motion trajectories and 3D Gaussian parameters from a sequence of motion-blurred images, inaccurate poses, and sparse point clouds. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality geometry and appearance from blurry inputs where standard 3D Gaussian Splatting fails due to unmodeled motion blur. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DeSplat and 360 Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling the physical motion blur formation process via virtual camera poses and optimizing the camera trajectory (start and end poses) alongside the Gaussians, rather than assuming static sharp inputs or using different blur kernels. Inputs: A sequence of N motion-blurred images \{Bk\}{k=0}^{N-1}, their corresponding inaccurate initial poses and sparse point clouds estimated from COLMAP. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity o, color c) and optimized camera start (T{start}) and end (T{end}) poses for each blurred image. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian: Parameterized by \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or its Cholesky decomposition/rotation/scale representation as in 3D-GS), o \in \mathbb{R}, and c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Camera Pose: T{start} and T{end} are parameterized by their corresponding Lie algebras of SE(3), represented by a 6D vector each. Virtual Poses: n discrete virtual camera poses interpolated between T{start} and T{end} to approximate the exposure time. Parameters: n: Number of discrete samples (virtual camera poses) used to approximate the motion blur integral. Typical value: 10. Learning rate for Gaussians: Identical to original 3D-GS. Learning rate for camera poses (T{start}, T{end}): Exponentially decreased from 1 \times 10^{-3} to 1 \times 10^{-5}. Optimizer: Adam. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians and camera poses using estimations obtained from COLMAP. 2. Virtual Pose Generation: For each blurred image k, define the start pose T{start}^{(k)} and end pose T{end}^{(k)}. Generate n virtual poses Ti^{(k)} for i=0 \dots n-1 by interpolating between T{start}^{(k)} and T{end}^{(k)}. The interpolation method can be linear or cubic B-spline. 3. Virtual Image Synthesis: For each virtual pose Ti^{(k)}, render a sharp virtual image Ci^{(k)}(u) using standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. The pixel value at location u is computed by sorting Gaussians front-to-back and compositing their contributions. The opacity contribution of a Gaussian i is given by: \alphai = oi \cdot \exp(-\sigmai) where oi is the learned opacity and \sigmai = \frac{1}{2} \Deltai^\top \Sigma'^{-1} \Deltai, with \Deltai being the offset between the pixel center and the 2D Gaussian center projected onto the image plane. 4. Blur Model Approximation: Compute the synthesized blurred image Bk(u) by averaging the virtual sharp images: Bk(u) \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} Ci^{(k)}(u) \quad (7). 5. Loss Computation: Calculate the photometric loss (e.g., L1 or SSIM) between the synthesized blurred image Bk(u) and the input blurred image Bk^{input}(u). 6. Gradient Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta and camera poses T. Gradient w.r.t. Gaussian parameters \theta: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial Bk} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \left( \frac{\partial Bi}{\partial Ci} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial Ci}{\partial \theta} \right) \quad (10) where \frac{\partial Bi}{\partial Ci} = \frac{1}{n}. Gradient w.r.t. Camera Poses T: \frac{\partial L}{\partial T} = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial Bk} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \left( \frac{\partial Bk}{\partial Ci} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial Ci}{\partial \theta} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial T} \right) \quad (11) Note: The source text contains a typo in the second term of the sum for Eq. 11, listing \frac{\partial Ci}{\partial \theta} instead of \frac{\partial Ci}{\partial T}, but the formula provided is used as written. The term \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial T} represents the Jacobian of the Gaussian parameters with respect to the camera pose. 7. Optimization: Update \theta and T using the Adam optimizer. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def renderblurredimage(gaussians, Tstart, Tend, nsamples, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Renders a motion-blurred image by averaging nsamples virtual sharp images. Args: gaussians: List of 3D Gaussian parameters (mu, sigma, opacity, color). Tstart: 6D vector representing start pose (Lie algebra of SE(3)). Tend: 6D vector representing end pose (Lie algebra of SE(3)). nsamples: Number of virtual poses to interpolate. imagewidth, imageheight: Dimensions of the output image. Returns: blurredimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3). """ # Interpolate virtual poses # Linear interpolation as a baseline; cubic B-spline can be used for complex trajectories virtualposes = [] for i in range(nsamples): t = i / (nsamples - 1) # Interpolate Lie algebra vectors Tvirtual = (1 - t) Tstart + t Tend virtualposes.append(Tvirtual) virtualimages = [] for Tv in virtualposes: # Render sharp image using standard 3D-GS rasterization # This function encapsulates the projection, sorting, and compositing of Gaussians sharpimage = rendersharp3dgs(gaussians, Tv, imagewidth, imageheight) virtualimages.append(sharpimage) # Average virtual images to approximate blur blurredimage = torch.stack(virtualimages, dim=0).mean(dim=0) return blurredimage def trainbadgaussians(blurredimages, initialgaussians, initialTstart, initialTend, nsamples=10): """ Training loop for BAD-Gaussians. """ # Initialize parameters gaussians = initialgaussians.clone().requiresgrad(True) Tstart = initialTstart.clone().requiresgrad(True) Tend = initialTend.clone().requiresgrad(True) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([{'params': gaussians}, {'params': [Tstart, Tend]}], lr=1e-3) # Learning rate schedule for poses poselr = 1e-3 for step in range(numtrainingsteps): # Exponential decay for pose learning rate currentposelr = 1e-3 (1e-5 / 1e-3) (step / numtrainingsteps) for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: if paramgroup['params'] == [Tstart, Tend]: paramgroup['lr'] = currentposelr else: paramgroup['lr'] = 1e-3 # Original 3D-GS LR for Gaussians optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0 for blurredimg in blurredimages: # Render blurred image renderedblur = renderblurredimage(gaussians, Tstart, Tend, nsamples, blurredimg.shape[1], blurredimg.shape[2]) # Compute photometric loss loss = F.l1loss(renderedblur, blurredimg) totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return gaussians, Tstart, Tend Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance Saturation: Increasing n beyond 10 yields diminishing returns. Performance reaches a saturation point, so n=10 is recommended for the trade-off between performance and efficiency. Trajectory Representation: Cubic interpolation (B-spline) improves performance in scenes with complex camera trajectories (e.g., MBA-VO and Deblur-NeRF-R) compared to linear interpolation. Pose Accuracy Sensitivity: The method is sensitive to the accuracy of initial poses. Methods like Deblur-NeRF and DP-NeRF show a significant performance gap when trained with COLMAP poses versus ground-truth poses, highlighting the importance of good initialization. Time Complexity: Training time is approximately 30 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. This is significantly faster than competing methods like Deblur-NeRF, DP-NeRF, and BAD-NeRF, which take more than 10 hours. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Rendering Efficiency: Achieves over 200 FPS rendering efficiency. In contrast, Deblur-NeRF, DP-NeRF, and BAD-NeRF fall below 1 FPS. Strengths: High rendering speed, fast training time, ability to handle motion blur and inaccurate poses jointly. Limitations: Sensitive to initial pose accuracy. Performance gains from increasing n saturate quickly. When to use: When reconstructing scenes from motion-blurred images with inaccurate camera poses and sparse initialization. When not to use: When high-precision camera poses are already available and images are sharp (standard 3D-GS is sufficient and simpler). BAD-Gaussians was introduced in the paper "BAD-Gaussians: Bundle Adjusted Deblur Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [15] and addresses the limitations of NeRF-based deblurring methods (Deblur-NeRF [26], BAD-NeRF [46]) which are computationally expensive and slow to render. The method leverages the geometry within multi-view blurry images to reconstruct a high-quality 3D scene by minimizing the photometric error between input blurred images and synthesized blurred images based on a physical motion blur image formation model. name: LiteTex-GS
body: LiteTex-GS is a fast and lightweight texturing framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples geometry from appearance by assigning independent local RGB texture maps to each Gaussian primitive. It solves the computational overhead of high-resolution texturing by initializing compact low-resolution maps and progressively allocating higher resolution only to primitives with significant reconstruction errors, using a global-to-local capacity allocation strategy. Unlike prior methods that statically allocate texture resolution, LiteTex-GS uses a frequency-aware scheduler to coordinate image supervision, texture-cap release, and primitive densification, while employing a contribution- and area-aware pruning strategy to eliminate low-utility Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images \{Im\}, camera poses, and an initial set of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, rotation, scale, opacity) initialized with minimal 2x2 local texture maps. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity) and local RGB texture maps Ti for each primitive. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive i: pos: 3D position vector. rot: Quaternion or rotation matrix. scale: 3D scale vector. opacity: Scalar opacity value. Ti: Local RGB texture map. Initially 2x2. Can grow to rectangular dimensions up to a personal ceiling R{max,i} and global cap u(t). Rmax,i: Personal resolution ceiling for texture growth. patience: Integer counter for pruning protection. stats: Accumulated projected area ai, contribution ci, and normalized error ei. Frequency Significance Image F{img}: Precomputed 2D array representing scene frequency content. Scheduler State: Current iteration t. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize each Gaussian primitive with a 2x2 RGB texture map Ti. Set personal resolution ceilings R{max,i} to the initial texture size (2). Initialize accumulated statistics ai, ci, ei to zero for all primitives. Initialize patience counters to zero. 2. Preprocessing (Frequency-Aware Scheduling Setup): For each training image Im: Convert to grayscale \bar{I}m. Compute gradient magnitude Gm = \sqrt{(Sobelx \bar{I}m)^2 + (Sobely \bar{I}m)^2}. Normalize Gm to \tilde{G}m via min-max normalization. Compute weight map Wm = \text{clip}(w{min} + \alpha \tilde{G}m, w{min}, w{max}) with \alpha=1.5, w{min}=1.0, w{max}=3.0. Compute weighted image Wm \odot Im and transform to frequency domain: Fm = |\text{fftshift}(\mathcal{F}(Wm \odot Im))|. Compute F{img} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^M Fm. Calculate total energy E{total} = \sum{u,v} F{img}(u,v). Determine coarsest scale parameters: E{min} = E{total} / \beta with \beta=3. Generate frequency stages by sampling at most L=32 targets between E{min} and E{total}, mapping targets to render scales via binary search on accumulated energy within window (H/s) \times (W/s), and merging adjacent stages with identical integer scales. 3. Training Loop (per iteration t): Scheduler Query: Compute (r(t), u(t), \rho(t)) = \mathcal{S}(t; F{img}), where r(t) is render downsampling factor, u(t) is global texture resolution cap, and \rho(t) is densification rate. Rendering: For each pixel p in the rendered view: Identify influencing primitives N(p). For each primitive i \in N(p): Compute mapping \Phii(p): 1. Intersect camera ray of p with local tangent plane of Gaussian i. 2. Transform intersection point from view space to world space. 3. Project into primitive’s axis-aligned local frame. 4. Normalize canonical coordinate by primitive’s 2D scale. 5. Convert to texture coordinates based on current texel size and texture center offset. Check if \Phii(p) is within valid texture domain. If out of bounds, skip texture sampling for this primitive. Sample texture: val = S(Ti, \Phii(p)) using differentiable bilinear sampling S. Compute blending weight \omegai(p) = T^iv(p)\alpha^iv(p), where \alpha^iv(p) is opacity-weighted Gaussian response and T^iv(p) is accumulated transmittance. Compute rendered color: \hat{I}(p) = \sum{i \in N(p)} \omegai(p) S(Ti, \Phii(p)). Loss Computation: Compute per-pixel loss: Lv(p) = (1 - \lambda) ||Iv(p) - \hat{I}v(p)||1 + \lambda (1 - SSIMv(p)) with \lambda=0.2. Assign loss to primitives using blending weights \omegai(p). Statistics Accumulation: For each primitive i: Accumulate projected area n{i,v} (number of pixels with valid support). Accumulate contribution \sum{p \in \Omegav} \omega^iv(p). Accumulate error \sum{p \in \Omegav} Lv(p). Periodic Management (every 250 iterations): Normalization: ai = \frac{\sumv n{i,v}}{\sumv Wv Hv}. ci = \frac{\sumv \sum{p \in \Omegav} \omega^iv(p)}{\sumv Wv Hv}. ei = \frac{\text{accumulated error}}{ci}. ei = ei / \max(ej) (normalized). Pruning Check: For each primitive i: Determine low-utility status: mi^{(t)} = \mathbb{1}(ci^{(t)} < \tauc \lor ai^{(t)} < \taua) with \tauc=5\times10^{-6}, \taua=5\times10^{-5}. If mi^{(t)}=1, increment patience counter; else reset to 0. If patience counter \ge K=8, remove primitive. Note: Newly split primitives have a lower post-split opacity floor to prevent immediate removal. Texture Growth: Identify high-error subset H = \{i | ei > Qq(\{ej\})\} with q=0.85 (Mip-NeRF 360/DeepBlending) or q=0.60 (Tanks&Temples). For each i \in H: Update personal ceiling: R{max,i} \leftarrow \min(2R{max,i}, u(t)). Recompute active texture resolutions for all primitives based on support, texel size, and R{max,i}. If recomputed resolution exceeds current texture size: Upsample texture map Ti. Copy learned texels to initialize enlarged grid. Preserve Adam moments of existing texels. Initialize new texels with zero moments. Densification: Perform standard 3DGS densification with rate \rho(t). New primitives start with zero accumulated statistics and 2x2 textures. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def litetexgstraining(trainingimages, initialgaussians, config): """ Main training loop for LiteTex-GS. """ # 1. Preprocessing Fimg = computefrequencysignificanceimage(trainingimages, config.alpha, config.wmin, config.wmax) stages = generatefrequencystages(Fimg, config.beta, config.scfg, config.L) # 2. Initialization for g in initialgaussians: g.texture = np.zeros((2, 2, 3)) # 2x2 RGB g.Rmax = 2 g.patience = 0 g.stats = {'area': 0, 'contrib': 0, 'error': 0} gaussians = initialgaussians adammoments = {g.id: {'m': np.zeroslike(g.texture), 'v': np.zeroslike(g.texture)} for g in gaussians} for t in range(config.maxiterations): # 3. Scheduler rt, ut, rhot = schedulerquery(t, stages) # 4. Render and Accumulate Stats for view in trainingviews: renderedimage = renderscene(gaussians, view, rt) lossmap = computeloss(renderedimage, view.targetimage, config.lambdaval) for g in gaussians: # Accumulate stats based on rasterization weights g.stats['area'] += getprojectedarea(g, view) g.stats['contrib'] += getrenderingcontribution(g, view) g.stats['error'] += getaccumulatederror(g, view, lossmap) # 5. Optimization Step (Standard 3DGS Adam update) updategaussianparameters(gaussians, adammoments, config) # 6. Periodic Management (every 250 iterations) if t % 250 == 0: normalizestats(gaussians) # Pruning for g in gaussians: islowutility = (g.stats['contrib'] < config.tauc) or (g.stats['area'] < config.taua) if islowutility: g.patience += 1 else: g.patience = 0 if g.patience >= config.K: removegaussian(gaussians, g) # Texture Growth higherrorthreshold = quantile(gaussians, 'normalizederror', config.q) higherrorprimitives = [g for g in gaussians if g.stats['normalizederror'] > higherrorthreshold] for g in higherrorprimitives: g.Rmax = min(2 g.Rmax, ut) for g in gaussians: newres = computeactiveresolution(g) if newres > g.texture.shape[0]: # Assuming square for simplicity in check upsamplingtexture(g, newres, adammoments[g.id]) # Densification densifygaussians(gaussians, rhot) return gaussians def computefrequencysignificanceimage(images, alpha, wmin, wmax): M = len(images) Fimg = np.zeroslike(images[0]) for Im in images: Igray = grayscale(Im) Gm = sobelgradientmagnitude(Igray) Gnorm = minmaxnormalize(Gm) Wm = np.clip(wmin + alpha Gnorm, wmin, wmax) Fm = np.abs(np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft2(Wm Im))) Fimg += Fm return Fimg / M def upsamplingtexture(g, newres, adamid): oldtex = g.texture oldm = adammoments[adamid]['m'] oldv = adammoments[adamid]['v'] # Create new larger texture newtex = np.zeros((newres, newres, 3)) newm = np.zeros((newres, newres, 3)) newv = np.zeros((newres, newres, 3)) # Copy existing texels h, w, = oldtex.shape newtex[:h,:w,:] = oldtex newm[:h,:w,:] = oldm newv[:h,:w,:] = oldv g.texture = newtex adammoments[adamid]['m'] = newm adammoments[adamid]['v'] = newv Parameters: Initial texture resolution: 2x2. Sobel weight parameters: \alpha=1.5, w{min}=1.0, w{max}=3.0. Scheduler parameters: \beta=3, s{cfg}=4, L=32. Loss balance parameter: \lambda=0.2. Quantile parameter q: 0.85 for Mip-NeRF 360 and DeepBlending; 0.60 for Tanks&Temples. Pruning thresholds: \tauc=5\times10^{-6}, \taua=5\times10^{-5}. Patience counter K: 8. Pruning interval: 250 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pixels whose mapped texture coordinates fall outside the valid texture domain are marked as out of bounds and do not use texture sampling; wrapping or padding is not applied. Newly split primitives are protected by a lower post-split opacity floor to prevent immediate removal before accumulating reliable statistics. Texture resolution can be rectangular, allowing different primitives to allocate capacity according to local geometric extent. Time Complexity: The frequency-aware scheduling and per-primitive texture optimization add overhead compared to standard 3DGS, but the method is designed to be lightweight by initializing compact textures and only growing them when necessary. The preprocessing step is performed once and introduces negligible overhead. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is significantly reduced compared to high-resolution textured Gaussian methods because primitives start with 2x2 textures and only grow when needed. The contribution- and area-aware pruning further reduces memory by eliminating low-utility Gaussians. Measured Performance: LiteTex-GS achieves competitive or superior rendering quality while using substantially fewer parameters and less computational overhead than prior textured Gaussian methods. Strengths: Decouples geometry from appearance, allowing for efficient texturing; adapts texture resolution to visual difficulty; maintains a compact geometric scaffold. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of pruning thresholds and quantile parameters for different datasets; texture upsampling requires managing Adam moments to avoid gradient dilution. When to use: When high-quality texturing is required but computational resources are limited, or when standard 3DGS lacks sufficient detail. When not to use: When real-time rendering speed is the absolute priority and texture detail is not critical, standard 3DGS may be faster due to lower overhead. LiteTex-GS was proposed by Li and Guo et al. in 2026, published in the Eurographics proceedings. It addresses the challenge of balancing expressive detail with computational efficiency in Gaussian Splatting texturing. The method builds on the frequency-aware scheduling principle introduced by DashGaussian [CJJ 25] and extends it to coordinate image supervision, texture-cap release, and primitive densification. It is motivated by the limitations of opacity-based pruning in standard 3DGS [KKL 23] and the static texture allocation of prior methods [PKDD25, CTP 25]. LiteTex-GS: Fast and Lightweight Texturing for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70637, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Virtual Camera Optimization for Mirror Reflections
head: GSIM, Gaussian Splatting in Mirrors
body: Virtual Camera Optimization for Mirror Reflections (GSIM) is a method for rendering physically accurate mirror reflections in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) by modeling reflections as images captured by virtual cameras positioned symmetrically to the real camera across the mirror plane. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistencies and blurriness caused by 3D-GS misinterpreting reflections as virtual 3D space behind the mirror. Unlike NeRF-based methods that use ray tracing, this method maintains real-time rendering speeds by using standard rasterization from the virtual camera pose. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A trained 3D-GS scene representation (Gaussians), real camera poses [R|t], intrinsics K, and ground truth images. Outputs: Final rendered image \hat{C}{pred,f}, optimized mirror plane parameters [n, o], and virtual camera pose [R'|t']. Data Structures Gaussian Scene: Each Gaussian i is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity Oi, and spherical harmonic coefficients Ci \in \mathbb{C}^{N{sh}}. Mirror Plane: Defined by normal vector n \in \mathbb{R}^3 and origin point o \in \mathbb{R}^3 in world coordinates, denoted as [n, o]. Virtual Camera Extrinsic: A 3 \times 4 matrix [R'|t'] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4}. Mirror Mask: A binary mask identifying pixels PM belonging to the mirror region within the set of all pixels P{cam}. Numbered Steps 1. Depth and Normal Rasterization: Extend standard 3D-GS rasterization to render depth and normal maps for the current view. Depth Map (\hat{D}): Rendered via alpha-compositing of Gaussian centers' z-depths di: \hat{D} = \sum{i \in N} di \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Normal Map (\hat{N}): Rendered via alpha-compositing of Gaussian shortest axis normals ni: \hat{N} = \sum{i \in N} ni \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ni is the normalized vector of the shortest axis of the i-th Gaussian's covariance matrix. 2. Mirror Plane Prediction: Estimate the mirror plane [n, o] in world coordinates using the rendered depth and normal maps. Color Optimization: Replace mirror region colors in the ground truth image with a constant color to reconstruct the mirror surface geometry without texture interference. Depth Regularization: Apply a smoothness loss L{smooth} to ensure depth consistency, weighted by color similarity: L{smooth} = \sum{k \in P{cam}} \sum{q \in N(k)} \exp(-\gamma \| C'{gt}(k) - C'{gt}(q) \|) | \hat{D}{pred,r}(k) - \hat{D}{pred,r}(q) | where k and q are pixels, N(k) are 4-connected neighbors, C'{gt} is the modified ground truth color, and \gamma is a hyper-parameter controlling color influence. Normal Consistency: Use depth estimates to supervise normal consistency. 3. Virtual Camera Pose Computation: Compute the virtual camera extrinsic matrix [R'|t'] symmetric to the real camera [R|t] about the mirror plane [n, o]: \begin{bmatrix} R' & t' \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} I - 2nn^T & 2o \times n \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where I is the identity matrix and o \times n denotes the cross product. 4. Virtual Camera Rendering: Render the scene from the virtual camera using standard 3D-GS forward rasterization to obtain the reflected image \hat{C}{pred,v}. 5. Image Fusion: Fuse the virtual camera render and the real camera render \hat{C}{pred,r} using the mirror mask: \hat{C}{pred,f}(k) = \begin{cases} \hat{C}{pred,v}(k), & \text{if } k \in P{cam} \cap PM \\ \hat{C}{pred,r}(k), & \text{if } k \in P{cam} \setminus PM \end{cases} where PM is the set of pixels in the masked mirror region. 6. Optimization: Refine the mirror plane parameters [n, o] (and thus the virtual camera pose) via gradient descent during training to enhance reflection quality and resolve imperfections in the initial plane estimate. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computevirtualcameraextrinsic(realextrinsic, mirrornormal, mirrororigin): """ Computes the virtual camera extrinsic matrix [R'|t'] given the real camera extrinsic [R|t] and mirror plane [n, o]. Args: realextrinsic: 3x4 matrix [R|t] mirrornormal: 3x1 vector n mirrororigin: 3x1 vector o Returns: virtualextrinsic: 3x4 matrix [R'|t'] """ R = realextrinsic[:,:3] t = realextrinsic[:, 3] n = mirrornormal.flatten() o = mirrororigin.flatten() # Compute reflection matrix components # I - 2nn^T reflectionrot = np.eye(3) - 2.0 np.outer(n, n) # 2 (o x n) translationoffset = 2.0 np.cross(o, n) # Construct the 4x4 transformation matrix for the mirror reflection # [ I - 2nn^T 2o x n ] # [ 0 1 ] mirrortransform = np.eye(4) mirrortransform[:3,:3] = reflectionrot mirrortransform[:3, 3] = translationoffset # Append 1 to t to make it homogeneous thom = np.append(t, 1.0) # Apply mirror transform to the real camera pose # The formula in the paper is: [R' t'; 0 1] = MirrorTransform [R t; 0 1] # Note: The paper's formula implies matrix multiplication of the 4x4 homogeneous matrices. realcamhom = np.eye(4) realcamhom[:3,:3] = R realcamhom[:3, 3] = t virtualcamhom = mirrortransform @ realcamhom # Extract 3x4 extrinsic virtualextrinsic = virtualcamhom[:3,:] return virtualextrinsic def renderdepthandnormals(gaussians, cameraextrinsic, cameraintrinsics): """ Renders depth and normal maps from 3D-GS scene. This is a simplified representation of the alpha-compositing process. """ # Project Gaussians to screen space # This step involves standard 3D-GS projection logic screengaussians = projectgaussians(gaussians, cameraextrinsic, cameraintrinsics) # Sort by z-depth screengaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.zdepth) # Initialize maps height, width = screengaussians[0].imageshape depthmap = np.zeros((height, width)) normalmap = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) alphamap = np.zeros((height, width)) # Alpha compositing for g in screengaussians: # Get Gaussian properties in screen space alpha = g.alpha depth = g.zdepth normal = g.shortestaxisnormal # Normalized vector of shortest scaling axis # Update depth and normal using alpha compositing # Dnew = Dold (1 - alpha) + depth alpha # Nnew = Nold (1 - alpha) + normal alpha # Note: The paper uses the standard alpha compositing formula for accumulation # D = sum(di alphai prod(1-alphaj)) # For implementation, iterate pixels covered by the 2D Gaussian for y, x in g.screencoverage: transmittance = 1.0 - alphamap[y, x] depthmap[y, x] = depthmap[y, x] (1 - alpha) + depth alpha normalmap[y, x] = normalmap[y, x] (1 - alpha) + normal alpha alphamap[y, x] = alphamap[y, x] + alpha (1 - alphamap[y, x]) return depthmap, normalmap def optimizemirrorplane(depthmap, normalmap, gtcolor, mirrormask, gamma): """ Estimates mirror plane [n, o] from depth and normal maps. """ # This step typically involves fitting a plane to the depth/normal data # or optimizing parameters n and o to minimize reconstruction error. # The paper mentions using Lsmooth for depth regularization. # Placeholder for plane fitting/optimization logic # n, o = fitplane(depthmap, normalmap) # Apply smoothness loss if needed # Lsmooth = sum(exp(-gamma ||Cgt(k) - Cgt(q)||) |D(k) - D(q)|) return n, o def renderwithvirtualcamera(gaussians, virtualextrinsic, cameraintrinsics): """ Renders the scene using the virtual camera. """ # Standard 3D-GS rasterization return standardgsrasterize(gaussians, virtualextrinsic, cameraintrinsics) def fuseimages(realrender, virtualrender, mirrormask): """ Fuses real and virtual renders based on the mirror mask. """ finalimage = np.where(mirrormask, virtualrender, realrender) return finalimage Parameters \gamma: Hyper-parameter for the RGB-weighted depth smoothness regularization loss. n: Normal vector of the mirror plane in world coordinates. o: Origin point of the mirror plane in world coordinates. PM: Set of pixels belonging to the masked mirror region. P{cam}: Set of all pixels in the rendered image. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Misinterpretation of Reflections: Standard 3D-GS treats reflections as virtual 3D space, causing blurriness and multi-view inconsistencies. Imperfect Plane Estimates: Initial mirror plane estimates may be inaccurate, necessitating the optimization step to refine the virtual camera pose. Textureless Areas: Depth predictions may be unreliable in textureless regions, requiring the color replacement strategy during optimization. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering speeds are maintained, comparable to standard 3D-GS, as it avoids the computational expense of ray tracing. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional depth and normal maps during training, but no significant increase in scene representation size. Performance: Achieves comparable or superior results to state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing training time compared to NeRF-based approaches like Mirror-NeRF. Strengths: Physically-based reflection rendering, real-time capability, no need for additional depth supervision tailored specifically for mirrors (unlike Mirror-3DGS). Limitations: Relies on accurate mirror plane estimation; performance may degrade if the mirror mask is inaccurate. When to Use: Scenes with mirrors where high-quality, multi-view consistent reflections are required, and real-time rendering is desired. When Not to Use: Scenes without reflective surfaces, or where computational resources are extremely limited and even the overhead of depth/normal rendering is prohibitive. The method was proposed by Zihan Wang, Shuzhe Wang, Matias Turkulainen, Junyuan Fang, and Juho Kannala from Aalto University, University of Oulu, and ETH Zurich. It was published in the BMVC 2024 paper "Gaussian Splatting in Mirrors: Reflection-Aware Rendering via Virtual Camera Optimization". The work addresses the limitations of 3D-GS in handling specular reflections, which prior NeRF-based methods like Mirror-NeRF attempted to solve using ray tracing, but at the cost of training time and rendering speed. The method builds on the observation that mirror reflections can be modeled as images from a virtual camera symmetric to the real camera. name: Differentiable DOF Rendering
head: Differentiable Depth of Field Rendering
body: Differentiable DOF Rendering is a method that generates blurred images by convolving projected 2D Gaussians with depth-dependent blur kernels derived from a finite-aperture camera model, enabling the differentiable optimization of camera parameters and scene geometry. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling defocus blur as a differentiable operation, allowing the joint optimization of scene structure and camera intrinsic/extrinsic parameters (specifically focal distance and aperture) rather than treating them as fixed inputs. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{S}, camera parameters for each training view m (focal distance fm, aperture parameter Qm), and training images Im. Outputs: A rendered color image \tilde{I}, a depth map \tilde{D}, and a Circle of Confusion (CoC) map \tilde{M}^{(coc)}. Data Structures 3D Gaussian: Defined by position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients (standard 3DGS representation). 2D Gaussian (Gk'): The projection of a 3D Gaussian into screen space. Blur Kernel (Gk^{(coc)}): An isotropic 2D Gaussian kernel defined by covariance \Sigmak^{(coc)} = a \mathbf{I}, where a is a scalar derived from the CoC radius. Formulas The Circle of Confusion (CoC) radius Rk^{(coc)} for a Gaussian k with center depth zk is calculated as: Rk^{(coc)} = \frac{1}{2} Q \left| \frac{1}{zk} - \frac{1}{f} \right| where Q = \frac{F}{A} is the simplified aperture parameter (F is lens focal length, A is aperture), zk is the object point depth, and f is the focal distance. The blur kernel Gk^{(coc)} is defined as: Gk^{(coc)}(\mathbf{x}) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}^T \Sigmak^{(coc)} \mathbf{x} \right) where \Sigmak^{(coc)} = a \mathbf{I} is an isotropic covariance matrix. The scalar a is determined by minimizing the L2 distance between the Gaussian kernel and a uniform intensity distribution within the CoC radius, yielding: a = \frac{(Rk^{(coc)})^2}{2 \ln 4} The convolved 2D Gaussian Gk'' is obtained by convolving the projected Gaussian Gk' with the blur kernel: Gk'' = Gk' Gk^{(coc)} Since the convolution of two Gaussians is another Gaussian, Gk'' remains a valid Gaussian primitive, preserving the rasterization consistency. Numbered Steps 1. Projection: Project each 3D Gaussian k from the scene into 2D screen space to obtain Gk'. 2. CoC Calculation: For each projected Gaussian Gk', calculate its CoC radius Rk^{(coc)} using its center depth zk and the current camera parameters f, Q via Equation (7). 3. Kernel Construction: Construct the isotropic blur kernel Gk^{(coc)} using the calculated radius Rk^{(coc)} to determine the scalar a. 4. Convolution: Convolve the projected Gaussian Gk' with the blur kernel Gk^{(coc)} to produce the blurred Gaussian Gk''. 5. Re-evaluation: Re-evaluate the number of Gaussians linked to each pixel, denoted as N{x'}, because the convolution changes the spatial support and associations between Gaussians and pixels. 6. Compositing: Accumulate contributions from the convolved Gaussians Gk'' to render the final color image \tilde{I}, depth map \tilde{D}, and CoC map \tilde{M}^{(coc)}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiabledofrender(gaussians3d, cameraparams, imagewidth, imageheight): """ gaussians3d: List of 3D Gaussian primitives. cameraparams: Dict containing 'f' (focal distance) and 'Q' (aperture parameter). """ f = cameraparams['f'] Q = cameraparams['Q'] # Step 1: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D # Returns list of 2D Gaussians Gk' with properties: center (x, y), # covariance matrix Sigma2d, opacity alpha, color c, and depth zk projectedgaussians = projecttoscreen(gaussians3d, cameraparams) blurredgaussians = [] for gprime in projectedgaussians: # Step 2: Calculate CoC radius # Rcoc = 0.5 Q |1/zk - 1/f| zk = gprime.depth Rcoc = 0.5 Q abs(1.0 / zk - 1.0 / f) # Step 3: Construct blur kernel parameters # a = Rcoc^2 / (2 ln(4)) a = (Rcoc 2) / (2.0 math.log(4)) # The blur kernel is an isotropic Gaussian with covariance aI # Step 4: Convolve Gk' with blur kernel # Convolution of two Gaussians results in a Gaussian with summed covariances # Sigmablurred = Sigma2d + a I Sigmablurred = gprime.covariance + a np.eye(2) # Create the new blurred Gaussian Gk'' gdoubleprime = Gaussian2D( center=gprime.center, covariance=Sigmablurred, opacity=gprime.opacity, # Opacity remains unchanged by convolution in this model color=gprime.color) blurredgaussians.append(gdoubleprime) # Step 5 & 6: Re-evaluate pixel associations and composite # Sort blurredgaussians by depth for correct alpha blending blurredgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth, reverse=True) # Initialize output buffers colorimage = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) depthmap = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) cocmap = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # Standard alpha blending rasterization using the blurred Gaussians for g in blurredgaussians: # Rasterize g into the image buffers # This step involves re-evaluating which pixels are covered by g # due to the changed covariance Sigmablurred rasterizegaussian(g, colorimage, depthmap, cocmap) return colorimage, depthmap, cocmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The simplification of the CoC formula assumes F \ll f and F \ll zo. If these conditions are not met, the approximation error increases. Boundaries: The method assumes uniform depth across each 2D Gaussian’s support, set as the z-coordinate of the center position. This approximation may introduce artifacts for Gaussians with large depth variance or extreme perspective distortion. Degenerate Input: If zk = f, the CoC radius becomes zero, resulting in no blur. This is the focal plane. Time Complexity: The method adds a convolution step per Gaussian. However, since the convolution of Gaussians is closed-form (sum of covariances), the computational overhead is minimal compared to standard rasterization, provided the rasterization is CUDA-customized. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the additional blur kernel parameters (scalar a) and potentially re-evaluating pixel-Gaussian associations, which may increase memory bandwidth usage during the compositing pass. Strengths: Enables differentiable optimization of camera parameters (f, Q) and scene geometry simultaneously. It leverages natural defocus blur in training images as a geometric cue. Limitations: The assumption of uniform depth within a Gaussian's support may lead to reconstruction artifacts in regions with significant depth discontinuities or large Gaussians. When to use: When training data contains defocus blur and the goal is to reconstruct a scene with accurate geometry and potentially optimize camera intrinsics. When not to use: When high-precision depth estimation is required for very large primitives or when the camera model assumptions (F \ll f) are violated. Differentiable DOF Rendering was introduced in the paper "DOF-GS: Adjustable Depth-of-Field 3D Gaussian Splatting for Post-Capture Refocusing, Defocus Rendering and Blur Removal". It extends the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework to handle depth-of-field effects, allowing for post-capture refocusing and blur removal by making the blur process differentiable with respect to scene and camera parameters.
