name: ParetoGS Continuous-Budget Decoding
head: ParetoGS budget decoding, ParetoGS residual atlas encoding
body: ParetoGS Continuous-Budget Decoding is a runtime procedure that returns parameters for exactly K Gaussians at any valid integer budget by interpolating between nested adapted anchors using a compressed residual atlas and calibrated exponents. It differs from static compression methods like Data Compression and Storage Optimization by enabling smooth, continuous trade-offs between quality and performance without retraining, and from discrete pruning methods like Pruning and Density Control by preserving the full geometric fidelity of the original model through residual interpolation rather than hard selection. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of nested adapted anchors (including a Full model), the global nested member ordering, and pre-calibrated interval exponents (p, q). Outputs: Standard K-Gaussian parameters (position, log scale, quaternion, opacity logit, DC color, higher-order SH coefficients) for a specified integer budget K. Data Structures: Global Nested Ordering: A permutation of Gaussian IDs derived from concatenating entry sequences of contracted anchors. Full-model parameters are reordered to match this sequence. Compressed Residual Atlas: Stores orthogonal decompositions of non-full anchor residuals relative to the Full model. Layout: Stacked by member layer and parameter field. Precision: Quantization scales, anchor combination coefficients, and SH channel bases are stored in FP16. Quantization: Symmetric INT8 quantization applied independently to each channel within blocks of 64 Gaussian rows. Interval Exponents: For each interval between neighboring anchors, a pair (p, q) is stored. Member-Order Metadata: Tracks the entry sequence of Gaussians as budget increases. Runtime Cache: By default, caches the two most recently used endpoints. Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Global Nested Ordering: When contracting an upper anchor U to a lower anchor L, record the IDs of deleted Gaussians. Reverse each deletion trace to determine the order in which members enter as budget increases. Starting with the smallest anchor, concatenate these entry sequences to form the global nested ordering. Reorder full-model parameters and align all anchors to this ordering by ID. 2. Compute and Encode Residuals: Compute residuals of non-full anchors relative to the Full model in raw parameter coordinates (position, log scale, quaternion, opacity logit, DC color, higher-order SH coefficients). Convert non-full anchor residuals to FP16 and stack them by member layer and parameter field. Perform orthogonal decomposition along the anchor-state dimension for each layer. Retain all available components along the state dimension (maximum rank 10). For the 45 higher-order SH channels, use a rank-36 channel subspace, while ensuring decoding outputs all 45 channels. Apply symmetric INT8 quantization independently to each channel within blocks of 64 Gaussian rows using the following formulas: s{bc} = \frac{\max{i \in b} |x{ic}|}{127} q{ic} = \text{clip}\left(\text{round}\left(\frac{x{ic}}{s{bc}}\right), -127, 127\right) \hat{x}{bic} = q{ic} s{bc} where b is the block of 64 rows, c is the channel, x{ic} is the input value, s{bc} is the scale, and q{ic} is the quantized value. If a block is all-zero, the scale s{bc} defaults to 1. 3. Calibrate Interval Exponents: For each neighboring anchor pair, enumerate shared-state exponent p and entering-member gate exponent q from predefined discrete sets: P = \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6\} Q = \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3\} At rounded budgets corresponding to normalized progress t \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}, compare all 72 (p, q) pairs on up to ten training views. Views are midpoint selections from equally partitioned intervals of the training-camera list. Calculate the reconstruction loss \ell{v,h} for view v at the lower endpoint, three intermediate budgets, and upper endpoint, indexed by h=0, \dots, 4, using image loss \ell = 0.8 L1 + 0.2 (1 - SSIM). Compute loss delta, delta variance, and negative delta mean for each view: d{v,h} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{h=1}^{3} \frac{\ell{v,h} - \ell{v,h+1}}{t{h+1} - th} sv = \frac{1}{3} \sum{h=0}^{3} |d{v,h} - (\ell{v,0} - \ell{v,4})| mv = \frac{1}{4} \sum{h=0}^{3} \max(-d{v,h}, 0) Define Q^+ as the mean of the largest \lceil V/4 \rceil values in a set. Minimize the calibration objective: J(p, q) = \frac{1}{3V} \sum{v=1}^{V} \sum{h=1}^{3} \ell{v,h} + Q^+(\{mv\}) + 0.25 Q^+(\{sv\}) Store the minimizing p and q for each interval. Exact ties favor larger p, then larger q. Pitfall: Calibration must not update Gaussian parameters or use test views to avoid overfitting and ensure deployment stability. 4. Decode at Runtime for Budget K: If K matches an exact anchor, restore that anchor directly. If K=N (full count), use the Full model. For other counts, identify the two neighboring anchors between which K falls. Interpolate shared members in raw parameter coordinates using the shared-state exponent p. For entering members, use their upper-anchor state and multiply their activated opacity by t^q, where t is the normalized progress within the interval. Clip scaled opacity to [10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}], convert back to logit, and output standard K-Gaussian parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def decodeparetogs(K, fullmodel, anchors, ordering, atlas, exponents): """ Decode ParetoGS parameters for budget K. Args: K: Integer budget (number of Gaussians). fullmodel: Array of parameters for the full model, reordered by globalnestedordering. anchors: List of adapted anchors, each containing parameters for a subset of Gaussians. ordering: Global nested ordering of Gaussian IDs. atlas: Compressed residual atlas containing orthogonal decompositions. exponents: Dictionary mapping anchor intervals to (p, q) tuples. Returns: Parameters for exactly K Gaussians. """ N = len(ordering) # Case 1: Exact anchor match for anchor in anchors: if anchor.count == K: return anchor.parameters[ordering] # Case 2: Full model if K == N: return fullmodel[ordering] # Case 3: Interpolation between neighboring anchors # Find the two anchors between which K falls based on their counts # Assuming anchors are sorted by count loweranchor = None upperanchor = None for i in range(len(anchors) - 1): if anchors[i].count < K < anchors[i+1].count: loweranchor = anchors[i] upperanchor = anchors[i+1] break if loweranchor is None or upperanchor is None: raise ValueError("K does not fall within any anchor interval") # Get exponents for this interval p, q = exponents[(loweranchor.id, upperanchor.id)] # Calculate normalized progress t # t is the relative position of K between lower and upper anchor counts # Note: The source defines t based on normalized progress, # but for interpolation between discrete anchors, we assume t represents # the fraction of the way from lower to upper in terms of member inclusion. # The source mentions t in {0.25, 0.5, 0.75} for calibration, # implying t is a continuous variable in [0, 1] for decoding. t = (K - loweranchor.count) / (upperanchor.count - loweranchor.count) # Identify shared and entering members # Shared members are those present in both lower and upper anchors # Entering members are those present in upper but not lower lowerids = set(loweranchor.memberids) upperids = set(upperanchor.memberids) sharedids = lowerids & upperids enteringids = upperids - lowerids # Initialize output parameters # We need to reconstruct the full set of K parameters # The global ordering helps us map IDs to positions # Create a mapping from ID to index in the global ordering idtoidx = {gid: idx for idx, gid in enumerate(ordering)} # Parameters for shared members: interpolate in raw coordinates # The source says "shared members follow Equation (4) in raw parameter coordinates" # Equation (4) is not provided, but typically this implies linear interpolation # or interpolation based on the exponent p. # Given the context of "shared-state exponent p", it likely modulates the # contribution or the interpolation weight. # However, without Eq (4), we assume standard linear interpolation for shared members # as is common in such atlases, or that p affects the opacity/weighting. # Let's assume linear interpolation for raw parameters for shared members. # Parameters for entering members: use upper-anchor state, scale opacity by t^q # Opacity is stored as logit. outputparams = {} for gid in sharedids: idx = idtoidx[gid] # Interpolate raw parameters between lower and upper # Assuming parameters are aligned by ID in the anchors lowerp = loweranchor.parameters[gid] upperp = upperanchor.parameters[gid] # Linear interpolation for raw parameters # Note: The source mentions "shared-state exponent p". # If p is an exponent for the shared state, it might mean: # param = lowerp + t^p (upperp - lowerp) # Or it might affect the opacity specifically. # Given the ambiguity of Eq (4), and the explicit instruction for entering members, # we will use linear interpolation for shared parameters as a safe default # for "raw parameter coordinates" unless p is explicitly defined as a power law. # However, "shared-state exponent p" strongly suggests a power law interpolation. # Let's use t^p for the interpolation weight. weight = t p interpolatedp = lowerp + weight (upperp - lowerp) outputparams[gid] = interpolatedp for gid in enteringids: idx = idtoidx[gid] # Use upper-anchor state upperp = upperanchor.parameters[gid] # Scale opacity by t^q # Opacity is the 4th component (index 3) in the 59 scalar components # It is stored as a logit. opacitylogit = upperp[3] opacity = sigmoid(opacitylogit) # Scale opacity scaledopacity = opacity (t q) # Clip opacity scaledopacity = max(1e-6, min(1 - 1e-6, scaledopacity)) # Convert back to logit scaledopacitylogit = logit(scaledopacity) # Update the opacity logit in the parameter vector newp = upperp.copy() newp[3] = scaledopacitylogit outputparams[gid] = newp # Assemble the final parameter array in the global ordering finalparams = np.zeros((K, 59)) for i, gid in enumerate(ordering[:K]): finalparams[i] = outputparams[gid] return finalparams def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) def logit(x): return np.log(x / (1 - x)) Parameters: Scalar components per Gaussian: 59 at SH degree 3 (position, log scale, quaternion, opacity logit, DC color, higher-order SH coefficients). Quantization block size: 64 Gaussian rows per channel. All-zero block scale fallback: 1. Precision for quantization scales, anchor combination coefficients, and SH channel bases: FP16. Image loss composition: 0.8 L1 + 0.2 (1 - SSIM). Opacity clip range: [10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Calibration Overfitting: Calibration must not update Gaussian parameters or use test views to avoid overfitting and ensure deployment stability. No Per-Gaussian Progress Correction: Only interval-level exponents are cached; no per-Gaussian progress correction is stored. Precision: Quantization scales and coefficients are FP16; INT8 quantization is used for the atlas data. Time Complexity: Decoding is O(K) for assembling the K Gaussian parameters, assuming constant-time lookup of anchors and exponents. Calibration is O(V \cdot |P| \cdot |Q| \cdot H), where V is the number of views, |P| and |Q| are the sizes of the exponent sets, and H is the number of intervals. Memory Complexity: The compressed residual atlas reduces storage by using orthogonal decomposition (rank 10 for state, rank 36 for SH channels) and INT8 quantization. The exact memory savings depend on the number of anchors and the compression ratio of the atlas. Measured Performance: The method achieves high-quality continuous-budget rendering, with PSNR results comparable to full models at lower budgets. Strengths: Enables smooth quality-performance trade-offs without retraining; preserves geometric fidelity through residual interpolation; efficient runtime decoding. Limitations: Requires pre-calibration; calibration must be done carefully to avoid overfitting; no per-Gaussian progress correction. When to Use: When continuous budget control is needed for deployment on devices with varying capabilities or when dynamic quality adjustment is required. When Not to Use: When static compression is sufficient, or when per-Gaussian adaptive quality is needed. ParetoGS Continuous-Budget Decoding was introduced in the paper "ParetoGS: High-Quality Continuous-Budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Adapted Anchors". It builds on the concept of adapted anchors and residual encoding to provide a flexible rendering pipeline. name: SpotLessSplats (SLS)
body: SpotLessSplats (SLS) is a robust 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework that enables high-quality reconstruction from casually captured video data containing transient distractors (e.g., moving people, wind-blown elements). Unlike standard 3DGS which assumes static scenes, SLS uses unsupervised detection of outliers in training images by leveraging pre-trained text-to-image features and robust optimization to ignore these distractors. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DeSplat or 360 Gaussian Splatting by specifically addressing the problem of semantic outlier modeling in casual captures, using feature-space similarities rather than just photometric residuals to identify inliers and outliers. Inputs: A set of posed images \{In\}{n=1}^N from a casually captured scene, and a pre-trained 2D foundation model (e.g., DINOv2) to extract semantic feature maps F. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians optimized for novel view synthesis, with transient distractors effectively ignored. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Feature Map F: Semantic feature embeddings extracted from input images using the foundation model. Inlier Mask M: A binary or probabilistic mask indicating inlier pixels. Residual Histogram: A histogram with B buckets of width 10^{-3} tracking residual magnitudes over time. MLP Classifier H: A network with parameters \theta^{(t)} for spatio-temporal outlier detection. Parameters: \tau: Hyperparameter for generalized median cut-off percentile. Typical values: 0.5 (median) or 0.9. \kappa: Utilization-based pruning threshold. Value: 10^{-8}. T: Steps between utilization calculations. Value: 100. |NT(t)|: Number of images accumulated for utilization calculation. Value: 100. \lambda: Weight for regularization loss. Value: 0.5. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each training image In, extract semantic feature map Fn using the pre-trained foundation model. 2. Robust Masking (Photometric Baseline): Compute the 1-norm residual image Rn = \|In - \hat{I}n\|1 pixel-wise. Compute a generalized median \rho of residuals over multiple batches to handle skewed distributions (see Sub-step 2a). Compute the initial inlier mask Mn^{(t)} using a threshold \rho and a morphological dilation: Mn^{(t)} = \mathbb{1}\{Rn > \rho\} \circledast B > 0.5, \quad P(Rn > \rho) = \tau where \mathbb{1} is the indicator function, \circledast denotes convolution with a normalized 3 \times 3 box filter B, and the condition > 0.5 applies to the result of the convolution. 3. Outlier Detection (SLS-mlp): Train an MLP classifier H with parameters \theta^{(t)} to predict pixel-wise inlier probabilities M{mlp}^{(t)} = H(F; \theta^{(t)}). Architecture: H uses 1 \times 1 convolutions, acting i.i.d. across pixels. Loss Function: Minimize L(\theta^{(t)}) = L{sup}(\theta^{(t)}) + \lambda L{reg}(\theta^{(t)}). Supervision Loss: L{sup}(\theta^{(t)}) = \max(U^{(t)} - H(F; \theta^{(t)}), 0) + \max(H(F; \theta^{(t)}) - L^{(t)}, 0). Labels: U^{(t)} is Mn^{(t)} computed with \tau=0.5; L^{(t)} is Mn^{(t)} computed with \tau=0.9. Regularization: Minimize the Lipschitz constant of H via L{reg} as detailed in [Liu et al. 2022, Eq. (13)] to ensure similar features map to similar probabilities. Optimization Schedule: Parameters \theta^{(t)} are updated concurrently with 3DGS optimization, interleaved such that one is fixed while the other is optimized. Mask Selection: Use M{mlp}^{(t)} as the final inlier/outlier mask for training. 4. Residual Tracking (Sub-step 2a): To handle skewed outlier distribution across images, track residual magnitudes over multiple training batches. Discretize residuals into B histogram buckets of width 10^{-3}. Update bucket population via a discounted update similar to fast median filtering [Perreault and Hebert 2007]. Extract generalized median \rho as the \tau quantile in the histogram population. 5. Utilization-Based Pruning (UBP): Replace standard opacity reset with UBP to compress the scene representation. Track the gradient of rendered colors \hat{I}{h,w} with respect to the projected splat positions xg of each Gaussian g. Compute utilization ug: ug = \sum{t \in NT(t)} \mathbb{E}{w,h} \left[ M{h,w}^{(t)} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \hat{I}{h,w}^{(t)}}{\partial xg} \right)^2 \right] where the expectation is over image pixels (w,h). Average across the image (W \times H), computed every T=100 steps accumulated over |NT(t)|=100 images. Prune Gaussians if ug < \kappa (where \kappa = 10^{-8}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spotlesssplatstraining(images, poses, foundationmodel, numsteps): # Initialize 3D Gaussians gaussians = initialize3dgaussians() # Initialize MLP for outlier detection mlp = MLP1x1conv() theta = mlp.parameters() # Initialize residual histogram B = 1000 # Number of buckets bucketwidth = 1e-3 histogram = np.zeros(B) taumedian = 0.5 tauhigh = 0.9 lambdareg = 0.5 # Pruning parameters T = 100 NT = 100 kappa = 1e-8 utilizationbuffer = [] for step in range(numsteps): # 1. Sample a batch of images batchimages, batchposes = samplebatch(images, poses) # 2. Extract semantic features features = foundationmodel(batchimages) # 3. Render current Gaussians renderedimages = render3dgs(gaussians, batchposes) # 4. Compute residuals and update histogram residuals = np.abs(batchimages - renderedimages).mean(axis=-1) # 1-norm approx updatehistogram(histogram, residuals.flatten(), bucketwidth) # 5. Compute generalized median rho rhomedian = getquantile(histogram, taumedian) rhohigh = getquantile(histogram, tauhigh) # 6. Compute photometric masks maskmedian = (residuals > rhomedian) maskhigh = (residuals > rhohigh) # Apply morphological dilation (3x3 box filter) maskmedian = dilate(maskmedian) maskhigh = dilate(maskhigh) # 7. Update MLP (Interleaved with GS optimization) # If step is even, update MLP; if odd, update Gaussians (example schedule) if step % 2 == 0: # Compute MLP loss predinlier = mlp(features) U = maskmedian L = maskhigh lsup = np.maximum(U - predinlier, 0) + np.maximum(predinlier - L, 0) lsup = lsup.mean() # Compute Lipschitz regularization (simplified placeholder for Eq 13) lreg = computelipschitzreg(mlp, features) lossmlp = lsup + lambdareg lreg updateparameters(theta, lossmlp) # Use MLP mask for this step's GS update if MLP is active # In practice, SLS-mlp uses Mmlp as the mask finalmask = sigmoid(predinlier) # Or thresholded else: # Update 3D Gaussians # Use the mask from the previous step or current photometric mask # SLS-mlp uses Mmlp, so we assume finalmask is available lossgs = compute3dgsloss(renderedimages, batchimages, finalmask) updategaussians(gaussians, lossgs) # Track utilization for pruning if step % T == 0: # Compute gradient of rendered color w.r.t projected splat positions # This requires backprop through rendering to xg grads = computegradrenderedvsprojectedpos(gaussians, renderedimages, finalmask) utilizationbuffer.append(grads) if len(utilizationbuffer) >= NT: # Compute utilization ug utilizations = np.zeros(numgaussians) for gidx in range(numgaussians): # Average over accumulated images and pixels # E{w,h} [ M{h,w} (dI/dxg)^2 ] # Simplified: sum over buffer and average utilizations[gidx] = np.mean([ np.mean(buf[gidx] 2) for buf in utilizationbuffer ]) # Prune gaussians = prunegaussians(gaussians, utilizations, kappa) # Reset buffer utilizationbuffer = [] # Reset histogram or continue tracking? # Sources say "tracking residual magnitudes over multiple training batches" # implying continuous tracking. Subtopics: SLS-mlp (Spatio-temporal Clustering): Uses an MLP classifier trained unsupervised to predict inlier probabilities based on semantic features. It differs from spatial clustering by leveraging temporal consistency across the dataset. Choose when semantic information is strong and distractors are complex. Spatial Clustering: Uses non-parametric clustering of local feature embeddings to find image regions of structured outliers. Simpler but less robust to temporal variations than SLS-mlp. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for feature extraction (foundation model) and MLP training, but the MLP is lightweight (1 \times 1 convs). The interleaved optimization ensures convergence. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature maps and the MLP parameters. The histogram tracking uses constant memory. UBP reduces memory usage by pruning Gaussians. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality on casually captured scenes. Reduces the number of Gaussians by 2-4 times while maintaining quality. Strengths: Robust to transient distractors (people, wind) without manual annotation. Avoids overfitting to distractors with colors similar to the background, a common failure mode of residual-only methods like RobustNeRF. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained foundation model. Performance depends on the quality of semantic features. When to use: Casual captures with transient objects. When not to use: Static, controlled environments where standard 3DGS suffices, or when computational resources for foundation model inference are limited. SpotLessSplats was introduced by Sabour, Goli, Kopanas, Mathews, and Lagun from Google Deepmind and University of Toronto. It addresses the limitation of 3DGS which requires highly controlled environments (no moving people, consistent lighting). The method builds on prior work like RobustNeRF [Sabour et al. 2023] and NeRF-W, but improves upon them by using semantic features instead of just photometric residuals. It also incorporates insights from [Goli et al. 2024] for utilization-based pruning. name: TruncGradGS
head: Piecewise truncated gradient, Truncated Gradient Updates
body: TruncGradGS is a modification to the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rasterization gradient computation that replaces near-zero Gaussian derivative tails with a linear surrogate to solve the vanishing gradient problem in dynamic scenes with large inter-frame displacements. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by ensuring that Gaussians discarded by the alpha-blending threshold still receive gradient updates, thereby maintaining gradient flow for primitives that are distant or rapidly moving. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \sigma), 2D pixel coordinates p, the alpha-blending discard threshold \tau, and the linear slope parameter m. Outputs: Modified gradient \nabla G with respect to the Gaussian parameters (specifically the mean \Delta x). Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS primitive representation: Mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (positive definite) Opacity \sigma \in \mathbb{R} Color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 (view-dependent) Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Squared Mahalanobis Distance: For a query pixel p and a Gaussian with mean \mu, calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance d(p)^2 using the inverse covariance matrix \Sigma^{-1}: d(p)^2 = (\mu - p)^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mu - p) Note: In the context of the 2D projection used for rasterization, \Sigma refers to the projected 2D covariance, and p, \mu are 2D coordinates. 2. Determine Boundary Point (xb): The truncation boundary is defined by the Gaussian isocontour where the density equals the threshold \tau: G{2D}(xb) = \tau. This corresponds to a squared Mahalanobis distance of -2 \log \tau. To find the scalar distance s from the pixel p to the boundary point xb along the ray direction, parametrize the ray as: xb = p + s \frac{\mu - p}{\|\mu - p\|} Substitute this into the distance equation (\mu - xb)^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mu - xb) = -2 \log \tau to form a quadratic equation in s. The solution for s is: s = \|\mu - p\| \sqrt{1 \pm \frac{-2 \log \tau}{K}} where K is defined as: K = a(\mux - px)^2 + 2b(\mux - px)(\muy - py) + c(\muy - py)^2 The coefficients a, b, c come from the un-normalized general Gaussian 2D function (conic form): f(x, y) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} [a(\mux - x)^2 + c(\muy - y)^2] - b(\mux - x)(\muy - y)\right) Select the appropriate root for s that places xb on the Gaussian splat. 3. Calculate True Gradient: Compute the true partial derivative of the 2D Gaussian function G{2D} with respect to the mean parameter \Delta x (representing the mean offset). The derivative contains interaction terms with the Gaussian function: \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x} (Specific analytical forms depend on the exact parameterization of \Delta x, but it is the standard backpropagated gradient from the rasterizer). 4. Apply Piecewise Truncated Gradient: Determine the gradient update g based on the squared Mahalanobis distance d(p)^2 relative to the threshold -2 \log \tau and the sign of the gradient: Case 1 (Inside Threshold): If -2 \log G < -2 \log \tau (i.e., the pixel is within the effective support), use the true partial derivative: g = \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x} Case 2 (Outside Threshold): If the Gaussian is outside the threshold, apply a linear surrogate. First, calculate the bias b to ensure continuity at the boundary xb: b = \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}(xb) - m xb Then, apply the piecewise rule based on the sign of the gradient at the boundary \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}(xb): If \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}(xb) < 0: g = \min(m \cdot x + b, \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}) If \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}(xb) > 0: g = \max(-m \cdot x + b, \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}) Note: The variable x in the linear terms mx+b represents the distance coordinate along the ray from the pixel to the boundary, effectively scaling the linear surrogate. 5. Loss Sign Guard: Only apply the truncated gradient if the Gaussian is decreasing the loss via alpha-blending, i.e., \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai} < 0. If \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai} \ge 0, do not apply the truncated gradient. Applying it when the loss is increasing causes long-range push forces that make Gaussians repel each other. Parameters: \tau: The density threshold determining the boundary point. Set to the alpha-blending discard threshold of the rasterizer (typically 1/255). m: The slope of the linear surrogate gradient. A model parameter controlling the linear scaling of the gradient magnitude. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Repulsion: Applying the truncated gradient when \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai} \ge 0 causes Gaussians to repel each other due to long-range push forces. Discontinuity: The method ensures gradient continuity at the boundary xb by matching the linear surrogate to the true gradient value at that point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def truncgradgsgradientupdate(mean2d, covinv2d, pixel2d, truegradient, alpha, sigma, tau, m, lossgradalpha): """ Computes the truncated gradient for a 3D Gaussian splat at a specific pixel. Args: mean2d: np.array, 2D mean of the Gaussian [mux, muy] covinv2d: np.array, 2x2 inverse covariance matrix of the projected Gaussian pixel2d: np.array, 2D pixel coordinate [px, py] truegradient: float, the standard backpropagated gradient dG/dDeltax alpha: float, the projected density of the Gaussian at the pixel sigma: float, the opacity of the Gaussian tau: float, the alpha-blending discard threshold (e.g., 1/255) m: float, the slope parameter for the linear surrogate lossgradalpha: float, the gradient of the loss with respect to alpha (sigma alpha) Returns: float: The modified gradient to be used for optimization """ # Step 1: Compute Squared Mahalanobis Distance diff = mean2d - pixel2d # d(p)^2 = (mu - p)^T Sigma^-1 (mu - p) mahalanobissq = np.dot(diff, np.dot(covinv2d, diff)) # Step 2: Determine if we are inside or outside the threshold # Threshold condition: -2 log(G) < -2 log(tau) # Since G = exp(-0.5 mahalanobissq), -2 log(G) = mahalanobissq # So we check if mahalanobissq < -2 log(tau) thresholdval = -2.0 math.log(tau) if mahalanobissq < thresholdval: # Case 1: Inside threshold, use true gradient grad = truegradient else: # Case 2: Outside threshold, use linear surrogate # Check loss sign guard if lossgradalpha >= 0: # Do not apply truncated gradient if it increases the loss # Return 0 or the original gradient? The source says "do not apply". # In standard 3DGS, discarded Gaussians get 0 gradient. # TruncGradGS applies surrogate ONLY if it helps. # If it increases loss, we treat it as standard discarded Gaussian (0 gradient) # or potentially the true gradient if it was computed? # Source: "do not apply the truncated gradient... causes long-range push" # Implies we fall back to standard behavior (0 gradient for discarded) # or simply skip the surrogate. Given it's discarded, standard is 0. grad = 0.0 else: # Calculate boundary point distance s # K = a(dx)^2 + 2b(dx)(dy) + c(dy)^2 # Note: The source defines K using coefficients a,b,c from the conic form. # In standard 3DGS, the projected covariance Sigma2D is related to a,b,c. # For implementation, we need to solve for s. # s = ||mu - p|| sqrt(1 + (-2 log tau) / K) # However, K is derived from the conic coefficients. # If we only have covinv, we can derive the boundary distance directly. # The distance from center to boundary along the ray is determined by: # (mu - (p + s dir))^T Sigma^-1 (mu - (p + s dir)) = -2 log tau # Let dir = (mu - p) / ||mu - p|| # Let u = mu - p. Then mu - xb = u - s (u/||u||) = (||u|| - s) (u/||u||) # So (mu - xb)^T Sigma^-1 (mu - xb) = (||u|| - s)^2 (u/||u||)^T Sigma^-1 (u/||u||) # Let Q = (u/||u||)^T Sigma^-1 (u/||u||) # Then (||u|| - s)^2 Q = -2 log tau # ||u|| - s = sqrt(-2 log tau / Q) # s = ||u|| - sqrt(-2 log tau / Q) distmup = np.linalg.norm(diff) if distmup < 1e-8: grad = truegradient # Degenerate case, treat as center else: direction = diff / distmup Q = np.dot(direction, np.dot(covinv2d, direction)) # Solve for s # We want the point on the ray from p towards mu that is at distance threshold # The distance from mu to boundary is sqrt(-2 log tau / Q) # The distance from p to mu is distmup # The boundary is between p and mu if the pixel is outside? # Actually, the ray is from p to mu. # xb = p + s direction # mu - xb = mu - p - s direction = (distmup - s) direction # Mahalanobis sq at xb = (distmup - s)^2 Q = -2 log tau # distmup - s = sqrt(-2 log tau / Q) # s = distmup - sqrt(-2 log tau / Q) sqrtterm = math.sqrt(max(0, -2.0 math.log(tau) / Q)) s = distmup - sqrtterm # Calculate bias b for continuity # b = grad(xb) - m xb # Here x in the formula mx+b refers to the coordinate along the ray. # We need the true gradient at the boundary point xb. # However, the source defines the surrogate as min(mx + b, grad). # And b is derived from matching at xb. # We approximate the gradient at the boundary or use the current truegradient? # The source says: "match the linear surrogate... to the true gradient at the boundary point xb" # We don't have the true gradient at xb easily without re-evaluating G. # But we can approximate or use the current truegradient if it's close? # Strictly, we should evaluate truegradient at xb. # For implementation simplicity, if we assume the gradient doesn't change drastically # or we just use the current truegradient as a proxy for the boundary value? # No, the source explicitly derives b from grad(xb). # Let's assume we can compute gradatboundary. # Since we don't have the full function G(x) here, we use the provided truegradient # as an approximation or note that it requires re-evaluation. # Implementation note: To be precise, evaluate the true Gaussian gradient # at the boundary point xb = pixel2d + s direction. # For this pseudocode, we use the passed truegradient as a placeholder # for grad(xb) if re-evaluation is not possible, but ideally: # gradatboundary = computetruegradientat(mean2d, covinv2d, pixel2d + s direction) # Using the current truegradient as a proxy for grad(xb) is an approximation. # A more robust implementation would re-calculate G and dG/dx at xb. gradatboundary = truegradient # Placeholder for re-evaluation at xb b = gradatboundary - m s # Apply piecewise rule # If grad(xb) < 0: min(mx + b, grad) # If grad(xb) > 0: max(-mx + b, grad) # Here x is the distance from p, which is s? Or the coordinate? # The source uses x in mx+b. In the context of the ray parametrization, # x likely refers to the distance along the ray from the pixel. # So we use s. if gradatboundary < 0: linearval = m s + b grad = min(linearval, truegradient) else: linearval = -m s + b grad = max(linearval, truegradient) return grad TruncGradGS is designed to be compatible with dynamic frameworks like 4DGS, addressing the specific challenge of large temporal divergence where primitives move significantly between frames. Standard 3DGS discards Gaussians with contribution scalar \sigmai \alphai below a threshold, resulting in zero gradients. TruncGradGS applies the linear surrogate to these discarded Gaussians to maintain gradient flow. Time Complexity: The method adds a constant-time overhead per Gaussian-pixel interaction to compute the Mahalanobis distance, solve for the boundary, and apply the piecewise logic. It does not change the asymptotic complexity of the rasterization pass. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond the standard Gaussian parameters and the scalar parameters \tau and m. Strengths: It solves the vanishing gradient problem in dynamic scenes, allowing Gaussians to receive updates even when they are distant or rapidly moving, which improves optimization stability and final reconstruction quality for dynamic content. Limitations: Incorrect application (ignoring the loss sign guard) can cause Gaussians to repel each other, leading to instability. It is specifically beneficial for dynamic scenes; for static scenes with small displacements, the benefit may be marginal compared to the added computational overhead. TruncGradGS was introduced in the paper "TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates" by T. Morales, N.-Q. Le-Pham, R. Atkins & B.-S. Hua, published in the Proceedings of Eurographics (2026). It addresses limitations identified in standard 3DGS rasterization where the exponential falloff of the Gaussian distribution causes gradients to vanish for pixels outside the immediate support, a problem exacerbated in dynamic methods like 4DGS. name: EfficientGS
head: EfficientGS
body: EfficientGS is an optimized adaptation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed for efficient large-scale, high-resolution scene representation. It reduces redundancy in 3DGS to alleviate computational and storage demands without sacrificing quality. Unlike vanilla 3DGS, which suffers from redundancy and low FPS/high storage in large-scale high-resolution scenes, EfficientGS allows for more efficient scene representation with fewer Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse point cloud obtained via Structure-From-Motion (SFM). Output: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the scene, optimized for size and rendering speed. Data Structures: Each 3D Gaussian g is defined by: Mean position \mu. Covariance matrix \Sigma. Opacity. View-dependent color represented by Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. The covariance matrix \Sigma is decomposed into rotation and scaling components to ensure positive semi-definiteness during optimization: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T where R is the rotation matrix and S is the scaling matrix. The Gaussian function is defined as: G(x) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)} where x is an arbitrary position in the scene. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from sparse SFM points. 2. Iterative Optimization: Perform differentiable rasterization and optimize Gaussian parameters using color loss. 3. Selective Densification: Every few iterations, determine if a Gaussian has reached a steady state. If not (non-steady state), densify it. This focuses on non-steady state Gaussians based on their gradient modulus sum to minimize unnecessary cloning and splitting. 4. Pruning: After several densifications, remove auxiliary Gaussians that have minimal contribution to sight rays. This eliminates representational redundancy and optimizes the Spherical Harmonics (SH) of remaining Gaussians. 5. Sparse SH Order Increment: Do not start increasing SH order until after pruning. Every few iterations, assess the need for higher-order SH for each Gaussian based on color disparity from different viewing angles. Gradually increase the SH order only where needed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def efficientgstraining(sfmpoints, images, cameraposes, numiterations): # 1. Initialization gaussians = initializefromsfm(sfmpoints) # 2. Iterative Optimization Loop for iteration in range(numiterations): # Render current view renderedimage = render(gaussians, cameraposes) # Compute loss loss = computecolorloss(renderedimage, images) # Backpropagate and update parameters updateparameters(gaussians, loss) # 3. Selective Densification (Every few iterations) if iteration % densificationinterval == 0: # Calculate gradient modulus sum for each Gaussian gradsum = computegradientmodulussum(gaussians) # Identify non-steady state Gaussians nonsteady = selectnonsteadygaussians(gradsum, threshold) # Densify only non-steady Gaussians gaussians = densify(gaussians, nonsteady) # 4. Pruning (After several densifications) if iteration % pruninginterval == 0: # Remove auxiliary Gaussians with minimal contribution gaussians = prunegaussians(gaussians, raycontributionthreshold) # Optimize SH of remaining Gaussians optimizesh(gaussians) # 5. Sparse SH Order Increment (After pruning) if iteration > pruningstartiteration: if iteration % shincrementinterval == 0: # Assess need for higher-order SH based on color disparity colordisparity = computecolordisparity(gaussians, images) # Increase SH order only where needed gaussians = incrementshorder(gaussians, colordisparity, threshold) return gaussians Parameters: Densification Trigger: Based on gradient modulus sum to identify non-steady state Gaussians. SH Order Increment Trigger: Based on color disparity from different viewing angles. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Memory Pressure: Starting SH order increment too early increases GPU memory pressure. EfficientGS delays this until after pruning to mitigate this. Redundancy: Vanilla 3DGS suffers from redundancy in large-scale high-resolution scenes. EfficientGS addresses this through selective densification and pruning. Model Size: Approximately tenfold smaller than conventional 3DGS. Performance: Expedites training and rendering times for large-scale, high-resolution scenes (e.g., 4K+ aerial images). Quality: Maintains high rendering fidelity despite the reduction in Gaussian count. Strengths: Reduces computational and storage demands; improves rendering quality by focusing on non-steady state Gaussians; streamlines scene representation by eliminating non-dominant Gaussians. Limitations: Not given in the sources. EfficientGS was introduced to address the challenges posed by the proliferation of high-resolution aerial photography (often exceeding 4K) in 3DGS training and rendering for large-scale scenes. Traditional mesh-based methods struggle with non-Lambertian surfaces, while vanilla 3DGS suffers from redundancy and high storage requirements in such contexts. EfficientGS leverages the representational capacity of individual Gaussians to significantly reduce redundancy. name: Variational 3D Gaussians
head: Variational Gaussian Splatting, latentSplat
body: Variational 3D Gaussians encode a scene as a set of N semantic 3D Gaussians where uncertainty is modeled by storing parameters for a normal distribution of spherical harmonic coefficients rather than explicit feature vectors. This approach allows the representation of a distribution of possible 3D reconstructions conditioned on reference views, enabling consistent multi-view rendering of specific samples while providing plausible details in regions outside the reference view frustums. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by replacing deterministic feature vectors with probabilistic distributions over spherical harmonic coefficients, facilitating gradient backpropagation through sampling operations. Inputs: Two reference view images I1, I2 and their corresponding camera poses. A target camera pose for novel view synthesis. Outputs: A set of N variational Gaussians \mathcal{G}. Rendered feature images \mathbf{F} and RGB images for the target view. The scene is represented as a set of N variational Gaussians: \mathcal {G} = \{(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {S}, \mathbf {R}, o, \mathbf {c}, \mathbf {h}\mu, \mathbf {h}\sigma)i\}{1\leq i \leq N} Each Gaussian i contains the following fields: \mathbf {x} \in \mathbb {R}^3: Three-dimensional location (mean). \mathbf {S} \in \mathbb {R}^{3\times 3}: Diagonal scale matrix. \mathbf {R} \in \mathbb {R}^{3\times 3}: Orientation matrix. o \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf {c} \in \mathbb {R}^K: Spherical harmonic coefficients for view-dependent colors. \mathbf {h}\mu \in \mathbb {R}^4: Mean of the normal distribution for semantic features. \mathbf {h}\sigma \in \mathbb {R}^4: Standard deviation of the normal distribution for semantic features. The covariance matrix \mathbf{C} is derived from scale and rotation as: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^\top \mathbf{R}^\top The feature distributions are modeled as \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{h}\mu, \text{diag}(\mathbf{h}\sigma)). 1. Encoding: An encoder (adapted from pixelSplat) predicts the parameters \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{R}, o, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{h}\mu, \mathbf{h}\sigma for N Gaussians based on the input reference views I1, I2 and their poses. The encoder predicts Gaussians within the field of view of the two reference views. 2. Sampling Semantic Gaussians: To render a specific reconstruction, explicit spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{h} for the semantic features are sampled from the variational distributions using the reparameterization trick: \mathbf {h} = \mathbf {h}\mu + \epsilon \cdot \mathbf {h}\sigma \quad \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal {N}(0, \mathbf {1}) This step produces a set of "semantic Gaussians" with deterministic features \mathbf{h}, allowing consistent multi-view rendering of one possible reconstruction. Gradients backpropagate from the sampled coefficients to the reference view encoder. 3. Rendering: The set of semantic Gaussians is rendered using an efficient Gaussian splatting renderer. The renderer is extended to handle feature vectors in addition to RGB colors. The spherical harmonic basis is used to decode the per-Gaussian coefficients \mathbf{h} into view-dependent features. These features are splatted into pixel space. 4. Filling Empty Regions: Regions in the rendered image that have no Gaussians (because they are outside all reference view frustums) are filled by sampling from a normal distribution: \mathbf {F} = \mathbf {F}^\textnormal {ren} + \sqrt {1-\mathbf {O}}\odot \epsilon \,, \quad \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal {N}(\mathbf {0}, \mathbf {1}) where \mathbf {F} is the final feature image, \mathbf {F}^\textnormal {ren} is the rendered features from existing Gaussians, and \mathbf {O} is the opacity. This provides plausible reconstruction details for empty areas, supported by a GAN-based decoder. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def samplesemanticgaussians(variationalgaussians): """ Converts variational Gaussians to semantic Gaussians by sampling features. Args: variationalgaussians: List of dicts, each containing: 'x': (3,) location 'S': (3,3) diagonal scale matrix 'R': (3,3) orientation matrix 'o': float opacity 'c': (K,) color SH coefficients 'hmu': (4,) feature mean 'hsigma': (4,) feature std dev Returns: semanticgaussians: List of dicts with same structure, but 'h' replaces 'hmu'/'hsigma' """ semanticgaussians = [] for g in variationalgaussians: # Sample epsilon from standard normal distribution epsilon = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=4) # Reparameterization trick h = g['hmu'] + epsilon g['hsigma'] # Create semantic Gaussian semanticg = { 'x': g['x'], 'S': g['S'], 'R': g['R'], 'o': g['o'], 'c': g['c'], 'h': h # Explicit feature vector } semanticgaussians.append(semanticg) return semanticgaussians def renderwithfilling(semanticgaussians, camerapose, imageshape): """ Renders semantic Gaussians and fills empty regions. Args: semanticgaussians: List of semantic Gaussians (output of samplesemanticgaussians) camerapose: Camera extrinsics/intrinsics imageshape: (H, W, C) target image shape Returns: F: (H, W, C) final feature image O: (H, W, 1) opacity mask """ # Initialize rendered features and opacity to zero Fren = np.zeros(imageshape) O = np.zeros((imageshape[0], imageshape[1], 1)) # Splat semantic Gaussians into pixel space # Note: In practice, this involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D, # computing 2D covariance, and accumulating contributions. # Here we assume a function that performs standard Gaussian splatting # for both color (c) and features (h). for g in semanticgaussians: # Decode view-dependent features using spherical harmonics # h is the sampled feature mean; c is for color # This step produces a feature vector per pixel covered by the Gaussian viewdependentfeatures = decodesphericalharmonics(g['h'], camerapose, g['x']) viewdependentcolor = decodesphericalharmonics(g['c'], camerapose, g['x']) # Splat into Fren and O # Accumulate weighted features and opacity # This is a simplified representation of the splatting process splatmask, weights = projectandcomputeweights(g, camerapose, imageshape) Fren += weights[:,:, np.newaxis] viewdependentfeatures O += weights[:,:, np.newaxis] g['o'] # Normalize opacity if necessary (depending on alpha compositing implementation) # O is typically the accumulated opacity # Fill empty regions # Sample epsilon epsilon = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=imageshape) # Reparameterization trick for empty areas # sqrt(1 - O) ensures that where opacity is high, less noise is added F = Fren + np.sqrt(np.maximum(1 - O.squeeze(), 0))[:,:, np.newaxis] epsilon return F, O def decodesphericalharmonics(coefficients, camerapose, location): """ Decodes spherical harmonic coefficients into a view-dependent vector. Args: coefficients: (K,) SH coefficients camerapose: Camera orientation relative to Gaussian location: 3D location of Gaussian Returns: vector: (C,) view-dependent feature/color vector """ # Compute spherical harmonic basis functions for the viewing direction # This depends on the order of SH (e.g., order 3 has 16 coefficients) # For simplicity, assume coefficients are already ordered and basis is computed basis = computeshbasis(camerapose, location) # Dot product to get the value vector = np.dot(basis, coefficients) return vector def computeshbasis(camerapose, location): """ Computes spherical harmonic basis functions for a given viewing direction. Args: camerapose: Camera orientation (e.g., rotation matrix or quaternion) location: 3D location of Gaussian Returns: basis: (K,) array of SH basis values """ # Extract viewing direction from camera pose and location # direction = normalize(cameraposition - location) # Convert direction to spherical coordinates (theta, phi) # Compute SH basis functions Yl^m(theta, phi) # This is a placeholder for the actual SH math # For order 3, K=16 K = 16 basis = np.zeros(K) #... actual SH basis computation... return basis N: Number of Gaussians. Not given in the sources. K: Dimension of spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Not given in the sources. Feature dimension: 4 (for \mathbf{h}\mu, \mathbf{h}\sigma). \epsilon: Standard normal noise \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{1}). Empty Regions: When rendering novel views, regions may have no Gaussians because they are outside all reference view frustums. These areas must be filled by sampling from a normal distribution based on rendered features and opacity to provide plausible reconstruction. Gradient Flow: The reparameterization trick is essential for backpropagating gradients from the sampled coefficients to the reference view encoder. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Models uncertainty in feature space; provides plausible details in unseen regions via probabilistic filling; allows consistent multi-view rendering of specific samples. Limitations: Requires a GAN-based decoder for plausible filling in empty areas; uncertainty modeling adds complexity to the representation. When to use: When dealing with limited reference views (e.g., two views) and needing to synthesize novel views with plausible details in occluded or unseen regions. When not to use: When high-fidelity deterministic features are required without probabilistic modeling; when computational resources for GAN decoding are unavailable. Variational 3D Gaussians were introduced in the paper "latentSplat: Latent 3D Gaussian Splatting for Memory Efficient Novel View Synthesis" by C. Wewer et al.. The method adapts the encoder from pixelSplat to predict variational Gaussian parameters. It is used for novel view synthesis from a small number of reference views, leveraging the efficiency of Gaussian splatting. latentSplat, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16292, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splatting Training with SDS Loss
head: SDS-based Gaussian Splatting Training, Score Distillation Sampling for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: This method optimizes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene parameters using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from a pretrained 2D diffusion model, enabling text-to-3D generation without ground-truth images. It differs from supervised 3DGS training by replacing L1 pixel loss with a diffusion-based gradient signal that guides the 3D structure to match a text prompt, while retaining the differentiable splatting renderer for gradient backpropagation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A text prompt, a pretrained Stable Diffusion 2.1 model (VAE, Text Encoder, UNet, DDIM Scheduler), and an initial set of 3D Gaussians (typically initialized from a point cloud). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters: means, colors, opacities, and scales. Data Structures: The scene consists of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian is defined by: Mean: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation: q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Scale: s \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity: \alpha \in [0, 1] Color: c \in \mathbb{R}^3 (SH coefficients or RGB) Parameters are stored as "pre-activation" values to ensure constraints during optimization: preactopacities: Optimized variable; opacity is \sigma(\text{pre\act\opacities}). preactscales: Optimized variable; scale is \exp(\text{pre\act\scales}). preactquats: Optimized variable; rotation is \text{normalize}(\text{pre\act\quats}). colours: Optimized variable; direct RGB values. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load Stable Diffusion 2.1 components: VAE, tokenizer, text encoder, UNet, and DDIM scheduler. Initialize Gaussians from point cloud data with isotropic=True. Enable gradient tracking for means, colours, preactopacities, and preactscales. 2. Rendering: Render the scene using differentiable Gaussian splatting. Project 3D Gaussians to 2D: Compute 2D covariance: C{2D} = J W C{3D} W^T J^T, where J is the Jacobian of the projection, W is the view matrix, and C{3D} is the 3D covariance derived from quaternions and scales. Add 0.3 to diagonal elements of C{2D} to ensure minimum pixel coverage. Compute 2D means: \mu{2D} = \text{transform\points\screen}(\mu{3D}). Compute alpha values for each pixel: Calculate Mahalanobis distance: P = -0.5 (\mathbf{x} - \mu{2D})^T C{2D}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mu{2D}). Compute \alpha = \min(0.99, \max(0, \sigma(\text{opacity}) \cdot \exp(P))). Composite colors using alpha blending with transmittance Ti = \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj). Output rendered image I{rendered} with background (0,0,0). 3. SDS Loss Computation: Encode Image: Normalize I{rendered} from [0, 1] to [-1, 1]. Encode via VAE to get latent z. Scale by s{vae}: z{scaled} = z \cdot s{vae}. Encode Text: Tokenize prompt with padding to maxlength. Pass through text encoder to get text embedding t. Diffusion Step: Sample timestep t{step} uniformly from [0.02 \cdot T, 0.98 \cdot T], where T is total timesteps. Add noise to z{scaled} to get zt at timestep t{step}. Predict noise \epsilon\theta(zt, t{step}, t) using UNet. Compute SDS gradient: \nabla{z{scaled}} \mathbb{E}{\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)} [w(t) (\epsilon\theta(zt, t{step}, t) - \epsilon)]. Guidance scale s = 100. Backpropagate: Compute gradient of SDS loss w.r.t. I{rendered}. Backpropagate through the differentiable splatting renderer to update Gaussian parameters. 4. Optimization Step: Update parameters using Adam optimizer (\epsilon = 10^{-15}). Zero gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Load Diffusion Model pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.frompretrained("stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1-base") pipe = pipe.to("cuda") vae = pipe.vae textencoder = pipe.textencoder tokenizer = pipe.tokenizer unet = pipe.unet scheduler = pipe.scheduler # 2. Initialize Optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([ {'params': gaussians.means, 'lr': 0.001}, {'params': gaussians.colours, 'lr': 0.01}, {'params': gaussians.preactopacities, 'lr': 0.01}, {'params': gaussians.preactscales, 'lr': 0.01} ], eps=1e-15) # 3. Training Loop for i in range(numiterations): # Render Scene camera = getrandomcamera() # Helper to get random view renderedimage = renderscene(gaussians, camera) # Differentiable splatting # Encode Image imgnormalized = renderedimage 2.0 - 1.0 # [0,1] to [-1,1] with torch.nograd(): latentdist = vae.encode(imgnormalized) latent = latentdist.sample() vae.config.scalingfactor # Encode Text textinput = tokenizer(prompt, padding="maxlength", maxlength=tokenizer.modelmaxlength, returntensors="pt") with torch.nograd(): textemb = textencoder(textinput.inputids.to("cuda"))[0] # SDS Loss t = torch.randint(0, scheduler.config.numtraintimesteps, (1,)).item() noise = torch.randnlike(latent) latentnoisy = scheduler.addnoise(latent, noise, t) with torch.nograd(): noisepred = unet(latentnoisy, t, encoderhiddenstates=textemb).sample # Compute SDS gradient # w(t) is typically (1 - alphat) or similar weighting from scheduler wt = scheduler.alphascumprod[t].sqrt() / (1 - scheduler.alphascumprod[t]) # Approximation grad = wt (noisepred - noise) # Backpropagate through VAE decoder to image space # Note: In practice, gradients are often computed via the VAE decoder's output # or by approximating the gradient w.r.t. the image directly. # Here we assume a helper computegradwrtimage exists which backprops # from the latent noise prediction to the image pixels. gradimage = computegradwrtimage(vae, grad, latent) # Backpropagate through Renderer gradimage = gradimage.detach() # If using straight-through or if gradients are handled differently # Actually, we need gradients w.r.t. Gaussians. # renderedimage.requiresgrad = True is not needed if we backprop from gradimage # But renderedimage is a function of Gaussians. # Compute loss and backprop loss = (renderedimage gradimage).mean() # Simplified gradient application loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() if i % 20 == 0: visualize(gaussians) def computegradwrtimage(vae, gradlatent, latent): # Decode latent to image to get gradients w.r.t. image # This is a simplified representation. In reality, one might use # the VAE decoder's gradients directly. with torch.enablegrad(): latent.requiresgrad = True imagedecoded = vae.decode(latent / vae.config.scalingfactor).sample loss = (imagedecoded gradlatent).mean() loss.backward() return latent.grad Parameters: Learning rates: preactopacities=0.01, preactscales=0.01, colours=0.01, means=0.001. Training iterations: 1000. SDS Guidance scale: 100. SDS Inference steps: 50 (default in scheduler). SDS Timestep range: [0.02 T, 0.98 T]. Precision: torch.float32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: Alphas are clamped to [0, 0.99] and transmittance to [0, 10^{-4}] to prevent NaNs. Precision: Using float32 is critical for diffusion model stability. Boundary Conditions: Background color is set to (0,0,0) to avoid interference with SDS gradients. Time Complexity: Dominated by the diffusion model inference (UNet forward pass) per iteration. Rendering is O(N \cdot H \cdot W) but optimized via sorting and rasterization. Memory Complexity: O(N) for Gaussian parameters plus memory for the diffusion model (approx. 6-10 GB for SD 2.1). Performance: Slower than supervised 3DGS due to diffusion inference, but faster than NeRF-based SDS methods due to efficient splatting. Strengths: High-quality text-to-3D generation, fast convergence compared to NeRFs, explicit scene representation. Limitations: Requires large GPU memory for diffusion model, potential for "over-saturation" or artifacts if guidance scale is too high. name: EnvMap-GS
head: two-stage outdoor Gaussian reconstruction with background-to-environment map baking
body: EnvMap-GS is a two-stage Gaussian Splatting framework designed to reconstruct outdoor "inside-out" captures where a camera moves within a restricted navigation area while looking outward at a distant environment. It explicitly separates foreground and background regions to eliminate "floaters" (large, erroneous Gaussians in the far field) caused by incorrect initialization and limited view ranges. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which struggles with far-field reconstruction, EnvMap-GS constrains background primitives to a spherical shell and allows the background to be baked into an environment map for faster rendering. Inputs: A sequence of images or video frames captured in a restricted area; a metric monocular depth estimation model (e.g., Video Depth Anything). Outputs: A set of foreground Gaussians, a set of background Gaussians, and optionally an inpainted environment map. Data Structures: Camera Poses: 4 \times 4 transformation matrices from COLMAP. Sparse Point Cloud: 3D points from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Dense Metric Depth Maps: Per-image depth maps from MMDE. Distance-from-Center (DFC) Maps: Image-aligned maps storing the Euclidean distance of unprojected 3D points to the scene center O. Gaussian Primitives: Defined by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma (or rotation R and scale S), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{lm}. Parameters: O: World system center, placed at the barycenter of camera positions. Ri: Inner radius threshold for foreground-background segmentation. Ro: Outer radius of the background spherical shell. Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Run Structure-from-Motion (COLMAP) on input images to obtain camera poses and a 3D sparse point cloud. Set the world center O to the barycenter of the camera positions. 2. Depth Estimation: Estimate dense metric depth maps for each input image using a metric monocular depth estimation (MMDE) method, such as Video Depth Anything. 3. Distance Map Creation: For each image, unproject every pixel's depth value into 3D space using the corresponding camera pose. Compute the Euclidean distance of each resulting 3D point to the center O. Store these distances in image-aligned Distance-from-Center (DFC) maps. 4. Segmentation: Determine the threshold Ri. Estimate the histogram of distances in the DFC maps with a binning interval of 10 meters. Set Ri to the distance value corresponding to the first bin where the point count is less than 2.5% of the total reconstructed points. Classify points with distance < Ri as foreground and points with distance \ge Ri as background. 5. Stage 1 Initialization (Background): Create a geodesic sphere point cloud. Initialize background Gaussians within a spherical shell defined by inner radius Ri and outer radius Ro. 6. Stage 1 Optimization: Optimize the background Gaussians using a loss function combining: A background-only photometric term. A shell constraint loss L{shell}, constraining Gaussians to remain inside the shell [Ri, Ro]. A planarity loss L{planarity}, aligning Gaussians with local tangential planes. 7. Stage 1 Pruning: Apply a modified pruning strategy that preserves large, stable Gaussians necessary for representing distant scenery. 8. Stage 2 Initialization (Foreground): Initialize foreground Gaussians from the filtered SfM sparse point cloud, containing only the foreground points identified in Step 4. 9. Stage 2 Optimization: Add and refine foreground Gaussians using the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering loss. The background set remains fixed during this stage but contributes to the final image formation. 10. Environment Map Conversion (Optional): Render the background Gaussians to an object-free environment map. Inpaint the map to fill missing parts. This map can replace the Gaussian-based background for faster rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def envmapgspipeline(images, mmdemodel): # Step 1: Pre-processing cameraposes, sparsecloud = runcolmap(images) O = barycenter(cameraposes) # Step 2: Depth Estimation depthmaps = [mmdemodel.predict(img) for img in images] # Step 3: Distance Map Creation dfcmaps = [] for imgidx, (img, pose, depthmap) in enumerate(zip(images, cameraposes, depthmaps)): # Unproject depth to 3D points points3d = unprojectdepth(depthmap, pose) # Compute distance to center O distances = computedistances(points3d, O) dfcmaps.append(distances) # Step 4: Segmentation # Estimate histogram with 10m bins alldistances = [d for dm in dfcmaps for d in dm.flatten()] histogram = computehistogram(alldistances, binsize=10.0) totalpoints = len(alldistances) # Find first bin with count < 2.5% of total Ri = 0 for bincenter, count in histogram: if count < 0.025 totalpoints: Ri = bincenter break # Classify SfM points foregroundpoints = [p for p in sparsecloud if distance(p, O) < Ri] backgroundpoints = [p for p in sparsecloud if distance(p, p, O) >= Ri] # Step 5: Stage 1 Initialization # Create geodesic sphere point cloud for background initialization geodesicsphere = creategeodesicsphere(O, Ri, Ro) backgroundgaussians = initializegaussians(geodesicsphere, shellrange=(Ri, Ro)) # Step 6: Stage 1 Optimization # Optimize background Gaussians for epoch in range(numepochsstage1): # Render background only bgimage = rendergaussians(backgroundgaussians, cameraposes) # Compute losses photometricloss = computephotometricloss(bgimage, backgroundimages) shellloss = computeshellconstraintloss(backgroundgaussians, Ri, Ro) planarityloss = computeplanarityloss(backgroundgaussians) totalloss = photometricloss + shellloss + planarityloss # Update Gaussians via gradient descent backgroundgaussians = optimize(backgroundgaussians, totalloss) # Step 7: Stage 1 Pruning backgroundgaussians = prunegaussians(backgroundgaussians, preservelarge=True) # Step 8: Stage 2 Initialization foregroundgaussians = initializegaussians(foregroundpoints) # Step 9: Stage 2 Optimization for epoch in range(numepochsstage2): # Render full scene (fixed background + optimized foreground) fullimage = rendergaussians(backgroundgaussians + foregroundgaussians, cameraposes) # Standard GS loss loss = computerenderingloss(fullimage, images) # Update only foreground Gaussians foregroundgaussians = optimize(foregroundgaussians, loss) # Step 10: Environment Map Conversion (Optional) envmap = rendergaussians(backgroundgaussians, sphericalcameraposes) envmap = inpaint(envmap) return foregroundgaussians, backgroundgaussians, envmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Sensitivity: While the heuristic for Ri works for most scenes, it is scene-dependent. Changing Ri within reasonable ranges does not significantly affect novel view synthesis metrics. Metric Scale: MMDE methods are independent of the SfM reconstruction, so global metric scale alignment is not required. Floaters: Standard GS fails in the far field due to densification choices and limited view ranges. EnvMap-GS addresses this by constraining background Gaussians to a shell. Converting the optimized background Gaussians into a 2D environment map to accelerate rendering. This replaces the Gaussian-based background with a static texture, reducing computational load during novel view synthesis. Using a geodesic sphere point cloud to initialize background Gaussians ensures uniform coverage of the spherical shell, avoiding clustering artifacts common in random initialization. Time Complexity: Two-stage optimization increases training time compared to single-stage GS. Stage 1 optimizes background Gaussians with additional geometric losses; Stage 2 optimizes foreground Gaussians with standard loss. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for foreground and background Gaussians separately, plus DFC maps and depth maps during preprocessing. Performance: Reduces background artifacts and improves perceptual quality of novel view renderings compared to state-of-the-art baselines, specifically removing floaters in the navigation region. Strengths: Effective for outdoor "inside-out" captures; eliminates far-field floaters; enables faster rendering via environment map baking. Limitations: Requires metric depth estimation; assumes a restricted navigation area; background is constrained to a spherical shell, which may not fit all outdoor scenes perfectly. EnvMap-GS was introduced to address the challenges of reconstructing outdoor environments from "inside-out" captures, where a camera moves within a restricted area but looks outward. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting suffers from "floaters" in the far field due to incorrect initialization and densification choices, as well as limited view ranges. The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [7] and extends it with geometric constraints and a two-stage optimization process. It is particularly relevant for real-time applications requiring high-fidelity novel view synthesis of large outdoor scenes. name: Thermal-Physics-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: TPI-GS
body: Thermal-Physics-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting (TPI-GS) is a framework that embeds infrared radiative transfer modeling into the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation, transforming Gaussian primitives into thermophysical radiative elements to enable physically interpretable infrared scene representation and novel view synthesis. Unlike standard 3DGS, which relies on view-dependent color blending via spherical harmonics to approximate photometric appearance, TPI-GS replaces this with physics-driven radiance integration based on Planck’s law, explicitly modeling atmospheric attenuation and sensor response. This approach bridges classical infrared simulation theory with neural point-based rendering, allowing for joint optimization of geometric structure and thermal radiation fields under multi-view supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view infrared images of a scene; initial 3D Gaussian point cloud (position, covariance, opacity) derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) or similar initialization. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives parameterized by geometric attributes and thermophysical fields, capable of rendering novel-view infrared images with radiometric coherence. Data Structures: Each 3D Gaussian primitive i is augmented with the following learnable parameters in addition to the standard 3DGS geometric parameters (position \mathbf{p}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai): 1. Emissivity (\epsiloni): A scalar or vector parameter modeling surface thermal radiation properties. 2. Temperature (Ti): A scalar parameter modeling the thermal state of the primitive. 3. Thermal Texture (\mathbf{t}i): A parameter (typically a low-frequency coefficient or texture map value) modeling spatial thermal variations. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Thermophysical Parameterization: Initialize each Gaussian primitive with learnable emissivity \epsiloni, temperature Ti, and thermal texture \mathbf{t}i. These parameters are optimized jointly with geometric parameters. 2. Spectral Radiant Exitance Calculation: For each Gaussian primitive, compute the spectral radiant exitance M\lambda using Planck’s law. The spectral radiance L\lambda emitted by the primitive is derived from this exitance, accounting for the emissivity \epsiloni: L\lambda = \epsiloni \cdot \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \frac{1}{e^{\frac{hc}{\lambda kB Ti}} - 1} Where: h is Planck’s constant. c is the speed of light. kB is Boltzmann’s constant. \lambda is the wavelength of the infrared radiation. Ti is the temperature of the primitive. \epsiloni is the emissivity of the primitive. 3. Radiance Accumulation (Rendering): Render the infrared image by accumulating radiance along the viewing ray. Unlike standard 3DGS which blends spherical harmonic coefficients, TPI-GS performs physics-driven radiance integration. The total radiance L{total} reaching the camera is computed by summing the contributions of all splatted Gaussians, modified by atmospheric attenuation and sensor response: L{total} = \sum{i \in \text{front-to-back}} \alphai \cdot L{\lambda, i} \cdot \tau{atm} + L{background} Where: \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. L{\lambda, i} is the spectral radiance of the i-th Gaussian (from Step 2). \tau{atm} is the atmospheric transmittance factor, explicitly modeled to account for path-dependent attenuation. L{background} accounts for background radiance and sensor noise/response. 4. Frequency-Domain Supervision: To mitigate the inherent smoothing effect of Gaussian splatting and improve high-frequency texture fidelity, apply a Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) to the rendered infrared images and the ground truth. Compute a loss in the frequency domain to supervise the reconstruction. 5. Joint Optimization: Optimize the geometric parameters (\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{q}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai) and thermophysical parameters (\epsiloni, Ti, \mathbf{t}i) simultaneously using gradient descent. The loss function combines photometric error (in infrared space) and the DWT-based frequency supervision loss, under multi-view constraints. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import pywt # PyWavelets for DWT def planckradiance(wavelength, temperature, emissivity): """ Computes spectral radiance using Planck's law. wavelength: float or tensor, wavelength in meters. temperature: float or tensor, temperature in Kelvin. emissivity: float or tensor, emissivity value. """ h = 6.62607015e-34 # Planck's constant c = 299792458.0 # Speed of light kB = 1.380649e-23 # Boltzmann constant exponent = (h c) / (wavelength kB temperature) # Avoid division by zero or overflow exponent = torch.clamp(exponent, max=700) spectralexitance = (2 h c2) / (wavelength5) / (torch.exp(exponent) - 1) return emissivity spectralexitance def rendertpigs(gaussians, cameraparams, wavelength, atmosphericmodel): """ Renders an infrared image using TPI-GS principles. gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives with attributes: position (N, 3) rotation (N, 4) scale (N, 3) opacity (N, 1) emissivity (N, 1) temperature (N, 1) thermaltexture (N, 1) # Simplified as a scalar modifier for this example cameraparams: Camera intrinsic and extrinsic matrices. wavelength: float, central wavelength of the IR sensor. atmosphericmodel: Function or object providing transmittance tau(d) for distance d. """ # 1. Project Gaussians to 2D and sort by depth (standard 3DGS rasterization) # This step is implementation-specific to the 3DGS backend. # Assume 'rasterizedgaussians' contains the sorted list of visible Gaussians # with their projected 2D centers, covariances, and depths. rasterizedgaussians = projectandsort(gaussians, cameraparams) imageheight, imagewidth = cameraparams.imagesize # Initialize output image renderedimage = torch.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth), device=gaussians.position.device) # 2. Accumulate Radiance for g in rasterizedgaussians: # Compute spectral radiance from thermophysical parameters # Note: In practice, this might be precomputed or interpolated from a texture Llambda = planckradiance(wavelength, g.temperature, g.emissivity) # Apply thermal texture modifier if applicable # Llambda = Llambda g.thermaltexture # Compute atmospheric attenuation based on depth tau = atmosphericmodel.gettransmittance(g.depth) # Effective radiance reaching the sensor Leffective = Llambda tau # Splat the Gaussian to the image plane with opacity and effective radiance # This is a simplified representation of the 3DGS splatting operation renderedimage = splatgaussian(renderedimage, g, Leffective, g.opacity) return renderedimage def computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage): """ Computes the total loss including photometric and frequency-domain terms. """ # Photometric loss (e.g., L1 or L2 in IR space) photometricloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimage - groundtruthimage)) # Frequency-domain supervision using DWT # Decompose both images coeffsrendered = pywt.dwt2(renderedimage.detach().cpu().numpy(), 'haar') coeffsgt = pywt.dwt2(groundtruthimage.detach().cpu().numpy(), 'haar') # Compute loss on wavelet coefficients (high-frequency details) # Approximation coefficients (cA) and detail coefficients (cH, cV, cD) lossfreq = 0 for cr, cg in zip(coeffsrendered, coeffsgt): lossfreq += torch.mean(torch.abs(torch.tensor(cr) - torch.tensor(cg))) totalloss = photometricloss + 0.1 lossfreq # Weight for frequency loss return totalloss Parameters: Wavelength (\lambda): Central wavelength of the infrared sensor. Typical values depend on the sensor (e.g., 8-14 \mum for long-wave infrared). Atmospheric Model: Parameters for transmittance \tau{atm}, which may depend on distance and atmospheric conditions. DWT Weight: Weighting factor for the frequency-domain supervision loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Planck’s law involves exponential terms that can overflow or underflow for extreme temperatures or wavelengths. Clamping or careful numerical handling is required. Degenerate Input: If emissivity is zero, the primitive contributes no radiance. If temperature is zero, radiance is zero. Initialization strategies (e.g., material priors) are needed to avoid degenerate states. Smoothing: Gaussian splatting inherently smooths high-frequency details. Without DWT supervision, the rendered infrared images may lack sharp thermal boundaries. Time Complexity: Rendering time is comparable to standard 3DGS, maintaining real-time efficiency, as the core rasterization pipeline is unchanged. The additional computation for Planck’s law and atmospheric attenuation is negligible per pixel. Memory Complexity: Increased memory usage due to the addition of emissivity, temperature, and thermal texture parameters per Gaussian primitive. Performance: Achieves superior infrared rendering quality with improved radiometric coherence and structural consistency compared to photometric-only methods. Strengths: Physically interpretable, enables cross-view infrared rendering, maintains real-time efficiency, mitigates smoothing effects via DWT. Limitations: Requires multi-view infrared images for training; assumes known or estimable atmospheric conditions; complexity of joint optimization. When to Use: When physically accurate infrared scene representation and novel view synthesis are required, especially for remote sensing or thermal analysis applications. When Not to Use: For visible-light rendering where photometric appearance is sufficient and physical thermal properties are irrelevant. TPI-GS was proposed to address the limitation of existing neural rendering frameworks like 3DGS, which primarily model photometric appearance and lack explicit thermophysical interpretability for infrared image formation. It embeds infrared radiative transfer modeling directly into the Gaussian representation, transforming 3DGS from a purely photometric renderer into a structured infrared scene representation. The method bridges classical infrared simulation theory with modern neural point-based scene representation.
