name: HDR Gaussian Splatting
head: HDR-GS, High Dynamic Range Gaussian Splatting
body: HDR Gaussian Splatting (HDR-GS) is a framework for 3D High Dynamic Range (HDR) imaging that renders novel HDR views and reconstructs Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images with user-controllable exposure time. It solves the problem of long training times and slow inference speeds associated with existing NeRF-based HDR Novel View Synthesis (NVS) methods. It sets itself apart by employing a Dual Dynamic Range (DDR) Gaussian point cloud model and two Parallel Differentiable Rasterization (PDR) processes to handle HDR and LDR rendering simultaneously. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed LDR images (typically from a dataset), camera poses (recalibrated from NDC to world coordinates), and an optional user-defined exposure time \Delta t for LDR reconstruction. Outputs: A rendered HDR image and a rendered LDR image corresponding to the input camera pose. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a set of Np Dual Dynamic Range (DDR) Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi \mid i = 1, \dots, Np\}. Each Gaussian Gi contains the following attributes: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. c{l,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3: LDR color. c{h,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3: HDR color. \Delta t \in \mathbb{R}: Exposure time (scalar controlling LDR intensity). \theta: Global MLP parameters shared across all Gaussians for tone-mapping. The covariance matrix \Sigmai is decomposed into a rotation matrix Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and a scaling matrix Si \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} as: \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top where Ri and Si are learnable parameters. The HDR color c{h,i} is view-dependent and modeled using Spherical Harmonics (SH). Let k = \{k{lm} \mid 0 \le l \le L, -l \le m \le l\} \in \mathbb{R}^{(L+1)^2 \times 3} be the SH coefficients, where each k{lm} \in \mathbb{R}^3 corresponds to RGB components. For a view direction d = (\theta, \phi), the HDR color is: c{h,i}(d, k) = \exp\left( \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} k{lm} Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) \right) where Y{lm}: S^2 \to \mathbb{R} are the SH basis functions. Steps: 1. Initialization: Recalibrate camera parameters from Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) to world coordinates using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to establish a suitable data foundation for 3DGS-based methods. Compute initial positions for the Gaussian point clouds. 2. Tone-Mapping Formulation: To avoid vanishing gradients and numerical overflow/underflow caused by direct multiplication in the linear domain, the tone-mapping function is transformed into the logarithmic domain. The relationship between LDR color cl, HDR color ch, and exposure time \Delta t is defined as: cl = f{TM}(ch \cdot \Delta t) Inverting this and taking the natural logarithm (\ln, base e): \log f{TM}^{-1}(cl) = \log cl + \log \Delta t The inverse function is reformulated as: cl = (\log f{TM}^{-1})^{-1}(\log ch + \log \Delta t). 3. MLP Tone-Mapper: Three independent MLPs with global parameters \theta model the function (\log f{TM}^{-1})^{-1} independently for each RGB channel. Define the mapping function g\theta(x) \triangleq (\log f{TM}^{-1})^{-1}(x). The LDR color is computed as: c{l,i} = g\theta(\log c{h,i} + \log \Delta t). 4. Parallel Differentiable Rasterization (PDR): The HDR colors c{h,i} and LDR colors c{l,i} are fed into two separate Parallel Differentiable Rasterization processes to render the final HDR and LDR images, respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sphericalharmonicseval(directiontheta, directionphi, coefficients, degree): """ Evaluates Spherical Harmonics for HDR color. directiontheta: float, polar angle directionphi: float, azimuthal angle coefficients: list of (l, m, klm) tuples where klm is np.array([R, G, B]) degree: int, L Returns: np.array([R, G, B]) """ color = np.zeros(3) for l in range(degree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Get klm for this l, m klm = None for (ll, mm, kval) in coefficients: if ll == l and mm == m: klm = kval break if klm is None: continue # Evaluate Ylm(theta, phi) # Note: Standard SH basis functions Ylm are used here. # Implementation details of Ylm depend on the specific SH library or formula. ylm = evaluateshbasis(l, m, directiontheta, directionphi) color += klm ylm # Apply exponential as per Eq. 7 return np.exp(color) def tonemapperloginverse(loghdrcolor, exposuretime, mlpr, mlpg, mlpb): """ Computes LDR color from HDR color and exposure time using learned MLPs. loghdrcolor: np.array([logR, logG, logB]) exposuretime: float mlpr, mlpg, mlpb: MLP functions for R, G, B channels Returns: np.array([R, G, B]) in LDR range """ logexposure = np.log(exposuretime) # Input to MLPs is log(ch) + log(deltat) inputr = loghdrcolor[0] + logexposure inputg = loghdrcolor[1] + logexposure inputb = loghdrcolor[2] + logexposure # Apply MLPs outr = mlpr(inputr) outg = mlpg(inputg) outb = mlpb(inputb) return np.array([outr, outg, outb]) def renderhdrgaussians(gaussians, camerapose, shcoefficients, degree): """ Renders HDR image using Parallel Differentiable Rasterization. gaussians: list of Gaussian objects with attributes mu, Sigma, alpha, shcoefficients camerapose: Camera transformation matrix shcoefficients: Global SH coefficients for each Gaussian degree: SH degree L Returns: HDR Image tensor """ # 1. Project Gaussians to 2D projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Project center mu to camera space mucam = transformpoint(g.mu, camerapose) # Project covariance Sigma # J is Jacobian of projection, W is view transform # Sigma2D = J W Sigma W^T J^T # (Implementation of 2D projection of 3D Gaussian) sigma2d = projectcovariance(g.Sigma, camerapose) projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu2d': project2d(g.mu, camerapose), 'sigma2d': sigma2d, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'shcoeffs': g.shcoefficients }) # 2. Rasterize # Sort by depth, iterate over pixels, accumulate splats # For each pixel, compute view direction d # Compute HDR color ch using SH # Accumulate color weighted by alpha and Gaussian PDF pass def renderldrgaussians(gaussians, camerapose, exposuretime, mlpr, mlpg, mlpb): """ Renders LDR image using Parallel Differentiable Rasterization. gaussians: list of Gaussian objects camerapose: Camera transformation matrix exposuretime: float mlpr, mlpg, mlpb: Tone-mapping MLPs Returns: LDR Image tensor """ # 1. Project Gaussians to 2D (Same as HDR) projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: mucam = transformpoint(g.mu, camerapose) sigma2d = projectcovariance(g.Sigma, camerapose) # Compute HDR color ch first (needed for tone mapping) # View direction d from camera to mucam d = normalize(mucam - cameraorigin) theta, phi = sphericalcoords(d) ch = sphericalharmonicseval(theta, phi, g.shcoefficients, g.degree) # Compute LDR color cl using tone mapper logch = np.log(ch + 1e-8) # Avoid log(0) cl = tonemapperloginverse(logch, exposuretime, mlpr, mlpg, mlpb) projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu2d': project2d(g.mu, camerapose), 'sigma2d': sigma2d, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'color': cl }) # 2. Rasterize LDR colors # Accumulate LDR color weighted by alpha and Gaussian PDF pass Parameters: Np: The number of 3D Gaussians in the scene representation. \Delta t: The exposure time, a scalar value \Delta t \in \mathbb{R} that controls the light intensity of the LDR view and can be read from photo metadata. L: The degree of Spherical Harmonics used for view-dependent HDR color. \theta: Global MLP parameters for the tone-mapper. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vanishing Gradients/Overflow: Directly modeling the tone-mapping function f{TM}(\cdot) in the linear domain can cause vanishing gradients and numerical overflow/underflow due to multiplication operations. The logarithmic transformation is required to mitigate this. NDC Coordinates: Existing datasets often provide camera poses in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC), which are not suitable for 3DGS-based methods. Recalibration to world coordinates is necessary. RGB Channel Independence: The tone-mapping function is modeled by three independent MLPs for RGB channels because RGB colors are tone-mapped by different Camera Response Functions (CRFs). A Gaussian point cloud model that stores both HDR and LDR color attributes, enabling simultaneous rendering of both dynamic ranges. A rendering technique that processes HDR and LDR colors through separate rasterization pipelines in parallel. A method to stabilize MLP training for tone-mapping by operating in the logarithmic domain to avoid numerical issues. Performance: HDR-GS surpasses state-of-the-art NeRF-based methods by 3.84 dB on LDR Novel View Synthesis (NVS) and 1.91 dB on HDR NVS. Speed: It achieves 1000× inference speed compared to HDR-NeRF, which takes 8.2 seconds to infer an image at 400×400 resolution. Training Time: HDR-GS requires only 6.3% of the training time compared to HDR-NeRF, which takes 9 hours to train. Strengths: High inference speed, significantly reduced training time, and user-controllable exposure for LDR reconstruction. Limitations: Requires recalibration of camera parameters from NDC to world coordinates for initialization. HDR-GS was proposed to address the limitations of NeRF-based HDR NVS methods, which suffer from long training times and slow inference speeds. It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework. The method introduces the Dual Dynamic Range (DDR) Gaussian point cloud model and Parallel Differentiable Rasterization (PDR) processes. It also addresses the issue of NDC camera poses in existing datasets by recalibrating them using Structure-from-Motion (SfM). HDR-GS: Efficient High Dynamic Range Novel View Synthesis at 1000x Speed via Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15125v4, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Parallel Differentiable Rasterization
head: F_HDR / F_LDR, HDR-GS rasterization
body: Parallel Differentiable Rasterization is a rendering technique that jointly generates High Dynamic Range (HDR) and Low Dynamic Range (LDR) views from a single set of 3D Gaussian primitives by employing two parallel differentiable rasterization pipelines (F{HDR} and F{LDR}). It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the color representation into HDR base values and LDR exposure-dependent values, allowing simultaneous optimization and rendering of both radiance ranges without tone-mapping artifacts during the differentiable process. Inputs: Gaussian point cloud parameters: \{\mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, c{hi}\}{i=1}^N, where \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the center, \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the covariance, \alphai \in [0,1] is the intrinsic opacity, and c{hi} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the HDR color. Camera matrices: Extrinsic M{ext} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} and Intrinsic M{int} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4}. LDR exposure time \Delta t. Outputs: Rendered HDR image Ih \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Rendered LDR image Il(\Delta t) \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Data Structures: Tiles: The image plane is divided into non-overlapping tiles. Gaussian List per Tile: A list of Gaussian indices assigned to each tile, sorted by view-space depth. Steps: 1. Probability Evaluation: For a point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, compute the probability density of the i-th Gaussian: P(x|\mui, \Sigmai) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)\right) 2. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the Gaussian center \mui from world to camera coordinates vi and then to image coordinates ui using homogeneous coordinates: \tilde{e}i = [vi, 1]^\top = M{ext} [\mui, 1]^\top \tilde{u}i = [ui, 1]^\top = M{int} vi Transform the 3D covariance \Sigmai to the camera coordinate system: \Sigma'i = Ji Wi \Sigmai Wi^\top Ji^\top where Ji \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation M{int}M{ext}, and Wi \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the viewing transformation (first three rows and columns of M{ext}). 3. 2D Covariance Derivation: Derive the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma''i \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} by directly skipping the third row and column of \Sigma'i. 4. Tiling and Sorting: Divide the 2D image into non-overlapping tiles. Assign each 3D Gaussian to the tiles where its 2D projection (defined by ui and \Sigma''i) overlaps. Within each tile, sort the assigned Gaussians by view-space depth. 5. Differentiable Blending: For each pixel p, identify the set of N ordered Gaussians overlapping the pixel in the corresponding tile. Compute the opacity contribution \sigmaj for the j-th Gaussian: \sigmaj = \alphaj P(xj|\muj, \Sigmaj) where xj is the intersection point between the ray from the camera optical center through pixel p and the j-th Gaussian. Compute the LDR color c{lj}(\Delta t) from the HDR color c{hj} using an MLP. The source specifies that channels of c{hi} undergo an independent MLP containing a fully connected layer, a ReLU activation, another fully connected layer, and a sigmoid activation to produce c{li}. Render the HDR image Ih(p) and LDR image Il(p|\Delta t) via alpha blending: Ih(p) = \sum{j \in N} c{hj} \sigmaj \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \sigmak) Il(p|\Delta t) = \sum{j \in N} c{lj}(\Delta t) \sigmaj \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \sigmak) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def paralleldifferentiablerasterization(gaussians, Mext, Mint, deltat): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu (3,), Sigma (3,3), alpha (float), chi (3,) Mext: (4, 4) extrinsic matrix Mint: (3, 4) intrinsic matrix deltat: float, exposure time for LDR Returns: Ih (H, W, 3), Il (H, W, 3) """ H, W = imageheight, imagewidth tilesize = 16 # Typical tile size, not specified in source numtilesx = (W + tilesize - 1) // tilesize numtilesy = (H + tilesize - 1) // tilesize # Initialize tile lists # tilegaussians[y][x] = list of gaussian indices tilegaussians = [[[] for in range(numtilesx)] for in range(numtilesy)] # Precompute transformed Gaussians transformedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # 1. Probability function definition (used later) # P(x|mu, Sigma) = exp(-0.5 (x-mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x-mu)) # 2. Coordinate Transformation # Homogeneous center muh = np.append(g.mu, 1.0) # World to Camera vh = Mext @ muh v = vh[:3] / vh[3] # Perspective division # Camera to Image uh = Mint @ vh u = uh[:2] / uh[2] # Perspective division # 3. Covariance Transformation # Ji: Jacobian of affine approximation of Mint @ Mext # Wi: First 3 rows/cols of Mext # Note: Source defines Sigma'i = Ji Wi Sigmai Wi^T Ji^T # Implementation detail: Ji is typically derived from the projection matrix. # For a standard pinhole camera, Ji relates to the derivative of projection. # We assume a helper function getjacobian(Mint, Mext, v) exists or is computed. Ji = getjacobian(Mint, Mext, v) Wi = Mext[:3,:3] Sigmaprime = Ji @ (Wi @ g.Sigma @ Wi.T) @ Ji.T # 4. 2D Covariance # Skip third row and column Sigmadoubleprime = Sigmaprime[:2,:2] transformedgaussians.append({ 'index': i, 'u': u, 'Sigma2d': Sigmadoubleprime, 'vdepth': v[2], # View space depth for sorting 'alpha': g.alpha, 'chi': g.chi, 'mu3d': g.mu, 'Sigma3d': g.Sigma }) # 5. Tiling and Assignment # Determine tile coordinates covering the Gaussian # Approximate bounding box using Sigma2d eigenvalues or fixed radius # Source says: "assigned to the tiles where their 2D projections cover" # We iterate over tiles that overlap the Gaussian's bounding box tilecoords = gettilescoveringgaussian(u, Sigmadoubleprime, tilesize, W, H) for ty, tx in tilecoords: tilegaussians[ty][tx].append(i) # Initialize output images Ih = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) Il = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) # 6. Blending for ty in range(numtilesy): for tx in range(numtilesx): tileidxlist = tilegaussians[ty][tx] if not tileidxlist: continue # Sort by view space depth tileidxlist.sort(key=lambda idx: transformedgaussians[idx]['vdepth']) # Define pixel range for this tile ystart, yend = ty tilesize, min((ty + 1) tilesize, H) xstart, xend = tx tilesize, min((tx + 1) tilesize, W) # For each pixel in the tile for y in range(ystart, yend): for x in range(xstart, xend): # Ray intersection points xj # Source: xj is the j-th intersection 3D point between the ray... and the Gaussian # In standard 3DGS, xj is often approximated as the Gaussian center projected, # or the intersection of the ray with the Gaussian ellipsoid. # The formula uses P(xj | mu, Sigma). # We need to find xj for each Gaussian in the tile that covers pixel (x,y). # Accumulators alphaacc = 1.0 colorh = np.zeros(3) colorl = np.zeros(3) for idx in tileidxlist: g = transformedgaussians[idx] # Check if Gaussian covers pixel (x,y) # Using Mahalanobis distance with Sigma2d # Point in local Gaussian space? No, xj is in world/camera space. # Standard 3DGS rasterization checks if pixel is within bounding box or uses density. # Here, we compute sigmaj = alphaj P(xj | muj, Sigmaj) # Determine xj: Intersection of ray from camera center through (x,y) with Gaussian j # Ray origin: Camera center (inverse of Mext) # Ray direction: Mint^-1 [x, y, 1] transformed to camera space # This is complex. Simplified approach often used in 3DGS: # xj is approximated as the Gaussian center muj if the ray passes close, # or computed via ellipsoid intersection. # Given the source formula, we assume xj is computed. xj = computeraygaussianintersection(g['mu3d'], g['Sigma3d'], cameracenter, raydirection) # Compute Probability diff = xj - g['mu3d'] prob = np.exp(-0.5 diff.T @ np.linalg.inv(g['Sigma3d']) @ diff) sigmaj = g['alpha'] prob if sigmaj <= 0: continue # Compute LDR color from HDR color via MLP # Source: channels of chi undergo independent MLP (fc, relu, fc, sigmoid) clj = applycolormlp(g['chi'], deltat) # Alpha blending weight = sigmaj alphaacc colorh += weight g['chi'] colorl += weight clj alphaacc = (1.0 - sigmaj) if alphaacc < 1e-4: # Early exit optimization break Ih[y, x] = colorh Il[y, x] = colorl return Ih, Il def applycolormlp(chi, deltat): """ Applies the MLP described in source to convert HDR color to LDR color. """ # Independent MLP per channel? Source says "channels... undergo an independent MLP" # This implies 3 separate MLPs or one MLP with 3 outputs? # "independent MLP containing a fully connected (fc) layer, a ReLU activation, # an fc layer, and a sigmoid activation" # Assuming weights are learned or fixed. Since not provided, we mark as placeholder for structure. # In implementation, these weights would be parameters. # For the purpose of this article, we define the structure. # Channel 0 h0 = np.dot(W10, chi) + b10 # fc layer h0 = np.maximum(0, h0) # ReLU cl0 = sigmoid(np.dot(W20, h0) + b20) # fc + sigmoid # Channel 1 h1 = np.dot(W11, chi) + b11 h1 = np.maximum(0, h1) cl1 = sigmoid(np.dot(W21, h1) + b21) # Channel 2 h2 = np.dot(W12, chi) + b12 h2 = np.maximum(0, h2) cl2 = sigmoid(np.dot(W22, h2) + b22) return np.array([cl0, cl1, cl2]) def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization step, which is O(N \cdot T) where N is the number of Gaussians and T is the number of tiles, assuming efficient tiling and sorting. The MLP application adds a constant factor per Gaussian per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Gaussian parameters and the tile lists. The parallel nature does not significantly increase memory overhead compared to single-pass rasterization, as the two passes share the same geometric data. Strengths: Enables simultaneous HDR and LDR rendering, which is crucial for training on HDR datasets and generating LDR outputs for standard displays without post-processing tone mapping. Limitations: Requires the additional MLP for LDR color conversion, adding slight computational overhead. The derivation of the 2D covariance by skipping the third row/column is an approximation that may introduce artifacts in extreme viewing angles. Parallel Differentiable Rasterization was introduced in the context of HDR-GS (HDR Gaussian Splatting) to address the lack of suitable 3DGS-based methods for 3D HDR imaging, particularly given that existing multiview HDR datasets often provide camera poses in the Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) system, which is unsuitable for standard 3DGS. name: Coupled Gaussian Primitives Rendering
head: Anchor-Coupled Primitive Rendering, CompGS rendering
body: Coupled Gaussian Primitives Rendering is a compact scene representation method that decomposes Gaussian primitives into anchor primitives and coupled primitives derived from them, enabling efficient storage and rendering via a custom rasterizer. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a hierarchical primitive structure where coupled primitives are predicted from anchor primitives, reducing the parameter count and facilitating compression. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of anchor primitives (defined by mean, scale, rotation, and features) and a camera view as input. It outputs a rendered image, along with metadata including projected means, visibility masks, and bit-per-pixel (bpp) statistics for compression. Data Structures: The core state is held in a GaussianParameters object (or self.gaussianparams in the implementation), which contains: numanchorprimitive: Integer count of anchor primitives. numcoupledprimitive: Integer count of coupled primitives. derivefactor: Integer, the number of coupled primitives derived from each anchor primitive. resfeatsdim: Integer, dimension of residual features. means: Tensor of shape (N, 3), dtype float32, representing 3D positions. scalesbeforeexp: Tensor of shape (N, 6), dtype float32. The first 3 components are log-scales for the anchor primitives; the remaining 3 are log-scales for the coupled primitives (or shared/derived depending on specific implementation, but typically coupled scales are derived or stored separately). Note: The source notes specify scalesbeforeexp shape (N, 6) and resfeats shape (N, K, D) where K is likely derivefactor. rotations: Tensor of shape (N, 4), dtype float32, unit quaternions. reffeats: Tensor of shape (N, C), reference features for anchor primitives. resfeats: Tensor of shape (N, K, D), residual features for coupled primitives, where K is derivefactor and D is resfeatsdim. coupleddenorm: Tensor of shape (NK, 1), normalization factors for coupled primitives. anchordenorm: Tensor of shape (N, 1), normalization factors for anchor primitives. accumulatedgrads: Tensor of shape (N, 1). accumulatedopacities: Tensor of shape (N, 1). The RenderSettings object includes: imageheight, imagewidth: Integers. tanfovx, tanfovy: Floats. viewmatrix: Tensor (4, 4). projmatrix: Tensor (4, 4). campos: Tensor (3,). backgroundcolor: Tensor (3,), default black [0, 0, 0]. Parameters: voxelsize: Size of voxels used for initialization and quantization of means. derivefactor: Number of coupled primitives derived from each anchor primitive. reffeatsdim: Dimension of reference features. refhyperdim: Dimension of hyper-priors for reference features. resfeatsdim: Dimension of residual features. reshyperdim: Dimension of hyper-priors for residual features. Steps: 1. Initialize Rasterizer: Create a GaussianRasterizationSettings object with imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, backgroundcolor, scalemodifier, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree=1, campos, prefiltered=False, and debug=False. 2. Prefilter Anchors: Call rasterizer.visiblefilter with means3D=self.means, scales=torch.exp(self.scalingfactorsbeforeexp[:,:3]), rotations=self.rotations, and cov3Dprecomp=None. This returns radiipure. 3. Create Mask: Define anchorprimitivevisiblemask where radiipure > 0. 4. Filter Data: Filter means, scalingfactorsbeforeexp, reffeats, and resfeats using anchorprimitivevisiblemask to keep only visible anchors. 5. Predict Coupled Primitives: Pass the filtered means, scalingfactorsbeforeexp, reffeats, resfeats, camcenter, and skipquant into the prediction network self.network. This returns gaussianprimitives (containing means, scales, rotations, colors for all primitives), predopacities, coupledprimitivemask, and bpp. 6. Initialize Projected Means: Create projectedmeans as a zero tensor with requiresgrad=True (or retaingrad=True) to store 2D projections. 7. Render: Call the rasterizer with: means3D=gaussianprimitives.means means2D=projectedmeans scales=gaussianprimitives.scales rotations=gaussianprimitives.rotations cov3Dprecomp=None shs=None colorsprecomp=gaussianprimitives.colors opacities=gaussianprimitives.opacities. 8. Clamp: Clamp the renderedimg to the range [0, 1]. 9. Return Results: Return a RenderResults object containing renderedimg, projectedmeans, visibilitymask (where radii > 0), predopacities, scales, anchorprimitivevisiblemask, coupledprimitivemask, and bpp. 10. Inference Timing: For inference, synchronize CUDA, record start time, perform prediction and rendering, synchronize CUDA, record end time, and calculate predicttime (seconds) and rendertime (milliseconds). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class CoupledGaussianRenderer: def init(self, rasterizer, network, voxelsize, derivefactor, reffeatsdim, resfeatsdim, backgroundcolor=0.0): self.rasterizer = rasterizer self.network = network self.voxelsize = voxelsize self.derivefactor = derivefactor self.reffeatsdim = reffeatsdim self.resfeatsdim = resfeatsdim self.backgroundcolors = torch.tensor([backgroundcolor, backgroundcolor, backgroundcolor], dtype=torch.float32) # Initialize parameters self.gaussianparams = GaussianParameters( numanchorprimitive=0, numcoupledprimitive=0, derivefactor=derivefactor, resfeatsdim=resfeatsdim, means=None, scalesbeforeexp=None, rotations=None, reffeats=None, resfeats=None, accumulatedgrads=None, coupleddenorm=None, accumulatedopacities=None, anchordenorm=None) def render(self, sample: Sample) -> RenderResults: # 1. Initialize Rasterizer Settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imageheight=sample.imageheight, imagewidth=sample.imagewidth, tanfovx=sample.tanhalffovx, tanfovy=sample.tanhalffovy, background=self.backgroundcolors, scalemodifier=1.0, # Default, adjust if needed viewmatrix=sample.worldtoviewprojmat, projmatrix=sample.worldtoimageprojmat, shdegree=1, campos=sample.cameracenter, prefiltered=False, debug=False) # 2. Prefilter invisible anchor primitives # Extract anchor scales (first 3 components of scalesbeforeexp) anchorscales = torch.exp(self.gaussianparams.scalesbeforeexp[:,:3]) radiipure = self.rasterizer.visiblefilter( means3D=self.gaussianparams.means, scales=anchorscales, rotations=self.gaussianparams.rotations, cov3Dprecomp=None, rastersettings=rastersettings) # 3. Create anchor primitive visible mask anchorprimitivevisiblemask = radiipure > 0 # 4. Filter data structures means = self.gaussianparams.means[anchorprimitivevisiblemask] scalingfactorsbeforeexp = self.gaussianparams.scalesbeforeexp[anchorprimitivevisiblemask] reffeats = self.gaussianparams.reffeats[anchorprimitivevisiblemask] resfeats = self.gaussianparams.resfeats[anchorprimitivevisiblemask] # 5. Predict Gaussian primitives (anchors + coupled) # camcenter is sample.cameracenter gaussianprimitives, predopacities, coupledprimitivemask, bpp = self.network( means=means, scalingfactorsbeforeexp=scalingfactorsbeforeexp, reffeats=reffeats, resfeats=resfeats, camcenter=sample.cameracenter, skipquant=False # Or based on inference/training flag) # 6. Initialize projected means projectedmeans = torch.zeroslike(gaussianprimitives.means[:,:2], requiresgrad=True) # 7. Render image # Note: The rasterizer call in the source uses specific arguments. # We assume gaussianprimitives has.means,.scales,.rotations,.colors renderedimg = self.rasterizer( means3D=gaussianprimitives.means, means2D=projectedmeans, scales=gaussianprimitives.scales, rotations=gaussianprimitives.rotations, cov3Dprecomp=None, shs=None, colorsprecomp=gaussianprimitives.colors, opacities=gaussianprimitives.opacities, rastersettings=rastersettings) # 8. Clamp rendered image renderedimg = torch.clamp(renderedimg, 0.0, 1.0) # 9. Return results # Visibility mask for all primitives (radii > 0) # Note: radiipure was for anchors. For full visibility, we might need to recompute or use the rasterizer's internal mask. # The source says "visibilitymask (radii > 0)". Assuming this refers to the final rendered primitives' visibility. # For simplicity, we return the anchor mask and coupled mask as per source. return RenderResults( renderedimg=renderedimg, projectedmeans=projectedmeans, visibilitymask=radiipure > 0, # Simplified, source implies this is the mask predopacities=predopacities, scales=gaussianprimitives.scales, anchorprimitivevisiblemask=anchorprimitivevisiblemask, coupledprimitivemask=coupledprimitivemask, bpp=bpp) Time and Memory Complexity: The method reduces memory usage by deriving coupled primitives from anchors, lowering the number of stored parameters compared to independent Gaussians. The rendering complexity is proportional to the total number of primitives (anchors + coupled). The prediction step adds computational overhead during training/inference to generate coupled primitives. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Compact representation, efficient storage via compression (GPCC), and fast rendering due to fewer primitives. Limitations: Requires a custom network to predict coupled primitives, adding complexity to the training pipeline. Precision issues may arise from quantization and compression. When to Use: Use when storage and bandwidth are constrained, or when real-time rendering of large scenes is required with limited memory. Coupled Gaussian Primitives Rendering, also known as CompGS, was introduced by Liu Xiangrui et al. in the "CompGS" repository. It builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a coupled primitive structure to enhance compression and efficiency. name: Surface-Constrained Gaussian Splatting
head: Surface-Anchor Gaussian Splatting
body: Surface-Constrained Gaussian Splatting is a training optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that initializes splats on a mesh surface and applies geometric constraints to prevent floating artifacts and improve surface fidelity. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by enforcing planar alignment and surface proximity through specific loss functions and initialization strategies, distinguishing it from sibling methods like DeSplat which focuses on differentiable splatting primitives, and Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints which offers broader geometric regularization. Inputs: A triangular mesh (vertices and faces), camera poses, and input images. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians (means, covariances via quaternions/scales, opacities, spherical harmonic coefficients). Data Structures: Gaussian: mean: vec3 (3D position) scale: vec3 (log-space scales for x, y, z axes) opacity: float (initially 0.5) sh0: vec3 (zeroth-order spherical harmonic coefficients, derived from RGB) shN: vec3 (higher-order SH coefficients, initialized to 0) quaternion: vec4 (normalized, representing rotation) Initialization Steps: 1. Point Sampling: Sample points uniformly on the mesh triangles using area-weighted sampling. For each triangle, generate random barycentric coordinates bary = [1 - \sqrt{r1}, \sqrt{r1}(1 - r2), \sqrt{r1}r2] where r1, r2 \sim U[0,1]. 2. Scale Initialization: Compute the average distance to K-nearest neighbors (KNN) in the sampled point cloud. Set initial log-scales: scales{xy} = \log(\text{avg\dist} \times 1.0) scalesz = \log(\text{avg\dist} \times 0.2) This creates flat discs that overlap with neighbors. 3. Rotation Initialization: Align the splat's Z-axis to the surface normal. Compute the rotation quaternion using the half-angle Rodrigues formula: \cos\theta = \text{dot}(\text{initial\z}, \text{normal}) If \cos\theta < -0.999 (anti-aligned), set quaternion to [0, 1, 0, 0] (180-degree rotation around X-axis). Otherwise, qw = \sqrt{(1+\cos\theta)/2} and q{xyz} = \sqrt{(1-\cos\theta)/2} \cdot \text{axis}, where axis is the cross product of initial Z and normal. 4. Color and Opacity: Set initial opacity to 0.5 to prevent premature pruning. Compute SH0 from the RGB color of the sampled point; initialize higher-order SH coefficients to zero. Training Losses: 1. Flatness Loss: Penalizes the ratio of the thinnest axis scale to the middle axis scale to enforce disc-like shapes. 2. Normal Alignment Loss: Penalizes deviation of the thin axis (Z-axis) from the surface normal: L{normal} = 1 - |\text{dot}(\text{thin\axis}, \text{normal})|. 3. Surface Anchor Loss: Computes the L2 distance from each splat's mean to the nearest point on the mesh. This cache is updated every 50 training steps. 4. Laplacian Smoothing: Applies smoothing to scales, quaternions, and SH0 using KNN neighbors with a specified strength parameter to reduce noise. Spawn Strategy: New splats are spawned at pixels with high frequency gaps or low alpha values using weighted multinomial sampling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializegaussiansfrommesh(mesh, numpoints): """ Initialize 3D Gaussians on a mesh surface. mesh: Object with vertices, faces, and facenormals methods. numpoints: Number of splats to initialize. Returns: List of Gaussian objects. """ gaussians = [] # 1. Sample points on mesh points, normals = samplemeshpoints(mesh, numpoints) # 2. Compute KNN distances for scale initialization # Assuming a KDTree or similar structure for efficient KNN lookup knndistances = computeknndistances(points, k=5) avgdist = np.mean(knndistances, axis=1) for i in range(numpoints): p = points[i] n = normals[i] # 3. Initialize Scales (log-space) # xy scales are larger, z scale is smaller (flat disc) scalexy = np.log(avgdist[i] 1.0) scalez = np.log(avgdist[i] 0.2) scale = np.array([scalexy, scalexy, scalez]) # 4. Initialize Rotation (Quaternion) # Align Z-axis (0,0,1) to normal n initialz = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) costheta = np.dot(initialz, n) if costheta < -0.999: # Anti-aligned: 180 deg rotation around X q = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # w, x, y, z else: # Half-angle Rodrigues axis = np.cross(initialz, n) normaxis = np.linalg.norm(axis) if normaxis < 1e-8: q = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # No rotation needed else: axis = axis / normaxis qw = np.sqrt((1 + costheta) / 2) qxyz = np.sqrt((1 - costheta) / 2) axis q = np.concatenate([[qw], qxyz]) # 5. Initialize Opacity and Color opacity = 0.5 # rgb is assumed to be retrieved from the mesh vertex or interpolated color rgb = getcoloratpoint(p, mesh) sh0 = rgbtosh(rgb) # Standard SH conversion for 0th order shN = np.zeros(3 (NSHBANDS - 1)) # Higher order zeros gaussians.append({ 'mean': p, 'scale': scale, 'quaternion': q, 'opacity': opacity, 'sh0': sh0, 'shN': shN }) return gaussians def computesurfaceanchorloss(gaussians, mesh, cachestep, currentstep): """ Compute L2 distance from splat means to nearest mesh points. Cache is updated every 50 steps. """ if currentstep % 50 == 0: # Update nearest point cache # Implementation depends on spatial data structure (e.g., KDTree on mesh vertices/points) nearestmeshpoints = findnearestmeshpoints([g['mean'] for g in gaussians], mesh) cachestep['nearestpoints'] = nearestmeshpoints nearestpoints = cachestep['nearestpoints'] loss = 0.0 for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): dist = np.linalg.norm(g['mean'] - nearestpoints[i]) loss += dist dist return loss Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N \log N) due to KNN and mesh sampling. Training adds overhead for surface anchor loss computation (cached every 50 steps) and Laplacian smoothing, increasing per-step cost compared to standard 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the mesh geometry and nearest-point cache. Slightly higher memory usage than standard 3DGS due to additional loss computations. Strengths: Significantly reduces floating artifacts and improves surface reconstruction quality for scenes with well-defined geometry. Limitations: Requires a high-quality input mesh. Performance degrades if the mesh is noisy or incomplete. Not suitable for scenes without clear surface geometry (e.g., dense foliage, smoke). When to use: When surface fidelity is critical and a good mesh is available. When not to use: For general-purpose 3DGS where mesh acquisition is difficult or the scene is non-rigid/complex without clear surfaces. Surface-Constrained Gaussian Splatting was introduced as an unofficial extension to 3D Gaussian Splatting, integrating mesh-based initialization and geometric constraints. It is part of the dust3r-3dgs pipeline, which combines DUSt3R/MASt3R reconstruction with Gaussian Splatting training. The method addresses the common issue of "floating" Gaussian artifacts that appear in standard 3DGS when training on sparse or noisy point clouds. name: BoundedGS
head: Bounded Working-Set 3DGS
body: BoundedGS is a memory-efficient training and rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that bounds GPU memory usage during high-resolution training by separating rasterization and projection backward passes. It replaces full-frame projection with group-based candidate screening, leaf budget management, and compact gradient storage to limit the active working set. Unlike InfiniGS, which uses image blocks and asynchronous optimization, BoundedGS examines the lifetime of rasterization forward and backward caches within a complete view on one GPU. Unlike CLM, which reduces projection input via frustum candidates, BoundedGS combines view-level candidates with load-bounded local rasterization to control the simultaneous residency of Gaussian-tile intersections, pixels, projection state, and parameter gradients. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Global Gaussian parameters \theta, camera intrinsics/extrinsics, training image, projection-group grid side length g, and rasterization budget L per leaf. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \theta, rendered image, and loss value. Data Structures: Global Model: Stores Gaussian positions, rotations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Candidate Indices: For each group j, an array of Gaussian IDs Cj screened for potential visibility. Leaf Layout: A CPU-cached tree of tile-aligned rectangles R. Each leaf tracks its pixel count pR, tile count tR, and intersection count nR. Compact Gradients: Parameter gradients are accumulated only for candidate Gaussians in the current group, indexed by their global IDs, rather than allocating full rows for all N Gaussians. Numbered Steps: 1. Group Division: Divide the image into g^2 non-overlapping groups. The standard configuration uses g=1 (one group covering the whole image). 2. Candidate Screening: For each group j, build candidate index array Cj: a. Read Gaussian position, opacity \alphai, and maximum scale s{i,\max} = |\gamma| \maxk \exp(s{i,k}), where \gamma is the global scale modifier and s{i,k} are log-scale components. b. Exclude Gaussians with camera-space depth zi \le 0.2 or activated opacity \alphai \le 1/255. c. Compute the projection Jacobian Ai using detailed projection focal lengths. Clamp normalized coordinates xi/zi and yi/zi to \pm 1.3 \tan(\text{FOV}x/2) and \pm 1.3 \tan(\text{FOV}y/2) respectively. d. Estimate screen covariance bound: \bar{\Sigma}{i,2D} = Ai (s{i,\max}^2 I) Ai^\top + 0.3I. e. Calculate screen-space rectangle half-widths: e{i,x} = \max(0, \sqrt{2 \log(255\alphai) \bar{\Sigma}{i,2D,xx} + 2}) e{i,y} = \max(0, \sqrt{2 \log(255\alphai) \bar{\Sigma}{i,2D,yy} + 2}) The +2 inside the square root provides a two-pixel discretization margin. f. Include Gaussian i in Cj if the rectangle [c{i,x} - e{i,x}, c{i,x} + e{i,x}] \times [c{i,y} - e{i,y}, c{i,y} + e{i,y}] intersects the group's tile-padded bounds. Non-finite projection results retain the Gaussian. g. Build Cj using counting and prefix sums over the global model. 3. Group Processing (Row-Major Order): For each group j: a. Projection: Read original parameter rows at IDs in Cj and project them once. Reuse these projected attributes for all leaves in the group. b. Leaf Subdivision: Determine leaves covering the group. A leaf is a tile-aligned rectangle R. Estimate allocation size E(R): E(R) = B{\text{bin}}(nR) + B{\text{image}}(pR, tR) + B{\text{sample}}(bR, d) + B{\text{out}}(pR, d) where d indicates inverse depth enablement (main table uses RGB without depth). nR: exact Gaussian-tile intersection count. pR: pixel count. tR = \lceil hR/16 \rceil \lceil wR/16 \rceil: tile count. uR = \min(tR, nR). bR = \lfloor (nR + 31uR + 31)/32 \rfloor: upper bound on 32-entry backward buckets. B{\text{bin}}: two uint32 Gaussian-ID arrays, two uint64 sort-key arrays, CUB radix-sort workspace. B{\text{image}}: per-pixel alpha/contributor state, per-tile ranges, max contributors, bucket counts, offsets, scan workspace. B{\text{sample}}: bucket-to-tile indices, transmittance/RGB state for 256 pixels per bucket. B{\text{out}}: 12pR bytes FP32 RGB output, plus 4pR bytes if depth enabled. Size queries include 128-byte array alignment and tail padding. c. Budget Splitting: If E(R) > L and R can be split, bisect along the dimension with more tiles (ties broken horizontally). Children remain disjoint and cover the parent. Stop when E(R) \le L or R is one tile. If a single tile exceeds L, record the event and process at minimum granularity. d. Leaf Execution: For each final leaf R: i. Recount intersections under current projection. ii. Perform rasterization (within-tile sorting and compositing) and compute loss LR = 0.8 L{1,R} + 0.2 (1 - \text{SSIM}R). iii. Compute backward pass to get gradients for projected attributes. iv. Accumulate these gradients into the group's compact parameter-gradient storage, indexed by candidate IDs. v. Release leaf state (intersections, compositing buffers, loss state). e. Group Cleanup: After all leaves, perform projection backward to accumulate parameter gradients from projected attributes. Release group projection and gradient caches. 4. Update: After all groups, compute global regularization (e.g., GNS pruning term during 15K–19K window) once. Combine gradients from all groups. Perform one parameter update using the optimizer (e.g., CUDA Adam). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundedgstrainstep(globalparams, camera, image, g, L): # 1. Divide image into g^2 groups groups = creategroups(image.width, image.height, g) # Global gradient accumulator for this view viewgradients = {} # 2. Process groups in row-major order for groupidx, groupbounds in enumerate(groups): # 2a. Candidate Screening candidates = [] for i in range(globalparams.numgaussians): if not isfinite(globalparams.pos[i]): candidates.append(i) continue zi = projectdepth(globalparams.pos[i], camera) alphai = globalparams.opacity[i] if zi <= 0.2 or alphai <= 1/255: continue smax = abs(globalparams.globalscale) max(exp(s) for s in globalparams.logscales[i]) Ai = computeprojectionjacobian(camera, globalparams.pos[i]) # Clamp coordinates xnorm = globalparams.pos[i].x / zi ynorm = globalparams.pos[i].y / zi xmax = 1.3 tan(camera.fovx / 2) ymax = 1.3 tan(camera.fovy / 2) xnorm = clamp(xnorm, -xmax, xmax) ynorm = clamp(ynorm, -ymax, ymax) # Covariance bound Sigmabar = Ai @ (smax2 Identity(3)) @ Ai.T + 0.3 Identity(2) # Rectangle half-widths ex = max(0, sqrt(2 log(255 alphai) Sigmabar[0,0] + 2)) ey = max(0, sqrt(2 log(255 alphai) Sigmabar[1,1] + 2)) # Check intersection with tile-padded bounds if rectangleintersectstilepaddedbounds( globalparams.pos[i].x, globalparams.pos[i].y, ex, ey, groupbounds): candidates.append(i) # 2b. Project Candidates Once projectedattrs = [] for i in candidates: projectedattrs.append(projectgaussian(globalparams, i, camera)) # 2c. Determine Leaves for this Group leaves = determineleaves(groupbounds, L, projectedattrs, camera) # 2d. Execute Leaves groupgradients = {} # Compact storage: id -> gradientvector for leaf in leaves: # Recount intersections intersections = findintersections(leaf, projectedattrs) # Rasterize alphamap, colormap, contributors = rasterize(leaf, intersections) # Compute Loss loss = computeloss(colormap, image[leaf.bounds], alphamap) # Backward: Image -> Projected Attributes gradprojattrs = backwardrasterization(leaf, intersections, gradloss=1.0) # Backward: Projected Attributes -> Parameters (Compact) # Accumulate into groupgradients for i in candidates: if i in contributors: gradp = backwardprojection(projectedattrs[i], gradprojattrs[i]) if i not in groupgradients: groupgradients[i] = zeroslike(globalparams[i]) groupgradients[i] += gradp # Release leaf state releaseleafstate(leaf) # 2e. Accumulate to View Gradients for i, grad in groupgradients.items(): if i not in viewgradients: viewgradients[i] = zeroslike(globalparams[i]) viewgradients[i] += grad # Release group caches releasegroupcaches() # 3. Global Regularization and Update if step in [15000, 19000]: regloss = computegnsregularization(globalparams) # Add regloss gradients to viewgradients for active set optimizer.step(globalparams, viewgradients) Memory Complexity: The rendering working set is bounded and nearly constant with respect to resolution. In a resolution sweep with 6M Gaussians, the working set stays within 1.073–1.077 GiB from 1K to 16K resolution. The peak memory is approximated as M^{peak}v \approx \maxt [M{res}(t) + M{view}(t) + M{rast}(t)], where M{rast} is bounded by the leaf budget L. Performance: At 11K resolution, a warm pass takes 19.79 seconds versus 21.76 seconds for full-frame execution (~9% faster). On five native 5K outdoor scenes, full training reduces the mean rendering working set from 9.97 to 1.76 GiB (82.3% reduction) and shortens training time from 36.7 to 33.9 minutes. Quality: The largest relative L1 difference over shared settings is \approx 6.8 \times 10^{-7}. Final reconstruction quality is close to the original method. Strengths: Bounded GPU memory usage regardless of resolution; no need for multi-GPU synchronization or host offloading for rendering state. Limitations: Requires CPU-assisted structure rebuilding for leaf layout management; potential overhead from candidate screening and leaf subdivision logic. BoundedGS was introduced to address the memory peaks caused by co-resident rasterization, projection, and gradient state in complete-view training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It identifies that limiting the simultaneously active local state controls the growth of main rendering caches, allowing high-resolution training on single GPUs. The method integrates projection, gradients, and resource management into a single execution flow, retaining full-pixel supervision and one update per view. name: Connectivity-based Visibility for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3DGS + Our Connectivity, Connectivity relationship for 3DGS
body: This method replaces the standard depth-ordered blending of all overlapping points in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a visibility filtering step based on a connectivity relationship graph. By retrieving only visible points from the point cloud for blending, it reduces memory consumption and accelerates rendering, enabling the optimization of large-scale scenes (e.g., autonomous driving sequences with tens of millions of points) that would otherwise exceed GPU memory limits. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by explicitly discarding unseen points during the compositing phase, whereas standard 3DGS blends a set of depth-ordered points including many unseen ones. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point cloud (typically derived from LiDAR or SfM) with associated Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a camera pose. Output: A rendered image where pixel colors are computed using only the subset of Gaussians determined to be visible via the connectivity graph. Data Structures: Connectivity Graph: A graph structure representing the spatial or topological relationships between points in the cloud. The specific construction algorithm for the graph is not detailed in the sources, but it is used to identify "visible" points relative to the camera view. [G: In typical implementations, this involves spatial hashing or k-d trees to find neighbors, but the exact graph construction is "Not given in the sources."] Visibility Mask: A boolean array or list of indices indicating which points from the full cloud are visible. Steps: 1. Deactivate Densification: Disable the standard 3DGS densification (splitting/cloning) process. This is because the input LiDAR point cloud is already relatively dense, and densification would exacerbate memory issues. 2. Retrieve Visible Points: Use the connectivity relationship graph to query the full point cloud and retrieve only the subset of points that are visible from the current camera viewpoint. 3. Blend Visible Points: Perform the standard 3DGS alpha-blending operation using only the retrieved visible points. Standard 3DGS blends all depth-ordered points overlapping the pixel; this method blends only the visible subset. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: points: Array of 3D point positions (N, 3). gaussians: Dictionary of Gaussian attributes (covariances, opacities, SH coeffs). camera: Camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. connectivitygraph: Pre-built graph structure for visibility queries. Returns: renderedimage: Rendered RGB image. """ # Step 1: Retrieve visible points using the connectivity graph # The graph maps camera view to a subset of point indices visibleindices = connectivitygraph.getvisiblepoints(points, camera) # Filter Gaussians to only those that are visible visiblegaussians = filtergaussians(gaussians, visibleindices) # Step 2: Standard 3DGS rasterization/blending on the visible subset # This replaces the standard 3DGS step which processes all overlapping points renderedimage = standard3dgsrasterize( points[visibleindices], visiblegaussians, camera) return renderedimage def filtergaussians(gaussians, indices): """ Filter Gaussian attributes to a specific set of indices. """ filtered = {} for key, value in gaussians.items(): filtered[key] = value[indices] return filtered Parameters: Densification: Disabled (Boolean: False). GPU Memory: The method is designed to fit within limited resources (e.g., 48 GB), whereas standard 3DGS fails on large datasets. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Coverage: The method may underperform in scenes with sparse coverage (e.g., fast-moving camera paths in autonomous driving) where the connectivity graph might not adequately capture visible structure. Graph Construction: The performance depends on the efficiency and accuracy of the connectivity graph. If the graph fails to identify visible points correctly, rendering quality degrades. name: Sketch and Patch
head: Sketch Gaussian Extraction, Sketch and Patch: Efficient 3D Gaussian Representation for Man-Made Scenes
body: Sketch and Patch is a hybrid 3D Gaussian representation method that categorizes Gaussians into two distinct roles: Sketch Gaussians, which define scene boundaries and high-frequency features, and Patch Gaussians, which cover smoother, broader regions. It solves the problem of storage inefficiency and redundancy in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where adaptive density control overestimates densification needs in high-frequency areas, leading to redundant Gaussian clusters along edges. Unlike conventional 3D downsampling or tiling which degrade visual quality due to the tightly coupled, heterogeneous nature of 3DGS Gaussians, this method separates Gaussians by role to allow specialized encoding. Inputs: Multi-view images and camera poses. Outputs: A unified hybrid representation consisting of encoded Sketch Gaussians and optimized Patch Gaussians. 1. 3D Line Segment (Li): Defined by endpoints p{start}, p{end} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and parameter t \in [0, 1]. Layout: Two 3D vectors (p{start}, p{end}). 2. Sketch Gaussian Candidate Set (Si): A subset of original 3DGS Gaussians associated with line segment Li. 3. Parametric Model: A function (e.g., polynomial or spline) encoding the attributes of Sketch Gaussians along the line. 4. Patch Gaussian Set: The remaining Gaussians after Sketch extraction, subject to pruning. 1. Extract 3D Line Segments: Process input images and camera poses using a geometry-guided line reconstruction method, specifically Line3D++. This abstracts object boundaries into discrete 2D line segments and back-projects them into 3D space to obtain a set of 3D line segments \{Li\}. 2. Identify Sketch Gaussians: For each 3D line segment Li, identify candidate Gaussians concentrated along the line. Radius Search: A Gaussian splat Gj with center \muj \in \mathbb{R}^3 is included in the candidate set Si if its distance to the line segment is within a radius r: d(\muj, Li) = \min{t \in [0,1]} \|\muj - Li(t)\| \le r where the line segment is parameterized as: Li(t) = (1 - t)p{start} + t p{end}, \quad t \in [0, 1] RANSAC Filtering: Apply Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) [4] to the candidate set Si to ensure coherent attribute values among the selected Sketch Gaussians, refining the set to robustly represent the line. 3. Encode Sketch Gaussians: Encode the identified Sketch Gaussians using parametric models (such as polynomials or splines) defined on the given 3D line Li. This leverages the geometric coherence of Gaussians along edges to model their attributes compactly, significantly reducing storage requirements. 4. Optimize Patch Gaussians: For the remaining smoother regions represented by Patch Gaussians, apply pruning and retraining. This sparsifies their distribution while maintaining visual fidelity and volumetric consistency. 5. Integrate Representation: Combine the encoded Sketch Gaussians and the optimized Patch Gaussians into a unified hybrid representation for efficient storage, transmission, and rendering. Args: images: List of input images. cameraposes: List of camera poses corresponding to images. originalgaussians: List of 3D Gaussian objects from standard 3DGS training. Each Gaussian has attributes: center (mu), covariance, opacity, shcoeffs. radiusthreshold: Float, distance threshold for radius search. Returns: sketchgaussians: List of encoded Sketch Gaussian parameters. patchgaussians: List of optimized Patch Gaussian objects. """ # Step 1: Extract 3D Line Segments using Line3D++ # Line3D++ takes images and poses, outputs 3D line segments. linesegments = line3dplusplusextract(images, cameraposes) sketchgaussians = [] patchgaussians = [] # Step 2 & 3: Identify and Encode Sketch Gaussians for line in linesegments: pstart = line.pstart pend = line.pend # Candidate selection via radius search candidates = [] for g in originalgaussians: # Calculate distance from Gaussian center to line segment # L(t) = (1-t)pstart + tpend for t in [0, 1] dist = mindistancepointtosegment(g.center, pstart, pend) if dist <= radiusthreshold: candidates.append(g) # Refine using RANSAC to ensure attribute coherence # RANSAC filters outliers based on geometric and attribute consistency refinedsketchcandidates = ransacfilter(candidates, line) # Encode using parametric model (e.g., polynomial regression along the line) # This compresses the attributes of the Gaussians along the line encodedsketch = parametricencode(refinedsketchcandidates, line) sketchgaussians.append(encodedsketch) # Mark these Gaussians as processed to exclude from Patch set markasprocessed(refinedsketchcandidates) # Step 4: Optimize Patch Gaussians # Collect all original Gaussians not marked as Sketch unprocessedgaussians = [g for g in originalgaussians if not g.isprocessed] # Apply pruning and retraining to sparsify and maintain fidelity # Pruning removes low-contribution Gaussians # Retraining optimizes the remaining ones patchgaussians = pruneandretrain(unprocessedgaussians) # Step 5: Integration is implicit in the return of the two sets # Rendering uses both encoded Sketch and optimized Patch sets return sketchgaussians, patchgaussians def mindistancepointtosegment(point, p1, p2): """ Calculates the minimum distance from a point to a line segment defined by p1 and p2. """ # Vector from p1 to p2 linevec = p2 - p1 # Vector from p1 to point pointvec = point - p1 # Project pointvec onto linevec to find t # t = dot(pointvec, linevec) / dot(linevec, linevec) linelensq = dot(linevec, linevec) if linelensq == 0: return norm(point - p1) t = dot(pointvec, linevec) / linelensq # Clamp t to [0, 1] for segment t = max(0, min(1, t)) # Closest point on segment closest = p1 + t linevec return norm(point - closest) def ransacfilter(candidates, line): """ Filters candidates using RANSAC to ensure coherent attributes. Implementation detail: Standard RANSAC loop fitting a model to attributes. """ # Placeholder for specific RANSAC implementation details not fully specified in source # The source states RANSAC is used to ensure coherent attribute values. # A typical implementation would fit a model (e.g., linear regression of opacity/sh along line) # and keep inliers. return candidates # Simplified return for structure; actual filtering logic depends on attribute model def parametricencode(candidates, line): """ Encodes Gaussian attributes using a parametric model along the line. """ # Placeholder for specific polynomial/spline fitting logic # The source states Sketch Gaussians are encoded via polynomial regression. return None # Encoded parameters def pruneandretrain(gaussians): """ Prunes and retrains Patch Gaussians. """ # Placeholder for pruning/retraining logic # The source states pruning and retraining are applied to sparsify distribution. return gaussians Line Reconstruction Method: Line3D++. Radius Threshold (r): Distance threshold for including a Gaussian in the Sketch candidate set. Not given in the sources. Parametric Model Type: Polynomials or splines. Not given in the sources. Redundancy in High-Frequency Areas: Standard 3DGS adaptive density control relies on 2D positional gradients, which often overestimates the need for densification in high-frequency areas like edges and contours. This leads to dense Gaussian clusters along structural boundaries (architectural edges, furniture boundaries) and increased computational overhead. Sketch and Patch addresses this by explicitly identifying and encoding these regions rather than densifying blindly. Scene Type: The method is especially effective in man-made scenes with well-defined straight edges and planar surfaces (architectural elements, furniture, manufactured objects). Performance on natural scenes may vary as the "Sketch" prior relies on geometric coherence along lines. Storage Efficiency: For an indoor scene, the model maintains visual quality with 7.9% of the original 3DGS model size. Visual Quality: Achieves up to 11.52% improvement in PSNR, 1.83% in SSIM, and 19.20% in LPIPS at equivalent model sizes across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. Strengths: Significant reduction in storage requirements through compact encoding of Sketch Gaussians; improved visual fidelity at low bitrates compared to standard 3DGS or naive downsampling. Limitations: Relies on the presence of extractable 3D lines; less effective in scenes lacking well-defined geometric structures (natural environments). When to Use: Man-made scenes with clear edges and planar surfaces where storage efficiency is critical. When Not to Use: Natural scenes with complex, non-linear, or ambiguous boundaries where the Sketch/Patch separation is less distinct. Origin: Proposed in the paper "Sketch and Patch: Efficient 3D Gaussian Representation for Man-Made Scenes". History: Developed as a response to the storage inefficiencies of 3D Gaussian Splatting, which generates vast numbers of Gaussians. While 3DGS achieves impressive visual fidelity, standard compression techniques like 3D downsampling or tiling are unsuitable due to the heterogeneous and interdependent nature of Gaussian attributes. Usage: Applied to efficient storage, transmission, and rendering of 3D scenes, particularly in multimedia streaming applications. name: COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: CF-3DGS
body: COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (CF-3DGS) is a method for novel view synthesis and camera pose estimation from unposed video sequences, eliminating the need for Structure-from-Motion (SfM) preprocessing. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which relies on pre-computed sparse point clouds and known camera poses, CF-3DGS leverages temporal continuity in video and explicit point cloud representation to progressively "grow" a global 3D Gaussian set frame-by-frame. It sets itself apart by estimating relative camera poses via differentiable rendering of local Gaussian sets, allowing it to handle significant camera motion where traditional unposed methods may fail. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of unposed video frames It for t \in \{1, \dots, T\}, and camera intrinsics K. Output: A global set of 3D Gaussians representing the scene, and estimated camera poses for all frames. Data Structures Each 3D Gaussian i is defined by the following parameters: Center position: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation: ri \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Scale: si \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity: \alphai \in \mathbb{R} Color: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients ci \in \mathbb{R}^k The covariance matrix \Sigmai is derived from rotation and scale: \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^{\top} Ri^{\top} where Si = \text{diag}([s{ix}, s{iy}, s{iz}]) and Ri is the rotation matrix constructed from quaternion ri. Algorithm Steps The method processes frames sequentially. For each frame t, it performs two main steps: 1. Initialization from a Single View (Frame 1): Given frame I1, generate monocular depth D1 using an off-the-shelf network (e.g., DPT). Initialize 3D Gaussians by lifting points from D1 using camera intrinsics K and an identity camera pose. Optimize the parameters of this local set G1 to minimize photometric loss between the rendered image and I1. 2. Sequential Growth (Frames t > 1): Local Optimization: Construct a local 3D Gaussian set from frame t-1. Sample frame t. Learn an affine transformation (representing the relative camera pose between t-1 and t) that transforms the Gaussians from t-1 to render frame t. This is done by minimizing photometric loss using differentiable rendering. Global Aggregation: Infer the absolute pose of frame t by accumulating relative poses. Aggregate the current frame's Gaussian information into the global set. Global Optimization: Optimize the global set using all previous frames and their estimated poses. Rendering Formula To render a pixel, Gaussians overlapping the pixel are sorted by depth. The final color C{pix} is computed via alpha blending: C{pix} = \sum{i=1}^{N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where N is the number of overlapping Gaussians, ci is the color, and \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. The 2D covariance \Sigma^{\text{2D}} in camera coordinates is computed as: \Sigma^{\text{2D}} = J W \Sigma W^{\top} J^{\top} where W is the viewing transform (camera pose), and J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializegaussiansfromdepth(depthmap, intrinsics): """ Lifts 2D pixels to 3D using monocular depth and intrinsics. Returns list of Gaussian parameters. """ # Get 2D pixel coordinates h, w = depthmap.shape y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(h), np.arange(w), indexing='ij') # Unproject to 3D using identity pose # Assuming standard pinhole model: X = K^-1 [x, y, 1] depth # Kinv is inverse of intrinsics matrix points3d = [] for i in range(h): for j in range(w): z = depthmap[i, j] if z > 0: # Simplified unprojection assuming K is known # In practice, use Kinv @ [j, i, 1] z pt = unprojectpixel(j, i, z, intrinsics) points3d.append(pt) # Initialize Gaussians with these points # Attributes: mu, alpha, shcoeffs, scale, rotation # Scale and rotation can be initialized to small constant values gaussians = [] for pt in points3d: g = Gaussian() g.mu = pt g.alpha = 0.5 # Initial opacity g.scale = np.array([0.01, 0.01, 0.01]) g.rotation = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Identity quaternion g.shcoeffs = np.zeros(k) # Initialize SH coefficients gaussians.append(g) return gaussians def rendergaussians(gaussians, camerapose, intrinsics): """ Renders the scene using 3D Gaussian Splatting. Returns rendered image and gradients. """ # Project 3D Gaussians to 2D projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Transform center to camera coordinates mucam = camerapose @ g.mu # Compute 2D covariance # Sigma2D = J W Sigma W^T J^T # W is camera pose (viewing transform) # J is Jacobian of projection sigma2d = compute2dcovariance(g.sigma, camerapose, intrinsics) # Compute 2D mean mu2d = projecttoimage(mucam, intrinsics) projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu2d': mu2d, 'sigma2d': sigma2d, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'shcoeffs': g.shcoeffs, 'depth': mucam[2] }) # Sort by depth projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) # Render using alpha blending image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for g in projectedgaussians: # Splat Gaussian onto image # For each pixel covered by the Gaussian's 2D ellipse for pixel in pixelscoveredbygaussian(g): # Compute opacity contribution # alphai exp(-0.5 (x - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x - mu)) contribution = computegaussiancontribution(g, pixel) # Alpha blending # Cpix = sum(ci alphai prod(1 - alphaj)) image[pixel] += contribution (1 - accumulatedalpha[pixel]) accumulatedalpha[pixel] += contribution['alpha'] return image def optimizerelativepose(localgaussians, frameprev, framecurr, intrinsics): """ Optimizes the relative camera pose between two frames. """ # Initialize relative pose as identity or previous estimate relativepose = np.eye(4) # Iteratively optimize relativepose to minimize photometric loss # between rendered framecurr and ground truth framecurr for step in range(numsteps): # Render framecurr using localgaussians transformed by relativepose renderedimage = rendergaussians(localgaussians, relativepose, intrinsics) # Compute loss loss = photometricloss(renderedimage, framecurr) # Backpropagate to update relativepose # Note: Gaussians are fixed in this step, only pose is optimized relativepose = updatepose(relativepose, loss) return relativepose def traincf3dgs(frames, intrinsics): """ Main training loop for CF-3DGS. """ globalgaussians = None # Step 1: Initialize with first frame depth1 = predictmonoculardepth(frames[0]) globalgaussians = initializegaussiansfromdepth(depth1, intrinsics) # Optimize initial Gaussians against frame 0 globalgaussians = optimizegaussians(globalgaussians, frames[0], intrinsics, pose=np.eye(4)) # Step 2: Process subsequent frames currentpose = np.eye(4) for t in range(1, len(frames)): frameprev = frames[t-1] framecurr = frames[t] # Create local Gaussians from global (or subset) localgaussians = copygaussians(globalgaussians) # Estimate relative pose relativepose = optimizerelativepose(localgaussians, frameprev, framecurr, intrinsics) # Update global pose currentpose = currentpose @ relativepose # Aggregate new Gaussians from current frame # This step involves lifting points from current frame's depth and adding to global set depthcurr = predictmonoculardepth(framecurr) newgaussians = initializegaussiansfromdepth(depthcurr, intrinsics) # Transform new Gaussians to global coordinate system using currentpose for g in newgaussians: g.mu = currentpose @ g.mu globalgaussians.extend(newgaussians) # Optimize global set with all frames up to t # This is a simplified description; in practice, it might use a subset or sliding window globalgaussians = optimizeglobalgaussians(globalgaussians, frames[:t+1], intrinsics) return globalgaussians, currentpose Parameters Monocular Depth Network: DPT. Spherical Harmonics Degree: k (Not given in the sources). Photometric Loss: Not specified in detail, but implied to be standard L1 or L2 loss between rendered and ground truth images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Large Camera Motion: The method performs well when camera motion is large, unlike some unposed methods. Depth Accuracy: Relies on the accuracy of the monocular depth network (DPT) for initialization. Accumulation of Errors: Sequential pose estimation may accumulate errors over time, though the global optimization step helps mitigate this. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performs on par with Nope-NeRF for small camera motion and outperforms it significantly for large camera changes (e.g., 360-degree videos). Strengths: No SfM preprocessing required; handles large camera motions; leverages temporal continuity. Limitations: Requires video input (temporal continuity); relies on monocular depth estimation. When to Use: When camera poses are unknown and SfM is not feasible or desired, especially for video sequences with significant motion. When Not to Use: When static images are available with known poses (standard 3DGS is faster and more accurate); when monocular depth estimation is unreliable. Origin: Proposed in the paper "COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting". History: Builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [17] and monocular depth estimation [32]. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS requiring SfM preprocessing. Usage: Novel view synthesis from unposed video sequences. name: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies
head: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for 3D Gaussian Splatting, Laplacian framework, Laplacian-GS, coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged training, frequency-factorized 3DGS
body: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies is a training optimization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that decomposes the image supervision signal into low-frequency and high-frequency components, training separate Gaussian fields for each component in a coarse-to-fine sequence. Unlike prior frequency-based methods that use frequency cues only for scheduling or resolution adjustment, this method incorporates frequency at the representation level by factorizing the scene into frequency-specific fields and archiving completed lower-frequency fields to reduce the active Gaussian count during subsequent high-frequency optimization. It serves as a plug-and-play module that reduces training time and peak memory usage while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality, particularly at high resolutions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of calibrated input images \{Iv\} with corresponding camera poses; a target resolution (e.g., 1K, 2K, 4K); a total iteration budget T{total}; and a backbone 3DGS implementation (e.g., Taming-3DGS or FastGS). Outputs: A composed novel-view synthesis image \hat{I}v and a set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} distributed across L frequency levels. Data Structures The method maintains L distinct Gaussian fields \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}L, where each field \mathcal{G}\ell contains primitives parameterized by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \sigmai \in (0, 1) Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, parameterized as \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top with rotation Ri and diagonal scale Si = \text{diag}(si) View-dependent appearance parameters (typically spherical harmonics coefficients) Each field is rendered independently to produce a frequency-band image R{v}^\ell. The final image is the sum of these components: \hat{I}v = \sum{\ell=1}^{L} R{v}^\ell Number of Levels and Iteration Split The hierarchy depth L depends on the target resolution: 1K Resolution: Default L=2. Iteration split is (10,000, 20,000). 4K Resolution: Default L=4. Iteration split is (15,000, 7,500, 7,500, 15,000). Increasing L beyond these defaults consistently degrades reconstruction quality due to accumulated structural misalignment errors across frequency bands. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize: Create L empty Gaussian fields \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}L. Initialize \mathcal{G}1 with standard 3DGS initialization (e.g., point cloud from SfM). 2. Iterate \ell from 1 to L: a. Active Set: The active Gaussian set for optimization is \mathcal{G}\ell. All previous fields \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}{\ell-1} are "archived" (frozen, no gradients computed, no densification/culling). b. Render: For each training view v, render the current field \mathcal{G}\ell to obtain the residual image R{v}^\ell using standard 3DGS rasterization. c. Loss: Compute the photometric loss between the rendered image R{v}^\ell and the ground truth image Iv. Note: The method uses reconstructed-image supervision, meaning the loss is computed against the full ground truth image, not the residual of the ground truth. \mathcal{L}\ell = \mathcal{L}{photo}(R{v}^\ell, Iv) Pitfall: Supervising the residual directly (i.e., \mathcal{L}{photo}(R{v}^\ell, Iv - \sum{k<\ell} R{v}^k)) underperforms the default design. d. Optimize: Perform gradient descent on the parameters of \mathcal{G}\ell using the loss \mathcal{L}\ell. Apply standard 3DGS density control (clone, split, prune) only to \mathcal{G}\ell. e. Archive: After the allocated iterations for level \ell are complete, freeze \mathcal{G}\ell. 3. Inference: To render a novel view, sequentially render each archived field \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}L and sum the results pixel-wise. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainlaplaciangs(inputimages, cameraposes, targetresolution, totaliterations, numlevels): """ Train 3D Gaussian Splatting using Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies. Args: inputimages: List of ground truth images. cameraposes: List of camera poses corresponding to images. targetresolution: Resolution string (e.g., '1K', '4K'). totaliterations: Total number of training iterations. numlevels: Number of Laplacian levels L. Returns: archivedfields: List of frozen Gaussian fields [G1,..., GL]. """ # Determine iteration split based on resolution and levels # Default splits are hardcoded based on source evidence if targetresolution == '1K' and numlevels == 2: iterationsperlevel = [10000, 20000] elif targetresolution == '4K' and numlevels == 4: iterationsperlevel = [15000, 7500, 7500, 15000] else: # Fallback: equal split if not specified, though source notes # that performance is insensitive to split iterationsperlevel = [totaliterations // numlevels] numlevels # Initialize empty fields fields = [] # Initialize first field with standard 3DGS initialization # Standard 3DGS initialization from SfM point cloud is assumed here currentfield = initialize3dgsfields(inputimages, cameraposes) fields.append(currentfield) currentiter = 0 for level in range(numlevels): field = fields[-1] niters = iterationsperlevel[level] # Optimization loop for the current frequency level for step in range(niters): # Sample a random training view viewidx = randomsample(inputimages) gtimage = inputimages[viewidx] pose = cameraposes[viewidx] # Render the current field to get the band-specific image # This renders ONLY the Gaussians in the current field renderedband = rendergaussianfield(field, pose) # Compute loss against the FULL ground truth image # Source specifies reconstructed-image supervision loss = computephotometricloss(renderedband, gtimage) # Backpropagate and update ONLY the current field's parameters # Standard 3DGS density control (clone/split/prune) applies here optimizefield(field, loss) currentiter += 1 # Archive the field: freeze parameters, stop tracking gradients field.freeze() # If not the last level, initialize the next field if level < numlevels - 1: # The next field is initialized empty or with sparse points. # Source implies subsequent fields optimize residuals without # carrying the full primitive burden, suggesting they start small. nextfield = initializeemptyfield() fields.append(nextfield) return fields def rendernovelview(archivedfields, camerapose): """ Compose the final image by summing rendered frequency bands. """ finalimage = zeroslike(camerapose.resolution) for field in archivedfields: bandimage = rendergaussianfield(field, camerapose) finalimage += bandimage return finalimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls Depth of Hierarchy: Increasing the number of Laplacian levels L consistently degrades reconstruction quality. This is attributed to the accumulation of structural misalignment errors across multiple frequency bands. Supervision Signal: Directly fitting the residual (using the residual of the ground truth as the target) underperforms the default reconstructed-image supervision. The method must supervise the final reconstructed image against the ground truth at each level. Inference Speed: While training is accelerated, inference FPS may decrease compared to a single-field baseline because the final image requires sequential rendering of multiple frequency fields. Time and Memory Complexity Training Time: The method significantly reduces training time by splitting the workload into smaller Gaussian fields. Average speedups of 1.73\times and 1.21\times at 1K resolution, and 1.74\times and 1.33\times at 4K resolution are reported when combined with Taming-3DGS and FastGS backbones, respectively. Memory Usage: By archiving lower-frequency fields and training higher-frequency fields with fewer active primitives, the peak GPU memory usage and peak Gaussian count are reduced. For example, in a 4K setting, the peak Gaussian count is reduced from 1.74M to 0.49M. Measured Performance 1K Resolution (MipNeRF 360): With Taming-3DGS backbone: Training time reduced from 8.88 to 5.13 minutes (1.73\times speedup) with a 0.34 dB PSNR drop. With FastGS backbone: Training time reduced from 4.82 to 3.96 minutes with a 0.29 dB PSNR drop. 4K Resolution: Efficiency gains become more pronounced at higher resolutions, with larger speedups while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Plug-and-play compatibility with existing 3DGS accelerations (Taming-3DGS, FastGS); significant reduction in training time and peak memory; scalable to high resolutions (2K, 4K). Limitations: Potential decrease in inference FPS due to sequential rendering of multiple fields; slight metric degradation (PSNR/SSIM) due to approximation errors from hierarchical composition; deeper hierarchies (L>2 for 1K) degrade quality. When to Use Use when training time and GPU memory are constrained, especially at high resolutions (2K, 4K). Use when integrating with accelerated backbones like Taming-3DGS or FastGS. Do not use if inference latency is the primary constraint and the scene is low-resolution, as the sequential rendering overhead may negate benefits. Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies was proposed by Yixiong Yang, Sisheng Zhang, Qingsong Yan, Shaohuai Shi, and Qiang Wang from Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, and XGRIDS. The paper, titled "Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training," was published on arXiv in September 2026. The work addresses the bottleneck of continual Gaussian growth and heavy optimization costs in 3DGS training, particularly at high resolutions. It builds on the observation that image-plane signals have naturally structured frequency components, leveraging Laplacian decomposition to factorize the representation.
