name: Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian
head: MaGS representation
body: Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian (MaGS) is a hybrid scene representation that combines a triangular mesh with 3D Gaussians, where Gaussians are "adsorbed" to mesh facets rather than being rigidly anchored in free space. This allows Gaussians to "roam" on the surface, increasing their degrees of freedom for movement and deformation. It is designed to facilitate the reconstruction and simulation of dynamic 3D objects by providing a structured yet flexible primitive layout. Inputs: A triangular mesh defined by vertices, facets, and normals; a set of 3D Gaussians initialized with logical coordinates and facet assignments. Outputs: Spatial positions, orientations, scales, opacities, and colors for each Gaussian, ready for splatting. Data Structures: Mesh: vertices: Array of N vectors vi \in \mathbb{R}^3 for i=1..N. facets: Array of M triplets of vertex indices. normals: Array of M vectors nj \in \mathbb{R}^3 for j=1..M. Gaussian i: MeshId: Integer index j identifying the facet j on which the Gaussian resides. w: Logical coordinates w \in [0, 1]^3. Standard 3D Gaussian attributes: mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients. Step 1: Initialization Gaussians are randomly initialized. The logical coordinate components w1, w2 are generated randomly within [0,1]. The third component w3 is also generated randomly. The MeshId is assigned such that Gaussians are evenly distributed across all M facets, ensuring an equal number of Gaussians per facet. Step 2: Normal Calculation For any position on a facet, the normal is calculated by linearly interpolating the normals at the three vertices of that facet. Step 3: Spatial Position Computation To compute the spatial mean \mui of Gaussian i on facet j, the following procedure is used: 1. Define the interpolation function f: f(w, x, y, z) = w1 x + w2 y + (1 - w1 - w2)z where w are the logical coordinates and x, y, z are values at the three vertices of the facet. 2. Calculate the scaling factor lj for facet j: lj = \frac{|v{j1}v{j2}| |v{j1}v{j3}|}{|v{j1}v{j2} \times v{j1}v{j3}|} where v{j1}, v{j2}, v{j3} are the spatial coordinates of the three vertices of facet j. 3. Compute the mean position \mui: \mui = f(wi, v{j1}, v{j2}, v{j3}) + w{i3} nj lj where nj is the normal vector of facet j. Step 4: Deformation (Optional/Contextual) In dynamic scenarios, deformation networks (MPE-Net, RMD-Net, RGD-Net) adjust the mesh and Gaussian parameters. The mesh deformation updates the vertex positions v and normals n, which implicitly updates \mui via the formulas above. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Gaussian Hover: If w{i3} \neq 0, the Gaussian does not lie directly on the mesh surface but hovers above it. This increases the degree of freedom for the Gaussian to move across the mesh but may introduce artifacts if the hover distance is too large relative to the scene scale. Precision: The scaling factor lj involves cross products and lengths; degenerate triangles (zero area) will cause division by zero. Ensure facet area is non-zero before computing lj. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a structured initialization for Gaussians based on geometry, facilitating dynamic simulation and deformation. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the underlying mesh; complex topology may require careful handling of facet assignments. MaGS was introduced in the paper "Reconstructing and Simulating Dynamic 3D Objects with Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian Splatting". It extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by integrating mesh-based constraints to better handle dynamic scenes and simulations. name: Gradient-Aware Super Sampling (GASS)
head: GASS module, Gradient-Aware Interpolation
body: Gradient-Aware Super Sampling (GASS) is a post-rendering module that leverages the continuous differentiability of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to extract image gradients, which guide a refinement network to enable high-fidelity super sampling from low-resolution inputs. It addresses aliasing artifacts and detail loss inherent in standard 3DGS rendering by combining low-resolution frame intensities with their spatial gradients and historical features. Unlike UpscaleGS, which uses image-space gradients to fit a bicubic spline function, GASS employs a network to leverage geometric and historical priors for more robust interpolation. GASS consists of two main components: Gradient-aware interpolation and Geometry-temporal recurrent refinement. Inputs: Low-resolution rendered image I. Image-space gradients G (computed from I). Depth map D. Normal-view inner product map Nv. Warped historical feature \tilde{h} from the previous frame. Outputs: High-resolution image \hat{I}. Updated historical feature h. Low-Resolution Image I: 2D array of pixel intensities. Gradients G: 2D arrays for \frac{\partial I}{\partial x} and \frac{\partial I}{\partial y}. Depth Map D: 2D array of depth values. Normal-View Map Nv: 2D array of dot products between surface normals and view directions. Feature Map F: 3D tensor with height/width matching I and channels CF. The number of channels CF must exceed \min\{S^2, 27\} to ensure the coefficient matrix M has full column or row rank. Historical Feature \tilde{h}: 3D tensor aligned to the current frame via warping. The rendered image I(x, y) is differentiable with respect to 2D spatial coordinates (x, y). The gradients are computed by blending weighted per-Gaussian gradients. For N Gaussians, the x-gradient is: \frac {\partial I(x, y)}{\partial x}=\sum {i=1}^N ci\left(\frac {\partial Ti}{\partial x} \alpha i+Ti \frac {\partial \alpha i}{\partial x}\right) where ci is the view-dependent color, \alphai is the opacity, and Ti is the transmittance. The differential of transmittance Ti with respect to x is recursively expanded as: \frac {\partial Ti}{\partial x} = - \frac {\partial \alpha {i-1}}{\partial x}T{i-1} + (1 - \alpha {i-1}) \frac {\partial T{i-1}}{\partial x} The y-gradient \frac {\partial I(x, y)}{\partial y} follows an analogous form. This step maps a low-resolution block to a high-resolution block using a bivariate polynomial constrained by function values and derivatives. 1. Block Definition: For each pixel (x0, y0) in I, consider it and its eight adjacent pixels to form a 3 \times 3 block of interpolation nodes. 2. Polynomial Constraints: A bivariate polynomial f(x, y) is defined such that for i, j \in \{-1, 0, 1\}: \begin{aligned} f(x0+i, y0+j) &= I(x0+i, y0+j) \\ \frac {\partial }{\partial x}f(x0+i, y0+j) &= \frac {\partial }{\partial x}I(x0+i, y0+j) \\ \frac {\partial }{\partial y}f(x0+i, y0+j) &= \frac {\partial }{\partial y}I(x0+i, y0+j) \end{aligned} 3. Mapping: Under an S \times S super-sampling setting, the 3 \times 3 block in I centered at (x0, y0) maps to an S \times S block in \hat{I} centered at (\hat{x}0, \hat{y}0). 4. Linear Combination: Each pixel in the high-resolution block is a linear combination of the low-resolution intensities and their spatial gradients, weighted by a coefficient matrix M: \mathrm {Vec}(\hat {I}{S\times S}(\hat {x}0, \hat {y}0)) = \mathbf {M} \begin {bmatrix} \mathrm {Vec}(I{3\times 3}(x0, y0)) \\ \mathrm {Vec}(\frac {\partial }{\partial x}I{3\times 3}(x0, y0))\\ \mathrm {Vec}(\frac {\partial }{\partial y}I{3\times 3}(x0, y0)) \end {bmatrix} where \mathrm {Vec}(\cdot) denotes column-wise vectorization. 5. Implementation: This operation is implemented by cascading a convolution layer with a transposed-convolution layer: F = \operatorname {Conv}(I) \hat {I} = \operatorname {TConv}(F) where \operatorname {Conv}(\cdot) is a 3 \times 3 convolution layer and \operatorname {TConv}(\cdot) is an S \times S transposed-convolution layer. F acts as the coefficient vector in the polynomial space. To mitigate aliasing artifacts caused by gradient sampling frequency limits, a refinement network updates the feature map using geometric and temporal priors. 1. Refinement Network Input: The network takes I, G, D, Nv, and the warped historical feature \tilde{h}. 2. Feature Update: The historical feature is updated via a modified GRU architecture: h = \operatorname {RefineNet}(G, D, Nv, \tilde{h}) 3. Residual Generation: A residual feature \Delta F is generated from the updated historical feature: \Delta F = \operatorname {Conv}(h) 4. Feature Map Update: The feature map F is updated as: F \leftarrow F + \Delta F This updated F is then used in the transposed convolution step to produce the final high-resolution image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GASSModule(nn.Module): def init(self, supersamplefactor=2): super(GASSModule, self).init() self.S = supersamplefactor # Convolution layers for interpolation # Input channels: 1 (for I) -> Output channels: CF # CF must be > min(S^2, 27) self.convinterpolation = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Transposed convolution for upsampling self.tconvinterpolation = nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 1, kernelsize=S, stride=S) # Refinement Network components # Simplified GRU-like structure for feature update self.refineconv = nn.Conv2d(32, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Inputs to RefineNet: G (2 channels), D (1 channel), Nv (1 channel), htilde (32 channels) self.refinenetinputconv = nn.Conv2d(2 + 1 + 1 + 32, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Parameters self.lambda1 = 0.1 def computegradients(self, I): """ Computes image-space gradients G from low-res image I. Assumes I is differentiable with respect to x and y. In practice, this might use finite differences or the analytical 3DGS gradient formula. Here we use Sobel filters as a proxy for the analytical gradient extraction described. """ # I shape: (B, 1, H, W) # Gradient kernels sobelx = torch.tensor([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]], dtype=I.dtype, device=I.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3) sobely = torch.tensor([[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]], dtype=I.dtype, device=I.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3) # Pad I for convolution Ipadded = F.pad(I, (1, 1, 1, 1), mode='reflect') # Compute gradients gradx = F.conv2d(Ipadded, sobelx, padding=0) grady = F.conv2d(Ipadded, sobely, padding=0) return torch.cat([gradx, grady], dim=1) # Shape: (B, 2, H, W) def forward(self, I, D, Nv, htilde): """ I: Low-res image (B, 1, H, W) D: Depth map (B, 1, H, W) Nv: Normal-view inner product map (B, 1, H, W) htilde: Warped historical feature (B, 32, H, W) """ # 1. Compute Gradients G = self.computegradients(I) # 2. Gradient-Aware Interpolation # F = Conv(I) F = self.convinterpolation(I) # 3. Geometry-Temporal Recurrent Refinement # Concatenate inputs for RefineNet: G, D, Nv, htilde # G: (B, 2, H, W), D: (B, 1, H, W), Nv: (B, 1, H, W), htilde: (B, 32, H, W) refineinput = torch.cat([G, D, Nv, htilde], dim=1) # h = RefineNet(G, D, Nv, htilde) # Simplified: Convolution on concatenated inputs to produce updated feature h h = self.refinenetinputconv(refineinput) # Delta F = Conv(h) deltaF = self.refineconv(h) # F <- F + Delta F F = F + deltaF # 4. Upsample # Ihat = TConv(F) Ihat = self.tconvinterpolation(F) return Ihat def computeloss(self, Ihat, Igt): """ Computes GASS loss: L = LC + lambda1 Llap LC: Charbonnier loss Llap: Laplacian loss ||grad^2 X - grad^2 Y||1 """ # Charbonnier loss epsilon = 1e-3 LC = torch.mean(torch.sqrt((Ihat - Igt)2 + epsilon2)) # Laplacian loss # Approximate Laplacian using 2nd order derivatives # Simple 2D Laplacian kernel laplaciankernel = torch.tensor([[0, 1, 0], [1, -4, 1], [0, 1, 0]], dtype=Ihat.dtype, device=Ihat.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3) Ihatlap = F.conv2d(F.pad(Ihat, (1, 1, 1, 1), mode='reflect'), laplaciankernel, padding=0) Igtlap = F.conv2d(F.pad(Igt, (1, 1, 1, 1), mode='reflect'), laplaciankernel, padding=0) Llap = torch.mean(torch.abs(Ihatlap - Igtlap)) L = LC + self.lambda1 Llap return L Super-sampling factor S: Determines the output resolution relative to input. Typical values depend on the desired output resolution (e.g., S=2 for 2x upscaling). Number of channels in F (CF): Must exceed \min\{S^2, 27\}. \lambda1: Weighting factor for Laplacian loss. Value is 0.1. Gradient Sampling Frequency: Gradients are derived from partial derivatives of the original continuous image function, so they remain constrained by the sampling frequency, making it difficult to avoid aliasing artifacts without refinement. Rank of Matrix M: The number of channels in F must be sufficient to ensure the coefficient matrix M has full column or row rank; otherwise, the interpolation may not capture higher-order relationships. Historical Feature Alignment: The warped historical feature \tilde{h} must be accurately aligned to the current frame; misalignment can introduce temporal inconsistencies. Time Complexity: GASS is designed to be lightweight and computationally efficient, reducing average rendering time per frame by enabling lower-resolution rendering followed by super-sampling. The use of convolutional layers and a compact GRU-like backbone contributes to this efficiency. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for low-resolution images, gradients, depth maps, normal maps, and historical features. The feature map F size depends on the chosen number of channels. Strengths: Effectively leverages geometric and historical priors for superior super-sampling performance compared to gradient-free methods; reduces aliasing artifacts; improves rendering efficiency. Limitations: Relies on the availability of accurate depth and normal maps; performance may degrade if historical features are poorly aligned; gradients are still limited by the initial sampling frequency. When to Use: When real-time rendering of large-scale 3DGS scenes is required, and high-resolution output is needed without the computational cost of rendering at full resolution directly. When Not to Use: When geometric information (depth, normals) is unavailable or unreliable; when temporal coherence is not a factor (e.g., single static image). GASS was introduced in the paper "3DGS^3: Joint Super Sampling and Frame Interpolation for Real-Time Large-Scale 3DGS Rendering" by Y. Zhao et al.. It is part of a unified framework that jointly performs super-sampling and frame interpolation to accelerate 3DGS rendering. The method builds on the differentiable nature of 3DGS-rendered images and incorporates insights from Hermite interpolation. It is designed to work collaboratively with a Lightweight Temporal Frame Interpolation (LTFI) module to reduce computational cost. 3DGS^3: Joint Super Sampling and Frame Interpolation for Real-Time Large-Scale 3DGS Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37314-430, fetched 2026-10-29

name: CLM
head: Early Adam Update, CLM Pipelining, CPU-GPU Memory Barrier Removal, Smart Caching Policy for Gaussian States
body: CLM is a training optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes the GPU memory barrier by offloading Gaussian states to CPU memory and overlapping CPU-side optimizer updates with GPU rendering. It solves the problem of VRAM exhaustion and communication stalls in large-scale scenes by implementing a smart caching policy that keeps frequently updated Gaussians on the GPU while streaming others. Unlike baseline offloading which incurs significant latency, CLM uses pipelining and early Adam updates to hide communication overhead, enabling training of scenes that exceed GPU memory on a single device. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of training views (microbatches), the current set of 3D Gaussian parameters \theta (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients), and the Adam optimizer state. Output: Updated Gaussian parameters \theta' and rendered images. Data Structures: 1. CPU Memory Buffer: Stores the full set of Gaussian attributes. Attributes are concatenated and padded to be contiguous and cache-line aligned. 2. GPU Memory Buffer: Stores a subset of "in-frustum" Gaussians required for the current microbatch. 3. Double Buffer: Used in the pipelining stage to enable parameter prefetching and delayed gradient offloading. 4. Signal Buffer: A buffer in CPU pinned memory used to synchronize the GPU communication stream and the CPU Adam thread. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-compute Finalization Microbatch (Lg): For each Gaussian g in the scene, determine the microbatch index Lg at which it is "finalized." A Gaussian is finalized in microbatch j if it is accessed in microbatch j but not in any subsequent microbatch k > j within the current training batch B. Lg = \max \{ i \mid g \in Si \} where Si is the set of Gaussians accessed in microbatch i. If g is not accessed in the batch, Lg = 0. 2. Microbatch Scheduling: Schedule the order of microbatches to maximize two factors: Spatial Locality: Maximize the intersection |S{i+1} \cap Si| to improve GPU caching efficiency. Early Finalization: Arrange microbatches so that more Gaussians are finalized in earlier indices, allowing more CPU Adam updates to overlap with GPU work. 3. Selective Loading (GPU-initiated): Instead of using standard cudaMemcpy, a custom CUDA kernel initiates data transfer from pinned CPU memory to GPU registers, then to GPU memory. The kernel splits the contiguous CPU buffer and concatenates only the in-frustum Gaussian attributes into GPU memory. This avoids CPU-GPU coordination overhead and utilizes PCIe bandwidth efficiently. 4. Forward and Backward Pass: The GPU renders the current microbatch using the loaded Gaussians and computes gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}. 5. Gradient Offloading: A custom kernel transfers gradients from GPU memory to CPU memory. The kernel fetches previously accumulated gradients, adds the new gradients in CUDA registers, and stores the sum back to CPU memory. 6. Early CPU Adam Update: A dedicated CPU thread executes the Adam optimizer. At the end of every microbatch j, the CPU thread updates all Gaussians g where Lg = j. The Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is released during this process to allow concurrent execution with the primary thread. Synchronization is handled via the signal buffer: the GPU sets a signal via DMA when gradients are ready, triggering the CPU update. Gaussians finalized in the last microbatch (Lg = B) do not have their Adam computation overlapped with subsequent GPU work. 7. Caching Policy: The system maintains a cache of frequently updated Gaussians on the GPU. Gaussians not in the cache are streamed from CPU memory as needed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainbatch(batchviews, gaussians, optimizerstate): # 1. Determine finalization microbatch for each Gaussian # Si is the set of Gaussians accessed in microbatch i Lg = {} for g in gaussians: accessedmicrobatches = [i for i, view in enumerate(batchviews) if g in view.frustumgaussians] if accessedmicrobatches: Lg[g] = max(accessedmicrobatches) else: Lg[g] = 0 # 2. Schedule microbatches to maximize overlap (implementation detail omitted) scheduledviews = schedulemicrobatches(batchviews) # 3. Initialize double buffers for pipelining gpuparamsbuffer = allocategpubuffer() cpugradbuffer = allocatecpupinnedbuffer() # 4. Process microbatches for j, view in enumerate(scheduledviews): # Selective Loading: Load in-frustum Gaussians from CPU to GPU # Initiated by GPU kernel to avoid CPU-GPU coordination infrustumgaussians = getinfrustumgaussians(view, Lg) selectiveloadkernel(infrustumgaussians, gpuparamsbuffer) # Forward and Backward Pass renderoutput = forwardpass(gpuparamsbuffer, view) gradients = backwardpass(renderoutput, view) # Gradient Offloading: Accumulate gradients in CPU memory # Kernel adds new gradients to existing accumulated gradients accumulategradientskernel(gradients, cpugradbuffer) # Signal GPU communication stream completion signalbuffer.setsignal() # Early CPU Adam Update # Update Gaussians finalized in this microbatch gaussianstoupdate = [g for g, l in Lg.items() if l == j] if gaussianstoupdate: cpuadamthread.update(gaussianstoupdate, cpugradbuffer, optimizerstate) return gaussians A framework that stores the full scene in CPU RAM and dynamically streams only visible Gaussians to GPU memory, enabling training and rendering of scenes exceeding VRAM on a single consumer GPU. It uses a lightweight caching system to track recently used Gaussians and reduce CPU-GPU data transfer. A pitfall is that a single distant view may require access to the full scene, causing high transfer overhead. A custom CUDA kernel that loads Gaussian parameters from pinned CPU memory to GPU registers and then to GPU memory, initiated from the GPU to avoid CPU-GPU coordination overhead. It stores offloaded Gaussian attributes in pinned CPU memory, concatenated and padded for cache-line alignment. The kernel splits attributes from the contiguous CPU buffer and concatenates only in-frustum attributes into GPU memory. A similar kernel is used to transfer gradients from GPU to CPU. Memory Usage: Significantly reduces GPU memory usage for Gaussian model states by offloading them to CPU RAM. It slightly increases "other" memory usage due to the double buffer design for pipelining. Performance: Reduces training time by overlapping communication and CPU Adam computation with GPU computation. In naive offloading, communication and CPU Adam overheads account for >50% of training time; CLM reduces this by hiding these costs. Scalability: Enables training on scenes that exceed VRAM on a single GPU. Hardware: Requires pinned CPU memory and a dedicated CPU thread for Adam updates. Tested on RTX 2080 Ti and RTX 4090. Limitations: The effectiveness of overlapping CPU Adam depends on the scene; scenes with fewer early-finalized Gaussians see less benefit. CLM was introduced in the paper "CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It extends the Grendel training framework and incorporates gsplat rasterization kernels. The method addresses the limitations of naive offloading and distributed training approaches like Grendel-GS. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3779212.3790140, fetched 2026-10-31 A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.01110, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Gaussians Cache Mechanism
head: Gaussian Cache, Reference View Cache
body: The Gaussians Cache Mechanism is a dynamic memory management module designed to accelerate the training and inference of pose-free generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting by eliminating redundant Gaussian prediction computations. It solves the problem of re-inferencing Gaussian points for reference views that share identical relative poses and features across consecutive optimization iterations. Unlike the baseline which re-predicts Gaussians for all input pairs every step, this method stores, queries, and releases cached Gaussian states based on image IDs, achieving a 2× speedup in training and an 8× speedup in inference without degrading reconstruction quality (PSNR). The mechanism operates as a dynamic store, query, and release system that maps image identifiers to pre-computed Gaussian point sets. It prevents the computational overhead of re-running the Gaussian prediction network (e.g., G-3DG model) for reference views that have already been processed in the immediate previous iteration. Input: A set of reference views I^1r \cdots I^Nr with corresponding image IDs \{1, \dots, N\} and their predicted Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i from the current or previous iteration. Output: A cache data structure containing stored Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i indexed by image ID i, and the retrieved subset of Gaussians for the current rendering step. The cache is a dynamic store mapping image IDs to Gaussian point sets. Structure: A hash map or dictionary Cache. Key: Image ID i (integer). Value: Predicted Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i (set of 3D Gaussians with attributes: position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Size: Variable, determined by the number of unique reference views processed in recent iterations. 1. Store: In training or inference step t, the system predicts Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i for each reference view i in the current batch. These points \mathbf{G}i are stored in the cache associated with their image ID i. 2. Query: In step t+1, the system identifies the set of image IDs required for the current iteration. It queries the cache using these IDs to retrieve previously stored Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i. 3. Combine: The retrieved cached Gaussians are combined with any newly predicted Gaussians (for views not found in the cache or if the cache was cleared) to form the complete set of Gaussians for splatting. 4. Release: After querying all necessary IDs for the current iteration, the cache identifies any remaining stored Gaussians that were not accessed (unmatched). These unmatched Gaussians are released (deleted) from the cache to optimize memory usage. This ensures that stale data from previous iterations that are no longer relevant does not accumulate, reducing the memory footprint without compromising performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class GaussiansCache: def init(self): # Dictionary mapping imageid -> GaussianPoints self.cache = {} def store(self, imageid, gaussianpoints): """ Stores predicted Gaussian points for a specific image ID. """ self.cache[imageid] = gaussianpoints def query(self, requiredimageids): """ Retrieves cached Gaussian points for the required image IDs. Returns a dictionary of {imageid: gaussianpoints} for found IDs. """ retrieved = {} for imgid in requiredimageids: if imgid in self.cache: retrieved[imgid] = self.cache[imgid] return retrieved def release(self, requiredimageids): """ Removes cached Gaussians that were not accessed in the current query. This optimizes memory usage by clearing stale data. """ # Identify keys in cache that are NOT in the required set keystoremove = [key for key in self.cache if key not in requiredimageids] # Delete the unmatched entries for key in keystoremove: del self.cache[key] def processiteration(self, currentimageids, predictionnetwork): """ Full workflow for one training/inference iteration. """ # 1. Query cache for previously computed Gaussians cachedgaussians = self.query(currentimageids) # 2. Identify IDs not in cache (need new prediction) uncachedids = [imgid for imgid in currentimageids if imgid not in cachedgaussians] # 3. Predict Gaussians for uncached IDs newgaussians = {} for imgid in uncachedids: # Predict Gaussians from reference views # Assumes predictionnetwork takes image and returns Gaussian points newgaussians[imgid] = predictionnetwork.predict(imgid) # 4. Combine cached and new Gaussians for rendering allgaussians = {cachedgaussians, newgaussians} # 5. Render/Splat using allgaussians renderresult = splat(allgaussians) # 6. Store newly predicted Gaussians into cache for next iteration for imgid, gpoints in newgaussians.items(): self.store(imgid, gpoints) # 7. Release unmatched Gaussians to free memory self.release(currentimageids) return renderresult Typical Values: On a single RTX 3090 GPU, this mechanism reduces training time from 4s/iter to 2s/iter and inference time from 1.02s/iter to 0.13s/iter. Precision/Identity: The cache relies on exact image ID matching. If the same physical view is assigned a different ID in consecutive steps, it will be treated as a new view, leading to redundant computation. Memory Management: The release step is critical. If the release step is omitted, the cache grows indefinitely with every unique view ever processed, leading to excessive memory consumption. Time Complexity: Reduces per-iteration computation by avoiding redundant forward passes through the Gaussian prediction network for repeated views. Memory Complexity: Bounded by the number of unique reference views processed in the immediate vicinity of the current iteration, as stale entries are released. Performance: Achieves a 2× speed increase during training and an 8× boost during inference compared to the baseline without the cache. Quality: Maintains identical PSNR (32.34 dB) compared to the baseline, indicating no negative impact on reconstruction accuracy. Strengths: Significant reduction in training and inference latency; effective for pose-free generalizable methods where reference views are reused across iterations. Limitations: Requires consistent image ID assignment across iterations to benefit from caching. Does not handle long-term temporal coherence beyond the immediate release cycle. The Gaussians Cache Mechanism was introduced in the GGRt (Generalizable Gaussian Splatting in Real-time) paper by Li et al.. GGRt is a pose-free generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that aims to achieve real-time rendering (\ge 100 FPS) and fast inference (\ge 5 FPS) without requiring explicit camera pose information. The cache mechanism was specifically designed to address the computational bottleneck of re-inferencing Gaussian points for reference views that share the same relative pose and features across consecutive training and inference steps. It builds on the G-3DG model and IPO-Net components of the GGRt architecture. GGRt: Towards Pose-Free Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting in Real-Time, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73209-619, fetched 2026-10-29

name: FastGS
head: FastGS framework, Multi-View Consistent Densification and Pruning (VCD/VCP)
body: FastGS is a general acceleration framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that significantly reduces training time by regulating the number of Gaussians based on multi-view consistency, dispensing with explicit budgeting mechanisms. It re-engineers the training loop using dynamic sparse rasterization and fast gradient checkpointing to skip negligible computations. Unlike sibling methods that rely on Gaussian-associated properties (Taming-3DGS) or indirect gradient approximations (Speedy-Splat), FastGS directly evaluates each Gaussian's contribution to multi-view reconstruction quality to guide densification and pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud, multi-view images. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonic coefficients). Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive Gi is parameterized as follows: Mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation ri \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \sigmai \in \mathbb{R} Color coefficients ci \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 3} (view-dependent spherical harmonics, degree 3) The covariance matrix is defined as \Sigmai^{3D} = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top, where Ri and Si are rotation and scale matrices derived from ri and si. Rendering and Projection: To render, Gaussians are projected into the 2D image plane. Given a viewing transformation W, the covariance in camera coordinates is computed as: \Sigmai^{\prime 3D} = J W \Sigmai^{3D} W^\top J^\top where J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. The projected 2D covariance \Sigmai^{2D} is obtained by marginalizing \Sigmai^{\prime 3D} along the viewing direction. The 2D Gaussian contribution to pixel p is: Gi^\prime(p) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (p - \mui^{2D})^\top (\Sigmai^{2D})^{-1} (p - \mui^{2D})\right) Color is accumulated via alpha blending: C(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \quad \alphai = \sigmai Gi^\prime(p) Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using SfM point clouds. 2. Dynamic Sparse Rasterization: During rendering, skip tiles with negligible transmittance to reduce computation. 3. Gradient Checkpointing: Use a fast gradient checkpointing scheme that recomputes only necessary intermediate values during the backward pass to save memory. 4. Multi-View Score Computation (VCD/VCP): Sample training views and generate per-pixel L1 loss maps between ground truth and rendered images. For each sampled view, compute a multi-view score for each Gaussian by counting the number of high-error pixels within its 2D footprint. High-error pixels are identified solely from the per-pixel L1 loss. 5. Adaptive Densification (VCD): Use the multi-view score to guide densification. If a Gaussian contributes beneficially to multi-view rendering quality (low error contribution), it is retained or densified. This avoids the redundancy seen in methods using Gaussian-associated scores. 6. Adaptive Pruning (VCP): Remove Gaussians that are useless to multi-view rendering quality (high error contribution or low importance). 7. Optimization: Update parameters using the accumulated gradients. The method does not require a global budget mechanism for the number of Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastgstrain(sfmpoints, multiviewimages, numiterations): # Initialize Gaussians from SfM gaussians = initializefromsfm(sfmpoints) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample views and render sampledviews = sampleviews(multiviewimages) renderedcolors = [] gtcolors = [] for view in sampledviews: # Dynamic sparse rasterization skips low-transmittance tiles color = renderdynamicsparse(gaussians, view.camera) renderedcolors.append(color) gtcolors.append(view.gtimage) # 2. Compute Multi-View Scores (VCD/VCP) # Calculate L1 loss maps lossmaps = computel1loss(renderedcolors, gtcolors) # Compute importance score for each Gaussian based on high-error pixels in footprint gaussianscores = computemultiviewscores(gaussians, lossmaps) # 3. Adaptive Densification (VCD) # Densify Gaussians that have low error contribution (high importance) # but are currently sparse or small gaussians = densifyvcd(gaussians, gaussianscores, thresholdlowerror) # 4. Adaptive Pruning (VCP) # Remove Gaussians with high error contribution (low importance) gaussians = prunevcp(gaussians, gaussianscores, thresholdhigherror) # 5. Backward Pass with Gradient Checkpointing # Recompute only necessary intermediates to save memory gradients = backwardpasscheckpointed(gaussians, sampledviews, gtcolors) # 6. Optimizer Step updategaussians(gaussians, gradients) return gaussians Parameters: Training time target: ~100 seconds for static scenes (e.g., Tanks & Temples train scene). Loss weights: Standard 3DGS loss weights apply (\lambda{SSIM}, etc.). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundancy: Methods relying on Gaussian-associated scores (like Taming-3DGS) lead to excessive growth of redundant Gaussians because they do not leverage actual contribution to rendering quality. Quality Degradation: Methods relying on gradients (like Speedy-Splat) lead to significant degradation in rendering quality because they indirectly enforce multi-view consistency. Precision: Dynamic sparse rasterization requires careful handling of transmittance thresholds to avoid artifacts. A strategy to improve training time efficiency by separating higher SH bands from the 0th band within the rasterizer, reducing the number of updates for higher SH bands compared to diffused colors. It modifies the rasterizer to split SH bands from the diffused color, updating SH bands every 16 iterations while updating diffused color at every step. It also optimizes SSIM loss calculation by replacing the standard 11x11 2D Gaussian kernel with two smaller 1D Gaussian kernels, calculated via a fused CUDA kernel. The total loss is defined as L = (1 - \lambda{SSIM})L1 + \lambda{SSIM} L{D-SIM} + \lambdam Lm + \lambda{sh} L{sh}. Restructuring splat attributes (color, bounding box, position) into 128-bit aligned vectors to utilize optimized memory load instructions and reduce the total number of memory operations. The new structure packs: Field 1: Color (4D float vector, 128 bits, padded from original 96-bit 3D float); Field 2: Bounding Box (4D unsigned integer vector, 64 bits, 16-bit uints in pixel space); Field 3: Screen Position (2D float vector, 64 bits). The Bounding Box and Screen Position are packed to form a single 128-bit structure alongside the Color. This trades additional compute instructions for unpacking data for further reductions in memory operation instructions. Using the original 96-bit 3D float vector for color lacks optimized load instructions, leading to inefficient memory access. Time Complexity: Significantly reduced training time. Achieves 3.29× faster training than state-of-the-art methods on Mip-NeRF 360 dataset. Achieves 15.45× faster training than vanilla 3DGS on Deep Blending dataset. Memory Complexity: Reduced via gradient checkpointing and dynamic sparse rasterization. Performance: Completes training on Tanks & Temples train scene in approximately 100 seconds. Scaling: Demonstrates 2.82× faster training for dynamic scene reconstruction and 2.24× faster for surface reconstruction. Strengths: General applicability to static, dynamic, surface, sparse-view, large-scale reconstruction, and SLAM tasks. No budgeting mechanism required. Limitations: Relies on accurate multi-view consistency; performance may degrade if multi-view data is insufficient or noisy. FastGS was proposed as a general acceleration framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting to address the trade-off between training time and rendering quality. It was introduced in a preprint in December 2025. The method builds on the foundational differentiable rasterization and gradient accumulation principles of 3DGS [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. It specifically targets the inefficiencies of existing densification and pruning strategies by introducing multi-view consistent evaluation metrics. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) FastGS: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting in 100 Seconds, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2511.04283, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Trick-GS: A Balanced Bag of Tricks for Efficient Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/icassp49660.2025.10889395, fetched 2026-10-30 Warp-Level Culling for Efficient Blending in 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3820019, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Fused Backward and Optimizer
head: Fused Adam Update, Fused optimizer-backward pass, Fused updates, Fusing Backward and Optimizer
body: Fused Backward and Optimizer is a training optimization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates the Adam optimizer step directly into the backward pass of the differentiable rasterizer. It solves the bottleneck where parameter updates consume 40–60% of training time by eliminating separate optimizer kernels and reducing VRAM usage through the avoidance of intermediate parameter buffers. It differs from sibling methods like FastGS by prioritizing memory efficiency and correctness over maximum speed, whereas FastGS and CLM focus on skipping computations for invisible Gaussians to achieve higher speedups at the cost of potential quality degradation or inconsistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} computed by the rasterizer's backward pass; current first and second moment estimates mt, vt for Adam; hyperparameters \alpha (learning rate), \beta1, \beta2, \epsilon. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \theta{t+1}; updated moments m{t+1}, v{t+1}. Data Structures: Gaussian Parameters: Stored in contiguous GPU memory. Fields include position, covariance (6 values), opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Adam Moments: Two buffers per parameter set, matching the size of the parameters, storing mt and vt. Gradients: Buffer matching parameter size, populated by the rasterizer backward pass. Numbered Steps: 1. Gradient Computation: The differentiable rasterizer computes pixel colors and gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} for all visible Gaussians. For Gaussians outside the viewing frustum, gradients are explicitly set to zero. 2. Moment Loading: Load current first and second moment estimates mt and vt from global memory into registers or shared memory for the active Gaussians. 3. Fused Update Kernel: Launch a single CUDA kernel that performs the Adam update logic for all parameters in parallel: Compute biased first moment: m{t+1} = \beta1 mt + (1 - \beta1) \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}. Compute biased second moment: v{t+1} = \beta2 vt + (1 - \beta2) \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}\right)^2. Compute bias-corrected estimates: \hat{m}{t+1} = \frac{m{t+1}}{1 - \beta1^{t+1}}, \hat{v}{t+1} = \frac{v{t+1}}{1 - \beta2^{t+1}}. Update parameters: \theta{t+1} = \thetat - \alpha \frac{\hat{m}{t+1}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}{t+1}} + \epsilon}. Write updated moments m{t+1}, v{t+1} and parameters \theta{t+1} back to global memory. 4. Memory Management: No intermediate buffers for raw parameters are allocated during the update, as updates are written directly to the parameter storage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fusedadambackward(grads, params, m, v, alpha, beta1, beta2, eps, t): """ Fuses Adam update into the backward pass. grads: Tensor of gradients dL/dtheta. params: Tensor of current parameters thetat. m: Tensor of first moment estimates mt. v: Tensor of second moment estimates vt. alpha: Learning rate. beta1, beta2: Adam decay rates. eps: Adam epsilon. t: Current training step index (1-based). """ # Compute bias correction terms bias1 = 1.0 - beta1 t bias2 = 1.0 - beta2 t # Update first moment mnew = beta1 m + (1.0 - beta1) grads # Update second moment vnew = beta2 v + (1.0 - beta2) (grads 2) # Bias-corrected moments mhat = mnew / bias1 vhat = vnew / bias2 # Parameter update paramsnew = params - alpha (mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + eps)) # Write back m[:] = mnew v[:] = vnew params[:] = paramsnew Parameters: \alpha: Learning rate (typically 1.6 \times 10^{-2} for position, 1.0 \times 10^{-3} for other parameters in standard 3DGS, but specific values for the fused variant are not explicitly differentiated in the source). \beta1, \beta2: Adam momentum coefficients (typically 0.9, 0.999). \epsilon: Adam epsilon (typically 10^{-15}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradients: To maintain correctness with respect to the original Adam step, parameter updates must be performed even for parameters receiving a gradient of zero (e.g., Gaussians outside the viewing frustum). Skipping these updates breaks the moment estimation consistency. Performance Trade-off: While this approach reduces VRAM, it does not skip computations for invisible Gaussians, limiting the speedup compared to methods that do skip them. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of Gaussian parameters. The fused kernel reduces kernel launch overhead and memory bandwidth pressure by combining gradient accumulation and update into one pass. Memory Complexity: O(N) for parameters and moments. VRAM is reduced because no additional buffers for intermediate parameter states are required during the update step. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 outdoor scenes with an RTX 4090, training time reduced from 5m31s to 5m04s, and VRAM usage decreased from 6.0GiB to 5.6GiB, with PSNR increasing slightly from 24.72 to 24.73. Strengths: Significant VRAM reduction, especially beneficial for large scenes with many Gaussians. Maintains strict numerical equivalence with the standard Adam optimizer. Limitations: Attainable performance improvements are smaller compared to methods that skip updates for invisible Gaussians. After integration, parameter updates remain a significant bottleneck, consuming a large fraction of the remaining runtime. When to Use: When VRAM is the primary constraint or when strict adherence to the original 3DGS optimization trajectory is required without risking quality degradation from skipped updates. When Not to Use: When maximum training speed is the priority and slight quality inconsistencies are acceptable; in such cases, skipping updates for invisible Gaussians (as in FastGS) is preferred. The method was introduced in "Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization". Profiling of the original 3DGS implementation revealed that the Adam update routine consumed 40–60% of total training time. The authors proposed fusing the optimizer step into the rasterizer's backward pass to alleviate this bottleneck. The approach is presented as a foundational optimization that can be combined with other techniques like skipping invisible Gaussian updates, though the latter is noted as an optional extension that may introduce inconsistencies. Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic and Temporal Modeling
head: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting, Dynamic Neural Rendering, On-the-Fly Training
body: Dynamic and Temporal Modeling extends static volumetric representations to handle non-rigid motion and time-varying scenes by parameterizing attributes as functions of time or modeling temporal deformation fields. It solves the limitation of static radiance fields and fixed Gaussian sets, which cannot represent evolving geometry or appearance. It sets itself apart from static methods by introducing explicit temporal dependencies, either through canonical space deformation [13852-deformation-field-modeling.md] or direct time-conditioned attribute prediction [17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md], and distinguishes itself from offline 4D reconstruction methods by supporting on-the-fly or incremental training strategies [7582-on-the-fly-dynamic-nerf-training.md][9203-3dgstream.md]. The family shares the following core mechanisms for handling temporal dynamics: 1. Temporal Parameterization: Attributes that vary with time, such as position \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, density \sigma, or color \mathbf{c}, are expressed as functions of time t [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Common functional forms include: Polynomial/Linear: \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{q}0 + \mathbf{m}t [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Fourier Series: \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{c}0 + \sum{k=0}^{K} (\mathbf{a}k \cos(k \omega t) + \mathbf{b}k \sin(k \omega t)) [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Neural Deformation: A neural network \Psit(x, t) predicts a displacement \Delta x to warp dynamic coordinates to a canonical space [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Implicit Fields: Time-dependent NeRFs map (x, d, t) to density and color, often using local neighborhoods of frames [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. 2. Canonical Space Mapping: Many methods (e.g., D-NeRF, Nerfies) introduce a canonical configuration, typically at t=0, where the scene is static. A deformation network maps dynamic coordinates x at time t to canonical coordinates x': x' = x + \Psit(x, t) The radiance field is then queried in the canonical space: [\sigma, c] = \Psix(x', d) [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. 3. Rendering with Dynamics: The rendering process integrates time-dependent attributes. For Gaussian-based methods, position and rotation are computed for the specific time t of the camera ray before rasterization [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. For NeRF-based methods, density \sigma and color c are queried at the deformed or time-conditioned point [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. 4. Loss Functions: Optimization typically minimizes photometric loss (L1 or LPIPS) between rendered and ground truth images [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Additional constraints often include: Temporal Smoothness: Penalizing abrupt changes in attributes between adjacent frames [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Rigid/Flow Constraints: Using optical flow or KNN rigid loss to guide deformation [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Regularization: Elastic or background regularization to prevent overfitting in deformation fields [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. An on-the-fly training method that replaces temporal deformation fields with a NeRF model conditioned on multi-view projected colors. It leverages the invariance of projected color for corresponding 3D points across consecutive frames to implicitly track correspondence, allowing it to utilize radiance fields from previous frames to render the current frame with minimal optimization iterations. Unlike sibling methods that use explicit temporal inputs or deformation networks which extrapolate poorly to unseen times, OD-NeRF requires the minimum number of optimization iterations per new frame. Choose this method when streaming dynamic scenes with minimal per-frame optimization latency is required and specular/occlusion artifacts are manageable. A method for training dynamic Neural Radiance Fields concurrently with the acquisition of training frames, enabling the streaming of dynamic scenes as they unfold. It estimates the radiance field for the current time step tk using only the images up to tk and the radiance field from the previous step t{k-1}. It is distinguished by its application of a first-order Markov assumption to decouple current estimation from the entire history, allowing for minimal optimization iterations per frame and interactive-speed streaming. Choose this method for real-time dynamic scene reconstruction where scalability to long sequences is critical. A method for online training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in dynamic scene reconstruction. It models the transformation between frames as a neural transformation cache and adaptively adds 3D Gaussians to handle emerging objects. It is distinguished from static 3DGS by its ability to incrementally update the scene representation as new video frames arrive, rather than requiring offline batch optimization of a fixed set of Gaussians. Choose this method when explicit Gaussian representation is preferred over neural fields for dynamic scenes, especially with emerging geometry. This family addresses the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when applied to dynamic scenes, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging, and real-world captures with optical artifacts. It extends the static Gaussian representation to handle temporal dynamics, transient occluders, and blur effects. It differs from sibling NeRF-based methods (e.g., D-NeRF) by maintaining a unified, explicit Gaussian representation rather than a neural field, which yields efficiency and state-of-the-art results on diverse photo scenes without requiring explicit transient labels. Choose this method when handling complex optical artifacts or transient objects in dynamic scenes. Deformation Field Modeling addresses the problem of reconstructing and rendering dynamic scenes from static image or video sequences by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of geometry and appearance. It solves the limitation of static radiance fields by mapping dynamic, time-varying coordinates to a static canonical space where the radiance field is defined. What sets this approach apart from siblings like Dynamic Object Embedding in Static Scenes (which isolates motion to specific objects) or Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (which uses explicit parametric functions) is its reliance on a learned implicit function (typically an MLP) to predict continuous displacement vectors or feature transformations, allowing for complex, non-rigid, and global deformations without assuming a specific motion prior. Choose this method for complex non-rigid deformations where explicit parametric motion models are insufficient. 4D-GS extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by parameterizing Gaussian attributes as functions of time, enabling the reconstruction and rendering of non-rigidly deforming objects. It distinguishes itself from sibling NeRF-based dynamic methods by retaining the efficient splatting rasterization pipeline while replacing static positional encoding with multi-resolution hexplane voxels to capture spatiotemporal correlations. Choose this method when high-fidelity dynamic reconstruction is needed with the efficiency of Gaussian splatting, particularly for scenes with complex spatiotemporal correlations. Temporal Input Conditioning is a family of techniques that parameterize scene attributes—such as position, rotation, opacity, density, or color—as explicit functions of time t to enable the synthesis of novel views for dynamic scenes. It solves the problem of representing non-rigid motion and temporal evolution in volumetric data without requiring ground-truth geometry or multi-view stereo data at every instant. It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into a static canonical space and a learned deformation field, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture. Unlike DaReNeRF, which focuses on specific direction-aware wavelet decompositions, this family establishes the foundational canonical-space paradigm for dynamic neural rendering. Choose this method as a general-purpose approach for dynamic scene representation using canonical space and deformation fields. A method that introduces a temporal radial basis function to represent temporal opacity, modeling emerging or vanishing content. Polynomial functions model motion and rotation. Spherical harmonics are replaced with features consisting of base color, view-related feature, and time-related feature. The latter two are translated into residual color through an MLP added to the base color. During optimization, new 3D Gaussians are sampled at under-optimized positions based on training error and coarse depth. A procedure coupled with the two-step DynART/P-DVC algorithm to handle large displacement amplitudes by resolving large-scale features first and progressively enriching with finer details. Resolve large-scale features of both microstructure and motion. Progressively enrich the description with finer details. An explicit deformation modeling method using parametric functions to ensure temporal continuity and robustness, where the number of parameters is independent of time. 1. Use a Fourier series to fit changes in the Gaussian’s position. 2. Approximate rotation by a linear function. 3. Keep other attributes unchanged over time. 4. Use dynamic optimization to optimize the parameters of the Fourier series and the linear function. Introduce a bidirectional optical flow loss in addition to image losses. Dynamic and Temporal Modeling in volumetric rendering originated from the need to extend static Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting to 4D scenes. Early works like D-NeRF introduced canonical space deformation for dynamic NeRFs [13852-deformation-field-modeling.md]. The adaptation to 3D Gaussian Splatting followed, with methods like 4D-GS and 3DGStream introducing explicit temporal parameterization and neural transformation caches [17368-4d-gs.md][9203-3dgstream.md]. On-the-fly training methods like OD-NeRF further enabled real-time streaming by leveraging Markov assumptions [7582-on-the-fly-dynamic-nerf-training.md]. These methods are widely used in dynamic novel view synthesis, AR/VR, and video compression. name: Projected Color-Guided Dynamic NeRF
head: OD-NeRF
body: Projected Color-Guided Dynamic NeRF (OD-NeRF) is an on-the-fly training method for dynamic scenes that replaces temporal deformation fields with a NeRF model conditioned on multi-view projected colors. By leveraging the invariance of projected color for corresponding 3D points across consecutive frames, the model implicitly tracks correspondence, allowing it to utilize radiance fields from previous frames to render the current frame with minimal optimization iterations. Unlike sibling methods that use explicit temporal inputs or deformation networks which extrapolate poorly to unseen times, OD-NeRF requires the minimum number of optimization iterations per new frame. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of multi-view images representing a dynamic scene. For synthetic datasets, the method builds upon the TiNeuVox architecture; for real-world datasets, it builds upon InstantNGP (via NerfAcc). Outputs: A radiance field representation that can render novel views for any frame in the sequence, updated incrementally frame-by-frame. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy Grid: A spatial structure used for efficient sampling, transited and updated from the previous frame in synthetic datasets. In real-world datasets, the hash voxel grid from InstantNGP serves this purpose. 2. NeRF MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron that maps concatenated spatial features and projected color statistics to density and color. 3. Spatial Feature: The feature vector queried from the voxel grid at a sampled point's location. Parameters: \sigma{\min}: Density threshold for rejection sampling. Not given in the sources. R: Fixed interval for rejection sampling. Not given in the sources. Warm-up Duration: 2 seconds for the first frame in synthetic datasets to compensate for slower convergence of hashed voxels compared to multi-scale voxels. Optimization Schedule: Intensity scaled from 1 (frame 1) to 0.05 (frame 10) for better convergence. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: For the first frame, initialize the radiance field. For synthetic datasets, apply a 2-second warm-up period. 2. Sampling: Sample points along rays. Synthetic: Use rejection sampling based on the transited occupancy grid from the previous frame. A sample xi is rejected if its occupancy value \sigma{\text{occ}}(xi) is below \sigma{\min} AND it is not on a fixed interval R: \text{reject } xi \text{ if } (\sigma{\text{occ}}(xi) < \sigma{\min}) \land \neg(i \mod R \equiv R//2) Real-world: Use the standard sampling strategy of InstantNGP. 3. Projected Color Computation: For each sampled point, compute the mean and variance of its projected colors from the training views. 4. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the mean and variance of the projected colors with the spatial feature queried from the voxel grid at the point's location. 5. NeRF Query: Input the concatenated feature vector into the NeRF MLP to predict density and color. 6. Rendering: Render the image using standard volume rendering integration. 7. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between the rendered image and the ground truth image. Real-world Specific: Add a depth smoothness regularization loss L{\text{depth}} calculated over any 3 \times 3 patch of rays: L{\text{depth}} = \frac{\text{std}(d{\text{far}} / d{3 \times 3})}{\text{std}(c{3 \times 3})} where d{\text{far}} is the depth of the farthest sample, d{3 \times 3} is the mean depth of the 3 \times 3 patch, and c{3 \times 3} is the mean color of the patch. 8. Transition and Update: Update the occupancy grid for the next frame based on the current frame's results to guide sampling for the subsequent frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trainodnerfframebyframe(videosequence, config): # Initialize NeRF MLP and occupancy grid model = NeRFMLP() if config['datasettype'] == 'synthetic': occupancygrid = OccupancyGrid() if config.get('warmupduration', 2.0) > 0: time.sleep(config['warmupduration']) else: occupancygrid = HashVoxelGrid() for frameidx, framedata in enumerate(videosequence): # Optimization schedule: scale from 1.0 (frame 1) to 0.05 (frame 10) optscale = max(0.05, 1.0 - (frameidx / 10.0) 0.95) for camera in framedata.cameras: rays = createrays(camera) renderedcolors = [] for ray in rays: samples = [] # Step 2: Sampling if config['datasettype'] == 'synthetic': uniformsamples = sampleuniformalongray(ray) for i, xi in enumerate(uniformsamples): sigmaocc = occupancygrid.query(xi) # Rejection sampling condition if not (sigmaocc < config['sigmamin'] and not (i % config['R'] == config['R'] // 2)): samples.append(xi) else: samples = sampleinstantngp(ray, occupancygrid) # Step 3: Projected Color Computation projectedcolors = computeprojectedcolors(samples, videosequence[:frameidx]) meancolor = np.mean(projectedcolors, axis=0) varcolor = np.var(projectedcolors, axis=0) # Step 4: Feature Concatenation spatialfeature = occupancygrid.queryspatialfeatures(samples) inputfeature = np.concatenate([spatialfeature, meancolor, varcolor], axis=-1) # Step 5: NeRF Query density, color = model.forward(inputfeature) # Step 6: Rendering (Standard volume rendering integration) T = 1.0 renderedcolor = np.zeros(3) for j in range(len(samples)): dist = np.linalg.norm(samples[j] - samples[j-1]) if j > 0 else 1.0 alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density[j] dist) renderedcolor += color[j] alpha T T = (1.0 - alpha) renderedcolors.append(renderedcolor) # Step 7: Optimization gtimages = framedata.gtimages loss = np.mean(np.abs(np.array(renderedcolors) - np.array(gtimages))) optscale # Real-world specific depth regularization if config['datasettype'] == 'real': depthloss = computedepthsmoothness(renderedcolors, samples) loss += depthloss model.backward(loss) # Step 8: Transition and Update updateoccupancygridfromrender(occupancygrid, samples, density) def NeRFMLP(): pass def OccupancyGrid(): pass def HashVoxelGrid(): pass def createrays(camera): pass def sampleuniformalongray(ray): pass def sampleinstantngp(ray, grid): pass def computeprojectedcolors(samples, prevframes): pass def updateoccupancygridfromrender(grid, samples, density): pass def computedepthsmoothness(renderedcolors, samples): pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Surfaces: Specular highlights violate the assumption of projected color invariance, leading to artifacts. Occlusions: Occluded points also violate relative invariance, causing artifacts. Filtering these outliers may incur significant computational costs. Convergence Speed: Hashed voxels converge slower than multi-scale voxels, necessitating the warm-up period for synthetic datasets. Planar Backgrounds: Real-world datasets with large planar backgrounds (e.g., walls, tables) may fail to converge well even for the first frame, requiring the depth smoothness regularization. Speed: Achieves an interactive speed of 6 FPS for both training and rendering on synthetic dynamic scenes on-the-fly. It provides a significant speed-up compared to state-of-the-art methods on real-world dynamic scenes. Optimization Efficiency: Requires the minimum number of optimization iterations for each new frame compared to models with temporal input dimensions or deformation fields. Extrapolation: Exhibits excellent temporal extrapolation capability, unlike deformation-based models that extrapolate poorly to unseen times. Memory: Uses hash voxel grids (InstantNGP) or multi-scale voxel grids (TiNeuVox), which are generally more memory-efficient than dense 3D grids. Limitations: Performance degrades on scenes with strong specularities or significant occlusions due to the reliance on projected color invariance. OD-NeRF was introduced in the paper "OD-NeRF: Efficient Training of On-the-Fly Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the challenge of efficient on-the-fly training, where the radiance field is trained and rendered frame-by-frame, effectively utilizing the radiance field estimated from previous frames. The method was implemented on top of TiNeuVox for synthetic datasets and InstantNGP (via NerfAcc) for real-world datasets. name: On-the-Fly Dynamic NeRF Training
head: OD-NeRF
body: On-the-fly Dynamic NeRF Training (OD-NeRF) is a method for training dynamic Neural Radiance Fields concurrently with the acquisition of training frames, enabling the streaming of dynamic scenes as they unfold. Unlike traditional dynamic NeRFs that require full video sequences for offline 4D reconstruction, this approach estimates the radiance field for the current time step tk using only the images up to tk and the radiance field from the previous step t{k-1}. It is distinguished by its application of a first-order Markov assumption to decouple current estimation from the entire history, allowing for minimal optimization iterations per frame and interactive-speed streaming. Inputs: C{0:k}: The set of multi-view images captured up to the current time step tk. F{k-1}: The radiance field function estimated at the previous time step t{k-1}. Outputs: Fk: The updated radiance field function at time tk, parameterized by spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. The method relies on standard NeRF representations: 1. Radiance Field Fk: A neural network mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \sigma \in \mathbb{R} is volume density and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is RGB color. For dynamic scenes, this may implicitly or explicitly encode time via deformation fields or 4D expansion, but the core optimization target is the field state Fk. 2. Occupancy Grid Gk: A sparse data structure used for efficient ray sampling, which is updated via a transition function from G{k-1}. 1. Initialize: Start with an initial radiance field F0. The occupancy grid G0 is initialized to cover the scene volume. 2. Receive Data: At time step k, acquire the new set of images Ck. 3. Markov Simplification: Apply the first-order Markov assumption to simplify the probability model. Assume conditional independence such that the current radiance field Fk is independent of all previous images \{C{0:k-1}\} and fields \{F{0:k-2}\} given the current images Ck and previous field F{k-1}: Fk \perp\!\!\!\perp \{C{0:k-1}, F{0:k-2}\} \mid \{Ck, F{k-1}\} This reduces the estimation objective to: Fk = \arg\max{Fk} P(Fk \mid Ck, F{k-1}) 4. Define Loss: Minimize the rendering loss between the rendered image \hat{C}k(r) and the ground truth image Ck(r) for all rays r \in R: Fk = \arg\min{Fk} \sum{r \in R} ||\hat{C}k(r) - Ck(r)||^22 5. Volume Rendering: For each ray r, compute the rendered color \hat{C}k(r) by aggregating N points along the ray with intervals \deltai: \hat{C}k(r) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where the transmittance Ti is: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) Here, \sigmai and ci are the density and color queried from Fk at the i-th point on the ray. 6. Optimization: Update the parameters of Fk (and potentially Gk) using gradient descent to minimize the loss defined in Step 4. The optimization starts from the state F{k-1} to ensure continuity and minimize the number of iterations required. 7. Transition: Update the occupancy grid Gk from G{k-1} using a simple transition function to maintain efficient sampling. 8. Stream: Render novel views using Fk at time tk. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ontheflytrainingstep(Fprev, imagesCk, camerask, numiterationsperframe, delta): # Initialize current field parameters from previous step Fcurr = copy.deepcopy(Fprev) # Volume rendering function matching the formula exactly using forward accumulation def volumerender(points, directions): # points: (N, 3), directions: (N, 3) sigma, color = Fcurr(points, directions) # sigma: (N,), color: (N, 3) rendered = np.zeros(3) T = 1.0 for i in range(len(sigma)): alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma[i] delta) rendered += T alpha color[i] T = (1.0 - alpha) return rendered # Loss computation over all cameras and pixels def computeloss(): totalloss = 0.0 for cam in camerask: for u, v in cam.pixelcoordinates: rayorigin = cam.position raydirection = normalize(cam.focalmatrix @ np.array([u, v, 1.0]) - rayorigin) points = rayorigin + np.array([raydirection (i delta) for i in range(N)]) rendered = volumerender(points, raydirection) gt = cam.image[u, v] totalloss += np.sum((rendered - gt) 2) return totalloss # Optimization loop for in range(numiterationsperframe): loss = computeloss() gradients = computegradient(loss, Fcurr.weights) Fcurr.weights -= learningrate gradients return Fcurr Number of optimization iterations per frame: The exact number is not given in the sources. Number of samples N: Not given in the sources. Interval \delta: Not given in the sources. Camera Setup: The method is limited to dynamic scenes captured by multi-view forward-facing cameras. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the radiance field Fk and the occupancy grid Gk. Scalability: Estimating Fk conditioned on all previous images C{0:k} is not scalable as time tk increases. The Markov assumption is critical to mitigate this complexity growth. Camera Setup: The method is limited to dynamic scenes captured by multi-view forward-facing cameras. Monocular setups are excluded due to the need for camera movement, which is cumbersome for prolonged streaming. 360-degree inward-facing setups are also excluded due to hardware complexity. Continuity: The optimization must start from F{k-1} to ensure smooth transitions and minimize optimization steps. Precision: The volume rendering loop must use forward transmittance accumulation to avoid numerical underflow or off-by-one errors when rays start inside volumes or use fine step sizes. Time Complexity: The method aims for interactive speed by minimizing optimization iterations per frame. It avoids the O(K) complexity of processing all K frames jointly, instead operating in O(1) per frame with respect to the history length, thanks to the Markov assumption. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the radiance field Fk and the occupancy grid Gk. It does not need to store the full history of radiance fields or images, only the current state and the immediate previous state. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables real-time streaming of dynamic scenes as they happen. Scalable to long-duration events by avoiding history accumulation. Compatible with NeRF acceleration techniques (e.g., occupancy grids). Limitations: Limited to multi-view forward-facing camera setups. Requires careful initialization and transition between time steps to maintain quality with minimal iterations. Use when the goal is to stream a dynamic scene in real-time or near-real-time, and the camera setup allows for multi-view forward-facing capture. Do not use with monocular or complex multi-view inward-facing setups. The method was introduced in the paper "OD-NeRF: Efficient Training of On-the-Fly Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields". Traditional dynamic NeRFs (e.g., D-NeRF, Nerfies) focus on reconstructing 4D space-time from full video sequences. OD-NeRF addresses the limitation that these methods cannot stream the event while it is happening. It builds on the success of NeRF acceleration techniques that allow training small scenes in seconds, extending this to dynamic scenes on-the-fly. The method enables applications in social media, VR/AR, and gaming industries where real-time streaming of dynamic 3D content is valuable. name: 3DGStream
head: Neural Transformation Cache for 3DGS
body: 3DGStream is a method for online training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in dynamic scene reconstruction. It models the transformation between frames as a neural transformation cache and adaptively adds 3D Gaussians to handle emerging objects. It is distinguished from static 3DGS by its ability to incrementally update the scene representation as new video frames arrive, rather than requiring offline batch optimization of a fixed set of Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of images (video frames) with known camera poses, arriving online. Output: A dynamic 3DGS representation consisting of a set of 3D Gaussians whose attributes (position, rotation, scale, opacity, color) vary with time, managed via a neural transformation cache. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS attributes: mean position \mathbf{\mu}, covariance (defined by rotation \mathbf{q} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}. Neural Transformation Cache: A neural network that predicts the transformation (displacement and/or rotation) required to map a Gaussian's canonical state to its state at a specific time t. The exact architecture and input/output dimensions of this cache are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: The scene is initialized with a point cloud. For scenes with large static parts, the point cloud is randomly initialized into dynamic and static subsets, which are optimized separately to decouple dynamic and static components. 2. Neural Transformation Cache Modeling: The transformation between frames is modeled using a neural transformation cache. This cache likely takes the canonical Gaussian attributes and time t as input to predict the dynamic attributes. 3. Online Training: The 3DGS is trained online as new frames arrive. The rendering process uses the transformed Gaussians for the current frame's time t. 4. Adaptive Gaussian Addition: New 3D Gaussians are adaptively added to the scene to handle emerging objects that were not present in previous frames. This likely involves splitting or cloning existing Gaussians based on rendering error or depth uncertainty, similar to standard 3DGS densification, but applied dynamically over time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializescene(images): # Randomly initialize point cloud into dynamic and static subsets # if large static parts are detected. gaussians = randominitializepointcloud(images[0]) cache = NeuralTransformationCache() # Architecture not specified return gaussians, cache def onlinetrainingstep(gaussians, cache, newimage, camerapose, timet): # 1. Transform Gaussians using the neural transformation cache # The cache predicts transformation based on time t and canonical attributes transformedgaussians = cache.transform(gaussians, timet) # 2. Render the image using transformed Gaussians # Standard 3DGS rasterization is used with the time-specific attributes renderedimage = render3dgs(transformedgaussians, camerapose) # 3. Compute loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS) between rendered and ground truth loss = computeloss(renderedimage, newimage) # 4. Backpropagate to update Gaussians and Cache # Gradients flow through the cache transformation to update canonical attributes updateparameters(gaussians, cache, loss) # 5. Adaptively add new Gaussians for emerging objects # This step likely involves densification based on error or depth gaussians = adaptiveaddgaussians(gaussians, renderedimage, newimage) return gaussians, cache gaussians, cache = initializescene(videoframes) for t, (image, pose) in enumerate(videoframes): gaussians, cache = onlinetrainingstep(gaussians, cache, image, pose, t) Parameters: Learning rate for Gaussians and Cache: Not given in the sources. Time frequency \omega for Fourier-based temporal modeling (if used): Not given in the sources. 3DGStream uses a neural cache, not explicitly Fourier series, though the parent family mentions Fourier as a common form. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Emerging Objects: If new objects appear rapidly, the adaptive addition mechanism must be robust to avoid artifacts or slow convergence. Static/Dynamic Decoupling: Incorrect initialization of static vs. dynamic subsets may lead to poor reconstruction of static parts. Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues in 3DGS rasterization and neural network training apply. A method for modeling temporal transformations using a neural network. It sets itself apart from polynomial or Fourier-based parameterization by learning the transformation directly from data. Choose it when the motion is complex and not easily modeled by simple functions. See Deformation Field Modeling. A technique for dynamically adding Gaussians during training. It sets itself apart from fixed-set methods by allowing the scene complexity to grow. Choose it for scenes with occlusions or emerging objects. See Dynamic and Temporal Modeling. Time Complexity: Online training implies per-frame processing time. The complexity depends on the number of Gaussians and the cost of the neural transformation cache. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and the size of the neural transformation cache. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables online reconstruction of dynamic scenes; handles emerging objects; decouples static and dynamic parts. Limitations: Requires careful initialization; performance depends on the neural cache's capacity and training stability. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic scenes from video in an online or incremental manner. When not to use: For static scenes or when offline batch optimization is feasible and preferred for higher quality. 3DGStream was introduced as a method for online training of 3DGS in dynamic scene reconstruction. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and extends them to handle temporal dynamics through a neural transformation cache and adaptive Gaussian addition. It is part of the broader family of dynamic 3DGS methods, which also includes approaches like 4D Gaussian Splatting and GaussianFlow.
