name: Blur and Transient Modeling
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to handle temporal dynamics, transient occluders, and real-world optical artifacts like motion and defocus blur. It distinguishes itself from sibling NeRF-based methods by relying on explicit Gaussian primitives rather than implicit neural fields, enabling efficient rendering without requiring explicit transient labels. The family builds on the parent's mechanisms for temporal parameterization, canonical space mapping, and dynamic rendering Parent. NeTF is a neural modeling framework for Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging that recovers the 5D transient function (spatial location and direction) implicitly represented by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) [4692-neural-transient-field-netf.md]. It solves the inverse problem of reconstructing hidden 3D scenes from sparse, unbalanced time-resolved measurements captured by Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) arrays [4692-neural-transient-field-netf.md]. Unlike sibling methods that use Cartesian rays, NeTF parametrizes input training data on spherical wavefronts and employs Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to handle sparse sampling, producing sharper edges in semi-occluded scenes [4692-neural-transient-field-netf.md]. Choose it for NLOS reconstruction where sparse time-of-flight data must be mapped to 3D density volumes [4692-neural-transient-field-netf.md]. SWAG extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by conditioning Gaussians on learned appearance embeddings to handle dynamic scenes [6875-swag.md]. It specifically addresses transient occluders (e.g., pedestrians, moving vehicles) by training unsupervised transient Gaussians that learn to ignore these distractors, yielding state-of-the-art results on diverse photo scenes [6875-swag.md]. It is distinguished from siblings like NeTF by its reliance on explicit Gaussian primitives with appearance conditioning rather than implicit neural fields [6875-swag.md]. Choose it when reconstructing static scenes with moving occluders in standard RGB datasets [6875-swag.md]. Techniques to explicitly incorporate blur modeling during training to address real-world capture issues like motion blur and defocus blur. It employs coarse-to-fine kernel optimization and photometric bundle adjustment. Choose it when standard 3DGS produces artifacts due to camera motion or defocus in real-world captures. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) excels on carefully curated datasets, but real-world captures often suffer from blurs such as motion blur and defocus blur. Recent approaches explicitly incorporated blur modeling during training to address this challenge. While the approximations made in GS contribute to its efficiency, they also underlie artifacts such as aliasing and blur, and limit the accuracy of illumination estimation and the modeling of challenging objects. Most existing efforts focus on specific failure modes rather than providing a universal solution, requiring practitioners to diagnose scene issues and apply targeted optimization strategies. name: Neural Transient Field (NeTF)
body: Neural Transient Field (NeTF) is a neural modeling framework for Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging that recovers the 5D transient function (spatial location and direction) implicitly represented by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Unlike NeRF, which parametrizes input training data along lines (rays), NeTF parametrizes input training data on spherical wavefronts. It sets itself apart from siblings like SWAG by explicitly modeling the transient field in NLOS contexts, handling sparse and unbalanced sampling via MCMC, and producing sharper edges in semi-occluded scenes compared to Phasor Field or DLCT. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse set of transient measurements captured by a SPAD (Single-Photon Avalanche Diode) at specific spots on a relay wall. Measurements are parameterized on spherical wavefronts. Output: A 3D density volume implicitly represented by the MLP, which corresponds to the hidden scene. The final mesh is extracted via thresholding and Marching Cubes. Data Structures: MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes 5D coordinates (3D spatial position + 2D direction on the spherical wavefront) as input and outputs the transient density/value. Sampling Spots: A set of 2D coordinates on the relay wall where measurements are taken. In experiments, these are often arranged in a grid (e.g., 256 \times 256). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the MLP parameters. 2. Training (One-Stage Baseline): Sample points in the 3D volume and directions on the spherical wavefront. Query the MLP to predict the transient value. Compute the loss between predicted and measured transients at every measuring spot on the relay wall. Update MLP parameters to minimize loss. 3. Two-Stage Training (Optional but recommended for sparse data): Stage 1: Conduct training using all initial samples to obtain an initial reconstruction. Loss Calculation: Calculate the loss function between the predicted and measured transients at every measuring spot on the relay wall. PDF Formation: Normalize the calculated loss to form a Probability Density Function (PDF). Higher loss implies undersampling. Resampling: Resample detection spots using the PDF. A higher loss corresponds to a higher PDF and is more densely sampled. Stage 2: Build a new training dataset from the resampled spots and retrain the network to refine reconstruction. 4. MCMC Sampling: Use Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to account for sparse and unbalanced sampling in the transient field during the rendering/integration process. 5. Surface Extraction: Map the implicit volume to surfaces by thresholding the density values followed by Marching Cubes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Sample 3D points and directions (spherical wavefronts) # Note: Specific sampling strategy for spherical wavefronts is implied by points3d, directions = samplesphericalwavefronts() # 2. Query MLP # Input: 5D (3D pos + 2D direction) predictedtransient = mlpforward(mlpparams, points3d, directions) # 3. Compute Loss # Compare predicted transient with measured transient at corresponding spots loss = computeloss(predictedtransient, measurements, currentspots) # 4. Update MLP mlpparams = updateparameters(mlpparams, loss) # End of Stage if stage < numstages: # Two-stage training: Resample spots based on loss # Calculate loss at every measuring spot spotlosses = [] for spotidx, spot in enumerate(currentspots): # Predict transient for this spot pred = predictforspot(mlpparams, spot, measurements) # Compute loss for this spot l = computespotloss(pred, measurements[spotidx]) spotlosses.append(l) # Normalize loss to form PDF pdf = normalize(spotlosses) # Resample detection spots using PDF # Higher loss -> higher PDF -> more densely sampled currentspots = resamplespots(currentspots, pdf) return mlpparams def extractmesh(mlpparams, threshold=0.5): """ Extract mesh from implicit volume. """ # 1. Evaluate density on a 3D grid griddensity = evaluategrid(mlpparams) # 2. Thresholding binaryvolume = griddensity > threshold # 3. Marching Cubes mesh = marchingcubes(binaryvolume) return mesh Parameters: MLP Architecture: Not specified in sources [G: Standard MLP layers with ReLU activations are typical for such implicit fields, but exact layer counts/sizes are "Not given in the sources"]. Threshold: Value for Marching Cubes. Not specified in sources [G: Typical values range 0.1-1.0 depending on normalization, but "Not given in the sources"]. Sampling Grid: 256 \times 256 spots used in Bunny dataset experiments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Confocal vs. Non-Confocal: NeTF does not separately treat confocal and non-confocal setups in its current form. Occlusion: Sparse sampling can lead to strong reconstruction artifacts if occlusions are not handled properly. NeTF uses MCMC and two-stage training to mitigate this. Noise: Learning-based techniques are substantially more computationally expensive than previous optimization techniques. Surface Smoothness: Brute-force Marching Cubes on the implicit volume may lead to noise on smooth surfaces. A training strategy to address sampling bias (undersampling) in NLOS reconstruction by resampling detection spots based on reconstruction loss. It addresses the long-tailed classification problem analogy where high-loss spots (undersampled regions) are oversampled in the second stage. It is chosen when the initial reconstruction fails to recover fine details (e.g., bunny ears) due to sparse sampling. It sets itself apart from one-stage training by dynamically adjusting the sampling distribution based on error. Time Complexity: Substantially more computationally expensive than previous optimization techniques (e.g., F-K, DLCT). Memory Complexity: Implicitly represented by MLP, so memory usage depends on MLP size and grid resolution for extraction [G: Not given in the sources]. Measured Performance: Bunny (Confocal): MAE of 2.65 cm (vs. 2.38 cm for DLCT, 2.43 cm for F-K). Bunny (Non-Confocal): MAE of 7.45 cm (vs. 3.77 cm for FBP, 7.02 cm for BP). Indonesian (Confocal): MAE of 0.31 cm (vs. 0.61 cm for F-K, 0.30 cm for DLCT). Z (Non-Confocal): MAE of 0.60 cm (vs. 0.46 cm for FBP). Strengths: Produces sharper edges for both front and back planes in semi-occluded scenes compared to Phasor Field and DLCT/F-K. Manages to separate different parts of a mesh, whereas DLCT exhibits adhesion. Incurs much lower noise than SOTA methods, similar to NeRF. Robust to low-resolution inputs (e.g., 8 \times 8 spots). Limitations: Computationally expensive. Does not distinguish between confocal and non-confocal setups. MAE may not fully reflect reconstruction quality (e.g., NeTF may have higher MAE than FBP on Z letter but better silhouette preservation). When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction of hidden scenes is required, especially in semi-occluded scenarios or when noise reduction is critical. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited or when confocal/non-confocal specific optimizations are needed. NeTF was introduced in the paper "Non-line-of-Sight Imaging via Neural Transient Fields". It is inspired by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) but adapts the concept to NLOS imaging by parameterizing data on spherical wavefronts instead of rays. It uses MCMC to handle sparse sampling. Tested on synthetic and real NLOS data including Bunny, Lucy, Indonesian, Bike, Letter Z, and semi-occluded scenes. name: SWAG
head: Unsupervised Transient Gaussian Splatting, Unsupervised Transient Gaussians
body: SWAG is a method for unsupervised transient modeling in 3D Gaussian Splatting that extends the standard representation by conditioning Gaussians on learned appearance embeddings. It solves the problem of transient occluders (e.g., pedestrians, moving vehicles) in casual photo captures by training dedicated transient Gaussians that are explicitly optimized to ignore occlusion, yielding state-of-the-art results on diverse photo scenes. It differs from sibling methods like Wild-GS, which aligns pixel appearance features from image triplanes to 3D Gaussians using depth regularization and visibility maps, by focusing on unsupervised transient Gaussian training rather than triplane alignment. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of unposed or loosely posed images of a scene containing transient objects. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the static scene geometry and appearance, plus a set of transient Gaussians representing occluders. Data Structures: The method maintains two sets of Gaussians: 1. Static Gaussians: Standard 3DGS parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) conditioned on learned appearance embeddings. 2. Transient Gaussians: A separate set of Gaussians optimized to model transient distractors. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a set of 3D Gaussians from the input images. 2. Appearance Conditioning: Learn appearance embeddings for the Gaussians to handle view-dependent effects and static appearance variations. 3. Transient Gaussian Training: Introduce transient Gaussians into the scene representation. These are trained unsupervised to model pixels that are occluded or inconsistent with the static scene model. 4. Occlusion Ignorance: The transient Gaussians are optimized to "ignore" occluders, meaning they absorb the error caused by transient objects, allowing the static Gaussians to reconstruct the underlying static scene geometry without being corrupted by moving elements. 5. Rendering: Render the scene by compositing contributions from both static and transient Gaussians. The static Gaussians provide the consistent background, while transient Gaussians capture the dynamic elements. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Yields state-of-the-art results on diverse photo scenes. Strengths: Robustness to transient occluders in casual captures; unsupervised training (no need for explicit transient labels). Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When reconstructing scenes from casual photo captures with transient objects (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles) and unsupervised learning is preferred. When not to use: When explicit transient modeling is not required or when posed data with known camera parameters is available and transient objects are not a concern. SWAG was introduced as an extension to 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle transient objects in unstructured photo collections. It builds on the parent's mechanisms for temporal parameterization, canonical space mapping, and dynamic rendering Parent. It is related to Wild-GS, which uses triplane features and depth regularization, and SpotlessSplats, which uses pre-trained feature spaces for outlier detection. name: Deformation Field Modeling
head: Dynamic Deformation, Canonical Space Warping, Time-Dependent Coordinate Mapping
body: Deformation Field Modeling addresses the problem of reconstructing and rendering dynamic scenes from static image or video sequences by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of geometry and appearance. It solves the limitation of static radiance fields by mapping dynamic, time-varying coordinates to a static canonical space where the radiance field is defined. What sets this approach apart from siblings like Dynamic Object Embedding in Static Scenes (which isolates motion to specific objects) or Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (which uses explicit parametric functions) is its reliance on a learned implicit function (typically an MLP) to predict continuous displacement vectors or feature transformations, allowing for complex, non-rigid, and global deformations without assuming a specific motion prior. The family shares the following core mechanisms for handling temporal dynamics: 1. Temporal Parameterization: Attributes that vary with time, such as position \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, density \sigma, or color \mathbf{c}, are expressed as functions of time t. Common functional forms include: Polynomial/Linear: \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{q}0 + \mathbf{m}t. Fourier Series: \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{c}0 + \sum{k=0}^{K} (\mathbf{a}k \cos(k \omega t) + \mathbf{b}k \sin(k \omega t)) [9168-dynamic-3d-gaussian-splatting-katsumata-et-al.md]. Neural Deformation: A neural network \Psit(x, t) predicts a displacement \Delta x to warp dynamic coordinates to a canonical space. Implicit Fields: Time-dependent NeRFs map (x, d, t) to density and color, often using local neighborhoods of frames. 2. Canonical Space Mapping: Many methods (e.g., D-NeRF, Nerfies) introduce a canonical configuration, typically at t=0, where the scene is static. A deformation network maps dynamic coordinates x at time t to canonical coordinates x': x' = x + \Psit(x, t) The radiance field is then queried in the canonical space: [\sigma, c] = \Psix(x', d). 3. Rendering with Dynamics: The rendering process integrates time-dependent attributes. For Gaussian-based methods, position and rotation are computed for the specific time t of the camera ray before rasterization [9168-dynamic-3d-gaussian-splatting-katsumata-et-al.md]. For NeRF-based methods, density \sigma and color c are queried at the deformed or time-conditioned point. 4. Loss Functions: Optimization typically minimizes photometric loss (L1 or LPIPS) between rendered and ground truth images. Additional constraints often include: Temporal Smoothness: Penalizing abrupt changes in attributes between adjacent frames. Rigid/Flow Constraints: Using optical flow or KNN rigid loss to guide deformation. Regularization: Elastic or background regularization to prevent overfitting in deformation fields. This method integrates dynamic advertising objects into static NeRF scenes by ensuring perspective consistency through spatial alignment and joint rendering with alpha blending. It addresses the high computational cost of traditional dynamic NeRFs (e.g., DyNeRF), which require over 100M parameters and independent models per time step, by using a static NeRF for static areas and a lightweight deformation field for dynamic regions. Unlike siblings like Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting which may model global dynamics, this approach isolates motion to specific objects, reducing parameters by 95%. Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting models dynamic scenes by keeping Gaussian properties (scale, opacity, spherical harmonics) unchanged over time while parameterizing position and orientation as continuous functions of time. It distinguishes itself from implicit deformation networks by using explicit, time-independent Fourier series for position and linear functions for rotation, ensuring temporal continuity and reducing overfitting. A method that divides the dynamic sequence into different windows based on motion amount, training separate dynamic 3DGS models in different windows with different canonical spaces and deformation fields. The deformation field uses a tunable MLP that focuses more on modeling the dynamic part of the scene. Fine-tuning ensures temporal consistency between windows using overlapping frames to add constraints. The MLP is fixed and only the canonical representation is optimized during fine-tuning. A NeRF model built using a deformation field to improve performance in the presence of non-rigid transformations (dynamic scenes). Introduce an additional MLP that maps input observation frame coordinates to deformed canonical coordinates. Add elastic regularization, background regularization, and coarse-to-fine deformation regularization by adaptive masking the positional encoding. Query time-dependent features: hidden = self.querytime(raysptsemb, scalesemb, rotationsemb, timefeature, timeemb). Compute a mask for static vs dynamic regions: if args.staticmlp is true, mask = self.staticmlp(hidden); else if args.emptyvoxel, mask = self.emptyvoxel(raysptsemb[:,:3]); else mask = torch.oneslike(opacityemb[:,0]).unsqueeze(-1). Compute position deformation: if args.nodx is false, dx = self.posdeform(hidden) and pts = raysptsemb[:,:3]mask + dx. Compute scale deformation: if args.nods is false, ds = self.scalesdeform(hidden) and scales = scalesemb[:,:3]mask + ds. Compute opacity deformation: if args.nodo is false, do = self.opacitydeform(hidden) and opacity = opacityemb[:,:1]mask + do. Compute SHS deformation: if args.nodshs is false, dshs = self.shsdeform(hidden).reshape([shsemb.shape[0],16,3]) and shs = shsembmask.unsqueeze(-1) + dshs. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deformgaussians(raysptsemb, scalesemb, rotationsemb, opacityemb, shsemb, timeemb, args): # 1. Query time-dependent features hidden = querytime(raysptsemb, scalesemb, rotationsemb, timeemb) # 2. Compute mask for static vs dynamic regions if args.staticmlp: mask = staticmlp(hidden) elif args.emptyvoxel: mask = emptyvoxelquery(raysptsemb[:,:3]) else: mask = torch.oneslike(opacityemb[:, 0]).unsqueeze(-1) # 3. Compute position deformation if not args.nodx: dx = posdeform(hidden) means3D = raysptsemb[:,:3] mask + dx else: means3D = raysptsemb[:,:3] # 4. Compute scale deformation if not args.nods: ds = scalesdeform(hidden) scales = scalesemb[:,:3] mask + ds else: scales = scalesemb[:,:3] # 5. Compute opacity deformation if not args.nodo: do = opacitydeform(hidden) opacity = opacityemb[:,:1] mask + do else: opacity = opacityemb[:,:1] # 6. Compute SHS deformation if not args.nodshs: dshs = shsdeform(hidden).reshape([shsemb.shape[0], 16, 3]) shs = shsemb mask.unsqueeze(-1) + dshs else: shs = shsemb # 7. Rasterize renderedimage, radii, depth = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=None, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=None, opacities=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotationsemb, cov3Dprecomp=None) return { "render": renderedimage, "viewspacepoints": None, "visibilityfilter": radii > 0, "radii": radii, "depth": depth } The concept of deformation fields for dynamic scenes originated with the introduction of Nerfies by Park et al. in November 2020. Nerfies introduced an additional MLP to map input observation frame coordinates to deformed canonical coordinates, enabling the reconstruction of non-rigid transformations that baseline NeRFs failed to handle. This was followed by concurrent work like NerFace (December 2020) and subsequent extensions like HyperNeRF (June 2021). In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, methods like SWAGS have adapted these principles by dividing sequences into motion-based windows and using tunable MLPs for localized deformation. name: Dynamic Object Embedding in Static Scenes
head: Lightweight Dynamic NeRF Modeling via Local Deformation Field, Local deformation field model
body: This method integrates dynamic advertising objects into static NeRF scenes by ensuring perspective consistency through spatial alignment and joint rendering with alpha blending. It addresses the high computational cost of traditional dynamic NeRFs (e.g., DyNeRF), which require over 100M parameters and independent models per time step, by using a static NeRF for static areas and a lightweight deformation field for dynamic regions. Unlike siblings like Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting which may model global dynamics, this approach isolates motion to specific objects, reducing parameters by 95%. Inputs: 1. Sparse video frames of the static scene (exhibition stand + background). 2. Sparse video frames of the dynamic object (e.g., rotating watch). 3. Four corresponding marking points (e.g., corners) in both the static scene and dynamic object for alignment. Outputs: A rendered frame at time t combining the static scene and the dynamically deformed object. Data Structures: 1. Static NeRF Model (F{static}): A standard NeRF representation with fixed parameters, no time dimension, and no deformation field. 2. Deformation Field (\Delta): A 3-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Input: Spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and time t \in \mathbb{R}. Hidden Layers: Two hidden layers, each with dimension 128. Output: Displacement vector \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: Total 5 million parameters. Steps: 1. Static Scene Reconstruction: Generate a static NeRF model for the advertising scene using sparse input reconstruction. The model parameters are fixed and do not include a time dimension. 2. Dynamic Object Modeling: Train a local deformation field model on the dynamic object using sparse video acquisition (e.g., 25-30 frames). The model learns the displacement \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t) of spatial points over time. 3. Spatial Alignment: Select four marking points in both the static scene and the dynamic object. Use the RANSAC algorithm to align the coordinate system of the dynamic object with the static scene. This ensures perspective consistency with an alignment error of less than 1 pixel. 4. Joint Rendering: For a given time t: a. Calculate the deformation position of the dynamic object using the local deformation field: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t). b. Input the deformed coordinates \mathbf{x}' into the static NeRF model F{static} to obtain color and density. c. Fuse the dynamic object with the static scene using alpha blending with a blending factor of 0.95. Formulas: The dynamic radiation field is expressed as: F(\mathbf{x}, t) = F{static}(\mathbf{x} + \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t)) where F(\mathbf{x}, t) is the output radiance field at spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} and time t, F{static} is the static NeRF query function, and \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t) is the displacement predicted by the deformation field. Parameters: Deformation Field Architecture: 3-layer MLP. Hidden Layer Dimension: 128. Total Parameters: 5 million. Alpha Blending Factor: 0.95. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alignment Error: Must be kept below 1 pixel to ensure perspective consistency. Sparse Input: The method is designed for sparse input reconstruction, which may affect reconstruction quality compared to dense inputs. Dynamic Region Size: The method is most effective when the dynamic region constitutes \le 20\% of the scene. Temporal Discontinuity: Visual discontinuities such as color jumps or sudden light/shadow changes can occur without temporal consistency constraints. Parameter Efficiency: Uses 5M parameters, which is 95% less than DyNeRF's 100M+ parameters. Performance: PSNR increased by 2.3 \pm 0.2 dB under sparse input (mean \pm std over 10 trials). Temporal Consistency: Achieves SSIM \ge 0.92. Suitability: Suitable for VR devices due to lower parameter count and computational load compared to traditional dynamic NeRFs. Limitations: Requires sparse input reconstruction and is constrained to dynamic regions comprising \le 20\% of the scene. This method was proposed to address the limitations of traditional dynamic NeRFs like DyNeRF, which require independent models for each time step and over 100M parameters, making them unsuitable for VR devices. It introduces a local deformation field model to efficiently model motion displacement in dynamic advertising objects embedded in static scenes. name: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (Katsumata et al.)
head: Dynamic 3DGS, Fourier-based Dynamic 3DGS, Katsumata et al
body: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting models dynamic scenes by keeping Gaussian properties (scale, opacity, spherical harmonics) unchanged over time while parameterizing position and orientation as continuous functions of time. It distinguishes itself from implicit deformation networks by using explicit, time-independent Fourier series for position and linear functions for rotation, ensuring temporal continuity and reducing overfitting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians with static attributes and a sequence of training images with known camera poses and timestamps t. Output: Optimized Fourier series coefficients for position and linear coefficients for rotation, minimizing rendering and flow losses. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: 1. Static Attributes: Base position \mathbf{c}0 \in \mathbb{R}^3, base rotation \mathbf{q}0 \in \mathbb{R}^4, scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH}. 2. Dynamic Parameters: Position: Fourier series coefficients \{\mathbf{a}k, \mathbf{b}k\}{k=0}^{K} for each spatial dimension. Rotation: Linear coefficients \mathbf{m}q \in \mathbb{R}^4 representing the rate of change of quaternion components. The total number of dynamic parameters per Gaussian is independent of time. Formulas: The position \mathbf{c}(t) and rotation \mathbf{q}(t) at time t are computed as: \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{c}0 + \sum{k=0}^{K} \left( \mathbf{a}k \cos(k \omega t) + \mathbf{b}k \sin(k \omega t) \right) \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{q}0 + \mathbf{m}q t where \omega is the base frequency. Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a static reconstruction. Set dynamic coefficients \mathbf{a}k, \mathbf{b}k, \mathbf{m}q to zero or small random values. 2. Forward Pass: For each training image at time t: Compute \mathbf{c}(t) and \mathbf{q}(t) using the formulas above. Rasterize the Gaussians using standard 3DGS rasterization with the time-dependent position and rotation. Render the image \hat{I}. 3. Loss Calculation: Image Loss: Compute image losses between the rendered image \hat{I} and the ground truth I{gt}. Optical Flow Loss: Compute bidirectional optical flow between rendered frames or between rendered and ground truth frames, and add L{flow} to penalize temporal inconsistencies. Total Loss: L = L{img} + \lambda{flow} L{flow}. 4. Backpropagation: Update Fourier coefficients and linear rotation parameters using gradient descent to minimize the total loss. Parameters: K: Number of Fourier harmonics. Not given in the sources. \omega: Base frequency. Not given in the sources. \lambda{flow}: Weight for optical flow loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Periodicity Assumption: The Fourier series assumes periodic motion, which aligns with the observation that human and articulated object motion often exhibits periodic characteristics. Non-periodic motions may require higher K or hybrid models. Temporal Continuity: The parametric functions are continuous with respect to time, which ensures temporal continuity and robustness for novel view synthesis. Time Complexity: Optimization time is independent of the number of time steps because the parameterization is time-independent. Rendering time per frame is comparable to static 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Storage increases by O(K) per Gaussian for Fourier coefficients and O(1) for linear rotation parameters. Strengths: Fast training due to explicit parameterization; temporal continuity ensured by continuous functions; robust against overfitting compared to implicit deformation fields. Limitations: Assumes smooth or periodic motion; may struggle with abrupt, non-periodic changes without high-frequency terms. Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting was proposed by Katsumata et al.. It was introduced as an explicit deformation method to address the overfitting and high parameter count associated with implicit deformation modeling in NeRF-based approaches. The method leverages the observation that human and articulated object motion often exhibits periodic characteristics, justifying the use of Fourier series for position modeling. name: Deformation Network (Dynamic)
body: The Deformation Network (Dynamic) is a method for modeling temporal dynamics in 3D Gaussian Splatting by predicting time-dependent deformations for Gaussian attributes. It solves the problem of animating static Gaussian splats by warping their means, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients based on a query time t. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Dynamic Object Embedding by applying explicit displacement fields to the Gaussian parameters rather than relying on static scene embeddings or separate dynamic object tracking. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray-point embeddings raysptsemb (containing 3D coordinates), pre-computed Gaussian attributes scalesemb, rotationsemb, opacityemb, and shsemb (Spherical Harmonics coefficients), and a scalar time value timeemb. Outputs: Deformed Gaussian attributes (means3Dfinal, scalesfinal, opacityfinal, shsfinal) ready for rasterization. Data Structures: raysptsemb: Tensor of shape [N, D{pts}], where N is the number of Gaussian points and D{pts} includes spatial coordinates and potentially other embeddings. scalesemb: Tensor of shape [N, 3]. rotationsemb: Tensor of shape [N, 4] (quaternions). opacityemb: Tensor of shape [N, 1]. shsemb: Tensor of shape [N, K, 3], where K is the number of SH bands (e.g., 16 for degree 2). timeemb: Scalar or tensor representing the normalized time t \in [0, 1]. Parameters: args.staticmlp: Boolean flag. If true, uses a static MLP to compute a mask. args.emptyvoxel: Boolean flag. If true, uses empty voxel queries for masking. args.nodx: Boolean flag. If false, predicts position deformation. args.nods: Boolean flag. If false, predicts scale deformation. args.nodo: Boolean flag. If false, predicts opacity deformation. args.nodshs: Boolean flag. If false, predicts SH deformation. Steps: 1. Query Time-Dependent Features: Compute a hidden representation by concatenating spatial, scale, rotation, and time embeddings and passing them through a time-query network \Psit. \text{hidden} = \Psit(\text{rays\pts\emb}, \text{scales\emb}, \text{rotations\emb}, \text{time\feature}, \text{time\emb}) 2. Compute Mask: Determine a mask m to distinguish static from dynamic regions or to handle empty space. If args.staticmlp is true: m = \sigma(\text{StaticMLP}(\text{hidden})). Else if args.emptyvoxel is true: m = \text{EmptyVoxelQuery}(\text{rays\pts\emb}[:,:3]). Else: m = \mathbf{1} (all ones). 3. Deform Position: If args.nodx is false, predict displacement \Delta x and update means. \Delta x = \text{PosDeform}(\text{hidden}) \mathbf{c}{new} = \mathbf{c}{old} \cdot m + \Delta x 4. Deform Scale: If args.nods is false, predict scale change \Delta s and update scales. \Delta s = \text{ScalesDeform}(\text{hidden}) \mathbf{s}{new} = \mathbf{s}{old} \cdot m + \Delta s 5. Deform Opacity: If args.nodo is false, predict opacity change \Delta \alpha and update opacity. \Delta \alpha = \text{OpacityDeform}(\text{hidden}) \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} \cdot m + \Delta \alpha 6. Deform SH Coefficients: If args.nodshs is false, predict SH changes \Delta \text{SH} and update coefficients. \Delta \text{SH} = \text{SHSDeform}(\text{hidden}).\text{reshape}([N, 16, 3]) \text{SH}{new} = \text{SH}{old} \cdot m{\text{unsqueeze}} + \Delta \text{SH} 7. Rasterize: Pass the final deformed attributes to the rasterizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deformgaussians(raysptsemb, scalesemb, rotationsemb, opacityemb, shsemb, timeemb, args): # 1. Query time-dependent features # Assumes querytime is a defined MLP or network hidden = querytime(raysptsemb, scalesemb, rotationsemb, timeemb) # 2. Compute mask for static vs dynamic regions if args.staticmlp: mask = staticmlp(hidden) elif args.emptyvoxel: mask = emptyvoxelquery(raysptsemb[:,:3]) else: mask = torch.oneslike(opacityemb[:, 0]).unsqueeze(-1) # 3. Compute position deformation if not args.nodx: dx = posdeform(hidden) means3D = raysptsemb[:,:3] mask + dx else: means3D = raysptsemb[:,:3] # 4. Compute scale deformation if not args.nods: ds = scalesdeform(hidden) scales = scalesemb[:,:3] mask + ds else: scales = scalesemb[:,:3] # 5. Compute opacity deformation if not args.nodo: do = opacitydeform(hidden) opacity = opacityemb[:,:1] mask + do else: opacity = opacityemb[:,:1] # 6. Compute SHS deformation if not args.nodshs: dshs = shsdeform(hidden).reshape([shsemb.shape[0], 16, 3]) shs = shsemb mask.unsqueeze(-1) + dshs else: shs = shsemb # 7. Rasterize renderedimage, radii, depth = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=None, # screenspacepoints computed internally shs=shs, colorsprecomp=None, opacities=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotationsemb, cov3Dprecomp=None) return { "render": renderedimage, "viewspacepoints": None, "visibilityfilter": radii > 0, "radii": radii, "depth": depth } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Masking Logic: The mask multiplication m applies to the base attributes. If m=0, the deformation is zeroed out, effectively keeping the attribute static or zeroed. Implementers must ensure m is correctly normalized if it represents a probability. SH Reshaping: The SH deformation output must be reshaped to match the input SH tensor dimensions before addition. Time Normalization: timeemb should be normalized to a consistent range (e.g., [0, 1]) across the dataset. A method for updating 3D Gaussian kernels after deformation to prevent "spike-like" artifacts by preserving surface coverage without geometric proxies. Choose when naive affine transformations fail to represent the occupancy region. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians N for the deformation network forward pass, plus the standard O(N) rasterization cost. The deformation network query is typically a small MLP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the deformation network weights and the additional deformation fields for position, scale, opacity, and SH. This increases memory usage compared to static 3DGS. Strengths: Allows for continuous time interpolation and smooth animation of Gaussian attributes. Limitations: Performance depends on the capacity of the deformation network; overfitting can occur if not regularized. When to use: When animating dynamic scenes with continuous motion is required. When not to use: For static scenes or when computational resources are severely limited. The Deformation Network (Dynamic) approach is implemented in the unofficial 4DGS repository by ElenaViewSynthesis. It builds on the principles of dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting, where time is treated as an additional input to predict attribute variations. name: Surface-Preserving Kernel Adaptation
head: Laplacian-Based Deformation Adaptation
body: Surface-Preserving Kernel Adaptation is a method for updating 3D Gaussian kernels after a deformation field has been applied to their means, ensuring that the kernels maintain their original surface coverage on the deformed geometry. It solves the problem of "spike-like" artifacts that arise when naive local affine transformations are estimated from partial neighborhoods, which fail to represent the transformation of the entire occupancy region. It sets itself apart from prior works that use geometric proxies like bounding scales or splitting by operating in a proxy-free scenario, directly adapting the kernel parameters to preserve the underlying surface manifold. Inputs: Deformed Gaussian means \{\phi\Delta(pi)\}{i=1}^N, where \phi\Delta is the deformation map. Original Gaussian means \{pi\}{i=1}^N. Original Gaussian axes \{v{i,1}, v{i,2}\} representing the major and minor axes of the occupancy region \Omegai. Splat graph structure defining adjacency. Outputs: Adapted Gaussian kernels G{\phi\Delta, i} with updated parameters (position, scale, orientation) that preserve surface coverage. Data Structures: Splat Graph: An implicit or explicit graph where nodes are Gaussian kernels and edges connect adjacent kernels based on spatial proximity or splat overlap. Adjacency is determined by graph distance. Inscribed Triangle Ti: A set of three vertices \{t{i,1}, t{i,2}, t{i,3}\} representing the occupancy region \Omegai of Gaussian Gi. Steps: 1. Define Inscribed Triangle Proxy: For each Gaussian kernel Gi with mean pi and axes v{i,1} (major) and v{i,2} (minor), define the inscribed triangle of maximum area Ti = \{t{i,k}\}{k=1}^3 as a proxy for its occupancy region \Omegai. The vertices are computed as: t{i,1} = pi + v{i,1} t{i,2} = pi - \frac{1}{2}v{i,1} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}v{i,2} t{i,3} = pi - \frac{1}{2}v{i,1} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}v{i,2} 2. Identify Adjacent Gaussians: For each triangle vertex t{i,k}, identify a set of adjacent Gaussians M(t{i,k}) from the splat graph. The selection is based on graph distance to ensure the adjacency of the surface. 3. Transfer Displacement to Vertices: The deformation map \phi\Delta is defined only on the Gaussian means. To find the deformed position of each triangle vertex t{i,k}, compute the displacement using inverse distance weighting from the adjacent Gaussians in M(t{i,k}). The deformed vertex t'{i,k} is: t'{i,k} = t{i,k} + \frac{\sum{j \in M(t{i,k})} w{ij} (\phi\Delta(pj) - pj)}{\sum{j \in M(t{i,k})} w{ij}} where the weight w{ij} is the inverse squared distance: w{ij} = \|t{i,k} - pj\|^{-2} 4. Recover Adapted Kernel Parameters: Compute the Steiner circumellipse of the deformed triangle T'i = \{t'{i,1}, t'{i,2}, t'{i,3}\}. The parameters of the adapted Gaussian kernel G{\phi\Delta, i} (position, scale, and orientation) are uniquely recovered from this ellipse to preserve the original surface coverage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeinscribedtriangle(mean, majoraxis, minoraxis): """ Computes the vertices of the inscribed triangle of maximum area for a Gaussian kernel defined by its mean and axes. Args: mean: np.array, shape (3,), the Gaussian mean pi. majoraxis: np.array, shape (3,), the major axis vi,1. minoraxis: np.array, shape (3,), the minor axis vi,2. Returns: np.array, shape (3, 3), vertices ti,1, ti,2, ti,3. """ t1 = mean + majoraxis t2 = mean - 0.5 majoraxis + (np.sqrt(3) / 2) minoraxis t3 = mean - 0.5 majoraxis - (np.sqrt(3) / 2) minoraxis return np.array([t1, t2, t3]) def inversedistanceweighteddisplacement(vertex, adjacentmeans, deformedmeans, graphadjacency): """ Computes the displaced position of a triangle vertex using inverse distance weighting from adjacent Gaussians. Args: vertex: np.array, shape (3,), the original triangle vertex ti,k. adjacentmeans: list of np.array, shape (3,), means pj of adjacent Gaussians. deformedmeans: list of np.array, shape (3,), deformed means phidelta(pj). graphadjacency: list of bool/int, indicating which adjacent Gaussians are in M(ti,k). In practice, this filters the lists above to only include valid neighbors. Returns: np.array, shape (3,), the deformed vertex position t'i,k. """ # Filter to only adjacent Gaussians based on graph distance validindices = [j for j, isadj in enumerate(graphadjacency) if isadj] if not validindices: # Fallback if no neighbors found return vertex neighborsp = [adjacentmeans[j] for j in validindices] neighborspprime = [deformedmeans[j] for j in validindices] displacements = [np.array(pprime) - np.array(p) for p, pprime in zip(neighborsp, neighborspprime)] weights = [] for p in neighborsp: distsq = np.sum((vertex - p) 2) # Avoid division by zero if distsq < 1e-8: distsq = 1e-8 weights.append(1.0 / distsq) weights = np.array(weights) weightssum = np.sum(weights) if weightssum == 0: return vertex weighteddisplacement = np.zeros(3) for w, disp in zip(weights, displacements): weighteddisplacement += w disp return vertex + weighteddisplacement / weightssum def steinercircumellipseparameters(vertices): """ Recovers Gaussian kernel parameters (position, scale, orientation) from the vertices of the Steiner circumellipse. Note: The exact mathematical derivation for recovering Gaussian parameters from the Steiner circumellipse vertices is referenced as [47] in the source. This implementation assumes a standard geometric reconstruction. For a 2D Gaussian in 3D space, this typically involves finding the center, principal axes, and eigenvalues of the ellipse defined by the three points. Args: vertices: np.array, shape (3, 3), deformed triangle vertices t'i,1, t'i,2, t'i,3. Returns: dict with keys 'mean', 'majoraxis', 'minoraxis'. """ # Compute centroid as the new mean newmean = np.mean(vertices, axis=0) # Compute covariance-like matrix to find axes # Center the vertices centered = vertices - newmean cov = np.dot(centered.T, centered) # Eigen decomposition to find orientation and scale eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) # Sort by eigenvalue magnitude idx = eigenvalues.argsort()[::-1] eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx] eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx] # Scale factors proportional to sqrt(eigenvalues) # Note: Exact scaling factor for Steiner circumellipse to Gaussian parameters # depends on the specific definition in [47]. Here we use a proportional scaling. scale1 = np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) scale2 = np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) # Ensure real positive scales scale1 = max(scale1, 1e-6) scale2 = max(scale2, 1e-6) return { 'mean': newmean, 'majoraxis': eigenvectors[:, 0] scale1, 'minoraxis': eigenvectors[:, 1] scale2 } def surfacepreservingkerneladaptation(gaussians, deformationmap, splatgraph): """ Main adaptation routine. Args: gaussians: list of dicts with 'mean', 'majoraxis', 'minoraxis'. deformationmap: function phidelta that takes a mean and returns deformed mean. splatgraph: object or structure providing getadjacentgaussians(vertex, gaussians). Returns: list of adapted Gaussian parameters. """ adaptedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): pi = g['mean'] v1 = g['majoraxis'] v2 = g['minoraxis'] # Step 1: Define inscribed triangle triangle = computeinscribedtriangle(pi, v1, v2) # Step 2 & 3: Transfer displacement to vertices deformedtriangle = np.zeroslike(triangle) for k in range(3): tk = triangle[k] # Get adjacent Gaussians for this vertex # splatgraph.getadjacentgaussians should return list of indices or objects # For this pseudocode, we assume it returns a list of adjacent Gaussian indices adjindices = splatgraph.getadjacentgaussians(tk, gaussians) if not adjindices: deformedtriangle[k] = tk # No change if no neighbors continue adjmeans = [gaussians[j]['mean'] for j in adjindices] adjdeformedmeans = [deformationmap(gaussians[j]['mean']) for j in adjindices] # Create adjacency mask (all returned are adjacent) adjmask = [True] len(adjindices) deformedtriangle[k] = inversedistanceweighteddisplacement( tk, adjmeans, adjdeformedmeans, adjmask) # Step 4: Recover adapted kernel params = steinercircumellipseparameters(deformedtriangle) adaptedgaussians.append(params) return adaptedgaussians Parameters: M(t{i,k}): Set of adjacent Gaussians to vertex t{i,k}, chosen based on graph distance on the splat graph. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Naive Affine Estimation Failure: Estimating a local affine transformation from a neighborhood that only partially covers a subset of a Gaussian's occupancy region \Omega causes the kernel to deviate from the underlying surface, leading to spike-like artifacts. No Adjacent Neighbors: If a vertex has no adjacent Gaussians in the splat graph, the displacement cannot be computed via weighting. A fallback (e.g., identity) is required. Precision: Inverse distance weighting involves division by squared distances; small distances can lead to numerical instability if not clamped. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N and the average degree of the splat graph. For each Gaussian, 3 vertices are processed, and each vertex queries adjacent Gaussians. If K is the average number of adjacent Gaussians per vertex, complexity is O(N \cdot K). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the Gaussians and the splat graph structure. Strengths: Preserves geometric structure and visual fidelity by maintaining original surface coverage; avoids spike-like artifacts common in naive deformation approaches; works in a proxy-free scenario. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the splat graph for adjacency; computationally more expensive than simple affine transformation if the graph is dense; requires the deformation map to be defined on means. When to Use: When deforming 3D Gaussian Splatting representations where preserving surface fidelity is critical and proxy-based methods (bounding scales, splitting) are not applicable or desired. When Not to Use: If computational efficiency is paramount and some artifact tolerance is acceptable; if the splat graph is poorly constructed or sparse. The method was introduced in "Proxy-Free Gaussian Splats Deformation with Splat-Based Surface Estimation". It addresses limitations in existing deformation techniques for 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly the failure of naive local affine transformations to preserve surface coverage. The approach builds on the foundation of 2D Gaussian Splatting, which encourages each kernel to act as a local patch covering the underlying surface. It references Steiner circumellipse [47] and inverse distance weighting [48] as mathematical foundations. The method was evaluated using Laplacian-based deformation techniques such as As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) [1] and Bounded Biharmonic Weights (BBW) [2] on synthetic objects from ShapeNet, Objaverse, and Sketchfab. name: Relative Mesh Deformation Network
head: RMD-Net
body: The Relative Mesh Deformation Network (RMD-Net) is a component of the Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian Splatting (MaGS) framework that refines dynamic mesh deformations by learning motion priors from video data. It predicts the relative displacement between a coarse guide mesh and a refined mesh, ensuring that the underlying mesh structure accurately drives the deformation of associated 3D Gaussians. Unlike methods that anchor Gaussians rigidly to mesh facets, RMD-Net operates within a system that allows Gaussians to roam on the mesh surface, adjusting their logical coordinates in response to mesh changes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: EM: Embedding of the guide mesh. E{Vi}: Embedding of the i-th vertex of the guide mesh. Outputs: A tuple of relative deformation parameters for vertex i: (\Delta v, \Delta q, \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c)i. \Delta v: Vertex displacement. \Delta q: Vertex rotation. \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c: Parameters utilized in Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian rendering, not directly corresponding to mesh deformation geometry. Data Structures: The network outputs a fixed-size vector per vertex. The exact internal bit-packing or tensor layout of the embeddings EM and E{Vi} is not specified in the sources. The output is a tuple of five components per vertex. Algorithm: 1. Embedding Extraction: Compute the global mesh embedding EM and the per-vertex embedding E{Vi} for the guide mesh. 2. Network Forward Pass: Pass the embeddings into the RMD-Net function: (\Delta v, \Delta q, \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c)i = \text{RMD}(EM, E{Vi}) 3. Deformation Application: The predicted \Delta v and \Delta q are used to refine the guide mesh deformation. The parameters \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c are passed to the Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian rendering pipeline to adjust Gaussian properties. 4. Gaussian Update: The refined mesh deformation influences the Gaussians. The final deformed Gaussians are derived by interpolating the Gaussian properties (w{gaussians}) with the mesh properties (v{mesh}) adjusted by the relative displacements: (w{gaussians} + \Delta w) \times (v{mesh} + \Delta v) \rightarrow \text{Final Deformed Gaussians} where \times denotes the interpolation operation used by MaGS. Parameters: \lambda{ssim}: Weight for the SSIM loss component. Typical value not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The parameters \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c do not correspond directly to mesh deformation but are critical for the rendering step. The method relies on the differentiability of the entire pipeline, including the interpolation operation, to enable backpropagation through the deformation network. A network that calculates changes in logical coordinates \Delta w during mesh deformation, allowing Gaussians to roam on the mesh surface rather than being anchored to a facet. It takes the mesh embedding EM, the vertex embeddings of the three vertices of the facet containing Gaussian i (E{V1}, E{V2}, E{V3}), and the Gaussian's current logical coordinate wi as input, outputting \Delta wi. Formula: \Delta wi = \text{RGD}(EM, E{V1}, E{V2}, E{V3}, wi). Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables joint optimization of mesh deformation and Gaussian properties through backpropagation based on rendering errors. Allows Gaussians to roam on the mesh surface, providing flexibility in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the guide mesh and the learned motion priors. The exact computational cost of the network is not specified. When to Use: Use when reconstructing dynamic 3D objects where mesh-guided deformation is preferred over point-based deformation, and when the ability to simulate physics on the reconstructed mesh is required. The Relative Mesh Deformation Network was introduced in the paper "Reconstructing and Simulating Dynamic 3D Objects with Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian Splatting". It is part of the MaGS framework, which combines mesh-based deformation with Gaussian Splatting for dynamic scene reconstruction and simulation. The method builds on the concept of Mesh-adsorbed Gaussians, where Gaussians are associated with mesh facets but can adjust their positions relative to the mesh during deformation. name: 4D-GS
head: 4D Gaussian Splatting
body: 4D-GS extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by parameterizing Gaussian attributes as functions of time, enabling the reconstruction and rendering of non-rigidly deforming objects from multi-view video. It distinguishes itself from other dynamic Gaussian methods by replacing standard positional encoding with multi-resolution hexplane voxels for spatiotemporal information and employing a two-stage optimization process that first stabilizes the static scene before learning the deformation field. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images \{Iv\} with known camera poses and timestamps t. Outputs: A set of 4D Gaussians, where each Gaussian is defined by a base set of static attributes and a time-dependent deformation field. Data Structures: 1. Static Gaussians: Each Gaussian i stores base attributes: position \mathbf{c}i, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, SH}. 2. Hexplane Voxels: A multi-resolution structure encoding spatiotemporal information. It consists of six 2D planes (hexplanes) representing the 2D projections of the 3D space and time dimension. Each plane is a grid of learnable features. 3. Attribute MLPs: Compact Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) dedicated to predicting delta values for specific attributes (e.g., position, rotation, scale) based on inputs from the hexplane voxels and the query time t. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a static 3D Gaussian point cloud using standard 3DGS initialization (e.g., from SfM points). 2. Stage 1: Static Optimization: Optimize the static Gaussian attributes (\mathbf{c}i, \mathbf{q}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}{i, SH}) using standard 3DGS rendering and photometric loss until convergence. This establishes a stable baseline for the scene. 3. Stage 2: Deformation Field Learning: Voxel Encoding: For each Gaussian i and query time t, encode its spatial position \mathbf{c}i and time t into the multi-resolution hexplane voxels. This replaces positional encoding. Temporal Smoothing: Add linearly decaying Gaussian noise to the encoded time vector to improve temporal smoothing without additional computational overhead. Delta Prediction: Pass the encoded spatiotemporal features through attribute-specific compact MLPs to predict delta values (\Delta \mathbf{c}, \Delta \mathbf{q}, \Delta \mathbf{s}, etc.). Attribute Update: Compute the dynamic attributes for time t: \mathbf{c}i(t) = \mathbf{c}i + \Delta \mathbf{c}i(t) \mathbf{q}i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}i + \Delta \mathbf{q}i(t)) \mathbf{s}i(t) = \mathbf{s}i + \Delta \mathbf{s}i(t) Rendering: Render the scene using the time-dependent attributes \mathbf{c}i(t), \mathbf{q}i(t), \mathbf{s}i(t) for the camera timestamp t. Optimization: Minimize photometric loss (L1) between rendered and ground truth images. Optimize the MLP weights and the static Gaussian attributes jointly. Parameters: Hexplane Resolution: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Compact MLPs; specific layer sizes not given in the sources. Noise Schedule: Linearly decaying Gaussian noise on the time vector; decay rate not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Artifacts: Without noise injection, time interpolation can amplify artifacts. Optimization Stability: Jointly optimizing static and dynamic attributes from scratch can be unstable; the two-stage approach mitigates this. Complexity: Rendering complexity is similar to 3DGS, but training involves additional overhead from hexplane voxel lookups and MLP inference for each Gaussian at each time step. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Stable training via two-stage optimization; efficient spatiotemporal encoding via hexplanes; robust temporal smoothing via noise injection. Limitations: Requires a static baseline; performance on highly dynamic scenes with large non-rigid deformations may be limited by the capacity of compact MLPs. 4D-GS was introduced as an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle dynamic scenes. It builds on the principles of temporal parameterization and canonical space mapping shared by its siblings. The method was developed to address the instability of directly optimizing dynamic Gaussians and the inefficiency of positional encoding for spatiotemporal data. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: GraphiXS
head: GraphiGS, GraphiTS, Graphical X Splatting
body: GraphiXS is a probabilistic graphical model for 4D Gaussian Splatting that reformulates reconstruction as a Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation problem, introducing structured dependencies among cameras, time, and components to handle uncertainty. Unlike deterministic 4DGS methods that minimize photometric error directly, GraphiXS uses stochastic priors and Bayesian inference to regularize dynamics and component visibility, making it robust to sparse views and missing frames. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 2D images I{ct} indexed by camera c and time t; camera poses C; time indices T. Outputs: A set of 4D Gaussian components parameterized by \theta, including mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, base opacity o, spherical harmonics color sh, appearance time g, duration u, velocity v, acceleration a, jerk j, and snap s. Data Structures: Each component p stores: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (symmetric positive definite). o \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity. sh: Spherical harmonics coefficients for color. g \in \mathbb{R}: Appearance time. u \in \mathbb{R}: Duration of existence. v, a, j, s \in \mathbb{R}^3: Velocity, acceleration, jerk, and snap parameters for dynamics. Generative Process: The model defines a generative process with four steps: 1. Component Selection: Given mixture model F, camera c \sim C, and time t \sim T, sample a subset of components \{\alphai\} with L components for image I{ct}. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel X{c,d}^t, cast a ray R{c,d}^t from camera c at time t. 3. Intersection: Identify the subset of components \{\betaj\} from \{\alphai\} that intersect with ray R{c,d}^t. 4. Rasterization: Generate the color for pixel X{c,d}^t based on \{\betaj\} and ray R{c,d}^t. Factorized Likelihood: The likelihood is factorized according to the graphical dependencies: P(X | \cdot) = P(X | \beta, R) P(\beta | \alpha, R) P(R | C, T) P(\alpha | \delta\theta, C, T) where X is the image, \beta are per-pixel components, R is the ray, \alpha are per-image components, and \delta\theta is the mixture model. Rendering (Rasterization): The rendering step P(X | \beta, R) is implemented as standard alpha blending: Ras(X; \beta, R) = \sum{i=1}^N \lambdai \beta{2D}^i(X) where \lambdai = si oi \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj \beta{2D}^j(X)) is the transmittance/weight, si is a scale/color factor, oi is opacity, and \beta{2D}^i(X) is the projected 2D Gaussian. Image Loss (Energy-based Likelihood): The baseline rendering loss is converted into an energy-based likelihood: P(I | \beta, R, \theta, C, T) \propto \exp \left( - \sum{t} \sum{c}^{M} L{img}(I{ct}) \right) where the image loss L{img} is: L{img} = (1 - \epsilonD - SSIM) L1 + (\epsilonD - SSIM) L{D-SSIM} + \epsilono \sumi ||oi||1 + \epsilon\Sigma \sum{i,j} ||\lambda{i,j}||1 Here, L1 and L{D-SSIM} are L1 and Deep-SSIM losses, \lambda{i,j} are eigenvalues of covariance \Sigma, and \epsilon terms are hyperparameters. Priors: The prior P(\theta) regularizes the parameters to ensure well-behaved dynamics and structure: 1. Mean Dynamics (Brownian Motion): The mean \mu evolves via Brownian motion with a deterministic drift f(\mu, t): \frac{d\mu}{dt} = f(\mu, t) + \mathcal{N}(0, \epsilon^2 I) Discretized as: \mu(t) = \mu(t-1) + f(\mu, t)\Delta t + \mathcal{N}(0, \epsilon^2 I)\Delta t The drift function f(\mu, t)\Delta t uses higher-order derivatives: f(\mu, t)\Delta t = v(t-g) + \frac{1}{2}a(t-g)^2 + \frac{1}{6}j(t-g)^3 + \frac{1}{24}s(t-g)^4 where v, a, j, s are velocity, acceleration, jerk, and snap, and g is the appearance time. 2. Opacity Prior: P(o) \propto \frac{1}{N1} \sum{i=1}^N oi^2 \exp\left(-\frac{(t-g)^2}{2u^2}\right) \psi(\cdot) where u is the duration a component lasts, N1 is a normalization constant, and \psi(\cdot) is the splatting response. 3. Dynamics Prior: P(vp, ap, jp, sp) \propto \exp\left(-\lambdah \sum{t=1}^{Nt} \frac{||vp||^2 + ||ap||^2 + ||jp||^2 + ||sp||^2}{|\det(\Sigmap)|^{1/2}}\right) This prefers slowly moving components, weighted by the volume proxy |\det(\Sigmap)|. 4. Covariance Prior: P(\Sigmap) \propto \exp\left(-\lambda\sigma \frac{1}{Nt} \sum{p} ||\Sigmap - \hat{\Sigma}t||F^2\right) where \hat{\Sigma}t is the mean covariance of components at time t. 5. Component Confidence: A metric to prefer components visible across all frames: P(\alpha | \delta\theta, C, T) = E\{P(r{c,d}^t | \alpha)\} \approx \frac{\sum{c,t,d} P(r{c,d}^t | \alpha)}{\sum{p,c,t,d} P(r{c,d}^t | \delta{\thetap})} The numerator is the soft visibility of component \alpha to all pixels; the denominator is the sum of soft visibility of all components. Full Prior: P(\theta(t)) = P(o) P(\mu(1)) \prod{t=2}^K \mathcal{N}(\mu(t-1) + f(\mu, t), \epsilon^2 I) \prod{t=1}^K P(v, a, j, s) P(\Sigma) [ S1 ] Optimization (MAP): The objective is to maximize the posterior: \arg\max\theta \log P(X | R, \beta, \alpha, C, T, \theta) P(\theta) Equivalent to minimizing: L{full} = -\log P(I | \cdot) - \log P(\alpha | \cdot) - \log P(\theta) L{full} = L{img} + L\alpha + L\theta [ S1 ] Algorithm: Optimization uses Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingraphixs(images, cameras, times, initialcomponents, numiterations): # Initialize parameters theta for all components # theta includes mu, Sigma, o, sh, g, u, v, a, j, s theta = initializeparameters(initialcomponents) # SGHMC parameters frictioncoefficient = 120 noisescale = 1.0 burniniterations = 7000 burninfriction = 5e5 browniannoisestd = 1e-4 # Loss weights lambdaalpha = 1e-3 temporalopacityweight = 0.01 lambdah = 1e-4 epsilonDSSIM = 0.2 # Example value, check source for exact if needed, source implies structure epsilono = 0.01 epsilonSigma = 0.01 for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample a batch of (camera, time) pairs batchcameras, batchtimes = samplebatch(cameras, times) # Anneal learning rates for dynamics parameters lrv, lra, lrj, lrs, lru = anneallearningrate(iteration, start=1e-2, end=1e-4) # Compute gradients grads = computegradients(theta, batchcameras, batchtimes, images, lambdaalpha, temporalopacityweight, lambdah, epsilono, epsilonSigma) # SGHMC Update if iteration < burniniterations: currentfriction = burninfriction else: currentfriction = frictioncoefficient # Add SGHMC noise noise = samplenormalnoise(grads, noisescale, currentfriction) # Update parameters theta = updateparameters(theta, grads, noise, lrv, lra, lrj, lrs, lru) # Handle component addition/removal if using stochastic strategy # Note: Deterministic variant uses top-N selection theta = managecomponents(theta, images, batchcameras, batchtimes) return theta Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Methods relying on a canonical Gaussian set deformed via a neural field (e.g., HexPlane or MLP) cannot be upgraded directly; instead, GraphiXS priors must be applied to the displaced components at each sampled timestamp with gradients backpropagated through the deformation network. The deterministic variant replaces SGHMC with Adam, disables component confidence loss, removes Brownian motion noise, and uses deterministic top-N selection for densification. Time and Memory Complexity: The method involves millions of parameters, requiring significant memory for storing component states and gradients. Optimization uses SGHMC, which adds computational overhead due to noise injection and momentum tracking compared to standard Adam. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The total number of components is capped at 1.5 million in experiments. Strengths: Robust to sparse views and missing frames due to probabilistic modeling of uncertainty and component confidence. Handles arbitrary and potentially discontinuous motions via Brownian motion and higher-order derivatives. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to SGHMC and large parameter space. Not directly applicable to implicit deformation-based methods without modification. When to use: When dealing with dynamic scenes with uncertainty, sparse views, or missing temporal data, and when using explicit 3D/4D Gaussians or similar primitives (e.g., FTGS, Ex4DGS, 4DGS-1). GraphiXS was introduced by Zhu et al. in 2025. It generalizes the unnormalized mixture model of 3D/4DGS by introducing structured dependencies among random variables to enable Bayesian inference and regularization. It builds on the framework of 4D Gaussian Splatting. name: Temporal Input Conditioning
head: Time-conditioned rendering, Dynamic scene parameterization
body: Temporal Input Conditioning is a family of techniques that parameterize scene attributes—such as position, rotation, opacity, density, or color—as explicit functions of time t to enable the synthesis of novel views for dynamic scenes. It solves the problem of representing non-rigid motion and temporal evolution in volumetric data without requiring ground-truth geometry or multi-view stereo data at every instant. It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into a static canonical space and a learned deformation field, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture. Unlike DaReNeRF, which focuses on specific direction-aware wavelet decompositions, this family establishes the foundational canonical-space paradigm for dynamic neural rendering. The family shares the following core mechanisms for handling temporal dynamics: 1. Temporal Parameterization: Attributes that vary with time, such as position \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, density \sigma, or color \mathbf{c}, are expressed as functions of time t. Common functional forms include: Polynomial/Linear: \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{q}0 + \mathbf{m}t. Fourier Series: \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{c}0 + \sum{k=0}^{K} (\mathbf{a}k \cos(k \omega t) + \mathbf{b}k \sin(k \omega t)). Neural Deformation: A neural network \Psit(x, t) predicts a displacement \Delta x to warp dynamic coordinates to a canonical space. Implicit Fields: Time-dependent NeRFs map (x, d, t) to density and color, often using local neighborhoods of frames. 2. Canonical Space Mapping: Many methods (e.g., D-NeRF, Nerfies) introduce a canonical configuration, typically at t=0, where the scene is static. A deformation network maps dynamic coordinates x at time t to canonical coordinates x': x' = x + \Psit(x, t) The radiance field is then queried in the canonical space: [\sigma, c] = \Psix(x', d). 3. Rendering with Dynamics: The rendering process integrates time-dependent attributes. For Gaussian-based methods, position and rotation are computed for the specific time t of the camera ray before rasterization. For NeRF-based methods, density \sigma and color c are queried at the deformed or time-conditioned point. 4. Loss Functions: Optimization typically minimizes photometric loss (L1 or LPIPS) between rendered and ground truth images. Additional constraints often include: Temporal Smoothness: Penalizing abrupt changes in attributes between adjacent frames. Rigid/Flow Constraints: Using optical flow or KNN rigid loss to guide deformation. Regularization: Elastic or background regularization to prevent overfitting in deformation fields. D-NeRF synthesizes novel views at arbitrary time instances for dynamic scenes with complex non-rigid geometries, optimizing a deformable volumetric function from a sparse set of monocular input images without ground-truth geometry or multi-view stereo data. It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into a static canonical space and a learned deformation field, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture. Unlike DaReNeRF, which focuses on specific deformation regularizations, D-NeRF establishes the foundational canonical-space paradigm for dynamic neural rendering. DaReNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes that employs a direction-aware representation to capture scene dynamics from six distinct orientations. It addresses the shift variance and direction ambiguity (checkerboard artifacts) inherent in traditional 2D Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DWT) by utilizing the Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform (DTCWT). Unlike standard plane-based decompositions, DaReNeRF models features from six different directions to eliminate ghosting artifacts around moving objects. A NeRF variant that represents scene geometry and appearance at each specific time step t, trained using neighboring frames around time t, to capture local scene geometry and motion. Represent scene appearance using mapping function c = ϕc(x, d) taking point x ∈ R3 and viewing direction d ∈ R2 to predict color c ∈ R3. Represent scene geometry via mapping function s = ϕg(x) which maps a 3D point x to a signed distance value s ∈ R. For a camera ray r(h) = o + hd, sample K 3D points {xi(r) = r(hi) | i = 1,..., K, hi < hi+1}. Use the time-dependent NeRF to compute SDF flows, which are used to constrain the learning of continuous camera motion via the linear relationship between SDF flow and scene flow. Convert signed distance si to density σi using: σi = max((Φ(si) - Φ(si+1))/Φ(si), 0), where Φ(s) = 1/(1+e^(1-γs)), γ is a learnable parameter, and i is the point index. Render pixel color Ĉ(r) via volume rendering: Ĉ(r) = Σ(i=1 to K) Li σi ci, where Li = Π(j=1 to i-1) (1 - σj) is the accumulated transmittance. The concept of temporal input conditioning in neural rendering originated with D-NeRF, which introduced the canonical space paradigm for dynamic scenes. This approach allows for the decomposition of dynamic scenes into static geometry and time-varying deformations, addressing the limitations of direct 6D mappings. Subsequent works like DaReNeRF have refined this by introducing direction-aware representations to mitigate artifacts such as shift variance and checkerboard effects. More recent developments, such as the time-dependent NeRF described in, integrate these concepts with continuous camera motion optimization, using local temporal neighborhoods to constrain SDF flows and improve pose estimation.
