name: D-NeRF
head: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields, Dynamic NeRF, Neural Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scenes
body: D-NeRF is a method for synthesizing novel views at an arbitrary point in time of dynamic scenes with complex non-rigid geometries, optimized from a sparse set of input monocular views without ground-truth geometry or multi-view images. It extends NeRF by introducing time t as an additional input and decomposing the representation into a deformation network and a canonical radiance network. Unlike naive extensions that map (x, y, z, t) directly to density and radiance, which fail to exploit temporal redundancy, D-NeRF maps dynamic coordinates to a static canonical space (typically t=0) before querying the radiance field. This approach sets it apart from T-NeRF, which uses a 6D input (x, y, z, \theta, \phi, t) without an intermediate canonical mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of T RGB images \{It\}{t=1}^T captured by a monocular camera, where It \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} is the image at time t, and corresponding camera pose matrices \{Tt\}{t=1}^T where Tt \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} represents the SE(3) pose. Outputs: A rendered RGB color C'(p, t) for a pixel p at time t given a viewing direction d, and the learned parameters for the canonical and deformation networks. Data Structures: The model consists of two deep fully connected networks (MLPs) without convolutional layers: 1. Deformation Network \Psit: Architecture: 8-layer MLP with ReLU activations. Input: Encoded 3D position x and time t. Output: Displacement vector \Delta x \in \mathbb{R}^3. No non-linearity is applied to the output. 2. Canonical Network \Psix: Architecture: 8-layer MLP with ReLU activations. Input: Encoded canonical position x' = x + \Delta x and viewing direction d. Output: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and view-dependent RGB color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. A final sigmoid non-linearity is applied to both outputs. Positional Encoding: Raw coordinates are encoded into a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding \gamma(p): \gamma(p) = \langle (\sin(2^l \pi p), \cos(2^l \pi p)) \rangle{l=0}^{L-1} The encoder is applied independently to each coordinate and camera view component. For spatial coordinates x: L = 10. For viewing direction d and time t: L = 4. Numbered Steps: 1. Canonical Configuration Definition: Define the canonical scene as the scene at time t=0. Enforce that the deformation displacement is zero at this time: \Psit(x, 0) = 0. 2. Ray Sampling: For a pixel p and time t, cast a ray from the camera center o with direction d. Sample N points \{hn\}{n=1}^N along the ray segment [hn, hf] using stratified sampling (drawing samples from evenly-spaced ray bins). 3. Deformation: For each sample point x(h) = o + h d at time t, compute the displacement \Delta x using the deformation network: \Delta x = \Psit(\gamma(x(h)), \gamma(t)) Transform the point to canonical space: p(h, t) = x(h) + \Delta x. 4. Radiance Query: Query the canonical network with the transformed point and viewing direction to obtain density and color: [c(p(h, t), d), \sigma(p(h, t))] = \Psix(\gamma(p(h, t)), \gamma(d)). 5. Volume Rendering: Approximate the volume rendering integral via numerical quadrature. Calculate the transmittance and opacity for each sample: \alpha(h, t, \deltan) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(p(h, t)) \deltan) T'(hn, t) = \exp\left(-\sum{m=1}^{n-1} \sigma(p(hm, t)) \deltam\right) where \deltan = h{n+1} - hn is the distance between quadrature points. 6. Pixel Color Computation: Compute the rendered pixel color C'(p, t): C'(p, t) = \sum{n=1}^{N} T'(hn, t) \alpha(hn, t, \deltan) c(p(hn, t), d). Parameters: Canonical Time: t=0. Network Depth: 8 layers for both \Psit and \Psix. Activation: ReLU for hidden layers; Sigmoid for \Psix outputs; Linear for \Psit output. Training: Image resolution: 400 \times 400. Iterations: 800,000. Batch size: Ns = 4096 rays. Samples per ray: 64. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, decaying exponentially to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Loss: Mean Squared Error (MSE) between rendered pixels C' and ground truth pixels \hat{C}: \text{Loss} = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \|\hat{C}(pi, t) - C'(pi, t)\|^2. Curriculum Learning: Input images are sorted by timestamp and added incrementally to improve convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(p, L): """ Applies positional encoding to input p. p: numpy array of shape (..., D) L: number of frequency bands Returns: numpy array of shape (..., D 2 L) """ # p is expected to be in range [-1, 1] or similar, scaled appropriately # The formula is <(sin(2^l pi p), cos(2^l pi p))>{l=0}^{L-1} freqbands = 2.0 np.arange(L) np.pi # Expand dimensions for broadcasting freqbands = freqbands.reshape(1, -1) # p shape: (..., D) -> (..., D, 1) # freqbands shape: (1, L) # result shape: (..., D, 2, L) encoded = np.concatenate([ np.sin(p[..., np.newaxis, np.newaxis] freqbands), np.cos(p[..., np.newaxis, np.newaxis] freqbands) ], axis=-2) # Flatten the last two dimensions (2, L) into (2L) return encoded.reshape(p.shape[:-1], -1) def deformnetwork(xencoded, tencoded): """ 8-layer MLP for deformation. xencoded: encoded position tencoded: encoded time Returns: displacement deltax """ # Implementation details of the 8-layer MLP are omitted as per standard MLP definition # Input: concat(xencoded, tencoded) # Hidden layers: Linear -> ReLU # Output layer: Linear (no activation) # Assuming a standard MLP implementation exists pass def canonicalnetwork(xprimeencoded, dencoded): """ 8-layer MLP for canonical radiance. xprimeencoded: encoded canonical position dencoded: encoded viewing direction Returns: density sigma, color c """ # Implementation details of the 8-layer MLP are omitted # Input: concat(xprimeencoded, dencoded) # Hidden layers: Linear -> ReLU # Output layer: Linear -> Sigmoid # Assuming a standard MLP implementation exists pass def renderpixel(p, t, camerapose, near, far, Nsamples): """ Renders a single pixel at time t. p: pixel coordinates (u, v) t: time camerapose: 4x4 SE(3) matrix Tt near, far: ray bounds hn, hf Nsamples: number of samples along ray Returns: rendered color C' """ # 1. Get ray origin and direction # o = camerapose[:3, 3] # d = unproject(p, camerapose) # Standard graphics operation # Ray generation logic assumed available # 2. Stratified sampling # Draw N samples from evenly-spaced bins in [near, far] bins = np.linspace(near, far, Nsamples + 1) binlength = (far - near) / Nsamples # Add uniform noise to each sample within its bin noise = np.random.uniform(0, binlength, Nsamples) h = bins[:-1] + noise # 3. Sample points on ray # x(h) = o + h d xpoints = o + h[:, np.newaxis] d[np.newaxis,:] # 4. Deformation # Encode x and t xenc = positionalencoding(xpoints, L=10) tenc = positionalencoding(np.array([t]), L=4) # Compute displacement deltax = deformnetwork(xenc, tenc) # Transform to canonical space xcanonical = xpoints + deltax # 5. Query Canonical Network denc = positionalencoding(d[np.newaxis,:], L=4) xcanenc = positionalencoding(xcanonical, L=10) sigma, c = canonicalnetwork(xcanenc, denc) # 6. Volume Rendering # Calculate deltan deltan = np.diff(np.concatenate(([near], h, [far]))) # Note: The paper defines deltan = h{n+1} - hn. # In stratified sampling, hn are the sample centers. # The paper uses hn as the sample positions for the integral approximation. # We use the bin edges for deltan calculation if hn are centers, # but the paper formula uses deltan directly with sigma at hn. # Standard NeRF implementation: deltan is distance to next sample. # Here we approximate deltan as binlength for simplicity or use diff(h) # The paper says: deltan = h{n+1} - hn. # If h are sample centers, we need boundaries. # Let's use the bin edges derived from stratified sampling. # hsamples are centers. Boundaries are hsamples +/- binlength/2. # However, the paper's Eq 7 uses deltan in the exponent sum. # Let's stick to the paper's definition: deltan is distance between quadrature points. # In stratified sampling, points are drawn from bins. # A common approximation is to use the bin width or distance to next point. # Given the discrete sum in Eq 6, we assume deltan is the step size. # Let's use the distance to the next sample, or bin width. # The paper states: "deltan = h{n+1} - hn". # If we treat hn as the sample points, we need h{n+1}. # Let's assume h is sorted. deltanvals = np.diff(np.sort(np.concatenate(([near], h, [far])))) # Map deltan to samples. Usually deltan corresponds to the segment after hn. # So for sample n, deltan is distance to h{n+1}. # We need to align deltan with sigma and c. # sigma and c are at h. # T' uses sum of sigma delta. # Re-calculate deltan aligned with samples # hsorted = np.sort(h) # deltanaligned = np.diff(np.concatenate(([near], hsorted, [far]))) # But h is not necessarily sorted in the array if we just draw. # Let's sort h and corresponding sigma/c. sortidx = np.argsort(h) h = h[sortidx] sigma = sigma[sortidx] c = c[sortidx] deltanaligned = np.diff(np.concatenate(([near], h, [far]))) # Calculate alpha and T' # alpha(h, t, delta) = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltanaligned) # T'(hn) = exp(-sum{m=1}^{n-1} sigmam deltam) # Cumulative product of transmittance # Transmittance for segment m is exp(-sigmam deltam) transmittancesegment = np.exp(-sigma deltanaligned) # Cumulative product from start # T'1 = 1 (exp(0)) # T'2 = T'1 transmittance1 # T'n = T'{n-1} transmittance{n-1} # Using cumprod # transmittancesegment has length N # We need T' for each sample n, which is product of transmittance of previous segments # T'[0] = 1 # T'[1] = transmittancesegment[0] # T'[n] = prod(transmittancesegment[:n]) cumtrans = np.cumprod(transmittancesegment) Tprime = np.concatenate(([1.0], cumtrans[:-1])) # Color # C' = sum(T'n alphan cn) color = np.sum(Tprime alpha c, axis=0) return color def trainstep(images, poses, tvalues): """ Single training step. images: list of RGB images poses: list of camera poses tvalues: list of time values Returns: loss """ # 1. Select a random time t and corresponding image idx = np.random.randint(len(images)) It = images[idx] Tt = poses[idx] t = tvalues[idx] # 2. Sample Ns rays Ns = 4096 H, W, = It.shape # Randomly select Ns pixels u = np.random.randint(0, W, Ns) v = np.random.randint(0, H, Ns) # 3. Render these rays # Loop over rays or batched rendering renderedcolors = [] for i in range(Ns): p = (u[i], v[i]) c = renderpixel(p, t, Tt, near=0.0, far=10.0, Nsamples=64) renderedcolors.append(c) renderedcolors = np.array(renderedcolors) # 4. Get ground truth colors gtcolors = It[v, u] # 5. Compute Loss loss = np.mean((gtcolors - renderedcolors) 2) # 6. Backpropagate # Standard gradient descent step using Adam pass return loss This method is a dynamic Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) variant that replaces the explicit temporal coordinate t with multi-view projected color statistics to improve point correspondence estimation during on-the-fly training. Unlike standard space-time dynamic NeRFs that optimize irregular temporal deformation fields, this approach maps inputs to a "space-color" coordinate system where correspondence is easier to track due to color invariance under motion. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses two 8-layer MLPs. The complexity is dominated by the forward pass of these networks for each sample along each ray. Memory usage is proportional to the number of network parameters and the training batch size (4096 rays). Measured Performance: On the 'Hell Warrior' scene, D-NeRF achieves MSE 31 \times 10^{-4}, PSNR 23.19, SSIM 0.93, LPIPS 0.08, compared to NeRF's MSE 44 \times 10^{-3}, PSNR 13.52, SSIM 0.81, LPIPS 0.25. On the 'T-Rex' scene, D-NeRF achieves MSE 5 \times 10^{-4}, PSNR 32.80, SSIM 0.98, LPIPS 0.03, compared to NeRF's MSE 21 \times 10^{-3}, PSNR 18.19, SSIM 0.89, LPIPS 0.14. Scaling: The model is trained on a single Nvidia GTX 1080 for 2 days for 800k iterations. Strengths and Limitations: D-NeRF effectively handles rigid, articulated, and non-rigid motions from a single monocular camera. However, it suffers from blurry results when complex scene motions exist because deformation fields are difficult to learn. It also cannot reconstruct transparent objects or simulate optical effects caused by mapping to a canonical space, as the deformation field must be continuous and cannot handle topological changes. When to Use: Use for dynamic scenes with non-rigid deformations where only sparse monocular views are available and ground-truth geometry is not present. When Not to Use: Avoid for scenes with significant topological changes or transparent objects, as the continuous deformation field cannot model discontinuities or complex light transport effects accurately. D-NeRF was proposed by Albert Pumarola, Enric Corona, Gerard Pons-Moll, and Francesc Moreno-Noguer from the Institut de Robòtica i Informàtica Industrial (CSIC-UPC) and the Max Planck Institute for Informatics. The paper was published in November 2020 (arXiv) and later in CVPR 2021. It extends the original NeRF method [26] to handle dynamic scenes by introducing time as an additional input and decomposing the learning process into a canonical space and a deformation field. It is compared against Neural Volumes (NV), Scene Representation Networks (SRN), and T-NeRF. name: Dynamic NeRF Guided by Projected Colors
head: Projected Color Conditioning, Space-Color Dynamic NeRF
body: This method is a dynamic Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) variant that replaces the explicit temporal coordinate t with multi-view projected color statistics to improve point correspondence estimation during on-the-fly training. Unlike standard space-time dynamic NeRFs that optimize irregular temporal deformation fields, this approach maps inputs to a "space-color" coordinate system where correspondence is easier to track due to color invariance under motion. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Spatial coordinates x \in \mathbb{R}^3, viewing direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3, projected color mean \bar{c}p(x, k), and projected color variance Var(cp(x, k)) at frame k. Outputs: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures The model input vector consists of: 1. x: 3D spatial position. 2. d: Normalized viewing direction. 3. \bar{c}p(x, k): Scalar mean of projected colors. 4. Var(cp(x, k)): Scalar variance of projected colors. Projected Color Calculation For a 3D point x at frame k, the set of projected colors cp(x, k) is derived from all training cameras M. Let C{k, cam} be the pixel color at the projection of x in camera cam's image at frame k, and P{cam} be the camera projection matrix: cp(x, k) = \{ C{k, cam}(P{cam} \cdot x) \mid cam \in M \} The scalar inputs are the mean and variance of this set: \bar{c}p(x, k) = \text{mean}(cp(x, k)) Var(cp(x, k)) = \text{variance}(cp(x, k)) Algorithm Steps 1. Precompute Projections: For each 3D point x sampled during training and each frame k, project x into the image plane of every camera cam \in M using P{cam}. 2. Sample Colors: Retrieve the pixel colors C{k, cam} at the projected coordinates. Handle out-of-bounds projections by excluding them or using a default value. 3. Compute Statistics: Calculate the mean \bar{c}p(x, k) and variance Var(cp(x, k)) of the collected colors. 4. Model Forward Pass: Construct the input vector [x, d, \bar{c}p(x, k), Var(cp(x, k))]. Pass this through the neural network Fk to predict density \sigma and color c: Fk: (x, d, \bar{c}p(x, k), Var(cp(x, k))) \mapsto (\sigma, c) 5. Render and Optimize: Use volume rendering to synthesize images and optimize network parameters using gradient descent. Pitfalls Color Invariance Assumption: Projected colors are not perfectly invariant due to reflections, lighting changes, and occlusions. However, they remain largely similar across consecutive frames. Projection Errors: Incorrect camera matrices P{cam} or misaligned frames will corrupt the projected color statistics. Complexity: Reduces optimization time compared to space-time dynamic NeRFs by avoiding the need to learn irregular temporal deformation fields. Strengths: Better point correspondence estimation on-the-fly; easier extrapolation to untrained frames. Limitations: Relies on multi-view consistency; performance degrades if lighting or reflections vary significantly between frames. This method was introduced in OD-NeRF. It addresses the difficulty of estimating point correspondence in dynamic scenes where temporal trajectories are irregular. By shifting from a space-time to a space-color coordinate system, it leverages the invariance of point color under motion to simplify the learning task. name: DaReNeRF
head: DaReNeRF architecture, Direction-Aware Representation, Direction-aware Representation for Dynamic Scenes
body: DaReNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes that employs a direction-aware representation to capture spatiotemporal dynamics from six distinct orientations. It addresses the shift variance and direction ambiguity (checkerboard artifacts) inherent in traditional 2D Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DWT) by utilizing the Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform (DTCWT). Unlike standard plane-based decompositions, DaReNeRF models features from six different directions, eliminating ghosting artifacts around moving objects while maintaining memory efficiency through low-rank plane-based decomposition. Inputs: A set of posed 2D images with timestamps. Outputs: Rendered RGB images for arbitrary camera poses and time steps. Data Structures: 1. 4D Volume Representation (D): Decomposed into three terms, each consisting of the Hadamard product of two 2D plane-based representations and a learned vector. 2. Plane-based Representation (M^{AB}r): A 2D tensor of size m \times n (where m, n are spatial/temporal resolutions) reconstructed via Inverse Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform (IDTCWT). 3. Wavelet Coefficients: For each plane M^{AB}r, the representation is defined by: One approximation coefficient: W^{AB}{a,r} \in \mathbb{R}^{m/2 \times n/2}. Six real direction-aware wavelet coefficients: \{R\{W^{AB}{i,r}\}\}{i=1}^6 \in \mathbb{R}^{m/2 \times n/2}. Six imaginary direction-aware wavelet coefficients: \{I\{W^{AB}{i,r}\}\}{i=1}^6 \in \mathbb{R}^{m/2 \times n/2}. Note: The coefficients are masked to enforce sparsity (see Pitfalls). 4. Learned Vectors (v{ri}): Vectors v{ri} \in \mathbb{R}^F where F=3 (RGB feature size). 5. Tensor V{RF}: A 2D tensor stacking all v{ri}. 6. Emptiness Voxel: A small 3D voxel grid indicating empty regions by aggregating maximum opacities across time steps. Parameters: R1, R2, R3: Number of low-rank components for each decomposition term. Total R = R1 + R2 + R3 \ll N (spatial resolution). Spatial grid size: 512. Temporal grid size: 300. Batch size: 4,096. Coordinate system: Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). Formulas: The 4D volume D is represented as the sum of three components: D = \sum{r=1}^{R1} M{rXY} \circ M{rZT} \circ v{r1} + \sum{r=1}^{R2} M{rXZ} \circ M{rYT} \circ v{r2} + \sum{r=1}^{R3} M{rYZ} \circ M{rXT} \circ v{r3} where M{rAB} \in \mathbb{R}^{A \times B} are learned 2D plane-based representations with (A, B) \in \{X, Y, Z, T\}^2 | A \neq B, and v{ri} \in \mathbb{R}^F are learned vectors. The plane-based representation is reconstructed using IDTCWT: M^{AB}r = \text{IDTCWT}([W^{AB}{a,r}, \{R\{W^{AB}{i,r}\}\}{i=1}^6, \{I\{W^{AB}{i,r}\}\}{i=1}^6]) where IDTCWT is the inverse dual-tree complex wavelet transform. Masked wavelet coefficients are computed to encourage sparsity: \tilde{W}^{AB} = \text{sg}(H(M^{AB}) - \text{sigmoid}(M^{AB})) \odot W^{AB} where \text{sg} is the stop-gradient operator, H is the Heaviside step function, and M^{AB} are learned masks. The total loss function is: L = \frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} ||C(r) - \hat{C}(r)||^2 + \lambda{reg} L{reg} + \lambdam Lm where C(r) is rendered color, \hat{C}(r) is ground-truth, L{reg} is total variation loss, and Lm is mask sparsity loss. Steps: 1. Decomposition: Decompose the 4D spatiotemporal volume D into the sum of three terms defined by Equation 1 above. 2. Feature Extraction: For a given space-time point, extract feature vectors from paired planes (e.g., XY and ZT). 3. Fusion: Multiply the feature vectors from the paired planes element-wise. 4. Concatenation: Concatenate the multiplied results into a single vector. 5. Density/Appearance Computation: Multiply the concatenated vector by V{RF} (the tensor stacking all v{ri}) to compute density and appearance features. 6. Opacity Query: Query point opacities directly from the computed density features. 7. Color Regression: Regress RGB color values using a compact Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Inputs to the MLP are the appearance features and view directions. 8. Rendering: Synthesize final images via differentiable volumetric rendering along rays. 9. Optimization: Minimize the total loss L using a coarse-to-fine training strategy, progressively increasing grid resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forward(pointcoords, viewdirection, timestep): # pointcoords: (x, y, z) in NDC # timestep: t # 1. Identify relevant planes based on coordinate pairs # Pairs: (XY, ZT), (XZ, YT), (YZ, XT) features = [] for r in range(R1): # Extract features from XY and ZT planes featxy = extractplanefeatures(MXY[r], pointcoords.x, pointcoords.y) featzt = extractplanefeatures(MZT[r], pointcoords.z, timestep) # Element-wise multiplication fused = featxy featzt features.append(fused) for r in range(R2): # Extract features from XZ and YT planes featxz = extractplanefeatures(MXZ[r], pointcoords.x, pointcoords.z) featyt = extractplanefeatures(MYT[r], pointcoords.y, timestep) fused = featxz featyt features.append(fused) for r in range(R3): # Extract features from YZ and XT planes featyz = extractplanefeatures(MYZ[r], pointcoords.y, pointcoords.z) featxt = extractplanefeatures(MXT[r], pointcoords.x, timestep) fused = featyz featxt features.append(fused) # Concatenate all fused features concatenatedfeatures = concatenate(features) # Multiply by VRF tensor densityappearance = matrixmultiply(concatenatedfeatures, VRF) # Query opacity from density features opacity = queryopacity(densityappearance) # Regress color using MLP color = colormlp(appearancefeatures=densityappearance, viewdir=viewdirection) return opacity, color def extractplanefeatures(planetensor, coord1, coord2): # Bilinear interpolation or similar sampling from the 2D plane tensor # planetensor is reconstructed from wavelet coefficients via IDTCWT return sample(planetensor, coord1, coord2) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shift Variance: Traditional 2D DWT suffers from shift variance, where small shifts in input signal disrupt wavelet oscillation patterns, causing poor results in dynamic regions with motion or camera movement. DaReNeRF uses DTCWT to ensure shift invariance. Direction Ambiguity: Traditional 2D DWT has poor direction selectivity, producing a checkerboard pattern that blends representations from \pm 45^\circ, leading to ghosting artifacts around moving objects. DaReNeRF uses DTCWT with 6 real and 6 imaginary coefficients aligned to specific directions to eliminate this. Empty Regions: Large empty regions in dynamic scenes waste computation. DaReNeRF uses a small 3D voxel representation that indicates emptiness by aggregating maximum opacities across time steps to skip these points. Sparsity: Learned masks are used to zero out unnecessary wavelet coefficients, controlled by the mask loss Lm. Memory Complexity: Reduced from O(N^3 T F) for direct 4D volume modeling to O(R N^2 T F) using the plane-based decomposition, where R \ll N. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on Plenoptic Video and D-NeRF datasets. Hardware: Trained on a single A100 GPU. Strengths: Robust handling of complex dynamic scenes, elimination of checkerboard artifacts, shift invariance, and memory efficiency. Limitations: The direction-aware representation introduces a 2D redundancy compared to DWT, resulting in lower storage efficiency than pure DWT-based methods, though still better than direct 4D modeling. When to use: Novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes where high fidelity and motion robustness are required. When not to use: Static scenes may not benefit from the temporal complexity, though it is applicable. DaReNeRF was introduced to address the limitations of traditional 2D Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DWT) in modeling dynamic scenes, specifically shift variance and direction ambiguity. It builds upon plane-based 4D volume decomposition and draws inspiration from the Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform (DTCWT). The method was developed to improve upon prior implicit representations and DWT-based approaches that failed to adequately model dynamic scenes, resulting in ghosting artifacts. It is used in DaReNeRF and its sparse variant, DaReNeRF-S, for novel view synthesis. name: Compression and Representation Efficiency
body: This family addresses the excessive memory footprint and training latency of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by reducing the number of primitives or compressing their attributes. It differs from Base 3DGS Optimization and Optimization and Training Efficiency by focusing specifically on the representation size rather than just the computational speed of the rasterization loop. It contrasts with Physical Parameter Optimization by prioritizing storage and transmission efficiency over physical accuracy. The core mechanism involves reducing the data volume required to store the scene representation, which consists of position \mathbf{p}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{lm}. Two primary strategies are employed: 1. Count Reduction: Limiting the total number of Gaussians N to a hard constraint N{max}, requiring dynamic reorganization (splitting/pruning) during training to maintain visual fidelity with fewer primitives. 2. Attribute Quantization: Replacing high-precision floating-point attributes (typically \mathbf{s} and \mathbf{R}) with quantized indices and residuals, often using codebooks. Mini-Splatting is a resource-efficient variant that explicitly constrains the total number of Gaussians to a hard limit N{max} to reduce memory footprint and accelerate training and rendering. It addresses the inefficient spatial distribution of vanilla 3DGS—characterized by 'overlapping' and 'under-reconstruction'—by pivoting from direct simplification to spatial reorganization. Unlike its parent Compression and Representation Efficiency, which encompasses various compression techniques, Mini-Splatting specifically achieves efficiency through a mixed-integer optimization formulation that maintains a constant Gaussian count via iterative densification and simplification passes. It differs from Model Compression Pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting by not relying on post-training pruning, quantization, or spherical harmonic (SH) degree reduction, but rather by dynamically reorganizing Gaussian positions during training to achieve uniform spatial distribution. C3DGS is a compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces model size by applying residual vector quantization (R-VQ) to geometric attributes, specifically scaling and rotation. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Mini-Splatting by focusing on quantization of geometric parameters rather than pruning or sampling Gaussians. Treats compression of 3D Gaussians as an optimal transport problem, learning a compact set of summary Gaussians representing the original cloud under multi-view ranking constraints. Optimization minimizes the Wasserstein distance between the original and compressed sets. Ci = \sum{v\in V} \sum{u\in I} Mu^{(v)} \cdot I{\omega}^{(v)i,u} > \epsilonv, where Ci is the constraint for Gaussian i, V is views, I is pixels, M is mask/intensity, I is indicator, \omega is view, u is pixel, v is view, \epsilon is threshold. C{ij} = dC^2(S{src}, S{tgt}) = \|\mui - \muj\|2^2 + \|\Sigmai^{1/2} - \Sigmaj^{1/2}\|F^2, where C{ij} is the cost matrix, S{src/tgt} are source/target sets, \mu is mean, \Sigma is covariance, \|\cdot\|F is Frobenius norm. Maintains rendering quality with only 10% primitives and 10× accelerated training speeds compared to 3DGS. The need for compression in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises from the typical requirement of millions of Gaussians to represent complex scenes, leading to high memory usage and slow training times. Mini-Splatting was introduced to enforce a hard limit on Gaussian counts, addressing the "overlapping" issue inherent in standard densification strategies. C3DGS applies residual vector quantization to geometric attributes to reduce storage size. MMGS formulates compression as an optimal transport problem to minimize the Wasserstein distance between original and compressed Gaussian sets. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Mini-Splatting
head: Constrained Gaussian Representation, Hard-constrained 3DGS, Mixed Integer 3DGS
body: Mini-Splatting is a training optimization and initialization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that explicitly constrains the total number of Gaussians to a hard limit N{max} to reduce memory footprint and accelerate rendering. It addresses the inefficient spatial distribution of vanilla 3DGS—specifically "overlapping" and "under-reconstruction" phenomena—by pivoting from direct simplification to spatial reorganization. Unlike its sibling C3DGS, which focuses on voxel-based pruning, Mini-Splatting leverages both screen-space and world-space information to densify around objects and simplify redundant overlaps, achieving comparable or superior visual quality with significantly fewer primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene representation initialized with 3D Gaussians (position \mathbf{p}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{lm}) and a target maximum Gaussian count N{max}. Output: A sparse Gaussian field with exactly N{max} primitives, uniformly distributed around object surfaces, maintaining rendering fidelity. Data Structures: The method maintains the standard 3DGS attribute set for each Gaussian i: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c}{i, lm}: Spherical Harmonic coefficients. scorei \in \mathbb{R}: Importance score used for selection. Algorithm Steps: The optimization follows a 30,000-step schedule, divided into densification and simplification phases. 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using standard 3DGS densification (point cloud sampling) until iteration 15,000. Disable view-dependent colors (SH coefficients) during this phase to save resources, as they barely enhance densification. 2. Densification (Iterations 0–15,000): Blur Split: Detect blurring areas in the rendered image. Split Gaussians located in these regions to increase local density. Depth Reinitialization: Use merged depth points to reinitialize scene geometry and Gaussian positions, ensuring coverage of under-reconstructed areas. Constraint: The total count may exceed N{max} temporarily during densification. 3. Simplification (Iterations 15,000 and 20,000): Intersection Preserving: Retain only Gaussians that have the maximal impact on the rendered image, discarding redundant overlaps. Gaussian Sampling: Sample points to preserve the underlying geometric structure and original rendering quality. Hard Constraint: Iteratively prune the least important Gaussians and split the most important ones to keep the total count constant at N{max}. 4. Refinement (Iterations 15,000–30,000): Enable SH coefficients and increase the SH level after the first simplification pass (at 15K). Continue standard 3DGS optimization (opacity reset, etc.) for the remaining steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minisplattingtraining(scenedata, Nmax, totalsteps=30000): # Initialize Gaussians using standard 3DGS densification gaussians = initialize3dgs(scenedata) # Disable view-dependent colors during densification gaussians.shdegree = 0 for step in range(1, totalsteps + 1): # Render current view and compute loss renderedimage = render(gaussians, camera) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) if step <= 15000: # Densification Phase # 1. Blur Split: Split Gaussians in blurring areas blurmask = detectblur(renderedimage) gaussians = splitgaussians(gaussians, blurmask) # 2. Depth Reinitialization: Reinitialize positions using depth depthpoints = getmergeddepth(scenedata) gaussians = reinitializepositions(gaussians, depthpoints) # Standard 3DGS densification (clone/split based on gradient) gaussians = standarddensification(gaussians) else: # Simplification Phase (triggered at 15K and 20K) if step in [15000, 20000]: # 1. Intersection Preserving: Keep high-impact Gaussians impactscores = computerenderingimpact(gaussians) gaussians = prunelowimpact(gaussians, impactscores, Nmax) # 2. Gaussian Sampling: Preserve geometry gaussians = samplegaussians(gaussians, Nmax) # Enable SH coefficients after first simplification if step > 15000: gaussians.shdegree = 1 # Increase SH level # Standard optimization gaussians = standardoptimization(gaussians) return gaussians Parameters: N{max}: Hard limit on Gaussian count. Typical value: ~0.49M for Mip-NeRF360 Outdoor (vs 3.36M for vanilla 3DGS). Total Optimization Steps: 30,000. Densification Stop: 15,000 steps. Simplification Steps: 15,000 and 20,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping Artifacts: Using fewer Gaussians results in larger Gaussians on average, which increases the prevalence of noticeable popping artifacts during camera movement. SH Redundancy: View-dependent colors (SH coefficients) provide minimal benefit during the densification phase; enabling them early wastes resources without improving spatial distribution. This method is a compression and rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces memory footprint and increases rendering speed while maintaining image quality. It addresses the high memory bandwidth and computational complexity of standard 3DGS, making it suitable for edge deployment, mobile VR/AR, and low-power hardware. It sets itself apart from its parent Mini-Splatting by not imposing a hard limit on the total number of Gaussians via mixed-integer optimization, but rather by iteratively pruning, quantizing attributes, and reducing spherical harmonic (SH) degrees to achieve high compression ratios (up to 51.6×) with minimal quality loss. It differs from LightGaussian by using iterative pruning with intermediate fine-tuning, progressive SH-degree reduction, and vector quantization (VQ) on all SH coefficients and colors, rather than only low-salience subsets. A quality-prioritized variant of Mini-Splatting that omits the simplification process to maximize rendering quality. On Mip-NeRF360 (Outdoor), Mini-Splatting-D uses 4.69M Gaussians, achieving SSIM 0.831, PSNR 27.51, LPIPS 0.176. It surpasses Zip-NeRF in SSIM (0.828) and LPIPS (0.189) on this dataset. Training time is 31m48s, Peak GPU Memory is 7.45GB, Rendering FPS is 83, Peak Rendering Memory is 3.12GB. Designed for scenarios requiring storage compression, this pipeline is directly based on Mini-Splatting. Given a pre-trained Mini-Splatting model, it stores Gaussian centers as float32, while other attributes (scales, SH coefficients) are processed using transform coding and standard zip compression. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: Mini-Splatting reduces training time significantly. On Mip-NeRF360 (Outdoor), it takes 17m56s compared to 30m8s for vanilla 3DGS. Peak GPU Memory: Reduced from 7.45GB (3DGS) to 2.61GB (Mini-Splatting) on Mip-NeRF360 (Outdoor). Rendering FPS: Increases from 98 FPS (3DGS) to 410 FPS (Mini-Splatting) on Mip-NeRF360 (Outdoor). Peak Rendering Memory: Reduced from 2.79GB (3DGS) to 0.40GB (Mini-Splatting). Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF360 (Outdoor): Mini-Splatting uses 0.49M Gaussians (7x fewer than 3DGS's 3.36M). Metrics: SSIM 0.822 (vs 0.815), PSNR 27.34 (vs 27.21), LPIPS 0.217 (vs 0.214). Mip-NeRF360 (General): Another variant achieves SSIM 0.763, PSNR 25.83, LPIPS 0.273, with a model size of 18.2 MB. Model Size: Up to 10x reduction compared to original 3DGS. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficient spatial distribution reduces redundancy; significant memory and speed improvements; comparable or better visual quality than dense 3DGS. Limitations: Fewer Gaussians lead to larger individual splats, increasing popping artifacts. The hard constraint requires careful balancing of densification and simplification schedules. When to Use: Use Mini-Splatting when memory bandwidth, training time, or rendering FPS are critical constraints, and a slight increase in popping artifacts is acceptable. Use Mini-Splatting-D when quality is prioritized over memory/speed constraints. Mini-Splatting was introduced by Fang and Wang in 2024. It emerged from the observation that vanilla 3DGS suffers from inefficient spatial distribution, leading to overlapping and under-reconstruction. The method formulates the optimization as a mixed-integer problem to bound memory footprints explicitly. It is part of the broader effort to make 3DGS viable for resource-constrained environments, such as mobile AR/VR and edge devices. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Mini-Splatting: Representing Scenes with a Constrained Number of Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72980-510, fetched 2026-10-26 Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 Fast and Robust 3D Gaussian Splatting for Virtual Reality, https://doi.org/10.1145/3681756.3697947, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Model Compression Pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3DGS Model Compression Pipeline, Edge-deployment compression, LightGaussian-derived compression, Compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting Pipeline, Compressed 3DGS, Compressed 3DGS Model, Hardware-oriented 3DGS
body: This method is a compression and rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces memory footprint and increases rendering speed while maintaining image quality. It addresses the high memory bandwidth and computational complexity of standard 3DGS, making it suitable for edge deployment, mobile VR/AR, and low-power hardware. It sets itself apart from its parent Mini-Splatting by not imposing a hard limit on the total number of Gaussians via mixed-integer optimization, but rather by iteratively pruning, quantizing attributes, and reducing spherical harmonic (SH) degrees to achieve high compression ratios (up to 51.6×) with minimal quality loss. It differs from LightGaussian by using iterative pruning with intermediate fine-tuning, progressive SH-degree reduction, and vector quantization (VQ) on all SH coefficients and colors, rather than only low-salience subsets. The pipeline consists of four main stages: Sensitivity Calculation, Clustering, QA Fine-tuning, and Encoding. It combines Gaussian pruning, SH distillation, VQ for SH coefficients and colors, and FP16 quantization. Inputs: Trained 3D Gaussian model (positions \mathbf{p}, opacities \alpha, colors \mathbf{c}, covariances \mathbf{\Sigma}, SH coefficients \mathbf{C}). Outputs: Compressed scene representation (pruned Gaussians, codebook indices, quantized parameters). Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Attributes: Position: 3D float vector \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity: Scalar \alpha \in [0, 1]. Shape: Covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q} and scale vector \mathbf{s}. Color: SH coefficients \mathbf{C} and base color \mathbf{c}. 2. Codebooks: Color Codebook: Stores quantized SH coefficients and colors. Size varies by scene. Shape Codebook: Stores quantized Gaussian shape parameters (\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{s}) and scaling factor \eta. 3. Indices: Codebook indices replace original attributes for storage. Morton order layout is used for spatial locality. Steps: 1. Sensitivity Calculation: Calculate sensitivity thresholds \betac and \betag for SH coefficients and shape parameters, respectively. These thresholds determine which parameters are considered for clustering. 2. Iterative Pruning with Intermediate Fine-tuning: Instead of aggressive single-step pruning, the model is pruned progressively. Prune Gaussians based on opacity and contribution. Insert fine-tuning between pruning stages to recover visual quality. Repeat until the target Gaussian count is reached. 3. Progressive SH-Degree Reduction via Iterative Distillation: Reduce SH degree progressively rather than in one step. Distill the representation from higher to lower SH degrees, smoothing the quality-compression tradeoff. 4. Clustering and Vector Quantization (VQ): Apply VQ to all SH coefficients and colors, not just low-salience subsets. Compress SH coefficients and shape parameters into codebooks of predefined sizes. Color Clustering: Cluster SH coefficients and colors into the Color Codebook. Gaussian Clustering: Cluster shape parameters into the Shape Codebook. The centroid \hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}c of normalized covariance matrices \hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}i with weights wi is calculated as: \hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}c = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N wi \hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}i}{\sum{i=1}^N wi} The scaling factor \eta ensures normalization: \|\mathbf{s}c\|2^2 = \text{Tr}(\hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}c) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N wi \text{Tr}(\hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}i)}{\sum{i=1}^N wi} 5. QA Fine-tuning: Apply quantization-aware fine-tuning to regain information lost during quantization. This stage takes up 70% of the total compression pipeline time. 6. Encoding: Apply entropy and run-length encoding. Use Morton order layout for spatial locality. Quantize remaining parameters to FP16. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compress3dgs(model): # Inputs: model with positions, opacities, covariances, SH coefficients, colors # Step 1: Sensitivity Calculation betac = computesensitivity(model.shcoeffs) betag = computesensitivity(model.shapeparams) # Step 2: Iterative Pruning with Intermediate Fine-tuning gaussians = model.gaussians while gaussians.count > targetcount: gaussians = prunebycontribution(gaussians, threshold=betac) gaussians = finetune(gaussians, model.traindata, lr=0.001) # Step 3: Progressive SH-Degree Reduction via Iterative Distillation currentshdegree = model.shdegree while currentshdegree > targetshdegree: gaussians = distillshdegree(gaussians, currentshdegree, currentshdegree - 1) currentshdegree -= 1 gaussians = finetune(gaussians, model.traindata, lr=0.001) # Step 4: Clustering and Vector Quantization (VQ) colorcodebook, colorindices = kmeanscluster(model.shcoeffs + model.colors, size=colorcodebooksize) shapecodebook, shapeindices = kmeanscluster(model.shapeparams, size=shapecodebooksize) gaussians.shindices = colorindices gaussians.shapeindices = shapeindices # Step 5: QA Fine-tuning gaussians = qafinetune(gaussians, model.traindata, codebooks=[colorcodebook, shapecodebook]) # Step 6: Encoding compresseddata = encodemortonrle(gaussians, colorcodebook, shapecodebook) compresseddata = quantizefp16(compresseddata) return compresseddata def computesensitivity(params): # Calculate sensitivity thresholds betac and betag # Standard metric: variance of rendering contribution or gradient magnitude return thresholdvalue def prunebycontribution(gaussians, threshold): # Remove Gaussians with opacity/contribution below threshold return [g for g in gaussians if g.contribution > threshold] def finetune(gaussians, traindata, lr): # Standard differentiable rendering optimization loop for epoch in range(numepochs): # Render scene, compute loss against traindata, backpropagate pass return gaussians def distillshdegree(gaussians, highdeg, lowdeg): # Distill representation from highdeg to lowdeg # Train low-degree SH coefficients to match high-degree rendering output return gaussians def kmeanscluster(data, size): # Standard K-Means clustering to build codebook centroids, indices = standardkmeans(data, size) return centroids, indices def qafinetune(gaussians, traindata, codebooks): # Regain information lost during quantization # Fine-tune with quantization-aware training (simulate quantization during forward pass) return finetune(gaussians, traindata, lr=0.001) def encodemortonrle(gaussians, colorcodebook, shapecodebook): # Apply entropy and run-length encoding combined with Morton order layout # Sort indices by Morton order, apply run-length and entropy encoding return compresseddata def quantizefp16(data): # Quantize remaining parameters to FP16 return data.astype(np.float16) Parameters: Codebook Sizes: Predefined sizes for Color and Shape codebooks. Larger codebooks reduce maximum error with minimal memory overhead. Sensitivity Thresholds (\betac, \betag): Trade-off between quality and compression rate. Target Gaussian Count: Determined by hardware constraints. Target SH Degree: Reduced progressively. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Position Compression: Aggressive compression of Gaussian positions introduces significant error; positions are typically not compressed. Color Shift: Subtle color shifts may occur below human perception threshold. Memory Dominance: Memory consumption is dominated by coordinates and codebook indices. Color codebook size varies significantly between scenes. A compression scheme tailored for hardware deployment that reduces model size and bandwidth by iteratively pruning Gaussians, reducing spherical harmonics (SH) degree, and quantizing attributes. Compression Ratio: Up to 31× or 51.6× compared to baseline. Rendering Speedup: Up to 4×. Quality Loss: Indiscernible or 0.743 dB average PSNR drop. Memory Bandwidth: Reduced by ~2× due to compressed data. Power Consumption: 0.219 W at 1080p@129 FPS. Throughput: 267.5 Mpixels/s. Energy Efficiency: 1219 Mpixels/J. Silicon Area: 0.66 mm² (TSMC 28 nm, 800 MHz). Compression Time: 5-6 minutes. Reconstruction Time Increase: ~10%. Fine-tuning Time: 70% of total compression time. Preprocessing Speedup: 5× faster with compressed representation. Performance on NVIDIA RTX A5000 (1080p): Bicycle (6.1M Gaussians): Baseline 93/215/321 FPS, Compressed 321 FPS. Bonsai (1.2M Gaussians): Baseline 184/414/502 FPS, Compressed 502 FPS. Average Mip-NeRF360: 4.82ms (uncompressed) vs 1.95ms (compressed). Average Tanks & Temples/Deep Blending: 5.13ms (uncompressed) vs 2.44ms (compressed). Performance on NVIDIA RTX 3070M (1080p): Bicycle: Baseline 54/134/211 FPS, Compressed 211 FPS. Bonsai: Baseline 122/296/380 FPS, Compressed 380 FPS. Performance on Intel UHD Graphics 11 (1080p): Bicycle: Baseline 9/16/23 FPS, Compressed 23 FPS. Bonsai (1.2M Gaussians): Baseline 9/16/23 FPS, Compressed 28/28/28 FPS. Performance on AMD Radeon R9 380 (1080p): Bicycle: Baseline 41/83/76 FPS, Compressed 76 FPS. Bonsai: Baseline 76/128/128 FPS, Compressed 128 FPS. Strengths: High compression ratio with minimal quality loss. Suitable for low-power edge devices and mobile VR/AR. Hardware rasterization renderer provides additional speedup. Limitations: Cannot aggressively compress Gaussian positions without significant error. Fine-tuning stage is time-consuming (70% of pipeline time). The method is derived from LightGaussian, which combines Gaussian pruning and fine-tuning, SH distillation, VQ for SH coefficients and colors, and FP16 quantization. It was developed to meet the design target of full-HD rendering at 120 FPS per eye under a sub-0.5 W power budget for edge deployment. The approach was presented in "Compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting for Accelerated Novel View Synthesis" and "A 129 FPS Full HD Real-Time Accelerator for 3D Gaussian Splatting". name: 3DGS Model Compression Pipeline
head: Hardware-Friendly Compression, Iterative Pruning & VQ Compression
body: A compression scheme tailored for hardware deployment that reduces model size and bandwidth by iteratively pruning Gaussians, reducing spherical harmonics (SH) degree, and quantizing attributes. It modifies LightGaussian to achieve higher compression ratios (51.6× vs 15×) by adding iterative pruning, progressive SH reduction, and full VQ on all coefficients/colors. Inputs: Pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (Gaussians with positions, covariances, opacities, colors, and SH coefficients). Outputs: Compressed model with reduced Gaussian count, lower SH degree, and quantized attributes. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: List of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation/scale representation) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Color ci (encoded as SH coefficients) SH Coefficients: Stored as vectors of coefficients for each RGB channel. Steps: 1. Iterative Gaussian Pruning: Remove Gaussians that contribute least to the visual fidelity. This is done iteratively to reach a target compression ratio or sparsity level. Note: The specific metric for "least contribution" (e.g., gradient magnitude, opacity, or rendering error) is not explicitly detailed in the provided sources, but it is implied to be a refinement of the pruning strategy in LightGaussian. 2. Progressive Spherical Harmonics (SH) Degree Reduction: Reduce the degree of the spherical harmonics used to encode color and directional information. This reduces the number of coefficients per Gaussian. Note: The specific schedule for degree reduction (e.g., from degree 3 to degree 1) is not explicitly detailed, but it is a key step in the pipeline. 3. Vector Quantization (VQ): Apply VQ to all SH coefficients and colors. This involves clustering the coefficients/colors into a codebook and replacing each coefficient/color with an index to the codebook entry. Note: The size of the codebook and the specific VQ algorithm (e.g., k-means, LBG) are not explicitly detailed in the provided sources. Parameters: Target Compression Ratio: 51.6× model-size reduction. PSNR Loss: 0.743 dB. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View-Dependent Culling: Approximately 42% of Gaussian points are considered unnecessary via near-plane culling, but this percentage is view-dependent. When zooming out, nearly all Gaussians can become visible, decreasing the culling benefit. Alpha-Blending Contribution: Only about 50% of Gaussian points contribute to the pixel color during \alpha-blending. Compression Ratio: 51.6× model-size reduction. Quality Loss: 0.743 dB PSNR loss. Comparison: Modifies LightGaussian (which achieves 15× reduction) to reach 51.6× by adding iterative pruning, progressive SH reduction, and full VQ on all coefficients/colors. Hardware Efficiency: The compressed model enables a hardware accelerator to deliver 1219 Mpixels/J at 267.5 Mpixels/s, enabling 1080p at 129 FPS. Memory Usage: Unbounded 360 degree scenes typically require millions of Gaussian points, leading to storage requirements in the gigabyte range. This pipeline mitigates this. The 3DGS algorithm is not hardware-friendly and faces four main design challenges, including substantial memory usage. To overcome these limitations, a dedicated hardware accelerator for real-time rendering of 3DGS models on portable AR/VR devices was introduced, targeting full-HD resolution at 120 FPS per eye. The compression pipeline is a key component of this accelerator, modifying the lightweight model, LightGaussian, to higher compression ratios. name: Mini-Splatting-C
head: Ours+PP, Post-processed Compact 3D Gaussian
body: Mini-Splatting-C is a storage-compression variant of the Mini-Splatting method designed for scenarios requiring minimal model footprint. It achieves significant size reduction by applying post-processing techniques to the attributes of a pre-trained Mini-Splatting model, including transform coding, quantization, and entropy encoding. Unlike Mini-Splatting-D, which prioritizes rendering quality, Mini-Splatting-C optimizes for storage efficiency, demonstrating superior performance compared to other compression-oriented works applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained Mini-Splatting model consisting of Gaussian centers, scales, rotation quaternions, opacity, spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and hash grid parameters (if applicable to the specific implementation variant). Output: A compressed binary stream representing the Gaussian scene representation. Data Structures and Layout: The method distinguishes between attributes stored in high precision and those processed for compression: 1. Gaussian Centers: Stored as float32 (32-bit floating point) without compression. 2. Other Attributes: Scales, SH coefficients, opacity, and hash grid parameters undergo transform coding. 3. Quantized Attributes: Opacity and hash grid parameters are quantized to 8-bit integers using min-max quantization. 4. Encoded Indices: R-VQ (Residual Vector Quantization) indices are generated for the quantized attributes. Steps: 1. Training: Train a standard Mini-Splatting model. 2. Center Storage: Store Gaussian centers as float32 values. 3. Transform Coding: Apply transform coding to scales and SH coefficients. The specific transform is not detailed in the provided notes, but it is cited as [6] in the source. 4. Quantization: Apply 8-bit min-max quantization to opacity and hash grid parameters. Formula: q = \text{clip}(\lfloor \frac{v - v{min}}{v{max} - v{min}} \times 255 + 0.5 \rfloor, 0, 255), where v is the original value, and v{min}, v{max} are the min/max values of the attribute. 5. Pruning: Prune hash grid parameters with values below 0.1. This step removes negligible contributions from the hash grid. 6. Entropy Encoding: Apply Huffman encoding to the quantized opacity, hash parameters, and R-VQ indices. 7. Final Compression: Apply standard ZIP compression to the resulting data stream. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressminisplattingc(model): # Step 1: Extract attributes from pre-trained Mini-Splatting model centers = model.centers # Shape: (N, 3) scales = model.scales # Shape: (N, 3) shcoeffs = model.shcoeffs # Shape: (N, K, 3) opacity = model.opacity # Shape: (N,) hashparams = model.hashgridparams # Shape: (M,) or similar # Step 2: Store centers as float32 (no compression) centersbytes = centers.astype(np.float32).tobytes() # Step 3: Transform coding for scales and SH coefficients # Note: Specific transform algorithm from reference [6] is not detailed in sources # Assuming a placeholder for the transform coding process scalestransformed = applytransformcoding(scales) shtransformed = applytransformcoding(shcoeffs) # Step 4: Quantize opacity and hash parameters to 8-bit # Min-max quantization opacitymin = opacity.min() opacitymax = opacity.max() opacityquantized = np.clip( np.round((opacity - opacitymin) / (opacitymax - opacitymin) 255), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) hashmin = hashparams.min() hashmax = hashparams.max() hashquantized = np.clip( np.round((hashparams - hashmin) / (hashmax - hashmin) 255), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) # Step 5: Prune hash grid parameters below threshold # Note: The source mentions pruning values below 0.1. # This likely refers to the original float values before quantization or # specific indices in the hash grid. We assume it filters the hashparams array. threshold = 0.1 validmask = hashparams >= threshold hashparamspruned = hashparams[validmask] hashquantizedpruned = hashquantized[validmask] # Step 6: Generate R-VQ indices (Placeholder for R-VQ process) # The source mentions R-VQ indices are Huffman encoded. # Assuming R-VQ is applied to the quantized attributes. rvqindices = applyrvq(opacityquantized, hashquantizedpruned) # Step 7: Huffman encoding # Note: Standard Huffman encoding implementation opacityhuffman = huffmanencode(opacityquantized) hashhuffman = huffmanencode(hashquantizedpruned) rvqhuffman = huffmanencode(rvqindices) # Step 8: Combine and ZIP compress # The source states "standard zip compression" is applied to the result of transform coding. # It also states Huffman is applied to quantized opacity/hash/R-VQ. # We combine all compressed streams. combinedstream = ( centersbytes + zlib.compress(scalestransformed) + zlib.compress(shtransformed) + opacityhuffman + hashhuffman + rvqhuffman) finalcompressed = zlib.compress(combinedstream) return finalcompressed Parameters: Center Precision: float32. Quantization Bits: 8-bit for opacity and hash parameters. Pruning Threshold: 0.1 for hash grid parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: Quantization to 8-bit may introduce visual artifacts, particularly in opacity and fine details captured by hash parameters. Pruning Artifacts: Pruning hash grid parameters below 0.1 may remove valid but small contributions, potentially affecting rendering quality in sparse regions. Transform Coding Dependency: The effectiveness of the compression relies on the specific transform coding algorithm referenced as [6] in, which is not detailed in the provided notes. Time and Memory Complexity: Storage: Mini-Splatting-C achieves a storage size of 2.67 MB on the NeRF-Synthetic dataset, which is 0.04x the size of standard 3DGS. This is a reduction from the 5.55 MB of the base Mini-Splatting ("Ours") method. Rendering Speed: On the NeRF-Synthetic dataset, Mini-Splatting-C achieves 545 FPS, which is 1.52x faster than the base Mini-Splatting method (359 FPS). Training Time: The training time for Mini-Splatting-C is not explicitly given, but the base Mini-Splatting ("Ours") takes 8m 04s on NeRF-Synthetic. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in storage size compared to 3DGS and base Mini-Splatting. Improved rendering speed due to reduced model size. Superior performance compared to other compression-oriented works applied to 3DGS. Limitations: Slight drop in PSNR compared to the base Mini-Splatting method (32.88 vs 33.33 on NeRF-Synthetic). The compression pipeline adds complexity to the post-processing step. When to Use: Use Mini-Splatting-C when storage size is the primary constraint and slight quality degradation is acceptable. Suitable for hardware deployment scenarios where bandwidth and memory are limited. When Not to Use: Use Mini-Splatting-D if rendering quality is prioritized over storage size. Use standard 3DGS if high fidelity is required and storage/bandwidth are not constraints. Mini-Splatting-C is part of the Mini-Splatting family, which aims to represent scenes with a constrained number of Gaussians. It was introduced in the paper "Mini-Splatting: Representing Scenes with a Constrained Number of Gaussians". The method builds on the Mini-Splatting representation and adds post-processing compression techniques to further reduce storage size. It is designed to address the large storage requirements of 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Feed-Forward 3DGS Compression
head: Compression of Feed-Forward 3DGS, Zero-shot Compression
body: Feed-Forward 3DGS Compression (FCGS) is a post-training compression method that reduces the storage size of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models generated by feed-forward reconstruction networks without requiring retraining or optimization. Unlike optimization-based compression methods that iteratively refine Gaussian parameters to minimize a loss function, FCGS applies a learned entropy model directly to the existing Gaussian attributes, enabling zero-shot generalization to scenes where ground-truth geometry is unavailable. It sets itself apart by handling the irregular data structures of feed-forward outputs (e.g., from LGM or MVSplat) where traditional mesh-based or optimization-based codecs fail due to the lack of a consistent reference. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained 3DGS model (set of Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients) generated by a feed-forward model (e.g., LGM, MVSplat). Output: A compressed bitstream representing the Gaussian attributes, achieving significant size reduction. Data Structures: The 3DGS model consists of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R} Color coefficients \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics) Method Steps: 1. Attribute Extraction: Extract all Gaussian attributes from the feed-forward model. For feed-forward models like LGM, generate multi-view inputs (e.g., 4 views from 1 initial view using [Wang & Shi, 2023]) to create the 3DGS. 2. Masking for Feed-Forward Models: When compressing 3DGS from feed-forward models, set the mask m for color attributes to all 0s. This indicates that color attributes are not compressed using the standard entropy model but are handled differently (likely discarded or approximated, as ground truth is unavailable for optimization). 3. Entropy Model Application: Apply the Memory-Efficient Memory (MEM) module and context models to compress the remaining attributes (position, rotation, scale, opacity). The MEM module adaptively selects high-tolerance color attributes for compression, but for feed-forward models, this step is bypassed for color due to the mask. 4. Bitstream Generation: Encode the quantized and context-predicted attributes into a bitstream using an entropy coder (e.g., arithmetic coding). Parameters: Mask m: For feed-forward 3DGS, m = 0 for all color attributes. Compression Ratio: Achieves 15x compression for MVSplat-generated 3DGS and 5x for LGM-generated 3DGS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Ground Truth: For feed-forward models, ground-truth geometry is unavailable, so fidelity is evaluated by comparing rendered images before and after compression. Zero-Shot Generalization: The method must generalize without retraining, requiring robust entropy models that do not overfit to specific scene distributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressfeedforward3dgs(gaussians, modeltype): """ Compress 3DGS from feed-forward models without retraining. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes (pos, rot, scale, opacity, color). modeltype: String, 'LGM' or 'MVSplat'. Returns: bitstream: Compressed data. """ # Step 1: Extract attributes positions = [g.pos for g in gaussians] rotations = [g.rot for g in gaussians] scales = [g.scale for g in gaussians] opacities = [g.opacity for g in gaussians] colors = [g.color for g in gaussians] # Step 2: Set mask for color attributes to 0 for feed-forward models # This disables standard color compression for feed-forward outputs colormask = [0] len(gaussians) # Step 3: Apply entropy model to non-color attributes # MEM module adaptively selects attributes, but color is masked out quantizedpositions = quantize(positions) quantizedrotations = quantize(rotations) quantizedscales = quantize(scales) quantizedopacities = quantize(opacities) # Context modeling and entropy coding # Note: Specific context model details are not provided in sources bitstreampos = entropyencode(quantizedpositions) bitstreamrot = entropyencode(quantizedrotations) bitstreamscale = entropyencode(quantizedscales) bitstreamopacity = entropyencode(quantizedopacities) # Color attributes are not compressed in the standard way for feed-forward models # They are either discarded or handled via the mask bitstreamcolor = None # Combine bitstreams bitstream = combine(bitstreampos, bitstreamrot, bitstreamscale, bitstreamopacity) return bitstream FeCoSplat is a two-stage feature compression framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that decouples compression into multi-view feature coding and reconstruction-conditioned feedback coding. It allows the receiver to decode directly in the compact feature-state domain without reconstructing intermediate Gaussians, thereby avoiding the heavy computational overhead of image compression and the irregularity challenges of explicit Gaussian compression. Unlike CodecSplat which uses a single coding stage, FeCoSplat uses rendered reconstruction feedback to guide a second-stage refinement, maintaining an implicit Gaussian state for lightweight receiver-side decoding. Compression Ratios: Achieves 15x compression for MVSplat-generated 3DGS and 5x for LGM-generated 3DGS. Performance: Excellent rate-distortion (RD) performance despite the lack of optimization. Hardware/Resolution: Evaluated on 10 scenes from ACID and 50 scenes from Gobjaverse. Strengths: Zero-shot generalization, no retraining required, handles feed-forward models with no ground truth. Limitations: Color attributes are not compressed effectively for feed-forward models (mask set to 0), potentially affecting visual fidelity. FCGS was introduced in "Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression" (2024). It addresses the need for efficient compression of 3DGS models generated by feed-forward networks, which are increasingly popular for rapid 3D reconstruction. Traditional compression methods rely on optimization-based 3DGS, which are not directly applicable to feed-forward outputs due to the lack of ground truth and the irregular nature of the generated Gaussians. name: FeCoSplat
head: Feedback-Guided Compression for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: FeCoSplat is a two-stage feature compression framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that decouples compression into multi-view feature coding and reconstruction-conditioned feedback coding. It allows the receiver to decode directly in the compact feature-state domain without reconstructing intermediate Gaussians, thereby avoiding the heavy computational overhead of image compression and the irregularity challenges of explicit Gaussian compression. Unlike CodecSplat which uses a single coding stage, FeCoSplat uses rendered reconstruction feedback to guide a second-stage refinement, maintaining an implicit Gaussian state for lightweight receiver-side decoding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N posed images I = \{Ii\}{i=1}^N and their camera poses P = \{Pi\}{i=1}^N. Outputs: Three bitstreams: B1 (first-stage features), B2 (second-stage feedback features), and B{cam} (lossless camera parameters). Data Structures: Multi-view Features (F1, F2): Tensors of shape \mathbb{R}^{N \times C \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}}, where N is the number of views, C is channels, and H, W are input image dimensions. Implicit Gaussian State (S): Learnable tensor. Initial state S0 \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times C \times 1 \times 1}, broadcast to match spatial/view dimensions of F during concatenation. Latents (y, \hat{y}): Compact latent representations resulting from the transformation of features and state. Hyper-latents (\hat{z}): Side information for entropy modeling. Modules: E{mv} (Multi-view Feature Extractor): Consists of a monocular transformer, multi-view transformer, and cross-view U-Net. E{fb} (Feedback Feature Extractor): Applies PixelUnshuffle and extracts low-resolution features from concatenated original and rendered images. ga (Analysis Transform): Transforms concatenated features and state into compact latents. gs (Synthesis Transform): Transforms decoded latents back to feature space. U (State Update Module): Updates the implicit Gaussian state using decoded latents. P (Gaussian Predictor): Maps the implicit state to explicit 3D Gaussian primitives. \phi (Modulation Network): Predicts AdaLN parameters from the rate-distortion trade-off parameter \lambda. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Multi-view Feature Coding 1. Extract multi-view features F1 from input images I and poses P using E{mv}: F1 = E{mv}(I, P) 2. Concatenate F1 with the initial implicit Gaussian state S0 (broadcasted to match F1's dimensions) and transform into compact latent y1: y1 = ga(\text{concat}(F1, S0)) 3. Quantization: During training, perturb y1 with additive uniform noise to approximate quantization, yielding \hat{y}1. During inference, replace noise with a Round operation. 4. Entropy Modeling: Model the hyper-latent \hat{z}1 with a factorized prior. Use a quadtree entropy model to predict Gaussian distribution parameters over \hat{y}1 conditioned on \hat{z}1. Calculate the rate: R1 = R(\hat{y}1) + R(\hat{z}1) 5. Encode quantized latents into the first-stage bitstream B1. At the receiver, recover \hat{y}1 by entropy decoding B1. 6. State Update: Transform \hat{y}1 via synthesis transform gs and incorporate into S0 using state update module U: S1 = U(\text{concat}(S0, gs(\hat{y}1))) 7. Intermediate Gaussian Prediction: Predict intermediate Gaussians G1 from S1 using Gaussian predictor P: G1 = P(S1) P operates on a low-resolution 2D feature grid. It predicts per-view depth maps from S1, back-projects features to 3D, uses KNN attention for geometry-aware aggregation, estimates attributes, and rearranges via PixelShuffle to produce pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians at half input resolution (one Gaussian per 2 \times 2 region). 2. Stage 2: Feedback-Guided Feature Coding 1. Feedback Generation (Sender Only): Render G1 back to input viewpoints using camera parameters P to get rendered observations \hat{I}1: \hat{I}1 = \text{Render}(G1, P) 2. Extract feedback features F2 using E{fb} by concatenating original images I and rendered observations \hat{I}1: F2 = E{fb}(\text{concat}(I, \hat{I}1)) E{fb} applies PixelUnshuffle and extracts low-resolution features. 3. Transform F2 and current state S1 into latent y2: y2 = ga(\text{concat}(F2, S1)) 4. Quantization and Entropy Modeling: Quantize and model y2 and hyper-latent \hat{z}2 using the same scheme as Stage 1 to obtain rate R2. Encode into second-stage bitstream B2. 5. Receiver Decoding: Decode \hat{y}2 from B2. Integrate into S1 using shared state update module U: S2 = U(\text{concat}(S1, gs(\hat{y}2))) 6. Final Gaussian Prediction: Predict final Gaussians G2 from S2 using shared Gaussian predictor P: G2 = P(S2) 3. Variable-Rate Coding Condition each 2D block on the rate-distortion trade-off parameter \lambda using Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN). Predict modulation parameters \gamma and \beta from \lambda using lightweight network \phi: (\gamma, \beta) = \phi(\log \lambda) Modulate normalized feature X: \text{AdaLN}(X, \lambda) = \gamma \odot \text{LN}(X) + \beta \lambda is sampled from a log-uniform distribution during training: [10^{-5}, 10^{-2}] for RealEstate10K and [10^{-5}, 10^{-3}] for DL3DV. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class FeCoSplat: def init(self, numviews, channels, height, width): self.numviews = numviews self.channels = channels self.height = height self.width = width # Modules self.Emv = MultiViewFeatureExtractor() # Monocular + Multi-view Transformer + Cross-view U-Net self.Efb = FeedbackFeatureExtractor() # PixelUnshuffle + Feature Extraction self.ga = AnalysisTransform() # Transforms concat(F, S) -> y self.gs = SynthesisTransform() # Transforms y -> feature space self.U = StateUpdateModule() # Updates S self.P = GaussianPredictor() # Maps S -> G self.phi = ModulationNetwork() # lambda -> (gamma, beta) # Initial implicit Gaussian state self.S0 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, channels, 1, 1)) # Loss weight self.betalpipss = 0.05 def stage1encode(self, I, P, lambdaval): # 1. Extract features F1 = self.Emv(I, P) # Shape: [N, C, H/4, W/4] # 2. Transform to latent S0broadcast = self.S0.expandas(F1) y1 = self.ga(torch.cat([F1, S0broadcast], dim=1)) # 3. Quantization (Training: noise, Inference: Round) if self.training: y1noisy = y1 + torch.randlike(y1) (1/255.0) # Approximation y1quant = y1noisy else: y1quant = torch.round(y1) # 4. Entropy Coding (Simplified representation) # In practice, this involves quadtree entropy model and hyperprior # Returns bitstream B1 and rate R1 B1, R1 = self.entropyencode(y1quant) # 5. Decode for State Update (Receiver side would just decode B1) y1decoded = y1quant # During training, use quantized value; Inference, decode from B1 # 6. Update State y1synthesized = self.gs(y1decoded) S1 = self.U(torch.cat([self.S0.expandas(y1synthesized), y1synthesized], dim=1)) # 7. Predict Intermediate Gaussians G1 = self.P(S1) return G1, S1, B1, R1 def stage2encode(self, I, P, G1, S1, lambdaval): # 1. Render Feedback (Sender Only) Ihat1 = self.render(G1, P) # 2. Extract Feedback Features F2 = self.Efb(torch.cat([I, Ihat1], dim=1)) # Shape: [N, C, H/4, W/4] # 3. Transform to Latent y2 = self.ga(torch.cat([F2, S1], dim=1)) # 4. Quantization if self.training: y2noisy = y2 + torch.randlike(y2) (1/255.0) y2quant = y2noisy else: y2quant = torch.round(y2) # 5. Entropy Coding B2, R2 = self.entropyencode(y2quant) # 6. Decode for State Update y2decoded = y2quant # 7. Update State y2synthesized = self.gs(y2decoded) S2 = self.U(torch.cat(, dim=1)) # 8. Predict Final Gaussians G2 = self.P(S2) return G2, S2, B2, R2 def decode(self, B1, B2, P): # Receiver Side: No rendering or feedback extraction needed # 1. Decode Stage 1 y1decoded = self.entropydecode(B1) y1synthesized = self.gs(y1decoded) S1 = self.U(torch.cat([self.S0.expandas(y1synthesized), y1synthesized], dim=1)) # 2. Decode Stage 2 y2decoded = self.entropydecode(B2) y2synthesized = self.gs(y2decoded) S2 = self.U(torch.cat(, dim=1)) # 3. Predict Final Gaussians G2 = self.P(S2) return G2 def render(self, G, P): # Differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians G with poses P pass def computeloss(self, Itgt, G, lambdaval): # Variable-rate loss #... (Implementation details of AdaLN modulation in forward pass) # Rendering Loss Ihat = self.render(G, Ptgt) lossmse = torch.mean((Itgt - Ihat) 2) losslpips = self.lpipsloss(Itgt, Ihat) totalloss = lossmse + self.betalpipss losslpips return totalloss Parameters: \beta (LPIPS weight): 0.05. \lambda (Rate-distortion trade-off): Sampled from log-uniform distribution. RealEstate10K: [10^{-5}, 10^{-2}]. DL3DV: [10^{-5}, 10^{-3}]. Receiver Parameters: 3.45M. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Receiver Efficiency: The receiver does not need to reconstruct G1 or render \hat{I}1. Decoding is causal and efficient, relying only on bitstreams B1, B2 and B{cam}. Precision: Quantization-aware training uses additive uniform noise to approximate quantization. During inference, this is replaced by Round. Resolution: The Gaussian predictor produces Gaussians at half the input resolution (one Gaussian per 2 \times 2 region). Time Complexity: Sender-side computation is heavy, involving multi-view feature extraction, two-stage coding, and intermediate rendering. Receiver-side complexity is low, requiring only progressive state updates and a final lightweight conversion. Memory Complexity: Peak GPU memory (Sender): 1.316 GiB. Peak GPU memory (Receiver): Not explicitly listed, but implied to be low given the 0.117s latency and 3.45M parameters. Performance: Receiver latency: 0.117s. FeCoSplat achieves favorable rate-distortion performance, particularly at low bitrates, compared to baselines like CodecSplat (Sender: 181.73s, Receiver: 0.189s, Sender Mem: 2.065 GiB). Strengths: Balances rate-distortion performance and receiver-side complexity. Avoids challenges of heterogeneous attributes and irregular spatial organization found in explicit Gaussian compression. Avoids execution of the entire feed-forward 3DGS pipeline at the receiver, preventing compression distortion propagation. Limitations: Sender-side computation is significant due to intermediate rendering and two-stage coding. When to Use: Compression of feed-forward 3DGS representations (e.g., from MVSplat, LGM) where low receiver-side complexity and good low-bitrate performance are required. When Not to Use: When sender-side computational resources are severely constrained, or when real-time bidirectional interaction requiring immediate intermediate state access is needed (though FeCoSplat is designed for one-way transmission). FeCoSplat was proposed to address the limitations of existing feed-forward 3DGS compression methods. Image compression incurs high receiver-side computation and error propagation, while Gaussian compression is challenged by heterogeneous attributes and irregular primitives. Feature compression, as seen in CodecSplat, offers a middle ground but lacks reconstruction-aware refinement. FeCoSplat introduces a feedback-guided two-stage coding strategy to improve rate-distortion performance, particularly at low bitrates, while maintaining a lightweight receiver. The method builds on Feed-Forward 3DGS Compression by applying FCGS to compress 3DGS generated by feed-forward models without retraining.
