name: Hybrid Compression Framework
head: Adaptive Voxelization and GPCC Compression for 3DGS
body: The Hybrid Compression Framework is a post-training compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces model size and bandwidth by combining adaptive voxelization with Generalized Prediction Context Coding (GPCC). It addresses the impracticality of generative compression, which requires retraining distinct models for each bitrate, and the quality degradation of standard post-training methods due to parameter distortion. By quantizing mean positions to voxel centers and fine-tuning remaining attributes, it achieves higher quality at lower bitrates compared to sibling methods like Mini-Splatting-C. Inputs: Pre-trained 3DGS model G = \{\mui, \Sigmai, Ci, \alphai\}{i=1}^N, where \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 are means, \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} are covariances, Ci are spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and \alphai \in [0,1] are opacities. Training images \{\tilde{I}i\}{i=1}^k and camera views \{\tilde{\theta}i\}{i=1}^k. Outputs: Compressed bitstream containing GPCC-coded positions, covariances, SH coefficients, and opacities. Data Structures: 1. Voxelized Model \tilde{G}: A set of M Gaussians (M < N). \hat{\mu}i: Quantized mean position (voxel center). \tilde{\Sigma}i: Fine-tuned covariance. \tilde{C}i: Fine-tuned SH coefficients. \tilde{\alpha}i: Fine-tuned opacity. 2. GPCC Context: Octree structure for position coding; transform coding context for attributes. Parameters: Q{dc}: Quantization parameter for low-frequency SH coefficients (DC/base color). Set relatively small. Q{ac}: Quantization parameter for high-frequency SH coefficients (AC). Set relatively large compared to Q{dc}. Q{op}: Quantization parameter for opacity. Set relatively small compared to Q{ac}. J: Number of octree partitioning levels (resolution). Steps: 1. Adaptive Voxelization: Define the bounding box of the Gaussian volume. Partition the space into an octree. At each level, occupied voxels are subdivided up to level J. Quantize each Gaussian mean \mui to the center of its containing voxel \hat{\mu}i. Merge Gaussians falling into the same voxel. Let the unique voxel centers be \{\hat{\mu}i\}{i=1}^M. 2. Attribute Initialization: For each unique voxel center \hat{\mu}i, initialize the remaining attributes \Sigmai, Ci, \alphai by averaging the attributes of all original Gaussians mapped to that voxel. 3. Fine-Tuning: Keep the quantized mean positions \{\hat{\mu}i\}{i=1}^M fixed. Optimize the remaining attributes \{\tilde{\Sigma}i, \tilde{C}i, \tilde{\alpha}i\}{i=1}^M by minimizing the training loss L{train} until the rendering quality matches the input model G. The training loss is defined as: L{train} = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^k \frac{1}{2} \| R{\tilde{\theta}i}(\tilde{G}) - \tilde{I}i \|F where R{\theta} is the rendering function for view \theta, and \| \cdot \|F is the Frobenius norm. 4. Compression: Positions: Losslessly compress the voxelized positions \{\hat{\mu}i\}{i=1}^M using GPCC (octree coding + entropy coder). Covariances: Compress \{\tilde{\Sigma}i\}{i=1}^M using vector quantization. SH and Opacity: Compress \{\tilde{C}i, \tilde{\alpha}i\}{i=1}^M using transform coding with quantization parameters Q{dc}, Q{ac}, Q{op} via GPCC. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridcompression(3DGSmodel, trainingdata, Qdc, Qac, Qop, octreelevels): # 1. Adaptive Voxelization # Determine bounding box and build octree up to octreelevels voxelcenters = {} for gaussian in 3DGSmodel: voxelid = getvoxelid(gaussian.mean, octreelevels) if voxelid not in voxelcenters: voxelcenters[voxelid] = [] voxelcenters[voxelid].append(gaussian) voxelizedgaussians = [] for voxelid, gaussiansinvoxel in voxelcenters.items(): # Quantize mean to voxel center mean = getvoxelcenter(voxelid) # Initialize attributes by averaging cov = averagecovariances([g.cov for g in gaussiansinvoxel]) shcoeffs = averagesh([g.sh for g in gaussiansinvoxel]) opacity = averageopacities([g.alpha for g in gaussiansinvoxel]) voxelizedgaussians.append({ 'mean': mean, 'cov': cov, 'sh': shcoeffs, 'alpha': opacity }) # 2. Fine-Tuning # Fix means, optimize other attributes for gaussian in voxelizedgaussians: gaussian.mean = gaussian.mean # Fixed # Minimize Ltrain using gradient descent on attributes # Ltrain = (1/k) sum(0.5 ||Rtheta(G) - I||F^2) voxelizedgaussians = finetuneattributes(voxelizedgaussians, trainingdata) # 3. Compression # Compress positions with GPCC posbitstream = gpccencodepositions([g['mean'] for g in voxelizedgaussians]) # Compress covariances with vector quantization covbitstream = vectorquantizecovariances([g['cov'] for g in voxelizedgaussians]) # Compress SH and opacity with GPCC transform coding shbitstream = gpccencodetransform([g['sh'] for g in voxelizedgaussians], Qdc, Qac) alphabitstream = gpccencodetransform([g['alpha'] for g in voxelizedgaussians], Qop) return posbitstream + covbitstream + shbitstream + alphabitstream Time Complexity: Requires a fine-tuning phase after voxelization, which incurs retraining costs proportional to the number of voxels and training iterations. Memory/Bandwidth: Significantly reduces model size compared to the original 3DGS by merging Gaussians and compressing attributes. Quality: Achieves higher quality at equivalent bitrates compared to standard post-training PCC methods by mitigating distortion through fine-tuning. Strengths: No need to retrain the entire model from scratch for different bitrates (unlike generative compression). Limitations: The fine-tuning step adds computational overhead during compression. The method was proposed in "Adaptive Voxelization for Transform Coding of 3D Gaussian Splatting Data" (2025). It builds on the observation that 3DGS data can be viewed as a 3D point cloud (3DPC). Previous post-training methods relied on point cloud compression (PCC) but suffered from quality loss due to parameter distortion. Generative compression methods, while efficient, require retraining for each rate-distortion point, making them impractical for multi-rate applications. This framework combines adaptive voxelization with GPCC to balance compression efficiency and rendering quality. name: Prune2TargetSize
head: Top-down pruning and recovery
body: Prune2TargetSize is an algorithm designed to reduce a pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model to a precise target number of splats while maintaining visual quality. It solves the problem of unpredictable model size in standard 3DGS training, where hyperparameters like cloning thresholds and densification intervals interact in complex, scene-dependent ways, making it impossible to guarantee a specific final splat count. Unlike bottom-up approaches that grow splats to a target, this method uses a top-down strategy of iterative pruning and recovery, which has been found to perform better in practice. Inputs: G: A pretrained 3DGS model. d: The target number of splats for the output layer. r: The maximum pruning ratio per iteration (hyperparameter). I: Training view images. P: Camera poses associated with images I. Outputs: GL: A list of d splats, sorted in descending order of global significance score. Data Structures: The 3DGS model G consists of a set of splats Gi. Each splat typically includes position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients, though the internal layout is inherited from the base 3DGS implementation [15] cited in. Global significance score S: A scalar value for each splat, computed by CalGS. The exact formula for CalGS is not provided in the source text, but it references external work [10] for the calculation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize G^ \leftarrow G. 2. Compute current splat count n = \text{NumOfGS}(G^). 3. While n > d: a. Compute global significance scores S for all splats in G^ using I and P via CalGS. b. If n \times (1 - r) > d: i. Prune the bottom r fraction of splats (those with the lowest S) from G^. ii. Run Recovery training on the pruned G^ with IsRefinementIteration=True. This allows cloning, splitting, and pruning. iii. Update n = \text{NumOfGS}(G^). c. Else (if n \times (1 - r) \le d): i. Prune G^ to remove exactly n - d splats (lowest S). ii. Run Finetune training on G^ with IsRefinementIteration=False. This disables cloning, splitting, and pruning. iii. Update n = \text{NumOfGS}(G^). 4. Compute final global significance scores S for the pruned model G^. 5. Sort splats in G^ in descending order of S to produce GL. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Prune2TargetSize(Gpretrained, targetsized, maxpruningratior, imagesI, posesP): """ Reduces a pretrained 3DGS model to a precise target number of splats. Args: Gpretrained: Pretrained 3DGS model. targetsized: Target number of splats. maxpruningratior: Max fraction of splats to prune in one step. imagesI: List of training images. posesP: List of camera poses. Returns: GL: List of splats sorted by significance. """ # Initialize Gstar = Gpretrained n = countsplats(Gstar) while n > targetsized: # Compute global significance scores # Note: CalGS implementation details are in external reference [10] scores = CalGS(Gstar, imagesI, posesP) # Determine pruning strategy if n (1 - maxpruningratior) > targetsized: # Prune a fraction r numtoprune = int(n maxpruningratior) # Identify indices of splats with lowest scores sortedindices = argsortasc(scores) pruneindices = sortedindices[:numtoprune] # Prune splats Gstar = removesplats(Gstar, pruneindices) # Recovery training: allows cloning, splitting, pruning Gstar = RecoveryTraining(Gstar, imagesI, posesP, isrefinement=True) # Update count n = countsplats(Gstar) else: # Prune to exact target numtoprune = n - targetsized sortedindices = argsortasc(scores) pruneindices = sortedindices[:numtoprune] # Prune splats Gstar = removesplats(Gstar, pruneindices) # Finetune training: disables cloning, splitting, pruning Gstar = FinetuneTraining(Gstar, imagesI, posesP, isrefinement=False) # Update count n = countsplats(Gstar) # Final sorting finalscores = CalGS(Gstar, imagesI, posesP) sortedindices = argsortdesc(finalscores) GL = [Gstar[i] for i in sortedindices] return GL Parameters: r: Max pruning ratio. Typical values are not specified in the sources. d: Target number of splats. Scene-dependent. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard 3DGS hyperparameters (e.g., \taup for cloning/splitting, densification interval) do not allow precise control over the total splat count because their interactions are complex and scene-dependent. The mapping between hyperparameter settings and total splat count is unclear and can change across different 3D scenes. The algorithm assumes CalGS can compute a consistent global significance score for all splats. A sibling compression method. A sibling compression method. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The iterative nature (prune then recover) implies multiple training passes, which is computationally expensive compared to single-pass pruning. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides precise control over the final model size (number of splats). The top-down approach (prune then grow) is preferred over bottom-up approaches because it worked better in practice. Limitations: Requires a pretrained model as a starting point. The iterative process may be slow due to repeated training steps. When to use: When hardware deployment requires a strict upper bound on model size or bandwidth, and visual quality must be preserved as much as possible. When not to use: When computational resources for iterative training are limited, or when an approximate size is acceptable. Prune2TargetSize was introduced in the paper "L3GS: Layered 3D Gaussian Splats for Efficient 3D Scene Delivery" published at ACM MOBICOM ’25 in November 2025. It is part of the L3GS pipeline, which aims to create layered 3DGS models for efficient scene delivery. The method addresses the lack of precise control over model size in standard 3DGS training. name: SUNDAE
head: Spectrally Pruned Gaussian Fields with Neural Compensation
body: SUNDAE is a graph-based compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces computational load by pruning redundant Gaussians while preserving key scene details. It distinguishes itself from direct splatting by shifting to feature splatting, utilizing a neural compensation head to interpolate features and recover fine details lost during pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} with attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients, color). Output: A pruned subset of Gaussians and a neural network model for feature reconstruction. Data Structures: Gaussian Graph: Nodes represent Gaussians. Edges represent spatial relationships or proximity between Gaussians. Neural Compensation Head: A lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN). Steps: 1. Graph Construction: Construct a graph where nodes are the 3D Gaussians. Edges are established to capture spatial relationships between Gaussians. 2. Spectral Pruning: Apply a band-limited graph filter to the constructed graph. This filter selectively down-samples (prunes) the Gaussians, removing redundant ones while attempting to preserve key scene details. 3. Feature Splatting Setup: Instead of rendering directly from the pruned Gaussians' full attributes, the method shifts to feature splatting. 4. Neural Compensation: Employ a lightweight neural network-based feature interpolation head (CNN) to recover fine details that were potentially lost during the pruning process. This compensates for the information loss from down-sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with position, covariance, opacity, SH, color. Returns: prunedgaussians: Subset of input Gaussians. neuralhead: Trained CNN for feature interpolation. """ # Step 1: Construct graph based on spatial relationships # graph = buildgraph(gaussians) # Step 2: Apply band-limited graph filter to prune # prunedgaussians = applybandlimitedgraphfilter(graph, gaussians) # Step 3: Train neural compensation head # # The head interpolates features to recover lost details. # Training likely involves minimizing reconstruction error between # original rendering and pruned+compensated rendering. neuralhead = traincnnhead(prunedgaussians, gaussians) return prunedgaussians, neuralhead def buildgraph(gaussians): """ Construct a graph where nodes are Gaussians and edges represent spatial relationships. """ # Implementation detail not provided in sources. # Typically involves k-NN or distance-based thresholding. pass def applybandlimitedgraphfilter(graph, gaussians): """ Apply a band-limited graph filter to select a subset of Gaussians. """ # Implementation detail not provided in sources. pass def traincnnhead(prunedgaussians, originalgaussians): """ Train a lightweight CNN to interpolate features and recover fine details. """ # Implementation detail not provided in sources. pass Parameters: Band-limited graph filter cutoff: Not given in the sources. Neural network architecture: Lightweight CNN. Specific layers or dimensions are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Information Loss: Pruning may remove critical details; the neural compensation head is designed to counteract this. Graph Construction: The method relies on capturing spatial relationships; the specific metric for edge creation is not defined in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory usage by pruning Gaussians and using a lightweight neural network for compensation. Performance: The method aims to balance efficient Gaussian placement with the preservation of visual quality. Strengths: Preserves key scene details while reducing redundancy; shifts to feature splatting for potentially more efficient representation. Limitations: Requires training and storing a neural network for compensation. When to use: When hardware-oriented deployment requires reduced computational complexity and memory usage for 3DGS. When not to use: When real-time inference without neural network overhead is required. SUNDAE (Spectrally Pruned Gaussian Fields with Neural Compensation) is a graph-based compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was introduced to push contextual modeling in 3DGS to a finer granularity. The method is cited as reference [39] in and [54] in. name: Fast Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting (FCGS)
head: Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression
body: FCGS is an optimization-free, feed-forward compression pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that compresses representations in a single pass without per-scene finetuning, aiming to reduce compression time from minutes to seconds while maintaining fidelity. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Model Compression Pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting and 3DGS Model Compression Pipeline by eliminating the need for iterative per-scene optimization, which typically takes 10–28 minutes, by using an autoencoder-based structure with a Multi-path Entropy Module (MEM) to balance compression size and fidelity. Inputs and outputs: Input: A trained 3DGS representation consisting of unstructured Gaussian blobs with attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color, spherical harmonics coefficients). Output: A compressed bitstream representing the latent space of the Gaussian attributes. Data structures: The method treats Gaussian attributes as a set of unstructured blobs. The core data structure is the latent vector \mathbf{z} derived from the analysis transform. Attributes \mathbf{x}: The raw Gaussian parameters. Latent \mathbf{y}: The output of the analysis transform ga(\mathbf{x}). Hyperprior \mathbf{z}: The output of the hyperanalysis transform, used to model the entropy of \mathbf{y}. Quantized Latent \hat{\mathbf{y}}: The discretized latent representation. Method steps: 1. Analysis Transform: Map input Gaussian attributes \mathbf{x} into a latent space \mathbf{y} using an analysis transform network ga. This step is inspired by image compression autoencoders. 2. Multi-path Entropy Module (MEM): Determine the processing path for each attribute group based on sensitivity. If an attribute is geometry-sensitive (e.g., position, scale, rotation), it bypasses the autoencoder and is directly quantized: \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}. If an attribute is color-sensitive (e.g., SH coefficients, opacity), it passes through the autoencoder: \mathbf{y} = ga(\mathbf{x}). This prevents model collapse caused by geometry deviations that would break rasterization. 3. Quantization: Quantize the latent variables \mathbf{y} to obtain \hat{\mathbf{y}}. 4. Context Modeling: Eliminate redundancies among parameters using customized context models: Inter-Gaussian Context: Models dependencies between different Gaussians. Intra-Gaussian Context: Models dependencies within the parameters of a single Gaussian. These context models are lightweight and efficient. 5. Hyperprior Encoding: Encode the quantized latent \hat{\mathbf{y}} into a hyperprior \mathbf{z} using a hyperanalysis transform to estimate the probability distribution for entropy coding. 6. Entropy Coding: Encode the residuals and hyperprior using the estimated probabilities to produce the final bitstream. 7. Decoding (Reverse): Decode the bitstream to recover \hat{\mathbf{y}} and \hat{\mathbf{z}}. Use the hyperprior \hat{\mathbf{z}} to predict the distribution of \hat{\mathbf{y}}. Apply the synthesis transform gs (if applicable for color attributes) to reconstruct the attributes. Directly use the quantized geometry attributes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fcgcompress(gaussians): """ Compress 3DGS using FCGS. gaussians: dict or object containing attributes: pos: (N, 3) scale: (N, 3) rot: (N, 4) opacity: (N, 1) shcoeffs: (N, K, 3) """ # Step 1 & 2: Analysis and MEM Path Selection # Geometry attributes are directly quantized to preserve rasterization integrity posq = quantize(gaussians.pos) scaleq = quantize(gaussians.scale) rotq = quantize(gaussians.rot) # Color attributes pass through the autoencoder # y = ga(x) for color attributes colorlatent = analysistransform(gaussians.opacity, gaussians.shcoeffs) colorlatentq = quantize(colorlatent) # Step 3 & 4: Context Modeling # Inter- and intra-Gaussian context models are applied to predict probabilities # This step is implicit in the entropy coding process using the context models # hinter and hintra are used to condition the probability distribution # Step 5: Hyperprior hyperprior = hyperanalysistransform(colorlatentq) hyperpriorq = quantize(hyperprior) # Step 6: Entropy Coding # Encode quantized values using the context models and hyperprior bitstream = entropyencode( pos=posq, scale=scaleq, rot=rotq, colorlatent=colorlatentq, hyperprior=hyperpriorq, contextmodels=getcontextmodels() # Inter and Intra) return bitstream def fcgdecompress(bitstream): """ Decompress 3DGS using FCGS. """ # Step 6 (Reverse): Entropy Decoding posq, scaleq, rotq, colorlatentq, hyperpriorq = entropydecode( bitstream, contextmodels=getcontextmodels()) # Step 2 (Reverse): MEM Path Reversal # Geometry attributes are directly used pos = dequantize(posq) scale = dequantize(scaleq) rot = dequantize(rotq) # Color attributes pass through synthesis transform # x = gs(y) for color attributes opacity, shcoeffs = synthesistransform(colorlatentq, hyperpriorq) return { 'pos': pos, 'scale': scale, 'rot': rot, 'opacity': opacity, 'shcoeffs': shcoeffs } Parameters: Compression Ratio: Over 20×. Compression Time: Seconds (compared to 10-28 minutes for optimization-based methods). Edge cases and pitfalls: Geometry Sensitivity: Directly quantizing geometry attributes is critical; processing them through the autoencoder leads to model collapse because rasterization fails due to deviations. Color Attributes: Allowing all color attributes to be processed by the autoencoder without fixing geometry can lead to densification issues and suboptimal fidelity. A technique to boost compression performance by applying FCGS to 3DGS that have been pruned using techniques like Trimming or Mini-Splatting. When combined with pruning (e.g., Mini+Ours on Deep Blending dataset), FCGS achieves a compression ratio of 100× over vanilla 3DGS. The size of compressed 3DGS using FCGS (at the highest rate) is only 40% that of MSC (Model Compression Pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting) with the same fidelity. Time Complexity: O(1) per scene in terms of optimization iterations, as it is a single feed-forward pass. Compression time is reduced from minutes to seconds. Memory Complexity: Depends on the autoencoder and context model sizes, but described as lightweight and efficient. Measured Performance: Achieves a compression ratio of over 20× while maintaining fidelity, surpassing most SOTA per-scene optimization-based methods. When combined with pruning, it achieves 100× compression ratio. Strengths: Fast, optimization-free, high compression ratio, compatible with pruning techniques. Limitations: May have lower fidelity than optimization-based methods if not carefully tuned, though it surpasses most SOTA methods. When to use: When rapid compression is required, or when per-scene optimization is computationally prohibitive. When not to use: When maximum possible fidelity is required and optimization time is not a constraint. FCGS was introduced in 2024 by Yihang Chen et al. as a solution to the storage challenges posed by the vast number of Gaussians in 3DGS. It is inspired by image compression methods, specifically autoencoder-based structures like those proposed by Ballé et al. (2018). The method addresses the limitation of previous compression techniques that required per-scene optimization, making them sluggish and slow. name: C3DGS
head: Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: C3DGS is a compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces storage requirements by applying residual vector quantization (R-VQ) to geometric attributes, specifically scaling and rotation. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Mini-Splatting by focusing on attribute quantization rather than count reduction via sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained set of N 3D Gaussians with full-precision attributes: position \mathbf{p}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{lm}. Output: A compressed representation using codebooks and residuals, achieving a scene size of 48.8 MB on the MipNeRF360 dataset. Data Structures: 1. Codebook: A finite set of representative vectors for scaling and rotation. 2. Indices: Quantized indices pointing to entries in the codebook. 3. Residuals: Small correction values stored for each Gaussian to recover precision. Method Steps: 1. Attribute Selection: Identify geometric attributes for quantization: scaling \mathbf{s} and rotation \mathbf{R}. 2. Residual Vector Quantization (R-VQ): Cluster the geometric attributes into a codebook using R-VQ. For each Gaussian, find the nearest codebook entry. Compute the residual between the original attribute and the codebook entry. Store the codebook index and the residual. 3. Non-Quantized Attributes: Position \mathbf{p} and opacity \alpha are not quantized. Sharing these attributes across Gaussians would result in overlapping Gaussians, which degrades quality. 4. Reconstruction: During rendering, retrieve the codebook entry and add the residual to reconstruct the full-precision attribute. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressc3dgs(gaussians): # gaussians: list of objects with attributes p, R, s, alpha, clm codebooks = buildcodebook([g.s for g in gaussians], method='R-VQ') codebookR = buildcodebook([g.R for g in gaussians], method='R-VQ') compressedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Find nearest codebook entry idxs = findnearest(codebooks, g.s) idxR = findnearest(codebookR, g.R) # Compute residuals ress = g.s - codebooks[idxs] resR = g.R - codebookR[idxR] # Store compressed data compressedgaussians.append({ 'p': g.p, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'clm': g.clm, 'idxs': idxs, 'idxR': idxR, 'ress': ress, 'resR': resR }) return compressedgaussians, codebooks, codebookR def decompressc3dgs(compressedgaussians, codebooks, codebookR): gaussians = [] for cg in compressedgaussians: s = codebooks[cg['idxs']] + cg['ress'] R = codebookR[cg['idxR']] + cg['resR'] gaussians.append({ 'p': cg['p'], 'R': R, 's': s, 'alpha': cg['alpha'], 'clm': cg['clm'] }) return gaussians Parameters: Codebook size: Not given in the sources. Residual precision: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Overlapping Gaussians: Avoid quantizing position and opacity to prevent this. Size: 48.8 MB on MipNeRF360. Quality: SSIM 0.798, PSNR 27.08, LPIPS 0.247 on MipNeRF360. Comparison: Outperforms 3DGS (750 MB) and Compact3D (not given) in size, while maintaining competitive quality. C3DGS was introduced in [54] (cited as). It builds on the principle of vector quantization in signal processing. name: CompGS
head: Efficient 3D Scene Representation via Compressed Gaussian Splatting
body: CompGS is a compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces representation size by introducing a hybrid primitive structure consisting of anchor and coupled primitives. It differs from sibling methods like Mini-Splatting and C3DGS by explicitly modeling the dependency between primitives to predict coupled attributes from anchors, rather than relying solely on global quantization or structural pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of trained 3D Gaussians with attributes \{\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{R}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}{i}\}. Output: A compressed bitstream representing the scene. Data Structures: The method partitions the Gaussian set into two groups: 1. Anchor Primitives: Stored with full precision or high-fidelity quantization. 2. Coupled Primitives: Attributes are predicted from nearby anchors, storing only residuals or indices. Steps: 1. Hybrid Structure Construction: Partition Gaussians into anchors and coupled primitives. The specific selection criteria (e.g., random, based on importance) are not detailed in the provided sources. 2. Attribute Prediction: For each coupled primitive, predict its attributes (position, rotation, scale, opacity, SH coefficients) based on the attributes of associated anchor primitives. 3. Residual Encoding: Compute the difference (residual) between the actual attributes of the coupled primitive and the predicted attributes. Encode these residuals compactly. 4. Rate-Constrained Optimization: Optimize the representation by jointly minimizing rendering distortion and bit rate. 5. Entropy Estimation: Model the bit rate for both anchor and coupled primitives using entropy estimation to guide the quantization and coding process. Formulas: The optimization objective is a rate-distortion cost function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{D} + \lambda \mathcal{R} Where: \mathcal{D} is the rendering distortion. \mathcal{R} is the total bit rate, modeled via entropy estimation for anchors and coupled primitives. \lambda is the Lagrange multiplier controlling the trade-off. Parameters: \lambda: Not given in the sources. Number of anchors/coupled split ratio: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Prediction accuracy for coupled primitives depends on the spatial coherence of the scene. Degenerate cases where anchors are too far from coupled primitives may lead to large residuals. Entropy estimation accuracy is critical for rate modeling; poor estimation may lead to suboptimal quantization. A progressive compression framework that jointly and adaptively controls the quantity and quality of Gaussians to enable incremental bitstreams. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to standard 3DGS due to compact residual representations and entropy coding. Performance: Achieves high compression ratios while maintaining visual fidelity. Strengths: Effective hybrid structure reduces redundancy; rate-distortion optimization ensures efficient bit usage. Limitations: Complexity of predicting coupled attributes and entropy modeling. When to use: When storage or transmission bandwidth is constrained. When not to use: When real-time decoding complexity is a primary concern and compression is not critical. CompGS was proposed in the paper "CompGS: Efficient 3D Scene Representation via Compressed Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the high memory footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a hybrid primitive structure and rate-constrained optimization. 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: PCGS (Progressive Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting)
head: Progressive Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: PCGS is a progressive compression framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that jointly and adaptively controls both the quantity and quality of anchor primitives to enable effective progressivity for on-demand applications. Unlike single-rate compression methods or progressive methods that only adjust quantity, PCGS allows incremental bitstreams to refine fidelity by decoding additional anchors and progressively refining existing ones. It builds on CompGS via the Scaffold-GS representation and improves upon HAC++ by introducing a quantization context model that exploits correlations across progressive levels. Inputs: A trained 3DGS scene represented by Scaffold-GS anchors. A set of progressive levels s \in \{1, \dots, S\}. Trade-off parameters \lambdas for each level s. Outputs: A progressive bitstream consisting of a header and incremental payloads for each level s. The header contains shared components: MLPs, anchor locations xa, hash grid H, and masks mg. Incremental payloads contain quantized attributes for newly decoded anchors and refined values for previously decoded anchors. Anchor Representation (Scaffold-GS): Each anchor i consists of: Location: xa^{[i]} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Anchor Feature: f^{[i]} \in \mathbb{R}^{Da}. Scaling: l^{[i]} \in \mathbb{R}^6. Learnable Offsets: o^{[i]} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times K}. Masks: Base masking feature: f{base} (learnable). Level-specific masking feature: f{sm} (learnable). Anchor-level mask at level s: m{as}^{[i]}. Gaussian-level mask at level s: m{gs}^{[i]}. Global mask mg from which m{as} is derived. Hash Grid: Binary hash grid H used to capture correlations among anchors. Hash feature fh obtained via interpolation from H. Entropy Model Parameters: Quantization step size (predicted by hash feature). Gaussian distribution parameters (mean and variance) for newly decoded anchors. Trinomial distribution parameters for refining previously decoded anchors. 1. Training Phase: 1. Initialize Scaffold-GS anchors and parameters (MLPs, xa, H, f{base}, f{sm}). 2. For each iteration: a. Randomly sample a progressive level s from the set of levels. b. Retrieve the corresponding trade-off parameter \lambdas. c. Compute the anchor-level mask m{as}^{[i]} and Gaussian-level mask m{gs}^{[i]} for each anchor i using f{base} and f{sm}. d. Determine the state of each anchor: If m{as}^{[i]} = 0: Anchor remains undecoded. If m{as}^{[i]} transitions from 0 to 1: Anchor is newly decoded. If m{as}^{[i]} = 1 and was decoded in a previous level: Anchor is refined. e. Encode attributes: For newly decoded anchors: Use Gaussian distribution entropy modeling. For refined anchors: Use progressive quantization with trinomial distribution entropy modeling. f. Compute loss: \text{Loss} = L{Scaffold} + \lambdas \frac{1}{Na (Da + 6 + 3K)} (L{entropy} + L{hash}) where L{Scaffold} is the reconstruction loss, L{entropy} is the entropy rate, and L{hash} is the hash grid regularization. g. Update parameters using gradient descent. 3. Train for 40k iterations for full optimization, or 30k for fair comparison with standard protocols. 2. Encoding Phase (Progressive Bitstream Generation): 1. Header Encoding: a. Encode anchor locations xa using GPCC (Group Prediction and Context-based Coding). All valid anchor locations are encoded together in the header to reduce bit consumption, rather than incrementally. b. Encode shared MLPs, hash grid H, and global masks mg. 2. Level s=1 Encoding: a. Identify anchors with m{as}^{[i]} = 1. b. Quantize attributes (f, l, o) for these anchors. c. Encode quantized values using Gaussian distribution entropy modeling. 3. Level s \ge 2 Encoding: a. Identify newly decoded anchors (m{as}^{[i]} transitions 0 to 1). Quantize and encode their attributes using Gaussian distribution entropy modeling. b. Identify refined anchors (previously decoded). Apply progressive quantization (trit-plane division) to refine their attributes. c. Encode the refinement residuals using trinomial distribution entropy modeling, exploiting correlations with previous quantization levels. 3. Decoding Phase: 1. Header Decoding: a. Decode MLPs, anchor locations xa, hash grid H, and masks mg. 2. Level s=1 Decoding: a. Decode attributes for valid anchors using Gaussian distribution entropy modeling. 3. Level s \ge 2 Decoding: a. Refine already decoded anchors using progressive quantization and trinomial distribution probability estimation. b. Decode newly introduced anchors and Gaussian offsets via Gaussian distribution. 4. Rendering: a. Reconstruct Gaussians from anchors using Scaffold-GS MLPs. b. Render using \alpha-composed blending: C = \sumi ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where C \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the pixel color, ci is view-dependent color, and \alphai is opacity after 2D projection. Gaussian Function: G(x) = \exp \left( - \frac{1}{2} (x - xg)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - xg) \right) where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a random 3D location, xg \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the Gaussian mean, and \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top is the covariance matrix with scaling S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and rotation R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Rendering Equation: C = \sumi ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alpha \in \mathbb{R} is opacity and c \in \mathbb{R}^3 is view-dependent color. Training Loss: \text{Loss} = L{Scaffold} + \lambdas \frac{1}{Na (Da + 6 + 3K)} (L{entropy} + L{hash}) where \lambdas balances Rate-Distortion at level s. \lambdas: Trade-off parameter for level s, varying to balance R-D performance. Training Iterations: 40k for sufficient optimization covering all rates; 30k for fair comparison with standard protocols. Na: Number of anchors. Da: Dimension of anchor feature. K: Dimension of offset matrix. Anchor Location Encoding: Anchor locations are encoded using GPCC, which relies on mutual information among anchors. Encoding all valid anchor locations together in the header is required to reduce bit consumption; incremental encoding increases bit usage. Probability Estimation: Replacing the trinomial distribution with a Gaussian distribution for previously decoded anchors leads to inaccurate probability estimation because it fails to exploit quantization context across levels. Loss Design: Using accumulated entropy from all previous and current levels as rate regularization causes fidelity degradation. Incorporating fidelity at previous levels into optimization worsens performance by introducing excessive complexity. Progressive Masking: Masks must be monotonically non-decreasing across levels to ensure smooth progression. Time Complexity: Training is performed in a single session for all levels, requiring 30k-40k iterations, compared to 60k iterations per rate for methods like HEMGS. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of anchors and the size of the hash grid. Progressive compression allows variable memory usage based on the decoded level. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360, PCGS (40k) achieves 28.0 dB PSNR at ~10 MB, compared to GoDe (30k+30k) at 27.8 dB and HEMGS (60k) at 26.9 dB. Scaling: PCGS scales well with progressive levels, allowing adaptive bitstreams for dynamic bandwidth and storage constraints. Strengths: Joint optimization of quantity and quality; effective progressivity; comparable performance to single-rate methods; efficient entropy coding using trinomial distribution. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \lambdas; complexity in entropy modeling due to trinomial distribution. When to Use: On-demand applications with dynamic bandwidth/storage constraints; scenarios requiring progressive refinement of 3DGS scenes. When Not to Use: Single-rate compression requirements where progressivity is not needed; scenarios with strict latency constraints where decoding all levels is prohibitive. PCGS was proposed in 2025 by the authors of the paper "PCGS: Progressive Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds on Scaffold-GS and improves upon HAC++ by introducing progressive compression capabilities. The method addresses the lack of progressivity in existing 3DGS compression techniques, which waste resources in on-demand applications. name: SLAM and Mapping
head: SLAM, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping, Neural SLAM, Gaussian SLAM
body: SLAM and Mapping in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) refers to the joint estimation of camera poses and the optimization of a 3D Gaussian scene representation from a sequence of images or RGB-D frames. It solves the problem of reconstructing a consistent 3D model while tracking the camera trajectory in real-time or offline. Unlike standard 3DGS training which assumes known camera poses, SLAM methods must handle pose uncertainty, often integrating geometric constraints, depth information, or neural field representations to maintain consistency. This family distinguishes itself by coupling the differentiable rendering of Gaussians (or hybrid neural fields) with optimization loops that update both the scene geometry/appearance and the camera extrinsics simultaneously. The core mechanism of 3DGS-based SLAM involves an iterative loop that alternates between or jointly optimizes camera poses T and Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} (position \mathbf{p}, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}, and spherical harmonics coefficients). 1. Differentiable Rendering: The scene is rendered from the current camera pose T to produce an image \hat{I} and/or depth map \hat{D}. This is typically done via alpha-compositing of 3D Gaussians projected onto the image plane. 2. Loss Computation: A loss function \mathcal{L} is computed between the rendered output and the ground-truth input (image I, depth D, or semantic labels). Common terms include photometric loss (\mathcal{L}{rgb}) and geometric loss (\mathcal{L}{depth}). 3. Gradient Propagation: Gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial T} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathcal{G}} are backpropagated through the differentiable renderer. 4. Optimization: Camera poses and Gaussian parameters are updated using gradient descent (e.g., Adam) or bundle adjustment. Key challenges addressed by specific methods include: Pose Drift: Accumulated errors in camera trajectory estimation. Geometric Consistency: Ensuring that the reconstructed geometry aligns with observed depth or structure. Representation Choice: Using explicit 3D Gaussians, implicit neural fields (NeRF), or hybrid representations (neural points + MLPs) to balance rendering speed and reconstruction quality. CG-SLAM is a SLAM method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates an uncertainty map derived from rendered depth into the training process. It addresses the reconstruction quality limitations of standard differentiable rendering pipelines by leveraging explicit geometry representation to alleviate viewpoint misalignment. It extends the standard 3DGS optimization loop by incorporating depth-based uncertainty. Mechanism: It renders a depth map \hat{D} from the current Gaussians and camera pose. An uncertainty map U is computed from \hat{D} (formula not specified in sources). This map modulates the loss function, reducing the influence of pixels with high depth uncertainty (e.g., low texture, occlusions) during optimization. When to choose: Use when depth information is available and geometric consistency is critical, particularly in textureless regions where standard photometric loss may fail. Link: CG-SLAM Mapping strategies define the mechanism for aligning pixels or features between two scenes or observations to facilitate spatial correspondence, pose estimation, or scene fusion. They solve the problem of establishing accurate geometric and semantic links between distinct viewpoints or temporal states in SLAM and 3D reconstruction pipelines. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on discrete feature matching or dense neural field optimization alone, these strategies range from direct pixel identity assumptions to semantic-aware correspondences and joint optimization windows. Identity Mapping: Assumes direct pixel correspondence (u,v) \to (u,v) or rigid transformation. Lacks accuracy under significant viewpoint changes. Semantic Correspondence: Uses Vision Transformers (ViT/DINO) to extract dense semantic features F \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} and matches them via cosine similarity. Improves matching in textureless regions. Co-segmentation: Segments images into K parts using DINO clustering, then matches regions semantically before refining pixel-level correspondence. Enforces structural consistency. Joint Mapping and Pose Update: Fuses tracked RGB-D frames into an existing map by jointly optimizing geometry, poses, and features. Uses a sliding window of N{kf} keyframes and Nm sampled rays to mitigate network forgetting in online incremental learning. When to choose: Choose Identity for simple rigid motions; Semantic/Co-segmentation for textureless or repetitive environments; Joint Mapping for online incremental reconstruction. Link: Mapping Strategies Semantic-aware mapping integrates semantic information into the SLAM loop to improve robustness and consistency. It typically involves extracting semantic features (e.g., via DINO or other encoders) and using them to guide feature matching, loop closure, or regularization. This helps in handling dynamic objects and textureless regions where photometric cues are insufficient. When to choose: Use in environments with significant semantic structure or dynamic elements where geometric consistency alone is ambiguous. Link: Semantic-aware mapping Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representation is a method for modeling 3D scenes using continuous volumetric functions, typically implemented as multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) or hybrid grid-MLP architectures, that map spatial coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis by learning a scene's appearance and geometry implicitly, allowing for photorealistic rendering from arbitrary camera poses. Unlike explicit representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting which store millions of discrete primitives, NeRF stores the scene implicitly within network weights, offering high compression ratios at the cost of slower rendering speeds. Mechanism: A network f\theta maps (\mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Rendering uses volume rendering equation: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k. Hybrid variants (e.g., Instant NGP) use hash grids for acceleration. When to choose: Use when high-fidelity appearance is prioritized over real-time rendering speed, or when integrating with existing NeRF-based SLAM pipelines. Link: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) Representation Combines an existing frame-based tracking system (ORB-SLAM) with 3DGS mapping. ORB-SLAM recovers poses, and 3DGS is trained with poses and sensor depth of keyframes, equivalent to offline splatting. Performance: On EuRoC Machine Hall (Stereo Depth), ATE RMSE (m): ORB-SLAM3 0.052, Ours 3.190. Point-SLAM fails on all sequences. Comparison: ORB-SLAM achieves best ATE, but combined approach shows no significant difference in rendering metrics compared to unified 3DGS SLAM. Unified approach is preferred for exploring 3DGS throughout the entire algorithm. When to choose: Use when robust pose estimation is required from classical methods, or for offline reconstruction where real-time tracking is not needed. A neural point-based hybrid neural field SLAM system enabling multi-agent cooperative localization and mapping with loop closure. Mechanism: Uses a keyframe-associated neural point representation inspired by PointNeRF, allowing per-point features to be adjusted during pose graph optimization. Employs a two-stage distributed-to-centralized training scheme: initial decoders are trained separately for each agent, then fused and fine-tuned jointly. Integrates odometry, loop detection, sub-map fusion, and global refinement. When to choose: Use for multi-agent cooperative SLAM scenarios requiring loop closure and consistent map fusion. The first fully distributed multi-agent neural SLAM framework enabling accurate collaborative mapping and robust camera tracking without centralized training or raw data exchange. Mechanism: Uses a triplane+MLP hybrid neural field representation as a mapping module. Introduces an intra-to-inter loop closure strategy to reduce pose drift and align submaps across agents through peer-to-peer feature sharing and global consistency loss. When to choose: Use for distributed multi-agent systems where bandwidth constraints prevent raw data exchange. A SLAM method employing a novel multiscale patch-based loss that aligns feature points, maps, and RGB-D pixels through warpings. Mechanism: Uses an INGP-like multiresolution hybrid feature grid+MLP representation for neural SDF learning. Extensive evaluations show superior performance and robustness over prior implicit field-based SLAM methods, especially under challenging conditions. When to choose: Use for high-accuracy RGB-D SLAM in challenging environments requiring robust feature alignment. A globally consistent SLAM system using a point-based implicit neural (PIN) representation. Mechanism: Replaces grid structures with neural feature points, offering spatial flexibility and elastic correction during loop closure. Mapping alternates with odometry. Mapping step is based on a hybrid neural SDF representation with explicit neural points and implicit MLP decoders. Odometry is performed correspondence-free via second-order scan-to-map optimization. A sliding window replay buffer ensures stable incremental updates. Loop closures trigger pose graph optimization and elastic deformation of neural points, enabling consistent large-scale mapping. When to choose: Use for large-scale mapping requiring global consistency and elastic correction during loop closure. An active SLAM approach that plans camera trajectories to maximize information gain during reconstruction. Mechanism: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D bounding box, uniformly sample goal-state candidates Sg from view space, initialize DVGO coarse model M(c) and agent state s0, append initial image to database \{I\}. 2. Global Policy: Select next-best-view s^g from goal candidates Sg using criterion: s^g = \arg\min{sg \in Sg} (\lambda{cp} l{cp}(x{sg}) - \lambda{ig} Es(sg)), where x{sg} is 3D location of sg. 3. Local Policy: Execute planning optimization to obtain optimized trajectory S^ and local next-best view s^. 4. Action: Move agent to s^. 5. Observation: Obtain new image observation It. 6. Update Database: Add new observation to database \{I\}{i=0}^{t+1}. 7. Mapping Optimization: Optimize DVGO model Mt to M{t+1} by sampling pixels from database, including synchronizing entropy volume V(E,c). 8. Stop Check: Stop if (1) change in entropy volume is below threshold, or (2) maximum information gain of feasible goal candidates is below threshold. 9. Fine Stage: After exploration, initialize DVGO fine model M(f) with trained coarse model MT(c). Perform stochastic training by sampling pixels from database \{I\}{i=0}^T for N iterations, optimizing every m iterations. When to choose: Use for autonomous exploration tasks where maximizing reconstruction quality per unit of motion is required. A camera tracking method that decouples lightness from the image to handle lighting changes, by converting images to LAB space and discarding the L (lightness) channel during comparison. Mechanism: 1. Parameterize camera pose as T = (t, q) with 3D translation t and rotation quaternion q. 2. Initialize camera pose assuming constant camera velocity. 3. Convert input image C and rendered image \hat{C} to LAB space using \rho. 4. Discard the L channel. 5. Minimize L{tracking} using color (A/B channels) and depth differences. Formula: L{tracking} = \lambda{color} |\rho(\hat{C}) - \rho(C)| + \lambda{depth} |\hat{D} - D|, where \rho is the operation of converting the image from RGB to LAB space, C is the input image, \hat{C} is the rendered image, D is the input depth, and \hat{D} is the rendered depth. Parameters: \lambda{color} = 0.5, weight for the color term in the tracking loss. \lambda{depth} = 1.0, weight for the depth term in the tracking loss. When to choose: Use in environments with significant lighting variations where photometric consistency is compromised. Extends passive mapping with active view selection to maximize information gain. Mechanism: Reconstruct environment using 3D Gaussians (e.g., via SplaTAM). Propose path candidates using frontier-based exploration. Sample cameras along the path concerning the mobility of the agent. Compute EIG for each path and choose the one with the highest EIG to continue exploration. Formula: Pj = \arg \max{Pj} \text{tr} \left( \sum{x{acqi} \in Pj} H''[y{i\acq}|x{acqi}, w] \right) H''[w|D{train}]^{-1}. When to choose: Use for autonomous mapping where efficient exploration is required to minimize reconstruction time or energy. SLAM has a long history in computer vision, traditionally relying on feature-based methods (e.g., ORB-SLAM) or direct methods (e.g., DSO, LSD-SLAM). The advent of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [Mildenhall et al. 2020] introduced implicit neural representations for novel view synthesis, leading to "Neural SLAM" methods that optimize neural fields jointly with camera poses. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting [Kerbl et al. 2023] has been adapted for SLAM (e.g., SplaTAM, Gaussian Splatting SLAM) due to its fast rendering speed and explicit representation, offering a balance between the quality of NeRF and the efficiency of traditional point-based methods. Hybrid approaches combining neural fields and Gaussians (e.g., PIN-SLAM, CP-SLAM) are also emerging to leverage the strengths of both representations. name: CG-SLAM
body: CG-SLAM is a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM method that improves reconstruction quality by incorporating an uncertainty map derived from rendered depth into the training process. It leverages the explicit geometry of 3D Gaussians to enable flexible reprojection, addressing viewpoint misalignment more effectively than NeRF-based methods. CG-SLAM operates within the iterative loop defined by SLAM and Mapping, specifically modifying the loss computation and gradient propagation steps to account for depth uncertainty. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera poses T, 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} (position \mathbf{p}, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}, spherical harmonics coefficients), and ground-truth depth D. Outputs: Updated camera poses T', updated Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}', and a refined 3D map. Data Structures: Uncertainty Map (U): A 2D image map aligned with the rendered depth, where each pixel value represents the estimated uncertainty of the corresponding depth measurement. The specific formula for generating U from rendered depth is not detailed in the sources [G: Typically derived from the variance of depth estimates or consistency checks across frames]. Steps: 1. Differentiable Rendering: Render the current scene state to produce a depth map \hat{D} and an RGB image \hat{I} using alpha-compositing of projected 3D Gaussians. 2. Uncertainty Estimation: Generate an uncertainty map U based on the rendered depth \hat{D}. This map quantifies the reliability of the depth predictions. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}, which includes standard photometric and geometric terms, but is weighted or regularized by the uncertainty map U. The introduction of U into the training process is the key differentiator that greatly improves reconstruction quality. 4. Gradient Propagation: Backpropagate gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial T} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathcal{G}} through the differentiable renderer, accounting for the uncertainty-weighted loss. 5. Optimization: Update T and \mathcal{G} using gradient descent (e.g., Adam) or bundle adjustment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cgslamstep(cameraposes, gaussians, gtdepth, gtrgb): # 1. Render scene rendereddepth, renderedrgb = rendergaussians(cameraposes, gaussians) # 2. Generate uncertainty map from rendered depth # Note: Specific formula for uncertainty generation is not provided in sources uncertaintymap = computeuncertaintyfromdepth(rendereddepth) # 3. Compute loss with uncertainty weighting # Standard losses (photometric, geometric) are modified by uncertainty loss = computeuncertaintyawareloss(renderedrgb, rendereddepth, gtrgb, gtdepth, uncertaintymap) # 4. Backpropagate gradients = computegradients(loss, cameraposes, gaussians) # 5. Update parameters cameraposes = updateparameters(cameraposes, gradients['poses']) gaussians = updateparameters(gaussians, gradients['gaussians']) return cameraposes, gaussians Parameters: Uncertainty weighting scheme: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not given in the sources (standard Adam or BA likely used). Edge Cases: Degenerate depth values (e.g., infinity) in rendered depth may require masking before uncertainty computation. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is enabled by the 3DGS representation, making it suitable for SLAM applications. Memory Complexity: Explicit 3D Gaussian representation requires memory proportional to the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Better reconstruction quality compared to NeRF-based methods due to explicit geometry and flexible reprojection. Real-time rendering capability. Limitations: Specific quantitative performance metrics are not provided in the sources. When to use: When high-quality reconstruction and real-time performance are required for robotics tasks like relocalization, navigation, and manipulation. CG-SLAM was introduced in reference [189] (cited as in the provided text). It is part of the broader trend of using 3D Gaussian Splatting for SLAM, leveraging its explicit geometry for better reconstruction than implicit NeRF representations. name: Mapping Strategies
head: Pixel mapping strategies, Scene alignment strategies
body: Mapping strategies define the correspondence mechanism between pixels or features of two distinct scenes (e.g., a source and a target scene) to enable alignment, fusion, or editing. They solve the problem of spatial misalignment that arises when direct pixel-to-pixel correspondence is invalid due to viewpoint changes, object deformation, or semantic differences. Unlike sibling methods such as CG-SLAM which rely on geometric feature matching, or NeRF Representation which optimizes continuous fields, these strategies explicitly define how visual information is transferred or matched between discrete scene representations. The method consists of three primary strategies for establishing correspondence, followed by a resampling technique to enforce geometric consistency. Inputs: Two scenes (Source and Target), represented as images or radiance fields. Outputs: A mapping function or set of correspondences between pixels/features of the two scenes. Definition: Assumes a direct 1:1 pixel correspondence between the source and target images. Mechanism: Maps pixel (u, v) in the source directly to (u, v) in the target. Limitation: Lacks spatial alignment accuracy; fails when scenes differ in viewpoint or scale. Definition: Uses deep learning features to establish dense semantic matching. Mechanism: 1. Extract dense semantic features from both scenes using Vision Transformers (ViT) [Dosovitskiy 2020] and DINO [Amir et al. 2021]. 2. Compute similarity metrics (e.g., cosine similarity) between feature vectors of pixels in the source and target. 3. Establish correspondences based on feature proximity. Advantage: Improves spatial matching over identity mapping by leveraging semantic context. Definition: Refines alignment by segmenting images into semantically meaningful parts. Mechanism: 1. Use DINO’s clustering capabilities to segment both scenes into coherent regions. 2. Establish correspondences at the region level rather than pixel level. 3. Map pixels within corresponding semantic segments. Advantage: Yields finer correspondence and maintains semantic boundaries, handling intra-class variations better than dense feature matching. To align geometry and color after establishing correspondence, a density-based resampling strategy is applied along corresponding rays. 1. Problem: Initial uniform sampling fails due to misalignment between scenes. 2. Method: Identify density peaks along each ray in the source scene. 3. Adjustment: Adjust sampling points in the target scene to align with these density peaks. 4. Result: Ensures improved color-geometry consistency and realistic fusion of visual attributes. Parameters: Sampling density along rays: Not given in the sources. Threshold for density peaks: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Misalignment: Identity mapping fails completely under viewpoint changes. Semantic Ambiguity: Co-segmentation may fail if DINO clustering produces inconsistent regions across scenes. iMAP is the first NeRF-based dense online SLAM model that jointly optimizes camera pose and an implicit scene representation. It solves the problem of simultaneous localization and mapping by treating the scene as a continuous radiance field rather than a discrete mesh or point cloud. It sets itself apart from its siblings by being the foundational method that introduced the iterative two-step approach of tracking and mapping to NeRF-based SLAM, upon which NICE-SLAM and subsequent methods build. RNR-Map Construction embeds visual information from an RGB-D image into a 2D grid map (RNR-Map) using a pretrained encoder and inverse camera projection. It differs from sibling methods like iMAP by operating directly on latent codes to bypass the computationally expensive differentiable rendering step required for alignment, enabling high-frequency mapping. A mapping subroutine that fuses tracked RGB-D frames into the existing scene map by jointly optimizing scene geometry, camera poses, and feature embeddings using a sliding window of keyframes. Steps: 1. Randomly select N{kf} keyframes for each frame to form an optimization window. 2. For each frame in the optimization window, randomly sample Nm rays and transform them into the world coordinate system with estimated frame poses. 3. Sample points within sparse voxels, render pixels, and calculate loss functions using the method from Section 4.1 of. Parameters: N{kf}: Number of keyframes randomly selected for the optimization window. Nm: Number of rays randomly sampled for each frame in the optimization window. Identity Mapping: O(1) per pixel; extremely fast but inaccurate for non-aligned scenes. Semantic Mapping: High computational cost due to ViT/DINO inference; robust to viewpoint changes. Co-Segmentation: Moderate to high cost due to clustering; robust to semantic variations. Resampling: Adds overhead proportional to ray length and sampling density; improves fusion quality. Joint Mapping: Depends on window size N{kf} and ray count Nm; prone to network forgetting if not jointly optimized. Mapping strategies in the context of 3D editing and SLAM emerged with the need to transfer visual attributes between scenes or align incremental maps. Generalized TensoRF introduced these strategies for view-consistent 3D editing. Vox-Fusion adapted similar concepts for dense tracking and mapping using voxel-based neural implicit representations. name: iMAP
head: implicit mapping
body: Sucar et al. introduced iMAP as the first NeRF-based dense online SLAM model. It solves simultaneous localization and mapping by treating the scene as a continuous radiance field rather than a discrete mesh or point cloud. iMAP employs an iterative two-step approach consisting of tracking and mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of RGB images from a moving camera. Outputs: Camera poses for each frame and a continuous implicit scene representation (NeRF). Data Structures: Keyframe Set: A sparse, incrementally selected set of images used for optimization. Algorithm Steps: 1. Keyframe Selection: Select a sparse subset of images from the input stream to serve as keyframes for optimization. 2. Tracking (Pose Optimization): Optimize the camera pose with respect to the current NeRF model. This step is computationally faster than mapping. 3. Mapping (Bundle Adjustment): Perform joint optimization of the camera pose and the NeRF model parameters. This step is computationally slower than tracking. 4. Parallel Execution: Run the tracking step in parallel with the mapping process to maintain tracking speed close to the camera framerate. Parameters and Edge Cases: Performance is limited by the computational cost of the NeRF-based mapping step. Combined with the slower mapping step, the method is far from achieving real-time performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imap(imagesequence): # Initialize NeRF model with random weights nerfmodel = NeuralNetwork() # Initialize keyframe set with initial frames keyframes = imagesequence[:initialk] # Initialize poses for keyframes poses = {kfid: identitypose() for kfid in keyframes} for frameid, image in enumerate(imagesequence): # Step 1: Tracking (Pose Optimization) # Optimize pose for current frame relative to current NeRF # Standard gradient descent on pose parameters minimizing rendering loss currentpose = optimizepose(image, nerfmodel, poses.get(frameid)) poses[frameid] = currentpose # Step 2: Mapping (Bundle Adjustment) # Jointly optimize poses and NeRF parameters using keyframes # Standard bundle adjustment minimizing photometric and geometric losses nerfmodel, poses = bundleadjustment(keyframes, poses, imagesequence, nerfmodel) # Incrementally select new keyframes if necessary if shouldaddkeyframe(image, poses): keyframes.add(frameid) return poses, nerfmodel NICE-SLAM is an improvement on iMAP that uses a hierarchical grid-based representation to fill gaps in large-scale unobserved scene features. It achieves lower pose estimation errors and better scene reconstruction results than iMAP while using approximately one-quarter of the FLOPs, one-third of the tracking time, and half of the mapping time. It is still far from achieving real-time performance. NICER-SLAM is an end-to-end dense SLAM system that performs simultaneous tracking and mapping using only RGB inputs. It uses a hierarchical neural implicit representation based on signed distance functions (SDFs). It leverages monocular geometric cues, optical flow, and a warping loss to guide optimization without depth supervision. It proposes a locally adaptive SDF-to-density transformation tailored for indoor scene dynamics. Tracking Speed: Pose tracking speed is close to camera framerate. Overall Performance: Combined with the slower NeRF-based mapping step, iMAP is far from achieving real-time performance. Efficiency: NICE-SLAM (the direct successor) uses approximately one-quarter of the FLOPs of iMAP, one-third of the tracking time, and half of the mapping time. Accuracy: NICE-SLAM achieves lower pose estimation errors and better scene reconstruction results than iMAP. Limitations: The NeRF-based mapping step is computationally expensive, preventing real-time operation. iMAP was introduced by Sucar et al. in March 2021. It is the first NeRF-based dense online SLAM model. It was followed by NICE-SLAM in December 2021. name: RNR-Map Construction
head: Feature Registration
body: RNR-Map Construction embeds visual information from an RGB-D image into a 2D grid map (RNR-Map) using a pretrained encoder and inverse camera projection. It differs from sibling methods like iMAP by operating directly on latent codes to bypass the computationally expensive differentiable rendering step required for alignment, enabling high-frequency mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An RGB-D image It \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 4}, where the first three channels are RGB and the fourth is depth. A relative pose \Delta pt = (\Delta xt, \Delta yt, \Delta at) representing the change in x, y position and heading angle \alpha from the previous pose. Output: A local RNR-Map mt^l \in \mathbb{R}^{U \times V \times D} and a local mask nt^l \in \mathbb{Z}^{U \times V}. Data Structures: RNR-Map (m): A 2D grid of size U \times V. Each cell m(u,v) stores a latent code vector of dimension D (m(u,v) \in \mathbb{R}^D). Mask (n): A 2D grid of size U \times V. Each cell n(u,v) stores an integer count of the number of latent codes averaged into the corresponding map cell. Parameters: D: The channel size (dimensionality) of the latent code feature vector. K: Camera intrinsic matrix. \theta{enc}: Parameters of the pretrained encoder. s: Grid resolution (size of each cell in world units). Not explicitly defined in sources, but implied by the floor division in the mapping formula. Steps: 1. Pose Accumulation: Compute the absolute pose pt by cumulating relative pose differences from the start pose p0 = (0, 0, 0). 2. Encoding: Encode the input image It using the pretrained encoder \theta{enc} to produce a feature map Ct \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}. 3. Inverse Projection: For each pixel (h, w) in Ct, calculate its 3D world position [qx, qy, qz]^T using the camera intrinsic K, the extrinsic matrix derived from pt, and the depth value d{h,w} from It. 4. Grid Mapping: Map the 3D world position to 2D grid coordinates (u, v) using the grid resolution s: u = \left\lfloor \frac{qx(h,w)}{s} \right\rceil, \quad v = \left\lfloor \frac{qy(h,w)}{s} \right\rceil 5. Feature Registration: Update the map cell m(u,v) and mask cell n(u,v) by averaging the incoming feature c{h,w} with existing features in that cell: m(u,v) = \frac{1}{n(u,v)} \sum{ci \in X{(u,v)}} ci, \quad n(u,v) = |X{(u,v)}| where X{(u,v)} is the set of features mapped to cell (u,v). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rnrmapconstruction(It, deltapt, pprev, K, thetaenc, s): """ Construct/update RNR-Map from a single RGB-D frame. Args: It: RGB-D image tensor of shape (H, W, 4). deltapt: Relative pose (dx, dy, da) from previous step. pprev: Previous absolute pose (x, y, alpha). K: Camera intrinsic matrix. thetaenc: Pretrained encoder network. s: Grid cell size in world units. Returns: mlocal: Local RNR-Map tensor of shape (U, V, D). nlocal: Local mask tensor of shape (U, V). """ # 1. Compute absolute pose pt = pprev + deltapt # Note: Exact pose composition (e.g., SE(2) transformation) is not detailed in sources # 2. Encode image Ct = thetaenc(It) # Shape: (H, W, D) # 3. Initialize local map and mask # Dimensions U, V depend on the extent of the scene covered by the current frame # For implementation, these are typically derived from the bounding box of projected points U, V = computegriddimensions(pt, K, It.depthchannel, s) mlocal = zeros((U, V, D)) nlocal = zeros((U, V), dtype=int) # 4. Inverse projection and registration for h in range(H): for w in range(W): # Extract depth d = It[h, w, 3] # Skip invalid depth if d <= 0: continue # Get feature vector c = Ct[h, w,:] # Inverse camera projection to get 3D world position # Using K and extrinsic matrix derived from pt # Let R, t be the rotation and translation from pt # Pixel coordinates (upx, vpx) = (w, h) # Homogeneous pixel coordinate pcam = inv(K) @ [w, h, 1] # Scale by depth pcam = d # Transform to world frame q = R @ pcam + t # Map to 2D grid # Using floor rounding as per source formula u = floor(q[0] / s) v = floor(q[1] / s) # Check bounds if 0 <= u < U and 0 <= v < V: # Update mask nlocal[u, v] += 1 # Update map with running average # m(u,v) = (1/n) sum(ci) # This can be implemented incrementally: # mnew = ((nold mold) + c) / (nold + 1) nold = nlocal[u, v] - 1 if nold > 0: mlocal[u, v] = (nold mlocal[u, v] + c) / nlocal[u, v] else: mlocal[u, v] = c return mlocal, nlocal Determines an agent's position within an RNR-Map using a single query image by operating directly on latent codes, bypassing rendering. Time Complexity: The mapping process operates at 91.9 Hz. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates the rendering step in mapping, allowing for high-frequency updates suitable for navigation systems. Limitations: Requires a pretrained encoder and decoder pair; relies on accurate pose estimation for correct spatial alignment. The RNR-Map was introduced by Songhwai Oh et al. in 2023. It is designed as a navigation map that supports camera tracking, image-based localization, and image-goal navigation. The method uses an autoencoder-like framework where the encoder embeds pixel features into the 2D grid map. name: Image-Based Localization (Floc)
head: Heatmap Generation, Target Localization, RNR-Map-based localization
body: Image-Based Localization (Floc) determines an agent's position within a Renderable Neural Radiance Map (RNR-Map) using a single query image, bypassing the computationally expensive rendering step required by traditional inverse volume rendering methods. Unlike sibling methods that rely on differentiable rendering to match observed pixels with rendered views, Floc operates directly on the latent codes embedded in the RNR-Map, outputting a spatial heatmap and a predicted orientation to identify the most probable location and viewing angle. Inputs and Outputs Input: A target query image I{trg} and the global RNR-Map m. Output: A heatmap E \in \mathbb{R}^{U \times V} representing the probability distribution of the target location (u{trg}, v{trg}) across the map grid, and a predicted orientation \hat{a}{trg}. Data Structures RNR-Map (m): A 2D grid map where each cell (u,v) contains a latent code vector c{u,v} derived from the encoder. The map also stores occupancy counts n(u,v). Local Map (m{trg}): A temporary grid representation of the query image, generated by the registration function F{reg} using a hypothetical origin pose p0 = (0,0,0). Processed Maps (m'k, m'q): Feature maps extracted from m and m{trg} by CNNs Fk and Fq. Numbered Steps 1. Local Map Generation: Transform the target image I{trg} into a local map m{trg} using the registration encoder F{reg}(I{trg}, p0; \theta{enc}), where p0 is the fixed origin pose (0,0,0). 2. Feature Extraction: Process the global RNR-Map m through convolutional network Fk to obtain m'k. Simultaneously, process the local map m{trg} through convolutional network Fq to obtain m'q. 3. Orientation Rotation: Generate R rotated versions of the query feature map m'q. For each rotation index r \in \{1, \dots, R\}, apply rotation Rotr corresponding to angle \thetar = 360^\circ \times \frac{r-1}{R} to produce (m'q)r. 4. Cross-Correlation: Perform cross-correlation (denoted as \mathrm{Conv}) between the global feature map m'k and each rotated query feature map (m'q)r. This acts as a sliding window filter to find spatial matches. 5. Heatmap and Orientation Prediction: Forward the outputs of the cross-correlation operations into a final CNN FE. FE produces the heatmap E and the orientation prediction \hat{a}{trg}. Formulas The localization function F{loc} is defined as: F{loc}(m, m{trg}; \theta{loc}) = FE\left(\mathrm{Conv}\left(Fk(m), \{Fq(m{trg})r\}{r=1}^R\right)\right) where \{Fq(m{trg})r\}{r=1}^R are the R rotated versions of the processed target map. The training loss minimizes the error between the predicted outputs and ground truth: \mathrm{Loss}(\theta{loc}) = D{KL}(E{gt}, \hat{E}) + CE(a{trg}, \hat{a}{trg}) where D{KL} is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the ground truth heatmap E{gt} and predicted heatmap \hat{E}, and CE is the cross-entropy loss for the orientation a{trg}, which is discretized into 18 bins. Parameters R (Rotations): The number of discrete orientation angles to search. The source specifies 18 bins for orientation classification. p0: The initial pose used for encoding the query image, fixed at (0,0,0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Unknown Position: The method assumes the agent does not know the target location, necessitating the use of the origin pose p0 for the initial encoding of I{trg}. Orientation Ambiguity: Visual similarity can cause confusion between visually similar places; the rotation search and orientation head mitigate this but require sufficient training data. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def floclocalization(globalmapm, targetimageItrg, R=18): # Step 1: Transform target image to local map using origin pose p0=(0,0,0) # Freg is the registration encoder from RNR-Map Construction localmapmtrg = Freg(Itrg, p0=(0,0,0)) # Step 2: Process global and local maps through CNNs # Fk and Fq are feature extraction networks mprimek = Fk(globalmapm) mprimeq = Fq(localmapmtrg) # Step 3: Rotate query map into R different angles rotatedqueries = [] for r in range(1, R + 1): # Angle calculation: 360 (r-1) / R angle = 360.0 (r - 1) / R # Rotr represents the rotation operation rotatedmprimeq = Rotr(mprimeq, angle) rotatedqueries.append(rotatedmprimeq) # Step 4: Cross-correlation (Conv) between global map and each rotated query # Conv denotes cross-correlation convoutputs = [] for qrot in rotatedqueries: # Conv(mprimek, qrot) slides qrot over mprimek output = Conv(mprimek, qrot) convoutputs.append(output) # Step 5: Forward to CNN FE to produce heatmap and orientation # FE takes the list of convoutputs (or concatenated features) heatmapE, orientationpred = FE(convoutputs) return heatmapE, orientationpred Speed: The localization framework operates at 56.8 Hz. This is significantly faster than rendering-based optimization methods (e.g., camera tracking at 5 Hz) because it eliminates the rendering step. Accuracy: In curved scenarios of the NRNS dataset, the navigation framework utilizing this localization achieves a 65.7% success rate, an improvement of 18.6% over the state-of-the-art (55.4%). Strengths: Direct utilization of latent codes allows for fast, real-time localization without rendering. It is robust under odometry and actuation noises. Limitations: It relies on the quality of the latent codes embedded in the RNR-Map. If the RNR-Map is poorly constructed or lacks visual information, localization accuracy degrades. It is less precise than rendering-based camera tracking for fine-level localization. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Renderable Neural Radiance Map for Visual Navigation". Context: It addresses the challenge of visual navigation by explicitly embedding 3D visual information into a 2D grid form (RNR-Map) and leveraging the implicit visual information of latent codes for reasoning about the environment. Development: The work was supported by the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation (IITP). It is presented as the first method combining explicit grid embedding, renderability, and fast latent-code-based localization for navigation.
