name: Semantic-aware mapping
head: Semantic 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM, Semantic-aware Gaussian Mapping
body: Semantic-aware mapping extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM by integrating 2D semantic segmentation priors into the optimization loop to produce semantically labeled 3D maps. It distinguishes itself from standard radiance-field optimization by distilling 2D semantic labels to guide the Gaussian representation, enabling semantic-aware mapping. This family addresses the limitation of purely geometric SLAM by providing class-level understanding of the scene, which aids in dynamic object handling, loop closure, and high-level reasoning. The family builds on SLAM and Mapping. The core mechanism involves augmenting the standard 3D Gaussian parameter set with semantic attributes and modifying the loss function to include semantic consistency terms. 1. Semantic Augmentation: Each 3D Gaussian i is assigned a semantic label li. This label can be a discrete class identifier or a probability vector over semantic classes. 2. Semantic Distillation: 2D semantic masks are obtained from a pre-trained 2D segmentation network or dataset annotations. These 2D labels are projected or back-projected to align with the 3D Gaussians. 3. Semantic Loss: A semantic distillation loss \mathcal{L}{sem} is computed between the rendered semantic features (or projected labels) and the 2D semantic masks. 4. Combined Optimization: The total loss \mathcal{L} combines photometric reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{rgb} and the semantic loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{sem} \mathcal{L}{sem} where \lambda{sem} is the weight for the semantic loss. Gradients from both terms are backpropagated to update Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color, semantics) and camera poses. 5. Semantic-Guided Control: Adaptive control mechanisms (splitting and pruning) may be guided by semantic boundaries to avoid redundant splitting in homogeneous semantic regions. SemGauss-SLAM is a SLAM method that integrates semantic information into the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework. It distinguishes itself from standard radiance-field optimization by distilling 2D semantic labels to guide the Gaussian representation, enabling semantic-aware mapping. It is chosen when a dense, semantically labeled 3D map is required for tasks like navigation or scene understanding. Unsupervised Asset Grouping is a method for categorizing discovered objects in a scene by comparing the distributions of color and semantic features among image patches using Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) and agglomerative clustering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SemGauss-SLAM by operating on a discretized ground feature plane to group assets without requiring explicit object pose information or supervised labels, enabling the construction of a cross-scene asset library. A SLAM method that considers Gaussian’s semantic information in the simultaneous localization and mapping process by distilling 2D semantic information which can be obtained using 2D segmentation methods or provided by the dataset. A SLAM system that integrates semantic priors with NeRF-based representation to distinguish between dynamic and static objects. Separates tracking and NeRF-based mapping into four threads: segmentation, tracking, mapping, and loop detection. Segmentation thread identifies and suppresses dynamic feature points and regions. Tracking thread extracts features, filters them via semantic and geometric cues, computes static optical flow, and produces camera poses and keyframes. Mapping thread integrates input sparse point cloud to guide NeRF-based ray sampling and uses dynamic-aware masks to drive keyframe selection and volume rendering, preserving static surface geometry. Loop detection thread detects revisited areas and performs global bundle adjustment, enhancing long-range consistency. A dense semantic-aware SLAM framework using class-wise scene decomposition with a hybrid point-based Neural Field mapping module. Introduces a multi-class neural scene representation that explicitly links object classes to NeRF camera poses. Leverages 2D semantic priors and multiview image features to strengthen pose estimation through back-projected geometric constraints. Trains a lightweight coarse model via self-supervision to accelerate tracking. Refines geometry by supervising occupancy with Gaussian-distributed priors. The integration of semantic information into 3D Gaussian Splatting for SLAM emerged as a natural extension of both semantic SLAM and 3DGS. Early works like LIVGaussMap [184] focused on geometric initialization using LiDAR. Subsequently, methods such as SGS-SLAM [185], NEDS-SLAM [186], and SemGauss-SLAM [187] incorporated semantic information by distilling 2D semantic labels. Concurrently, other approaches like DDN-SLAM [251] and DNS-SLAM [254] explored semantic priors within NeRF-based or hybrid neural field representations to handle dynamic scenes and improve pose estimation. These methods aim to enhance the robustness of SLAM in complex environments by leveraging high-level semantic cues alongside low-level photometric and geometric constraints. name: SemGauss-SLAM
head: SGS-SLAM, NEDS-SLAM
body: SemGauss-SLAM is a simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) method that integrates semantic information into the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework. It distinguishes itself from standard radiance-field optimization by distilling 2D semantic labels to guide the Gaussian representation, enabling semantic-aware mapping. Inputs: A sequence of RGB-D images (or RGB images with depth estimation), camera poses (initially estimated via visual odometry), and 2D semantic segmentation masks. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with semantic attributes, optimized camera poses, and a semantic map. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Each Gaussian i is defined by position \mui, covariance \Sigmai (or rotation Ri and scale si), opacity \alphai, spherical harmonics coefficients ci, and a semantic label li. Semantic Label: li is a discrete class identifier or a probability vector over semantic classes. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using visual features or LiDAR points if available. 2. Forward Rendering: Render the scene to obtain RGB and depth images using differentiable rasterization. 3. Semantic Distillation: Obtain 2D semantic masks from a pre-trained 2D segmentation network or dataset annotations. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss between rendered and input RGB images. Compute a semantic consistency loss between the rendered semantic features and the 2D semantic masks. 5. Optimization: Update Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color, semantics) and camera poses to minimize the combined loss. 6. Adaptive Control: Apply Gaussian splitting and pruning based on opacity and gradient magnitude, potentially guided by semantic boundaries to avoid redundant splitting. Formulas: Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{sem} \mathcal{L}{sem}. \mathcal{L}{rgb}: Photometric reconstruction loss. \mathcal{L}{sem}: Semantic distillation loss, measuring the discrepancy between projected 2D semantic labels and rendered semantic features. \lambda{sem}: Weight for the semantic loss. Parameters: \lambda{sem}: Not given in the sources. Semantic segmentation model: Not specified, but implied to be a standard 2D method. Edge cases and pitfalls: Semantic ambiguity in textureless regions may lead to incorrect label propagation. Misalignment between 2D semantic masks and 3D Gaussians due to depth errors can degrade map quality. SGS-SLAM: A variant that considers Gaussian semantic information. NEDS-SLAM: Another variant integrating semantic information into SLAM. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables semantic understanding in the reconstructed map, useful for robotics tasks like navigation and manipulation. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of 2D semantic segmentation. Origin: SemGauss-SLAM, along with SGS-SLAM and NEDS-SLAM, was introduced to enhance 3D Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM by incorporating semantic information. History: It builds on earlier methods like LIVGaussMap which used LiDAR for initialization. Usage: Used in robotics for relocalization, navigation, and 6D pose estimation. name: Unsupervised Asset Grouping
head: Asset Grouping via JSD Clustering
body: Unsupervised Asset Grouping is a method for categorizing discovered objects in a scene by comparing the distributions of color and semantic features among image patches using Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) and agglomerative clustering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SemGauss-SLAM by operating on a discretized ground feature plane to group assets without requiring explicit object pose information or supervised labels, enabling the construction of a cross-scene asset library. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An inferred RGB-DINO ground feature plane M{\text{rgb-dino}}, where each pixel (x, y) is interpolated from discrete grids M{\text{rgb}} and M{\text{dino}} via decoders \text{Dec}{\text{rgb}} and \text{Dec}{\text{dino}} to form m{\text{rgb-dino}} = \text{Interp}(M{\text{rgb-dino}}, (x, y)). Output: A set of labeled object feature patches K, grouped into clusters, with a selected template object per cluster and a BEV layout defined by rotation angles \theta. Data Structures: M{\text{rgb-dino}}: A 2D grid of features combining color and semantic (DINO) embeddings. K: A set of object feature patches, each enclosed in a bounding box. P{\text{rgb-dino}}: The set of all RGB-DINO feature patches in the scene. \hat{p}: The template RGB-DINO feature patch selected from a cluster. H = (H\sigma, H{\text{rgb}}): Shared vertical feature axes (used in cross-scene extension). Steps: 1. Discretization: Discretize the continuous feature plane M{\text{rgb-dino}} using a clustering algorithm (e.g., K-means) to identify distinct regions. This results in a set of labeled object feature patches K. 2. Similarity Measurement: For any two object patches ki, kj \in K, compute the similarity between them using the Jensen-Shannon Divergence over the distribution of their labels, denoted as \text{JSD}(ki || kj). 3. Clustering: Perform agglomerative clustering on the patches in K using the JSD values as the distance metric. The number of clusters is determined by inspecting training views and can be flexibly adjusted to control categorization granularity. 4. Template Selection: Select one template object from each resulting cluster. This selection can be random or user-defined. 5. Layout Extraction: For each template \hat{p} and its copies p \in P{\text{rgb-dino}}, extract the scene layout in Bird's Eye View (BEV) by optimizing a rotation angle \theta. The optimal angle \theta^ minimizes the pixel-wise squared error between the template and the rotated copy: \theta^ = \arg\min\theta \sumi \|\hat{p}i - R\theta(pi)\|2^2 where R\theta rotates the input feature patch p by angle \theta. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def unsupervisedassetgrouping(Mrgbdino): # Step 1: Discretize feature plane into labeled patches # K is a list of patches, each with a bounding box and label distribution K = kmeansclustering(Mrgbdino) # Step 2 & 3: Compute JSD distances and perform agglomerative clustering # Distance matrix D where D[i,j] = JSD(K[i], K[j]) D = computejsddistancematrix(K) # Perform agglomerative clustering with JSD metric # numclusters is determined by inspecting training views clusters = agglomerativeclustering(K, D, numclusters) # Step 4: Select templates templates = [] for cluster in clusters: # Random or user-defined selection template = random.choice(cluster) templates.append(template) # Step 5: Extract BEV layout via rotation optimization layout = {} for template in templates: phat = template.patch # Find all copies of this asset in the scene copies = findsimilarpatches(phat, Mrgbdino) besttheta = 0 minloss = infinity # Optimize rotation angle theta for theta in range(0, 360, 1): # Discrete search or gradient descent # Rotate copy patches by theta rotatedcopies = [rotatepatch(p, theta) for p in copies] # Compute pixel-wise loss loss = sumsquarederror(phat, rotatedcopies) if loss < minloss: minloss = loss besttheta = theta layout[template.id] = besttheta return clusters, templates, layout def computejsddistancematrix(patches): n = len(patches) D = zeros((n, n)) for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1, n): # JSD over label distributions of patches i and j D[i, j] = jensenshannondivergence(patches[i].labels, patches[j].labels) D[j, i] = D[i, j] return D Parameters: Clustering Algorithm: K-means is used for initial discretization. Distance Metric: Jensen-Shannon Divergence. Number of Clusters: Not fixed; set by inspecting training views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Absence of Pose Information: Pixel-wise comparison is not ideal without pose; JSD on distributions is required. Granularity: The number of clusters must be manually adjusted based on user intent or scene complexity. A framework that represents a scene using template feature patches, BEV layout, shared vertical feature axes, and MLP decoders, enabling cross-scene asset discovery by sharing vertical axes among different scenes. It constructs a library storing template feature patches by sharing vertical axes across scenes, allowing newly configured scenes to be rendered directly without retraining by using the shared axes and decoders with new template patches and layouts. This overcomes limitations of voxel-based representations that lack constraints for cross-scene analogue discovery. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of patches N and the clustering algorithm. Agglomerative clustering is typically O(N^3) or O(N^2 \log N) depending on implementation. Optimization of \theta for each template adds a cost proportional to the number of copies and the search space for \theta. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the feature plane M{\text{rgb-dino}}, the patches K, and the distance matrix D (O(N^2)). Strengths: Enables unsupervised categorization and cross-scene asset reuse without retraining. Limitations: Requires a synthetic dataset or pre-trained feature extractors (RGB-DINO); granularity is user-dependent. When to Use: When building a reusable asset library from multiple scenes or when unsupervised object categorization is needed in ground feature plane representations. Originated in the paper "AssetField: Assets Mining and Reconfiguration in Ground Feature Plane Representation" (2023). It addresses the lack of constraints in previous voxel-based neural representations that prevented cross-scene analogue discovery, leveraging the potential of neural representations to share vertical feature axes across scenes. name: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) Representation
head: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (INGP), Photon Field Networks, Photon Fields
body: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representation is a method for encoding a 3D scene as a continuous volumetric function using a neural network, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis from sparse 2D images. It solves the problem of reconstructing complex lighting and geometry without explicit mesh extraction by mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Unlike explicit representations like Gaussian Splatting which store millions of discrete blobs, NeRF stores the scene implicitly within a network, trading higher memory usage for compactness and smoother interpolation, though it typically requires significantly more training time and slower rendering speeds. The NeRF representation generally refers to the implicit neural field formulation introduced by Mildenhall et al., though the provided notes also detail specific variants like Photon Field Networks (INGP) and the explicit Gaussian Splatting representation often grouped under this family in SLAM contexts. The core NeRF mechanism involves training a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict volume density and view-dependent color. Inputs: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and a 2D view direction vector \vec{\omega} = (\theta, \phi). Outputs: Volume density \sigma (scattering coefficient) and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} = (R, G, B). Neural Network: A fully connected MLP. Standard configurations use 8 layers with 256 hidden units, using ReLU activations, with positional encoding applied to inputs. Positional Encoding: Inputs \mathbf{x} and \vec{\omega} are mapped to higher dimensions using sine and cosine functions at multiple frequencies to help the network learn high-frequency details. Volumetric Rendering: The scene is rendered by sampling points along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\vec{\omega}. 1. Initialization: Collect a set of images with known camera poses (e.g., from Structure from Motion like COLMAP). 2. Sampling: For each pixel in a training image, cast a ray from the camera origin through the pixel. Sample N points along the ray within the scene bounds. 3. Network Evaluation: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i and view direction \vec{\omega}, pass the encoded inputs through the MLP to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. 4. Alpha Compositing: Compute the final pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) by integrating along the ray using alpha compositing: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity of the i-th segment, \deltai is the distance between samples, and Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance. 5. Loss Computation: Compare the rendered image with the ground truth image using a loss function, typically combining L1 loss and Structural Similarity (SSIM). 6. Optimization: Backpropagate the loss to update the MLP weights using gradient descent (e.g., Adam). Radiance Estimation (Photon Fields variant): For Photon Field Networks, the field approximates indirect radiance Li: P{\phi}(x, g, \vec{\omega}) \approx Li(x, \vec{\omega}) = \int{\Omega{4\pi}} pg(x, \vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i) L(x, \vec{\omega}i) d\omegai \quad (4) where g is the phase function coefficient. KNN Radiance Estimation: Li(x, \vec{\omega}) \approx \sum{n=1}^K pg(x, \vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}n) \frac{\Phin}{4\pi r^3} \quad (5) where r is the distance to the farthest photon, \Phin is photon intensity, and pg is the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Target Encoding: Li'(x, \vec{\omega}) = \begin{cases} -\frac{\log{10}(Li(x, \vec{\omega}))}{\psi} & \text{if } Li(x, \vec{\omega}) > \frac{1}{10^{\psi}} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (6) where \psi is the precision parameter (typically 4-6). Inverse Transformation: Li(x, \vec{\omega}) = 10^{-Li'(x, \vec{\omega})} \cdot \Psi \quad (7). \psi: Maximum desired floating point precision in digits beyond zero. Values of 4 to 6 are sufficient. G: Set of discrete phase coefficients for photon assignment. G = \{-0.75, 0.0, 0.75\} is a common compromise. K: Number of neighbors in KNN query. K=1024 is used in Photon Fields. Batch Size: 2^{16} samples per batch for training. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, network, numsamples): # Sample points along the ray tvals = linspace(raynear, rayfar, numsamples) points = rayorigin + outerproduct(tvals, raydirection) # Encode inputs (positional encoding omitted for brevity) encodedpoints = positionalencoding(points) encodeddirs = positionalencoding(raydirection) # Evaluate network densities, colors = network(encodedpoints, encodeddirs) # Compute alphas and transmittance deltas = diff(tvals) alphas = 1.0 - exp(-densities deltas) transmittance = exp(-cumsum(densities deltas)) # Composite color weights = alphas transmittance finalcolor = sum(weights colors) return finalcolor def trainphotonfield(photonmap, network, batchsize=216, psi=4): kdtree = buildkdtree(photonmap) for step in range(numsteps): # Generate random samples x = randomuniformgrid(batchsize) omega = randomuniformdirections(batchsize) g = randomchoice([-0.75, 0.0, 0.75], batchsize) # Estimate ground truth radiance using KNN Li = estimateradianceknn(kdtree, x, omega, g, K=1024) # Encode target Liprime = encodetarget(Li, psi) # Forward pass Lipred = network(x, omega, g) # Compute loss and update loss = mse(Lipred, Liprime) network.backward(loss) network.update() Precision: Radiance values can vary widely; logarithmic encoding is necessary to normalize targets to [0,1] for stable training. Boundaries: Ray sampling must be bounded to avoid infinite integration; near and far clipping planes are required. Degenerate Input: If camera poses are inaccurate, the network may learn inconsistent geometry, leading to artifacts. Isolates static background by training exclusively on background pixels, using an emptiness regularizer [12484-scene-nerf.md]. Decomposes scenes into albedo, geometry, and lighting for outdoor relighting, unlike standard NeRF's Lambertian assumption [14477-nerf-osr.md]. Uses an explicit RGB\alpha volume for real-time rendering, avoiding per-ray neural evaluation [15335-explicit-volumetric-rendering-with-multiple-view-aggregation.md]. Models facial dynamics using morphable model parameters, requiring only monocular input [16398-dynamic-neural-radiance-fields.md]. Compresses NeRF by pruning MLP weights, reducing storage and inference time [17703-neural-network-pruning-for-nerf.md]. Encodes images into voxel grids via CNN, enabling latent compression [17789-scene-auto-encoder.md]. Coarse-to-fine tracking with KL regularization over ray termination. Dense RGB-D SLAM with hierarchical semantic encoding. Integrates local feature correspondences for pose initialization. Merges traditional SLAM with NeRF for online reconstruction, using IMU error correction. Time Complexity: Training is slow, often taking hours to days, as the network must converge to represent the entire scene. Rendering is slow (seconds per image) because it requires evaluating the network at many points along each ray. Memory Complexity: The network weights are compact (few megabytes), but training requires storing large datasets of images and poses. Performance: On standard hardware, NeRF achieves high visual quality but low frame rates. Gaussian Splatting variants offer >100 FPS but use hundreds of megabytes of memory. Strengths: High-quality novel view synthesis, handles complex lighting and reflections implicitly, no explicit mesh required. Limitations: Slow training and rendering, prone to floating artifacts and aliasing in sparse regions, difficult to extract clean meshes. When to Use: When visual quality is paramount and real-time performance is not required, or for offline content creation. When Not to Use: For real-time applications requiring high frame rates, or when explicit geometry extraction is needed. NeRF was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020, revolutionizing novel view synthesis by using neural networks to represent 3D scenes implicitly. The concept of Photon Field Networks (INGP) was later introduced to accelerate global illumination computation by replacing expensive photon tracing with neural inference. Gaussian Splatting, introduced by Kerbl et al. at SIGGRAPH 2023, offers an explicit alternative that trades memory for speed. These methods are widely used in virtual reality, film, robotics, and cultural heritage preservation. name: Scene NeRF
body: Scene NeRF is a method for isolating and rendering the static background of a scene by training a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) exclusively on pixels identified as background via human segmentation masks. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly excluding dynamic foreground elements (e.g., humans) from the training data and employing an emptiness regularizer to prevent artifacts in empty space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A video sequence of the scene; human segmentation masks for each frame; camera poses and sparse scene model from COLMAP; multi-view stereo (MVS) depth maps; dense monocular depth maps. Outputs: A trained Scene NeRF model \mathcal{N}s that renders background colors and densities. Data Structures: Segmentation Mask M(\mathbf{r}): A binary value for each ray \mathbf{r}. M(\mathbf{r}) = 1 if the ray intersects the human/foreground, M(\mathbf{r}) = 0 if it corresponds to the background. Fused Depth Map D{fuse}(\mathbf{r}): A depth estimate for each ray, obtained by fusing MVS and monocular depth maps. Preprocessing: 1. Use COLMAP to obtain camera poses, sparse scene model, and MVS depth maps D{mvs}. 2. Retrieve human segmentation maps using Mask-RCNN. 3. Fill holes in D{mvs} using dense monocular depth maps D{mono} (e.g., Miangoleh et al.). 4. Fuse D{mvs} and D{mono} into D{fuse} by finding a linear mapping between the two depth maps using pixels with both estimates, then transforming D{mono} values to match the D{mvs} scale. Training Steps: For each ray \mathbf{r} sampled from the camera: 1. Determine Mask: Check if the ray corresponds to the human or background using the segmentation mask M(\mathbf{r}). 2. Sample Terminating Depth: Determine the terminating depth \hat{z}\mathbf{r} for the emptiness regularizer by querying the fused depth map: \hat{z}\mathbf{r} = D{fuse}(\mathbf{r}). 3. Compute RGB Loss: Calculate the reconstruction loss only for background pixels. If M(\mathbf{r}) = 1, the loss is zero. If M(\mathbf{r}) = 0, the loss is the difference between the rendered color \mathbf{C}s(\mathbf{r}) and the ground-truth color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}): \mathcal{L}{s,rgb}(\mathbf{r}) = (1 - M(\mathbf{r})) \| \mathbf{C}s(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) \| 4. Compute Emptiness Regularizer: Calculate the integral of the scene density \sigmas from the near plane tn to a slack margin \alpha \hat{z}\mathbf{r}. This forces density to be zero in the empty space between the camera and the estimated scene surface: \mathcal{L}{s,empty}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{\alpha \hat{z}\mathbf{r}} \sigmas(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt where \alpha = 0.8 is a slack margin to avoid strong regularization when depth estimates are inaccurate. 5. Compute Total Loss: Sum the RGB loss and the emptiness regularizer weighted by \lambda{empty}: \mathcal{L}{s} = \mathcal{L}{s,rgb}(\mathbf{r}) + \lambda{empty} \mathcal{L}{s,empty}(\mathbf{r}) where \lambda{empty} = 0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computescenenerfloss(rays, gtcolors, masks, fuseddepths, lambdaempty=0.1, alpha=0.8, tn=0.0): """ Computes the total training loss for Scene NeRF over a batch of rays. Assumes a standard volume rendering forward pass is available. """ totalloss = 0.0 for r, cgt, m, zfuse in zip(rays, gtcolors, masks, fuseddepths): # Standard volume rendering forward pass to obtain rendered color Cs, # density samples sigmas, and depth samples tsamples along the ray cs, sigmas, tsamples = volumerenderforwardpass(r) # 1. RGB Loss: weighted by background mask M(r) # If m=1 (human), loss is 0. If m=0 (background), loss is L2 norm difference. rgbloss = (1.0 - m) norm(cs - cgt) # 2. Emptiness Regularizer: integral of density from tn to alpha zfuse maxdepth = alpha zfuse densityintegral = 0.0 for i in range(len(tsamples) - 1): tcurr, tnext = tsamples[i], tsamples[i+1] # Clamp integration interval to [tn, maxdepth] upper = min(tnext, maxdepth) lower = max(tcurr, tn) if upper > lower: densityintegral += sigmas[i] (upper - lower) emptyloss = densityintegral # 3. Total Loss loss = rgbloss + lambdaempty emptyloss totalloss += loss return totalloss Parameters: \lambda{empty}: Hyperparameter controlling the weight of the emptiness regularizer. Set to 0.1 in all experiments. \alpha: Slack margin for the emptiness regularizer. Set to 0.8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hazy Objects: Simply minimizing the RGB reconstruction loss leads to 'hazy' objects floating in the scene. This is resolved by adding the emptiness regularizer. Inaccurate Depth: The slack margin \alpha = 0.8 is used to avoid strong regularization when depth estimates are inaccurate. Single Human Assumption: The method assumes a single human being in the scene, though it can be trivially extended. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Effectively isolates static background from dynamic foreground (humans). Limitations: Requires accurate human segmentation masks and depth estimates. Performance degrades if depth estimates are inaccurate without the slack margin. When to Use: When the goal is to reconstruct the static background of a scene with dynamic foreground elements, given video input and segmentation masks. Origin: The method is described in "NeuMan: Neural Human Radiance Field from a Single Video" by W. Jiang et al.. History and Development: The approach builds on traditional motion detection work by using a NeRF for the background model. It follows the approach of Video-NeRF in using an emptiness regularizer. Where it is Used: Used for reconstructing static backgrounds in videos containing human subjects. NeuMan: Neural Human Radiance Field from a Single Video, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-324, fetched 2026-10-29

name: NeRF-OSR
head: NeRF-OSR Baseline, Neural Radiance Fields for Outdoor Scene Relighting
body: NeRF-OSR is a neural radiance field approach for outdoor scene relighting that learns a neural representation of scene geometry, diffuse albedo, and illumination-dependent shadows from a set of images capturing the same site from different viewpoints and at different times, enabling simultaneous editing of both the scene’s lighting and viewpoint. Unlike standard NeRF which learns a Lambertian model under fixed lighting, NeRF-OSR decomposes the scene into spatial occupancy, illumination, shadowing, and diffuse albedo reflectance, trained in a self-supervised manner from outdoor data captured from various viewpoints and at different illuminations. It sets itself apart from siblings like Scene NeRF by providing explicit intrinsic decomposition (albedo, geometry, lighting) rather than just view-dependent appearance, allowing for physical relighting and albedo editing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multiple RGB images of a single scene, shot at different timings (illumination conditions) and from different viewpoints. Output: A neural representation of the scene that can render novel views under arbitrary lighting conditions, specified by the user via environment maps or Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Data Structures: The method relies on two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to model the scene properties: 1. Density MLP: Takes 3D position x as input and outputs density \sigma(x). 2. Albedo MLP: Takes 3D position x as input and outputs diffuse albedo c{albedo}(x). NeRF-OSR modifies the color output to be albedo and combines it with an explicit lighting model. The final color is not directly predicted by the MLP but is computed as a function of albedo, geometry, and lighting. Illumination and Shadow Model: The method uses an explicit 2nd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) illumination model. The rendering equation is adapted to separate intrinsic properties from lighting: C(o, d) = \sum{i=1}^{N{depth}} T(ti) \alpha(\sigma(xi)\deltai) c(xi) where c(xi) is the color at point xi, derived from the albedo and the illumination model. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Data Pre-processing: Discard dynamic objects (cars, people, bikes) from the training stage using segmentation masks. Estimate masks for sky and vegetation and exclude them from evaluation due to highly varying appearance across weather seasons. Split data into training and testing sets based on recording sessions. 2. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, cast a ray from camera origin o in direction d. Sample N{depth} points \{xi\}{i=1}^{N{depth}} along the ray, where xi = o + ti d. 3. Hierarchical Sampling: To capture small details, perform a coarse pass with stratified sampling. Use the densities from the coarse pass for importance sampling in the final pass. 4. Neural Network Forward Pass: For each sampled point xi, query the Density MLP to get \sigma(xi). Query the Albedo MLP to get c{albedo}(xi). Compute the final color c(xi) by combining c{albedo}(xi) with the scene illumination (SH coefficients) and shadow term. The sources state the model is an explicit function of geometry, albedo, shadow, and lighting conditions. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute transmittance T(ti) = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{N{depth}-1} \sigma(xj)\deltaj). Compute opacity \alpha(y) = 1 - \exp(-y). Compute ray color: C(o, d) = \sum{i=1}^{N{depth}} T(ti) \alpha(\sigma(xi)\deltai) c(xi). Here, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 6. Optimization: Train the MLPs in a self-supervised manner using the observed ground-truth per-pixel colors. Supervise the rendered pixel colors of both the coarse and fine passes with the ground-truth colors. Estimate per-image illumination (SH coefficients) during training. 7. Geometry Extraction (Optional for Real-time): Extract geometry and albedo from the learned model as a mesh using Marching Cubes [16] at resolution 1000^3 voxels. Use the extracted mesh and albedo in an interactive renderer (e.g., OpenGL) for real-time VR rendering. Lighting model for real-time: C{interactive} = C{ambient} + s \odot C{sun} \max\{0, D{sun} \cdot N\}, where C{ambient} is ambient color, s is 0/1 based on shadow map occlusion, C{sun} is sun color, D{sun} is sun direction, and N is mesh normal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderneurospatialray(o, d, densitymlp, albedomlp, shcoeffs, shadowmap): # 1. Stratified sampling from near to far camera plane tcoarse = stratifiedsamplenearfar(o, d) xcoarse = o + tcoarse d sigmacoarse = densitymlp(xcoarse) # 2. Importance sampling for fine pass based on coarse densities tfine = importancesample(tcoarse, sigmacoarse) xfine = o + tfine d sigmafine = densitymlp(xfine) albedofine = albedomlp(xfine) # 3. Compute color from albedo, SH illumination, and shadow cfine = computecolorwithlighting(albedofine, shcoeffs, shadowmap, xfine) # 4. Volume rendering with transmittance and opacity delta = tfine[1:] - tfine[:-1] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmafine delta) T = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigmafine[:-1] delta, dim=0)) color = torch.sum(T alpha cfine, dim=0) return color Parameters: N{depth}: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. Marching Cubes Resolution: 1000^3 voxels. SH Order: 2nd-order. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Inaccuracies: Tiny bumps in learned geometry lead to significant changes in normals and illumination errors. The model may smooth geometry to achieve more accurate lighting, resulting in some blur. Dynamic Objects: Must be masked out; otherwise, they corrupt the static scene representation. Sky/Vegetation: Highly variable appearance makes evaluation difficult; masks should be used to exclude these regions from metrics. Standard NeRF Limitation: Standard NeRF formulation learns a Lambertian model under fixed lighting because c(x) is defined only through an MLP without encoding lighting. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Site 1 PSNR: 19.86 (d/s) and 18.72 (full). Site 2 PSNR: 15.83 (d/s) and 15.43 (full). Site 3 PSNR: 17.38 (d/s) and 16.65 (full). Outperforms Yu et al. [46] and Philip et al. [27] on all sites. Real-time Demo: Runs in real-time on Intel i7-4770 CPU, Nvidia GeForce GTX 970 (4GB VRAM) GPU, Oculus Rift S HMD. System RAM usage below 3 GB. Strengths: Simultaneous novel view and novel lighting generation; explicit intrinsic decomposition (albedo, geometry, lighting); ability to edit albedo and shadows; handles uncontrolled outdoor settings. Limitations: Geometry inaccuracies can cause lighting errors; requires posed images with varying illumination; sky and vegetation are difficult to evaluate due to seasonal changes. When to use: When simultaneous viewpoint and lighting editing of outdoor scenes is required, and intrinsic decomposition is needed. When not to use: When the scene contains significant dynamic objects that cannot be masked, or when only static lighting editing of a single view is needed (simpler methods may suffice). NeRF-OSR was introduced by Viktor Rudnev, Mohamed Elgharib, William Smith, Lingjie Liu, Vladislav Golyanik, and Christian Theobalt from MPI for Informatics, SIC, and University of York. It was published in arXiv:2112.05140v2 on 21 Jul 2022. It is the first neural radiance fields approach for outdoor scene relighting, enabling the learning of scene intrinsics (geometry, albedo, illumination, shadows) from uncontrolled outdoor data. It builds on the original NeRF representation [12096-neural-radiance-field-nerf-representation.md] but extends it with explicit lighting and shadow models. It is used for real-time interactive rendering in VR, albedo editing, and shadow editing. name: Explicit Volumetric Rendering with Multiple View Aggregation
head: Pooled Latent Volume Rendering, RGBα Volume Rendering
body: This method models scene geometry and appearance as an explicit RGBα volume to amortize rendering across multiple views, solving the computational inefficiency of NeRF-like methods where per-ray sampling is independent and not reusable across different viewing angles. Unlike its siblings Scene NeRF, NeRF-OSR, and Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields, which typically rely on implicit field evaluations or sparse ray sampling, this approach generates a dense volumetric representation that enables real-time rendering and the use of structural losses like SSIM during training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of n source views S = \{I1, \dots, In\} with corresponding camera poses P = \{P1, \dots, Pn\} and intrinsic parameters. Outputs: An RGBα volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times ds \times h \times w} and rendered target images \hat{C}. Data Structures: Latent Volume (Zi): An intermediate volumetric representation for each source view i. The exact dimensions are not specified in the sources, but it is processed by a 3D U-Net. RGBα Volume (V): A 4D tensor with channels for Red, Green, Blue, and Alpha (transparency). It has dimensions 4 \times ds \times h \times w, where ds is the number of depth samples, and h, w are the spatial dimensions of the viewing frustum. Numbered Steps: 1. Encode Source Views: For each source view i \in \{1, \dots, n\}, encode the image Ii into a latent volume Zi using the encoding process described in the parent article's Section 3.1. 2. Select Origin: Select an arbitrary source view i^ from the set of source views to serve as the origin of the coordinate system. 3. Align Volumes: Align each latent volume Zi to the origin i^ using the relative transformation P{i, i^} between the pose Pi of view i and the pose P{i^} of the origin. Let \mathcal{T}(P{i, i^}, Zi) denote this aligned volume. 4. Pool Volumes: Compute the pooled volumetric latent \bar{Z} by taking the mean of the aligned latent volumes across all n views: \bar{\mathbf{Z}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i \in n} \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}{i, i^}, \mathbf{Z}i) 5. Generate RGBα Volume: Feed the pooled latent \bar{Z} into a 3D U-Net to generate the explicit RGBα volume V. 6. Perspective Deformation: Apply perspective deformation to the viewing frustum using the intrinsic camera parameters. This is achieved via inverse warping and trilinear sampling. 7. Render: For a given pixel location (i, j), calculate the expected color \hat{C}{i,j} by integrating along the depth samples k=1 \dots ds: \hat{C}{i,j} = \sum{k=1}^{ds} T{i,j}^k \alpha{i,j}^k \mathbf{c}{i,j}^k where the transmittance T{i,j}^k is defined as: T{i,j}^k = \prod{m=1}^{k-1} (1-\alpha{i,j}^m) Here, \mathbf{c}{i,j}^k is the color value from the first 3 channels of V at sample k, and \alpha{i,j}^k is the alpha value from the last channel of V at sample k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderexplicitvolume(sourceviews, poses, intrinsics, originindex): """ sourceviews: List of images [I1,..., In] poses: List of camera poses [P1,..., Pn] intrinsics: Camera intrinsic parameters originindex: Index i of the reference view """ n = len(sourceviews) alignedlatents = [] # Step 1 & 2 & 3: Encode and Align for i in range(n): # Encode view i into latent volume Zi # Note: Exact encoding architecture details are in parent article Sect 3.1 Zi = encodeview(sourceviews[i]) # Calculate relative transformation from view i to origin view Pistar = poses[originindex] Pi = poses[i] Prel = computerelativetransform(Pi, Pistar) # Align Zi to the origin coordinate system Zaligned = transformvolume(Zi, Prel) alignedlatents.append(Zaligned) # Step 4: Pool aligned volumes # Sum the aligned volumes and divide by n pooledlatent = alignedlatents[0] for k in range(1, n): pooledlatent = pooledlatent + alignedlatents[k] pooledlatent = pooledlatent / n # Step 5: Generate RGBα Volume # Feed pooled latent to 3D U-Net V = generatergbalphavolume(pooledlatent) # Step 6 & 7: Render # Apply perspective deformation and integrate renderedimage = perspectivedeformandrender(V, intrinsics) return renderedimage def perspectivedeformandrender(V, intrinsics): """ V: RGBα volume [4, ds, h, w] intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrix K """ # Inverse warping and trilinear sampling based on intrinsics # This step maps the volume V to the target image plane # The exact implementation of inverse warping is referenced in Appendix of # For implementation, one would typically: # 1. Define a grid of 3D points in the camera coordinate system # 2. Project them to 2D pixel coordinates using K # 3. Sample V at these 3D locations using trilinear interpolation # 4. Perform alpha compositing along the ray # Placeholder for the specific inverse warping logic detailed in Appendix # Since the exact warping code is not provided in the main text, # we assume standard inverse warping using K. # Rendered color calculation per pixel (i,j) # See formula in text for integration over ds samples pass Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the SSIM loss in the training objective. Typical value not given in the sources. ds: Number of depth samples. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate System Alignment: The choice of origin view i^ is arbitrary, but all latent volumes must be consistently aligned to this origin to ensure correct pooling. Precision: Trilinear sampling is used for perspective deformation; care must be taken with boundary conditions and interpolation artifacts. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a valid set of source views with known poses. If poses are inaccurate, the alignment and pooling steps will produce incorrect volumetric representations. Scene NeRF Scene NeRF: Focuses on large-scale scene reconstruction. Choose when scalability to large environments is required. NeRF-OSR NeRF-OSR: Handles out-of-sample rendering. Choose when generalizing to unseen objects is critical. Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields: Models time-varying scenes. Choose when dealing with dynamic content. Time Complexity: Rendering is amortized across views. Per-view rendering time is 0.0178s (56 FPS) on an NVIDIA Tesla V100. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the RGBα volume V and latent volumes Zi. Exact memory footprint not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA Tesla V100, rendering 250 views takes 1.022s (245 FPS), which is a 400x speedup over pixelNeRF's 474.8606s (0.5 FPS). Per-view, it is 100x faster than pixelNeRF's 1.9047s. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; supports structural losses like SSIM during training because it renders full images rather than sparse rays. Limitations: Requires explicit volumetric storage; performance depends on the resolution of the RGBα volume. When to Use: When real-time novel view synthesis is required and multiple source views are available. Evaluated on ShapeNet chairs and cars. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and explicit volumes cannot be stored, or when only a single view is available for initialization. The method was introduced in "Fast and Explicit Neural View Synthesis". It addresses the limitation of NeRF-like methods where rendering cannot be amortized across views because each ray integral is independent. By using an explicit RGBα volume, the method allows for efficient rendering and the application of structural losses, which are not directly applicable to NeRF-like methods due to their sparse ray sampling. It has been evaluated on ShapeNet chairs and cars categories, demonstrating competitive visual quality and significant speed improvements over baselines like pixelNeRF. Fast and Explicit Neural View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv51458.2022.00009, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields
head: 4D Facial Avatar Reconstruction, Dynamic NeRF, Dynamic Neural Radiance Field (Dynamic NeRF) for Facial Avatars, Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields for Monocular 4D Facial Avatar Reconstruction, Dynamic Neural Scene Representation Network, Dynamic Radiance Field
body: Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (Dynamic NeRF) is a method for modeling the appearance and dynamics of a human face using an implicit volumetric representation. It combines a neural scene representation network with a low-dimensional morphable model to handle facial dynamics, allowing novel viewpoint and expression synthesis from monocular input. Unlike static NeRF methods, this approach handles dynamically changing surfaces by conditioning the neural network on morphable model expression parameters and a per-frame latent code. It differs from other volumetric approaches by requiring only a single view from a fixed camera (e.g., webcam) instead of an expensive calibrated multi-view rig. Inputs and Outputs Input: A monocular portrait video sequence of a subject, a static background image B (captured without the subject), and a 3D morphable model (3DMM). Output: A rendered RGB image for a specified head pose and facial expression. Data Structures Morphable Model Parameters: Pose Pi \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}: Rigid pose matrix (rotation and translation) for frame i. Expression \deltai \in \mathbb{R}^{76}: Coefficients of a low-dimensional delta-blendshape basis. Latent Code: \gammai \in \mathbb{R}^{32}: A learnable per-frame latent code vector. Network Weights: \theta{coarse}: Weights for the coarse dynamic radiance field MLP. \theta{fine}: Weights for the fine dynamic radiance field MLP. Positional Encoding: Position p: Encoded with 10 frequencies. Viewing direction \vec{v}: Encoded with 4 frequencies. Numbered Steps 1. Preprocessing (Tracking): Apply facial expression tracking using a 3D morphable model to estimate pose parameters Pi and expression parameters \deltai for each frame i in the training video. 2. Ray Dispatch: For each frame to be synthesized, dispatch rays in a canonical space shared by all frames. Transform the rays from camera space to this canonical space using the pose parameters Pi from the morphable model. 3. Coarse Sampling: Perform stratified sampling of 64 points along each viewing ray. 95% of rays correspond to pixels within the head bounding box. Sample 2048 viewing rays per training image/iteration. 4. Coarse Network Evaluation: For each sample point t on ray r, input its canonical position p, view direction \vec{v}, expression parameters \deltai, and latent code \gammai into the coarse dynamic radiance field MLP D{\theta{coarse}}. The MLP outputs density \sigma and color RGB. 5. Importance Sampling: Use the density distribution predicted by the coarse network to guide importance sampling for the fine network. 6. Fine Sampling: Re-sample 64 points along the ray based on the coarse density distribution. 7. Fine Network Evaluation: For each fine sample point, input p, \vec{v}, \deltai, and \gammai into the fine dynamic radiance field MLP D{\theta{fine}}. The MLP outputs density \sigma and color RGB. 8. Volumetric Integration: Compute the expected color C(r) for the ray by integrating the density and color values predicted by the fine network along the ray. The transmittance T(t) is accumulated along the ray. 9. Background Handling: For the last sample point of each ray (representing the background), set the color to the corresponding value from the static background image B. The network learns to predict low density for foreground samples if the ray hits a background pixel, and high density for foreground pixels, achieving self-supervised foreground-background decomposition. 10. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss for both coarse and fine networks against the ground truth image Ii. 11. Optimization: Update \theta{coarse}, \theta{fine}, and \gammai using the Adam optimizer. 12. Test Time Synthesis: At test time, always employ the latent code \gamma from the first frame of the training set. Formulas The dynamic radiance field MLP D\theta takes position p, view direction \vec{v}, facial expression dynamics \delta, and a per-frame latent code \gamma as inputs, and outputs color (RGB) and density (\sigma): D\theta (p, \vec{v}, \delta, \gamma) = (RGB, \sigma) The expected color C(r) of a camera ray r(t) = c + t\vec{d} with camera center c, viewing direction \vec{d}, and near/far bounds z{near}, z{far} is evaluated as: C(r; \theta, P, \delta, \gamma) = \int{z{near}}^{z{far}} \sigma\theta(r(t)) \cdot RGB\theta(r(t), \vec{d}) \cdot T(t) \, dt Where T(t) is the accumulated transmittance along the ray. The total loss is the sum of losses for the coarse and fine networks: L{total} = \sum{i=1}^M (Li(\theta{coarse}) + Li(\theta{fine})) Where the loss for a single image i is: Li(\theta) = \sum{j \in pixels} ||C(rj; \theta, Pi, \deltai, \gammai) - Ii[j]||^2 Parameters Positional Encoding: 10 frequencies for position p, 4 frequencies for viewing direction \vec{v}. Latent Code Regularization: L2 loss with weight decay \lambda = 0.05. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate lr = 0.0005. Training Resolution: 512 \times 512 images. Training Duration: 400k iterations. Sampling: 64 points for coarse, 64 points for fine. Ray Batch: 2048 rays per iteration. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Eye Dynamics: The morphable model does not model eye blinks or eye movements explicitly. These cannot be directly controlled, though they are implicitly correlated with other expression parameters. Data Requirements: Requires more training data than static NeRF (which needs ~100 posed images) because it must generalize over the space of expression vectors. Test Time Latent Code: At test time, the latent code from the first frame of the training set must be used, not a new random or optimized code. Pseudocode Unverified code. Returns shape (..., 3) return points Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses two MLPs (coarse and fine), each with 8 backbone layers of 256 neurons and a color branch of 4 layers of 128 neurons. The training requires 400k iterations. Measured Performance: On a dataset of monocular portrait videos, the method achieves an LPIPS of 0.06 (full training data). With latent codes, LPIPS is 0.059, compared to 0.068 without. PSNR is 26.85, SSIM is 0.95, and L1 is 0.019. Scaling: The method requires more training data than static NeRF. Training on half or quarter of the data significantly degrades quality. Strengths: Captures arbitrary geometry and topology such as hair, eyeware, and hats, which explicit geometry methods struggle with. Generates 3D-consistent results with view-dependent effects (e.g., glasses reflections). Allows explicit control over head pose and expressions. Requires only a single view from a fixed camera. Limitations: Does not explicitly model eye blinks or eye movements. Requires a large training corpus to generalize over the space of expression vectors. Focuses on the human head; upper body dynamics are not modeled. Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields were introduced in the paper "Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields for Monocular 4D Facial Avatar Reconstruction". The method builds on the static NeRF approach by Mildenhall et al.. It was developed to address the challenge of reconstructing 4D models of humans, especially the human face, for AR and VR telepresence applications. The method allows for the reconstruction of 4D facial avatars from monocular video sequences, making it suitable for capturing avatars of end users at home using only 2 minutes of their time. name: Neural Network Pruning for NeRF
head: Global Pruning, Magnitude Pruning, Model Pruning, Neural Network Pruning for 3D Scene Compression
body: This method compresses a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by removing weights with the smallest magnitudes from the fully-connected neural network representing the scene, thereby reducing storage size and inference time. Unlike traditional 3D compression which stores and compresses redundant 2D images, this approach compresses the functional representation directly, avoiding the inefficiency of decoding multiple images before rendering. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Scene NeRF and NeRF-OSR by its reliance on unstructured magnitude pruning of the MLP weights rather than structural changes to the scene representation or octree-based optimizations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model, defined as a fully-connected neural network (MLP) that maps a 5D coordinate (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) to volume density \sigma and view-dependent emitted radiance c. Output: A pruned NeRF model with reduced weight count and a retrained version of the pruned model. Data Structures: The NeRF model consists of fully-connected layers. The weights W are stored in standard dense tensor formats. Pruning creates a sparse mask M where M{ij} = 1 if the weight is kept, and 0 if removed. The compressed model stores only the non-zero weights and their indices. Parameters: Pruning Ratio (p): The fraction of weights to remove. Typical values used in experiments are 30%, 50%, 70%, and 90%. Pruning Strategy: Global magnitude pruning. A single threshold \tau is calculated across all layers of the network. Weights with absolute magnitude |w| < \tau are set to zero. Retraining Duration: 500 iterations. Retraining Hyperparameters: Identical to the hyperparameters of the corresponding iterations in the original NeRF paper. Steps: 1. Calculate Threshold: Compute the pruning threshold \tau for the global magnitude pruning. Sort all weights w in the network by absolute magnitude |w|. Select the threshold such that the bottom p percent of weights are below \tau. 2. Apply Mask: Create a binary mask M where M{ij} = 0 if |W{ij}| < \tau, and M{ij} = 1 otherwise. Update the weights: W{pruned} = W \odot M (element-wise multiplication). 3. Initialize Retraining: Load the pruned weights W{pruned} as the initialization for the training process. 4. Retrain: Perform gradient descent optimization for 500 iterations using the original NeRF training loss (MSE between rendered and ground truth colors) and the original hyperparameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pruneandretrain(nerfmodel, pruningratio, retrainiterations=500): """ Compress a NeRF model using global magnitude pruning and retrain. Args: nerfmodel: The trained NeRF MLP model. pruningratio: Float between 0 and 1, fraction of weights to remove. retrainiterations: Number of optimization steps for retraining. Returns: retrainedmodel: The pruned and retrained NeRF model. """ # 1. Collect all weights allweights = [] for param in nerfmodel.parameters(): allweights.extend(param.data.abs().flatten().tolist()) # 2. Determine threshold for global pruning # Sort weights to find the value at the pruningratio percentile allweights.sort() thresholdindex = int(len(allweights) pruningratio) threshold = allweights[thresholdindex] if thresholdindex < len(allweights) else 0.0 # 3. Apply pruning mask to each layer for param in nerfmodel.parameters(): mask = (param.data.abs() >= threshold).float() param.data = param.data mask # 4. Retrain the pruned model # Note: In a real implementation, this involves setting up the optimizer # and the NeRF rendering loss function. # The hyperparameters (learning rate, etc.) must match the original NeRF paper # for the corresponding iteration count. optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(nerfmodel.parameters(), lr=5e-4) # Typical NeRF LR for i in range(retrainiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Render a batch of rays using the pruned model # This involves sampling points along rays and passing them through the MLP renderedcolors = renderrays(nerfmodel, raybatch) # Calculate loss against ground truth colors loss = mseloss(renderedcolors, raybatch.gtcolors) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerfmodel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts without Retraining: Pruning without retraining causes visible artifacts in geometry and coloring starting at 50% pruning ratio, with disturbing quality degradation at 70% and severe artifacts at 90%. Retraining Limitations: Retraining fixes most artifacts, but quality remains significantly degraded at 90% pruning ratio. Global vs. Structured: Global pruning is chosen over structured pruning for flexibility in adjusting sparsity across different layers, yielding a better performance-compression trade-off. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The storage size is reduced by a factor of 1/(1-p), where p is the pruning ratio. For example, 90% pruning yields a compression factor of \times 10.00. Inference Time: Pruning speeds up inference compared to other neural network compression approaches, providing faster rendering. Measured Performance: Fern Dataset: Original: PSNR 24.73, MSE 0.0066, Compression \times 1.00. 30% Pruned: PSNR 25.41, MSE 0.0067, Compression \times 1.43. 30% Retrained: PSNR 25.45, MSE 0.0062, Compression \times 1.43. 50% Pruned: PSNR 22.48, MSE 0.0116, Compression \times 2.00. 50% Retrained: PSNR 24.78, MSE 0.0071, Compression \times 2.00. 70% Pruned: PSNR 20.97, MSE 0.0165, Compression \times 3.33. 70% Retrained: PSNR 22.51, MSE 0.0134, Compression \times 3.33. 90% Pruned: PSNR 16.87, MSE 0.0706, Compression \times 10.00. 90% Retrained: PSNR 20.25, MSE 0.0318, Compression \times 10.00. Lego Dataset: Original: PSNR 31.70, MSE 0.0028, Compression \times 1.00. 30% Pruned: PSNR 29.14, MSE 0.0034, Compression \times 1.43. 30% Retrained: PSNR 30.43, MSE 0.0029, Compression \times 1.43. 50% Pruned: PSNR 25.32, MSE 0.0077, Compression \times 2.00. 50% Retrained: PSNR 26.97, MSE 0.0051, Compression \times 2.00. 70% Pruned: PSNR 21.70, MSE 0.0144, Compression \times 3.33. 70% Retrained: PSNR 25.26, MSE 0.0085, Compression \times 3.33. 90% Pruned: PSNR 15.99, MSE 0.0786, Compression \times 10.00. 90% Retrained: PSNR 20.42, MSE 0.0352, Compression \times 10.00. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Intuitive implementation; speeds up inference; avoids redundancy of storing 2D images. Limitations: High pruning ratios (e.g., 90%) lead to severe quality loss even after retraining; requires retraining to mitigate artifacts. When to Use: Use this method when storage size and inference speed are critical constraints for a NeRF application, and moderate compression ratios (30-70%) are acceptable. Avoid for very high compression ratios (>90%) due to significant quality degradation. This method was introduced in a 2021 project by Stanford CS 231A students. It applies neural network compression techniques, specifically magnitude pruning, to the regression task of rendering 3D scenes, extending the success of pruning in classification tasks to neural functional representations. It is applied to NeRF models trained on the Lego and Fern datasets. Neural 3D Scene Compression via Model Compression, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2105.03120, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Scene Auto-Encoder
head: NFLDM Scene Auto-Encoder, Neural Field Voxel Grid Construction
body: The Scene Auto-Encoder is a method that encodes a set of RGB images with known camera poses and depth measurements into a 3D neural field represented as density and feature voxel grids, enabling novel view synthesis and serving as input for latent compression. It differs from its siblings, such as Scene NeRF and NeRF-OSR, by explicitly constructing a discrete voxel-based representation via a 2D CNN encoder and frustum lifting, rather than relying solely on a continuous MLP to map coordinates to radiance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N RGB images i, their corresponding camera poses \kappa, and depth measurements \rho (sparse or dense). Outputs: A shared 3D neural field represented as a density voxel grid V{Density} and a feature voxel grid V{Feat}, and reconstructed images \hat{i}. Data Structures: Voxel Grids (V{Density}, V{Feat}): 3D grids with spatial dimensions 32 \times 128 \times 128 (Z \times X \times Y). V{Density} stores density values \sigma. V{Feat} stores feature vectors of dimension C. Voxel sizes vary by dataset: VizDoom (4 \text{ game units})^3, Replica (0.125\text{m})^3, Carla (0.75\text{m})^3, AVD (non-uniform: 0.2\text{m} center, 1.6\text{m} horizontal/2.4\text{m} vertical furthest). Frustum (F): A discrete 3D structure of size H \times W \times D for each input image, where H, W are the spatial dimensions of the encoded feature map (smaller than input image size) and D is the number of depth samples. Encoded Tensor: For each image, a 2D tensor of dimension H \times W \times (D+C) produced by the encoder. Steps: 1. Image Encoding: Encode each of the N input images independently using an EfficientNet-B1 encoder. Replace Batchnorm layers with Instance normalization. Modify the second and eighth blocks' padding and stride to preserve spatial resolutions, resulting in an 8x downsampling factor. Replace the EfficientNet-B1 head with a bilinear upsampling layer, concatenate with features before the last downsampling layer, and pass through two Conv2d-ReLU-BatchNorm2d layers (first Conv2D increases channels from 432 to 512). Process features through two separate two-layer Conv networks to reduce channel dimensions to C (features) and D (density) for each pixel. Clamp density values to [-10, 10] and apply softplus activation. 2. Frustum Construction: For each image i with pose \kappa: Build a discrete frustum of size H \times W \times D using camera poses \kappa. The frustum contains image features and density values for each pixel along a pre-defined discrete set of D depths. Assign density values: The d-th channel of the CNN’s output at pixel (h, w) becomes the density value \sigma{(h,w,d)} of the frustum entry at (h, w, d). Calculate occupancy weight O(h,w,d) for each element in the frustum: O(h,w,d) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=0}^{d-1} \sigma{(h,w,j)}\deltaj\right)(1-\exp(-\sigma{(h,w,d)}\deltad)) where h, w are pixel coordinates, \sigma is density, and \deltaj is the distance between each depth in the frustum. Populate the frustum F: F(h,w,d) = [O(h,w,d)\phi(h,w), \sigma(h,w,d)] where \phi(h, w) is the C-channeled feature vector at pixel (h, w) scaled by O(h, w, d). 3. Voxel Grid Fusion: Transform frustums to world coordinates and fuse them into the shared voxel grids V{Density} and V{Feat}. For each voxel indexed by (x,y,z), pool all densities and features from corresponding frustum entries. The implementation takes the mean of the pooled features. 4. Volumetric Rendering: Project the voxel grids to 2D feature maps using camera poses \kappa. Trilinearly interpolate values on each voxel to get feature and density for each sampling point along camera rays. Feed 2D features into a decoder to produce output images \hat{i}. Decoder Architecture: Ten StyledConv blocks. The fourth layer's convolution is replaced with a transposed convolution to upsample by a factor of 2. Style modulation is skipped by feeding a constant vector of 1s. 5. Training and Optimization: Loss Functions: Image reconstruction loss: ||i - \hat{i}|| with coefficient 1. Perceptual loss is used in practice. Depth supervision: MSE loss on pixels with ground truth depth, weighted by 5. Regularization: Sum over entropy of sampled opacity values, weighted by 0.01. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 0.0002, betas (0., 0.99). Post-training Improvement: Add adversarial loss using StyleGAN2’s discriminator with R1 gradient regularization. Per-Scene Optimization: Optionally perform 60 steps by randomly sampling input views and reducing image reconstruction loss per encoded scene voxel to capture missing details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SceneAutoEncoder: def init(self, H, W, D, C, voxelsizez=32, voxelsizex=128, voxelsizey=128): """ Initialize the Scene Auto-Encoder. H, W: Spatial dimensions of the encoded feature map (input image size / 8). D: Number of depth samples in the frustum. C: Number of feature channels. """ super().init() self.H = H self.W = W self.D = D self.C = C # Encoder: EfficientNet-B1 based self.encoder = EfficientNetB1Encoder(H, W, D, C) # Decoder: StyleGAN2 based self.decoder = StyleGAN2Decoder() # Voxel Grids self.voxelsizez = voxelsizez self.voxelsizex = voxelsizex self.voxelsizey = voxelsizey # Voxel grids are typically initialized to zeros or small values # In training, these are updated via backprop or per-scene optimization self.Vdensity = None self.Vfeat = None def encodeimage(self, image): """ Encode a single RGB image into density and feature maps. Args: image: Tensor of shape (B, 3, Himg, Wimg) Returns: densitymap: Tensor of shape (B, D, H, W) featuremap: Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) """ # EfficientNet-B1 with Instance Norm and modified strides # Output of base encoder: (B, 432, H/8, W/8) -> adjusted to (B, 432, H, W) via stride/padding mods # Head replacement: Bilinear upsample, concat, Conv2d(432->512), Conv2d(512->C+D) x = self.encoder(image) # Split into density (D channels) and features (C channels) # Assuming the final conv layer outputs D+C channels # Note: The source says "two separate two-layer Conv networks", # but pseudocode simplifies to a split after a combined projection for clarity, # or we can implement the two separate networks explicitly. # Implementation of the two separate two-layer Conv networks as per source: # This part is complex to write fully without the exact layer definitions, # so we assume a projection layer outputs D+C channels, then split. # Or strictly following: "processed by two seperate two-layer Conv networks" # Let's assume x is the output of the head (B, 512, H, W) # Then two separate networks reduce to C and D. densitymap = self.densityhead(x) # (B, D, H, W) featuremap = self.featurehead(x) # (B, C, H, W) # Clamp density to [-10, 10] and apply softplus densitymap = torch.clamp(densitymap, -10, 10) densitymap = torch.nn.functional.softplus(densitymap) return densitymap, featuremap def buildfrustum(self, densitymap, featuremap, cameraposes): """ Build discrete frustums for each image. Args: densitymap: (B, D, H, W) featuremap: (B, C, H, W) cameraposes: List of camera pose matrices Returns: frustums: List of tensors, each (H, W, D, 1+C) containing [Ophi, sigma] """ frustums = [] for b in range(densitymap.shape[0]): sigma = densitymap[b] # (D, H, W) phi = featuremap[b] # (C, H, W) # Calculate deltaj (distance between depth samples) # Assuming uniform depth sampling for simplicity, delta is constant delta = 1.0 # Placeholder for actual depth interval # Calculate occupancy weights # O(h,w,d) = exp(-sum{j=0}^{d-1} sigma{(h,w,j)}delta) (1 - exp(-sigma{(h,w,d)}delta)) # We need to compute cumulative sum of sigma along D dimension sigmacumsum = torch.cumsum(sigma, dim=0) # (D, H, W) # Term 1: exp(-sum{j=0}^{d-1} sigma delta) # For d=0, sum is 0, so exp(0)=1. # We shift sigmacumsum to get sum{j=0}^{d-1} sigmaprev = torch.cat([torch.zeros((1, sigma.shape[1], sigma.shape[2]), device=sigma.device), sigmacumsum[:-1]], dim=0) term1 = torch.exp(-sigmaprev delta) # Term 2: (1 - exp(-sigma delta)) term2 = 1 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) O = term1 term2 # (D, H, W) # Scale features by occupancy # phi is (C, H, W), O is (D, H, W) # We need to broadcast O to (D, C, H, W) or reshape Oexpanded = O.unsqueeze(1) # (D, 1, H, W) phiscaled = phi.unsqueeze(0) Oexpanded # (D, C, H, W) # Stack features and density # F(h,w,d) = [O(h,w,d)phi(h,w), sigma(h,w,d)] # Shape: (D, C+1, H, W) frustumdata = torch.cat([phiscaled, sigma.unsqueeze(1)], dim=1) # Transform to world coordinates and store # This step involves geometric transformation which is complex to pseudocode without specific coordinate system details # We assume a function transformtoworld handles this frustumworld = transformtoworld(frustumdata, cameraposes[b]) frustums.append(frustumworld) return frustums def fusefrustums(self, frustums): """ Fuse frustums into voxel grids. Args: frustums: List of transformed frustum tensors Returns: Vdensity, Vfeat """ # Initialize voxel grids # Size: 32 x 128 x 128 Vdensity = torch.zeros((self.voxelsizez, self.voxelsizex, self.voxelsizey)) Vfeat = torch.zeros((self.voxelsizez, self.voxelsizex, self.voxelsizey, self.C)) # For each frustum, map its entries to voxel indices and accumulate # This requires inverse projection from camera space to world voxel space for frustum in frustums: # frustum shape: (D, C+1, H, W) # Map each (h, w, d) to voxel (x, y, z) # Accumulate density and features # Simple mean pooling as per source pass # Note: The actual implementation of mapping and pooling is non-trivial # and depends on the specific coordinate system and voxel grid definition. # The source states: "For each voxel indexed by (x,y,z), we pool all densities # and features of the corresponding frustum entries... simply take the mean" return Vdensity, Vfeat def render(self, Vdensity, Vfeat, cameraposes): """ Volumetric rendering using Mip-NeRF implementation. Args: Vdensity: Density voxel grid Vfeat: Feature voxel grid cameraposes: List of camera poses for rendering Returns: renderedimages: List of reconstructed images """ renderedfeatures = [] for pose in cameraposes: # Trilinear interpolation and volume rendering # This calls the Mip-NeRF implementation features = mipnerfrender(Vdensity, Vfeat, pose) renderedfeatures.append(features) # Decode features to images images = [] for features in renderedfeatures: image = self.decoder(features) images.append(image) return images def computeloss(self, images, targetimages, depthmeasurements): """ Compute training loss. Args: images: Reconstructed images targetimages: Ground truth images depthmeasurements: Ground truth depth Returns: totalloss """ # Image reconstruction loss (Perceptual Loss) imgloss = perceptualloss(images, targetimages) # Depth supervision loss # MSE loss on pixels with ground truth depth depthloss = mselosswithmask(images, targetimages, depthmeasurements) # Regularization: Entropy of sampled opacity values # This requires access to the opacity values from rendering opacityentropy = computeopacityentropy(images) totalloss = imgloss + 5 depthloss + 0.01 opacityentropy return totalloss Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables novel view synthesis and serves as input for latent compression. The voxel-based representation allows for efficient fusion of multi-view information. Limitations: The voxel size is fixed per dataset, which may limit flexibility. The method relies on accurate camera poses and depth measurements. When to use: When a 3D neural field representation is needed for generative modeling or latent compression. When not to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis without generative constraints is the primary goal, as other methods like NeRF-OSR might be more suitable. The Scene Auto-Encoder is part of the NeuralField-LDM (NFLDM) framework, introduced in "NeuralField-LDM: Scene Generation with Hierarchical Latent Diffusion Models". It builds on previous work in lifting 2D image features to 3D, such as LiftSplat-Shoot (LSS), and uses a voxel-based representation similar to optimization-based scene reconstruction methods. The method is used for scene generation and can be combined with hierarchical latent diffusion models.
