name: Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion
head: BNV-Fusion
body: Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion (BNV-Fusion) is a dense 3D reconstruction method that incrementally integrates noisy depth maps into a global neural implicit representation using a bi-level fusion strategy. It combines local-level weighted averaging for efficient integration with global-level neural rendering optimization to ensure geometric coherence. Unlike sibling methods that either rely solely on latent code integration (e.g., NeuralFusion, DI-Fusion) or single-MLP global representations (e.g., iMAP), BNV-Fusion uses a volume of latent codes to encode local geometry, improving detail and scalability while maintaining near real-time performance. Inputs: A sequence of depth maps \{D0,..., Dn\} and associated extrinsic camera-to-world transformation matrices \{T{cw}^0,..., T{cw}^n\}, where T{cw}^t denotes the rigid transformation from camera ct to the world coordinate. Outputs: A global implicit neural volume Vw representing the scene geometry, from which a mesh can be extracted via Marching Cubes. Data Structures: 1. Implicit Neural Volume (Vw): Defined as a weighted sum of decoder outputs conditioned on latent codes. It consists of a grid of latent codes \{\bm{l}i\} located at positions \{\bm{p}i\}. 2. Local Shape Embedding: Comprises an encoder E (modified PointNet) and a decoder \mathcal{D} (4-layer MLP). 3. Single-View Neural Volume (Vc^t): A set of latent codes representing local geometry for a specific depth map Dt. Method Steps: 1. Encoding: For each depth map Dt at frame t: Unproject the depth map into a point cloud. Pass the point cloud through the encoder E to extract deep features for each point by aggregating information within a local region. Map these features to a set of latent codes to form the single-view neural volume Vc^t. 2. Local-Level Fusion: Integrate Vc^t into the global volume Vw: Perform weighted averaging of the new latent codes into the global volume Vw using weights Wc^t. This step efficiently integrates new information but is susceptible to depth outliers as it lacks global context. 3. Global-Level Fusion: Optimize the global volume Vw: Iteratively optimize the latent codes in Vw by minimizing the discrepancy between Signed Distance Function (SDF) values extracted from the volume and actual depth measurements along camera rays. The decoder \mathcal{D} parameters are frozen during this optimization; only the latent codes are updated. This step encourages coherent global reconstruction and corrects errors from the local-level fusion. Implicit Neural Volume Definition: The SDF value s at a query point is computed using trilinear interpolation of latent codes: s = \sum{i=0}^{N=7} w(\bar{\bm{x}}i, \bm{p}i)\mathcal{D}(\bm{l}i, \bar{\bm{x}}i) Where: N=7: The number of neighboring latent codes used for trilinear interpolation. w(\cdot, \cdot): The weight function for trilinear interpolation, dependent on the query point \bar{\bm{x}}i and the latent code position \bm{p}i. \mathcal{D}: The decoder network (MLP) that maps a latent code and a 3D coordinate to an SDF value. \bm{l}i: The latent code for the i-th neighbor. \bar{\bm{x}}i: The 3D coordinate of the query point relative to the i-th latent code. Local Shape Embedding Training: The encoder E and decoder \mathcal{D} are trained jointly in a supervised manner using object CAD models from ShapeNet. The loss function for a training sample pair (\bm{p}, \bm{x}) is: \mathcal{L}(\theta{\mathcal{E}}, \theta{\mathcal{D}}) = \|\mathcal{D}{\theta{\mathcal{D}}}(\mathcal{E}{\theta{\mathcal{E}}}(\bm{p}), \bm{x}) - s^{gt}{\bm{x}} \|1 Where: \bm{p}: A local point cloud with normals of a local surface patch. \bm{x}: A sampled point around the surface. s^{gt}{\bm{x}}: The ground-truth SDF value for point \bm{x}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. globalvolume = InitializeImplicitNeuralVolume() # Grid of latent codes li at positions pi decoderD = LoadTrainedDecoder() # 4-layer MLP, parameters frozen during fusion encoderE = LoadTrainedEncoder() # Modified PointNet def encodedepthmap(depthmap, poseTcw): """ Converts a depth map into a single-view neural volume (set of latent codes). """ # Unproject depth map to 3D point cloud pointcloud = unprojectdepth(depthmap, poseTcw) # Extract deep features and map to latent codes # E is modified PointNet aggregating local region info latentcodes = encoderE(pointcloud) return latentcodes def locallevelfusion(globalvolume, newlatentcodes, weights): """ Integrates new latent codes into the global volume via weighted averaging. """ for newcode in newlatentcodes: # Find corresponding location in global volume # Update global volume latent code using running average weighted by Wcst globalvolume.updateweightedaverage(newcode, weights) return globalvolume def globallevelfusion(globalvolume, depthmap, poseTcw, numiterations): """ Optimizes latent codes in the global volume using neural rendering. """ # Unproject depth map to get measurement points and values measurementpoints, measurementsdfs = unprojectdepthwithsdf(depthmap, poseTcw) for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample points along camera rays or use measurement points # Compute SDF from global volume using trilinear interpolation predictedsdfs = [] for pt in measurementpoints: # Get 8 neighbors for trilinear interpolation neighbors = gettrilinearneighbors(globalvolume, pt) sdfval = 0.0 for i, neighbor in enumerate(neighbors): # w is trilinear weight, D is frozen decoder w = computetrilinearweight(pt, neighbor.pos) # Input to D: latent code li and relative coord xbari relcoord = pt - neighbor.pos sdfval += w decoderD(neighbor.code, relcoord) predictedsdfs.append(sdfval) # Compute loss: discrepancy between predicted SDFs and actual measurements loss = sum((pred - meas)2 for pred, meas in zip(predictedsdfs, measurementsdfs)) # Backpropagate to update latent codes only (decoder D is frozen) updatelatentcodes(globalvolume, loss) return globalvolume for t in range(numframes): Dt = getdepthmap(t) Tcwt = getpose(t) # Step 1: Encoding Vct = encodedepthmap(Dt, Tcwt) # Step 2: Local-Level Fusion globalvolume = locallevelfusion(globalvolume, Vct, weights=Wct) # Step 3: Global-Level Fusion globalvolume = globallevelfusion(globalvolume, Dt, Tcwt, numiterations=K) mesh = marchingcubes(globalvolume) Time Complexity: The method runs in near real-time, approximately 2 Hz without proper code optimization. Memory Complexity: The implicit neural volume allows surface extraction at any resolution via Marching Cubes without increasing memory usage, unlike TSDF volumes which discretize at a pre-defined resolution. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality over existing methods; captures fine details that traditional volumetric fusion approaches tend to miss; scalable due to volume-based representation of local geometry. Limitations: Local-level fusion is susceptible to depth outliers because it only integrates measured surfaces and their surroundings without global context. Updating the global representation in the latent space using an additive scheme does not always lead to correct geometry. When to use: Dense 3D reconstruction from depth maps where global consistency and fine detail are required, and incremental integration is needed. When not to use: When robustness to severe depth outliers is critical without the global optimization step, or when real-time performance significantly faster than 2 Hz is required. Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion (BNV-Fusion) was introduced to address the limitations of TSDF volume representations in balancing robustness to noisy measurements and maintaining level of detail. It leverages recent advances in neural implicit representations and neural rendering for dense 3D reconstruction. The method was evaluated on 312 sequences of various indoor environments in the ScanNet dataset. It differs from NeuralFusion and DI-Fusion by optimizing latent codes via neural rendering for global consistency, rather than only integrating measurements in the latent code domain. It also differs from iMAP by using a volume of latent codes to encode local geometry, improving detail and scalability, whereas iMAP uses a single MLP that loses details and does not scale well. name: Application-Specific Reconstructions
head: Domain-Specific 3DGS Training, Specialized Reconstruction Priors
body: Application-Specific Reconstructions refers to the modification of the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training pipeline to address domain-specific challenges such as dynamic human avatars, displaced objects, or physical plausibility constraints. While Base 3DGS Optimization provides a generic differentiable rendering loop, this family introduces structural changes—such as physical priors, generative inpainting, or mesh-embedded representations—to handle ambiguities inherent in monocular video or specific geometric constraints. It sets itself apart from siblings like WildGaussians (which handles wild/non-rigid motion via generic deformation) by enforcing explicit domain rules (e.g., canonical space physics or mesh topology) rather than relying solely on learned deformation fields. The core mechanism shared by all methods in this family is the integration of domain-specific constraints or post-processing steps into the optimization loop defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Training. 1. Constraint Injection: Unlike vanilla 3DGS which minimizes photometric loss \mathcal{L}{photo} alone, these methods add regularization terms or structural constraints. For example, GaussianBody adds a physical prior loss \mathcal{L}{phys}, while SplattingAvatar enforces mesh adherence. 2. Representation Modification: The Gaussian attributes or their initialization are modified to fit the domain. GauHuman redesigns densification primitives; SplattingAvatar embeds Gaussians in mesh tangent space with trainable embeddings; Inpainting for Displaced Objects modifies the kernel set by removing and reinitializing specific subsets. 3. Specialized Initialization: Standard SfM initialization is often replaced or augmented. GaussianBody initializes in canonical space based on parametric models; SplattingAvatar initializes one Gaussian per mesh triangle. What it is: A method for dynamic digital human modeling from monocular video. Distinction: It focuses on re-engineering the prune/split/clone densification mechanisms and incorporating pose refinement and weight field modules, rather than relying on physical-based priors in canonical space like GaussianBody. When to choose: When high-fidelity detail learning for dynamic humans is required without explicit parametric body model constraints. What it is: A method for dynamic digital human modeling that leverages physically-based priors to regularize 3D Gaussians in canonical space. Distinction: It addresses artifacts in dynamic cloth reconstruction by enforcing physical constraints on deformation, distinguishing it from GauHuman which uses redesigned densification, and SplattingAvatar which uses mesh embeddings. When to choose: When reconstructing dynamic cloth or soft tissue where physical plausibility is critical to avoid monocular ambiguity artifacts. What it is: A technique to remedy "black smudges" and missing background textures when objects are displaced in a scene. Distinction: It uses generative AI (LaMa) to inpaint missing background regions and reinitializes Gaussian kernels with these colors, unlike vanilla 3DGS which leaves empty spots or blends irrelevant kernels. When to choose: When the training data contains scenes where objects move, revealing previously occluded background areas that are absent from the input training images. What it is: A real-time human avatar rendering method that embeds 3D Gaussians onto a driving mesh (FLAME). Distinction: It avoids noise from nearest-triangle sampling by using trainable embeddings for motion control and enforces "walking on triangle" constraints, distinguishing it from canonical-space methods like GaussianBody. When to choose: When non-ambiguous motion control and high-fidelity rendering of complex geometries (eyes, hair) are required using a parametric mesh as a driver. Definition: Adapts the feature rendering pipeline for robotics simulation, achieving real-time open-vocabulary segmentation by fusing 3DGS with a lightweight 2D segmentation network. Definition: Applies 3DGS to create digital plant assets, leveraging alpha blending and feature fields to accurately reconstruct translucent leaf structures. Definition: A method for defining unknown scatterers in radiative transfer contexts using a grid mapper and extinction transform. Steps: 1. Define unknown scatterers using the grid mapper and an extinction transform that maps the abstract state vector to a grid mask: unknownscatterers = at3d.containers.UnknownScatterers(at3d.medium.UnknownScatterer(gridtoopticalproperties, extinction=(None, at3d.transforms.StateToGridMask(mask=cloudmask)))). 2. Initialize the state generator with the reconstruction solver dictionary, unknown scatterers, surfaces, numerical parameters, sources, Stokes counts, and background scatterers: stategen = at3d.medium.StateGenerator(solversreconstruct, unknownscatterers, surfaces, numericalparameters, sources, numstokes, backgroundopticalscatterers). Parameters: cloudmask: boolean array identifying cloud regions, derived from solvers[wvl].medium['cloud'].extinction.data > 0. uncertaintymodel: radiometric noise uncertainty applied to sensors, initialized with parameters 1e-5 and 1e-3. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [Kerbl et al., 2023] provides a robust baseline for static scene reconstruction. However, dynamic scenes, specific geometric constraints, and occlusion handling require specialized adaptations. GauHuman and GaussianBody address the long-standing problem of dynamic human avatars from monocular video, where depth ambiguity leads to artifacts in clothing and body shape. Inpainting for Displaced Objects addresses the specific failure mode of 3DGS when objects move, exposing unseen background. SplattingAvatar integrates 3DGS with parametric meshes (FLAME) to provide stable, controllable avatars. These methods represent a shift from generic scene representation to domain-aware reconstruction, leveraging the differentiable nature of 3DGS to incorporate physical, geometric, or generative priors. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) lforster/hybridCT, https://github.com/lforster/hybridCT, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GauHuman
head: HUGS (Human Gaussian Splats)
body: GauHuman is a method for high-fidelity dynamic human reconstruction from monocular video that adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to the specific geometry and topology of the human body. It solves the problem of inefficient optimization and artifact generation in dynamic scenes by redesigning the densification primitives and incorporating pose refinement. It sets itself apart from vanilla 3DGS by replacing standard density-based splitting with a human-aware prune/split/clone mechanism, and from other body methods like GaussianBody by focusing on efficient optimization speed rather than physical cloth priors. GauHuman builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Training by modifying the densification and optimization steps to handle dynamic human motion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of monocular RGB images of a human subject performing actions; an initial SMPL or similar parametric human model estimate (for pose); camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the human body and clothing, optimized for novel view synthesis and real-time rendering. Data Structures: The method maintains the standard 3DGS Gaussian attributes: position \mathbf{p}, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}, and covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} (parameterized as rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}). Additionally, it incorporates: 1. Pose Refinement Module: A network or optimization variable that refines the global pose parameters over time. 2. Weight Field Module: A lightweight MLP or set of weights that modulates Gaussian contributions to capture fine details (e.g., clothing folds) that standard Gaussians might miss. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians based on the initial human pose estimate. Unlike standard SfM points, these are distributed over the human surface or volume. 2. Joint Optimization: Optimize Gaussian attributes (\mathbf{p}, \alpha, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{s}), pose parameters, and weight field parameters simultaneously. 3. Redesigned Densification: Prune: Remove Gaussians with low opacity or those not contributing to the human silhouette, using a threshold adapted for dynamic motion. Split/Clone: Instead of splitting based solely on gradient magnitude, the method uses a human-aware criterion. Gaussians are split if they are located on high-curvature regions of the human body or if the pose refinement indicates significant motion in that region. This prevents the "exploding" Gaussian artifacts common in dynamic scenes. 4. Pose Refinement: Update the global pose parameters to align the canonical human shape with the observed frames, reducing misalignment artifacts. 5. Weight Field Learning: Train the weight field to adjust the opacity or color of Gaussians, allowing for finer detail representation without increasing the Gaussian count excessively. 6. Rendering: Render the scene using standard differentiable rasterization of Gaussians, weighted by the learned weight field. Formulas: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a combination of photometric loss and regularization terms specific to the human domain: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambda{pose} \mathcal{L}{pose} + \lambda{weight} \mathcal{L}{weight} Where \mathcal{L}{photo} is the standard L1 + SSIM loss. \mathcal{L}{pose} regularizes the pose refinement to stay within plausible human motion bounds. \mathcal{L}{weight} ensures the weight field does not overfit. The exact formulation of \mathcal{L}{pose} and \mathcal{L}{weight} is not detailed in the provided sources, but they serve to constrain the optimization to physically plausible human dynamics. Parameters: Training time: Minutes (specifically, efficient enough for minute-level training). Rendering speed: 166 FPS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: Monocular input can lead to ambiguity. The method mitigates this by using the human prior (SMPL-like structure) during initialization and optimization. Dynamic Clothing: Fast-moving clothing can cause artifacts. The weight field module helps capture these fine details, but extreme occlusion may still result in floating Gaussians if not handled by the joint optimization with the scene (see Subtopics). This variant optimizes human and scene Gaussians jointly. The human model acts as a constraint for the scene reconstruction, which helps mitigate floating Gaussians (floaters) that typically appear in areas around intersections or occlusions when using sparse input views. This approach contrasts with sequential optimization (scene first, then human) which is prone to such artifacts. Time Complexity: Training is highly efficient, completing in minutes. This is a significant improvement over iterative neural radiance field methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Achieves real-time rendering at 166 FPS. Strengths: Minute-level training time; real-time rendering; high-fidelity dynamic human reconstruction from monocular video. Limitations: Relies on monocular input, which may suffer from depth ambiguity without strong priors; performance may degrade with extreme occlusions or very sparse views unless joint optimization is used. When to use: When real-time rendering and fast training are required for dynamic human avatars from monocular video. When not to use: When multi-view stereo data is available and higher geometric accuracy is needed without relying on human priors; when physical cloth simulation is required (use GaussianBody instead). GauHuman was introduced as part of the recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting applications for dynamic digital human modeling. It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS in dynamic scenes by redesigning the densification process. It is cited alongside other methods like GaussianBody, GaussianAvatar, and SplattingAvatar in surveys of 3DGS advancements. The method is also known as HUGS (Human Gaussian Splats) in some contexts. name: GaussianBody
body: GaussianBody is a method for dynamic digital human modeling from monocular video that leverages physically-based priors to regularize 3D Gaussians in canonical space. It solves the problem of visual artifacts in dynamic cloth reconstruction caused by the ambiguity of monocular input. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by enforcing geometric consistency in the canonical domain rather than relying solely on photometric loss in the image domain. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Monocular video sequence of a human subject; a parametric body model (e.g., SMPL) providing canonical space geometry. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians with attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) that can be rendered into novel views and poses. Data Structures: Gaussians are stored in canonical space. Each Gaussian i has attributes: mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and color coefficients ci. The parametric model provides a mesh surface M in canonical space. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians based on the parametric body model in canonical space. 2. Deformation Prediction: Predict the deformation from canonical space to the observed pose space using a deformation network or field. 3. Regularization: Apply physically-based priors to regularize the Gaussians in canonical space. This involves constraining the Gaussians to adhere to the geometry priors of the parametric model to ensure pose-dependent cloth deformation. 4. Rendering: Transform Gaussians from canonical to view space based on the predicted deformation and camera parameters. Render the image using standard 3DGS rasterization. 5. Optimization: Minimize a combined loss function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \mathcal{L}{phys} where \mathcal{L}{photo} is the photometric reconstruction loss and \mathcal{L}{phys} is the physical prior loss enforcing geometric consistency in canonical space. Parameters: Weight of physical prior loss \lambda{phys}: Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular ambiguity can lead to artifacts in dynamic cloth if physical priors are not strong enough. Precision issues in canonical space deformation prediction may cause misalignment. HAHA attaches Gaussians to the surface of a mesh and combines rendered results from a textured human body mesh and Gaussians to reduce the number of Gaussians required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids artifacts in dynamic cloth from monocular video; generalizes to novel poses effectively. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the parametric body model and physically-based priors. When to use: Dynamic digital human modeling from monocular video where cloth artifacts are a concern. When not to use: When high-fidelity static geometry is sufficient or when multi-view data is available. GaussianBody was introduced in [214] (cited as) for dynamic digital human modeling based on monocular video. It builds on 3DGS by incorporating physically-based priors to regularize Gaussians in canonical space. It is part of the family of application-specific reconstructions that modify the 3DGS optimization loop with domain-specific constraints [Parent]. name: Inpainting for Displaced Objects
head: GSP Inpainting, LaMa Inpainting
body: This method remedies black smudges and dirty textures caused by displaced objects exposing unseen areas that 3DGS cannot recover from input images. Unlike vanilla 3DGS which leaves empty spots and dirty textures blended from irrelevant kernels when objects are displaced, this method ameliorates the issue using generative AI inpainting. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Training by modifying the kernel set to remove and reinitialize specific subsets [Parent]. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian kernels \mathcal{G} representing the scene, including those belonging to objects that may be displaced. A rendered image I{rendered} of the current view. A segmentation mask or identification of the Gaussian kernels belonging to the displaced object. Outputs: Updated Gaussian kernels \mathcal{G}' with corrected colors, opacity, and specular properties. An inpainted image I{inpainted} (intermediate). Data Structures: Gaussian Kernel: Contains position \mathbf{p}, covariance \Sigma (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients (defining color c), and potentially separate diffuse/specular color components. Inpainting Model: LaMa or Stable Diffusion. Steps: 1. Remove Displaced Kernels: Identify all Gaussian kernels \mathcal{G}{obj} \subset \mathcal{G} belonging to the object that may be displaced. Remove these kernels from the scene representation. Note: This creates "holes" or missing regions in the rendered view corresponding to the object's previous position. 2. Render Current View: Render the scene using the remaining kernels \mathcal{G} \setminus \mathcal{G}{obj} to obtain I{rendered} and an alpha mask indicating the missing regions (holes). 3. Inpaint Image: Use a generative inpainting model (LaMa or Stable Diffusion) to fill the holes in I{rendered} using the alpha mask. Let the result be I{inpainted}. LaMa Specifics: The model generates plausible textures for the missing areas based on surrounding context. Stable Diffusion Specifics: Generates missing texture in masked regions. 4. Trace Rays and Record Colors: For each pixel (u, v) in the hole region of I{rendered}: Emit a ray from the camera through (u, v). Find the first Gaussian kernel \mathcal{G}i encountered by this ray in the original scene (before removal) or in the current scene if the ray intersects remaining geometry. Correction based on: The text states "assign them to the first Gaussian kernel encountered by the rays emitted from these pixels." In the context of GSP, this likely refers to mapping the new pixel color back to the Gaussian that would have been there or the nearest remaining kernel if the object is gone. However, explicitly says: "assign them to the first Gaussian kernel encountered by the rays emitted from these pixels." Since the object is removed, this ray might not hit the object. The standard interpretation in such "inpainting trick" papers is that the ray hits the background or remaining geometry, but the color is assigned to the removed Gaussian's slot if it were to be re-initialized, or more likely, the method re-initializes the removed Gaussians with the inpainted color. Refined Interpretation from: "Note the new colors of pixels originally in spots and assign them to the first Gaussian kernel encountered by the rays emitted from these pixels." This implies that for the pixels that were occluded by the displaced object, we now have a new color from the inpainting. We need to assign this color to the Gaussians that were in that spot. Since they are removed, we must re-initialize them. The text says "assign them to the first Gaussian kernel encountered". If the object is gone, the ray hits something else. This step is ambiguous. Let's look at the next step: "Average the recorded colors on all noted Gaussian kernels". This implies multiple rays might hit the same Gaussian or we are collecting colors for the re-initialized Gaussians. Practical Implementation: For each removed Gaussian \mathcal{G}j \in \mathcal{G}{obj}, determine its screen-space projection. For each pixel in its projection, if it was in a hole, take the color from I{inpainted} at that pixel. Collect these colors for \mathcal{G}j. 5. Update Gaussian Attributes: For each removed Gaussian \mathcal{G}j \in \mathcal{G}{obj}: Diffuse Color: Calculate the average of all recorded colors assigned to \mathcal{G}j. Set this as the new diffuse color. Opacity: Set opacity \alpha = 1. Specular Color: Set specular color to 0 (or black) to prevent highlights, as the inpainted texture is assumed to be diffuse. 6. Re-insert Kernels: Add the updated kernels \mathcal{G}j back into the scene representation \mathcal{G}'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inpaintdisplacedobjects(Gaussians, Camera, InpaintingModel): """ Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes (pos, cov, alpha, color, etc.) Camera: Camera parameters for rendering InpaintingModel: Function to inpaint image given mask """ # 1. Identify and remove displaced Gaussians # Assume we have a mask or list of indices for displaced objects displacedindices = getdisplacedgaussianindices(Gaussians) displacedgaussians = [Gaussians[i] for i in displacedindices] remaininggaussians = [G for i, G in enumerate(Gaussians) if i not in displacedindices] # 2. Render scene with remaining Gaussians renderedimage, alphamask = render(remaininggaussians, Camera) # 3. Inpaint the holes # alphamask indicates where Gaussians are missing (holes) inpaintedimage = InpaintingModel(renderedimage, alphamask) # 4. Assign new colors to displaced Gaussians for G in displacedgaussians: # Project G to screen to find its pixel footprint screenpixels = projecttoscreen(G, Camera) collectedcolors = [] for pixel in screenpixels: # Check if this pixel was in a hole (missing from original render) # In practice, we know these pixels correspond to the displaced object # so we take the inpainted color directly newcolor = inpaintedimage[pixel] collectedcolors.append(newcolor) # 5. Update attributes if collectedcolors: # Average colors for diffuse component avgcolor = sum(collectedcolors) / len(collectedcolors) G.diffusecolor = avgcolor G.opacity = 1.0 G.specularcolor = 0.0 # Prevent highlights else: # Fallback if no pixels were recorded (e.g., object completely out of view) G.opacity = 0.0 # 6. Reconstruct full Gaussian set newGaussians = remaininggaussians + displacedgaussians return newGaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accuracy of the inpainted color depends on the quality of the generative model. LaMa may produce blurry textures if the context is insufficient. Boundaries: The transition between the inpainted region and the rest of the scene must be seamless. The method assumes the inpainted texture matches the surrounding geometry's lighting and material properties. Degenerate Input: If the displaced object is completely outside the camera view, no rays will hit its previous position, and no colors will be recorded. In this case, the Gaussian should be removed entirely (opacity 0). A sequential pipeline to fill occluded/missing regions in rendered novel views while maintaining 3D consistency, leveraging the constraint that Gaussians do not hallucinate details. Unlike the single-view LaMa approach, this method uses Stable Diffusion for texture generation and Poisson blending for depth consistency. It is chosen when 3D consistency across multiple novel views is required, particularly in sparse view synthesis scenarios. Steps: 1. Render a novel view with holes and an alpha mask. 2. Use Stable Diffusion inpainting to generate missing texture in the masked regions. 3. Estimate monocular depth on the inpainted image. 4. Use the gradient of this depth to fill in rendered depth in the masked regions using Poisson blending. 5. Project Gaussians to the scene using the inpainted depth and image. 6. Repeat the process sequentially for a few novel views until the scene is 3D consistent and renderable from any view without holes. Time Complexity: Depends on the inpainting model. LaMa is relatively fast, but Stable Diffusion is computationally expensive. The sequential nature of the 3D Inpainting Pipeline adds further time cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the inpainted images and intermediate depth maps. No significant additional memory overhead for the Gaussian kernels themselves, as they are re-initialized. Measured Performance: GSP (Gaussian Splashing) with inpainting shows improved visual quality in scenes with displaced objects, removing black smudges and dirty textures. CoherentGS outperforms DNGaussian visually and numerically on sparse view synthesis, avoiding blurry textures and distracting artifacts. Strengths: Effectively handles unseen areas caused by object displacement; leverages state-of-the-art generative models for realistic texture synthesis; maintains 3D consistency in the sequential pipeline. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the inpainting model; may introduce artifacts if the context is ambiguous; not suitable for dynamic scenes where the displacement is not known or segmented. When to Use: When objects in the scene are displaced or removed, exposing background areas not present in the input images. When sparse view synthesis is required and standard methods produce blurry textures. When Not to Use: When the scene is static and fully captured in the input images; when real-time performance is critical and generative inpainting is too slow. The method was introduced in the context of Gaussian Splashing (GSP), a unified particle-based framework for versatile motion synthesis and rendering. The authors observed that standard 3DGS fails to recover color and texture information for areas exposed by displaced objects, leading to visual artifacts. They proposed using LaMa, a large kernel mask inpainting model, to remedy this issue. The 3D Inpainting Pipeline variant was introduced in CoherentGS for sparse novel view synthesis, leveraging the constraint that Gaussians do not hallucinate details to safely use generative inpainting. name: SplattingAvatar
head: SplattingAvatar: Realistic Real-Time Human Avatars with Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Splatting
body: SplattingAvatar is a real-time human avatar rendering method that embeds 3D Gaussians directly onto a driving mesh (FLAME or SMPL-X) in mesh tangent space. It solves the noise and instability associated with nearest-triangle sampling in canonical space, particularly for complex geometries like eyes and hair. It sets itself apart from siblings like GauHuman and GaussianBody by using trainable embeddings for motion control rather than physical priors or redesigned densification primitives, and avoids the artifacts of Inpainting for Displaced Objects by maintaining strict mesh adherence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view video of a human subject; a parametric head/body model (FLAME or SMPL-X) fitted to the subject; camera poses and intrinsics. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with attributes (position, covariance, color, opacity) embedded in mesh tangent space; a trained embedding network for motion control; a Unity-compatible rendering implementation. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i has: Position \mathbf{p}i in mesh tangent space (local to the mesh triangle). 3D covariance \Sigmai (represented as rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{s}i). Color \mathbf{c}i (SH coefficients). Opacity \alphai. Trainable embedding vector \mathbf{e}i used for pose/expression conditioning. Mesh: Parametric mesh (FLAME/SMPL-X) with vertices \mathbf{V}, faces \mathbf{F}, and UV coordinates. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Fit a parametric mesh (FLAME or SMPL-X) to the input video using a fitting tool (e.g., MICA/DECA). Initialize one Gaussian per mesh triangle in the mesh tangent space. 2. Embedding-Based Motion Control: Instead of deforming Gaussians via nearest-triangle sampling in canonical space (which causes noise), use trainable embeddings \mathbf{e}i to predict pose- and expression-dependent offsets. These embeddings are ported to compute shaders for real-time motion control. 3. Training Optimization: Total iterations: 30,000. Loss weights: \lambdal = 0.01 for L1 loss. Other weights: \lambdas = 1.0, Ts = 10.0, Tr = 0.008. Iterations 0–599: No densification/pruning. Iterations 600–14,999: Densify and prune every 100 iterations. Every 3,000 iterations: Reset all Gaussian opacities to zero to remove redundant Gaussians. Iterations 15,000–29,999: No densification/pruning/opacity reset. "Walking on triangle" step: Performed after densifying and pruning to ensure Gaussians remain within their assigned mesh triangles. 4. Rendering: Draw one quad primitive per Gaussian in a Unity implementation, using \alpha^-blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainsplattingavatar(mesh, images, poses, expressions, numiterations=30000): # 1. Initialization gaussians = initializegaussianspertriangle(mesh) # One Gaussian per triangle embeddings = inittrainableembeddings(gaussians) for iter in range(numiterations): # 2. Motion Control via Embeddings # Predict offsets based on pose/expression and embeddings offsets = predictoffsets(embeddings, poses[iter], expressions[iter]) gaussians.positions += offsets # 3. "Walking on Triangle" Step # Ensure Gaussians stay within their mesh triangle boundaries gaussians = walkingontriangle(gaussians, mesh) # 4. Rendering and Loss Calculation renderedimage = rendergaussians(gaussians, cameraparams) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, images[iter], lambdal=0.01) # 5. Optimization Step optimize(gaussians, embeddings, loss) # 6. Densification and Pruning Schedule if 600 <= iter < 15000: if iter % 100 == 0: gaussians = densifyandprune(gaussians, threshold=0.008) if iter % 3000 == 0: gaussians.opacity = 0 # Reset opacity to remove redundant Gaussians return gaussians, embeddings def walkingontriangle(gaussians, mesh): # Clip Gaussian positions to their assigned mesh triangle in tangent space # This prevents Gaussians from sticking to triangle boundaries for g in gaussians: g.position = cliptotriangle(g.position, g.triangleindex, mesh) return gaussians Parameters: \lambdal (L1 loss weight): 0.01. \lambdas (SSIM loss weight): 1.0. Ts (Scale threshold): 10.0. Tr (Rotation threshold): 0.008. Total iterations: 30,000. Densify/Prune frequency: Every 100 iterations (iterations 600–14,999). Opacity reset frequency: Every 3,000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nearest-Triangle Sampling: Using nearest-triangle sampling for deformation (as in INSTA) causes unstable sampling in canonical space and strong noise in complex geometries like the eye region. SplattingAvatar avoids this by using embeddings-based motion control. Disabling "Walking on Triangle": Disabling this mechanism and clipping UV values causes Gaussians to stick and pile up on the boundaries of mesh triangles, leading to performance drops in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Over 300 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU in a Unity implementation. Quantitative Results (Head Avatar Dataset): Ours+FLAME: PSNR 28.19, SSIM 0.931, LPIPS 0.063. Ours+NHA: PSNR 28.86, SSIM 0.931, LPIPS 0.060. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High-fidelity rendering of complex geometries (eyes, hair, glasses); non-ambiguous motion control; real-time performance; significant improvement in photometric quality over mesh-based methods like FLARE. Limitations: Does not focus on accurate geometry and materials reconstruction compared to methods like FLARE. Performance can drop if "walking on triangle" is disabled. When to use: When real-time, high-quality human avatar rendering is required, especially for complex facial features. When not to use: When accurate geometry and materials reconstruction are the primary goals (use FLARE instead). SplattingAvatar was introduced in the paper "SplattingAvatar: Realistic Real-Time Human Avatars with Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and addresses limitations in previous avatar methods like INSTA and FLARE. It is part of the family of application-specific reconstructions in differentiable volume rendering. name: Geometry and Surface Priors
head: Geometric constraints, Surface alignment, Depth priors
body: This family of methods addresses the fundamental limitation of vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the production of "floating" volumetric ellipsoids that lack an explicit, watertight geometric boundary. By aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with continuous geometric priors (such as SDFs, depth maps, or explicit meshes), these methods enforce positional and normal consistency to enable accurate mesh extraction, physically-based rendering, and robust initialization. Unlike sibling methods that may rely solely on photometric loss or implicit constraints, this family explicitly integrates geometric supervision into the training or post-processing pipeline to ensure the Gaussians conform to physical surfaces. All methods in this family share the goal of aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with a continuous geometric prior. The core mechanism involves adding geometric loss terms to the standard photometric rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rgb}. These losses typically enforce two properties: 1. Positional Consistency: Gaussian centers \mathbf{c}i are encouraged to lie on the zero-level set of a distance function (SDF or UDF) or align with metric depth estimates. 2. Normal Consistency: The orientation of the Gaussians (derived from their covariance matrix or rotation quaternion) is aligned with the surface normal estimated from the geometric prior. The total loss function generally takes the form: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \mathcal{L}{geo} is the geometric consistency loss and \mathcal{L}{norm} is the normal consistency loss. The weights \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} are hyperparameters that balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Integrates the NeuS implicit surface reconstruction method into 3DGS to transfer explicit surface properties to discrete Gaussian primitives. Sets itself apart by directly coupling a NeuS-style Signed Distance Function (SDF) with a Gaussian rasterizer, unlike siblings that use monocular depth or explicit mesh extraction. Choose when watertight surface extraction and explicit SDF guidance are required over photometric-only training. A post-optimization step that resolves the up-to-scale ambiguity in multi-view reconstruction by aligning optimized 3D Gaussians with metric-scale monocular depth estimates. Sets itself apart by operating after standard optimization, fixing Gaussian parameters and optimizing only a global scale factor, unlike siblings that embed depth priors during training. Choose when metric scale recovery is needed without retraining. Addresses 3D reconstruction from sparse-view inputs where standard 3DGS suffers from geometric ambiguity due to insufficient multi-view constraints. Sets itself apart by explicitly integrating depth priors from pre-trained 2D monocular depth estimation networks to supervise Gaussian distribution, rather than relying solely on implicit neural fields. Choose when multi-view cues are insufficient and external depth estimates are available. Aligns the discrete 3D Gaussian representation with a continuous SDF prior to enhance geometry reconstruction quality. Sets itself apart by explicitly transferring surface properties from a neural SDF to the Gaussians, encouraging centers on the zero-level set and normals to align with the SDF gradient, unlike siblings like NeuSG. Choose when explicit SDF alignment is preferred over implicit NeuS coupling. Mitigates reconstruction artifacts and improves geometric fidelity by introducing a progressive propagation strategy. Sets itself apart by explicitly enforcing normal consistency between neighboring views and introducing planar constraints, ensuring discrete Gaussians align with continuous surface geometry. Choose when "popping" artifacts and planar surface alignment are critical. Encourages consistency between SDF and 3DGS to enhance geometry reconstruction quality. Sets itself apart by directly optimizing SDF-Gaussian alignment without auxiliary networks. Choose when lightweight SDF consistency is needed. Uses pretrained volume rendering priors (UDF) to push Gaussians toward true surfaces by optimizing along increasing rendering weights, avoiding off-surface drift and discreteness. Sets itself apart as a post-training refinement strategy effective for open and thin structures, outperforming closed-surface-tailored methods. Choose when refining existing reconstructions for thin/open structures without retraining. The problem of "floating" Gaussians in standard 3DGS has been a primary driver for geometric priors. Early works like NeuSG adapted implicit surface representations (NeuS) to guide Gaussian placement. Subsequent works such as GSDF and 3DGSR encouraged consistency between SDFs and Gaussian attributes. More recent approaches leverage monocular depth estimators for scale alignment or sparse-view reconstruction. Volume rendering priors, such as those in VRP-UDF, have been used to refine surfaces, particularly for thin structures where standard methods fail. name: GaussianPro
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Progressive Propagation
body: GaussianPro is a training optimization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that mitigates reconstruction artifacts (such as "popping" Gaussians) and improves geometric fidelity by introducing a progressive propagation strategy. Unlike standard densification which relies solely on position gradients, GaussianPro utilizes propagated depth and normal maps from neighboring views to guide the growth and adjustment of Gaussians. It sets itself apart by explicitly enforcing normal consistency between neighboring views and introducing planar constraints, ensuring that the discrete Gaussian representation aligns more closely with continuous surface geometry. GaussianPro operates by integrating geometric priors into the densification and optimization pipeline. It generates initial depth and normal maps, propagates these values across neighboring pixels using patch matching, and uses the propagated information to identify regions requiring new Gaussians. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}, where each gi is defined by center \mathbf{c}i, covariance \Sigmai (or rotation Ri and scale Si), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients Ci. Input images from multiple views. Initial depth and normal estimates (e.g., from a monocular estimator or SfM). Outputs: Optimized set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with improved geometric alignment and reduced artifacts. The method relies on standard 3D Gaussian Splatting data structures but augments the densification logic with geometric filters. Gaussian Attributes: Standard fields: \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (scale), \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, \mathbf{c}{sh} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 3} (SH coefficients). Geometric Maps: Depth map D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} and Normal map N \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} for each view. Propagated Maps: D{prop} and N{prop}, generated via patch matching. 1. Generate Initial Geometric Priors: Compute initial depth D and normal N maps for each input view. These serve as the source for propagation. 2. Patch Matching Propagation: For each pixel p in a target view, propagate depth and normal information from neighboring pixels in adjacent views. This generates propagated depth D{prop}(p) and normal N{prop}(p). Note: Patch matching involves searching for corresponding patches in neighboring views to fill in missing or unreliable depth/normal values. 3. Geometric Filtering and Selection: Identify pixels p that require additional Gaussians. This is done by comparing the rendered depth/normal with the propagated depth/normal or by detecting regions where the current Gaussian density is insufficient relative to the geometric detail. Pixels with high discrepancy or low coverage are marked for densification. 4. Gaussian Initialization: Initialize new Gaussians at the locations corresponding to the selected pixels. The initial position \mathbf{c}{new} is derived from the propagated depth D{prop}(p) and the camera projection. The initial orientation is aligned with the propagated normal N{prop}(p). 5. Optimization with Geometric Losses: During training, minimize the total loss \mathcal{L}{total}, which includes photometric loss and specific geometric terms: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{planar} \mathcal{L}{planar} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} \mathcal{L}{rgb}: Standard photometric reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS). \mathcal{L}{planar}: Planar loss that encourages Gaussians to lie on planar surfaces, ensuring they match real surfaces more closely. \mathcal{L}{norm}: Normal consistency loss enforcing alignment between the Gaussian's rendered normal and the propagated normal N{prop}. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{norm}): Enforces consistency between the Gaussian's rendered normal \mathbf{n}{rendered} and the propagated normal \mathbf{n}{prop}. \mathcal{L}{norm} = \mathcal{L}{1}(\mathbf{n}{rendered}, \mathbf{n}{prop}) + \mathcal{L}{angular}(\mathbf{n}{rendered}, \mathbf{n}{prop}) Where \mathcal{L}{1} is the L1 distance and \mathcal{L}{angular} is the angular difference (e.g., 1 - \mathbf{n}{rendered} \cdot \mathbf{n}{prop}). Planar Loss (\mathcal{L}{planar}): Encourages Gaussians to conform to planar structures. While the exact formula is not explicitly detailed in the provided snippets, it is described as a constraint ensuring Gaussians match real surfaces more closely. Typically, this involves minimizing the distance of Gaussian centers to a fitted plane or penalizing deviations from planarity within local neighborhoods. Progressive Propagation: The strategy updates Gaussians progressively by considering normal consistency between neighboring views. This implies that the propagation and densification steps are not one-off but integrated into the iterative training loop, allowing Gaussians to grow and adjust based on evolving geometric estimates. \lambda{planar}: Weight for the planar loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{norm}: Weight for the normal consistency loss. Not given in the sources. Patch matching window size: Not given in the sources. Popping Artifacts: Standard 3DGS can suffer from "popping" Gaussians due to discrete depth sorting. GaussianPro mitigates this by ensuring consistent sorting and geometric alignment, though it does not replace tile-based sorting (like StopThePop) if used in conjunction. Propagation Errors: If the initial depth/normal estimates are noisy, patch matching may propagate errors. Geometric filtering is used to identify reliable pixels, but poor initial priors can still lead to misaligned Gaussians. Degenerate Input: In textureless or reflective regions, depth and normal estimation may fail. The method relies on the robustness of the patch matching and geometric filtering to handle these cases. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianprotrainingstep(gaussians, images, cameras, initialdepth, initialnormal): """ One step of GaussianPro training. """ # 1. Render current Gaussians renderedimage, rendereddepth, renderednormal = render(gaussians, cameras) # 2. Propagate geometric information from neighboring views # Assuming 'images' contains multiple views propagateddepth, propagatednormal = patchmatchpropagation( initialdepth, initialnormal, cameras, images) # 3. Compute Photometric Loss lossrgb = computephotometricloss(renderedimage, targetimage) # 4. Compute Normal Consistency Loss # Align rendered normal with propagated normal lossnorm = l1loss(renderednormal, propagatednormal) + \ angularloss(renderednormal, propagatednormal) # 5. Compute Planar Loss # Encourage Gaussians to lie on planes lossplanar = computeplanarloss(gaussians) # 6. Total Loss totalloss = lossrgb + lambdanorm lossnorm + lambdaplanar lossplanar # 7. Backpropagate and Update Gaussians gaussians.backward(totalloss) gaussians.update() # 8. Densification based on Geometric Filtering # Identify pixels needing new Gaussians pixelstodensify = geometricfilter( rendereddepth, propagateddepth, renderednormal, propagatednormal) for p in pixelstodensify: # Initialize new Gaussian using propagated info newgaussian = initializegaussianfrompropagation( p, propagateddepth[p], propagatednormal[p], cameras) gaussians.add(newgaussian) return totalloss The broader family of methods that align Gaussians with geometric priors. GaussianPro is a specific implementation within this family that uses progressive propagation [9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment]. Uses neural implicit surfaces to guide Gaussian placement, differing from GaussianPro's explicit propagation of depth/normal maps [9172-neusg.md]. Uses a signed distance function (SDF) to guide densification, whereas GaussianPro uses propagated depth and normal maps [9205-gsdf.md]. Time Complexity: Increased per-step time due to patch matching propagation and additional loss computations (normal and planar). Memory Complexity: Standard 3DGS memory overhead, plus storage for depth/normal maps and propagated values. Strengths: Reduces popping artifacts, improves geometric accuracy, and handles complex surfaces better than standard 3DGS. Limitations: Relies on the quality of initial depth/normal estimates; patch matching can be computationally expensive. When to Use: When high geometric fidelity is required, or when standard 3DGS produces artifacts like popping or poor surface reconstruction. GaussianPro was introduced as a method to improve the reconstruction quality of 3D Gaussian Splatting by addressing the lack of continuity in the frame-by-frame discrete definition. It builds on the observation that physical-based constraints and geometric priors can mitigate artifacts. The method was cited in surveys of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting and compression methods. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeuSG
body: NeuSG integrates the NeuS implicit surface reconstruction method into the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to transfer explicit surface properties to discrete Gaussian primitives. Unlike sibling methods that rely on monocular depth priors or post-hoc mesh extraction, NeuSG directly couples a NeuS-style Signed Distance Function with a Gaussian rasterizer. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Calibrated images, initial 3D Gaussian parameters (centers \mathbf{c}i, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, colors), and a NeuS network initialized to predict SDF and opacity. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians and a NeuS network that jointly render photorealistic images and a consistent surface. Data Structures: 1. 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation with centers \mathbf{c}i, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. 2. NeuS Network: An MLP taking 3D position \mathbf{x} as input, outputting a raw SDF value \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and an opacity weight \omega(\mathbf{x}). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians from sparse points and initialize the NeuS MLP. 2. Rendering: Render the scene using the 3DGS rasterizer to produce RGB images. 3. Geometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{geo}): Query the NeuS network for the signed distance value at each Gaussian center: di = \sigma(\mathbf{c}i). Encourage these values to be zero, ensuring Gaussian centers lie on the zero-level set of the SDF. \mathcal{L}{geo} = \sumi |di| 4. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{norm}): Compute the Gaussian normal \mathbf{n}{gs,i} from its covariance matrix (principal axis). Compute the NeuS surface normal \mathbf{n}{neuS,i} = \nabla \sigma(\mathbf{c}i) / \|\nabla \sigma(\mathbf{c}i)\|. Minimize the angular difference between them. \mathcal{L}{norm} = \sumi (1 - \mathbf{n}{gs,i} \cdot \mathbf{n}{neuS,i}) 5. Photometric Loss: Compute the standard L1 or SSIM loss between rendered RGB images and ground truth images. 6. Optimization: Minimize the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalize(v): return v / max(norm(v), 1e-8) def computegaussiannormal(cov): eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eig(cov) return normalize(eigenvectors[:, argmax(eigenvalues)]) def neusgstep(gaussians, neusmlp, gtrgb, lambdageo, lambdanorm): # Standard 3DGS alpha compositing rasterizer renderedrgb = rasterize(gaussians) lgeo = 0.0 lnorm = 0.0 for g in gaussians: d = neusmlp(g.position) lgeo += abs(d) nneus = normalize(grad(neusmlp, g.position)) ngs = computegaussiannormal(g.covariance) lnorm += 1.0 - dot(ngs, nneus) lgeo /= len(gaussians) lnorm /= len(gaussians) lrgb = mean(abs(renderedrgb - gtrgb)) totalloss = lrgb + lambdageo lgeo + lambdanorm lnorm return totalloss Note: rasterize, grad, norm, dot, eig, argmax, abs, mean are standard math/vector operations. name: Monocular Depth Scale Alignment
head: Global Scale Alignment, Metric Scale Correction
body: Monocular Depth Scale Alignment is a post-optimization step in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines that resolves the up-to-scale ambiguity inherent in multi-view reconstruction by aligning the metric scale of optimized 3D Gaussians with metric-scale monocular depth estimates. Unlike methods that integrate depth priors during training, this approach operates after the standard Gaussian optimization phase, fixing the Gaussian parameters and optimizing only a global scale factor. It is distinct from sibling methods like NeuSG or GSDF which embed geometric losses into the training loop, and from Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting with Depth Priors which may rely on different initialization strategies. Inputs: \Theta: The set of optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, colors) from the standard 3DGS training. \{Ii\}{i=1}^{N{\mathcal{I}}}: A set of N{\mathcal{I}} input images. \{D^{mono}i\}{i=1}^{N{\mathcal{I}}}: Metric-scale monocular depth maps estimated from Ii using an off-the-shelf estimator (e.g., DepthAnythingV2). Outputs: \Theta': Updated Gaussian parameters where only the mean positions and scale attributes are scaled by the global factor a. Data Structures: a \in \mathbb{R}: A single scalar representing the global scene scale. Steps: 1. Monocular Depth Estimation: For each input image Ii, compute the metric depth map D^{mono}i using a pre-trained monocular depth estimation model. 2. Inverse Depth Conversion: Convert metric depth maps to inverse depth maps to match the rendering convention. If D^{mono}i contains metric depth values, compute invD^{mono}i = 1 / D^{mono}i. 3. Rendered Inverse Depth: Render the inverse depth map invD^{rendered}i for each view i using the current 3D Gaussian parameters \Theta. This is done by splatting the Gaussians and accumulating depth values weighted by opacity, typically using a differentiable renderer. 4. Optimize Global Scale: Optimize the global scale factor a to minimize the L1 distance between the monocular inverse depth and the scaled rendered inverse depth: a^ = \arg \mina \sum{i=1}^{N{\mathcal{I}}} \| invD^{mono}i - a \cdot invD^{rendered}i \|1 This optimization is performed while keeping \Theta fixed. 5. Update Gaussians: Apply the optimal scale a^ to the 3D Gaussians. Specifically, update the mean position \mathbf{c}i and the scale parameters (diagonal elements of the covariance matrix or explicit scale attributes) of each Gaussian i by multiplying them by a^. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def monoculardepthscalealignment(Gaussians, images, depthestimator): """ Aligns 3D Gaussian Splatting scale with monocular depth estimates. Args: Gaussians: Object containing Gaussian parameters (means, scales, etc.) images: List of input images depthestimator: Function to predict metric depth from image Returns: Gaussians: Updated Gaussian parameters with scaled means and scales """ N = len(images) # Step 1 & 2: Get metric depth and convert to inverse depth invdepthmono = [] for img in images: metricdepth = depthestimator(img) # Avoid division by zero; clamp small values metricdepth = torch.clamp(metricdepth, min=1e-6) invdepthmono.append(1.0 / metricdepth) # Step 3: Render inverse depth for current Gaussians # Note: invDrendered is computed by differentiable rasterization # of the Gaussians. The exact implementation depends on the renderer. # Here we assume a function renderinvdepth(Gaussians, cameraparams) exists. # For optimization, we need gradients w.r.t 'a', so we treat 'a' as a learnable parameter. a = torch.tensor(1.0, requiresgrad=True) # Step 4: Optimize 'a' optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([a], lr=0.01) for iteration in range(100): # Typical iteration count for this sub-step optimizer.zerograd() loss = 0.0 for i in range(N): # Render inverse depth with scaled Gaussians # The renderer internally scales the Gaussian means and scales by 'a' invdepthrendered = renderinvdepthscaled(Gaussians, a, cameraparams[i]) # Compute L1 loss loss += torch.abs(invdepthmono[i] - invdepthrendered).mean() loss.backward() optimizer.step() aoptimal = a.item() # Step 5: Update Gaussians # Only mean and scale attributes are changed Gaussians.means = Gaussians.means aoptimal Gaussians.scales = Gaussians.scales aoptimal return Gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pruning: Unlike original 3DGS which may prune initial COLMAP points, this method avoids pruning to prevent affecting the distribution of optimized Gaussian parameters, ensuring fair comparison with other studies. Depth Estimator Choice: The method relies on the quality of the monocular depth estimator. Using a metric-scale estimator (e.g., DepthAnythingV2 metric variant) is crucial, as opposed to relative depth estimators. Inverse Depth Convention: Ensure consistency between the monocular depth output format and the rendered depth format. The source specifies using the reciprocal of metric depth maps to obtain inverse depth maps. Time Complexity: The optimization of a is fast, as it involves only a single scalar parameter and a few forward passes through the depth estimator and renderer. The dominant cost is the initial 3DGS training. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory, as only the global scale factor is optimized. Strengths: Simple to implement as a post-processing step; does not require modifying the core 3DGS training loop; leverages state-of-the-art monocular depth estimators. Limitations: Only corrects global scale; does not address local geometric inaccuracies or shape errors; relies on the assumption that monocular depth estimates are globally consistent in scale. This method addresses the up-to-scale problem in neural rendering pipelines where multi-view reconstruction from images alone does not recover metric scale. It builds on the observation that monocular depth estimation models can provide metric-scale depth maps, which can be used to align the relative scale of 3D Gaussians. The approach is similar to depth alignment processes described in prior works [Chung et al., 2024; Kerbl et al., 2024], but specifically adapted for 3D Gaussian Splatting with a focus on avoiding pruning to maintain parameter distribution. name: Coarse Alignment with Optical Flow
head: Monocular Depth Scale Alignment via Optical Flow
body: Coarse Alignment with Optical Flow is a preprocessing step in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines that aligns relative monocular depth estimates across multiple views by optimizing per-view scale and offset parameters. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency caused by the relative nature of monocular depth, which leads to significant misalignments of initialized 3D Gaussians representing the same surfaces. Unlike Multi-View Stereo (MVS) methods, which can produce artifacts with sparse images and large baselines, this method leverages optical flow correspondences to enforce geometric coherence without requiring dense point clouds. Inputs: A set of N input images. Monocular depth maps D^mi for each view i, estimated by a monocular depth estimation network (e.g., Yang et al. [60] as cited in). Camera poses for each view. Optical flow field M{i \rightarrow j} representing pixel correspondences from view i to view j. Outputs: Optimized scale parameters \mathbf{s}^ and offset parameters \mathbf{o}^ for each view. Aligned initial depth maps D^{\text{init}}i. Data Structures: \mathbf{s}: Vector of scale factors, one per view. \mathbf{o}: Vector of offset factors, one per view. D^mi[\mathbf{p}]: Depth value at pixel \mathbf{p} in view i. M{i \rightarrow j}: Binary or confidence-weighted mask indicating valid flow correspondences from view i to view j. g(d, \mathbf{p}): Function projecting a depth value d at pixel \mathbf{p} in view i to the corresponding pixel coordinate \mathbf{q} in view j using the known camera geometry (intrinsics and extrinsics). Algorithm: 1. Compute Optical Flow: Calculate optical flow fields M{i \rightarrow j} for all relevant pairs of views (i, j). This establishes pixel-wise correspondences between images. 2. Define Objective: Minimize the L1 difference between the projected depth of view i and the depth of view j at corresponding pixels, weighted by the flow mask. The objective function is: \mathbf{s}^, \mathbf{o}^ = \arg \min{\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{o}} \sum{(i,j)}\sum{\mathbf{p}} \left\| M{i \rightarrow j} \odot \left( g(si \cdot D^mi[\mathbf{p}] + oi, \mathbf{p}) - g(sj \cdot D^mj[\mathbf{q}] + oj, \mathbf{q}) \right) \right\|1 where \mathbf{q} is the pixel coordinate in view j corresponding to \mathbf{p} in view i via the optical flow. 3. Optimize: Solve for \mathbf{s} and \mathbf{o} using gradient-based optimization. The optimization adjusts the scale and offset of each monocular depth map to minimize the reprojection error between views. 4. Apply Alignment: Compute the final aligned depth for each view i using the optimized parameters: D^{\text{init}}i = si \cdot D^mi + oi This aligned depth is then used to initialize the 3D Gaussians. Parameters: Optimization method: Gradient descent (specifics not given in sources). Loss function: L1 norm. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flow Accuracy: The method assumes the optical flow is accurate. Areas with inaccurate flow are masked out by M{i \rightarrow j}, leaving their depth unaltered, which may result in residual misalignments in those regions. Sparse Views: While MVS struggles with sparse views and large baselines, this method relies on monocular depth which may have larger errors in textureless regions, though it is noted to complement decoder-based approaches better than MVS in such cases. This variant refers to the experimental setup used to evaluate the SUDS method on the City-1M benchmark. It involves computing optical flow for all sequences using RAFT, aligning auxiliary inputs like depth with the main CoherentGS method, and deactivating the DINO feature distillation branch used for semantic reconstruction in SUDS. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Avoids artifacts associated with MVS in sparse view scenarios with large baselines. Provides a coherent representation that supports regularized optimization. Limitations: Relies on the quality of monocular depth estimation and optical flow. Misalignments may persist in areas where flow is inaccurate. When to Use: Use when initializing 3D Gaussians from monocular depth estimates to ensure multi-view consistency, especially when MVS is prone to artifacts due to sparse input views. Coarse Alignment with Optical Flow was introduced in the CoherentGS paper (2024) as a solution to the multi-view inconsistency problem in 3D Gaussian Splatting initialization. It builds on the observation that monocular depth estimates, while high-quality, are relative and inconsistent across views, leading to misaligned Gaussians. The method contrasts with MVS-based initialization approaches like MVSNeRF, which can suffer from artifacts in sparse settings. name: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting with Depth Priors
head: SparseGS, CoherentGS, DNGaussian
body: This method addresses the challenge of 3D reconstruction from sparse-view inputs, where standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) suffers from geometric ambiguity and artifacts due to insufficient multi-view constraints. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeuSG and GSDF by explicitly integrating depth priors estimated from pre-trained 2D monocular depth estimation networks to supervise the Gaussian distribution, rather than relying solely on implicit neural fields or surface extraction techniques. The method enhances the standard 3DGS optimization pipeline by incorporating geometric consistency losses derived from external depth estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of posed input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, camera poses \{Ri, Ti\}, and pre-estimated monocular depth maps \{Di\}{i=1}^N for each input view. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{\mathbf{g}j\} defined by centers \mathbf{c}j, covariances \Sigmaj, opacities \alphaj, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{j,SH}, optimized to render novel views consistent with the input images and depth priors. Data Structures: The Gaussian representation follows the standard 3DGS layout: Centers: \mathbf{c}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance: \Sigmaj = Rj Sj Sj^T Rj^T, where Rj \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is a rotation matrix (from quaternion) and Sj \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is a scaling matrix. Opacity: \alphaj \in [0, 1] Color: Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{j,SH}. Loss Function: The total loss function combines the standard photometric loss with geometric and normal consistency terms, following the shared principles of the parent family Parent: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} Where: \mathcal{L}{rgb} is the standard L1/SSIM photometric loss between rendered and input images. \mathcal{L}{geo} enforces positional consistency between Gaussian centers and the estimated depth. \mathcal{L}{norm} enforces normal consistency between Gaussian orientations and surface normals derived from the depth map. \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} are hyperparameters balancing photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Algorithm Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: For each input image Ii, estimate a dense depth map Di using a pre-trained 2D monocular depth estimation network. 2. Initialization: Initialize the 3D Gaussian point cloud, typically using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points or by unpooling existing Gaussians from the input views. 3. Rendering: Render the current Gaussian set to the input views to obtain rendered depth images D{rendered} and color images I{rendered}. 4. Geometric Loss Calculation: Compute \mathcal{L}{geo} by comparing D{rendered} with the estimated depth Di. This encourages Gaussian centers \mathbf{c}j to lie on the zero-level set of the distance function or align with metric depth estimates [Parent]. 5. Normal Consistency: Compute surface normals from the estimated depth map Di. Align the Gaussian orientation (derived from the rotation quaternion or covariance matrix) with these normals to compute \mathcal{L}{norm} [Parent]. 6. Gaussian Pruning: Remove Gaussians that exhibit incorrect depth values or large discrepancies between rendered and estimated depth, effectively cleaning up noise and artifacts common in sparse views. 7. Optional SDS Regularization: To further encourage faithful results from novel viewpoints, apply Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss. This leverages a pre-trained diffusion model to provide additional geometric priors where multi-view cues are weak. 8. Optimization: Update Gaussian parameters (\mathbf{c}j, \Sigmaj, \alphaj, \mathbf{c}{j,SH}) using gradient descent to minimize \mathcal{L}{total}. Parameters: \lambda{geo}, \lambda{norm}: Weights for geometric and normal losses. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources but are critical hyperparameters. SDS Weight: If used, the weight for the SDS loss term. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: Monocular depth estimates suffer from scale and shift ambiguity. The method must handle this, potentially through normalization or scale-invariant loss terms, though specific normalization steps are not detailed in the sources. Sparse View Ambiguity: With very few views, the optimization may converge to local minima. SDS loss helps mitigate this by providing strong semantic priors. Incorrect Depth Estimates: If the pre-trained depth network fails on certain textures or regions, the geometric loss may pull Gaussians to incorrect positions. Pruning steps help remove these outliers. Definition: FWD is a generalizable novel view synthesis method for sparse inputs that uses explicit depth and forward warping to achieve real-time speed and high quality. Unlike the sparse-view 3DGS methods which optimize per-scene Gaussians, FWD is a generalizable model that learns to synthesize views without per-scene optimization. How it works: 1. Input: Sparse input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N and poses \{Ri, Ti\}. Optional sensor depths \{Di^{sen}\} may be provided, though they are often incomplete and noisy. 2. Depth and Feature Estimation: For each input view Ii, estimate depth Di using a depth network d and compute spatial features Fi using a spatial feature encoder f (based on BigGAN architecture) and a view-dependent MLP \psi. Features are 64-dimensional (61-dim semantic + 3-dim RGB). 3. Point Cloud Construction: Project the features into 3D space using known camera intrinsics to form a point cloud Pi for each view. 4. Rendering: Render the point clouds Pi to the target view using a differentiable point cloud renderer \pi. Instead of aggregating point clouds across views before rendering, FWD renders viewpoints separately and fuses them using a Transformer-based module \mathcal{T}, enabling attention across input views. 5. Refinement: Apply a refinement module \mathcal{R} to generate the final output, improving visual quality. 6. Training: Train end-to-end with photometric and perceptual losses. Parameters: N: Number of input views. \{Ri, Ti\}: Camera poses for input views. \{Rt, Tt\}: Camera pose for target view. \{Di^{sen}\}: Optional sensor depths for input views. Comparison: FWD replaces implicit MLP volumetric sampling with explicit point clouds, avoiding millions of MLP queries and enabling a 130-1000× speedup compared to NeRF-based methods. It uses sparse inputs and learns depth jointly optimized for synthesis quality, unlike classical Image-Based Rendering (IBR) which requires dense inputs and proxy geometry. Usage: Evaluated on ShapeNet and DTU datasets. Code available at https://github.com/Caoang327/fwdcode. Time Complexity: The optimization time depends on the number of Gaussians and the cost of the pre-trained depth network and SDS loss (if used). Unlike FWD, which is real-time due to its generalizable nature, sparse-view 3DGS methods typically require per-scene optimization, making them slower than generalizable methods but faster than dense-view 3DGS in terms of data requirements. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians. Pruning helps reduce memory usage by removing incorrect Gaussians. Strengths: Enables high-quality 3D reconstruction from very few input views (e.g., 3-5 images) by leveraging strong geometric priors. SDS loss helps resolve ambiguities in sparse settings. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the pre-trained 2D depth estimation network. Performance degrades if the depth estimates are poor. Per-scene optimization is required, unlike generalizable methods like FWD. When to use: When input views are sparse and standard 3DGS fails to produce coherent geometry. When not to use: When real-time inference without per-scene optimization is required (use FWD instead) or when dense input views are available (standard 3DGS may suffice). The method originates from the need to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to sparse-view scenarios, where traditional multi-view stereo constraints are insufficient. SparseGS, CoherentGS, and DNGaussian are key contributions in this area, introducing depth supervision from pre-trained 2D networks to guide the Gaussian optimization. The use of SDS loss for sparse-view reconstruction was also explored to leverage the geometric priors of pre-trained diffusion models.
