name: GSDF
head: Gaussian SDF, Gaussian Signed Distance Function
body:
GSDF is a training optimization technique that aligns the discrete 3D Gaussian representation with a continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) prior to enhance geometry reconstruction quality. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeuSG by explicitly transferring surface properties from a neural SDF to the Gaussians, encouraging Gaussian centers to lie on the zero-level set and normals to align with the SDF gradient. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (centers \mathbf{c}i, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, colors \mathbf{c}i), a pre-trained or concurrently trained neural SDF field S(\mathbf{x}), and input images with camera poses. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians suitable for high-fidelity rendering and mesh extraction. Data Structures: Neural SDF: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} to a scalar distance value S(\mathbf{x}). Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes. The covariance matrix \Sigmai defines the orientation and scale, from which the normal direction is derived. Method Steps: 1. Render: Perform standard differentiable volume rendering to generate predicted images and depth maps. 2. Evaluate SDF: For each Gaussian center \mathbf{c}i, query the neural SDF to obtain S(\mathbf{c}i). 3. Compute Geometric Loss: Calculate the loss encouraging Gaussians to lie on the surface: \mathcal{L}{geo} = \sumi |S(\mathbf{c}i)| This term minimizes the signed distance of Gaussian centers to the zero-level set. 4. Compute Normal Loss: Estimate the surface normal from the SDF gradient 
abla S(\mathbf{c}i) and the Gaussian orientation. The Gaussian normal \mathbf{n}i is derived from the eigenvector of the covariance matrix \Sigmai corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue (or the rotation quaternion's forward vector). The loss minimizes the angular difference: \mathcal{L}{norm} = \sumi (1 - \mathbf{n}i \cdot  rac{
abla S(\mathbf{c}i)}{\|
abla S(\mathbf{c}i)\|}) This ensures the Gaussian orientation aligns with the SDF surface normal. 5. Optimize: Minimize the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \mathcal{L}{rgb} is the photometric rendering loss. Parameters: \lambda{geo}, \lambda{norm}: Hyperparameters balancing geometric consistency against photometric fidelity. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Gaussians: If Gaussians become flat or elongated incorrectly, the normal estimation from covariance may become unstable. SDF Accuracy: The method relies on the quality of the underlying neural SDF. Poor SDF training leads to incorrect geometric priors. Complexity: Adds overhead of querying the neural SDF MLP for each Gaussian center during training. Strengths: Recovers more detailed mesh structures compared to standard 3DGS. Enhances geometry reconstruction quality. Limitations: Requires a reliable neural SDF prior. Performance depends on the accuracy of the SDF field. When to use: When high-quality surface reconstruction and mesh extraction are required from 3DGS. GSDF was introduced to leverage neural signed distance functions (SDFs) for surface reconstruction, inspired by similar approaches in NeRF-based methods. It was extended in subsequent works like 2DGS, which replaced 3D Gaussians with 2D Gaussians for more accurate ray-splat intersection. It is closely related to other methods such as 3DGSR and GSPull that also encourage consistency between SDF and 3DGS. name: Surface and Geometry Alignment
head: Geometric Priors for 3DGS, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
body: This family of methods addresses the fundamental limitation of vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the production of "floating" volumetric ellipsoids that lack an explicit, watertight geometric boundary. By aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with continuous geometric priors (such as SDFs, depth maps, or explicit meshes), these methods enforce positional and normal consistency to enable accurate mesh extraction, physically-based rendering, and robust initialization. Unlike sibling methods that may rely solely on photometric loss or implicit constraints, this family explicitly integrates geometric supervision into the training or post-processing pipeline to ensure the Gaussians conform to physical surfaces. All methods in this family share the goal of aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with a continuous geometric prior. The core mechanism involves adding geometric loss terms to the standard photometric rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rgb}. These losses typically enforce two properties: 1. Positional Consistency: Gaussian centers \mathbf{c}i are encouraged to lie on the zero-level set of a distance function (SDF or UDF) or align with metric depth estimates. 2. Normal Consistency: The orientation of the Gaussians (derived from their covariance matrix or rotation quaternion) is aligned with the surface normal estimated from the geometric prior. The total loss function generally takes the form: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \mathcal{L}{geo} is the geometric consistency loss and \mathcal{L}{norm} is the normal consistency loss. The weights \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} are hyperparameters that balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. A post-hoc method that converts trained 3DGS into a watertight mesh via self-regularization and Poisson reconstruction. It differs from siblings by operating after training rather than during, solving the "floating" ellipsoid problem for downstream mesh applications. A training optimization that re-projects Gaussians onto a canonical surface mesh to resolve unbalanced aggregation from densification. Unlike SuGaR or Geo-Splatting, it explicitly repositions Gaussians to a known geometry rather than relying on loss-driven alignment. A physically-based inverse rendering method that differentiably constructs surface-aligned Gaussians from an explicit mesh to improve normal estimation and light transport. It distinguishes itself by using ray tracing on the mesh for accurate PBR, avoiding the approximated normals of standard 3DGS. A geometric contrastive embedding method that aligns token similarity with 3D proximity to ensure clustering by physical surface. Unlike hard positional constraints, it uses soft contrastive targets derived from unprojected depths to shape the latent space. The concept of aligning Gaussian representations with geometric priors emerged as a solution to the lack of explicit geometry in 3D Gaussian Splatting. While 3DGS excels at novel view synthesis, its volumetric nature makes mesh extraction difficult. Early works like SuGaR introduced post-hoc regularization to flatten Gaussians into surfels. Subsequent methods like Geo-Splatting integrated explicit meshes for physically-based rendering, while others like GeoCE Loss focused on feature-space geometric consistency. The family continues to evolve with methods addressing initialization and sparse-view constraints. SuGaR: Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for Efficient 3D Scene Reconstruction and High-Quality Mesh Reconstruction, https://sugar-iseg.github.io/, 2023 Geo-Splatting: Geometrically-Accurate Gaussian Splatting for View-Dependent Appearance and Accurate Geometry, https://github.com/ingra14d/Geo-Splatting, 2024

name: SuGaR
head: SuGaR: Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for Realistic Head Avatar Reconstruction, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
body: SuGaR is a post-hoc surface alignment method that converts the discrete, volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation into a continuous, watertight triangle mesh. It solves the problem that vanilla 3DGS produces "floating" ellipsoids with no explicit geometric boundary, making it difficult to extract meshes for downstream applications like animation or physics. Unlike sibling methods that enforce surface constraints during training (e.g., Geo-Splatting), SuGaR operates after the initial 3DGS optimization, using a self-regularization loss to flatten and align Gaussians to a surface, followed by Poisson reconstruction. Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} with positions \mathbf{c}i, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, and colors \mathbf{c}i^{color}) and a set of multi-view images with known camera poses. Outputs: A triangle mesh \mathcal{M} and a modified set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' pinned to the mesh surface. Data Structures: Gaussian i: \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (derived from scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c}i^{color}: Spherical Harmonics coefficients or RGB color. Steps: 1. Render Depth and Opacity: Render the current 3DGS model to obtain a depth map D and an opacity map \alpha for each input view. The depth di for a pixel is the weighted average of the distances of the splatted Gaussians along the ray. 2. Compute Self-Regularization Loss: Apply a penalty to encourage Gaussians to lie on the surface. The loss \mathcal{L}{reg} constrains the distance between the camera and the closest Gaussian to match the rendered depth. \mathcal{L}{reg} = \sum{i} \left( \mathbf{c}i \cdot \mathbf{r}i - di \right)^2 Where \mathbf{r}i is the ray direction for the pixel corresponding to Gaussian i's projection, and di is the rendered depth value. Note: Sources describe this as constraining the "distance between the camera and the closest Gaussian". 3. Flatten and Align Gaussians: Optimize the Gaussian parameters to minimize \mathcal{L}{reg}. This process flattens the Gaussians (reducing the scale along the normal direction) and aligns their orientation with the surface normal estimated from the depth/position data. The Gaussians become "surfels" (surface elements). 4. Poisson Mesh Reconstruction: Extract the surface geometry from the aligned Gaussians. Sample points from the centers \mathbf{c}i of the flattened Gaussians. Estimate normals for these points using the aligned Gaussian orientations or gradients of the depth map. Run Poisson surface reconstruction on these points and normals to generate the triangle mesh \mathcal{M}. 5. Pin Gaussians to Mesh (Optional for Hybrid Representation): To create a hybrid representation, project the Gaussian centers onto the extracted mesh \mathcal{M} and update their positions \mathbf{c}i' to lie exactly on the surface. Parameters: Weight of the regularization loss \lambda{reg}: Not given in the sources. Poisson reconstruction depth: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Fuzzy Materials: SuGaR is limited in reconstructing fuzzy materials and volumetric effects, as it forces a surface-based representation. Discrete Nature: Due to the discrete nature of 3DGS, the resulting geometry may be comparable or worse than implicit methods (like NeuS) if the Gaussian distribution is sparse or noisy. Time Complexity: Post-hoc optimization adds training time proportional to the number of Gaussians and views for the regularization step. Poisson reconstruction is O(N \log N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the original 3DGS plus the mesh data. No significant additional memory during optimization compared to standard 3DGS. Strengths: Provides a watertight mesh suitable for DCC pipelines, animation, and physics. Simple to implement as a post-processing step. Limitations: Decreases rendering performance compared to vanilla 3DGS due to the flattening constraint and potential loss of volumetric detail. Geometry quality may lag behind continuous implicit methods. When to use: When a mesh is required for downstream applications and the scene is primarily opaque/surface-based. When not to use: For scenes with significant transparency, fog, or volumetric effects. SuGaR was introduced by Guédon and Lepetit. It is cited as the pioneering work that builds 3D surfaces from multi-view images using the 3DGS representation. It addresses the lack of structure in the raw 3DGS point cloud, which makes it difficult for artists to modify or animate. name: Surface-guided Gaussian Re-initialization
head: GVA
body: Surface-guided Gaussian Re-initialization (GVA) is a training optimization method that resolves the unbalanced aggregation of 3D Gaussians caused by densification and splitting operations. It achieves this by re-initializing Gaussian parameters based on a surface prior, ensuring the discrete representation better fits the input monocular video. Unlike its siblings SuGaR and Geo-Splatting, which primarily rely on loss terms for alignment, GVA explicitly repositions Gaussians to a canonical surface geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of trained 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} with positions \mathbf{c}i, covariances \Sigmai, and a canonical surface mesh \mathcal{M} (e.g., a human body mesh). Output: Re-initialized Gaussians \{G'i\} whose centers are projected onto the surface \mathcal{M}. Data Structures: Canonical Mesh \mathcal{M}: Defined by vertices \mathbf{V} and faces \mathcal{F}. Each face f \in \mathcal{F} has vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 and a normal \mathbf{n}f. Gaussian Gi: Defined by center \mathbf{c}i, rotation Ri, scale Si, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Steps: 1. Identify Unbalanced Aggregation: Detect Gaussians that have clustered excessively due to densification/splitting. 2. Project to Canonical Space: For each Gaussian Gi with center \mathbf{c}i, find the closest point on the canonical mesh \mathcal{M}. 3. Compute Barycentric Coordinates: Determine the barycentric coordinates (u, v, w) of the projection point relative to the triangle vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. 4. Re-initialize Position: Set the new center \mathbf{c}'i to the projected point on the surface. 5. Align Orientation: Adjust the rotation R'i such that the Gaussian's principal axis aligns with the surface normal \mathbf{n}f at the projection point. 6. Update Covariance: Recompute \Sigma'i based on the new orientation and scale. Formulas: The new position \mathbf{c}'i is calculated as: \mathbf{c}'i = u \mathbf{v}1 + v \mathbf{v}2 + w \mathbf{v}3 where u, v, w are barycentric coordinates. Parameters: Mesh Resolution: Not given in the sources. Re-initialization Frequency: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: If the closest point falls on an edge or vertex, barycentric coordinates may become unstable. Occlusion: The canonical mesh may not represent occluded regions accurately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reinitializegaussians(gaussians, mesh): """ Re-initialize Gaussian positions and orientations based on a canonical mesh. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: center: numpy array (3,) rotation: numpy array (3,3) or quaternion scale: numpy array (3,) mesh: Mesh object with attributes: vertices: numpy array (N, 3) faces: numpy array (M, 3) indices into vertices getclosestpointandnormal(center): returns (point, normal) Returns: List of re-initialized Gaussian objects """ reinitializedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Step 1: Find closest point on mesh closestpoint, surfacenormal = mesh.getclosestpointandnormal(g.center) # Step 2: Re-initialize position g.center = closestpoint # Step 3: Align orientation with surface normal # Assuming 'alignrotationtonormal' is a helper that rotates a base vector (e.g., z-axis) # to align with the given normal. g.rotation = alignrotationtonormal(g.rotation, surfacenormal) # Step 4: Recompute covariance from rotation and scale # Sigma = R S S^T R^T scalematrix = np.diag(g.scale) g.covariance = g.rotation @ (scalematrix @ scalematrix.T) @ g.rotation.T reinitializedgaussians.append(g) return reinitializedgaussians def alignrotationtonormal(currentrotation, targetnormal): """ Adjust rotation so that the Gaussian's principal axis (e.g., z-axis) aligns with targetnormal. This is a placeholder for the specific alignment logic used in GVA. """ # Standard approach: compute rotation matrix that aligns z-axis (0,0,1) to targetnormal zaxis = np.array([0, 0, 1]) if np.allclose(zaxis, targetnormal): return currentrotation # Compute rotation axis and angle rotationaxis = np.cross(zaxis, targetnormal) rotationangle = np.arccos(np.dot(zaxis, targetnormal)) # Convert to rotation matrix (Rodrigues' formula) # Note: This is a simplified implementation. GVA may use a specific alignment strategy. k = rotationaxis / np.linalg.norm(rotationaxis) K = np.array([ [0, -k[2], k[1]], [k[2], 0, -k[0]], [-k[1], k[0], 0] ]) Ralign = np.eye(3) + np.sin(rotationangle) K + (1 - np.cos(rotationangle)) (K @ K) return Ralign @ currentrotation Uses a canonical mesh (e.g., FLAME for faces, SMPL for bodies) as the geometric prior. Sets it apart by providing a consistent topology for re-initialization. Choose when dealing with articulated or deformable subjects. Attaches Gaussians directly to the mesh surface. Sets it apart by reducing the number of Gaussians needed for high-fidelity geometry. Choose when computational efficiency is critical. Time Complexity: Depends on the mesh traversal for closest point queries. Typically O(N \log M) or O(N) with spatial hashing, where N is the number of Gaussians and M is the number of mesh faces. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the canonical mesh and its acceleration structure. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Resolves unbalanced aggregation; improves geometric fidelity on monocular video. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the canonical mesh; may introduce artifacts if the mesh is incomplete or inaccurate. When to Use: Human avatar reconstruction from monocular video. When Not to Use: Scenes without a clear canonical surface prior. GVA was proposed in the context of human avatar reconstruction from monocular video. It addresses the issue of Gaussian aggregation during training, which can degrade geometric accuracy. The method builds on the idea of embedding Gaussians onto a canonical human body mesh, similar to SplattingAvatar and GoMAvatar. name: Geo-Splatting
body: Geo-Splatting is a physically-based inverse rendering method that augments 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with explicit geometric guidance to improve normal estimation and light transport modeling. It addresses the inaccuracies in material decomposition and relighting caused by the approximated normals and semi-transparent nature of standard Gaussian points. Unlike sibling methods like SuGaR which rely on implicit geometric constraints or approximated normals, Geo-Splatting differentiably constructs surface-aligned Gaussian points from an optimizable explicit mesh, leveraging well-defined mesh normals and an opaque mesh surface for accurate light transport. Inputs: Multi-view images, camera poses. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (centers, covariances, colors, opacities), explicit triangular mesh, material properties (albedo, roughness, normal), and environment light. Data Structures: 1. Learnable Isovalue Grid: A 3D scalar field representing the implicit surface distance function. 2. Triangular Mesh: Extracted from the isovalue grid using FlexiCubes. 3. 3D Gaussian Points: Structured points generated on the mesh surface. Each Gaussian i is defined by center \mathbf{c}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (decomposed into scale \mathbf{S}i and rotation \mathbf{R}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color/view-dependent appearance. 4. BVH (Bounding Volume Hierarchy): Acceleration structure built on the explicit mesh for ray tracing. Steps: 1. Geometry Extraction: Extract an intermediate triangular mesh from the learnable isovalue grids using FlexiCubes. This provides an explicit, differentiable geometric prior. 2. Gaussian Generation (MGadapter): Use the Mesh-to-Gaussian adaptor (MGadapter) to generate 3DGS points on the mesh surface in a differentiable manner. This ensures that Gaussian centers lie on the mesh surface and their orientations align with the mesh normals. This step differentiably constructs structured Gaussian points grounded on the mesh geometry. 3. Light Transport Evaluation: Perform BVH-accelerated ray tracing on the extracted mesh to evaluate light transport. This step accounts for self-occlusion and inter-reflection, which split-sum approximations lack. Monte Carlo sampling is used to evaluate the rendering equation [19] on the explicit mesh proxy. 4. PBR Color Computation: Compute per-Gaussian physically-based rendering (PBR) colors by evaluating the rendering equation [19] using the light transport results and material properties (albedo, roughness, normal). 5. Rendering: Composite the shaded Gaussian points into final images using the standard 3DGS rasterization algorithm. 6. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian parameters, mesh, and material properties end-to-end by minimizing the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \mathcal{L}{rgb} is the photometric loss, \mathcal{L}{geo} is the geometric consistency loss, and \mathcal{L}{norm} is the normal consistency loss. The weights \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. mesh = FlexiCubes.extract(isovaluegrid) gaussians = MGadapter.generate(mesh) # Differentiable construction bvh = BVH.build(mesh) for step in range(numsteps): # 1. Render Image # Ray trace on mesh for light transport lighttransport = BVH.trace(bvh, rays) # Compute PBR colors for each Gaussian for g in gaussians: g.color = PBR.evaluate(g.material, lighttransport, g.normal) # Composite using 3DGS rasterizer renderedimage = Rasterizer.render(gaussians) # 2. Compute Losses lossrgb = MSE(renderedimage, targetimage) lossgeo = GeometricLoss(gaussians.center, mesh) lossnorm = NormalLoss(gaussians.normal, mesh.normal) totalloss = lossrgb + lambdageo lossgeo + lambdanorm lossnorm # 3. Backpropagate totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: \lambda{geo}, \lambda{norm}: Hyperparameters for loss weighting. Values not given in the sources. FlexiCubes: Used for isosurface extraction. MGadapter: Differentiable module for mesh-to-Gaussian conversion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Existing 3DGS-based inverse methods suffer from inaccuracies in normal estimation due to approximated normals and semi-transparent Gaussian points, leading to noisy material decomposition and flawed relighting. Geo-Splatting mitigates this by using explicit mesh normals. Split-sum approximation lacks self-occlusion modeling, leading to inaccurate decomposition under strong shadow effects. Geo-Splatting uses ray tracing to handle this. Spherical Gaussian (SG) methods struggle with reflective cases due to low-frequency nature. Geo-Splatting uses Monte Carlo sampling with ray tracing on an explicit mesh proxy to handle reflective surfaces. Time Complexity: Training time is 9 minutes on the reported dataset, compared to 56 minutes for R3DG and 13 minutes for GS-IR. This efficiency is attributed to the use of BVH-accelerated ray tracing on the explicit mesh proxy rather than direct ray tracing on 3D Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Relighting PSNR of 29.5dB, compared to 26.6dB for R3DG and 20.4dB for GS-IR. Strengths: Superior decomposition and relighting quality; excellent training efficiency; accurate light transport modeling via explicit mesh normals and ray tracing; handles self-occlusion and reflective surfaces. Limitations: Requires explicit mesh extraction and BVH construction; relies on the quality of the initial isovalue grid and FlexiCubes extraction. When to use: When high-fidelity material decomposition and relighting are required, especially in scenes with strong shadows or reflective surfaces. When not to use: When computational resources for BVH construction and ray tracing are limited, or when simple photometric reconstruction without physical accuracy is sufficient. Geo-Splatting was proposed by Wenzheng Chen, Guanbin Li, et al. from Sun Yat-sen University and Peking University. It was published in ICCV 2025. The work addresses limitations in existing 3DGS-based inverse rendering methods like R3DG and GS-IR, which rely on approximated normals and split-sum approximations. It builds on prior works in isosurface extraction [41] and physically-based rendering [19]. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GeoSplatting: Towards Geometry Guided Gaussian Splatting for Physically-Based Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51701.2025.02692, fetched 2026-10-30

name: GeoCE Loss
head: Geometric Contrastive Loss
body:
GeoCE (Geometric Contrastive Embedding) is a geometric supervision method used in 3D Gaussian Splatting training to ensure that learned scene tokens cluster by physical surface rather than by viewpoint. It solves the problem where feature-space similarity does not guarantee geometric consistency, by explicitly aligning token cosine similarities with 3D proximity. Unlike sibling methods that enforce hard constraints on Gaussian positions or normals, GeoCE shapes the latent token space using a soft contrastive target derived from unprojected patch depths, allowing multiple patches observing the same surface to share high similarity weights. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N geometry tokens \{\mathbf{g}i\}{i=1}^N, where each token \mathbf{g}i corresponds to an image patch observed from a specific camera view. Ground-truth camera poses and intrinsics for the training views. Depth maps for the training views (precomputed, e.g., by DA3-Giant). Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{geo}} that penalizes discrepancies between token similarity and 3D proximity. Data Structures Tokens: \mathbf{g}i \in \mathbb{R}^d, \ell2-normalized. Anchors: A subset of tokens sampled as anchors. The method samples 2048 tokens per scene as anchors during training. 3D Points: For each anchor i, a 3D point \mathbf{p}i is computed by unprojecting the median-depth pixel of its associated patch using the ground-truth camera. Bandwidths: A scalar \sigmai for each anchor, derived from local patch texture. Parameters 	au = 0.1: Temperature parameter for the softmax. \lambda{\mathrm{geo}} = 0.05: Weight for the GeoCE loss in the total objective. K = 2048: Number of anchor tokens sampled per scene. Grid size: 4 	imes 4 pixels for depth averaging. Algorithm Steps 1. Anchor Sampling: Randomly sample K tokens from the current batch of scene tokens to serve as anchors. 2. 3D Unprojection: For each anchor i, identify its associated image patch. Compute the median depth di of the valid pixels in this patch. Unproject the center of the patch (or the median-depth pixel) using the ground-truth camera intrinsics and pose to obtain the 3D anchor point \mathbf{p}i. 3. Validity Check: Exclude anchors whose patches have valid depth on fewer than half of their pixels. 4. Bandwidth Calculation: Compute the base bandwidth \sigma as the scene-wise median 3D distance between adjacent patch points. For each anchor i, compute the mean image-gradient energy of its patch to rank texture complexity. Calculate the per-token bandwidth \sigmai by log-interpolating between \sigma (for the flattest patch) and 0.4\sigma (for the most textured patch), based on the patch's rank in gradient energy. 5. Target Weight Computation: For each pair of anchors (i, j) with i 
eq j, compute the soft target weight w{ij} based on their 3D Euclidean distance: w{ij} \propto \exp \left( - rac{\|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}j\|^2}{2\sigmai \sigmaj} ight) The weight w{ij} represents the probability that tokens i and j observe the same surface region. Patches with high 3D proximity receive high weights. Normalize w{ij} such that \sum{j 
eq i} w{ij} = 1 for each i (implicit in the cross-entropy formulation). 6. Loss Computation: Compute the cosine similarity between all pairs of anchor tokens: s{ij} = \mathbf{g}i^	op \mathbf{g}j (assuming \ell2-normalized tokens). Calculate the GeoCE loss using cross-entropy between the target distribution w{ij} and the predicted similarity distribution: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{geo}} = -\sum{i} \sum{j 
eq i} w{ij} \log  rac{\exp(\mathbf{g}i^	op \mathbf{g}j / 	au)}{\sum{k 
eq i} \exp(\mathbf{g}i^	op \mathbf{g}k / 	au)} This loss pushes the token cosine similarities to match the soft target distribution weighted by 3D proximity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geoceloss(geometrytokens, anchorsindices, cameras, depthmaps, sigmabase, tau=0.1): """ Computes the GeoCE loss for a batch of scene tokens. Args: geometrytokens: Tensor of shape (N, D), L2-normalized geometry tokens. anchorsindices: List of K indices into geometrytokens to use as anchors. cameras: List of camera objects with intrinsics and poses for the views. depthmaps: Dictionary mapping viewid to depth map tensor. sigmabase: Base bandwidth (scene-wise median 3D distance). tau: Temperature parameter. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ K = len(anchorsindices) anchorstokens = geometrytokens[anchorsindices] # Shape (K, D) # Step 2 & 3: Unproject and filter anchors validanchors = [] anchorpoints = [] anchorgradenergies = [] for idx in anchorsindices: # Identify the view and patch associated with token idx # Implementation detail: assumes a mapping from token index to (viewid, patchbbox) exists. viewid, patchbbox = gettokenviewandpatch(idx) depthmap = depthmaps[viewid] patchdepths = extractpatchdepths(depthmap, patchbbox) # Check validity: at least half pixels must have valid depth if countvaliddepth(patchdepths) < 0.5 patchdepths.numel(): continue # Compute median depth mediandepth = torch.median(patchdepths[patchdepths > 0]) # Unproject to 3D pi = unprojectpixel(viewid, patchbbox.center, mediandepth, cameras[viewid]) # Compute gradient energy for bandwidth interpolation gradenergy = computemeangradientenergy(viewid, patchbbox) validanchors.append(idx) anchorpoints.append(pi) anchorgradenergies.append(gradenergy) if len(validanchors) < 2: return 0.0 Kvalid = len(validanchors) anchorpoints = torch.stack(anchorpoints) # Shape (Kvalid, 3) anchortokens = geometrytokens[validanchors] # Shape (Kvalid, D) # Step 4: Calculate per-token bandwidths # Rank patches by gradient energy sortedindices = torch.argsort(anchorgradenergies) # Log-interpolate sigmai from sigmabase (flattest) to 0.4 sigmabase (most textured) # Assuming linear rank mapping to log-space interpolation minsigma = 0.4 sigmabase maxsigma = sigmabase sigmas = [] for rank, idx in enumerate(sortedindices): # Normalize rank to [0, 1] t = rank / (Kvalid - 1) # Log-interpolation: log(sigmai) = (1-t)log(maxsigma) + tlog(minsigma) logsigma = (1 - t) torch.log(torch.tensor(maxsigma)) + t torch.log(torch.tensor(minsigma)) sigmas.append(torch.exp(logsigma)) sigmas = torch.tensor(sigmas) # Step 5: Compute target weights # Compute pairwise distances dists = torch.cdist(anchorpoints, anchorpoints) # Shape (Kvalid, Kvalid) # Compute weights wij proportional to exp(-dist^2 / (2 sigmai sigmaj)) # Using broadcasting for sigmai and sigmaj sigmamatrix = sigmas.unsqueeze(1) sigmas.unsqueeze(0) weights = torch.exp(-dists2 / (2 sigmamatrix)) # Exclude self-connections weights = weights (1 - torch.eye(Kvalid, device=weights.device)) # Normalize weights for each row i weights = weights / (weights.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) # Step 6: Compute loss # Compute cosine similarities (tokens are L2-normalized) similarities = anchortokens @ anchortokens.T # Shape (Kvalid, Kvalid) # Softmax over j != i # Subtract max for numerical stability expsim = torch.exp(similarities / tau) expsim = expsim (1 - torch.eye(Kvalid, device=expsim.device)) sumexpsim = expsim.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) logprobs = torch.log(expsim / (sumexpsim + 1e-8) + 1e-8) # Cross-entropy: - sumi sumj wij log(pj|i) loss = -torch.sum(weights logprobs) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Invalid Depth: Patches with insufficient valid depth are excluded. If too few anchors remain valid, the loss cannot be computed. Precision: Median depth computation should handle outliers in depth maps. Bandwidth Scaling: The bandwidth \sigmai scales with local patch spacing. Incorrect scaling can lead to overly local or overly global similarity targets. Time Complexity: O(K^2) per batch, where K is the number of sampled anchors (2048). This is negligible compared to the rendering and clustering steps. Memory Complexity: O(K^2) to store the pairwise distance and weight matrices. Performance: GeoCE enables the formation of compact, surface-aligned Gaussian clusters, improving reconstruction quality (PSNR) while reducing the number of required Gaussians. Strengths: Explicitly enforces geometric consistency in the latent space, preventing viewpoint-based clustering artifacts. Works with unposed cameras when combined with TokenBA. Limitations: Requires accurate depth maps (or depth estimation) for the training views. Performance depends on the quality of the median depth and the validity of the 3D unprojection. GeoCE was introduced in the ZipSplat paper (2026) as part of a framework for few-shot 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitation of previous methods where clustering in feature space did not guarantee geometric coherence. By aligning token similarity with 3D proximity, it enables more robust scene representation, particularly in scenarios with limited views or unposed cameras. ZipSplat: Fewer Gaussians, Better Splats, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.05102, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Cone Loss
body:
The Cone Loss is a geometric regularization term used in ZipSplat to ground 3D Gaussian tokens to their specific source image patches, preventing decoded Gaussians from drifting arbitrarily in 3D space. Unlike frustum-based constraints that merely ensure visibility, this loss explicitly ties each token’s geometry to the observation that produced it, ensuring an observation-grounded scene representation. It serves as a sibling to the GeoCE Loss, which handles token merging, while the Cone Loss handles the initial spatial anchoring of individual tokens. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: K: Total number of scene tokens. 
gs: Number of Gaussians per token. \gmean{kj}: The 3D mean position of the j-th Gaussian belonging to token k. \pik: The projection function mapping 3D points into the 2D image plane of token k's source view. \{u}k: The 2D center coordinate of the source image patch for token k. Outputs: A scalar loss value \loss{\mathrm{cone}} representing the total reprojection error. Data Structures Token indices k \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Gaussian indices j \in \{1, \dots, 
gs\}. Coordinates are measured in "patch units" (where the patch width/height is normalized to 1 unit). Algorithm The loss is computed by summing a robust penalty ho over all Gaussians of all tokens. The penalty is based on the Euclidean distance between the projected Gaussian center and the source patch center. 1. For each token k from 1 to K: 2. For each Gaussian j from 1 to 
gs: 3. Project the Gaussian mean \gmean{kj} into the source view of token k using \pik to obtain the 2D point \mathbf{p} = \pik(\gmean{kj}). 4. Check if the Gaussian projects behind the camera plane of the source view. If yes, assign a sentinel distance d = 20 patch units. Note that this distance yields no lateral gradient. If no, compute the Euclidean distance in patch units: d = \| \mathbf{p} - \{u}k \|. 5. Apply the hinged Cauchy penalty function ho(d) to d. 6. Accumulate ho(d) into the total loss. Formula The total Cone Loss is defined as: \loss{\mathrm{cone}} = \sum{k=1}^{K} \sum{j=1}^{
gs} ho \left( \left\| \pik(\gmean{kj}) - \{u}k ight\| ight) Where: \pik(\gmean{kj}) is the 2D projection of the j-th Gaussian of token k into its source view. \{u}k is the center of the source patch for token k. The norm \|\cdot\| is the Euclidean distance measured in patch units. ho is a robust penalty function (hinged Cauchy). Robust Penalty Function ho The function ho(d) is a hinged Cauchy function of the distance d in patch units. It has the following properties: 1. Hinge (Zero-cost region): For d \le 2, ho(d) = 0. This allows Gaussians to extend up to 2 patch units past their source observation, accommodating flat surfaces or occluded regions. 2. Smooth Ramp: For 2 < d \le 4, the penalty ramps smoothly with C^1 continuity. 3. Saturation: For d > 4, the penalty saturates to limit the influence of distant outliers. Parameters Weight \lambda{\mathrm{cone}} = 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Behind-view Gaussians: Gaussians projecting behind the source view receive a fixed sentinel distance of 20 patches. This provides a large penalty value but no lateral gradient, preventing optimization from pushing these Gaussians laterally into the view. Depth Independence: The loss constrains only the lateral position relative to the viewing cone. Depth is left to be determined by the rendering loss. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coneloss(gmeans, projections, patchcenters, numtokens, numgs): """ Computes the Cone Loss for ZipSplat. Args: gmeans: Tensor of shape (numtokens, numgs, 3), 3D means of Gaussians. projections: Function or Tensor mapping gmeans to 2D source view coordinates. If Tensor, shape (numtokens, numgs, 2). patchcenters: Tensor of shape (numtokens, 2), centers of source patches. numtokens: Integer K. numgs: Integer ngs. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ totalloss = 0.0 for k in range(numtokens): for j in range(numgs): # Get 3D mean mean3d = gmeans[k, j] # Project to 2D source view # Note: In a real implementation, projections[k, j] would be precomputed # or computed via camera intrinsics/extrinsics for token k. proj2d = projections[k, j] # Get patch center uk = patchcenters[k] # Compute distance in patch units # Check if behind view (implementation dependent on projection method) # Assuming projections handles visibility or we check depth buffer/z-value # If the source does not provide explicit visibility mask, we assume # standard projection logic where invalid projections are handled. # Based on notes: "Gaussians that project behind a member view receive # a sentinel distance of 20 patches". if isbehindview(mean3d, k): # Helper to check z-depth relative to camera d = 20.0 else: # Euclidean distance in 2D patch units d = torch.norm(proj2d - uk) # Apply hinged Cauchy penalty totalloss += hingedcauchy(d) return totalloss def isbehindview(mean3d, tokenidx): """ Placeholder for camera-specific visibility check. Returns True if the point is behind the camera plane of the source view. It addresses the issue that without geometric supervision, decoded Gaussians in token-based representations can drift from their source patches, leading to merging errors where tokens from different surfaces are combined. name: Neural Network and Feed-Forward Approaches
head: Feed-forward 3DGS, Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: This family encompasses methods that replace or augment the iterative per-scene gradient descent optimization of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent] with neural networks. These approaches either regress Gaussian parameters directly from input images in a single forward pass (feed-forward) or use neural priors to guide the optimization process. They are distinguished from sibling methods like Base 3DGS Optimization by their reliance on learned generalization or implicit constraints rather than direct parameter tuning, and from WildGaussians by their focus on static scene reconstruction or generalizable priors rather than explicit temporal modeling. All methods in this family utilize a differentiable rendering pipeline to connect neural network outputs to image-space losses. The core mechanism involves predicting high-dimensional representations (either Gaussian primitives or implicit fields) and optimizing them via backpropagation through the rasterizer. MVSplat is a feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing the per-scene gradient descent optimization loop required by standard 3DGS. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like VRP-UDF by combining multi-view feature extraction via transformers and cost volumes with a U-Net decoder to predict Gaussian primitives, enabling rapid inference without iterative scene-specific optimization. See MVSplat for implementation details. VRP-UDF is a neural network-based volume rendering prior that learns unsigned distance functions (UDFs) to guide the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of inaccurate surface reconstruction and depth errors common in standard Gaussian splatting by providing dense, geometrically consistent queries around the UDF zero-level set. Unlike sibling methods like MVSplat which primarily regress Gaussian parameters directly from images, VRP-UDF introduces an intermediate implicit surface representation (the UDF) that regularizes the Gaussian distribution, particularly improving thin structure recovery. See VRP-UDF Training & Rendering Setup for implementation details. GS-Net is a 3D neural network that predicts high-dimensional feature vectors for optimized 3D Gaussians, using Q-Render to efficiently render these features into 2D maps for distillation from 2D foundation models. Unlike methods that force per-scene feature optimization, GS-Net predicts features in a generalizable manner using a 3D neural network. Definition: Given optimized 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N, a 3D neural network predicts a set of C-dimensional Gaussian features \mathcal{F} = \{fi\}{i=1}^N where fi \in \mathbb{R}^C. Voxelization: To ensure compatibility with typical 3D backbones like Point Transformer v3 (PTv3) and MinkUnet, 3D Gaussians are voxelized by sampling their center location \mu. De-voxelization: Predicted voxel features are converted back into predicted Gaussian features \mathcal{F}. Rendering: Q-Render transforms predicted Gaussian features into rendered feature maps. Training: The 3D neural network is trained to minimize the rendering loss between the rendered feature maps and target 2D feature maps extracted from CLIP’s vision encoder. Q-Render accelerates training by leveraging the inductive bias of the 3D neural network, which predicts spatially smooth Gaussian features, allowing sparse sampling of quantile Gaussians instead of dense ray sampling. This approach uses a masked autoencoder to learn a generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting-based representation. It combines a masked autoencoder (MAE) with a 3D transformer-based architecture to enable reconstruction of unseen scenes and support transfer learning. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent] requires per-scene optimization, which is computationally expensive and limits scalability. Feed-forward approaches emerged to address this by learning a mapping from images to Gaussians. MVSplat pioneered the use of cost volumes and U-Nets for direct regression. Subsequent works like GS-Net and MAE-based methods extended this to high-dimensional feature distillation and generalizable representations. VRP-UDF introduced implicit surface priors to improve geometric fidelity during the optimization phase. name: MVSplat
head: Amortized 3D Reconstruction, Feed-forward 3DGS, Feedforward 3D Reconstruction, Single-pass 3DGS
body: MVSplat is a feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing the per-scene gradient descent optimization loop required by standard 3DGS. It builds upon PixelSplat by combining multi-view feature extraction through transformers and cost volumes, which are then processed by a U-Net. Unlike iterative methods that optimize primitives for a specific scene, MVSplat provides a universal reconstruction model trained on diverse object types, offering useful 3D priors for subsequent 3D optimizations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N sparse multi-view images of a scene. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives, defined by their position, covariance (scale and rotation), opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Data Structures: The network architecture processes image features into a cost volume, which is decoded into Gaussian parameters. The specific internal tensor layouts for the transformer tokens and U-Net feature maps are not detailed in the sources [G: Standard transformer encoder/decoder and U-Net convolutional block structures are assumed]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Multi-view Feature Extraction: Extract features from the input images using a transformer-based backbone. This step generalizes features between views, similar to the epipolar transformer used in PixelSplat. 2. Cost Volume Construction: Construct a cost volume representing the similarity or correlation of features across the input views. This volume encodes depth information. 3. Depth and Gaussian Regression: Process the cost volume through a U-Net architecture. The U-Net decodes the cost volume to predict depth maps and directly regresses the 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. 4. Rendering (Optional for Training): The predicted 3D Gaussians are rendered into novel views using the differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer to compute photometric losses. Formulas: The sources do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the feature extraction or U-Net decoding steps. The training objective minimizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered novel views and the ground truth novel views. Parameters: Training Views: 20 source images are used as inputs during training. Evaluation Views: 5 novel views are used for calculating MSE losses during training evaluation. Finetuning Inputs: 80 views are used as inputs to the feed-forward model for initialization in the finetuning regime. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: The method is designed for sparse inputs, but performance may degrade if the input views have insufficient overlap or extreme baseline differences not covered in the training distribution. Scale Ambiguity: Unlike methods that use known camera poses, MVSplat relies on the cost volume and transformer generalization. If the input views lack sufficient geometric cues, scale ambiguity may arise, though the sources note that NoPoSplat addresses this specifically by eliminating known camera pose requirements. Addresses reconstructing 3D scenes from a limited number of input views (sparse views) or even a single image, bypassing the iterative per-scene optimization required by standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. It achieves this by employing learned priors within a feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian parameters from input images in a single pass. This approach favors inference speed and cross-scene generalization over the high geometric fidelity typically achieved by regularization-based methods that rely on per-scene gradient descent. VolSplat is a feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing the per-scene gradient descent optimization required by standard 3DGS Parent. It distinguishes itself by lifting 2D features into a sparse 3D voxel grid via plane-sweep depth prediction and predicting one Gaussian primitive per occupied voxel, ensuring scene-adaptive primitive allocation while maintaining stable sparse 3D decoding. Time Complexity: The method performs inference in a single forward pass, making it significantly faster than iterative optimization methods that require hundreds or thousands of gradient descent steps per scene. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is determined by the neural network's parameter count and the intermediate feature maps during the forward pass. It does not require storing large per-scene optimization states or dense point clouds during the initial reconstruction phase. Measured Performance: The model generates compelling reconstructions with just a single forward pass. After fine-tuning, it is on par with overfitting baselines in color accuracy (PSNR, LPIPS) but largely outperforms hash-based baselines in depth error. Strengths: Bypasses per-scene gradient descent; provides useful 3D priors for subsequent 3D optimizations; works on a variety of object types. Limitations: As a feed-forward model, it may not achieve the same level of geometric fidelity as iterative methods that overfit to a specific scene's data, particularly in areas with limited viewpoint coverage. MVSplat was introduced as a method to combine multi-view feature extraction through transformers and cost volumes, processed by a U-Net, building upon the foundations of PixelSplat. It is part of a broader trend towards amortized 3D reconstruction, where a neural network is trained to generalize across scenes rather than optimizing for a single instance. The model was trained on all CO3Dv2 categories to create a universal reconstruction model capable of handling various object types. name: Sparse Input Reconstruction via Generalizability
head: Feed-Forward Gaussian Models, Learned Prior 3D GS
body: Sparse Input Reconstruction via Generalizability refers to methods that leverage learned priors to reconstruct 3D scenes, enabling reconstruction from a single input image or a very sparse set of views after training on multiple views. Unlike regularization-based methods that rely on strong constraints and per-scene optimization to favor geometric quality, these generalizability-based methods use learned priors for fast feed-forward inference, prioritizing speed and cross-scene generalization. This approach bypasses the iterative gradient descent required by standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressing the limitation where regularization techniques diminish in efficacy with limited views. The core mechanism involves training a model on a dataset of multi-view images to learn the mapping from 2D image features to 3D Gaussian parameters. During inference, the model directly generates the properties of a set of 3D Gaussians from the input images in a single pass. Inputs and Outputs: Input: One or more input images (often just a single image for generalizable models). Output: A set of 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) representing the scene. Data Structures: The output is a list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (often parameterized by rotation Ri and scale Si) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics coefficients c{i, l} for color representation. Steps: 1. Training Phase: The network is trained on a dataset of scenes with multiple views. The loss function typically includes rendering loss (comparing rendered images to ground truth) and potentially regularization terms to ensure geometric consistency. 2. Inference Phase: a. Extract features from the input image(s) using a backbone network (e.g., CNN or Transformer). b. Predict Gaussian parameters directly from these features. c. Render the predicted Gaussians using differentiable rasterization to verify consistency if needed, but the primary output is the Gaussian set itself. Variants: PixelSplat: Samples Gaussians from dense probability distributions. Splatter Image: Uses a 2D image-to-image network to map an input image to a 3D Gaussian per pixel. Pitfalls: Computational Intensity of Augmentation: If the method relies on synthesizing additional views through generative models to augment input data, this process is computationally intensive and bounded by the capabilities of the generative model. Distribution Issues: In pixel-aligned approaches like Splatter Image, generated Gaussians are distributed nearly evenly in space. This uniform distribution struggles to represent high-frequency details and smoother regions with an appropriate number of Gaussians, leading to potential loss of detail or inefficient memory usage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generalizablereconstruction(inputimages): """ Reconstructs 3D Gaussians from input images using a pre-trained feed-forward model. Args: inputimages: Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) representing input images. Returns: gaussians: List of Gaussian parameters (mu, sigma, alpha, shcoeffs). """ # Step 1: Feature Extraction # The specific backbone architecture (e.g., ResNet, ViT) is implementation-dependent. features = featureextractor(inputimages) # Step 2: Gaussian Parameter Prediction # This step varies by variant (PixelSplat vs Splatter Image). # For a generic feed-forward model: gaussians = gaussianpredictor(features) # Step 3: Return Gaussians return gaussians Sparse View Input Scalability is the capability of a generalizable neural rendering method to handle an arbitrary number of input views, where reconstruction quality improves progressively as more views are added. It distinguishes itself from single-view methods (like PixelSplat or SplatterImage) by leveraging multi-view geometric constraints via cost volumes, and from iterative optimization methods by enabling direct inference from sparse inputs without per-scene tuning. Speed: Significantly faster than iterative optimization methods (like standard 3DGS) because it avoids per-scene gradient descent. Inference is a single forward pass. Generalization: Excels at cross-scene generalization due to learned priors. Geometric Fidelity: May suffer from lower geometric fidelity compared to regularization-based methods, especially in complex scenes or with very sparse inputs, as the learned prior may not capture all scene-specific details. Memory: Memory usage depends on the number of Gaussians predicted. Pixel-aligned methods may use more Gaussians than necessary for smooth regions. Limitations: Performance is bounded by the training data distribution. Out-of-distribution scenes may yield poor results. The reliance on generative models for view synthesis (if used) adds computational overhead and potential artifacts. The challenge of 3D Gaussian Splatting for sparse inputs centers on how priors are modeled, whether through depth information, generative models, or feed-forward Gaussian models. Traditional regularization-based methods rely on strong constraints and per-scene optimization, favoring geometric quality but incurring higher computation. Generalizability-based methods emerged to address the inefficiency of per-scene optimization, particularly when dealing with a limited number of views or even just one, where the efficacy of regularization techniques tends to diminish. Key developments include: PixelSplat: Proposed sampling Gaussians from dense probability distributions. Splatter Image: Introduced a 2D image-to-image network that maps an input image to a 3D Gaussian per pixel. Cost Volume Representations: Some approaches use cost volume representations to provide geometry cues, although this can be challenging with very few views. Future research directions include exploring adaptive mechanisms to control the trade-off between speed and geometric fidelity, such as learned confidence measures or context-aware prior selection. Additionally, extending these approaches to dynamic scenarios, handling temporal consistency and motion-induced artifacts, is an active area of interest. name: Sparse View Input Scalability
head: Arbitrary View Count Scalability, MVSplat, Progressive Multi-View Reconstruction, Sparse Input Reconstruction via Generalizability
body: Sparse View Input Scalability is the capability of a generalizable neural rendering method to handle an arbitrary number of input views, where reconstruction quality improves progressively as more views are added. It distinguishes itself from single-view methods (like PixelSplat or SplatterImage) by leveraging multi-view geometric constraints via cost volumes, and from iterative optimization methods by enabling direct inference from sparse inputs without per-scene tuning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images (where N \ge 2), typically calibrated with intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian attributes (mean, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) defined in a canonical space, which can be rendered via differentiable rasterization. Data Structures: Cost Volume: A 3D tensor representing geometric consistency across views. For a target view, features from source views are warped into the target view's coordinate system. The volume aggregates these features to identify depth hypotheses. Attribute Prediction Network: A neural network (typically a U-Net or similar encoder-decoder) that takes the cost volume and/or image features as input and outputs Gaussian attributes. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract multi-scale features from each input image using a shared encoder (e.g., ResNet or ConvNet). 2. Cost Volume Construction: For a target view, warp features from source views into the target view's space using estimated depth hypotheses or inverse depth planes. Aggregate the warped features and the target view's own features to form a cost volume. This volume encodes geometric consistency across the N views. 3. Attribute Prediction: Pass the cost volume (and potentially the original image features) through the attribute prediction network. The network outputs the parameters for each Gaussian: position (\mu), covariance (\Sigma), opacity (\alpha), and color/diffuse properties (SH coefficients). 4. Rendering: Render the predicted Gaussians using standard differentiable splatting to produce the output image. The rendering loss is used during training of the network. Formulas: The cost volume C at depth d for a pixel p in the target view is computed by aggregating features from source views vi: C(p, d) = \text{Aggregate}(F{target}(p), F{source}(warp(p, d, vi))) where warp projects the point from the target view to the source view using camera geometry and depth d. The Gaussian attributes A are predicted by the network f\theta: A = f\theta(C, F{images}) where A includes \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \text{SH}. Parameters: Number of Views (N): The method supports N \ge 2. Typical experiments use N \in [2, 8]. Depth Planes: The number of depth hypotheses used in cost volume construction. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Few Views (N=2): The method can produce plausible geometries with only 2 views, but accuracy is lower than with more views. Degenerate Input: If input views have insufficient overlap or extreme baselines, cost volume construction may fail to find consistent matches. Not given in the sources. Precision: Cost volume construction requires precise camera calibration. Errors in extrinsics can lead to incorrect depth estimates. Time Complexity: Inference time is constant with respect to scene complexity but depends on the number of views N and the resolution of the cost volume. Typically faster than iterative optimization methods. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the size of the cost volume, which depends on the number of views, image resolution, and depth planes. Not given in the sources. Performance: On the DTU dataset (Scan105), the method produces plausible geometries with 2 views. Quality progressively improves and converges to low error as views increase from 2 to 8. Strengths: Generalizable to unseen scenes; handles arbitrary view counts; smoother surfaces compared to density-based methods like MVSNerf. Limitations: Performance degrades with very sparse views compared to dense inputs; requires accurate camera calibration. When to Use: When a quick reconstruction from a few calibrated views is needed, and iterative optimization is too slow. When Not to Use: When single-view reconstruction is required without priors (use PixelSplat) or when dense input is available and iterative optimization is feasible for higher quality. The concept of handling arbitrary view counts in generalizable neural rendering was demonstrated in SparseNeuS, which showed progressive improvement from 2 to 8 views on the DTU dataset. The specific integration of cost volume representations into Gaussian Splatting for sparse view reconstruction was introduced by MVSplat, building on earlier work like PixelNeRF and PixelSplat. name: VolSplat Architecture and Training Pipeline
head: VolSplat
body: VolSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that regresses scene parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself by lifting 2D features into a sparse 3D voxel grid via plane-sweep depth prediction and predicting exactly one Gaussian primitive per occupied voxel, ensuring scene-adaptive allocation with stable sparse decoding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N{\text{in}} = 6 input views at 256 \times 256 resolution. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}, each defined by a 38-dimensional parameter vector, for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: 1. Multi-scale Feature Maps: Extracted per view via a weight-sharing ResNet backbone. 2. Cost Volume: Constructed via plane-sweep with D = 128 inverse-depth candidates per reference view. 3. Sparse Voxel Grid: World-coordinate representation where only occupied cells are materialized, processed via MinkowskiEngine. 4. Gaussian Primitive Parameter Vector \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{38}: Comprises opacity \alpha, center offset \Delta \mathbf{x}, anisotropic scale \mathbf{s}, quaternion rotation \mathbf{q}, and degree-2 spherical-harmonic color coefficients \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract multi-scale feature maps from each input view using a weight-sharing ResNet backbone. 2. Refine features via a cross-view interaction module using local window attention to enhance multi-view consistency. 3. Construct a cost volume for each reference view using a plane-sweep strategy with D = 128 inverse-depth candidates. 4. Perform local neighbor matching on the cost volume to predict robust depth maps. 5. Lift the 2D features into 3D space using the predicted depth maps, building the representation in world coordinates. 6. Process the lifted features as a sparse voxel set where only occupied cells are materialized, applying sparse 3D refinement via MinkowskiEngine. 7. Predict one Gaussian primitive per occupied voxel, outputting the 38-dimensional parameter vector \mathbf{p}. Formulas: The parameter vector \mathbf{p} is defined as: \mathbf{p} = [\alpha, \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, sx, sy, sz, qw, qx, qy, qz, c0, \dots, c{37}] where \alpha \in [0,1] is opacity, (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) is the center offset, (sx, sy, sz) is the anisotropic scale, (qw, qx, qy, qz) is the quaternion rotation, and c0 \dots c{37} are the degree-2 spherical-harmonic color coefficients. Parameters: Inverse-depth candidates: 128 per reference view. Gaussian parameter vector dimension: 38. Input views per training sample: 6. Target views per training sample: 8. Input resolution: 256 \times 256 pixels. Optimizer: AdamW with decoupled weight decay. Learning rate: Two separate groups for the pretrained monocular branch and the remaining trainable parameters. Stability mechanism: Gradient clipping is enabled during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse grid initialization: Only occupied cells are materialized to avoid computational redundancy of a dense global grid. Depth prediction errors: Robust depth prediction via local neighbor matching is critical for accurate feature lifting. Anchor gap selection: The progressive expansion of the anchor-gap range during early training iterations is required for stable convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Weight-sharing ResNet backbone for multi-scale feature extraction self.backbone = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 7, stride=2, padding=3, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(64), nn.ReLU(inplace=True)) # Cross-view interaction via local window attention self.crossviewattn = nn.MultiheadAttention(embeddim=256, numheads=8, batchfirst=True) # Depth prediction head self.depthhead = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(256, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(128, 1, 3, padding=1)) # Sparse 3D refinement layers self.sparserefine = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(256, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm3d(256), nn.ReLU(inplace=True)) # Gaussian parameter predictor self.gaussianhead = nn.Conv3d(256, 38, 1) def forward(self, inputviews): # inputviews: Tensor of shape (Nin, 3, 256, 256) # Step 1: Feature Extraction features = self.backbone(inputviews) # Shape: (Nin, C, H, W) # Step 2: Cross-View Interaction B, C, H, W = features.shape featflat = features.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(B, HW, C) refinedfeat, = self.crossviewattn(featflat, featflat, featflat) refinedfeatures = refinedfeat.reshape(B, H, W, C).permute(0, 3, 1, 2) # Step 3 & 4: Cost Volume Construction and Depth Prediction # Construct cost volume with 128 inverse-depth candidates # Perform local neighbor matching to predict depth maps depthmaps = [] for i in range(B): # Sources do not specify the exact cost volume aggregation and matching logic costvol = self.buildcostvolume(refinedfeatures[i:i+1]) depthmap = self.localneighbormatching(costvol) depthmaps.append(depthmap) depthmaps = torch.stack(depthmaps, dim=0) # Shape: (Nin, H, W) # Step 5: Feature Lifting # Lift 2D features to 3D space using predicted depth maps in world coordinates # Sources do not specify the exact lifting/ray-casting logic liftedfeatures = self.liftfeatures(refinedfeatures, depthmaps) # Step 6: Sparse 3D Refinement # Create sparse voxel set, materializing only occupied cells # Sources do not specify the exact sparse tensor creation logic sparsetensor = self.createsparsetensor(liftedfeatures) refinedsparse = self.sparserefine(sparsetensor) # Step 7: Gaussian Parameter Prediction # Predict one Gaussian primitive per occupied voxel gaussianparams = self.gaussianhead(refinedsparse) return gaussianparams def buildcostvolume(self, reffeat): # Plane-sweep cost volume construction with 128 candidates # Sources do not specify the exact implementation return torch.zeros(1, 1, 256, 256, 128) def localneighbormatching(self, costvolume): # Local neighbor matching on cost volume # Sources do not specify the exact implementation return torch.zeros(1, 256, 256) def liftfeatures(self, features, depthmaps): # Lift 2D features to 3D using depth maps # Sources do not specify the exact implementation return torch.zeros(1, 256, 16, 16, 16) def createsparsetensor(self, liftedfeatures): # Create sparse voxel set from lifted features # Sources do not specify the exact implementation return torch.zeros(1, 256, 16, 16, 16) Training Data Sampling: Each sample uses N{\text{in}} = 6 input views and N{\text{target}} = 8 target views. Two input views are selected as boundary anchors with a randomly sampled frame gap within a predefined range. The remaining input views are sampled between the anchors. The anchor-gap range is progressively expanded during early training iterations. Target novel views are chosen from disjoint camera positions not included in the inputs. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU with 6 input views. VolSplat achieves a superior balance between reconstruction quality and resource consumption compared to state-of-the-art baselines on RealEstate10K. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Scene-adaptive primitive allocation, stable sparse 3D decoding, efficient sparse 3D refinement using MinkowskiEngine. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When a feed-forward approach for 3DGS is required, especially for scenes with sparse input views Parent. When not to use: When per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher quality is needed Parent. The method builds on previous work in feed-forward 3DGS, such as MVSplat Parent, and incorporates techniques from 4D spatio-temporal convnets (MinkowskiEngine) for efficient sparse 3D processing. Training is performed on RealEstate10K and fine-tuned on ScanNet, with zero-shot evaluation on ACID. name: VRP-UDF Training & Rendering Setup
head: UDF-Gaussian Joint Training, Volume Rendering Prior Network
body: This method integrates a neural network-based volume rendering prior (VRP) that learns Unsigned Distance Functions (UDFs) to guide the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of inaccurate surface reconstruction and depth estimation in Gaussian splatting by providing dense, geometrically consistent queries around the UDF zero-level set. Unlike sibling methods like MVSplat which rely on explicit multi-view stereo consistency or pure geometric priors, this approach uses a differentiable UDF field to regularize the Gaussian primitives, ensuring unbiased learning from ground truth UDFs and depths while mitigating the ambiguities inherent in standard SDF-based normal estimation. The method employs a joint training pipeline where a set of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) model the UDF and color fields, which are then used to refine Gaussian Splatting parameters. Inputs: Multi-view images, camera poses, and ground truth unsigned distance values (or depth maps) for the scene. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and the learned UDF/Color fields. The volume rendering prior consists of four distinct MLPs, all utilizing 256 hidden units. The architecture is defined as follows: 1. Feature Network (f{w1}): Structure: 3 layers. Input: 3D coordinates. Output: Feature vectors. 2. Weight Network (f{w2}): Structure: 6 layers with skip connections. Input: Feature vectors from f{w1} and 3D coordinates. Output: Weights for the UDF and color prediction. 3. UDF Network (fu): Structure: 8 layers with skip connections. Input: Feature vectors and 3D coordinates. Output: Unsigned distance value. Activation: A Softplus activation function is applied to the final output layer to enforce non-negative outputs (d \ge 0). 4. Color Network (fc): Structure: 2 layers. Input: Feature vectors and 3D coordinates. Note: Normal vectors are explicitly excluded from the input. Output: Color values. The training process is divided into specific phases with a total duration of 30,000 iterations. 1. Initial Phase (Iterations 0–9,000): Standard Gaussian Splatting optimization is performed without the UDF prior. 2. Prior Introduction (Iteration 9,000): Training of the UDF networks (fu) and color networks (fc) begins. The learning rate and decay scheduler for these networks follow established conventions from prior works [1, 24] (exact numerical values are not specified in the source). 3. Refinement Phase (Iterations 20,000–30,000): During the final 10,000 iterations, the Gaussians are refined using the learned prior. Ray Casting: Rays are cast with a batch size of 2,048. Sampling: 64 points are sampled along each ray. Rendering: The UDF and color networks are queried at these sample points to compute volume rendering losses, which are backpropagated to update both the Gaussian parameters and the network weights. The following pseudocode outlines the refinement step during the final training phase. It assumes standard differentiable rendering primitives are available. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainvrpudfgaussian(gaussians, cameras, images, totaliterations=30000, udfstartiter=9000, refinementstartiter=20000): """ Joint training loop for VRP-UDF and 3D Gaussian Splatting. """ # Initialize networks fw1 = MLP(layers=3, hidden=256) fw2 = MLP(layers=6, hidden=256, skipconnections=True) fu = MLP(layers=8, hidden=256, skipconnections=True) fc = MLP(layers=2, hidden=256) # Optimizers optgaussians = Optimizer(gaussians.parameters()) optnetworks = Optimizer([fw1, fw2, fu, fc].parameters()) for iteration in range(1, totaliterations + 1): # Sample a batch of camera views batchcameras, batchimages = samplebatch(cameras, images) # Forward pass: Render current Gaussians renderedimages, rendereddepths = rendergaussians(gaussians, batchcameras) # Compute standard Gaussian Splatting losses (color, depth, etc.) lossgs = computegaussianlosses(renderedimages, batchimages, rendereddepths) if iteration >= udfstartiter: # Query UDF and Color networks for sample points # In practice, sample points are derived from ray casting through Gaussians # or random hierarchical sampling near the zero-level set. samplepoints = getsamplepoints(gaussians, batchcameras, numsamples=64) # Get features features = fw1(samplepoints) weights = fw2(features, samplepoints) # Predict UDF (apply Softplus to ensure non-negativity) udfvalues = fu(features, samplepoints) udfvalues = softplus(udfvalues) # Predict Color (no normals in input) colors = fc(features, samplepoints) # Compute UDF/Color losses against ground truth UDFs/Depths # Note: Ground truth UDFs are assumed to be available or derived from depth lossudf = computeudfloss(udfvalues, groundtruthudfs) losscolor = computecolorloss(colors, groundtruthcolors) # Combine losses if iteration >= refinementstartiter: # Refinement phase: Higher weight on UDF consistency to guide Gaussians totalloss = lossgs + lambdaudf lossudf + lambdacolor losscolor else: # Initial prior training phase totalloss = lossgs + lambdaudf lossudf + lambdacolor losscolor # Backpropagation optnetworks.zerograd() optgaussians.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optnetworks.step() optgaussians.step() else: # Standard Gaussian Splatting update optgaussians.zerograd() lossgs.backward() optgaussians.step() def softplus(x): """Enforce non-negative output.""" return torch.log(1 + torch.exp(x)) Normal Ambiguity: Normal vectors must not be included in the input to the color network (fc). At the zero-level set of a UDF, the gradient is non-differentiable and normals are ambiguous, which can degrade color prediction. Sampling Inaccuracies: Random hierarchical sampling and the ill-defined nature of UDF fields near surfaces can cause rendering inaccuracies. This is a common issue in volume rendering frameworks, leading to depth discrepancies even with theoretically unbiased mappings. Convergence Parameters: Excessively large convergence parameters (such as the "flip factor" in NeuralUDF) can cause the UDF to flip into an SDF prematurely, before the true surface is reached, resulting in depth rendering errors. Time Complexity: The method adds significant computational overhead during the refinement phase due to the forward passes through four MLPs (f{w1}, f{w2}, fu, fc) for every sample point. The training duration is fixed at 30,000 iterations, with the prior active for the latter 21,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases due to the storage of the four MLPs (totaling 19 layers with 256 hidden units each) and the gradients for both the Gaussians and the networks. Performance: The method achieves high accuracy in surface reconstruction and depth estimation, outperforming baselines like NeUDF and VRPrior on complex indoor scenes and thin structures (e.g., eggshells, plant branches). It provides the best accuracy among tested renderers for both UDFs and SDFs. Limitations: Despite being unbiased in theory, practical inaccuracies persist due to sampling noise and UDF ill-definition near surfaces. It may struggle to capture extremely thin structures completely without advanced extraction techniques. The VRP-UDF method originates from the paper "VRP-UDF: Toward Unbiased Learning of Unsigned Distance Functions From Multi-View Images With Volume Rendering Priors". It builds upon the principles of differentiable volume rendering and unsigned distance function learning, extending them to the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting. The approach addresses limitations in previous UDF-based methods (like NeuralUDF) where premature flipping and normal ambiguity hindered high-fidelity reconstruction. It is particularly relevant for applications requiring precise geometric details from multi-view images, such as digital heritage (e.g., potted flowers, paper boats) and complex indoor scenes.
