name: Scale Decay
body: Scale Decay is a training-time regularization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that gradually reduces Gaussian scales to control final primitive sizes and encourage pruning of redundant or occluded Gaussians. It trades a slight decrease in reconstruction quality for significantly higher rendering FPS and reduced memory footprint. Input: The current set of N active Gaussians, each defined by position, rotation, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Output: The updated set of Gaussians with scaled-down \mathbf{s} values after each training iteration. Gaussians store scale as a 3D vector \mathbf{s} = [sx, sy, sz]. The decay is applied directly to these scale components at every training iteration. \eta{decay}: Multiplicative decay factor applied per iteration. Typical value: 0.999875. Tested values: 0.999875, 0.999900, 0.999925, 0.999950. Disabled state: "NoDecay" (equivalent to \eta{decay} = 1.0). 1. After the standard gradient update for a training iteration, retrieve the current scale vector \mathbf{s} for each active Gaussian. 2. Multiply each scale component by the decay factor: \mathbf{s} \leftarrow \mathbf{s} \times \eta{decay}. 3. Proceed to the next iteration; the reduced scales encourage Gaussians to fall below visibility thresholds or become occluded, triggering existing pruning heuristics. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyscaledecay(gaussians, etadecay): """Applies multiplicative scale decay to all active Gaussians.""" for g in gaussians: g.scale = g.scale etadecay Pruning Interaction: Scale Decay works in conjunction with pruning heuristics; reducing scale encourages the removal of occluded or out-of-view primitives, which is critical for the observed reduction in Gaussian count. Quality-Speed Trade-off: Stronger decay (lower \eta{decay}) increases FPS and reduces final Gaussian counts and average scales, but slightly degrades reconstruction quality metrics. The source text claims that "increasing \eta{decay} consistently improves FPS", but the provided empirical data confirms that lower values yield higher FPS and smaller scales. Log-Scale Storage: If an implementation stores scales in log-space (\mathbf{s}{\text{log}} = \log(\mathbf{s})) to ensure positivity, the decay must be applied as an additive shift: \mathbf{s}{\text{log}}^{\text{new}} = \mathbf{s}{\text{log}}^{\text{old}} + \log(\eta{decay}). Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration for the decay operation, where N is the number of active Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Reduces final model memory footprint by decreasing the total Gaussian count through induced pruning. Performance Metrics (15K iterations, \eta{decay}=0.999875 vs disabled): FPS: Increases from 157 to 248. Final Gaussian Count: Decreases from 1.73M to 1.52M. Final Average Scale: Decreases from 0.0211 to 0.016. Quality: PSNR decreases from 26.00 to 26.47, and LPIPS increases from 0.231 to 0.236. (Note: Table 16 in the source reports PSNR as 26.60 for NoDecay, indicating minor reporting variance across tables.) Strengths: Highly effective lever for balancing quality and speed; encourages pruning of redundant Gaussians. Limitations: Slight degradation in visual quality metrics; requires tuning \eta{decay} to avoid excessive detail loss. Scale Decay was introduced in the GRay paper as a regularization technique to optimize the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It was found to effectively control final Gaussian sizes and encourage pruning of occluded or out-of-view primitives, leading to noticeable FPS improvements with minimal quality impact. name: DARBF-Splatting
head: DARB-Splatting, Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions Splatting
body: DARBF-Splatting is a method that replaces the standard Gaussian kernel in 3D Gaussian Splatting with a class of non-exponential, decaying anisotropic radial basis functions (DARBFs). It solves the limitation of the exponential family by allowing kernels like half-cosine or inverse multiquadric, which span larger regions with higher opacity for the same variance, thereby reducing the number of primitives needed and improving training efficiency. Unlike standard 3DGS, it introduces a scalar correction factor to approximate the closed-form integration shortcut of Gaussians, preserving computational efficiency while enabling differentiable rendering with non-Gaussian kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D primitives (positions, covariances, colors, opacities) initialized from an SfM pipeline (e.g., COLMAP). Output: A rendered 2D image and optimized primitive attributes via backpropagation. Data Structures: The primitive i retains the standard 3DGS structure but uses a DARBF kernel instead of a Gaussian: Position: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite). Parameterized by rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{s}i as in [Parent]. Color: \mathbf{c}i (e.g., spherical harmonics coefficients). Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1]. Correction Factor: \psi \in \mathbb{R} (scalar). Method Steps: 1. 3D to 2D Projection: Transform the 3D primitive into the camera coordinate system. Project the 3D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i to a 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i by skipping the third row and column of the transformed 3x3 matrix. This bypasses costly integration, a property specific to the Gaussian family that DARBF-Splatting approximates. 2. Compute Mahalanobis Distance: For a pixel center x' in the 2D image plane, calculate the Mahalanobis distance dM from the projected primitive center \boldsymbol{\mu}' using the 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i: dM(x'; \boldsymbol{\mu}', \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i) = \sqrt{(x' - \boldsymbol{\mu}')^T (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i)^{-1} (x' - \boldsymbol{\mu}')} where \boldsymbol{\mu}' is the 2D projection of \mathbf{p}i. 3. Evaluate DARBF Kernel: Compute the kernel value K(dM) using a chosen DARBF function. The function must be non-negative, decaying, and anisotropic (via dM). Half-Cosine Kernel: K{hc}(dM) = \begin{cases} \cos\left(\frac{dM^2}{\xi}\right) & \text{if } dM^2 < \frac{\xi \pi}{2} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \xi > 0 is a shape parameter. Inverse Multiquadric (Inverse MQ): K{imq}(dM) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + dM^2}} (Note: Specific parameterization for Inverse MQ in the source is implied by the formula structure, but exact scaling factors are not explicitly detailed beyond the general form). Other DARBFs: Modified raised cosine, modular sinc. 4. Apply Correction Factor: Since non-Gaussian functions do not naturally integrate to a closed-form constant like Gaussians do during projection, apply a scalar correction factor \psi to the kernel value to approximate the Gaussian's integration shortcut: \sigmai(x') = \alphai \cdot \psi \cdot K{hc}(dM) The value of \psi is precomputed via closed-form regression experiments to ensure comparable accumulated opacity to Gaussians. 5. Rasterization and Blending: Sort primitives by depth. For each pixel, accumulate color using alpha blending [Parent]: C(x') = \sum{i \in N} \mathbf{c}i \sigmai(x') \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj(x')) where \sigmai(x') is the effective opacity contribution of primitive i at pixel x'. 6. Optimization: Backpropagate the pixel error to optimize \mathbf{p}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \mathbf{c}i, \alphai and potentially \psi if learned (though the source selects a precomputed scalar \psi for efficiency). Parameters: Kernel Type: Half-cosine, Inverse MQ, etc.. Shape Parameter (\xi): Controls the width of the half-cosine kernel. Typical values are not explicitly given, but \beta=2 is mentioned for modified half-cosine in Table 1 context (likely related to \xi or variance scaling). Correction Factor (\psi): Scalar precomputed from regression. Specific values are not listed, but its inclusion improves metrics (Table 6). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Functions: Growing functions cause instability and are omitted; only decaying functions are used. Integration Cost: Using functions outside the Gaussian family typically incurs costly integration. The correction factor \psi is critical to avoid this. Precision: The half-cosine kernel has finite support (dM^2 < \frac{\xi \pi}{2}), which must be checked to avoid evaluating cosine outside the valid domain. Allows negative opacity values to cancel out artifacts. Negative Gaussian Splatting Wraps primitives around surfaces using a scaffold structure. Scaffold-GS Enforces geometric constraints on primitives. GeoGaussian Injects differentiable blur kernels into rasterization. Grid-based Blur Kernel Time Complexity: Training convergence is 34% faster than standard 3DGS with the half-cosine kernel. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by 15% compared to standard 3DGS with the half-cosine kernel. Performance: Achieves comparable PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS results to 3DGS on Mip-NeRF 360 scenes. Strengths: More efficient training and lower memory footprint; wider-spread kernels (half-cosine, Inverse MQ) reduce the need for multiple splats to achieve the same accumulated value. Limitations: Requires precomputed correction factors for non-Gaussian kernels; not all DARBFs perform equally (e.g., radial cosine had lower SSIM than half-cosine in Table 6). When to use: When computational savings (training time, memory) are critical and comparable visual quality to 3DGS is acceptable. When not to use: When the absolute highest fidelity of the Gaussian kernel's integration properties is required without approximation. DARBF-Splatting was introduced by Hashiru Pramuditha, Vinasirajan Viruthshaan, Vishagar Arunan, Saeedha Nazar, Sameera Ramasinghe, Simon Lucey, and Ranga Rodrigo from the University of Moratuwa and University of Adelaide. It was published in 2026 in the IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV). The work generalizes splatting techniques beyond the exponential family, addressing the underexplored area of non-Gaussian reconstruction kernels in 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Grid-based Blur Kernel
head: Sharpness-indexed Blur Kernels, Trainable Grid-based Blur Kernels
body: Grid-based Blur Kernels address the challenge of modeling spatially-varying blurriness in radiance field optimization by replacing MLP-generated blur kernels with a set of learnable, indexed grid kernels. Unlike Negative Gaussian Splatting which modifies primitive attributes, or Scaffold-GS which constrains geometry, this method injects a differentiable blur convolution into the rendering pipeline to explicitly deblur or model defocus. It sets itself apart from previous works that use MLPs to generate kernels by allowing expressivity improvements via grid size expansion without additional computational cost for kernel generation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training views (images), a sharpness level map L (precomputed), and the number of blur kernels Nk. Outputs: A blurred image Ib that approximates the ground truth I{gt}, and optimized blur kernels \mathcal{B}. Data Structures: Blur Kernel Tensor \mathcal{B}: A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{N{img} \times Nk \times K \times K \times C}. N{img}: Number of training views. Nk: Number of unique sharpness groups (blur kernels). K: Kernel size (spatial dimension). C: Number of color channels. Note: The channel dimension C is often omitted for brevity in formulas. Sharpness Level Map L: A map where each pixel is assigned an integer value from 0 to Nk-1, indicating its sharpness group. Cropped Image I'c: A tensor of shape P' \times P' \times K \times K derived from the clean image Ic. Parameters: K: Kernel size. Typical value: 11. Nk: Number of blur kernels. Typical value: 400. Learning Rate: 0.05 for the kernel. Initialization: 2D Gaussian distribution. P': Patch size dimension. Typical value: 22 (patch size P=22). Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Sharpness Prior): Estimate a spatially varying defocus map for every training view using a Defocus Map Estimation Network (DMENet). Quantize this map uniformly into Nk values to create the sharpness level map L. Optionally, segment the scene based on depth information (e.g., from MIDAS) to assess focus levels within segments. This step is performed once before training. 2. Kernel Indexing: For each pixel x in a training view, determine its sharpness level Lx from the map L. Map this level to a specific blur kernel wx from the grid \mathcal{B} using a mapping function F: wx = F(\mathcal{B}, L, x) Here, F simply indexes \mathcal{B} using the view index and the sharpness level Lx. 3. Image Cropping: Crop the clean image Ic along height and width with stride 1 to obtain I'c of shape P' \times P' \times K \times K. This creates a local neighborhood window for each pixel in the target patch. 4. Blurred Image Convolution: Compute the blurred image Ib at pixel coordinates (h, w) by convolving the cropped clean image with the indexed kernel wx: Ib[h,w] = \sum{i=0}^{K} \sum{j=0}^{K} I'c[h,w,i,j] wx[h,w,i,j] where h, w are indices along the height and width of the image and blur kernels, respectively. 5. Optimization: Optimize both the blur kernels \mathcal{B} and the underlying neural fields (e.g., NeRF) jointly using the reconstruction loss: \mathcal{L}{recon} = ||Ib - I{gt}||2 where I{gt} is the ground truth image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gridbasedblurkernelrendering(trainingviews, sharpnessmapL, B, K, Nk): """ trainingviews: List of images or patches. sharpnessmapL: Tensor of shape (H, W) with integer values in [0, Nk-1]. B: Tensor of shape (Nimg, Nk, K, K, C). K: Kernel size. Nk: Number of blur kernels. """ # Step 1: Preprocessing is assumed done externally to produce L. # Step 2 & 3: For each training view (indexed by vidx): for vidx in range(len(trainingviews)): Ic = trainingviews[vidx] # Shape: (H, W, C) Pprime = Ic.shape[0] # Assuming square patches for simplicity # Crop Ic to get Ic' for convolution # Ic' shape: (Pprime, Pprime, K, K, C) # This involves gathering neighbors for each pixel in the patch Icprime = cropimagewithstride(Ic, K) # Initialize blurred image Ib = zeroslike(Ic) # Get sharpness map for this view Lview = sharpnessmapL[vidx] # Shape: (Pprime, Pprime) # Step 4: Convolution with indexed kernels for h in range(Pprime): for w in range(Pprime): # Get sharpness level for pixel (h, w) sharpnesslevel = Lview[h, w] # Index the blur kernel from the grid B # wx shape: (K, K, C) wx = B[vidx, sharpnesslevel,:,:,:] # Perform convolution for this pixel # Icprime[h, w,:,:,:] is the KxKxC patch centered at (h,w) patch = Icprime[h, w,:,:,:] # Element-wise multiply and sum Ib[h, w,:] = sum(sum(patch wx)) # Step 5: Compute Loss # Lrecon = ||Ib - Igt||2 # Backpropagate to update B and neural fields computelossandupdate(Ib, Igt, B) def cropimagewithstride(Ic, K): """ Crops the image Ic to create a tensor of local neighborhoods. Returns tensor of shape (H, W, K, K, C) """ H, W, C = Ic.shape Icprime = zeros((H, W, K, K, C)) for h in range(H): for w in range(W): # Extract KxK neighborhood centered at (h, w) # Handle boundaries by padding or clamping as needed hstart = max(0, h - K // 2) hend = min(H, h + K // 2 + 1) wstart = max(0, w - K // 2) wend = min(W, w + K // 2 + 1) # Extract patch patch = Ic[hstart:hend, wstart:wend,:] # Resize or pad patch to exactly KxK if boundaries are hit # For simplicity, assume valid padding or that K is small relative to H,W # In practice, this step gathers the neighbors for the convolution Icprime[h, w,:,:,:] = patch # Simplified; actual implementation requires precise indexing return Icprime Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Sharpness Groups: Pixels in groups with high sharpness values (clear regions) may skip convolution to save computation. The method skips convolution for pixels in 100 groups of each view with high sharpness values. Boundary Conditions: The cropping operation requires handling image boundaries. The sources do not specify padding strategy, but standard practice involves zero-padding or replication. Initialization: Blur kernels are initialized with a 2D Gaussian distribution to provide a reasonable starting point for optimization. This variant refers to the preprocessing step used to generate the sharpness level map L. It estimates a spatially varying defocus map for every training view using DMENet, an end-to-end CNN framework. The defocus map is quantized uniformly into Nk values to create the sharpness level map L, which divides pixels into Nk groups based on their degree of sharpness. Additionally, the method may segment the scene based on depth information (from MIDAS) to assess the focus level within each segment, improving the extraction of sharp regions. This step is generic and can use any operator that reliably measures sharpness, but DMENet and MIDAS are the specific tools cited. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of required neighboring rays per ray from K^2 to \frac{K^2}{P'^2} compared to random ray sampling in NeRF, due to random patch sampling. The sharpness prior computation takes less than a couple of minutes and does not affect training or testing times. Memory Complexity: The blur kernel tensor \mathcal{B} has size N{img} \times Nk \times K \times K \times C. With N{img} views, Nk=400, K=11, and C=3, this is a significant but manageable memory footprint. Performance: The method successfully renders clean images even from harshly defocused regions. It improves expressivity by increasing grid size without extra cost for kernel generation. Strengths: Joint optimization with neural fields allows rapid convergence. The grid-based approach is more efficient than MLP-based kernel generation. Limitations: Requires a preprocessing step for sharpness estimation. Performance depends on the accuracy of the defocus map estimation. The method originates from "Sharp-NeRF: Grid-based Fast Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields using Sharpness Prior". It was proposed to address the limitations of NeRF and its derivatives in handling defocus blur by leveraging a sharpness prior and grid-based blur kernels. The work contrasts with previous methods that used MLPs to generate blur kernels, offering a more scalable and expressive alternative. name: TideGS Trajectory Ordering
head: Clustered TSP ordering for 3DGS, Trajectory-aware view ordering
body:
TideGS Trajectory Ordering is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces standard randomized view shuffling with a trajectory-aware ordered sequence of views to improve optimization stability and convergence for large-scale scenes. Unlike standard 3DGS which samples views with random shuffling, TideGS uses a clustered traveling-salesperson (TSP) ordering to preserve trajectory continuity, reducing gradient variation between consecutive steps. It builds on Base 3DGS Optimization by modifying the view sampling schedule while retaining the standard masked update mechanism. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M training views with camera poses; the current state of Gaussian parameters 	heta; a fixed block size B. Outputs: A permutation \pi of view indices; updated parameters 	heta{t+1} after processing one epoch. Data Structures: 1. Spatial Blocks: Gaussians are partitioned into K spatial blocks using Morton-code ordering. Each block contains a fixed number of primitives B. The block-index universe is \mathcal{K} = \{0, \dots, K-1\}. These blocks serve as the basic unit for SSD–CPU–GPU streaming. Bit-packing details for Morton codes are Not given in the sources. 2. View Permutation: An ordered sequence \pi = (\pi1, \dots, \piM) generated by clustered TSP over camera poses. This is a permutation of view indices, not spatial blocks. 3. Active Set \mathcal{I}t: At iteration t, the set of Gaussian indices and parameter coordinates that are visible and selected for update after coarse-to-fine filtering. Numbered Steps: 1. Block Partitioning: Partition all Gaussian primitives into spatial blocks using Morton-code ordering. Each block k \in \mathcal{K} contains exactly B Gaussians. 2. Trajectory Construction: Apply a clustered traveling-salesperson (TSP) algorithm to the camera poses of the M training views to generate the permutation \pi = (\pi1, \dots, \piM). 3. Training Loop: Iterate through the views in the order defined by \pi. For each iteration t from 1 to M: a. Block Selection: Perform coarse block-wise frustum culling to select the working set of blocks Kt \subseteq \mathcal{K} relevant to the current view \pit. b. Active Set Determination: Perform coarse-to-fine filtering to determine the Gaussian-level active set \mathcal{I}t. Only Gaussians in the selected blocks that are visible in view \pit are included. c. Gradient Computation: Compute the photometric loss f{\pit}(	heta) and its gradient 
abla f{\pit}(	heta) for the active Gaussians. d. Masked Update: Update the parameters using the masked update rule: 	heta{t+1}^{(j)} =  egin{cases} 	hetat^{(j)} - \etat \cdot ut^{(j)}, & j \in \mathcal{I}t, \ 	hetat^{(j)}, & 	ext{otherwise,} \end{cases} where ut^{(j)} is the optimizer's update direction (e.g., Adam moments) and \etat is the learning rate. e. State Preservation: Parameters not in \mathcal{I}t are not updated, preserving their state and preventing interference from distant regions. Formulas: Objective Function: The goal is to minimize the average photometric loss over M training views: \min{	heta} F(	heta):=  rac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^M fi(	heta) where fi(	heta) is the photometric loss for view i and 	heta \in \mathbb{R}^d is the concatenation of all Gaussian parameters. Gradient-Variation Surrogate: To analyze ordering stability, the following surrogate measures the squared norm difference between consecutive per-view gradients along the permutation \pi: V\pi(\{	hetat\}):= \sum{t=1}^{M-1} \left\| 
abla f{\pit}(	hetat) - 
abla f{\pi{t+1}}(	hetat) ight\|^2 This term is smaller for \pi{TSP} than for random permutations, indicating reduced gradient drift. Parameters: B: The fixed number of primitives (Gaussians) contained in each spatial block (typical value: e.g., B Gaussians). K: The total number of spatial blocks. M: The total number of training views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stale Optimizer State: Sequentially correlated samples in non-shuffled training may introduce bias or cause optimizer state (e.g., momentum) to become stale or misaligned. Mitigation: The masked update in TideGS acts as a safeguard against stale optimizer state by updating optimizer state only on active coordinates, preventing distant regions from interfering with each other. Visibility Sparsity: Most parameters are untouched at each step. Inactive parameters are not repeatedly perturbed by unrelated views, and their update history is dominated by iterations where they are visible. An oracle-efficient active next-best-view selection framework for 3DGS that reduces computational cost by evaluating only a randomized subset of candidate views per iteration. It differs from TideGS by focusing on memory-efficient rendering and stochastic submodular optimization rather than trajectory-aware view ordering. Choose it when minimizing oracle complexity for view selection is the priority. Training-time techniques that replace randomized view shuffling with deterministic sequences to optimize Gaussian caching and reduce CPU optimizer communication overhead. Unlike TideGS which targets gradient stability via TSP ordering, these strategies focus on caching efficiency and CPU-side throughput. Choose them when CPU-bound optimizer performance is the bottleneck. Time Complexity: The TSP ordering is computed once during initialization. The training loop processes each view exactly once per epoch, similar to standard 3DGS, but with the overhead of block-wise frustum culling and Morton-code based spatial partitioning. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for spatial blocks and Morton codes. The out-of-core streaming capability allows handling large scenes by loading only active blocks into GPU memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces gradient drift; mitigates stale optimizer state through masked updates; enables scalable training via out-of-core optimization. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of TSP order; relies on visibility-induced sparsity for effectiveness. When to use: Large-scale scenes where standard random shuffling leads to unstable convergence or slow training. When not to use: Small scenes where random shuffling is sufficient and the overhead of TSP ordering is unjustified. TideGS was introduced in the paper "TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization". It departs from standard randomized view order to address scalability and stability issues in large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting training. The method leverages empirical properties of visibility-induced sparsity and trajectory continuity to improve optimization. TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.20150, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LiTe-GS
head: Oracle-Efficient NBV Selection for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: LiTe-GS is an oracle-efficient active next-best-view (NBV) selection framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces the computational cost of Fisher-information-based view selection by evaluating only a randomized subset of candidate views at each iteration rather than exhaustively scoring the full pool. It formulates NBV selection as the cardinality-constrained maximization of Fisher-information gain, leveraging stochastic submodular optimization to balance estimation accuracy with oracle efficiency, thereby achieving O(M \log(1/\epsilon)) oracle complexity independent of the selection cardinality K. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: H0: The prior block-diagonal Fisher information matrix obtained from an initial 3DGS reconstruction trained on a small set of seed views V0. Vc: A pool of M candidate viewpoints for acquisition. K: The selection cardinality, i.e., the number of views to select in each acquisition batch. \epsilon: An accuracy parameter controlling the trade-off between oracle efficiency and approximation quality. Outputs: S: A set of K selected views. Data Structures: Fisher Information Matrix (H): Stored as a block-diagonal matrix where each block corresponds to the parameters of an individual Gaussian primitive i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. Hv \approx \text{blkdiag}(Hv(\hat{\theta}1), Hv(\hat{\theta}2), \dots, Hv(\hat{\theta}N)). Each block Hv(\hat{\theta}i) is computed as \sigma^{-2} J{v,i}^\top J{v,i}, where J{v,i} is the Jacobian of the rendered observations for view v with respect to the parameters of Gaussian i. Priority Queue (Q): A max-priority queue storing candidate views from the current sampled subset P, ordered by their cached marginal gains \gammav. Formulas: 3D Gaussian Density: Gi(x) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (x - \mui)^\top \Pii^{-1} (x - \mui) \right). Covariance Parameterization: \Pii = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top, where Ri \in SO(3) and Si is a scaling matrix. Image-Space Covariance: \Pi'i = JW \Pii W^\top J^\top, where W is the viewing transformation and J is the Jacobian of the projective transformation. Rendered Color: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai (1 - \sum{j < i} \alphaj), where N is the set of Gaussians along the pixel’s viewing ray. Fisher Information for View v: Hv(\hat{\Theta}) \approx \sigma^{-2} \sum{\text{pixels}} Jv^\top Jv, where Jv = \frac{\partial fv}{\partial \Theta}|{\hat{\Theta}} is the Jacobian of the rendering function. Marginal Gain: \rho(\{v\} | Sq) is the marginal information gain computed via oracle evaluation, which constructs and accumulates the Fisher-information contribution Hv. The marginal gain is the reduction in uncertainty (increase in information) by adding view v to the selected set Sq. Subset Size: p = \frac{M}{K} \log \frac{1}{\epsilon}. Parameters: \epsilon: Typical value 0.1. Tested values include 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6. K: Tested values 3, 4, 6. \delta: Small regularization parameter for ill-conditioning, applied as H0 \leftarrow H0 + \delta I. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize selected set S = \emptyset. Initialize current information matrix H = H0. Precondition H0 by adding regularization: H0 \leftarrow H0 + \delta I. Initialize cached marginal gains \gammav \leftarrow \infty for all v \in Vc. 2. Iterative Selection (for q = 1 to K): Sample Subset: Sample a subset P \subset (Vc \setminus S) of size p = \frac{M}{K} \log \frac{1}{\epsilon}. Initialize Queue: Initialize a max-priority queue Q over views in P using their cached gains \gammav. Lazy Evaluation Loop: Repeat: Pop view v with the largest cached gain from Q. Oracle Evaluation: Recompute the true marginal gain \Deltav = \rho(\{v\} | Sq) by constructing and accumulating the Fisher information contribution Hv. Update cached gain \gammav \leftarrow \Deltav. Re-insert v into Q with updated priority \gammav. Until \gammav = \max{u \in P} \gammau (i.e., the popped view's true gain is greater than or equal to the cached gains of all other views in Q). Select and Update: Add selected view v to S: S \leftarrow S \cup \{v\}. Update information matrix: H \leftarrow H + Hv. 3. Return: Selected set S. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import random import heapq def logdet(M): """Computes the natural logarithm of the determinant of matrix M.""" return np.linalg.slogdet(M)[1] def computejacobian(view): """Computes the Jacobian Jv = d(fv)/d(Theta) for the given view.""" # Standard differentiable rendering computes this via backpropagation. return view.renderjacobian() def computefisherblock(jacobian, sigma2inv): """Computes Hv = sigma^-2 Jv^T Jv.""" return sigma2inv (jacobian.T @ jacobian) def liTegs(h0, candidateviews, k, epsilon, delta, sigma2inv): m = len(candidateviews) # Precondition H0 with regularization h = h0 + delta np.eye(h0.shape[0]) s = [] remainingviews = list(candidateviews) cachedgains = {v: float('inf') for v in candidateviews} for q in range(1, k + 1): # Sample subset P of size p psize = int((m / k) np.log(1 / epsilon)) psize = min(psize, len(remainingviews)) p = random.sample(remainingviews, psize) # Max-heap using negative gains heap = [(-cachedgains[v], v) for v in p] heapq.heapify(heap) selectedview = None while heap: neggain, v = heapq.heappop(heap) # Oracle evaluation: recompute true marginal gain jacobian = computejacobian(v) hv = computefisherblock(jacobian, sigma2inv) truegain = logdet(h) - logdet(h + hv) cachedgains[v] = truegain # Check if truegain >= max cached gain of remaining views in heap if heap: maxothercached = -heap[0][0] else: maxothercached = -float('inf') if truegain >= maxothercached: selectedview = v h = h + hv break else: heapq.heappush(heap, (-truegain, v)) if selectedview is None: selectedview = p[0] jacobian = computejacobian(selectedview) hv = computefisherblock(jacobian, sigma2inv) h = h + hv s.append(selectedview) remainingviews.remove(selectedview) return s Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The prior information matrix H0 can be ill-conditioned. This is handled by preconditioning with a small regularization parameter \delta: H0 \leftarrow H0 + \delta I. Subset Size: The subset size p depends on \epsilon. If \epsilon is large, p becomes small, potentially leading to poor selection quality if the subset does not contain informative views. Dynamic Resampling: LiTe-GS dynamically resamples candidate subsets at each acquisition step. This differs from Static-Subset Greedy (SSG), which samples once per stage. Dynamic resampling prevents the algorithm from being permanently restricted to a potentially unfavorable subset realization. A baseline method that uses the same Fisher-information-based objective but evaluates the full oracle over all candidate views at each iteration, resulting in higher oracle complexity. A baseline that samples a fixed subset of candidates once per acquisition stage and keeps it fixed, whereas LiTe-GS dynamically resamples candidate subsets at each acquisition step. Time and Memory Complexity: Oracle Complexity: Expected O(M \log(1/\epsilon)) oracle evaluations with respect to the number of candidate views M, independent of the selection cardinality K. Memory: The block-diagonal approximation of the Fisher information matrix makes storage tractable, scaling with the number of Gaussian primitives N but avoiding the full dense matrix. Measured Performance: On Blender (Ship) with K=6, \epsilon=0.1: 208 oracle evaluations, PSNR 25.49, SSIM 0.830, LPIPS 0.158. Increasing K from 3 to 6 increases POP-GS evaluations from 275 to 549, while LiTe-GS remains nearly constant (210, 209, 208). For fixed K=6, increasing \epsilon from 0.1 to 0.6 reduces evaluations from 208 to 44, yielding 80.42% and 91.99% reductions respectively. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly reduces oracle evaluations compared to exhaustive methods like POP-GS while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality. Provides an explicit trade-off between efficiency and accuracy via \epsilon. Limitations: Approximation quality depends on \epsilon. A fixed subset (SSG) can occasionally outperform LiTe-GS if the fixed subset is favorable, but LiTe-GS is more robust across different scenes due to dynamic resampling. LiTe-GS was proposed in the paper "LiTe-GS: Oracle-Efficient Next Best View Selection for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the computational bottleneck of information-driven view selection in 3DGS, where repeated evaluations of expensive information-gain oracles become prohibitive as the number of candidate views increases. The method leverages stochastic submodular optimization techniques to design an efficient active-view selection strategy. name: View Ordering Strategies
head: Camera Order, GS Count Order, TSP Order
body: View ordering strategies determine the sequence in which training views are processed during 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to improve training efficiency and stability. Unlike randomized shuffling, these methods leverage geometric or visibility information to reduce communication overhead between CPU and GPU memory. They are primarily used in conjunction with Gaussian caching mechanisms to minimize redundant data transfers. Inputs: A set of training views V = \{v1, \dots, vN\}, their camera poses, and the current set of 3D Gaussians G. Outputs: A permutation \pi of view indices representing the processing order. The strategies operate by sorting the views based on specific criteria: 1. Random Order: Views are shuffled uniformly at random. This serves as the baseline for comparison. 2. Camera Order: Views are sorted by the coordinate of their camera center along the scene’s principal axis. This creates a spatially coherent traversal path. 3. GS Count Order: Views are sorted in descending order by the number of Gaussians visible in each view. Prioritizing views with higher Gaussian counts allows the CPU Adam optimizer to update a larger number of Gaussians earlier in the training process, thereby reducing its relative overhead. 4. TSP Order: Views are ordered using a Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) heuristic to find a sequence that maximizes the overlap of visible Gaussians between successive views. This strategy is specifically designed to enhance the effectiveness of Gaussian caching by keeping frequently accessed Gaussians resident in GPU memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Computation: GS Count Order and TSP Order require computing view-Gaussian visibility, which adds preprocessing overhead. Scene Scale: In scenes with very low Gaussian sharing between images (low \rho), such as "BigCity," the benefits of TSP-based caching are reduced because fewer Gaussians are shared between successive views. Conversely, in scenes with high Gaussian density per image, such as "Bicycle," caching benefits are more significant. This is a combined optimization technique used in CLM that caches Gaussian parameters across views and applies TSP-based ordering to minimize redundant CPU-to-GPU transfers. By maintaining a cache of recently accessed Gaussians, the system avoids reloading them from CPU memory. When combined with TSP order, CLM reduces communication volume by 37% (in the Alameda scene) to 82% (in the BigCity scene) compared to naive offloading without caching. In scenes with low inter-image Gaussian sharing, the caching benefit is smaller, but the ordering still contributes to overall efficiency. Communication Reduction: CLM with Gaussian Caching and TSP Order significantly reduces the volume of parameters transferred from CPU to GPU memory compared to naive offloading. Overhead: GS Count Order and TSP Order require additional processing to compute visibility or solve the TSP problem, unlike Camera Order or Random Order. Performance: The choice of ordering affects training throughput. TSP Order is shown to improve throughput on hardware such as RTX 2080 Ti and RTX 4090 when used with CLM. Scalability: The effectiveness of caching-dependent strategies (TSP) scales with the degree of Gaussian overlap between views; it is less effective in sparse or highly fragmented scenes. These strategies were introduced in the context of CLM (CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting) to address the bottleneck of transferring Gaussian parameters between CPU and GPU memory during training. The ablation study in the source paper evaluates these ordering methods to isolate the impact of view sequence on communication volume and training speed. CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3779212.3790140, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Gradient Computation and Back-Propagation
head: Differentiable Back-Propagation, Gradient Flow in Gaussian Splatting
body: Gradient Computation and Back-Propagation refers to the mechanism of calculating the derivatives of a rendering loss with respect to the learnable parameters of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, color, and spherical harmonic coefficients) to enable end-to-end training via gradient descent [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. It differs from standard rasterization by propagating gradients through the differentiable alpha-compositing equation and the 2D projection approximation, allowing the scene representation to be optimized [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. This family includes specialized variants for specific signal models (e.g., ToF), feature fields, skew-normal distributions, and memory-efficient training strategies [9733-tof-gradient-computation-for-gaussian-splatting.md][9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection.md][10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q.md][13506-deferred-back-propagation.md]. The core mechanism relies on the differentiable alpha-compositing equation. For a pixel \mathbf{x}, the rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) is computed as: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}k \alphak(\mathbf{x}) Tk(\mathbf{x}) where \mathbf{c}k is the color of the k-th Gaussian, \alphak(\mathbf{x}) is its opacity at pixel \mathbf{x}, and Tk(\mathbf{x}) is the transmittance up to the k-th Gaussian: Tk(\mathbf{x}) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(\mathbf{x})) The Gaussians are sorted by depth from closest to farthest [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. The gradient of the loss L with respect to the parameters \thetak of the k-th Gaussian is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \thetak} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})} \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})} \frac{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \thetak} The term \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})} represents the contribution of the k-th Gaussian to the pixel color gradient. It is computed efficiently using recursive accumulators traversed in reverse depth order to avoid O(N^2) complexity [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Specifically: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})} = Tk(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{c}k - \alphak(\mathbf{x}) \sum{j=k+1}^{N} \mathbf{c}j \alphaj(\mathbf{x}) Tj(\mathbf{x}) \frac{1}{1-\alphak(\mathbf{x})} In practice, this is implemented by maintaining a running transmittance T and a running accumulated color C{acc} [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. The term \frac{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \thetak} depends on the parameterization: Opacity: \alphak is typically the sigmoid of a learnable scalar. The gradient is \frac{\partial \alphak}{\partial \text{opacity}{raw}} = \alphak (1 - \alphak) [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. 2D Projection: The 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} is derived from the 3D covariance \Sigma{3D} and the view matrix. The conic matrix C = \Sigma{2D}^{-1} is used for efficient evaluation. Gradients \frac{\partial \alphak}{\partial C} are computed based on the Gaussian PDF derivative [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. 3D Covariance: \Sigma{3D} is parameterized by scale and rotation (\Sigma{3D} = R S S^T R^T). Gradients flow to scale and rotation via the chain rule through \Sigma{3D} and then to \Sigma{2D} [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Color/SH: \mathbf{c}k is computed from spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Gradients flow directly to SH coefficients based on the basis function evaluation at the viewing direction [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Computes gradients for Time-of-Flight (ToF) signals (e.g., quad pixel signals) by introducing recursive accumulation terms that account for squared transmittance factors. Unlike standard RGB rendering where the gradient depends linearly on transmittance, ToF gradients require a backward pass that squares the transmittance terms, making the computation distinct from sibling methods that rely on simple chain rules. A training-free method for rendering feature fields by aggregating 2D feature embeddings from training views into pre-trained 3D Gaussians. It uses the rendering gradients (opacity \times transmittance) as weights to back-project features, offering a significant speedup over iterative optimization-based alternatives like Feature 3DGS. Computes exact gradients for 3D Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS) by decoupling the interaction between rotation and scale matrices. It introduces an intermediate variable Q = ARS to reformulate the 2D Skew-Normal density, allowing for direct, closed-form gradient computation of the skew parameter k, mean \mu, and shape matrix Q, avoiding the high complexity of differentiating coupled RS terms directly. A training optimization technique that suppresses specular reflection artifacts while preserving transmission details. It modulates the gradients of the transmission color component using a local variance-based gating factor during the backward pass, ensuring the forward pass remains unchanged. A memory-efficient technique that decouples the high-memory forward rendering pass from the backward gradient computation pass. It renders the full-resolution image without gradients, computes the loss and cached image gradients, and then performs patch-wise re-rendering with gradients enabled to compute parameter updates. This enables the use of full-resolution image losses (e.g., CNN-based style losses) despite limited GPU memory. Computes gradients for a depth rendering formulation that uses softmax scaling to bias accumulation toward high-weight Gaussians. It solves the problem of mode-selection depth, which restricts gradients to the single highest-weight Gaussian, by approximating mode depth while maintaining gradient flow to all contributing Gaussians, modulated by a temperature parameter \beta. The standard backward pass for 3DGS that computes gradients of a rendering loss with respect to all learnable parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color, SH coefficients). It differs from standard rasterization by propagating gradients through the differentiable alpha-compositing equation and the 2D projection approximation, enabling end-to-end training. A gradient computation method using half-precision (FP16) arithmetic to optimize accuracy-throughput trade-off, omitting block-local reductions. It calculates \frac{\partial I}{\partial Mi} using Eqs. (3, 4, 5), \frac{\partial Mi}{\partial u} using Eq. (2) and bilinear interpolation, and geometric derivatives from Eq. (1). The gradient of image I w.r.t. primitive position xi is \frac{\partial I(x,y)}{\partial xi} = \frac{\partial I(x,y)}{\partial Mi(x,y)} \left( \frac{\partial Mi(x,y)}{\partial u} \frac{\partial u}{\partial xi} + \frac{\partial Mi(x,y)}{\partial v} \frac{\partial v}{\partial xi} \right), where Mi is the primitive mask and u,v are local coordinates. It differs from standard implementations by using half precision and omitting block-local reductions to align with accuracy-throughput goals. A 2D tensor allocated per Gaussian to store gradients written by the CUDA backward pass, separating standard and absolute gradient channels. It is allocated as a tensor of shape (N, 4) with dtype matching xyz, setting requiresgrad=trackgradients and attempting to call retaingrad() to preserve gradients for intermediate computations, catching exceptions if unsupported. The layout is (N, 4) float32, where channels 0-1 are standard screen-space gradients and channels 2-3 are absolute gradients used by ABSGS and ImprovedGS. Implementation: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. screenspacepoints = torch.zeros( (pc.getxyz.shape[0], 4), dtype=pc.getxyz.dtype, requiresgrad=trackgradients, device=pc.getxyz.device,) if trackgradients: try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except Exception: pass A pitfall is that retaingrad() may raise an exception in older PyTorch versions or specific execution contexts, requiring a try/except block to prevent crashes. An optimization step where appearance features on each point are updated via backpropagation through the aggregation and rendering network. The gradient on point feature i is updated using the chain rule: \Delta Fi = -lr \times w(p,h,w)i \times g(p,h,w), where g(p,h,w) is the gradient from the loss function and lr is the learning rate. To freeze weights for specific attributes in the Gaussian model, iterate through the list of attribute names (screenlist). For each attribute, get its gradient tensor. Multiply the gradient tensor by a mask (element-wise) or set to zero if no mask is provided. For freezweightsbymasknounsqueeze, the mask is multiplied directly with the gradient tensor without unsqueezing. For freezweightsbymask, the mask is unsqueezed by 1 dimension before multiplication. The screenlist contains strings representing the names of the Gaussian model attributes whose gradients are to be modified (e.g., ['omega'], ['rotation']). A module integrated into Deferred Back-propagation (DBP) to maintain consistency between the forward-only rendering step and the gradient-based re-rendering step. Without Local Self-Attention, the rendered images between the first (Render w/o Grad) and second (Re-Render w/ Grad) steps of DBP are inconsistent, causing the loss from the forward-only pass to fail as a gradient guide, which drops PSNR after ~1,500 training steps. With Local Self-Attention, PSNR remains stable at 32.34 dB throughout training, whereas without it, PSNR drops significantly. The foundational differentiable rasterization for 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023, establishing the chain rule propagation through alpha-compositing and 2D projection [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Subsequent work extended this to specialized signal models, such as Time-of-Flight (ToF) signals, which require squared transmittance factors in the gradient computation [9733-tof-gradient-computation-for-gaussian-splatting.md]. Memory-efficient training strategies like Deferred Back-propagation were developed to handle full-resolution losses that exceed GPU memory limits [13506-deferred-back-propagation.md]. Variants for feature fields, skew-normal distributions, and specular artifacts have been proposed to enhance the expressiveness and quality of the reconstructed scenes [9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection.md][10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q.md][13432-specular-aware-gradient-gating.md]. name: ToF Gradient Computation for Gaussian Splatting
head: Opacity gradient for ToF image formation, Recursive gradient for quad pixels
body: This method computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to the opacity parameters of 3D Gaussians specifically for Time-of-Flight (ToF) image formation models, such as those generating phasor or quad pixel signals. It extends the standard differentiable alpha-compositing gradient used in RGB rendering by introducing recursive accumulation terms that account for the squared transmittance factors inherent in ToF signal models. Unlike standard color rendering where the gradient depends linearly on transmittance, ToF gradients require a backward pass that squares the transmittance terms, making the computation less trivial and distinct from sibling methods that rely on simple chain rules or intermediate variable optimizations. The method computes the gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphak} for the opacity \alphak of the k-th Gaussian sorted by depth. The computation relies on a backward recursive pass to accumulate contributions from Gaussians with greater depth (higher index k). Inputs: L: The scalar loss function. \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})}: The gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered ToF signal (e.g., quad pixel signal) at pixel \mathbf{x}. N: The total number of Gaussians sorted by depth for the pixel. \alphak: The opacity of the k-th Gaussian. \mathbf{q}k: The ToF signal contribution (e.g., quad value) of the k-th Gaussian. Tk: The transmittance up to the k-th Gaussian, defined as Tk = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj). Outputs: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphak}: The gradient of the loss with respect to the opacity of the k-th Gaussian. The algorithm requires two scalar/vector accumulators for each pixel, initialized to zero before the backward pass: 1. \text{acc}k^q: The accumulated ToF signal contribution from Gaussians k+1 to N. 2. (Implicit) The transmittance Tk is computed during the forward pass or stored. 1. Initialize Accumulator: Set \text{acc}{N+1}^q = 0. 2. Backward Recursion: Iterate k from N down to 1: a. Compute the gradient of the signal with respect to opacity using the recursive formula: \frac{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak} = Tk^2 \left( \mathbf{q}k + 2(\alphak - 1)\text{acc}k^q \right) b. Compute the final opacity gradient using the chain rule: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphak} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})} \frac{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak} c. Update the accumulator for the next iteration (previous Gaussian in depth order): \text{acc}k^q = \alpha{k+1} \mathbf{q}{k+1} + (1 - \alpha{k+1})^2 \text{acc}{k+1}^q Note: For k=N, \text{acc}{N+1}^q is 0, so \text{acc}N^q = \alpha{N+1} \mathbf{q}{N+1} is not applicable as N+1 does not exist. The base case for the accumulator update is handled by the loop structure where the update uses the next Gaussian's data. Specifically, the recurrence for \text{acc}k^q depends on \text{acc}{k+1}^q. The definition in is: \text{acc}k^q = \begin{cases} \alpha{k+1} \mathbf{q}{k+1} + (1 - \alpha{k+1})^2 \text{acc}{k+1}^q, & k < N \\ 0, & k = N \end{cases} Correction on Step 2c logic based on definition: The accumulator \text{acc}k^q is defined for index k. The recurrence calculates \text{acc}k^q using values from k+1. Therefore, the loop should compute \text{acc}k^q after computing the gradient for k, or the gradient for k uses \text{acc}k^q which was computed in the previous iteration (for k+1). Let's align with the standard backward pass pattern: Revised Step 2: Initialize \text{acc}{N+1}^q = 0. For k = N down to 1: 1. Calculate \frac{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak} = Tk^2 (\mathbf{q}k + 2(\alphak - 1)\text{acc}k^q). Wait, the definition of \text{acc}k^q in is: \text{acc}k^q = \begin{cases} \alpha{k+1} \mathbf{q}{k+1} + (1 - \alpha{k+1})^2 \text{acc}{k+1}^q, & k < N \\ 0, & k = N \end{cases} This implies \text{acc}k^q is the accumulation starting from k+1. So for k=N, \text{acc}N^q = 0. For k=N-1, \text{acc}{N-1}^q = \alphaN \mathbf{q}N + (1-\alphaN)^2 \text{acc}N^q. Therefore, the algorithm is: 1. Set \text{acc}{N+1}^q = 0. 2. For k = N down to 1: a. Determine \text{acc}k^q: If k < N: \text{acc}k^q = \alpha{k+1} \mathbf{q}{k+1} + (1 - \alpha{k+1})^2 \text{acc}{k+1}^q. If k = N: \text{acc}k^q = 0. b. Compute signal gradient: \frac{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak} = Tk^2 (\mathbf{q}k + 2(\alphak - 1)\text{acc}k^q). c. Compute loss gradient: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphak} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})} \frac{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak}. 1. Chain Rule: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphak} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})} \frac{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak} 2. Signal Gradient: \frac{\partial \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak} = Tk^2 \left( \mathbf{q}k + 2(\alphak - 1)\text{acc}k^q \right) 3. Accumulator Recurrence: \text{acc}k^q = \begin{cases} \alpha{k+1} \mathbf{q}{k+1} + (1 - \alpha{k+1})^2 \text{acc}{k+1}^q, & k < N \\ 0, & k = N \end{cases} Tk: Transmittance up to Gaussian k. \mathbf{q}k: Quad contribution of Gaussian k. \alphak: Opacity of Gaussian k. Squared Transmittance: The presence of Tk^2 in the gradient formula makes the computation distinct from standard RGB rendering, where the factor is Tk. This increases the sensitivity to depth ordering and opacity values. Recursion Base Case: The accumulator \text{acc}N^q must be explicitly initialized to 0. Failure to do so leads to incorrect gradient accumulation for the deepest Gaussian. Precision: The squared terms (1-\alpha{k+1})^2 can lead to numerical instability if opacities are very close to 1 or 0, though this is inherent to the ToF model. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetofopacitygradient( gradlosssignal, # dL/dq(x), scalar or vector qcontributions, # List of qk for k=1..N alphas, # List of alphak for k=1..N transmittances # List of Tk for k=1..N): """ Computes dL/dalphak for ToF quad pixel signals. Args: gradlosssignal: Gradient of loss w.r.t. rendered signal q(x). qcontributions: Array of shape (N,) containing qk. alphas: Array of shape (N,) containing alphak. transmittances: Array of shape (N,) containing Tk. Returns: gradalphas: Array of shape (N,) containing dL/dalphak. """ N = len(alphas) gradalphas = [0.0] N acckq = 0.0 # This will hold acc{k+1}^q in the loop, initialized to acc{N+1}^q = 0 # Iterate backwards from N-1 to 0 (indices 0..N-1) for k in range(N - 1, -1, -1): # k is the current index (0-based) # Corresponds to Gaussian k+1 in 1-based indexing from sources # 1. Compute acck^q (accumulation from k+1 onwards) # In 1-based indexing: acck^q = alpha{k+1} q{k+1} + (1-alpha{k+1})^2 acc{k+1}^q # In 0-based indexing: current k, next is k+1 # acckq currently holds acc{k+1}^q from the previous iteration (which was k+1 in 0-based, i.e., k+2 in 1-based) # Wait, let's trace carefully. # Loop starts at k = N-1 (last Gaussian). # acckq is initialized to 0 (acc{N+1}^q). # For k = N-1: # We need acc{N-1}^q (1-based index N). # Formula: accN^q = 0 (base case). # So for the last element, acc is 0. if k == N - 1: acccurrent = 0.0 else: # acccurrent = alpha{k+1} q{k+1} + (1 - alpha{k+1})^2 accnext # In 0-based: next index is k+1 alphanext = alphas[k+1] qnext = qcontributions[k+1] acccurrent = alphanext qnext + (1.0 - alphanext)2 acckq # 2. Compute signal gradient d q(x) / d alphak # Formula: Tk^2 (qk + 2(alphak - 1)acck^q) Tk = transmittances[k] qk = qcontributions[k] alphak = alphas[k] gradsignal = (Tk 2) (qk + 2.0 (alphak - 1.0) acccurrent) # 3. Compute loss gradient gradalphas[k] = gradlosssignal gradsignal # 4. Update acckq for the next iteration (which is k-1) # The next iteration needs acc{k-1}^q? No, the next iteration is k-1. # It will need acc{k-1}^q which depends on acck^q. # So we store acccurrent as acckq for the next loop step. acckq = acccurrent return gradalphas Focuses on feature gradients rather than opacity/photometric gradients. Uses an intermediate variable Q to optimize the backward pass for standard splatting. Gates gradients based on specular components, not specific to ToF. Defers gradient computation for memory efficiency. Derives gradients for depth estimation using softmax, distinct from ToF quad pixel gradients. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel for the backward pass, where N is the number of Gaussians. This is comparable to the forward pass but requires an additional recursive accumulator. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel for the accumulator, assuming transmittances and contributions are available. Strengths: Enables end-to-end training of 3D Gaussian Splatting models for ToF data, allowing optimization of geometry and appearance based on depth/reflectivity signals. Limitations: The squared transmittance terms can make gradients more sensitive to noise and numerical precision compared to RGB rendering. The method is specific to ToF signal models (phasor/quad) and does not apply to standard RGB rendering without modification. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models on Time-of-Flight datasets (e.g., depth, quad pixels) and gradients with respect to opacity are required. When not to use: For standard RGB rendering where the simpler linear transmittance gradient suffices. The method was introduced in the context of optimizing depth indirectly in dynamic radiance fields using 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the gap in differentiable rendering for ToF sensors, where the image formation model involves phasor or quad pixel signals that differ from standard RGB alpha-compositing. The key insight is that the gradient of the ToF signal with respect to opacity involves a recursive accumulation with squared transmittance terms, necessitating a specialized backward pass. name: Gradient-Weighted Feature Back-Projection
head: Back-Projection Equation, Expected Feature Back-Projection, FBP, Feature Back-Projection
body: Gradient-Weighted Feature Back-Projection is a training-free method for rendering feature fields in 3D Gaussian Splatting by aggregating 2D feature embeddings from training views into pre-trained 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of assigning semantic or visual features to 3D Gaussians without the computational cost of training a separate feature field or distilling features from a 2D foundation model. Unlike training-based alternatives like Feature 3DGS, which require iterative optimization of feature parameters, this method computes features in a single pass using the rendering gradients as weights, offering a significant speedup while maintaining high-quality 3D segmentation results. The method leverages the differentiable nature of the alpha-compositing equation to determine the influence of each Gaussian on the final rendered image. It back-projects 2D features (e.g., from LSeg or DINOv2) into 3D space by weighting the contribution of each Gaussian based on its opacity and transmittance. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians with fixed parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) obtained from a standard 3DGS reconstruction. A set of V training views, each with a corresponding 2D feature map \mathbf{F}{2D} generated by a pre-trained model (e.g., LSeg, DINOv2). The camera parameters for each training view. Outputs: A feature vector \mathbf{f}k \in \mathbb{R}^D for each Gaussian k, where D is the feature dimension. Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian k stores its 3D feature vector \mathbf{f}k. Initially, this may be zero or uninitialized. 2D Feature Map: For each view n, a 2D array \mathbf{F}{2D}(x, y, n) of shape H \times W \times D, where H, W are image dimensions. 1. Render and Compute Gradients: For each training view n: Render the scene using the current Gaussian parameters to obtain the rendered color \mathbf{C}n(x, y) and depth/alpha information. The rendering follows the standard alpha-compositing equation: \mathbf{C}n(x, y) = \sum{k=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}k \alphak(x, y, n) Tk(x, y, n) where \mathbf{c}k is the color of the k-th Gaussian, \alphak(x, y, n) is its opacity at pixel (x, y) in view n, and Tk(x, y, n) is the transmittance up to the k-th Gaussian: Tk(x, y, n) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(x, y, n)) Compute the gradient of the rendered color with respect to the k-th Gaussian's color \mathbf{c}k. This gradient serves as the weight for back-projection: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}n(x, y)}{\partial \mathbf{c}k} = \alphak(x, y, n) Tk(x, y, n) Let wk(x, y, n) = \alphak(x, y, n) Tk(x, y, n). 2. Accumulate Features: For each Gaussian k, accumulate the weighted 2D features from all views n where the Gaussian contributes to the pixel. Expected Feature Back-Projection (Normalized): \mathbf{f}k = \frac{\sum{n} \sum{(x,y) \in \text{pixels}} \mathbf{F}{2D}(x, y, n) wk(x, y, n)}{\sum{n} \sum{(x,y) \in \text{pixels}} wk(x, y, n)} Accumulated Feature Back-Projection (Unnormalized): \mathbf{f}k = \sum{n} \sum{(x,y) \in \text{pixels}} \mathbf{F}{2D}(x, y, n) wk(x, y, n) Note: If Euclidean normalization is applied to \mathbf{f}k after calculation, the normalized and unnormalized variants become equivalent. 3. Pruning: Calculate the numerator of the back-projection equation for each Gaussian. If the numerator is zero (indicating no influence on any screen pixel), prune the Gaussian or mark it as invalid to avoid division by zero or irrelevant data during inference. 4. Completion: The back-projection is completed in a single pass through all training views. No iterative optimization is required. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientweightedfeaturebackprojection(gaussians, views, featuremodel): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: position (3,) scale (3,) rotation (4,) opacity (scalar) color (3,) feature (D,) # To be filled views: List of view dictionaries with attributes: cameraparams gtimage (H, W, 3) gtfeatures (H, W, D) # Pre-computed by featuremodel featuremodel: Function to compute 2D features from an image. """ # Initialize features to zero for g in gaussians: g.feature = np.zeros(D) g.featureweightsum = 0.0 # Step 1 & 2: Render and Accumulate for view in views: # Render the scene to get alpha and transmittance for each Gaussian at each pixel # This typically involves a rasterization pass. # For each pixel (x, y), we get a list of overlapping Gaussians sorted by depth. # We compute alphak(x,y) and Tk(x,y) for each Gaussian k. # Efficient implementation: Use a tile-and-bin CUDA pipeline or similar # to compute contributions. Here we describe the logical accumulation. for k in range(len(gaussians)): g = gaussians[k] # Get the contribution of Gaussian k to all pixels in this view # In a real implementation, this is done via rasterization buffers. # weights[k] is a (H, W) array where weights[k][x,y] = alphak Tk weights = computegaussianweights(g, view.cameraparams) # Accumulate weighted features # Feature map F2D is (H, W, D) # We need to sum F2D[x,y] weights[x,y] for all x,y # Vectorized operation: # weightedfeatures = sum over x,y of (weights[x,y] F2D[x,y]) weightedfeatures = np.sum(weights[:,:, np.newaxis] view.gtfeatures, axis=(0, 1)) g.feature += weightedfeatures g.featureweightsum += np.sum(weights) # Step 3: Normalize and Prune for g in gaussians: if g.featureweightsum > 0: # Expected Feature Back-Projection g.feature = g.feature / g.featureweightsum else: # Prune or mark as invalid g.feature = None g.ispruned = True return gaussians Feature Model: Pre-trained models such as LSeg or DINOv2 are used to generate \mathbf{F}{2D}. Rasterizer: The gsplat library is used for rendering. Hardware: Experiments are performed on NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Zero Influence: If a Gaussian has no influence on any pixel (numerator is zero), it should be pruned before inference to prevent division by zero or irrelevant data. Normalization: The normalized (expected) and unnormalized (accumulated) variants are equivalent if Euclidean normalization is applied to the result. This variant uses the back-projected features for semantic segmentation. It obtains feature vectors \{\mathbf{f}k\} \in \mathbb{R}^D for each Gaussian. A query embedding \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^D is extracted from a language query or another modality. Segmentation is performed by computing the similarity sim(\mathbf{f}k, \mathbf{q}) (typically cosine similarity) and thresholding: G = \{gk \mid \text{sim}(\mathbf{f}k, \mathbf{q}) > \theta\}, where \theta is a user-defined threshold. 2D segmentation masks are derived similarly by querying rendered 2D features. This variant encodes each object with a unique vector and back-projects these vectors into the 3D scene. Two approaches are used: 1. Orthogonal Encoding: Procedurally generated orthogonal vectors are assigned to objects to maximize separation. This is limited by the embedding dimension D. 2. Contrastive Encoding: Non-orthogonal vectors are made distinct through contrastive learning, which maximizes distance between different objects. The loss function is \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{classification}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{orthogonality}}, where \mathcal{L}{\text{classification}} = \text{CrossEntropy}(\hat{y}, y) and \mathcal{L}{\text{orthogonality}} = \|\mathbf{E}\mathbf{E}^T - \mathbf{I}\|F. This variant transfers annotated regions from source images to a target object. DINOv2 features are transferred to the target scene via back-projection. The closest matching source annotation for each Gaussian is identified by performing k-nearest neighbors (kNN) classification on the feature space. Time Complexity: The method requires a single pass through all training views. The feature back-projection process takes an average of 2-3 minutes for the entire pipeline, including ground truth feature map generation. Inference Speed: Object segmentation (including text encoding and similarity calculation) takes 30 ms. Similarity calculation alone takes less than 1 ms. Speedup: The method achieves a 900x speedup compared to segmentation using masked gradients. It is 10x faster than Feature 3DGS (2.5 mins vs 20-30 mins for 7000 iterations) because it does not train a feature field. Memory: Memory usage is comparable to standard 3DGS, with the addition of storing feature vectors for each Gaussian. Strengths: Training-free, fast, scalable, high-quality 3D segmentation. Limitations: Requires pre-trained 3D Gaussians and 2D feature maps from training views. Performance depends on the quality of the 2D feature model. The method was introduced by Bharadwaj Amrutur and Shalabh Bhatnagar from the Indian Institute of Science. It addresses the limitations of training-based feature field rendering methods, which often perform poorly at 3D segmentation without post-processing. The approach leverages the gradient of the rendering equation to weight feature contributions, providing a computationally efficient alternative to distillation or feature field training.
