name: Sliced Wasserstein-based Gaussian Cloning Update
head: Slice-based Scale Update, Sliced Wasserstein Cloning
body: A method to determine the scale update for cloned Gaussians by minimizing the difference between the integrated color of the new and old Gaussians along arbitrary 1D slices passing through their centers, ensuring rasterization integral conservation. It sets itself apart from standard densification by enforcing a specific integral constraint on 1D projections rather than relying solely on position gradient magnitudes, leading to improved PSNR, SSIM, and lower LPIPS compared to base 3DGS. Inputs: A set of N cloned Gaussians with new opacity o^{\text{new}} and sliced covariance \Sigma^{\text{new}}. The corresponding old Gaussians with opacity o^{\text{old}} and sliced covariance \Sigma^{\text{old}}. A set of arbitrary 1D slices \mathcal{S} passing through the Gaussian centers. Outputs: Updated scale parameters for the cloned Gaussians that satisfy the integral conservation constraint. Data Structures: Gaussians are represented by their mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity o, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. The derivation sets the mean \mu to zero without loss of generality to simplify the equations. The 'sliced' covariance \Sigma denotes the 1D variance of the Gaussian along an arbitrary slice direction S(\cdot). Steps: 1. Define the Objective: Minimize the squared L2 norm of the difference between the integrals of the new and old color functions \mathbf{C} over the entire real line for all slices \mathcal{S}: \left\| \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathbf{C}^{\text{new}}(x) dx - \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathbf{C}^{\text{old}}(x) dx \right\|2^2, \quad \forall \mathcal{S}. This ensures that the rasterization integral remains equal before and after cloning for any arbitrary slice. 2. Derive Color Function for New Gaussians: The color function \mathbf{C}^{\text{new}}(x) along the slice is derived from the standard 3DGS rasterization equation. For N Gaussians, it is given by: \mathbf{C}^{\text{new}}(x) = \sum{i=1}^N o^{\text{new}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\Sigma^{\text{new}}}\right) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \left(1 - o^{\text{new}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\Sigma^{\text{new}}}\right)\right). 3. Apply Binomial Expansion: Using the binomial expansion for p < 1 where (1-p)^{i-1} = \sum{k=0}^{i-1} \binom{i-1}{k} (-1)^k p^k, let p = o^{\text{new}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\Sigma^{\text{new}}}\right). The color function becomes: \mathbf{C}^{\text{new}}(x) = \sum{i=1}^N \sum{k=0}^{i-1} \binom{i-1}{k} (-1)^k (o^{\text{new}})^{k+1} \exp\left(-\frac{(k+1)x^2}{2\Sigma^{\text{new}}}\right). 4. Compute Integrals: The integral of \mathbf{C}^{\text{new}}(x) over x \in (-\infty, \infty) is computed analytically using the standard Gaussian integral \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp(-ax^2) dx = \sqrt{\pi/a}. Substituting a = \frac{k+1}{2\Sigma^{\text{new}}} yields a closed-form expression for the integrated color. Similarly, the integral for \mathbf{C}^{\text{old}}(x) is computed using its parameters. 5. Solve for Scale Update: Equating \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathbf{C}^{\text{new}}(x) dx = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathbf{C}^{\text{old}}(x) dx and solving for \Sigma^{\text{new}} provides the scale update, as detailed in the source's equation (9). Parameters: Number of Gaussians N: Not given in the sources. Opacity o^{\text{new}}: Not given in the sources. Sliced Covariance \Sigma^{\text{new}}: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The binomial expansion assumes p < 1, i.e., o^{\text{new}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\Sigma^{\text{new}}}\right) < 1. The derivation assumes the mean \mu is zero. The method relies on the assumption that integrating over 1D slices is sufficient to preserve the rasterization integral, an approximation inspired by sliced Wasserstein methods. Time Complexity: The analytical integration is O(1) per term, but the double summation in the expanded color function scales as O(N^2) per slice. Memory Complexity: Operates on existing Gaussian parameters with no additional significant memory overhead compared to standard 3DGS. Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic dataset with the same number of Gaussians, the method achieves higher PSNR, SSIM, and lower LPIPS than base 3DGS. For example, on the 'Mic' scene, PSNR is 37.29 vs 35.35 for 3DGS. Average PSNR is 33.80 for the proposed method vs 33.42 for 3DGS. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) without increasing the number of Gaussians. Limitations: The method is specific to the cloning step and does not replace the entire training loop. It relies on the validity of the 1D slice approximation. The method is introduced in "3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo". It draws inspiration from sliced Wasserstein methods to enforce integral conservation during the cloning operation in 3D Gaussian Splatting training. 3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, https://ubc-vision.github.io/3dgs-mcmc/, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Cross-Structure Collaboration Module
body: The Cross-Structure Collaboration Module (CSCM) is a feature extraction mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates global tri-plane features with local context-aware grid features to generate Hierarchical Dense Embedded (HDE) features. It solves feature misalignment and insufficient geometric constraints in large-scale scenes by preserving global coherence while capturing local detail. It sets itself apart from standard tri-plane methods by adding a context grid interpolation step and from pure grid methods by maintaining a static global tri-plane backbone. The CSCM divides training into three levels (coarse to fine) to reduce feature misalignment caused by the disparity between tri-plane feature map size and grid resolution. It consists of three components: Tri-plane Feature Acquisition, Context Interpolation, and Cross-Structure Hierarchical Compensation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A query 3D point p (Gaussian center), the current point cloud state, and the tri-plane feature maps. Output: The Hierarchical Dense Embedded feature fh for the query point. Data Structures 1. Tri-Plane Features (F): A static 3D instance of k-planes factorization. It consists of three m-channel feature plane maps F \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h \times m} corresponding to the axis-aligned planes: xy, xz, and yz, with spatial resolution w \times h. 2. Context Grid (G): A resolution grid created for the current point cloud based on a given resolution parameter \alpha. 3. Vertex Features (fg): Features associated with the vertices v of the grid G. Defined as fg = [fp, p, O, s], where fp is the inherent features of the query point, p is position, O is the offset of the neural Gaussian center, and s is the scale. Steps 1. Tri-plane Feature Acquisition: Generate attention-enhanced tri-plane features F^TA using a tri-plane attention module TA. The attention operation TA for dimension i \in \{xy, xz, yz\} is defined as: F^T{A,i} = TA(Fi) = \rhoi (SA(CA(||{j \in \{xy,xz,yz\}} (Fj)))) Where ||{j \in \{xy,xz,yz\}} (\cdot) concatenates feature planes along the channel dimension in the order xy, xz, yz. CA(\cdot) is the channel attention operation. SA(\cdot) is the spatial attention operation. \rhoi(\cdot) extracts the feature map for dimension i from the concatenated result. Next, project the query point p onto the planes using projection function \pii(\cdot) and perform bi-linear interpolation \psi(\cdot) on both the original features Fi and the attention-enhanced features F^T{A,i}. Concatenate the interpolated features from all three orientations along the channel dimension and pass them through the tri-plane decoder \phit to obtain the tri-plane feature ft: ft = \phit (||{i \in \{xy,xz,yz\}} (\psi(Fi, \pii(p)), \psi(F^T{A,i}, \pii(p)))) 2. Context Interpolation: Create the resolution grid G for the current point cloud based on resolution \alpha. Identify the vertices v of the grid G that contain the query point p. Calculate the weight wv for each vertex v based on the normalized absolute distance between p and v along each axis: wv = \prod{dim \in \{x,y,z\}} (1 - \{p{dim} - v{dim}\}) Where \{\cdot\} computes the normalized absolute distance along each axis. Perform weighted aggregation of the vertex features fg and decode using \phic to obtain the contextual feature fc: fc = \phic \left( \frac{\sum{v \in G} wv \times fg}{\sum{v \in G} wv} \right) 3. Cross-Structure Hierarchical Compensation: Concatenate the tri-plane feature ft and the contextual feature fc to form the final Hierarchical Dense Embedded (HDE) feature fh: fh = [ft, fc] Parameters Resolution \alpha: Determines the granularity of the context grid G. Not given in the sources. Tri-plane Resolution (w, h): Spatial resolution of the feature planes. Not given in the sources. Channels (m): Number of channels in the tri-plane feature maps. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Overfitting: Gaussians may cluster extremely close to the camera plane, lacking geometric validity for novel viewpoints. This is exacerbated in large-scale scenes with limited viewpoint overlap. The CSCM itself does not solve this; a separate Cross-View Consistency Module (CVPM) handles it. Feature Misalignment: Caused by the size difference between tri-plane feature maps and grid resolution. Mitigated by the coarse-to-fine training levels. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Significantly improves the quality of rendering details in subsequent novel view synthesis. Strengths: Integrates global perception (tri-plane) with local sensitivity (context grid). Reduces feature misalignment via hierarchical compensation. Limitations: Requires maintaining both tri-plane structures and dynamic context grids. Does not inherently solve geometric validity issues caused by camera clustering (requires CVPM). When to use: Large-scale scenes where detail preservation and global coherence are critical. The CSCM was proposed in "SplatCo: Structure-View Collaborative Gaussian Splatting for Detail-Preserving Rendering of Large-Scale Unbounded Scenes". It is inspired by Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN). name: Structure-View Co-learning
body: Structure-View Co-learning (SVC) is a training module that combines structural and view-dependent gradients to enable robust joint optimization of Gaussian positions and appearance. It addresses the limitations of single-view optimization schemes, which often suffer from local minima and visual artifacts, by enforcing global coherence and local detail preservation simultaneously. Unlike methods that treat geometry and appearance independently, SVC integrates a Cross-View Consistency Loss with a geometric pruning mechanism to reduce redundancy while maintaining structural integrity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with parameters \{xa, \alpha, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{s}\} (location, opacity, rotation, scale), a set of training views with camera poses xp, and target RGB images. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters and rendered RGB images. Data Structures: Each Gaussian stores standard 3DGS parameters. SVC introduces additional learnable parameters for view-dependent color modeling. In the Spherical Voronoi variant, each Gaussian is equipped with additional parameters \{\tauk\}, \{sk\}, \{ck\}. Spherical Voronoi Sites: Each site k stores three floats for location (sk \in \mathbb{R}^3) and three floats for radiance (ck \in \mathbb{R}^3). Memory Footprint: The total learnable parameters per Gaussian for the view-direction parameterization is 48 floats (16 sites \times 3 floats for location + 16 sites \times 3 floats for radiance). The temperature \tauk is not stored but computed on the fly from the site norm. Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted combination of view gradient loss \mathcal{L}V and structure gradient loss \mathcal{L}S: \mathcal{L} = \lambda (\lambdaV \mathcal{L}V + \lambdaS \mathcal{L}S) where \lambda is a global scaling factor, and \lambdaV, \lambdaS are weights for the respective components. The structure component often includes a Cross-View Consistency Loss (L{CVC}) to ensure geometric consistency across different viewpoints. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Spherical Voronoi sites uniformly using Fibonacci sampling on the sphere S^2. For 3DGS, equip each Gaussian with the additional parameters \{\tauk\}, \{sk\}, \{ck\}. 2. Forward Pass (Rendering): For each Gaussian, evaluate the radiance f{SV}(\omega; \tau, s, c): S^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3 based on the view direction \omega. In the weighted variant, compute the unit direction \hat{s}k = sk / \|sk\| and implicit temperature \tauk = \|sk\| for each site. Render the image using standard alpha-blending of Gaussians. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the view-dependent loss \mathcal{L}V (e.g., L1 or SSIM between rendered and target images). Compute the structural loss \mathcal{L}S. This may involve a Cross-View Consistency Loss (L{CVC}) comparing features or depths from different views. Combine losses: \mathcal{L} = \lambda (\lambdaV \mathcal{L}V + \lambdaS \mathcal{L}S). 4. Backpropagation and Update: Compute gradients for all parameters, including Gaussian positions and the new view-dependent parameters. Update parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). 5. Cross-View Pruning (CVPM): Periodically, evaluate consistency between views. If the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) between views i and j is high (> 0.6), compute L{CVC}. Prune unexpected Gaussians based on geometric consistency criteria, such as depth discrepancies or distance thresholds (e.g., di(p) < 0.01 \land dj(p) < 0.5 \lor di(p) > 3\sigma). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def structureviewcolearning(gaussians, views, targetimages, lambdav, lambdas, lambdaglobal): """ Performs one step of Structure-View Co-learning. """ # 1. Forward pass: Render images renderedimages = [] for view in views: # Evaluate radiance using Spherical Voronoi if applicable # For each Gaussian, compute color based on view direction omega # fsv = sphericalvoronoiradiance(omega, sites, colors, temperatures) image = rendergaussians(gaussians, view.camera) renderedimages.append(image) # 2. Compute Losses # View-dependent loss (e.g., L1 or SSIM) lossv = 0 for rendered, target in zip(renderedimages, targetimages): lossv += l1loss(rendered, target) lossv /= len(views) # Structural loss (e.g., Cross-View Consistency) losss = crossviewconsistencyloss(gaussians, views) # Combined loss totalloss = lambdaglobal (lambdav lossv + lambdas losss) # 3. Backpropagation totalloss.backward() # 4. Optimization Step optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # 5. Pruning (optional, periodic) if step % pruneinterval == 0: prunegaussians(gaussians, views, threshold=0.6) return totalloss Parameters: \lambdaV, \lambdaS: Weights for view and structure losses. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Number of Spherical Voronoi sites: 8 sites per Gaussian for standard benchmarks, 128 for synthetic scenes, 1024 for real scenes. SSIM Threshold for pruning: 0.6. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The temperature \tauk is computed from the norm of the site vector, which may lead to numerical instability if the site vector is near zero. Boundaries: The Spherical Voronoi parameterization assumes the view direction is on the unit sphere S^2. Degenerate Input: If views are too similar, the consistency loss may not provide sufficient gradient for geometry updates. A method that replaces traditional spherical harmonics with a Spherical Voronoi partition of the sphere to model view-dependent color. It treats the sites' locations, radiance, and implicit temperatures as jointly learnable parameters. It is chosen when high-fidelity view-dependent effects (e.g., glossy reflections) are required, as it offers higher expressiveness than spherical harmonics. It uses 48 learnable parameters per Gaussian (16 sites \times 6 floats). Time Complexity: The rendering complexity is dominated by the Gaussian splatting process, which is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. The additional cost of evaluating the Spherical Voronoi function is proportional to the number of sites K per Gaussian, making it O(N \cdot K). Memory Complexity: The memory footprint increases by 48 floats per Gaussian for the Spherical Voronoi parameters. Performance: The Spherical Voronoi formulation yields consistent improvements over baselines, achieving higher PSNR than spherical harmonics, spherical Gaussians, and spherical bicubics on standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, DeepBlending, Tanks&Temples, NeRF-Synthetic). Strengths: Robust joint optimization of geometry and appearance; better handling of complex directional behaviors like reflections. Limitations: Increased memory usage per Gaussian; requires careful initialization of Voronoi sites. Structure-View Co-learning was introduced in the context of large-scale unbounded scene reconstruction to address the limitations of existing 3DGS methods that suffer from detail loss or lack global spatial awareness. The Spherical Voronoi parameterization was proposed to provide a more expressive representation for view-dependent color, building on the idea of differentiable partitions of the sphere. name: Resource Peak Management in Full Training
head: BoundedGS Image Supply, BoundedGS Structure Updates
body: This method manages memory peaks during the structure updates (density control) and image supply phases of 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It solves the problem of high GPU memory usage caused by concurrent old and new state layouts during densification and high-resolution image decoding. It sets itself apart from standard implementations by deferring layout rebuilding until after view caches are released and using bounded prefetch queues for image supply, thereby decoupling memory peaks from the Gaussian count and image resolution. The method consists of two primary subsystems: Structure Update Management and Image Supply Management. Inputs: List of Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, SH coefficients, opacity), optimizer states, statistics, and a set of training images (compressed). Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters, optimizer states, and statistics ready for the next training step, with bounded peak memory usage. 1. Gaussian State: Contains parameters, optimizer state, and statistics. Layout is rebuilt only once per density control cycle. 2. Prefetch Queue: A fixed-capacity queue holding decoded images. Capacity is bounded to limit residency. 3. Pinned Memory Buffer: Used for transferring leaf regions. Standard methods rebuild the Gaussian layout after every clone, split, parent removal, or pruning action, creating intermediate layouts with concurrent old and new state. BoundedGS defers this: 1. Candidate Grouping: Group candidates and accumulate repeated IDs before a single update. 2. Selection: Density control selects retained and new Gaussians based on thresholds. 3. Cache Release: Ensure view caches are released before rebuilding. 4. Final Mapping: Perform one final mapping to construct the new parameters, optimizer state, and statistics. 5. CPU-Assisted Upload: Hold the target layout on the host (CPU) memory. Release the old device (GPU) layout. Upload the target layout to the GPU. Note: This trades host memory and transfer time for reduced GPU overlap peaks. To manage the memory cost of high-resolution images: 1. Host Storage: Keep compressed images (e.g., JPEG) on the host CPU. 2. Prefetch Queue: Decode images through a fixed-capacity prefetch queue. 3. Overlap: Overlap CPU decoding work with GPU training. 4. Bounded Residency: Bound the number of decoded images in memory. 5. Leaf Transfer: Pack each leaf’s region in pinned memory. Transfer as uint8 on a separate CUDA stream. Convert to floating-point supervision when used. Release the memory after loss backward. Prefetch holds at most the current and next leaf. Decoded Image Memory Cost: If retaining every decoded uint8 image, the cost is: M{images} \approx 3 \sum{v} Pv \text{ bytes} Where v is the number of RGB images and Pv is the number of pixels per image. Prefetch Queue Capacity: Bounded to hold at most the current and next leaf. Image Format: Compressed (JPEG) on host, uint8 during transfer, float for supervision. Host Memory Pressure: The CPU-assisted path increases host RSS. In experiments, RSS rose from 6.30 GiB to 13.37 GiB. Transfer Overhead: Uploading the target layout from host to device adds training time (11.7% increase in one benchmark). Precision: Images are transferred as uint8 and converted to float later. Ensure conversion happens before loss computation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundedgstrainingstep(gaussians, optimizer, imagescompressed, config): """ One training step with resource peak management. """ # 1. Structure Update (Density Control) # Step 1: Group candidates and accumulate repeated IDs candidates = groupcandidates(gaussians) # Step 2: Density control selects retained and new Gaussians retainedids, newgaussians = densitycontrol(gaussians, candidates) # Step 3: Release view caches to free GPU memory releaseviewcaches() # Step 4: Final mapping on Host (CPU) # Hold target layout on host targetlayouthost = constructlayouthost(retainedids, newgaussians, optimizer, gaussians.stats) # Release old device layout releaseolddevicelayout(gaussians) # Upload target to GPU gaussians = uploadtodevice(targetlayouthost) # 2. Image Supply # Keep compressed images on host # Decode through fixed-capacity prefetch queue currentleaf = prefetchqueue.getcurrentleaf() nextleaf = prefetchqueue.peeknextleaf() # Transfer leaf region leafregionuint8 = packleafregion(currentleaf, pinnedmemory) leafregionfloat = transferandconvert(leafregionuint8, stream) # Compute loss and backward loss = computeloss(gaussians, leafregionfloat) loss.backward() # Release leaf memory after backward releaseleafmemory(leafregionfloat) # Update optimizer optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return gaussians Stores predecoded images on the host CPU to reduce GPU structure-update peaks during training. It uses CPU assistance for structure updates instead of repeated GPU rebuilding. This lowers the structure-update peak from 12.83 to 8.68 GiB (32.4% reduction), but raises RSS from 6.30 to 13.37 GiB and adds 11.7% training time on five 5K scenes. It exchanges transfer or decoding overhead for lower resource peaks compared to repeated GPU rebuilding. Memory Peaks: Structure-update peak: Reduced from 12.83 GiB to 8.68 GiB (32.4% reduction) compared to repeated GPU rebuilding. Host RSS: Increased from 6.30 GiB to 13.37 GiB. Rendering working set: Held near 1.76 GiB. Performance: Training time: Increased by 11.7% compared to repeated GPU rebuilding (33.95 min vs 30.39 min). Compared to host-resident predecoded images, bounded JPEG supply lowers RSS from 17.60 to 13.37 GiB (24.0% reduction) at a 5.5% training-time cost. Scaling: Larger Gaussian counts (e.g., 12M SH3 budget) increase the expected benefit of avoiding overlapping layouts. Higher resolution images (8K or 16K) increase the expected host-memory benefit of bounded JPEG supply. Strengths: Controls high-resolution working sets effectively. Reduces GPU memory peaks during structure updates. Limitations: Increases host memory usage. Adds training time due to CPU-GPU transfers and decoding overhead. When to Use: When GPU memory is the bottleneck during structure updates. When training on high-resolution images (5K and above). When Not to Use: When host memory is limited. When training time is critical and GPU memory is sufficient. Originated in the BoundedGS paper (2026) by the authors of "BoundedGS: Memory-Efficient High-Resolution Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting". The method addresses the memory peaks observed in full training of 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly during density control and image supply phases. It was tested on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples datasets. name: GauFRe
head: Gaussian Deformation Fields
body: GauFRe is a method for real-time dynamic novel view synthesis that represents dynamic scenes using deformable 3D Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of reconstructing non-rigid motion from monocular video by employing a forward-warping deformation field, which explicitly models the temporal evolution of scene geometry. Unlike backward-warping approaches common in NeRFs that require querying a canonical space, GauFRe predicts the deformed primitive system at a specific time directly, making it efficient for explicit primitive-based rendering. It distinguishes itself by decoupling static and dynamic regions into separate Gaussian sets and applying exponential/normalization constraints to scale and rotation parameters for stable optimization. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of monocular RGB images (video) of a dynamic scene. Optionally, a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud for initialization. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives representing the scene at any queried time t, allowing for novel view synthesis at arbitrary viewpoints and timestamps. Data Structures The scene is represented by two disjoint sets of Gaussian primitives: 1. Dynamic Set: Resides in a canonical space. Each primitive i is defined by: Position \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, factored into rotation Ri and scale si Scalar density \sigmai \in \mathbb{R} View-dependent color ci (represented by m-order spherical harmonics) 2. Static Set: A non-deforming set of Gaussians initialized around SfM-derived 3D points. The deformation is modeled by a time-conditioned Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) \mathcal{F}{DF}, which takes canonical position \mathbf{x}i and time t as input and outputs delta values for position, rotation, and scale. Formulas 1. Covariance Factorization: To ensure positive semi-definiteness, the covariance matrix is factored as: \Sigmai = Ri \text{Exp}(si) \text{Exp}(si)^T Ri^T where Ri is derived from a unit-length quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4, and \text{Exp}(si) is a diagonal matrix with entries e^{s{i,j}}. 2. Forward-Warping Deformation: The MLP predicts deltas \Delta \mathbf{x}, \Delta q, \Delta s. The deformed attributes at time t are computed as: Position: \mathbf{x}i(t) = \mathbf{x}i + \Delta \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{x}i, t) Rotation: qi(t) = \text{Normalize}(qi + \Delta q(\mathbf{x}i, t)) Scale: si(t) = \text{Exp}(si + \Delta s(\mathbf{x}i, t)) The exponential operation is applied to the scale delta to ensure positive scales, and normalization is applied to the rotation delta to maintain unit quaternions. 3. Screen-Space Projection: For a camera with view transformation V and projection matrix K, the 2D mean and covariance are: \mathbf{u}i = K V \mathbf{x}i(t) \Sigma'i = J V \Sigmai(t) V^T J^T where J is the Jacobian of the projection matrix K evaluated at the transformed point. Parameters Resolution: Experiments reported at 480x270. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090. Training Time: Approximately 20 minutes for real-world scenes. Pseudocode The following pseudocode outlines the optimization loop and rendering process. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Convert unit quaternion [w, x, y, z] to 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2)] ]) def normalizequaternion(q): """Ensure quaternion remains a unit vector.""" return q / np.linalg.norm(q) def computecovariance(q, s): """Factorize rotation and scale into covariance matrix.""" R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) Sdiag = np.diag(np.exp(s)) return R @ Sdiag @ Sdiag.T @ R.T def projecttoscreen(x, V, K): """Compute 2D mean and covariance from 3D position and camera matrices.""" uhomogeneous = K @ V @ x u2d = uhomogeneous[:2] / uhomogeneous[2] # Jacobian J of perspective projection K evaluated at transformed point z = uhomogeneous[2] J = np.array([[1.0/z, 0.0, -u2d[0]/(z2)], [0.0, 1.0/z, -u2d[1]/(z2)]]) return u2d, J def ellipticalweightedaveragesplatting(projectedgaussians, resolution): """Rasterize 2D Gaussians using elliptical weighted average splatting.""" # Standard rasterization loop over screen pixels and Gaussians # (Implementation details omitted; follows standard 3DGS splatting) pass def initializegaussians(imagesequence, usesfm=True): """Initialize dynamic and static Gaussian sets.""" if usesfm: staticpositions = getsfmpoints() # Standard SfM output staticgaussians = [{'position': p, 'quaternion': np.array([1,0,0,0]), 'scale': np.zeros(3), 'density': 1.0, 'color': np.zeros(3)} for p in staticpositions] else: staticgaussians = [] dynamicpositions = np.random.rand(1000, 3) # Random initialization fallback dynamicgaussians = [{'position': p, 'quaternion': np.array([1,0,0,0]), 'scale': np.zeros(3), 'density': 1.0, 'color': np.zeros(3)} for p in dynamicpositions] dfmlp = lambda x, t: (np.random.rand(3), np.random.rand(4), np.random.rand(3)) # Placeholder for trained MLP return dynamicgaussians, staticgaussians, dfmlp def computedeformedattributes(g, dfmlp, timet): """Apply forward-warping deformation to a single dynamic Gaussian.""" x = g['position'] q = g['quaternion'] s = g['scale'] deltax, deltaq, deltas = dfmlp(x, timet) newx = x + deltax newq = normalizequaternion(q + deltaq) news = s + deltas Sigma = computecovariance(newq, news) return {'position': newx, 'covariance': Sigma, 'density': g['density'], 'color': g['color']} def renderframe(dynamicgaussians, staticgaussians, dfmlp, V, K, timet, resolution): """Render a single frame at time t.""" deformeddynamic = [computedeformedattributes(g, dfmlp, timet) for g in dynamicgaussians] allgaussians = deformeddynamic + staticgaussians projectedgaussians = [] for g in allgaussians: u, J = projecttoscreen(g['position'], V, K) Sigmaprime = J @ V @ g['covariance'] @ V.T @ J.T projectedgaussians.append({'mean': u, 'covariance': Sigmaprime, 'density': g['density'], 'color': g['color']}) return ellipticalweightedaveragesplatting(projectedgaussians, resolution) def optimize(imagesequence, dynamicgaussians, staticgaussians, dfmlp, maxepochs=1000, pruneinterval=100): """End-to-end optimization loop with self-supervised loss.""" optimizerstate = {'lr': 0.001, 'params': dynamicgaussians + staticgaussians + [dfmlp]} # Adam optimizer initialization for epoch in range(maxepochs): for frameidx, (image, V, K, timet, resolution) in enumerate(imagesequence): renderedimage = renderframe(dynamicgaussians, staticgaussians, dfmlp, V, K, timet, resolution) loss = np.mean((renderedimage - image)2) # Self-supervised rendering loss # Backpropagate and step (standard Adam update rule) if epoch % pruneinterval == 0: # Periodic cloning, splitting, and pruning dynamicgaussians = [g for g in dynamicgaussians if g['density'] > 0.01] staticgaussians = [g for g in staticgaussians if g['density'] > 0.01] return dynamicgaussians, staticgaussians, dfmlp Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The exponential activation on scale deltas is critical; without it, negative scales could arise, leading to invalid covariance matrices. Boundaries: The static component is initialized using SfM points. If SfM fails or is sparse, the static regions may be poorly represented. Degenerate Input: Random initialization of the dynamic point cloud is used if SfM is not available, which may lead to slower convergence or local minima. A variant that improves convergence and model capacity by learning scale residuals rather than absolute scales. It initializes the scale vector \mathbf{s}{init} using the average distance of K nearest neighbors via the KNN algorithm. A decoder \mathcal{D}{cov} predicts the scale residual \Delta \mathbf{s} from volume latent features \mathbf{f}i. The final scale is computed as \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s}{init} + \Delta \mathbf{s}. This allows independent optimization of scaling (via vector \mathbf{s}) and rotation (via quaternion \mathbf{q}). Time Complexity: Optimization is significantly faster than NeRF-based methods due to the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting. Training takes approximately 20 minutes for real-world scenes. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N. The method maintains two sets of Gaussians (dynamic and static), potentially increasing memory usage compared to single-set methods, but the static set avoids deformation field queries. Measured Performance: Achieves 96 FPS real-time rendering on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU at 480x270 resolution. Quality: On the D-NeRF dataset, GauFRe achieves a PSNR of 34.80, SSIM of 0.985, and LPIPS of 0.028. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; explicit modeling of non-rigid transformations via forward-warping; efficient handling of static regions via a separate component. Limitations: Requires a deformation field MLP, which adds complexity to the optimization; performance depends on the quality of the initial point cloud (SfM or random). When to use: Real-time dynamic novel view synthesis from monocular video where high efficiency is required. When not to use: Static scene reconstruction (use standard 3DGS); scenes with extremely complex non-rigid motion that cannot be captured by a forward-warping field. GauFRe (Gaussian Deformation Fields) was proposed to address the challenges of real-time dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular video. Traditional NeRF-based methods use backward-warping deformation fields, which are inefficient for explicit primitive-based systems like 3D Gaussian Splatting because they require querying a canonical space for every ray sample. GauFRe introduces a forward-warping deformation field that predicts the deformed primitive system at a given time, aligning with the explicit nature of Gaussians. It also incorporates a GS-specific static component to handle static regions separately, improving reconstruction quality in dynamic scenes. The method builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md] and optimizes end-to-end with a self-supervised rendering loss. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization
head: Original 3DGS Loss
body: This method optimizes a set of 3D Gaussian primitives by rendering them to 2D images and comparing the result against ground truth views using a distortion loss, while dynamically modulating the Gaussian count via adaptive densification. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly linking the optimization objective (loss scale) to the structural evolution of the scene representation, where gradient magnitudes drive both parameter updates and the addition/removal of primitives. Inputs and Outputs Input: A collection of N 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gi is defined by position \mathbf{p}i, rotation qi, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients ci [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. A set of training views (camera poses and intrinsics) and corresponding ground truth images \mathbf{x}. Output: Optimized Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}^ and the final scene representation. Data Structures The Gaussian parameters are stored in contiguous arrays or structures of arrays (SoA) for efficient GPU access: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center coordinates. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Unit quaternion for rotation. \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale factors (typically exponentiated during storage to ensure positivity). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. ci: Spherical harmonic coefficients (e.g., SH0, SH1, \dots). Numbered Steps 1. Random Camera Selection: Select a single training view (camera pose and intrinsics) randomly from the dataset. This provides the stochastic flavor of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). 2. Differentiable Rendering: Project each 3D Gaussian Gi to 2D screen space using the camera projection matrix and the Gaussian's covariance \Sigmai [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. Sort the projected Gaussians by depth (z-buffer) [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. Alpha-blend the Gaussians in depth order to produce the rendered image \hat{\mathbf{x}} [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the distortion loss D(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{x}}) between the ground truth image \mathbf{x} and the rendered image \hat{\mathbf{x}}. The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = \gamma \, D(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{x}}) where \gamma is a scalar weighting factor. Common choices for D include L1 loss, Structural Similarity (SSIM), or perceptual loss (LPIPS). 4. Backpropagation: Propagate the pixel error backward through the alpha compositing and 2D projection operations to compute gradients for every parameter of every Gaussian Gi that contributed to the rendered pixels. This uses the chain rule. 5. Parameter Update: Update the Gaussian parameters using the Adam optimizer [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. Adam maintains running averages of gradients and squared gradients to adapt per-parameter step sizes. Different parameter types (e.g., position vs. opacity) use different base learning rates. 6. Adaptive Densification and Pruning: Densification: Analyze the gradient magnitudes of the position parameters \mathbf{p}i for each Gaussian. If the gradient magnitude exceeds a threshold, split the Gaussian into two new primitives (copying parameters and adjusting scales/opacities). Pruning: Remove Gaussians with opacity \alphai below a specified threshold. These decisions are driven by the gradients from the distortion loss, meaning the optimization objective influences the evolution of the Gaussian count. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn gamma = 1.0 # Scalar weighting factor for distortion loss optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(gaussianparams, lr=baselr) # Adam optimizer def render(gaussians, camera): """ Differentiable renderer. Projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, sorts by depth, and alpha-blends. Returns rendered image xhat and intermediate data for backprop. """ # 1. Project Gaussians to 2D screen space # 2. Sort by depth # 3. Alpha blend in depth order # Returns: xhat, rendercontext pass def computeloss(xhat, xgt, gamma): """ Computes distortion loss D(x, xhat) scaled by gamma. D can be L1, SSIM, or LPIPS. """ distortion = L1Loss(xhat, xgt) # Example: L1 loss return gamma distortion def updategaussians(gaussians, rendercontext, densificationthreshold, pruningthreshold): """ Adaptive densification and pruning based on gradients. """ # 1. Compute gradient magnitudes for positions from rendercontext posgradmags = getpositiongradientmagnitude(rendercontext) # 2. Densification: Split Gaussians with high gradient magnitude for i in range(len(gaussians)): if posgradmags[i] > densificationthreshold: splitgaussian(gaussians, i) # 3. Pruning: Remove Gaussians with low opacity for i in range(len(gaussians) - 1, -1, -1): if gaussians[i].opacity < pruningthreshold: removegaussian(gaussians, i) for step in range(numsteps): # 1. Randomly select a camera view camera = randomtrainingview() xgt = getgroundtruthimage(camera) # 2. Render xhat, rendercontext = render(gaussians, camera) # 3. Compute Loss loss = computeloss(xhat, xgt, gamma) # 4. Backpropagate loss.backward() # 5. Update Parameters with Adam optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # 6. Adaptive Densification/Pruning updategaussians(gaussians, rendercontext, densificationthreshold, pruningthreshold) Parameters \gamma: Scalar weighting factor for the distortion loss. It varies across datasets to align Gaussian counts across methods, as adaptive densification relies on gradient magnitude. Optimizer: Adam, which keeps a running sense of each parameter's recent gradients and adapts a per-parameter step size. Base Learning Rates: Different for position, rotation, scale, opacity, and SH coefficients. Densification Threshold: Gradient magnitude threshold for splitting Gaussians. Pruning Threshold: Opacity threshold for removing Gaussians. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Gradient magnitudes for position updates must be computed accurately to avoid over-splitting or under-splitting. Boundaries: Pruning must handle the case where all Gaussians are removed (though unlikely with proper initialization). Degenerate Input: If the initial Gaussian count is too low, densification may not recover the scene structure quickly enough. GS-SLAM is a Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) method that simultaneously estimates camera poses and reconstructs 3D scenes using 3D Gaussians. It distinguishes itself from other radiance-field SLAM approaches by employing an adaptive 3D Gaussian expanding strategy to dynamically add new Gaussians and delete unreliable ones based on captured depth and rendered opacity. SplaTAM is an RGB-D Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) method that represents the world as a collection of 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of online tracking and mapping by using depth and photometric Iterative Closest Point (ICP) for pose estimation and densification. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Gaussian-SLAM and Gaussian Splatting SLAM by its specific use of view-independent colors and a densification mask to prevent duplicate Gaussian creation. Gaussian-SLAM is a keyframe-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) method that utilizes 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense scene representation. It solves the problem of real-time, photorealistic mapping and localization by fusing sub-maps derived from keyframes, addressing the drift and consistency issues common in online streaming approaches. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SplaTAM (which uses online densification and depth/photometric ICP) and MonoGS (which is monocular) by employing a sub-map fusion strategy to maintain global consistency. Gaussian Splatting SLAM is a simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) method that reconstructs a scene as a collection of 3D Gaussians while estimating camera poses, building on 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization. It differs from siblings like SplaTAM and Gaussian-SLAM by explicitly minimizing a combined photometric and geometric residual for both tracking and mapping, and by applying isotropic scale regularization to stabilize localization. Differentiable Pose Estimation optimizes camera poses by backpropagating photometric loss gradients through a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renderer. It solves the problem of recovering accurate camera extrinsics when initial poses are noisy or unknown, specifically enabling applications like motion deblurring where camera motion during exposure must be modeled. It distinguishes itself from SLAM-based siblings like SplaTAM and Gaussian-SLAM by focusing on batch optimization of poses for a static scene (or trajectory) rather than incremental online tracking, often leveraging the equivalence between camera transformation and Gaussian position transformation to simplify gradient computation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P) per step, where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels, due to projection and blending [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. The number of Gaussians N grows during training due to densification. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian parameters [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales to large scenes due to the efficiency of the splatting renderer, but the number of Gaussians can become very large, requiring compression or pruning. Strengths: Differentiable rendering allows for end-to-end optimization of geometry and appearance. Adaptive densification allows the representation to adapt to scene complexity. Limitations: The number of Gaussians is not fixed and can grow uncontrollably without proper pruning. The optimization is sensitive to the initial Gaussian distribution and hyperparameters like \gamma. When to use: When high-fidelity, photorealistic reconstruction is required and computational resources allow for a large number of primitives. When not to use: When memory or rendering speed is strictly constrained and a compact representation is needed. The method originates from the 3D Gaussian Splatting paper [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md], which introduced the use of 3D Gaussians as a scene representation for real-time novel view synthesis. The optimization procedure leverages the differentiability of the splatting renderer to optimize Gaussian parameters using standard gradient-based optimizers like Adam [3761-3d-gaussian-splatting-training.md]. The adaptive densification strategy was introduced to address the limitation of fixed Gaussian counts, allowing the representation to evolve during training. name: GS-SLAM
body: GS-SLAM is a Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) method that simultaneously estimates camera poses and reconstructs 3D scenes using 3D Gaussians. It distinguishes itself from other radiance-field SLAM approaches by employing an adaptive 3D Gaussian expanding strategy to dynamically add new Gaussians and delete unreliable ones based on captured depth and rendered opacity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: RGB-D image frames (color and depth), initial camera poses, and an initial set of 3D Gaussians. Outputs: Optimized camera poses, updated 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), and a dense 3D scene representation. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Each Gaussian i is defined by a mean position \mui, a covariance matrix \Sigmai (parameterized by rotation Ri and scale Si), an opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{i,lm} for view-dependent color. Depth Buffer: Captured depth values from the RGB-D sensor for each pixel. Opacity Buffer: Rendered opacity values for each pixel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the scene with a sparse set of 3D Gaussians, typically derived from initial pose estimates or feature points. 2. Rendering: For each incoming RGB-D frame, render the current set of 3D Gaussians to produce predicted color and opacity images using differentiable volume rendering. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss between the rendered color and the observed RGB image. Compute a depth loss between the rendered depth (or expected depth from Gaussians) and the captured depth. 4. Adaptive Expanding (Adding Gaussians): Identify regions where the rendered opacity is low or the depth error is high, indicating missing geometry. Add new 3D Gaussians in these regions. The position of new Gaussians can be sampled from the depth map or existing Gaussian distributions. 5. Pruning (Deleting Gaussians): Evaluate the reliability of existing Gaussians. Delete Gaussians that are deemed unreliable. Criteria include low opacity and/or high discrepancy with captured depth. 6. Optimization: Update the parameters of all active Gaussians (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) and the camera pose using stochastic gradient descent to minimize the combined loss. 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-6 for subsequent frames. Formulas: Photometric Loss: L{rgb} = ||I{rendered} - I{observed}||1. Depth Loss: L{depth} = ||D{rendered} - D{observed}||1. Total Loss: L = L{rgb} + \lambda L{depth}, where \lambda is a weighting factor. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for depth loss. Not given in the sources. Opacity threshold for pruning: Not given in the sources. Depth error threshold for adding Gaussians: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Densification: Without careful management, new Gaussians may be added in regions already well-represented. GS-SLAM avoids this by using captured depths and rendered opacity to guide expansion. Unreliable Gaussians: Gaussians with low opacity or high depth error should be removed to maintain efficiency and accuracy. Initialization: Poor initial poses or sparse initial Gaussians can lead to convergence issues. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gsslamloop(frames, initialgaussians, initialposes): gaussians = initialgaussians poses = initialposes for frame in frames: rgb = frame.rgb depth = frame.depth # Render current scene renderedrgb, renderedopacity, rendereddepth = render(gaussians, poses[-1]) # Compute losses lossrgb = l1loss(renderedrgb, rgb) lossdepth = l1loss(rendereddepth, depth) loss = lossrgb + lambdadepth lossdepth # Backpropagate to update Gaussians and Pose updategaussiansandpose(gaussians, poses, loss) # Adaptive Expanding # Identify regions with low opacity or high depth error lowopacitymask = renderedopacity < opacitythreshold highdeptherrormask = abs(rendereddepth - depth) > deptherrorthreshold expandmask = lowopacitymask | highdeptherrormask # Add new Gaussians in expanded regions newgaussians = addgaussians(gaussians, poses[-1], depth, expandmask) gaussians = gaussians + newgaussians # Prune unreliable Gaussians # Remove Gaussians with low opacity or high depth error gaussians = prunegaussians(gaussians, renderedopacity, depth) poses.append(poses[-1]) # Update pose estimate return gaussians, poses The pseudocode assumes standard differentiable rendering and optimization routines. Specific thresholds and addition/pruning heuristics are not detailed in the sources and would require implementation-specific tuning. Uses view-independent colors and a densification mask to avoid duplicate densification. Uses an extra scale regularization loss to encourage isotropic Gaussians. Uses an extra scale regularization loss to encourage isotropic Gaussians. Focuses on the pose estimation component within the SLAM framework. Performance: On the Replica dataset, GS-SLAM achieves a PSNR of 31.56, SSIM of 0.97, and LPIPS of 0.094. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Adaptive strategy allows for dynamic scene reconstruction and handling of unseen areas. Limitations: Performance is lower than some other 3DGS SLAM methods like GaussianSplattingSLAM (PSNR 38.90) on the Replica dataset. GS-SLAM was proposed in the context of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting for SLAM applications. It addresses the limitations of implicit representation-based methods by using explicit 3D Gaussians, which can be more efficiently optimized and rendered. head: SplaTAM System
body: SplaTAM is an RGB-D Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) method that represents the world as a collection of 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of online tracking and mapping by using depth and photometric Iterative Closest Point (ICP) for pose estimation and densification. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Gaussian-SLAM and Gaussian Splatting SLAM by its specific use of view-independent colors and a densification mask to prevent duplicate Gaussian creation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: RGB-D image frames. Outputs: Camera trajectory and 3D Gaussian map. Data Structures: Representation: 3D Gaussians. Densification Mask: Binary mask indicating regions in the new frame that require new Gaussians based on the discrepancy between current Gaussians and captured depth. Steps: 1. Tracking: Estimate the current camera pose using depth and photometric ICP against the existing Gaussian map. 2. Rendering: Render the current frame from the estimated pose using differentiable Gaussian rasterization to obtain rendered depth and color. 3. Densification Decision: Compute a densification mask by comparing the rendered depth/opacity with the captured depth of the new frame. 4. Densification: Add new Gaussians in regions indicated by the mask where current Gaussians do not adequately cover the captured depth. 5. Optimization: Optimize Gaussian parameters and camera pose using photometric and depth losses. Formulas: Photometric and depth loss formulations: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Depth loss weight (\lambda): Not given in the sources. Densification threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Densification: SplaTAM avoids this by using view-independent colors and a specific densification mask. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatamstep(rgbframe, depthframe, gaussianmap, camerapose): # 1. Tracking: Estimate pose using depth and photometric ICP against existing Gaussians # Standard ICP aligns rendered depth to captured depth; photometric aligns colors newcamerapose = optimizeposeicp(gaussianmap, rgbframe, depthframe, camerapose) # 2. Rendering: Alpha-blend projected Gaussians to obtain rendered frame rendereddepth, renderedcolor = alphablendgaussians(gaussianmap, newcamerapose) # 3. Densification Decision: Compute mask based on depth/opacity discrepancy densificationmask = computedepthdiscrepancymask(rendereddepth, depthframe, gaussianmap) # 4. Densification: Spawn new Gaussians at masked pixel locations using view-independent colors gaussianmap = spawngaussians(gaussianmap, rgbframe, depthframe, densificationmask) # 5. Optimization: Update Gaussian parameters and pose via gradient descent gaussianmap, newcamerapose = gradientdescentstep(gaussianmap, newcamerapose, rgbframe, depthframe) return gaussianmap, newcamerapose Keyframe-based with sub-map fusion. Monocular RGB-only with online optimization. Uses differentiable rendering for pose tracking. Time Complexity: Online, real-time capable. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of Gaussians. Measured Performance: On the Replica dataset, SplaTAM achieves PSNR 34.11, SSIM 0.97, and LPIPS 0.10. Strengths: Online mapping, real-time performance, high-quality reconstruction. Limitations: Requires RGB-D input. SplaTAM was introduced as an RGB-D SLAM method that maps the world as 3D Gaussians. It uses depth and photometric ICP to track and densify online. The method is cited in "Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting". head: Yugay et al. 2024 SLAM
body: Gaussian-SLAM is a keyframe-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) method that utilizes 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense scene representation. It solves the problem of real-time, photorealistic mapping and localization by fusing sub-maps derived from keyframes, addressing the drift and consistency issues common in online streaming approaches. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SplaTAM (which uses online densification and depth/photometric ICP) and MonoGS (which is monocular) by employing a sub-map fusion strategy to maintain global consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: RGB image sequences, camera intrinsics, and initial pose estimates. Outputs: A dense 3D Gaussian map, camera poses, and rendered photorealistic images. Data Structures: The method maintains a global map composed of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian is defined by: Mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (parameterized by rotation R \in SO(3) and scale S \in \mathbb{R}^3) Opacity \alpha \in [0, 1] Spherical harmonics coefficients for color c Steps: 1. Keyframe Selection: Identify keyframes from the input stream based on motion or coverage criteria to form sub-maps. 2. Sub-map Optimization: Optimize the Gaussians within each sub-map independently to minimize rendering loss against the corresponding keyframe images. 3. Sub-map Fusion: Align and fuse the optimized sub-maps into a global map. This involves estimating the relative poses between sub-maps and merging overlapping Gaussian representations. 4. Scale Regularization: Apply an extra scale regularization loss on the scale of Gaussians to encourage isotropic shapes, stabilizing localization and mapping. 5. Pose Estimation: Update camera poses by minimizing the photometric reprojection error between the rendered image and the observed image. Formulas: The total loss function L includes the rendering loss L{render} and the scale regularization loss L{scale}: L = L{render} + \lambda L{scale} Where L{scale} penalizes deviations from isotropic scales, encouraging \sigmax \approx \sigmay \approx \sigmaz. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for scale regularization. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: Poor lighting or textureless regions may lead to ambiguous pose estimates. Precision: Floating-point precision in covariance matrix decomposition can affect stability during optimization. A monocular RGB-only SLAM method with online optimization using Gaussian Splatting. It differs from Gaussian-SLAM by not relying on keyframe-based sub-map fusion, instead optimizing the map continuously online. It is chosen when depth sensors are unavailable and real-time online mapping is preferred over batch-like sub-map fusion. A hybrid SLAM system combining a voxel-based neural implicit surface representation with an octree structure for dynamic scene expansion. It encodes and optimizes each scene voxel implicitly, supporting incremental mapping without prior environment knowledge and leveraging a multi-process framework for heightened speed. It demonstrates improved accuracy and completeness compared to prior methods. An end-to-end simultaneous localization and mapping approach that produces dense, photorealistic maps while tracking camera pose, replacing sparse classical SLAM outputs. The pipeline involves: 1. Tracking the current frame against the existing map. 2. Updating the map with new views by inserting new Gaussians where coverage is poor and refining existing ones. 3. Optional loop closure to detect revisited locations and correct drift. 4. Continuously rendering the photorealistic map. It is dense and photorealistic, supporting relighting and rendering downstream, but requires heavier compute and is less mature for real-time on edge hardware compared to classical SLAM. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the Replica dataset, Gaussian-SLAM achieves a PSNR of 37.50, SSIM of 0.96, and LPIPS of 0.07. Strengths: Provides dense, photorealistic maps and supports downstream rendering tasks. The sub-map fusion approach helps maintain global consistency. Limitations: Heavier compute requirements compared to classical SLAM. Less mature for real-time deployment on edge hardware. When to Use: When photorealistic dense mapping is required and computational resources are sufficient. When Not to Use: When real-time performance on resource-constrained devices is critical. Gaussian-SLAM was introduced by Yugay et al. in 2024. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting, leveraging its differentiable rendering capabilities for SLAM tasks. The method represents a shift from sparse classical SLAM outputs to dense, neural-renderable maps, addressing the limitations of earlier NeRF-based SLAM systems in terms of editing and real-time performance. name: Gaussian Splatting SLAM
head: Gaussian Splatting SLAM Tracking and Mapping Optimization, GaussianSplattingSLAM, Monocular Gaussian SLAM, RGB-D SLAM with Gaussian Splatting
body: Gaussian Splatting SLAM is a simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) method that reconstructs a scene as a collection of 3D Gaussians while estimating camera poses, building on 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization. It differs from siblings like SplaTAM and Gaussian-SLAM by explicitly minimizing a combined photometric and geometric residual for both tracking and mapping, and by applying isotropic scale regularization to stabilize localization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current camera pose T{CW}, current Gaussian set \mathcal{G}, incoming RGB-D frame (color image I, depth map D). Outputs: Updated camera pose T{CW}, updated Gaussian parameters (positions, scales, colors, opacities). Data Structures: Gaussians (\mathcal{G}): Each Gaussian g has position \boldsymbol{\mu}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}, color \mathbf{c}, opacity \alpha. Keyframes (\mathcal{W}): A set of selected keyframes used for mapping. Steps: 1. Tracking: Estimate the current camera pose T{CW} by minimizing the tracking loss. Perform up to 100 iterations per frame. Terminate iterations early if the magnitude of the pose update becomes less than 10^{-4}. For monocular settings, increase the learning rate of the Gaussian positions \boldsymbol{\mu}W by a factor of 10. For RGB-D experiments, use standard learning rates (rotation: 0.003, translation: 0.001). 2. Mapping: Update the Gaussian parameters and keyframe poses. Perform 150 iterations for the single-process implementation. Minimize the mapping loss over all Gaussians \mathcal{G} and keyframes k \in \mathcal{W}. 3. Keyframing: Select new keyframes based on Gaussian covisibility. Calculate the Intersection of Union (IOU) and Overlap Coefficient (OC) between current keyframe i and candidate j. IOU{cov}(i, j) = \frac{|Gi^v \cap Gj^v|}{|Gi^v \cup Gj^v|}. OC{cov}(i, j) = \frac{|\mathcal{G}i \cap \mathcal{G}j|}{\min(|\mathcal{G}i^v|, |\mathcal{G}j^v|)}. Here, Gi^v denotes the set of Gaussians visible in keyframe i. Formulas: Tracking Loss: \min{T{CW} \in SE(3)} \lambda{pho} E{pho} + (1 - \lambda{pho}) E{geo}, where E{pho} is the photometric residual and E{geo} is the geometric residual. Mapping Loss: \min{\mathcal{G}, k \in \mathcal{W}} \sum{k \in \mathcal{W}} (\lambda{pho} E{pho}^k + (1 - \lambda{pho}) E{geo}^k) + \lambda{iso} E{iso}, where E{iso} is the isotropic regularization term. Parameters: Photometric loss weight \lambda{pho} = 0.9 for all RGB-D experiments. Isotropic regularization weight \lambda{iso} = 10 for both monocular and RGB-D experiments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular tracking requires higher learning rates for positions to stabilize convergence. Isotropic scale regularization is critical for stabilizing localization and mapping. Performance: On the Replica dataset, GaussianSplattingSLAM achieves PSNR 38.90, SSIM 0.99, and LPIPS 0.07. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High reconstruction quality and stable localization via isotropic regularization. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rates for monocular settings. Gaussian Splatting SLAM was introduced in the paper "Gaussian Splatting SLAM" (arXiv:2312.06741). It extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to SLAM by integrating tracking and mapping modules that optimize both camera poses and Gaussian parameters simultaneously. name: Differentiable Pose Estimation
head: Pose Estimation via 3DGS Gradients
body: Differentiable Pose Estimation optimizes camera poses by backpropagating photometric loss gradients through a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renderer. It solves the problem of recovering accurate camera extrinsics when initial poses are noisy or unknown, specifically enabling applications like motion deblurring where camera motion during exposure must be modeled. It distinguishes itself from SLAM-based siblings like SplaTAM and Gaussian-SLAM by focusing on batch optimization of poses for a static scene or trajectory rather than incremental online tracking, often leveraging the equivalence between camera transformation and Gaussian position transformation to simplify gradient computation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N images, initial camera poses Ti (often initialized via COLMAP), initial 3D Gaussian parameters (positions mi, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, and spherical harmonic color coefficients ci), and camera intrinsics K. Outputs: Optimized camera poses Ti or a global transformation \hat{T}. Data Structures: Camera Pose: Represented as a 4x4 transformation matrix T or a 6-DOF vector. In the Deblur-GS variant, poses are parameterized as control points of a Bézier curve trajectory. 3D Gaussians: Defined by position mi, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color ci. Loss Function: The total loss L combines L1 and D-SSIM terms: L = \lambda L1 + (1 - \lambda) L{D-SSIM} Typical value: \lambda = 0.2. Gradient Derivation: The gradient of the loss with respect to the camera pose T is derived by splitting the chain rule into three components: color, covariance, and position: \frac{\partial L}{\partial T} = \sum{i \in N} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{C}} \left( \frac{\partial \hat{C}}{\partial ci} \frac{\partial ci}{\partial T} + \frac{\partial \hat{C}}{\partial \alphai} \frac{\partial \alphai}{\partial \Sigma'i} \frac{\partial \Sigma'i}{\partial T} + \frac{\partial \hat{C}}{\partial \alphai} \frac{\partial \alphai}{\partial m'i} \frac{\partial m'i}{\partial T} \right) Where \hat{C} is the rendered color, ci is the Gaussian color, \alphai is opacity, \Sigma'i is the projected 2D covariance, and m'i is the projected 2D position. Simplifications and Pitfalls: 1. Color Term Elimination: The term \frac{\partial ci}{\partial T} is eliminated. The assumption is that during short optimization steps, the view-dependent color encoded in spherical harmonics remains effectively unchanged. 2. Covariance Term Ignorance: The term involving \frac{\partial \Sigma'i}{\partial T} is ignored. If Gaussians form elongated ellipsoids, this term becomes large and causes instability. Ignoring it enhances robustness. 3. Position Term and Pose-Position Equivalence: The remaining term involves \frac{\partial m'i}{\partial T}. The method exploits the equivalence: K(T \hat{T})mi = K T (\hat{T} mi) Where \hat{T} is an external transformation applied to the pose T, which is mathematically equivalent to applying \hat{T} to the Gaussian position mi. Instead of differentiating T directly, the method optimizes a global transformation \hat{T} applied to all Gaussian positions mi. The gradient is computed as: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{T}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{m}} \frac{\partial \hat{m}}{\partial \hat{T}} The differentiable renderer provides \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{m}}, and automatic differentiation handles \frac{\partial \hat{m}}{\partial \hat{T}}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize 3D Gaussians and camera poses (e.g., via COLMAP). 2. For each training iteration: a. Select a camera view or trajectory segment. b. Forward pass: Render the image using the current Gaussian parameters and camera pose/transformation. c. Compute Loss L against the target image. d. Backward pass: i. Compute \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{m}} from the renderer's output. ii. Compute \frac{\partial \hat{m}}{\partial \hat{T}} using automatic differentiation. iii. Combine to get \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{T}}. e. Update parameters using an Adam optimizer. 3. Repeat until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizepose(gaussians, cameraposes, images, intrinsics, numiterations, lambdal1=0.2, scenelr=1e-3, poselr=1e-3, decaystart=50000, decayend=1e-5): sceneparams = gaussians.parameters() poseparams = cameraposes.parameters() for i in range(numiterations): viewidx = i % len(images) targetimage = images[viewidx] T = cameraposes[viewidx] # Forward pass: rasterize Gaussians with current pose renderedimage = rasterizeforward(gaussians, T, intrinsics) # Compute photometric loss explicitly l1term = sum(abs(renderedimage - targetimage)) / renderedimage.numel() ssimterm = computessim(renderedimage, targetimage) loss = lambdal1 l1term + (1 - lambdal1) ssimterm # Backward pass through differentiable renderer loss.backward() # Update scene parameters with fixed learning rate for p in sceneparams: if p.grad is not None: p.data -= scenelr p.grad # Update pose parameters with exponential decay progress = max(0, i - decaystart) / (numiterations - decaystart) currentposelr = poselr (decayend / poselr) progress for p in poseparams: if p.grad is not None: p.data -= currentposelr p.grad # Zero gradients for next iteration for p in sceneparams: if p.grad is not None: p.grad.zero() for p in poseparams: if p.grad is not None: p.grad.zero() A specific implementation of differentiable pose estimation designed for motion-blurred images. It extends the differentiable Gaussian splatting rasterizer to support depth, pose, and cumulative opacity for both forward and backward propagation. It uses two separate Adam optimizers for Gaussian scene parameters and camera pose parameters. The pose learning rate exponentially decays from 1 \times 10^{-3} to 1 \times 10^{-5}. Camera motion is modeled using 7th-order Bézier interpolation with 31 sampled points on the trajectory. Training runs for 90K iterations on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. A post-processing step used in pose-free reconstruction settings where ground-truth poses are unavailable. Since multiple 3D scenes and camera configurations can explain the same unposed inputs, the reconstructed scene may not align with the ground-truth evaluation frame. To resolve this, the reconstructed 3D Gaussians are frozen, and each target camera pose is optimized for 200 iterations using an L2 loss. This alignment is not used if ground-truth poses are available. A method to reduce inconsistency between multi-cameras and ameliorate error introduced in SLAM algorithms for static background scenes in self-driving data, where standard SfM fails due to fewer view overlaps. It implicitly learns a pair of refinement offsets \Delta P = (\Delta R, \Delta T) for each original camera pose P = [R, T], where R \in SO(3) and T \in \mathbb{R}^3. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N and the rasterization cost. Each iteration requires a forward render and backward pass. Deblur-GS uses 90K iterations. Memory Complexity: Stores Gaussian parameters and gradients for both scene and pose. The extension to support depth and cumulative opacity increases memory overhead slightly. Strengths: Robust to elongated Gaussian shapes by ignoring covariance gradients. Efficiently handles pose optimization by leveraging position-pose equivalence. Limitations: Assumes short optimization steps for color invariance. Requires good initialization (e.g., COLMAP). Pose-free settings require additional evaluation-time alignment. When to use: When optimizing camera poses for a static scene with known or roughly estimated initial poses, particularly in deblurring or novel view synthesis contexts. When not to use: For online SLAM where incremental tracking is required; use SplaTAM or Gaussian-SLAM instead. The method originates from the need to handle camera motion blur in 3D Gaussian Splatting, leading to the Deblur-GS paper. It builds on the differentiable rasterization of 3DGS. The equivalence between camera transformation and Gaussian position transformation is a key theoretical insight enabling efficient gradient computation. Evaluation-time pose alignment protocols were later formalized in pose-free reconstruction benchmarks. Camera pose refinement for static backgrounds was introduced to address multi-camera inconsistency in self-driving datasets where SfM struggles. name: Global 3DGS with Progressively Growing
head: Progressive Global 3DGS, Sequential Global 3DGS
body: Global 3DGS with Progressively Growing is a sequential reconstruction method that learns a global 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model by incrementally integrating frames, using estimated relative poses to update the scene representation and densify Gaussians to cover new views. It differs from standard global 3DGS by avoiding the accumulation of noisy relative pose errors across long sequences; instead, it grows the model frame-by-frame, aligning densification intervals with the addition of new frames to ensure continuous coverage of unobserved regions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of images \{It\}, where t is the frame index. Outputs: A global set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} with attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and estimated camera poses for all frames. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Set \mathcal{G}: A collection of K Gaussians. Each Gaussian k has: Position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation Rk \in SO(3) (represented as quaternion or rotation matrix) Scale Sk \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphak \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics coefficients ck Camera Poses: For each frame t, a pose Pt consisting of rotation qt \in SO(3) and translation tt \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: N: Number of optimization iterations per step. This value is set equal to the interval between adding new frames and performing densification. Initial learning rate for pose optimization: 10^{-5}, decaying to 10^{-6}. Densification threshold: Based on the average magnitude of viewspace position gradients. Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with the first frame It. Initialize a set of 3D Gaussian points (e.g., via depth estimation or feature matching, though the source specifies starting from frame It with an orthogonal camera pose). Set the initial camera pose for It as orthogonal. 2. Relative Pose Estimation: Use Local 3DGS to estimate the relative camera pose between the current frame It and the next frame I{t+1}. 3. Global Update: Update the global 3D Gaussian set \mathcal{G} and all its attributes over N iterations. The optimization uses the estimated relative pose and the two observed frames (It, I{t+1}) as inputs. 4. Pose Representation: Camera poses are optimized in the representation of quaternion rotation q \in SO(3) and translation vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3. 5. Progression: When the next frame I{t+2} becomes available, repeat the process: estimate the relative pose between I{t+1} and I{t+2}, and infer the relative pose between It and I{t+2}. 6. Densification: Densify the global 3DGS every N steps (aligned with the pace of adding new frames). Candidates for densification are determined by the average magnitude of viewspace position gradients. Gaussians with large average magnitude of viewspace position gradients indicate under-reconstruction and are split or cloned. 7. Opacity Reset: Keep resetting the opacity of Gaussians until the end of the training process to enable integration of new frames into the existing model. 8. Continuous Growth: Continue growing the 3D Gaussian points (densification) until the end of the input sequence, rather than stopping in the middle of training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def global3dgsprogressivegrowth(imagesequence): # Initialize global Gaussian set with the first frame # Assume orthogonal pose for the first frame G = initializegaussians(imagesequence[0], pose='orthogonal') # Set optimization parameters N = 1000 # Number of steps for adding new frames and densification intervals lrposeinit = 1e-5 lrposefinal = 1e-6 for t in range(1, len(imagesequence)): It = imagesequence[t-1] Inext = imagesequence[t] # Estimate relative pose between It and Inext using Local 3DGS relativepose = local3dgsestimatepose(It, Inext) # Update global 3DGS over N iterations for step in range(N): # Decay learning rate for pose optimization lrpose = lrposeinit (lrposefinal / lrposeinit) (step / N) # Optimize global Gaussians and poses using It, Inext and relativepose # The relative pose helps align Inext to the global coordinate system optimizeglobal3dgs(G, It, Inext, relativepose, lrpose) # Reset opacity to allow integration of new frames resetopacity(G) # Densify Gaussians every N steps # Target Gaussians with large average magnitude of viewspace position gradients densifygaussians(G, threshold=getgradientthreshold(G)) return G Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Relative Poses: Accumulated noise in relative poses can dramatically impact the optimization of the global 3DGS for the whole scene. The progressive approach mitigates this by limiting the propagation of errors. Under-reconstruction: Unobserved frames may contain regions not yet well reconstructed. The optimization tries to move Gaussians to correct this with large gradient steps, which is why densification targets these regions. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of frames, as each frame is processed sequentially with N iterations of optimization and densification. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians, which grows progressively with the number of frames. Performance: Evaluated on Tanks and Temples and CO3D-V2 datasets. Achieves photo-realistic reconstruction and accurate camera pose estimation. Strengths: Avoids error accumulation from noisy relative poses; continuously covers new views; integrates new frames effectively. Limitations: Requires sequential processing; densification must be carefully timed with frame addition. Origin: Proposed in "COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting" (CVPR 2024). History: Builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [17] and Local 3DGS. Addresses issues with global 3DGS optimization when relative poses are noisy. Usage: Used for novel view synthesis and pose estimation on real-world datasets like Tanks and Temples and CO3D-V2.
