name: Contribution-based ordering
head: Contribution score, Contribution-based progressive rendering, Euclidean distance from center, Gcontr, PRoGS Contribution Metric
body: Contribution-based ordering is a post-training method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that sorts primitives by their visual importance to enable progressive rendering. It solves the problem of inefficient data streaming by ensuring high-impact splats are transmitted and rendered first. Unlike EAGLES which uses this metric during training to prune splats, this method operates on the fully trained model to select impactful splats for independent streaming. Inputs: A trained set of M 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^M, each defined by position \mathbf{x}i, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color ci. A set of training viewpoints V. Outputs: A sorted list of Gaussian IDs based on their contribution score, or a spatially refined ordering using an octree. Data Structures: 1. Contribution Map: A hash map or array indexed by Gaussian ID, storing the scalar contribution score B{id}. 2. Octree (Optional): A spatial subdivision structure (typically depth 3) used to refine global ordering. Each leaf node stores a local ranking of Gaussians within its bounds. Steps: 1. Render Training Views: For each viewpoint v \in V, render the scene using standard 3DGS volume splatting Gaussian Splatting. 2. Calculate Per-Pixel Contribution: For each pixel p in each view, identify the N overlapping Gaussians. The color C is computed as: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where Ti is the transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) The contribution of the i-th Gaussian to pixel p is defined as the weight factor: w{i,p} = Ti \alphai Store the top K contributing Gaussians per pixel. 3. Aggregate Global Contribution Score: Sum the contributions of each Gaussian across all pixels P and all views V: B{id} = \sum{v \in V} \sum{p \in P} (T{id} \alpha{id}) where T{id} and \alpha{id} are the transmittance and opacity of Gaussian id at pixel p in view v. 4. Refine with Octree (Optional): To prevent bias towards densely captured areas, insert all Gaussians into an octree. For each leaf node, sort the contained Gaussians by their local contribution. This ensures spatial distribution of high-contribution splats, preventing sparsely captured regions from being unfairly under-reconstructed. 5. Alternative Metric: Euclidean Distance: An alternative metric used in some implementations (e.g., three.js) orders Gaussians by Euclidean distance from the scene center (0,0,0): G{contr} = \sqrt{(x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2} where (x1, y1, z1) is the camera position (or center) and (x2, y2, z2) is the Gaussian center. The center is taken as (0,0,0). Parameters: K: The number of highest contributing Gaussians per pixel used to decide on the ordering. Typical value: 20. Octree depth: Controls spatial subdivision granularity. Typical value: 3. Pitfalls: Size Bias: Large splats covering multiple pixels inherently receive higher scores than small splats, as each pixel's contribution is capped at 1. Small splats must have high opacity or cover many pixels to compete. Density Bias: Without octree refinement, Gaussians in densely captured areas dominate the score, leading to poor reconstruction of sparse regions. Frustum Culling Margin: When enabling frustum culling, boundaries should be increased by 30% to avoid clipping visible splats at chunk boundaries. Integrates this ordering into compression pipelines to stream high-contribution primitives first, prioritizing semantic importance over spatial/Morton order. Complexity: Requires a full forward pass over all training views to compute contributions. Performance: Significantly improves perceptual quality at low bitrates compared to distance-based or random ordering. Strengths: Maximizes visual fidelity for the first few chunks sent; effective for progressive web streaming. Limitations: Computationally expensive pre-processing step; large splats are favored, potentially delaying fine details. When to use: Optimal for bandwidth-constrained progressive delivery where early perceptual quality is prioritized. When not to use: Unsuitable for training-time pruning or scenes where uniform spatial coverage is required without octree refinement. Originating in the PRoGS (Progressive Rendering of Gaussian Splats) paper, this method was developed to address the inefficiency of transmitting full 3DGS models for real-time web viewing. It distinguishes itself from training-time pruning methods like EAGLES by operating post-training to optimize data transmission order. name: Contribution-based compression integration
head: Compression Integration, Integration with compression, PRoGS with Vector Quantization, Progressive compression integration
body: This method integrates contribution-based ordering into existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) compression pipelines, specifically Niedermayr et al.'s approach, to improve visual quality at the time to First Paint (TFP) by streaming high-contribution primitives first. It ensures that spatial or Morton ordering typically applied for storage efficiency does not overwrite the semantic importance ordering derived from rendering contribution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A compressed 3DGS scene file (specifically the method by Niedermayr et al.), contribution values per Gaussian, and Gaussian IDs. Output: A chunked compressed file where chunks are ordered by Gaussian contribution, allowing progressive rendering with higher initial quality. Data Structures: Chunk: A subset of Gaussians stored together. Each chunk must contain its own minimum and maximum values for vector quantization if rendered independently. Gaussian Data: Per-Gaussian data must be stored with ID mapping; fully aggregated codebooks without ID mapping are insufficient for this method. Steps: 1. Adapt Renderer: Modify the rendering engine to return contribution values and corresponding Gaussian IDs for each splat. 2. Calculate Ordering: Sort the Gaussians based on their calculated contribution values. 3. Rewrite Save Functionality: Group Gaussians into chunks according to the calculated contribution-based order. For each chunk, calculate and store the minimum and maximum values required for vector quantization dequantization. The base compression method (Niedermayr et al.) sorts Gaussians in Morton order before saving to improve compression ratios; this step voids the contribution-based ordering. In the implementation, this Morton sorting was disabled because it affects only final storage requirements and not the selected splats for progressive rendering. If Morton sorting is re-enabled, it must be applied to the already sorted indices. 4. Save Scene: Write the chunks to disk in the contribution-based order, explicitly skipping Morton sorting to preserve the progressive order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def savecompressedscene(gaussians, contributionvalues, chunksize): # Step 1: Pair Gaussians with their contribution values and IDs indexedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): indexedgaussians.append((i, g, contributionvalues[i])) # Step 2: Sort by contribution (descending, assuming higher contribution is better) indexedgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x[2], reverse=True) # Step 3: Chunk the sorted list chunks = [] for i in range(0, len(indexedgaussians), chunksize): chunkdata = indexedgaussians[i: i + chunksize] # Step 4: Calculate min/max for vector quantization for this chunk # Standard min/max calculation over all Gaussian attributes (mean, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients) chunkmin = [min(attr[j] for attr in chunkdata) for j in range(len(chunkdata[0]))] chunkmax = [max(attr[j] for attr in chunkdata) for j in range(len(chunkdata[0]))] # Step 5: Quantize and store chunk # The exact vector quantization routine from Niedermayr et al. is not provided in the sources. # The min and max values must be included in every chunk for dequantization. quantizedchunk = chunkdata # Quantization routine omitted; min/max stored separately. chunks.append({ 'min': chunkmin, 'max': chunkmax, 'data': quantizedchunk }) # Step 6: Write chunks to file in contribution-based order # Morton order sorting is explicitly skipped to preserve contribution order. with open('scene.bin', 'wb') as f: for chunk in chunks: f.write(chunk['min']) f.write(chunk['max']) f.write(chunk['data']) Parameters: Chunk Size: Not given in the sources. Compression Method: Specifically tested with Niedermayr et al.. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Morton Order Conflict: Applying Morton order sorting after contribution-based sorting destroys the progressive quality benefit. Independent Chunk Rendering: If chunks are rendered independently, min/max values must be included in every chunk for correct dequantization. Codebook Usage: This method requires per-Gaussian data storage with ID mapping. It is incompatible with compression schemes that use fully aggregated codebooks without ID mapping. Quality: Achieves similar quality per percentage of splats compared to the base approach on standard 3DGS. Memory: In actually required memory, there is a smaller difference compared to non-compressed progressive methods because the shared codebook reduces Gaussian-specific data. Performance: Improves quality at the time to First Paint (TFP). Limitations: Requires modification of the renderer to pass back contribution values and IDs. Requires per-Gaussian data storage. Origin: Proposed in PRoGS (Progressive Rendering of Gaussian Splats). Development: The method was validated on the MiPNeRF360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending datasets using the original 3DGS code. Usage: Used to facilitate progressive streaming of 3DGS, reducing bandwidth requirements while maintaining visual quality during loading. PRoGS: Progressive Rendering of Gaussian Splats, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00308, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D Convex Splatting
head: Convex Splatting
body: 3D Convex Splatting is a neural rendering method that replaces standard 3D Gaussian primitives with smooth convex shapes to represent scenes. It solves the limitation of Gaussians in accurately modeling flat surfaces and sharp edges, offering greater geometric flexibility and requiring fewer primitives for equivalent fidelity. Unlike its parent Gaussian Splatting, which relies on covariance matrices and elliptical distributions, this method represents each point as a 3D convex polyhedron defined by six vertices without explicit scale or rotation parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud where each point is a 3D convex polyhedron defined by six vertices, along with opacity and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color. Output: A rendered 2D image via volume splatting. Data Structures: The view-dependent state per point consists of 29 elements totaling 116 bytes: means2d (2 elements, 8 B, 2D projected center of the convex in pixel space), normals (12 elements, 48 B, 2D outward normals for each of the 6 projected hull vertices), offsets (6 elements, 24 B, line-offsets for each hull edge in the 2D indicator function), opacities (1 element, 4 B, alpha transparency for blending the convex splat), colors (3 elements, 12 B, RGB color coefficients for shading), radii (1 element, 4 B, projected radius in pixels for culling), depths (1 element, 4 B, Z-depth of the convex center for depth sorting), delta (1 element, 4 B, smoothness parameter controlling edge curvature), sigma (1 element, 4 B, sharpness parameter controlling boundary transition), pointsview (1 element, 4 B, number of vertices in the 2D convex hull, ≤ 6). Steps: 1. Frustum Culling: Test intersection of the camera frustum with each 3D convex polyhedron. Because each point lacks the scale and rotation parameters used in 3DGS, a different intersection test is required. 2. Projection & Hull Reconstruction: Project all six vertices of in-frustum 3D convex shapes onto the image plane, where they may no longer remain convex. Recompute the 2D convex hull from the projected 2D points to form the view-dependent splat geometry. 3. Color Computation: Compute view-dependent color using the camera pose and spherical harmonic coefficients stored in the point cloud. 4. Rasterization: Render the projected 2D convex hulls using an efficient CUDA rasterizer, which improves fidelity while reducing memory usage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ptssplatting(view, PC, infrustumids): SP = EmptyViewDependentSplats() # Project all vertices of each 3D convex shape onto 2D positions2d, SP.depth = Project3DCXTo2D(view.pose, PC.vertices[infrustumids]) # Recompute the convex hull from the 2D points SP.vertices2d = Compute2DConvexHull(positions2d) # Not given in the sources. # Compute view-dependent color SP.color = ComputeColorGivenView(view.pose, PC.sh[infrustumids]) return SP Parameters: delta: Smoothness parameter controlling edge curvature. sigma: Sharpness parameter controlling boundary transition. pointsview: Number of vertices in the 2D convex hull, bounded by 6. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The projection of 3D vertices to 2D may result in non-convex point sets, necessitating explicit convex hull recomputation. The absence of explicit scale/rotation parameters requires a custom frustum intersection test distinct from standard Gaussian rasterizers. A rendering strategy for non-elliptical primitives (lines, triangles) that decomposes them into vertices and re-sketches the shape. It is chosen when mixed-primitive frameworks are needed for sharp edges. Generates initial elliptical surface patches from point clouds via local PCA. It is chosen for initializing splat models from sparse data, differing from convex shapes by using elliptical primitives. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory usage compared to Gaussian Splatting by requiring fewer primitives to represent the scene. Performance: Coupled with an efficient CUDA rasterizer, it improves fidelity while reducing memory overhead. Strengths: Greater flexibility than Gaussians; more accurate representation of flat surfaces and sharp edges; fewer primitives required. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When accurate representation of sharp edges and flat surfaces is critical, and memory efficiency is a concern. When not to use: Not given in the sources. 3D Convex Splatting was introduced as the first work to move beyond Gaussian primitives by introducing smooth convex shapes. It is followed by Triangle Splatting and MeshSplatting in a lineage that progressively enhances visual quality and integration with classical graphics pipelines. It is especially well-suited for capturing the structured geometry of manufactured space objects, achieving more compact and clutter-free representations than Gaussian Splatting. name: Compositional Splatting Strategy
head: Compositional Splatting, Gaussian Line Splatting, Gaussian lines, Line-segment-centered primitive splatting, MP-GS Compositional Splatting
body: Compositional Splatting is a rendering strategy for non-elliptical primitives, specifically Gaussian lines and Gaussian triangles, which decomposes the primitive into its constituent vertices, splats them individually using point-based techniques, and re-sketches the final shape on the image plane. It solves the problem of rendering primitives that lack a simple elliptical boundary, enabling mixed-primitive Gaussian Splatting frameworks to accurately reconstruct object surfaces. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which renders ellipses directly, this method constructs the primitive's silhouette from the common tangents of vertex-based boundary ellipses. The method renders Gaussian lines and Gaussian triangles by treating them as compositions of their vertices. The process involves primitive formulation, compositional splatting of vertices, boundary ellipse formulation, common tangent calculation, and modified alpha blending. Inputs: Primitive type: Gaussian line (2 vertices) or Gaussian triangle (3 vertices). Viewpoint parameters: Projection matrix P, world-to-view transformation W, and Jacobian J. Primitive parameters: Gaussian Line: Two 3D vertex coordinates \mu1, \mu2. Gaussian Triangle: First vertex 3D coordinate \mu1 \in \mathbb{R}^3, second and third vertices 2D relative coordinates \mu2, \mu3 \in \mathbb{R}^2, rotation matrix R, and shared covariance matrix \Sigma. Rendering parameters: Opacity \alpha, color c. Outputs: Image plane pixels with color and opacity values derived from the re-sketched primitive. Gaussian Triangle: \mu1: \mathbb{R}^3 (3D coordinate of the first vertex). \mu2: \mathbb{R}^2 (2D relative coordinate of the second vertex in the triangle's local plane). \mu3: \mathbb{R}^2 (2D relative coordinate of the third vertex in the triangle's local plane). R: 3 \times 3 rotation matrix defining the triangle's orientation. \Sigma: 3 \times 3 covariance matrix (shared by all three vertices). Gaussian Line: \mu1, \mu2: \mathbb{R}^3 (3D coordinates of the two endpoints). \Sigma: 3 \times 3 covariance matrix (shared by both vertices). Step 1: Primitive Formulation (3D to Local 2D). For a Gaussian triangle, reconstruct the 3D coordinates of the second and third vertices using the first vertex and the rotation matrix: \mu2^{3D} = \mu1 + \mu2[0] \times (R[:, 0]^T) + \mu2[1] \times (R[:, 1]^T) \mu3^{3D} = \mu1 + \mu3[0] \times (R[:, 0]^T) + \mu3[1] \times (R[:, 1]^T) For a Gaussian line, the vertices are already in 3D space. Step 2: Compositional Splatting (Projection). Project each vertex and the shared covariance to the 2D image plane. Let P be the projection matrix and W be the world-to-view transformation. \mu1^{2D} = (PW\mu1)[:2] \mu2^{2D} = (PW\mu2^{3D})[:2] \quad (\text{or } (PW\mu2)[:2] \text{ for lines}) \mu3^{2D} = (PW\mu3^{3D})[:2] \quad (\text{for triangles}) \Sigma^{2D} = (J W \Sigma W^T J^T)[:2,:2] Step 3: Re-sketching on the Image Plane. This step constructs the boundary of the primitive on the image plane. Step 3.1: Boundary Ellipse Formulation. Define the boundary ellipse for each vertex i as the contour where the Gaussian value is 1/255. The contour is the set of points (x,y) satisfying gi^{ct} = 0: gi^{ct} = -2 \ln(255) + \frac{c\Sigma(x{\mui} - x)^2 + a\Sigma(y{\mui} - y)^2 + b\Sigma(x{\mui} - x)(y{\mui} - y)}{a\Sigma c\Sigma - b\Sigma^2} = 0 Here, \Sigma^{2D} is decomposed into symmetric matrix elements a\Sigma, b\Sigma, c\Sigma. The equation is expanded into the general quadratic form: gi^{ct} = ai x^2 + bi xy + ci y^2 + di x + ei y + fi = 0 The coefficients ai, bi, ci, di, ei, fi are derived from \mui^{2D} and \Sigma^{2D}. Step 3.2: Common Tangent Line Measurement. Calculate the common tangent lines between pairs of boundary ellipses. This is done by finding the intersection of their dual ellipses. 1. Compute the dual ellipse function gi^{dual} for each boundary ellipse using projective geometry duality: gi^{dual} = \left[ -\frac{1}{4}(ei)^2 + ci fi \right] x^2 + \left[ \frac{1}{2} di ei - bi fi \right] xy + \left[ -\frac{1}{4}(di)^2 + ai fi \right] y^2 + \left[ -ci di + \frac{1}{2} bi ei \right] x + \left[ \frac{1}{2} bi ei - ai ei \right] y - \frac{1}{4}(bi)^2 + ai ci = 0 2. Solve the system g1^{dual}=0, g2^{dual}=0 for the intersection point (xs, ys). 3. The common tangent line is given by: xs x + ys y + 1 = 0 This calculation has O(1) time complexity. Step 4: Rendering. Perform image rendering over the re-sketched primitives using a modified alpha-blending function. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compositionalsplatting(primitivetype, vertices3d, rotationmatrix, covariance3d, P, W, J): """ Renders a Gaussian line or triangle using compositional splatting. Args: primitivetype: 'line' or 'triangle' vertices3d: List of coordinates. For line: [mu13d, mu23d]. For triangle: [mu13d, mu22drel, mu32drel] rotationmatrix: 3x3 R matrix (required for triangle) covariance3d: 3x3 Sigma matrix P: Projection matrix W: World-to-view transformation matrix J: Jacobian of the projective transformation Returns: Rendered image contribution (color, opacity) for the primitive. """ # Step 1: Formulate 3D coordinates for all vertices if primitivetype == 'triangle': mu13d = vertices3d[0] mu2rel = vertices3d[1] mu3rel = vertices3d[2] mu23d = mu13d + mu2rel[0] rotationmatrix[:, 0] + mu2rel[1] rotationmatrix[:, 1] mu33d = mu13d + mu3rel[0] rotationmatrix[:, 0] + mu3rel[1] rotationmatrix[:, 1] vertex3ds = [mu13d, mu23d, mu33d] else: # line mu13d = vertices3d[0] mu23d = vertices3d[1] vertex3ds = [mu13d, mu23d] numvertices = len(vertex3ds) # Step 2: Compositional Splatting (Project to 2D) vertex2ds = [] for mu3d in vertex3ds: mu2d = (P @ W @ mu3d)[:2] vertex2ds.append(mu2d) # Project Covariance to 2D WsigmaWT = W @ covariance3d @ W.T JWsigmaWTJT = J @ WsigmaWT @ J.T sigma2d = JWsigmaWTJT[:2,:2] # Step 3: Re-sketching # Step 3.1: Boundary Ellipse Formulation boundaryellipses = [] for i in range(numvertices): mui = vertex2ds[i] asig = sigma2d[0, 0] bsig = sigma2d[0, 1] csig = sigma2d[1, 1] denom = asig csig - bsig2 logterm = -2 math.log(255) # Expand gi^ct = 0 to aix^2 + bixy + ciy^2 + dix + eiy + fi = 0 ai = csig / denom ci = asig / denom bi = bsig / denom di = (-2 csig mui[0] - bsig mui[1]) / denom ei = (-2 asig mui[1] - bsig mui[0]) / denom fi = logterm + (csig mui[0]2 + asig mui[1]2 + bsig mui[0] mui[1]) / denom boundaryellipses.append({'a': ai, 'b': bi, 'c': ci, 'd': di, 'e': ei, 'f': fi}) # Step 3.2: Common Tangent Line Measurement tangentlines = [] if numvertices == 2: pairs = [(0, 1)] else: # triangle pairs = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)] for i, j in pairs: elli = boundaryellipses[i] ellj = boundaryellipses[j] # Calculate dual ellipse coefficients for i Ai = -0.25 elli['e']2 + elli['c'] elli['f'] Bi = 0.5 elli['d'] elli['e'] - elli['b'] elli['f'] Ci = -0.25 elli['d']2 + elli['a'] elli['f'] Di = -elli['c'] elli['d'] + 0.5 elli['b'] elli['e'] Ei = 0.5 elli['b'] elli['e'] - elli['a'] elli['e'] Fi = -0.25 elli['b']2 + elli['a'] elli['c'] # Calculate dual ellipse coefficients for j Aj = -0.25 ellj['e']2 + ellj['c'] ellj['f'] Bj = 0.5 ellj['d'] ellj['e'] - ellj['b'] ellj['f'] Cj = -0.25 ellj['d']2 + ellj['a'] ellj['f'] Dj = -ellj['c'] ellj['d'] + 0.5 ellj['b'] ellj['e'] Ej = 0.5 ellj['b'] ellj['e'] - ellj['a'] ellj['e'] Fj = -0.25 ellj['b']2 + ellj['a'] ellj['c'] # Solve system Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0 for intersection (xs, ys) # The source does not provide the specific algebraic solver for conic intersection. # xs, ys = solveconicintersection(Ai, Bi, Ci, Di, Ei, Fi, Aj, Bj, Cj, Dj, Ej, Fj) # Tangent line: xs x + ys y + 1 = 0 # tangentlines.append((xs, ys)) # Step 4: Rendering # The source does not provide the exact implementation of the modified alpha-blending function. # return rendermodifiedalphablend(vertex2ds, tangentlines, primitivetype) pass Threshold: The boundary ellipse is defined at Gaussian value 1/255. Points outside this contour are truncated to zero. Complexity: Calculating the common tangent line between each pair of boundary ellipses has O(1) time complexity. Pitfalls: Numerical instability may occur if the covariance matrix is singular or near-singular. The source notes that avoiding numerical instability is a reason for the 1/255 truncation. Time Complexity: The core geometric operation (common tangent calculation) is O(1) per pair of vertices. The overall complexity depends on the number of primitives and the cost of the modified alpha blending. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional parameters for non-elliptical primitives (relative 2D coordinates for triangles) compared to standard Gaussian ellipses. Strengths: Enables accurate reconstruction of object surfaces using mixed primitives (Gaussian lines and triangles). Limitations: More complex rendering pipeline due to the need for re-sketching and dual ellipse calculations. Not directly compatible with standard Gaussian Splatting pipelines without modification. When to use: Not given in the sources. Compositional Splatting was introduced in the MP-GS (Mixed-Primitive-based Gaussian Splatting) framework. It addresses the limitations of standard Gaussian Splatting, which uses only ellipsoidal primitives, by introducing Gaussian lines and triangles. The method leverages the observation that line segments and triangles can be represented as compositions of their vertices, allowing for a compositional splatting approach. A Mixed-Primitive-based Gaussian Splatting Method for Surface Reconstruction, https://core.ac.uk/works/308836756, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Base Splat Model Generation
head: Elliptical Splat Generation, PCA-based Splat Fitting
body: Base Splat Model Generation replaces isolated 3D points with elliptical surface patches (splats) that approximate the underlying local surface geometry, addressing the limitation of points as mere isolated samples. It differs from its parent, 3D Convex Splatting, by using PCA-derived elliptical primitives rather than smooth convex shapes, and from its sibling, Compositional Splatting Strategy, by generating the initial model via local neighbor statistics rather than compositional merging [S1, 13273-compositional-splatting-strategy.md]. Inputs: A sparse 3D point cloud P = \{pi\}{i=0}^{M-1} where each pi \in \mathbb{R}^3, and for each point, the camera position ci that observed it. Outputs: A set of splats, each defined by a center si, a normal vector ni, and two orthogonal tangential vectors ui, vi representing the major and minor axes. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D grid used to accelerate neighbor search. Points are hashed into voxels based on their coordinates. Neighbor List Nr(pi): The set of points within a fixed radius r of pi. Parameters: r: Fixed search radius for neighbors. Threshold: Empirical threshold for the flatness coefficient fi to decide splat center placement. Steps: 1. Voxelization: Discretize the 3D space into voxels. Assign each point pi to its corresponding voxel. 2. Neighbor Search: For each point pi, identify neighbors Nr(pi) by checking the point's voxel and its 26 adjacent voxels. Filter points within distance r. 3. PCA Computation: Perform Principal Component Analysis on the neighbor set Nr(pi): Compute the average point \bar{p}i = \frac{1}{|Nr(pi)|} \sum{q \in Nr(pi)} q. Compute the covariance matrix of the neighbors. Solve the eigenvalue problem to obtain three eigenvalues \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 and their corresponding eigenvectors w1, w2, w3. 4. Orientation and Axis Calculation: Set the normal vector ni = w3 (eigenvector of smallest eigenvalue). Compute the tangential vectors (axes): ui = \sqrt{\lambda1} \cdot w1 vi = \sqrt{\lambda2} \cdot w2 Normal Flipping: Ensure ni points outwards from the model interior. If ni \cdot (ci - pi) < 0, flip the orientation of ni and adjust ui, vi to maintain the right-handed cross-product relationship (ui \times vi = ni). 5. Flatness Coefficient: Calculate the planarity measure: fi = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda1} + \sqrt{\lambda2}}{\sqrt{\lambda1} + \sqrt{\lambda2} + \sqrt{\lambda3}} fi = 1 indicates a completely planar area (\lambda3 = 0). fi = 2/3 indicates a perfectly isotropic point set (\lambda1 = \lambda2 = \lambda3). 6. Splat Center Determination: If fi is high (above the empirical threshold), set the splat center si = pi. If fi is low, set the splat center si = \bar{p}i (the average point from PCA) to reduce holes in flat regions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def basesplatgeneration(points, camerapositions, radius, flatnessthreshold): """ Generate base splats from a point cloud using PCA. Args: points: Array of shape (M, 3) containing 3D coordinates. camerapositions: Array of shape (M, 3) containing camera position for each point. radius: Search radius for neighbors. flatnessthreshold: Empirical threshold for flatness coefficient. Returns: splats: List of dictionaries with keys 'center', 'normal', 'u', 'v'. """ M = points.shape[0] splats = [] # Step 1: Voxelization # Hash points to voxels. Assuming a simple grid for illustration. voxelsize = radius voxelmap = {} # Key: (vx, vy, vz), Value: list of point indices for i, p in enumerate(points): vx, vy, vz = int(p[0] / voxelsize), int(p[1] / voxelsize), int(p[2] / voxelsize) if (vx, vy, vz) not in voxelmap: voxelmap[(vx, vy, vz)] = [] voxelmap[(vx, vy, vz)].append(i) # Step 2 & 3: Neighbor Search and PCA for i in range(M): pi = points[i] ci = camerapositions[i] # Find neighbors in 27 voxels (current + 26 adjacent) vx, vy, vz = int(pi[0] / voxelsize), int(pi[1] / voxelsize), int(pi[2] / voxelsize) neighbors = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: key = (vx + dx, vy + dy, vz + dz) if key in voxelmap: for j in voxelmap[key]: distsq = np.sum((points[j] - pi)2) if distsq <= radius2: neighbors.append(points[j]) if len(neighbors) < 3: # Degenerate case: not enough neighbors for PCA # Default to identity orientation if insufficient neighbors splats.append({ 'center': pi, 'normal': np.array([0, 0, 1]), 'u': np.array([1, 0, 0]), 'v': np.array([0, 1, 0]) }) continue neighborsarr = np.array(neighbors) # PCA meanp = np.mean(neighborsarr, axis=0) centered = neighborsarr - meanp cov = np.cov(centered, rowvar=False) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) # Sort eigenvalues and eigenvectors in descending order idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx] eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx] w1, w2, w3 = eigenvectors[:, 0], eigenvectors[:, 1], eigenvectors[:, 2] lambda1, lambda2, lambda3 = eigenvalues[0], eigenvalues[1], eigenvalues[2] # Step 4: Orientation and Axes ni = w3 ui = np.sqrt(lambda1) w1 vi = np.sqrt(lambda2) w2 # Flip normal if pointing towards camera if np.dot(ni, ci - pi) < 0: ni = -ni # Adjust tangents to maintain right-handed system: u x v = n # If we flip n, we can flip u or v. Flipping u is sufficient. ui = -ui # Step 5: Flatness Coefficient sqrtl1 = np.sqrt(lambda1) sqrtl2 = np.sqrt(lambda2) sqrtl3 = np.sqrt(lambda3) fi = (sqrtl1 + sqrtl2) / (sqrtl1 + sqrtl2 + sqrtl3) # Step 6: Splat Center if fi > flatnessthreshold: si = pi else: si = meanp splats.append({ 'center': si, 'normal': ni, 'u': ui, 'v': vi }) return splats A variant that explicitly solves the eigenvalue/eigenvector problem from local neighbors to align splats with minimal curvature. It differs from the base method by focusing on surface-aligned orientations and is chosen when shape-aware, rotationally invariant orientations are required, though it may produce less coherent fields than global methods. Time Complexity: Dominated by neighbor search. With voxelization, average case is O(M) for M points, assuming constant average neighbors within radius r. Without voxelization, it is O(M^2). PCA is O(k) where k is the number of neighbors (typically small constant). Memory Complexity: O(M) to store the point cloud, voxel grid, and resulting splats. Strengths: Adapts splat shape to local geometry; reduces holes in flat regions by moving centers to the local mean; filters noise via fixed-radius search. Limitations: Requires dense enough sampling for PCA to be meaningful; sensitive to the choice of radius r and flatness threshold; local orientation may lack global coherence compared to methods using global tangent fields. When to use: When starting from a sparse or moderately dense point cloud and needing an initial approximation of surface geometry with elliptical primitives. When not to use: When global surface coherence is critical without post-processing, or when the point cloud is extremely sparse (PCA fails). The method was introduced in the context of textured splat-based point clouds for rendering on handheld devices. It builds on earlier work by Pauly et al. [2002] for hierarchical clustering and Wu and Kobbelt [2004; 2005] for optimized subsampling, but specifically adapts PCA to define elliptical splat shapes from local neighbor statistics. The approach aims to improve model compactness and rendering quality, particularly for multi-texturing, by replacing isolated points with surface-adaptive patches. Textured splat-based point clouds for rendering in handheld devices, https://doi.org/10.1145/2775292.2782779, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Covariance Matrix (CM) Splatting
head: Plane Principal Component Analysis
body: Covariance Matrix (CM) Splatting is a surface-aligned splatting technique that orients elliptical surface patches by solving the eigenvalue and eigenvector problems associated with a covariance matrix computed from local neighbor points. It aligns splats with the direction of minimal curvature, providing shape-aware, rotationally invariant orientations. Unlike the Householder (HH) method, which computes globally coherent tangent fields without considering surface curvature, CM relies solely on local geometric statistics, resulting in less coherent fields and more discontinuities between splats. Inputs: A set of 3D points P = \{pi\} with associated precomputed normal vectors ni, and a kernel radius r = 5\epsilon, where \epsilon is the estimated average point distribution. Outputs: For each splat center c, a normal vector v0, two tangent vectors v1, v2, and eigenvalues \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2 defining the splat's orientation and scale. Data Structures: Covariance Matrix C: A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. Eigenvalues \lambda: A vector of three scalar values, sorted such that \lambda0 \le \lambda1 \le \lambda2. Eigenvectors v: A set of three orthogonal unit vectors corresponding to \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2. Steps: 1. Identify Neighbors: For a splat center c, identify all points pi within the kernel radius r = 5\epsilon. 2. Compute Centroid: Calculate the centroid c{local} of the neighbor points: c{local} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} pi where N is the number of neighbors. 3. Compute Covariance Matrix: Calculate the covariance matrix C using the average squared sum of distances between the neighbor points and the centroid: C = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (pi - c{local})(pi - c{local})^T. 4. Solve Eigenproblem: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2 and corresponding eigenvectors v0, v1, v2 of C. 5. Assign Vectors: The eigenvector v0 corresponding to the lowest eigenvalue \lambda0 is assigned as the estimated normal vector. The eigenvectors v1 and v2 corresponding to the greatest eigenvalues \lambda1 and \lambda2 are assigned as the two tangent vectors. 6. Define Splat Size: Use the eigenvalues \lambda1 and \lambda2 to define the size (scale) of the splat along the tangent directions. Parameters: Kernel Size: 5\epsilon, where \epsilon is the estimated average point distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Sensitivity: CM reacts poorly to noise. Even in close neighborhoods with similar normal vectors, noise causes increasing variations in tangent vector directions. Discontinuities: The method creates more discontinuities (holes) between splats compared to Householder splatting. Local Coherence: Because CM aligns splats only locally, the resulting tangent fields are less coherent than those produced by HH. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Local angular deviation of the tangent vector fields was measured on several models with varying noise levels (\epsilon0, \epsilon1, \epsilon2). Lower deviation indicates better coherence with precomputed normals. | Model | Noise Level | CM Deviation (\epsilon0) | CM Deviation (\epsilon1) | CM Deviation (\epsilon2) | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Armadillo | \epsilon0 | 2.29, 7.62 | - | - | | Armadillo | \epsilon1 | - | 17.03, 63.35 | - | | Armadillo | \epsilon2 | - | - | 20.06, 69.69 | | Buddah | \epsilon0 | 2.43, 9.94 | - | - | | Buddah | \epsilon1 | - | 15.49, 57.89 | - | | Buddah | \epsilon2 | - | - | 15.74, 58.06 | | Bunny | \epsilon0 | 2.31, 8.26 | - | - | | Bunny | \epsilon1 | - | 13.04, 50.56 | - | | Bunny | \epsilon2 | - | - | 18.61, 62.77 | | Dragon | \epsilon0 | 2.30, 7.88 | - | - | | Dragon | \epsilon1 | - | 16.73, 63.28 | - | | Dragon | \epsilon2 | - | - | 21.54, 68.95 | | Bee | \epsilon0 | 2.22, 11.49 | - | - | | Bee | \epsilon1 | - | 19.73, 68.12 | - | | Vase | \epsilon0 | 1.77, 4.96 | - | - | | Vase | \epsilon1 | - | 15.06, 59.01 | - | | Cathedral | \epsilon0 | 1.06, 18.67 | - | - | | Cathedral | \epsilon1 | - | 12.74, 49.37 | - | | Male | \epsilon0 | 3.04, 15.96 | - | - | | Male | \epsilon1 | - | 14.28, 51.95 | - | Note: The table in the source lists two values for each CM entry (e.g., "2.29, 7.62"). The source does not explicitly define what these two numbers represent, but they are consistently paired with CM results. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Rotationally invariant; produces shape-aware directions; eigenvalues allow for dynamic resizing of splats. Limitations: Poor performance on noisy data; less coherent tangent fields than Householder; creates more discontinuities; strictly local alignment. When to use/not use: Use CM when the input data is clean and rotational invariance is required. Avoid CM for noisy data (e.g., depth sensor scans) where Householder splatting provides significantly lower angular deviation and better coherence. CM Splatting was introduced as a standard method for surface-aligned splatting in non-photorealistic rendering. It relies on Plane Principal Component Analysis [Rus09] to estimate splat normal vectors and orientations from 3D point data. It was compared against the Householder (HH) formula in a study by Anjos et al. [dARLP17] to evaluate rendering quality on noisy meshes and point clouds. name: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Feed-forward Reconstruction Model
body: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting explicitly represents a 3D scene as a collection of anisotropic Gaussian distributions to enable real-time novel view synthesis via splatting. It predicts Gaussian primitives directly from N input images using a multi-view Transformer and linear projection, bypassing iterative optimization. Inputs: N RGB images of resolution H \times W with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Outputs: A set of K 3D Gaussian primitives, where each primitive k is defined by parameters \mathbf{G}k and feature vector \mathbf{F}k. Data Structures: 1. Input Images: N tensors of shape (H, W, 3). 2. Ray Embeddings: Plücker ray embeddings computed per pixel. 3. Patch Features: Extracted via a shallow CNN, shape (N, \frac{HW}{p^2}, C). 4. Token Sequence: Flattened patch features, shape (N \times \frac{HW}{p^2}, C). 5. Latent Features: Output of the multi-view Transformer, shape (N \times \frac{HW}{p^2}, C{\text{latent}}). 6. Gaussian Primitives: Each includes center \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} parameterized by orthogonal rotation R and diagonal scale S such that \Sigma = RSS^T R^T, spherical harmonic coefficients c{\text{SH}} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times (k+1)}, opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^1, and additional feature vector \mathbf{F}k. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Concatenate RGB values with Plücker ray embeddings per pixel. 2. Patch Encoding: Group features into non-overlapping p \times p patches. Encode with a shallow CNN to obtain patch features of channel dimension C. 3. Tokenization: Flatten patch features from all N views into a sequence \{\mathbf{X}\} of length N \times \frac{HW}{p^2}. 4. Transformer Processing: Process \{\mathbf{X}\} with a multi-view Transformer to produce latent features \{\mathbf{Z}\}: \{\mathbf{Z}\} = \text{Transformer}{\text{MV}}(\{\mathbf{X}\}). 5. Primitive Prediction: Apply a linear projection to each latent token to produce \{\mathbf{G}k, \mathbf{F}k\} = \text{Linear}(\{\mathbf{Z}\}). 6. Rendering: Project each 3D Gaussian onto the 2D image plane for a target viewpoint. Compute pixel color via front-to-back alpha compositing. Formulas: Covariance Parameterization: \Sigma = RSS^T R^T, where R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is an orthogonal rotation matrix and S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is a diagonal scale matrix. 2D Projection: \mu{2D} = PW \mu, \Sigma{2D} = JW \Sigma J^T, where \mu{2D} and \Sigma{2D} are the center and covariance of the projected Gaussian, W is the viewing transformation matrix, P is the projective transformation matrix, and J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. Alpha Compositing: C(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^K \mathbf{c}i \alphai \mathcal{G}i^{\text{2D}}(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj \mathcal{G}j^{\text{2D}}(\mathbf{p})), where \mathcal{G}i^{\text{2D}}(\mathbf{p}) is the 2D projection of the i-th Gaussian at pixel \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{c}i is the color, \alphai is opacity, and K is the number of splats. Parameters: Patch size p: Not given in the sources. CNN channel dimension C: Not given in the sources. Transformer latent dimension C{\text{latent}}: Not given in the sources. SH order k: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Covariance PSD: The covariance matrix \Sigma must remain positive semi-definite. The method ensures this by parameterizing \Sigma = RSS^T R^T, where R is an orthogonal rotation matrix and S is a diagonal scale matrix. Patch Alignment: The patch size p must divide H and W evenly to form non-overlapping patches. Ray Embeddings: Plücker coordinates are computed from ray origins and directions derived from known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeplucker(origins, directions): """Compute Plücker coordinates L = o x d for each pixel.""" return np.cross(origins, directions) def computeraydata(camera, H, W): """Compute ray origins and directions from camera matrices.""" K = camera['intrinsics'] Rcam, t = camera['extrinsics'][:3,:3], camera['extrinsics'][:3, 3] origin = -Rcam.T @ t invK = np.linalg.inv(K) y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing='ij') hom = np.stack([x, y, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1).astype(np.float32) dirs = (invK @ hom.reshape(-1, 3).T).T.reshape(H, W, 3) dirs = (Rcam.T @ dirs.reshape(-1, 3).T).T.reshape(H, W, 3) return origin, dirs def extractpatches(features, patchsize): """Extract non-overlapping p x p patches from N views.""" N, H, W, Cin = features.shape patches = features.reshape(N, H // patchsize, patchsize, W // patchsize, patchsize, Cin) patches = patches.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5) return patches.reshape(N, (H // patchsize) (W // patchsize), patchsize patchsize Cin) def shallowcnn(patches, outchannels): """Apply a shallow CNN to patch features. Architecture not specified in sources.""" return patches @ np.zeros((patches.shape[-1], outchannels)) def multiheadattention(x, dim, numheads): """Simplified multi-view transformer block. Exact architecture not specified in sources.""" qkv = x @ np.zeros((dim 3, dim)) q, k, v = np.split(qkv, 3, axis=-1) scale = 1.0 / np.sqrt(dim // numheads) attn = np.exp(q @ k.T scale) attn = attn / attn.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) return attn @ v def reconstructcovariance(Rflat, Sflat): """Reconstruct covariance from rotation and scale parameters: Sigma = R S S^T R^T.""" R = Rflat.reshape(3, 3) S = np.diag(Sflat) return R @ S @ S.T @ R.T def feedforwardgaussiansplatting(images, cameras, patchsize=16): """ Predicts 3D Gaussian primitives from N RGB images. Args: images: List of N numpy arrays, shape (H, W, 3), dtype float32, normalized [0, 1]. cameras: List of N camera objects with 'extrinsics' (4x4) and 'intrinsics' (3x3). patchsize: Integer, size of non-overlapping patches. Returns: gaussians: List of dictionaries, each containing 'mu', 'cov', 'alpha', 'shcoeffs', 'features'. """ N = len(images) H, W, = images[0].shape numpatchesh = H // patchsize numpatchesw = W // patchsize numpatches = numpatchesh numpatchesw # Step 1: Feature Extraction pixelfeatures = [] for i in range(N): origins, directions = computeraydata(cameras[i], H, W) plucker = computeplucker(origins, directions) pluckerexpanded = np.repeat(plucker[:,:, np.newaxis,:], 3, axis=2).reshape(H, W, 6) combined = np.concatenate([images[i], pluckerexpanded], axis=-1) pixelfeatures.append(combined) # Step 2: Patch Encoding patches = extractpatches(np.stack(pixelfeatures, axis=0), patchsize) cnnoutput = shallowcnn(patches.reshape(-1, patches.shape[-1]), outchannels=64) patchfeatures = cnnoutput.reshape(N, numpatches, 64) # Step 3: Tokenization tokens = patchfeatures.reshape(-1, 64) # Step 4: Transformer Processing latents = multiheadattention(tokens, dim=512, numheads=8) # Step 5: Primitive Prediction # Linear projection outputs parameters for Gaussian primitives Dout = 3 + 9 + 3 + 1 + 27 + 32 # mu, R, S, alpha, SH, features linearlayer = np.zeros((latents.shape[1], Dout)) predictions = latents @ linearlayer # Step 6: Parse predictions into Gaussian primitives gaussians = [] for k in range(predictions.shape[0]): pred = predictions[k] mu = pred[0:3] Rflat = pred[3:12] Sflat = pred[12:15] alpha = pred[15] shcoeffs = pred[16:43] features = pred[43:] cov = reconstructcovariance(Rflat, Sflat) gaussians.append({ 'mu': mu, 'cov': cov, 'alpha': alpha, 'shcoeffs': shcoeffs, 'features': features }) return gaussians Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Enables real-time novel view synthesis after a single forward pass. Quality is competitive with NeRF. Strengths: Fast reconstruction without per-scene training. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting builds on Gaussian Splatting. The specific feed-forward reconstruction model is based on the architecture from GS-LRM. name: GaussianShader
body: GaussianShader enriches 3D Gaussians with physical material parameters—specifically diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, and normals—to enable the rendering of specular and reflective objects. It extends the standard Gaussian representation to support physically-based appearance for novel view synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for color, and additional material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, normals). Outputs: A rendered 2D image using the enriched material parameters. Data Structures: Each Gaussian stores: 1. Position (\mathbf{p}) and 3D covariance (\Sigma). 2. Opacity (\alpha). 3. SH coefficients for view-dependent color. 4. Material parameters: diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, and surface normal. 5. Projected 2D covariance and screen-space position (computed during preprocessing). Steps: 1. Preprocess (Culling): Discard Gaussians whose 99% confidence interval does not intersect the view frustum after projection. 2. Preprocess (Color Computation): Compute the direction-dependent color using the stored SH coefficients. 3. Preprocess (Buffering): Store the computed color, opacity, projected screen-space position, and 2D covariance values in an atomic linear-append buffer. The 2D covariance indicates the orientation and size of the projected 2D Gaussian. 4. Preprocess (Sorting): Depth-sort the Gaussians using the Onesweep sorting algorithm on the GPU to enable order-dependent blending. 5. Rendering (Rasterization): Render the sorted Gaussians via GPU rasterization. For each Gaussian, render one planar quad (splat) consisting of two triangles. 6. Vertex Shader: Compute the screen-space vertex positions of the splat from the 2D covariance information. The size of the splat is set to cover the 99% confidence interval of the projected Gaussian. Output the precomputed color and 2D splat center to the pixel shader. 7. Pixel Shader: Discard fragments outside the 99% confidence interval. For remaining fragments, compute the exponential color and opacity falloff based on the distance to the splat center. Blend the final colors into the framebuffer. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Splat Size: Set to cover the 99% confidence interval of the projected Gaussian. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on accurate projection of 3D covariance to 2D to determine splat size and falloff. Material Parameters: The specific integration of material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, normals) into the shading model is not detailed in the provided sources, only that they are stored and used to handle specular/reflective objects. This variant utilizes hardware rasterization for fast novel view synthesis, particularly on low-power GPUs. It employs the preprocessing, sorting, and rasterization steps described in the main method to achieve real-time performance. Time and Memory Complexity: Sorting: Uses the Onesweep algorithm, which offers consistent performance suitable for real-time applications. Memory: Requires storage for material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, normals) in addition to standard Gaussian attributes. Measured Performance: Designed for acceleration on low-power GPUs by leveraging hardware rasterization instead of software rasterization. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables physically accurate rendering of specular and reflective objects; efficient real-time rendering via hardware rasterization and Onesweep sorting. Limitations: Specific details on the shading model's complexity and computational overhead of material parameter evaluation are not provided. When to Use: When rendering scenes with specular or reflective objects using 3D Gaussians. When real-time performance on low-power hardware is required. GaussianShader was introduced to address the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in handling specular and reflective objects. It enriches the Gaussian representation with material parameters such as diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, and normals. The method has been used as a foundation for subsequent techniques, such as Gaussian Splashing, which builds upon it for physical simulations using Position-Based Fluids. name: SpotlessSplats
body: SpotlessSplats is a robustness-enhancing method for Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction that improves reconstruction quality in casual captures by detecting and ignoring transient distractors. Unlike SWAG, which trains unsupervised transient Gaussians to ignore occluders, SpotlessSplats operates in a richer, pre-trained feature space to filter noise. Inputs and Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Project deformed Gaussians into a pre-trained feature space. 2. Outlier Detection: Identify Gaussians corresponding to transient distractors by detecting outliers in this feature space. 3. Filtering: Ignore or suppress the contribution of detected outlier Gaussians during the differentiable rendering process. Formulas: Specific mathematical formulations for the feature extractor or outlier detection function are not provided in the sources. The method modifies the standard differentiable rendering pipeline to exclude identified outliers. Parameters: Feature space dimension, outlier threshold, and feature extractor architecture are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes avatar geometry is stable and distinct from transient elements; severe occlusion or extreme pose changes may lead to incorrect outlier classification. Effectiveness depends on the quality of the pre-trained feature space. Point Rasterization is a neural point rendering technique from DGNR, not explicitly part of SpotlessSplats, but related to the rendering pipeline. Definition: Density points from space P are projected using camera model C to create images of dimensions W \times H, assigning points passing the depth test to neural density features. Steps: 1. Convert real-valued projection Qs(pr) to integer pixel coordinates qr by rounding to nearest integer: qr = \lfloor Qs(pr) \rceil. 2. Encode pixels qr into neural density features \tau through a 1 \times 1 convolution kernel, encoding local 3D scene context around pr. Formula: World point pr is projected to layer l image space: Qs(pr) = \frac{1}{2^l} C(R(pr) + T) where C is the camera model, and (R, T) is the rigid transformation from world to camera space. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: SpotlessSplats yields improved reconstruction quality in casual captures by ignoring transient distractors. It builds on SWAG by further enhancing robustness. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enhanced robustness to transient distractors in casual captures; improved reconstruction quality. Limitations: Relies on a pre-trained feature space; specific implementation details (thresholds, feature dimensions) are not provided. When to use: When capturing casual videos with transient distractors (e.g., moving people, shadows) that degrade standard Gaussian Splatting reconstruction. When not to use: Not given in the sources. SpotlessSplats was introduced as an extension to 3D Gaussian Splatting for robust reconstruction. It builds on SWAG, which uses unsupervised transient Gaussians, by detecting outliers in a richer, pre-trained feature space. name: Gaussian Avatars
head: FLAME Gaussian Splatting, PSAvatar, PSAvatar / Relightable Avatar, Relightable Avatar [S2, unofficial]
body: Gaussian Avatars reconstructs photorealistic, animatable head avatars by anchoring 3D Gaussians to a parametric FLAME mesh. It associates each FLAME mesh triangle with a Gaussian that is optimized for the scene while being constrained to remain within its corresponding triangle. Unlike methods that predict Gaussian parameters via feedforward networks conditioned on pose, Gaussian Avatars optimizes the Gaussian ellipsoid parameters directly while enforcing geometric constraints, enabling high-fidelity rendering and relighting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view video of a talking head; pre-fitted FLAME model parameters (pose, expression, shape). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians associated with FLAME mesh triangles, optimized for appearance and geometry. Data Structures: Gaussian: Each Gaussian i is associated with a specific triangle t of the FLAME mesh. Constraint: The Gaussian position \mathbf{p}i is computed from barycentric coordinates (u, v, w) relative to its associated triangle vertices. Steps: 1. Initialization: Fit a FLAME model to the input video frames using tools like MICA or DECA to obtain initial mesh parameters. 2. Gaussian Association: Initialize one Gaussian per triangle of the FLAME mesh in tangent space. 3. Constrained Optimization: Optimize Gaussian parameters using differentiable rendering. The position \mathbf{p}i is constrained to remain within the barycentric coordinates of triangle t. The FLAME mesh deforms according to the current pose and expression parameters, and the Gaussians follow the deformation while maintaining their triangle constraints. 4. Rendering: Render the scene using standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. 5. Loss Function: Minimize photometric loss (\mathcal{L}{L1}) and perceptual loss (\mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM}) between rendered and ground truth images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingaussianavatars(videoframes, cameraparams, flamemeshinit): # Initialize one Gaussian per FLAME mesh triangle gaussians = [] for tri in flamemeshinit.triangles: gaussians.append({ 'triid': tri.id, 'barycentric': np.array([0.33, 0.33, 0.34]), # Initialized inside triangle 'scale': np.array([0.01, 0.01, 0.01]), 'rotation': np.eye(3), 'opacity': 1.0, 'sh': np.zeros(48) }) # Training loop for frameidx, frame in enumerate(videoframes): cam = cameraparams[frameidx] pose, expr = flameparams[frameidx] # Deform FLAME mesh vertices using pose and expression parameters meshverts = deformflame(flamemeshinit.vertices, pose, expr) # # Update Gaussian positions constrained to their associated triangles for g in gaussians: v0, v1, v2 = meshverts[g['triid']] g['pos'] = g['barycentric'][0] v0 + g['barycentric'][1] v1 + g['barycentric'][2] v2 # Render scene using standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization renderedimage = rasterizegaussians3dgs(gaussians, cam) # # Compute photometric and perceptual losses loss = np.mean(np.abs(renderedimage - frame)) + 0.2 msssim(renderedimage, frame) # # Backpropagate gradients and update Gaussian parameters optimizerstep(gaussians, loss) # return gaussians, flameparams Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Number of Gaussians: One per triangle of the FLAME mesh. Edge Cases: Degenerate triangles: Ensure barycentric coordinates are valid. Precision: Barycentric coordinate optimization must maintain non-negativity and sum-to-one constraint. A method that combines parametric morphable face models (e.g., FLAME) with deformable 3D Gaussians, employing diffusion strategies and expression-aware deformation fields to disentangle rigid head poses from non-rigid facial movements. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by leveraging the topological consistency and editability of parametric meshes to solve the cross-frame correspondence and topology flexibility challenges inherent in unstructured Gaussian splatting for dynamic faces. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of triangles in the FLAME mesh. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Riggable; photorealistic head rendering. Limitations: Limited to head avatars; requires FLAME fitting. When to use: When high-fidelity, animatable head avatars are needed. When not: For full-body avatars or scenes without a parametric head model. Gaussian Avatars was introduced to reconstruct human avatars using 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses challenges such as handling dynamic Gaussians and supporting relighting. The method trains a FLAME model of the bust, associating each triangle with a Gaussian. It is also known as PSAvatar or Relightable Avatar. name: Head Avatar Modeling
body: A method that combines parametric morphable face models (e.g., FLAME) with deformable 3D Gaussians, employing diffusion strategies and expression-aware deformation fields to disentangle rigid head poses from non-rigid facial movements. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by leveraging the topological consistency and editability of parametric meshes to solve the cross-frame correspondence and topology flexibility challenges inherent in unstructured Gaussian splatting for dynamic faces. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view video sequences of a human head; FLAME model parameters (identity, pose, expression) or a pre-fitted FLAME mesh. Outputs: Deformable 3D Gaussians conditioned on the parametric head state, enabling real-time rendering of novel views and expressions. Data Structures: 1. FLAME Model: A parametric 3D morphable model defining the head geometry, controlled by identity, pose, and expression parameters. 2. Gaussian Primitives: Each Gaussian is associated with a location on the FLAME mesh surface or within the head volume, with attributes optimized during training. Steps: 1. Initialization: Generate an initial human mesh using the FLAME model. If a well-fitting pre-existing mesh is not available, fit the FLAME model to the input data. 2. Deformation Field Learning: Train an expression-aware deformation field that maps FLAME expression parameters to 3D Gaussian displacements, disentangling rigid head poses from non-rigid facial movements. 3. Gaussian Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian attributes while constraining them to remain consistent with the parametric head model to ensure topological flexibility and multi-view consistency. 4. Rendering: Render the scene using 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization with Gaussians deformed by the learned expression-aware field. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: FLAME parameters control facial expressions and geometry, though typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mesh-Free Input: When no well-fitting mesh is available, the method may train Gaussians with flat Gaussians and construct a "Triangle Soup" during training, which can pose challenges for large faces or unbounded scenes. Precision: Disentangling rigid pose from non-rigid expression requires careful initialization to avoid artifacts in complex expressions like eye closure or mouth opening. A 3D head avatar framework that overcomes global expression conditioning limitations by proposing Spatially-Varying Expression (SVE). Unlike prior methods using uniform global expression codes, SVE integrates both spatial and expression features to enable fine-grained control over facial geometry and rendering. A generation network produces SVE by combining 3DMM expression parameters with position-specific features. It uses a coarse-to-fine training strategy to refine geometry and rendering through initialization and adaptive sampling, capturing intricate details like wrinkles and eye motion with significantly higher fidelity than global-expression-based NeRFs. A technique to generate and modify human facial meshes using FLAME parameters, enabling animation of expressions like smiling, sadness, eye closure, and mouth opening. It involves generating an initial human mesh using the FLAME model and adjusting FLAME parameters to manipulate expressions directly. If a well-fitting pre-existing mesh is not available, the FLAME model is fitted to the data. Compared to static models, FLAME-based conditioning enables editable animations but shows lower PSNR metrics on facial reconstruction. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Qin et al.'s SVE method renders at 2K resolution, trains 4–5× faster than prior work, and runs in real-time. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Exploits the speed advantage and editability of Gaussian Splatting to enable fast training, real-time rendering, and precise control over deformations. Addresses challenges in cross-frame correspondence and topology flexibility. Limitations: FLAME-based conditioning shows lower PSNR metrics on facial reconstruction compared to some baselines. Reconstruction in challenging scenes (e.g., occlusions, sparse single-view inputs, or loose clothing) remains a critical challenge. When to use: When real-time rendering of dynamic facial expressions with high editability is required. When not: When maximum photometric fidelity (PSNR) is the sole priority and real-time performance is not critical. Originating from the convergence of parametric morphable models (like FLAME) and 3D Gaussian Splatting, this method addresses the need for expressive, real-time head avatars. The FLAME model, originally developed for facial animation, provides a structured representation of head geometry. The integration with Gaussian Splatting allows for efficient rendering and novel view synthesis, overcoming the limitations of global expression conditioning found in earlier NeRF-based methods. Recent developments include the introduction of 4K multi-view datasets for 16 identities to support these frameworks. name: Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars
head: GHG, GoHA, GoHA / GHG, Relightable Gaussian head methods using FLAME rig
body: Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars (GHG) is a method for reconstructing 3D head avatars that supports dynamic relighting under novel illumination conditions. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Avatar methods by using a FLAME-rigged Gaussian representation and a relightable BRDF to enable high-fidelity synthesis under arbitrary lighting. Inputs: Video capture of a talking head; initial FLAME mesh fit via MICA or DECA. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and material parameters for a relightable BRDF. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Primitives: Each Gaussian i stores position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and BRDF parameters (albedo, roughness). 2. FLAME Rig: Parametric head model with pose \theta, expression \beta, and identity \gamma. 3. Deformation Network: A lightweight MLP or explicit offset field mapping canonical positions to deformed positions conditioned on pose and expression. Steps: 1. Initialization: Fit a FLAME mesh to the input video to obtain identity \gamma. Initialize one Gaussian per triangle of the FLAME mesh in the canonical rest pose, stored in tangent space. 2. Deformation: For a target pose \theta and expression \beta, compute the rigid transformation from FLAME. Apply pose-conditioned offsets \Delta \mathbf{p} predicted by the deformation network to correct non-rigid skin deformation. Update covariance \Sigmai using the Jacobian J of the deformation map: \Sigma'i = J \Sigmai J^T + \sigma^2 I. 3. Relightable Rendering: Project deformed Gaussians to screen space and accumulate contributions front-to-back. Compute color using a relightable BRDF fr(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p}) parameterized by view \mathbf{v}, light \mathbf{l}, normal \mathbf{n}, and material \mathbf{p}. This replaces static spherical harmonics to allow rendering under arbitrary light environments \mathbf{L}. 4. Optimization: Minimize photometric \mathcal{L}{L1} and perceptual \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} losses between rendered and ground truth images. Freeze geometry and train the relightable BRDF parameters in a second stage if needed. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Focuses on volume visualization scenes with composable primitives and Blinn-Phong relighting, distinct from GHG's head-specific FLAME rig and BRDF approach. Memory: Compresses to \le 30 MB for a full avatar, including BRDF parameters. Strengths: Supports diverse lighting conditions and dynamic relighting. Limitations: Relighting quality depends on BRDF accuracy and FLAME fit quality. Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars were introduced to enable dynamic lighting changes for virtual production and telepresence. The method builds on Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction principles, specifically using the FLAME parametric head model for rigging. name: iVR-GS Relighting via Gaussian Primitives
head: iVR-GS
body: iVR-GS is a novel view synthesis (NVS) framework for volume visualization (VolVis) scenes that leverages composable and editable 3D Gaussian primitives to enable flexible exploration without direct access to volume data. It distinguishes itself from baseline 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and NeRF-based methods (Plenoxels, CCNeRF) by explicitly modeling lighting effects via the Blinn-Phong model, allowing for high-quality relighting and scene editing. Unlike simple image-space interpolation, iVR-GS reconstructs underlying geometry to ensure physically plausible relighting results. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input views of a VolVis scene. Outputs: Relit images of the scene under varying light source polar angles. Data Structures: The method represents the scene using 3D Gaussian primitives. The exact parameterization of each primitive is not given in the sources. Method Steps: 1. Light Source Configuration: Fix the azimuthal angle of the light source to be identical to the camera's azimuthal angle. 2. Polar Angle Adjustment: Vary the polar angle of the light source from -90^\circ (bottom) to 90^\circ (top). 3. Sampling: Uniformly sample 180 images along this light source trajectory. 4. Rendering: Render the scene using the Blinn-Phong lighting model applied to the Gaussian primitives. Formulas: The lighting effect is modeled using the Blinn-Phong model. The specific mathematical formulation for the Blinn-Phong shading is not detailed in the provided text, but it is applied to the Gaussian primitives to compute the final color. Parameters: Number of sampled images: 180. Polar angle range: [-90^\circ, 90^\circ]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lighting Model Mismatch: iVR-GS relies on the Blinn-Phong model. It may encounter challenges when handling VolVis scenes that employ different lighting models, potentially requiring a redesign of the lighting representation. Interpolation Failure: Linear interpolation (LERP) of the first and last relit images fails to produce faithful results because it ignores geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
