Azimuth is in the XY plane, polar is elevation from XY plane.""" azrad = math.radians(azimuthdeg) polrad = math.radians(polardeg) cospol = math.cos(polrad) return (cospol math.cos(azrad), cospol math.sin(azrad), math.sin(polrad)) def relightivrgs(gaussians, cameraazimuth, numsamples=180): """Relight a scene represented by 3D Gaussian primitives using iVR-GS.""" images = [] polarangles = linspace(-90.0, 90.0, numsamples) for polarangle in polarangles: lightdir = sphericaltocartesian(cameraazimuth, polarangle) # The specific Blinn-Phong shading formula and Gaussian rasterization pipeline are not given in the sources. image = None images.append(image) return images Extends the framework by parameterizing each Gaussian with explicit shading attributes and using a palette-based color representation for decoupled geometry and appearance editing. The parent method introducing relightable Gaussian avatars supporting diverse lighting conditions. Quality: Produces higher-quality reconstruction results compared to Plenoxels, CCNeRF, and base 3DGS. Real-time: Supports real-time scene editing and exploration. Limitations: The reliance on the Blinn-Phong model limits its applicability to scenes with different lighting models. Comparison: Outperforms linear interpolation (LERP) for relighting tasks by modeling geometry, whereas LERP fails to produce faithful results. iVR-GS (Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting) was presented as a novel NVS framework for VolVis scenes. It addresses limitations in existing NVS methods by leveraging composable and editable Gaussian primitives. The method was evaluated on datasets such as "chameleon" and "supernova". iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Editable Gaussian Representation
head: Editable Gaussian, iVR-GS Gaussian
body: Editable Gaussian Representation extends the iVR-GS framework [7018-ivr-gs-relighting-via-gaussian-primitives.md] by parameterizing each Gaussian primitive with explicit shading attributes, enabling direct manipulation of color, opacity, and lighting effects. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which treats color as a static view-dependent attribute, this method decouples geometry from shading, allowing for scene recoloring and light editing by modifying specific primitive parameters rather than retraining the entire model. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-view images of a scene; initial Gaussian parameters (geometry and shading); ground-truth color images for regularization. Output: A collection of N editable Gaussian primitives, each defined by geometry and shading attributes, optionally compressed via Vector Quantization (VQ) and composed into a single model. Data Structures: Each editable Gaussian i is parameterized with two sets of attributes: 1. Geometry Attributes: mean position \mui, rotation quaternion qi, scale si, opacity oi, and normal ni. 2. Shading Attributes: offset color \Delta ci, ambient coefficient k{ia}, diffuse coefficient k{id}, specular coefficient k{is}, and shininess \betai. A global Palette Color cp \in \mathbb{R}^3 is maintained per basic scene. Rendering Formula: The voxel color cv is expressed as cv = cp + \Delta ci. The final rendered color is accumulated using standard alpha compositing, where the contribution of Gaussian i depends on its opacity \alphai (derived from oi) and depth-based transmittance Ti. Training and Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians with geometry attributes. Set the palette color cp to the mean color value of the input multi-view images. 2. Regularization: During optimization, apply the following loss terms alongside the standard 3DGS photometric loss: Opacity L1 Regularization: Encourages opacity to be low to neutralize the tendency to use more Gaussians for compact surfaces, facilitating removal. (Specific formula not provided in the sources.) Offset Color Sparsity: Prevents significant palette color shifts. Defined as the L1 loss of the rendered offset color map \Delta C = \sum{i \in N} Ti \alphai \Delta ci. Bilateral Smoothness: Ensures shading attributes do not change significantly in smooth-color regions. For the ambient coefficient map Ka = \sum{i \in N} Ti \alphai k{ia} and ground-truth color c{\text{GT}}, the loss is L{\text{smooth}} = \| \nabla Ka \| \exp(-\| \nabla c{\text{GT}} \|). This regularization is similarly applied to kd, ks, and \beta. 3. Pruning: Periodically remove low-opacity Gaussians to reduce model size, similar to base 3DGS. 4. Compression & Composition: To recover all visible parts, multiple basic iVR-GS models are composed into a single model. Before composition, VQ using k-means clustering is applied to extract a more compact form of editable Gaussians for each basic model. The exact compression ratio and compression time are not given in the sources. Parameters: Palette Color (cp): Fixed during training as the mean color of input images; adjustable during inference for scene recoloring. Offset Color (\Delta c): Added to enhance the expressiveness of cp. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Compact Surfaces: The model tends to utilize more Gaussians to reconstruct compact surfaces because color depends on the normal attribute, making opacity L1 regularization critical to neutralize this effect. Palette Shifts: Without sparsity regularization on \Delta c, the offset color may cause significant deviations from the intended palette. Text-Driven Gaussian Editing modifies the appearance of VolVis scenes represented by textured Gaussian primitives using natural language text prompts while preserving underlying geometry and lighting. It distinguishes itself from iterative baseline methods by employing a one-time update strategy that applies image-to-image (IP2P) editing only once on a small subset of multi-view images, significantly reducing editing time and avoiding blurriness in semi-transparent scenes. Choose this variant when text-based appearance editing is required without altering scene geometry or requiring iterative optimization. Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to base 3DGS with additional regularization overhead. Memory Complexity: The base model size is larger than standard 3DGS due to additional shading attributes per Gaussian, but VQ reduces the final model size. Performance: Enables real-time scene editing (recoloring, opacity adjustment, light direction) without retraining. Strengths: Explicit control over lighting and color; composability of scenes; reduced model size via pruning and VQ. Limitations: Requires multi-view input for training; complexity in managing shared codebooks for composition. The Editable Gaussian Representation was introduced in the iVR-GS paper, which proposes Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds upon the iVR-GS method which models lighting effects using the Blinn-Phong model [7018-ivr-gs-relighting-via-gaussian-primitives.md]. The method was developed to address the lack of explicit editability in standard 3DGS for volume visualization scenes. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Text-Driven Gaussian Editing
head: One-time IP2P Text Editing for Gaussians, TexGS-VolVis Text-Driven Editing, Text-Driven NPSE
body: Text-Driven Gaussian Editing modifies the appearance of volume visualization (VolVis) scenes represented by textured Gaussian primitives using natural language text prompts, while preserving the underlying geometry and lighting. It distinguishes itself from iterative baseline methods by employing a one-time update strategy that applies image-to-image (IP2P) editing only once on a small subset of multi-view images, significantly reducing editing time. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-reconstructed textured Gaussian representation of a VolVis scene and a text prompt describing the desired style or appearance change. Output: An edited Gaussian representation where the texture attributes are updated to reflect the text prompt, while geometry remains fixed. Data Structures: The method operates on textured Gaussian primitives. Each primitive stores geometry attributes (position, rotation, scale) and appearance attributes (opacity, base color, and texture attributes). The text-driven editing process specifically targets the texture attributes for appearance modification. Steps: 1. Subset Selection: Select a small subset of multi-view images from the training set. 2. IP2P Editing: Apply an image-to-image (IP2P) diffusion model to the selected subset of images using the text prompt to generate edited target images. 3. Texture Update: Optimize only the texture attributes of the Gaussian primitives to match the edited target images from Step 2. The geometry and base color are kept fixed to ensure geometry consistency. 4. Rendering: Render the edited Gaussian representation to verify the result. Parameters: Number of primitives: 108,119 for 512×512 resolution. Editing Time: 1.6 minutes for 512×512 resolution. Rendering Resolution: 512×512. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Elliptical Artifacts: IP2P editing results are not always geometry-consistent with scene content, and updating the model on a small subset of multi-view images amplifies these inaccuracies, leading to visible elliptical artifacts in the rendered output. Geometry Consistency: Unlike methods that update geometry or require iterative multi-view consistency updates, this method relies on fixed geometry, which prevents geometric distortion but may limit expressiveness if the texture attribute alone cannot capture complex styles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def textdrivengaussianediting(gaussians, textprompt, multiviewimages, subsetindices): # Step 1: Select subset of images selectedimages = [multiviewimages[i] for i in subsetindices] # Step 2: Apply IP2P editing to generate target images editedimages = applyip2pdiffusion(selectedimages, textprompt) # Step 3: Update only texture attributes of Gaussians to match edited images for primitive in gaussians: primitive.texture = optimizetextureattribute(primitive, editedimages, selectedimages) return gaussians def applyip2pdiffusion(images, prompt): # Standard IP2P diffusion: encode images to latent space, # condition on text prompt, denoise, decode to edited images. return [diffusionmodel.edit(img, prompt) for img in images] def optimizetextureattribute(primitive, editedimages, originalimages): # Gradient descent to update texture parameter lr = 0.01 for step in range(100): rendered = renderprimitive(primitive, originalimages) loss = sum((r - e)2 for r, e in zip(rendered, editedimages)) gradient = computegradient(loss, primitive.texture) primitive.texture -= lr gradient return primitive.texture def renderprimitive(primitive, images): # Standard Gaussian splatting render for a single primitive across viewpoints return [splat(primitive, view) for view in images] def computegradient(loss, texture): # Standard backpropagation through the rendering and loss function return gradientdescentstep(loss, texture) Stylizes VolVis scenes using text instructions while keeping geometry fixed and updating only texture attributes. It uses a one-time update strategy to avoid the blurriness associated with iterative approaches in semi-transparent scenes. It sets itself apart from siblings like StyleSplat by embedding texture maps within Gaussian primitives to express complex style patterns and reduce elliptical artifacts. Choose this when geometry consistency and detailed style patterns are required without iterative multi-view updates. Time and Memory Complexity: Editing Time: TexGS-VolVis takes 1.6 minutes for 512×512 resolution, compared to 7.2 minutes for DGE, 38.3 minutes for IG2G, and 44.69 minutes for IN2N. Rendering Time: Mean/Max rendering time for TexGS-VolVis is 7.21/9.93 ms at 512×512 resolution. Model Size: TexGS-VolVis uses 221 MB for 108,119 primitives, which is larger than DGE (87 MB) and IG2G (57 MB) but smaller than IN2N (1,150 MB). Scaling: The method scales well with editing time due to the one-time update strategy, but rendering time depends on the number of primitives and resolution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High CLIP directional similarity (0.174) compared to IN2N (0.043), IG2G (0.134), and DGE (0.133). Produces detailed and accurate 3D edits that align closely with text prompts. Geometry-consistent editing. Limitations: May exhibit elliptical artifacts if IP2P results are not geometry-consistent. Less expressive than methods that update geometry, potentially resulting in low-frequency appearances if the texture attribute cannot capture complex styles. When to Use: Use when fast editing is required and geometry consistency is critical. Suitable for VolVis scenes where detailed style patterns are needed without iterative multi-view updates. When Not to Use: Avoid when the desired edit requires significant geometric changes or when the texture attribute alone is insufficient to express the desired style. Text-Driven Gaussian Editing is part of the TexGS-VolVis framework, which focuses on expressive scene editing for volume visualization using textured Gaussian splatting. It was introduced to address the limitations of iterative editing methods, which are slow. The method leverages the one-time update strategy to achieve faster editing times while maintaining high-quality results. name: Text-Driven Non-Photorealistic Scene Editing
head: Image-driven NPSE, Text-Driven Gaussian Editing (for VolVis), Text-driven NPSE, Texture-Attribute Non-Photorealistic Scene Editing (NPSE)
body: Text-Driven Non-Photorealistic Scene Editing (NPSE) stylizes volume visualization (VolVis) scenes represented by textured Gaussian primitives using text instructions, while Image-Driven NPSE performs the same task using a reference image prompt. Both variants optimize only the texture attributes of the Gaussian representation to preserve the underlying geometry and lighting, distinguishing them from methods that alter geometry or require iterative multi-view consistency updates. It sets itself apart from siblings like StyleSplat by embedding texture maps within Gaussian primitives to express complex style patterns and reduce elliptical artifacts, leveraging a one-time update strategy for text-driven editing to avoid the blurriness associated with iterative approaches in semi-transparent scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained TexGS-VolVis scene (Gaussian primitives with geometry \mu, shading \beta, and texture attributes), a text prompt (for text-driven) or an image prompt I{prmt} (for image-driven), and optionally a 2D segmentation mask for region-specific editing. Outputs: An optimized TexGS-VolVis scene with modified texture attributes that reflect the stylized appearance. Data Structures: The method operates on Gaussian primitives enhanced with a texture attribute. Each primitive stores: Geometry attributes (e.g., mean position \mu). Shading attributes (e.g., \beta). Texture attributes: A texture map (set of texels) associated with the primitive. Opacity: A scalar value controlling transparency. View-independent color c{ind}: Used only if the texture attribute is disabled. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: For Image-Driven NPSE: Randomly initialize all Gaussian texture maps. Define the view-independent color using the texture-sampled color, ignoring palette colors. For Text-Driven NPSE: Initialize the scene opacity at 2\times its target value. Fix all geometry attributes (\mu) and shading attributes (\beta) to preserve consistent geometry and lighting. 2. Prompt Generation (Text-Driven Only): Use the IP2P model (based on Stable Diffusion) to generate edited images from unedited multi-view images and the text instruction. Set classifier-free guidance scale for input multi-view images to 1.25. Set classifier-free guidance scale for text prompts to 12.5. Ensure the IP2P model is loaded and configured with the specified guidance scales before inference. 3. Optimization Loop: Select training views. For text-driven NPSE, use only six views (front, back, left, right, top, bottom) to reduce ambiguity. For image-driven NPSE, use the full set of training views (e.g., 162 uniformly sampled via icosphere sampling). Render the scene R from the selected training views using Blinn-Phong shading. Calculate the loss function based on the editing type: Image-Driven: Use L{img} (defined below). Text-Driven: Use an RGB reconstruction loss between the rendered image R and the IP2P-generated edited image. Update only the texture attributes (or c{ind} if texture is disabled) via gradient descent. Opacity Adjustment (Text-Driven Only): Gradually reduce the scene's opacity from the initial 2\times target value to 0.5\times over fixed iteration intervals to prevent occlusion of unedited primitives and reduce blurriness from inconsistent edits. 4. Iteration Count: For Image-Driven NPSE: Optimize for 3,000 iterations. For Text-Driven NPSE: Optimize for 1,500 iterations using the IP2P editing images. 5. Region-Specific Editing (Optional): If editing specific regions, use a 2D-lift-3D segmentation approach: Render a view from TexGS-VolVis. Use a 2D segmentation model (e.g., SAM) with user-specified point prompts to generate a 2D mask. Lift the 2D mask to 3D by identifying and segmenting the corresponding Gaussian primitives. Apply the editing optimization only to the primitives in the segmented group. Formulas: The loss function for image-driven NPSE is: L{img} = \lambdas L{NNFM}(R, I{prmt}) + (1 - \lambdas) \| C(R) - C(I{prmt}) \|2 Where: R is the rendered image from TexGS-VolVis. I{prmt} is the image prompt. C is a pretrained CLIP model. L{NNFM} is the Neural Network Feature Matching (NNFM) loss using a pretrained VGG-16 network to capture fine stylization details. \| C(R) - C(I{prmt}) \|2 is the L2 distance between feature vectors extracted by CLIP, encouraging global style consistency. \lambdas is the hyperparameter balancing fine details and global style. If the texture attribute is not used, the appearance is edited by updating the view-independent color c{ind} within each primitive. Parameters: \lambdas: Hyperparameter balancing fine stylization details and global style consistency. \lambdas = 0.0: Emphasizes global style patterns. \lambdas = 0.5: Intermediate balance. \lambdas = 0.9: Emphasizes finer, more localized style details (default). \lambdas = 1.0: Maximum emphasis on fine details. Training Image Resolution: 800×800 for image-driven editing (balances quality and fitting time). 512×512 for text-driven editing (avoids out-of-memory issues with IP2P). Training Views: 162 uniformly sampled via icosphere sampling is sufficient; increasing beyond this yields marginal gains. Iterations: 3,000 for image-driven; 1,500 for text-driven. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Text Prompt Accuracy: Text-based editing relies heavily on the IP2P model. Inaccurate or vague text prompts lead to erroneous editing results. Opacity Issues: High opacity causes occlusion, leaving uncovered primitives unedited. Low opacity leads to blurry stylization due to inconsistent IP2P edits across views. The gradual opacity reduction strategy mitigates this. Storage: The texture attribute can occupy significant storage space, especially with high texel counts, resulting in larger model sizes compared to other Gaussian Splatting methods. Segmentation Efficiency: The 2D-lift-3D segmentation method requires identifying and segmenting corresponding Gaussian primitives for each 2D mask, which can be inefficient for scenes requiring multiple rounds of segmentation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def textdrivennpse(texgsvolvis, textprompt, numiterations=1500): # 1. Generate edited images using IP2P model on 6 training views trainingviews = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # front, back, left, right, top, bottom editedimages = [] for viewidx in trainingviews: uneditedimage = render(texgsvolvis, viewidx) # IP2P model (Stable Diffusion-based) generates edited image # Classifier-free guidance scales: 1.25 for image, 12.5 for text editedimg = ip2pgenerate(uneditedimage, textprompt, 1.25, 12.5) editedimages.append(editedimg) # 2. Initialize opacity at 2x target value targetopacity = texgsvolvis.gettargetopacity() currentopacity = 2.0 targetopacity texgsvolvis.setopacity(currentopacity) # 3. Fix geometry and shading attributes texgsvolvis.freezegeometry() texgsvolvis.freezeshading() # 4. Optimization loop for i in range(numiterations): # Gradually reduce opacity to 0.5x target over fixed iteration intervals progress = i / max(numiterations - 1, 1) currentopacity = targetopacity (2.0 - 1.5 progress) texgsvolvis.setopacity(currentopacity) # Render and compute RGB reconstruction loss totalloss = 0.0 for viewidx, editedimg in zip(trainingviews, editedimages): renderedimg = render(texgsvolvis, viewidx) loss = F.mseloss(renderedimg, editedimg) totalloss += loss # Update only texture attributes (or cind if texture is disabled) texgsvolvis.textureattributes.retaingrad() totalloss.backward() texgsvolvis.textureattributes.data -= 0.01 texgsvolvis.textureattributes.grad return texgsvolvis def imagedrivennpse(texgsvolvis, imageprompt, lambdas=0.9, numiterations=3000): # 1. Initialize texture maps randomly texgsvolvis.initializetexturemapsrandomly() # Define view-independent color using texture-sampled color texgsvolvis.setviewindependentcolorfromtexture() # 2. Fix geometry and shading attributes texgsvolvis.freezegeometry() texgsvolvis.freezeshading() # 3. Optimization loop for i in range(numiterations): # Select a random training view viewidx = random.randint(0, len(texgsvolvis.trainingviews) - 1) renderedimg = render(texgsvolvis, viewidx) # Compute Limg loss # NNFM loss using pretrained VGG-16 for fine details nnfmloss = nnfmlossfunction(renderedimg, imageprompt) # CLIP loss for global style consistency clipfeatr = clipmodelencode(renderedimg) clipfeatp = clipmodelencode(imageprompt) cliploss = F.mseloss(clipfeatr, clipfeatp) loss = lambdas nnfmloss + (1 - lambdas) cliploss # Update texture attributes texgsvolvis.textureattributes.retaingrad() loss.backward() texgsvolvis.textureattributes.data -= 0.01 texgsvolvis.textureattributes.grad return texgsvolvis def render(texgsvolvis, viewidx): # Standard differentiable splatting/volume rendering return texgsvolvis.render(viewidx) def ip2pgenerate(image, prompt, scaleimg, scaletxt): # Calls pretrained IP2P model with given guidance scales # Returns edited image tensor return image def nnfmlossfunction(rendered, prompt): # Computes Neural Network Feature Matching loss using pretrained VGG-16 # Returns scalar loss return F.mseloss(rendered, prompt) def clipmodelencode(image): # Extracts feature vector using pretrained CLIP model return image Stylizes volume visualization scenes by transferring the artistic style of a reference image onto a 3D Gaussian representation, ensuring multi-view consistency. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like StyleSplat by embedding texture attributes within Gaussian primitives, allowing each primitive to express multiple colors and reducing elliptical artifacts, while leveraging a combined NNFM and CLIP loss strategy to capture both local and global style patterns. Time Complexity: The method requires iterative optimization. Image-driven NPSE takes approximately 3,000 iterations, while text-driven NPSE takes 1,500 iterations. Fitting time is influenced by the number of primitives and training image resolution. Memory Complexity: The texture attribute can occupy significant storage space, especially as the number of texels increases, resulting in a larger model size than other Gaussian Splatting methods. Text-driven editing uses lower resolution (512×512) to avoid out-of-memory issues with the IP2P model. Strengths: Real-time rendering, expressive style patterns via texture attributes, geometry-consistent editing without iterative updates for text-driven NPSE, and flexible partial editing via 2D-lift-3D segmentation. Limitations: High storage requirements for texture attributes, reliance on IP2P model quality for text-driven editing, and potential inefficiency in 2D-lift-3D segmentation for complex scenes. When to Use: When high-quality, expressive non-photorealistic stylization of volume visualization scenes is required, and real-time rendering is needed. When Not to Use: When storage space is limited, or when precise text prompts are not available for text-driven editing. TexGS-VolVis is the first 2DGS-based framework in VolVis aimed at expressive scene editing. It builds upon existing NeRF and 3DGS scene editing approaches guided by text instructions. The method was introduced in the paper "TexGS-VolVis: Expressive Scene Editing for Volume Visualization via Textured Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the challenges of applying iterative editing strategies to complex and semi-transparent VolVis scenes, which often result in blurry appearances or geometry-inconsistent edits. name: Image-Driven Non-Photorealistic Scene Editing (NPSE)
head: Image-Driven NPSE, TexGS-VolVis Image-Driven NPSE
body: Image-Driven Non-Photorealistic Scene Editing (NPSE) stylizes volume visualization scenes by transferring the artistic style of a reference image onto a 3D Gaussian representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like StyleSplat by embedding texture attributes within Gaussian primitives, allowing each primitive to express multiple colors and reducing elliptical artifacts, while leveraging a combined NNFM and CLIP loss strategy to capture both local and global style patterns. Inputs: A set of multi-view input images of the scene. A reference style image. Text prompts (optional, used for classifier-free guidance in the IP2P model). Outputs: A set of textured Gaussian primitives representing the stylized scene. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Defined by position, covariance, opacity, base color, and a texture attribute. The texture attribute allows the primitive to store multiple color values, enabling complex style expression. Model Storage: The model size is dominated by the texture attributes, which constitute over 90% of the total storage. Parameters: Classifier-free guidance scale: Set to 1.25 for input multi-view images and 12.5 for text prompts when using the Stable Diffusion model IP2P. Rendering Resolution: 800×800 pixels in reported experiments. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives from the input multi-view images. 2. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, base color, and texture attributes) to match the reference style. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss using a combination of: Neural Style Loss (NNFM): To preserve detailed style patterns and ensure multi-view consistency. CLIP Loss: To capture global style patterns from the reference image. Note: While other methods may use only VGG-based losses, TexGS-VolVis explicitly combines NNFM and CLIP. 4. Rendering: Render the scene using the optimized textured Gaussian primitives. The texture attribute allows each Gaussian to express multiple colors during rendering, enhancing expressive capacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizegaussiansforstyle(gaussians, inputimages, referencestyleimage, textprompt, maxiterations=1000): """Optimizes Gaussian primitives to match a reference style.""" # Initialize Gaussians from input multi-view images gaussians = initializegaussiansfromviews(gaussians, inputimages) # IP2P classifier-free guidance scales guidancescaleimage = 1.25 guidancescaletext = 12.5 # Loss functions nnfmlossfn = NeuralStyleLoss() cliplossfn = CLIPLoss() for iteration in range(maxiterations): totalloss = 0.0 for renderedimg in renderallviews(gaussians): # NNFM loss preserves detailed style and multi-view consistency totalloss += nnfmlossfn(renderedimg, referencestyleimage) # CLIP loss captures global style patterns totalloss += cliplossfn(renderedimg, referencestyleimage) # Backpropagate and update all Gaussian parameters updategaussians(gaussians, totalloss) return gaussians def renderallviews(gaussians, views): """Renders scene using textured Gaussian primitives.""" images = [] for view in views: projected = projectgaussiansto2d(gaussians, view) sortedgaussians = sortbydepth(projected) image = rasterizewithtexturemapping(sortedgaussians) images.append(image) return images def initializegaussiansfromviews(gaussians, inputimages): # Standard backprojection initialization return gaussians def projectgaussiansto2d(gaussians, view): # Apply view-projection matrix to 3D positions and covariances return gaussians def sortbydepth(projectedgaussians): # Sort primitives by distance to camera center return projectedgaussians def rasterizewithtexturemapping(sortedgaussians): # Alpha-blend 2D ellipses using texture attributes for color return image def updategaussians(gaussians, loss): # Gradient descent step on all parameters pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Elliptical Artifacts: Vanilla Gaussian primitives (representing only a single color) can lead to unnatural elliptical distortions, particularly at object boundaries like wood textures. The texture attribute mitigates this. Performance: The additional lighting and texture mapping computations make rendering slightly slower than methods like StyleSplat. Optimization Time: Using both VGG and CLIP during optimization makes TexGS-VolVis slightly slower than ARF and StyleSplat in terms of editing time. The primary implementation of Image-Driven NPSE described in the sources. It uses textured Gaussian primitives and a combined NNFM/CLIP loss. Choose this when high-fidelity, multi-color style transfer with multi-view consistency is required. TexGS-VolVis A baseline method using vanilla Gaussian primitives (single color per primitive). It is faster and has a smaller model size but produces less detailed results and suffers from elliptical artifacts. StyleSplat A NeRF-based baseline using Plenoxels and NNFM loss. It requires significantly more storage due to its explicit feature grid. ARF A NeRF-based baseline using a palette color network and unrestricted color network with NNFM loss. It has the slowest rendering time among the compared methods. StyleRF-VolVis Time and Memory Complexity: Editing Time: TexGS-VolVis takes 8.0 minutes for 800×800 resolution, compared to 6.9 minutes for StyleSplat and 5.9 minutes for ARF. Model Size: TexGS-VolVis uses 223 MB, significantly larger than StyleSplat (89 MB) due to texture attributes, but smaller than ARF (975 MB). Rendering Time: TexGS-VolVis has a mean/max rendering time of 11.82/13.32 ms, which is faster than StyleRF-VolVis (243.61/348.58 ms) but slightly slower than StyleSplat (6.11/10.27 ms). Primitive Count: TexGS-VolVis uses 129,857 primitives, far fewer than StyleSplat's 357,090, while producing more detail-rich results. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Produces more detailed and expressive results than baselines, captures local and global style patterns, and uses fewer primitives. Limitations: Slower optimization due to CLIP loss, larger model size than StyleSplat, and slightly slower rendering than StyleSplat. When to Use: Use when high-quality, multi-color stylization with multi-view consistency is needed, and storage/compute for optimization is available. Avoid if minimal model size or fastest rendering speed is the primary constraint, in which case StyleSplat is preferable. TexGS-VolVis was introduced in the paper "TexGS-VolVis: Expressive Scene Editing for Volume Visualization via Textured Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the Gaussian Splatting technique and extends it with texture attributes for non-photorealistic rendering in volume visualization contexts. The method addresses the limitations of single-color Gaussian primitives in capturing complex artistic styles. name: NoPoSplat
body: NoPoSplat is a 3D Gaussian Splatting method that eliminates the requirement for known camera poses during training. It solves the problem of pose ambiguity by anchoring the scene representation to a canonical coordinate system derived from a single input view and introducing intrinsics token embeddings to resolve scale ambiguity. This approach achieves superior novel view synthesis quality, particularly in scenarios with minimal view overlap, distinguishing it from sibling methods that rely on pre-calibrated camera parameters. Inputs: A set of input images, typically sparse views. No known camera poses or intrinsics are required. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined in a canonical coordinate system. Data Structures: Canonical Coordinate System: A fixed reference frame anchored to the geometry of the single input view used as the reference. Intrinsics Token Embeddings: Learnable embeddings that encode camera intrinsic parameters to infer projection geometry without explicit pose input. Steps: 1. Canonical Anchoring: Establish a fixed reference frame anchored to the geometry observed in a single input view. 2. Intrinsics Encoding: Generate intrinsics token embeddings to represent camera intrinsic parameters. 3. Scale Resolution: Apply the intrinsics token embeddings to resolve the scale ambiguity inherent in monocular or sparse-view reconstruction. 4. Differentiable Rendering: Project the Gaussians from the canonical coordinate system to target views and compute gradients for optimization. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: Without known poses, scale ambiguity is a critical issue; NoPoSplat addresses this via intrinsics token embeddings. Minimal View Overlap: The method is specifically noted for superior performance in scenarios with minimal view overlap. No subtopics. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Eliminates the need for known camera poses and achieves superior novel view synthesis quality in scenarios with minimal view overlap. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Use when camera poses are unknown or unreliable, especially in sparse-view settings with minimal overlap. name: SplatArmor
head: SplatArmor [S1]
body: SplatArmor is a method for reconstructing animatable human avatars using drivable 3D Gaussians. It addresses the limitation of standard rigid deformation in capturing large, non-rigid motions and pose-dependent appearance effects. It sets itself apart by leveraging two distinct Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to predict large motions and employing SE(3) fields to model pose-dependent effects, enabling more detailed geometry and appearance reconstruction than methods relying solely on Linear Blend Skinning (LBS). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view video frames of a human subject; SMPL mesh parameters (pose \theta, shape \beta) corresponding to each frame. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the avatar, parameterized to be drivable by SMPL parameters, allowing rendering of novel poses and views. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Position \mathbf{p}, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}. SMPL Model: Parametric human body model providing a canonical mesh and skinning weights. MLPs: Two separate neural networks used for motion prediction. SE(3) Fields: A field representation encoding pose-dependent transformations. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians on the canonical SMPL mesh surface. 2. Large Motion Prediction: Use two different MLPs to predict large motions. These MLPs operate on inputs derived from the SMPL space and the canonical space. 3. Pose-Dependent Effects: Apply SE(3) fields to capture pose-dependent effects. This allows the avatar's appearance and geometry to change dynamically based on the pose \theta. 4. Deformation: Combine the rigid LBS deformation (from the parent method) with the predicted large motions and SE(3) field adjustments to transform canonical Gaussians to the target pose. 5. Rendering: Render the deformed Gaussians using differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. 6. Training: Optimize Gaussian parameters and MLP weights by minimizing photometric and perceptual losses against input video frames. Formulas: Large Motion Prediction: Let M{SMPL} and M{Canonical} be the two MLPs. The predicted motion \Delta \mathbf{p}{large} is derived from these networks. \Delta \mathbf{p}{large} = f(M{SMPL}, M{Canonical}, \theta, \beta) (Specific internal structure of M{SMPL} and M{Canonical} is not detailed in the sources.) SE(3) Fields: The SE(3) field provides a pose-dependent transformation T{SE3}(\theta). \mathbf{p}{final} = T{SE3}(\theta) \cdot (\mathbf{p}{LBS} + \Delta \mathbf{p}{large}) (Exact formulation of the SE(3) field application is not detailed in the sources.) Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Performance: The sources do not provide specific performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) for SplatArmor. Strengths: Capable of capturing more dynamic details and pose-dependent effects compared to methods using only LBS. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of dynamic human avatars with significant non-rigid motion and pose-dependent appearance changes is required. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and simpler deformation methods (like pure LBS) are sufficient, or when real-time performance is critical and the overhead of MLP inference is prohibitive. SplatArmor was introduced in the context of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting for human avatar reconstruction. It is cited as a method that improves upon basic drivable 3D Gaussians by incorporating more sophisticated motion prediction and pose-dependent modeling. name: SMPL-based rigid/non-rigid deformation
head: SMPL-driven Gaussian deformation, Parametric Gaussian Avatar deformation
body: This family of methods reconstructs animatable human avatars by anchoring 3D Gaussians to the surface of the SMPL parametric body model and deforming them from a canonical rest pose to a target pose \theta and expression \beta. It solves the problem of dynamic human reconstruction by providing a geometric prior that ensures topological consistency and enables real-time novel view synthesis and animation. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Gaussian Splatting by its explicit reliance on a parametric mesh for initialization and deformation, and from Gaussian Avatar by its use of explicit rigid/non-rigid transformation pipelines (LBS + residual) rather than purely feedforward parameter prediction. The family shares the following mechanisms, terms, and math, building on the splatting principles of primitive representation, transformation, rasterization, and compositing [23-splatting.md]. Parametric Anchoring: Gaussians are initialized on the surface of a parametric mesh (e.g., SMPL, FLAME) in a canonical rest pose [S1, 1477-gaussian-avatars.md, 1482-relightable-gaussian-codec-avatars.md]. Each Gaussian i is associated with a specific triangle t or vertex of the mesh. Deformation Pipeline: To animate the avatar, Gaussians are deformed from the canonical pose to a target pose \theta and expression \beta [S1, 8385-smpl-based-rigid-non-rigid-deformation.md]. 1. Rigid Deformation: The canonical position \mathbf{p}i is transformed using Linear Blend Skinning (LBS): \mathbf{p}{rigid} = \sum{j=1}^{N{bones}} w{i,j} \mathbf{T}j(\theta) \mathbf{p}i where w{i,j} are skinning weights and \mathbf{T}j(\theta) are bone transformation matrices. 2. Non-Rigid Deformation: A residual offset \Delta \mathbf{p} is predicted by a deformation network (e.g., MLP) conditioned on pose and/or canonical position. The final position is: \mathbf{p}'i = \mathbf{p}{rigid} + \Delta \mathbf{p} Some methods predict parameters directly via a feedforward network, implicitly handling deformation. 3. Covariance Update: The covariance matrix \Sigmai is transformed using the Jacobian J of the deformation map with respect to the canonical position: \Sigma'i = J \Sigmai J^T + \sigma^2 I where \sigma^2 I is a small regularization term to ensure positive definiteness. The Jacobian J includes contributions from both LBS and the non-rigid deformation network [G, 11805-full-body-avatar-modeling.md]. Differentiable Rendering: The deformed Gaussians are rendered using differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. Gradients are computed from the rendered image to the Gaussian parameters and network weights. Loss Function: Training minimizes a combination of photometric and perceptual losses [S1, 1477-gaussian-avatars.md, 1482-relightable-gaussian-codec-avatars.md]: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the L1 loss between rendered and ground truth images, and \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} is the multi-scale structural similarity loss. Gaussian Avatar is a method for reconstructing animatable full-body human avatars from video by leveraging the SMPL parametric model as a geometric prior. It solves the problem of dynamic human reconstruction by using a feedforward network to predict Gaussian parameters directly from pose features, enabling real-time novel view synthesis and animation. It is distinguished from siblings like 3DGS-Avatar by its reliance on a feedforward prediction of parameters via pose features rather than explicit per-Gaussian rigid/non-rigid transformation pipelines during inference. 3DGS-Avatar reconstructs full-body human avatars by combining 3D Gaussians with rigid and non-rigid transformations of an underlying SMPL model. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by replacing spherical harmonics with a shallow MLP to model per-Gaussian color, enabling pose-dependent appearance modeling. Animatable Gaussians is a method for reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) driven by the SMPL-X parametric model. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity, real-time renderable human avatars from monocular video by explicitly modeling pose-conditioned deformation offsets. It is distinguished from sibling methods like 3DGS-Avatar, which uses per-Gaussian deformation MLPs, and GaussianAvatars, which focuses on head-driven avatars using the FLAME model. UV-based motion parameterization is a method for modeling dynamic human deformation by reparameterizing 3D spatial coordinates into 2D surface-level UV coordinates combined with time. It solves the problem of high-dimensional motion field learning by exploiting the prior that human motion occurs primarily at the surface level, reducing the input dimensionality from 4D space-time (x, y, z, t) to 3D surface-time (u, v, t). This approach is distinct from volumetric parameterizations because it leverages the parametric mesh's surface topology to enforce spatial coherence among nearby surface points, resulting in significantly lower memory usage and faster convergence. It builds on SMPL-based rigid/non-rigid deformation by predicting residual offsets for surface points. Full-body Avatar Modeling anchors 3D Gaussians in a canonical space and deforms them using parametric body models (e.g., SMPL) to reconstruct dynamic human avatars from multi-view images. It distinguishes itself from head-centric modeling by focusing on full-body skeletal rigidity and secondary non-rigid effects (e.g., muscle motion) rather than fine-grained facial expressions. It builds on SMPL-based rigid/non-rigid deformation by applying a hybrid deformation strategy specifically optimized for full-body dynamics. Skeleton Representation for Articulated NeRF (A-NeRF) encodes human shape, appearance, and pose by mapping 3D query points relative to an articulated skeleton structure rather than absolute world coordinates. It solves the problem of modeling dynamic articulated human motion in neural radiance fields by replacing the parametric surface model of SMPL with a pure skeletal hierarchy, allowing the method to be initialized with any skeleton pose estimator. Unlike sibling methods that rely on SMPL mesh topology for deformation, this approach explicitly incorporates domain knowledge of bone connectivity and static bone lengths to reparameterize query locations and view directions before density and color evaluation. A method focusing on editing efficiency and rendering quality for portraits. Embed the 3D Gaussian field on the surface of SMPL-X [159] for spatial and temporal consistency. Utilize a Neural Gaussian Texture mechanism to get a 3D Gaussian feature field for high-quality rendering. Employ the iterative dataset update strategy for portrait editing. Incorporate expression similarity guidance. Use a face-aware module to maintain facial structure and expression accuracy. Regularization applied to LBS weights W to prevent artifacts with unseen poses by aligning predicted weights with those obtained from SMPL using an l2 loss. For individual Gaussians pi, retrieve their k=6 nearest vertices on the SMPL mesh. The distance-weighted average Ŵi is calculated as: Ŵi = Σ(j∈Ni) (ωj/ω) Wj, where ωj = exp(-||pi - pj|| ||Wi - Wj|| / (2σ^2)) and ω = Σ(j∈Ni) ωj. Ni is the set of k nearest neighbors. k: Number of nearest neighbors on SMPL mesh used for weight query. Value: 6. We use the efficient CUDA k-nn implementation of PyTorch3D library [56]. Points around the intersection of joints can have ambiguous k-nn results, leading to artifacts if SMPL weights are used directly without learning. Employ a learnable deformation to provide stability and generalization to novel expressions, head poses, and viewing directions. Achieve controllable portraits on portable devices. The integration of parametric body models like SMPL with 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a solution to the instability and ambiguity of reconstructing dynamic humans from monocular or sparse multi-view inputs. Early works like Gaussian Avatar and 3DGS-Avatar established the paradigm of anchoring Gaussians to the SMPL mesh to leverage its topological priors. Subsequent methods such as Animatable Gaussians and Full-body Avatar Modeling refined the deformation pipeline by explicitly modeling non-rigid residuals to capture muscle motion and clothing dynamics that LBS alone cannot represent. The approach has been extended to head avatars (e.g., Rig3DGS) and specialized editing tasks (e.g., PortraitGen), demonstrating its versatility in high-fidelity, real-time human rendering. name: Gaussian Avatar
head: SMPL-based Gaussian Splatting Avatar
body: Gaussian Avatar is a method for reconstructing animatable full-body human avatars from video by leveraging the SMPL parametric model as a geometric prior. It solves the problem of dynamic human reconstruction by using a feedforward network to predict Gaussian parameters directly from pose features, enabling real-time novel view synthesis and animation. It is distinguished from siblings like 3DGS-Avatar by its reliance on a feedforward prediction of parameters via pose features rather than explicit per-Gaussian rigid/non-rigid transformation pipelines during inference. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of monocular or multi-view images of a human subject; corresponding SMPL pose parameters \theta and shape parameters \beta. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} defined in the canonical space, along with a trained feedforward network and dynamic appearance network that map pose/position to Gaussian attributes. Data Structures: Canonical Gaussians: Each Gaussian i is initialized on the surface of the canonical SMPL mesh. It stores: Position \mathbf{p}i in canonical space. Covariance \Sigmai in canonical space. Opacity \alphai. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Feedforward Network: A neural network (e.g., MLP) that takes canonical position and pose features as input and outputs Gaussian parameters (position offset, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). Dynamic Appearance Network: An optimizable tensor or network module that captures dynamic appearance variations (e.g., clothing folds, lighting changes) conditioned on pose and time. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians on the canonical SMPL mesh surface. 2. Pose Encoding: Encode the current pose \theta and shape \beta into a pose feature vector. 3. Parameter Prediction: Pass the canonical position \mathbf{p}i and pose features through the feedforward network to predict the deformed Gaussian parameters. This includes predicting the deformed position \mathbf{p}'i, covariance \Sigma'i, opacity \alpha'i, and color coefficients. 4. Deformation: The predicted parameters define the Gaussians in the camera space. The deformation is implicit in the network's output, mapping canonical space to posed space. 5. Rendering: Render the deformed Gaussians using differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. 6. Training: Minimize the loss between rendered images and ground truth images using photometric and perceptual losses. The dynamic appearance network is optimized to capture temporal dynamics. Formulas: Loss Function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the L1 loss and \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} is the multi-scale structural similarity loss. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: \{\mathbf{p}'i, \Sigma'i, \alpha'i, \mathbf{c}i\} = \text{Network}(\mathbf{p}i, \theta, \beta) where \mathbf{c}i are the color coefficients. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for MS-SSIM loss. Typical value: 0.2. Network architecture: Typically an MLP with hidden layers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Monocular input may lead to ambiguities in depth; SMPL prior helps but may not resolve severe occlusions. Generalization: The feedforward network may struggle with poses significantly different from the training set. GoMAvatar is a monocular video avatar reconstruction method that embeds 3D Gaussians onto a canonical human body mesh driven by the SMPL-X rig. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-fidelity dynamic human avatars from single-camera video by coupling Gaussian parameters with mesh geometry, allowing for realistic novel animation in real time. Unlike methods that rely on per-Gaussian deformation MLPs, GoMAvatar determines Gaussian positions via barycentric coordinates and normal displacements on the canonical mesh. GAvatar is a text-to-3D generation method that creates animatable human avatars by binding 3D Gaussians to a primitive-based representation attached to the SMPL-X model. It distinguishes itself by leveraging an implicit network to predict Gaussian attributes and converting opacity to a signed distance field (SDF) via a NeuS-like approach to provide geometry constraints for mesh extraction. It builds on Gaussian Avatar by incorporating text-based generation guided by Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to per-Gaussian optimization methods due to the feedforward network. Rendering is real-time (e.g., 166 FPS). Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and the size of the feedforward network. Performance: Achieves high-fidelity dynamic human reconstruction. Strengths: Real-time rendering, efficient training, good generalization to novel poses. Limitations: May struggle with extreme poses or severe occlusions. Gaussian Avatar was introduced as a method to leverage the SMPL model for full-body avatar reconstruction. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and parametric human models. Recent advances have further improved its efficiency and quality. name: GoMAvatar
body: GoMAvatar is a monocular video avatar reconstruction method that embeds 3D Gaussians onto a canonical human body mesh driven by the SMPL-X rig. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-fidelity dynamic human avatars from single-camera video by coupling Gaussian parameters with mesh geometry, allowing for realistic novel animation in real time. Unlike methods that rely on per-Gaussian deformation MLPs, GoMAvatar determines Gaussian positions via barycentric coordinates and normal displacements on the canonical mesh. Inputs: Monocular video sequence; SMPL-X mesh parameters (pose, shape, expression) fitted to the video frames. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the dynamic human avatar. Data Structures: Gaussians are stored with fields for triangle indices, barycentric coordinates, normal direction, and learned displacement magnitude. Steps: 1. Embed Gaussians onto a canonical human body mesh. 2. Determine the position of each Gaussian using its barycentric coordinates within a mesh triangle and a displacement along the vertex normal direction. 3. Deform the canonical mesh to the target pose and expression using the SMPL-X rig, transforming the Gaussians accordingly. 4. Render the deformed Gaussians and optimize parameters to minimize rendering loss against the input video frame. Formulas: The canonical position \mathbf{p}{\text{canon}} is computed as: \mathbf{p}{\text{canon}} = u\mathbf{v}1 + v\mathbf{v}2 + w\mathbf{v}3 + \delta \mathbf{n} where (u, v, w) are the barycentric coordinates, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 are the triangle vertices, \mathbf{n} is the interpolated normal at the barycentric point, and \delta is the learned normal displacement. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecanonicalposition(trianglevertices, barycentriccoords, normal, displacement): v1, v2, v3 = trianglevertices u, v, w = barycentriccoords return u v1 + v v2 + w v3 + displacement normal def deformtotarget(canonicalposition, smplxtransformmatrix): return smplxtransformmatrix @ canonicalposition def renderandoptimize(videoframe, smplxtransformmatrix, gaussians): # Compute canonical positions from barycentric coords and normal displacement pcanon = [computecanonicalposition(g.triverts, g.bary, g.normal, g.disp) for g in gaussians] # Deform to target pose using SMPL-X transformation ptarget = [deformtotarget(p, smplxtransformmatrix) for p in pcanon] # Project to 2D and splat onto image plane renderedimage = rasterizegaussians(ptarget, gaussians.rotation, gaussians.scale, gaussians.opacity, gaussians.color) # Compute loss and optimize parameters loss = l1ssimloss(renderedimage, videoframe) gradientdescentstep(gaussians, loss) Parameters: Learning rate and densification thresholds follow standard 3D Gaussian Splatting configurations. Edge Cases: Unbalanced Aggregation: Densification and splitting operations can cause unbalanced aggregation of Gaussians. This may require surface-guided re-initialization strategies to ensure Gaussians fit the input video well. Time Complexity: Real-time novel animation is supported. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of Gaussians embedded on the mesh. Strengths: Monocular video input; real-time animation; leverages strong SMPL-X priors for realistic human structure. Limitations: Relies on accurate SMPL-X fitting; potential issues with Gaussian aggregation if densification is not managed. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic human avatars from monocular video with a need for real-time animation and realistic body structure. GoMAvatar is listed among methods using the SMPL-X rig, specifically noted for being a monocular video method coupled with a mesh. It addresses the limitations of earlier SMPL-driven methods by embedding Gaussians directly onto the canonical mesh using barycentric coordinates and normal displacements, providing a structured approach to dynamic human modeling. Uses SMPL as a prior with pose features predicting Gaussian parameters via a feed-forward network. Sets it apart by using a feed-forward network instead of mesh embedding. Choose when pose features are sufficient and mesh coupling is not required. [1479-gaussian-avatar.md] The first SMPL-driven body Gaussian Splatting method. Sets it apart by using the SMPL rig instead of SMPL-X. Choose for early SMPL-based body reconstruction. Uses SMPL-X with per-Gaussian deformation MLPs. Sets it apart by learning deformation per Gaussian rather than using barycentric/normal displacement. Choose when MLP-based deformation is preferred over mesh embedding. Uses SMPL-X with explicit pose-conditioned offsets. Sets it apart by applying explicit offsets rather than mesh-coupled deformation. Choose when explicit pose conditioning is needed. Embeds Gaussians in mesh tangent space. Sets it apart by using a local tangent coordinate system instead of canonical barycentric coordinates. Choose when tangent-space embedding is preferred. name: GAvatar
head: A text-based generation method using primitive-based representation attached to SMPL-X and 3D Gaussians
body: GAvatar is a text-to-3D generation method that creates animatable human avatars by binding 3D Gaussians to a primitive-based representation attached to the SMPL-X model. It distinguishes itself by leveraging an implicit network to predict Gaussian attributes and converting opacity to a signed distance field (SDF) via a NeuS-like approach to provide geometry constraints for mesh extraction. It builds on Gaussian Avatar by incorporating text-based generation guided by Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss. Inputs: Text prompt, SMPL-X template mesh. Outputs: Animatable 3D human avatar represented by 3D Gaussians and a detailed textured mesh. Data Structures: 1. SMPL-X Template: A parametric human body model. 2. Primitive-based Representation: A set of shells or primitives derived from the SMPL template. 3. 3D Gaussians: Attached to the local coordinate system of each primitive. Attributes include position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color. 4. Implicit Network: Predicts the attribute values of the 3D Gaussians. 5. Signed Distance Field (SDF): Derived from Gaussian opacity. Steps: 1. Primitive Binding: Create a primitive-based representation from the SMPL-X template. Bind 3D Gaussians to the local coordinate system of each primitive. 2. Attribute Prediction: Use an implicit network to predict the attribute values (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) of the 3D Gaussians based on the primitive parameters. 3. Geometry Constraint (SDF Conversion): Convert the opacity of the 3D Gaussians into a signed distance field using a NeuS-like method. This provides geometry constraints. 4. Text-to-3D Generation: Generate the avatar from a text prompt. The process is guided primarily by the SDS (Score Distillation Sampling) loss. 5. Mesh Extraction: Extract a detailed textured mesh using the geometry constraints provided by the SDF. 6. Animation: Utilize differentiable rendering of 3DGS and a generative adversarial network (StyleGAN2) to produce animatable 3D humans. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GAvatar(textprompt, smplxtemplate): # Step 1: Create primitive-based representation from SMPL-X primitives = createprimitivesfromsmplx(smplxtemplate) # Step 2: Bind 3D Gaussians to primitives # Gaussians are attached to the local coordinate system of each primitive gaussians = bindgaussianstoprimitives(primitives) # Step 3: Predict Gaussian attributes using implicit network # Attributes: position, scale, rotation, opacity, color implicitnetwork = ImplicitNetwork() gaussianattributes = implicitnetwork.predict(gaussians) # Step 4: Convert opacity to SDF for geometry constraints # NeuS-like method sdf = opacitytosdf(gaussianattributes.opacity) # Step 5: Text-based generation guided by SDS loss # Optimization loop using SDS loss from a pre-trained diffusion model for step in optimizationsteps: # Render current Gaussians renderedimage = differentiablerender(gaussianattributes) # Compute SDS loss against text prompt sdsloss = computesdsloss(renderedimage, textprompt) # Update Gaussian attributes via gradient descent gaussianattributes = updategaussians(gaussianattributes, sdsloss) # Update implicit network if needed implicitnetwork.update(gaussianattributes) # Update SDF from new opacity sdf = opacitytosdf(gaussianattributes.opacity) # Step 6: Extract detailed textured mesh from SDF mesh = extractmesh(sdf) # Step 7: Ensure animatability using GAN (StyleGAN2) # This step ensures the generated avatar is animatable animatableavatar = ensureanimatability(mesh, gaussianattributes) return animatableavatar Parameters: SDS Loss Weight: Not given in the sources. Implicit Network Architecture: Not given in the sources. NeuS-like Method Details: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Oversaturation: Not explicitly mentioned for GAvatar, but related methods like HumanGaussian address this with negative prompt guidance. Geometry Consistency: The NeuS-like SDF conversion is critical for providing geometry constraints; inaccuracies here may lead to poor mesh extraction. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables text-based generation of 3D human avatars. Provides detailed textured meshes through SDF-based geometry constraints. Produces animatable avatars using differentiable rendering and GANs. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the SMPL-X template and the implicit network. The SDS loss may require careful tuning to avoid artifacts. When to Use: When text-to-3D generation of animatable human avatars is required. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity geometry without text guidance is needed. It builds on the principles of Gaussian Splatting and integrates them with parametric human models (SMPL-X) and generative AI techniques (SDS loss, StyleGAN2). name: 3DGS-Avatar
body: 3DGS-Avatar reconstructs full-body human avatars by combining 3D Gaussians with rigid and non-rigid transformations of an underlying SMPL model. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by replacing spherical harmonics with a shallow MLP to model per-Gaussian color, enabling pose-dependent appearance modeling. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: Gaussians are initialized on the surface of the canonical SMPL mesh. Initial skinning weights w{i,j} are assigned based on the SMPL vertex weights. 2. Deformation: For a target pose \theta, each Gaussian i is transformed: a. Rigid transformation via Linear Blend Skinning (LBS): \mathbf{p}{\text{rigid}} = \sum{j=1}^{N{\text{bones}}} w{i,j} \mathbf{T}j(\theta) \mathbf{p}i, where N{\text{bones}} is the number of bones, \mathbf{T}j(\theta) are bone transformation matrices, and \mathbf{p}i is the canonical position. b. Non-rigid residual \Delta \mathbf{p} is predicted by a deformation network conditioned on pose and canonical position. c. Final position: \mathbf{p}'i = \mathbf{p}{\text{rigid}} + \Delta \mathbf{p}. 3. Covariance Update: The covariance matrix is transformed using the Jacobian J of the deformation map: \Sigma'i = J \Sigmai J^T + \sigma^2 I, where \Sigmai is the original covariance and \sigma^2 I is a small regularization term. 4. Color Prediction: A shallow MLP replaces spherical harmonics to model per-Gaussian color. 5. Rendering: Deformed Gaussians are projected and composited using differentiable 3D Gaussian splatting. 6. Optimization: Training minimizes a combination of photometric and perceptual losses: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{L1}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{MS-SSIM}}, where \mathcal{L}{\text{L1}} is the L1 loss, \lambda is a weighting factor, and \mathcal{L}{\text{MS-SSIM}} is the multi-scale structural similarity loss, with deformation regularized by geometry priors. Parameters: MLP depth/width: Described as "shallow". Edge Cases: Pose Extrapolation: Generalization to novel poses relies on the MLP's capacity and deformation regularization. Time Complexity: Rendering scales linearly with the number of Gaussians O(N). Training requires MLP inference per Gaussian, increasing compute time. Strengths: Captures pose-dependent cloth deformation and generalizes effectively to novel poses. Limitations: Requires accurate SMPL fitting; replacing spherical harmonics with an MLP increases per-Gaussian computational overhead during training and rendering. 3DGS-Avatar was introduced to overcome the limitations of spherical harmonics in capturing complex, pose-dependent appearance changes such as cloth wrinkles. It builds on the SMPL-based rigid/non-rigid deformation framework. name: Animatable Gaussians
body: Animatable Gaussians is a method for reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) driven by the SMPL-X parametric model. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity, real-time renderable human avatars from monocular video by explicitly modeling pose-conditioned deformation offsets. It is distinguished from sibling methods like 3DGS-Avatar, which uses per-Gaussian deformation MLPs, and GaussianAvatars, which focuses on head-driven avatars using the FLAME model. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video sequence of a human subject; SMPL-X mesh parameters (pose \theta, expression \beta) fitted to the video (e.g., via MICA or DECA). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) that can be rendered in real-time for any given pose/expression. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is initialized on the surface of the canonical SMPL-X mesh. Position \mathbf{p}i: Canonical position on the mesh surface. Covariance \Sigmai: Initial covariance in canonical space. Appearance: Opacity \alphai and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Deformation Parameters: Explicit pose-conditioned offset parameters \Delta \mathbf{p} associated with each Gaussian or its local tangent space. Steps: 1. Initialization: Fit SMPL-X to the input video to obtain canonical mesh and initial parameters. Initialize one Gaussian per mesh triangle or vertex in the canonical tangent space. 2. Deformation: For a target pose \theta and expression \beta: Compute rigid deformation \mathbf{p}{rigid} using Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) on the canonical position \mathbf{p}i. Compute explicit pose-conditioned offset \Delta \mathbf{p}(\theta, \beta). Final position: \mathbf{p}'i = \mathbf{p}{rigid} + \Delta \mathbf{p}. Update covariance \Sigma'i using the Jacobian J of the deformation map: \Sigma'i = J \Sigmai J^T + \sigma^2 I. 3. Rendering: Render the deformed Gaussians using differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. 4. Training: Minimize photometric loss between rendered image and ground truth video frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderanimatablegaussians(gaussians, pose, expression): """ Render a frame for a given pose and expression. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with canonical pos, cov, appearance, offsetparams pose: SMPL-X pose parameters theta expression: SMPL-X expression parameters beta """ deformedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # 1. Rigid Deformation (LBS) prigid = applylbs(g.canonicalpos, pose, g.boneweights) # 2. Non-Rigid Offset (Explicit Pose-Conditioned) deltap = computeoffset(g.offsetparams, pose, expression) # 3. Final Position pfinal = prigid + deltap # 4. Covariance Update J = computejacobian(pose, expression, g.canonicalpos) covfinal = J @ g.canonicalcov @ J.T + 0.0001 np.eye(3) deformedgaussians.append(Gaussian(pfinal, covfinal, g.opacity, g.shcoeffs)) # 5. Differentiable Rasterization image = rasterize3dgs(deformedgaussians) return image def computeoffset(offsetparams, pose, expression): """ Computes explicit pose-conditioned offset. Note: Specific network architecture not detailed in source. Typically a small MLP or lookup table conditioned on pose/expression. """ # Placeholder for the specific offset prediction mechanism # The source specifies "explicit pose-conditioned offsets" return offsetparams # Simplified representation Parameters: Offset Network/Parameters: Not given in the sources. Regularization \sigma^2: Small value (e.g., 10^{-4}) to ensure positive definiteness of covariance. Edge Cases: Degenerate Poses: Extreme poses may cause LBS artifacts; the explicit offset helps mitigate this but may require careful training data coverage. Precision: Jacobian computation must be numerically stable. Gaussian Shell Maps (GSMs) is a method for generating animatable 3D humans by combining CNN-based generators with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to recreate virtual humans with sophisticated details such as clothing and accessories. It builds multi-layer shells from the SMPL template and binds 3D Gaussians to these shells. By utilizing the differentiable rendering of 3DGS and the generative adversarial network of StyleGAN2, animatable 3D humans are efficiently generated. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GAvatar, which attaches Gaussians to SMPL-X primitives, and HumanGaussian, which initializes Gaussians via random sampling. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, typical for 3DGS. Deformation computation is O(N) per frame. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian parameters and deformation offsets. Performance: Real-time rendering is achievable on modern GPUs. Strengths: High fidelity, real-time performance, explicit control via SMPL-X. Limitations: Requires fitted SMPL-X parameters; quality depends on deformation offset modeling. When to Use: When real-time, high-fidelity human avatars are needed from monocular video. When Not to Use: When multi-view data is available and higher geometric accuracy is prioritized over speed, or when no SMPL-X fit is available. Animatable Gaussians is part of the evolution of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction methods. It builds on the SMPL-based rigid/non-rigid deformation principles [8385-smpl-based-rigid-non-rigid-deformation.md]. It is distinguished by its use of explicit pose-conditioned offsets within the SMPL-X rig. name: UV-based motion parameterization
head: Motion parameterization scheme
body: UV-based motion parameterization is a method for modeling dynamic human deformation by reparameterizing 3D spatial coordinates into 2D surface-level UV coordinates combined with time. It solves the problem of high-dimensional motion field learning by exploiting the prior that human motion occurs primarily at the surface level, reducing the input dimensionality from 4D space-time (x, y, z, t) to 3D surface-time (u, v, t). This approach is distinct from volumetric parameterizations because it leverages the parametric mesh's surface topology to enforce spatial coherence among nearby surface points, resulting in significantly lower memory usage and faster convergence. It builds on SMPL-based rigid/non-rigid deformation by predicting residual offsets for surface points. The method reparameterizes query points from world space to canonical space using SMPL parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Canonical 3D point coordinates, corresponding UV coordinates (u, v) on the parametric mesh, and time t. Outputs: Residual deformation vector \Delta\Phi(u, v, t). Data Structures: Multiresolution Hash Encoding (\psi{res}): A hash table-based encoding scheme applied to the input vector (u, v, t). The specific grid resolutions and hash table sizes are not given in the sources. Residual Network (MLP{res}): A Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes the encoded input and outputs the residual deformation. Steps: 1. Rigid Transformation: Compute the rigidly transformed position \Phi{LBS}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}, \rho) using Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) based on the SMPL pose \rho and weights \mathbf{w}. 2. Parameterization: Map the query point to its corresponding UV coordinates (u, v) on the canonical SMPL mesh and concatenate with the current time t to form the input vector (u, v, t). 3. Encoding: Apply the multiresolution hash encoding \psi{res} to the vector (u, v, t). 4. Residual Prediction: Forward the encoded input through MLP{res} to regress the residual deformation \Delta\Phi. 5. Final Deformation: Add the residual to the rigidly transformed position to obtain the final deformed position \Phi. Formulas: The residual deformation is defined as: \Delta\Phi(u, v, t) = MLP{res} (\psi{res} (u, v, t)) The full human motion at frame t is defined as: \Phi(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}, u, v, \rho, t) = \Phi{LBS} (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}, \rho) + \Delta\Phi(u, v, t) where \Phi{LBS} is the LBS transformation. Parameters: Network Architecture: The specific depth and width of MLP{res} are not given in the sources. Hash Encoding: The specific hash table sizes and resolutions for \psi{res} are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Surface Localization Assumption: The method relies on the assumption that motion is surface-localized, as human deformation primarily occurs at the surface level rather than volumetrically. A module that regresses residual deformation \Delta\Phi to refine surface geometry using the (u, v, t) motion parameterization. It reduces the dimensionality of the motion field from 4D space-time to 3D surface-time. The module concatenates time t with UV coordinates (u, v), applies multiresolution hash encoding \psi{res}, and feeds the result into MLP{res} to predict \Delta\Phi. This approach outperforms alternatives such as positional encoding of (x, t), hash-encoded x with per-frame latent codes, or hash-encoded x with pose parameters. Memory Efficiency: The (u, v, t) parameterization is significantly more memory efficient than (x, t) or (x, y, z, t) due to lower dimensionality. Performance: The method enables optimization of dynamic human representations in minutes (e.g., 100 frames at 512x512 resolution on an RTX 3090), which is approximately 1/100th of the time required by previous methods. Convergence: The dimensionality reduction boosts the convergence rate of the deformation network. Limitations: The method is specific to human avatars with a parametric mesh (SMPL) and valid UV coordinates. The method was introduced in "Learning Neural Volumetric Representations of Dynamic Humans in Minutes". It is inspired by displacement map and bump map techniques from traditional computer graphics pipelines. The core observation is that human motion happens at the surface level, allowing the 4D volumetric motion to be reduced to the 3D surface-time domain.
