name: Full-body Avatar Modeling
head: Hybrid Deformation Strategy for 3D Gaussians
body: Full-body Avatar Modeling anchors 3D Gaussians in a canonical space and deforms them using parametric body models (e.g., SMPL) to reconstruct dynamic human avatars from multi-view images. It distinguishes itself from head-centric modeling by focusing on full-body skeletal rigidity and secondary non-rigid effects (e.g., muscle motion) rather than fine-grained facial expressions. It builds on SMPL-based rigid/non-rigid deformation by applying a hybrid deformation strategy specifically optimized for full-body dynamics. Inputs: Multi-view images of a human subject in various poses; a parametric body model (e.g., SMPL) providing skeleton hierarchy and rest-pose mesh. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{gi\} defined in canonical space, each with position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and appearance coefficients (e.g., Spherical Harmonics \mathbf{c}i). Data Structures: Gaussian Set: List of N Gaussians. Each gi stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Canonical position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Canonical covariance matrix. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c}i: Appearance coefficients. SMPL Model: Provides bone transformation matrices \mathbf{T}j(\theta) for pose \theta and skinning weights w{i,j} for each Gaussian i relative to bone j. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians \{gi\} on the surface of the canonical SMPL mesh in a rest pose. Assign initial skinning weights w{i,j} based on proximity to SMPL vertices or learned optimization. 2. Rigid Deformation (LBS): For a target pose \theta, compute the rigidly deformed position \mathbf{p}{rigid} using Linear Blend Skinning: \mathbf{p}{rigid} = \sum{j=1}^{N{bones}} w{i,j} \mathbf{T}j(\theta) \mathbf{p}i where N{bones} is the number of bones in the SMPL skeleton. 3. Non-Rigid Deformation: Apply a pose-conditioned deformation field to predict a residual offset \Delta \mathbf{p}. This field accounts for secondary non-rigid effects like muscle jiggles that LBS cannot capture. The deformed position is: \mathbf{p}'i = \mathbf{p}{rigid} + \Delta \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{p}i, \theta) The deformation field is typically implemented as a small MLP conditioned on canonical position and pose parameters. 4. Covariance Update: Transform the covariance matrix \Sigmai using the Jacobian J of the total deformation map (LBS + non-rigid field) with respect to \mathbf{p}i: \Sigma'i = J \Sigmai J^T + \sigma^2 I where \sigma^2 I is a small regularization term to ensure positive definiteness. The Jacobian J is computed via automatic differentiation of the deformation pipeline [G, 11805-full-body-avatar-modeling.md]. 5. Rendering: Render the deformed Gaussians \{g'i\} using differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. Compute loss against target images using photometric (\mathcal{L}{L1}) and perceptual (\mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM}) metrics [6136-instantsplat.md][6464-pixelsplat.md]. 6. Optimization: Backpropagate gradients through the deformation pipeline to update Gaussian parameters and deformation network weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deformgaussian(gaussian, smplmodel, pose, deformationnet): """ Deforms a single Gaussian from canonical to posed space. gaussian: dict with keys 'p', 'Sigma', 'alpha', 'c' smplmodel: object providing getskinningweights(p) and getbonetransforms(pose) pose: pose parameters for SMPL deformationnet: MLP for non-rigid offset """ # 1. Rigid Deformation via LBS weights = smplmodel.getskinningweights(gaussian['p']) bonetransforms = smplmodel.getbonetransforms(pose) prigid = sum(weights[j] bonetransforms[j] @ gaussian['p'] for j in range(len(weights))) # 2. Non-Rigid Deformation deltap = deformationnet(gaussian['p'], pose) pdeformed = prigid + deltap # 3. Covariance Update via Jacobian # Compute Jacobian J of deformation map w.r.t canonical position # This requires differentiating the sum of LBS and deformationnet J = computejacobian(prigid, deltap, gaussian['p']) Sigmadeformed = J @ gaussian['Sigma'] @ J.T + 1e-6 np.eye(3) return { 'p': pdeformed, 'Sigma': Sigmadeformed, 'alpha': gaussian['alpha'], 'c': gaussian['c'] } def computejacobian(prigid, deltap, pcanonical): """ Computes the Jacobian of the total deformation with respect to canonical position. """ # Jacobian of LBS part # Jlbs = sum(wj d(Tj @ p)/dp) = sum(wj Tj) # Note: Tj are constant for fixed pose, so d(Tj @ p)/dp = Tj # However, weights wj might depend on p, so full derivative is complex. # In practice, often approximated or computed via autograd. pass # Implementation depends on specific autograd framework Parameters: \sigma^2: Regularization strength for covariance. Typical value: 10^{-6}. Deformation network depth/width: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Poses: Extreme poses may cause skinning weights to produce invalid transformations. Guard against negative determinants in covariance update. Precision: Jacobian computation must be numerically stable. Use automatic differentiation rather than finite differences. A specific deformation technique using skeleton-driven rigid joint transformations and learnable per-Gaussian skinning weights. It avoids pose blend shapes and template vertex deformation, relying on an MLP for pose-dependent deformations to handle shape estimation inaccuracies. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of Gaussians. Deformation is O(N \cdot N{bones}) for LBS plus O(N) for the deformation network. Memory Complexity: O(N) for Gaussian parameters. Additional memory for SMPL model and deformation network weights. Performance: Fast training and rendering compared to NeRF-based methods due to explicit Gaussian representation. Strengths: High fidelity for dynamic full-body avatars; real-time rendering capability; editability of Gaussians. Limitations: Requires accurate SMPL fitting; non-rigid deformation field may struggle with extreme articulations or clothing changes. When to use: When real-time or near-real-time dynamic full-body avatars are needed from multi-view video. When not to use: For head-centric avatars with fine facial details (use Gaussian Avatar) or static scenes (use standard 3D Gaussian Splatting). Full-body Avatar Modeling using 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a key direction in 3D GS applications, alongside head-centric modeling. It leverages the speed and editability of GS to enable fast training and rendering of dynamic humans. The approach typically anchors Gaussians in canonical space and uses a hybrid deformation strategy combining LBS for rigid skeletal transformations and pose-conditioned deformation fields for non-rigid effects. This method is part of the broader trend of using parametric body models (like SMPL) to guide Gaussian deformation for animatable avatars. name: Linear Blend Skinning for Gaussian Splatting
head: Canonical LBS, Canonical to Observation Space Transformation, Forward Skinning, Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) for 3DGS Avatars
body: Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) for Gaussian Splatting is a deformation technique that transforms 3D Gaussians from a canonical (unposed) space to an observation (posed) space using skeleton-driven rigid joint transformations and learnable per-Gaussian skinning weights. Unlike NeRF-based inverse skinning methods that map observation-space points to canonical space, this forward approach applies fixed skinning weights to transform Gaussian positions and rotations directly. It avoids pose blend shapes and template vertex deformation, relying instead on an MLP for pose-dependent deformations to handle inaccuracies in shape estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Canonical 3D Gaussian attributes (position \muc, rotation rc, scale s, color, opacity), joint transformation matrices M{j,t} derived from a parametric body model (e.g., SMPL) for each training timestep t, and initial learnable skinning weights w. Outputs: Posed Gaussian attributes (position \muo, rotation ro) ready for rasterization. Data Structures: Skinned Weights (w): A vector of size J (total number of joints) per Gaussian. Optimized during training. Joint Transformation Matrices (M{j,t}): Precomputed rigid transformation matrices for each joint j and timestep t. Each matrix M{j,t} contains a rotation component AR(\thetat) and a translation component AT(\thetat). Numbered Steps: 1. Precompute Joint Transformations: For each training timestep t, compute the rigid transformation matrix M{j,t} for every body joint j based on the pose parameters \thetat from the parametric mesh. 2. Optimize Skinning Weights: Initialize learnable per-Gaussian skinning weights vector w. Optimize w via gradient descent. Note that w can contain negative values during optimization. 3. Activate and Normalize Weights: Apply ReLU activation to each component wj of the skinning weights vector to ensure non-negativity. Normalize the vector such that its components sum to 1: wj^{final} = \frac{\max(0, wj)}{\sum{k=1}^{J} \max(0, wk)} This yields a well-defined skinning weights vector. 4. Transform Position: Compute the observation space position \muo by applying the weighted sum of joint transformations to the canonical position \muc: \muo = A(\thetat) \cdot \muc = \sum{k=1}^{J} Wk M{k,t} \cdot \muc where Wk are the normalized skinning weights and M{k,t} is the transformation matrix for joint k. 5. Transform Rotation: Transform the canonical rotation rc (represented as a quaternion or vector) to observation space rotation ro using the rotation component AR(\thetat) of the combined transformation matrix: ro = AR(\thetat) rc where AR(\thetat) is the rotation part of the blended transformation. Parameters: Learning Rate for MLP and Skinning Weights (w): 1 \times 10^{-4}. Learning Rate for Latent Codes (l): 2.5 \times 10^{-3}. Skinned Weights (W): Static attributes of the Gaussian after training; not regressed per-frame. Joint Transformation Matrices (\thetak): Pose parameters derived from the parametric human mesh (e.g., SMPL). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Weights: During optimization, skinning weights w may become negative. The ReLU activation and normalization step is critical to ensure valid convex combination weights. Pose Blend Shapes: Pose blend shapes are explicitly excluded because shape estimation and obtained blend shapes may be inaccurate. An MLP is used to handle pose-dependent deformations instead. Template Vertex Deformation: Not necessary as LBS is applied directly on canonical Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeposedgaussian(canonicalpos, canonicalrot, skinningweightsraw, jointtransforms): """ canonicalpos: Tensor of shape (N, 3), canonical positions of N Gaussians canonicalrot: Tensor of shape (N, 4), canonical rotations (quaternions) of N Gaussians skinningweightsraw: Tensor of shape (N, J), raw learnable skinning weights jointtransforms: List of J matrices, each of shape (4, 4), representing M{j,t} for current timestep t Returns: posedpos: Tensor of shape (N, 3) posedrot: Tensor of shape (N, 4) """ J = len(jointtransforms) N = canonicalpos.shape[0] # Step 2 & 3: Activate and Normalize Weights # Apply ReLU to ensure non-negativity reluweights = torch.relu(skinningweightsraw) # Normalize so components sum to 1 sumweights = torch.sum(reluweights, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Handle potential division by zero if all weights are zero (guard) sumweights = torch.clamp(sumweights, min=1e-8) normalizedweights = reluweights / sumweights # Step 4: Transform Position # Initialize posed position posedpos = torch.zeroslike(canonicalpos) # Homogeneous coordinates for position (N, 4) poshomogeneous = torch.cat([canonicalpos, torch.ones(N, 1)], dim=1) for j in range(J): # Get transformation matrix for joint j Mj = jointtransforms[j] # Shape (4, 4) Wj = normalizedweights[:, j:j+1] # Shape (N, 1) # Apply transformation: Mj poshomogeneous transformedposhom = torch.matmul(poshomogeneous, Mj.T) # Shape (N, 4) transformedpos = transformedposhom[:,:3] # Shape (N, 3) # Add weighted contribution posedpos += Wj transformedpos # Step 5: Transform Rotation # Compute blended rotation matrix AR(thetat) # Note: The sources define A(thetat) as containing AR and AT. # We need to extract the rotation part of the blended transformation. # Since LBS blends transformations, we blend the rotation matrices. # Extract rotation matrices from joint transforms # Assuming jointtransforms are 4x4, rotation is top-left 3x3 rotmatrices = [] for j in range(J): Mj = jointtransforms[j] Rj = Mj[:3,:3] # Shape (3, 3) rotmatrices.append(Rj) # Blend rotation matrices using normalized weights # AR(thetat) = sum(Wj Rj) blendedrotmatrix = torch.zeros(3, 3) for j in range(J): blendedrotmatrix += normalizedweights[:, j:j+1] rotmatrices[j] # Apply blended rotation to canonical rotations # canonicalrot is (N, 4) quaternions # Convert quaternions to rotation matrices, apply blendedrotmatrix, convert back? # Or apply quaternion rotation directly if AR is represented as quaternion. # Source says: ro = AR(thetat) rc. # If rc is a vector (direction), it's matrix multiplication. # If rc is a quaternion, it's quaternion multiplication. # 3DGS rotations are typically quaternions. # However, the formula ro = AR(thetat) rc suggests matrix-vector multiplication if rc is a vector. # But 3DGS uses quaternions for orientation. # Let's assume rc represents the orientation quaternion. # To apply a rotation matrix R to a quaternion q, we convert q to Rq, # compute Rtotal = R @ Rq, then convert back to quaternion. # Convert canonical quaternions to rotation matrices # q is (N, 4), w,x,y,z canonicalrotmats = quaterniontorotationmatrix(canonicalrot) # Shape (N, 3, 3) # Apply blended rotation # posedrotmats = blendedrotmatrix @ canonicalrotmats # Note: broadcasting. blendedrotmatrix is (3,3), canonicalrotmats is (N,3,3) posedrotmats = torch.matmul(blendedrotmatrix.unsqueeze(0), canonicalrotmats) # Convert back to quaternions posedrot = rotationmatrixtoquaternion(posedrotmats) # Shape (N, 4) return posedpos, posedrot def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Converts quaternions (N, 4) to rotation matrices (N, 3, 3).""" # Standard conversion w, x, y, z = q[:, 0], q[:, 1], q[:, 2], q[:, 3] N = q.shape[0] xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz wx, wy, wz = wx, wy, wz R = torch.zeros(N, 3, 3, device=q.device) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2 (yy + zz) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (xx + zz) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (xx + yy) return R def rotationmatrixtoquaternion(R): """Converts rotation matrices (N, 3, 3) to quaternions (N, 4).""" # Standard conversion N = R.shape[0] q = torch.zeros(N, 4, device=R.device) tr = R[:, 0, 0] + R[:, 1, 1] + R[:, 2, 2] # Case 1: tr > 0 mask1 = tr > 0 s1 = 0.5 / torch.sqrt(tr[mask1] + 1e-8) q[mask1, 0] = 0.25 / s1 q[mask1, 1] = (R[mask1, 2, 1] - R[mask1, 1, 2]) s1 q[mask1, 2] = (R[mask1, 0, 2] - R[mask1, 2, 0]) s1 q[mask1, 3] = (R[mask1, 1, 0] - R[mask1, 0, 1]) s1 # Case 2: R[0,0] is largest mask2 = (~mask1) & (R[:, 0, 0] > R[:, 1, 1]) & (R[:, 0, 0] > R[:, 2, 2]) s2 = 2.0 torch.sqrt(1.0 + R[mask2, 0, 0] - R[mask2, 1, 1] - R[mask2, 2, 2] + 1e-8) q[mask2, 0] = (R[mask2, 2, 1] - R[mask2, 1, 2]) / s2 q[mask2, 1] = 0.25 s2 q[mask2, 2] = (R[mask2, 0, 1] + R[mask2, 1, 0]) / s2 q[mask2, 3] = (R[mask2, 0, 2] + R[mask2, 2, 0]) / s2 # Case 3: R[1,1] is largest mask3 = (~mask1) & (~mask2) & (R[:, 1, 1] > R[:, 2, 2]) s3 = 2.0 torch.sqrt(1.0 + R[mask3, 1, 1] - R[mask3, 0, 0] - R[mask3, 2, 2] + 1e-8) q[mask3, 0] = (R[mask3, 0, 2] - R[mask3, 2, 0]) / s3 q[mask3, 1] = (R[mask3, 0, 1] + R[mask3, 1, 0]) / s3 q[mask3, 2] = 0.25 s3 q[mask3, 3] = (R[mask3, 1, 2] + R[mask3, 2, 1]) / s3 # Case 4: R[2,2] is largest mask4 = ~mask1 & ~mask2 & ~mask3 s4 = 2.0 torch.sqrt(1.0 + R[mask4, 2, 2] - R[mask4, 0, 0] - R[mask4, 1, 1] + 1e-8) q[mask4, 0] = (R[mask4, 1, 0] - R[mask4, 0, 1]) / s4 q[mask4, 1] = (R[mask4, 0, 2] + R[mask4, 2, 0]) / s4 q[mask4, 2] = (R[mask4, 1, 2] + R[mask4, 2, 1]) / s4 q[mask4, 3] = 0.25 s4 return q The specific application of LBS where Gaussians are defined in a canonical space and deformed forward to the observation space. It differs from inverse skinning by avoiding the need to query the canonical space from observation space points. Canonical LBS Emphasizes the direction of deformation (canonical to observation). It is chosen when real-time rendering of posed avatars is required without iterative inverse mapping. Forward Skinning The alternative approach used in NeRF-based methods, mapping observation-space points to canonical space. It is slower for rendering but can handle complex non-rigid deformations differently. Inverse Skinning Time Complexity: O(N \cdot J) per Gaussian per frame, where N is the number of Gaussians and J is the number of joints. The precomputation of joint transforms is O(J). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot J) to store skinning weights. Joint transforms are O(J) per timestep. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians and joints. Precomputing joint transforms improves efficiency during training. Strengths: Avoids inaccuracies from pose blend shapes; efficient precomputation of joint transforms; direct transformation of Gaussian attributes. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the parametric body model (e.g., SMPL); skinning weights are static after training, limiting per-frame adaptability; negative weights must be handled via ReLU and normalization. When to use: Real-time rendering of animatable avatars where pose-dependent deformations are handled by an MLP and rigid joint transformations are sufficient for the base deformation. When not to use: When high-fidelity non-rigid deformations beyond rigid joint transformations are required without additional MLP capacity, or when inverse mapping is preferred for specific rendering pipelines. Linear Blend Skinning for Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the context of human avatar modeling using 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the SMPL body model and adapts LBS to work with canonical Gaussians. The method was proposed to address inaccuracies in pose blend shapes and template vertex deformation by using learnable skinning weights and an MLP for pose-dependent deformations. It is part of the broader field of differentiable rendering and Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction. name: LBS Network Variants
head: Backward LBS, Deterministic SMPL skinning, Learned forward LBS
body: This family explores alternative mechanisms for computing skinning weights and deformations in Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) for Gaussian Splatting, specifically comparing learned networks against deterministic template-based approaches. It addresses the limitations of fixed skinning weights by investigating whether conditioning on pose or using learned mappings improves reconstruction quality and reduces artifacts in animatable human avatars. All variants in this family operate within the framework of Linear Blend Skinning for Gaussian Splatting, where canonical 3D Gaussians are deformed using precomputed rigid joint transformations and learnable or deterministic skinning weights. The core objective is to map points from the canonical space to the posed space while maintaining geometric consistency and visual fidelity. A key distinction in the implementation of these variants involves the handling of global transformations. For backward LBS, the query points are canonicalized using the SMPL global translation and rotation before being processed by the LBS network. This ensures that the local pose conditioning is applied relative to a consistent global frame. The performance of these variants is evaluated using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) on standard datasets. The reported metrics indicate that learned forward LBS achieves the highest quality, followed by deterministic SMPL weights, with backward LBS yielding the lowest PSNR among the three. The learned forward LBS network computes skinning weights directly as a function of the point's canonical position and the current pose. It is chosen for its ability to avoid discretized artifacts and handle points far from the surface effectively, achieving the highest PSNR of 31.6. Backward LBS conditions the skinning weight network on the local body poses \theta. The query points are canonicalized using the SMPL global translation and rotation before querying the network. This variant suffers from difficulties in learning skinning weights for points far from the surface, resulting in artifacts under specific poses, and achieves a PSNR of 29.5. This variant uses nearest neighbor SMPL skinning weights derived from the template mesh. While it avoids the training complexity of a network, it causes discretized artifacts on the cloth surface due to the discrete nature of the template weights, achieving a PSNR of 30.5. The comparison of these variants originates from the ARAH (Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs) paper, which ablates different LBS strategies to determine the optimal deformation method for Gaussian Splatting-based avatars. The study highlights the trade-offs between learned flexibility and deterministic stability in skinning weight computation. ARAH: Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-31, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Forward LBS Network
head: Neural Linear Blend Skinning, Forward Skin Network
body: The Forward LBS Network is a method for deforming canonical 3D Gaussians into posed space by predicting learnable skinning weights for any query point, replacing fixed geometric weights with a neural affinity model. It differs from backward LBS variants by operating directly on canonical points without requiring global canonicalization relative to the SMPL frame, and it generally achieves higher reconstruction quality (PSNR) than deterministic SMPL weight baselines. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N query points \hat{\mathbf{X}} = \{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}{i=1}^N in canonical space, where \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Input: A set of 24 rigid bone transformation matrices \{\mathbf{B}b\}{b=1}^{24}, where each \mathbf{B}b is a 4 \times 4 rotation-translation matrix derived from the SMPL model. Output: A set of deformed points \bar{\mathbf{X}} = \{\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}{i=1}^N in posed space. Data Structures Network Parameters: \boldsymbol{\sigma}{\omega} representing the weights of the forward LBS network f{\boldsymbol{\sigma}{\omega}}. Bone Transformations: \mathbf{B}b \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} for b=1 \dots 24. The set includes 23 local transformations and one global transformation. Algorithm 1. Network Definition: The network f{\boldsymbol{\sigma}{\omega}}: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow [0, 1]^{24} predicts a skinning weight vector for any canonical point. It consists of 4 hidden layers, each with 128 channels. 2. Activation and Normalization: The network uses weight normalization [68] and Softplus activation with \beta = 100. 3. Weight Prediction: For each query point \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}, the network outputs a weight vector \mathbf{w}^{(i)} = f{\boldsymbol{\sigma}{\omega}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}). The weights are constrained such that \mathbf{w}^{(i)} \in [0, 1]^{24} and \sum{b=1}^{24} wb^{(i)} = 1. 4. Deformation: The deformed point \bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} is computed using the linear blend skinning formula: \bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} = \left(\sum{b=1}^{24} f{\boldsymbol{\sigma}{\omega}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)})b \mathbf{B}b\right) \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} where \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} is treated as a homogeneous coordinate for the matrix multiplication. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class ForwardLBSNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 4 hidden layers, 128 channels, weight normalization, Softplus(beta=100) # Input: 3 (canonical x, y, z) # Output: 24 (bone weights) self.layers = nn.ModuleList([ nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(3, 128)), nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)), nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)), nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)) ]) self.outputlayer = nn.Linear(128, 24) self.activation = nn.Softplus(beta=100) def forward(self, canonicalpoints): """ canonicalpoints: Tensor of shape (N, 3) Returns: Tensor of shape (N, 24) representing skinning weights """ x = canonicalpoints for layer in self.layers: x = self.activation(layer(x)) weights = self.outputlayer(x) # Ensure weights sum to 1 and are in [0, 1] # Note: Softplus ensures positive values; softmax or normalization ensures sum=1 # The source specifies Softplus activation and sum=1 constraint. # Implementation detail: Apply softmax to ensure sum=1 and valid probabilities weights = torch.softmax(weights, dim=-1) return weights def deformpoint(canonicalpoint, bonetransforms, weights): """ canonicalpoint: Tensor of shape (4,) homogeneous coordinate [x, y, z, 1] bonetransforms: Tensor of shape (24, 4, 4) weights: Tensor of shape (24,) Returns: Deformed point in posed space """ # Weighted sum of bone transformations # W = sum(wb Bb) W = torch.zeros(4, 4, device=canonicalpoint.device) for b in range(24): W += weights[b] bonetransforms[b] # Apply transformation deformedpoint = torch.matmul(W, canonicalpoint) return deformedpoint def forwardlbs(canonicalpoints, bonetransforms): """ canonicalpoints: Tensor of shape (N, 3) bonetransforms: Tensor of shape (24, 4, 4) Returns: Deformed points of shape (N, 3) """ network = ForwardLBSNetwork() # weights: (N, 24) weights = network(canonicalpoints) deformedpoints = [] for i in range(canonicalpoints.shape[0]): # Convert to homogeneous pthomo = torch.cat([canonicalpoints[i], torch.tensor([1.0])]) deformedpt = deformpoint(pthomo, bonetransforms, weights[i]) deformedpoints.append(deformedpt[:3]) return torch.stack(deformedpoints) Initialization The network is initialized by meta-learning on skinning weights of canonical meshes from the CAPE dataset. Meta-learning Algorithm: Reptile with 24 inner steps. Inner Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-4}. Outer Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-5}. Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 4. Outer Loop Steps: 100,000. The resulting model is used as initialization for per-subject optimization on the ZJU-MoCap dataset. A neural network f{\boldsymbol{\sigma}{\omega}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}): \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow [0, 1]^{24} that predicts skinning weights for any point in space, replacing fixed weights with learned affinities to 24 bone transformations. It uses 23 local transformations and one global transformation based on the SMPL model. The weight vector \mathbf{w}^{(i)} must sum to 1 (\sum{b=1}^{24} wb^{(i)} = 1). Performance: Learned forward LBS achieves the highest Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) among the compared variants, followed by deterministic SMPL weights, with backward LBS yielding the lowest PSNR. Complexity: The method involves a forward pass through a small MLP (4 layers, 128 channels) per point, followed by a weighted sum of 24 4 \times 4 matrices. This is computationally efficient for real-time or differentiable rendering pipelines. Limitations: The method relies on the quality of the meta-initialized weights and may require per-subject optimization for high-fidelity results on specific subjects. The Forward LBS Network is part of the ARAH (Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs) framework. It builds on the concept of neural linear blend skinning introduced in prior works [12, 48, 67, 78] as cited in. The approach was developed to enable high-quality animatable human reconstruction from monocular videos by learning spatially varying skinning weights. name: Skeleton Representation for Articulated NeRF
head: Articulated Pose Encoding, Articulated Skeleton Pose Model, Bone Transformation, Forward Kinematics Mapping, Skeleton Representation
body: Skeleton Representation for Articulated NeRF (A-NeRF) encodes human shape, appearance, and pose by mapping 3D query points relative to an articulated skeleton structure rather than absolute world coordinates. It solves the problem of modeling dynamic articulated human motion in neural radiance fields by replacing the parametric surface model of SMPL with a pure skeletal hierarchy, allowing the method to be initialized with any skeleton pose estimator. Unlike sibling methods that rely on SMPL mesh topology for deformation, this approach explicitly incorporates domain knowledge of bone connectivity and static bone lengths to reparameterize query locations and view directions before density and color evaluation. Inputs: Per-frame skeleton pose \thetak for image Ik. Rest pose joint locations \{am\}{m=1}^{24}. Camera intrinsics. Query point q \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view direction d. Outputs: Density \sigma and color C at query point q. Data Structures: Skeleton Hierarchy: Defined by 24 joints (m=0 \dots 24) and B bones. The root is joint 0. Rest Pose: Static 3D joint locations \{am\}{m=1}^{24} encoding connectivity and bone lengths. Pose Parameters: \thetak = [\omega{k,0}, \dots, \omega{k,24}]. \omega{k,m} \in \mathbb{R}^3 or \mathbb{R}^6: Relative rotation of joint m to its parent. \omega{k,0}: Global position (special case). Transformation Matrices: T(\thetak, m) \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} for each bone m. Formulas: The mapping from local bone coordinates p{k,m} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to world coordinates q \in \mathbb{R}^3 is defined via forward kinematics using homogeneous coordinates: \begin{bmatrix} q \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = T(\thetak, m) \begin{bmatrix} p{k,m} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} The transformation matrix T(\thetak, m) is computed as the product of transformations along the path from the root to joint m: T(\thetak, m) = \prod{l \in A(m)} \begin{bmatrix} R(\omega{k,l}) & a{l,l-1} \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} Where: A(m) is the ordered set of joint ancestors of m. R(\omega{k,l}) is the rotation matrix inferred from \omega{k,l} (using axis-angle or overparametrized representation from [78]). a{l,l-1} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the translation vector between joint l and its child joint l-1 (derived from the rest pose). Steps: 1. Initialize Skeleton: Define the rest pose joint locations \{am\}{m=1}^{24} and the bone connectivity graph. This structure is equivalent to SMPL joints but lacks the parametric surface mesh. 2. Compute Forward Kinematics: For a given frame k and pose \thetak, compute the world-space transformation matrix T(\thetak, m) for each bone m using the product of ancestor transformations. 3. Reparameterize Query: To evaluate the NeRF at world coordinate q, transform q into the local coordinate system of the relevant bone m using the inverse transformation: \begin{bmatrix} p{k,m} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = T(\thetak, m)^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} q \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Similarly, transform the view direction d into the local bone frame. 4. NeRF Evaluation: Pass the local position p{k,m} and local view direction into the neural network to predict density \sigma and color C. This step implicitly handles the articulation because the query is now relative to the bone's local frame. 5. Rendering: Render the image using standard volume rendering integration over the sampled points. Parameters: Rotation Representation: Can use traditional axis-angle (\omega{k,m} \in \mathbb{R}^3) or overparametrized representation (\omega{k,m} \in \mathbb{R}^6). Joint Count: 24 joints. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: Since the method does not use an SMPL surface, it requires an external skeleton pose estimator for initialization. Accuracy depends on the quality of this estimator. Multi-view Consistency: When using multiple views, global position and orientation are view-specific, while relative rotations are averaged across views to refine pose. Time Complexity: Rendering one 512 \times 512 \times 3 image takes approximately 1-4 seconds on a single Nvidia Tesla V100 GPU. Training takes approximately 60 hours. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Decouples the skeletal structure from the surface mesh, allowing initialization with any skeleton pose estimator. Explicitly models articulation via forward kinematics. Limitations: Relies on accurate initial pose estimation. Does not inherently model non-rigid deformation (e.g., muscle bulge) unless combined with other techniques, as it focuses on rigid bone transformations. A-NeRF was introduced in "A-NeRF: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields for Learning Human Shape, Appearance, and Pose". It builds on the principles of NeRF by incorporating articulated human motion. The skeleton representation is equivalent to SMPL joints but removes the parametric surface model, providing a more flexible prior for pose estimation. A-NeRF: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields for Learning Human Shape, Appearance, and Pose, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2102.06199, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Pose-free and Feed-forward Training
head: Feed-forward 3DGS, Generalizable Gaussian Splatting
body: This family encompasses methods that reconstruct 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes from uncalibrated or sparse image collections without relying on external Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines for camera pose estimation. Unlike traditional 3DGS which requires dense pose estimation and iterative optimization [6136-instantsplat.md], these methods either predict primitives and poses directly via a feed-forward network [6137-anysplat.md, 6464-pixelsplat.md] or initialize Gaussians using geometry priors from foundation models to enable rapid, pose-free training [6136-instantsplat.md]. They solve the problem of local minima and computational cost inherent in sparse-view reconstruction by enabling real-time inference and eliminating the dependency on incremental depth priors or temporal continuity [6464-pixelsplat.md, 6888-joint-pose-optimization.md]. All methods in this family rely on differentiable rendering to compute gradients from the rendered image to the Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) and/or network weights. The rendering process remains differentiable with respect to the scene representation. Loss functions typically combine photometric reconstruction error, such as \mathcal{L}{L1} or \mathcal{L}{MSE}, with perceptual or structural metrics like \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} or \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} [6136-instantsplat.md][6464-pixelsplat.md]. InstantSplat is a pose-free, sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) method that eliminates the need for Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines by leveraging geometry priors from foundation models like MASt3R or VGGT. It enables training in seconds by directly initializing Gaussians from these priors, distinguishing itself from feed-forward methods like pixelSplat which regress primitives directly from images, and from traditional 3DGS which requires dense pose estimation. AnySplat is a pose-free, feed-forward network that reconstructs 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes from uncalibrated image collections without requiring camera pose annotations. It differs from sibling methods like InstantSplat and pixelSplat by handling arbitrary multi-view inputs (dense or sparse) in a single forward pass, yielding both scene primitives and per-image intrinsics/extrinsics simultaneously. This enables zero-shot evaluation on casual captures where pose data is unavailable, matching the quality of pose-aware baselines while maintaining real-time rendering latency. pixelSplat is a feed-forward model that learns to reconstruct 3D radiance fields parameterized by 3D Gaussian primitives from pairs of images, enabling real-time and memory-efficient rendering and fast 3D reconstruction at inference time. It solves the problem of local minima inherent to sparse and locally supported representations in generalizable novel view synthesis, where non-differentiable pruning/splitting (used in single-scene optimization) cannot be used because gradients must back-propagate through the representation. Unlike light-field transformers which do not reconstruct editable 3D scene representations, pixelSplat generates an explicit 3D representation that is renderable in real time, remains editable, and is cheap to train. Joint Pose Optimization (JPO) eliminates the dependency on external Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines by simultaneously optimizing camera poses and the scene representation (neural or Gaussian) from unposed images. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on incremental depth priors or temporal continuity, JPO directly minimizes photometric reconstruction error to solve for both geometry and pose. It is distinct from feed-forward methods that predict poses via a separate network, as JPO treats poses as learnable parameters optimized via gradient descent. Loss scheduling for the candidate head is a training strategy that gradually reduces the influence of an image-dependent 'candidate head' (\hat{C}i) during optimization, transitioning to a shared representation (\hat{C}) to stabilize pose estimation for hard-pose images. It prevents the shared representation from being distracted by wrong supervision introduced by hard-pose images in the early stages, allowing the model to assimilate these images into the shared representation once the shared model is accurate enough. This method is distinct from sibling methods like InstantSplat and pixelSplat by explicitly decoupling the training influence of per-image heads via a cosine schedule rather than relying solely on joint pose optimization or fixed head structures. An extension to handle noisy camera poses, following SHARE implementation with modified input module. Use three 1x1 2D convolutional layers to reduce channel dimension of feature maps from 768 to 128, matching SHARE input dimension. Each conv layer preceded by normalization and Swish activation. M (number of fine-grained primitives per voxel): 8 (due to GPU memory constraints). On CO3D dataset, Oursext yields PSNR 21.62, SSIM 0.864, LPIPS 0.211. The family originates from the need to generalize 3D Gaussian Splatting beyond single-scene optimization, which is computationally expensive and requires accurate initial poses [6464-pixelsplat.md]. Early work like pixelSplat [6464-pixelsplat.md] introduced feed-forward architectures to predict Gaussian primitives directly from image pairs, addressing the local minima issues of traditional splatting. Subsequent developments like InstantSplat [6136-instantsplat.md] and AnySplat [6137-anysplat.md] incorporated foundation model priors (e.g., MASt3R, VGGT) to enable pose-free reconstruction from sparse or uncalibrated views, significantly reducing training time to seconds. Joint Pose Optimization [6888-joint-pose-optimization.md] provides an alternative by treating poses as learnable parameters rather than predicting them via a network. These methods are used in generalizable novel view synthesis, 3D object reconstruction from sparse views, and applications requiring real-time rendering from casual captures [6464-pixelsplat.md, S1]. VS-Splat: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse-views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.12343, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: InstantSplat
head: MASt3R/VGGT-guided 3DGS, Pose-free 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: InstantSplat is a pose-free, sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) method that eliminates the need for Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines by leveraging geometry priors from foundation models like MASt3R or VGGT. It enables training in seconds by directly initializing Gaussians from these priors, distinguishing itself from feed-forward methods like pixelSplat which regress primitives directly from images, and from traditional 3DGS which requires dense pose estimation. Inputs: A sparse set of uncalibrated images (typically 3–10 views). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives optimized for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Primitives: Standard 3DGS representation. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, parameterized by a rotation matrix \mathbf{R}i and scaling vector \mathbf{s}i such that \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^\top \mathbf{R}i^\top. Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for color c. 2. Geometry Priors: Depth maps and relative camera poses generated by MASt3R or VGGT from the input image pairs. Steps: 1. Prior Extraction: For each input image pair, run MASt3R or VGGT to obtain dense depth maps and relative camera poses. 2. Point Cloud Generation: Back-project pixels using the estimated depth and camera intrinsics to form a 3D point cloud. 3. Gaussian Initialization: Initialize the mean positions \boldsymbol{\mu}i of the Gaussians from the generated point cloud. 4. Differentiable Rendering: Render the scene using standard 3DGS differentiable rasterization. 5. Optimization: Optimize Gaussian parameters (positions, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients) using a loss function combining photometric error (\mathcal{L}{L1}) and perceptual loss (\mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM}). The optimization converges significantly faster than standard 3DGS due to the high-quality initialization from priors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def instantsplat(inputimages, intrinsicslist, numsteps=1000): # 1. Extract geometry priors via MASt3R/VGGT depthmaps, relativeposes = extractpriors(inputimages) # 2. Back-project depth to 3D point cloud pointcloud = backprojectdepth(depthmaps, intrinsicslist, relativeposes) # 3. Initialize Gaussian primitives gaussians = initializegaussians(pointcloud) # 4. Differentiable optimization loop for step in range(numsteps): renderedimages = render(gaussians, relativeposes) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, inputimages) gaussians = optimize(gaussians, loss) return gaussians def extractpriors(images): # Foundation model inference for depth and relative poses depthmaps = [model.predictdepth(img) for img in images] relativeposes = [model.predictpose(img1, img2) for img1, img2 in zip(images[:-1], images[1:])] return depthmaps, relativeposes def backprojectdepth(depthmaps, intrinsicslist, relativeposes): points = [] for depth, intrinsics, pose in zip(depthmaps, intrinsicslist, relativeposes): h, w = depth.shape u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w), np.arange(h)) z = depth[v, u] x = (u - intrinsics.cx) z / intrinsics.fx y = (v - intrinsics.cy) z / intrinsics.fy homogenous = np.stack([x, y, z, np.oneslike(z)], axis=-1) worldpoints = (pose @ homogenous.T).T[:,:3] points.append(worldpoints) return np.vstack(points) def initializegaussians(pointcloud): means = pointcloud covariances = computecovariancefromscaleandrotation(pointcloud) opacities = np.full(len(pointcloud), 0.5) shcoeffs = np.zeros((len(pointcloud), 16, 3)) return {'means': means, 'covariances': covariances, 'opacities': opacities, 'shcoeffs': shcoeffs} def render(gaussians, poses): return differentiablerasterize(gaussians['means'], gaussians['covariances'], gaussians['opacities'], gaussians['shcoeffs'], poses) def computeloss(rendered, target): return np.mean(np.abs(rendered - target)) + msssim(rendered, target) def optimize(gaussians, loss): grads = computegradients(loss, gaussians) return applysgd(gaussians, grads, lr=0.0001) def computecovariancefromscaleandrotation(points): # Standard initialization: uniform scale and identity rotation scale = np.ones((len(points), 3)) 0.1 rotation = np.tile(np.eye(3), (len(points), 1, 1)) S = np.diag(scale, axis1=-2, axis2=-1) return rotation @ S @ S.T @ rotation.T def differentiablerasterize(means, covs, opacities, shcoeffs, poses): # Standard 3DGS differentiable rasterizer return rasterizerprojectandshade(means, covs, opacities, shcoeffs, poses) def msssim(rendered, target): return structuralsimilarityindex(rendered, target) def computegradients(loss, gaussians): return gradientof(loss, gaussians) def applysgd(gaussians, grads, lr): for key in gaussians: gaussians[key] = gaussians[key] - lr grads[key] return gaussians Parameters: Training time: Typically completes in seconds due to high-quality initialization. Learning rate: Standard 3DGS learning rates apply. Edge Cases: Degenerate Input: If priors are noisy or missing, initialization may fail. Precision: Depth estimation errors propagate to Gaussian positions. A prior-aided monocular dynamic Gaussian Splatting method using CoTracker, VGG-T, DUSt3R, or metric-depth priors. A prior-aided monocular dynamic Gaussian Splatting method using CoTracker, VGG-T, DUSt3R, or metric-depth priors. A module that enhances existing feed-forward models by merging and refining Gaussian primitives in a canonical 3D space using a hybrid Splat-Voxel representation. Steps: 1. Input: Initial set of Gaussian primitives from existing pixel-aligned feed-forward models (from current frame or warped from previous frames). 2. Splat-to-Voxel Transfer: Aggregate local features from Gaussian primitives into a voxel representation. 3. Voxel Hierarchy: Construct a coarse-to-fine voxel hierarchy by adaptively sparsifying the high-resolution voxel grid. 4. Transformer Processing: Apply a sparse voxel transformer to features at the coarse resolution to capture global context. 5. Refinement: Generate refined Gaussian primitives at the high-resolution level from the processed voxel features. Parameters: Processing time: The module merges 200K Gaussian primitives in 15 ms. Performance: Quality improvement: PSNR improvement of around 2 dB compared to pixel-aligned reconstruction approaches. A feed-forward framework for novel-view synthesis that builds a hierarchical voxel-based scene representation and predicts 3D Gaussians from sparse input views. It provides a training and evaluation pipeline specifically for the RealEstate10K (RE10K) dataset. Evaluation uses six views using a fixed index file located at assets/re10kevaluation/evaluationindexre10k.json. Time complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to standard 3DGS due to better initialization, often completing in seconds. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates the need for SfM (COLMAP), enabling pose-free training. Fast training time. Works with sparse views. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the geometry priors (MASt3R/VGGT). Performance may degrade if priors are inaccurate. When to use: When SfM fails or is too slow, or when working with sparse/unstructured image collections. When not to use: When high-precision dense reconstruction is required and priors are unreliable. InstantSplat was introduced as a solution to the bottleneck of Structure-from-Motion (SfM) in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It leverages recent advances in foundation models for geometry estimation (MASt3R, VGGT) to provide robust initial geometry, allowing for rapid optimization. It is part of the broader trend of pose-free and feed-forward training methods in 3DGS. name: Feature-3DGS
head: N2F2
body: Feature-3DGS is a method for open-vocabulary 3D segmentation that stores per-Gaussian language features, such as CLIP or LSeg embeddings. It is distinguished as the first method for feature field distillation based on 3D Gaussian Splatting, leveraging guidance from 2D foundation models to learn semantic features for each 3D Gaussian. It employs a low-dimensional feature field upsampled via a convolutional decoder to improve rendering efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images, camera poses, and 2D foundation model features extracted from input views. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with associated low-dimensional semantic feature vectors, and a convolutional decoder for upsampling. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian: Standard 3DGS attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color) plus a per-Gaussian semantic feature vector. Feature Vector: A low-dimensional embedding representing the semantic content. Convolutional Decoder: A neural network module that upsamples the sparse feature field to pixel space. Steps: 1. Learn semantic features for each 3D Gaussian. 2. Leverage guidance from 2D foundation models during training. 3. Employ a low-dimensional feature field. 4. Upsample the sparse feature field using a convolutional decoder to improve rendering efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectgaussians(gaussians, camera): """Project 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and compute 2D covariance.""" projected = [] for g in gaussians: # Transform to camera space, project via intrinsic matrix, # compute 2D covariance via Jacobian, apply screen-space bounding box. proj = standard3dgsprojection(g, camera) projected.append(proj) return sorted(projected, key=lambda p: p.depth) def alphablendfeatures(projectedgaussians, imagewidth, imageheight, featuredim): """Alpha-blend low-dimensional feature vectors per pixel.""" features = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, featuredim)) alphas = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) for g in projectedgaussians: bbox = g.screenboundingbox for y in range(bbox.ymin, bbox.ymax): for x in range(bbox.xmin, bbox.xmax): weight = g.opacity g.gaussianweight(x, y) features[y, x] += weight g.featurevector alphas[y, x] += weight features = features / (alphas[:,:, None] + 1e-5) return features def computefeatureloss(renderedfeatures, targetfeatures): """Compute feature distillation loss.""" return meansquarederror(renderedfeatures, targetfeatures) def forwardpass(gaussians, camera, decoder, imagewidth, imageheight, featuredim): projected = projectgaussians(gaussians, camera) sparsefeatures = alphablendfeatures(projected, imagewidth, imageheight, featuredim) densefeatures = decoder(sparsefeatures) return densefeatures def trainstep(gaussians, camera, decoder, optimizer, images, foundationmodelfeatures): renderedfeatures = forwardpass(gaussians, camera, decoder, images.shape[2], images.shape[3], foundationmodelfeatures.shape[-1]) loss = computefeatureloss(renderedfeatures, foundationmodelfeatures) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss Parameters: Foundation Model: CLIP or LSeg. Decoder Architecture: Convolutional decoder. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Provides a robust initialization strategy for Gaussians to improve semantic alignment. It sets itself apart by focusing on initialization quality rather than rendering or grouping. Choose it when starting training from sparse or noisy geometry. Holistic Gaussian Initialization Focuses on re-splatting techniques for efficient rendering. It differs by optimizing the rasterization pass rather than feature learning. Choose it when rendering speed is the primary bottleneck. ReSplat Uses adaptive entropy-based splatting to optimize rendering. It stands out by dynamically adjusting splat density based on feature entropy. Choose it when memory or compute limits restrict dense feature field rendering. AESplat Strengths: Enables open-vocabulary 3D segmentation and achieves efficient rendering via low-dimensional features and convolutional upsampling. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on the quality and coverage of the underlying 2D foundation models. Feature-3DGS was introduced as the first method for feature field distillation based on 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on 2D foundation models like CLIP and LSeg, adapting them to the 3D Gaussian representation. It follows a series of works leveraging 2D priors for 3D tasks, such as SAGA and Gaussian Grouping. name: Holistic Gaussian Initialization
body: Holistic Gaussian Initialization (HGI) is a strategy to generate dense and accurate initialized 3D Gaussians within seconds for endoscopic scenes, replacing the time-consuming and sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipeline (e.g., COLMAP) used in standard 3DGS. It works for both binocular and monocular input sequences by leveraging depth estimation models to back-project pixels into world coordinates, creating a dense point cloud that serves as the initial state for Gaussian optimization. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by eliminating the need for sparse SfM points, thereby accelerating initialization and improving density. It builds on InstantSplat and relates to siblings Feature-3DGS, ReSplat, and AESplat. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^T (either binocular pairs \{I^li, I^ri\} or monocular \{Ii\}), camera intrinsic parameters \mathbf{K}, and extrinsic parameters \mathbf{T}i for each view. For binocular input, a stereo depth estimation model is required. For monocular input, a monocular depth estimation model is required. Outputs: A set of initialized 3D Gaussians (positions, orientations, scales, opacities, colors) derived from the back-projected point clouds. Data Structures: Depth Maps: \mathbf{D}i, a 2D array of depth values for each view i. Binary Mask: \mathbf{M}i, a 2D array of the same resolution as the image, where 1 indicates valid scene pixels and 0 indicates invalid pixels (e.g., surgical tools). Point Cloud: \mathbf{P}i, a set of 3D points in world coordinates for view i. Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: For binocular input, use a stereo depth estimation model to predict metric depth maps \{\mathbf{D}i\}{i=1}^T for the left views. For monocular input, use a monocular depth estimation model to predict relative depth maps \{\mathbf{D}i\}{i=1}^T. 2. Re-projection: For each view i, re-project the pixels of the image Ii into world coordinates to obtain the partial point cloud \mathbf{P}i using: \mathbf{P}i = \mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{T}i\mathbf{D}i(\mathbf{I}i \odot \mathbf{M}i) where \odot denotes element-wise product, \mathbf{K} is the camera intrinsic matrix, \mathbf{T}i is the camera extrinsic matrix, and \mathbf{D}i is the depth map. The term \mathbf{D}i(\mathbf{I}i \odot \mathbf{M}i) applies the depth value at each pixel location, masked by \mathbf{M}i. 3. Combination: Combine the partial point clouds \{\mathbf{P}i\}{i=1}^T from all views into a single holistic point cloud. 4. Gaussian Initialization: Initialize the Gaussians using the points from the combined point cloud. Positions are set to the 3D coordinates. Orientations \mathbf{q} are aligned with normal directions estimated from the initial point cloud. One scaling axis is set smaller than the others to encourage disc-like surfels. Opacities and colors are initialized based on the input image colors and standard opacity values. Parameters: Number of initialization points: 1M back-projected points from the training dataset sensor depths. Depth Models: Stereo depth estimation model [11] (EndoNeRF) for binocular input; monocular depth estimation model [25] for monocular input. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular Scale Ambiguity: Relative depth maps from monocular models lose scale information, but accurate reconstruction is still achieved because the Gaussian optimization process incorporates explicit geometric constraints from real poses and rendered images. Tool Occlusion: Binary masks \mathbf{M}i are used to filter out surgical tool pixels, which are not part of the scene geometry. Limited Perspective: A single image contains a limited perspective, so combining multiple views is necessary for a holistic point cloud. This variant initializes the Gaussian scene using back-projected sensor depth readings for dense initialization, rather than sparse SfM points. It is chosen when sensor depth data is available. The steps are: 1. Back-project sensor depths into world coordinates. 2. Estimate normal directions from the initial point cloud using [61]. 3. Align Gaussian orientations \mathbf{q} with estimated normals using Eq. (7). 4. Set one scaling axis smaller than the others. The number of initialization points is 1M back-projected points from the training dataset sensor depths. Time Complexity: Initialization takes seconds, significantly faster than the minutes required for SfM pipelines. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of points (e.g., 1M points) and the resolution of depth maps. Strengths: Generates dense and accurate initialized points quickly; works for both binocular and monocular inputs; avoids sparse SfM limitations. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of depth estimation models; monocular input requires scale recovery during optimization. When to use: When fast initialization is required, especially in endoscopic scenes where SfM may fail or be too slow. Holistic Gaussian Initialization was introduced in the EndoGaussian paper. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which relies on sparse SfM points for initialization, leading to longer optimization times and potential inaccuracies in dynamic endoscopic scenes. The method leverages recent advances in depth estimation models to provide a dense and accurate initial point cloud. name: ReSplat
head: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting
body: ReSplat is a feed-forward recurrent Gaussian splatting model that iteratively refines 3D Gaussian primitives without explicitly computing gradients, using rendering error as a feedback signal to guide updates. It operates in a compact subsampled 3D space to reduce the Gaussian count while improving performance and generalization. Unlike single-step feed-forward models, ReSplat leverages a weight-sharing recurrent network for multi-step refinement, enabling robust generalization across diverse datasets, view counts, and resolutions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N (where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}), intrinsic matrices \{Ki\}{i=1}^N (Ki \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}), and extrinsic matrices \{(Ri, ti)\}{i=1}^N (where Ri \in SO(3), ti \in \mathbb{R}^3). Output: A set of M 3D Gaussian primitives G = \{(\muj, \alphaj, \Sigmaj, shj)\}{j=1}^M, where \muj is position, \alphaj is opacity, \Sigmaj is covariance, and shj represents spherical harmonics coefficients. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A set of M points \{(pj, fj)\}{j=1}^M, where pj \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the 3D position and fj \in \mathbb{R}^{C0} is the feature vector. Context-Aggregated Features: \{fj^\}{j=1}^M, where fj^ \in \mathbb{R}^{C0}. Gaussian Parameters: gj \in \mathbb{R}^{C1}, where C1 = 59 is the concatenation of all Gaussian parameters (\muj, \alphaj, \Sigmaj, shj) for the j-th Gaussian. Hidden State: zj \in \mathbb{R}^{C0}, representing the latent state for the j-th Gaussian. Parameters: Subsampling Factor: 16. The initial reconstruction operates in a 16x subsampled 3D space. Feature Dimension (C0): 256 for the small model, 512 for the base model. Number of Attention Blocks: Six alternating blocks of kNN attention and global attention. Number of Recurrent Steps (T): The total number of refinement iterations. Input Views (N): Tested with 2, 8, 16, and 32 views. Image Resolution: Tested from 256x256 to 540x960. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (Iteration 0): Point Cloud Generation Predict per-view depth maps at 1/4 resolution. Unproject and transform them into a point cloud with image features \{(pj, fj)\}{j=1}^M, where M = N \times H \times W / 16 is the number of points. \{Ii, Ki, Ri, ti\}{i=1}^N \rightarrow \{(pj, fj)\}{j=1}^M \quad (1) 2. Context Aggregation Use six alternating blocks of kNN attention and global attention to model local and global 3D contexts. This produces context-aggregated features fj^ \in \mathbb{R}^{C0} with increased expressiveness. \{(pj, fj)\}{j=1}^M \rightarrow \{(pj, fj^)\}{j=1}^M \quad (2) 3. Initial Gaussian Prediction Reconstruct an initial set of 3D Gaussians \{(gj^0, zj^0)\}{j=1}^M in the 16x subsampled 3D space. The point cloud \{pj\}{j=1}^M serves as the Gaussian centers. Other Gaussian parameters are decoded using a lightweight Gaussian head (two-layer MLP) from the context-aggregated features \{fj^\}{j=1}^M. 4. Recurrent Update Step t (for t = 1 to T): a. Rendering: Render the input views using the current Gaussian prediction Gt = \{(gj^t, zj^t)\}{j=1}^M. b. Error Computation: Compute the rendering errors \hat{E}t between the rendered views and the ground-truth input views. Derive the rendering error vector ej^t for each Gaussian. c. Error Propagation: Apply global attention on the rendering error to propagate these errors to the 3D Gaussians. d. Parameter Update: A kNN attention-based update module takes as input the concatenation of the current Gaussian parameters gj^t, the hidden state zj^t, and the rendering error ej^t. It predicts the incremental updates \Delta gj^t and \Delta zj^t. e. State Update: Update the Gaussian parameters and hidden state: gj^{t+1} = gj^t + \Delta gj^t zj^{t+1} = zj^t + \Delta zj^t 5. Iteration: Iterate the recurrent update process for a total of T steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resplat(inputimages, intrinsics, extrinsics, numviews, height, width, featuredim, numrecurrentsteps, subsamplingfactor=16): """ ReSplat: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting Args: inputimages: List of N images, shape (H, W, 3) intrinsics: List of N intrinsic matrices, shape (3, 3) extrinsics: List of N extrinsic matrices (R, t), shape (3, 3) and (3,) numviews: N height: H width: W featuredim: C0 (256 or 512) numrecurrentsteps: T Returns: gaussianparams: Array of shape (M, C1) points: Array of shape (M, 3) """ M = numviews height width // (subsamplingfactor 2) C1 = 59 # Concatenated Gaussian parameters # Step 1: Initialization - Point Cloud Generation points = [] features = [] for i in range(numviews): # Predict depth map at 1/4 resolution depthmap = predictdepth(inputimages[i]) # Shape (H/4, W/4) # Unproject to 3D using Ki, Ri, ti and extract features pts, feats = unprojectandextractfeatures(depthmap, intrinsics[i], extrinsics[i]) points.append(pts) features.append(feats) points = np.concatenate(points, axis=0) # Shape (M, 3) features = np.concatenate(features, axis=0) # Shape (M, C0) # Step 2: Context Aggregation # 6 alternating blocks of kNN and global attention contextfeatures = applycontextaggregation(points, features) # Shape (M, C0) # Step 3: Initial Gaussian Prediction # Centers are points, other params decoded via 2-layer MLP gaussianparams = decodegaussians(points, contextfeatures) # Shape (M, C1) hiddenstates = contextfeatures.copy() # Initialize zj^0 # Step 4: Recurrent Update for t in range(numrecurrentsteps): # Render input views using current Gaussians renderedimages = rendergaussians(gaussianparams, points, intrinsics, extrinsics) # Compute rendering errors (MSE) renderingerrors = computerenderingerror(renderedimages, inputimages) # Propagate errors to Gaussians via global attention errorfeatures = propagateerrors(renderingerrors, points) # Shape (M, C0) # Parameter Update # Concatenate current params, hidden state, and error features inputtoupdate = np.concatenate([gaussianparams, hiddenstates, errorfeatures], axis=-1) # Predict incremental updates using kNN attention-based module deltaparams, deltastates = updatemodule(inputtoupdate) # Shape (M, C1) and (M, C0) # Update Gaussians and hidden states gaussianparams = gaussianparams + deltaparams hiddenstates = hiddenstates + deltastates return gaussianparams, points def predictdepth(image): """Standard depth estimation network.""" return image # Placeholder for actual depth model output def unprojectandextractfeatures(depthmap, K, Rt): """Unproject depth to 3D, transform to world space, and extract image features.""" # Standard inverse projection and feature sampling return np.zeros((depthmap.shape[0] depthmap.shape[1], 3)), np.zeros((depthmap.shape[0] depthmap.shape[1], 256)) def applycontextaggregation(points, features): """Six alternating blocks of kNN attention and global attention.""" # Standard attention block implementation return features # Placeholder for actual aggregated features def decodegaussians(points, features): """Two-layer MLP decoding Gaussian parameters from features.""" # Standard MLP forward pass return np.zeros((features.shape[0], 59)) # Placeholder for actual params def rendergaussians(gaussianparams, points, intrinsics, extrinsics): """Standard 3D Gaussian splatting rasterization.""" return np.zeroslike(intrinsics[0]) # Placeholder for rendered images def computerenderingerror(rendered, groundtruth): """Mean squared error between rendered and ground truth images.""" return np.mean((rendered - groundtruth) 2) def propagateerrors(errors, points): """Global attention over rendering error features to propagate to Gaussians.""" return np.zeros((points.shape[0], 256)) # Placeholder for propagated features def updatemodule(inputtensor): """kNN attention-based update module predicting incremental updates.""" # Standard kNN attention forward pass return np.zeros((inputtensor.shape[0], 59)), np.zeros((inputtensor.shape[0], 256)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Naive Prediction: Naively predicting Gaussian parameters from subsampled point features leads to considerable performance loss. This is compensated by using kNN and global attention layers to encode 3D context. Unbounded Scenes: Unlike SplatFormer, which relies on Point Transformer V3 requiring a proper grid size for point cloud serialization (challenging for unbounded scenes), ReSplat handles diverse scene-level datasets without this limitation. Initialization: ReSplat predicts initial Gaussians directly from posed images, without requiring any initial 3D points, unlike G3R which requires well-covered 3D points for initialization. Time Complexity: ReSplat is 100x faster than optimization-based 3DGS due to its feed-forward design. Rendering speed is 4x faster than per-pixel baselines like MVSplat and DepthSplat due to the 16x fewer Gaussians. It is 20x faster than LVSM due to the explicit 3D Gaussian representation. Memory Complexity: Uses 1/16 of the Gaussians compared to per-pixel baselines. Performance: On DL3DV with 8 input views at 512x960 resolution, ReSplat improves PSNR by 3.5dB, uses 1/16 of the Gaussians, and achieves 4x faster rendering speed compared to baselines. On DL3DV with 16 input views at 540x960 resolution, it outperforms Long-LRM by 0.8dB PSNR while using 4x fewer Gaussians. On DL3DV with 8 input views at 256x448 resolution, full ReSplat achieves PSNR 29.07, SSIM 0.902, LPIPS 0.105. Strengths: Feed-forward design, iterative refinement without explicit gradients, robust generalization across datasets/view counts/resolutions, handles scene-level datasets, explicit 3D Gaussian representation for fast rendering. Limitations: Requires posed input images. When to use: Sparse view synthesis, scene-level reconstruction, when computational efficiency and generalization are prioritized over per-scene optimization. When not to use: When unposed images are available (requires pose estimation), when extremely dense point clouds are needed for specific applications. ReSplat was introduced by Haofei Xu, Daniel Barath, Andreas Geiger, and Marc Pollefeys in the paper 'ReSplat: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting'. It addresses the limitations of existing feed-forward Gaussian splatting models, which are constrained by relying on a single forward pass for inference. The method builds on the concept of learning to optimize, but differs from approaches like G3R by being gradient-free and from SplatFormer by being recurrent and handling scene-level datasets. name: AESplat
head: AESplat: Advancing Pose-Free Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting via Decoupled Appearance Modeling
body: AESplat is a pose-free, feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework that improves novel view synthesis by decoupling appearance modeling into view-independent (zeroth-order spherical harmonics) and view-dependent (higher-order spherical harmonics) components. Unlike unified prediction paradigms that regress all SH coefficients jointly, AESplat derives the zeroth-order coefficient directly from input pixel RGB values without training, while predicting higher-order coefficients using a shallow MLP conditioned on 3D-aware inductive biases. This approach addresses the suboptimal rendering quality of existing pose-free methods that overlook the fundamental distinction between diffuse base appearance and specular/view-dependent variations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N unposed images \{Iv\}{v=1}^N, comprising NC context images IC and NT target images IT. The input resolution is 224 \times 224 pixels. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \{G{v \to 1}\} in the canonical frame of the first view, and camera parameters (extrinsics P{v \to 1} and intrinsics Kv) for all views. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive Gj: Defined in the canonical frame of the first view. Center \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation r \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Scale s \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R} SH Coefficients c \in \mathbb{R}^{(l+1)^2 \times 3}, where l is the SH degree. Camera Parameters: Extrinsics P{v \to 1}: 6D rotation representation + 4D homogeneous translation vector, converted to a homogeneous transformation matrix. Intrinsics Kv: Field of View (FOV), assuming equal horizontal/vertical FOV and centered principal point. Method Steps: 1. Multi-View Feature Extraction: Input images are patchified and encoded by a DINOv2 backbone into image features Fv. These are concatenated with learnable camera tokens gv. A ViT-based encoder-decoder with Alternating-Attention aggregates information. Masked attention restricts context tokens to attend only to context tokens, while target tokens attend to both, preventing target-view leakage into Gaussian reconstruction. 2. Camera Parameter Estimation: Refined camera tokens \hat{g}v are passed to a camera head to predict extrinsics P{v \to 1} and intrinsics Kv for each view. The first view is defined as the canonical frame. 3. Gaussian Geometry Prediction: Refined context tokens \hat{F}v^C are processed by two DPT heads: One predicts depth to recover Gaussian centers \mu. The other predicts rotation r, scale s, opacity \alpha, and initial SH coefficients. All Gaussians are transformed into the canonical frame of the first view: \{G{v \to 1}\}{v=1}^N = \{(\muj, rj, sj, \alphaj, cj)\}{j=1}^{H \times W} where \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, r \in \mathbb{R}^4, s \in \mathbb{R}^3, \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, c \in \mathbb{R}^{(l+1)^2 \times 3}. 4. View-Independent Appearance Modeling (VIAM): The zeroth-order SH coefficient c{00} is derived directly from the input image pixel RGB value Cj^v \in \mathbb{R}^3 for pixel-aligned Gaussians, without training. This is termed Image-to-Direct Component (I2DC). The formula is: c{00}^{(v,j)} = \frac{Cj^v - 0.5}{Y{00}} where Y{00} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}} is the constant zeroth-order SH basis function. 5. name: AnySplat
head: Pose-free feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: AnySplat is a pose-free feed-forward network that reconstructs 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes from uncalibrated image collections without requiring camera pose annotations. It solves the dependency on explicit pose estimation by predicting 3D Gaussian primitives and per-image intrinsics and extrinsics in a single forward pass. body: FreeSplat is a feed-forward framework that reconstructs geometrically consistent global 3D Gaussian Splatting from long, sparse image sequences to support free-view synthesis across wide view ranges. It differs from pixelSplat and MVSplat, which are limited to narrow-range interpolation due to heavy transformer backbones, by using pure CNN-based backbones and a Pixel-aligned Triplet Fusion (PTF) module to handle arbitrary view counts and wide baselines. Inputs: A sparse sequence of T posed RGB images \{It\}{t=1}^T with known camera poses \{Pt\}{t=1}^T. Outputs: Global 3D Gaussian primitives \{\Sigma, \alpha, s\} and depths d. Data Structures: Local Gaussian Triplet Map (F{lt}): Tensor of shape R^{C \times H \times W} containing latent features for each pixel. Local Gaussian Centers (\mu{tl}): Tensor of shape R^{3 \times H \times W}. Local Gaussian Weights (\omega{lt}): Tensor of shape R^{1 \times H \times W}, values in (0, 1). Local Gaussian Features (f{lt}): Tensor of shape R^{(C-1) \times H \times W}. Global Gaussian Centers (\mug): Tensor of shape R^{3 \times M}, where M is the number of global Gaussians. Global Gaussian Weights (\omegag): Tensor of shape R^{1 \times M}. Global Gaussian Features (fg): Tensor of shape R^{C \times M}. Cost Volume (F{cv}^t): Tensor of shape R^{K \times 4 \times 4} (or similar channel dimension depending on f\theta). Parameters: N: Number of nearby views selected for cost volume construction. K: Number of virtual depth planes. [d{near}, d{far}]: Depth range for virtual planes. \delta: Ratio threshold for pixel-wise alignment depth difference check. Value not specified in sources. T: Number of context views sampled during Free-View Training. Typical value: between 2 and 8. Learning Rate: 1e-4 (Adam optimizer). Image Resolution: 384 \times 512. Steps: 1. 2D Feature Extraction: Feed the sparse sequence of posed images \{It\}{t=1}^T into a shared CNN-based 2D backbone to extract multi-scale embeddings F{et} and matching features Fm. 2. Adaptive Cost Volume Construction: For the current view It with pose Pt and matching feature Fm: a. Select N nearby views \{I{tn}\}{n=1}^N based on pose proximity. b. Define K virtual depth planes \{dk\}{k=1}^K uniformly spaced in [d{near}, d{far}]. c. Warp nearby view features to each depth plane: \tilde{F}m^{tn,k} = \text{Trans}(P{tn}, Pt)Fm, where \text{Trans} denotes the transformation from pose P{tn} to Pt. d. Compute the cost volume F{cv}^t \in R^{K \times 4 \times 4}: F{cv}^t[k] = f\theta\left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^N \cos(Fm, \tilde{F}m^{tn,k}) \oplus \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^N \tilde{F}m^{tn,k} \right) where \cos(\cdot) is cosine similarity, \oplus is feature-wise concatenation, and f\theta(\cdot) is a 1 \times 1 CNN mapping to dimension 1. 3. Multi-Scale Feature Aggregation: Pass F{cv}^t through a multi-scale encoder-decoder structure (UNet++-like). Concatenate encoder output with multi-scale image features \{F{st}\} before the decoder to upsample to full resolution. Predict a depth candidates map D{ct} \in R^{K \times H \times W} and a Gaussian triplet map F{lt} \in R^{C \times H \times W}. 4. Depth Prediction: Predict the depth map Dt via soft-argmax to bound depth between near and far: Dt = \sum{k=1}^K \text{softmax}(D{ct})k \cdot dk. 5. Unprojection: Unproject the pixel-aligned Gaussian triplet map F{lt} to 3D Gaussian triplets \{\mu{tl}, \omega{lt}, f{lt}\}, where \mu{tl} \in R^{3 \times HW} are centers, \omega{lt} \in R^{1 \times HW} are weights in (0,1), and f{lt} \in R^{(C-1) \times HW} are features. 6. Pixel-wise Triplet Fusion (PTF): Initialize global Gaussians as empty. For t=1 to T: a. Global Projection: Project global Gaussian centers \mu{t-1}^g \in R^{3 \times M} onto the t-th view: p{tg}:= \{x{tg}, y{tg}, d{tg}\} = Pt \mu{t-1}^g where [x{tg}, y{tg}, d{tg}] \in R^{3 \times M} are projected 2D coordinates and depths. b. Correspondence: For the i-th local Gaussian with 2D coordinate [x{tl}(i), y{tl}(i)] and depth d{tl}(i), find the intra-pixel global projection set S{ti}: S{ti}:= \{j \mid \lfloor x{tg}(j) \rfloor = \lfloor x{tl}(i) \rfloor, \lfloor y{tg}(j) \rfloor = \lfloor y{tl}(i) \rfloor\} where \lfloor \cdot \rfloor is the rounding operator. Find valid correspondence mi: mi = \begin{cases} \arg \min{j \in S{ti}} d{tg}(j) & \text{if } |d{tl}(i) - \min{j \in S{ti}} d{tg}(j)| < \delta \cdot d{tl}(i) \\ \emptyset & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Define the valid correspondence set \mathcal{F}t:= \{(i, mi) \mid i = 1, \dots, HW; mi \neq \emptyset\}. c. Gaussian Triplet Fusion (Geometric): For each pair (i, mi) \in \mathcal{F}t, compute weighted sum of centers and sum weights: \mu{tg}(mi) = \frac{\omega{lt}(i)\mu{tl}(i) + \omega{t-1}^g(mi)\mu{t-1}^g(mi)}{\omega{lt}(i) + \omega{t-1}^g(mi)} \omega{t}^g(mi) = \omega{lt}(i) + \omega{t-1}^g(mi). d. Gaussian Triplet Fusion (Feature): Aggregate aligned local and global Gaussian latent features through a lightweight GRU: f{gt}(mi) = \text{GRU}(f{lt}(i), f{t-1}^g(mi)) Append unaligned local Gaussian triplets to the global set. 7. Gaussian Primitives Decoding: Decode global Gaussian triplets into primitives: \Sigma, \alpha, s = \text{MLP}d(fg^T) \mu = \mug^T. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
