head: ZipSplat: Fewer Gaussians, Better Splats
body: ZipSplat is a feed-forward method that reconstructs scenes from unposed, uncalibrated images as compact, observation-grounded scene tokens, each derived from a source patch and decoded into freely placed Gaussians. It solves the problem of redundant, misaligned Gaussian predictions across views by aggregating multi-view observations into a fixed set of learned tokens, while allowing the reconstruction budget to be adjusted at inference without retraining. It sets itself apart from its parent AnySplat and sibling FreeSplat by deriving tokens directly from image patches rather than learned queries, and by using a cone loss to ground decoded Gaussians to their source observations, preventing spatial drift. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N unposed and uncalibrated images \mathcal{I} = \{In \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}\}{n=1}^N. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians and estimated camera parameters. Data Structures: Geometry Tokens (\mathbf{g}): One token per image patch, extracted from a multi-view backbone. Scene Tokens (\mathbf{z}): A compact set of K tokens derived by clustering geometry tokens. Gaussians (\mathcal{G}): Each scene token k decodes into G Gaussians. Each Gaussian j is parameterized by: Center \boldsymbol{\mu}{kj} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scales \mathbf{s}{kj} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}{kj} \in \mathbb{R}^4 Opacity \alpha{kj} \in [0, 1] Color coefficients \mathbf{c}{kj} \in \mathbb{R}^C (using degree-1 spherical harmonics). Algorithm Steps: 1. Token Extraction: A multi-view backbone extracts per-patch visual tokens at multiple layers. These are merged into geometry tokens \mathbf{g}, one per image patch. 2. Clustering: Geometry tokens are clustered into K scene tokens using k-means. The number of tokens K is determined by a compression ratio r at inference: K = r \cdot T (where T is the total number of geometry tokens). Clustering is guided by the GeoCE loss to ensure patches observing the same surface are merged. 3. Token Fusion (Refinement): Scene tokens are refined through alternating cross- and self-attention to recover detail lost during cluster averaging. For l=1, \ldots, L: \mathbf{z}k^l = \operatorname{SA}\left( \operatorname{CA} (\mathbf{z}k^{l-1}, \mathbf{g}, \mathbf{v}k^l) \right) where geometry tokens \mathbf{g} serve as keys and backbone features \mathbf{f}^l provide values. Final residual cross-attention incorporates color features: \mathbf{z}k = \mathbf{z}k^L + \operatorname{CA} (\mathbf{z}k^L, \mathbf{g}, \mathbf{v}k^{\mathrm{col}}). 4. Gaussian Decoding: An MLP decoder \mathcal{D} maps each scene token \mathbf{z}k into G freely placed Gaussians: \mathcal{G}k = \left\{ \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}{kj}, \mathbf{s}{kj}, \mathbf{q}{kj}, \alpha{kj}, \mathbf{c}{kj} \right) \right\}{j=1}^{G} = \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}k) The full scene is assembled from all K tokens. 5. Geometric Grounding (Cone Loss): To prevent decoded Gaussians from drifting from their source patch, a cone loss penalizes the reprojection distance between Gaussian centers and the source patch center \mathbf{u}k: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{cone}} = \sum{k=1}^{K} \sum{j=1}^{G} \rho \left( \left\| \pik(\boldsymbol{\mu}{kj}) - \mathbf{u}k \right\| \right) where \pik projects into the source view of token k, distances are measured in patch units, and \rho is a robust penalty. 6. Token Shaping (GeoCE Loss): To ensure clustering merges patches observing the same surface, a geometric consistency loss aligns token similarity with 3D proximity. Each token's patch is unprojected to a 3D anchor \mathbf{p}i using median depth. A soft target distribution is constructed: w{ij} \propto \exp \left( -\frac{\|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}j\|^2}{2\sigmai\sigmaj} \right), \quad j \neq i where \sigmai scales with local patch spacing. 7. TokenBA Refinement: Cameras and tokens are refined using robust PnP on patch-Gaussian correspondences and updating scene tokens through the frozen decoder using photometric error on input views. Parameters: G=32: Number of Gaussians per scene token. L=3: Number of cross- and self-attention blocks for fusion. r: Compression ratio, sampled uniformly from [0.2/N, 1] during training to enable adjustable budget at inference. Loss weights: \lambda{geo}=0.05, \lambda{cone}=0.01, \lambda{pose}=0.05. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gaussian Drift: Without geometric constraints (cone loss), the decoder can place Gaussians anywhere in 3D, drifting from the source patch. Surface Mixing: Clustering can merge tokens from different surfaces if not guided by geometric consistency (GeoCE). Token Fusion is the refinement stage where scene tokens are updated through alternating cross- and self-attention to recover detail lost during the cluster averaging step. It uses geometry tokens as keys to bias retrieval toward relevant observations across views and backbone features as values. It is chosen when high-frequency detail recovery is needed after aggressive compression. Time and Memory Complexity: The method produces a compact representation where the number of Gaussians scales with the compression ratio r rather than the number of input views, allowing for a continuous quality-efficiency trade-off. Measured Performance: Trained on RealEstate10K and DL3DV at 256 \times 256 resolution for 450K steps on 16 GH200 GPUs. Strengths: Adjustable reconstruction budget at inference; observation-grounded tokens prevent redundancy; pose-free operation. Limitations: Requires a multi-view backbone and attention mechanisms, which may increase inference latency compared to simpler splatting methods. When to use: When reconstructing scenes from uncalibrated, unposed image collections with a need for adjustable memory/compute budgets. ZipSplat was introduced in a preprint in 2026 by the authors of the arXiv paper "ZipSplat: Fewer Gaussians, Better Splats". It builds on the lineage of pose-free feed-forward training methods like AnySplat, addressing the limitation of pixel-to-Gaussian mappings that scale with input size rather than scene complexity. name: SHARE (Pose-free 3D Gaussian Splatting via Shape-Ray Estimation)
head: Pose-free 3D Gaussian Splatting via Shape-Ray Estimation
body: SHARE is a pose-free, feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework that jointly estimates relative camera poses and reconstructs accurate 3D geometry by operating in latent space rather than explicit 3D space, mitigating pose-induced geometry misalignment. Unlike methods that transform 3D geometries from each viewpoint into a reference camera coordinate using predicted poses, SHARE constructs a unified cost volume in latent space, bypassing erroneous 3D space transformation. It sets itself apart from siblings like FreeSplat and ZipSplat by using Plücker rays to guide multi-view feature fusion directly, avoiding the sequential estimation of pose and shape that leads to significant geometric errors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M unposed images I = \{Ii\}{i=1}^M. Output: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gn\}{n=1}^N and relative camera poses \{Ri, Ti\}{i=1}^M. Each Gaussian Gn is defined by position \mun, opacity \alphan, covariance matrix \Sigman, and color cn. Data Structures: Multi-view Features: Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times C}, extracted per view. Plücker Rays: P{li} \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times 6}, defined per spatial patch l for view i. Each ray consists of direction d and momentum m, denoted P = \langle d, m \rangle. Cost Volumes: Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times D} for each view i, where D is the number of hypothetical depth candidates. Spatial Weights: Wi \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}} used to account for view-dependent effects. Fused Feature: Vg, the canonical volume representation. Parameters: \Phi\theta denotes the network mapping. Numbered Steps: 1. Joint Feature Extraction: Estimate multi-view features Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times C} using a matching transformer backbone. 2. Ray Estimation: Estimate patch-wise Plücker rays P{li} \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times 6} through an additional two-layer lightweight transformer. Each ray is defined by direction d and momentum m. 3. Cost Volume Construction: For each viewpoint i, construct cost volumes Ci by extending 2D features into 3D along hypothetical planes and projecting onto other views. Compute channel-wise correlations between the reference feature Fi and warped features F{dj \to i} for D depth candidates. The cost volume Ci is computed as: Ci = \sum{j \neq i} \frac{Fi \cdot F{j \to i}}{\sqrt{C}} \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times D} where D is the number of hypothetical depth candidates. 4. Pose-aware Cost Aggregation: Refine cost volumes through cost aggregation conditioned on predicted Plücker rays. Use patch-wise cross-attention to embed pose awareness into the cost volumes. Since rays are locally defined in spatial patches, they are seamlessly integrated with image features, introducing geometric bias into the cost volumes. 5. Canonical Volume Formation: Select one viewpoint as the canonical view. Align remaining views to the canonical space using the pose-aware cost volumes and spatial weights Wi to account for occlusion and lighting, building a fused feature Vg. 6. Anchor Prediction: Use fused features Vg to predict pixel-aligned coarse geometry (anchors). 7. Anchor-aligned Gaussian Prediction: Use fused features Vf (derived from Vg) to predict offset vectors from the coarse anchors to spread to adjacent regions. Predict k Gaussians per region for fine-grained reconstruction. Formulas: The objective mapping function is: \Phi\theta: \{Ii\}{i=1}^M \rightarrow \{Gn\}{n=1}^N, \{Ri, Ti\} = \Psi(\{P{li}\}{l=1}^{Ph \times Pw}) where Gn = \{\mun, \alphan, \Sigman, cn\}, P = \langle d, m \rangle, and \Psi converts Plücker rays to camera parameters (R, T). Parameters: Ph, Pw: Spatial patch resolution used for defining Plücker rays and cost volumes. D: Number of hypothetical depth candidates used in cost volume construction. Pitfalls: Sequential estimation of camera pose and shape leads to significant geometry misalignment if pose estimates are inaccurate. SHARE avoids this by joint estimation in latent space. Inaccurate pose estimates in traditional methods cause errors when transforming 3D geometries into a reference coordinate system. SHARE bypasses this by fusing features in latent space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shareforward(images): """ Input: images - List of M unposed images Ii. Output: Gaussians {Gn}, Camera Poses {Ri, Ti} """ # Step 1: Joint Feature Extraction # Fi in R^(H/4 x W/4 x C) features = [] for img in images: # Using a matching transformer backbone Fi = matchingtransformerbackbone(img) features.append(Fi) # Step 2: Ray Estimation # Pli in R^(H/4 x W/4 x 6) # Plucker rays P = <d, m> rays = [] for Fi in features: # Using a two-layer lightweight transformer Pi = lightweighttransformer(Fi) rays.append(Pi) # Step 3: Cost Volume Construction # Ci in R^(H/4 x W/4 x D) costvolumes = [] for i in range(len(images)): Ci = torch.zeros((H/4, W/4, D)) for j in range(len(images)): if i != j: # Warp features from view j to view i based on hypothetical depth # F{j->i} in R^(H/4 x W/4 x C) Fjtoi = warpfeatures(features[j], hypotheticaldepths, rays[j]) # Channel-wise correlation # Ci += (Fi. Fj->i) / sqrt(C) correlation = torch.sum(features[i] Fjtoi, dim=-1) / math.sqrt(C) Ci += correlation costvolumes.append(Ci) # Step 4: Pose-aware Cost Aggregation # Refine cost volumes using patch-wise cross-attention with rays refinedcostvolumes = [] for i in range(len(images)): # Cross-attention between cost volume and Plucker rays Cprimei = patchwisecrossattention(costvolumes[i], rays[i]) refinedcostvolumes.append(Cprimei) # Step 5: Canonical Volume Formation # Select view 0 as canonical canonicalviewindex = 0 # Align other views to canonical space using refined cost volumes and weights # Wi in R^(H/4 x W/4) accounts for view-dependent effects # Vg is the fused feature Vg = aligntocanonical(refinedcostvolumes, weights, canonicalviewindex) # Step 6: Anchor Prediction # Predict coarse geometry anchors from Vg anchors = predictanchors(Vg) # Step 7: Anchor-aligned Gaussian Prediction # Predict offsets from anchors to spread to adjacent regions # Predict k Gaussians per region offsets = predictoffsets(Vg, anchors) gaussians = spreadgaussians(anchors, offsets) # Convert Plucker rays to camera parameters # Psi converts P = <d, m> to R, T poses = [] for Pi in rays: Ri, Ti = convertpluckertopose(Pi) poses.append((Ri, Ti)) return gaussians, poses Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On real-world datasets including DTU, BlendedMVS, RealEstate10K, and ACID, SHARE achieves robust performance compared to existing generalizable pose-free approaches. It outperforms these baselines even when compared to pose-dependent Gaussian splatting methods. In specific comparisons with MVSplat, SHARE shows higher PSNR (e.g., 18.46dB vs 11.88dB in noisy pose scenarios). Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Robust to pose noise; avoids geometry misalignment caused by inaccurate pose estimates; efficient and scalable pose-free novel view synthesis via a single feed-forward pipeline. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use it: When precise camera poses are unavailable or noisy, and robust 3D reconstruction is required from unposed image collections. When not: When precise camera poses are already available and explicit 3D transformation is preferred. SHARE was introduced to address the challenge of obtaining accurate camera poses in real-world scenarios, which often leads to noisy pose estimates and geometric misalignments. It was developed as a pose-free, feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework that overcomes these ambiguities by joint shape and camera rays estimation. The method builds on the principles of multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques, specifically cost volume construction and aggregation, but adapts them to latent space for Gaussian splatting. It is used for novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction from sparse unposed images. name: pixelSplat
head: 3D Gaussian Splats from Image Pairs, Epipolar Transformer Gaussian Splatting
body: pixelSplat is a feed-forward model that reconstructs a 3D radiance field parameterized by 3D Gaussian primitives from a pair of input images, enabling real-time and memory-efficient rendering. It solves the problem of local minima inherent to sparse, locally supported representations in generalizable novel view synthesis, where non-differentiable pruning or splitting (used in single-scene optimization) cannot be applied because gradients must back-propagate through the representation. Unlike light-field transformers which produce black-box ray colors, pixelSplat generates an explicit, editable 3D representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pair of images I1, I2 and their associated camera parameters (poses T and intrinsics K). Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, and scale S (or spherical harmonics coefficients for color). Data Structures: The model predicts a dense probability distribution over 3D space for each pixel. The Gaussian parameters are predicted per pixel u in the reference image. Features: Pixel-aligned features \mathbf{F}[u] are generated by summing outputs from a ResNet-50 and a ViT-B/8 vision transformer, both pre-trained with a DINO objective. Gaussian Parameters: For each pixel u, a neural network f predicts \phi, \boldsymbol{\delta}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \mathbf{S}. These are mapped to the final Gaussian attributes: Mean: \boldsymbol{\mu} = \text{ray}(u) + \boldsymbol{\delta} (where \text{ray}(u) is the camera ray direction/origin for pixel u). Covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is predicted directly or derived from scale and rotation. Opacity: \alpha is predicted. Scale: S is predicted. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass each reference image through a ResNet-50 and a ViT-B/8 (DINO-pretrained). Sum their pixel-wise outputs to generate initial features. 2. Epipolar Transformer: Perform two rounds of epipolar cross-attention to encode features between the two views. This step uses frequency-based positional encoding of depth to resolve scale ambiguity. The transformer infers a per-scene scale factor si to handle the arbitrary scale of SfM poses. 3. Probability Distribution Prediction: Predict a dense probability distribution over 3D space (specifically along the camera rays) conditioned on the epipolar features. 4. Differentiable Sampling (Reparameterization Trick): Sample Gaussian means \boldsymbol{\mu} from the predicted dense probability distribution. The sampling operation is made differentiable via a reparameterization trick that couples the density of a sampled Gaussian primitive to the probability of that location. Mechanism: When a gradient increases the opacity of a Gaussian at a 3D location, the model increases the probability that a Gaussian will be sampled at that location in future training steps, implicitly spawning or deleting primitives. 5. Attribute Prediction: Use a neural network f conditioned on the feature \mathbf{F}[u] for each pixel u to output the remaining Gaussian parameters: mean offset \boldsymbol{\delta}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, and scale S. \phi, \boldsymbol{\delta}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \mathbf{S} = f(\mathbf{F}[u]) \quad (8) 6. Rendering: Render the predicted Gaussians using standard differentiable Gaussian splatting rasterization. 7. Loss Computation: Compute the loss between the rendered image and the target image using a combination of Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Perceptual Distance (LPIPS). 8. Optimization: Update network weights using the Adam optimizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pixelsplatforward(imagepair, cameraparams): """ imagepair: List of two images [I1, I2] cameraparams: List of two camera pose/intrinsic tuples [(T1, K1), (T2, K2)] Returns: Rendered image, Gaussian parameters (for loss/visualization) """ # 1. Feature Extraction # ResNet-50 and ViT-B/8 are pre-trained DINO models featuresresnet = [] featuresvit = [] for img in imagepair: featuresresnet.append(resnet50dino(img)) featuresvit.append(vitb8dino(img)) # Sum pixel-wise outputs featuressum = [fres + fvit for fres, fvit in zip(featuresresnet, featuresvit)] # 2. Epipolar Transformer # Two rounds of epipolar cross-attention with frequency-based depth encoding # Infers per-scene scale factor to resolve SfM scale ambiguity epipolarfeatures = epipolarcrossattention( featuressum[0], featuressum[1], cameraparams[0], cameraparams[1]) # 3. & 4. Probability Distribution and Differentiable Sampling # Predict dense probability distribution over 3D space (depth along rays) probdist = predictprobabilitydistribution(epipolarfeatures) # Sample Gaussian means from the distribution using reparameterization trick # This makes sampling differentiable w.r.t. the distribution parameters sampleddepths = samplefromdistribution(probdist) sampledmeans = rayorigin + sampleddepths raydirection # 5. Attribute Prediction # Neural network f predicts attributes conditioned on features # Note: In practice, features are aligned to pixels. # The sampling step ensures gradients flow through the location selection. # The network f predicts delta, sigma, alpha, S for each pixel. # The mean is refined by the sampled depth or predicted delta. # Based on Eq 8: phi, delta, Sigma, S = f(F[u]) # We assume the probabilistic sampling handles the mean location, # and f handles the other attributes, or f predicts all and sampling is used for training stability. # The paper states: "predict a dense probability distribution... and sample Gaussian means... # predict Gaussian parameters using a neural network f conditioned on the feature F[u]" # It implies f predicts the attributes, and the mean is either sampled or predicted. # Given "sample Gaussian means from the predicted dense probability distribution", # the mean is likely derived from the sample. # Let's assume f predicts delta, sigma, alpha, S. # Mean is constructed from the sampled depth. gaussianparams = [] for u in pixels: # Get feature for pixel u from epipolar features Fu = getpixelfeature(epipolarfeatures, u) # Predict attributes phi, delta, Sigma, S = neuralnetworkf(Fu) # Construct mean. # If sampling is used for mean, delta might be residual or not used for mean. # The paper says "sample Gaussian means... predict attributes...". # It is likely that the mean is the sampled point, and f predicts Sigma, Alpha, S, Color. # However, Eq 8 includes delta. # Interpretation: The probability distribution is over depth. # The sample gives the depth. The network f predicts the offset delta? # Or f predicts the attributes and the sampling is a separate mechanism for training? # "We make this sampling operation differentiable... allowing us to back-propagate gradients # through the Gaussian splatting representation." # "When receiving a gradient that would increase the opacity... increase the probability..." # This suggests the sampling is integral to the forward pass for training. # Let's assume Mean is sampled, and f predicts the rest. # But Eq 8 has delta. # Alternative: f predicts delta, and the distribution is over delta? # "predict a dense probability distribution over 3D space" # "sample Gaussian means from that probability distribution" # So Mean is sampled. # Then what is delta in Eq 8? # Maybe delta is the residual from the ray? # If Mean is sampled, it is already absolute. # Let's stick to the text: "sample Gaussian means... predict attributes...". # We will assume the sampled mean is used, and f predicts Sigma, Alpha, S, Color. # If delta is present, it might be a residual correction. # To be safe and complete based on Eq 8: # Mean = Ray(u) + delta? No, sampling is explicit. # Let's assume the sampling provides the primary location, and delta is a small residual. # Or, the probability distribution is over the offsets? # "dense probability distribution over 3D space" -> Absolute space. # Implementation detail: # The sampling step is the key differentiable component for location. # The network f predicts the other parameters. mean = sampledmeans[u] # From sampling # If delta is predicted, it might be ignored for mean if sampling is primary, # or used to adjust mean. Given "sample Gaussian means", sampling is primary. gaussian = Gaussian( mean=mean, covariance=Sigma, opacity=alpha, scale=S, color=phi # Assuming phi maps to color/SH) gaussianparams.append(gaussian) # 6. Rendering renderedimage = gaussiansplattingrasterize(gaussianparams, cameraparams[0]) return renderedimage, gaussianparams def pixelsplatloss(renderedimage, targetimage): # Combination of MSE and LPIPS mseloss = meansquarederror(renderedimage, targetimage) lpipsloss = lpipsdistance(renderedimage, targetimage) return mseloss + lpipsloss Parameters: Training Resolution: 256 \times 256 pixels. Loss Function: Mean Squared Error (MSE) + Perceptual Distance (LPIPS). Optimizer: Adam. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: SfM poses are scaled by an arbitrary unknown scalar si. The model handles this by inferring the scale via an epipolar transformer that finds cross-view pixel correspondences. Without this, ghosting artifacts occur. Local Minima: Gaussian primitives have local support; gradients vanish if the distance to the correct location exceeds a few standard deviations. The probabilistic sampling avoids this by allowing gradients to flow through the probability distribution, implicitly spawning/deleting primitives. Without this, speckling artifacts occur. Out-of-Distribution Poses: Reflective surfaces may appear transparent, and Gaussians may appear billboard-like when viewed from out-of-distribution camera poses. Defines the training pipeline for Splatt3R, a feed-forward model that predicts 3D Gaussian primitives directly from uncalibrated stereo image pairs. It distinguishes itself from pixelSplat by eliminating explicit pose regression overhead and using a specific loss masking strategy to prevent hallucinating geometry in occluded regions. Time Complexity: Inference cost is approximately 650 times less than the next-fastest baseline for encoding one scene and rendering 100 images. Rendering is accelerated by 2.5 orders of magnitude compared to state-of-the-art light field transformers. Memory Complexity: Memory-efficient rendering due to rasterization-based volume rendering of Gaussians, significantly less memory per ray at training time compared to ray-marching NeRFs. Performance: Benchmarked on wide-baseline novel view synthesis on RealEstate10k and ACID datasets. Outperforms baselines like pixelNeRF, GPNR, and Du et al.'s light field transformer in PSNR and LPIPS. Strengths: Real-time rendering, editable 3D representation, fast 3D reconstruction at inference, handles scale ambiguity, avoids local minima via differentiable sampling. Limitations: Struggles with reflective surfaces (transparency) and out-of-distribution views (billboard effect). Requires paired images with known poses (though scale is handled). pixelSplat was introduced by Charatan, Li, Tagliasacchi, and Sitzmann from MIT and Simon Fraser University/University of Toronto. It was presented at CVPR 2024. The method addresses the limitations of previous generalizable novel view synthesis methods, which were either slow (ray-marching NeRFs) or lacked explicit 3D representations (light-field transformers). It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting for single-scene optimization [19] and adapts it for the generalizable, feed-forward setting. name: Splatt3R Training Procedure with Loss Masking
head: Splatt3R Training, Loss-Masked Gaussian Splatting Training
body: This method defines the training pipeline for Splatt3R, a feed-forward model that predicts 3D Gaussian primitives directly from uncalibrated stereo image pairs to enable real-time novel view synthesis. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like pixelSplat by eliminating explicit pose regression overhead and using a specific loss masking strategy to prevent the model from hallucinating geometry in regions occluded from the context views. Inputs and Outputs Input: A batch of context image pairs (two input images) and target images (three novel view images) sampled from a scene. Output: Predicted 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) and rendered RGB images for the target views. Data Structures Gaussian Primitives: Defined by position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Loss Mask: A binary mask M \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W} indicating valid pixels for supervision. Parameters \phi = 0.3: Minimum fraction of pixels in the second context image with direct correspondences in the first. \psi = 0.3: Minimum fraction of pixels in target images present in at least one context image. \lambda{MSE} = 1.0: Weight for Mean Squared Error loss. \lambda{LPIPS} = 0.25: Weight for LPIPS perceptual loss. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 1.0 \times 10^{-5}, weight decay 0.05, gradient clipping norm 0.5. Resolution: 512 \times 512 pixels. Epochs: 2000 (approx. 500,000 iterations). Steps 1. Sampling: For each training step, randomly sample two context images and three target images from a scene in the training split (e.g., ScanNet++). 2. View Selection: Select target view positions such that the angular parameters \phi and \psi are satisfied, ensuring sufficient overlap between context and target views. 3. Forward Pass: Render the predicted 3D Gaussians at 512 \times 512 resolution for each target view using differentiable splatting. 4. Mask Generation: Generate a loss mask M that identifies pixels in the target view that are visible from the context views. Pixels not visible in any context view are masked out. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss between the rendered image I{render} and the target image I{target}: L = \lambda{MSE} \cdot \text{MSE}(I{render}, I{target}) + \lambda{LPIPS} \cdot \text{LPIPS}(I{render}, I{target}) The loss is computed only on pixels where M=1. Metrics (PSNR, LPIPS) are reported both across the entire image and averaged across just the pixels in the loss mask. 6. Backpropagation: Apply the loss mask to the gradients before backpropagating to update the Gaussian parameters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstep(contextimages, targetimages, model, optimizer): # 1. Forward pass: predict Gaussians from context images gaussians = model.encode(contextimages) # 2. Render target views renderedimages = [] for targetview in targetimages: # Render using differentiable splatting img = splatrender(gaussians, targetview.cameraparams) renderedimages.append(img) # 3. Compute Loss Mask # Mask M identifies pixels visible from context views # Implementation detail: M is derived from visibility checks or # correspondence maps between context and target views masks = computevisibilitymasks(contextimages, targetimages, gaussians) # 4. Compute Loss with Masking totalloss = 0.0 for renderedimg, targetimg, mask in zip(renderedimages, targetimages, masks): # Apply mask to images maskedrendered = renderedimg mask maskedtarget = targetimg mask # Compute MSE and LPIPS on masked regions mseloss = meansquarederror(maskedrendered, maskedtarget) lpipsloss = lpipslossfunction(maskedrendered, maskedtarget) # Weighted sum loss = 1.0 mseloss + 0.25 lpipsloss totalloss += loss # 5. Backpropagation optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() # Gradient clipping torch.nn.utils.clipgradnorm(model.parameters(), maxnorm=0.5) optimizer.step() return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Unbounded Gaussian Growth: Omitting the loss masking strategy causes Gaussian sizes to grow unboundedly, eventually exhausting VRAM and halting training. Hallucination: Without masking, the model attempts to reconstruct areas not visible to the context views, leading to poor accuracy and artifacts. Time Complexity: The method runs at approximately 4 FPS for full scene reconstruction at 512 \times 512 resolution on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti. Memory Complexity: VRAM usage is sensitive to the loss masking; without it, memory consumption grows unboundedly due to Gaussian size explosion. Strengths: Eliminates explicit pose estimation overhead by predicting all Gaussians in a shared coordinate space. Generalizes well to in-the-wild data captured by mobile phones. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of the underlying feature extractor (e.g., MASt3R) for generating initial correspondences. When to Use: Suitable for feed-forward 3D reconstruction from uncalibrated stereo pairs where real-time rendering is required and camera poses are unknown. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenarios requiring explicit pose estimation or when ground truth poses are available and can be leveraged for higher accuracy (e.g., pixelSplat with GT poses). Splatt3R was introduced as a feed-forward generalizable model for generating 3D Gaussian Splats from uncalibrated stereo images. It builds on the MASt3R architecture, which provides robust feature matching, and adapts it to predict 3D Gaussian parameters directly. The method was evaluated on the ScanNet++ dataset and in-the-wild mobile captures. It represents a shift from traditional multi-view stereo systems that rely on explicit pose estimation and depth information. name: Joint Pose Optimization
head: BARF, Unposed images methods
body: Joint Pose Optimization (JPO) refers to methods that simultaneously optimize camera poses and the scene representation (neural fields or Gaussian splats) to eliminate the dependency on pre-computed Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines. This approach relaxes the strict requirement for known camera parameters, allowing novel-view synthesis from unposed images using only photometric loss. It distinguishes itself from pose-free feed-forward methods by iteratively refining poses during training rather than predicting them in a single forward pass, though it typically requires rough initialization and is limited to small motions. All methods in this family rely on differentiable rendering to compute gradients from the rendered image to the Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) and/or network weights. The rendering process remains differentiable with respect to the scene representation. Loss functions typically combine photometric reconstruction error, such as \mathcal{L}{L1} or \mathcal{L}{MSE}, with perceptual or structural metrics like \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} or \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} [6136-instantsplat.md][6464-pixelsplat.md]. 1D Signal Alignment is a simplified analytical model used to investigate the local convergence behavior of joint camera pose and scene reconstruction optimization. It reduces the complex 3D joint optimization problem into a 1D signal alignment task to analyze how the signal spectrum affects gradient stability. Unlike full 3D joint optimization methods which suffer from high-frequency spectral noise causing local optima, this method demonstrates that applying a Gaussian filter to the signal spectrum stabilizes gradients and ensures convergence to the global optimum within a specific initial range. IPO-Net is a generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting network trained in a self-supervised manner without relying on pre-acquired camera poses or depth. It extracts features Fr and Ft from reference images Ir and target image It using a Shared Image Encoder (ResNet backbone pre-trained with DINO augmented with FPN). It iteratively updates pose and depth for K iterations using a Conv-GRU module: T{r \rightarrow t}^{(k)}=T{r \rightarrow t}^{(k-1)}+\Delta T{r \rightarrow t} and Dt^{(k)}=Dt^{(k-1)}+\Delta Dt, where \Delta T and \Delta D are predicted differences. It transfers pre-estimated relative poses \mathbf {T}{r\rightarrow t} between reference views and target view to relative poses \mathbf {T}{r\rightarrow r+1} between nearby reference views for Gaussians prediction. Joint pose optimization emerged to address the limitations of traditional pipelines that depend on off-the-shelf pose estimation methods, which increase inference time and fail in texture-less regions or when images lack overlap. Early works proposed joint optimization for both static [HJS∗ 23,WWX∗ 21,CL23a,LMTL21,SCW∗ 25] and dynamic settings [LGM∗ 23]. However, these methods still require rough pose initialization and are limited to small motions. Alternative solutions followed incremental approaches, leveraging mono-depth prior [BWL∗ 23] or temporal continuity [FLK∗ 24]. More recent extensions enable generalizable representations [CL23b,HJS∗ 23,XLC∗ 25], enabling joint pose prediction and representation learning from sparse image collections. Ye et al. [YLX∗ 25] demonstrated efficient pose estimation and novel-view synthesis from unposed images using only photometric loss, though limited to static scenes. name: 1D Signal Alignment for Joint Optimization Analysis
head: 1D Signal Alignment, 1D Signal Alignment Pilot Study
body: 1D Signal Alignment is a simplified analytical model used to investigate the local convergence behavior of joint camera pose and scene reconstruction optimization. It reduces the complex 3D joint optimization problem into a 1D signal alignment task to analyze how the signal spectrum affects gradient stability. Unlike full 3D joint optimization methods which suffer from high-frequency spectral noise causing local optima, this method demonstrates that applying a Gaussian filter to the signal spectrum stabilizes gradients and ensures convergence to the global optimum within a specific initial range. Inputs: Ground truth 1D signal f{GT}: Continuous, bounded, with finite support. Translated versions f1, f2: Generated by translating f{GT} by unknown parameters p1, p2. Gaussian kernel N: Used for spectral filtering (default variance \sigma^2 = 4). Outputs: Estimated signal g. Estimated translation parameters q1, q2. Relative pose error u = (p1 - p2) - (q1 - q2). The method operates on continuous 1D signals. For implementation, these are discretized into arrays. Signal Array: 1D array representing f{GT}, g, f1, f2. Parameters: Scalars q1, q2 (or their difference u). Frequency Domain: Arrays for Fourier transforms \mathcal{F}[f{GT}] and \mathcal{F}[N]. 1. Define Ground Truth and Targets: Define the ground truth signal f{GT}(x). Generate two target signals f1 and f2 by translating f{GT} by random offsets p1 and p2: fi(x) = f{GT}(x - pi), \quad i \in \{1, 2\} where the translation operator is W{1d}(f, p)(x) = f(x - p). 2. Initialize Estimates: Initialize the estimated signal g(x) (e.g., as a copy of f{GT} or random noise) and the estimated translation parameters q1, q2. 3. Define Reconstruction Loss: The loss function L{1d} measures the squared L2 distance between the translated estimate and the targets: L{1d}(g, q1, q2) = \sum{i \in [1,2]} \int \| W{1d}(g, qi)(x) - fi(x) \|^2 dx Substituting the translation definition: L{1d}(g, q1, q2) = \sum{i \in [1,2]} \int \| g(x) - f{GT}(x - pi + qi) \|^2 dx The global optimum is achieved when q1 - q2 = p1 - p2 and g = W{1d}(f{GT}, p1 - q1). 4. Spectral Analysis of Gradient: The gradient of the loss with respect to the relative pose error u = (p1 - p2) - (q1 - q2) is derived in the frequency domain: \frac{d L{1d}}{du} = \int \| \mathcal{F}[f{GT}] \|^2 \cdot H(u, k) \, dk where k is the wavenumber, \mathcal{F}[f{GT}] is the Fourier transform of the ground truth signal, and: H(u, k) = 4\pi k \sin(2\pi k u). 5. Apply Gaussian Filtering (Mitigation): High-frequency components cause H(u, k) to alternate in sign and grow in magnitude, leading to noisy gradients and local optima. To mitigate this, convolve f{GT} with a Gaussian kernel N. This is equivalent to modulating H(u, k) by the squared magnitude of the kernel's Fourier transform: \frac{d \tilde{L}{1d}}{du} = \int \| \mathcal{F}[f{GT}] \|^2 \cdot \tilde{H}(u, k) \, dk where: \tilde{H}(u, k) = \| \mathcal{F}[N] \|^2 \cdot H(u, k). 6. Iterative Optimization: Perform gradient descent on g, q1, q2 (or directly on u) using the filtered gradient \frac{d \tilde{L}{1d}}{du}. Translation Operator: W{1d}(f, p)(x) = f(x - p). Loss Function: L{1d}(g, q1, q2) = \sum{i=1}^{2} \int \| g(x) - f{GT}(x - pi + qi) \|^2 dx. Unfiltered Gradient Kernel: H(u, k) = 4\pi k \sin(2\pi k u). Filtered Gradient Kernel: \tilde{H}(u, k) = \| \mathcal{F}[N] \|^2 \cdot H(u, k). Optimality Condition: q1 - q2 = p1 - p2 \quad \text{and} \quad g = f{GT}(x - (p1 - q1)). Gaussian Variance: The variance of the Gaussian kernel N is set to 4 in the pilot study. Convergence Radius: With variance 4, gradient descent converges to u=0 if the initial magnitude |u| < 6.0. High-Frequency Signals: Signals with spreading high-frequency spectra cause H(u, k) to alternate signs rapidly as k increases. This results in large, noisy gradients that trap optimization in local optima. Initial Pose Error: Without filtering, the "well-behaved" region of the gradient is narrow. If the initial relative pose error u is large, the optimizer may fail to converge. Saddle Points: A suitable learning rate is required to prevent getting stuck on saddle points, although the filtered region is quasi-convex. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussiankernel1d(size, variance): """ Creates a 1D Gaussian kernel. Args: size: Length of the kernel. variance: Variance (sigma^2) of the Gaussian. Returns: Normalized 1D numpy array. """ x = np.linspace(-size//2, size//2, size) kernel = np.exp(-x2 / (2 variance)) return kernel / np.sum(kernel) def computegradientfiltered(u, fgtfft, kernelvariance, dx): """ Computes the gradient of the 1D alignment loss with respect to u, using Gaussian filtering to stabilize high frequencies. Args: u: Relative pose error (scalar). fgtfft: FFT of the ground truth signal fGT. kernelvariance: Variance of the Gaussian filter N. dx: Spatial step size. Returns: Gradient dLtilde1d / du. """ # Frequency domain coordinates n = len(fgtfft) k = np.fft.fftfreq(n, d=dx) # H(u, k) = 4 pi k sin(2 pi k u) H = 4.0 np.pi k np.sin(2.0 np.pi k u) # Fourier transform of Gaussian kernel N # FN = sqrt(2pisigma^2) exp(-2pi^2sigma^2k^2) # We need ||F[N]||^2 # Note: The variance in the source is for the kernel N. # Standard Gaussian: exp(-x^2 / (2sigma^2)). # Source sets variance of N to 4. Assuming this refers to sigma^2. sigmasq = kernelvariance FNsq = 2.0 np.pi sigmasq np.exp(-2.0 np.pi2 sigmasq k2) # Modulated kernel Htilde Htilde = FNsq H # Integrate ||F[fGT]||^2 Htilde # ||F[fGT]||^2 is real and non-negative integrand = np.abs(fgtfft)2 Htilde # Numerical integration (trapezoidal or simple sum dk) dk = k[1] - k[0] if len(k) > 1 else 1.0 gradient = np.sum(integrand) dk return gradient def optimize1dalignment(fgt, p1, p2, variance=4.0, lr=0.01, steps=1000): """ Simulates the 1D Signal Alignment optimization. Args: fgt: 1D numpy array representing ground truth signal. p1: True translation for signal 1. p2: True translation for signal 2. variance: Variance of the Gaussian filter. lr: Learning rate. steps: Number of optimization steps. Returns: Estimated relative pose error u. """ # Discretization parameters dx = 1.0 / len(fgt) # Assuming normalized domain # Generate targets # Shift fgt by p1 and p2. # Note: In discrete domain, shifting by non-integer requires interpolation. # For this pilot study analysis, we assume continuous domain properties # or integer shifts for simplicity in implementation context. # Here we assume p1, p2 are integers or we use FFT-based shifting. # FFT of ground truth fgtfft = np.fft.fft(fgt) # Initialize relative pose error u # We optimize u = (p1 - p2) - (q1 - q2). # Let's initialize u randomly or as 0. u = np.random.uniform(-5.0, 5.0) for in range(steps): grad = computegradientfiltered(u, fgtfft, variance, dx) u = u - lr grad return u Extends the 1D analysis to 2D planar images to further validate the spectral effects on joint optimization. The parent method that 1D Signal Alignment analyzes. It jointly optimizes camera poses and neural representations [6888-joint-pose-optimization.md]. Time Complexity: The analysis is computational and analytical. The optimization step involves FFTs (O(N \log N)) and integration, making it efficient for analysis but not a direct rendering method. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the signal length N for storing the signal and its FFT. Strengths: Provides theoretical insight into why coarse-to-fine training schedules work. Demonstrates that Gaussian filtering stabilizes gradients by suppressing high-frequency noise. Guarantees convergence to the global optimum if the initial error is within a specific radius (|u| < 6.0 with variance 4). Limitations: It is a simplified 1D model and does not directly replace 3D joint optimization. Requires careful tuning of the Gaussian variance to balance smoothing and gradient accuracy. When to use: Use this analysis to understand convergence issues in joint pose optimization or to justify the use of spectral filtering/coarse-to-fine schedules in 3D neural rendering. Origin: Introduced in the paper "Improving Robustness for Joint Optimization of Camera Pose and Decomposed Low-Rank Tensorial Radiance Fields" (AAAI 2024). Purpose: The authors conducted this pilot study to analyze the effect of the signal spectrum on the joint optimization process, specifically addressing the instability caused by high-frequency components. Development: The work builds on the observation that joint optimization is highly influenced by the structural bias of the underlying representation. It aligns with motivations behind coarse-to-fine training schedules in prior works like [Lin et al. 2021] and [Heo et al. 2023]. name: Loss Scheduling for Candidate Head
head: candidate scheduling, v scheduling
body: Loss scheduling for the candidate head is a training strategy that gradually reduces the influence of an image-dependent 'candidate head' (\hat{C}i) during optimization, transitioning to a shared representation (\hat{C}) to stabilize pose estimation for hard-pose images. It prevents the shared representation from being distracted by wrong supervision introduced by hard-pose images in the early stages, allowing the model to assimilate these images into the shared representation once the shared model is accurate enough. This method is distinct from sibling methods like InstantSplat and pixelSplat by explicitly decoupling the training influence of per-image heads via a cosine schedule rather than relying solely on joint pose optimization or fixed head structures. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training progress l \in [0, 1]; hyperparameters u (start of transition) and v (end of transition); rendered color from shared head \hat{C}; rendered color from candidate head \hat{C}i; ground truth image I. Outputs: Scheduled loss value \mathcal{L}. Data Structures: l: Scalar float representing normalized training progress (0 to 1). u, v: Scalar floats in [0, 1] defining the schedule boundaries. \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\cdot): Photometric loss function (e.g., \mathcal{L}{L1} or \mathcal{L}{MSE}). Parameters: u: Start of transition phase. Typical value: 0.1. v: End of transition phase. Typical value: 0.5. Steps: 1. Calculate the scheduling weight w{u,v}(l) based on current training progress l and hyperparameters u, v. 2. Compute the photometric loss for the shared head: \mathcal{L}{shared} = \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C} | C). 3. Compute the photometric loss for the candidate head: \mathcal{L}{candidate} = \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}i | C). 4. Combine losses using the schedule: \mathcal{L} = w{u,v} \mathcal{L}{shared} + (1 - w{u,v}) \mathcal{L}{candidate}. Formulas: The scheduling weight w{u,v}(l) is defined as: w{u,v}(l) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } l < u \\ 1 - \frac{\cos(\pi(l - u)/(v - u))}{2} & \text{if } u \le l < v \\ 1 & \text{if } l \ge v \end{cases} The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = w{u,v} \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C} | C) + (1 - w{u,v}) \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}i | C) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelossschedule(l, u, v, lossshared, losscandidate): """ Computes the scheduled loss for candidate head training. Args: l (float): Training progress in [0, 1]. u (float): Start of transition phase. v (float): End of transition phase. lossshared (float): Photometric loss from shared head. losscandidate (float): Photometric loss from candidate head. Returns: float: Scheduled loss value. """ if l < u: w = 0.0 elif l < v: # Cosine interpolation from 0 to 1 # Formula: 1 - cos(pi (l - u) / (v - u)) / 2 w = 1.0 - (math.cos(math.pi (l - u) / (v - u)) / 2.0) else: w = 1.0 # Weighted combination # When w=0, only candidate head contributes. # When w=1, only shared head contributes. scheduledloss = w lossshared + (1.0 - w) losscandidate return scheduledloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If u \ge v, the transition interval is invalid or empty. The sources assume u < v. Precision issues in the cosine calculation near boundaries u and v are mitigated by the piecewise definition ensuring continuity (w=0 at l=u, w=1 at l=v). The candidate head size (embedding \elli) should be adjusted based on the challenge of the image poses, acting as a regularizer for 'slack' variables. This variant replaces the photometric loss \mathcal{L}{rgb} with a feature-based loss \mathcal{L}{feat} during the early training stage (l < u) to stabilize training against appearance changes (weather/time). It uses deep features from a Vision Transformer (ViT) as a surrogate for RGB values, which are less sensitive to appearance changes. Steps: 1. Render features \hat{F}i(r) using volume rendering with feature field f(t), shared density \sigma(t), candidate feature fi(t), and candidate density \sigmai(t). 2. Compute feature loss: \mathcal{L}{feat}(r) = \| Fi(r) - \hat{F}i(r) \|2^2, where Fi(r) is the 2D deep feature from a pretrained model (e.g., DINO). 3. Replace \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}i | Ci) with \mathcal{L}{feat}(\hat{F}i | Fi) for l < u. 4. Optimize static color \hat{C}i^{(a)}(r) jointly with transient color \hat{C}i^{(\tau)}(r) using volume rendering with appearance-dependent color ci^{(a)}(t) and \sigma(t). Formulas: Feature field: f(t) = \Pi{\theta2}(z(t)), where z(t) is positional encoding. No viewing direction is used for f(t). Candidate head feature/density: [fi(t), \sigmai(t)] = \Pi{\theta3}(z(t), \elli^{(c)}), where \Pi{\theta3} is the candidate head MLP and \elli^{(c)} is the candidate embedding. Appearance-dependent static color: ci^{(a)}(t) = \Pi{\theta4}(f(t), \gammad(d), \elli^{(a)}), where d is viewing direction and \elli^{(a)} is appearance embedding. When to choose: Use this variant when training on unconstrained images with diverse appearances due to different weather or times, where RGB values of corresponding pixels are not guaranteed to be the same. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead to the training loop as it only involves computing a scalar weight and combining two pre-computed loss values. The computational cost is dominated by the rendering of the candidate and shared heads. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for both the shared head and the candidate head. The size of the candidate embedding \elli can be adjusted based on pose difficulty. Performance: Enables high-quality NeRF model training with perfect camera poses even for hard-pose images that would otherwise distract the shared representation. It allows the model to converge where methods like BARF fail. Strengths: Stabilizes pose estimation for hard-pose images; prevents shared representation corruption; robust to appearance changes when combined with feature surrogates. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters u and v; relies on the candidate head architecture being sufficiently expressive. When to use: When training pose-free, feed-forward models on unconstrained image sets with varying poses and appearances. When not to use: When camera poses are known and fixed, or when the scene has consistent appearance across all views. The method originates from UP-NeRF (Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields). It addresses the challenge of training NeRFs without camera pose priors on unconstrained image collections, where hard-pose images can introduce wrong supervision. The approach builds on the principle that the shared representation should not be distracted by hard-pose images initially, allowing the candidate head to handle them until the shared representation is robust enough. The scheduling parameters u and v are set to 0.1 and 0.5 respectively, aligning with coarse-to-fine training strategies. name: Point-Based Neural Renderer Architecture
head: Neural Renderer
body: The Point-Based Neural Renderer is a differentiable rendering module that projects a 3D point cloud and camera pose into a 2D feature map by splatting points and blending them via alpha-compositing. It enables end-to-end training by allowing photometric and perceptual loss gradients to propagate back to optimized point attributes and network weights. Unlike methods that rely on a single input image, this architecture requires fusing multiple input views and renders each point cloud individually at target viewpoints before fusion. Inputs: 1. A set of N input views, each providing a rasterized point cloud with attributes: color, depth, normal, uncertainty, and a 6-component latent feature vector. 2. Camera poses for the input views and the target novel view. 3. A set of selected input views for the target view, determined by a camera selection algorithm. Outputs: 1. A final rendered image (RGB) for the target novel view. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of points Pi for each view i, where each point stores position, color, depth, normal, uncertainty, and a 6-component latent feature vector. Rasterized View: A 2D image grid where each pixel stores accumulated attributes from splatted points, primarily the latent feature vector extended by input color channels. Feature Map: An intermediate representation of size H \times W \times F, where H and W are image dimensions and F is the feature space dimension. Parameters: F: Feature space dimension. Typical value: 64. \lambda: Temporal filtering adaptation rate. Typical value: 0.05. Steps: 1. Reprojection and Splatting: For each selected input view i, reproject the 3D points to the 2D plane of the target novel view using point splatting. Generate attribute layers for each view containing input-view colors and optimized latent features. 2. Encoding: Encode each view's rasterized point cloud into a feature space of F dimensions using a series of convolutional residual blocks. The weights of these convolutional blocks are shared across all input views. 3. Weight Calculation: Compute the final blending weight w for each point/pixel contribution from view i. The weight is the product of three terms: w = w{CS} \cdot w{TS} \cdot w{PD} where: w{CS}: Camera selection weight. If view i is selected, si = 1.0; otherwise, si = 0.0. w{TS}: Temporal smoothing weight. It is updated recursively to handle temporal instability: w{t,i} = \lambda si^t + (1.0 - \lambda) w{t-1,i} where t is the frame index, si^t is the selection score for view i at frame t, and \lambda = 0.05. w{PD}: Point visibility weight. It accounts for point visibility and penalizes pixels at grazing angles to increase the influence of front-facing views. The exact formula for w{PD} is not given in the sources. 4. Weighted Average Pooling: Apply weighted average pooling to the encoded feature maps from all selected views to produce a single F-channel image. The pooling normalizes the sum of weights per pixel: \text{PooledFeature}{x,y} = \frac{\sum{i} wi \cdot \text{EncodedFeature}{i,x,y}}{\sum{i} wi} This normalization ensures that changing the number of selected views does not require retraining, as the magnitude distribution of features remains stable for the decoder. 5. Decoding: Decode the pooled features using consecutive convolutional residual blocks to generate the final rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convresidual(inputtensor, weights, bias): """Standard 2D convolution followed by ReLU and residual addition.""" out = inputtensor for w, b in zip(weights, bias): H, W, Cin = out.shape kH, kW,, Cout = w.shape newout = [[[0.0]Cout for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): for cout in range(Cout): acc = b[cout] for ky in range(kH): for kx in range(kW): for cin in range(Cin): acc += out[y][x][cin] w[ky][kx][cin][cout] newout[y][x][cout] = acc out = newout out = [[[max(0.0, v) for v in row] for row in layer] for layer in out] out = [[[out[y][x][c] + inputtensor[y][x][c] for c in range(Cout)] for x in range(W)] for y in range(H)] return out def pointbasedneuralrenderer(pointclouds, poses, targetpose, selectedindices, F=64, lambdatemp=0.05): # Step 1: Splat attributes to 2D grids for each selected view H, W = imagedimensions rasterized = [] for idx in selectedindices: grid = [[[0.0]14 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for point in pointclouds[idx]: x, y = project3dto2d(point.position, poses[idx], targetpose) if 0 <= x < W and 0 <= y < H: for c in range(14): grid[y][x][c] += point.attributes[c] rasterized.append(grid) # Step 2: Encode each view with shared convolutional residual blocks sharedconvweights = [...] # Parameters for convolutional residual blocks sharedconvbias = [...] encoded = [convresidual(view, sharedconvweights, sharedconvbias) for view in rasterized] # Step 3: Compute blending weights w = wCS wTS wPD weights = [] for i, idx in enumerate(selectedindices): wcs = 1.0 # Camera selection score wtsprev = getprevioustemporalweight(idx) # From previous frame state wts = lambdatemp wcs + (1.0 - lambdatemp) wtsprev wpd = computevisibilityweight(rasterized[i]) # Visibility/grazing angle penalty (formula not given in sources) weights.append(wcs wts wpd) # Step 4: Weighted average pooling per pixel pooled = [[[0.0]F for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): sumfeatures = [0.0]F sumw = 0.0 for i, view in enumerate(encoded): w = weights[i] for c in range(F): sumfeatures[c] += w view[y][x][c] sumw += w if sumw > 1e-8: for c in range(F): pooled[y][x][c] = sumfeatures[c] / sumw else: for c in range(F): pooled[y][x][c] = sumfeatures[c] # Step 5: Decode pooled features decweights = [...] # Parameters for decoder convolutional residual blocks decbias = [...] return convresidual(pooled, decweights, decbias) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Instability: When cameras appear or disappear, the camera selection score si changes abruptly. This is mitigated by temporal filtering with \lambda = 0.05. Grazing Angles: Pixels at grazing angles have lower visibility. The weight w{PD} penalizes these pixels to increase the influence of front-facing views. Variable View Count: Changing the number of selected views does not require retraining because the weighted average pooling normalizes the sum of weights per pixel. A differentiable rendering module that projects a 3D point cloud and camera pose into a 2D feature map by splatting points and blending them via alpha-compositing. It solves the problem of generating geometrically consistent feature maps for novel view synthesis by allowing photometric and perceptual loss gradients to propagate back to point positions and features during end-to-end training. Unlike SynSin, which relies on a single input image, this method requires fusing multi-view inputs, rendering each point cloud individually at target viewpoints before fusion. Choose it when generating novel views from a set of input images with known camera poses and a point cloud representation of the scene. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improved temporal stability compared to previous neural renderers. Allows changing the number of selected views without retraining. Limitations: Requires multi-view inputs. The exact formula for w{PD} is not given in the sources. When to use: When generating novel views from a set of input images with known camera poses and a point cloud representation of the scene. The Point-Based Neural Renderer was introduced in "Point-Based Neural Rendering with Per-View Optimization". The method was developed to address the limitations of previous neural renderers, such as temporal instability and the need for retraining when the number of input views changes. name: Neural Point Cloud Renderer
head: differentiable point cloud renderer, $\pi$
body: The Neural Point Cloud Renderer (\pi) is a differentiable rendering module that projects a 3D point cloud and camera pose into a 2D feature map by splatting points and blending them via alpha-compositing. It solves the problem of generating geometrically consistent feature maps for novel view synthesis by allowing photometric and perceptual loss gradients to propagate back to point positions and features during end-to-end training. Unlike SynSin [82], which relies on a single input image, this method requires fusing multi-view inputs, rendering each point cloud individually at target viewpoints before fusion. Inputs: A 3D point cloud Pi containing points with 3D coordinates, features, and depths. Camera pose P defining the target view. Parameters: Point radius r, number of nearest points K, output resolution, and feature dimension. Outputs: Rendered feature map \tilde{F} of shape H \times W \times C (e.g., 150 \times 200 \times 64). Rendered depth map D of shape H \times W. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list or tensor of points. Each point x has a 3D position, a feature vector F, and a depth d. Pixel: Identified by index l. Invisible pixels are filled with 64-dimensional zeros. Parameters: Point radius in NDC coordinates: r = 1.5 pixels. Number of nearest points to blend per pixel: K = 16. Output feature map resolution: 150 \times 200 pixels. Feature dimension per pixel: C = 64. Blending weight clamp range: [10^{-3}, 1.0]. Steps: 1. Transformation: Transform the point cloud Pi from world coordinates to the target view coordinates based on the camera pose P. 2. Projection: Project the 3D points to the 2D image plane to obtain their splatted centers. 3. Distance Calculation: For each pixel l, compute the Euclidean distance s between the pixel center and the splatted center of each 3D point x. 4. Blending Weight Computation: Compute the blending weight \alpha for each point based on the distance s and the point radius r in NDC coordinates. 5. Sorting: Sort the feasible points for each pixel by their depth values (z-buffer depths). 6. Alpha-Compositing: Blend the top K nearest points using alpha-compositing to compute the rendered feature Fl and depth Dl for pixel l. 7. Invisible Pixel Handling: Fill pixels with no feasible points with 64-dimensional zeros. Formulas: The blending weight \alpha is computed as: \alpha = 1 - \text{clamp}\left(\frac{r^2}{s^2}, 10^{-3}, 1.0\right) where s is the Euclidean distance between the splatted point center and the pixel, and r is the point radius in NDC coordinates. The rendered feature Fl for pixel l is computed by blending the top K points: Fl = \sum{i=1}^{K} \alphai Fi \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where Fi and \alphai are the feature and blending weight of the i-th point (sorted by depth). The rendered depth Dl for pixel l is computed as: Dl = \sum{i=1}^{K} \alphai di where di is the depth of the i-th point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def neuralpointcloudrenderer(points, camerapose, K=16, rndc=1.5, outh=150, outw=200, featdim=64): """ Renders a point cloud to a feature map using differentiable splatting. Args: points: Tensor of shape (N, 3 + featdim + 1) representing N points. Columns: [x, y, z, f1,..., f64, depth] camerapose: Camera extrinsics/intrinsics to transform points to view space. K: Number of nearest points to blend per pixel. rndc: Point radius in NDC coordinates. outh, outw: Output image height and width. featdim: Feature dimension per pixel. Returns: renderedfeatures: Tensor of shape (outh, outw, featdim) rendereddepth: Tensor of shape (outh, outw) """ # 1. Transform and project points to target view coordinates # Apply camera extrinsics (rotation R, translation t) to get view coordinates, # then apply perspective division and intrinsics to map to pixel coordinates. viewcoords = points[:,:3] @ camerapose[:3,:3].T + camerapose[:3, 3] # Perspective projection to pixel space x = viewcoords[:, 0] / (viewcoords[:, 2] + 1e-8) camerapose[0, 0] + camerapose[0, 2] y = viewcoords[:, 1] / (viewcoords[:, 2] + 1e-8) camerapose[1, 1] + camerapose[1, 2] z = viewcoords[:, 2] coords = torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=1) features = points[:, 3:3+featdim] depths = points[:, -1] # 2. Initialize output tensors renderedfeatures = torch.zeros(outh, outw, featdim, device=points.device) rendereddepth = torch.zeros(outh, outw, device=points.device) # 3. Compute distances and weights for all points ygrid, xgrid = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(outh), torch.arange(outw), indexing='ij') pixelgrid = torch.stack([xgrid, ygrid], dim=-1).float() # Euclidean distance squared between pixel centers and point splat centers distsq = torch.sum((pixelgrid.unsqueeze(-2) - coords[:,:2].unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0))2, dim=-1) # 4. Compute blending weights rsq = rndc 2 alpha = 1.0 - torch.clamp(rsq / (distsq + 1e-8), min=1e-3, max=1.0) # 5. Sort points by depth for each pixel sorteddepths, sortedindices = torch.sort(depths.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), dim=-1) topkindices = sortedindices[...,:K] # Gather features and alphas based on sorted indices idxexpanded = topkindices.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, -1, featdim) gatheredfeatures = torch.gather(features.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), 2, idxexpanded) gatheredalphas = torch.gather(alpha, 2, topkindices) gathereddepths = torch.gather(sorteddepths, 2, topkindices) # 6. Alpha-compositing oneminusalpha = 1.0 - gatheredalphas # Cumulative product of (1 - alpha) for j < i cumprod = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(oneminusalpha[...,:1]), torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha[...,:-1], dim=-1)], dim=-1) weightedfeatures = gatheredalphas.unsqueeze(-1) gatheredfeatures cumprod.unsqueeze(-1) renderedfeatures = torch.sum(weightedfeatures, dim=-2) weighteddepths = gatheredalphas gathereddepths rendereddepth = torch.sum(weighteddepths, dim=-1) return renderedfeatures, rendereddepth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invisible Pixels: Pixels with no feasible points (no points within the blending radius or occluded) are filled with 64-dimensional zeros. Depth Inaccuracy: Naive fusion of point clouds from multiple views is vulnerable to inaccurate depths, where points with wrong depths may occlude points from other views, leading to degraded results. This method avoids naive fusion by rendering each point cloud individually and fusing the results via a Transformer. Precision: The blending weight is clamped to a minimum of 10^{-3} to prevent numerical instability when s is very large or r is small relative to s. Renders Plenoptic Point Clouds (PPCs) by directly projecting occupied voxels visible in the viewing direction over each training viewpoint, using the same projection scheme as colorization. Unlike NeRF-like solutions that use ray-marching via the Volume Rendering equation, this method projects explicit occupied voxels. Performs novel-view synthesis for canonical space using a neural point cloud representation. The point cloud is structured as P = \{(xi, fi, \gammai) \mid i = 1, \dots, N\}, where each point i has a location xi, a neural feature fi, and a scale confidence value \gammai \in [0, 1]. Treats rendering as an image inpainting problem using a U-Net backbone, replacing ordinary convolution with gate convolution (GateConv) and sparse convolution (SparseConv) to fill irregular holes. Directly inpainting sparse point cloud images generates blurry results compared to this method because the color of directly projected points differs from ground truth images due to view-dependent effects (e.g., specular highlights) and different exposure times. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fully differentiable, allowing end-to-end training with photometric and perceptual losses. Geometrically consistent across views due to explicit geometry transformation. Limitations: Vulnerable to depth inaccuracies if not handled properly (mitigated by individual rendering and fusion). Requires multi-view inputs. When to use: When generating novel views from a constructed point cloud with multi-view inputs and requiring differentiable rendering for optimization. Implementation: Pytorch3D. The Neural Point Cloud Renderer \pi is introduced in the context of real-time novel view synthesis with forward warping and depth. It builds on the differentiable renderer design of SynSin [82] but extends it to handle multi-view inputs by rendering each point cloud individually and fusing the results. The method is implemented using Pytorch3D. name: Point Cloud Inpainting via Gate/Sparse Convolution
head: Gate Convolution Inpainting, Image Inpainting Baseline for Point Cloud Rendering, Point Cloud Inpainting, Sparse Convolution Inpainting
body: This method serves as a baseline for evaluating neural point cloud rendering by treating the completion of sparse point cloud projections as a standard 2D image inpainting problem. It addresses the challenge of filling missing regions in rendered views derived from incomplete 3D point clouds. It differs from the parent Neural Point Cloud Renderer by bypassing explicit 3D-to-2D splatting blending logic in favor of direct 2D convolutional synthesis, and from Implicit Neural Point Clouds (INPC) by operating on discrete image grids rather than implicit fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D image representation of a sparse point cloud projected from a target viewpoint. This image contains valid pixel colors where points project and empty/invalid regions where no points exist. Output: A completed 2D image with filled-in colors for the missing regions. Data Structures: The input is treated as a standard 2D tensor (image) with channels (e.g., RGB). No explicit 3D data structures are used in this specific baseline step; the 3D point cloud Pi has already been projected to form the 2D input. Method Steps: 1. Projection: Project the 3D point cloud Pi onto the 2D image plane of the target camera view. For each pixel, if a point projects to it, store its color; otherwise, mark the pixel as invalid/empty. 2. Backbone Selection: Adopt a U-Net architecture as the backbone network. The U-Net consists of an encoder path to capture context and a decoder path to reconstruct the image, connected by skip connections. 3. Convolution Replacement: Replace standard convolution operations within the U-Net with two specialized variants: Gate Convolution (GateConv): Uses a gating mechanism to modulate feature maps, allowing the network to focus on relevant features for inpainting. Sparse Convolution (SparseConv): Operates efficiently on sparse data structures, reducing computational cost for irregular holes. 4. Training/Inference: The network is trained or applied to predict the missing pixel values based on the surrounding valid context. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointcloudinpaintingbaseline(pointcloud, cameraparams): """ Baseline inpainting method using U-Net with Gate/Sparse Convolution. """ # Step 1: Project 3D points to 2D image # Initialize image with invalid markers h, w = cameraparams.imageheight, cameraparams.imagewidth inputimage = np.full((h, w, 3), np.nan, dtype=np.float32) for point in pointcloud: # Project 3D point to 2D pixel coordinates u, v = project3dto2d(point, cameraparams) if 0 <= u < w and 0 <= v < h: inputimage[v, u] = point.color # Step 2: Initialize U-Net with Gate/Sparse Convolution layers # The U-Net structure is predefined. # Key modification: Replace nn.Conv2d with GateConv or SparseConv layers. model = UNetBackbone( encoderchannels=[64, 128, 256, 512], convolutiontype='gate' # or 'sparse') # Step 3: Forward pass through the network # The network learns to fill NaN regions based on valid neighbors completedimage = model(inputimage) return completedimage Parameters: U-Net Depth: Not specified in sources, but standard U-Net depths (4-5 levels) are implied. Convolution Type: Either GateConv or SparseConv. Training Data: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blurry Results: Directly inpainting sparse point cloud images generates blurry results compared to methods that account for 3D structure. This occurs because the color of directly projected points differs from ground truth images due to view-dependent effects (e.g., specular highlights) and different exposure times. Irregular Holes: The method is designed to handle irregular holes in the projected image, which correspond to missing parts of the 3D object. The Completion Framework is a method for repairing and complementing incomplete point clouds derived from RGB or RGB-D frames that only partially capture an object. It distinguishes itself from standard completion methods by using two separate encoders to produce distinct latent representations for the existing and missing parts of the point cloud, which are then concatenated and decoded to output the weights of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). This approach allows for the generation of a complete, colored point cloud by enforcing a Gaussian prior on the missing part's latent space while maintaining multi-view consistency with scanned images. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The baseline produces blurry results compared to the proposed method in the source paper. It is less effective at handling view-dependent effects like specularities. Strengths: Simple to implement as it leverages existing 2D image inpainting architectures (U-Net) and operations (GateConv, SparseConv). Limitations: Fails to capture 3D geometric consistency and view-dependent appearance, leading to blurriness. When to use: As a baseline for comparison against more advanced neural point cloud rendering methods. When not to use: When high-fidelity, sharp rendering of specular or view-dependent effects is required. This method was introduced as a baseline in the paper "Neural Point Cloud Rendering via Multi-Plane Projection". It utilizes techniques from state-of-the-art image inpainting, specifically Gate Convolution [6] and Sparse Convolution [5], to address the problem of incomplete point cloud projections. The authors found that direct 2D inpainting of projected point clouds resulted in blurry outputs, motivating the development of their more advanced neural point cloud rendering approach.
