name: Completion Framework
head: GPN Completion Framework
body: The Completion Framework is a method for repairing and complementing incomplete point clouds derived from RGB or RGB-D frames that only partially capture an object. It distinguishes itself from standard completion methods by using two separate encoders to produce distinct latent representations for the existing and missing parts of the point cloud, which are then concatenated and decoded to output the weights of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). This approach allows for the generation of a complete, colored point cloud by enforcing a Gaussian prior on the missing part's latent space while maintaining multi-view consistency with scanned images. The framework operates by mapping an incomplete point cloud to a continuous parameterization of a 3D object space via NeRF weights. Inputs and Outputs Input: An incomplete point cloud P obtained from RGB/RGB-D scanning, split into two disjoint subsets: Pe (existing parts) and Pm (missing parts). Output: The weights \phi of a NeRF model \Phi\phi, which can render the complete point cloud and match the input cloud and existing scanning images. Data Structures Point Cloud Subsets: Pe and Pm are disjoint subsets of the input point cloud P. Latent Representations: ze = \varepsilone(Pe): Latent code for existing parts. zm = \varepsilonm(Pm): Latent code for missing parts. Combined Latent: z = ze \oplus zm, where \oplus denotes concatenation. NeRF Weights: \phi = \Psi\psi(z), where \Psi\psi is the decoder network. Numbered Steps 1. Split Input: Divide the input point cloud P into disjoint subsets Pe (existing) and Pm (missing). 2. Encode Existing Parts: Process Pe with encoder \varepsilone to produce latent representation ze. This encoder is used only for reconstruction. 3. Encode Missing Parts: Process Pm with encoder \varepsilonm to produce latent representation zm. This encoder renders a generative model, forcing zm to follow a Gaussian prior. 4. Concatenate Latents: Combine ze and zm into a single latent vector z = ze \oplus zm. 5. Decode NeRF Weights: Pass z through decoder \Psi\psi to output NeRF weights \phi. 6. Inference Optimization: During inference, the encoder predicts an initial latent code and generates a unique NeRF model. Perform latent-based conditional optimization to refine the predicted NeRF model to match the reconstructed cloud and existing scanning images. Formulas The training loss function combines a color rendering loss and a KL divergence term: L{color} = \sum{r \in R} ||\Phi{\phi=\Psi\psi(\varepsilone(Pe) \oplus \varepsilonm(Pm))}(r) - C(r)||^2 L = L{color} + D{KL}(\varepsilone(Pe) \oplus \varepsilonm(Pm), \mathcal{N}(0, I)) Where: R is the set of rays. \Phi\phi is the NeRF model parameterized by weights \phi. C(r) is the color of ray r from the input data. D{KL} is the Kullback-Leibler divergence. \mathcal{N}(0, I) is the standard normal distribution, serving as the prior for the latent space. Parameters Latent Combination: The operation \varepsilone(Pe) \oplus \varepsilonm(Pm) represents the concatenation of the two latent representations. Prior: The latent code for the missing part zm is forced to follow a Gaussian prior \mathcal{N}(0, I). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def completionframeworktraining(Pe, Pm, R, C): """ Pe: Point cloud subset for existing parts Pm: Point cloud subset for missing parts R: Set of rays for rendering C: Ground truth colors for rays R """ # Step 1: Encode existing parts ze = encodere(Pe) # Step 2: Encode missing parts zm = encoderm(Pm) # Step 3: Concatenate latent representations zcombined = concatenate(ze, zm) # Step 4: Decode NeRF weights phi = decoder(zcombined) # Step 5: Render colors using NeRF renderedcolors = [] for r in R: color = nerfrender(phi, r) renderedcolors.append(color) # Step 6: Calculate Color Loss Lcolor = sumsquarederror(renderedcolors, C) # Step 7: Calculate KL Divergence Loss # Assuming encoderm outputs mean and log-variance for Gaussian prior # DKL(zm, N(0, I)) Lkl = kldivergence(zm, mean=0, var=1) # Step 8: Total Loss L = Lcolor + Lkl return L def completionframeworkinference(Pincomplete): """ Pincomplete: Incomplete point cloud to be completed """ # Split into existing and missing parts # Note: In practice, Pm might be inferred or sampled based on occlusion/masking Pe, Pm = splitpointcloud(Pincomplete) # Encode ze = encodere(Pe) zm = encoderm(Pm) # Concatenate and Decode zcombined = concatenate(ze, zm) phi = decoder(zcombined) # Refine via latent-based conditional optimization # This step adjusts the latent code or NeRF weights to match # the reconstructed cloud and existing scanning images phirefined = optimizeneuralradiancefield(phi, Pincomplete) return phirefined Edge Cases and Pitfalls Missing Part Definition: The method assumes a predefined split of the point cloud into Pe and Pm. Determining Pm for real-world scans where the "missing" geometry is unknown requires careful handling, potentially relying on the generative capability of \varepsilonm. Gaussian Prior Enforcement: The requirement for zm to follow \mathcal{N}(0, I) is critical for the generative aspect. Failure to enforce this may result in poor generalization to unseen objects. Optimization Stability: The latent-based conditional optimization during inference adds complexity. Improper initialization or learning rates may lead to divergence or suboptimal completions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on ShapeNet categories (cars and chairs). The framework uniformly samples 16,384 colored points on each 3D model and uses 100 views for rendering. Strengths: Lightweight, generalizable, and capable of completing unseen portions of real-world objects with colors, unlike methods that only reconstruct synthetic objects. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial split between existing and missing parts. Performance depends on the ability of the encoders to disentangle and complement the latent representations. When to Use: Suitable for RGB/RGB-D scanning reconstruction applications where objects are partially captured and color completion is required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for complete point clouds where no completion is needed, or for applications requiring explicit mesh output rather than implicit NeRF representations. The Completion Framework is part of the GPN (Generative Point-Based NeRF) framework, proposed by Haipeng Wang et al.. It builds upon the "Generation Framework" and is inspired by Hyperpocket. The method addresses the limitation of existing point cloud completion techniques that rely on learning to reconstruct synthetic objects rather than completing the unseen portions of real-world objects. It was evaluated on standard shape generation benchmarks, specifically cars and chairs, using the ShapeNet dataset. name: Partial Point Cloud Completion Optimization
head: Shape completion, free-space optimization
body: This method optimizes an object-level latent code to reconstruct a complete 3D shape from a partial point cloud, using a pre-trained generative prior (ObjectNet) to infer missing geometry, followed by a patch-level refinement stage to recover high-frequency details. It distinguishes itself from global implicit field methods by decoupling the coarse shape completion (via the object prior) from local detail recovery (via patch latent codes), allowing for generalizable completion without per-scene network training. Inputs: Partial point cloud derived from depth maps at fixed and per-scene random viewpoints. Pre-trained ObjectNet (trained on the target category) and PatchNet (pre-trained on a different category, kept fixed). Initial object latent code estimate. Outputs: Optimized object latent code z{obj} and patch latent codes z{patch} representing the completed 3D shape. Data Structures: Object Latent Code (z{obj}): A vector sampled from a multivariate Gaussian fitted to object latent codes obtained during ObjectNet training. Patch Latent Codes (z{patch}): Intermediate variables representing local patches of the shape, regressed during optimization. Extrinsics: Camera parameters associated with the input depth maps. Formulas and Losses: 1. Reconstruction Loss: Measures the discrepancy between the rendered output and the input partial point cloud. 2. L2 Regularizer: Applied to the latent codes to prevent overfitting. 3. Coverage Loss: Ensures the generated shape covers the visible region of the input. 4. Free-Space Loss: Encourages the network to regress positive values for samples located between the surface and the camera. This is applied to 30% of the sampled points. 5. Extrinsics Losses: Explicitly excluded during optimization to avoid detrimental effects on patches outside the partial point cloud. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute the average of the object latent codes obtained during ObjectNet training. Initialize z{obj} with this average. 2. Global Optimization (600 iterations): Sample 8,000 points per iteration. Optimize z{obj} and intermediate variables (including z{patch} and extrinsics) to minimize the sum of Reconstruction Loss, L2 Regularizer, Coverage Loss, and Free-Space Loss. Update learning rate: Start at \eta = 0.01. Halve \eta every 200 iterations. 3. Local Refinement (Last 100 iterations): Fix the extrinsics. Optimize only the patch latent codes z{patch}. Use a learning rate of \eta = 0.001. This step integrates details not captured by the object-level prior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partialpointcloudcompletion(partialpointcloud, objectnet, patchnet): # 1. Initialization # Fit multivariate Gaussian to object latent codes from training # Sample initial zobj from the fitted Gaussian, or use the mean zobj = mean(objectlatentcodesfromtraining) # Initialize patch latent codes and extrinsics as intermediate variables zpatch = initializepatchlatents() extrinsics = initializeextrinsics() # 2. Global Optimization learningrate = 0.01 numglobaliters = 600 lrdecaystep = 200 for i in range(numglobaliters): # Decay learning rate if i > 0 and i % lrdecaystep == 0: learningrate /= 2.0 # Sample 8k points samples = samplepoints(count=8000) # Compute losses # Reconstruction loss between rendered output and partialpointcloud lossrecon = computereconstructionloss(samples, zobj, zpatch, extrinsics, objectnet, patchnet) # L2 regularizer on latent codes lossreg = l2regularizer(zobj, zpatch) # Coverage loss losscov = computecoverageloss(samples, zobj, zpatch, extrinsics) # Free-space loss (30% of samples) freespaceratio = 0.3 freespacesamples = selectrandomsubset(samples, freespaceratio) lossfree = computefreespaceloss(freespacesamples, zobj, zpatch, extrinsics) # Total loss (exclude extrinsics losses) totalloss = lossrecon + lossreg + losscov + lossfree # Backpropagate and update zobj, zpatch, extrinsics updatevariables(zobj, zpatch, extrinsics, totalloss, learningrate) # 3. Local Refinement # Fix extrinsics extrinsics.requiresgrad = False refinementlr = 0.001 numrefinementiters = 100 for i in range(numrefinementiters): # Sample points (implementation detail: reuse or resample) samples = samplepoints(count=8000) # Compute losses lossrecon = computereconstructionloss(samples, zobj, zpatch, extrinsics, objectnet, patchnet) lossreg = l2regularizer(zobj, zpatch) losscov = computecoverageloss(samples, zobj, zpatch, extrinsics) freespacesamples = selectrandomsubset(samples, freespaceratio) lossfree = computefreespaceloss(freespacesamples, zobj, zpatch, extrinsics) totalloss = lossrecon + lossreg + losscov + lossfree # Backpropagate and update ONLY zpatch updatevariables(zpatch, totalloss, refinementlr) return zobj, zpatch Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Extrinsics Losses: Including extrinsics losses during optimization has a detrimental effect on patches outside the partial point cloud; they must be excluded. PatchNet Pre-training: PatchNet is pre-trained on a different object category and kept fixed, making the task more challenging than if it were category-specific. Baseline Comparison: Baselines use versions where the eight final layers are pre-trained on all categories and fine-tuned on the target shape category. Performance: On the ShapeNet dataset, the method achieves higher F-scores than baselines (DeepSDF and other baselines) across sofas and airplanes, both fixed and random viewpoints. For example, on sofas (fixed viewpoint), it achieves an accuracy of 0.091 and F-score of 48.1, improving to 0.053 accuracy and 52.4 F-score after refinement (Note: The source text lists "0.052 / 53.6" for "ours+refined" in the notes, but Table 5 in the source text shows "0.053 / 52.4" for sofas random and "0.052 / 53.6" is not explicitly in the provided Table 5 snippet for sofas fixed. The notes say "sofas fixed 0.091 / 48.1 (ours), 0.052 / 53.6 (ours+refined)". Table 5 snippet shows "ours" as 0.091/48.1. The refined values are not fully visible in the snippet but the notes provide them. We rely on the notes for the refined values). Complexity: The method requires 600 iterations of global optimization and 100 iterations of local refinement, using 8,000 samples per iteration. Strengths: The two-stage approach allows the object prior to handle global shape completion while patch-level refinement captures local details. Limitations: The method relies on a pre-trained ObjectNet and PatchNet, limiting its applicability to categories covered by these networks. The method is part of the PatchNets framework, which introduces patch-based generalizable deep implicit 3D shape representations. It builds upon the Completion Framework, which uses two encoders for existing and missing parts [Parent]. The optimization strategy is inspired by techniques for shape completion from depth maps, such as those by Park et al.. name: Implicit Neural Point Clouds (INPC)
body: Implicit Neural Point Clouds (INPC) is a point-based neural radiance field method that represents the scene as an implicit point cloud structure using a multi-resolution hash grid and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for rendering. It solves the problem of high-quality novel view synthesis by combining the efficiency of point-based splatting with the flexibility of neural implicit representations. Unlike its sibling Neural Point Cloud Renderer, which typically relies on explicit Gaussian or spherical harmonics features attached to points, INPC uses a hash-encoded MLP to predict appearance and opacity, allowing for denser and more continuous feature representation. It distinguishes itself from other neural implicit methods by utilizing differentiable bilinear splatting for rasterization, enabling efficient gradient-based optimization of both the point positions and the neural network parameters. Inputs: C: Camera model (intrinsics and extrinsics). P: Set of 3D point positions. A: Set of point opacities. F: Set of point features (initially empty or initialized from SfM). I{prior}: Optional prior point cloud to influence initial sampling probabilities. Outputs: I: Rendered image. Point Probability Octree: The scene is represented by an octree structure where leaf nodes define the sampling distribution for points. Each leaf node stores: ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center of the voxel in world space. li \in \mathbb{N}0: Current subdivision level. pi \in [0, 1]: Sampling probability. qi \in [0, 1]: Subdivision probability. Hash Grid and MLP (via TCNN): Hash Grid: Multi-resolution hash grid configuration: otype: 'Grid' type: 'Hash' nlevels: 10 nfeaturesperlevel: 4 log2hashmapsize: 23 baseresolution: 16 perlevelscale: 2.0 interpolation: 'Linear' Feature MLP: otype: 'FullyFusedMLP' activation: 'ReLU' outputactivation: 'None' nneurons: 64 nhiddenlayers: 1 Background MLP: 4 hidden layers, 128 neurons each, ReLU activations. Encoding: Normalized viewing direction encoded using spherical harmonics of degree 3 (implemented in TCNN as 'degree': 4 with input directions mapped to [0, 1]^3). CNN Post-Processing: Standard three-layer U-Net with 64 initial filters. Activations: GELU. Downsampling: Average pooling. Upsampling: Bilinear interpolation followed by point-wise convolution. Residual Block: One block based on Fast Fourier Convolution (FFC) with \alpha{in} = 0.75, \alpha{out} = 0.75. 1. Bounding Box: Define b{min}, b{max} \in \mathbb{R}^3 as the axis-aligned bounding box of the Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud, enlarged by 10%. If no SfM cloud is available, use the smallest axis-aligned box enclosing the viewing frusta of all training cameras. 2. Scene Normalization: Apply a world-space transformation to camera poses and SfM point cloud so they fit inside a cube [-1, 1]^3. Set near plane to 0.01 and far plane to 100. 3. Octree Initialization: Initialize the octree as a regular grid of cube-shaped voxels with resolution R (a power of 2) within the bounding box. The initial subdivision level for all leaf nodes is li = \log2(R). 4. Sampling Probability Initialization: If a prior point cloud I is provided, let |Ii| be the number of points inside the volume of the i-th leaf node and Q be the 0.95-quantile of these point counts. Compute initial probability as |IQ| / |Ii|, clipping values to [0.1, 1.0] for robustness. The rendering process uses differentiable bilinear splatting. Algorithm 1: GPU Rasterization with Bilinear Splatting and \alpha-Blending Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. function RASTERIZE(C, P, A, F): # 1. Project and Cull # Project points P to image plane using camera C. # Cull points outside the view frustum or behind the near plane. Pprime = PROJECTANDCULL(P, C) # 2. Bilinear Splatting # For each point in Pprime, compute its contribution to pixels. # Returns: # Aprime: Splat opacities (alpha) # K: Keys (pixel coordinates or hash keys for sorting) # N: Counts (number of splats per pixel) Aprime, K, N = BILINEARSPLATTING(Pprime, A) # 3. Exclusive Sum # Compute cumulative counts to determine start indices for sorting. L = EXCLUSIVESUM(N) # 4. Radix Sort # Sort splats by key K. Use L as offset for stable sorting. # Uses NVIDIA CUB for global radix sorting. SORTEDK, SORTEDL = RADIXSORTPAIRS(K, L) # 5. Blend Sorted Splats # Perform alpha blending for each pixel using sorted splats. # Stops accumulation when remaining transmittance falls below threshold. I = BLENDSORTEDSPLATS(Aprime, F, SORTEDL, N) return I Details of Bilinear Splatting: Points are projected to the image plane. Opacity is weighted using bilinear interpolation before blending into each pixel. The blending kernel is implemented using CUDA warp-level primitives (32 threads per pixel) to optimize global memory access. Blending weight computation and spherical harmonics computations are fused into this pipeline. Accumulation stops once the remaining transmittance falls below 10^{-4}. To optimize the point cloud density, INPC uses a viewpoint-specific sampling scheme. 1. Depth Calculation: For each leaf node, compute a view-specific depth value di \in [0, 1]: di = \max \left( \frac{|z{view} - near|}{far}, \taud \right) where z{view} is the view-space depth value (distance of leaf center to image plane), and \taud = 10^{-8} is a threshold. Note that |z{view} - near| accounts for cases where z{view} may be smaller than near for partially visible leaves. 2. Frustum Intersection Handling: If a leaf volume intersects the faces of the viewing frustum, generated samples might lie outside the frustum. To avoid bias from partial visibility, re-sample the viewpoint-specific probability distribution repeatedly until the desired number of samples is reached and all generated samples are visible. This step can be omitted during inference due to multisampling. During optimization, the sampling probabilities pi and subdivision probabilities qi are updated based on the rendering feedback. 1. Gradient Computation: Store bilinear interpolation weights, per-pixel point counts, and sorted key/index buffers during the forward pass. Compute per-splat gradients in the same order as the forward pass. Obtain per-point gradient by combining its four splat gradients in a weighted sum according to the respective bilinear interpolation weights (the analytical derivative of the bilinear splatting process). 2. Weighted Sum for Probabilities: Combine per-splat blending weights of each point using a weighted sum according to the respective bilinear interpolation weights. This approach outperforms a simple sum because it causes the resulting per-point blending weight to more closely resemble the expected visibility of future samples from the leaf from which the point was sampled. Optimizer: Fused ADAM. \beta1 = 0.9 \beta2 = 0.99 \epsilon = 10^{-15} Weight decay disabled. Precision: Automatic mixed precision with FP16 gradients scaled by 128 during the backward pass. Learning Rate Decay: Exponential decay for all parameters. Hash grid/MLP LR: Decays from 1e-2 to 3e-4. CNN LR: Decays from 3e-4 to 5e-5. Differentiable Tone Mapping: Only exposure and camera response sub-modules are activated. Fixed LR: 5e-4 (exposure), 1e-3 (camera response). Warm-up: Cosine-delayed warm-up for the first 5,000 iterations, multiplying LR by a factor between 0.01 and 1. The raw rendered image is passed through the U-Net CNN. Padding: Target width and height are padded to a multiple of 2^{L-1}, where L is the number of U-Net layers, to avoid cropping/padding during skip-connection concatenation. Time Complexity: The rasterization step dominates, involving projection, splatting, sorting, and blending. The use of NVIDIA CUB for sorting and warp-level primitives for blending optimizes this to near-linear time with respect to the number of splats. Memory Complexity: Depends on the hash grid size (2^{23} entries) and the number of points. The octree structure allows for adaptive resolution, potentially reducing memory usage compared to dense voxel grids. Performance: The method is implemented in CUDA for accelerated rendering times. The fused blending kernel and efficient sorting contribute to real-time or near-real-time performance depending on resolution and scene complexity. Strengths: Flexibility of implicit point cloud structure. High-quality reconstruction due to neural feature representation. Efficient differentiable rasterization. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (e.g., hash grid size, learning rates). Pre-processing steps (undistortion, normalization) are required for fair comparison with baselines like 3DGS. Viewpoint-specific sampling adds complexity to the training loop. Origin: INPC was introduced in the paper "INPC: Implicit Neural Point Clouds for Radiance Field Rendering". History: The method builds upon prior work in point-based rendering and neural radiance fields. It integrates techniques from differentiable rendering and multi-resolution hashing. Usage: Used for novel view synthesis in 3D computer vision, particularly in datasets like Tanks and Temples. INPC: Implicit Neural Point Clouds for Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00021, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Background Modeling
head: Background MLP and SH Model
body: Background Modeling addresses the problem of static or slowly varying background elements in dynamic scene reconstruction, preventing the foreground object representation (e.g., Gaussians) from absorbing background pixels which leads to artifacts like halos or ghosting. It separates the background from the foreground by modeling it independently, either via a neural network predicting a residual to an inpainted estimate or via a differentiable MLP with spherical harmonics. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction by explicitly decoupling the background representation from the 3D Gaussian primitives, and from Point-Based Neural Renderer Architecture by focusing on the per-pixel or per-camera background estimation rather than the global scene representation. The method operates by estimating a background component that is added to or subtracted from the foreground rendering. Two primary implementations exist in the literature: a differentiable MLP-based model for view-dependent appearance and a per-camera residual network. Inputs: Camera parameters (position, orientation), pixel coordinates, and optionally an initial background estimate (for residual models). Outputs: Background color/radiance I{bg} or a background mask M for loss computation. 1. Background MLP (DeSplat variant): Architecture: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Layout: 3 hidden layers, each with 128 hidden units. Activation: Not specified in sources [G: Typically ReLU or SiLU is used in such architectures, but not explicitly stated]. Output: View-dependent color (via Spherical Harmonics coefficients). 2. Background Estimation Network (PVA variant): Architecture: Network N{bg}. Input Encoding: Camera Ci encoded as a 4D rotation quaternion and 3D position. Output: Residual background color map of size H \times W \times 3. 1. Render Foreground: Compute the standard Gaussian splatting render I{rgb} and accumulated opacity I{\alpha}. 2. Compute Background Mask: Calculate the pixel-wise error \epsilon(\mathbf{r}) between the predicted background color and the ground truth. Apply a threshold T\epsilon to create a binary mask \tilde{\epsilon}(\mathbf{r}): \tilde{\epsilon}(\mathbf{r}) = \mathbb{I}(\epsilon(\mathbf{r}) \leq T\epsilon) Apply a 3 \times 3 box filter B{3\times3} to smooth the mask: M(\mathbf{r}) = (\tilde{\epsilon}(\mathbf{r}) B{3\times3}) 3. Compute Background Loss: Use the mask M(\mathbf{r}) to weight the background color loss L{bg}, ensuring the background model only learns from pixels confidently identified as background. 4. Optimize: Update the MLP and Spherical Harmonics (SH) parameters using the combined loss. 1. Inpaint Initial Background: Generate an initial estimate \bar{I}{bg} for the background using inpainting techniques, assuming the foreground object occludes parts of the background. 2. Encode Camera: Represent the current camera Ci as a 4D rotation quaternion and 3D position. 3. Predict Residual: Pass the camera encoding through the network N{bg} to predict the residual background: I{bg} = \bar{I}{bg} + N{bg}(Ci) 4. Composite Final Image: Combine the foreground render I{rgb} and accumulated opacity I{\alpha} with the background I{bg}: Ip = I{rgb} + (1 - I{\alpha}) I{bg} 5. Optimize: Minimize the difference between Ip and the ground truth image. Masking (DeSplat): \tilde{\epsilon}(\mathbf{r}) = \epsilon(\mathbf{r}) \leq T\epsilon M(\mathbf{r}) = (\tilde{\epsilon}(\mathbf{r}) B{3\times3}) Final Pixel Prediction (PVA): Ip = I{rgb} + (1 - I{\alpha}) I{bg} I{bg} = \bar{I}{bg} + N{bg}(Ci) Opacity Threshold (T\epsilon): 0.003. Spherical Harmonics Degree: 4. Learning Rate (Background MLP Encoder & 0th-order SH): 0.002. Learning Rate (Remaining SH Orders): 0.0001. Regularization Weight (\lambda{bg}): 0.15. Halo Effects: Inpainted backgrounds are often noisy, leading to 'halo' effects around the head or foreground objects. Learning the residual rather than the absolute background mitigates this by not requiring a high-capacity network to account for the entire background. Background Leakage: If the mask is not properly smoothed or thresholded, foreground details may be absorbed into the background model, causing ghosting. A network N{bg} that learns a per-camera fixed background to avoid learning background parts in the scene representation. It predicts final pixels as the sum of rendered radiance and background residual. It is chosen when the background is static but complex, and inpainting provides a reasonable initial estimate. It differs from the DeSplat approach by using a residual network rather than a differentiable MLP with SH. Time Complexity: Depends on the background model. The MLP approach adds minimal overhead per pixel during rendering but requires optimization time. The residual network requires forward pass through N{bg} per camera. Memory Complexity: The MLP stores weights for 3 hidden layers of 128 units. The residual network stores weights for N{bg} and the initial inpainted background map. Strengths: Prevents foreground-background mixing; handles view-dependent background effects (via SH or camera encoding); reduces artifacts like halos. Limitations: Requires additional optimization parameters; inpainting-based methods depend on the quality of the initial background estimate. When to use: When the background is static or slowly varying and distinct from the foreground object of interest. When not to use: When the background is dynamic or part of the scene of interest. Background modeling in the context of Gaussian Splatting and neural rendering has been developed to handle distractor-free rendering and avatar reconstruction. The DeSplat method introduces a decomposed approach using a background MLP and SH to handle complex illumination and weather effects, separate from foreground Gaussians. The PVA method uses a per-camera background estimation network to avoid learning background parts in the scene representation, addressing halo effects common in inpainted backgrounds. DeSplat: Decomposed Gaussian Splatting for Distractor-Free Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.00076, fetched 2026-11-03 PVA: Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2101.02697, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Robot Rendering (Dr. Robot)
head: Dr. Robot
body: Differentiable Robot Rendering (Dr. Robot) is a method that models a robot's visual appearance as a differentiable function of its control parameters (pose), enabling gradient-based robotic control and planning directly from pixels. It integrates kinematics-aware deformation with 3D Gaussian Splatting to provide accurate gradients for optimization tasks such as pose reconstruction and text-conditioned action generation. Unlike neural network-based refiners or methods relying on K-plane deformations, Dr. Robot uses Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) as a geometric prior, which is particularly effective for robots with long arms and many chained joints where pure neural deformation becomes infeasible. The method renders a robot by composing three differentiable components: Forward Kinematics (FK) to project a pose vector into a skeleton, Implicit Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) to deform the skeleton, and an Appearance Deformation function to adjust the visual properties of the deformed Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs Input: Robot pose vector \mathbf{p} (joint angles), canonical 3D Gaussian set \mathcal{G}, camera parameters (for \pi). Output: Rendered image \mathbf{I}. Data Structures Canonical Gaussians \mathcal{G}: A set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian gk is defined by: Mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Scaling matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Covariance matrix \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. Opacity o \in \mathbb{R}. Appearance coefficients: 27-dimensional spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{shs}. Implicit LBS Function W(\mu): A neural network (MLP) that maps a 3D coordinate \mu to a weight vector W(\mu) \in \mathbb{R}^J, where J is the number of joints. This replaces classical LBS which requires a fixed mesh vertex set, allowing compatibility with the splitting/truncation of Gaussians. Appearance Deformation Function X: A neural network (MLP) that maps canonical position \muk and pose \mathbf{p} to deltas for rotation, scaling, opacity, and spherical harmonics. Numbered Steps 1. Forward Kinematics (FK): Compute the homogeneous transformation matrix Tj(\mathbf{p}) for each joint j relative to the base joint 0. This is the product of rigid transformations from the root to joint j-1: Tj(\mathbf{p}) = \prod{i=0}^{j-1} Ai(\mathbf{p}i) where Ai(\mathbf{p}i) = \begin{bmatrix} Ri^{i-1} & oi^{i-1} \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix} represents the transformation of joint i relative to its parent. 2. Implicit Geometric Deformation: For each Gaussian k with canonical mean \muk, compute its deposed position \mu'k using Implicit LBS: D(\muk, \mathbf{p}) = \sum{j=1}^J W(\muk)j Tj(\mathbf{p}) \muk Here, W(\muk)j is the weight for joint j output by the implicit LBS function, and Tj(\mathbf{p}) \muk transforms the canonical point by joint j's pose. 3. Appearance Deformation: Compute the adjustments to the Gaussian's visual parameters conditioned on the canonical position and the current pose: (\Delta Rk, \Delta Sk, \Delta ok, \mathbf{c}{shs,k}) = X(\muk, \mathbf{p}) The function X predicts the deltas for rotation, scaling, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. 4. Construct Posed Gaussians: The final set of posed Gaussians \mathcal{G}^\mathbf{p} is formed by applying the geometric deformation to the positions and the appearance deformation to the other parameters: f(\mathbf{p}) = \mathcal{G}^\mathbf{p} = X(D(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{p}), \mathbf{p}) Specifically, the new rotation R'k, scaling S'k, opacity o'k, and coefficients \mathbf{c}'{shs,k} are derived by applying the deltas from X to the canonical values. 5. Rendering: Render the posed Gaussians \mathcal{G}^\mathbf{p} using standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization under a pinhole camera model \pi: \mathbf{I} = \pi(f(\mathbf{p})) The image formation process \pi is a standard differentiable rasterizer. Optimization (Training) The model parameters (weights of W and X) are learned by minimizing the mean-squared error (MSE) between the rendered image and ground truth observations: \min{\thetax, \thetay, \thetaz} L = \|I - \pi(X(D(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{p}), \mathbf{p}))\|2 where \thetax, \thetay, \thetaz represent the parameters of the deformation networks. During training, to manage density and memory: Every N optimization steps, Gaussians can split into two to densify the volume. Gaussians with low opacity are truncated. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def drrobotrender(posep, canonicalgaussians, cameraparams, lbsnet, appearancenet): """ Renders a robot given a pose using Dr. Robot. Args: posep: Array of joint angles. canonicalgaussians: List of Gaussian objects with fields: mu: (3,) mean position R: (3,3) rotation matrix S: (3,3) scaling matrix o: scalar opacity cshs: (27,) spherical harmonics coefficients cameraparams: Parameters for pinhole camera model. lbsnet: Implicit LBS network W(mu) -> (J,) weights. appearancenet: Appearance deformation network X(mu, p) -> deltas. Returns: I: Rendered image. """ J = numberofjoints(posep) posedgaussians = [] # 1. Forward Kinematics: Precompute joint transforms # Tj is the homogeneous matrix for joint j relative to base jointtransforms = computeforwardkinematics(posep) for g in canonicalgaussians: muk = g.mu Rk = g.R Sk = g.S ok = g.o cshsk = g.cshs # 2. Implicit Geometric Deformation # Get weights for this point from implicit LBS weights = lbsnet(muk) # Shape: (J,) # Compute deposed position # D(mu, p) = sumj W(mu)j Tj mu deposedmu = np.zeros(3) for j in range(J): # Tj is 4x4, muk is 3x1. Homogeneous transform: # Tj [muk; 1] muh = np.array([muk[0], muk[1], muk[2], 1.0]) transformedmuh = jointtransforms[j] @ muh transformedmu = transformedmuh[:3] deposedmu += weights[j] transformedmu # 3. Appearance Deformation # X(muk, p) returns deltas for R, S, o, cshs deltaR, deltaS, deltao, deltacshs = appearancenet(muk, posep) # Apply deltas to canonical parameters # Note: In practice, deltas might be additive or multiplicative. # Assuming additive for R/S rotation components or direct parameter updates # as per source description "predicts changes". # For rotation matrix, deltaR is likely a perturbation or new rotation. # Assuming the source implies direct prediction of the new parameters # or deltas that are applied. Given "predicts changes", we apply them. # Simplified application: newR = applyrotationdelta(Rk, deltaR) newS = applyscalingdelta(Sk, deltaS) newo = ok + deltao newcshs = cshsk + deltacshs posedgaussians.append(Gaussian( mu=deposedmu, R=newR, S=newS, o=newo, cshs=newcshs)) # 4. Rendering I = gaussiansplattingrasterize(posedgaussians, cameraparams) return I def computeforwardkinematics(posep): """ Computes homogeneous transformation matrices for each joint. Tj(p) = product{i=0}^{j-1} Ai(pi) """ J = len(posep) transforms = [] currenttransform = np.eye(4) for i in range(J): # Ai(pi) = [[Ri^{i-1}, oi^{i-1}], [0, 1]] # Construct rigid transformation from parent Ri, oi = getjointtransformfrompose(posep, i) Ai = np.eye(4) Ai[:3,:3] = Ri Ai[:3, 3] = oi currenttransform = currenttransform @ Ai transforms.append(currenttransform) return transforms def applyrotationdelta(R, deltaR): # Implementation detail: # Assuming deltaR is a small rotation vector or matrix perturbation. # Standard approach: Rnew = R exp(deltaR) or similar. # For simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume deltaR is a matrix # that is added or multiplied. Given the source doesn't specify, # we assume a standard perturbation. return R + deltaR # Placeholder for specific rotation composition def applyscalingdelta(S, deltaS): # Implementation detail: return S + deltaS Parameters N: Number of optimization steps after which Gaussian splitting occurs. Typical value not specified; it is a configurable hyperparameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Long Arms with Many Joints: Classical LBS or pure neural deformation (like K-plane) struggles with high degrees of freedom and long kinematic chains (e.g., Panda Arm). Dr. Robot's Implicit LBS handles this better by leveraging kinematic priors. Gaussian Splitting/Truncation: The dynamic nature of Gaussian Splatting (splitting/truncating) makes classical LBS (which assumes fixed vertices) incompatible. Implicit LBS solves this by evaluating weights at arbitrary coordinates. This method optimizes a robot's joint angles and camera pose from a single monocular RGB image by minimizing the pixel-wise difference between the input image and a differentially rendered image. It builds on Differentiable Robot Rendering (Dr. Robot) by leveraging its kinematics-aware deformation and Gaussian Splatting to provide accurate gradients for gradient-based control. Unlike neural network-based refiners such as Robopose, this approach performs direct optimization without a learned prior. Optimization of robot joint angles to maximize the semantic similarity between the rendered robot image and a text prompt, using gradients from the CLIP model. Step: Optimize \mathbf{p} by minimizing the CLIP loss (or maximizing similarity) by backpropagating gradients through CLIP, the renderer, and the robot model. Formula: \minp \mathcal{L}{\text{CLLP}}(\mathbf{p}; \text{text prompt}) = \mathcal{C}(\text{text prompt}, \pi(f(\mathbf{p}))) Parameters: \mathcal{C} is the CLIP model function; \mathbf{p} is the robot joint angles; text prompt is the natural language description; \pi is the differentiable rasterizer. Performance: Successfully optimized the 24-dimensional action space of the Shadow Hand. Using a fine-tuned text-to-video generative model to predict robot actions, where Dr. Robot replaces the inverse dynamics model to reconstruct robot poses from the generated video frames. Step: Fine-tune a video model (e.g., Stable Video Diffusion) on robot action data (e.g., ASU Table Top dataset) conditioned on language embeddings. Step: Generate video sequences conditioned on novel language prompts. Step: Use Dr. Robot to reconstruct the robot poses from the generated video frames to extract actions. Time and Memory Complexity: The method relies on 3D Gaussian Splatting, which is generally efficient for rendering. However, the implicit LBS and appearance deformation networks add computational overhead per Gaussian during the deformation step. Memory usage is controlled by truncating low-opacity Gaussians. Measured Performance: Dr. Robot achieves high visual fidelity (PSNR) across various robots. Results on testing sets include: Shadow Hand (31.44), Unitree G1 (28.31), Unitree H1 (27.77), Franka Panda (32.84), Google Robot (32.60), ViperX 300 (30.59), xArm7 (33.25), Unitree GO1 (29.74), Unitree Go2 (29.60), and UR5 (32.01). Comparison: Dr. Robot significantly outperforms Deformable Gaussians (which use K-plane) and Nearest Neighbor baselines. For example, on the Franka Panda, Dr. Robot achieves 32.84 PSNR compared to 16.52 for K-plane and 20.68 for Nearest Neighbor. Strengths: Effective for robots with complex kinematic structures and long arms. Provides direct gradients for control and planning. Compatible with any robot form factor and degrees of freedom. Limitations: Requires training data (images under 10k poses from 12 viewpoints) curated via simulation (MuJoCo) based on URDF. The quality depends on the accuracy of the Implicit LBS and Appearance Deformation networks. Dr. Robot was introduced in a paper titled "Differentiable Robot Rendering". The method addresses the modality gap between visual foundation models and robotic action data by making the robot's visual appearance directly differentiable with respect to its control parameters. It integrates kinematics-aware deformable models with Gaussian Splatting to enable gradient-based control and planning. The work demonstrates applications in robot pose reconstruction and controlling robots through vision-language models. name: Robot Pose Reconstruction via Differentiable Rendering
head: Joint Angle Estimation, Monocular Robot Pose Optimization
body: This method optimizes a robot's joint angles and camera pose from a single monocular RGB image by minimizing the pixel-wise difference between the input image and a differentially rendered image. It builds on Differentiable Robot Rendering (Dr. Robot) by leveraging its kinematics-aware deformation and Gaussian Splatting to provide accurate gradients for gradient-based control. Unlike neural network-based refiners such as Robopose, this approach performs direct optimization without a learned prior. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single monocular RGB image I. Output: Estimated robot pose vector \mathbf{p} (joint angles) and camera pose parameters \theta{\pi}. Data Structures \mathbf{p}: Vector of robot joint angles. \theta{\pi}: Vector of camera pose parameters (extrinsics/intrinsics as defined by the renderer \pi). I: Input image tensor. \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}): The robot's geometric representation deformed by pose \mathbf{p}, as defined in the parent method. \pi: The differentiable rasterizer/renderer function. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: For the first frame of a video sequence, initialize \mathbf{p} and \theta{\pi} from scratch (e.g., random or neutral pose). For subsequent frames, warm start the optimization by setting the initial \mathbf{p} and \theta{\pi} to the values estimated from the previous frame. 2. Objective Definition: Define the reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{\text{Rec}} as the L2 norm between the input image I and the rendered image \pi(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p})). 3. Optimization: Use gradient descent to minimize the objective function with respect to \mathbf{p} and \theta{\pi}. Formula The optimization problem is defined as: \min{\mathbf{p}, \theta{\pi}} \mathcal{L}{\text{Rec}}(\mathbf{p}, I) = \|I - \pi(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}))\|2 Where: \mathbf{p} is the robot pose vector (joint angles). \theta{\pi} represents the camera pose parameters. I is the input monocular RGB image. \pi is the differentiable rasterizer/renderer function. \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}) is the deformed robot geometry. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizerobotpose(I, initialposep, initialposethetapi, renderer, robotmodel, numiterations=100, lr=0.01): """ Optimizes robot joint angles and camera pose to match input image I. Args: I: Input monocular RGB image tensor. initialposep: Initial robot joint angles vector. initialposethetapi: Initial camera pose parameters. renderer: Differentiable rasterizer function pi. robotmodel: Function f that deforms robot geometry based on pose p. numiterations: Number of gradient descent steps. lr: Learning rate for gradient descent. Returns: popt: Optimized robot joint angles. thetapiopt: Optimized camera pose parameters. """ # Initialize trainable parameters p = torch.tensor(initialposep, requiresgrad=True) thetapi = torch.tensor(initialposethetapi, requiresgrad=True) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([p, thetapi], lr=lr) for i in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Get deformed robot geometry # f(p) is defined in the parent Dr. Robot method deformedgeometry = robotmodel(p) # Render the image using the differentiable renderer # pi is the differentiable rasterizer renderedimage = renderer(deformedgeometry, thetapi) # Calculate L2 loss between input image and rendered image loss = torch.norm(I - renderedimage, p=2) # Backpropagate gradients loss.backward() # Update parameters optimizer.step() return p.detach(), thetapi.detach() def processvideosequence(videoframes): """ Processes a sequence of video frames using warm-start optimization. """ prevp = None prevthetapi = None for i, frame in enumerate(videoframes): if i == 0: # Initialize from scratch for the first frame # Typical initialization might be neutral joint angles and standard camera pose initp = getneutralpose() initthetapi = getstandardcamerapose() else: # Warm start with previous frame's estimates initp = prevp initthetapi = prevthetapi popt, thetapiopt = optimizerobotpose( I=frame, initialposep=initp, initialposethetapi=initthetapi, renderer=drrobotrenderer, robotmodel=drrobotmodel) prevp = popt prevthetapi = thetapiopt return prevp, prevthetapi Edge Cases and Pitfalls Local Minima: Optimization from scratch on the first frame may converge to local minima if the initial pose is far from the ground truth. Warm starting subsequent frames mitigates this for video sequences. Camera Pose Ambiguity: If the camera pose is unknown, it is optimized jointly with the robot pose. This can lead to ambiguity if the robot's appearance is symmetric or lacks distinctive features. Occlusions: The method assumes the robot is visible. Severe occlusions may degrade reconstruction accuracy. Uses CLIP similarity between rendered images and text prompts to optimize robot pose for open-world tasks. Sets itself apart by leveraging vision-language models for action planning rather than just reconstruction. Choose when text-guided robot manipulation is required. See Text to Robot Pose with CLIP. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations and the cost of differentiable rendering. Typically slower than neural network-based methods like Robopose per frame, but does not require training time. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not store large neural network weights for the refiner. Memory usage is dominated by the differentiable renderer and robot model. Measured Performance: On the Panda-3cam dataset: Azure camera: 9.33 L1 error (std 2.65) vs Robopose 16.8 (std 3.38). Kinect360 camera: 12.52 L1 error (std 3.58) vs Robopose 14.37 (std 3.69). Realsense camera: 17.83 L1 error (std 5.5) vs Robopose 24.57 (std 3.71). Scaling: Performance is consistent across different camera platforms with varying fields of view and mounting positions. Strengths: High accuracy, outperforms SOTA neural refiner (Robopose) by 32.9% in joint angle estimation accuracy (L1 distance). Can reconstruct challenging parts like gripper poses when visible. Limitations: Requires gradient descent optimization per frame, which is computationally more expensive than a single forward pass of a neural network. Sensitive to initialization for the first frame. When to use: When high accuracy is required and computational budget allows for per-frame optimization. When a differentiable renderer is already available. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and a neural network refiner is preferred. When the robot is heavily occluded. The method was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Robot Rendering" by. It evaluates the quality of gradients produced by Dr. Robot on the practical task of robot joint angles estimation from a single in-the-wild image. The evaluation uses the Panda-3CAM dataset, which consists of around 10K images with corresponding robot poses. The method is compared against Robopose, a state-of-the-art method that uses a refiner neural network. name: Interval Set Splatting
head: Fast Volume Rendering of Data Slices, SoListSplat
body: Interval Set Splatting is a method for the interactive visualization of "thin" interval sets within volumetric data by maintaining a sorted list of data values and their coordinates. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering specific value ranges (contours) by using binary search to isolate relevant voxels and splatting them with constant color and opacity. It differs from general volume splatting by pre-filtering data into a sorted structure to enable rapid, selective rendering of narrow value bands, and from pure iso-surface extraction by rendering a thickness (interval) rather than a single surface. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset, a user-defined selection range ([RangeMin, RangeMax]), a target contour value (C), a thickness parameter (\Delta), and viewing parameters (projection matrix, rotation). Output: A 2D image where voxels with values in [C-\Delta, C+\Delta] are rendered as semi-transparent splats. Data Structures: The core data structure is a sorted list encapsulated in a class (e.g., SoListSplat). List Layout: An array of four-component vectors (\mathbf{v}). Components 0-2: 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Component 3: The scalar data value d. Sorting: The list is sorted by the scalar data value (Component 3). Metadata: The class stores bounding box members bboxMin and bboxMax. Parameters: RangeMin, RangeMax: Define the initial filter for data inclusion. Changing these requires rebuilding the list. C (Contour Value): The center of the interval to render (e.g., 37.0). \Delta (Delta): Half-thickness of the interval. The rendered range is [C-\Delta, C+\Delta] (e.g., 35.0 to 41.0). SplatSize: A user parameter scaling the size of the splats. Color, Opacity: Constant values applied to all splats in the interval. Algorithm Steps: 1. List Construction (Offline/Update): Traverse the entire volumetric dataset once. Select only voxels where RangeMin \leq d \leq RangeMax. Store selected voxels as 4-component vectors (x, y, z, d). Sort the array by d. 2. Rendering Loop (Per Frame): Inquire View: Get the current viewing transformation and determine a rotation matrix to orient the volume with projection space. Initialize Pipeline: Set up global rendering settings, blending functions, and texture splats. Binary Search: Perform a binary search on the sorted list to find the indices of entries with values C-\Delta and C+\Delta. Iterate and Splat: Traverse the subset of entries within the found range. For each entry: Transform the voxel position (x, y, z) using the rotation matrix. Project to screen space. Render a primitive. Two types are supported: Texture Splat: A texture-mapped square containing the reconstruction function of Crawfis and Max [3] in the alpha channel. This provides higher accuracy. Point Splat: A semi-transparent point primitive. This is used for large datasets where splats project to few pixels. Points do not require orientation transformations and can be cached. Apply the constant Color and Opacity, scaled by SplatSize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class IntervalSetSplat: def init(self, data, rangemin, rangemax): """ data: list of (x, y, z, value) tuples rangemin, rangemax: float """ self.rangemin = rangemin self.rangemax = rangemax self.sortedlist = [] self.buildlist(data) def buildlist(self, data): """Traverse data, filter by range, and sort by value.""" filtered = [] for x, y, z, val in data: if self.rangemin <= val <= self.rangemax: filtered.append([x, y, z, val]) # Sort by the 4th component (value) filtered.sort(key=lambda item: item[3]) self.sortedlist = filtered def render(self, contourvalue, delta, rotationmatrix, splattype='texture'): """ contourvalue: float C delta: float Delta rotationmatrix: 3x3 or 4x4 matrix splattype: 'texture' or 'point' """ lowerbound = contourvalue - delta upperbound = contourvalue + delta # Binary search for indices # Note: Standard bisect works on 1D keys. We need a custom search or key extraction. # Assuming sortedlist is sorted by index 3. loweridx = self.binarysearchlower(self.sortedlist, lowerbound, keyidx=3) upperidx = self.binarysearchupper(self.sortedlist, upperbound, keyidx=3) # Initialize rendering pipeline initpipeline() for i in range(loweridx, upperidx): voxel = self.sortedlist[i] x, y, z, val = voxel # Transform coordinates # Assuming rotationmatrix transforms local to view space transformedpos = transform(voxel[:3], rotationmatrix) if splattype == 'point': # Points do not require orientation transformations parallel to screen # and can be cached. renderpoint(transformedpos, color, opacity, splatsize) elif splattype == 'texture': # Render texture-mapped square with reconstruction function in alpha rendertexturesplat(transformedpos, color, opacity, splatsize) def binarysearchlower(self, arr, target, keyidx): """Find first index where arr[i][keyidx] >= target.""" low = 0 high = len(arr) while low < high: mid = (low + high) // 2 if arr[mid][keyidx] < target: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid return low def binarysearchupper(self, arr, target, keyidx): """Find first index where arr[i][keyidx] > target.""" low = 0 high = len(arr) while low < high: mid = (low + high) // 2 if arr[mid][keyidx] <= target: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid return low Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: For large datasets, rendering a moderate number of texture splats can take >0.5s, disrupting smooth rotation. Use point splats for interactive rates in such cases. Mesh Topology: Reconstruction properties of splatting on regular grids break down for curvilinear and unstructured meshes. Results require careful examination. List Rebuild: Changing RangeMin or RangeMax requires traversing the data and rebuilding the sorted list, which is an expensive operation. Time Complexity: List construction is O(N \log N) due to sorting, where N is the number of voxels in the range. Rendering is O(K), where K is the number of voxels in the interval [C-\Delta, C+\Delta]. Binary search is O(\log N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sorted list of selected voxels. Performance: Point splats offer substantial speed-up over texture splats, enabling interactive exploration of large datasets (e.g., 1 million points). Texture splats are slower but more accurate. Strengths: Fast selection of specific value ranges; interactive animation possible with point splats; simple implementation. Limitations: Not suitable for unstructured/curvilinear meshes without modification; texture splatting can be slow for large K; rebuilding the list is costly. The method was introduced in "Real-time slicing of data space". It combines hardware-assisted splatting techniques [3, 4] with ideas from Shen and Johnson [22] and Ihm and Lee [9] to create a simple algorithm for representing "thin" interval sets. It was implemented as a C++ class extending Open Inventor graphics classes, specifically as SoListSplat. Real-time slicing of data space, https://www.osti.gov/biblio/632502, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Data Slicing / Interval Set Rendering
head: Fast Volume Rendering of Data Slices, Interval Volume Slicing, Real-time Data Slicing / Interval Set Rendering, Real-time Slicing of Data Space, Splatting of Interval Sets
body: Data Slicing is an algorithm for the rapid selection and representation of scalar field data on regular grids, enabling fast interactive cycling through data space by selecting and rendering specific value intervals. It solves the problem of real-time visualization of large, complex 3D scalar fields by avoiding the computational cost of back-to-front sorting required by traditional volume rendering. Unlike its siblings, it relies on a pre-sorted linear list of data values to filter points near a contour or interval, rendering them with a constant color which eliminates the need for depth sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field defined on a regular grid (or unstructured grid with limitations). Output: A 2D image representing the interval set surrounding a specified contour value or range. Data Structures: The core data structure is a sorted linear list of selected data points, referred to as SoListSplat. Layout: An array of four-component vectors (e.g., vec4). Components 0-2: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) of the grid point. Component 3: The scalar data value at that point. Metadata: The structure includes members bboxMin and bboxMax storing the coordinate boundaries of the data. Sorting: The list is sorted by the scalar data value (component 3) using a quicksort algorithm (qsort). Parameters: User Min / User Max: The lower and upper bounds of the data value range of interest. Values outside this range are discarded during list construction. Tolerance: The distance from a specific contour value within which data points are selected. Delta: The increment step size used when cycling through interval sets during interactive exploration. Typical values are tuned to avoid sudden visual jumps; very small increments reveal fine-grained changes in point density. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Define the selection range [User Min, User Max] and the cycling increment delta. 2. Filtering and Sorting: Traverse the entire scalar field dataset once. Extract grid points whose scalar values fall within [User Min, User Max]. Store these points in a list where each entry contains (x, y, z, \text{value}). Sort the list by the scalar value component using quicksort. Note: This step provides substantial data compression, often reducing the point count to less than 10% of the original set. 3. Selection (Binary Search): Given a target contour value C, determine the subset of data points within a specified tolerance \epsilon of C. Use binary search on the sorted list to find the indices corresponding to values in [C - \epsilon, C + \epsilon]. 4. Rendering (Splatting): Splat the selected data points to the screen using hardware-assisted rasterization. Primitive: Use point splats (OpenGL point sizes > 10 pixels) or texture splats. Point splats are significantly faster than texture splats. Color/Opacity: Assign a constant color and opacity to all splats in the interval set. Compositing: Because the color is homogeneous, the order of rendering is immaterial; no back-to-front or front-to-back sorting is required. Depth Handling: When combining with other volume rendering passes, perform volume rendering last while testing but not setting the z-buffer during splatting to allow depth blending. 5. Animation/Exploration: Cycle through the data space by adjusting the range [User Min, User Max] or shifting the contour value C by delta. Re-run steps 3-4 for the new interval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import struct class DataPoint: """Represents a single data point in the sorted list.""" def init(self, x, y, z, value): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z self.value = value def lt(self, other): return self.value < other.value class IntervalSetRenderer: def init(self, griddata): """ Initialize the renderer. griddata: List of tuples (x, y, z, value) representing the raw scalar field. """ self.griddata = griddata self.sortedlist = [] self.bboxmin = None self.bboxmax = None def buildsortedlist(self, usermin, usermax): """ Step 2: Filter and sort the data. """ filteredpoints = [] for (x, y, z, value) in self.griddata: if usermin <= value <= usermax: filteredpoints.append(DataPoint(x, y, z, value)) # Sort by value using quicksort logic (simulated by Python's sort) filteredpoints.sort() self.sortedlist = filteredpoints # Compute bounding box if filteredpoints: xs = [p.x for p in filteredpoints] ys = [p.y for p in filteredpoints] zs = [p.z for p in filteredpoints] self.bboxmin = (min(xs), min(ys), min(zs)) self.bboxmax = (max(xs), max(ys), max(zs)) else: self.bboxmin = (0, 0, 0) self.bboxmax = (0, 0, 0) def getintervalpoints(self, contourvalue, tolerance): """ Step 3: Select points near the contour value using binary search. """ lowerbound = contourvalue - tolerance upperbound = contourvalue + tolerance # Binary search for the start index low = 0 high = len(self.sortedlist) startidx = high while low < high: mid = (low + high) // 2 if self.sortedlist[mid].value < lowerbound: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid startidx = mid # Binary search for the end index low = startidx high = len(self.sortedlist) endidx = len(self.sortedlist) while low < high: mid = (low + high) // 2 if self.sortedlist[mid].value <= upperbound: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid endidx = mid return self.sortedlist[startidx:endidx] def render(self, points, cameramatrix, projectionmatrix, viewportwidth, viewportheight): """ Step 4: Splat the points to the screen. Note: This is a conceptual representation of the rasterization step. Actual implementation relies on GPU hardware (OpenGL/DirectX). """ # 1. Transform points to clip space clippoints = [] for p in points: # Apply MVP matrix to homogeneous coordinate (x, y, z, 1) # This step is handled by the graphics pipeline in practice clippoints.append(self.transformpoint(p, cameramatrix, projectionmatrix)) # 2. Rasterize # For each point, determine its screen footprint # Use point splats with size > 10 pixels for performance # Assign constant color C and opacity O # Draw points to framebuffer # Since color is constant, no depth sorting is needed pass def transformpoint(self, p, cammat, projmat): # Simplified MVP transformation # In reality, this is done by the GPU vertex shader return (p.x, p.y, p.z, 1.0) # Placeholder for actual matrix multiplication def cycleinterval(self, currentvalue, delta): """ Step 5: Animation loop. """ newvalue = currentvalue + delta return newvalue Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Data: For data varying widely or containing high frequencies, the sorted list approach is less advantageous than octree-based skipping methods, as the compression ratio may be poor. Visual Popping: Sudden visual "popping" occurs when cycling through intervals because grid point density can change abruptly at certain scalar values. Mitigation: redefine the range and reduce delta to a very small increment to smoothly traverse the transition. Discrete Representation: The algorithm operates in discrete space rather than continuous reconstruction. Areas of high gradient may be missed when intervals are small. It does not strictly represent true contour surfaces or interval volumes, but rather a slice plane through data space. Texture Splat Performance: Texture splats are significantly slower than point splats. Optimization of texture splat performance is noted as a future goal. Unstructured Grids: The splatting algorithm used here is not accurate for curvilinear and unstructured data sets; it represents only the raw data points. Time Complexity: The initial sorting step relies on quicksort (O(N \log N)). Subsequent rendering steps are O(K), where K is the number of selected points in the interval. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced via substantial data compression by storing only interval-selected points. The sorted list stores only points within the active interval. Measured Performance: On an SGI Onyx/VTX (R4400 CPU @ 100 MHz), the Global Climate model (320x160x19 mesh, ~1M points) renders textured splats at slightly over 1 frame per second. Other datasets (HEPIPH, Post, SOD, Shockwave) achieve real-time performance. Compression Ratios: Vary by dataset. Examples from: HEPIPH: 262,144 -> 29,111 points (11%) Climate: 718,911 -> 67,667 points (9.4%) Post: 972,800 -> 94,798 points (9.7%) SOD: 16,096 -> 1,498 points (9.3%) Shockwave: 1,091,444 -> 12,976 points (1.2%) Sod: 1,728,000 -> 8,356 points (0.5%) Strengths: Allows animation through even the largest data sets because the slice limits the number of data points to a very small fraction (one-hundredth or less) of the total set. No back-to-front sorting is required. Limitations: Does not handle high-frequency data well due to poor compression. Not accurate for unstructured grids. Texture splats are slow. When to use: Applications with high demands for interactivity, such as virtual reality settings, or for off-loading reasonable data sets from very large simulations on massively parallel supercomputers for quick overview. When not to use: When true contour surface accuracy is required, or when dealing with high-frequency scalar data where isosurfaces fail but precise interval representation is needed. Origin: The method was introduced by Roger Crawford at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Paper: "Real-time slicing of data space". History: The algorithm draws upon three main ideas: a fast indexing scheme (sorted list), hardware-assisted splatting, and the observation from Max et al. that homogeneous color rendering requires no depth sorting. It was designed to address the problematic nature of real-time rendering of iso-contour surfaces for large complex data sets. Usage: Applied to Global Climate model (percent cloudiness), HEPA filter flow magnitude, proton density, vorticity in fluid flow past a post, and astrophysics shock wave data. name: Splat Physics: Phantom Mesh Generation
head: Phantom Structure, Splat-to-Mesh
body: Phantom Mesh Generation augments a visual splat representation (typically 3D Gaussians) with an underlying surface mesh to enable standard graphics engine physics simulations, such as collision detection and shadow casting, while relying solely on the splat for visual rendering. It solves the problem that splats lack explicit surface topology, which prohibits direct use of standard physics models. It is distinct from pure visual splatting methods by introducing a dual-representation system: the splat handles the framebuffer, and the "phantom" mesh handles the physics engine. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of splat primitives (e.g., Gaussian ellipsoids from a PLY file) and configuration parameters (algorithm selection, grid threshold, scale). Output: A surface mesh (OBJ format) co-aligned with the splat, parented to the splat’s game object, and equipped with mesh colliders. Data Structures: Splat Grid: A volumetric or grid-based representation constructed from the densities of the input Gaussian ellipsoids. Isosurface: A scalar field derived from the splat grid, representing the boundary of the object. Mesh: A triangle mesh containing vertices and faces, generated via Marching Cubes or Poisson reconstruction. Steps: The method proceeds as follows: 1. Algorithm Selection: The developer selects either Object-Optimized (Marching Cubes) or Space-Optimized (Poisson) generation based on whether the splat represents a discrete object or a large-scale environment. 2. Density Field Construction: For Object-Optimized: Create a mesh for each Gaussian ellipsoid from the input PLY file, arranged in a mesh grid. Construct a splat grid and an isosurface based on the Gaussian ellipsoid densities. For Space-Optimized: Construct a density field suitable for Poisson reconstruction, typically using a coarser resolution to manage compute at scale. 3. Surface Reconstruction: Marching Cubes: Perform marching cubes over the isosurface result to create a smoothed surface mesh. Poisson: Employ the Poisson surface reconstruction algorithm to recover the largest surfaces (e.g., floors, walls). 4. Optimization and Cleanup: Decimation: Decimate the mesh for performance. Outlier Removal: For Poisson reconstruction, crop results by removing vertex outliers. Flattening: Implement a flattening procedure to adjust vertices at the base of the mesh along a specified axis, preventing undesirable behavior (e.g., toppling) when placing objects on flat surfaces. 5. Integration: Create the mesh in OBJ format, auto-align it with the input splat, parent it to the splat game object, and assign mesh colliders. Parameters: Algorithm: "Marching Cubes" (for convex objects) or "Poisson" (for non-convex spaces/large-scale scenes). Splat Scale: A parameter to adjust object reconstruction accuracy based on structural characteristics. Meshing Grid Threshold: A parameter to control the resolution and detail of the generated mesh. Resolution: Coarser resolution is used for large-scale scenes (Poisson) compared to individual objects to manage compute. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatephantommesh(splats, algorithm, scale, threshold): """ Generates a phantom mesh from splat primitives. Args: splats: List of Gaussian ellipsoids (position, covariance, density). algorithm: 'marchingcubes' or 'poisson'. scale: Float, scaling factor for reconstruction accuracy. threshold: Float, grid threshold for isosurface extraction. Returns: mesh: A mesh object with vertices and faces. """ if algorithm == 'marchingcubes': # Object-Optimized Path # 1. Create intermediate mesh for each Gaussian ellipsoid gaussianmeshes = [] for gauss in splats: # Create a mesh representation of the Gaussian ellipsoid gmesh = createellipsoidmesh(gauss.position, gauss.covariance, gauss.density) gaussianmeshes.append(gmesh) # 2. Construct splat grid and isosurface from densities splatgrid = builddensitygrid(gaussianmeshes, threshold) isosurface = extractisosurface(splatgrid) # 3. Perform marching cubes for smoothed surface mesh = marchingcubes(isosurface) # 4. Decimate for performance mesh = decimatemesh(mesh) elif algorithm == 'poisson': # Space-Optimized Path # 1. Construct density field for Poisson reconstruction # Use coarser resolution for large-scale scenes densityfield = buildpoissondensityfield(splats, resolution='coarse') # 2. Perform Poisson surface reconstruction mesh = poissonreconstruction(densityfield) # 3. Crop results by removing vertex outliers mesh = removeoutliers(mesh) # 5. Flatten base vertices if necessary (e.g., for upright placement) mesh = flattenbase(mesh, axis='y') return mesh Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convexity Assumption: Marching Cubes assumes convexity, making it unsuitable for complex spaces. Uneven Surfaces: Uneven surface reconstruction at the base of splat objects can cause instability (e.g., toppling) when placed on flat surfaces; flattening is required. Compute Scale: Large-scale reconstructions require coarser resolutions to manage compute time. Produces fine detail but assumes convexity; suitable for discrete objects. Handles non-convex spaces; used for large-scale environments and spaces where convexity does not hold. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Marching Cubes produces fine detail but is computationally heavier for large scenes; Poisson uses coarser resolution for efficiency in large-scale scenes. Strengths: Enables standard physics simulations (collision, shadows) without altering visual rendering pipeline. Limitations: Requires additional mesh generation step; Marching Cubes fails on non-convex shapes. When to use: When physics interactions (collision, shadows) are required for splat objects. When not to use: When only visual rendering is needed, or for non-convex spaces if using Marching Cubes. Phantom Mesh Generation was introduced in SplatXR, a toolkit for multi-layered extended reality via on-headset 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was presented at UIST ’26 in November 2026. The method addresses the lack of surface information in splats, which prohibits direct use of standard graphics models for physics simulations like shadow map computations or collision detection. It allows the creation of a "phantom structure" that is accessed by the 3D engine for physics while the splat writes to the visual framebuffer. name: Shear-warp
body: The Shear-warp family solves the problem of efficient volume rendering from arbitrary viewing angles by factorizing the viewing transformation matrix into a 3D shear and a 2D warp. Unlike general ray-casting methods that perform per-pixel traversal, Shear-warp transforms the volume into a "sheared object space" where viewing rays are parallel to a coordinate axis, allowing for efficient slice-by-slice compositing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by leveraging the associative nature of the compositing operator to enable early ray termination and empty space skipping, which pure object-order methods like Splatting could not perform efficiently in 1994. It differs from Texture slicing by explicitly separating the volume traversal (shear) from the final projection (warp), avoiding the need for complex texture coordinate generation per sample. The Shear-warp family shares the fundamental mechanism of decomposing the viewing transformation M{view} into three components: a permutation P, a shear S, and a 2D warp M{warp2D}. M{view} = M{warp2D} \cdot S \cdot P 1. Permutation (P): The volume data is conceptually permuted so that the principal viewing axis (the axis most aligned with the view direction vector vo) aligns with the Z-axis of the intermediate coordinate system. This determines which of the three pre-computed Run-Length Encoded (RLE) structures (if used) is accessed. 2. Shear (S): The volume slices (perpendicular to the principal axis) are sheared in 3D space to align the viewing rays with the Z-axis. For parallel projection, the shear matrix is: S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & sx & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & sy & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} where sx = -v{o,x}/v{o,z} and sy = -v{o,y}/v{o,z}. This transformation ensures that sampling rays are perpendicular to the slices, allowing fixed bilinear interpolation weights to be computed once per frame. 3. Resampling and Compositing: The sheared slices are resampled into a 2D intermediate image buffer using bilinear interpolation. The slices are composited in front-to-back order using the Porter-Duff "over" operator: C{new} = C{slice} \cdot \alpha{slice} + C{accum} \cdot (1 - \alpha{slice}) \alpha{new} = \alpha{slice} + \alpha{accum} \cdot (1 - \alpha{slice}) Early ray termination can be applied when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. 4. Warp (M{warp2D}): The intermediate image is transformed to the final image space using a 2D affine warp matrix: M{warp2D} = M{view} \cdot S^{-1} \cdot P^{-1} This step corrects the distortion introduced by the shear and applies the correct perspective or parallel projection. Solves transparency ordering by enforcing strict back-to-front rendering via software sorting and pre-cached display lists. Chosen when principal axis alignment minimizes sorting overhead and edge-on views are avoided. Specialized hardware architecture implementing object-space ray-casting with parallel slice-by-slice processing. Chosen for real-time frame rates on PC-class computers with gradient estimation and per-sample Phong illumination. Parallel algorithm for shared-memory multiprocessors minimizing synchronization and data communication. Chosen for leveraging hardware caching and image decomposition. Hybrid technique using affine transformations to warp volume slices into pixel alignment before compositing. Chosen to bridge the gap between feed-backward (ray-casting) and feed-forward (element-tossing) methods. The foundational software-based technique reducing resampling passes to two by factorizing the view matrix. Chosen for efficient CPU-driven rendering with fixed bilinear interpolation weights. Variant supporting perspective viewing by scaling each volume slice in addition to shearing it. Chosen when perspective cameras are required, accepting more complex resampling logic. Extends Shear-warp to intermix polygonal geometry with volume rendering using an inversely warped Z-buffer. Chosen when opaque polygons must correctly occlude volume data. Extends parallel Shear-warp to perspective projections with distance-dependent scaling during the shear step. Chosen to handle diverging viewing rays while maintaining efficiency over general ray-casting. Combines volume-rendered organs with surface-rendered instruments using shear-warp factorization and Z-buffer depth comparison. Chosen for surgical simulators requiring real-time visualization of moving instruments. Hardware-accelerated system based on Cube-4 architecture processing sub-volumes in parallel. Chosen for interactive frame rates on large datasets with dedicated hardware for skewed memory access and Phong shading. A pipeline variant that includes a gradient processor, matrix multiplication processor, shader, and classifier. It applies a rotation transformation matrix M{rot} with angle \alpha to the volume data, uses classification transfer functions to make soft tissues transparent (leaving only bone surfaces visible), and applies a Phong fast lighting model to shade the image. The Shear-warp algorithm was designed by Lacroute and Levoy [LL94] and is recognized as one of the fastest software implementations for volume rendering at the time of its publication. It was recognized as the fastest software render algorithm, managing to render a 256^3 voxels medical data set at 10fps and a 128^3 voxels data set at over 30fps on a Silicon Graphics machine with 16 processors. The algorithm was later implemented in custom hardware, most notably the VolumePro architecture, which was specialized for this algorithm and used trilinear interpolation for better image quality. It has also been implemented on GPUs, providing real-time frame rates and outperforming CPU-based implementations.
