name: Bounding Box Raymarching
head: Back-face ray casting, Raycasting via Bounding Box Rendering, Two-pass ray casting, WebGL Two-Pass Volume Ray Casting with Back-Face Culling
body: Bounding Box Raymarching is a GPU-accelerated volume rendering technique that determines ray segment endpoints by rasterizing the back faces of the volume's bounding box into a texture, then performing front-to-back ray marching in a second pass using those endpoints. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which pixels correspond to rays intersecting the volume and correctly defining the ray start and end positions in world or texture space, thereby avoiding the computational waste of marching rays through empty space outside the volume. It sets itself apart from standard texture slicing by performing integration along rays completely inside a fragment shader rather than in the vertex stage, and from Entry Point Buffer with Back-to-Front Projection by explicitly storing the back-face coordinates in a dedicated texture buffer during a pre-pass rather than relying solely on depth buffer comparisons or entry-point buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D volume dataset (stored as a 3D texture or 2D texture atlas), a bounding box geometry (typically a unit cube or axis-aligned box), camera matrices (Model-View-Projection), and rendering parameters (number of steps, transfer function). Outputs: A 2D color buffer containing the rendered volume image with front-to-back compositing. Data Structures: 1. Bounding Box Geometry: Defined by 8 vertices and 12 triangles (6 faces). For a unit cube, vertices are at coordinates (0,0,0) to (1,1,1). Indices define the triangles in counter-clockwise order. 2. Back-Face Texture (Exit Points): A 2D texture (e.g., 512x512 RGBA) attached to a Framebuffer Object (FBO). It stores the world-space or texture-space coordinates of the back-face intersection points. Internal format is often GLRGBA16F or GLRGBA. 3. Volume Texture: A 3D texture (sampler3D) or a 2D texture atlas acting as a 3D volume. If a 2D atlas is used, it maps 3D coordinates to 2D UVs using tile indices. 4. Transfer Function: A 1D texture (sampler1D) mapping scalar density values to RGBA color and opacity. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a Framebuffer Object (FBO) with a 2D color attachment texture (for back-face coordinates) and a depth buffer. Load the volume data into a 3D texture or 2D texture atlas. Load the transfer function into a 1D texture. Define the bounding box geometry (vertices and indices). 2. Pass 1: Back-Face Rasterization (Coordinate Generation): Bind the FBO. Enable depth testing and back-face culling. Configure culling to discard front-facing polygons (gl.CULLFACE with gl.FRONT) so that only the back faces of the bounding box are rendered. This ensures that for each pixel, we capture the entry point of the ray into the volume (from the camera's perspective, the "back" of the box is the far boundary). Note: Terminology varies; some sources call the first pass "back-face" rendering to get the exit point, while the second pass renders the front face to get the entry point. The key is capturing the two boundaries. Render the bounding box geometry. The fragment shader outputs the world-space (or texture-space) coordinates of the back-facing fragments. Store these coordinates in the FBO's color texture. 3. Pass 2: Ray Marching and Compositing: Bind the default framebuffer (screen). Disable back-face culling or enable front-face culling (gl.FRONT) to render only the front faces of the bounding box. This triggers the fragment shader for pixels inside the volume projection. Vertex Shader: Pass the current fragment's world-space (or texture-space) coordinates as a varying attribute. This represents the ray origin (entry point). Fragment Shader: a. Retrieve Endpoints: Sample the back-face texture using the current pixel's screen coordinates (or projected texture coordinates) to get the ray destination (exit point). Formula: backPos = texture2D(backFaceTexture, texCoord).xyz. Front Position: frontPos = varyingWorldCoords. b. Compute Ray Parameters: Calculate ray direction: dir = backPos - frontPos. Calculate ray length: rayLength = length(dir). Calculate step size: delta = 1.0 / steps (if using normalized texture space) or stepSize = rayLength / steps. Calculate direction vector per step: deltaDirection = normalize(dir) delta. c. Initialize Accumulators: accumulatedColor = vec4(0.0). accumulatedAlpha = 0.0. currentPosition = frontPos. d. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate for a fixed number of steps (MAX\STEPS) or until the ray exits the volume. Sample the volume at currentPosition: dataSample = sampleVolume(currentPosition). Extract color and alpha from the sample (using transfer function if necessary). Front-to-Back Compositing: Standard/Absorption Mode: sample.a = dataSample.a \times uOpacityVal sample.rgb = dataSample.rgb \times uColorVal accumulatedColor += (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha) sample.rgb accumulatedAlpha += sample.a MIP Mode: Track the maximum density value and replace accumulation. Termination Conditions: Break if: accumulatedAlpha \ge 1.0 (opaque). accumulatedLength \ge rayLength (reached back face). currentPosition is outside volume bounds (if not using bounding box endpoints). Advance Ray: currentPosition += deltaDirection. e. Output: Write accumulatedColor to the screen. Formulas: Ray Direction: dir = backPos - frontPos. Step Size (Normalized): delta = 1.0 / steps. Step Size (World/Texture Space): stepSize = length(dir) / steps. Compositing (Front-to-Back): C{out} = C{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \times C{sample} \times \alpha{sample}. Texture Atlas Mapping (if applicable): nTiles = dataDims.z tileWidth = 1.0 / nTiles p = pos.y \times tileWidth + pos.x / nTiles q = pos.z sample = texture2D(tex, vec2(p, q)). Parameters: steps / uSteps: Number of samples per ray. Default/Typical: 256 or 512. alphaCorrection / uOpacityVal: Opacity multiplier per sample. Default: 0.08. MAXSTEPS: Hard limit for loop iterations. Value: 512 or 4095. gstepSize: Fixed step size for marching. Value: 0.001f. volExtentMin / volExtentMax: Volume bounds in texture space. Typically [0,0,0] to [1,1,1] or [-1,-1,-1] to [1,1,1]. camera: Camera position in texture space. Calculated as (worldCameraPosition - volExtentMin) / (volExtentMax - volExtentMin). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Loading: If the voxel texture is not loaded before the render pass, the render function may return early. Accumulator Type: Using vec4 for accumulatedColor and multiplying by alphaSample (which includes the alpha channel) causes incorrect blending because the alpha channel is treated as color data. Use vec3 for color accumulation. Camera Clipping: If the camera is inside the volume, the near plane can clip the view. Minimize by using a smaller near plane value, but avoid excessive smallness due to floating-point precision artifacts. Warping Artifacts: If the volume texture wrapping mode is not set correctly (e.g., GLCLAMP), warping artifacts can occur at corners during rotation. A one-pixel empty margin should be present in the volume texture. Matrix Order: Transformation order must be Identity -> Rotate -> Translate. Applying translation before rotation causes the object to orbit the origin instead of rotating in place. Depth Texture Support: Requires WEBGLdepthtexture extension for some implementations. Ray Direction Logic: If only the front or back surface is rendered incorrectly, check the ray direction and start point relative to the camera. Precomputes ray entry points and marching distances into a 2D "RayData" texture during a geometry prepass, allowing the fragment shader to sample these values directly rather than recalculating intersections. Chosen when explicit ray segment encoding is needed for early termination or occlusion checks. Time Complexity: O(P \times S), where P is the number of pixels inside the volume projection and S is the number of steps per ray. The two-pass approach adds a constant overhead for the back-face rasterization. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the back-face coordinate texture, plus memory for the volume texture and transfer function. Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on the number of steps and the density of the volume. Early termination (when alpha reaches 1.0) can significantly reduce average step count for opaque volumes. Strengths: Efficiently culls pixels outside the volume by only rendering the bounding box faces. Handles zooming and rotation correctly by recalculating ray endpoints per frame. Simple implementation using standard GPU rasterization and fragment shaders. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence if not adaptive. Requires two render passes, increasing overhead compared to single-pass methods if the volume is small or sparse. Precision issues can arise with very small near planes or large view distances. When to Use: Suitable for real-time volume rendering on GPUs where the volume is dense and fits within a bounding box, and when hardware acceleration for ray-cube intersection is desired without complex ray-tracing cores. When Not to Use: Not ideal for highly sparse volumes where most rays do not intersect, or for scenes requiring complex lighting interactions that cannot be approximated by simple front-to-back compositing. Bounding Box Raymarching, also known as back-face ray casting, originated as a method to leverage the GPU's rasterization pipeline for volume rendering, avoiding the need for explicit ray-triangle intersection calculations in shaders. It was popularized in WebGL implementations for browser-based volume visualization, where hardware acceleration is critical. The technique builds on the concept of using the depth buffer and back-face culling to determine ray boundaries, a principle also used in Entry Point Buffer with Back-to-Front Projection. name: Volume Ray Casting with RayData Texture
head: Deferred Volume Rendering, GS Raymarch Pass, Ray-marching pixel shader, Raymarching Pass, Volume Ray Marching, Volume Ray-Casting (Simple), Volume Raycasting Pass
body: Volume Ray Casting with RayData Texture renders a 3D scalar field by precomputing ray entry points and marching distances into a 2D "RayData" texture during a geometry prepass, then executing a single-pass ray-marching fragment shader. It sets itself apart from standard back-face rasterized volume rendering by explicitly encoding the ray origin (in texture space) and traversal length (depth) into a dedicated render target, allowing the fragment shader to sample these values directly rather than recalculating ray-cube intersections or relying solely on depth buffer comparisons. This method solves the problem of efficiently determining valid ray segments for volume rendering while supporting early termination and scene occlusion checks. The method consists of a prepass to populate the RayData texture and a main rendering pass to execute the ray march. Inputs: 3D Volume Texture (mpVolumeSRV): Contains scalar data (8-bit or 16-bit RAW), normalized to [0, 1]. RayData Texture (mpFarNearSRV): 2D texture storing ray entry coordinates (RGB) and marching distance (Alpha). Scene Depth Buffer: Used for occlusion culling. Camera Matrices: View and Projection matrices provided via constant buffer mpCBperFrame. Outputs: Output Render Target (mpOutputRTV): Final composited volume image, typically DXGIFORMATR16G16B16A16FLOAT. 1. RayData Texture: Format: DXGIFORMATR16G16B16A16FLOAT (16-bit float per channel). Layout: RGB: Texture-space coordinates of the ray entry point (front face intersection). A: Distance from the eye to the back face of the volume (marching distance). 2. Volume Texture: Format: SurfaceFormat.Single (float) or equivalent 16/32-bit float. Dimensions: (mWidth, mHeight, mDepth). Data: Normalized scalar values [0, 1]. 3. Front/Back Position Textures (Alternative Implementation): In some implementations, front and back face positions are stored in separate 2D textures (mFront, mBack) to compute ray direction, rather than using a single RayData texture with precomputed depth. 1. Draw Back Faces: Render the six back-facing quads of the simulation volume bounding box. Shader Output: Distance from the eye (view space) to the fragment is written to the Alpha channel of the RayData texture. 2. Draw Front Faces: Render the six front-facing quads of the simulation volume bounding box. Shader Output: Texture-space coordinates of the fragment are written to the RGB channel. Blending: Enable subtractive blending for the Alpha channel to compute the depth through the volume: OutputColor.rgb = SourceColor.rgb OutputColor.a = DestinationColor.a - SourceColor.a Note: If the camera is inside the volume or the near plane clips the front faces, this step requires correction (see Near Plane Clipping Correction). 1. Setup: Bind sampler mpGenSampler (Trilinear, Clamped) at slot 0. Bind Geometry Shader mpRaymarchGS (if generating rays) and Fragment Shader mpRayCastingPS. Bind Constant Buffer mpCBperFrame to GS and PS. Bind Shader Resources: mpVolumeSRV at slot 0, mpFarNearSRV at slot 2. Bind Output Render Target mpOutputRTV. 2. Execute Draw Call: Draw a full-screen quad (or single primitive if using GS). 3. Fragment Shader Execution (Per Pixel): Lookup Ray Data: Sample mpFarNearSRV to get: EntryPoint: Ray entry position in texture space (from RGB). MarchingDistance: Total depth through the volume (from A). Calculate Ray Direction: Vector from Eye to EntryPoint (both in texture space). Alternative: If using Front/Back textures, calculate dir = normalize(BackPos - FrontPos). Initialize: pos: Ray origin (Entry Point). dst: Accumulated color (0, 0, 0, 0). StepSize: Typically half a voxel. Step: dir StepSize. Marching Loop: For each iteration (up to Iterations): 1. Sample Volume: Sample scalar value v from 3D texture at pos. 2. Transfer Function: Map v to color/alpha. Example: src.a = v 0.5. 3. Composite (Front-to-Back): FinalColor.rgb += SampleColor.rgb \times SampleColor.a \times (1 - FinalColor.a) FinalColor.a += SampleColor.a \times (1 - FinalColor.a) 4. Early Termination: Break if FinalColor.a > 0.99 (or 0.95 in some implementations). 5. Advance: pos += Step. 6. Bounds Check: Break if pos exceeds volume bounds (e.g., > 1.0 in texture space). Scene Occlusion Check: Calculate scene distance from depth buffer. Limit marching to \min(\text{BackFaceDistance}, \text{SceneDistance}). If front face is occluded by scene geometry, output a large negative value in the red channel of RayData to prevent sampling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def float3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def float4(x, y, z, w): return (x, y, z, w) def distanceeyetofragment(viewpos): return viewpos.z def texturespacecoordinates(pixel): return pixel.xy def reverseprojectdepth(depthbufferval, invprojmatrix): return depthbufferval def enableblendmode(blendop): pass def disableblendmode(): pass def prepasspopulateraydata(backfaces, frontfaces, raydatatexture): # 1. Draw back faces: output view-space distance to Alpha for pixel in backfaces: raydatatexture[pixel].rgb = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) raydatatexture[pixel].a = distanceeyetofragment(pixel.viewpos) # 2. Draw front faces: output texture-space coordinates to RGB, subtractive blend for Alpha enableblendmode(blendop="SUBTRACTALPHA") for pixel in frontfaces: raydatatexture[pixel].rgb = texturespacecoordinates(pixel) raydatatexture[pixel].a = 0.0 disableblendmode() def raycastingfragmentshader(pixelcoord, raydatatexture, volumetexture, scenedepthtexture): # 1. Lookup Ray Data raydata = raydatatexture[pixelcoord] entrypointtex = raydata.rgb marchingdist = raydata.a # Check for occlusion marker (large negative red value) if entrypointtex[0] < -1000.0: return float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 2. Calculate Ray Direction # Vector from eye to entry point in texture space eyepostex = float3(0.5, 0.5, 0.0) raydir = normalize(entrypointtex - eyepostex) # 3. Scene Occlusion Check scenedepth = reverseprojectdepth(scenedepthtexture[pixelcoord]) effectivedist = min(marchingdist, scenedepth) # 4. Initialize pos = entrypointtex dstcolor = float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) stepsize = 0.5 stepvec = raydir stepsize # 5. Marching Loop maxiterations = int(effectivedist / stepsize) for i in range(maxiterations): # Sample Volume scalarval = volumetexture.sample(pos).r srccolor = float4(scalarval, scalarval, scalarval, scalarval 0.5) # Front-to-Back Blending srccolor.rgb = srccolor.a dstcolor = (1.0 - dstcolor.a) srccolor + dstcolor # Early Termination if dstcolor.a > 0.99: break # Advance pos = pos + stepvec # Bounds Check if any(p > 1.0 for p in pos): break return dstcolor Step Size: Typically half a voxel. Iterations: Proportional to marching distance. Opacity Threshold: 0.95 or 0.99. Sampler: Trilinear filtering, clamped addressing. Camera Inside Volume: If the camera is inside the volume or the near plane clips the front faces, the RayData texture contains incorrect entry points and depths. Requires correction via channel marking and depth subtraction. Scene Occlusion: Rays may march through volume parts behind scene geometry. Must compare volume depth with scene depth. Banding Artifacts: Caused by integral numbers of equally spaced samples, especially with rapidly changing depth. Hardware Requirements: Shader Model 3.0 and RGBA16F support for 2D/3D textures are required. Compiler Warnings: Older DirectX SDK compilers may error on warnings (X4121). Near Plane Clipping Correction is a technique for rendering volumetric data when the camera is located inside the volume bounds or when the camera's near clipping plane intersects the front faces of the volume bounding box. It solves the problem of incorrect ray entry points and depth values that occur when the front faces are clipped, which would otherwise cause the raymarching algorithm to sample outside the volume or miss the entry point entirely. It sets itself apart from standard back-face rasterized volume rendering by explicitly detecting clipped regions via channel marking and correcting the ray origin and depth for those specific pixels. Scene Depth Clipping for Volume Occlusion modifies ray marching to stop when rays hit scene geometry or are occluded by it, preventing rendering of volume parts behind obstacles. It calculates scene distance by reading the scene depth and reverse projecting it to view space to find the distance from the eye to the closest obstacle. The ray marching limit uses the minimum of the back-face distance (from RayData) and the scene distance to determine where ray marching terminates. If the front face is occluded by scene geometry, the shader outputs a large negative red value in the RayData texture, ensuring the final texture-space position falls outside the volume so no samples are taken for that ray. A pitfall occurs if the depth buffer cannot be read as a texture (e.g., Direct3D 10 with multisample antialiasing), requiring scene distance computation in the main scene rendering pass using multiple render targets. Banding Suppression via Weighted Sampling suppresses banding artifacts caused by integral numbers of equally spaced samples, especially with rapidly changing depth values. It takes one additional sample beyond the calculated number of samples. The additional sample's contribution is weighted by d / \text{sampleWidth}, where d is the difference between the scene distance at the fragment and the total distance traveled by the ray at the last sample, and \text{sampleWidth} is the typical step size. Banding may remain if there are high-frequency variations in volume density or the transfer function, requiring solutions like increasing sampling frequency, jittering, or higher-order filters. Hellgate: London used trilinear jittered sampling at a frequency of twice per voxel. Off-Screen Ray Marching with Edge Detection renders fluid into a smaller off-screen render target to save performance when simulation grid resolution is low compared to screen resolution, then composites the result into the final image. It renders pixels in detected problematic areas at screen resolution, while rendering most smoke at low resolution. Artifacts appear near sharp depth discontinuities in scene geometry and where the camera clips the fluid volume. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of samples per ray (proportional to volume depth). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient for GPU implementation as it reduces per-pixel intersection calculations to texture lookups. Performance degrades if the volume is large and sampling steps are high. Strengths: Simple implementation, supports early termination, integrates with deferred shading pipelines. Limitations: Artifacts near sharp depth discontinuities, banding without jittering, limited by texture resolution for RayData. When to Use: Real-time fluid rendering where performance is critical and volume resolution is moderate. When Not to Use: High-precision scientific visualization requiring exact ray-cube intersections or complex transfer functions with high-frequency variations. The method originates from real-time fluid rendering techniques used in games like Hellgate: London and described in GPU Gems 3. It is very similar to the approach described in Scharsach 2005. The technique requires Shader Model 3.0 hardware for RGBA16F texture support. pengliu916/DynamicVolumeRayCasting, https://github.com/pengliu916/DynamicVolumeRayCasting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Graphics Runner – Volume Rendering 101, http://graphicsrunner.blogspot.com.ar/2009/01/volume-rendering-101.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Near Plane Clipping Correction
head: Camera Inside Volume Handling, Inside-Volume Volume Rendering via Backface Raycasting, Near Clipping Plane Hole Filling
body: Near Plane Clipping Correction is a technique for rendering volumetric data when the camera viewpoint is located inside the volume bounds, a scenario where standard bounding-box ray setups fail because the near clipping plane intersects the front faces of the volume, creating holes in the ray entry data. It extends the image-based ray setup by intersecting rays with explicit polygonal geometry to correctly determine entry points and clip internal surfaces, allowing for hybrid rendering of isosurfaces and direct volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera position in world coordinates, volume bounding box defined by axes and lengths, RayData texture storing precomputed ray entry points and marching distances, and near clipping plane geometry. Output: Corrected ray origins and entry distances for pixels where the camera is inside the volume or the near plane clips the front faces. Data Structures: Volume Box Matrix (M{vol}): A 4 \times 4 matrix defining the local coordinate system of the volume. Columns 0-2 contain vec4(axisdirection length, 0) for the x, y, and z axes respectively. Column 3 contains vec4(tx, ty, tz, 1) representing the box position. Inverse Volume Box Matrix (M{inv}): The inverse of M{vol}, used to transform world coordinates to the local unit cube (0,0,0)-(1,1,1). RayData Texture: A texture storing ray entry positions and depths. It is cleared to zero before rendering. AABB Structure: Defines the unit bounding box with min at (0,0,0) and max at (1,1,1). Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate System Transformation: Construct M{vol} using the volume box axes and their lengths. Compute M{inv} = M{vol}^{-1}. Transform the camera position from world coordinates to the local unit cube coordinate system: \mathbf{p}{local} = M{inv} \cdot [\mathbf{p}{cam}, 1]^T. The resulting \mathbf{p}{local} is passed to the shader as LOCALCAMPOS. 2. Marking Clipped Regions (Back-face Rasterization): Clear the RayData texture to zero. Render only the back faces of the volume bounding box (vertices at (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) in the local system). Pass the interpolated local unit texture coordinates (vLocalUnitTexCoord) to the shader. In the fragment shader, write a negative color value into the green channel of the RayData texture for these pixels. This marks pixels where back faces were rendered but front faces were clipped by the near plane. 3. Rasterization Sequence for Depth Correction: describes a multi-pass rasterization approach to fill holes using depth buffer information. Step 3.1: Disable depth buffer, enable color buffer. Rasterize the entire near clipping plane. Step 3.2: Enable depth buffer, disable color buffer. Rasterize the nearest back faces of active bricks. Step 3.3: Enable depth buffer, enable color buffer. Rasterize the nearest front faces of active bricks. 4. Shader Correction for Marked Pixels: Identify pixels where the green channel is negative (indicating clipped front faces). For these pixels, explicitly initialize the ray entry position to the texture-space position of the corresponding point on the near plane. Correct the depth value read from the RayData texture by subtracting the distance from the eye to the corresponding point on the near plane. 5. Ray Setup and Marching Start Position: Define the ray origin as LOCALCAMPOS. Define the ray direction as the normalized vector from the camera to the back-face vertex coordinate. Calculate the entry distance t to the unit AABB (0,0,0)-(1,1,1) using the slab method. Determine the start position for the raymarching loop by mixing between the camera position and the front-face intersection point based on the sign of t. If t > 0 (camera outside), use the front face intersection; if t \le 0 (camera inside), use the camera position. Formulas: \mathbf{r}{dir} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}{LocalUnitTexCoord} - \mathbf{LOCAL\CAM\POS}) \mathbf{r}{InvDir} = 1.0 / \mathbf{r}{dir} (with zero-component handling) \mathbf{t}{Minima} = (\mathbf{b}{min} - \mathbf{r}{origin}) \cdot \mathbf{r}{InvDir} \mathbf{t}{Maxima} = (\mathbf{b}{max} - \mathbf{r}{origin}) \cdot \mathbf{r}{InvDir} \mathbf{t}{Entries} = \min(\mathbf{t}{Minima}, \mathbf{t}{Maxima}) t{MaxEntry} = \max(\mathbf{t}{Entries}.x, \mathbf{t}{Entries}.y, \mathbf{t}{Entries}.z) \mathbf{p}{front} = \mathbf{r}{origin} + \mathbf{r}{dir} \cdot t \mathbf{useFrontCoord} = 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot \text{sign}(t) \mathbf{startPos} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{LOCAL\CAM\POS}, \mathbf{p}{front}, \mathbf{useFrontCoord}) Where \mathbf{r}{origin} is LOCALCAMPOS, \mathbf{v}{LocalUnitTexCoord} is the interpolated back-face coordinate, \mathbf{b}{min} and \mathbf{b}{max} are the unit AABB bounds, and \text{sign}(t) returns 1 for t>0, 0 for t=0, and -1 for t<0. Parameters with Typical Values: Volume Box: Defined by axes and lengths. The local coordinate system maps to (0,0,0)-(1,1,1). RayData Texture: Cleared to zero before rendering. Green Channel Marker: Negative value used to indicate clipped front faces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Camera Inside Volume: Standard bounding-box ray setups fail because the near clipping plane intersects the front faces, creating holes in the ray entry data. Precision: The slab method for AABB intersection must handle cases where ray direction components are zero or near-zero to avoid division by zero or precision issues. Degenerate Input: If the camera is exactly on the boundary of the volume, the sign of t determines the behavior. The mix function with sign(t) handles this by preferring the camera position if t \le 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getunitaabbentry(origin, direction): # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0.0 else 1e30 for d in direction] bmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] bmax = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] tminima = [(bmin[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmaxima = [(bmax[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tentries = [min(tminima[i], tmaxima[i]) for i in range(3)] # Find first real entry value: max of minimums across x, y, z tmaxentry = max(tentries[0], tentries[1], tentries[2]) return tmaxentry def getcloserpos(camera, frontfaceintersection, t): usefront = 0.5 + 0.5 (1.0 if t > 0.0 else (-1.0 if t < 0.0 else 0.0)) return [camera[i] + usefront (frontfaceintersection[i] - camera[i]) for i in range(3)] def computeraysetup(localcampos, vlocalunittexcoord): origin = localcampos direction = [vlocalunittexcoord[i] - localcampos[i] for i in range(3)] mag = (sum(xx for x in direction)) 0.5 direction = [d / mag for d in direction] t = getunitaabbentry(origin, direction) frontfacelocal = [origin[i] + direction[i] t for i in range(3)] startpos = getcloserpos(localcampos, frontfacelocal, t) return origin, direction, startpos, vlocalunittexcoord This method enables volume ray casting when the camera viewpoint is located inside the volume (e.g., virtual colonoscopy), a scenario where standard bounding-box ray setups fail because the near clipping plane intersects the front faces of the volume, creating holes in the ray entry data. It extends the image-based ray setup by intersecting rays with explicit polygonal geometry to correctly determine entry points and clip internal surfaces, allowing for hybrid rendering of isosurfaces and direct volume rendering. Time Complexity: The correction adds a constant number of rasterization passes (back faces, near plane, front faces) and a simple shader calculation per pixel. The complexity is dominated by the raymarching loop, which is unchanged. Memory Complexity: Requires the RayData texture to store entry points and depths. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the resolution of the RayData texture and the number of samples in the raymarching loop. Strengths: Correctly handles camera positions inside the volume and near-plane clipping artifacts, enabling immersive viewing experiences like virtual colonoscopy. Limitations: Requires explicit rasterization of the volume bounding box and near clipping plane. May introduce artifacts if the near plane is very close to the camera or if the volume geometry is complex. When to Use: When the camera viewpoint is inside the volume or when the near clipping plane intersects the front faces of the volume. When Not to Use: When the camera is always outside the volume and the near plane does not intersect the front faces. Origin: The technique is described in the context of GPU-based volume raycasting, particularly for handling fluid volumes and immersive viewpoints. History and Development: The method is detailed in "Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids" (GPU Gems 3) and "Advanced Illumination Techniques for GPU-Based Volume Raycasting". Where it is Used: Virtual colonoscopy, immersive fluid visualization, and any application requiring camera movement inside volumetric data. name: Viewpoint Inside Volume Ray Setup
head: Endoscopic Raycasting, Hybrid ray setup, Polygonal geometry intersection
body: This method enables volume ray casting when the camera viewpoint is located inside the volume (e.g., virtual colonoscopy), a scenario where standard bounding-box ray setups fail because the near clipping plane intersects the front faces of the volume, creating holes in the ray entry data. It extends the image-based ray setup by intersecting rays with explicit polygonal geometry to correctly determine entry points and clip internal surfaces, allowing for hybrid rendering of isosurfaces and direct volume rendering. The method builds on the image-based ray setup described in Near Plane Clipping Correction. It computes ray parameters per pixel using a pre-rendering step followed by the ray casting pass. Inputs: Volume texture V. Polygonal geometry mesh M representing internal surfaces or the volume boundary. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Ray step size s and maximum ray length L{max}. Outputs: Final color image C. Data Structures: 1. Ray Start Position Image (I{start}): A 2D texture storing the 3D world-space starting position of the ray for each pixel. 2. Ray Length Image (I{len}): A 2D texture storing the total length of the ray segment to be marched. 3. Modified Ray Length Image (I{len}'): Intermediate texture storing the clipped ray length after polygon intersection. 4. Compositing Buffer: The final rendered image buffer. Steps: 1. Compute Starting Position Image (I{start}): For each pixel (u, v), compute the ray origin. If the viewpoint is inside the volume, the origin is the camera position. If outside, it is the intersection with the near plane or bounding box. This step builds on the base image-based ray setup. 2. Compute Ray Length Image (I{len}): For each pixel, compute the initial ray length, typically the distance from the ray origin to the far plane or bounding box exit point. Store the length in I{len}. 3. Render Polygonal Geometry to Modify Ray Length: This step clips the rays at internal surfaces or corrects entry points. a. Fill Holes: If the near clipping plane clips into front faces, rasterize the near clipping plane geometry to fill gaps where no ray origin was defined. b. Intersect with Polygonal Mesh: Rasterize the polygonal mesh M using a depth buffer. For each pixel, if a polygon is visible, compute the intersection distance d{int} from the ray origin \mathbf{p}0 along the ray direction \mathbf{d}. c. Clip Length: Update the ray length in I{len}' to the minimum of the current length and the intersection distance. The depth buffer ensures only the nearest surface is considered. 4. Raycasting: For each pixel, retrieve \mathbf{p}0 from I{start} and L' from I{len}'. March the ray from \mathbf{p}0 along \mathbf{d} for length L', sampling the volume V and compositing the result into the compositing buffer. 5. Blending: Composite the result into the final image. If hybrid rendering is used, the polygonal geometry may be rendered separately as an opaque surface, and the volume ray casting is performed only for the interior or exterior regions as defined by the geometry. Parameters: Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The near clipping plane may clip into the front faces of the volume, creating holes that must be filled using the near clipping plane or depth buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupviewpointinsidevolume(volume, mesh, camera, stepsize): # Step 1: Compute Starting Position Image Istart = empty((height, width, 3)) for u, v in pixels: raydir = unproject(u, v, camera) if camera.positioninsidevolume(volume): Istart[u, v] = camera.position else: Istart[u, v] = intersectnearplane(camera, raydir) # Step 2: Compute Ray Length Image Ilen = empty((height, width)) for u, v in pixels: raydir = unproject(u, v, camera) Ilen[u, v] = intersectfarplane(Istart[u, v], raydir, camera) # Step 3: Render Polygonal Geometry to Modify Ray Length Ilenmod = copy(Ilen) depthbuffer = initializedepthbuffer() # Fill holes from near clipping plane rasterizenearplane(Ilenmod, camera) # Intersect with polygonal mesh for triangle in mesh: hitdist = intersectraytriangle(Istart, unprojectdirections, triangle) depth = projectdepth(Istart + hitdist unprojectdirections) for u, v in pixels: if hitdist[u, v] < Ilenmod[u, v] and depth[u, v] < depthbuffer[u, v]: Ilenmod[u, v] = hitdist[u, v] depthbuffer[u, v] = depth[u, v] # Step 4: Raycasting compbuffer = empty((height, width, 3)) for u, v in pixels: p0 = Istart[u, v] L = Ilenmod[u, v] raydir = unproject(u, v, camera) color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < L: sample = samplevolume(p0 + t raydir, volume) color, alpha = composite(color, alpha, sample) t += stepsize compbuffer[u, v] = color # Step 5: Blending finalimage = copy(compbuffer) rasterizemesh(finalimage, mesh, camera) return finalimage Time Complexity: O(N) for ray casting, where N is the number of pixels. The pre-pass is O(P), where P is the number of polygons in the mesh. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the ray start and length images. Additional memory for the depth buffer during the polygon rasterization pass. Strengths: Enables realistic endoscopic visualization; allows hybrid rendering. Limitations: Requires explicit polygonal geometry. When to use: Virtual colonoscopy, internal organ visualization, any scenario where the camera is inside the volume. When not to use: Simple bounding-box volumes where the camera is outside. The method was developed as an extension of image-based volume ray casting to support viewpoints inside the volume. It was presented in the context of advanced illumination techniques for GPU-based volume ray casting. The approach builds on earlier work by Scharsach et al. (2006) for handling near clipping plane issues. It is particularly relevant for medical visualization, such as virtual colonoscopy, where the camera navigates inside the body. name: Multi-pass GPU Ray Casting on Virtual Globe
head: GPU-based Direct Volume Ray-Casting on Virtual Globe, Multi-pass GPU ray-casting for EME, Spherical coordinate DVR
body: This method renders 3D volumetric data stored in spherical coordinates onto a virtual globe by transforming bounding box positions to Cartesian space, generating rays in Cartesian coordinates, and sampling the spherical texture front-to-back. It differs from standard GPU-based ray-casting because the voxel positions use a spherical coordinate system which is irregular, requiring explicit Cartesian coordinate transformation for ray generation and texture sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volumetric data (e.g., electromagnetic power density) stored in a 3D floating-point texture using spherical coordinates (latitude, longitude, altitude layers). Input: A volume bounding box mesh representing the extent of the volumetric data. Input: User-defined transfer function parameters (via color picker). Output: A 2D composite image of the volumetric data blended onto the scene. Data Structures: 1. 3D Floating-Point Texture: Stores the volumetric data. The voxels are organized in a spherical coordinate system. The 3D space is divided into n layers along the altitude direction. Each layer is divided into m \times k grids along the longitude and latitude directions. 2. Back Face Position Texture: A 2D RGB texture used to store the termination points of rays entering the volume. This is rendered using a Frame Buffer Object (FBO). 3. Bounding Box Mesh: A proxy mesh representing the volume bounds. Its vertex colors are assigned the 3D texture coordinates corresponding to the voxel positions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-computation of Volumetric Data (Optional/Contextual): The volumetric data (e.g., EME power density) is computed on the GPU using fragment shaders. The power density P at a point is calculated based on radio device parameters. For a single radio, the radiated power density is: P = Pt - L - Ls where Pt is the radio's power, L is the total propagation loss, and Ls represents other losses (system loss, operation loss). The total propagation loss L is the sum of free space propagation loss L{fs} and terrain/obstruction loss A{ref}: L = L{fs} + A{ref} The free space propagation loss is: L{fs} = 32.45 + 20 \lg f + 20 \lg d where f is the frequency of the radio and d is the distance. If there are N radio devices, the total power density is the summation: P = \sum{i=1}^{N} Pi where Pi is the power density of the i-th radio. This data is stored in the 3D texture. 2. First Pass: Render Back Faces: Render the back faces of the volume bounding box to the Back Face Position Texture (2D RGB texture) using an FBO. The vertex shader assigns the 3D texture coordinates (spherical coordinates mapped to the bounding box) to the vertex colors of the bounding box. The fragment shader outputs these colors, effectively storing the entry/termination points of rays into the volume in Cartesian space (derived from the transformed vertex positions). 3. Second Pass: Ray Casting and Compositing: Render the front faces of the volume bounding box. Vertex Shader: Transform the vertex position to eye coordinates space and pass it to the fragment shader. Fragment Shader: 1. Fetch the termination point (entry point) for the current fragment from the Back Face Position Texture using the transformed vertex position. 2. Compute the projecting ray direction \vec{d} as the difference between the current fragment's position (or vertex color representing the exit point) and the fetched termination point: \vec{d} = \text{CurrentPosition} - \text{TerminationPoint} 3. Transform the ray direction and positions to align with the spherical coordinate system of the 3D texture if necessary, or sample the texture directly if the texture coordinates are mapped appropriately. Note: The source states rays are generated in Cartesian coordinates to sample the spherical texture, implying a coordinate transformation step occurs during sampling or ray definition. 4. Sample the 3D texture of the volumetric data from front to back along the ray direction. 5. Assign color to each sample using a transfer function based on user interactive input. 6. Composite each sample color along the ray direction using front-to-back compositing to produce the final fragment color. 4. Final Pass: Blending: Blend the resulting 2D volume image to the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbackfaces(): bindfbo(backfacepositiontexture) drawmesh(boundingboxmesh, faceculling=FRONT) # Render only back faces # Vertex shader outputs vertex color = 3D texture coordinates (spherical -> cartesian mapping handled by hardware/vertex data) unbindfbo() def renderfrontfaces(): bindfbo(scenecolorbuffer) drawmesh(boundingboxmesh, faceculling=BACK) # Render only front faces # Vertex Shader # Input: Vertex position V, Vertex Color C (3D texture coords) # Output: FragPosEye (eye space position), FragColor (exit point in cartesian) # Fragment Shader # Input: FragPosEye, FragColor (exit point) # Uniform: backfacepositiontexture (entry points), volumetexture (3D data) entrypoint = texture(backfacepositiontexture, FragColor).rgb exitpoint = FragColor # Or derived from FragPosEye transformed back # Compute ray direction in Cartesian space raydir = exitpoint - entrypoint # Normalize and step along ray numsteps = 100 # Not given in sources, typical value stepsize = length(raydir) / numsteps raydir = normalize(raydir) accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 currentpos = entrypoint for i in range(numsteps): # Sample 3D texture # Note: The source implies sampling the spherical texture. # The ray is in Cartesian, but the texture is spherical. # A transformation from Cartesian ray position to Spherical texture coordinates is required. # This is marked as as the exact transformation matrix is not provided in the text, # but the concept of "transforming bounding box positions to Cartesian... and sampling spherical texture" is explicit. sphericalcoords = cartesiantospherical(currentpos) density = texture(volumetexture, sphericalcoords).r # Transfer function color = transferfunction(density) alpha = opacityfunction(density) # Front-to-back compositing if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break # Standard front-to-back blending # Cout = Cin + (1 - Ain) Csample Asample # Aout = Ain + (1 - Ain) Asample weight = (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha accumulatedcolor += weight color accumulatedalpha += weight currentpos += raydir stepsize return accumulatedcolor def blendtoscene(): # Render a fullscreen quad with the result of Pass 2 # Blend mode: Source Alpha, One drawfullscreenquad(resulttexturefrompass2) Parameters: Pt: Radio's power. Ls: Other losses (system loss, operation loss). N: Number of radio devices within the frequency bands. Pi: Power density of the i-th radio. n: Number of layers along the altitude direction for grid division. m \times k: Grid dimensions along longitude and latitude direction per layer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Irregular Coordinates: Spherical voxel coordinates are irregular, so standard regular volume rendering approaches fail. Explicit coordinate transformation to Cartesian space is required for ray casting. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The method relies on the bounding box to define the ray entry and exit points. Degenerate bounding boxes (zero volume) would result in zero-length rays. Time Complexity: Designed for interactive frame rates using high dense parallel computation on GPU. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D volumetric texture (m \times k \times n samples) and the 2D back-face position texture. Scaling: The computation of 3D EME power density is independent at each grid, making it suitable for parallel computing on GPU. Strengths: Allows dynamic visualization of 3D EME power density coverage by adjusting radio device parameters; leverages GPU hardware for high-performance rendering. Limitations: Requires complex coordinate transformations due to the spherical nature of the data; not directly applicable to regular Cartesian volumes without adaptation. When to use: When visualizing 3D electromagnetic environment (EME) data on a virtual globe where data is naturally structured in spherical coordinates. When not: For regular Cartesian volumetric data where simpler ray-marching techniques (like Bounding Box Raymarching) are sufficient. Origin: The method inherits from GPU-based Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) using 3D textures [9], extended to visualize 3D Electromagnetic Environment (EME) on a virtual globe with spherical coordinates. History: Proposed in 2010 by authors publishing in the I.J. Image, Graphics and Signal Processing. It builds upon earlier work on GPU-based DVR [9] and general-purpose GPU computation [17, 18]. Usage: Used for visualizing 3D electromagnetic environment (EME) on a virtual globe in the described system. name: Entry Point Buffer with Back-to-Front Projection
head: Back-to-Front Projection for Entry Points, Block Projection Entry Point Method
body: This method determines the first intersection of each viewing ray with the visible volume to skip transparent data during raycasting. It establishes an entry point buffer storing depth values and block indices, populated by projecting non-transparent blocks back-to-front. It sets itself apart from standard bounding box raymarching by using block-level visibility culling and hidden surface removal to initialize rays precisely at the volume surface rather than the bounding box. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset organized into blocks, transfer function, viewing transformation (parallel projection assumed for simplification). Output: Entry point buffer containing depth values and block indices for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Block Metadata: Stores minimum and maximum sample values for each block. 2. Summed Area Table (SAT): Precomputed table of the opacity transfer function to quickly determine block visibility. 3. Entry Point Buffer: Array sized to the image plane. Each entry stores: relativedepth: Z-value of the generic template. blockindex: Unique identifier for the block. Steps: 1. Block Visibility Culling: Identify blocks containing only transparent data. A block is considered transparent if its min/max sample values, when evaluated against the opacity transfer function and summed area table, yield zero opacity. 2. Template Generation: For parallel projection, generate one geometric template representing the block's projection under the current viewing transformation. 3. Back-to-Front Projection: Traverse the list of non-transparent blocks in reverse order (back-to-front). For each block, translate the template by vector \mathbf{t} = (tx, ty, tz), where tx, ty are the block's position on the image plane and tz is the depth offset. Write the Z-value of the generic template into the entry point buffer for covered pixels, along with the block's unique index. Use a Z-buffer algorithm to ensure correct visibility (only the closest entry point is stored). 4. Ray Initialization: In the ray setup phase, use the depth values and block indices from the entry point buffer to calculate the absolute ray start position. The absolute depth is found by adding the stored relative depth to the block's tz value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeentrypoints(blocks, transferfunction, sat, imagewidth, imageheight): # 1. Cull transparent blocks using min/max values and SAT visibleblocks = [] for block in blocks: if not isblocktransparent(block.minval, block.maxval, transferfunction, sat): visibleblocks.append(block) # 2. Generate template for parallel projection # Rasterize the block's projected quad under viewing transformation template = generateblocktemplate(blocks[0]) # 3. Initialize entry point buffer entrypointbuffer = [None] (imagewidth imageheight) # 4. Back-to-front projection for block in reversed(visibleblocks): tx, ty = block.positiononimageplane tz = block.depthoffset for pixel in template.pixels: screenx = pixel.x + tx screeny = pixel.y + ty if 0 <= screenx < imagewidth and 0 <= screeny < imageheight: idx = screeny imagewidth + screenx newdepth = pixel.z # Z-buffer logic: keep the closest (smallest) depth value if entrypointbuffer[idx] is None or newdepth < entrypointbuffer[idx]['relativedepth']: entrypointbuffer[idx] = { 'relativedepth': newdepth, 'blockindex': block.id } return entrypointbuffer def isblocktransparent(minval, maxval, transferfunction, sat): opacity = computeblockopacity(minval, maxval, transferfunction, sat) return opacity == 0 def computeblockopacity(minval, maxval, transferfunction, sat): # Standard SAT lookup: sum opacity values for the range [minval, maxval] return sat[maxval] - sat[minval - 1] if minval > 0 else sat[maxval] def generateblocktemplate(block): # Rasterize block under viewing transformation to get relative Z-values per pixel pixels = [] for y in range(block.height): for x in range(block.width): pixels.append({'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': block.basedepth + (x + y) block.depthstep}) return pixels Parameters: Summed Area Table: Used to quickly determine block visibility based on min/max sample values and opacity transfer function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance Overhead: Using addition and depth test at every pixel of the template for each block is expensive. Mitigation: The back-to-front projection and storing indices/relative depths reduces the number of operations in the ray setup phase, as additions are only performed for rays that actually hit a block. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of visible blocks and their projected area. The projection step involves iterating over template pixels for each block. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the entry point buffer (depth + index per pixel) and block metadata. Strengths: Effectively skips transparent data, allowing interactive transfer function modification due to fast block-level visibility checks. Limitations: The projection step can be expensive due to per-pixel additions and depth tests. When to Use: Suitable for large medical datasets with significant transparent regions where interactive exploration is required. Developed for efficient volume visualization of large medical datasets. The method leverages block-based processing and GPU-friendly rasterization techniques to optimize raycasting initialization. name: Triton-accelerated Volume Raycasting
head: FlashDRR Triton Kernel, Triton-based Volume Raycasting, fused volume rendering
body: Triton-accelerated Volume Raycasting is a fused GPU rendering technique using the Triton programming language to perform volume raycasting, avoiding the materialization of intermediate ray-sample tensors in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to reduce memory footprint and increase speed. It differs from standard PyTorch implementations by fusing CUDA kernels, which reduces iteration time and memory overhead, particularly at high resolutions. While standard PyTorch execution degrades super-linearly beyond 1024x1024 resolution due to memory bandwidth limits and cache thrashing, Triton maintains predictable linear scaling proportional to the total number of rays rendered. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: mu: A 5D tensor of shape (B, C, D, H, W) representing volume density or scatter coefficients, where B is batch size, C is channels, and D, H, W are volume dimensions. viewmat: A camera view matrix. ras2ijk: A transformation matrix mapping raster coordinates to voxel indices. triton: A boolean flag. If True, the fused Triton kernel is used; if False, the standard PyTorch implementation is used. raysamples: Number of samples per ray, typically 384 or 512. resolution: Output image resolution, e.g., 1024x1024 or 2048x2048. Outputs: Rendered image tensor of shape (B, C, Hout, Wout). Data Structures The method avoids allocating large intermediate tensors for ray samples, maintaining a near-constant memory footprint below 430 MiB. Standard PyTorch implementations typically allocate tensors of size Rays × Samples/Ray in HBM. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: The VolumeRaycaster is instantiated with parameters raysamples and resolution; the triton flag is set to True to enable the fused kernel. 2. Ray Generation: Rays are generated per-pixel using viewmat and ras2ijk to determine entry and exit points into the volume [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md]. 3. Fused Kernel Execution: The Triton kernel launches a grid of threads, where each block handles a tile of the output image. Threads load ray parameters and iterate through raysamples. Volume values are sampled using trilinear interpolation [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md]. Front-to-back compositing updates accumulated color C' and opacity \alpha' using the emission-absorption model: C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Accumulation occurs in on-chip memory, avoiding intermediate HBM writes. Final pixel values are written to global memory using atomic addition. 4. Early Ray Termination (ERT): Rays terminate when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95 or 1.0) [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md]. 5. Output Assembly: Final accumulated color and opacity tensors are returned. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tritonvolumeraycastkernel(mu, viewmat, ras2ijk, out, raysamples, strideh, stridew, blockh, blockw, stepsize): # Grid coordinates for the tile pidh = 0 pidw = 0 # Initialize accumulators for the tile acccolor = torch.zeros((blockh, blockw), dtype=torch.float32) accalpha = torch.zeros((blockh, blockw), dtype=torch.float32) # Compute ray origin and direction from viewmat and ras2ijk for each pixel in the tile origins, directions = computerayparams(pidh, pidw, strideh, stridew, blockh, blockw, viewmat, ras2ijk) for s in range(raysamples): # Compute sample position along ray and transform to voxel coordinates t = origins + s directions voxelcoords = transformtovoxel(t, viewmat, ras2ijk) # Sample volume density density = mu[voxelcoords] # Compute opacity and color contribution alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-density stepsize) color = density alpha # Front-to-back compositing acccolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accalpha) color accalpha = accalpha + (1.0 - accalpha) alpha # Early Ray Termination if torch.max(accalpha) > 0.95: break # Write results to global memory using atomic addition for h in range(blockh): for w in range(blockw): idx = pidh strideh + h jdx = pidw stridew + w atomicadd(out[0, idx, jdx], acccolor[h, w]) atomicadd(out[1, idx, jdx], accalpha[h, w]) Parameters triton: Boolean flag. True enables the fused kernel. raysamples: Number of samples per ray. Typical values are 384 or 512. resolution: Output image resolution. Typical values are 1024x1024 or 2048x2048. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Nondeterminism: The Triton kernel uses tl.atomicadd, which is order-nondeterministic. Gradient checks require a looser tolerance (atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-3) and nondettol=1e-6 to account for this noise. Precision: The method supports both fp32 and fp16/bf16. Verification shows that Triton results match standard PyTorch results within atol=1e-4 for both precisions. Memory Scaling: Standard PyTorch execution degrades super-linearly beyond 1024x1024 resolution due to memory bandwidth limits and cache thrashing. Per-ray register accumulation is a forward-pass optimization for direct volume ray casting that eliminates per-sample global-memory read-modify-write operations by accumulating RGB, depth, and opacity values in per-thread stack-allocated registers. It differs from the baseline implementation by writing each per-ray output exactly once to global memory after the ray marching loop completes, thereby significantly reducing global memory traffic. Time and Memory Complexity Time: Triton maintains predictable linear scaling proportional to the total number of rays rendered. Standard PyTorch execution time degrades super-linearly beyond 1024x1024 resolution. Memory: The Triton version reduces peak VRAM usage from scaling linearly with total samples (Rays × Samples/Ray) to a near-constant footprint below 430 MiB, achieving a 99.5% memory reduction at high workloads. Measured Performance Speedup: At 2048x2048 resolution with 256 ray samples, the Triton kernel reduces iteration time from 1,804.32 ms to 9.16 ms, a 197x speedup compared to the non-Triton version. Memory Usage: At 1024x1024 resolution with 512 samples, standard PyTorch evaluation memory is ~12.4 GB, while Triton evaluation memory is 110.7 MiB. Training Overhead: At 1024x1024 resolution with 512 samples, Triton training step time is 15.4 ms. Triton training adds ~3.05x overhead compared to its own evaluation, while standard PyTorch adds ~1.31x overhead. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Significant reduction in memory footprint and iteration time at high resolutions. Predictable linear scaling. Limitations: Nondeterministic gradient updates due to atomic operations. Requires Triton support. Triton-accelerated Volume Raycasting is part of the FlashDRR project, which aims to provide fast, differentiable volume rendering for medical imaging applications. The method leverages the Triton programming language to fuse CUDA kernels, addressing the memory bottlenecks of standard PyTorch implementations. pcarnah/flashdrr, https://github.com/pcarnah/flashdrr, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Per-ray register accumulation for volume rendering
head: Residual Accumulation, Residual Accumulator Optimization, Stage 1 optimization, register accumulation
body: Per-ray register accumulation is a forward-pass optimization for direct volume ray casting that eliminates per-sample global-memory read-modify-write operations by accumulating RGB, depth, and opacity values in per-thread stack-allocated registers. It differs from the baseline implementation by writing each per-ray output exactly once to global memory after the ray marching loop completes, thereby significantly reducing global memory traffic. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, volume density/opacity samples, transfer function parameters, bounding box, and step size. Outputs: outRGB (accumulated color), outDepth (accumulated depth), outOpacity (accumulated opacity). Data Structures: The method uses per-thread local storage to hold intermediate state. accRgb[MAXVOLUMERENDERCHANNELS]: A stack-allocated array for RGB accumulation, typically unrolled via #pragma unroll. depth: A scalar variable for depth accumulation. opacity: A scalar variable for accumulated alpha/opacity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each ray processed by a thread, initialize accRgb to zero, depth to 0, and opacity to 0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate through the volume samples along the ray. Sample the volume density and color at the current step. Compute the step opacity alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) and transmittance T = exp(-opacity). Compute the contribution weight w = alpha T and update the registers: accRgb[c] += w color[c], depth += w (t - tmin), opacity += alpha. Residual Accumulation for Depth: To save arithmetic operations, a residual accumulator s can replace direct depth accumulation. Initialize s on each row i with z{i,i-1} - z{i-1,i-1}. Update rules are s \leftarrow s + r{i,j} and zj \leftarrow zj + s, allowing overwriting of z{i-1,j} with z{i,j} in the same column and requiring only one row buffer. 3. Final Write: After the loop completes, write the final accumulated values from the per-thread registers to the global output tensors outRGB, outDepth, and outOpacity exactly once per ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MAXVOLUMERENDERCHANNELS = 3 # Compile-time constant def perrayregisteraccumulation(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, stepsize, volumesampler): # 1. Initialize per-thread registers accrgb = [0.0] MAXVOLUMERENDERCHANNELS depth = 0.0 opacity = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 # 2. Accumulate in registers numsteps = max(1, int(round((tmax - tmin) / stepsize))) for i in range(numsteps): t = tmin + (i + 0.5) stepsize # Mid-point sampling pos = rayorigin + t raydirection density, color = volumesampler.sample(pos) # Standard direct volume rendering compositing alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) weight = alpha transmittance for c in range(MAXVOLUMERENDERCHANNELS): accrgb[c] += weight color[c] depth += weight (t - tmin) # Relative depth accumulation opacity += alpha transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early termination guard if transmittance < 1e-4: break # 3. Write final results to global memory exactly once outrgb = accrgb outdepth = depth outopacity = opacity return outrgb, outdepth, outopacity Parameters: MAXVOLUMERENDERCHANNELS: Compile-time constant defining the maximum number of RGB channels supported in the accumulation register array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Accumulating in registers changes the order of floating-point operations compared to global memory accumulation, which may yield minor precision differences. Early Termination: If early termination is triggered, the final write must still occur, outputting the partial accumulation state. Backward Pass: This optimization applies strictly to the forward pass; the backward pass is handled separately via a Python torch.autograd.Function wrapper to avoid storing per-sample weights. Performance: In a fire renderer at 256 spp, this optimization reduced the volumerender stage time from 8772.5 ms to 6171.4 ms (-29.7%) and reduced end-to-end walltime by 17.8% (saving 2.57 s). Memory Traffic: Significantly reduces global memory read-modify-write operations on outRGB, outDepth, and outOpacity. Scalability: Performance gains are most significant when global memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck. Strengths: Reduced global memory traffic, lower latency per ray, and simpler memory access patterns for output tensors. Limitations: Performance is bounded by hardware register limits; excessive channels or auxiliary variables may cause register spilling to local memory, negating bandwidth benefits. This optimization was introduced alongside the migration of the autograd layer to Python in the fvdb-core pull request "Optimizations for volumerender and move its autograd layer to Python". It was designed to address the performance bottleneck of the volumerender stage, which previously accounted for 60.7% of the total runtime. The technique builds on standard GPU programming principles that use per-thread registers to minimize global memory accesses. name: GPU Ray Casting for Light Field Display
head: Direct Volume Rendering on Light Field Display, Interactive Light Field Volume Rendering, MCOP Ray Casting with Adaptive Mipmap Level Selection, MCOP projection, Multi-viewer 3D Volume Rendering
body: This method implements direct volume rendering on an interactive light field display by computing rays from projector positions through screen pixels into the volume using Multi-Camera Optical Projection (MCOP). It solves the problem of incorrect per-pixel ray parameter values caused by standard vertex attribute interpolation in non-linear projections, ensuring a fully continuous perceived image for multiple viewers. Unlike traditional multiview technologies that force users into fixed positions due to abrupt view changes, this approach provides smooth parallax and accommodation cues. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume texture: A single 4-component 3D texture where RGB channels store the unscaled precomputed gradient and the A channel stores the voxel value. LUT: A 1D RGBA texture containing an interactively modifiable look-up table. Uniforms: Projector position Ew (float3), Virtual observer distance Vd (float), Virtual observer height Vh (float), \log2 V (float, log2 of voxel size), DL (float, step size), S0 (float, screen pixel size), \tan \Phi (float, angular spread factor), a{max} (float, opacity termination threshold). Matrices: OpenGL model-view matrix and its inverse. Outputs: Fragment color and opacity (float4). Data Structures: The method uses the following structures: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. org = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) dir = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) length = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Steps: 1. Proxy Geometry Setup: Render a coarsely tessellated proxy geometry (8x8 quads) of a slightly enlarged bounding volume. This avoids the interpolation errors inherent in standard fixed-function pipelines for MCOP projections. 2. Vertex Shader Projection: In the vertex shader, perform MCOP projection on the proxy vertices. Pass both normalized and unnormalized projected coordinates to the fragment stage. 3. Ray Origin Computation: In the fragment shader, receive the unnormalized projected position S from the vertex stage. S represents the screen pixel’s position in the display reference frame. 4. Ray Direction Calculation: Compute the ray direction d passing through point S using the MCOP projection parameterized by emitter E and virtual viewer parameters V: d = \left[ \frac{Sx - Ex}{Ez}, \frac{Sy - Vy}{Vz}, -1 \right] Note: The source code in Appendix A of uses a simplified calculation for rayd based on Ew, Vd, Vh and pixel coordinates x,y: \text{ray\d} = \left[ -\frac{E{w,x} - x}{E{w,z}}, \frac{Vh - y}{Vd}, -1, 0 \right] 5. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the infinite ray defined by S and d into local volume coordinates (coincident with texture coordinates) by applying the world-to-texture homogeneous transform matrix (inverse model-view matrix). 6. Ray Clipping and Validation: Clip the line against the unit box to compute the ray entry point and integration lengths. If the ray length is null (or less than epsilon), discard the fragment as invalid. 7. Ray Marching Loop: Step through the ray in a loop, performing volume resampling and compositing until the volume is exited or full opacity is reached. 8. Mipmap Level Selection: At each sampling step, compute the depth z of the current sample by transforming its position in texture space to world (screen-aligned) space using a single dot product. Compute the mipmap level l using the equation: l = \text{median}\left(0, L{max}, \left\lfloor \log2 \frac{s(z)}{v0} \right\rfloor \right) Where s(z) is the variable step-size, L{max} is the maximum available mipmap level, and v0 is the voxel size at the finest mipmap level. The implementation uses a derived formula: \text{mipmap\l} = \log2(S0 + 2 \cdot \tan \Phi \cdot z) - \log2 V 9. Texture Sampling: Access the volume texture using the tex3Dlod intrinsic (or equivalent) with the computed mipmap level. 10. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. 11. Transfer Function: Apply the transfer function and shading to get color Ci and opacity \alphai. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode is derived from Appendix A of. All helper functions are defined inline to ensure self-containment. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math Ew = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Projector position Vd = 0.0 # Virtual observer distance Vh = 0.0 # Virtual observer height log2V = 0.0 # log2 voxel size DL = 0.0 # stepsize S0 = 0.0 # screen pixel size tanPhi = 0.0 # angular spread factor amax = 1.0 # opacity termination threshold def normalize(v): """Standard vector normalization.""" mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if mag == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def mulvec(mat, vec): """Matrix-vector multiplication for 4x4 matrix and 4D vector.""" return ( mat[0][0]vec[0] + mat[0][1]vec[1] + mat[0][2]vec[2] + mat[0][3]vec[3], mat[1][0]vec[0] + mat[1][1]vec[1] + mat[1][2]vec[2] + mat[1][3]vec[3], mat[2][0]vec[0] + mat[2][1]vec[1] + mat[2][2]vec[2] + mat[2][3]vec[3], mat[3][0]vec[0] + mat[3][1]vec[1] + mat[3][2]vec[2] + mat[3][3]vec[3]) def cliptounitbox(origin, direction): """Standard slab method to clip ray to unit box.""" tmin = -1e9 tmax = 1e9 for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0.0: if origin[i] < 0.0 or origin[i] > 1.0: return (0.0, 0.0) else: t1 = (0.0 - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (1.0 - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return (0.0, 0.0) return (tmin, tmax) def mipmapvalue(uvw, level): """3D texture sampling with explicit LOD.""" # Uses tex3Dlod intrinsic return texture3D(uvw, level) def rayatxy(x, y, mvinv): """Compute ray passing through pixel in world coords.""" rayo = (x, y, 0.0, 0.0) rayd = (-(Ew[0] - a) Ci[0], I[1] + (1.0 - a) Ci[1], I[2] + (1.0 - a) Ci[2]) a = a + (1.0 - a) ai # Step along ray uvw = (uvw[0] + deltadir[0], uvw[1] + deltadir[1], uvw[2] + deltadir[2]) return (I[0], I[1], I[2], a) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertex Attribute Interpolation Error: Standard vertex attribute interpolation does not produce correct per-pixel ray parameter values for MCOP. This is mitigated by using the proxy geometry and computing projections in the vertex shader. Tile Misalignment Artifacts: On the specific hardware (96 projectors updated in batches of 16), misalignment between tiles can become visible if objects are moved with a slow refresh rate. Out of Bounds: If the clipped ray length is null or less than epsilon, the fragment is discarded. Performance: At full resolution (1 ray/pixel, 1 sample/voxel), millions of rays require hundreds of steps, limiting interactive frame rates. The method suggests lowering sampling rate during interaction by reducing pixel count (2.5mm precision) and doubling the integration step-size. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays (pixels). The number of samples N is determined by the ray length divided by the step size DL. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D volume texture (4-component) and the 1D LUT. Measured Performance: The method was demonstrated on a display with 96 projectors. Performance was limited by single GPU volume renderer performance at full resolution, necessitating reduced sampling rates for interactivity. Strengths: Provides a fully continuous perceived image for multiple viewers, unlike discrete multiview systems. Supports parallax, accommodation, and stereo cues. Limitations: Requires a specific light field display hardware setup. Tile misalignment artifacts can occur with slow refresh rates. When to use: Interactive direct volume rendering on multi-viewer light field displays where continuous viewing zones are required. When not to use: Standard single-viewer rendering or displays without light field capabilities. Origin: The method was introduced by Agus et al. in 2008. History: It was developed to address the limitations of contemporary multiview technologies that forced users into fixed positions due to abrupt view-image changes. The approach builds on GPU-accelerated ray casting techniques and MCOP projection models. Usage: Used for interactive light field volume rendering, allowing users to manipulate objects with 6-DOF trackers and modify transfer functions while maintaining multi-user capability.
