name: Planes Method
head: Compositing on the CPU, RealityEngine Volume Rendering with CPU Compositing
body: The Planes Method is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that leverages 3D texture mapping hardware to resample volumetric data into planes coplanar with rays ending in a row of pixels, then performs shading and front-to-back compositing on the CPU. It solves the problem of view-dependent shading and interactive classification in texture-mapped rendering by offloading the computationally intensive Phong shading and compositing logic to the processor, allowing for optimization techniques like early ray termination and low-opacity skipping. Unlike Shear-Warp, which performs classification before bilinear resampling and requires a final warp step, the Planes method performs trilinear interpolation followed by classification and requires no final warp, resulting in higher image quality and consistent performance for perspective projections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset where each voxel consists of four 8-bit values: three gradient components (Gx, Gy, Gz) and raw density (\rho). Input: A viewing volume defined by parallel or perspective projection parameters. Input: Transfer functions for opacity and reflectance (Phong shading parameters). Output: A 2D image frame buffer with composited color and opacity values. Data Structures: The voxel data is loaded into an RGB-type 3D texture map. Although the texture format is RGB, the fields store three gradient values and raw density. The gradients are precomputed offline using high-quality Sobel operators. Algorithm Steps: The method utilizes a master-slave parallel architecture on symmetric multi-processor (SMP) systems, where the master handles texture mapping and slaves handle raycasting. The core rendering loop processes scanlines sequentially but interlaces CPU and GPU work. 1. Preprocessing: Compute Sobel gradients for the volume offline. Load the gradient/density data into the 3D texture map. 2. Initialization: Load the texture rotation matrix corresponding to the current view. 3. First Plane Resampling: Resample the first plane of orthogonal rays into the frame buffer using 3D texture mapping hardware. 4. Memory Transfer: Read the first plane from the frame buffer into main memory. 5. Scanline Loop: For each remaining scanline y: a. Resample: Resample the next plane of orthogonal rays into the frame buffer. b. Column Loop: For each column x in the previous plane (which corresponds to a ray): i. Initialize: Set integration variables (accumulated color C{acc}=0, accumulated opacity A{acc}=0). ii. Ray Marching Loop: While the sample position is within bounds and the ray is not opaque (A{acc} < 1.0): 1. Sample: Retrieve density \rho and gradients \mathbf{G} from the resampled plane data at the current sample position. The hardware performs trilinear interpolation of these values. 2. Opacity Lookup: Lookup opacity \alpha in the transfer function using \rho. 3. Skip Check: If \alpha is below a threshold, skip shading and compositing for this sample (space leaping). 4. Shading: If \alpha > threshold, lookup shade in reflectance map to generate Phong shaded RGB. 5. Composite: Update accumulated color and opacity using front-to-back compositing: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - A{acc}) A{acc} = A{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - A{acc}) 6. Early Termination: If A{acc} \ge 1.0, terminate the ray marching loop (early ray termination). iii. Store: Store ray color in previous row of image. c. Next Plane: Read next plane from frame buffer into memory. 6. Final Plane: Shade and composite final plane as above. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planesmethod(volumetexture, viewmatrix, opacityfunc, reflectancefunc, imagewidth, imageheight, numsamples, opacitythreshold): # Precomputed gradients are in volumetexture as RGB (Gx, Gy, Gz) + Density # Load texture rotation matrix texturerotation = viewmatrix # Resample first plane into frame buffer resampleplaneintoframebuffer(0, texturerotation) # Read first plane from frame buffer into memory planedata = readframebuffertomemory(0) # Loop over all remaining scanlines for y in range(1, imageheight): # Interlace: Initiate texture mapping for next scanline initiatetexturemapping(y + 1, texturerotation) # Resample next plane into frame buffer resampleplaneintoframebuffer(y, texturerotation) # Loop over all columns in the previous plane for x in range(imagewidth): # Initialize integration variables acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 # While within bounds and ray not opaque for s in range(numsamples): # Get sample data from currentplanedata at column x, sample s density = planedata[x, s, 3] gradients = planedata[x, s,:3] # Lookup opacity in transfer function alpha = opacityfunc(density) # If sample opacity > threshold: Lookup shade in reflectance map if alpha > opacitythreshold: samplecolor = reflectancefunc(gradients, viewmatrix) else: samplecolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Composite ray color OVER sample weight = alpha (1.0 - accopacity) acccolor[0] += samplecolor[0] weight acccolor[1] += samplecolor[1] weight acccolor[2] += samplecolor[2] weight accopacity += weight # Early ray termination (ray not opaque) if accopacity >= 1.0: break # Store ray color in previous row of image setpixelcolor(x, y, acccolor) # Read next plane from frame buffer into memory planedata = readframebuffertomemory(y) # Shade and composite final plane as above def loadtexturerotationmatrix(matrix): # Loads the view matrix into the 3D texture mapping hardware's rotation register pass def resampleplaneintoframebuffer(scanlineidx, rotationmatrix): # Forwards a polygon coplanar with rays ending in a row of pixels to the graphics pipeline. # Hardware performs trilinear interpolation of the 3D texture map and writes to frame buffer pass def readframebuffertomemory(scanlineidx): # Reads the resampled plane data from the frame buffer into main memory as a 2D array [width, samples, 4] pass def initiatetexturemapping(scanlineidx, rotationmatrix): # Queues the texture mapping calculation for the next scanline to interleave CPU and GPU work pass def setpixelcolor(x, y, color): # Writes the accumulated color to the image buffer at pixel coordinates (x, y) pass def reflectancemap(gradients, viewmatrix): # Computes Phong shaded RGB using the interpolated gradients and view parameters pass Parameters: Opacity Threshold: A value below which shading and compositing are skipped. Gradient Computation: High-quality Sobel gradients are computed serially offline. Hardware: Onyx 2 workstation with Infinite Reality graphics. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Memory Limits: The volume size is limited by available texture memory due to storing gradients, causing texture paging for large volumes. Sequential Bottleneck: The parallel speedup is limited by the time it takes to perform texture mapping for all planes, which must be performed sequentially because there is only one graphics pipeline. Precision: The method relies on 3D texture mapping hardware for interpolation. The sources state that assuming a piecewise linear gradient function, this method produces the same gradient values at sample locations as if gradients were computed at unit voxel distances from the sample point. This method renders regular volumetric grids by leveraging 3D texture mapping hardware to resample density and pre-computed gradients, then transferring the raw sample data to main memory for CPU-based Phong shading and compositing. It solves the problem of view-dependent shading in texture-mapped rendering by avoiding the need to re-shade and reload textures for every frame change, and by circumventing the infeasibly large lookup tables required by post-texturing gradient indexing. Unlike the Planes Method, which may rely on hardware blending for final compositing without explicit CPU shading, this method explicitly offloads the lighting calculation to the CPU to support arbitrary dynamic lights and non-linear transfer functions without hardware interpolation artifacts. Image-Parallel Ray Casting via 2D Texture Mapping is an object-space volume rendering technique that accelerates direct volume rendering by projecting parallel slices of volumetric data onto the image plane and compositing them using graphics hardware rasterization and blending. It replaces standard ray casting by treating the volume as a stack of 2D texture-mapped rectangles, leveraging hardware-accelerated texture sampling and alpha blending to achieve rendering speeds dependent only on image size rather than scene complexity. Unlike its sibling Texture-Mapped Volume Rendering with CPU Shading, this method performs the compositing entirely within the GPU pipeline using standard blending operators. Time Complexity: The rendering time is dominated by the texture mapping operations (sequential) and the CPU-based raycasting/compositing (parallelizable). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the volume data in 3D texture memory. Measured Performance: CT scanned Head dataset (bone structures) at 200x200 resolution: 0.44 seconds. Lobster dataset (sampling resolution 512x512x64): 1.88 seconds. Opaque Sphere dataset: 1.84 seconds. Translucent Lobster dataset: 2.78 seconds (12 times faster than Sommer et al.). 128x128 image of Opaque Sphere with 84 samples per ray: 0.19 seconds. Lobster dataset (128x128 image, 84 samples per ray): 0.24 seconds. Time to perform texture mapping of 128x128x84 planes: 0.12 seconds. Strengths: Supports arbitrary parallel and perspective projections in the same time (unlike Shear-Warp). No final warp step required, removing a filtering step and resulting in higher image quality. Supports interactive segmentation/classification (unlike Shear-Warp which requires multiple copies of compressed data structures). Allows for CPU-based optimizations like early ray termination and low-opacity skipping. Produces high-quality Phong shading with specular highlights. Limitations: The parallel speedup is bounded by the time required for sequential texture mapping Tt, as there is only one graphics pipeline. Limited by available texture memory for large volumes. Slower than methods that do not employ directional shading (e.g., Cabral et al.). When to use: When high-quality view-dependent shading (Phong) is required, interactive classification is needed, or perspective projections are used, and hardware supports 3D texture mapping. When not to use: When maximum frame rate is critical and shading quality is secondary, or when the volume size exceeds available texture memory. The Planes Method was developed for use on Silicon Graphics Onyx 2 workstations with Infinite Reality graphics hardware. It was presented as an alternative to shear-warp and other texture-mapped methods to achieve high-quality, accurately shaded volume rendering at interactive frame rates. The method builds on the concept of using 3D texture mapping hardware for resampling but diverges by performing the compositing and shading on the CPU to leverage software optimizations. name: Texture-Mapped Volume Rendering with CPU Shading
head: Hardware resampling with software shading, Our architecture
body: This method renders regular volumetric grids by leveraging 3D texture mapping hardware to resample density and pre-computed gradients, then transferring the raw sample data to main memory for CPU-based Phong shading and compositing. It solves the problem of view-dependent shading in texture-mapped rendering by avoiding the need to re-shade and reload textures for every frame change, and by circumventing the infeasibly large lookup tables required by post-texturing gradient indexing. Unlike Planes Method, which may rely on hardware blending for final compositing without explicit CPU shading, this method explicitly offloads the lighting calculation to the CPU to support arbitrary dynamic lights and non-linear transfer functions without hardware interpolation artifacts. Inputs: A regular 3D volume grid of density values D. Pre-computed gradients \nabla D for each voxel. Camera parameters (view direction, projection type). Lighting parameters (light position, color, material properties for Phong shading). Transfer function parameters (mapping density to opacity \alpha). Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity from the volume. Data Structures: 1. Texture Memory: A 3D texture object storing density values and their corresponding gradients. Layout: Stored as a solid texture in graphics hardware texture memory. The source notes specify 32-bits per voxel for density storage in the context of memory capacity. 2. Sample Buffer: A buffer in main memory (CPU-accessible) to store the resampled density and gradient values for each sample point along each ray. 3. Frame Buffer: Standard display buffer for final image output. Steps: 1. Load Data: Store the volume density and pre-computed gradients into the graphics hardware's 3D texture memory. This is done once per volume dataset, not per frame. 2. Resample: Use hardware texture interpolation to resample the 3D texture by rendering planes parallel to the image plane (or along rays) through the volume. The hardware interpolates the density and gradient values at the sample points defined by the ray casting geometry. 3. Transfer: Read back the resampled sample data (density and gradient values) from the texture memory into a buffer in main memory. 4. Shade: For each sample point in the buffer, compute the shading on the CPU. Estimate the surface normal \mathbf{n} from the interpolated gradient \nabla D. Map the density value to opacity \alpha using the transfer function. Apply the full Phong lighting equation using the estimated normal, light direction, view direction, and material properties. 5. Composite: Composite the shaded samples along each ray into a final image color using back-to-front compositing, either in main memory or via frame buffer blending hardware. Formulas: Phong Shading: The intensity I at a sample point is calculated as: I = Ia ka + \sum{j} I{lj} \left( kd (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}j) + ks (\mathbf{r}j \cdot \mathbf{v})^{\alpha{spec}} \right) Where: Ia is ambient light intensity, ka is ambient reflectivity. I{lj} is the intensity of the j-th light, \mathbf{l}j is the light direction vector. kd is diffuse reflectivity. ks is specular reflectivity, \alpha{spec} is the specular exponent. \mathbf{n} is the surface normal (derived from gradient). \mathbf{r}j is the reflection vector of the light. \mathbf{v} is the view direction vector. The source explicitly states a "full Phong lighting equation" is used for software classification and shading. The standard equation is provided here as a standard implementation gap. Compositing (Back-to-Front): C{out} = C{in} (1 - \alpha{sample}) + C{sample} \alpha{sample} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} (1 - \alpha{sample}) + \alpha{sample} Where C{sample} is the shaded color and \alpha{sample} is the opacity derived from the transfer function. Parameters: Texture Memory Size: Typical high-end graphics systems have 64 MB of texture memory, which can hold volumes up to 256^3 with 32-bits per voxel. Sampling Rate: Determined by the image size and number of samples along each ray. The source notes that 64 sampling planes were used for 512 \times 512 windows in performance tests. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation Artifacts: If RGB values are interpolated by texture hardware directly (as in traditional architectures), non-linear mappings from density to RGB produce incorrect interpolated samples. This method avoids this by interpolating raw density and gradients, then applying non-linear shading in software. Memory Limits: The volume data must fit in the texture memory of the graphics system. If the volume is larger than physical texture memory, hardware paging may be used, but performance may degrade. Gradient Storage: The method requires pre-computed gradients for each voxel, which are stored in the texture and interpolated by hardware. Time Complexity: The rendering time is dominated by the texture resampling (hardware accelerated) and the CPU shading/compositing. On a four Raster Manager SGI RealityEngine Onyx with one 150MHz CPU, a 512 \times 512 \times 64 volume rendered into a 512 \times 512 window in 0.1 seconds. Memory Complexity: Requires texture memory proportional to the volume size (N^3 voxels). Typical limit is 64 MB for 256^3 volumes. Strengths: Supports arbitrary and dynamically changing directional lights and viewing parameters without re-loading textures. Avoids incorrect interpolation artifacts from non-linear transfer functions by shading in software. Avoids the infeasibly large lookup tables required by post-texturing LUTs. Limitations: Requires transferring sample data from texture memory to main memory, which can be a bottleneck if the bandwidth is low. Limited by the physical texture memory size of the graphics hardware. When to use: When high-quality view-dependent shading is required, and the hardware supports 3D texture mapping but lacks sufficient post-texturing LUT capabilities or when dynamic lighting changes make pre-shading impractical. Suitable for SGI Reality Engine and Onyx workstations. This method was presented by Frank Dachille, Kevin Kreeger, Baoquan Chen, Ingmar Bitter, and Arie Kaufman from the Center for Visual Computing (CVC) and Department of Computer Science at the State University of New York at Stony Brook. It builds on the idea of using 3D texture mapping hardware for volume rendering, first mentioned by Akeley on the SGI Reality Engine. The method addresses limitations of traditional texture-mapped volume rendering architectures, such as the need to re-shade and reload textures for every view change, and the inaccuracies of hardware-interpolating RGB values with non-linear transfer functions. It is an alternative to Van Gelder and Kim's "Ideal architecture" which uses a post-texturing LUT indexed by gradient, which requires an infeasibly large LUT size. The method was used on SGI Reality Engine and Onyx workstations with Raster Manager. High-Quality Volume Rendering Using Texture Mapping Hardware, https://cfcs.pku.edu.cn/baoquan/docs/20180622110034067331.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Image-Parallel Ray Casting via 2D Texture Mapping
head: 2D Texture-Mapped Volume Rendering, 2D Texture Mapping Volume Rendering, Texture-Mapped Volume Rendering (2D), 2D Texture Slicing, 2D texture slice rendering
body: Image-Parallel Ray Casting via 2D Texture Mapping is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that replaces per-ray traversal with the projection of parallel object-aligned slices onto the image plane, leveraging graphics hardware rasterization and blending. It solves the performance bottleneck of software ray casting by projecting slices slice-by-slice, making it particularly effective for large volumetric datasets where 3D texture memory bandwidth becomes a limiting factor. Unlike its sibling Texture-Mapped Volume Rendering with CPU Shading, which offloads shading to the CPU, this method performs shading and compositing within the GPU's fragment shader and blending units. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset V of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Output: A 2D image buffer containing the composited volume rendering. Data Structures: Texture Memory: Three 2D textures, each of size Dx \times Dy, Dy \times Dz, and Dx \times Dz respectively, storing one copy of the volume for each slicing direction. Gradient Storage: Pre-computed gradients are stored in the RGB channels of the texture to allow bi-linear interpolation in screen space. Polygon Geometry: Each slice is represented by a proxy polygon covering the extent of the slice in screen space, as there are no volumetric primitives in graphics hardware. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Slicing Direction (Base Plane): Compute the viewing direction vector \vec{v}. Calculate the angle between \vec{v} and the three primary axes of the volume data (normals \vec{n}x, \vec{n}y, \vec{n}z). Select the axis with the minimum angle to the viewing direction as the "base plane" normal. This determines which of the three texture stacks to use. In case of a tie at 45 degrees, an arbitrary choice is made. 2. Generate Slice Stack: Define a set of parallel planes orthogonal to the viewing direction. Pre-computed Slices: If slices are pre-computed orthogonal to a primary axis, they are stored as 2D textures. For arbitrary viewpoints, these must be re-projected, which distorts the slice views. View-Aligned Slices: For optimal quality, slices are generated orthogonal to the viewing direction for each frame. These slices may have complex shapes (triangles to hexagons) and require regeneration every frame. Interpolation: To mitigate aliasing and popping artifacts, additional intermediate slices may be interpolated and shifted such that sample spacing along viewing rays is practically constant, independent of viewing direction. 3. Project and Rasterize Slices: For each slice in the stack: Project the slice polygon onto the image plane. Assign texture coordinates (s, t) to the polygon vertices corresponding to the 2D volume slice. Rasterize the polygon. The graphics hardware performs bi-linear interpolation of the texture values (scalar field and pre-computed gradients) for each covered pixel. Gradient Normalization: In the fragment shader, normalize the interpolated gradients to ensure high image quality during shading. 4. Shading and Classification: For each pixel covered by the slice: Retrieve the interpolated scalar value and gradient. Apply the transfer function to compute color C and opacity \alpha. Classification can occur pre- or post-interpolation. Opacity Correction: Scale the opacity linearly according to the distance between samples to approximate the integration along the ray. 5. Compositing: Blend the slice onto the image plane using the standard front-to-back or back-to-front compositing operator provided by the graphics hardware. C{out} = C{in} \cdot (1 - \alpha{slice}) + C{slice} \cdot \alpha{slice} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} \cdot (1 - \alpha{slice}) + \alpha{slice} The method is exactly equivalent to standard ray casting unless precision is lost due to integer arithmetics in the compositing step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderimageparallel2dtexture(volumedata, viewdirection, imagewidth, imageheight): # Handle list input to avoid AttributeError on.shape if isinstance(volumedata, list): Dz, Dy, Dx = len(volumedata), len(volumedata[0]), len(volumedata[0][0]) else: Dz, Dy, Dx = volumedata.shape # 1. Determine base plane axis vx, vy, vz = viewdirection norm = (vx2 + vy2 + vz2)0.5 vx, vy, vz = vx/norm, vy/norm, vz/norm cosx, cosy, cosz = abs(vx), abs(vy), abs(vz) if cosx >= cosy and cosx >= cosz: baseaxis = 'x' elif cosy >= cosx and cosy >= cosz: baseaxis = 'y' else: baseaxis = 'z' # 2. Prepare texture stacks # Three 2D textures are stored in memory, one for each slicing direction # Pre-compute gradients and store in RGB channels gradients = computegradients(volumedata) # 3. Generate slice stack # Determine number of slices N based on volume depth and desired sample spacing # Interpolate in-between slices to eliminate popping artifacts slices = generateslicestack(volumedata, viewdirection, baseaxis, imagewidth, imageheight) # 4. Render loop framebuffer = [{'color': (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 'alpha': 0.0} for in range(imagewidth imageheight)] for slicedata in slices: # Project slice polygon to screen space screencoords = projecttoscreen(slicedata.polygon, viewdirection, imagewidth, imageheight) # Rasterize and interpolate # Hardware performs bi-linear interpolation of texture values for i, j in screencoords: scalarval = sampletexture(slicedata.texture, slicedata.u, slicedata.v) grad = gradients[slicedata.u, slicedata.v] grad = normalizevector(grad) # Fragment shader normalization color, alpha = applytransferfunction(scalarval, grad) alpha = alpha slicedata.sampledistance # Opacity correction # Composite onto framebuffer using hardware blending framebuffer = blendslice(framebuffer, i, j, color, alpha, imagewidth) return framebuffer def computegradients(vol): # Pre-compute gradients for RGB channel storage Dz, Dy, Dx = len(vol), len(vol[0]), len(vol[0][0]) return [[[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(Dx)] for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dz)] def generateslicestack(vol, viewdir, axis, w, h): # Generate parallel planes orthogonal to viewing direction # Return list of slice objects with polygon, texture ref, u, v, sampledistance return [] def projecttoscreen(polygon, viewdir, w, h): # Map 3D polygon vertices to 2D screen coordinates return [(i, j) for i in range(w) for j in range(h)] def sampletexture(tex, u, v): # Bi-linear interpolation of 2D texture return 0.0 def normalizevector(v): n = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[0]/n, v[1]/n, v[2]/n] if n > 0 else v def applytransferfunction(scalar, grad): # Compute color and opacity from scalar and gradient return (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), 0.1 def blendslice(fb, i, j, color, alpha, imgw): # Front-to-back or back-to-front compositing idx = i + j imgw fb[idx]['color'] = tuple(c1 (1 - a2) + c2 a2 for c1, c2 in zip(fb[idx]['color'], color)) fb[idx]['alpha'] = fb[idx]['alpha'] (1 - alpha) + alpha return fb Parameters and Edge Cases: Sample Spacing: Must be chosen to balance performance and quality. Too large causes aliasing; too small wastes bandwidth. View Direction Parallel to Slices: If the view direction is parallel to the primary axes of pre-computed slices, the projection distorts the slice views, degrading image quality. In the extreme case where the view direction is parallel to the slices, no image is generated. Aliasing: Lack of interpolation between slices may lead to aliasing artifacts if the scalar field or transfer functions contain high frequencies. Popping Artifacts: Sudden changes in slicing direction can cause popping. This is worse for anisotropic data. Interpolating in-between slices mitigates this. This method renders deformed volumetric data, specifically video volumes bent into a horseshoe shape, by distorting texture coordinates rather than geometry. It enables the use of standard planar, view-aligned texture slicing (as described in Image-Parallel Ray Casting via 2D Texture Mapping) on non-planar data by computing inverse mappings in the fragment shader. Unlike forward mapping, it avoids gaps and overlaps inherent in geometry deformation, ensuring every pixel is covered by a valid texture lookup. Time Complexity: Rendering speed depends only on image size, not scene complexity. It is generally faster than software ray casting for large volumes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing three copies of the volume in texture memory (one for each slicing direction). Performance: 2D texture slicing outperforms 3D texture slicing for large volumes due to coherent memory accesses and higher performance of bi-linear interpolation compared to tri-linear. Performance factors include software sampling rate, texture download rate, and polygon scan conversion rate. Strengths: Simple implementation, leverages standard graphics hardware, fast rendering of large datasets, no complex geometric models required. Limitations: Lower image quality compared to 3D texture mapping if only trilinear interpolation is used on 3D data. Distortion artifacts if pre-computed slices are used for arbitrary viewpoints. Popping artifacts when switching slicing directions. When to Use: Large volumetric datasets where interactive frame rates are required and 3D texture memory is insufficient or too slow. When Not to Use: When high image quality is critical and 3D texture mapping is available, or when the view direction is frequently parallel to the primary axes of pre-computed slices. The method originated as a solution to the lack of 3D texture mapping hardware in early graphics pipelines. Historically, it was used when 3D texture mapping was unavailable and remains relevant today for large volumes due to its performance characteristics. The approach was formalized by Cullip and Neumann (1993), Guan and Lipes (1994), and Cabral et al. (1994). Rezk-Salama et al. (2000) improved the method by addressing popping artifacts and opacity correction. name: Distorted Video Volumes (Horseshoe Mapping)
head: Backward-mapping for deformed volumes, Horseshoe Volume Rendering
body: This method renders deformed volumetric data, specifically video volumes bent into a horseshoe shape, by distorting texture coordinates rather than geometry. It enables the use of standard planar, view-aligned texture slicing (as described in Image-Parallel Ray Casting via 2D Texture Mapping) on non-planar data by computing inverse mappings in the fragment shader. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A video volume V consisting of N consecutive 2D frames Ii, conceptually divided into bricks Bk for rendering. Input: Rendering parameters: inner radius r{min}, outer radius r{max}, y-scaling factor ys, and a scale/offset vector g{vScaleCrd} for temporal mapping. Input: Fragment shader input TextureCoord0 representing the physical position (xP, yP, zP) on the slice plane. Output: Texture coordinates (xC, yC, tC) in computation space C, used to sample the video volume. Data Structures: Video Volume V: Array of 2D images. Parameters: r{min}, r{max}: Floats defining the radial range of the horseshoe. ys: Float scaling the vertical dimension. g{vScaleCrd}: Vector (\text{offset}, \text{scale}) for temporal coordinate adjustment. Transformation Formulas: The mapping from Computation Space C (where xC, yC, tC \in [0, 1]) to Physical Space P (where the slice lies) is defined by cylindrical coordinates: \begin{aligned} xP &= -r \cos(\pi tC) \\ yP &= ys yC \\ zP &= r \sin(\pi tC) \end{aligned} where the radius r varies linearly with xC: r = r{min} + \Delta r xC, \quad \Delta r = r{max} - r{min} The inverse mapping (Physical P to Computation C) is required for backward mapping: 1. Compute radius rp and angle \theta from xP, zP: rp = \sqrt{xP^2 + zP^2}, \quad \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(zP, xP) 2. Compute xC: xC = \frac{rp - r{min}}{r{max} - r{min}} 3. Compute yC: yC = \frac{yP}{ys} 4. Compute tC: tC = \left(\frac{\theta}{\pi} - \text{offset}\right) \times \text{scale} where \text{offset} and \text{scale} are the components of g{vScaleCrd}. The angle \theta ranges from (-\pi, \pi], and the linear transform maps this range to the desired temporal coordinate range. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the inverse mapping within a fragment program, matching the source HLSL snippet. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. txCrdx = ((txCrd.x 2.0) - 1.0) (-1.0) rpx = sqrt(txCrdx txCrdx + txCrd.z txCrd.z) rpy = atan2(txCrd.z, txCrdx) lkupx = (rpx - gfInRad) / (gfOutRad - gfInRad) lkupy = txCrd.y / ys # Source code omits division, assuming ys=1 or pre-scaled input lkupz = ((rpy / PI) - gvScaleCrd.x) gvScaleCrd.y Parameters: r{min}, r{max}: Define the inner and outer radii of the horseshoe geometry. ys: Scaling factor for the y dimension. g{vScaleCrd}: Vector (\text{offset}, \text{scale}) applied to the normalized angle to compute the temporal coordinate tC. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Transformation: Since video volumes are typically unlit, the transformation of volume gradients for lighting calculations can be omitted. If shading is required, the Jacobian of the transformation must be applied to gradients. Angle Continuity: atan2 has a discontinuity at the branch cut. Ensure texture coordinates wrap correctly if the horseshoe is not a full circle or if interpolation artifacts are visible. Radius Bounds: If rp < r{min} or rp > r{max}, xC will be outside [0,1]. Clamp or handle out-of-bounds sampling. Opaque flow geometry (arrows, lines) can be added to the scene to visualize optical flow fields alongside the distorted volume. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment for the coordinate transformation. The cost is dominated by the texture lookup and compositing from the parent method. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for temporary variables in the shader. Strengths: No geometric deformation overhead; compatible with standard hardware texture mapping; handles complex deformations like horseshoes easily. Limitations: Requires inverse mapping functions (atan2, sqrt) which may be slightly more expensive than linear transforms, though negligible on modern GPUs. Not suitable for lighting without gradient transformation. The method was introduced by Botchen, Chen, Weiskopf, and Ertl in their work on GPU-assisted multi-field video volume visualization. It builds on the concept of backward mapping for deformed volumes proposed by Ropinski et al. [RSSSG01], adapting it for video data rendered via texture slicing. GPU-assisted Multi-field Video Volume Visualization, https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/b3eb5a9069e8d00fa52149b0ff85554801f0f917, fetched 2026-11-04 (unofficial)

name: 3D Pixel Texture Classification
head: VGH Lookup
body: 3D Pixel Texture Classification maps three voxel attributes (Data Value, Gradient Magnitude, and Second Derivative) to color and opacity by storing the classification function in a 3D pixel texture. It differs from lower-dimensional lookup tables by explicitly incorporating curvature information via a specialized "sheet" representation for the signed second derivative axis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume samples containing Data Value (D), Gradient Magnitude (G), and Second Derivative (S). Output: Color (C) and Opacity (\alpha) for the sample. Data Structures: A 3D pixel texture stores the transfer function. Axis 1 (Data Value): 8-bit resolution (256 entries). Axis 2 (Gradient Magnitude): 8-bit resolution (256 entries). Axis 3 (Second Derivative): Limited resolution representing "sheets" for specific second derivative values. Steps: 1. Attribute Computation: Compute D, G, and S for each sample point. 2. Sign Maintenance: Apply a scale and bias transformation to S to maintain its sign and map it to the texture coordinate range for proper interpolation. 3. Texture Lookup: Sample the 3D pixel texture using (D, G, S') as coordinates. 4. Sheet Representation: Structure the second derivative axis as three control points ("sheets") for negative, zero, and positive values. 5. Opacity Interpolation: Control the opacity on the center sheet (zero second derivative) directly via classification widgets, and scale the opacity on the outer sheets (positive/negative second derivative) from the center sheet opacity according to a boundary emphasis slider. Parameters: Resolution: 256 \times 256 \times N for the texture, where N is the number of second derivative control points (typically 3 sheets). Boundary Emphasis: A scalar parameter controlling the relative opacity scaling between outer and center sheets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifyvoxel(datavalue, gradientmagnitude, secondderivative, texture, boundaryemphasis, smin, smax): # 1. Scale and bias second derivative to maintain sign and fit texture coordinate range [0.0, 1.0] # Exact transformation formula is not provided in the sources. scoord = (secondderivative - smin) / (smax - smin) scoord = max(0.0, min(1.0, scoord)) # 2. Sample the 3D pixel texture # Data Value and Gradient Magnitude use full 8-bit resolution (0-255) # Second Derivative uses limited resolution (3 sheets) # Perform trilinear interpolation color, alpharaw = texture[datavalue, gradientmagnitude, scoord] # 3. Apply boundary emphasis scaling # Opacity on outer sheets is scaled from the center sheet opacity according to the boundary emphasis slider. # Exact modulation formula is not provided in the sources. alpha = alpharaw boundaryemphasis return color, alpha A technique included in a real-time raycaster built by Roettger et al. to exploit the intrinsically parallel nature of GPUs, along with volume clipping. It addresses the inefficiency of multi-pass rendering pipelines by using a single-pass framework. Memory: The 3D texture size is 256 \times 256 \times N. Full 8-bit resolution on all three axes (256^3 entries) would be prohibitively expensive, so the second derivative axis resolution is limited. Performance: Performance relies on hardware-accelerated 3D texture sampling. Limitations: The second derivative axis uses limited resolution, as the method prioritizes zero-crossing detection over high-fidelity curvature representation. The method was described in the context of interactive volume rendering using multi-dimensional transfer functions. It leverages the capabilities of 3D pixel textures available in graphics hardware at the time of publication. name: Hardware Shading via Pixel Texture
head: Quantized Normal Shading, Volume Ray Tracing via 2D Texture Packing
body: Hardware Shading via Pixel Texture is a technique for adding lighting calculations to texture-memory based volume rendering, addressing the common limitation where such methods lack shading. It distinguishes itself from standard hardware interpolation by encoding surface normals into a 2D pixel texture and using nearest-neighbor lookups to avoid redundancy and truncation errors. This approach increases rendering quality with negligible cost by decoupling shading from the primary volume sampling pipeline. Inputs: Volume data consisting of density and radiance fields. View direction. Quantized normal data. Outputs: Shaded volume image. Data Structures: 2D Pixel Texture (Shading Texture): Stores lighting information and quantized normals. Quantized Normal Encoding: Format: 16-bit integer per normal vector. Channel Layout: The first 8 bits of the quantized normal are stored in the Red channel; the second 8 bits are stored in the Green channel. Interpolation Mode: Nearest-neighbor. Steps: 1. Volume Ray Tracing/Sampling: Pack all sample points into a 2D texture representation. Draw a quad of the same size as the texture to trigger the pixel shader. Perform volume ray tracing within the shader. Terminate ray tracing if the ray exits the volume. Note: If using ray marching with RBFs, intersect RBFs with slices perpendicular to the view direction, render slices far-to-near with alpha blending (GLONE, GLSRCALPHA), and retrieve density D(x) and source radiance Lx from 3D textures. Set RGB output to D(x)Lx and alpha to differential transmittance. 2. Normal Encoding: Encode surface normals using a 16-bit quantization scheme. Split the 16-bit value: assign the first 8 bits to the Red channel and the second 8 bits to the Green channel of the pixel texture. 3. Shading Lookup: Perform a nearest-neighbor lookup on the 2D pixel texture containing the quantized normals. Use nearest-neighbor interpolation specifically to avoid redundancy and truncation errors associated with standard hardware interpolation. 4. Lighting Calculation: Light the quantized normals using the 2D pixel texture. The process is equivalent to a 16-bit 1D nearest-neighbor pixel texture lookup or an 8-bit per-axis 2D nearest-neighbor texture lookup. Generate the shading pixel texture on a per-view basis in software. Formulas: Radiance Retrieval (if using RBF ray marching): \text{RGB} = D(x) Lx Where D(x) is density and Lx is source radiance retrieved from 3D textures. Normal Encoding: \text{Red} = \text{QuantizedNormal} \gg 8 \text{Green} = \text{QuantizedNormal} \ \& \ 0xFF Where >> is bitwise right shift and & is bitwise AND. Parameters: Quantization Bits: 16 bits per normal. Interpolation: Nearest-neighbor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation Artifacts: Using linear interpolation for normals causes redundancy and truncation errors; nearest-neighbor is required. Performance Cost: Generating the shading pixel texture per-view in software has minimal cost but could be performed in hardware. A variant that explicitly encodes surface normals into a 2D pixel texture to provide shading while avoiding redundancy and truncation errors. It uses a dedicated 2D texture lookup for lighting calculations. Choose this when high-quality shading is needed without interpolation artifacts. A technique for visualizing 3D vector fields by compositing semitransparent line segments. It builds on this method by extending the concept of splats to composite collections of antialiased lines in a back-to-front manner. Choose this for directional vector field visualization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The performance cost of generating the shading pixel texture is minimal. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Dramatically increases rendering quality with negligible cost; avoids interpolation artifacts for normals. Limitations: Previous work often lacked shading; requires per-view generation of shading texture (though minimal cost). When to use: When texture-memory based volume rendering requires shading without significant performance overhead. Originating from work on interactive volume rendering using multi-dimensional transfer functions, this method was introduced to address the lack of shading in texture-memory based volume rendering. It was developed to provide a natural and efficient way to express information about the shape of structures in the volume. The technique was implemented on hardware such as the Octane2 and GeForce3. name: Quantized Normal Shading via Pixel Texture
head: Quantized Normal Shading
body: Quantized Normal Shading via Pixel Texture is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that encodes surface normals into a 2D pixel texture to provide shading while avoiding the redundancy and truncation errors associated with standard hardware interpolation. It distinguishes itself from standard volume texture sampling by using a dedicated 2D texture lookup for lighting calculations, ensuring that the quantized normal data is retrieved without interpolation artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset containing multi-dimensional components (e.g., V, G, H) and a current view vector. Output: A shaded 2D image composited into the frame buffer. Data Structures: Shading Pixel Texture: A 2D texture where the red channel stores the first 8 bits of the quantized normal, and the green channel stores the second 8 bits. Scratch/Auxiliary Buffer: A temporary buffer used to render individual slices before they are composited into the final frame buffer. Quantization Scheme: Normals are quantized using a 16-bit scheme. The normal vector \mathbf{n} is mapped to a 16-bit integer index, which is then split into two 8-bit values: 1. First 8 bits \rightarrow Red channel (R) 2. Second 8 bits \rightarrow Green channel (G) Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate Shading Texture: For the current view direction, compute the quantized normals for all relevant data points and encode them into the 2D pixel texture. This is typically performed in software on a per-view basis. Alternatively, quantized normals can be rendered as points with hardware lighting and copied from the frame buffer to the pixel texture, though some hardware implementations lack the flexibility for this operation. 2. Render Slice to Scratch Buffer: Render the current slice of the volume data (using the appropriate transfer function components) into the scratch/auxiliary buffer. 3. Apply Shading via Pixel Texture: Use a glCopyPixels() operation to render the slice from the scratch buffer while applying the shading pixel texture. On hardware like the SGI Octane 2 with V-series cards, pixel texture lookup does not occur directly on a per-fragment basis during standard rasterization, necessitating this two-step buffer approach. Nearest-neighbor interpolation must be used for the pixel texture lookup to preserve the quantized normal values. 4. Composite: Blend the shaded slice from the scratch buffer into the main frame buffer, combining it with previously rendered slices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateshadingtexture(volumedata, viewvector): """ Encodes quantized normals into a 2D texture for the current view. """ texture = [[None for in range(volumedata.width)] for in range(volumedata.height)] for y in range(volumedata.height): for x in range(volumedata.width): normal = computesurfacenormal(volumedata, x, y, viewvector) quantizedindex = int(normal.x 32767 + 32768) & 0xFFFF redchannel = quantizedindex & 0xFF greenchannel = (quantizedindex >> 8) & 0xFF texture[y][x] = (redchannel, greenchannel, 0, 0) return texture def renderslicewithshading(volumedata, viewvector, framebuffer, scratchbuffer, shadingtexture): """ Renders a single slice with quantized normal shading and composites it. """ currentshadingtexture = generateshadingtexture(volumedata, viewvector) renderslicetobuffer(volumedata, scratchbuffer) for y in range(scratchbuffer.height): for x in range(scratchbuffer.width): shade = shadingtexture[y][x] applyshadingtopixel(scratchbuffer, x, y, shade) compositeslices(scratchbuffer, framebuffer) def computesurfacenormal(volumedata, x, y, viewvector): """Computes the surface normal at a data point using gradient estimation.""" dx = volumedata[x+1, y] - volumedata[x-1, y] dy = volumedata[x, y+1] - volumedata[x, y-1] dz = 0.0 length = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 return (dx/length, dy/length, dz/length) def renderslicetobuffer(volumedata, buffer): """Samples volume data and applies transfer function to fill buffer.""" for y in range(volumedata.height): for x in range(volumedata.width): value = volumedata[x, y] buffer[y][x] = applytransferfunction(value) def applyshadingtopixel(buffer, x, y, shade): """Modulates pixel color using nearest-neighbor pixel texture lookup.""" r, g, b, a = buffer[y][x] shader, shadeg,, = shade buffer[y][x] = (r shader / 255.0, g shadeg / 255.0, b, a) def compositeslices(scratchbuffer, framebuffer): """Blends scratch buffer contents into the frame buffer.""" for y in range(scratchbuffer.height): for x in range(scratchbuffer.width): s = scratchbuffer[y][x] f = framebuffer[y][x] framebuffer[y][x] = ( f[0] + s[0] s[3] / 255.0, f[1] + s[1] s[3] / 255.0, f[2] + s[2] s[3] / 255.0, f[3] + s[3] (1.0 - f[3] / 255.0)) Parameters: Quantization Bits: 16 bits total (8 bits per channel for R and G). Interpolation Mode: Nearest-neighbor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Flexibility: Some hardware implementations are not flexible enough to support rendering quantized normals as points with hardware lighting and copying them to a pixel texture. The authors currently generate the shading pixel texture on a per-view basis in software, noting it could easily be performed in hardware as well. Rasterization Limitations: On certain architectures (e.g., SGI Octane 2), pixel texture lookup is not available during standard per-fragment rasterization, necessitating the use of an auxiliary buffer and glCopyPixels(). Performance Cost: Generating the shading pixel texture on a per-view basis in software has a minimal performance cost. A lighting method using texture-shader features (e.g., Nvidia GeForce 3) where the normal vector at each point is encoded in the three color values of an RGB texture. The GeForce 3 interpolates these values for each pixel, computes the dot product with the current view vector, and uses the result as a lookup into a texture that encodes a reflection map. This method provides better precision than the normal index method but costs more memory. A hardware lighting method encoding normal information in a separate set of textures. It encodes the normal at each data point as an 8-bit index indicating one of 256 direction vectors uniformly distributed in 3-space. These textures are drawn in a separate pass using a palette to map each normal index to a specular light value for the current view vector. This method has lower precision than the RGB texture method but uses less memory. Time Complexity: The generation of the shading pixel texture is performed on a per-view basis, with a minimal performance cost when done in software. Memory Complexity: The method requires a scratch/auxiliary buffer for each slice. The shading texture size depends on the quantization scheme (16-bit per normal). Performance: The method is implemented on SGI Octane 2 with V-series graphics cards and nVidia GeForce3 series. The performance cost of generating the shading texture is minimal. Strengths: Avoids hardware interpolation redundancy and truncation errors associated with standard normal interpolation. Limitations: Requires an auxiliary buffer on some hardware due to rasterization limitations. Some hardware does not support the alternative hardware lighting path. When to Use: When high-quality shading is required in volume rendering and the hardware supports pixel texture operations (or can be emulated via copy operations). When Not to Use: When hardware flexibility is limited and the software-based texture generation becomes a bottleneck, or when memory constraints are severe (compared to normal index methods). The method was developed for interactive volume rendering using multi-dimensional transfer functions. It was implemented on the SGI Octane 2 with V-series graphics cards and the nVidia GeForce3 series graphics adaptor. The approach leverages the texture-shader features of hardware like the GeForce 3 to perform lighting calculations in hardware, enhancing the geometry and structure of the rendered data. The key observation in the implementation is that pixel texture operations only need to be applied to the portion of the volume currently changing (e.g., when the transfer function is manipulated). name: Line Bundles
head: Anisotropic textured volume rendering using line segments, Fiber Bundles
body: Line Bundles is a hardware-accelerated technique for visualizing 3D vector fields by rendering and compositing many semitransparent line segments to produce an anisotropic volume rendering result. It solves the problem of conveying both velocity magnitude and directionality simultaneously, addressing the limitation of standard volume rendering which may lack clear directionality. Unlike standard volume rendering, Line Bundles clearly evidences directionality by orienting the line segments along the flow field. It builds on Hardware Shading via Pixel Texture by extending the concept of splats to composite collections of antialiased lines in a back-to-front manner. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D vector field (flow field) and optionally a scalar field (e.g., velocity magnitude). Output: A 2D image with an anisotropic, fibrous appearance where line orientations indicate flow direction and color indicates magnitude or other scalar data. Data Structures: Splat Data: Each data point in the volume is associated with a 3D bounding box. Line Bundle: A pre-computed set of rendered line segments. The bundle consists of N line segments (typically N > 300). Color Encoding: The primary color can be fixed for the entire volume or vary per splat. If fixed, the bundle can be precomputed into a GL object for rapid reorientation. If variable, it encodes vector magnitude, a separate scalar field, or a positional indicator. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Optional): If a single primary color is used, precompute the line bundle into a GL object. This allows rapid reorientation and redrawing at each data point. 2. Sorting: Sort all data points (splats) in back-to-front order relative to the view direction. 3. Iteration: For each data point in sorted order: a. Define Bounding Box: Establish a 3D bounding box associated with the current splat. b. Perturbation: For each line segment in the bundle: i. Position Jitter: Randomly scatter the line segment within the 3D bounding box. Perturb the center position within the box. ii. Color Jitter: Randomly perturb the hue, saturation, and value of the line segment's color. If the primary color varies per splat, use the splat-specific color; otherwise, use the fixed primary color. iii. Orientation: Orient the line segment in the direction of the flow field at that data point. c. Rendering: Render the collection of antialiased lines. The lines must have transparent heads and tails to avoid unwanted edges. d. Compositing: Composite the rendered lines into the frame buffer using back-to-front compositing. This creates a thin, wispy appearance. 4. Completion: Repeat for all data points. The jittering of color and position produces an anisotropic texture oriented in the direction of the flow field, even when lines are dense with no space between them. Parameters: Number of Lines per Splat (N): In excess of 300 line segments per data point can be used with no degradation in real-time performance on mid- to high-end graphical workstations. Bounding Box Size: Not given in the sources. Jitter Range: Not given in the sources. Controlled jittering is required to avoid regular patterns or completely filled regions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Regular Patterns: Uncontrolled jittering can lead to regular patterns or completely filled regions. Controlled jittering is essential. Hard Edges: Lines without antialiasing or with opaque heads/tails create unwanted edges. Antialiased lines with transparent heads and tails are required. Directionality Loss: Standard volume rendering may lack clear directionality. Line Bundles address this by orienting lines with the flow. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlinebundles(vectorfield, scalarfield, viewdirection, fixedcolor=None, linecount=300, bboxsize=1.0): # 1. Sort data points back-to-front relative to view direction # Dot product with view direction determines depth; reverse=True sorts far to near sortedpoints = sorted(vectorfield.keys(), key=lambda p: sum(p[i] viewdirection[i] for i in range(3)), reverse=True) # 2. Precompute line bundle geometry if primary color is fixed if fixedcolor is not None: baselines = generatelinebundle(count=linecount) else: baselines = None for point in sortedpoints: flowdirection = normalize(vectorfield[point]) magnitude = scalarfield[point] # Determine primary color for this splat if fixedcolor is not None: primarycolor = fixedcolor else: primarycolor = mapmagnitudetocolor(magnitude) # Standard scalar-to-color mapping # Define bounding box for the splat bboxcenter = point bboxextent = bboxsize / 2.0 for line in baselines: # i. Position Jitter: Randomly scatter within bounding box jitteroffset = [random.uniform(-bboxextent, bboxextent) for in range(3)] jitteredcenter = [bboxcenter[i] + jitteroffset[i] for i in range(3)] # ii. Color Jitter: Perturb hue, saturation, value jitteredcolor = perturbhsv(primarycolor) # iii. Orientation: Align line with flow direction orienteddir = flowdirection # Render line with antialiasing and transparent ends # Standard GPU rasterization with alpha blending and line antialiasing drawantialiasedline(jitteredcenter, orienteddir, jitteredcolor, alpha=0.5) def generatelinebundle(count): # Generate base line segment geometries (e.g., unit vectors at various offsets) return [createunitline() for in range(count)] def mapmagnitudetocolor(mag): # Map scalar magnitude to RGB color return magtorgb(mag) def perturbhsv(colorrgb): # Convert RGB to HSV, add small random offsets to H, S, V, convert back h, s, v = rgbtohsv(colorrgb) h = (h + random.uniform(-0.05, 0.05)) % 1.0 s = max(0.0, min(1.0, s + random.uniform(-0.1, 0.1))) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v + random.uniform(-0.1, 0.1))) return hsvtorgb(h, s, v) def normalize(v): length = (sum(xx for x in v)) 0.5 return [x / length for x in v] def createunitline(): return {'center': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'direction': [0.0, 1.0, 0.0], 'length': 1.0} def rgbtohsv(rgb): # Standard conversion r, g, b = rgb maxc = max(r, g, b) minc = min(r, g, b) l = (maxc + minc) / 2.0 if maxc == minc: return 0.0, 0.0, l d = maxc - minc s = d / (2.0 - maxc - minc) if l > 0.5 else d / (maxc + minc) if maxc == r: h = ((g - b) / d) % 6 elif maxc == g: h = (b - r) / d + 2 else: h = (r - g) / d + 4 return h / 6.0, s, l def hsvtorgb(h, s, v): # Standard conversion i = int(h 6) % 6 f = h 6 - i p = v (1.0 - s) q = v (1.0 - f s) t = v (1.0 - (1.0 - f) s) if i == 0: return v, t, p elif i == 1: return q, v, p elif i == 2: return p, v, t elif i == 3: return p, q, v elif i == 4: return t, p, v else: return v, p, q Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Fiber bundles with in excess of 300 line segments per data point can be used with no degradation in real-time performance on mid- to high-end graphical workstations. Strengths: Allows viewing velocity magnitude like normal volume rendering while clearly evidencing directionality. Produces a thin, wispy appearance. Limitations: Requires back-to-front compositing, which can be challenging on some hardware without proper support. Dense lines may obscure underlying structures if not carefully tuned. When to use: When visualizing 3D vector fields where both magnitude and direction are critical, and anisotropic texture is desired. When not to use: When precise quantitative analysis of the vector field is required, as the aesthetic nature may obscure details. Line Bundles (also known as Fiber Bundles) was developed by R. Crawfis, H. Shen, and N. Max. The technique was presented in the context of flow visualization techniques for CFD using volume rendering and was applied to visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. The authors developed several more techniques to represent flow fields using anisotropic or textured volume rendering. The technique relies on graphics hardware to create texture by rendering and compositing many semitransparent line segments. It extends the concept of splats to composite collections of antialiased lines in a back-to-front manner. name: Spherical Coordinate Volume Rendering
head: Geodetic Volume Rendering, Spherical Coordinate Volume Rendering for Atmospheric Data, Spherical coordinate volume ray casting, Weather radar volume rendering implementation
body: Spherical Coordinate Volume Rendering is a volume ray casting technique designed to render radar or atmospheric data directly in spherical coordinates, eliminating the need for preprocessing or resampling to a uniform Cartesian grid. It solves the accuracy loss and memory trade-offs associated with Cartesian resampling or the geometric gaps left by textured conic surface approximations. Unlike standard texture slicing which relies on parallel planar cuts, this method operates on the intrinsic curvilinear structure of the data, making it distinct from siblings like View-Aligned Slicing with 3D Textures which assume regular grid structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset stored as stacked 2D images representing radar sweeps, where each image corresponds to a specific elevation angle. The dataset contains non-uniform elevation spacing. Output: A rendered 2D image (e.g., 800×800 canvas) composited via hardware alpha blending. Data Structures: The volume is stored in memory as a single large image formed by stacking 2D images vertically. Image Layout: Each 2D image represents one elevation sweep. Columns: 360 columns, spaced 1 degree apart in azimuth (\phi). Rows: 400 rows, spaced 250 meters apart in range (r). Coordinate System: The data is indexed by spherical coordinates (r, \phi, \theta), where \theta is the elevation angle. Algorithm Steps: The method extends general volume ray casting by modifying the sample lookup process to handle spherical coordinates and non-uniform elevation spacing. 1. Ray Traversal: For each pixel, traverse the ray through the volume in tens to hundreds of steps (e.g., 200 steps for an 800×800 canvas). 2. Coordinate Conversion: At each step, let the current sample point in Cartesian coordinates be (x, y, z). Convert these to spherical coordinates (r, \phi, \theta) using the following equations: r = \sqrt{(x - 0.5)^2 + (y - 0.5)^2 + (z - 0.5)^2} \phi = \arctan(y, x) + \pi \theta = \arccos(z/\phi) Note: The source uses \phi in the denominator of the \theta equation, which is mathematically inconsistent with standard spherical definitions where \phi is the azimuth. However, this is the exact formula provided in the source. 3. Azimuth and Range Lookup: Map \phi to the column index (0–359). Map r to the row index within the elevation slice (0–399). 4. Elevation Search (Handling Non-Uniform Spacing): Because elevation angles are not uniformly incremented, there is no direct linear mapping from \theta to the slice index in the stacked image. Perform a search to find the two elevation slices (images) immediately above and below the current sample point's \theta value. 5. Interpolation: Retrieve the values from the two bounding elevation slices at the calculated (r, \phi) position. Interpolate between these two values to determine the final volume value at the sample point. 6. Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity of the sample using the standard hardware alpha blending equation, processing slices in depth order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersphericalvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, elevationangles): """ rayorigin: (x, y, z) raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) volumedata: List of 2D arrays (images), one per elevation angle. Each image is 400 rows (range) x 360 cols (azimuth). elevationangles: List of theta values corresponding to each image in volumedata. """ numsteps = 200 stepsize = length(raydirection) # Assumed normalized or derived from scene bounds accumulatedcolor = (0, 0, 0) accumulatedopacity = 0 # Precompute elevation angle bounds for faster search if needed, # but source implies a search process is required. for i in range(numsteps): # Current point in Cartesian coordinates t = i stepsize x = rayorigin.x + raydirection.x t y = rayorigin.y + raydirection.y t z = rayorigin.z + raydirection.z t # Convert to spherical coordinates r = sqrt((x - 0.5)2 + (y - 0.5)2 + (z - 0.5)2) phi = atan2(y, x) + pi # Note: Source formula uses phi in denominator, potentially erroneous # but implemented as specified. theta = acos(z / phi) # 1. Find bounding elevation slices # Search for indices k such that elevationangles[k] <= theta < elevationangles[k+1] # This requires a search process due to non-uniform spacing. loweridx, upperidx = findboundingelevation(theta, elevationangles) # 2. Map r and phi to image coordinates # Range resolution: 250m per row. Azimuth: 1 deg per col. # Assuming r and phi are normalized or scaled appropriately to indices. rowidx = r / 250.0 colidx = phi / (2 pi) 360.0 # Clamp indices to valid range [0, 399] and [0, 359] rowidx = clamp(rowidx, 0, 399) colidx = clamp(colidx, 0, 359) # 3. Interpolate between elevation slices # Interpolate factor based on theta distance between lower and upper angles thetalower = elevationangles[loweridx] thetaupper = elevationangles[upperidx] ttheta = (theta - thetalower) / (thetaupper - thetalower) # Get values from the two slices at the same (row, col) vallower = volumedata[loweridx][rowidx][colidx] valupper = volumedata[upperidx][rowidx][colidx] volumevalue = lerp(vallower, valupper, ttheta) # 4. Apply transfer function to get color and opacity color, opacity = transferfunction(volumevalue) # 5. Composite # Standard alpha blending: Cdest = Csrc Asrc + Cdest (1 - Asrc) # references general volume ray casting compositing alphacontrib = opacity (1 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color alphacontrib accumulatedopacity += alphacontrib if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor Parameters: Ray Traversal Steps: Tens to hundreds per ray. Example: 200 steps for 800×800 rendering. Azimuth Resolution: 360 columns, 1 degree spacing. Range Resolution: 400 rows, 250 meters spacing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Uniform Elevation Spacing: The irregular spacing of elevation angles prevents direct index calculation, necessitating a search process to find bounding slices, which increases computational complexity. Precision: The conversion formulas must be implemented carefully. The source formula for \theta uses \phi in the denominator, which may lead to division by zero or incorrect values if \phi is near 0 or if the standard definition of spherical coordinates is assumed. Performance: The method requires a high number of non-trivial computations (trigonometric functions, searches, interpolations) per pixel, resulting in complex shaders. Time Complexity: High per-pixel cost due to trigonometric conversions and elevation searches for every sample point along every ray. Memory Complexity: Efficient in terms of preprocessing; no resampling to a larger Cartesian grid is required, avoiding the memory bloat associated with uniform grid resampling. Performance: Requires powerful hardware and specific WebGL implementations (e.g., Firefox with native OpenGL, Opera) to compile and run the complex shaders efficiently. Not feasible for real-time use on older or less capable hardware. Strengths: Preserves original data detail without resampling artifacts; avoids gaps associated with conic surface approximations. Limitations: Computationally intensive; dependent on specific browser/hardware capabilities for WebGL shader compilation. The method was developed for real-time interactive weather radar data visualization using WebGL. It addresses issues identified in previous approaches where resampling caused memory/detail trade-offs and textured conic surfaces left geometric gaps. The specific implementation details and formulas are documented in a book chapter by John Edgar Congote et al.. A related concept for curvilinear grids is discussed in research on volume rendering for unstructured grids, which highlights the benefits of using spherical coordinates to avoid Cartesian-to-geodetic conversion errors. name: Slice Polygon Computation (3D Texture)
body: Slice Polygon Computation (3D Texture) is a texture-based volume rendering method that generates proxy geometry by intersecting slicing planes with the volume's bounding box, then mapping the resulting polygons using 3D texture coordinates. It differs from the alternative approach of storing data as 2D texture slices, which uses pre-aligned rectangular proxy polygons, by dynamically computing arbitrary slice polygons and relying on 3D texture lookups. Inputs: A volumetric dataset stored as a 3D texture object. A viewing direction defining a series of parallel slicing planes. The bounding box of the volume. Outputs: A sequence of textured polygons (proxy geometry) representing the intersection of the slicing planes with the volume. Data Structures: Vertex arrays containing 3D positions and corresponding 3D texture coordinates. The 3D texture object containing the scalar field data. Steps: 1. Intersect Slicing Planes with Bounding Box: Calculate the intersection points between the slicing planes and the edges of the volume's bounding box. 2. Sort Vertices: Sort the resulting intersection vertices in a clockwise or counterclockwise direction around their center to form a valid polygon. 3. Calculate Texture Coordinates: For each vertex of the generated polygon, calculate the corresponding 3D texture coordinate. This can be done on the CPU, in a vertex program, or via automatic texture-coordinate generation. 4. Render: Pass the vertex arrays to the graphics library to render the textured polygons. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, o): return Vector3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def add(self, o): return Vector3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def dot(self, o): return self.xo.x + self.yo.y + self.zo.z def cross(self, o): return Vector3(self.yo.z-self.zo.y, self.zo.x-self.xo.z, self.xo.y-self.yo.x) def length(self): return (self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2)0.5 def normalize(self): l = self.length(); return Vector3(self.x/l, self.y/l, self.z/l) if l > 1e-9 else Vector3(0,0,0) class Plane: def init(self, p0, normal): self.p0, self.normal = p0, normal def intersectlineplane(p1, p2, plane): linevec = p2 - p1 denom = linevec.dot(plane.normal) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return None t = (plane.p0 - p1).dot(plane.normal) / denom if 0 <= t <= 1: return p1 + linevec t return None def computecenter(points): if not points: return Vector3(0, 0, 0) s = Vector3(0, 0, 0) for p in points: s = s + p return s (1.0 / len(points)) def sortclockwisearoundcenter(points, center, normal): if len(points) <= 2: return points ref = Vector3(0, 1, 0) if abs(normal.y) < 0.9 else Vector3(1, 0, 0) u = normal.cross(ref).normalize() v = u.cross(normal) projected = [] for p in points: vec = p - center projected.append((vec.dot(u), vec.dot(v), p)) # A pseudo-angle can be used to avoid trigonometric functions projected.sort(key=lambda pt: math.atan2(pt[1], pt[0])) return [pt[2] for pt in projected] def mappositiontotexturecoord(position, bboxmin, bboxmax): dx = bboxmax.x - bboxmin.x dy = bboxmax.y - bboxmin.y dz = bboxmax.z - bboxmin.z if dx == 0 or dy == 0 or dz == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Guard against degenerate bounding box return ((position.x - bboxmin.x) / dx, (position.y - bboxmin.y) / dy, (position.z - bboxmin.z) / dz) def computeslicepolygons(volumebboxmin, volumebboxmax, slicingplanes): polygons = [] # Standard 12 bounding box edges edges = [ (volumebboxmin, Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmin.y, volumebboxmin.z)), (Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmin.y, volumebboxmin.z), volumebboxmax), (volumebboxmin, Vector3(volumebboxmin.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmin.z)), (Vector3(volumebboxmin.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmin.z), volumebboxmax), (volumebboxmin, Vector3(volumebboxmin.x, volumebboxmin.y, volumebboxmax.z)), (Vector3(volumebboxmin.x, volumebboxmin.y, volumebboxmax.z), volumebboxmax), (Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmin.y, volumebboxmin.z), Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmin.z)), (Vector3(volumebboxmin.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmin.z), Vector3(volumebboxmin.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmax.z)), (Vector3(volumebboxmin.x, volumebboxmin.y, volumebboxmax.z), Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmin.y, volumebboxmax.z)), (Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmin.y, volumebboxmax.z), Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmax.z)), (Vector3(volumebboxmin.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmax.z), Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmax.z)), (Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmin.z), Vector3(volumebboxmax.x, volumebboxmax.y, volumebboxmax.z)) ] for plane in slicingplanes: intersectionpoints = [] for p1, p2 in edges: pt = intersectlineplane(p1, p2, plane) if pt is not None: intersectionpoints.append(pt) center = computecenter(intersectionpoints) sortedpts = sortclockwisearoundcenter(intersectionpoints, center, plane.normal) vertices = [] for pt in sortedpts: tex = mappositiontotexturecoord(pt, volumebboxmin, volumebboxmax) vertices.append((pt, tex)) polygons.append(vertices) return polygons Parameters: Slicing plane spacing: Determines the number of slices. Bounding box: Defines the spatial extent of the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues in clipping: The brute-force approach of generating a large triangle and clipping it to the data set can suffer from precision issues when generating texture coordinates for clipped triangles. The slice polygon computation method avoids this by intersecting directly with the bounding box edges. Degenerate input: If a slicing plane does not intersect the bounding box, no vertices are generated, and the slice is skipped. A method to efficiently generate a stack of oblique slices orthogonal to the viewing direction by treating each slice as a 2D 'scanplane' and exploiting scanplane coherence, avoiding polygon clipping. It differs from the brute-force approach (calculate plane equation, generate large triangle, clip to data set, generate texture coordinates) by generating slices directly with no clipping, avoiding precision problems and artifacts from numeric imprecision in clipping. It is chosen when oblique slices are required and efficiency is a concern. See also Polygon-based Volumetric Rendering with Depth Peeling, Object Aligned Planes Volume Rendering, and 3D Texture Slicing with Back-to-Front Blending. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids precision issues associated with polygon clipping. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When using 3D textures and dynamic slicing planes are required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is described in GPU Gems Chapter 39, "Volume rendering techniques". It is a standard technique in texture-based volume rendering, building on the principles of texture slicing.
