name: Projective Space Texture Mapping with Multi-Resolution Templates
head: Inverse/Forward Projection Texture Indexing, Plenoptic Surface Texture Mapping, Projective Space Texture, Projective Texture Mapping for Volume, Pseudo-Solid Texturing
body: Projective Space Texture Mapping with Multi-Resolution Templates is a technique that assigns solid textures to any position within a volume object using plenoptic projection functions as pseudo-procedure functional models. It solves the problem of intermixing volumetric rendering with solid texturing without requiring explicit uv-parameterization of the volume geometry. Unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed geometric parameterizations, this approach connects 3D positions in the volume to 2D projective positions on a plenoptic surface, and then to integral coordinates in a morphed texture image. It is distinguished by its use of multi-resolution intermediate templates generated via forward projection (DVR/DSR) and inverse projection (projective texture mapping) to mitigate aliasing artifacts known as the "cliff effect". The method operates in two distinct phases: forward projection to generate multi-resolution intermediate templates, and inverse projection to map textures from a morphed image onto the volume. Inputs: Volume object data, a morphed texture image (2D array of color/texture values), a plenoptic primitive centroid (Ox, Oy, Oz), and resolution parameters for templates and patches. Outputs: A textured volume rendering and intermediate templates (images) at various resolutions. 1. Morphed Texture Image: A 2D grid of size W \times H storing color/texture values. Coordinates (u, v) are normalized continuous variables in [0, 1]. 2. Intermediate Template: A 2D image representing the plenoptic surface, indexed by integral coordinates (x, y) corresponding to resolution intervals \Delta u, \Delta v. 3. High-Resolution Patch: A sub-region of the morphed texture image defined by vertices (u{a1}, v{a1}) and (u{a2}, v{a2}). Plenoptic Surface Parameterization: Defined by two continuous variables u \in [0, 1] and v \in [0, 1]. Resolution Intervals (Forward Projection): For an intermediate template with dimensions xd \times yd: \Delta u = \frac{1}{xd - 1} \Delta v = \frac{1}{yd - 1} A pixel at continuous position (u, v) is indexed by integral pair (x, y) where: u = x \cdot \Delta u v = y \cdot \Delta v High-Resolution Patch Indexing (Inverse Projection): For a patch with vertices (u{a1}, v{a1}) and (u{a2}, v{a2}) where u{a1} < u{a2} and v{a1} < v{a2}, the position (xa, ya) in the patch for a texture coordinate (u, v) is: (xa, ya) = \left( \frac{u - u{a1}}{\Delta ua}, \frac{v - v{a1}}{\Delta va} \right) where \Delta ua and \Delta va are the resolution intervals (width/height) of the patch. Ray Origin Adjustment (Forward Projection): For a new high-resolution representation of a region with positions (u1, v1) and (u2, v2), and new resolution intervals \Delta u1 = \frac{1}{x{d1}-1} and \Delta v1 = \frac{1}{y{d1}-1}, the new origin of the tracing ray is: Origin(u, v) = \left( u1 + x1 \cdot (u2 - u1) \cdot \Delta u1, \quad v1 + y1 \cdot (v2 - v1) \cdot \Delta v1 \right) where 0 \le x1 \le x{d1}-1 and 0 \le y1 \le y{d1}-1. Phase 1: Forward Projection (Template Generation) 1. Define the plenoptic surface parameterization using continuous variables u \in [0, 1] and v \in [0, 1]. 2. Select a resolution xd \times yd for the intermediate template. Calculate intervals \Delta u = 1/(xd - 1) and \Delta v = 1/(yd - 1). 3. Iterate through integral coordinates (x, y) for the template. Calculate continuous positions u = x \cdot \Delta u and v = y \cdot \Delta v. 4. Use u and v to adjust the origin and direction of the tracing ray for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) or Direct Surface Rendering (DSR). The ray origin is adjusted according to the formula: Origin(u, v) = \left( u1 + x1 \cdot (u2 - u1) \cdot \Delta u1, \quad v1 + y1 \cdot (v2 - v1) \cdot \Delta v1 \right) where x1, y1 correspond to the current template grid indices. 5. Render the ray to generate the pixel value for the intermediate template at (x, y). 6. Repeat for desired resolutions to create a multi-resolution representation of the intermediate template. Phase 2: Inverse Projection (Volume Texturing) 1. For each voxel p(X, Y, Z) in the volume object, define a ray passing through p(X, Y, Z) and the plenoptic primitive centroid (Ox, Oy, Oz). 2. Determine the 2D projective position (u, v) on the plenoptic surface where this ray intersects or is parameterized. 3. Identify the corresponding high-resolution patch in the morphed texture image that covers (u, v). Let the patch vertices be (u{a1}, v{a1}) and (u{a2}, v{a2}). 4. Calculate the integral coordinates (xa, ya) in the morphed texture image using: (xa, ya) = \left( \frac{u - u{a1}}{\Delta ua}, \frac{v - v{a1}}{\Delta va} \right) where \Delta ua, \Delta va are the patch resolution intervals. 5. Sample the texture value from the morphed texture image at (xa, ya). 6. Assign this texture value to the voxel p(X, Y, Z). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocate2darray(width, height): return [[0.0] width for in range(height)] def allocate3darray(dims): return [[[0.0] dims[0] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[2])] def normalizevector(v): length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def samplebilinear(texture, u, v): # Standard bilinear interpolation for continuous texture coordinates tu, tv = u, v x0, y0 = int(tu), int(tv) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 x0 = max(0, min(x0, len(texture[0]) - 1)) x1 = max(0, min(x1, len(texture[0]) - 1)) y0 = max(0, min(y0, len(texture) - 1)) y1 = max(0, min(y1, len(texture) - 1)) sx, sy = tu - x0, tv - y0 top = texture[y0][x0] (1 - sx) + texture[y0][x1] sx bottom = texture[y1][x0] (1 - sx) + texture[y1][x1] sx return top (1 - sy) + bottom sy def computeuvfromray(rayorigin, raydirection, centroid): # The source states a ray through p(X,Y,Z) and centroid indexes the texture, # but does not provide the explicit algebraic formula for mapping the 3D ray to 2D (u,v). # This implements a standard projective mapping onto a reference plane. dx, dy, dz = raydirection if abs(dz) < 1e-6: return 0.5, 0.5 t = 1.0 / dz projx = rayorigin[0] + dx t projy = rayorigin[1] + dy t return projx + 0.5, projy + 0.5 def renderray(volumedata, rayorigin, raydirection): # Standard DVR/DSR ray marching implementation. # Returns a color value by accumulating opacity and color along the ray. return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) def generateintermediatetemplate(volumedata, centroid, width, height): deltau = 1.0 / (width - 1) deltav = 1.0 / (height - 1) template = allocate2darray(width, height) u1, v1 = 0.0, 0.0 u2, v2 = 1.0, 1.0 for y in range(height): for x in range(width): u = x deltau v = y deltav originx = u1 + x (u2 - u1) deltau originy = v1 + y (v2 - v1) deltav rayorigin = (originx, originy, 0.0) raydirection = normalizevector((centroid[0] - rayorigin[0], centroid[1] - rayorigin[1], centroid[2] - rayorigin[2])) color = renderray(volumedata, rayorigin, raydirection) template[y][x] = color return template def texturevolume(volumedata, morphedtexture, centroid): texturedvolume = allocate3darray(volumedata.shape) ua1, va1 = 0.0, 0.0 ua2, va2 = 1.0, 1.0 texwidth, texheight = len(morphedtexture[0]), len(morphedtexture) deltaua = 1.0 / (texwidth - 1) deltava = 1.0 / (texheight - 1) for z in range(volumedata.shape[2]): for y in range(volumedata.shape[1]): for x in range(volumedata.shape[0]): voxelpos = (x, y, z) rayorigin = voxelpos raydirection = normalizevector((centroid[0] - rayorigin[0], centroid[1] - rayorigin[1], centroid[2] - rayorigin[2])) u, v = computeuvfromray(rayorigin, raydirection, centroid) if not (ua1 <= u <= ua2 and va1 <= v <= va2): continue texx = (u - ua1) / deltaua texy = (v - va1) / deltava texturevalue = samplebilinear(morphedtexture, texx, texy) texturedvolume[z][y][x] = texturevalue return texturedvolume Morphed Texture Image Size: Experiments show that 128 \times 128 pixels results in prominent cliff effects, while 1024 \times 1024 pixels greatly improves image quality. Resolution Intervals: Determined by the dimensions of the intermediate template or patch (xd, yd). Cliff Effect: A single pixel projected onto a surface almost parallel to the direction of projection is smeared over a relatively large area of solid, introducing alias artifacts. Mitigation: Use high-resolution texture images and high-resolution intermediate templates to eliminate these artifacts reasonably. Degenerate Input: If the ray direction is parallel to the surface normal or the projection plane, the (u, v) coordinates may become undefined or infinite. Standard projective geometry techniques (e.g., clipping or fallback coordinates) are required to handle this. Used in the forward projection phase to generate intermediate templates. Sets itself apart by rendering the volume/surface from adjusted ray origins defined by the plenoptic parameters. Used in the inverse projection phase. Sets itself apart by mapping the morphed texture directly to volume voxels via ray indexing, avoiding explicit mesh parameterization. A sibling method that applies additional geometric constraints to the projective mapping process. Sets itself apart by enforcing stricter alignment rules between texture and volume geometry. Choose it when strict geometric fidelity is required over flexible solid texturing. See Multi-constraints-based projective texture mapping. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of voxels and the cost of DVR/DSR for template generation. Inverse projection requires ray tracing for each voxel to determine (u, v) and texture sampling. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, the morphed texture image, and potentially multiple intermediate templates if multi-resolution is used. Strengths: Avoids degradation of rendered image quality while interpolating texture to resolutions exceeding the texture map. Eliminates the need for uv-parameterization. Limitations: Finite resolution of the morphed texture image can still introduce alias artifacts (cliff effect) if not sufficiently high. When to Use: When texturing complex volumetric scenes without explicit surface parameterization is required, and high-quality solid texturing is needed. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited and high-resolution textures cannot be afforded, leading to visible aliasing. The method was introduced in the paper "Texture Mapping Volume Objects". It builds on the concept of plenoptic functions and solid textures, addressing the intermixing of volumetric rendering and solid texturing. It references earlier work on two-part texture mapping by Bier and Sloan [ES86] and solid texture models by Winter [Win02]. The approach uses plenoptic indexing functions to substitute mathematical/procedure models for projective space texturing. name: 3D Texture Generation
body: This family encompasses methods for storing volumetric scalar field data directly into a 3D texture object, allowing the graphics hardware to perform volume rendering operations such as ray casting or slicing via hardware-accelerated texture lookups. It solves the problem of high computational cost associated with per-voxel integration on the CPU or in custom shaders by offloading the volume composition operator and interpolation to the GPU's texture unit. Unlike sibling methods that may use post-packing, isotropic synthesis, or specific engine integrations, this family focuses on the fundamental mechanism of populating a 3D texture array for direct hardware sampling. (Empty) Stores scalar field data as color and opacity values within a 3D texture object to facilitate hardware-accelerated rendering. It is distinguished by its reliance on pre-defined linear texture coordinates for parallel polygons, which allows the geometry to be cached in a display list. Choose it when caching geometry and avoiding non-linear depth integration formulae is prioritized. Constructs a 3D texture object from volumetric data by rendering 2D slices of the scene to a 2D texture, reading the resulting pixels, and assembling them into a 3D texture. It is described as one of the simplest methods for volume visualization. Choose it for straightforward voxel data generation without post-packing optimizations. A corrective stage applied after greedy packing to optimize inefficiently packed layouts by enforcing a global slice orientation. It addresses memory waste caused by mixing tall and wide slices in the final 3D texture. Choose it when initial greedy packing fails or increases memory requirements. Generates volumetric textures that exhibit uniform distribution in 3D space, with no dependency on position or orientation. It sets itself apart by using standard 2D texture synthesis on a single cross-section, avoiding the complexity and performance costs of full 3D volumetric synthesis. Choose it for materials like sponges or sausages where cross-sections appear similar regardless of location or cutting angle. Step: Import noiseShape.tga and noiseErosion.tga into Unity. Set Format to RGBA 32 Bit, disable alpha is transparency, disable generate mipmaps, disable sRGB, enable read-write, and set max size to 4096 (or higher via script). Split the 2D textures into 3D textures using the SplitSelectedTexture function (Tools/Textures/Split Texture2D To Texture3D Cube). This creates NoiseShape.asset and NoiseErosion.asset Texture3D assets. Pitfall: noiseShape.tga has a width of 16384, which exceeds the default Unity max size. Use Tools/Textures/Set Max Size To 16384 to allow full-size import. Definition: Rendering large volumes by maintaining a full-resolution 3D texture for MPR (Multi-Planar Reformation) views and a reduced-resolution 'context volume' for the 3D pane to save GPU memory. Step: Calculate context volume dimensions as half per axis (1/2 reduction) relative to the full-resolution volume. Parameter: maxTextureDimension3D runtime limit. Default WebGPU guarantee is 2048, but actual adapter limits may differ. Must compare each volume dimension against device.limits.maxTextureDimension3D. Pitfall: Context volume still requires significant GPU memory (~1 GB for 1024×1024×4096). End-to-end renderability depends on runtime GPU memory, CPU cache capacity, and active MPR views. The column 'Renderable with context?' should be renamed to '3D texture payload fits' and made conditional. If even the context volume exceeds limits, a second reduction level or bricking with a page table is required for out-of-core data. Number: Memory usage for 512×512×400: 210 MB full-res, 26 MB context. For 512×512×2000: 1.05 GB full-res, 131 MB context. For 1024×1024×2000: 4.2 GB full-res, 524 MB context. For 1024×1024×4096: 8.6 GB full-res, 1.05 GB context. Not given in the sources. name: AR mapping to 3D texture
head: 3D texture mapping, texture-based volume rendering
body: AR mapping to 3D texture is an object-order volume rendering technique that maps a 3D scalar field directly into a 3D texture unit, using parallel polygon slices to composite the volume via linear alpha blending. It solves the problem of high computational cost associated with ray-casting by leveraging hardware-accelerated texture interpolation and framebuffer compositing. Unlike 3D Texture Generation via Slicing, which explicitly calculates ray intersections and integrates transfer functions, this method avoids non-linear formulae by relying on a linear mapping of color and opacity into the texture coordinates, allowing for pre-cached geometry in display lists. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar field (volume data), a transfer function mapping scalars to color and opacity, and a set of parallel polygons (typically quads) representing the view-aligned slices. Output: A 2D image rendered to the framebuffer. Data Structures 3D Texture: A 3D texture object with dimensions matching the volume data resolution. Each texel stores a 4-component vector (RGBA). The RGB components store the mapped color, and the A component stores the mapped opacity. Polygon Set: A collection of parallel quads. The texture coordinates for these quads are defined once and remain constant regardless of view rotation. Steps 1. Texture Population: Map the scalar values from the input volume data into the 3D texture. For each voxel at position (i, j, k) with scalar value s, compute the color C and opacity \alpha using the transfer function T(s) = (R, G, B, \alpha). Store (R, G, B, \alpha) in the texel at (i, j, k). 2. Coordinate Definition: Define texture coordinates for the parallel polygons. The coordinates are linearly mapped to the 3D texture space. Because the mapping is linear, the texture coordinates do not need to be recalculated when the view rotates. 3. Geometry Setup: Place the set of parallel polygons into a display list. A display list is a group of precomputed OpenGL commands cached for later execution, improving performance when redrawing the same geometry multiple times. 4. Rendering: a. Enable 3D texture mapping and linear interpolation (trilinear filtering). b. Enable alpha blending with the standard linear alpha blending equation: C{out} = C{src} \cdot \alpha{src} + C{dst} \cdot (1 - \alpha{src}). c. Render the parallel polygons in back-to-front order (or front-to-back with appropriate blending setup) through the 3D texture. The hardware interpolates the RGBA values from the 3D texture based on the polygon's position and the linear texture coordinates. d. Composite the results into the framebuffer. Parameters Framebuffer Resolution: A color/RGBA resolution of at least 16 bits is desirable for good quality. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is used for texture sampling. Pitfalls Quality Limitation: The quality is limited due to the lack of bit accuracy and the approximation inherent in linear blending and interpolation. Off-Axis Degradation: Image quality degrades at off-axis views compared to on-axis views. Estimation Error: The linear estimation method for texture coordinate mapping is likely worse than Wilson's depth integration, but visualizations remain effective. Screen Size Threshold: There is a critical screen size where the cost of increased trilinear interpolations overtakes the cost of footprint mappings. A data layout strategy storing gradients in RGB and isovalue in Alpha, enabling hardware-accelerated normal interpolation. The foundational structured mesh data structure for storing scalar fields, enabling efficient spatial indexing. An object-order technique using 3D textures and pre-integration in a lookup table to support arbitrary transfer functions. Time Complexity: Sub-second rendering times for moderately-sized datasets. The cost is dominated by texture interpolation and framebuffer compositing. Memory Complexity: Requires memory proportional to the volume resolution for the 3D texture (O(N^3) for N \times N \times N volume). Performance: High performance due to hardware acceleration of texture mapping and blending. Strengths: Simple implementation, high frame rates for moderate resolutions, effective visualization. Limitations: Limited quality due to lack of bit accuracy, degradation at off-axis views, and potential artifacts from linear interpolation. Not suitable for high-precision requirements or complex transfer functions that require non-linear integration. When to Use: When high performance is required for moderately-sized datasets and high visual fidelity is not critical. When Not to Use: When high bit accuracy, off-axis quality, or complex transfer function integration is required. The method was described in the context of Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration. It is also discussed in A Practical Evaluation of Popular Volume Rendering Algorithms. The approach leverages early OpenGL capabilities for 3D texture mapping and display lists to achieve real-time performance. Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration, https://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/bitstream/10012/1104/1/jlmckinl2002.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Practical Evaluation of Popular Volume Rendering..., https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/PracticalEvaluationofVolumeRenderingAlgorithms.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Gradient-Isosurface Texture Packing
head: Gradient Packing in Alpha Channel
body:
Gradient-Isosurface Texture Packing is a data layout strategy for 3D volume textures that stores surface gradients in the RGB components and the original scalar isovalue in the Alpha component. This allows a single texture to serve as both the data source for shading (via interpolated normals) and the classification source (via the isovalue), eliminating the need for a second texture copy or runtime gradient calculation. It sets itself apart from AR mapping to 3D texture by embedding geometric shading information directly into the texture coordinates, and from Uniform Grid by enabling hardware-accelerated normal interpolation during ray casting. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset with scalar values V(x,y,z) and computed gradient vectors 
abla V(x,y,z) = (Gx, Gy, Gz). Outputs: A 3D volume texture T with internal format supporting 4 components (e.g., RGBA16F or RGBA8). Data Structures: The texture stores four components per voxel: R = Gx (Gradient X component) G = Gy (Gradient Y component) B = Gz (Gradient Z component) A = V (Original scalar/isovalue) Steps: 1. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient 
abla V for each voxel. The sources cite two approaches: Central differences for accuracy. Sobel filters for high-quality offline computation. Optional filtering: A simple averaging of neighbors or a separable 3D Gaussian kernel to smooth gradients. 2. Normalization: Normalize the gradient vector to unit length to store as a normal. \hat{G} =  rac{
abla V}{\|
abla V\|} If \|
abla V\| = 0, the gradient is undefined. 3. Pack Data: Construct a HalfVector4 (or equivalent 16-bit float vector) for each voxel: P(x,y,z) = (\hat{G}x, \hat{G}y, \hat{G}z, V(x,y,z)) 4. Upload: Upload the packed array to the GPU as a 3D texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packgradients(volumedata: Array3D[float], resolution: int): """ Pack gradients and isovalue into a 3D texture format. volumedata: 3D array of scalar values. resolution: N x N x N grid size. Returns: 3D array of HalfVector4 (or equivalent packed structure). """ packedvolume = emptyarray(resolution, resolution, resolution, dtype=HalfVector4) # 1. Compute Gradients (Central Difference) gradients = emptyarray(resolution, resolution, resolution, dtype=Vector3) for z in range(resolution): for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): # Central difference approximation # Handle boundaries by clamping or assuming zero gradient gx = sample(volumedata, x+1, y, z) - sample(volumedata, x-1, y, z) gy = sample(volumedata, x, y+1, z) - sample(volumedata, x, y-1, z) gz = sample(volumedata, x, y, z+1) - sample(volumedata, x, y, z-1) grad = Vector3(gx, gy, gz) norm = length(grad) if norm > 0.0: grad = normalize(grad) gradients[x, y, z] = grad # 2. Pack into Texture Format for z in range(resolution): for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): g = gradients[x, y, z] val = volumedata[x, y, z] # Store gradient in RGB, value in Alpha packedvolume[x, y, z] = HalfVector4(g.x, g.y, g.z, val) return packedvolume def samplepackedtexture(tex: Texture3D, pos: Vector3): """ Sample the packed texture to retrieve normal and isovalue. """ # Hardware interpolation handles the linear interpolation of RGB (normal) and A (value) vec4 = tex3Dlod(tex, pos) normal = normalize(vec4.rgb) # Ensure normalization after interpolation isovalue = vec4.a return normal, isovalue Parameters: Gradient Filter: Sobel or Central Difference. Sobel is preferred for offline quality. Texture Format: Must support 4 components. 16-bit floats (HalfVector4) are recommended for gradient precision. Edge Cases: Zero Gradient: If the gradient magnitude is zero (flat region), normalization fails. Set gradient to (0,0,0) or a default normal. Boundary Conditions: Central differences require neighbors outside the volume. Clamp coordinates to the nearest boundary voxel. Precision: Storing normalized gradients in 8-bit integers (as mentioned in for older hardware) loses precision. 16-bit floats are standard for modern implementations. A technique where volume gradients are pre-computed and stored in texture memory alongside density data, allowing the texture mapping hardware to interpolate both density and gradients during resampling. It sets itself apart from Sommer et al.'s method, which computes gradients from a second copy of the volume in main memory (slower for translucent projections), by using hardware interpolation for throughput. Choose this when dynamic lighting and high-quality shading are required without reloading textures. Time Complexity: Gradient computation is O(N^3) offline. Rendering is O(1) per sample for shading (no extra texture fetches for normals). Memory Complexity: Requires 4 components per voxel. If gradients were computed on-the-fly, an additional texture or memory would be needed. Performance: On a 200MHz CPU, computing gradients for a 256^3 volume takes 12 seconds. Rendering speed depends on the base ray-casting implementation but benefits from reduced memory bandwidth for shading data. Strengths: Enables dynamic lighting changes without reloading texture memory. Hardware-accelerated interpolation of normals. Limitations: Gradients are static; cannot handle dynamic volume changes without recomputation. Offline computation cost. Originated from early 3D texture mapping hardware acceleration research. Cullip and Neumann described a method utilizing the PixelFlow machine that pre-computed gradient components. Sommer et al. proposed resampling texture volumes in planes parallel to image pixels. The specific packing of gradients into RGB and isovalue into Alpha is detailed in unofficial tutorials. Volume Rendering 102: Transfer Functions, http://graphicsrunner.blogspot.com/2009/01/volume-rendering-102-transfer-functions.html, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) High-Quality Volume Rendering Using Texture Mapping..., https://cfcs.pku.edu.cn/baoquan/docs/20180622110034067331.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Rendering Iso-surfaces via 3D Textures
head: Non-polygonal 3D texture based iso-surface rendering
body:
A hardware-accelerated method to render shaded iso-surfaces on a per-pixel basis using 3D texture mapping and OpenGL alpha testing, avoiding polygonal reconstruction. It sets itself apart from polygonal approaches (e.g., Marching Cubes) by eliminating the need for surface fitting and handling enormous triangle counts, and from pre-computed lighting methods by allowing dynamic lighting changes without reloading texture memory. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (scalar field X), an iso-value threshold T, a light direction vector \vec{L}, a model rotation matrix M{rot}, diffuse reflectivity kd, and ambient intensity Ia. Output: A 2D image of the shaded iso-surface. Data Structures: 3D Texture: A 4-component texture (RGBA). RGB Components: Store the material gradient vector 
abla X at each voxel. Alpha Component: Store the scalar material value X at each voxel. Frame Buffer: Stores the rendered pixel colors. Preprocessing (Gradient Packing): Gradients must be packed into the [0, 1] range for storage in standard 8-bit or floating-point textures. 1. Compute the gradient \vec{G} = 
abla X = (Gx, Gy, Gz) for each voxel. 2. Scale and translate components: C{rgb} = 0.5 \cdot \vec{G} + 0.5 This maps \vec{G} \in [-1, 1] to C{rgb} \in [0, 1]. 3. Assign C{rgb} to the RGB channels and X to the Alpha channel of the 3D texture. Rendering Steps: 1. Iso-surface Extraction (Alpha Testing): Enable OpenGL alpha testing with a reference value equal to the iso-value T. Perform texture-mapped volume rendering (e.g., ray casting or slicing) through the 3D texture. The alpha test rejects pixels where the sampled alpha value X < T. Only pixels passing the depth test and having X \ge T are drawn. This effectively selects the first surface point along the view ray. Result: The frame buffer now contains the unshaded surface points. In Gradient Shading, the RGB channels contain the packed gradients; in Gradientless Shading, the RGB channels may contain arbitrary values or the material values themselves, depending on the specific implementation variant, but the alpha channel holds the material value X. 2. Shading (Two Variants): Variant A: Gradient Shading (Matrix Multiplication) This method uses the stored gradients to compute lighting via a Color Matrix (CM) applied during a frame buffer copy operation. Color Matrix Construction: The Color Matrix combines light direction, rotation, and unpacking scaling. CM =  egin{pmatrix} Lx & Ly & Lz & 0 \ Lx & Ly & Lz & 0 \ Lx & Ly & Lz & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} M{rot}  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 2 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} Note: The source text provides a specific matrix form for the scaling/bias part. The standard interpretation of unpacking [0,1] to [-1,1] is 2x - 1. The source matrix shows:  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 & -1 \ 2 & 2 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} However, standard affine unpacking is diagonal. The source text explicitly writes: CM =  egin{pmatrix} Lx & Ly & Lz & 0 \ Lx & Ly & Lz & 0 \ Lx & Ly & Lz & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} M{rot}  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 & -1 \ 2 & 2 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} We retain the source's explicit matrix definition. Execution: Copy the frame buffer contents onto itself using the Color Matrix. This operation multiplies each pixel vector by CM.  egin{bmatrix} Ia \ Ia \ Ia \ 0 \end{bmatrix} +  egin{bmatrix} kd \ kd \ 1 \end{bmatrix} \odot \left( CM  egin{bmatrix} R \ G \ B \ \alpha \end{bmatrix} ight) =  egin{bmatrix} kd(L \cdot N{rot}) + Ia \ kd(L \cdot N{rot}) + Ia \ kd(L \cdot N{rot}) + Ia \ \alpha \end{bmatrix} Where R, G, B are the unpacked gradients (rotated normals N{rot}), L is the light direction, and \odot denotes component-wise multiplication for the scalar factors kd and 1. Variant B: Gradientless Shading (Forward Differences) This method approximates the diffuse term Id \approx 
abla X \cdot \vec{L} using forward differences of the material values, avoiding the need to store gradients. Formula: Id \approx  rac{\partial X}{\partial L} = X(\vec{p}0) - X(\vec{p}0 + \Delta \cdot \vec{L}) Where \vec{p}0 is the surface point, \vec{L} is the light direction, and \Delta is a small step size. Execution: 1. Render the iso-surface as in Step 1. The frame buffer contains X(\vec{p}0). 2. Render the iso-surface again, but shift the texture coordinates or sampling position towards the light source by \Delta \cdot \vec{L}. This yields X(\vec{p}0 + \Delta \cdot \vec{L}). 3. Use OpenGL blending (e.g., GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA or specific arithmetic blending) to compute the difference between the two passes. 4. Combine the result with ambient lighting Ia and diffuse reflectivity kd. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Limited frame buffer precision can result in slightly less contrast compared to software ray-casting. Gradient Clamping: Gradients must be properly scaled to [0,1] for storage and unscaled for lighting. Incorrect scaling leads to incorrect normal directions. Lighting Changes: Unlike pre-computed lighting textures, this method handles dynamic light direction changes by updating the Color Matrix or sampling offset, requiring no texture reload. Performance: Achieved approximately 6 frames per second for realistically sized datasets on the hardware tested, compared to roughly 9 seconds for a software-based ray-caster rendering the same surface. Memory: Requires a 4-component 3D texture. Gradient shading stores gradients + values. Gradientless shading stores only values (potentially saving memory if gradients are not pre-computed, but requiring multiple rendering passes). Strengths: Avoids polygonal reconstruction overhead (Marching Cubes). Interactive manipulation of isovalue is possible. Dynamic lighting without texture reloading. Smooth shading (limited only by hardware interpolation and frame buffer precision). Limitations: Dependent on 3D texture hardware support and OpenGL alpha testing capabilities. Frame buffer precision limits final image contrast. Gradientless shading requires multiple rendering passes and careful handling of sampling offsets. This method was presented in the context of volume visualization and rendering techniques, specifically addressing the limitations of polygonal iso-surface extraction for interactive applications. It builds on the concept of hardware-accelerated volume rendering via 3D texture maps. It contrasts with pre-computed lighting approaches (where ambient and reflected light are stored in the texture) and normal-mapping approaches (where normal orientation is stored and indexed into a color table), which suffer from texture reloading requirements and quantization artifacts, respectively. Volume Visualization and Volume Rendering Techniques, https://www.cs.unh.edu/~cs880/visualization/Meissner-VolRenderingEGTutorial-rdb.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Uniform Grid
head: Uniform Mesh
body: A uniform grid is a structured mesh where vertices are spaced uniformly along each axis, with geometry and connectivity defined implicitly by bounding box limits and vertex counts. Inputs and Outputs: aabbmin: Minimum corner of the axis-aligned bounding box. Default: [-1, -1, -1]. aabbmax: Maximum corner of the axis-aligned bounding box. Default: [1, 1, 1]. xext, yext, zext: Number of vertices along each axis. defaultvalue: Initial scalar value for all points. Default: float('inf'). getpoints(): Returns a (X, Y, Z, 3) float32 tensor containing 3D coordinates of all grid points. getvalues(): Returns a (X, Y, Z) float32 tensor containing scalar values at each vertex. setvalues(tensor): Updates the scalar field with a (X, Y, Z) float32 tensor. Data Structure: The grid is defined by the positions of the minimum vertex (x0, y0, z0) and maximum vertex (x1, y1, z1), and the number of vertices along each axis (x\ext, y\ext, z\ext). Geometry and micro-topology are given implicitly; the connectivity of quadrilateral cells is computed trivially from the min/max positions and vertex counts. Additional data attributes can be associated with each vertex. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Allocate memory for scalar values of size x\ext \times y\ext \times z\ext and fill with defaultvalue. 2. Coordinate Computation: For any vertex at indices (i, j, k) where 0 \le i < x\ext, 0 \le j < y\ext, 0 \le k < z\ext: x = x0 + i \cdot \frac{x1 - x0}{x\ext - 1} y = y0 + j \cdot \frac{y1 - y0}{y\ext - 1} z = z0 + k \cdot \frac{z1 - z0}{z\ext - 1} 3. Access: Retrieve or update values via the getvalues() and setvalues() methods, which return or accept a (X, Y, Z) float32 tensor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class UniformGrid: def init(self, xext, yext, zext, aabbmin=(-1.0, -1.0, -1.0), aabbmax=(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), defaultvalue=float('inf')): self.xext = xext self.yext = yext self.zext = zext self.aabbmin = aabbmin self.aabbmax = aabbmax self.values = [[[defaultvalue for in range(zext)] for in range(yext)] for in range(xext)] def getpoint(self, i, j, k): dx = self.aabbmax[0] - self.aabbmin[0] if self.xext > 1 else 0.0 dy = self.aabbmax[1] - self.aabbmin[1] if self.yext > 1 else 0.0 dz = self.aabbmax[2] - self.aabbmin[2] if self.zext > 1 else 0.0 x = self.aabbmin[0] + i (dx / (self.xext - 1)) if self.xext > 1 else self.aabbmin[0] y = self.aabbmin[1] + j (dy / (self.yext - 1)) if self.yext > 1 else self.aabbmin[1] z = self.aabbmin[2] + k (dz / (self.zext - 1)) if self.zext > 1 else self.aabbmin[2] return (x, y, z) def getpoints(self): points = [] for i in range(self.xext): for j in range(self.yext): for k in range(self.zext): points.append(self.getpoint(i, j, k)) return points def getvalues(self): return self.values def setvalues(self, newvalues): self.values = newvalues Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Dimensions: If any extent is 1, the denominator (extent - 1) becomes zero. The coordinate formula must handle this by returning the minimum bound for that axis. Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors may occur during coordinate computation for large extents; recomputing coordinates from indices per ray/cell is standard practice. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Trivial computation of coordinates and connectivity; suitable for regularly sampled data. Limitations: Cannot represent non-uniform sampling or complex geometries. When to Use: Regular, structured data like CT/MRI scans or terrain models. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Uniform grids were introduced as a standard method for representing structured meshes in computational geometry and volume rendering. They are widely used in digital terrain models and medical imaging (CT, MRI) due to their simplicity and efficiency. name: Röttger et al. Rendering
head: 3D Texture Volume Rendering with Pre-Integration, Texture-Based Volume Rendering with Pre/Post-Classification, Texture-based VR
body: Röttger et al. Rendering is an object-order volume rendering technique that utilizes 3D textures and view-port aligned slices to achieve high-quality visualization through pre-integration. It solves the problem of high computational cost and artifacts associated with integrating arbitrary (non-linear) transfer functions during rendering by approximating the volume rendering integral in a pre-computed 3D lookup table. Unlike its siblings, it specifically enables hardware-accelerated interpolation along the ray within a tetrahedral cell to support arbitrary transfer functions, including isosurface effects, which linear transfer functions cannot handle without artifacts. Inputs: A scalar volume dataset. A transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Camera parameters (position, orientation). Lighting parameters (ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients, light position, eye position). Outputs: A rendered 2D image with correct color and opacity composition. 1. Pre-Integration Lookup Table (LUT) A 3D texture map parameterized by three axes: X-axis: Front scalar value (sf) at the cell entry point. Y-axis: Back scalar value (sb) at the cell exit point. Z-axis: Distance through the cell (l) or thickness. Content: The texture stores the pre-integrated color and opacity resulting from the volume rendering integral for the given parameters. Note on 2D Transfer Functions: For transfer functions dependent on both scalar and gradient magnitude, a 4D table is infeasible. Instead, a 3D table is used where each slice corresponds to a constant gradient magnitude, assuming the gradient is constant per ray segment. 2. Volume Data Texture A 3D texture cube storing the volume data for rendering: Dimensions: 256^3 \times 4 voxels (float type). RGB Channels: Normalized gradient values in range [0, 1]. Alpha Channel: Opacity values in range [0, 1]. Gradient Storage: Raw gradients can be negative. They are normalized to [-1, 1] via scaling, then shifted to [0, 1] for storage using the equation: \text{stored\value} = \frac{\nabla f(x) + 1.0}{2.0}. 1. Data Loading and Gradient Calculation: Obtain opacity values for the volume class. Calculate the gradient of each volume element using central differences. Normalize gradients to [-1, 1] and shift to [0, 1] for texture storage. 2. Texture Creation and Loading: Reserve memory space for a 3D texture cube with dimensions being the smallest powers of two that can contain the data. Fill the space with zeros. Load the gradient data into the RGB channels and opacity into the Alpha channel of the 3D texture. Upload the texture to GPU memory. 3. Pre-Integration Table Generation (Offline): Compute the 3D table of colors and opacities for discrete front scalar values (sf), back scalar values (sb), and distances (l). For arbitrary transfer functions, this table allows the hardware to look up the integrated color directly. Partial Pre-Integration: To allow interactive changes to the transfer function, store static components (exponentiation of distances) separately from dynamic components (color and opacity). 4. Rendering (Object-Order Slicing): Determine the object axis (X, Y, or Z) most parallel to the projection axis. Select the texture slice furthest from the camera along that axis. Rotate the camera around the object and draw the texture slices starting from the furthest one. During rasterization, use a fragment shader to perform shading and blending. 5. Fragment Shader Processing: Sample the volume data texture at the fragment position. Expand the stored gradient values from [0, 1] back to [-1, 1] for lighting calculations. Apply the lighting model (ambient, diffuse, specular) using the expanded normal and the stored opacity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. function expand(v: float3) -> float3: """ Reverses the normalization of gradient values stored in [0,1]. Returns values in [-1, 1]. """ return (v - 0.5) 2.0 function main( texPos0: float3, # Texture coordinates globalAmbient: float3, # Ambient light color lightColor: float3, # Light source color lightPosition: float3, # Light position eyePosition: float3, # Camera/Eye position Ka: float3, # Ambient reflection coefficient Kd: float3, # Diffuse reflection coefficient Ks: float3, # Specular reflection coefficient shininess: float, # Shininess exponent samplerTex0: sampler3D # 3D texture containing gradient (RGB) and opacity (A)) -> float4: # Initialize output OUT = float4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Sample the volume data texture # RGB: Normalized gradient [0,1] # A: Opacity [0,1] texvalue = tex3D(samplerTex0, texPos0) # Recover normal vector from stored gradient normal = expand(texvalue.rgb) # Set output alpha to sampled opacity OUT.a = texvalue.a # Only compute lighting if opacity is non-zero if OUT.a > 0.0: # Ambient component ambient = lightColor Ka # Diffuse component # Note: Source uses dot(lightPosition, normal). # Standard Phong usually uses dot(normal, lightdirection). # We follow the source code exactly. diffuse = max(dot(lightPosition, normal), 0.0) Kd lightColor # Specular component # Calculate halfway vector between light and eye halfway = normalize(lightPosition - eyePosition) specular = pow(dot(halfway, normal), shininess) Ks # Combine lighting components OUT.rgb = ambient + diffuse + specular return OUT Transfer Function: Must be arbitrary; supports non-linear functions and isosurface effects. Lighting Model Components: Ambient (Ka), Diffuse (Kd), Specular (Ks), Shininess, Light Color, Light Position, Eye Position. 3D Texture Limit: 512^3 voxels on tested hardware (GeForce FX). Volume Data Texture Size: 256^3 \times 4 voxels (float). Gradient Sign Preservation: Gradients can be negative. They must be normalized to [-1, 1] and shifted to [0, 1] for storage in the texture. Failure to do so results in incorrect normals. Performance Limitation: 3D texture access is slower than 2D due to irregular memory access patterns and higher computational cost (trilinear interpolation requires 8 texture accesses vs. 4 for bilinear). Fill Rate Limit: Performance is primarily limited by fill rate. High zoom levels decrease FPS significantly because larger primitives generate more fragments. Alpha Test Effectiveness: The benefit of alpha testing (skipping transparent fragments) is inversely proportional to data density. Higher density reduces the benefit because more fragments are opaque and require blending. 4D Table Infeasibility: Standard pre-integration for 2D transfer functions (scalar + gradient) requires a 4D table, which is infeasible. The method uses a 3D table assuming constant gradient per segment. Pre-computation: Computing the lookup table is costly, especially when the transfer function changes. Partial pre-integration mitigates this by separating static and dynamic components. Rendering: The rendering step involves texture lookups and fragment shading. The complexity is dominated by the fill rate and the cost of 3D texture sampling. Hardware: Tested on GeForce FX chip. Fill Rate: The GeForce FX has a fill rate of 1.6 billion texels per second. Zoom Impact: High zoom levels significantly decrease FPS due to increased fragment generation. Strengths: Substantial performance improvements over standard integration. Supports arbitrary (non-linear) transfer functions without artifacts. Superior image quality compared to 2D textures due to trilinear interpolation, avoiding banding artifacts. Allows interactive changes to optical properties with virtually no overhead if partial pre-integration is used. Limitations: 3D texture access is slower than 2D. Limited by 3D texture size (e.g., 512^3 voxels). Performance degrades with high zoom levels. Alpha testing benefits diminish with high data density. When high-quality visualization with arbitrary, non-linear transfer functions is required. When hardware acceleration for volume integration is needed. When the volume size fits within the 3D texture limits of the target hardware. When the transfer function changes frequently and partial pre-integration is not implemented (due to high LUT recomputation cost). When the volume data exceeds the 3D texture size limits of the hardware. When fill rate is a critical bottleneck and high zoom levels are expected. The method was introduced by Röttger et al. [272] as an extension of pre-integrated volume rendering. It builds on the concept of pre-integration proposed by Engel et al. [EKE01] for 1D transfer functions using 2D tables. Röttger et al. extended this to allow arbitrary transfer functions by creating a 3D texture map parameterized by front scalar value, back scalar value, and distance. Engel et al. [EKE01]: Demonstrated pre-integration for 1D transfer functions using 2D tables. Röttger et al.: Introduced the 3D texture map for arbitrary transfer functions, solving artifacts associated with linear transfer functions. Kniss et al. [KPI 03]: Proposed a special type of 2D transfer function representation based on the sum of Gaussians for analytical pre-integration. Partial Pre-Integration: Moreland and Angel [04] proposed storing static components separately to allow interactive transfer function changes. STF Guided Segmentation: Used for automatic setup of multi-dimensional transfer functions. High-Quality Visualization: Applied in various practical examples for volume visualization. Object-Oriented Geometry Rendering: Supports rendering of structured grids using object-space algorithms. name: 3D Texture Generation via Slicing
head: 3D Texture Slicing, Slice-based Volume Generation
body: 3D Texture Generation via Slicing is a method for constructing a 3D texture from volume data by approximating slices of that data. It solves the problem of populating a 3D texture resource by rendering 2D slices of a scene to a 2D texture, reading the resulting pixels, and assembling them into a 3D texture. It is described as one of the simplest methods for volume visualization. It differs from AR mapping to 3D texture by relying on explicit pixel extraction and assembly rather than direct mapping, and from 3D Texture Generation via Vertex Shader Iteration by using multiple draw calls (one per slice) rather than a single draw call with layer targeting. Inputs: Volume data values, target 3D texture dimensions (assumed cubic for the primary implementation described). Outputs: A populated 3D texture. Data Structures: Uint8Array: A flat 1D array representing the 3D data, sized width width width. Render Target: A 2D texture or framebuffer attachment used for intermediate rendering. Pixel Buffer: A temporary buffer to read pixels from the render target. Steps: 1. Initialize a Uint8Array for 3D data of size width width width. 2. Loop i from 0 to width - 1: a. Set the material slice parameter to i / width. b. Render the mesh to the render target. c. Read pixels from the render target. d. Extract the red channel from the pixel data. If pixels are stored as RGBA, the red channel for pixel j is at index 4 j. Store these in pixelsRed. e. Copy pixelsRed to the 3D data array at the current offset corresponding to slice i. 3. Create a 3D texture and upload the assembled data with format R8. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generate3dtextureviaslicing(width, rendermesh, getpixels, createtexture, uploadtexture): # Initialize flat array for 3D volume data # Size is width width width volumedata = Uint8Array(width width width) # Loop through each slice for i in range(width): # Set slice parameter for the renderer # Normalized slice index sliceparam = i / width rendermesh.material.slice = sliceparam # Render the mesh to the 2D render target rendertotarget(rendermesh) # Read pixels from the render target # Assuming RGBA format, 8-bit per channel pixelbuffer = getpixels() # Extract red channel # For each pixel j, red is at index 4j pixelsred = [] for j in range(width width): pixelsred.append(pixelbuffer[4 j]) # Copy to 3D data array # Offset for slice i is i width width offset = i width width for k in range(width width): volumedata[offset + k] = pixelsred[k] # Create and upload 3D texture texture = createtexture(format="R8") uploadtexture(texture, volumedata) return texture Parameters: width: The dimension of the cubic volume. Typical values depend on resolution requirements. format: The texture format, typically R8 for single-channel data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: This method requires one draw call per slice. For large volumes, this results in significant overhead. Precision: Reading pixels back from the GPU to CPU memory can be slow and may introduce precision loss if not handled carefully. Boundary Conditions: The slice parameter i / width assumes a specific mapping between the normalized value and the volume coordinate system. Incorrect mapping may result in missing or duplicated slices. This method renders to a specific slice of a 3D texture in a single draw call by iterating over texels of a source depth buffer in the vertex shader and projecting them into the 3D volume. It solves the performance penalty of multiple draw calls (one per slice) and redundant sampling of the depth texture for every slice. It differs from the primary slicing method by avoiding the CPU-GPU round-trip for each slice and by using glLayer to target slices directly. Steps: 1. Draw points, with the number of points equal to the depth buffer resolution or less. 2. In the vertex shader, fetch the depth buffer value for the current point. 3. Project the fetched depth value into the cube covered by the 3D texture to determine the Z-coordinate (slice). 4. Set the target slice for rendering using the glLayer variable in the vertex shader. 5. In the fragment shader, perform the desired calculations (e.g., processing color textures) and write to the 3D texture slice. Parameters: glLayer: A built-in variable used to specify the layer/slice index for rendering to a 3D texture or array texture. Pitfalls: The glLayer variable in the vertex shader is not part of the core OpenGL specification prior to version 4.2; it requires the GLAMDvertexshaderlayer extension or a geometry shader pass-through. Time Complexity: O(N^3) for a volume of size N \times N \times N, due to N draw calls and N^2 pixels per slice. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for storing the volume data. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. However, it is noted as "terribly slow" compared to single-draw-call methods when dealing with large volumes due to the overhead of multiple draw calls. Scaling: Scales poorly with volume size due to the linear increase in draw calls. Strengths: Simple to implement; described as one of the simplest methods for volume visualization. Limitations: High CPU overhead due to multiple draw calls; slow pixel readback from GPU to CPU. When to use: Small volumes or prototyping where simplicity is prioritized over performance. When not to use: Large volumes or real-time applications requiring high performance. This method is described as one of the simplest methods for volume visualization. It is commonly used in educational contexts and simple volume renderers. The vertex shader iteration variant was discussed in a 2013 Stack Exchange post as an optimization for rendering to 3D textures. name: Voxel Generation via 2D Slice Texture
head: 2D Slice Texture Voxel Generation
body: This method generates billions of explicit voxels without using 3D textures or compression by treating a single large 2D texture as a column of 2D slices. It solves the memory bottleneck of storing full 3D volumes by rendering voxel data to a bitmap (chunk/page) and discarding it immediately after use. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly generating every voxel in a shader rather than sampling implicit data, and by reusing a single 2D texture buffer for multiple chunks to minimize VRAM allocation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D texture representing a column of slices, 2D texture coordinates (u, v), world bounds (worldMin, worldMax), and the voxel pitch (voxels per chunk side). Output: 3D world coordinates for each voxel in the current chunk, which are then used to generate voxel data (density, color, etc.) and render depth/normals to screen. Data Structures: Slice Texture: A 2D texture with dimensions 128 \times 16384 (width \times height). The width (128) represents the slice thickness/width, and the height (16384) is the maximum texture width supported by most modern graphics cards. This texture is treated as a column of slices. Parameters: volumePitch: Number of voxels per chunk side. worldMin, worldMax: Minimum and maximum coordinates defining the chunk's world space bounds. Texture dimensions: 128 \times 16384. Steps: 1. Run Voxel Generation Shader: Execute the shader on the 2D slice texture. 2. Map 2D Coordinates to 3D: For each point on the 2D slice texture, determine the corresponding 3D point clamped in the 0-1 range. The x coordinate is derived directly from the 2D texture's x coordinate. The z coordinate (slice number) is derived from the 2D texture's y coordinate. The y coordinate (distance from top of slice) is derived from the 2D texture's y coordinate. 3. Calculate World Coordinates: Convert the normalized 3D coordinates to world space using linear interpolation (mix) between worldMin and worldMax. 4. Generate Voxel Data: Use the calculated world coordinates to generate voxel properties (e.g., density, material). 5. Render Chunk: Render the generated voxel data to the screen by shooting a ray from the front of the chunk to the back. The volume cube is isometric, shaped like an imperfect hexagon with sides having a 0.5 slope. 6. Render Auxiliary Data: Render depth, normals, and texture information to a 2D texture for each chunk. 7. Composite: Render chunks to screen in back-to-front order. 8. Reuse Memory: Reuse textures for closer chunks as older ones fall out of distance. Pseudocode: The following GLSL-like pseudocode maps 2D texture coordinates to 3D voxel coordinates within a chunk. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. // Helper for integer modulo int intMod(int lhs, int rhs) { return lhs - ((lhs / rhs) rhs); } void main() { // Input: 2D texture coordinates (0.0 to 1.0) vec2 xyCoordsIn = vec2(TexCoord0); // Output: 3D normalized coordinates (0.0 to 1.0) vec3 xyzCoordsOut = vec3(0.0); // Parameters int iVolumePitch = int(volumePitch); // Calculate integer position in the 2D texture column // yPos represents the linear index along the height of the 2D texture int yPos = int(volumePitch volumePitch xyCoordsIn.y); // Map 2D coordinates to 3D coordinates // x remains the same xyzCoordsOut.x = xyCoordsIn.x; // y is the offset within the current slice (row within the slice) // intMod(yPos, iVolumePitch) gives the row index within the slice xyzCoordsOut.y = float(intMod(yPos, iVolumePitch)) / float(volumePitch); // z is the slice number (column index in the 2D texture column) // yPos / iVolumePitch gives the slice index xyzCoordsOut.z = float(yPos / iVolumePitch) / float(volumePitch); // Convert normalized 3D coordinates to world space vec3 worldPosInVoxels = vec3( mix(worldMin.x, worldMax.x, xyzCoordsOut.x), mix(worldMin.y, worldMax.y, xyzCoordsOut.y), mix(worldMin.z, worldMax.z, xyzCoordsOut.z)); // Use worldPosInVoxels to generate voxel data (e.g., density, color) //... } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on integer arithmetic for coordinate mapping to avoid floating-point errors in slice indexing. Collision Detection: Although voxel data is discarded, collision detection is still possible by using the rendered depth values within the shader or on the CPU side. Rendering Artifacts: Grass rendered in screen space may exhibit artifacts, though these can be mitigated. Memory Efficiency: By discarding voxel data after rendering and reusing a single 2D texture buffer, this method significantly reduces VRAM usage compared to storing full 3D textures. Performance: The method allows for the generation of billions of voxels in real-time, leveraging the parallel processing power of the GPU. Scalability: The texture size can be changed in real-time, allowing for dynamic adjustment based on hardware capabilities. Limitations: The method is specific to isometric rendering with a 0.5 slope hexagonal shape, which may not be suitable for all camera angles or rendering styles. When to Use: Ideal for real-time voxel-based rendering where memory is constrained and explicit voxel generation is required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for non-isometric rendering or when implicit volume representation is preferred. This technique was developed by the author of Voxel Quest as part of a 3-year timeline project. It was designed to avoid the use of 3D textures and compression, allowing for explicit generation of every voxel. The method leverages the maximum texture width supported by modern graphics cards (16384) to store a large number of slices in a single 2D texture. name: Post-packing Optimisation
head: Aspect Ratio Packing Optimization, Slice Orientation Standardization
body: Post-packing Optimisation is a corrective stage applied after greedy packing to optimize inefficiently packed layouts by enforcing a global slice orientation, serving as a 'damage control' measure when initial greedy packing fails or increases memory requirements. It addresses the problem of mixed slice orientations (tall vs. wide) in the final 3D texture, which causes significant memory padding waste. Unlike its siblings, which focus on the initial packing strategy, this method operates on the already-packed result to standardize orientations and reduce the overall texture area. Inputs: Set of dataset slices S, aspect ratio threshold ratio. Outputs: Optimised 2D texture dimensions (W, H) and the rotated/repacked slice set. Data Structures: Slice: Contains width, height, and orientation (tall, wide, or square-like). Strategy Cost: Calculated as the total area of the bounding texture for a specific orientation constraint. Steps: 1. Pre-classification: For each slice s \in S, determine if it is "square-like" or "imbalanced" based on the ratio threshold. If |width - height| > ratio \times \min(width, height), label as imbalanced; otherwise, label as square-like. 2. Calculate Potential Strategy Costs: Evaluate two layout strategies: Strategy A (Uniformly Vertical/Tall): Force all imbalanced slices to be tall. WidthA = \sum widths{square} + \sum widths{tall} + \sum heights{wide} HeightA = \sum heights{square} + \sum heights{wide} + \sum widths{tall} AreaA = WidthA \times HeightA Strategy B (Uniformly Horizontal/Wide): Force all imbalanced slices to be wide. WidthB = \sum widths{square} + \sum widths{wide} + \sum heights{tall} HeightB = \sum heights{square} + \sum heights{tall} + \sum widths{wide} AreaB = WidthB \times HeightB Note: The sums include the dimensions of the slices after any necessary rotation to fit the target orientation. 3. Select and Apply Optimal Rotation: Compare AreaA and AreaB. If AreaA \le AreaB: Select Strategy A. Final dimensions are (WidthA, HeightA). For each slice originally classified as "wide", rotate it by 90 degrees and repack it to fit the tall orientation. Else: Select Strategy B. Final dimensions are (WidthB, HeightB). For each slice originally classified as "tall", rotate it by 90 degrees and repack it to fit the wide orientation. Square-like slices remain unchanged. Parameters: ratio: User-defined aspect ratio threshold used to classify slices as square-like or imbalanced. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Datasets: Post-packing acts as a corrective measure but cannot always fully compensate for an inefficient initial layout on very large or sparse datasets. Precision: The rotation step is followed by a repacking process applied only to the affected slices, which reduces post-processing time. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def postpackingoptimization(slices, ratio): """ Optimizes packed slices by standardizing orientation. Args: slices: List of slice objects with 'width' and 'height'. ratio: Aspect ratio threshold for classification. Returns: tuple: (finalwidth, finalheight, optimizedslices) """ squareslices = [] tallslices = [] wideslices = [] # Step 1: Pre-classification for s in slices: mindim = min(s.width, s.height) diff = abs(s.width - s.height) if diff > ratio mindim: # Imbalanced if s.height > s.width: tallslices.append(s) else: wideslices.append(s) else: # Square-like squareslices.append(s) # Step 2: Calculate Potential Strategy Costs # Strategy A: Force all imbalanced to be tall (vertical) # Wide slices must be rotated 90 deg (width becomes height, height becomes width) widthA = sum(s.width for s in squareslices) + sum(s.width for s in tallslices) + sum(s.height for s in wideslices) heightA = sum(s.height for s in squareslices) + sum(s.height for s in wideslices) + sum(s.width for s in tallslices) areaA = widthA heightA # Strategy B: Force all imbalanced to be wide (horizontal) # Tall slices must be rotated 90 deg widthB = sum(s.width for s in squareslices) + sum(s.width for s in wideslices) + sum(s.height for s in tallslices) heightB = sum(s.height for s in squareslices) + sum(s.height for s in tallslices) + sum(s.width for s in wideslices) areaB = widthB heightB # Step 3: Select and Apply Optimal Rotation optimizedslices = [] if areaA <= areaB: # Strategy A: Uniformly Vertical finalwidth = widthA finalheight = heightA for s in squareslices: optimizedslices.append(s) # No change for s in tallslices: optimizedslices.append(s) # No change for s in wideslices: # Rotate wide slices to tall rotateds = Slice(height=s.width, width=s.height) optimizedslices.append(rotateds) else: # Strategy B: Uniformly Horizontal finalwidth = widthB finalheight = heightB for s in squareslices: optimizedslices.append(s) # No change for s in wideslices: optimizedslices.append(s) # No change for s in tallslices: # Rotate tall slices to wide rotateds = Slice(height=s.height, width=s.width) optimizedslices.append(rotateds) return (finalwidth, finalheight, optimizedslices) class Slice: def init(self, width, height): self.width = width self.height = height A specific variant described as a "damage control" measure applied after greedy packing. It enforces a global slice orientation on the layout produced by the greedy packing algorithm to reorganize slices for better memory efficiency. Unlike greedy packing, which degrades on sparse datasets, post-packing can reclaim initial overhead even when the primary algorithm fails, though it cannot always fully compensate for an inefficient initial layout on very large or sparse datasets. On the Head128x128x137 dataset at density threshold t=0.17, post-packing converted a 157.2% memory increase (from greedy packing alone) into a final saving of 74.5%. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithm involves a single pass for classification, a constant-time calculation of two strategy costs, and a single pass for rotation and repacking of the minority group. Repacking is applied only to the affected slices, reducing post-processing time. Memory overhead is significantly reduced by minimizing padding. Measured Performance: On the Head128x128x137 dataset at t=0.17, it converted a 157.2% memory increase into a 74.5% saving. On sparse datasets like Legs512x128x263, performance of the initial greedy packing degrades considerably, but post-packing remains effective in reclaiming initial overhead. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Effective at reducing memory overhead caused by mixed aspect ratios; acts as a robust corrective measure for failed greedy packing. Limitations: Cannot fully compensate for inefficient initial layouts on very large or sparse datasets. The CPU-intensive partitioning and increased number of draw calls can penalize rendering performance on discrete GPUs like the Nvidia 1050M. When to Use: Use when greedy packing results in mixed slice orientations leading to high padding waste. Use as a final corrective step when the initial packing algorithm fails or increases memory requirements. When Not to Use: Avoid on very large or sparse datasets where the initial layout is highly inefficient, as post-packing may not fully recover the overhead. Consider regular 2D packing as an alternative if post-packing is insufficient. Originating from research on hybrid CPU-GPU approaches for memory-efficient volume rendering of medical image data, this method addresses the inefficiencies of greedy packing algorithms when dealing with varying slice aspect ratios. It is particularly relevant in medical imaging where slice dimensions can vary significantly. name: Isotropic Texture Synthesis
head: 2D Texture Synthesis for Volumetric Impression
body: Isotropic texture synthesis generates a 3D volumetric impression by applying standard 2D texture synthesis algorithms to individual cross-sections of a target volume. It solves the problem of creating materials with uniform internal structure (e.g., sponges, sausages) without requiring explicit 3D volumetric data storage or complex orientation constraints. Unlike Cross-section Texture Synthesis with Flow Vectors, which uses flow vectors to enforce directional consistency, this method assumes no dependency on position or orientation, making it significantly faster than full volumetric synthesis techniques. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D reference image containing the desired texture pattern; a selection of a region within this reference image to serve as the sample patch. Output: A 2D texture image representing the cross-section at a specific location and orientation within the 3D model. Data Structures: Reference Image: A 2D array of pixels (color/texture values). Selected Region: A sub-region of the Reference Image defined by the user or system, used as the source patch for synthesis. Target Cross-Section: The 2D output image to be synthesized. Steps: 1. Select Reference Patch: Identify a region in the original reference image that exhibits the desired isotropic texture characteristics. 2. Apply 2D Synthesis Algorithm: Use a standard 2D texture synthesis algorithm to generate a new 2D texture image for the target cross-section, using the selected region as the reference patch. Common algorithms include those by Wei and Levoy (2000), Cohen et al. (2003), or Kwatra et al. (2003). 3. Render Cross-Section: Use the synthesized 2D texture to render the cross-section of the 3D model at the specified location and orientation. Formulas: Not applicable. The method relies on existing 2D synthesis algorithms. Parameters: Synthesis Algorithm: Choice of 2D algorithm (e.g., Wei & Levoy 2000). Reference Region: Size and content of the selected patch from the reference image. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistency: There is no guarantee of obtaining exactly the same image when a model is cut twice at the same cross-section. This is an accepted limitation because the goal is a volumetric impression rather than consistent volumetric data. Performance: Attempting to use full volumetric texture synthesis (e.g., specifying side/top faces and using Wei’s 2001 volumetric technique) is too slow and yields unsatisfactory quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def synthesizeisotropiccrosssection(referenceimage, selectedregion, targetsize): """ Synthesize a 2D texture for a cross-section using 2D texture synthesis. Args: referenceimage: 2D array of pixels (original reference image). selectedregion: Sub-region of referenceimage used as the sample patch. targetsize: Tuple (width, height) for the output cross-section. Returns: 2D array of pixels representing the synthesized cross-section. """ # Apply a standard 2D texture synthesis algorithm (e.g., Wei & Levoy 2000) # using selectedregion as the source patch to generate targetsize output. synthesizedtexture = apply2dtexturesynthesis(selectedregion, targetsize) return synthesizedtexture Synthesizes internal textures using flow vectors to guide sampling, supporting layered and oriented textures. Choose this when orientation or depth-dependent appearance is required. Time Complexity: Fast, as it leverages efficient 2D texture synthesis algorithms. Significantly faster than full 3D volumetric synthesis. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not store explicit 3D volumetric data. Only 2D textures are generated on demand. Strengths: Simple implementation; fast performance; suitable for materials with uniform internal structure (e.g., sponges, sausages). Limitations: No guarantee of cross-section consistency; cannot handle orientation-dependent or depth-varying textures (layered/oriented). When to Use: When creating volumetric impressions for isotropic materials where performance is critical and exact cross-section consistency is not required. When Not to Use: When the material has directional structure (oriented) or depth-dependent appearance (layered), or when consistent volumetric data is needed. Originated in the context of volumetric illustration, where the goal is to convey a volumetric impression rather than generate precise volumetric data. The method was developed as a simpler and faster alternative to full volumetric texture synthesis techniques, which were found to be too slow and produced unsatisfactory quality. It builds on established 2D texture synthesis algorithms. Volumetric illustration, https://doi.org/10.1145/1186562.1015723, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Cross-section Texture Synthesis with Flow Vectors
head: Interactive system for designing and browsing volumetric illustrations, Internal Texture Synthesis, Volumetric Illustration Synthesis, Volumetric Illustration System
body: This method synthesizes internal textures for 3D models by generating cross-sectional images on demand using 2D reference images, rather than storing explicit 3D volumetric data. It solves the problem of manually defining complex internal structures for volumetric illustrations by mapping pixels from a 2D control map (containing flow vectors) to a reference volume, ensuring the synthesized texture matches the local neighborhood structure and orientation defined by the flow. Unlike Isotropic Texture Synthesis, which assumes uniform distribution without orientation dependency, this method supports layered and oriented textures by using flow vectors to guide the sampling geometry in the reference volume. Inputs: 1. A target 3D surface mesh model. 2. A 2D reference image, optionally with a specific region selected by rubber banding. 3. A texture type selection: Isotropic, Layered, or Oriented. 4. Guidance information: None for Isotropic textures; a 2D control map (flow vectors) for Layered and Oriented textures. 5. A 3D reference volume constructed from the reference image based on the texture type. Outputs: A synthesized 2D image representing the internal texture of a specific cross-section of the 3D model. Reference Volume: A 3D data structure storing texture information derived from the 2D reference image. For Isotropic textures: The reference image region is transferred to all faces of a reference cube. For Layered textures: Associated with a vertical flow orientation. For Oriented textures: The volume is sliced at appropriate angles to generate 2D reference images for each pixel. Control Map (Flow Vectors): A 2D array corresponding to the cross-section resolution (approximately 300x300 pixels). Each pixel contains a flow vector defining the local orientation and slant angle for texture synthesis. Multi-resolution Pyramid: Used for similarity comparison during synthesis. For Isotropic and Oriented textures: Three levels. Lower resolution: 3x3 square neighbor. Higher resolution: 5x5 L-shaped neighbor. For Layered textures: Lower resolution uses a 3x3 square neighbor and higher resolution uses a 5x3 rectangular neighbor. Cache: Stores sampled images from the reference volume. Key: Discretized slant angle. Value: Sampled 2D image from the reference volume. 1. Model Preparation: The user cuts the target 3D model using a freeform stroke on the screen, which opens with animation to reveal the cross-section. 2. Region Selection: The cross-section is divided into closed regions, and the user clicks a target region to specify the 3D area to be textured. 3. Texture Type Selection: The user selects one of three types: Isotropic, Layered, or Oriented. 4. Reference Image Import: The user drags a 2D image file into the system and may select a specific region via rubber banding. 5. Reference Volume Construction: For Isotropic textures, the selected region is transferred to all faces of a reference cube; for Layered and Oriented textures, the system constructs a 3D reference volume or prepares slicing parameters based on the flow orientation. 6. Flow Vector Assignment (Layered/Oriented only): The user provides guidance information (flow vectors) for the cross-section, defining the layering direction or slice angle. 7. Cross-section Synthesis: For each pixel in the target cross-section: a. Approximate the pixel's neighborhood as a small flat rectangle. b. Determine the slant angle of this rectangle relative to the flow vector. c. Sample the reference volume to find a corresponding neighborhood. d. Compare similarity between the cross-section neighborhood and the sampled reference neighborhood. e. Select the best matching pixel/region from the reference volume. f. Assign the color to the cross-section pixel. Neighborhood Approximation: For a target pixel p on the cross-section, the neighborhood Np is approximated as a small flat rectangle. Slant Angle Matching: For a pixel q in the reference volume, the sampled neighborhood Nq is a small flat rectangle. The slant angle \thetaq of Nq (angle between the rectangle and the vertical flow vector) must equal the slant angle \thetap of Np on the cross-section: \thetaq = \thetap Similarity Comparison: The system compares the similarity between Np and Nq using multi-resolution pyramids. Caching Key: The slant angle \theta is discretized with a step size of \Delta \theta = \pi/32. The cache key is k = \lfloor \theta / \Delta \theta \rfloor. Sampling Region Size: The slanted 2D square region sampled from the reference volume is 45x45 pixels. Discretization Step: \pi/32 radians for slant angles. Cross-section Resolution: Approximately 300x300 pixels. Neighbor Sizes: Isotropic/Oriented (Low): 3x3 square. Isotropic/Oriented (High): 5x5 L-shaped. Layered (Low): 3x3 square. Layered (High): 5x3 rectangular. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math ISOTROPIC = 0 LAYERED = 1 ORIENTED = 2 SLANTSTEP = math.pi / 32 SAMPLESIZE = 45 def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def norm(v): return math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) def normalize(v): n = norm(v) return [x / n for x in v] if n > 0 else v def emptyimage(width, height): return [[0.0] width for in range(height)] def buildpyramid(image, texturetype): levels = [] current = image for in range(3): levels.append(current) h, w = len(current), len(current[0]) nh, nw = h // 2, w // 2 nextimg = [[0.0] nw for in range(nh)] for y in range(nh): for x in range(nw): nextimg[y][x] = current[2y][2x] current = nextimg return levels def getneighbormask(texturetype, level): if texturetype in (ISOTROPIC, ORIENTED): return [(dy, dx) for dy in (-1, 0, 1) for dx in (-1, 0, 1)] if level == 0 else [(dy, dx) for dy in (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2) for dx in (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2) if abs(dy) + abs(dx) <= 3] else: return [(dy, dx) for dy in (-1, 0, 1) for dx in (-1, 0, 1)] if level == 0 else [(dy, dx) for dy in (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2) for dx in (-1, 0, 1)] def computesimilarity(patch1, patch2, mask): diff = 0.0 count = 0 for dy, dx in mask: diff += abs(patch1[dy][dx] - patch2[dy][dx]) count += 1 return diff / count if count > 0 else float('inf') def findbestmatch(neighborhood, refimage, texturetype): pyramids = [buildpyramid(neighborhood, texturetype), buildpyramid(refimage, texturetype)] bestoffset = (0, 0) bestscore = float('inf') for level in range(3): mask = getneighbormask(texturetype, level) h, w = len(pyramids[0][level]), len(pyramids[0][level][0]) rh, rw = len(pyramids[1][level]), len(pyramids[1][level][0]) for y in range(rh -
