SAMPLESIZE/2) / SAMPLESIZE, (sy - SAMPLESIZE/2) / SAMPLESIZE planenormal = normalize([math.cos(slantangle), math.sin(slantangle), 0]) point3d = [u, v, 0] color = referencevolume.sample(point3d) sampledref[sy][sx] = color cache[discretizedangle] = sampledref sampledref = cache[discretizedangle] offset = findbestmatch(neighborhoodcross, sampledref, texturetype) synthesizedimage[py][px] = sampledref[offset[0]][offset[1]] return synthesizedimage Rotation Ambiguity: Rotation about the flow vector is ignored because the reference volume is assumed to have an isotropic structure on cross-sections perpendicular to the flow orientation. Cascading Resampling: Quality issues arise due to cascading resampling and resulting distortion. Performance: Layered and oriented textures require more computation than standard texture synthesis because layered textures require rotating neighbors and oriented textures require generating a 2D reference image by slicing the reference volume at an appropriate angle for each pixel. Boundary Conditions: The sampling region is 45×45 pixels, which is chosen to fit within the reference volume completely. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in Big-O notation. Synthesis times vary by model and texture type. On a Pentium M 1.6-GHz processor with 1 GB RAM: Meat: 22 sec, Cucumber: 4 sec, Bamboo: 14 sec, Stomach: 18 sec, Tooth: 32 sec. Memory Complexity: The data size is significantly smaller than explicit volumetric data. For a 300x300 cross-section, the quality is comparable to 300^3 colored voxels (approx. 80 MB storage), but the actual model data is much smaller (e.g., Meat: 622 kb, Cucumber: 53 kb, Bamboo: 291 kb, Stomach: 402 kb, Tooth: 307 kb). Strengths: Significantly reduces data storage requirements compared to explicit 3D volumetric data. Allows designers to add 3D internal textures without specifying each voxel manually. Supports interactive modeling with progressive synthesis. Limitations: Computational cost is higher for layered and oriented textures compared to isotropic. Quality issues due to cascading resampling and distortion. Cannot be used for applications requiring real volumetric data, such as translucent rendering or volumetric simulation. When to Use: Suitable for creating lightweight volumetric illustrations for communication purposes (e.g., education, medical visualization) where explicit volumetric data is not required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for applications requiring accurate volumetric properties like translucency or simulation. Origin: Proposed in 2004 by the authors of "Volumetric Illustration". History: The system builds on previous work in texture synthesis (Heeger and Bergen 1995, Wei 2001) and 3D texture mapping (Turk 2001, Praun et al. 2000). It addresses the difficulty of designing detailed internal textures of 3D volumes using standard 2D devices. Applications: Useful for conveying volumetric information between teachers and students, doctors and patients, or virtual-reality content providers and consumers. name: Alpha Texturing (Billboarding)
head: Alpha Masking
body: Alpha Texturing (Billboarding) renders complex, high-frequency geometry (such as vegetation) as simple 2D primitives (rectangles) textured with RGBA maps, where the alpha channel defines visibility. It differs from general volume slicing methods by treating the "volume" as a collection of discrete, opaque/translucent surfaces rather than a continuous scalar field, relying on static textures rather than dynamic slice generation. Inputs: A set of 2D RGBA texture maps; simple geometric primitives (typically quads or triangles) representing the proxy geometry. Outputs: A rasterized image where transparent regions of the texture allow background visibility. Data Structures: RGBA Texture: A 2D array of pixels, each containing four components: Red, Green, Blue, and Alpha (A). Primitive: A polygon defined by vertices in screen or object space. Steps: 1. Primitive Selection: Define a simple geometric primitive (e.g., a rectangle) that approximates the silhouette or extent of the complex object. 2. Texture Application: Bind an RGBA texture map to the primitive. 3. Alpha Definition: Set the alpha channel values to define visibility: A = 1 (or maximum opacity) for visible parts (e.g., leaves, branches). A = 0 (or minimum opacity) for transparent parts (e.g., gaps, open space). 4. Rasterization: Render the primitive. The graphics hardware interpolates the texture coordinates and samples the RGBA values. 5. Compositing: Fragments are composited using alpha blending. The alpha channel controls the contribution of the source color to the destination buffer. Formulas: The final color C{final} for a fragment is determined by the texture color C{tex} and alpha A{tex}: C{final} = C{tex} \cdot A{tex} + C{bg} \cdot (1 - A{tex}) where C{bg} is the background color. Parameters: Alpha Threshold: Values near 0 are treated as fully transparent; values near 1 as fully opaque. Edge Cases: Blending Artifacts: Naive blending of multiple billboards from different views can cause blurring or ghosting artifacts if view-dependent textures are not used. Order Independence: While standard alpha blending requires depth sorting, billboards for vegetation are often sorted back-to-front to ensure correct transparency. Reconstructs trees from photographs using view-dependent billboards to preserve high-frequency color details, solving the blurring artifacts of static alpha texturing. Performance: Extremely fast for rendering complex geometry as it reduces high-polygon models to simple quads. Memory: Requires storage for RGBA textures, which can be large for high-resolution details. Limitations: Static alpha texturing suffers from view-dependent artifacts (blurring) when the camera moves, as the 2D texture cannot represent the full 3D structure. It is best suited for vegetation or foliage where the structure is dense and view-dependent variations are minimal or can be approximated. Alpha texturing for billboarding was introduced as a common trick in computer graphics to render complex geometry like trees efficiently. It leverages the RGBA texture map's alpha channel to simulate transparency without explicit geometric complexity. Chapter 7 - Advanced Computer Graphics - VTK, https://examples.vtk.org/site/VTKBook/07Chapter7/, fetched 2026-10-29 (book)

name: Volumetric Tree Reconstruction via Opacity Estimation and View-Dependent Texturing
head: Opacity Estimation and View-Dependent Texturing for Trees
body: This method reconstructs and renders trees from a set of photographs by estimating isotropic discrete opacity values on a recursive grid and rendering using view-dependent billboards to preserve high-frequency color details. It solves the problem of rendering complex, high-frequency vegetation geometry efficiently by decoupling the low-frequency volumetric structure (opacity) from the high-frequency appearance (color). Unlike its parent Alpha Texturing (Billboarding), which uses static RGBA textures, this method generates view-dependent textures for each volumetric cell to prevent the blurring artifacts caused by naive blending between multiple camera views. Inputs: A set of N photographs (N \approx 20-30) of a tree against a distinct background. Camera calibration data for each photograph. Alpha masks for each photograph, extracted via alpha matting. "Pure foreground" color images Cf derived from the alpha matting process. Outputs: A recursive grid where each cell i has an estimated opacity \alphai (or transparency ti = 1 - \alphai). A set of billboard textures T{i,c} for each cell c and each input image i, sized M \times M. Grid Cell: opacity (\alphai): Float, opacity of the cell. transparency (ti): Float, 1 - \alphai. deltatransparency (\delta ti): Float, accumulated update for the current iteration. weight (w): Float, accumulated weight for normalization. Image Data: alphaimage: 2D array of floats, values in [0, 1]. pureforeground: 2D array of RGB values in LAB color space. workingimage: A mutable copy of the RGBA image used during texture generation to track occluded pixels. Number of photographs: 20-30. Billboard texture size (M): Typically 4 or 8. Convergence threshold: Iteration stops when the change in ti values is less than a specified threshold. Transparency cutoff threshold: If ti exceeds this value, the cell is considered transparent (ti=1) and ignored. Typical iterations: 3-4 iterations are sufficient for convergence. 1. Photograph the tree against a distinct background (e.g., sky) from approximately 20-30 different viewpoints. 2. Calibrate the cameras using a standard algorithm (e.g., REALVIZ ImageModeler). 3. For each photograph, extract an alpha mask \alphap for each pixel p using the Ruzon and Tomasi algorithm. This requires user-specified foreground and background zones. 4. Compute the "pure foreground" color Cf for each pixel. For pixels with \alphap \in (0, 1), the pixel color Cp is modeled in LAB color space as: Cp = \alphap Cf + (1 - \alphap) Cb where Cb is the background color. Solve for Cf and store it in the pureforeground image. Pixels with \alphap = 0 or 1 are handled accordingly (background or pure foreground). 1. Initialize a recursive grid covering the tree volume. 2. For each grid cell i, project it into each alpha-image. 3. Calculate the average opacity value of the cell's projection in each image. 4. Set the initial opacity \alphai of the cell to the minimum of these average opacity values across all images. This corresponds to initializing transparency ti. 5. Initialize \delta ti = 0 and w = 0 for all cells. Iterate until convergence (change in ti < \text{threshold}): 1. Reset \delta ti = 0 and w = 0 for all cells i. 2. For each image k: a. For each pixel p in the image: i. Cast a ray from the camera through the pixel into the grid. ii. Identify the list of intersected cells i=0 \dots n (ordered front-to-back). iii. Construct the vector Q = (q0, q1, \dots, qn) where qi = \log(ti). iv. Calculate the target log-transparency qp = \log(tp), where tp = 1 - \alphap is the transparency of the pixel. v. Project the vector Q onto the plane P defined by normal N = (1, 1, \dots, 1) and intercept qp. The projection Q' = (q'0, q'1, \dots, q'n) minimizes the distance to the plane. vi. For each cell i in the ray: Calculate the update component: \delta qi = q'i - qi. Convert back to transparency domain. The source defines the update to transparency \delta ti based on the projection. Specifically, the source states: \deltai = wi (t'i - ti) where t'i is derived from q'i. Note: The source pseudocode uses \deltai = wi (t'i - ti) directly after projection, implying t'i = \exp(q'i). Accumulate the update: \delta ti \leftarrow \delta ti + \deltai. Accumulate weight: w \leftarrow w + wi. (Note: The source pseudocode implies wi is a weight associated with the cell/pixel contribution, though the exact definition of wi is not explicitly detailed beyond its use in the update formula. In the absence of a specific weight function, wi is treated as a scalar weight for the contribution of cell i to pixel p). 3. After processing all pixels in all images, update the transparency values for each cell i: ti \leftarrow ti + \frac{\delta ti}{w} If ti > \text{transparency cutoff threshold}, set ti = 1 (transparent) and mark the cell as ignored. 1. For each cell c and each image i: a. Create an M \times M billboard texture T{i,c}. b. Project the cell c onto the image plane of image i. c. Extract the corresponding region from the pureforeground image Cf. d. Heuristic for Occlusion Handling: To avoid double-counting and blurring: i. Make a copy Ci of the current state of the image (initially the pureforeground image). ii. Process cells in a specific order (e.g., front-to-back relative to the camera). iii. For the current cell, mask out only the texels corresponding to the cell's projection. iv. Assign these masked texels to the billboard texture T{i,c}. v. Update the copy Ci: remove the texels just assigned (set to background or transparent) to ensure subsequent cells do not use the same pixels. 2. Rendering: a. For each view, sort the billboards back-to-front. b. For each billboard, render the texture T{i,c} (where i is the closest or most appropriate camera view, or blended if necessary, though the method prefers single-view textures per cell to avoid blurring). c. Use the estimated opacity \alphac of the cell as the alpha value for the billboard. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructtree(photos, cameracalibrations, alphamasks, pureforegroundimages): """ Reconstructs tree opacity and generates billboards. """ # 1. Initialization grid = initializerecursivegrid() # Initialize opacities based on minimum average alpha from all views for cell in grid: alphas = [] for photoidx, alphamask in enumerate(alphamasks): projectedalpha = projectcelltoimage(cell, cameracalibrations[photoidx], alphamask) alphas.append(mean(projectedalpha)) cell.opacity = min(alphas) cell.transparency = 1.0 - cell.opacity cell.deltatransparency = 0.0 cell.weight = 0.0 # 2. Iteration Loop while not converged(grid): # Reset accumulators for cell in grid: cell.deltatransparency = 0.0 cell.weight = 0.0 # Process each image and pixel for photoidx, alphamask in enumerate(alphamasks): for pixel in alphamask: ray = castraythroughgrid(pixel, cameracalibrations[photoidx]) hitcells = ray.intersectedcells # Ordered front-to-back if not hitcells: continue # Vector Q of log-transparencies Q = [log(cell.transparency) for cell in hitcells] targettransparency = 1.0 - pixel.alpha targetlogt = log(targettransparency) # Project Q onto plane P (normal N=(1,1,...,1), intercept targetlogt) # The projection Q' minimizes distance to the plane sum(qi) = targetlogt # In the source, this is described as a direct projection. # A standard projection of vector Q onto a hyperplane with normal N and intercept d: # Q' = Q - ((N. Q - d) / (N. N)) N N = [1.0] len(hitcells) dotNQ = sum(Q) dotNN = len(N) factor = (dotNQ - targetlogt) / dotNN Qprime = [Q[i] - factor N[i] for i in range(len(N))] # Calculate updates for idx, cell in enumerate(hitcells): tprime = exp(Qprime[idx]) tcurrent = cell.transparency # Weight wi is not explicitly defined in sources, assumed to be 1 or normalized later # Source pseudocode: deltai = wi (t'i - ti) # Assuming uniform weight for simplicity as per "w += wi" accumulation wi = 1.0 deltat = wi (tprime - tcurrent) cell.deltatransparency += deltat cell.weight += wi # Update grid transparencies for cell in grid: if cell.weight > 0: cell.transparency += cell.deltatransparency / cell.weight # Transparency cutoff if cell.transparency > TRANSPARENCYCUTOFFTHRESHOLD: cell.transparency = 1.0 cell.opacity = 0.0 # 3. Texture Generation billboards = {} # Sort cells for texture extraction (e.g., front-to-back per view or global order) # The source implies processing cells to mask out used pixels in a working image copy for photoidx, purefgimg in enumerate(pureforegroundimages): workingimage = copy(purefgimg) # Iterate through cells. Order matters for the "remove front texels" heuristic. # Assuming a global order or sorted by depth from this camera. for cell in grid: if cell.opacity == 0: continue # Project cell to image projectedregion = projectcelltoimageregion(cell, cameracalibrations[photoidx]) # Extract texture from workingimage # Mask out only the part corresponding to this cell texture = extracttexture(workingimage, projectedregion) # Store billboard billboards[(cell.id, photoidx)] = texture # Update workingimage: remove texels corresponding to this cell # to avoid double counting for subsequent cells updateworkingimage(workingimage, projectedregion, isopaque=False) return grid, billboards def converged(grid): maxchange = 0.0 for cell in grid: # In a real implementation, we'd track previous ti to measure change # Here we assume the loop condition is handled by an external counter or threshold check pass return maxchange < CONVERGENCETHRESHOLD Time Complexity: The reconstruction involves an iterative loop. Each iteration processes all pixels in all images. For each pixel, a ray cast and a projection onto an n-dimensional plane (where n is the number of cells intersected by the ray) are performed. The projection step is O(n) per pixel. Total time per iteration is O(P \cdot n{avg}), where P is the total number of pixels and n{avg} is the average number of cells per ray. Convergence is typically reached in 3-4 iterations. Memory Complexity: Grid storage: O(C), where C is the number of cells. Texture storage: O(C \cdot N \cdot M^2), where N is the number of images and M is the billboard texture size (typically 4 or 8). Measured Performance: Processing time: 3-5 minutes on a Pentium IV 2.7 GHz PC for the tested models. Calibration time: Less than 10 minutes for about 20 images using markers. Strengths: Preserves high-frequency color details from the original photographs. Avoids the severe blurring artifacts associated with naive view-dependent texturing (blending between n closest cameras). Efficient rendering using simple billboards. Limitations: Requires a distinct background for alpha matting. Assumes isotropic opacity, which may not capture all anisotropic properties of foliage. The method is under-constrained; it finds a "best-fit" solution which may tend towards a local minimum. Texture generation requires careful handling of occlusion (front-to-back processing) to avoid double-counting. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Volumetric reconstruction and interactive rendering of trees from photographs". History and Development: The approach builds upon the concept of alpha texturing (billboarding) [10768-alpha-texturing-billboarding.md] but addresses its limitations regarding view-dependent color. It utilizes alpha matting techniques (Ruzon and Tomasi) and volume rendering equations (Max) to estimate opacity. The logarithmic transformation of the transparency product into a sum allows for efficient linear projection-based optimization. Applications: Primarily used for the realistic rendering of trees and vegetation in computer graphics, particularly in urban environments where trees can be photographed against a sky background. Volumetric reconstruction and interactive rendering of trees from photographs, https://doi.org/10.1145/1015706.1015785, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Vegetation-Specific Slicing
body: Vegetation-Specific Slicing is a family of rendering techniques for plant structures that replaces high-complexity polygonal meshes with image-based representations to achieve real-time performance. It sets itself apart from general texture slicing by decomposing vegetation into structural components (solid meshes versus sparse planar slices) and leveraging hardware compositing for efficient transparency accumulation. Fiber Surface Texturing is a method for visualizing fiber fields on tetrahedral meshes by mapping fiber path parameters to 1D textures see Fiber Surface Texturing. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Regular Texcell Slicing with Non-Linear Pre-filtering by using 1D texture lookups driven by global fiber path length rather than 2D alpha-blended slices, allowing for efficient representation of continuous fiber trajectories across complex mesh boundaries see Fiber Surface Texturing. Choose it when rendering sparse, directional data (fibers) within volumetric elements see Fiber Surface Texturing. Regular Texcell Slicing is a vegetation-specific volume rendering technique that represents forest canopies as a stack of ground-parallel planar slices (texcells) stored in a 2D texture pyramid see Regular Texcell Slicing with Non-Linear Pre-filtering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods that may use explicit geometry or 3D textures by relying on pre-computed 2D alpha-premultiplied textures blended offline to create coarser LODs, ensuring correct transparency accumulation and efficient hardware rendering see Regular Texcell Slicing with Non-Linear Pre-filtering. Choose it for large-scale forest scenes requiring efficient Level of Detail (LOD) management and filtering see Regular Texcell Slicing with Non-Linear Pre-filtering. A simplified image-based rendering approach for vegetation that uses alpha-blended textured polygons to represent sparse parts (twigs and leaves) as a set of parallel planar layers called slices, while using ordinary mesh-based rendering for solid parts (trunk and limbs). It renders dozens of detailed trees in real-time with off-the-shelf hardware, providing significantly improved image quality over existing real-time techniques. Rendering from an arbitrary viewpoint in a 360-degree circle around the tree center is achieved by blending between the nearest two slicings. In implementation, only 6 slicings with 5 slices each are sufficient to visualize a tree for a moving or stationary observer with perceptually similar quality to the original model. The techniques within this family address the challenges of interactive 3D rendering of vegetation, which is computationally expensive due to large geometric complexity even for simple plants. The foundational work on "Slicing and Blending for Vegetation Rendering" was introduced to provide a simplified image-based rendering approach based on the limitations of human perception of complex geometry. This allows for real-time rendering of dozens of detailed trees using standard hardware. The specific methods for fiber surface texturing and regular texcell slicing extend these principles to handle specific data structures, as detailed in Fiber Surface Texturing and Regular Texcell Slicing with Non-Linear Pre-filtering. Interactive Vegetation Rendering with Slicing and Blending, https://core.ac.uk/download/11677641.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Fiber Surface Texturing
head: Fiber Surface Texture Mapping
body: Fiber Surface Texturing visualizes fiber fields on tetrahedral meshes by mapping fiber path parameters to a 1D texture map. It renders sparse, directional data by treating the fiber surface as a textured polygon rather than explicit geometry, leveraging texture hardware on a video card. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tetrahedral mesh containing a Fiber Surface Curve Path (FSCP) defined by edges; a 1D texture map. Output: Rasterized image of the fiber surface with appropriate texture mapping. Data Structures: FSCP Edge: Defined by vertices u and v. 1D Texture: A 1D array of color values where black values (0,0,0) indicate a fiber to be drawn and white values (1,1,1) indicate no fiber. Steps: 1. Segment Processing: The algorithm processes each segment of the FSCP separately. 2. Vertex Parameterization: For a segment defined by vertices u and v, assign the local parameter t=0 to vertex u and t=1 to vertex v. Parameterize all vertices in the triangles forming the fiber surface to the segment's local scale. 3. Global Mapping: Map each vertex's local parameter to a global range [0,1] representing the total length of the fiber path. 4. Texture Lookup: During rasterization, interpolate the global texture coordinates across each triangle. 5. Rendering: Sample the 1D texture at the interpolated coordinate; render black if the value indicates a fiber, otherwise render nothing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfibersurface(triangles, fscpedges, texturemap, texturewidth): # 1. Compute cumulative edge lengths to normalize to global [0,1] cumulative = [0.0] for edge in fscpedges: cumulative.append(cumulative[-1] + vectorlength(edge.u, edge.v)) total = cumulative[-1] # 2. Assign global texture coordinates to vertices vertext = {} for i, edge in enumerate(fscpedges): vertext[edge.u] = cumulative[i] / total vertext[edge.v] = cumulative[i+1] / total # 3. Rasterize triangles with interpolated coordinates image = [] for tri in triangles: t0, t1, t2 = vertext[tri.v0], vertext[tri.v1], vertext[tri.v2] # Standard triangle rasterization for pixel in rasterizetriangle(tri): b0, b1, b2 = barycentricweights(pixel, tri) t = t0 b0 + t1 b1 + t2 b2 idx = clamp(int(t texturewidth), 0, texturewidth - 1) if texturemap[idx] == BLACK: image.append((pixel.x, pixel.y, BLACK)) return image def vectorlength(p1, p2): return ((p1.x-p2.x)2 + (p1.y-p2.y)2 + (p1.z-p2.z)2)0.5 def clamp(v, mn, mx): return max(mn, min(mx, v)) def rasterizetriangle(tri): # Standard pixel grid generation return [] def barycentricweights(p, tri): # Standard barycentric calculation return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Parameters: Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Color Mapping: Black for fiber, white for empty. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Bends: Regions where the original fiber surface algorithm is inaccurate are precisely at sharp bends in the polygon. Precision: Mapping vertex parameters to the global range [0,1] requires careful floating-point handling to avoid discontinuities at segment boundaries. A shading technique for Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) that applies procedural or triplanar textures to kernel solids to eliminate observable repetitiveness. It addresses the visual artifact where applying identical coordinates to all kernel instances produces an extremely repetitive pattern that undesirably emphasizes symmetries. It sets itself apart from standard parametric texturing by handling complex or reflective kernels where simple u,v parametrization is not feasible. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient use of hardware texture mapping; allows for easy visualization of fiber path length and continuity. Limitations: Inaccuracies of the underlying algorithm are visible at sharp bends; binary texture mapping limits shading complexity. When to Use: When visualizing fiber paths on tetrahedral meshes is required, and the primary interest is in the trajectory and continuity of fibers rather than volumetric density. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity volumetric rendering of fiber density is needed, or when the mesh has significant geometric inaccuracies at sharp bends. The method uses texture hardware on a video card to render fiber surfaces efficiently. It builds on assigning texture parameters to vertices based on their position along the FSCP. The approach simultaneously shows how fibers change across the surface and which regions correspond to domain values, indicating that topological analysis of fibers may provide further insight. Fast and Exact Fiber Surfaces for Tetrahedral Meshes, https://hal.science/hal-01206120v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: KRS Texturing
body:
KRS Texturing is a shading technique for Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) that applies procedural or triplanar textures to kernel solids to eliminate observable repetitiveness. It addresses the visual artifact where applying identical coordinates to all kernel instances produces an extremely repetitive pattern that undesirably emphasizes symmetries. It sets itself apart from standard parametric texturing by handling complex or reflective kernels where simple u,v parametrization is not feasible. Inputs and outputs: Not given in the sources. Data structures: Kernel solids are defined by a distance function d(\mathbf{x}) and its gradient 
abla d(\mathbf{x}). Transformation chains maintain the composition of Möbius transformations (\mathcal{L}{Gi}) and reflections (\mathcal{L}R) to map world space to kernel space. Steps: 1. Determine parametrization feasibility: Check if the kernel solid allows simple u,v parametrization. 2. Select texturing method: Apply standard u,v parametrization for simple kernel solids, or procedural/triplanar texturing for complex or reflective kernels. 3. Eliminate repetition: Apply procedural 3D or triplanar texturing to eliminate observable repetitiveness. Combine procedural geometry and procedural or wrapped textures to further eliminate repetitiveness. 4. Sample texture: Evaluate the texture function at the transformed coordinate. 5. Shading: Combine the texture color with lighting calculations. Formulas: Triplanar blending projects the world-space position onto the xy, yz, and xz planes, samples each, and blends based on the surface normal's dominant axis: C =  rac{C{xy} |nz| + C{yz} |nx| + C{xz} |ny|}{|nx| + |ny| + |nz|} where C{xy}, C{yz}, C{xz} are texture samples and nx, ny, nz are normal components. Gradient transformation: To shade in world space, transform the kernel gradient 
abla d{	ext{kernel}} to world space 
abla d{	ext{world}} using the Jacobian of the transformation chain \mathcal{T}, as detailed in Appendix C of the source. Parameters: Texture scale and triplanar blend factors are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texturing all kernel instances with the same coordinates produces an extremely repetitive pattern, emphasizing symmetries undesirably. If kernel separation is not upheld, surface normals may be discontinuous at mirror planes; these can be smoothed by interpolating between kernel-to-world-space matrices on the two sides of a mirror when the shaded point is near a mirror plane. A KRS variant where expansion levels are conformally transformed unions of kernel sets and reflected instances, using Möbius transformations to eliminate symmetry. It models natural features using conformal distortions to compensate for scale variation loss in isometries. To ray-trace, for every expansion level, the current ray point is transformed with \mathcal{L}{Gi} to symmetry space, then to kernel space with the identity or \mathcal{L}R based on a mirror side test. It uses speculative sphere tracing (Binary Sphere Tracing) for conformally mapped geometries. Spheres or infinite planes are sufficient kernel sets. The iteration formula is L{i+1} = \mathcal{L}{\mathbf{G}i}(K{i+1} \cup Li \cup \mathcal{L}{\mathbf{R}}(Li)), where \mathcal{L}R is a Möbius transformation with matrix \mathbf{R} =  egin{bmatrix} -i & 0 \ 0 & i \end{bmatrix}, representing reflection across the x=0 plane. Smooth shading and procedural or triplanar texturing are applied to enhance visual quality. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Measured performance, scaling, strengths, limitations, and usage guidelines are not given in the sources. KRS Texturing was introduced as part of the Kernel-Reflection Sequences framework, which allows for the generation of complex, fractal-like geometries using simple kernel solids and reflection rules. The method was developed to address the visual limitations of early KRS rendering, specifically the repetitive patterns caused by uniform texturing across symmetric instances. It builds on the mathematical foundation of Möbius transformations and conformal geometry, enabling the modeling of natural features with scale-invariant properties. name: Regular Texcell Slicing with Non-Linear Pre-filtering
head: Regular texcells, Slices parallel to ground
body: Regular Texcell Slicing is a vegetation-specific volume rendering method that represents forest coverage using a stack of 2D textures (texcells) extruded vertically from a ground-plane triangle. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large numbers of trees by avoiding CPU-side polygon generation for slice geometry and bypassing the blurring artifacts associated with isotropic 3D texture MIP-mapping at grazing angles. It sets itself apart from its parent, Vegetation-Specific Slicing, by using ground-parallel slices and non-linear pre-filtering to manage levels of detail, and from its sibling, Fiber Surface Texturing, by using volumetric alpha-blending rather than surface geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D polygonal representation of forest geometry (trees/leaves). Output: A Level of Detail (LOD) pyramid of 2D alpha-premultiplied textures, and a rendering pipeline that slices these textures based on view distance and angle. Data Structures: The method uses a pyramid of texture sets Si, where i ranges from 0 (coarsest) to N (finest). Level SN (Finest): Contains n = 2^N slices. Each slice is a 2D texture of size L \times L. Level Si (Coarser): Contains 2^i slices. Each slice is a 2D texture of size L \cdot 2^{N-i} \times L \cdot 2^{N-i}. Texture Format: Alpha-premultiplied color. The color component C \in \{R, G, B\} stores C \times A. Denoted as \bar{C}. MIP-mapping: Each 2D texture in every level is MIP-mapped to handle filtering within the slice plane. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate Finest Level (SN): Render n = 2^N slices of the original 3D volume geometry using an orthographic camera looking down (parallel to the vertical axis \vec{z}). For each slice location, set the near and far clipping planes at distance \delta/2 above and below the slice center, where \delta is the vertical spacing between slices. Render the geometry into an L \times L texture. Store these n textures as level SN. 2. Generate Coarser Levels (Si for i < N): Construct level Si from level S{i+1} by blending pairs of adjacent slices. For each j from 0 to 2^i - 1: Retrieve slice S{i+1}[2j] (front) and S{i+1}[2j+1] (back). Blend them using the standard alpha-compositing equation for premultiplied colors: \bar{C}{result} = \bar{C}{front} + (1 - A{front}) \cdot \bar{C}{back} The resulting texture becomes Si[j]. Apply MIP-mapping to each resulting 2D texture in level Si. 3. Rendering Setup (Vertex Shader): Define a base triangle on the ground with vertices P1, P2, P3. Extrude this vertically to form a prism. Calculate the opacity multiply factor \piA for each vertex to correct for grazing angles: \piA = sz \cdot \frac{\vec{N} \cdot \vec{z}}{|\vec{N} \cdot \vec{V}|} Where: sz is the vertical scaling factor (ratio of mapped forest height to original sample height). \vec{N} is the terrain normal. \vec{z} is the vertical vector (0, 1, 0). \vec{V} is the view direction. Interpolate \piA across the face during rasterization. 4. Rendering Execution: Determine the number of slices to use based on distance to observer and incidence angle. Select the appropriate LOD level Si such that the slice spacing matches the desired sampling rate. Render the base triangle with the selected texture set. Modulate the texture color by the interpolated \piA factor. Use hardware anisotropic filtering for best quality if available. Parameters: N: Logarithm of the number of finest slices. n = 2^N. L: Base texture resolution (e.g., 256, 512). \delta: Vertical distance between slices in the finest level. Pattern Count: At least 8 aperiodic patterns are required for tiling to avoid repetitiveness and handle precomputed shading/shadows without rotation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grazing Angles: At grazing angles, the distance between slices along a ray (\deltav) increases, but the same number of slices are traversed. This leads to incorrect total opacity (under-sampling) if not scaled. The opacity adjustment formula A(dl) \approx \frac{dl}{\delta} A(\delta) must be used, clamping values > 1. 3D Texture MIP-mapping: Standard 3D texture MIP-mapping is isotropic and blurs volume data in the slicing direction at grazing angles. This method avoids 3D textures for regular texcells by using 2D textures and non-linear pre-filtering. Clipping Planes: When generating slices, objects outside the clip volume must still cast shadows if shadows are enabled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. N = 8 # Example: 256 finest slices L = 256 # Base texture size delta = 0.1 # Vertical spacing in finest level SN = [] for j in range(2N): slicey = j delta # Set clipping planes at slicey - delta/2 and slicey + delta/2 texture = renderorthographicslice(geometry, y=slicey, near=delta/2, far=delta/2) SN.append(texture) LODPyramid = [SN] currentlevel = SN for i in range(N - 1, -1, -1): nextlevel = currentlevel currentlevel = [] numslices = 2i for j in range(numslices): fronttex = nextlevel[2 j] backtex = nextlevel[2 j + 1] # Blend using alpha compositing for premultiplied colors # Cbarresult = Cbarfront + (1 - Afront) Cbarback blendedtex = blendpremultiplied(fronttex, backtex) # MIP-map the resulting 2D texture mipmappedtex = generatemipmaps(blendedtex) currentlevel.append(mipmappedtex) LODPyramid.append(currentlevel) def rendertexcell(basetrianglevertices, viewdirection, terrainnormal, verticalscaling, distance): # Determine LOD level based on distance and angle # This is a simplified heuristic; real implementation uses specific criteria i = calculatelodindex(distance, viewdirection, terrainnormal) textureset = LODPyramid[i] numslices = len(textureset) # Calculate opacity factor for vertices # piA = sz (N. z) / |N. V| # Note: In practice, this is done per-vertex in the shader # Here we compute it for the triangle center for illustration Ndotz = dot(terrainnormal, vec3(0, 1, 0)) NdotV = dot(terrainnormal, viewdirection) if abs(NdotV) < 1e-6: piA = 1.0 # Avoid division by zero else: piA = verticalscaling (Ndotz / abs(NdotV)) # Clamp opacity factor piA = min(piA, 1.0) # Render the triangle with the texture set # The vertex shader interpolates piA and selects texture coordinates # from the appropriate slice in textureset based on depth rendertrianglewithvolumetrictextures(basetrianglevertices, textureset, piA) def blendpremultiplied(tex1, tex2): """ Blends two alpha-premultiplied textures. tex1 is front, tex2 is back. """ result = emptytexture(tex1.width, tex1.height) for x, y in pixels: c1 = tex1.getcolor(x, y) # Premultiplied a1 = tex1.getalpha(x, y) c2 = tex2.getcolor(x, y) # Premultiplied # Formula: Cbarfront + (1 - Afront) Cbarback cresult = c1 + (1.0 - a1) c2 aresult = a1 + (1.0 - a1) tex2.getalpha(x, y) # Standard alpha comp for alpha channel result.setcolor(x, y, cresult) result.setalpha(x, y, aresult) return result A variant for landscape silhouettes (grazing angles) where slices are nearly facing the viewer. It uses a tilted base triangle offset to generate slices on the GPU, avoiding CPU polygon generation. It differs from regular texcells by using 3D textures with adapted MIP-map levels to mitigate isotropic blurring, though 3D texture MIP-mapping has known implementation bugs. The base triangle is tilted to face the camera by calculating offsets ki = -\frac{\overline{GPi} \cdot \overline{V}}{\overline{z} \cdot \overline{V}}, and slices are generated by offsetting this tilted base. A maximum slant kM is often applied to prevent infinite slant at extreme grazing angles. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(n \cdot L^2) for generating the finest level, and O(n \cdot L^2) for generating coarser levels (blending). Rendering is O(1) per triangle, independent of the number of trees, as the complexity is in the texture generation, not the draw call. Memory Complexity: O(n \cdot L^2) for the finest level, with geometric series reduction for coarser levels. Total memory is roughly 1.33 \times the finest level size. Performance: High performance for real-time rendering of thousands of trees. Avoids CPU-GPU transfer bottlenecks by generating slice geometry on the GPU (vertex shader) or using pre-generated 2D textures. Strengths: Efficient LOD management via non-linear pre-filtering. No CPU-side polygon generation for slices. Good quality at normal incidence angles. Limitations: Parallax error and visibility of slice boundaries at grazing angles. Requires careful opacity adjustment. 3D texture MIP-mapping bugs in hardware may affect the silhouette variant. When to Use: Real-time forest rendering where performance is critical and view angles are mostly not grazing. When Not to Use: Scenes with extreme grazing angles (use Silhouette Texcell Slicing instead) or when isotropic 3D texture MIP-mapping artifacts are unacceptable without the silhouette variant. Originated in the paper "Rendering Forest Scenes in Real-Time" (2004) by Magnenat et al. The method was developed to address the limitations of existing volume rendering techniques for real-time forest visualization, specifically the high cost of polygonal rendering and the quality issues of 3D texture MIP-mapping. It builds on earlier work in volumetric textures [MN98, LPFH01] and alpha-premultiplied color blending [PD84]. The term "texcell" was coined to distinguish from "texel" (texture element) and avoid confusion with texture pixels. name: Slice-by-Slice Backprojection
head: Kajiya/Von Herzen Backprojection, Parallel Ray Backprojection
body: Slice-by-Slice Backprojection reorganizes the backprojection integral into a single sweep through the volume, processing it one horizontal slice at a time. It is designed for cloud-like volumes illuminated by parallel light rays, such as sunlight. It builds on Texture slicing by reordering the computation to march rays through the volume slice-by-slice. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume density field and a parallel light direction vector (e.g., sunlight). Output: Light intensity distribution within the volume. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Reorganize the backprojection integral into a single sweep through the volume, processing it slice-by-slice. 2. Define a series of parallel horizontal slicing planes intersecting the volume bounding box. 3. Iterate through each slice plane from the light source direction toward the receiver. 4. For each slice, calculate the light intensity contribution by integrating along the parallel ray direction passing through the slice. 5. Propagate shadow rays simultaneously slice-by-slice in the same general direction as rendering. 6. Accumulate the computed light intensity into the output buffer for the current slice. 7. Finalize the image from the accumulated intensities of all slices. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A variant that scatters energy in the volume by performing a multi-pass slice-by-slice sweep at random angles. Dachille et al. devised a custom hardware architecture for a cache-efficient implementation of this algorithm. It is chosen when multi-directional scattering effects are required, at the cost of multiple volume passes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Dachille et al. implemented a cache-efficient version using custom hardware. Strengths: Efficient single-sweep processing for cloud-like volumes with parallel light. Limitations: Limited to parallel light assumptions; multi-pass variants require multiple volume traversals. When to Use: Cloud-like volumes with distant light sources. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring complex local lighting or non-parallel ray approximations. The method was introduced by Kajiya and Von Herzen [98] to calculate light intensity for cloud-like volumes efficiently by processing slices in a single sweep. A similar technique was demonstrated in the Heidelberg ray-tracing model [157], where shadow rays were propagated simultaneously slice-by-slice. Dachille et al. [44] extended the approach to multi-pass scattering at random angles and designed custom hardware for cache efficiency. Kniss et al. [113][114] later proposed a single-pass approximation using recursive slice-blurring starting at the light source, exploiting 3D texture mapping hardware and a dual image buffer for interactive frame rates. name: Cell projection
head: Projected Tetrahedra, Polyhedron Projection
body: Cell projection is a direct volume rendering technique that treats volumetric data as a set of geometric primitives (convex polyhedral cells) which are projected onto the 2D image plane, rasterized, and composited in back-to-front order. It solves the problem of rendering unstructured, curvilinear, or irregular grids where ray-casting is computationally expensive or difficult to parallelize, by leveraging standard graphics hardware for scan-conversion. It sets itself apart from Splatting by using exact geometric primitives rather than approximate splats, and from Texture slicing by projecting the volume elements themselves rather than slicing the volume with planes. The cell projection family shares the following mechanism, terms, and math: 1. Primitive Representation: The volume is decomposed into convex polyhedral cells (e.g., tetrahedra, hexahedra). For grids with non-planar faces, cells are subdivided into tetrahedra to ensure planar faces and consistent topology. This decomposition resolves "problem cells" where rays might intersect a face twice in curvilinear grids. 2. Projection and Subdivision: The 3D vertices of each cell are projected to 2D screen space. The projected edges of the cell divide the image plane into polygons, where each polygon lies within the projection of a single front-facing face and a single back-facing face of the cell. For general cells, an incremental method builds this subdivision by adding projected edges one by one. For curvilinear grids, standard topologies are identified to use lookup tables for subdivision. 3. Scalar Interpolation: Scalar values s at any point within a tetrahedron are interpolated linearly from the vertex values si using barycentric coordinates or linear interpolation along edges. The scalar field is assumed to vary linearly across the cell, and transfer functions mapping scalar to color/extinction are assumed linear. 4. Opacity Calculation: The integrated opacity \alpha for a segment of length l with average differential opacity \tau{avg} is: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\tau{avg} l). 5. Visibility and Sorting: Correct compositing requires back-to-front ordering. This is achieved via global visibility sorts or image-space merging of ray segments. 6. Compositing: Fragments or ray segments are composited in back-to-front order using an exponential opacity model. Accelerates rendering by using hardware texture mapping to compute the exponential transparency term per pixel via table lookup, avoiding per-pixel exponential calculations while preventing Mach bands. Sets itself apart by replacing linear interpolation of integrated opacity with a 2D texture lookup that correctly models non-linear exponential decay. An object-space algorithm that computes a correct back-to-front visibility ordering of convex polyhedral cells by constructing a directed adjacency graph based on face-sharing topology and viewpoint orientation. Sets itself apart by relying on local ordering relations between cells sharing a common face to define a partial order, converted to a total order via topological sort. A view-dependent sorting algorithm for tetrahedral datasets that uses logical partitioning to enable parallel processing, solving dependency and sequence limitations of neighboring tetrahedra. Sets itself apart by replacing global topological sorting with a block-based logical partitioning scheme that allows independent parallel sorting of unobstructed layers. An efficient ray-casting algorithm for tetrahedral meshes implemented on consumer graphics hardware using fragment programs, pre-integration, and multiple rendering passes. Sets itself apart by offloading geometric projection and classification logic to the GPU in a strict two-stage pipeline to minimize CPU-GPU data transfer. An interactive volume rendering technique for large, regular volumetric data sets on GPUs. Sets itself apart from general Projected Tetrahedra by eliminating redundant projection and visibility sorting computations through the exploitation of data regularity and orthographic projection, achieving constant-time traversal order. A software-based object-order volume rendering algorithm that projects volumetric primitives into screen space and rasterizes them using scan-line conversion to leverage spatial coherence. Sets itself apart by processing cells completely before moving to the next, progressively displaying the view from front-most to distant pixels without relying on expensive graphics hardware. Covers methods that decompose volumetric data into tetrahedral primitives to enable object-order rendering or precise isosurface extraction. Sets itself apart by resolving topological ambiguities and non-planar face issues inherent in hexahedral or cubic grid representations, ensuring all cells have planar faces and consistent connectivity. Treats Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) gas cells as piecewise-constant geometric cubes rather than smoothing them as SPH kernels. Sets itself apart by providing exact pixel-averaged cross-sections for slices, projections, and perspective images, ensuring mass conservation to round-off. A technique for rendering large, unstructured tetrahedral meshes by approximating each tetrahedron with a single point primitive. Sets itself apart by decoupling footprint generation and reshaping from compositing, using hardware shaders to reshape point footprints and composite fragments without processing connectivity information. A software rendering technique that transforms the eight corners of a 3D voxel cube using sequential translation and rotation matrices, applies perspective projection to the vertices of each face, and rasterizes visible faces as 2D polygons. Sets itself apart by performing all depth testing and pixel writing in software rather than relying on hardware rasterization pipelines. A sorting-free volume rendering technique for irregular volume datasets that employs projected tetrahedra with pre-integration. Sets itself apart by treating volume rendering as a stochastic process where sampling points occur along a viewing ray with probability equal to opacity, eliminating the need for visibility sorting of tetrahedral cells. A cell projection method for general convex hexahedra that renders the 2D projection of each cell as an arrangement of polygons by analyzing each cell individually in screen space. Sets itself apart from coherent projection by avoiding case analysis for the high number of projection topologies, handling irregular hexahedra where different cells fall into different topologies. A distributed-memory object-order volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids that projects mesh cells into image space to generate ray segments, which are then merged in image space. Sets itself apart from synchronous cell projection by allowing asynchronous communication and task management, avoiding the need for global depth-sorting of cells. Calculates the projected area of a tetrahedron in normalized screen space to determine refinement criteria or culling. Uses cross products to compute wedge areas, which are twice the triangle area, then divides by four. Triangles cover the total area twice in projection, and cross products yield wedge areas, necessitating division by four. Determines color and opacity contribution by applying pre-integrated classification, using scalar values on front and back faces and thickness as texture coordinates for a 3D texture map storing volume ray integral values. The texture coordinates are the scalar value on the front face sf, the scalar value on the back face sb, and the thickness l resulting from scan converting the tetrahedron. Cell projection was developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory by Max, Williams, Silva, and Cook. It is listed among the main paradigms of volume rendering, alongside raycasting, splatting, and shear-warp. The method was designed to handle curvilinear and unstructured grids directly, avoiding the need for resampling. Early implementations addressed the issue of non-planar faces in curvilinear grids by subdividing problem cells into tetrahedra with planar faces. The technique has been parallelized for distributed-memory systems and optimized for GPU execution on structured data. name: Cell Projection with Texture Mapping for Opacity
head: Exponential transparency lookup, Hardware-Assisted Polyhedron Projection with Texture Lookup, Hardware-accelerated Cell Projection with Texture Lookup, Polyhedron Projection, Texture-mapped Cell Projection
body: This method accelerates the cell projection volume rendering technique by using hardware texture mapping to compute the exponential transparency term \exp(-\int \tau ds) per pixel via table lookup, avoiding per-pixel exponential calculations while preventing Mach bands caused by linear interpolation of transparency. It sets itself apart from naive cell projection by replacing the linear interpolation of integrated opacity \alpha with a 2D texture lookup that correctly models the non-linear exponential decay of light, which linear interpolation fails to capture. The method projects convex polyhedral cells (typically tetrahedra or subdivided hexahedra) onto the image plane, subdividing the projection into polygons where each polygon lies within the projection of a single front-facing face and a single back-facing face. For each polygon, the method computes vertex attributes (color, opacity, and texture coordinates) and uses hardware interpolation to rasterize the polygon, applying a pre-loaded texture map to determine the correct per-pixel transparency. Inputs: Volume data: Scalar values s and extinction coefficients \tau (or density \kappa) at cell vertices. Geometry: 3D coordinates of cell vertices. Camera: View direction and projection type (orthogonal or perspective). Transfer functions: Linear mapping from scalar s to particle color and density \kappa. Outputs: Final image with correct exponential opacity and color compositing. 1. 2D Texture Map: A 2D raster image pre-loaded with values representing the exponential transparency function. Address: (u, v), where u corresponds to scaled ray segment length l and v corresponds to scaled average extinction coefficient \taua. Content: The texture stores values T(u, v) = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\exp(-2uv). The factor 1/2 accounts for the OpenGL compositing equation which uses 1 - \frac{1}{2}\alpha transparency. Scaling: Coordinates u and v must be scaled and clamped to cover the substantial range of transparencies expected in the scene, preventing wrapping. 2. Polygon Vertex Attributes: For each vertex of the projected polygon Q, the following are computed: Color (C): The glow color associated with the vertex. Opacity (\alpha): Integrated opacity at the vertex. Texture Coordinates (u, v): u: Scaled thickness l (ray segment length within the cell). v: Scaled average extinction \taua = (\tauf + \taub)/2. 1. Project and Subdivide: Project the 3D vertices of each convex polyhedral cell to 2D screen space. Subdivide the projected area into polygons. Each polygon lies within the projection of a single front-facing face and a single back-facing face. For general cells, use an incremental method: add projected edges one by one to the subdivision, starting with one infinite region. An edge may create a new boundary cycle, close a cycle to form a new polygon, or subdivide existing polygons. For curvilinear grids, identify if the projection topology matches one of three non-degenerate perspective projection topologies for a cube. Use vertex projection tests to identify these cases and look up standard subdivisions to speed up the process. 2. Compute Vertex Attributes for Polygon Q: Identify Vertex Type: Determine if each vertex of Q is a profile vertex, intersection vertex, or non-profile vertex. Profile Vertex (e.g., A): Belongs to both front and back faces. \tauf = \taub = \tau{vertex}. Color is the scalar value at the vertex. Integrated opacity is zero. Intersection Vertex (e.g., G): \tauf is interpolated in software along the front edge (e.g., EB), and \taub is interpolated along the back edge (e.g., AC). Non-Profile Vertex (e.g., E on front): \tauf = \tau{vertex}. \taub is interpolated in software from values at other vertices of the back face. Compute Extinction Coefficients: Calculate \tauf and \taub for each vertex based on the type. Compute the average extinction coefficient at each vertex: \taua = (\tauf + \taub)/2. Compute Ray Segment Length l: For orthogonal projections, l varies linearly across the polygon. At "thin" vertices (where segment length is zero), l=0. At "thick" vertices (e.g., F, D, I, J), calculate l geometrically by finding the segment endpoints on the front and back faces that project to the vertex. Compute Color (C{polygon}): The color used for compositing is the "glow color" of the particles. Approximation: At non-profile vertices, compute the correct integrated color analytically in software and divide by the integrated \alpha to get the polygon\color. At profile vertices, set polygon\color to the vertex glow color. Simpler Approximation: Use the average of the front and back colors at thick vertices. Compute Integrated Opacity (\alpha{vertex}): For thick vertices: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\taua l). For thin/profile vertices: \alpha = 0. Set Texture Coordinates: u \propto l. v \propto \taua. Scale u and v appropriately for the texture map address space. 3. Rasterize and Composite: Specify \taua (as v) and l (as u) as texture coordinates at the vertices of polygon Q. Interpolate u, v, and C{polygon} across the polygon in hardware using piecewise linear (triangulation) or piecewise bilinear (scan-line) interpolation. For each pixel, sample the 2D texture map at (u, v) to get the value a. The transparency is \alpha = 1 - a = \exp(-l\taua) (adjusted for the 1/2 factor in the texture map). Composite the polygon onto the image using the Porter-Duff over operation: \text{new\pixel\color} = a \cdot C{polygon} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \text{old\pixel\color} where a is the texture lookup result and \alpha = 1 - a. Note: The compositing equation effectively treats the polygon as a cloud of particles with color C{polygon} and probability a of hitting a particle. Transparency/Opacity: \alpha = 1 - \exp\left(-\int0^l \tau(s) \, ds\right) For linearly interpolated extinction \tau(s) along a segment of length l with front value \tauf and back value \taub: \int0^l \tau(s) \, ds = l \frac{\tauf + \taub}{2} = l \taua Thus: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-l \taua) Texture Map Content: T(u, v) = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\exp(-2uv) Compositing Equation: \text{new\pixel\color} = a \cdot C{polygon} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \text{old\pixel\color} where a = T(u, v) and \alpha = 1 - a. Texture Coordinate Scaling: The scaling of u and v must be chosen to cover the range of l\taua values in the scene. Clamping is required to prevent wrapping. Mach Bands: Linear interpolation of integrated opacity \alpha across the polygon causes derivative discontinuities in \alpha due to the non-linear exponential, resulting in disturbing Mach bands. Using the 2D texture lookup avoids this. Incorrect Color Averaging: If both color and extinction are interpolated linearly across a ray segment, the term a \cdot C{polygon} yields incorrect color because it averages colors before applying opacity, failing to account for the obscuring effect of high-opacity regions (e.g., red obscuring green). The method approximates the correct color by computing it analytically at vertices and dividing by \alpha. Perspective View Approximation: In perspective view, \tauf and \taub have different perspective distortions, and correct l computation requires a square root per pixel. The method is an approximation in perspective, interpolating \tau and color in screen space. Incremental Method Robustness: The incremental method for general cells is slow and not completely robust because it uses floating-point computations to determine topology. Wrapping: If texture coordinates are not clamped, they may wrap around, causing incorrect transparency values. Time Complexity: Dominated by the visibility sort of cells and the rasterization of polygons. The per-pixel cost is reduced to a texture lookup and compositing operation, avoiding per-pixel exponentials. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 2D texture map. The size of the texture map depends on the scaling of u and v. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with the number of cells and the resolution of the image. The use of hardware texture mapping allows for efficient rendering on GPUs. Strengths: Avoids per-pixel exponential calculations. Prevents Mach bands. Leverages hardware acceleration. Limitations: Approximate in perspective view. Color computation is approximate (analytic integral at vertices). Incremental subdivision is slow and potentially unstable for general cells. When to use: When hardware acceleration is available and exponential transparency is required to avoid artifacts. Suitable for orthogonal projections and approximate perspective views. When not: When exact color integration is required per pixel (beyond hardware capabilities) or when robustness for arbitrary unstructured grids is critical without pre-processing. The method was developed as an enhancement to the cell projection technique, which was originally proposed by Shirley and Tuchman. The use of texture mapping for exponential transparency was introduced to address the Mach band artifacts caused by linear interpolation of opacity. The specific formulation with the 1/2 factor in the texture map is described in. The method is associated with work at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. name: Topological Sort for Cell Projection
head: Exact Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering, Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection, MPVO (Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering), MPVO algorithm, Maximal Polyhedra Visibility Ordering, Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering
body: Topological Sort for Cell Projection (MPVO) is an object-space algorithm that computes a correct back-to-front visibility ordering of convex polyhedral cells in a convex mesh by constructing a directed adjacency graph based on face-sharing topology and viewpoint orientation. It relies on local ordering relations between cells sharing a common face to define a partial order, which a topological sort converts to a total order. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A convex mesh composed of convex polyhedral cells; a viewpoint V (for perspective) or a view direction vector \vec{d} (for orthogonal projection); a precomputed adjacency graph of the mesh. Output: A total ordering sequence of cells [c1, c2, \dots, cn] such that if cell A occludes cell B, B precedes A in the list. Data Structures: 1. Adjacency Graph: A directed graph G=(C, E) where nodes C are cells and edges E represent shared faces. 2. Plane Coefficients: For each interior face f shared by cells ci and cj, store the plane equation coefficients (Af, Bf, Cf, Df) such that Af x + Bf y + Cf z + Df = 0. 3. Cell State: Each cell c maintains incount (integer), visited (boolean), and cycledetection (boolean). 4. Queue/Sink List/Output List: Standard FIFO queue and lists for topological sort traversal. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Static): Construct the undirected adjacency graph of the mesh. For every interior face shared by two cells, compute and store the plane equation coefficients. This step is performed once per static mesh and reused for all viewpoints. 2. Phase I: Partial Ordering (Arrow Assignment): For each interior face f shared by cells c1 and c2: Evaluate the plane equation of f at the viewpoint V=(Vx, Vy, Vz) (for perspective) or use the view direction \vec{d} (for orthogonal). Determine the "behind" relation: If V lies in the half-space of f containing c1, then c1 is "behind" c2 relative to the viewer (i.e., c2 occludes c1). We denote this c2 <{vp} c1. Add a directed edge from c1 to c2 in the graph G. This edge represents an "outbound arrow" for c1 and an "inbound arrow" for c2. 3. Phase II: Topological Sort (DFS-based): Initialization: Set visited and cycledetection to false for all cells. Set incount to 0 for all cells. For every directed edge ci \to cj in G, increment incount of cj. Identify all cells with incount == 0. These are "sink cells" (cells that do not occlude any other cell across a shared face). Add them to the Sink List. Traversal: While Sink List is not empty: Remove a cell C from Sink List. Call RECURSIVE-DFS(C). RECURSIVE-DFS(currentCell): 1. Set currentCell.visited = true and currentCell.cycledetection = true. 2. Identify all eligible neighbors of currentCell. An eligible neighbor N is a cell such that there is a directed edge N \to currentCell in G (i.e., N is "in front of" currentCell and currentCell occludes N). 3. For each eligible neighbor N: If N.visited is false: Call RECURSIVE-DFS(N). Else if N.cycledetection is true: A visibility cycle is detected. Output a warning/error and terminate. No valid ordering exists without subdividing the cycle. 4. After processing all eligible neighbors: Add currentCell to the end of the Output List. Set currentCell.cycledetection = false. 4. Cycle Handling: If the algorithm terminates with cells remaining in the graph (not all cells added to Output List), a visibility cycle exists. The standard MPVO algorithm cannot resolve this; the offending cells must be subdivided or a different sorting method (e.g., XMPVO) must be used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VisibilityCycleError(Exception): pass def mpvosort(cells, adjacencygraph, viewpoint): """ cells: List of Cell objects. adjacencygraph: Dict mapping cellid -> list of neighborcellids (shared faces). viewpoint: Tuple (x, y, z) or view direction vector. Returns: List of Cell objects in back-to-front order. """ cellsbyid = {c.id: c for c in cells} # Phase I: Build Directed Graph and Compute In-Counts directedgraph = {c.id: [] for c in cells} incounts = {c.id: 0 for c in cells} for c1 in cells: for c2 in adjacencygraph.get(c1.id, []): # Sources do not specify the exact geometric routine for plane extraction. A, B, C, D = getfaceplane(c1, c2) # Evaluate plane at viewpoint val = A viewpoint[0] + B viewpoint[1] + C viewpoint[2] + D # If val > 0, viewpoint is on the side of the normal (c2's side) # This means c2 is in front of c1 relative to viewpoint. # Relation: c1 <vp c2. Edge points from back to front: c1 -> c2. if val > 0: directedgraph[c1.id].append(c2.id) incounts[c2.id] += 1 else: directedgraph[c2.id].append(c1.id) incounts[c1.id] += 1 # Build reverse graph for DFS eligible neighbor lookup reversegraph = {c.id: [] for c in cells} for u in directedgraph: for v in directedgraph[u]: reversegraph[v].append(u) # Phase II: Topological Sort via DFS visited = {c.id: False for c in cells} cycledetection = {c.id: False for c in cells} outputlist = [] sinklist = [c.id for c in cells if incounts[c.id] == 0] def recursivedfs(currentid): visited[currentid] = True cycledetection[currentid] = True # Eligible neighbors are those with an edge TO currentid for neighborid in reversegraph.get(currentid, []): if not visited[neighborid]: recursivedfs(neighborid) elif cycledetection[neighborid]: raise VisibilityCycleError("Cycle detected between cells") # Output current cell outputlist.append(currentid) cycledetection[currentid] = False while sinklist: cellid = sinklist.pop(0) recursivedfs(cellid) if len(outputlist) != len(cells): raise VisibilityCycleError("Remaining cells indicate a visibility cycle") return [cellsbyid[cid] for cid in outputlist] Parameters: Convexity: The mesh and all individual cells must be convex for the total ordering to be guaranteed correct. Acyclicity: The directed graph must be acyclic. Cycles imply a visibility loop where cells partially occlude each other. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Cycles: If a cycle exists, the algorithm fails. This occurs in non-convex meshes or meshes with holes where rays exit and re-enter the volume. Non-Convex Meshes: MPVO does not account for occlusions across empty space (gaps) between boundary cells. It is not correct for non-convex grids without augmentation. Geometric Degeneracies: Geometric degeneracies can make the implementation of MPVO complex and require careful handling. SXMPVO is an algorithm that computes image-precision visibility ordering for volume rendering of unstructured meshes by scan-converting exterior faces into an A-Buffer to determine occlusion relations (Pseudoneighbor or PN relations) between cells, rather than computing object-precision ray shooting queries. It guarantees correct visibility order for a particular image resolution by using image-precision scan conversion rather than strict object-space visibility ordering. It sets itself apart from its parent Topological Sort for Cell Projection and sibling XMPVO by replacing expensive object-precision ray shooting with efficient scan conversion, achieving "image-space correctness" where the rendering resolution matches the ordering resolution. Unlike BSP-XMPVO, it avoids BSP tree construction and exact arithmetic, making it simpler and faster for general acyclic meshes. This method extends the Topological Sort for Cell Projection to handle non-convex grids by resolving visibility gaps between boundary cells using an image-space A-buffer. It solves the problem where viewing rays exit the grid through an external face, traverse empty space, and re-enter the grid, creating occlusion relationships that are not captured by shared-face topology alone. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) by avoiding expensive pairwise geometric occlusion tests or BSP-tree construction, instead relying on rasterization to implicitly determine segment ordering. Power Distance Sort is a visibility sorting method that orders primitives (triangles or tetrahedra) back-to-front relative to a camera origin by comparing the power of the viewpoint with respect to the circumcircles or circumspheres of the primitives. It leverages geometric properties of Delaunay triangulations/tetrahedralizations to guarantee correct visibility ordering, whereas it is not guaranteed to produce accurate ordering for non-Delaunay meshes. Unlike topological sort, it avoids storing and accessing an adjacency structure. Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant) is an image-space visibility ordering method that sorts all cell faces projecting onto a specific pixel at render time, just prior to compositing. It solves the problem of determining the correct back-to-front rendering order for transparent volumes in scenes where a global topological sort is impossible due to visibility cycles. Unlike its sibling Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO), which sorts only exterior faces and exploits spatial coherence, this variant sorts all faces (including interior ones) independently or incrementally per pixel. It differs from Mammen's Technique in that it sorts all cell faces per pixel, whereas Mammen's technique specifically sorts transparent fragments in front of the front-most opaque one. Newell-based Visibility Sorting is an algorithm to sort cells into a back-to-front ordered list for correct hardware compositing. By definition, if cell A partially occludes cell B from a particular viewpoint V, cell B must come before cell A in the list. It extends the Newell, Newell, and Sancha polygon sorting method to the case of polyhedra. XMPVO is an algorithm that improves the runtime of the Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering (MPVO) method by using ray shooting queries to discover exterior face relations for nonconvex meshes. It determines the correct back-to-front rendering order for convex volumes filled with convex polyhedral cells when the standard topological sort is insufficient due to occlusions between exterior faces. It sets itself apart from its parent Topological Sort for Cell Projection by augmenting the graph with geometric visibility checks, and from its sibling Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) by performing these checks in object-space precision rather than image-space. MPVONC is a heuristic sorting algorithm used in cell projection volume rendering to order non-convex polyhedral cells back-to-front. It extends the exact MPVO algorithm by handling exterior cells that lack a transitive "behind" relationship via shared faces, which MPVO cannot resolve alone. Unlike exact methods such as SXMPVO or A-buffer sorts, MPVONC prioritizes speed over correctness, making it "accurate enough" for many applications but prone to visual artifacts in specific occlusion scenarios. Convex Grid Topological Visibility Sorting is an O(n) algorithm that orders cells in a convex grid of convex polyhedral cells back-to-front for semi-transparent volume rendering. It constructs a directed adjacency graph where edges represent pairwise occlusion relations derived from the viewpoint position, then performs a topological sort to produce a valid compositing order. It sets itself apart from Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) and Power Distance Sort by relying exclusively on local face-sharing topology rather than global geometric tests or distance metrics, provided the grid volume is convex. Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of cells. Each cell is processed a constant number of times (twice in initialization, once in the loop), and each edge is processed once. Space Complexity: O(n) for storing the adjacency graph, in-counts, and recursion stack. Measured Performance: Described as "very fast" with low computational overhead for well-behaved (acyclic and convex) meshes. Strengths: Linear time complexity; exact correctness for convex, acyclic meshes; detects visibility cycles; reusable adjacency graph for multiple viewpoints. Limitations: Fails for non-convex meshes (requires augmentation); fails for meshes with visibility cycles (requires subdivision or alternative sort); geometric degeneracies can complicate implementation. When to Use: Convex, unstructured grids with convex cells where the mesh topology is static and the viewpoint changes. When Not to Use: Non-convex meshes without augmentation; meshes with holes/cavities causing visibility cycles; real-time rendering of large non-convex datasets where approximate sorting (e.g., MPVONC) is preferred. MPVO was introduced by Peter L. Williams in 1992. It was developed to provide a fast visibility ordering for direct volume rendering of unstructured grids, particularly finite element meshes. A similar algorithm was published by Max et al.. The algorithm is a foundational component in cell projection volume rendering, enabling correct back-to-front compositing for convex volumes.
