name: Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO)
head: SXMPVO (Image-Space Visibility Ordering), SXMPVO algorithm, Scanning Exact MPVO, Scanning Exact Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering
body: SXMPVO is an algorithm that computes image-precision visibility ordering for volume rendering of unstructured meshes by scan-converting exterior faces into an A-Buffer to determine occlusion relations (Pseudoneighbor or PN relations) between cells, rather than computing object-precision ray shooting queries. It guarantees correct visibility order for a particular image resolution by using image-precision scan conversion rather than strict object-space visibility ordering. It sets itself apart from its parent Topological Sort for Cell Projection and sibling XMPVO by replacing expensive object-precision ray shooting with efficient scan conversion, achieving "image-space correctness" where the rendering resolution matches the ordering resolution. Unlike BSP-XMPVO, it avoids BSP tree construction and exact arithmetic, making it simpler and faster for general acyclic meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unstructured mesh (tetrahedral, hexahedral, or "zoo" mesh) consisting of n cells. The mesh must be acyclic. Cells may have nonplanar surfaces provided their edges do not project to crossing lines ("bow tie" projections). Output: A total ordering sequence of cells b = c{im} < c{im-1} < \dots < c{i1} < c{i0} = a, where b comes before a in the sorted sequence (back-to-front). Data Structures: 1. MPVO Structures: Standard adjacency graph, cell vertices, plane equation coefficients, arrows on shared faces, and a sink cell flag per cell. Storage: 4f + 14n words, where f is the number of interior faces (O(n)). 2. Exterior Face List: A list holding a record for each exterior face. Each record contains: pointer to the face, pointer to the owning cell, face centroid, and next pointer. Storage: O(b) words, where b is the number of exterior cells. 3. A-Buffer: Implemented as an array of pixel (PIX) lists, one per pixel in the screen image (w \times h). PIX Entry: Contains: distance z from the screen to the intersection point where the ray through pixel p intersects face f, pointer to face f, and next pointer for the PIX list. Storage: O(wh + a) words, where a is the total projected area (number of pixels scanned). 4. PN List: Every cell has a PN list pointer (initially NULL). The PN list for a cell contains all exterior cells it occludes (its dependencies). PN Entry: Contains: cell number of the occluded cell, and next pointer. Storage: O(a) words for entries, plus O(n) words for head pointers. Algorithm Steps: 1. Phase I: Create Partial Ordering (Interior) Traverse all cells to mark arrows on shared faces exactly as in MPVO Phase I, determining "behind" relations for adjacent cells. Set a sinkcell flag in each cell to true or false based on the arrows. Complexity: O(n). 2. Phase II: Sort Exterior Faces Create the exterior face list. Sort the exterior faces by increasing distance from the screen to the face's centroid. Complexity: O(b \log b). 3. Phase III: Scan Faces and Add Dependencies Create the A-Buffer (array of PIX lists). Remove exterior faces from the sorted queue one at a time. Scan-convert the interior of each exterior face f in 3D (sampling at pixel centers). For each pixel p of face f enumerated by scan conversion: Create a PIX entry with z (distance to intersection), pointer to f, and next pointer. Insert the PIX entry into the PIX list for pixel p in the A-Buffer in order of decreasing z. Use an efficient insertion sort. Because faces are sorted by centroid distance, insertions occur at or near the beginning of the list. After rasterizing all exterior faces, process each PIX list: Discard the first entry of every PIX list (the back-facing face where the ray exits the mesh for the last time, which has no matching front-facing face behind it). If the viewpoint is outside the mesh, also discard the last entry (the face where the ray enters the mesh for the first time). Traverse the remaining PIX lists to discover Pseudoneighbor (PN) relations: Between each consecutive front-facing/back-facing face pair on the PIX list, there is a "ray-gap". The two cells whose faces make up this pair are pseudoneighbors (PNs). The cell contributing the back-facing face is the occluding PN. The other cell (contributing the front-facing face) is the occluded PN. Add a PN entry (cell number of occluded PN) to the PN list of the occluding PN. Set the sinkcell flag of the occluded PN to false. Duplicate Handling: Check if the PN relation is already in the occluding PN's PN list. If not, add it to the head. If found, move it to the head to exploit coherence. This reduces search cost to O(1) in practice, avoiding O(b^2) or O(a^2/b) costs. Complexity: O(wh + a) for most data sets. 4. Phase IV: Depth First Search (DFS) Examine each cell to identify those still marked as sink cells (cells with no outbound arrows AND not an occluded PN). Execute a Depth First Search (DFS) on the directed graph to determine the final visibility order. Traverse each edge in the directed graph twice. Modification: Occluded neighbors (cells on the PN list of cell c) are now eligible neighbors of c in the recursive DFS step. Complexity: O(n + a). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sxmpvo(mesh, imagewidth, imageheight, viewpoint, viewpointoutside): cells = mesh.cells cellsbyid = {c.id: c for c in cells} for cell in cells: cell.sinkflag = True cell.pnlisthead = None cell.outboundneighbors = [] # Phase I: Mark arrows on shared faces (MPVO Phase I) for cell in cells: for face in cell.faces: if face.isshared: neighbor = face.othercell(cell) viewdir = normalize(viewpoint - face.centroid) if dot(face.normal, viewdir) > 0: cell.outboundneighbors.append(neighbor) neighbor.sinkflag = False # Phase II: Sort Exterior Faces exteriorfaces = [f for f in mesh.faces if not f.isshared] exteriorfaces.sort(key=lambda f: distance(viewpoint, f.centroid)) # Create A-Buffer abuffer = [[] for in range(imagewidth imageheight)] # Phase III: Scan Faces and Add Dependencies for face in exteriorfaces: # Standard scan conversion to get pixelscovered pixelscovered = [] for p in pixelscovered: z = distance(viewpoint, p.intersectionpoint) pixentry = {'z': z, 'face': face, 'next': None} pixlist = abuffer[p.index] # Insert in decreasing z order prev = None curr = pixlist[0] if pixlist else None while curr and curr['z'] > z: prev = curr curr = curr['next'] if prev: prev['next'] = pixentry else: pixlist.insert(0, pixentry) pixentry['next'] = curr for pixlist in abuffer: if not pixlist: continue # Discard first entry (back-facing face exiting mesh last) pixlist.pop(0) if viewpointoutside and pixlist: # Discard last entry (face entering mesh first) pixlist.pop() for i in range(len(pixlist) - 1): entry1 = pixlist[i] entry2 = pixlist[i+1] # Check face orientation relative to view direction if isbackface(entry1.face) and isfrontface(entry2.face): occludingcell = entry1.face.cell occludedcell = entry2.face.cell addpnrelation(occludingcell, occludedcell) occludedcell.sinkflag = False # Phase IV: DFS sinkcells = [c for c in cells if c.sinkflag] sortedorder = [] for sink in sinkcells: if not sink.visited: dfs(sink, sortedorder, cellsbyid) return sortedorder[::-1] def addpnrelation(occludingcell, occludedcell): current = occludingcell.pnlisthead while current: if current.cellid == occludedcell.id: if current != occludingcell.pnlisthead: # Move to head prev = None temp = occludingcell.pnlisthead while temp != current: prev = temp temp = temp.next if prev: prev.next = current.next else: occludingcell.pnlisthead = current.next current.next = occludingcell.pnlisthead occludingcell.pnlisthead = current return current = current.next newentry = {'cellid': occludedcell.id, 'next': occludingcell.pnlisthead} occludingcell.pnlisthead = newentry def dfs(cell, order, cellsbyid): cell.visited = True order.append(cell) for neighbor in cell.outboundneighbors: if not neighbor.visited: dfs(neighbor, order, cellsbyid) currentpn = cell.pnlisthead while currentpn: occludedid = currentpn.cellid occludedcell = cellsbyid[occludedid] if not occludedcell.visited: dfs(occludedcell, order, cellsbyid) currentpn = currentpn.next Combines BSP tree of exterior faces with MPVO adjacency to handle non-convex meshes. Chosen when object-precision exactness is required or when scan-conversion is insufficient, but at the cost of higher complexity and memory. Completes SXMPVO by generating a global topological sort using Pseudo-Neighbor relations derived from image-space occlusion. Chosen when a strict total order is needed for rendering pipelines that require it. Time Complexity: Overall: O(wh + a + n) for most data sets, where w, h are image dimensions, a is the projected area (pixels scanned), and n is the number of cells. Expected cost: O(wh(\hat{d}e + 1) + n), where \hat{d}e is the average depth complexity of exterior faces. Phase I: O(n). Phase II: O(b \log b). Phase III: O(wh + a). Phase IV: O(n + a). Memory Complexity: MPVO structures: 4f + 14n words (O(n)). A-Buffer: O(wh + a) words. PN Lists: O(a) words for entries, O(n) for head pointers. Exterior Face List: O(b) words. Total overhead over MPVO is modest. For helix3.5 (3.57M cells, 375x450 image), SXMPVO uses 367 MB vs MPVONC's 347.4 MB. Performance: On a 250 MHz MIPS R10000: 0.32s for 187,395 cells; 10.85s for 4,500,000 cells. On a 2.53 GHz Pentium 4: 500K-600K tetrahedra per second for a 1,050,000 pixel image. Faster than all published exact visibility ordering algorithms in object or image space. Slower than MPVONC but generates exact images at comparable speed for datasets >100,000 cells. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simpler and more stable than extending MPVO to exact object-space ordering. No extra preprocessing compared to MPVO. Handles nonconvex boundaries, disconnected meshes, and mixed cell types (zoo meshes). Faster than BSP-XMPVO. Limitations: Requires the mesh to be acyclic. Sorting errors may occur for "tiny cells" (not projecting to any pixel) if antialiasing via splatting is used, as the behind relation is only guaranteed across continuous adjacent cells or sampled ray-gaps. Image-space correctness is tied to the rendering resolution. SXMPVO was introduced to address the failure of MPVO on nonconvex meshes, where ray-gaps between cells cause incorrect ordering. It was developed as a more stable and simple alternative to conceptually extending MPVO with strict object-space visibility ordering. It improves upon XMPVO by using image-precision ray shooting via scan conversion and an A-Buffer, rather than object-precision queries. It is used in volume rendering systems for unstructured grids, specifically tetrahedral and zoo meshes. name: BSP-XMPVO
head: Binary Space Partition - Extended Monotone Polygon Visibility Ordering, Binary Space Partition MPVO, Fast Polyhedral Cell Sorting
body: BSP-XMPVO is a visibility sorting algorithm for unstructured and curvilinear grids that combines a Binary Space Partition (BSP) tree of exterior faces with the adjacency-based ordering of MPVO to handle non-convex meshes. It augments the partial order from MPVO with dependencies derived from the BSP tree to resolve occlusions between non-adjacent cells, achieving exact sorting with linear time complexity relative to the number of cells, O(n + bp), where n is the total cells, b is the boundary cells, and p is the small number of partially projected cells. Unlike MPVO, which assumes convexity and produces artifacts on non-convex meshes, BSP-XMPVO provides exact ordering for general acyclic meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unstructured mesh S with convex cells (e.g., tetrahedra, hexahedra). The mesh must be acyclic. The data structure must support cell-to-cell adjacency (e.g., a facet-edge structure). Output: A total visibility ordering of the cells in S for a given viewpoint v. Data Structures: 1. Adjacency Graph G: Undirected graph where nodes are cells. Edges connect adjacent cells. 2. BSP Tree T: Built from the set of boundary facets B. Internal nodes store a plane equation (from a boundary facet). Leaves contain fragments of boundary facets. 3. Dependency Counters: For each cell Ci, three integer counters track unresolved dependencies: numinbound(Ci): Count of <ADJ dependencies (neighbors behind Ci). bspdepcount(Ci): Count of <BSP dependencies (boundary fragments of Ci not yet projected). ppcdepcount(Ci): Count of <PPC dependencies (partially projected cells behind Ci). 4. PPC-List: A list of cells that are "partially projected" (some fragments projected, some not). Preprocessing (View-Independent): 1. Adjacency Graph Construction: Build G from mesh topology. If raw data lacks topology, compute it using hashing in O(n \log n) worst-case time. 2. BSP Tree Construction: Let B be the set of boundary facets (facets incident to only one cell). Recursively partition B using a plane passing through one of the facets in B. Heuristic: At each node, select a small number of candidate cuts (e.g., 10) at random from the facets in the current region. Choose the cut that minimizes the number of split elements. Split facets into fragments if they intersect the cutting plane. Store fragments in leaves. The tree size b' (number of fragments) is \Theta(b^2) worst-case but near-linear O(b) in practice. Runtime Algorithm (Per Viewpoint v): The algorithm runs a BSP-tree traversal and an MPVO-like topological sort in lockstep. It maintains a queue of projectable cells (counters all zero). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def BSPXMPVO(viewpoint): # 1. Orient adjacency graph G for viewpoint for edge (Cprev, Ccurr) in G.edges: if CprevbehindCcurr(Cprev, Ccurr, viewpoint): orientedge(Cprev, Ccurr) else: orientedge(Ccurr, Cprev) # 2. Initialize counters for C in Cells: numinbound[C] = indegree(C) bspdepcount[C] = numboundaryfacets(C) ppcdepcount[C] = 0 ppclist = [] queue = PriorityQueue() for C in Cells: if numinbound[C] == 0 and bspdepcount[C] == 0 and ppcdepcount[C] == 0: queue.enqueue(C) # 3. BSP Traversal BSPXMPVOtraversal(rootnode, viewpoint) # 4. MPVO Traverse while not queue.empty(): C = queue.dequeue() output(C) for i in range(numfaces(C)): if arrow(i, C) == INBOUND: neighbor = getneighbor(C, i) numinbound[neighbor] -= 1 if numinbound[neighbor] == 0 and bspdepcount[neighbor] == 0 and ppcdepcount[neighbor] == 0: queue.enqueue(neighbor) def BSPXMPVOtraversal(node, viewpoint): if node.isleaf(): BSPXMPVOupdatedep(node) return # Traverse child not containing viewpoint first BSPXMPVOtraversal(node.childnotcontaining(viewpoint), viewpoint) BSPXMPVOupdatedep(node) BSPXMPVOtraversal(node.childcontaining(viewpoint), viewpoint) def BSPXMPVOupdatedep(node): cutcells = getcellsonplane(node.plane) # Check PPC dependencies for Cj in ppclist: for Ci in cutcells: if CjbehindCi(Cj, Ci, viewpoint): ppcdepcount[Ci] += 1 # Update PPC list and decrement BSP deps for Ci in cutcells: bspdepcount[Ci] -= 1 if bspdepcount[Ci] == 1: ppclist.append(Ci) elif bspdepcount[Ci] == 0: ppclist.remove(Ci) # Enqueue projectable cells for Ci in cutcells: if numinbound[Ci] == 0 and bspdepcount[Ci] == 0 and ppcdepcount[Ci] == 0: queue.enqueue(Ci) Parameters: Candidate Cuts: Number of random candidate planes considered during BSP construction. Default is 10. n: Total number of cells. b: Number of boundary cells (or boundary facets). p: Size of the PPC-list. Typically 0.1–0.3% of total cells. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: BSP Tree Depth: The BSP tree can become deep and unbalanced, leading to O(b) cost per search and potentially O(b^2) overall flavor if not balanced. PPC List Growth: If mesh elements "spike in" behind others, the PPC list can grow. In practice it remains small (avg 0.1%, max 0.3% of elements) because most mesh elements are well-shaped. Topological Data: If the input lacks adjacency pointers, preprocessing takes O(n \log n). Time Complexity: O(n + bp) per viewpoint, where n is total cells, b is boundary cells, and p is the number of partially projected cells. This is an improvement over XMPVO's O(b^2 + n). Preprocessing Time: Building the BSP tree is slow. For a 13,000 cell dataset, it took 3.0 seconds; for 190,000 cells, 6.4 seconds; for 240,000 cells, 5.8 seconds. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of cells and boundary facets. The BSP tree size is \Theta(b^2) worst-case but near-linear O(b) in practice. Performance: On a 13,000 cell dataset, BSP-XMPVO took 0.37 seconds (vs 3.5s for XMPVO, 0.07s for MPVONC). On 190,000 cells, 2.5s (vs 25s for XMPVO). On 240,000 cells, 2.9s (vs 48s for XMPVO). Strengths: Exact sorting for non-convex meshes; significantly faster than XMPVO; near-linear runtime for typical meshes. Limitations: Slow preprocessing; BSP tree can be unbalanced; PPC dependencies add overhead if the mesh has many non-convex interlocking structures. When to Use: Interactive rendering of unstructured grids where exact visibility is required for non-convex meshes and preprocessing cost is acceptable. When Not to Use: If the mesh is convex (use MPVO for speed); if preprocessing time is prohibitive; if the mesh has extreme non-convexities causing large PPC lists or deep BSP trees. BSP-XMPVO was proposed by Comba et al. in 1999. It builds on MPVO by Williams (1992) and XMPVO by Silva et al.. It is used for interactive rendering of unstructured grids, aiming to close the gap between rendering regular and irregular grids. name: SXMPVO Total Ordering (Phase II Modification)
head: Phase II of MPVO with modifications
body: This method completes the Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) algorithm by generating a global topological sort of mesh cells. It extends the standard MPVO Phase II by incorporating Pseudo-Neighbor (PN) relations derived from image-space occlusion, ensuring a correct segment sorting order for volume rendering on unstructured meshes. The method operates on the data structures and intermediate results (PIX lists) produced by the SXMPVO Phase I (scan conversion). Inputs: A set of mesh cells, each with a sinkcellflag (boolean) and a PNlist (linked list of PN entries). An A-Buffer containing PIX lists, one per screen pixel. Each PIX list entry (PIX entry) contains: z (distance from screen to intersection, float/double), faceptr (pointer to exterior face), and next (pointer to next PIX entry). Each exterior face list record contains: pointer to face, pointer to owning cell, face centroid, and next pointer. Outputs: A total ordering of all cells in the mesh, suitable for front-to-back or back-to-front volume rendering. Data Structures: PN Entry: Contains occludedcellnumber (integer) and next (pointer). PIX List: A singly linked list of PIX entries, sorted by decreasing z. Algorithm Steps: 1. Extract Pseudo-Neighbor (PN) Relations: Iterate through every PIX list in the A-Buffer. Discard the first entry (back-facing face where the ray exits the mesh). If the viewpoint is outside the mesh, discard the last entry (back-facing face where the ray enters the mesh). Iterate through the remaining consecutive pairs of entries. Identify pairs where the first entry refers to a front-facing face and the second refers to a back-facing face. Let C{back} be the cell owning the back-facing face (occluding PN) and C{front} be the cell owning the front-facing face (occluded PN). Add a PN entry containing C{front} to the PNlist of C{back}. Apply the move-to-front heuristic: if C{front} is already in C{back}'s PNlist, move it to the head. Set sinkcellflag of C{front} to false. 2. Identify Sink Cells: Traverse all cells in the mesh to find those whose sinkcellflag is still true. These cells have no outbound PN or MPVO relations pointing away from them in the dependency graph. 3. Perform Recursive Depth-First Search (DFS): Initialize an empty output list orderedcells. Define a function RECURSIVE-DFS(cell c). Mark c as visited. For each neighbor n in the union of MPVO neighbors and PN neighbors (cells listed in c's PNlist), if n is not visited, call RECURSIVE-DFS(n). Append c to orderedcells. 4. Finalize Order: The orderedcells list contains the cells in reverse topological order (back-to-front). Reverse this list to obtain the front-to-back rendering order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class PNList: def init(self): self.entries = [] def addormovetofront(self, cellnum): if cellnum not in self.entries: self.entries.insert(0, cellnum) elif self.entries[0] != cellnum: self.entries.remove(cellnum) self.entries.insert(0, cellnum) def extractpnrelations(abuffer): for pixlist in abuffer.values(): if len(pixlist) < 2: continue start = 1 end = len(pixlist) - 1 for i in range(start, end - 1, 2): celloccluding = pixlist[i+1].faceptr.owningcell celloccluded = pixlist[i].faceptr.owningcell celloccluding.pnlist.addormovetofront(celloccluded) celloccluded.sinkcellflag = False def sxmpvototalordering(cells, abuffer): extractpnrelations(abuffer) visited = set() orderedcells = [] def recursivedfs(c): visited.add(c) neighbors = c.mpvoneighbors + c.pnlist.entries for n in neighbors: if n not in visited: recursivedfs(n) orderedcells.append(c) for c in cells: if c.sinkcellflag and c not in visited: recursivedfs(c) return orderedcells[::-1] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping Faces: If faces overlap but are not sampled at points within the overlap region, the generated sort may not be a strict visibility ordering. However, the image-space rendering remains correct because faces are sampled at actual pixel locations. Viewpoint Position: If the viewpoint is outside the mesh, the PIX lists have an even number of entries, so the last entry is also discarded. This is the core modification of Phase II. It defines occlusion relations based on consecutive front-facing/back-facing face pairs on a PIX list. The cell contributing the back-facing face is the "occluding PN," and the other is the "occluded PN". This method captures image-space occlusion that may not be represented by explicit mesh topology (MPVO relations). It is chosen when exact image-space visibility is required for unstructured meshes with complex boundaries or disconnected components. It relies on the coherence of scan conversion to keep PN lists short and efficient via the move-to-front heuristic. Time Complexity: Dominated by the scan conversion (Phase I) and the DFS. The PN extraction iterates through PIX lists. The move-to-front heuristic ensures that frequently encountered PN relations are found quickly, keeping list traversal efficient. The DFS is linear in the number of cells and relations. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for PIX lists (proportional to image resolution and mesh complexity) and PN lists (proportional to the number of PN relations). Strengths: Handles nonconvex boundaries and disconnected components. Provides exact image-space visibility ordering. Limitations: Requires image-space sampling (scan conversion). Performance depends on the coherence of the scan conversion process. When to use: Unstructured mesh volume rendering where exact visibility is critical and the mesh is acyclic. When not to use: Structured grids where simpler sorting methods suffice, or when the mesh contains cycles. The SXMPVO algorithm extends the MPVO algorithm by incorporating image-space information (PIX lists) to derive additional occlusion relations (PN relations). This allows for a more accurate visibility ordering in image space, particularly for meshes with nonconvex boundaries or disconnected components. The method builds on the MPVO algorithm's Phase II but modifies the neighbor definition to include PN neighbors. name: A-buffer visibility sort for non-convex grids
head: A-buffer, Topological Sort with A-Buffer for Non-Convex Grids, Visibility sorting for non-convex grids
body: This method extends the Topological Sort for Cell Projection to handle non-convex grids by resolving visibility gaps between boundary cells using an image-space A-buffer. It solves the problem where viewing rays exit the grid through an external face, traverse empty space, and re-enter the grid, creating occlusion relationships that are not captured by shared-face topology alone. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) by avoiding expensive pairwise geometric occlusion tests or BSP-tree construction, instead relying on rasterization to implicitly determine segment ordering. The algorithm integrates an A-buffer into the topological sort pipeline to extract "gap relations" between boundary cells. Inputs: A non-convex curvilinear or unstructured grid. A list of exterior faces (faces belonging to boundary cells that are not shared with another cell). Image dimensions w \times h. Camera parameters defining viewing rays corresponding to pixel centers. Outputs: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) of cell ordering relations, including both shared-face relations (from the parent method) and gap relations (from the A-buffer). Data Structures: 1. A-Buffer: A 2D array of size w \times h. Each element A[y][x] is a pointer to a sorted linked list of fragments. 2. Fragment: A structure stored in the linked lists containing: depth: The distance from the viewpoint to the intersection point along the viewing ray. faceid: Identifier of the exterior face intersected. next: Pointer to the next fragment in the list. The lists are maintained in increasing order of depth (front-to-back). Steps: 1. Sort Exterior Faces: Sort the list of all exterior faces by the depth of their centroids relative to the viewpoint. This heuristic ensures that when rasterizing, new intersections are likely to occur at the head of the A-buffer lists, minimizing list maintenance cost. 2. Initialize A-Buffer: Allocate the w \times h array. Initialize all pixel entries to NULL or an empty list. This step incurs an overhead proportional to the number of pixels wh. 3. Rasterize and Collect Intersections: For each exterior face in the sorted order: a. Scan-convert the face into the image space. b. For each pixel (x, y) covered by the face, compute the intersection of the viewing ray for that pixel with the face. c. Calculate the intersection depth d. d. Insert a new fragment with depth = d and faceid into the linked list at A[y][x]. e. Maintain the sorted order of the list by depth. Since faces are processed in centroid-depth order, insertion is typically efficient. 4. Extract Gap Relations: Iterate through every pixel (x, y) that has a non-empty A-buffer list. a. Traverse the linked list of fragments. b. For every pair of successive fragments in the list, let Fi be the fragment with depth di and F{i+1} be the fragment with depth d{i+1}, where di < d{i+1}. c. The face Fi is in front of face F{i+1} along this specific viewing ray. d. Add a directed edge (relation) from the cell containing face Fi to the cell containing face F{i+1} in the topological sort graph. This represents the occlusion across the gap. 5. Process Topological Sort: Combine the relations extracted from shared faces (as defined in Topological Sort for Cell Projection) with the gap relations extracted in Step 4. Perform the topological sort on the resulting graph to obtain the final visibility ordering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def abuffervisibilitysort(exteriorfaces, grid, w, h, getviewingray, intersectface): # Step 1: Sort exterior faces by centroid depth # Source specifies sorting by centroid depth to keep insertion at head inexpensive. for face in exteriorfaces: face.centroiddepth = computecentroiddepth(face) # exteriorfaces.sort(key=lambda f: f.centroiddepth) # Step 2: Initialize A-Buffer # Overhead proportional to number of pixels wh. abuffer = [[None] w for in range(h)] # Step 3: Rasterize exterior faces for face in exteriorfaces: # Scan-convert face into image space. coveredpixels = scanconvertface(face, w, h) # for (x, y) in coveredpixels: ray = getviewingray(x, y) depth = intersectface(face, ray) # if depth is not None: fragment = Fragment(depth=depth, faceid=face.id) abuffer[y][x] = insertintosortedlist(abuffer[y][x], fragment) # Step 4: Extract Gap Relations gaprelations = [] for y in range(h): for x in range(w): head = abuffer[y][x] if head is None: continue prev = head curr = head.next while curr is not None: # Successive fragments Fi (prev) and F{i+1} (curr) with di < d{i+1}. # Face Fi is in front of F{i+1} along this viewing ray. cellprev = grid.facetocell(prev.faceid) # cellcurr = grid.facetocell(curr.faceid) # # Add directed edge from cell containing Fi to cell containing F{i+1}. gaprelations.append((cellprev, cellcurr)) prev = curr curr = curr.next # Step 5: Process Topological Sort # Combine gap relations with shared-face relations from parent method. # Perform topological sort to obtain final ordering. sharedrelations = getsharedfacerelations(grid) # allrelations = sharedrelations + gaprelations return topologicalsort(grid.cells, allrelations) # class Fragment: def init(self, depth, faceid): self.depth = depth self.faceid = faceid self.next = None def insertintosortedlist(head, newfragment): """ Inserts newfragment into the linked list starting at head, maintaining order by depth. Assumes newfragment is likely to be near the head due to sorting heuristic. """ if head is None: return newfragment if newfragment.depth < head.depth: newfragment.next = head return newfragment curr = head while curr.next is not None and curr.next.depth < newfragment.depth: curr = curr.next newfragment.next = curr.next curr.next = newfragment return head Parameters and Edge Cases: Sorting Heuristic: Sorting by centroid depth is critical for performance. The source states that this ensures "a new intersection almost always occurs at the head of the A-buffer list for each pixel, so maintaining the list per pixel is inexpensive". Non-Planar Faces: In curvilinear grids, quadrilateral faces may be non-planar. A viewing ray can leave and re-enter the same cell across the same face, making a strict visibility sort impossible for that specific ray. Approximation: The method does not produce a true global visibility sort because occlusions along rays not passing through pixel centers are ignored. However, since the A-buffer rays match the pixel sample rays used in final hardware rendering, the resulting image is correct. ZSWEEP is an exact, object-order cell projection algorithm for volume rendering on unstructured grids that optimizes for sorting efficiency and memory usage. It solves the problem of correctly ordering cell segments for front-to-back compositing without the high memory overhead of ray-casting or the complexity of true global visibility sorts. It sets itself apart from its parent A-buffer visibility sort for non-convex grids by using a sweep-plane approach that exploits the implicit global ordering induced by vertex z-coordinates, rather than maintaining full A-buffer lists for all pixels simultaneously. k-Buffer Analysis is a software-based diagnostic method that determines the optimal fixed buffer size k for the k-buffer visibility sorting algorithm in hardware-assisted volume rendering. It measures the required k by recording insertion depths into an ideal A-buffer, avoiding the unbounded memory of a true A-buffer while offering a less conservative sorting scheme than ZSWEEP. The k-buffer is a fixed-depth fragment sorting structure used in image-space volume rendering to manage visibility for non-convex grids. It acts as a hardware-efficient alternative to the unbounded A-buffer by storing only a constant number k of fragments per pixel, combining incoming fragments with stored ones and discarding the farthest (for front-to-back) or closest (for back-to-front) to manage memory. It is chosen when the fragment stream is approximately sorted (k-nearly sorted), allowing exact visibility sorting on the GPU with O(n) complexity, whereas the unbounded A-buffer requires potentially unbounded memory and the Z-buffer only handles single-layer visibility. Time Complexity: O(b \log b + wh + a + n), where b is the number of exterior faces, w and h are image dimensions, a is the projected area of external faces in pixels, and n is the number of relations across shared faces (or number of cells). b \log b: Sorting exterior faces. wh: Overhead for setting up and checking A-buffer lists. a: Cost of scan-converting faces and extracting relations. n: Processing shared-face relations. Memory Complexity: Substantial. The A-buffer requires storing a linked list of fragments for every pixel. Strengths: Faster than pairwise occlusion tests (O(b^2)) or BSP-tree based methods for general non-convex grids. It avoids complex preprocessing. Limitations: High memory consumption due to per-pixel linked lists. It is an approximation; it does not guarantee true visibility for rays not aligned with pixel centers, though it guarantees image correctness for the rendered pixels. The A-buffer was originally proposed by Loren Carpenter in 1984 to resolve visibility and aliasing problems by using multiple fragments per pixel. It was extended in the context of volume rendering for unstructured grids by Silva et al. to handle non-convex grids where simple topological sorts fail due to gaps between boundary cells. The approach shifts the visibility determination from object-space geometric tests to image-space rasterization, leveraging the hardware's rasterization capabilities (or software equivalents) to implicitly sort fragments. name: ZSWEEP
head: ZSWEEP mapper, ZSweep, ZSweep Algorithm
body: ZSWEEP is an exact, object-order cell projection algorithm for volume rendering on unstructured grids that sweeps a plane parallel to the viewing plane through the data in order of increasing z to sort and render cells. It differs from its parent A-buffer visibility sort for non-convex grids by optimizing specifically for memory usage and sorting efficiency through a sweep-based approach rather than a general A-buffer intersection list management, and it is substantially faster than its sibling k-Buffer Analysis while using much less memory than ray-casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unstructured dataset containing tetrahedral and/or hexahedral cells. A viewing direction defining the z-axis for the sweep. Output: A rendered image with correct visibility and opacity accumulation. Data Structures: Active Cell Set: A data structure holding only the cells currently intersected by the sweep plane. This keeps the memory footprint low. Face Intersection List: A short list of ordered face intersections for each pixel, known to be correct and complete at the instant each stage of computation is completed. Auxiliary Data Structures: Store partial information taken from a small number of "slices" of the dataset. Steps: 1. Sweep: Sweep a plane parallel to the viewing plane through the data in order of increasing z. 2. Exploit Ordering: Exploit the implicit (approximate) global ordering that the z-ordering of the vertices induces on the cells incident to them. 3. Project Faces: As vertices are encountered by the sweep plane, project the faces of cells incident to those vertices. Special care is taken to avoid double projection of internal faces. Correctness in the projection order is assured. 4. Rasterize: Rasterize cell faces as they are encountered by the sweep plane. 5. Compute Contribution: Compute the contribution for each pixel in stages during the sweep, using the short list of ordered face intersections. Ensure the list of face intersections is correct and complete at the instant that each stage of the computation is completed. 6. Integrate: Use a pre-integrated table for integration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zsweeprender(mesh, viewdirection, preintegrationtable): # 1. Sort vertices by their coordinate along the view direction (z) sortedvertices = sorted(mesh.vertices, key=lambda v: dot(v.position, viewdirection)) # 2. Initialize active cell set and auxiliary data structures activecells = set() pixelintersections = {} # Maps pixelid to list of (face, depth, celldata) # 3. Sweep plane moves from front to back (increasing z) for vertex in sortedvertices: # Identify cells incident to the current vertex incidentcells = mesh.getcellsincidentto(vertex) # Add incident cells to the active set if not already present for cell in incidentcells: activecells.add(cell) # 4. Project faces of cells incident to the current vertex # Avoid double projection of internal faces projectedfaces = [] for cell in activecells: for face in cell.faces: if face.isboundary or face.owner == cell: projectedfaces.append(face) # 5. Rasterize and update pixel intersection lists for face in projectedfaces: screencoords = projecttoscreen(face, viewdirection) pixelid = getpixelid(screencoords) if pixelid not in pixelintersections: pixelintersections[pixelid] = [] pixelintersections[pixelid].append((face, face.centerdepth, cell.data)) # 6. Compute pixel contributions using the ordered intersection lists # The list is guaranteed to be correct and complete at this stage for pixelid in list(pixelintersections.keys()): intersections = pixelintersections[pixelid] intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) # Sort front-to-back color, opacity = 0.0, 0.0 for face, depth, celldata in intersections: samplecolor, sampleopacity = preintegrationtable.lookup(celldata) alpha = 1.0 - opacity color += samplecolor sampleopacity alpha opacity += sampleopacity alpha if opacity >= 1.0: break del pixelintersections[pixelid] # Clear after processing # Remove cells from active set if they are no longer intersected by the sweep plane activecells = {c for c in activecells if c.isbehindsweepplane(vertex)} return pixelintersections def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def projecttoscreen(face, viewdir): return [v - dot(v, viewdir) viewdir for v in face.vertices] def getpixelid(coords): return (int(coords[0]), int(coords[1])) Parameters: Cell Types: Handles datasets containing tetrahedral and/or hexahedral cells. Integration: Uses a pre-integrated table for integration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Compatibility: There is no simple way to map this algorithm into currently available graphics hardware. It is a software rendering technique. Internal Faces: Double projection of internal faces must be avoided to ensure correctness. Ordering: The algorithm relies on the implicit global ordering induced by vertex z-ordering; correctness in projection order must be assured. Out-of-Core ZSWEEP is a direct volume rendering technique for large unstructured grids that extends the in-core ZSWEEP algorithm to handle datasets exceeding available RAM by processing data in tiles and loading meta-cells from disk only when needed. It differs from its sibling MIR by being substantially faster and leveraging the ZSWEEP optimization of front-to-back sorting, at the cost of more complex preprocessing and higher main-memory requirements. This variant involves processing scanlines from bottom to top. For each scanline, a 'critical section' of code is entered, where only one processor can run at a time. The surviving polygons of the previous pixel's x-actives list must be updated with newly interpolated values of field data and screen-z. New screen-z values may require rearrangement of polygons among survivors to maintain screen-z order. Taking into account the line-of-sight distance between the two polygons, the color-opacity contribution for that inter-polygon region is calculated and composited into a software floating point frame buffer using standard equations. Performance: The method is up to 5 times faster than the best previously-known exact algorithms that use comparable amounts of memory. Memory Usage: It has excellent memory efficiency, using much less memory than ray-casting. The memory footprint is kept low by holding only the active cell set in memory. Auxiliary data structures only store partial information from a small number of "slices" of the dataset. Hardware Mapping: There is no simple way to map this algorithm into currently available graphics hardware. It is implemented as a software rendering technique. Strengths: Fast, memory-efficient, exact rendering of unstructured datasets, simple enough to be readily adaptable to general (non-tetrahedral) cell formats. Limitations: Hardware incompatibility, potential bottleneck in parallel implementations due to critical sections. ZSWEEP was developed by Ricardo Farias, Joseph S. B. Mitchell, and Claudio Silva, combining the approaches of sweeping, projection, and A-buffers. It was presented in a conference paper in January 2000. The algorithm is an example of an A-Buffer technique that optimizes for sorting and memory usage. name: Out-of-Core ZSWEEP
head: OOC-ZSWEEP
body: Out-of-Core ZSWEEP is a direct volume rendering technique for large unstructured grids that extends the in-core ZSWEEP algorithm to handle datasets exceeding available RAM by processing data in tiles and loading meta-cells from disk only when needed. It differs from its sibling MIR by being substantially faster and leveraging the ZSWEEP optimization of front-to-back sorting, at the cost of more complex preprocessing and higher main-memory requirements. The algorithm is divided into two distinct phases: a view-independent preprocessing phase performed once to generate disk files, and a view-dependent rendering phase. Input: An unstructured volumetric grid defined by vertices and cells. Output: A rendered image (pixel colors/compositing results). The preprocessing generates two primary files on disk: 1. Meta-cell File: A small file containing a high-level description for each meta-cell. Each entry includes: Bounding box. Number of vertices. Number of cells. Pointer to the start of the meta-cell's data in the main data file. 2. Meta-cell Data File: A larger file containing the actual list of vertices and cells for each meta-cell. Vertices and cells may appear repeated across different meta-cells because each meta-cell is a self-contained unit. During rendering, the following in-memory structures are used: Pixel Intersection Lists: For each pixel in the current tile, a sorted list of intersections storing z-values and auxiliary information. Vertex Queue: A queue used for sweeping vertices. Vertices are tagged as either 'bounding-box' or 'dataset' vertices. Meta-cell Memory Buffer: Holds the vertices and cells of the currently active meta-cell(s) loaded from disk. 1. Chunk Creation (Meta-cell Generation): Let v be the total number of vertices and m be the target number of vertices per meta-cell. Externally sort all vertices by their x-values. Partition the sorted vertices into v/m consecutive parts. For each part, externally sort its vertices by y-values. Partition each part into v/m sub-parts. For each refined part, externally sort its vertices by z-values. Take the final parts as chunks (meta-cells). These chunks have roughly the same number of vertices but may differ in volume. 2. Meta-cell Association: Compute which cells spatially intersect each meta-cell and identify the vertices belonging to those cells. This is performed in external memory. The output is the two files described above. Note: Unlike the meta-cells in Chiang et al. [2], a cell in this variant can belong to as many meta-cells as it spatially intersects. The rendering is performed tile by tile. 1. Tile Division: Subdivide the screen into tiles. 2. Tile Processing: For each tile: 1. Compute the set of meta-cells that project into (intersect) the current tile. 2. Sort these meta-cells in a front-to-back order based on their depth relative to the camera. 3. Initialize the vertex queue and pixel intersection lists for the tile. 4. Sweep Loop: While the queue is not empty: Dequeue the next vertex v. If v is a bounding-box vertex: If the meta-cell m associated with this bounding box has not been loaded: Retrieve all vertices and cells of m from the disk files. Transform the vertices to view space. Insert these vertices into the queue, tagging them as dataset vertices. Increment the counter of bounding-box vertices seen for meta-cell m. If the counter for m reaches 8: Deallocate the memory for meta-cell m (free memory from disk). If v is a dataset vertex: Project the faces incident to v. For each pixel covered by the face, compute the intersection of the ray emanating from the pixel with the face. Store the z-value and auxiliary information in the pixel's intersection list in sorted order. Compositing: As the sweep plane reaches the "target Z" plane for each pixel, perform compositing using the accumulated intersection list for that pixel. Target vertices per meta-cell (m): Determines the size of the chunks. The number of meta-cells should be small enough to fit in memory. Tile Size: Determines the granularity of screen subdivision. Memory Usage: Main memory usage is dominated by pixel intersection lists and the "use set" of each vertex (cells incident to each vertex) for the currently loaded meta-cells. Cell Overlap: A single cell may be stored in multiple meta-cells if it spatially intersects multiple meta-cells. This increases disk space but simplifies the rendering logic by making meta-cells self-contained. Bounding Box Count: The algorithm assumes 8 bounding-box vertices per meta-cell (likely corresponding to a hexahedral bounding box). Memory Complexity: Constant memory usage with respect to dataset size. For a large 2048-by-2048 image of the Delta dataset, in-core ZSWEEP requires over 380 MB, while OOC-ZSWEEP requires about 24 MB. Time Complexity: Rendering times depend on the number of cells and resolution. For the SPX3 dataset at 2048^2 resolution, OOC-ZSWEEP took 1157 seconds to generate the image, with a cost of 174 µs per cell. Comparison with MIR: OOC-ZSWEEP is usually more efficient than MIR (Memory Insensitive Rendering), sometimes by a factor of 10 or more. However, it requires preprocessing and uses more memory than MIR. MIR is simpler to implement but considerably slower due to more sorting and disk I/O. Strengths: Enables rendering of datasets larger than RAM; faster than purely disk-based methods like MIR; leverages ZSWEEP's early compositing and sorting optimizations. Limitations: Complex preprocessing; higher memory usage than MIR; implementation complexity due to lazy loading and queue management. Out-of-Core ZSWEEP was introduced by Farias et al. as an extension of the ZSWEEP algorithm [4] to handle unstructured grids that do not fit in main memory. It builds on the meta-cell concept from Chiang et al. [2], adapting it for the specific needs of the ZSWEEP sweep process. The method was designed to address the limitations of in-core algorithms when dealing with large scientific datasets, providing a balance between the speed of in-core rendering and the capacity of out-of-core techniques. name: k*-Buffer Analysis
head: k-value Analysis
body: k-Buffer Analysis is a software-based diagnostic method that determines the optimal fixed buffer size k for the k-buffer visibility sorting algorithm in hardware-assisted volume rendering. It measures the required k by recording insertion depths into an ideal A-buffer, avoiding the unbounded memory of a true A-buffer while offering a less conservative sorting scheme than ZSWEEP. The method consists of two phases: the operational logic of the k-buffer itself and the analytical procedure to derive the required k. Inputs: A stream of fragments generated from 3D primitives (e.g., tetrahedra or triangles). A camera viewpoint and projection parameters. A target resolution (e.g., 512 \times 512). Outputs: The maximum required k (k{max}) for the dataset. The distribution of pixels requiring specific k values (e.g., count of pixels where k > 2 or k > 6). Identification of geometric degeneracies (e.g., sliver cells) causing high k requirements. A-Buffer (for Analysis): A 2D array of lists, one per pixel. Each list stores fragments sorted by depth (distance from viewpoint) in increasing order. k-buffer (for Operational Logic): A fixed-size array of k entries per pixel. Each entry contains the distance of the fragment from the viewpoint. In hardware implementations, entries are kept unsorted to simplify logic, relying on the property that the input sequence is k-nearly sorted. This phase simulates an ideal A-buffer to measure the true sorting distance of fragments. 1. Initialize an A-buffer for the target resolution. Each pixel contains an empty sorted list. 2. Rasterize the dataset from the viewpoint, generating a stream of fragments. 3. For each fragment f{new} with depth d{new}: a. Find the correct insertion position in the pixel's sorted A-buffer list such that depths are in increasing order (for front-to-back compositing). b. Let i be the index of the insertion position (0-based). c. Record the insertion depth metric: k{pixel} = \max(k{pixel}, i). The definition of k in the analysis is "the number of positions any fragment had to move to its correct position in the sorted order minus one for compositing". Effectively, if a fragment must be inserted at index i, it implies that up to i closer fragments exist. 4. Aggregate results: a. k{max} = \max{\text{pixels}} (k{pixel}). b. Count pixels where k{pixel} > 2. c. Count pixels where k{pixel} > 6. 5. Visualize (optional) the spatial distribution of k requirements to identify problematic regions (e.g., sliver cells). This phase describes how the determined k is used during rendering. 1. Initialize a k-buffer of size k for each pixel. 2. For each fragment f{new} arriving at a pixel: a. If the k-buffer is not full: insert f{new} into the buffer. b. If the k-buffer is full: determine if f{new} should replace an existing fragment. For front-to-back compositing, each time a new fragment f{new} is inserted, it dislodges the first entry (f1). Discard the fragment with the largest depth to maintain the closest fragments for compositing. c. In practice, hardware implementation is simplified by keeping the k-buffer entries unsorted. 3. Compositing: a. Retrieve the k fragments from the buffer. b. Sort them by depth (if not kept sorted). c. Perform front-to-back compositing using the pre-integrated table lookup. Note that k+1 entries are required for correct compositing of a k-nearly sorted sequence because the closest and second closest must be available for the lookup. k: The number of fragment entries stored per pixel. Typical Value: 6 is the standard value in existing HAVS implementations. Experimental Values: 6, 8, 10, 12. Trade-off: Larger k yields more precise results but lower efficiency (higher memory and processing time). Highly Out-of-Order Input: If the incoming fragment sequence is not k-nearly sorted, the output will be incorrect and artifacts may be visible. Sliver Cells: Large, thin cells with bad aspect ratios cause high k requirements. Solution 1: Subdivide degenerate cells into smaller, more symmetric cells using Delaunay tetrahedralization properties (empty circumsphere). Solution 2: Mesh smoothing operations to eliminate bad cells without creating additional tetrahedra. Artifact Visibility: Artifacts from limited k are often hard to notice, especially with transparent transfer functions. In worst-case scenarios (e.g., Torso dataset), only a small percentage of pixels (0.6%) were truly incorrect. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kbufferanalysis(primitives, resolution, camera): """ Performs k-Buffer Analysis to determine the required k for a dataset. Returns maxk and pixel distribution stats. """ # Initialize A-buffer: list of lists, one per pixel abuffer = [[[] for in range(resolution[1])] for in range(resolution[0])] kperpixel = [[0 for in range(resolution[1])] for in range(resolution[0])] # Generate fragments from dataset (standard rasterization step) fragments = rasterize(primitives, camera, resolution) for frag in fragments: u, v = frag['screencoords'] depth = frag['depth'] # Find insertion index in sorted A-buffer (increasing depth) pixellist = abuffer[u][v] insertidx = len(pixellist) for i, existingfrag in enumerate(pixellist): if depth < existingfrag['depth']: insertidx = i break # Insert fragment pixellist.insert(insertidx, frag) # Record k requirement: number of positions moved minus one for compositing kperpixel[u][v] = max(kperpixel[u][v], insertidx) maxk = 0 countkgt2 = 0 countkgt6 = 0 for u in range(resolution[0]): for v in range(resolution[1]): kval = kperpixel[u][v] if kval > maxk: maxk = kval if kval > 2: countkgt2 += 1 if kval > 6: countkgt6 += 1 return {"maxk": maxk, "pixelskgt2": countkgt2, "pixelskgt6": countkgt6, "distribution": kperpixel} def kbufferinsert(buffer, frag, k): """ Inserts a fragment into a k-buffer of size k. Keeps the k closest fragments. Entries are kept unsorted for hardware simplicity. """ if len(buffer) < k: buffer.append(frag) return # Find fragment with largest depth (furthest) furthestidx = 0 maxdepth = buffer[0]['depth'] for i in range(1, k): if buffer[i]['depth'] > maxdepth: maxdepth = buffer[i]['depth'] furthestidx = i # If new fragment is closer than the furthest in buffer, replace it if frag['depth'] < maxdepth: buffer[furthestidx] = frag A sibling method that uses a conservative technique for compositing samples to avoid memory space explosion in the A-buffer. The k-buffer offers a less conservative sorting scheme but requires analysis to ensure k is sufficient. Choose the k-buffer when memory is constrained but fragment ordering is nearly sorted. The parent method that uses an unbounded buffer. k-buffer analysis determines the fixed size k needed to approximate the A-buffer's behavior efficiently. Choose the k-buffer when rendering non-convex grids with high depth complexity but limited VRAM. Time Complexity: Analysis: O(N \log K) or O(N \cdot K) depending on implementation, where N is the number of fragments. The source notes that sorting n fragments with a k-nearly sorted property can be done in O(n) time. Rendering: O(1) per fragment insertion if k is fixed and small. Memory Complexity: O(k \cdot W \cdot H), where W, H are image dimensions. This is significantly less than the unbounded A-buffer O(N \cdot W \cdot H) in worst cases. Measured Performance: Hardware: Intel Pentium Dual 1.60GHz, NVIDIA GeForce9800 GTX. Datasets: F117: 2,517,674 fragments, Max A-buffer 481, Max k 15. 7,632 pixels require k > 2, 71 pixels require k > 6. Kew: 2,813,532 fragments, Max k 3. 0 pixels require k > 2, 0 pixels require k > 6. Spx2: 6,615,778 fragments, Max k 22. 10,626 pixels require k > 2, 512 pixels require k > 6. Torso: 7,223,435 fragments, Max k 15. 43,317 pixels require k > 2, 1,683 pixels require k > 6. Fighter: 5,414,884 fragments, Max k 3. 1 pixel requires k > 2, 0 pixels require k > 6. Strengths: Reduces memory requirements compared to A-buffer. Simple enough for hardware implementation. Artifacts are often unnoticeable, especially with transparency. Limitations: Requires preprocessing/analysis to determine optimal k. Sensitive to sliver cells, which can inflate k requirements. Fixed k may lead to incorrect ordering if the dataset has high depth complexity in specific regions. Origin: The k-buffer was introduced as part of the Hardware-Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) algorithm for unstructured grid volume rendering. History: Developed by Steve Callahan and colleagues, as detailed in the MS thesis "The k-Buffer and Its Applications to Volume Rendering". The analysis method was used to validate the effectiveness of the k-buffer on various datasets (F117, Kew, Spx2, Torso, Fighter). Development: Subsequent work optimized the HAVS algorithm by adjusting k values (6, 8, 10, 12) to balance precision and efficiency, showing that higher k improves precision but reduces performance. Optimization and Implementation of Unstructured Grid Volume Rendering Algorithm, https://doi.org/10.2991/iccasm.2012.373, fetched 2026-10-26 THE K-BUFFER AND ITS APPLICATIONS TO VOLUME RENDERING, https://ctsilva.github.io/thesis/steve-callahan-ms-thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: k-buffer
head: fixed depth A-buffer, modified A-buffer of fixed depth
body: The k-buffer is a fixed-depth fragment sorting structure used in image-space volume rendering to manage visibility for non-convex grids. It acts as a hardware-efficient alternative to the unbounded A-buffer by storing only a constant number k of fragments per pixel, combining incoming fragments with stored ones and discarding the farthest (for front-to-back) or closest (for back-to-front) to manage memory. It is chosen when the fragment stream is approximately sorted (k-nearly sorted), allowing exact visibility sorting on the GPU with O(n) complexity, whereas the unbounded A-buffer requires potentially unbounded memory and the Z-buffer only handles single-layer visibility. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of fragments generated by rasterization. Each fragment has a view-space distance d, a scalar data value v (e.g., density), and color/opacity. The fragments are assumed to be partially sorted in object space by the CPU. Output: An accumulated color and opacity in the framebuffer, and the remaining k-1 fragments written back to the k-buffer for subsequent processing. Data Structures: k-buffer: For each pixel, stores k entries. Each entry contains: d: Distance of the fragment from the viewpoint (view-space depth). v: Scalar data value associated with the fragment. Note: In the hardware implementation, entries are kept unsorted to simplify logic. Framebuffer: Stores the accumulated color c and opacity \alpha of the ray segment processed so far. Preintegrated Texture: A 3D texture used to look up the color and opacity contribution of a ray segment between two scalar values and distance. Parameters: k: The number of fragments stored per pixel. Typical value k=3. Threshold: Opacity threshold for early ray termination. Algorithm Steps: The k-buffer operates as a fragment stream sorter. For each incoming fragment f{new}, the following steps are performed in the fragment shader: 1. Read Accumulated Color: Read the current accumulated color c1 and opacity from the framebuffer. 2. Early Ray Termination: If c1 is opaque (opacity above threshold), terminate execution for this fragment (discard f{new}). 3. Fetch k-buffer Entries: Read the current k fragments (f1, \dots, fk) from the k-buffer buffers. 4. Identify Closest Fragments: Find the single closest fragment n1 among f{new} and the k stored entries based on distance d. Identify the remaining fragments r1, \dots, r{k-1} (excluding n1). Find the second closest fragment n2 among the remaining fragments r1, \dots, r{k-1}. 5. Compute Segment Properties: Let d1 be the depth of n1 and d2 be the depth of n2. Let v1 be the scalar value of n1 and v2 be the scalar value of n2. Compute the distance d = d2 - d1. 6. Lookup Contribution: Read the color c2 and opacity \alpha2 from the preintegrated texture using v1, v2, and d. 7. Composite: Composite c2 and \alpha2 into the framebuffer color c1. 8. Update k-buffer: Write the remaining fragments r1, \dots, r{k-1} back into the k-buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Fragment: def init(self, d, v, color, opacity): self.d = d self.v = v self.color = color self.opacity = opacity FRAMEBUFFER = {'color': (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 'opacity': 0.0} KBUFFER = [] # List of k Fragment objects THRESHOLD = 0.99 def preintegratedlookup(v1, v2, d): # Standard 3D texture lookup for preintegrated volume rendering return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 def processfragment(fnew): # Stage 1: Read accumulated color c1 = FRAMEBUFFER['color'] a1 = FRAMEBUFFER['opacity'] # Early ray termination if a1 >= THRESHOLD: return # Stage 2: Fetch k-buffer entries candidates = [fnew] + KBUFFER # Find closest fragment n1 n1 = min(candidates, key=lambda f: f.d) # Identify remaining fragments remaining = [f for f in candidates if f is not n1] # Find second closest fragment n2 from remaining n2 = min(remaining, key=lambda f: f.d) # Get properties d1 = n1.d d2 = n2.d v1 = n1.v v2 = n2.v # Compute distance between the two closest fragments d = d2 - d1 # Lookup color/opacity for the segment between n1 and n2 c2, a2 = preintegratedlookup(v1, v2, d) # Composite result into framebuffer FRAMEBUFFER['color'] = c1 + c2 a2 (1.0 - a1) FRAMEBUFFER['opacity'] = a1 + a2 (1.0 - a1) # Write remaining fragments back to k-buffer KBUFFER[:] = remaining Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Cases: f{new} may be inserted at the beginning (if closer than all others) or end (if further) of the sorted order. Out-of-Order Input: If the incoming sequence is highly out of order (worse than k-nearly sorted), the output will be incorrect, leading to visible artifacts. Screen-Space Interpolation: Projecting vertices to screen to compute 2D texture coordinates for screen-space buffer lookups yields incorrect results due to perspective-correct texture coordinate interpolation. Read-Write Race Condition: Simultaneously reading and writing a buffer in the same rendering pass is undefined. Holes in Data: Vertices on the boundary must be tagged. Ray segments with both vertices on the boundary are assigned zero color and opacity. A second tag indicates if a k-buffer entry is internal or external. This logic exceeds current hardware capabilities in the original implementation, so holes are not handled properly. Tags can be stored as the signs of v and d. Time Complexity: O(n) to sort a k-nearly sorted sequence of n fragments. Memory Complexity: Fixed memory per pixel: k entries. Performance: Achieved rendering rates of over six frames per second for datasets with over 1.4 million cells on tested hardware. Strengths: Reduces memory requirement compared to unbounded A-buffer; simple enough to implement on existing graphics architectures; shifts sorting burden to GPU. Limitations: Less conservative than ZSWEEP; incorrect output if input is highly out of order; limited handling of holes due to hardware instruction limits. When to Use: When fragments are partially sorted in object space (k-nearly sorted) and GPU-based visibility sorting is desired. When Not to Use: When fragments are highly unsorted or when exact handling of holes is required with current hardware limitations. The k-buffer was introduced by Steve Silva et al. in the context of Hardware-Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) for unstructured volume rendering. It builds on the A-buffer concept by Carpenter [5] and Danskin and Hanrahan [15], aiming to shift sorting burden to the GPU. The implementation utilized the ATIdrawbuffers OpenGL extension for multiple render targets. It is a generalized version of the Z-buffer, with classic Z-buffer corresponding to k=1 and Z3 buffer to k=3. name: Power Distance Sort
head: Circumsphere radius sort, Delaunay power sort, Power Distance Sort for Delaunay Tetrahedralization, Power Distance Sorting, Power Sorting, Radical axis sorting, Visibility sorting via circumcircles
body: Power Distance Sort is a visibility sorting method for Delaunay tetrahedralizations that orders cells in back-to-front order relative to a viewpoint using the power of the viewpoint with respect to each cell's circumsphere. It solves the problem of determining correct rendering order without constructing an adjacency graph or handling visibility cycles, which are required by topological sort methods. Unlike Topological Sort for Cell Projection, which guarantees correctness for any convex grid via graph traversal, Power Distance Sort relies on the geometric properties of Delaunay meshes; it is not guaranteed to produce accurate visibility ordering for non-Delaunay meshes. Inputs: A set of tetrahedra Ti forming a Delaunay tetrahedralization. A viewpoint (camera origin) \mathbf{o}. Outputs: A list of tetrahedra sorted in decreasing order of power distance from \mathbf{o}, which corresponds to a correct back-to-front visibility order for Delaunay meshes. Data Structures: Each tetrahedron T requires the precomputed center \mathbb{O}(T) and radius \mathbb{R}(T) of its circumsphere. A list of tuples (powerdistance, tetrahedronindex) for sorting. Formulas: The power of the viewpoint \mathbf{o} relative to the circumsphere of tetrahedron T is defined as: P(T) = \|\mathbb{O}(T) - \mathbf{o}\|2^2 - \mathbb{R}(T)^2 Where: \mathbb{O}(T) is the 3D center of the circumsphere of T. \mathbb{R}(T) is the radius of the circumsphere of T. \mathbf{o} is the 3D position of the camera origin. \|\cdot\|2 denotes the Euclidean norm. Alternatively, if d is the distance from \mathbf{o} to \mathbb{O}(T) and r is the radius \mathbb{R}(T), the power distance is d^2 - r^2. Steps: 1. For each tetrahedron Ti in the mesh, compute the center \mathbb{O}(Ti) and radius \mathbb{R}(Ti) of its circumsphere. 2. For each tetrahedron Ti, calculate the power distance P(Ti) using the formula above. 3. Sort the tetrahedra in decreasing order of P(Ti) (largest power distance first, i.e., furthest back). 4. Render the tetrahedra in the sorted order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computecircumsphere(tetrahedron): """ Computes the center and radius of the circumsphere of a tetrahedron. tetrahedron: list of 4 vertices, each a tuple (x, y, z). Returns: (center, radius) """ # Implementation of circumsphere calculation for 3D tetrahedron # Let vertices be v0, v1, v2, v3 v0, v1, v2, v3 = tetrahedron # Vector differences d1 = [v1[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] d2 = [v2[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] d3 = [v3[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] # Cross products cross1 = [d2[1]d3[2] - d2[2]d3[1], d2[2]d3[0] - d2[0]d3[2], d2[0]d3[1] - d2[1]d3[0]] cross2 = [d3[1]d1[2] - d3[2]d1[1], d3[2]d1[0] - d3[0]d1[2], d3[0]d1[1] - d3[1]d1[0]] cross3 = [d1[1]d2[2] - d1[2]d2[1], d1[2]d2[0] - d1[0]d2[2], d1[0]d2[1] - d1[1]d2[0]] # Dot product of d1 with cross1 dot = d1[0]cross1[0] + d1[1]cross1[1] + d1[2]cross1[2] if abs(dot) < 1e-9: # Degenerate tetrahedron (coplanar vertices) # Return a large radius or handle as error return ([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], float('inf')) # Center calculation # O = v0 + 0.5 ( (|d2|^2 cross1 + |d3|^2 cross2 + |d1|^2 cross3) / dot) # Note: The standard formula involves cross products of the edge vectors. # Using the determinant form or vector algebra: # C = v0 + ( (|d2|^2 (d1 x d3) + |d3|^2 (d3 x d1) + |d1|^2 (d1 x d2)) / (2 d1. (d2 x d3))) # Let's use the cross products computed above which correspond to parts of the denominator/numerator structure. # Actually, the standard vector formula for circumcenter O relative to v0 is: # O = v0 + 0.5 ( (|d2|^2 (d1 x d3) + |d3|^2 (d3 x d1) + |d1|^2 (d1 x d2)) / (d1. (d2 x d3))) # Note: d1 x d3 is -cross1? No. # Let's stick to a robust geometric library or explicit determinant if needed. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a helper getcircumsphere exists or is implemented via standard linear algebra. # Simplified implementation for clarity: # Using the property that the circumcenter is equidistant from all 4 vertices. # Solve linear system for center (cx, cy, cz). # This is a standard computational geometry task. # We will assume a function computecircumcenterandradius is available. pass def powerdistancesort(tetrahedra, viewpoint): """ Sorts tetrahedra by power distance from viewpoint. tetrahedra: list of tetrahedra (each is list of 4 vertices). viewpoint: tuple (x, y, z). Returns: list of tetrahedra sorted back-to-front. """ poweredtetrahedra = [] for i, tet in enumerate(tetrahedra): center, radius = computecircumsphere(tet) # Calculate squared distance from viewpoint to center dx = center[0] - viewpoint[0] dy = center[1] - viewpoint[1] dz = center[2] - viewpoint[2] distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz # Power distance power = distsq - radiusradius poweredtetrahedra.append((power, i)) # Sort by power distance in decreasing order (largest power = furthest) poweredtetrahedra.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) sortedtetrahedra = [tetrahedra[idx] for, idx in poweredtetrahedra] return sortedtetrahedra Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Delaunay Meshes: The method is not guaranteed to produce accurate visibility ordering unless the mesh is a Delaunay triangulation. There is no way to tell in advance whether a given non-Delaunay mesh will be correctly sorted. Degenerate Tetrahedra: If vertices are coplanar, the circumsphere is undefined (infinite radius). This must be handled, potentially by skipping or treating as a special case. Viewpoint Position: The sort order is relative to the ray origin, making it valid for fisheye and distorted projections. However, simple schemes may fail from certain viewpoints or viewing directions if the Delaunay property is not strictly maintained. Implements a specialized quicksort to optimize data movement for power distance sorting, yielding significant speed improvements over generic sorts. Time Complexity: Theoretical time complexity is O(n \log n) due to the sorting step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the power distance for each tetrahedron, O(n). Performance: In practice, it is competitive with topological sort (O(n)) because it avoids the overhead of storing and accessing an adjacency structure. It has very small constant computations and is straightforward to implement. Strengths: Fast, simple implementation, no adjacency graph required, works with distorted projections. Limitations: Only guaranteed correct for Delaunay tetrahedralizations; incorrect for general meshes. Power Distance Sort was described by Cignoni et al. and Wittenbrink. Edelsbrunner (1989) proved that for a Delaunay tetrahedralization, no visibility cycles are possible, and that sorting by power distance yields a correct visibility order. The method relies on the geometric property that the shared face of two adjacent tetrahedra lies on the radical plane of their circumspheres, which divides the space into regions where the viewpoint has a lower power distance to one circumsphere or the other. name: Customized Quicksort for Visibility Sorting
head: Customized Quicksort
body: This method implements a specialized quicksort algorithm to sort volume rendering cells (tetrahedra) for visibility determination. It addresses the performance bottleneck of generic sorting routines by optimizing data movement for the specific structure required by power distance sorting. It is distinguished from generic library sorts (like qsort) by its ability to handle the coupled data structures of tangential distance and cell index efficiently, yielding a 75% to 89% improvement in speed. Inputs: A list of N tetrahedral cells. For each cell, the precomputed tangential squared distance to the circumscribing sphere, denoted as d^2. The tetrahedral index, denoted as idx. Outputs: A sorted list of tetrahedral indices ordered by increasing tangential squared distance d^2. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on an array of structures or parallel arrays containing two fields per element: 1. dist: A float representing the tangential squared distance. 2. index: An integer representing the tetrahedral index. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the list of tetrahedra with their associated tangential squared distances and indices. 2. Partitioning: Select a pivot element from the current sub-array. The pivot selection strategy is critical for performance on nearly sorted data (see View Coherence Optimization). 3. Comparison: Compare the dist field of elements against the pivot's dist. 4. Swapping: When swapping elements during partitioning, move both the dist (float) and the index (integer) together to maintain the association between the distance metric and the cell identifier. 5. Recursion: Recursively apply the sort to the sub-arrays created by the partition. 6. Termination: Stop when sub-arrays are of size 0 or 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def customizedquicksort(cells, low, high): """ Sorts the cells array in-place based on the 'dist' field. cells: List of objects/tuples with attributes 'dist' (float) and 'index' (int). low: Start index of the sub-array. high: End index of the sub-array. """ if low < high: # Partition the array and get the pivot index pivotindex = partition(cells, low, high) # Recursively sort elements before and after partition customizedquicksort(cells, low, pivotindex - 1) customizedquicksort(cells, pivotindex + 1, high) def partition(cells, low, high): """ Partitions the array such that elements with dist <= pivot.dist are on the left, and elements with dist > pivot.dist are on the right. """ # Select pivot. For view coherence, the last element is often efficient if data is nearly sorted. pivotdist = cells[high].dist pivotindex = high i = low - 1 # Index of smaller element for j in range(low, high): # Compare only the distance field if cells[j].dist <= pivotdist: i = i + 1 # Swap both dist and index to keep them coupled swap(cells, i, j) # Place pivot in correct position swap(cells, i + 1, high) return i + 1 def swap(cells, i, j): """ Swaps two elements in the cells array. Moves both the tangential squared distance (float) and the tetrahedral index (int). """ tempdist = cells[i].dist tempindex = cells[i].index cells[i].dist = cells[j].dist cells[i].index = cells[j].index cells[j].dist = tempdist cells[j].index = tempindex Parameters and Edge Cases: Pivot Selection: The choice of pivot significantly impacts performance. Standard random or median-of-three pivots are common, but for view coherence, using the last element of the previous frame's sorted order is effective. Precision: The distance is stored as a float. Precision issues may arise if distances are extremely close, potentially affecting strict visibility ordering. Degenerate Input: If the input is already sorted or nearly sorted, a naive quicksort may degrade to O(N^2) without proper pivot selection or hybridization (e.g., switching to insertion sort for small sub-arrays). The custom implementation exploits view coherence to mitigate this. Accelerates sorting by leveraging the similarity between consecutive camera viewpoints, using the previous frame's sorted order as a starting point. Time Complexity: Average case O(N \log N). Best case O(N \log N) or better with view coherence on nearly sorted data. Worst case O(N^2) if pivot selection is poor and data is structured adversarially, though mitigated by the custom implementation's design. Memory Complexity: O(\log N) stack space for recursion. In-place sorting requires no additional memory for the data structures. Performance: Provides a 75% to 89% improvement over the C library utility qsort(). The rate varies between 600,000 to 2 million cells per second depending on the hardware and scene complexity. Strengths: High efficiency due to optimized data movement (moving only two values: float and int) and avoidance of generic sorting overhead. Limitations: Not guaranteed to produce accurate visibility ordering unless the mesh is a Delaunay triangulation (inherited from the underlying Power Distance Sort method). This method is described in the context of unstructured volume rendering, specifically for sorting tetrahedral cells based on tangential distances to circumscribing spheres, a technique originally proposed by Cignoni et al. and Karasick et al.. The customized quicksort was developed to overcome the inefficiencies of generic sorting routines when handling the specific data structures required for this visibility sorting task.
