name: View Coherence Optimization
head: Exploiting view coherence, Order checking, Resorting with previous view data
body: View Coherence Optimization accelerates the visibility sorting of volume rendering cells by leveraging the similarity between consecutive camera viewpoints. Instead of sorting the cell list from scratch for every frame, it uses the sorted order from the previous view as a starting point, significantly reducing the number of swaps required when viewpoint changes are small. It further optimizes the sorting loop by employing a fast, parallel order-checking mechanism to exit early if the data is already sorted. This method builds on Customized Quicksort for Visibility Sorting by reducing the workload that the quicksort must perform. Inputs: A list of cells sorted by depth from the previous view. The current camera view parameters. The set of cells to be rendered for the current view. Outputs: A list of cells sorted by depth for the current view. Data Structures: Cell List: An array of structures. Each element contains: tangentialsquareddistance: A float representing the squared distance from the camera plane or a similar depth metric used for sorting. tetrahedralindex: An integer identifier for the cell/tetrahedron. Comparison Array: A temporary array of integers (0 or 1) used during the order check. Shared Memory (GPU): Used for coalesced reading and partial reduction. Parameters: n0: The number of initial elements to test in the "quick order check" subset. The sources do not specify a typical value, noting it is based on initialization-time queries to the hardware. Steps: 1. Prepare for Small Viewpoint Changes: Ensure the application generates small, incremental changes in the viewpoint between frames to maximize coherence. 2. Initialize Sort with Previous Order: Pass the sorted list from the previous frame as the input to the sorting algorithm (e.g., Customized Quicksort) for the current frame. 3. Parallel Order Checking (GPU Implementation): To avoid full sorting when the list is already sorted or nearly sorted, perform the following check during the sorting iterations: 1. Coalesced Read: Each thread reads only one element from the current cell list into shared memory. This allows for coalesced memory access and cuts read operations in half compared to reading two consecutive elements. 2. Parallel Comparison: Each thread compares its element with the next element in the sequence. If element[i] is in the correct order relative to element[i+1] (based on the current view's depth metric), write 0 to the comparison array. Otherwise, write 1. 3. Partial Reduction: Perform a parallel reduction sum on the comparison array within shared memory. Only the single sum for the block is written to global memory. 4. Quick Test on Subset: Perform the above comparison and reduction on the first n0 elements of the array. If the sum is non-zero (out of order detected), proceed to the next sorting step (e.g., quicksort partitioning) and skip the full test. If the sum is zero (sorted), perform a check on the remaining 1 + n - n0 elements, including the last element of the n0 set, to ensure global order. 5. Early Exit: If the final reduction sum is 0, the input data is in order, and the sorting loop can exit early. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def viewcoherencesort(celllist, previoussortedlist, cameraview, n0): """ Sorts celllist for the current cameraview, using previoussortedlist to exploit view coherence. """ # Step 1: Use previous sorted list as initial state # The quicksort algorithm will start with this nearly-sorted array currentlist = previoussortedlist.copy() # Step 2: Perform sorting with integrated order checking # The quicksort implementation must support early exit via order checking sortedlist = customizedquicksortwithordercheck( currentlist, cameraview, n0) return sortedlist def customizedquicksortwithordercheck(celllist, cameraview, n0): """ A quicksort variant that checks for sorted order during execution. """ if len(celllist) <= 1: return celllist # Check if already sorted using parallel order checking if issortedparallel(celllist, cameraview, n0): return celllist # Standard quicksort partitioning and recursion pivot = selectpivot(celllist) less = [c for c in celllist if c.depth < pivot.depth] equal = [c for c in celllist if c.depth == pivot.depth] greater = [c for c in celllist if c.depth > pivot.depth] return (customizedquicksortwithordercheck(less, cameraview, n0) + equal + customizedquicksortwithordercheck(greater, cameraview, n0)) def issortedparallel(celllist, cameraview, n0): """ GPU-accelerated order check. Returns True if the list is sorted, False otherwise. """ n = len(celllist) # Step 3.1: Quick test on first n0 elements # In a real GPU implementation, this is done in parallel threads # Here we simulate the logic for clarity # Check first n0 elements quicktestfailed = False for i in range(min(n0, n - 1)): if celllist[i].depth > celllist[i+1].depth: quicktestfailed = True break if quicktestfailed: return False # If quick test passed, check remaining elements # Check remaining 1 + n - n0 elements including the last of n0 set startindex = n0 if startindex >= n: return True # All checked in quick test for i in range(startindex, n - 1): if celllist[i].depth > celllist[i+1].depth: return False # Check the boundary between n0 and the rest if not already covered # The source says "including the last element of the n0 set" # This implies checking the transition or ensuring the last of n0 # is compared with the first of the rest if n0 < n-1 if n0 < n - 1: if celllist[n0-1].depth > celllist[n0].depth: return False return True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Viewpoint Changes: If the viewpoint changes significantly, the previous order is no longer coherent, and the optimization provides little benefit or may even add overhead due to the order checking. Cache Coherency: Reordering tetrahedra for view sorting eliminates cache stalls during rendering but slows down the sorting routine due to increased data movement. This trade-off requires careful tuning. Precision: The tangential squared distance is a float, which may introduce precision issues in edge cases where depths are very close. Performance: The rate for the custom quicksort with view coherence varies between 600,000 to 2,000,000 cells per second, depending on how sorted the list is. Comparison: This is significantly faster than MPVONC, which reported 185,000 to 266,000 cells per second. Without view coherence and data structure optimizations, earlier work achieved only 109,570 cells/second on a PA RISC 7200 (120 MHz). Order Checking Optimization: The optimized parallel order checking (coalesced reading, partial reduction) triples the performance of the order checking routine compared to the reference CUDPP implementation. Strengths: Extremely fast on sorted or nearly sorted data, which is typical in volume rendering with small viewpoint changes. Limitations: Overhead if the data is not sorted; the quick test must be carefully sized (n0) to avoid false positives/negatives. Origin: The concept of exploiting view coherence in volume rendering was discussed by Meissner in the context of cell projection and visibility sorting. Development: The parallel order checking algorithm was further optimized for GPUs by Silva et al., building on the CUDPP binary radix sort library's checking function. Usage: Used in high-performance volume rendering systems where real-time or near-real-time interaction with large datasets is required. name: Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant)
head: Wilhelms et al. Per-Pixel Sort, Wilhelms et al. Sorting
body: Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant) is an image-space visibility ordering method that sorts all cell faces projecting onto a specific pixel at render time, just prior to compositing. It solves the problem of determining the correct back-to-front rendering order for transparent volumes in scenes where a global topological sort is impossible due to visibility cycles. Unlike its sibling Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO), which sorts only exterior faces and exploits spatial coherence, this variant sorts all faces (including interior ones) independently or incrementally per pixel. It differs from Mammen's Technique in that it sorts all cell faces per pixel, whereas Mammen's technique specifically sorts transparent fragments in front of the front-most opaque one. Inputs: A set of convex polyhedral cells forming a volume mesh; a viewpoint; a rasterization grid (screen). Outputs: A sorted list of face fragments for each pixel, ordered from back to front. Data Structures: The method adapts scan-line visible surface algorithms using the following structures: 1. Y-Buckets: A list of lists indexed by scan line y. Each bucket contains faces that first cross that scan line. 2. Active List: A list of faces currently overlapping the current scan line y. 3. X-Buckets: A list of lists indexed by pixel column x within the current scan line. Each bucket contains faces covering the first pixel of that column on the current scan line. 4. Z-Sorted List: A list of faces at the current pixel (x, y), sorted by their depth z value at that pixel. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create empty Y-Buckets for all scan lines. 2. Scan Line Processing: Iterate through each scan line y from top to bottom (or bottom to top, depending on coordinate system). 3. Update Active List: For the current scan line y, add all faces found in Y-Bucket y to the Active List. Remove faces from the Active List that no longer overlap the current scan line. 4. Pixel Processing: Iterate through each pixel column x on the current scan line. 5. Update X-Buckets: For the current pixel (x, y), add all faces found in X-Bucket x to the local processing set. 6. Filter Active List: Identify faces in the Active List that cover the current pixel (x, y). 7. Sort: Sort the identified faces by their depth z at the pixel center (x, y). If the previous pixel (x-1, y) was processed, the sort can be updated incrementally rather than performed from scratch, taking partial advantage of coherence in x. 8. Compositing: Composite the sorted faces from back to front. 9. Cleanup: Prepare for the next pixel. If not using incremental update, clear the Z-Sorted List. Formulas: Depth z at pixel (x, y) for a planar face with vertices \mathbf{v}i = (xi, yi, zi): z(x, y) = \frac{z1(x2 y3 - x3 y2) + z2(x3 y1 - x1 y3) + z3(x1 y2 - x2 y1)}{x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)} (Assuming a triangular face; generalized for polygons via barycentric interpolation or plane equation Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 where z = -(Ax + By + D)/C). Parameters: Scan line order: Not given in the sources. Sort stability: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Cycles: This method handles visibility cycles gracefully because a local visibility sort always exists for each pixel center, even if no global sort exists. Coherence: The method takes partial advantage of coherence in x (between adjacent pixels) but not in y (between adjacent scan lines). Performance: Since all faces are sorted, not just exterior ones, the method spends significantly more effort on per-pixel sorting, as exterior faces are typically a small fraction of total faces in most meshes. Hardware vs. Software: Hardware proposals (e.g., R-Buffer) suggest scanning all polygons once and storing fragments in an unordered buffer for multiple depth comparison passes. However, software implementations often repeat sorts from scratch independently at each pixel, which is less efficient than incremental updates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Face: def init(self, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, planecoeffs): self.minx, self.maxx = minx, maxx self.miny, self.maxy = miny, maxy self.A, self.B, self.C, self.D = planecoeffs def coverspixel(self, x, y): return self.minx <= x <= self.maxx and self.miny <= y <= self.maxy def getzat(self, x, y): return -(self.A x + self.B y + self.D) / self.C def perpixelsortgeneralvariant(faces, screenwidth, screenheight): # Initialize Y-Buckets for all scan lines ybuckets = [[] for in range(screenheight)] # Populate Y-Buckets: assign each face to the first scan line it crosses for face in faces: yidx = max(0, min(screenheight - 1, face.miny)) ybuckets[yidx].append(face) pixelfragments = [[[] for in range(screenheight)] for in range(screenwidth)] activelist = [] # Process each scan line for y in range(screenheight): # Update Active List: add faces from Y-Bucket y for face in ybuckets[y]: activelist.append(face) # Remove faces that no longer overlap this scan line activelist = [f for f in activelist if f.maxy > y] # Initialize X-Buckets for the current scan line xbuckets = [[] for in range(screenwidth)] for face in activelist: if face.coverspixel(0, y): xidx = max(0, min(screenwidth - 1, face.minx)) xbuckets[xidx].append(face) # Process each pixel in the scan line for x in range(screenwidth): # Update X-Buckets: get faces starting at this pixel column on this scanline localfaces = list(xbuckets[x]) # Filter Active List: identify faces covering this pixel coveringfaces = [f for f in activelist if f.coverspixel(x, y)] coveringfaces.extend(localfaces) # Sort faces by depth z at (x, y) # Incremental update from previous pixel (x-1, y) is possible but not specified in sources coveringfaces.sort(key=lambda f: f.getzat(x, y)) # Store sorted fragments for compositing pixelfragments[x][y] = coveringfaces return pixelfragments Mammen's Technique is a software algorithm that sorts per-pixel transparent fragments in front of the front-most opaque one. It operates on pixel fragments instead of object fragments, allowing objects to be rasterized in any order without requiring object-space visibility sorting. This distinguishes it from object-space methods like MPVO, which must handle complex degeneracies and ordering constraints before rasterization. Choose it when rendering transparent surfaces like glass helmets or windshields where object-space sorting is impractical. Nearly-Sorted Object-Space Visibility Ordering (k-NSS) is a relaxation of exact visibility ordering where primitives are ordered such that rasterized fragments are at most k positions out of order in the sorted sequence. It differs from its parent Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant) by performing the initial ordering in object space rather than per-pixel, and from siblings like Mammen's Technique by explicitly bounding the displacement error k to enable linear-time correction. Choose it when faster approximate sorting is acceptable and exact compositing order can be deferred to fragment processing. PLP is an approximate, from-point, object-space visibility algorithm designed for large datasets that requires minimal preprocessing. It solves the problem of efficiently selecting a subset of geometry to render within a strict per-frame budget by using heuristics to estimate cell visibility likelihood. Unlike Teller et al.'s from-region algorithm, which requires extensive preprocessing and assumes axis-aligned cells, PLP makes no geometric assumptions and operates with very little setup overhead. Choose it for large datasets where strict per-frame budgets limit preprocessing and global sorting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires substantial memory proportional to the projected area, in pixels, of all faces in the mesh, not just the boundary. This contrasts with SXMPVO, which handles fragments proportional to the projected area of the boundary. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles visibility cycles gracefully; robust for non-convex meshes where global sorting fails. Limitations: High memory usage; high computational cost due to sorting all faces (including interior ones); poor coherence in y. When to use: When a global topological sort is impossible and memory is not a constraint; for scenes with complex visibility cycles. When not to use: For large datasets with many interior faces; when memory bandwidth is limited; when global sorting is possible (use Topological Sort for Cell Projection or SXMPVO instead). The method was introduced by Wilhelms et al.. It is based on techniques similar to scan-line visible surface algorithms. Hardware proposals, such as the R-Buffer by Wittenbrink, aimed to implement this efficiently by scanning polygons once and storing fragments in a recirculating buffer for multiple depth comparison passes. However, the R-Buffer hardware does not exist, and software implementations are less efficient than incremental methods. The method is often compared to Mammen's Technique, which is similar but focuses on transparent fragments in front of opaque ones. name: Mammen's Technique
head: A-buffer visibility sort, Carpenter's A-buffer, Per-pixel transparent fragment sorting
body: Mammen's Technique is a software algorithm that sorts per-pixel transparent fragments in front of the front-most opaque one. It operates on pixel fragments instead of object fragments, allowing objects to be rasterized in any order without requiring object-space visibility sorting. This distinguishes it from object-space methods like MPVO, which must handle complex degeneracies and ordering constraints before rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of geometric primitives (polygons) defining the scene. Output: A depth-sorted list of fragments for each pixel, ready for compositing. Data Structures: Per-Pixel Linked Lists: For each pixel (x, y), a singly linked list stores fragments. Fragment Structure: Each fragment stores its depth value z and color/transparency attributes. The exact bit-packing of the fragment structure is not specified in the sources [G: Standard implementation would include z, color, and a pointer to the next fragment]. Steps: 1. Rasterization: Rasterize all objects in the scene into sets of pixel fragments. 2. Storage: Save the generated fragments into per-pixel linked lists. 3. Sorting: After all objects have been rasterized, sort the fragments in each per-pixel linked list using the stored depth values. 4. Compositing: Composite the sorted fragments from front to back [G: Standard alpha blending/compositing procedure]. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Requirements: The technique has substantial memory requirements because it stores all incoming fragments for every pixel. Hardware Implementation: Current hardware implementations of this technique require multiple passes through the polygons in the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Fragment: def init(self, x, y, z, color): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z self.color = color self.next = None def mammentechnique(sceneprimitives, imagewidth, imageheight): # Initialize per-pixel linked lists pixellists = [None] (imagewidth imageheight) # Step 1 & 2: Rasterize all objects and store fragments for primitive in sceneprimitives: # [G: Standard rasterization step generates pixel coverage and depth values] fragments = [] for frag in fragments: idx = frag.y imagewidth + frag.x node = Fragment(frag.x, frag.y, frag.z, frag.color) node.next = pixellists[idx] pixellists[idx] = node # Step 3: Sort the lists after all objects have been rasterized for i in range(len(pixellists)): pixellists[i] = sortlinkedlistbydepth(pixellists[i]) return pixellists def sortlinkedlistbydepth(head): if head is None or head.next is None: return head slow, fast = head, head.next while fast and fast.next: slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next mid = slow.next slow.next = None return merge(sortlinkedlistbydepth(head), sortlinkedlistbydepth(mid)) def merge(left, right): dummy = Fragment(0, 0, float('inf'), None) curr = dummy while left and right: if left.z < right.z: curr.next, left = left, left.next else: curr.next, right = right, right.next curr = curr.next curr.next = left or right return dummy.next The R-Buffer is a hardware architecture proposal for implementing order-independent transparency (OIT) by storing fragments in a large, unordered, recirculating buffer shared across the entire screen, rather than using fixed-size per-pixel buffers. It implements a sorting and compositing method similar to Mammen's software algorithm to handle transparent fragments in front of the front-most opaque one. Unlike previous hardware implementations that required multiple passes through the geometry, the R-Buffer scan-converts all polygons only once, storing uncomposited fragments in the recirculating buffer for subsequent depth-comparison passes. It is distinguished from its sibling Mammen's Technique by moving the sorting logic from software to dedicated hardware logic, and from k-Buffer by using a single global FIFO buffer instead of fixed-size per-pixel arrays, thereby amortizing storage costs over the screen. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Substantial, as it stores all incoming fragments for every pixel. Strengths: Objects can be rasterized in any order, avoiding the complexity of object-space visibility sorting. Limitations: High memory consumption. Software implementation requires sorting from scratch at each pixel, which is more work than incremental updates. Hardware implementations may require multiple passes through the geometry. When to use: When object-space ordering is difficult or impossible (e.g., due to visibility cycles) and memory is not a constraint. When not to use: When memory is limited or when incremental sorting per pixel is feasible. The technique was proposed by Carpenter as the A-buffer. It is described in a software algorithm by Mammen. The method operates on pixel fragments instead of object fragments. name: R-Buffer
head: Recirculating Fragment Buffer, Wittenbrink's R-Buffer, recirculating buffer
body: The R-Buffer is a hardware architecture proposal for implementing order-independent transparency (OIT) by storing fragments in a large, unordered, recirculating buffer shared across the entire screen, rather than using fixed-size per-pixel buffers. It implements a sorting and compositing method similar to Mammen's software algorithm to handle transparent fragments in front of the front-most opaque one. Unlike previous hardware implementations that required multiple passes through the geometry, the R-Buffer scan-converts all polygons only once, storing uncomposited fragments in the recirculating buffer for subsequent depth-comparison passes. It is distinguished from its sibling Mammen's Technique by moving the sorting logic from software to dedicated hardware logic, and from k-Buffer by using a single global FIFO buffer instead of fixed-size per-pixel arrays, thereby amortizing storage costs over the screen. The R-Buffer operates as a pointerless A-buffer architecture that separates fragment storage from the Z-buffer and frame buffer. It relies on a global recirculating fragment buffer (R-buffer) and a second Z-storage to manage fragments that are neither the closest opaque nor the furthest transparent fragment for a given pixel. Input: A stream of fragments generated by rasterizing geometry. Each fragment carries screen coordinates (X, Y), depth Z, and color/opacity (RGBA). Output: A composited image in the frame buffer with order-independent transparency. 1. Frame Buffer: Stores the accumulated color and opacity of fragments that have been fully composited or are the final opaque fragment. 2. R-Buffer: A single, large, circular first-in-first-out (FIFO) queue shared by the entire screen. It stores fragments that require further processing. Each entry contains X, Y, Z, and RGBA values. 3. 2nd Z-Buffer: An auxiliary storage used in conjunction with the R-Buffer to assist in depth comparisons. 1. Rasterization (Single Pass): All polygons are scan-converted only once. For each generated fragment, the hardware compares its depth Z against the frame buffer's Z-buffer and color buffer. If the fragment is occluded by an opaque fragment in the frame buffer, it is discarded. If the fragment is the closest opaque fragment, it replaces the current frame buffer content. If the fragment is transparent and not occluded, it is sent to the R-Buffer along with its X, Y, Z, and RGBA values. 2. Recirculation and Compositing (Multiple Passes): Fragments are retrieved from the R-Buffer in FIFO order. The R-Buffer comparison and control logic performs depth sorting for fragments targeting the same pixel. The two closest fragments to the eye (or the closest fragment and the current frame buffer content) are selected for compositing. The selected fragments are composited using Porter-Duff operations into the frame buffer. Any remaining fragments that were not composited are written back into the R-Buffer. This process repeats until the R-Buffer is empty or an early ray termination condition is met (e.g., accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold). The following pseudocode implements the R-Buffer's global FIFO recirculation and Porter-Duff compositing logic as described in the hardware proposal. All helper functions are defined to ensure self-containment. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FrameBuffer = {} # Maps (x, y) -> (color, opacity, z) RBuffer = [] # Global FIFO queue of fragments: (x, y, z, r, g, b, a) THRESHOLD = 0.99 # Early ray termination threshold def porterduffover(c1, a1, c2, a2): aout = a1 + a2 (1.0 - name: Nearly-Sorted Object-Space Visibility Ordering
head: k-NSS, k-Nearly Sorted Sequence
body: Nearly-Sorted Object-Space Visibility Ordering (k-NSS) is a relaxation of exact visibility sorting where primitives are ordered such that rasterized fragments are at most k positions out of order in the sorted sequence. This allows for the use of faster, approximate object-space sorting algorithms while deferring the guarantee of correct compositing to an exact sorting step during fragment processing. It differs from its parent Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant) by performing the initial ordering in object space rather than per-pixel, and from siblings like Mammen's Technique by explicitly bounding the displacement error k to enable linear-time correction. Inputs: A set of 3D primitives P. A viewpoint v. A parameter k, the maximum allowed displacement in positions. Outputs: A sequence of rasterized fragments that is k-nearly sorted, requiring exact sorting during the compositing stage. Data Structures: k-Nearly Sorted Sequence (k-NSS): A tuple (b1, \dots, bn) of distinct integer values representing the positions of fragments in the nearly sorted order. Exactly Sorted Sequence (ESS): A tuple (a1, \dots, an) of distinct integer values representing the positions of fragments in the exact sorted order. Definitions: A tuple (b1, \dots, bn) is a k-NSS of a sequence S if: \max(|a1 - b1|, |a2 - b2|, \dots, |an - bn|) = k where (a1, \dots, an) is the ESS of S. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Object-Space Ordering): Generate a nearly-sorted sequence of primitives using one of the following methods: BSP-Tree Method: Hierarchically build a Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) tree from the primitives P. Ensure no leaf node contains more than k primitives, which may involve splitting original primitives into multiple ones. Perform a back-to-front traversal of the BSP tree. Render the set of \le k primitives in each leaf node in any order. Simple Sorting Method: Sort primitives by their centroid distance from the viewpoint, or by the distance of their first vertex. This is often sufficient for well-behaved datasets. 2. Rasterization: Rasterize the primitives in the order generated by Step 1. This produces a stream of fragments that is k-nearly sorted with respect to the exact visibility order. 3. Fragment Processing (Exact Sorting): The nearly-sorted fragment stream must be sorted exactly before compositing to ensure correctness. This is typically handled by a k-buffer (or similar structure) which sorts the incoming k-nearly sorted sequence in O(n) time. The k-buffer requires k+1 entries to ensure both the closest and second-closest fragments are available for pre-integrated table lookups. In practice, the hardware implementation is simplified by keeping the k-buffer entries unsorted. Parameters: k: The maximum number of positions a fragment can be out of order from its exact sorted position. It determines the size of the k-buffer and the maximum leaf size in the BSP tree. Typical values are small integers (e.g., k=1, 2). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Primitive Splitting: The BSP-tree method may split original primitives, increasing the primitive count. Incorrect Output: If the incoming sequence is highly out of order (displacement > k), the k-buffer output will be incorrect, which may be noticeable in the images. Memory: The k-buffer size scales with k. A larger k increases memory usage but allows for coarser initial sorting. Time Complexity: The k-buffer can sort a k-nearly sorted sequence of n fragments in O(n) time. The object-space sorting step complexity is Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The k-buffer requires k+1 entries per pixel (or per active fragment stream). The BSP tree requires additional memory for node storage and potentially split primitives. Strengths: Allows for faster object-space sorting algorithms; handles visibility cycles gracefully by deferring exact sort to fragment processing. Limitations: Requires exact sorting during fragment processing; incorrect if k is too small for the dataset's complexity. When to use: When object-space sorting is significantly faster than per-pixel sorting and the dataset is well-behaved enough that simple sorting yields a small k. When not to use: When the dataset produces sequences with displacement > k, as the k-buffer output will be incorrect. The concept was introduced in the context of Hardware-Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) for unstructured volume rendering. It builds on the observation that simple sorting techniques (like centroid sorting) often produce nearly sorted sequences in practice, as exploited in the ZSWEEP algorithm. The k-buffer mechanism was developed to efficiently correct these nearly sorted sequences. name: Prioritized-Layered Projection (PLP)
body: PLP is an approximate, from-point, object-space visibility algorithm designed for large datasets that requires minimal preprocessing. It solves the problem of efficiently selecting a subset of geometry to render within a strict per-frame budget by using heuristics to estimate cell visibility likelihood. Unlike Teller et al.'s from-region algorithm, which requires extensive preprocessing and assumes axis-aligned cells, PLP makes no geometric assumptions and operates with very little setup overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset partitioned into cells; a user-defined budget B representing the maximum amount of geometry to be rendered per frame; the current viewpoint. Outputs: An approximate visible set of cells. Data Structures: 1. Spatial Partitioning: A structure organizing the dataset cells for efficient spatial queries. Not given in the sources. 2. Cell Statistics: For each cell, simple statistics are precomputed. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Build a spatial partitioning for the dataset and compute simple statistics for each cell. 2. Runtime Visibility Estimation: Use heuristics to estimate how likely it is for each cell to be visible. 3. Budgeted Selection: Add cells to an approximate visible set up to the user-defined budget. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: B: User-defined budget of geometry to be rendered per frame. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation Error: As an approximate algorithm, PLP does not guarantee finding all visible primitives. Heuristic Quality: The effectiveness of the algorithm depends heavily on the chosen heuristic. Pseudocode: Not provided in the sources. cPLP is a conservative, image-space algorithm developed by Klosowski and Silva. It uses PLP to obtain an initial guess of the visible set and then augments this approximate set to make it conservative. Time and Memory Complexity: Preprocessing requires building a spatial partitioning and computing cell statistics. The exact complexity is not given in the sources. Runtime complexity depends on the heuristic calculation and prioritization. The sources do not provide specific complexity bounds. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics, hardware, resolution, or scene details are not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Requires very little preprocessing and makes no assumptions about the geometry of the model, unlike Teller et al.'s algorithm which requires long preprocessing and assumes axis-aligned cells. Limitations: Does not guarantee exact visibility and may miss visible cells. When to Use: Use PLP when rendering large datasets with limited preprocessing time and when an approximate visible set is sufficient to meet a strict per-frame rendering budget. When Not to Use: Do not use PLP if exact visibility is required or if the dataset allows for extensive preprocessing and axis-aligned geometry assumptions, in which case Teller et al.'s algorithm might be more suitable. PLP was developed by Klosowski and Silva. The algorithm is contrasted with from-region visibility algorithms like Teller et al.'s, which require long preprocessing times and assume axis-aligned cells. cPLP is also attributed to Klosowski and Silva. name: Newell-based Visibility Sorting
head: Newell, and Sancha (NNS), Newell and Sancha sort, NNS algorithm, Extended Newell, Visibility Sorting (Newell-based)
body: Newell-based Visibility Sorting is an O(n²) algorithm for ordering convex polyhedra back-to-front to enable correct hardware compositing in volume rendering. It generalizes the Newell, Newell, and Sancha polygon sorting algorithm to 3-D volume elements, specifically handling unstructured meshes where topological adjacency information is unavailable. Unlike sibling methods that rely on grid topology (e.g., Topological Sort for Cell Projection) or exact geometric intersection checks (e.g., SXMPVO), this method uses a sequence of increasingly difficult geometric tests to determine occlusion between arbitrary pairs of cells. It is distinguished by its iterative list-reordering strategy and its explicit handling of visibility cycles through subdivision requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n convex polyhedra (cells) defined by their vertices. A viewpoint V. Output: A list of cells sorted in back-to-front order (from farthest to nearest relative to V). Data Structures: Cell: A convex polyhedron. Precomputed data includes: Vertices: List of 3D coordinates. Faces: List of polygons (planar faces). Bounding Box: Extents along x, y, and z axes in screen space. Bounding Sphere (Optional): Center and radius for alternative tests. Sort List: A dynamic list of cell indices. Moved Flag: A boolean flag per cell to detect cycles. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Apply viewing transformations to all vertices to obtain screen coordinates with perspective-corrected Z values. Precompute bounding boxes (and optionally bounding spheres) for each cell. 2. Initial Sort: Sort the cells from back to front based on the depth coordinate (Z) of their rear-most (farthest) vertex. Let this list be L. 3. Iterative Testing: Initialize an empty output list O. While L is not empty: Take the rearmost cell A from L (the cell with the largest Z value in the current list order). Iterate through the remaining cells in L to find if A occludes any other cell B. Occlusion Test: For each candidate cell B in L (excluding A), determine if A obscures B from viewpoint V. Use the sequence of tests below. Test 1 (Z-extent): Check if the z-extent of B is entirely in front of the z-extent of A. If true, A cannot obscure B. Terminate search for obscured cells for A early if this test passes for all remaining B. Test 2 (X-overlap): Check if the x-extents of A and B do not overlap on the image plane. If true, A cannot obscure B. Test 3 (Y-overlap): Check if the y-extents of A and B do not overlap on the image plane. If true, A cannot obscure B. Test 4 (Front-face separation): Check if all vertices of B lie in front of the plane of one of the front-facing faces of A. If true, A cannot obscure B. Test 5 (Back-face separation): Check if all vertices of A lie in back of the plane of one of the back-facing faces of B. If true, A cannot obscure B. Alternative Tests (Bounding Spheres): If bounding spheres are available: Test 19: Check if the cones from the viewpoint to the bounding spheres of A and B are disjoint. Test 29: Check if the bounding sphere for A is disjoint from and lies behind the bounding sphere for B. Definitive Test: If none of the above eliminate occlusion, perform a definitive search. Option A: Search for a separating plane between the cells using linear programming (Newell 1974). Option B: Search for an intersection between the projections of an edge of A and an edge of B. If an intersection exists, the ray through it passes through both cells; determine which cell is in front by comparing Z values at the intersection point. Result Handling: If A does not occlude any other cell in L: Remove A from L and append it to the output list O. If A does occlude a cell B: Move B to the rearmost position (head) of the initial list L and restart the testing process with B as the new candidate A. Cycle Detection: Mark B as "moved". If B is already marked as moved and is about to be moved again, a visibility cycle is detected. No visibility sort is possible without subdivision. 4. Early Termination Optimization: To maintain the validity of the Z-sort early termination (Test 1), track the position in list L after which the Z-order is still undisturbed. When a cell is moved to the head, only test against cells up to this undisturbed boundary. 5. Window Optimization (Optional): Divide the image plane into windows. Maintain a farthest-Z-sorted list of cells overlapping each window. For a candidate cell A, only check lists for windows that A overlaps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: cells: List of Cell objects. viewpoint: 3D point representing the camera position. Returns: List of Cell objects sorted back-to-front. """ # Stage 1: Preprocessing for cell in cells: cell.transform(viewpoint) cell.computeboundingbox() # Optional: cell.computeboundingsphere() # Stage 2: Initial Sort # Sort by the Z-coordinate of the farthest vertex cells.sort(key=lambda c: c.farthestz, reverse=True) outputlist = [] movedflags = {id(c): False for c in cells} # List of remaining cells to process remaining = list(cells) while remaining: # Take the rearmost cell A A = remaining[0] occludedcell = None occludedindex = -1 # Test A against all other cells in remaining # Optimization: Track undisturbed Z-order boundary # For simplicity, we iterate through the rest of the list for i in range(1, len(remaining)): B = remaining[i] # Test if A obscures B if doesaobscureb(A, B, viewpoint): occludedcell = B occludedindex = i break # Found an obscured cell, stop searching for A if occludedcell is None: # A does not obscure any remaining cell # Remove A from remaining and add to output remaining.pop(0) outputlist.append(A) else: # A obscures B. Move B to the front of remaining. # Mark B as moved. if movedflags[id(occludedcell)]: # Cycle detected raise VisibilityCycleError("Visibility cycle detected. Subdivision required.") movedflags[id(occludedcell)] = True # Move B to the front (rearmost position in list context) bcell = remaining.pop(occludedindex) remaining.insert(0, bcell) # Restart testing with B as the new A # Note: The loop continues, but effectively we restart the outer logic # by keeping A (now B) at index 0 and re-evaluating. # To implement cleanly, we continue the while loop, # but we must ensure we don't re-test A against itself. # The structure above handles this by picking remaining[0] again. pass return outputlist def doesaobscureb(cella, cellb, viewpoint): """ Sequence of tests to determine if cella obscures cellb. Distance = dot(N, V - P) # Front means distance > 0 (assuming normal points out) return dot(plane.normal, vertex - plane.point) > 0 def allvertexinback(vertex, plane): return dot(plane.normal, vertex - plane.point) < 0 def hasseparatingplane(cella, cellb): # Linear programming or geometric check # Returns True if a plane exists separating A and B return False # Placeholder for LP implementation def noedgeintersectionprojections(cella, cellb): # Check if projections of edges intersect # If no intersection, they are disjoint in projection return False # Placeholder for edge intersection check A three-stage sorting algorithm for rendering convex polyhedra (volume primitives) in correct back-to-front depth order, specifically designed to handle non-planar faces and rendering cycles in unstructured volume data. It extends the Newell-based visibility sorting approach by introducing a rigorous "fine-tuning" stage that uses plane separation tests and edge intersection checks to resolve ambiguities that a simple Z-depth sort cannot handle. Unlike the parent method which relies on Newell's basic plane tests, this method explicitly handles cycles by reordering the list and detecting circular dependencies, ensuring correct hardware compositing for primitives like tetrahedra, pyramids, and bricks. Time Complexity: O(n²) in the worst case, as it performs pairwise occlusion tests for n cells. The initial sort is O(n log n). Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the cells and the sort list. Performance: The algorithm is slow for large grids due to the quadratic number of tests. However, early termination tests (Z, X, Y extents) often eliminate pairs quickly, improving average-case performance. Strengths: Handles unstructured meshes without topological adjacency information. Simple to implement compared to BSP-tree based methods. Provides a clear mechanism for detecting visibility cycles. Limitations: Cannot handle visibility cycles without subdividing cells. Does not handle non-planar faces natively; requires preprocessing or subdivision. Performance degrades significantly with large numbers of cells. When to use: Suitable for small to medium-sized unstructured grids where topological information is unavailable and exact geometric sorting is required. When not to use: For large grids, structured grids with topological data, or when real-time performance is critical. The Newell, Newell, and Sancha (NNS) algorithm was originally developed for sorting polygons. It was extended to 3-D polyhedra for volume rendering of unstructured grids. The method is based on the work of Newell, Newell, and Sancha (1972) and Newell (1974). It serves as a basis for more recent techniques in volume rendering of unstructured data. The algorithm is particularly relevant for visualizing simulation data from curvilinear grids and finite element analysis where cells may be deformed and non-planar. name: Polyhedron Sorting with Fine-Tuning
head: Hidden surface removal for volume primitives, Shirley-Tuckman extension for unstructured data
body: A three-stage sorting algorithm for rendering convex polyhedra (volume primitives) in correct back-to-front depth order, specifically designed to handle non-planar faces and rendering cycles in unstructured volume data. It extends the Newell-based visibility sorting approach by introducing a rigorous "fine-tuning" stage that uses plane separation tests and edge intersection checks to resolve ambiguities that a simple Z-depth sort cannot handle. Unlike the parent method which relies on Newell's basic plane tests, this method explicitly handles cycles by reordering the list and detecting circular dependencies, ensuring correct hardware compositing for primitives like tetrahedra, pyramids, and bricks. The algorithm sorts a list of N convex polyhedra into back-to-front order relative to the viewer. It consists of three stages: viewing transformation, rough sorting, and fine-tuning. Input: A list H of N convex polyhedra. Each polyhedron P is defined by a set of vertices and faces. Each face is defined by an ordered list of vertices. Output: A sorted list H where Pi precedes Pj if Pi is behind Pj (i.e., Pj obscures Pi). Polyhedron P: vertices: List of 3D points (x, y, z). faces: List of faces. facenormals: Pre-computed average outward normals for each face. faceplanes: Pre-computed plane coefficients (a, b, c, d) for each face. Zrearmost: The maximum Z coordinate of all vertices after viewing transformation (used for rough sort). Face Plane: Defined by ax + by + cz + d = 0. Edge: Defined by two vertices. 1. Viewing Transformation: Apply viewing and projection transformations to all vertices. Scale Z such that the eye looks down the Z axis towards negative infinity in a right-handed coordinate system. Sort by increasing Z (smaller Z is further away, larger Z is closer). 2. Face Normal and Plane Calculation: For each face with n vertices (xi, yi, zi), calculate the average outward normal (a, b, c) using Newell's method: a = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} (yi - yj)(zi + zj) b = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} (zi - zj)(xi + xj) c = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} (xi - xj)(yi + yj) where j = (i+1) \pmod n. 3. Plane Coefficient d: Calculate d using the centroid of the face (\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z}) as a point on the plane: d = -(a\bar{x} + b\bar{y} + c\bar{z}) where \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum xi, etc.. 4. Face Classification: Determine if a face is front-facing or back-facing based on the Z component of its outward normal. In a right-handed system where the eye looks down the Z axis, a positive Z component of the normal indicates a front-facing polygon; a negative or zero component indicates a back-facing polygon. 5. Tolerance \delta: For each face, calculate \delta as the maximum deviation of any vertex of that face from its average plane. This tolerance is used to handle non-planar faces and round-off errors. The fine-tuning stage iterates through the list H to correct the order established by the rough sort. For each pair of adjacent polyhedra P and Q (where P is currently before Q in the list), the algorithm determines if they are in the correct order. If not, Q is moved to the head of the list, and the process repeats with Q as the new P. Step 1: Test if P is behind Q (Separating Plane Test) Check if all vertices of P lie behind a plane defined by any back-facing polygon of Q. For each back-facing face of Q with plane equation f(x,y,z) = ax+by+cz+d: f(xj, yj, zj) \ge -\delta \quad \forall \text{ vertices } j \in P If this holds for at least one back-facing face of Q, then P is behind Q. The order is correct. Return True. Step 2: Test if Q is in front of P (Separating Plane Test) Check if all vertices of Q lie in front of a plane defined by any front-facing polygon of P. For each front-facing face of P with plane equation f(x,y,z) = ax+by+cz+d: f(xj, yj, zj) \ge -\delta \quad \forall \text{ vertices } j \in Q If this holds for at least one front-facing face of P, then Q is in front of P. The order is correct. Return True. Step 3: Edge Intersection Test If Tests 1 and 2 fail, call EdgeIntersection(P, Q). 1. Project all edges of P and Q onto the screen plane. 2. Find all intersection points between edges of P's projection and edges of Q's projection. 3. If no intersections are found: If the projections are disjoint, the order does not matter. Return True. If the projections overlap but no edges intersect (e.g., one is inside the other), assume the polyhedron with the larger Z{rearmost} is in front. If Z{rearmost}(Q) > Z{rearmost}(P), return True. Else, return False. 4. If intersections are found: For each intersection point, calculate the Z coordinate on the surface of P (ZP) and on the surface of Q (ZQ). If none found, return False (ambiguous/cycle). Step 4: Cycle Handling and Resolution If EdgeIntersection returns False (indicating Q obscures P or a cycle exists): 1. Move Q to the head of the list H. 2. Repeat the fine-tuning process with Q as the new P and the next polyhedron as Q. 3. Cycle Detection: Tag polyhedra that have been moved to the head. If a polyhedron Q is already tagged when it becomes the new P, a cycle has been detected (e.g., A obscures B, B obscures C, C obscures A). 4. Limitations: Quadratic worst-case time complexity makes it unsuitable for very large datasets without acceleration structures. It extends the work of Michael E. Newell on procedure models for digital image synthesis. name: XMPVO
body: XMPVO is an algorithm that improves the runtime of the Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering (MPVO) method by using ray shooting queries to discover exterior face relations for nonconvex meshes. It determines the correct back-to-front rendering order for convex volumes filled with convex polyhedral cells when the standard topological sort is insufficient due to occlusions between exterior faces. It sets itself apart from its parent Topological Sort for Cell Projection by augmenting the graph with geometric visibility checks, and from its sibling Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) by performing these checks in object-space precision rather than image-space. Inputs: A set of n convex polyhedral cells forming a mesh, a viewpoint position, and a projection matrix. Outputs: A topologically sorted list of cells suitable for back-to-front volume rendering. Data Structures: A directed visibility graph where nodes represent cells and edges represent visibility relations. The graph is initialized with parent MPVO edges based on shared faces and viewpoint containment, then augmented with additional edges representing exterior face occlusions discovered via ray shooting. A projection complex stores the 2D intersections of projected cell edges and the projected vertices on the image plane. Steps: 1. Construct Projection Complex: Project the 3D cell edges and vertices onto the image plane. Compute the intersections of these projected edges to form the projection complex. 2. Identify Query Points: Identify all edge intersections and vertices within the projection complex. 3. Ray Shooting Queries: For each point identified in Step 2, perform a ray shooting query from the viewpoint through that point into the scene to discover which exterior faces occlude other exterior faces. If face A occludes face B at a query point, add a directed edge from the cell containing A to the cell containing B in the visibility graph. 4. Topological Sort: Perform a topological sort on the augmented visibility graph (containing both MPVO relations and discovered exterior face relations) to determine the final rendering order. Formulas: Time Complexity: O(n + b^2), where n is the number of cells and b is the number of exterior faces. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The ray shooting queries are performed in object-precision (3D space), which is expensive and makes it hard to avoid redundant queries. Robustness: Robustly computing the intersections of the projections of cell edges is difficult and may require exact arithmetic packages, which slows down performance. Redundancy: Due to the object-precision nature, redundant queries are hard to avoid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def xmpvo(cells, viewpoint, projectionmatrix): # Step 1: Construct Projection Complex projectedvertices = [project3dto2d(v, projectionmatrix) for v in cells.vertices] projectededges = [projectedge(e, projectionmatrix) for e in cells.edges] projectioncomplex = compute2dlineintersections(projectededges) # Step 2: Identify Query Points querypoints2d = list(projectioncomplex.vertices) + list(projectioncomplex.edgeintersections) # Step 3: Ray Shooting Queries # Initialize directed graph with parent MPVO edges based on shared faces and viewpoint containment visibilitygraph = {cell: set() for cell in cells} for p2d in querypoints2d: rayorigin = viewpoint raydirection = unproject2dto3d(p2d, projectionmatrix, viewpoint) raydirection = normalize(raydirection) # Find exterior faces intersected by the ray, sorted by distance faces = rayshootmesh(rayorigin, raydirection, cells.exteriorfaces) for i in range(len(faces) - 1): celloccluder = faces[i].owner celloccluded = faces[i+1].owner if celloccluded not in visibilitygraph[celloccluder]: visibilitygraph[celloccluder].add(celloccluded) # Step 4: Topological Sort return topologicalsort(visibilitygraph) def topologicalsort(graph): indegree = {node: 0 for node in graph} for u in graph: for v in graph[u]: indegree[v] += 1 queue = [node for node in graph if indegree[node] == 0] sortedcells = [] while queue: u = queue.pop(0) sortedcells.append(u) for v in graph[u]: indegree[v] -= 1 if indegree[v] == 0: queue.append(v) return sortedcells def rayshootmesh(origin, direction, faces): intersections = [] for face in faces: t = intersectrayface(origin, direction, face) if t > 0: intersections.append((t, face)) intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [face for, face in intersections] def project3dto2d(vertex, projectionmatrix): # Standard perspective/orthographic projection return (projectionmatrix @ vertex)[:2] def projectedge(edge, projectionmatrix): return (project3dto2d(edge.start, projectionmatrix), project3dto2d(edge.end, projectionmatrix)) def compute2dlineintersections(edges): # Standard 2D line intersection routine intersections = set() for i in range(len(edges)): for j in range(i + 1, len(edges)): pt = intersect2dlines(edges[i], edges[j]) if pt is not None: intersections.add(pt) return type('ProjectionComplex', (), {'vertices': set(), 'edgeintersections': intersections})() def unproject2dto3d(p2d, projectionmatrix, viewpoint): # Standard inverse projection to get ray direction return normalize(p2d - viewpoint) def intersectrayface(origin, direction, face): # Standard ray-polygon intersection returning distance t return 0.0 def intersect2dlines(e1, e2): # Standard 2D line intersection returning point or None return None The Kraus and Ertl method handles visibility cycles in convex meshes during cell projection volume rendering. It addresses cases where a global topological sort of cells is impossible due to cyclic visibility dependencies, while a local sort still exists for each pixel center. Time Complexity: O(n + b^2), where n is the number of cells and b is the number of exterior faces. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves runtime over the O(n^2) Stein et al. method by reducing visibility checks to only those involving exterior faces. Limitations: Performs ray shooting queries in object-precision, which is expensive. Hard to avoid redundant queries due to object-precision. Robustly computing intersections of projected edges is difficult and may require exact arithmetic packages, slowing performance. When to use: When dealing with nonconvex meshes where MPVO is insufficient, and the number of exterior faces b is small relative to n, making O(n + b^2) faster than O(n^2). When not to use: When high precision is required for edge intersections, or when the overhead of exact arithmetic is prohibitive. In such cases, image-space variants like SXMPVO are used instead. XMPVO was developed by Silva et al.. It was introduced as an improvement over the MPVO algorithm to handle nonconvex meshes more efficiently. The method relies on the observation that extra visibility relationships only occur when an exterior face in the mesh occludes another exterior face. name: Kraus and Ertl Method
body: The Kraus and Ertl method handles visibility cycles in convex meshes during cell projection volume rendering. It addresses cases where a global topological sort of cells is impossible due to cyclic visibility dependencies, while a local sort still exists for each pixel center. Inputs and Outputs: Input: MPVO sorting results identifying cyclic visibility dependencies. Output: Scan-converted cycle regions resolved via hardware compositing. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Apply the basic MPVO sorting algorithm to detect and isolate pixels where cell ordering forms a cycle. 2. Use special hardware compositing methods to scan-convert each isolated cycle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def krausandertlmethod(mpvosortresults): outputbuffer = {} cyclepixels = [] for pixel, sortdata in mpvosortresults.items(): if sortdata.hascycle: cyclepixels.append(pixel) for pixel in cyclepixels: cyclecells = sortdata.cyclecells # The source does not specify the exact hardware compositing # or scan-conversion algorithm used to resolve the cycle. outputbuffer[pixel] = cyclecells return outputbuffer Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rendering costs per cycle increase quadratically in the number of cells involved in the cycle. The method is designed for convex meshes. Time Complexity: Rendering costs per cycle increase quadratically in the number of cells involved in the cycle. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles visibility cycles gracefully for convex non-overlapping cells. For convex non-overlapping cells, there is always a visibility sort for each pixel center even if there is no global visibility sort of the cells. Limitations: Quadratic cost per cycle. Limited to convex meshes in its original form. When to use: When rendering convex meshes with potential visibility cycles where standard MPVO fails. When not to use: Rendering non-convex meshes without extension to SXMPVO. The method was introduced by Kraus and Ertl. The method could be extended to nonconvex meshes using the SXMPVO algorithm. name: MPVONC
head: MPVO, MPVO Non-Convex, MPVO with Non-Convexities, MPVONC heuristic
body: MPVONC is a heuristic sorting algorithm used in cell projection volume rendering to order non-convex polyhedral cells back-to-front. It extends the exact MPVO algorithm by handling exterior cells that lack a transitive "behind" relationship via shared faces, which MPVO cannot resolve alone. Unlike exact methods such as SXMPVO or A-buffer sorts, MPVONC prioritizes speed over correctness, making it "accurate enough" for many applications but prone to visual artifacts in specific occlusion scenarios. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh of polyhedral cells defining a volume; a viewpoint position \mathbf{v}; the geometric definition of each cell (vertices, faces). Output: A total ordering of cells from back to front for rendering. Data Structures: Cell List: A list of all cells in the mesh. Adjacency Graph: Implicitly or explicitly defined by shared faces. For MPVO, this is a directed graph where an edge Cj \to Ci exists if Cj is "behind" Ci across a shared face [Parent]. MPVO Adjacency List: A dictionary mapping each cell ID to a list of cell IDs behind it, derived from the directed graph [Parent]. Visited Set: A boolean array or hash set tracking cells included in the DFS traversal to ensure each cell is processed exactly once. Steps: 1. Identify Exterior Front-Facing Cells: Iterate over all cells. A cell C is an "exterior front-facing cell" if it has at least one face on the boundary of the mesh and that exterior face is front-facing with respect to the viewpoint \mathbf{v}. Let E be the set of these cells. 2. Sort Exterior Cells: Sort the cells in E by decreasing distance of their centroids to the viewpoint. For two cells Ca, Cb \in E, Ca precedes Cb if \|\mathbf{c}a - \mathbf{v}\| > \|\mathbf{c}b - \mathbf{v}\|. 3. Depth-First Search (DFS) Traversal: Initialize an empty list orderedcells and an empty visited set. For each cell C{start} in the sorted list E, if C{start} is not in visited, perform a DFS starting from C{start} to find all reachable cells via the MPVO "behind" relationships (edges in the directed graph), appending them to orderedcells in post-order to yield a back-to-front sequence. The sources state the DFS constructs the total visibility ordering from <vp relations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mpvonc(cells, viewpoint, mpvoadj): # mpvoadj: dict mapping cellid -> list of cellids behind it exteriorfrontcells = [] for cell in cells: for face in cell.faces: if face.isboundary and dot(viewpoint - cell.centroid, face.normal) > 0: exteriorfrontcells.append(cell) break exteriorfrontcells.sort(key=lambda c: norm(c.centroid - viewpoint), reverse=True) orderedcells = [] visited = set() def dfscollect(cellid): visited.add(cellid) # Recursively visit cells behind the current cell for behindid in mpvoadj.get(cellid, []): if behindid not in visited: dfscollect(behindid) # Post-order append yields back-to-front rendering order orderedcells.append(cellid) for startcell in exteriorfrontcells: if startcell.id not in visited: dfscollect(startcell.id) return orderedcells Parameters: None. The algorithm is deterministic given the geometry and viewpoint. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray-Gap Occlusion Failure: The method may fail when one cell occludes another across a region where ray-gaps are possible, specifically if the occluding cell's centroid is farther from the viewpoint than the occluded cell's centroid. Non-Exactness: The sorting is not exact, leading to certain visual artifacts, though it is considered fast and "accurate enough" for most applications. A method that removes the assumption that the mesh is convex by means of a sweep algorithm used in conjunction with the MPVO method. It is substantially faster than previous exact methods for general meshes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Considered "very fast" and "accurate enough" for most applications. Strengths: Simple to implement, fast, handles non-convex meshes approximately. Limitations: Not exact; prone to visual artifacts in cases of complex occlusion or ray-gaps where centroid distance does not correlate with visibility order. When to use: When rendering speed is critical and minor visual artifacts are acceptable, or for convex/weakly non-convex meshes. When not to use: When exact visibility is required, or in scenes with complex interpenetrating non-convex geometry where ray-gaps are likely. MPVONC was proposed by Peter L. Williams. It was developed to extend the MPVO algorithm, which works for convex meshes, to non-convex meshes. It is commonly used in combination with the Projected Tetrahedra (PT) technique for volume rendering of unstructured grids. name: Convex Grid Topological Visibility Sorting
head: Teller et al. Visibility Algorithm, Adjacency graph sort, Convex Grid Topological, Visibility Sorting (Convex Grid)
body: Convex Grid Topological Visibility Sorting is an O(n) algorithm that orders cells in a convex grid of convex polyhedral cells back-to-front for semi-transparent volume rendering. It constructs a directed adjacency graph where edges represent pairwise occlusion relations derived from the viewpoint position, then performs a topological sort to produce a valid compositing order. It sets itself apart from Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO) and Power Distance Sort by relying exclusively on local face-sharing topology rather than global geometric tests or distance metrics, provided the grid volume is convex. Inputs: A grid of n convex polyhedral cells. An adjacency structure mapping each face of each cell to the index of the neighboring cell sharing that face, or a null value if the face is on the boundary. A viewpoint position V in 3D space. Outputs: A list of cell indices sorted in back-to-front order (from farthest to nearest relative to V). Data Structures: Cell Node: Contains an integer incount initialized to 0, representing the number of incoming edges in the directed graph. Adjacency List: For each cell, a list of neighbor cell indices corresponding to its faces. Queue: A FIFO queue storing cell indices with incount equal to 0. Output List: A dynamic array or linked list storing the sorted cell indices. Definitions: Let F be a common face shared by cells A and B. Let PF be the plane equation of face F. The partial order relation B <{vp} A holds if cell B must precede cell A in the visibility sort. B <{vp} A is true if the viewpoint V is on the same side of the plane PF as cell A. In this case, A occludes B across face F, but B cannot occlude A. The directed graph has a node for each cell and a directed edge from B to A whenever B <{vp} A. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Counts: For all cells C in the grid, set C.incount = 0. 2. Build Directed Graph: For each cell A and each of its faces F with neighbor B: evaluate the plane equation PF at V and at A. If V and A are on the same side of PF, the relation B <{vp} A holds; add a directed edge from B to A and increment A.incount by 1. If V and A are on opposite sides, the relation A <{vp} B holds; add a directed edge from A to B and increment B.incount by 1. 3. Initialize Queue: For all cells C, if C.incount == 0, add C to the Queue. 4. Topological Sort: While the Queue is not empty, remove a cell C from the Queue, add C to the end of the Output List, and for each neighbor B with a directed edge from C to B, decrement B.incount by 1. If any B.incount reaches 0, add B to the Queue. 5. Cycle Detection: If the Output List contains fewer than n cells, a visibility cycle exists. The algorithm fails to produce a total order for the remaining cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convexgridtopologicalsort(cells, adjacency, viewpoint): """ Sorts cells in back-to-front order for a convex grid. Args: cells: List of cell objects. Each cell has a method getcentroid(). adjacency: List of lists. adjacency[i][f] is the index of the neighbor sharing face f of cell i, or -1 if boundary. viewpoint: 3D vector (x, y, z). Returns: List of cell indices in back-to-front order. """ n = len(cells) incount = [0] n graph = [[] for in range(n)] # Standard vector operations def dot(v1, v2): return sum(v1[i] v2[i] for i in range(3)) def planevalue(point, normal, p0): """Returns signed distance of point from plane defined by normal and p0.""" return dot([point[i] - p0[i] for i in range(3)], normal) # Face geometry retrieval is assumed available from the grid structure. # The sources do not specify how face normals/points are stored, # so we assume a helper that returns (normal, pointonplane) for a given cell and face. def getfacegeometry(cellidx, faceidx): # Placeholder for grid-specific face geometry lookup pass for cellidx in range(n): cell = cells[cellidx] for faceidx, neighboridx in enumerate(adjacency[cellidx]): if neighboridx == -1: continue # Boundary face, no directed edge normal, p0 = getfacegeometry(cellidx, faceidx) valv = planevalue(viewpoint, normal, p0) vala = planevalue(cell.getcentroid(), normal, p0) # Check if V and A are on the same side of the plane if (valv > 0 and vala > 0) or (valv < 0 and vala < 0): # B <vp A holds. B is neighboridx, A is cellidx. graph[neighboridx].append(cellidx) incount[cellidx] += 1 elif (valv < 0 and vala > 0) or (valv > 0 and vala < 0): # A <vp B holds. graph[cellidx].append(neighboridx) incount[neighboridx] += 1 else: # Degenerate case: V or A lies exactly on the plane. # A small epsilon tolerance should be used when comparing plane values. pass queue = [] for i in range(n): if incount[i] == 0: queue.append(i) outputlist = [] head = 0 while head < len(queue): c = queue[head] head += 1 outputlist.append(c) for b in graph[c]: incount[b] -= 1 if incount[b] == 0: queue.append(b) if len(outputlist) < n: raise ValueError("Visibility cycle detected. Grid is not convex or topology is invalid.") return outputlist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Cycles: If the queue becomes empty before all cells are processed, a cycle exists. This indicates the grid is not convex or contains cavities/concavities where viewing rays exit and re-enter the grid. The cells involved must be subdivided. Non-Convex Grids: The algorithm is not correct for non-convex grids because viewing rays may leave the grid volume through an external face, cross a gap, and re-enter another cell. Cells with external faces are called boundary cells. Boundary Cells: For non-convex grids, the algorithm can be extended by adding directed edges between boundary cells whenever a viewing ray crosses both. This requires O(b^2) pairwise tests for b boundary cells. Plane Evaluation Precision: If the viewpoint V lies exactly on a face plane, the side determination is ambiguous. A small epsilon tolerance should be used when comparing plane values. An algorithm to generate a visibility ordering for cells in a curvilinear grid (hexahedra) to support semi-transparent rendering, using a combination of undirected breadth-first search and directed depth-first searches on the adjacency graph. It sets itself apart from Convex Grid Topological Visibility Sorting by handling non-convex volumes without requiring a convex decomposition, leveraging the implicit topology of curvilinear grids to avoid auxiliary data structures. Time Complexity: O(n) for convex grids with adjacency structures, where n is the number of cells, assuming each cell has at most six faces. The extended algorithm for non-convex grids with b boundary cells is O(n + b^2). An optimized version by Silva et al. (1998) achieves O((b + I)\log2 b + n), where I is the number of crossings among exterior face edges. Memory Complexity: O(n + e), where e is the number of edges in the directed graph. Since each cell has a constant number of faces (e.g., 6), e = O(n), so memory is O(n). Strengths: Linear time complexity for convex grids; simple implementation; reuses adjacency graph and plane equations across views if geometry is static, requiring only edge direction updates per viewpoint. Limitations: Fails for non-convex grids without extension; requires adjacency structure; visibility cycles may occur in complex geometries requiring subdivision. When to Use: Ideal for convex grids (e.g., structured hexahedral meshes) where performance is critical and the grid topology is well-defined. When Not to Use: Non-convex grids without boundary cell extensions; grids lacking precomputed adjacency structures. Origin: The algorithm is based on pairwise ordering relations between cells sharing a common face. It was described in the context of volume rendering for curvilinear and unstructured grids. History: Teller et al. developed a from-region visibility algorithm used by Funkhouser et al. in their walkthrough system, which requires long preprocessing times and assumes axis-aligned cells. The O(n) topological sort for convex grids is a more efficient variant that does not require such strict assumptions. Usage: Used in hardware-assisted polyhedron projection for volume rendering.
