name: Spatial Decomposition for Adaptive Projection
head: AMRRegion decomposition, Image plane decomposition
body: Spatial Decomposition for Adaptive Projection is a parallelization strategy for inherently spatial volume rendering tasks, specifically designed to distribute the computational load of adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) projection across multiple processors. It solves the problem of efficiently generating line integrals in parallel by decomposing the image plane rather than the data domain, ensuring that each processor handles a distinct spatial region of the final output. Unlike methods that require frequent synchronization or complex data redistribution, this approach guarantees non-overlapping results, minimizing communication overhead to a single final merge step. The method decomposes the computational domain into subdomains realized as individual data containers for independent processing. The core mechanism involves distributing the image plane equally among processors, with each processor responsible for a specific rectangular prism of the volume along the line of sight. Input: The full AMR dataset (grids and field values), the projection direction (line of sight), and the total number of processors P. Output: A global set of unique points (xp, dxp, yp, dyp, v) representing the adaptive projection, constructed by merging local results from all processors. The primary data structure for a processor's workload is the AMRRegion, defined as a rectangular prism. Dimensions: (Li, Lj, Ld). Coordinate System: Axes are rotated such that the line of sight corresponds to the third dimension (Ld). Constraints: Li \times Lj is constant across all processors, representing the fixed area of the image plane assigned to each processor. Ld spans the entire computational domain along the axis of projection. Local Result: Each processor maintains a list of points (xp, dxp, yp, dyp, v) constrained to lie within its assigned AMRRegion. 1. Domain Decomposition: Divide the computational domain such that the image plane is distributed equally among the P processors. 2. Prism Allocation: For each processor k (where k \in [0, P-1]), allocate a rectangular prism AMRRegion with dimensions (Li, Lj, Ld). Ensure the axes are rotated so the projection axis aligns with Ld. The area Li \times Lj must be identical for all k. 3. Local Projection: Each processor independently executes the Adaptive Projection algorithm on the AMR data. The algorithm computes line integrals along the sight-line. Constraint: Only points (xp, dxp, yp, dyp, v) that fall within the processor's allocated AMRRegion are included in the local result set. 4. Result Merging: After all processors complete their local projections, they join their image arrays. Since the AMRRegions are spatially disjoint in the image plane, the resulting sets of points are guaranteed to be unique, requiring no deduplication logic beyond simple concatenation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatialdecompositionadaptiveprojection(amrdata, numprocessors, projectionaxis): """ Performs adaptive projection using spatial decomposition. Args: amrdata: The full AMR dataset. numprocessors: Total number of MPI ranks. projectionaxis: The direction of projection (used to define Ld). Returns: Global list of unique points (xp, dxp, yp, dyp, v). """ # 1. Determine image plane dimensions and split # Let total image plane area be Atotal. # Each processor gets area Aproc = Atotal / numprocessors. # Dimensions Li, Lj are chosen such that Li Lj = Aproc. # Ld spans the entire domain along the projection axis. Li, Lj = calculateimageplanedims(numprocessors) Ld = getdomainextentalongaxis(projectionaxis) localresults = [] # 2. Each processor determines its specific region in the image plane # The image plane is divided into a grid of Li x Lj blocks. # Processor rank 'rank' is assigned a specific offset (ox, oy) in the image plane. ox, oy = getprocessorimageoffset(rank, numprocessors, Li, Lj) # Define the bounding box for this processor's AMRRegion # In the rotated coordinate system where projection axis is z: regionmin = (ox, oy, 0) regionmax = (ox + Li, oy + Lj, Ld) # 3. Perform local adaptive projection # The adaptive projection algorithm generates line integrals. # We filter results to only include points within the region. for grid in amrdata.grids: # Project grid data along the line of sight # This returns a list of points (xp, dxp, yp, dyp, v) # Note: xp, yp are coordinates in the image plane (rotated frame) localpoints = adaptiveprojectionsinglegrid(grid, projectionaxis) # Filter points based on the allocated rectangular prism for point in localpoints: xp, dxp, yp, dyp, v = point if (regionmin[0] <= xp < regionmax[0] and regionmin[1] <= yp < regionmax[1]): localresults.append(point) # 4. Merge results # In a real MPI implementation, this would involve MPIGather or similar. # Since regions are non-overlapping, simple concatenation suffices. globalresults = mergelocalresults(localresults) return globalresults File Format Compatibility: Enzo and Orion output formats store one file per processor with unordered grids. This lack of spatial decomposition in the input files causes poor scaling, as processors must read grid datasets from many files to find relevant data. Scaling Limit: Strong scaling holds well between 4 and 64 processors for the Santa Fe Light Cone dataset. At 128 processors, algorithmic overhead dominates disk I/O cost, causing deviation from ideal scaling. Communication Overhead: Negligible. Processors only communicate at the end of the projection to share non-overlapping final results, avoiding frequent synchronization. Scaling: Strong scaling is effective up to 64 processors for the Santa Fe Light Cone dataset (512^3 resolution, 5.5 \times 10^8 elements). Beyond this, algorithmic overhead becomes the dominant cost, surpassing disk I/O. Strengths: Minimal communication; simple merge logic due to spatial disjointness. Limitations: Performance degrades significantly if the input data format is not spatially decomposed (e.g., Enzo/Orion formats), leading to excessive I/O. This method is implemented within the yt analysis toolkit, which provides a ParallelAnalysisInterface for spatially-aware decomposition. It was developed to address the parallelization needs of adaptive projection in astrophysical simulation data, where data is inherently spatial and often stored in formats that do not align with processor boundaries. name: Cell integration rendering
body: Cell integration rendering is a volume visualization technique that renders data by integrating optical properties over each individual cell and then processing every pixel covered by the cell's projection onto the viewing plane. It is distinguished from its parent method, Cell Projection with Scan-line Conversion, by performing explicit integration within the cell volume rather than simple projection, resulting in significantly higher image quality. However, this approach is computationally prohibitive compared to ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset defined by a grid of cells; camera parameters defining the viewing plane; optical properties (density, color, opacity) associated with the cells. Output: A 2D image where pixel values represent accumulated intensity. Data Structures: Grid: A structured or unstructured set of cells. The specific layout depends on the underlying data representation (e.g., rectangular grid). Pixel Buffer: An image plane storing accumulated intensity and opacity for each pixel. Steps: 1. Projection: For each cell in the volume, project the cell geometry onto the viewing plane to determine the set of pixels covered by the cell's footprint. 2. Integration: For each pixel covered by the cell's projection, determine the specific integration volume within the cell that corresponds to that pixel. 3. Intensity Calculation: Perform an intensity calculation over the bounds of the integration volume. The intensity I is calculated by integrating the contribution of density emitters within the volume. The formula is: I(u) = \int \frac{x}{y} \frac{z}{d} \rho(d) O(s) \left[ Ka(u)Ia + Kd(u, S, M)(N \cdot Lj)Ij \right] + (1 - \rho(d)bc(u)) \, dxdydz Where: u represents spatial coordinates or parameters within the integration volume. x, y, z, d are geometric factors related to the projection and depth. \rho(d) is the density as a function of depth d. O(s) is the opacity as a function of scalar value s. Ka(u) is the ambient color coefficient. Ia is the ambient light intensity. Kd(u, S, M) is the diffuse color coefficient, dependent on position u, scalar S, and material M. N is the surface normal. Lj is the light direction vector for light source j. Ij is the intensity of light source j. bc(u) is a term related to back-scattering or attenuation that modifies the density contribution. The integration is performed over the volume element dxdydz. 4. Accumulation: Add the calculated intensity to the corresponding pixel values in the image buffer. 5. Termination Check: If a pixel's accumulated opacity reaches unity (1.0), set a flag for that pixel to skip further processing. Parameters: Grid Size: The resolution of the input data. Image Size: The resolution of the output image. Transfer Functions: Mapping from scalar values to density \rho(d) and opacity O(s). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The method is extremely slow. On a Sun 4 workstation, rendering a single image required between two and twelve CPU hours, depending on grid and image size. Incremental Display: While the front-to-back processing order allows for incremental display, stopping early may result in images that are not representative of the final result. Sampling Artifacts: While cell integration reduces sampling artifacts compared to image-order methods, the computational cost makes it impractical for interactive exploration. A hybrid technique where an image-order ray-casting method is used within each cell. Cells are processed in a front-to-back order: first by plane (closest to viewpoint first), then by cell within the plane (closest to viewpoint first). For each cell, the algorithm determines which pixels are affected by the cell's scan lines and defines an integration volume for each pixel. Intensity is accumulated into pixel values, and if a pixel's opacity reaches unity, it is flagged and skipped. This allows for incremental display, though early termination yields non-representative results. Time Complexity: Extremely high. Rendering times of 2–12 CPU hours per image were observed on a Sun 4 workstation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Produces far superior image quality compared to simpler projection methods. Strengths: High visual fidelity; reduction of sampling artifacts inherent in image-order rendering. Limitations: Prohibitively slow for most applications; not recommended for research projects requiring parameter tuning due to excessive processing time. When to use: Only when image quality is the absolute priority and computational time is not a constraint. When not to use: For interactive visualization, large datasets, or when rapid iteration is needed; ray casting is much faster and preferred. The cell integration method was discussed in the context of volume visualization research in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It was identified as an alternative to reduce sampling artifacts but was ultimately deemed impractical due to its computational cost compared to ray casting. The concept of treating volumetric data as a field of density emitters, which underpins the intensity calculation in cell-by-cell processing, was also explored during this period. name: Tetrahedral representation and traversal
body: This family covers methods that decompose volumetric data into tetrahedral primitives to enable object-order rendering or precise isosurface extraction. It solves the problem of rendering unstructured or irregular grids by providing a topology that guarantees planar faces and consistent ray-cell intersection logic, avoiding the "problem cells" found in hexahedral grids. Unlike Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm, which extracts an isosurface, standard projected tetrahedra render the volume interior (opacity/color). It differs from Ray Marching by leveraging hardware rasterization or explicit geometric traversal rather than per-pixel sampling, offering efficiency for unstructured grids. This family builds on the shared principles of Cell projection. Projected Tetrahedra (PT) is an object-order volume rendering technique that decomposes a volume into tetrahedral cells, projects them onto the 2D image plane, and rasterizes the resulting triangles using hardware acceleration. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering unstructured or irregular grids by leveraging the graphics pipeline's scan conversion and compositing capabilities, avoiding the memory bandwidth and cache inefficiencies of ray casting. Unlike Tetrahedral Volume Rendering, which may use differentiable rasterization or two-pass GPU pipelines for unstructured data, standard PT generates a continuous stream of triangles in software (or via vertex shaders) that are sorted and composited. It differs from Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm by rendering the volume interior (opacity/color) rather than extracting an isosurface. The Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm (MTA) is an iso-surface extraction method that decomposes volumetric grid cells (typically cubes) into tetrahedra to resolve topological ambiguities inherent in cube-based methods like Marching Cubes. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a tetrahedral decomposition to ensure consistent, planar intersections within each cell, thereby avoiding the "problem cells" where rays might intersect a face twice or where topology is ambiguous. Early Tetrahedron Termination is a rendering optimization technique that reduces the computational load by skipping the processing of tetrahedra that are fully occluded by previously rendered, opaque geometry. It operates on the principle that if a ray has already accumulated sufficient opacity to block further contributions, subsequent tetrahedra along that ray do not need to be evaluated. This method is distinct from general opacity culling, which removes primitives with zero intrinsic opacity before rendering; Early Tetrahedron Termination removes primitives based on the accumulated opacity of the scene during the rendering phase. Adaptive Delaunay Update is a strategy for maintaining the topological connectivity of a tetrahedral mesh during optimization-based volume rendering, specifically when vertex positions change dynamically. It addresses the problem of keeping the mesh valid (Delaunay) without incurring the prohibitive cost of full recomputation at every iteration. It differs from static triangulation methods by incrementally updating topology based on vertex movement thresholds, balancing GPU acceleration speed with geometric accuracy. Grid-based Traversal is a method for rendering irregular volume data (tetrahedral meshes) at interactive rates by partitioning the volume into a hierarchical grid structure to quickly determine candidate tetrahedra. It sets itself apart from its siblings by avoiding explicit connectivity information between tetrahedra, instead relying on spatial hashing into a grid to manage the large number of primitives. Unlike Projected Tetrahedra, which projects primitives to screen space, this method operates in object space using ray-tetrahedron intersection tests within grid cells. This method enables parallel volume rendering of large unstructured tetrahedral grids by partitioning the data using a kd-tree and applying a traditional sort-last compositing algorithm. It renders unstructured grids natively without sampling into a regular grid, avoiding the oversampling/undersampling issues and parallel distribution complexities associated with grid-based sampling approaches. Unlike other parallel rendering approaches that require continuous cell transfer, this method requires no further cell transfer once distributed; only image data is communicated between processes for final composition. Tetrahedral Mesh Connectivity Encoding, specifically the Basic Cut-Border Machine (CBM), is a region-growing compression scheme that encodes the connectivity of a tetrahedral mesh by traversing it and generating a stream of opcodes. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and transmitting mesh topology by describing the position of new vertices relative to a growing boundary (the cut-border). It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Projected Tetrahedra by focusing on lossless connectivity compression rather than direct rasterization, and from Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm by preserving the explicit mesh structure rather than extracting an isosurface. This method constructs a tetrahedral mesh from arbitrarily distributed 3D points by enforcing the Delaunay property: no point lies within the circumsphere of any tetrahedron in the mesh. It serves as an alternative to silhouette-based methods like Visual Hull Methods (VMC), which suffer from threshold sensitivity and discontinuous surfaces. Unlike its sibling Local Convex Hull (LCH), which uses convex hull algorithms for local surface construction, this method relies on Delaunay triangulation to generate the tetrahedral representation. TetraSDF is an analytic isosurface extraction framework for neural Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) that represents the SDF as a ReLU Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) composed with a multi-resolution tetrahedral positional encoder. It solves the problem of discretization error inherent in sampling-based methods like Marching Cubes, which deviate from the true zero-level set, and the lack of high-frequency detail capture in plain ReLU MLPs with analytic marching. It sets itself apart by preserving a global Continuous Piecewise Affine (CPWA) structure via barycentric interpolation, enabling exact zero-level set extraction without grid resolution artifacts. Tetrahedral Primitive Representation is a family of volume rendering techniques that decompose a volumetric dataset into tetrahedral cells to serve as the fundamental geometric primitives for projection and compositing. It solves the problem of rendering unstructured or curvilinear grids by providing a topology that guarantees planar faces and consistent ray-cell intersection logic, avoiding the "problem cells" found in hexahedral grids. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the primitive-level data structures (such as strips, fans, or specific basis vectors) and the explicit projection of these tetrahedra to screen space, rather than just the traversal algorithm or the surface extraction logic. Lookup tables defining neighbor configurations for the tetrahedral grid, divided into face, edge, and vertex neighbors, used for analytic traversal. Edge definitions are e0 = \{v0, v1\}, e1 = \{v0, v2\}, e2 = \{v0, v3\}, e3 = \{v1, v2\}, e4 = \{v1, v3\}, e5 = \{v2, v3\}. For a tetrahedron T with ordered vertices (v0, v1, v2, v3), the face index f \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} refers to the face opposite vertex vf, and the edge index e \in \{0, \dots, 5\} refers to specific vertex pairs. The face neighbor lookup table (Table A6) takes tetra offset t \in \{0, \dots, 5\} and local face index f \in \{0, \dots, 3\} as input, and outputs neighbor index i \ge 1, anchor displacement \Deltai = (\Delta{x,i}, \Delta{y,i}, \Delta{z,i}) \in \mathbb{Z}^3, and neighbor tetra offset ti. The edge neighbor lookup table (Table A7) takes edge (t, e) as input and outputs neighbor index i \ge 1, anchor displacement \Deltai, and neighbor tetra offset ti. The use of tetrahedra in volume rendering originated from the need to handle unstructured grids and resolve topological ambiguities in regular grids. The Marching Tetrahedrons algorithm was developed as an improvement over Marching Cubes to ensure planar faces. Projected Tetrahedra was introduced to leverage hardware rasterization for unstructured data. More recent developments include TetraSDF for neural implicit surfaces and LinPrim for differentiable rendering. name: Projected Tetrahedra
head: Shirley and Tuchman, Shirley-Tuchman Method
body: Projected Tetrahedra (PT) is an object-order (cell-projection) volume rendering technique that renders unstructured tetrahedral meshes by projecting individual tetrahedra onto the screen, decomposing them into triangles, and compositing them in back-to-front order. It solves the problem of visualizing complex, non-convex, or disconnected unstructured data (such as finite element meshes) with high geometric fidelity, avoiding the stair-stepping artifacts of voxel-based methods. Unlike Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm, which extracts an isosurface mesh, PT renders the volume itself using translucent triangles. Unlike Early Tetrahedron Termination or TetraSDF, PT relies on explicit geometric decomposition and hardware rasterization rather than ray-marching or signed distance fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tetrahedral mesh MT where each vertex Vi has an associated scalar value si. The mesh may be derived from decomposing hexahedral cells (typically 5 tetrahedra per cube). Output: A 2D image with color and opacity per pixel, composited via the Porter-Duff "over" operator. Data Structures: Tetrahedron: Defined by 4 vertices V0, V1, V2, V3. Basis Graph (GPU Implementation): A fixed topology of 5 vertices: the 4 real tetrahedron vertices plus 1 "phantom" vertex VP. The topology is a GLTRIANGLEFAN starting at VP, then V0, V1, V2, V3, closing back to V0. This allows a single vertex shader program to handle all projection classes by dynamically computing coordinates or swapping vertices. Classification Texture (GPU): A 1D texture mapping test permutations to projection class and vertex order. Transfer Function: A lookup table (LUT) or 2D texture mapping scalar values to color C(s) and extinction coefficient \tau(s). Pre-integrated tables (e.g., \psi table) may be used to support arbitrary transfer functions. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (View-Dependent): Calculate plane equations for each face of every tetrahedron to determine visibility relative to the viewpoint. Compute the gradient \bar{g} of the scalar field within each tetrahedron. Initialize the view matrix and projection matrix. 2. Visibility Sorting: Sort all tetrahedra in back-to-front order with respect to the eyepoint. Common approximation: Sort by centroid depth. For higher accuracy, use Williams' MPVO (Maximum Projection Volume Order) or k-buffer sorting. 3. Projection and Classification (Per Tetrahedron): Transform the four vertices V0..V3 to screen space. Classify the tetrahedron based on the visibility of its faces relative to the viewpoint. The classification is determined by the signs of the dot products of the view vector with the face normals, or equivalently by the z-components of cross products in screen space. There are four projection classes: Class 1: All 4 faces visible (+ + + +). Decomposes into 3 triangles. Class 2: 3 faces visible, 1 hidden (+ + + -). Decomposes into 4 triangles. Class 3: 2 faces visible, 2 hidden (+ + - - or + - + -). Degenerate case of Class 1 or 2. Class 4: 1 face visible, 3 hidden (+ - - -). Degenerate case. Handle degenerate cases (Class 3/4) by creating zero-area triangles or skipping them. 4. Decomposition into Triangles: Decompose the projected outline of the tetrahedron into one to four triangles based on the classification. Identify the "thick vertex" vt: the point on the ray segment traversing the maximum distance through the tetrahedron. For Class 2, vt is the intersection of the front and back edges. For other classes, vt is one of the projected vertices. The other vertices are "thin vertices". 5. Attribute Computation (Color and Opacity): Compute the scalar values at the ray's entry (sf) and exit (sb) points. For thin vertices, sf = sb = sv (the scalar value at the vertex). For the thick vertex, interpolate sf and sb from the thin vertices if necessary. Compute the thickness l of the cell along the viewing ray (distance traversed by the ray segment). Map sf and sb to chromaticity C(s) and extinction coefficient \tau(s) using the transfer function. Compute opacity \alpha for the thick vertex: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\tau{avg} \cdot l} where \tau{avg} = (\tau(sf) + \tau(sb)) / 2. Compute color C for the thick vertex as the average of C(sf) and C(sb). Thin vertices are rendered with zero opacity and their original chromaticity C(sv). In GPU implementations, these values are often computed in a vertex shader or fragment shader using texture lookups. 6. Rasterization and Compositing: Render the decomposed triangles using hardware rasterization. Use backface culling to render only front faces if applicable. Composite the fragments into the framebuffer in back-to-front order using the Porter-Duff "over" operator: I{new} = \alpha C + (1 - \alpha) I where I is the previous framebuffer color, C is the fragment color, and \alpha is the fragment opacity. Pseudocode (CPU/GPU Hybrid Approach): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderprojectedtetrahedra(tetrahedra, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, transferfunction, width, height): # Step 1: Preprocessing for tet in tetrahedra: tet.computeplaneequations() tet.computegradient() # Step 2: Visibility Sorting def centroiddepth(tet): cx = sum(v.x for v in tet.vertices) / 4.0 cy = sum(v.y for v in tet.vertices) / 4.0 cz = sum(v.z for v in tet.vertices) / 4.0 return viewmatrix.projectz(cx, cy, cz) tetrahedra.sort(key=centroiddepth) # Step 3 & 4: Projection, Classification, Decomposition trianglestorender = [] for tet in tetrahedra: screenverts = [projectionmatrix.transform(v) for v in tet.vertices] v0, v1, v2, v3 = screenverts # Classify using cross products in screen space c1 = (v1[0]-v0[0])(v2[1]-v0[1]) - (v1[1]-v0[1])(v2[0]-v0[0]) c2 = (v1[0]-v0[0])(v3[1]-v0[1]) - (v1[1]-v0[1])(v3[0]-v0[0]) c3 = (v2[0]-v0[0])(v3[1]-v0[1]) - (v2[1]-v0[1])(v3[0]-v0[0]) test1 = (c1 c2 < 0) test2 = (c1 c3 > 0) classid = 1 if (test1 and test2) else (2 if test1 else 3) # Decompose into triangles if classid == 1: triindices = [(0, 1, 2), (0, 2, 3)] else: triindices = [(0, 1, 2), (0, 2, 3), (0, 3, 1)] # Step 5: Attribute Computation l = tet.computethickness(viewmatrix) g = tet.gradient d = viewmatrix.direction sf = tet.scalaratentry(g, d) sb = sf + (g.dot(d)) l tauavg = (transferfunction.tau(sf) + transferfunction.tau(sb)) / 2.0 alphathick = 1.0 - math.exp(-tauavg l) colorthick = (transferfunction.color(sf) + transferfunction.color(sb)) / 2.0 for tri in triindices: verts = [screenverts[i] for i in tri] attrs = [] for i in tri: if i == 0: # Thick vertex placeholder for Class 1/2 attrs.append({'pos': verts[i], 'alpha': alphathick, 'color': colorthick}) else: attrs.append({'pos': verts[i], 'alpha': 0.0, 'color': transferfunction.color(tet.scalarat(i))}) trianglestorender.append({'verts': verts, 'attrs': attrs}) # Step 6: Rasterization and Compositing framebuffer = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0] for in range(width height)] for tridata in trianglestorender: for y in range(int(min(v[1] for v in tridata['verts'])), int(max(v[1] for v in tridata['verts']))): for x in range(int(min(v[0] for v in tridata['verts'])), int(max(v[0] for v in tridata['verts']))): alphaf, colorf = interpolatebarycentric(x, y, tridata['verts'], tridata['attrs']) if alphaf > 0.0: idx = y width + x prevc, preva = framebuffer[idx] newc = alphaf colorf + (1.0 - alphaf) prevc newa = alphaf + preva (1.0 - alphaf) framebuffer[idx] = (newc, newa) def interpolatebarycentric(x, y, verts, attrs): # Standard barycentric interpolation for fragment attributes v0, v1, v2 = verts a0, a1, a2 = attrs denom = (v1[1]-v2[0])(v0[0]-v2[0]) + (v2[0]-v1[0])(v0[1]-v2[1]) w0 = ((v1[1]-v2[1])(x-v2[0]) + (v2[0]-v1[0])(y-v2[1])) / denom w1 = ((v2[1]-v0[1])(x-v2[0]) + (v0[0]-v2[0])(y-v2[1])) / denom w2 = 1.0 - w0 - w1 alphaf = w0a0['alpha'] + w1a1['alpha'] + w2a2['alpha'] colorf = w0a0['color'] + w1a1['color'] + w2a2['color'] return alphaf, colorf Parameters: Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to color and opacity. Can be a 1D LUT or 2D texture (indexed by scalar and thickness). Sorting Algorithm: Centroid sort (fast, approximate) or MPVO/k-buffer (accurate, slow). Basis Graph: Fixed 5-vertex topology for GPU vertex shaders. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting Accuracy: Centroid sorting is not 100% accurate and can lead to visual artifacts, especially with elongated cells or complex overlaps. Degeneracy: Classes 3 and 4 are degenerate cases where a vertex is projected onto an edge or another vertex. Precision: Linear interpolation of opacity can cause Mach banding artifacts. GPU Constraints: Vertex shaders lack branching and dynamic vertex creation, requiring redundant calculations for all projection classes. Edge Artifacts: Interpolation weights becoming zero at edges can cause loss of classification and erroneous zero thickness lookup. Tetrahedral Volume Rendering (Tetrahedral VR) is a cell-projection technique that renders unstructured tetrahedral meshes by projecting individual tetrahedra onto the screen and compositing them in depth order. It solves the problem of visualizing complex, non-convex, or disconnected unstructured data (such as finite element meshes) with high geometric fidelity, avoiding the stair-stepping artifacts of voxel-based methods. Unlike Projected Tetrahedra, which generates triangles for hardware rasterization, this method typically follows a two-pass GPU pipeline or a differentiable rasterization approach. The core logic involves projecting tetrahedra, determining their screen-space geometry, computing ray intersections, and accumulating color/opacity. This method addresses the data transfer bottleneck between the CPU and the graphics board in unstructured volume visualization by employing a view-independent description of the mesh. It builds a fixed set of data in a preprocessing step that is reused every frame, allowing for caching and pre-compilation of transfer data. Unlike its sibling Projected Tetrahedra, which produces a continuous stream of triangles that cannot be combined to blocks without significant overhead, this approach pre-defines the geometry to optimize bandwidth usage through OpenGL mechanisms. Alternating Tetrahedral Decomposition is a method for converting a structured hexahedral grid into a tetrahedral mesh by partitioning each cubic cell into five tetrahedra. It solves the topological consistency problem inherent in decomposing cubes, where using a single decomposition pattern for all cells creates T-junctions and discontinuities at shared faces. It sets itself apart from non-alternating schemes by ensuring that adjacent cells share common faces, maintaining the manifold topology required for correct ray-primitive traversal and data interpolation. Hardware-Assisted Projection is a family of volume rendering techniques that project 3D geometric primitives (tetrahedra, polyhedra, or hexahedra) onto the 2D image plane to leverage the graphics pipeline's rasterization and blending hardware. It solves the performance bottleneck of software-based raycasting by replacing irregular memory access with global back-to-front sorting and hardware-accelerated compositing. Unlike sibling methods that may use local sorting, additive accumulation, or specific decomposition strategies, this family is defined by the reliance on explicit depth sorting of cells to ensure correct alpha blending via the Porter-Duff "over" operator, or additive accumulation in absorption-only regimes. Sorting-free Projected Tetrahedra (SPT) is a volume rendering technique for irregular tetrahedral datasets that approximates back-to-front accumulation using stochastic color composition, thereby eliminating the need for explicit visibility sorting. Unlike its sibling Projected Tetrahedra, which requires sorting tetrahedra before rendering, SPT controls particle rendering via opacity as a probability in the rasterization process, avoiding the sorting artifacts inherent in k-buffer methods like Hardware-Assisted Projection (HAVS). GPU-based Projected Tetrahedra is a method for interactive volume rendering of unstructured tetrahedral data that shifts the geometric classification and decomposition of cells from the CPU to the GPU using programmable vertex shaders. It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional Projected Tetrahedra (PT) by avoiding redundant projections and pre-processing, allowing for the rendering of large datasets at interactive rates. It differs from standard PT by executing the classification logic within the vertex shader program rather than on the CPU, and from ray-casting approaches by occupying a substantially smaller memory footprint while achieving competitive frame rates. Texture-Encoded Isosurfacing is a GPU-based technique for extracting isosurfaces from unstructured tetrahedral grids by using 2D texturing hardware to compute intersections. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Projected Tetrahedra by using the decomposition step of the PT algorithm to create smaller tetrahedra instead of triangles, then projecting their front and back faces to leverage a checkerboard texture for intersection computation. A method for irregular grids that projects volumetric primitives (tetrahedra) onto screen space to determine visibility order, then casts rays through the resulting 2D triangle list to fetch scalar values. It decomposes each volumetric primitive into faces, projects all triangles onto the screen to determine visibility order, and casts a ray through the projected triangles to generate a depth-sorted list of intersections. Volume rendering is performed by linearly interpolating between adjacent faces, assuming linear opacity and intensity contribution for each tetrahedron. The list of triangles per pixel must be updated whenever the viewpoint changes, requiring a sorting step. Rendering time was 11 seconds for a 256^2 viewport and up to 100 seconds for a 1024^2 viewport on an SGI Power Challenge, with a sorting step time of ~2 seconds per viewpoint change. A software algorithm for interactive unstructured volume rendering that moves computations for order-independent transparency and volume scan conversion from CPU to graphics hardware, eliminating the need for a software sorting pass. It preprocesses the dataset, visibility sorts cells back-to-front, tests plane equations to determine class (1-4), projects and splits cell unique front/back faces, computes color and opacity for the thick vertex, and scanconverts new triangles in hardware. In the original CellFast implementation on OpenGL accelerated desktops, Steps II-V (visibility sorting, plane equation testing, projection/splitting, and color/opacity computation) saturate the host CPU, leaving the graphics hardware running below capacity. An average of 3.4 triangles are written per tetrahedron during the splitting process. A technique to approximate a tetrahedron's projection by finding the enclosing ellipsoid with the smallest volume, used to simplify constrained minimization over integrals with no closed form. It notes that the unit sphere is the min-volume ellipsoid for the unit tetrahedron, applies the transformation T associated with the specific tetrahedron to the unit sphere, and transfers the transform T, point position, and scalar value to the GPU. A simple raycaster determines the projection of the ellipsoid, transforming rays using T to cull fragments on the GPU based on simple ray-sphere intersection. The volume scaling factor is \det(T), where T is the transformation matrix mapping the unit tetrahedron to the target tetrahedron. Sub-pixel tetrahedra do not require reshaping, providing speedups. The most popular technique for rendering unstructured tetrahedral meshes, combining Projected Tetrahedra with the MPVO with Non-Convexities sorting algorithm. MPVONC sorting is not exact, leading to visual artifacts, but is fast and 'accurate enough' for most applications. PT has accuracy and implementation issues leading to incorrect images, particularly regarding perspective projection and compositing accuracy on existing GPUs. Most existing codes do not generate strictly correct images and are often limited to parallel projections due to implementation limitations. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of tetrahedra. The visibility sorting step is a bottleneck, often O(N \log N) or worse depending on the algorithm. Memory Complexity: Substantially less than ray casting approaches because no topology information (e.g., adjacency lists) needs to be stored for traversal. Memory usage is approximately 20 bytes per tetrahedron (assuming 4 tets per vertex) in GPU implementations. Measured Performance: Interactive rates (up to 2.0 M Tets/s) can be achieved on current graphics hardware with GPU-based implementations. Software implementations are significantly slower (seconds to minutes per frame). Scaling: Performance scales with the number of tetrahedra and the complexity of the transfer function. Sorting performance degrades with complex overlaps. Strengths: High geometric fidelity, efficient use of graphics hardware for rasterization and compositing, low memory footprint compared to ray casting. Limitations: Requires visibility sorting, which is a bottleneck and can be inaccurate. Degenerate cases and edge artifacts can occur. Linear interpolation of opacity can cause Mach banding. When to Use: Interactive visualization of unstructured tetrahedral meshes where geometric fidelity is important and sorting overhead is acceptable. When Not to Use: When exact visibility ordering is critical and sorting is too slow, or when the dataset is too large for the sorting bottleneck. Projected Tetrahedra was proposed by Shirley and Tuchman in 1990. It was one of the first algorithms for projecting cells of unstructured grids, designed to utilize the geometry acceleration and rasterization of polygon rendering available in graphics hardware. The method has been widely adopted and extended, including GPU-based implementations using vertex shaders (e.g., GATOR algorithm) and optimizations for data transfer and sorting. It is a foundational technique in the field of unstructured volume rendering. Contains 4 unsigned integer indices to retrieve vertex data. 2. Vertex Texture: RGBA texture, 32 bits per component. RGB fields store vertex coordinates (x, y, z); A field stores the scalar value s. 3. Gradient Texture: RGB texture, 32 bits per component. Stores precomputed gradient vectors at vertices. Same size and indexing as Vertex Texture. 4. Classification Texture: 1D texture containing a Ternary Truth Table. Maps combined cross-product test results to projection class indices. 5. Preprocessing (CPU): For each tetrahedron, determine if it contributes to the visualization. First Pass (GPU Fragment Shader): Setup: Render the Tetrahedral Texture as a quadrilateral with screen-space size. This ensures one fragment shader invocation per tetrahedron. Approximate Cell Sampling is a method for sampling cell-centered data in tetrahedral volume rendering that estimates the contribution of neighboring tetrahedra without performing a full tree traversal to locate their vertices. It solves the problem of accessing neighbor geometry when vertex data is not stored for non-coarse elements, using volume ratios and face normals to approximate neighbor centroids. It is distinguished from Simple Cell Sampling by weighting samples by the inverse distance to the estimated centroids, and from Vertex-centered Data Sampling by operating on cell-centered data rather than vertex-centered data. Vertex-centered Data Sampling reconstructs scalar field values within a tetrahedral element by interpolating the scalar data stored at the element's four vertices using the sample point's barycentric coordinates. It is distinguished from its sibling Cell-centered Data Sampling by relying on vertex-local data rather than averaging cell-centered values from face neighbors. DiffTetVR is a differentiable direct volume renderer for tetrahedral meshes that enables optimization of vertex positions, colors, opacities, and local mesh subdivision without multigrid methods. It solves the limitation of previous differentiable volume rendering works restricted to regular grids. Unlike sibling methods that use ray marching or approximate cell sampling, DiffTetVR uses a rasterization-based approach with per-pixel linked lists to efficiently handle unstructured geometry. High Accuracy Volume Rendering (HIAC) is a software-based cell projection renderer designed for high-quality batch-mode generation of images from unstructured finite element data. It solves the problem of rendering complex, non-convex, or disconnected meshes with mathematical exactness, avoiding the approximations typically introduced for efficiency. Unlike its siblings, which may prioritize interactivity or approximate sampling, HIAC guarantees high accuracy by using exact solutions for radiance integrals and interpolation, extending hardware-assisted projection to arbitrary convex polyhedra. This method represents the result of convolving an arbitrary scalar-valued volumetric function with a reconstruction filter as a BT Volume, provided the filter itself is a BT Volume sharing a similar \kappa function. It solves the problem of generating high-quality, continuous volumetric data from discrete samples by exploiting the closure of BT Volumes under addition. Unlike standard convolution which sums kernel functions, this method ensures that the discrete convolution produces a single BT Volume where each tetrahedron is covered by one tetrahedron from each piecewise BT kernel in the sum. A volume rendering approach for phase space tessellations that combines state-of-the-art order-independent transparency methods to manage the extreme depth complexity of tetrahedral meshes. It proposes a view-dependent multiresolution representation of the data and a tile-based rendering strategy. This addresses the issue where phase space tessellation techniques for N-body dark matter simulations yield density fields with a vast amount of elements and self-intersections, causing interactive visualization methods to either employ simplified rendering integrals or suffer from artifacts. A direct volume rendering method for high-resolution irregular tetrahedral grids that supports current and upcoming graphics hardware architectures, large and deformable grids, and arbitrary encoding of deformations within the mesh. It handles meshes with high element counts (e.g., 1600k tetrahedral elements) and uses a 3D texture (e.g., 256^2 \times 110) storing volume data bound to the tetrahedral mesh. It must support arbitrary encoding of deformations within the mesh, allowing for dynamic changes to the volume geometry during rendering. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of tetrahedra N and the sorting cost. Sorting is O(N \log N) or O(N) with bucket sort. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for textures (Tetrahedral, Vertex, Gradient, Classification) and MRTs. BT Volumes have large space requirements, limited by graphics card memory. Limitations: Requires sorting (view-dependent); perspective projection breaks certain optimizations; BT Volumes have high memory usage; numerical instability of erfi function requires approximation. When to use: When visualizing unstructured finite element data or phase space tessellations where geometric fidelity is critical and regular grids are unsuitable. When not to use: When extreme performance is required on highly perspective-heavy scenes with limited GPU memory, or when regular grid data is available (use Volume Ray Casting instead). The Basis Tensor (BT) Volume approach was introduced to support arbitrary isosurface values and efficient GPU rendering using DirectX 10 and geometry shaders. The PTINT (Projected Tetrahedra with Partial Pre-Integration) method extended this by integrating partial pre-integration techniques to improve visual quality while maintaining interactivity. More recently, DiffTetVR introduced differentiable rendering capabilities for unstructured meshes, enabling gradient-based optimization of mesh parameters. The method is used in scientific visualization, particularly for dark matter simulations and engineering prototyping. It solves the problem where a viewing ray intersects the same non-planar face twice, making back-to-front compositing impossible. Unlike view-independent methods that always subdivide all non-planar faces, this approach is viewpoint-dependent, subdividing only "problem" cells to minimize polygon count and rendering overhead. Inputs: Grid vertices: Array of 3D positions \mathbf{P}i and scalar values si. Cells: List of cells, each defined by an ordered list of vertex indices. Transfer functions: Linear or piecewise linear mappings from scalar s to RGB color and differential opacity \tau. Viewpoint: Camera position \mathbf{V} and projection parameters. Outputs: A set of polygons (triangles, quads, or tetrahedral projections) ready for rasterization and compositing. Data Structures: Vertex List: Stores \mathbf{P}i and si. Face Diagonals: Implicitly defined by the lowest-index vertex rule; no explicit storage needed if recomputed or cached per face. Steps: 1. Face Triangulation (Consistent Subdivision): For every quadrilateral face shared by two cells, determine the diagonal. The diagonal must connect the vertex with the lowest index in the face's vertex list to the opposite vertex. This ensures that both adjacent cells agree on the triangulation of the shared face. Let the face vertices be v0, v1, v2, v3 with indices idx0, idx1, idx2, idx3. Find v{min} such that idx{min} = \min(idx0, idx1, idx2, idx3). The diagonal connects v{min} to the vertex opposite it in the quad. This splits the quad into two triangles. 2. Problem Cell Detection: A cell is a "problem cell" if a viewing ray can intersect it in more than one disjoint segment. This occurs if the ray intersects multiple triangles of the cell's triangulated boundary in a way that implies entering and exiting the cell multiple times. For each cell, check if the viewpoint \mathbf{V} and the cell's geometry allow for multiple intersections. This can be tested using the plane equations of the triangulated faces and the relative positions of \mathbf{V} and the cell vertices. If the cell contains contour surfaces (scalar values crossing transfer function breakpoints), it is also marked as a problem cell for subdivision purposes. 3. Cell Subdivision (if Problem Cell): If a cell is marked as a problem cell, subdivide it into tetrahedra. Identify the vertex v{cell\min} with the lowest index among all vertices of the cell. For each face of the cell that does not contain v{cell\min}, the face is already triangulated (from Step 1). Create tetrahedra by connecting v{cell\min} to each of these triangles. This decomposition is consistent with the face triangulation because v{cell\min} is also the lowest-index vertex for any face sharing it. If the cell contains contour surfaces or transfer function breakpoints, further subdivide the resulting tetrahedra into slabs based on the contour planes or breakpoint scalar values. 4. Projection and Polygon Generation: Project the cell (or its tetrahedral subdivisions) onto the image plane. The projected edges divide the image plane into polygons (triangles and quadrilaterals). For non-subdivided cells, the projection is of the original polyhedron. For subdivided cells, the projection is of the constituent tetrahedra. 5. Attribute Computation: For each polygon, compute vertex attributes: RGB color, integrated opacity \alpha, and ray segment length l (or differential opacity \tau) at the front and back endpoints of the viewing ray segment through the cell. Profile Vertices: Vertices on the silhouette. Set color from scalar s, set integrated opacity \alpha = 0. Thick Vertices: Internal vertices (e.g., interior to a face). Compute integrated opacity \alpha = 1 - e^{-\tau \cdot l}, where \tau = (\tauf + \taub)/2 and l is the ray segment length. Compute color: Either as the average of front and back colors or analytically integrated color divided by \alpha. Length Approximation: In perspective views, l varies nonlinearly. Approximate by computing l at vertices and interpolating linearly across the polygon in screen space. 6. This method avoids defects in per-vertex classification during rasterization by ensuring that at least one vertex on a shared edge carries the correct visibility classification of the adjacent face. It addresses artifacts caused by per-vertex computations where edge visibility is ambiguous, ensuring the correct classification affects the entire edge during rasterization. Unlike Viewpoint-dependent subdivision of non-planar faces, which subdivides non-planar faces based on the viewpoint, this method relies on vertex attributes to propagate visibility information across shared edges in a view-independent manner. A method to subdivide nonconvex problem cells (like hexahedra with nonplanar quadrilateral faces) into tetrahedra with consistent diagonals on shared faces, avoiding gaps or overlaps. A strategy to handle non-planar quadrilateral faces in curvilinear grids that cause self-intersection or multiple intersections with a single viewing ray, by temporarily subdividing only the affected 'problem cells' into tetrahedra while leaving other cells as quadrilaterals. Time Complexity: Detection of problem cells is O(1) per cell (using plane equations). Subdivision is only performed on problem cells. Sorting is O(N) with MPVO. Rendering is proportional to the number of projected polygons. Memory Complexity: Requires storing grid topology and potentially subdivided cells. The BSP-MPVO variant may require additional memory for the BSP tree. Performance: Faster than subdividing all cells into tetrahedra because only problem cells are subdivided. However, subdividing all quadrilaterals increases polygon count (e.g., 7 to 25 polygons for a hexahedron) and OpenGL data output, though fragment count remains the same. Strengths: Handles general curvilinear and unstructured grids directly without resampling. Avoids visibility cycles and bow-tie artifacts. Consistent face triangulation prevents gaps/overlaps between adjacent cells. Limitations: Approximations in perspective views (linear interpolation of \tau and l) can introduce errors like Mach bands. Hardware color interpolation is not mathematically equivalent to analytic integration unless strict conditions are met (orthogonal view, planar faces, linear scalar, constant color per cell). When to use: Curvilinear or unstructured grids with non-planar faces where visibility sorting is critical. When not to use: Regular grids (use ray casting or texture-based methods) or when high accuracy in perspective views with non-linear transfer functions is required without hardware approximations. The method was developed to address the limitations of cell projection on curvilinear and unstructured grids, where faces are not necessarily planar. It builds on earlier work by Shirley and Tuchman and the MPVO sorting algorithm. The specific viewpoint-dependent subdivision strategy for non-planar faces was introduced in the context of volume rendering for curvilinear grids. It allows for direct rendering of complex geometries like airplane wings or ship hulls without resampling. name: Hexahedron Projection for Curvilinear Grids
body: Hexahedron Projection is a cell projection method for direct volume rendering of curvilinear hexahedral grids that classifies the 2D projection of each hexahedron into specific topological cases and renders them as pre-defined triangle fans or strips. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering non-planar faces in hardware by avoiding the computational geometry complexity of general line-sweep subdivision or full tetrahedral decomposition. Unlike its siblings, which may rely on view-independent classification or full subdivision into tetrahedra, this method uses viewpoint-dependent case analysis to minimize vertex and fragment operations, offering a significant speedup over subdividing all cells into five tetrahedra. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A curvilinear hexahedral grid where each hexahedron is defined by 8 vertices V0 \dots V7. Output: A stream of triangle fans and triangle strips suitable for hardware rasterization. Data Structures: Hexahedron Vertices: An array of 8 3D points defining the cell. Projected Vertices: The 2D screen-space coordinates of the 8 vertices. Case Classification: An integer count (0, 1, 2, or 4) and boolean flags for bow-tie or degenerate status. New Vertices: Temporary 2D points (V8, V9, \dots) computed as intersections of projected edges. Algorithm Steps: 1. Bow-Tie and Degeneracy Check: Iterate through the 6 quadrilateral faces of the hexahedron. For each face, compute the line equations for its 4 projected edges. For each edge line, check if the other 2 vertices of that face lie on the same side of the line. If any vertex lies on a different side, the face projection is a self-intersecting "bow-tie". If any vertices coincide, the cell is degenerate. For bow-tie or degenerate cells, subdivide the hexahedron into 5 tetrahedra and render using Shirley-Tuchman triangle fans. 2. Containment Test: For non-degenerate, non-bow-tie cells, select a reference face. Compute line equations for the 4 edges of this reference face. Test the 4 non-face vertices against these 4 line equations to determine if they lie inside the projected quadrilateral. Let count be the number of contained vertices, which can be 0, 1, 2, or 4 (a count of 3 implies a bow-tie). 3. Vertex Permutation: Permute the vertex indices so that the vertices of the reference face containing the projected vertices are mapped to indices 0, 1, 2, 3. Apply further rotation permutations to ensure that in the count = 1 case, the contained vertex is mapped to index 7, and in the count = 2 case, the contained vertices are mapped to indices 6 and 7. 4. Case-Specific Rendering: Generate triangle fans or strips based on the count and intersection availability. Count = 1 (Standard): Find intersection V8 of edges V7V4 and V0V1, and V9 of edges V7V6 and V1V2. Fan 1: 8, 1, 5, 4, 0, 3, 7, 1. Fan 2: 9, 7, 3, 2, 6, 5, 1, 7. Count = 1 (Alternate A): If V8 is not found at V7V4/V0V1, find V8 at the intersection of V7V4 and V1V2, and V{10} at the intersection of V7V4 and V1V5. Fan 1: 9, 6, 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 5, 6. Fan 2: 8, 7, 3, 0, 1. Fan 3: 10, 8, 1, 0, 4, 5. Count = 1 (Alternate B): If V9 is not found at V7V6/V1V5, find V9 at the intersection of V7V6 and V0V1, and V{10} at the intersection of V7V6 and V1V5. Fan 1: 10, 5, 6, 2, 1, 9, 8, 4, 5. Fan 2: 9, 1, 2, 3, 7. Fan 3: 8, 9, 7, 3, 0, 4. Count = 1 (Alternate C): If V{10} is not found at V7V4/V1V5, find V{10} at the intersection of V1V2 and V4V0. Fan 1: 9, 2, 3, 7, 8, 4, 5, 6, 2. Fan 2: 10, 7, 3, 0, 1, 5, 4, 8, 7. Count = 1 (Alternate D): If V{10} is not found at V7V6/V1V5, find V{10} at the intersection of V2V6 and V1V5. Fan 1: 8, 4, 0, 3, 7, 9, 6, 5, 4. Fan 2: 10, 6, 9, 7, 3, 2, 1, 5, 6. Count = 4: No extra vertices needed. Fan 1: 4, 0, 3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 0. Fan 2: 6, 7, 3, 2, 1, 5. Count = 2: Find V8 at the intersection of V7V4 and V0V1, and V9 at the intersection of V6V5 and V0V1. Fan: 7, 8, 0, 3, 2, 6, 9, 8. The source mentions a triangle strip is used but does not explicitly list its vertex indices. Count = 0: The projected vertices form a convex octagon. Permute indices counter-clockwise around the octagon. If vertex 0 connects to vertex 5 (the i-3 case), renumber by replacing index i with 8-i. Find V8 at the intersection of V0V3 and V1V6, V9 at V0V3 and V2V5, V{10} at V4V7 and V2V5, and V{11} at V4V7 and V1V6. Fan: 8, 0, 1, 2, 9, 10, 11, 7, 0. Strip: 7, 6, 11, 5, 10, 4, 3, 9, 2. Parameters: Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating Point Precision: General line-sweep methods suffer from inconsistent topological tests (e.g., point vs. line) due to finite precision. This method avoids this by using pre-classified triangle fans for specific projection topologies. Bow-Tie Faces: Self-intersecting face projections make visibility sorting impossible for back-to-front compositing. These must be detected and handled via tetrahedral subdivision. Degenerate Cells: Cells with coincident vertices (common in cylindrical/spherical coordinates) must be subdivided into tetrahedra. A direct volume rendering technique that determines cell traversal by projecting cell faces onto the 2D image plane. It solves the problem of efficiently finding entry and exit points in irregular meshes by avoiding complex 3D geometric intersection tests, relying instead on 2D screen-space projection and ray-crossing tests. Unlike general traversal methods that require pre-computed topological structures, this method uses on-the-fly decomposition and 2D projection, making it suitable for irregular sampling densities. A projection-based direct volume rendering method for curvilinear grids where each data value is mapped to color and opacity, and cell faces are drawn as Gouraud-shaded polygons. Depth is not considered during compositing. It sets itself apart from its parent Hexahedron Projection for Curvilinear Grids by bypassing complex topological classification into triangle fans or strips, opting instead for a simpler polygonal projection that prioritizes speed over physical accuracy. Unlike its sibling Projection-Based Ray Casting for Curvilinear Grids, it does not cast rays through the volume but projects the mesh geometry directly to the screen. Time Complexity: The method involves a constant number of geometric tests per hexahedron (bow-tie check, containment test, intersection calculations), with classification dominating CPU time. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storing the grid vertices and temporary intersection points without large pre-computed topological structures. Measured Performance: On an 800 MHz Pentium4 Xeon and nVidia 5900FXUltra, rendering 141,960 hexahedra (including 50,352 degenerate and 924 bow-tie) took 5.27 seconds total: 0.13s data read, 3.5s case classification, 1.51s rendering. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of hexahedra. Strengths: Faster than subdividing all cells into five tetrahedra because it requires fewer vertex and fragment operations. Handles non-planar faces in curvilinear grids effectively. Limitations: Requires handling many specific topological cases (standard and alternates for count=1). Bow-tie and degenerate cases still require tetrahedral subdivision. When to Use: When rendering curvilinear hexahedral grids on hardware that supports triangle fans/strips, and performance is critical. When Not to Use: When the grid has a high proportion of bow-tie or degenerate cells, or when a simpler, more robust (but slower) method like full tetrahedral subdivision is preferred for simplicity. Origin: Proposed by Nelson Max at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. History: The method builds on earlier work by Schussman and Max for perspective views of cubes, extending it to curvilinear grids where faces are non-planar. It addresses the limitations of line-sweep methods by Wilhelms and Van Gelder and incremental methods by Max, Williams, and Silva, which were difficult to implement robustly due to floating-point precision issues. Usage: Used in direct volume rendering of curvilinear grids, particularly in scientific visualization contexts where performance on hardware is important. name: Projection-Based Ray Casting for Curvilinear Grids
head: Curvilinear Grid Ray Casting, Hong and Kaufman hexahedron traversal, Hong and Kaufman method
body: A projection-based ray-casting algorithm for curvilinear grids (hexahedra) that finds the first face by scan-converting boundary faces, then projects all faces to find exit points. It is a very fast ray-casting technique exploiting the special topology of curvilinear grids. It sets itself apart from its parent, Hexahedron Projection for Curvilinear Grids, by using a projection-based traversal strategy rather than hardware rasterization of triangle fans/strips, and from its sibling Depthless Cell Face Projection by explicitly handling the non-planar geometry of curvilinear hexahedra via on-the-fly triangulation and ray-crossing tests. Inputs: Curvilinear grid data (hexahedral cells with non-planar faces). Viewpoint and projection parameters. Scalar field values associated with grid nodes. Outputs: Rendered image with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Hexahedron representation: 8 vertices per cell, each with 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Face representation: Each hexahedron has 6 faces. Each face is decomposed into 2 triangles, resulting in 12 triangles per hexahedron. Image plane: 2D coordinate system for projection. Steps: 1. Find Entry Face: Scan-convert all boundary faces of the hexahedron onto the image plane to find the first face along the ray observed from the viewpoint. This is done before depth-sorting along the given viewing ray. 2. Triangulation: Decompose all faces of a hexahedron on the fly into twelve triangles. This is necessary because the faces of a curvilinear hexahedron are non-planar. 3. Projection: Project all twelve triangles onto the image plane for intersection calculation to traverse cells. 4. Ray-Triangle Intersection: Compute interpolated scalar values along the ray together with depth as part of the ray-triangle intersection test. This allows for volume rendering integration during traversal. 5. Find Exit Face: Original Approach: Test the remaining eleven triangles sequentially until an intersected triangle (exit face) is found. One triangle is already known as the entry face. Follow-up Approach: Group the remaining eleven triangles and project them onto the image plane. Find the exiting triangle using a ray-crossing technique [Haines94]. A point P is inside a 2D polygon if a horizontal ray from P to the right crosses polygon edges an odd number of times. By checking how many times this horizontal ray crosses the edges of tested triangles, the exiting triangle, and hence the exiting face, can be determined. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercurvilineargrid(grid, viewpoint, imagewidth, imageheight): # Initialize image buffer image = createimagebuffer(imagewidth, imageheight) # Pre-process: Scan-convert boundary faces to find entry points # This step finds the first face along the ray for each pixel entryfaces = scanconvertboundaryfaces(grid, viewpoint) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Construct ray from viewpoint through pixel (x, y) ray = constructray(viewpoint, x, y, imagewidth, imageheight) # Find entry face using pre-computed entryfaces entryface = entryfaces[y][x] if entryface is None: continue # Decompose hexahedron containing entryface into 12 triangles triangles = decomposehexahedron(entryface.hexahedron) # Remove entry triangle from list of triangles to test for exit entrytriangle = gettrianglefromface(entryface) triangles.remove(entrytriangle) # Project all triangles to image plane projectedtriangles = [projecttoimageplane(t, viewpoint) for t in triangles] # Find exit triangle using ray-crossing technique exittriangle = findexittriangleraycrossing(ray, projectedtriangles, entrytriangle) if exittriangle is not None: # Compute intersection point and depth intersectionpoint, depth = raytriangleintersection(ray, exittriangle) # Interpolate scalar value at intersection point scalarvalue = interpolatescalar(grid, intersectionpoint) # Accumulate color and opacity (volume rendering integration) accumulatepixel(image, x, y, scalarvalue, depth) def findexittriangleraycrossing(ray, projectedtriangles, entrytriangle): # Ray-crossing technique: A point P is inside a 2D polygon if a horizontal ray # from P to the right crosses polygon edges an odd number of times. # We need to find which triangle contains the ray's intersection point with the # hexahedron's exit face. # Get the intersection point of the ray with the hexahedron's bounding volume # or use the entry point and ray direction to determine the exit face. # For simplicity, assume we have a point P on the ray that is inside the hexahedron # but outside the entry triangle's plane. # In practice, this involves checking the ray's path through the projected triangles. # The exit triangle is the one where the ray exits the hexahedron. # Using the ray-crossing rule: # For each projected triangle, check if the ray's intersection point with the # hexahedron's exit plane is inside the triangle. # However, the source describes projecting triangles and using ray-crossing to find # the exit triangle. This implies checking the winding or crossing number of the # ray relative to the projected triangles. # A more precise interpretation: # The ray intersects the hexahedron at two points: entry and exit. # The entry point is known. The exit point is on one of the remaining 11 triangles. # We project these 11 triangles to the image plane. # We then use the ray-crossing technique to determine which triangle contains the # exit point's projection. # Let Pexit be the exit point on the ray. # We don't know Pexit yet. Instead, we use the ray's direction and the entry point # to define a line in 2D image space. # We then check which triangle this line exits from. # Simplified implementation: # For each projected triangle, compute the intersection of the ray's 2D projection # with the triangle's edges. Count the number of crossings. # The triangle with an odd number of crossings (or the one that contains the ray's # exit point) is the exit triangle. # Since the ray enters through one triangle and exits through another, and the # hexahedron is convex (or treated as such for traversal), the exit triangle is # the one where the ray leaves the hexahedron. # Using the ray-crossing rule for point-in-polygon: # We need a point P that is known to be inside the hexahedron but outside the # entry triangle. A point slightly along the ray from the entry point works. Pinside = entrypoint + raydirection epsilon # Project Pinside to image plane Pinside2D = projecttoimageplane(Pinside, viewpoint) exittriangle = None for tri in projectedtriangles: if ispointinpolygon2d(Pinside2D, tri): # This triangle contains the projected point inside the hexahedron. # The exit triangle is the one where the ray exits the hexahedron. # This logic needs refinement. The ray-crossing technique is used to find # the exit triangle from the set of projected triangles. pass # Correct interpretation from source: # "The exiting triangle can then be found by applying a ray-crossing technique. # Accordingly, a point P is inside a 2D polygon if and only if the horizontal ray # starting from P and shooting infinitely to the right crosses the polygon edges # an odd number of times. By checking how many times this horizontal ray crosses # the edges of tested triangles, the exiting triangle, and hence the exiting face, # can be determined." # This implies that for each triangle, we check if the ray's intersection point # (or a point along the ray) is inside the triangle's projection. # The exit triangle is the one that contains the exit point. # Since we don't know the exit point, we use the ray's path. # The ray enters the hexahedron at the entry triangle and exits at the exit triangle. # The exit triangle is the one where the ray leaves the hexahedron. # A robust way: # For each projected triangle, compute the intersection of the ray with the triangle's plane. # Check if the intersection point is inside the triangle. # The triangle with the farthest intersection point (along the ray) is the exit triangle. # However, the source specifically mentions the ray-crossing technique. # This suggests a 2D point-in-polygon test on the projected triangles. # Let's assume we have a point P on the ray that is inside the hexahedron. # We project P to 2D. # We then check which projected triangle contains P2D. # This triangle is the exit triangle. # But P is inside the hexahedron, so it might be inside multiple triangles if they overlap in projection. # The exit triangle is the one where the ray exits the hexahedron. # Correct logic: # The ray enters the hexahedron at the entry triangle. # The ray exits the hexahedron at the exit triangle. # The exit triangle is the one where the ray leaves the hexahedron. # We can find this by checking the intersection of the ray with each of the 11 triangles. # The triangle with the farthest intersection point is the exit triangle. # The ray-crossing technique is an optimization to avoid computing all intersections. # It uses the fact that the exit triangle is the one where the ray crosses from inside to outside. # Implementation: # For each projected triangle, check if the ray's 2D projection crosses the triangle's edges. # The triangle with an odd number of crossings is the exit triangle. for tri in projectedtriangles: # Check if the ray's 2D projection crosses the triangle's edges an odd number of times if raycrossestriangle2d(ray2d, tri): exittriangle = tri break return exittriangle def raycrossestriangle2d(ray2d, triangle): # Count the number of times the horizontal ray from a point on the ray crosses the triangle's edges # This is a standard point-in-polygon test using the ray-crossing rule pass Parameters: Viewport resolution: e.g., 300^2. Hardware: SGI Octane (198 MHz MIPS). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-planar faces: Must be decomposed into triangles on the fly. Precision: Ray-crossing technique may have issues with degenerate cases (e.g., ray passing through vertices or edges). Performance: Original approach is slower than follow-up approach. A method for direct volume rendering of data sampled on a curvilinear grid (six-sided cells with non-planar, non-orthogonal faces) by casting rays directly through the volume without interpolating to a rectilinear grid first. It is less prone to accumulation of interpolation errors and easily accommodates irregular sampling densities compared to interpolation-based methods, but is generally slower because it cannot make the simplifying assumptions in traversing regular grids. Exterior-Face Ray Casting is a parallel volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids (tetrahedral and hexahedral) that restricts ray casting to visible exterior faces of subvolumes, traversing elements until exiting another exterior face. It sets itself apart from its parent, Projection-Based Ray Casting for Curvilinear Grids, by explicitly identifying and projecting only the visible exterior faces of partitioned subdomains to define the exact screen area for ray casting, thereby avoiding redundant traversal of invisible internal boundaries. Time Complexity: The follow-up algorithm is twice as fast as the original implementation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: 3.45 seconds for a 300^2 viewport rendering of the Blunt-fin data set on SGI Octane (198 MHz MIPS processors). Strengths: Very fast ray-casting technique exploiting the special topology of curvilinear grids. Limitations: Still requires significant computation for large viewports (up to 100 seconds for 1024^2 viewport). Sorting step on each viewpoint change is around two seconds, which is negligible even for larger resolutions (greater than 512^2). Origin: Hong and Kaufman [Hong98] suggested a projection-based ray-casting algorithm for curvilinear grids. A follow-up paper by Hong and Kaufman [Hong99] suggested an optimization using a ray-crossing technique [Haines94]. name: Ray-casting Curvilinear Volumes
head: Direct ray-casting of curvilinear volumes
body: A method for direct volume rendering of data sampled on a curvilinear grid (six-sided cells with non-planar, non-orthogonal faces) by casting rays directly through the volume without interpolating to a rectilinear grid first. It is less prone to accumulation of interpolation errors and easily accommodates irregular sampling densities compared to interpolation-based methods, but is generally slower because it cannot make the simplifying assumptions in traversing regular grids. Inputs: Curvilinear volume data (scalar values associated with nodes of a curvilinear grid); camera parameters (ray origin and direction); transfer function. Outputs: Rendered image (pixel colors). Data Structures: 1. Curvilinear Grid Representation: The volume is divided into six-sided cells. To facilitate intersection calculations, each curvilinear element (cell) is represented as being bounded by twelve triangles. This triangulation ensures planarity for the intersection primitives. 2. Scan Line List: A data structure supporting the organization of elements along scan lines to reduce the number of intersection calculations. 3. Active Element List: A data structure maintaining the subset of elements currently intersected by the current ray or scan line, further reducing intersection tests. Algorithm Steps: 1. Grid Triangulation: For each six-sided curvilinear cell, decompose the non-planar faces into triangles. The source specifies that each element is bounded by twelve triangles to ensure planarity for intersection calculations. The specific triangulation scheme (e.g., how vertices are paired) is not detailed in the provided text, but the result is a set of planar triangle primitives bounding the cell. 2. Ray Casting: Cast rays from the camera through the volume. 3. Intersection Testing: For each ray, determine intersections with the curvilinear elements. Assume the curvilinear elements are convex. If a ray intersects a convex element, it generates exactly two intersection points (entry and exit). Compute these intersections using the standard technique for triangle primitives. This involves solving for the intersection of the ray with each of the twelve triangles bounding the element and selecting the valid entry/exit points within the element's bounds. 4. Optimization: Use the scan line list and active element list to cull elements that do not intersect the current ray or scan line, reducing the number of intersection calculations required. 5. Shading and Compositing: For the segment of the ray inside the element, apply shading methods similar to those used for rectilinear volumes. This typically involves sampling the scalar data within the element, mapping it to color/opacity via a transfer function, and compositing the result along the ray. Parameters: Triangulation: 12 triangles per cell. Convexity Assumption: Elements are assumed convex. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-planar Faces: Curvilinear faces are inherently non-planar. The method relies on triangulation to approximate them as planar, which introduces geometric approximation error. Degenerate Faces: Faces bounding the element may be degenerate, requiring robust handling in the intersection code. Performance: The number of elements can be quite large, necessitating the use of spatial acceleration structures (scan line/active lists) to avoid O(N) intersection tests per ray. A volume rendering technique for 3D scalar fields defined on curvilinear grids that renders by casting rays along grid lines, where each ray deposits a scalar result on a vertex of the grid's face using a deposition function applied to intersected data points. It is much faster than traditional ray casting volume rendering on identical workstation hardware and is somewhat faster than traditional ray casting on a massively parallel supercomputer. It is used for quick look surveys of scalar fields to find features of interest. The technique is O(n) where n is the number of grid nodes. Interpretation of results can be difficult. Time Complexity: Generally slower than interpolation-based methods because it cannot make the simplifying assumptions in traversing regular grids. The specific complexity depends on the acceleration structures used (scan line/active lists) but is higher than rectilinear ray casting. Gridigration, a variant, is O(n). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the curvilinear grid and the triangulated representation (12 triangles per cell). Strengths: Less prone to accumulation of interpolation errors; easily accommodates irregular sampling densities. Limitations: Generally slower than interpolation-based methods; non-planar faces require triangulation approximation; degenerate faces can cause issues. When to Use: When preserving the original sampling density and avoiding interpolation artifacts is critical, and performance constraints allow for direct ray casting. When Not to Use: When high performance is required and the grid is regular or can be efficiently interpolated to a rectilinear grid. Originated in the context of direct volume rendering for curvilinear grids, extending ray casting methods for rectilinear volumes. The approach was explored to address the limitations of interpolating curvilinear volumes to rectilinear grids, which can introduce errors and fail to accommodate irregular sampling densities. The method is described in a paper discussing direct volume rendering of curvilinear volumes. Gridigration, a related fast technique, was developed by A. Globus as part of the Gridigrator software module.
