name: Exterior-Face Ray Casting
head: Distributed-memory volume ray-casting, Parallel Volume Ray-Casting on Unstructured Grids, Visible Exterior Face Rendering
body: Exterior-Face Ray Casting is a parallel volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids (tetrahedral and hexahedral) that restricts ray casting to visible exterior faces of subvolumes, traversing elements until exiting another exterior face. It sets itself apart from its parent, Projection-Based Ray Casting for Curvilinear Grids, by explicitly identifying and projecting only the visible exterior faces of partitioned subdomains to define the exact screen area for ray casting, thereby avoiding redundant traversal of invisible internal boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Unstructured grid data (elements, connectivity, scalar values), viewing position, transfer function (mapping scalar to color/opacity), and image resolution. Outputs: Final composited image. Data Structures: Exterior Face List: A list of all faces on the boundary of the local subvolume. Each face stores vertex coordinates, normal vector, and element connectivity. Visible Face List: A subset of the Exterior Face List containing only faces visible from the current viewing position. Ray Buffer: A two-dimensional array of linked lists. Each processor maintains a local buffer corresponding to its assigned image region. Incoming ray segments are sorted into linked lists by pixel address. Preprocessing: 1. View-Independent (Once): Find connectivity between elements. Identify all exterior faces of the subvolume. Calculate face normals. 2. View-Dependent (Per View): Extract visible faces from the Exterior Face List by checking face normals against the viewing direction. Orthographically project visible exterior faces onto the screen to produce a set of convex polygons in screen coordinates. Ray Casting Loop: 1. Traverse the Visible Face List in scanline order. 2. For each visible face, cast rays from the eye. 3. A ray enters the data domain through an exterior face and marches element by element using connectivity information until it exits through another exterior face. Due to concavity, holes, or saw-toothed partition boundaries, a ray may enter and exit multiple exterior faces. 4. Segmentation: Break the ray into segments based on element boundaries. The compositing operation is associative, allowing segments to be processed independently. 5. Sampling: Adaptive (Expensive): For a linear element with interpolation function f(x,y,z), ray P(t) = P(0) + td, entry a, exit b, and constant k (sampling rate for unit change in function value), the sample rate r is defined as: r = \frac{|f(P(b)) - f(P(a))|}{b - a} \cdot k This is noted as expensive and often not used in practice. Fixed (Practical): Precompute a fixed sampling interval dt. A good principle for linear elements is to sample at least one additional point c between entering point a and leaving point b. Estimate dt using: dt = 0.5 \times \min\left(\frac{lx}{ne}, \frac{ly}{ne}, \frac{lz}{ne}\right) where lx, ly, lz are bounding box sizes and ne is the total number of elements. Note: Source cites an alternative estimation: dt = \frac{lx + ly + lz}{ne}. Use the Trapezoid rule to calculate the value of the interval between sample points. Gaussian Quadrature Approximation: For linear elements, approximate intensity by computing the value at the middle of the segment. For quadratic elements, sample two points; for cubic elements, three points. This approximates a polynomial of degree 2n-1 using n points. 6. Color/Opacity Mapping: At each sample point, use the interpolated function value to obtain color and opacity from a look-up table. 7. Intensity Calculation: Compute intensity for a segment from entry a to exit b using: I(a, b) = \inta^b e^{-\inta^s \alpha(s') ds'} I(t) dt where \alpha (or c) is the attenuation coefficient and I(t) is the intensity at point t. 8. Compositing: Form the final image value by compositing front-to-back the intensity values of sample points along the ray. 9. Early Ray Termination: Terminate a ray when the accumulated opacity value reaches unity. Parallel Compositing: Ray segments contributing to a pixel cannot be combined until all are received and sorted in visibility order by the responsible processor. Approach 1: Separate local rendering from global compositing. Send all segments after local tracing finishes. Causes large messages and network congestion. Approach 2: Overlap rendering and compositing. Send segments immediately after generation. Improves overall image compositing performance by as much as 40%. Image Partitioning: Image space is partitioned evenly into horizontal strips for simplicity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exteriorfaceraycasting(grid, eyepos, transferfunc, imgw, imgh): # 1. View-Independent Preprocessing (Done Once) exteriorfaces = [] for elem in grid.elements: for faceidx in range(elem.numfaces): face = elem.faces[faceidx] if not face.isshared: exteriorfaces.append(face) face.normal = crossproduct(face.edge1, face.edge2) # 2. View-Dependent Preprocessing (Per View) visiblefaces = [] viewdir = normalize(eyepos) for face in exteriorfaces: if dot(face.normal, viewdir) > 0: visiblefaces.append(face) screenpolygons = {} for face in visiblefaces: screenpolygons[face] = orthographicproject(face.vertices, eyepos, imgw, imgh) # 3. Initialize Ray Buffer for Parallel Compositing raybuffer = [[[] for in range(imgw)] for in range(imgh)] # 4. Ray Casting Loop for face in visiblefaces: for pixel in screenpolygons[face]: rayorigin = eyepos raydir = normalize(pixel - eyepos) segments = traceraythroughelements(rayorigin, raydir, grid) segmentresults = [] for seg in segments: samples = samplesegment(seg.entry, seg.exit, seg.dir, seg.grid, transferfunc) intensity = 0.0 alpha = 0.0 for s in samples: c, a = transferfunc(s.value) # Front-to-back compositing alphaout = alpha + (1.0 - alpha) a intensityout = intensity + (1.0 - alpha) c a intensity, alpha = intensityout, alphaout if alpha >= 1.0: break segmentresults.append({ 'x': pixel.x, 'y': pixel.y, 'intensity': intensity, 'opacity': alpha, 'depth': seg.depth }) for res in segmentresults: raybuffer[res['y']][res['x']].append(res) # 7. Global Compositing finalimage = compositeraybuffer(raybuffer, imgw, imgh) return finalimage def samplesegment(a, b, raydir, grid, transferfunc): dt = 0.5 min(grid.bbox.x / grid.numelements, grid.bbox.y / grid.numelements, grid.bbox.z / grid.numelements) samples = [] t = a while t <= b: point = a + t raydir val = interpolategrid(grid, point) samples.append({'point': point, 'value': val}) t += dt if t > b: t = b return samples def traceraythroughelements(origin, direction, grid): segments = [] currentpos = origin currentdir = direction maxsteps = 1000 for in range(maxsteps): hitelem, hitt, hitnormal = findfirstelementintersection(currentpos, currentdir, grid) if hitelem is None: break segexit = currentpos + hitt currentdir segments.append({'entry': currentpos, 'exit': segexit, 'dir': currentdir, 'depth': hitt}) currentpos = segexit + 1e-6 currentdir currentdir = reflectortransmit(currentdir, hitnormal, hitelem) return segments def compositeraybuffer(buffer, w, h): image = [[(0.0, 0.0) for in range(w)] for in range(h)] for y in range(h): for x in range(w): segs = sorted(buffer[y][x], key=lambda s: s['depth']) intensity, alpha = 0.0, 0.0 for s in segs: alphaout = alpha + (1.0 - alpha) s['opacity'] intensityout = intensity + (1.0 - alpha) s['intensity'] intensity, alpha = intensityout, alphaout image[y][x] = (intensity, alpha) return image A memory-efficient variant that reduces memory footprint by storing only the face data of the most recent traversals, exploiting ray coherence among neighboring pixels. It sets itself apart from Exterior-Face Ray Casting by explicitly managing a temporary buffer to cache internal face parameters for the current visible set, thereby avoiding redundant geometric computations for rays traversing the same internal boundaries. Time Complexity: Dependent on the number of visible exterior faces and the number of elements traversed per ray. Adaptive sampling increases complexity significantly. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the exterior face list, visible face list, and the Ray Buffer. The Ray Buffer size grows during rendering and depends on viewing position, data shape, and partitioning. Measured Performance: Overlapping ray casting and compositing can improve overall image compositing performance by as much as 40%. Scaling: Load balancing is affected by early ray termination. Subvolumes with larger projected areas of high-density regions (high opacity) cause rays to terminate earlier, traversing fewer elements, leading to uneven load distribution. Strengths: Efficiently handles unstructured grids with concavities and holes; parallelizable via associative compositing. Limitations: Adaptive sampling is expensive; Ray Buffer management can be complex; load balancing issues due to variable ray traversal lengths. The method was developed for parallel volume rendering on distributed-memory architectures using unstructured grids. It addresses the challenges of rendering irregular, partitioned data volumes where traditional regular grid ray casting is not applicable. name: Visible Faces Driven Ray Casting
head: VF-Ray
body: Visible Faces Driven Ray Casting (VF-Ray) is a memory-efficient ray casting algorithm for unstructured tetrahedral and hexahedral grids that exploits ray coherence to minimize memory footprint. It reduces the storage of expensive face plane parameters by processing pixels in groups defined by visible exterior faces, storing only the face data for the current traversal set in a temporary buffer. Unlike its parent, Exterior-Face Ray Casting, which casts rays through all visible exterior faces of subvolumes, VF-Ray explicitly manages the lifecycle of face data structures to avoid storing adjacency information for the entire volume, making it suitable for large datasets where memory is constrained. Inputs: Unstructured grid (vertices, cells), scalar field values, viewing direction, screen resolution. Outputs: Rendered image (color and opacity per pixel). Data Structures: 1. Vertices List: Array of vertex coordinates. 2. Cells List: Array of cell definitions (e.g., tetrahedra indices). 3. Useset: For each vertex v, a list of all cells incident to v. This structure is used to handle degeneracies. 4. Face Data: A structure containing geometry and plane equation constants for a face. This is the most memory-intensive component. 5. computedFaces: A temporary buffer storing face data for internal faces intersected by rays within the current visible set. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Create the list of vertices and cells. Build the Useset for each vertex, storing all incident cells. 2. Visibility Determination: Identify external faces: faces belonging to only one cell. Identify visible faces: external faces whose normal vector \mathbf{n} makes an angle greater than 90^\circ with the viewing direction \mathbf{v} (i.e., \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} < 0). 3. Processing Loop (per visible face): Project the current visible face onto the screen to determine the visible set (the set of pixels covered by the face's projection). Initialize the computedFaces buffer as empty. For each pixel p in the visible set: 1. Cast a ray from the camera through pixel p. 2. Perform ray traversal through the volume. 3. Compute intersections with cell faces. 4. Degeneracy Handling: If the ray hits a vertex v, scan the Useset of v to find the next valid intersection. If the ray hits an edge v0v1, scan the Useset of v0 and v1 to find the next valid intersection. 5. Identify internal faces intersected by the ray. 6. Face Data Caching: If an intersected internal face is already in computedFaces, read its parameters from the buffer. Otherwise, compute the face parameters (plane equation constants) and store them in computedFaces. 7. Rendering: Use the face data to evaluate the traversed distance d within the current cell. Retrieve entry scalar value s0 and exit scalar value s1. Compute the cell contribution to the pixel's color and opacity using d, s0, s1, and an illumination integral. Clear the computedFaces buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vfraycast(vertices, cells, scalarfield, viewdirection, screenresolution): # 1. Preprocessing useset = builduseset(vertices, cells) externalfaces = findexternalfaces(cells) visiblefaces = [f for f in externalfaces if dot(f.normal, viewdirection) < 0] image = emptyimage(screenresolution) # 2. Process each visible face for face in visiblefaces: visibleset = projectfacetopixels(face, screenresolution) computedfaces = {} # Temporary buffer: faceid -> facedata # 3. Process pixels in the visible set for pixel in visibleset: ray = castraythroughpixel(pixel) currentpos = ray.origin color = (0, 0, 0) opacity = 0 # Ray traversal loop while not rayexitedvolume(ray, cells): # Find intersection with current cell faces intersection, hitfaceid = findintersection(ray, currentpos, cells) # Handle degeneracies using Useset if isvertexhit(intersection): hitvertex = intersection hitfaceid = findnextintersectionviauseset(hitvertex, useset, ray) elif isedgehit(intersection): hitedge = intersection hitfaceid = findnextintersectionviauseset(hitedge.v0, useset, ray) if hitfaceid is None: hitfaceid = findnextintersectionviauseset(hitedge.v1, useset, ray) # Get or compute face data if hitfaceid in computedfaces: facedata = computedfaces[hitfaceid] else: facedata = computefacedata(hitfaceid, vertices, cells) computedfaces[hitfaceid] = facedata # Evaluate traversal d = evaluatetraverseddistance(currentpos, intersection, ray.direction) s0 = interpolatescalar(scalarfield, currentpos, cells) s1 = interpolatescalar(scalarfield, intersection, cells) # Compute contribution cellcolor, cellopacity = computecellcontribution(d, s0, s1, facedata) color = blendcolor(color, cellcolor, opacity, cellopacity) opacity = blendopacity(opacity, cellopacity) currentpos = intersection image[pixel] = color, opacity # Clear buffer for next visible face computedfaces.clear() return image def builduseset(vertices, cells): useset = {v: [] for v in vertices} for cell in cells: for vertex in cell.vertices: useset[vertex].append(cell) return useset def findexternalfaces(cells): facecounts = {} for cell in cells: for face in cell.faces: faceid = getfaceid(face) facecounts[faceid] = facecounts.get(faceid, 0) + 1 return [face for faceid, count in facecounts.items() if count == 1] def findnextintersectionviauseset(vertexoredge, useset, ray): # Scan incident cells to find the next valid intersection along the ray candidates = [] if isinstance(vertexoredge, Vertex): incidentcells = useset[vertexoredge] else: # Edge incidentcells = set(useset[vertexoredge.v0]) & set(useset[vertexoredge.v1]) for cell in incidentcells: dist = rayintersectcell(ray, cell) if dist > 0: candidates.append((dist, cell)) if not candidates: return None candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return candidates[0][1].faceid # Return the face ID of the next intersection A GPGPU implementation of VF-Ray that parallelizes visibility determination, projection, and ray traversal across CUDA kernels, using a hash-based local memory buffer to minimize global memory bandwidth. Time Complexity: The algorithm's performance depends on the number of visible faces and the coherence of rays within each visible set. Processing each visible face involves projecting it and traversing rays for the covered pixels. The use of computedFaces reduces redundant plane equation computations for neighboring rays. Memory Complexity: VF-Ray significantly reduces memory footprint compared to methods storing full adjacency structures. It only stores Useset (incident cells per vertex) and the computedFaces buffer, which contains face data only for the current visible set. The computedFaces buffer is cleared after each visible face is processed, keeping memory usage proportional to the maximum number of internal faces intersected by rays in a single visible set. Strengths: Memory efficiency for large unstructured grids. Exploits ray coherence to improve caching performance. Handles degeneracies (vertex/edge hits) correctly using Useset. Limitations: Requires building and storing the Useset structure, which can be memory-intensive for highly connected meshes. Performance may degrade if ray coherence is low (e.g., complex geometry causing many distinct visible faces with small pixel sets). Not given in the sources: Specific scaling behavior on multi-core CPUs vs. GPUs is not detailed in the base algorithm description, though a GPU variant exists. VF-Ray was introduced as a memory-efficient ray casting algorithm for unstructured grids, specifically addressing the high memory cost of storing face plane parameters in traditional ray casting methods. It builds on the concept of ray coherence, where neighboring rays tend to intersect the same internal faces. The algorithm was developed to handle the limitations of previous approaches, such as Bunyk's method, which could fail to continue ray traversal when hitting edges or vertices. The method is cited in the context of volume rendering for unstructured tetrahedral and hexahedral meshes. name: VF-Ray-GPU
head: Memory Efficient GPU-Based Ray Casting
body: VF-Ray-GPU is a GPGPU implementation of the VF-Ray algorithm designed for memory-efficient ray casting on unstructured tetrahedral volumes. It solves the problem of rendering large datasets on GPUs with limited memory by avoiding explicit adjacency structures (like Useset) and pre-computed normals, instead computing face parameters and volume integrals on-the-fly. It sets itself apart from its parent, Visible Faces Driven Ray Casting, by fully parallelizing the visibility determination, projection, and ray traversal across CUDA kernels, utilizing a hash-based local memory buffer for traversal state to minimize global memory bandwidth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: vertList (vertex coordinates and scalar values), tetList (tetrahedron vertex indices), conTet (tetrahedron connectivity), extFaces (pre-computed external faces). Outputs: Rendered image. Data Structures: 1. vertList: Stores x, y, z coordinates and scalar value s for each vertex. 2. tetList: Stores vertex IDs vi composing each tetrahedron. 3. conTet: Stores tetrahedron ID ti sharing a specific face. 4. extFaces: List of external faces, pre-computed similarly to Bunyk's method. 5. visFaces: List of visible faces storing tetrahedron ID ti, face ID fi, and interpolation parameters z and s. 6. projVisFaces: List of projected visible faces storing bounding boxes in screen space. 7. computedFaces: 1D buffer in CUDA local memory per thread. Stores ti, fi, and face parameters. Indexed by a hash table based on the z-coordinate centroid of the face. MinZ maps to the first position, maxZ to the last. Face Identification: The vertices of face fi of tetrahedron ti are identified by indices vi, v{(i+1)\mod 4}, and v{(i+2)\mod 4} from tetList, avoiding explicit face storage. Algorithm Steps: The algorithm is divided into three CUDA kernels. Kernel 1: Find Visible Faces Thread Organization: One thread per external face. Total threads = number of external faces. Process: 1. Read external face from extFaces (texture memory). 2. Compute plane equation coefficients for z and s interpolation by solving two 3 \times 3 linear systems. 3. Perform visibility test: Compare the z-coordinate of the fourth vertex (not on the face) with the projected z-coordinate on the face using the computed interpolation parameters. 4. If projected z < fourth vertex z, the face is visible. 5. Store z and s interpolation parameters in visFaces (global memory). Cost: Less than 5% of total time and memory. Kernel 2: Project Visible Faces Thread Organization: One thread per visible face. Process: 1. Read vertex coordinates from vertList (texture memory) using IDs from tetList (global memory). 2. Project visible faces to screen space. 3. Compute bounding box of the projection. 4. Store bounding box in projVisFaces (global memory). Kernel 3: Ray Casting Thread Organization: CUDA grid divided into blocks; one block per visible face. Each block divided into threads; each thread computes a small set of pixels. Threads finishing early are reused by the hardware driver. Process: 1. Read visFaces and projVisFaces. 2. Determine visible face pixels using the bounding box and a point-in-triangle test (cross product). 3. For each pixel, trigger ray casting using the visible face as the first entry face. 4. Traverse tetrahedra: Compute face parameters on-the-fly (replacing pre-computed normals/gradients). Store next faces in computedFaces buffer. Hash index is the z-coordinate centroid of the face. Handle hash collisions: Check stored ti and fi to ensure the correct face is read. 5. Compute volume rendering integral on-the-fly for each cell contribution using Bunyk's method. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kernelfindvisiblefaces(extfaceidx): # Get face vertices from tetList using extFace data # Face fi of tetrahedron ti uses vertices vi, v(i+1)%4, v(i+2)%4 tid, fid = getfaceinfo(extfaceidx) v0 = vertList[tetList[tid][fid]] v1 = vertList[tetList[tid][(fid + 1) % 4]] v2 = vertList[tetList[tid][(fid + 2) % 4]] v3 = vertList[tetList[tid][(fid + 3) % 4]] # Fourth vertex # Compute plane equation coefficients for z and s interpolation # Solve 3x3 linear systems for z and s zcoeffs = solvelinearsystem(v0, v1, v2, v0.z, v1.z, v2.z) scoeffs = solvelinearsystem(v0, v1, v2, v0.s, v1.s, v2.s) # Project v3 onto the plane defined by v0, v1, v2 projectedz = interpolatez(v0, v1, v2, v3, zcoeffs) # Visibility test: back-face culling if projectedz < v3.z: # Store visible face parameters visFaces.append((tid, fid, zcoeffs, scoeffs)) def kernelprojectvisiblefaces(visiblefaceidx): tid, fid, zcoeffs, scoeffs = visFaces[visiblefaceidx] # Get vertex coordinates v0 = vertList[tetList[tid][fid]] v1 = vertList[tetList[tid][(fid + 1) % 4]] v2 = vertList[tetList[tid][(fid + 2) % 4]] # Project to screen space p0 = projecttoscreen(v0) p1 = projecttoscreen(v1) p2 = projecttoscreen(v2) # Compute bounding box minx = min(p0.x, p1.x, p2.x) miny = min(p0.y, p1.y, p2.y) maxx = max(p0.x, p1.x, p2.x) maxy = max(p0.y, p1.y, p2.y) projVisFaces.append((tid, fid, minx, miny, maxx, maxy)) def kernelraycasting(pixelx, pixely, visiblefaceidx): # Check if pixel is inside the bounding box bbox = projVisFaces[visiblefaceidx] if not (bbox.minx <= pixelx <= bbox.maxx and bbox.miny <= pixely <= bbox.maxy): return # Point-in-triangle test tid, fid, zcoeffs, scoeffs = visFaces[visiblefaceidx] v0 = vertList[tetList[tid][fid]] v1 = vertList[tetList[tid][(fid + 1) % 4]] v2 = vertList[tetList[tid][(fid + 2) % 4]] if not pointintriangle(pixelx, pixely, v0, v1, v2): return # Initialize ray rayorigin = screentoworld(pixelx, pixely) raydirection = computeraydirection(pixelx, pixely) # First entry face currenttid = tid currentfid = fid # Local buffer for computed faces computedfaces = [] # Fixed size buffer in local memory while true: # Get current face vertices v0 = vertList[tetList[currenttid][currentfid]] v1 = vertList[tetList[currenttid][(currentfid + 1) % 4]] v2 = vertList[tetList[currenttid][(currentfid + 2) % 4]] # Compute face parameters on-the-fly # Replace pre-computed normals/gradients facenormal = crossproduct(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) # Find intersection with ray t, hitpoint = rayplaneintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, v0, facenormal) if t < 0: break # Ray missed or went backwards # Compute integral contribution for the segment # Use Bunyk's method for integration contribution = computevolumeintegral(rayorigin, hitpoint, currenttid) accumulatecolor(contribution) # Find next face # Compute centroid z for hashing centroidz = (v0.z + v1.z + v2.z) / 3.0 hashindex = mapztobufferindex(centroidz) # Check local buffer for cached face nextface = None if hashindex < len(computedfaces): cached = computedfaces[hashindex] if cached.tid == currenttid and cached.fid != currentfid: # Verify it's the correct face (handle collisions) # Check if this face is shared by current tetrahedron nextface = cached if nextface is None: # Compute next face explicitly # Determine which vertex was not hit (or use connectivity) # Find adjacent tetrahedron sharing the face # This replaces Useset nexttid, nextfid = findnextface(currenttid, currentfid, hitpoint) # Store in local buffer if hashindex < len(computedfaces): computedfaces[hashindex] = (nexttid, nextfid,...) else: computedfaces.append((nexttid, nextfid,...)) nextface = (nexttid, nextfid) currenttid, currentfid = nextface # Handle degeneracies by perturbing ray if isdegenerate(hitpoint): rayorigin = hitpoint + epsilon raydirection else: rayorigin = hitpoint def solvelinearsystem(v0, v1, v2, val0, val1, val2): # Solve for plane equation ax + by + cz = d # Returns coefficients for interpolation pass def interpolatez(v0, v1, v2, v3, coeffs): # Project v3 onto plane of v0,v1,v2 using z interpolation pass def projecttoscreen(vertex): # Apply projection matrix pass def pointintriangle(x, y, v0, v1, v2): # Cross product test pass def rayplaneintersection(origin, direction, point, normal): # Standard ray-plane intersection pass def computevolumeintegral(origin, hit, tid): # On-the-fly integration using Bunyk's method pass def findnextface(tid, fid, hitpoint): # Find adjacent tetrahedron and face # Uses conTet or vertex connectivity pass def isdegenerate(hitpoint): # Check if hit is on edge or vertex pass Time Complexity: Slower than HARC and HARC-Partial due to on-the-fly face parameter computations and lack of pre-computed normals/gradients. Memory Complexity: Very low. 38 bytes/tetrahedron. Blunt Fin: 7,029 KB. Oxygen Post: 19,494 KB. Fighter+: 426 MB. F16: 239 MB. Performance (Hardware): Intel Pentium Core 2 Duo 6400 (2.13 GHz), 2 GB RAM, nVidia GeForce 8800 Ultra (768 MB). Blunt Fin: 186 ms. Oxygen Post: 370 ms. Fighter+: 3,081 ms. F16: 804 ms. Scaling: Handles large datasets (1.1M-1.9M vertices) that exceed the 768 MB memory of the GeForce 8800 Ultra for other algorithms. Strengths: Low memory footprint allows rendering of large datasets on limited hardware; ~4x faster and ~50% less memory than CPU-based VF-Ray. Limitations: Slower than HARC/HARC-Partial; approximate results for degenerate cases due to ray perturbation. When to use: When memory is the primary constraint and the dataset is too large for other GPU ray casting methods. When not to use: When maximum performance is required and memory is sufficient (use HARC). Origin: Based on VF-Ray, described in [APCBRF07] A. Maximo et al., 'Memory efficient and robust software implementation of the raycast algorithm', WSCG’07 (2007). Development: Implemented using CUDA to exploit GPGPU parallelism. Usage: Tested on Blunt Fin, Oxygen Post, Fighter, and F16 datasets. name: Depthless Cell Face Projection
body: Depthless Cell Face Projection is a projection-based direct volume rendering method for curvilinear grids where each data value is mapped to color and opacity, and cell faces are drawn as Gouraud-shaded polygons without considering depth during compositing. It sets itself apart from its parent Hexahedron Projection for Curvilinear Grids by avoiding complex topological classification into triangle fans or strips, opting instead for direct polygonal projection prioritized for speed. Unlike its sibling Projection-Based Ray Casting for Curvilinear Grids, it projects mesh geometry directly to the screen rather than casting rays through the volume. Inputs: A curvilinear grid mesh and a scalar field defined at each vertex. Outputs: A 2D image with color and opacity values. Data Structures: Data structures record information for three adjoining faces of each cell to ensure each face is drawn only once. The exact layout is not specified in the sources, but they must support efficient lookup to prevent duplicate rendering of shared faces between adjacent cells. Steps: 1. Map each data value to a color and an opacity value. 2. Draw the faces of each curvilinear grid cell as Gouraud-shaded polygons, using the mapped values at the vertices. 3. Store information for three adjoining faces of the cell in data structures to ensure each face is drawn only once. Parameters: Opacity: Typically set to zero for maximum speed. Shading: Gouraud shading is used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Cells: Small cells contribute the same intensity as large cells because depth is not considered. On grids where cell size is inversely proportional to interest (finely gridded in areas of interest), this automatic weighting may be preferred by some scientists. Hardware Compositing Limitations: Hardware compositing uses 8-bit intensity/opacity resolution. Small cells may contribute well under 1/256 of the maximum possible intensity and thus never appear in the image if depth were considered. The depthless method avoids ignoring data entirely but weights it improperly. Visual Artifacts: Noticeable visual artifacts appear from some angles because the distance between cell faces is not taken into account. These artifacts tend to delineate cell boundaries and probably would not be misinterpreted as data information. A projection-based direct volume rendering method for curvilinear grids that addresses the lack of depth consideration in the depthless method. It maps sample locations to screen space and calculates depth, average color, and opacity for vertices, allowing opacity to be taken into consideration more accurately than its sibling Depthless Cell Face Projection. Choose this variant when physical depth weighting and accurate opacity accumulation are required over maximum rendering speed. Cell Face Projection with Depth Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Approximately one second for 40,000 cells on a uniprocessor R3000-based Silicon Graphics VGX. Strengths: Extremely fast and trivial to implement. It prevents small cells from being ignored due to hardware compositing resolution limits. Limitations: Lacks physical depth weighting, leading to improper weighting of cell contributions. Produces visual artifacts delineating cell boundaries from certain angles. When to Use: When speed is the primary concern and the grid has many small cells that might be lost in hardware compositing. When the automatic weighting of small cells (often high-interest areas) is desirable. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy of depth and opacity accumulation is required. When visual artifacts from cell boundaries are unacceptable. The method was described in the 1993 paper "Rapid Exploration of Curvilinear Grids Using Direct Volume Rendering". It was developed as a simple, fast alternative to more complex volume rendering techniques for exploring curvilinear grids. The method is part of a suite of techniques designed to handle the specific challenges of curvilinear meshes, such as non-planar faces and varying cell sizes. name: Cell Face Projection with Depth
body: Cell Face Projection with Depth is a projection-based direct volume rendering method for curvilinear grids that addresses the lack of depth consideration in the depthless method. It maps sample locations to screen space and calculates depth, average color, and opacity for vertices, allowing opacity to be taken into consideration more accurately than its sibling Depthless Cell Face Projection. Inputs: Curvilinear grid cell vertex positions, per-vertex data values, and the current camera viewpoint. Outputs: Screen-space image with color and opacity values. Data Structures: Cell Data Structure: Stores precomputed vertex attributes for the current viewpoint. Fields: vertexcount, vertices[]. vertices[i] contains: screenpos: 2D screen coordinates. depth: Average depth through the cell at this projected location. color: Average color. opacity: Average opacity. isonconvexhull: Boolean flag. iscoalesced: Boolean flag (true if two vertices map to the same screen location). Steps: 1. Identify Vertex Addresses and Locations: Determine the vertex addresses and spatial locations for each cell. 2. Map to Screen Space: Map all sample locations (vertices) of the cell to screen space based on the current viewpoint. 3. Identify Convex Hull: For each cell, identify the vertices that lie on the convex hull of the projected cell in screen space. 4. Process Convex Hull Vertices: Check Coalescence: Determine if convex hull vertices are coalesced (i.e., two distinct vertices map to the same screen space location). If Not Coalesced: The depth through the cell at that point is zero. The vertex does not contribute color or opacity. If Coalesced (e.g., looking straight on at a regular cell): Record a depth for that vertex and take the data value as the average of the two vertices' data values. Map this average to color and opacity. Depth Recording: If a vertex appears on the convex hull from certain angles, record its depth; if it appears on the opposite face, take the average of the two vertex depths. 5. Process Interior Vertices: For interior vertices, locate the point at the same projected location on the opposite cell exterior, find data values for that point by interpolation, calculate depth and average color and opacity, and store them in the vertex data structure. 6. Store Precomputed Data: This information (depth, color, opacity) is calculated whenever the viewpoint is changed and stored with the cell data structure. 7. Rendering: Draw each face once for each cell (twice overall, except on the boundary). Scale color and opacity based on the depth of the vertex during rendering. Scaling intensity can be used to take care of intensity problems this may cause. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def crossproduct2d(o, a, b): return (a[0] - o[0]) (b[1] - o[1]) - (a[1] - o[1]) (b[0] - o[0]) def compute2dconvexhull(screenverts): pts = sorted([(v['sx'], v['sy'], v['idx']) for v in screenverts]) hull = [] for p in pts: while len(hull) >= 2 and crossproduct2d(hull[-2][:2], hull[-1][:2], p[:2]) <= 0: hull.pop() hull.append(p) return [h[2] for h in hull] def projecttodepth(pos3d, viewpointmatrix): clip = viewpointmatrix @ np.append(pos3d, 1.0) if clip[3] <= 0: return 0.0 return clip[2] / clip[3] def interpolatedataat(targetpos, cellvertices): # Standard barycentric or trilinear interpolation from cell vertices return np.mean([v[1] for v in cellvertices]) def interpolateoppositeboundary(startpos, sx, sy, cellvertices): # Ray-cast from camera through (sx, sy) to find opposite cell boundary return startpos + np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.1]) def transferfunction(dataval): # Standard transfer function mapping data value to (color, opacity) return (dataval, dataval) def rasterizepolygon(faceverts, scaledcolor, scaledopacity): # Standard polygon rasterization with per-vertex attributes pass def preprocesscell(cellvertices, cellfaces, viewpointmatrix, transferfunction): # 1. Map sample locations to screen space screenverts = [] for i, (pos3d, dataval) in enumerate(cellvertices): clip = viewpointmatrix @ np.append(pos3d, 1.0) if clip[3] <= 0: continue ndc = clip[:3] / clip[3] screenverts.append({ 'idx': i, 'pos3d': pos3d, 'data': dataval, 'sx': ndc[0], 'sy': ndc[1], 'depth': ndc[2] }) # 2. Identify convex hull vertices in screen space hullindices = compute2dconvexhull(screenverts) # 3. Calculate depth, color, opacity for each vertex vertexdata = [] for v in screenverts: ishull = v['idx'] in hullindices depth = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) opacity = 0.0 if ishull: coalesced = None for other in screenverts: if other['idx'] != v['idx'] and other['idx'] in hullindices: if abs(other['sx'] - v['sx']) < 1e-6 and abs(other['sy'] - v['sy']) < 1e-6: coalesced = other break if coalesced is None: # Not coalesced: depth through cell is zero, no contribution depth = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) opacity = 0.0 else: # Coalesced: record depth, average data values depth = (v['depth'] + coalesced['depth']) / 2.0 avgdata = (v['data'] + coalesced['data']) / 2.0 color, opacity = transferfunction(avgdata) else: # Interior vertex: locate point on opposite exterior at same projected location opppos = interpolateoppositeboundary(v['pos3d'], v['sx'], v['sy'], cellvertices) oppdata = interpolatedataat(opppos, cellvertices) oppdepth = projecttodepth(opppos, viewpointmatrix) depth = (v['depth'] + oppdepth) / 2.0 color, opacity = transferfunction(oppdata) vertexdata.append({'sx': v['sx'], 'sy': v['sy'], 'depth': depth, 'color': color, 'opacity': opacity, 'ishull': ishull}) return vertexdata, hullindices def rendercell(vertexdata, hullindices, cellfaces): # 4. Render faces for face in cellfaces: faceverts = [vertexdata[i] for i in face if i in hullindices] if len(faceverts) < 3: continue for fv in faceverts: # Scale color and opacity based on depth scaledcolor = tuple(c fv['depth'] for c in fv['color']) scaledopacity = fv['opacity'] fv['depth'] rasterizepolygon(faceverts, scaledcolor, scaledopacity) Parameters: Viewpoint: Changes the screen projection and triggers recalculation of precomputed values. Scaling intensity: A parameter to adjust for intensity problems caused by double drawing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coalesced Vertices: If convex hull vertices are not coalesced, the depth is zero and the vertex contributes nothing. Artifacts: Produces noticeable artifacts at angles close to 90 degrees for regular cells. These artifacts tend to delineate cell boundaries and probably would not be misinterpreted as data information. Performance: Much slower for new orientations than the depthless method because precomputation must be recalculated whenever the viewpoint is changed. Time Complexity: Slower than the depthless method for new orientations due to the need to recalculate depth, color, and opacity for all vertices whenever the viewpoint changes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing precomputed vertex attributes (depth, color, opacity) with the cell data structure for each viewpoint. Accuracy: Takes opacity into consideration more accurately than the depthless method, providing a more "realistic" rendering assuming a physical, colored medium. Strengths: More realistic appearance; accounts for depth and opacity. Limitations: Noticeable artifacts at near-90-degree angles for regular cells; slower performance for dynamic viewpoints. When to use: When realistic opacity handling is prioritized over performance and viewpoint stability. When not to use: When rapid exploration with frequent viewpoint changes is required, or when artifacts at specific angles are unacceptable. Development: Developed as an improvement over the "Depthless Cell Face Projection" method to address the lack of depth consideration in compositing. Usage: Used for direct volume rendering of curvilinear grids, particularly in scientific visualization contexts where realistic opacity is desired. name: Per-vertex edge classification for view-independent cell projection
head: Edge classification for cell projection
body: This method avoids defects in per-vertex classification during rasterization by ensuring that at least one vertex on a shared edge carries the correct visibility classification of the adjacent face. It addresses artifacts caused by per-vertex computations where edge visibility is ambiguous, ensuring the correct classification affects the entire edge during rasterization. Unlike Viewpoint-dependent subdivision of non-planar faces, which subdivides non-planar faces based on the viewpoint, this method relies on vertex attributes to propagate visibility information across shared edges in a view-independent manner. Inputs: Vertex positions of the tetrahedron faces, face normals, adjacency information specifying which faces share an edge, and the view direction. Outputs: Modified texture coordinates, specifically the r component, for each vertex to encode the visibility classification of adjacent faces. Data Structures: Each vertex stores standard attributes (position, normal) plus additional texture coordinates. Specifically, the r texture coordinate encodes the classification of the adjacent face sharing an edge. Steps: 1. Define Edge Directions: Utilize the counterclockwise winding order of each face to define a directed edge for each vertex. For a face with vertices v0, v1, v2, each vertex vi is considered the start of the edge from vi to v{i+1 \pmod 3}. 2. Supply Adjacent Face Normal: For each directed edge starting at vertex v, supply the normal of the adjacent face sharing that edge as a vertex attribute to v. This allows the vertex shader to access the geometry of the neighboring face. 3. Check for Entering Face: In the vertex program, determine if the adjacent face is potentially entering relative to the view direction. 4. Modify Texture Coordinate: If the adjacent face is potentially entering, set the r texture coordinate of the start vertex to a large positive value instead of 0. If not, leave it unchanged. This ensures that the edge classification is correctly propagated during rasterization. Example: Consider two adjacent faces f0 and f1 sharing an edge between vertices v2 and v3. For face f1, vertex v3 is the start of the edge from v3 to v2. The vertex program checks if f1 is entering; if so, it sets the r coordinate of v3 to a large positive value, while the r coordinate of v2 remains unchanged for rendering f1. For face f0, vertex v2 is the start of the edge from v2 to v3. The vertex program checks if f1 is entering; if so, it modifies the r component of v2 since f1 is potentially entering for all fragments of f0. Pitfalls: Unclassified Endpoint: One endpoint of the edge remains unclassified. Computing full classification would require normals of all three remaining faces per vertex, requiring more per-vertex parameters. This problem is considered negligible as mistakes occur at singular positions, affecting at most one pixel per tetrahedron. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: View-independent, avoids complex geometric subdivision, minimal additional memory overhead. Limitations: May result in minor classification errors at singular positions, affecting at most one pixel per tetrahedron. This method is part of the hardware-based view-independent cell projection approach, which aims to render curvilinear grids efficiently on modern graphics hardware. It addresses the limitations of per-fragment classification by using per-vertex attributes to propagate visibility information. The technique was introduced by Weiler and Kraus in their work on hardware-based view-independent cell projection. name: Consistent Tetrahedral Subdivision
head: Linear order diagonal selection, Nielson and Sung (1997) method simplification
body: Consistent Tetrahedral Subdivision is a method for decomposing non-convex problem cells, such as hexahedra with non-planar quadrilateral faces, into tetrahedra using diagonals that are consistent across shared faces. It solves visibility sort failures and geometric gaps or overlaps in curvilinear grid rendering by ensuring that adjacent cells sharing a quadrilateral face agree on the diagonal used to split that face, without requiring explicit mesh connectivity data. Inputs: 1. A set of cells (pyramids, prisms, or hexahedra) to be subdivided. 2. A linear order on the set of all vertices in the grid, derived from integer indices assigned to each vertex. Outputs: 1. A set of tetrahedra that exactly fill the volume of the original cells. 2. Consistent diagonal choices for all quadrilateral faces shared between adjacent cells. Vertex Index: Each vertex v has an associated integer index I(v) representing its position in the linear order. Cell Vertices: Each cell is defined by its vertices. For a hexahedron, vertices are labeled A through H, where A is the smallest vertex in the linear order, and G is the vertex farthest from A (the opposite corner). For any quadrilateral face defined by four vertices, the diagonal is chosen based on the linear order: 1. Identify the vertex with the smallest index among the four vertices of the quadrilateral. Let this vertex be V{min}. 2. The chosen diagonal connects V{min} to the vertex opposite it in the quadrilateral. This rule is applied independently to each quadrilateral face. Because the decision depends only on the four vertices of the face, adjacent cells sharing that face will always select the same diagonal, ensuring consistency without connectivity pointers. A pyramid consists of a quadrilateral base and an apex vertex. 1. Apply the Decision Rule to the quadrilateral base to select the diagonal starting from the smallest base vertex. 2. The plane defined by this diagonal and the apex vertex divides the pyramid into two tetrahedra. Result: 2 tetrahedra. A triangular prism has two triangular bases and three quadrilateral lateral faces. 1. Identify the unique smallest vertex L in the linear order among all vertices of the prism. 2. Identify the two quadrilateral faces that share vertex L. 3. Apply the Decision Rule to these two faces. Since L is the smallest vertex in the entire prism, it is also the smallest in these two faces. Thus, both diagonals start at L. 4. The plane defined by these two diagonals divides the prism into one tetrahedron and one pyramid. 5. Subdivide the resulting pyramid using the Decision Rule on its quadrilateral base. Result: 3 tetrahedra. A hexahedron has 8 vertices. Let A be the vertex with the smallest index in the linear order. Let G be the vertex farthest from A (the opposite corner). 1. Initial Diagonals: Apply the Decision Rule to the three quadrilateral faces that meet at vertex A. The diagonals on these faces start at A. 2. Count Diagonals at G: Examine the diagonals chosen for the remaining three quadrilateral faces (those not meeting at A). Count how many of these diagonals have G as an endpoint. Let this count be k. Case 0: k = 0 1. The three diagonals chosen for the faces not meeting at A, combined with the three diagonals already chosen for the faces meeting at A, form the six edges of a central tetrahedron. 2. Removing this central tetrahedron leaves four other tetrahedra filling the remaining volume. Result: 5 tetrahedra (1 central + 4 surrounding). Case k > 0: 1. At least one diagonal among the remaining three faces has G as an endpoint. Let this diagonal be d. 2. This diagonal d, together with the parallel face diagonal starting at A (from the initial step), defines a quadrilateral "slice" that cuts through the hexahedron. 3. This slice divides the hexahedron into two triangular prisms. 4. Apply the Decision Rule to the slice quadrilateral: Since A is the smallest vertex of the hexahedron, it is also the smallest in the slice. The Decision Rule selects the diagonal connecting A to the opposite vertex in the slice. 5. Subdivide each of the two resulting triangular prisms using the Prism Subdivision method. Result: 6 tetrahedra (3 from each prism). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getsmallestvertex(indices): """Returns the vertex index with the minimum value.""" return min(indices) def choosediagonalquad(indices): """ Chooses the diagonal for a quadrilateral defined by four vertices. indices: list of 4 vertex indices ordered around the quad perimeter [v0, v1, v2, v3]. Returns tuple of two indices forming the diagonal. """ smallest = min(indices) idx = indices.index(smallest) # Opposite vertex in a quad is at (idx + 2) % 4 return (smallest, indices[(idx + 2) % 4]) def subdividepyramid(baseindices, apexindex): """ Subdivides a pyramid into 2 tetrahedra. baseindices: list of 4 vertex indices forming the quadrilateral base. apexindex: vertex index opposite the base. Returns list of 2 tetrahedra, each a list of 4 vertex indices. """ d0, d1 = choosediagonalquad(baseindices) v0, v1, v2, v3 = baseindices # Diagonal splits quad into two triangles sharing the diagonal. # Tetrahedron 1: apex + triangle 1 # Tetrahedron 2: apex + triangle 2 if d0 == v0: return [[apexindex, v0, v1, v2], [apexindex, v0, v2, v3]] elif d0 == v1: return [[apexindex, v1, v2, v3], [apexindex, v1, v3, v0]] elif d0 == v2: return [[apexindex, v2, v3, v0], [apexindex, v2, v0, v1]] else: # d0 == v3 return [[apexindex, v3, v0, v1], [apexindex, v3, v1, v2]] def subdivideprism(indices): """ Subdivides a triangular prism into 3 tetrahedra. indices: list of 6 vertex indices. Standard topology assumed: [t0, t1, t2, b0, b1, b2] where t-triangles are bases, and vertical edges connect ti to bi. Returns list of 3 tetrahedra. """ # Define the three quadrilateral lateral faces quads = [ [indices[0], indices[1], indices[4], indices[3]], [indices[1], indices[2], indices[5], indices[4]], [indices[2], indices[0], indices[3], indices[5]] ] L = min(indices) # Identify the two quadrilateral faces sharing L quadswithL = [q for q in quads if L in q] d1 = choosediagonalquad(quadswithL[0]) d2 = choosediagonalquad(quadswithL[1]) # Extract non-L endpoints of the diagonals x = d1[1] if d1[0] == L else d1[0] y = d2[1] if d2[0] == L else d2[0] # The plane through d1 and d2 divides the prism into a tetrahedron and a pyramid. # The tetrahedron uses L, x, y, and the vertex that completes the base triangle. # In standard prism topology, the vertex connecting x and y on the same base is: basevertex = indices[(x + y) % 6] if (x + y) % 6 != L else indices[5 - (x + y) % 6] tetra = [L, x, y, basevertex] # The remaining volume is a pyramid. Subdivide it. # The pyramid base is the quadrilateral formed by the remaining vertices. # We reconstruct the pyramid base vertices from the prism minus the tetrahedron. remainingvertices = [v for v in indices if v not in tetra] # The apex of the pyramid is the vertex not on the base quadrilateral. # In this split, the apex is the vertex opposite the base quadrilateral in the original prism. # We pass the remaining vertices as the base and the opposite vertex as apex. # To maintain correct topology for subdividepyramid, we order the base vertices. # The base quadrilateral consists of the two non-L endpoints of d1/d2 and the two vertices not in the tetrahedron. # We simply pass the 4 base vertices and the apex to the pyramid function. # For simplicity and correctness per source: pyramidbase = [x, y, remainingvertices[0], remainingvertices[1]] pyramidapex = remainingvertices[2] return [tetra] + subdividepyramid(pyramidbase, pyramidapex) def subdividehexahedron(indices): """ Subdivides a hexahedron into 5 or 6 tetrahedra. indices: list of 8 vertex indices. Standard topology assumed: [0,1,2,3] bottom face, [4,5,6,7] top face, verticals (0,4),(1,5),(2,6),(3,7). Returns list of 5 or 6 tetrahedra. """ A = min(indices) # G is the vertex farthest from A (opposite corner) G = indices[7 - indices.index(A)] # Identify the three quadrilateral faces meeting at A # Assuming standard ordering where A is indices[0] if indices.index(A) != 0: raise ValueError("Hexahedron vertices must be ordered with A at index 0") quadsatA = [ [indices[0], indices[1], indices[5], indices[4]], # Front [indices[0], indices[3], indices[7], indices[4]], # Left [indices[0], indices[1], indices[2], indices[3]] # Bottom ] diagA1 = choosediagonalquad(quadsatA[0]) diagA2 = choosediagonalquad(quadsatA[1]) diagA3 = choosediagonalquad(quadsatA[2]) # Identify the remaining three quadrilateral faces quadsrem = [ [indices[1], indices[2], indices[6], indices[5]], # Right [indices[2], indices[3], indices[7], indices[6]], # Back [indices[4], indices[5], indices[6], indices[7]] # Top ] diagRem1 = choosediagonalquad(quadsrem[0]) diagRem2 = choosediagonalquad(quadsrem[1]) diagRem3 = choosediagonalquad(quadsrem[2]) # Count diagonals with G as an endpoint among the remaining three k = 0 if G in diagRem1: k += 1 if G in diagRem2: k += 1 if G in diagRem3: k += 1 if k == 0: # Case 0: 5 tetrahedra # The three diagonals from QRem and the three from QA form a central tetrahedron. # Central tetrahedron vertices: A and the three non-A endpoints of diagAi # plus the three non-G endpoints of diagRemj. Actually, the source states: # "the three diagonals in this set plus the three diagonals already shown... are the six edges of a central tetrahedron." # This implies the central tetrahedron is formed by the four vertices that are endpoints of these 6 diagonals. # Since A is endpoint of 3 diagA, and G is not endpoint of any diagRem, the other 3 vertices are the non-A endpoints. V1 = diagA1[1] V2 = diagA2[1] V3 = diagA3[1] centraltetra = [A, V1, V2, V3] # The remaining 4 tetrahedra fill the rest. # T1: A, V1, V2, indices[1] (if V1,V2 correspond to faces sharing edge A-1) # To be strictly correct without hardcoding topology assumptions beyond the source: # We return the central tetrahedron and the 4 surrounding ones. # Surrounding tetrahedra are formed by the faces of the central tetrahedron and the hexahedron faces. return [centraltetra, [A, V1, V2, indices[1]], [A, V2, V3, indices[3]], [A, V3, V1, indices[4]], [V1, V2, V3, indices[5]]] # Simplified topology fill else: # Case >0: 6 tetrahedra # Find a diagonal among QRem that has G as an endpoint diagG = diagRem1 if G in diagRem1 else (diagRem2 if G in diagRem2 else diagRem3) # The slice is defined by diagG and the parallel diagonal starting at A # Parallel face to the one containing diagG is one of the quadsatA # We find which quadatA is parallel to the quad containing diagG # For standard hexahedron, parallel faces are opposite. # Slice vertices: endpoints of diagG and endpoints of parallel diagA # This slice divides hexahedron into two prisms # We extract prism vertices and subdivide them # Prism 1 vertices: A, diagG endpoints, and adjacent vertices # Prism 2 vertices: remaining vertices # For implementation completeness: prism1verts = [A] + list(diagG) + [indices[1], indices[4]] # Example topology prism2verts = [indices[2], indices[3], indices[5], indices[6], indices[7]] # Example topology # Apply Decision Rule to slice quadrilateral (A, diagG endpoints, parallel diagA endpoint) # Since A is smallest, slice diagonal is (A, G) # Subdivide each prism return subdivideprism(prism1verts) + subdivideprism(prism2verts) Linear Order: The integer index assigned to each vertex. This is the primary parameter controlling the subdivision geometry. Precision: The method relies on integer indices, so floating-point precision issues in vertex coordinates do not affect the consistency of the diagonal selection. Boundaries: The method assumes a closed or properly bounded grid. Boundary faces do not have adjacent cells, so consistency is not required, but the diagonal choice is still made for the purpose of subdivision. Degenerate Input: If a hexahedron is degenerate (e.g., volume zero), the subdivision may produce degenerate tetrahedra. Time: O(N), where N is the number of cells. Each cell is processed independently in constant time for a fixed cell type. Memory: O(N), to store the resulting tetrahedra. The method does not require additional connectivity data structures. Not given in the sources. The method scales linearly with the number of cells. It is suitable for large grids because it avoids global connectivity analysis. Strengths: Ensures consistent diagonals across shared faces without mesh connectivity. Simple to implement. Deterministic. Limitations: The resulting tetrahedra may not be optimal for rendering (e.g., they may be sliver-like). The number of tetrahedra per hexahedron varies (5 or 6), which may complicate data structures. Does not guarantee visibility sort correctness for all view directions, only that the subdivision is consistent. Use when rendering curvilinear grids with non-planar faces and when mesh connectivity is not available or expensive to compute. Use when a consistent tetrahedral decomposition is required for volume rendering or finite element analysis. Use when optimal tetrahedra quality is critical. Use when the grid is already well-connected and a more sophisticated subdivision method can be applied. The method was developed as a simplification of the Nielson and Sung (1997) method, which was originally designed for a more specific purpose. The authors of the current method discovered this simplification independently. It is used in the context of approximate volume rendering for curvilinear and unstructured grids, specifically to handle problem cells that cause visibility cycles due to non-convex projections. The method contradicts part of the report by Guy and Crawfis (1997) regarding the subdivision of cubes. name: Problem Cell Subdivision for Curvilinear Grids
head: Problem face detection, Temporary tetrahedral subdivision
body: Problem Cell Subdivision is a viewpoint-dependent strategy for handling non-planar quadrilateral faces in curvilinear grids that cause self-intersection or multiple intersections with a single viewing ray. It solves the visibility sort failure inherent in projecting distorted hexahedra by temporarily subdividing only the affected "problem cells" into tetrahedra, while leaving other cells as quadrilaterals. Unlike full tetrahedral subdivision, which significantly increases rasterization overhead, this method limits computational cost by applying subdivision only where the viewing geometry necessitates it. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A curvilinear mesh (hexahedral cells), a viewpoint V, and a BSP tree constructed from exterior faces. Outputs: A visibility-sorted list of cells ready for compositing, with problem cells temporarily modified into tetrahedral representations. Data Structures: Faces: Each quadrilateral face F is associated with two triangular subfaces, S and T, determined by a diagonal from a specific vertex (typically the "smallest" vertex). Each subface stores: 1. Plane equation. 2. Two cell pointers (to the adjacent cells sharing the face, or one if exterior). Tetrahedra: When a cell is subdivided, new tetrahedra are created. Each new tetrahedron has a parent pointer to the original cell. Subdivisions are stored in memory blocks of size 2, 3, 5, or 6 tetrahedra, allocated from four large arrays with used/unused lists for reuse. New tetrahedra and their separating interior faces are stored together in blocks to provide memory locality. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Static): Subdivide all exterior non-planar quadrilaterals into triangles permanently. Construct the BSP tree using these exterior triangles for accurate visibility sorting. Determine the two triangular subfaces for every interior quadrilateral face based on mesh topology. 2. Viewpoint Update (Dynamic): For each cell A and current viewpoint V: Identify the quadrilateral face F of A divided into triangles S and T by a diagonal from vertex L. Determine if F is a "problem face" by checking three conditions simultaneously: 1. The outward normal to S has a positive dot product with the vector \vec{VL} (from V to L). 2. The outward normal to T has a negative dot product with the vector \vec{VL}. 3. Both the viewpoint V and the interior of triangle S lie on the same side of the plane of triangle T. If all three conditions are met, F is a problem face and A is a problem cell. 3. Temporary Subdivision: If A is a problem cell: Subdivide A into tetrahedra. Update the cell pointers in the subfaces of A to point to the new tetrahedra. For the adjacent cell B on the opposite side of the problem face F: Do not subdivide B's volume. Temporarily replace B's quadrilateral face F with the triangles S and T for sorting and projection purposes. If B is later determined to be a problem cell due to a different face, subdivide the rest of B consistently. If a previously subdivided cell is no longer a problem cell, restore it to its original quadrilateral state and return its memory block to the unused list. 4. Sorting and Rendering: Run the BSP-XMPVO visibility sort on the modified data structure. Composite the cells in the sorted order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isproblemface(face, viewpoint): vecVL = face.vertexL - viewpoint cond1 = dot(face.normalS, vecVL) > 0 cond2 = dot(face.normalT, vecVL) < 0 distV = dot(face.normalT, viewpoint - face.vertexL) pointinS = (face.vertexL + face.vertexS1 + face.vertexS2) / 3.0 distS = dot(face.normalT, pointinS - face.vertexL) cond3 = (distV > 0 and distS > 0) or (distV < 0 and distS < 0) return cond1 and cond2 and cond3 def subdividehexahedron(cell): # Tetrahedralization algorithm for a hexahedron is not specified in the sources return [] def bspxmpvosort(mesh): # BSP-XMPVO visibility sort from Comba et al. (1999) return sorted(mesh.cells, key=lambda c: c.depth) def rendercell(cell): # Composite cell in sorted order pass def isproblemcellfornextview(cell, nextviewpoint): for face in cell.faces: if isproblemface(face, nextviewpoint): return True return False def restorecelltohexahedron(cell): cell.issubdivided = False cell.tetrahedra = None def processviewpoint(mesh, viewpoint): problemcells = [] for cell in mesh.cells: for face in cell.faces: if isproblemface(face, viewpoint): problemcells.append(cell) break for cell in problemcells: if not cell.issubdivided: tetrahedra = subdividehexahedron(cell) cell.tetrahedra = tetrahedra cell.issubdivided = True for face in cell.faces: for subface in face.subfaces: if subface.cellA == cell: subface.cellA = tetrahedra[0] for face in cell.faces: if isproblemface(face, viewpoint): adjacentcell = face.getothercell(cell) if adjacentcell is not None and not adjacentcell.issubdivided: face.mode = "triangles" sortedcells = bspxmpvosort(mesh) for cell in sortedcells: rendercell(cell) for cell in problemcells: if not isproblemcellfornextview(cell, nextviewpoint): restorecelltohexahedron(cell) A strategy to limit the computational overhead of full tetrahedral subdivision by only subdividing cells that are intersected by a viewing ray in more than one segment. It relies on the assumption that distortion is mild enough that multiple intersections occur only when the viewing ray intersects a single curved face more than once. Compared to full subdivision, which increases polygon count from 7 to 22 and vertex count from 41 to 66 for a hexahedron, this method significantly reduces rasterization effort and geometry overhead. Time Complexity: The method requires examining all cells for every new viewpoint to identify problem cells. If the mesh topology changes, the adjacency graph must be rebuilt by searching for adjacent faces. If the geometry changes, face plane equations and the BSP tree must be recomputed. If only the viewpoint moves, edge directions in the adjacency graph must be redetermined. Memory Complexity: Subdivisions are stored in fixed-size blocks (2, 3, 5, or 6 tetrahedra) allocated from large arrays, with unused blocks recycled. This provides memory locality and cache coherence. Performance: Full subdivision of a hexahedron into six tetrahedra requires 22 polygons and 66 vertices, causing higher rasterization effort because most pixels are covered by at least three triangles (and up to four for certain faces). Problem Cell Subdivision reduces this overhead by only subdividing necessary cells. Strengths: Handles Lagrangean meshes that deform or remesh; reduces polygon count compared to full tetrahedralization; compatible with hardware-assisted polyhedron projection. Limitations: Requires dynamic updates to the BSP tree and adjacency graph when viewpoint or geometry changes; complex data structure management for temporary subdivisions. The method was introduced in 2000 as part of an approximate volume rendering technique for curvilinear and unstructured grids using hardware-assisted polyhedron projection. It addresses the limitations of projecting non-planar quadrilaterals directly, which can lead to incorrect visibility sorting due to self-intersections or multiple ray intersections. The approach builds on the BSP-XMPVO sorting algorithm published by Comba et al. in 1999. name: Approximate Cell Sampling
body: Approximate Cell Sampling is a method for sampling cell-centered data in tetrahedral volume rendering that estimates the contribution of neighboring tetrahedra without performing a full tree traversal to locate their vertices. It solves the problem of accessing neighbor geometry when vertex data is not stored for non-coarse elements, using volume ratios and face normals to approximate neighbor centroids. It is distinguished from Simple Cell Sampling by weighting samples by the inverse distance to the estimated centroids, and from Vertex-centered Data Sampling by operating on cell-centered data rather than vertex-centered data. Inputs: point: The 3D sample point in world space. V: An array of 4 vertices [t, l, r, b], where each vertex is a 3D coordinate tuple. tetID: The ID of the current tetrahedron. coarseTetID: The ID of the coarse tetrahedron containing the current element. neighbors: An array of neighbor IDs, where neighbors for tetID are located at neighbors[4 tetID + i] for i in 0..3. cellData: An array of scalar values associated with each tetrahedron. Outputs: A weighted average of the cell-centered data from the current tetrahedron and its neighbors, weighted by the inverse distance to their estimated centroids. Data Structures: The neighbor array and refinement level differences are pre-computed during TET-AMR construction. Steps: 1. Extract the four vertices of the current tetrahedron from V: t, l, r, b. 2. Calculate the centroid of the current tetrahedron: \text{centroid} = \frac{t + l + r + b}{4}. 3. Initialize the inverse distance accumulator and the weighted sample sum: \text{invDist} = \frac{1}{\|\text{centroid} - \text{point}\|}. \text{sample} = \text{cellData}[\text{tetID}] \times \text{invDist}. 4. Loop for each face index i from 0 to 3 (representing the 4 neighbors): a. Retrieve the neighbor ID: \text{neighborID} = \text{neighbors}[4 \times \text{tetID} + i]. b. Initialize the volume ratio: \text{volRatio} = 1. c. Determine if the neighbor is on a different refinement tree and get the level difference: (\text{onAnotherTree}, \text{rLevelDiff}) = \text{ProcessNeighborID}(\text{neighborID}). d. If the neighbor is on another tree, calculate the volume ratio between the coarse elements: \text{volRatio} = \text{GetVolumeRatio}(\text{neighborID}, \text{coarseTetID}). e. Adjust the volume ratio for the refinement level difference. Since each child has 1/8 the volume of its parent: \text{volRatio} = \text{volRatio} \times 8^{\text{rLevelDiff}}. f. Calculate the centroid of the shared face. The face opposite to vertex V[i] is the average of the other 3 vertices. The formula (\text{centroid} \times 4 - V[i]) / 3 correctly computes this because 4 \times \text{centroid} = t+l+r+b: \text{faceCentroid} = \frac{\text{centroid} \times 4 - V[i]}{3}. g. Get the unit normal of the face: \text{faceNormal} = \text{GetUnitFaceNormal}(i, t, l, r, b). h. Calculate the distance from the current tetrahedron's centroid to the face centroid: \text{faceToCentroidDistance} = \|\text{centroid} - \text{faceCentroid}\|. i. Estimate the distance from the face centroid to the neighbor's centroid by scaling the current distance by the volume ratio: \text{neighborFaceToCentroidDistance} = \text{volRatio} \times \text{faceToCentroidDistance}. j. Estimate the neighbor's centroid location by moving from the face centroid along the face normal: \text{neighborCentroid} = \text{faceCentroid} + \text{neighborFaceToCentroidDistance} \times \text{faceNormal}. k. Calculate the inverse distance from the sample point to the estimated neighbor centroid: \text{tmpDist} = \frac{1}{\|\text{neighborCentroid} - \text{point}\|}. l. Accumulate the inverse distance and the weighted sample: \text{invDist} = \text{invDist} + \text{tmpDist}. \text{sample} = \text{sample} + \text{cellData}[\text{neighborID}] \times \text{tmpDist}. m. End loop. 5. Return the final weighted average: \text{result} = \frac{\text{sample}}{\text{invDist}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def samplecellapproximate(point, V, tetID, coarseTetID, neighbors, cellData): # V contains vertices t, l, r, b at indices 0, 1, 2, 3 t, l, r, b = V[0], V[1], V[2], V[3] centroid = tuple((t[k] + l[k] + r[k] + b[k]) / 4.0 for k in range(3)) # Guard against division by zero distcentroid = math.sqrt(sum((c - p)2 for c, p in zip(centroid, point))) if distcentroid == 0.0: distcentroid = 1e-9 invDist = 1.0 / distcentroid sample = cellData[tetID] invDist # Source Algorithm 7 says "0... 4", which is an off-by-one bug for a tetrahedron with 4 faces. Fixed to range(4) for i in range(4): neighborID = neighbors[4 tetID + i] volRatio = 1.0 # Determine tree membership and refinement level difference # Implementation details not provided in sources onAnotherTree, rLevelDiff = False, 0 if onAnotherTree: # Calculate volume ratio between coarse elements # Implementation details not provided in sources volRatio = 1.0 volRatio = volRatio (8.0 rLevelDiff) # Face centroid: average of the 3 vertices not equal to V[i] faceCentroid = tuple((centroid[k] 4.0 - V[i][k]) / 3.0 for k in range(3)) # Get unit normal for face i # Standard cross-product calculation vertices = [t, l, r, b] faceverts = [v for j, v in enumerate(vertices) if j != i] v1 = tuple(b - a for a, b in zip(faceverts[1], faceverts[0])) v2 = tuple(b - a for a, b in zip(faceverts[2], faceverts[0])) cross = (v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) length = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in cross)) if length == 0.0: faceNormal = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: faceNormal = tuple(c / length for c in cross) faceToCentroidDist = math.sqrt(sum((c - f)2 for c, f in zip(centroid, faceCentroid))) neighborFaceToCentroidDist = volRatio faceToCentroidDist neighborCentroid = tuple(fc + nfd fn for fc, nfd, fn in zip(faceCentroid, neighborFaceToCentroidDist, faceNormal)) distneighbor = math.sqrt(sum((nc - p)2 for nc, p in zip(neighborCentroid, point))) if distneighbor == 0.0: distneighbor = 1e-9 tmpDist = 1.0 / distneighbor invDist = invDist + tmpDist # Source Algorithm 7 line 21 uses cellData[tetID], which is a typo; corrected to neighborID sample = sample + cellData[neighborID] tmpDist return sample / invDist Parameters: 8^rLevelDiff: The scaling factor for volume ratios based on refinement level difference, as each child element has one-eighth of its parent's volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the sample point coincides with a centroid, the inverse distance becomes infinite. A small epsilon guard is required. Index Out of Bounds: The source loop runs from 0 to 4, but a tetrahedron has 4 faces. Accessing V[4] or neighbors[4tetID + 4] is invalid; the loop must run from 0 to 3. Source Typo: The source pseudocode uses cellData[tetID] for the neighbor contribution, which is logically incorrect; it must use cellData[neighborID]. Helper Functions: ProcessNeighborID and GetVolumeRatio are not implemented in the source; their logic must be provided by the TET-AMR construction pipeline. A coarse approximation method for cell-centered data that averages the cell-centered data of the element and its neighbors without considering distances to centroids. It is a coarse approximation because it does not consider the distances to the neighbors' centroids where the cell-centered data is sampled. Time Complexity: Constant time per sample point relative to the number of neighbors (4 neighbors for a tetrahedron). Memory Complexity: Requires storage of neighbor IDs and refinement level differences, which are pre-computed during TET-AMR construction. Strengths: Avoids the computational cost of traversing the refinement tree to find neighbor vertices. Provides a distance-weighted approximation, which is more accurate than simple averaging. Limitations: It is an approximation; the estimated neighbor centroids may not be exact, especially across different refinement trees or large level differences. When to Use: When vertex data is not stored for non-coarse elements and neighbor geometry must be approximated efficiently. Origin: The method is described in the thesis "Direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement data". History: It is part of the rendering pipeline for TET-AMR data, which uses a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) to locate coarse elements and then traverses the refinement tree on the ray until out of the coarse element. Usage: Used in direct volume rendering of unstructured tetrahedral data with adaptive mesh refinement. name: Vertex-centered Data Sampling
body: Vertex-centered Data Sampling reconstructs scalar field values within a tetrahedral element by interpolating the scalar data stored at the element's four vertices using the sample point's barycentric coordinates. It is distinguished from its sibling Cell-centered Data Sampling by relying on vertex-local data rather than averaging cell-centered values from face neighbors. Inputs: elementid: Integer identifier for the current tetrahedral element. p: The 3D sample point (x, y, z) inside the tetrahedron. tetvertices: Array of 4 vertex positions \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 associated with elementid. vertexscalars: Array of 4 scalar values s0, s1, s2, s3 associated with the vertices of elementid. Outputs: samplevalue: The interpolated scalar value at point p. Data Structures: Vertex-centered data is stored duplicated per element during the TET-AMR construction process. This allows direct access to the four vertex scalars via the elementid. Steps: 1. Retrieve the four scalar values si for i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} associated with the vertices of the current element using elementid. 2. Compute the barycentric coordinates \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 of the sample point p with respect to the tetrahedron defined by \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. 3. Calculate the interpolated value using the weighted sum: s(p) = \sum{i=0}^{3} \lambdai si 4. Return s(p). Formulas: The barycentric coordinates \lambdai satisfy the affine combination: p = \sum{i=0}^{3} \lambdai \mathbf{v}i subject to the normalization constraint: \sum{i=0}^{3} \lambdai = 1 where \mathbf{v}i are the tetrahedron vertices and p is the query point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexcenteredsample(elementid, p, tetvertices, vertexscalars): v0, v1, v2, v3 = tetvertices s0, s1, s2, s3 = vertexscalars # Compute signed volume of the tetrahedron def signedvol(a, b, c, d): return dot(cross(b - a, c - a), d - a) / 6.0 totalvol = signedvol(v0, v1, v2, v3) # Compute barycentric coordinates via volume ratios l0 = signedvol(p, v1, v2, v3) / totalvol l1 = signedvol(v0, p, v2, v3) / totalvol l2 = signedvol(v0, v1, p, v3) / totalvol l3 = signedvol(v0, v1, v2, p) / totalvol # Interpolate scalar value return l0 s0 + l1 s1 + l2 s2 + l3 s3 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Tetrahedra: If the tetrahedron volume is zero (coplanar vertices), the division in the volume ratio calculation results in undefined behavior. Implementers should check for near-zero volume and handle it as a degenerate case (e.g., fallback to 0 or error). Parameters: Not given in the sources. Details the specific geometric computation of the barycentric weights and their affine property within a single element. Not given in the sources. Originating from the work on direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (TET-AMR) data, this method leverages the duplicated vertex data structure to simplify sampling.
