name: Hardware-Assisted Polyhedron Projection
head: Approximate Volume Rendering for Curvilinear and Unstructured Grids by Hardware-Assisted Polyhedron Projection, CP scheme, Parallel Cell-Projection Volume Rendering, Polyhedron Projection
body: Hardware-Assisted Polyhedron Projection is a technique for volume rendering arbitrary unstructured grids composed of convex polyhedral cells by projecting 3D cells into 2D screen space and using hardware rasterization to compute optical properties per pixel. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex, non-uniform volumetric data by leveraging the graphics pipeline for scan conversion and compositing, avoiding the memory bandwidth bottlenecks of raycasting. Unlike raycasting, which groups connected cells to exploit coherence, this method disperses connected cells widely to achieve static load balancing in parallel environments. It builds on Hardware-Assisted Projection by providing the specific geometric subdivision and data distribution strategies required for arbitrary convex polyhedra. The method projects each convex polyhedral cell onto the image plane, subdivides the projection into regions where optical thickness varies linearly, computes color and opacity for these regions, and composites them in back-to-front order using hardware blending. Inputs: A set of convex polyhedral cells defining an unstructured grid; scalar values at nodes mapped to color and extinction coefficient \tau; camera parameters (viewpoint, projection matrix). Outputs: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. Ray Segment A data structure used during scan conversion and composition, consisting of four parameters: RGB: Color (3 floats or fixed-point). \alpha: Opacity (1 float). zfront: Depth of the front intersection point. zback: Depth of the back intersection point. Winged-Edge Subdivision Structure Used to represent the projection of a polyhedron P on the image plane. It stores vertices, edges, and faces, allowing efficient traversal and modification as projected edges are added. Cell Storage Each cell stores four node indices (16 bytes). Node Storage Each node stores three coordinates and one scalar value (16 bytes). 1. Projection Phase: Project the 3D vertices of a cell P to 2D screen space. Construct a winged-edge subdivision structure for the projection of P. Add the projected edges of P one by one to this structure by moving along a new edge and finding its intersections with existing edges. Create a new vertex at each intersection (unless it coincides with an existing vertex) and modify the winged-edge structure, potentially dividing one of the existing polygons in two. The projected edges divide the image plane into polygonal regions. 2. Region Analysis: For each polygon Q in the final subdivision, identify that it lies in the projection of one front face and one back face of P. Assume viewing rays are parallel (viewpoint at infinity) or approximate perspective as linear variation for small/distant cells, such that the thickness (length of viewing ray segment in P) varies linearly over Q. Compute thickness as zero at profile vertices and compute thickness from the geometry of P and viewing ray at non-profile vertices and projected edge intersections. 3. Analytic Integration: Compute colors and opacities for viewing rays through the region's vertices by analytic integration. The intensity I(s) along a ray with extinction coefficient \tau(s) satisfies: \frac{dI(s)}{ds} = -\tau(s)I(s) Integrating along a ray segment of length l yields: I(l) = I(0) \exp\left(-\int0^l \tau(s) \, ds\right) Transparency is defined as: T = \exp\left(-\int0^l \tau(s) \, ds\right) If \tau is constant, transparency reduces to \exp(-l \cdot \tau). 4. Scan Conversion: For each pixel P(x, y) in the projection area R of the cell, calculate the cell's contribution (color RGB and opacity \alpha) and depth values (z{front} and z{back}) for front and back intersection points. This set of four parameters is called a 'ray segment'. Compute ray segments for every cell. 5. Partial Composition (Optional): During scan conversion, if two neighboring ray segments in the list are derived from neighboring cells contacting each other along the ray, perform composition of these segments. The resultant is again a ray segment. This reduces the length of the ray-segment list. 6. Depth Sorting: For each pixel on the screen, gather ray segments corresponding to the pixel and make a depth-sorted list. Cells must be sorted in back-to-front order relative to the viewpoint to ensure correct compositing. 7. Hardware Compositing: Interpolate and composite using polygon rendering hardware, avoiding linear interpolation of vertex transparency to prevent Mach bands. Use a texture map for hardware lookup of the exponential: for constant \tau, use product l \cdot \tau as a 1D texture coordinate; for varying \tau, use l and \tau as a 2D texture coordinate pair. Composite depth-sorted ray segments from front to back using alpha blending with Porter-Duff's over operation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwareassistedpolyhedronprojection(cells, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Render unstructured grid cells using hardware-assisted polyhedron projection. Args: cells: List of convex polyhedra, each defined by vertices and node indices. camera: Camera object with projection matrix and view direction. imagewidth: Width of the output image in pixels. imageheight: Height of the output image in pixels. Returns: Rendered image buffer. """ # Initialize image buffer image = createimagebuffer(imagewidth, imageheight) # Global sorting of cells back-to-front relative to viewpoint sortedcells = sortcellsbacktofront(cells, camera) # Precompute texture map for exponential lookup # For constant tau, map l tau -> exp(-l tau) # For varying tau, map (l, tau) -> exp(-integral tau ds) exptexture = createexponentialtexture() for cell in sortedcells: # Step 1: Project cell to screen space projectedvertices = projectvertices(cell.vertices, camera.projectionmatrix) # Step 2: Construct winged-edge subdivision subdivision = constructwingededgesubdivision(projectedvertices, cell.edges) # Step 3: Identify regions and compute vertex properties regions = subdivision.getpolygons() regiondata = [] for region in regions: # Identify front and back faces for this region frontface, backface = identifyfaces(region, cell) # Compute thickness at region vertices # Thickness is zero at profile vertices, computed from geometry otherwise thicknesses = computethicknessatvertices(region.vertices, frontface, backface, camera.viewdirection) # Compute color and opacity at vertices via analytic integration vertexcolors = [] vertexopacities = [] for i, vertex in enumerate(region.vertices): # Get scalar value at vertex node scalar = getscalaratnode(vertex.nodeindex) # Map scalar to extinction coefficient tau tau = mapscalartotau(scalar) # Compute thickness l for this vertex l = thicknesses[i] # Compute transparency T = exp(-integral tau ds) # If tau is constant: T = exp(-l tau) # If tau varies, use precomputed integral or 2D texture lookup if istauconstant(): transparency = exp(-l tau) # Use 1D texture coordinate l tau texcoord = l tau else: # Use 2D texture coordinate (l, tau) texcoord = (l, tau) transparency = lookuptexture(exptexture, texcoord) # Compute color I(l) = I(0) T # Assuming I(0) = 1 (white light source) color = mapscalartocolor(scalar) transparency vertexcolors.append(color) vertexopacities.append(1.0 - transparency) # Opacity = 1 - Transparency regiondata.append({ 'vertices': region.vertices, 'colors': vertexcolors, 'opacities': vertexopacities, 'thicknesses': thicknesses, 'taus': [gettauatnode(v.nodeindex) for v in region.vertices] }) # Step 4: Scan conversion using hardware rasterization for regioninfo in regiondata: # Rasterize the polygon region with hardware # Interpolate colors and texture coordinates across the polygon # Avoid linear interpolation of transparency to prevent Mach bands # For each pixel in the bounding box of the region: for pixelx, pixely in getpixelcoordsinregion(regioninfo['vertices']): # Interpolate texture coordinate for exponential lookup if istauconstant(): u = interpolatevalue(regioninfo['thicknesses'], regioninfo['vertices'], pixelx, pixely) v = 0.0 # Not used for 1D texture texcoord = (u, v) else: u = interpolatevalue(regioninfo['thicknesses'], regioninfo['vertices'], pixelx, pixely) v = interpolatevalue(regioninfo['taus'], regioninfo['vertices'], pixelx, pixely) texcoord = (u, v) # Lookup transparency from texture transparency = lookuptexture(exptexture, texcoord) # Compute color by interpolating vertex colors color = interpolatecolor(regioninfo['colors'], regioninfo['vertices'], pixelx, pixely) # Create ray segment # Compute zfront and zback for this pixel zfront = interpolatedepth(regioninfo['vertices'], pixelx, pixely, face='front') zback = interpolatedepth(regioninfo['vertices'], pixelx, pixely, face='back') raysegment = { 'color': color, 'opacity': 1.0 - transparency, 'zfront': zfront, 'zback': zback } # Add ray segment to pixel's list addraysegmenttopixel(pixelx, pixely, raysegment) # Step 5: Composition Phase for pixelx in range(imagewidth): for pixely in range(imageheight): raysegments = getraysegmentsforpixel(pixelx, pixely) # Sort ray segments by zfront (back-to-front) raysegments.sort(key=lambda seg: seg['zfront'], reverse=True) # Composite ray segments using Porter-Duff over operation accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 for seg in raysegments: # Porter-Duff over: # Cout = Cfg alphafg + Cbg alphabg (1 - alphafg) # alphaout = alphafg + alphabg (1 - alphafg) fgcolor = seg['color'] fgalpha = seg['opacity'] accumulatedcolor = fgcolor fgalpha + accumulatedcolor accumulatedopacity (1.0 - fgalpha) accumulatedopacity = fgalpha + accumulatedopacity (1.0 - fgalpha) # Early ray termination if fully opaque if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break setpixelcolor(pixelx, pixely, accumulatedcolor) return image Cell storage size: 16 bytes per cell (four node indices). Node storage size: 16 bytes per node (three coordinates and a scalar value). Transparency: \exp\left(-\int0^l \tau(s) \, ds\right). Mach Bands: Linear or bilinear interpolation of vertex transparency causes distracting Mach bands because opacity is a nonlinear function of thickness. Use texture mapping for exponential lookup. Curvilinear Cells: Faces may not be planar. Modifications must be made to approximate curvilinear cells, whose faces may not be planar. The method gives only an approximation to the correct volume rendering for curved finite elements. Load Imbalance: Grouping connected cells together causes severe load imbalances during zoom-in viewing, as a few processors handle all calculations while others go idle. Disperse connected cells widely to avoid this. Unstructured Meshes: Irregular cell sizes and shapes make balanced load distribution difficult due to variations in projected image area and scan conversion costs. Time Complexity: Dominated by global sorting of cells (O(N \log N)) and scan conversion/compositing per pixel. Parallel implementation reduces per-processor load via round-robin distribution. Memory Complexity: Cell storage is 16 bytes per cell, node storage is 16 bytes per node. In worst-case no sharing, 80n bytes transferred for n cells. Spatial partitioning tree reduces runtime memory consumption. Measured Performance: On IBM SP2, 2 frames per second for a 400x400-pixel image using 128 processors on a dataset with half a million tetrahedral cells. Scaling: Good scalability on distributed-memory supercomputers due to static load balancing via round-robin distribution. Strengths: Flexible data distribution, efficient use of hardware rasterization, good parallel scalability. Limitations: Requires global sorting for back-to-front compositing. Approximation for curvilinear cells. Load imbalance if connected cells are grouped. Origin: Proposed by Nelson Max, Peter L. Williams, and Cláudio T Silva in 2000. Development: Builds on earlier work by Shirley and Tuchman (1990) and Wilhelms and Van Gelder (1991) on polygon subdivision for hardware rendering. Extended to parallel environments by Max et al. (1997) for distributed-memory supercomputers. Usage: Used for volume rendering of unstructured grids, particularly in scientific visualization of aerodynamics and other complex geometries. Approximate volume rendering for curvilinear and unstructured grids by hardware-assisted polyhedron projection, https://doi.org/10.1002/(sici)1098-1098(2000)11:1<53::aid-ima6>3.0.co;2-7, fetched 2026-10-25 PDF Cell-projection Parallel Volume Rendering With Early Ray Termination, http://www.tomitaken.org/project/papers/ReVolver/2004/VIIP.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF A Scalable Parallel Cell-Projection Volume Rendering Algorithm for..., https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~ma/papers/PRS97.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (PDF) Image-space visibility ordering for cell projection volume..., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/8193687Image-spacevisibilityorderingforcellprojectionvolumerenderingofunstructureddata, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hardware-Assisted Projected Tetrahedra
head: CellFast algorithm, HAPT, Hardware CellFast
body: Hardware-Assisted Projected Tetrahedra (HAPT) is a flexible, highly efficient volume rendering method that adapts the original Projected Tetrahedra (PT) algorithm to exploit programmable graphics hardware. It solves the visibility ordering and rendering bottleneck of irregular tetrahedral meshes by streaming sorted tetrahedra as point primitives, decomposing them into triangles in a geometry shader, and evaluating the volume ray integral per fragment during rasterization. Unlike its sibling PTINT, which requires a two-pass approach with GPU read-back, HAPT performs the entire rendering pipeline in a single GPU pass, eliminating auxiliary data structures and reducing GPU memory consumption. HAPT builds on Hardware-Assisted Projection by replacing software-based cell projection with hardware rasterization. The method consists of two main phases: sorting and rendering. Input: An unstructured tetrahedral mesh where each vertex has a scalar value. The data may be static or time-varying. Output: A 2D image composited from back-to-front, representing direct volume rendering (DVR) or iso-surface rendering. Tetrahedra are streamed to the GPU as point primitives. To minimize data throughput, each point primitive represents one tetrahedron and carries the following attributes: 1. Position: The position of one vertex of the tetrahedron (e.g., v0). 2. Texture Coordinates: The positions of the other three vertices (v1, v2, v3) are passed as texture coordinates. 3. Scalar Value: The scalar value of the primary vertex is passed as the w coordinate of the vertex. Before rendering, tetrahedra must be sorted in back-to-front order relative to the viewpoint. HAPT supports multiple sorting strategies: CPU Methods: STL-based introsort or MPVONC (Meshed Polyhedra Visibility Ordering for Non-Convex meshes). MPVONC is exact but requires auxiliary adjacency lists and precomputed face normals, increasing CPU memory by ~4x the volume size. GPU Methods: CUDA-based quicksort or bitonic sort. Bitonic sort requires power-of-two array sizes, which may slow performance if padding is needed. Approximate Sorting: Centroid sorting is used for GPU methods (except MPVONC). It is significantly faster but approximate, potentially inverting adjacent tetrahedra. The error is low (average ~1 RGB unit on [0,255] scale) and visually imperceptible in most cases. The rendering is performed in a single pass through the GPU pipeline. 1. Vertex Shader (VS): Receives the point primitives. If time-varying data is used, an early discard test removes empty tetrahedra (all vertices mapped to zero opacity). 2. Geometry Shader (GS): Decomposes the point primitive into one to four triangles based on the tetrahedron's projection case. Determines the projection case using PTINT's classification strategy: four cross products and a table lookup. Computes three attributes for each generated vertex: traversal length l, scalar front sf, and scalar back sb. Vertex Types: Thick Vertex: The entry point where the ray traverses the maximum distance l. Its scalar value must be interpolated, and l may need to be computed if it is not an edge length. This vertex may not be one of the original four projected vertices. Thin Vertices: All other projected vertices. For these, sf = sb (original scalar value) and l = 0, as the ray traverses no distance at these extremities. Stores sf, sb, l as RGB color attributes of the vertices to pass information to the fragment shader. For iso-surface rendering, the GS extracts the iso-surface as one or two triangles with face normals. 3. Rasterization: The hardware rasterizer processes the triangles. 4. Fragment Shader (FS): Interpolates sf, sb, l per fragment. Computes the volume ray integral using partial pre-integration. Accesses a pre-computed table using indices derived from l and the front/back colors (extracted from sf/sb via the transfer function). Composites the result using hardware blending. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def haptrender(tetrahedra, viewpoint, transferfunction, preinttable): # 1. Sorting # Sort tetrahedra back-to-front. # Example: Use CUDA quicksort on indices. sortedindices = cudaquicksort(tetrahedra, viewpoint) # 2. Stream to GPU # Create point primitives. # Each primitive: pos=v0, texcoords=(v1, v2, v3), w=scalar(v0) pointprimitives = [] for idx in sortedindices: tet = tetrahedra[idx] pointprimitives.append({ 'pos': tet.v0, 'texcoords': (tet.v1, tet.v2, tet.v3), 'w': tet.scalarv0 }) # 3. Geometry Shader Execution (per tetrahedron) triangles = [] for prim in pointprimitives: # Decompose into triangles based on projection case # Case determination: 4 cross products + table lookup case = determineprojectioncase(prim.pos, prim.texcoords, viewpoint) generatedtriangles = decomposetetrahedron(case, prim.pos, prim.texcoords) for tri in generatedtriangles: # Compute attributes for each vertex of the triangle verts = [] for v in tri.vertices: # Determine if v is a 'thick' or 'thin' vertex if isthickvertex(v, case): # Thick vertex: max traversal distance l = computetraversallength(v, case) sf = interpolatescalar(v, case, prim) sb = interpolatescalar(v, case, prim) else: # Thin vertex: no traversal l = 0.0 sf = getscalar(v, prim) sb = getscalar(v, prim) # Store as RGB color for interpolation color = rgbfromvalues(sf, sb, l) verts.append({'pos': v, 'color': color}) triangles.append(verts) # 4. Rasterization and Fragment Shader Execution image = emptyimage() for tri in triangles: # Rasterize triangle fragments = rasterize(tri) for frag in fragments: # Interpolated values from vertex colors sf = frag.color.r sb = frag.color.g l = frag.color.b # Partial Pre-Integration # Extract colors from transfer function cfront = transferfunction(sf) cback = transferfunction(sb) # Compute indices for pre-integration table idx1 = computeindex(l) idx2 = computeindexfromcolors(cfront, cback) # Lookup result result = preinttable[idx1][idx2] # Composite into image (back-to-front) image.composite(frag.pos, result) return image def decomposetetrahedron(case, v0, v1, v2, v3): # Returns list of triangles based on PTINT classification # Case 1: 3 triangles # Case 2: 2 triangles # Case 3: 2 triangles # Case 4: 1 triangle (degenerate) # Implementation details depend on specific PTINT table pass def isthickvertex(v, case): # Returns True if v is the entry point with max traversal distance # Depends on the specific projection case pass def computetraversallength(v, case): # Computes Euclidean distance. # May require square root (lookup table in hardware) pass def interpolatescalar(v, case, prim): # Interpolates scalar value at thick vertex pass def getscalar(v, prim): # Returns original scalar value of vertex v pass def rgbfromvalues(sf, sb, l): # Maps sf, sb, l to RGB color components # sf -> R, sb -> G, l -> B return (sf, sb, l) def computeindex(l): # Maps traversal length to table index pass def computeindexfromcolors(cfront, cback): # Maps front/back colors to table index pass Sorting Error: Centroid sorting is approximate and may invert adjacent tetrahedra. While visually imperceptible in most cases, it introduces error (avg ~1 RGB unit). MPVONC Degeneracy: MPVONC does not perform correct visibility ordering in some degenerated cases, though it works for most meshes. Bitonic Sort Padding: Bitonic sort requires power-of-two array sizes, which may slow performance if padding is needed. Empty Regions: Early discard in the vertex shader is only profitable if the volume has large empty regions, due to texture fetch overhead. Iso-surface Normals: Normals are restricted to faces (flat shading) unless adjacency info is carried, which impacts memory/performance. A hybrid method that uses pre-integrated optical depth tables. HAPT builds on this by leveraging GPU rasterization for cell projection, removing the need for GPU read-back and auxiliary basis graphs. Time Complexity: Sorting dominates the pre-processing time. GPU sorting (quicksort) is fast, achieving over 6 M Tet/s. Rendering is a single pass, efficient due to hardware rasterization. Memory Complexity: Low GPU memory consumption. Tetrahedra are streamed as point primitives, avoiding the need to store the entire volume in GPU memory. This allows rendering of volumes with several million tetrahedra. CPU memory for MPVONC is ~4x the volume size. Performance: Blunt fin (187 K Tet): 19.2 fps. Oxygen post (513 K Tet): 8.1 fps. Turbulent jet (1 M Tet/frame): 17.5 fps. spx2 (828 K Tet): 7.4 fps (DVR), 8.2 fps (Iso-surface). Strengths: Single-pass rendering, low GPU memory usage, support for time-varying data, hybrid DVR/iso-surface rendering. Limitations: Requires geometry shader. Centroid sorting is approximate. MPVONC is memory-intensive and has degenerate cases. Flat shading for iso-surfaces unless adjacency info is carried. When to use: Large unstructured tetrahedral datasets where GPU memory is a constraint, or time-varying data requires streaming. When not to use: When exact visibility ordering is critical and CPU memory is limited (MPVONC). When smooth iso-surface normals are required without adjacency overhead. HAPT was introduced by A. Maximo, R. Marroquim, and R. Farias in 2010, published in the Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques. It is an adaptation of the PTINT method, designed to exploit programmable graphics hardware by performing the entire algorithm in a single GPU pass. It addresses the visibility ordering problem using fast sorting algorithms (quicksort, MPVONC) and leverages the geometry shader for triangle decomposition. name: Tetrahedral Projection with Partial Pre-integration
head: PT algorithm, PTINT (Projected Tetrahedra with Partial Pre-Integration), Projected Tetrahedra with Partial Pre-Integration
body: Tetrahedral Projection with Partial Pre-integration (PTINT) is a hybrid volume and isosurface rendering method that projects tetrahedra onto the screen and computes fragment colors using pre-integrated optical depth tables. It solves the performance bottleneck of explicit isosurface extraction by computing isosurfaces per fragment within the rendering pipeline, avoiding the case-handling complexity of marching tetrahedra. Unlike full pre-integration, PTINT uses a transfer-function-independent \psi table, allowing interactive transfer function editing without expensive table recomputation. It builds on Hardware-Assisted Projected Tetrahedra by leveraging GPU rasterization for cell projection. Inputs: Regular 3D scalar volume data (stored as hexahedral volunits), viewing vector \vec{v}, isovalue (optional), transfer function (TF), Phong illumination coefficients (optional). Outputs: Final color buffer. Data Structures: 1. Volume Data: Regular grid of hexahedral volunits, each decomposed into 5 tetrahedra. 2. Exponential Texture: 1D texture (256 entries) storing e^{-u} for u \in [0,1]. 3. \psi Table: 2D texture storing partial pre-integration integral values, independent of the transfer function. 4. Transfer Function Texture: 1D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA colors. 5. Vertex/Color/Normal Arrays: Fixed-size arrays passed to glMultiDrawElements, containing data for 5 tetrahedra per volunit (4 vertices + 1 thick vertex per tetrahedron). 6. Index Arrays: 5 arrays of indices defining the triangle fan order for the 5 tetrahedra, created once for all volunits. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sorting: Determine traversal order based on viewing vector \vec{v} = \{vx, vy, vz\}. If vx > 0, traverse x-indices ascending; else descending. If vy > 0, traverse y-indices ascending; else descending. If vz > 0, traverse z-indices ascending; else descending. The relative order of axes traversal does not matter for regular data. Only 8 traversal permutations are required to cover all viewing angles. 2. Data Preparation (CPU): For each volunit, compute vertex positions and colors. Compute normal vectors (valid for all volunits, computed once). Upload vertex, color, and normal arrays to GPU memory. If isosurfaces/lighting are disabled, skip gradient computation and normal interpolation. 3. Rendering (GPU Vertex Shader): Read basis hexahedron information from global uniform variables. Displace vertices correctly using the basis information. Pass vertex attributes (position, color, normal) to the fragment shader. 4. Rasterization: Render each volunit as 5 triangle fans (one per tetrahedron). Interpolate color attributes across the triangles. 5. Fragment Color Computation (Fragment Shader): Isosurface Rendering (Optional): Check if isovalue is within the scalar range of the current fragment. Retrieve front gradient \vec{g}f and back gradient \vec{g}b. Compute normal vector \vec{n} by combining \vec{g}f and \vec{g}b with weights relative to the distance between the isosurface and the front/back intersection points. Compute Phong illumination (diffuse, specular, ambient) using \vec{n}. Volume Rendering: Retrieve front color Cf and back color Cb from the transfer function texture using scalar values at the front and back intersections. Retrieve thickness l (optical depth or geometric thickness). Compute indices for the \psi table using Cf, Cb, and l. Lookup value from the \psi table. Compute final fragment color using the \psi table value. Alternative (Simpler/Faster): Compute chromaticity as average of Cf and Cb. Compute opacity \alpha = 1 - e^{-\tau \cdot l}, where \tau is mean alpha. Use exponential texture for e^{-u} lookup. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computefragmentcolor(frontscalar, backscalar, thicknessl, isosurfaceenabled, isovalue, viewvector): # 1. Transfer function lookup Cf = tftexture[frontscalar] Cb = tftexture[backscalar] # 2. Exponential lookup for opacity u = thicknessl expval = exptexture[u] alpha = 1.0 - expval # 3. Partial pre-integration lookup # Compute indices for psi table using Cf, Cb, and l # (Exact indexing formula not given in sources) psiidx = computepsiindex(Cf, Cb, thicknessl) psivalue = psitable[psiidx] # 4. Final color composition # (Exact composition formula not given in sources) finalcolor = psivalue # 5. Isosurface contribution (optional) if isosurfaceenabled: if min(frontscalar, backscalar) <= isovalue <= max(frontscalar, backscalar): # Retrieve gradients gf = gradientarray[frontscalar] gb = gradientarray[backscalar] # Compute distances to intersection points df = distancetofrontintersection(frontscalar) db = distancetobackintersection(backscalar) diso = distancetoisosurfaceintersection(isovalue) # Weights relative to distance between isosurface and intersection points wf = abs(diso - df) wb = abs(diso - db) # Combine gradients for normal n = normalize(wf gf + wb gb) # Phong illumination isocolor = phonglighting(n, viewvector) finalcolor = isocolor + finalcolor return finalcolor def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def phonglighting(normal, viewdir): # Standard Phong model using pre-loaded coefficients diffuse = max(0.0, sum(n l for n, l in zip(normal, lightdir))) specular = max(0.0, sum(n r for n, r in zip(normal, reflectdir))) 4.0 return (diffuse ambient + specular specularcoeff, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) def computepsiindex(cf, cb, l): # Placeholder for exact indexing logic return (int(cf 255), int(cb 255)) def distancetofrontintersection(scalar): # Placeholder for ray-tetrahedron intersection math return 0.0 def distancetobackintersection(scalar): return 0.0 def distancetoisosurfaceintersection(iso): return 0.0 Parameters: Exponential Texture Size: 256 entries. Storage per Tetrahedron: 24 bytes (assuming 4 tets per vertex, 16 bytes per texture element). Traversal Orders: 8 possible permutations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clipping: Clipping must be parallel to the volume's bounding box sides to maintain regular properties required for implicit sorting. Memory: The entire dataset must fit in main memory to avoid swapping, as no extra data structures are created. Performance: Partial pre-integration is slower than simple scalar averaging but necessary for interactive TF editing. Full pre-integration requires expensive table recomputation on TF change. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(1) due to regular data spacing and implicit 3D array structure. Rendering is proportional to the number of tetrahedra. Memory Complexity: 24 bytes per tetrahedron on GPU memory. No extra data structures beyond volume data. Performance: On Intel Pentium IV 3.6 GHz, GeForce 6800, 512x512 viewport: Blunt Fin: 11.30 fps (PTINT) vs 4.07 fps (GATOR), 5.20 fps (VICP), 4.47 fps (HARC), 6.09 fps (HAVS). Oxygen Post: 4.49 fps (PTINT) vs 8.63 fps (HARC). Fuel (1.2M tet): 70.78 fps, 5.99 M tet/s. Tooth (5M tet): 1.22 fps, 6.30 M tet/s. Aneurism (83M tet): 2.42 fps, 5.35 M tet/s. Rendering time accounts for >60% of total time for most datasets. Strengths: High frame rates, interactive transfer function editing, no explicit isosurface case handling, low memory footprint compared to ray casting. Limitations: Limited to regular data, clipping constraints, slower than simple averaging, requires data to fit in memory. PTINT is based on the Projected Tetrahedra (PT) method by Roettger et al. (2000) and partial pre-integration by Moreland and Angel (2004). It was developed to leverage GPU acceleration for cell projection while maintaining interactive capabilities for volume visualization. name: Röttger 3D Texture Mapping
head: Hardware-Assisted Projected Tetrahedra with 3D Texture Mapping, Pre-integrated Volume Rendering for Tetrahedra, Röttger et al. 3D Texture Mapping
body: Röttger 3D Texture Mapping is an extension of the projected tetrahedra algorithm that enables hardware-accelerated rendering of volumetric data with arbitrary transfer functions. It solves the limitation of earlier hardware-assisted methods that could only handle linear transfer functions without artifacts by introducing pre-integrated volume rendering. Unlike siblings that rely on linear interpolation of opacity, this method uses a 3D texture map to accurately compute the optical thickness and resulting color/opacity along the ray segment within a tetrahedron, approximated via 2D texture mapping hardware. Inputs and Outputs Input: A tetrahedral mesh representing the volume data; a transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity; camera parameters. Output: A 2D image with correct compositing of volumetric data. Data Structures Pre-integration Texture: A 3D texture map used to store pre-computed integration results. Layout: The texture has three coordinates. 1. u: Corresponds to the scalar value at the cell entry point. 2. v: Corresponds the scalar value at the cell exit point. 3. w: Corresponds to the distance (optical thickness) through the cell along the ray. Content: The texture stores the integrated color and opacity resulting from the transfer function applied over the segment defined by the entry/exit values and the path length. Steps 1. Pre-computation (Offline): For a range of possible entry values, exit values, and path lengths, compute the volume rendering integral using the specific transfer function. Store the resulting color and opacity in the 3D texture map at coordinates corresponding to the entry value, exit value, and path length. 2. Projection and Rasterization: Project the tetrahedra vertices to screen space. Rasterize the projected tetrahedra. During rasterization, interpolate the scalar values at the entry and exit points of the ray segment passing through the tetrahedron for each pixel. Calculate the geometric length of the ray segment within the tetrahedron for each pixel. 3. Texture Lookup: Use the interpolated entry value, exit value, and segment length as texture coordinates (u, v, w) to sample the pre-integration texture. The hardware texture unit performs trilinear interpolation within the 3D texture to retrieve the pre-computed color and opacity. 4. Approximation via 2D Mapping: The 3D texture map is approximated using two-dimensional texture mapping hardware to accelerate the lookup process. This involves mapping the 3D coordinates to a 2D texture space, likely by packing or projecting the dimensions, allowing standard 2D texture hardware to perform the interpolation. 5. Compositing: Composite the retrieved color and opacity values using hardware blending operations in back-to-front order. Formulas The volume rendering integral is approximated by the lookup in the pre-integration texture. The differential equation for intensity I(s) along a ray is: \frac{dI(s)}{ds} = -\tau(s)I(s) The transparency T for a segment of length l is: T = \exp\left(-\int0^l \tau(s) \, ds\right) The pre-integration texture stores the result of this integral for arbitrary transfer functions, avoiding the need for per-pixel numerical integration. Parameters Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Range of Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The accuracy depends on the resolution of the pre-integration texture. Insufficient resolution may lead to artifacts. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes the entry and exit values and the path length are within the bounds of the pre-computed texture. Extrapolation may cause artifacts. Arbitrary Transfer Functions: The method supports arbitrary transfer functions, unlike earlier hardware-assisted methods. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is offline. Runtime complexity is dominated by rasterization and texture lookup, which is efficient on modern hardware. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D pre-integration texture. Size depends on the resolution of the texture and the range of values/path lengths. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports arbitrary transfer functions; hardware-accelerated; avoids artifacts associated with linear interpolation of opacity. Limitations: Requires pre-computation; memory usage for the 3D texture; approximation via 2D mapping may introduce errors. When to use: When arbitrary transfer functions are required and hardware acceleration is desired. When not to use: When memory is constrained or pre-computation is not feasible. Origin: Introduced by Röttger et al. [RKE00] as an extension of the projected tetrahedra algorithm [ST90]. History: The method was developed to address the limitations of earlier hardware-assisted volume rendering techniques that could only handle linear transfer functions. It introduced the concept of pre-integrated volume rendering. Usage: Used in interactive volume rendering of volumetric data. name: Absorption-Only Radiography via Unsorted Hexahedron Projection
head: Unsorted Hexahedron Projection, Absorption-Only Radiography
body: This method simulates X-ray radiographs for curvilinear hexahedral meshes by accumulating optical thickness additively, thereby eliminating the need for a global back-to-front visibility sort. It differs from its parent Hardware-Assisted Projection by exploiting the commutative property of addition in the absorption-only regime (J=0) to allow unsorted rendering, and from Hardware-Assisted Projected Tetrahedra by supporting direct projection of hexahedral cells to reduce mesh storage and rendering overhead. Inputs: A curvilinear hexahedral mesh where each cell has an extinction coefficient Kv and geometric definition. An image plane resolution. Outputs: A radiograph image representing accumulated optical thickness (or intensity) per pixel. Data Structures: Mesh Cell: Defined by 8 vertices. Each vertex v has an associated extinction coefficient Kv and a precomputed thickness tv. P-buffer: A floating-point off-screen buffer (texture) storing the accumulated attenuation \tau{acc} for each pixel. Initialized to zero. Projection Geometry: For each hexahedron, a set of triangle fans or strips is generated based on the projection of its faces. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Software): For each hexahedral cell, compute the thickness tv for each vertex v using the cell's geometry. Compute the vertex attenuation av = Kv \cdot tv. Determine if the hexahedron can be projected directly. A hexahedron is valid for direct projection if: It is non-degenerate (no coinciding vertices). The projection of each of its 6 faces is a convex quadrilateral. If valid, generate triangle fans or strips for the hexahedron using the method of Max [12]. If invalid (degenerate or non-convex face projections), subdivide the hexahedron into 5 tetrahedra. Note: If these tetrahedra share non-planar faces with adjacent non-subdivided cells, gaps or overlaps may occur, introducing small errors. 2. Rendering Passes (Hardware): Initialize the P-buffer texture with zero attenuation. Group cells into batches of non-overlapping cells to minimize P-buffer to texture copies. For each batch: 1. Render the triangles (fans/strips) of the cells in the batch. 2. Fragment Program: For each fragment covered by a triangle: Interpolate the vertex attenuations av from the triangle's vertices to get the local attenuation \tau{cell} for the fragment. Read the current accumulated attenuation \tau{acc} from the P-buffer texture at the fragment's screen position. Compute the new accumulated attenuation: \tau{new} = \tau{acc} + \tau{cell}. Write \tau{new} to the P-buffer. 3. After rendering the batch, copy the P-buffer contents to the input texture for the next batch. This copy is necessary because writes to output buffers are not guaranteed to be in polygon order, and texture caching does not account for on-the-fly texture changes. 3. Final Compositing (Software or Hardware): After all cells are processed, the P-buffer contains the total optical thickness \tau{total} for each pixel. Compute the final intensity I for each pixel using the absorption-only recurrence: I = I0 \exp(-\tau{total}) where I0 is the incident X-ray intensity. Alternatively, if multiple wavelength bands are used, accumulate them in parallel in the RGBA channels of the P-buffer and compute the final intensity for each band separately. Formulas: Vertex Attenuation: av = Kv \cdot tv. Accumulation: \tau{new} = \tau{acc} + \tau{cell}. Final Intensity: I = I0 \exp(-\tau{total}). Recurrence (Conceptual): IV[i+1] = e^{-\tau[i]} IV[i]. Parameters: Floating Point Precision: 32-bit floating point is required for the P-buffer to maintain accuracy in attenuation computation. Parallelism: Up to 4 wavelength bands can be accumulated in parallel using the RGBA channels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Hexahedra: Must be subdivided into tetrahedra. Non-Convex Face Projections: Must be subdivided into tetrahedra. Non-Planar Faces: Subdividing a hexahedron into tetrahedra may create non-planar faces with adjacent non-subdivided cells, leading to gaps or overlaps in viewing ray segments and small errors in total absorption. Texture Copy Overhead: Copying the P-buffer to a texture after every cell is slow; batching non-overlapping cells is necessary for performance. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of cells, assuming constant-time projection and fragment processing. The number of texture copies depends on the batching strategy. Memory Complexity: O(R) where R is the number of pixels in the image, for the P-buffer. Strengths: No global sort required; supports curvilinear hexahedral meshes directly; parallel accumulation of multiple wavelength bands. Limitations: Limited to absorption-only regime (J=0); potential errors from subdivision of degenerate/non-convex cells; texture copy overhead. When to Use: Industrial and medical X-ray simulation where emissivity is negligible and hexahedral meshes are used. When Not to Use: When emissivity is significant; when tetrahedral meshes are used and hexahedral projection is not applicable; when high precision is required and subdivision errors are unacceptable. This method was developed for industrial and medical settings where X-ray self-emission is negligible. It builds on the polyhedron projection method and uses the method of Max [12] for hexahedral projection and Shirley and Tuchman [16] for tetrahedral projection. The technique addresses the need for floating-point accuracy in attenuation computation, which is not supported by standard framebuffer compositing operations. name: Sorting-free Projected Tetrahedra
head: Stochastic Projected Tetrahedral
body: Sorting-free Projected Tetrahedra (SPT) is a volume rendering technique for irregular tetrahedral datasets that approximates back-to-front accumulation using stochastic color composition, thereby eliminating the need for explicit visibility sorting. Unlike its sibling Projected Tetrahedra, which requires sorting tetrahedra before rendering, SPT controls particle rendering via opacity as a probability in the rasterization process, avoiding the sorting artifacts inherent in k-buffer methods like Hardware-Assisted Projection (HAVS). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tetrahedral mesh (irregular volume data), a transfer function, and a repetition level N (or Lr). Output: A rendered image where brightness is the ensemble average of N stochastic passes. Data Structures: 1. Pre-integration Lookup Table: A 3D texture mapping three integration parameters to pre-integrated color C and opacity \alpha. Fields: Scalar value at the front (sf), scalar value at the back (sb), and segment length (d). Mapping: C = C(sf, sb, d) and \alpha = \alpha(sf, sb, d). Note: The pre-integrated color is opacity-weighted (divided by the corresponding opacity). 2. Geometry Shader Outputs: For each split triangle, the "thickest" vertex passes: Front scalar (sf) Back scalar (sb) Distance value (d) Algorithm Steps: 1. Classification and Decomposition (Geometry Shader): Input: A single tetrahedron (4 vertices). Classify the tetrahedron into 4 classes of projection patterns based on its intersection with the view frustum/image plane. Decompose the tetrahedron into triangles. Emit one or two triangle strips (triangle fans are not supported by geometry shaders). Calculate parameters (sf, sb, d) for vertices on each triangle. Pass these through the "thickest" vertex of the split triangle. 2. Stochastic Color Composition (Fragment Shader) - Repeated N times: For each fragment generated by the rasterized triangles: Look up the pre-integrated transfer function in the 3D texture using the interpolated (sf, sb, d) to obtain color C and opacity \alpha. Stochastic Discard: Generate a random number r \in [0, 1]. If r > \alpha, discard the fragment. Otherwise, proceed. Brightness Assignment: If the fragment is not discarded, it represents a particle. The luminosity of the particle nearest to the viewpoint is assigned to the brightness value for this pass. Note: In the basic SPT algorithm, particle depth is determined as that of a pre-defined location (front, back, or middle point on the ray segment). 3. Accumulation: Repeat Steps 1-2 for N independent ensembles (repetitions). Calculate the average of the brightness values from all N repetitions to obtain the final pixel color. Formulas: Probability of Brightness: The probability that the k-th luminosity equals the brightness is defined as the event where there is no particle from the first to the (k-1)-th ray-segments and more than one particle in the k-th ray segment. Particle Distribution: The number of particles follows a Poisson distribution along the viewing ray segment intersecting the tetrahedral cell. The particle spacing follows an exponential distribution. Variance of Total Brightness: Since variances are identical and covariance is zero (independent occurrences): Var(B{total}) = \frac{Var(B^{(i)})}{N} where B^{(i)} is the brightness value of the i-th ensemble. Deviation: \sigma{total} = \sqrt{\frac{Var(B^{(i)})}{N}} Complexity: The computational complexity of the standard stochastic approach is O(n^2), but SPT's complexity is proportional to the repetition level N and the number of cells. Parameters: Repetition Level (N or Lr): The number of times Steps 1-2 are repeated. Controls the level of detail and noise. Larger deviation allows smaller N. Typical values tested: 1, 25, 100, 144. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Triangle Fans: Geometry shaders do not support triangle fans. Workaround: Emit one or two triangle strips instead. Multiple Volumes: The basic SPT algorithm causes prominent artifacts when treating multiple volumes because it controls particles stochastically in the image plane but not in the depth direction. Sorting Errors: Unlike HAVS, SPT avoids rendering artifacts caused by visibility sorting errors. A technique applied to multiple volumes to resolve the depth-direction artifact of the SPT algorithm by accurately determining particle positions along the ray. It constructs a cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the particle spacing and develops a technique for calculating the nearest particle along the interval using the CDF. Time Complexity: Proportional to the repetition level N and the number of cells. Memory Complexity: Depends on VRAM. On an NVIDIA GeForce 9600GT (512MB VRAM), it supports up to ~24.5 million tetrahedral cells at 1024x1024 resolution. Performance: Computing time: ~1.4 seconds per repetition for 24.5 million cells at 1024x1024. Construction time: ~100 milliseconds to construct the 3D texture for pre-integrated classification. Generation time: ~17.4 seconds to generate particles (if using particle-based comparison models like PBVR). Strengths: No visibility sorting required, avoiding k-buffer artifacts. No extra buffer space for candidate fragments. Can visualize continuous iso-surfaces of precipitous transfer functions better than PBVR. Suitable for high-resolution displays (e.g., tiled-display walls). Limitations: Noise decreases with N, requiring higher N for high quality, which increases compute time. Basic SPT has artifacts with multiple volumes. Construction/generation times are significant when transfer functions change or for time-varying datasets. When to Use: When the number of tetrahedral cells is smaller than 24.5 million and particle count is larger than 24 million, or when sorting artifacts are unacceptable. When Not to Use: For datasets with >24.5 million cells (PBVR is preferred) or when real-time performance is critical and high N is required. Sorting-free Projected Tetrahedra was introduced as a sorting-free volume rendering technique for irregular tetrahedral datasets. It builds on the concept of Projected Tetrahedra but replaces the sorting step with stochastic color composition. The method was developed to overcome drawbacks of visibility sorting (like in HAVS) and particle-based methods (like PBVR). It was tested on datasets with up to 1.25 million cells and later scaled to 24.5 million cells. A later extension addressed the multiple volume artifact by introducing nearest particle calculation techniques. name: GPU-based Projected Tetrahedra
head: Two-Shader PT, Vertex Shader PT, Tetrahedral Projection using Vertex Shaders
body: GPU-based Projected Tetrahedra is a method for interactive volume rendering of unstructured tetrahedral data that shifts the geometric classification and decomposition of cells from the CPU to the GPU using programmable vertex shaders. It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional Projected Tetrahedra (PT) by avoiding redundant projections and pre-processing, allowing for the rendering of large datasets at interactive rates. It differs from standard PT by executing the classification logic within the vertex shader program rather than on the CPU, and from ray-casting approaches by occupying a substantially smaller memory footprint while achieving competitive frame rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unstructured tetrahedral mesh data (vertices and connectivity). Output: A composited image in the framebuffer. Data Structures: Basis Graph: A fixed topology used for all tetrahedra. It consists of four vertices representing the cell's corners and one additional "phantom" vertex. Triangle Fan: The primitive type sent to the GPU, comprising the four vertices and the phantom vertex. Texture Memory: Used to store the model data to avoid redundant projections and improve access speed. Algorithm Steps: 1. Data Upload: Store the tetrahedral model in GPU texture memory. 2. Primitive Submission: Send the four vertices of a tetrahedron and an invalid/placeholder phantom vertex to the GPU as a triangle fan. 3. Vertex Shader Classification: A vertex program performs geometric tests on the input vertices to determine the classification of the cell relative to the view direction. 4. Basis Graph Mapping: Based on the classification, map the four vertices to the basis graph topology. 5. Phantom Vertex Calculation: Calculate the position of the phantom vertex based on the classification results. 6. Thickness Interpolation: Determine the thickness of the cell at the phantom vertex by linearly interpolating the values (e.g., density or scalar field) at the four vertices. 7. Attribute Assignment: Assign color and opacity to the phantom vertex using a lookup table indexed by the calculated thickness. 8. Rasterization and Compositing: Rasterize the modified faces (triangles formed by the basis graph) and composite them into the framebuffer using hardware blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(positions, scalars): """ positions: array of 4 vec3, the vertices of the tetrahedron scalars: array of 4 float, the scalar values at the vertices Returns: modified positions and scalars for the 5 vertices (4 corners + 1 phantom) """ # 1. Perform geometric tests to classify the tetrahedron # This determines the projection order and which faces are visible classification = classifytetrahedron(positions) # 2. Map vertices to the fixed basis graph topology # The basis graph always has 5 vertices: 4 real, 1 phantom mappedpositions = maptobasisgraph(positions, classification) # 3. Calculate the phantom vertex position # The position depends on the classification (e.g., centroid, projection center) phantompos = calculatephantomvertex(mappedpositions, classification) # 4. Determine thickness at the phantom vertex # Linear interpolation of scalar values at the 4 corners thickness = interpolatethickness(scalars, classification) # 5. Assign color and opacity based on thickness # Uses a pre-defined lookup table (transfer function) color, opacity = lookupcoloropacity(thickness) # 6. Return the 5 vertices with updated attributes # The first 4 are the mapped corners, the 5th is the phantom finalpositions = append(mappedpositions, phantompos) finalscalars = append(scalars, thickness) # Or just pass thickness to fragment shader return finalpositions, finalscalars, color, opacity def fragmentshader(positions, scalars, color, opacity): """ Renders the triangles formed by the basis graph. """ # Standard rasterization and blending # The opacity and color are interpolated across the triangle faces return blendintoframebuffer(color, opacity) Parameters: Lookup Table: Maps thickness (scalar value) to color and opacity. Size depends on the transfer function resolution. Basis Graph Topology: Fixed for all cells. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Constraints: Current GPUs cannot change the topology of graphics primitives dynamically. Therefore, the most general topology (the basis graph with 5 vertices) must always be sent, even if the classification results in a simpler geometry. Data Independence: No data can be saved across vertex primitives. Each primitive must be sent with all relevant data structures, as the GPU does not maintain state between independent draw calls for different tetrahedra. Precision: Linear interpolation of thickness may introduce approximation errors in regions of high gradient. This method extends GPU-based Projected Tetrahedra by pre-computing volume rendering integrals into texture maps, enabling hardware-accelerated compositing of semi-transparent triangles [1996-cell-projection-with-3d-2d-textures.md]. It solves the limitation of standard projected tetrahedra by supporting arbitrary transfer functions via pre-integration, at the cost of increased memory usage for 3D textures or approximation errors for 2D textures. It differs from Sorted Rasterization of Projected Tetrahedra by relying on texture-based integral approximation rather than explicit sorting of all triangles, and from On-the-fly Shell Geometry Construction by using pre-computed textures instead of dynamic geometry generation. Sorted Rasterization of Projected Tetrahedra is a GPU-based direct volume rendering (DVR) method for unstructured tetrahedral data that achieves interactive rates by treating each tetrahedron as a distinct primitive and rasterizing them using hardware operations. It differs from traditional ray casting by leveraging hardware rasterization and blending to compute pixel color, avoiding explicit per-pixel ray-tetrahedron intersection tests. On-the-fly shell geometry construction is a method for generating shell geometry (tetrahedrons or prisms) dynamically on the GPU during runtime, enabling shell mapping techniques to be applied to animated surfaces rather than requiring static, offline CPU preprocessing. It differs from traditional shell mapping by eliminating data-dependent preprocessing steps; instead, it uses a deterministic, data-independent rule based on vertex indices to ensure consistency between adjacent prisms, allowing for full parallelization in compute shaders. This variant optimizes the GPU-based PT method by maintaining a buffer holding the four vertices of the current tetrahedron and the additional fifth vertex sometimes created by the algorithm. It swaps the vertices in the buffer as necessary to follow the direction of the strip and caches edge lengths and face areas computed for the current tetrahedron, as these are required by the PT algorithm and are reused by the next tetrahedron in a strip. A pitfall is that computing edge lengths and face areas requires a square root, which impacts running time and complexity. A hybrid approach for tetrahedral meshes that projects the complete mesh onto the screen to simplify the problem from 3D to 2D, using precomputed adjacency information for correct accumulation order. The step involves projecting the complete mesh onto the screen. A method for projecting cells onto the detector, specifically used to simulate the initial set of radiation leaving the hohlraum. It subdivides collapsed cells (single point) and cells with coinciding vertices or nonconvex quadrilateral faces into tetrahedra, and projects remaining hexahedra using the method of Max. Performance: Capable of rendering over 2.0 million tetrahedra per second (Tet/s) on current graphics hardware. Memory Footprint: Occupies a substantially smaller memory footprint compared to ray-casting approaches. Pre-processing: Requires no pre-processing of the data and no additional data structures. Scalability: Allows interactive viewing of large unstructured datasets on a desktop personal computer. Strengths: High performance, low memory usage, no pre-processing required, leverages hardware acceleration. Limitations: Requires sending the most general topology (basis graph) for all cells, which may involve redundant computation for simple cases; no data persistence across primitives limits optimization strategies that rely on inter-primitive state. The method was introduced by Wylie et al. in 2002 as an extension of the Projected Tetrahedra (PT) algorithm. It was designed to leverage the programmable vertex shaders available on commodity graphics cards to perform classification and decomposition of volume cells on the GPU. This shifted the processing burden from the CPU to the GPU, enabling interactive visualization of unstructured data sets. The approach is based on the PT algorithm by Shirley and Tuchman. name: Cell Projection with 3D/2D Textures
head: Röttger et al. Cell Projection with 3D/2D Textures
body: This method extends GPU-based Projected Tetrahedra by pre-computing volume rendering integrals into texture maps, enabling hardware-accelerated compositing of semi-transparent triangles. It solves the limitation of standard projected tetrahedra by supporting arbitrary transfer functions via pre-integration, at the cost of increased memory usage for 3D textures or approximation errors for 2D textures. It differs from Sorted Rasterization of Projected Tetrahedra by relying on texture-based integral approximation rather than explicit sorting of all triangles, and from On-the-fly Shell Geometry Construction by using pre-computed textures instead of dynamic geometry generation. Inputs: A volume dataset, a transfer function, and a viewing direction. Outputs: A rendered image. Data Structures: 1. 3D Texture Map (Optional/Original): Stores pre-integrated color and opacity. Dimensions correspond to cell entry values, exit values, and distance through the cell. 2. 2D Texture Map 1 (Approximation): Stores dependencies of the volume rendering integral with respect to the length between two sample points, approximated in linear terms. 3. 2D Texture Map 2 (Residual): Stores remaining parts of the integral that depend only on sample values. 4. Projected Tetrahedra Geometry: Each tetrahedron is decomposed into triangles. Vertices are assigned all associated triangles. Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Compute the volume rendering integral for each cell. If using 3D textures: Store color and opacity directly in a 3D texture map. If using 2D textures: Approximate dependencies on sample point distance linearly and store in the first 2D texture map. Store remaining sample-value-dependent integral parts in the second 2D texture map. 2. Decomposition: Decompose each volume cell into tetrahedra, then into triangles. 3. Projection: Project the tetrahedra onto the screen. 4. Triangle Assignment: Assign all associated triangles to each vertex of each projected tetrahedron. 5. Rendering: Compute opacity and color at the thickest point for each tetrahedron. Perform linear interpolation between the triangle faces pierced by the ray. Blend the triangles into the frame-buffer using back-to-front compositing (Painter's Algorithm). Parameters: Texture resolution: Not given in the sources. Transfer function: Arbitrary (if 3D texture) or Linear (if 2D texture approximation is used without pre-integration extensions). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: 3D textures are memory-consuming. Transfer Function Limitations: The 2D texture approximation method can only handle linear transfer functions without artifacts. Approximation Error: Linear approximation of integral dependencies may introduce errors for non-linear volume properties. Sorts the cells before they are split into tetrahedra to ensure correct depth ordering. Utilizes 2D texture mapping hardware to accelerate opacity interpolation and provide correct per-pixel opacity values. This method can only handle linear transfer functions without artifacts. Time Complexity: Pre-processing is required to compute texture maps. Rendering time is reduced to texture lookups and compositing. Memory Complexity: High for 3D texture approach; moderate for 2D texture approach. Measured Performance: Interactive rendering times were achieved on an SGI Octane MXE with up to 5 fps. Strengths: Supports arbitrary transfer functions (with 3D textures); leverages hardware texture interpolation. Limitations: High memory consumption for 3D textures; 2D approximation limited to linear transfer functions; requires pre-processing. When to use: When arbitrary transfer functions are needed and memory is sufficient, or when linear transfer functions are acceptable and memory is constrained. When not to use: When memory is extremely limited and linear transfer functions are insufficient, or when dynamic transfer functions are required without pre-computation. Originated with Röttger et al. [Röttger00], who introduced pre-integrated volume rendering for projected tetrahedra. The method was extended by Guthe et al. [Guthe02] to add hardware-accelerated pre-integration [Engel01]. It builds on earlier parallel cell projection work by Lucas [Lucas92] and Stein et al. [243]. name: Sorted Rasterization of Projected Tetrahedra
head: GPU DVR for unstructured data via sorted PT, Radiance Mesh Rendering via Hardware Rasterization, Tet-by-Tet Ray Casting
body: Sorted Rasterization of Projected Tetrahedra is a GPU-based direct volume rendering (DVR) method for unstructured tetrahedral data that achieves interactive rates by treating each tetrahedron as a distinct primitive and rasterizing them using hardware operations. It differs from traditional ray casting by leveraging hardware rasterization and blending to compute pixel color, avoiding explicit per-pixel ray-tetrahedron intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tetrahedral mesh where each tetrahedron k has constant density \sigmak and color fields \mathbf{c}k(\mathbf{r}) defined at any point \mathbf{r} within it. The camera position (origin) is required for sorting. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color C and opacity \alpha based on the compositing order. Data Structures: Tetrahedron Attributes: For each tetrahedron k, store: Vertices: 4 vertices defining the geometry. Density: Scalar \sigmak. Color Fields: Functions or values defining \mathbf{c}k^{\text{in}} and \mathbf{c}k^{\text{out}} at entry and exit points. Circumsphere Power: A scalar value used for sorting relative to the camera origin. Sorted List: Tetrahedra sorted by their circumsphere power relative to the camera, loaded from back to front. Numbered Steps: 1. Sorting: Sort all tetrahedra based on the power of their circumspheres relative to the camera origin to establish a back-to-front order. 2. Rendering Setup: Without Mesh Shaders: Use instanced shaders. Draw an instance of a triangle strip for each tetrahedron. The vertex shader uses the instance index to load tetrahedron attributes and plane equations. Each tetrahedron is loaded 4 times, once per vertex. With Mesh Shaders: Replace vertex shaders with mesh shaders. An entire thread block collaboratively generates mesh data passed directly to the hardware rasterizer. Use warp shuffle operations to share data loaded within each tetrahedron, loading each tetrahedron only once. 3. Vertex Processing: For each tetrahedron, emit 4 vertices with tetrahedron data attached to each to the interpolation registers. 4. Fragment Shader Execution: For each pixel hit by a tetrahedron, read back the whole tetrahedron data attached to the triangle hit to reconstruct the back intersection. Compute the entry point tk^{\text{in}} and exit point tk^{\text{out}} along the ray \mathbf{r} for the tetrahedron. Calculate the optical depth dk and opacity \alphak: dk = (tk^{\text{out}} - tk^{\text{in}}) \sigmak \alphak = 1 - e^{-dk} Evaluate the color at the entry and exit points: \mathbf{c}k^{\text{in}} = \mathbf{c}k(\mathbf{r}(tk^{\text{in}})) \mathbf{c}k^{\text{out}} = \mathbf{c}k(\mathbf{r}(tk^{\text{out}})) Compute the color change \Delta \mathbf{C}k using the closed-form solution: \Delta \mathbf{C}k = \left(1 - \frac{\alphak}{dk}\right) \mathbf{c}k^{\text{in}} + \left(\frac{\alphak}{dk} - e^{-dk}\right) \mathbf{c}k^{\text{out}} 5. Compositing: Blend the pre-sorted tetrahedra along the ray. The final pixel color is: C = \sumk wk \Delta Ck where the weight wk = \prod{l=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha\ell) is efficiently computed using hardware blending operations. The compositor composites the fragment according to the back-to-front load order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computedeltaC(alphak, dk, cin, cout): """Computes the color change for a tetrahedron.""" if dk < 1e-6: # Limit as dk -> 0 yields deltaC -> 0 return np.zeroslike(cin) alphaoverd = alphak / dk return (1.0 - alphaoverd) cin + (alphaoverd - math.exp(-dk)) cout def sortedrasterizationpipeline(sortedtets, rayorigin, raydir): """ Algorithmic representation of the GPU rasterization and compositing steps. Hardware rasterization handles triangle setup and interpolation. Hardware blending computes the weight product wk. """ accumulatedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 weight = 1.0 # wk = product of (1 - alpha) for previous tets for tet in sortedtets: # Hardware rasterization finds intersection interval [tin, tout] tin, tout = tet.rayintersect(rayorigin, raydir) if tin is None: continue sigma = tet.density dk = (tout - tin) sigma alphak = 1.0 - math.exp(-dk) if alphak < 1e-6: continue cin = tet.colorfield(rayorigin + raydir tin) cout = tet.colorfield(rayorigin + raydir tout) deltaC = computedeltaC(alphak, dk, cin, cout) # Hardware blending computes: accumulatedcolor += weight deltaC # and updates weight = (1 - alphak) accumulatedcolor += weight deltaC weight = (1.0 - alphak) accumulatedopacity += weight alphak if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity Parameters: Density (\sigmak): Constant for each tetrahedron. Color Fields (\mathbf{c}k): Defined by the dataset. Sorting Criterion: Power of circumsphere relative to camera origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: When dk approaches zero, the ratio \frac{\alphak}{dk} approaches 1. The limit yields \Delta \mathbf{C}k \to \mathbf{0}, which is handled by a threshold check. Precision: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Tetrahedra: Not given in the sources. A specific implementation of sorted rasterization of projected tetrahedra that treats each tetrahedron as a distinct primitive and outputs individually wound tetrahedra. A rendering technique used when mesh shaders are not available, drawing an instance of a triangle strip for each tetrahedron. A modern GPU feature that allows collaborative generation of mesh data, reducing redundant data loads. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves interactive rates on commodity GPUs. Mesh shaders provide the fastest rendering approach by reducing redundant data loads. Strengths: Leverages hardware rasterization and blending, avoiding explicit ray casting per pixel. Efficient for unstructured data. Limitations: Requires sorting of tetrahedra. When to Use: Interactive volume rendering of unstructured tetrahedral data on modern GPUs. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method is part of the broader field of GPU-based direct volume rendering for unstructured data. It builds on the concept of projected tetrahedra and optimizes it for hardware rasterization. The specific implementation using mesh shaders and warp shuffle operations is described in. name: On-the-fly Shell Geometry Construction
head: GPU shell construction, Parallel prism construction, Real-time shell geometry construction
body: On-the-fly shell geometry construction is a method for generating shell geometry (tetrahedrons or prisms) dynamically on the GPU during runtime, enabling shell mapping techniques to be applied to animated surfaces rather than requiring static, offline CPU preprocessing. It differs from traditional shell mapping by eliminating data-dependent preprocessing steps; instead, it uses a deterministic, data-independent rule based on vertex indices to ensure consistency between adjacent prisms, allowing for full parallelization in compute shaders. The method constructs shell geometry in two distinct stages to optimize memory and time consumption, ensuring that the resulting geometry is consistent across adjacent faces without requiring random assignment or correction of edge patterns. Input: A base mesh S defined by vertices V, vertex normals N, and face connectivity (triangles). Output: Three buffers: 1. Vertex Data Buffer: Contains vertices for the transformed base mesh and the offset surface. 2. Shell Data Buffer: Contains the constructed tetrahedrons/prisms with intersection data. 3. Index Buffer: Maps indices from the Shell Data Buffer to the Vertex Data Buffer for vertex shader access. The implementation relies on three specific buffers: 1. Vertex Data Buffer: Stores the positions of the transformed base mesh vertices (St) and the offset surface vertices (S't). 2. Shell Data Buffer: Stores the geometric data for each tetrahedron or prism, including the calculated intersections with tetrahedron planes required for ray tracing. 3. Index Buffer: Stores integer indices pointing to entries in the Vertex Data Buffer. Each entry in the Shell Data Buffer references these indices to retrieve the correct vertex positions during rendering. The construction is performed per face of the base mesh in parallel. Step 1: Vertex Transformation 1. Transform the base mesh S into St using standard vertex shader transformations (model-view-projection). 2. Construct an offset surface S't by shifting each vertex of St along its vertex normal N by a predefined distance d. 3. Store all resulting vertices (St and S't) into the Vertex Data Buffer. Step 2: Shell Construction 1. For each face of the base mesh, construct the shell tetrahedrons or prisms. 2. Determine the direction of the splitting edge for each prism side to preserve consistency between adjacent prisms. This is done using the Edge Direction Rule: An edge is defined as 'rising' if it goes from a base mesh vertex with a lower index to a vertex with a higher index, and 'falling' otherwise. 3. Use the determined edge directions to split the prism sides consistently. 4. Calculate intersections with tetrahedron planes, which are required for further ray tracing during rendering. 5. Store the resulting shell geometry data into the Shell Data Buffer. 6. Populate the Index Buffer with indices linking the Shell Data Buffer entries to the corresponding vertices in the Vertex Data Buffer. The following pseudocode illustrates the parallel construction process per face. It assumes a compute shader environment where each work group or thread handles one or more faces. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. OFFSETDISTANCE = 0.01 # Predefined distance for offset surface def constructshellgeometry(basemesh): # Stage 1: Vertex Transformation # Parallelized over all vertices transformedvertices = [] offsetvertices = [] for vertex in basemesh.vertices: # Transform base vertex (e.g., model-view-projection) stpos = transformvertex(vertex.position) # Calculate offset vertex # Shift along vertex normal by predefined distance stnormal = transformnormal(vertex.normal) stnormal = normalize(stnormal) sprimetpos = stpos + (stnormal OFFSETDISTANCE) transformedvertices.append(stpos) offsetvertices.append(sprimetpos) # Store in Vertex Data Buffer vertexdatabuffer = list(transformedvertices + offsetvertices) # Stage 2: Shell Construction # Parallelized over all faces shelldata = [] indexdata = [] for face in basemesh.faces: v0, v1, v2 = face.vertices idx0, idx1, idx2 = face.vertexindices # Get transformed positions for base vertices p0 = transformedvertices[idx0] p1 = transformedvertices[idx1] p2 = transformedvertices[idx2] # Get offset positions for base vertices o0 = offsetvertices[idx0] o1 = offsetvertices[idx1] o2 = offsetvertices[idx2] # Determine edge directions for consistency # Edge is 'rising' if index goes from lower to higher # Edge is 'falling' if index goes from higher to lower # Example: Constructing a prism/tetrahedron structure # The specific geometric decomposition depends on the shell mapping variant, # but the splitting edge direction is determined by the index rule. # Determine direction of edge (v0, v1) if idx0 < idx1: edge01direction = 'rising' else: edge01direction = 'falling' # Determine direction of edge (v1, v2) if idx1 < idx2: edge12direction = 'rising' else: edge12direction = 'falling' # Determine direction of edge (v2, v0) if idx2 < idx0: edge20direction = 'rising' else: edge20direction = 'falling' # Construct tetrahedrons/prisms based on these directions # This ensures adjacent prisms share consistent splitting edges # The exact geometric construction of the tetrahedrons from these vertices # and directions follows the standard shell mapping decomposition, # adapted to use the determined edge directions. # Construct shell geometry data (positions, normals, intersections) # Intersections with tetrahedron planes are calculated here shellentry = constructtetrahedron(p0, p1, p2, o0, o1, o2, edge01direction, edge12direction, edge20direction) shelldata.append(shellentry) # Create index mapping # Indices into vertexdatabuffer for the vertices of this shell entry # The exact indices depend on the layout of vertexdatabuffer # Assuming transformed vertices are first, then offset vertices baseindices = [idx0, idx1, idx2] offsetindices = [idx0 + len(basemesh.vertices), idx1 + len(basemesh.vertices), idx2 + len(basemesh.vertices)] # Store indices for this shell entry indexdata.append(baseindices + offsetindices) # Store results shelldatabuffer = list(shelldata) indexbuffer = list(indexdata) return vertexdatabuffer, shelldatabuffer, indexbuffer def constructtetrahedron(p0, p1, p2, o0, o1, o2, dir01, dir12, dir20): """ Constructs the shell geometry (tetrahedrons/prisms) for a face. The specific decomposition depends on the shell mapping algorithm, but uses the edge directions to ensure consistency. """ # The exact geometric decomposition of the tetrahedrons/prisms from the six vertices # and edge directions follows standard shell mapping. # This part is implementation-specific to the shell mapping variant. # The key is that the splitting edge is determined by the index rule. return { 'base': [p0, p1, p2], 'offset': [o0, o1, o2], 'edgedirections': [dir01, dir12, dir20] } def transformvertex(v): # Applies standard model-view-projection transformation as in a vertex shader return v def transformnormal(n): # Applies inverse-transpose normal transformation as in a vertex shader return n Offset Distance (d): The predefined distance by which vertices are shifted along their normals to create the offset surface S't. The value is not specified in the sources. Number of Depth Peeling Passes: Empirically, 3-4 passes are enough to produce good quality results for order-independent transparency. Animated Surfaces: The method is specifically designed to handle animated surfaces, avoiding the static limitation of offline preprocessing. Consistency: The edge direction rule guarantees consistency between adjacent prisms, preventing gaps or overlaps that could occur with random edge pattern assignment. Rasterization Overhead: All tetrahedrons must be rasterized each pass, even with culling. The vertex processing and rasterization work occur before the z-test, which can be a performance bottleneck. Mip-map Construction: Simple mip-map construction with linear downscaling does not produce correct results for 3D textures, especially at very low scales. Time Complexity: The method is data-independent and parallelizable, allowing tetrahedrons to be constructed in parallel for each face of the base mesh. The process is split into two stages to optimize time consumption. Memory Complexity: The method uses three buffers (Vertex Data, Shell Data, Index Buffer) to store the geometry and connectivity. This structure is designed to reduce memory usage compared to storing full geometry data redundantly. Performance: The method was tested on multiple scenes against shell mapping techniques, showing applicability for real-time rendering. Performance gains are expected with advanced lighting calculations due to reduced overdraw. Strengths: Enables real-time rendering of animated surfaces with small-scale volumetric structures. Data-independent and parallelizable, suitable for GPU compute shaders. Ensures consistency between adjacent prisms without complex preprocessing. Limitations: Requires rasterization of all tetrahedrons each pass, which can be inefficient. Simple mip-map construction is not suitable for 3D textures in this context. May benefit from hardware ray tracing in the future, as current rasterization-based approach has overhead. When to Use: Suitable for real-time rendering of animated surfaces with small-scale volumetric features (e.g., knitwear, fur, grass, forests) where offline preprocessing is not feasible. When Not to Use: Not suitable for static surfaces where offline preprocessing is acceptable and may offer better optimization opportunities. Also, simple mip-map techniques are not appropriate for 3D textures in this context. The method was introduced in the paper "Real-time Rendering of Small-scale Volumetric Structure on Animated Surfaces" (2021). It addresses the limitation of previous shell mapping techniques, which required offline CPU preprocessing and static surfaces. Previous methods assigned edge patterns randomly and corrected inconsistencies, making the process data-dependent and non-parallelizable. This method simplifies the prism pattern defining process by using vertex indices to determine edge directions, enabling on-the-fly construction on the GPU. It is part of the broader field of real-time rendering, shell mapping, and levels of detail.
