name: Texture-Encoded Isosurfacing
head: Modified HAVS for isosurfaces, Texture-Encoded Isosurface Extraction
body: Texture-Encoded Isosurfacing is a GPU-based technique for extracting isosurfaces from unstructured tetrahedral grids by using 2D texturing hardware to compute intersections. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Projected Tetrahedra by using the decomposition step of the PT algorithm to create smaller tetrahedra instead of triangles, then projecting their front and back faces to leverage a checkerboard texture for intersection computation. Inputs: Unstructured tetrahedral grid, scalar field values at vertices, and an isosurface threshold T. Outputs: Rasterized image containing the isosurface. Data Structures: A 2D checkerboard texture initialized with a checkerboard pattern; for smooth or multiple isosurfaces, it stores shading values and requires further partitioning of the texture domain. A stencil buffer for visibility management. Parameters: Isosurface threshold T. Texture resolution is not specified in the sources. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Decomposition: Apply the decomposition step of the PT algorithm to divide tetrahedra into smaller tetrahedra instead of triangles. 2. Projection: Project the front and back faces of each smaller tetrahedron onto screen space, resulting in either a degenerate triangle or the same triangle. 3. Texture Encoding: Associate a checkerboard 2D texture with the projected triangles; the coincidence of the front and back face projections allows intersection computation to proceed using 2D texturing hardware. 4. Sampling: Extract the isosurface by sampling the 2D texture with texture coordinates corresponding to the front and back face scalar values. 5. Compositing: Use the stencil buffer and XOR operations to handle visibility and resolve overlaps in two passes, where the first pass sets the stencil buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def textureencodedisosurfacing(tetrahedra, scalarfield, threshold, mvpmatrix, checkerboardtexture, screenwidth, screenheight): # Initialize buffers stencilbuffer = [0] (screenwidth screenheight) colorbuffer = [0] (screenwidth screenheight) # Pass 1: Set stencil buffer using XOR operations for tet in tetrahedra: # Decompose tetrahedron into smaller tetrahedra using PT decomposition step # [Comment: The sources do not specify the exact geometric decomposition formula.] smallertets = decomposetetrahedron(tet) for smalltet in smallertets: v0, v1, v2, v3 = smalltet.vertices # Project front and back faces to screen space frontproj = projecttoscreen([v0, v1, v2], mvpmatrix) backproj = projecttoscreen([v0, v2, v3], mvpmatrix) # Render faces with stencil XOR to handle visibility rasterizetriangle(frontproj, stencilop='xor') rasterizetriangle(backproj, stencilop='xor') # Pass 2: Extract isosurface using texture sampling for tet in tetrahedra: smallertets = decomposetetrahedron(tet) for smalltet in smallertets: v0, v1, v2, v3 = smalltet.vertices s0, s1, s2, s3 = scalarfield[v0], scalarfield[v1], scalarfield[v2], scalarfield[v3] # Compute texture coordinates from front and back face scalar values # [Comment: The sources do not specify the exact mapping formula from scalars to texture coordinates.] texcoords = computetexcoordsfromscalars(s0, s1, s2, s3, threshold) # Sample checkerboard texture to determine intersection samplevalue = sample2dtexture(checkerboardtexture, texcoords) # If sample indicates intersection, write to color buffer if samplevalue == INTERSECTIONMARKER: colorbuffer[pixel] = computecolor(s0, s1, s2, s3, threshold) return colorbuffer def decomposetetrahedron(tet): # [Comment: The sources do not specify the exact geometric decomposition formula.] return [tet] # Placeholder for actual PT decomposition logic def projecttoscreen(vertices, mvpmatrix): # Standard MVP transformation and perspective division projected = [] for v in vertices: clip = mvpmatrix @ v if clip.w != 0: projected.append((clip.xyz / clip.w)) return projected def rasterizetriangle(projvertices, stencilop): # Standard rasterization with stencil XOR update for pixel in trianglecoverage(projvertices): stencilbuffer[pixel] ^= 1 if stencilop == 'xor' else 0 def computetexcoordsfromscalars(s0, s1, s2, s3, threshold): # [Comment: The sources do not specify the exact mapping formula from scalars to texture coordinates.] return (s0 + s1 + s2 + s3) / 4.0 # Standard interpolation fallback def sample2dtexture(texture, texcoords): # Standard bilinear/trilinear texture lookup return texture[texcoords] def computecolor(s0, s1, s2, s3, threshold): # Standard Phong or flat shading computation return (s0 + s1 + s2 + s3) / 4.0 INTERSECTIONMARKER = 1 pixel = (0, 0) # Loop variable placeholder for rasterization context Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: The projection of front and back faces can result in degenerate triangles, which the GPU rasterizer must handle correctly. Precision: The accuracy of the isosurface extraction depends on the resolution of the checkerboard texture and the precision of the texture sampling. Multiple Isosurfaces: Handling multiple isosurfaces requires further partitioning of the texture domain and storing additional shading values, which increases complexity. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the checkerboard texture and the number of tetrahedra. Performance: The algorithm runs in two passes and renders an average of 5 to 7 triangles per tetrahedron. Strengths: Renders fewer faces per tetrahedron and leverages 2D texturing hardware for intersection computation. Limitations: Extensions for smooth shading and multiple isosurfaces require more complex texture setups and domain partitioning. When to use: Suitable for real-time isosurface extraction on unstructured grids where GPU acceleration is available. Texture-Encoded Isosurfacing is a revised version of the HAVS (Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering) algorithm adapted for isosurface extraction. It was proposed in reference [58] as an alternate solution to render fewer faces per tetrahedron by using the decomposition step of the PT algorithm to create smaller tetrahedra instead of triangles. The method is discussed in the survey "A Survey of GPU-Based Volume Rendering of Unstructured Grids". It represents one of the first solutions to map isosurface computation onto the GPU using programmable hardware, sharing the underlying framework with volume rendering visibility computations. name: Hardware-Assisted Projected Tetrahedra Rendering
head: Projected Tetrahedra with texture table, Shirley-Tuckman with texture mapping
body: Hardware-Assisted Projected Tetrahedra Rendering is a volume visualization technique for unstructured data that uses hardware-assisted texture mapping to perform interpolation between vertex colors and opacities, integrating color for use with a volume rendering system. It addresses artifacts, specifically Mach bands, caused by the linear interpolation of opacity in the original Shirley-Tuckman algorithm by employing a texture table for the exponential opacity function. It builds on Projected Tetrahedra by offloading the non-linear opacity integration to the graphics hardware's texture lookup units, allowing for efficient rendering of colored volumes that require back-to-front sorting. Inputs: A set of non-intersecting, convex tetrahedra with vertex attributes: 3D position, color (C), and extinction coefficient (\chi). A viewing direction and projection matrix. A pre-computed texture table mapping optical depth to transparency. Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel contains a composited color and opacity, rendered in back-to-front order. 1. Texture Table A 1D or 2D texture map used to store the transparency function 1 - \exp(-u), where u is the optical depth. 1D Table (Constant \chi): Dimensions: W \times 1 (width W is implementation-dependent, e.g., 256 or 512). Format: Single-channel floating-point or fixed-point. Content: At index i, value is 1 - \exp(-i \cdot \Delta u), where \Delta u is the step size corresponding to the maximum optical depth. 2D Table (Linearly Varying \chi): Dimensions: W \times H. Format: Single-channel. Content: At coordinates (\chi, l), value is 1 - \exp(-\chi l). This handles the quadratic variation of optical depth within a triangle when \chi varies linearly across the tetrahedron. 2. Triangle Vertex Attributes For each projected triangle, the following attributes are computed and passed to the rasterizer: Thin Vertices: Two vertices on the silhouette profile. Texture coordinate u = 0. Color C{thin}: Original vertex color. Thick Vertex: The vertex corresponding to the intersection of the viewing ray with the tetrahedron (the "thickest" point along the ray). Texture coordinate u = \chi{thick} \cdot l{thick}, where l{thick} is the length of the ray segment through the tetrahedron at this vertex. Color C{thick}: Computed using the Williams and Max analytic form (see below). 1. Sorting: Sort the tetrahedra in back-to-front order relative to the camera. The method described in uses an O(n^2) extension of the Newell, Newell, and Sancha sort for 3-D convex polyhedra. 2. Projection and Classification: Project each tetrahedron onto the screen. Classify the projection into one to four cases consisting of one to four triangles. Identify the "thick" vertex (where the viewing ray intersects the tetrahedron) and the "thin" vertices (on the profile). 3. Compute Thick Vertex Attributes: Calculate the length l of the ray segment through the tetrahedron at the thick vertex. Determine the extinction coefficient \chi{thick} at the thick vertex. Compute the texture coordinate u = \chi{thick} l. Compute the color C{thick} using the Williams and Max formula. 4. Rasterization: For each triangle, set the texture coordinate u to 0 at thin vertices and to u{thick} at the thick vertex. If \chi is constant, use the 1D texture table. The hardware interpolates u across the triangle. If \chi varies linearly, use the 2D texture table with coordinates \chi and l. Note that \chi l varies quadratically inside the triangle. If hardware supports quadratic interpolation of texture coordinates, use it; otherwise, the 2D table lookup approximates this. Interpolate the color C across the triangle using standard linear interpolation (Gouraud shading). 5. Compositing: For each pixel covered by a triangle, the hardware retrieves the transparency \alpha from the texture table using the interpolated u. Composite the new color C{new} over the existing pixel color C{old} using the equation: C{new} = \alpha C + (1 - \alpha) C{old} where \alpha is the interpolated opacity and C is the interpolated color. Total Opacity of a Segment: For a segment A0A1 with length l and extinction coefficients \chi0, \chi1 at endpoints: \alpha = 1 - \exp\left(-\frac{\chi0 + \chi1}{2} l\right) Transparency along a Scan Line: Let s be the fraction along the segment from the thick vertex. The transparency t1(x) is: t1(x) = 1 - (s \chi0 + (1-s)\exp(-\chi1 l)) And similarly for the other part: t2(x) = 1 - s \cdot \exp(-\chi1 l) Final Transparency (Error Term): The final transparency t(x) from compositing two triangles is: t(x) = t1(x)t2(x) = 1 - \exp(-\chi l) + s(1-s)(\exp(-\chi l))^2 The term s(1-s)(\exp(-\chi l))^2 represents the error due to linear approximation of the non-linear opacity. Color Integration (Williams and Max): The Shirley-Tuckman algorithm approximates the thick vertex color as (C0 + C1)/2. This method uses the exact analytic form from Williams and Max [4], which weights the frontmost color more heavily than the rear color. The specific formula is not provided in the text, but it is noted that it requires supplementary arithmetic beyond practical hardware limits, so it is computed on the CPU and passed as a vertex attribute. Texture Table Resolution: Not given in the sources. Sorting Complexity: O(n^2) for n polyhedra. Mach Bands: Linear interpolation of opacity causes Mach bands, particularly at faces parallel to the viewing direction. This is caused by the quadratic error term in the transparency function. Intersecting Polyhedra: The sorting algorithm performs no subdivisions for intersecting polyhedra or cycles and arbitrarily chooses a drawing order, which may produce incorrect results. Quadratic Interpolation: If hardware does not support quadratic interpolation of texture coordinates, the 2D texture table is used as an approximation for linearly varying \chi. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwareassistedprojectedtetrahedra(tetrahedra, camera, texturetable1d, texturetable2d): """ Renders a list of tetrahedra using hardware-assisted texture mapping. Args: tetrahedra: List of Tetrahedron objects with vertices containing pos, color, chi. camera: Camera object with projection matrix and view direction. texturetable1d: 1D array for constant chi. texturetable2d: 2D array for varying chi. Returns: Image buffer. """ # Step 1: Sort tetrahedra back-to-front sortedtetrahedra = sortpolyhedrabacktofront(tetrahedra) # Initialize image buffer image = initializeimagebuffer() for tet in sortedtetrahedra: # Step 2: Project and classify projectedtriangles = projectandclassify(tet, camera) for tri in projectedtriangles: # Identify thick and thin vertices thickv, thinv1, thinv2 = classifyvertices(tri) # Step 3: Compute thick vertex attributes # Calculate ray segment length at thick vertex lthick = computeraylength(thickv, camera.viewdirection) chithick = thickv.chi # Compute texture coordinate u = chi l uthick = chithick lthick # Compute color using Williams and Max formula # Note: This is computed on CPU as it's too complex for hardware cthick = williamsmaxcolorintegration(thickv, thinv1, thinv2, lthick) # Set vertex attributes for rasterization # Thin vertices have u=0 tri.vertices[0].u = 0.0 tri.vertices[0].color = thinv1.color tri.vertices[1].u = 0.0 tri.vertices[1].color = thinv2.color tri.vertices[2].u = uthick tri.vertices[2].color = cthick # Step 4: Rasterize and Composite # The hardware interpolates u and color across the triangle # and uses u to lookup alpha from the texture table rasterizetriangle(tri, texturetable1d, texturetable2d, image) return image def williamsmaxcolorintegration(thickv, thinv1, thinv2, l): """ Computes the color at the thick vertex using the exact analytic form. This weights the frontmost color more heavily. """ # Exact formula from Williams and Max [4] # Not provided in source text, but implied to be more accurate than (C0+C1)/2 # Placeholder for the actual complex formula return computeexactcolor(thickv, thinv1, thinv2, l) def rasterizetriangle(tri, tex1d, tex2d, image): """ Simulates hardware rasterization. In reality, this is done by the GPU. """ for pixel in tri.boundingbox: if pixel inside tri: # Barycentric interpolation s, t, r = barycentriccoords(pixel, tri.vertices) # Interpolate u (texture coordinate) u = s tri.vertices[0].u + t tri.vertices[1].u + r tri.vertices[2].u # Interpolate color c = s tri.vertices[0].color + t tri.vertices[1].color + r tri.vertices[2].color # Lookup alpha from texture table # If chi varies, use 2D table with chi and l # For simplicity, assuming constant chi case here alpha = tex1d[u] # Composite oldc = image[pixel] newc = alpha c + (1 - alpha) oldc image[pixel] = newc Time Complexity: Sorting: O(n^2) for n polyhedra. Rendering: Linear in the number of triangles, with constant-time texture lookups and compositing per pixel. Memory Complexity: Texture table size depends on resolution. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient use of hardware acceleration for opacity integration. Correctly handles colored volumes with back-to-front sorting. More accurate color integration than the original Shirley-Tuckman algorithm by using the Williams and Max formula for the thick vertex. Limitations: Mach bands can still occur due to linear interpolation of opacity. Sorting is O(n^2), which may be slow for large datasets. Intersecting polyhedra are not handled correctly; the sort arbitrarily chooses an order. The exact Williams and Max color formula requires supplementary arithmetic not available in hardware, so it must be computed on the CPU. When to Use: When rendering unstructured data with color and opacity variations that require sorting. When hardware acceleration is available and the dataset size is manageable for O(n^2) sorting. When Not to Use: When intersecting polyhedra are present and correct sorting is critical. When high performance is required for very large datasets due to the sorting complexity. Origin: The method was presented by Clifford Stein, Barry Becker, and Nelson Max from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the paper "Sorting and Hardware Assisted Rendering for Volume Visualization". History and Development: The project grew out of the need to visualize unstructured meshed vector fields from finite element analysis code. It is an extension of the Shirley-Tuckman algorithm, which classifies the projection of tetrahedra into triangles and renders them using hardware. The authors identified artifacts in the original algorithm, particularly Mach bands from linear opacity interpolation, and introduced texture tables to handle the exponential opacity function. They also extended the Newell, Newell, and Sancha sort for polygons to handle 3-D convex polyhedra. Usage: It is used in volume visualization tools for unstructured data, such as finite element analysis results. name: Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm
body: The Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm (MTA) is an iso-surface extraction method that converts a volumetric grid into a polygonal mesh by decomposing each cubic cell into tetrahedra and determining intersections within them. It builds on the shared principles of Cell projection but distinguishes itself from its sibling Marching Cubes by resolving topological ambiguities inherent in cubic decomposition through specific tetrahedral tessellation patterns. Unlike Projected Tetrahedra which projects primitives to screen space, MTA operates in object space to generate a watertight manifold. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field defined on a regular 3D grid of voxels. Each voxel has 8 vertices with associated scalar values vi. Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface at a specified threshold value T. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D array of vertices. Each vertex Vi has coordinates (xi, yi, zi) and a scalar value vi. Tetrahedra: Each cubic cell is decomposed into 6 tetrahedra. The decomposition is fixed and non-symmetric, introducing directional bias. Steps: 1. Grid Traversal: Iterate through every cubic cell in the grid. 2. Tetrahedral Decomposition: Subdivide the current cubic cell into 6 tetrahedra. A common decomposition connects the center of the cube to the faces, or uses a fixed set of diagonals. The specific connectivity must be consistent across the grid to ensure manifold continuity. 3. Vertex Classification: For each tetrahedron, determine the state of its 4 vertices relative to the isosurface threshold T. A vertex is "inside" if vi < T (or vi > T, depending on convention) and "outside" otherwise. This yields 2^4 = 16 possible configurations. 4. Intersection Calculation: For each edge of the tetrahedron where the scalar values change sign (one vertex inside, one outside), calculate the intersection point P using linear interpolation: P = Va + \frac{T - va}{vb - va} (Vb - Va) where Va, Vb are the endpoints of the edge and va, vb are their scalar values. 5. Triangle Generation: Based on the configuration of inside/outside vertices, select the pre-defined set of triangles that connect the intersection points. The lookup table for MTA is derived from the valid triangulations of the tetrahedron that are consistent with the global topology, avoiding the ambiguities present in Marching Cubes. 6. Mesh Assembly: Collect all generated triangles. Ensure shared edges between adjacent tetrahedra/cells are handled consistently to produce a watertight mesh. Parameters: Isosurface Threshold (T): The scalar value defining the surface. Typical values depend on the data range. Tetrahedral Decomposition Pattern: The specific way cubes are split. Must be chosen to minimize directional bias, though perfect symmetry is impossible. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Directional Ambiguities: Because a cube cannot be subdivided into tetrahedra symmetrically, the MTA exhibits directional ambiguities. The resulting surface may vary slightly depending on the orientation of the grid or the specific decomposition pattern used. Missed Boundaries: The algorithm can miss material boundaries if the isosurface enters a tetrahedron but only intersects one edge. Detection relies on vertex information, so a single-edge intersection without vertex sign changes may be undetected. Degenerate Triangles: Standard MTA can produce thin, degenerate triangles that degrade interpolated shading. This is addressed in variants like Regularised Marching Tetrahedra. Regularised Marching Tetrahedra (RMT) is an iso-surface extraction algorithm that combines the topological consistency of the Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm with vertex clustering to generate simplified surfaces with improved triangle aspect ratios. Unlike standard MTA, which can produce thin, degenerate triangles, RMT reduces the triangle count by approximately 70% while preserving the original topology by basing clustering on the tetrahedral lattice. Choose this when shading quality and mesh simplification are priorities over raw geometric fidelity. Regularised Marching Tetrahedra The Subgrid Pipeline is a method for extracting isosurfaces from tetrahedral grids by resolving topological ambiguities within individual tetrahedra using subgrid-accurate intersection data. It distinguishes itself from standard MTA by explicitly handling open, scoop, and normal boundary curves to ensure watertightness, allowing multiple intersection vertices per edge to represent complex topology. It builds on Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm by replacing the fixed lookup table with a local reconstruction procedure that processes boundary curves. Choose this for complex topologies where standard MTA fails to capture fine details. Subgrid Pipeline This method computes smooth isosurface normals for tetrahedral meshes by calculating vertex normals weighted by the volume of connected tetrahedra. It solves the problem of severe visual discontinuities that arise when using the constant cell normal Nt directly, which decreases rendering quality significantly. It differs from its siblings, such as Regularised Marching Tetrahedra which modifies the topology, by retaining the standard Marching Tetrahedrons topology but enhancing the shading data through pre-computed vertex attributes. Choose this when smooth shading is required without altering the mesh geometry. Tetrahedral Normal Calculation McGrids is an iso-surface extraction method that constructs adaptive, non-uniform tetrahedral grids using an iterative Monte Carlo process to estimate a probability density function (PDF) based on the implicit field, followed by a refinement step and mesh extraction via Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform grid sampling by concentrating grid points near surfaces and geometric details, significantly reducing the number of implicit field queries and memory usage compared to uniform grids. Unlike Regularised Marching Tetrahedra or Subgrid Pipeline which may rely on fixed or hierarchical structures, McGrids dynamically adapts the grid topology through probabilistic sampling and Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation (CVT) relaxation. Choose this for large datasets with sparse features to optimize performance. McGrids Exact Fiber Surface Extraction computes the pre-image of a 1-manifold path (Fiber Surface Control Polygon, FSCP) in the range of a bivariate field f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2 over a tetrahedral mesh. It solves the problem of approximating these surfaces using signed distance fields, which fail to capture sharp bends and complex topologies. Unlike Regularised Marching Tetrahedra which smooths geometry, this method guarantees planar pre-images within each tetrahedron by decomposing the extraction into base surface generation and precise clipping. Choose this for bivariate field visualization requiring exact topological preservation. Exact Fiber Surface Extraction Marching Tetrahedra Reconstruction is a surface reconstruction method that converts a set of input vertices and normals into a 3D mesh by computing an implicit field using the Welland function, sampling it on a tetrahedral grid, and extracting the zero-level set via Marching Tetrahedra. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by using a tetrahedral decomposition of the grid cells, which eliminates the ambiguity cases inherent in cube-based extraction. It builds on Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm but replaces the standard linear interpolation with a Welland-based implicit field evaluation. Choose this for point cloud reconstruction where topological correctness is critical. Marching Tetrahedra Reconstruction The Raster Algorithm for Fiber Surface Extraction approximates fiber surfaces by extracting the 0 level-set of a signed range distance field to the Fiber Surface Control Polygon (FSCP). It reduces the computational cost of distance field evaluation by rasterizing the scalar field range into a 2D grid, trading geometric accuracy for speed. Unlike exact methods, it imposes a lower bound on Hausdorff distance near FSCP bends and only handles closed FSCPs. Choose this for real-time applications where approximate fiber surfaces are sufficient. Raster Algorithm for Fiber Surface Extraction The Keppel Heuristic is a local decision method used in contour tiling to determine how to connect two parallel contour segments during volume rendering. It resolves the ambiguity of the next vertex to connect by comparing the volumes of two candidate tetrahedra formed with interior reference points. Choose this when resolving contour connections in tetrahedral-based contouring. Keppel Heuristic Tetrahedralization Schemes decompose volumetric grid cells into tetrahedra to facilitate isosurface extraction via the Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm. They resolve topological ambiguities inherent in cubic grid decomposition by providing specific tessellation patterns. This family is distinguished from its siblings, such as Regularised Marching Tetrahedra and Subgrid Pipeline, by the specific lattice structure (BCC, Diamond, or Centered Cubic) and the resulting tetrahedral connectivity used to define the local cell geometry. Choose this when the underlying grid structure is non-cubic or requires specific connectivity properties. Tetrahedralization Schemes MTCut is a real-time volume cutting algorithm that modifies isosurfaces generated by the Marching Tetrahedra (MT) algorithm using a user-defined cutting tool. Unlike traditional tetrahedral mesh cutting strategies that require a pre-computed tetrahedrization of the entire volume, MTCut computes the tetrahedrization of only the intersected cells on-the-fly, enabling interactive performance for complex meshes. It produces a watertight manifold model, distinguishing it from approaches like Zachow et al. [ZGSZ03] that yield open surfaces with borders. Choose this for interactive volume cutting applications. MTCut The Nielson-Franke Generalization is a direct generalization of Nielson's and Franke's algorithm for multi-material interfaces. It reduces to the Nielson-Franke algorithm when material fractions are restricted such that exactly one li=1 at each vertex. It uses a clipping algorithm (e.g., BSP) to calculate material boundaries within tetrahedra and maps them back to physical space. In the three-material case, it assumes a "Y" shaped subdivision in the barycentric triangle centered at c = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). Choose this for multi-material volume rendering where material interfaces need to be explicitly resolved. Nielson-Franke Generalization (Note: No dedicated article exists, so linked to parent context or sibling if applicable, but here listed as minor variant). Time Complexity: The algorithm runs in effectively the same time as the marching cubes/tetrahedra algorithm, i.e., linear with respect to the number of cells/vertices in the grid. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra generated. The output mesh size is proportional to the surface area of the isosurface. Measured Performance: Performance is comparable to Marching Cubes, but the overhead of tetrahedral decomposition and lookup may be slightly higher. The algorithm is efficient for uniform grids. Strengths: Resolves topological ambiguities present in Marching Cubes; produces watertight meshes; well-understood and widely implemented. Limitations: Directional ambiguities due to non-symmetric tetrahedral decomposition; can produce degenerate triangles; may miss boundaries if only one edge is intersected. When to Use: When topological correctness is more important than avoiding directional bias, or when working with tetrahedral meshes directly. When Not to Use: When directional bias is unacceptable and cannot be mitigated by grid alignment; when performance is critical and Marching Cubes is sufficient; when dealing with multi-material interfaces requiring complex boundary handling (use Nielson-Franke Generalization or Subgrid Pipeline). The Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm was developed as an improvement over Marching Cubes to address topological ambiguities. The history of the Marching Cubes Algorithm (MCA) is detailed in, noting that initial implementations overlooked certain cases, resulting in holes. The MTA was introduced to provide a more robust topological structure by decomposing cubes into tetrahedra, although it introduces its own directional ambiguities. It is widely used in scientific visualization and medical imaging for iso-surface extraction. name: Regularised Marching Tetrahedra
head: RMT
body: Regularised Marching Tetrahedra (RMT) is an iso-surface extraction algorithm that combines the topological consistency of the Marching Tetrahedra Algorithm with vertex clustering to generate simplified surfaces with improved triangle aspect ratios. Unlike standard Marching Tetrahedra, which can produce thin, degenerate triangles that degrade interpolated shading, RMT reduces the triangle count by approximately 70% while preserving the original topology by basing clustering on the tetrahedral lattice. Inputs: A scalar field defined on a 3D grid (or implicit surface definition) and an iso-value threshold. Outputs: A triangular mesh representing the iso-surface. Data Structures: 1. Lattice: A tessellation of the data volume into tetrahedra, constructed from the underlying grid cells. 2. Vertex Clusters: A mapping from original sample points (grid vertices) to clustered representative points. Since RMT clusters before triangulation, the primary data structure is the set of unique clustered vertices. 3. Edge Intersections: For each tetrahedral edge crossing the iso-surface, the intersection point is calculated. Steps: 1. Construct Lattice: Decompose the volume grid into tetrahedra. 2. Vertex Clustering: Perform vertex clustering on the sampled data vertices before triangulation. Identify vertices that are spatially close to each other. Cluster these vertices into single representative points. Crucial Constraint: The clustering must be based on the original tetrahedral lattice structure. Vertices belonging to the same tetrahedron or sharing a common edge/face in the lattice are considered for clustering together. This specific constraint preserves the topological consistency of the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm, which is not guaranteed by generic vertex clustering. The position of the clustered vertex is typically the centroid or average of the clustered original vertices. 3. Triangulation: For each tetrahedron in the lattice: Determine which edges intersect the iso-surface by comparing the scalar values at the tetrahedron's vertices against the iso-value. Calculate the intersection points on these edges using linear interpolation. Use the standard Marching Tetrahedra lookup table to determine the connectivity of the triangles, but use the clustered vertex positions instead of the original grid vertex positions. This results in a mesh of near-regular triangles. 4. Gradient and Curvature Estimation (Optional/Post-processing): To estimate the gradient or curvature at a surface vertex: Identify all tetrahedra that contain the edge associated with that vertex. Use only the scalar data from the vertices of these specific tetrahedra to compute the gradient/curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def regularisedmarchingtetrahedra(grid, isovalue): # 1. Construct Tetrahedral Lattice # Decompose each grid cell into tetrahedra using a fixed diagonal rule. tetrahedra = [] for x in range(grid.dimx - 1): for y in range(grid.dimy - 1): for z in range(grid.dimz - 1): v = [ grid.vertexindex(x, y, z), grid.vertexindex(x+1, y, z), grid.vertexindex(x, y+1, z), grid.vertexindex(x+1, y+1, z), grid.vertexindex(x, y, z+1), grid.vertexindex(x+1, y, z+1), grid.vertexindex(x, y+1, z+1), grid.vertexindex(x+1, y+1, z+1) ] # Split cube into 6 tetrahedra tetrahedra.append((v[0], v[1], v[2], v[3])) tetrahedra.append((v[0], v[3], v[4], v[7])) tetrahedra.append((v[3], v[7], v[2], v[6])) tetrahedra.append((v[2], v[6], v[5], v[1])) tetrahedra.append((v[1], v[5], v[4], v[0])) tetrahedra.append((v[4], v[5], v[6], v[7])) # 2. Vertex Clustering clusteredvertices = clustervertices(grid.vertices, tetrahedra) vertexmap = buildvertexmap(grid.vertices, clusteredvertices) triangles = [] # 3. Triangulation for tet in tetrahedra: vals = [grid.values[tet[i]] for i in range(4)] # Determine which edges intersect the iso-surface intersectingedges = [] edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)] for i, j in edges: if (vals[i] - isovalue) (vals[j] - isovalue) < 0: intersectingedges.append((i, j)) if not intersectingedges: continue # Calculate intersection points using clustered positions intersectionpoints = [] for edge in intersectingedges: v0idx, v1idx = edge p0 = clusteredvertices[vertexmap[v0idx]] p1 = clusteredvertices[vertexmap[v1idx]] val0 = vals[v0idx] val1 = vals[v1idx] t = (isovalue - val0) / (val1 - val0) pintersect = lerp(p0, p1, t) intersectionpoints.append(pintersect) # Generate triangles using the standard Marching Tetrahedra lookup table edgemask = 0 for idx, in enumerate(intersectingedges): edgemask |= (1 << idx) # Standard MT lookup table maps the 6-bit edge mask to triangle indices # Implementation uses a precomputed 256-entry table triindices = mtlookuptable[edgemask] for tri in triindices: triangles.append((intersectionpoints[tri[0]], intersectionpoints[tri[1]], intersectionpoints[tri[2]])) return triangles def clustervertices(originalvertices, tetrahedra): # Group vertices that are spatially close and topologically connected # via the tetrahedral lattice. Return a list of unique representative points. # Implementation detail: Use a spatial hash or grid to find neighbors, # then merge based on lattice connectivity. pass def buildvertexmap(originalvertices, clusteredvertices): # Map each original vertex index to the index of its representative # in the clusteredvertices list. pass Parameters: Iso-value: The scalar threshold for surface extraction. Clustering Threshold: The maximum distance between vertices to be considered for clustering. Not explicitly given in sources, but implied by "spatially close". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clustering Topology: If clustering is not strictly bound by the tetrahedral lattice, topological errors (holes, non-manifold edges) may occur. Accuracy vs. Simplification: The vertex clustering method is not optimal for minimizing surface area, volume, or curvature errors. More accurate positioning would require principal curvature calculations, which are more complex. Gradient Estimation: Gradient estimation must be limited to the local tetrahedral neighborhood to maintain consistency with the simplified mesh. An iso-surface extraction algorithm that iterates over a volume grid to extract intersections within tetrahedral cells, specifically designed for objects represented using radial basis functions. It differs from its parent, Regularised Marching Tetrahedra, by omitting the vertex clustering step, thereby lacking the mesh simplification and improved triangle aspect ratios provided by the full method. It is chosen over Marching Squares to avoid topological ambiguities. Triangle Count: Typically reduces the triangle count by 70% compared to Marching Tetrahedra (MT) and by 40% compared to Marching Cubes (MC). Performance: The additional time required for clustering is offset by the reduction in points and triangles stored, resulting in a fast algorithm that can be generated in nearly the same time as MT alone. Visual Quality: Significantly improves interpolated shading (especially Gouraud shading) by eliminating sharp edges and points caused by thin/small triangles in MT and MC. Accuracy: Volume and surface area error differences compared to MT are much less than the error inherent in the sampling resolution. Limitations: The vertex clustering is not optimal for minimizing surface area, volume, or curvature errors. Regularised Marching Tetrahedra was introduced to address the issues of mesh simplification and poor triangle aspect ratios in standard iso-surface extraction methods. While mesh simplification algorithms exist, they often fail to maintain topology. RMT combines the topological robustness of Marching Tetrahedra with the simplification benefits of vertex clustering, specifically tailored to preserve topology by leveraging the tetrahedral lattice structure. It is suitable for implicit surfaces, thresholded medical data, and surfaces created from object cross-sections. head: Iso-surface extraction using Radial Basis Functions, Marching Tetrahedral
body: An iso-surface extraction algorithm that iterates over a volume grid to extract intersections within tetrahedral cells, specifically designed for objects represented using radial basis functions. It differs from its parent, Regularised Marching Tetrahedra, by omitting the vertex clustering step, thereby lacking the mesh simplification and improved triangle aspect ratios provided by the full method. It is chosen over Marching Squares to avoid topological ambiguities. Inputs: A bounding box (AxisAlignedBox3) defining the spatial extent of the volume. A resolution parameter reso controlling the grid density. A scalar field evaluation function evaluatefn(Vector3) that returns the value at a given point. An iso-value threshold for surface extraction. Outputs: A list of vertices (list<Vector3>) representing the iso-surface. Data Structures: noplanes: A vector of 3 unsigned integers storing the number of planes in X, Y, and Z dimensions. gridlines: A vector of 4 vectors of floats. gridlines[0]: X coordinates for the primary grid. gridlines[1]: X coordinates for the secondary (shifted) grid. gridlines[2]: Y coordinates. gridlines[3]: Z coordinates. Tetrahedral: A structure containing 4 Vector3 vertices. Parameters: distx: Distance scaling factor for X-axis tetrahedra. Value: \sqrt{2.0}. disty: Distance scaling factor for Y-axis tetrahedra. Value: 0.5. distz: Distance scaling factor for Z-axis tetrahedra. Value: 1/\sqrt{2.0}. Steps: 1. name: Subgrid Pipeline
head: Subgrid Marching Pipeline
body: The Subgrid Pipeline extracts isosurfaces from tetrahedral grids by resolving topological ambiguities within individual tetrahedra using subgrid-accurate intersection data. It distinguishes itself from standard Marching Tetrahedrons by explicitly handling open, scoop, and normal boundary curves to process complex intersection configurations. It builds on Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm by replacing the fixed lookup table with a local reconstruction procedure that processes boundary curves. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A range of tetrahedra in a grid, a scalar field defined on vertices, an isovalue, and configuration options (mod2, greedy, computenormals). Output: A global TriangleSoup containing the extracted surface triangles. Data Structures: EdgeInts: A structure storing intersection data for the 6 edges of a tetrahedron. Fields: ne01, ne02, ne03, ne12, ne13, ne23. Each neij represents the number of intersections on edge (i,j). In the standard pipeline, these are integers derived from t-values. In the Mod2 Reduction variant, they are reduced modulo 2. CombFace: Represents a boundary curve (open, scoop, or normal). Contains a list of vertices defining the curve. TriangleSoup: A collection of triangles (triplets of vertices) accumulated from all tetrahedra. Steps: 1. Iterate Tetrahedra: Loop through each tetrahedron in the input range using a TetRange iterator. 2. Query Intersections: For the current tetrahedron, query the edge intersections. Request t-values (positions) and normals for all 6 edges if computenormals is true. Compute the intersection count for each edge based on the scalar field values at the vertices and the isovalue. Let N{ij} be the number of intersections on edge (i,j). 3. Mod2 Reduction (Optional): If the mod2 option is enabled, apply modulo-2 reduction to the intersection data. If the reduction results in a configuration that implies no surface, skip processing this tetrahedron. 4. Construct Boundary Curves: Call boundarycombcurves with the tetrahedron indices, intersection counts, and edge occupation flags. This function analyzes the intersection topology to identify three types of curves: opencurves, scoopcurves, and normalcurves. 5. Track Statistics (Optional): Increment a counter for "non-even" tetrahedra if opencurves is not empty. Increment a counter for "non-normal" tetrahedra if opencurves is empty AND scoopcurves is empty. 6. Construct Local Surface: Create a local TriangleSoup for the current tetrahedron. Use the subgridsurface method for general cases or subgridgreedy for optimized performance, based on the opts.greedy flag. 7. Merge: Append the local TriangleSoup to the global result soup. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def subgridpipeline(tetrange, scalarfield, isovalue, opts): globalsoup = [] nonevencount = 0 nonnormalcount = 0 for tet in tetrange: # Step 2: Query edge intersections edgeints = [0] 6 normals = [None] 6 edgeintersections = [None] 6 for edgeidx in range(6): v0, v1 = tet.edges[edgeidx] s0 = scalarfield(v0) s1 = scalarfield(v1) # Compute intersection count and t-value if (s0 - isovalue) (s1 - isovalue) < 0: t = (isovalue - s0) / (s1 - s0) edgeintersections[edgeidx] = v0 + t (v1 - v0) edgeints[edgeidx] = 1 if opts.computenormals: grad = (scalarfield.gradient(v1) - scalarfield.gradient(v0)) normals[edgeidx] = grad / max(norm(grad), 1e-8) else: edgeints[edgeidx] = 0 # Step 3: Mod2 Reduction if opts.mod2: for edgeidx in range(6): edgeints[edgeidx] %= 2 if sum(edgeints) == 0: continue # Step 4: Construct boundary curves opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves = boundarycombcurves( tet.indices, edgeints, edgeintersections, normals) # Step 5: Track statistics (optional) if opts.trackstats: if opencurves: nonevencount += 1 if not opencurves and not scoopcurves: nonnormalcount += 1 # Step 6: Construct local surface if opts.greedy: localsoup = subgridgreedy(tet, opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, edgeints) else: localsoup = subgridsurface(tet, opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, edgeints) # Step 7: Merge globalsoup.extend(localsoup) return globalsoup def computeedgeintersections(edge, scalarfield, isovalue): v0, v1 = edge s0 = scalarfield(v0) s1 = scalarfield(v1) if (s0 - isovalue) (s1 - isovalue) < 0: t = (isovalue - s0) / (s1 - s0) return v0 + t (v1 - v0) return None def computenormal(edge, scalarfield, isovalue): v0, v1 = edge grad = scalarfield.gradient(v1) - scalarfield.gradient(v0) return grad / max(norm(grad), 1e-8) def boundarycombcurves(tetindices, edgeints, intersections, normals): # Standard Marching Tetrahedrons curve construction opencurves = [] scoopcurves = [] normalcurves = [] # Map edge indices to intersection points edgepts = {i: intersections[i] for i in range(6) if intersections[i] is not None} # Generate open curves from paired edge intersections if len(edgepts) == 2: pts = list(edgepts.values()) opencurves.append([pts[0], pts[1]]) elif len(edgepts) == 4: pts = list(edgepts.values()) opencurves.append([pts[0], pts[1]]) opencurves.append([pts[2], pts[3]]) return opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves def subgridsurface(tet, opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, edgeints): # Standard Marching Tetrahedrons triangle generation triangles = [] for curve in opencurves: if len(curve) == 2: triangles.append(curve) return triangles def subgridgreedy(tet, opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, edgeints): # Greedy variant fallback return subgridsurface(tet, opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, edgeints) Parameters: mod2: Boolean. If true, reduces intersection counts modulo 2. greedy: Boolean. If true, uses the optimized subgridgreedy reconstruction. computenormals: Boolean. If true, computes normals for intersection points. trackstats: Boolean. If true, collects statistics on curve types. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Subgrid methods require accurate computation of intersection positions; floating-point errors can lead to non-watertight surfaces if not handled carefully. Degenerate Input: Tetrahedra with zero volume or collinear vertices may cause division-by-zero or invalid t-values in intersection computation. Complex Topology: The ability to handle multiple intersections per edge allows for complex topologies, but increases computational cost. Mod2 Reduction is an ablation of the Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra method that provides exact input intersection locations but limits the output to at most one intersection per edge. It uses the parity of the intersection count to determine connectivity, effectively restoring the single-surface-per-edge constraint of classic Marching Tetrahedra while utilizing subgrid-accurate vertex positions. It is distinguished from its sibling Subgrid Surface Reconstruction by its strict limitation to one output vertex per edge, whereas the full subgrid method allows multiple vertices to represent complex topology. Subgrid Surface Reconstruction is a method for extracting a triangle soup from a tetrahedral grid by processing individual tetrahedra to resolve topological ambiguities in isosurface extraction. It distinguishes itself from standard Marching Tetrahedrons by explicitly handling open, scoop, and normal boundary curves to ensure watertightness, offering two variants: subgridsurface for general cases and subgridgreedy for optimized performance. Subgrid Marching Triangles is a 2D contouring algorithm that reconstructs curves within a single triangle using a subgrid procedure, applied to all triangles in a 2D triangular grid given intersection counts on grid edges. Unlike 3D subgrid marching tets, this 2D variant does not need to worry about compatibility between neighboring cells, allowing for the specific modification in the odd sum case: rather than subtracting 1 from all 3 edge coordinates in a face, subtract 1 from the largest edge coordinate, breaking ties arbitrarily. For the dual method, it uses the same regularized QEF as in Section 3.3.2 of, but in two dimensions. It can be applied to arbitrary unstructured triangulations, including surface meshes, as it makes no assumptions about the structure of the triangle grid. Time Complexity: The per-tetrahedron cost is greater than that of marching tets because it may produce more polygons per tet and involves additional logic for local reconstruction. However, the amortized cost per output triangle is quite comparable. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of output triangles and temporary storage for boundary curves and local triangle soups during processing. Performance: Speed improvements can be achieved by precomputing a table of common stencils if speed or thread synchronization is critical. Strengths: Handles multiple intersections per edge; applicable to arbitrary unstructured grids. Limitations: Higher per-tetrahedron computational cost compared to classic marching tets; potential for increased output polygon count. The Subgrid Pipeline originates from the work on Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra, which aims to improve the accuracy of isosurface extraction by considering subgrid details within each tetrahedron. The 2D variant, Subgrid Marching Triangles, extends these concepts to two-dimensional contouring. hbaktash/subgrid-marching, https://github.com/hbaktash/subgrid-marching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra, https://doi.org/10.1145/3811358, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mod2 Reduction
head: Modulo-2 Reduction, Subgrid Mod 2 Algorithm
body: Mod2 Reduction is an ablation of the Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra method that provides exact input intersection locations but limits the output to at most one intersection per edge. It uses the parity of the intersection count to determine connectivity, effectively restoring the single-surface-per-edge constraint of classic Marching Tetrahedra while utilizing subgrid-accurate vertex positions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: For each edge of a tetrahedron, a list of intersection parameter values (t) where the scalar field crosses the isovalue, and the total count of these intersections. Output: A single aggregated intersection location (vertex position) for the edge, and a boolean flag indicating whether the current tetrahedron should be skipped in the pipeline. Data Structures: Edge Intersections: A list of floating-point values representing the parametric position t \in [0, 1] along the edge where the isosurface is crossed. Intersection Count: An integer representing the size of the list above. Steps: 1. Parity Check: Calculate the parity of the intersection count N for the edge: p = N \pmod 2. 2. Connectivity Determination: If p = 1, the two endpoints of the edge are on different sides of the surface. If p = 0, the endpoints are on the same side of the surface. 3. Aggregation: If p = 1, calculate the aggregated intersection location V{agg} by averaging all true intersection positions ti found along the edge: V{agg} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} ti This position is used as the primal vertex for the edge in the mesh construction. 4. Pipeline Integration: In the dual subgrid pipeline, this function is called if the opts.mod2 flag is true. If the function returns true, the current tetrahedron is skipped. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mod2reduction(edgeintersections: list[float], edgecount: int) -> tuple[bool, float]: """ Determines connectivity and aggregated position for an edge. Args: edgeintersections: List of t-values where the isosurface crosses the edge. edgecount: Number of intersections (len(edgeintersections)). Returns: (shouldskip, aggregatedt) shouldskip: True if the edge does not cross the surface (even parity). aggregatedt: The average t-value if odd parity, otherwise undefined. """ # Step 1 & 2: Parity check if edgecount % 2 == 0: # Even number of intersections: endpoints are on the same side. # Skip this edge for connectivity. return (True, 0.0) # Step 3: Aggregation # Odd number of intersections: endpoints are on different sides. # Calculate average of all intersection positions. sumt = 0.0 for t in edgeintersections: sumt += t avgt = sumt / edgecount # Return False to indicate the edge IS active (should not skip) return (False, avgt) Parameters: opts.mod2: A boolean flag in the pipeline configuration. When true, Mod2 Reduction is applied instead of the full subgrid intersection handling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Averaging multiple t values assumes the intersections are distinct and well-separated. Degenerate Input: If edgecount is 0, the parity is even, and the edge is skipped. Implementation Note: The function convertmod2intersections was moved to query/mod2reduction.h in the reference implementation. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of intersections per edge, requiring a single pass over the intersection list. Memory Complexity: Minimal overhead; requires storing the list of intersections temporarily for averaging. Performance: In a 100^3 grid comparison, Subgrid Mod 2 shows slightly better geometric quality than classic Marching Tetrahedra but cannot produce more than one disc per tetrahedron. Strengths: Improves the accuracy of primal vertex positions compared to classic Marching Tetrahedra by using exact intersection locations. Limitations: Produces much more distortion than the full Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra algorithm because it cannot handle multiple intersections per edge. It produces the same mesh connectivity as classic Marching Tetrahedra. When to use: When the surface topology is simple (no multiple intersections per edge) but higher vertex accuracy than classic Marching Tetrahedra is desired. When not to use: When the surface requires multiple intersections per edge, as the method averages them into a single vertex. The Subgrid Mod 2 Algorithm was introduced as an ablation study to determine the essential components of the Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra method. It was proposed by the authors of the Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra paper to isolate the contribution of exact intersection locations versus the ability to handle multiple intersections per edge. name: Subgrid Surface Reconstruction
body: Subgrid Surface Reconstruction extracts a triangle soup from a tetrahedral grid by processing individual tetrahedra. It distinguishes itself from standard Marching Tetrahedrons by accepting pre-computed boundary curves (open, scoop, normal) and edge occupation flags to guide triangle generation, offering two variants: subgridsurface for general cases and subgridgreedy for optimized performance. Inputs and Outputs: The method processes a single tetrahedron. Inputs include tetrahedron vertex positions, global vertex indices, pre-computed edge intersection times, boundary curve definitions (open, scoop, normal), non-normal edge occupation flags, and flags for scoop mid-vertices and bulge magnitude. The output is a triangle soup representing the isosurface segment within that tetrahedron. Data Structures: Tetrahedron: 4 vertex positions (3D coordinates) and 4 global indices (integers). Edge Intersections: 6 intersection times (floats), one per edge. Boundary Curves: Lists of vertices or edges defining open, scoop, and normal boundaries. Flags: Boolean flags for scoop mid-vertices and bulge magnitude. Steps: 1. Filter Unoccupied Edges: Use unoccupiededgeisectts to filter edge intersection times, returning only times for edges that are not occupied. 2. Reconstruct Surface: Pass the filtered intersection times, tetrahedron positions, global indices, boundary curves, occupation flags, and magnitude flags to either subgridsurface or subgridgreedy to generate the local triangle soup. 3. Aggregate: Combine the triangle soups from all processed tetrahedra into a global mesh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Scoop Mid-Vertices: Input flag indicating the presence of mid-vertices for scoop boundaries. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Even-Sum Condition: If the even-sum condition is not satisfied, the output might not be orientable and might have open holes, typically due to non-watertight input or grid edge-intersection issues. Resolution/Perturbation: Changing the resolution or applying perturbation may help resolve intersection issues if the even-sum condition fails. It is distinguished from Subgrid Surface Reconstruction by its explicit dual grid structure and support for robust intersection queries with optional regularization. Choose it when robust intersection handling and regularization are required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Requires pre-computed boundary curves and edge intersections. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. name: Dual Subgrid Pipeline
body: The Dual Subgrid Pipeline extracts an isosurface from a scalar function defined on a triangle mesh or Signed Distance Field (SDF) by constructing a dual mesh representation within a tetrahedral grid. It processes tetrahedra individually to generate a triangle soup, querying edge intersections and constructing boundary curves (open, scoop, normal) before generating the final surface via a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) solve or centroid placement. It is distinguished from its parent, Subgrid Surface Reconstruction, by its explicit use of a dual grid structure to resolve topological ambiguities and its support for robust intersection queries with optional regularization. Inputs: 1. Source Data: Exactly one of the following: a triangle mesh file (OBJ, OFF, PLY), a named built-in SDF (e.g., Sphere, Torus), or a precomputed.npz file containing tetrahedral mesh data and precomputed intersections. 2. Configuration: DualSubgridPipelineOpts struct. 3. Grid Resolution: tetGridResolution (n^3), default 64. Outputs: DualSubgridPipelineResult struct containing: soup (TriangleSoup), nonzerotets (int), totaltets (int), nonnormaltets (int), noneventets (int), isecttime (double), constructiontime (double). Optionally, a saved OBJ mesh file. DualSubgridPipelineOpts Fields: mod2 (bool): Use mod2 intersection reduction. userobust (bool): Enable robust ray-intersection queries (FCPW watertight test + iterative all-hits). Always false in standard builds due to performance cost (~2x slower) with negligible robustness gain. showprogress (bool): Display progress bar. regalpha (double): Regularization weight for QEF solve. Default 0.1. projectduals (bool): Project dual vertices to the local grid cell. nonormal (bool): Ignore normals; place dual points at boundary-polygon centroids. Required for.npz inputs lacking normals. DualSubgridPipelineResult Fields: soup, nonzerotets, totaltets, nonnormaltets, noneventets, isecttime, constructiontime. Edge Intersection Data Stored in two arrays indexed by edge pair (0-5): edgeisectts: std::array<std::vector<double>, 6> storing intersection parameters (t). edgeisectnormals: std::array<std::vector<Vector3>, 6> storing intersection normals. Edge Index Mapping Edges are mapped to indices 0-5 based on vertex pairs (vi, vj) where i < j: 0: (0, 1), 1: (0, 2), 2: (0, 3), 3: (1, 2), 4: (1, 3), 5: (2, 3). 1. Input Validation and Preprocessing: Ensure exactly one input mode is active (--input, --inputSDF, or --npz). If input is a mesh, read it into a SimplePolygonMesh, normalize scale to 0.98, and apply rigid decorrelation translation using a seed (default 1). If input is.npz, verify it was passed via --npz, not -i. 2. Query Handler Initialization: Create InputQueryHandler based on input type: SDFQueryHandler for SDFs (epsilon \epsilon = 10^{-3}), MeshQueryHandler for standard meshes, or CGALQueryHandler if --cgal flag is set (requires build with -DSUBGRIDWITHCGAL=ON). 3. Pipeline Execution Loop: Iterate over each tetrahedron T in the tetrahedral grid range. Query Intersections: For all 6 edges of T, query the InputQueryHandler for intersections. Store parameters t and normals n. Call handler with recordNormals = !opts.nonormal. Count Intersections: Use countsfromisectts to count intersections per edge. If the sum of counts is 0, skip T. Mod2 Reduction: If opts.mod2 is true, apply mod2 reduction to intersection data. If this results in a skip condition, continue to next T. Construct Boundary Curves: Call boundarycombcurves using intersection data. This returns opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, and populates edgeoccupations. Generate Local Surface: Call dualsubgridsurface with tetrahedron positions, indices, intersection data, curves, and options (regalpha, projectduals, usenormals). If opts.nonormal is true, place each dual point at the centroid of the boundary polygon. Otherwise, solve the QEF to determine dual vertex positions. Accumulate Result: If localsoup.faces is not empty, append it to the global result soup. 4. Post-Processing: Construct primal and dual meshes from face-per-edge data. If the primal mesh is not manifold, throw an error. Optionally save the dual mesh as an OBJ file. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import time from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import List, Tuple, Dict @dataclass class TriangleSoup: vertices: List[List[float]] faces: List[List[int]] @dataclass class DualSubgridPipelineResult: soup: TriangleSoup nonzerotets: int totaltets: int nonnormaltets: int noneventets: int isecttime: float constructiontime: float @dataclass class DualSubgridPipelineOpts: mod2: bool userobust: bool showprogress: bool regalpha: float projectduals: bool nonormal: bool def rundualsubgridpipeline(inputsource, opts, tetgridresolution): # 1. Input Handling if inputsource.type == 'mesh': mesh = loadmesh(inputsource.path) mesh.scale = 0.98 mesh.translatedecorrelated(seed=1) queryhandler = MeshQueryHandler(mesh) elif inputsource.type == 'sdf': queryhandler = SDFQueryHandler(inputsource.name, epsilon=1e-3) elif inputsource.type == 'npz': raise NotImplementedError("NPZ handling uses a separate pipeline function.") else: raise ValueError("Exactly one input mode (--input, --inputSDF, or --npz) must be provided.") tetgrid = generatetetrahedralgrid(tetgridresolution) globalsoup = TriangleSoup(vertices=[], faces=[]) totaltets = 0 nonzerotets = 0 noneventets = 0 nonnormaltets = 0 starttime = time.time() # 2. Main Loop for tet in tetgrid: totaltets += 1 tetindices = tet.vertexindices tetpositions = tet.vertexpositions edgeisectts = [[] for in range(6)] edgeisectnormals = [[] for in range(6)] edgepairs = [(0,1), (0,2), (0,3), (1,2), (1,3), (2,3)] for edgeidx, (vi, vj) in enumerate(edgepairs): ts, normals = queryedgeintersections(queryhandler, tetpositions[vi], tetpositions[vj]) edgeisectts[edgeidx] = ts if not opts.nonormal: edgeisectnormals[edgeidx] = normals counts = [len(ts) for ts in edgeisectts] if sum(counts) == 0: continue nonzerotets += 1 if opts.mod2: for i in range(6): edgeisectts[i] = edgeisectts[i][:len(edgeisectts[i]) % 2] if sum(len(ts) for ts in edgeisectts) == 0: continue opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, edgeoccupations = \ boundarycombcurves(edgeisectts, edgeisectnormals, opts) localsoup = dualsubgridsurface( tetpositions=tetpositions, tetindices=tetindices, edgeisectts=edgeisectts, edgeisectnormals=edgeisectnormals, opencurves=opencurves, scoopcurves=scoopcurves, normalcurves=normalcurves, opts=opts) if len(localsoup.faces) > 0: globalsoup.vertices.extend(localsoup.vertices) globalsoup.faces.extend(localsoup.faces) endtime = time.time() constructiontime = endtime - starttime return DualSubgridPipelineResult( soup=globalsoup, nonzerotets=nonzerotets, totaltets=totaltets, nonnormaltets=nonnormaltets, noneventets=noneventets, isecttime=0.0, constructiontime=constructiontime) def dualsubgridsurface(tetpositions, tetindices, edgeisectts, edgeisectnormals, opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, opts): localsoup = TriangleSoup(vertices=[], faces=[]) dualvertices = [] allcurves = opencurves + scoopcurves + normalcurves for curve in allcurves: if opts.nonormal: centroid = computecentroid(curve.vertices) dualvertices.append(centroid) else: A, b = buildqefsystem(curve, edgeisectnormals) alpha = opts.regalpha I3 = np.eye(3) dualvertex = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + alpha I3, A.T @ b) if opts.projectduals: dualvertex = projecttolocalgridcell(dualvertex, tetpositions) dualvertices.append(dualvertex) faces = generatefacesfromcurvesandduals(allcurves, dualvertices) localsoup.vertices = dualvertices localsoup.faces = faces return localsoup def loadmesh(path): # Standard mesh loader returning object with.vertices,.faces,.scale,.translatedecorrelated pass def MeshQueryHandler(mesh): return type('MeshQueryHandler', (), {'mesh': mesh}) def SDFQueryHandler(name, epsilon): return type('SDFQueryHandler', (), {'name': name, 'epsilon': epsilon}) def generatetetrahedralgrid(res): # Returns list of tetrahedra objects with.vertexindices and.vertexpositions pass def queryedgeintersections(handler, p0, p1): d = np.array(p1) - np.array(p0) ts, normals = [], [] for tri in handler.mesh.faces: v0, v1, v2 = handler.mesh.vertices[tri[0]], handler.mesh.vertices[tri[1]], handler.mesh.vertices[tri[2]] e1, e2 = np.array(v1) - np.array(v0), np.array(v2) - np.array(v0) n = np.cross(e1, e2) denom = np.dot(d, n) if abs(denom) > 1e-8: f = 1.0 / denom s = np.array(p0) - np.array(v0) u = f np.dot(s, n) v = f np.dot(np.cross(d, s), e2) w = f np.dot(np.cross(e1, s), e1) if 0 <= u <= 1 and 0 <= v <= 1 and 0 <= u + v <= 1: t = f np.dot(s, e2) if 0 <= t <= 1: ts.append(t) normals.append(n / np.linalg.norm(n)) return ts, normals def boundarycombcurves(ts, normals, opts): # Sources do not specify the exact curve construction algorithm; standard subgrid logic groups edge intersections into open, scoop, and normal curves. opencurves = [] scoopcurves = [] normalcurves = [] edgeoccupations = {} return opencurves, scoopcurves, normalcurves, edgeoccupations def computecentroid(vertices): return np.mean(vertices, axis=0).tolist() def buildqefsystem(curve, normals): A = [] b = [] for edge in curve.edges: n = edge.normal p = edge.midpoint A.append(n) b.append(np.dot(n, p)) return np.array(A), np.array(b) def projecttolocalgridcell(point, tetpos): return np.clip(point, np.min(tetpos, axis=0), np.max(tetpos, axis=0)).tolist() def generatefacesfromcurvesandduals(curves, dualverts): # Sources do not specify the exact face generation algorithm; standard logic connects dual vertices to form triangles based on boundary curves. faces = [] for i in range(len(dualverts) - 2): faces.append([0, i+1, i+2]) return faces tetGridResolution: Integer n. The grid is n \times n \times n tetrahedra. Default: 64. regAlpha: Double. Regularization weight for QEF. Default: 0.1. mod2: Boolean. Enables mod2 intersection reduction. projectDuals: Boolean. Projects dual vertices to the local grid cell. noNormal: Boolean. Ignores normals, using centroid placement. Required for.npz inputs without normals. USEROBUSTQUERIES: Static boolean. Always false in standard builds. Even-Sum Condition: If result.noneventets > 0, the output may not be orientable and may have open holes. This is likely caused by a non-watertight input or a grid edge-intersection issue. Changing the resolution or perturbation may help. NPZ Input Normals: If loading from.npz and opts.nonormal is false, the.npz file must contain an isectnormals array. If missing, a runtime error is thrown. Robust Queries: Enabling robust queries (USEROBUSTQUERIES = true) makes the method ~2x slower with negligible effect on robustness, so it is disabled by default. Input Mode Conflict: Passing a.npz file via --input (or -i) instead of --npz causes an error. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra in the grid, O(n^3), where n is tetGridResolution. Each tetrahedron is processed independently. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra and the number of intersections per edge. The TriangleSoup size depends on the surface area relative to the grid resolution. Not given in the sources. The source provides timing breakdowns (query, construction, primal, dual) but no absolute performance metrics for specific hardware or resolutions. Scaling is determined by the grid resolution n. Higher resolutions increase accuracy but linearly increase the number of tetrahedra and thus computation time and memory usage. Strengths: Robust intersection queries (when enabled, though disabled by default), support for both mesh and SDF inputs, optional regularization for smooth dual vertex placement, and mod2 reduction for topological simplification. Limitations: Potential for non-orientable output if the even-sum condition is not met, dependency on grid resolution for accuracy, and performance cost of robust queries (if enabled). Use when extracting isosurfaces from complex meshes or SDFs where topological robustness is critical, and when a dual grid representation is preferred for subsequent processing (e.g., dual mesh construction). Avoid if real-time performance is critical and robust queries are needed (due to ~2x slowdown). Avoid if the input is known to be non-watertight and the even-sum condition cannot be satisfied. The Dual Subgrid Pipeline is part of the Subgrid Marching framework, developed by H. Baktash. It is described in the repository hbaktash/subgrid-marching. The method is an evolution of the Subgrid Surface Reconstruction technique, introducing a dual mesh representation to handle complex intersection patterns within tetrahedral cells. It supports various input types (mesh, SDF, precomputed NPZ) and offers configurable options for regularization and normal handling. It is used in computer graphics for isosurface extraction, particularly in contexts requiring robust handling of topological ambiguities and integration with dual mesh structures. hbaktash/subgrid-marching, https://github.com/hbaktash/subgrid-marching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tetrahedral Normal Calculation
head: Vertex-weighted tetrahedral normal
body: This method computes smooth isosurface normals for tetrahedral meshes by calculating vertex normals weighted by the volume of connected tetrahedra. It solves the problem of severe visual discontinuities that arise when using the constant cell normal Nt directly, which decreases rendering quality significantly. It differs from its siblings, such as Regularised Marching Tetrahedra which modifies the topology, by retaining the standard Marching Tetrahedrons topology but enhancing the shading data through pre-computed vertex attributes. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh where each tetrahedron ht has four vertices. Scalar field values at the vertices (used implicitly to determine the plane orientation, though the normal is constant per cell). The connectivity list of tetrahedra. Outputs: A vertex normal vector Nv for each mesh vertex, stored in the data file. During rendering, a smooth interpolated normal for any intersection point on the isosurface. Data Structures: Vertex Normal Array: An array of 3D vectors, one per vertex. Tetrahedron Data: For each tetrahedron, the pre-computed plane normal Nt and volume V(ht). Steps: 1. Compute Tetrahedron Plane Normal (Nt): For each tetrahedron ht, determine the normal Nt = (a, b, c)^T of the plane describing the iso-surface within that cell. This normal is constant within the cell because the orientation of the plane is independent of the iso-value. Note: The specific geometric calculation of Nt from vertex positions and scalar values is assumed to be handled by the parent Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm. This method assumes Nt is available. 2. Compute Vertex Normals (Nv): For each vertex v in the mesh, calculate its normal Nv by summing the contributions of all tetrahedra ht connected to v. The contribution is weighted by the volume of the tetrahedron V(ht). The formula is: Nv = \sum{t=0}^{n} Nt V(ht) where: n is the number of tetrahedra connected to vertex v. Nt is the plane normal of tetrahedron ht. V(ht) is the volume of tetrahedron ht. After the summation, normalize the resulting vector: Nv \leftarrow \frac{Nv}{\|Nv\|} Store Nv for each vertex. 3. Interpolate Normal at Intersection Point: During ray traversal, when an intersection point P is found within a tetrahedron ht: a. Calculate the 3D barycentric coordinates (\lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) of P with respect to the four vertices of ht. This extends the 2D barycentric coordinate system used for triangles to the 3D tetrahedral case. b. Interpolate the pre-computed vertex normals using these barycentric coordinates: N{interp} = \sum{i=0}^{3} \lambdai N{v,i} where N{v,i} is the pre-computed normal of the i-th vertex of the tetrahedron. c. Normalize the interpolated vector: N{final} = \frac{N{interp}}{\|N{interp}\|} d. Use N{final} for shading calculations. Parameters: None specific to the calculation itself, other than the mesh geometry and scalar field. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuities: Using the constant cell normal Nt directly results in severe discontinuities between tetrahedra surfaces. This method mitigates that by smoothing across vertices. Zero Volume: If a tetrahedron has zero volume (degenerate), it contributes nothing to the sum. Ensure degenerate tetrahedra are handled or excluded during pre-computation. Normalization: Failure to normalize Nv after summation and N{interp} after interpolation will result in incorrect lighting intensity and direction. This method computes smooth isosurface normals for newly generated triangles created by cutting tetrahedra during the Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm. It specifically addresses triangles that lie strictly inside the isosurface (i.e., the parent tetrahedron contains only cutting planes, not the isosurface itself). It differs from gradient-based approximations by averaging the normals of the intersecting cutting planes, providing a geometrically consistent normal for interior cut faces [11806-average-normal-calculation-for-cut-triangles.md]. In a fragment shader implementation, the interpolated normal vector is output as the color. The step involves setting the fragment color to the normal vector: FragColor = vec4(oNormal, 1.0);. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is O(V \cdot T{avg}) where V is the number of vertices and T{avg} is the average number of tetrahedra per vertex. Rendering interpolation is O(1) per intersection point. Memory Complexity: Requires storing one 3D vector per vertex. Strengths: Produces smooth shading across the isosurface, significantly improving visual quality over flat shading with cell normals. Limitations: Requires pre-computation and storage of vertex normals. Does not address topological artifacts, only shading artifacts. When to use: When smooth shading is required for tetrahedral volume rendering and the parent algorithm provides tetrahedron plane normals. This method was described in the context of fast ray traversal of tetrahedral and hexahedral meshes for direct volume rendering. It addresses the visual quality issues inherent in the basic Marching Tetrahedrons algorithm when using flat shading. name: Average Normal Calculation for Cut Triangles
head: Cut Plane Normal Averaging, Interior Tetrahedra Normal Calculation
body: This method computes surface normals for newly generated triangles created when cutting tetrahedra that contain only cutting planes (interior to the isosurface). It differs from gradient-based approximations by averaging the normals of the intersecting cutting planes, providing a geometrically consistent normal for interior cut faces. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Identify new triangles belonging to tetrahedra that only contain cutting planes (interior to the isosurface). 2. Compute the cutting plane normal for each vertex using the distance of the vertex's tetrahedron to the plane, as described in [ABE+03]. 3. Calculate the average normal by summing the cutting plane normals and normalizing the result. 4. Output the averaged normal for shading. Formulas: \mathbf{n}{avg} = \frac{\sum{i=0}^{3} \mathbf{n}{cut, i}}{\|\sum{i=0}^{3} \mathbf{n}{cut, i}\|} [G: Standard vector normalization], where \mathbf{n}{cut, i} is the cutting plane normal for vertex i and \mathbf{n}{avg} is the resulting averaged normal. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: This specific normal calculation must be performed in the vertex shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateaveragenormalcuttriangle(distances, vertexpositions): # Step 1: Identify interior tetrahedra triangles (handled by traversal) # Step 2: Compute cutting plane normals from vertex distances # Not given in the sources. Implementation depends on [ABE+03]. # Compute normal from distance of vertex's tetrahedron to the plane. cutnormals = [] for i in range(4): ni = computecuttingplanenormal(distances[i], vertexpositions[i]) cutnormals.append(ni) # Step 3: Average the cutting plane normals sumnormal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for n in cutnormals: sumnormal[0] += n[0] sumnormal[1] += n[1] sumnormal[2] += n[2] # Step 4: Normalize and return magnitude = (sumnormal[0]2 + sumnormal[1]2 + sumnormal[2]2)0.5 if magnitude > 0.0: return [sumnormal[0]/magnitude, sumnormal[1]/magnitude, sumnormal[2]/magnitude] else: return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] This variant approximates the normal from the gradient at the fragment's position using volume information stored in a 3D texture. It is used for new triangles of the cut that belong to tetrahedra containing the isosurface. It differs from the average normal method by using local gradient information rather than averaging cutting plane normals. It must be performed in the fragment shader because 3D texture access is extremely slow at the vertex shader level. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Performance testing was conducted on a Pentium IV PC with 1 GB RAM and a GeForce 6800 Ultra graphics card with 256 MB memory, showing real-time framerates for interactive cutting on models like the heart, jaw, hip, and head. Strengths include smooth normals for interior cut faces and efficient vertex shader execution. Limitations include applicability only to tetrahedra containing only cutting planes. Use for interior cut faces in Marching Tetrahedrons when vertex shader performance is critical; avoid for tetrahedra containing the isosurface. This method is part of the MTCut algorithm, which extends the Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm to support interactive cutting of isosurfaces. The specific normal calculation for interior tetrahedra relies on the cutting plane normal computation described in [ABE+03]. The method was tested on a Pentium IV PC with a GeForce 6800 Ultra graphics card, demonstrating its efficiency for real-time haptic and visual feedback.
