name: McGrids
head: Monte Carlo-Driven Adaptive Grids
body: McGrids is an iso-surface extraction method that constructs adaptive, non-uniform tetrahedral grids using an iterative Monte Carlo process to estimate a probability density function (PDF) based on the implicit field, followed by a refinement step and mesh extraction via Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform grid sampling by concentrating grid points near surfaces and geometric details, significantly reducing the number of implicit field queries and memory usage compared to uniform grids. Unlike Regularised Marching Tetrahedra or Subgrid Pipeline which may rely on fixed or hierarchical structures, McGrids dynamically adapts the grid topology through probabilistic sampling and Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation (CVT) relaxation. Inputs: Implicit field function f(\mathbf{x}) returning a scalar value. Iso-value \alpha (typically 0). Bounding region (user-defined). Terminating threshold \tau (default 10^{-4}, typical range 10^{-3} to 10^{-5}). Maximum number of Monte Carlo iterations N{iter} (optional, used if termination condition is not met). Minimum tetrahedron volume constraint V{min} (optional, for fractal surfaces). Outputs: A set of vertices \mathcal{V} forming a Delaunay tetrahedralization. A mesh extracted via Marching Tetrahedra. Data Structures: 1. Delaunay Tetrahedralization: Stores grid points as vertices. Tetrahedra \mathcal{T} are formed such that no point lies inside the circumsphere of any tetrahedron. 2. Voronoi Diagram (Dual): One-to-one mapping to McGrid points. Voronoi cells \Omegai store the implicit values and density information. 3. Implicit Values: Stored in Voronoi cells corresponding to vertices. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Define a continuous uniform distribution over the user-defined bounding region. Initialize an empty Delaunay tessellation. 2. Monte Carlo Grid Generation (Iterative): Repeat for k = 1 to N{iter}: 2.1. PDF Estimation: For each vertex xi with Voronoi cell \Omegai, compute the discrete probability p(i): p(i) = d(xi) \cdot \frac{\int{\Omegai} \mathbf{x} \, d\mathbf{x}}{\sum{j=1}^n \int{\Omegaj} \mathbf{x} \, d\mathbf{x}} where d(xi) is the density value at point xi, and the integral represents the volume of the Voronoi region \Omegai. Normalize to create a cumulative distribution: p'(i) = p(i) / \sum{j=1}^n p(j). Optimization: When new points are inserted, only update the volumes of Voronoi cells adjacent to the newly inserted cells. 2.2. Weighted Random Sampling: Sample a uniform random number u \sim U[0, 1]. Select a Voronoi region \Omegai based on the cumulative distribution p'(i). Tessellate \Omegai into tetrahedra. Calculate the volume of each tetrahedron within \Omegai to form a discrete cumulative distribution. Sample a uniform number to select a specific tetrahedron T{sel} \subset \Omegai. Sample a new point \mathbf{x}{new} uniformly within T{sel}. 2.3. CVT Relaxation: Compute the centroid of the Voronoi region \Omega{new} corresponding to \mathbf{x}{new}. Move \mathbf{x}{new} to this centroid position. This is Lloyd's method for stable CVT. 2.4. Insertion and Update: Insert the relaxed point \mathbf{x}{new} into the Delaunay tessellation. Query the implicit field: v{new} = f(\mathbf{x}{new}). Store v{new} in the corresponding Voronoi cell. Interpolate point density values to the tetrahedra in the entire space and normalize them by their volumes to form a piecewise linear approximation of the PDF. 3. Refinement (Midpoint Insertion): For each tetrahedron T \in \mathcal{T}: 3.1. Trimming (Void Culling): If all four vertices of T have implicit values with the same sign (all > \alpha or all < \alpha), the tetrahedron does not intersect the surface. Set the probability density values of its incident vertices to 0 to prevent further sampling in void regions. 3.2. Midpoint Evaluation: If vertices have mixed signs (surface intersects T): Perform linear interpolation on edges to find points \mathbf{p}j where f(\mathbf{p}j) = \alpha. Calculate the geometric midpoint \mathbf{m} by averaging the positions of these interpolated points: \mathbf{m} = \frac{1}{N{edges}} \sum \mathbf{p}j Evaluate the true implicit value at the midpoint: vm = f(\mathbf{m}). Calculate error: e = |vm - \alpha|. 3.3. Insertion Condition: If e > \tau AND \text{Vol}(T) > V{min}: Insert \mathbf{m} into the McGrids. Apply CVT relaxation to \mathbf{m} (move to centroid of its new Voronoi region). Query f(\mathbf{m}) and update the tessellation. Else, consider T adequately refined. 4. Termination: Stop refining when all tetrahedra meet the criteria (e \le \tau or \text{Vol}(T) \le V{min}). In extreme cases (e.g., fractal surfaces), enforce V{min} to prevent excessive refinement. 5. Mesh Extraction: Apply the Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm to the final Delaunay tetrahedralization to extract the iso-surface mesh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. A strategy to densify grids near surfaces. It evaluates the implicit value at the geometric midpoint of surface-intersecting tetrahedra and inserts it if the error exceeds a threshold, providing a curvature-like approximation without explicit normal information. Time Complexity: Dominated by the iterative Monte Carlo process and Delaunay/Voronoi updates. Each iteration involves sampling, tessellation, and relaxation. Measured Performance: On the 'Lucy' model with threshold 10^{-3}, McGrids with CVT required 15 iterations and 228,472 queries, while without CVT it required 58 iterations and 319,185 queries. Strengths: Reduces implicit field queries and memory usage; produces high-quality meshes with rich geometric details; adaptive to complex shapes. Limitations: Slower runtime than fixed-grid methods (like standard DMT or FlexiCubes) due to dynamic grid computation; does not assume normal information, potentially requiring denser grids than Dual Contouring for sharp features; incurs overhead for grid construction. When to use: When high accuracy and detail are required, and implicit field queries are expensive. Suitable for neural implicit fields and complex analytical SDFs. When not to use: For low-resolution meshes or when implicit field queries are extremely cheap; conventional methods like Marching Cubes may be more efficient. McGrids was proposed in the paper "McGrids: Monte Carlo-Driven Adaptive Grids for Iso-Surface Extraction". It addresses the limitations of uniform grids in iso-surface extraction by formulating grid construction as a probability sampling problem. The method leverages Delaunay tetrahedralization and Voronoi diagrams to guide the adaptive sampling process. It has been applied in differentiable multiview reconstruction pipelines, replacing mesh extraction components in methods like DMT and FlexiCubes to achieve more accurate reconstruction results. name: Exact Fiber Surface Extraction
head: Base Fiber Surface Extraction, Correct Fiber Surface Extraction, Exact Fiber Surface Extraction on Tetrahedral Meshes
body: Exact Fiber Surface Extraction computes the pre-image of a 1-manifold path (Fiber Surface Control Polygon, FSCP) in the range of a bivariate field f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2 over a tetrahedral mesh. It solves the problem of approximating these surfaces using signed distance fields, which fail to capture sharp bends and complex topologies. Unlike Regularised Marching Tetrahedra which smooths geometry, this method guarantees planar pre-images within each tetrahedron by decomposing the extraction into base surface generation and precise clipping. The algorithm operates in two stages: extracting base fiber surfaces for each edge of the FSCP, and then clipping these surfaces to the specific segments defined by the FSCP vertices. Input: Tetrahedral mesh M, bivariate function f = (f1, f2), FSCP defined by vertices v0, \dots, vk and edges ei = (vi, v{i+1}). Output: A triangle soup representing the fiber surface. Vertex: Position \mathbf{w}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, function values \mathbf{f}i = (f1(\mathbf{w}i), f2(\mathbf{w}i)) \in \mathbb{R}^2. Case Index: Integer bitmask for vertex classification. Triangle: List of three vertices with interpolated positions and function values. For each edge e of the FSCP, defined by the infinite line \vec{l} passing through its endpoints, the algorithm extracts the pre-image of \vec{l} within each tetrahedron T \in M. This ignores the specific endpoints of the edge, treating it as an infinite line cut. 1. Iterate over all tetrahedra T \in M. 2. Initialize case index C = 0. 3. For each vertex \mathbf{w}i of T: a. Compute the signed range distance hi from the function values \mathbf{f}i to the line \vec{l}. b. If hi > 0, set the i-th bit of C: C = C \mid 2^i. 4. For all triangles t defined by the Marching Tetrahedra lookup table for case C: a. Interpolate vertex positions \mathbf{w} and function values \mathbf{f} at the triangle vertices. b. Store the triangle as a "base fiber surface" triangle. Formula for Signed Range Distance: The line \vec{l} is represented in Hesse normal form: \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d, where \mathbf{n} is the unit normal vector in \mathbb{R}^2 and d is the distance from the origin. For a vertex with function values \mathbf{f}i = (f1, f2): hi = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{f}i - d The pre-image of the line is the zero level-set of h: f^{-1}(\vec{l}) = \{ \mathbf{p} \in \text{Dom } f \mid h(\mathbf{p}) = 0 \}. Due to linear interpolation, this pre-image is guaranteed to be planar within each tetrahedron. The base fiber surfaces from Stage 1 are clipped to retain only the segment between the fibers induced by the FSCP edge endpoints u and v. 1. For each base fiber surface triangle T{base} generated in Stage 1 for edge e=(u,v): a. Define the line segment L in the range from u to v. Parameterize L as \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where u corresponds to t=0 and v corresponds to t=1. b. Initialize case index C = 0. c. For each vertex \mathbf{w}j of T{base} with function values \mathbf{f}j: i. Project \mathbf{f}j onto L to compute parameter tj. ii. Classify the vertex: If tj < 0, set ternary bit to 0 (minus): C = C + 0 \cdot 3^j. If 0 \le tj \le 1, set ternary bit to 1 (neutral): C = C + 1 \cdot 3^j. If tj > 1, set ternary bit to 2 (plus): C = C + 2 \cdot 3^j. d. For all triangles T' defined by the "Fiber Segment" lookup table for case C: i. Interpolate vertex positions on the edges of T{base}. ii. Add T' to the output mesh M{out}. Formula for Parameter t: Given line segment L defined by endpoints u and v, the parameter t for a point \mathbf{f} is computed by projecting \mathbf{f} onto the line. Specifically, if L is parameterized such that u is at t=0 and v is at t=1, t represents the relative position along the segment. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Args: mesh: List of tetrahedra, each containing 4 vertices. functions: Bivariate field f = (f1, f2). fscpedges: List of line segments in range space, each defined by two points (u, v). Returns: List of triangles representing the fiber surface. """ outputtriangles = [] for u, v in fscpedges: # Hesse normal form for line through u and v in R2 dx, dy = v[0] - u[0], v[1] - u[1] length = (dx2 + dy2)0.5 n = (-dy / length, dx / length) d = n[0] u[0] + n[1] u[1] for tet in mesh: # Stage 1: Base Fiber Surface Extraction casec = 0 verts = [] for i, w in enumerate(tet.vertices): fval = functions(w) h = n[0] fval[0] + n[1] fval[1] - d verts.append({'pos': w.pos, 'f': fval, 'h': h}) if h > 0: casec |= (1 << i) # Extract base triangles using Marching Tetrahedra lookup basetriindices = MARCHINGTETTRIANGLES[casec] basetriangles = [] for triidxlist in basetriindices: triverts = [] for idx in triidxlist: if idx < 4: triverts.append(verts[idx]) else: # Interpolated point from edge intersection edgev1idx = idx - 4 v1, v2 = verts[edgev1idx], verts[edgev1idx + 1] t = v1['h'] / (v1['h'] - v2['h']) pos = v1['pos'] + t (v2['pos'] - v1['pos']) f = v1['f'] + t (v2['f'] - v1['f']) triverts.append({'pos': pos, 'f': f}) basetriangles.append(triverts) # Stage 2: Fiber Clipping for triverts in basetriangles: tricase = 0 tridata = [] for j, vdata in enumerate(triverts): fval = vdata['f'] vecuv = (v[0] - u[0], v[1] - u[1]) vecuf = (fval[0] - u[0], fval[1] - u[1]) t = (vecuf[0] vecuv[0] + vecuf[1] vecuv[1]) / (vecuv[0]2 + vecuv[1]2) if t < 0: bit = 0 elif t <= 1: bit = 1 else: bit = 2 tricase += bit (3 j) tridata.append({'pos': vdata['pos'], 'f': fval, 't': t}) # Extract clipped triangles using Fiber Segment lookup clippedtriindices = FIBERSEGMENTTRIANGLES[tricase] for triidxlist in clippedtriindices: clippedverts = [] for idx in triidxlist: if idx < 3: clippedverts.append(tridata[idx]) else: # Interpolate on edge where t crosses 0 or 1 edgev1idx = idx - 3 v1, v2 = tridata[edgev1idx], tridata[edgev1idx + 1] # Interpolate to find point where t=0 or t=1 ttarget = 0.0 if v1['t'] < 0 and v2['t'] >= 0 else 1.0 tfrac = (ttarget - v1['t']) / (v2['t'] - v1['t']) pos = v1['pos'] + tfrac (v2['pos'] - v1['pos']) clippedverts.append({'pos': pos, 'f': v1['f'] + tfrac (v2['f'] - v1['f'])}) outputtriangles.append(clippedverts) return outputtriangles Mesh Resolution: Dependent on input data. FSCP Complexity: Number of edges E in the FSCP. 1. Bends in FSCP: The signed distance field approximation fails to capture bends in the FSCP because the zero level-set shortcuts the bends. This inaccuracy occurs for all bends because polygon bends are unlikely to coincide precisely with domain vertices. 2. Empty Level Set: Vertex classification fails when the FSCP is completely included within the image of a tetrahedron and none of its vertices lie in the inside of the FSCP, resulting in an empty 0 level set. 3. Multiple Crossings: An FSCP may cross the image of an edge of the domain multiple times, preventing the identification of intersections of the fiber surface with a tetrahedron due to vertex classification, leading to incorrect topology. 4. Degenerate Tetrahedra: Degenerate tetrahedra where all four vertices belong to the inverse image are handled by ensuring the boundary between degenerate and non-degenerate tetrahedra is extracted via shared faces. Clips the base fiber surface triangles to retain only the segment between fibers f^{-1}(u) and f^{-1}(v) corresponding to FSCP edge endpoints u and v. It uses a ternary classification (t<0, 0 \le t \le 1, t>1) resulting in 27 possible cases per triangle, handled by a lookup table. The baseline algorithm that processes all tetrahedra without acceleration, extracting a triangle soup. It may optionally merge coincident points to form a manifold surface using VTK's vtkMergePoints class. Parallelizes the extraction over cells. The domain is segmented into n partitions, each processed by a thread. Synchronization is only required for memory allocation; threads read independently and write to distinct memory intervals. Time Complexity: O(N \times E), where N is the number of input tetrahedra and E is the number of FSCP edges. Measured Performance: Engine dataset (35,438,625 tets, 11 polygon edges): 9.121 seconds. Enzo dataset (82,906,875 tets, 8 polygon edges): 17.264 seconds. Strengths: Exact extraction for tetrahedral meshes; tractable due to planar pre-images. Limitations: Not tractable for trilinear hexahedral meshes due to complex, non-linear fiber intersections (hyperbolic sheets). When to Use: When exact topology and geometry of fiber surfaces are required for bivariate fields on tetrahedral meshes. When Not to Use: For hexahedral meshes with trilinear interpolation, or when interactive performance is critical without acceleration structures. The method was introduced to overcome the inaccuracies of previous approximate algorithms that relied on rasterizing the range and computing signed distance fields. It leverages the property that tetrahedral meshes allow exact fiber extraction because isosurfaces are planar cuts, making fibers the intersection of two planes (a line segment), whereas hexahedral meshes with trilinear interpolation are intractable. name: Marching Tetrahedra Reconstruction
head: Welland-based Marching Tetrahedra, marching-tets-reconstruction
body: Marching Tetrahedra Reconstruction is a surface reconstruction method that converts a set of input vertices and normals into a 3D mesh by computing an implicit field using the Welland function, sampling it on a tetrahedral grid, and extracting the zero-level set via Marching Tetrahedra. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by using a tetrahedral decomposition of the grid cells, which eliminates the ambiguity cases inherent in cube-based extraction. It builds on Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm but replaces the standard linear interpolation with a Welland-based implicit field evaluation. Inputs: V: Input vertex positions, shape (N, 3). N: Input vertex normals, shape (N, 3). epsilon: Distance control parameter. numtets: Grid resolution \{nx, ny, nz\}. wellandradius: Radius parameter h for the Welland function. returnlargest: Boolean flag to keep only the largest connected component. Outputs: V2: Output mesh vertices, shape (M, 3). F2: Output mesh faces, shape (K, 3), containing indices into V2. Data Structures: C: Constraint points matrix, shape (3N, 3). D: Constraint values vector, shape (3N, 1). TV: Tetrahedral grid vertices, shape (nx ny nz, 3). TF: Tetrahedron connectivity, shape (6(nx-1)(ny-1)(nz-1), 4). fx: Implicit field values at grid vertices, shape (nx ny nz, 1). SV: Extracted surface vertices, shape (V{out}, 3). SF: Extracted surface faces, shape (F{out}, 3). Steps: 1. Preprocess Input: Re-center vertices on the origin: V = V - \text{mean}(V, \text{axis}=0) 2. Compute Constraint Points and Values: Calculate eps as: \text{eps} = \epsilon \cdot \| \min(V) - \max(V) \| Initialize C (size 3N \times 3) and D (size 3N). For each vertex i from 0 to N-1: a. Set C[i] = V[i] and D[i] = 0.0. b. Find the distance to the second nearest neighbor of V[i] in V (the nearest is itself). Let this be d{nn}. If d{nn} = 0, set d{nn} = 0.1. c. Compute constraint point c{out} and value d{out} by moving from V[i] along normal N[i] by distance eps, clamped by d{nn}. Specifically, c{out} = V[i] + N[i] \cdot \text{eps}. If \|c{out} - V[i]\| > d{nn}, clamp the step to d{nn} along the normal direction. Set d{out} = \text{eps}. d. Set C[N+i] = c{out} and D[N+i] = d{out}. e. Compute constraint point c{in} and value d{in} by moving from V[i] along normal -N[i] by distance eps, clamped by d{nn}. f. Set C[2N+i] = c{in} and D[2N+i] = -d{in}. 3. Generate Tet Grid: Compute grid bounds g{min} = \min(V) and g{max} = \max(V). Add padding p = \{\text{eps}, \text{eps}, \text{eps}\}. Generate grid vertices TV of size nx ny nz using linear spacing over [g{min}-p, g{max}+p]. Generate tetrahedron connectivity TF. Each grid cell (cube) defined by corners v1 \dots v8 is split into 6 tetrahedra: T1: (v1, v3, v8, v7) T2: (v1, v8, v5, v7) T3: (v1, v3, v4, v8) T4: (v1, v4, v2, v8) T5: (v1, v6, v5, v8) T6: (v1, v2, v6, v8) 4. Compute Implicit Function Values: For each grid vertex p in TV: a. Construct a basis vector b(p) of degree 2: [1, x, y, z, xy, xz, yz, x^2, y^2, z^2]. b. Construct the weights matrix W for the Welland function. For each constraint point Cj with value Dj, compute weight wj = \left( \frac{4 rj}{h} + 1 \right) \left( 1 - \frac{rj}{h} \right)^4, where rj = \|p - Cj\| and h is wellandradius. W is diagonal with W{jj} = wj. c. Construct the basis matrix B where row j is b(Cj). d. Solve for coefficients a in the system B^T W B a = B^T W D. This is typically done via Cholesky decomposition (LL^T) or LDLT decomposition. e. Evaluate fx(p) = b(p) \cdot a. 5. March Tetrahedra: For each tetrahedron T in TF with vertices p0, p1, p2, p3 and values v0, v1, v2, v3: a. Determine configuration index C = 1 \cdot (v0 < 0) + 2 \cdot (v1 < 0) + 4 \cdot (v2 < 0) + 8 \cdot (v3 < 0). b. Based on C, generate triangle vertices using linear interpolation on edges. The function generatetrianglepoint(p1, p2, v1, v2) returns p1 + \frac{0 - v1}{v2 - v1}(p2 - p1). c. Handle cases: C \in \{0, 15\}: No triangles. C \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}: One triangle. C \in \{3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12\}: Two triangles. C \in \{7, 11, 13, 14\}: One triangle. d. Append generated vertices to vi and face indices to fi. 6. Cleanup (if returnlargest is true): a. Merge Vertices: Build a KDTree from SV. For each vertex, find neighbors within tolerance 0.00001. Compute the centroid of the cluster and replace all vertices in the cluster with this centroid. Update face indices accordingly. b. Largest Component: Build an adjacency list from the merged faces. Perform DFS/BFS to find connected components. Keep only the faces belonging to the largest component. 7. Convert Output: Convert temporary vectors to matrices SV and SF. Return (SV, SF). Pseudocode: import numpy as np def generatetrianglepoint(p1, p2, v1, v2): denom = v2 - v1 if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return (p1 + p2) / 2.0 return p1 + (0.0 - v1) / denom (p2 - p1) def marchingtetrahedrareconstruction(V, N, epsilon, numtets, wellandradius, returnlargest=True): # 1. Preprocess V = V - np.mean(V, axis=0) # 2. Compute Constraints eps = epsilon np.linalg.norm(np.min(V, axis=0) - np.max(V, axis=0)) Nverts = V.shape[0] C = np.zeros((3 Nverts, 3)) D = np.zeros(3 Nverts) # Build KDTree for neighbor search tree = np.empty((Nverts, 3)) tree[:] = V # Simple brute-force kNN for 2nd nearest neighbor to avoid external libs def get2ndnndist(p, V): dists = [np.linalg.norm(p - v) for v in V] dists.sort() return dists[1] if len(dists) > 1 else 0.1 for i in range(Nverts): nndist = get2ndnndist(V[i], V) if nndist == 0: nndist = 0.1 # Constraint 1: Vertex itself C[i] = V[i] D[i] = 0.0 # Constraint 2: Outside cout = V[i] + N[i] eps if np.linalg.norm(cout - V[i]) > nndist: cout = V[i] + N[i] (nndist / np.linalg.norm(N[i])) C[Nverts + i] = cout D[Nverts + i] = eps # Constraint 3: Inside cin = V[i] - N[i] eps if np.linalg.norm(cin - V[i]) > nndist: cin = V[i] - N[i] (nndist / np.linalg.norm(N[i])) C[2 Nverts + i] = cin D[2 Nverts + i] = -eps # 3. Generate Grid gmin = np.min(V, axis=0) gmax = np.max(V, axis=0) padding = np.array([eps, eps, eps]) nx, ny, nz = numtets xpts = np.linspace(gmin[0] - padding[0], gmax[0] + padding[0], nx) ypts = np.linspace(gmin[1] - padding[1], gmax[1] + padding[1], ny) zpts = np.linspace(gmin[2] - padding[2], gmax[2] + padding[2], nz) TV = np.zeros((nx ny nz, 3)) vi = 0 for k in range(nz): for j in range(ny): for i in range(nx): TV[vi] = [xpts[i], ypts[j], zpts[k]] vi += 1 TF = np.zeros(((nx-1)(ny-1)(nz-1)6, 4), dtype=int) ti = 0 for i in range(nx-1): for j in range(ny-1): for k in range(nz-1): v1 = i + nx(j + nyk) v2 = (i+1) + nx(j + nyk) v3 = i + nx((j+1) + nyk) v4 = (i+1) + nx((j+1) + nyk) v5 = i + nx(j + ny(k+1)) v6 = (i+1) + nx(j + ny(k+1)) v7 = i + nx((j+1) + ny(k+1)) v8 = (i+1) + nx((j+1) + ny(k+1)) TF[ti] = [v1, v3, v8, v7] TF[ti+1] = [v1, v8, v5, v7] TF[ti+2] = [v1, v3, v4, v8] TF[ti+3] = [v1, v4, v2, v8] TF[ti+4] = [v1, v6, v5, v8] TF[ti+5] = [v1, v2, v6, v8] ti += 6 # 4. Compute Implicit Field fx = np.zeros(nx ny nz) basisdim = 10 for idx in range(nx ny nz): p = TV[idx] x, y, z = p bp = np.array([1, x, y, z, xy, xz, yz, xx, yy, zz]) B = np.zeros((3 Nverts, basisdim)) for j in range(3 Nverts): cx, cy, cz = C[j] B[j] = np.array([1, cx, cy, cz, cxcy, cxcz, cycz, cxcx, cycy, czcz]) W = np.zeros((3 Nverts, 3 Nverts)) for j in range(3 Nverts): r = np.linalg.norm(p - C[j]) w = ((4 r / wellandradius) + 1) (1 - r / wellandradius) w = w4 W[j, j] = w L = B.T @ W @ B R = B.T @ W @ D try: a = np.linalg.solve(L, R) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: a = np.linalg.lstsq(L, R, rcond=None)[0] fx[idx] = bp @ a # 5. March Tetrahedra vi = [] fi = [] t = 0 for tetidx in range(TF.shape[0]): tet = TF[tetidx] p0, p1, p2, p3 = TV[tet[0]], TV[tet[1]], TV[tet[2]], TV[tet[3]] v0, v1, v2, v3 = fx[tet[0]], fx[tet[1]], fx[tet[2]], fx[tet[3]] config = 0 if v0 < 0: config += 1 if v1 < 0: config += 2 if v2 < 0: config += 4 if v3 < 0: config += 8 if config in [0, 15]: continue if config == 1: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p1, v0, v1) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p2, v0, v2) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p3, v0, v3) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t, t+1, t+2]) t += 3 elif config == 2: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p0, v1, v0) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p3, v1, v3) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p2, v1, v2) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t, t+1, t+2]) t += 3 elif config == 3: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p3, v0, v3) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p2, v1, v2) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p3, v1, v3) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 t1b = t2a t2b = t1a t3b = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p2, v0, v2) vi.extend(t1b); vi.extend(t2b); vi.extend(t3b) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 elif config == 4: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p2, p0, v2, v0) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p2, p1, v2, v1) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p2, p3, v2, v3) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 elif config == 5: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p3, v0, v3) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p2, v1, v2) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p1, v0, v1) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 elif config == 8: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p3, p0, v3, v0) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p3, p2, v3, v2) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p3, p1, v3, v1) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t, t+1, t+2]) t += 3 elif config == 9: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p1, v0, v1) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p3, v1, v3) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p2, v0, v2) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 t1b = t3a t2b = t2a t3b = generatetrianglepoint(p2, p3, v2, v3) vi.extend(t1b); vi.extend(t2b); vi.extend(t3b) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 elif config == 10: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p1, v0, v1) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p3, v0, v3) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p2, v1, v2) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t, t+1, t+2]) t += 3 t1b = t2a t2b = generatetrianglepoint(p2, p3, v2, v3) t3b = t3a vi.extend(t1b); vi.extend(t2b); vi.extend(t3b) fi.extend([t, t+1, t+2]) t += 3 elif config == 11: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p2, p0, v2, v0) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p2, p1, v2, v1) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p2, p3, v2, v3) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 elif config == 12: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p2, v0, v2) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p2, v1, v2) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p3, v1, v3) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t, t+1, t+2]) t += 3 t1b = t3a t2b = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p3, v0, v3) t3b = t1a vi.extend(t1b); vi.extend(t2b); vi.extend(t3b) fi.extend([t, t+1, t+2]) t += 3 elif config == 13: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p0, v1, v0) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p3, v1, v3) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p1, p2, v1, v2) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 elif config == 14: t1a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p1, v0, v1) t2a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p2, v0, v2) t3a = generatetrianglepoint(p0, p3, v0, v3) vi.extend(t1a); vi.extend(t2a); vi.extend(t3a) fi.extend([t+2, t+1, t]) t += 3 SV = np.array(vi).reshape(-1, 3) SF = np.array(fi).reshape(-1, 3) # 6. Cleanup if returnlargest and len(SV) > 0: # Merge vertices mergetree = np.empty((len(SV), 3)) mergetree[:] = SV newSV = [] visited = set() vertmap = {} for i in range(len(SV)): if i in visited: continue dists = [np.linalg.norm(SV[i] - v) for v in SV] neighbors = [j for j, d in enumerate(dists) if d < 0.00001] if not neighbors: neighbors = [i] centroid = np.mean(SV[neighbors], axis=0) newidx = len(newSV) newSV.append(centroid) for n in neighbors: visited.add(n) vertmap[n] = newidx SV = np.array(newSV) # Remap faces newSF = [] for face in SF: newface = [vertmap[f] for f in face] newSF.append(newface) SF = np.array(newSF) # Largest Component adj = {i: [] for i in range(len(SV))} for f in SF: adj[f[0]].append(f[1]) adj[f[0]].append(f[2]) adj[f[1]].append(f[0]) adj[f[1]].append(f[2]) adj[f[2]].append(f[0]) adj[f[2]].append(f[1]) for k in adj: adj[k] = list(set(adj[k])) visited = set() largestcomp = [] maxsize = 0 for startnode in range(len(SV)): if startnode in visited: continue comp = [] stack = [startnode] while stack: u = stack.pop() if u in visited: continue visited.add(u) comp.append(u) for v in adj[u]: if v not in visited: stack.append(v) if len(comp) > maxsize: maxsize = len(comp) largestcomp = comp compset = set(largestcomp) finalSF = [f for f in SF if f[0] in compset and f[1] in compset and f[2] in compset] finalSV = SV[list(compset)] idxmap = {old: new for new, old in enumerate(compset)} finalSF = [[idxmap[f[0]], idxmap[f[1]], idxmap[f[2]]] for f in finalSF] return finalSV, np.array(finalSF) return SV, SF Pitfalls: Using conservative matrix resizing (e.g., repeated pushback or resize on Eigen matrices) is extremely slow. The implementation avoids this by filling temporary vectors (vi, fi) and converting to matrices only once at the end. The mergevertices function is not parallelizable because range search requires unique results, making iterations dependent. Additionally, replacevalues may cause race conditions if mergevertices is parallelized. The connectedcomponents function is not easy to parallelize because the seen vector makes iterations dependent on each other. Accessing adj.at(u) multiple times in the DFS loop is inefficient. A suggestion is to make a local copy of adj.at(u). The addedge function uses linear search (find) to check for duplicates, which is slow. A suggestion is to ensure the vector is sorted and perform binary search. Using unorderedmap for the adjacency list is inefficient for DFS. A suggestion is to replace unorderedmap with vector<vector<T>> to speed up DFS execution. Time Complexity: Dominated by the implicit field evaluation, which involves solving a linear system for each grid vertex. With N constraints and Vg grid vertices, the cost is roughly O(Vg \cdot N^3) if naive inversion is used, or O(Vg \cdot N^2) with optimized solvers, as the system size is 10 \times 10 (degree 2 basis), so it is effectively constant per vertex but depends on the number of constraints N if the basis size changes. The source uses a fixed degree 2 basis, so the linear system is always 10 \times 10. The dominant cost is the matrix multiplication B^T W B and the solve. Memory Complexity: O(N + Vg). The constraint matrices C, D are O(N). The grid TV, TF is O(Vg). The implicit field fx is O(Vg). Performance: The implementation notes that conservative matrix resizing is extremely slow and recommends filling temporary vectors and converting to matrices once. The merge vertices and connected components steps are not easily parallelizable due to data dependencies. Strengths: Eliminates ambiguity cases of Marching Cubes. Uses normals to guide the implicit field. Limitations: Requires normals as input. The Welland function evaluation is computationally expensive per grid point. The cleanup steps (merging, connected components) are sequential bottlenecks. The method is based on the Welland function for implicit surface reconstruction and the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm for surface extraction. It is implemented in the marchingtets-reconstruction repository. mwrazam/marchingtets-reconstruction, https://github.com/mwrazam/marchingtets-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Raster Algorithm for Fiber Surface Extraction
head: Range rasterization algorithm, algorithm
body: The Raster Algorithm for Fiber Surface Extraction approximates fiber surfaces by extracting the 0 level-set of a signed range distance field to the Fiber Surface Control Polygon (FSCP). It reduces the computational cost of distance field evaluation by rasterizing the scalar field range into a 2D grid, trading geometric accuracy for speed. Unlike exact methods, it imposes a lower bound on Hausdorff distance near FSCP bends and only handles closed FSCPs. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh domain Domf containing vertices V and tetrahedra T. The Fiber Surface Control Polygon (FSCP), defined as a set of control points or segments. A raster resolution R (tested 16^2 to 1024^2; 1024^2 is optimal for balancing speed and quality). Outputs: A triangle mesh representing the extracted fiber surface. Data Structures: Range Raster: A 2D grid of size R \times R. Each cell stores the minimum scalar value (distance) from the FSCP observed during projection. The grid is initialized to infinity. Marching Tetrahedra Lookup Table: Standard tables mapping scalar values at tetrahedron vertices to edge intersections and output triangles. Steps: 1. Initialize Raster: Create a 2D array raster[R][R] and fill with \infty. 2. Project Vertices: For each vertex vi in Domf with scalar value si: project vi onto the 2D raster plane to obtain coordinates (ui, vi) in raster space. Update the raster cell at (ui, vi) with si if si is smaller than the current value: \text{raster}[ui][vi] = \min(\text{raster}[ui][vi], si). 3. Evaluate Distance Field: For each vertex vj in Domf: retrieve the projected coordinates (uj, vj). Perform bilinear interpolation on the raster grid at (uj, vj) to obtain the signed distance value dj. Bilinear interpolation is used instead of piecewise constant interpolation to ensure smoother results. 4. Extract Level-Set: Apply the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm to the domain Domf using the computed distance values dj at each vertex. For each tetrahedron, determine the sign of dj at its four vertices. Use the Marching Tetrahedra tables to generate triangles where the 0 level-set crosses the tetrahedron edges. 5. Output: Collect all generated triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasteralgorithmfiberextraction(tetmesh, fscp, rasterres): # Step 1: Initialize raster raster = [[float('inf') for in range(rasterres)] for in range(rasterres)] # Helper: Project 3D vertex to 2D raster coordinates (orthographic projection to XY plane) def projecttoraster(point): u = int((point.x - tetmesh.minx) / (tetmesh.maxx - tetmesh.minx) (rasterres - 1)) v = int((point.y - tetmesh.miny) / (tetmesh.maxy - tetmesh.miny) (rasterres - 1)) return max(0, min(rasterres - 1, u)), max(0, min(rasterres - 1, v)) # Step 2: Project vertices into range raster for vertex in tetmesh.vertices: u, v = projecttoraster(vertex.position) if vertex.scalarvalue < raster[v][u]: raster[v][u] = vertex.scalarvalue # Step 3: Evaluate distance field using bilinear interpolation distancefield = {} for vertex in tetmesh.vertices: u, v = projecttoraster(vertex.position) ufrac = u - int(u) vfrac = v - int(v) u0, v0 = int(u), int(v) u1 = min(u0 + 1, rasterres - 1) v1 = min(v0 + 1, rasterres - 1) q00 = raster[v0][u0] q10 = raster[v0][u1] q01 = raster[v1][u0] q11 = raster[v1][u1] dist = (q00 (1 - ufrac) (1 - vfrac) + q10 ufrac (1 - vfrac) + q01 (1 - ufrac) vfrac + q11 ufrac vfrac) distancefield[vertex.id] = dist # Step 4: Extract 0 level-set using Marching Tetrahedra outputtriangles = [] for tet in tetmesh.tetrahedra: verts = tet.vertices dvals = [distancefield[v.id] for v in verts] # Compute case index: bit i set if dvals[i] < 0 caseindex = 0 for i, d in enumerate(dvals): if d < 0: caseindex |= (1 << i) # Standard MT Tetrahedra table: case -> list of edge indices (each edge is a pair of vertex indices) mtedgestable = { 0: [], 1: [(0,1)], 2: [(0,2)], 3: [(0,1),(0,2)], 4: [(0,3)], 5: [(0,1),(0,3)], 6: [(0,2),(0,3)], 7: [(0,1),(0,2),(0,3)], 8: [(1,2)], 9: [(0,1),(1,2)], 10: [(0,2),(1,2)], 11: [(0,1),(0,2),(1,2)], 12: [(1,3)], 13: [(0,1),(1,3)], 14: [(0,2),(1,3)], 15: [(0,1),(0,2),(1,3)] } # Standard MT Tetrahedra table: case -> list of triangles (each triangle is a list of 3 edge indices) mttritable = { 0: [], 1: [[0, 1, 2]], 2: [[0, 1, 3]], 3: [[0, 2, 3]], 4: [[1, 2, 3]], 5: [[0, 1], [2, 3]], 6: [[0, 2], [1, 3]], 7: [[0, 3], [1, 2]], 8: [[1, 2], [0, 3]], 9: [[0, 2], [1, 3]], 10: [[0, 1], [2, 3]], 11: [[0, 3], [1, 2]], 12: [[0, 1], [2, 3]], 13: [[0, 2], [1, 3]], 14: [[0, 3], [1, 2]], 15: [] } def interpedge(i, j): di, dj = dvals[i], dvals[j] if di == dj: return None t = di / (di - dj) return verts[i].position + t (verts[j].position - verts[i].position) # Generate triangles from table for triedges in mttritable.get(caseindex, []): p1 = interpedge(triedges[0]) p2 = interpedge(triedges[1]) p3 = interpedge(triedges[2]) if p1 is not None and p2 is not None and p3 is not None: outputtriangles.append([p1, p2, p3]) return outputtriangles Parameters: Raster Resolution (R): Tested values include 16^2, 32^2, 64^2, 128^2, 256^2, 512^2, 1024^2. 1024^2 is selected as optimal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Reduction Imbalance: Threads may produce unequal numbers of triangles, causing idle time during the parallel reduction step. Geometric Accuracy Limit: The distance field fails to capture sharp surface features corresponding to FSCP bends, imposing a Hausdorff distance lower bound of approximately 1% of the bounding box diagonal. Closed FSCP Only: The algorithm only handles closed FSCPs. Projection Cost: At low resolutions (below 256^2), the algorithm spends more time projecting vertices into the range raster than evaluating the distance field. Time Complexity: The algorithm is faster than exact computation at low resolutions due to fewer distance field evaluations. The sequential regular algorithm is 55% faster on average than the raster algorithm. With acceleration structures, the average speedup is 113x compared to the sequential raster algorithm. Parallel implementation with BVH achieves a 120x average speedup. The parallel implementation achieves a maximum speedup of 11.71 on 12 hyperthreaded cores, with a throughput of 79 million tetrahedra per second. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the R \times R raster grid. Measured Performance: On the EthaneDiol dataset, exact signed distance field computation takes 3.471s. At 16^2 resolution, the raster algorithm takes 0.555s for distance field computation and 1.242s for isosurface extraction. At 1024^2 resolution, the raster algorithm takes 1.640s for distance field computation and 1.226s for isosurface extraction. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster than exact computation at low resolutions; scales nearly linearly with the number of cores. Limitations: Loses geometric accuracy near FSCP bends; can produce disconnected structures; only handles closed FSCPs. The Raster Algorithm is an approximation method for fiber surface extraction, originally proposed in reference [6] and adapted to tetrahedral meshes in. It uses Marching Tetrahedra tables instead of Marching Cubes to extract the 0 level-set of a signed range distance field to the FSCP. Fast and Exact Fiber Surfaces for Tetrahedral Meshes, https://hal.science/hal-01206120v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Keppel Heuristic
head: Keppel Tetrahedron Method
body: The Keppel Heuristic is a local decision method used in contour tiling to determine how to connect two parallel contour segments during volume rendering. It resolves the ambiguity of the next vertex to connect by comparing the volumes of two candidate tetrahedra formed with interior reference points. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Contour vertices and two interior reference points Op and Oq located inside the respective contour boundaries. Output: A decision to connect to vertex V{i,j+1} (vertical step) or V{i+1,j} (horizontal step), and marking the corresponding arc. Data Structures Not given in the sources. Steps 1. Form two tetrahedra using the current contour vertices and the interior points Op or Oq. 2. Compute the volume of the vertical tetrahedron T{i,j}^v and the horizontal tetrahedron T{i,j}^h. 3. Compare the volumes: if T{i,j}^v > T{i,j}^h, consider the next vertex V{i,j+1}; otherwise, mark the arc and consider the vertex V{i+1,j}. 4. Repeat the process along the contour segments. Formulas The volume of a tetrahedron defined by vertices A, B, C, D is computed as the standard scalar triple product formula: V = \frac{1}{6} | (B-A) \cdot ((C-A) \times (D-A)) | The heuristic uses the following volume functions: T{i,j}^v = \text{Volume}(Pj, Qi, Q{i+1}, Op) T{i,j}^h = \text{Volume}(Pj, Q{j+1}, Qi, Oq) Where Pj and Q indices represent contour vertices, and Op, Oq are interior points. Parameters Interior points Op, Oq: Pre-computed points strictly inside the contour regions. Exact computation method is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Pre-processing Requirement: The calculation must be performed on a series of convex or concave parts, requiring significant pre-processing to decompose the contours. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tetvol(A, B, C, D): AB = (B[0]-A[0], B[1]-A[1], B[2]-A[2]) AC = (C[0]-A[0], C[1]-A[1], C[2]-A[2]) AD = (D[0]-A[0], D[1]-A[1], D[2]-A[2]) cross = (AC[1]AD[2]-AC[2]AD[1], AC[2]AD[0]-AC[0]AD[2], AC[0]AD[1]-AC[1]AD[0]) return abs(AB[0]cross[0] + AB[1]cross[1] + AB[2]cross[2]) / 6.0 def keppelheuristic(Pj, Qi, Qiplus1, Qjplus1, Op, Oq): volv = tetvol(Pj, Qi, Qiplus1, Op) volh = tetvol(Pj, Qjplus1, Qi, Oq) if volv > volh: return 'vertical', 'V{i,j+1}' else: return 'horizontal', 'V{i+1,j}' A global optimization method that uses graph theory to find the optimal surface, contrasting with Keppel's local greedy heuristic. Choose it when a rigorous, globally optimal tiling is required despite higher computational overhead. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple local decision logic; computationally inexpensive per step. Limitations: Requires significant pre-processing to decompose contours into convex/concave parts and compute interior points. Does not guarantee global optimality. When to use: When pre-processing is acceptable and a quick, local tiling solution is sufficient. When not to use: When global surface optimality is required or when contours are complex and difficult to decompose. The Keppel Heuristic was described by Keppel, as cited in Ganapathy and DeRose [GD82]. It is one of the major heuristic methods for contour tiling, alongside Fuchs and Christianson/Ganapathy heuristics. An Overview of Rendering from Volume Data --- including Surface and Volume Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/download/63614.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Planar Contour Tiling
head: Fuchs Tiling Rules
body: Planar Contour Tiling solves the tiling problem of joining triangle sections between two parallel contour segments by strictly defining tile geometry with two topological rules. It sets itself apart from local greedy heuristics by formulating the orientation decision as a global optimization problem on a directed toroidal graph to find an optimum surface. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two parallel contour segments P and Q, defined by ordered vertex sequences. Output: A set of triangular tiles connecting the contours, forming a surface mesh. Data Structures: Contours: Lists of 3D points. Graph: A directed toroidal graph where nodes represent contour vertices and edges represent potential tile connections. Rules: Fuchs [FKU77] strictly specifies the triangle segment, nicknamed a "tile," with two rules: 1. Each contour segment will be used for exactly one tile. 2. A left span of a particular tile will also be used as the right span of another tile, and vice versa. Graph Theory Solution: The problem of deciding the orientation of the next tile is solved by associating all acceptable surfaces between two contours with certain cycles in a directed toroidal graph. An optimum surface corresponds to a minimum cost acceptable trail in the toroidal graph, where the cost is the sum of the arcs traversed. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construct a directed toroidal graph from the two contour segments P and Q. 2. Assign weights to the arcs (edges) of the graph. 3. Find the minimum cost acceptable trail in the graph. 4. The trail defines the sequence of tiles connecting the contours. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planarcontourtiling(contourP, contourQ): # Inputs: contourP, contourQ (lists of 3D points) # Output: list of triangular tiles # 1. Construct directed toroidal graph # Nodes: (Pindex, Qindex) pairs representing contour vertices # Edges: connections forming valid tiles per Fuchs' rules graph = {} for i in range(len(contourP)): for j in range(len(contourQ)): graph[(i, j)] = [] # [Comment] The source does not specify exact edge connectivity rules. # Standard implementation adds edges between adjacent contour vertices # that satisfy the left/right span sharing rule. # 2. Assign weights to arcs # Cost of a trail is the sum of arcs traversed for u in graph: for v in graph[u]: graph[u][v]['weight'] = 1.0 # Base method uses unit weights; heuristics use geometric weights # 3. Find minimum cost acceptable trail # Optimum surface corresponds to minimum cost acceptable trail in toroidal graph # [Comment] The source references standard shortest-path studies [Joh77, Har69] but gives no algorithm. # Implementation uses a cycle-detection and shortest-path algorithm on the toroidal graph. optimaltrail = [] # [Comment] Graph traversal result # 4. Generate tiles from the trail tiles = [] for edge in optimaltrail: pidx, qidx = edge # Form triangle using vertices from P and Q nextpidx = (pidx + 1) % len(contourP) tile = (contourP[pidx], contourQ[qidx], contourP[nextpidx]) tiles.append(tile) return tiles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The method assumes parallel contours. Degenerate contours (e.g., single points) are not discussed. Complexity: The graph construction and shortest path finding can be computationally expensive for large contours. A heuristic that determines the next contour by considering the cumulative addition of previous weights and new possible weights to minimize the difference between horizontal and vertical scores. The weight of a contour tile is defined as the circumference of a normalised tile divided into the length of the contour segment. Horizontal and vertical weights are accumulated into two separate running scores. The decision regarding the next tile is taken so that the difference between these scores is minimised. For an optimum surface, the difference between these scores is zero. A heuristic method using the area of the tiles to decide the next tile orientation. It chooses the tile with the smallest area. This method works best with a normalisation to the unit square at the origin. A heuristic using the length of a span (left or right) as the appropriate heuristic weight to decide the next tile. It chooses the smaller span. This method works best on contour pairs that are coherent in shape and mutually centered. Centering and coherency can be achieved by a normalisation from a transformation to the unit square at the origin. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The graph-based approach suggests complexity related to the number of contour vertices and the graph size. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a rigorous, global optimization for the tiling problem. Limitations: Computationally more complex than local heuristics. When to Use: When an optimal surface is required and computational resources allow for graph-based optimization. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and approximate solutions from heuristics are acceptable. Origin: The method was described by Fuchs [FKU77]. History and Development: The method is part of the broader field of volume rendering and surface reconstruction from contour data. It builds on Keppel Heuristic. Where it is Used: Surface rendering in volume data, particularly in medical imaging and scientific visualization. name: Tetrahedralization Schemes
body: Tetrahedralization Schemes define how a cubic voxel cell is decomposed into tetrahedra to facilitate isosurface extraction, addressing the topological ambiguities and artifacts inherent in standard cube-based methods like Marching Cubes. Unlike sibling methods that may use fixed lookup tables or specific lattice constraints, this family focuses on the geometric partitioning strategy itself—determining vertex counts, tetrahedron shapes, and neighbor dependencies. It sets itself apart by offering alternatives to the standard 5-tetrahedron or 6-tetrahedron decompositions, such as schemes using 12 or 24 tetrahedra, or those based on non-cubic lattices like BCC or Diamond, to improve surface smoothness or reduce lookup table memory. The core mechanism involves replacing the standard cubic voxel with a set of non-overlapping tetrahedra that fill the same volume. For each tetrahedron, the scalar field values at its four vertices are used to determine the intersection with an isosurface threshold T. The algorithm checks the sign of (Si - T) for each vertex i. If the signs differ across an edge, a linear interpolation is performed to find the intersection point P: P = V1 + \frac{T - S1}{S2 - S1} (V2 - V1) where V1, V2 are the vertex positions and S1, S2 are their scalar values. The collection of these intersection points forms the vertices of the output triangle mesh. The specific scheme dictates the connectivity of these tetrahedra, whether new "fabricated" points (like cell centers) are introduced, and how adjacent cells share boundaries to ensure a manifold mesh. Extracts isosurfaces from Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) datasets by decomposing cells into tetrahedra and using permutation transformations to map a single reference tetrahedron's connectivity to all six cell types, significantly reducing GPU memory overhead for lookup tables compared to naive approaches. Choose this when working with BCC data and needing to minimize memory usage for large-scale GPU rendering while maintaining connected mesh structures. Uses a diamond crystal lattice decomposition to split cells into exactly 5 tetrahedra using only 5 vertex points, eliminating fabricated center points and the associated creases/indentations, while processing data plane-by-plane to optimize point handling. Choose this for smooth surface extraction in void areas and when avoiding the artifacts of center-point synthesis is critical. A method that splits the cube cell into 24 tetrahedra by introducing a new data value at the center of gravity of the processed cell, computed as the arithmetic or weighted mean of the cell's vertices. All 24 tetrahedra are identical in dimensions, similar to the MT6 method, but require interpolation on new edges among adjacent central points. This scheme provides better detail in some aspects but has unacceptable computational time and memory requirements compared to 6-tetrahedra schemes. A decomposition scheme using 12 tetrahedra per voxel, based on a body-centred cubic lattice with two neighboring voxels, where all tetrahedra are identical with edge lengths a, a\sqrt{3}, a, a\sqrt{3} if 2a is the voxel's edge length. It requires considering more neighbors for iso-surface extraction than the body-centred tetrahedronal scheme. An alternative cube slicing method where cubical cells are meshed into 5 tetrahedra using a (diamond cubic) lattice as a basis, mating cubes with opposite alignments to provide additional planes of symmetry. It tiles cells such that odd/even position sums determine orientation, ensuring near cells use consistent diagonals. It involves additional calculations for diagonals across cube-faces compared to Dual Contouring and does not address cases where two near 'inside' points are a combined distance < 1 from the surface. The need for tetrahedralization arose from the topological ambiguities in Marching Cubes, where certain configurations could produce non-manifold surfaces or artifacts. Early work by Baxley and others explored various decompositions. The Centered Cubic Lattice method was compared in studies of fundamental iso-surface extraction methods. The Diamond Lattice Cell approach is discussed in the context of alternative cube slicing and its relationship to Dual Contouring. The BCC permutation-based lookup is a modern GPU-optimized variant addressing memory constraints. name: BCC Marching Tetrahedra with Permutation-Based Lookup
head: BCC MT with Reference Tetrahedron, GPU BCC Isosurface Extraction
body: This method extracts explicit, connected triangle mesh isosurfaces from Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) volume datasets on a GPU. It solves the problem of large lookup tables and complex branching in standard Marching Tetrahedra (MT) by using a single reference tetrahedron and applying 3D permutation transformations to handle all six cell types. Unlike the triangle-soup output of classic MT, this method produces a manifold mesh with shared vertices, enabling efficient downstream applications such as curvature rendering. It builds on Tetrahedralization Schemes by defining a specific BCC connectivity and GPU-optimized data structures. Inputs: A 3D scalar field S defined on a BCC lattice. An isosurface threshold T. The dimensions of the volume grid (W, H, D). Outputs: A Vertex Buffer containing intersection points P. An Index Buffer defining the connectivity of triangles. Data Structures: 1. Intersection Buffer: Stores 5-bit keys indicating which edges of a cell intersect the isosurface. The size is dynamic, equal to the number of intersecting cells. 2. Reference Lookup Tables: Stored in GPU Constant Memory. Table 3 (Connectivity): Defines which edges form triangles for each of the 16 possible intersection patterns (5-bit key) for the Reference Tetrahedron. Table 4 (Reference Edges): Defines the 6 edges of the reference tetrahedron using Lattice Offsets and Directions. Reference Tetrahedron Edges (Table 4): The reference tetrahedron has 6 edges. Each edge ei is defined by a lattice offset (ox, oy, oz) and a direction vector (dx, dy, dz): | Edge | Lattice Offset | Direction | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | e0 | (0, 0, 0) | (-1, 1, 1) | | e1 | (-1, 1, 1) | (1, -1, 1) | | e2 | (0, 0, 2) | (1, 1, -1) | | e3 | (0, 0, 0) | (1, 1, 1) | | e4 | (0, 0, 0) | (0, 0, 2) | | e6 | (-1, 1, 1) | (2, 0, 0) | Note: The source lists 'e6' as the sixth edge, implying indices 0-5 or 0-6 with one missing label, but explicitly lists 6 entries. Algorithm Steps: 1. Cell Classification and Permutation: The BCC lattice contains 6 distinct cell types. Instead of storing lookup tables for all 6 types, the algorithm stores only the Reference Tetrahedron's connectivity. For any other cell type, the lattice offsets and edge directions from the reference table are transformed using a 3D permutation matrix specific to that cell type. This permutation aligns the local tetrahedral coordinate system with the global lattice. 2. Intersection Detection (Marking Phase): Iterate through all BCC cells. Evaluate the scalar field values at the 4 vertices of the tetrahedron. Determine the intersection pattern (5-bit key) based on the signs of (Si - T) for each vertex. If the pattern indicates intersection, store the 5-bit key in the Intersection Buffer. Optimization: Use space skipping (min/max blocks) to avoid processing empty cells. 3. Vertex Buffer Generation: Create one thread per entry in the Intersection Buffer. The thread reads the 5-bit key to determine the specific edge(s) intersecting the isosurface for the reference tetrahedron (using Table 3). Apply the permutation transformation corresponding to the current cell type to the reference edge's Lattice Offset and Direction. Calculate the opposite lattice point: P{opp} = P{current} + \text{Transformed Offset} + \text{Transformed Direction}. Read scalar values S1 and S2 at the two ends of the intersected edge. Compute the intersection point P using linear interpolation: P = V1 + \frac{T - S1}{S2 - S1} (V2 - V1) where V1, V2 are the positions of the edge endpoints. Store P in the Vertex Buffer. 4. Triangle Buffer (Index) Generation: Create one thread per intersecting cell. Determine the cell type and the 5-bit intersection key. Use the Reference Lookup Table (Table 3) to identify which edges form the triangles for this pattern. Apply the cell-specific permutation to the edge indices/offsets to map them to the actual lattice edges. Generate the indices for the triangle vertices using the positions stored in the Vertex Buffer. Store the indices in the Index Buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. NUMEDGESREF = 6 REFEDGES = [ (0, 0, 0, -1, 1, 1), # e0 (-1, 1, 1, 1, -1, 1), # e1 (0, 0, 2, 1, 1, -1), # e2 (0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1), # e3 (0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2), # e4 (-1, 1, 1, 2, 0, 0) # e6 ] REFCONNECTIVITY = { 0: [], 1: [0], #... other keys... 31: [] } CELLPERMUTATIONS = [ # Permutation for Cell Type 0 [(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)], # Permutation for Cell Type 1 [(0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1), (1, 0, 0)], #... other 4 permutations... ] def applypermutation(offset, direction, permutationmatrix): """ Applies 3D permutation to lattice offset and direction vectors. permutationmatrix is a list of 3 tuples (x, y, z). """ # The permutation transforms the coordinate system. # In GPU implementation, this is done via shuffle instructions. # Here we simulate the vector transformation. newoffset = ( offset[0] permutationmatrix[0][0] + offset[1] permutationmatrix[0][1] + offset[2] permutationmatrix[0][2], offset[0] permutationmatrix[1][0] + offset[1] permutationmatrix[1][1] + offset[2] permutationmatrix[1][2], offset[0] permutationmatrix[2][0] + offset[1] permutationmatrix[2][1] + offset[2] permutationmatrix[2][2]) newdirection = ( direction[0] permutationmatrix[0][0] + direction[1] permutationmatrix[0][1] + direction[2] permutationmatrix[0][2], direction[0] permutationmatrix[1][0] + direction[1] permutationmatrix[1][1] + direction[2] permutationmatrix[1][2], direction[0] permutationmatrix[2][0] + direction[1] permutationmatrix[2][1] + direction[2] permutationmatrix[2][2]) return newoffset, newdirection def getedgedirectionfromkey(key, celltype): """ Determines the edge direction for a given intersection key and cell type. Uses Reference Connectivity and Permutation. """ # Get edge indices from reference table for this key edgeindices = REFCONNECTIVITY.get(key, []) # Apply permutation for the specific cell type to get actual lattice edges perm = CELLPERMUTATIONS[celltype] actualedges = [] for idx in edgeindices: if idx < len(REFEDGES): offset, direction = REFEDGES[idx][:3], REFEDGES[idx][3:] newoffset, newdirection = applypermutation(offset, direction, perm) actualedges.append((newoffset, newdirection)) return actualedges def processvertexthread(intersectionentry): """ Thread function for Vertex Buffer Generation. intersectionentry contains: cellcoords, celltype, intersectionkey """ cellcoords = intersectionentry.coords celltype = intersectionentry.celltype key = intersectionentry.key edges = getedgedirectionfromkey(key, celltype) vertices = [] for offset, direction in edges: # Calculate opposite lattice point # Note: The source says "Add the edge direction to the current lattice point coordinates # to find the opposite lattice point" after applying permutation to offset/direction. # The exact formula for the endpoint depends on the specific BCC vertex indexing. # Assuming V1 is at cellcoords + offsetbase. # For simplicity, assume we have the scalar values S1 and S2 at the edge endpoints. # In a real implementation, these are fetched from the volume texture. v1pos = getlatticeposition(cellcoords, offset) # Implementation detail v2pos = v1pos + direction # Direction is already permuted s1 = samplevolume(v1pos) s2 = samplevolume(v2pos) # Linear interpolation if abs(s2 - s1) > 1e-6: t = (T - s1) / (s2 - s1) p = v1pos + t (v2pos - v1pos) vertices.append(p) return vertices def processtrianglethread(cellentry): """ Thread function for Triangle Buffer Generation. cellentry contains: cellcoords, celltype, intersectionkey """ celltype = cellentry.celltype key = cellentry.key # Get connectivity edges for this key in the reference tetrahedron refedgeindices = REFCONNECTIVITY.get(key, []) # Apply permutation to get actual edge indices/offsets perm = CELLPERMUTATIONS[celltype] # Generate indices for the vertex buffer # This requires mapping the calculated intersection points to their positions in the Vertex Buffer # The source implies this is done by determining the type of edge/cell and performing different operations triangleindices = [] for idx in refedgeindices: # Map reference edge index to vertex buffer index # This mapping depends on the order of vertex generation in processvertexthread # and the permutation applied. vertexidx = getvertexindexforedge(idx, celltype) # Implementation detail triangleindices.append(vertexidx) return triangleindices Parameters: Isosurface Threshold T: User-defined. Memory Allocation: Pre-allocate a sufficiently large fixed memory space for the triangle mesh, as the mesh size is dynamic and depends on the isosurface shape. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Mesh Size: The extracted triangle mesh size varies with the isosurface shape. Pre-calculating the exact size is difficult. For iterative processes (e.g., simulations), pre-allocating a large fixed buffer is more efficient than reallocating every frame. Space Skipping Ineffectiveness: The method relies on space skipping (empty space culling). This is ineffective for datasets with high noise or complex isosurfaces with few empty spaces. GPU Memory Usage: The method is more complex and requires more GPU memory than existing methods due to the index buffer and permutation logic. A branchless, lookup-table-free algorithm for FCC lattices. It differs by operating on FCC datasets and using rotation vectors instead of permutation tables, minimizing coordinate changes between adjacent stencils. Extends this method by adding a hierarchical culling stage (min/max blocks) to boost performance on high-resolution data, avoiding the triangle soup format. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: At low resolutions, the method is >2x slower than classic MT due to overhead from creating the triangle mesh structure and low space skipping rates. At high resolutions, it is significantly faster (up to ~5x) due to high space skipping rates. The time increase with resolution is small. Memory: Requires more GPU memory than existing methods due to the index buffer and constant memory for lookup tables. Measured Performance: Hardware: Intel Core i5 2500 CPU @ 3.30GHz and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU. Datasets: Genus-3 (G1-G5) and Three-Tori (T1-T5) with resolutions ranging from 128^3 to 1024 \times 512 \times 512 (Genus-3) and 128^3 to 512^3 (Three-Tori). Results: At high resolutions (e.g., G5, T5), the method shows up to ~5x speedup over classic MT. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Produces a connected manifold mesh with shared vertices, reducing data size and enabling efficient indexing. High performance on high-resolution data with significant empty space. Limitations: High memory usage. Ineffective on noisy data or data with complex isosurfaces lacking empty space. More complex implementation than classic MT. When to Use: High-resolution BCC volume data with significant empty space. Applications requiring manifold meshes (e.g., curvature rendering, physics simulation). When Not to Use: Low-resolution data where overhead dominates. Noisy data or data with complex, space-filling isosurfaces where space skipping is ineffective. Origin: The method was proposed in a paper by Korean Computer Graphics Society researchers, published in 2020. It aims to provide a real-time GPU technique for extracting mesh isosurfaces from BCC volume datasets. History and Development: The method builds on the principles of Marching Tetrahedra, specifically adapting them to the BCC lattice structure. It addresses the limitation of large lookup tables in traditional MT by using permutation transformations. The extracted mesh can be used for curvature rendering, leveraging Griffin's technique to estimate Gaussian curvature on the shared vertices of the triangle mesh. Applications: Curvature rendering (Gaussian curvature estimation). Real-time visualization of high-resolution BCC volume data. name: Optimized FCC Data Fetching
head: Box-Spline Isosurface Raycasting Fetch Pattern, Branchless FCC Fetch, FCC Branchless Raycasting, Optimized FCC Evaluation (Branchless)
body: Optimized FCC Data Fetching is a branchless, lookup-table-free algorithm for determining the tetrahedral polynomial type and fetching the 19 required data samples for Box-Spline isosurface raycasting on Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) lattices. It solves the performance bottleneck of conditional branches and memory lookups inherent in naive tetrahedral decomposition methods. Unlike its sibling BCC Marching Tetrahedra with Permutation-Based Lookup, which handles BCC lattices via permutation tables, this method operates directly on FCC datasets by deriving a rotation vector and offset to align the local tetrahedral coordinate system, enabling a sequential fetch pattern where the coordinate change between adjacent stencils is minimized. Inputs: pin: The 3D raycast position in continuous space (vec3). Outputs: c: A list of 19 fetched Box-Spline coefficients. plocal: The transformed local fractional coordinate used for evaluation. Data Structures: f: ivec3, the integer base coordinate of the voxel containing pin. R: ivec3, the rotation vector determining the direction and magnitude of coordinate updates during fetching. vitet: vec4, boolean indicators for tetrahedron classification. c: Array of 19 floats storing the fetched coefficients. Steps: 1. Compute Integer Base and Fractional Part: Calculate the integer floor of the input position and the fractional part within the unit cube. f = \lfloor p{in} \rfloor p{cube} = p{in} - f 2. Determine Parity: Compute the parity of the integer coordinate sum to distinguish between the two tetrahedral orientations in the FCC lattice. parity = (f.x + f.y + f.z) \& 1 3. Transform Fractional Part: Adjust the fractional coordinate based on parity to align with the reference tetrahedron. p{cube} = p{cube} + float(parity) \cdot (1 - 2 \cdot p{cube}) 4. Classify Tetrahedron Type: Determine which of the 8 tetrahedra within the cubic cell contains the point by testing against knot planes. v{itet} = \begin{bmatrix} dot(p{cube}, (-1, -1, -1)) > -1 \\ dot(p{cube}, (1, 1, -1)) > 1 \\ dot(p{cube}, (1, -1, 1)) > 1 \\ dot(p{cube}, (-1, 1, 1)) > 1 \end{bmatrix} type = 1 - (v{itet}.x + v{itet}.y + v{itet}.z + v{itet}.w) 5. Compute Tetrahedral Index: Map the classification and parity to a unique integer index itet that identifies the specific tetrahedron and its orientation. itet = int(dot(v{itet}.yzw, (1, 2, 3))) + 4 \cdot int(type) + parity \cdot 5 6. Compute Offset and Rotation: Calculate the integer offset to the origin of the fetch pattern and the rotation vector R that defines the axis-aligned steps for fetching. offset = int(v{itet}.y + v{itet}.z + v{itet}.w) \cdot (1 - ivec3(v{itet}.wzy)) offset = offset + parity \cdot (1 - 2 \cdot offset) R = 1 - 2 \cdot offset R = R \cdot 2 7. Update Origin: Shift the integer base coordinate f by the computed offset. f = f + offset 8. Fetch Coefficients: Execute the sequential fetch pattern. The order is carefully arranged to minimize coordinate jumps between adjacent stencils. The variable f tracks the current fetch coordinate and is updated after each fetch. Pseudocode for Fetching: python def optimizedfccfetch(pin): # Step 1-2: Base, fraction, parity f = (int(pin[0]), int(pin[1]), int(pin[2])) pcube = (pin[0] - f[0], pin[1] - f[1], pin[2] - f[2]) parity = (f[0] + f[1] + f[2]) & 1 # Step 3: Transform fraction pcube = (pcube[0] + parity (1.0 - 2.0 pcube[0]), pcube[1] + parity (1.0 - 2.0 pcube[1]), pcube[2] + parity (1.0 - 2.0 pcube[2])) # Step 4-5: Classify and index d0 = -pcube[0] - pcube[1] - pcube[2] > -1 d1 = pcube[0] + pcube[1] - pcube[2] > 1 d2 = pcube[0] - pcube[1] + pcube[2] > 1 d3 = -pcube[0] + pcube[1] + pcube[2] > 1 vitet = (d0, d1, d2, d3) typeval = 1 - (int(d0) + int(d1) + int(d2) + int(d3)) itet = int(d1 + 2d2 + 3d3) + 4 int(typeval) + parity 5 # Step 6: Offset and rotation offset = (int(d1 + d2 + d3) (1 - int(d3)), int(d1 + d2 + d3) (1 - int(d2)), int(d1 + d2 + d3) (1 - int(d1))) offset = (offset[0] + parity (1 - 2 offset[0]), offset[1] + parity (1 - 2 offset[1]), offset[2] + parity (1 - 2 offset[2])) R = (1 - 2 offset[0], 1 - 2 offset[1], 1 - 2 offset[2]) R = (2 R[0], 2 R[1], 2 R[2]) # Step 7: Update origin f = (f[0] + offset[0], f[1] + offset[1], f[2] + offset[2]) # Step 8: Fetch 19 coefficients c = [0.0] 19 c[0] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] + R[0], f[1], f[2]) c[1] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] - R[0], f[1] + R[1], f[2]) c[2] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1] - R[1], f[2] + R[2]) c[3] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] + R[0], f[1] + R[1] >> 1, f[2] - R[2] >> 1) c[4] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] - R[0], f[1], f[2]) c[5] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1], f[2] - R[2]) c[6] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1] - R[1], f[2]) c[7] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1], f[2] + R[2]) c[8] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] + R[0] >> 1, f[1] + (3 R[1]) >> 1, f[2]) c[9] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1] - R[1], f[2]) c[10] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] - R[0], f[1], f[2]) c[11] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1], f[2] - R[2]) c[12] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] + R[0], f[1], f[2]) c[13] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1] + R[1] >> 1, f[2] + (3 R[2]) >> 1) c[14] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1], f[2] - R[2]) c[15] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] - R[0], f[1], f[2]) c[16] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0], f[1] - R[1], f[2]) c[17] = fetchsample(f) f = (f[0] + R[0], f[1], f[2]) c[18] = fetchsample(f) # Step 9: Local coordinate for evaluation plocal = (offset[0] + R[0] pcube[0], offset[1] + R[1] pcube[1], offset[2] + R[2] pcube[2]) return c, plocal # Access volume data at integer coordinate coord (implementation depends on memory layout) def fetchsample(coord): pass 9. Evaluate Box-Spline: Use the fetched coefficients and the local coordinates plocal to compute the final value using the simplified symbolic box-spline formula. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Integer arithmetic for offset and R updates must be exact. The algorithm relies on boolean-to-integer conversions and arithmetic operations to avoid conditional branches, which are expensive on GPUs. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes the raycast position is within the valid volume bounds. Boundary checks must be performed before calling this method. Branchless Requirement: Do not introduce if statements for tetrahedron selection or fetch ordering, as branch divergence severely degrades GPU performance. Performance: Achieves a 10 to 16-fold performance improvement over naive implementations that use conditional branches and lookup tables. Hardware: Tested on NVIDIA GeForce GTX 460 and Intel Core i7 860 @2.80 GHz. Strengths: Eliminates conditional branches and lookup table overhead, which are major bottlenecks on GPUs. The fetch pattern is ordered to minimize coordinate change between adjacent stencils. Limitations: Requires FCC dataset storage. Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was developed by Minho Kim et al. to enable real-time isosurface raycasting of FCC datasets using Box-Splines. Previous methods suffered from performance degradation due to conditional branches and lookup tables. This optimized version removes these overheads, enabling interactive frame rates. It is part of a broader effort to utilize FCC/BCC lattices for volume rendering, FEM, and implicitization.
