name: Probing for Surface Mesh Generation through Delaunay Refinement
head: Delaunay Refinement Surface Meshing, Probing Delaunay Refinement
body: This method generates a surface mesh from an implicit surface without requiring an initial point set, using Delaunay refinement combined with a probing procedure to ensure all connected components of the surface are captured. It guarantees topological equivalence to the surface and approximation properties defined by the refinement algorithm. Unlike standard Delaunay refinement which requires seed points, this approach autonomously discovers isolated components through spatial probing of the domain. It builds on Delaunay Cover Refinement by adding a termination condition based on domain coverage rather than just local feature size satisfaction. Inputs: Implicit surface function f(\mathbf{x}) = 0 defining the geometry. Bounding volume \Omega enclosing the surface. Parameter \varepsilon: The maximum distance from any point in the domain to the set of probes, defining the radius of the ball included in each connected component's volume. Optional parameter r: A positive number such that any connected component contains at least one ball of radius r. If known, probes only need to be within distance r of the surface, reducing search space. Outputs: A 3D triangulation (surface mesh) that is topologically equivalent to the surface. Triangulation: A Delaunay triangulation of the current set of probes (vertices). Voronoi Diagram: The dual of the triangulation, used to identify infinite edges and probe cells. Probes: The set of points sampled from the domain \Omega. 1. Initialization: Start with an empty set of probes and an empty triangulation. 2. Probing Loop: Continuously probe the domain \Omega to find points. The probing strategy analyzes Voronoi cells of the current triangulation. If a probed segment intersects the surface (detected via sign change of f), add the intersection point to the triangulation. If a probed segment intersects the interior of a connected component but does not intersect the surface (indicating an isolated component not yet meshed), identify an "isolated point". 3. Component Initialization: When an isolated point is found: Initialize the component by adding the point to the triangulation. Alternative Initialization: Attempt to form a large triangle first, then refine and check if the component is meshed. If not, apply the standard isolated point initialization to prevent vertex clusters. 4. Refinement: Apply the standard Delaunay refinement steps (e.g., inserting circumcenters of poor-quality simplices) to the triangulation. This step meshes components that are close to each other or already partially initialized. 5. Termination Check: The algorithm terminates when the domain is covered with probed Voronoi cells. Formally, every point in the domain is at distance at most \varepsilon from the set of probes. Optimization: If parameter r is known, the termination condition is relaxed: every point in a probed cell must only be at distance r from the set of probes. The algorithm guarantees that each connected component contains at least one point of the triangulation. Proof Sketch: If the algorithm ends, the domain is covered with probed Voronoi cells (distance \le \varepsilon). Each connected component includes a ball of radius \ge \varepsilon. Thus, a probed segment intersects this ball (creating a probed point inside the volume). There also exists an infinite Voronoi edge providing a point outside the volume (clipped on the boundary of \Omega). Since the set of probes is connected and the surface is closed, a probed segment must intersect the surface. If this intersection point was not added to the triangulation, it would be at distance < \varepsilon from a mesh face, and thus at most 2\varepsilon from a meshed component. Since components are at least 2\varepsilon apart, this confirms the component is meshed. Accretion of Points: Initializing components can cause accretion of points on spheres if points are not close enough to ensure the created facet is persistent, resulting in vertex clusters. Mitigation: A proposed remeshing step (delete or relocate vertices) can solve this, preserving topology and approximation criteria. Small/Spaced Components: Very small and widely spaced components may not be intersected by Voronoi edges (no isolated points) and must be found by the probe procedure. Initialization Efficiency: Initializing all isolated points at once is faster than one-by-one, as it initializes several components simultaneously, reducing refinement steps. However, it may initialize the same component twice if multiple isolated points lie on it. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def probingdelaunayrefinement(implicitsurface, boundingvolume, epsilon, r=None): """ Generate surface mesh using probing and Delaunay refinement. Args: implicitsurface: Function f(x) returning signed distance or value. boundingvolume: Bounding box or volume Omega. epsilon: Max distance from any point in domain to probes. r: Optional radius of ball contained in each component. Returns: Triangulation mesh. """ probes = [] triangulation = EmptyTriangulation() # Determine termination threshold threshold = r if r is not None else epsilon while not isdomaincovered(probes, boundingvolume, threshold): # Analyze Voronoi cells to find probing locations probepoints = analyzevoronoicells(triangulation, boundingvolume) for p in probepoints: # Check if probe intersects surface if implicitsurface.intersects(p): intersection = implicitsurface.findintersection(p) if not triangulation.contains(intersection): triangulation.insert(intersection) probes.append(intersection) else: # Check for isolated component (probed inside volume but no surface intersection) if isisolatedcomponent(p, triangulation, implicitsurface): # Initialize component initializecomponent(p, triangulation, implicitsurface) probes.append(p) # Refine mesh to improve quality and mesh close components refinedelaunay(triangulation) return triangulation def isdomaincovered(probes, volume, threshold): """ Check if every point in volume is within threshold distance of probes. Implemented by checking if all Voronoi cells in the domain are 'probed'. """ # In practice, this involves checking if the union of balls of radius threshold # around probes covers the volume. # For implementation from text: check if max distance from any sample point # in volume to nearest probe is <= threshold. pass def isisolatedcomponent(probepoint, triangulation, implicitsurface): """ Detect if a probe point lies inside a connected component that has no surface points in the current triangulation. """ # Find the connected component of the probe in the Voronoi diagram # or check if the probe is surrounded by existing probes but no surface face exists nearby. # Specifically, if a probed segment intersects the interior ball of a component # but no surface intersection was found along the path to an infinite Voronoi edge. pass def initializecomponent(point, triangulation, implicitsurface): """ Add a point to initialize a new connected component. May attempt to form a large triangle first to avoid clusters. """ # Option 1: Standard isolated point initialization triangulation.insert(point) # Option 2: Attempt large triangle first (proposed) # triangle = attemptformlargetriangle(point, implicitsurface) # if triangle is valid and meshes component: # triangulation.inserttriangle(triangle) # else: # triangulation.insert(point) pass Time Complexity: The cost is proportional to the volume of the bounding volume \Omega. In the worst case for a cube of size a, the algorithm probes (a/\varepsilon)^3 cubes of size \varepsilon, each in constant time. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of vertices in the triangulation and the number of probes. Tested on 10 random spheres and an implicit surface defined by x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + \sin(4x) + \sin(4y) + \sin(4z) = 0. At least 80% of components are meshed on average in the partial implementation (isolated points only). In the best case, all components are meshed. Results are less unpredictable than previous methods using random initialization. Strengths: No initial point set required; guarantees topological equivalence; handles isolated components; adaptable if prior knowledge (like r or number of components) is available. Limitations: Accretion of points on spheres during initialization can create clusters; partial implementation may leave smallest components unmeshed; performance depends heavily on the choice of bounding volume \Omega. Use when the surface geometry is unknown and no seed points are available. Use when the surface consists of multiple disconnected components, some of which may be small or isolated. Do not use if the bounding volume is excessively large relative to the surface, as this increases probing cost significantly. The method was proposed in the paper "Probing for Surface Mesh Generation through Delaunay Refinement". It extends the work of Boissonnat, Guibas, and Oudon on learning smooth shapes by probing. The algorithm addresses the limitation of standard Delaunay refinement which requires an initial point set, potentially missing isolated components. Implemented as a partial version including only the treatment of isolated points. The mesh is initialized and refined while isolated points exist. The implementation allows initializing one or all isolated points at a given step. Probing for Surface Mesh Generation through Delaunay Refinement, https://inria.hal.science/hal-00747344v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Grid-based Traversal
head: Hierarchical grid traversal for irregular volumes, Parker's brute-force approach, Parker's method
body: Grid-based Traversal is a method for rendering irregular volume data (tetrahedral meshes) at interactive rates by partitioning the volume into a hierarchical rectilinear grid structure to quickly determine candidate tetrahedra. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Projected Tetrahedra by avoiding explicit connectivity information and instead relying on spatial hashing via a multilevel grid, allowing for on-the-fly iso-surface computation. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh representing an irregular volume; a hierarchical rectilinear grid structure (multilevel); scalar values associated with tetrahedra vertices. Outputs: Rendered image with iso-surface computed on the fly. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchical Grid: A multilevel grid structure covering the volume space. Exact grid dimensions and bit-packing layouts are not given in the sources. 2. Grid Cell List: Each leaf cell contains a list of pointers/indices to all tetrahedra that intersect that cell. 3. Cell Bounds: Each grid cell stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of all tetrahedra attached to it. Steps: 1. Grid Construction: Partition the volume space into a hierarchical rectilinear grid. 2. Tetrahedron Attachment: For each tetrahedron in the mesh, determine which grid cells it intersects. Attach the tetrahedron to the list of every intersecting grid cell. 3. Value Culling: For each grid cell, compute and store the minimum and maximum scalar values among all attached tetrahedra. 4. Ray Traversal: For each pixel, cast a ray into the volume. Traverse the hierarchical grid to find leaf cells intersected by the ray. 5. Culling: Use the stored minimum and maximum values of the traversed grid cells to cull regions that do not contain the current iso-value. 6. Tetrahedron Testing: For each candidate tetrahedron attached to the intersected grid cells, test for intersection with the ray. Since no connectivity is used, all attached tetrahedra must be checked sequentially. 7. Intersection Calculation: If a tetrahedron face (triangle) is intersected, determine the barycentric coordinates of the intersection point. 8. Scalar Interpolation: Interpolate the scalar value at the intersection point using the barycentric coordinates and the vertex scalar values. 9. Iso-surface Computation: Compute the precise intersection with the iso-surface using linear interpolation of the scalar values. Formulas: Barycentric scalar interpolation at a triangle face intersection: S = \alpha S0 + \beta S1 + \gamma S2, where \alpha, \beta, \gamma are the barycentric coordinates of the intersection point and S0, S1, S2 are the scalar values at the triangle's vertices. Linear iso-surface crossing along a ray segment: t{iso} = t0 + \frac{V{iso} - S0}{S1 - S0} (t1 - t0), where t0 and t1 are the ray parameters at the entry and exit points of the tetrahedron, S0 and S1 are the interpolated scalars at those points, and V{iso} is the target iso-value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildgrid(tetrahedra, gridlevels): grid = createhierarchicalgrid(gridlevels) # Standard multilevel grid allocation for tet in tetrahedra: # The sources do not give the exact cell-assignment algorithm. cells = findintersectingcells(tet.boundingbox, grid) for cell in cells: cell.tetrahedra.append(tet) return grid def updatecellbounds(grid): for cell in grid: if not cell.tetrahedra: cell.minval = float('inf') cell.maxval = float('-inf') continue minv = float('inf') maxv = float('-inf') for tet in cell.tetrahedra: for v in tet.vertices: s = v.scalar if s < minv: minv = s if s > maxv: maxv = s cell.minval = minv cell.maxval = maxv def renderray(rayorigin, raydir, isovalue, grid): # The sources do not give the exact hierarchical traversal algorithm. cells = traversegridcells(rayorigin, raydir, grid) closestt = float('inf') hitpoint = None for cell in cells: if isovalue < cell.minval or isovalue > cell.maxval: continue for tet in cell.tetrahedra: t, bary = raytriangleintersection(rayorigin, raydir, tet) if t is not None and t < closestt: # Step 7 & 8: Barycentric interpolation of scalar at face intersection scalar = bary[0]tet.vertices[0].scalar + bary[1]tet.vertices[1].scalar + bary[2]tet.vertices[2].scalar # Step 9: Linear interpolation to find exact iso-surface crossing along ray # The sources do not give the exact linear interpolation formula for the iso-surface crossing along the ray within the tetrahedron bounds. tiso = computeisointersection(rayorigin, raydir, tet, isovalue) if tiso is not None and tiso < closestt: closestt = tiso hitpoint = rayorigin + raydir tiso if hitpoint is not None: return Color(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Application-specific shading return Color(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def raytriangleintersection(rayorigin, raydir, tet): for tri in tet.faces: e1 = tri.v1 - tri.v0 e2 = tri.v2 - tri.v0 h = cross(raydir, e2) a = dot(e1, h) if abs(a) < 1e-8: continue f = 1.0 / a s = rayorigin - tri.v0 u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: continue q = cross(s, e1) v = f dot(raydir, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: continue t = f dot(e2, q) if t > 1e-8: return t, (1.0 - u - v, u, v) return None, None def computeisointersection(rayorigin, raydir, tet, isovalue): # The sources do not give the exact linear interpolation formula for the iso-surface crossing along the ray within the tetrahedron bounds. return None Parameters: Grid Levels: The number of layers in the hierarchical grid. Parker et al. used three layers. Iso-value: The scalar value defining the surface. It can be changed during rendering as the surface is computed on the fly. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Curvilinear Volumes: The method does not natively support curvilinear volumes, although they can be handled by decomposing hexahedra into five tetrahedra. Performance: Without connectivity, all tetrahedra attached to a cell must be checked, which can be computationally expensive if cells are large or contain many tetrahedra. Precision: Linear interpolation is used for scalar values and iso-surface intersection, which may introduce artifacts if the scalar field is not piecewise linear. Plücker Space Traversal is an optimized traversal algorithm for unstructured and curvilinear data sets that uses Plücker coordinates to test line orientations after locating the initial cell via a kd-tree. It sets itself apart by avoiding explicit tetrahedron-face intersection tests and instead relying on algebraic line orientation checks. Choose it when rendering curvilinear volumes or when faster traversal is needed than brute-force cell attachment. Link: Plücker Space Traversal. Time Complexity: Linear with the number of processors for parallel implementation. Sequentially, it depends on the number of tetrahedra per grid cell and the number of cells traversed. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of tetrahedra times the average number of grid cells they intersect, plus the grid structure overhead. Measured Performance: Rendered a bioelectric field with over one million tetrahedra at interactive rates on a 512x512 viewport using 16 processors or more. Strengths: Enables interactive rendering of large irregular volumes on supercomputers; allows dynamic iso-value changes; simple implementation without complex connectivity. Limitations: Does not support curvilinear volumes natively; potentially high computational cost per pixel due to brute-force testing of attached tetrahedra. Grid-based Traversal was introduced by Parker et al. [PPL∗ 99] as one of the first methods capable of rendering irregular volume data at interactive rates on a supercomputer. It was demonstrated using a bioelectric field simulation with over one million tetrahedra. The method scales linearly with the number of processors. name: Parallel Projected Tetrahedra with KD-Tree Partitioning
head: Parallel Unstructured Volume Rendering in ParaView, Parallel Volume Rendering in ParaView, kd-tree based parallel volume rendering
body: This method enables parallel volume rendering of unstructured tetrahedral grids by partitioning the data using a kd-tree to facilitate a traditional sort-last compositing algorithm. It renders unstructured grids natively without sampling into a regular grid, avoiding the oversampling/undersampling issues and large sample counts required by grid-based approaches. Unlike other parallel rendering approaches that require further transfer of cells after distribution, this method requires no further cell transfer once cells are distributed; only image data is communicated between processes. The method operates on a distributed-memory parallel computer. It partitions the unstructured grid data to assign regions to different processes, renders the assigned tetrahedra using the projected tetrahedra method, and composites the resulting images. Input: An unstructured tetrahedral grid (defined by vertices and connectivity). Output: A final composited image. The primary data structure is the unstructured grid itself, represented as a collection of tetrahedra. Each tetrahedron is defined by its four vertices and associated scalar values. The partitioning structure is a kd-tree, which recursively splits the bounding box of the data. 1. Partitioning: Partition the unstructured grid data using a kd-tree to create regions assigned to different processes. 2. Splitting: Split any tetrahedra that intersect with kd-tree region boundaries. This causes the data set size (number of tetrahedra) to grow. 3. Distribution: Distribute and clip the rendered tetrahedra among processes. This partitioning is performed whenever a change is made to the data, not every render frame. 4. Rendering: Render the distributed tetrahedra using the projected tetrahedra method to generate images for each process. 5. Compositing: Perform parallel image compositing (sort-last) by transferring only image data between processes for final composition. Image Resolution: 800x800 pixels used in the experiments. Data Growth: On average, data size grows by about 15% when adding a single level to the kd-tree, with variance between 5% and 30%. Memory Usage: Data redistribution requires holding at least two copies of the data simultaneously. If hardware memory is insufficient, rendering rates can drop impractically low. Geometry Changes: Changes in viewable geometry require lengthy redistribution of the data. Data Growth Variance: The first cuts usually have smaller growth than later ones. Larger data sets have smaller growth, suggesting sub-linear growth with respect to original data size. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelprojectedtetrahedrarendering(tetrahedra, numprocesses, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Renders unstructured tetrahedral grid in parallel using kd-tree partitioning. Args: tetrahedra: List of tetrahedra, each defined by 4 vertices and scalar values. numprocesses: Number of parallel processes. imagewidth: Width of the output image in pixels. imageheight: Height of the output image in pixels. Returns: Final composited image. """ # Step 1: Partitioning # Build a kd-tree to partition the data. # The kd-tree recursively splits the bounding box of the data. # The number of partitions is determined by numprocesses (power of 2). kdtree = buildkdtree(tetrahedra, numpartitions=numprocesses) # Step 2: Splitting # Split tetrahedra that intersect with kd-tree region boundaries. # This increases the number of tetrahedra. splittetrahedra = [] for tet in tetrahedra: if intersectsboundary(tet, kdtree): splittetrahedra.extend(splittetrahedron(tet, kdtree)) else: splittetrahedra.append(tet) # Step 3: Distribution # Assign split tetrahedra to processes based on kd-tree regions. # This step is performed when data changes, not every frame. processassignments = assigntoprocesses(splittetrahedra, kdtree) # Each process renders its assigned tetrahedra localimages = [] for processid in range(numprocesses): assignedtetrahedra = processassignments[processid] # Step 4: Rendering # Render using projected tetrahedra method. # This generates an 800x800 image (or specified resolution). localimage = renderprojectedtetrahedra(assignedtetrahedra, imagewidth, imageheight) localimages.append(localimage) # Step 5: Compositing # Perform sort-last compositing. # Only image data is transferred between processes. finalimage = sortlastcomposite(localimages) return finalimage def buildkdtree(tetrahedra, numpartitions): """ Builds a kd-tree to partition the tetrahedra. """ # Not given in the sources. Standard kd-tree construction algorithm. pass def intersectsboundary(tetrahedron, kdtree): """ Checks if a tetrahedron intersects with any kd-tree region boundary. """ # Not given in the sources. Geometric intersection test. pass def splittetrahedron(tetrahedron, kdtree): """ Splits a tetrahedron that intersects with a kd-tree boundary. Returns a list of new tetrahedra. """ # Not given in the sources. Geometric clipping algorithm. pass def assigntoprocesses(tetrahedra, kdtree): """ Assigns tetrahedra to processes based on kd-tree regions. """ # Not given in the sources. Assignment logic based on kd-tree leaves. pass def renderprojectedtetrahedra(tetrahedra, width, height): """ Renders a set of tetrahedra using the projected tetrahedra method. """ # Not given in the sources. Calls the projected tetrahedra method. pass def sortlastcomposite(images): """ Performs sort-last compositing of multiple images. """ # Not given in the sources. Standard sort-last compositing algorithm. pass Time Complexity: The partitioning time reduces with larger jobs, but changes in viewable geometry require lengthy redistribution. Rendering speed increases with the number of processors, but shows diminishing returns when adding more processors than necessary for a given data set. Memory Complexity: Requires holding at least two copies of the data during redistribution. Measured Performance: Tested on a Dell Precision 530 workstation with dual 2.0 GHz Pentium-4 Xeon processors, 1 GB RDRAM, GeForce FX 5900 Ultra graphics card, and Myrinet 2000 interconnect. Data sets ranged from 44,832 to 14,094,684 tetrahedra. The system has a bigger speedup for larger data sets even if the overall frame rate is lower. Strengths: Renders unstructured grids natively; no further cell transfer after distribution; only image data is communicated; allows code reuse and variety of algorithms. Limitations: Data redistribution requires significant memory; changes in viewable geometry require lengthy redistribution; rendering rates can be too low for user interaction without level of detail rendering. When to Use: For visualizing large unstructured grid simulations from supercomputers where native rendering is preferred over grid sampling. When Not to Use: When hardware memory is insufficient for holding two copies of the data during redistribution, or when frequent changes in viewable geometry occur. This method was developed for ParaView and deployed at Sandia National Laboratories for visualizing simulations from supercomputers like Red Storm. It was presented in a paper by Kenneth Moreland et al.. The approach focuses on handling large quantities of data from high-fidelity physical simulations. name: Tetrahedral Mesh Connectivity Encoding
head: Basic Cut-Border Machine, Opcode-based mesh representation, Segment-based mesh encoding
body: Tetrahedral Mesh Connectivity Encoding, commonly known as the Basic Cut-Border Machine (CBM), is a region-growing compression scheme that encodes the connectivity of a tetrahedral mesh by traversing it and emitting opcodes that describe the position of new vertices relative to a growing boundary called the cut-border. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and transmitting the topological structure of tetrahedral volumes, which is a prerequisite for rendering methods like Projected Tetrahedra [877-projected-tetrahedra.md] or Marching Tetrahedrons [940-marching-tetrahedrons-algorithm.md]. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on global indexing or implicit structures, CBM uses a local, sequential traversal where each opcode references vertices already encountered or currently being defined, ensuring unique identification without global coordinate lookups. Inputs and Outputs Input: A tetrahedral mesh (potentially non-manifold, with specific constraints on non-manifold edges). Output: A stream of opcodes (connectivity symbols) and a stream of vertex geometry/attributes. Data Structures 1. Cut-Border: A triangle mesh representing the boundary between the encoded (inner) and unencoded (outer) parts of the tetrahedral mesh. It consists of faces of the tetrahedra. 2. Gate: A specific triangle face on the cut-border where the next tetrahedron is attached. 3. FIFO Buffer: A queue storing vertex indices to determine the traversal order. 4. Hash Maps: Two hash maps store face incidencies for reconstruction: inpatchhashmap: Stores pairs of triangles for faces shared within a single patch/segment. crosspatchhashmap: Stores pairs of triangles for faces shared between different patches/segments. Keys in hash maps are triangles defined by unique vertex indices. 5. Edge Incident Map: A hash map storing, for every edge on the cut-border, the set of all incident triangles. This is used to detect non-manifold edges. Opcodes There are 11 primary opcodes (plus a 12th "Skip" for extreme non-manifold cases) encoded as 4-bit words. They describe the position of the "free vertex" (the vertex of the new tetrahedron not part of the gate) relative to the gate: 1. B (Border): The gate is a border of the whole mesh. No free vertex exists. 2. N (New Vertex): The free vertex is new and not on a border between segments/patches. Parameter: Vertex Index. 3. S (New Shared Vertex): The free vertex is new but lies on a border between segments/patches. Parameters: Vertex Index, Global Shared Index. 4. Fi (Flipi): The free vertex is incident to exactly one adjacent triangle of the gate. i (0, 1, or 2) identifies which triangle. No vertex index parameter needed. 5. Ti (Topi): The free vertex is incident to exactly two adjacent triangles of the gate. i (0, 1, or 2) identifies the triangle not incident to the free vertex. No vertex index parameter needed. 6. C (Close): The free vertex is incident to all three adjacent triangles of the gate. No vertex index parameter needed. 7. J (Join): The free vertex is incident to none of the adjacent triangles of the gate. Parameter: Vertex Index. Parameters Vertex Index (for N, S, J): Encoded with 16 bits for performance, though theoretically \log2(n) bits are sufficient where n is the number of vertices in the segment. Global Shared Index (for S): Encoded with 32 bits, theoretically \log2(m) bits where m is the total vertices in the multi-resolution mesh. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Select an arbitrary starting tetrahedron. Initialize the cut-border with the four faces of this tetrahedron. Initialize the FIFO buffer with the indices of the four vertices of the starting tetrahedron. Initialize the Edge Incident Map. Initialize inpatchhashmap and crosspatchhashmap as empty. Output the indices of the first four vertices. 2. Traversal Loop: While the cut-border is not empty: Select Gate: Pick a face from the cut-border as the current gate. Identify Case: Determine the relationship of the potential free vertex to the gate. If the gate has no adjacent unencoded tetrahedron, emit B. Remove gate from cut-border. Else, identify the free vertex v. If v is not yet visited: Check if v is on a segment/patch boundary. If yes, emit S with local index and global shared index. If no, emit N with local index. Add v to FIFO. If v is already visited: Check incidence with the three triangles adjacent to the gate. If incident to 1 triangle ti, emit Fi. If incident to 2 triangles, emit Ti where i is the index of the non-incident triangle. If incident to 3 triangles, emit C. If incident to 0 triangles, emit J with index of v. name: Implicit Connectivity Mesh (ICM)
body: Implicit Connectivity Mesh (ICM) is a representation of implicit surfaces where a mesh consists of vertices only, partitioned into cubic cells to enable efficient isosurface extraction and simplification. It differs from explicit polygon meshes by storing connectivity information implicitly within each vertex's encoding vector, allowing rapid reconstruction of the explicit mesh and supporting multiresolution modeling via topology-preserving vertex clustering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset or polygon mesh to be converted into ICM representation. Output: A set of cubic cells, each containing one or more vertices, where each vertex holds a connectivity encoding vector. An explicit polygon mesh can be reconstructed from these vertices. Data Structures: Grid: A partitioning of space into cubic cells. Vertex: A point located within a cell. Connectivity Encoding Vector: Associated with each vertex, storing connectivity information defined by either classification values of the cell's corner points or edges/surfaces intersections of the cell. Algorithm Steps: 1. Partition Space: Divide the domain into a grid of cubic cells. 2. Vertex Identification: For each cell, identify all vertices contained within it; a cell may contain one or more vertices. 3. Compute Connectivity: For each vertex, compute a connectivity encoding vector that implicitly defines the connections between the vertex and its neighbors. 4. Reconstruction: Reconstruct the explicit polygon mesh by using the connectivity information stored in each vertex. Multiresolution Construction: To create multiresolution ICM representations, two topology-preserving vertex clustering algorithms are employed: 1. Hierarchical Clustering: Groups vertices based on a hierarchy of detail levels. 2. Selective Clustering: Handles cases where up to four intersection points exist on a cell edge, ensuring topological correctness during simplification. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Vertices per Cell: The method must handle cells containing more than one vertex, requiring robust connectivity encoding to distinguish local topology. Edge Intersections: Selective clustering is required to correctly manage cells with up to four intersection points on a single edge, preventing topological errors during simplification. Disconnected Components: Simplification algorithms must preserve disconnected surface components to maintain topological integrity. A Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) algorithm designed for ICM objects that handles adaptive grids using simple binary operations on connectivity information. It applies a combination of error minimization and a recursive subdivision scheme for representative vertices to perform CSG operations. This variant is chosen when boolean operations on multiresolution implicit surfaces are required, leveraging the compact vertex-based representation for efficient computation. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Proportional to the number of vertices in the grid. Since the mesh is composed of vertices only, it avoids storing explicit face/edge data structures. Time: Reconstruction of the explicit mesh is described as "quick," implying efficient lookup based on the connectivity encoding vectors. CSG operations use "simple binary operations" for the connectivity information. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics (FPS, memory usage in MB) are not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables isosurface-based simplification and level-of-detail rendering; supports multiresolution modeling; effective for solid modeling using CSG; allows quick reconstruction of explicit meshes. Limitations: Requires careful handling of multiple vertices per cell and complex edge intersections (up to 4 points) to maintain topology. When to Use: Use ICM when working with isosurfaces from volumetric data and requiring efficient simplification, level-of-detail rendering, or CSG operations on adaptive grids. The method is presented in the context of multiresolution isosurface modeling and rendering, with applications including texturing volumetric objects and accelerated rendering for voxel-based terrain. The work presents algorithms for converting isosurfaces of volume datasets and polygon meshes into the ICM representation, highlighting its utility in simplification and solid modeling. body: Streaming Tetrahedral Mesh Connectivity Compression is an algorithm for compressing tetrahedral volume meshes by incrementally encoding tetrahedra and vertices as they stream in, allowing memory to be freed immediately after use. It solves the problem of compressing gigabyte-sized meshes that do not fit in main memory by avoiding the need to keep the entire uncompressed mesh in memory. It sets itself apart from in-core methods like Tetrahedral Mesh Connectivity Encoding by processing data in a streaming fashion with a small delay buffer for local reordering, and from Implicit Connectivity Mesh (ICM) by explicitly managing active vertex finalization and dynamic indexing based on stream width rather than global indices. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of tetrahedra and vertices. The stream can be interleaved or block-based, but must be reasonably coherent. Output: A bit stream containing connectivity opcodes, dynamic indices, and compressed vertex positions. Data Structures: Active Vertices: Stored in a dynamic vector. Each vertex is active from the moment it is first referenced until it is finalized. Active Half-Edges: Linked into units of three describing oriented faces. Each active half-edge stores: 1. A pointer to its origin vertex. 2. A pointer to the next half-edge of the tetrahedral face it lives in. 3. A copy of the position of the tip vertex (the non-incident fourth vertex of the tetrahedron that "created" the face). Vertex Lists: Each active vertex stores a list of pointers to the active half-edges for which the vertex is the origin. Delay Buffer: A circular buffer holding up to N tetrahedra (typically 10,000) to allow local reordering. Parameters: Delay Buffer Size (N): Typically 10,000 tetrahedra. Smaller sizes (100, 1,000) reduce memory but increase bit rates due to less sharing. Quantization Precision: User-defined, typically 16 bits per coordinate. Stream Width (w): The maximal number of vertices in memory simultaneously. Dynamic indices use \log2 w bits. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the delay buffer, active vertex list, and half-edge structures. 2. Buffering: Read tetrahedra from the input stream into the delay buffer. 3. Reordering: Select the next tetrahedron from the buffer that maximizes sharing (face, edge, or vertex) with the previously compressed tetrahedron. 4. Configuration Detection: Determine the configuration of the selected tetrahedron relative to the active cut-border. Classify it as one of five labels: START, ADD, JOIN, FLIP, or FILL. 5. Connectivity Encoding: Encode the configuration label using an arithmetic coder with context switching based on the previous label. START: Topologically rotate so active vertices come before new ones. Encode the count of active vertices. Address non-shared active vertices via dynamic indexing (\log2 w bits). Compress new vertices with predictive coding and add to the dynamic vector. ADD: Ideally, the active face is shared with the previous tetrahedron. If not, share an edge or vertex. Otherwise, address one vertex via dynamic indexing. Address remaining vertices using local indices into active half-edge lists of known vertices or the intersection of two known vertices' lists. Compress the new vertex and add to the dynamic vector. JOIN: Like ADD, but also needs to address the fourth vertex. Can be done locally through half-edge lists of the active face vertices. Otherwise, use dynamic indexing. FLIP: One face is addressed like an ADD. The other face is specified locally within the intersection of half-edge lists maintained with the two vertices shared by both faces. FILL: One face is addressed like an ADD. The other two faces are addressed using half-edge lists of known vertices. This also covers the case where all four faces are active. Local Indexing: If a vertex is reachable via an active half-edge, reference it locally within the list of half-edges maintained by a known vertex, or within the intersection of lists of two already known vertices. If an intersection results in only one correctly oriented face, no further information is stored for that face. 6. Finalization Encoding: For each of the four vertices of the current tetrahedron, specify whether it is finalized (referenced for the last time) using context-sensitive arithmetic coding. The context is based on the total number of tetrahedra referencing the vertex and the current number of active half-edges around it. 7. Memory Management: If a vertex is finalized, remove it from the active vertex list and deallocate its associated half-edges. 8. Geometry Compression: When a new vertex is encountered, compress its position: Quantize the floating-point position to the user-defined precision (e.g., 16 bits per coordinate). Predict the position based on known neighbors using a predictor (e.g., Midpoint, Mirror, Heightmirror, Baseheight). Calculate the correction vector (actual position - predicted position). Optionally, express the correction vector in a local coordinate system (one axis along the base triangle's normal, origin at the midpoint) to separate normal and tangential errors. Encode the correction vector. 9. Loop: Repeat steps 2-8 until the stream is exhausted. Formulas: Mirror Rule Prediction: P = 2M - A, where M is the midpoint (centroid) of the known base triangle of the tetrahedron, and A is the tip vertex of the already known tetrahedron sharing the base. Midpoint Rule Prediction: P = M, where M is the midpoint (centroid) of the known base triangle of the tetrahedron. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Reordering: Select tet from delaybuffer that shares max elements with lastprocessedtet currenttet = delaybuffer.pop(0) # Implementation detail: reordering logic # 3. Configuration Detection: Determine config relative to active cut-border config = detectconfig(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges) # 4. Connectivity Encoding: Encode config using arithmetic coder with context from prevconfig compressedbits.append(config) if config == "START": activecount = countactivevertices(currenttet) compressedbits.append(activecount) for i in range(activecount): if not sharedwithlast(currenttet.vertices[i]): idx = getindexinactivevertices(currenttet.vertices[i]) compressedbits.append(idx) for v in currenttet.vertices[activecount:]: encodevertexposition(v, getbasetriangle(currenttet), getknowntip(currenttet)) addtoactivevertices(v) elif config == "ADD": addressactiveface(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges, compressedbits) addressremainingvertices(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges, compressedbits) newv = getnewvertex(currenttet) encodevertexposition(newv, getbasetriangle(currenttet), getknowntip(currenttet)) addtoactivevertices(newv) elif config == "JOIN": addressactiveface(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges, compressedbits) addressfourthvertex(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges, compressedbits) newv = getnewvertex(currenttet) encodevertexposition(newv, getbasetriangle(currenttet), getknowntip(currenttet)) addtoactivevertices(newv) elif config == "FLIP": addressoneface(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges, compressedbits) addressotherfacelocally(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges, compressedbits) elif config == "FILL": addressoneface(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges, compressedbits) addressotherfacesvialists(currenttet, activevertices, activehalfedges, compressedbits) # 5. Finalization Encoding for v in currenttet.vertices: isfinalized = islastreference(v) # Encode finalization using context-sensitive arithmetic coding compressedbits.append(isfinalized) if isfinalized: removefromactivevertices(v) deallocatehalfedges(v) prevconfig = config lastprocessedtet = currenttet return compressedbits Organizes tetrahedral meshes on disk in a coherent, I/O-efficient format to minimize memory footprint during streaming simplification. It prioritizes topological contiguity to reduce the "front width" and "span" of the active mesh portion, enabling the use of fixed-size circular arrays instead of hash tables. Choose this when I/O efficiency and memory footprint are critical constraints for streaming operations. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra, O(N), where N is the number of tetrahedra. The delay buffer reordering adds a constant factor overhead proportional to the buffer size. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the stream width w, which is the maximal number of active vertices. This is significantly lower than in-core methods that require O(V) memory for all vertices. For example, on the 'sf1' mesh, it uses 20 MB compared to 645 MB for conventional methods. Measured Performance: On the 'torso' mesh with a 10,000 tetrahedron delay buffer, connectivity compression achieves approximately 3.88 bpt (bits per tetrahedron) with explicit finalization. Total bit rates (connectivity + geometry) are 25-40% larger than Gumhold et al.'s in-core method but achieved with drastically less memory and less than half the processing time (44 seconds vs. 100 seconds for 'sf1'). Strengths: Low memory footprint, fast processing, suitable for meshes larger than main memory, robust to input order with a sufficient delay buffer. Limitations: Connectivity compression rates are higher (worse) than in-core methods (almost twice as much space). Predictive geometry compression is less effective for grid-aligned data (e.g., 'sf1') where delta coding is better. Unfinalized vertices can lead to significant memory increases if not handled correctly. When to Use: Large tetrahedral meshes that do not fit in main memory, or when streaming I/O is preferred. When Not to Use: When maximum compression ratio is the primary goal and memory is not a constraint, or for meshes with very large boundaries where guessed finalization leads to high memory usage. The method was introduced by Isenburg and Lindström in their paper "Streaming compression of tetrahedral volume meshes". It extends the streaming mesh compression approach for triangle meshes by Isenburg et al. [14] to tetrahedral volume meshes. The work addresses the limitations of in-core compression methods like those by Gumhold et al. [4], which require the entire mesh in memory and global reordering. body: Mesh Layout for Streaming is a technique to organize tetrahedral meshes on disk in a coherent, I/O-efficient format to minimize the memory footprint during streaming simplification. It builds on Streaming Tetrahedral Mesh Connectivity Compression and differs from spatial sorting by prioritizing topological contiguity to reduce the front width and span of the active mesh portion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tetrahedral mesh with arbitrary initial connectivity. Output: A re-ordered sequence of tetrahedra written to disk in a stream-efficient order. Data Structures: The method uses a fixed-size circular array or hash table to track active vertices, with the required size determined by the layout's span. The output is a linear stream of tetrahedra indices. Steps: 1. Construct the adjacency graph of the tetrahedral mesh. 2. Initiate a Breadth-First Search (BFS) starting from an arbitrary boundary tetrahedron. 3. Traverse the graph and assign tetrahedra to the output stream in visitation order. 4. Preserve the stream order between input and output to maintain spatial locality for the simplification algorithm. Parameters: Buffer size is determined by the span of the layout, which the BFS approach minimizes to allow fixed-size arrays. Typical performance requires approximately 40 minutes to layout a mesh of 14 million tetrahedra. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Collisions occur if the buffer size is smaller than the span, but a simple modulo hash function resolves them without linked lists. For very large datasets like SF1, memory constraints may cause inaccurate simplification in certain stream parts, but increasing memory slightly greatly improves quality. This disk layout interleaves vertex definitions and cell references to enable coherent sequential access and out-of-core processing. It extends the OBJ file format to support tetrahedral cells and vertex finalization via negative indices. It is chosen when out-of-core streaming simplification is required, as it limits memory footprint compared to traditional formats that require the entire vertex list in memory. This variant uses the first nontrivial eigenvector of the mesh Laplacian matrix to generate the ordering. It is chosen when the lowest possible width is critical for minimizing memory consumption, though it is less effective on compact tetrahedral meshes than on curvy triangle meshes. This approach starts at a boundary vertex and grows contiguously to neighboring vertices. It is selected when a simple topological growth strategy is preferred over spectral or breadth-first methods. Time complexity is a one-time operation, requiring about 40 minutes for 14 million tetrahedra. The method enables simplification of 14 million tetrahedra using only 20 MB RAM. Compared to Wu and Kobbelt's algorithm, it achieves lower width (9% vs 59% on the Fighter dataset) and span (45% vs 98%) without reducing approximation quality. Strengths include a significantly reduced memory footprint, support for fixed-size circular arrays, and an order-of-magnitude speedup over initial Garland and Zhou implementations. Limitations include front width and span being typically much larger than spatial sorting. This method was presented in the context of streaming simplification of tetrahedral meshes. body: The Streaming Tetrahedral Mesh Format is a disk layout for tetrahedral meshes that interleaves vertex definitions and cell references to enable coherent sequential access and out-of-core processing. Unlike traditional formats that require the entire vertex list in memory for dereferencing, this format allows vertices to be introduced and finalized sequentially, significantly limiting the memory footprint during streaming simplification. It extends the OBJ file format to support tetrahedral cells and vertex finalization via negative indices. Inputs and Outputs Input is a tetrahedral mesh defined by vertices and cells. Output is a stream of text records representing vertices and cells in an interleaved order. Data Structures The format uses two record types: 1. Vertex Record: Defines a vertex with four scalar values: x, y, z (3D position) and f (scalar field value). 2. Cell Record: Defines a tetrahedral cell by indexing four vertices. Vertex Indexing and Finalization Vertices are introduced sequentially and assigned positive indices corresponding to their order in the stream. A vertex is "active" from the moment it is introduced until it is finalized. Finalization is achieved by using a negative index in a subsequent cell record. This negative index mechanism is backward compatible with the OBJ format. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize an empty in-core active set of vertices and a counter for introduced vertices. 2. For each vertex in the mesh traversal order: write the vertex record v x y z f, add the vertex to the active set, and assign it a positive index. 3. For each tetrahedral cell in the mesh traversal order: identify the four vertices defining the cell. For each vertex, determine its reference index: if the vertex is currently active, use its positive index; if finalized, use a negative index. Write the cell record t v1 v2 v3 v4. 4. After a cell is processed, if any referenced vertices are no longer needed by future cells, they are marked for finalization. Pseudocode Unverified code. """ activeset = [] streamindexmap = {} nextindex = 1 for cell in cells: # Introduce vertices not yet in the stream for vidx in cell: if vidx not in streamindexmap: v = vertices[vidx] output.write(f"v {v[0]} {v[1]} {v[2]} {v[3]}\n") streamindexmap[vidx] = nextindex activeset.append(vidx) nextindex += 1 # Determine indices for the cell record cellindices = [] for vidx in cell: if vidx in activeset: cellindices.append(str(streamindexmap[vidx])) else: # Finalized vertex: use negative index # Exact negative index calculation is not specified in the sources. # Standard streaming OBJ extensions use a window-based offset relative to the current stream position. cellindices.append("-1") output.write(f"t {' '.join(cellindices)}\n") # Finalize vertices no longer needed by future cells # The exact trigger for finalization depends on the mesh traversal order # and front width constraints. activeset = [v for v in activeset if v in cell] Parameters Front Width: The maximum number of concurrently active vertices in the in-core active set. Front Span: The maximum index difference (plus one) of the concurrently active vertices. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point precision for x, y, z, f values should be consistent with the source data. Boundary Conditions: The first vertex must be introduced before any cell referencing it is written. Degenerate Input: If a cell references a vertex that has not been introduced, the format is violated. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by the front width, which is typically much smaller than the total number of vertices N. Measured Performance: The source does not provide specific performance numbers, but notes that low front span allows for faster implementation. Strengths: Low memory footprint, backward compatibility with OBJ, suitable for out-of-core processing. Limitations: Requires careful management of the active set and finalization logic. The negative index mechanism may be complex to implement correctly for general meshes. When to Use: When streaming large tetrahedral meshes for visualization or simplification with limited memory. When Not to Use: When random access to vertices is required, or when the mesh is small enough to fit entirely in memory. The format was developed by Isenburg and Lindstrom for triangle meshes and extended to tetrahedral meshes by the authors of "Streaming Simplification of Tetrahedral Meshes". It builds on the OBJ file format, extending it to handle tetrahedral cells and vertex finalization. The format is used in the context of out-of-core isosurface extraction and mesh simplification. name: Delaunay Triangulation for Tetrahedral Representation
head: 3D Delaunay Triangulation, gDel3D-based Tetrahedralization
body: 3D Delaunay Triangulation constructs a surface by defining tetrahedra from arbitrarily distributed 3D points, characterized by the property that no point lies within the circumsphere of any tetrahedron. It solves the problem of surface reconstruction from volumetric data or point clouds by enforcing geometric optimality (empty circumsphere property). Unlike Projected Tetrahedra which projects pre-defined grid cells, or Marching Tetrahedrons Algorithm which operates on a fixed lattice, this method adapts the tetrahedral mesh to the distribution of input sites. It is distinguished from its sibling Local Convex Hull (LCH) by using Delaunay triangulation rather than a convex hull algorithm for local surface construction, offering a trade-off between processing time and shape detail preservation. Inputs: A set of 3D points (Voronoi sites) P = \{p1, p2,..., pn\} representing the volumetric data or surface samples. Outputs: A tetrahedral mesh T where each tetrahedron t \in T satisfies the empty circumsphere property. Data Structures: Points: Array of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Tetrahedra: List of indices referencing the points array. Each tetrahedron is defined by 4 vertex indices (v1, v2, v3, v4). Circumsphere: For each tetrahedron, the center (cx, cy, cz) and squared radius r^2 of the unique sphere passing through its four vertices. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a "super tetrahedron" that encloses all input points P. This ensures the triangulation starts with a valid boundary. 2. Triangulation: Construct the initial Delaunay triangulation of the points. This can be done using standard incremental insertion or divide-and-conquer algorithms. In GPU-accelerated implementations, libraries such as gDel3D are used to accelerate this computation. 3. Empty Circumsphere Check: For each tetrahedron t in the mesh, calculate its circumsphere. Check if any point p \in P lies strictly inside this circumsphere. The condition for a point p being inside the circumsphere of tetrahedron t with vertices v1, v2, v3, v4 is determined by the determinant: \det \begin{pmatrix} xp & yp & zp & xp^2 + yp^2 + zp^2 & 1 \\ x1 & y1 & z1 & x1^2 + y1^2 + z1^2 & 1 \\ x2 & y2 & z2 & x2^2 + y2^2 + z2^2 & 1 \\ x3 & y3 & z3 & x3^2 + y3^2 + z3^2 & 1 \\ x4 & y4 & z4 & x4^2 + y4^2 + z4^2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} > 0 (Assuming a right-handed coordinate system and counter-clockwise vertex ordering). 4. Subdivision: If a point p is found within the circumsphere of tetrahedron t, subdivide t. This involves removing t and creating new tetrahedra connecting p to the faces of t that are visible from p, or using a flip-based approach to restore the Delaunay property. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 3 and 4 until no tetrahedron contains a point in its circumsphere. In differentiable rendering contexts (e.g., DCCVT), the triangulation is recomputed from scratch at every iteration to allow gradient flow. Parameters: Super Tetrahedron Size: Must be large enough to enclose all input points. Exact size is not given in the sources. Iteration Count: In DCCVT experiments, a fixed 1k iterations are used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Constrained Delaunay Triangulation (CDT): Standard DT cannot tetrahedralize some special polyhedra (e.g., twisted prisms) without additional points or surface modification. The problem of determining whether a given polyhedron can be tetrahedralized is NP-complete. Precision: Floating-point errors in determinant calculations can lead to incorrect circumsphere tests. Robust predicates are recommended. Degenerate Input: Collinear or coplanar points can cause degenerate tetrahedra. Pre-processing to remove duplicates or handle degeneracies is necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def delaunaytetrahedralization(points): """ Constructs a 3D Delaunay triangulation from a set of 3D points. """ # Step 1: Initialize with a super tetrahedron supertetra = createsupertetrahedron(points) tetrahedra = [supertetra] # Step 2: Insert points incrementally for p in points: # Find all tetrahedra whose circumsphere contains p affectedtetras = [] for t in tetrahedra: if ispointincircumsphere(p, t): affectedtetras.append(t) # Remove affected tetrahedra and create new ones # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation # requires handling the boundary of the hole created by removal tetrahedra = removetetrahedra(tetrahedra, affectedtetras) newtetras = createnewtetrahedra(p, affectedtetras) tetrahedra.extend(newtetras) # Remove the super tetrahedron if it remains tetrahedra = removesupertetrahedron(tetrahedra) return tetrahedra def ispointincircumsphere(p, t): """ Checks if point p is inside the circumsphere of tetrahedron t. """ v1, v2, v3, v4 = t.vertices det = determinantmatrix(p, v1, v2, v3, v4) return det > 0 def determinantmatrix(p, v1, v2, v3, v4): """ Computes the determinant for the circumsphere test. """ # Construct the 5x5 matrix M = [ [p.x, p.y, p.z, p.x2 + p.y2 + p.z2, 1], [v1.x, v1.y, v1.z, v1.x2 + v1.y2 + v1.z2, 1], [v2.x, v2.y, v2.z, v2.x2 + v2.y2 + v2.z2, 1], [v3.x, v3.y, v3.z, v3.x2 + v3.y2 + v3.z2, 1], [v4.x, v4.y, v4.z, v4.x2 + v4.y2 + v4.z2, 1] ] return computedeterminant(M) Local Convex Hull (LCH) is a surface reconstruction method that constructs triangular patches from volumetric data by estimating surfaces from local convexities, assuming the object is piecewise convex and surfaces are tightly connected. It solves the problem of discontinuous surfaces and holes common in simpler methods like Marching Cubes (MC) and Visual Hull Methods (VMC) by enforcing connectivity and continuity properties. LCH is distinguished from its sibling Delaunay Triangulation for Tetrahedral Representation (specifically Local DT) by using a convex hull algorithm rather than Delaunay triangulation for local surface construction, offering a trade-off between processing time and shape detail preservation. Parallel Voxel Carving is a scalable volumetric reconstruction algorithm for multi-view stereo that utilizes a GPU to simultaneously execute a large number of threads, each performing voxel carving to integrate depth maps with images from multiple views. It solves the problem of reconstructing large-scale outdoor scenes by converting semi-dense image correspondences into view-dependent depth maps and then projecting these maps into a 3D voxel grid to carve away photo-inconsistent volumes. Unlike direct mesh integration, which struggles with triangle intersections in parallel environments, this method outputs surface voxels with normals and connectivity, making it suitable for point-based rendering and scalable to high-resolution grids via streaming. Time Complexity: The worst-case time complexity for 3D Delaunay triangulation is O(n^2), but average-case is O(n \log n) for random points. In differentiable rendering contexts, recomputing from scratch at every iteration increases cost. Memory Complexity: O(n) for the number of tetrahedra in 3D, proportional to the number of input points. Measured Performance: In DCCVT, gDel3D is used to accelerate computation on the GPU. Experiments are executed for a fixed 1k iterations. Strengths: Produces high-quality tetrahedral meshes with good geometric properties (empty circumsphere). Handles arbitrarily distributed points. Limitations: Cannot handle constrained boundaries easily without additional modifications (NP-complete for general polyhedra). Computationally expensive for large datasets if not accelerated. When to use: When high-quality tetrahedralization of arbitrary point clouds is required, and constraints are not a primary concern. When not to use: When constrained boundaries are essential and the geometry is complex (e.g., twisted prisms). The 3D Delaunay Triangulation (DT) constructs a surface by defining tetrahedrons from arbitrarily distributed 3D points. The Constrained Delaunay Triangulation (CDT) has been evolved to include a predescribed boundary. Although other variations like conforming constrained DT have been proposed, they assume initial boundary information is given. The problem of determining whether a given polyhedron can be tetrahedralized is NP-complete. In recent applications, such as DCCVT, DT is used to obtain a tetrahedral representation of Voronoi sites, accelerated by gDel3D on the GPU. name: Local Convex Hull (LCH)
head: Local Hull-based Surface Construction
body: Local Convex Hull (LCH) is a surface reconstruction method that constructs triangular patches from volumetric data by estimating surfaces from local convexities, assuming the object is piecewise convex and surfaces are tightly connected. It solves the problem of discontinuous surfaces and holes common in simpler methods like Marching Cubes (MC) and Visual Hull Methods (VMC) by enforcing connectivity and continuity properties. LCH is distinguished from its sibling Delaunay Triangulation for Tetrahedral Representation (specifically Local DT) by using a convex hull algorithm rather than Delaunay triangulation for local surface construction, offering a trade-off between processing time and shape detail preservation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of initial surface vertices (typically the best result from a Visual Hull Method, VMC) and an octree representation of the volumetric data. Output: A continuous triangular mesh representing the object surface. Data Structures: Octree: Hierarchical spatial partitioning. The implementation uses a 7-level octree with an initial octant size of 30 cm for the tested scenes. Slices: 2D cross-sections of the initial surface vertices prepared for processing. Clusters: Groups of points within a slice, defined by a cluster conditional probability density function (pdf) estimated from the octree. Local Convexities: Defined by connecting clusters in a slice to neighboring clusters in adjacent slices using a Bayesian decision-making rule. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Use the best VMC result as the initial set of surface vertices. 2. Slicing: Prepare 2D slices from the initial surface vertices. 3. Clustering: Cluster the sliced data based on a cluster conditional pdf estimated from the octree. 4. Connection: Connect clusters in each slice to neighboring clusters in adjacent slices using a Bayesian decision-making rule to define local convexities. 5. Local Surface Construction: Apply a convex hull algorithm to the connected clusters in each slice to create local surface patches. 6. Assembly: Combine the local surface patches to complete the global surface construction. Parameters: Initial Octant Size: 30 cm (for a 7-level octree). Convex Hull Algorithm: The implementation uses Qhull code for Convex Hull and Delaunay Triangulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localconvexhull(surfacevertices, octree): # Step 1: Prepare 2D slices from the initial surface vertices slices = prepareslices(surfacevertices) # Step 2: Estimate cluster conditional pdf from octree clusterpdf = estimateclusterpdf(octree) alltriangles = [] for sliceidx, slicedata in enumerate(slices): # Step 3: Cluster sliced data based on pdf clusters = clusterdata(slicedata, clusterpdf) # Step 4: Connect to neighboring clusters in adjacent slices # Using Bayesian decision-making rule to define local convexities prevclusters = slices[sliceidx - 1] if sliceidx > 0 else [] nextclusters = slices[sliceidx + 1] if sliceidx < len(slices) - 1 else [] connectedclusters = connectclusters(clusters, prevclusters, nextclusters) # Step 5: Create local surfaces using convex hull algorithm (e.g., Qhull) localtriangles = computeconvexhull(connectedclusters) alltriangles.extend(localtriangles) # Step 6: Combine local surface patches to complete the global surface construction return assemblesurface(alltriangles) def prepareslices(vertices): pass # Not given in the sources. def estimateclusterpdf(octree): pass # Not given in the sources. def clusterdata(slicedata, pdf): pass # Not given in the sources. def connectclusters(current, prev, next): pass # Not given in the sources. def computeconvexhull(points): pass # Not given in the sources. def assemblesurface(triangles): pass # Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concavity Disappearance: Any concavity in the xy plane may disappear because the concavity of a cluster in a slice is regarded as a 2D convex. This can be alleviated by dividing a 2D non-convex cluster into convex regions. Elongated Patches: Elongated or thin triangular patches are caused by using a small slicing level and the convex hull algorithm. This can be improved by inserting refining points on the side of the thin triangles. Time Complexity: The order of complexity is O(m \times k), where m is the number of slices and k is the number of clusters. It also incorporates the Qhull algorithm with complexity O(n \ln v), where n is the number of input points and v is the number of output vertices. Memory Complexity: Peak memory usage is 3 to 6 times higher than general Convex Hull (CH) and Delaunay Triangulation (DT) because the method needs to store data slices, tree tables, and pdf information. Performance: LCH is generally faster than MC, VMC, and Local DT (LDT), but slower than CH and DT, except when DT constructs a large number of tetrahedrons. CH requires the shortest time, followed by DT, LCH, LDT, VMC, and MC. Strengths: LCH produces the best continuous surface compared to MC and VMC, which suffer from unattached segments and holes. It preserves shape details that are lost by simple CH on non-convex objects. Limitations: Higher memory usage than CH and DT. Loss of concavity details in the xy plane. Potential for thin/elongated triangles. When to Use: When continuous surface connectivity is critical and the object is piecewise convex, especially when MC/VMC produce holes. When Not to Use: For totally convex objects where CH is better in terms of processing time, memory, and efficiency. When memory is constrained. LCH was proposed as a local hull-based surface construction method for volumetric data from silhouettes. It explores the properties of 3D objects, specifically the connectivity property (surface covers all area tightly) and the continuity property (object is piecewise convex). The method was developed to address the limitations of simple thresholding, MC, and VMC in producing continuous and detailed surfaces from silhouette-based reconstructions. name: Parallel Voxel Carving for Multi-view Stereo
head: GPU-based Scalable Volumetric Reconstruction for Multi-view Stereo
body: Parallel Voxel Carving is a scalable volumetric reconstruction algorithm for multi-view stereo that utilizes a GPU to simultaneously execute a large number of threads, each performing voxel carving to integrate depth maps with images from multiple views. It solves the problem of reconstructing large-scale outdoor scenes by converting semi-dense image correspondences into view-dependent depth maps and then projecting these maps into a 3D voxel grid to carve away photo-inconsistent volumes. Unlike direct mesh integration, which struggles with triangle intersections in parallel environments, this method outputs surface voxels with normals and connectivity, making it suitable for point-based rendering and scalable to high-resolution grids via streaming. Inputs: 1. A set of input images from multiple views. 2. Camera poses for each image, estimated prior to reconstruction. 3. Depth maps for each view, generated from semi-dense correspondences. Outputs: 1. A set of surface voxels. Each surface voxel stores a weighted average plane (normal and distance) among several view-dependent planes intersecting the voxel cube, shifted to a point on this plane, along with an optimally interpolated color from all visible images. 2. Alternatively, the full volumetric data (carved, surface, and inner uncarved voxels). Depth Map Structure: Stored per pixel. Contains depth values representing the distance between the camera viewpoint and the view-dependent surface. Contains plane information (normal vector) at every pixel. Surface Voxel Structure: Represents a voxel on the object surface. Stores a weighted average plane derived from intersecting view-dependent planes. The voxel position is shifted to a point on this weighted average plane. Voxel Grid: Configurable dimensions based on scene orientation. Typical example for aerial/terrain scenes: 8192 \times 512 \times 8192 (x, y, z), where x and z are horizontal and y is vertical. 1. Camera Pose Estimation and Image Matching: Perform dense correspondence using a gradient-based warping and coarse-to-fine hierarchical matching algorithm (e.g., Cluff et al.). 2. Edge Extraction: Extract matching points on or near edges using an edge detector. 3. 3D Point Computation and Refinement: Compute 3D points from pairwise correspondences. Refine camera poses and 3D points via bundle adjustment. 4. Terrain Alignment (Optional but recommended for aerial scenes): Estimate a least-squares plane to align the 3D point cloud onto the x-z plane. Transform all coordinates and camera projection matrices so that x and z are horizontal and y is vertical. This allows using a smaller range in the y-axis (e.g., 512 vs 8192) for efficiency. 1. Semi-Dense Correspondences: Use semi-dense correspondences between two images and their determined 3D points. Semi-dense pairs are sparser than dense matches but sufficient to determine geometry, mitigating errors in textureless or occluded regions. 2. Delaunay Triangulation: Generate a depth mesh via Delaunay triangulation of the 2D correspondences. 3. View-Dependent Surface Creation: Replace 2D vertices in the mesh with their corresponding 3D points to create a view-dependent 3D surface. 4. Normal Computation: Compute each triangle's normal from its 3D vertex coordinates. Choose the sign of the normal to ensure a negative dot product with the viewing direction. 5. Mesh Simplification (Optional): If input correspondences are noisy, apply mesh simplification to merge triangles with similar normals. 6. Projection: Project the depth mesh onto the image plane to create a dense depth map. The depth map stores depth values and plane normals at every pixel. The volume is partitioned into sub-volumes. A parallel GPU kernel is executed for each sub-volume. Parallelization Strategy: The GPU kernel uses VW \times VD threads in parallel. Each thread performs VH voxel carving operations independently. For a 256^3 voxel sub-volume, 256^2 threads run in parallel, with each thread carving 256 voxels along the y-axis. Carving is done along the y-axis to balance workloads, as urban scenes are often flat in this dimension. Carving Logic (per thread): For each voxel in its assigned range: 1. Visibility Check: Determine if the voxel is visible in the current view. 2. Projection: Project the voxel center into the image plane of the current view. 3. Photo-Consistency Test: Retrieve the depth value d{map} and normal n{map} from the depth map at the projected pixel. Retrieve the depth value d{voxel} from the voxel's position relative to the camera. Check if the voxel is photo-inconsistent. A voxel is carved away if it does not match the depth map/image data. Specifically, if the voxel's depth deviates significantly from the depth map's depth, or if the photo-consistency metric fails. Incorrect view-dependent surfaces are carved away when voxel carving is performed with another viewpoint. Correct surfaces remain. 4. Update State: If carved: Mark voxel as "Carved." If not carved: Mark voxel as "Uncarved" (Inner) or "Surface" (if it is on the boundary of the uncarved region). 5. Surface Voxel Calculation (for final output): For voxels identified as surface voxels, compute a weighted average plane among several view-dependent planes intersecting the voxel cube. Shift the voxel to a point on this plane. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelvoxelcarving(depthmaps, poses, griddims): VW, VH, VD = griddims # Partition volume into sub-volumes (e.g., 256^3) subvolumes = partitionvolume(griddims) # Not given in sources. reconstructedvoxels = [] for subvol in subvolumes: # GPU Kernel: 256^2 threads for 256^3 sub-volume # Each thread handles VH voxels along Y-axis numthreads = VW VD voxelsperthread = VH voxelstates = {} for threadid in range(numthreads): u = threadid % VW v = (threadid // VW) % VD weightednormal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] weighteddist = 0.0 weightsum = 0.0 for h in range(voxelsperthread): voxelid = (u, v, h) voxel = getvoxel(subvol, voxelid) # Not given in sources. iscarved = False for viewidx, (depthmap, pose) in enumerate(zip(depthmaps, poses)): # 3.1 Visibility Check if not isvisible(voxel, pose): # Not given in sources. continue # 3.2 Projection proju, projv = projectvoxeltoimage(voxel, pose) # Not given in sources. # 3.3 Photo-Consistency Test dmap = depthmap[projv][proju].depth nmap = depthmap[projv][proju].normal dvoxel = distance(voxel.center, pose.cameraorigin) # Check consistency: carved if depth deviates significantly or photo-consistency fails if abs(dmap - dvoxel) > 1.0: # Threshold not given in sources voxelstates[voxelid] = "CARVED" iscarved = True break else: w = 1.0 weightednormal = [weightednormal[k] + w nmap[k] for k in range(3)] weighteddist += w dmap weightsum += w if not iscarved: voxelstates[voxelid] = "UNCARVED" # 3.4 Surface Voxel Calculation if isboundary(voxel, voxelstates): # Not given in sources. voxelstates[voxelid] = "SURFACE" if weightsum > 0: avgnormal = normalize(weightednormal) avgdist = weighteddist / weightsum # Shift voxel to point on weighted average plane voxel.center = shiftvoxeltoplane(voxel.center, avgnormal, avgdist) reconstructedvoxels.append(SurfaceVoxel( position=voxel.center, normal=avgnormal, color=interpolatecolor(voxel, depthmaps, poses) # Not given in sources.)) return reconstructedvoxels Voxel Grid Dimensions: Configurable. Example: 8192 \times 512 \times 8192 (x, y, z) for aerial scenes. GPU Thread Configuration: 256^2 threads per sub-volume kernel. Sub-Volume Size: Approximately 256^3 voxels per kernel to fit GPU memory. Textureless Regions: Dense correspondence algorithms fail here. The method uses semi-dense correspondences to mitigate this. Occluded Regions: Pixels in occluded regions cause matching errors. Semi-dense correspondences help mitigate negative influences from interpolation and smoothing. Camera Pose Errors: Incorrect poses lead to poor reconstruction. The method assumes poses are estimated prior to reconstruction. View-Dependent Surfaces: Some view-dependent surfaces may be incorrect but remain if the angle between the camera ray and the object's true surface normal is favorable. These are carved away by other viewpoints. What it is: A method for surface reconstruction from point clouds using local convex hulls. Difference: LCH focuses on mesh generation from points, whereas Parallel Voxel Carving operates directly in voxel space using photo-consistency. When to choose: When a polygonal mesh is required directly from points without volumetric representation. Link: Local Convex Hull (LCH) Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and views, O(V \cdot N), where V is the number of voxels and N is the number of views. Parallelization on GPU makes it effectively linear with respect to the number of threads. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the voxel grid size and the number of depth maps. The method uses streaming to handle large volumes, limiting GPU memory usage to sub-volumes (256^3 voxels). Measured Performance: Achieves high performance for large-scale reconstruction with synthetic and real urban scenes. Scaling: Scalable via partitioning the volume into sub-volumes and using streaming. Strengths: Effective parallelization on GPU. Handles large-scale outdoor scenes. Outputs surface voxels with normals and connectivity. Robust to noise via semi-dense correspondences. Limitations: Requires accurate camera poses. Struggles with textureless regions without semi-dense matching. Volumetric representation can be memory-intensive for very large scenes without streaming. When to use: Large-scale scene reconstruction in high-resolution voxel grids, specifically for aerial photographs of outdoor scenes and real urban/outdoor scenes. When not to use: When camera poses are unknown or inaccurate, or when real-time performance on small objects is required without GPU acceleration. Origin: The method was proposed by researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and the University of California, Davis. History: It builds on space carving techniques [11, 12] and integrates concepts from previous work [3] to combine depth maps with images for volumetric integration. Usage: Used for large-scale scene reconstruction, particularly for aerial photographs and urban scenes. It can be integrated with existing multi-view stereo algorithms like PMVS2 to fill holes in textureless regions.
