name: Debug Voxel Visualization
head: DisplayVolume, Voxel Debug Rendering, Voxel Sphere Debug, VoxelMap::visualize
body: Debug Voxel Visualization renders a 3D voxel grid as individual geometric primitives (typically cubes or spheres) for each active voxel by iterating through the voxel data array and drawing a pre-loaded model at every non-transparent position. It solves the problem of visualizing the discrete structure and spatial distribution of voxel data in a scene, distinct from surface extraction methods. It differs from Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Geometry and Bounding Box Drawing by rendering individual voxel instances rather than aggregate bounding volumes, allowing for per-voxel inspection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 1D array of voxel data (typically RGBA bytes), metadata defining the grid dimensions (w, h, d), a threshold value for voxel activation, and a pre-loaded geometric model (cube or sphere). Output: A set of transformed geometric primitives submitted to the graphics pipeline, positioned at their respective grid coordinates. Data Structures: Voxel Data: A 1D array of GLubyte (RGBA) with size w \times h \times d \times 4 bytes. VolumeMetadata: Parsed from a JSON file (e.g., in StreamingAssets), containing dimensions and validation checks ensuring the dimension length is exactly 3. Voxel Model: A pre-loaded 3D cube or sphere mesh, centered at the origin. Parameters: intensityThreshold (float, 0.0–1.0): Voxels with alpha below this value are skipped. dontDraw (float, default 0.0f): Alternative alpha threshold for skipping voxels. sphereRadius (float, default 0.5f): Radius of the debug sphere in mm before scaling. voxelOffset (vec3): Offset applied to align the centered cube model origin to the voxel grid position. Calculated as (1.0f / voxelmap\size, 1.0f / voxelmap\size, 1.0f / voxelmap\size). maxSpheres (int, default 5000): Safety cap for spawned debug spheres. Steps: 1. Load metadata JSON and parse into VolumeMetadata. Validate that the dimension length is 3. 2. Iterate through the voxel grid coordinates x \in [0, w-1], y \in [0, h-1], z \in [0, d-1]. 3. Calculate the 1D array index for the current voxel using row-major ordering: arrayPos = 4 \times (x + y \times voxelmap\size + z \times voxelmap\size \times voxelmap\size) where voxelmap\size is the dimension size (assuming a cubic grid where w=h=d=size). 4. Extract the alpha channel from the RGBA byte at index arrayPos + 3. 5. If the alpha value exceeds the threshold (intensityThreshold or dontDraw): a. Normalize the RGB values by dividing by 255.0f. b. Set the shader color to the normalized RGB values. c. Compute the world position using the voxel offset and grid coordinates: \mathbf{p}{world} = \mathbf{voxelOffset} + \text{vC\to\wC}(\text{glm::vec3}(x, y, z), voxelmap\size) where \text{vC\to\wC} converts voxel coordinates to world coordinates based on the grid size. d. Draw the voxel model at \mathbf{p}{world} with the set color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def debugvoxelvisualize(voxeldata: list, metadata: dict, threshold: float, model: Mesh): """ Renders active voxels as geometric primitives. Args: voxeldata: 1D list of RGBA bytes (GLubyte). metadata: Dict with 'width', 'height', 'depth', 'size'. threshold: Alpha threshold for activation (0.0-1.0). model: Pre-loaded geometric mesh (cube/sphere). """ w = metadata['width'] h = metadata['height'] d = metadata['depth'] size = metadata['size'] # Assuming cubic grid for index formula # Validate dimensions if len([w, h, d]) != 3: raise ValueError("Metadata must contain exactly 3 dimensions") # Calculate voxel offset for centering voxeloffset = (1.0 / size, 1.0 / size, 1.0 / size) # Iterate through all voxels for z in range(d): for y in range(h): for x in range(w): # Calculate 1D array index (row-major, 4 bytes per pixel) arraypos = 4 (x + y size + z size size) # Extract alpha channel (RGBA layout) alpha = voxeldata[arraypos + 3] # Check threshold if alpha > threshold: # Normalize RGB r = voxeldata[arraypos] / 255.0 g = voxeldata[arraypos + 1] / 255.0 b = voxeldata[arraypos + 2] / 255.0 # Compute world position # vCtowC converts voxel coords to world coords # Assuming simple scaling for demonstration voxelcoords = (x, y, z) worldpos = ( voxeloffset[0] + voxelcoords[0] (1.0 / size), voxeloffset[1] + voxelcoords[1] (1.0 / size), voxeloffset[2] + voxelcoords[2] (1.0 / size)) # Draw model drawmodel(model, position=worldpos, color=(r, g, b)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when converting voxel coordinates to world space if the grid size is very large. Boundaries: The voxelOffset calculation assumes a specific alignment; incorrect offsets may cause voxels to be misaligned or clipped. Degenerate Input: If the voxel data array is empty or dimensions are invalid, the loop will not execute or may throw errors. Validation of metadata is crucial. Performance: Iterating through all voxels and drawing individual models can be expensive for large grids. The maxSpheres cap helps prevent excessive draw calls. A visual effect that draws outlines of the voxel shapes on the grid with a specified width. It differs from solid voxel rendering by highlighting the boundaries between voxels, useful for inspecting grid structure. Parameter: width (float) defining the edge thickness. A technique for inspecting dense voxel grids by plotting central slices along X, Y, and Z axes, optionally overlaying hierarchy information from an octree. It differs from full-volume rendering by reducing visual clutter and focusing on specific cross-sections. Steps: Load voxel grid, build octree (maxdepth=8), plot central slices (maxdepth=5) with optional red hierarchy overlays. A real-time debug overlay highlighting active Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) field mutations and non-Euclidean portal throats using concentric distance rings. It differs from standard voxel visualization by focusing on SDF-based CSG operations and portal effects. Formula: max(dTrack, -dSphere) for CSG union operations. Parameters: uPortalsA/B for portal throats. An animated vertical laser scanner curtain used to sweep across the scene for SDF X-Ray visualization. It differs from static visualization by providing a dynamic, animated view of the internal structure. Step: Render an animated vertical curtain sweeping across the viewport. Time Complexity: O(N) where N = w \times h \times d, as every voxel must be checked. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the voxel data array. Performance: Performance degrades linearly with grid size. The maxSpheres cap limits draw calls but may truncate visualization for large grids. Strengths: Simple to implement, provides direct per-voxel visibility, easy to debug individual voxel states. Limitations: High draw call overhead for large grids, not suitable for real-time visualization of very large volumes without instancing or culling. When to Use: Debugging voxel data integrity, small-scale voxel worlds, educational purposes. When Not to Use: Large-scale production rendering, real-time visualization of massive voxel grids. Debug Voxel Visualization is a fundamental technique in voxel-based applications, originating from the need to inspect discrete volumetric data. It is commonly used in voxel editors, game engines, and scientific visualization tools. The method described here is based on implementations in open-source projects like VXCT and VRDF SDK. guillaume-schneider/vrdf-sdk, https://github.com/guillaume-schneider/vrdf-sdk, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Helliaca/VXCT, https://github.com/Helliaca/VXCT, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Milestone 13: MagicaVoxel look (.vox, DDA voxel grid, sun/sky, bloom, style voxel), https://github.com/adriendjn/mypbr/pull/10, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) hsafari68/Voxelerate, https://github.com/hsafari68/Voxelerate, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) feat(sdf-wizard): [W] 20-Second SDF X-Ray & Measurement Wizard (uDebugVizMode 1..5 + live caliper), https://github.com/bourkefloyd/gemini-4-argon-sfhackathon-2026/pull/23, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Wireframe Block Highlighter
head: Voxel Block Wireframe Outline
body:
The Wireframe Block Highlighter renders a visible outline around a target voxel block to assist in debugging or user interaction within a voxel world. It solves the problem of identifying specific block coordinates in a dense voxel grid by drawing a wireframe box slightly larger than the block itself. It differs from face-based highlighting methods by enclosing the entire volume of the block rather than marking a specific surface normal, making it suitable for general selection or debugging where the block's position is the primary concern rather than its orientation. Inputs: Target block position (x, y, z) in voxel space. Outline padding parameter p. Line width parameter w. Outline color C. Outputs: 12 line segments defining the cube edges. Data Structures: Edges Array: A static array of 12 pairs of corner indices. Each pair defines a line segment between two vertices of the unit cube. The indices correspond to the 8 corners of the cube, indexed 0–7. Layout: [{0,1}, {1,2}, {2,3}, {3,0}, {4,5}, {5,6}, {6,7}, {7,4}, {0,4}, {1,5}, {2,6}, {3,7}]. Corner mapping (standard unit cube): 0: (0,0,0) 1: (1,0,0) 2: (1,1,0) 3: (0,1,0) 4: (0,0,1) 5: (1,0,1) 6: (1,1,1) 7: (0,1,1) Parameters: Line width w = 0.025. Outline padding p = 0.01. Outline color C = 	ext{Color.black}. Steps: 1. Calculate Block Bounds: Define the block's local bounds in voxel space: 	ext{min}{local} = (x, y, z) 	ext{max}{local} = (x+1, y+1, z+1) Apply padding to create the wireframe bounds: 	ext{min}{wire} = 	ext{min}{local} - (p, p, p) 	ext{max}{wire} = 	ext{max}{local} + (p, p, p) 2. Compute Corner Vertices: Generate the 8 vertices of the padded cube using 	ext{min}{wire} and 	ext{max}{wire}. Let Vi be the vertex corresponding to corner index i. Example for V0: V0 = (	ext{min}{wire}.x, 	ext{min}{wire}.y, 	ext{min}{wire}.z) Example for V6: V6 = (	ext{max}{wire}.x, 	ext{max}{wire}.y, 	ext{max}{wire}.z) 3. Generate Line Segments: Iterate through the 12 edge pairs in the Edges array. For each pair \{i, j\}, create a line segment from vertex Vi to vertex Vj. Render these segments using a line renderer with width w and color C. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderwireframehighlight(blockpos: Vector3, padding: float, linewidth: float, color: Color): # 1. Calculate padded bounds minwire = blockpos - Vector3(padding, padding, padding) maxwire = blockpos + Vector3(1.0 + padding, 1.0 + padding, 1.0 + padding) # 2. Define the 8 corners of the padded cube # Indices: 0:(0,0,0), 1:(1,0,0), 2:(1,1,0), 3:(0,1,0), # 4:(0,0,1), 5:(1,0,1), 6:(1,1,1), 7:(0,1,1) corners = [ Vector3(minwire.x, minwire.y, minwire.z), # 0 Vector3(maxwire.x, minwire.y, minwire.z), # 1 Vector3(maxwire.x, maxwire.y, minwire.z), # 2 Vector3(minwire.x, maxwire.y, minwire.z), # 3 Vector3(minwire.x, minwire.y, maxwire.z), # 4 Vector3(maxwire.x, minwire.y, maxwire.z), # 5 Vector3(maxwire.x, maxwire.y, maxwire.z), # 6 Vector3(minwire.x, maxwire.y, maxwire.z) # 7 ] # 3. Define the 12 edges as pairs of corner indices edges = [ (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0), # Bottom face (4, 5), (5, 6), (6, 7), (7, 4), # Top face (0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7) # Vertical edges ] # 4. Render lines for startidx, endidx in edges: startpoint = corners[startidx] endpoint = corners[endidx] LineRenderer.drawline(startpoint, endpoint, linewidth, color) This variant highlights a specific face of the voxel block rather than the entire block outline. It is chosen when the user needs to identify the surface normal or the specific side of a block being targeted, rather than just the block's location. It differs from the Wireframe Block Highlighter by adjusting the highlight position based on the face normal to avoid z-fighting and by rotating the highlight mesh to align with the face. Steps: 1. Convert global voxel coordinates to local coordinates using the world's coordinate system. 2. Calculate the distance d from the camera to the highlight position. 3. Iterate over the 3 axes (x, y, z). For each axis i: If the normal component ni is 0, add 0.5 to the position to center the highlight on the face: posi += 0.5. If ni 
eq 0, add an offset based on the normal direction: posi +=  egin{cases} 1 + 	ext{slop} & 	ext{if } ni > 0 \ -	ext{slop} & 	ext{if } ni < 0 \end{cases} where 	ext{slop} = 0.001 + 0.001 	imes d. 4. Apply the calculated position to the highlight mesh. 5. Set rotation based on the normal axes: If ny 
eq 0, set rotation.x = \pi/2. If nx 
eq 0, set rotation.y = \pi/2 [G: Assumes axis-aligned faces; other orientations may require quaternion rotation]. Parameters: slop: Z-fighting avoidance offset, calculated as 0.001 + 0.001 	imes 	ext{distance}. Pitfalls: Z-fighting is avoided by the distance-dependent slop offset. The rotation logic assumes axis-aligned faces; it sets X or Y rotation to 90 degrees based on normal components. Time Complexity: O(1) per highlighted block, as it always renders exactly 12 line segments regardless of block content. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the edge definitions and temporary vertex calculations. Performance: Very high performance due to minimal geometry. Suitable for highlighting many blocks simultaneously if the line renderer supports instancing or batched rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement, visually unambiguous for block selection, low overhead. Limitations: Does not indicate surface orientation or normal direction. May obscure the block's texture if the line width is too large or color contrast is poor. The Wireframe Block Highlighter is a common technique in voxel-based game development and debugging tools. It is used in projects such as Voxel Forge to provide visual feedback for block selection and interaction. The method is often paired with raycasting to determine the target block and then rendered as a debug overlay. philip2012/voxel-forge, https://github.com/philip2012/voxel-forge, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) fenomas/noa, https://github.com/fenomas/noa, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Matplotlib 3D Voxel Rendering with Internal Faces
head: Matplotlib internal_faces parameter, ax.voxels monkey patch
body: This method enables the rendering of all voxel faces in a 3D volume, including occluded internal faces, by overriding the standard Matplotlib voxels method. The standard method only renders surface faces, hiding internal voxels even if they have alpha transparency. It sets itself apart from siblings like the Wireframe Block Highlighter by explicitly generating geometry for internal boundaries rather than just highlighting existing structures. The method implements a monkey patch for Axes3D.voxels that iterates through all voxel coordinates and their neighbors to determine which faces to render based on the internalfaces flag. Inputs and Outputs: Input: filled: 3D boolean NumPy array of shape (X, Y, Z) defining voxel presence. Input: x, y, z: Optional 3D coordinate arrays of shape (X+1, Y+1, Z+1). If None, generated via np.indices. Input: internalfaces: Boolean keyword argument. If True, renders faces between adjacent filled voxels. Input: facecolors: Optional 4D array (X, Y, Z, 4) or broadcastable color. Output: A Matplotlib Axes3D object containing Poly3DCollection objects for each voxel's visible faces. Data Structures: voxelfaces: A defaultdict(list) mapping voxel coordinates (i, j, k) to a list of vertex arrays defining the faces to be drawn for that voxel. square: A 4 \times 3 integer array defining the four corners of a unit square face: \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Parse Arguments: Extract filled and optional x, y, z. If x, y, z are None, generate them using np.indices((size+1, size+1, size+1)). 2. Validate Dimensions: Ensure filled.ndim == 3. 3. Handle Colors: Broadcast facecolors and edgecolors to match filled.shape if provided, or use defaults. 4. Initialize Storage: Create voxelfaces = defaultdict(list). 5. Iterate Axes Permutations: Define a generator permutationmatrices(3) that yields cyclic permutation matrices for the 3 axes. For each permutation matrix permute: a. Calculate dimensions pc, qc, rc along the permuted axes. b. Rotate the base square: squarerot = square.dot(permute.T). c. Iterate over p \in [0, pc) and q \in [0, qc): i. Calculate base index i0 for (p, q, 0) in the original coordinate system. ii. If filled[i0] is true, add the base face (at r=0) to voxelfaces[i0] using squarerot. iii. Iterate through adjacent pairs along the third axis r: for r1, r2 in zip(range(rc-1), range(1, rc)): 1. Calculate indices i1 (at r1) and i2 (at r2). 2. Internal Face Logic: If filled[i1] is true AND (internalfaces is true OR filled[i2] is false): Add the face between i1 and i2 to voxelfaces[i1]. If filled[i2] is true AND (internalfaces is true OR filled[i1] is false): Add the face between i2 and i1 to voxelfaces[i2]. iv. Boundary Face Logic: For the last index rc-1: 1. Calculate index ik at rc-1 and vertex position p{k2} at rc. 2. If filled[ik] is true, add the outer boundary face to voxelfaces[ik]. 6. Generate Geometry: Iterate over voxelfaces. For each coordinate and list of face indices: a. Convert indices to 3D positions using x, y, z arrays if provided, or use indices directly. b. Create a Poly3DCollection for the faces. c. Assign facecolors and edgecolors. d. Add the collection to the axes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from collections import defaultdict from matplotlib.cbook import backports def voxelsinternalfaces(ax, filled, x=None, y=None, z=None, internalfaces=False, facecolors=None, edgecolors=None): """ Monkey-patched voxels method to render internal faces. """ if filled.ndim != 3: raise ValueError("Argument filled must be 3-dimensional") size = np.array(filled.shape, dtype=np.intp) coordshape = tuple(size + 1) if x is None: x, y, z = np.indices(coordshape) else: x, y, z = (backports.broadcastto(c, coordshape) for c in (x, y, z)) # Handle colors def broadcastcolorarg(color, name): if np.ndim(color) in (0, 1): return backports.broadcastto(color, filled.shape + np.shape(color)) elif np.ndim(color) in (3, 4): if np.shape(color)[:3] != filled.shape: raise ValueError(f"When multidimensional, {name} must match the shape of filled") return color else: raise ValueError(f"Invalid {name} argument") if facecolors is None: facecolors = ax.getpatchesforfill.getnextcolor() facecolors = broadcastcolorarg(facecolors, 'facecolors') if edgecolors is None: edgecolors = 'black' # Default edge color if not specified edgecolors = broadcastcolorarg(edgecolors, 'edgecolors') ax.autoscalexyz(x, y, z) square = np.array([ [0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0] ], dtype=np.intp) voxelfaces = defaultdict(list) def permutationmatrices(n): mat = np.eye(n, dtype=np.intp) for in range(n): yield mat mat = np.roll(mat, 1, axis=0) for permute in permutationmatrices(3): pc, qc, rc = permute.T.dot(size) pinds = np.arange(pc) qinds = np.arange(qc) rinds = np.arange(rc) squarerot = square.dot(permute.T) for p in pinds: for q in qinds: p0 = permute.dot([p, q, 0]) i0 = tuple(p0) if filled[i0]: voxelfaces[i0].append(p0 + squarerot) for r1, r2 in zip(rinds[:-1], rinds[1:]): p1 = permute.dot([p, q, r1]) p2 = permute.dot([p, q, r2]) i1 = tuple(p1) i2 = tuple(p2) # Face between i1 and i2 if filled[i1] and (internalfaces or not filled[i2]): voxelfaces[i1].append(p2 + squarerot) if filled[i2] and (internalfaces or not filled[i1]): voxelfaces[i2].append(p2 + squarerot) # Upper boundary face pk = permute.dot([p, q, rc-1]) pk2 = permute.dot([p, q, rc]) ik = tuple(pk) if filled[ik]: voxelfaces[ik].append(pk2 + squarerot) # Create Poly3DCollections for coord, facesinds in voxelfaces.items(): # Convert indices to 3D positions # Note: facesinds contains vertex offsets relative to the voxel corner # We need to map the voxel coordinate to the actual grid position # The coordinate 'coord' is the index in the filled array (0..size-1) # The vertices are defined by the grid points (0..size) # Reconstruct vertices for this voxel # The logic in the source adds 'p2 + squarerot' to the face list. # 'p2' is the permuted coordinate of the neighbor. # We need to map these integer grid coordinates back to x, y, z values. vertices = [] for faceverts in facesinds: # faceverts is an array of 4 integer grid coordinates # Map to actual x,y,z pts = [] for v in faceverts: # v is a tuple of indices (ix, iy, iz) # x, y, z are the coordinate arrays pts.append([x[v[0], v[1], v[2]], y[v[0], v[1], v[2]], z[v[0], v[1], v[2]]]) vertices.append(np.array(pts)) # Determine color for this voxel # coord is the index in filled array fc = facecolors[coord] if facecolors.ndim > 0 else facecolors ec = edgecolors[coord] if edgecolors.ndim > 0 else edgecolors poly = ax.addcollection3d( art3d.Poly3DCollection(vertices, facecolors=fc, edgecolors=ec, linewidths=0.5)) return ax Parameters: internalfaces: False by default. Set to True to render faces between adjacent filled voxels. filled: 3D boolean NumPy array. facecolors: 4D NumPy array (X, Y, Z, 4) or broadcastable color. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Standard Matplotlib voxels does not render internal faces, causing occluded voxels to be hidden. Performance: Rendering all internal faces can be computationally expensive and visually cluttered for large volumes. Coordinate Mismatch: If x, y, z are provided, they must have shape (X+1, Y+1, Z+1). Time Complexity: O(V \cdot F), where V is the number of voxels and F is the number of faces per voxel (up to 6). The algorithm iterates through all voxel neighbors. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot F) to store the voxelfaces dictionary and the resulting Poly3DCollection objects. Strengths: Allows visualization of internal structure in transparent volumes. Limitations: Can produce visually dense output; not suitable for large datasets without culling. When to use: Debugging voxel data, visualizing internal structures in small transparent volumes. When not to use: Large-scale volume rendering where performance is critical or visual clarity is preferred over completeness. This technique was proposed as a solution to the limitation in Matplotlib's standard voxels method, which only renders surface faces. The official Matplotlib example solves occlusion by offsetting voxel faces slightly, but this method explicitly generates internal faces via the internalfaces flag. It was discussed in a Stack Overflow question and a Matplotlib issue regarding missing internal faces. name: Diagonal Voxel Peek Rendering
head: DenseVoxelDraw Diagonal, DenseVoxelDraw DiagonalPeek
body: Diagonal Voxel Peek Rendering is a debug and visualization method for rendering 3D voxel grids from a diagonal (isometric-like) perspective. It maps pixel columns to diagonals in the X-Y plane at fixed Z heights, drawing visible top, left, and right faces of voxels. It sets itself apart from standard axis-aligned debug renderers by providing a "peek" capability: it draws the top face of a voxel if it is on the top boundary or if there is empty space above it, revealing the internal structure of the volume. Unlike Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Geometry which renders wireframes or solid boxes, this method rasterizes specific faces to simulate a 3D view without full ray-marching. Inputs: model: A 3D voxel grid of bytes (or similar scalar type). Dimensions are SizeX, SizeY, SizeZ. scaleX: Horizontal scaling factor (default 4). scaleY: Vertical scaling factor (default 6). Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel column corresponds to a diagonal slice of the voxel volume. Data Structures: The voxel model is accessed as model[x, y, z]. Coordinates are integer indices. Algorithm: The rendering is performed in two passes or variants: the basic Diagonal pass and the Diagonal Peek pass. Both iterate over screen coordinates (pixelX, pixelY). 1. Calculate Screen Dimensions: pixelWidth = model.SizeX + model.SizeY. The vertical screen range is 0 to model.SizeZ. 2. Loop over Screen Pixels: Loop pixelY from 0 to model.SizeZ. Loop pixelX from 0 to pixelWidth with a step of 2. 3. Calculate Voxel Start Coordinates: startX = max(pixelX - model.SizeY + 1, 0). startY = max(model.SizeY - 1 - pixelX, 0). voxelZ = model.SizeZ - 1 - pixelY. 4. Handle Right Edge: If pixelX >= pixelWidth - 1 and model[SizeX-1, 0, voxelZ] is a non-zero byte rightEdge: Draw a Right face rect at (pixelX, pixelY). Continue to the next pixelX iteration. 5. Scan Diagonal: Initialize leftDone = false, rightDone = false. Loop voxelX from startX and voxelY from startY while voxelX <= model.SizeX and voxelY <= model.SizeY and !(leftDone && rightDone), incrementing both voxelX and voxelY. 6. Check Left Boundary (Right Face): If !leftDone and voxelX > 0 and model[voxelX-1, voxelY, voxelZ] is a non-zero byte voxelRight: Draw a Right face rect at (pixelX, pixelY). Set leftDone = true. 7. Check Bottom Boundary (Left Face): If !rightDone and voxelY > 0 and model[voxelX, voxelY-1, voxelZ] is a non-zero byte voxelLeft: Draw a Left face rect at (pixelX+1, pixelY). Set rightDone = true. 8. Check Current Voxel: If model[voxelX, voxelY, voxelZ] is a non-zero byte voxel: If !leftDone, draw a Left face rect at (pixelX, pixelY). If !rightDone, draw a Right face rect at (pixelX+1, pixelY). Break the voxel loop. 9. Peek Logic (for Diagonal Peek variant): The basic logic above is extended with a peek boolean parameter in the drawing functions. For the Right Edge check: Call DrawRight with peek true if voxelZ >= model.SizeZ OR (voxelZ < SizeZ-1 and model[SizeX-1, 0, voxelZ+1] is non-zero). For the Left Boundary check: Call DrawRight with peek true if voxelZ == SizeZ-1 OR (voxelZ < SizeZ-1 and model[voxelX-1, voxelY, voxelZ+1] is zero). For the Bottom Boundary check: Call DrawLeft with peek true if voxelZ == SizeZ-1 OR (voxelZ < SizeZ-1 and model[voxelX, voxelY-1, voxelZ+1] is zero). Helper Functions: DrawRight(x, y, peek): If peek is true: Draw a Top rect at (xscaleX, yscaleY) with size scaleX by 1. Draw a Right rect at (xscaleX, yscaleY+1) with size scaleX by scaleY-1. Else: Draw a single Right rect at (xscaleX, yscaleY) with size scaleX by scaleY. DrawLeft(x, y, peek): If peek is true: Draw a Top rect at (xscaleX, yscaleY) with size scaleX by 1. Draw a Left rect at (xscaleX, yscaleY+1) with size scaleX by scaleY-1. Else: Draw a single Left rect at (xscaleX, yscaleY) with size scaleX by scaleY. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderdiagonalpeek(model, scaleX=4, scaleY=6): width = model.SizeX + model.SizeY height = model.SizeZ for pixelY in range(height): for pixelX in range(0, width, 2): startX = max(pixelX - model.SizeY + 1, 0) startY = max(model.SizeY - 1 - pixelX, 0) voxelZ = model.SizeZ - 1 - pixelY # Right Edge Check if pixelX >= width - 1: if model[model.SizeX - 1, 0, voxelZ] != 0: rightedge = model[model.SizeX - 1, 0, voxelZ] # Peek logic for right edge peekright = False if voxelZ >= model.SizeZ: peekright = True elif voxelZ < model.SizeZ - 1 and model[model.SizeX - 1, 0, voxelZ + 1] != 0: peekright = True drawright(pixelX, pixelY, scaleX, scaleY, peekright) continue leftdone = False rightdone = False voxelx = startX voxely = startY while voxelx <= model.SizeX and voxely <= model.SizeY and not (leftdone and rightdone): # Check Left Boundary (Right Face) if not leftdone and voxelx > 0: if model[voxelx - 1, voxely, voxelZ] != 0: voxelright = model[voxelx - 1, voxely, voxelZ] peekright = False if voxelZ == model.SizeZ - 1: peekright = True elif voxelZ < model.SizeZ - 1 and model[voxelx - 1, voxely, voxelZ + 1] == 0: peekright = True drawright(pixelX, pixelY, scaleX, scaleY, peekright) leftdone = True # Check Bottom Boundary (Left Face) if not rightdone and voxely > 0: if model[voxelx, voxely - 1, voxelZ] != 0: voxelleft = model[voxelx, voxely - 1, voxelZ] peekleft = False if voxelZ == model.SizeZ - 1: peekleft = True elif voxelZ < model.SizeZ - 1 and model[voxelx, voxely - 1, voxelZ + 1] == 0: peekleft = True drawleft(pixelX + 1, pixelY, scaleX, scaleY, peekleft) rightdone = True # Check Current Voxel if model[voxelx, voxely, voxelZ] != 0: voxel = model[voxelx, voxely, voxelZ] if not leftdone: # For the current voxel, peek logic isn't explicitly detailed for the main body in the source, # but typically the 'peek' applies to the top face visibility. # Based on the helper functions, we assume standard drawing for the main voxel body # unless specified otherwise. The source notes focus on boundary peeking. drawleft(pixelX, pixelY, scaleX, scaleY, False) if not rightdone: drawright(pixelX + 1, pixelY, scaleX, scaleY, False) break voxelx += 1 voxely += 1 def drawright(x, y, scaleX, scaleY, peek): if peek: # Draw Top rect drawrect(x scaleX, y scaleY, scaleX, 1) # Draw Right rect drawrect(x scaleX, y scaleY + 1, scaleX, scaleY - 1) else: drawrect(x scaleX, y scaleY, scaleX, scaleY) def drawleft(x, y, scaleX, scaleY, peek): if peek: # Draw Top rect drawrect(x scaleX, y scaleY, scaleX, 1) # Draw Left rect drawrect(x scaleX, y scaleY + 1, scaleX, scaleY - 1) else: drawrect(x scaleX, y scaleY, scaleX, scaleY) A rendering method similar to Front but with scaling and 'peek' capability, drawing top and front faces if the voxel is on the top boundary or has empty space above it. Choose this when a front-facing orthographic view with peek is needed instead of a diagonal view. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) where W, H, D are the dimensions of the voxel grid, as each diagonal line is scanned. The inner loop runs until a voxel is found or boundaries are hit. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, excluding the output image buffer. Performance: Performance depends on the density of the voxel grid. Sparse grids may terminate loops early. Strengths: Provides a quick 3D-like visualization of voxel data without complex ray-marching. The peek feature helps visualize the top surface of volumes. Limitations: Not a physically accurate rendering method. Artifacts may occur at boundaries. The diagonal projection can distort perception of depth compared to perspective views. When to use: Debugging voxel data, quick visualization of large voxel grids, educational purposes. When not to use: Production-quality rendering, scenes requiring accurate lighting or shadows. name: Rasterizing Proxy Geometry
head: Liu et al. proxy rasterization
body: Rasterizing proxy geometry converts volumetric data into simplified geometric primitives (lines, planes, or octree cuts) submitted to the graphics pipeline for specific sampling or visibility tasks. Unlike full volume rendering, it exploits proxy geometry freedom to perform ray-casting, arbitrary slicing, and page visibility determination without traversing hierarchy structures on the GPU. It sets itself apart by using rasterization hardware to generate linear probes or per-pixel lists of non-empty ray segments, thereby avoiding expensive empty-space skipping data structure lookups. The method relies on generating specific proxy primitives that represent a view-dependent cut or probe through the volume, then rasterizing them to extract volumetric information into frame buffers or visibility buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric data (scalar field), camera parameters, proxy geometry definition (line, plane, or octree cut), and deformation parameters (if applicable). Outputs: A buffer containing sampled volume data (e.g., alpha values, gradients) or a list of active page IDs/visible segments. Data Structures: Proxy Geometry: Application-defined primitives representing the sampling path or visibility cut (line segment for linear probes, plane for slicing, view-dependent cut of octree nodes for Liu et al.). Frame Buffer / Visibility Buffer: Stores fragment shader outputs; back frame buffer for linear probes, visibility buffer for page visibility. Steps: 1. Define Proxy Geometry: Create primitives representing the desired sampling path or visibility cut (line segment for linear probes, view-dependent cut of octree nodes for Liu et al.). 2. Transform Geometry: For linear probes, rotate object space to align the desired line parallel to the image plane. For Liu et al., transform proxy geometry into clip space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. 3. Rasterize: Submit proxy geometry to the rasterizer. For linear probes, direct fragment shader output (volume sampling) to the back frame buffer. For Liu et al., rasterize to determine visibility or generate per-pixel lists of non-empty ray segments. 4. Sample Volume (Fragment Shader): For linear probes, the fragment shader samples the deformed volume along the line, avoiding encapsulating deformation inside the shader by pre-aligning the line. For Liu et al., use rasterized output to skip empty-space lookups. 5. Post-Processing / Readback: For linear probes, copy line data from frame buffer to main memory for UI use. For Liu et al., reduce visibility buffer to active page IDs using a compute shader reduction step. Formulas: Linear Probe Alignment: Rotate object space so line vector \vec{L} is parallel to the image plane. Interaction Criteria: Scan sampled line for first non-zero alpha (\alpha > 0), first gradient with magnitude |\nabla V| > T{grad}, or sum of alpha values \sum \alpha > 1 (infinite absorption). Parameters: Line Resolution: Determined by rasterization resolution (e.g., 512x512x106 volume). Thresholds: Gradient magnitude threshold T{grad} and alpha sum threshold (1.0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deformation Complexity: If proxy geometry does not account for deformation, the line must be divided into segments for piece-wise linear approximation, increasing complexity. Memory Bandwidth: Liu et al. address performance bottlenecks of atomic operations in concurrent thread updates by using compute shader reduction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizeproxygeometry(volumedata, camera, proxytype, deformation=None): if proxytype == "LINEARPROBE": # 1. Define line segment in object space linestart = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) lineend = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # 2. Rotate object space to align line parallel to image plane # Align line vector with camera's right vector (image plane axis) linevec = (lineend[i] - linestart[i] for i in range(3)) # Rotation matrix to align Z-axis line with X-axis rotmat = ((0, 0, 1), (0, 1, 0), (-1, 0, 0)) def applyrotation(pt, mat): return tuple(sum(p m for p, m in zip(pt, col)) for col in zip(mat)) alignedline = (applyrotation(linestart, rotmat), applyrotation(lineend, rotmat)) # 3. Rasterize line and sample volume in fragment shader numsamples = 100 samples = [] for t in range(numsamples): tnorm = t / (numsamples - 1) pos = tuple(alignedline[0][i] + tnorm (alignedline[1][i] - alignedline[0][i]) for i in range(3)) # Volume sampling along the aligned line alpha = volumesample(volumedata, pos) gradientmag = abs(volumegradient(volumedata, pos)) samples.append({'alpha': alpha, 'gradient': gradientmag}) # 4. Copy to main memory (simulated by keeping list) linedata = samples # 5. Scan for interaction criteria firstnonzeroalpha = next((s for s in linedata if s['alpha'] > 0), None) firstlargegradient = next((s for s in linedata if s['gradient'] > 0.5), None) sumalpha = 0.0 infiniteabsorption = None for s in linedata: sumalpha += s['alpha'] if sumalpha > 1.0: infiniteabsorption = s break return firstnonzeroalpha, firstlargegradient, infiniteabsorption elif proxytype == "OCTREECUT": # 1. Define proxy geometry as view-dependent cut of octree nodes proxymesh = [] for node in volumeoctree: if node.isvisible(camera): proxymesh.append(node.tomesh()) # 2. Rasterize to generate per-pixel lists of non-empty ray segments visibilitybuffer = [] for mesh in proxymesh: visibilitybuffer.extend(mesh.rasterize(camera)) # 3. Reduce visibility buffer to active page IDs using compute shader activepages = list(set(visibilitybuffer)) return activepages def volumesample(data, pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation return 0.5 def volumegradient(data, pos): # Standard finite difference return 0.3 Proxy Mesh Rendering for Page Visibility determines which virtual memory pages are visible in a scene by rendering a simplified proxy mesh to a visibility buffer and reducing that buffer to a list of active page IDs. It differs from standard visibility buffers by encoding depth information to support Level of Detail (LOD) selection and by utilizing a compute shader reduction step to minimize memory bandwidth, addressing the performance bottlenecks of atomic operations in concurrent thread updates. Linear Probe via Ray Picking uses a line as proxy geometry to perform a linear probe (similar to ray casting) through the deformed volume. It involves rotating object space to align the desired line parallel to the image plane, rasterizing the line to direct fragment shader output (volume sampling) to the back frame buffer, and copying the line data to main memory for user interface use. It allows for interaction criteria such as finding the first non-zero alpha, first large gradient, or sum of alpha values exceeding one. Time Complexity: Linear probes are O(N) where N is the number of pixels covered by the line, avoiding full volume traversal. Liu et al. approach avoids hierarchy traversal, reducing look-ups into empty-space skipping data structures. Memory Complexity: Requires frame buffer storage for the proxy output or visibility buffer for page visibility. Strengths: Avoids expensive empty-space skipping data structure lookups; simplifies linear probes by handling deformation alignment in object space rather than fragment shader; supports interactive user interfaces like ray picking. Limitations: Requires careful alignment of proxy geometry for deformation; compute shader reduction is needed for page visibility to avoid atomic operation bottlenecks. When to Use: When interactive probing (ray picking, slicing) is required without full volume rendering overhead; when page visibility determination for virtual memory management is needed. When Not to Use: When full volume visualization with complex lighting and shading is required. The concept of using proxy geometry for volume rendering was proposed by Liu et al. [LCDP13] to rasterize proxy geometry representing a view-dependent cut of octree nodes, optimizing look-ups into empty-space skipping data structures. Hadwiger et al. [HAAB+ 18] also utilized rasterization hardware to avoid hierarchy traversal on the GPU by rasterizing occupancy geometry. The linear probe technique was discussed in the context of integrating dynamic deformations into interactive volume visualization, allowing for high-resolution sampling of deformed space without complex fragment shader deformation logic. name: Proxy Mesh Rendering for Page Visibility
head: Visibility Buffer Reduction
body: Proxy Mesh Rendering for Page Visibility determines which virtual memory pages are visible in a scene by rendering a simplified proxy mesh to a visibility buffer and reducing that buffer to a list of active page IDs. The method encodes depth information to support Level of Detail (LOD) selection and uses a compute shader reduction step to minimize memory bandwidth. Inputs and Outputs Input: A proxy mesh representing the geometry of the scene, where each face is associated with a specific virtual memory page ID. Output: A CPU-accessible array of page IDs. Entries are zero for invisible pages and contain integer depth values for visible pages. Data Structures Visibility Buffer: A single-channel, 32-bit unsigned integer image rendered at low resolution to enhance performance. Page ID Buffer: A buffer passed to the fragment shader containing the page ID for each face, indexed by the face index. Steps 1. Vertex Shader Execution: The vertex shader receives vertex positions and applies model and camera transformations. 2. Fragment Shader Execution: For each rasterized fragment, the fragment shader retrieves the page ID corresponding to the input face index. Background and unassigned faces output a zero page ID, which is ignored in later steps. 3. Visibility Buffer Reduction: A compute shader processes the visibility buffer to generate a list of required page IDs. It updates each pixel's list entry in parallel, encoding depth as integers that decrease with greater depth. The atomicMax() function ensures only the closest depth value is written to the buffer. The shader iterates through linked pages per pixel to set buffer entries, connecting nearby pages to mitigate the effects of low resolution. 4. Data Transfer: The buffer is transferred to CPU memory. The resulting array contains zeroes for unneeded pages and depth values for needed pages. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. WORKGROUPSIZE = 256 # Workgroup size for shared memory optimization def vertexshader(position, modelmatrix, cameramatrix): # Apply model and camera transformations return cameramatrix @ (modelmatrix @ position) def fragmentshader(faceindex, pageidbuffer): # Retrieve page ID for the current face pageid = pageidbuffer[faceindex] # Background and unassigned faces result in zero page # Sources do not specify how to detect background or unassigned faces if pageid is None: return 0 return pageid def computeshaderthread(pixelidx, visibilitybuffer, linkedpages, depthvalues): # Shared memory optimization suggested to avoid atomic contention shareddepth = [0] WORKGROUPSIZE # Encode depth as integers that decrease with greater depth newdepth = depthvalues[pixelidx] # Use atomicMax to ensure only the closest (maximum integer) depth is kept visibilitybuffer[pixelidx] = atomicmax(visibilitybuffer[pixelidx], newdepth) # Iterate through linked pages per pixel to set buffer entries for linkedpage in linkedpages[pixelidx]: visibilitybuffer[linkedpage] = atomicmax(visibilitybuffer[linkedpage], newdepth) def atomicmax(current, new): # Simulates hardware atomicMax operation return new if new > current else current def transfertocpu(visibilitybuffer): # Transfer buffer to CPU memory return list(visibilitybuffer) Parameters Resolution: The visibility buffer is rendered at low resolution to enhance performance, as atomic operations are avoided in favor of shared memory in workgroups. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Race Conditions: Finding the minimum depth for LOD communication can lead to race conditions. atomicMax() is employed but has an adverse performance impact on concurrent thread updates. Primitive ID Performance: Using glPrimitiveID has a negative performance impact. The implementation uses the leading vertex to determine triangle primitive IDs instead. Distant Page Misses: Low resolution can cause distant pages to be missed in virtual texturing. However, overlapping Gaussians cause nearby pages to remain memory-bound, making the trade-off acceptable. Performance: Rendering at low resolution improves performance by reducing the number of atomic operations required. However, atomic operations themselves have an adverse performance impact on concurrent thread updates. Memory: The method reduces memory bandwidth usage by transferring a reduced list of page IDs rather than full visibility data. Accuracy: Low resolution may cause distant pages to be missed. This is mitigated by page linking, which connects nearby pages. When to use: Suitable for virtual texturing systems where nearby pages are memory-bound due to overlapping geometry (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting). When not to use: Not suitable when precise visibility of distant, non-overlapping pages is critical, as low resolution may miss them. The method is described in the context of virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on techniques discussed by Hable regarding primitive ID performance and Mayer regarding small visibility buffers for virtual texturing. The implementation is part of a Vulkan-based system described by Haberl. Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://zenodo.org/records/19690968, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Point-Based Chunk Rendering
head: GL_POINTS Chunk Draw, Hardware Accelerated Point Rendering with Distance Attenuation, OpenGL point rendering, Vertex Point Rendering, Scaled point rendering
body: Point-Based Chunk Rendering is a technique that renders volumetric data by representing occupied voxels as point primitives (GLPOINTS) whose sizes are dynamically scaled based on their distance to the image plane, approximating surface continuity. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by avoiding fixed-size cubes and manual glPointSize calls; instead, it enables the use of vertex arrays and display lists for high-performance rendering by precomputing geometry while handling distance attenuation in the shader. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A chunk of voxel data (typically 32^3 or similar block size) containing occupied and empty cells. Output: A stream of point primitives submitted to the GPU for rasterization. Data Structures: The method relies on a Vertex Array Object (VAO) storing attributes for each occupied voxel in the chunk. The layout is defined as follows: Attribute 0 (Position): 3 floats (vec3), stride 12 bytes, offset 0. Attribute 1 (Normal/Extents): 3 floats (vec3), stride 12 bytes, offset 0. Attribute 2 (Texcoords): 2 floats (vec2), stride 8 bytes, offset 0. Buffers are uploaded with GLSTATICDRAW. Steps: 1. Voxel to Point Conversion: Iterate through the chunk's voxel grid. For each occupied voxel, calculate its world-space position P{world} using the transformation P{world} = I{voxel} \times V{size} for unit voxels, as defined in Voxels rasterized as geometry. 2. Attribute Population: Populate the VAO buffers with the position, normal, and texture coordinates for each occupied voxel. Empty voxels are skipped. 3. Shader Setup: Bind the chunk VAO. Set the Model, View, and Projection matrices via shader uniforms. 4. Distance Attenuation: In the vertex shader, calculate the distance d between the vertex position and the camera. Scale the point size S based on this distance to approximate the voxel's physical size in screen space. This replaces the need for glPointSize, which is viewpoint-dependent and prevents the use of vertex arrays. 5. Rendering: Call glDrawArrays(GLPOINTS, 0, numoccupiedvoxels). 6. Cleanup: Unbind the VAO. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderchunk(chunkvao, numoccupied, modelmatrix, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix): # Bind the vertex array object to the graphics pipeline activevao = chunkvao # Set model, view, and projection matrices as shader uniforms shaderuniforms["umodel"] = modelmatrix shaderuniforms["uview"] = viewmatrix shaderuniforms["uprojection"] = projectionmatrix # Issue draw call for point primitives drawprimitives(primitivetype="GLPOINTS", startindex=0, count=numoccupied) # Unbind the vertex array object activevao = None Vertex Shader Logic (Python-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(aposition, anormal, atexcoord, modelmatrix, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, basepointsize): worldpos = modelmatrix vec4(aposition, 1.0) viewpos = viewmatrix worldpos dist = length(viewpos.xyz) glPointSize = basepointsize (1.0 / dist) glPosition = projectionmatrix viewpos return glPointSize, glPosition Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Meshes: Meshes must be updated on the GPU even if they are empty to prevent floating quads or artifacts when destroying blocks near chunk borders. Quality vs. Speed: While point generation is significantly faster than triangle generation (e.g., Marching Cubes), the image quality is generally not superior to Marching Cubes. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Primitive generation is O(N) where N is the number of occupied voxels. Rendering is faster than triangle-based methods because point primitives are simpler to process by the GPU. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing vertex attributes (position, normal, texcoord) for each occupied voxel. Strengths: High performance for large volumes; enables use of vertex arrays/display lists; simple implementation. Limitations: Lower visual quality compared to surface-based methods like Marching Cubes; potential for gaps or artifacts if point size attenuation is not tuned correctly. When to use: When rendering speed is critical and approximate surface visualization is acceptable. When not to use: When high-fidelity surface details are required. This technique was proposed in "Hardware Accelerated Point Rendering of Isosurfaces" (2003) as an alternative to triangle-based surface visualization. It addresses the limitation of OpenGL's glPointSize being viewpoint-dependent, which prevents precomputation of point sizes in vertex arrays. The method leverages hardware acceleration to scale points based on distance, enabling fast rendering of volumetric data. name: Hexagonal Prism Voxel Rendering
head: HEXAGON, HexRender
body: Hexagonal Prism Voxel Rendering is a geometry-based volume rendering technique that represents occupied voxels as hexagonal prisms to reduce aliasing and improve visual quality compared to cubic voxels. It differs from cubic voxel methods by utilizing a specific hexagonal vertex layout and instanced rendering to optimize draw calls. Inputs: A voxel grid defined by integer coordinates (x, y, z) within the bounds [0, 255] inclusive. A palette ID or texture index associated with each voxel. Scene parameters including camera matrix, world transform, scale, and rotation. Outputs: Rasterized hexagonal prisms submitted to the graphics pipeline via an instanced draw call. Hexagonal Prism Geometry (Static) The geometry consists of a single hexagonal prism unit. Vertices: 36 vertices total. Each vertex is 6 floats: 3 for position (x, y, z) and 3 for normal (nx, ny, nz). Faces: The prism comprises a top face, a bottom face, and 6 side faces. Indices: 36 indices total. Top face indices: 0–5. Bottom face indices: 6–11. Side face indices: 12–35. Local Space Coordinates: The prism is defined in a local space where x \in [-0.5, 1.5] and y \in [0, \sqrt{3}]. Top face z = 1, Bottom face z = 0. Top face normals: (0, 0, 1). Bottom face normals: (0, 0, -1). Side face normals point outward in the xy-plane and are calculated based on hexagon geometry involving \sqrt{3}. Grid placement offset is calculated as: \text{offset} = (1.5 \times x, \sqrt{3} \times y + (x \bmod 2) \times 0.5 \times \sqrt{3}, z). Attribute 1: Normal (from VBO). 3. Attribute 2: Palette Index (from Instance VBO, divisor 1). 4. Attribute 3: Voxel Position (from Instance VBO, divisor 1). 1. Voxel Trimming (TrimVoxels): Goal: Remove internal voxels, keeping only exposed ones. Pass 1: Insert all non-hole voxel positions into an unorderedset. Pass 2: For each non-hole voxel, check its 6 neighbors using displacement arrays: dx = \{-1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0\} dy = \{0, 0, -1, 1, 0, 0\} dz = \{0, 0, 0, 0, -1, 1\}. Exposure Check: A voxel is marked as exposed if any neighbor is out of bounds (<0 or >255) or not present in the set. Result: Add exposed voxels to the trimmed list. 3. Geometry Generation: Create Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) and Element Buffer Object (EBO) for the hexagonal prism geometry. Create Instance VBO (instaceVBO) populated with MVVoxel data for all trimmed voxels. Link vertex attributes as defined in the Data Structures section. 4. Returns vertices (list of 6-float tuples) and indices (list of ints). Matches source layout: 36 vertices, 36 indices. """ vertices = [] indices = [] def addvertex(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz): vertices.append((x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)) # Top Face (z=1, normal 0,0,1) - 6 vertices, indices 0-5 topybase = SQRT3 for i in range(6): angle = i math.pi / 3 # Standard hexagon vertices mapped to local space bounds x = 0.5 + 0.5 math.cos(angle) y = 0.5 SQRT3 + 0.5 SQRT3 math.sin(angle) addvertex(x, y, 1, 0, 0, 1) # Bottom Face (z=0, normal 0,0,-1) - 6 vertices, indices 6-11 for i in range(6): angle = i math.pi / 3 x = 0.5 + 0.5 math.cos(angle) y = 0.5 SQRT3 + 0.5 SQRT3 math.sin(angle) addvertex(x, y, 0, 0, 0, -1) # Side Faces - 24 vertices (4 per face 6 faces), indices 12-35 # Each side face connects a top edge to a bottom edge for i in range(6): anglecurr = i math.pi / 3 anglenext = ((i + 1) % 6) math.pi / 3 x1 = 0.5 + 0.5 math.cos(anglecurr) y1 = 0.5 SQRT3 + 0.5 SQRT3 math.sin(anglecurr) x2 = 0.5 + 0.5 math.cos(anglenext) y2 = 0.5 SQRT3 + 0.5 SQRT3 math.sin(anglenext) # Calculate outward normal for the side face nx = math.cos((anglecurr + anglenext) / 2) ny = math.sin((anglecurr + anglenext) / 2) # Quad split into 2 triangles (6 indices per face) baseidx = 12 + i 6 # Triangle 1 indices.extend([baseidx, baseidx+1, baseidx+2]) indices.extend([baseidx, baseidx+2, baseidx+3]) # Triangle 2 indices.extend([baseidx, baseidx+3, baseidx+4]) indices.extend([baseidx, baseidx+4, baseidx+5]) # Add 6 vertices for this side face (top 3, bottom 3) addvertex(x1, y1, 1, nx, ny, 0) addvertex(x2, y2, 1, nx, ny, 0) addvertex(x1, y1, 0, nx, ny, 0) addvertex(x2, y2, 0, nx, ny, 0) addvertex(x1, y1, 1, nx, ny, 0) addvertex(x2, y2, 1, nx, ny, 0) return vertices, indices def trimvoxels(voxelset): """ Removes internal voxels by keeping only exposed ones. voxelset: set of (x,y,z) tuples representing non-hole voxels. name: Voxelization via Rasterization
body: Voxelization via Rasterization converts 3D geometric primitives (typically triangle meshes) into a discrete 3D voxel grid by leveraging the graphics pipeline's rasterization hardware. It is distinguished from ray-marching or signed distance field (SDF) methods by its reliance on standard GPU rasterization primitives, though it may require specific techniques like conservative rasterization to avoid gaps. Builds on Voxels rasterized as geometry. This method converts two-dimensional surface geometry into a three-dimensional voxel grid by performing three rasterization passes along the principal axis-aligned directions (X, Y, and Z). It produces a 6-separating voxelization, which is sparse enough to support 6-connected ray marching without penetrating the original surface. It is distinguished from 26-separating methods by its sparsity, and from other 6-separating approaches like Schwarz and Seidel [SS10] by being minimal, as it corresponds exactly to the crosshairs intersection target rather than a superset. This method rasterizes a triangle mesh directly into a 2D UV texture space in memory-friendly chunks, storing the triangle (face) ID in the alpha channel of the resulting texture. This allows for per-texel face identification and subsequent interpolation of 3D vertex positions, effectively converting geometric mesh data into a volumetric representation without explicit ray marching or signed distance field computation. It differs from sibling methods like 3-axis rasterization by processing faces in arbitrary batches rather than axis-aligned slices, and from Triangle Projection Voxelization by explicitly managing VRAM constraints through chunked execution loops. Triangle Projection Voxelization renders input mesh triangles directly into a 3D voxel grid using a union-based accumulation strategy, where overlapping projections are resolved by retaining the maximum coverage or depth value. It differs from sibling methods like 3-axis rasterization voxelization by treating the voxel grid as a volumetric render target rather than a set of discrete 2D slices, allowing for a single-pass (or few-pass) projection that inherently handles complex geometry intersections without explicit geometric clipping. This method leverages the DirectX 11.1 "Forced Sample Count" feature to perform Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) rasterization without requiring a bound MSAA render target. It serves as a memory-efficient alternative to standard MSAA voxelization, which necessitates allocating an MSAA render target in video memory (vidmem). By decoupling the rasterization sample count from the render target format, it reduces vidmem overhead while providing coverage-based voxelization. This method enables real-time rendering of bone-animated voxel characters by converting a skeletal mesh into voxel data at editor time and switching between static and bone-driven voxel chunks at runtime based on asset data. It differs from standard voxelization by baking bone weights and grouping voxels per bone to allow rigid-body animation of voxel chunks, avoiding per-vertex skinning costs in the voxel shader. Cascaded Voxel Cone Tracing Voxelization is a technique that renders scene geometry into a 3D texture (Geometry Volume, GV) using an orthographic camera aligned with the light direction, organized into cascades to handle varying distances and resolutions. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly separating the voxelization into multiple cascaded volumes, where each cascade covers a volume twice as large as the previous one, allowing for high-resolution detail near the light source and coarser resolution at a distance. Definition: A technique to fix 'holes' introduced by switching projection directions in different primitives. Standard rasterization invokes the pixel shader only if a primitive covers the pixel center; this method expands primitive edges to ensure all pixels touched by the primitive are covered. Step: Expand primitive edges in the Geometry Shader to ensure all pixels touched by the primitive are covered by the rasterizer. Pitfall: Edge expansion causes extra pixels to be shaded (yellow pixels in Figure 9), particularly for thin triangles, leading to unnecessary pixel shader calls. These extra voxels must be culled later using voxel-primitive intersection tests. Definition: Using hardware-supported conservative rasterization available on Maxwell base chipsets or higher via NVAPI. It avoids artifacts from manual edge expansion and eliminates the need for subsequent voxel-primitive intersection tests. Parameter: Hardware Requirement: Maxwell base chip set or higher. Comparison: Unlike manual edge expansion, hardware conservative rasterization does not produce extra shaded pixels, so voxel-primitive intersection tests are not needed. The method originated from the need to efficiently voxelize triangle meshes for real-time global illumination and ray tracing on GPUs. Early implementations relied on standard rasterization, which suffered from gaps ("holes") when primitives fell between pixel centers or when projection directions changed. The introduction of conservative rasterization techniques, both manual (via geometry shader edge expansion) and hardware-supported (starting with NVIDIA's Maxwell architecture), provided robust solutions to these artifacts. The technique is widely used in real-time rendering engines for voxel cone tracing, voxel-based lighting, and volumetric data visualization. name: 3-axis rasterization voxelization
head: 6-separating voxelization of 2D input, CNS*11 method, FBP09 method
body: This method produces a 6-separating voxelization of two-dimensional input geometry by rasterizing primitives along three axis-aligned projection directions in three separate passes. It is designed for applications where ray marching follows 6-connected paths, allowing for a sparser voxel set than 26-separating methods while still guaranteeing that discretized rays do not penetrate separating surfaces. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Triangle Projection Voxelization by its reliance on point-depth evaluation at pixel centers rather than full geometric intersection tests, and from Chunked UV Rasterization with Face ID Storage by its specific 3-pass axis-aligned structure. Inputs: A set of two-dimensional input primitives (e.g., triangles) defined in three-dimensional space. Outputs: A set of occupied voxels Sd that form a 6-separating cover. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array or hash map storing voxel occupancy. Render Target: A 2D buffer corresponding to the projection plane for each pass. Parameters: Projection Axes: The three axis-aligned directions: X, Y, and Z. Voxel Size: The physical dimension of a voxel. Pixel-to-Voxel Mapping: The transformation from screen space to voxel grid coordinates. Steps: 1. Initialize the output voxel set Sd as empty. 2. For each of the three axes A \in \{X, Y, Z\}: a. Project the input primitives onto the 2D plane perpendicular to axis A. b. Rasterize the projected primitives into a 2D render target. c. For each pixel p in the render target that is covered by the rasterization: i. Determine the center of the voxel column corresponding to pixel p along axis A. ii. Evaluate the depth of the input primitive at the center Cp. iii. Identify the voxel whose center is closest in depth to the evaluated primitive depth. iv. Add this voxel to Sd. 3. Return Sd. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def threeaxisrasterizationvoxelization(primitives, voxelsize, gridorigin, gridextent): """ primitives: List of geometric primitives. voxelsize: Scalar physical dimension of a voxel. gridorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the grid's minimum corner. gridextent: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the grid's maximum corner. Returns: Set of occupied voxel indices (ix, iy, iz). """ occupiedvoxels = set() axes = [0, 1, 2] # X, Y, Z for axis in axes: projaxes = [a for a in axes if a != axis] uaxis, vaxis = projaxes[0], projaxes[1] # The sources do not specify the exact rasterization traversal. for uidx in range(gridextent[uaxis] - gridorigin[uaxis]): for vidx in range(gridextent[vaxis] - gridorigin[vaxis]): # The sources do not specify the exact rasterization coverage test. if rasterizecoverage(primitives, uidx, vidx, uaxis, vaxis): ucenter = gridorigin[uaxis] + (uidx + 0.5) voxelsize vcenter = gridorigin[vaxis] + (vidx + 0.5) voxelsize # The sources do not specify the exact depth evaluation routine. depthval = evaluateprimitivedepth(primitives, ucenter, vcenter, axis) # Include voxel whose center is closest in depth to the evaluated primitive depth colz = int(round((depthval - gridorigin[axis]) / voxelsize)) occupiedvoxels.add((uidx, vidx, colz)) return occupiedvoxels Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Point Evaluation: The method requires point evaluations of depth. 6-Separation Guarantee: The method produces 6-separating results even for curved primitives, a property that is difficult to ascertain without topological analysis. Symmetry: The crosshairs target is a symmetrical realization of the general intersection target. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces a sparse voxel set compared to 26-separating methods. Simple to implement on GPU using standard rasterization pipelines. Works with curved primitives. Limitations: Only 6-separating, not 26-separating. Requires three passes. Precision of depth evaluation can affect accuracy. When to Use: When 6-connected ray marching is sufficient and sparsity is desired. When Not to Use: When 26-connected paths are required or when higher separability is needed. The method is equivalent to the GPU-based methods used by Forest et al. [FBP09] and Crassin et al. [CNS11]. The theoretical foundation for separability requirements is provided by Cohen-Or and Kaufman [COK97]. The crosshairs intersection target is a minimal 6-separating target for two-dimensional input in three-dimensional space. name: Chunked UV Rasterization with Face ID Storage
head: UV Space Rasterization for Voxelization
body: This method rasterizes a 3D mesh in UV space in memory-friendly chunks, storing the face ID in the alpha channel to enable per-texel face identification and subsequent 3D position interpolation. It builds on Voxelization via Rasterization. Inputs: outvertices: Tensor of vertex positions, shape (N, 3). outfaces: Tensor of face indices, shape (M, 3). outuvs: Tensor of UV coordinates, shape (N, 2). texturesize: Integer resolution of the 2D rasterization buffer. chunksize: Integer number of faces per rasterization call, typically 100,000. Outputs: rast: Rasterization buffer tensor, shape (1, \text{texture\size}, \text{texture\size}, 4). pos: Interpolated 3D positions for valid pixels, shape (\text{texture\size}, \text{texture\size}, 3). Data Structures: rast: A 4-channel float32 tensor where channel 3 (alpha) stores the accumulated face ID. mask: Boolean tensor indicating valid pixels where rast[..., 3] > 0. Steps: 1. Prepare UV Coordinates: Scale UVs to [-1, 1] and pad with z=0 and w=1 to form clip-space coordinates. \text{uvs\rast} = \text{torch.cat}([\text{out\uvs} \times 2 - 1, \text{torch.zeros\like}(\text{out\uvs}[:,:1]), \text{torch.ones\like}(\text{out\uvs}[:,:1])], \text{dim}=-1).\text{unsqueeze}(0) 2. Initialize Rasterization Buffer: Create a zero-initialized tensor for the rasterization output. \text{rast} = \text{torch.zeros}((1, \text{texture\size}, \text{texture\size}, 4), \text{device}=\text{'cuda'}, \text{dtype}=\text{torch.float32}) 3. Chunked Rasterization Loop: Iterate over faces in chunks of 100,000. For each chunk index i from 0 to M with step chunksize: a. Rasterize the chunk: (\text{rast\chunk}, \) = \text{rasterize}(\text{ctx}, \text{uvs\rast}, \text{out\faces}[i:i+\text{chunk\size}], \text{resolution}=[\text{texture\size}, \text{texture\size}]). b. Compute the mask for the current chunk: \text{mask\chunk} = \text{rast\chunk}[..., 3:4] > 0. c. Update the face ID in the alpha channel by adding the global face index i: \text{rast\chunk}[..., 3:4] += i. Pitfall: Face IDs are stored in the alpha channel by adding the loop index i, which overwrites the original alpha value; the mask must be recomputed or stored separately before merging. d. Merge the chunk result into the global rast buffer: \text{rast} = \text{torch.where}(\text{mask\chunk}, \text{rast\chunk}, \text{rast}). 4. Extract Valid Pixel Mask: \text{mask} = \text{rast}[0,..., 3] > 0. 5. Interpolate 3D Positions: Use the rasterization buffer and face indices to interpolate vertex positions for the valid pixels: \text{pos} = \text{interpolate}(\text{out\vertices}.\text{unsqueeze}(0), \text{rast}, \text{out\faces})[0][0]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def chunkeduvrasterization(outvertices, outfaces, outuvs, texturesize, chunksize=100000, ctx=None): # 1. Prepare UV coordinates uvsrast = torch.cat([ outuvs 2 - 1, torch.zeroslike(outuvs[:,:1]), torch.oneslike(outuvs[:,:1]) ], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0) # 2. Initialize rasterization buffer rast = torch.zeros((1, texturesize, texturesize, 4), device=outvertices.device, dtype=torch.float32) # 3. Chunked rasterization loop numfaces = outfaces.shape[0] for i in range(0, numfaces, chunksize): endidx = min(i + chunksize, numfaces) faceschunk = outfaces[i:endidx] # Standard GPU rasterization call (e.g., diff-renderer) rastchunk, = rasterize(ctx, uvsrast, faceschunk, resolution=[texturesize, texturesize]) # Compute mask before modifying alpha to avoid overwriting the hit flag maskchunk = rastchunk[..., 3:4] > 0 # Update alpha channel with global face index rastchunk[..., 3:4] += i # Merge into global buffer rast = torch.where(maskchunk, rastchunk, rast) # 4. Extract valid pixel mask mask = rast[0,..., 3] > 0 # Standard barycentric interpolation call pos = interpolate(outvertices.unsqueeze(0), rast, outfaces)[0][0] return rast, pos A compact encoding for face identity within a voxel chunk. It uses a uint64t to store: bits 0–5 for u coordinate (6 bits), bits 6–11 for v coordinate (6 bits), bits 12–17 for depth (6 bits), bits 18–20 for axis (3 bits), bit 21 for positive direction flag (1 bit), and bits 22–31 for material (10 bits). A structure used to define the orientation and boundary of a face within a padded voxel chunk. It contains fixedaxis (the axis perpendicular to the face), fixedvalue (the coordinate value on that axis), iteraxes (the two axes spanning the face), and paddedboundaryindex (the index in the padded buffer). Padded coordinates are calculated as coords[iteraxes[0]] = u + 1, coords[iteraxes[1]] = v + 1, and coords[fixedaxis] = paddedboundaryindex. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables voxelization of large meshes by breaking them into manageable chunks to limit VRAM usage. Face ID storage allows for accurate 3D position interpolation and per-texel face identification. Limitations: The alpha channel is overwritten by the face ID index, requiring the mask to be recomputed or stored separately before merging. When to use: When processing large meshes that exceed available VRAM and per-voxel face identification is required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Triangle Projection Voxelization
head: Union-based Voxelization, VoxelizationByUnionPass
body: Triangle Projection Voxelization is a rasterization-based voxelization technique that renders 3D mesh triangles directly into a 3D voxel grid using a union-based accumulation approach. It differs from sibling methods by projecting triangles onto a single view volume and resolving coverage via multiple render targets or passes, rather than iterating over axes or processing chunks. It builds on Voxelization via Rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh (vertex indices and positions), voxel grid dimensions, and a boolean flag msolid indicating whether to render solid or translucent geometry. Output: A 3D voxel grid stored in a Unordered Access View (UAV). Data Structures: The method utilizes a specific pipeline layout named PASSVOXELIZEUNION. Descriptor Range 0: Constant Buffer View (CBV), count 1, offset 0, flags DATASTATIC. Descriptor Range 1: Constant Buffer View (CBV), count 1, offset 0, flags DATASTATIC. Descriptor Range 2: Unordered Access View (UAV), count numUAVs, offset 0, flags DATASTATICWHILESETATEXECUTE. Shader Stages: Vertex Shader (VS), Pixel Shader (PS). Steps: 1. Reset the command allocator and command list for the frame. 2. Bind the descriptor heap containing CBV, SRV, and UAV descriptors. 3. Set up resource barriers to transition the render target to RENDERTARGET state. 4. If msolid is false, clear the render target view with a clear color (e.g., {CLEARCOLOR, 0.0f}). 5. Clear the depth stencil view with a depth value of 1.0. 6. Configure the voxelization pass: set layoutIdx to PASSVOXELIZEUNION, set pipeIdx to PASSVOXELIZEUNIONSOLID if depthPeel is true otherwise PASSVOXELIZEUNION, and set instanceCount to 3. 7. Bind the pipeline state using vertex shader VSTRIPROJUNION and pixel shader PSTRIPROJUNION. 8. Bind the descriptor ranges for the two CBVs and the UAV array. 9. Call DrawIndexed(mnumIndices, instanceCount, 0, 0, 0) to execute the rasterization pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervoxelizationunion(meshindices, voxelgriduavcount, issolid, depthpeel): # 1. Reset command allocator and command list # (Host API initialization assumed; not detailed in sources) # 2. Bind descriptor heap containing CBV, SRV, and UAV descriptors # (Host API initialization assumed; not detailed in sources) # 3. Set up resource barriers to transition render target to RENDERTARGET state # (Host API initialization assumed; not detailed in sources) # 4. Clear render target if not rendering solid geometry if not issolid: clearrendertarget([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # 5. Clear depth stencil view cleardepthstencil(1.0) # 6. Configure voxelization pass parameters layoutid = PASSVOXELIZEUNION pipeid = PASSVOXELIZEUNIONSOLID if depthpeel else PASSVOXELIZEUNION instancecount = 3 # 7. Bind pipeline layout and state with VS and PS shaders bindpipelinelayout(layoutid) bindpipelinestate(pipeid) bindvertexshader("VSTRIPROJUNION") bindpixelshader("PSTRIPROJUNION") # 8. Bind descriptor ranges: two CBVs and numUAVs UAVs binddescriptorrange("CBV", 1, 0, "DATASTATIC") binddescriptorrange("CBV", 1, 0, "DATASTATIC") binddescriptorrange("UAV", voxelgriduavcount, 0, "DATASTATICWHILESETATEXECUTE") # 9. Execute indexed draw call executedrawindexed(indexcount=len(meshindices), instancecount=instancecount, firstindex=0, vertexoffset=0, firstinstance=0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The instanceCount is hardcoded to 3, which may imply rendering the same geometry for multiple depth layers or axes, though the exact semantic is not detailed in the source. Precision issues may arise if the triangle projection does not align with voxel boundaries, leading to gaps or overlaps. The depthPeel flag determines whether solid or translucent voxelization logic is used, requiring careful state management. A geometry shader technique that projects triangles onto the 2D plane aligned with the axis most perpendicular to the face normal, minimizing distortion and overlap artifacts. Limitations: Requires multiple UAVs or passes for full coverage; hardcoded instance count may limit flexibility. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Axis-Aligned Projection via Face Normal
head: Face Normal Axis Selection, Optimal Axis Projection
body: This method is a geometry shader technique used in rasterization-based voxelization to project 3D mesh triangles onto a 2D plane aligned with the axis most perpendicular to the triangle's face normal. By selecting the optimal viewing axis (X, Y, or Z) for each triangle, it minimizes projection overlap and distortion, ensuring that the triangle's area is preserved as much as possible in the chosen projection plane. This approach adapts the projection direction per primitive, which is particularly useful for reducing artifacts in voxel grids where triangles might otherwise be foreshortened or occluded incorrectly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle strip consisting of vertices, each with a world-space position, a normal vector, and texture UV coordinates. Output: A geometry stream containing transformed clip-space positions, world-space positions, and texture UVs, ready for rasterization into a voxel texture or buffer. Data Structures: Vertex Input: Contains vertex.xyz (world position), normal (world normal), and uv (texture coordinates). Geometry Output: Contains positionCS (clip space position), positionWS (world space position), and uv (texture coordinates). Steps: 1. Calculate Face Normal: Compute the average of the three input vertex normals and normalize the result to obtain the triangle's face normal. \mathbf{n}{face} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{n}0 + \mathbf{n}1 + \mathbf{n}2) 2. Determine Optimal Axis: Calculate the absolute dot product of the face normal with the three world-space axes (\mathbf{x}=(1,0,0), \mathbf{y}=(0,1,0), \mathbf{z}=(0,0,1)). Select the axis with the maximum dot product. dx = |\mathbf{n}{face} \cdot \mathbf{x}|, \quad dy = |\mathbf{n}{face} \cdot \mathbf{y}|, \quad dz = |\mathbf{n}{face} \cdot \mathbf{z}| The axis index is determined as follows: If dx is maximum, select the X-axis (projection onto the ZY plane). If dy is maximum, select the Y-axis (projection onto the XZ plane). If dz is maximum, select the Z-axis (projection onto the XY plane). 3. Transform to Clip Space: For each vertex, transform its world-space position to clip space. \mathbf{p}{clip} = \text{TransformWorldToHClip}(\mathbf{p}{world}) 4. Normalize to NDC: Divide the clip space position by its w-component to normalize to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). \mathbf{p}{ndc} = \frac{\mathbf{p}{clip}}{w} 5. Adjust Z Range (Platform Specific): If the platform uses a 0-1 Z range for clip space (e.g., DirectX), convert the Z coordinate from 0-1 to -1-1 range. This is typically checked using a platform-specific constant like UNITYNEARCLIPVALUE. \text{if } \text{UNITY\NEAR\CLIP\VALUE} \ge 0: \quad z{ndc} = z{ndc} \times 2.0 - 1.0 6. Permute Coordinates: Swap the XYZ coordinates of the NDC position to align the selected projection axis with the depth (Z) axis for rasterization. If X-axis is dominant (Index 0): Swap to ZY. \mathbf{p}{permuted} = (z, y, x). If Y-axis is dominant (Index 1): Swap to XZ. \mathbf{p}{permuted} = (x, z, y). If Z-axis is dominant (Index 2): No swap. \mathbf{p}{permuted} = (x, y, z). 7. Restore Z Range (Platform Specific): If the platform uses a 0-1 Z range, convert the Z coordinate back from -1-1 to 0-1. \text{if } \text{UNITY\NEAR\CLIP\VALUE} \ge 0: \quad z{permuted} = z{permuted} \times 0.5 + 0.5 8. De-normalize: Multiply the permuted position by w to restore the clip space scale. \mathbf{p}{final} = \mathbf{p}{permuted} \times w 9. Output: Output the final clip space position, the original world space position, and the texture UV to the geometry stream. Restart the triangle strip. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
