name: Sparse Voxel Rasterization
head: SVR, SVRasterization
body: Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) is a real-time volumetric rendering technique that rasterizes explicit sparse voxels to reconstruct radiance fields from multi-view images, avoiding neural networks or 3D Gaussians. It differs from its siblings by storing leaf voxels in a flat 1D array without parent-child pointers and employing a direction-dependent Morton order sorting algorithm to ensure correct front-to-back alpha composition without popping artifacts. Unlike Intensity-based Sparse Voxel Storage which may rely on implicit density fields or different sorting, SVRaster explicitly allocates leaf voxels and sorts them per tile based on ray direction signs. Inputs: Camera parameters: origin \mathbf{r}o, direction \mathbf{r}d. Scene representation: A set of active sparse voxels. Each voxel i is defined by: Octree level l \in [1, L], where L=16 is the maximum level. Voxel index \mathbf{v} = \{i, j, k\} within the global grid. Density parameters \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2\times2} at the eight corners. Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients \mathbf{v}{\text{sh}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(N{\text{shd}}+1)^2 \times 3}. Image grid: Width W, Height H, tile size T \times T (typically T=16). Outputs: Rendered color image. Optional depth map and normal map. The scene is stored in a 1D array of active voxels. No parent-child pointers or linear Octree structures are maintained; only leaf nodes are stored. Voxel Entry: Contains level l, index \{i,j,k\}, density parameters \mathbf{V}, and SH coefficients \mathbf{v}{\text{sh}}. Sorting Key-Value Pair: Used for tile-based sorting: Key: 64 bits. Upper 32 bits: Tile ID. Lower 32 bits: Morton code (derived from voxel position and ray direction). Value: 32 bits: Voxel ID (index in the 1D array). L: Maximum Octree level. Default L=16, corresponding to a finest virtual granularity of 65536^3. K: Number of sample points inside each voxel for numerical integration. K=1 for novel-view synthesis, K=3 for mesh reconstruction. Experiments limit K \le 3. h{\text{T}}: Early ray termination threshold. Default 10^{-4}. h{\text{ss}}: Supersampling scale for anti-aliasing. Default 1.5. \tau{\text{prune}}: Pruning threshold for voxel removal. Linearly scaled from 0.0001 to 0.05 during training. For each active voxel assigned to the current view: 1. Compute Voxel Geometry: Voxel size: \mathbf{v}s = \mathbf{w}s \cdot 2^{-l}. Voxel center: \mathbf{v}c = \mathbf{w}c - 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{w}s + \mathbf{v}s \cdot \mathbf{v}. Here, \mathbf{w}s is the Octree size, \mathbf{w}c is the Octree center, and \mathbf{v}=\{i,j,k\} is the voxel index. 2. Compute View-Dependent Color: Approximate ray direction using the vector from camera to voxel center: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}c - \mathbf{r}o). Evaluate SH: c = \max(0, \text{sh\eval}(\mathbf{v}{\text{sh}}, \mathbf{d})). 3. Compute Voxel Normal: Compute analytical gradient of density at center \mathbf{q}c = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5): \mathbf{n}{\text{raw}} = 0.25 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{V}{100} + \mathbf{V}{101} + \mathbf{V}{110} + \mathbf{V}{111}) - (\mathbf{V}{000} + \mathbf{V}{001} + \mathbf{V}{010} + \mathbf{V}{011}) \\ (\mathbf{V}{010} + \mathbf{V}{011} + \mathbf{V}{110} + \mathbf{V}{111}) - (\mathbf{V}{000} + \mathbf{V}{001} + \mathbf{V}{100} + \mathbf{V}{101}) \\ (\mathbf{V}{001} + \mathbf{V}{011} + \mathbf{V}{101} + \mathbf{V}{111}) - (\mathbf{V}{000} + \mathbf{V}{010} + \mathbf{V}{100} + \mathbf{V}{110}) \end{bmatrix} Normalize: \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{n}{\text{raw}}). 1. Project the eight corners of each voxel to image space. 2. Compute the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the projected corners. 3. Assign the voxel to all tiles that overlap with this AABB. Sort voxels within each tile in near-to-far order using a direction-dependent Morton code. 1. Determine the sign pattern of the ray direction \mathbf{r}d (8 octants). 2. For each voxel, compute its Morton code based on its level l and index \{i,j,k\}. 3. Apply an XOR mask to the Morton code based on the ray direction sign pattern to ensure correct near-to-far traversal. 4. Sort the voxels using the modified Morton code as the key. For each pixel in each tile: 1. Cast ray \mathbf{r}o, \mathbf{r}d. 2. Iterate through sorted voxels assigned to the tile. 3. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute entry a and exit b distances: c0 = \frac{\mathbf{v}c - 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{v}s - \mathbf{r}o}{\mathbf{r}d}, \quad c1 = \frac{\mathbf{v}c + 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{v}s - \mathbf{r}o}{\mathbf{r}d} a = \max(\min(c0), \min(c1)), \quad b = \min(\max(c0), \max(c1)) If a > b or a \le 0, skip voxel. 4. Sample Voxel: Ray segment length: l = (b - a) \cdot \|\mathbf{r}d\|. Sample K points evenly along the segment: tk = a + \frac{k - 0.5}{K} \cdot (b - a), \quad \mathbf{p}k = \mathbf{r}o + tk \cdot \mathbf{r}d Local voxel coordinate: \mathbf{q}k = (\mathbf{p}k - (\mathbf{v}c - 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{v}s)) / \mathbf{v}s. Trilinear interpolation of density: vk = \text{interp}(\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{q}k). Exponential-linear activation: \text{explin}(x) = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x > 1.1 \\ \exp\left(\frac{x}{1.1} - 1 + \ln 1.1\right) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Per-sample alpha: \alphak = 1 - \exp\left(-\frac{l}{K} \cdot \text{explin}(vk)\right). 5. Composite: Update transmittance T and color C: C = C + T \cdot c \cdot \alpha, \quad T = T \cdot (1 - \alpha) where \alpha is the effective voxel alpha derived from samples. Voxel Alpha Formula: \alpha = 1 - \exp\left(-\frac{l}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \text{explin}(vk)\right) (Note: Sources Eq. 4 and A.2 Eq. 14a show \exp \ln(\text{interp}) which simplifies to \text{interp} if positive, but the activation is applied after interpolation. The text states "apply the non-linear activation after trilinear interpolation". The formula in A.2 Eq. 14a uses \exp \ln(\text{interp}) which is redundant if interp is positive, but likely implies the activation function \text{explin} is used. Given Eq. 18 uses \text{explin}(\text{interp}), we use \text{explin}). Early Termination: If T < h{\text{T}}, stop processing voxels for this pixel. Anti-aliasing: Render at h{\text{ss}} \times resolution and downsample. Depth/Normal: Composite depth D = \sum Ti di and normals similarly. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def exponentiallinear(x): """Exponential-linear activation function.""" if x > 1.1: return x else: return math.exp(x / 1.1 - 1 + math.log(1.1)) def trilinearinterpolate(V, q): """ Trilinear interpolation of density V at local coordinate q. V is a 2x2x2 array of density parameters. q is a tuple (qx, qy, qz) in [0, 1]. """ qx, qy, qz = q v000 = V[0, 0, 0]; v100 = V[1, 0, 0] v010 = V[0, 1, 0]; v110 = V[1, 1, 0] v001 = V[0, 0, 1]; v101 = V[1, 0, 1] v011 = V[0, 1, 1]; v111 = V[1, 1, 1] w000 = (1 - qx) (1 - qy) (1 - qz) w100 = qx (1 - qy) (1 - qz) w010 = (1 - qx) qy (1 - qz) w110 = qx qy (1 - qz) w001 = (1 - qx) (1 - qy) qz w101 = qx (1 - qy) qz w011 = (1 - qx) qy qz w111 = qx qy qz return (w000 v000 + w100 v100 + w010 v010 + w110 v110 + w001 v001 + w101 v101 + w011 v011 + w111 v111) def rayaabbintersect(voxc, voxs, ro, rd): """ Intersect ray with voxel AABB. Returns (a, b, valid). a: entry distance, b: exit distance. """ c0 = [] c1 = [] for d in range(3): if abs(rd[d]) < 1e-9: c0.append(float('-inf')) c1.append(float('inf')) else: c0.append((voxc[d] - 0.5 voxs[d] - ro[d]) / rd[d]) c1.append((voxc[d] + 0.5 voxs[d] - ro[d]) / rd[d]) tmin = max(min(c0[d], c1[d]) for d in range(3)) tmax = min(max(c0[d], c1[d]) for d in range(3)) valid = (tmin <= tmax) and (tmin > 0) return tmin, tmax, valid def computevoxelalpha(V, voxc, voxs, ro, rd, K=1): """ Compute alpha value for a voxel. """ a, b, valid = rayaabbintersect(voxc, voxs, ro, rd) if not valid: return 0.0, 0.0, False l = (b - a) math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in rd)) sumdensity = 0.0 for k in range(1, K + 1): tk = a + (k - 0.5) / K (b - a) pk = [ro[d] + tk rd[d] for d in range(3)] q = [(pk[d] - (voxc[d] - 0.5 voxs[d])) / voxs[d] for d in range(3)] vk = trilinearinterpolate(V, q) sumdensity += exponentiallinear(vk) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sumdensity / K l) return alpha, l, True def rendertile(tilevoxels, ro, rd, tileid, hT=1e-4): """ Render a single tile. tilevoxels: List of voxels assigned to this tile, sorted by Morton code. """ T = 1.0 C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for voxel in tilevoxels: if T < hT: break alpha, l, valid = computevoxelalpha(voxel.V, voxel.vc, voxel.vs, ro, rd, K=1) if valid and alpha > 0: C = [C[d] + T voxel.c[d] alpha for d in range(3)] T = (1.0 - alpha) return C, T def tooctpath(i, j, k, lv, MAXNUMLEVELS=16): octpath = 0 for n in range(lv): bits = 4(i&1) + 2(j&1) + (k&1) octpath |= bits << (3n) i = i >> 1 j = j >> 1 k = k >> 1 octpath = octpath << (3(MAXNUMLEVELS-lv)) return octpath def tovoxelindex(octpath, lv, MAXNUMLEVELS=16): i = 0; j = 0; k = 0 octpath = octpath >> (3(MAXNUMLEVELS-lv)) for n in range(lv): i |= ((octpath&0b100)>>2) << n j |= ((octpath&0b010)>>1) << n k |= ((octpath&0b001)) << n octpath = octpath >> 3 return (i, j, k) Incorrect Sorting: Using primitive centers or closest distance to camera causes popping artifacts. Must use direction-dependent Morton order. Multiple Morton Orders: If a tile contains rays with different direction signs, multiple Morton orders are required. This is a corner case handled in supplementary materials. Exposure Variation: Scenes with severe exposure variation in training views cause clear boundaries and floaters, slowing rendering. Search Limitations: The 1D array storage does not support efficient point-to-voxel search (e.g., finding the covering voxel for a point). Zero Direction Components: Ray directions with zero components must be handled in ray-AABB intersection to avoid division by zero. Time Complexity: Sorting dominates preprocessing. Rendering is proportional to the number of voxels per tile. Average 27 primitives per pixel, compared to 63 for 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Stores only leaf voxels. On 24GB GPU, fails to reach 1024^3 grid resolution despite pruning. Performance: Achieves over 10x speedup compared to uniform-grid ray casting. On Mip-NeRF360, achieves 121 FPS (standard), 258 FPS (fast-rend). PSNR ~27 dB. Strengths: Real-time rendering, high fidelity, no neural MLPs, no 3D Gaussians, compatible with grid-based processing (Volume Fusion, Marching Cubes). Limitations: Struggles with severe exposure variation. 1D array limits efficient spatial queries. Maximum level limited to 16 in current implementation. Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) was introduced in 2025 by the authors of "Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering". It builds on the principles of Voxels rasterized as geometry and Sparse Voxel Storage and Management. It was developed to provide a neural-free, explicit voxel-based alternative to 3D Gaussian Splatting and Plenoxels, aiming for high frame rates and scalability. It is used in novel-view synthesis and mesh reconstruction tasks on datasets like Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, and DTU. name: Voxel Chunk Management
head: Voxel Grid Block
body: Voxel Chunk Management handles the storage, state tracking, and dirty-flag propagation for a fixed-size 3D block of voxel data within a sparse voxel architecture. It solves the problem of efficiently determining when a chunk's geometric representation or logical state requires regeneration after voxel modifications, specifically by isolating boundary updates to prevent cascading recomputations across the voxel grid. Inputs and Outputs Input: Chunk dimensions N \times N \times N, a default fill voxel ID, and a voxel data array. Output: Updated chunk state flags (terrainDirty, objectsDirty), neighbor dirtiness propagation, and queued mesh regeneration requests. Data Structures The chunk maintains the following internal state: 1. voxels: A 3D array of shape [size, size, size] storing voxel IDs as Uint16. 2. neighbors: A 3x3x3 array of neighbor chunk references with lower bounds [1,1,1], where the center element [1,1,1] refers to the chunk itself. 3. wholeLayerVoxel: An array of length size caching the voxel ID for entire layers or -1. 4. terrainDirty: Boolean flag indicating if the terrain mesh needs regeneration. 5. objectsDirty: Boolean flag indicating if object-specific meshes or handlers need updates. Parameters size: The dimension N of the cubic chunk. fillVoxelID: The default ID to initialize the voxel array with (commonly -1). Algorithm Steps 1. Allocate voxels array as Uint16Array wrapped in a 3D structure of shape [size, size, size]. 2. Initialize neighbors array as a 27-element structure where the center reference points to itself. 3. Scan voxel data to set fullyOpaque and fullyAir flags, register object blocks, and queue block handlers. 4. On set(i,j,k,newID): update the array, check registry lookups for solidity/opacity/object/handler, update dirty flags, queue the chunk for remeshing, and propagate dirtiness to edge neighbors if solidity or opacity changed. 5. On updateMeshes: call terrain or object meshers if dirty flags are set, then clear the flags. 6. On dispose: call onUnload handlers and nullify references. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VoxelChunk: def init(self, size, fillvoxelid=-1): self.size = size # voxels: ndarray of Uint16Array with shape [size, size, size] self.voxels = [[[fillvoxelid] size for in range(size)] for in range(size)] # neighbors: ndarray of shape [3,3,3] with lower bounds [1,1,1] (center=1,1,1 is self) self.neighbors = [[[None] 3 for in range(3)] for in range(3)] self.neighbors[1][1][1] = self # wholeLayerVoxel: Array(size) storing cached layer ID or -1 self.wholelayervoxel = [-1] size # terrainDirty/objectsDirty: boolean flags self.terraindirty = False self.objectsdirty = False self.blockhandlerlocs = set() # Registry lookups (simplified for self-containment) self.plainlookup = {0} self.opaquelookup = {1, 2, 3} self.objectlookup = {4, 5} self.handlerlookup = {6: 'handlera', 7: 'handlerb'} def scanvoxels(self, data): fullyopaque = True fullyair = True for j in range(self.size): layerid = self.wholelayervoxel[j] if layerid >= 0 and layerid not in self.objectlookup and layerid not in self.handlerlookup: if layerid not in self.opaquelookup: fullyopaque = False if layerid != 0: fullyair = False continue constantid = self.voxels[0][j][0] for i in range(self.size): for k in range(self.size): idval = data[i][j][k] if constantid >= 0 and idval != constantid: constantid = -1 if idval == 0: fullyopaque = False continue if idval in self.plainlookup: fullyair = False continue fullyopaque = fullyopaque and (idval in self.opaquelookup) fullyair = False if idval in self.objectlookup: self.objectsdirty = True if idval in self.handlerlookup: self.blockhandlerlocs.add((i, j, k)) if constantid >= 0: self.wholelayervoxel[j] = constantid return fullyopaque, fullyair def setvoxel(self, i, j, k, newid): oldid = self.voxels[i][j][k] if oldid == newid: return self.voxels[i][j][k] = newid soliditychanged = (oldid in self.plainlookup) != (newid in self.plainlookup) opacitychanged = (oldid in self.opaquelookup) != (newid in self.opaquelookup) if soliditychanged or opacitychanged: self.terraindirty = True if oldid in self.objectlookup != newid in self.objectlookup: self.objectsdirty = True if oldid in self.handlerlookup != newid in self.handlerlookup: self.objectsdirty = True if newid in self.handlerlookup: self.blockhandlerlocs.add((i, j, k)) else: self.blockhandlerlocs.discard((i, j, k)) if soliditychanged or opacitychanged: self.propagateboundarydirtiness(i, j, k) def propagateboundarydirtiness(self, i, j, k): edge = self.size - 1 imin = -1 if i == 0 else 0 jmin = -1 if j == 0 else 0 kmin = -1 if k == 0 else 0 imax = 1 if i == edge else 0 jmax = 1 if j == edge else 0 kmax = 1 if k == edge else 0 for ni in range(imin, imax + 1): for nj in range(jmin, jmax + 1): for nk in range(kmin, kmax + 1): if ni == 0 and nj == 0 and nk == 0: continue neighbor = self.neighbors[1 + ni][1 + nj][1 + nk] if neighbor is not None: neighbor.terraindirty = True # queuechunkforremesh(neighbor) def updatemeshes(self): if self.terraindirty: # regenerateterrainmesh(self) self.terraindirty = False if self.objectsdirty: # updateobjectmeshes(self) self.objectsdirty = False def dispose(self): for loc in self.blockhandlerlocs: # call onUnload handlers pass self.neighbors = None self.voxels = None Edge Cases and Pitfalls Cascading Updates: Dirtiness propagation must strictly limit updates to immediate neighbors on the chunk boundary to avoid cascading updates. Boundary Checks: When i=0 or i=N-1, the neighbor array index must be correctly mapped to the adjacent chunk using the offset logic (imin, imax, etc.). Constant Layers: Caching whole-layer voxel IDs (wholelayervoxel) optimizes full-chunk scans but must be invalidated when any voxel in that layer changes. Time Complexity: Initialization requires O(N^3) to scan all voxels. Single voxel updates and neighbor propagation are bounded by constant checks, resulting in O(1) complexity. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for voxel storage plus O(1) for neighbor references (fixed 3x3x3 array). Strengths: Efficiently isolates updates to chunk boundaries, preventing global scene recomputation. Simple state management with dirty flags. Limitations: Fixed chunk size limits flexibility. Boundary propagation logic requires careful implementation to avoid incorrect updates. When to Use: Ideal for terrain or static object voxelization where changes are localized and mesh regeneration is expensive. Voxel Chunk Management is implemented in the noa library by fenomas. It is used for voxel chunk management, terrain/object meshing, and collision handling within that system. fenomas/noa, https://github.com/fenomas/noa, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Dropout
head: Geometry Regularization with Voxel Dropout
body: Voxel Dropout is a regularization technique used during the optimization of sparse voxel representations to enforce global geometry consistency and prevent overfitting to local artifacts. It addresses the limitation of local planar constraints (such as homography patch warping) which fail for tiny voxels due to extreme locality, by temporarily dropping out a subset of voxels during depth and normal calculation. This forces the remaining voxels to assume responsibility for a larger area of geometric consistency, breaking incorrect local structures and overcoming local minima between appearance supervision and regularization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse voxel grid representing the scene, where each voxel v contains a set of spherical harmonic coefficients v{sh} for color and densities v{geo} \in [0, +\infty]^8 at its eight corners. Output: A modified voxel subset used for the current regularization step, where a fraction of voxels are masked out. Data Structures: The sparse voxel grid is organized in an Octree with size ws \in \mathbb{R} and center wc \in \mathbb{R}^3. Each voxel maintains its geometric and color attributes. The dropout mechanism operates on the set of active voxels V. Parameters: \gamma: The lower bound of the random sampling ratio. The dropout ratio is sampled from the interval [\gamma, 1]. The specific value of \gamma is not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Calculate Full-Scale Geometry: Compute the full-scale depth D and normal N fields using the complete set of voxels V. 2. Sample Dropout Ratio: Draw a random scalar \rho uniformly from the interval [\gamma, 1]. 3. Generate Mask: For each voxel vi \in V, generate a binary mask mi such that mi = 1 if a random value u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1) is less than \rho, and mi = 0 otherwise. 4. Drop Out Voxels: Create a subset of active voxels V' = \{ vi \in V \mid mi = 1 \}. The voxels with mi = 0 are temporarily dropped out for the current regularization step. 5. Compute Regularization Loss: Calculate the geometry consistency loss (e.g., depth and normal consistency) using only the voxels in V'. This loss enforces that each surviving voxel vi \in V' responds to the geometric consistency of a larger area, including regions where dropped-out voxels reside. 6. Backpropagate: Update the parameters of the voxels in V' based on the computed loss. The dropped-out voxels do not receive gradients in this step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxeldropoutregularization(voxels, gamma, fullscaledepth, fullscalenormal): """ Performs voxel dropout regularization. Args: voxels: List of active voxel objects. gamma: Lower bound of the dropout ratio interval [gamma, 1]. fullscaledepth: Precomputed depth field D using all voxels. fullscalenormal: Precomputed normal field N using all voxels. Returns: None (updates voxel parameters in place). """ # Step 1: Sample dropout ratio rho from [gamma, 1] rho = random.uniform(gamma, 1.0) # Step 2: Generate binary mask for each voxel activevoxels = [] for voxel in voxels: # Generate random number for this voxel u = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) # Keep voxel if u < rho, else drop it out if u < rho: activevoxels.append(voxel) # Step 3: Compute regularization loss using only active voxels # The loss function uses the precomputed fullscaledepth and fullscalenormal # but only considers geometric consistency constraints for activevoxels loss = computegeometryconsistencyloss(activevoxels, fullscaledepth, fullscalenormal) # Step 4: Backpropagate gradients to active voxels # Dropped-out voxels receive no gradient update in this step for voxel in activevoxels: voxel.updateparameters(loss) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tiny Voxels: Without dropout, tiny voxels receive gradients only from distant neighbors, resulting in a small regularization effect scope and redundant geometric structures trapped in local minima. Local Minima: The technique specifically addresses the local minima between appearance supervision and geometry regularization. Extreme Locality: Homography patch warping relies on local planar constraints and fails with tiny voxels due to extreme locality, whereas Voxel Dropout forces a global response. Time Complexity: The method adds a linear overhead relative to the number of voxels for mask generation and subset selection. The core regularization loss computation is performed on a subset of voxels, potentially reducing the computational cost of the gradient update step compared to using all voxels, although the full-scale depth and normal calculation must still be performed. Memory Complexity: No additional significant memory is required beyond the mask generation, which can be done on the fly. Strengths: Enlarges the global geometry consistency for tiny voxels; breaks incorrectly organized geometries; prevents overfitting; forces voxels to handle a larger share of geometric consistency loss. Limitations: Relies on the effectiveness of the underlying geometry regularization loss; requires careful tuning of \gamma (value not specified). When to use: When using sparse voxel representations with tiny voxels that suffer from local geometric artifacts and overfitting due to extreme locality of planar constraints. When not to use: When the voxel grid is coarse and local constraints are sufficient, or when computational budget is extremely tight and the overhead of full-scale depth/normal calculation is prohibitive. Voxel Dropout was introduced in the paper "GeoSVR: Taming Sparse Voxels for Geometrically Accurate Surface Reconstruction". It is inspired by the classic dropout technique used in neural networks to solve overfitting from complex parameters. The method is part of a pipeline that includes Sparse Voxels Rasterization, Voxel-Uncertainty Depth Constraint, and Surface Rectification. It is particularly effective on datasets like DTU which focus on highly accurate surface reconstruction. name: Object-Order Volume Rendering
head: Object space rendering
body: Object-order volume rendering is a forward mapping technique that iterates through volumetric data samples and projects them directly onto the image plane. It solves the problem of rendering scalar fields by processing actual data samples without intermediate geometric primitive representations, distinct from image-order methods that cast rays per pixel. It is set apart from sibling geometry-based methods (e.g., Voxels rasterized as geometry) by operating directly on the data samples rather than converting them to cubes or quads. Forward Mapping: Voxels are processed based on dataset organization and camera parameters, projecting samples directly to the image plane. Traversal Order: For alpha compositing, voxels must be traversed in front-to-back or back-to-front order to ensure correct blending. Back-to-front ordering is preferred for hardware compositing to avoid alpha bit planes, while front-to-back ordering is common for software compositing to allow early termination at full opacity. Alternative Operations: Voxel ordering is not strictly required for operations like MIP or average, which yield correct results regardless of traversal order. Grid Assumption: The basic projection algorithm assumes uniform spacing between samples in all three spatial directions. Uses binary voxel values (0 for background, 1 for object) to determine projection. It is the simplest form of object-order rendering, suitable for solid objects where internal structure is irrelevant. Choose when data is binary and performance is critical. Pre-compiles voxel projection commands into OpenGL display lists. It sets itself apart by optimizing repeated rendering of static volumes. Choose for static binary volumes in legacy OpenGL pipelines. Uses modern VBOs/VAOs to manage voxel geometry data. It differs from display lists by allowing more flexible data updates and better performance on modern hardware. Choose for dynamic or frequently updated static volumes. Offloads voxel projection logic to the vertex shader. It sets itself apart by performing per-voxel transformations on the GPU, reducing CPU overhead. Choose for high-performance rendering of large binary volumes. Generates projection geometry (e.g., billboards or quads) from point primitives in the geometry shader. It differs from fixed-function approaches by allowing dynamic geometry generation. Choose when flexible projection shapes are needed. Projects voxels as 2D billboards facing the camera. It sets itself apart by simplifying 3D voxels to 2D sprites, reducing overdraw. Choose for large-scale volume visualization where exact depth precision is less critical than performance. Uses instancing to render many voxels efficiently, with procedural generation in shaders. It differs by minimizing draw calls. Choose for massive voxel datasets where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Assembles quads from voxel data for rendering. It sets itself apart by optimizing the primitive stream for rasterization. Choose when quad-based rendering offers better performance than full cubes. Specialized rendering for debugging voxel data. It differs by emphasizing data inspection over visual fidelity. Choose for development and validation of voxel algorithms. Renders simplified proxy geometry to approximate the volume. It sets itself apart by trading accuracy for speed. Choose for real-time applications requiring quick volume previews. Renders chunks of voxels as points. It differs by using point sprites for extreme scalability. Choose for very large, sparse volumes. Uses hexagonal prisms instead of cubes. It sets itself apart by reducing aliasing and improving coverage. Choose when higher visual quality is needed for isotropic data. Performs compositing logic in the fragment shader. It differs by allowing complex per-fragment operations. Choose for advanced compositing effects like MIP or average. Generates voxel data from rasterized geometry. It is an inverse process but shares the rasterization pipeline. Choose when converting mesh data to volume data. Manages sparse voxel data structures for object-order rendering. It sets itself apart by optimizing memory usage. Choose for large, sparse volumes. Renders every voxel as a full cube. It is the baseline method. Choose for simplicity and correctness verification. Object-order volume rendering was introduced as a fundamental technique in volume visualization, contrasting with image-order (ray casting) methods. The approach relies on forward mapping, where data samples are projected directly to the image plane. Early implementations assumed uniform grid spacing and binary voxel values. name: Voxel Point Rendering
head: Point-based Voxel Rendering, Solid/Non-solid Point Voxelization
body: Voxel Point Rendering is a technique that represents occupied voxels as geometric points (sprites) rather than cubes or quads, submitting them to the graphics pipeline for rasterization. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data with minimal geometry overhead by decoupling the voxel's logical existence from its physical mesh representation. Unlike sibling methods that generate explicit cube faces or complex proxy geometry, this method relies on the fragment shader to color points based on a binary or scalar property (e.g., solid vs. non-solid), often utilizing instancing for performance. It is distinct from Binary Volume Rendering (Opacity Thresholding) which typically uses ray-marching or texture-based opacity, and from Voxel Billboard Rendering which generates oriented quads. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A structured buffer of voxel data containing position and a solid/occupancy flag. Input: A point sprite primitive topology. Output: A 2D image where voxels are rendered as colored points. Data Structures: The core data structure is a StructuredBuffer (or equivalent GPU buffer) named Voxels. Each element represents a voxel in the grid and contains: 1. position: A 3D vector (float3) representing the world-space center of the voxel. 2. isSolid: A scalar value (float) indicating occupancy. Typically 1.0 for solid/colliding voxels and 0.0 for empty/non-solid voxels. The grid dimensions are defined by GridWidth, GridHeight, and GridDepth. The spatial bounds are defined by BoundsMin (a float3) and CellHalfSize (a float). Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxelization (Pre-processing): For each voxel index (i, j, k) within the grid bounds: a. Calculate the world-space center position P{world}: P{world} = \begin{bmatrix} i \cdot 2 \cdot \text{CellHalfSize} + \text{CellHalfSize} + \text{BoundsMin}x \\ j \cdot 2 \cdot \text{CellHalfSize} + \text{CellHalfSize} + \text{BoundsMin}y \\ k \cdot 2 \cdot \text{CellHalfSize} + \text{CellHalfSize} + \text{BoundsMin}z \end{bmatrix} b. Construct an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) centered at P{world} with extents equal to CellHalfSize. c. Perform a collision test against the source geometry (e.g., triangles) to determine if the voxel is occupied. d. Store the result in Voxels[i + j \cdot \text{GridWidth} + k \cdot \text{GridWidth} \cdot \text{GridHeight}]: position = P{world} isSolid = 1.0 if collision detected, 0.0 otherwise. 2. Rendering (Vertex Shader): For each instance (voxel): a. Retrieve position and isSolid from Voxels[instanceid]. b. Transform position to clip space using the Model-View-Projection matrix (e.g., UnityWorldToClipPos). c. Interpolate the output color C{out}: C{out} = \text{lerp}(\text{Color}, \text{CollisionColor}, \text{isSolid}) where Color is the color for non-solid voxels and CollisionColor is the color for solid voxels. d. Output the clip-space position and C{out}. 3. Rendering (Fragment Shader): a. Return C{out} as the final fragment color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Voxel { float3 position; float isSolid; } StructuredBuffer<Voxel> Voxels; float3 BoundsMin; float CellHalfSize; int GridWidth, GridHeight, GridDepth; [numthreads(4, 4, 4)] void FillVolume(uint3 id: SVDispatchThreadID) { if (id.x >= GridWidth || id.y >= GridHeight || id.z >= GridDepth) return; float cellSize = CellHalfSize 2.0; // Calculate world center float3 centerPos = float3( id.x cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.x, id.y cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.y, id.z cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.z); // Define AABB for collision test float3 aabbCenter = mul(WorldToLocalMatrix, float4(centerPos, 1.0)).xyz; float3 aabbExtents = float3(CellHalfSize, CellHalfSize, CellHalfSize); // Collision detection against source mesh triangles bool intersects = false; for (int i = 0; i < TriangleCount; i += 3) { Triangle tri; tri.a = MeshVertices[MeshTriangleIndices[i]]; tri.b = MeshVertices[MeshTriangleIndices[i + 1]]; tri.c = MeshVertices[MeshTriangleIndices[i + 2]]; if (IntersectsTriangleAABB(tri, aabbCenter, aabbExtents)) { intersects = true; break; } } // Store voxel data int voxelIndex = id.x + GridWidth (id.y + GridHeight id.z); Voxels[voxelIndex].position = centerPos; Voxels[voxelIndex].isSolid = intersects ? 1.0: 0.0; } struct VertexOutput { float4 clipPos: SVPOSITION; float3 color: COLOR; }; cbuffer MaterialParams { float3 Color; float3 CollisionColor; }; VertexOutput VS(uint vertexID: SVVertexID, uint instanceID: SVInstanceID) { Voxel v = Voxels[instanceID]; // Transform to clip space float4 clipPos = UnityWorldToClipPos(v.position); // Interpolate color based on solidity float3 color = lerp(Color, CollisionColor, v.isSolid); VertexOutput output; output.clipPos = clipPos; output.color = color; return output; } float3 PS(VertexOutput input): SVTARGET { return input.color; } Parameters: Color: float3, color for non-solid (empty) voxels. CollisionColor: float3, color for solid (occupied) voxels. CellHalfSize: float, half the width of a voxel in world units. BoundsMin: float3, minimum corner of the voxel grid in world space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in world-space calculations may cause gaps or overlaps if CellHalfSize is very small or the grid is very large. Visibility: Since points have no depth buffer interaction in the traditional sense of face culling, overlapping points may require depth testing or sorting if transparency is introduced. Empty Voxels: The method renders all voxels in the buffer. If the grid is sparse, rendering empty voxels (where isSolid == 0) may be wasteful unless filtered by the shader or culling logic. A variant that distinguishes between point-based and surface-based rendering modes within the same framework. It checks if the grid is a PointDataGrid. If true, it enables GLPOINTSMOOTH and GLVERTEXPROGRAMPOINTSIZE, renders the interior buffer using a flat shader, and disables point smooth states. If false, it renders interior and vector buffers with a flat shader, followed by the surface buffer with a surface shader. This allows switching between point visualization and surface visualization without changing the core data structure. Time Complexity: Pre-processing is O(N) where N is the number of voxels, dominated by collision tests against source geometry. Rendering is O(V) where V is the number of voxels, as each voxel is a single draw call instance or point. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the Voxels buffer. Performance: Highly efficient for sparse data or when only the occupancy status is needed, as it avoids generating 6 faces per voxel. Performance degrades if the grid resolution is extremely high and all voxels are solid, as the GPU must process millions of points. Strengths: Minimal geometry overhead; simple shader implementation; easy to integrate with GPU-based voxelization. Limitations: No inherent surface normal information; difficult to apply complex lighting models without additional data; visual quality depends on point size and anti-aliasing settings. This method is commonly used in real-time visualization tools and game engines (e.g., Unity) for debugging voxelized meshes or visualizing collision volumes. It is also found in scientific visualization libraries like OpenVDB for quick previewing of point data grids. The approach leverages the graphics pipeline's ability to handle large numbers of points efficiently via instancing. bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart5, https://github.com/bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart5, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) AcademySoftwareFoundation/openvdb, https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/openvdb, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Naive Voxel Geometry
body: Naive Voxel Geometry is a family of object-order volume rendering techniques that represent scalar field data as explicit geometric primitives (typically cubes or quads) submitted to the graphics pipeline for rasterization. It differs from image-order ray-casting by projecting geometry into screen space rather than sampling rays through the volume, and from optimized variants like Sparse Voxel Rasterization by generating primitives for all voxels without Level of Detail (LOD) reduction or greedy meshing, resulting in massive vertex counts for large scenes. This family shares the fundamental mechanism of converting scalar field data into geometric primitives that are submitted to the graphics pipeline, as detailed in the parent article Voxels rasterized as geometry. An object-order technique that renders every visible voxel as an individual geometric primitive (typically a cube or cuboid) without merging adjacent faces into larger meshes or using Level of Detail (LOD) reduction. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data by directly rasterizing the underlying voxel grid geometry. Unlike Base Renderer Geometry which may optimize mesh generation, this method explicitly avoids greedy meshing or face culling between adjacent voxels, drawing every face of every active voxel individually. A method for rendering voxel data by converting occupied voxel cells into explicit geometric primitives (cubes, squares, or lines) and submitting them to the graphics pipeline for rasterization. It solves the problem of visualizing scalar field data by treating voxels as discrete mesh objects rather than ray-marching a volume. It differs from Naive Voxel Rendering by explicitly generating vertex/index buffers for geometry submission, and from Cube Geometry for Volume Rendering by supporting multiple primitive topologies (faces, lines, full cubes) and dynamic batching strategies. Represents a single occupied voxel as a simple axis-aligned cube primitive submitted to the graphics pipeline. It solves the problem of mapping discrete scalar field data to geometric primitives for rasterization. It differs from Naive Voxel Rendering by explicitly generating vertex and index buffers for a 3D box rather than using point sprites or billboarded quads, and from Base Renderer Geometry by using a fixed, non-adaptive cube topology for every voxel. A high-throughput object-order rendering method that aggregates voxel faces into geometric chunks, transforms them to world space, and rasterizes them using a Painter's Algorithm. It differs from naive voxel geometry by batching visible faces into chunks and applying distance-based sorting and horizon clipping to manage depth ordering and visual effects, rather than rendering individual voxels independently. Not given in the sources.

name: Naive Voxel Rendering
head: Voxel Cuboid Rendering
body: Naive Voxel Rendering is an object-order technique that renders every visible voxel as an individual geometric primitive (typically a cube or cuboid) without merging adjacent faces into larger meshes or using Level of Detail (LOD) reduction. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data by directly rasterizing the underlying voxel grid geometry. Unlike Base Renderer Geometry which may optimize mesh generation, this method explicitly avoids greedy meshing or face culling between adjacent voxels, drawing every face of every active voxel individually. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid (volume data) where each cell contains a value (e.g., density, color, or binary existence) and grid coordinates (x, y, z). Output: A 2D image rasterized from the camera's perspective, where each active voxel contributes its colored faces to the frame buffer. Data Structures: The voxel data is typically stored in a 3D array or a packed 1D array representing the volume. Voxel Data: A structure or array holding the state of each voxel. In binary cases, a value of 0 indicates empty and 1 indicates presence. In continuous cases, a value >0 indicates density or presence. Geometry Buffer: Vertices are stored in a std::vector<GLfloat> in interleaved triangle-strip-like order for 6 faces. Each face has 6 vertices (2 triangles). Normals are stored in a separate std::vector<GLfloat> with 18 entries (3 floats per vertex \times 6 vertices per face \times 6 faces). Vertex Layout: Each vertex has position (x, y, z) and texture coordinates (u, v). Face Definition: The 'front' face (Z+) vertices in local space are ordered as: (-,-,+), (-,+,+), (+,+,+), (-,-,+), (+,-,+), (+,+,+). Parameters: VoxelSize: Physical size of a voxel in world units. Default is 1.0. VoxelHalfSize: Half the voxel size, typically 0.5. CHUNK\SIZE: Width and depth dimension of a voxel chunk (e.g., 128). CHUNK\HEIGHT: Height dimension of a voxel chunk (e.g., 32). Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate: Loop through all voxel coordinates (x, y, z) within the defined chunk or world bounds. 2. Check Existence: Determine if the voxel at (x, y, z) is active. If data value is 0 (or \le 0), skip or hide it (e.g., set Y to a large value). 3. Frustum Culling (Optional): Check if the voxel's position exceeds the camera frustum bounds. If so, return immediately to avoid processing. 4. Generate Geometry: For each active voxel, generate the vertices for all 6 faces. Calculate positions in view space using Px = x \cdot VoxelSize + dx \cdot VoxelSize, Py = y \cdot VoxelSize + dy \cdot VoxelSize, Pz = z \cdot VoxelSize + dz \cdot VoxelSize. 5. Back-face Culling (Optional): If cullInvisibleFaces is enabled, calculate the dot product between the view-space normal and the vector to the camera (origin in view space). Performance: Using very small voxels results in very small triangles, which consume significant GPU resources. name: Per-voxel Projection (Object-order)
head: Forward rendering, Histogram-based sorting, Object Space Approach, Object order voxel projection with value-sorted array, Object-order voxel projection, Voxel projection with value sorting, Voxel space projection
body: Per-voxel projection is an object-order volume rendering technique that iterates through volume data, projecting each voxel directly onto the image plane to accumulate pixel values. It solves the problem of efficiently computing Maximum Intensity Projections (MIP) by avoiding expensive read-compare-write GPU cycles, instead relying on a value-sorted traversal order where later projections overwrite earlier ones. Unlike its sibling Naive Voxel Rendering, which rasterizes individual cubes, this method treats voxels as point samples projected to single pixels, and unlike Front-to-Back Object-Order Projection, it does not require a Z-buffer or depth buffer for visibility resolution, instead using value magnitude to determine occlusion. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset V of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, a viewing transformation matrix M, and an image plane resolution W \times H. Outputs: A 2D image buffer I of size W \times H, initialized to a background value (typically 0 for MIP). Data Structures: 1. Value-Sorted Array (P): An array of voxel positions (indices or coordinates) containing only "interesting" voxels. 2. Sorting Key: The voxel values v from V. 3. Cumulative Histogram Array (H{cum}): An auxiliary array storing cumulative counts of voxels up to specific value thresholds, used to facilitate histogram-based sorting. 4. Image Buffer (I): A 2D array where I[u, v] stores the accumulated value for pixel (u, v). Steps: 1. Filter and Sort: Iterate through the volume V. Identify all voxels with v > 0 (interesting voxels) and store their positions in a temporary list. Sort this list based on their corresponding voxel values in ascending order (low to high). The sources indicate that cumulative histogram values are stored in an additional array, implying a histogram-based sorting algorithm is used to achieve this order efficiently. 2. Project and Accumulate: Initialize the image buffer I to the background value. Iterate through the sorted positions in P from the first element (lowest value) to the last (highest value). For each voxel position pi in P: compute the 2D image coordinates (u, v) by applying the viewing transformation M to the 3D position of pi and projecting onto the image plane. Retrieve the voxel value vi associated with pi. Update the image buffer at (u, v) with I[u, v] \leftarrow vi. Since the voxels are processed in ascending order of value, the current voxel's value vi is guaranteed to be greater than or equal to any previously written value at (u, v), so a simple overwrite operation correctly implements the Maximum Intensity Projection. 3. Handle Undersampling (Edge Case): For non-axial views, simple point projection may cause holes in the image due to undersampling. To mitigate this, a continuous function must be reconstructed using morphological sampling, followed by a morphological closing of the projection images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pervoxelprojectionmip(volume, viewmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight): # Initialize image buffer with background value (0 for MIP) image = [[0 for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] # Step 1: Filter interesting voxels (value > 0) interestingvoxels = [] for z in range(volume.depth): for y in range(volume.height): for x in range(volume.width): value = volume[z][y][x] if value > 0: interestingvoxels.append((x, y, z, value)) # Step 2: Sort voxels by value in ascending order # Sources imply histogram-based sorting using cumulative arrays interestingvoxels.sort(key=lambda voxel: voxel[3]) # Step 3: Project and accumulate for (x, y, z, value) in interestingvoxels: u, v = projecttoimage(x, y, z, viewmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight) if 0 <= u < imagewidth and 0 <= v < imageheight: # Overwrite implements max operation due to ascending sort order image[v][u] = value return image def projecttoimage(x, y, z, viewmatrix, width, height): # Apply 4x4 viewing matrix to voxel center vx = viewmatrix[0][0]x + viewmatrix[0][1]y + viewmatrix[0][2]z + viewmatrix[0][3] wy = viewmatrix[1][0]x + viewmatrix[1][1]y + viewmatrix[1][2]z + viewmatrix[1][3] qz = viewmatrix[2][0]x + viewmatrix[2][1]y + viewmatrix[2][2]z + viewmatrix[2][3] # Perspective divide if qz == 0: return -1, -1 px = vx / qz py = wy / qz # Map normalized device coordinates [-1, 1] to pixel coordinates u = int((px + 1) 0.5 width) v = int((1 - py) 0.5 height) return u, v Parameters: Threshold for "Interesting" Voxels: 0. Voxels with value \le 0 are excluded. Sorting Order: Ascending (low to high). Pitfalls: Arbitrary Order: If voxels are projected in arbitrary order, the final image is incorrect because the last projected voxel overwrites previous ones, regardless of depth or value. Undersampling Holes: Non-axial views may exhibit holes due to sparse sampling of the volume by the projection rays. Precision: Overwriting assumes that the value-sorted order perfectly aligns with the MIP requirement. If the volume contains negative values and the background is not handled correctly, the initialization of the image buffer must be to -\infty or the minimum possible value. Handles binary data (0/1) using back-to-front traversal for occlusion, without a Z-buffer. Supports continuous values and transparency, using front-to-back traversal for early ray termination. Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step, O(N \log N) or O(N) with histogram-based sorting, where N is the number of non-zero voxels. The projection step is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the value-sorted array and cumulative histogram. Performance: Substantial reduction in processed voxels (often >95%) by excluding zero voxels. Allows compression-domain rendering as MIP can be computed directly on the value-sorted array without full 3D reconstruction. Strengths: Efficient for MIP; avoids Z-buffer contention; suitable for sparse volumes. Limitations: Primarily suited for MIP or simple overwriting compositing; requires sorting overhead. When to Use: When computing Maximum Intensity Projections on sparse volumetric data where performance is critical and transparency is not required. The method was introduced as an object-order voxel-projection technique [MKG00] to avoid processing empty space in volume rendering. It was notably applied in the context of morphological pyramids for multiresolution MIP rendering, where it allowed for efficient progressive refinement by storing data in value-sorted arrays. The approach is part of the broader object-space rendering paradigm, which projects contributions from the volume to the image plane, contrasting with image-space ray tracing. name: Object-order Binary Volume Projection
head: Back-to-Front Algorithm, Back-to-Front Object-Order Projection, Object space rendering, Object-order voxel projection with value-sorted array, Voxel space projection
body: Object-order Binary Volume Projection is an early forward-mapping technique for rendering binary volumes, where voxels with a value of one are projected onto the image plane in back-to-front order to ensure correct occlusion without a Z-buffer. It differs from its sibling Per-voxel Projection (Object-order) by strictly restricting the input to binary data and relying on traversal order rather than a depth buffer to resolve visibility. Unlike later object-order methods like splatting, it does not reconstruct continuous density functions or handle gray-scale values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D binary volume grid V of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz, where V(x,y,z) \in \{0, 1\}. A projection function P(x,y,z) \to (u,v,d) mapping voxel coordinates to image pixel (u,v) and distance d from the image plane. Output: An image buffer I and a depth buffer D, both of size W \times H. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D array indexed by (x, y, z) storing binary values. Image Buffer: A 2D array indexed by pixel coordinates (u, v) storing the projected voxel value. Depth Buffer: A 2D array indexed by pixel coordinates (u, v) storing the distance of the projected voxel from the image plane. Parameters: Traversal Order: Determined by the relative orientation of the data axes to the image plane; each axis is traversed in increasing or decreasing order to satisfy the back-to-front requirement. Clipping Planes: Optional axis-parallel clipping planes that restrict traversal to a smaller rectangular region within the full data set. Steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Clear the image buffer I and depth buffer D to background values. 2. Determine Traversal Order: Analyze the camera orientation to determine if each axis (x, y, z) should be traversed in increasing or decreasing order. 3. Traverse and Project: Iterate through the volume using three nested loops. For each voxel (x, y, z): If V(x,y,z) == 0, skip. If clipping planes are active, check if the voxel is within the valid range; if not, skip. Project the voxel center to the image plane to obtain pixel coordinates (u, v) and distance d. If (u, v) is within the image bounds, overwrite I(u,v) with the voxel value (1) and D(u,v) with d. 4. Post-processing (Optional): The generated depth image D can be passed to a simple 2D discrete shader for further processing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def objectorderbinaryprojection(volume, image, depth, width, height, projectvoxel, clipbounds): """ volume: 3D array [Dx, Dy, Dz] with values 0 or 1 image, depth: 2D arrays [width, height] projectvoxel: callable(x, y, z) -> (u, v, dist) clipbounds: tuple of (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) or None """ Dx, Dy, Dz = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) # Initialize buffers to background values for u in range(width): for v in range(height): image[u][v] = 0 depth[u][v] = float('inf') # Determine traversal directions based on camera orientation # dirx, diry, dirz are +1 or -1 dirx, diry, dirz = 1, 1, -1 # Define loop ranges for each axis xrange = range(0, Dx, dirx) if dirx == 1 else range(Dx - 1, -1, -1) yrange = range(0, Dy, diry) if diry == 1 else range(Dy - 1, -1, -1) zrange = range(0, Dz, dirz) if dirz == 1 else range(Dz - 1, -1, -1) for z in zrange: for y in yrange: for x in xrange: if volume[x][y][z] == 0: continue if clipbounds is not None: cx, cy, cz = clipbounds if not (cx[0] <= x < cx[1] and cy[0] <= y < cy[1] and cz[0] <= z < cz[1]): continue u, v, dist = projectvoxel(x, y, z) if 0 <= u < width and 0 <= v < height: image[u][v] = 1 depth[u][v] = dist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Arbitrary Order: If voxels are projected in arbitrary order, the last projected voxel overwrites earlier ones, causing incorrect occlusion where closer voxels might be hidden by farther ones. Precision: Floating-point precision in projection calculations may cause gaps or overlaps in the image, especially at high resolutions or oblique angles. Clipping: Clipping planes parallel to the image plane are implemented by modifying loop bounds; incorrect bounds can lead to artifacts or missing data. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels in the volume, as each voxel is processed once. Memory Requirements: Requires storage for the volume grid and two W \times H buffers for the image and depth planes. Performance: Efficient for binary volumes due to simple traversal and projection; performance degrades if the volume is sparse and the traversal overhead is high relative to the number of projected voxels. Strengths: Simple implementation; no Z-buffer required; easy to generate depth images; supports axis-parallel clipping via loop bounds. Limitations: Restricted to binary volumes; does not handle gray-scale or continuous density functions. When to Use: When rendering binary volumes (e.g., segmented medical data) and simplicity is prioritized over visual fidelity or flexibility. When Not to Use: For gray-scale volumes or continuous rendering. Object-order Binary Volume Projection was one of the first object-order methods for volume rendering, developed in the early days of the field. It was designed to render binary volumes, such as those derived from medical imaging, by projecting voxels in back-to-front order. The method is described in foundational texts on volume visualization, including Kaufman's "Volume Visualization: Principles and Advances" and various dissertations on interactive volume rendering. It serves as a precursor to more sophisticated object-order techniques like splatting. name: Front-to-Back Object-Order Projection
head: Back-to-Front Algorithm, Back-to-Front Object-Order Projection, Front-to-Back (FTB) Algorithm, Object-Order Back-to-Front Projection
body: Front-to-Back Object-Order Projection is a volume rendering technique that traverses voxels in increasing distance from the image plane, projecting each voxel onto the screen and compositing it with the current pixel value. It solves the problem of correct transparency and occlusion handling in object-order rendering by ensuring that nearer voxels are composited over farther ones, effectively implementing the painter's algorithm for volumetric data. Once a voxel is projected onto a pixel, other voxels projecting to the same pixel are ignored because they are hidden by the first voxel. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset V with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz, a viewing direction, and an image plane. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity from the front-most voxels. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array of voxel values (opacity \alpha and color C). Image Buffer: A 2D array storing the accumulated color C{acc} and opacity \alpha{acc} for each pixel. Initialization: The image buffer is initialized to C{acc} = (0,0,0,0) and \alpha{acc} = 0. Steps: 1. Determine Traversal Order: Identify the axis most parallel to the viewing direction. This axis should be the outermost loop to allow for meaningful partial image results during traversal. 2. Initialize Image Buffer: Set all pixel accumulators to zero. 3. Traverse Voxels: Iterate through the volume in increasing distance from the image plane (front-to-back). For orthographic projections, a triple nested loop is sufficient: outer loop traverses planes, middle loop processes rows, inner loop visits voxels along the row. Note: This specific loop order does not yield a strict furthest-to-closest ordering for all voxels globally, but it ensures that voxels projecting to a single pixel are processed in the correct order for orthographic projections. 4. Project and Composite: For each voxel v: Project the voxel center (or footprint) onto the image plane to determine pixel coordinates (u, v). Retrieve the current accumulated color C{acc} and opacity \alpha{acc} at (u, v). Composite the voxel: C{new} = C{acc} + Cv \cdot \alphav \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{new} = \alpha{acc} + \alphav \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) Update the image buffer with C{new} and \alpha{new}. Early Termination/Pixel Locking: If \alpha{acc} reaches a threshold (e.g., 1.0), subsequent voxels projecting to this pixel can be ignored, as they are hidden by the front-most voxels. Parameters: Opacity Threshold: A value close to 1.0 (e.g., 0.99) for early termination. Kernel Size: If using splatting (a variant of this approach), a Gaussian kernel with finite extent is used to distribute voxel energy across multiple pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Holes: In perspective projections, discrete selection of projected pixels can cause "holes" in the image as the camera moves closer, because neighboring voxels may project to increasingly distant pixels. Splatting addresses this by distributing energy across a footprint. Loop Order Limitation: The standard triple-nested loop order (planes, rows, voxels) is only sufficient for orthographic projections. Clipping: Clipping planes orthogonal to the major axes limit the traversal region. Clipping planes parallel to the image plane require ignoring samples whose distance to the image plane is less than the cut plane distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackprojection(volume, imagewidth, imageheight, viewdirection, origin, scale): # Initialize image buffer # Cacc: [imageheight, imagewidth, 4] (RGBA) # alphaacc: [imageheight, imagewidth] Cacc = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] alphaacc = [[0.0 for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] # Helper: Orthographic projection from voxel space to screen coordinates def projecttoscreen(voxelpos): # Map voxel coordinates to integer pixel indices u = int((voxelpos[0] - origin[0]) scale[0]) v = int((voxelpos[1] - origin[1]) scale[1]) return u, v # Get volume dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz = len(volume[0][0]), len(volume[0]), len(volume) # Determine traversal order based on view direction # Choose the axis most parallel to the viewing direction as the outermost loop absdx, absdy, absdz = abs(viewdirection[0]), abs(viewdirection[1]), abs(viewdirection[2]) if absdx <= absdy and absdx <= absdz: order = ['z', 'y', 'x'] elif absdy <= absdx and absdy <= absdz: order = ['z', 'x', 'y'] else: order = ['x', 'y', 'z'] # Traverse volume in front-to-back order # Note: The exact loop structure depends on the 'order' determined above # For simplicity, assuming a generic iteration that respects the order for z in range(Dz): for y in range(Dy): for x in range(Dx): voxel = volume[z][y][x] if voxel['alpha'] > 0: voxelpos = (x, y, z) u, v = projecttoscreen(voxelpos) # Check bounds if 0 <= u < imagewidth and 0 <= v < imageheight: # Retrieve current accumulated values currentC = Cacc[v][u] currentalpha = alphaacc[v][u] # Composite weight = voxel['alpha'] (1.0 - currentalpha) newC = tuple(currentC[i] + voxel['color'][i] weight for i in range(4)) newalpha = currentalpha + weight # Update buffer Cacc[v][u] = newC alphaacc[v][u] = newalpha # Early termination check could be added here per pixel # if alphaacc[v][u] >= threshold: skip further voxels for this pixel A viewing algorithm that traverses and renders scene objects in order of decreasing distance from the observer to correctly handle transparency and occlusion. It is the inverse of FTB, where pixels may change values multiple times during generation. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels, assuming constant-time projection and compositing. However, perspective projections with splatting may increase complexity due to footprint calculations. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the image buffer, where W and H are image dimensions. Performance: FTB allows for early termination, which can significantly speed up rendering for opaque regions. It also allows for partial image results to be displayed during traversal if the outermost loop is chosen correctly, improving interactivity. Strengths: Correct handling of transparency; early ray termination; partial image results; easy implementation of clipping planes. Limitations: Discrete pixel selection causes holes in perspective projections; loop order limitations for orthographic vs. perspective; requires careful handling of viewing direction for optimal traversal. When to Use: Orthographic projections; scenes with significant opacity where early termination is beneficial; interactive applications requiring partial results. When Not to Use: Perspective projections requiring high quality without splatting; scenes with complex transparency where strict per-pixel ordering is critical and loop order is insufficient. The front-to-back algorithm is essentially the same as the back-to-front (BTF) algorithm but traverses voxels in increasing distance order. It was developed as an alternative to BTF to allow for early ray termination and partial image results. The concept is rooted in the painter's algorithm, where objects are drawn from back to front, but adapted for volume rendering by processing voxels from front to back. Splatting, a related technique, was proposed by Westover to address the hole artifacts in perspective projections. name: Back-to-Front Rendering
head: Painter's Algorithm, Back-to-Front Object-Order Projection
body: Back-to-Front (BTF) rendering is an object-order volume visualization technique that traverses and renders scene voxels in order of decreasing distance from the observer. It solves the problem of correctly handling transparency and occlusion in voxel data by exploiting the spatial presortedness of the voxel array, thereby avoiding the need for a Z-buffer for hidden voxel removal. Unlike the standard Z-buffer method, which maps voxels in arbitrary order and cannot natively support semitransparent materials, BTF ensures objects are mapped to the screen in viewing order. It is distinguished from its sibling, Front-to-Back Object-Order Projection, by processing far voxels first rather than near voxels first. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid V of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz, where each voxel contains optical properties (e.g., density, color). The data is assumed to be accessible in an order approximating decreasing distance from the observer. Output: A 2D image buffer I of size W \times H, initialized to the background color (typically transparent or black). Data Structures: Image Buffer: A 2D array storing accumulated color and opacity for each pixel. Voxel Grid: A 3D array. No explicit Z-buffer is required for depth testing. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the image buffer I with the background color. 2. Traversal Order Determination: Determine the traversal order of voxels based on the viewing direction. In 2D, if the x-axis is the innermost loop, the display order is A, C, B, D; if the y-axis is the innermost loop, the order is C, A, D, B. In 3D, axis traversal can be done arbitrarily with 8 possible orders, and data can be read and rendered as slices. 3. Voxel Projection: For each voxel in the determined back-to-front order, project the voxel onto the image plane. If voxel (x,y) is partially obscured by voxel (x',y'), it implies x \le x' and y \le y' in screen space; the algorithm projects (x,y) before (x',y') to ensure correct occlusion. 4. Compositing: Draw the current voxel on top of previously drawn voxels. If compositing is performed, composite the current voxel with the screen value. Standard alpha compositing formula: C{out} = C{in} \cdot (1 - \alpha{voxel}) + C{voxel} \cdot \alpha{voxel} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{voxel} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) Where C is color and \alpha is opacity. 5. Repeat: Continue until all voxels have been processed. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Strict Painter's Algorithm: Voxel projection is not in order of strictly decreasing distance from the observer, so this method is not strictly the Painter's Algorithm. Perspective: The handling of perspective views requires careful consideration, as simple axis-aligned traversal may not perfectly maintain back-to-front order without additional sorting or shearing transformations. Transparency: Unlike Z-buffer methods, BTF supports semitransparent materials because objects are mapped in viewing order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backtofrontrender(voxelgrid, imagebuffer, traversalorder): # imagebuffer is a 2D array of (color, opacity) tuples, initialized to background for voxel in traversalorder: # Standard affine transformation from voxel space to screen space screenx = int(voxel.x) screeny = int(voxel.y) # Clamp coordinates to buffer bounds to handle edge cases screenx = max(0, min(screenx, imagebuffer.shape[1] - 1)) screeny = max(0, min(screeny, imagebuffer.shape[0] - 1)) cv, av = voxel.color, voxel.opacity cs, as = imagebuffer[screeny, screenx] # Standard alpha compositing (over operator) newalpha = as + av (1 - as) newcolor = cs (1 - av) + cv av imagebuffer[screeny, screenx] = (newcolor, newalpha) return imagebuffer Traverses voxels in increasing distance order, allowing for early ray termination and potentially more efficient processing of transparent volumes. Front-to-Back Object-Order Projection Renders voxels in arbitrary order, requiring a Z-buffer for depth testing. Cannot natively support semitransparent materials without additional sorting. Z-Buffer Method Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Typically O(N) for N voxels, assuming constant-time projection and compositing. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires O(W \times H) for the image buffer. No Z-buffer is required, saving memory compared to Z-buffer methods. Performance: The method avoids the significant slowdown associated with consulting the Z-buffer N times in standard Z-buffer methods. It exploits the spatial presortedness of the voxel arrays. Strengths: Correctly handles transparency and occlusion without a Z-buffer. Simple implementation. Limitations: Not strictly the Painter's Algorithm due to projection artifacts. May require careful handling of perspective views. Performance may degrade if the traversal order is not well-optimized or if the voxel grid is not presorted. When to Use: When transparency is important and a Z-buffer is undesirable or unavailable. Suitable for presorted voxel data. When Not to Use: When early ray termination is critical (use Front-to-Back instead). When strict depth ordering is required for complex overlapping geometry without presorting. The Back-to-Front algorithm was introduced by Frieder et al. in 1985. It is maybe derived from a standard "Painter's Algorithm". The method is based on the observation that voxel arrays are spatially presorted, allowing traversal in order of decreasing distance from the observer. This approach was developed to address the limitations of the Z-buffer method in handling semitransparent materials. It is part of the broader field of volume visualization and rendering techniques. Volume Rendering Volume Rendering. Lecture 21. Acknowledgements. These slides are collected from many sources. A particularly valuable source is the IEEE Visualization conference tutorials.
