name: Basic Opaque Voxel Rendering Pipeline
head: Basic Opaque Rendering Pipeline
body: This method implements a minimal, high-performance rendering pipeline for opaque voxel geometry, typically targeting modern graphics APIs like WebGPU. It solves the problem of efficiently displaying static or semi-static voxel worlds by treating occupied voxels as opaque geometric primitives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by enforcing a strict single-pipeline architecture with fixed lighting models (sun, sky, baked-AO) and specific depth buffer configurations, avoiding the complexity of transparency handling or dynamic shader compilation found in more advanced variants. The pipeline converts voxel data into GPU-drawable geometry and renders it using a fixed-function shading model. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of voxel definitions (cell types) and a volume data structure containing cell instances with positions and orientations. Output: Rasterized images (e.g., RGB/RGBA with depth) representing the opaque voxel scene. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Definition: An immutable structure defining the visual properties of a cell type (e.g., stone, dirt). It is shared across instances. 2. Voxel Volume: A dense or sparse grid of cells. Constructed via a Builder pattern where cells are placed at specific indices (i, j, k) with specific orientations. 3. Model: An immutable mesh representation generated from the Volume. It contains opaque and transparent mesh subsets, though this specific pipeline only utilizes the opaque subset. 4. Assembly: A copyable container of Models, allowing local transforms to be applied to groups of voxels (e.g., a character body part). 5. Vertex/Index Buffer: A single, growing, reusable buffer managed by a MeshUploader. It has an explicit byte budget; uploads exceeding this budget are rejected. Pipeline Configuration: The rendering pipeline is configured with the following fixed states: Front Face: Counter-Clockwise (CCW). Depth Buffer: Depth32Float. Culling: Back-face culling is enabled. Coordinate System: Targets WebGPU NDC where z \in [0, 1]. Rendering Steps: 1. Volume Construction: The application constructs a Voxel::Volume using a Builder. Cells are added with specific definitions and orientations. 2. Meshing (Baking): A VoxelMesher synchronously processes the Volume to generate an immutable Model. This step converts logical voxel data into geometric primitives (vertices and indices). 3. Assembly Composition: The application composes Models into an Assembly, applying local transforms. The assembly state is invalidated if transforms change. 4. Entity Binding: An AssemblyRenderingComponent is attached to a 3D Entity, binding the assembly without owning it. 5. Batching: A VoxelRenderingSystem collects these components via a Registry. It reconstructs compact batches every frame. For each non-empty bucket, a new Storage Buffer (SSBO) is created. 6. Draw Commands: The system emits instanced draw commands. No per-instance update commands are used; all instance data is pushed via the SSBOs. 7. Culling: Frustum culling is applied using the Gribb–Hartmann algorithm to exclude voxels outside the camera view. 8. Shading: The fragment shader applies a lighting model combining direct sunlight, sky ambient, and baked ambient occlusion (AO). 9. Capture (Optional): For debugging or testing, the scene can be rendered offscreen to an Rgba8UnormSrgb texture with depth, read back, and saved as PNGs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. stonedef = VoxelDefinition(material="stone", color=[0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) volumebuilder = VoxelVolumeBuilder(dimensions=(16, 16, 16)) cell = VoxelCell(definition=stonedef, orientation=Identity) volumebuilder.set(position=(2, 4, 1), cell=cell) volume = volumebuilder.build() model = mesher.bake(volume) # Returns immutable Model with opaque meshes assembly = VoxelAssembly() assembly.addpart("body", model, transform=Identity) for frame in frames: # Update assembly if transforms changed if assembly.needsupdate: assembly.updatetransforms() # System collects components and builds batches batches = voxelrenderingsystem.collectbatches([assembly]) # Create SSBOs for each bucket for bucket in batches: ssbo = createssbo(bucket.instancedata) # Issue instanced draw call drawinstanced( pipeline=pipeline, # CCW, Depth32Float, BackFaceCull vertexbuffer=meshbuffer, indexbuffer=meshindexbuffer, instancebuffer=ssbo, instancecount=bucket.instancecount, indexcount=bucket.indexcount) A specific implementation of the basic opaque pipeline within the Sparkle engine context. It differs by introducing a high-level abstraction layer involving Volume, Model, and Assembly objects, and relies on a registry-based system for rendering components. It emphasizes synchronous baking and per-frame batch reconstruction with SSBOs for instance data, avoiding per-instance update commands. Time Complexity: Meshing is synchronous and occurs during volume construction or explicit bake calls, not per-frame. Rendering is O(N) with respect to the number of visible voxel instances, dominated by draw call overhead and vertex processing. Memory Complexity: The vertex/index buffer grows with the number of visible faces. The SSBOs scale with the number of instances per bucket. The MeshUploader's byte budget limits peak memory usage per frame. Performance: Efficient for static or slowly changing scenes due to immutable models and instanced rendering. The Gribb–Hartmann culling reduces overdraw. Limitations: Only supports opaque rendering. Transparency is handled by a separate mesh subset in the model but not rendered by this specific pipeline configuration. Lighting is static (baked AO), limiting dynamic shadowing capabilities. When to use: Ideal for voxel-based games or simulations where performance is critical, lighting requirements are simple, and transparency is not needed or handled separately. When not to use: When dynamic lighting, complex shadows, or transparency are required. This pipeline originates from the spall project, specifically the spallrender module, which provides a baseline implementation for WebGPU-based voxel rendering. It is designed as a minimal, reference-quality implementation to validate the meshing and rendering logic before adding more complex features. The approach of using instanced rendering with SSBOs for instance data is a common optimization in modern graphics programming for large numbers of similar objects. The Sparkle engine's implementation adapts these principles into a more structured, entity-component-system (ECS) friendly architecture. name: Voxel Rendering Pipeline
head: Sparkle Voxel Engine Architecture
body: The Voxel Rendering Pipeline is a CPU-driven batching and GPU instancing method for rendering opaque voxel geometry within the Sparkle engine. It solves the problem of efficiently drawing large, dynamic voxel scenes by decoupling static geometry baking from per-frame rendering state. Unlike generic voxel renderers that may update vertex buffers every frame, this pipeline reconstructs compact draw batches on the CPU and emits single instanced draw commands per bucket, avoiding per-instance update commands. The pipeline operates in two distinct phases: an offline/synchronous baking phase and a per-frame rendering phase. Inputs: Voxel::Volume: A mutable collection of voxel cells with definitions and orientations. Assembly: A copyable container of Model instances with local transforms. Entity3D registry: Contains AssemblyRenderingComponent instances. Outputs: GPU draw calls (instanced) via a Metal command buffer. Updated SSBOs (Shader Storage Buffer Objects) containing batch data. 1. Voxel::Definition: Immutable, shareable definition of a voxel type (e.g., stone). 2. Voxel::Cell: Lightweight copy of a Definition plus an orientation. 3. Voxel::Volume::Builder: Builder pattern for constructing a Volume. Layout: Internal array of cells, indexed by 3D coordinates. Size: Configurable (e.g., {16, 16, 16}). 4. Voxel::Model: Immutable mesh data generated by the mesher. Contains opaque and transparent meshes. 5. Voxel::Assembly: Copyable structure containing named parts (e.g., "torso"), each referencing a Model and a local transform. 6. AssemblyRenderingComponent: Attached to Entity3D, binds an Assembly without owning it. 7. SSBO (Batch Buffer): One SSBO created per non-empty bucket per frame. Contains instance data for instanced rendering. 1. Volume Construction: The game constructs a Voxel::Volume using a Voxel::Volume::Builder. python # Example construction definition = getdefinition("stone") cell = Cell(definition, orientation) builder = VolumeBuilder(size=(16, 16, 16)) builder.set(position=(2, 4, 1), cell=cell) volume = builder.build() 2. Mesh Baking: The VoxelMesher synchronously bakes the Volume into an immutable Model. python model = mesher.bake(volume) 3. Assembly Composition: The game composes Models into a copyable Assembly. python assembly = Assembly() assembly.addpart("torso", model, transform) If transforms change, the assembly state is invalidated. 4. Entity Binding: An AssemblyRenderingComponent is attached to an Entity3D, binding the assembly. 5. Frame Rendering (VoxelRenderingSystem): a. Collection: The system collects AssemblyRenderingComponent instances from the Registry. b. Batch Reconstruction: Every frame, compact batches are reconstructed. c. SSBO Creation: A new SSBO is created for each non-empty bucket. d. Draw Emission: Instanced draw commands are emitted. No per-instance update commands are used. Bucketing Strategy: Not specified in sources. Typically involves spatial partitioning or material grouping. SSBO Size: Determined by the number of instances in the bucket. Transform Changes: The assembly state must be invalidated when transforms change to ensure correct rendering. Synchronous Baking: The mesher operates synchronously, which may block the main thread during volume updates. Memory Management: New SSBOs are created every frame for non-empty buckets. Efficient reuse or pooling is not described and may be a performance pitfall. Time Complexity: Per-frame complexity is dominated by batch reconstruction and SSBO creation. Since no per-instance updates are used, draw call overhead is minimized. Memory Complexity: Requires storing Model data (immutable) and per-frame SSBOs. Performance: Optimized for instanced rendering. Avoids frequent CPU-GPU synchronization for instance data. Strengths: Simple CPU-side logic, efficient GPU draw calls, clear separation of static and dynamic data. Limitations: Synchronous baking can cause stalls. Per-frame SSBO allocation may lead to memory fragmentation or allocation overhead. When to Use: Scenes with moderate dynamic voxel activity where per-frame CPU processing is acceptable. When Not to Use: Highly dynamic scenes requiring frequent per-instance updates or extremely large volumes where synchronous baking is prohibitive. The Voxel Rendering Pipeline is part of the Sparkle engine, specifically the V0.1.4 branch. It is designed for a voxel-based game, leveraging Metal for GPU rendering. The architecture emphasizes a clear separation between volume construction, mesh baking, and rendering, using an entity-component system for assembly management. V0.1.4 — Voxel engine design and implementation specification, https://github.com/EreliaStudio/Sparkle/pull/37, fetched 2026-10-26

name: WorldRenderer Multi-Pass Pipeline
head: VoxelKit GPU rendering engine
body: WorldRenderer is the GPU rendering engine for VoxelKit, implemented as a multi-pass Metal pipeline that draws five distinct world layers (Structure, Object, Zone, IoT, Agent) into a single MTKView-backed drawable. It is designed specifically for Apple Silicon hardware (e.g., M1 Pro 16-core GPU) and distinguishes itself through CPU-side frustum culling, hardware-aware quality presets, and instanced rendering of voxel geometry. Unlike generic voxel renderers, it integrates specific application logic such as zone triangulation, IoT billboard sprites, and agent trajectory lines within a unified Metal command buffer. Inputs: World Data: MergedVoxel buffers (CPU-updated, GPU-read), ChunkKey bounding boxes, Zone polygons, IoT device anchors, and Agent trajectory points. Camera State: View-projection matrix, camera position, viewport size, height cutoff, and fog density. Hardware Info: MTLDevice name used to select a quality preset. Outputs: A single composited image rendered to the MTKView drawable. CameraUniforms Passed to all shaders via setVertexBytes:. The layout is: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct CameraUniforms { float4x4 viewProjection; float3 cameraPosition; float voxelSize; float2 viewportSize; float heightCutoff; float fogDensity; }; MergedVoxel Buffer Storage Mode: MTLStorageMode.shared (allows CPU updates and GPU reads of the same physical memory). Content: Center position and half-size of each voxel. Zone Triangulation Buffer Content: Vertices for zone polygons, triangulated on the CPU. Method: Centroid computed via Accelerate.vDSP; fan triangulation for convex polygons, ear-clip for concave. IoT Icon Atlas Format: MTLTexture, 128×128 pixels. Hardware Preset Table Used at initialization to map MTLDevice.name substrings to quality settings: | Chip Generation | Preset | Max Instances | LOD Scale | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | M4 Pro / M4 Max | ultra | 50M | 1.0 | | M3 / M4 | high | 20M | 1.0 | | M1 Pro / M2 Pro | high | 10M | 1.0 | | M1 / M2 | medium | 5M | 0.8 | | iPhone A17 / A18 | medium | 3M | 0.7 | | iPhone A15 / A16 | low | 1M | 0.5 | 1. Initialization: Detect chip generation by checking MTLDevice.name for substrings (e.g., "M4 Pro", "A17"). Map result to the Hardware Preset Table to determine LOD aggressiveness, shadow quality, and max instance count. Create MTLRenderPipelineDescriptor for each pass (Structure, Zone, IoT, Agent) with appropriate vertex/fragment functions. Configure MTLDepthStencilState: depth write enabled for Structure/Object passes; disabled for Zone/IoT/Agent passes. 2. Per-Frame Render Loop (draw(in view: MTKView)): Update CameraUniforms with current camera state. Frustum Culling: Perform Gribb-Hartmann 6-plane AABB test on CPU for each ChunkKey bounding box. Eliminate off-screen chunks to reduce draw calls by ≥ 50% when the camera faces a wall. LOD Selection: Query ChunkedOctree at a depth based on distance(cameraPosition, chunkCenter). Encode StructurePass: Set vertex buffer with MergedVoxel data. Issue instanced draw call: drawPrimitives(type:.triangle, vertexStart:0, vertexCount:36, instanceCount: mergedVoxels.count). Encode ZonePass: Upload pre-triangulated zone vertices to MTLBuffer. Draw zone polygons. Encode IoTPass: Draw billboard sprites using the 128×128 icon atlas. Draw labels using textures baked from CoreText → CGContext. Encode AgentPass: Draw pulsing rings (instanced). Draw trajectories using MTLPrimitiveType.lineStrip. Draw predicted paths with fading alpha. Present: Present the drawable. 3. Frame Rate Control: Use CADisplayLink with preferredFrameRateRange. Locked Mode: Set minimum = preferred = maximum = targetFps (options: 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 120). Adaptive Mode: Set minimum = 24, preferred = 120, maximum = 120 (matches ProMotion). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initrenderer(device: MTLDevice): # Detect chip and set preset devicename = device.name if "M4 Pro" in devicename or "M4 Max" in devicename: preset = Preset(ultra, maxinstances=50000000, lodscale=1.0) elif "M3" in devicename or "M4" in devicename: preset = Preset(high, maxinstances=20000000, lodscale=1.0) elif "M1 Pro" in devicename or "M2 Pro" in devicename: preset = Preset(high, maxinstances=10000000, lodscale=1.0) elif "M1" in devicename or "M2" in devicename: preset = Preset(medium, maxinstances=5000000, lodscale=0.8) elif "A17" in devicename or "A18" in devicename: preset = Preset(medium, maxinstances=3000000, lodscale=0.7) elif "A15" in devicename or "A16" in devicename: preset = Preset(low, maxinstances=1000000, lodscale=0.5) else: preset = Preset(low, maxinstances=1000000, lodscale=0.5) # Default fallback # Create pipeline states structurepipeline = createpipeline(structurevertex, structurefragment, depthwrite=True) zonepipeline = createpipeline(zonevertex, zonefragment, depthwrite=False) iotpipeline = createpipeline(iotvertex, iotfragment, depthwrite=False) agentpipeline = createpipeline(agentvertex, agentfragment, depthwrite=False) # Create buffers mergedvoxelbuffer = device.newbuffer(size=mergedvoxels.count sizeof(MergedVoxel), options=MTLStorageMode.shared) zonebuffer = device.newbuffer(size=zonevertices.count sizeof(float3), options=MTLStorageMode.private) iconatlas = loadtexture("ioticons128x128.png") # Setup display link displaylink = CADisplayLink(target=self, selector="draw:") displaylink.preferredFrameRateRange = FrameRateRange(min=24, preferred=120, max=120) displaylink.addtorunloop() def draw(self, view: MTKView): # 1. Update Uniforms camerauniforms = CameraUniforms( viewProjection=view.camera.projectionMatrix view.camera.viewMatrix, cameraPosition=view.camera.position, voxelSize=1.0, # Assumed unit voxel size based on context viewportSize=view.drawableSize, heightCutoff=currentheightcutoff, fogDensity=currentfogdensity) commandbuffer.setvertexbytes(camerauniforms, offset=0, index=0) # 2. Frustum Culling & LOD visiblechunks = [] for chunk in allchunks: if gribbhartmanntest(chunk.boundingbox, view.camera.frustumplanes): dist = distance(view.camera.position, chunk.center) if dist < 20.0: loddepth = 5 # 3.125 cm elif dist < 100.0: loddepth = 3 # 12.5 cm else: loddepth = 1 # 50 cm # Apply LOD scale from preset effectivelod = loddepth preset.lodscale visiblechunks.append((chunk, effectivelod)) # 3. Encode Structure Pass encoder = commandbuffer.rendercommandencoder(pipelinestate=structurepipeline) encoder.setvertexbuffer(mergedvoxelbuffer, offset=0, index=0) # 36 vertices = 12 triangles = 6 faces of cube encoder.drawprimitives(type=MTLPrimitiveType.Triangle, vertexstart=0, vertexcount=36, instancecount=len(visiblechunks)) encoder.endencoding() # 4. Encode Zone Pass # Triangulate on CPU if data changed if zoneschanged: zonevertices = [] for zone in zones: centroid = vDSPcomputecentroid(zone.polygon) if isconvex(zone.polygon): zonevertices.extend(fantriangulate(zone.polygon, centroid)) else: zonevertices.extend(earcliptriangulate(zone.polygon)) zonebuffer.replace(range=0, length=len(zonevertices)sizeof(float3), bytes=zonevertices) encoder = commandbuffer.rendercommandencoder(pipelinestate=zonepipeline) encoder.setvertexbuffer(zonebuffer, offset=0, index=0) encoder.drawprimitives(type=MTLPrimitiveType.Triangle, vertexstart=0, vertexcount=len(zonevertices)) encoder.endencoding() # 5. Encode IoT Pass encoder = commandbuffer.rendercommandencoder(pipelinestate=iotpipeline) encoder.setvertexbuffer(iotbuffer, offset=0, index=0) encoder.setfragmenttexture(iconatlas, index=0) encoder.drawprimitives(type=MTLPrimitiveType.Triangle, vertexstart=0, vertexcount=iotvertexcount) encoder.endencoding() # 6. Encode Agent Pass encoder = commandbuffer.rendercommandencoder(pipelinestate=agentpipeline) # Pulsing rings encoder.setvertexbuffer(agentringbuffer, offset=0, index=0) encoder.setuniform("time", currenttime) encoder.drawprimitives(type=MTLPrimitiveType.Triangle, vertexstart=0, vertexcount=ringvertexcount, instancecount=agentcount) # Trajectories encoder.setvertexbuffer(agenttrajectorybuffer, offset=0, index=0) encoder.drawprimitives(type=MTLPrimitiveType.LineStrip, vertexstart=0, vertexcount=trajectoryvertexcount) encoder.endencoding() commandbuffer.presentdrawable(view.currentDrawable) Exponential Fog Factor \text{fogFactor} = 1 - \exp(-\text{fogDensity} \times \text{depth}) Where fogDensity is from CameraUniforms and depth is the fragment depth. Billboard Right Vector \text{right} = \text{cross}(\text{cameraUp}, \text{toCamera}) Computed in the vertex shader so the sprite always faces the camera. Key Light Direction: (0.577, 0.577, 0.577). Fill Light Direction: (-0.577, 0.2, -0.577). Ambient Light: 0.3. Zone Alpha: 0.25. LOD Band 0: Distance 0–20 m, Octree depth 5 (effective 3.125 cm). LOD Band 1: Distance 20–100 m, Octree depth 3 (effective 12.5 cm). LOD Band 2: Distance 100+ m, Octree depth 1 (effective 50 cm). Precision: Use MTLStorageMode.shared for MergedVoxel buffers to ensure CPU updates and GPU reads access the same physical memory without unnecessary copies. Boundaries: The Gribb-Hartmann test must be performed per 1 m³ chunk to effectively cull off-screen geometry. Degenerate Input: Zone triangulation must handle both convex (fan) and concave (ear-clip) polygons; failure to distinguish may result in incorrect rendering. Height Cutoff: Geometry with worldPos.y > heightCutoff is clipped in the fragment shader. Renders the primary voxel geometry using instanced cubes with two-directional diffuse lighting and depth fog. Chosen when rendering the bulk of the world volume. Link Renders semi-transparent (alpha 0.25) overlapping zone polygons using additive blending. Chosen for area-based metadata visualization. Link Renders IoT device icons as billboards and text labels. Chosen for sparse, high-priority object markers. Link Renders agent positions as pulsing rings and trajectories as line strips. Chosen for dynamic entity tracking. Link Time Complexity: Frustum culling is O(C) where C is the number of chunks. LOD query is O(1) per chunk. Rendering is dominated by the number of visible instances. Memory Complexity: O(V) for voxel data, where V is the number of occupied voxels. Zone and Agent data are O(Z) and O(A) respectively. Measured Performance: Designed to render 100,000 occupied voxels at native monitor refresh rate (up to 120 fps) on an M1 Pro 16-core GPU. Scaling: Frustum culling reduces draw calls by ≥ 50% when the camera faces a wall (half map off-screen). Strengths: High performance on Apple Silicon via instanced rendering and CPU-side culling. Hardware-aware presets ensure consistent performance across device generations. Limitations: CPU-side triangulation for zones may become a bottleneck for highly complex concave polygons. LOD transitions must be tuned to avoid visual popping. When to Use: Real-time visualization of voxel-based worlds on iOS/macOS devices with Metal support. When Not to Use: Non-Apple platforms, or scenes requiring dynamic global illumination beyond simple diffuse lighting. WorldRenderer is part of the VoxelKit project, an open-source voxel engine. The specific multi-pass pipeline design was documented in GitHub Issue #14 by user plagness in 2024. It was developed to address the need for efficient rendering of five distinct world layers on mobile and desktop Apple Silicon hardware, leveraging Metal's instancing capabilities and CPU-GPU shared memory features. WorldRenderer: Metal pipeline for all five map layers, https://github.com/plagness/VoxelKit/issues/14, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Two-Pass Voxel Shading Pipeline
head: Voxel-shader rendering pipeline
body: The Two-Pass Voxel Shading Pipeline is a rendering technique for voxel meshes that separates solid (opaque) geometry from porous (translucent) geometry to handle alpha blending correctly. It builds on Voxel Rendering Pipeline by explicitly dividing the draw calls into two distinct phases: one for opaque surfaces using an ambient occlusion (AO) shader, and a second for translucent surfaces using a custom model shader with blending enabled. This approach distinguishes itself from single-pass voxel renderers by ensuring that translucent blocks do not incorrectly occlude or blend with opaque blocks behind them due to depth buffer ordering issues. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A voxel mesh data structure containing vertexArrayObjects for both surface (solid) and porous (translucent) triangles; a camera providing view and projection matrices; optional texture maps (tileMap or texture). Outputs: A rendered frame on the GPU framebuffer. Data Structures: meshes: An object or array of mesh chunks. Each mesh contains: vertexArrayObjects: An object with keys surface and porous. surface: An array of triangle indices or VAO references for opaque geometry. porous: An array of triangle indices or VAO references for translucent geometry. modelMatrix: A 4x4 transformation matrix for the mesh. shader: The AO shader program for solid blocks. shader2: The custom model shader for porous blocks. Parameters: cameraNear: Near clipping plane, default 0.1. cameraFar: Far clipping plane, default 200.0. cameraFOV: Field of view in degrees, default 45.0. perspectiveResize: Boolean, default true. If true, updates the projection matrix on window resize. Steps: 1. Initialization (gl-init): Create the AO shader (this.shader) and the custom model shader (this.shader2). Initialize the projection matrix using mat4.perspective with cameraFOV, aspect ratio, cameraNear, and cameraFar. Listen for gl-render events to start the render loop. 2. Render Loop: Enable face culling and depth testing: gl.enable(gl.CULLFACE) and gl.enable(gl.DEPTHTEST). Update the view matrix from the camera. Pass 1: Solid Blocks Disable blending: gl.disable(gl.BLEND). Bind the AO shader (this.shader). Set uniforms: projection, view, tileCount, and optionally tileMap if a texture exists. Iterate over all meshes in this.meshes. For each mesh, if mesh.vertexArrayObjects.surface exists and is non-empty: Set the model uniform to mesh.modelMatrix. Bind the surface VAO. Draw triangles: gl.drawArrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, triangleVAO.length). Pass 2: Porous Blocks Set blend function to gl.blendFunc(gl.ONE, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA). Enable blending: gl.enable(gl.BLEND). Bind the custom model shader (this.shader2). Set uniforms: view, projection, and optionally texture if a texture exists. Iterate over all meshes in this.meshes. For each mesh, if mesh.vertexArrayObjects.porous exists and is non-empty: Set the model uniform. Bind the porous VAO. Draw triangles: gl.drawArrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, blockMesh.length). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def init(): # Create shaders shader = createaoshader() shader2 = createcustommodelshader() # Initialize projection matrix aspect = width / height fovrad = camerafov pi / 180 projectionmatrix = mat4.perspective(fovrad, aspect, cameranear, camerafar) # Listen for events on('gl-init', lambda: (shader.bind(), shader2.bind(), updateprojectionmatrix())) on('gl-render', render) if perspectiveresize: on('gl-resize', updateprojectionmatrix) def updateprojectionmatrix(): aspect = width / height fovrad = camerafov pi / 180 mat4.perspective(projectionmatrix, fovrad, aspect, cameranear, camerafar) emit('updateProjectionMatrix', projectionmatrix) def render(): gl = getglcontext() gl.enable(gl.CULLFACE) gl.enable(gl.DEPTHTEST) # Get view matrix viewmatrix = camera.getviewmatrix() # Pass 1: Solid blocks gl.disable(gl.BLEND) shader.bind() shader.setuniform('projection', projectionmatrix) shader.setuniform('view', viewmatrix) shader.setuniform('tileCount', stitcher.tilecount) if textureexists: shader.setuniform('tileMap', texture.bind()) for mesh in meshes: surfacevaos = mesh.vertexarrayobjects.get('surface') if surfacevaos and len(surfacevaos) > 0: shader.setuniform('model', mesh.modelmatrix) for vao in surfacevaos: vao.bind() gl.drawarrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, vao.length) vao.unbind() # Pass 2: Porous blocks gl.blendfunc(gl.ONE, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) # TODO: premult alpha? gl.enable(gl.BLEND) shader2.bind() shader2.setuniform('view', viewmatrix) shader2.setuniform('projection', projectionmatrix) if textureexists: shader2.setuniform('texture', texture.bind()) for mesh in meshes: porousvaos = mesh.vertexarrayobjects.get('porous') if porousvaos and len(porousvaos) > 0: shader2.setuniform('model', mesh.modelmatrix) for vao in porousvaos: vao.bind() gl.drawarrays(gl.TRIANGLES, 0, vao.length) vao.unbind() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Premultiplied Alpha: The implementation uses gl.ONE and gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA blending, which assumes non-premultiplied alpha. Premultiplied alpha is not handled, which may lead to incorrect blending results for translucent blocks. Shader Initialization: Rendering fails if render() is called before gl-init has bound the shaders. Camera Dependency: The pipeline requires a camera plugin that provides a valid view matrix; otherwise, it throws an error. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of meshes and triangles, as each mesh is iterated twice (once for solid, once for porous). Memory complexity depends on the storage of vertexArrayObjects for both surface and porous geometry per mesh. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of meshes and the density of solid vs. porous blocks. The separation allows for optimized shading (AO for solid, simpler texture lookup for porous). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Correctly handles alpha blending for translucent voxel blocks by rendering opaque geometry first, preventing depth buffer artifacts. Allows different shading logic for opaque vs. translucent geometry. Limitations: Does not handle premultiplied alpha, which may cause visual artifacts with certain textures. Requires two draw passes per mesh, potentially increasing overhead compared to a single-pass approach if blending is not needed. When to use it and when not: Use when rendering voxel meshes with both opaque and translucent blocks that require correct alpha blending. Do not use if all blocks are opaque, as the second pass is unnecessary overhead. The Two-Pass Voxel Shading Pipeline was developed by Mikola Lysenko (2013) and deathcap (2014) as part of the voxel-shader plugin for the Voxel.js ecosystem. It is designed to work with the voxel-stitch and game-shell-fps-camera plugins, leveraging their meshing and camera systems. The technique addresses the common issue in voxel rendering where translucent blocks (like glass or water) incorrectly interact with opaque blocks due to depth sorting and blending order. voxel/voxel-shader, https://github.com/voxel/voxel-shader, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Shader-based Rendering
head: GPU-accelerated Voxel Rendering, Shader-driven Voxelization
body: Shader-based Rendering offloads the generation and processing of voxel geometry to the GPU, utilizing vertex and fragment shaders to handle primitive assembly, visibility culling, and shading calculations. It solves the CPU bottleneck associated with generating and uploading vertex buffers for large voxel worlds by performing these operations procedurally or via texture lookups during the rendering pipeline. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Instancing with Procedural/Shader Generation by its specific reliance on GPU-side data structures (such as texture buffers) for attribute storage and its ability to reconstruct complex topology (e.g., 54,000 faces per cell) without explicit geometry shaders. The family shares the fundamental mechanism of converting scalar field data into geometric primitives that are submitted to the graphics pipeline. 1. Primitive Generation: Each occupied voxel is represented by one or more geometric primitives. The most common representation is a cube (6 faces, 8 vertices for shared shading, or 24 vertices for flat shading) or a set of quads representing visible faces. 2. Coordinate Transformation: Voxel indices (i, j, k) are transformed into world space. For a dense grid with bounds P{min} and P{max} and dimension N{dim}, the world position P{world} of a voxel center is calculated as: P{world} = P{min} + \frac{I{voxel}}{N{dim}} \times (P{max} - P{min}) For unit voxels, this simplifies to P{world} = I{voxel} \times V{size}, where V{size} is the voxel dimension. 3. Rasterization: The generated primitives are transformed into clip space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix and rasterized. Visibility is determined by the depth buffer (z-buffer) or a back-to-front painter's algorithm if transparency is required. 4. Culling: To manage performance, frustum culling is applied to exclude voxels outside the camera view. Back-face culling is often enabled to discard faces oriented away from the camera, calculated by the dot product of the view-space normal and the view vector. The ClearView Vertex Shader is a geometry reconstruction technique that generates voxel face geometry entirely within the vertex shader using glVertexID, eliminating the need for CPU-side vertex attribute buffers or geometry shaders. It reconstructs 54,000 faces per cell, each consisting of 4 vertices and 2 triangles, by fetching pre-packed face, vertex, and edge data from GPU textures. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Instancing with Procedural/Shader Generation by its explicit reliance on texture-based attribute lookups for LOD and line-drawing logic, and from Geometry Shader Processing by performing primitive assembly in the vertex stage rather than the geometry stage. Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering is a technique that renders voxels as solid cubes by performing ray-AABB intersection in screen space. It computes surface normals, samples colors, and applies fog entirely within the fragment shader. A GLSL shader program that renders voxel terrain using packed integer attributes for position, texture ID, and normal direction, with uniform matrices for transformation and lighting. Vertex Attribute 0: 'attrib1' (int), containing packed position, texture ID, and dimensions. Vertex Attribute 1: 'attrib2' (int), containing packed normal direction and side information. Uniform 'transformationMatrix': 4x4 matrix for model transformation. Uniform 'projectionMatrix': 4x4 matrix for perspective projection. Uniform 'viewMatrix': 4x4 matrix for camera view transformation. Uniform 'sunColor': 3D vector for directional light color. Uniform 'sunPosition': 3D vector for directional light position. Uniform 'uvscale': 2D vector for UV scaling. The approach leverages the parallel processing capabilities of modern GPUs to handle the high vertex counts typical of voxel-based environments. Early implementations relied on CPU-side mesh generation, which became a bottleneck as world sizes increased. The shift to shader-based methods, such as those seen in projects like knaxel/Voxel-Engine-Example, allows for dynamic LOD and procedural generation directly on the GPU, reducing memory bandwidth usage and CPU overhead. This technique is widely used in real-time voxel engines, Minecraft-like games, and scientific visualization tools where dynamic terrain modification is required. knaxel/Voxel-Engine-Example, https://github.com/knaxel/Voxel-Engine-Example, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: ClearView Vertex Shader
head: HexMeshUnified Vertex
body: The ClearView Vertex Shader is a geometry reconstruction technique that generates face primitives from sparse texture buffers using glVertexID, eliminating the need for vertex attribute buffers. It solves the problem of rendering complex volumetric or mesh data with minimal GPU memory bandwidth by fetching vertex and edge attributes on-the-fly. It differs from sibling methods like Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering by deferring attribute lookup to the vertex stage and relying on explicit face indexing rather than implicit voxel topology. Inputs and Outputs: The shader takes no vertex attributes. It reads from three texture buffers: uFaceTex (face connectivity), uVertexTex (vertex positions/attributes), and uEdgeTex (edge attributes/LOD). It outputs glPosition and varying attributes for the fragment shader. Data Structures: 1. Face Buffer (uFaceTex): RG32UI texture. Width W{face}, height H{face} = \lceil N{faces} \times 2 / W{face} \rceil. Each face is stored in two consecutive texels (linear index 2i and 2i+1). Texel 2i: Vertex indices vIdx[0..3] packed in RGBA. Texel 2i+1: Edge indices eIdx[0..3] packed in RGBA. 2. Vertex Buffer (uVertexTex): RGBA32F texture. Width W{vert}, height H{vert} = \lceil N{verts} / W{vert} \rceil. Each texel stores position (x,y,z) in RGB and scalar attribute a in A. 3. Edge Buffer (uEdgeTex): RG32F texture. Width W{edge}, height H{edge} = \lceil N{edges} / W{edge} \rceil. Each texel stores line attribute r and LOD value g in RG. Steps: 1. Calculate Face ID: Compute F = \lfloor \text{gl\VertexID} / 6 \rfloor. 2. Fetch Face Data: Fetch faceVertices from uFaceTex at linear index 2F. Extract vIdx[0..3] from RGBA. Fetch faceEdges from uFaceTex at linear index 2F+1. Extract eIdx[0..3] from RGBA. 3. Fetch Vertex/Edge Attributes: Initialize arrays vVertexPositions[4], vVertexAttributes[4], vLineAttributes[4], vEdgeLodValues[4]. For i = 0 to 3: Fetch vData from uVertexTex at index vIdx[i]. Set vVertexPositions[i] = vData.xyz, vVertexAttributes[i] = vData.a. Fetch eData from uEdgeTex at index eIdx[i]. Set vLineAttributes[i] = eData.r, vEdgeLodValues[i] = eData.g. 4. Determine Corner ID: Map glVertexID % 6 to a corner index C for the two triangles of the quad face: Vertex 0 \rightarrow Corner 0 Vertex 1 \rightarrow Corner 3 Vertex 2 \rightarrow Corner 1 Vertex 3 \rightarrow Corner 2 Vertex 4 \rightarrow Corner 1 Vertex 5 \rightarrow Corner 3 5. Transform and Output: Fetch thisVertexData from uVertexTex at index vIdx[C]. Compute world position: P{world} = M{model} \times \text{vec4}(thisVertexData.xyz, 1.0). Set vFragmentPositionWorld = Pworld.xyz. Set glPosition = M{mvp} \times \text{vec4}(thisVertexData.xyz, 1.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. faceid = glVertexID / 6 corneridmap = [0, 3, 1, 2, 1, 3] cornerid = corneridmap[glVertexID % 6] faceverticestexel = texelFetch(uFaceTex, vec2(faceid 2 % uTexWidth, faceid 2 / uTexWidth), 0) faceedgestexel = texelFetch(uFaceTex, vec2((faceid 2 + 1) % uTexWidth, (faceid 2 + 1) / uTexWidth), 0) vidx = faceverticestexel.rgba eidx = faceedgestexel.rgba vpos = vec4[4] vattr = vec4[4] lattr = vec4[4] elod = vec4[4] for i in 0..3: vdata = texelFetch(uVertexTex, vec2(vidx[i] % uTexWidth, vidx[i] / uTexWidth), 0) vpos[i] = vdata.xyz vattr[i] = vdata.a edata = texelFetch(uEdgeTex, vec2(eidx[i] % uTexWidth, eidx[i] / uTexWidth), 0) lattr[i] = edata.r elod[i] = edata.g currentvidx = vidx[cornerid] currentvdata = texelFetch(uVertexTex, vec2(currentvidx % uTexWidth, currentvidx / uTexWidth), 0) worldpos = uModelMatrix vec4(currentvdata.xyz, 1.0) vFragmentPositionWorld = worldpos.xyz glPosition = uModelViewProjection vec4(currentvdata.xyz, 1.0) Parameters and Edge Cases: uModelMatrix, uModelViewProjection: Standard transformation matrices. uTexWidth: Texture width used for linear indexing. Precision: Linear indexing assumes integer arithmetic. Ensure uTexWidth is large enough to avoid overflow for large meshes. Boundaries: glVertexID must be within 0, 6 \times N{faces}). A variant optimized for hexahedral meshes, sharing the same reconstruction principle but with specific topology assumptions. [HexMeshUnified Vertex Handles the per-fragment rendering, including line drawing, LOD-based opacity, and alpha blending. ClearView Fragment Shader Time Complexity: O(1) per vertex, but involves multiple texture fetches (4 per vertex: 2 face, 4 vertex/edge, 1 current vertex). Total fetches \approx 6 per vertex. Memory Complexity: O(N{faces} + N{verts} + N{edges}) in texture memory. No vertex buffer object (VBO) memory required for attributes. Strengths: Reduces VRAM usage by removing vertex attributes from VBOs. Flexible topology. Limitations: High texture fetch overhead. Cache misses on uVertexTex and uEdgeTex can degrade performance. Not suitable for extremely high-frequency vertex access patterns without careful texture tiling. When to use: Sparse or dynamic meshes where vertex attributes change frequently or memory is constrained. When not to use: Static meshes with simple topology where VBOs are more efficient. The ClearView Vertex Shader is part of the ClearView rendering system, developed for interactive visualization of large-scale volumetric and mesh data. It was introduced in the context of the HexVolumeRenderer project, aiming to balance visual fidelity with performance on consumer hardware. The method avoids traditional vertex buffer overhead by encoding geometry in texture buffers. Amory0709/geresim-spike, https://github.com/Amory0709/geresim-spike, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering
body:
Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering is a fragment-shader-based technique that renders voxels as solid cubes by performing ray-AABB (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box) intersection in screen space. It computes surface normals, samples colors, and applies fog effects entirely within the fragment shader, bypassing the need for explicit geometry generation for every voxel face. This method distinguishes itself from sibling approaches like ClearView Vertex Shader by deferring the geometric intersection logic to the fragment stage, allowing for per-fragment precision in ray-casting against voxel bounds. Inputs: vColor (vec3): Vertex color. vVert (vec3): Voxel center coordinates in world space. ndotl (float): Dot product of the normal and light direction. uinvprojviewrot (mat4): Inverse projection-view rotation matrix. ufar (float): Far plane distance of the camera. uViewport (vec2): Viewport dimensions (width, height). ulod (float): Level of detail or voxel size parameter. Outputs: outColor (vec4): Final fragment color. The method operates on standard GLSL types. The voxel is defined implicitly by its center vxl (derived from vVert) and size ulod. The AABB bounds are: minV = vxl - 0.5 	imes u\lod maxV = vxl + 0.5 	imes u\lod 1. Ray Direction Calculation: Compute the world-space ray direction from the fragment's screen coordinates. Normalize screen coordinates to [0,1] using uViewport. Convert to clip space [-1,1] with z=-1. Transform by uinvprojviewrot and normalize the resulting vector. 2. Ray-AABB Intersection: Perform ray-AABB intersection against the voxel defined by minV and maxV. The ray origin is (0,0,0) in the local voxel space. 3. Hit Point Calculation: Calculate the hit point hit relative to the voxel center. The hit point is in the range [-0.5 	imes u\lod, 0.5 	imes u\lod]. 4. Normal Determination: Determine the surface normal by finding the maximum absolute component of hit. The normal is a unit vector along the axis corresponding to the maximum absolute dimension, signed by the sign of the hit coordinate. 5. Texture Coordinate Calculation: Calculate texture coordinates uv based on the normal. Offset uv by 0.5. 6. Depth Setting: Set the fragment depth to result.x / ufar. 7. Fog Application: Apply fog by calculating a fog factor based on depth and mixing the calculated color with a fog color (0.5, 0.5, 0.7). Ray Direction: ray = 	ext{normalize}\left(  rac{(u\inv\proj\viewot 	imes vec4(x 	imes 2 - 1, y 	imes 2 - 1, -1, 1)).xyz}{(u\inv\proj\viewot 	imes vec4(x 	imes 2 - 1, y 	imes 2 - 1, -1, 1)).w} ight) where x and y are normalized screen coordinates. AABB Intersection: invR = 1.0 / ray tbot = (minV - ro) 	imes invR ttop = (maxV - ro) 	imes invR tmin = \min(ttop, tbot) tmax = \max(ttop, tbot) t0 = \max(\max(tmin.x, tmin.y), tmin.z) t1 = \min(\min(tmax.x, tmax.y), tmax.z) Hit if t0 \le t1. Hit Point: hit = vxl - ray 	imes result.x where result.x is the intersection distance t0. UV Coordinates: If normal.y 
eq 0: uv.y = hit.x, uv.x = hit.z 	imes normal.y If normal.x 
eq 0: uv.y = hit.y, uv.x = hit.z 	imes normal.x If normal.z 
eq 0: uv.y = hit.y, uv.x = hit.x 	imes -normal.z Finally, uv = uv + 0.5. Fog: fog\start = 256.0 / u ar fog = 	ext{pow}(\max(gl\FragDepth - fog\start, 0.0001), 0.5) out\Color = 	ext{mix}(calculated\color, vec4(0.5, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0), fog). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragmentshader(vcolor, vvert, ndotl, uinvprojviewrot, ufar, uviewport, ulod): """ Renders a voxel as a solid cube using ray-AABB intersection in screen space. Args: vcolor (vec3): Vertex color. vvert (vec3): Voxel center in world space. ndotl (float): Dot product of normal and light. uinvprojviewrot (mat4): Inverse projection-view rotation matrix. ufar (float): Far plane distance. uviewport (vec2): Viewport dimensions (width, height). ulod (float): Voxel size parameter. Returns: vec4: Final fragment color. """ # 1. Compute screen coordinates normalized to [0, 1] # Assuming glFragCoord is available in the shader environment x = glFragCoord.x / uviewport.x y = glFragCoord.y / uviewport.y # 2. Convert to clip space [-1, 1] with z = -1 clippos = vec4(x 2 - 1, y 2 - 1, -1, 1) # 3. Transform by inverse projection-view rotation # Note: The source uses uinvprojviewrot directly. # In a standard pipeline, this might be invProj invView, but we follow the source. transformed = uinvprojviewrot clippos # 4. Calculate ray direction ray = normalize(transformed.xyz / transformed.w) # 5. Define voxel AABB bounds vxl = vvert minv = vxl - 0.5 ulod maxv = vxl + 0.5 ulod # 6. Ray-AABB Intersection # Ray origin is (0,0,0) in local voxel space ro = vec3(0, 0, 0) invr = 1.0 / ray tbot = (minv - ro) invr ttop = (maxv - ro) invr tmin = min(ttop, tbot) tmax = max(ttop, tbot) t0 = max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y), tmin.z) t1 = min(min(tmax.x, tmax.y), tmax.z) # Check for hit if t0 > t1: # No hit, discard or return background color return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) resultx = t0 # 7. Calculate hit point relative to voxel center hit = vxl - ray resultx # 8. Determine surface normal # Find the maximum absolute component abshit = abs(hit) if abshit.x >= abshit.y and abshit.x >= abshit.z: normal = vec3(sign(hit.x), 0.0, 0.0) elif abshit.y >= abshit.x and abshit.y >= abshit.z: normal = vec3(0.0, sign(hit.y), 0.0) else: normal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, sign(hit.z)) # 9. Calculate texture coordinates (uv) uv = vec2(0.0, 0.0) if normal.y != 0.0: uv.y = hit.x uv.x = hit.z normal.y elif normal.x != 0.0: uv.y = hit.y uv.x = hit.z normal.x else: # normal.z != 0.0 uv.y = hit.y uv.x = hit.x -normal.z uv = uv + 0.5 # 10. Set fragment depth glFragDepth = resultx / ufar # 11. Calculate color (simplified, as texture sampling is commented out in source) # Using vertex color and ndotl as a placeholder for actual color calculation # In a real implementation, sample texture using uv color = vcolor (0.5 + 0.5 ndotl) # Simple diffuse lighting approximation # 12. Apply fog fogstart = 256.0 / ufar fogfactor = pow(max(glFragDepth - fogstart, 0.0001), 0.5) fogcolor = vec4(0.5, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0) outcolor = mix(color, fogcolor, fogfactor) return outcolor uinvprojviewrot: Inverse projection-view rotation matrix. ufar: Far plane distance of the camera. uViewport: Viewport dimensions (width, height). uTex: Texture sampler (declared but commented out in color calculation). ulod: Level of detail or size parameter used to define the voxel bounds relative to its center vxl. Precision: The ray direction calculation involves division by the w-component of the transformed clip coordinate. If this value is near zero, it may cause instability. Boundaries: The AABB intersection assumes the ray origin is at (0,0,0) in the local voxel space. If the voxel is not centered at the origin in its local coordinate system, the intersection logic will fail. Degenerate Input: If ulod is zero or negative, the voxel bounds will be invalid. Fog Calculation: The fog factor uses glFragDepth, which must be set before the fog calculation to ensure correct depth-based fogging. Time Complexity: The fragment shader performs a constant number of operations per fragment, including ray-AABB intersection and normal calculation. The complexity is O(1) per fragment. Memory Complexity: The method requires minimal memory, primarily storing the voxel center and size parameters. No additional geometry buffers are needed. Performance: Performance depends on the number of fragments processed. Since each voxel is rendered as a cube, the number of fragments is proportional to the surface area of the voxel grid visible to the camera. Strengths: No need to generate explicit geometry for each voxel face. Per-fragment precision in ray-casting allows for accurate surface detection. Simple implementation within the fragment shader. Limitations: May be slower than vertex-based methods for large voxel grids due to the high number of fragment shader invocations. Limited to solid voxels; transparency requires additional handling (e.g., back-to-front rendering). When to Use: Suitable for real-time rendering of voxel-based scenes where geometry generation overhead is a concern, and per-fragment precision is beneficial. When Not to Use: Not ideal for scenes with high transparency requirements or when vertex-based culling is more efficient. Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering is an unofficial technique described in the voxplat repository by kosshi-net. It leverages modern GPU capabilities to perform ray-casting in the fragment shader, providing a flexible approach to voxel rendering. The method is part of a broader family of shader-based rendering techniques for voxels. kosshi-net/voxplat, https://github.com/kosshi-net/voxplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Domain-transform methods
head: Fourier-space techniques, frequency-domain methods
body: Domain-transform methods solve the problem of high computational complexity in spatial-domain volume rendering by transforming volumetric data into an alternative domain (typically frequency, compression, or wavelet) where projections can be generated more efficiently. Unlike object-order methods that rasterize primitives, these techniques compute a global transformation of the entire volume, extract a slice or representation in the transformed domain, and inverse-transform to obtain the final image. This approach reduces per-view rendering complexity to O(N^2) (disregarding the one-time preprocessing cost), making it suitable for interactive X-ray simulation and medical imaging where occlusion effects are not required. The primary drawback is the inability to interactively modify display parameters such as opacity or lighting after the initial transformation. All domain-transform methods follow a three-stage pipeline: Global Transformation, Slice Extraction (or Domain Evaluation), and Inverse Transformation. 1. Global Transformation: The input 3D scalar volume f(x, y, z) is transformed into a global representation in an alternative domain. For frequency-domain methods, this is a 3D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) or Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT). For compression-based methods, it involves transforming coefficients into a compressed block format. This step is performed once per volume and has a computational complexity of O(N^3 \log N) using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithms. 2. Slice Extraction: A 2D slice or projection is extracted from the global representation corresponding to the desired viewing direction. In frequency-domain methods, this relies on the Projection-Slice Theorem, which states that the 2D Fourier transform of a projection is equal to a central slice of the 3D Fourier transform perpendicular to the viewing direction. Since the slicing plane rarely aligns with the discrete lattice of the transformed data, interpolation (e.g., trilinear, tri-cubic, or windowed sinc) is required to resample the data onto a 2D grid. 3. Inverse Transformation: The extracted 2D slice is inverse-transformed back to the spatial domain to produce the final 2D projection image. For frequency methods, this is a 2D Inverse FFT (IFFT). Common Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: Transforms assume periodic boundary conditions. Discontinuities at volume boundaries cause high-frequency artifacts (ghosting). Mitigation includes zero-padding the volume by a factor of k2 (typically 4/3) and applying vignetting correction (premultiplying by the reciprocal of the interpolation filter response). Aliasing: Insufficient output resolution violates the Nyquist criterion, causing aliasing. Fixed Parameters: Once transformed, parameters like opacity and lighting cannot be changed interactively. Generates attenuation-only, X-ray-like projections by exploiting the Fourier projection-slice theorem. It reduces per-view complexity to O(N^2 \log N) by transforming the volume into the frequency domain once. Choose it for interactive X-ray simulation and medical imaging where occlusion is not required. Hardware-accelerated method for computing the DFT on GPUs, adapted for the domain-transform pipeline. It sets itself apart by utilizing texture memory and fragment shaders for parallel butterfly operations. Choose it when rendering performance is bottlenecked by 2D slice transformations. Replaces the standard DFT with the Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) to map real-valued spatial data directly to real-valued spectra. It sets itself apart by eliminating complex number arithmetic, reducing memory requirements by half compared to a full complex spectrum. Choose it when memory bandwidth is a constraint. Transforms scalar data to the frequency domain, extracts a 2D projection slice, and inverse-transforms to the spatial domain. It sets itself apart by decoupling rendering performance from dataset resolution via the Projection-Slice Theorem. Choose it for large volumes where rendering speed depends primarily on output image resolution. Creates infinite, periodic repetitions of an object in space by wrapping query coordinates using modulo arithmetic. It sets itself apart by tiling geometry without increasing polygon count. Choose it for rendering infinite grids of primitives. Converts a 3D scalar volume into the frequency domain to enable rendering via the Projection-Slice Theorem. It sets itself apart by performing a global transformation that allows efficient convolution but requires significant preprocessing memory. Choose it when global frequency-domain operations are needed. Renders 3D fluorescence microscopy images by convolving a parameterized fluorophore density with a translation-invariant Point Spread Function (PSF) in the Fourier domain. It sets itself apart by modeling physical blurring and enabling gradient-based inference of shape and optical properties. Choose it for differentiable 3D image synthesis and microscopy optimization. Represents a 3D scalar volume using cosine waves as basis functions, mapping real input values to real output values. It sets itself apart by operating on compressed spatial blocks rather than a global frequency domain, allowing out-of-core rendering. Choose it for massive time-series data that exceeds main memory capacity. A real-valued integral transform that maps a real input function to a real spectrum, serving as an alternative to the complex DFT. It sets itself apart by using the \cos + \sin kernel instead of the complex exponential, avoiding complex arithmetic. Choose it for real-valued signal processing in domain-transform pipelines. Represents 4D spacetime volumetric data as a superposition of Fourier basis functions, utilizing CP tensor decomposition to reduce memory and computation. It sets itself apart by operating orthogonally to spatial decomposition and focusing on explicit spectral representation. Choose it for compact storage and reconstruction of dynamic volumetric data. Domain-transform methods, also known as Fourier-space techniques, were introduced to include algorithms working in the frequency domain. The basic idea is to compute the 3D Fourier transformation of the entire volume in a pre-processing step, extract a slice image in the frequency domain, and transform it back into the spatial domain using the 2D inverse Fourier transformation. The main advantage is the computational complexity of O(N^2) for the projection, disregarding the one-time 3D Fourier transformation pre-processing step. The major drawback is that they do not allow an interactive modification of any display parameter other than the viewing direction. These methods fall under the broader category of domain methods, where spatial data is transformed into an alternative domain (such as compression, wavelet, or frequency domain) from which a projection is directly generated. name: Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering
head: FT-based DVR, Fourier Domain Volume Rendering, Fourier projection rendering
body: Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering (FDVR) is an indirect volume rendering technique that generates attenuation-only, X-ray-like projections of a 3D scalar volume by exploiting the Fourier projection-slice theorem. It solves the problem of high computational complexity in spatial domain ray-casting by transforming the volume into the frequency domain once, then generating views via 2D resampling and inverse transforms, reducing per-view complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^2 \log N). Unlike Ray Casting or Digital Compositing, FDVR produces line-integral projections without hidden surface effects or direct transparency control, making it suitable for interactive X-ray simulation and medical imaging where occlusion is not required. The method follows the three-stage pipeline of domain-transform methods: Global Transformation, Slice Extraction, and Inverse Transformation. Input: A 3D scalar volume f(x, y, z) of size N \times N \times N (typically N is a power of two for FFT efficiency). Output: A 2D projection image I(u, v) of resolution M \times M (typically M=N) representing the density integral along viewing rays. Parameters: V: Normalized viewing direction vector (points away from the eye). W: Nonzero width of the interpolating filter used during slice extraction (typical value: 4). k2: Zero-padding factor (typical value: 4/3, i.e., 16% margin). 1. Input Volume: Scalar array, typically 8 bits per voxel. 2. 3D Spectrum: Array of N^3 complex coefficients (or real if using Hartley Transform). Requires 32-bit floating point precision (16 bytes per voxel if complex double precision is used). 3. 2D Slice: Array of M^2 complex coefficients extracted from the 3D spectrum. 1. Preprocessing (Global Transformation): Zero-Padding: To mitigate ghosting artifacts caused by periodic boundary conditions of the DFT, zero-pad the input volume f(x) by a factor of k2. This creates a margin of zeros around the data. Vignetting Correction: Premultiply the padded volume data f(x) by the reciprocal of the interpolation filter response Pm(x) = 1/H(x) before the forward transform. This ensures that the filter response H(s) and Pm(s) cancel during interpolation, preventing attenuation of the image periphery. 3D FFT: Compute the 3D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the corrected volume to obtain the frequency domain representation F(s). If memory efficiency is prioritized, a Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) may be used, though it requires a correction pass as it is not separable. Origin Shift: Rearrange the spectrum so that the origin (zero frequency) is at the center of the 3D array. 2. Per-View Rendering (Slice Extraction): Define Slice Plane: Define a 2D plane passing through the origin of the frequency domain and perpendicular to the viewing direction V. Interpolation: Since the arbitrary plane does not align with the integer lattice of the 3D spectrum, interpolate the values of F(s) along the plane using a filter H(s) (e.g., tricubic spline). This step has complexity O(W^3 N^2). Resampling: Resample the interpolated values onto a regular 2D grid to form the 2D spectrum I(u, v). 3. Inverse Transformation: 2D IFFT: Perform a 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) on the 2D slice I(u, v) to obtain the spatial domain projection image. Scaling: Rescale the resulting intensity values to the valid display range. The 3D Fourier transform of the spatial density function f(x, y, z) is: F(\omega1, \omega2, \omega3) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y, z) e^{-i2\pi(x\omega1 + y\omega2 + z\omega3)} dx dy dz \quad The Fourier projection-slice theorem states that the 2D Fourier transform of the projection is equal to a central slice of the 3D Fourier transform: I(u, v) = F(\omega1(u, v), \omega2(u, v), \omega3(u, v)) \quad The rendering operator \PiV is defined as: \PiV(f) = F2^{-1} \{ F3 \{ f \} \deltaV^{-1} \} \quad where \deltaV^{-1} restricts the spectrum to a plane passing through the origin and perpendicular to viewing direction V, and FN, FN^{-1} are forward and inverse N-dimensional Fourier transforms. Self-contained Python-like pseudocode. No external libraries used. Mitigation includes zero-padding (increasing memory by k2^3) or using wider interpolation filters (increasing per-view time by k1^3). Vignetting: Unless an ideal lowpass filter is used, the filter response attenuates the periphery of the volume. Mitigation involves premultiplying the volume by the reciprocal of the filter response before the forward transform. Aliasing: The output image resolution must meet the Nyquist criterion. If the projection slice resolution is too low, overlapping copies of rendered data occur. Memory Cost: The frequency domain representation requires 16 bytes per voxel (complex double precision), significantly higher than the 1 byte per voxel in the spatial domain. Lack of Occlusion: The method produces line integrals where voxels on a viewing ray contribute equally regardless of distance, resulting in no occlusion or hidden surface removal. This article details the specific algorithmic steps, data structures, and parameter choices required to implement Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) as described in the foundational literature. It solves the practical engineering problems of spectral leakage (ghosting), numerical stability in frequency-domain operations, and performance optimization for the 3D FFT and slice extraction pipeline. It sets itself apart from generic descriptions by providing exact margin sizes, interpolation kernels, and stability thresholds for degenerate cases, building on Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering. This method approximates the perceptual depth cues of exponential attenuation in volume rendering by replacing the variable absorption coefficient with a linear function of position, enabling the integrand to be evaluated as a Fourier projection. It sets itself apart from standard exponential attenuation models by allowing efficient computation via the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) is a direct volume rendering technique that computes X-ray-like attenuation-only projections of a three-dimensional dataset by exploiting the Fourier projection-slice theorem. It reduces the per-view computational complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^2 \log N) by computing a 3D frequency transform once during preprocessing, then generating views via 2D resampling and inverse transforms. Unlike Ray Casting or Digital Compositing, FVR produces line-integral projections without hidden surface effects or direct transparency control. A technique to compute integrals over irregular spatial domains by decomposing the domain into spatially disjoint intervals and summing their Fourier projection-slice integrals. It decomposes the ray segment connecting two interior points into spatially disjoint intervals, computes each interval integral using the projection-slice theorem, and applies recursive subdivision of volumes into octants. Time complexity is O(N^2 \log^2 N) for the octant subdivision algorithm. Applications include rendering spatially clipped volumes for medical visualization, fast calculation of inter-element attenuation for zonal radiosity algorithms, and approximate visibility determination for geometrically defined scenes. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(N^3 \log N) for the 3D FFT. Per-view rendering is O(M^2 \log M) for the 2D IFFT plus O(W^3 N^2) for slice extraction, where W is the filter width. For N=256, preprocessing is ~16M operations, while per-view is significantly faster than spatial domain O(N^3). Memory Complexity: Requires O(N^3) memory for the 3D spectrum. Complex arithmetic doubles the storage requirement compared to real-valued spatial data (16 bytes/voxel for double precision complex vs 1 byte/voxel for 8-bit spatial). Performance: Achieves interactive framerates on GPU hardware for typical volume sizes. The interpolation step is often the bottleneck due to high constant factors. Strengths: Fast generation of attenuation-only projections; suitable for X-ray simulation and MR angiography; allows filtering (lowpass, highpass) with little overhead. Limitations: No occlusion or hidden surface removal; limited to parallel projection; cannot model complex optical phenomena like emission or scattering directly; high memory usage; sensitive to interpolation artifacts (ghosting). When to Use: When speed is prioritized over occlusion, such as in medical X-ray simulation or quick previews. When Not to Use: When occlusion, hidden surface removal, or complex optical phenomena (emission, scattering) are required. FDVR was first applied by Dunne, Malzbender, and Napel et al. in the early 1990s for attenuation-only rendering and MR angiography. Levoy and Totsuka independently generalized the method to include shading and depth cueing in the frequency domain. The method was later implemented on graphics hardware (GPU) by Jansen et al. and Viola et al. to achieve interactive framerates. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) was originally introduced by Cooley, and the Fast Hartley Transform (FHT) was proposed by Bracewell and Hao as an alternative.
