head: Fourier Volume Rendering Implementation, Fourier Volume Rendering with Zero Padding and Tricubic Interpolation, Implementation Details for Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering
body: This article details the specific algorithmic steps, data structures, and parameter choices required to implement Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) as described in the foundational literature. It solves the practical engineering problems of spectral leakage (ghosting), numerical stability in frequency-domain operations, and performance optimization for the 3D FFT and slice extraction pipeline. It sets itself apart from generic descriptions by providing exact margin sizes, interpolation kernels, and stability thresholds for degenerate cases, building on Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering. Inputs: 1. Input Volume (V): A 3D scalar field of density/attenuation values. 2. Viewing Direction (\mathbf{v}): A 3D unit vector defining the camera orientation. 3. Lighting Direction (\mathbf{l}): A 3D unit vector defining the light source orientation (optional, for shading models). 4. Image Resolution (R): The desired output image dimensions, typically 128 \times 128. Outputs: 1. Rendered Image (I): A 2D array of pixel values (attenuation or shaded intensity) of size R \times R. 1. Zero-Padded Volume (V{pad}): Layout: 3D array of size (Nx + 2M, Ny + 2M, Nz + 2M), where N are original dimensions and M is the zero-padding margin. Content: Original volume data centered in the array; the outer M voxels on all sides are set to 0. 2. Frequency Spectrum (\hat{V}): Layout: 3D complex-valued array of the same size as V{pad}. Content: Result of the 3D FFT of V{pad}. 3. Extracted Slice (\hat{S}): Layout: 2D complex-valued array of size R \times R. Content: A planar slice extracted from \hat{V} along the viewing direction, interpolated using tricubic splines. 1. Edge Enhancement and Windowing: Apply edge sharpening operators to the input volume V. Apply nonlinear windowing to adjust the density range (optional, depending on the specific shading model or visual requirement). Note: These operations are performed in the spatial domain before the forward transform. 2. Zero Padding: Surround the processed volume with a margin of zeros. Margin Size: 16% of the volume width (or side length). Purpose: To avoid the "ghosting problem" caused by spectral leakage due to the discontinuity at the volume boundaries. 3. 3D FFT: Compute the 3D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of the zero-padded volume V{pad} to obtain the frequency spectrum \hat{V}. Optimization: The fftshift operation may be required to center the zero-frequency component at the origin of the frequency space, depending on the FFT library implementation. 1. Slice Extraction: For the current viewing direction \mathbf{v}, define a 2D plane in the frequency domain passing through the origin. Extract a slice of width equal to the spectrum's extent (or appropriate resolution R) from \hat{V} using tricubic interpolating spline interpolation. Note: Tricubic interpolation is used to approximate the continuous Fourier slice from the discrete voxel grid. 2. 2D Inverse FFT: Apply the 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) to the extracted slice \hat{S} to obtain the projection in the spatial domain. 3. Weighting: Apply weighting factors based on the viewing direction \mathbf{v} and lighting direction \mathbf{l} (if applicable) to the projected data. For attenuation-only rendering, this may be a simple scaling. For shading models, this involves computing diffuse/specular terms in the frequency domain or applying them post-projection. 4. Summation: Sum the weighted projections to produce the final R \times R image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def preprocessvolume(V, marginpercent=0.16): """ Preprocesses the input volume with edge enhancement, windowing, and zero padding. Assumes V has already undergone edge enhancement and nonlinear windowing. """ N = V.shape padsize = [int(n marginpercent) for n in N] # Create zero-padded volume paddedV = np.zeros((N[0] + 2padsize[0], N[1] + 2padsize[1], N[2] + 2padsize[2]), dtype=V.dtype) # Center the original volume start = padsize end = [start[i] + N[i] for i in range(3)] paddedV[start[0]:end[0], start[1]:end[1], start[2]:end[2]] = V # Compute 3D FFT and shift zero-frequency to center spectrum = np.fft.fftn(paddedV) spectrum = np.fft.fftshift(spectrum) return spectrum, padsize def tricubicsample(spectrum, gridcoords, padsize, originalshape): """ Samples the 3D spectrum at arbitrary coordinates using a 4x4x4 tricubic kernel. gridcoords: Nx3 array of (x,y,z) coordinates in the spectrum grid. """ # Determine grid spacing and bounds Ny, Nx, Nz = spectrum.shape x, y, z = gridcoords[:, 0], gridcoords[:, 1], gridcoords[:, 2] # Clamp coordinates to valid range x = np.clip(x, 0, Nx - 1) y = np.clip(y, 0, Ny - 1) z = np.clip(z, 0, Nz - 1) # Extract 4x4x4 neighborhood for each point and evaluate tricubic kernel # (Implementation details omitted for brevity; standard tricubic kernel evaluation) # Returns complex values interpolated from spectrum return np.zeros(len(gridcoords), dtype=np.complex128) def extractslicetricubic(spectrum, viewdirection, imageresolution, padsize, originalshape): """ Extracts a 2D slice from the 3D frequency spectrum using tricubic interpolation. """ # Define 2D grid on the plane orthogonal to viewdirection # Map 2D pixel coordinates to 3D frequency coordinates # (Geometric projection logic omitted; standard plane-to-grid mapping) gridcoords = np.zeros((imageresolution imageresolution, 3)) # Sample spectrum slicevalues = tricubicsample(spectrum, gridcoords, padsize, originalshape) return slicevalues.reshape(imageresolution, imageresolution) def renderfvr(spectrum, viewdirection, lightingdirection=None, imageresolution=128): """ Renders a single view using the precomputed spectrum. """ # Extract slice slice2d = extractslicetricubic(spectrum, viewdirection, imageresolution, padsize, originalshape) # Inverse FFT to get spatial projection projection = np.fft.ifftn(slice2d) projection = np.fft.ifftshift(projection) # Apply weighting based on view/lighting directions # For attenuation-only, this is identity or simple scaling if lightingdirection is not None: # Apply shading weights (model-specific) projection = applyshadingweights(projection, viewdirection, lightingdirection) # Return final image return np.abs(projection) def applyshadingweights(projection, viewdirection, lightingdirection): """ Applies shading weights to the projection. # The exact weighting function depends on the chosen shading model. # For directional shading, this typically combines view and light vectors. """ return projection Zero Padding Margin: 16% of the volume width. Interpolation Kernel: Tricubic interpolating spline. Image Resolution: Typically 128 \times 128 in the original implementation. 1. Ghosting Artifacts: Caused by spectral leakage due to discontinuities at the volume boundaries. Mitigated by adding a 16% margin of zeros around the input data. 2. Numerical Stability in Triangle FT: When computing the Fourier Transform of triangle meshes, denominators in the FT formula can approach zero, leading to divergence. This occurs when floating-point precision limits make it impossible to distinguish small differences in edge projections. A threshold \epsilon is used to detect these cases, and exact limit expressions are substituted. Formula for t=u (or permutations): g(t, t, u) = i \frac{e^{-it}}{t-u} + \frac{e^{-it}}{(t-u)^2} - \frac{e^{-iu}}{(t-u)^2} Formula for t=u=v: g(u, u, u) = \frac{e^{-iu}}{2} 3. Preprocessing Recalculation: Edge sharpening and nonlinear windowing are applied before the 3D FFT. Changing these operators requires recomputing the entire 3D Fourier spectrum, which hinders interactive data segmentation if hardwired into the preprocessing pipeline. 4. Memory Usage: Memory requirements vary based on the shading model complexity, ranging from 48 MB to 256 MB for a 128^3 volume in the original implementation. Adaptive Frequency Domain Filtering is an optimization technique for frequency domain volume rendering that reduces interpolation cost by selectively applying larger or smaller interpolation filters based on local spectral properties marked during preprocessing. It solves the performance bottleneck of slice extraction in Fourier-based rendering by identifying regions of the 3D spectrum where the signal magnitude is sufficiently low to permit coarser approximation without visible quality loss. It sets itself apart from standard frequency domain methods by introducing a preprocessing step that marks voxels, allowing the extraction phase to skip expensive multi-voxel support checks. See Adaptive Frequency Domain Filtering. FDK Pre-Filtering applies the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) pre-processing step to raw projection data, preparing it for backprojection in explicit cone-beam geometry. It solves the problem of correcting for the divergent ray paths and high-frequency attenuation inherent in cone-beam acquisitions by combining geometric cone weighting with a 1D ramp filter. Unlike parallel-beam Filtered Back Projection (FBP), this method accounts for the distance from the source to the detector and the angle of incidence, ensuring accurate reconstruction for divergent beams. It sets itself apart from Adaptive Frequency Domain Filtering by using a fixed ramp kernel rather than adaptive frequency masks, and from Hybrid CPU-GPU FVR Pipeline by being the explicit CPU-side implementation of this specific pre-filtering stage. See FDK Pre-Filtering (Ramp Filter + Cone Weighting). Gamma-Corrected Hemispherical Shading (GCHS) is a method for computing diffuse illumination in Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) that approximates the non-linear max(0, N·L) operator with a cubic polynomial of the gradient and light direction, enabling efficient evaluation in the frequency domain. It improves upon standard hemispherical shading by raising the term to the power of three, which effectively culls back-lit surfaces and preserves visual contrast without requiring non-linear operations that break Fourier linearity. See Gamma-Corrected Hemispherical Shading. The Hybrid CPU-GPU FVR Pipeline is a heterogeneous implementation strategy for Fourier Volume Rendering that partitions the computational workload between the CPU and the GPU. The CPU handles the heavy numerical computations, specifically the 3D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and resampling, while the GPU handles the rendering context, including texture management, projection-slice extraction via OpenGL, and final display. This approach leverages the hardware-accelerated interpolation and texture handling of OpenGL to simplify the representation of the 3D spectral volume, offering a middle ground between fully CPU-based pipelines and fully GPU-based implementations. See Hybrid CPU-GPU FVR Pipeline. Pre-FFT Edge Sharpening and Nonlinear Windowing involves applying edge sharpening and nonlinear density range windowing operators directly to the input volume data before computing the forward 3D Fourier transform. Modifying these operators requires recomputing the entire 3D Fourier spectra, which hinders interactive data segmentation if hardwired into the preprocessing pipeline. Numerical Stability for Triangle FT handles numerical divergence when denominators in the triangle FT formula approach zero due to floating-point precision limits. It uses exact limit expressions for degenerate cases. The steps are: 1. Calculate denominators s, t, u (projections of edges onto frequency vector \boldsymbol{\xi}). 2. Check if any pair (a,b) among (s,t,u) satisfies |a-b| < \epsilon (where \epsilon is floating-point threshold). 3. If |a-b| < \epsilon, use the special case formula instead of the general formula. The special case formula for t=u is g(t,t,u) = i \frac{e^{-it}}{t-u} + \frac{e^{-it}}{(t-u)^2} - \frac{e^{-iu}}{(t-u)^2}. GPU-Accelerated FVR Implementation is a high-performance implementation of the FVR pipeline mapped to run entirely on CUDA-enabled GPUs, achieving a speed-up of 117x compared to a single-threaded hybrid CPU/GPU implementation. The implementation addresses resampling issues and ghosting artifacts by using FFT-shift stages, zero-padding, and high-order interpolation filters. Preprocessing: O(N^3 \log N) for the 3D FFT, where N is the volume dimension. Per-View Rendering: O(R^2 \log R) for the 2D IFFT of the extracted slice, where R is the image resolution. The slice extraction itself is O(R^2) with tricubic interpolation. Memory: Varies based on the shading model. In the original implementation, memory requirements ranged from 48 MB to 256 MB for a 128^3 volume. Hardware: Tested on a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX using a sequential C implementation. Per-View Time: Varied from 6 seconds (for simpler shading models) to over a minute (for more complex models, due mostly to paging). GPU Acceleration: A CUDA-based implementation achieved a 117x speed-up compared to a single-threaded hybrid CPU/GPU implementation. The algorithm is asymptotically less expensive than conventional volume rendering for very large volumes, but the high constant factor makes it slower for smaller volumes. Parallelization can be achieved at a fine grain (within the FFT) or a coarse grain (between slices) for greater speedups. Strengths: Efficient computation of projections using the Fourier projection-slice theorem; ability to incorporate shading models in the frequency domain; potential for hardware acceleration. Limitations: High memory requirements for large volumes; sensitivity to preprocessing changes (requiring full spectrum recomputation); potential for ghosting artifacts if zero-padding is insufficient. Use when rendering large volumes where the cost of traditional ray-casting is prohibitive. Use when attenuation-only or simple shading models are sufficient. Use when hardware acceleration (GPU) is available. Avoid when interactive data segmentation with frequent changes to edge enhancement/windowing is required, as this necessitates full spectrum recomputation. Avoid when rendering very small volumes, as the algorithm's high constant factor makes it slower than conventional methods. Fourier Volume Rendering was introduced by Marc Levoy in 1990. The method exploits the Fourier projection-slice theorem to compute volume projections efficiently. The initial implementation was tested on a Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX. Subsequent developments included GPU-accelerated implementations using CUDA, achieving significant speed-ups. Variants such as adaptive frequency domain filtering and hybrid CPU-GPU pipelines have been developed to address performance and quality issues. FVR has been used in various scientific and engineering arenas such as medical imaging, geoscience, microscopy, and mechanical engineering. It is particularly useful for visualizing complex structures and phenomena where efficient rendering of large volumes is required. It solves the performance bottleneck of slice extraction in Fourier-based rendering by identifying regions of the 3D spectrum where the signal magnitude is sufficiently low to permit coarser approximation without visible quality loss. It sets itself apart from standard frequency domain methods by introducing a preprocessing step that marks voxels, allowing the extraction phase to skip expensive multi-voxel support checks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume data V. Output: 2D projection image. Intermediate: 3D spectrum S (computed via Hartley or Fourier transform). Data Structures: Spectrum (S): A 3D grid of complex (or real-valued Hartley) values. The sources note that due to the wide dynamic range, a floating-point format (e.g., 64-bit double) is necessary. Mark Array (M): A boolean grid of the same dimensions as S. M[i,j,k] = \text{true} indicates the voxel is "marked" and eligible for the smaller filter. Parameters: Larger Filter Size: 3 \times 3 \times 3. Smaller Filter Size: 1 \times 1 \times 1 (point sampling). Threshold (\epsilon): The maximum difference in response allowed. The sources specify a value of 0.3. This threshold determines the boundary for switching filters. Marking Condition: A voxel is marked if its magnitude satisfies a specific equation (referred to as Equation 16 in or 1G in). The exact formula for Equation 16/1G is not provided in the source text, but it is defined as "magnitude is small enough". Steps: 1. Transform: Compute the 3D spectrum S of the volume data V using the Hartley transform or Fourier transform. 2. Preprocess (Marking): Iterate through every voxel in S. Check if the voxel's magnitude satisfies the threshold condition (Equation 16/1G). Optimized Marking: To avoid testing all neighbors during extraction, mark a voxel v only if: 1. v satisfies the threshold condition. 2. All neighboring voxels within a distance equal to one-half of the support of the larger filter (3 \times 3 \times 3) also satisfy the threshold condition. Store the result in M. This process is done only once after transformation. 3. Slice Extraction: For each sample point on the slice plane: Identify the spectrum voxel v closest to the sample position. Check if M[v] is true. If true, use the smaller filter (1 \times 1 \times 1). If false, use the larger filter (3 \times 3 \times 3). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivefrequencydomainfiltering(volumedata, sliceplanesamples): # Step 1: Transform to frequency domain # Standard discrete Hartley or Fourier transform spectrum = hartleytransform(volumedata) dimx, dimy, dimz = len(spectrum), len(spectrum[0]), len(spectrum[0][0]) # Step 2: Preprocess - Mark voxels # Initialize 3D boolean grid marked = [[[False for in range(dimz)] for in range(dimx)] for in range(dimy)] # Larger filter is 3x3x3, so half-support distance covers immediate neighbors (radius 1) supportradius = 1 for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): # Check if current voxel satisfies threshold condition if issmallenough(spectrum[x][y][z], threshold=0.3): # Check all neighbors within supportradius allneighborsok = True for dx in range(-supportradius, supportradius + 1): for dy in range(-supportradius, supportradius + 1): for dz in range(-supportradius, supportradius + 1): if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz # Boundary Conditions: The marking step requires checking neighbors if 0 <= nx < dimx and 0 <= ny < dimy and 0 <= nz < dimz: if not issmallenough(spectrum[nx][ny][nz], threshold=0.3): allneighborsok = False break if not allneighborsok: break if not allneighborsok: break if allneighborsok: marked[x][y][z] = True # Step 3: Slice Extraction projection = [] for samplepoint in sliceplanesamples: # Standard coordinate rounding to find closest grid voxel x, y, z = round(samplepoint.x), round(samplepoint.y), round(samplepoint.z) if marked[x][y][z]: # Use smaller filter (1x1x1) value = spectrum[x][y][z] else: # Use larger filter (3x3x3) # Standard box/convolution filter over 3x3x3 neighborhood value = interpolatelargefilter(spectrum, x, y, z) projection.append(value) # Standard inverse transform image = inversehartleytransform(projection) return image def issmallenough(value, threshold): # Checks if magnitude satisfies the threshold condition (Equation 16/1G) return abs(value) <= threshold def interpolatelargefilter(spectrum, x, y, z): # Standard 3x3x3 box filter averaging over neighborhood total = 0.0 count = 0 dimx, dimy, dimz = len(spectrum), len(spectrum[0]), len(spectrum[0][0]) for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dz in range(-1, 2): nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz if 0 <= nx < dimx and 0 <= ny < dimy and 0 <= nz < dimz: total += spectrum[nx][ny][nz] count += 1 return total / count if count > 0 else 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The spectrum requires floating-point representation due to wide dynamic range. Using integer formats will cause significant error. Boundary Conditions: The marking step requires checking neighbors. Boundary voxels must be handled carefully to avoid out-of-bounds access. Threshold Selection: The threshold of 0.3 is specific to the implementation described. Changing it affects the trade-off between speed and accuracy. Time Complexity: The preprocessing step is O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the spectrum, with a constant factor depending on the filter support size (3 \times 3 \times 3). The extraction step is O(M) where M is the number of slice samples, with O(1) cost for marked voxels and O(K) for unmarked voxels (K is filter support size). The overall frequency domain projection operator is O(n^2 \log n). Memory Complexity: The spectrum requires floating-point storage. The sources note that a double-precision format consumes 16 times more memory than a spatial domain algorithm using 1-byte voxels. Using the Hartley transform and shorter number representations can control this explosion. Performance: The scheme reduced the cost of interpolation to about 15% of the non-adaptive case. Accuracy: Relative error was always below 40dB, a level at which image differences are not visible. Strengths: Significant reduction in interpolation cost; maintains high image quality. Limitations: Requires additional preprocessing step; high memory usage for spectrum storage. Origin: The method was introduced by Takashi Totsuka and Marc Levoy in their 1993 paper "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering". History: It was developed as part of the broader research into Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering. The technique leverages the properties of the Hartley transform to reduce memory costs compared to the standard Fourier transform. Usage: It is used in frequency domain volume rendering systems to optimize the slice extraction phase. name: FDK Pre-Filtering (Ramp Filter + Cone Weighting)
head: CPU FDK Pre-Filter, FDK Filter Application, Ramp Filter Kernel Mapping, applyFDKPreFilter
body: FDK Pre-Filtering applies the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) pre-processing step to raw projection data, preparing it for backprojection in explicit cone-beam geometry. It solves the problem of correcting for the divergent ray paths and high-frequency attenuation inherent in cone-beam acquisitions by combining geometric cone weighting with a 1D ramp filter. It sets itself apart from Adaptive Frequency Domain Filtering by using a fixed ramp kernel rather than adaptive frequency masks, and from Hybrid CPU-GPU FVR Pipeline by being the explicit CPU-side implementation of this specific pre-filtering stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D array of projections projections of shape (P, H, W) or (P, W, H) depending on axis orientation, where P is the number of views, H is the number of detector rows, and W is the number of detector columns. Parameters include voxelSize (mm), pixelSize (mm), sdd (Source-to-Detector Distance in mm), and axis (integer indicating the filtering dimension, typically -1 for the last dimension). Output: A 3D array of filtered projections of the same shape as the input. Data Structures: projections: std::vector<float> or torch.Tensor containing raw projection values. filterkernel: std::vector<double> or torch.Tensor representing the ramp filter in the frequency domain. rowvector: std::vector<std::complex<double>> used for intermediate FFT storage. Numbered Steps: 1. Axis Normalization: If the axis parameter is not -1, transpose the projections array so that the filtering dimension is always the last one (columns). 2. Cone Weighting: For each projection p in 0..P-1: Calculate the center coordinates for each detector pixel. For column index u in 0..W-1 and row index v in 0..H-1: a = -(u - 0.5(W-1)) \times \text{pixelSize} b = (v - 0.5(H-1)) \times \text{pixelSize} Calculate the geometric cone weight cw: cw = \frac{\text{sdd}}{\sqrt{\text{sdd}^2 + a^2 + b^2}} Apply the weight and normalize by voxel size: \text{proj}[u, v] = \frac{\text{proj}[u, v]}{\text{voxelSize}} \times cw 3. FFT Preparation: For each row v in 0..H-1 of the current projection: Extract the row data into a temporary vector. Determine the padded length padN for the FFT. The sources provide two strategies: Strategy A (from): padN = nextPow2(W), where nextPow2(n) returns the smallest power of 2 greater than or equal to n. Strategy B (from): padded = max(64, 1 << (2 length - 1).bitlength()). Zero-pad the row to length padN. 4. Ramp Filter Construction: Build the ramp filter kernel of size padN. Initialize a real-valued vector f of size padN with zeros. Set f[0] = 0.25. For odd indices i from 1 to padN/2: f[1 + 2i] = \frac{-1.0}{\pi^2 i^2} For odd indices i from padN/2 - 1 down to 1: f[1 + 2i] = \frac{-1.0}{\pi^2 i^2} Convert f to a complex vector fc. Perform an in-place FFT on fc with sign -1 (forward transform). Multiply each element fc[k] by 2.0 real(fc[k]). The resulting real parts form the filter kernel applied to the projection rows. 5. Frequency Domain Filtering: For each row v in 0..H-1: Perform an in-place FFT on the zero-padded row vector with sign -1. Multiply each element of the transformed row by the corresponding element of the pre-computed ramp filter kernel. Perform an in-place FFT on the result with sign +1 (inverse transform). Normalize the result: \text{norm} = \frac{1.0}{\text{padN} \times 2.0} Update the original projection row proj[u, v] with the real part of the first W elements of the inverse FFT result, scaled by norm. 6. Chunking (Optional Optimization): If processing large batches, the filtering can be applied in chunks. Calculate chunk = max(1, FILTERCHUNK // (batch count padded)). Apply the filter to slices lines[:, 0, start: start + chunk] and concatenate the results. 7. Axis Restoration: If the axis parameter was not -1, transpose the output array back to the original orientation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath def nextpow2(n): """Returns the smallest power of 2 greater than or equal to n.""" if n <= 0: return 1 return 1 << (n - 1).bitlength() def fftinplace(a, sign): """ Performs an in-place FFT on a list of complex numbers. sign: -1 for forward, +1 for inverse. """ N = len(a) # Bit-reversal permutation j = 0 for i in range(1, N): bit = N >> 1 while j & bit: j ^= bit bit >>= 1 j ^= bit if i < j: a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i] length = 2 while length <= N: angle = sign 2.0 math.pi / length wlen = cmath.exp(complex(0, angle)) for i in range(0, N, length): w = complex(1, 0) for j in range(length // 2): u = a[i + j] v = a[i + j + length // 2] w a[i + j] = u + v a[i + j + length // 2] = u - v w = wlen length = 2 def buildrampfilter(size): """ Builds the ramp filter kernel in the frequency domain. Returns a list of real numbers representing the filter response. """ f = [0.0] size f[0] = 0.25 half = size // 2 # Collect odd indices 1..half and half-1..1 n = list(range(1, half + 1, 2)) + list(range(half - 1, 0, -2)) for i in n: if 1 + 2 i < size: f[1 + 2 i] = -1.0 / (math.pi math.pi i i) # Convert to complex and perform forward FFT fc = [complex(x, 0) for x in f] fftinplace(fc, -1) # Multiply each element by 2.0 real(fc[i]) for i in range(size): fc[i] = complex(2.0 fc[i].real, 0) return [x.real for x in fc] def applyfdkprefilter(projections, P, W, H, voxelsize, sdd, pixelsize): """ Applies FDK pre-filtering (cone weighting + ramp filter) to projections. projections: flattened list of shape (P, W, H) or (P, H, W) depending on layout. Returns filtered projections as a flattened list. """ out = [0.0] (P W H) padn = nextpow2(W) ramp = buildrampfilter(padn) for p in range(P): # 1. Cone Weighting for u in range(W): a = -(u - 0.5 (W - 1)) pixelsize for v in range(H): b = (v - 0.5 (H - 1)) pixelsize cw = sdd / math.sqrt(sdd sdd + a a + b b) out[p W H + u H + v] = (projections[p W H + u H + v] / voxelsize) cw # 2. FFT Filtering per row for v in range(H): # Extract row and zero-pad row = [complex(0, 0)] padn for u in range(W): row[u] = complex(out[p W H + u H + v], 0) # Forward FFT fftinplace(row, -1) # Multiply by filter for u in range(padn): row[u] = row[u] ramp[u] # Inverse FFT fftinplace(row, 1) # Normalize and store back norm = 1.0 / (padn 2.0) for u in range(W): out[p W H + u H + v] = row[u].real norm return out Parameters: P: Number of projections (views). Typical values: 360–1000. W: Detector width in pixels. H: Detector height in pixels. voxelSize: Physical size of a voxel in the output volume (mm). sdd: Source-to-Detector Distance (mm). pixelSize: Physical size of a detector pixel (mm). FILTERCHUNK: Chunk size for memory optimization. Calculated as max(1, FILTERCHUNK // (batch count padded)). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The FFT implementation uses double precision for intermediate calculations to maintain accuracy, especially for the ramp filter construction and multiplication. Boundary Conditions: The zero-padding to the next power of 2 handles the circular convolution artifact of the FFT, assuming the ramp filter is correctly constructed for the padded length. Degenerate Input: If W is 0 or H is 0, the loops will not execute, returning an empty result. If sdd is 0, division by zero occurs in the cone weight calculation. Computes the geometric weighting factors required for the backprojection step of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm in explicit cone-beam geometry. It solves the problem of correctly weighting each ray's contribution based on the angle between the ray and the detector panel normal, as well as the distance from the source to the detector. It sets itself apart from parallel-beam FBP by accounting for the divergent cone-beam geometry through a |dS · ν| / D' weighting scheme, which simplifies to Feldkamp's cosine weight for circular orbits and upright panels. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot H \cdot W \log W) due to the 1D FFT performed on each of the P \times H rows of length W. Memory Complexity: O(P \cdot H \cdot W) for the input and output projections, plus O(W) for the temporary row vectors and filter kernel. Measured Performance: On a system with 360 views and 128 detector rows, the total work-items processed are 360 \times 128 = 46,080. The CPU implementation validates against a Python reference with MSE < 10^{-2}. Strengths: Explicitly handles cone-beam geometry, providing accurate pre-filtering for FDK reconstruction. The FFT-based approach is efficient for large detector widths. Limitations: Requires padding to power-of-2 lengths, which may increase memory usage slightly. When to Use: When performing explicit cone-beam reconstruction using the FDK algorithm and a CPU-based pre-filtering pipeline is required or preferred for validation. The FDK algorithm was introduced by Feldkamp, Davis, and Kress in 1984 for cone-beam CT reconstruction. The specific implementation details provided in the sources are from unofficial repositories (,) that implement and validate this step for CPU and GPU pipelines. itu-biai/torchtomo, https://github.com/itu-biai/torchtomo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: FDK Geometry Weight Calculation
head: Cone Weighting, Feldkamp's cosine weight, Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) Geometry Weight Calculation
body: Computes the geometric weighting factors required for the backprojection step of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm in explicit cone-beam geometry. It solves the problem of correctly weighting each ray's contribution based on the angle between the ray and the detector panel normal, as well as the distance from the source to the detector. It sets itself apart from parallel-beam FBP by accounting for the divergent cone-beam geometry through a |dS · ν| / D' weighting scheme, which simplifies to Feldkamp's cosine weight for circular orbits and upright panels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: sources: Tensor of shape [views, 3], source positions in 3D space. detectors: Tensor of shape [views, rows, columns, 3], detector pixel centers. center: Tensor of shape [3], center of rotation. rows, columns: Integers, detector dimensions. Outputs: weights: Tensor of shape [views, rows, columns], the computed geometric weights. matrices: Tensor of shape [views, 12], projection matrices for mapping voxel coordinates to detector pixels. Data Structures: lattice: Tensor of shape [views, rows, columns, 3], representing the expected flat detector panel positions. ViewColumn: A helper structure (conceptual) containing the 12 floats defining the projection geometry for a single view, derived from matrices. Parameters: FLATNESS: Float 1e-2, tolerance for panel flatness validation. FILTERCHUNK: Integer 1 << 25 (33,554,432), padded samples per filter call to bound FFT memory. (Note: This parameter is used in the parent pre-filtering step, not directly in weight calculation, but is part of the context). Steps: 1. Validate Detector Panel: If rows < 2 or columns < 2, raise ValueError. 2. Calculate Panel Geometry: origin = detectors[:, 0, 0]. rowstep = (detectors[:, -1, 0] - origin) / (rows - 1). columnstep = (detectors[:, 0, -1] - origin) / (columns - 1). Construct lattice: lattice = origin[:, None, None] + row rowstep[:, None, None] + column columnstep[:, None, None]. Calculate pitch: pitch = torch.minimum(rowstep.norm(dim=-1), columnstep.norm(dim=-1)).min(). 3. Validate Flatness: If (detectors - lattice).norm(dim=-1).amax() > FLATNESS pitch, raise ValueError. 4. Calculate Source Steps: Pad sources: before = 2 sources[:1] - sources[1:2], after = 2 sources[-1:] - sources[-2:-1]. padded = torch.cat([before, sources, after], dim=0). sourcesteps = (padded[2:] - padded[:-2]) / 2. 5. Calculate Redundancy Factor: radial = (sources - center).detach().double(). steps = F.cosinesimilarity(radial[1:], radial[:-1], dim=-1).clamp(-1, 1).acos(). turn = steps.sum() + steps.median(). redundancy = 0.5 if turn > 2 math.pi - steps.median() / 2 else 1.0. 6. Determine Filter Axis: alongcolumns = torch.sum(sourcesteps columnstep, dim=-1). alongrows = torch.sum(sourcesteps rowstep, dim=-1). axis = -1 if alongcolumns >= alongrows else -2. 7. Calculate Panel Normal and Depth: normal = unit(torch.linalg.cross(columnstep, rowstep)). Adjust sign: if torch.dot(normal, origin - sources) < 0, normal = -normal. paneldepth = dot(origin - sources, normal). 8. Define Coordinate System: filterstep = rowstep if axis == -2 else columnstep. along = unit(filterstep). across = torch.linalg.cross(normal, along). principal = sources + paneldepth[:, None] normal. 9. Compute Coordinates: Helper coordinate(direction): diff = detectors - principal[:, None, None, None]. coords = torch.sum(diff direction[None, None, None,:], dim=-1). u = coordinate(along). v = coordinate(across). 10. Calculate Weights: depth = paneldepth. linedepth = (depth.square() + v.square()).sqrt(). motionintoline = dot(sourcesteps, normal). motionintolinenormalized = motionintoline / linedepth. acrossray = dot(sourcesteps, across). weights = redundancy acrossray / (linedepth pitch). 11. Construct Projection Matrices: gram = sourcesteps @ sourcesteps.transpose(1, 2). Solve for topixels using gram and detector positions. Calculate offset, inverse depth, and stack into matrices of shape [views, 12]. Formulas: Backprojection weight for a voxel: W = \frac{D^2}{l^2}, where l is the depth along the panel normal and D is the panel's depth. For circular orbit and upright panel, this corresponds to Feldkamp's cosine weight: W = \frac{1}{U^2}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-flat detector panels: Validated by FLATNESS tolerance. If violated, raise ValueError. Degenerate detector dimensions: rows < 2 or columns < 2 raises ValueError. Precision: Use double for redundancy calculation to avoid numerical instability in cosine similarity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math import torch.nn.functional as F def unit(v): return v / v.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) def dot(a, b): return torch.sum(a b, dim=-1) def fdkgeometryweightcalculation(sources, detectors, center, rows, columns, FLATNESS=1e-2): """ Computes FDK geometry weights and projection matrices. Args: sources: [views, 3] detectors: [views, rows, columns, 3] center: [3] rows: int columns: int FLATNESS: float Returns: weights: [views, rows, columns] matrices: [views, 12] """ if rows < 2 or columns < 2: raise ValueError("Detector dimensions must be at least 2x2") # Step 2: Panel Geometry origin = detectors[:, 0, 0] # [views, 3] rowstep = (detectors[:, -1, 0] - origin) / (rows - 1) # [views, 3] columnstep = (detectors[:, 0, -1] - origin) / (columns - 1) # [views, 3] # Construct lattice rowindices = torch.arange(rows, device=sources.device).float() columnindices = torch.arange(columns, device=sources.device).float() rowgrid, columngrid = torch.meshgrid(rowindices, columnindices, indexing='ij') rowgrid = rowgrid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1).expand(sources.shape[0], -1, -1, -1) # [views, rows, columns] columngrid = columngrid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1).expand(sources.shape[0], -1, -1, -1) # [views, rows, columns] lattice = origin[:, None, None,:] + rowgrid[:,:,:, None] rowstep[:, None, None,:] + columngrid[:,:,:, None] columnstep[:, None, None,:] # [views, rows, columns, 3] pitch = torch.minimum(rowstep.norm(dim=-1), columnstep.norm(dim=-1)).min() # Step 3: Flatness Validation flatnesserror = (detectors - lattice).norm(dim=-1).amax() if flatnesserror > FLATNESS pitch: raise ValueError("Detector panel is not flat enough") # Step 4: Source Steps before = 2 sources[:1] - sources[1:2] after = 2 sources[-1:] - sources[-2:-1] paddedsources = torch.cat([before, sources, after], dim=0) sourcesteps = (paddedsources[2:] - paddedsources[:-2]) / 2 # Step 5: Redundancy Factor radial = (sources - center).detach().double() steps = F.cosinesimilarity(radial[1:], radial[:-1], dim=-1).clamp(-1, 1).acos() turn = steps.sum() + steps.median() redundancy = 0.5 if turn > 2 math.pi - steps.median() / 2 else 1.0 # Step 6: Filter Axis alongcolumns = torch.sum(sourcesteps columnstep, dim=-1) alongrows = torch.sum(sourcesteps rowstep, dim=-1) axis = -1 if alongcolumns >= alongrows else -2 # Step 7: Panel Normal and Depth normal = unit(torch.linalg.cross(columnstep, rowstep)) dotproduct = dot(normal, origin - sources) normal = torch.where(dotproduct < 0, -normal, normal) paneldepth = dot(origin - sources, normal) # Step 8: Coordinate System filterstep = rowstep if axis == -2 else columnstep along = unit(filterstep) across = torch.linalg.cross(normal, along) principal = sources + paneldepth[:, None] normal # Step 9: Coordinates diff = detectors - principal[:, None, None,:] # [views, rows, columns, 3] u = torch.sum(diff along[None, None, None,:], dim=-1) v = torch.sum(diff across[None, None, None,:], dim=-1) # Step 10: Weights depth = paneldepth linedepth = (depth.square() + v.square()).sqrt() motionintoline = dot(sourcesteps, normal) motionintolinenormalized = motionintoline / linedepth acrossray = dot(sourcesteps, across) weights = redundancy acrossray / (linedepth pitch) # Step 11: Projection Matrices # Simplified: Gram matrix and solving for projection parameters # This part is complex and depends on specific implementation details not fully provided in sources # For the purpose of this article, we assume a helper function exists matrices = constructprojectionmatrices(sources, detectors, rows, columns, axis) return weights, matrices def constructprojectionmatrices(sources, detectors, rows, columns, axis): # Placeholder for the complex matrix construction logic # In a real implementation, this would involve solving linear systems # to map voxel coordinates to detector pixels views = sources.shape[0] matrices = torch.zeros(views, 12, device=sources.device) #... detailed implementation... return matrices Applies the ramp filter and cone weighting to projections before backprojection. Choose this when you need to pre-process projections for FDK backprojection. FDK Pre-Filtering (Ramp Filter + Cone Weighting) Uses Fourier transform properties for volume rendering. Choose this for frequency-domain based rendering. Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering Time Complexity: O(V \cdot R \cdot C) for weight calculation, where V is views, R is rows, C is columns. Backprojection is O(V \cdot R \cdot C \cdot X \cdot Y \cdot Z). Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot R \cdot C) for weights and matrices. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with number of views and detector resolution. Strengths: Accurate geometric weighting for cone-beam geometry, handles non-flat panels with validation. Limitations: Requires flat detector panel validation, may be computationally intensive for large volumes. When to Use: When using FDK algorithm for cone-beam CT reconstruction. When Not to Use: For parallel-beam geometry or when high accuracy is not required. The FDK algorithm was introduced by Feldkamp, Davis, and Kress in 1984. It is a widely used method for cone-beam CT reconstruction, extending the FBP algorithm to 3D cone-beam geometry. The geometry weight calculation is a crucial part of the FDK algorithm, ensuring accurate reconstruction by accounting for the divergent beam geometry. itu-biai/torchtomo, https://github.com/itu-biai/torchtomo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gamma-Corrected Hemispherical Shading
head: Cubic Shading in Fourier Domain, Fourier Domain Gamma-Corrected Shading, Gamma-Corrected Shading
body:
Gamma-Corrected Hemispherical Shading (GCHS) is an illumination model for Fourier Volume Rendering that approximates the non-linear diffuse operator \max(0, \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}) by raising the hemispherical term (1 + \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L})/2 to a gamma power. It replaces linear hemispherical shading with a cubic polynomial expansion, which culls back-lit surfaces more effectively and reduces erroneous energy on rear-facing surfaces compared to linear approximations. Unlike the non-linear max operator, GCHS expands into a sum of geometric terms weighted by lighting coefficients, allowing geometric components to be pre-computed in the Fourier domain and re-evaluated for changing light directions via linear combinations. Inputs: Volume data f(\mathbf{x}). Light direction vector \mathbf{L} = (l1, l2, l3), normalized. Gamma exponent g=3. Outputs: Shaded volume rendering contribution in the Fourier domain, ready for back-projection or further processing. Data Structures: F(\mathbf{\Omega}): The 3D Fourier transform of the volume data f. \mathbf{\Omega} = (\omegax, \omegay, \omegaz): The frequency vector. Basis images: Twenty 8-bit sample basis images storing the geometric terms Vi. Coefficient matrix: A 20 	imes 20 matrix derived from corresponding lighting directions for the coefficients ai. Method: The method approximates the diffuse shading by expanding the cubic hemispherical term into a polynomial of dot products between the gradient 
abla f and the light vector \mathbf{L}, normalized by the gradient magnitude \|
abla f\|. 1. Define the Shading Operator: The base hemispherical shading operator is E =  rac{1}{2}(1 + \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}), where \mathbf{N} is the normalized surface normal. For GCHS, this is raised to the power g=3 and scaled: E{GCHS} =  rac{1}{8}(1 + \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L})^3 2. Expand the Polynomial: Substitute the normal \mathbf{N} =  rac{
abla f}{\|

Parameters: Gamma exponent g=3. This is the smallest integer power producing an inflection point, minimizing error in both zero and non-zero portions of the shading curve. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-linearity: The standard \max(0, \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}) cannot be projected into the Fourier basis. GCHS avoids this by using a polynomial approximation. Negative Intensity: Ignoring visibility (using simple hemispherical shading) results in negative image intensity values and reduced contrast. GCHS eliminates negative intensity without the max operator. Light Direction Changes: The convolution terms in the quadratic and cubic equations require a convolution with the full volume. This can only be precomputed for a constant light source. If the light direction changes, these terms must be recomputed. Performance: Cubic shading has lower frame rates than linear shading due to additional calculations. Time Complexity: The method requires computing convolutions of the volume data in the Fourier domain. The quadratic and cubic terms involve convolutions with the full volume, which are computationally expensive. The source notes that these terms must be recomputed if the light direction changes. Memory Complexity: Storage optimization uses twenty 8-bit sample basis images for the geometric terms and a 20 	imes 20 matrix for lighting coefficients. Measured Performance: For a 128^3 synthetic sphere: Traditional FVR is 36 fps (no depth cueing) and 27 fps (with depth cueing). Linear and cubic illuminations are 32 fps (no depth cueing) and 25 fps (with depth cueing). Strengths: Higher accuracy than linear hemispherical shading by better approximating the \max function. Reduces erroneous energy on surfaces back-facing the light. Produces images visually almost indistinguishable from normal diffuse shading. Allows re-evaluation for changing lights via linear combinations of pre-computed geometric terms. Limitations: Lower frame rates compared to linear shading. Requires recomputation of convolution terms for changing light directions. Not fully linear; the polynomial coefficients depend on the light direction. Origin: GCHS was proposed by Scoggins et al. as an improvement over the hemispherical shading method by Totsuka and Levoy. Development: Totsuka and Levoy replaced the non-linear \max(0, \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}) with the linear hemispherical term (1 + \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L})/2, which allowed Fourier projection but resulted in poor image quality (reduced contrast, negative intensities). Scoggins et al. raised this term to the cube (g=3) to better approximate the max operator, culling back-lit surfaces more effectively. Entezari et al. adapted this method for Fourier Volume Rendering, providing the Fourier domain implementation formulas. Usage: Used in Fourier Volume Rendering to incorporate better illumination models, specifically for constant light sources where the convolution terms can be precomputed. name: Hybrid CPU-GPU FVR Pipeline
head: Heterogeneous FVR Pipeline, CPU-Computational/GPU-Rendering FVR
body: The Hybrid CPU-GPU FVR Pipeline is a heterogeneous implementation strategy for Fourier Volume Rendering that partitions the computational workload between the CPU and the GPU. The CPU handles the heavy numerical computations, specifically the 3D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and resampling, while the GPU handles the rendering context, including texture management, projection-slice extraction via OpenGL, and final display. This approach leverages the hardware-accelerated interpolation and texture handling of OpenGL to simplify the representation of the 3D spectral volume, offering a middle ground between fully CPU-based pipelines and fully GPU-based implementations. The pipeline operates by alternating between a CPU computational context and GPU rendering contexts. The process begins on the CPU and concludes on the GPU's on-screen frame buffer. Input: A 3D volumetric dataset stored as a 3D array on the CPU. Output: A 2D reconstructed projection image displayed on the screen. 1. 3D Spectral Volume: A 3D texture object allocated in GPU memory that stores the frequency spectrum of the input volume. 2. Frame Buffer Object (FBO): An OpenGL object used for off-screen rendering. 3. 2D Texture (Intermediate): A 2-component 2D texture attached to the FBO, storing the extracted projection-slice. 4. 2D Texture (Final): A 2D texture uploaded to GPU memory containing the final reconstructed image for display. 1. Load the 3D dataset into CPU memory. 2. Perform a spatial shift on the 3D dataset. 3. Compute the forward 3D FFT of the shifted volume to obtain its frequency spectrum. 4. Activate an OpenGL off-screen rendering context. 5. Allocate a 3D OpenGL texture in GPU memory and upload the 3D spectral volume from the CPU to this texture. 6. Define a proxy quadrant (plane) passing through the origin of the frequency domain. 7. Intersect this proxy quadrant with the 3D spectral texture to extract the projection-slice. 8. Render the intersection result into the Frame Buffer Object (FBO). 9. Pack the FBO contents into a 2-component 2D texture attached to the FBO. 10. Switch back to the CPU computational context. 11. Download the 2-component 2D texture (containing the projection-slice) from GPU memory to CPU memory. 12. Resample the downloaded projection-slice on the CPU to remove ghosting artifacts. 13. Perform an inverse 2D FFT on the resampled slice to produce a shifted image in the spatial domain. 14. Perform a 2D fft-shift operation on the image to rearrange it correctly. 15. Pack the final reconstructed image into a 2D OpenGL texture. 16. Upload this texture to GPU memory using glTex2D. 17. Activate the on-screen rendering context. 18. Send the final texture to the frame buffer for display. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridfvrpipeline(volume3d): # 1. Load Data # volume3d is a 3D array on CPU # 2. Preprocessing (CPU) # Perform spatial shift on 3D array shiftedvolume = spatialshift(volume3d) # Compute forward 3D FFT using FFTW spectralvolume3d = fft3(shiftedvolume) # 3. GPU Context Activation (Off-screen) # Activate OpenGL off-screen rendering context activateopengloffscreencontext() # Allocate 3D OpenGL texture in GPU memory gpu3dtexture = allocate3dtexture(spectralvolume3d.shape) # Upload spectral volume from CPU to GPU texture uploadtogpu(gpu3dtexture, spectralvolume3d) # 4. Projection-Slice Extraction (GPU) # Create Frame Buffer Object (FBO) fbo = createframebufferobject() # Attach 2-component 2D texture to FBO attach2dtexturetofbo(fbo) # Define proxy quadrant through origin and intersect with 3D texture # Render intersection result to FBO renderprojectionslice(gpu3dtexture, fbo) # 5. Data Transfer (GPU to CPU) # Switch back to CPU computational context switchtocpucontext() # Download 2-component 2D texture from GPU to CPU projectionslice2d = downloadfromgpu(fbo) # 6. Resampling (CPU) # Resample slice to remove ghosting artifacts using nested loops resampledslice = resampleslice(projectionslice2d) # 7. Inverse Transform (CPU) # Perform inverse 2D FFT to produce shifted image shiftedimage = ifft2(resampledslice) # Perform 2D fft-shift to rearrange image finalimage = fftshift2d(shiftedimage) # 8. Final Upload (CPU to GPU) # Pack final image into 2D OpenGL texture finaltexture = create2dtexture(finalimage.shape) # Upload texture to GPU memory using glTex2D uploadtogpu(finaltexture, finalimage) # 9. Display (GPU) # Activate on-screen rendering context activateopenglonscreencontext() # Send texture to frame buffer for display displaytexture(finaltexture) def spatialshift(vol): return vol # Perform spatial shift on 3D array def fft3(vol): return vol # Compute forward 3D FFT using FFTW def activateopengloffscreencontext(): pass # Activate OpenGL off-screen context def allocate3dtexture(shape): return None # Allocate 3D OpenGL texture in GPU memory def uploadtogpu(tex, data): pass # Upload data to GPU texture def createframebufferobject(): return None # Create FBO def attach2dtexturetofbo(fbo): pass # Attach 2D texture to FBO def renderprojectionslice(tex, fbo): pass # Intersect texture with quadrant and render to FBO def switchtocpucontext(): pass # Switch execution context to CPU def downloadfromgpu(fbo): return None # Download FBO texture data to CPU def resampleslice(slice2d): return slice2d # Resample slice to remove ghosting artifacts def ifft2(slice2d): return slice2d # Perform inverse 2D FFT def fftshift2d(img): return img # Perform 2D fft-shift def create2dtexture(shape): return None # Create 2D OpenGL texture def activateopenglonscreencontext(): pass # Activate OpenGL on-screen context def displaytexture(tex): pass # Send texture to frame buffer Data Transfer Bottleneck: The frequent switching between CPU and GPU contexts requires transferring data back and forth, which limits the overall performance of the pipeline to the bandwidth of the communication channel between the CPU and GPU, which is significantly lower than internal GPU bandwidth. Resampling Cost: The resampling stage represents the most critical bottleneck in the pipeline. It involves four nested for loops (two for slice dimensions, two for filter kernel). For a projection-slice of size 512x512, this operation takes considerable time and blocks a real-time rendering loop. 3D FFT Latency: The 3D FFT operation on the CPU (using FFTW) is slow for volumes of size 64^3 or larger. Although executed once during preprocessing, performing it on several volumes elongates the pre-processing stage. 2D FFT Latency: The inverse 2D FFT is executed on a per-frame basis, and reducing its time consumption directly enhances the frame rate. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The pipeline lacks interactivity due to bottlenecks in data transfer and CPU-based resampling. The communication channel bandwidth between CPU and GPU limits the overall performance. Strengths: Easier to handle than a full CPU-based pipeline because the 3D spectral volume can be efficiently represented by 3D OpenGL textures with hardware-accelerated interpolation and built-in interpolation schemes. Limitations: Not suitable for real-time rendering of large volumes due to CPU resampling and data transfer overheads. The 3D FFT on CPU is a preprocessing bottleneck for large volumes (64^3+). When to use: When OpenGL texture handling is preferred for spectral volume representation and full GPU implementation is not feasible or desired. When not to use: When real-time performance is required for large volumes, or when the overhead of CPU-GPU data transfer and CPU-based resampling is unacceptable. The Hybrid CPU-GPU FVR Pipeline was proposed as an improvement over single-threaded CPU-based FVR implementations. It builds on the strategy of using heterogeneous computing to leverage the strengths of both CPU (computation) and GPU (rendering/texture handling). The reference implementation was adopted from a previous single-threaded version discussed in [24] (cited in). The approach aims to increase flexibility and efficiency in designing GPU pipelines by utilizing OpenGL for rendering contexts. name: Depth Cueing via Linear Attenuation
head: Approximate exponential attenuation, Linear attenuation shading model, X-rays with depth cueing
body: This method approximates the perceptual depth cues of exponential attenuation in volume rendering by replacing the variable absorption coefficient with a linear function of position, enabling the integrand to be evaluated as a Fourier projection. It sets itself apart from standard exponential attenuation models by allowing efficient computation via the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume density function \rho(x,y,z), volume color function C(x,y,z), constant opacity/absorption coefficient \tau, viewing direction vector \mathbf{V}, ray segment bounds a and b, linear depth constants m and \mathbf{b}, ray origin, and ray direction. Output: Total energy IP arriving at the end of the viewing ray. Data Structures: \rho: Scalar field representing density. C: Vector field representing color/emission. \mathbf{V}: Normalized 3D vector pointing away from the eye. \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}): Linear position function \mathbf{D} = m\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{b}, where m is a scalar and \mathbf{b} is a 3D vector constant defining the depth cueing geometry. Steps: 1. Define the viewing ray \mathbf{P}(t) parameterized by length t. 2. Construct the linear depth function \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)) = m\mathbf{P}(t) + \mathbf{b}. 3. Compute the dot product \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V} to determine the local attenuation weight. 4. Evaluate the integrand: \rho(\mathbf{P}(t)) C(\mathbf{P}(t)) [\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} (\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V})]. 5. Integrate the result from t=a to t=b. Formula: The total energy IP arriving at point \mathbf{P}(b) is given by: IP = \int{a}^{b} \rho(\mathbf{P}(t)) C(\mathbf{P}(t)) \left[ \frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} (\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V}) \right] dt Where: \rho(\mathbf{P}(t)): Density at position \mathbf{P}(t). C(\mathbf{P}(t)): Color/emission at position \mathbf{P}(t). \tau: Constant opacity/absorption coefficient. \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}(t)): Linear function of position, \mathbf{D} = m\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{b}. \mathbf{V}: Normalized viewing direction vector (points away from the eye). a, b: Start and end parameters of the ray segment. Note: The constant vector \mathbf{b} in the depth function is distinct from the scalar ray endpoint parameter b. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelinearattenuationenergy(rho, color, tau, m, bvec, v, rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, tend, numsamples): """ Computes the integrated energy for linear depth cueing. Args: rho: Function returning density scalar at (x,y,z). color: Function returning color vector at (x,y,z). tau: Constant opacity coefficient. m: Scalar constant for linear depth function. bvec: 3D vector constant for linear depth function (distinct from scalar limit b). v: Normalized 3D viewing direction vector (away from eye). rayorigin: 3D vector for ray origin. raydirection: 3D vector for ray direction. tstart: Start parameter 'a'. tend: End parameter 'b'. numsamples: Number of integration steps. Returns: Total energy IP. """ dt = (tend - tstart) / numsamples totalenergy = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tstart + i dt pt = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) dt = (m pt[0] + bvec[0], m pt[1] + bvec[1], m pt[2] + bvec[2]) dotproduct = dt[0] v[0] + dt[1] v[1] + dt[2] v[2] weight = (tau / 2.0) + (tau / 2.0) dotproduct density = rho(pt) c = color(pt) energysample = density c weight totalenergy += energysample dt return totalenergy Edge Cases: If \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{V} results in negative weights, the physical interpretation of attenuation may break down, though the formula remains mathematically valid. Precision issues may arise if \tau is very large or very small relative to the integration step size. A shading model that enhances depth perception in X-ray projections by weighting volume points based on their distance from the viewer, without introducing occlusion. It replaces per-voxel shading followed by projection with projection followed by per-pixel shading, allowing depth cueing (linear attenuation) to be computed efficiently by factoring the viewing direction out of the integral. Unlike opaque volume renderings, this method produces X-ray-like projections with no occlusion, but the linear shading provides sufficient shape cues for spatial understanding, especially in motion. Time Complexity: O(N^2 \log N) per view when implemented via the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, avoiding the O(N^3) cost of digital compositing. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient rendering of depth-cued X-ray images; leverages fast Fourier transforms. Limitations: Approximates exponential attenuation; does not model occlusion; accuracy depends on the linearity assumption of the depth cue. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced by Marc Levoy in his work on volume rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. It addresses the computational cost of exponential attenuation by linearizing the absorption term, allowing the use of frequency domain methods for shading. The approach is based on the observation that linear attenuation with a constant coefficient can be expressed as a Fourier projection, enabling efficient rendering. name: Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem
head: Fourier Projection-Slice Depth Cueing, Linear Attenuation via Fourier Projection-Slice, Linear Depth Cueing
body: A shading model that enhances depth perception in X-ray projections by weighting volume points based on their distance from the viewer, without introducing occlusion. It replaces per-voxel shading followed by projection with projection followed by per-pixel shading, allowing depth cueing (linear attenuation) to be computed efficiently by factoring the viewing direction out of the integral. Unlike opaque volume renderings, this method produces X-ray-like projections with no occlusion, but the linear shading provides sufficient shape cues for spatial understanding, especially in motion. Inputs: Volume density \rho(x,y,z) and emission coefficient C(x,y,z), combined as f(x,y,z) = \rho(x,y,z)C(x,y,z). Normalized viewing direction vector \mathbf{V} = (Vx, Vy, Vz), pointing away from the eye. Constant linear attenuation coefficient \tau. Linear depth function \mathbf{D}(P) = mP + b, where P is position along the ray. Outputs: 2D projection image I. Data Structures: Four 3D spectra (frequency domain representations) of the volume, each of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz (complex values). Two-dimensional slices extracted from these spectra for inverse transformation. Steps: 1. Precomputation: Create four copies of the volume data f(x,y,z). Multiply the first copy by 1. Multiply the second copy by Dx(x,y,z), the x-component of the depth function. Multiply the third copy by Dy(x,y,z), the y-component of the depth function. Multiply the fourth copy by Dz(x,y,z), the z-component of the depth function. Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of each of the four modified volumes to yield four 3D spectra: \mathcal{F}\{f\}, \mathcal{F}\{Dx f\}, \mathcal{F}\{Dy f\}, and \mathcal{F}\{Dz f\}. 2. Per-view Rendering: For the current viewing direction \mathbf{V}, extract 2D slices from each of the four 3D spectra corresponding to the projection plane defined by \mathbf{V}. Compute the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform of each extracted slice to obtain spatial domain images. Weight the inverse-transformed images by the components of \mathbf{V} and the constant terms derived from the attenuation model: Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dx f\} by Vx. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dy f\} by Vy. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{Dz f\} by Vz. Multiply the image from \mathcal{F}\{f\} by the constant c1 = \tau/2 - \tau/2 (Vx + Vy + Vz). Sum the four weighted images to produce the final output image I. Formula: The intensity I at a pixel is given by: I = Vx \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dx \right) \rho C \right] + Vy \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dy \right) \rho C \right] + Vz \Pi{\mathbf{V}} \left[ \left(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} Dz \right) \rho C \right] + c1 \Pi{\mathbf{V}} [\rho C] where \Pi{\mathbf{V}} is the projection operator, Dx, Dy, Dz are components of \mathbf{D}, and c1 = \tau/2 - \tau/2 (Vx + Vy + Vz). The underlying integral being approximated is: IP = \inta^b \rho(P(t)) C(P(t)) \left[ \frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} (\mathbf{D}(P(t)) \cdot \mathbf{V}) \right] dt where \mathbf{D} = mP + b is a linear function of position. Parameters: \tau: Constant linear attenuation coefficient. \mathbf{V}: Normalized viewing direction vector. m, b: Constants defining the linear depth function \mathbf{D}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ghosting: To avoid ghosting artifacts caused by spectral leakage, the input volume must be surrounded by a margin of zeros. The margin width is N(k2-1)/2 on each side, where k2 is the factor by which the volume width is increased. Viewing Direction Convention: \mathbf{V} must point away from the eye, not towards it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputespectra(rho, C, Dx, Dy, Dz): """ Precomputes the four 3D spectra required for linear depth cueing. Args: rho: 3D array of density values. C: 3D array of emission coefficients. Dx, Dy, Dz: 3D arrays of depth function components. Returns: spectra: List of four 3D complex arrays [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz]. """ f = rho C # Standard 3D FFT implementation Sf = fft3d(f) SDx = fft3d(f Dx) SDy = fft3d(f Dy) SDz = fft3d(f Dz) return [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz] def renderlineardepthcueing(spectra, V, tau): """ Renders a single view using linear depth cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Args: spectra: List of four 3D complex arrays [Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz]. V: Tuple (Vx, Vy, Vz) normalized vector pointing away from eye. tau: Constant linear attenuation coefficient. Returns: image: 2D array representing the rendered projection. """ Sf, SDx, SDy, SDz = spectra Vx, Vy, Vz = V c1 = tau / 2.0 - (tau / 2.0) (Vx + Vy + Vz) # Extracts a 2D slice from the 3D spectrum along the plane orthogonal to V, per the Fourier slice theorem slicef = extractslice(Sf, V) sliceDx = extractslice(SDx, V) sliceDy = extractslice(SDy, V) sliceDz = extractslice(SDz, V) # Standard 2D IFFT implementation imgf = ifft2d(slicef) imgDx = ifft2d(sliceDx) imgDy = ifft2d(sliceDy) imgDz = ifft2d(sliceDz) # Weight and sum according to the projection formula # The tau/2 factor is applied here to match the exact mathematical formulation termbase = c1 imgf termDx = Vx (tau / 2.0) imgDx termDy = Vy (tau / 2.0) imgDy termDz = Vz (tau / 2.0) imgDz image = termbase + termDx + termDy + termDz return image.real Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading is a frequency-domain rendering technique that simultaneously applies linear depth cueing (attenuation) and hemispherical directional shading to volume data. It solves the problem of efficiently computing both effects within the Fourier Projection-Slice framework, where naive spatial-domain computation would be prohibitively expensive. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, by combining the attenuation model with a hemispherical illumination model that avoids the nonlinear absolute value operator, allowing the lighting direction to be factored out of the integral. This requires 16 precomputed spectra and is slower than individual models due to a high constant factor, though asymptotically less expensive than conventional rendering. Memory: 48 megabytes for the 128^3 voxel cube implementation described. Performance: Rendering time was approximately 6 seconds per view on a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX for the linear depth cueing equation (approx. 1.5 seconds per extracted slice). Scaling: Per-view processing time increases by a factor of k2^2 if the volume width is increased by a factor of k2 due to zero padding. Memory requirements increase by a factor of k2^3. Strengths: Efficient computation of depth cueing in the frequency domain; produces X-ray-like projections with shape cues. Limitations: No occlusion; requires zero-padding to avoid ghosting artifacts. Originated in the work of Marc Levoy, described in "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem". The method is part of a family of algorithms for generating realistically shaded renderings of volume data using the Fourier projection-slice theorem. name: Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading
head: Composite Shading Model, Hemispherical Illumination Shading
body: Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading is a frequency-domain volume rendering technique that integrates linear attenuation (depth cueing) and hemispherical directional shading into a single rendering pass. It solves the problem of high computational cost associated with applying both effects in the spatial domain by leveraging the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Unlike standard spatial rendering which requires O(n^3) operations for these effects, this method reduces complexity to O(n^2). It is distinct from its sibling Combined Depth Cueing and Shading by specifically addressing the order of operations to optimize performance, often using a "reversed order" approximation to avoid multiple convolutions. The method replaces parallel illumination with illumination from an emissive hemisphere to avoid the nonlinear absolute value operator |N \cdot L|, allowing the lighting direction to be factored out of the integral for Fourier projection-slice evaluation. It combines linear attenuation and hemispherical illumination, requiring 16 precomputed spectra. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Volume of albedo \Omega(x,y,z). Orientation field N(x,y,z), typically estimated from scalar input data using a central difference operator. Viewing direction V and Lighting direction L (unit vectors). Attenuation coefficient \tau. Outputs: Rendered image intensity I. Data Structures The algorithm relies on 16 precomputed 3D spectra derived from the volume and orientation fields. VL Vector: A 12-element vector of products of viewing direction components V and lighting direction components L: VL = (Vx Lx, Vx Ly, Vx Lz, Vy Lx, Vy Ly, Vy Lz, Vz Lx, Vz Ly, Vz Lz, Vx, Vy, Vz, Lx, Ly, Lz) Note: The source lists 13 elements in the formula definition but refers to a 12-element vector in the text description. The formula explicitly lists 13 terms. DN Vector: A 12-element vector of products of displacement direction components D and orientation components N: DN = (Dx Nx, Dx Ny, Dx Nz, Dy Nx, Dy Ny, Dy Nz, Dz Nx, Dz Ny, Dz Nz, Dx, Dy, Dz, Nx, Ny, Nz) Note: Similar to VL, the formula lists 13 terms. Steps 1. Precomputation: a. Create four copies of the volume \Omega(x,y,z). b. Multiply each copy by the appropriate component of the orientation field N: one by 1, one by Nx, one by Ny, and one by Nz. c. Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of these four modified volumes to yield four 3D spectra. d. To support the composite model, the integrand is multiplied by linear attenuation and hemispherical illumination terms, resulting in a total of 16 precomputed spectra. 2. Per-view Rendering: a. For the current viewing direction V and lighting direction L, extract slices from each of the 16 precomputed spectra. b. Inverse Fourier Transform each slice to obtain spatial domain images. c. Weight each inverse-transformed slice by the corresponding component of the current lighting direction L (and viewing direction V for attenuation). d. Sum the weighted slices to produce the final image. Formulas The intensity I is computed as: I = \tau \frac{\pi}{2} VL \cdot \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} DN(x,y,z)\right) Is \Omega(x,y,z) \right] + \tau \frac{\pi}{2} c3 \PiV [Is \Omega(x,y,z)] Where: \PiV is the Fourier projection operator along viewing direction V. Is is the intensity of the light source. c3 is a constant term defined as: c3 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sumi VLi Note: The summation index i ranges over the components of the VL vector. Parameters \Omega(x,y,z): Volume of albedo. c3: Constant term dependent on V and L. Edge Cases and Pitfalls The composite model ignores emission \rho C from the depth cueing equation. In this context, emission can be interpreted as ambient illumination. The high constant factor makes the algorithm slower than conventional rendering for small volumes, despite being asymptotically less expensive. Combined Depth Cueing and Shading is a frequency-domain volume rendering technique that integrates linear attenuation (depth cueing) and hemispherical directional shading into a single rendering pass. It solves the problem of high computational cost associated with applying both effects in the spatial domain by leveraging the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Unlike standard spatial rendering which requires O(n^3) operations for these effects, this method reduces complexity to O(n^2). It is distinct from its sibling Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading by specifically addressing the order of operations to optimize performance, often using a "reversed order" approximation to avoid multiple convolutions. Time Complexity: Asymptotically O(n^2), which is less expensive than conventional spatial rendering O(n^3). Memory Complexity: Requires 16 precomputed spectra. For a 128^3 voxel cube implementation, memory usage is 256 megabytes. Measured Performance: On a 36 MHz Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX with a sequential C implementation, rendering time was over a minute per view for the composite model, mostly due to paging. This is significantly slower than the 6 seconds required for simpler models (e.g., linear depth cueing alone) on the same hardware. Strengths: Avoids the nonlinear absolute value operator |N \cdot L| present in parallel illumination models, allowing efficient Fourier evaluation. The resulting shading is less sensitive to surface orientation, similar to perception on a cloudy day, and avoids negative light artifacts from backward-facing normals. Limitations: High constant factor makes it slower than conventional rendering for small volumes. Ignores emission/ambient illumination. The method was developed by Marc Levoy as part of his work on volume rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. It extends earlier work on linear depth cueing and hemispherical illumination by combining them into a single composite model. The approach is based on the observation that the integrand can be expressed as a linear combination of Fourier projections, allowing the use of the projection-slice theorem for efficient rendering.
