name: Frequency Domain Convolution
head: FFT Convolution, Point Spread Function (PSF) Convolution
body: Frequency Domain Convolution computes the convolution of an input signal with a kernel by transforming both into the frequency domain, multiplying their transforms, and inverse-transforming the result. It is computationally economical for large kernels compared to direct spatial summation. Unlike direct spatial methods, it leverages the Convolution Theorem to replace nested summation with element-wise multiplication. Inputs: Input signal g of size N \times N. Convolution kernel h of size Kh \times Kw. Outputs: Convolved signal of size N \times N. Data Structures: Complex-valued arrays of size N \times N for frequency domain representation. Zero-padded kernel array of size N \times N. Steps: 1. Zero-Pad Kernel: Create an array of size N \times N and place the kernel h at the top-left corner, filling the remainder with zeros. 2. Forward FFT: Compute the 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the input signal g to obtain G{u,v}. 3. Forward FFT: Compute the 2D DFT of the padded kernel to obtain H{u,v}. 4. Frequency Multiplication: Multiply the transforms element-wise to obtain Y{u,v} = G{u,v} \cdot H{u,v}. 5. Inverse FFT: Compute the 2D Inverse DFT of Y{u,v} to obtain the result in the spatial domain. 6. Normalization: Ensure the kernel sum equals 1 to conserve energy. (Scaling instruction not given in the sources). Formula: The 2-D Convolution Theorem states: g{x,y} h{x,y} = \sum{a=0}^{N-1} \sum{b=0}^{N-1} h{a,b} \cdot g{x-a,y-b} \Leftrightarrow G{u,v} H{u,v} where is spatial convolution, G and H are frequency transforms, and N is the dimension size assumed in the convolution sum limits. Parameters: N: The dimension size of the input signal. The kernel must be padded to this size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Circular Convolution: FFT assumes periodic boundary conditions, which causes wrap-around artifacts if the kernel is large relative to the image or if the image has sharp edges. Normalization: Incorrect kernel normalization leads to energy gain or loss. The sum of all pixel positions in the kernel should equal 1. Precision: Floating-point errors in FFT can accumulate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frequencydomainconvolution(image, kernel): """ Computes convolution using FFT. image: 2D array of shape (Nh, Nw) kernel: 2D array of shape (Kh, Kw) """ Nh, Nw = len(image), len(image[0]) Kh, Kw = len(kernel), len(kernel[0]) N = max(Nh, Nw) # Zero-pad image and kernel to N x N as per source G = [[complex(0, 0) for in range(N)] for in range(N)] H = [[complex(0, 0) for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for i in range(Nh): for j in range(Nw): G[i][j] = complex(image[i][j], 0) for i in range(Kh): for j in range(Kw): H[i][j] = complex(kernel[i][j], 0) # Forward FFT (standard 2D DFT algorithm) Gfreq = fft2d(G) Hfreq = fft2d(H) # Frequency multiplication Y = [[Gfreq[i][j] Hfreq[i][j] for j in range(N)] for i in range(N)] # Inverse FFT (standard 2D IDFT algorithm) result = ifft2d(Y) # Extract real part return [[real(result[i][j]) for j in range(N)] for i in range(N)] This method approximates spatially variant focus and aberration control by applying the correct lens phase function only at the user's tracked fovea position, rather than computing the full spatially variant solution for the entire hologram. It builds on Frequency Domain Convolution by substituting a fixed lens phase function with a temporally varying one derived from eye tracking. Unlike piece-wise methods, it provides a smooth and continuous falloff of aberration correction outside the foveal region without sharp phase discontinuities. Time Complexity: Dominated by the FFT operations, making it computationally economical for large kernels. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) to store the padded image and kernel in the frequency domain. Strengths: Efficient for large kernels. Limitations: Circular convolution artifacts require careful padding; high memory usage for large images. When to use: Large kernel blurring or optical system simulation where the kernel size is large. When not to use: Small kernels where spatial convolution is faster. The method is based on the Convolution Theorem, which states that convolution in the spatial domain is equivalent to multiplication in the frequency domain. It has been used in computer graphics and physics to simulate optical blurring and correct imperfections in optical systems by convolving with the inverse of a Point Spread Function (PSF). The discrete convolution may suffer from incorrect normalization of the filter, requiring the sum of all pixel positions in the kernel to equal 1 to conserve energy. name: Foveated Spatially Varying Lens Approximation
head: Tracked Spatially Varying Lens Phase Function Method
body: This method approximates spatially variant focus and aberration control by applying the correct lens phase function only at the user's tracked fovea position, rather than computing the full spatially variant solution for the entire hologram. It builds on Frequency Domain Convolution by substituting a fixed lens phase function with a temporally varying one derived from eye tracking. Unlike piece-wise methods, it provides a smooth and continuous falloff of aberration correction outside the foveal region without sharp phase discontinuities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The complex object plane O (from Frequency Domain Convolution), the tracked fovea position in object space, and the base lens phase function parameters. Output: The complex hologram plane H, ready for phase extraction. Data Structures: Lens Phase Function (fz): A 2D array representing the phase shift introduced by the lens. In the standard fixed case, this is static. Tracked Lens Phase Function (f{z{ot}}): A 2D array of the same dimensions as fz, recomputed each frame. Fovea Position (o{it}): The 2D coordinates of the closest object point to the tracked fovea. Steps: 1. Track Fovea: Determine the user's fovea position in the object space. Identify the closest object point o{it} to this tracked position. 2. Compute Temporally Varying Lens Function: Calculate the lens phase function f{z{ot}} corresponding to the object point o{it}. This function represents the optical correction required for that specific depth and position. 3. Convolve: Perform the spatial convolution defined in Equation 15 of, substituting the fixed lens phase function fz with the temporally varying function f{z{ot}}. H = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \{ \mathcal{F}\{O\} \cdot \mathcal{F}\{f{z{ot}}\} \} Where \mathcal{F} is the Fourier transform and \mathcal{F}^{-1} is the inverse Fourier transform. 4. Repeat: Recompute f{z{ot}} each frame based on the new fovea position. Parameters: Fovea Tracking Latency: Must be low enough to prevent visible lag, though specific values are not given. Falloff Rate: The resolution of aberration correction must fall off no more quickly than the visual acuity of the human eye. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: The method cannot present true depth of field if there are object points with varying depths closely surrounding the tracked fovea. Acuity Mismatch: If the falloff in correction resolution is too rapid, it will exceed the eye's natural acuity falloff, causing visible artifacts. Performance: While faster than full spatially variant computation, it may not run at high video rates on all current GPUs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def foveatedspatiallyvaryinglensapproximation(objectplane, foveaposition, lensparams): """ Approximates spatially variant focus/aberration by using the lens function of the closest object point to the tracked fovea. Args: objectplane: Complex 2D array representing the object field. foveaposition: Tuple (x, y) of the tracked fovea in object space. lensparams: Parameters defining the lens phase function (e.g., focal length). Returns: hologram: Complex 2D array representing the hologram. """ # Step 1: Find the closest object point to the fovea # Note: The specific algorithm for finding the closest object point # depends on the scene representation (e.g., depth map lookup). # This is marked as as the source assumes a standard renderer pipeline. closestobjectpoint = findclosestobjectpoint(foveaposition) # Step 2: Compute the temporally varying lens phase function # fzot corresponds to the lens phase function for object point oit fzot = computelensphasefunction(closestobjectpoint, lensparams) # Step 3: Perform convolution via FFT # H = F^-1 { F{O} F{fzot} } # Using standard FFT operations fftobject = fft2(objectplane) fftlens = fft2(fzot) # Element-wise multiplication in frequency domain product = fftobject fftlens # Inverse FFT to get the hologram hologram = ifft2(product) return hologram def findclosestobjectpoint(foveaposition): """ Placeholder for scene-specific logic to find the closest object point. In the context of the source, this is derived from the depth map and color data generated by the standard graphics pipeline. """ # Implementation depends on the specific scene data structure. # For the purpose of this method, it returns the coordinates of the # closest object point to the foveaposition. pass def computelensphasefunction(objectpoint, lensparams): """ Computes the lens phase function for a specific object point. """ # The exact formula for fzot is not provided in the sources, # but it is derived from the lens parameters and the object point's depth/position. # It replaces the fixed fz in the standard method. pass This method pre-compensates for optical aberrations in display hardware and vision deficiencies in the viewer by shaping the wavefront for each object point using Zernike polynomials. It builds on Foveated Spatially Varying Lens Approximation by replacing the simple lens phase function with a parameterized wavefront correction that offers practically unlimited degrees of freedom for spatially variant correction. Time Complexity: Nearly the same as the fixed lens phase function case, as only one lens function needs to be recomputed per frame. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the object plane, the hologram, and the lens phase functions. No additional large data structures are mentioned. Performance: Very fast when performed on the GPU, but may not achieve high video rates on all current hardware. Strengths: Smooth and continuous falloff of aberration correction outside the foveal region; avoids sharp phase discontinuities found in piece-wise methods. Limitations: Cannot present true depth of field for closely spaced points at varying depths around the fovea; limited by the eye's visual acuity falloff. When to Use: When computational resources are limited and the user's gaze is tracked, and true depth of field for closely spaced objects is not critical. This method was introduced in the context of holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality. It was implemented on holographic display prototypes, with eye position simulated using a mouse cursor in lieu of an actual eye tracker. The method addresses the accommodation-convergence conflict by adjusting focus and addressing aberrations, while approximating depth of field in image space. name: Aberration and Vision Correction via Zernike Polynomials
head: Zernike Wavefront Shaping, Zernike-based Aberration Correction
body: This method pre-compensates for optical aberrations in display hardware and vision deficiencies in the viewer by shaping the wavefront for each object point using Zernike polynomials. It builds on Foveated Spatially Varying Lens Approximation by replacing the simple lens phase function with a parameterized wavefront correction that offers practically unlimited degrees of freedom for spatially variant correction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured Zernike coefficients a{jo} for a set of object points; object position \vec{o}; hologram plane geometry. Output: Complex phase function fz(\rho, \theta)o for each object point, which modulates the hologram to correct aberrations. Data Structures: Coefficients a{jo}: Array of floating-point values representing the magnitude of each Zernike term for object point o. Polar coordinates (\rho, \theta): Normalized radius and angle relative to the center of the sub-hologram for object point o. Steps: 1. Calibrate Coefficients: Determine the measured Zernike coefficients a{jo} for a sparse set of object points via user feedback (see Subtopics). 2. Adjust for Depth: Adjust the focus coefficient a{3o} from its measured value based on the focal depth of the imagery. 3. Correct Object Phase: Calculate the consistent object phase \phio at the hologram plane to handle widely varying object depths: \phio = -\frac{2\pi}{\lambda} (kp \|\vec{o}\| - l\|\vec{k}\| + kp \|\vec{o}\| - \vec{o}\|\vec{k}\|) where \vec{p}{co} is the center point of the sub-hologram for object point \vec{o}, \lambda is the wavelength, and kp, l, \vec{k} are geometric constants related to the propagation path. 4. Compute Zernike Terms: For each relevant Zernike polynomial j, compute the term Zj(\rho, \theta)o using the normalized polar coordinates \rho and \theta: Focus (j=3): Z3(\rho, \theta)o = a{3o} \frac{(2\rho^2 - 1)^2}{2} Vertical Astigmatism (j=4): Z4(\rho, \theta)o = a{4o} \frac{(\rho \cos^2\theta)^2}{2} Oblique Astigmatism (j=5): Z5(\rho, \theta)o = a{5o} \frac{(\rho \sin^2\theta)^2}{2} Horizontal Coma (j=6): Z6(\rho, \theta)o = a{6o} \frac{((3\rho^2 - 2)\rho \cos\theta)^2}{2} Vertical Coma (j=7): Z7(\rho, \theta)o = a{7o} \frac{((3\rho^2 - 2)\rho \sin\theta)^2}{2} 5. Combine Phase: Compute the total lens phase function fz(\rho, \theta)o by summing the object phase and the Zernike terms: fz(\rho, \theta)o = e^{i(\phio + \sumj Zj(\rho, \theta)o)} 6. Encode: Convert the complex value fz into a double-phase hologram representation for display on a phase-only spatial light modulator (SLM). Parameters: a{jo}: Measured Zernike coefficients. Typical values depend on the user's specific aberrations and the display's optical errors. \rho, \theta: Polar radius and angle, normalized to the sub-hologram center. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Measurement Impracticality: It is impractical to measure fz for all millions of object points. Coefficients must be measured for a sparse subset and interpolated. Phase Consistency: Without the object phase correction \phio, widely varying object depths produce poor results due to inconsistent phase at the hologram plane. Resolution Loss: Encoding complex values into double-phase holograms results in a corresponding loss in resolution. Interpolation: Aberrations are assumed to vary smoothly; interpolation is used for unmeasured points. A procedure to obtain Zernike coefficients a{jo} for the lens phase function fz by treating the display and eye optics as a black box. The display presents a single object point o to the user, represented in the hologram as fz(\rho, \theta)o. The user adjusts the coefficients a{jo} until the most tightly focused spot is seen. This process is repeated for additional object points o. The effect of adjusting various coefficients is orthogonal and corresponds roughly to familiar geometric operations (scale, squash, rotate, etc.). It is impractical to measure fz for all object points (millions); coefficients are measured for a subset (e.g., 15 points for highly aberrated systems, 1 point for non-aberrated displays) and interpolated. Complexity: The method adds a per-object-point phase computation cost. Interpolation of coefficients for unmeasured points adds a lookup/interpolation step. Performance: The correction is applied during hologram generation. The double-phase encoding step is trivial to compute after the complex-valued hologram is obtained. Strengths: Offers spatially variant correction with practically unlimited degrees of freedom, akin to using an independently customized complex lens for each point. Corrects both display hardware aberrations and viewer vision deficiencies. Limitations: Limited by the angular steering capability of the SLM. Resolution loss due to double-phase encoding. Requires user calibration, which is time-consuming if many points are measured (though interpolation mitigates this). When to use: When high-quality vision correction or hardware aberration correction is required for holographic near-eye displays. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and interpolation errors are unacceptable, or when the SLM's angular steering capability is insufficient for the required correction range. Originated in the context of holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality. The method leverages the optical correction capabilities of Fresnel holograms, which can arbitrarily shape the wavefront for each object point. The specific Zernike polynomials and calibration procedure were detailed in work by Maimone et al.. Holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality, https://doi.org/10.1145/3072959.3073624, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Split-Stream-FFT
body: Split-Stream-FFT is a GPU-optimized implementation of the Fast Fourier Transform designed to map the recursive structure of the FFT to the stream architecture of graphics hardware. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for volume rendering and other DSP applications by leveraging the parallel processing capabilities of commodity GPUs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of N complex samples f(n), where 0 \le n < N and N is a power of 2. Output: The frequency domain representation F(k), where 0 \le k < N, initially in bit-reversed order. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on a 1D array of complex numbers. No explicit tree structures are used; the recursion is implicit in the stage-based processing. Memory layout: A contiguous array of size N for input and output. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the input signal f(n) into the GPU memory. 2. Recursive Decomposition (DIF): Perform \log2 N stages of butterfly operations. In each stage, the data is divided into smaller DFTs. The division occurs in the frequency domain. The standard DFT definition includes a constant factor 1/N. This factor is discarded during the recursive steps to maintain a strict recursive structure without scaling at every level. The decomposition for a sequence of size N splits the input into even-indexed and odd-indexed frequency components based on the following relations for 0 \le n < N/2: e(n) = f(n) + f(n + N/2) o(n) = (f(n) - f(n + N/2)) e^{-2\pi i n / N} The resulting frequency values are computed as: F(k) = Fe(k) + WN^k Fo(k) \quad \text{for even } k F(k) = Fe(k) - WN^k Fo(k) \quad \text{for odd } k where Fe and Fo are the DFTs of the even and odd indexed input samples respectively, and WN^k = e^{-2\pi i k / N} is the twiddle factor. 3. Post-Processing: After all \log2 N stages are complete, the resulting frequency distribution is in the wrong order (bit-reversed). A bit-reversal (or tangling) operation is performed to re-sort the values into natural order. 4. Scaling: Multiply the final result by the constant factor 1/N to correct for the scaling discarded in step 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def splitstreamfft(f, N): """ Computes the FFT of input array f of size N using DIF approach. Returns F in bit-reversed order, then applies bit-reversal and scaling. """ # f is a list of complex numbers of length N # N must be a power of 2 numstages = int(math.log2(N)) # Stage-based DIF butterfly operations for stage in range(numstages): blocksize = 2 (stage + 1) halfblock = blocksize // 2 for i in range(0, N, blocksize): for j in range(halfblock): idxeven = i + j idxodd = i + j + halfblock # Twiddle factor W{blocksize}^j twiddle = complex(math.cos(-2 math.pi j / blocksize), math.sin(-2 math.pi j / blocksize)) valeven = f[idxeven] valodd = f[idxodd] # Butterfly operation t = valodd twiddle f[idxeven] = valeven + t f[idxodd] = valeven - t # Bit-reversal permutation numbits = int(math.log2(N)) result = [0] N for i in range(N): rev = 0 temp = i for in range(numbits): rev = (rev << 1) | (temp & 1) temp >>= 1 result[rev] = f[i] # Post-multiply by 1/N for i in range(N): result[i] = result[i] / N return result Parameters: N: Input size, must be a power of 2. Typical values depend on the volume resolution (e.g., 128^3, 256^3). Reconstruction Filter: The source mentions using a Lanczos windowed-sinc function for resampling in the frequency domain, but this is part of the broader FVR pipeline, not the FFT itself. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate during the recursive stages. Boundaries: The algorithm assumes N is a power of 2. Non-power-of-2 sizes require padding or a different algorithm. Ordering: The output is in bit-reversed order. Failure to perform the bit-reversal step results in incorrect frequency ordering. Scaling: Forgetting to multiply by 1/N at the end results in an amplitude error. Uses the FFT to perform convolution efficiently. Split-Stream-FFT provides the transform component. GPU-based FFT Convolution Split-Stream-FFT is a specific implementation within this category, focusing on the GPU mapping of the FFT recursion. Domain-transform methods Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for N input values. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the input and output arrays. Performance: The method is designed for superior speed performance on commodity graphics hardware compared to naive implementations. Strengths: Efficient mapping to GPU stream architecture; high performance for DSP and volume rendering applications. Limitations: Requires N to be a power of 2; output is in bit-reversed order; subject to under-/oversampling and aliasing issues inherent to the DFT. When to use: When high-performance FFT computation is needed on a GPU for volume rendering or general DSP. When not to use: When the input size is not a power of 2 and padding is undesirable; when natural order output is required without post-processing. Split-Stream-FFT was introduced in the context of Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) on the GPU. The paper "Fourier volume rendering on the GPU using a split-stream-FFT" describes this novel implementation designed to take advantage of commodity graphics hardware features. It was developed to address the limitations of previous FVR approaches and to provide an efficient FFT implementation for volume visualization, which is seen as the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction. The method uses the Decimation-in-Frequency (DIF) approach and incorporates a Lanczos windowed-sinc function for reconstruction filtering. (PDF) Fourier volume rendering on the GPU using a split-..., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220838994FouriervolumerenderingontheGPUusingasplit-stream-FFT, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction
head: Hartley Transform for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Hartley Transform for Real-Valued Spectra, Hartley-based Volume Rendering, Real-valued Fourier Transform, Real-valued frequency domain rendering
body: Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction is a frequency-domain volume rendering technique that replaces the standard Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) with the Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) to map real-valued spatial data directly to real-valued spectra. This eliminates the need for complex number arithmetic, thereby reducing memory requirements by half compared to storing a full complex spectrum, and by a factor of 16 compared to double-precision complex Fourier transforms. It sets itself apart from standard Fourier-based frequency rendering by avoiding the complexity of handling Hermitian symmetry during slice extraction, which would otherwise be required to save memory in the Fourier domain. It builds on Domain-transform methods by providing the specific spectral representation and memory optimization strategies. The method follows the three-stage pipeline of domain-transform methods: Global Transformation, Slice Extraction, and Inverse Transformation [S1, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md, 895-hartley-transform-for-memory-reduction.md, 5396-dct-based-volume-rendering.md, unofficial]. Input: A 3D scalar volume f(x, y, z) of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Output: A 2D projection image I(u, v) for a given viewing direction. Spectrum Array: A 3D array of real-valued numbers. Format: 16-bit floating point is used to represent the spectrum to reduce memory cost. Memory Reduction: This format reduces the memory cost factor to 2 compared to the original volume size (assuming 1-byte voxels), whereas a 64-bit double precision format would occupy 8 times more memory than the original volume. Precision: 64-bit double precision is considered a safe choice for representing the spectrum of a 256^3 volume due to its wide dynamic range, but 16-bit is used for efficiency. The continuous Hartley transform is defined as: FH(s) = \int{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x) \text{cas}(2\pi s x) dx where the kernel function \text{cas}(\theta) is defined as: \text{cas}(\theta) = \cos(\theta) + \sin(\theta) For the discrete case, the transform maps the real spatial domain volume to a real frequency domain spectrum. Floating Point Precision: 16-bit floating point is used to reduce memory cost. Volume Size: Examples include 128^3 (human head CT) and 256^3 (Utah teapot, turbine blade). 1. Preprocessing (Zero-Padding): Apply zero-padding to the input volume to mitigate boundary artifacts and aliasing, as the transform assumes periodic boundary conditions [S3, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md, 952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md, unofficial]. 2. Global Transformation (Forward Hartley Transform): Compute the 3D Hartley Transform of the preprocessed volume to obtain the real-valued frequency spectrum FH(\omega1, \omega2, \omega3). Store the spectrum in the 16-bit floating point format. 3. Slice Extraction: Define a 2D plane passing through the origin of the frequency domain and perpendicular to the viewing direction vector V [S3, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md, 6324-hartley-transform.md, unofficial]. Resample the 3D spectrum onto this 2D plane to obtain a 2D slice I(u, v). Since the slicing plane rarely coincides with the integer lattice of the discrete spectrum, interpolation is required [S3, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md, 6324-hartley-transform.md, unofficial]. Adaptive filtering can be used to reduce interpolation cost; relative error was always below 40dB, a level at which image differences are not visible. 4. Inverse Transformation: Apply the Inverse Hartley Transform to the extracted 2D slice to return to the spatial domain. 5. Post-processing: Convert the result from the 16-bit floating point format to the machine's native format for compositing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hartleytransformvolumerendering(volume, viewdirection): # 1. Preprocessing: Zero-pad to mitigate boundary artifacts # Standard practice: pad volume dimensions to next power of 2 for transform efficiency paddedvolume = zeropad(volume) # 2. Global Transformation: Compute 3D Hartley Transform spectrum = fasthartleytransform3d(paddedvolume) # Convert to 16-bit float for memory reduction spectrum16bit = quantizeto16bitfloat(spectrum) # 3. Slice Extraction: Define 2D plane perpendicular to viewdirection # Standard practice: construct orthonormal basis vectors u, v for the plane uvec, vvec = computeorthonormalbasis(viewdirection) width, height = computeoutputresolution(spectrum16bit.shape, viewdirection) ucoords = [u for u in linspace(-width / 2, width / 2, width)] vcoords = [v for v in linspace(-height / 2, height / 2, height)] # Resample spectrum onto the 2D plane using adaptive filtering slicedata = resamplespectrum(spectrum16bit, uvec, vvec, ucoords, vcoords) # 4. Inverse Transformation: Apply 2D Inverse Hartley Transform # The inverse Hartley transform is identical to the forward transform scaled by 1/N N = len(slicedata) len(slicedata[0]) inverseslice = fasthartleytransform2d(slicedata) / N # 5. Post-processing: Convert to native format image = converttonativeformat(inverseslice) return image def zeropad(data): # Implementation detail: Pad with zeros to next power of 2 newshape = tuple(2 int(ceil(log2(s))) for s in data.shape) padded = [[[[0.0 for in range(newshape[2])] for in range(newshape[1])] for in range(newshape[0])] for in range(1)] for i in range(data.shape[0]): for j in range(data.shape[1]): for k in range(data.shape[2]): padded[0][i][j][k] = data[i][j][k] return padded[0] def fasthartleytransform3d(data): # Apply 1D FHT along each axis sequentially temp = apply1dfhtalongaxis(data, axis=0) temp = apply1dfhtalongaxis(temp, axis=1) return apply1dfhtalongaxis(temp, axis=2) def apply1dfhtalongaxis(data, axis): # Compute 1D DHT along the specified axis # DHT of a signal x[n] of length N: X[k] = sum{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] cas(2pikn/N) N = data.shape[axis] result = [[[0.0 for in range(data.shape[2])] for in range(data.shape[1])] for in range(data.shape[0])] n = list(range(N)) k = list(range(N)) # Precompute cas kernel caskernel = [[cos(2 pi kval nval / N) + sin(2 pi kval nval / N) for nval in n] for kval in k] # Apply transform along axis for i in range(data.shape[axis]): for j in range(data.shape[1]): for l in range(data.shape[2]): val = 0.0 for m in range(N): val += data[m][j][l] caskernel[i][m] result[i][j][l] = val return result def computeorthonormalbasis(viewdirection): # Standard practice: find two vectors orthogonal to viewdirection vx, vy, vz = viewdirection if abs(vz) < 0.9: uvec = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: uvec = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Subtract projection onto viewdirection dot = uvec[0]vx + uvec[1]vy + uvec[2]vz uvec = [uvec[i] - dot viewdirection[i] for i in range(3)] norm = sqrt(sum(xx for x in uvec)) uvec = [x / norm for x in uvec] # Cross product for vvec vvec = [uvec[1]vz - uvec[2]vy, uvec[2]vx - uvec[0]vz, uvec[0]vy - uvec[1]vx] norm = sqrt(sum(xx for x in vvec)) vvec = [x / norm for x in vvec] return uvec, vvec def computeoutputresolution(spectrumshape, viewdirection): # Standard practice: determine output grid size based on bandwidth return (spectrumshape[0], spectrumshape[1]) def resamplespectrum(spectrum, uvec, vvec, ucoords, vcoords): # Standard practice: trilinear or adaptive filtering interpolation slicedata = [[0.0 for in vcoords] for in ucoords] for i, u in enumerate(ucoords): for j, v in enumerate(vcoords): # Map 2D coordinates to 3D frequency domain coordinates freqx = u uvec[0] + v vvec[0] freqy = u uvec[1] + v vvec[1] freqz = u uvec[2] + v vvec[2] slicedata[i][j] = interpolate3d(spectrum, freqx, freqy, freqz) return slicedata def interpolate3d(data, x, y, z): # Standard practice: trilinear interpolation ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz ix = max(0, min(ix, len(data) - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, len(data[0]) - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, len(data[0][0]) - 1)) c00 = data[ix][iy][iz] (1 - fx) (1 - fy) (1 - fz) c10 = data[ix + 1][iy][iz] fx (1 - fy) (1 - fz) c01 = data[ix][iy + 1][iz] (1 - fx) fy (1 - fz) c11 = data[ix + 1][iy + 1][iz] fx fy (1 - fz) c00z = data[ix][iy][iz + 1] (1 - fx) (1 - fy) fz c10z = data[ix + 1][iy][iz + 1] fx (1 - fy) fz c01z = data[ix][iy + 1][iz + 1] (1 - fx) fy fz c11z = data[ix + 1][iy + 1][iz + 1] fx fy fz return c00 + c10 + c01 + c11 + c00z + c10z + c01z + c11z def quantizeto16bitfloat(data): # Implementation detail: map 64-bit float to 16-bit float representation return [[float16(data[i][j][k]) for k in range(len(data[0][0]))] for j in range(len(data[0])) for i in range(len(data))] def converttonativeformat(data): return [[float32(data[i][j]) for j in range(len(data[0]))] for i in range(len(data))] Precision: Round-off error from using 16-bit floating point format resulted in a relative difference below 50dB compared to 64-bit double precision images, which is generally acceptable. Hermitian Symmetry: Unlike the Fourier transform, the Hartley transform does not produce a Hermitian symmetric spectrum for real inputs, so no half-spectrum storage is needed, simplifying slice extraction. Boundary Artifacts: The transform assumes periodic boundary conditions; failure to zero-pad or apply vignetting correction can lead to aliasing and boundary artifacts [S3, 824-fourier-projection-slice-volume-rendering.md, 952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md, unofficial]. Hartley Transform Volume Rendering is a frequency-domain technique that replaces spatial domain projection, shading, and depth cueing computations with frequency domain operations using the Hartley transform to reduce memory cost and computational complexity. It sets itself apart from standard Fourier-based frequency rendering by using real-valued kernels, which eliminates complex number arithmetic and simplifies slice extraction compared to handling Hermitian symmetry. It builds on Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction by providing the complete rendering pipeline, including adaptive filtering and format conversion. The GPU-based Fast Hartley Transform (FHT) is a frequency-domain volume rendering method that replaces the Fourier transform with the Hartley transform to map real-valued input data directly to real-valued spectra. This reduces memory requirements by half compared to the standard GPU-based Fourier transform. It builds on Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction by providing a specific GPU shader implementation using double butterfly passes and dual lookup textures. Time Complexity: The frequency domain method grows much slower than the O(n^3) spatial domain method. Memory Complexity: The Hartley transform reduces memory requirements by half compared to storing a full complex spectrum, and by a factor of 16 compared to double-precision complex Fourier transforms. Using 16-bit floating point format reduces the memory cost factor to 2 compared to the original volume size. Measured Performance: Rendering times were measured on an IRIS Crimson with a 50Mhz R4000 processor using non-optimized code. For a 128^3 volume, frequency domain rendering took 0.54 seconds compared to 1.77 seconds for spatial domain rendering. For a 256^3 volume, frequency domain rendering took 2.03 seconds compared to 24.29 seconds for spatial domain rendering. Strengths: Significant memory reduction, faster rendering for large volumes, simplified slice extraction compared to Fourier-based methods with half-spectrum storage. Limitations: Requires preprocessing (transform and inverse transform), potential precision loss with 16-bit format (though generally acceptable), and assumes periodic boundary conditions. When to Use: Suitable for large volumes where memory is a constraint and real-time or near-real-time rendering is not strictly required, or when hardware supports efficient Hartley transforms. When Not to Use: When complex number arithmetic is already optimized in hardware, or when the volume size is small enough that memory is not a bottleneck. The Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction was introduced by Takashi Totsuka and Marc Levoy in their 1993 paper "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering". The paper demonstrated the use of the Hartley transform to avoid complex number arithmetic in frequency domain volume rendering, thereby reducing memory requirements. The method was tested on human head CT data, Utah teapot, and turbine blade volumes, showing significant performance improvements over spatial domain rendering. The Hartley transform is a direct relative of the Fourier transform, defined by the kernel \text{cas}(\theta) = \cos(\theta) + \sin(\theta). name: Hartley Transform Volume Rendering
head: Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) Volume Rendering, Fourier Volume Rendering (using Hartley), Hartley-based Volume Rendering, Hartley-based frequency domain rendering, Real-valued frequency domain rendering
body: Hartley Transform Volume Rendering is a frequency-domain technique that replaces spatial domain projection, shading, and depth cueing computations with frequency domain operations using the Hartley transform to reduce memory cost and computational complexity. It sets itself apart from standard Fourier-based frequency rendering by using real-valued kernels, which eliminates complex number arithmetic and simplifies slice extraction compared to handling Hermitian symmetry. It builds on Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction by providing the complete rendering pipeline, including adaptive filtering and format conversion. Inputs: 3D volume data V(x,y,z) (typically padded to powers of 2, e.g., 128^3 or 256^3). Outputs: 2D projected image. Data Structures: Volume Data: 3D array of real values. Spectrum: 3D array of real values representing the Hartley transform of the volume. Format: 16-bit floating point format is used for the spectrum to reduce memory cost. Parameters: Floating Point Format: 16-bit float; 64-bit double precision is considered safe for 256^3 volumes but consumes significantly more memory. Adaptive Filtering Threshold (d{max}): 0.3, controlling the switch between filter sizes. Steps: 1. Pre-multiplication: Pre-multiply the volume data before transforming to handle the wide dynamic range of spectra. 2. Forward Hartley Transform: Perform the Hartley transform on the volume data to obtain the 3D spectrum H(sx, sy, sz). The Hartley transform is defined as: H\{f(\mathbf{x})\} = \int{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(\mathbf{x}) \text{cas}(2\pi \mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{x}) d\mathbf{x} where \text{cas}(x) = \cos(x) + \sin(x). 3. Frequency Domain Shading and Depth Cueing: Apply shading and depth cueing in the frequency domain. Multiple light sources are handled by shading the volume data (e.g., using gradient vectors for orientation intuition) before or during the transform process. For example, multiple lights can be applied to create color cues for gradient orientation. 4. Slice Extraction: For each frame, extract the relevant slice from the 3D spectrum corresponding to the current view angle. This involves interpolation and resampling. 5. Adaptive Filtering: Perform adaptive filtering on the extracted slice to reduce interpolation cost. Use a 3 \times 3 \times 3 filter and a 1 \times 1 \times 1 filter. The switch between filters is determined by the maximum difference in response (d{max}) of 0.3. If the difference is below d{max}, the smaller filter is used. 6. Inverse Hartley Transform: Perform the inverse Hartley transform on the filtered slice to return to the spatial domain. 7. Format Conversion: Convert the result from the 16-bit floating point format to the machine's native format for display. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def hartleytransformvolumerendering(volumedata, viewangle, dmax=0.3): # Step 1: Pre-multiply volume data to handle wide dynamic range of spectra # Specific pre-multiplication factor not given in sources. premultipliedvolume = volumedata # Step 2: Forward Hartley Transform to obtain 3D spectrum # Standard relation: H(s) = Re(F(s)) - Im(F(s)) where F is DFT fourierspectrum = np.fft.fftn(premultipliedvolume) spectrum = np.real(fourierspectrum) - np.imag(fourierspectrum) # Step 3: Frequency Domain Shading and Depth Cueing # Shading modifies spectrum based on light sources and gradient vectors shadedspectrum = applyfrequencydomainshading(spectrum, viewangle) # Step 4: Slice Extraction for current view angle extractedslice = extractslicefromspectrum(shadedspectrum, viewangle) # Step 5: Adaptive Filtering to reduce interpolation cost filteredslice = adaptivefilter(extractedslice, dmax) # Step 6: Inverse Hartley Transform to return to spatial domain # Inverse DHT of real spectrum is equivalent to Inverse DFT real part spatialresult = np.real(np.fft.ifftn(filteredslice)) # Step 7: Format Conversion to machine native format finalimage = converttonativeformat(spatialresult) return finalimage def applyfrequencydomainshading(spectrum, viewangle): # Sources do not provide exact mathematical formulation for frequency domain shading. # Implementation applies lighting model to spectrum coefficients. return spectrum def extractslicefromspectrum(spectrum, viewangle): # Sources do not specify exact interpolation/resampling algorithm. # Implementation extracts 2D slice from 3D spectrum along view direction. return spectrum def adaptivefilter(slicedata, dmax): # Sources specify 3x3x3 and 1x1x1 filters with dmax=0.3 threshold # Implementation switches filter size based on maximum response difference. return slicedata def converttonativeformat(data): # Converts 16-bit float representation to standard float32/float64 return data.astype(np.float32) Pitfalls: The algorithm does not allow non-linear attenuation due to the linear nature of the transform. Using Fourier transform with Hermitian symmetry unnecessarily complicates slice extraction compared to the real-valued Hartley transform. Time Complexity: Spatial domain projection complexity is O(n^3). Frequency domain projection complexity is O(n^2 \log n). Shading and depth cueing in the frequency domain are O(n^2). Memory Complexity: A straightforward double precision 3D spectrum implementation consumes 16 times more memory than a spatial domain algorithm (assuming 1 byte per voxel). Using Hartley + 16-bit float reduces this factor to 2. Measured Performance: On an IRIS Crimson with a 50Mhz R4000 processor, a 128^3 volume can be rendered in a fraction of a second. Interpolation Cost: Adaptive filtering reduces interpolation operations to ~15% of the non-adaptive case (e.g., 17.1% for Head, 12.9% for Teapot, 16.2% for Turbine). Relative Error: Adaptive filtering relative error is always below 40dB, where image differences are not visible. Round-off Error: Using 16-bit float causes relative difference from 64-bit double precision images below 50dB. Strengths: Significant speed advantages over spatial domain methods; allows shading/depth cueing to be factored out; reduced memory usage with 16-bit float; real-valued arithmetic simplifies implementation. Limitations: Non-occluding projection operator results in a loss of realism (no shadows/occlusion); does not allow non-linear attenuation due to the linear nature of the transform. When to use: When speed is critical and occlusion/shadows are not required; when memory is a constraint and 16-bit precision is acceptable; when implementing on DSPs due to high data level parallelism. When not to use: When realistic shadows and occlusion are required; when non-linear attenuation effects are necessary. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering". History: The paper demonstrates the use of the Hartley transform to replace spatial domain computations with frequency domain operations. It highlights the benefits of real-valued arithmetic and reduced memory usage. Usage: Experiments used Human skull (CT data, 106^3 padded to 128^3), Utah teapot (3D scanconverted to 256^3), and Turbine blade (256^3). Hardware: Suggested for implementation on Digital Signal Processors (DSPs) due to high data level parallelism and convolution/FFT core computations. name: GPU-based Fast Hartley Transform (FHT)
head: Fast Hartley Transform, GPU-based FHT, Hartley Transform Implementation
body: The GPU-based Fast Hartley Transform (FHT) is a frequency-domain volume rendering method that replaces the Fourier transform with the Hartley transform to map real-valued input data directly to real-valued spectra. This reduces memory requirements by half compared to the standard GPU-based Fourier transform. It builds on Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction by providing a specific GPU shader implementation using double butterfly passes and dual lookup textures. The FHT implementation on the GPU follows the structure of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) but modifies the butterfly operation and data storage to handle real-valued arithmetic. Input: A 3D volume dataset of real-valued samples (e.g., density values). Output: A 3D volume dataset of real-valued Hartley coefficients. The implementation requires two lookup textures to store the parameters for the butterfly operations, replacing the single complex-weight texture used in FFT. 1. FHT Lookup Texture 1: Format: Three-channel (RGB) texture. Content: Stores three integer addresses (indices) of the input samples that contribute to the final butterfly result. 2. FHT Lookup Texture 2: Format: Two-channel (LUMINANCE ALPHA) texture. Content: Stores precomputed weights for the cosine and sine terms required for the Hartley kernel. The transform is performed in passes. For multi-dimensional data, the separable approach is used: 1D transforms are performed along each axis, followed by a correction pass. 1. Scrambling: Perform the bit-reversal permutation (scrambling) exactly as in the standard FFT. 2. Butterfly Passes: Perform "double butterfly" passes instead of standard FFT butterfly passes. For each butterfly operation, the shader performs four texture fetches from the input data using the addresses stored in Lookup Texture 1. Let the four fetched values be v1, v2, v3, v4. Retrieve the precomputed cosine (c) and sine (s) weights from Lookup Texture 2. Compute the Hartley butterfly result by multiplying the input values with the trigonometric weights and summing them. The shader performs four texture fetches, sums them together, and performs correction according to equations 4 and 5 in the source literature. 3. Multi-dimensional Correction: In the multi-dimensional case, the product of the one-dimensional transforms for each direction is not yet the correct multi-dimensional Hartley transform. A final correction pass is applied to the product of the 1D transforms to yield the correct multi-dimensional result. The following pseudocode describes the GPU fragment shader logic for a single 1D butterfly pass. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fhtbutterflypass(inputvolume, lookuptex1, lookuptex2, outputvolume, coords): # Fetch three sample addresses from the 3-channel lookup texture idx1, idx2, idx3 = lookuptex1[coords] # The source specifies four texture fetches total; the fourth index logic is not detailed in the sources idx4 = coords # Fourth address derivation not provided in sources # Fetch precomputed cosine and sine weights from the 2-channel lookup texture cosw, sinw = lookuptex2[coords] # Perform four texture fetches as specified in the source v1 = inputvolume[idx1] v2 = inputvolume[idx2] v3 = inputvolume[idx3] v4 = inputvolume[idx4] # Multiply cos and sin terms with corresponding input values and sum them together # Exact coefficients and signs follow equations 4 and 5 in the source literature result = (v1 cosw) + (v2 sinw) + (v3 cosw) + (v4 sinw) outputvolume[coords] = result def fhtcorrectionpass(input1dtransforms, output3dtransform, coords): # Fetch 1D transform results for each dimension valx = input1dtransforms[coords[0]] valy = input1dtransforms[coords[1]] valz = input1dtransforms[coords[2]] # Apply correction to the product of 1D transforms # Exact correction formula not provided in sources; standard separable transform correction applies result = valx valy valz output3dtransform[coords] = result Lookup Textures: Must be precomputed and uploaded to GPU memory before rendering. Multi-dimensional Case: Requires a separate correction pass after the 1D transforms. Precision: The method relies on texture fetches and floating-point arithmetic. Precision errors may accumulate in deep butterfly hierarchies. Boundary Conditions: The scrambling and butterfly operations assume power-of-two dimensions for efficient bit-reversal and indexing. Memory Usage: Reduces memory requirements by half compared to FFT-based methods. The FHT lookup structure stores five values (three addresses and two weights) across two textures, whereas the FFT stores a complex weight, addresses, and a sign in a single texture. Performance: Tested on an ATI Radeon 9800 XT with 256 MB memory. Test Data: X-mas Tree volume of size 256^3. Resolutions: Tested at projection slice resolutions of 256^2 and 512^2 pixels. Interpolation: Performance was measured with nearest neighbor, trilinear, tri-cubic, and windowed sinc (Blackman window, width 4) interpolation. Strengths: Lower memory footprint than FFT; similar computational structure to FFT allows for optimized GPU shader implementation. Limitations: Requires two lookup textures instead of one, increasing texture memory bandwidth usage. The multi-dimensional correction pass adds an extra stage. The Fast Hartley Transform (FHT) was introduced as an alternative to the Fourier transform to reduce memory requirements by half. The theoretical basis is attributed to Bracewell [Bracewell 1986]. The GPU-based implementation for volume rendering was developed by Viola et al.. The work builds on Hart's implementation of FFT on the GPU [Engel 2003]. name: Frequency Domain Volume Rendering
head: Frequency Domain Volume Rendering (FVR) on GPU, GPU FVR, GPU-based Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Hardware-Accelerated FVR
body: Frequency Domain Volume Rendering (FVR) is a volume rendering technique that transforms scalar data from the spatial domain to the frequency domain, extracts a 2D projection slice, and inverse-transforms the result to the spatial domain, thereby avoiding the O(N^3) computational complexity of spatial projection methods. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on the Projection-Slice Theorem to decouple the rendering step from the dataset resolution, allowing the rendering performance to depend primarily on the output image resolution rather than the input volume size. The method follows the three-stage pipeline of domain-transform methods: Global Transformation, Slice Extraction, and Inverse Transformation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume f(x, y, z) of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Output: A 2D projection image of size Mx \times My. Data Structures: 1. Frequency Volume: A 3D texture storing complex numbers. In GPU implementations, this is typically a two-channel 32-bit floating-point 3D texture (real and imaginary parts). If the input dimensions are not powers of two, zero-padding is applied in the frequency domain to meet hardware texture dimension constraints. 2. Kernel Texture: A 1D floating-point RGBA texture storing the discretized filter kernel. For a kernel of width four, each channel stores one tile of the kernel. A single texture fetch at position X returns four weight values. 3. Scramble Lookup Texture: A texture containing pre-computed bit-reversal indices for the FFT scrambling phase. 4. Roots of Unity Texture: A texture storing the principal N-th roots of unity required for butterfly passes. 5. Ping-Pong Buffers: Two 2D textures used as source and destination buffers for iterative passes (scrambling and butterfly). Parameters: Interpolation Scheme: Nearest Neighbor (NN), Tri-linear (TL), Tri-cubic (TC), or Windowed Sinc. Window Function: For Windowed Sinc, a Blackman window of width four is used. Kernel Resolution: The discretized kernel has a resolution of 64 samples per filter tile. Samples per Tile: For cubic B-spline, the number of samples per filter tile can be 1, 4, or 16, influencing image quality. Projection Slice Resolution: Typically 256 \times 256 or 512 \times 512. Steps: 1. Pre-processing (CPU): 1. Rearrange spatial data to move the origin from the corner [0,0,0] to the center (wrap-around operation). 2. Perform a 3D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on the rearranged data. 3. Rearrange the transformed data to center low frequencies. 4. Upload the complex data to the GPU as a 3D texture. Optional: Suppress vignetting by spatially premultiplying the original volume with the reciprocal of the interpolation filter's frequency response. 2. Slicing Setup (GPU): 1. Map the 3D frequency texture onto a proxy geometry (a single quad) stretched over the rendering target. 2. Set texture coordinates to cover the entire 3D texture. 3. Rotate the texture around the frequency volume origin to define the viewing direction. The slice is perpendicular to the viewing direction and intersects the origin of the frequency spectrum. 3. Slice Extraction (Resampling): 1. For each fragment (pixel) in the rendering target, determine the corresponding 3D coordinate in the frequency texture based on the rotated texture coordinates. 2. Estimate blending factors by multiplying texture coordinates with the original texture resolution; the blending factors are the fractional parts of these new coordinates. 3. Fetch neighboring voxels from the 3D texture using the chosen interpolation scheme (NN, TL, TC, or Windowed Sinc). 4. Compute the weighted sum of the fetched voxels to produce the 2D slice value. Note: Higher-order filters (TC, Windowed Sinc) require more surrounding voxels (e.g., 64 for a 5 \times 5 \times 5 filter) compared to Tri-linear (8 voxels). 4. Inverse Transformation (GPU): 1. Perform a 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) on the extracted 2D slice. 2. Split the 2D IFFT into two passes: rows then columns. 3. Scrambling Phase: Swap samples at position x and y, where y is the bit-reversal of x. Use the scramble lookup texture for efficient swapping. 4. Butterfly Passes: Perform \log2(N) butterfly passes, where N is the number of rows or columns. Use ping-pong buffer swapping between source and destination textures. Fetch addresses of two contributing samples (a, b) and the principal N-th root of unity (w) from lookup textures. Perform complex multiplication and two additions: a' = a + w \cdot b, b' = a - w \cdot b. 5. Scale the final output by N^{-1} (where N is the total number of points in the 2D transform). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frequencydomainvolumerendering(volume3d, viewingdirection, outputsize): # Step 1: Pre-processing (CPU) volumecentered = rearrangeorigintocenter(volume3d) freqvolume3d = fft3d(volumecentered) freqvolumecentered = fftshift(freqvolume3d) gpufreqtexture = uploadtogpu(freqvolumecentered) # Step 2 & 3: Slicing (GPU Shader) slice2d = resampleslice(gpufreqtexture, viewingdirection, outputsize) # Step 4: Inverse 2D FFT (GPU Shader) # Transform rows slicerowstransformed = ifft1drows(slice2d) # Transform columns slicecolstransformed = ifft1dcols(slicerowstransformed) # Scale by N^-1 finalimage = slicecolstransformed / (outputsize[0] outputsize[1]) return finalimage def ifft1drows(data2d): for i in range(data2d.shape[0]): data2d[i,:] = ifft1dpass(data2d[i,:], data2d.shape[1]) return data2d def ifft1dcols(data2d): for i in range(data2d.shape[1]): data2d[:, i] = ifft1dpass(data2d[:, i], data2d.shape[0]) return data2d def ifft1dpass(arr, N): # Scrambling phase scrambled = bitreversescramble(arr) # Butterfly passes buffera = scrambled bufferb = [0.0] N numpasses = int(math.log2(N)) for i in range(numpasses): w = getrootofunity(i, N) for j in range(N): idxa, idxb = getbutterflyindices(j, i, N) vala = buffera[idxa] valb = buffera[idxb] prod = complexmultiply(w, valb) bufferb[j] = complexadd(vala, prod) bufferb[(j + N // 2) % N] = complexsub(vala, prod) buffera, bufferb = bufferb, buffera return buffera Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: The rendering target resolution must meet the Nyquist criterion. Low resampling quality introduces ghosts or non-existent frequencies. Ghosting/Copy Artifacts: Caused by the absence of zero-padding in the spatial domain, resulting in visible copies of the dataset. Vignetting Artifact: Central values of the final image are overemphasized due to the frequency response of the interpolation filter. Mitigated by spatial premultiplication with the reciprocal of the filter's frequency response. Overlapping Artifacts: Occur if the projection slice resolution is insufficient for the dataset resolution (e.g., a 256^3 dataset requires at least a 512 \times 512 slice). Hardware Limitations: NVIDIA GPUs do not natively support floating-point 3D textures, requiring storage in four-channel fixed-point textures and additional conversion before interpolation. Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering is a technique that performs the shear transformation of the shear-warp factorization in the frequency domain using the shifting theorem, allowing for arbitrary, view-independent sampling distances along viewing rays via zero-padding interpolation. Unlike standard shear-warp algorithms where sampling distance is coarse and view-dependent, this method decouples sampling density from the viewing direction by resampling in the frequency domain, thereby avoiding the large spatial zero-padding required by spatial-domain shear methods. A hardware realization of the FVR algorithm consisting of a memory block, a resampling block, and an Inverse FHT/FFT block. For a 256^3 dataset and 25 frames/sec frame rate, one interpolation step for a 512 \times 512 plane must be done within approximately 150 ns. This timing allows for a single interpolation unit and memory addressing logic without parallelization. A 5 \times 5 \times 5 filter (like tri-cubic spline or POCS) requires 64 surrounding voxels per sample point, which can be handled using a lookup table (e.g., EPROM) for precomputed function values. Time Complexity: The global transformation is O(N^3 \log N) and performed once offline. The rendering step is O(M^2 \log M), where M is the projection slice resolution. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D frequency volume (O(N^3)) and intermediate buffers for the 2D IFFT. Performance: Rendering performance depends on the resolution of the projection slice, not explicitly on the dataset resolution. Dataset resolution affects texture cache efficiency; higher resolution leads to more cache misses, causing slight performance differences (± 2 fps for a 512 \times 512 slice). Measured Performance: On an ATI Radeon 9800 XT, at 256 \times 256 resolution: NN=400 fps, TL=1050 fps, TC=180 fps, IFFT 2D=153 fps. At 512 \times 512 resolution: NN=500 fps, TL=350 fps, TC=45 fps, IFFT 2D=35 fps. The GPU implementation achieves a speed-up factor of approximately 17 compared to a CPU-based approach (17 fps on AMD Athlon XP 2200+). Strengths: High performance for static views; decouples rendering speed from dataset size. Limitations: Limited interactivity for display parameters other than viewing direction; requires significant preprocessing; sensitive to interpolation quality and resolution. When to use: When rendering large static volumes with high performance requirements and fixed viewing parameters. When not to use: When interactive modification of opacity, lighting, or other transfer function parameters is required. Frequency Domain Volume Rendering was introduced by Ivan Viola, Armin Kanitsar, and Eduard Gröller in 2004. The method leverages the Projection-Slice Theorem to accelerate volume rendering by moving the computationally expensive projection step into the frequency domain, where it becomes a simple slice extraction. The GPU-based implementation was recognized with the second-best paper award at SCCG 2004. name: Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering
head: FDVR, Fourier Volume Rendering, Resampling in the Frequency Domain
body: Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering is a technique that performs the shear transformation of the shear-warp factorization in the frequency domain using the shifting theorem, allowing for arbitrary, view-independent sampling distances along viewing rays via zero-padding interpolation. Unlike standard shear-warp algorithms where sampling distance is coarse and view-dependent, this method decouples sampling density from the viewing direction by resampling in the frequency domain, thereby avoiding the large spatial zero-padding required by spatial-domain shear methods. The method builds on Frequency Domain Volume Rendering by replacing the spatial shear stage with frequency-domain operations. Inputs and Outputs Input: Volume dataset V of size N \times N \times N (cubiform, power of two), viewing vector \vec{v}{so}, desired sampling distance s', slice distance dk. Output: Rendered image with arbitrary sampling distance s' along viewing rays. Data Structures Volume Data: 3D array of voxel values. Frequency Domain: 3D complex array resulting from FFT. Slices: 2D arrays representing planes perpendicular to the viewing direction. Numbered Steps 1. Permutation: Change the storage order of voxels in memory to maximize cache coherency, such that the (i, j) plane is most perpendicular to the viewing direction. The volume starts in the standard object coordinate system, already permuted such that the (i, j) plane is most perpendicular to the viewing direction. 2. 3D Fourier Transform: Compute the 3D Fourier transform of the permuted volume to reach the frequency domain representation. 3. Calculate Pre-Resampling Sampling Distance (s): Compute the sampling distance along the viewing rays before resampling using the viewing vector and slice distance. Normalize the viewing vector \vec{v}{so} = (v{so,i}, v{so,j}, v{so,k}) in the k direction by dividing each component by v{so,k}, yielding \vec{v}'{so} = (v'{so,i}, v'{so,j}, v'{so,k}) with v'{so,k} = 1.0. Calculate s using the formula: s = dk \sqrt{(v'{so,i})^2 + (v'{so,j})^2 + (v'{so,k})^2} where s is the sampling distance before resampling, dk is the distance between volume slices along the k axis, and v'{so,i}, v'{so,j}, v'{so,k} are the components of the normalized viewing vector. 4. Calculate Post-Resampling Slice Count (K'): Determine the number of slices needed after resampling to achieve the desired sampling distance s' using the ratio of desired to current sampling distance and the current slice count K. The relationship is given by: \frac{s'}{s} = \frac{K}{K'} Solve for K': K' = \frac{sK}{s'} Round K' to the closest integer K0^{pad} \in \mathbb{N}. 5. Zero-Padding: Append zeros in the frequency domain along the k direction to increase the number of slices from K to K0^{pad}, exploiting the packing theorem (zero-padding interpolation property). The difference between K0^{pad} and K is the amount of zero-padding necessary for the selected sampling distance s'. Note: For K0^{pad} > 50, the deviation from the desired sampling distance s' is below \pm 1.0\%. 6. Inverse Fourier Transform in k: Apply an inverse Fourier transform in the k direction while keeping the i and j directions in the frequency domain to obtain sheared slices. This stage effectively performs the shear transformation via the shifting theorem in the frequency domain. 7. Compositing: Perform numeric integration along the viewing rays on the resampled slices. This stage uses the arbitrary sampling distance s' independent of the viewing direction. 8. Warping: Transform the intermediate image of the compositing stage into the final image. The warping in this method remains similar to the standard shear-warp algorithm. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def frequencydomainshearwarp(volume, dk, sprime, K, vprimei, vprimej): """ Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering pipeline. volume: 3D array of shape (N, N, N) dk: slice distance along k axis sprime: desired sampling distance along viewing rays K: number of slices in k direction (typically N) vprimei, vprimej: normalized viewing vector components (vprimek = 1.0) """ N = volume.shape[0] # Step 1: Permutation (conceptual, assumes input is already aligned) # In practice, axes are permuted so the k-axis aligns with the dominant viewing direction. # Step 2: 3D Fourier Transform freqvolume = np.fft.fftn(volume) # Step 3: Calculate Pre-Resampling Sampling Distance (s) vprimek = 1.0 s = dk math.sqrt(vprimei2 + vprimej2 + vprimek2) # Step 4: Calculate Post-Resampling Slice Count (K') Kprimefloat = (s K) / sprime K0pad = int(round(Kprimefloat)) # Step 5: Zero-Padding in frequency domain along k paddedfreq = np.zeros((K0pad, N, N), dtype=complex) paddedfreq[:N,:,:] = freqvolume # Step 6: Inverse Fourier Transform in k shearedslicesfreq = np.fft.ifft(paddedfreq, axis=0) # Step 7: Compositing (numeric integration along viewing rays) # The exact compositing formula is not provided in the sources; standard front-to-back integration is used. # Numpy's ifft normalizes by N^3, so slice data must be scaled back to physical density units. image = np.zeros((N, N), dtype=np.float32) T = np.ones((N, N), dtype=np.float32) # Transmission for k in range(K0pad): # Scale back to density units and apply step size s' for numeric integration density = np.real(shearedslicesfreq[k]) (N3) alpha = density sprime alpha = np.clip(alpha, 0.0, 1.0) image += T alpha T = (1.0 - alpha) if np.all(T == 0): break # Step 8: Warping (conceptual, maps intermediate image to screen coordinates) # Standard shear-warp warping applies affine transformations to map the permuted coordinate system to screen space. return image Parameters Desired Sampling Distance (s'): The target sampling distance along the viewing rays, which is independent of the view direction. Slice Distance (dk): The distance between volume slices along the k axis in the object coordinate system. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Spatial Domain Zero-Padding: If spatial domain zero-padding is too small in shear-based methods, data passes over the border and re-enters from the other side due to periodicity, an error amplified by consecutive shears. This method avoids this by not requiring large spatial domain zero-padding. Rounding Error: Zero-padding can only be applied in discrete steps, so K0^{pad} is rounded to the closest integer. For K0^{pad} > 50, the deviation from the desired sampling distance s' is below \pm 1.0\%. Time Complexity: For a cubiform dataset with edge length N (power of two), the computational complexity is 6 \cdot N^3 \log2 N, consisting of one 3D FFT (3 \cdot N^3 \log2 N), N^2 1D IFFTs (N^3 \log2 N), and N^2 2D IFFTs (N^3 \log2 N). Memory Complexity: The method does not require large spatial domain zero-padding, resulting in significantly lower memory consumption compared to methods like Li et al.'s, which requires memory >5x higher. Performance: Experimental results show that the presented method outperforms established algorithms in the quality of the produced images. If the data is sampled above the Nyquist rate, the method is capable of perfect reconstruction of the original function. Strengths: Allows arbitrary, view-independent sampling distances; avoids periodicity errors from spatial shear; high reconstruction quality. Limitations: Requires FFT computation; rounding of slice count may introduce minor sampling distance deviations (negligible for K0^{pad} > 50). Origin: The method was introduced in a paper by researchers from the University of Technology, Austria, and Simon Fraser University, Vancouver, Canada. History: It is conceptually based on the shear-warp factorization, which consists of permutation, shearing, compositing, and warping stages. The method proposes performing the shear transformation in the frequency domain using the shifting theorem. Usage: Used for high-quality volume rendering, particularly where view-independent sampling and high reconstruction quality are required. name: Domain Repetition
head: Modular repetition, Tiling via modulo
body: Domain Repetition is a technique for creating infinite, periodic repetitions of an object in space by wrapping query coordinates using modulo arithmetic. It allows rendering an infinite grid of primitives by modifying the position before querying the base signed distance field (SDF). It builds on Domain-transform methods by applying a coordinate transformation stage to tile geometry without increasing polygon count. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point p = (px, py, pz) in world space, and repetition grid dimensions gx, gz for the x and z axes. The y-axis is typically left unmodified to allow vertical stacking or single-layer tiling. Output: A transformed point p' suitable for querying a base SDF, and the resulting distance value. Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values and vectors. Steps: 1. Modulo Wrapping: Apply the modulo operation to the x and z coordinates of the point p using the grid dimensions gx and gz. This maps the infinite space into a periodic interval 0, gx) and [0, gz). 2. Centering: Shift the result by -0.5 \times g to center the repeated domain around the origin. This ensures that the base primitive (e.g., a sphere or cube centered at the origin) is repeated symmetrically around each grid cell center. 3. Evaluation: Evaluate the base distance field function (e.g., cube, sphere) on the transformed point p'. Formulas: The transformation for the x and z coordinates is defined as: p'x = \text{mod}(px, gx) - \frac{gx}{2} p'z = \text{mod}(pz, gz) - \frac{gz}{2} The y coordinate remains unchanged: p'y = py Parameters: gx, gz: The width and depth of the repeating cell. Typical values depend on the scene scale (e.g., 1.0 for unit cubes). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts: Distorting the distance field can cause "nasty artifacts" during raymarching. Mitigation: A suggested solution is to step shorter in the raymarching function than the distance field returns to avoid overshooting across tile boundaries. Boundary Conditions: The modulo operation assumes periodic boundary conditions. If the base SDF is not periodic or symmetric, visible seams may appear. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def mod(a, b): return a - b math.floor(a / b) def domainrepetition(p: Vector3, gx: float, gz: float) -> Vector3: """ Transforms point p by repeating it in the xz-plane with grid sizes gx and gz. """ px = mod(p.x, gx) - gx 0.5 pz = mod(p.z, gz) - gz 0.5 return Vector3(px, p.y, pz) def cube(p: Vector3) -> float: """ Standard SDF for a unit cube centered at the origin. """ q = Vector3(abs(p.x), abs(p.y), abs(p.z)) return max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)) - 0.5 def repeatedcubes(p: Vector3) -> float: """ Example: Repeated cubes in the xz-plane with grid size 1.0. """ transformedp = domainrepetition(p, 1.0, 1.0) return cube(transformedp) [Space Repetition is a domain-transform technique that creates infinite, periodic repetitions of a signed distance field (SDF) in 3D space by wrapping query coordinates using modulo arithmetic. It tiles space with a rectangular (Cartesian) cell structure, unlike Polar Modulo which repeats objects in a polar/cylindrical arrangement. Choose it for linear grid tiling. Polar Modulo repeats a 2D pattern around the origin by a fixed angle determined by the number of repetitions. It applies modulo arithmetic to the angular coordinate rather than Cartesian coordinates, enabling radial symmetry. Choose it for concentric or angular sectors. Time Complexity: O(1) per raymarch step. The modulo and arithmetic operations are constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the base SDF evaluation. Strengths: Extremely efficient for creating infinite environments or tiled patterns without increasing geometric complexity. Limitations: Can introduce visual artifacts at tile boundaries if not handled carefully (e.g., via smaller raymarch steps). The distance field is no longer globally smooth, which may affect gradient-based operations like normals if not computed carefully. When to use: When rendering infinite grids, tiled floors, or periodic structures. When not to use: When global smoothness or non-periodic boundaries are required. Domain Repetition is a technique popularized in the context of raymarching signed distance fields (SDFs) for real-time graphics. The method leverages the mathematical property of the modulo operator to map infinite space onto a finite repeating domain.
