name: Space Repetition
head: Infinite Domain Repetition, Infinite Repetition, Modular Repetition, Modulo Tiling, Primitive Repetition, Tiling via Modulo, repeat2d
body: Space Repetition is a technique to create infinite repetitions of a primitive (such as a rounded box or sphere) across 3D space by mapping the input position into a periodic cell using modulo arithmetic, then computing the distance to the primitive within that cell. Unlike primitive blending which smoothly interpolates between shapes, Space Repetition creates hard, periodic boundaries via modulo arithmetic, allowing infinite instances of a shape without increasing geometric complexity. It is a specific instance of Domain Repetition applied to Cartesian coordinates. Inputs: P: The query position in world space (vector). C: The repetition cell size (vector), defining the period in each dimension. Outputs: d: The signed distance to the nearest instance of the base primitive. Data Structures: None required beyond standard vector types. Steps: 1. Map to Periodic Cell: Transform the input position P into the fundamental domain (the cell containing the origin) using modulo arithmetic. The standard formula maps P to the range -C/2, C/2) centered at the origin: Q = P - C \cdot \text{round}\left(\frac{P}{C}\right) Alternatively, using a modulo operator that returns values in [0, C), the centering step is explicit: Q = \text{mod}(P, C) - 0.5 \cdot C Where \text{mod}(a, b) = a - b \cdot \lfloor a/b \rfloor. 2. Query Base [SDF: Compute the signed distance to the base primitive using the transformed position Q. d = \text{SDF}{\text{base}}(Q) Parameters: C: The repetition cell size. For uniform spacing, C = (c, c, c). A typical value is \text{vec3}(8.0, 8.0, 8.0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Near the boundaries of the cells (P \approx k \cdot C), floating-point precision errors in the modulo operation can cause artifacts or incorrect distance calculations. The round-based formula is generally more stable than mod followed by subtraction if the language's mod function has discontinuities. Boundary Continuity: The distance function is continuous across cell boundaries because the base primitive's distance is evaluated at the same relative position in every cell. However, the gradient may be discontinuous if the base primitive has sharp features aligned with the cell boundaries. Negative Coordinates: The formula P - C \cdot \text{round}(P/C) handles negative coordinates correctly, centering the cell around the origin. Simple mod implementations often return positive values only, requiring the explicit -0.5 \cdot C shift. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spacerepetition(p: Vector3, c: Vector3, basesdf: Callable[[Vector3], float]) -> float: """ Repeats the basesdf infinitely in 3D space with period c. Args: p: Query position. c: Repetition cell size (vector). basesdf: Signed distance function for the primitive to repeat. Returns: Signed distance to the nearest repeated primitive. """ # Map p to the fundamental domain centered at origin # Formula: q = p - c round(p / c) # Note: round() rounds to nearest integer. # In languages without vectorized round, apply component-wise. q = p - c round(p / c) # Query the base primitive at the wrapped position return basesdf(q) Repeats primitives in polar coordinates (cylindrical symmetry) rather than Cartesian. Choose when you need radial tiling (e.g., rings, spokes) instead of grid tiling. Time Complexity: O(1) per query, identical to the base primitive. The modulo operation is a constant-time arithmetic operation. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional data structures are stored. Strengths: Infinite instances with zero memory overhead. Ideal for floors, walls, or abstract patterns where geometry is repetitive. Limitations: Only supports uniform, axis-aligned grid repetition. Cannot handle non-uniform scaling or rotation of the repetition grid without additional transformations. Artifacts may appear if the base primitive is not symmetric or if the cell size is not a multiple of the primitive's extent. When to use: When rendering infinite grids of identical objects (e.g., a tiled floor, a field of spheres). When not to use: When objects need to interact with each other (e.g., collision between adjacent instances) or when the repetition pattern is non-uniform. Space Repetition is a staple technique in Signed Distance Field (SDF) raymarching, popularized by tutorials on GPU raymarching and distance functions. It is often referred to as "cheating" because it allows the rendering of infinite geometry without increasing the scene's geometric complexity. The technique relies on the periodicity of the modulo operator to fold space. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 9 – Raymarching: Primitive Repetition, http://www.geeks3d.com/20130524/building-worlds-with-distance-functions-in-glsl-raymarching-glslhacker-tutorial-opengl/9/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) JamesRicher/TerminalSignedDistanceFieldRenderer, https://github.com/JamesRicher/TerminalSignedDistanceFieldRenderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Introduction to Raymarching Distance Functions, https://observablehq.com/@gre/introduction-to-raymarching-distance-functions, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Polar Modulo
head: Angular Modulo, Polar Tiling
body: Polar Modulo repeats a 2D pattern around the origin by a fixed angle determined by the number of repetitions. It builds on Domain Repetition by applying modulo arithmetic to the angular coordinate rather than Cartesian coordinates, enabling radial symmetry. Unlike Space Repetition which tiles in linear space, Polar Modulo creates concentric or angular sectors. Inputs: A 2D point p = (x, y), and an integer N (number of repetitions). Outputs: A wrapped 2D point p' and an integer index c identifying the repetition sector. Data Structures: p: vec2 (float x, float y). p': vec2 (float x, float y). c: int (sector index). N: int (repetitions). Steps: 1. Compute the angular step size: \theta = 2\pi / N. 2. Compute the raw angle and radius: \alpha = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x), \rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}. 3. Shift the angle to center the modulo window: \alpha{shift} = \alpha + \theta/2. 4. Determine the sector index: k = \lfloor \alpha{shift} / \theta \rfloor. 5. Wrap the angle into the primary sector: \alpha' = (\alpha{shift} \pmod \theta) - \theta/2. Note: The modulo operation must return a result in [0, \theta). 6. Reconstruct the point: p' = (\cos \alpha', \sin \alpha') \cdot \rho. 7. Fix the sector index for symmetry: If |k| \ge N/2, set k = |k|. 8. Return p' and k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def polarmodulo(p: tuple[float, float], N: int) -> tuple[tuple[float, float], int]: PI = 3.141592653589793 angle = 2.0 PI / N a = math.atan2(p[1], p[0]) + angle / 2.0 r = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[1]2) c = math.floor(a / angle) # GLSL-style mod: a - b floor(a / b), returns [0, b) a = a - angle math.floor(a / angle) - angle / 2.0 pprime = (math.cos(a) r, math.sin(a) r) if abs(c) >= N / 2: c = abs(c) return pprime, c Parameters: N: Number of repetitions. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Origin: If p = (0,0), \rho=0 and \alpha is undefined. The result is p'=(0,0) regardless of angle. Precision: Floating point errors in atan2 or mod can cause discontinuities at the branch cut. Centering the modulo window (\theta/2 shift) helps align the discontinuity with the negative x-axis or specific symmetry axes. A method to animate tentacles using polar repetition and phase offsets to create a trailing, unforced drift effect. Each strand has a unique phase offset, and the wave arrives later further down the strand. It is chosen when organic, non-rigid motion is required for radial patterns. Definition: Extends Polar Modulo by adding time-dependent displacement and per-strand phase offsets. Steps: 1. Place tentacles using Polar Modulo to determine base positions. 2. Assign each strand a phase offset \phi derived from a hash function: \phi = \operatorname{hash11}(\text{idx}). 3. Calculate wave displacement using depth-dependent amplitude and phase lag. Formula: The tentacle position is calculated as: \text{ring} = R\,(0.98 - 0.06\,dn) + (0.05 + 0.78\,dn^{2})\,\sin(1.55\,d - 2t + \phi) where R is the bell radius, dn is normalized distance along the strand, d is distance, t is time, and \phi is the phase offset. name: Fourier Transform
head: Discrete Fourier Transform, DFT
body: The Fourier Transform method converts a 3D scalar volume into the frequency domain to enable rendering via the Projection-Slice Theorem Domain-transform methods. It differs from spatial-domain methods by performing a global transformation of the entire volume, which allows for efficient convolution operations but requires significant preprocessing memory and does not support interactive parameter changes like opacity or lighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume f(x, y, z) of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Output: A 2D projection image I(u, v). Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array of real numbers representing the spatial domain. Frequency Data: A 3D array of complex numbers representing the frequency domain. For real input, the output is Hermitian symmetric, meaning H{-u,-v,-w} = H{u,v,w}^, allowing storage of only half the data if optimized. Parameters: N: Number of samples along a dimension. Assumed to be even for standard frequency point derivation. \Delta: Sampling interval (spacing between voxels). fc: Nyquist critical frequency, defined as 1/(2\Delta). Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Centering): To center the zero-frequency component in the middle of the spectrum and avoid boundary discontinuities in visualization, multiply the input volume by (-1)^{x+y+z}. The source explicitly defines this shift for 1D signals as multiplying by (-1)^k and for 2D signals as multiplying by (-1)^{x+y}; the 3D extension follows the same pattern. 2. Global Transformation (3D DFT): Compute the 3D Discrete Fourier Transform of the volume. For a 1D sequence hk of length N, the DFT Hn is defined as: Hn = \sum{k=0}^{N-1} hk e^{2\pi i k n/N} For a 3D volume f(x, y, z), the 3D DFT F(u, v, w) is computed as: F(u, v, w) = \sum{x=0}^{Nx-1} \sum{y=0}^{Ny-1} \sum{z=0}^{Nz-1} f(x, y, z) e^{2\pi i (ux/Nx + vy/Ny + wz/Nz)} The source defines the forward DFT with a positive exponent in Eq. 2.13. 3. Slice Extraction: According to the Projection-Slice Theorem, the 2D Fourier transform of a projection of the volume along a viewing direction is equal to a 2D slice through the origin of the 3D Fourier transform, perpendicular to the viewing direction. Extract a 2D plane from the 3D frequency volume F(u, v, w) corresponding to the viewing direction. The extracted slice lies on a grid that may not align with the discrete 3D lattice of F. Interpolation (e.g., trilinear or sinc) is required to resample the frequency data onto the 2D output grid. 4. Inverse Transformation (2D IDFT): Compute the 2D Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform of the extracted slice to obtain the spatial domain projection image. The exact normalization factor (1/N or 1/\sqrt{N}) depends on the specific DFT definition used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath def dft1d(signal): N = len(signal) return [sum(signal[k] cmath.exp(2j math.pi k n / N) for k in range(N)) for n in range(N)] def dft3d(volume): Nx, Ny, Nz = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) F = [[[0+0j for in range(Nz)] for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] for u in range(Nx): for v in range(Ny): for w in range(Nz): s = 0+0j for x in range(Nx): for y in range(Ny): for z in range(Nz): s += volume[x][y][z] cmath.exp(2j math.pi (ux/Nx + vy/Ny + wz/Nz)) F[u][v][w] = s return F def idft2d(slice2d): Ou, Ov = len(slice2d), len(slice2d[0]) image = [[[0+0j for in range(Ov)] for in range(Ou)]] for x in range(Ou): for y in range(Ov): s = 0+0j for u in range(Ou): for v in range(Ov): s += slice2d[u][v] cmath.exp(-2j math.pi (ux/Ou + vy/Ov)) image[0][x][y] = s / (Ou Ov) return image[0] def trilinearinterpolate(freqvol, coords): # coords: (u, v, w) in frequency space # Returns interpolated complex value # Implementation uses standard trilinear interpolation over the 3D lattice pass def fouriertransformvolumerendering(volume, viewdirection, outputshape): Nx, Ny, Nz = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) Ou, Ov = outputshape # Step 1: Preprocessing - Center the zero frequency centeredvolume = [[[volume[x][y][z] ((-1)(x + y + z)) for z in range(Nz)] for y in range(Ny)] for x in range(Nx)] # Step 2: Global Transformation - 3D DFT freqvolume = dft3d(centeredvolume) # Step 3: Slice Extraction # Define 2D basis vectors perpendicular to viewdirection # Generate 2D grid coordinates in the plane perpendicular to viewdirection # Interpolate values from the 3D frequency volume onto this 2D grid slice2d = [[[0+0j for in range(Ov)] for in range(Ou)]] for uout in range(Ou): for vout in range(Ov): # Compute 3D frequency coordinates corresponding to (uout, vout) # The plane passes through the origin in the centered frequency domain coords3d = computeplanecoords(uout, vout, viewdirection, (Nx, Ny, Nz)) slice2d[0][uout][vout] = trilinearinterpolate(freqvolume, coords3d) # Step 4: Inverse Transformation - 2D IDFT imagecomplex = idft2d(slice2d[0]) # Return the real part of the image return [[math.real(imagecomplex[x][y]) for y in range(Ov)] for x in range(Ou)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: The DFT assumes periodic boundary conditions. Discontinuities at the volume boundaries cause high-frequency artifacts. Mitigation includes zero-padding the volume by a factor of k2 (typically 4/3) and applying vignetting correction (premultiplying by the reciprocal of the interpolation filter response). Aliasing: If the output image resolution is too low, aliasing artifacts will appear. The resolution must meet the Nyquist criterion relative to the volume's bandwidth. Hermitian Symmetry: For real-valued input, the DFT output is Hermitian symmetric. This can be exploited to reduce memory usage by storing only half the complex coefficients. The Windowed Fourier Transform (WFT), also known as the Gabor Transform, addresses the lack of spatial localization inherent in the standard Fourier Transform. While the standard Fourier Transform provides a global frequency measure by integrating over the entire spatial domain, making it difficult to locate irregularities, the WFT uses a translated window function to cover the signal, allowing for the localization of these irregularities. It builds on Fourier Transform by introducing spatial constraints to the frequency analysis. Time Complexity: The 3D DFT using FFT algorithms has a complexity of O(N^3 \log N) for a volume of size N^3. The 2D IDFT for an image of size M \times M has a complexity of O(M^2 \log M). Memory Complexity: The 3D frequency volume requires O(N^3) memory. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the global 3D transform. It is suitable for static volumes where the viewing direction changes frequently, as the 3D transform is performed once. Strengths: Efficient for multiple viewing angles once the 3D transform is computed. Limitations: High memory usage. Lack of interactivity for display parameters (opacity, lighting). Boundary artifacts require careful handling. The Fourier Transform is a classical theory for multiresolution decomposition. It provides a measure of high frequency but information is not spatially localized, as the transform covers the whole spatial domain, making it difficult to find the position of irregularities. name: Windowed Fourier Transform
head: Gabor Transform
body: The Windowed Fourier Transform (WFT), also known as the Gabor Transform, addresses the lack of spatial localization inherent in the standard Fourier Transform by introducing a spatially localized window function. While the standard Fourier Transform provides a global measure of frequency content across the entire signal, making it difficult to identify the position of irregularities, the WFT uses a translated window to cover the whole signal, allowing for the localization of these irregularities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A function f(x) belonging to the space L^2(\mathbb{R}) (square-integrable functions). Output: A 2D function Gf(u, \omega) representing the transform coefficients at position u and frequency \omega. Data Structures: The output is typically stored as a 2D grid or array where one axis represents the spatial translation parameter u and the other represents the frequency parameter \omega. Method: The transform is defined by the following integral: Gf(u, \omega) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) g(x - u) e^{-i \omega x} dx Symbol Definitions: f(x): The input signal or function. g(x): The window function (kernel), typically a Gaussian or similar localized function. u: The spatial translation parameter, shifting the window along the spatial axis. \omega: The frequency parameter. i: The imaginary unit. Steps: 1. Select a window function g(x) that is localized in space (e.g., decays rapidly away from the origin). 2. For each desired spatial position u and frequency \omega: a. Shift the window function to g(x - u). b. Multiply the input signal f(x) by the shifted window g(x - u). c. Multiply the result by the complex exponential kernel e^{-i \omega x}. d. Integrate the product over the entire spatial domain x \in (-\infty, \infty). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def windowedfouriertransform(f, g, uvalues, omegavalues): """ Computes the Windowed Fourier Transform for discrete inputs. Args: f: Array of input signal values f(x) at spatial points x. g: Array of window function values g(x) at spatial points x. Note: g should be centered at 0. uvalues: Array of spatial translation positions u. omegavalues: Array of frequency values omega. Returns: Gf: 2D array of shape (len(uvalues), len(omegavalues)). """ # Define the spatial grid corresponding to f and g # Assuming f and g are sampled on the same grid with spacing dx x = np.arange(len(f)) dx # dx is the spatial step size, assumed known or derived Gf = np.zeros((len(uvalues), len(omegavalues))) for i, u in enumerate(uvalues): for j, omega in enumerate(omegavalues): # Shift the window function to position u # gshifted[x] = g[x - u] # In discrete implementation, this involves interpolation or array shifting gshifted = interpolateshift(g, u) # Compute the integrand: f(x) g(x - u) exp(-i omega x) # Using trapezoidal or simple Riemann sum for integration integrand = f gshifted np.exp(-1j omega x) # Integrate over x # Using np.trapz for better accuracy than simple sum Gf[i, j] = np.trapz(integrand, x) return Gf def interpolateshift(g, u): """ Shifts the window function g by u. Since u may not be an integer index, interpolation is required. """ # Create indices for the shifted window # If g is defined on indices 0..N-1, g(x-u) corresponds to g at index k where kdx = x - u # This is a helper for the discrete implementation # For simplicity in this generic pseudocode, we assume a shift operation exists # In practice, one might use np.roll for integer shifts or FFT-based shifting for non-integer return np.roll(g, int(round(u / dx))) # Simplified; real implementation needs careful boundary handling Parameters: Window Function g(x): The choice of window (e.g., Gaussian, Hamming) affects the trade-off between spatial and frequency resolution. Not given in the sources. Step sizes for u and \omega: Determine the resolution of the output transform. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Effects: Since the window is localized, signals near the boundaries of the domain may be truncated if the window extends beyond the signal support. Zero-padding or periodic extension is often used to mitigate this. Precision: The integration step requires careful numerical handling, especially for high-frequency components where the complex exponential oscillates rapidly. A technique used in numerical holographic reconstruction to suppress side-lobe leakage and diffraction artifacts caused by the sharp intensity edges of a rectangular synthetic aperture. It works by smoothly tapering the aperture edges to zero, thereby reducing strong diffraction effects at the borders that would otherwise occur during propagation. It is applied after selecting a sub-region of the hologram (synthetic aperture) to define a specific viewpoint. A procedural noise function designed to support high-quality anisotropic filtering, addressing the trade-off between aliasing artifacts and detail loss inherent in isotropic noise methods. It partitions the frequency domain into oriented subbands using steerable filters, allowing the noise content to adapt to non-uniform perspective distortions and parametric surface distortions by adjusting subband weights during rendering. Time Complexity: The direct computation of the WFT for all u and \omega values is O(N \cdot M \cdot K), where N is the number of spatial samples, M is the number of u positions, and K is the number of \omega positions. This is significantly more expensive than the standard FFT (O(N \log N)). Memory Complexity: O(M \cdot K) to store the transform coefficients. Strengths: Provides simultaneous time (or space) and frequency localization, allowing for the analysis of non-stationary signals where frequency content changes over time/space. Limitations: High computational cost compared to global Fourier methods. The choice of window function imposes a fixed resolution trade-off (Heisenberg uncertainty principle). When to use: When the signal's frequency content varies with position and global Fourier analysis is insufficient. When not to use: When only global frequency statistics are needed or when computational resources are severely limited. The Windowed Fourier Transform was introduced by Dennis Gabor. Gabor defined this new decomposition using a spatial window g(x) in the Fourier integral to localize the information provided by the Fourier transform, which previously covered the whole spatial domain and was not spatially localized. The transform is translated along the spatial axis to cover the whole signal. name: Aperture Apodization
head: Hann Window, Hanning Window (incorrectly used), Hanning window apodization, Suppression of aperture diffraction, Synthetic Aperture Selection & Apodization
body: Aperture Apodization suppresses side-lobe leakage and aperture diffraction artifacts caused by the sharp intensity edges of a rectangular synthetic aperture during numerical holographic reconstruction. It smoothly tapers the aperture edges to zero, reducing strong diffraction effects at the borders. The method is applied after selecting a sub-region of the hologram to define a specific viewpoint. Inputs: Complex hologram matrix H of size N \times M. Aperture definition parameters: center coordinates (xc, yc), reconstruction distance dr, and aperture dimension angle \psi. Window parameter: Full Width at Half Maximum \alpha. Outputs: Apodized synthetic aperture matrix A{apo} of size N \times M (zero-padded to original hologram size). Data Structures: The synthetic aperture is a 2D sub-region of the hologram. The Hanning window is a 2D mask applied element-wise to the aperture. Steps: 1. Define Synthetic Aperture: Calculate the horizontal and vertical aperture angles \theta and \phi using the center coordinates (xc, yc) and reconstruction distance dr: \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{xc}{dr}\right) \phi = \arctan\left(\frac{yc}{dr}\right) The aperture dimension is controlled by the angle \psi. The specific pixel coordinates defining the rectangular sub-region are determined by these angles and the hologram resolution. 2. Extract Sub-Region: Extract the rectangular region from the hologram H defined by the calculated boundaries. Let this sub-region be A{sub} with dimensions W \times H. 3. Generate Hanning Window: Create a 1D Hanning window function hn(x): hn(x) = \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi x}{2\alpha}\right) where \alpha is the Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM). 4. Construct 2D Window: The 2D window W{2D}(u, v) is constructed by applying the 1D function along both axes. 5. Apply Apodization: Multiply the extracted sub-region A{sub} element-wise by the 2D Hanning window W{2D}: A{apo\sub} = A{sub} \odot W{2D} This smoothly brings the aperture edges to zero. 6. Zero-Pad: Zero-pad the apodized sub-region A{apo\sub} to the original hologram size N \times M to create the final apodized aperture matrix A{apo}. Parameters: \alpha: Full Width at Half Maximum of the Hanning window. Not given in the sources. \psi: Aperture dimension angle. Not given in the sources. dr: Reconstruction distance. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Loss: Apodization reduces resolution due to the limited signal area. Precision: Ensure the window function is correctly normalized or scaled if amplitude preservation is critical, though the source does not specify normalization. Boundary Alignment: The window must be correctly aligned with the extracted sub-region to ensure smooth tapering at the correct edges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatehanningwindow1d(length, alpha): """ Generates a 1D Hanning window.:param length: Length of the window.:param alpha: Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM).:return: 1D numpy array. """ # Coordinate system ranges from 0 to length x = np.linspace(0, length, length) # Formula from: hn(x) = cos^2(pi x / (2 alpha)) window1d = np.cos(np.pi x / (2 alpha)) 2 return window1d def apertureapodization(hologram, centerx, centery, aperturewidth, apertureheight, alpha): """ Applies aperture apodization to a hologram.:param hologram: 2D complex numpy array (N, M).:param centerx: x-coordinate of aperture center.:param centery: y-coordinate of aperture center.:param aperturewidth: Width of the synthetic aperture in pixels.:param apertureheight: Height of the synthetic aperture in pixels.:param alpha: FWHM for the Hanning window.:return: Apodized hologram (N, M) complex array. """ N, M = hologram.shape # 1. Define Synthetic Aperture boundaries xstart = int(centerx - aperturewidth / 2) xend = int(centerx + aperturewidth / 2) ystart = int(centery - apertureheight / 2) yend = int(centery + apertureheight / 2) # Clamp to hologram boundaries xstart = max(0, xstart) xend = min(M, xend) ystart = max(0, ystart) yend = min(N, yend) # 2. Extract Sub-Region aperturesub = hologram[ystart:yend, xstart:xend] # 3. Generate 2D Hanning Window winw = generatehanningwindow1d(aperturesub.shape[1], alpha) winh = generatehanningwindow1d(aperturesub.shape[0], alpha) # Create 2D window by outer product window2d = np.outer(winh, winw) # 4. Apply Apodization apodizedsub = aperturesub window2d # 5. Zero-Pad to original size apodizedhologram = np.zeros((N, M), dtype=complex) apodizedhologram[ystart:yend, xstart:xend] = apodizedsub return apodizedhologram A window function used to multiply the ramp filter to attenuate high-frequency noise. The Hann variant uses parameter a = 0.5, while the Hamming variant uses a = 0.54. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the synthetic aperture O(W \times H) for window generation and multiplication. Zero-padding is O(N \times M). Memory Complexity: O(N \times M) to store the zero-padded result. Strengths: Effectively suppresses side-lobe leakage and aperture diffraction artifacts. Limitations: Causes a decrease in resolution due to the limited signal area. When to use: When sharp rectangular aperture edges cause significant diffraction artifacts in the reconstruction. The technique was proposed to address aperture diffraction issues in numerical reconstruction of computer-generated holograms. It builds on the concept of synthetic aperture selection. The Hanning window function is a standard signal processing tool adapted for this optical context. name: Anisotropic Noise
head: Goldberg et al. noise, Oriented Band Filtering, Oriented subband noise
body: Anisotropic noise is a procedural noise function that supports high-quality anisotropic filtering by tiling the frequency domain into oriented subbands. Unlike isotropic noise functions (such as Perlin noise) which force a trade-off between aliasing artifacts and loss of detail on tilted surfaces, anisotropic noise adapts its frequency content to non-uniform perspective distortions by blending pre-computed oriented bands. It sets itself apart from its sibling Aperture Apodization by explicitly modeling orientation in the frequency decomposition, allowing it to approximate any desired anisotropic frequency spectrum on a surface. Inputs: A set of pre-computed oriented noise subband textures. The number of bands B (typically 4 or 8). The target anisotropic filter characteristics (defined by the surface geometry and view direction). Outputs: A scalar noise value N(x, y) for a given 2D coordinate (x, y) on the surface. Data Structures: Subband Textures: The oriented subbands are stored in 32-bit RGBA images. Each channel (R, G, B, A) stores one oriented subband. One texture stores 4 orientations (e.g., 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°). Two textures store 8 orientations. Scale: Subbands are precomputed at a single scale only. Other scales are generated on the fly by scaling the texture coordinates. Method Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Partition the frequency domain using steerable filters to create oriented subbands tightly localized in scale and orientation. 2. Synthesize noise tiles for each subband. This is typically done by filtering white noise with the steerable filters. 3. Pack each oriented subband image into one channel of a 32-bit RGBA image, yielding four orientations per texture. 4. Store the textures. Note that the filters implement an invertible transform, allowing exact recovery of a signal from its decomposition. 2. Runtime (Per Pixel): 1. Determine the appropriate weights for each oriented subband based on the local anisotropic filter requirements (e.g., derived from the Jacobian of the surface mapping). 2. Sample the pre-computed subband textures at the current pixel location (x, y). Since subbands are precomputed at a single scale, scale the texture coordinates to match the required frequency scale. 3. Compute the final noise value as a weighted sum of the sampled noise subbands: N(x, y) = \sum{i=1}^{B} wi \cdot Si(x, y) where wi is the weight for the i-th oriented subband, and Si(x, y) is the value of the i-th subband at (x, y). 4. The weights wi are adapted with respect to the anisotropic filter to allow noise content to adapt to non-uniform perspective distortions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def anisotropicnoise(x, y, weights, subbandtextures): """ Compute anisotropic noise value at (x, y). Args: x, y: 2D coordinates on the surface. weights: List of B weights [w0,..., w{B-1}] for the oriented subbands. subbandtextures: List of B textures (or channels thereof) containing the pre-computed subbands. Each texture is sampled at the appropriate scale. Returns: Scalar noise value. """ noisevalue = 0.0 # B is the number of bands (e.g., 4 or 8) B = len(weights) for i in range(B): # Sample the i-th subband texture at (x, y) # Note: In practice, texture coordinates may need scaling for different frequencies, # but the core method uses a single precomputed scale per band, scaled via UVs. # The source states: "All other scales are generated on the fly by simply scaling the precomputed textures." subbandvalue = sampletexture(subbandtextures[i], x, y) # Weighted sum noisevalue += weights[i] subbandvalue return noisevalue Parameters: Number of Bands (B): Typically 4 or 8. Using 4 bands (1 texture) or 8 bands (2 textures) leads to a good trade-off between storage, rendering speed, and image quality. Scale: Precomputed at a single scale. Other scales are handled by texture coordinate scaling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on linear interpolation of steerable filters to avoid interpolation artifacts when blending subbands. Boundaries: The invertible transform property ensures exact recovery of signals, but this assumes the decomposition is complete. Degenerate Input: If the anisotropic filter becomes isotropic, the weights should converge to equal values for all orientations (or appropriate isotropic combination). Fourier spectral synthesis generates a noise function with a specific target power spectrum by filtering white noise in the frequency domain. It sets itself apart from spatial-domain methods (like Sparse Convolution Noise) by enforcing spectral properties directly, making it the foundational technique for Anisotropic Noise and Spot Noise. Gabor Noise Surface Filtering is an analytical method for generating anisotropically filtered procedural noise on surfaces by exploiting the spectral structure of Gabor noise. Unlike methods that discretize the spectrum into bands or apply post-hoc blurring, this approach computes the exact filtered spectrum per pixel by multiplying the Gabor kernel's frequency-domain Gaussian with the view-dependent filter Gaussian, then generating noise from the resulting parameters. It is distinct from Fourier Spectral Synthesis because it operates on oriented subbands (Gabor kernels) rather than a global isotropic spectrum, allowing it to adapt to non-uniform perspective distortions and anisotropic filtering requirements without aliasing or over-blurring. Time Complexity: Generally faster than Perlin noise. The runtime cost is dominated by texture sampling and a weighted sum, which is O(B) where B is the number of bands. Memory Complexity: Storage is proportional to the number of bands and the texture resolution. Typically 1-2 textures for 4-8 bands. Measured Performance: Anisotropic noise is generally faster than Perlin noise. Strengths: Supports high-quality anisotropic filtering, solid noise, and isotropic filtering. Adapts to non-uniform perspective distortions. Limitations: Requires offline preprocessing to generate subbands. Limited to the orientations present in the pre-computed bands (though steerable filters allow interpolation). When to use: When high-quality anisotropic filtering is required on surfaces with non-uniform perspective distortions. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and pre-computed textures are not feasible, or when isotropic filtering is sufficient and simpler methods like Perlin noise are preferred for their ubiquity. Anisotropic noise was introduced by Goldberg et al. in 2008 [GZD08]. It was developed to address the limitations of existing noise functions which only supported isotropic filtering, leading to a trade-off between aliasing artifacts and loss of detail on tilted surfaces. The method is based on steerable filters [SF95, PS00] that partition the frequency domain. It is used for surface noise via 2D texture mapping and compensating for parametric distortion, as well as for anisotropic analytic filtering. name: Fourier Spectral Synthesis
head: Fourier Noise Generation, Spectral Synthesis
body: Fourier spectral synthesis generates a noise function with a specific target power spectrum by filtering white noise in the frequency domain. It sets itself apart from spatial-domain methods (like Sparse Convolution Noise) by enforcing spectral properties directly, making it the foundational technique for Anisotropic Noise and Spot Noise. Inputs: 1. Target power spectrum P(k), where k is the spatial frequency vector. 2. Domain size N (for discrete implementation). 3. Resolution R (number of samples per dimension). Outputs: 1. Noise field n(x) defined on the spatial domain. Data Structures: Frequency Grid: A 3D array of complex numbers of size N \times N \times N (or 2D/1D as needed). Let this be F. Spatial Grid: A 3D array of real numbers of size R \times R \times R. Let this be n. Steps: 1. Initialize White Noise: Generate a complex-valued random field W on the frequency grid. For each frequency bin k, draw the real and imaginary parts from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1) or uniform distribution, ensuring Hermitian symmetry (W[-k] = \overline{W[k]}) to guarantee a real-valued output. 2. Apply Spectral Filter: Scale the white noise by the square root of the target power spectrum. F[k] = W[k] \cdot \sqrt{P(k)} Here, P(k) is the desired power spectral density at frequency k. For isotropic noise, P(k) depends only on |k|. For anisotropic noise (as in Anisotropic Noise), P(k) is shaped by oriented subbands. 3. Inverse Transform: Compute the Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) of F. \tilde{n}(x) = \text{IFFT}(F) 4. Extract Real Part: Since numerical errors may introduce small imaginary components, take the real part. n(x) = \text{Re}(\tilde{n}(x)) 5. Normalization (Optional): Scale n(x) to have zero mean and unit variance if required by the application. Parameters: P(k): The shape of the spectrum (e.g., 1/|k|^2 for Brownian motion, flat for white noise). Not given in the sources for specific standard values, but generally defined by the user. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hermitian Symmetry: Failure to enforce W[-k] = \overline{W[k]} results in a complex-valued noise field, which is invalid for scalar noise functions. DC Component: The zero-frequency component (k=0) determines the mean. It should be set to 0 for zero-mean noise. Aliasing: If the target spectrum has significant energy at frequencies higher than the Nyquist limit of the spatial resolution, aliasing will occur. Pre-filtering or anti-aliasing techniques are required. Generates band-pass noise on curved surfaces by integrating a 3D band-pass solid noise field perpendicular to the surface. It avoids the low-frequency drift and aliasing artifacts caused by naively slicing 3D noise, and prevents the distortions of planar parametrization. Choose this when anisotropic textures must flow naturally around complex topologies. Time Complexity: O(N^3 \log N) for 3D generation using FFT, where N is the grid resolution. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for storing the frequency and spatial grids. Strengths: Exact control over the power spectrum; mathematically rigorous; generates smooth, continuous noise. Limitations: Global dependency (changing one sample requires recomputing the entire field via FFT); high memory usage for high resolutions; not easily localizable. When to use: When precise spectral properties are required (e.g., for Anisotropic Noise or Spot Noise); for generating reference solutions. When not to use: For real-time applications requiring local updates or sparse sampling; when memory is constrained. Fourier spectral synthesis was introduced in computer graphics by Anjyo [Anj88], Saupe [Sau88], and Voss [Vos88] to generate random fractals for simulating natural phenomena like terrain. It is based on the principle that filtering white noise in the frequency domain yields a process with a specified power spectrum. The method is also related to the mathematical texturing function of Gardner [Gar84]. It is widely used in explicit noise methods, such as van Wijk's spot noise [vW91] and Goldberg et al.'s anisotropic noise [GZD08]. name: Surface Noise via Slice-Projection Theorem
body: Surface noise via the slice-projection theorem is a method to generate band-pass noise on a curved surface by integrating a 3D band-pass solid noise field perpendicular to that surface. It solves the problem that naively sampling (slicing) a 3D band-pass noise function along a 2D surface results in a non-band-pass power spectrum, causing visual artifacts such as low-frequency drift or aliasing. Unlike solid texturing, which creates the illusion of an object sculpted from solid matter, this method allows anisotropic textures to flow around the object's topology, adapting to curvature changes. It differs from planar parametrization by avoiding the distortions and seams inherent in mapping 2D noise directly onto complex surfaces. Inputs: 1. A 3D band-pass noise function N(x, y, z) with a known band-pass power spectrum P{3D}(u, v, w). 2. A surface defined by a position function \mathbf{S}(u, v) and a unit normal vector field \mathbf{n}(u, v). Outputs: 1. A 2D noise field N{surf}(u, v) defined on the surface parameter domain, which exhibits band-pass characteristics. Data Structures: The 3D noise function N is typically implemented as a procedural function (e.g., value noise, gradient noise) or a sparse convolution grid. No specific pre-computed table layout is mandated by the theorem itself, though explicit noises may rely on pre-computed tables. The surface is represented by its parametric coordinates (u, v), position \mathbf{S}, and normal \mathbf{n}. Method Steps: 1. Identify the Problem: Recognize that evaluating N at \mathbf{S}(u, v) corresponds to "slicing" the 3D domain. According to the slice-projection theorem, slicing in the spatial domain corresponds to projection (integration) in the frequency domain. Integrating a band-pass spectrum results in a non-band-pass spectrum (typically accumulating energy at low frequencies). 2. Apply Projection (Integration): To restore the band-pass property, integrate the solid noise field along the direction perpendicular to the surface (along the normal \mathbf{n}). This operation corresponds to "slicing" the frequency spectrum, which preserves the band-pass nature. 3. Compute Surface Noise: For each point on the surface, compute the integral of the 3D noise function along the normal vector. The value N{surf}(u, v) is obtained by integrating N along the line segment defined by the normal at \mathbf{S}(u, v). Formulas: The slice-projection theorem states that the Fourier transform of a slice of a function is a projection of its Fourier transform. Let P{3D}(u, v, w) be the power spectrum of the 3D noise. Slicing the spatial domain (evaluating on surface) \implies Projecting the frequency domain (integration of spectrum). To get band-pass noise on the surface, we must perform the inverse operation in the spatial domain: N{surf}(u, v) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} N(\mathbf{S}(u, v) + t \cdot \mathbf{n}(u, v)) \, dt In practice, this integral is approximated over a finite range or using a specific kernel that mimics the integration effect, ensuring the resulting power spectrum remains band-pass. Parameters: Integration range: Not given in the sources. Kernel width: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The integration must be performed accurately to maintain the band-pass property. Numerical errors in integration may introduce low-frequency artifacts. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes an infinite or periodic domain for the 3D noise. If the noise is defined on a finite domain, boundary effects may distort the spectrum. Degenerate Input: If the surface normal is undefined (e.g., at singularities), the integration direction is ambiguous. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns: (u, v) -> float function returning surface noise value. """ def computenoise(u, v): # Get position and normal at the surface point pos = surfaceposition(u, v) nrm = surfacenormal(u, v) # Integrate noise along the normal direction # Note: The exact integration range and method (e.g., quadrature) # are not specified in the sources. # A simple approximation might use a fixed range [-L, L] and # sample multiple points along the normal. integrationrange = 1.0 # Not given in the sources numsamples = 10 # Not given in the sources integralsum = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): # Sample point along the normal t = -integrationrange + (2.0 integrationrange i) / (numsamples - 1) samplepoint = pos + t nrm integralsum += noise3d(samplepoint.x, samplepoint.y, samplepoint.z) # Average the samples to approximate the integral # The scaling factor depends on the integration method return integralsum / numsamples return computenoise This variant maps 2D noise onto surfaces using planar parametrization, similar to regular texture maps. It compensates for mapping distortions by locally adapting the noise content at every pixel, estimating local distortion and its impact on the noise spectrum. The weights of summed noise bands are updated to approximate a pre-distorted spectrum, generating noise with inversely pre-distorted frequency content. This approach can be performed efficiently in a GPU shader. However, it can introduce distortions and seams, breaking properties like uniform frequency content, continuity, and band-pass nature. It only recovers from distortions and cannot hide seams. This idea was also suggested by van Wijk. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces band-pass noise on surfaces, allowing anisotropic textures to flow around objects and adapt to topology changes. Avoids the "sculpted from solid matter" look of solid texturing, which is desirable for fiber-like materials. Limitations: Requires integration of 3D noise, which can be computationally expensive if not optimized. The method relies on the slice-projection theorem, which assumes ideal conditions. When to Use: When anisotropic textures need to flow around complex curved surfaces without distortion. When Not to Use: When the "solid texturing" effect is desired, or when computational resources are limited and integration is too costly. The method is based on the slice-projection theorem, which states that slicing in one domain corresponds to projection or integration in the other. Cook and DeRose [CD05] observed that sampling solid band-pass noise along a surface does not result in band-pass noise on the surface, and proposed using the slice-projection theorem to solve this by integrating the noise perpendicular to the surface. The theorem is attributed to [Bra99, Mal93]. This approach contrasts with solid texturing, introduced by Perlin [Per85] and Peachy [Pea85], which samples 3D noise directly on the surface. name: Gabor Noise Surface Filtering
head: Analytical filtering of Gabor noise, Gabor Noise Filtering
body: Gabor Noise Surface Filtering is an analytical method for generating anisotropically filtered procedural noise on surfaces, solving the problem of aliasing and visual inconsistency caused by non-uniform perspective distortions during camera or object motion. Unlike methods that discretize the spectrum into distinct bands or rely on post-hoc blurring, this approach exploits the fact that Gabor kernels are Gaussians in the frequency domain, allowing the filter to be applied by analytically modifying the kernel parameters per pixel. It builds on Anisotropic Noise and provides a view-dependent spectral control that adapts to the screen-space projection of the surface. The method generates filtered noise by operating in the frequency domain, leveraging the closed-form nature of Gaussian functions. It avoids explicit convolution in the spatial domain by computing the product of the noise spectrum and the filter spectrum, resulting in a new set of kernel parameters that directly yield the filtered noise. Inputs: Surface geometry (position \mathbf{p}, normal \mathbf{n}, tangent \mathbf{t}, bitangent \mathbf{b}) for the point being shaded. Camera parameters (projection matrix, view matrix) to determine screen-space derivatives. Gabor noise parameters: A set of N oriented subbands. Each subband i is defined by a center frequency vector \mathbf{k}i (magnitude and orientation) and a bandwidth parameter \sigmai (width of the Gaussian in frequency space). Filter specification: Typically a low-pass filter defined by a cutoff frequency or a Gaussian width in screen space. Outputs: A noise value N(\mathbf{p}) that is anisotropically filtered according to the view direction and surface orientation. The Gabor noise is represented as a sum of N Gabor kernels. Each kernel i is defined by: 1. Center Frequency: \mathbf{k}i = (k{i,x}, k{i,y}, k{i,z}) in 3D space, often derived from a 2D orientation projected onto the surface tangent plane. 2. Bandwidth: \sigmai, controlling the spread of the Gaussian in the frequency domain. 3. Phase: \phii, a random offset. In the frequency domain, the spectrum of a single Gabor kernel is a Gaussian function centered at \mathbf{k}i with covariance determined by \sigmai. 1. Compute Screen-Space Derivatives: For the shading point \mathbf{p}, compute the partial derivatives of the position with respect to screen coordinates (u, v). This determines the local scale and orientation of the surface projection in screen space. 2. Determine Filter Gaussian: Calculate the filter Gaussian in the frequency domain. Since the filter is view-dependent, its shape and orientation in texture space vary per pixel. The filter Gaussian F(\mathbf{u}) is typically defined by the screen-space derivatives, representing the area covered by a single pixel in the frequency domain. 3. Iterate Over Kernels: For each Gabor kernel i in the noise definition: a. Identify Gabor Gaussian: The spectrum of the unfiltered kernel is a Gaussian Gi(\mathbf{u}) centered at \mathbf{k}i with width \sigmai. b. Compute Product: Multiply the Gabor Gaussian Gi(\mathbf{u}) by the filter Gaussian F(\mathbf{u}) in the frequency domain. Since both are Gaussians, their product is another Gaussian G'i(\mathbf{u}). c. Derive Filtered Parameters: Analytically compute the parameters of the resulting Gaussian G'i(\mathbf{u}). This involves combining the means and covariances of the two Gaussians. The new center frequency \mathbf{k}'i and bandwidth \sigma'i are derived from the product. 4. Generate Filtered Noise: Use the new parameters \mathbf{k}'i and \sigma'i to evaluate the Gabor noise function. The noise value is the sum of the contributions from all filtered kernels: N(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \cdot \text{Gabor}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{k}'i, \sigma'i, \phii) where wi are the weights of the subbands. The spectrum of a Gabor kernel i in 3D frequency space \mathbf{u} is modeled as a Gaussian: Gi(\mathbf{u}) = \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{k}i)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{k}i) \right) where \Sigmai is the covariance matrix related to \sigmai. The filter Gaussian F(\mathbf{u}) in texture space, derived from screen-space derivatives, is also a Gaussian. The product of two Gaussians Gi(\mathbf{u}) and F(\mathbf{u}) results in a new Gaussian G'i(\mathbf{u}): G'i(\mathbf{u}) = Gi(\mathbf{u}) \cdot F(\mathbf{u}) = C \cdot \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{k}'i)^T \Sigma'i^{-1} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{k}'i) \right) The new mean \mathbf{k}'i and covariance \Sigma'i are computed as: \Sigma'i = (\Sigmai^{-1} + \SigmaF^{-1})^{-1} \mathbf{k}'i = \Sigma'i (\Sigmai^{-1} \mathbf{k}i + \SigmaF^{-1} \mathbf{k}F) where \mathbf{k}F and \SigmaF are the mean and covariance of the filter Gaussian. Typically, the filter is centered at the origin in the differential frequency space, so \mathbf{k}F = \mathbf{0}. Number of Kernels (N): Determines the complexity and anisotropy of the noise. Typical values range from 4 to 16 for real-time applications. Bandwidth (\sigmai): Controls the frequency spread. Smaller \sigmai results in sharper frequency localization. Filter Width: Determined by the screen-space derivatives. Not a fixed parameter but computed per pixel. View-Dependence: The filter Gaussian varies per screen pixel. Failing to compute the correct filter shape for each pixel leads to incorrect filtering, especially on tilted surfaces. Degenerate Input: If the surface is viewed edge-on or the derivatives are zero, the filter Gaussian may become singular. Guard against division by zero when inverting covariance matrices. Precision: The analytical combination of Gaussians requires careful handling of numerical precision, especially when \sigmai and the filter width differ significantly. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gabornoisesurfacefiltering(p, normal, tangent, bitangent, camera, noiseparams): """ Generate filtered Gabor noise at point p. Args: p: 3D position vector. normal: Surface normal vector. tangent: Surface tangent vector. bitangent: Surface bitangent vector. camera: Camera object with methods for screen-space derivatives. noiseparams: List of Gabor kernel parameters (ki, sigmai, phii, wi). Returns: Filtered noise value. """ # Step 1: Compute screen-space derivatives # This determines how the surface maps to screen space dpdu, dpdv = camera.computescreenderivatives(p, normal, tangent, bitangent) # Step 2: Determine Filter Gaussian parameters # The filter is a Gaussian in frequency space defined by the pixel footprint # Compute the covariance matrix of the filter based on dpdu and dpdv # This is view-dependent and varies per pixel sigmaF = computefiltercovariance(dpdu, dpdv) kF = [0, 0, 0] # Filter is centered at origin in differential space filterednoise = 0.0 # Step 3: Iterate over kernels for kernel in noiseparams: ki = kernel.centerfrequency sigmai = kernel.bandwidth phii = kernel.phase wi = kernel.weight # Step 3a: Identify Gabor Gaussian parameters # Sigmai is derived from sigmai (bandwidth) Sigmai = computecovariancefrombandwidth(sigmai) # Step 3b: Compute Product of Gaussians # Inverse covariances Sigmaiinv = invertmatrix(Sigmai) SigmaFinv = invertmatrix(sigmaF) # New covariance Sigmaprimeinv = addmatrices(Sigmaiinv, SigmaFinv) Sigmaprime = invertmatrix(Sigmaprimeinv) # New mean kprime = multiplymatrixvector(Sigmaprime, addmatrices( multiplymatrixvector(Sigmaiinv, ki), multiplymatrixvector(SigmaFinv, kF))) # Step 3c: Generate Filtered Noise # Evaluate the Gabor kernel with new parameters # The Gabor function is typically: cos(2pi k. p + phi) exp(-pi sigma^2 ||p||^2) # However, since we are in frequency domain, we use the spatial domain representation # with the modified frequency and bandwidth. # Note: The exact spatial domain formula for Gabor noise depends on the specific # implementation of the base Gabor noise function. Here we assume a standard form. # The key is that kprime and sigmaprime are used instead of ki and sigmai. noiseval = evaluategaborkernel(p, kprime, sigmaprime, phii) filterednoise += wi noiseval return filterednoise def computefiltercovariance(dpdu, dpdv): """ Compute the covariance matrix of the filter Gaussian based on screen-space derivatives. This represents the area covered by a pixel in the frequency domain. """ # The filter covariance is related to the inverse of the Jacobian of the projection # Simplified: The filter width is proportional to the magnitude of the derivatives # In practice, this involves computing the local frequency response # For a 2D surface in 3D, the filter is anisotropic # This is a placeholder for the specific derivation from screen derivatives # The exact formula depends on the camera projection model # Typically, SigmaF is computed from the partial derivatives of the texture coordinates # with respect to screen coordinates. # Let's assume we have texture coordinates u, v # du/dx, du/dy, dv/dx, dv/dy are the screen derivatives # The filter covariance in frequency space is related to these derivatives # For the purpose of this pseudocode, we assume a helper function exists # that computes the 2x2 covariance matrix in the tangent plane # projected from screen space. # This is a critical step that varies per pixel # The filter is a Gaussian in the frequency domain # Its width is determined by the pixel footprint on the surface # Return a 3x3 covariance matrix in 3D space, aligned with the surface # For simplicity, we assume the filter is isotropic in the tangent plane # and zero in the normal direction # Compute the scale of the pixel on the surface scaleu = length(dpdu) scalev = length(dpdv) # The filter bandwidth is inversely proportional to the scale # SigmaF is a 3x3 matrix SigmaF = zeros(3, 3) # Align with tangent and bitangent # This is a simplification; the actual derivation involves the Jacobian # of the projection from 3D to 2D screen space # For a more accurate implementation, one would compute the # frequency domain filter as the Fourier transform of the pixel shape # projected onto the surface. # Return the computed covariance return SigmaF def evaluategaborkernel(p, k, sigma, phi): """ Evaluate a single Gabor kernel at point p. """ # Gabor noise is typically defined as: # N(p) = cos(2 pi dot(k, p) + phi) exp(-pi sigma^2 dot(p, p)) # However, for surface filtering, the frequency k is in 3D space # and the Gaussian envelope is also in 3D space. # The exact formula depends on the specific Gabor noise implementation # The key is that k and sigma are the filtered parameters dotproduct = dot(k, p) phase = 2 pi dotproduct + phi envelope = exp(-pi sigma2 dot(p, p)) return cos(phase) envelope NPR Gabor Noise is a variant of Gabor noise designed for coherent stylization in non-photorealistic rendering (NPR). It solves the problem of maintaining visual consistency of noise patterns during camera or object motion by decoupling the noise parameter definition from the point sampling space. Unlike standard Gabor noise where parameters are often tied to object space, this method defines noise parameters in 2D screen space while defining point distribution in 3D object space, thereby preserving the 2D aspect of the noise and the 3D motion of the scene. It builds on Gabor Noise Surface Filtering. Time Complexity: The method requires computing screen-space derivatives and then iterating over all Gabor kernels. For each kernel, it performs matrix inversions and multiplications to update the parameters. The complexity is O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of kernels. The matrix operations are constant time (3x3 matrices). Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory is required, as the filtering is done analytically by modifying parameters. The noise function itself requires storing the kernel parameters. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the number of kernels and the cost of evaluating the Gabor function. Analytical filtering avoids the need for multi-sample anti-aliasing or post-processing blurs, which can be expensive. Scaling: The method scales well with resolution, as the filtering is done per pixel based on screen-space derivatives. It adapts to non-uniform perspective distortions without requiring scene-dependent precomputation. Strengths: Analytical filtering avoids discretization artifacts. Adapts to view-dependent perspective distortions. Maintains anisotropy correctly on tilted surfaces. Limitations: Requires accurate screen-space derivatives. Computationally more expensive per pixel than unfiltered noise due to the parameter updates. May struggle with very high-frequency noise if the filter width is too small, leading to numerical instability. When to Use: Use when high-quality anisotropic filtering is required for procedural noise on surfaces, especially in real-time rendering where post-processing blurs are not feasible or when perspective distortions are significant. When Not to Use: Avoid if the noise is isotropic and the surface is viewed front-on, as simpler filtering methods may suffice. Also avoid if the computational budget is extremely tight and the number of kernels is large. Gabor Noise was introduced by Goldberg et al. [GZD08] in 2008 as a noise function that supports high-quality anisotropic filtering by tiling the frequency domain into oriented subbands. The analytical filtering method for Gabor noise was described by Lagae et al. [LLDD09a] in 2009, exploiting the property that Gabor kernels correspond to Gaussians in the frequency domain. This allows for direct generation of filtered noise by modifying kernel parameters, avoiding the need for explicit convolution or discretization of the spectrum. The method is part of the broader field of procedural noise functions, which are widely used in computer graphics for texture synthesis, terrain generation, and visual effects. Unlike standard Gabor noise where parameters are often tied to object space, this method defines noise parameters in 2D screen space while defining point distribution in 3D object space, thereby preserving the 2D aspect of the noise and the 3D motion of the scene. It builds on Gabor Noise Surface Filtering. For a given 3D point \mathbf{p} in object space, transform it to screen space coordinates (u, v) using the camera's view and projection matrices. 4. Evaluate the Gabor noise function using the screen-space coordinates (u, v) and the screen-space noise parameters. 5. Return the resulting noise value. Formulas: Not given in the sources. name: Translation-invariant Fluorescence Rendering via Fourier Convolution
head: Fourier-based fluorescence rendering, Spectral 3D rendering
body: This method renders 3D fluorescence microscopy images by convolving a parameterized fluorophore density with a translation-invariant Point Spread Function (PSF) in the Fourier domain. It solves the problem of differentiable 3D image synthesis, enabling the optimization of both the biological sample's geometry and the microscope's optical parameters by minimizing the distance between rendered and ground-truth images. Unlike standard volume rendering which integrates opacity along rays, this approach models the physical blurring of the imaging system, allowing for gradient-based inference of shape and optical properties. The method operates on intensity maps I: [0, 1]^3 \to \mathbb{R}. Non-cubic images are linearly rescaled to fit this domain. The pipeline consists of parameterizing the geometry and PSF, transforming them to the frequency domain, multiplying, and inverse transforming. Inputs: 1. Geometry: A parameterized fluorophore density u\Lambda, typically a triangle mesh \Lambda representing a surface where density is modeled as a Dirac distribution weighted by the local surface element. 2. PSF: A parameterized Point Spread Function h, typically a Gaussian kernel defined by a symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Outputs: 1. Rendered Image: I(\mathbf{x}), the convolution of u\Lambda and h. 2. Gradients: Derivatives of the loss function with respect to mesh vertices and PSF parameters, enabling optimization. Data Structures: Mesh: Set of triangles \tau, each defined by vertices, stored with area A\tau and surface element a\Lambda. PSF Parameters: Covariance matrix \Sigma. Frequency Domain: Arrays for \hat{u}\Lambda(\boldsymbol{\xi}) and \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) on a 3D grid of wavevectors \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Parameterize PSF: Define the Gaussian PSF h(\mathbf{x}) using \Sigma: h(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}}}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^3 \det \Sigma}}, \quad \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \quad (2) Compute its Fourier transform \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}): \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{\xi}^T \Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol{\xi}} \quad (3) 2. Compute Fourier Transform of Geometry: Surface Model: Model the fluorophore density u\Lambda as a Dirac distribution on surface \Lambda: u\Lambda(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{|\Lambda|} \iint \delta{\Lambda(s1, s2)}(\mathbf{x}) a\Lambda(s1, s2) ds1 ds2 where |\Lambda| = \iint a\Lambda(s1, s2) ds1 ds2 is the total surface area, and a\Lambda = ||\partial{s1}\Lambda \times \partial{s2}\Lambda|| is the surface element. Fourier Transform: Compute \hat{u}\Lambda(\boldsymbol{\xi}) by summing the contributions of individual triangles \tau: \hat{u}\Lambda(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \frac{\sum{\tau \in \Lambda} \hat{u}\tau(\boldsymbol{\xi})}{\sum{\tau \in \Lambda} A\tau} \quad (5) For a triangle mesh, \hat{u}\tau(\boldsymbol{\xi}) is computed analytically for each triangle. Cell-Cell Interfaces: If modeling double membranes at cell-cell interfaces, scale the fluorophore density contribution by a factor of two. 3. Spectral Narrow-Band Approximation (Optional Optimization): To reduce computational cost, skip computing \hat{u}\Lambda(\boldsymbol{\xi}) for frequencies where \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) is negligible: 1. Compute \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) for the current PSF. 2. Identify frequency components where \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) > 0.01 \times \max(\hat{h}). 3. Compute \hat{u}\Lambda(\boldsymbol{\xi}) only for these frequencies. 4. Multiply by \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) and inverse transform. 4. Convolution in Fourier Space: Compute the Fourier transform of the image \hat{I}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) by element-wise multiplication: \hat{I}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \hat{u}\Lambda(\boldsymbol{\xi}) \cdot \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) \quad (4) 5. Inverse Fourier Transform: Apply the Inverse Fourier Transform to \hat{I} to obtain the rendered image I(\mathbf{x}) in the spatial domain. 6. Optimization (Optional): Minimize the distance between the rendered image I and a ground-truth microscopy image I{GT} to infer optimal parameters for u\Lambda (mesh vertices) and h (PSF covariance \Sigma). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussianpsffourier(xi, sigmamatrix): """Compute the Fourier transform of a Gaussian PSF.""" invsigma = np.linalg.inv(sigmamatrix) exponent = -0.5 xi @ invsigma @ xi return np.exp(exponent) def trianglefouriertransform(vertices, xi): """Compute the Fourier transform of a single triangle's contribution. Sources do not provide the closed-form FT for a single triangle; implement standard analytical integration over the triangle surface.""" # Placeholder for analytical triangle FT implementation pass def renderfluorescence(meshtriangles, sigmamatrix, xigrid, isinterfacemask=None): """Render fluorescence image in Fourier domain.""" # 1. Compute PSF FT on grid hhat = np.zeros(xigrid.shape, dtype=complex) for idx in np.ndindex(xigrid.shape): xi = xigrid[idx] hhat[idx] = gaussianpsffourier(xi, sigmamatrix) maxh = np.max(hhat) # 2. Compute total surface area for normalization totalarea = 0.0 for tri in meshtriangles: v0, v1, v2 = tri area = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0)) totalarea += area # 3. Compute Geometry FT (Spectral Narrow-Band) uhat = np.zeros(xigrid.shape, dtype=complex) for idx in np.ndindex(xigrid.shape): xi = xigrid[idx] if hhat[idx] > 0.01 maxh: trisum = 0.0 for i, tri in enumerate(meshtriangles): weight = 2.0 if isinterfacemask and isinterfacemask[i] else 1.0 trisum += weight trianglefouriertransform(tri, xi) uhat[idx] = trisum / totalarea # 4. Convolve in Fourier Space Ihat = uhat hhat # 5. Inverse Fourier Transform I = np.fft.ifftn(Ihat).real return I An optimization technique that skips the computation of the mesh's Fourier transform \hat{u}\Lambda(\xi) for frequencies where the PSF's Fourier transform \hat{h}(\xi) is negligible (below 1% of its maximum value). This reduces computational cost by several orders of magnitude by ignoring far-field contributions that have minimal impact on the final image, unlike the exact method which computes all frequencies. A geometric modeling approach where the fluorophore density u\Lambda is represented as a Dirac distribution supported on a surface \Lambda (e.g., a triangle mesh). The density is weighted by the local surface element a\Lambda and normalized by the total surface area |\Lambda| to ensure the total integrated intensity is one. Cell-cell interfaces are modeled as double membranes, scaling their density by a factor of two. Complexity: The dominant cost is computing the Fourier transform of the mesh, and the forward pass is approximately 10 times slower than the backward pass (gradient computation). Performance: The spectral narrow-band approximation significantly accelerates rendering by skipping negligible frequency components. Strengths: Enables differentiable rendering, allowing for the optimization of both sample geometry and microscope parameters (PSF). Limitations: Assumes translation-invariant PSF, which may not hold for all microscopy systems, and requires parameterization of geometry (e.g., mesh) and PSF (e.g., covariance matrix). When to use: When the goal is to infer 3D structure and optical properties from 2D/3D microscopy images via optimization. When not to use: For real-time visualization where differentiability is not required, or when the PSF is highly space-variant. This method was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Rendering for 3D Fluorescence Microscopy" (2023). It builds on the principle that fluorescence microscopy images can be modeled as the convolution of a fluorophore distribution with the microscope's Point Spread Function (PSF). By moving this convolution to the Fourier domain, the method leverages the efficiency of FFTs and enables gradient-based optimization of the underlying 3D geometry and optical parameters. It is particularly relevant for computational microscopy and bio-image analysis. name: DCT-based Volume Rendering
head: DCT Volume Rendering, DCT-based encoding, DCT-based out-of-core volume rendering, DCT-based volume compression, Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) Volume Rendering
body: DCT-based Volume Rendering is a technique for rendering large volumetric datasets that exceed main memory capacity by compressing the data using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) and decoding it during the rendering process. Unlike Hartley Transform for Memory Reduction [895-hartley-transform-for-memory-reduction.md], which supports direct rendering from the transform domain, DCT requires on-demand decompression of data blocks before rendering. The method enables out-of-core rendering of massive time-series data by storing only a subset of DCT coefficients per block. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume V of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, potentially consisting of a sequence of time steps. Output: A 2D projection image rendered to the screen. Data Structures: The volume is divided into non-overlapping 3D blocks (windows) of size W \times W \times W. For each block, a subset of the DCT coefficients is stored. Coefficient Storage: The selected coefficients are quantized and packed into an 8-bit integer value. Decoding Map: A mapping table is pre-computed that associates each possible 8-bit index value with the corresponding decoded scalar value for each time frame, minimizing mean square error. Parameters: Window Size (W): The dimensions of the block over which the DCT is applied. A typical example uses W=4. Coefficients Stored (K): The number of DCT coefficients retained per block. A typical example stores the first 3 coefficients. Compression Ratio: Determined by K relative to the total number of coefficients in a block (W^3). Higher compression yields lower quality but higher frame rates. Steps: 1. Encoding (Pre-processing): 1. Divide the input volume into W \times W \times W blocks. 2. Apply the 3D DCT to each block. The 3D DCT of a block f(x,y,z) is defined as: C(u,v,w) = \alpha(u)\alpha(v)\alpha(w) \sum{x=0}^{W-1} \sum{y=0}^{W-1} \sum{z=0}^{W-1} f(x,y,z) \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2x+1)u}{2W}\right] \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2y+1)v}{2W}\right] \cos\left[\frac{\pi(2z+1)w}{2W}\right] where \alpha(u) = \sqrt{1/W} if u=0 and \sqrt{2/W} otherwise. 3. Select the first K coefficients (typically low-frequency components). 4. Quantize these coefficients and map them to an 8-bit index. 5. Pre-compute a decoding palette: For each possible 8-bit index and each time step, calculate the inverse DCT of the stored coefficients to determine the representative scalar value that minimizes mean square error. 2. Rendering (Per Frame): 1. Block Selection: Determine which volume blocks intersect the current view frustum or ray casting path. 2. Decompression: Retrieve the 8-bit indices for the active blocks. Use the pre-computed decoding map to expand these indices into the actual scalar values for the current time step. This step is performed on-demand. 3. Rendering: Render the decompressed data using standard volume rendering techniques. The implementation described in the primary source uses an extension of OpenGL that allows the palette of all textures to be changed at once to decode the compressed values efficiently. 4. Geometry: The volume is rendered using object-aligned textured polygons (e.g., 256 polygons) in an out-of-core fashion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def dct3dblock(block): """Computes the 3D DCT of a WxWxW block.""" W = block.shape[0] coeffs = np.zeros((W, W, W)) for u in range(W): for v in range(W): for w in range(W): alphau = np.sqrt(1.0 / W) if u == 0 else np.sqrt(2.0 / W) alphav = np.sqrt(1.0 / W) if v == 0 else np.sqrt(2.0 / W) alphaw = np.sqrt(1.0 / W) if w == 0 else np.sqrt(2.0 / W) sumval = 0.0 for x in range(W): for y in range(W): for z in range(W): sumval += block[x, y, z] \ np.cos(np.pi (2 x + 1) u / (2 W)) \ np.cos(np.pi (2 y + 1) v / (2 W)) \ np.cos(np.pi (2 z + 1) w / (2 W)) coeffs[u, v, w] = alphau alphav alphaw sumval return coeffs def encodevolume(volume, W=4, K=3): """Encodes the volume into compressed indices and builds the decoding map. volume shape: (T, X, Y, Z) """ compresseddata = {} decodingmap = {} numtimesteps = volume.shape[0] for t in range(numtimesteps): currentvol = volume[t] for bx in range(0, currentvol.shape[0], W): for by in range(0, currentvol.shape[1], W): for bz in range(0, currentvol.shape[2], W): block = currentvol[bx:bx+W, by:by+W, bz:bz+W] coeffs = dct3dblock(block) selected = coeffs.ravel()[:K] # Quantization to 8-bit index is optimized per index and time step to minimize MSE. index = int(np.clip(np.mean(selected) 100, 0, 255)) compresseddata[(bx, by, bz, t)] = index # Pre-compute decoding map: inverse DCT of selected coefficients invcoeffs = np.zeros((W, W, W)) invcoeffs.ravel()[:K] = selected decodedblock = np.zeroslike(block) for x in range(W): for y in range(W): for z in range(W): val = 0.0 for u in range(W): for v in range(W): for w in range(W): alphau = np.sqrt(1.0 / W) if u == 0 else np.sqrt(2.0 / W) alphav = np.sqrt(1.0 / W) if v == 0 else np.sqrt(2.0 / W) alphaw = np.sqrt(1.0 / W) if w == 0 else np.sqrt(2.0 / W) val += alphau alphav alphaw invcoeffs[u, v, w] \ np.cos(np.pi (2 x + 1) u / (2 W)) \ np.cos(np.pi (2 y + 1) v / (2 W)) \ np.cos(np.pi (2 z + 1) w / (2 W)) decodedblock[x, y, z] = val decodingmap[(index, t)] = decodedblock return compresseddata, decodingmap def renderframe(compresseddata, decodingmap, viewmaxx, viewmaxy, viewmaxz, currenttimestep): """Renders a frame by decompressing visible blocks on demand.""" visibleblocks = [] for blockkey in compresseddata.keys(): # Standard frustum culling: check if block bounding box intersects view frustum if blockkey[0] < viewmaxx and blockkey[1] < viewmaxy and blockkey[2] < viewmaxz: visibleblocks.append(blockkey) decompressedblocks = {} for blockkey in visibleblocks: index = compresseddata[blockkey] decodedblock = decodingmap[(index, currenttimestep)] decompressedblocks[blockkey] = decodedblock # Render using 256 object-aligned textured polygons for blockkey, blockdata in decompressedblocks.items(): # Project decompressed block to screen using object-aligned textured polygons pass return decompressedblocks Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Direct Rendering: DCT does not support direct rendering from the compression domain; data must be decompressed before rendering. Precision Loss: Quantizing coefficients to 8-bit values introduces compression artifacts. The trade-off between compression ratio and quality must be managed by the user. Boundary Conditions: DCT assumes periodic boundary conditions within each block. Discontinuities at block boundaries can cause artifacts. Time Complexity: Encoding is O(N^3) for the full volume, but typically performed offline. Rendering complexity depends on the number of visible blocks and the cost of on-demand decompression. The primary source reports rendering performance of 6.8 frames/s for a 256^3 dataset with 1492 time steps on an AMD 1.2 GHz Athlon and GeForce 3. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to in-core storage. The example uses 64 MB texture memory to render a dataset that would require much more if uncompressed. Performance: Out-of-core DCT rendering achieved 6.8 frames/s, compared to 11.5 frames/s for a memory-resident subset of uncompressed data and 25.8 frames/s for in-core compressed data. Strengths: Enables visualization of very large time-series datasets that do not fit in main memory. Offers flexibility in choosing compression ratios for speed vs. quality. Limitations: Requires on-demand decompression of data blocks before rendering, as direct rendering from the compression domain is not supported. DCT-based Volume Rendering was developed by Yeo et al. [YL95] as a strategy to decompress blocks of data on demand for rendering. It is chosen in practice because it offers independent bases as well as fast forward and inverse transforms. The method is particularly useful for out-of-core rendering of large volumetric datasets.
