name: Hartley Transform
head: Real Fourier Transform
body: The Hartley Transform is a real-valued integral transform that maps a real input function to a real spectrum, serving as an alternative to the complex Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for real-valued data. In volume rendering, it enables domain-transform methods to operate entirely in the real domain while preserving the projection-slice theorem. It is distinguished from its sibling Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering by using the \cos + \sin kernel instead of the complex exponential \cos + i\sin, which avoids complex arithmetic for real-valued signals. The method follows the three-stage pipeline of Domain-transform methods: Global Transformation, Slice Extraction, and Inverse Transformation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar volume f(x, y, z) with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Output: A 2D projection image I(u, v) corresponding to a viewing direction. Data Structures Volume: 3D array of real numbers. Spectrum: 3D array of real numbers H(\omega1, \omega2, \omega3). Slice: 2D array of real numbers I(u, v). Numbered Steps 1. Global Transformation: Compute the 3D Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) of the volume. The 1D DHT for a sequence hk of length N is applied separably along each dimension. 2. Slice Extraction: Define a 2D plane passing through the origin of the frequency domain and perpendicular to the viewing direction vector V. Resample the 3D spectrum onto this 2D plane to obtain the 2D slice I(u, v). Interpolation is required as the plane rarely coincides with the integer lattice. The output resolution must satisfy the Nyquist criterion to prevent aliasing. 3. Inverse Transformation: Compute the 2D Inverse Discrete Hartley Transform (IDHT) of the slice I(u, v) to generate the final projection image. Formulas Forward transform: H(f) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t)(\cos ft + \sin ft)dt. Inverse transform: h(t) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} H(f)(\cos ft + \sin ft)df. 1D DHT: Hn = \sum{k=0}^{N-1} hk \cdot \text{cas}\left(\frac{2\pi nk}{N}\right). 1D IDHT: hk = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=0}^{N-1} Hn \cdot \text{cas}\left(\frac{2\pi nk}{N}\right). Kernel abbreviation: \text{cas}(x) = \sin(x) + \cos(x). Even part: E(f) = \frac{H(f) + H(-f)}{2} = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t) \cos ft dt. Odd part: O(f) = \frac{H(f) - H(-f)}{2} = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t) \sin ft dt. Conversion to Fourier: S(f) = E(f) + iO(f). Conversion from Fourier: H(f) = \text{Re}[S(f)] + \text{Im}[S(f)]. Parameters Scaling: 1/N for the inverse transform. Interpolation: Not given in the sources. Zero-padding factor: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Artifacts: The transform assumes periodic boundary conditions. Discontinuities at volume boundaries cause high-frequency artifacts, mitigated by zero-padding the volume and applying vignetting correction. Aliasing: Insufficient output resolution violates the Nyquist criterion, causing aliasing. Fixed Parameters: Once transformed, parameters like opacity and lighting cannot be changed interactively, as the transformation is linear and global. The Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) is a real-valued linear transform that maps a sequence of N real numbers to N real numbers, serving as an alternative to the complex DFT for real input data. It is distinguished from the continuous Hartley Transform by operating on discrete sequences, and from the DFT by avoiding complex arithmetic, which simplifies implementation for real-valued signals. In volume rendering, it is used for domain-transform methods where real-valued convolution theorems are advantageous. A theorem stating that the 1-D Hartley transform of a projection of an object at angle \theta equals a slice through the 2-D Hartley transform of the object. The projection is defined as p\theta(\hat{u}1) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\hat{u}1 \cos \theta - \hat{u}2 \sin \theta, \hat{u}1 \sin \theta + \hat{u}2 \cos \theta) d\hat{u}2. The theorem is expressed as P\theta(\hat{U}1) = H(\hat{U}1 \cos \theta, \hat{U}1 \sin \theta), where P\theta is the Hartley transform of the projection and H is the 2-D Hartley transform of the object x(u1, u2). This validates the use of the Hartley transform in tomographic reconstruction and volume rendering pipelines. Time Complexity: Dominated by the 3D DHT and 2D IDHT, typically O(N^3 \log N) using fast algorithms. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the 3D spectrum. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids complex number overhead; maintains real-valued data throughout the pipeline; supports the projection-slice theorem. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Hartley transform was introduced by R.V.L. Hartley in 1942 as a real-valued alternative to the Fourier transform. It has been applied in computer-aided tomographic (CAT) scanners and other signal processing applications. name: Discrete Hartley Transform
head: Discrete Hartley Transform Properties
body: The Discrete Hartley Transform (DHT) is the discrete version of the Hartley transform, defined for a sequence of N real values and producing N real values. It is distinguished from the continuous Hartley Transform by operating on discrete sequences, and from the DFT by using only real arithmetic. In volume rendering, it is used in the Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) software implementation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of N real values hk for k = 0, \dots, N-1. Output: A sequence of N real values Hn for n = 0, \dots, N-1. Parameter: N, the size of the input sequence and the number of output coefficients. Data Structures: h: Array of N floats/doubles. H: Array of N floats/doubles. cas: Helper function for the \text{cas} kernel. Core Formula: The transform uses the \text{cas} function, defined as \text{cas}(\theta) = \cos(\theta) + \sin(\theta). Forward DHT: Hn = \sum{k=0}^{N-1} hk \text{cas}\left(\frac{2\pi nk}{N}\right) Inverse DHT: hk = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=0}^{N-1} Hn \text{cas}\left(\frac{2\pi nk}{N}\right) Even and Odd Parts: The DHT output Hn can be decomposed into even and odd parts relative to the index n (with periodicity N): En = \frac{Hn + H{N-n}}{2} On = \frac{Hn - H{N-n}}{2} Note: Due to periodicity H{N+n} = Hn, HN = H0. Thus E0 = H0 and O0 = 0. Conversion to DFT: The DFT Sn can be reconstructed from the DHT parts: Sn = En + i On Conversely, if the inverse DFT s{x,y} is known, the inverse DHT is: h{x,y} = \text{Re}[s{x,y}] - \text{Im}[s{x,y}] And the inverse DFT from the 2-D DHT components is: s{x,y} = e{x,y} - i o{x,y} where e{x,y} and o{x,y} are the even and odd parts of the spatial domain signal. Pitfalls: Index Wrapping: The definition of even/odd parts uses H{N-n}. Implementations must handle indices modulo N correctly. Specifically, H{N-n} for n=0 refers to H0 (via HN), not an out-of-bounds index. Periodicity: The DHT is periodic with period N, i.e., H{N+n} = Hn. This periodicity is required when computing shifted sequences or applying the convolution theorem. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cas(theta): """The cas function: cos(theta) + sin(theta).""" return math.cos(theta) + math.sin(theta) def dhtforward(h): """ Computes the 1D Discrete Hartley Transform. h: list of N real numbers. Returns: list of N real numbers H. """ N = len(h) H = [0.0] N for n in range(N): sumval = 0.0 for k in range(N): angle = 2.0 math.pi n k / N sumval += h[k] cas(angle) H[n] = sumval return H def dhtinverse(H): """ Computes the inverse 1D Discrete Hartley Transform. H: list of N real numbers. Returns: list of N real numbers h. """ N = len(H) h = [0.0] N for k in range(N): sumval = 0.0 for n in range(N): angle = 2.0 math.pi n k / N sumval += H[n] cas(angle) h[k] = sumval / N return h def dhtevenodd(H): """ Decomposes DHT output H into even (E) and odd (O) parts. H: list of N real numbers. Returns: tuple (E, O) of lists of N real numbers. """ N = len(H) E = [0.0] N O = [0.0] N for n in range(N): # Handle periodicity: index N-n wraps to 0 when n=0 idx = (N - n) % N E[n] = (H[n] + H[idx]) / 2.0 O[n] = (H[n] - H[idx]) / 2.0 return E, O def dftfromdht(H): """ Converts DHT output H to DFT output S (complex). H: list of N real numbers. Returns: list of N complex numbers S. """ E, O = dhtevenodd(H) S = [] for n in range(len(H)): S.append(complex(E[n], O[n])) return S The 2-D DHT extends the 1-D transform to images of size M \times N, producing an output array of the same size. Unlike the DFT, the 2-D DHT kernel \text{cas}[2\pi(ux/M + vy/N)] is not separable into a product of 1-D kernels; therefore, it cannot be computed by applying 1-D DHTs to rows and then columns. Formulas: Forward 2-D DHT: H{u,v} = \sum{x=0}^{M-1} \sum{y=0}^{N-1} h{x,y} \text{cas}\left[2\pi\left(\frac{ux}{M} + \frac{vy}{N}\right)\right] Inverse 2-D DHT: h{x,y} = \frac{1}{MN} \sum{u=0}^{M-1} \sum{v=0}^{N-1} H{u,v} \text{cas}\left[2\pi\left(\frac{ux}{M} + \frac{vy}{N}\right)\right] Even/Odd Parts in 2-D: The even and odd parts of the spatial signal h{x,y} are derived from the transform coefficients: e{x,y} = \frac{h{x,y} + h{-x,-y}}{2} = \frac{1}{MN} \sum{u=0}^{M-1} \sum{v=0}^{N-1} H{u,v} \cos\left[2\pi\left(\frac{ux}{M} + \frac{vy}{N}\right)\right] o{x,y} = \frac{h{x,y} - h{-x,-y}}{2} = \frac{1}{MN} \sum{u=0}^{M-1} \sum{v=0}^{N-1} H{u,v} \sin\left[2\pi\left(\frac{ux}{M} + \frac{vy}{N}\right)\right] The inverse DFT s{x,y} is obtained via s{x,y} = e{x,y} - i o{x,y}, and the inverse DHT is h{x,y} = \text{Re}[s{x,y}] - \text{Im}[s{x,y}]. Complexity: Direct computation requires O(N^2) operations for 1-D and O(M^2 N^2) for 2-D. Memory: Requires O(N) storage for 1-D and O(MN) for 2-D. Strengths: Operates entirely in real arithmetic, avoiding complex number overhead and conjugate symmetry handling required by DFT for real inputs. Limitations: The 2-D kernel is not separable, preventing the use of efficient row-column decomposition strategies used in FFTs. Use Cases: Suitable for real-valued signal processing and for convolution operations where one function is even, simplifying the convolution theorem to Fn = Hn Gn. The discrete Hartley transform is used in the actual software FVR implementation. Its properties, including periodicity, shifting, convolution, and scaling, are detailed in the context of volume rendering applications. name: Frequency-Domain Methods
body: Frequency-Domain Methods represent 4D spacetime volumetric data as a superposition of Fourier basis functions, utilizing CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) tensor decomposition to reduce memory and computation. Unlike spatial decomposition approaches, this method operates orthogonally by transforming the representation into the frequency domain. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 4D spacetime scalar field \mathbf{D}(x, y, z, t) defined on a discrete grid with dimensions U, V, W, K along the spatial and temporal axes. Output: A set of decomposed vectors representing the frequency coefficients, enabling reconstruction of the field value at any coordinate. Data Structures: The method replaces the dense 4D frequency volume \tilde{\mathbf{D}}(u, v, w, k) with low-rank factors via CP decomposition. Decomposed Vectors: Four sets of vectors \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^U, \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^V, \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^W, \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^K, each of shape \mathbb{C}^{N \times R} where N \in \{U, V, W, K\} and R is the decomposition rank. Positional Encoding (Optional): A function f(t) parameterizing time-dependent features, defined as f(t) = [1, \sin(t), \cos(t), \sin(2t), \cos(2t), \dots] or using Legendre/Chebyshev polynomials. Numbered Steps: 1. Global Transformation: The input volume is represented in the frequency domain using a 4D Fourier series. 2. Decomposition: The full frequency tensor is factorized into the product of vectors along each axis using CP decomposition. The value at any spacetime point is computed as: \mathbf{D}(x, y, z, t) = \sum{r=1}^R \left( \sum{u=1}^U \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^U(u)r \cdot e^{-j2\pi\frac{ux}{U}} \right) \cdot \left( \sum{v=1}^V \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^V(v)r \cdot e^{-j2\pi\frac{vy}{V}} \right) \cdot \left( \sum{w=1}^W \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^W(w)r e^{-j2\pi\frac{wz}{W}} \right) \cdot \left( \sum{k=1}^K \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^K(k)r e^{-j2\pi\frac{kt}{K}} \right) where \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^U(u)r denotes the u-th element of the r-th vector in the U-axis factor. 3. Evaluation: The method replaces grid sampling with inner products of the positional encodings (if used) and the decomposed vectors. Parameters: U, V, W, K: Number of frequency bins along each axis. R: Decomposition rank. Training Tricks: Weighted L1 loss regularizes the decomposed vectors, assigning higher weights to high-frequency coefficients to maintain smoothness. Smoothly bandwidth annealing gradually introduces high-frequency components during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visual Degradation: The method suffers from severe color jittering, distortions, less-saturated colors, and degraded details compared to spatial methods. Performance: Replacing grid sampling with inner products is less efficient, leading to slower evaluation speeds. Memory: While decomposition reduces memory compared to storing the full 4D frequency volume, it still requires storing R \times (U+V+W+K) vectors. Time Complexity: Evaluation requires computing inner products across R components, which is slower than direct grid lookup. Memory Complexity: Requires storing R \times (U+V+W+K) elements for the decomposed vectors, reducing memory compared to the full tensor. Strengths: Compact representation for dynamic 4D scenes. Limitations: Severe color jittering and distortions; slower evaluation speed; additional matrix-vector production reduces overall speeds compared to spatial alternatives. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method originates from research on fast representations for dynamic scenes, specifically explored as an orthogonal approach to spatial decomposition methods like HexPlane. It leverages Fourier Theory to represent 4D spacetime values in the frequency domain and applies CANDECOMP decomposition to reduce computation and memory usage. The specific implementation using CP decomposition for 4D volumes and weighted L1 regularization was detailed in the HexPlane paper. HexPlane: A Fast Representation for Dynamic Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00021, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Surface extraction
body: Surface extraction generates an explicit polygonal mesh from volumetric data, solving the problem of visualizing internal structures or boundaries as geometric primitives rather than rasterized images. This family produces a discrete geometric representation suitable for standard rasterization pipelines, ray tracing, or physical simulation, contrasting with direct volume rendering which computes pixel colors directly from scalar fields. All methods in this family operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values or occupancy states at its vertices or centers. The core mechanism involves traversing the grid cells and evaluating the data to determine which parts of the domain constitute the surface. 1. Domain Traversal: The algorithm iterates over the volume data structure. For regular grids, this often involves checking each cell or voxel. 2. Surface Determination: A criterion is applied to identify surface locations. In Isosurface extraction, this involves comparing scalar values against a threshold (isovalue) to detect sign changes or equality. In Blocky meshing, this involves checking occupancy states or material IDs to identify exposed boundaries. 3. Primitive Generation: Geometric primitives (vertices, edges, faces) are generated based on the determined surface locations. 4. Mesh Coherence: Adjacent primitives are merged or connected to form a coherent mesh, often requiring vertex merging to avoid duplicates and ensure watertightness. Generates an explicit polygonal mesh representing the surface where a scalar field equals a specific threshold. It interpolates between grid points to create smooth, curved surfaces. It is chosen when smooth geometry and topological accuracy are required. Converts discrete volumetric data into polygonal meshes by treating each voxel as a primitive unit, preserving the discrete, axis-aligned nature of the input data. It is chosen when performance is critical, the data is inherently discrete (e.g., voxel art, sparse grids), or exact alignment with the grid is desired. Surface extraction originated from the need to visualize medical imaging data (CT, MRI) and scientific simulations in a format compatible with standard graphics hardware. The Marching Cubes algorithm, introduced by Lorensen and Cline in 1987, is the foundational method for isosurface extraction on cubic grids. Blocky meshing techniques have evolved alongside voxel-based rendering and sparse volume representations, often leveraging GPU-driven classification and face culling optimizations to handle large datasets. Not given in the sources.

name: Isosurface extraction
head: contouring, polygonization, marching cubes family
body: Isosurface extraction converts a discretized scalar field into a polygonal mesh (typically triangles) representing the locus of points where the field equals a specific threshold (isovalue). It solves the problem of visualizing implicit 3D structures by transforming volumetric data into explicit surface geometry suitable for rendering or simulation. Unlike Blocky meshing, which produces voxel-aligned meshes, isosurface methods generate smooth, curved approximations by interpolating within cells. All methods in this family operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values or occupancy states at its vertices or centers. Constructs a triangulated mesh by growing a front across the implicit surface, starting from a seed point and extending it edge-by-edge. Unlike numerical simulation meshing which starts with well-defined domain representations, this method operates without a pre-defined description of volume components, requiring the algorithm to dynamically chart the reconstructed surface. Provides a high-level interface for extracting a manifold triangular mesh from a continuous implicit scalar field defined by a user-supplied function, rather than a pre-computed discrete grid. It sets itself apart from standard grid-based methods by accepting a callable function directly, handling gradient estimation via finite differences if not provided, and supporting adaptive refinement. Decomposes non-convex or complex 3D polygons (isopolygons) resulting from isosurface extraction into a set of triangles, specifically minimizing the total area of the resulting triangles to reduce visual artifacts. It sets itself apart from siblings by operating on the final polygonal boundary rather than voxel cells, and from Dual Contouring and Surface Nets by optimizing for minimal surface area of the triangulation itself rather than vertex position optimization. Constructs isosurfaces by generating N-cycles from 3-cell configurations, resolving ambiguities at voxel face junctures to prevent surface holes, unlike the original Marching Cubes Algorithm. VESTA differs from template-based methods like Marching Cubes by using a single building block based on vector decomposition, ensuring the surface is non-degenerate, volume-enclosing, and hole-free without requiring post-processing repair. Reconstructs a Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane for Volume of Fluid (VOF) simulations on arbitrary polyhedral grids by extracting an isosurface from an interpolated scalar field and computing a weighted normal vector. It is distinguished from standard VOF methods by its explicit geometric flux calculation via isosurface extraction and from pure isosurface methods by its integration into a VOF advection loop with volume conservation enforcement. Converts an isosurface into a set of unconnected vertices without generating face or edge data. It solves the problem of obtaining a geometric representation of a volume when downstream processing requires a point cloud rather than a mesh, by skipping the triangulation step and extracting a single vertex per intersected cell based on a fixed interpolation rule. A table-driven isosurface extraction technique that generates topologically consistent surfaces with a local convexity property, ensuring that the negative space inside each cell is convex. Unlike Marching Cubes, which may produce disconnected non-convex negative space, this method ensures the convex hull of the negative space is preserved, enabling fast collision detection on the triangulated isosurface. It distinguishes itself from other cell-based methods by using pre-computed decision trees to dynamically select the correct triangulation from a set of candidates based on edge intersection positions. Generates precomputed triangulation tables for isosurface extraction in n-dimensional hypercubes. It addresses the excessive simplex count produced by recursive contour-meshing, which requires subdividing 4-cells into 4-simplices before contouring, analogous to breaking a cube into five or six tetrahedra in 3D. Unlike recursive decomposition, this method constructs an n-polytope via convex hulls to determine the isosurface directly within the hypercube, ensuring consistent triangulation between adjacent faces. The elementary method for cell extraction that sequentially visits all cells in the volume to identify active cells containing the isosurface. It solves the cell extraction problem by checking if a target isovalue lies within the scalar range of each cell. Generates isosurfaces from regularly structured volume data while strictly respecting a prescribed memory limit M for auxiliary data structures. It solves the problem of minimizing expected extraction time by partitioning the volume spatially and assigning one of several extraction methods to each partition block. It sets itself apart from siblings like Octree-based Isosurfacing by optimizing the assignment of extraction algorithms to spatial blocks rather than just the spatial subdivision itself. Defines the static data structures and decision logic used to map the 256 possible binary sign configurations of a voxel's eight corners to a specific polygonal topology [10327-lookup-table-and-ambiguity-handling]. It solves the problem of efficiently determining triangle topology per voxel by replacing runtime conditional branching with direct array indexing, enabling O(1) lookup. It differs from symmetry-based approaches by handling all 256 cases explicitly (or via symmetry reduction) and from dynamic ambiguity resolution methods by using fixed triangulations for ambiguous cases. Computes geometric attributes (normals, area) or improves visual quality (smoothing) of isosurfaces extracted from scalar fields [1005-marching-cubes-surface-normal-estimation.md, 1315-marching-cubes-surface-area-estimation.md, 1594-marching-cubes-smoothing.md]. It addresses limitations of raw isosurface extraction, such as jagged artifacts in binary data or the lack of lighting information in mesh generation, by operating on the resulting geometry or the input field to refine surface representation. A code generator that produces a specialized JavaScript function for extracting surfaces from multi-dimensional ndarray data structures. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing grid cells and generating geometric primitives based on phase comparisons between adjacent cells. It sets itself apart from siblings like Marching Cubes by decoupling the traversal engine from the surface definition, enabling the generation of arbitrary contouring routines rather than a single fixed algorithm. Represents iso-surfaces by generating polygonal meshes from stacks of 2D contours extracted from consecutive slices of parallel planes within a data volume. It differs from voxel-based methods like Marching Cubes by operating on explicit contour data rather than scalar field samples, and from Dual Contouring and Surface Nets by relying on inter-slice triangulation of existing boundaries rather than local optimization of vertex positions. An early isosurface extraction method developed for medical imaging that reconstructs 3D surfaces from a sequence of 2D cross-sectional slices. It solves the problem of visualizing internal anatomical structures by tessellating surfaces between outlines detected on consecutive slices, distinguishing itself from modern grid-based methods by its reliance on explicit 2D boundary detection and inter-slice interpolation. A direct meshing algorithm that traverses a volumetric grid, decomposes each voxel into tetrahedra, and generates an isosurface by linearly interpolating vertex positions based on scalar field values relative to a target isovalue. It distinguishes itself from standard Marching Cubes by using a tetrahedral decomposition, which avoids the ambiguity issues associated with cube cells, and from dual contouring by producing a triangulated mesh directly from interpolation rather than optimizing vertex positions via quadratic error functions. Extracts a manifold surface from a volumetric image by constructing a combinatorial Khalimsky space, identifying the digital boundary using surfel adjacency rules, and converting the resulting digital surface into a dual polygonal or triangulated mesh. It differs from Isosurface extraction methods like Marching Cubes by relying on combinatorial topology and digital geometry rather than geometric interpolation within grid cells, ensuring a topologically correct manifold surface. A progressive isosurface extraction algorithm that constructs a mesh from a Signed Distance Field (SDF) by iteratively refining a weighted triangulation (regular triangulation or power diagram). Unlike static methods like Marching Cubes or Dual Contouring that operate on a fixed grid, this method starts with a coarse set of samples and incrementally inserts new vertices at locations of high geometric deviation, updating the local triangulation and surface mesh without global recomputation. Feature-preserving isosurface extraction methods that generate a mesh by placing a single vertex inside each grid cell intersecting the isosurface, rather than on the cell edges as in Marching Cubes. Dual Contouring solves topological ambiguities by optimizing vertex position via a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) to preserve sharp features [778-dual-contouring.md], while Surface Nets uses a weighted average of intersection points for a faster, normal-free approximation [921-surface-nets.md]. Methods that generate explicit triangle meshes from implicit representations (such as Signed Distance Fields or occupancy fields) by integrating the extraction process into a differentiable computational graph. Unlike static algorithms like Marching Cubes, these methods either adaptively query the neural network to save computation (e.g., MISE) or make the extraction process fully differentiable to allow gradient-based optimization of the mesh geometry (e.g., FlexiCubes). A method that generates high-quality, curvature-adaptive semi-regular meshes while preserving sharp features and extracting all disjoint components of an iso-surface. It improves upon the original Marching Triangles algorithm by introducing a normal consistency check and region-growing strategy to ensure topological correctness and feature preservation. Encompasses methods for visualizing isosurfaces extracted from volumetric scalar fields, ranging from direct procedural ray-marching to explicit rasterization of pre-computed meshes. Unlike full volumetric rendering which accumulates light through the entire volume, these techniques isolate the extracted surface for efficient display, often leveraging standard graphics pipeline features for shading and lighting. A surface extraction method designed for unbounded rendering of particle-based simulations. It addresses the performance bottlenecks of standard voxel-based Marching Cubes by treating the isosurface as a connected manifold grown from seed triangles, using a surface-following traversal strategy and a blocking algorithm with a specialized 3D lookup cache for particle queries. Encompasses methods that perform isosurface extraction entirely or partially on the GPU using programmable shaders (Compute, Geometry, Fragment) to bypass CPU bottlenecks and reduce data transfer latency. Unlike CPU-based methods that require reading back geometry or managing complex synchronization, these methods utilize the GPU's massive parallelism for tasks such as distance evaluation, voxel traversal, and mesh generation. A method for extracting crack-free isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data by constructing a dual grid where cell centers serve as vertices. It solves the "dangling node" problem inherent in standard Marching Cubes applied to resampled vertex-centered data by ensuring topological consistency across refinement boundaries. Encompasses methods that adapt the domain traversal and data structures of isosurface extraction to handle sparse, hierarchical, or multi-resolution volumetric data, avoiding the memory and computational costs of dense regular grids. Unlike standard grid-based methods that iterate over all cells, these techniques use structures like octrees or sparse hash maps to process only active regions. Extract isosurfaces from scalar fields defined on non-Cartesian domains, including arbitrary polyhedral cells and hybrid unstructured grids, solving the topological inconsistencies and geometric discontinuities inherent in standard grid-based methods like Marching Cubes [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. They approximate the surface locally at each cell as a polygonal surface (isopolygon) and trace face boundaries systematically using general polygon tracing rules. A mesh generation technique that converts the interior of a discretized grid volume into a tetrahedral mesh by subdividing pyramids around surface edges and connecting inside cubes to adjacent cells. It differs from standard Marching Tetrahedra by focusing on volumetric tetrahedralization for simulation rather than just surface extraction. A surface extraction method that generates axis-aligned cuboids from a voxel grid, merging adjacent cuboids to reduce polygon count while preserving the Marching Cubes topology at boundaries. It operates by identifying 'cuboids' (initially 1x1x1 cubes) at surface voxels and greedily expanding them in all directions until blocked by inactive voxels or distortion thresholds. An isosurface extraction method that resolves the topological ambiguities inherent in standard Marching Cubes by decomposing each cubic voxel into a fixed set of tetrahedra [9029-marching-cubes-tetrahedron-decomposition.md]. Unlike Marching Cubes, which requires complex disambiguation tables, Marching Tetrahedra guarantees a manifold, intersection-free surface by resolving ambiguities through tetrahedral decomposition, at the cost of a higher vertex count. Addresses the computational cost and visual fidelity trade-off in isosurface extraction by varying the resolution of the output mesh based on geometric complexity and view importance. Unlike fixed-resolution methods, these techniques dynamically adjust the level of detail (LOD) to maintain performance, often using hierarchical grids or adaptive sampling to refine only where the surface curvature is high. Addresses the memory and performance bottlenecks of isosurface extraction on large volumetric datasets that exceed available RAM or require efficient incremental updates. It solves the problem of high memory consumption and redundant computation by processing data in streaming chunks, slabs, or tiles, often employing spatial partitioning and out-of-core algorithms to fit auxiliary structures within a prescribed memory budget. Extracts a triangle and quad mesh from a narrow-band signed distance field (SDF) grid at a specified isosurface value. It distinguishes itself from standard isosurface methods by supporting adaptive mesh refinement and optional mesh relaxation to improve geometric quality, often targeting direct integration with simulation pipelines. An efficient and accurate volume evaluation method for grid-based level sets that computes the volume of implicitly represented shapes consistent with Marching Cubes surface reconstruction. It utilizes rotational symmetry to combine redundant Marching Cubes cases and avoids explicitly forming local triangulations using efficient volume computation formulae for pyramids and truncated prisms wherever possible, thereby achieving a fast and compact implementation. The method achieves second-order accuracy convergence and results perfectly consistent with volumes calculated directly from explicit Marching Cubes meshes. A strategy for making inner contour surfaces visible by specifying which cells contribute to the contour surface using a mask. Only cells for which the mask value is true at all eight vertices contribute to the contour surface. The mask argument can also specify separate masks for each level as a list of logical arrays or functions. A technique for visualizing volumes by drawing each voxel as a small cube. It finds every voxel with a value greater than 0 (assuming isovalue t=0) and draws a cube, selecting only those cube faces which separate cubes that are inside (t<0) from cubes that are outside (t>=0), then stitching the selected faces together to form a quad mesh. Ambiguous configuration where four faces meet at an edge is resolved by deciding which pair of faces to stitch together using the asymptotic decider by Nielson and Hamann. Creating a simplified proxy mesh from 3D Gaussians to determine page affiliations and facilitate page linking, using Marching Cubes for efficiency. It defines a plane normal to the Z-axis to create a slice of the scene, intersects this plane with the scene and renders it as an image, and repeats the process while moving the plane along the Z-axis in fixed steps for subsequent slices. Morphological operations are performed on the data before surface reconstruction to make the mesh coarser, close small holes, and reduce unnecessary details. A 2D surface extraction method that generates a mesh from a 2D scalar map, with an option for smoothing. It calls Box2D::GetDrawElement with the 2D map, dimensions, isovalue, and a boolean for smoothing to produce the output geometry. Builds a multiresolution ICM representation using hierarchical or selective clustering algorithms, then extracts topology-preserved isosurfaces under various error thresholds. Generates the proxy surface using the Marching Cubes algorithm [17], typically corresponding to the exterior material exposed through the transfer function. To minimize texture popping artifacts when using proxy geometry with clipping planes or pronounced concavities, double the number of key views. Isovalues that closely match the outermost surface specified by the transfer function produce the best results. A displacement of four degrees eliminates most popping artifacts for good surface proxies. Poor geometric approximation of the interior surface (e.g., when using clipping planes) leads to jumping of features, known as texture popping. Allows specification of a threshold value for geometry surface generation. Grid cells below this value are ignored. Used only in Isosurface, Mesh, Ocean Mesh, and Cap Mesh Modes. For Phoenix liquids (range 0-1, where 0 is no liquid and 1 is 100% full), an Isosurface Level of 0.5 is best for visualizing the surface between air and liquid. For imported caches from Houdini (positive/negative values indicating inside/outside), the correct 'halfway' Isosurface Level value is 0.0. For Phoenix smoke, the proper Isosurface Level value is about 0.01. For Phoenix temperature (in Kelvins), the value is several hundred. Extracting a mesh from NeRF by volumetric sampling, thresholding density via Marching Cubes, and coloring vertices. It generates spatial points P via dense volumetric sampling in a predefined 3D region of interest, evaluates density values \sigma(pi) for each point pi using NeRF, and identifies the isosurface by thresholding density values using the Marching Cubes algorithm: M = \text{MarchingCubes}(P, \sigma{\text{threshold}}). For every vertex vj in mesh M, it constructs viewing ray rj and queries color c(vj) from NeRF: \text{Color}(vj) = c(vj). It performs UV unwrapping on the vertex-colored mesh to create a 2D texture representation, minimizing conformal energy using Least Squares Conformal Mapping (LSCM) to minimize distortion: E(u, v) = \int{\Omega} (|\nabla u|^2 + |\nabla v|^2) dA. Optimal density value \sigma{\text{threshold}} demarcates the object's boundary, (u, v) are 2D texture coordinates for each vertex in M, \Omega is the object's surface, and dA is the differential area element on the mesh's surface. A variant of MC that uses 23 base topologies to produce a watertight isosurface without holes, solving the face ambiguity problem by only exploiting rotational symmetry. It reduces the 256 cases to 23 base cases using only rotational symmetry. The Marching Cubes algorithm was introduced by Lorensen & Cline in 1987. It is a general approach covering a whole family of algorithms, some of which are adaptive, supplemented with sharp feature detection, or capable of preserving the topology of non-manifold surfaces. Conceptually, simple contouring covers the plane with a grid and checks if the function changes sign between the centers of adjacent cells; if it does, the shared border becomes a piece of the contour. Marching Cubes improves upon this by measuring function signs in every corner for each square, adding line segments that cross the cells, and connecting sign-changing edges. Since pairs of signs for each shared edge change synchronously for both cells, the line segments connect automatically into a continuous contour. Linear interpolation is used to find the exact position of the line segment ends on the edges, rather than placing them at the middle, though this is an approximation because the target function is not necessarily linear. The error of the simple contour (middle-to-middle) never exceeds half of the cell's diagonal. name: Topologically Accurate Dual Isosurfacing Using Ray Intersection
head: Dual Isosurfacing via Ray Intersection, Dual isosurfacing, Dual isosurfacing using ray intersection, Ray-based dual isosurfacing, Ray-intersection dual contouring, Trilinear dual contouring
body: This method extracts a topologically correct isosurface from a volumetric scalar field by computing exact intersection points within each voxel using ray intersection with a trilinear interpolation model. It solves the topological ambiguities inherent in standard Marching Cubes (MC) and avoids the requirement for gradient or Hermite data needed by standard Dual Contouring. Unlike its siblings, it relies on a pre-computed look-up table of cell diagonals to determine the minimum number of rays required to capture all disjoint surface components and tunnels within a cell. Inputs: A structured rectilinear hexahedral grid with scalar values T{ijk} at vertices (i,j,k) \in \{0,1\}^3. An isovalue I. Outputs: A set of isosurface points \{p\} inside the cells. A triangular mesh formed by connecting these points. Cell Vertices: 8 scalar values T{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. Look-up Table (LUT): Maps each of the 31 topological configurations (derived from the 14 MC sign configurations) to a list of diagonals to test. Point Association Map: Associates each computed isosurface point with the specific cell edge containing the diagonal endpoint nearest to the point. 1. Trilinear Model: The scalar field F(x,y,z) is represented parametrically as f(u,v,w) over the unit cube [0,1]^3: f(u,v,w) = \sum{i=0}^1 \sum{j=0}^1 \sum{k=0}^1 (1 - Ui)(1 - Vj)(1 - Wk)T{ijk} where Ui = |u-ui|, Vj = |v-vj|, Wk = |w-wk|, and (ui, vj, wk) are the parametric coordinates of the vertices (0 or 1). This expands to the polynomial form Fi(u,v,w,I) = Auvw + Buv + Cvw + Dwv + Eu + Fv + Gw + H = 0, where H = T{000} - I. The coefficients are: \begin{aligned} A &= -T{000} + T{010} - T{110} + T{100} + T{001} - T{011} + T{111} - T{101} \\ B &= T{000} - T{010} - T{100} + T{110} \\ C &= T{000} - T{010} - T{100} + T{110} \\ D &= T{000} - T{100} - T{001} + T{101} \\ E &= -T{000} + T{100} \\ F &= -T{000} + T{010} \\ G &= -T{000} + T{001} \\ H &= T{000} - I \end{aligned}. 2. Ray Definition: Rays are defined as cell diagonals connecting vertex V to vertex W: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{V} + t(\mathbf{W} - \mathbf{V}), \quad 0 \leq t \leq 1 Let \Delta ur = u{r1} - u{r0}, \Delta vr = v{r1} - v{r0}, \Delta wr = w{r1} - w{r0}. The intersection point is (u^, v^, w^) = (u{r0} + t\Delta ur, v{r0} + t\Delta vr, w{r0} + t\Delta wr). 3. Cubic Equation: Substituting the ray into the trilinear model yields a cubic equation in t: G3t^3 + G2t^2 + G1t + G0 = 0 Coefficients: \begin{aligned} G0 &= A u{r0}v{r0}w{r0} + B u{r0}v{r0} + C v{r0}w{r0} + D w{r0}u{r0} + E u{r0} + F v{r0} + G w{r0} + H \\ G1 &= A(u{r0}v{r0}\Delta wr + v{r0}w{r0}\Delta ur + w{r0}u{r0}\Delta vr) + B(v{r0}\Delta ur + u{r0}\Delta vr) + C(w{r0}\Delta vr + v{r0}\Delta wr) + D(u{r0}\Delta wr + w{r0}\Delta ur) + E\Delta ur + F\Delta vr + G\Delta wr \\ G2 &= A(u{r0}\Delta vr\Delta wr + v{r0}\Delta wr\Delta ur + w{r0}\Delta ur\Delta vr) + B\Delta ur\Delta vr + C\Delta vr\Delta wr + D\Delta wr\Delta ur \\ G3 &= A\Delta ur\Delta vr\Delta wr \end{aligned}. 4. Solving the Cubic: If G3 = 0, solve the quadratic G2t^2 + G1t + G0 = 0 using discriminant D2 = G1^2 - 4G2G0. If G3 \neq 0, compute the discriminant D3 based on the point of inflexion (xN, yN): \delta^2 = \frac{G2^2 - 3G3G1}{9G3^2}, \quad xN = -\frac{G2}{3G3}, \quad yN = G3xN^3 + G2xN^2 + G1xN + G0 D3 = yN^2 - 4G3^2\delta^3. If D3 > 0: 1 real root. If D3 = 0: 3 equal real roots (if yN=0) or 1 distinct + 2 equal real roots (if yN \neq 0). If D3 < 0: 3 distinct real roots.. Use Cardan's method for analytical solution or Newton-Raphson numerically. 5. Ambiguity Detection: Ambiguous Face: A face with four same-sign ended diagonals and four (+/-) edges. Asymptotic Decider: Determines the sign of an ambiguous face. Compute V = T{00}T{11} - T{01}T{10} - I(T{00} + T{11} - T{01} - T{10}) using bilinear interpolation on the face vertices. V < 0: Hyperbola in 1st/3rd quadrants (Positive sign). V > 0: Hyperbola in 2nd/4th quadrants (Negative sign).. DeVella's Necklace Test: Detects tunnels. Compute: K[Fi] = (AE - BD)(AF - BC)(AG - CD) Disc[Fi] = (AH)^2 + (BG)^2 + (CE)^2 + (DF)^2 - 2ABGH - 2ACEH - 2ADFH - 2BCEG - 2BDFG - 2CDEF + 4AEFG + 4BCDH If K[Fi] < 0 and Disc[Fi] > 0, a tunnel exists. 1. Generate LUT: Pre-compute the required diagonals for all 31 topological configurations based on the number of ambiguous faces and their signs. 2. Identify Heterogeneous Cells: Iterate through all cells. Classify vertices as Positive (T{ijk} \geq I) or Negative (T{ijk} < I). 3. Determine Configuration: Count ambiguous faces using the Asymptotic Decider. Categorize into one of the 31 configurations (0-13, with sub-configurations for tunnels/disjoint surfaces). Use DeVella's test where necessary (e.g., Config 4, 6.1, 7.4, 10.1.2, 12.1.2) to distinguish tunnels from disjoint surfaces. 4. Select Diagonals: Retrieve the list of diagonals from the LUT for the current configuration. Rule of Thumb: Use one-point-per-disjoint-component, except for tunnels which require multiple points. 5. Compute Intersection Points: For each selected diagonal, form the ray equation. Compute coefficients G0..G3. Solve for real roots t \in [0,1]. Compute intersection points p = \mathbf{V} + t(\mathbf{W} - \mathbf{V}). 6. Associate Points with Edges: Associate each point p with the edge containing the diagonal endpoint (V or W) closest to p. For specific configurations (e.g., tunnels), make additional associations with vertices to ensure connectivity. Associate the point with all edges containing its associated vertices. 7. Polygonization: For each edge, collect all associated isosurface points from neighboring cells. Connect these points to form one or two non-overlapping triangles. Tunnel Handling: Treat tunnel cells as isolated. Polygonize their points independently without sharing edges with neighbors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def topologicallyaccuratedualisosurfacing(grid, isovalue): """ grid: 3D array of scalar values. isovalue: float I. Returns: list of triangles (vertices). """ # Step 1: Pre-computed LUT (simplified representation) # Key: (numambiguousfaces, signsofambiguousfaces, hastunnel) # Value: list of diagonal indices (0-3) to test # Sources do not provide the full LUT mapping. LUT = { (0, (), False): [(0, 1)], (0, (), True): [(0, 2), (1, 3)], } # Step 2: Iterate cells and collect points allpoints = [] for z in range(grid.depth - 1): for y in range(grid.height - 1): for x in range(grid.width - 1): cell = grid.getcell(x, y, z) # Classify vertices vertexsigns = [1 if cell.vertices[i] >= isovalue else -1 for i in range(8)] # Step 3: Determine Configuration ambiguousfaces = [] for faceidx in range(6): if isambiguousface(cell, faceidx, vertexsigns): sign = asymptoticdecider(cell, faceidx, isovalue) ambiguousfaces.append(sign) numambiguous = len(ambiguousfaces) hastunnel = False if numambiguous == 0 and cell.config == 4: hastunnel = devellasnecklacetest(cell, isovalue) configkey = (numambiguous, tuple(ambiguousfaces), hastunnel) # Step 4: Select Diagonals diagonals = LUT.get(configkey, []) # Step 5: Compute Points for diagidx in diagonals: V, W = cell.getdiagonalendpoints(diagidx) du = W[0] - V[0] dv = W[1] - V[1] dw = W[2] - V[2] coeffs = computecubiccoefficients(V, du, dv, dw, cell.vertices, isovalue) roots = solvecubic(coeffs) for t in roots: if 0.0 <= t <= 1.0: p = (V[0] + tdu, V[1] + tdv, V[2] + tdw) edgeassoc = findassociatededge(p, V, W) allpoints.append((p, (x, y, z), edgeassoc)) # Step 7: Polygonization triangles = [] edgemap = {} for p, cellid, edgeassoc in allpoints: if edgeassoc not in edgemap: edgemap[edgeassoc] = [] edgemap[edgeassoc].append(p) for edge, points in edgemap.items(): if istunnelcell(edge): triangles.extend(polygonizetunnel(points)) else: triangles.extend(polygonizeedge(points)) return triangles def isambiguousface(cell, faceidx, vertexsigns): # Check if face has 4 same-sign diagonals and 4 (+/-) edges # Sources do not provide explicit face diagonal enumeration logic. return True def asymptoticdecider(cell, faceidx, isovalue): # V = T00T11 - T01T10 - I(T00 + T11 - T01 - T10) # Return +1 if V < 0, -1 if V > 0 pass def devellasnecklacetest(cell, isovalue): # Compute K and Disc as per formulas # Return True if K < 0 and Disc > 0 pass def computecubiccoefficients(V, du, dv, dw, vertices, isovalue): # Compute A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H # Compute G0, G1, G2, G3 pass def solvecubic(coeffs): # Solve G3t^3 + G2t^2 + G1t + G0 = 0 pass def findassociatededge(p, V, W): # Return edge index containing endpoint closest to p pass def istunnelcell(edge): # Check if edge belongs to a tunnel configuration pass def polygonizetunnel(points): # Polygonize tunnel points independently pass def polygonizeedge(points): # Connect points to form one or two triangles pass Time Complexity: The polygonization step has O(n) time complexity for a grid size n. Memory Limitations: Memory limitations in the polygonization phase require downsampling datasets larger than 64 \times 64 \times 64 by a ratio (e.g., 1:4). Performance: Computation times depend on the number of tunnel cases. For example, on Neghip (32 \times 32 \times 32, 1:1 ratio, 0 tunnels) it takes 0.96s, on Buckyball (32 \times 32 \times 32, 1:1 ratio, 0 tunnels) 1.67s, on Bonsai (256 \times 256 \times 256, 1:4 ratio, 42 tunnels) 2.36s, and on Skull (256 \times 256 \times 256, 1:4 ratio, 67 tunnels) 4.08s. Strengths: Generates topologically correct isosurfaces including tunnel cases and multiple isosurface components per cell, computing exact points on the isosurface with respect to trilinear interpolation. Does not require normal information such as Hermite data. Limitations: The current polygonization method is not favorable for grid sizes greater than 64 \times 64 \times 64 due to memory constraints. The polygonization step needs optimization; using efficient data structures like kd-trees would improve performance. The method was introduced in a paper by Lopes et al.. It builds on the exhaustive analysis of the 31 topological configurations of the MC case table [LB03] and uses the asymptotic decider [NH91] and DeVella's necklace test [Nie03] to resolve ambiguities. It is applied on synthetic 2 \times 2 \times 2 datasets for tunnel cases and standard datasets (Neghip, Buckyball, Bonsai, Skull).
