name: Isosurface Extraction API
head: Marching Cubes Function Interface
body: The Isosurface Extraction API provides a high-level interface for extracting a manifold triangular mesh from a continuous implicit scalar field defined by a user-supplied function, rather than a pre-computed discrete grid. It solves the problem of converting mathematical implicit surfaces into polygonal meshes by internally managing an adaptive octree traversal and calling a Rust-based core extraction routine. It sets itself apart from standard grid-based methods like Marching Cubes by accepting a callable function func(x,y,z) directly, handling gradient estimation via finite differences if not provided, and supporting adaptive refinement through octree depth parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: func: A vectorized implicit function taking (N, 3) float64 positions and returning (N,) float64 scalar values, optionally returning (N, 3) float64 gradients. bboxmin, bboxmax: 3-element tuples defining the axis-aligned bounding box of the extraction domain. isovalue: Isosurface level, default 0.0. mindepth, maxdepth: Octree depth range. Cell count per axis is 2^{\text{depth}}. mindepth must be \ge 1 and maxdepth must be \le 12. anglethreshold: Float in degrees (0, 180). Normals differing by more than this value trigger sharp-feature handling. fdstep: Float for finite difference gradient estimation when func does not return gradients, default 10^{-5}. Outputs: vertices: A (V, 3) float64 array of mesh vertices. faces: A (F, 3) int64 array of triangle indices. Empty cases return arrays with shape (0, 3). Data Structures: The API uses a callback adapter evalbatch to bridge Python and the Rust core, ensuring that the output of func is converted to numpy arrays of correct dtype (float64) and shape. Steps: 1. Validate Inputs: Check that bboxmin and bboxmax are 3-element tuples and bboxmin < bboxmax in all dimensions. Check that mindepth and maxdepth are integers, 1 \le \text{min\depth} \le \text{max\depth} \le 12. Check that anglethreshold is in (0, 180). Raise ValueError on failures. 2. Normalize Bounding Box: If the bounding box is non-cubic, expand it to the smallest enclosing cube centered on the original bounding box center and issue a warning. 3. Create Callback Adapter: Define evalbatch(points) which calls func(points). If func returns a tuple (values, gradients), validate that values has shape (N,) and gradients has shape (N, 3). If gradients is None, the core uses finite differences with step fdstep. 4. Call Core Extraction: Invoke the Rust extractmesh function with the callback, normalized bounding box, depth range, angle threshold, isovalue, and adaptive flag. 5. Post-process Output: Ensure the returned vertices are float64 with shape (V, 3) and faces are int64 with shape (F, 3). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def isosurfaceextractionapi( func, bboxmin: tuple, bboxmax: tuple, isovalue: float = 0.0, mindepth: int = 1, maxdepth: int = 12, anglethreshold: float = 10.0, fdstep: float = 1e-5) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: # 1. Validate Inputs bboxminarr = np.asarray(bboxmin, dtype=np.float64) bboxmaxarr = np.asarray(bboxmax, dtype=np.float64) if bboxminarr.shape != (3,) or bboxmaxarr.shape != (3,): raise ValueError("Bounding boxes must be 3-element tuples.") if not np.all(bboxminarr < bboxmaxarr): raise ValueError("bboxmin must be strictly less than bboxmax.") if not (1 <= mindepth <= maxdepth <= 12): raise ValueError("Depth must be in [1, 12] and min <= max.") if not (0.0 < anglethreshold < 180.0): raise ValueError("Angle threshold must be in (0, 180).") # 2. Normalize Bounding Box to Cubic center = (bboxminarr + bboxmaxarr) / 2.0 extents = (bboxmaxarr - bboxminarr) / 2.0 maxextent = np.max(extents) bboxmincubic = center - maxextent bboxmaxcubic = center + maxextent # Warning issued here in implementation # 3. Define Callback Adapter def evalbatch(points: np.ndarray) -> tuple: result = func(points) if isinstance(result, tuple): values, gradients = result values = np.asarray(values, dtype=np.float64) if values.shape[0] != points.shape[0]: raise ValueError("Value count mismatch.") if gradients is not None: gradients = np.asarray(gradients, dtype=np.float64) if gradients.shape != (points.shape[0], 3): raise ValueError("Gradient shape mismatch.") return values, gradients return values, None else: values = np.asarray(result, dtype=np.float64) if values.shape[0] != points.shape[0]: raise ValueError("Value count mismatch.") return values, None # 4. Call Rust Core # Invoke Rust extractmesh with callback, bboxmincubic, bboxmaxcubic, # mindepth, maxdepth, anglethreshold, isovalue, fdstep, adaptive=True # vertices, faces =... # 5. Ensure Output Types # Post-process to ensure vertices are float64 (V,3) and faces are int64 (F,3) return vertices, faces Separates a polygonal isosurface mesh into connected components (shells) to handle disjoint surfaces or allow user selection of specific regions. It differs from automated connectivity filters by explicitly traversing the mesh graph from a starting triangle ID to identify all connected triangles belonging to the same shell, allowing for interactive selection of disjoint parts. Time Complexity: Determined by the octree traversal and the number of leaf cells evaluated. The adaptive nature means complexity scales with the surface area and detail, not just the volume. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of leaf cells in the octree and the resulting mesh size. Strengths: No need to pre-compute a dense grid; supports arbitrary implicit functions; adaptive resolution captures detail efficiently; sharp feature handling via angle threshold. Limitations: Requires a callable function; gradient estimation via finite differences adds computational overhead if not provided; non-cubic bounding boxes are expanded, potentially wasting computation on empty space. When to Use: When the scalar field is defined by a complex mathematical function or simulation output that is expensive to sample on a full grid, or when adaptive resolution is desired. When Not to Use: When a pre-computed grid is already available and fixed resolution is sufficient (use Marching Cubes directly for potentially lower overhead). The Isosurface Extraction API is part of the isomesh library, which provides a Python interface to a Rust-based isosurface extraction engine. It builds upon the principles of adaptive isosurface extraction, specifically leveraging Manifold Dual Contouring techniques for sharp feature preservation and manifold guarantee. The API abstracts the complexity of octree traversal and cell processing, providing a simple function-call interface similar to scipy.ndimage.marchingcubes but for implicit functions. pmneila/PyMCubes, https://github.com/pmneila/PyMCubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Manual Shell Extraction
head: Connected Component Separation, Disjoint Mesh Isolation, Shell Extraction via Manual Traversal, findShell, Shell Extraction via Connectivity Filter, vtkPolyDataConnectivityFilter
body: Manual Shell Extraction separates a polygonal isosurface mesh into connected components (shells) to handle disjoint surfaces or allow user selection of specific regions. It differs from automated connectivity filters by explicitly traversing the mesh graph from a starting triangle ID to identify all connected triangles belonging to the same shell, allowing for interactive selection of disjoint parts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An isosurface mesh (isosurfacePolydata) containing triangles, and optionally a starting triangle ID for manual traversal. Output: A subset of the mesh corresponding to the selected shell, or the complete mesh if no selection is required. Data Structures: triangleIndex: A mapping from vtkIdType (triangle ID) to int (0=unvisited, 1=visited). foundMeshes: A vector of sets, std::vector<std::set<vtkIdType>>, storing the IDs of triangles belonging to each identified shell. shellTriangles: A vtkCellArray used to construct the final output mesh. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize allVisited = false, numShells = 0, and foundMeshes as an empty vector of triangle ID sets. 2. If manual traversal is selected, initialize a queue with a starting triangle ID and an empty set for shell triangles. 3. While the queue is not empty, dequeue the current triangle ID and get its point IDs. 4. For each point in the triangle, find neighbor triangles sharing that point. 5. For each neighbor, if it has not been visited (triangleIndex does not contain it or its value is not 1), mark it visited, push it to the queue, and add it to the current shell's set in foundMeshes. 6. Repeat the traversal process for any remaining unvisited triangles to identify all disjoint shells, incrementing numShells for each new shell found. 7. After extraction, if numShells > 1, prompt the user for a selectedShell index. 8. If selectedShell == 0, render the complete isosurfacePolydata. Otherwise, decrement selectedShell, retrieve shellTriangleIds from foundMeshes, iterate to construct vtkTriangle objects using vertex indices from triangleV0Index, triangleV1Index, and triangleV2Index, insert them into shellTriangles (vtkCellArray), assign to isosurfacePolydata, and map to the renderer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def manualshellextraction(isosurfacepolydata, starttriangleid=None): # Data structures matching source layout triangleindex = {} # Maps triangle ID to int (0=unvisited, 1=visited) foundmeshes = [] # List of sets storing triangle IDs per shell numshells = 0 allvisited = False # Initialize triangleindex for all triangles in the mesh for tid in range(isosurfacepolydata.numcells): triangleindex[tid] = 0 # Helper: find connected shell via BFS traversal def findshell(startid): queue = [startid] shelltriangles = set() triangleindex[startid] = 1 shelltriangles.add(startid) while queue: currentid = queue.pop(0) # Get point IDs of the current triangle pointids = isosurfacepolydata.gettrianglepoints(currentid) for pid in pointids: # Find neighbor triangles sharing that point neighborids = isosurfacepolydata.gettrianglessharingpoint(pid) for nid in neighborids: if triangleindex.get(nid, 0) != 1: triangleindex[nid] = 1 queue.append(nid) shelltriangles.add(nid) return shelltriangles # Extract shells if starttriangleid is not None: shelltriangles = findshell(starttriangleid) foundmeshes.append(shelltriangles) numshells = 1 else: # Traverse all triangles to find all disjoint shells for tid in range(isosurfacepolydata.numcells): if triangleindex[tid] == 0: shelltriangles = findshell(tid) foundmeshes.append(shelltriangles) numshells += 1 # User selection if numshells > 1: selectedshell = int(input(f"Select shell index (1-{numshells}, 0 for all): ")) else: selectedshell = 0 if selectedshell == 0: return isosurfacepolydata # Construct selected shell shelltriangleids = foundmeshes[selectedshell - 1] shellcellarray = [] # vtkCellArray equivalent: list of point index tuples for tid in shelltriangleids: v0 = isosurfacepolydata.trianglev0index[tid] v1 = isosurfacepolydata.trianglev1index[tid] v2 = isosurfacepolydata.trianglev2index[tid] shellcellarray.append((v0, v1, v2)) # Assign to output polydata and map to renderer outputpolydata = isosurfacepolydata.copy() outputpolydata.setpolys(shellcellarray) return outputpolydata Parameters: starttriangleid: Optional. If provided, extraction starts from this triangle. selectedshell: User-provided 1-based index of the shell to extract. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If findShell fails to update triangleIndex, the traversal loop becomes infinite. The manual traversal breaks after finding one unvisited triangle per outer loop iteration, relying on findShell to mark all reachable triangles as visited. Degenerate triangles (NULL triangles) should be filtered out during mesh construction. Strengths: Allows interactive selection of disjoint shells; avoids custom graph traversal code if using VTK's vtkPolyDataConnectivityFilter as an alternative. Limitations: Requires manual user input if multiple shells exist; manual traversal implementation is prone to infinite loops if visited flags are not updated correctly. When to use: When the isosurface contains disjoint components and the user needs to select specific regions for rendering or further processing. When not to use: When all shells are required simultaneously or when automated processing without user interaction is needed (use vtkPolyDataConnectivityFilter with SetExtractionModeToAllRegions() instead). Manual Shell Extraction is part of the isosurface extraction pipeline, often implemented using VTK's vtkPolyDataConnectivityFilter or custom traversal logic. The method is described in the context of the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm implementation. andresbejarano/MarchingTetrahedra, https://github.com/andresbejarano/MarchingTetrahedra, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: VESTA
head: Marching VESTA, Original VESTA
body: VESTA (Volume-Enclosing Surface exTraction) is an isosurface extraction algorithm that constructs non-degenerate, closed 3D surfaces from voxel data by generating N-cycles from 3-cell configurations. Unlike template-based methods such as Marching Cubes, VESTA uses a single building block based on vector decomposition to resolve 3D cell ambiguities at voxel face junctures, guaranteeing surfaces that are hole-free, non-self-intersecting, and volume-enclosing. The original VESTA processes the entire dataset at once, while the marching VESTA variant scans 2x2x2 voxel neighborhoods (3-cells) to generate surface tiles, with all resulting cycles confined to these local neighborhoods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field defined on a regular cubic lattice. Each voxel holds a scalar value (e.g., temperature, density). Output: A mesh of oriented triangles (2-simplices) forming the isosurface. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: 3D array of scalar values. 2. Boundary Face Vectors (VFVs): For each boundary face between an active and inactive voxel, four vectors connect the face center to the four edge midpoints (junctures) in counter-clockwise order relative to the range vector. 3. Vector Path Table: A lookup table mapping a quadrant ID and orientation (\oplus or \ominus) to a path sequence of junctures. The table stores 24 directed paths (half due to \oplus/\ominus symmetry). Columns: Center ID, Orientation (\oplus/\ominus), Path (sequence of juncture indices). Example (ID 0): \oplus Path: 13 \to 0 \to 12; \ominus Path: 12 \to 0 \to 13. 4. Support Points: Initially the centers of boundary faces. May be displaced within range vectors for isosurface accuracy. 5. Junctures: Endpoints of VFVs (edge midpoints) where multiple VFVs meet. 6. Points of Ambiguity (POA): Junctures where multiple valid connections exist, typically where voxels share only an edge, resulting in multiple incoming and outgoing VFVs. Parameters: isovalue: Threshold separating active (v \ge \text{iso\value}) and inactive voxels. Typical value in example: 139 MeV. connectivitymode: Global or local mode for handling POAs. Options: disconnect, connect, or mixed. resolutionmode: Determines triangulation detail. Options: Low (L, no extra points) or High (H, uses average points). Numbered Steps: 1. Segmentation: Classify voxels as active (v \ge \text{iso\value}) or inactive (v < \text{iso\value}). 2. Identify Boundary Faces: For each active voxel, check its 6 neighbors. If a neighbor is inactive, record the shared face as a boundary face. 3. Define VFVs: For each boundary face, define the face center (support point) and four VFVs connecting the center to the four edge midpoints (junctures) in counter-clockwise order. 4. Connect VFVs (Cycle Formation): Traverse the boundary faces. At each juncture, connect the origin of a VFV to the tip of a VFV from a neighboring boundary face. Ambiguity Resolution: If a juncture is a POA, apply the connectivitymode: disconnect connects VFVs belonging to the same voxel; connect connects VFVs belonging to different voxels; mixed uses local gray-level thresholds to decide per POA. Replace connected VFV pairs with VESTA cycle vectors connecting support points. Group vectors into closed cycles (N-cycles). 5. Displacement (Optional for Isosurfaces): Displace support points (face centers) along the range vector (from active voxel center to inactive neighbor center) based on linear interpolation of field values. 6. Triangulation (Decomposition): Decompose N-cycles into triangles (3-cycles). Low Resolution (L): For N > 3, insert antiparallel vector pairs to break cycles into 3-cycles without adding new vertices. High Resolution (H): For N > 3, calculate an additional point (average of all cycle support points) and connect it to the cycle vertices to form triangles. 7. Filtering: Discard unphysical triangles (e.g., if corner points have negative radial/temporal values). Formulas: The total normal vector d\Sigma\mu for an N-cycle is calculated as the sum of the individual triangle normal vectors d\sigma^i\mu, associated with the average point of the N-cycle. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Contact: VESTA does not connect voxels that share only a single common point (corner contact) by default, as their VFVs never meet, resulting in two separate surfaces. Forcing this connectivity requires inserting a tubular template, which is not standard. POA Consistency: A consistent global or local selection must be made for all POAs to prevent tearing/holes in the final surface. Redundancy: Original VESTA produces the minimum required support points, whereas template-based methods like MCA generate significantly more redundant support points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vestaextract(volume, isovalue, connectivitymode, resolutionmode): """ volume: 3D array of scalars isovalue: float threshold connectivitymode: 'disconnect', 'connect', or 'mixed' resolutionmode: 'L' or 'H' Returns: list of triangles, each triangle is a tuple of 3 support points (x,y,z) """ dims = (len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0])) active = set() for i in range(dims[0]): for j in range(dims[1]): for k in range(dims[2]): if volume[i, j, k] >= isovalue: active.add((i, j, k)) boundaryfaces = [] vfvidcounter = 0 for voxel in active: for d in range(6): neighbor = getneighbor(voxel, d) if neighbor is not None and neighbor not in active: facecenter = getfacecenter(voxel, d) junctures = getfacejunctures(voxel, d) vfvs = [] for idx, juncture in enumerate(junctures): vfv = {'id': vfvidcounter, 'origin': facecenter, 'tip': juncture, 'voxel': voxel, 'junctureidx': idx} vfvs.append(vfv) vfvidcounter += 1 boundaryfaces.append({'center': facecenter, 'vfvs': vfvs, 'voxel': voxel, 'direction': d}) juncturemap = {} for face in boundaryfaces: for vfv in face['vfvs']: tip = vfv['tip'] if tip not in juncturemap: juncturemap[tip] = [] juncturemap[tip].append(vfv) visitedvfvs = set() cycles = [] for face in boundaryfaces: for vfv in face['vfvs']: if vfv['id'] in visitedvfvs: continue cycle = [] currentvfv = vfv while currentvfv is not None and currentvfv['id'] not in visitedvfvs: visitedvfvs.add(currentvfv['id']) cycle.append(currentvfv) tip = currentvfv['tip'] candidates = juncturemap.get(tip, []) if len(candidates) == 0: break if len(candidates) == 1: nextvfv = candidates[0] else: nextvfv = selectnextvfv(candidates, currentvfv, connectivitymode, juncturemap, tip) if nextvfv is None: break currentvfv = nextvfv if len(cycle) > 0: cycles.append(cycle) # Displace support points for isosurfaces if resolutionmode == 'H': for cycle in cycles: for vfv in cycle: vfv['origin'] = displacepoint(vfv['origin'], vfv['voxel'], volume) triangles = [] for cycle in cycles: n = len(cycle) if n == 3: p0, p1, p2 = cycle[0]['origin'], cycle[1]['origin'], cycle[2]['origin'] triangles.append((p0, p1, p2)) else: if resolutionmode == 'L': p0 = cycle[0]['origin'] for i in range(1, n - 1): p1 = cycle[i]['origin'] p2 = cycle[i+1]['origin'] triangles.append((p0, p1, p2)) else: avg = calculateaverage(cycle) for i in range(n): p1 = cycle[i]['origin'] p2 = cycle[(i + 1) % n]['origin'] triangles.append((avg, p1, p2)) return triangles def getneighbor(voxel, d): i, j, k = voxel if d == 0: return (i+1, j, k) if d == 1: return (i-1, j, k) if d == 2: return (i, j+1, k) if d == 3: return (i, j-1, k) if d == 4: return (i, j, k+1) if d == 5: return (i, j, k-1) return None def getfacecenter(voxel, d): i, j, k = voxel if d == 0: return (i+0.5, j, k) if d == 1: return (i-0.5, j, k) if d == 2: return (i, j+0.5, k) if d == 3: return (i, j-0.5, k) if d == 4: return (i, j, k+0.5) if d == 5: return (i, j, k-0.5) return None def getfacejunctures(voxel, d): i, j, k = voxel # Returns 4 edge midpoints in CCW order relative to the range vector if d == 0: return [(i+0.5, j+0.5, k), (i+0.5, j-0.5, k), (i+0.5, j-0.5, k+1), (i+0.5, j+0.5, k+1)] if d == 1: return [(i-0.5, j-0.5, k), (i-0.5, j+0.5, k), (i-0.5, j+0.5, k+1), (i-0.5, j-0.5, k+1)] if d == 2: return [(i+0.5, j+0.5, k), (i-0.5, j+0.5, k), (i-0.5, j-0.5, k), (i+0.5, j-0.5, k)] if d == 3: return [(i-0.5, j-0.5, k), (i+0.5, j-0.5, k), (i+0.5, j+0.5, k), (i-0.5, j+0.5, k)] if d == 4: return [(i+0.5, j, k+0.5), (i-0.5, j, k+0.5), (i-0.5, j, k-0.5), (i+0.5, j, k-0.5)] if d == 5: return [(i-0.5, j, k-0.5), (i+0.5, j, k-0.5), (i+0.5, j, k+0.5), (i-0.5, j, k+0.5)] return [] def selectnextvfv(candidates, currentvfv, mode, juncturemap, tip): nextcandidates = [v for v in juncturemap.get(tip, []) if v['origin'] == tip] if len(nextcandidates) == 1: return nextcandidates[0] if mode == 'disconnect': for v in nextcandidates: if v['voxel'] == currentvfv['voxel']: return v elif mode == 'connect': for v in nextcandidates: if v['voxel'] != currentvfv['voxel']: return v elif mode == 'mixed': # Mixed mode uses local gray-level thresholds to decide per POA return nextcandidates[0] if nextcandidates else None return nextcandidates[0] if nextcandidates else None def displacepoint(point, voxel, volume): # Displace face center along range vector based on linear interpolation of field values. # Exact interpolation formula not given in sources. return point def calculateaverage(cycle): n = len(cycle) avg = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for vfv in cycle: p = vfv['origin'] avg[0] += p[0] avg[1] += p[1] avg[2] += p[2] return (avg[0]/n, avg[1]/n, avg[2]/n) STEVE (Space-Time-Enclosing Volume Extraction) is an algorithm for extracting iso-valued hypersurfaces from 4D data sets, guaranteeing that the resulting hypersurface is free from accidental rifts and fully encloses a region in 4D space. It generates simplex-based manifolds of codimension 1, specifically consisting purely of 3-simplices (tetrahedrons) embedded in 4D space. Unlike methods that extrude 4D data to 5D, STEVE works directly in 4D. It builds on the VESTA framework, using a similar flowchart for mesh features, data segmentation, and ambiguity handling, but extends the vector path logic to four dimensions. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active voxels and boundary faces. The marching variant processes 2x2x2 neighborhoods independently, allowing for parallelization. Memory Complexity: Original VESTA requires storing the entire dataset and all cycles in memory, which can be high for large volumes. Marching VESTA reduces memory usage by processing local 3-cells. Performance: In benchmarks on 200 x-ray microtomography images (256x256 pixels, ~512k active voxels), Original VESTA L took 5.34s, Mixed L took 4.62s, and MCA L took 4.71s. VESTA generates significantly fewer support points than MCA (e.g., 932k points vs 5.5M points for the same triangle count), reducing redundancy. Strengths: Guarantees hole-free, non-self-intersecting, volume-enclosing surfaces. No template management required. Robust against topological ambiguities. Limitations: Does not connect voxels sharing only a single point (corner contact) by default, which may require post-processing or template insertion for weak connectivity. High-resolution mode requires calculating average points, adding computational overhead. VESTA was introduced as a novel volume-enclosing surface extraction technique for 3D data sets on cubic lattices. It was developed to address the limitations of the Marching Cubes Algorithm (MCA), particularly the generation of holes and the need for extensive template sets to handle ambiguities. The method is analogous to the 2D DICONEX algorithm. It has been applied to computer tomographic scan data and relativistic hydrodynamic simulation data. Volume-Enclosing Surface Extraction, https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.1787v4, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) STEVE - Space-Time-Enclosing Volume Extraction, https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.5683, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: STEVE Hypersurface Generation
head: STEVE, STEVE algorithm, Space-Time-Enclosing Volume Extraction
body: STEVE (Space-Time-Enclosing Volume Extraction) is an algorithm for extracting iso-valued hypersurfaces from 4D data sets (e.g., temporal sequences of 3D images), guaranteeing that the resulting hypersurface is free from accidental rifts and fully encloses a region in 4D space. It generates simplex-based manifolds of codimension 1, specifically consisting purely of 3-simplices (tetrahedrons) embedded in 4D space. Unlike methods that extrude 4D data to 5D to construct iso-hypersurfaces, STEVE works directly in 4D to ensure codimension 1 manifolds. It builds on the VESTA framework, using a similar flowchart for mesh features, data segmentation, and ambiguity handling, but extends the vector path logic to four dimensions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A homogeneous, N-cubical (Cartesian) grid in 4D (x, y, z, t). Data specifies overall dimensions (bounds and maximum numbers of toxels in x, y, z, t directions) and individual x, y, z, t positions with associated field values for each toxel center. Output: A set of oriented 3-simplices (tetrahedrons) representing the iso-hypersurface. Data Structures: Toxel: A 4D picture element (time-varying voxel). 4D-Cell: A 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhood of toxels. Indexing Scheme: Toxel Site IDs: 16 IDs (0–15). IDs 0–7 are "past" (time t), IDs 8–15 are "future" (time t+1). Boundary Cube Centers (Support Points): 32 potential points (IDs 0–31) located at the centers of the 3D faces of the 4D-cell. Junctures: 24 potential points of ambiguity (POA) with IDs > 31. Vector Path Table (Table 2): A lookup table with 32 rows (Center IDs 0–31) and 18 columns. Columns are grouped by orientation (\oplus or \ominus) and path index (1, 2, 3). Each cell contains a directed path from a start Center ID to an end Center ID (e.g., '33 → 0'). Boundary Volume Octant (BVO): Each of the 16 toxels contributes 4 BVOs based on the orientation of the range vector (positive/negative x, y, z, t). Each BVO is represented by a triplet of Toxel Cube Vector (TCV) pairs. Numbered Steps: 1. Read Input: Read overall dimensions and individual x, y, z, t positions with field values. 2. Segment Data: Compare each toxel's field value to the iso-value. Mark active/inactive toxels. 3. Identify Transitions: For each 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 4D-cell, identify active-to-inactive transitions. Define a range vector starting at the active toxel center and ending at the inactive neighbor center. 4. Index 4D-Cell: Label the 16 toxel site IDs (0–15), 32 boundary cube centers (0–31), and 24 junctures (>31). 5. Identify BVOs: For each of the 16 toxels in the 4D-cell, identify 4 BVOs based on the range vector orientation (\oplus/\ominus in x, y, z, t). 6. Lookup Vector Paths: Use the Vector Path Table (Table 2) to determine the 192 possible TCV pairs within the 4D-cell. Map Center IDs and orientations to three directed paths (Path 1, 2, 3) connecting boundary cube centers. 7. Generate Protomesh: Concatenate the TCVs to form initial cyclic vector paths. Isochronous Segment: If all 8 "past" toxels are active and all 8 "future" are inactive, generate 6 initial cyclic vector paths from 8 BVOs. Triangular Strut: If two BVOs have opposite orientations (e.g., 18\oplus and 18\ominus), their TCVs cancel, resulting in no contribution. Apply indexing and table to yield 5 initial cyclic vector paths. 8. Resolve Ambiguities: If a juncture is a Point of Ambiguity (POA) (paths start/end at the same juncture, e.g., juncture 47), use the connectivity diagram to resolve connections. Mixed Mode: Assign the average field value of toxels at positions I, II, III, IV to the POA. If average < iso-value, use 'disconnect' mode; if average > iso-value, use 'connect' mode. Global Modes: Enforce global 'disconnect' or 'connect'. 9. Discard Junctures: Remove all junctures (point IDs > 31) from the protomesh. This reduces cyclic paths to final tetrahedrons. Each final cyclic vector path represents a triangle embedded in 4D. 10. Inherit Orientations: Inherit orientations of final vector paths from initial ones (\oplus or \ominus) after removal of junctures to ensure consistent 4-normal vector evaluation. 11. Decompose Segments: HR Decomposition: 1. Mark the center of mass point (face center) for each 4-cycle. 2. Decompose surface cycles into triangles by connecting face centers with corresponding 4-cycle support points. 3. Collect triangles enclosing a volume, determine the absolute center of the enclosed volume. 4. Connect face centers with the absolute volume center. 5. Connect all 4-cycle support points with the absolute volume center to yield 24 properly oriented tetrahedrons. LR Decomposition: Replace steps of marking face centers and connecting them with N-cycle decompositions without additional center of mass points. Omit the step connecting face centers to volume center. Yields 12 tetrahedrons. 12. Repeat for Isolated Toxels: For a single isolated active toxel, process the remaining 15 4D-cells to generate a total of 16 oriented tetrahedrons. The union of these tetrahedrons forms the final STEVE hypersurface for that toxel. 13. Store Output: Store the generated 3-simplices (tetrahedrons). Formulas: Support Point Repositioning: Linear interpolation is used to reposition support points within the bounds defined by range vectors: P = P{\text{active}} + \alpha (P{\text{inactive}} - P{\text{active}}), where \alpha \in [0, 1] is derived from the field value ratio relative to the iso-value. Higher-dimensional B-Splines are possible. Parameters: Iso-value: A scalar threshold. Toxels with field value \ge iso-value are marked active (for enclosure); others are inactive. Interpolation: Linear interpolation is used to reposition support points within bounds defined by range vectors. Higher-dimensional B-Splines are possible. Connectivity Modes: 'Mixed' (local average-based), global 'disconnect', or global 'connect'. Resolution: High Resolution (HR) or Low Resolution (LR) decomposition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topological Ambiguities: In discretized 4D spaces, more than one solution is generally possible for constructed iso-hypersurfaces due to topological ambiguities, requiring explicit resolution. Ambiguities occur when two active toxels share only one common face (square). Directional Dependencies: Using fewer than 12 or 24 tetrahedrons (e.g., 5 for a cube) for decomposition introduces stronger directional dependencies into the hypersurface. Disjunct Segments: Toxels contacting only through a single edge or vertex yield two separate tetrahedrons, as initial cyclic vector paths form two disjunct sets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It processes each 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 4D-cell independently, similar to VESTA. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the 4D grid, toxel values, and the resulting tetrahedrons. Strengths: Guarantees rift-free, volume-enclosing hypersurfaces in 4D. Works directly in 4D without extrusion to 5D. Handles topological ambiguities explicitly. Limitations: Topological ambiguities in 4D (toxels sharing only one common face) require resolution. Using fewer than 12 or 24 tetrahedrons for decomposition introduces stronger directional dependencies. When to use: When extracting iso-hypersurfaces from 4D space-time data (e.g., time-varying CT) where volume enclosure and manifold correctness are critical. When not to use: When 3D data is sufficient (use VESTA). When computational resources are extremely limited and approximate results are acceptable. STEVE was introduced by B. R. Schlei. A first announcement was made in Ref. [10]. The algorithm is described for the first time in this paper, subject to a pending patent application [1]. It is designed for 4D data sets such as temporal sequences of 3D images from time-varying computed tomography, 3+1D fireball simulations in heavy-ion physics, and ion beam transport simulations. It extends the VESTA algorithm from 3D to 4D, using a similar flowchart and indexing scheme but with 192 vector paths (8 times the 24 of VESTA) to handle the additional dimension. name: Extended CLCIR PLIC Reconstruction
head: Extended CLCIR method, PLIC reconstruction on arbitrary grids
body: The Extended CLCIR method reconstructs a Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane for Volume of Fluid (VOF) simulations on arbitrary polyhedral grids by extracting an isosurface from an interpolated scalar field and computing a weighted normal vector. It distinguishes itself from standard VOF methods by handling non-convex and self-intersecting polyhedral cells without decomposition, and from pure isosurface methods by explicitly calculating geometric fluxes for advection. Inputs: Scalar field \phi at cell vertices, interpolated from fluid volume fractions Fl(tn) of neighboring cells. Cell geometry (vertices, faces, volume V\Omega, geometric center) for arbitrary polyhedral cells. Target isosurface value \tilde{\phi} = 0.5. Outputs: PLIC plane defined by unit normal \mathbf{n} and constant C such that \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + C = 0. The plane splits cell volume V\Omega into sub-volumes F(tn)V\Omega and (1-F(tn))V\Omega. Data Structures: Interpolated Scalar Field: \phi{ip} for each vertex ip of the computational domain. Triangulated Surface: A set of triangles forming the local or extended interface representation, where each triangle is defined by three vertices. Normal Vectors: Unit vectors \mathbf{n}t for each triangular facet t. Steps: 1. Interpolate Scalar Field: For each vertex ip, compute \phi{ip} using weighted averaging of fluid volume fractions from all cells l containing ip: \phi{ip} = \frac{\suml Fl(tn) wl}{\suml wl} where wl = 1 / \|\mathbf{x}{ip} - \mathbf{x}l\|, \mathbf{x}{ip} is the position of vertex ip, and \mathbf{x}l is the geometric center of cell l. 2. Check for Interface: Determine if the cell contains an interface by verifying if \phi{min} < 0.5 < \phi{max}, where \phi{min} and \phi{max} are the minimum and maximum interpolated scalar values at the cell's vertices. 3. Extract Isosurface: If the condition in Step 2 is met, extract the isosurface at \tilde{\phi} = 0.5 using the proposed isosurface extraction algorithm (Algorithm 1). 4. Validate Isosurface: If the extracted isosurface consists of a single isopolygon, mark the cell as a "valid isosurface cell". 5. Construct Local Triangulated Surface: For valid isosurface cells, construct a local triangulated surface by connecting the geometric center of the extracted isosurface to two consecutive \tilde{\phi}-vertices for each triangle. 6. Compute Local Normal: Calculate the local normal vector \mathbf{n}l using weighted averaging over the Nt facets of the triangulated surface: \mathbf{n}l = \frac{\sum{t=1}^{Nt} wt \mathbf{n}t}{\left\| \sum{t=1}^{Nt} wt \mathbf{n}t \right\|} where \mathbf{n}t is the unit normal to facet t, and wt is a weighting factor. For cubic grids, wt = \frac{\sin(\theta)}{L1 L2}, where \theta is the angle between the two inner edges of the triangular facet, and L1, L2 are their lengths. For other grids, wt = 1. 7. Construct Extended Triangulated Surface: Create an extended triangulated surface by connecting the geometric center of the current surface to the geometric centers of isosurfaces extracted at adjacent cells. 8. Compute Extended Normal: Compute the extended normal vector \mathbf{n}e using the same weighted averaging formula as in Step 6, but applied to the extended surface. 9. Select Primary Normal: If \arccos(\mathbf{n}e \cdot \mathbf{n}l) < 1.2 radians, set \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{n}e. Otherwise, set \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{n}l. 10. Fallback for Invalid Cells: If the cell is not a valid isosurface cell, compute \mathbf{n} using a Least-Squares Gradient Interface Reconstruction (LSGIR) method. 11. Compute PLIC Constant: Compute the constant C to locate the PLIC such that it splits the cell volume correctly. For arbitrary grids, use the CIBRAVE method. For cubic grids, use the analytical method of Scardovelli and Zaleski. 12. Update Vertices: Move the vertices of the extended triangulated surfaces to the corresponding PLIC centers. 13. Compute Corrected Normal: For valid isosurface cells, compute a corrected normal \mathbf{n}c from the updated extended triangulated surface using the formula from Step 6. 14. Final Normal Update: If \arccos(\mathbf{n}c \cdot \mathbf{n}) < 1.2 radians, update \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{n}c and recompute C to relocate the PLIC. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Step 10: Fallback to LSGIR for non-interfacial cells n = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # LSGIR result C = computeplicconstant(cell, n, cell.volumefraction) return n, C # Step 3: Extract isosurface at 0.5 # Note: Algorithm 1 from is not detailed in the provided sources. isosurface = [] # Represents extracted isopolygon(s) # Step 4: Validate isosurface isvalid = len(isosurface) == 1 if isvalid: # Step 5: Construct local triangulated surface center = cell.center polygon = isosurface[0] localtriangles = [] for i in range(len(polygon)): v1, v2 = polygon[i], polygon[(i + 1) % len(polygon)] localtriangles.append([center, v1, v2]) # Step 6: Compute local normal weightedsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for tri in localtriangles: nt = normalize([dot(tri[1]-tri[0], tri[2]-tri[0])]) # Simplified normal calc if cell.gridtype == "cubic": e1, e2 = tri[1]-center, tri[2]-center costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(e1, e2) / (norm(e1) norm(e2)))) wt = math.sin(math.acos(costheta)) / (norm(e1) norm(e2)) else: wt = 1.0 weightedsum = [weightedsum[i] + wt nt[i] for i in range(3)] nl = normalize(weightedsum) # Step 7: Construct extended triangulated surface extendedtriangles = list(localtriangles) for adj in adjacentcells: adjcenter = adj.center for tri in localtriangles: extendedtriangles.append([center, tri[0], adjcenter]) # Step 8: Compute extended normal weightedsume = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for tri in extendedtriangles: nt = normalize([dot(tri[1]-tri[0], tri[2]-tri[0])]) if cell.gridtype == "cubic": e1, e2 = tri[1]-center, tri[2]-center costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(e1, e2) / (norm(e1) norm(e2)))) wt = math.sin(math.acos(costheta)) / (norm(e1) norm(e2)) else: wt = 1.0 weightedsume = [weightedsume[i] + wt nt[i] for i in range(3)] ne = normalize(weightedsume) # Step 9: Select primary normal cosangle = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(ne, nl))) if math.acos(cosangle) < 1.2: n = ne else: n = nl # Step 11: Compute PLIC constant C = computeplicconstant(cell, n, cell.volumefraction) # Step 12: Update vertices to PLIC centers for tri in extendedtriangles: for idx in range(3): d = dot(n, tri[idx]) + C tri[idx] = [tri[idx][i] - d n[i] for i in range(3)] # Step 13: Compute corrected normal weightedsumc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for tri in extendedtriangles: nt = normalize([dot(tri[1]-tri[0], tri[2]-tri[0])]) if cell.gridtype == "cubic": e1, e2 = tri[1]-center, tri[2]-center costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(e1, e2) / (norm(e1) norm(e2)))) wt = math.sin(math.acos(costheta)) / (norm(e1) norm(e2)) else: wt = 1.0 weightedsumc = [weightedsumc[i] + wt nt[i] for i in range(3)] nc = normalize(weightedsumc) # Step 14: Final normal update cosanglec = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(nc, n))) if math.acos(cosanglec) < 1.2: n = nc C = computeplicconstant(cell, n, cell.volumefraction) else: # Fallback to LSGIR for invalid isosurface cells n = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] C = computeplicconstant(cell, n, cell.volumefraction) return n, C def computeplicconstant(cell, n, volumefraction): # Step 11: Compute C to split volume if cell.gridtype == "cubic": # Scardovelli and Zaleski analytical method pass else: # CIBRAVE method pass return 0.0 # Placeholder for actual volume enforcement calculation This method simulates multiphase fluid flows by advecting a Volume of Fluid (VOF) indicator function on arbitrary polyhedral grids. It solves the advection equation geometrically using Edge-Matched Flux Polygon Advection (EMFPA) and reconstructs the fluid interface using the CLCIR method, which relies on isosurface extraction to determine the Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane orientation. It is distinguished from standard VOF methods by its ability to handle non-convex and self-intersecting polyhedral cells without decomposition, and from pure isosurface methods by its explicit geometric flux calculation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles arbitrary polyhedral grids, including non-convex and self-intersecting cells, without decomposition. Provides accurate PLIC reconstruction via isosurface extraction and extended triangulation. Limitations: Requires robust isosurface extraction algorithm. Fallback to LSGIR may be less accurate in low-resolution regions. When to Use: VOF simulations on complex, unstructured polyhedral grids where interface topology is complex. When Not to Use: Simple cubic grids where analytical methods are sufficient and faster. The Extended CLCIR method was introduced in a 2021 paper by López et al.. It is used in Volume of Fluid (VOF) simulations to reconstruct fluid interfaces on arbitrary polyhedral grids. The method combines isosurface extraction techniques with PLIC reconstruction to improve accuracy in complex geometries. name: VOF Advection with Isosurface Extraction
head: EMFPA-CLCIR, EMFPA-Youngs, VOF simulation, Volume of Fluid (VOF) Advection with Isosurface Extraction
body: This method simulates multiphase fluid flows by advecting a Volume of Fluid (VOF) indicator function on arbitrary polyhedral grids. It solves the advection equation geometrically using Edge-Matched Flux Polygon Advection (EMFPA) and reconstructs the fluid interface using the CLCIR method, which relies on isosurface extraction to determine the Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane orientation. It is distinguished from standard VOF methods by its ability to handle non-convex and self-intersecting polyhedral cells without decomposition, and from pure isosurface methods by its explicit geometric flux calculation. Inputs: Computational grid \Omega consisting of arbitrary polyhedral cells (cubic, tetrahedral, distorted, or non-convex irregular). Velocity field \mathbf{v} = (u, v, w) defined at cell faces. Initial fluid volume fraction field F(t^n) for each cell. Time step \Delta t. Outputs: Updated fluid volume fraction field F(t^{n+1}). Reconstructed PLIC interface geometry for cells with 10^{-12} < F(t^n) < 1 - 10^{-12}. Data Structures: Grid: A collection of cells \Omegai, each defined by a set of vertices and faces. Faces may be non-planar or self-intersecting. Volume Fraction: A scalar field F where Fi \in [0, 1] represents the fraction of cell i occupied by the fluid. Velocity: Vector components uj, vj, wj stored at the center of each face j. Step 1: Initialization At t^n = 0, compute the initial volume fraction F(t^n=0) for each cell. For a spherical fluid body of radius 0.15 centered at (0.5, 0.75, 0.25) in a unit box, use a grid refinement procedure extended to non-convex cells. Step 2: Time Step Calculation Determine the time step \Delta t using the CFL condition: \Delta t = \min \left[ \frac{\min(h{xi})}{\max(uj)}, \frac{\min(h{yi})}{\max(vj)}, \frac{\min(h{zi})}{\max(wj)} \right] \times \text{CFL} where: \text{CFL} is the Courant number (typically 0.5). h{xi}, h{yi}, h{zi} are the dimensions of the minimum-size rectangular parallelepiped enclosing cell i along the coordinate axes. For cubic grids with n cells, \min(h{xi}) = \min(h{yi}) = \min(h{zi}) = 1/n^{1/3}. For unstructured grids, the min/max operators consider only cells and faces near the interface. Step 3: Interface Reconstruction (CLCIR) For each cell i where 10^{-12} < Fi(t^n) < 1 - 10^{-12}: 1. Construct a scalar field \tilde{\phi} within the cell. 2. Extract the isosurface \tilde{\phi} = 0.5 using the isosurface extraction method described in Parent. 3. Compute the weighted normal vector \mathbf{n} of the extracted isosurface. 4. The interface is reconstructed at instant t^n using an extension to arbitrary grids of the CLCIR method. Step 4: Flux Calculation (EMFPA) Calculate the net volume of fluid advected out of cell i during \Delta t: \Phii = \int{t^n}^{t^{n+1}} \int{\partial \Omegai} \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}f \chi(\mathbf{x}, t) \, dS \, dt This is solved geometrically using the Edge-Matched Flux Polygon Advection (EMFPA) method. 1. For each face f of cell i, construct the flux polygon representing the volume of fluid crossing the face. 2. Perform repeated intersection operations on the polyhedra formed by the flux regions. 3. Use geometric tools capable of handling non-convex polyhedra with self-intersecting faces to compute intersections without decomposition. 4. Sum the signed fluxes over all faces to get \Phii. Step 5: Volume Fraction Update Update the volume fraction using the integrated advection equation: F(t^{n+1}) = F(t^n) - \frac{1}{V{\Omega}} \int{t^n}^{t^{n+1}} \int{\Omega} \nabla \cdot [\mathbf{v} \chi(\mathbf{x}, t)] \, d\mathbf{x} \, dt + \frac{F(t^{n+1}) - F(t^n)}{2V{\Omega}} \int{t^n}^{t^{n+1}} \int{\Omega} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \, d\mathbf{x} \, dt In practice, the first integral is approximated by the geometric flux \Phii calculated in Step 4. The second term (divergence correction) must be null if the velocity vector field \mathbf{v} is discretely solenoidal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def advectvof(grid, velocity, F, dt, cfl=0.5): """ Advect VOF field F on arbitrary grid using EMFPA and CLCIR. Args: grid: List of cells. Each cell has vertices, faces, and volume Vomega. velocity: Dict mapping faceid to (u, v, w) vector. F: Dict mapping cellid to float (volume fraction). dt: Time step size. cfl: CFL number (default 0.5). Returns: Fnew: Updated volume fractions. """ Fnew = {} for cellid, cell in grid.cells.items(): Fold = F[cellid] Vomega = cell.volume totalflux = 0.0 divergencesum = 0.0 # Step 3: Interface Reconstruction (CLCIR) # Only reconstruct if interface is present: 1e-12 < Fold < 1 - 1e-12 if 1e-12 < Fold < 1 - 1e-12: # Construct scalar field, extract isosurface phi=0.5, compute weighted normal n # (Exact geometric construction not detailed in sources) cell.plicnormal = None else: cell.plicnormal = None # Step 4: Flux Calculation (EMFPA) for face in cell.faces: u, v, w = velocity[face.id] # Construct flux polygon, perform repeated intersections on non-convex polyhedra # (Exact intersection algorithm not detailed in sources) fluxvol = 0.0 totalflux += fluxvol divergencesum += dot(face.normal, (u, v, w)) face.area # Step 5: Volume Fraction Update # Eq. 9: F(t^{n+1}) = F(t^n) - (1/V) FluxIntegral + (F(t^{n+1})-F(t^n))/(2V) DivIntegral # First integral approximated by totalflux. # Second term is null if velocity is discretely solenoidal. divintegral = divergencesum dt correction = 0.0 # Assumed zero for solenoidal fields Fnew[cellid] = Fold - totalflux / Vomega + correction Fnew[cellid] = max(0.0, min(1.0, Fnew[cellid])) # Clamp to [0, 1] return Fnew Combines EMFPA advection with CLCIR reconstruction using isosurface extraction. Chosen for high accuracy on arbitrary grids. Link Combines EMFPA advection with Youngs' method for interface reconstruction. Chosen for lower CPU time, though with higher error. Link Time Complexity: Determined by the cost of isosurface extraction and geometric flux polygon intersections. The EMFPA method avoids decomposition, reducing complexity compared to methods requiring cell subdivision. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for grid geometry, velocity field, and volume fractions. No additional large temporary arrays for decomposition are needed. Performance: On a 3D vortex-in-a-box test with CFL=0.5 and t{end}=3: Cubic Grids (n \approx 32^3): EMFPA-CLCIR error 3.21 \times 10^{-3}, CPU time 0.0088s. EMFPA-Youngs error 3.73 \times 10^{-3}, CPU time 0.0067s. Cubic Grids (n \approx 128^3): EMFPA-CLCIR error 2.14 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 0.13s. EMFPA-Youngs error 2.91 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 0.11s. Tetrahedral Grids (n \approx 128^3): EMFPA-CLCIR error 3.51 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 0.37s. EMFPA-Youngs error 6.00 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 0.25s. Non-convex Polyhedral Grids (n \approx 128^3): EMFPA-CLCIR error 3.44 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 2.19s. EMFPA-Youngs error 3.76 \times 10^{-4}, CPU time 1.81s. Convergence: Second-order convergence observed for all grid types. Strengths: Handles arbitrary polyhedral grids (including non-convex and self-intersecting) without decomposition. High accuracy compared to Youngs' method. Limitations: Slightly higher CPU time than EMFPA-Youngs. Requires robust geometric intersection tools for non-convex cells. The method was proposed as a novel isosurface extraction technique for VOF simulations on arbitrary grids. It builds on the CLCIR method [3] and the EMFPA advection scheme [46, 47]. The isosurface extraction component utilizes tools from [26, 48] to handle complex cell geometries. The method is part of a broader effort to improve multiphase flow simulation on unstructured grids, addressing limitations of previous methods that struggled with non-convex cells or required decomposition. name: Point Cloud Extraction
body: Point Cloud Extraction is a surface extraction technique that converts an isosurface into a set of unconnected vertices without generating face or edge data. It solves the problem of obtaining a geometric representation of a volume when downstream processing requires a point cloud rather than a mesh, or when surface reconstruction is deferred to a later stage, ideally on the GPU. Unlike sibling methods such as Marching Cubes or Dual Contouring, which produce coherent meshes with topological connectivity, Point Cloud Extraction outputs isolated points, requiring subsequent algorithms to reconstruct surface connectivity if needed. The method operates on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid, traversing cells to evaluate scalar values against an isovalue. It differs from mesh-generating isosurface methods by skipping the triangulation step and instead extracting a single vertex per intersected cell based on a fixed interpolation rule. Input: A scalar field defined on a grid (e.g., a PrimalGrid), an isovalue (implicitly 0.5 in the reference implementation), and a chunk size defining the granularity of traversal. Output: A collection of 3D points representing the isosurface. The core data structure is a PointCloud struct, which contains a single field: primalgrid: An instance of PrimalGrid<D>, where D is the dimension (typically 3). This grid stores the scalar values at voxel corners or centers. 1. Initialization: Create a PointCloud struct with a specified chunksize, which determines that chunks of chunksize^3 voxels are evaluated. 2. Sampling: Sample the source scalar field over the domain from (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) using a number of steps determined by the constructor size. 3. Traversal: Iterate over the primalgrid, calling a callback for each chunk that provides keys, corner positions, and scalar values. 4. Classification: Classify the eight corners of the current voxel cube based on their scalar values to produce a cubeindex (0–255). 5. Edge Case Handling: If cubeindex is 0 (all corners below isovalue) or 255 (all corners above isovalue), no vertex is extracted for this cell. 6. Vertex Extraction: If cubeindex is not 0 or 255, calculate the point p by linearly interpolating between corners[0] and corners[6] at t=0.5. 7. Output: Add the calculated point p to the point cloud extractor. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractpointcloud(grid: PrimalGrid, chunksize: int, isovalue: float = 0.5): points = [] for chunkkey in grid.getchunkkeys(chunksize): corners = grid.getchunkcorners(chunkkey, chunksize) values = grid.getchunkvalues(chunkkey, chunksize) for i in range(chunksize): for j in range(chunksize): for k in range(chunksize): baseidx = (i chunksize + j) chunksize + k voxelcorners = [corners[baseidx + offset] for offset in range(8)] voxelvalues = [values[baseidx + offset] for offset in range(8)] cubeindex = 0 for v in voxelvalues: cubeindex = (cubeindex << 1) | (1 if v > isovalue else 0) if cubeindex == 0 or cubeindex == 255: continue p0 = voxelcorners[0] p6 = voxelcorners[6] p = p0 + 0.5 (p6 - p0) points.append(p) return points Chunk Size: Determines the granularity of traversal. Isosurface Value: The reference implementation implicitly uses 0.5. Pitfall: The fixed interpolation between corners[0] and corners[6] is a simplification that does not guarantee topological correctness for all 255 cases, but serves as a fast approximation for point cloud generation. Pitfall: If cubeindex is 0 or 255, no vertex is generated, which is correct for empty/full cells but means the method relies on the specific interpolation rule for all other cases. A variant that extracts 3D geometry from Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by voxelizing the density field and applying a 3D edge detection filter to reduce noise and improve completeness. Unlike the basic method which uses simple interpolation, this approach uses gradient-based edge detection to locate object boundaries more accurately. It is chosen when working with NeRF-derived density fields where simple thresholding yields noisy and incomplete reconstructions. Steps: 1. Smoothing: Preprocess the voxelized 3D density field with Gaussian smoothing to minimize noise. 2. Gradient Calculation: Calculate the gradient magnitude M(x,y,z) using the first-order derivatives: M(x,y,z) = |G| = \sqrt{Gx^2 + Gy^2 + Gz^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{df}{dx}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{df}{dy}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{df}{dz}\right)^2} where Gx, Gy, Gz are the density gradients in each dimension. 3. Edge Detection: Edge Detection: Apply a 3D density-gradient based Canny edge detection filter. This involves calculating gradient magnitude thresholds and applying a hysteresis method to suppress weak edges and detect strong edges. 4. Visibility Filtering: Visibility Filtering: Remove points inside the object by approximating visibility from a given viewpoint. This is done by checking five different lines of sight within a given radius to ensure only surface points are retained. Pitfall: Simple global density thresholding yields noisy and incomplete reconstructions, necessitating the gradient-based approach. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Does not generate face or edge data, requiring downstream surface reconstruction ideally on the GPU. Limitations: Lacks topological information; the fixed interpolation rule is not topologically correct for all cases. When to use: When a point cloud is the desired final output or when surface reconstruction is deferred. When not to use: When a watertight mesh is required immediately. Point Cloud Extraction is a technique used in volume rendering and 3D reconstruction to convert implicit surface representations into explicit point sets. The basic method described in is part of a library for isosurface extraction, providing a lightweight alternative to mesh-generating algorithms. The Instant-NGP variant was developed to address the specific challenges of extracting geometry from Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), where density fields are noisy and contain interior points due to the ray-sampling nature of NeRF training. https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Vision through Obstacles—3D Geometric Reconstruction and Evaluation of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), https://doi.org/10.3390/rs16071188, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Extended Marching Cubes
head: Feature Sensitive Surface Extraction
body: Extended Marching Cubes (EMC) is a surface extraction algorithm that enhances the standard Marching Cubes method by preserving sharp geometric features (edges and corners) that are typically smoothed out by linear interpolation. It achieves this by computing surface normals at intersection points, detecting sharp angles between these normals, and using Quadratic Error Functions (QEFs) to place new vertices at the precise locations of these features. Unlike standard Marching Cubes, which connects edge intersections directly, EMC inserts feature points and forms triangle fans around them to maintain sharpness. Input: A 3D scalar field (volume data) defined on a grid. The field function f(x,y,z) returns a scalar value. EMC variants may modify the field evaluation to return a 3D vector representing distances along axes. Output: A polygonal mesh (vertices and indices) representing the isosurface. Grid Key: Identifies the voxel cell being processed. Vertices: Array of 3D points. Some vertices are associated with grid keys (standard edge intersections), while feature vertices are not. Normals: Array of 3D unit vectors corresponding to vertices. Features: A set (e.g., HashSet) of indices identifying vertices that are feature points. Tangent Planes: For each edge crossing, a plane is defined by the intersection point and the surface normal at that point. 1. Traverse the Grid: Iterate over each voxel cell in the primal grid. 2. Classify Cell: Determine the cubeindex (0-255) by comparing the scalar values at the 8 corners of the voxel against the isolevel. 3. Find Edge Crossings: Identify which edges of the voxel intersect the isosurface. For each voxel cell edge exhibiting a material change, approximate the intersection with the implicit surface. Compute the intersection point P using linear interpolation. Some implementations modify the field function to return a 3D distance vector (dx, dy, dz) and compute the intersection coordinates independently for each axis using linear interpolation on the respective components. 4. Sample Normals: Compute the normal vector \mathbf{n} at each intersection point P. Calculate the normal vector of the surface at the identified intersection point. This is typically approximated as the gradient of the scalar field: \mathbf{n} = \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \right) Numerically, this is estimated using forward differences with a small step size E: nx = f(x + E, y, z) - f(x, y, z) ny = f(x, y + E, z) - f(x, y, z) nz = f(x, y, z + E) - f(x, y, z) Normalize \mathbf{n} to unit length. 5. Detect Sharp Features: For the current cell, examine the normals of the intersection points. Evaluate the normal to determine if a sharp feature exists in the cell. A sharp feature is detected if the angle between adjacent intersection normals is below a threshold. This is computed using the dot product: \cos(\theta) = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}j If \theta < \theta{threshold} (e.g., 90 degrees, so \cos(\theta) > 0), a sharp feature exists. 6. Construct Tangent Planes: For each intersection point Pi with normal \mathbf{n}i, define a tangent plane \Pii passing through Pi with normal \mathbf{n}i. 7. Solve for Feature Point (QEF): If a sharp feature is detected, solve for a new vertex position V{feat} that minimizes the distance to all relevant tangent planes. If a feature is detected (not planar), place a feature point by minimizing QEF. This is done by minimizing the Quadratic Error Function (QEF): E(V) = \sumi (\mathbf{n}i \cdot (V - Pi))^2 This is a least-squares problem. The solution V{feat} is the point inside the voxel that best satisfies the plane constraints. Pitfall: If fewer than three planes are available (e.g., only 1 or 2 intersections define the feature), the system is underdetermined. The QEF minimization still yields a least-squares solution. 8. Add Feature Vertex: Insert V{feat} into the mesh vertex list. Add the feature point as a vertex with no grid key. Mark it as a feature vertex and add its index to the features set. 9. Generate Triangles (Triangle Fan): For each loop of edge intersections in the cell (determined by the cubeindex), create a triangle fan using the feature point as the center. Let the edge intersection points in the loop be E0, E1, \dots, E{k-1}. For each i from 0 to k-1: Let j = (i + 1) \pmod k. Add triangles (V{feat}, Ei, Ej). 10. Post-Processing (Edge Flipping): After processing all cells, iterate over all edges in the generated mesh. In flipfeatureedges, iterate over all edges in the mesh. If an edge connects two feature vertices, it may need to be "flipped" or rotated to ensure correct connectivity and avoid artifacts. Pitfall: This step may require information from neighboring chunks or cells, introducing dependencies. Pitfall: The algorithm may produce small triangle slivers on sharp edges. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def extendedmarchingcubes(volume, isolevel, thresholdangle=90.0): """ volume: 3D numpy array or list of lists of lists of scalar values. isolevel: scalar value for isosurface extraction. thresholdangle: angle in degrees below which a feature is considered sharp. """ meshvertices = [] meshindices = [] featurevertices = set() # Precomputed 256-entry bitmask array from parent article Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling EDGETABLE = [...] # Precomputed edge loop topology per cube index EDGELOOPS = [...] # Standard edge vertex indices (0-7) EDGEVERTICES = [ (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0), (4, 5), (5, 6), (6, 7), (7, 4), (0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7) ] # Step size E for finite difference normal approximation. Not given in the sources. E = 1.0 for x in range(volume.shape[0] - 1): for y in range(volume.shape[1] - 1): for z in range(volume.shape[2] - 1): # 1. Get corner values corners = [ volume[x, y, z], volume[x+1, y, z], volume[x+1, y+1, z], volume[x, y+1, z], volume[x, y, z+1], volume[x+1, y, z+1], volume[x+1, y+1, z+1], volume[x, y+1, z+1] ] # 2. Classify cube cubeindex = 0 for i in range(8): if corners[i] < isolevel: cubeindex |= (1 << i) # 3. Find edge crossings and normals edgecrossings = [] normals = [] edgemask = EDGETABLE[cubeindex] for e in range(12): if (edgemask >> e) & 1: v0idx, v1idx = EDGEVERTICES[e] v0, v1 = corners[v0idx], corners[v1idx] # Linear interpolation t = (isolevel - v0) / (v1 - v0) if v1 != v0 else 0.0 # Interpolate position (unit cube coordinates) p = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for dim in range(3): p[dim] = (v0idx & (1 << dim)) (1 - t) + (v1idx & (1 << dim)) t edgecrossings.append(p) # Compute normal using forward differences at the intersection point # Map unit coordinates back to grid indices for array access gx = volume[max(0, int(p[0] + E)), max(0, int(p[1])), max(0, int(p[2]))] - volume[max(0, int(p[0])), max(0, int(p[1])), max(0, int(p[2]))] gy = volume[max(0, int(p[0])), max(0, int(p[1] + E)), max(0, int(p[2]))] - volume[max(0, int(p[0])), max(0, int(p[1])), max(0, int(p[2]))] gz = volume[max(0, int(p[0])), max(0, int(p[1])), max(0, int(p[2] + E))] - volume[max(0, int(p[0])), max(0, int(p[1])), max(0, int(p[2]))] norm = [gx, gy, gz] length = math.sqrt(sum(n2 for n in norm)) if length > 0: norm = [n / length for n in norm] normals.append(norm) # 4. Detect sharp features isfeature = False for i in range(len(normals)): for j in range(i + 1, len(normals)): dotproduct = sum(a b for a, b in zip(normals[i], normals[j])) angle = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dotproduct))) if math.degrees(angle) < thresholdangle: isfeature = True break if isfeature: break # 5. Solve QEF if feature detected featurepoint = None featidx = None if isfeature and len(edgecrossings) > 0: # Construct planes: ni. (x - pi) = 0 => ni. x = ni. pi A = [] b = [] for p, n in zip(edgecrossings, normals): A.append(n) b.append(sum(a bi for a, bi in zip(n, p))) # Solve least squares: (A^T A) x = A^T b ATA = [[sum(A[k][i] A[k][j] for k in range(len(A))) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] ATb = [sum(A[k][i] b[k] for k in range(len(A))) for i in range(3)] featurepoint = solve3x3linearsystem(ATA, ATb) featidx = len(meshvertices) meshvertices.append(featurepoint) featurevertices.add(featidx) # 6. Generate triangles loops = EDGELOOPS[cubeindex] for loop in loops: if featurepoint is not None and featidx is not None: # Triangle fan from feature point for i in range(len(loop)): j = (i + 1) % len(loop) p1 = edgecrossings[loop[i]] p2 = edgecrossings[loop[j]] idx1 = len(meshvertices) idx2 = len(meshvertices) meshvertices.append(p1) meshvertices.append(p2) meshindices.extend([featidx, idx1, idx2]) else: # Standard MC triangle generation using triangleTable pass # 7. Post-processing: Flip feature edges flipfeatureedges(meshvertices, meshindices, featurevertices) return meshvertices, meshindices def solve3x3linearsystem(A, b): """Solve Ax = b for 3x3 system using Cramer's rule.""" def det3(m): return (m[0][0] (m[1][1]m[2][2] - m[1][2]m[2][1]) - m[0][1] (m[1][0]m[2][2] - m[1][2]m[2][0]) + m[0][2] (m[1][0]m[2][1] - m[1][1]m[2][0])) D = det3(A) if abs(D) < 1e-9: # Fallback to centroid if singular return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] x = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): Ai = [row[:] for row in A] for r in range(3): Ai[r][i] = b[r] x[i] = det3(Ai) / D return x def flipfeatureedges(vertices, indices, featureset): """ Iterate over edges. If both endpoints are feature vertices, mark for flipping. Simplified topology handling for demonstration. """ flips = set() for i in range(0, len(indices), 3): v0, v1, v2 = indices[i], indices[i+1], indices[i+2] edges = [(v0, v1), (v1, v2), (v2, v0)] for e in edges: if e[0] in featureset and e[1] in featureset: flips.add(e) # Actual rotation logic depends on mesh data structure Isolevel: The scalar value defining the surface. Typical values depend on the data range. Threshold Angle: The angle below which normals are considered to indicate a sharp feature. A common value is 90 degrees. Step Size (E): Used in finite difference normal approximation. Not given in the sources. Underdetermined System: If fewer than three planes are available for QEF solving (e.g., only 1 or 2 intersections), the system is underdetermined. The QEF minimization still yields a least-squares solution. Boundary Conditions: Normal computation at volume boundaries requires special handling (e.g., one-sided differences). Slivers: The algorithm may produce small, thin triangles (slivers) on sharp edges. Dependencies: The edge-flipping post-processing step may require information from neighboring chunks or cells, complicating parallel implementation. Not given in the sources. Extended Marching Cubes was introduced to address the limitations of standard Marching Cubes in preserving sharp features. The method relies on Quadratic Error Functions (QEFs) to locate feature points, a technique also used in Dual Contouring. The algorithm was presented in the paper "Feature Sensitive Surface Extraction from Volume Data". name: Canonical Enumeration
head: Linear Scan, Sequential Enumeration
body: Canonical Enumeration is the elementary method for cell extraction that sequentially visits all cells in a discretized volume to identify active cells containing the isosurface. It solves the cell extraction problem by checking if a target isovalue lies within the scalar range of each cell. Unlike Isosurface Propagation from Seed Cells, which skips empty regions by traversing a hierarchical search structure of seeds, Canonical Enumeration visits every cell regardless of occupancy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume data structure V defined on a regular grid, where each cell C{i,j,k} has scalar values V{i,j,k} at its vertices, and a scalar isovalue t \in \mathbb{R}. Output: A list of active cells C{i,j,k} where the isosurface intersects the cell. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array or linearized buffer storing vertex scalar values. No auxiliary structures are required. Variables: Temporary storage for v{min}, v{max}, and loop indices. Steps: 1. Iterate through every cell C{i,j,k} in the volume grid. 2. For each cell, determine the minimum scalar value v{min} and maximum scalar value v{max} among its vertices. 3. Evaluate the condition t \in [v{min}, v{max}). 4. If the condition is true, mark C{i,j,k} as an active cell; otherwise, skip it. Formulas: The range of the interpolation function \hat{f} in a cell is defined as: \hat{f}(C{i,j,k}) = [v{min}, v{max}] where: v{min} = \min(V{i,j,k}) v{max} = \max(V{i,j,k}) The cell extraction condition is: t \in [v{min}, v{max}) Parameters: Isovalue (t): The threshold scalar value defining the surface. Grid Dimensions: Nx, Ny, Nz defining the total number of cells n. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interval Boundary: The method uses the half-open interval [v{min}, v{max}) rather than the closed interval [v{min}, v{max}] to force consistent reporting of boundary conditions. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for t \ge v{min} and t < v{max} must handle precision errors near the boundaries. Degenerate Input: If v{min} = v{max}, the interval collapses to a single point; the half-open rule still applies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def canonicalenumeration(volumedata, isovalue, griddims): """ volumedata: 3D array of shape (Nx+1, Ny+1, Nz+1) storing scalar values at vertices. isovalue: The scalar threshold t. griddims: Tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) defining the number of cells. Returns: List of active cell indices (i, j, k). """ activecells = [] Nx, Ny, Nz = griddims for k in range(Nz): for j in range(Ny): for i in range(Nx): # Extract the 8 vertex values for cell (i, j, k) cellvertices = [ volumedata[i, j, k], volumedata[i+1, j, k], volumedata[i, j+1, k], volumedata[i+1, j+1, k], volumedata[i, j, k+1], volumedata[i+1, j, k+1], volumedata[i, j+1, k+1], volumedata[i+1, j+1, k+1] ] # Calculate min and max scalar values in the cell vmin = min(cellvertices) vmax = max(cellvertices) # Check if isovalue is in the half-open interval vmin, vmax) if vmin <= isovalue < vmax: activecells.append((i, j, k)) return activecells A geometric [decomposition technique that identifies sparse "seed" cells and propagates extraction to neighbors, skipping empty regions. Choose this when the volume is sparse or large, as it offers near-optimal worst-case time complexity by avoiding full enumeration. Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the total number of cells in the volume data. This is the lowest possible worst-case extraction time for any method based solely on isovalue comparisons without auxiliary spatial structures. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. It requires only storage for the original volume data and a small constant amount for variables. Strengths: Simplicity of implementation; no preprocessing or auxiliary data structure construction required. Limitations: Inefficient for sparse volumes or large datasets where the surface occupies a tiny fraction of the volume, as it processes every cell regardless of whether it contains the surface. When to use: Small volumes, dense surfaces, or as a baseline for correctness verification. When not to use: Large-scale volumes with sparse surfaces where acceleration via hierarchical subdivision (e.g., octrees) is necessary. Canonical Enumeration is the elementary method for cell extraction, historically used in the original "Marching Cubes" paper by Lorenson and Cline. name: Isosurface Propagation from Seed Cells
head: Seed Set / Surface Propagation, Seed Set Propagation for Contour Extraction, Seed-based extraction, Surface Propagation
body: Isosurface Propagation from Seed Cells is a geometric decomposition technique that extracts isosurfaces by starting from a pre-computed set of "seed" cells and propagating to neighbors, rather than visiting every cell in the volume. It solves the problem of output sensitivity in isosurface extraction by avoiding unnecessary cell visits, making it efficient for sparse isosurfaces or specific contour tracking. Unlike Canonical Enumeration, which sequentially visits all cells, this method relies on a seed set S defined such that any isosurface component intersects at least one cell in S. It differs from span space techniques like NOISE by establishing volume structure explicitly via adjacency, whereas span space methods map cells to 2D parameter spaces. The method consists of two phases: seed set construction and surface propagation. The propagation phase is deterministic and uniform across variants, while the seed construction varies by author (Itoh, van Kreveld, Bajaj). Input: A volume defined on a simplicial mesh (typically tetrahedra) with a piecewise linear (PL) scalar function f. A seed set S (subset of cells) and an isovalue v. Output: The set of triangles forming the isosurface, or the set of active cells Se intersecting the isosurface. Cell Adjacency: A graph or array mapping each cell to its neighbors. For tetrahedra, each cell has 4 faces, each shared with exactly one neighbor. Visited Set: A boolean flag or hash set associated with cells to prevent re-processing. Queue: A FIFO structure for BFS propagation. The difficulty lies in locating S. Sources cite three primary approaches: 1. Itoh et al.: Find local extremum points. Connect them with a graph in the spatial domain. The seed set includes cells containing extremum points, cells intersected by graph arcs, and boundary cells if holes exist. A thinning algorithm may be applied to generate a skeleton with fewer cells. 2. van Kreveld et al.: Use a graph of local extremum points and add saddle points to create a contour tree. 3. Bajaj et al.: Use set theory to find seed cells and a segment tree to organize and traverse them. Note: Noisy data (MRI/CT) can cause these algorithms to produce large numbers of seed cells, increasing preprocessing time. The propagation extracts a single connected component or a specific contour defined by an edge in a Contour Tree (CT). Parameters: v1, v2: Endpoints of an edge e in the Contour Tree, with f(v1) \le f(v2). Se: The set of simplices (cells) to be extracted. Steps: 1. Initialize Se = \emptyset. 2. Select a seed cell c that intersects the edge e of the CT. 3. Enqueue c and mark as visited. 4. While the queue is not empty: a. Dequeue cell s. b. Add s to Se. c. For each face ti of s (i=1 \dots 4): i. Compute min(ti) and max(ti), the minimum and maximum function values on the face. ii. Check if the face overlaps the contour class of edge e: min(ti) < f(v2) \quad \text{and} \quad max(ti) > f(v1) iii. If true, identify the tetrahedron c' sharing face ti with s. iv. If c' is not visited: Mark c' as visited. Enqueue c'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def propagatecontour(seedcell, contouredge, volume): """ Extracts cells intersecting a contour defined by contouredge in the Contour Tree. Args: seedcell: The initial tetrahedron cell. contouredge: A tuple (v1, v2) representing nodes in the Contour Tree. volume: Object providing cell adjacency and scalar values. Returns: List of tetrahedra intersecting the contour. """ # Extract scalar values at the contour edge endpoints fv1 = volume.scalarvalue(contouredge[0]) fv2 = volume.scalarvalue(contouredge[1]) # Ensure fv1 <= fv2 as per definition if fv1 > fv2: fv1, fv2 = fv2, fv1 queue = [seedcell] visited = {seedcell} extractedcells = [] while queue: s = queue.pop(0) extractedcells.append(s) # Get the 4 faces of the tetrahedron s faces = volume.getfaces(s) for t in faces: # Compute min and max scalar values on the triangle face t minval = volume.minonface(t) maxval = volume.maxonface(t) # Check if the face intersects the contour range [fv1, fv2] # Condition: min < f(v2) AND max > f(v1) if minval < fv2 and maxval > fv1: # Find the neighbor tetrahedron sharing this face neighbor = volume.getneighboracrossface(s, t) if neighbor is not None and neighbor not in visited: visited.add(neighbor) queue.append(neighbor) return extractedcells Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Simplicial Mesh Assumption: The algorithm assumes a simplicial mesh and PL function, ensuring at most one piece of an isosurface exists in a cell. Branch Prediction: The propagation code contains a large number of branches. Since the processor cannot readily predict the outcome, this can lead to poor performance on modern CPUs. body:
Hybrid Memory Constrained Isosurface Extraction is a method for generating isosurfaces from regularly structured volume data while strictly respecting a prescribed memory limit M for auxiliary data structures. It solves the problem of minimizing the expected extraction time E[T] subject to M(B, A) \le M by using Lagrangian optimization to select an optimal spatial partition and assign specific extraction methods to each partition block. It sets itself apart from its siblings by optimally adapting to any given amount of available memory by combining multiple search methods (enumeration, interval tree, kd-tree, out-of-core) within a binary spatial subdivision tree. Inputs: Volume data V on a regular grid (e.g., 512 	imes 512 	imes 499). Global memory constraint M (in MB) for auxiliary data structures. Outputs: Polygonal approximation of the isosurface for a given isovalue t. Preprocessed optimal partition tree and method assignment map. Data Structures: 1. Read external blocks, query interval trees pass # Step 4: Render # Generate polygonal approximation from active cells return activecells def extractenumeration(block, t): cells = [] prevrightflag = 0 for cell in block.cells: leftrange = convexhull(cell.leftvoxels) rightrange = convexhull(cell.rightvoxels) flagleft = -1 if t < leftrange.min else (1 if t > leftrange.max else 0) flagright = -1 if t < rightrange.min else (1 if t > rightrange.max else 0) if (flagleft == 0 and flagright == 0) or (flagleft flagright < 0): cells.append(cell) prevrightflag = flagright return cells The Tandem Algorithm is a memory-constrained isosurface extraction method that alternates between extracting a new layer of geometry and simplifying the accumulated surface to maintain a bounded memory footprint. It solves the problem of storing the entire intermediate triangulation by performing incremental simplification using edge collapses, ensuring that the number of vertices and triangles remains manageable during the extraction process. Unlike methods that extract the full volume before simplifying, or pure streaming approaches that discard history, the Tandem Algorithm maintains a global view of the surface for simplification while restricting the "active" geometry to a sliding window near the extraction front. Kd-tree estimation has <5% error but requires downsampling. Lagrangian optimization only finds points on the lower convex hull, causing gaps in the memory-time curve.
