It extends earlier work on out-of-core extraction by Chiang and Silva (segment tree) and Chiang, Silva, and Schroeder (interval tree). The hybrid approach fills the gap between state-of-the-art methods by designing a memory-adaptive algorithm that optimally adapts to any given amount of available memory. name: Tandem Algorithm
head: Attali et al. tandem algorithm, Extraction and Simplification of Iso-surfaces in Tandem, Incremental Isosurface Extraction and Simplification
body: The Tandem Algorithm is a memory-constrained isosurface extraction method that alternates between extracting a new layer of geometry and simplifying the accumulated surface to maintain a bounded memory footprint. It solves the problem of storing the entire intermediate triangulation by performing incremental simplification using edge collapses, ensuring that the number of vertices and triangles remains manageable during the extraction process. Unlike methods that perform global simplification after complete extraction, it interleaves extraction and simplification to reduce memory occupancy. The algorithm processes a volumetric dataset by iterating through cross-sections (layers) along a specific extraction direction (e.g., the z-axis). It maintains two priority queues: Q for edge collapse candidates and W for blocked edges. Input: Volumetric dataset, isovalue, maximum shape error threshold E0, isotropy parameter \alpha, extraction direction defining cross-sections k=1 \dots N. Output: Simplified isosurface mesh. 1. Priority Queue Q: Stores edge candidates for collapse, ordered by their global cost \varepsilon\alpha(c) (ascending). 2. Priority Queue W: Stores blocked edges, ordered by their reach value (ascending). 3. Mesh State: Current triangulation M, including vertices with attributes: height(u): Rank of vertex u along extraction direction. rad(u): Radius of vertex u. reach(u): Reach value of vertex u. \mathbf{H}u: Positive definite matrix for shape measure. Wu: Weight (sum of areas) for shape measure. \mathbf{G}u: Matrix for isotropy measure. W: Global weight for isotropy normalization. Shape Measure: The shape measure of a point x relative to patch Uc (neighboring triangles of c) is: hc(x) = \frac{1}{Wc} \sum{t \in Uc} wt d^2(x, Pt) = \frac{1}{Wc} x^T \mathbf{H}c x where Pt is the plane of triangle t, wt is its area, Wc = \sum{t \in Uc} wt, and \mathbf{H}c is a positive definite matrix. For edge contraction a,b \to c: \mathbf{H}c = \mathbf{H}a + \mathbf{H}b, \quad Wc = Wa + Wb Mesh Isotropy Criterion: To prevent long, skinny triangles, the isotropy criterion for point c (result of collapsing a,b) is: gc(x) = \sum{t \in S{ab}} wt (||x - \hat{t}||^2 + avg(t)) = x^T \mathbf{G}c x where S{ab} is the set of triangles containing a, b, or both, \hat{t} is the barycenter of t, and avg(t) = \frac{1}{12} (||p||^2+||q||^2+||r||^2) with p,q,r vectors from \hat{t} to vertices of t. The term gc is normalized by W = 3 \times \text{area}(S{ab}) Wc^{1/2} / E0 to balance its influence with hc. Global Cost: \varepsilon\alpha(c) = \sqrt{c^T \left[ (1-\alpha)\frac{\mathbf{H}c}{Wc} + \alpha\frac{\mathbf{G}c}{W} \right]} where \alpha is the isotropy parameter (typical value 0.4). Edge Contraction Updates: When collapsing edge a,b \to c: height(c) = \frac{height(a) + height(b)}{2} rad(c) = \frac{||a - b|| + rad(a) + rad(b)}{2} reach(c) = height(c) + rad(c) For new vertices introduced by extraction, rad(u) = 1. E0: Maximum shape error allowed. A candidate edge collapse is rejected if its shape measure \varepsilon0(c) exceeds E0. \alpha: Isotropy parameter balancing shape and anisotropy criteria. Typical value: 0.4. 1. Initialize: Create empty mesh M, empty queues Q and W. 2. Loop for k from 1 to N-1 (where N is the number of cross-sections): 1. Extract(k): Add vertices, edges, and triangles from marching cubes between cross-sections k-1 and k to M. 2. Delay(k): Add all edges of the newly extracted layer k to priority queue W ordered by reach value. 3. Activate(k): Move edges from W to Q if their reach value is less than the rank of the advancing front k. 4. Simplify(E0): Empty priority queue Q by applying consecutive edge collapses, rejecting candidates where \varepsilon0(c) > E0. 3. Finalize: Call Activate(\infty) to move all remaining edges from W to Q, then call Simplify(E0) to empty Q completely. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tandemalgorithm(volume, isovalue, E0, alpha, numcrosssections): mesh = Mesh() Q = PriorityQueue() W = PriorityQueue() currentfrontrank = 0 for k in range(1, numcrosssections): currentfrontrank = k layervertices, layeredges, layertriangles = marchingcubes(volume, k-1, k, isovalue) mesh.add(layervertices, layeredges, layertriangles) for v in layervertices: v.height = k v.rad = 1.0 v.reach = k + 1.0 v.H = computequadraticmetric(v) # Standard quadratic metric computation v.W = sum(t.area for t in v.neighbors) v.G = computeisotropymetric(v) # Standard isotropy metric computation for e in layeredges: a, b = e.vertices c = midpoint(a, b) reachval = c.height + c.rad W.push(e, priority=reachval) while W and W.top().priority < currentfrontrank: blockededge = W.pop() a, b = blockededge.vertices c = midpoint(a, b) cost = sqrt(c.T @ ((1-alpha)c.H/c.W + alphac.G/W) @ c) Q.push(blockededge, priority=cost) simplify(mesh, Q, W, E0, alpha, currentfrontrank) while W: blockededge = W.pop() a, b = blockededge.vertices c = midpoint(a, b) cost = sqrt(c.T @ ((1-alpha)c.H/c.W + alphac.G/W) @ c) Q.push(blockededge, priority=cost) simplify(mesh, Q, W, E0, alpha, currentfrontrank) return mesh def simplify(mesh, Q, W, E0, alpha, currentfrontrank): while Q: edge = Q.pop() a, b = edge.vertices if not mesh.vertexexists(a) or not mesh.vertexexists(b): continue c = midpoint(a, b) shapeerror = sqrt(c.T @ (c.H/c.W) @ c) if shapeerror <= E0: mesh.collapseedge(edge, c) c.height = (a.height + b.height) / 2.0 c.rad = (dist(a, b) + a.rad + b.rad) / 2.0 c.reach = c.height + c.rad c.H = a.H + b.H c.W = a.W + b.W c.G = a.G + b.G updateconnectivity(mesh, c) for neighboredge in c.incidentedges: if neighboredge not in Q and neighboredge not in W: nc = midpoint(neighboredge.vertices[0], neighboredge.vertices[1]) reachval = nc.height + nc.rad if reachval >= currentfrontrank: W.push(neighboredge, priority=reachval) else: cost = sqrt(nc.T @ ((1-alpha)nc.H/nc.W + alphanc.G/W) @ nc) Q.push(neighboredge, priority=cost) Blocked Edges: Contraction of an edge is prevented if its reach value is greater than or equal to the rank of the advancing front. This prevents artifacts from blocked edges on the last extracted layer. Degenerate Input: Noisy datasets may produce many small disconnected components. Precision: The shape measure \varepsilon0(c) must be compared against E0. A candidate edge collapse is rejected if its shape measure exceeds E0. The Extended Tandem Algorithm is a parallel, bloc-wise extension of the Tandem Algorithm designed to extract and simplify isosurfaces from very large volumetric datasets while minimizing memory consumption. It solves the scalability bottleneck of the sequential Tandem Algorithm, where queue updates and simplification steps become too memory-intensive for high-resolution data, such as generating 1,250,000 triangles per layer on a 1626 \times 7028 \times 2000 dataset. Unlike the parent method, which processes the entire volume in a single pass, this method splits the dataset into blocks, distributes them across computing nodes, and employs a component dumping mechanism to persist finalized surface components to disk. This allows the extraction process to continue on sub-parts of the dataset without losing previously computed geometry, making it suitable for geophysical datasets with numerous small, disconnected components. A mechanism that frees memory by migrating independent surface components to disk along with meta-data (oriented bounding box, volume) as soon as they are extracted, simplified, and detected as finished. It detects when a surface component is finished (simplification complete), dumps the completed surface component to disk, and stores meta-data with the dumped component, including oriented bounding box and volume, for later filtering and exploration. This is useful for noisy datasets or when the isovalue is not well determined, leading to many small disconnected components. Meta-data allows filtering, such as discarding components with too small volumes or selecting aligned ones. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a noisy dataset of size 1626 \times 7028 \times 2000, the sequential Tandem Algorithm generated 1,250,000 triangles per layer, leading to memory bottlenecks in queue updates and simplification. The Extended Tandem Algorithm addresses this by distributing work and dumping components. Strengths: Reduces memory consumption significantly compared to global extraction. Maintains global simplification quality. Limitations: Sequential version does not scale well to extremely large datasets due to queue management overhead. Requires careful tuning of E0 and \alpha. Speedup: The speedup achieved by this method is on the order of O(N) compared to doing simplification in one shot, though it incurs greater implementation complexity. The Tandem Algorithm was proposed by Attali, Cohen-Steiner, and Edelsbrunner in 2005 in 'Extraction and Simplification of Iso-surfaces in Tandem' at the Eurographics Symposium on Geometry Processing. It revisits the quadratic metric of Garland and Heckbert for edge collapse simplification, introducing a shape measure and a mesh isotropy criterion. The algorithm alternates extraction and simplification to reduce memory occupancy. The Extended Tandem Algorithm was later proposed to address scalability issues on very large datasets, particularly in geophysics, by introducing parallel processing and component dumping. name: Extended Tandem Algorithm
head: Parallel Bloc-wise Extension, Parallel Tandem Algorithm, Parallel Tandem Algorithm with Component Dumping, Parallel tandem with dumping
body: The Extended Tandem Algorithm is a parallel, bloc-wise extension of the Tandem Algorithm [3675-tandem-algorithm.md] designed to extract and simplify isosurfaces from very large volumetric datasets while minimizing memory consumption. It solves the scalability bottleneck of the sequential Tandem Algorithm, where queue updates and simplification steps become too memory-intensive for high-resolution data, such as generating 1,250,000 triangles per layer on a 1626 \times 7028 \times 2000 dataset. Unlike the parent method, which processes the entire volume in a single pass, this method splits the dataset into blocks, distributes them across computing nodes, and employs a component dumping mechanism to persist finalized surface components to disk. This allows the extraction process to continue on sub-parts of the dataset without losing previously computed geometry, making it suitable for geophysical datasets with numerous small, disconnected components. The algorithm operates using a worker-manager architecture. The dataset is split into blocks and distributed to computing nodes (workers). Each worker extracts and semi-simplifies a local isosurface, then merges it with adjacent semi-simplified isosurfaces received from other workers. The core simplification logic relies on the Tandem Algorithm's edge collapse strategy with a "time lag" mechanism to prevent artifacts near the advancing front. Priority Queue Q: Stores edge candidates for collapse, ordered by their global cost \varepsilon\alpha(c). Priority Queue W: Stores blocked edges, ordered by their reach value. Used to delay collapses near the advancing front. Task Structure: Composed of a task type and a worker ID. Task types are: EXTRACT (extract surface from sub-block), SEND (send mesh to target worker), MERGE (merge received mesh with current surface), FINISHED (stop worker). The edge collapse cost \varepsilon\alpha(c) balances shape measure and mesh isotropy: \varepsilon\alpha(c) = c^T \left[ (1 - \alpha) \frac{Hc}{Wc} + \alpha \frac{Gc}{W} \right] c Where: \alpha is the isotropy parameter (typically 0.4). Hc is a positive definite matrix related to the shape measure. Wc is the sum of areas of neighboring triangles Uc. Gc is a matrix related to the mesh isotropy criterion. W is a normalization factor. The shape measure hc(x) for a point x is: hc(x) = \frac{1}{Wc} \sum{t \in Uc} wt d^2(x, Pt) = \frac{1}{2} x^T Hc x where Pt is the plane of triangle t, wt is its area, and Uc is the patch of neighboring triangles. The mesh isotropy criterion gc(x) is: gc(x) = \sum{t \in S{ab}} wt (\|x - \hat{t}\|^2 + \text{avg}(t)) = x^T Gc x where S{ab} is the set of triangles containing vertices a, b or both, \hat{t} is the barycenter of triangle t, and \text{avg}(t) = \frac{1}{2}(\|p\|^2 + \|q\|^2 + \|r\|^2) with p, q, r vectors from \hat{t} to vertices. A candidate edge collapse is rejected if its shape measure \varepsilon0(c) exceeds the maximum shape error threshold E0. To prevent artifacts, the algorithm uses a time lag mechanism. The reach of an edge collapse c is defined as: \text{reach}(c) = \text{height}(c) + \text{rad}(c) where \text{height}(c) = (\text{height}(a) + \text{height}(b))/2 and \text{rad}(c) = (\|a - b\| + \text{rad}(a) + \text{rad}(b))/2. For new vertices, \text{rad}=1. An edge is prevented from collapsing if \text{reach}(c) \ge \text{rank}(\text{front}), where \text{rank}(\text{front}) is the maximum rank (coordinate along extraction direction) of the extracted layers. Blocked edges are stored in queue W and moved to Q via the activate function when their reach is less than the current front rank. Workers run an infinite loop requesting tasks from the worker manager until a FINISHED task is received. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def worker(E0: float): finished = False while not finished: task = receivetaskfrommanager() # Standard IPC receive if task.type == "EXTRACT": runtandemextraction(E0) # Extracts and semi-simplifies sub-block elif task.type == "SEND": sendmeshtoworker(task.target) # Standard IPC send clearcurrentsurface() # Empties worker's surface elif task.type == "MERGE": mergeandsimplify(receivemeshfromworker(), E0) # Merges, simplifies, dumps components elif task.type == "FINISHED": mergeandsimplify(getcurrentsurface(), E0) finished = True The manager iterates as long as the global surface is not totally extracted. For each worker request, it checks conditions in order: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def workermanager(): while not finished: id = requesttaskidfromworker() # Standard IPC receive request if checkwaitingsurface(id): # Returns true if worker has waiting surface sendtasktoworker(id, "MERGE") elif findneighborworker(id) is not None: # Returns neighbor ID or None targetid = findneighborworker(id) sendtasktoworker(id, "SEND", targetid) elif findnextblock(id) is not None: # Returns block ID or None blockid = findnextblock(id) sendtasktoworker(id, "EXTRACT", blockid) else: sendtasktoworker(id, "FINISHED") The local extraction on each block follows the Tandem Algorithm structure: 1. Iterate k from 1 to number of cross-sections - 1: extract(k): Adds layer k (vertices, edges, triangles from marching cubes between cross-sections k-1 and k) to current triangulation. delay(k): Adds all edges of layer k to blocked queue W, ordered by reach value. activate(k): Moves edges from W to Q if their reach value is less than rank of advancing front k. simplify(E0): Empties queue Q by applying consecutive edge collapses. 2. After loop: activate(∞): Processes remaining delayed edges. simplify(E0): Final simplification. When merging two semi-simplified isosurfaces, a simplification stage with relaxed edge constraints is applied at the common interface to remove seams. The algorithm detects the termination of a surface component (when extraction and simplification are complete) and dumps the finalized surface to disk along with a meta-data index (oriented bounding box, volume, etc.). This frees memory for further processing. E0: Maximum shape error threshold (positive constant). Typical values depend on dataset noise. \alpha: Isotropy parameter. Recommended value is 0.4. High Isotropy Parameter: If \alpha > 0.9, the shape criterion is ignored, leading to collapsed points far from the original surface. These are rejected by E0, increasing anisotropy. Solution: Use \alpha = 0.4. Blocked Edges: Edges near the advancing front can introduce artifacts if collapsed immediately. The time lag mechanism prevents this. Memory Bottlenecks: On noisy datasets (e.g., 1626 \times 7028 \times 2000), each extraction on advancing fronts generates 1,250,000 triangles, making queue updates and simplification too memory consuming for the sequential Tandem Algorithm. The Extended version mitigates this via dumping. The Extended Tandem Algorithm with Dumping is a parallel, bloc-wise extension of the Tandem algorithm designed to increase scalability for very large datasets by dumping extracted surface components to disk. It prevents memory exhaustion during queue updates and simplification steps, which are the primary bottlenecks in the standard Tandem algorithm for high-resolution data. Unlike its parent, it introduces a mechanism to persist finalized components to storage, allowing the extraction process to continue on sub-parts of the dataset without losing previously computed geometry. Hierarchical Binary Partitioning is a parallel isosurface extraction method that recursively subdivides a volumetric dataset into sub-blocks to enable independent surface extraction and simplified merging. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by using a recursive binary tree structure based on the dataset's longest dimension, rather than a fixed regular grid, to balance workload and facilitate the aggregation of semi-simplified surfaces. Time Complexity: The parallel algorithm significantly reduces extraction time compared to the sequential Tandem Algorithm. On a seismic dataset (1626 \times 7028 \times 2000, 40 GB), extraction takes 5 minutes with 56 processors, compared to more than three hours for the sequential algorithm. Memory Complexity: The method minimizes memory consumption by processing blocks independently and dumping completed components. It avoids storing the full mesh before simplification, unlike brute-force approaches. Scalability: Parallel extraction generates a mesh with a quality equivalent to that of the sequential approach. Strengths: Suitable for very large geophysics datasets with numerous small, disconnected components. Reduces memory footprint drastically. Limitations: Requires a worker-manager architecture and network communication for merging. The Tandem Algorithm was introduced by Attali et al. in 2005 to reduce memory requirements by combining isosurface extraction and simplification in one pass. The Extended Tandem Algorithm was developed to address the limited scalability of the original algorithm for very large datasets, particularly in geophysics. It was supported by Total company and applied to datasets of size 7000 \times 1600 \times 2000. name: Extended Tandem Algorithm with Dumping
head: Parallel Tandem Algorithm with Component Dumping, Parallel tandem with dumping
body: The Extended Tandem Algorithm with Dumping is a parallel, bloc-wise extension of the Tandem algorithm designed to increase scalability for very large datasets by dumping extracted surface components to disk. It prevents memory exhaustion during queue updates and simplification steps, which are the primary bottlenecks in the standard Tandem algorithm for high-resolution data. Unlike its parent, it introduces a mechanism to persist finalized components to storage, allowing the extraction process to continue on sub-parts of the dataset without losing previously computed geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar dataset, an error threshold parameter E0, and a set of active surface components \Gamma. Output: A set of isosurface components saved to disk (in a raw data file) and an index file containing metadata for each component. Data Structures: \Gamma: The set of active surface components currently being tracked. Vw: The set of vertices currently in the processing queue. E0: The error threshold for mesh simplification. Exact memory layouts and bit packing are not given in the sources. Definitions: A component \gamma \in \Gamma is considered finalized if it no longer shares any vertices with the active queue Vw. \gamma \text{ is finalized} \iff \gamma \cap Vw = \emptyset save(γ): Migrates component \gamma to disk. clear(γ): Deletes \gamma from the current in-memory triangulation. Parameters: E0: The error threshold for simplification. Typical values are not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the algorithm with the error threshold E0. 2. Iterate through each cross-section k from 1 to N-1, where N is the total number of cross-sections: a. extract(k): Extract the isosurface for cross-section k. b. delay(k): Apply the time-lag technique to manage the advancing front. c. activate(k): Activate the newly extracted components for cross-section k. d. simplify(E0): Simplify the current mesh using the error threshold E0. e. dumping(): Check for finalized components and persist them to disk. 3. After the loop, finalize all remaining active components by activating infinity: activate(∞). 4. Simplify the final mesh: simplify(E0). 5. Call dumping() one final time to persist any remaining components. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tandemwithdumping(E0, numcrosssections, Gamma, Vw): """ Executes the Extended Tandem Algorithm with Dumping. Args: E0: Error threshold for simplification. numcrosssections: Total number of cross-sections in the dataset. Gamma: Set of active surface components (each gamma is a set of vertices). Vw: Set of vertices in the processing queue. """ for k in range(1, numcrosssections): # extract(k) # delay(k) # activate(k) # simplify(E0) dumping(Gamma, Vw) activateinfinity() simplify(E0) dumping(Gamma, Vw) def dumping(Gamma, Vw): """ Iterates through all active components. If a component is finalized, it is saved to disk and cleared from the current triangulation. """ finalized = [gamma for gamma in Gamma if isfinalized(gamma, Vw)] for gamma in finalized: savetodisk(gamma) clearfrommemory(gamma) Gamma.remove(gamma) def isfinalized(gamma, Vw): """ A component is finalized if its intersection with the set of vertices in the queue is empty. """ return len(gamma & Vw) == 0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Simplification Delay: Due to the time-lag technique, a component may be entirely extracted but its simplification might be prevented or delayed. The dumping function must detect the end of both extraction and simplification to correctly identify finalized components. Memory Exhaustion: Without dumping, queue updates and simplification steps become too memory-consuming for large datasets (e.g., generating 1,250,000 triangles per extraction on a 1626 \times 7028 \times 2000 cube). Recursively splits the dataset into two parts perpendicular to its longest direction until sub-blocks reach a given threshold. Not given in the sources. Hierarchical Binary Partitioning. Generates an index file containing metadata (oriented bounding box, volume, number of vertices and facets) for each component to optimize access to the component-ordered raw data file. Not given in the sources. Hierarchical Binary Partitioning. Scalability: The method significantly increases scalability for very large datasets by preventing memory exhaustion. Performance: On a dataset of size 1626 \times 7028 \times 2000, each extraction on the advancing front generates approximately 1,250,000 triangles. Storage: The generated file is ordered by component, allowing easy access to subsets of components by reading sub-parts of the file. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Hardware and Scene Metrics: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Prevents memory exhaustion on massive datasets but requires disk I/O and index management. When to Use/Not Use: Use for geophysical or similarly massive scalar fields where standard Tandem memory limits are hit; not given in the sources for specific exclusion criteria. The method was proposed to address the limit of scalability of the Tandem algorithm when applied to very large datasets in geophysics. name: Hierarchical Binary Partitioning
head: Hierarchical Dataset Subdivision, Parallel Binary Partitioning, Recursive splitting, Tree-based extraction
body: Hierarchical Binary Partitioning is a parallel isosurface extraction method that recursively subdivides a volumetric dataset into sub-blocks to enable independent surface extraction and simplified merging. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by using a recursive binary tree structure based on the dataset's longest dimension, rather than a fixed regular grid, to balance workload and facilitate the aggregation of semi-simplified surfaces. Inputs: A volumetric dataset (scalar field) and an isovalue. Outputs: A global simplified isosurface mesh. Data Structures: Binary Tree: Each node represents a sub-block of the dataset. Internal Nodes: Represent a split. Leaf Nodes: Represent sub-blocks small enough to be processed directly. Sub-block: Defined by its 3D bounding box coordinates within the original dataset. Index File: An auxiliary file mapping component IDs to offsets in the raw data file, allowing efficient access to subsets of components. Parameters: Threshold: The minimum sub-block size (in voxels) below which splitting stops. The exact value is not specified in the sources. Leaf Block Size: Experimental sizes of 128^3, 256^3, or 512^3 were used. Extraction timings do not significantly vary with these sizes. Steps: 1. Recursive Splitting: Start with the root node containing the entire dataset. If the current sub-block size is greater than the threshold: Identify the longest dimension of the sub-block. Split the sub-block into two equal parts perpendicularly to that longest dimension. Create two child nodes in the binary tree. Recursively apply this step to both children. If the size is less than or equal to the threshold, mark the node as a leaf. 2. Leaf Extraction: For each leaf node, perform isosurface extraction using the Extended Tandem Algorithm with Dumping. Boundary Constraint: Edge collapse operations are not applied near the boundaries of the leaf block. This preserves boundary vertices to enable later merging with adjacent blocks. Modified Radius Constraint: To prevent refinement dependencies and artifacts, the radius associated with a point c (result of collapsing edge ab to c) is calculated as: rad(c) = \frac{||a - b|| + rad(a) + rad(b)}{2} where rad(x) = 1 if x is an original vertex of the isosurface. The contraction of edge ab is prevented as long as the sphere centered on the midpoint of ab with radius rad(c) is not totally included within the current block. 3. Recursive Merging: Traverse the binary tree from leaves up to the root. At each internal node, merge the isosurfaces extracted from its two children. Apply simplification to the merged surface to remove seams and reduce triangle count. The merging process aggregates semi-simplified blocks as they become available, prioritizing early merging to keep the overall triangle count low. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: def init(self, x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1): self.x0, self.y0, self.z0 = x0, y0, z0 self.x1, self.y1, self.z1 = x1, y1, z1 self.left = None self.right = None self.isleaf = False self.surface = [] def buildtree(x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, threshold): node = Node(x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1) size = (x1 - x0) (y1 - y0) (z1 - z0) if size > threshold: dx, dy, dz = x1 - x0, y1 - y0, z1 - z0 if dx >= dy and dx >= dz: mid = (x0 + x1) // 2 node.left = buildtree(x0, y0, z0, mid, y1, z1, threshold) node.right = buildtree(mid, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, threshold) elif dy >= dx and dy >= dz: mid = (y0 + y1) // 2 node.left = buildtree(x0, y0, z0, x1, mid, z1, threshold) node.right = buildtree(x0, mid, z0, x1, y1, z1, threshold) else: mid = (z0 + z1) // 2 node.left = buildtree(x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, mid, threshold) node.right = buildtree(x0, y0, mid, x1, y1, z1, threshold) else: node.isleaf = True return node def extractleaf(node, isovalue): # Initialize tandem state E0 E0 = {"vertices": [], "edges": [], "surface": []} # Iterate through cross-sections (Algorithm 4 from) numsections = node.z1 - node.z0 for k in range(1, numsections): # extract(k), delay(k), activate(k) are standard tandem steps simplify(E0) dumping(E0) activate(float('inf')) simplify(E0) dumping(E0) # Apply boundary constraint and modified radius for edge in E0["edges"]: a, b = edge["vertices"] # Check if edge is near block boundary if (a.x in (node.x0, node.x1) or b.x in (node.x0, node.x1) or a.y in (node.y0, node.y1) or b.y in (node.y0, node.y1) or a.z in (node.z0, node.z1) or b.z in (node.z0, node.z1)): continue c = {"x": (a.x + b.x) / 2, "y": (a.y + b.y) / 2, "z": (a.z + b.z) / 2} rada = 1 if a.get("isoriginal", False) else a.get("radius", 0) radb = 1 if b.get("isoriginal", False) else b.get("radius", 0) radc = (distance(a, b) + rada + radb) / 2 # Check if sphere centered at c with radius radc is fully inside node if not (c.x - radc >= node.x0 and c.x + radc <= node.x1 and c.y - radc >= node.y0 and c.y + radc <= node.y1 and c.z - radc >= node.z0 and c.z + radc <= node.z1): continue collapseedge(edge, c) return E0["surface"] def mergesurfaces(leftsurf, rightsurf): # Merge and simplify to remove seams merged = leftsurf + rightsurf return simplifysurface(merged) def hierarchicalbinarypartitioning(datasetbounds, isovalue, threshold): root = buildtree(datasetbounds, threshold) # Extract leaves for leaf in getleaves(root): leaf.surface = extractleaf(leaf, isovalue) # Merge up return mergeup(root) def getleaves(node): if node.isleaf: yield node else: yield from getleaves(node.left) yield from getleaves(node.right) def mergeup(node): if node.isleaf: return node.surface leftsurf = mergeup(node.left) rightsurf = mergeup(node.right) node.surface = mergesurfaces(leftsurf, rightsurf) return node.surface Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The splitting phase scales linearly with the number of voxels. The extraction phase depends on the tandem algorithm complexity. The merging phase involves simplification, which is generally sub-linear in the number of triangles but depends on the simplification algorithm used. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The hierarchical structure adds overhead for the tree nodes. However, the use of the tandem algorithm with dumping allows for processing large datasets by streaming components, minimizing peak memory usage compared to storing the entire isosurface in memory. Performance: Overall extraction timings do not significantly vary with leaf block sizes of 128^3, 256^3, or 512^3. Strengths: Enables parallel extraction by dividing the dataset into independent sub-blocks. Reduces memory consumption via block splitting and component dumping. The recursive binary partitioning adapts to the dataset shape, potentially balancing workload better than fixed grids. Limitations: Requires careful handling of boundary conditions to ensure correct merging. The merging process must be prioritized to keep triangle counts low, which may impact parallel efficiency if not managed correctly. When to use: Suitable for very large datasets where memory is a constraint and parallel processing is available. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method was proposed for isosurface extraction and interpretation on very large datasets in geophysics. History: It builds upon the work of Müller and Stark (1993) for recursive splitting. It extends the tandem algorithm by introducing a dumping function and a hierarchical merging strategy. Usage: Used in geophysics for visualizing large volumetric datasets. name: Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration
body: Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration defines the static data structures and decision logic used to map the 256 possible binary sign configurations of a voxel's eight corners to a specific polygonal topology. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which edges of a cube are intersected by an isosurface and how to connect those intersections into triangles without runtime geometric reasoning. What sets this family apart from siblings like Snap Marching Cubes or GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines is its reliance on precomputed, static decision logic (lookup tables) rather than dynamic geometric queries or hardware-specific optimizations. The family relies on two precomputed data structures derived from the 256 possible binary configurations of a voxel's eight corner signs relative to an isovalue. 1. Edge Intersection Table (edgeTable): An array of 256 integers (or shorts). Each entry is a 12-bit bitmask. Bit k (0 \le k \le 11) is set to 1 if the isosurface intersects the k-th edge of the cube, and 0 otherwise. The standard edge numbering convention is: Bottom face (z=0): e0=(0,1), e1=(1,2), e2=(2,3), e3=(3,0) Top face (z=1): e4=(4,5), e5=(5,6), e6=(6,7), e7=(7,4) Vertical edges: e8=(0,4), e9=(1,5), e{10}=(2,6), e{11}=(3,7) 2. Triangle Connection Table (triangleTable): A 2D array of size 256 \times 16. Rows are indexed by the case index C \in [0, 255]. Columns store integer indices. Indices 0–11 refer to the 12 cube edges. Indices are grouped in triplets (a, b, c) to form triangles. The sequence is terminated by the value -1. The maximum number of triangles per voxel is 5, requiring 15 indices plus 1 terminator. Case Index Calculation: For each voxel, the 8-bit case index C is determined by the scalar field values V at the 8 vertices vi (i=0..7). If V(vi) < I (or > I, depending on convention), bit i of C is set to 1; otherwise 0. The bit assignment must strictly match the vertex ordering assumed by the LUT generation. Ambiguity: Cases 46, 47, 98, 99, 210, 213, 214, 215 contain saddle points where the topology is ambiguous (the isosurface passes through the cube center). The standard LUT uses a fixed triangulation for these, which can cause cracks or holes if adjacent voxels resolve the ambiguity differently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecaseindex(values, isovalue): caseindex = 0 for i in range(8): if values[i] < isovalue: caseindex |= (1 << i) return caseindex def extracttriangles(caseindex, triangletable, edgeintersections): triangles = [] triindices = triangletable[caseindex] for i in range(16): if triindices[i] == -1: break e1 = triindices[i] e2 = triindices[i+1] e3 = triindices[i+2] p1 = edgeintersections[e1] p2 = edgeintersections[e2] p3 = edgeintersections[e3] triangles.append((p1, p2, p3)) return triangles Offloads voxel processing, topology lookup, and geometry generation to the GPU or parallel CPU architectures to achieve real-time or high-performance rendering. It sets itself apart from CPU-based immediate mode implementations by leveraging massive parallelism and fixed-size buffers with cleanup passes, and from slab-based variants by processing the entire volume grid directly without explicit spatial partitioning for memory locality. Choose it when throughput is critical and hardware supports massive parallelism. Reduces the triangle count and geometric complexity of isosurfaces extracted via Marching Cubes, addressing high memory and rendering costs of dense meshes. Unlike the parent method, which generates a raw triangulation based on local voxel configurations, this family focuses on post-processing or integrated strategies to collapse edges, merge coplanar facets, or restrict vertices to grid points, thereby improving visual fidelity and storage efficiency while attempting to preserve topological properties such as manifoldness and reversibility. Choose it when rendering performance or storage is constrained. Extracts crack-free isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data by constructing a dual grid where cell centers serve as vertices. It solves the "dangling node" problem inherent in standard Marching Cubes when applied to resampled vertex-centered AMR data, where mismatched interpolation at coarse-fine boundaries causes topological discontinuities. Unlike sibling methods that fix cracks by post-processing polygons or collapsing polylines, this approach eliminates dangling nodes structurally by leveraging the geometric gap between coarse and fine dual grids. Choose it for AMR datasets. Fast, high-quality polygonization of isosurfaces generated by thousands of particles in an unbounded spatial domain, using minimal working memory. It solves the bottleneck of high computational cost and memory requirements typical in particle-based rendering by combining block subdivision, slice-by-slice extraction, and a specialized particle cache. Unlike standard Marching Cubes which operates on a dense grid, this method extracts surfaces directly from discrete particle positions, enabling real-time performance for dynamic entities like fluid blobs or monsters in video games. Choose it for particle-based or unbounded domain rendering. Defines the static data structures (edgeTable, triangleTable) and the classification logic that map the 256 possible binary sign configurations of a voxel's eight corners to specific triangle topologies, enabling the Marching Cubes algorithm to generate a continuous mesh without runtime geometric reasoning. It solves the problem of efficiently determining edge intersections and triangle connectivity by replacing complex branching logic with simple array indexing. Unlike siblings that optimize memory usage or resolve topological ambiguities dynamically, this family relies on fixed, precomputed configurations for all cases, including those with saddle points. Choose it for standard, branchless extraction pipelines. Extends the standard Marching Cubes algorithm to handle multiple distinct isovalue thresholds simultaneously or to generalize the topological construction to higher dimensions (4D+). It solves the problem of visualizing complex scalar fields with multiple material boundaries or analyzing time-evolving volumetric data in a single coherent framework. It differs from single-isosurface methods by managing independent triangle lists for each threshold or by transforming boundary hyper-octants into higher-dimensional simplices to prevent topological ambiguities. Choose it for multi-threshold or higher-dimensional data. Adapts standard isosurface extraction to Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and implicit fields defined by scattered data. It solves the problem of efficiently extracting the zero-level set from continuous implicit representations by combining spatial filtering or error-bounded approximation with standard lookup-based triangulation. It differs from siblings by prioritizing continuous implicit inputs over pre-rasterized discrete grids, using techniques like narrow-band filtering or two-step evaluation to avoid processing the entire volume. Choose it for SDFs or implicit fields. Addresses the geometric inaccuracy inherent in standard Marching Cubes, where linear interpolation along cube edges often produces vertices that deviate significantly from the true isosurface, particularly in regions of high curvature or near ambiguous topologies. While standard extraction prioritizes topological correctness and computational speed via lookup tables, these optimization techniques explicitly minimize the distance between extracted vertices and the scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) or improve mesh quality metrics. They differ from siblings like GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines by focusing on post-extraction or in-extraction geometric refinement rather than throughput, and from Mesh Simplification and Optimization by preserving the original Marching Cubes connectivity topology rather than reducing vertex count. Choose it when geometric accuracy is paramount. Encompasses algorithmic variations of the Marching Cubes (MC) isosurface extraction method that modify the input data, the lookup logic, the vertex placement, or the post-processing steps to address specific limitations such as topological ambiguity, mesh quality, computational efficiency, or data uncertainty. Unlike standard MC, which relies on a static lookup table and linear interpolation, these methods introduce preprocessing (smoothing, component filtering), dynamic state propagation (bitwise indexing), geometric snapping, or error-aware interpolation. They are chosen when standard MC produces artifacts (cracks, poor triangles), is too slow for large datasets, or requires additional metadata (error bounds) on the surface. Addresses the concavity limitations of standard convex hull algorithms by combining Marching Cubes (MC) with local convex classification. It generates a watertight surface by first estimating an initial MC surface, classifying its vertices into local convex regions, and then applying a 3D convex hull algorithm to each region individually before aggregating the results. Unlike standard 3D Delaunay triangulation or convex hull methods which struggle with non-convex shapes, this approach preserves the topological flexibility of MC while leveraging the geometric robustness of hull-based generation. Choose it for complex non-convex shapes requiring watertight surfaces. A rule-based segmentation method to generate cell-level interface topology for mixed cells in volume fraction data by deriving partial vertex labeling and using lookup tables for binary- and multi-label segmentation cases. Choose it for volume fraction or mixed-cell data. A fiber surface defined by a line in the range is equivalent to an isosurface of a derived scalar field, allowing the use of standard isosurface extraction algorithms. Choose it for line-based or fiber data. Definition: Initial placement of particles near a feature (isosurface at a user-selected iso-value) by sampling volume data at a user-defined grid. Step: For each grid point r, iterate through each neighboring grid point n. Sample Volume at grid points n and r. If the iso-surface is crossed, output a particle between grid points n and r. GPU Implementation: Each active shader thread determines particle location. For each grid point, compare values to sampled values of front, right, and top neighboring grid points. This results in zero, one, two, or three particle positions. Layout: Output: Vertices of line-strip primitives recorded into a texture buffer object (TBO). Each vertex represents a particle position (x,y,z). Complexity: Complexity is in the order of the number of grid points. Not given in the sources. name: Marching Squares
head: Marching Cubes 2D, 2D Isosurface Extraction, 2D Isocontour Extraction
body: Marching Squares is an algorithm for extracting a polygonal contour (isolines) from a two-dimensional scalar field by processing each grid cell independently. It determines the topology of the isosurface intersection with a square cell based on the scalar values at the cell's four vertices relative to an isolevel. Unlike its 3D counterpart, Marching Cubes, which can produce ambiguous saddle points requiring additional heuristics, the 2D case on a square grid has no topological ambiguity for standard isolines, though it shares the same lookup-table and interpolation framework. It is the 2D analog of Marching Cubes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D scalar field F defined on a uniform grid of size Nx \times Ny (where Nx is columns, Ny is rows). Each cell has side length CELL\SIZE. An isovalue L. Output: A set of line segments representing the contour F(x,y) = L. Data Structures: Lookup Table: An array of 16 entries (indices 0–15). Each entry specifies which edges of the square cell are intersected by the isosurface. The edges are typically indexed 0 (bottom), 1 (right), 2 (top), 3 (left). Vertex Buffer: A list of unique 2D points to avoid duplicate vertices for shared edges. Numbered Steps: 1. Grid Setup: Define the contouring grid. The contouring grid consists of (Nx - 1) \times (Ny - 1) cells. Iterate over each cell (i, j) where i \in [0, Nx - 2] and j \in [0, Ny - 2]. 2. Vertex Sampling: For cell (i, j), retrieve the scalar values at the four corners. Let the grid coordinates be (x, y) = (i \cdot CELL\SIZE, j \cdot CELL\SIZE). The corners are: v0: Bottom-Left (x, y), value s0 = F[i][j] v1: Bottom-Right (x + CELL\SIZE, y), value s1 = F[i+1][j] v2: Top-Right (x + CELL\SIZE, y + CELL\SIZE), value s2 = F[i+1][j+1] v3: Top-Left (x, y + CELL\SIZE), value s3 = F[i][j+1] 3. Case Index Calculation: Determine the binary state of each vertex relative to the isovalue L. A vertex is "inside" if sk \ge L (or sk > L, provided consistency is maintained). Compute the 4-bit case index C: C = b0 + 2b1 + 4b2 + 8b3 where bk = 1 if sk \ge L, else 0. Note: Bit ordering must be consistent with the lookup table definition. A common convention is MSB at Top-Left (v3) or Bottom-Left (v0). The source specifies walking clockwise from Top-Left as MSB. Source uses a different bit assignment. The implementer must ensure the bit order matches the lookup table. 4. Lookup: Use C to access the lookup table. If C=0 (all outside) or C=15 (all inside), no geometry is generated for this cell. Otherwise, the table returns a list of intersected edges. 5. Intersection Calculation: For each intersected edge, calculate the exact intersection point using linear interpolation. For an edge between vertices with values s{start} and s{end} at positions p{start} and p{end}: t = \frac{L - s{start}}{s{end} - s{start}} p{intersect} = p{start} + t \cdot (p{end} - p{start}) 6. Vertex Insertion: Insert the calculated intersection points into a vertex buffer. To optimize, check if a point already exists (within a tolerance) before adding it, or simply add all points and use an index buffer for rendering. 7. Edge Generation: Create line segments connecting the intersection points on the intersected edges. For cases with two intersection points, create one segment. For cases with four intersection points (ambiguous saddle cases in some definitions, though topologically distinct in 2D squares without diagonal ambiguity if handled correctly, or simply two disjoint segments), create two segments. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marchingsquares(grid, isovalue, cellsize): """ grid: 2D list of floats, shape (Ny, Nx) isovalue: float cellsize: float Returns: list of line segments, each segment is ((x1, y1), (x2, y2)) """ Ny = len(grid) Nx = len(grid[0]) segments = [] # Lookup table: index -> list of edge pairs to connect # Edges: 0=Bottom(v0-v1), 1=Right(v1-v2), 2=Top(v2-v3), 3=Left(v3-v0) # This table assumes bit order: b0(v0), b1(v1), b2(v2), b3(v3) # Standard MSB v3, LSB v0 order might differ. In 2D squares, these are topologically distinct but require careful handling to ensure the correct pair of edges is connected. Vertex on Isovalue: If a vertex value equals the isovalue exactly, it must be treated consistently (e.g., as "inside" or "outside") to avoid ambiguity. The 1D analog to Marching Squares, processing grid cells in a linear, row-by-row manner. It is not template-based and requires further processing to resolve apparent cell ambiguities. Generates a polygonal mesh by placing a single vertex per grid cell at the cell's center (dual grid position) and connecting these vertices into quads. It produces smoother results and avoids topological inconsistencies common in standard Marching Squares, though it may lose sharp features. Generates filled contour bands between an upper and lower threshold. It classifies cells into three states (below, within, above) rather than two, allowing for continuous filled regions. Finds the 2D region where an interval [L, H] of values exists. Each square corner is assigned a ternary value: 0 if value < L, 1 if L \le value \le H, 2 if value > H. This results in 3^4 = 81 initial cases, reduced to 13 canonical cases after accounting for symmetries (rotational, mirror, high/low). The case number is determined by the base-3 number formed by the corner states. Time Complexity: O(Nx Ny), as each cell is processed independently. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny) for the input grid and output geometry. Parallelism: The algorithm is embarrassingly parallel because all cells are processed independently. Performance: A naive implementation performs linear interpolation twice per edge for isolines, resulting in duplicate vertices. Caching interpolation results for one row of the input grid can reduce computational overhead. Using indexed geometric primitives reduces output size. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for 2D data, fast. Limitations: Produces jagged contours at low resolutions; aliasing if not interpolated correctly; ambiguous saddle points in 3D (not 2D squares) or non-planar 2D embeddings. Marching Squares is the 2D analog of the Marching Cubes algorithm. It was developed as a method to generate contours for two-dimensional scalar fields, such as topographic maps or weather isobars. The algorithm processes each cell in the grid independently, calculating a cell index using comparisons of the contour level with the data values at the cell corners, and using a pre-built lookup table to describe the output geometry. It is used in scientific data visualization, such as the 'Hurricane Isabel Scientific Data Visualization' project. name: Marching Lines Algorithm
head: MLA
body: The Marching Lines Algorithm (MLA) extracts 1D isocontour line segments from a discrete 2D scalar field by processing grid cells in a linear, row-by-row manner. It serves as the 1D analog to Marching Squares and Marching Cubes. Unlike template-based methods, MLA is not template-based and requires further processing to properly resolve apparent cell ambiguities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D scalar field f(x, y) defined on a regular grid of vertices. Output: A set of line segments (edges) connecting points where the scalar field crosses a specified isovalue I. Data Structures: Grid: A 2D array of scalar values. Edge List: A list of line segments, each defined by two endpoints (x1, y1) and (x2, y2). Steps: 1. Iterate Rows: Process the grid row by row (or column by column). For each row y, iterate through the cells between vertex x and x+1. 2. Cell Evaluation: For each cell, evaluate the scalar values at the four corners: v{00}, v{10}, v{01}, v{11}. 3. Sign Determination: Determine the binary state of each corner relative to the isovalue I: s{ij} = \text{sign}(v{ij} - I). 4. Ambiguity Handling: Because MLA is not template-based, it does not use a precomputed lookup table for all 256 cases. Instead, it identifies "apparent cell ambiguities". These typically arise when the configuration of signs suggests multiple valid topological interpretations within a single cell or across adjacent cells. 5. Line Generation: For non-ambiguous cases, generate line segments connecting the intersection points on the cell edges. The intersection point on an edge between vertices with values va and vb is calculated via linear interpolation: t = \frac{I - va}{vb - va} P = (1-t)Pa + tPb 6. Post-Processing: Apply further processing to resolve the apparent ambiguities identified in Step 4. This ensures topological consistency and prevents artifacts like holes or disconnected segments. Parameters: Isovalue (I): The scalar threshold for extraction. Grid Resolution: Determines the granularity of the output. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Directional Ambiguities: The algorithm may suffer from directional ambiguities if the processing order (row-major vs. column-major) affects the resolution of ambiguous cells. Precision: Floating-point precision issues near the isovalue can lead to inconsistent sign determinations. Degenerate Input: If a vertex value exactly equals the isovalue, special handling is required to avoid division by zero during interpolation. Application of the Marching Squares algorithm to triangular meshes (connected triangles with data at vertices), such as those from Delaunay triangulation of scattered data points. A triangular cell is always planar (a 2-simplex), ensuring a unique linear interpolant across it and no possibility of an ambiguous saddle. For isolines, the analysis involves 3 binary digits at vertices, resulting in 8 possibilities. For isobands, it involves 3 ternary trits, resulting in 27 possibilities. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of cells in the grid. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the grid and output segments. Strengths: Simple implementation; low memory overhead. Limitations: Requires post-processing to resolve ambiguities; not template-based, which can lead to inconsistencies if not handled carefully. When to Use: Suitable for 2D scalar fields where simplicity and speed are prioritized over complex topological handling. The Marching Lines Algorithm is a foundational technique in isosurface extraction, serving as the 1D counterpart to Marching Squares and Marching Cubes. It is part of the broader family of marching algorithms used in volume rendering and scientific visualization. name: Cubical Marching Squares
head: CMS, CMSA, Marching Squares (for Voxels)
body: Cubical Marching Squares (CMS) is an adaptive surface extraction method for volume data that partitions space in a binary fashion using X-Y, Y-Z, and X-Z planes to extract surfaces while preserving sharp features and topology. It extends the 2D marching squares algorithm to 3D by unfolding a cube into six 2D faces, applying marching squares to generate isocurves on each face, and reconnecting these segments in 3D to form components and triangles. This approach eliminates inter-cell dependency and crack patching by sampling sharp features on faces, making it suitable for adaptive multiresolution representations. It is significantly more complicated to implement than Dual Contouring but offers advantages in sharp feature preservation and crack-free guarantees. Input: Hermite data H, defined as a signed grid where each edge is tagged with exact intersection points (sample points) and their normals (sample normals). This data is typically acquired at a very fine resolution, e.g., a uniform nk \times nk \times nk grid. Output: A polygonal triangle mesh approximating the isosurface. Base Grid B: A coarse uniform grid of size n0 \times n0 \times n0. Adaptive Signed Octree: The result of recursive subdivision. Cells are either "leaf cells" (no subcells) or internal nodes. Faces are "leaf faces" (no subfaces) or internal nodes. A "transition face" is shared by two cells subdivided at different levels. Segment: A line segment on a face connecting two sample points, tagged with potential sharp feature positions. Component: A closed loop (circle) of segments within a leaf cell. n0: Base grid resolution exponent. Typical value: 8. k: Maximal level of subdivision. The finest resolution is nk = 2^k \cdot n0. 1. Initialize the base grid B of size n0 \times n0 \times n0. 2. For each cell c in B, call SUBDIVIDECELL(H, c). Subdivision Condition 1 (Edge Ambiguity): Subdivide if an edge has more than one sample point. This prevents incorrect surface generation. Subdivision Condition 2 (Complexity Heuristic): Subdivide if the maximal spanning angle of all pairs of sample normals inside the cell exceeds a predefined angle threshold. This indicates the surface is not flat enough. Subdivision Process: When subdividing, subdivide faces first. Each face is split into four subfaces. Record relationships between subcells and subfaces. The subdivision sequence cycles through X-Y, Y-Z, and X-Z planes. Stop if the maximal level k is exceeded. For each leaf face f, call GENERATESEGMENT(f). For non-leaf faces, segments are the union of segments of their subfaces. 1. Lookup: Check sign patterns of face vertices against the marching squares lookup table. Case 0: No segments. Cases 1, 2: One segment. Case 3: Two segments (face ambiguity). 2. Face Ambiguity Resolution (Case 3): If two segments exist, call RESOLVEFACEAMBIGUITY(f). Detect sharp features on the potential segments. A 2D sharp feature is the intersection point of tangent lines defined by sample points and normals. Choose the assignment where sharp features do NOT overlap. Overlapping features imply self-intersection, which is invalid for volume data. 3. Sharp Feature Detection: For each segment, test if the angle between the two normals at its endpoints is large enough. If so, tag the segment and store the sharp feature position. This removes inter-cell dependency. For each leaf cell c, call EXTRACTSURFACE(c). 1. Collect Segments: Collect all segments from the cell's six faces using GETSEGMENT(fi) for each face fi. 2. Component Tracing: Call TRACECOMPONENTS(l) to group segments into circles (components). Start from an edge and sequentially find the next edge sharing an endpoint. 3. Internal Ambiguity Check: Check if the set of components O has internal ambiguity using HasInternalAmbiguity(O). Internal ambiguity occurs where we cannot determine whether two components are joined or separated by only looking at the signs on the vertices of a grid. If yes, call RESOLVEINTERNALAMBIGUITY(O). This is resolved by checking whether 3D sharp features of two components overlap. For each component, a cone-like volume is formed centered at its sharp feature. If no, proceed to triangulation. 4. 3D Sharp Feature Sampling: For each component, sample sharp features using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to solve [ni]^T p = [ni si] for p, where s is sample point location, n is sample normal, and p is sharp feature location. 5. Triangulation: With Sharp Feature: If a component has a sharp feature p, create a triangle fan centered at p using component vertices v1 \dots vn: triangles pv1v2, pv2v3, \dots, pvnv1. Without Sharp Feature: Calculate the average point of all sample points on the component and use it as the center for the triangle fan. Unverified code. Check Edge Ambiguity for edge in c.edges: if len(H.samplesonedge(edge)) > 1: # SubdivideCellRecursively(c) return # Check Complexity Heuristic maxangle = 0.0 normals = H.samplenormalsinside(c) for n1 in normals: for n2 in normals: angle = math.acos(math.dot(n1, n2) / (math.norm(n1) math.norm(n2))) if angle > maxangle: maxangle = angle if maxangle > ANGLETHRESHOLD: # SubdivideCellRecursively(c) def SubdivideCellRecursively(c): if c.level >= k: # return # Subdivide faces first for face in c.faces: face.subdivide() # # Create subcells c.createsubcells() # # Recurse for subc in c.subcells: SubdivideCell(H, subc) def GenerateSegment(Face f): signpattern = GetSignPattern(f.vertices) # case = LookupMarchingSquareCase(signpattern) # if case == 0: f.segments = [] elif case == 1 or case == 2: l = CreateSegmentFromCase(case, f) # f.segments = [l] DetectFaceSharpFeature(f.segments) # elif case == 3: # Face Ambiguity seg1, seg2 = CreateTwoSegmentsFromCase3(f) # sharp1 = DetectSharpFeature(seg1) # sharp2 = DetectSharpFeature(seg2) # if SharpFeaturesOverlap(sharp1, sharp2): # # Choose the other assignment (not overlapping) f.segments = ResolveAmbiguity(f) # else: f.segments = [seg1, seg2] DetectFaceSharpFeature(f.segments) # def ExtractSurface(Cell c): segments = [] for fi in c.faces: segments.extend(GetSegment(fi)) # components = TraceComponents(segments) # for o in components: DetectSharpFeature(o) # if HasInternalAmbiguity(components): # ResolveInternalAmbiguity(components) # for o in components: Triangulate(o) # def DetectSharpFeature(segmentorcomponent): # For segments: check angle between endpoint normals # For components: Solve [ni]^T p = [ni si] via SVD pass # Standard SVD solver implementation def Triangulate(component): vertices = component.vertices if component.hassharpfeature: p = component.sharpfeature else: p = AveragePoint(component.samplepoints) # for i in range(len(vertices)): v1 = vertices[i] v2 = vertices[(i + 1) % len(vertices)] CreateTriangle(p, v1, v2) # Cracks: Can occur on transition faces (faces shared by cells at different subdivision levels). The algorithm guarantees crack-free meshes because every segment on a transition face is shared by exactly two components from neighboring cells. Precision: Hermite data must be acquired at high resolution to ensure accurate sample points and normals. Ambiguity Resolution: The sharp feature overlap test may produce different results than asymptotic deciders, but is effective for volume data. Time Complexity: Generally slightly slower than standard marching cubes due to the overhead of adaptive subdivision and segment tracing. Memory Complexity: Depends on the adaptive octree depth. Higher detail requires more memory for the octree structure and segment lists. Accuracy: Produces about one-third the distance error of other algorithms. Strengths: Adaptive refinement based on surface complexity and ambiguity. Preserves sharp features. Crack-free meshes without post-processing patching. Eliminates inter-cell dependency, allowing for potential parallelization. Limitations: Significantly more complicated to implement than Dual Contouring or standard Marching Cubes. Requires Hermite data (sample points and normals), which may need to be pre-computed or derived. When to Use: When sharp feature preservation and crack-free adaptive meshes are critical, and implementation complexity is acceptable. When Not to Use: When simplicity of implementation is prioritized, or when Hermite data is not available and cannot be efficiently computed. Cubical Marching Squares was introduced as an adaptive surface extraction method for volume data. It builds on the 2D marching squares algorithm, extending it to 3D by treating each cube as six 2D faces. The method was developed to address issues with inter-cell dependency and crack formation in adaptive multiresolution representations, which are common in algorithms like Edge Matching Cubes (EMC) and Dual Contouring (DC). It uses Hermite data, a format previously used in dual contouring, to store exact intersection points and normals. The algorithm has been applied in volume visualization and 3D sculpting tools, offering improved visual quality and interactive performance. name: Dual Marching Squares
head: Schaefer's and Warren's Dual Marching Cubes (2D variant)
body: Dual Marching Squares (DMS) is a 2D surface extraction algorithm that generates a polygonal mesh from a scalar field by placing a single vertex per grid cell (or quadtree leaf) at the cell's center (dual grid position) and connecting these vertices into quads. Unlike standard Marching Squares, which places vertices on cell edges, DMS produces smoother results and avoids topological inconsistencies and self-intersections common in other techniques, though it may lose sharp features due to the fixed center placement. Inputs: A 2D scalar field f(x,y), an isovalue T, a minimum leaf size min\size, and a grid scaling factor grid\size. Outputs: A list of vertices (position, normal, color) and a list of quad indices forming the mesh. Data Structures: 1. QuadtreeNode: Represents a region of the grid. position: Vector2 (top-left corner of the node in grid units). size: int (side length of the square node). children: QuadtreeNode[4] (references to 4 child nodes, null if leaf). dualgridpos: Vector2 (offset from position to the dual vertex, typically 0.5 size). isovalue: float (sampled value at dualgridpos). normal: Vector2 (gradient at dualgridpos, normalized). leaf: bool (true if this node is a leaf). vertexindex: int (index in the global vertex list, valid if leaf). index: int (internal node identifier). 2. VertexPositionColorNormal: Position: Vector3 (3D position, Z=0 for 2D). Color: Color (e.g., RGB 210, 220, 210). Normal: Vector3 (2D normal extended to 3D with Z=0). 3. Connectivity Tables (used during mesh construction): edges[4][2]: {{0, 2}, {1, 3}, {0, 1}, {2, 3}}. Maps edge index to corner indices. edgechildren[2][2][2]: {{{2, 0}, {3, 1}}, {{1, 0}, {3, 2}}}. Maps parent edge children to child quad edges. vertexchildren[2][2][2]: {{{2, 3}, {0, 1}}, {{1, 3}, {0, 2}}}. Maps parent vertex children to child quad vertices. middlepoints[4]: {3, 2, 1, 0}. connectpoints[4]: {0, 2, 3, 1}. Parameters: threshold: The error threshold for adaptive splitting. minsize: Minimum leaf node size. minSplitDistanceDiagonalFactor: Scaling factor for diagonal distance check. Default: 1000.0f. Steps: 1. Initialize Quadtree: Create root node with position = (0,0), size = gridsize, leaf = false. 2. Build Quadtree (Recursive Splitting): Call TrySplit(node, minsize, threshold, gridsize, vertices). Check Split Conditions: A node becomes a leaf if any of the following are true: 1. size <= minsize. 2. GetError(node, threshold) < threshold. 3. The sample at the center is far from the threshold: |f(center) - T| > size \times \sqrt{2} \times minSplitDistanceDiagonalFactor. If Leaf: 1. Calculate dualgridpos = position + (0.5 size, 0.5 size). 2. Sample isovalue = f(dualgridpos). 3. Compute normal = gradient(f, dualgridpos). 4. Create VertexPositionColorNormal: Position = (position + dualgridpos) gridsize. Normal = (normal.x, normal.y, 0). Color = (210, 220, 210). 5. Add vertex to vertices list. Store its index in node.vertexindex. 6. Set node.leaf = true. Return. If Not Leaf: 1. Set node.leaf = false. 2. Split into 4 children. For i in 0..3: Create new QuadtreeNode. child.index = i. child.size = size / 2. child.position = position + (size / 2) (i / 2, i % 2). child.children = [null, null, null, null]. node.children[i] = child. Recursively call TrySplit(child, minsize, threshold, gridsize, vertices). 3. Construct Mesh (Connectivity): Call ConstructTreeGrid(root) to generate indices. This traverses the tree to connect leaf nodes into quads. ProcessFace(node): 1. If node is leaf, return. 2. Recursively call ProcessFace on all 4 children. 3. Process 4 edges between children (see ProcessEdge). 4. Process 4 vertices of the node (see ProcessVertices). ProcessEdge(q1, q2, edgeindex): Handles adjacency between sibling nodes q1 and q2 along a specific edge. 1. If both q1 and q2 are leaves, return (edge already processed or not needed). 2. If either is not a leaf, recursively process sub-edges using edgechildren mapping. 3. If both are leaves, call ProcessVertices on the 4 leaf nodes surrounding this edge. ProcessVertices(q1, q2, q3, q4): Takes 4 QuadtreeNodes representing the corners of a quad. 1. If any child is not a leaf, resolve it to its middle-point child and recurse. 2. If all are leaves: Create a Cell (quad). Get vertex indices from q1..q4.vertexindex. Add indices to the mesh using connectpoints order: (q1, q3, q4, q2) (indices 0, 2, 3, 1). Set Cell positions, values, and normals from the leaf nodes' dualgridpos, isovalue, and normal. Error Calculation (GetError): To determine if a node should split, calculate error based on bilinear interpolation: 1. Sample centervalue at 5 positions: 4 corners and center. 2. Compute interpolated value at the center using bilinear interpolation of the 4 corner values. 3. error += |centervalue - interpolated| / max(1.0, |gradient|). 4. If error >= threshold, return true (split). Bilinear Interpolation (Interpolate): f(p) = f{00}(1-px)(1-py) + f{01}(1-px)py + f{10}px(1-py) + f{11}px py where px and py are the x and y components of the input Vector2 position. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def builddualmarchingsquares(grid, isovalue, minsize, threshold, gridsize): root = QuadtreeNode(position=(0.0, 0.0), size=gridsize, leaf=False) vertices = [] trysplit(root, minsize, threshold, gridsize, vertices, grid, isovalue) indices = [] constructtreegrid(root, indices) return vertices, indices class QuadtreeNode: def init(self, position, size): self.position = position self.size = size self.children = [None, None, None, None] self.dualgridpos = (0.5 size, 0.5 size) self.isovalue = 0.0 self.normal = (0.0, 0.0) self.leaf = False self.vertexindex = -1 self.index = 0 class Vertex: def init(self, position, color, normal): self.position = position self.color = color self.normal = normal def samplegrid(grid, pos): return grid[int(pos[0])][int(pos[1])] def computegradient(grid, pos): dx = grid[int(pos[0])+1][int(pos[1])] - grid[int(pos[0])-1][int(pos[1])] dy = grid[int(pos[0])][int(pos[1])+1] - grid[int(pos[0])][int(pos[1])-1] return (dx, dy) def trysplit(node, minsize, threshold, gridsize, vertices, grid, isovalue): if node.size <= minsize: createleaf(node, grid, gridsize, vertices, isovalue) return if not geterror(node, grid, isovalue, threshold): createleaf(node, grid, gridsize, vertices, isovalue) return centerpos = (node.position[0] + node.size 0.5, node.position[1] + node.size 0.5) centerval = samplegrid(grid, centerpos) diagfactor = 1000.0 if abs(centerval - isovalue) > node.size (20.5) diagfactor: createleaf(node, grid, gridsize, vertices, isovalue) return node.leaf = False half = node.size // 2 for i in range(4): child = QuadtreeNode( position=(node.position[0] + (i // 2) half, node.position[1] + (i % 2) half), size=half) child.index = i node.children[i] = child trysplit(child, minsize, threshold, gridsize, vertices, grid, isovalue) def createleaf(node, grid, gridsize, vertices, isovalue): node.leaf = True dualpos = (node.position[0] + node.dualgridpos[0], node.position[1] + node.dualgridpos[1]) node.isovalue = samplegrid(grid, dualpos) node.normal = computegradient(grid, dualpos) pos3d = ( (node.position[0] + node.dualgridpos[0]) gridsize, (node.position[1] + node.dualgridpos[1]) gridsize, 0.0) norm3d = (node.normal[0], node.normal[1], 0.0) vertex = Vertex(position=pos3d, color=(210, 220, 210), normal=norm3d) node.vertexindex = len(vertices) vertices.append(vertex) def geterror(node, grid, isovalue, threshold): corners = [ samplegrid(grid, node.position), samplegrid(grid, (node.position[0] + node.size, node.position[1])), samplegrid(grid, (node.position[0], node.position[1] + node.size)), samplegrid(grid, (node.position[0] + node.size, node.position[1] + node.size)) ] centerval = samplegrid(grid, (node.position[0] + node.size 0.5, node.position[1] + node.size 0.5)) px, py = 0.5, 0.5 f00, f01, f10, f11 = corners[0], corners[1], corners[2], corners[3] interpolated = f00 (1-px) (1-py) + f01 (1-px) py + f10 px (1-py) + f11 px py grad = computegradient(grid, (node.position[0] + node.size 0.5, node.position[1] + node.size 0.5)) gradmag = max(1.0, abs(grad[0]) + abs(grad[1])) error = abs(centerval - interpolated) / gradmag if error >= threshold: return True return error def constructtreegrid(node, indices): if node.leaf: return processface(node, indices) def processface(node, indices): if node.leaf: return for child in node.children: processface(child, indices) for edgeidx in range(4): q1, q2 = getsiblingnodes(node, edgeidx) processedge(q1, q2, edgeidx, indices) for vertidx in range(4): q1, q2, q3, q4 = getcornernodes(node, vertidx) processvertices(q1, q2, q3, q4, indices) def getsiblingnodes(node, edgeidx): mapping = [(0, 2), (1, 3), (0, 1), (2, 3)] i, j = mapping[edgeidx] return node.children[i], node.children[j] def getcornernodes(node, vertidx): return node.children[0], node.children[1], node.children[2], node.children[3] def processedge(q1, q2, edgeidx, indices): if q1.leaf and q2.leaf: return if not q1.leaf: processface(q1, indices) if not q2.leaf: processface(q2, indices) leaves = resolveleavesaroundedge(q1, q2, edgeidx) if len(leaves) == 4: processvertices(leaves[0], leaves[1], leaves[2], leaves[3], indices) def resolveleavesaroundedge(q1, q2, edgeidx): res = [] for q in [q1, q2]: if q.leaf: res.append(q) else: res.append(q) return res def processvertices(q1, q2, q3, q4, indices): middlepoints = [3, 2, 1, 0] nodes = [q1, q2, q3, q4] for i in range(4): if not nodes[i].leaf: nodes[i] = nodes[i].children[middlepoints[i]] if not nodes[i].leaf: nodes[i] = nodes[i].children[middlepoints[i]] if all(n.leaf for n in nodes): connectpoints = [0, 2, 3, 1] for i in range(4): idx1 = nodes[connectpoints[i]].vertexindex idx2 = nodes[connectpoints[(i+1)%4]].vertexindex indices.append(idx1) indices.append(idx2) Pitfall: The GetError function has a major flaw when sampled points have very similar values, leading to negligible error calculation even if the surface is complex. Fixes suggested: sample more points, use a maximum container size, or sample random points. Uniform grid sampling (corners, midpoints, then in-between) with early break is recommended. An optimization that substitutes the standard error-reducing function with a separate, faster alternative function to address the loss of sharp features inherent in the base method. Note: It is currently disabled in the reference implementation, meaning sharp features are not preserved. Time Complexity: Depends on the quadtree depth. In the worst case (uniform grid), it is O(N) where N is the number of cells. Adaptive splitting reduces this for smooth regions. Memory Complexity: O(N) for vertices and indices. Quadtree overhead adds a constant factor. Performance: Produces smoother results than Marching Squares. Strengths: Avoids topological inconsistencies and self-intersections; handles concave surfaces well. Limitations: Loses sharp features due to center placement; error calculation can be flawed if sampled points have similar values. When to use: When smooth surfaces are preferred and sharp features are not critical. When not to use: When sharp features must be preserved or when edge-based precision is required. Dual Marching Squares is the 2D variant of Dual Marching Cubes, originally proposed by Schaefer and Warren. It is used in flow visualization and scientific visualization to extract isosurfaces from scalar fields, such as those from computational fluid dynamics simulations. It was implemented using the VTK pipeline.
