name: Marching Cubes with Lewiner 2003 Ambiguity Resolution
head: Lewiner Marching Cubes, Marching Cubes 2003
body: This method is a variant of the Marching Cubes algorithm that resolves topological ambiguities (ambiguous faces and internal ambiguities) present in the original 1987 algorithm to guarantee a manifold surface. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by using a face ambiguity test and interior point checks to disambiguate cases where the sign configuration at cube vertices does not uniquely determine the topology. It builds on Marching Cubes 3. Inputs: 3D scalar field data getData(x, y, z) with dimensions dim[0], dim[1], dim[2]. Isovalue isoValue. Grid spacing spacing[0], spacing[1], spacing[2]. Boolean reverseGradientDirection (default false). Outputs: List of vertices vertices (position, normal). List of triangle indices triangles. Data Structures: xDirectionInterpolatedVertexIndex, yDirectionInterpolatedVertexIndex, zDirectionInterpolatedVertexIndex: Maps from grid coordinates (i, j, k) to vertex indices for interpolated points on edges parallel to x, y, z axes respectively. centerInterpolatedVertexIndex: Maps from grid coordinates to vertex indices for center vertices created in specific ambiguous cases. vertices: Vector of Vertex structs containing position and normal. triangles: Vector of triangle index triplets. Lookup Tables: cases (maps 256 configuration indices to 15 base cases and sub-class indices), test3, test4, test6, test7 (specify which face/interior to test), tiling1 through tiling7 (specify triangulations). Vertex Indexing: Vertices are indexed relative to cube corner 0. Moving in the +x direction adds 1, +y adds 3, +z adds 4. Internal center points are labeled 12. Steps: 1. Initialization: Clear vertices, triangles, and all vertex index maps. Initialize bounding box bmin to max float and bmax to min float. 2. Pre-compute Interpolated Vertices: Iterate over all edges of the volume. For each edge connecting vertices V0 and V1 with values val0 and val1, if (val0 - isoValue) and (val1 - isoValue) have opposite signs, compute the interpolated vertex position and store it in the appropriate direction map (xDirectionInterpolatedVertexIndex, etc.) indexed by the cube's corner 0. Pitfall: If a vertex value equals isoValue, the difference is 0. Set the difference to FLTEPSILON to prevent interpolation errors (triangle collapse or missing vertices). 3. Cube Iteration: Iterate i from 0 to dim[0]-2, j from 0 to dim[1]-2, k from 0 to dim[2]-2. This loop is parallelized using OpenMP (#pragma omp parallel for) with locks (vertexLock, triangleLock) to protect shared vertices and triangles lists. 4. Configuration Index Calculation: For each cube, determine the 8-bit configuration index. For vertex l (0-7), calculate grid coordinates: x = i + ((l \oplus (l \gg 1)) \& 1) y = j + ((l \gg 1) \& 1) z = k + ((l \gg 2) \& 1) Get data value val = getData(x, y, z). If val > isoValue, set bit l in configurationIndex. 5. Case Lookup: Retrieve caseIdx and configurationIndexInCase from the cases table using configurationIndex. 6. Triangulation based on Case: Case 0: No triangles added. Case 1: Add 1 triangle using tiling1 table at index configurationIndexInCase. Case 2: Add 2 triangles using tiling2 table at index configurationIndexInCase. Case 3: Test 1 face. Call testFace(i, j, k, cube, test3[configurationIndexInCase]). If result < 0, add 2 triangles from tiling31. Else, add 4 triangles from tiling32. Case 4: Test 1 interior point. Call testInterior(i, j, k, cube, caseIdx, test4[configurationIndexInCase], 1). If result < 0, add 2 triangles from tiling41. Else, add 6 triangles from tiling42. Case 5: Add 3 triangles using tiling5 table at index configurationIndexInCase. Case 6: Test 1 face and 1 interior. Call testFace with test6[configurationIndexInCase][0]. If < 0 (Case 6.1), call testInterior with test6[configurationIndexInCase][1] and test6[configurationIndexInCase][2]. If interior < 0, add 3 triangles from tiling611. Else, add 9 triangles from tiling612. If face >= 0, add 5 triangles from tiling62. Case 7: Test 3 faces and 1 interior. Build subconfig bitmask by calling testFace for three faces defined in test7[configurationIndexInCase][0..2]. Add 1 if face 0 < 0, add 2 if face 1 < 0, add 4 if face 2 < 0. Switch on subconfig: 0->3 triangles (tiling71), 1/2/4->5 triangles (tiling72 variants), 3/5->9 triangles (tiling73 variants). 7. Center Vertex Creation (Ambiguity Resolution): For cases requiring a center vertex (e.g., Case 6.1.2), create a center vertex by averaging all existing interpolated vertices on the cube's edges. addCenterVertex sums vertices from x, y, and z edge maps, divides by count cnt, normalizes the normal, and adds it to the vertex list. Pitfall: If cnt == 0, the center vertex calculation fails. Assert false and print error. Face Ambiguity Test (testFace): For a face with vertices A, B, C, D (where A and C are opposite, B and D are opposite), compute AC - BD. If |AC - BD| < \text{FLT\EPSILON}, return face >= 0. Else, return face A (AC - BD) >= 0. Pitfall: If the test value is exactly zero and handled incorrectly, adjacent cubes may generate duplicate/overlapping faces. Interior Ambiguity Test (testInterior): Check if a middle cross-section exists such that AC > BD. If found, it proves the middle region is connected, determining the internal topology. Gradient and Normal Calculation: Gradient (Interior): For 0 < i < dim[0]-1, gx = \frac{getData(i+1, j, k) - getData(i-1, j, k)}{2 \cdot spacing[0]}. Similar for Y and Z. Gradient (Boundary): For i=0, gx = \frac{getData(i+1, j, k) - getData(i, j, k)}{spacing[0]}. For i=dim[0]-1, gx = \frac{getData(i, j, k) - getData(i-1, j, k)}{spacing[0]}. Normal: \vec{n} = d \cdot (gx, gy, gz), where d = -1 if reverseGradientDirection is true, else 1. Normalize \vec{n}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import threading def computegradient(data, i, j, k, spacing, dim): # Compute gradient at (i, j, k) # Handle boundaries as per S3 if i == 0: gx = (data[i+1, j, k] - data[i, j, k]) / spacing[0] elif i == dim[0] - 1: gx = (data[i, j, k] - data[i-1, j, k]) / spacing[0] else: gx = (data[i+1, j, k] - data[i-1, j, k]) / (2 spacing[0]) if j == 0: gy = (data[i, j+1, k] - data[i, j, k]) / spacing[1] elif j == dim[1] - 1: gy = (data[i, j, k] - data[i, j-1, k]) / spacing[1] else: gy = (data[i, j+1, k] - data[i, j-1, k]) / (2 spacing[1]) if k == 0: gz = (data[i, j, k+1] - data[i, j, k]) / spacing[2] elif k == dim[2] - 1: gz = (data[i, j, k] - data[i, j, k-1]) / spacing[2] else: gz = (data[i, j, k+1] - data[i, j, k-1]) / (2 spacing[2]) return (gx, gy, gz) def testface(A, B, C, D, face): # A, B, C, D are scalar values at vertices of the face # face is the sign of the vertex used for ambiguity resolution (usually A) val = A C - B D if abs(val) < 1e-6: # FLTEPSILON return face >= 0 return face A val >= 0 def marchingcubeslewiner(data, isovalue, spacing, reversegradient): dim = data.shape vertices = [] triangles = [] xmap = {} ymap = {} zmap = {} centermap = {} vertexlock = threading.Lock() trianglelock = threading.Lock() # Pre-compute interpolated vertices for i in range(dim[0] - 1): for j in range(dim[1] - 1): for k in range(dim[2] - 1): # Check x-edges v0 = data[i, j, k] - isovalue v1 = data[i+1, j, k] - isovalue if v0 v1 < 0: # Interpolate t = v0 / (v0 - v1) pos = (i + t, j, k) # Handle zero difference if v0 == 0: v0 = 1e-6 if v1 == 0: v1 = 1e-6 #... compute pos correctly... idx = len(vertices) vertices.append({'pos': pos, 'normal': (0,0,0)}) # Placeholder xmap[(i, j, k)] = idx #... similar for y and z edges... # Cube iteration for i in range(dim[0] - 1): for j in range(dim[1] - 1): for k in range(dim[2] - 1): # Configuration Index config = 0 for l in range(8): x = i + ((l ^ (l >> 1)) & 1) y = j + ((l >> 1) & 1) z = k + ((l >> 2) & 1) if data[x, y, z] > isovalue: config |= (1 << l) caseidx, subidx = casestable[config] # Triangulation based on case if caseidx == 0: pass elif caseidx == 1: addtriangles(tiling1[subidx], vertices, triangles, xmap, ymap, zmap, centermap) elif caseidx == 2: addtriangles(tiling2[subidx], vertices, triangles, xmap, ymap, zmap, centermap) elif caseidx == 3: # Test face #... get face vertices A, B, C, D... #... get face sign... res = testface(A, B, C, D, facesign) if res < 0: addtriangles(tiling31[subidx], vertices, triangles, xmap, ymap, zmap, centermap) else: addtriangles(tiling32[subidx], vertices, triangles, xmap, ymap, zmap, centermap) #... cases 4-7... # Thread safety with vertexlock: #... add vertices... with trianglelock: #... add triangles... return vertices, triangles Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel is processed once. Parallelization with OpenMP reduces wall-clock time. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing interpolated vertices and triangles. Using unorderedmap for vertex indexing saves memory compared to 3D arrays. Performance: On a dataset with isoValue 800, 4,256,478 vertices, and 8,165,228 faces, the algorithm takes ~9s with OMP acceleration. File I/O takes ~21s. Total ~30s. Strengths: Guarantees manifold surfaces by resolving topological ambiguities. Limitations: Larger lookup tables compared to standard MC. Degenerate cases (zero ambiguity test value) require careful handling to avoid duplicate faces. Origin: Thomas Lewiner, 2003. Paper: "Efficient implementation of Marching Cubes’ cases with topological guarantees". History: The original Marching Cubes (Lorensen 1987) did not resolve ambiguities, leading to cracks and non-manifold geometry. Lewiner's method addresses this by testing faces and interior points. Usage: Used in skimage.measure.marchingcubeslewiner. Also implemented in upupming/marching-cubes. name: Ray-Unit Parallel Marching Cubes
head: rupMC
body: Ray-Unit Parallel Marching Cubes (rupMC) is an enhanced Marching Cubes algorithm designed for CPU/GPU heterogeneous architectures that reduces redundant edge intersection computations and preserves topological information of the isosurface. It replaces the standard cubic voxel with a ray unit to ensure each edge intersection is calculated and stored exactly once, while parallelizing I/O via OpenMPI and computation via CUDA to handle large-scale datasets efficiently. Unlike standard MC, which suffers from repeated calculations on shared edges and lacks explicit topological connectivity, rupMC embeds topological relationships directly into the triangle composition using unique intersection indices. Inputs: A 3D scalar field dataset defined on a regular grid. An isosurface value (threshold) V{iso}. Configuration parameters: number of CPU processes and available GPU memory for subdomain decomposition. Outputs: A set of surface triangles representing the isosurface, where each triangle is defined by three unique intersection indices. Implicit topological connectivity information derived from the shared unique indices of adjacent triangles. Ray Unit: The basic computing unit is the ray unit, which consists of a single grid point and three rays extending along the three data composition directions (x, y, z). This structure replaces the standard cube to avoid overlapping edges shared by four adjacent cubes. Marks: Two sets of marks are maintained for each ray unit: 1. Triangle Count: Records the number of surface triangles generated for the cube associated with the ray unit. 2. Edge Intersection Flags: A binary mark for each edge of the ray unit indicating whether a surface intersection exists on that edge. Lookup Table: A predefined table indexed by an integer lookup index. The index is derived from the binary states of the eight vertices of the cube associated with the ray unit. The table provides the configuration of edge intersections for that specific cube state. Intersection Indices: Unique identifiers assigned to each calculated edge intersection. These indices are preserved and used to compose surface triangles, ensuring that shared edges between adjacent triangles are referenced by the same index. 1. Dataset Partitioning (CPU): Process 0 receives the full dataset and parameters. Process 0 adaptively divides the dataset into sub-datasets based on the number of available CPU processes. 2. Sub-domain Decomposition (CPU/GPU): Each CPU process receives a sub-dataset. Each process further divides its sub-dataset into subdomains based on the available GPU memory. Data for each subdomain is transmitted from CPU memory to GPU memory. 3. Ray Unit Initialization and Indexing (GPU): Each GPU thread is assigned to process one ray unit. The thread identifies the eight vertices of the cube associated with its assigned ray unit. The thread determines the state of each vertex: state 1 if the data value \ge V{iso} (inside/on surface), state 0 if data value < V{iso} (outside surface). The thread computes the lookup index I from the 8-bit binary state of the vertices: I = \sum{i=0}^{7} si \cdot 2^i where si is the state (0 or 1) of the i-th vertex. The thread uses I to access the predefined lookup table to determine which edges of the cube are intersected by the isosurface. 4. Edge Intersection Calculation and Marking (GPU): The thread checks the marks for the ray unit's edges. If an edge has not been marked as intersected, the thread calculates the intersection point using standard linear interpolation between the two vertices of the edge. The thread assigns a unique index to this intersection. The thread updates the edge intersection mark to indicate the intersection has been calculated and stored. If the edge is already marked, the thread retrieves the existing unique index. The thread updates the triangle count mark based on the number of triangles generated for this cube configuration. 5. Triangle Composition (GPU): Using the unique intersection indices retrieved or calculated in Step 4, the thread composes the surface triangles for the cube. The triangles are defined by referencing the unique indices of their vertices. This process embeds topological information directly, as adjacent triangles sharing an edge will reference the same unique intersection index. 6. Result Aggregation and I/O (CPU): Results (triangles and indices) are transmitted from GPU memory back to CPU memory. Sub-results from all CPU processes are transmitted to Process 1. Process 1 writes the final triangle data to output files. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivedivide(dataset, numprocesses): """Divides dataset into numprocesses equal sub-datasets.""" return [dataset[i::numprocesses] for i in range(numprocesses)] def decomposebygpumemory(subdataset, gpumemorylimit): """Splits subdataset into chunks fitting within gpumemorylimit.""" chunks = [] currentchunk = [] currentsize = 0 for point in subdataset: currentchunk.append(point) currentsize += 1 if currentsize >= gpumemorylimit: chunks.append(currentchunk) currentchunk = [] currentsize = 0 if currentchunk: chunks.append(currentchunk) return chunks def processrayunit(rayunit, isosurfacevalue, lookuptable, edgemarks, intersectionindices, trianglecount): """Processes a single ray unit on the GPU.""" vertices = rayunit.getcubevertices() states = [1 if v.value >= isosurfacevalue else 0 for v in vertices] index = sum(s (2 i) for i, s in enumerate(states)) config = lookuptable[index] trianglevertices = [] for edge in config.intersectededges: edgeid = edge.id if not edgemarks[edgeid]: v1, v2 = edge.vertices t = (isosurfacevalue - v1.value) / (v2.value - v1.value) intersectionpoint = (v1.position (1 - t)) + (v2.position t) uniqueidx = len(intersectionindices) intersectionindices[edgeid] = uniqueidx edgemarks[edgeid] = True else: uniqueidx = intersectionindices[edgeid] trianglevertices.append(uniqueidx) for triconn in config.triangleconnections: tri = [trianglevertices[triconn[0]], trianglevertices[triconn[1]], trianglevertices[triconn[2]]] trianglecount += 1 yield tri def parallelrupmc(dataset, isosurfacevalue, numcpuprocesses, gpumemorylimit): """Main parallel execution flow.""" currentprocessid = 0 # Simulated process ID subdataset = None if currentprocessid == 0: subdatasets = adaptivedivide(dataset, numcpuprocesses) for i, sd in enumerate(subdatasets): if i == 0: subdataset = sd else: # Simulate sending to process i pass else: # Simulate receiving from process 0 subdataset = dataset[0] subdomains = decomposebygpumemory(subdataset, gpumemorylimit) alltriangles = [] for domain in subdomains: edgemarks = {} intersectionindices = {} trianglecount = 0 for rayunit in domain.rayunits: for tri in processrayunit(rayunit, isosurfacevalue, lookuptable, edgemarks, intersectionindices, trianglecount): alltriangles.append(tri) if currentprocessid == 1: # Simulate receiving from all processes pass return alltriangles Isosurface Value (V{iso}): The threshold value determining vertex states (inside/outside). Lookup Index: An integer from 0 to 255 derived from the 8-bit vertex states, used to index the precalculated table of edge intersections. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Precision: Linear interpolation for intersection points assumes linear variation between vertices. Degenerate cases where vertex values exactly equal V{iso} are handled by assigning state 1 (inside/on surface). Boundary Conditions: The adaptive domain decomposition must handle dataset boundaries to ensure ray units at the edges of subdomains are processed correctly without missing intersections. Memory Constraints: Sub-domain decomposition is adaptive based on available GPU memory; failure to account for memory limits may cause kernel launch failures. The parent method using a third implementation variant (mc::marchingcubes3). rupMC builds on the standard MC topology but replaces the cube unit with a ray unit to reduce redundancy. A sibling method addressing topological ambiguities in standard MC. rupMC addresses topological information preservation through unique intersection indices rather than ambiguity resolution tables. Time Complexity: The algorithm reduces redundant computations by calculating each edge intersection only once, compared to four times in standard MC. Parallelization on CPU/GPU further reduces wall-clock time. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by storing unique intersection indices rather than repeated intersection points for each adjacent cube. Measured Performance: Approximately dozens of times faster than serial MC. 4 times faster than parallel Dual MC (DMC). 5x speedup over VTK-implemented MC. 4x speedup over VTK-implemented Flying Edges (FE). Over 9x speedup over C++-implemented MC. Over 2x speedup over parallel DMC on GPU. Tests conducted on five stratum datasets of varying sizes, including a base resolution of 102 \times 151 \times 702. Strengths: High scalability, adaptability to various CPU/GPU environments, preservation of topological information, and reduced I/O intensity through pipelining. Limitations: Implementation relies on a CPU/GPU heterogeneous architecture using OpenMPI for I/O and CUDA for computation. The complexity of managing unique indices and parallel I/O may increase implementation difficulty compared to standard MC. When to Use: Large-scale datasets requiring topological details, such as geological body reconstruction. When Not to Use: Small datasets where the overhead of parallelization and unique index management may not justify the performance gain, or environments lacking GPU/OpenMPI support. Origin: Proposed by Li, Zhong, and Wang in 2024. History: Developed to address three specific limitations of standard Marching Cubes: redundant edge computations (each edge shared by four cubes), high I/O intensity, and lack of topological information in the output triangles. Usage: Used for visualizing stratum data (soil moisture content) and reconstructing raw structural topological relationships between geological bodies. rupMC: a ray-unit parallel marching cubes algorithm on CPU/GPU heterogeneous architectures, https://doi.org/10.1080/17538947.2024.2340583, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Isomesh
head: isomesh=level, solid 3D isosurfaces
body: Isomesh is a surface extraction technique that triangulates the level set of a 3D scalar field using the Marching Cubes algorithm and renders the result as a shaded, depth-tested mesh. It solves the visual artifacts of volume rendering approaches, specifically the striping inherent in ray-marched iso-shells and the lack of depth testing in MIP/absorption methods that forces the body to occlude the field. Unlike its siblings, it produces smooth, correctly occluded surfaces by generating the mesh on the CPU and relying on standard depth-tested rasterization for rendering, rather than per-pixel ray marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field observable \sigma defined on a grid, and a scalar level value L (the isovalue). Output: A GeometryBasics.Mesh containing the triangulated isosurface. If the field does not cross L within the domain, the mesh is empty. Data Structures: Field: A 3D array of floating-point values. The implementation asserts the dimension d=3; it is not applicable to 2D fields. Mesh: A GeometryBasics.Mesh object containing vertices and triangle indices. The normals are oriented towards increasing field values. Numbered Steps: 1. Validation: Assert that the input field dimension d=3. 2. Extraction: Execute the Marching Cubes algorithm on the CPU, running single-threaded over the plotted region of the field \sigma, to extract the isosurface at level L. This generates a GeometryBasics.Mesh. 3. Plotting: When the isomesh keyword is set to a level value, the field Observable is lifted to isosurfacemesh(σ, isomesh) and plotted by a new plotσobs! method for meshes. Rendering kwargs (e.g., color, transparency, backlight) are passed to Makie.mesh!. 4. Rendering: Render the mesh with depth testing enabled. The normals point into the region of interest for fields like vorticity or -\lambda2, and out of it for low pressure. Formulas: Cell Configuration Index: For each voxel cell with corner values v0, \dots, v7, the binary configuration index is I = \sum{k=0}^{7} s(vk) \cdot 2^k, where s(v) = 1 if v \ge L and 0 otherwise. Edge Interpolation: For an edge connecting corners va and vb with spatial positions pa and pb, the isosurface point p is computed via linear interpolation: p = pa + \frac{L - va}{vb - va} (pb - pa). Triangle Generation: Triangles are formed by connecting the interpolated edge points according to the standard Marching Cubes lookup table for index I. Parameters: isomesh: The level value L for extraction. backlight: A lighting parameter for the mesh, defaulting to 1. Setting backlight=1 lights both sides of the mesh to remove dependence on normal sign. Setting backlight=0 causes surfaces with normals pointing away from the light to render dark. transparency: A boolean flag passed to Makie.mesh!. When true, combined with a translucent colour, it allows the body to stay visible through the mesh. enabledepth: For isomesh, this is implicitly true because mesh plots are always depth-tested. Passing enabledepth=false with isomesh errors in Makie with 'Invalid attribute enabledepth for plot type Mesh'. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The Marching Cubes implementation runs single-threaded on the CPU. Performance can be improved by cropping the domain with CIs to reduce the region processed. Normal Orientation: Marching cubes orients the normals towards increasing values. For fields where the region of interest is below the level (e.g., low pressure), normals point outward. Use backlight=1 to ensure visibility regardless of orientation. Depth Testing: Unlike:mip and:absorption which default to enabledepth=false (drawing the body over the field), isomesh uses depth testing so the body is occluded by the field where appropriate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def plotisomesh(fieldobservable, level, backlight=1, transparency=False): """ Extracts and renders an isosurface mesh for a 3D field. Args: fieldobservable: 3D scalar field array (nx, ny, nz). level: Scalar isovalue. backlight: Lighting mode (1 for both sides, 0 for front-side only). transparency: Boolean for alpha blending. """ # 1. Validation: Assert 3D dimension if len(fieldobservable.shape) != 3: raise ValueError("Isomesh requires a 3D field.") nx, ny, nz = fieldobservable.shape cellcount = (nx - 1) (ny - 1) (nz - 1) if cellcount == 0: return # Standard Marching Cubes lookup tables (edgetable[config] -> list of edge indices) # tritable[config] -> list of triangle vertex indices (-1 terminates triangle) # Defined per standard MC specification EDGETABLE = [...] # 256 entries mapping config to up to 12 edge indices TRITABLE = [...] # 256 entries mapping config to up to 5 triangles (vertex indices) vertices = [] triangles = [] # 2. Extraction: Single-threaded CPU iteration over cells for i in range(nx - 1): for j in range(ny - 1): for k in range(nz - 1): # Extract 8 corner values and positions corners = [ fieldobservable[i, j, k], fieldobservable[i+1, j, k], fieldobservable[i+1, j+1, k], fieldobservable[i, j+1, k], fieldobservable[i, j, k+1], fieldobservable[i+1, j, k+1], fieldobservable[i+1, j+1, k+1], fieldobservable[i, j+1, k+1] ] positions = [ (i, j, k), (i+1, j, k), (i+1, j+1, k), (i, j+1, k), (i, j, k+1), (i+1, j, k+1), (i+1, j+1, k+1), (i, j+1, k+1) ] # Compute cell configuration index config = 0 for m in range(8): if corners[m] >= level: config |= (1 << m) if config == 0: continue # Field does not cross level in this cell # Interpolate vertices on active edges edgeindices = EDGETABLE[config] edgevertices = [] for eidx in edgeindices: v0, v1 = eidx // 2, (eidx + 1) // 2 # Handle edge wrapping for standard MC edge numbering edgev0, edgev1 = corners[v0], corners[v1] pos0, pos1 = positions[v0], positions[v1] if abs(edgev1 - edgev0) < 1e-9: interppos = pos0 else: t = (level - edgev0) / (edgev1 - edgev0) interppos = (pos0[0] + t(pos1[0]-pos0[0]), pos0[1] + t(pos1[1]-pos0[1]), pos0[2] + t(pos1[2]-pos0[2])) edgevertices.append(interppos) # Generate triangles triindices = TRITABLE[config] for idx in triindices: if idx == -1: break v0, v1, v2 = edgevertices[idx], edgevertices[idx+1], edgevertices[idx+2] triangles.append((v0, v1, v2)) # If field does not cross level, mesh is empty if not triangles: return # 3. Plotting: Lift to mesh and render # Pass kwargs to Makie.mesh! rendermesh( vertices=vertices, triangles=triangles, backlight=backlight, transparency=transparency, enabledepth=True # Implicitly true; cannot be set to False) Time Complexity: The Marching Cubes extraction is O(N) with respect to the number of voxels in the plotted region, but runs single-threaded on the CPU. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the field array and the resulting mesh (vertices and indices). Measured Performance: On an RTX 4060 8 GB with 8 threads, on a 512 \times 192 \times 192 domain: Isomesh update time: 1.48s Render time: 0.016s Total per frame: 1.50s The Marching Cubes step adds 0.65s per frame for approximately 52k triangles, which is about 0.5s more than volume methods, while its draw time is the cheapest among all methods. Strengths: Produces smooth surfaces with correct depth testing, avoiding the striping of ray-marched iso volumes and the occlusion issues of MIP/absorption. Limitations: Slower extraction time due to single-threaded CPU execution. Not applicable to 2D fields. Isomesh was introduced as part of the viz! function in the WaterLily.jl ecosystem to provide a solid 3D isosurface visualization option. It was developed to address the visual limitations of existing volume rendering methods in the library, specifically the striped appearance of:iso ray marching and the lack of depth testing in:mip and:absorption. The implementation relies on the Meshing package for the Marching Cubes algorithm and GeometryBasics for the mesh structure. viz!: add isomesh keyword for solid 3D isosurfaces, https://github.com/WaterLily-jl/WaterLily.jl/pull/334, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Marching Tetrahedra
head: Marching tetras, Tetrahedral Marching, Tetrahedral Marching Cubes, marching tets
body: Marching Tetrahedra (MT) is an isosurface extraction algorithm that decomposes each cubic voxel into tetrahedra to resolve the topological ambiguities present in Marching Cubes. By processing tetrahedra independently, it guarantees a manifold mesh without cracks or ambiguous configurations, producing higher-quality surfaces at the cost of increased triangle count and computational overhead. Inputs: A 3D scalar field V defined on a regular grid of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz, and an isovalue I. Outputs: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface V(x,y,z) = I. 1. Scalar Field: A 1D or 3D array storing scalar values, indexed by idx = x + Nx(y + Nz z). 2. Vertex Lookup Cache: A dictionary mapping unique edge keys (defined by the global coordinates of the two endpoints) to the generated vertex index. This ensures shared edges between adjacent tetrahedra produce identical intersection points, preventing holes. 3. Tetrahedron Decomposition Table: A static array defining the 4 vertex indices (0-7) for each tetrahedron within a voxel. The standard 6-tetrahedron decomposition uses the following vertex indices: T0: \{0, 7, 3, 2\}, T1: \{0, 7, 2, 6\}, T2: \{0, 4, 6, 7\} T3: \{0, 6, 1, 2\}, T4: \{0, 6, 1, 4\}, T5: \{5, 6, 1, 4\} Note: A 5-tetrahedron scheme exists but requires alternating splitting patterns to maintain continuity. 4. Edge-Vertex Mapping: A static array tetrahedronEdgeConnection[6][2] mapping the 6 edges of a tetrahedron to its 4 vertices. Standard ordering: Edge 0: \{0, 1\}, Edge 1: \{0, 2\}, Edge 2: \{0, 3\} Edge 3: \{1, 2\}, Edge 4: \{1, 3\}, Edge 5: \{2, 3\} 5. Triangle Lookup Table: A static array tetrahedronTriangles[16][7] mapping the 16 possible vertex sign configurations (4-bit index) to the resulting triangles. Each entry contains up to two triangles (3 edge indices each), terminated by -1. 1. Initialize: Create empty vertex list, index list, and edge cache. 2. Iterate Voxels: Loop through all voxels (x, y, z) in the grid. 3. Sample Vertices: Retrieve scalar values v0 \dots v7 and positions p0 \dots p7 for the 8 corners of the current voxel. 4. Decompose: For each of the 6 tetrahedra in the voxel: a. Get Vertices: Retrieve the 4 vertex indices (i0, i1, i2, i3) from the decomposition table. b. Compute Case Index: Determine the 4-bit configuration mask flagIndex: python flagIndex = 0 if v[i0] < I: flagIndex |= 1 if v[i1] < I: flagIndex |= 2 if v[i2] < I: flagIndex |= 4 if v[i3] < I: flagIndex |= 8 c. Lookup Triangles: Retrieve the triangle definitions from tetrahedronTriangles[flagIndex]. If the first entry is -1, continue to the next tetrahedron. d. Generate Vertices: For each triangle in the lookup result (up to 2): i. Get the 3 edge indices (ea, eb, ec) from the lookup table. ii. For each edge index, determine the two global vertex indices (u, v) using tetrahedronEdgeConnection. iii. Calculate the intersection point on the edge. If the edge has not been cached, compute it and store it in the cache using the key (\min(u,v), \max(u,v)). iv. Interpolation: Compute the intersection point P on the edge between vertices A and B with values fA and fB: t = \frac{I - fA}{fB - fA} P = A + t(B - A) Guard: If |fB - fA| < \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}), return the midpoint (A+B)/2 to avoid division by zero. v. Add the vertex to the mesh if new, or retrieve its index from the cache. e. Add Triangle: Add the 3 vertex indices to the mesh index list. Ensure consistent winding order (e.g., using a global WindingOrder array). Case Index: \text{flagIndex} = \sum{k=0}^{3} \mathbb{I}(vk < I) \cdot 2^k. Edge Intersection Parameter: t = \frac{I - fA}{fB - fA}. Intersection Point: P = A + t(B - A). Isovalue (I): The threshold scalar value. Default 0.0. Decomposition Scheme: 6 tetrahedra per voxel is standard for continuity. 5 tetrahedra is an alternative but requires alternating schemes to maintain continuity. Epsilon (\epsilon): Tolerance for degenerate cases (value == isovalue or equal edge values). Default 10^{-3}, with 10^{-6} used for near-identical vertex values. Ambiguity Resolution: Unlike Marching Cubes, MT has no topological ambiguities because a tetrahedron has only 4 vertices, reducing the case logic to 16 symmetric configurations. Mesh Holes: Without caching edge intersections, floating-point errors can cause gaps where tetrahedra share edges. Caching is mandatory for a manifold mesh. Degenerate Triangles: If a vertex lies exactly on the isovalue, the interpolation parameter t may be 0 or 1, resulting in duplicate vertices. These are filtered out or handled by tracking zero-isovalue points in a map. Winding Order: Incorrect vertex ordering in the decomposition table or lookup table leads to inverted normals. The ordering of the tetrahedrons matters to generate correctly sided output. Performance: MT generates more triangles than Marching Cubes (approx. 2-3x) and requires more memory for the vertex cache. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marchingtetrahedra(grid, dims, isovalue): vertices = [] indices = [] edgecache = {} # Maps (v0idx, v1idx) -> vertexindex # 6 tetrahedra per cube, each with 4 vertex indices (0-7) tetradecomp = [ [0, 7, 3, 2], [0, 7, 2, 6], [0, 4, 6, 7], [0, 6, 1, 2], [0, 6, 1, 4], [5, 6, 1, 4] ] # Edge-vertex mapping for a tetrahedron: 6 edges, each connects 2 vertices (0-3) edgevertices = [ [0, 1], [0, 2], [0, 3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3] ] # Triangle lookup table: 16 cases, each up to 2 triangles (3 edge indices each), -1 terminator trilookup = [...] # Standard 16-entry table, e.g., case 0: [-1], case 1: [0, 3, 2, -1, -1, -1, -1] for z in range(dims[2]): for y in range(dims[1]): for x in range(dims[0]): # Sample 8 voxel corners using linear index baseidx = x + dims[0] (y + dims[1] z) offsets = [0, 1, dims[0], dims[0]+1, dims[0]dims[1], dims[0]dims[1]+1, dims[0]dims[1]+dims[0], dims[0]dims[1]+dims[0]+1] voxelvals = [grid[baseidx + off] for off in offsets] voxelpos = [getgridposition(x, y, z, off) for off in offsets] for tet in tetradecomp: v0, v1, v2, v3 = tet vals = [voxelvals[v0], voxelvals[v1], voxelvals[v2], voxelvals[v3]] pos = [voxelpos[v0], voxelpos[v1], voxelpos[v2], voxelpos[v3]] # Compute case index flag = 0 if vals[0] < isovalue: flag |= 1 if vals[1] < isovalue: flag |= 2 if vals[2] < isovalue: flag |= 4 if vals[3] < isovalue: flag |= 8 # Lookup triangles tridefs = trilookup[flag] if tridefs[0] == -1: continue # Process up to 2 triangles for i in range(0, len(tridefs), 3): if tridefs[i] == -1: break e0, e1, e2 = tridefs[i], tridefs[i+1], tridefs[i+2] # Generate vertices for each edge verts = [] for e in [e0, e1, e2]: u, v = edgevertices[e] edgekey = (min(u, v), max(u, v)) if edgekey in edgecache: verts.append(edgecache[edgekey]) else: # Intersect edge fa, fb = vals[u], vals[v] if abs(fb - fa) < 1e-6: t = 0.5 else: t = (isovalue - fa) / (fb - fa) p = pos[u] + t (pos[v] - pos[u]) newidx = len(vertices) vertices.append(p) edgecache[edgekey] = newidx verts.append(newidx) indices.extend(verts) return vertices, indices A variant that decouples mesh resolution from Gaussian distribution, enabling fine meshing of restricted scene segments. It performs tetrahedralization of vertices, classifies tets as inside/outside based on sampled interior points, and extracts separating faces. It prioritizes smoothness and artifact reduction over raw metric gains, producing topologically clean surfaces for complex scenes like those in MipNeRF 360. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels. Each voxel is processed independently, making it highly parallelizable. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the scalar field. Additional memory is required for the output mesh, which is larger than Marching Cubes. The edge cache adds overhead proportional to the number of unique edges. Performance: Generally slower than Marching Cubes due to the higher number of tetrahedra (6 vs 1) and the cost of edge caching. Benchmarks report MT taking approximately 1.8x to 3.7x longer than Marching Cubes depending on the scene and implementation. Strengths: Topologically correct, no cracks, works on irregular tetrahedral meshes. Limitations: Higher triangle count, more complex implementation due to caching, potential for degenerate geometry if not handled. When to Use: When topological correctness is critical (e.g., medical imaging, simulation) and cracks are unacceptable. When working with unstructured tetrahedral grids. When Not to Use: When performance is the primary constraint and approximate surfaces are acceptable. Marching Tetrahedra was developed as an extension to Marching Cubes to circumvent the Marching Cubes patent (US 4,710,876) and to solve the topological ambiguity problem present in some Marching Cubes configurations. The patent expired in 2005. The method was introduced in 1991 and later applied natively to tetrahedral meshes by Doi and Koide. It is widely used in scientific visualization and medical imaging where mesh quality and topology are paramount. name: Topological Correctness Guarantees
head: Topologically Correct Marching Cubes, Asymptotic Decider, Connectedness Couples
body: Topological Correctness Guarantees is a family of isosurface extraction methods designed to resolve the topological ambiguities inherent in standard Marching Cubes [774-marching-cubes.md]. Standard Marching Cubes uses linear interpolation, which can produce incorrect connectivity (e.g., disconnected sheets instead of a tunnel) when the underlying trilinear interpolant has critical points within a voxel [1368-topologically-correct-marching-cubes.md]. This family ensures the output mesh is homeomorphic to the trilinear interpolant of the input scalar field or a valid 2-manifold for binary data, preventing non-manifold artifacts and self-intersections [1428-topologically-defined-isosurfaces.md]. Unlike standard implementations that rely on arbitrary lookup tables, these methods use geometric tests, vertex insertion, or global connectivity constraints to deterministically resolve ambiguous configurations [790-asymptotic-decider.md][1430-topologically-defined-isosurface-via-connectedness-couples.md]. All methods in this family address the "ambiguous face" and "interior tunnel" cases where the sign pattern of voxel corners does not uniquely determine the surface topology under linear interpolation. 1. Ambiguity Detection: The algorithms identify configurations where the standard 15-case table is insufficient. This typically occurs when a face has alternating signs (a saddle) or when the interior of the cube contains a critical point [790-asymptotic-decider.md][1368-topologically-correct-marching-cubes.md]. 2. Resolution Strategy: Geometric Tests: Methods like the Asymptotic Decider evaluate the bilinear interpolant on ambiguous faces to determine the correct saddle connectivity [790-asymptotic-decider.md]. Vertex Insertion: Methods like Topologically Correct Marching Cubes (TMC) insert additional vertices (e.g., at the cell center) to resolve interior tunnels, ensuring the mesh remains a 2-manifold [1368-topologically-correct-marching-cubes.md]. Connectivity Constraints: For binary data, methods like Topologically Defined Isosurfaces enforce valid foreground/background connectedness couples (e.g., 6-adjacency for background) to guarantee a singularity-free surface [1428-topologically-defined-isosurfaces.md]. Higher-Order Interpolation: Some approaches use Hermite interpolation or full case tables to resolve ambiguities based on gradient information or averaged values [961-marching-cubes-with-hermite-data-and-full-case-table.md]. 3. Manifold Guarantee: The primary goal is to produce a closed, oriented 2-manifold mesh. This requires handling degenerate cases (e.g., Q=0) and ensuring that shared edges between adjacent voxels are triangulated consistently [1368-topologically-correct-marching-cubes.md][1430-topologically-defined-isosurface-via-connectedness-couples.md]. Uses a geometric test on ambiguous faces by comparing the isovalue to the saddle point of the bilinear interpolant. It resolves face ambiguities but does not handle interior tunnels. Choose this for face-level correctness with minimal computational overhead. Extends MC with Hermite interpolation and a full case table to resolve ambiguities using second-order data. Choose this when higher geometric accuracy is needed alongside topological correctness, particularly for ambiguous faces. Guarantees the mesh is homeomorphic to the trilinear interpolant by inserting vertices in ambiguous cells (e.g., tunnels). Choose this for general scalar fields where watertight, manifold meshes are required regardless of interior critical points. Extracts isosurfaces from binary volumes using connectedness couples (e.g., 6-voxel foreground / 18-voxel background). Choose this for binary medical or segmented data where global connectivity constraints ensure validity. Similar to the above but focuses on precomputed lookup tables based on valid connectedness couples. Choose this for efficient binary volume extraction with guaranteed manifold properties. Extends MC33 by classifying vertices and using interior tests to distinguish between separated and joined vertex groups. Choose this when both topological correctness (handling all 33 cases) and high mesh quality (avoiding skinny triangles) are required. A differentiable loss function for neural networks that enforces topological consistency and normal alignment. Choose this for learning-based isosurface extraction where gradient-based optimization is used. The problem of topological ambiguity in Marching Cubes was first identified by Lorensen and Cline (1987), who proposed 15 unambiguous cases, leaving 18 ambiguous cases unresolved [774-marching-cubes.md]. Natarajan (1995) provided a rigorous test for these ambiguities using the trilinear interpolant [790-asymptotic-decider.md]. Subsequent work by Chernyaev (MC33) and others expanded the lookup tables to handle all 33 topological cases [1618-extended-trilinear-triangulation.md]. For binary volumes, combinatorial topology approaches by Coeurjolly et al. established the use of connectedness couples to guarantee manifold surfaces [1428-topologically-defined-isosurfaces.md]. Recent developments integrate these guarantees into differentiable rendering pipelines using consistency losses [4351-topology-normal-consistency-loss.md]. name: Asymptotic Decider
head: Nielson and Hamann decider, Nielson-Hamann Asymptotic Decider, Nielson-Hamann Face Disambiguation
body: The Asymptotic Decider (AD) is a geometric test used in Marching Cubes to resolve topological ambiguities on cube faces where the standard lookup table is insufficient. It determines the correct connectivity of intersection points on "saddle" faces by comparing the isovalue against the saddle point value of the bilinear interpolant. Unlike arbitrary case selection, AD uses vertex scalar values to dictate edge connections on ambiguous faces. The method operates on individual cube faces identified as ambiguous. It does not resolve interior ambiguities (tunnels) within the cube volume; those require extensions like Marching Cubes 33 or Natarajan's test. Input: Scalar values at the four corners of a cube face and an isovalue I. Output: A boolean or integer flag indicating which of the two possible triangulations to use for the ambiguous face. The algorithm requires access to the scalar values at the four vertices of the face. Let the vertices be indexed 0, 1, 2, 3 in counter-clockwise order around the face. V0: Top-Left V1: Top-Right V2: Bottom-Right V3: Bottom-Left Note: Standard Marching Cubes numbering for a cube face (e.g., the front face z=0) typically maps vertices 0, 1, 5, 4. The relative geometric positions (Top-Left, etc.) must be mapped to these indices based on the face orientation. 1. Identify Ambiguous Faces: A face is ambiguous if its four vertices have alternating signs relative to the isovalue I. Specifically, two diagonally opposite vertices are on one side of the isovalue, and the other two are on the opposite side. Condition: (V0 - I)(V2 - I) > 0 AND (V1 - I)(V3 - I) > 0 AND (V0 - I)(V1 - I) < 0. If the face is not ambiguous, use the standard lookup table case. 2. Compute the Decider Value (Q or V{decider}): Calculate the value that determines the saddle point topology. The sources provide equivalent formulations depending on whether the input is normalized to [0,1] or uses raw scalar values. Formulation A (Raw Scalar Values, from): Let T{ij} be the scalar value at corner (i,j) of the face. Q = T{00}T{11} - T{01}T{10} - I(T{00} + T{11} - T{01} - T{10}) Where: T{00} is the value at Top-Left (V0) T{11} is the value at Bottom-Right (V2) T{01} is the value at Top-Right (V1) T{10} is the value at Bottom-Left (V3) I is the isovalue. Formulation B (Simplified Product, from): If the isovalue is 0 (or if values are pre-shifted by subtracting I), the formula simplifies to: Q = V0 V2 - V1 V3 Where Vi are the values relative to the isovalue (i.e., Vi = \text{Scalar}i - I). 3. Determine Connectivity: If Q < 0: The isocontour forms a hyperbola in the first and third quadrants (connecting Top-Left to Bottom-Right). Use the triangulation that connects the vertices with the same sign (the "diagonal" connecting the positive corners). If Q > 0: The isocontour forms a hyperbola in the second and fourth quadrants (connecting Top-Right to Bottom-Left). Use the triangulation that connects the vertices with the same sign (the "diagonal" connecting the negative corners). If Q = 0: The saddle point lies exactly on the isovalue. In practice, this is treated as Q \ge 0 or handled via a small epsilon tolerance to avoid undefined behavior in subsequent gradient calculations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def asymptoticdecider(facevalues, isovalue): """ Resolves face ambiguity for Marching Cubes using the Nielson-Hamann test. Args: facevalues: List of 4 scalar values [V0, V1, V2, V3] corresponding to Top-Left, Top-Right, Bottom-Right, Bottom-Left vertices. isovalue: The threshold scalar value. Returns: int: 0 if connecting V0-V2 (Top-Left to Bottom-Right), 1 if connecting V1-V3 (Top-Right to Bottom-Left). Returns None if face is not ambiguous. """ V0, V1, V2, V3 = facevalues # Check for ambiguity: Alternating signs relative to isovalue s0 = 1 if V0 > isovalue else -1 s1 = 1 if V1 > isovalue else -1 s2 = 1 if V2 > isovalue else -1 s3 = 1 if V3 > isovalue else -1 # Ambiguous if diagonals have same sign and adjacent have different signs if not (s0 == s2 and s1 == s3 and s0 != s1): return None # Compute Q using raw values and isovalue (Formulation A from) Q = (V0 V2) - (V1 V3) - isovalue (V0 + V2 - V1 - V3) # Determine connection # Q < 0 -> Connect V0 and V2 (Top-Left to Bottom-Right) # Q >= 0 -> Connect V1 and V3 (Top-Right to Bottom-Left) # Q=0 is a degenerate saddle; defaulting to Q>0 branch maintains consistency if Q < 0: return 0 # Connect V0-V2 else: return 1 # Connect V1-V3 Isovalue (I): The scalar threshold defining the surface. Face Vertices: The four scalar values defining the face. Degenerate Saddle (Q=0): If the saddle point value equals the isovalue, the topology is undefined locally. Implementers should add a small epsilon (\epsilon) to the comparison or treat Q=0 as a specific case (e.g., default to Q>0) to maintain consistency. Interior Ambiguity: AD only resolves face ambiguities. It does not resolve the "tunnel" ambiguity inside the cube (where the surface passes through the cube center). Using AD alone with the standard 15-case table (or even the 23-case MC23) can still produce non-manifold geometry if interior ambiguities are present. Precision: Floating-point errors in Q calculation can flip the sign incorrectly. Standard practice recommends using double precision for intermediate calculations when inputs span large dynamic ranges. Ambiguous Face Triangulation is a technique to resolve topological ambiguity in cell triangulation when a single face has sign changes along all four edges, resulting in four vertices on that face. It sets itself apart from the parent Asymptotic Decider by using a geometric connectivity rule based on face orientation to determine the triangulation, ensuring that adjacent cells fit together topologically. An extension of Natarajan's tests to all ambiguous cases of Marching Cubes, including interior ambiguities. Proposed by Lopes and Brodlie in 2003. An alternative interpolant for ambiguous faces using the Asymptotic Decider to resolve ambiguity. It produces four triangular sections and a flat diamond in the middle. Time Complexity: O(1) per face. The test involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No additional data structures are required beyond the face vertex values. Performance: Adds negligible computational overhead compared to the table lookup. However, it increases implementation complexity. Strengths: Simple to implement; resolves the most common face-level topological errors; ensures continuity across shared faces between adjacent cubes. Limitations: Does not resolve interior ambiguities (tunnels). Requires scalar values at vertices (not just binary occupancy). When to use: When generating manifolds from scalar fields where face-level continuity is critical and interior ambiguities are either rare or handled by a separate step (e.g., MC33). The Asymptotic Decider was proposed by Nielson and Hamann in 1991. It was introduced to address the ambiguities in the original Marching Cubes algorithm identified by Dürst and others, specifically regarding the behavior of the bilinear interpolant on cube faces. The method was published in "The Asymptotic Decider: Resolving the Ambiguity in Marching Cubes". It was later observed by Natarajan (1994) that similar ambiguities exist in the interior of the cube, leading to further extensions like Marching Cubes 33. name: Ambiguous Face Triangulation for Regular Grid
body: Ambiguous Face Triangulation is a technique to resolve topological ambiguity in cell triangulation when a single face has sign changes along all four edges, resulting in four vertices on that face. It sets itself apart from the parent Asymptotic Decider by using a geometric connectivity rule based on face orientation to determine the triangulation, ensuring that adjacent cells fit together topologically. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A regular grid with a scalar field F. For each cell, the signs of F at the 8 vertices, specifically identifying configurations where exactly one face has sign changes on all four edges (Cases 4 and 6 in the standard 256-case classification). Output: A set of triangles forming the isosurface approximation within the cell and its neighbors. Data Structures: Grid vertices: V{ijk} with scalar values F{ijk}. Intersection points: Calculated via linear interpolation on edges where signs differ. Face configuration: A boolean mask or index identifying the ambiguous face. Steps: 1. Identify Ambiguity: Detect if a cell has a face where F changes sign on all four edges. Let this face be f. The four vertices of the triangulation lie on the edges of f. 2. Pairwise Connection: Connect the four vertices on face f pairwise. The connection segments must be parallel to one of the vectors (1,1,0), (1,0,1), or (0,1,1), depending on the orientation of the face. 3. Neighbor Consistency: Ensure the choice of pairing guarantees that the triangulations of two adjacent cells sharing the face f fit together. The ambiguity is due to the sign configuration on the shared face. 4. Block Analysis: Consider the block of two cubes adjacent to the ambiguous face. The border of the union of these two cubes does not contain ambiguities because the sign changes along the edges of the shared face prevent a parametrization in the direction of those edges. 5. Parametrization: Both cubes are parametrizable in the vertical direction (the direction perpendicular to the ambiguous face's plane). The vertical component of the gradient \nabla F does not disappear, so the union of the two cells is parametrizable in the vertical direction. 6. Joining Possibilities: There are only three possibilities to join two ambiguous cells, determined by the types of the two cells (Type 4 or Type 6). The valid joins are: two Type 4 cells, one Type 4 and one Type 6 cell, and two Type 6 cells. 7. Triangulation Choice: For the ambiguous face, there are two ways to connect the vertices pairwise. Both choices lead to the same isotopic approximation. Choose either way, provided the triangulations for both cells fit together. Formulas: Intersection point on edge between Va and Vb: P = Va + \frac{Fa}{Fa - Fb} (Vb - Va) Gradient condition for vertical parametrizability: \frac{\partial F}{\partial z} \neq 0 \quad \text{(in the vertical direction)} Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Closed Loop on Face: If the surface intersects a grid face in a closed curve lying completely within that face, special handling is required. Both adjacent cubes must be parametrizable in the direction perpendicular to the face. The "bubble" must not leave the cube on the opposite face, as this would require the gradient to change more than \pi/2. The bubble is continuously flattened towards the face by linear interpolation and pushed through to remove the intersection loop. Surface Passing Through Vertices: Handle by considering F to be strictly positive whenever F \ge 0. Multiple Intersections on Edge: If the surface intersects an edge more than once, the gradient must be perpendicular to the edge at some point between intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resolveambiguousface(F, i, j, k, facenormal): """ Resolves triangulation for a cell with an ambiguous face. F: 3D array of scalar values. i, j, k: integer indices of the cell's minimum corner. facenormal: tuple (nx, ny, nz) indicating the axis perpendicular to the ambiguous face. Returns: list of two triangles, each a tuple of 3 3D coordinates. """ # Cell vertex coordinates (unit grid spacing assumed) V = [ (i, j, k), (i+1, j, k), (i, j+1, k), (i+1, j+1, k), (i, j, k+1), (i+1, j, k+1), (i, j+1, k+1), (i+1, j+1, k+1) ] Vval = [F[i, j, k], F[i+1, j, k], F[i, j+1, k], F[i+1, j+1, k], F[i, j, k+1], F[i+1, j, k+1], F[i, j+1, k+1], F[i+1, j+1, k+1]] # Identify the 4 edges of the ambiguous face based on orientation if facenormal == (0, 0, 1): # XY face at z=k edgeindices = [(0, 1), (1, 3), (3, 2), (2, 0)] elif facenormal == (0, 0, -1): # XY face at z=k+1 edgeindices = [(4, 5), (5, 7), (7, 6), (6, 4)] elif facenormal == (0, 1, 0): # XZ face at y=k edgeindices = [(0, 1), (1, 5), (5, 4), (4, 0)] elif facenormal == (0, -1, 0): # XZ face at y=k+1 edgeindices = [(2, 3), (3, 7), (7, 6), (6, 2)] elif facenormal == (1, 0, 0): # YZ face at x=i edgeindices = [(0, 2), (2, 6), (6, 4), (4, 0)] else: # facenormal == (-1, 0, 0) YZ face at x=i+1 edgeindices = [(1, 3), (3, 7), (7, 5), (5, 1)] # Compute intersection points on the 4 edges intersections = [] for v1idx, v2idx in edgeindices: p1, p2 = V[v1idx], V[v2idx] f1, f2 = Vval[v1idx], Vval[v2idx] t = f1 / (f1 - f2) p = (p1[0] + t (p2[0] - p1[0]), p1[1] + t (p2[1] - p1[1]), p1[2] + t (p2[2] - p1[2])) intersections.append(p) # Pairwise connection: connect opposite vertices on the face # The diagonal connects intersections[0] with [2], and [1] with [3] # This ensures the segment is parallel to (1,1,0), (1,0,1), or (0,1,1) return [(intersections[0], intersections[1], intersections[2]), (intersections[0], intersections[2], intersections[3])] A variant handling the case where the surface intersects a grid face in a closed curve lying completely within that face. It requires verifying that both adjacent cubes are parametrizable in the direction perpendicular to the face and that the "bubble" does not leave the cube on the opposite face (which would imply a gradient change of more than \pi/2). The bubble is continuously flattened towards the face by linear interpolation and pushed through to remove the intersection loop. Time Complexity: Constant time per ambiguous face, as it involves a fixed number of geometric checks and interpolations. Memory Complexity: Constant, requiring only local vertex and edge data. Strengths: Guarantees topological correctness (isotopy) by ensuring adjacent cells fit together. Handles the specific ambiguity of 4 vertices on one face. Limitations: Only applies to regular grids. Requires the gradient to not vanish in the vertical direction for the block of two cells. Does not handle multiple intersections on a single edge without additional constraints. When to use: When using Marching Cubes on regular grids and encountering Cases 4 and 6 ambiguities. When not to use: When the grid is not regular, or when the gradient vanishes in the direction perpendicular to the ambiguous face. Originated in the context of isotopic approximation of implicit curves and surfaces on regular grids. The method addresses the topological ambiguities in Cases 4 and 6 of the Marching Cubes algorithm, where a single face has sign changes on all four edges. It was developed to ensure that the resulting triangulation is isotopic to the true isosurface, avoiding topological errors like tunnels or disconnected components. The approach relies on the geometric properties of the gradient and the structure of the regular grid. name: Marching Cubes with Hermite Data and Full Case Table
head: Hermite Marching Cubes, Full Case Table Marching Cubes, Quadratic Marching Cubes
body: This method extends the standard Marching Cubes algorithm by incorporating Hermite interpolation for zero-crossing estimation and a full case table to resolve topological ambiguities inherent in the original Lorensen and Cline implementation. It solves the problem of incorrect surface topology and inaccurate vertex placement in regions where linear interpolation fails to capture the true geometry of the implicit surface, specifically addressing ambiguous face configurations and saddle points. Unlike the Asymptotic Decider which uses local geometric tests on bilinear interpolants, this method relies on a pre-computed full case table and second-order Hermite interpolation derived from neighboring value differences. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A regularly sampled voxel grid of scalar values. Values are stored in binary format as either unsigned chars (1 byte) or floats (4 bytes), linearized in row-major order (x + y \cdot ResX + z \cdot ResX \cdot ResY). Parameters: --res <x-resolution y-resolution z-resolution>: Grid dimensions. If unspecified, assumes a cube grid and reads the first 4 bytes of the file as the resolution. --dim <x-scale y-scale z-scale>: Voxel physical scale. Default is (1, 1, 1). --iso <isovalue>: Extraction threshold. Default is 0. --sIters <smoothing iterations>: Number of 1-ring smoothing iterations applied to the voxel grid before extraction. Default is 0. --full: Enables the full case table. --quadratic: Enables Hermite interpolation. --polygon: Outputs raw iso-polygons instead of triangulated mesh. --nonManifold: Disables the insertion of a barycenter vertex to prevent non-manifold edges, potentially resulting in non-manifold output. Output: A PLY format mesh file containing the extracted isosurface. Data Structures: The implementation operates on a 3D grid of scalar values. No additional complex data structures are described beyond the standard voxel grid and the output triangle/polygon list. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Optional): If --sIters is greater than 0, apply 1-ring smoothing to the input voxel grid values. 2. Grid Iteration: Iterate through every voxel in the grid. For each voxel, identify the 8 corner vertices and their scalar values vi. 3. Hermite Data Generation (Conditional): If the --quadratic flag is specified, generate Hermite data by considering the difference between neighboring values. This data is used to define a second-order interpolant. 4. Zero-Crossing Interpolation: If --quadratic is set, use the second-order Hermite interpolant to determine the positions of zero-crossings on the voxel edges. Otherwise, use standard linear interpolation. 5. Case Table Lookup: Determine the sign pattern of the 8 voxel corners relative to the --iso value. If the --full flag is specified, use the Full Case Table to resolve the configuration. The Full Case Table specifically resolves the ambiguous case where a face has a zero-crossing and the values on the antipodal corners of that face are the same. To resolve this ambiguity, the algorithm uses the average value of the face corners. If --full is not specified, the standard 15-case table is used. 6. Polygon Generation: Generate the raw iso-polygons based on the resolved case. 7. Triangulation (Conditional): If the --polygon flag is NOT specified, triangulate the raw iso-polygons using a minimal-area-triangulation strategy. Manifold Guarantee: During triangulation, check if two polygons share two vertices that are not on a polygon edge. If this condition arises, the minimal-area-triangulation might introduce the same edge for both polygons, creating non-manifold edges. By default, if a non-manifold triangulation can arise, introduce an additional vertex at the plane's barycenter to ensure the output triangle mesh is manifold. If the --nonManifold flag is enabled, skip the barycenter insertion, which may result in non-manifold edges. 8. Output: Write the resulting mesh to the specified PLY file. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurface(voxelgrid, resolution, dim, isovalue, usefulltable, usehermite, smoothingiters, outputfile): # Apply smoothing if requested if smoothingiters > 0: voxelgrid = apply1ringsmoothing(voxelgrid, smoothingiters) triangles = [] # Iterate over all voxels for z in range(resolution.z - 1): for y in range(resolution.y - 1): for x in range(resolution.x - 1): # Get 8 corner values corners = getvoxelcorners(voxelgrid, x, y, z, resolution) cornerpositions = getvoxelcornerpositions(x, y, z, resolution, dim) # Determine sign pattern signs = [1 if v > isovalue else -1 for v in corners] caseindex = computecaseindex(signs) # Determine zero-crossing positions edgeintersections = [] for edge in voxeledges: v1, v2 = corners[edge.v1], corners[edge.v2] p1, p2 = cornerpositions[edge.v1], cornerpositions[edge.v2] if usehermite: # Generate Hermite data from neighboring differences # Use second-order interpolant t = interpolatehermite(v1, v2, edge, voxelgrid, x, y, z, resolution) else: # Standard linear interpolation t = (isovalue - v1) / (v2 - v1) pos = lerp(p1, p2, t) edgeintersections.append(pos) # Resolve case if usefulltable: # Check for ambiguous face: zero-crossing on face, antipodal corners same value # Use average value of face corners to resolve polygons = resolvefullcase(caseindex, edgeintersections, corners) else: polygons = resolvestandardcase(caseindex, edgeintersections) # Triangulate if not outputrawpolygons: # Minimal area triangulation for poly in polygons: tri = minimalareatriangulate(poly) # Check for non-manifold edges if not nonmanifoldmode: if potentialnonmanifold(tri, triangles): # Insert barycenter vertex barycenter = computebarycenter(poly) tri = insertbarycenter(tri, barycenter) triangles.extend(tri) else: triangles.extend(polygons) # Store as polygons if flag set writeply(outputfile, triangles) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-manifold edges: Two polygons may share two vertices that are not on a polygon edge. Minimal area triangulation might introduce the same edge for both polygons, creating non-manifold edges. The default behavior introduces a barycenter vertex to avoid this, but the --nonManifold flag disables this, potentially resulting in non-manifold output. Ambiguous Faces: The standard 15-case table fails when a face has a zero-crossing and the values on the antipodal corners are the same. The --full flag is required to resolve this using the average value of the face corners. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The algorithm iterates over each voxel once, performing constant-time lookups and interpolations per voxel. Hermite interpolation adds computational overhead compared to linear interpolation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the voxel grid and the output mesh. Strengths: Resolves topological ambiguities present in the original Lorensen and Cline implementation. Provides more accurate surface positions via second-order Hermite interpolation. Guarantees manifold output by default through barycenter insertion. Limitations: Hermite interpolation requires access to neighboring values, potentially increasing memory access patterns. The full case table increases the complexity of the lookup logic. Non-manifold mode can produce invalid meshes. When to use: When high topological correctness is required, especially in regions with saddle points or ambiguous faces, and when higher accuracy in vertex placement is desired via quadratic interpolation. When not to use: When performance is critical and the standard linear interpolation is sufficient. When memory bandwidth is a bottleneck due to Hermite data requirements. This method is an implementation of Marching-Cubes isosurface extraction that supports Hermite Data and a full case table to resolve the ambiguous cases present in the original Lorensen and Cline implementation. It was presented at 3DV 2015. The code is available from the Department of Computer Science at Johns Hopkins University. Implementations of Hermite interpolation on adapted octrees can also be found in the code for Poisson Surface Reconstruction, Floating Scale Surface Reconstruction, and Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees. name: Topologically Correct Marching Cubes
body: Topologically Correct Marching Cubes (TMC) is an extension to the standard Marching Cubes algorithm that guarantees the output mesh is homeomorphic to the trilinear interpolant of the input scalar field within each cell. It solves the problem of topological ambiguity in standard Marching Cubes, where specific vertex sign patterns (such as those forming a tunnel within a single cell) are incorrectly resolved into disconnected sheets. Unlike standard Marching Cubes, which may produce non-manifold artifacts or incorrect connectivity in these ambiguous cases, TMC inserts additional vertices to resolve complex features, ensuring a 2-manifold and watertight mesh provided the isosurface does not intersect the domain boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid (domain) with scalar values at vertices, and an isovalue. Output: A polygon mesh (list of points and polygons) representing the isosurface. Data Structures: The algorithm uses the standard Marching Cubes lookup table for the 15 topological cases, but augments the vertex generation phase. When an ambiguous configuration is detected, the algorithm allocates additional vertex structures within the cell to represent the internal topology. Steps: 1. Grid Traversal: Iterate over every voxel in the input domain. 2. Case Identification: Determine the standard Marching Cubes case index based on the signs of the scalar values at the 8 vertices of the voxel relative to the isovalue. 3. Ambiguity Detection: Identify if the current case corresponds to an ambiguous configuration where the standard linear interpolation fails to capture the true topology of the trilinear interpolant (e.g., the "tunnel" case). 4. Vertex Insertion: If an ambiguous case is detected: Insert additional vertices within the cell. Connect these new vertices to the edge intersections to form a triangulation that is homeomorphic to the trilinear surface. 5. Mesh Assembly: Collect all generated polygons and points to form the final mesh. Parameters: usetopologicallycorrectmarchingcubes: A boolean flag. Set to true to enable TMC; false for standard Marching Cubes. isovalue: The scalar threshold for surface extraction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Intersection: The guarantee of the mesh being 2-manifold and watertight holds only if the isosurface does not intersect the domain boundaries. If the surface touches or crosses the boundary, the topological guarantees may fail. Sharp Features: TMC does not guarantee the recovery of sharp features present in the input field; it focuses on topological correctness of the smooth trilinear interpolant. Complexity: The insertion of vertices increases the vertex count per cell compared to standard MC, potentially impacting memory and rendering performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def topologicallycorrectmarchingcubes(domain, isovalue): """ Extracts an isosurface using Topologically Correct Marching Cubes. Args: domain: A structure containing the voxel grid values and geometry. isovalue: The scalar threshold. Returns: points: List of 3D coordinates. polygons: List of polygon indices. """ points = [] polygons = [] vertexcache = {} # Standard MC ambiguous case indices (saddle/tunnel configurations) AMBIGUOUSCASES = {23, 26, 29, 30, 34, 37, 40, 43, 46, 49, 52, 55, 58, 61, 64, 67, 70, 73, 76, 79, 82, 85, 88, 91, 94, 97, 100, 103, 106, 109, 112, 115, 118, 121, 124, 127} for cell in domain.cells: vertexvalues = [domain.value(v) for v in cell.vertices] # 1. Determine case index caseindex = 0 for i, val in enumerate(vertexvalues): if val < isovalue: caseindex |= (1 << i) # 2. Compute edge intersections edgeintersections = computeedgeintersections(cell, vertexvalues, isovalue) # 3. Check for ambiguity isambiguous = caseindex in AMBIGUOUSCASES if isambiguous: # 4. Resolve ambiguity by inserting vertices centervertex = computecentervertex(cell, vertexvalues, isovalue) points.append(centervertex) centeridx = len(points) - 1 # Create topology-correct triangulation using the center vertex triangles = resolveambiguoustriangulation(caseindex, edgeintersections, centeridx) else: # 5. Standard Marching Cubes processing triangles = standardmarchingcubestriangulation(caseindex, edgeintersections) for tri in triangles: polygons.append(tri) return points, polygons def computeedgeintersections(cell, vertexvalues, isovalue): """ Computes the intersection points of the isosurface with the cell edges using linear interpolation. """ intersections = {} edges = [(0,1), (1,3), (3,2), (2,0), (4,5), (5,7), (7,6), (6,4), (0,4), (1,5), (3,7), (2,6)] for i, (v1idx, v2idx) in enumerate(edges): v1, v2 = cell.vertices[v1idx], cell.vertices[v2idx] val1, val2 = vertexvalues[v1idx], vertexvalues[v2idx] if (val1 - isovalue) (val2 - isovalue) < 0: t = (isovalue - val1) / (val2 - val1) point = lerp(v1, v2, t) intersections[i] = point return intersections def computecentervertex(cell, vertexvalues, isovalue): """ Computes a new vertex position within the cell to resolve topology. Uses the geometric center as a topological anchor. """ center = lerp(cell.vertices[0], cell.vertices[7], 0.5) return center def standardmarchingcubestriangulation(caseindex, edgeintersections): """ Generates triangles for a standard (non-ambiguous) case using the lookup table. """ # Compact representation of the 15 standard MC cases mapping edge indices to triangles cases = { 0: [], 255: [], 1: [(0,1,2)], 2: [(1,2,3)], 4: [(2,3,0)], 8: [(3,0,1)], 16: [(4,5,6)], 32: [(5,6,7)], 64: [(6,7,4)], 128: [(7,4,5)], 3: [(0,1,5), (0,5,4)], 5: [(0,1,3), (0,3,2)], 6: [(1,2,3), (1,3,0)], 9: [(0,1,5), (0,5,4)], 10: [(1,2,5), (1,5,4)], 12: [(2,3,5), (2,5,4)], 17: [(0,1,6), (0,6,4)], 20: [(1,2,6), (1,6,5)], 24: [(2,3,6), (2,6,7)], 34: [(0,1,7), (0,7,4)], 40: [(1,2,7), (1,7,5)], 48: [(2,3,7), (2,7,6)], 51: [(0,1,7), (0,7,3), (0,3,2)], 57: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 69: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,4)], 78: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 87: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 93: [(0,1,7), (0,7,3), (0,3,2)], 102: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 111: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 114: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 120: [(0,1,7), (0,7,3), (0,3,2)], 123: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 126: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 135: [(0,1,7), (0,7,3), (0,3,2)], 141: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 153: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,4)], 162: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 171: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 177: [(0,1,7), (0,7,3), (0,3,2)], 186: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 195: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 198: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 204: [(0,1,7), (0,7,3), (0,3,2)], 207: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 210: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 219: [(0,1,7), (0,7,3), (0,3,2)], 225: [(0,1,7), (0,7,5), (0,5,4)], 237: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,4)], 246: [(0,1,7), (0,7,6), (0,6,5)], 252: [(0,1,7), (0,7,3), (0,3,2)] } triindices = cases.get(caseindex, []) return [[edgeintersections[e] for e in tri] for tri in triindices] def resolveambiguoustriangulation(caseindex, edgeintersections, centeridx): """ Generates triangles for an ambiguous case using the inserted center vertex. Connects the center vertex to all edge intersections to form a fan topology. """ edgepoints = list(edgeintersections.values()) triangles = [] for i in range(len(edgepoints)): p1 = edgepoints[i] p2 = edgepoints[(i + 1) % len(edgepoints)] triangles.append([p1, p2, centeridx]) return triangles Improves aspect ratio of MC33 triangulations by modifying scalar field values near intersections while preventing topological errors. It correctly represents the topology of the trilinear interpolant even when \lambda=0, unlike Raman and Wenger. Time Complexity: Higher than standard Marching Cubes due to the overhead of ambiguity detection and vertex insertion calculations. The complexity remains linear with respect to the number of voxels, but the constant factor is larger. Memory Complexity: Increases vertex count per cell for ambiguous cases, leading to higher memory usage for the output mesh. Performance: Accurately represents small complex features (e.g., tunnels) that standard MC misses. However, it does not guarantee recovery of sharp features. Strengths: Guarantees a 2-manifold, watertight mesh homeomorphic to the trilinear interpolant, provided boundary conditions are met. Limitations: Fails to guarantee manifoldness if the isosurface intersects domain boundaries. Does not preserve sharp features. When to use: When topological correctness is critical (e.g., medical imaging, simulation) and the surface is expected to be smooth and contained within the domain. When not to use: When sharp feature preservation is required, or when the surface intersects the domain boundaries. Topologically Correct Marching Cubes was introduced by Roberto Grosso in the paper "Construction of topologically correct and manifold isosurfaces," published in Computer Graphics Forum, volume 35, pages 187–196, by Wiley Online Library in 2016. It is implemented in the CGAL "3D Isosurfacing" package, which became available in CGAL 6.1 (released fall 2025).
