name: Topology-aware mesh quality improvement for Marching Cubes 33
head: Labelle and Shewchuk integration with Extended MC33, Topology-preserving skinny triangle removal
body: This method improves the aspect ratio of triangulations generated by Marching Cubes 33 by modifying scalar field values near isosurface intersections, while preventing topological errors using a verification step. It combines the topological guarantees of Extended Marching Cubes 33 with the skinny triangle removal strategy of Labelle and Shewchuk. Unlike Raman and Wenger, this method correctly represents the topology of the trilinear interpolant even when \lambda=0, whereas Raman and Wenger cannot represent it correctly even at \lambda=0. Inputs: A scalar field grid V. An isovalue \alpha. A parameter \lambda \in [0, 0.5] determining the threshold for collapsing intersection points. Outputs: A manifold triangle mesh homeomorphic to the trilinear interpolant of the input scalar field. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D array of scalar values. Cube Status: A boolean mask for each cube indicating if it is "blocked" (preventing mesh improvement). Collapsed Vertices: A set of grid vertex coordinates identified for scalar field modification. Steps: 1. Grid Preprocessing: Eliminate ambiguous configurations that cause non-manifold edges in the Chernyaev lookup table by splitting faces at critical points where grid vertex scalar values equal the isovalue. The source proposes splitting all faces in the grid slice containing the problematic configuration to ensure robust handling. 2. Scalar Field Modification: Detect all intersected edges. If an intersection point is at distance d < \lambda \cdot L from a grid vertex (where L is the edge length), collapse the intersection point to the nearest grid vertex by modifying the scalar field value at that vertex. This modifies the grid V to V'. 3. Topology Verification: To prevent undesired topological changes caused by the scalar field modification, track isosurface topology changes in the interior of each cube. If a configuration is detected that could modify the global isosurface topology, mark the cube and its immediate neighbors as "blocked". 4. Mesh Extraction: Run the Marching Cubes 33 algorithm with the extended triangulation on the modified grid V'. Mesh improvements (triangle collapsing) are performed only in the cubes that are not in the neighborhood of the blocked cubes. 5. Geometry Preservation: Move each isosurface vertex located on a grid vertex (due to collapsing) to the location of the closest isosurface vertex in the original grid to preserve the original geometry. Quality Measure: Triangle quality is measured using the radii ratio q(t): q(t) = \frac{r{in}}{r{out}} where r{in} is the incircle radius and r{out} is the circumcircle radius of triangle t. The value q(t) \in [0, 0.5], where 0 is degenerate and 0.5 is equilateral. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def topologyawaremc33(grid, isovalue, lambdaparam): """ grid: 3D list of scalar values isovalue: float lambdaparam: float in [0, 0.5] """ Nx, Ny, Nz = len(grid), len(grid[0]), len(grid[0][0]) originalgrid = [row[:] for row in grid] modifiedgrid = [row[:] for row in grid] blocked = [[[False for in range(Nx-1)] for in range(Ny-1)] for in range(Nz-1)] verticestocollapse = set() # Step 1: Preprocessing # Split faces at critical points where vertex values equal isovalue # to resolve Chernyaev lookup table ambiguities. # Step 2: Scalar Field Modification for z in range(Nz - 1): for y in range(Ny - 1): for x in range(Nx - 1): # 12 edges of a cube edges = [ ((x, y, z), (x+1, y, z)), ((x, y, z), (x, y+1, z)), ((x, y, z), (x, y, z+1)), ((x+1, y, z), (x+1, y+1, z)), ((x+1, y, z), (x+1, y, z+1)), ((x, y+1, z), (x+1, y+1, z)), ((x, y+1, z), (x, y+1, z+1)), ((x, y, z+1), (x+1, y, z+1)), ((x, y, z+1), (x, y+1, z+1)), ((x+1, y, z+1), (x+1, y+1, z+1)), ((x+1, y, z+1), (x+1, y, z)), ((x, y+1, z+1), (x+1, y+1, z+1)) ] for v0, v1 in edges: val0, val1 = grid[v0[0]][v0[1]][v0[2]], grid[v1[0]][v1[1]][v1[2]] if (val0 - isovalue) (val1 - isovalue) <= 0: if val0 == val1: continue t = (isovalue - val0) / (val1 - val0) # Assume unit grid spacing L=1. Distance to v0 is t, to v1 is 1-t. if t < lambdaparam: verticestocollapse.add(v0) if (1.0 - t) < lambdaparam: verticestocollapse.add(v1) for v in verticestocollapse: modifiedgrid[v[0]][v[1]][v[2]] = isovalue # Step 3: Topology Verification for z in range(Nz - 1): for y in range(Ny - 1): for x in range(Nx - 1): if topologydiffers(originalgrid, modifiedgrid, (x, y, z), isovalue): blocked[z][y][x] = True for dz in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dx in range(-1, 2): nz, ny, nx = z+dz, y+dy, x+dx if 0 <= nz < Nz-1 and 0 <= ny < Ny-1 and 0 <= nx < Nx-1: blocked[nz][ny][nx] = True # Step 4 & 5: Mesh Extraction & Geometry Preservation mesh = [] for z in range(Nz - 1): for y in range(Ny - 1): for x in range(Nx - 1): usegrid = originalgrid if blocked[z][y][x] else modifiedgrid tri = mc33extendedtriangulation(usegrid, (x, y, z), isovalue) for v in tri.vertices: if v in verticestocollapse: v.pos = findclosestisosurfacevertex(originalgrid, v.gridpos, isovalue) mesh.extend(tri) return mesh def mc33extendedtriangulation(grid, cubeidx, isovalue): x, y, z = cubeidx signs = [ grid[x][y][z] > isovalue, grid[x+1][y][z] > isovalue, grid[x+1][y+1][z] > isovalue, grid[x][y+1][z] > isovalue, grid[x][y][z+1] > isovalue, grid[x+1][y][z+1] > isovalue, grid[x+1][y+1][z+1] > isovalue, grid[x][y+1][z+1] > isovalue ] case = sum(s << i for i, s in enumerate(signs)) # Standard MC33 lookup table maps case to triangle indices. # Computes edge intersections and assembles triangles per the extended table. return [] def topologydiffers(grida, gridb, cubeidx, isovalue): # Compares the connectivity of intersection points on the cube faces # between the original and modified grids. Returns True if topology changes. return False def findclosestisosurfacevertex(originalgrid, gridpos, isovalue): # Searches original grid edges for the intersection point closest to gridpos. # Returns the 3D coordinates of that intersection. return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Performance: In the Bonsai dataset with \lambda=0.2 and isovalue 39.5, only 0.63% of cubes intersected by the isosurface were blocked. For a randomly generated scalar field on a 6x6x6 grid, 6.73% of cubes were blocked for \lambda=0.1, and 31.1% were blocked for \lambda=0.2. Strengths: Correctly represents the topology of the trilinear interpolant even when \lambda=0. Improves aspect ratio of triangles. Limitations: The verification step can block a significant portion of cubes in random or highly complex fields (up to 31.1% in tested random fields). This method was proposed by the author of as an extension to Marching Cubes 33. It integrates the Labelle and Shewchuk algorithm with the Extended MC33 triangulation. The work addresses issues with the Chernyaev lookup table and non-manifold triangulations. An extended triangulation to the Marching Cubes 33 algorithm, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13173-019-0086-6, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Topologically Defined Isosurfaces
head: Digital Geometry Connectedness Marching Cubes
body: Topologically Defined Isosurfaces is a method for extracting a closed, oriented 2-manifold from a binary volumetric image that guarantees topological correctness by enforcing digital geometry connectedness constraints. Unlike standard Marching Cubes, which may produce self-intersections or incorrect topology in ambiguous configurations, this method modifies the local configuration table based on valid foreground/background connectedness couples (e.g., 6-voxel foreground / 18-voxel background) to ensure the resulting surface separates the foreground from the background without singularities. It builds on Topological Correctness Guarantees by providing a formal proof of validity for the generated surface using combinatorial manifold theory. Inputs: A binary volumetric image I (voxels are 0 or 1) and a valid connectedness couple (n, \lambda), where n is the connectivity for 1-voxels (foreground) and \lambda is the connectivity for 0-voxels (background). Outputs: A closed, oriented 2-manifold mesh representing the isosurface. Data Structures: Binary Picture I: A 3D grid of voxels. The source assumes the border of the support contains only 0-voxels or only 1-voxels. 8-cube: A set of 8 voxels v0 \dots v7 forming a unit cube in the grid, ordered by binary coding of the index. 4-face: An inner face of an 8-cube composed of 4 voxels. Each 4-face is shared by exactly two adjacent 8-cubes. Link: A pair of 6-connected voxels. Local Graph G{gs}: A directed graph constructed for each 8-cube, consisting of oriented edges and vertices lying on the 4-faces. Complete Graph G(I): The union of all local graphs from all 8-cubes in I. Parameters: Connectedness Couple (n, \lambda): Must be one of the valid couples: (6, 18), (6, 26), (18, 6), or (26, 6). n \in \{6, 18, 26\} for foreground (1-voxels). \lambda \in \{6, 18, 26\} for background (0-voxels). Invalid Couples: Couples such as (6,6), (18,18), (18,26), (26,18), (26,26) are invalid because they produce locally different surfaces in the inverse picture, violating the consistency property. Algorithm Steps: 1. Decomposition: Decompose the binary picture I into all possible 8-cubes. 2. Face Orientation: For each 8-cube, identify its six inner 4-faces. Orient each inner 4-face such that they are consistently ordered (e.g., clockwise when viewed from the outside of the 8-cube). 3. Link Identification: For each ordered 4-face, identify its four links (pairs of adjacent voxels on the face). Determine the value of each link based on the voxel values (0 or 1). 4. Local Graph Construction (4-face rules): Apply the following rules to each link on an ordered 4-face to generate vertices and oriented edges: If link value is (0,0) or (1,1): No vertex is created. If link value is (0,1): Create one vertex between the two voxels. Add an incoming oriented edge to this vertex that stays on the 4-face. If link value is (1,0): Create one vertex between the two voxels. Add an outgoing oriented edge from this vertex that stays on the 4-face. Note: Cases 6 and 9 of the 4-configuration (ambiguous faces) are handled implicitly by the global consistency of the valid connectedness couple. The source states that for valid couples, the generated surface follows the required properties, and arbitrary choices for invalid couples lead to inconsistencies. 5. Handle Strict 26-Adjacency: Check if the 8-cube contains two strictly 26-adjacent 1-voxels (if n=26) or two strictly 26-adjacent 0-voxels (if \lambda=26). If such a configuration exists, the local graph is transformed: the two disconnected loops generated on the 4-faces are triangulated (subdivided) to prevent the surface from intersecting the adjacency 3-map of the strictly adjacent voxels. 6. Assemble Local Graph: Gather all oriented edges generated on the six oriented inner 4-faces of the 8-cube to form the local graph G{gs} for that 8-cube. According to Theorem 3, for a valid couple, this graph is a set of oriented loops of length \ge 3, disconnected from each other. 7. Assemble Complete Graph: Extend the set of all local graphs from all 8-cubes to form the complete graph G(I). Each edge in the complete graph belongs to exactly two loops with different orientations. 8. Final Mesh Generation: Derive the final isosurface from the complete graph. If loops have length > 3, subdivide (triangulate) them to form a combinatorial manifold. The embedding of this redefined local graph in \mathbb{R}^3 does not intersect the adjacency 3-map of strictly 26-adjacent voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def topologicallydefinedisosurfaces(binaryimage, foregroundconn, backgroundconn): """ Extracts a topologically correct isosurface from a binary volume. Args: binaryimage: 3D numpy array of 0s and 1s. foregroundconn: Connectivity for 1-voxels (6, 18, or 26). backgroundconn: Connectivity for 0-voxels (6, 18, or 26). Returns: A list of triangles representing the closed 2-manifold. """ # Validate connectedness couple validcouples = [(6, 18), (6, 26), (18, 6), (26, 6)] if (foregroundconn, backgroundconn) not in validcouples: raise ValueError(f"Invalid connectedness couple {(foregroundconn, backgroundconn)}. Must be one of {validcouples}") # Initialize global edge-to-loop mapping # Key: (vertexid, vertexid), Value: list of loopids globaledges = {} # Key: loopid, Value: list of (vertexid, vertexid) edges globalloops = {} loopcounter = 0 # Get dimensions dims = binaryimage.shape # Iterate over all 8-cubes # An 8-cube is defined by its minimum corner (x, y, z) for x in range(dims[0] - 1): for y in range(dims[1] - 1): for z in range(dims[2] - 1): # Extract the 8 voxels of the 8-cube # Order: binary coding of index i = x + 2y + 4z? # Standard Marching Cubes ordering: # v0=(0,0,0), v1=(1,0,0), v2=(1,1,0), v3=(0,1,0), # v4=(0,0,1), v5=(1,0,1), v6=(1,1,1), v7=(0,1,1) voxels = [ binaryimage[x, y, z], binaryimage[x+1, y, z], binaryimage[x+1, y+1, z], binaryimage[x, y+1, z], binaryimage[x, y, z+1], binaryimage[x+1, y, z+1], binaryimage[x+1, y+1, z+1], binaryimage[x, y+1, z+1] ] # Identify the 6 inner 4-faces # Face 0: z=0 (v0, v1, v2, v3) # Face 1: z=1 (v4, v5, v6, v7) # Face 2: y=0 (v0, v1, v5, v4) # Face 3: y=1 (v3, v2, v6, v7) # Face 4: x=0 (v0, v3, v7, v4) # Face 5: x=1 (v1, v2, v6, v5) faces = [ [voxels[0], voxels[1], voxels[2], voxels[3]], # z=0 [voxels[4], voxels[5], voxels[6], voxels[7]], # z=1 [voxels[0], voxels[1], voxels[5], voxels[4]], # y=0 [voxels[3], voxels[2], voxels[6], voxels[7]], # y=1 [voxels[0], voxels[3], voxels[7], voxels[4]], # x=0 [voxels[1], voxels[2], voxels[6], voxels[5]] # x=1 ] # Process each 4-face for face in faces: # Identify 4 links (edges of the square face) # Links are pairs of adjacent voxels in the face # Order: clockwise? The source says "ordered 4-faces are coded with Hamming coding" # and links are in clockwise direction. # Let's assume standard clockwise order for the face vertices: v0, v1, v2, v3 links = [ (face[0], face[1]), (face[1], face[2]), (face[2], face[3]), (face[3], face[0]) ] for v1, v2 in links: val1 = v1 val2 = v2 # Create a unique ID for the link (edge in the voxel grid) # To ensure global consistency, we need a canonical representation of the link # The link is between two 6-connected voxels. # We can use the coordinates of the two voxels. # However, the pseudocode needs to map voxel values to geometric positions. # For simplicity, we assume a helper function getlinkid(v1pos, v2pos) # which returns a unique identifier for the edge between two voxel centers. linkid = getlinkid(v1, v2) # Implementation detail: map voxel indices to edge ID if val1 == val2: # (0,0) or (1,1): No vertex created continue elif val1 == 0 and val2 == 1: # (0,1): Incoming edge # Create vertex at midpoint vertexid = getvertexid(v1, v2) # Add edge to local graph # The edge is directed towards the vertex # We need to track loops. # Since we are building a global graph, we add this directed edge. adddirectededge(globaledges, globalloops, loopcounter, linkid, vertexid, direction='incoming') elif val1 == 1 and val2 == 0: # (1,0): Outgoing edge vertexid = getvertexid(v1, v2) adddirectededge(globaledges, globalloops, loopcounter, linkid, vertexid, direction='outgoing') # Handle strict 26-adjacency # Check if there are two strictly 26-adjacent 1-voxels (if foregroundconn == 26) # or two strictly 26-adjacent 0-voxels (if backgroundconn == 26) # Strict 26-adjacency means sharing a corner. # This requires checking all pairs of voxels in the 8-cube. # If found, triangulate the disconnected loops in the local graph. if isstrict26adjacent(voxels, foregroundconn, backgroundconn): triangulatelocalloops(globalloops, loopcounter) loopcounter += 1 # Or manage loop IDs differently # Final Mesh Generation # The complete graph G(I) is an oriented 2D combinatorial manifold. # Each edge belongs to exactly two loops with different orientations. # Subdivide loops of length > 3. triangles = [] for loopid, loopedges in globalloops.items(): if len(loopedges) > 3: # Subdivide the loop into triangles # A loop of length N can be triangulated by fan triangulation from the first vertex verticesinloop = getverticesfromedges(loopedges) triangles.extend(triangulateloop(verticesinloop)) else: # Length 3 is already a triangle verticesinloop = getverticesfromedges(loopedges) triangles.append(verticesinloop) return triangles def getlinkid(v1, v2): # Returns a unique ID for the edge between two voxel centers # This ensures that the same physical edge in the grid is identified globally # regardless of which 8-cube it is processed in. # The source implies that each link is an element of two 4-faces and is covered twice in both directions. # So we need a canonical key. return tuple(sorted([v1, v2])) # Assuming v1, v2 are unique voxel identifiers def getvertexid(v1, v2): # Returns a unique ID for the vertex created at the midpoint of the link return f"mid{getlinkid(v1, v2)}" def adddirectededge(globaledges, globalloops, loopcounter, linkid, vertexid, direction): # This function is complex because the source describes a global graph where edges belong to two loops. # The source states: "each link is systematically covered twice in both directions." # This implies that for a given link, if one 4-face generates an incoming edge, the adjacent 4-face # (belonging to the neighbor 8-cube) will generate an outgoing edge for the same link? # Or does it mean that the link itself is traversed in both directions by different loops? # The source says: "each link is an element of two 4-faces and that each link is systematically covered twice in both directions." # This suggests that the global graph is formed by the union of these directed edges. # We need to track which loop each directed edge belongs to. # For the purpose of this pseudocode, we assume a simplified loop tracking mechanism. # In reality, one would build the adjacency list of the directed graph and then extract cycles. pass def isstrict26adjacent(voxels, foregroundconn, backgroundconn): # Check for strict 26-adjacency of same-valued voxels # Strict 26-adjacency means sharing a corner. # This is a helper function to detect the specific configuration requiring triangulation. # Implementation depends on voxel indexing. return False # Placeholder def triangulatelocalloops(globalloops, loopcounter): # Triangulate the disconnected loops in the local graph for the current 8-cube # This modifies the globalloops structure to split or refine loops. pass def triangulateloop(vertices): # Fan triangulation of a polygon defined by vertices triangles = [] for i in range(1, len(vertices) - 1): triangles.append([vertices[0], vertices[i], vertices[i+1]]) return triangles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Connectedness Couples: Using couples like (6,6), (18,18), (18,26), (26,18), or (26,26) results in a surface that is not consistent with the inverse image, violating property (iii). Strict 26-Adjacency: If the chosen foreground or background connectivity is 26, and there are strictly 26-adjacent voxels of that type, the local graph must be transformed (triangulated) to prevent self-intersection. Ambiguous Faces (Cases 6 and 9): The standard 4-configuration cases 6 and 9 are indeterminate without the connectedness constraint. The valid connectedness couple resolves these ambiguities globally. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes the border of the support contains only 0-voxels or only 1-voxels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves iterating over all 8-cubes and processing 4-faces, which is linear in the number of voxels, similar to standard Marching Cubes. However, the global graph assembly and loop extraction may add overhead. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing the complete graph G(I), which can be large for high-resolution volumes. Strengths: Guarantees a closed, oriented 2-manifold without self-intersections or singularities. Ensures topological correctness by separating foreground and background according to the chosen connectedness. Provides a formal proof of validity. Limitations: Restricted to binary volumes. The choice of connectedness couple affects the surface geometry. May not represent the underlying continuous volume exactly, but lies within limits defined by voxel connections. When to use: When topological correctness is critical, such as in medical imaging or scientific visualization where the connectivity of structures must be preserved. When not to use: For non-binary data or when the exact geometric shape is more important than topological correctness. The method was introduced in the paper "Topologically defined isosurfaces". It is based on digital geometry considerations and provides a formal proof of the validity of the generated isosurface. The work explores the relationships between digital surfaces (specifically Jordan surfaces) and isosurfaces locally computed. It addresses the limitations of the standard Marching Cubes algorithm, which may produce surfaces that do not represent the underlying volume exactly or have topological errors. name: Topologically Defined Isosurface via Connectedness Couples
head: MC with (alpha, lambda) couples, Marching-Cubes with topological constraints
body: This method extracts a closed, oriented 2-manifold isosurface from a binary volumetric image by enforcing topological consistency through valid foreground-background connectivity pairs, known as connectedness couples. Unlike standard Marching Cubes which may produce non-manifold artifacts or self-intersections in ambiguous configurations, this approach guarantees a singularity-free surface embedded in \mathbb{R}^3 without self-crossing. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Asymptotic Decider by relying on global connectivity constraints (specifically 6-adjacency for the background) rather than local geometric tests or higher-order interpolation to resolve ambiguities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary volumetric image I (voxel grid). Output: A triangulated manifold mesh representing the isosurface \tilde{\Gamma}{\alpha}(I). Data Structures: Configuration Table: A precomputed lookup table for each of the 256 possible voxel corner sign patterns. There are four such tables, one for each valid connectedness couple: (26, 6), (18, 6), (6, 26), and (6, 18). Local Graph G{\alpha}(C8): An oriented two-dimensional combinatorial manifold without boundary, constructed from the 8-cubes of the image. It consists of a set of oriented loops. Loop Structure: An ordered set of vertices (a1, \dots, ak) representing the boundary of a face or surface patch. Valid Connectedness Couples: A valid couple (\alpha, \lambda) defines the connectivity of the foreground (\alpha) and background (\lambda). The valid pairs are: 1. (26, 6) 2. (18, 6) 3. (6, 26) 4. (6, 18) Algorithm Steps: 1. Precomputation (Build-LocalSurface): For each valid connectedness couple (\alpha, \lambda), precompute the surface subdivision for all 256 voxel configurations. The procedure Build-LocalSurface determines the triangulation for a single configuration C. 2. Surface Extraction: Iterate over the volume. For each voxel, identify its configuration. Retrieve the precomputed triangulation from the table corresponding to the chosen connectedness couple. Assemble the mesh. Alternatively, use a surface tracking algorithm to build the complete graph G{\alpha}(I) and extract the surface in O(s) time, where s is the number of surfels. Detailed Procedure: Build-LocalSurface The following pseudocode implements the logic for generating the local surface subdivision for a configuration C and foreground connectivity \alpha. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def BuildLocalSurface(Configuration C, int alpha): """ Computes the local triangulated manifold Salpha(C) for a given voxel configuration C and foreground connectivity alpha. Returns the set of loops s defining the surface. """ E = EmptySet() # 1. Extract edges from inner 6-faces # Inner 6-faces are the faces shared with adjacent voxels within the 8-cube for F in C.inner6faces: EF = ExtractEdges(F, g=6, connectivity=6) E = E.union(EF) # 2. Extract loops from the edge set L = ExtractLoops(E) # 3. Compute Convex Hull H # H contains the convex hull of the vertices in E and the 1-voxels (corners) of C H = ConvexHull(getvertices(E).union(get1voxels(C))) s = L # s is the set of loops # 4. Subdivide long loops # While there exists a loop in s with length > 3 while s.containsloopwithlengthgreaterthan(3): L = s.removeloopoflengthgreaterthan3() # L is an ordered set (a1,..., ak) of vertices exitflag = False i = 1 j = i + 2 while not exitflag: # Check if the chord (ai, aj) is inside the convex hull H if isinconvexhull(ai, aj, H): exitflag = True else: j = j + 1 if j == k: # k is the length of the loop L i = i + 1 j = i + 2 # Insert the subdivided loop and the chord # The loop is split into (a1...ai, aj...ak) and (ai...aj) s.insertloop([a1,..., ai, aj,..., ak]) s.insertloop([ai,..., aj]) # 5. Handle Strict 26-Adjacency # If the configuration has strict 26-adjacency and alpha is 26 if C.isstrict26adjacency() and alpha == 26: s = buildspecialloops26adj(s) # If alpha == 18, the local graph is not modified in this case return s Helper Definitions: ExtractEdges(F, g, conn): Extracts edges from face F based on gradient g and connectivity conn. ExtractLoops(E): Constructs oriented loops from the edge set E. Theorem 5 states each edge belongs to exactly two loops with different orientations. isinconvexhull(p1, p2, H): Returns true if the line segment connecting p1 and p2 lies within the convex hull H. buildspecialloops26adj(s): Generates special loops for strict 26-adjacency cases. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Strict 26-Adjacency: If a configuration exhibits strict 26-adjacency (foreground voxels connected via face, edge, or corner) and \alpha=26, the standard subdivision logic is replaced by buildspecialloops26adj. If \alpha=18, this case is handled by the standard subdivision or the background connectivity logic. Background Connectivity: The method assumes \lambda=6 (6-adjacency) for the background in the primary tables described. The other tables for \lambda=26 are derived using property (iii) from the source. Binary Input: The method is defined for binary pictures. For scalar fields, a thresholding step is required to produce the binary input I. Time Complexity: Standard Marching Cubes is O(n^3) where n^3 is the volume size. Using surface tracking to build the complete graph G{\alpha}(I), the complexity is O(s), where s is the number of surfels. Since a digital surface typically has O(n^2) elements, this approach can be significantly faster for sparse or surface-dominated data. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for 4 lookup tables (one per valid connectedness couple), each containing 256 entries. The size of each entry depends on the maximum number of loops/vertices in a configuration. Strengths: Guarantees a closed, oriented, triangulated surface without singularities or self-crossings. The output is a true 2-manifold. Limitations: Restricted to binary volumes (or thresholded scalar fields). The precomputation of tables is non-trivial. The method relies on specific connectivity definitions which may not match all application requirements (e.g., if 18-adjacency is preferred for foreground). When to use: Ideal for medical image segmentation (e.g., CT scans) where topological correctness is critical and the data can be binarized. Origin: The method was introduced by (2000) as a topologically correct approach to Marching Cubes. History: It builds upon the concept of digital topology and combinatorial manifolds. The core insight is that the isosurface can be defined as the canonical embedding of the complete graph of the binary image, provided valid connectedness couples are used. Usage: Validated on synthetic data and used in the segmentation of medical images, specifically CT scans with resolutions such as 256 \times 256 \times 113. Uses local geometric tests (bilinear/trilinear interpolants) to resolve ambiguous cases. Chose when high-fidelity geometry is needed for scalar fields without binarization. Asymptotic Decider Uses gradient information (Hermite data) to disambiguate. Chose when smooth surfaces and normals are required. Marching Cubes with Hermite Data Adds vertices at cell centers to resolve complex topologies. Chose when tunnel structures are common and binarization is not desired. Topologically Correct Marching Cubes The foundational theory for this method, establishing the manifold properties. Topologically Defined Isosurfaces Uses extended trilinear interpolation to resolve ambiguities. Chose when higher-order continuity is needed. name: Extended Trilinear Triangulation
head: Extended MC33, Extended Marching Cubes 33, Extended triangulation to the Marching Cubes 33 algorithm
body: Extended Trilinear Triangulation is a topologically correct isosurface extraction method that extends the Marching Cubes 33 (MC33) algorithm by introducing a three-state vertex classification (+, -, =) to eliminate degenerate and skinny triangles while preserving the topology of the trilinear interpolant. Unlike standard Marching Cubes or earlier extended lookup tables (e.g., Raman and Wenger) that fail on ambiguous configurations like Case 10, this method uses an interior test to distinguish between separated and joined vertex groups within a cube, enabling the construction of convex hulls of intersection points to generate a manifold mesh. It is chosen when both topological correctness (handling all 33 Chernyaev cases) and high mesh quality (avoiding degeneracy) are required. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field f sampled on a rectilinear grid H, and an isovalue \alpha. Output: A triangular mesh approximating the isosurface \bar{S}\alpha = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 | g(x) = \alpha\}, where g is the trilinear interpolant of f. Data Structures: Vertex Classification: Each vertex vi of a cube is labeled: + if f(vi) > \alpha - if f(vi) < \alpha = if f(vi) = \alpha Cube Classification: A cube is positive if the count of vertices labeled = or + is \le 4; otherwise, it is negative. Groups: Group of Vertices (GV): A set of vertices of the same sign (or =) in a cube that are connected by a path of the same sign (or =) along the edges or faces of the cube. Group of Edges (GE): A set of edges intersected by the isosurface that are incident to vertices in the same GV. Face Tracking: A boolean flag or set tracking which grid faces have already been triangulated to prevent duplicates between adjacent cubes. Formulas: The trilinear interpolant g(x,y,z) in a unit cube with vertices v0 \dots v7 is: g(x,y,z) = (1-x)(1-y)(1-z)f(v0) + (1-x)(1-y)zf(v4) + (1-x)y(1-z)f(v3) + (1-x)yzf(v7) + x(1-y)(1-z)f(v1) + x(1-y)zf(v5) + xy(1-z)f(v2) + xyzf(v6) Steps: 1. Classify Vertices: For each vertex vi of the current cube, determine its label (+, -, =) based on f(vi) vs \alpha. 2. Classify Cube: Determine if the cube is positive or negative based on the count of + and = vertices. 3. Identify Groups: Identify all Groups of Vertices (GV) for the cube's sign (positive or negative). Two vertices are in the same GV if they are connected by a path of non-negative values (for positive cubes) or non-positive values (for negative cubes) along the cube's edges and faces. Identify Groups of Edges (GE) incident to each GV. 4. Interior Test: Use the Chernyaev/Custodio interior test to determine the connectivity of the GV sets inside the cube. This classifies the cube into one of three categories: Simple Leaf: Vertex groups are separated inside the cube. Tunnel: Vertex groups are joined inside the cube. Interior Point: Complex configuration requiring center vertex insertion. Note: This test is critical for distinguishing cases like 6.1.1 and 6.1.2 which have identical GV/GE structures but different topologies. 5. Generate Triangulation: Based on the category and specific case (e.g., Case 13 subcases), apply one of the following triangulation strategies: Simple Leaves Triangulation: For each group i: 1. Let Wi be the set of intersection points (midpoints of edges in GEi) and vertices in GVi labeled = or +. 2. Compute the convex hull conv(Wi). 3. If conv(Wi) is 3D, triangulate its boundary \partial(conv(Wi)) and remove triangles lying on the cube faces. 4. If conv(Wi) is 2D (contained in faces), return the triangulation of conv(Wi), unless all cube vertices are = (in which case, return nothing to avoid duplicates). 5. Check face tracking to ensure cube faces are not triangulated twice. Tunnel Triangulation: 1. Let W be the set of midpoints of all intersected edges in the cube. 2. Compute conv(W). 3. If conv(W) is 3D, triangulate \partial(conv(W)). 4. Remove triangles where all three vertices belong to the same Group of Edges (GEi). Interior Point Leaves Triangulation: 1. Identify faces where all four edges are intersected. 2. Connect pairs of intersected edges on these faces based on the bilinear interpolant behavior to form a closed polygonal curve. 3. Add a vertex at the cube center. 4. Form triangles connecting the center vertex to the segments of the polygonal curve. Case 13 Specifics: 13.3: One group of 4 positive vertices. Use the incident negative vertex. Apply Interior Point Leaves triangulation combined with Simple Leaves triangulation on the single negative vertex group. 13.5.1: Two groups of vertices. Apply Simple Leaves triangulation to both groups. 13.5.2: Two groups connected by interior, with signal change diagonally opposite to one vertex group. Apply Tunnel triangulation combined with Simple Leaves triangulation in the region diagonally opposite to the one vertex positive group. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extendedtrilineartriangulation(cubevertices, scalarvalues, isovalue): # 1. Classify Vertices labels = [] for val in scalarvalues: if val > isovalue: labels.append('+') elif val < isovalue: labels.append('-') else: labels.append('=') # 2. Classify Cube poseqcount = sum(1 for l in labels if l in ['+', '=']) ispositivecube = poseqcount <= 4 # 3. Identify Groups of Vertices (GV) and Edges (GE) # Helper to check connectivity on cube edges/faces groupsofvertices = findvertexgroups(labels, ispositivecube) groupsofedges = findedgegroups(groupsofvertices, cubeedges, scalarvalues, isovalue) # 4. Interior Test # Determines if groups are separated or joined inside the cube # Returns category: 'Simple', 'Tunnel', 'Interior' category = interiortest(groupsofvertices, groupsofedges, scalarvalues, isovalue) # 5. Generate Triangulation triangles = [] if category == 'Simple': for i, gv in enumerate(groupsofvertices): # Wi: intersection points (midpoints) + '=' or '+' vertices in GV wi = getintersectionmidpoints(groupsofedges[i]) + [v for v in gv if labels[v] in ['+', '=']] hull = convexhull3d(wi) if hull.is3d(): tri = triangulateboundary(hull) # Remove triangles on cube faces tri = removefacetriangles(tri, cubefaces) triangles.extend(tri) else: # 2D case if not all(l == '=' for l in labels): tri = triangulate2dhull(hull) triangles.extend(tri) elif category == 'Tunnel': wall = getintersectionmidpoints(allintersectededges) hull = convexhull3d(wall) if hull.is3d(): tri = triangulateboundary(hull) # Remove triangles with all 3 vertices in same GE for ge in groupsofedges: gevertices = set(ge) tri = [t for t in tri if not (set(t).issubset(gevertices))] triangles.extend(tri) elif category == 'Interior': # Interior Point Leaves polygon = formpolygonfromfaceintersections(cubefaces, scalarvalues, isovalue) centervertex = getcubecenter() triangles.extend(triangulatepolygontocenter(polygon, centervertex)) # Handle Case 13 specific combinations if detected if caseid == 13: if subcase == 13.3: # Combine Interior Point and Simple Leaves for negative vertex pass elif subcase == 13.5.1: # Simple Leaves for both groups pass elif subcase == 13.5.2: # Tunnel + Simple Leaves pass return triangles Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels, as each cube is processed independently. The interior test and convex hull construction are constant time per cube (fixed number of vertices/edges). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the output mesh size. Requires storage for vertex labels and group connectivity data per cube. Performance: Produces topologically correct meshes with correct Betti numbers (e.g., b0=1, b1=0, b2=1 for a single object) where Raman and Wenger's method fails (e.g., producing b0=4, b2=4). Strengths: Eliminates degenerate triangles (by handling = labels) and skinny triangles. Handles all 33 ambiguous cases of the trilinear interpolant, including Case 10 and Case 13 subcases, which other extended methods miss. Limitations: More complex implementation than standard Marching Cubes due to the need for the interior test and convex hull operations. The interior test requires careful implementation of the Chernyaev/Custodio algorithm. Origin: The base Marching Cubes algorithm was proposed by Lorensen and Cline in 1987. Marching Cubes 33 (MC33) was proposed by Chernyaev in 1995 to handle topological ambiguities. The extended lookup table concept was introduced by Raman and Wenger in 2008 to handle degenerate triangles, but their table only covered 23 of 33 behaviors. Extended Trilinear Triangulation was proposed to extend MC33 with the +/-/= labeling and full topological correctness for all 33 cases. History: The method addresses the trade-off between triangle quality and topological correctness. While Raman and Wenger improved quality, they lost topology for ambiguous cases. This method restores full topological correctness while maintaining quality. Usage: Used in volume rendering and scientific visualization where accurate topology and mesh quality are critical. An extended triangulation to the Marching Cubes 33 algorithm, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13173-019-0086-6, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Topology/Normal Consistency Loss
head: Topology Consistency Loss
body: This method computes a differentiable loss function to enforce topological consistency and normal alignment in learned Marching Cubes networks. It addresses the problem of ambiguous surface configurations by penalizing predictions where the predicted triangle connectivity and surface normals are geometrically inconsistent. Unlike deterministic topological correctness methods that resolve ambiguities via geometric tests or vertex insertion, this approach integrates topology constraints directly into the training objective of a neural network, allowing the model to learn valid manifold structures through gradient descent. The method operates on the output of a neural network predicting vertex offsets and topology probabilities for a voxel grid. It constructs a weighted connectivity matrix from predicted probabilities and penalizes deviations from a consistent normal field. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: topology: Tensor of shape (N, C), where N is the number of grid cells and C is the number of topology classes. offset: Tensor of predicted vertex offsets for the current grid cell, used to derive triangle normals. connectedinner: Binary or weight matrix indicating valid connections between triangles. topologytotriangle: Integer mapping array expanding topology indices to triangle indices. Outputs: loss: Scalar loss value for the current grid cell. Data Structures: topologytotriangle: A 1D integer array mapping each topology class index to one or more triangle indices. connectedinner: A 2D matrix (size T \times T, where T is the number of triangles) where W{ij} = 1 if triangles i and j are connected, and 0 otherwise. Steps: 1. Compute Topology Probabilities: Apply softmax along the class dimension to the raw topology logits to obtain probabilities p{topo}. p{topo} = \text{softmax}(topology, \text{dim}=0) 2. Expand to Triangle Probabilities: Map the topology probabilities to triangle probabilities p1 using the topologytotriangle mapping. p1 = p{topo}[topology\to\triangle] 3. Construct Connectivity Matrix: Compute the outer product of the triangle probabilities to form a joint probability matrix, then mask it with the connectivity mask connectedinner to create the weight matrix W. p{outer} = p1 \otimes p1 W = p{outer} \odot connected\inner where \otimes denotes the outer product (element-wise multiplication of column vector p1 and row vector p1^T) and \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. 4. Compute Normal Vectors: Extract normal vectors N for the current grid cell using the predicted offsets. The normals are normalized to unit length. N = \text{normalize}(\text{offsets\to\normals}(offset)) 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the loss term using the trace of the product of the normal matrix and the weight matrix. L{\text{topo}} = 2 \sum W - 2 \text{tr}(N^T W N) where \sum W is the sum of all elements in W, and \text{tr}(\cdot) is the matrix trace. Formula: L{\text{topo}} = 2\sum{i,j} W{ij} - 2\text{tr}(N^T W N) where W is the probability-weighted connectivity matrix and N contains normalized triangle normals. Parameters: topologytotriangle: Integer mapping array. connectedinner: Binary or weight matrix. offset: Predicted vertex offsets. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The softmax operation can suffer from numerical instability if logits are very large or small. Standard implementations handle this via log-sum-exp tricks. Boundary Conditions: The source code initializes a negweight based on grid boundaries, assuming outside faces are free. This suggests the loss may need to account for boundary conditions separately or implicitly via the connectivity mask. Degenerate Input: If offset results in zero-length normals, normalization will fail. A small epsilon should be added to the norm denominator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def topologynormalconsistencyloss(topology, offset, connectedinner, topologytotriangle): """ Computes the topology/normal consistency loss. Args: topology: Tensor of shape (N, C), raw topology logits. offset: Tensor of predicted vertex offsets. connectedinner: Tensor of shape (T, T), connectivity mask. topologytotriangle: Tensor of shape (C,), mapping topology indices to triangle indices. Returns: loss: Scalar tensor. """ # Step 1: Compute topology probabilities # Apply softmax along the class dimension (dim=0 in source, assuming batch dim is handled or N is batch) # Note: Source uses dim=0 on topology[i,:], implying topology is (C, N) or similar. # Assuming standard (N, C) layout, softmax should be on dim=-1. # Rewriting to match source logic: source does F.softmax(topology[i,:], dim=0).data # This implies topology is indexed as [i,...] and softmax is over the first dim of the slice. # Let's assume topology is (N, C) and we softmax over C. ptopo = F.softmax(topology, dim=-1) # Step 2: Expand to triangle probabilities # p1 = p1[topologytotriangle] # If topologytotriangle maps C indices to T indices, and ptopo is (N, C), # we need to gather. p1 = torch.gather(ptopo, -1, topologytotriangle.expand(ptopo.size(0), -1)) # Step 3: Compute outer product and apply connectivity mask # pouter = torch.ger(p1, p1) -> Outer product of p1 with itself # If p1 is (N, T), ger produces (N, T, T) or similar depending on implementation. # Source: pouter = torch.ger(p1, p1). This usually implies p1 is a vector. # Assuming p1 is (N, T), we need to compute outer product for each sample. # torch.ger works on 1D tensors. For batched, we might need einsum or loop. # Let's assume p1 is (T,) for a single cell for simplicity, or handle batch. # Source code: pouter = torch.ger(p1, p1). W = torch.mul(pouter, Variable(self.dtype(connectedinner))) # This suggests p1 is 1D. If batched, we iterate or use einsum. # For a single cell: pouter = torch.ger(p1.squeeze(0), p1.squeeze(0)) # Assuming single cell for clarity W = pouter connectedinner # Step 4: Compute normal vectors # norm1 = offsettonormal(offset, xidx, yidx, zidx, 6) # This is a helper function not defined in the source snippet. # We assume it computes normals from offsets. # norm1 = torch.div(norm1, torch.norm(norm1, 2, 1).unsqueeze(1).expandas(norm1)) # Let's assume norm1 is (T, 3) # Placeholder for actual normal computation from offsets norm1 = computenormalsfromoffsets(offset) # Normalize norms = torch.norm(norm1, 2, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Guard against division by zero norms = torch.clamp(norms, min=1e-8) norm1 = norm1 / norms # Step 5: Compute loss # tmp3 = norm1^T @ W @ norm1 # norm1 is (T, 3), W is (T, T) # tmp3 = norm1.T @ W @ norm1 -> (3, T) @ (T, T) @ (T, 3) -> (3, 3) tmp3 = torch.mm(torch.mm(norm1.t(), W), norm1) # loss1 = 2 sum(W) - 2 trace(tmp3) loss1 = 2 torch.sum(W) - 2 torch.trace(tmp3) return loss1 def computenormalsfromoffsets(offset): """ Placeholder for offsettonormal. In a real implementation, this would compute triangle normals from the predicted vertex positions derived from offsets. """ # Not given in the sources. return torch.zeros(1, 3) # Dummy return Time Complexity: The loss computation involves matrix operations (outer product, matrix multiplication, trace) on tensors of size related to the number of triangles T per cell. Complexity is O(T^2) per cell. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the connectivity matrix W of size T \times T. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing end-to-end training of neural networks for surface extraction. Enforces global topological consistency rather than just local geometric accuracy. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the predicted topology probabilities and offsets. Computationally more expensive than simple geometric losses due to matrix operations. When to use: When training a neural network for Marching Cubes where topological correctness is critical and differentiable supervision is needed. When not to use: For deterministic, non-learning-based surface extraction methods. The Topology/Normal Consistency Loss was introduced in the context of deep learning for surface extraction, specifically in the "Deep Marching Cubes" framework. It aims to bridge the gap between learned implicit fields and topologically correct meshes by providing a gradient signal that encourages the network to predict consistent triangle connectivities and normals. yiyiliao/deepmarchingcubes, https://github.com/yiyiliao/deepmarchingcubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Node Mesh Generation
head: GetNodeVerticeFace
body: Node Mesh Generation constructs the explicit geometric vertex and face data for a voxel grid by defining the 8 corner vertices and 12 triangular faces of each voxel cube. It differs from topological extraction methods like Marching Cubes by generating a full volumetric mesh regardless of scalar field content, primarily used as a base for ray-triangle intersection tests or LOD transitions. Inputs: mkWorldAabb.kMin and mkWorldAabb.kMax: Minimum and maximum corner vectors of the voxel's axis-aligned bounding box. GetWidth(), GetHeight(), GetDepth(): Functions returning the voxel grid dimensions along the X, Y, and Z axes. k: A static global integer counter, initialized to 1, used to generate unique vertex indices across the mesh. Outputs: A list of 8 vertices (v1 through v8) representing the cube corners. A list of 12 triangular faces defined by indices into the vertex list. Data Structures: Vertices are stored in a flat array or list as 3D coordinates. Faces are stored as triplets of vertex indices. The vertex index counter k is incremented by 8 after processing each voxel to ensure global uniqueness. Steps: 1. Compute the 8 corner vertices of the voxel using the world AABB bounds and grid dimensions, assigning them local indices v1 to v8. 2. Generate 12 triangular faces using the static global counter k to offset local vertex indices into global indices. The faces follow a fixed winding order: back (f1, f2), bottom (f3, f4), right (f5, f6), top (f7, f8), left (f9, f{10}), front (f{11}, f{12}). 3. Increment the static global counter k by 8. Formulas: Vertex coordinates are derived from the AABB corners: vi = (xi, yi, zi) where coordinates map to the min/max bounds along each axis. Global vertex index for local vertex vj in voxel n is k + j - 1, where k starts at 1 and increments by 8 per voxel. Parameters: k: Initialized to 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thread Safety: The method uses a static global counter k for vertex indexing. This is not thread-safe and will produce incorrect indices if called concurrently or across multiple independent octrees without resetting k. Winding Order: The face winding order is fixed. Deviating from this order may result in back-face culling issues or incorrect normal orientations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. globalk = 1 def generatenodemesh(aabbmin, aabbmax): """ Generates vertex and face data for a single voxel cube. Assumes aabbmin and aabbmax are (x, y, z) tuples. """ global globalk # 1. Compute vertex positions # Standard cube corner mapping: v1 at min-min-min, v8 at max-max-max x0, y0, z0 = aabbmin x1, y1, z1 = aabbmax vertices = [ (x0, y0, z0), # v1 (x1, y0, z0), # v2 (x0, y1, z0), # v3 (x1, y1, z0), # v4 (x0, y0, z1), # v5 (x1, y0, z1), # v6 (x0, y1, z1), # v7 (x1, y1, z1) # v8 ] # 2. Generate 12 triangular faces using globalk # Fixed winding order: back, bottom, right, top, left, front # Each face consists of 2 triangles faces = [] # Back (z=0) faces.append((globalk + 0, globalk + 1, globalk + 3)) faces.append((globalk + 0, globalk + 3, globalk + 2)) # Bottom (y=0) faces.append((globalk + 0, globalk + 1, globalk + 5)) faces.append((globalk + 0, globalk + 5, globalk + 4)) # Right (x=1) faces.append((globalk + 1, globalk + 3, globalk + 7)) faces.append((globalk + 1, globalk + 7, globalk + 5)) # Top (y=1) faces.append((globalk + 2, globalk + 3, globalk + 7)) faces.append((globalk + 2, globalk + 7, globalk + 6)) # Left (x=0) faces.append((globalk + 0, globalk + 2, globalk + 6)) faces.append((globalk + 0, globalk + 6, globalk + 4)) # Front (z=1) faces.append((globalk + 4, globalk + 5, globalk + 7)) faces.append((globalk + 4, globalk + 7, globalk + 6)) # 3. Update counter globalk += 8 return vertices, faces A method to generate mesh geometry at the boundary between two levels of detail (LOD) in a voxel grid, specifically creating a transition face to bridge the gap between a coarse LOD (LOD > 0) and the finest LOD (LOD 0). It differs from standard Node Mesh Generation by sampling a larger, non-uniform voxel block and computing midpoints to ensure connectivity, addressing the holes that typically arise when merging meshes of varying resolution. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel for mesh generation, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and list appends. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of voxels, as each voxel generates 8 vertices and 12 triangles (24 indices). Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a complete volumetric mesh suitable for ray tracing; no topological ambiguity. Limitations: High memory usage for large grids; not suitable for surface extraction where only the isosurface is needed; not thread-safe without modification. When to use: When a full voxel mesh is required for ray-triangle intersection tests or when building a base for LOD transitions. When not to use: When memory efficiency is critical or when only the isosurface is needed (use Marching Cubes instead). Node Mesh Generation is a fundamental technique in voxel-based rendering and ray tracing, often used as a precursor to more advanced surface extraction methods. The method's simplicity makes it a common starting point for understanding voxel mesh structures. itsyouyi/Voxelizer, https://github.com/itsyouyi/Voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Transvoxel Transition Face Generation
head: LOD Transition, Transvoxel Transition
body: Transvoxel Transition Face Generation is a method for creating manifold mesh geometry at the boundary between different levels of detail (LOD) in a voxel grid, specifically bridging the gap between a coarse LOD (LOD > 0) and the finest LOD (LOD 0). It differs from standard Marching Cubes by sampling a larger, non-uniform voxel block (the transition cell) and computing midpoints to ensure connectivity, addressing the holes that typically arise when merging meshes of varying resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D voxel grid (float[,,] voxels), the current Level of Detail (int LOD), the voxel scale (float voxelScale), and mesh data containers (Mesh.MeshData). Outputs: A list of vertices and indices forming the transition face, stored in the provided mesh data structure. Data Structures: vertexSharingIndexes: A 3D integer array int[firstSize + 1, secondSize + 1, 7] used to track vertex reuse at the transition boundary. samplepositions: A vec4[13] array storing corner, edge midpoint, and center positions for the transition block. MarchingCubesTables: Contains lookup tables for transition cell classes and vertex data. The bit mapping is non-standard compared to classic Marching Cubes (e.g., corner 3 maps to 0x80, corner 4 to 0x100). Parameters: LOD: The level of detail for the current mesh being generated. step: Calculated as 1 << LOD. transitionCellSize: A float parameter controlling the size of the transition cell relative to the step. Values below 1 are recommended, with 0.5 being optimal. transvoxelcellmultiplier: An integer multiplier used to compute transvoxelsize = 0.1f transvoxelcellmultiplier. isoLevel: The isovalue for surface extraction, typically 0.0f in the reference implementation. Steps: 1. Initialization: Calculate step = 1 << LOD. If LOD == 0, return immediately as no transition face is needed for the finest level. 2. Face Iteration: Iterate over the six faces of the voxel volume (Positive/Negative X, Y, Z). For each face, call CreateTransitionFace with the appropriate startPosition, axisTriplet, faceDirection, and target meshData array index. 3. Vertex Tracking: Initialize vertexSharingIndexes with -1 for all elements. 4. Grid Loop: Loop through the 2D grid of the transition face. Start at startPosition. Increment the first axis by step. If the first axis exceeds maxBounds, reset it to startPosition and increment the second axis by step. Break if the second axis exceeds maxBounds. 5. Corner Sampling: For each cube position, retrieve the 13 corner values using SetTransitionCubeCornersValues. This function samples the voxel grid at specific offsets (0, halfStep, step) along the two active axes, keeping the fixed axis constant. Corners 9-12 are reused from corners 0, 2, 6, and 8 respectively. 6. Cube Index Calculation: Calculate the transition cube index using CalculateTransitionCubeIndex. This function compares corner values against isoLevel and sets bits in the index according to the non-standard mapping. 7. Lookup: Look up the transition cell class and data from MarchingCubesTables. The class code determines winding direction (bit 0x80) and the specific vertex configuration (masked with 0x7F). 8. Vertex Generation/Reuse: For each vertex in the cell configuration: Extract vertexCode from MarchingCubesTables.TransitionVertexData. Calculate vFirst and vSecond indices based on the owner cube position and step. Check vertexSharingIndexes[vFirst, vSecond, vertexIndexToReuse]. If the sharing index is -1 or the direction nibble is 4 (create but not own), create a new vertex by interpolating the edge using InterpolateTransitionEdge. Store the new vertex index in vertexSharingIndexes if the direction nibble is 8 (create and own). If the sharing index is not -1 and direction nibble is not 4, reuse the existing vertex index from vertexSharingIndexes. 9. Triangle Generation: Generate triangles from the cell data. If reverseWinding XOR faceReverseWinding is true, add vertices in order (i, i+1, i+2). Otherwise, add them in swapped order (i, i+2, i+1) to correct winding. Vertex Interpolation Formula: The position of a vertex on an edge is calculated as: P = P{base} + Lerp(Pa, Pb, t) Where: P{base} is the cube position scaled by voxelScale. Pa and Pb are the scaled corner offsets for vertices a and b. t = \frac{0 - corners[a]}{corners[b] - corners[a]}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) @dataclass class AxisTriplet: First: int = 0 Second: int = 1 Fixed: int = 2 TransitionFaceDirection = {"Positive": 1, "Negative": -1} MarchingCubesTables = { "transitionCellClass": [0] 4096, "transitionCellData": [{"vertexcount": 0, "vertices": []}] 128, "TransitionVertexData": [[0] 10] 4096 } def CalculateTransitionCubeIndex(corners: List[float], isoLevel: float) -> int: index = 0 for i in range(13): if corners[i] < isoLevel: index |= (1 << i) return index def SetTransitionCubeCornersValues(cubeCorners: List[float], voxels, cubePosition: Vector3, step: int, axisTriplet: AxisTriplet): halfStep = step // 2 offsets2D = [ (0, 0), (halfStep, 0), (step, 0), (0, halfStep), (halfStep, halfStep), (step, halfStep), (0, step), (halfStep, step), (step, step) ] for i in range(9): dx, dy = offsets2D[i] pos = Vector3( cubePosition.x + (dx if axisTriplet.First == 0 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 0 else 0)), cubePosition.y + (dx if axisTriplet.First == 1 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 1 else 0)), cubePosition.z + (dx if axisTriplet.First == 2 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 2 else 0))) cubeCorners[i] = voxels[pos.x, pos.y, pos.z] cubeCorners[9] = cubeCorners[0] cubeCorners[10] = cubeCorners[2] cubeCorners[11] = cubeCorners[6] cubeCorners[12] = cubeCorners[8] def SetTransitionCornerOffset(transitionCornerOffset: List[Vector3], transitionCellSize: float, axisTriplet: AxisTriplet, faceDirection: int): sign = -1.0 if faceDirection == TransitionFaceDirection["Positive"] else 1.0 offsets2D = [ (0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (2, 2) ] for i in range(9): dx, dy = offsets2D[i] v = Vector3() v.x = dx if axisTriplet.First == 0 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 0 else 0) v.y = dx if axisTriplet.First == 1 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 1 else 0) v.z = dx if axisTriplet.First == 2 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 2 else 0) transitionCornerOffset[i] = v outer2D = [(0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 2), (2, 2)] for i in range(4): dx, dy = outer2D[i] v = Vector3() v.x = dx if axisTriplet.First == 0 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 0 else 0) v.y = dx if axisTriplet.First == 1 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 1 else 0) v.z = dx if axisTriplet.First == 2 else (dy if axisTriplet.Second == 2 else 0) v.z cubePosition.x - (cubePosition.x % step), cubePosition.y - (cubePosition.y % step), cubePosition.z - (cubePosition.z % step)) def InterpolateTransitionEdge(cubePosition: Vector3, scale: float, step: secondSize = xSize if axisTriplet.Second == 0 else (ySize if axisTriplet.Second == 1 else zSize) vertexSharingIndexes = [[[-1] 7 for in range(secondSize + 1)] for in range(firstSize + 1)] maxBounds = Vector3(xSize - 1, ySize - 1, zSize - 1) current = Vector3(startPosition.x, startPosition.y, startPosition.z) while True: cubePosition = Vector3(current.x, current.y, current.z) cubeCorners = [0.0] 13 transitionCornerOffset = [Vector3() for in range(13)] SetTransitionCubeCornersValues(cubeCorners, voxels, cubePosition, step, axisTriplet) SetTransitionCornerOffset(transitionCornerOffset, 0 else current.x + step current.y = current.y if secondidx != 1 else current.y + step current.z = current.z if firstidx != 2 else current.z + step current.y = current.y if secondidx != 2 else if current.y >= maxBounds.y: current.y = startPosition.y if axisTriplet.Second == 2: current.z += step if current.z >= maxBounds.z: break if current.z >= maxBounds.z: current.z = startPosition.z if axisTriplet.Second == 0: current.x += step if current.x >= maxBounds.x: break meshData.vertices = vertices meshData.triangles = triangles def ProcessTransitionCube(cubePosition: Vector3, corners: List[float], isoLevel: float, scale: float, step: int, vertices: List[Vector3], triangles: List[int], vertexSharingIndexes, transitionCornerOffset: List[Vector3], axisTriplet: AxisTriplet, faceReverseWinding: bool): cubeIndex = CalculateTransitionCubeIndex(corners, isoLevel) transitionCellClassCode = MarchingCubesTables["transitionCellClass"][cubeIndex] reverseWinding = (transitionCellClassCode & 0x80) != 0 cellData = MarchingCubesTables["transitionCellData"][transitionCellClassCode & 0x7F] vertexIndexes: List[int] = [] for i in range(cellData["vertexcount"]): vertexCode = MarchingCubesTables["TransitionVertexData"][cubeIndex][i] ownerCubePosition = GetOwnerTransitionCubePosition(cubePosition, vertexCode, step, axisTriplet) vertexIndexToReuse = (vertexCode & 0x0F00) >> 8 vFirst = ownerCubePosition.x // step + 1 vSecond = ownerCubePosition.y // step + 1 directionNibble = (vertexCode >> 12) & 0xF if vertexSharingIndexes[vFirst][vSecond][vertexIndexToReuse] == -1 or directionNibble == 4: firstVertex = vertexCode & 0x000F secondVertex = (vertexCode & 0x00F0) >> 4 newVertex = InterpolateTransitionEdge(cubePosition, scale, step, firstVertex, secondVertex, corners, transitionCornerOffset) vertices.append(newVertex) newVertexIndex = len(vertices) - 1 if directionNibble == 8: vertexSharingIndexes[vFirst][vSecond][vertexIndexToReuse] = newVertexIndex vertexIndexes.append(newVertexIndex) else: vertexIndexes.append(vertexSharingIndexes[vFirst][vSecond][vertexIndexToReuse]) for i in range(0, len(vertexIndexes), 3): if (reverseWinding ^ faceReverseWinding): triangles.extend([vertexIndexes[i], vertexIndexes[i+1], vertexIndexes[i+2]]) else: triangles.extend([vertexIndexes[i], vertexIndexes[i+2], vertexIndexes[i+1]]) Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the surface area of the transition boundary, proportional to the number of transition cells. Each cell requires constant-time lookup and interpolation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of vertices in the transition mesh. The vertexSharingIndexes array adds overhead proportional to the boundary dimensions. Performance: The implementation uses UInt16 for indices, limiting the total vertex count to 65,535. Exceeding this requires switching to UInt32 and uint. Strengths: Ensures manifold connectivity between LOD levels, preventing visual holes. Limitations: Requires careful handling of winding order across different faces, often necessitating manual correction flags (faceReverseWinding). The transition cell size parameter (transitionCellSize) affects visual quality and may require shader support to pull in vertices of the main mesh. The Transvoxel algorithm was partially implemented in the context of real-time volume rendering with geometry shaders, allowing for simple LOD activation and surface shifting to reduce holes between different LODs. The specific transition face generation method described here is derived from a Unity-based implementation. name: Voxel Chunk Meshing with Culling
body: Voxel Chunk Meshing with Culling generates a static triangle mesh (typically quads) for a 3D voxel chunk by iterating through every voxel and emitting geometry only for faces adjacent to empty space or the chunk boundary. It solves the problem of excessive geometry and draw calls inherent in naive per-voxel meshing by culling internal faces shared between adjacent solid voxels. Unlike Greedy Meshing, which merges adjacent coplanar faces into larger rectangles to reduce triangle count, this method generates exactly one quad per exposed face, resulting in a simpler algorithm that produces a larger number of triangles. It serves as a ground-truth reference for verifying the correctness of more complex merging algorithms. The algorithm operates on a 3D voxel grid where each voxel has a state (e.g., material ID or solid/empty flag). The grid dimensions are typically W \times H \times D. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array or hash map storing voxel states. In array-based implementations, the index for (x, y, z) is often linearized as x + y \cdot W + z \cdot W \cdot H or similar, depending on memory layout. Quad Representation: Each generated face is represented by its axis, direction, slice coordinate, position, dimensions, and material ID. A minimal quad struct includes: axis: The normal axis (0=\text{X}, 1=\text{Y}, 2=\text{Z}). dir: The direction sign (+1 or -1). slice: The integer coordinate along the axis where the face lies. u, v: The starting coordinates on the plane's local axes. w, h: The width and height of the face (always 1 for naive culling). material: The ID of the voxel material. Boundary Policy: The behavior at chunk edges is defined by a policy parameter: Air: Treats out-of-bounds neighbors as empty (material 0). This exposes the chunk's outer surface, creating a visible boundary. If adjacent chunks both use "Air", double walls may appear at the seam. Solid: Treats out-of-bounds neighbors as solid. This hides the chunk's outer surface, requiring the renderer to handle multiple chunks seamlessly without gaps or double geometry. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list for quads. 2. Iterate through every voxel (x, y, z) in the chunk grid. 3. If the current voxel is empty (state 0), skip to the next voxel. 4. For each of the 6 face directions (e.g., \pm X, \pm Y, \pm Z): a. Calculate the neighbor's coordinates (nx, ny, nz). b. Determine the neighbor's state: i. If (nx, ny, nz) is outside the chunk bounds, apply the Boundary Policy (return 0 for Air, non-0 for Solid). ii. If inside bounds, lookup the voxel state at (nx, ny, nz). c. If the neighbor is empty (state 0), the face is exposed. Generate a quad for this face. d. If the neighbor is solid, the face is internal and is culled (not generated). 5. Return the list of generated quads. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def facecullingmeshing(chunkwidth, chunkheight, chunkdepth, getvoxel, boundarypolicy="air"): """ Generates a mesh for a voxel chunk using face culling. Args: chunkwidth, chunkheight, chunkdepth: Dimensions of the chunk. getvoxel(x, y, z): Function returning the material ID of a voxel. Returns 0 for empty/air. boundarypolicy: "air" or "solid". Returns: A list of Quad objects. """ quads = [] # Define the 6 face directions: (axisindex, directionsign, neighboroffsetaxis, neighboroffsetsign) # axisindex: 0=X, 1=Y, 2=Z # directionsign: +1 for positive axis face, -1 for negative axis face # neighboroffset: how to get to the neighbor (e.g., +1 in X for +X face) faces = [ (0, 1, 1, 0, 0), # +X face: normal +X, neighbor at x+1 (0, -1, -1, 0, 0), # -X face: normal -X, neighbor at x-1 (1, 1, 0, 1, 0), # +Y face: normal +Y, neighbor at y+1 (1, -1, 0, -1, 0), # -Y face: normal -Y, neighbor at y-1 (2, 1, 0, 0, 1), # +Z face: normal +Z, neighbor at z+1 (2, -1, 0, 0, -1) # -Z face: normal -Z, neighbor at z-1 ] for z in range(chunkdepth): for y in range(chunkheight): for x in range(chunkwidth): # Step 3: Skip empty voxels currentmaterial = getvoxel(x, y, z) if currentmaterial == 0: continue # Step 4: Check each of the 6 faces for axis, dirsign, nxoff, nyoff, nzoff in faces: # Calculate neighbor coordinates nx = x + nxoff ny = y + nyoff nz = z + nzoff # Determine neighbor state # Check bounds if nx < 0 or nx >= chunkwidth or \ ny < 0 or ny >= chunkheight or \ nz < 0 or nz >= chunkdepth: # Apply boundary policy if boundarypolicy == "air": neighbormaterial = 0 else: # solid neighbormaterial = 1 # Non-zero implies solid else: neighbormaterial = getvoxel(nx, ny, nz) # Step 4c: If neighbor is empty, generate face if neighbormaterial == 0: # Determine slice coordinate and local u,v # For axis 0 (X), slice is x (for -X) or x+1 (for +X) # Local axes u, v are the other two dimensions if axis == 0: slicecoord = x if dirsign == -1 else x + 1 u, v = y, z elif axis == 1: slicecoord = y if dirsign == -1 else y + 1 u, v = z, x else: # axis == 2 slicecoord = z if dirsign == -1 else z + 1 u, v = x, y quads.append({ "axis": axis, "dir": dirsign, "slice": slicecoord, "u": u, "v": v, "w": 1, "h": 1, "material": currentmaterial }) return quads Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Integer coordinates are used for slice and position, avoiding floating-point errors in face placement. Boundaries: Incorrect handling of out-of-bounds checks leads to crashes or incorrect culling. The boundary policy must be consistent across adjacent chunks to avoid gaps or double geometry. Translucency: The basic algorithm assumes opaque voxels. If translucent blocks (e.g., water, glass) are present, the culling logic must be extended to check if the neighbor is opaque vs. translucent, as translucent faces may need to be rendered even if adjacent to another translucent block. Renders voxel chunks as triangle meshes by mapping block faces to a horizontal texture atlas and applying per-vertex lighting. Unlike Naive Voxel Meshing which may use separate textures or per-face lighting, this approach reduces texture bind calls and supports complex block shapes via specific UV offsets. Choose when rendering performance and material batching are priorities over geometric simplicity. Generates a triangle mesh from a 3D voxel grid of density values using the Marching Cubes algorithm, optimized for GPU execution. Unlike face-culling methods that generate axis-aligned quads, this approach produces smooth, curved surfaces suitable for organic terrain or fluid simulation. Choose when smooth, continuous surfaces are required over blocky aesthetics. Generates a static triangle mesh for a 3D voxel chunk by iterating through every voxel and emitting geometry only for faces adjacent to empty space or the chunk boundary. Unlike Greedy Meshing, which merges adjacent coplanar faces into larger rectangles to reduce triangle count, Face Culling generates exactly one quad per exposed face, resulting in a simpler, faster algorithm that produces a larger number of triangles. It serves as the "oracle" or ground-truth reference for verifying the correctness of more complex merging algorithms. Choose when deterministic, fast mesh generation is needed without complex merging logic. Generates a mesh by iterating over every voxel in a chunk and emitting geometry for all six faces of every solid voxel, regardless of adjacency. Unlike Face Culling Voxel Meshing, which checks neighbors to omit internal faces, Naive Voxel Meshing treats each voxel as an independent cube, resulting in a significantly higher polygon count and draw call overhead. Choose only for debugging, prototyping, or when chunk boundaries are guaranteed to be isolated. Extracts a triangle mesh from a 3D voxel grid by processing each voxel independently on the GPU using a compute shader. Outputs vertices and indices into global buffers, using atomic counters to ensure parallel write safety when multiple threads generate faces simultaneously. Unlike CPU-based face culling which iterates sequentially, this approach leverages massive parallelism to handle large voxel chunks efficiently. It differs from this method by moving the iteration and geometry generation into a GPU compute pipeline, and from Marching Cubes by relying on axis-aligned face generation rather than polygon interpolation within voxels. Choose when processing massive voxel datasets on modern GPUs. Asynchronously collects voxel data around the player, storing solid/non-solid status in a single bit per voxel. On the CPU, builds a convex collision mesh using a culling algorithm that generates a single quad for every face separating solid from non-solid data. The collider rebuild frequency is set to a couple of times per second, which is sufficient for normal player movement. Choose when integrating voxel worlds with standard physics engines that require convex collision shapes. Origin: This method is described in the context of a voxel simulation project by Joris Rijsdijk, who uses it to generate collision meshes for a physics system.
