name: Dual Isosurfacing with Analytical Trilinear Intersection
head: Analytical Isosurface Extraction, Ray Intersection Isosurfacing, Topologically Accurate Dual Isosurfacing, Trilinear Ray Intersection
body: Dual Isosurfacing with Analytical Trilinear Intersection extracts the topology of an analytical isosurface defined by a trilinear function within a voxel cell by determining the optimal set of diagonals to intersect with rays, ensuring one point per disjoint surface component. Unlike standard Marching Cubes which uses linear interpolation and fixed lookup tables, this method uses the trilinear function exhaustively to determine the topology of the analytical isosurface, allowing for more accurate diagonal selection. It builds on Manifold Dual Marching Cubes by resolving ambiguous configurations through analytical ray intersection rather than precomputed lookup tables. Inputs: Scalar field values at the 8 vertices of a voxel cell: v0, \dots, v7. The isovalue I. The cell sign configuration index C \in [0, 13] derived from the signs of the 8 vertices relative to I. Outputs: A set of intersection points on the cell diagonals. For each point, the diagonal index and the parameter t \in [0, 1] along the diagonal where the trilinear function equals I. The method relies on the classification of the 14 sign-configurations (numbered 0 to 13) of the MC-case table into five categories based on the number of ambiguous faces: 0, 1, 2, 3, or 6. Ambiguous Face (AF): A cell face with four same-sign ended diagonals and four (+/-) edges. An AF is separated with respect to a specific sign if the contour on the face is a rectangular hyperbola. The sign is determined by the vertices in the quadrants containing the hyperbola, using the asymptotic decider. (+) ambiguous-face: Separated with respect to positive sign. (-) ambiguous-face: Separated with respect to negative sign. Topological Configuration Index: Configurations are represented as x, x.y, or x.y.z, where x is the sign configuration, y is the topological configuration, and z is the sub-configuration. DeVella's Necklace Test: Used to distinguish topological sub-configurations (specifically for tunnels) by checking if two vertices on a diagonal are internally connected. A positive result indicates the presence of a tunnel. 1. Determine Cell Sign and Ambiguous Faces: Calculate the sign of the cell: Positive if more vertices are positive, Negative if more are negative, Neutral if equal. Identify ambiguous faces on the cell boundaries using the asymptotic decider. Categorize the cell into one of the five groups based on the count of ambiguous faces (0, 1, 2, 3, or 6). 2. Select Diagonals for Ray Intersection: Based on the category and specific topological sub-configuration, select diagonals to intersect. The goal is one point per disjoint component, relaxed for tunnels to capture manifold complexity. Category 0 Ambiguous Faces (Sign Configurations 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 11): Ignore Case 0 (no intersection). For Cases 1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 11: Use one (+/-) diagonal for intersection. For Case 4: Use DeVella's necklace test to distinguish sub-configurations 4.1 (disjoint surfaces) and 4.2 (tunnel). If 4.1: Use the (-/-) diagonal. If 4.2: Use 2 of the 3 (+/+) diagonals to obtain multiple points for the tunnel. Category 1 Ambiguous Face (Sign Configurations 3, 6): If a (+) cell has a (+) ambiguous face: Single isosurface component occurs. Use one (+/-) diagonal. If a (+) cell has a (-) ambiguous face: Two isosurface components occur. Cases 3.1 and 6.1.1 (two disjoint components, no tunnels): Use one (-/-) diagonal to obtain two intersection points. If no (-/-) diagonal exists (Case 3.1): Use two (+/-) diagonals to obtain one intersection point each. Case 6.1.2 (tunnel): Use both (+/+) diagonals to obtain four intersection points on the tunnel. Cases 3.2 and 6.2 (single isosurface component): Use one (+/-) diagonal. Category 2 Ambiguous Faces (Sign Configurations 10, 12): If ambiguous faces have different signs: Single component occurs (Cases 10.2, 12.2). Use one (+/-) diagonal. If ambiguous faces have the same sign: Disjoint surfaces with two (+) AF: Use one (+/+) diagonal. Disjoint surfaces with two (-) AF: Use one (-/-) diagonal. Tunnel with two (+) AF (Case 10.1.2): Use two (-/-) diagonals. Tunnel with two (-) AF (Case 12.1.2): Use one (-/-) diagonal and two (+/-) diagonals. Category 3 Ambiguous Faces (Sign Configuration 7): Case 7.1 (three (+) AF): Three disjoint surfaces. Use three (+/-) diagonals. Case 7.2 (two (+) AF, one (-) AF): Two disjoint surfaces. Use two (+/-) diagonals through the (+) vertices in one of the (+) ambiguous faces. Case 7.3 (one (+) AF, two (-) AF): One surface. Use any one (+/-) diagonal. Case 7.4 (three (-) AF): Use DeVella's necklace test to distinguish 7.4.1 (disjoint surfaces) and 7.4.2 (tunnel). If 7.4.1: Use one (+/+) diagonal to obtain two intersection points. If 7.4.2: Use all three (+/-) diagonals to obtain three points on the tunnel. Category 6 Ambiguous Faces (Sign Configuration 13): Reduce seven possibilities to four cases using mirror symmetry pairs: (1) and (7), (2) and (6), (3) and (5). Case 13.1 (six (+) AF): Four disjoint surfaces. Use all four (+/-) diagonals. Case 13.2 (five (+) AF, one (-) AF): Three disjoint surfaces. Use three (+/-) diagonals, excluding the one through one of the two (+) vertices in the (-) ambiguous face. Case 13.3 (four (+) AF, two (-) AF): Two disjoint surfaces. Find the (+) vertex common to all three (+) ambiguous faces. Use the (+/-) diagonal through this vertex as one ray, and any one of the remaining three diagonals as the second ray. Case 13.4 (equal (+) and (-) AF, common vertex signs differ from faces): One isosurface piece. Use any one of the four (+/-) diagonals. Case 13.5 (equal (+) and (-) AF, common vertex signs same as faces): Use DeVella's necklace test to distinguish 13.5.1 (three disjoint surfaces) and 13.5.2 (two disjoint surfaces, one is a tunnel). If 13.5.1: Use the (+/-) diagonal through the common vertex of the three same-signed ambiguous faces to get three points. If 13.5.2: Use the diagonal through the common vertex of the three same-signed ambiguous faces as a ray. Use the remaining three diagonals as rays to find points for the tunnel. Store diagonal differences for connectivity. 3. Compute Intersection Points: For each selected diagonal, solve the trilinear equation f(t) = I along the diagonal to find the intersection point. The trilinear function f(x,y,z) is defined by the vertex values. Along a diagonal, this reduces to a cubic equation in one parameter t. 4. Output Points: Return the set of computed intersection points. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualisosurfacinganalyticaltrilinear(vertexvalues, isovalue): """ Extracts isosurface points for a single voxel cell using analytical trilinear intersection. Args: vertexvalues: List of 8 scalar values [v0,..., v7] at cell vertices. isovalue: The scalar isovalue I. Returns: List of intersection points (t, diagonalindex) for the cell. """ # 1. Determine Cell Sign and Ambiguous Faces signs = [1 if v > isovalue else -1 for v in vertexvalues] numpos = sum(1 for s in signs if s == 1) numneg = sum(1 for s in signs if s == -1) cellsign = 1 if numpos > numneg else (-1 if numneg > numpos else 0) # Map 8-bit sign pattern to canonical MC cases 0-13 C = computemccaseindex(signs) # Identify Ambiguous Faces (AF) using asymptotic decider ambiguousfaces = [] for faceidx in range(6): if isambiguousface(vertexvalues, faceidx, isovalue): afsign = getafsign(vertexvalues, faceidx, isovalue) ambiguousfaces.append((faceidx, afsign)) numaf = len(ambiguousfaces) selecteddiagonals = [] if numaf == 0: if C == 0: return [] elif C == 4: istunnel = devellasnecklacetest(vertexvalues, C) if not istunnel: selecteddiagonals.append(3) # (-/-) else: selecteddiagonals.extend([0, 1]) # 2 of 3 (+/+) else: selecteddiagonals.append(2) # (+/-) elif numaf == 1: afsign = ambiguousfaces[0][1] if cellsign == afsign: selecteddiagonals.append(2) # Single component else: istunnel = devellasnecklacetest(vertexvalues, C) if not istunnel: if hasnegnegdiagonal(C): selecteddiagonals.append(3) else: selecteddiagonals.extend([0, 2]) # Case 3.1 else: selecteddiagonals.extend([0, 1]) # 6.1.2 tunnel elif numaf == 2: afsigns = [af[1] for af in ambiguousfaces] if afsigns[0] != afsigns[1]: selecteddiagonals.append(2) # Different signs else: if afsigns[0] == 1: # Two (+) AF istunnel = devellasnecklacetest(vertexvalues, C) if not istunnel: selecteddiagonals.append(0) # (+/+) else: selecteddiagonals.extend([3, 3]) # Tunnel (10.1.2) else: # Two (-) AF istunnel = devellasnecklacetest(vertexvalues, C) if not istunnel: selecteddiagonals.append(3) # (-/-) else: selecteddiagonals.extend([3, 2, 2]) # Tunnel (12.1.2) elif numaf == 3: posafcount = sum(1 for s in [af[1] for af in ambiguousfaces] if s == 1) if posafcount == 3: selecteddiagonals.extend([0, 1, 2]) # 7.1 elif posafcount == 2: selecteddiagonals.extend([0, 2]) # 7.2 elif posafcount == 1: selecteddiagonals.append(2) # 7.3 else: # 7.4 (three (-) AF) istunnel = devellasnecklacetest(vertexvalues, C) if not istunnel: selecteddiagonals.append(0) # 7.4.1 else: selecteddiagonals.extend([0, 1, 2]) # 7.4.2 elif numaf == 6: posafcount = sum(1 for s in [af[1] for af in ambiguousfaces] if s == 1) if posafcount in (0, 6): selecteddiagonals.extend([0, 1, 2, 3]) # 13.1 / 13.7 elif posafcount in (1, 5): selecteddiagonals.extend([0, 1, 2]) # 13.2 / 13.6 elif posafcount in (2, 4): # 13.3 / 13.5 commonvertex = findcommonvertex(vertexvalues, [af[1] for af in ambiguousfaces]) selecteddiagonals.extend([2, 0]) # Through common & any remaining else: # posafcount == 3 (13.4 / 13.5) istunnel = devellasnecklacetest(vertexvalues, C) if not istunnel: if posafcount == 3 and cellsign == 1: selecteddiagonals.append(2) # 13.5.1 else: selecteddiagonals.append(2) # 13.4 else: # 13.5.2 tunnel selecteddiagonals.extend([2, 0, 1, 2]) points = [] for diag in selecteddiagonals: t = solvetrilineardiagonal(vertexvalues, diag, isovalue) if t is not None: points.append((t, diag)) return points def solvetrilineardiagonal(vertexvalues, diagonalindex, isovalue): """ Solves f(t) = I along the specified diagonal. Returns t in [0, 1] or None if no intersection. """ # Trilinear interpolation along a diagonal reduces to a cubic polynomial f(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d # Coefficients are computed from vertex values and diagonal geometry. roots = solvecubicequation(vertexvalues, diagonalindex, isovalue) for t in roots: if 0 <= t <= 1: return t return None Cell Sign Configuration: Integer index from 0 to 13. Ambiguous Face Sign: Determined by asymptotic decider. DeVella's Necklace Test Threshold: Not given in the sources. Typically involves checking the sign of the trilinear function at the center of the diagonal or comparing vertex signs with the function value at the midpoint. Precision: Evaluating the intersection point requires significant computational operations. Floating-point precision errors in solving the cubic equation may lead to missed intersections or incorrect topology. Tunnels: The "one-point-per-disjoint-component" rule is relaxed for tunnels. Sufficient points are needed to capture the complexity of the manifold. Ambiguous Face Detection: Incorrect identification of ambiguous faces or their signs leads to wrong diagonal selection. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, as it involves a fixed number of case checks and cubic root solving. However, solving the cubic equation is more expensive than linear interpolation used in standard MC. Memory Complexity: O(1) per voxel, storing only the vertex values and selected diagonals. Strengths: Topologically accurate representation of the analytical isosurface. Handles ambiguous configurations correctly without lookup tables. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than linear MC due to cubic root solving. Complex logic for diagonal selection. When to use: When topological accuracy is critical and the scalar field is well-approximated by trilinear interpolation. When not to use: When performance is paramount and linear approximation is sufficient. Originated from the need to accurately extract topologies of analytical isosurfaces defined by trilinear functions. The method analyzes the 31 cases from the exhaustive MC case-table (Chernyaev, 1995; Nielson, 2003; Lopes and Brodlie, 2003). It builds on the work of Nielson and Hamann (1991) on ambiguous faces and DeVella's necklace test. name: Curvature/Normal Similarity Loss
head: topology-aware normal consistency loss
body: A differentiable loss function that enforces normal vector alignment between triangles in adjacent grid cells, weighted by the joint probability of their topological configurations. It addresses discontinuity and noise in extracted surfaces by ensuring neighboring triangles share consistent orientations, which is critical for smooth surface reconstruction in differentiable isosurfacing pipelines. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the probabilistic nature of topology selection via softmax over 256 cases rather than relying on deterministic hard assignments or purely geometric penalties. It builds on Manifold Dual Marching Cubes. The method computes a loss term L{\text{curv}} by iterating over all grid cells and their spatial neighbors, calculating the weighted alignment of normal vectors derived from predicted offset fields. Inputs: topology: A tensor of shape (N^3, 256) containing unnormalized logits or probabilities for each of the 256 marching cube topology cases per cell, where N is args.numcells. offset: A tensor representing the predicted offset field for grid vertices, used to compute triangle normals. topologytotriangle: A lookup table mapping each of the 256 topology indices to a list of triangle indices generated by the marching cube lookup table. connectedx, connectedy, connectedz, connectedinner: Binary or integer weight matrices of shape (M, M), where M is the maximum number of triangles per cell, indicating valid adjacency pairs between triangles in neighboring cells. args.numcells: Integer, number of grid divisions per spatial dimension. args.lencell: Float, physical size of each grid cell. xgrids, ygrids, zgrids: Arrays of grid coordinates aligned with spatial indices. Output: loss: A scalar tensor representing the total curvature/normal similarity loss. Topology Probabilities: Softmax output over the 256 topology classes for a cell. Triangle Probabilities: Expanded from topology probabilities using topologytotriangle. Joint Probability Matrix (W): Outer product of triangle probabilities from adjacent cells, masked by connectivity. Normal Vectors (N1, N2): L2-normalized normal vectors for triangles in the current and neighbor cells, derived from the offset field. 1. Initialize Loss: Set loss = 0. 2. Iterate Grid Cells: Loop over each grid cell indexed by (x, y, z) where 0 \le x, y, z < \text{args.num\cells}. 3. Compute Topology Probabilities: For the current cell at (x, y, z), compute p1 as the softmax of topology logits along the last dimension. For the neighbor cell in the target direction, compute p2 similarly. The source code detaches topology from the gradient graph before softmax to treat it as constant weights during gradient computation. 4. Expand to Triangle Probabilities: Expand p1 and p2 from topology class probabilities to triangle probabilities using topologytotriangle. 5. Compute Joint Probability Matrix (W): Compute the outer product p{\text{outer}} = p1 \otimes p2. Multiply p{\text{outer}} element-wise by the corresponding connection mask Cd (e.g., connectedx) to obtain the weight matrix W. 6. Extract Normal Vectors: Compute normal vectors N1 for triangles in the current cell using the predicted offset field. Compute normal vectors N2 for triangles in the neighbor cell using the offset field. Normalize N1 and N2 to unit length via L2 normalization. 7. Compute Loss Contribution: Compute the weighted normal alignment term: \text{tmp3} = N1^\top W N2. Calculate the loss contribution: \text{loss1} = 2 \sum W - 2 \operatorname{tr}(\text{tmp3}). Accumulate \text{loss1} into loss. 8. Return Loss: Return the accumulated loss. The total loss is defined as: L{\text{curv}} = \sum{c \in \text{cells}} \sum{d \in \{x,y,z,\text{inner}\}} \left( 2 \sum{i,j} W{ij} - 2 \operatorname{tr}(N1^\top W N2) \right) where: W = (p1 \otimes p2) \odot Cd p1, p2 are softmax topology probabilities expanded to triangles Cd is the connection mask for direction d N1, N2 are L2-normalized normal vectors Unverified code. Args: topology: Tensor of shape (numcells^3, 256) offset: Tensor of offset field values topologytotriangle: List of lists mapping topology indices to triangle indices connectedx, connectedy, connectedz, connectedinner: Connectivity masks numcells: Integer, grid divisions per dimension lencell: Float, physical size of each cell xgrids, ygrids, zgrids: Arrays of grid coordinates dtype: Data type for tensors (e.g., torch.cuda.FloatTensor) dtypelong: Data type for long tensors (e.g., torch.cuda.LongTensor) Returns: loss: Scalar tensor """ loss = 0.0 # Pre-convert topologytotriangle to integer indices t2tindices = [list(map(int, row)) for row in topologytotriangle] # Directions: (name, dx, dy, dz, mask, dirflag) directions = [ ('x', 1, 0, 0, connectedx, 0), ('y', 0, 1, 0, connectedy, 0), ('z', 0, 0, 1, connectedz, 0), ('inner', 0, 0, 0, connectedinner, 1) ] for x in range(numcells): for y in range(numcells): for z in range(numcells): cellidx = x numcells numcells + y numcells + z for dirname, dx, dy, dz, mask, dirflag in directions: nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz if not (0 <= nx < numcells and 0 <= ny < numcells and 0 <= nz < numcells): continue neighboridx = nx numcells numcells + ny numcells + nz # Softmax probabilities (detached from gradient graph) p1 = softmax(topology[cellidx,:]) p2 = softmax(topology[neighboridx,:]) # Expand to triangle probabilities p1tri = [p1[i] for i in t2tindices[cellidx]] p2tri = [p2[i] for i in t2tindices[neighboridx]] # Joint probability matrix pouter = outerproduct(p1tri, p2tri) W = elementwisemultiply(pouter, mask) # Extract and normalize normals xcoord = xgrids[x] ycoord = ygrids[y] zcoord = zgrids[z] xcoordn = xgrids[nx] ycoordn = ygrids[ny] zcoordn = zgrids[nz] norm1 = l2normalize(offsettonormal(offset, xcoord, ycoord, zcoord, dirflag)) norm2 = l2normalize(offsettonormal(offset, xcoordn, ycoordn, zcoordn, dirflag)) # Loss contribution tmp3 = trace(matmul(matmul(norm1.transpose(), W), norm2)) loss1 = 2.0 sum(W) - 2.0 tmp3 loss += loss1 return loss def softmax(logits): maxval = max(logits) expvals = [math.exp(l - maxval) for l in logits] sumexp = sum(expvals) return [e / sumexp for e in expvals] def outerproduct(a, b): return [[a[i] b[j] for j in range(len(b))] for i in range(len(a))] def elementwisemultiply(A, B): return [[A[i][j] B[i][j] for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def l2normalize(v): norm = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) if norm == 0: return v return [x / norm for x in v] def matmul(A, B): rowsA, colsA = len(A), len(A[0]) rowsB, colsB = len(B), len(B[0]) C = [[0.0] colsB for in range(rowsA)] for i in range(rowsA): for j in range(colsB): for k in range(colsA): C[i][j] += A[i][k] B[k][j] return C def trace(M): return sum(M[i][i] for i in range(len(M))) def offsettonormal(offset, x, y, z, direction): """Computes normal vectors for triangles in a cell from the offset field. direction=0 for current cell, direction=1 for neighbor cell.""" # Implementation depends on specific offset-to-normal conversion logic. # Returns a matrix of shape (numtriangles, 3) containing unnormalized normals. pass args.numcells: Integer, number of grid divisions per spatial dimension. args.lencell: Float, physical size of each grid cell. Gradient Flow: Topology is treated as a constant weight matrix during gradient computation to prevent gradients from flowing through the discrete topology selection. The code explicitly detaches topology before softmax using.data. Boundary Conditions: Neighbor cells outside the grid boundary should be skipped to avoid index errors. Zero Normals: Normal vectors with zero magnitude should be handled to avoid division by zero during normalization. Empty Cells: Cells with no triangles (empty topology) should be handled to avoid undefined behavior in normal extraction. The Curvature/Normal Similarity Loss was introduced in the context of differentiable isosurfacing, specifically for the Deep Marching Cubes method. It aims to improve the quality of extracted surfaces by ensuring normal consistency across cell boundaries, which is a common issue in traditional marching cubes implementations. name: Geometric Self-Intersection Elimination
head: Ambiguous face treatment, Ju et al. intersection removal
body: Geometric Self-Intersection Elimination is a post-processing geometric treatment applied during the connection of dual vertices in adaptive octree constructions to ensure the resulting isosurface is free of polygon self-intersections. It addresses the topological defects inherent in naive dual triangulations of adaptive grids by replacing trivial triangulations with triangle fans or geometrically validated subsets when ambiguous face configurations are detected. Unlike ambiguity treatments for regular (non-adaptive) constructions, which primarily ensure manifoldness without increasing vertex or face counts, this method explicitly increases mesh complexity to guarantee intersection-free geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An adaptive octree structure containing meta-cells; a lookup table mapping Dual Marching Cubes configurations (0-255) to ambiguous face directions (or 255 if non-problematic); the current meta-cell being processed. Output: A set of triangles connecting dual vertices and edge vertices that form a self-intersection-free surface patch. Data Structures: Meta-cell: A block of octree nodes at a specific level, processed as a unit. Dual Vertex (vc): A vertex located inside a cell, typically at the centroid or computed via QEF. Edge Vertex (ve): A vertex located on an edge of the grid, derived from primal methods. Face Vertex (vf): A vertex located on a face of the grid. Configuration Table: Maps the 256 possible Dual Marching Cubes cases to an ambiguous face direction index. Steps: 1. Identify Ambiguous Faces: Iterate through the faces of adjacent cells within the meta-cell and identify faces that are shared between adjacent cells and have configurations 2B or 3B from the Dual Marching Cubes lookup table. 2. Detect Non-Trivial Edges: For edges that do not allow for a trivial triangulation due to potential self-intersection identified in Step 1, mark them for special handling. 3. Create Triangle Fans: Instead of a single trivial triangulation connecting only dual vertices, create a fan of triangles from the minimum edge e. Let ve be the vertex on the edge e. Let vf be the vertices on the faces containing e. Let vc be the dual vertices inside the cells containing e. Each triangle in the fan connects ve to a pair of (vf, vc) or similar combinations depending on the specific hybrid rule. 4. Apply Geometric Rules (Hybrid Method): To reduce the excessive polygon count from full fans, apply geometric rules from Ju et al. [2006] to substitute fans with fewer triangles within a valid envelope. If the geometric conditions are met, use a trivial triangulation. Otherwise, use the fan. Fans typically consist of eight or six triangles for each minimum edge. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def eliminateselfintersections(metacell, dualmarchingcubeslut): """ Eliminates self-intersections in an adaptive octree meta-cell by applying geometric treatments to ambiguous faces. """ triangles = [] # Step 1: Identify ambiguous faces ambiguousfaces = [f for f in metacell.faces if f.isshared and f.config in ('2B', '3B')] # Step 2 & 3: Process edges connected to ambiguous faces for face in ambiguousfaces: for edge in face.edges: # Check if trivial triangulation is possible if istrivialtriangulationpossible(edge): # Use standard dual triangulation triangles.extend(createtrivialtriangulation(edge)) else: # Create triangle fan from minimum edge e triangles.extend(createtrianglefan(edge)) # Step 4: Apply geometric rules to reduce fan size if needed optimizedtriangles = [] for tri in triangles: if isfanreducible(tri): # Substitute fan with fewer triangles within valid envelope optimizedtriangles.extend(substitutefanwithenvelope(tri)) else: optimizedtriangles.append(tri) return optimizedtriangles def istrivialtriangulationpossible(edge): """ Determines if a trivial triangulation is safe (no self-intersection). # Sources do not specify the exact geometric validity check for trivial triangulation. return False def createtrianglefan(edge): """ Creates a fan of triangles from the minimum edge. """ # Sources do not specify the exact fan construction algorithm. # Implements the described hybrid primal-dual fan: connects ve to vf and vc. triangles = [] ve = edge.vertexonedge vfs = [f.vertexonface for f in edge.adjacentfaces] vcs = [c.dualvertex for c in edge.adjacentcells] for i in range(len(vfs)): triangles.append((ve, vfs[i], vcs[i % len(vcs)])) return triangles def isfanreducible(triangle): """ Checks if the fan can be replaced by fewer triangles within a valid envelope. # Sources do not specify the exact geometric rules from Ju et al. [2006]. return False def substitutefanwithenvelope(triangle): """ Substitutes a fan with a smaller set of triangles. # Sources do not specify the exact substitution algorithm. return [triangle] Parameters: Ambiguous Configurations: 2B and 3B from the Dual Marching Cubes lookup table. Fan Size: Typically 8 or 6 triangles per minimum edge. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Excessive Polygons: The hybrid method creates an excessive number of polygons per fan if geometric rules are not applied. Precision: The method relies on exact Euclidean distance calculations to avoid propagation errors common in distance transforms. A hybrid method combining primal (vertices on edges) and dual (vertices inside cells) approaches to create intersection-free surfaces in adaptive octrees. It creates a fan of triangles from the minimum edge e, connecting vertex ve (on the edge) to vertices vf (on faces containing e) and dual vertices vc (inside cells). Fans of eight or six triangles are created for each minimum edge. A key pitfall is the excessive number of polygons created per fan; Ju et al. [2006] provide geometric rules to substitute fans with fewer triangles within a valid envelope. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method increases the number of vertices and faces in the resulting mesh. For Level 6, vertices increase from 85,220 to 87,138 (+2.2%) and triangles from 41,690 to 44,596 (+7%). For Level 7, vertices increase from 299,016 to 302,839 (+1.3%) and triangles from 148,188 to 154,248 (+4.1%). Time: Processing time for meta-cells increases slightly. For Level 6, meta-cell processing time increases from 144s to 154s (+10s) and the connection step increases by 2s. For Level 7, processing time increases from 161s to 171s. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Ensures a self-intersection-free surface, which is critical for volume rendering and simulation. Limitations: Increases mesh complexity (vertices and faces) compared to regular ambiguity treatments. The regular ambiguity treatment does not increase vertex or face count but only ensures manifoldness. When to Use: Use when constructing isosurfaces from adaptive octrees where self-intersections are unacceptable. Use when the scene requires exact Euclidean distance calculations without propagation errors. When Not to Use: Avoid if mesh size is a critical constraint and self-intersections can be tolerated or handled by other means. Avoid if processing time is extremely limited, as the geometric checks add overhead. The method is based on the work of Ju et al. [2006], who proposed a hybrid primal-dual approach for adaptive octrees. It was implemented and evaluated in the context of extracting isosurfaces from salt domes. The implementation uses a lookup table for Dual Marching Cubes configurations to identify ambiguous faces. name: Parallel Processing and Pipeline Optimization
body: This family covers parallel processing and pipeline optimization for Dual Marching Cubes surface extraction. It addresses topological consistency and parallel reconstruction by encoding neighborhood and connectivity information using a halfedge data structure. Unlike standard parallel extraction that produces unconnected primitives, it handles non-manifold edges (e.g., tunnels spanning two neighbor cells) and enables parallel mesh simplification. The pipeline operates on a regular 3D grid and processes cells in parallel. It resolves topological inconsistencies by generating a valid halfedge data structure that correctly handles non-manifold edges, such as tunnels spanning two neighbor cells. Connectivity and neighborhood information are encoded to support parallel processing and simplification. The specific grid definitions, lookup tables, and two-pass counting and generation structure are detailed in the child articles. The first phase of the algorithm. It determines exact memory requirements for vertex and quad buffers. It iterates over a voxel grid, classifying cells and accumulating counts based on precomputed lookup tables. It is read-only regarding output buffers. The complete surface extraction method. It generates a quadrilateral mesh with full connectivity information (1-ring neighbors). It combines static and dynamic lookup tables with parallel reduction algorithms. It builds on the Counting Pass but extends it for interactive performance on parallel hardware. A scheme to encode neighborhood and connectivity information in the DMC mesh, enabling parallel processing and simplification. Used to facilitate parallel simplification methods by identifying irregular elements based on face colors. The method originated in "A parallel dual marching cubes approach to quad only surface reconstruction". It addresses topological consistency and parallel reconstruction issues in Dual Marching Cubes. The approach was developed to handle ambiguous configurations and enable efficient parallel simplification of volume data. name: Dual Marching Cubes (Counting Pass)
head: DM counting pass, segment vertex/quad counter
body: The Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) Counting Pass is the first phase of a two-pass surface extraction pipeline that counts the number of vertices and quads required for a specific segment ID across a voxel grid, using corner bitmasks and precomputed lookup tables to avoid geometry generation overhead. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by relying on static lookup tables (DMVERTCOUNT, DMQUADCOUNT) to map cell configuration masks to exact memory requirements, deferring actual mesh construction to the subsequent pass. Inputs: voxelToSegId: A 1D array of uint16t mapping linear voxel indices to segment identifiers. segId: The target segment identifier to count geometry for. startX, startY, startZ, endX, endY, endZ: Inclusive bounding box coordinates defining the voxel grid region to traverse. XOFF, YOFF, ZOFF: Stride constants for 3D-to-1D index mapping. Outputs: vertCount: Total number of dual vertices required for the segment. quadCount: Total number of dual quads required for the segment. vertices: A dynamically allocated array of floats sized vertCount 3. counts: Temporary array storing accumulated corner bitmasks for each voxel in the bounding box. The result is packaged into a struct dmcresult: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct dmcresult { uint32t quadCount; uint32t vertCount; float vertices; float normals; uint32t triangles; }; DMVERTCOUNT[256]: A static const int8t array mapping cube configuration masks (0-255) to vertex counts. DMQUADCOUNT[256]: A static const int8t array mapping cube configuration masks (0-255) to quad counts. EDGETOCELLSEDGES[103]: Static const int8t array mapping edge indices to cell edge indices (triplets). EDGETOCELLSOFFS[103]: Static const int8t array mapping edge indices to cell edge offsets (triplets using XOFF, YOFF, ZOFF). The pass traverses the voxel grid in reverse order (from end to start) to handle index wrapping correctly. 1. Initialize Bounds: Decrement startX and startY by 1 to adjust for counting overshoot. Calculate window dimensions: X\WIN\SIZE = endX - startX + 1 Y\WIN\SIZE = endY - startY + 1 2. Initialize Accumulators: Set vertCount = 0 and quadCount = 0. Initialize counts array to zero for the bounding box region. 3. Traverse Voxel Grid: Initialize linear grid index i to endX + endY YOFF + endZ ZOFF. Iterate z from endZ down to startZ: Iterate y from endY down to startY: Iterate x from endX down to startX: a. Check Segment ID: If voxelToSegId[i] == segId: b. Compute Corner Mask: Compute wi = i - countoffset, where countoffset = startZ ZOFF. Accumulate corner bits into counts[wi] for each of the 8 voxel corners: python for c in range(8): counts[wi] |= (1 << c) c. Accumulate Counts: python vertCount += DMVERTCOUNT[counts[wi]] quadCount += DMQUADCOUNT[counts[wi]] d. Update Linear Index: Decrement i by 1. Adjust for Y-loop wrap: python i = i + XWINSIZE - YOFF Adjust for Z-loop wrap: python i = i + YWINSIZE YOFF - ZOFF 4. Allocate Buffers: Allocate vertex buffer: python vertices = [0.0] (vertCount 3) 5. Cleanup: Reset counts array to zero for the bounding box region to prepare for the next pass or segment. 6. Return Result: Populate and return struct dmcresult with vertCount, quadCount, and allocated buffers. XOFF, YOFF, ZOFF: Stride constants for 3D-to-1D index mapping. corner0 to corner7: Bit positions (0-7) representing the eight corners of a voxel cell, used to construct the 8-bit configuration mask. Grid Traversal Direction: The traversal is reversed (end to start). Explicit index reset logic using XWINSIZE, YWINSIZE, and stride constants is required to maintain correct 3D-to-1D mapping. Memory Allocation: Buffers are allocated based on counts. If vertCount or quadCount is zero, allocation should handle empty arrays gracefully. Segment ID Mismatch: Voxels not matching segId are skipped, contributing 0 to counts. Time Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of voxels in the bounding box. The pass performs a single iteration with constant-time bitmask updates and table lookups. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the counts array and O(1) for the lookup tables. The output buffers are allocated based on the result, but their size is not known until the pass completes. Strengths: Avoids geometry generation overhead; provides exact memory requirements for the subsequent generation pass. Limitations: Requires two passes; the counting pass alone does not produce a mesh. When to Use: When memory allocation must be precise and dynamic, or when implementing a parallel pipeline where the generation pass requires pre-allocated buffers. The Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) method is an alternative to the standard Marching Cubes algorithm, often used for its manifold properties and efficiency in parallel implementations. The counting pass is a specific optimization within the DMC pipeline, introduced in the context of GPU acceleration and parallel processing for volume rendering. It is part of a broader family of surface extraction techniques that separate memory sizing from geometry generation to facilitate parallel execution. chrisj/dual-marching-cubes, https://github.com/chrisj/dual-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Parallel Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) Pipeline
head: Multi-staged DMC pipeline, Parallel DMC on Regular Grids
body: The Parallel Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) Pipeline is a surface extraction method that generates a manifold quadrilateral mesh with full connectivity information (1-ring neighbors) from a regular 3D grid. It solves the problem of unconnected primitives and missing adjacency data inherent in standard parallel extraction by combining static and dynamic lookup tables with parallel reduction algorithms. Unlike standard parallel Marching Cubes which produces redundant and unconnected fragments, this method ensures topological consistency through a multi-staged pipeline that switches from block-based to cell-based processing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A regular 3D grid L of scalar values v{i,j,k} representing a function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, and an isovalue \alpha. Output: A manifold quadrilateral surface mesh with vertex positions, face connectivity, and 1-ring neighbor adjacency data. Data Structures: The pipeline relies on static lookup tables precomputed for all 23 canonical cell cases and dynamic tables generated during execution. 1. Vertex-Edges Table: Maps a cell case and a specific cell vertex to a 12-bit vector (1 bit per edge) representing the set of associated active edges. 2. Edge-Vertex Table: Maps a cell case and a specific edge to a 24-bit vector (2 bits per edge) identifying the associated cell vertex. 3. Vertex-Adjacencies Table: Maps a cell case and a cell vertex to a sorted set of tuples (V{zyx}, e), where V{zyx} is the offset to the adjacent cell and e is the associated edge, sorted in 1-ring order. 4. Case Table: A 3D array of dimensions (Nx - 1) \times (Ny - 1) \times (Nz - 1) storing the cell case for each cell in the volume. 5. Index Table: A 3D array of dimensions (Nx - 1) \times (Ny - 1) \times (Nz - 1) storing the index of the first face and vertex for each cell in the mesh buffers. For a cell (i,j,k) and its x-th vertex, the location in the vertex buffer is I{i,j,k} + x. Steps: 1. Block Selection: The volume is decomposed into blocks. For each block, the minimum and maximum density values are evaluated in parallel. If the condition \min \le \alpha < \max holds, the block is marked as selected, and its index is stored in a buffer. 2. Classification: One block is mapped to one thread group. Grid values for the block are loaded into local memory. For each cell (i,j,k) within the block, the 8 corner values are inspected relative to \alpha. A point v{i,j,k} is classified as inside if v{i,j,k} > \alpha and outside if v{i,j,k} \le \alpha. The resulting case is stored in the Case Table. 3. Indexing: A parallel all-prefix-sum (scan) algorithm is performed on vertex and face counts to compute total buffer sizes and map cells to unique locations in mesh buffers. The total count is transferred to the host for buffer allocation. During this scan, the number of relevant cells is counted, and their indices (i,j,k) are written to a buffer. This switches processing from block-based to cell-based. 4. Mesh Generation Phase 1 (Vertices): For each relevant cell, vertices are relocated using a Quadric Error Metric (QEM) based approach. The storage location in the mesh buffers is determined via dynamic lookup tables (derived from the Index Table). The 1-ring neighbors are gathered using the Vertex-Adjacencies Table. 5. Mesh Generation Phase 2 (Faces): Faces are generated using a parallel scheme where each cell chooses three edges sharing the same origin (along the x, y, and z axes). This results in four grid values being classified and 16 possible configurations. An extended Face Table maps local edges to adjacent cell edges to form quadrilaterals. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def paralleldmcpipeline(V, alpha, blocks): # 1. Block Selection selectedblocks = [] for block in blocks: minval, maxval = computeminmax(block) if minval <= alpha < maxval: selectedblocks.append(block.index) # 2. Classification (Parallel per block) casetable = empty3darray(Nx-1, Ny-1, Nz-1) for blockidx in selectedblocks: block = getblock(blockidx) # Load block values into local memory localV = loadlocalmemory(block) for cell in block.cells: i, j, k = cell.coords # Classify 8 corners insidemask = 0 for corner in cell.corners: if localV[corner] > alpha: insidemask |= (1 << cornerindex) casetable[i, j, k] = getcanonicalcase(insidemask) # 3. Indexing (Parallel Scan) # Compute vertex counts per cell based on casetable vertexcounts = computevertexcounts(casetable) # Parallel prefix sum (scan) # A'[i] = sum(A[0]...A[i-1]) vertexoffsets = parallelscan(vertexcounts) # Transfer total count to host totalvertices = vertexoffsets[-1] + vertexcounts[-1] host.allocatevertexbuffer(totalvertices) # Count relevant cells and store their indices relevantcells = [] for i in range(Nx-1): for j in range(Ny-1): for k in range(Nz-1): if casetable[i, j, k] != 0: # 0 is empty case relevantcells.append((i, j, k)) # 4. Mesh Generation Phase 1 (Vertices) for (i, j, k) in relevantcells: case = casetable[i, j, k] baseidx = vertexoffsets[i, j, k] # Get edges for this case and vertex # Vertex-Edges Table: (case, vertex) -> 12-bit vector # Edge-Vertex Table: (case, edge) -> 24-bit vector for vidx in range(numverticesforcase(case)): # Relocate vertex using QEM pos = relocatevertexqem(V, i, j, k, case, vidx) # Store in buffer bufferidx = baseidx + vidx vertexbuffer[bufferidx] = pos # Gather 1-ring neighbors using Vertex-Adjacencies Table # Table returns sorted tuples (Vzyx, e) neighbors = get1ringneighbors(case, vidx) adjacencybuffer[bufferidx] = neighbors # 5. Mesh Generation Phase 2 (Faces) # Face generation relies on parallel scheme [SDC09] # Each cell generates faces based on 3 edges sharing origin facecount = computefacecounts(casetable) faceoffsets = parallelscan(facecount) totalfaces = faceoffsets[-1] + facecount[-1] host.allocatefacebuffer(totalfaces) for (i, j, k) in relevantcells: case = casetable[i, j, k] basefaceidx = faceoffsets[i, j, k] # Choose 3 edges sharing same origin (x, y, z axes) # This defines 4 grid values and 16 configurations edges = selectoriginedges(case) # Use extended Face Table to map local edges to adjacent cell edges # Form quadrilaterals faces = generatequadrilaterals(case, edges, vertexbuffer) for fidx, face in enumerate(faces): facebuffer[basefaceidx + fidx] = face Parameters: Grid Spacing Factor: The regular grid definition uses a spacing factor of 4, defined as L = \{(i \cdot 4 \cdot x, j \cdot 4 \cdot y, k \cdot 4 \cdot z): i = 0,...,Nx; j = 0,...,Ny; k = 0,...,Nz\}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unconnected Primitives: Standard parallel processing analyzes cells independently, leading to unconnected primitives and redundant computations. This is mitigated by the static/dynamic lookup tables ensuring manifold connectivity. Precision: The classification uses strict inequality v{i,j,k} > \alpha for inside and \le \alpha for outside. Register Limits: The QEM-based vertex relocation is chosen over complex QEF minimization via pseudoinverse to avoid performance penalties from limited register counts on parallel hardware. Time Complexity: The pipeline is dominated by parallel operations: block selection, classification, and prefix sums (scan), all of which are O(N) where N is the number of cells or blocks. The mesh generation is also parallelized per cell. Memory Complexity: The method doubles memory effort due to the Case and Index tables, which are 3D arrays of size (Nx - 1) \times (Ny - 1) \times (Nz - 1). However, it only allocates memory for relevant parts of the volume if combined with block culling. Performance: The switch from block-based to cell-based processing in the Cell Selection stage significantly accelerates mesh generation. The QEM approach is less computationally complex than QEF minimization, avoiding register pressure penalties. Strengths: Generates a manifold surface with full connectivity and 1-ring neighborhood information, suitable for interactive applications. Limitations: The QEM-based relocation achieves lower quality than QEF minimization, though it is sufficient for preserving terrain volume. The method is based on Dual Marching Cubes by Nielson [Nie04], which provides high-quality manifold surfaces but lacks interactivity in parallel settings. The pipeline extends DMC with a novel parallel processing scheme using static and dynamic lookup tables and parallel reduction algorithms. It was developed to address the lack of 1-ring neighbor information in standard surface extraction algorithms, which typically requires extensive post-processing. The vertex relocation uses the Quadric Error Metric [GH97]. name: Dual Nodes Generation with Connectivity Inversion
head: DMC with Ambiguous Face Handling, Tunnel Recovery
body: This method resolves non-manifold edge configurations in Manifold Dual Marching Cubes (MDMC) by generating two dual nodes instead of one for cells sharing ambiguous faces, thereby recovering topological tunnels. It differs from standard Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) by analyzing the connectivity of both interior (blue) and exterior (white) vertex components to determine node placement, whereas standard DMC relies solely on interior components. Inputs: A voxel grid or octree cell c with 8 vertices. Scalar field values at vertices to determine inside/outside status relative to isosurface \partial V. The Manifold Dual Marching Cubes (MDMC) lookup table configuration for the cell. Outputs: A set of dual nodes (surface points) within cell c and its adjacent cells Ac. Connectivity information linking these nodes to form manifold triangles. Data Structures: Cell Graph: A graph G=(V, E) where V contains the 8 vertices of the cell and E contains the 12 edges connecting them. Vertex Status: Each vertex v \in V is classified as: Blue: Inside \partial V (scalar value indicates interior). White: Outside \partial V (scalar value indicates exterior). Connected Components: Sets of vertices connected by edges where both endpoints share the same status (Blue-Blue or White-White). Steps: 1. Graph Construction: Represent the current cell c as a graph with 8 vertices and 12 edges. 2. Vertex Classification: Classify each of the 8 vertices as Blue (inside) or White (outside) based on the scalar field threshold. 3. Component Identification: Identify all Blue Connected Components (BCCs): maximal sets of blue vertices connected by blue-blue edges. Identify all White Connected Components (WCCs): maximal sets of white vertices connected by white-white edges. 4. Ambiguity Check: Determine if the cell configuration corresponds to an ambiguous face case identified by the MDMC LUT. 5. Node Generation Logic: Standard Case: If the cell has a single Blue Connected Component and no ambiguous faces, generate one dual node per BCC using standard DMC rules. Ambiguous Case: If the cell has a single Blue Connected Component but contains one or more ambiguous faces: a. Enumerate the set of adjacent cells Ac that share these ambiguous faces. b. For each cell in Ac, extract its White Connected Components. c. Verify that the existence of an ambiguous face implies at least two White Connected Components in the local topology. d. Use the White Connected Components to generate dual nodes in cell c and all adjacent cells in Ac. This results in the creation of two dual nodes instead of one. 6. Tunnel Recovery: The generation of two nodes at ambiguous interfaces ensures that tunnels in \partial V are preserved and non-manifold edges are eliminated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatedualnodes(cell, scalarfield, mcmclut, adjacentcells): """ Generates dual nodes for a single cell using connectivity inversion. Args: cell: Object containing 8 vertex indices and 12 edge definitions. scalarfield: Array of scalar values at vertex positions. mcmclut: Lookup table from Manifold Dual Marching Cubes. adjacentcells: List of cell objects sharing faces with cell. Returns: List of dual node positions and connectivity data. """ # 1. Get vertex values and classify vertexvalues = [scalarfield[v] for v in cell.vertices] # Assume threshold is 0.0; inside if value > 0.0 isinside = [v > 0.0 for v in vertexvalues] # 2. Build adjacency graph for the cell edges = cell.edges # List of (v1idx, v2idx) # 3. Find Connected Components bluecomponents = findconnectedcomponents(isinside, edges, targetstatus=True) whitecomponents = findconnectedcomponents(isinside, edges, targetstatus=False) # 4. Check for ambiguous configuration via MDMC LUT configindex = 0 for i, inside in enumerate(isinside): if inside: configindex |= (1 << i) isambiguous = mcmclut.isambiguous(configindex) dualnodes = [] if isambiguous and len(bluecomponents) == 1: # Ambiguous case with single blue component requires connectivity inversion # Process adjacent cells sharing the ambiguous face for adjc in adjacentcells: adjvalues = [scalarfield[v] for v in adjc.vertices] adjinside = [v > 0.0 for v in adjvalues] adjwhite = findconnectedcomponents(adjinside, adjc.edges, targetstatus=False) # Existence of ambiguous face implies at least two white connected components if len(adjwhite) >= 2: # Generate dual nodes based on the separation of white components # Geometric placement uses the centroid of each white component node1 = computecentroid(adjwhite[0], adjc.vertices) node2 = computecentroid(adjwhite[1], adjc.vertices) dualnodes.append(node1) dualnodes.append(node2) else: # Fallback to standard single node if topology does not split node = computecentroid(bluecomponents[0], cell.vertices) dualnodes.append(node) else: # Standard DMC behavior: one node per blue component for comp in bluecomponents: node = computecentroid(comp, cell.vertices) dualnodes.append(node) return dualnodes def findconnectedcomponents(isinside, edges, targetstatus): """ Finds connected components of vertices that satisfy targetstatus. """ n = len(isinside) visited = [False] n components = [] adj = [[] for in range(n)] for v1, v2 in edges: if isinside[v1] == targetstatus and isinside[v2] == targetstatus: adj[v1].append(v2) adj[v2].append(v1) for i in range(n): if not visited[i] and isinside[i] == targetstatus: comp = [] stack = [i] visited[i] = True while stack: u = stack.pop() comp.append(u) for v in adj[u]: if not visited[v]: visited[v] = True stack.append(v) components.append(comp) return components def computecentroid(vertexindices, cellvertices): """ Computes the geometric centroid of the given vertices. """ coords = [cellvertices[i] for i in vertexindices] centroid = sum(coords) / len(coords) return centroid Parameters: Threshold: The scalar value separating inside/outside. Not given in the sources. \lambda (Curvature Parameter): Used in the broader adaptive extraction context to determine refinement. Typical value: 0.9. Max Octree Depth: Limits the resolution of the adaptive grid. Typical value: 7. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Manifold Edges: Standard DMC LUT may create non-manifold edges if it only considers blue connected components in cells sharing an ambiguous face. This method specifically addresses this by inverting to white components. Degenerate Triangles: Standard DMC2 can produce more degenerated triangles and struggle with sharp edges compared to this method. Multiple Ambiguous Faces: If a cell has multiple ambiguous faces (e.g., three), the logic must ensure that the white component analysis correctly separates all relevant surface portions. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of cells, with a constant factor increase due to the additional graph traversal for white components in ambiguous cases. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the graph structure for each cell and the connected components. Performance: On the 'Block' dataset (512x512x128 voxels, \lambda=0.9, max depth 7), this method produced 46,888 triangles, compared to 54,888 triangles for DMC2. Strengths: Recovers tunnels, eliminates non-manifold edges, produces fewer triangles, and captures sharp edges better than DMC2. Limitations: Requires analysis of adjacent cells for full connectivity resolution in some ambiguous configurations. This method was developed as part of an adaptive surface extraction algorithm from anisotropic volumetric data using generalized octrees. It addresses specific topological failures in Dual Marching Cubes when handling ambiguous face configurations, which are common in complex volumetric data. name: Mesh simplification via face coloring
head: Cell-based coloring, DMC simplification, Uniform structure coloring, Vertex and face coloring for parallel mesh processing
body: Mesh simplification via face coloring is a parallel method for reducing the element count of dual marching cubes (DMC) meshes by identifying and removing quadrilaterals based on vertex valence patterns. It solves the problem of excessive mesh density in isosurface extraction by leveraging the uniform structure of volume data to assign colors to cells, vertices, and faces, enabling conflict-free parallel simplification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dual marching cubes mesh consisting of quadrilaterals derived from Dual Mesh Building. Output: A simplified mesh with reduced element count and a recomputed halfedge data structure. Data Structures: Cell Index: 3D integer tuple (i, j, k) representing the position in the volume grid. Cell Color (cv): Integer in [0, 7] derived from the cell index. Edge Color (ce): Integer in [0, 23] derived from the cell color and local edge index. Quadrilateral Color (cq): Integer in [0, 4] after reduction. Vertex Valence: The number of quadrilaterals incident to a vertex. Formulas: 1. Cell Color: Derived from the 3D cell index (i, j, k) using bitwise operations: cv = (i \& 1) \ | \ ((j \& 1) \ll 1) \ | \ ((k \& 1) \ll 2) This results in 8 distinct colors. 2. Edge Color: Derived from the cell color cv and the local edge index e incident to vertex v0: ce = 3 \times cv + e where e \in \{0, 1, 2\} corresponds to local edges e0, e3, e8. This results in 24 distinct edge colors. 3. Quadrilateral Color: Each cell edge corresponds to a maximum of one quadrilateral, so the edge color is transferred directly to the quadrilateral. A reduction kernel then maps colors \ge 5 to the range [0, 4]. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Cell Colors: For every active cell in the volume grid, compute cv using the cell color formula. 2. Transfer Colors to Vertices: Vertices inherit colors from their adjacent cells because they only have neighbors in adjacent cells. 3. Compute Edge Colors: For each cell, compute the colors of its edges e0, e3, e8 using ce = 3 \times cv + e. 4. Transfer Colors to Quadrilaterals: Assign the computed edge color ce to the quadrilateral associated with that edge. 5. Reduce Quadrilateral Colors: A second kernel processes faces to reduce the number of quadrilateral colors to 5. It iterates through all quadrilaterals with colors \ge 5 and assigns a new color between 0 and 4 by checking which color does not yet appear in its neighborhood. 6. Identify Simplification Candidates: Identify quadrilaterals based on the valence patterns of their incident vertices. Pattern 3-X–3-Y: Vertices with valence 3, X, 3, Y (where X and Y are other valences). Pattern 3-3-3-3: All four incident vertices have valence 3. 7. Simplify Elements: Remove quadrilaterals identified in Step 6. For the 3-X–3-Y pattern, vertices are repositioned during simplification. For the 3-3-3-3 pattern, elements are removed directly. 8. Recompute Halfedge Data Structure: After each simplification step, the halfedge data structure must be recomputed to maintain connectivity integrity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecellcolor(i, j, k): """Compute cell color from 3D index using bitwise pattern.""" return (i & 1) | ((j & 1) << 1) | ((k & 1) << 2) def computeedgecolor(cellcolor, localedgeindex): """Compute edge color from cell color and local edge index e in {0, 1, 2}.""" return 3 cellcolor + localedgeindex def reducequadrilateralcolors(quads): """ Reduce quadrilateral colors to 5 colors. quads: list of quadrilaterals, each with a 'color' attribute and 'neighbors' list. """ for quad in quads: if quad.color >= 5: neighborcolors = {n.color for n in quad.neighbors} newcolor = 0 while newcolor in neighborcolors: newcolor += 1 quad.color = newcolor return quads def simplifymesh(mesh): """ Simplify the mesh based on valence patterns and face coloring. mesh: Dual marching cubes mesh object with cells, vertices, and quads. """ # Compute vertex valences from mesh connectivity vertexvalences = {} for quad in mesh.quads: for v in quad.vertices: vertexvalences[v.id] = vertexvalences.get(v.id, 0) + 1 quadstoremove = [] for quad in mesh.quads: valences = [vertexvalences[v.id] for v in quad.vertices] if all(v == 3 for v in valences): quadstoremove.append(quad) elif valences[0] == 3 and valences[2] == 3: quadstoremove.append(quad) for quad in quadstoremove: mesh.removequad(quad) # Recompute halfedge data structure after simplification mesh.recomputehalfedgestructure() return mesh Parameters: Number of cell colors: 8. Number of edge colors: 24. Final number of quadrilateral colors: 5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and Boundaries: Boundary cells do not generate quadrilaterals if an entry in the hash table bucket is an invalid index. Valence Patterns: The 3-X–3-Y pattern simplification repositions vertices, which increases the deviation from the iso-value. Quality Trade-off: Simplification improves quadrilateral quality but reduces triangle quality and increases the number of irregular vertices for triangular meshes. Halfedge Recomputation: The halfedge data structure must be recomputed after each simplification step, which is computationally expensive due to global memory access on the GPU. Generates the lookup tables for dual marching cubes. It sets itself apart by focusing on the topological rules for vertex placement rather than mesh simplification. Choose it when defining the core extraction logic. Link Ensures the resulting mesh is manifold. It sets itself apart by handling non-manifold configurations explicitly. Choose it when topological correctness is critical. Link Builds the connectivity structure for the mesh. It sets itself apart by providing the necessary data structure for operations like simplification. Choose it when you need to traverse or modify the mesh topology. Link Time Complexity: The coloring steps are parallel and efficient. The halfedge data structure computation is time-consuming due to many global memory accesses on the GPU. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for cell, edge, and quadrilateral colors. The reduction step requires temporary storage for neighbor checks. Measured Performance: For the human skull surface, 352,337 elements with the 3-X–3-Y pattern were simplified, compared to 167,537 with the previous method. The 3-3-3-3 pattern simplification reduces the total number of elements by 5%. Scaling: The method is designed for parallel execution on GPUs, leveraging the uniform structure of volume data. Strengths: Significantly reduces element count compared to previous methods. Improves quadrilateral quality. Limitations: Increases deviation from the iso-value for 3-X–3-Y patterns. Reduces triangle quality. Requires expensive halfedge recomputation. When to Use: When a high-quality quad-only mesh is desired and element count reduction is important. When Not to Use: When strict adherence to the iso-value is critical (due to vertex repositioning in 3-X–3-Y patterns) or when triangle quality is more important than quad quality. The method was introduced in a parallel dual marching cubes approach to quad-only surface reconstruction. It builds on the uniform structure of volume data to enable efficient parallel processing. The method was evaluated on various datasets including torso, body, synthetic iWP, and gen2 data sets. name: Halfedge Data Structure Construction
head: Dual mesh connectivity, Halfedge linking
body: This method constructs the connectivity information for the quadrilateral mesh generated by Dual Marching Cubes, specifically storing vertices, faces, next halfedges, and twin edge relationships. It solves the problem of efficiently linking halfedges across cell boundaries on the GPU by using a hash table to group halfedges by their incident vertex pairs, handling boundary and non-manifold edges in parallel. It builds on Dual Mesh Building and relates to Dual Marching Cubes Table Generation, Manifold Dual Marching Cubes, and Mesh simplification via face coloring. Inputs: List of quadrilateral faces, where each face is defined by four vertex indices. Outputs: vertexhalfedge: Array mapping each vertex index to the index of one outgoing halfedge. facehalfedge: Array mapping each face index to the index of its first halfedge. halfedgestartvertex: Array mapping each halfedge index to its start vertex. halfedgeface: Array mapping each halfedge index to its face index. halfedgenext: Array mapping each halfedge index to the index of the next halfedge in the face loop. halfedgetwin: Array mapping each halfedge index to its twin halfedge index (or -1 if boundary). Hash Table: Key: 64-bit unsigned integer (unsigned long long int). Bits 0–31: Smaller vertex index of the edge. Bits 32–63: Larger vertex index of the edge. This ordering ensures that distinct threads processing the same geometric edge compute the identical key. Value: A counter representing the number of halfedges currently stored in the bucket. Bucket Storage: An array or dynamic structure where halfedge indices are appended at the position determined by the counter value before incrementing. 1. Kernel 1 (Local Information): Each thread processes one quadrilateral face. For each of the four vertices, the thread determines the halfedge indices. For each of the four halfedges in the quadrilateral, the thread stores the index of the start vertex, the face index, and the index of the next halfedge. The thread computes a hash key from the start and end vertices, uses atomicAdd on the hash table counter for this key to find the insertion position within the bucket, and stores the halfedge index in the bucket at that position. The thread also updates the vertexhalfedge entry for the start vertex and the facehalfedge entry for the face. 2. Kernel 2 (Global Information): The kernel iterates through all entries in the hash table to connect twin edges. For each bucket (edge), if it contains only one halfedge, it is marked as a boundary edge. If it contains two halfedges, they are set as twins. If it contains four halfedges (non-manifold edge, e.g., a tunnel between cells), the algorithm connects twins by pairing halfedges that point in opposite directions to ensure consistent face orientation. Hash key construction: \text{key} = (\min(u, v) \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFFFFFF}) \ | \ ((\max(u, v) \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFFFFFF}) \ll 32) where u and v are the start and end vertex indices of the halfedge. Bucket insertion position: \text{pos} = \text{atomicAdd}(\text{counters}, \text{key}, 1). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kernellocalinfo(quads, hashtable, counters, hestartv, heface, henext, vertexhe, facehe): for faceidx, quad in enumerate(quads): v0, v1, v2, v3 = quad vertices = [v0, v1, v2, v3] for i in range(4): heidx = faceidx 4 + i startv = vertices[i] endv = vertices[(i + 1) % 4] nextheidx = faceidx 4 + ((i + 1) % 4) hestartv[heidx] = startv heface[heidx] = faceidx henext[heidx] = nextheidx if vertexhe[startv] == -1: vertexhe[startv] = heidx if facehe[faceidx] == -1: facehe[faceidx] = heidx u, v = (startv, endv) if startv < endv else (endv, startv) key = (u & 0xFFFFFFFF) | ((v & 0xFFFFFFFF) << 32) pos = atomicadd(counters[key], 1) hashtable[key].append(heidx) def kernelglobalinfo(hashtable, hestartv, hetwin): for key, bucket in hashtable.items(): halfedges = bucket n = len(halfedges) if n == 1: hetwin[halfedges[0]] = -1 elif n == 2: hetwin[halfedges[0]] = halfedges[1] hetwin[halfedges[1]] = halfedges[0] elif n == 4: minv = key & 0xFFFFFFFF maxv = (key >> 32) & 0xFFFFFFFF fwd = [h for h in halfedges if hestartv[h] == minv] bwd = [h for h in halfedges if hestartv[h] == maxv] hetwin[fwd[0]] = bwd[0] hetwin[bwd[0]] = fwd[0] hetwin[fwd[1]] = bwd[1] hetwin[bwd[1]] = fwd[1] Note: atomicadd is a standard GPU primitive for atomic addition. Atomic operations: atomicAdd used for counter increment. Hash table size: Not given in the sources. Non-manifold edges: Tunnels between cells may result in an edge containing four halfedges. Precision: The hash key uses 64-bit integers to avoid collisions. Vertex indices must fit within 32 bits. Boundary edges: Edges with only one halfedge are correctly identified as boundaries. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tested on Intel Core i7-8700, 32 GB memory, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti 11GB. Strengths: Parallel construction, handles non-manifold geometry, robust for volume rendering isosurfaces. Limitations: Hash table overhead, potential for collisions if vertex indices exceed 32 bits. The method is part of the Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) approach for quad-only surface reconstruction. It was developed to efficiently generate connectivity for the dual mesh on the GPU, addressing the limitations of previous methods that struggled with non-manifold cases or required sequential processing. name: Parallel Dual Marching Cube
body: Parallel Dual Marching Cube (PDMC) is an intersection-free iso-surface extraction method that processes a 3D signed distance field (SDF) grid on the GPU to produce a triangle or quadrilateral mesh. It is implemented as a CUDA kernel accessible via a PyTorch C++ extension. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D signed distance field (SDF) grid tensor grid of shape [dimX, dimY, dimZ] residing on a CUDA device. The values must be contiguous. Parameters: isovalue (scalar): The threshold for extraction. Default: 0.0. dtype (torch.float32 or torch.float64): Precision for vertex coordinates and grid processing. returnquads (bool): If True, output quad faces [F, 4]; if False, output triangle faces [F, 3]. normalize (bool): If True, vertices are normalized to [0, 1]; if False, they remain in [0, dim-1]. Outputs: verts: Tensor of shape [V, 3] containing vertex coordinates. faces: Tensor of shape [F, 3] or [F, 4] containing face indices (starting from 0). Data Structures: The CUDA kernel uses the following device storage structures: Vertex<T>: Struct with fields x, y, z of type T, stored contiguously. Quad<T>: Struct with fields i, j, k, l of type T, stored contiguously. Triangle<T>: Struct with fields i, j, k of type T, stored contiguously. Edge<T>: Struct with fields i, j of type T, stored contiguously. CUDualMC device storage: tempstorage: IndexType for prefix sums. firstcellused: IndexType. usedcellindex: IndexType. usedtofirstmcvert: IndexType. usedcellcode: uint8t. usedtofirstmcpatch: IndexType. mcverttocell: IndexType. mcverttoedge: Edge<Vertex<Scalar>>. mcverttype: uint8t (values 0-2 indicate x/y/z entering, 3-5 indicate x/y/z exiting). quads: Quad<IndexType>. tris: Triangle<IndexType>. firsttriscreate: IndexType. firstvertscreate: IndexType. verts: Vertex<Scalar>. Linearization Functions: To map 3D grid coordinates to 1D indices, the method uses: gA(x, y, z) = z + \text{dims}[2] \times (y + \text{dims}[1] \times x) where x is the slowest-varying dimension and z is the fastest. The inverse linearization functions are: gX(\text{id}) = \text{id} / (\text{dims}[2] \times \text{dims}[1]) gY(\text{id}) = (\text{id} / \text{dims}[2]) \% \text{dims}[1] gZ(\text{id}) = \text{id} \% \text{dims}[2] Algorithm Steps: 1. Degeneracy Check: Check if the input grid values are entirely above or below the isovalue; if so, return empty vertex and face tensors to skip degenerate cases. 2. Padding: Pad the input SDF grid with a 1-voxel border filled with isovalue + 1 on all six sides to handle boundary conditions during extraction. 3. Kernel Launch: Pass the padded grid and isovalue to the CUDA kernel, which populates device buffers for vertices, quads, and triangles. 4. Coordinate Offset: Subtract 1 from all output vertex coordinates to offset the padding added in step 2. 5. Normalization (Optional): If normalization is enabled, divide vertex coordinates by (dimX-1, dimY-1, dimZ-1) to map them to the [0, 1] range; otherwise, keep them in [0, dim-1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def paralleldualmarchingcube(grid, isovalue=0.0, returnquads=False, normalize=True, dtype=torch.float32): """ Extracts an isosurface from a 3D SDF grid using Parallel Dual Marching Cube. Args: grid: 3D tensor or nested list of shape (dimX, dimY, dimZ). isovalue: Scalar threshold. returnquads: If True, returns quad faces; else triangle faces. normalize: If True, normalizes vertices to [0, 1]. dtype: Precision type. Returns: verts: Tensor of shape (V, 3). faces: Tensor of shape (F, 3) or (F, 4). """ # Convert input to tensor to handle list inputs and ensure CUDA residency grid = torch.astensor(grid, dtype=dtype, device="cuda") # Step 1: Degeneracy Check if grid.min() >= isovalue or grid.max() <= isovalue: return torch.zeros((0, 3), dtype=dtype, device=grid.device), torch.zeros((0, 4), dtype=torch.int32, device=grid.device) dimX, dimY, dimZ = grid.shape # Step 2: Padding grid = F.pad(grid, (1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1), "constant", isovalue + 1) # Step 3: Kernel Launch # The CUDA kernel is invoked via a compiled C++ extension (e.g., C.CUDualMC.forward) # which populates device buffers for vertices, quads, and triangles. # A step the sources do not give is a comment saying so. vertsraw, quads, tris = cudakernelcall(grid, isovalue) # Step 4: Coordinate Offset verts = vertsraw - 1 # Step 5: Normalization (Optional) if normalize: verts = verts / (torch.tensor([dimX, dimY, dimZ], dtype=verts.dtype, device=grid.device) - 1) if returnquads: return verts, quads else: return verts, tris Dual Marching Cubes with GPU Mesh Simplification is a parallel isosurface extraction method that computes cell intersections using an asymptotic decider to resolve ambiguities, outputting a quadrilateral mesh stored in a halfedge data structure. It extends the Parallel Dual Marching Cube method by adding a GPU-based mesh simplification step to reduce vertex count and improve mesh quality. Unlike standard Marching Cubes which produces triangles, this method produces quadrilaterals. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Intersection-free extraction, parallel processing on GPU, supports both triangle and quad outputs. Limitations: Requires a CUDA-capable GPU; the input grid must be contiguous and reside on the CUDA device. When to use: When extracting isosurfaces from large 3D SDF grids on the GPU with a need for intersection-free results. When not to use: When running on CPU-only systems, or when the input grid is not a signed distance field or does not reside on the GPU. Parallel Dual Marching Cube was introduced as part of the PaMO (Parallel Mesh Optimization) project by Oh et al. in 2025. It is an intersection-free iso-surface extraction module used in PaMO. seonghunn/pdmc, https://github.com/seonghunn/pdmc, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Dual Marching Cubes with GPU Mesh Simplification
head: DMC with GPU Mesh Simplification, Parallel Dual Marching Cube with Simplification
body: Dual Marching Cubes with GPU Mesh Simplification is a parallel isosurface extraction method that computes cell intersections using an asymptotic decider to resolve ambiguities, outputting a quadrilateral mesh stored in a halfedge data structure. It extends the Parallel Dual Marching Cube method by adding a GPU-based mesh simplification step to reduce vertex count. Unlike standard Marching Cubes which produces triangles, this method produces quadrilaterals, offering better quadrilateral quality than Dual Contouring (DC) while maintaining topological correctness in most cases. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D signed distance field (SDF) grid defined on a regular voxel grid. Output: A quadrilateral mesh stored in a halfedge data structure. Data Structures: The method uses a halfedge data structure to store the resulting mesh. The specific field layouts for the halfedge structure are not detailed in the sources. Steps: 1. Parallel Cell Processing: Process each cell of the input grid in parallel on the GPU. For each cell, determine the intersection of the isosurface with the cell edges using the SDF values at the vertices. 2. Ambiguity Resolution: Use an asymptotic decider to resolve topological ambiguities within cells where the standard dual marching cubes configuration is ambiguous. 3. Quadrilateral Generation: Generate quadrilateral faces based on the resolved intersections. The output is a mesh composed entirely of quadrilaterals. 4. GPU Mesh Simplification: Perform mesh simplification on the GPU to reduce the number of vertices and quads. This step eliminates vertices and quadrilaterals based on specific vertex valence patterns. Simplification Criteria: Vertices and quads are eliminated if their vertex valence pattern matches either: 3-X-3-Y where X, Y \ge 5 3-3-3-3 Implementation: The simplification is implemented using a face coloring scheme with exactly 5 colors. This coloring scheme is executed on the GPU to identify eligible vertices/quads for elimination in parallel. 5. Output: Return the simplified quadrilateral mesh in the halfedge data structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualmarchingcubeswithsimplification(sdfgrid, isovalue): """ Extracts a quadrilateral mesh from an SDF grid using Dual Marching Cubes and simplifies it using a 5-color face coloring scheme. Args: sdfgrid: 3D array of signed distance values. isovalue: The scalar value defining the isosurface. Returns: simplifiedquads: List of quadrilaterals, each a list of 4 vertex indices. halfedges: List of halfedge records for the mesh. """ D, H, W = sdfgrid.shape quads = [] halfedges = [] # Step 1 & 2: Parallel cell processing and ambiguity resolution # Each thread block processes a subset of cells for d in range(D - 1): for h in range(H - 1): for w in range(W - 1): # Sample SDF at 8 corners of the cell vals = [sdfgrid[d+i, h+j, w+k] for i in (0,1) for j in (0,1) for k in (0,1)] # Determine which edges are intersected intersectededges = [] for eidx in range(12): v1, v2 = EDGEVERTICES[eidx] if (vals[v1] < isovalue) != (vals[v2] < isovalue): intersectededges.append(eidx) # Asymptotic decider resolves topology # Standard dual marching cubes configuration lookup table cellquads = asymptoticdecider(intersectededges, vals, isovalue) for q in cellquads: quads.append(q) # Step 3: Quadrilateral Generation & Halfedge construction for i, q in enumerate(quads): halfedges.append({'face': i, 'next': (i + 1) % len(quads), 'vertex': q[0]}) # Step 4: GPU Mesh Simplification # Compute vertex valences (number of quads sharing each vertex) valences = {} for q in quads: for v in q: valences[v] = valences.get(v, 0) + 1 # Identify vertices matching elimination patterns eligible = [] for v, val in valences.items(): # Pattern 3-3-3-3: vertex valence is 3, and all adjacent vertices in dual graph have valence 3 # Pattern 3-X-3-Y: vertex valence is 3, opposite neighbors have valence 3, others >= 5 # Simplified check for pseudocode completeness if val == 3: eligible.append(v) # 5-color face coloring scheme colors = [0] len(quads) for i in range(len(quads)): used = set() for j in range(len(quads)): if i == j: continue if any(v in quads[i] for v in quads[j]): used.add(colors[j]) for c in range(5): if c not in used: colors[i] = c break # Eliminate eligible vertices and associated quads simplifiedquads = [] for i, q in enumerate(quads): if any(v in eligible for v in q) and colors[i] % 2 == 0: continue simplifiedquads.append(q) return simplifiedquads, halfedges EDGEVERTICES = [ (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7), # bottom/top faces (0,2), (1,3), (4,6), (5,7), # side faces (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7) # vertical edges ] def asymptoticdecider(intersectededges, vals, isovalue): # Standard asymptotic decider logic resolves topological ambiguities # Returns list of quads, each quad is a list of 4 vertex indices return [] Parameters: Number of Colors: Exactly 5 colors are used for the face coloring scheme. Valence Thresholds: For the 3-X-3-Y pattern, X and Y must be \ge 5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tunnels: The algorithm cannot generate a topologically correct surface when a tunnel exists inside a single cell or spans across two neighboring cells. Non-manifold Vertices: DMC produces more non-manifold vertices than DMCS due to fewer total vertices, but DC generates one order of magnitude more non-manifold vertices than DMC and DMCS when a cell is intersected by more than one branch. Standard Marching Cubes (MC) and Triangulated Marching Cubes (TMC) do not generate non-manifold vertices, unlike DMC, DMCS, and DC. Time and Memory Complexity: The method is parallelized on the GPU, allowing for efficient processing of large datasets. Specific time and memory complexity formulas are not provided in the sources. Measured Performance: Performance benchmarks on various datasets are provided in: | Dataset | Dimensions | Voxels | Time (ms) | Vertices | Quads | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Male head (CT) | 256×256×113 | 616M | 113 | 611M | 189M | | Engine (CT) | 256×256×256 | 310M | 996 | 311M | 40M | | Knee (MRI) | 512×512×87 | 3,467M | 679 | 3,433M | 967M | | Kummer surface (Synth) | 256×256×256 | 265M | 752 | 263M | 856M | | Male head (MRI) | 256×256×256 | 1,979M | 810 | 1,962M | 482M | | Female head (MRI) | 256×256×109 | 732M | 292 | 724M | 980M | | Neovius surface (Synth) | 256×256×256 | 644M | 956 | 640M | 992M | | Porsche (CT) | 559×1023×347 | 1,420M | 200 | 1,420M | 238M | | Steiner surface (Synth) | 512×512×512 | 1,232M | 672 | 1,232M | 184M | Scaling: The method scales well with dataset size due to GPU parallelization. Performance varies based on dataset complexity and topology. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Generates better quadrilateral quality than Dual Contouring (DC). Generates better triangle quality than Marching Cubes (MC). GPU-based simplification reduces vertex count. Limitations: Cannot handle tunnels within or spanning cells correctly. Produces more non-manifold vertices than DMCS due to fewer total vertices. Generates non-manifold vertices, unlike standard MC and TMC. When to Use: Use when high-quality quadrilateral meshes are required from SDF data. Use when GPU acceleration is available and performance is critical. Avoid when topological correctness in the presence of tunnels is required. When Not to Use: Do not use if non-manifold vertices are unacceptable and DMCS is not an option. Do not use if the data contains tunnels within or spanning cells. Origin: The method is described in "A parallel dual marching cubes approach to quad only surface reconstruction". History and Development: The method builds on the Parallel Dual Marching Cube method. It adds GPU-based mesh simplification to reduce vertex count.
