name: Load-Balanced Isosurfacing on Multi-GPU Clusters
head: Cost-Heuristic Block Distribution, Preprocessing-Based Load Balancing
body: This method efficiently distributes isosurfacing workloads across multiple GPUs in a cluster by using preprocessing to estimate the computational cost of volume blocks, maximizing load uniformity over a user-defined range of isovalues. Unlike naive round-robin assignment which yields unpredictable speedups due to data-dependent work variance, this technique uses a linear cost heuristic derived from triangle counts and hardware profiling to assign blocks to GPUs, ensuring balanced work distribution. It builds on Marching Cubes Job Scheduling by providing the specific cost estimation and assignment algorithms required for multi-GPU clusters. Inputs: Volume data V of resolution Rx \times Ry \times Rz, treated as an array of cuboid blocks of cells. User-defined salient isovalue range [I{min}, I{max}]. Target cluster hardware configuration (GPU types, memory). Outputs: Block-to-GPU assignment map. Isosurface triangle vertex buffers for each block. Block Metadata (Preprocessing Output): Stored per block. Contains M entries. Each entry is a pair (Ik, Tk), where Ik is a probe isovalue and Tk is the triangle count for that isovalue in the block. Profiling Model: Linear function parameters (C, L) for each GPU type. C: Constant overhead factor (ms). L: Linear factor (ns per triangle). Isosurface Crossing Table: Byte-per-cell table at full block resolution. Stores indices of active cells (those crossing the isovalue) within each X row. One table stored per GPU. Minimum-Maximum Table: Stores min/max values for contiguous spans of cells (length 10-20) within each X row. Used to skip spans where the isovalue is not present. 1. Divide Volume: Partition the volume into roughly uniformly sized cuboid blocks. Typical block size is 128^3 cells. 2. Sort Data: For each block, sort the data values in ascending order. 3. Select Probe Isovalues: To find M probe isovalues for N sample values, select the value at every N/(M-1)'th position in the sorted list. 4. Count Triangles: For each probe isovalue Ik: Iterate through all cells in the block on the CPU. Classify each cell into a marching cubes case. Lookup the triangle count for the case from a standard table. Sum the counts to get Tk. 5. Store Metadata: Write the mapping (Ik, Tk) for all k \in [0, M-1] to a file for each block. 1. Generate Synthetic Volume: Create a test volume of size similar to a block (e.g., 128^3) using superimposed sinusoidal waves with random frequencies, directions, and amplitudes. 2. Measure Times: Compute isosurfaces for isovalues ranging from the minimum to the maximum value in the synthetic field. Record the isosurfacing time t for each triangle count T. 3. Fit Linear Model: Use linear least squares fitting to determine the parameters C and L for the equation: \text{Time} = C + L \times T where Time is in milliseconds, T is the number of triangles, C is the constant overhead, and L is the cost per triangle. Note: Perform this independently for each GPU type in the cluster. 1. Compute Mean Triangle Count: For each block, calculate the mean triangle count \bar{T} within the user-defined salient isovalue range [I{min}, I{max}]. Use linear interpolation between the preprocessed probe isovalues to estimate T for any isovalue in the range. Average these estimates over the range. 2. Evaluate Cost Heuristic: Compute the cost H for each block using the profiling model: H = C + L \times \bar{T}. 3. Initial Sort and Round-Robin: Sort all blocks by descending cost H. Assign blocks to GPUs in round-robin fashion. 4. Refinement (Variance Minimization): Initialize a counter for unsuccessful exchanges to 0. Loop until the counter exceeds a limit or variance drops below a threshold: 1. Pick a random pair of blocks (Bi, Bj) assigned to different GPUs (Ga, Gb). 2. Calculate the variance of the sum of costs H across all GPUs before and after swapping Bi and Bj. 3. If the swap decreases the variance, apply the swap and reset the unsuccessful counter to 0. 4. If the swap does not decrease the variance, increment the unsuccessful counter.. Each GPU processes its assigned blocks sequentially or in parallel depending on resources. For each block: Pass 1: Counting and Offsets 1. Triangle Counting: Compute the total triangle count for the block and the offset of triangles into the vertex buffer for each X row of cells. Do not compute spatial positions. Optimization: Use the Minimum-Maximum Table to skip spans of cells where the isovalue is not in [min, max]. 2. Prefix Sums: Apply exclusive prefix sums per X row to compute exact indices within the output vertex buffer for output triangles associated with each row. Implementation: Perform many independent serial prefix sums in parallel on the GPU, as the lists are small and of nearly uniform length. 3. Crossing Table: Record indices of active cells within each X row in the Isosurface Crossing Table. Pass 2: Creation 1. Thread Assignment: Assign each GPU thread to one X row of cells. 2. Triangle Generation: Compute isosurface triangles and normals for the assigned row. Optimization: Iterate through the Isosurface Crossing Table to apply marching cubes only to active cells. 3. Buffer Writing: Place triangles into the target vertex buffer using the offsets computed in Pass 1. 4. Normals: Compute normals for each vertex using finite differences on the gradient. Use ghost cells around blocks to ensure consistency. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def preprocessblock(blockdata, M): """ Preprocessing phase for a single block. blockdata: list of scalar values in the block. M: number of probe isovalues. Returns: list of (isovalue, trianglecount) pairs. """ sorteddata = sorted(blockdata) N = len(sorteddata) probeisovalues = [] # Select M probe isovalues uniformly from sorted data for i in range(M): index = int(i (N / (M - 1))) probeisovalues.append(sorteddata[index]) results = [] for iso in probeisovalues: # Count triangles for this isovalue tcount = countmarchingcubestriangles(blockdata, iso) results.append((iso, tcount)) return results def countmarchingcubestriangles(data, isovalue): """ Counts triangles for a block of data at a specific isovalue. Assumes data is a 3D grid flattened or accessible via indices. """ # Placeholder for actual marching cubes case classification logic # which iterates cells, classifies cases, and sums triangle counts. # This is a conceptual representation. totaltriangles = 0 # Iterate over all cells in the block for cell in data: case = classifymarchingcubescase(cell, isovalue) totaltriangles += TRIANGLECOUNTTABLE[case] return totaltriangles def profilegpu(blocksize, numsamples=100): """ Profiling phase. Determines C and L for a specific GPU. blocksize: dimensions of a block (e.g., 128). Returns: (C, L) tuple. """ # Generate synthetic volume syntheticvol = generatesyntheticvolume(blocksize) minval = min(syntheticvol) maxval = max(syntheticvol) trianglecounts = [] times = [] # Sample isovalues from min to max for i in range(numsamples): iso = minval + (maxval - minval) (i / (numsamples - 1)) tcount = countmarchingcubestriangles(syntheticvol, iso) # Measure time to isosurface this block ttime = measureisosurfacingtime(syntheticvol, iso) trianglecounts.append(tcount) times.append(ttime) # Linear least squares fitting: Time = C + L T # Using standard linear regression formulas n = len(trianglecounts) sumt = sum(trianglecounts) sumtime = sum(times) sumtt = sum(tt for t in trianglecounts) sumttime = sum(tti for t, ti in zip(trianglecounts, times)) denominator = n sumtt - sumt sumt if denominator == 0: return (0.0, 0.0) # Avoid division by zero L = (n sumttime - sumt sumtime) / denominator C = (sumtime - L sumt) / n return (C, L) def assignblocks(blocksmetadata, gpucosts, salientrange, maxunsuccessful=1000): """ Assignment phase. blocksmetadata: list of dicts, each containing 'probedata' (list of (iso, count)) gpucosts: dict mapping gpuid -> (C, L) salientrange: tuple (Imin, Imax) Returns: list of gpuids for each block. """ # Step 1: Compute cost for each block blockcosts = [] for i, meta in enumerate(blocksmetadata): # Interpolate mean triangle count over salient range meant = computemeantrianglecount(meta['probedata'], salientrange) # Use the cost model of the first GPU (or average if multiple types) # For simplicity, assume homogeneous GPUs or pick one representative C, L = gpucosts['gpu0'] cost = C + L meant blockcosts.append({'id': i, 'cost': cost}) # Step 2: Sort by descending cost blockcosts.sort(key=lambda x: x['cost'], reverse=True) # Step 3: Round-robin assignment numgpus = len(gpucosts) assignments = [None] len(blockcosts) for idx, block in enumerate(blockcosts): gpuid = idx % numgpus assignments[block['id']] = gpuid # Step 4: Refinement # Calculate initial variance gpusums = {g: 0.0 for g in gpucosts} for block in blockcosts: gpuid = assignments[block['id']] gpusums[gpuid] += block['cost'] variance = computevariance(gpusums.values()) unsuccessful = 0 while unsuccessful < maxunsuccessful: # Pick random pair of blocks on different GPUs b1idx, b2idx = random.sample(range(len(blockcosts)), 2) b1 = blockcosts[b1idx] b2 = blockcosts[b2idx] g1 = assignments[b1['id']] g2 = assignments[b2['id']] if g1 == g2: unsuccessful += 1 continue # Calculate variance after swap # Current sums s1 = gpusums[g1] s2 = gpusums[g2] # New sums after swap news1 = s1 - b1['cost'] + b2['cost'] news2 = s2 - b2['cost'] + b1['cost'] # Create new sums dict for variance calculation newsums = gpusums.copy() newsums[g1] = news1 newsums[g2] = news2 newvariance = computevariance(newsums.values()) if newvariance < variance: # Apply swap assignments[b1['id']] = g2 assignments[b2['id']] = g1 gpusums[g1] = news1 gpusums[g2] = news2 variance = newvariance unsuccessful = 0 else: unsuccessful += 1 return assignments def computemeantrianglecount(probedata, salientrange): """ Interpolates triangle counts over the salient range and returns the mean. probedata: list of (iso, count) sorted by iso. """ Imin, Imax = salientrange # Linear interpolation function def gett(iso): # Find bracketing probes for i in range(len(probedata) - 1): i1, t1 = probedata[i] i2, t2 = probedata[i+1] if i1 <= iso <= i2: # Linear interpolation if i2 == i1: return t1 return t1 + (t2 - t1) (iso - i1) / (i2 - i1) # If outside range, clamp to nearest if iso < probedata[0][0]: return probedata[0][1] return probedata[-1][1] # Sample mean over range # For implementation, integrate or sample densely numsamples = 100 totalt = 0 for i in range(numsamples): iso = Imin + (Imax - Imin) (i / (numsamples - 1)) totalt += gett(iso) return totalt / numsamples def computevariance(values): n = len(values) if n == 0: return 0 mean = sum(values) / n return sum((v - mean)2 for v in values) / n Block Size: 128^3 cells. Chosen as a compromise between overhead (smaller blocks) and load balancing granularity (larger blocks). Salient Isovalue Range: User-defined range [I{min}, I{max}]. Load balancing is maximized over this set. Span Length (Optimization): 10-20 cells for the Minimum-Maximum Table. Overhead Dominance: Even blocks with very few triangles may take substantial time to compute due to API and kernel startup overhead. The heuristic must account for this constant factor C. Heuristic Conditioning: The heuristic must be well-conditioned to avoid unreasonably large changes in estimates for small changes in input metadata. Metadata Completeness: The heuristic must be computable from compact metadata produced by preprocessing, as not all data can be loaded every time the heuristic is evaluated. Hardware Specificity: The relationship between overhead and actual work varies by platform. The heuristic must reflect the specific hardware platform being used. Arbitrary Assignment: Arbitrary block assignment (no cost heuristic) leads to varied and undefined performance because work distribution uniformity depends on the specific isovalue and dataset. Time and Memory Complexity: Preprocessing: O(B \cdot N \cdot M), where B is the number of blocks, N is the number of cells per block, and M is the number of probe isovalues. Sorting takes O(N \log N) per block. Profiling: O(S \cdot T{gpu}), where S is the number of synthetic samples and T{gpu} is the time to isosurface one block. Assignment: O(B \log B) for sorting, plus refinement iterations. Refinement is bounded by a limit on unsuccessful exchanges. Isosurfacing: O(N) per block for counting and creation, with optimizations reducing constant factors. Memory: Metadata is compact (M entries per block). Isosurface Crossing Table requires 1 byte per cell per GPU. Measured Performance: Platform: 12 Linux nodes, each with 2 NVIDIA Quadro FX5600s (1.5GiB memory), 2 quad-core AMD Opteron 2350 CPUs at 2GHz, 16GiB RAM, Infiniband. Constant Factor: ~1.2ms per 128^3 block on a single GPU, dominated by API and kernel startup time. Linear Factor: ~40ns per triangle on a single GPU. Throughput with Heuristic: ~250 million triangles per second on 24 GPUs for isovalue range 2.75-3.25. Throughput without Heuristic: ~175 million triangles per second on 24 GPUs for the same range. Scalability: The cost heuristic yields substantial performance improvements over naive round-robin distribution, particularly within the salient isovalue range. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Maximizes load uniformity over user-defined isovalues; enables improved scalability over naive approaches; handles large volumes that do not fit on a single node. Limitations: Requires preprocessing and profiling phases; performance peaks only within the salient isovalue range (though other ranges do not suffer unacceptable penalties); small scale variation in results occurs due to noise in isosurfacing times and cost heuristic accuracy. Origin: The method was proposed by Steven Martin, Han-Wei Shen, and Patrick McCormick from The Ohio State University and Los Alamos National Laboratory. It was published in the Eurographics Symposium on Parallel Graphics and Visualization (EGPGV) in 2010. History and Development: The technique addresses the challenge of distributing isosurfacing workloads on increasingly hierarchical parallel architectures (clusters with multiple nodes, each with multiple GPUs). It improves upon earlier cost heuristics by Zhang et al. [ZN03], which used active cells and hardcoded coefficients, and Scheidegger et al. [SSD08], which used isosurface statistics. This method uses sampled triangle counts and linear regression based on profiling the target system, providing a more accurate and less complex cost determination. Usage: Used in multi-GPU cluster environments for isosurfacing large volume datasets, specifically tested on NVIDIA Quadro FX5600 GPUs. name: Capacity-safe slab-based Marching Cubes
head: Capacity-safe slab-based isososurface extraction, Capacity-safe slab-based isosurface extraction pipeline, Capacity-safe tiled Marching Cubes, Two-pass tiled Marching Cubes, inclusive slab partitioning with exact allocation, slab-based two-pass GPU isosurface extraction
body: A GPU-accelerated isosurface extraction pipeline that uses inclusive slab partitioning and a two-pass counting/exact allocation strategy to prevent slab-boundary omissions and output-buffer overflow for large scalar grids. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by resolving topological discontinuities and holes via boundary-consistent slab processing, and differs from HistoPyramids/Flying Edges by specializing counting/compaction for tightly coupled extraction, rendering, and engine integration. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar volume V defined on a grid of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz, where V: \{0, \dots, Nx-1\} \times \{0, \dots, Ny-1\} \times \{0, \dots, Nz-1\} \to \mathbb{R}. An isovalue \tau \in \mathbb{R}. Output: A Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) containing two arrays: pos (positions) and nrm (normals). The total capacity is N vertices, where N is the exact sum of vertices generated by all cells. Each triangle writes 3 consecutive vertices. For each vertex, pos stores a 3D vector and nrm stores a 3D vector. Data Structures Grid Dimensions: Nx, Ny, Nz. Cell Index: (i, j, k) where 0 \le i \le Nx-2, 0 \le j \le Ny-2, 0 \le k \le Nz-2. Linear Index: lin(x, y, z) = (z Ny + y) Nx + x. Slab Configuration: The z-axis is partitioned into slabs of thickness S. The set of valid cells for slab s is defined as the closed interval \mathcal{K}s = \{k \mid k{begin}(s) \le k \le k{end}(s)\}. Count Arrays: For each slab s, a local count array counts indexed by linear cell index, and an exclusive prefix-sum array offsets. Lookup Tables: Uses the standard edgeTable and triangleTable from Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration. Parameters Slab Thickness (S): Recommended range [48, 96] for a 512^3 grid. Boundary Handling: If Nz-1 is not divisible by S, the final slab is processed as a partial slab without padding, with its upper cell index clamped to Nz-2. Algorithm Steps 1. Pass 1: Classify/Scan (Counting) Initialize global vertex count N \leftarrow 0. For each slab s: For each cell (i, j, k) with k \in [k{begin}(s), k{end}(s)]: Compute case index c = \text{caseIndex}(V, i, j, k, \tau). Retrieve vertex count n{ijk} = \text{numVerts}[c]. Store n{ijk} in counts[lin(i,j,k)]. Compute exclusive prefix-sum (scan) over counts to generate offsets. Calculate slab-level total Ns = \text{offsets}[\text{last}] + \text{count}s[\text{last}]. Set slab base offset \text{base}[s] = N. Update global count N \leftarrow N + Ns. Allocate an interoperable VBO with exactly N vertex capacity. 2. Pass 2: Generate (Writing) For each slab s: For each cell (i, j, k) with k \in [k{begin}(s), k{end}(s)]: Compute case index c = \text{caseIndex}(V, i, j, k, \tau). If \text{numVerts}[c] \neq 0: Compute edge vertices \text{edgeVerts}[0..11] \leftarrow \text{edge\lerp}(V, i, j, k, \tau). Determine destination address \text{dst} = \text{base}[s] + \text{offsets}[lin(i,j,k)]. Iterate through the triangle edge list \text{triTable}[c][t..t+2] for t from 0 to \text{numVerts}[c]-1 with step 3. If any edge index e0, e1, e2 is < 0, break the loop. Retrieve vertices \mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2 from \text{edgeVerts}. Compute face normal \mathbf{n} = \frac{(\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) \times (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0)}{\|(\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) \times (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0)\|} to enforce counterclockwise winding. Write positions \{\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2\} to \text{pos}[\text{dst}:\text{dst}+2] and normals \{\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{n}\} to \text{nrm}[\text{dst}:\text{dst}+2]. Increment \text{dst} \leftarrow \text{dst} + 3. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def capacitysafeslabmarchingcubes(V, Nx, Ny, Nz, tau, S): # Pass 1: Classify and Scan globalN = 0 slabbases = [] # Determine slab ranges numslabs = (Nz - 1 + S - 1) // S # Ceiling division for number of slabs # Note: Nz-1 is the max k index for cells. # Slab s covers k from sS to min((s+1)S - 1, Nz-2) for s in range(numslabs): kstart = s S kend = min((s + 1) S - 1, Nz - 2) # Local count array for this slab # Size depends on number of cells in slab slabcellcount = 0 for i in range(Nx - 1): for j in range(Ny - 1): for k in range(kstart, kend + 1): slabcellcount += 1 counts = [0] slabcellcount offsets = [0] slabcellcount # Fill counts idx = 0 for i in range(Nx - 1): for j in range(Ny - 1): for k in range(kstart, kend + 1): c = computecaseindex(V, i, j, k, tau) nverts = numvertstable[c] lin = (k Ny + j) Nx + i # Note: The source uses lin(i,j,k) as index into counts. # In a slab-local array, we map this linear index to a local index or use a global array. # The source implies a slab-local count array indexed by linear cell index. # To implement cleanly, we can use a global array or map. # Given the source says "counts[lin(i,j,k)]", and lin is global, # we assume counts is sized to cover the slab's linear indices or we map. # However, for exact allocation per slab, a local array is more efficient. # Let's assume a local mapping or that the source implies a global array for simplicity in description, # but for implementation, we'll use a local list indexed by a local counter for clarity, # or stick to the source's linear index if memory allows. # The source says "counts[lin(i,j,k)]". If Nz is large, this is sparse. # But for the algorithm description, we follow the source's logic: # Store nijk in a count array indexed by the linear cell index. # We will assume a global count array for Pass 1 to simplify the scan logic across slabs if needed, # but the source computes Ns per slab. # Let's use a global array for counts to match the "linear cell index" description strictly. counts[lin] = nverts idx += 1 # Exclusive Scan # Standard exclusive prefix sum currentsum = 0 for i in range(len(counts)): temp = counts[i] counts[i] = currentsum currentsum += temp # Calculate slab total # The source says Ns = offsets[last] + countss[last] # Here 'counts' holds the offsets after scan. 'countss' in source refers to the original counts. # We need the original counts to get the last element's contribution. # Let's re-read: "offsets[ℓ] for each cell ℓ. Calculate the slab-level total Ns = offsets[last] + countss[last]" # So we need to store original counts or recompute. # Let's assume we have a separate array for original counts or recompute. # For pseudocode clarity, we'll recompute the last count. lastlin = (kend Ny + (Ny - 1)) Nx + (Nx - 1) # Find the max linear index in this slab maxlin = 0 for i in range(Nx - 1): for j in range(Ny - 1): for k in range(kstart, kend + 1): lin = (k Ny + j) Nx + i if lin > maxlin: maxlin = lin # Recompute last count clast = computecaseindex(V, maxlin % (Nx-1), (maxlin // (Nx-1)) % (Ny-1), maxlin // (Nx Ny), tau) nlast = numvertstable[clast] Ns = counts[maxlin] + nlast slabbases.append(globalN) globalN += Ns # Allocate VBO # In a real implementation, this would be cudaMalloc or similar posbuffer = allocatebuffer(globalN 3) nrmbuffer = allocatebuffer(globalN 3) # Pass 2: Generate for s in range(numslabs): kstart = s S kend = min((s + 1) S - 1, Nz - 2) bases = slabbases[s] # We need the offsets for this slab. # In Pass 1, we computed offsets into a global array or slab-local array. # The source says "offsets[lin(i,j,k)]". # If we used a global array for offsets, we can access it directly. for i in range(Nx - 1): for j in range(Ny - 1): for k in range(kstart, kend + 1): c = computecaseindex(V, i, j, k, tau) nverts = numvertstable[c] if nverts != 0: edgeverts = computeedgeintersections(V, i, j, k, tau) lin = (k Ny + j) Nx + i dst = bases + offsets[lin] t = 0 while t < nverts: e0 = tritable[c][t] e1 = tritable[c][t+1] e2 = tritable[c][t+2] if e0 < 0 or e1 < 0 or e2 < 0: break p0 = edgeverts[e0] p1 = edgeverts[e1] p2 = edgeverts[e2] n = normalize(cross(p1 - p0, p2 - p0)) posbuffer[dst] = p0 posbuffer[dst+1] = p1 posbuffer[dst+2] = p2 nrmbuffer[dst] = n nrmbuffer[dst+1] = n nrmbuffer[dst+2] = n dst += 3 t += 3 def computecaseindex(V, i, j, k, tau): # Standard MC case index calculation # V is sampled at corners (i,j,k) to (i+1,j+1,k+1) # I(v < tau) c = 0 for z in range(2): for y in range(2): for x in range(2): val = V[i+x, j+y, k+z] if val < tau: c |= (1 << (x + 2y + 4z)) return c def computeedgeintersections(V, i, j, k, tau): # Linear interpolation on 12 edges # Returns array of 12 vertices verts = [None] 12 # Edge 0: (i,j,k) to (i+1,j,k) #... implementation of linear interpolation... return verts def normalize(v): return v / length(v) def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Cracks: Using inclusive slab indexing (\mathcal{K}s includes k{end}(s)) ensures that the k+1 corner access required by MC remains valid at slab boundaries, eliminating omissions/duplications and cracks caused by off-by-one inconsistencies. Empty Triangles: The algorithm checks if edge indices e0, e1, e2 are < 0. If so, it breaks the triangle loop, handling cases where the triangle table entry indicates no triangle for that specific triplet. Partial Slabs: If Nz-1 is not divisible by S, the final slab is processed as a partial slab without padding, with its upper cell index clamped to Nz-2. Time Complexity: O(M) for both passes, where M = (Nx-1)(Ny-1)(Nz-1) is the number of cells. Memory Complexity: The additional storage consists of the slab-local count and offset arrays, while the output buffers are allocated according to the exact number of generated vertices. The method uses less than 11 GB GPU memory for a 512^3 grid. Performance: On electromagnetic-potential fields with resolutions up to 512^3, the method generates approximately 42.81 million vertices in 44.7 ms, uses less than 11 GB GPU memory, and renders the resulting geometry at 28.6 FPS. Strengths: Prevents buffer overruns, eliminates boundary cracks, and enables zero-copy streaming to OpenGL buffers. Limitations: Less suitable for sharp-feature preservation than methods such as Dual Contouring or MC33. Limited to volumes that fit within the memory of a single GPU. The method was introduced in a paper presenting a GPU-accelerated visualization framework for interactive exploration of fusion-plasma simulation data. It combines inclusive slab partitioning with a two-pass counting and exact allocation strategy to prevent slab-boundary omissions and output-buffer overflow. The generated positions and normals are written directly to CUDA–OpenGL interoperable buffers, enabling standalone renderer display without intermediate CPU-side copy. The extracted geometry is integrated into Unreal Engine for volume rendering, explicit-isosurface inspection, particle-trajectory visualization, clipping, and VR-based spatial exploration. name: Capacity-Safe Marching Cubes Pipeline
head: Proposed Framework, Two-pass exact-allocation strategy
body: A GPU-based isosurface extraction method that avoids buffer overflow by determining the exact vertex count before geometry generation, using a two-pass approach: first computing counts/offsets, then allocating exact buffers and generating triangles. It sets itself apart from naive parallel Marching Cubes by avoiding buffer overflow and dynamic memory allocation during geometry generation through a two-pass counting and compaction strategy, building on GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines. Unlike fixed-capacity baselines that reserve static buffers, this method determines the exact vertex count before generation, ensuring stability and preventing buffer overflow without excessive static reservation. The extraction process consists of four sequential stages: cell classification, prefix-sum computation, exact VBO (Vertex Buffer Object) allocation, and triangle generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field V defined on a grid of resolution Nx \times Ny \times Nz. The scalar values are normalized to the range [0, 1] using the minimum and maximum values of the dataset. An isovalue \tau is specified within this normalized range. Output: A set of vertices and normals representing the isosurface, stored in a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO). Data Structures: 1. Edge Intersection Table (edgeTable): An array of 256 integers (or shorts). Each entry is a 12-bit bitmask. Bit k (0 \le k \le 11) is set to 1 if the isosurface intersects the k-th edge of the cube, and 0 otherwise. The standard edge numbering convention is: Bottom face (z=0): e0=(0,1), e1=(1,2), e2=(2,3), e3=(3,0) Top face (z=1): e4=(4,5), e5=(5,6), e6=(6,7), e7=(7,4) Vertical edges: e8=(0,4), e9=(1,5), e{10}=(2,6), e{11}=(3,7) [10327-lookup-table-and-ambiguity-handling] 2. Triangle Connection Table (triangleTable): A 2D array of size 256 \times 16. Rows are indexed by the case index C \in [0, 255]. Columns store integer indices. Indices 0–11 refer to the 12 cube edges. Indices are grouped in triplets (a, b, c) to form triangles. The sequence is terminated by the value -1. The maximum number of triangles per voxel is 5, requiring 15 indices plus 1 terminator [10327-lookup-table-and-ambiguity-handling]. Case Index Calculation: For each voxel, the 8-bit case index C is determined by the scalar field values V at the 8 vertices vi (i=0..7). If V(vi) < \tau (or > \tau, depending on convention), bit i of C is set to 1; otherwise 0. The bit assignment must strictly match the vertex ordering assumed by the LUT generation [10327-lookup-table-and-ambiguity-handling]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Cell Classification: For each voxel in the grid, compute the case index C based on the scalar values at its 8 corners relative to the isovalue \tau. Determine if the voxel is "active" (i.e., C \neq 0 and C \neq 255) and calculate the number of triangles Tv generated by this voxel using the triangleTable. The number of triangles is the count of non-terminating triplets in the row C of triangleTable. 2. Prefix-Sum Computation: Compute an exclusive prefix sum (scan) of the triangle counts Tv for all active voxels. This produces an offset array where each entry indicates the starting index in the output buffer for the triangles generated by the corresponding voxel. This step determines the exact total number of vertices required, as each triangle consists of 3 vertices. Let N{total} be the total number of triangles. The required vertex buffer size is 3 \times N{total} vertices. 3. Exact VBO Allocation: Allocate a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) and a Normal Buffer Object with exact sizes derived from the prefix sum. The size is 3 \times N{total} vertices. This prevents buffer overflow and avoids the need for large static reservations. 4. Triangle Generation: For each active voxel, use the case index C to look up the intersected edges in edgeTable. Interpolate the intersection points on the edges using the scalar values at the vertices. Use triangleTable to determine the connectivity of the triangles. Write the vertex positions and normals to the pre-allocated buffers at the offsets computed in Step 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def capacitysafemarchingcubes(volume, isovalue, resolution): """ volume: 3D array of scalar values, normalized to [0, 1] isovalue: float in [0, 1] resolution: tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) """ Nx, Ny, Nz = resolution # Step 1: Cell Classification # Compute case index and triangle count for each voxel # Initialize arrays to store triangle counts per voxel trianglecounts = zeros(Nx Ny Nz, dtype=int32) for z in range(Nz - 1): for y in range(Ny - 1): for x in range(Nx - 1): # Get scalar values at 8 corners v = [ volume[x, y, z], volume[x+1, y, z], volume[x+1, y+1, z], volume[x, y+1, z], volume[x, y, z+1], volume[x+1, y, z+1], volume[x+1, y+1, z+1], volume[x, y+1, z+1] ] # Compute case index C C = 0 for i in range(8): if v[i] < isovalue: # Convention: below isosurface is inside C |= (1 << i) # If voxel is active (not fully inside or outside) if C != 0 and C != 255: # Count triangles from triangleTable # triangleTable[C] is a list of 16 integers, terminated by -1 row = triangleTable[C] tcount = 0 idx = 0 while row[idx] != -1: tcount += 1 idx += 3 trianglecounts[z Nx Ny + y Nx + x] = tcount else: trianglecounts[z Nx Ny + y Nx + x] = 0 # Step 2: Prefix-Sum Computation # Compute exclusive prefix sum to get offsets offsets = exclusivescan(trianglecounts) totaltriangles = sum(trianglecounts) totalvertices = 3 totaltriangles # Step 3: Exact VBO Allocation # Allocate buffers on GPU vbopositions = allocatebuffer(totalvertices 3) # 3 floats per vertex vbonormals = allocatebuffer(totalvertices 3) # Step 4: Triangle Generation # Launch kernel to generate triangles # Each thread block handles a subset of voxels launchkernelgeneratetriangles(volume, isovalue, offsets, trianglecounts, vbopositions, vbonormals, resolution) return vbopositions, vbonormals def exclusivescan(arr): """ Compute exclusive prefix sum. result[i] = sum(arr[0]...arr[i-1]) """ n = len(arr) result = zeros(n, dtype=arr.dtype) if n == 0: return result currentsum = 0 for i in range(n): result[i] = currentsum currentsum += arr[i] return result def launchkernelgeneratetriangles(volume, isovalue, offsets, trianglecounts, vbopositions, vbonormals, resolution): """ GPU kernel to generate triangles. """ # Pseudocode for kernel logic # Each thread processes one voxel voxelidx = threadid() if voxelidx >= len(trianglecounts): return tcount = trianglecounts[voxelidx] if tcount == 0: return offset = offsets[voxelidx] # Get voxel coordinates Nx, Ny, Nz = resolution z = voxelidx // (Nx Ny) y = (voxelidx % (Nx Ny)) // Nx x = voxelidx % Nx # Get scalar values at 8 corners v = [ volume[x, y, z], volume[x+1, y, z], volume[x+1, y+1, z], volume[x, y+1, z], volume[x, y, z+1], volume[x+1, y, z+1], volume[x+1, y+1, z+1], volume[x, y+1, z+1] ] # Compute case index C C = 0 for i in range(8): if v[i] < isovalue: C |= (1 << i) # Look up edges and triangles edgemask = edgeTable[C] trirow = triangleTable[C] # Intersect edges to get points points = [] for e in range(12): if (edgemask >> e) & 1: # Interpolate on edge e p = interpolateedge(v, e, isovalue) points.append(p) # Generate triangles idx = 0 triidx = 0 while trirow[idx] != -1: e1 = trirow[idx] e2 = trirow[idx+1] e3 = trirow[idx+2] p1 = points[e1] p2 = points[e2] p3 = points[e3] # Compute normal n = cross(p2 - p1, p3 - p1) n = normalize(n) # Write to VBO base = offset + triidx 3 vbopositions[base 3] = p1.x vbopositions[base 3 + 1] = p1.y vbopositions[base 3 + 2] = p1.z vbonormals[base 3] = n.x vbonormals[base 3 + 1] = n.y vbonormals[base 3 + 2] = n.z vbopositions[(base + 1) 3] = p2.x vbopositions[(base + 1) 3 + 1] = p2.y vbopositions[(base + 1) 3 + 2] = p2.z vbonormals[(base + 1) 3] = n.x vbonormals[(base + 1) 3 + 1] = n.y vbonormals[(base + 1) 3 + 2] = n.z vbopositions[(base + 2) 3] = p3.x vbopositions[(base + 2) 3 + 1] = p3.y vbopositions[(base + 2) 3 + 2] = p3.z vbonormals[(base + 2) 3] = n.x vbonormals[(base + 2) 3 + 1] = n.y vbonormals[(base + 2) 3 + 2] = n.z triidx += 1 idx += 3 def interpolateedge(v, edgeidx, isovalue): """ Interpolate intersection point on edge. Edge indices: 0-3 bottom, 4-7 top, 8-11 vertical Vertices: 0-3 bottom, 4-7 top """ if edgeidx < 4: # Bottom face v0 = v[edgeidx] v1 = v[(edgeidx + 1) % 4] elif edgeidx < 8: # Top face v0 = v[edgeidx] v1 = v[(edgeidx + 1) % 4 + 4] else: # Vertical edges v0 = v[edgeidx - 8] v1 = v[edgeidx - 8 + 4] # Linear interpolation t = (isovalue - v0) / (v1 - v0) # Coordinates would be interpolated similarly # For simplicity, assume v contains coordinates or we map indices to coords # In reality, v is scalar values, we need vertex positions # This is a simplification for pseudocode return v0 + t (v1 - v0) # Placeholder for actual coordinate interpolation Parameters: Isovalues (\tau): Specified in the normalized scalar range [0, 1]. Typical tested values are 0.35, 0.50, and 0.65. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Buffer Overflow: Using a fixed-capacity single-pass output buffer causes failure at high resolutions (e.g., 512^3) because the generated output exceeds available buffer capacity, resulting in overwritten or missing vertex data and incomplete geometry. Ambiguity: Cases 46, 47, 98, 99, 210, 213, 214, 215 contain saddle points where the topology is ambiguous. The standard LUT uses a fixed triangulation for these, which can cause cracks or holes if adjacent voxels resolve the ambiguity differently [10327-lookup-table-and-ambiguity-handling]. The capacity-safe pipeline does not inherently resolve this; it relies on the underlying Marching Cubes implementation. A GPU-accelerated Marching Cubes pipeline that classifies voxels, uses exclusive prefix sums to count active voxels and required vertices, compacts the voxel index array to remove empty voxels, and extracts the isosurface only for active voxels. It sets itself apart from naive parallel Marching Cubes by avoiding buffer overflow and dynamic memory allocation during geometry generation through a two-pass counting and compaction strategy, building on the Capacity-Safe Marching Cubes Pipeline. This method is a six-stage hybrid CPU-GPU pipeline for isosurface extraction that maximizes performance by balancing memory hierarchy usage and parallelizing the Marching Cubes algorithm. It differs from sibling methods like Capacity-Safe Marching Cubes Pipeline by offloading the spatial traversal and active cell identification to the CPU using pre-constructed spatial data structures, while the GPU handles the exact buffer allocation and triangle generation in parallel. Unlike GPU Marching Cubes with Scan-Based Compaction, which typically handles all active cells on the GPU, this approach reduces GPU memory pressure and bandwidth by transferring only the necessary active cell indices from CPU to GPU. Time Complexity: The method involves a linear pass over all voxels for classification and prefix sum, followed by a linear pass for triangle generation. The complexity is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. Memory Complexity: Peak VRAM usage includes the input scalar volume, intermediate count and offset buffers, and the generated position and normal buffers. Measured Performance: At 512^3 resolution with isovalue 0.35, the method generates 42.81 million vertices in 44.7 ms with 10.9 GB peak VRAM usage, rendering at 28.6 FPS. At 128^3 resolution with isovalue 0.35, the method generates 1.28 million vertices in 5.8 ms with 1.9 GB peak VRAM usage, rendering at 221.4 FPS. At 128^3 resolution with isovalue 0.50, the method generates 0.94 million vertices in 4.9 ms with 1.7 GB peak VRAM usage, rendering at 264.7 FPS. At 128^3 resolution with isovalue 0.65, the method generates 0.61 million vertices in 4.1 ms with 1.6 GB peak VRAM usage, rendering at 312.5 FPS. Scaling: Increasing the grid resolution increases both the number of processed cells and the amount of generated geometry. Strengths: Ensures stability and prevents buffer overflow without excessive static reservation. Remains stable at high resolutions where fixed-capacity methods fail. Limitations: Requires two passes over the data (classification and generation), which may introduce overhead for very small datasets. The prefix sum computation can be a bottleneck if not optimized. When to use: When extracting isosurfaces from large volumes where the number of triangles is unknown or variable, and buffer overflow is a concern. When not to use: When the number of triangles is small and known in advance, or when memory bandwidth is extremely limited and the overhead of the prefix sum is prohibitive. The method was proposed in the context of visualizing 3D plasma simulation data, specifically for examining morphological changes and identifying regions of interest in simulated plasma fields. It was evaluated on a workstation equipped with an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX CPU, 256 GB of system memory, and an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU with 24 GB of VRAM. The evaluation focused on geometric continuity, extraction time, rendering performance, and GPU memory usage. Visual tools for 3D plasma simulation: GPU-based isosurface extraction..., https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13674866/, fetched 2026-10-30

name: GPU Marching Cubes with Scan-Based Compaction
head: Empty Space Skipping via Stream Compaction, MarchingCubesGPU, Stream Compaction for Empty Space Skipping
body: A GPU-accelerated Marching Cubes pipeline that classifies voxels, uses exclusive prefix sums to count active voxels and required vertices, compacts the voxel index array to remove empty voxels, and extracts the isosurface only for active voxels. It optimizes Marching Cubes by using stream compaction to avoid processing voxels that do not contain the isosurface. It builds on Capacity-Safe Marching Cubes Pipeline by implementing the two-pass capacity-safe approach on GPU hardware. Inputs: basePoint: World-space origin of the voxel grid (float3). gridSize: Dimensions of the voxel grid in voxels (uint3). voxelSize: Physical size of each voxel (float3). isoValue: Scalar threshold for isosurface extraction (float, default 0.2f). Implicit input: A scalar field function V(x, y, z) evaluated per voxel corner. In the reference implementation, this is V(x, y, z) = \cos(x)\sin(y) + \cos(y)\sin(z) + \cos(z)\sin(x). Outputs: resultPts: Array of float3 vertices representing the extracted isosurface. successful: Boolean indicating if extraction succeeded (false if no active voxels). Data Structures: Device arrays (all size numVoxels unless noted): dvoxelVerts: uint, stores the number of vertices generated per voxel. dvoxelOccupied: uint, binary occupancy flag per voxel (1 if active, 0 if empty). dvoxelVertsScan: uint, exclusive prefix sum of dvoxelVerts. dvoxelOccupiedScan: uint, exclusive prefix sum of dvoxelOccupied. dcompVoxelArray: uint, compacted array of indices for active voxels. dresult: float3, output vertex buffer, size numresultVertices sizeof(float3). Host pinned arrays: dvoxelOccupied: uint, size numVoxels. dvoxelVerts: uint, size numVoxels. Steps: 1. Allocation: Allocate device arrays dvoxelVerts, dvoxelOccupied, dvoxelVertsScan, dvoxelOccupiedScan, dcompVoxelArray and pinned host arrays dvoxelOccupied, dvoxelVerts of size sizeof(uint) numVoxels. 2. Voxel Classification: Launch classifyVoxel kernel. Grid configuration: dim3 grid((numVoxels + threads - 1) / threads, 1, 1). If grid.x > 65535, split into 2D: grid.y = grid.x / 32768; grid.x = 32768;. Block size: threads = 256. Each thread processes one voxel index i. Compute world coordinates of the 8 corners of voxel i. Evaluate the scalar field at each corner. Determine if the isosurface intersects the voxel (standard Marching Cubes classification). Write 1 to dvoxelOccupied[i] if active, 0 otherwise. Write the number of vertices generated for this voxel (0, 1, 2, or 3 triangles \times 3 vertices? No, Marching Cubes generates 0-4 triangles. The reference code implies counting vertices. Standard MC generates 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4 triangles. Each triangle has 3 vertices. However, shared vertices exist. The variable name dvoxelVerts suggests counting vertices. The formula for total vertices is derived from the sum of these counts. Let's assume dvoxelVerts[i] stores the number of output vertices contributed by voxel i. In a naive implementation, this is 3 \times \text{num\triangles}. In a shared-vertex implementation, it is more complex. The source code comment says "calculate number of vertices need per voxel". We will assume it counts the raw vertices before global deduplication, or the implementation handles deduplication locally. Given the simplicity of the scan-based approach, it likely counts 3 \times Ti where Ti is the number of triangles. 3. Occupancy Scan: Run exclusiveSumScan on dvoxelOccupied to produce dvoxelOccupiedScan. 4. Active Voxel Count: Copy the last element of dvoxelOccupied to host variable lastElement. Copy the last element of dvoxelOccupiedScan to host variable lastScanElement. Compute numactiveVoxels = lastElement + lastScanElement. If numactiveVoxels == 0, set numresultVertices = 0, mark successful = false, and return. 5. Voxel Compaction: Launch compactVoxels kernel. Grid: Same as classification. Each thread i checks dvoxelOccupied[i]. If true, write i to dcompVoxelArray at an index determined by the prefix sum. Specifically, the output index is dvoxelOccupiedScan[i]. 6. Vertex Count Scan: Run exclusiveSumScan on dvoxelVerts to produce dvoxelVertsScan. 7. Result Vertex Count: Copy the last element of dvoxelVerts to host variable lastElement2. Copy the last element of dvoxelVertsScan to host variable lastScanElement2. Compute numresultVertices = lastElement2 + lastScanElement2. 8. Result Buffer Allocation: Allocate dresult of size numresultVertices sizeof(float3). 9. Isosurface Extraction: Launch extractIsosurface kernel. Grid: dim3 grid2((numactiveVoxels + threads - 1) / threads, 1, 1). If grid2.x > 65535, split: grid2.y = grid2.x / 32768; grid2.x = 32768;. Note: The source mentions a potential bug where extraction code checks grid.x instead of grid2.x in the condition, but the correct logic is to check the extraction grid. Each thread j corresponds to an active voxel index idx = d\compVoxelArray[j]. Retrieve the 8 corner coordinates of voxel idx. Evaluate the scalar field at corners. Determine the Marching Cubes case index. Look up the triangle configuration from the MC lookup table. Compute intersection points on edges using linear interpolation: P = A + \frac{isoValue - V(A)}{V(B) - V(A)} (B - A). Write the resulting vertices to dresult at offsets provided by dvoxelVertsScan[idx]. 10. Copy Result: Copy dresult to host resultPts. 11. Cleanup: Free pinned memory (cudaFreeHost) and device arrays (cudaFree). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpumarchingcubesscancompact(basePoint, gridSize, voxelSize, isoValue): # Constants threads = 256 numVoxels = gridSize.x gridSize.y gridSize.z # 1. Allocate device arrays dvoxelVerts = cudamalloc(numVoxels sizeof(uint)) dvoxelOccupied = cudamalloc(numVoxels sizeof(uint)) dvoxelVertsScan = cudamalloc(numVoxels sizeof(uint)) dvoxelOccupiedScan = cudamalloc(numVoxels sizeof(uint)) dcompVoxelArray = cudamalloc(numVoxels sizeof(uint)) # Pinned host arrays for final copy hvoxelOccupied = cudamallochost(numVoxels sizeof(uint)) hvoxelVerts = cudamallochost(numVoxels sizeof(uint)) # 2. Classify Voxels # Grid setup with dimension limit handling gridx = (numVoxels + threads - 1) // threads gridy = 1 if gridx > 65535: gridy = gridx // 32768 gridx = 32768 grid = (gridx, gridy, 1) classifyVoxel<<<grid, threads>>>( dvoxelVerts, dvoxelOccupied, gridSize, numVoxels, basePoint, voxelSize, isoValue) cudaDeviceSynchronize() # 3. Scan Occupancy exclusiveSumScan(dvoxelOccupiedScan, dvoxelOccupied, numVoxels) # 4. Count Active Voxels lastElement = cudacopylasttohost(dvoxelOccupied, numVoxels) lastScanElement = cudacopylasttohost(dvoxelOccupiedScan, numVoxels) numactiveVoxels = lastElement + lastScanElement if numactiveVoxels == 0: numresultVertices = 0 successful = False # Cleanup and return return successful, [] # 5. Compact Voxels # Reuse grid for compaction (same size as numVoxels) compactVoxels<<<grid, threads>>>( dcompVoxelArray, dvoxelOccupied, dvoxelOccupiedScan, numVoxels) cudaDeviceSynchronize() # 6. Scan Vertex Counts exclusiveSumScan(dvoxelVertsScan, dvoxelVerts, numVoxels) # 7. Count Result Vertices lastElement2 = cudacopylasttohost(dvoxelVerts, numVoxels) lastScanElement2 = cudacopylasttohost(dvoxelVertsScan, numVoxels) numresultVertices = lastElement2 + lastScanElement2 # 8. Allocate Result Buffer dresult = cudamalloc(numresultVertices sizeof(float3)) # 9. Extract Isosurface # Grid setup for active voxels grid2x = (numactiveVoxels + threads - 1) // threads grid2y = 1 if grid2x > 65535: grid2y = grid2x // 32768 grid2x = 32768 grid2 = (grid2x, grid2y, 1) extractIsosurface<<<grid2, threads>>>( dresult, dcompVoxelArray, dvoxelVertsScan, numactiveVoxels, basePoint, voxelSize, isoValue) cudaDeviceSynchronize() # 10. Copy Result resultPts = cudamallochost(numresultVertices sizeof(float3)) cudamemcpy(resultPts, dresult, numresultVertices sizeof(float3)) # 11. Cleanup cudafreehost(hvoxelOccupied) cudafreehost(hvoxelVerts) cudafree(dvoxelVerts) cudafree(dvoxelOccupied) cudafree(dvoxelVertsScan) cudafree(dvoxelOccupiedScan) cudafree(dcompVoxelArray) cudafree(dresult) successful = True return successful, resultPts def classifyVoxel<<<grid, threads>>>(dvoxelVerts, dvoxelOccupied, gridSize, numVoxels, basePoint, voxelSize, isoValue): i = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x if i < numVoxels: # Compute voxel index to 3D coordinates x = i % gridSize.x y = (i // gridSize.x) % gridSize.y z = i // (gridSize.x gridSize.y) # Get 8 corner world coordinates corners = [] for dx in [0, 1]: for dy in [0, 1]: for dz in [0, 1]: wx = basePoint.x + (x + dx) voxelSize.x wy = basePoint.y + (y + dy) voxelSize.y wz = basePoint.z + (z + dz) voxelSize.z corners.append((wx, wy, wz)) # Evaluate scalar field values = [] for (wx, wy, wz) in corners: # Reference implementation uses: cos(x)sin(y) + cos(y)sin(z) + cos(z)sin(x) val = cos(wx) sin(wy) + cos(wy) sin(wz) + cos(wz) sin(wx) values.append(val) # Determine if active # Simple check: if all values are above or below isoValue, it's empty # More robust: check if any corner is above and any is below minval = min(values) maxval = max(values) if minval <= isoValue and maxval >= isoValue: dvoxelOccupied[i] = 1 # Count vertices (naive: 3 vertices per triangle) # Determine MC case caseindex = 0 for k, v in enumerate(values): if v > isoValue: caseindex |= (1 << k) # Lookup number of triangles numtriangles = mctablenumtriangles[caseindex] dvoxelVerts[i] = numtriangles 3 else: dvoxelOccupied[i] = 0 dvoxelVerts[i] = 0 def compactVoxels<<<grid, threads>>>(dcompVoxelArray, dvoxelOccupied, dvoxelOccupiedScan, numVoxels): i = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x if i < numVoxels: if dvoxelOccupied[i] == 1: outidx = dvoxelOccupiedScan[i] dcompVoxelArray[outidx] = i def extractIsosurface<<<grid, threads>>>(dresult, dcompVoxelArray, dvoxelVertsScan, numactiveVoxels, basePoint, voxelSize, isoValue): j = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x if j < numactiveVoxels: idx = dcompVoxelArray[j] # Get 8 corner world coordinates (same as classify) x = idx % gridSize.x y = (idx // gridSize.x) % gridSize.y z = idx // (gridSize.x gridSize.y) corners = [] for dx in [0, 1]: for dy in [0, 1]: for dz in [0, 1]: wx = basePoint.x + (x + dx) voxelSize.x wy = basePoint.y + (y + dy) voxelSize.y wz = basePoint.z + (z + dz) voxelSize.z corners.append((wx, wy, wz)) values = [] for (wx, wy, wz) in corners: val = cos(wx) sin(wy) + cos(wy) sin(wz) + cos(wz) sin(wx) values.append(val) caseindex = 0 for k, v in enumerate(values): if v > isoValue: caseindex |= (1 << k) # Lookup triangles triangles = mctabletriangles[caseindex] numtriangles = len(triangles) # Compute intersection points # Edge interpolation: P = A + (iso - Va) / (Vb - Va) (B - A) # This requires mapping edge indices to corner pairs # For brevity, assume a helper function exists points = [] for tri in triangles: for edgeidx in tri: p = interpolateedge(edgeidx, corners, values, isoValue) points.append(p) # Write to result offset = dvoxelVertsScan[idx] for k, p in enumerate(points): dresult[offset + k] = p def interpolateedge(edgeidx, corners, values, isoValue): # Map edge index to corner pair # Standard MC edge mapping edgepairs = [ (0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,0), # Bottom (4,5), (5,6), (6,7), (7,4), # Top (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7) # Vertical ] if edgeidx < 0 or edgeidx >= 12: return (0,0,0) # Should not happen c1idx, c2idx = edgepairs[edgeidx] c1 = corners[c1idx] c2 = corners[c2idx] v1 = values[c1idx] v2 = values[c2idx] denom = v2 - v1 if denom == 0: return c1 t = (isoValue - v1) / denom return ( c1[0] + t (c2[0] - c1[0]), c1[1] + t (c2[1] - c1[1]), c1[2] + t (c2[2] - c1[2])) A GPU compute pipeline that converts an octree of leaf nodes (extracted from a density field) into a compact triangle mesh using parallel index generation, prefix-sum compaction, and vertex attribute assembly. It builds on GPU Marching Cubes with Scan-Based Compaction by handling the final assembly of vertex attributes and index compaction for the extracted geometry. Time Complexity: O(N) for classification, scan, and extraction, where N is the number of voxels. The scans are parallel prefix sums, typically O(\log N) depth with O(N) work. Memory Complexity: O(N) for device arrays (dvoxelVerts, dvoxelOccupied, etc.) and O(V) for the result buffer, where V is the number of output vertices. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of voxels and GPU cores. The 2D grid splitting handles large voxel counts exceeding 65535 in one dimension. Strengths: Avoids buffer overflow by pre-calculating exact vertex counts. Skips empty voxels, reducing computation for sparse fields. Limitations: Requires multiple kernel launches and memory transfers. The naive vertex counting may overestimate if shared vertices are not handled locally. The reference implementation uses a specific scalar field function, not a general texture lookup. When to use: When the voxel grid is large and sparse, or when exact buffer sizing is required to avoid reallocation. When not to use: When the field is dense (many active voxels), the overhead of compaction may not be worth it. When vertex sharing/deduplication is critical for mesh quality, this method produces a non-manifold or duplicated vertex mesh unless post-processed. Originated from the ALGMarchingCubesGPU project by AlbertLiDesign. It is described as an optimization in Marching Cubes using stream compaction to avoid processing empty voxels. It is used in volume rendering and medical imaging contexts. name: QEF-based Octree Mesh Generation
head: Compute-based Isosurface Extraction, GPU Mesh Compaction Pipeline
body: A GPU compute pipeline that converts an octree of leaf nodes (extracted from a density field) into a compact triangle mesh using parallel index generation, prefix-sum compaction, and vertex attribute assembly. It builds on GPU Marching Cubes with Scan-Based Compaction by handling the final assembly of vertex attributes and index compaction for the extracted geometry. Inputs: octree: Contains dvertexPositions, dvertexNormals, dnodeMaterials. clipmapNodeSize: Spatial resolution of the current octree chunk. CLIPMAPLEAFSIZE: Constant defining the leaf node size. MAXMESHTRIANGLES, MAXMESHVERTICES: Hardware or implementation limits. Outputs: meshBuffer: A MeshBufferGPU structure containing the final mesh data. Data Structures: MeshBufferGPU: vertices: cl::Buffer (or equivalent GPU buffer) of type MeshVertex. countVertices: int. triangles: cl::Buffer of int indices. countTriangles: int. MeshVertex: Struct containing: position: vec4 (or equivalent 4-component vector). normal: vec4 (or equivalent 4-component vector). material: vec4 (or equivalent 4-component vector). Steps: 1. Allocate dindexBuffer of size numVertices 6 3 and dtrianglesValid of size numVertices 3. 2. Perform an exclusive scan on dtrianglesValid to produce dtrianglesScan and compute numTriangles. 3. If numTriangles <= 0, return early (0 indicates success with no triangles, <0 indicates error). 4. Multiply numTriangles by 2. 5. Assert numTriangles < MAXMESHTRIANGLES and numVertices < MAXMESHVERTICES. 6. Allocate dcompactIndexBuffer of size numTriangles 3. 7. Launch CompactMeshTriangles kernel with global size trianglesValidSize, passing dtrianglesValid, dtrianglesScan, dindexBuffer, dcompactIndexBuffer. 8. Allocate dvertexBuffer of size sizeof(MeshVertex) numVertices. 9. Compute colour = ColourForMinLeafSize(clipmapNodeSize / CLIPMAPLEAFSIZE) and pack into clfloat4 dcolour = {colour.x, colour.y, colour.z, 0.f}. 10. Launch GenerateMeshVertexBuffer kernel with global size numVertices, passing octree.dvertexPositions, octree.dvertexNormals, octree.dnodeMaterials, dcolour, dvertexBuffer. 11. Assign dvertexBuffer to meshBuffer->vertices, numVertices to meshBuffer->countVertices, dcompactIndexBuffer to meshBuffer->triangles, and numTriangles to meshBuffer->countTriangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatemesh(octree, clipmapNodeSize, CLIPMAPLEAFSIZE, MAXMESHTRIANGLES, MAXMESHVERTICES): # Step 1: Allocate buffers for index generation and validity tracking # Note: numVertices is assumed to be known from previous stages (e.g., voxel classification) dindexBuffer = allocatebuffer(numVertices 6 3) dtrianglesValid = allocatebuffer(numVertices 3) # Step 2: Exclusive scan to determine triangle counts dtrianglesScan, numTriangles = exclusivescan(dtrianglesValid) # Step 3: Early exit if no triangles if numTriangles <= 0: return createemptymeshbuffer() # Step 4: Scale triangle count (implementation-specific scaling) numTriangles = 2 # Step 5: Assert bounds assert numTriangles < MAXMESHTRIANGLES assert numVertices < MAXMESHVERTICES # Step 6: Allocate compact index buffer dcompactIndexBuffer = allocatebuffer(numTriangles 3) # Step 7: Compact triangles trianglesValidSize = numVertices 3 launchkernel(CompactMeshTriangles, globalsize=trianglesValidSize, args=[dtrianglesValid, dtrianglesScan, dindexBuffer, dcompactIndexBuffer]) # Step 8: Allocate vertex buffer dvertexBuffer = allocatebuffer(sizeof(MeshVertex) numVertices) # Step 9: Compute color for material assignment ratio = clipmapNodeSize / CLIPMAPLEAFSIZE colour = ColourForMinLeafSize(ratio) dcolour = [colour.x, colour.y, colour.z, 0.0] # Step 10: Generate vertex attributes launchkernel(GenerateMeshVertexBuffer, globalsize=numVertices, args=[octree.dvertexPositions, octree.dvertexNormals, octree.dnodeMaterials, dcolour, dvertexBuffer]) # Step 11: Assemble final mesh buffer meshBuffer = MeshBufferGPU() meshBuffer.vertices = dvertexBuffer meshBuffer.countVertices = numVertices meshBuffer.triangles = dcompactIndexBuffer meshBuffer.countTriangles = numTriangles return meshBuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: numTriangles <= 0: Handled by early return. Buffer overflows: Asserted against MAXMESHTRIANGLES and MAXMESHVERTICES. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. name: GPU-accelerated Marching Cubes Pipeline
head: Six-stage GPU-accelerated Marching Cubes methodology
body: This method is a six-stage hybrid CPU-GPU pipeline for isosurface extraction that maximizes performance by balancing memory hierarchy usage and parallelizing the Marching Cubes algorithm. It differs from sibling methods like Capacity-Safe Marching Cubes Pipeline by offloading the spatial traversal and active cell identification to the CPU using pre-constructed spatial data structures, while the GPU handles the exact buffer allocation and triangle generation in parallel. Unlike GPU Marching Cubes with Scan-Based Compaction, which typically handles all active cells on the GPU, this approach reduces GPU memory pressure and bandwidth by transferring only the necessary active cell indices from CPU to GPU. Inputs: Volume dataset V of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Isovalue h. Spatial data structure type (k-d tree, interval tree, quadtree, or octree). Outputs: Vertex buffer P containing 3D positions of isosurface vertices. Normal buffer N containing surface normals. Rendered isosurface. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored in Video Memory (VRAM) for GPU access. A copy may exist in RAM during preprocessing. Spatial Structure: Stored in Main Memory (RAM). Used for CPU-side traversal. Active Cell List: A list of indices corresponding to voxels intersecting the isosurface, transferred from CPU to GPU. Vertex Buffers (P, N): Allocated in VRAM with exact sizes determined in Stage 4. Lookup Tables: Stored in Texture Memory for fast read-only access by GPU kernels. Parameters: Block Size: The number of threads per block. Chosen to balance workload: not too low (to avoid underutilization) and not too high (to avoid thread launch/termination overhead). Memory Types: Texture Memory: Used for lookup tables and volume data. Shared Memory: Used for computing edge intersections within a thread block. Steps: 1. CPU: Data Loading and Allocation. Read volume dataset V (Nx \times Ny \times Nz). Allocate memory for V in both RAM and VRAM. Allocate extra memory for span-space related to volume data (if not using an octree). 2. CPU: Spatial Structure Construction. Construct the chosen spatial data structure from V. Store this structure in RAM. Free V from RAM, keeping it only in VRAM. 3. CPU: Active Cell Identification. Given isovalue h, traverse the spatial data structure to identify nodes corresponding to active volume cells (cells where the isosurface intersects). Create a list of these active cell indices. Transfer this list to the GPU via the communication bus. 4. GPU: Buffer Allocation. For each active cell in the list: Classify the cell into one of the 15 Marching Cubes cases by comparing h to the eight cell vertices. Determine the cell index. Calculate the number of vertices required for the isosurface in this cell. Sum the required vertices across all active cells to determine the total vertex count. Allocate exact sizes for vertex buffer P and normal buffer N in VRAM. 5. GPU: Triangle Generation. Traverse the list of active cells again. For each cell: Calculate intersections with the 12 edges of the cell by interpolating vertex values and normals from the volume data stored in VRAM. Use the cell index and intersections to determine the specific vertex and normal list for the isosurface. Write the vertices to buffer P and normals to buffer N. 6. GPU: Rendering. Render the volume data using the populated vertex buffers P and N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cpupreprocessing(volumedata, dimensions, structuretype): # Allocate volume data in RAM and VRAM ramvolume = allocate(volumedata) vramvolume = allocateinvram(volumedata) # Construct spatial structure in RAM spatialstructure = constructstructure(ramvolume, structuretype) # Free RAM volume, keep VRAM volume free(ramvolume) return spatialstructure, vramvolume def cpufindactivecells(spatialstructure, isovalue): activecells = [] # Traverse structure to find nodes intersecting isovalue for node in traverse(spatialstructure, isovalue): activecells.append(node.index) return activecells def gpuallocatebuffers(activecells, vramvolume, isovalue): totalvertices = 0 # Pre-pass to count vertices for cellindex in activecells: # Get 8 vertex values from vramvolume vertexvalues = getcellvertices(vramvolume, cellindex) # Classify cell into one of 15 cases cellindexmc = classifymarchingcubes(vertexvalues, isovalue) # Determine vertex count for this case verticesneeded = getvertexcount(cellindexmc) totalvertices += verticesneeded # Allocate exact buffers bufferP = allocatevram(totalvertices 3) # Assuming 3 floats per vertex bufferN = allocatevram(totalvertices 3) # Assuming 3 floats per normal return bufferP, bufferN def gpugeneratetriangles(activecells, vramvolume, bufferP, bufferN, isovalue): # Shared memory for edge intersections within a block sharedmem = allocatesharedmemory() for cellindex in activecells: # Re-calculate cell index (faster than storing/retrieving) vertexvalues = getcellvertices(vramvolume, cellindex) cellindexmc = classifymarchingcubes(vertexvalues, isovalue) # Compute intersections using shared memory for data sharing intersections = computeedgeintersections( vertexvalues, isovalue, sharedmem) # Get vertices and normals from lookup tables (texture memory) vertices, normals = getverticesnormals(cellindexmc, intersections) # Write to buffers writetobuffer(bufferP, vertices) writetobuffer(bufferN, normals) def gpurender(bufferP, bufferN): rendergeometry(bufferP, bufferN) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Block Size Selection: Choosing a block size that is too low underutilizes threads, while a size that is too high causes overhead in thread management. Redundant Calculation: The cell index calculation is performed in both Stage 4 and Stage 5. This is intentional as it is faster on the GPU to recompute than to store and retrieve from an array. Memory Hierarchy: Failure to use Texture Memory for read-only data (lookup tables, volume data) and Shared Memory for intra-block data sharing (edge intersections) will result in suboptimal performance. A variant that accelerates the search for active cells using spatial data structures (k-d tree, interval tree, quadtree, octree) implemented on the GPU, but where the search itself is performed on the CPU. Complexity: The CPU handles the spatial traversal (O(N) in worst case, but optimized by structure) and the GPU handles the parallel classification and interpolation (O(A) where A is the number of active cells). Performance: The method balances CPU and GPU tasks to maximize performance. It relies on the parallelization of the active cell list processing on the GPU. Memory: Requires allocation for volume data in VRAM, spatial structure in RAM, and exact-sized vertex buffers in VRAM. Extra memory for span-space is needed for non-octree structures. Strengths: Avoids buffer overflow by exact allocation; leverages CPU for spatial traversal which can be more efficient for sparse data; uses GPU memory hierarchy (Texture/Shared) for speed. Limitations: Requires data transfer between CPU and GPU for the active cell list; dependent on the efficiency of the spatial structure construction and traversal. The methodology was proposed to accelerate the Marching Cubes technique for volumetric visualization by properly utilizing the GPU memory hierarchy and parallel processing capabilities. It builds upon earlier proposals by Buatois et al., Johansson, Martin et al., Pascucci, Reck et al., and Tatarchuk et al.. The specific implementation details, including the six-stage scheme and CUDA kernel optimizations, are described in the source.
