name: Edge Transformations for Improving Mesh Quality of Marching Cubes
head: Edge Transformations for Marching Cubes, MC with Edge Transforms, Macet, Marching Cubes using Edge Transformations (Macet)
body:
Edge Transformations (Macet) is a method that improves the geometric quality of the worst triangles generated by Marching Cubes (MC) by repositioning the endpoints of active edges before calculating their intersections with the isosurface. Unlike post-processing smoothing, which incurs unbounded error and may not remove all degeneracies, Macet modifies the sampling grid geometry while strictly preserving the mesh topology and connectivity determined by the standard MC lookup tables. It addresses the specific failure mode where MC generates poor-quality triangles when active edges are nearly parallel to the isosurface. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) defined on a 3D grid, an isovalue I, and the standard Marching Cubes topology (active edges identified per cell). Output: A mesh M with the same connectivity as standard MC but with improved triangle quality (no degenerate triangles in tested datasets). Data Structures: Scalar Field Interpolant: A cubic spline interpolant is used to reconstruct the scalar field and its derivatives. This ensures C^1 continuity, which is required for gradient-based transforms, as trilinear interpolation is not differentiable at cell boundaries. Vertex Buffers: Two buffers store candidate vertex positions for each endpoint of an active edge: 1. gradientbuffer: Stores positions resulting from the Gradient Transformation. 2. tangentialbuffer: Stores positions resulting from the Tangential Transformation. Active Edge List: A list of edges where the function f^(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) - I has different signs at its endpoints v and w. Parameters: Displacement Limit (\alpha): The maximum displacement for the gradient transform is limited to 0.5 times the original edge length to avoid excessive computation and instability. Iteration Limit: The iterative selection process stops when mesh quality stabilizes or a maximum iteration count is reached. In experiments, this typically required fewer than four steps. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify Active Edges: For each cell, identify all active edges (v, w) where f^(v) and f^(w) have opposite signs. 2. Detach Edges: For each active edge, conceptually create a "detached" edge (v', w'). This allows shared endpoints to move independently without affecting the topology determined by the original cell configuration. 3. Compute Gradient Transform: For each endpoint p \in \{v, w\} of the detached edge, compute a new position pg by moving away from the isosurface in the direction of the gradient 
abla f: pg = p + \alpha 
abla f(p) where 
abla f points away from the isosurface. The scalar \alpha is chosen such that the displacement does not exceed 0.5 times the original edge length. 4. Compute Tangential Transform: For each endpoint p \in \{v, w\}, compute a displacement direction d(p) parallel to the isosurface. The new position pt is: pt = p + \alpha d(p) The direction d(p) is chosen to maximize the dot product \langle 
abla f(t), v' - w' angle, where t is the intersection of the transformed edge (v', w') with the isosurface. This effectively aligns the edge tangentially to the isosurface at the intersection point. 5. Iterative Selection (Greedy Optimization): Initialize the vertex position for each endpoint to its original grid position. Iterate through vertex pairs (endpoints of active edges). For each vertex, evaluate the triangle quality if the vertex is taken from gradientbuffer versus tangentialbuffer. Select the position that maximizes the quality of the worst triangle connected to that vertex. Use previously computed vertices as soon as they are available to update neighbor calculations. Repeat until the quality of the worst triangle no longer improves or the iteration limit is reached. 6. Recompute Intersection: For each transformed edge (v', w'), compute the intersection point t with the isosurface using a bisection-based root finding procedure. Linear interpolation is invalid because the edge endpoints have moved freely. 7. Generate Mesh: Use the computed intersection points and the original MC topology to generate the final triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def macetextractmesh(grid, isovalue): """ Extracts a high-quality mesh from a scalar grid using Edge Transformations. Assumes cubic spline interpolation is available for f(x) and gradf(x). """ # 1. Identify active edges and topology (Standard MC step) activeedges = [] for cell in grid.cells: # Determine cell configuration based on signs of f(v) - isovalue config = getmcconfig(cell.vertices, isovalue) # Get list of active edges for this configuration edges = getactiveedgesfromconfig(config) activeedges.extend(edges) # 2. Initialize buffers for vertex positions # Each edge has two endpoints. We store candidate positions. # gradientpos[edgeid][endpointindex] # tangentialpos[edgeid][endpointindex] gradientpos = {} tangentialpos = {} for edgeid, (v, w) in enumerate(activeedges): # 3. Gradient Transform # Move endpoints along gradient away from isosurface gradv = v + 0.5 length(v, w) normalize(gradf(v)) gradw = w + 0.5 length(v, w) normalize(gradf(w)) gradientpos[edgeid] = [gradv, gradw] # 4. Tangential Transform # Move endpoints to maximize alignment with isosurface tangent # This requires an iterative sub-step or approximation to find optimal alpha # For implementation, we approximate by moving perpendicular to gradient # and projecting onto the plane defined by the edge and gradient. # Simplified: d(p) is orthogonal to gradf(p) and lies in the plane # spanned by the edge vector and the gradient. # Calculate direction to maximize <gradf(t), v' - w'> # This is complex to solve analytically for t, so we use an iterative # refinement or a simplified heuristic as described in. # Here we assume a helper function that computes the optimal tangential shift. tanv = computetangentialshift(v, w, isovalue) tanw = computetangentialshift(w, v, isovalue) tangentialpos[edgeid] = [tanv, tanw] # 5. Iterative Selection # We need to select for each vertex whether to use gradient or tangential pos # to maximize the worst triangle quality. # Since vertices are shared, we process iteratively. # Map edge endpoints to global vertex IDs to handle sharing vertexcandidates = {} # vertexid -> [gradientpos, tangentialpos] for edgeid, (v, w) in enumerate(activeedges): # Note: v and w are local to the cell/edge context. # In a full implementation, we must map these to unique global vertex indices. # For this pseudocode, we assume a simplified unique edge processing # where shared vertices are resolved by the greedy pass. # Store candidates for the two endpoints of this edge # We need to aggregate candidates for shared vertices across cells. # This part requires a global vertex map. pass # Simplified Greedy Pass Logic (as per): # "The vertex pairs are processed one at a time, and the previously # computed vertices are used as soon as they are available." finalvertices = {} # vertexid -> finalposition # Iterate until convergence or max steps for iteration in range(MAXITERATIONS): improved = False for edgeid, (v, w) in enumerate(activeedges): # Get global IDs for v and w gidv = getglobalid(v) gidw = getglobalid(w) # If already decided, skip or use existing? # The paper says "previously computed vertices are used as soon as available". # This implies a dependency order or a relaxation method. # Evaluate quality for v using gradient pos vs tangential pos # considering the current positions of neighbors (including w) posgv = gradientpos[edgeid][0] postv = tangentialpos[edgeid][0] # We need to know the positions of the other endpoints of triangles # incident to v to calculate triangle quality. # This requires building the adjacency list or accessing cell data. qualityg = calculateworsttrianglequality(v, posgv, w, wpos, neighbors) qualityt = calculateworsttrianglequality(v, postv, w, wpos, neighbors) if qualityg > qualityt: newv = posgv else: newv = postv # Update global vertex if better or if not yet set if gidv not in finalvertices or newv is better: finalvertices[gidv] = newv improved = True if not improved: break # 6. Recompute Intersection and Generate Mesh meshtriangles = [] for cell in grid.cells: config = getmcconfig(cell.vertices, isovalue) activeedgesincell = getactiveedgesfromconfig(config) triangles = [] for edge in activeedgesincell: v, w = edge gidv = getglobalid(v) gidw = getglobalid(w) # Get final transformed positions vfinal = finalvertices[gidv] wfinal = finalvertices[gidw] # Bisection root finding for intersection on transformed edge t = bisectionintersection(vfinal, wfinal, isovalue) # Add triangle based on MC triangle table for this config # The triangle table indices depend on the config, not the positions triangles.extend(gettrianglesfromtable(config, t)) meshtriangles.extend(triangles) return Mesh(meshtriangles) def computetangentialshift(p1, p2, isovalue): """ Computes the tangential shift for endpoint p1 of edge (p1, p2). Maximizes <gradf(t), p1' - p2'>. """ # Simplified implementation: # Move p1 in direction orthogonal to gradf(p1) # such that the edge becomes more tangent to the isosurface. grad = gradf(p1) edgevec = p2 - p1 # Project edgevec onto plane orthogonal to grad # d = edgevec - projgrad(edgevec) # But we want to move p1, so we adjust p1. # A robust way is to find the point on the isosurface closest to the edge # and move towards it, or align the edge with the tangent plane. # The source states: "maximize <rf(t), v' - w'>". # This is an optimization problem. # Heuristic: Move p1 along the direction perpendicular to gradf(p1) # and perpendicular to the edge normal? # Let's use the projection method. # Direction d such that d. gradf(p1) = 0 # We want to maximize the component of the edge vector along the gradient # at the intersection. # For the purpose of implementation from text, we note that this requires # an iterative solver or a specific geometric construction. # We will return a placeholder comment for the exact geometric derivation # as it is complex, but the goal is clear. return p1 # Placeholder: Exact geometric derivation for tangential shift # maximizing <gradf(t), v'-w'> is non-trivial and requires # iterative refinement or solving for t. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiable Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is not differentiable at cell boundaries, causing unpredictable results for gradient-based transforms. This is handled by using cubic spline interpolation. Multiple Roots: Cubic spline interpolation may result in multiple roots in active edges. This presents no practical problem because topology is already determined by MC lookup tables and the intersection calculation returns only one vertex. Topology Preservation: The transformation must satisfy two conditions: 1) The active edge must keep only one intersection with the isosurface throughout the motion. 2) The intersection induced by the detached edge must not result in triangle flips. Linear Interpolation Invalid: Standard linear interpolation for intersection calculation is invalid after moving edge endpoints. Bisection-based root finding must be used. Time Complexity: The method incurs minimal computational overhead, requiring at most twice the execution time of the original Marching Cubes algorithm. The overhead decreases as the dataset size increases. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two additional vertex position buffers per active edge endpoint and the cubic spline coefficients for the scalar field. Performance: Experiments on a Pentium 4 3.0-GHz PC with 2-Gbyte RAM showed that Macet did not produce a single degenerate triangle in tested datasets (Silicium, Lobster, Engine), whereas standard MC and other methods produced degenerate triangles. Accuracy: The Hausdorff distance between the Macet mesh and the original MC mesh is very small, indicating that the mesh is very close to the MC mesh while having better quality. Strengths: Eliminates degenerate triangles; preserves MC topology; orthogonal to MC performance optimizations (e.g., out-of-core, acceleration structures); suitable for downstream processes like Constrained Delaunay Tetrahedralization (CDT) where mesh quality is critical (e.g., tetgen crashes on MC meshes for complex datasets but works on Macet meshes). Limitations: Does not explicitly aim for adaptive meshing or sharp feature preservation (unlike Dual Contouring); does not allow topological changes (unlike Warping Cubes). Origin: The method was introduced by Dietrich et al. in the paper "Edge Transformations for Improving Mesh Quality of Marching Cubes". History: The work was motivated by the observation that poor triangle quality in MC is correlated with cell edges nearly parallel to the isosurface. Previous methods like smoothing or decimation did not fully remove degeneracies and incurred unbounded error. Dual methods like Dual Contouring improved quality but focused on adaptive meshing and sharp features. Macet was designed specifically to improve mesh quality for high-fidelity visualization and downstream geometric processing. Usage: It is used in visualization pipelines where high-quality isosurfaces are required for rendering or further geometric processing, such as tetrahedralization for finite element analysis. name: Midpoint Marching Cubes
head: Proposed Marching Cubes Algorithm
body: Midpoint Marching Cubes is a surface extraction method that modifies the standard Marching Cubes algorithm by replacing linear scalar interpolation on cube edges with fixed midpoint selection. It reduces the 256 possible cube configurations to 15 basic patterns using reflective and rotational symmetries, thereby eliminating the need for scalar value interpolation during the intersection calculation phase. Unlike its siblings which optimize vertex positions or handle complex ambiguities, this method prioritizes computational simplicity by fixing intersection points to geometric centers, though it sacrifices accuracy for complex geometries and suffers from the "hole problem" due to reliance on complementary symmetry alone. Inputs: A regular 3-D grid derived from a volumetric dataset (e.g., endoscope scanning data), where each grid vertex has an associated binary occupancy state (1 if inside the surface, 0 if outside). Outputs: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface, rendered via OpenGL. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D array of vertices. Each vertex v at coordinates (i, j, k) holds a binary value b \in \{0, 1\}. Cube Index: An 8-bit integer representing the occupancy state of the 8 vertices of a logical cube. The bits correspond to vertices #1 through #8 as defined in the standard MC configuration. Lookup Table: A reduced table mapping the 8-bit index to one of 15 basic surface intersection patterns. This table accounts for reflective and rotational symmetries to collapse the standard 256 cases. Intersection Points: Pre-calculated or computed on-the-fly positions at the exact midpoints of the 12 edges of the cube. Steps: 1. Grid Generation: Convert the raw volumetric dataset into a regular 3-D grid. For each logical cube, determine the binary occupancy of its 8 vertices. A vertex is assigned binary 1 if its projection distance on the i, j, or k axis exceeds the midpoint threshold relative to the surface; otherwise, it is 0. 2. Index Calculation: Construct an 8-bit binary index for the current cube based on the occupancy states of its 8 vertices (vertices #1 to #8). 3. Pattern Lookup: Use the 8-bit index to retrieve the corresponding surface intersection pattern from the reduced lookup table (15 basic patterns). Pattern 0: No vertices inside (no triangles). Pattern 1: One vertex inside, etc. 4. Intersection Calculation: For each edge of the cube identified as intersected by the pattern, set the surface intersection point exactly at the midpoint of that edge. No linear interpolation based on scalar values is performed. 5. Triangle Generation: Generate triangles using the 12 possible midpoint positions on the cube edges as vertices, following the connectivity defined by the lookup table pattern. 6. Rendering: Render the resulting triangle vertex coordinates using OpenGL. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def midpointmarchingcubes(grid, lookuptable): """ grid: 3D array of binary occupancy values (0 or 1) for each vertex. lookuptable: Dictionary mapping 8-bit integer index to a list of triangle definitions. Each triangle definition is a list of 3 edge indices (0-11). """ triangles = [] # Iterate over all logical cubes in the grid # Assuming grid dimensions are (Dx, Dy, Dz) for i in range(grid.shape[0] - 1): for j in range(grid.shape[1] - 1): for k in range(grid.shape[2] - 1): # 1. Get the 8 vertices of the current cube # Vertices are ordered according to standard MC convention v0 = grid[i, j, k] v1 = grid[i+1, j, k] v2 = grid[i+1, j+1, k] v3 = grid[i, j+1, k] v4 = grid[i, j, k+1] v5 = grid[i+1, j, k+1] v6 = grid[i+1, j+1, k+1] v7 = grid[i, j+1, k+1] # 2. Calculate 8-bit index # Bit 0 corresponds to v0, Bit 1 to v1,..., Bit 7 to v7 index = (v0 << 0) | (v1 << 1) | (v2 << 2) | (v3 << 3) | \ (v4 << 4) | (v5 << 5) | (v6 << 6) | (v7 << 7) # 3. Lookup pattern # If index is 0 or 255, no triangles are generated (empty or full cube) if index == 0 or index == 255: continue # Get the list of edges that form triangles for this index # The lookup table returns edge indices (0-11) grouped into triangles edgeindices = lookuptable[index] # 4. Generate triangles # Process edge indices in groups of 3 to form triangles for triedges in edgeindices: # triedges is a list of 3 edge indices p1 = getmidpoint(i, j, k, triedges[0]) p2 = getmidpoint(i, j, k, triedges[1]) p3 = getmidpoint(i, j, k, triedges[2]) triangles.append([p1, p2, p3]) return triangles def getmidpoint(i, j, k, edgeindex): """ Returns the midpoint coordinates of a specific edge of the cube at (i,j,k). Edge indices 0-11 correspond to the 12 edges of a cube. Standard MC edge ordering is assumed. """ # Define the 8 corners of the cube corners = [ (i, j, k), # 0 (i+1, j, k), # 1 (i+1, j+1, k), # 2 (i, j+1, k), # 3 (i, j, k+1), # 4 (i+1, j, k+1), # 5 (i+1, j+1, k+1), # 6 (i, j+1, k+1) # 7 ] # Define the 12 edges as pairs of vertex indices edges = [ (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0), # Bottom face (4, 5), (5, 6), (6, 7), (7, 4), # Top face (0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7) # Vertical edges ] vstart, vend = edges[edgeindex] pstart = corners[vstart] pend = corners[vend] # Midpoint calculation mx = (pstart[0] + pend[0]) / 2.0 my = (pstart[1] + pend[1]) / 2.0 mz = (pstart[2] + pend[2]) / 2.0 return (mx, my, mz) Parameters: Threshold for Binary Assignment: The method relies on a binary classification of vertices. The source notes that a vertex is assigned 1 if its "projection distance on i and j axes exceeds the midpoint". The exact scalar threshold for this binary conversion is not explicitly defined in the provided text, but it implies a step function at the grid cell center or a specific depth threshold from the scanning system. Lookup Table Size: 15 basic patterns. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hole Problem: The method suffers from the "hole problem" because the lookup table depends only on complementary symmetry. This fails to resolve ambiguous cases correctly, potentially leading to topological errors or holes in the mesh. Accuracy Limitations: High accuracy is not guaranteed for complex geometries. The method is limited to objects with smooth, featureless surfaces. Ambiguity: Standard MC ambiguities (e.g., the tetrahedron case) are not addressed by midpoint selection alone, as the method relies on the reduced 15-pattern table which may not cover all topological configurations correctly without additional logic. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of cubes in the grid. The lookup is O(1) and midpoint calculation is O(1). No scalar interpolation is required, which is faster than standard MC. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the grid and the resulting mesh. The lookup table is constant size (15 patterns). Strengths: Simple implementation; no need for scalar value interpolation; reduced lookup table size (15 vs 256); fast rendering via OpenGL. Limitations: Low accuracy for complex or feature-rich surfaces; prone to the "hole problem" due to symmetry-only lookup; not suitable for high-fidelity reconstruction of detailed geometries. When to use: Suitable for real-time or resource-constrained applications involving smooth, featureless surfaces (e.g., endoscopic scanning of biological tissues) where speed is prioritized over geometric precision. When not to use: Not suitable for complex geometries, sharp features, or applications requiring high topological correctness and accuracy. The method was proposed in the context of 3-D surface reconstruction based on endoscope and optical fiber scanning systems. It was introduced as a "Proposed Marching Cubes Algorithm" to simplify the surface extraction process for volumetric data derived from endoscopic scans. The authors reduced the standard 256 cases to 15 basic patterns using reflective and rotational symmetries, a technique previously studied in other works. The method was evaluated using plane tests and endoscope scanning data, showing limitations in accuracy for non-smooth surfaces. A Marching Cubes Algorithm: Application for Three-dimensional Surface Reconstruction Based on Endoscope and Optical Fiber, https://inria.hal.science/hal-01205823v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Marching Cubes Boundary Cap
head: MC boundary cap, box-face crossing cap
body: Marching Cubes Boundary Cap is a post-processing step for Marching Cubes (MC) that closes open mesh boundaries when the isosurface exits the sample-cube boundary. It solves the problem of non-watertight meshes (IsWatertight = false) caused by insufficient bounding ranges, ensuring the output is a closed 2-manifold suitable for 3D printing. It differs from auto-sizing the bounding box by allowing users to force a too-small range while still producing a watertight mesh, and differs from general mesh simplification by specifically targeting boundary closure rather than complexity reduction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The mesh M generated by the Marching Cubes algorithm, consisting of vertices V, triangles T, and adjacency information. The scalar field values are already sampled on the face vertices from the MC pass. Output: A closed 2-manifold mesh where boundary edges on the cube faces are triangulated and welded to the existing MC boundary vertices. Data Structures: The mesh M consists of vertices V and triangles T. Adjacency information is derived from the edgeTable and triangleTable of the parent Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling. Boundary edges are identified as edges shared by only one triangle. Steps: 1. Check for Interior Surface: If the bounding range is auto-sized to enclose the set, the surface remains interior to the cube. In this case, the cap method is a no-op to maintain byte-identical output and performance. 2. Iterate Cube Faces: For each of the 6 cube faces, identify the cross-section polygon(s) where the scalar field intersects the face. 3. 2D Contour Extraction: Run a 2D Marching Squares contour algorithm on the face grid to extract the contour lines of the intersection between the isosurface and the cube face. 4. Triangulate Cap: Triangulate the interior (or exterior, depending on the field sign convention relative to the iso value) region enclosed by the contour lines to create a cap mesh. 5. Weld Vertices: Weld the vertices of the generated cap triangles to the existing boundary vertices of the MC mesh on that face to form a single closed 2-manifold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marchingcubesboundarycap(mesh, scalarfield, cubebounds, isovalue): """ Closes open boundaries of a Marching Cubes mesh if the isosurface exits the cube. Args: mesh: Object containing vertices V, triangles T, and adjacency info. scalarfield: Function or array providing scalar values at grid points. cubebounds: Bounding box of the sample cube. isovalue: The isovalue used for Marching Cubes. Returns: Closed 2-manifold mesh. """ # Step 1: Check if surface is interior (no-op case) # If the bounding range was auto-sized to enclose the set, the surface is interior. # This check ensures byte-identical output for the standard case. if issurfaceinterior(mesh, cubebounds, isovalue): return mesh # Step 2: Iterate over the 6 faces of the cube for face in cubefaces(cubebounds): # Step 3: Extract contour on the face using 2D Marching Squares # The scalar field values are already sampled on the face vertices. contourlines = marchingsquares2d(face.gridvertices, scalarfield, isovalue) # Step 4: Triangulate the region enclosed by the contour lines # Determine interior vs exterior based on field sign convention relative to isovalue. captriangles = triangulatecontour(contourlines, isovalue) # Step 5: Weld cap vertices to existing MC boundary vertices boundaryvertices = getboundaryvertices(mesh, face) weldedmesh = weldvertices(mesh, captriangles, boundaryvertices) mesh = weldedmesh return mesh def issurfaceinterior(mesh, cubebounds, isovalue): """ Helper to determine if the mesh is fully contained within the cube bounds. In practice, this might check if any boundary edges exist on the cube faces. If no boundary edges exist on the cube faces, the surface is interior. """ boundaryedgesoncube = findboundaryedgesoncubefaces(mesh, cubebounds) return len(boundaryedgesoncube) == 0 def marchingsquares2d(gridvertices, scalarfield, isovalue): """ Standard 2D Marching Squares implementation. Returns a list of contour line segments on the 2D grid. """ # Implementation details of 2D Marching Squares are assumed to be available # from the parent article or standard graphics libraries. pass def triangulatecontour(contourlines, isovalue): """ Triangulates the polygon(s) defined by contourlines. The choice of interior vs exterior depends on the sign of (scalarfield - isovalue). """ pass def getboundaryvertices(mesh, face): """ Returns vertices of the mesh that lie on the specified cube face and are part of boundary edges (edges shared by only one triangle). """ pass def weldvertices(mesh, captriangles, boundaryvertices): """ Merges captriangles with the existing mesh, ensuring vertices on the boundary are shared. """ pass Parameters: isovalue: The isovalue used for Marching Cubes. Typical values depend on the scalar field. cubebounds: The bounding box of the sample cube. If auto-sized, the cap is a no-op. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the bounding range is auto-sized to enclose the set, the surface remains interior to the cube. The cap method must be a no-op in this case to maintain byte-identical output and performance. Precision issues may arise when determining if the surface is exactly on the boundary. A small epsilon tolerance should be used when comparing vertex positions to the cube faces. An algorithm to universally enclose open reconstructed mesh surfaces (specifically those with a single hole) by appending a base plane, creating a closed mesh suitable for MPM/FEM simulation. It differs from the standard MC boundary cap by not relying on the grid structure of the Marching Cubes output, but rather on the boundary edges of any reconstructed mesh. It is chosen when the input mesh is not from a regular grid or when the boundary is not aligned with a cube face. Input: Mesh vertices \mathcal{V} and triangles \mathcal{F} structured in 2D arrays. Steps: 1. Construct boundary edges and organize in a list. 2. Classify edges using a non-manifold test (manifold edges are in 2 triangles; non-manifold are boundary edges). 3. Conduct BFS to sort boundary vertices into an ordered list. 4. Iteratively build a base plane of the soft tissue surface in the shape of the open mesh boundary. 5. Loop for each vertex v in the ordered edge list: find the projection of v in the appended base. 6. Connect the projection of the last v, the projection of the current v, and the center of the base plane to create new faces. Pitfall: Designed for input meshes with a single 'hole' (one connected edge). If there are two disjoint surfaces, run the algorithm separately for each surface. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of boundary edges on the cube faces. The 2D Marching Squares pass is linear with respect to the number of cells on the face. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of boundary edges, as new triangles are added for the cap. Measured Performance: In a validation test case with a sphere of radius r=1.8 inside a cube with half-extent 1.6, the uncapped MC mesh had 648 boundary edges and was not watertight. After capping, the mesh was watertight. Strengths: Ensures watertightness even with undersized bounding boxes. Maintains byte-identical output for the standard auto-sized case. Limitations: Only applies to boundaries on the cube faces. Does not handle holes in the interior of the mesh. When to use: When 3D printing or simulation requires a closed 2-manifold, and the bounding box cannot be guaranteed to enclose the entire isosurface. When not to use: When the bounding box is auto-sized to enclose the set, as the cap is a no-op and adds unnecessary complexity. Origin: The method was developed as part of the FracturingFog project, specifically in issue #422 and fixed in #425 by AloneButUnsober. It was implemented in the UserBulbMeshExporter and validated by MeshValidator to ensure SignedVolume > 0 and outward winding. The default mitigation was to auto-size the cube (UserBulbMeshExporter.ProbeBoundingRange), but this method allows users to force a too-small range while still producing a watertight mesh. name: Grid Structure and Topology
body: This family defines the geometric and topological data structures used to represent the scalar field domain for isosurface extraction. It solves the problem of mapping discrete volumetric data to a continuous mesh by establishing how grid vertices, cells, and boundaries are organized. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the underlying grid topology (structured, dual, or hierarchical) rather than the specific triangulation rules or ambiguity resolution strategies. The family relies on two precomputed data structures derived from the 256 possible binary configurations of a voxel's eight corner signs relative to an isovalue Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling. 1. Edge Intersection Table (edgeTable): An array of 256 integers (or shorts). Each entry is a 12-bit bitmask. Bit k (0 \le k \le 11) is set to 1 if the isosurface intersects the k-th edge of the cube, and 0 otherwise. The standard edge numbering convention is: Bottom face (z=0): e0=(0,1), e1=(1,2), e2=(2,3), e3=(3,0) Top face (z=1): e4=(4,5), e5=(5,6), e6=(6,7), e7=(7,4) Vertical edges: e8=(0,4), e9=(1,5), e{10}=(2,6), e{11}=(3,7) Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling 2. Triangle Connection Table (triangleTable): A 2D array of size 256 \times 16. Rows are indexed by the case index C \in [0, 255]. Columns store integer indices. Indices 0–11 refer to the 12 cube edges. Indices are grouped in triplets (a, b, c) to form triangles. The sequence is terminated by the value -1. The maximum number of triangles per voxel is 5, requiring 15 indices plus 1 terminator Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling Case Index Calculation: For each voxel, the 8-bit case index C is determined by the scalar field values V at the 8 vertices vi (i=0..7). If V(vi) < I (or > I, depending on convention), bit i of C is set to 1; otherwise 0. The bit assignment must strictly match the vertex ordering assumed by the LUT generation Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling. Ambiguity: Cases 46, 47, 98, 99, 210, 213, 214, 215 contain saddle points where the topology is ambiguous (the isosurface passes through the cube center). The standard LUT uses a fixed triangulation for these, which can cause cracks or holes if adjacent voxels resolve the ambiguity differently Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecaseindex(values, isovalue): caseindex = 0 for i in range(8): if values[i] < isovalue: caseindex |= (1 << i) return caseindex def extracttriangles(caseindex, edgetable, triangletable, edgeintersections): triangles = [] edgemask = edgetable[caseindex] triindices = triangletable[caseindex] for i in range(0, len(triindices), 3): if triindices[i] == -1: break e1, e2, e3 = triindices[i], triindices[i+1], triindices[i+2] p1 = edgeintersections[e1] p2 = edgeintersections[e2] p3 = edgeintersections[e3] triangles.append((p1, p2, p3)) return triangles Extracts a 3D polygonal mesh from a discretized scalar field defined on a regular Cartesian grid. It sets itself apart by operating directly on the structured IJK grid topology using a fixed lookup table for cell triangulation, whereas methods like Dual Contouring and Surface Nets optimize vertex positions for accuracy, and Marching Tetrahedra and Decomposition decompose cells to resolve topological ambiguities. Extracts crack-free isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data by constructing a dual grid where cell centers serve as vertices. It solves the "dangling node" problem inherent in standard Marching Cubes when applied to resampled vertex-centered AMR data, where mismatched interpolation at coarse-fine boundaries causes topological discontinuities. Unlike sibling methods that fix cracks by post-processing polygons or collapsing polylines, this approach eliminates dangling nodes structurally by leveraging the geometric gap between coarse and fine dual grids. The 3D analogous structure of a quadtree, partitioning a 3D space region into eight subregions (octants). The tree is built directly from the volume data. For non-regular grids (dimensions not power of two), subregions have different sizes as they partition cell regions. Not given in the sources. Marching cubes technique for volumetric visualization accelerated with graphics processing units, https://doi.org/10.1007/s13173-012-0097-z, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Marching Cubes on Structured Grids
head: MC extraction, Marching Cubes in IJK Coordinate Space, Marching Cubes mesh extraction from implicit volume
body: Marching Cubes on Structured Grids extracts a 3D triangular mesh from a scalar field defined on a regular 3D grid by evaluating the field at grid vertices, determining intersection cases, and interpolating edge crossings. It builds on Grid Structure and Topology by processing each voxel independently using precomputed lookup tables. Unlike Dual Grid Isosurface Extraction which operates on cell centers, this method operates directly on the grid vertices, making it the standard approach for extracting surfaces from implicit volumes, neural fields, and medical imaging data. Inputs: 1. Scalar Field (V): A 3D array of shape (Rx, Ry, Rz) containing scalar values at grid vertices. 2. Isovalue (I): The threshold scalar value defining the surface. 3. Grid Bounds: Lower bounds c1 = (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and upper bounds c2 = (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}) defining the physical extent of the grid. 4. Lookup Tables: edgeTable (256 entries, 12-bit masks) and triangleTable (256 entries, 16 integers) as defined in Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling. Outputs: 1. Vertices: A list of 3D coordinates (x, y, z) in physical space. 2. Triangles: A list of triplets of vertex indices. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D array V[i, j, k] where 0 \le i < Rx, 0 \le j < Ry, 0 \le k < Rz. Edge Intersections: Temporary storage for the 3D position of the isosurface intersection on a cube edge. Steps: 1. Evaluate Scalar Field: If the input is not a pre-computed grid (e.g., a neural network), evaluate the scalar field V at all grid vertices. For a neural implicit volume, this involves batching vertex queries to manage memory. Note: If the network uses view-dependent shading (viewdirs), the sigma value depends on direction. Standard MC assumes a static scalar field. A common workaround is to substitute fake viewdirs pointing to the origin, though this may produce incorrect geometry. 2. Iterate Voxels: Loop through each voxel (i, j, k) where 0 \le i < Rx-1, 0 \le j < Ry-1, 0 \le k < Rz-1. 3. Compute Case Index: Retrieve the 8 vertex values v0 \dots v7 for the current voxel. The vertex ordering must match the LUT convention (typically: v0=(0,0,0), v1=(1,0,0), \dots, v7=(1,1,1) in local IJK space). Calculate the case index C: C = \sum{m=0}^{7} bm 2^m where bm = 1 if vm < I (or vm > I, depending on the specific LUT convention used; consistency is key), and 0 otherwise. 4. Check Intersection: Look up edgeTable[C]. If the result is 0, the isosurface does not intersect this voxel; skip to the next voxel. 5. Compute Edge Intersections: For each edge e where the bit e is set in edgeTable[C]: Identify the two vertices va, vb connected by edge e. Calculate the intersection point P using linear interpolation: P = va + \frac{I - V(va)}{V(vb) - V(va)} (vb - va) Store P in local IJK coordinates or physical coordinates. 6. Generate Triangles: Look up triangleTable[C]. Iterate through the triplets (a, b, c) until the terminator -1 is reached. For each triplet, retrieve the pre-computed intersection points Pa, Pb, Pc and add the triangle (Pa, Pb, Pc) to the output mesh. 7. Coordinate Transformation: If intersections were computed in IJK (grid) space, transform them to XYZ (physical) space. The standard approach, often used for simplicity, is to map the grid coordinates directly: x = x{min} + \frac{i}{Rx} (x{max} - x{min}) y = y{min} + \frac{j}{Ry} (y{max} - y{min}) z = z{min} + \frac{k}{Rz} (z{max} - z{min}) Note: This linear mapping is not technically correct for non-uniform grids or if the grid spacing is not uniform, but for most applications the difference is negligible. For strict correctness, one should interpolate the physical coordinates of the vertices first. 8. Handle Ambiguities: For cases 46, 47, 98, 99, 210, 213, 214, 215, the standard LUT provides a fixed triangulation. This may cause topological errors (cracks) if adjacent voxels resolve the ambiguity inconsistently. Advanced implementations may use the Asymptotic Decider or Matveyev's algorithm to resolve these. Pre-calculate grid vertex physical coordinates to avoid repeated division # Note: Standard MC uses vertices of the voxel. # Voxel (i,j,k) has vertices at grid indices (i,j,k) to (i+1,j+1,k+1) for i in range(Rx - 1): for j in range(Ry - 1): for k in range(Rz - 1): # Edge 6: (6,7) if edgemask & 64: p6 = (c1[0] + (i+1)dx, c1[1] + (j+1)dy, c1[2] + (k+1)dz) p7 = (c1[0] + idx, c1[1] + (j+1)dy, c1[2] + (k+1)dz) edgeintersections[6] = interp(v[6], v[7], p6, p7) # Edge 7: (7,4) if edgemask & 128: p7 = (c1[0] + idx, c1[1] + (j+1)dy, c1[2] + (k+1)dz) p4 = (c1[0] + idx, c1[1] + jdy, c1[2] + (k+1)dz) edgeintersections[7] = interp(v[7], v[4], p7, p4) # It builds on Marching Cubes on Structured Grids by introducing a snapping mechanism that reduces geometric error, distinguishing it from standard UMC and other siblings like Bitwise Marching Cubes which prioritize bitwise operations over positional accuracy. Smart Conversion is an advanced, gradient-based voxel-to-mesh conversion algorithm that prioritizes accuracy by correcting errors from noise, multiple materials, or inaccurate iso-values. Unlike standard isosurface extraction methods such as Marching Cubes on Structured Grids which rely on fixed threshold crossings, Smart Conversion iteratively "pulls" the mesh to align with the true boundary of the scan by locating points of steepest gradient along local surface normals. This makes it particularly suitable for medical or high-precision industrial contexts where accuracy is paramount and the initial voxel data may contain flaws. Flying Edges is a parallel, threaded algorithm for volumetric isocontouring of continuous scalar fields that addresses the performance limitations of Marching Cubes by processing volume edges rather than voxel cells. It eliminates point merging bottlenecks by using an edge-based iterator to generate output points and triangle cells, avoiding the need for hashing duplicate points. This method finds the ray start point \hat{x}0 = D^{-1}(p) in undeformed space without computing the inverse deformation map D^{-1} directly. It solves the problem where D may not be invertible or well-defined at the camera position by intersecting the deformed view ray with a deformed explicit hull mesh that contains the surface. Dividing Cubes is an isosurface extraction method that replaces the triangular mesh primitives of Marching Cubes with 3D points. It solves the problem of excessive triangle counts and the subsequent scan-conversion overhead by adaptively subdividing cells intersected by the surface until each subcell projects onto a single pixel. Cell Subdivision Isosurface Extraction is a method for extracting isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data that retains the original identity of cells (vertex/node-centered data) to support debugging and patch tracking. Unlike dual-grid approaches that stitch cells together, this method eliminates non-linear hanging nodes by subdividing boundary cells into pyramids, allowing standard isosurface techniques (like Marching Cubes) to be applied directly to the subdivided geometry. It is chosen when preserving cell-to-triangle mapping is critical, at the cost of increased geometric complexity due to pyramid decomposition. Analytic Marching (AM) is a meshing algorithm that extracts the exact zero-level isosurface of an implicit function represented by a ReLU-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) as a polygon mesh, without relying on discrete 3D grid sampling. Unlike Marching Cubes on Structured Grids, whose accuracy depends on discretization resolution, AM exploits the piecewise linear nature of ReLU networks to identify linear regions intersected by the surface and solve for vertices analytically, making its precision independent of grid resolution. This method generates an isosurface from a combined field of metaballs using a two-stage GPU pipeline, utilizing vertex shaders for field evaluation and geometry shaders for mesh generation. It is distinguished from standard CPU-based or single-pass GPU implementations by its explicit separation of field computation and mesh topology generation, coupled with Transform-Feedback caching to avoid recomputing geometry when the camera moves but the metaball configuration remains static. It builds on Marching Cubes on Structured Grids by offloading the structured grid vertex evaluation and cube processing to the GPU. Matveyev's Algorithm is an algorithm based on a triangulation table that correctly represents trilinear interpolant behavior using intersections on cube diagonals. Proposed by Matveyev in 1999, it addresses the ambiguity problem in the interior of the cube by using diagonal intersections to determine the correct topology of the trilinear interpolant. Geomorph LOD Seam Handling is a technique to achieve watertight seams between fine and coarse LOD levels in Marching Cubes by geometrically deforming the fine surface at the boundary to match the coarse contour. It identifies boundary vertices between fine and coarse LOD levels, applies a geometric morph (bending) to fine surface vertices at the boundary, and deforms vertices toward the coarse contour to eliminate gaps. TexF with Implicit Geometry (SDF) is an extension where TexF shares a canonical grid with an implicit Signed Distance Field (SDF). The surface is extracted via Marching Cubes, and TexF attributes are transferred to vertices for standard vertex-color rendering, avoiding per-pixel TexF queries. The SDF and TexF share the same grid. After extracting a mesh with Marching Cubes, TexF attributes are transferred to its vertices using k-nearest-neighbor interpolation. The rasterizer then interpolates these vertex attributes across triangles, avoiding per-pixel TexF queries. 3-Edge Cube Sampling with Corner Extension is an optimization where, instead of calculating intersection points for all 12 edges of a cube, intersections are computed for only the 3 edges in the bottom-left corner of each cube. An extra row is added in the top-right corner of the processing zone to ensure all necessary grid values are accessible for the reduced edge set. The indexing logic requires a special upgrade/mapping to correctly access grid values, making it complicated to implement correctly. Octree-Based Isolevel Culling builds an octree structure over the volume to assess the ISO level distribution, allowing the algorithm to skip processing areas far from the target isolevel. Propagation-based culling methods are noted as unreliable and inefficient compared to direct octree assessment. Coarse Sampling Dead-Space Elimination performs an initial pass sampling the volume at a coarser spatial rate to identify and eliminate regions where field strength is well below the isolevel. However, coarse sampling provides virtually no performance gain for non-trivial fields, as safe sampling borders still capture most of the grid. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel is processed independently. The constant factor depends on the number of triangles generated per voxel (max 5). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the scalar field grid. The output mesh size depends on the surface complexity. Performance: The algorithm is highly parallelizable as voxels are independent. However, point merging (deduplication of vertices) can be a bottleneck on CPU implementations. GPU implementations like Flying Edges avoid this by processing edges. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for well-sampled data, widely supported. Limitations: Sensitive to grid resolution; aliasing artifacts if the grid is too coarse. Ambiguity cases (46, 47, etc.) can cause topological errors. View-dependent fields cannot be directly represented without approximation. When to use: When extracting surfaces from static, uniformly sampled scalar fields (e.g., medical CT/MRI, neural implicit volumes with fixed resolution). When not to use: When the field is view-dependent, when high precision is required without dense sampling (use Analytic Marching), or when dealing with AMR data (use Cell Subdivision). The Marching Cubes algorithm was originally developed and patented by GE Medical Systems for use in their CT and MRI equipment. The patent has since expired, placing the algorithm in the public domain. It is one of the most common visualization methods in use today and is used by several other algorithms such as Metaballs and Part Extraction. Modifications allow it to be performed in IJK coordinate space and interpolated back into XYZ space for any 3D structured grid. sxyu/pixel-nerf, https://github.com/sxyu/pixel-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Marching Cubes Marching Cubes, https://daac.hpc.mil/gettingStarted/MarchingCubes.html, fetched 2026-10-29 A Evolucao do Algoritmo Marching Cubes, https://doi.org/10.5540/03.2017.005.01.0107, fetched 2026-10-26 draquel/VoxelWorlds, https://github.com/draquel/VoxelWorlds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Beyond UV Mapping: Mesh Texture Compression via Surface-Aligned Texture Fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.23606, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) How to speed up marching cubes?, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/868831/how-to-speed-up-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

head: Uniform Marching Cubes
body: Uniform Marching Cubes with Snapping is a uniform-grid polygonization algorithm that computes cell topology masks from coarse grid vertex signs and optionally snaps iso-surface vertices to edges by minimizing distance to grid vertices. It builds on Marching Cubes on Structured Grids by introducing a snapping mechanism that reduces geometric error, distinguishing it from standard UMC and other siblings like Bitwise Marching Cubes which prioritize bitwise operations over positional accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A structured grid of scalar values, represented by gridsigns (signs of values relative to an isovalue), gridverts (vertex positions), and edges (edge definitions). Output: A list of output vertex indices (iout) and vertex attributes (vout), stored in a UMCChunk structure. Data Structures: The core state is held in struct UMCChunk: dim: uint32t grid dimensions. pem: int flag enabling/disabling snapping mode. snapthreshold: float threshold for snapping behavior. gridsigns: pointer to grid vertex signs. gridverts: pointer to grid vertex positions. edges: pointer to edge data. edgevindexes: pointer to edge vertex indices. vout: pointer to output vertex buffer. nout: pointer to output normal buffer. vnsize: uint32t vertex buffer size. vnnext: uint32t next vertex index. iout: pointer to output index buffer. isize: uint32t index buffer size. inext: uint32t next index index. vcount: uint32t vertex count. pcount: uint32t primitive count. snappedcount: uint32t count of snapped vertices. indexedprimitives: int flag for indexed rendering. initialized: int initialization flag. vao, ibo, vvbo, nvbo: GLuints for OpenGL resources. Parameters: ISOLEVEL: Fixed at 0.0f for sign comparison. snapthreshold: Float parameter controlling snapping threshold. pem: Integer flag to enable/disable snapping. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize UMCChunk with pem and snapthreshold. 2. Topology Mask Computation: For each cell, compute the topology mask by reading gridsigns at subdivided coordinates. The coordinates are calculated as (x+xoff)>>1, (y+yoff)>>1, (z+zoff)>>1. Set bit m in the mask based on the sign of the vertex. 3. Snapping Logic (if pem is enabled): Extract a 2-bit vertex state v from gridsigns. Add vm to the mask. If v==1, store a pointer to the corresponding grid vertex index in cell.isoverts[idx]. 4. Edge Snapping: For each edge: Check if endpoints differ (e->gridv0 != e->gridv1). Check if edge length is strictly positive. Check if the edge is not already snapped. Compute the normalized distance from the iso vertex to the grid vertex. Track the minimum distance edge for snapping. Update the maximum edge length. 5. Output Storage: Append output indices to a dynamically resized array iout. If outindsize is reached, double it via realloc before storing the next index. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Iterate over cells for cell in cells: # Compute topology mask mask = 0 for i in range(8): # Subdivided coordinates x = (cell.x + dx[i]) >> 1 y = (cell.y + dy[i]) >> 1 z = (cell.z + dz[i]) >> 1 # Read sign sign = gridsigns[index(x, y, z)] # Set bit m based on sign if sign > 0: mask |= (1 << i) # Snapping logic if enabled if chunk.pem: # Extract 2-bit vertex state v v = extractvertexstate(gridsigns, cell) # Add vm to mask mask += v mask # If v==1, store pointer to grid vertex index if v == 1: cell.isoverts[0] = getgridvertexindex(gridsigns, cell, 0) # Note: Other vertex indices would be stored similarly for the specific edge case # The source mentions storing a pointer to the corresponding grid vertex index in cell.isoverts[idx] # This implies a mapping for the specific vertex being snapped. # Edge processing for snapping mindist = infinity snappededge = None maxedgelen = 0.0 for edge in cell.edges: # Check endpoints differ if edge.gridv0 != edge.gridv1: # Check length > 0 length = distance(gridverts[edge.gridv0], gridverts[edge.gridv1]) if length > 0: # Check not already snapped if not issnapped(edge): # Compute normalized distance isovertex = computeisovertex(edge, gridverts, ISOLEVEL) gridvertex = gridverts[edge.gridv0] # Or v1, depending on convention dist = distance(isovertex, gridvertex) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist snappededge = edge if length > maxedgelen: maxedgelen = length # Perform snapping if mindist is within threshold if chunk.pem and snappededge is not None and mindist < chunk.snapthreshold: # Snap vertex to grid vertex snappedvertex = gridverts[snappededge.gridv0] # Store snapped vertex in vout idx = chunk.vnnext chunk.vout[idx] = snappedvertex chunk.vnnext += 1 chunk.snappedcount += 1 # Add index to iout if chunk.inext >= chunk.isize: chunk.iout = realloc(chunk.iout, chunk.isize 2) chunk.isize = 2 chunk.iout[chunk.inext] = idx chunk.inext += 1 else: # name: Smart Conversion
head: Gradient-based voxel-to-mesh conversion
body:
Smart Conversion is an advanced, gradient-based voxel-to-mesh conversion algorithm that prioritizes accuracy by correcting errors from noise, multiple materials, or inaccurate iso-values. Unlike standard isosurface extraction methods such as Marching Cubes on Structured Grids which rely on fixed threshold crossings, Smart Conversion iteratively "pulls" the mesh to align with the true boundary of the scan by locating points of steepest gradient along local surface normals. This makes it particularly suitable for medical or high-precision industrial contexts where accuracy is paramount and the initial voxel data may contain flaws. Smart Conversion operates as a post-processing refinement step applied to a mesh initially generated from voxel data. The algorithm refines the vertex positions by analyzing the local gradient field of the underlying voxel volume. Input: A triangular mesh (initially derived from voxels) and the corresponding scalar voxel volume data. Output: A refined triangular mesh where vertices are shifted to align with high-gradient regions of the voxel data. The method operates on the mesh vertex list and the voxel grid. The algorithm requires access to the mesh vertex positions and the 3D scalar voxel field. The following parameters control the behavior of the algorithm: Sampling Points (N): Defines the size of the neighborhood around each vertex considered when computing gradients. Intermediate Smoothing (\sigma{int}): Controls the amount of smoothing applied to the shift field at each iteration. Polynomial Degree (d): Determines the degree of the polynomial fitting the sampled points around each vertex. Iterations (K): Specifies the number of refinement cycles to perform. Outlier Threshold (T{out}): Dictates how outliers in the voxel data are handled. Preparation Smooth (\sigma{prep}): Sets the amount of smoothing before the main iterative process. The process consists of a preparation phase followed by iterative refinement: 1. Preparation: Apply smoothing to the voxel volume using \sigma{prep} if \sigma{prep} > 0. 2. Initialization: For each vertex v in the mesh, identify its local neighborhood in the voxel grid. 3. Iterative Refinement (for k = 1 to K): a. Gradient Approximation: For each vertex v, sample N points in its local neighborhood within the voxel volume. b. Polynomial Fitting: Fit a polynomial of degree d to the sampled voxel values to create a local continuous approximation P(x, y, z) of the scalar field. c. Normal and Gradient Calculation: Compute the gradient 
abla P at the current vertex position. The surface normal n is approximated by normalizing the gradient: n =  rac{
abla P}{\|
abla P\|}. d. Vertex Shift Calculation: Locate the point of steepest gradient along the normal n. The vertex is shifted by a displacement vector \Delta v towards this point to create a crisper boundary. e. Outlier Handling: If the computed shift or the local gradient statistics exceed the Outlier Threshold T{out}, discard or clamp the shift to prevent artifacts. f. Smoothing: Apply smoothing with parameter \sigma{int} to the collection of all computed shift vectors (the "shift field") to avoid overly sharp or inconsistent changes between adjacent vertices. g. Application: Update vertex positions: v{new} = v{old} + \Delta v{smoothed}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smartconversion(vertices, voxelvolume, params): # vertices: list of (x, y, z) tuples # voxelvolume: 3D array F[x][y][z] # params: dict containing N, sigmaint, d, K, Tout, sigmaprep # Step 1: Preparation if params['sigmaprep'] > 0: voxelvolume = smoothvolume(voxelvolume, params['sigmaprep']) for in range(params['K']): shifts = [] for v in vertices: # Step 2a: Gradient Approximation neighborhood = getneighborhood(v, voxelvolume, params['N']) # Step 2b: Polynomial Fitting poly = fitpolynomial(neighborhood, params['d']) # Step 2c: Normal and Gradient Calculation grad = poly.gradientat(v) mag = magnitude(grad) if mag < 1e-6: shifts.append((0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) continue normal = tuple(g / mag for g in grad) # Step 2d: Vertex Shift Calculation target = findsteepestgradientpoint(v, normal, poly, params['Tout']) shift = tuple(t - s for t, s in zip(target, v)) # Step 2e: Outlier Handling if magnitude(shift) > params['Tout']: shift = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) shifts.append(shift) # Step 2f: Smoothing smoothedshifts = smoothvectorfield(shifts, params['sigmaint']) # Step 2g: Application vertices = [tuple(v + s for v, s in zip(v, s)) for v, s in zip(vertices, smoothedshifts)] return vertices def magnitude(vec): return math.sqrt(sum(c c for c in vec)) def getneighborhood(vertex, volume, npoints): # Samples npoints in a spherical region around vertex mapped to voxel indices. # Returns list of (x, y, z, value) tuples. return [] def fitpolynomial(points, degree): # Uses least-squares regression to determine polynomial coefficients. # Returns an object with a gradientat method. class Poly: def gradientat(self, p): # Analytical gradient of the fitted polynomial at p return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return Poly() def findsteepestgradientpoint(vertex, normal, poly, threshold): # Searches along vertex + tnormal for t that maximizes ||grad(P)||. return vertex def smoothvolume(volume, sigma): # Applies Gaussian smoothing to the 3D voxel volume. return volume def smoothvectorfield(shifts, sigma): # Applies spatial smoothing to the list of shift vectors. return shifts Noise Sensitivity: If the voxel data is noisy, the gradient calculation may produce erratic shifts. The "Intermediate Smoothing" parameter is critical here; setting it too low preserves noise, while setting it too high blurs fine details. Multiple Materials: In regions with multiple materials, the gradient may be ambiguous. The algorithm attempts to correct for this by pulling the mesh to the "true boundary," but incorrect "Outlier Threshold" settings may discard valid boundary points. Artifact Introduction: High "Polynomial Degree" values may introduce artifacts if the local data does not support such complex variations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The source notes that higher "Sampling Points" and "Iterations" directly increase processing time. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method requires storage for the voxel volume, the mesh, and the shift field. Strengths: Produces crisper, more precise mesh boundaries than basic iso-value thresholds; corrects for noise and inaccurate iso-values; aligns mesh with the true scan boundary. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than standard Marching Cubes; requires careful tuning of multiple parameters (Smoothing, Degree, Threshold); may lose fine details if smoothing is too aggressive. When to Use: Medical imaging, high-precision industrial scanning, or any scenario where accuracy is paramount and the initial voxel-to-mesh conversion has flaws. When Not to Use: Real-time applications where performance is critical; clean data where standard methods are sufficient; scenes with extreme noise where smoothing cannot recover details. Smart Conversion is a feature of the MeshInspector software, described as a "smart alternative" to basic voxel-to-mesh conversion methods. It is designed for users who require higher fidelity than standard algorithms like Marching Cubes can provide, particularly in contexts where the initial data may be noisy or the iso-value is not perfectly representative of the physical object. The method is part of a workflow that includes visualization tools like "Distance Compare" to inspect the accuracy of the conversion. name: Flying Edges
head: vtkFlyingEdges3D
body: Flying Edges is a parallel, threaded algorithm for volumetric isocontouring of continuous scalar fields that addresses the performance limitations of Marching Cubes by processing volume edges rather than voxel cells. It eliminates point merging bottlenecks by using an edge-based iterator to generate output points and triangle cells, avoiding the need for hashing duplicate points. Inputs and outputs: Input: A structured grid (volume) with continuous scalar values at vertices, and an isovalue q. Output: A polygonal surface (polydata) consisting of points and triangle cells representing the isocontour. Data structures: The algorithm uses a multi-pass approach. 1. Pass 1 (Gathering): The algorithm iterates through the volume to gather information about the output size (number of points and triangles) without generating geometry. This enables precise, one-time memory allocation. 2. Pass 2 (Generation): Multiple threads simultaneously produce output using the pre-allocated memory, processing data along each edge independently. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize memory allocation for points and triangles based on the gathered information from Pass 1. 2. Divide the volume edges among available threads. 3. For each thread, iterate through its assigned edges: a. Retrieve the scalar values at the two endpoints of the edge. b. Check if the isovalue q lies between the endpoint values. c. If so, compute the intersection point using linear interpolation. d. Determine the triangle connectivity based on the surrounding cell topology. e. Write the point and triangle data directly into the pre-allocated buffers. 4. Finalize the output polydata structure. Formulas: For an edge with endpoints having scalar values v1 and v2, and spatial coordinates \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2, the intersection point \mathbf{p}{int} at isovalue q is calculated as: \mathbf{p}{int} = \mathbf{p}1 + \frac{q - v1}{v2 - v1} (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}1) This formula assumes v1 \neq v2. If v1 = v2, the edge is parallel to the isosurface and no intersection is generated. Parameters: Isovalue q: The threshold value for continuous scalar fields. Example: q=100 for CT-Angio (16-bit). Example: q=0.07 for SuperNova (32-bit float). Example: q=1800 for Nano (16-bit unsigned). Edge cases and pitfalls: Parallel efficiency declines as the number of threads increases, typically showing up when the number of threads approaches 20-40 CPU threads due to memory bus saturation, cache locality issues, and thread overhead. The algorithm assumes continuous scalar fields. Discrete or integer fields may require preprocessing or different handling. Time Complexity: The algorithm accesses voxel values only one time and performs edge intersections only once, compared to Marching Cubes which accesses each voxel value up to eight times and processes edges up to four times. Memory Complexity: Requires two passes: one for gathering output size and one for generation. Memory is allocated once based on the gathered size. Performance: Flying Edges is much faster than Marching Cubes even when run sequentially (with one thread). Performance improvements are typically one to two orders of magnitude greater than MC-based methods. Strengths: High performance, parallel efficiency (up to a point), no point merging bottleneck, precise memory allocation. Limitations: Parallel efficiency declines with high thread counts (20-40+ threads) due to memory bus saturation and cache issues. When to use: When high-performance isocontouring of continuous scalar fields is required, especially in parallel environments. When not to use: When the number of threads is very high (20-40+) and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck, or when discrete scalar fields are used. Flying Edges was developed by the VTK community to improve system performance for applications like ParaView, 3D Slicer, and trame. It was introduced in a blog post titled "Really Fast Isocontouring" by Will Schroeder and Spiros Tsalikis in June 2023. The algorithm is implemented in VTK as vtkFlyingEdges3D. Robert Maynard has also implemented Flying Edges in vtk-m. Really Fast Isocontouring, https://www.kitware.com/really-fast-isocontouring/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Undeformed Space Ray Start via Deformed Hull Intersection
head: Approximate Inverse via Hull, Dg^-1 approximation
body: This method finds the ray start point \hat{x}0 = D^{-1}(p) in undeformed space without computing the inverse deformation map D^{-1} directly. It solves the problem where D may not be invertible or well-defined at the camera position by intersecting the deformed view ray with a deformed explicit hull mesh that contains the surface. Inputs: Deformation function D(x) mapping undeformed space x to deformed space p. View ray in deformed space. Outputs: Approximate undeformed ray start point \hat{x}0. Data Structures: Hull Mesh: A triangle mesh defined in undeformed space with 3D vertex coordinates and triangle connectivity indices. The mesh must completely contain the target isosurface. Steps: 1. Generate Undeformed Hull: Create a low-resolution explicit hull in undeformed space that completely contains the isosurface. The default method is Marching Cubes because it is easy to implement efficiently on the GPU. To ensure the hull contains the surface, offset the original isosurface by the marching cubes diagonal cell size before generation. This is valid if the surface is defined by an SDF, as offsets correspond directly to distances. 2. Deform Hull: Apply the forward deformation transform D to all vertices of the hull mesh to create a deformed hull in deformed space. 3. Intersect Ray with Deformed Hull: Find the intersection point p between the deformed space view ray and the deformed hull mesh. Implementation can use rasterization of the hull mesh to find the primary intersection point, or explicit ray-triangle intersections. 4. Compute Approximate Inverse: Obtain the corresponding object-space location \hat{x} using the barycentric coordinates of the intersected triangle. This is performed automatically by hardware: object-space vertex positions are interpolated from vertex to fragment shading units by the rasterizer. The result is the approximate inverse Dg^{-1}(p) \approx D^{-1}(p). Formula: The approximate inverse is constructed as: Dg^{-1}(p) \approx D^{-1}(p) where Dg^{-1} is the inverse derived from the deformed hull's linear interpolation. Parameters: Hull Generation Method: Marching Cubes is used by default because it is easy to implement efficiently on the GPU. Alternatives like Wyvill et al. 1986 were not explored. Offset Distance: The marching cubes diagonal cell size. Pitfalls: Non-Conservative Extraction: Standard Marching Cubes is not conservative. If the hull does not completely contain the isosurface, parts of the surface outside the hull will not be rendered, and hull faces cutting through the isosurface will reveal the inside of the object. Precision: The method introduces error from the linearization of the inverse via hull interpolation and numerical integration of the trajectory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeundeformedraystart(viewrayorigin, viewraydirection, deformationfunc, sdffield, celldiagonalsize): # Step 1: Generate Undeformed Hull # Offset the SDF to ensure the hull completely contains the original isosurface. # For a standard SDF (inside < 0, outside > 0), extracting at -offset expands the mesh. offsetvalue = -celldiagonalsize hullundeformed = marchingcubesimpl(sdffield, isovalue=offsetvalue) # Step 2: Deform Hull deformedvertices = [deformationfunc(v) for v in hullundeformed.vertices] hulldeformed = TriangleMesh(vertices=deformedvertices, triangles=hullundeformed.triangles) # Step 3: Intersect Ray with Deformed Hull # Find primary intersection point p in deformed space. # Implementation uses rasterization or explicit ray-triangle intersections. hit = raytriangleintersect(viewrayorigin, viewraydirection, hulldeformed) if hit is None: return None p = hit.point triidx = hit.triangleindex bary = hit.barycentric # Step 4: Compute Approximate Inverse # Use barycentric coordinates to interpolate undeformed vertex positions. # This is performed automatically by hardware rasterization. tri = hullundeformed.triangles[triidx] v0 = hullundeformed.vertices[tri[0]] v1 = hullundeformed.vertices[tri[1]] v2 = hullundeformed.vertices[tri[2]] xhat = bary[0] v0 + bary[1] v1 + bary[2] v2 return xhat class TriangleMesh: def init(self, vertices=None, triangles=None): self.vertices = vertices if vertices is not None else [] self.triangles = triangles if triangles is not None else [] def marchingcubesimpl(sdffield, isovalue): # Sources do not provide Marching Cubes implementation details. # Standard algorithm generates a triangle mesh from a scalar field at the given isovalue. mesh = TriangleMesh() # Standard MC logic populates mesh.vertices and mesh.triangles. return mesh def raytriangleintersect(origin, direction, mesh): # Standard ray-triangle intersection (Möller–Trumbore algorithm). closestt = float('inf') closesthit = None for i, tri in enumerate(mesh.triangles): v0 = mesh.vertices[tri[0]] v1 = mesh.vertices[tri[1]] v2 = mesh.vertices[tri[2]] edge1 = v1 - v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 h = cross(direction, edge2) a = dot(edge1, h) if a > -1e-8 and a < 1e-8: continue f = 1.0 / a s = origin - v0 u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: continue q = cross(s, edge1) v = f dot(direction, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: continue t = f dot(edge2, q) if t > 1e-8 and t < closestt: closestt = t closesthit = {'point': origin + t direction, 'triangleindex': i, 'barycentric': (1.0 - u - v, u, v)} return closesthit Strengths: Avoids direct inversion of D, which may not exist or be well-defined. Efficient on GPU due to rasterization support. Limitations: Approximate; introduces error from linearization. Requires the hull to completely contain the surface, necessitating an offset. Error Sources: Numerical integration of the trajectory and approximation of the inverse via hull linearization. This method was introduced in the context of non-linear sphere tracing for rendering deformed signed distance fields. It generalizes the bounding-box technique for determining an initial value proposed by Barr [1986]. The approach leverages the efficiency of GPU rasterization to approximate the inverse deformation map, allowing for robust ray tracing in deformed spaces without explicit inverse functions. Non-linear sphere tracing for rendering deformed signed distance fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3355089.3356502, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Dividing Cubes
body: Dividing Cubes is an isosurface extraction method that replaces the triangular mesh primitives of Marching Cubes with 3D points. It solves the problem of excessive triangle counts and the subsequent scan-conversion overhead by adaptively subdividing cells intersected by the surface until each subcell projects onto a single pixel. Inputs: A structured volume dataset V with scalar values. An isovalue I defining the surface. Viewing direction and projection parameters to determine pixel coverage. Outputs: A set of 3D points representing the isosurface, each associated with an intensity or color value for rendering. Data Structures: Subcell List: A list of points (x, y, z) and their corresponding scalar/intensity values. Steps: 1. Identify Intersected Cells: Scan the volume grid to identify all voxels (cubes) where the isosurface passes through. 2. Subdivide Intersected Cells: For each identified voxel, recursively subdivide it into smaller subcells. 3. Determine Subdivision Depth: Select the subdivision depth such that the resulting subcells are small enough to project onto exactly one pixel on the image plane. 4. Render Subcells as Points: Project the calculated intensity for each subcell onto the viewing plane to form a gradient-shaded representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dividingcubes(volume, isovalue, cameraparams, imagewidth, imageheight): points = [] # Standard volume traversal for x in range(volume.width - 1): for y in range(volume.height - 1): for z in range(volume.depth - 1): voxel = volume.getcell(x, y, z) # Check if isovalue crosses the voxel by comparing with vertex values if isovalueexistsinvoxel(voxel, isovalue): # Compute depth so subcell projects to one pixel depth = computesubdivisiondepth(voxel, cameraparams, imagewidth, imageheight) subcells = subdividevoxel(voxel, depth) for subcell in subcells: # Linear interpolation to find intersection point on subcell edge point = estimateintersection(subcell, isovalue) # Intensity from subcell scalar value intensity = subcell.scalar points.append((point, intensity)) return points Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Voxels on the boundary of the volume must be handled correctly to avoid out-of-bounds access during subdivision and intersection estimation. Uses bitwise operations to optimize the lookup table and configuration steps of Marching Cubes. It still generates triangles but improves performance. Bitwise Marching Cubes Applies snapping to vertex positions to reduce geometric errors in the generated mesh. Uniform Marching Cubes with Snapping Optimizes the conversion of volume data to surface representations. Smart Conversion A method that avoids the voxel grid structure by operating on the edges of the volume, potentially offering better performance and accuracy. Flying Edges A technique for ray casting in deformed volumes. Undeformed Space Ray Start via Deformed Hull Intersection Uses a dual grid structure to extract isosurfaces, potentially offering different trade-offs in accuracy and performance. Dual Grid Isosurface Extraction Time Complexity: The complexity depends on the number of intersected voxels and the required subdivision depth. Strengths: Eliminates scan conversion overhead; adapts to viewing angle and resolution; produces smooth, gradient-shaded images. Limitations: Does not produce a connected mesh. When to Use: When rendering large datasets for visualization where a connected mesh is not required, and performance of scan conversion is a bottleneck. Dividing Cubes was developed as a variation of the Marching Cubes algorithm to address the computational cost of scan conversion when dealing with large numbers of small triangles. It was introduced in the context of volume visualization, where the goal is to efficiently render complex surfaces from volumetric data.
