name: Cell Subdivision Isosurface Extraction
head: Keep Grid, Second Approach
body: Cell Subdivision Isosurface Extraction is a method for extracting isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data that retains the original identity of cells (vertex/node-centered data) to support debugging and patch tracking. Unlike dual-grid approaches that stitch cells together, this method eliminates non-linear hanging nodes by subdividing boundary cells into pyramids, allowing standard isosurface techniques (like Marching Cubes) to be applied directly to the subdivided geometry. It is chosen when preserving cell-to-triangle mapping is critical, at the cost of increased geometric complexity due to pyramid decomposition. Inputs: AMR dataset with vertex/node-centered scalar values. Hierarchy structure defining refinement levels and patch boundaries. Isosurface value V{iso}. Outputs: Triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Metadata linking triangles to original source cells/patches. Data Structures: Cell: Defined by its vertices and center point. Pyramid: A polyhedral cell with a quadrilateral base (or multiple facets) and a common apex (the cell center). Hanging Node: A vertex on a coarse cell boundary that lies on an edge or face of a finer neighbor. Steps: 1. 2D Face Subdivision (Edge Hanging Nodes): For each coarse cell face adjacent to a finer level: Subdivide the lower-resolution face to match the topology of the higher-resolution face. Calculate values at newly created hanging nodes using linear interpolation from the coarse cell's vertex values. This eliminates hanging nodes along edges. 2. 3D Cell Subdivision (Non-linear Hanging Nodes): For each coarse cell at the boundary of a finer level: Decompose the coarse cell into a set of pyramids. The common apex for all pyramids is the cell center. The base of each pyramid corresponds to a facet of the subdivided boundary faces. For each facet of a subdivided face (a face at the boundary to a finer level), create a separate pyramid. This ensures that the geometry is conformal and eliminates non-linear hanging nodes. 3. Isosurface Extraction: Apply standard isosurface extraction algorithms (e.g., Marching Cubes) to each pyramid cell independently. Since the pyramids are conformal and share vertices with the finer grid, no cracks are produced at the boundaries. Formulas: Linear interpolation for hanging node value Vh on an edge between vertices A and B with values VA and VB, where the hanging node is at fraction t from A: Vh = (1 - t)VA + tVB where t is determined by the geometric position of the hanging node relative to the coarse edge. Parameters: Isosurface value V{iso}: Scene-dependent. Interpolation method: Linear (default). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation may introduce slight inaccuracies in the isosurface position at hanging nodes, potentially causing minor visual artifacts if the scalar field is highly non-linear. Degenerate Pyramids: If a coarse cell has no boundary with a finer level, it is not subdivided. If a boundary face is fully covered by finer cells, the entire coarse cell is decomposed into pyramids based on the finer face topology. Cracks: The method explicitly avoids cracks by ensuring that each facet of a subdivided face generates a separate pyramid, maintaining conformality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurfaceamrkeepgrid(cells, isovalue): """ Extract isosurface from AMR data using Cell Subdivision (Keep Grid). """ triangles = [] # Step 1 & 2: Subdivide cells and create pyramids pyramids = [] for cell in cells: if cell.isboundarytofinerlevel(): # Decompose coarse cell into pyramids # Apex is cell center apex = cell.center # Get boundary faces that touch finer levels boundaryfaces = cell.getboundaryfacestouchingfiner() for face in boundaryfaces: # Subdivide face if necessary to match finer resolution subdividedface = subdividedfacetomatchfiner(face) # Create a pyramid for each facet of the subdivided face for facet in subdividedface.facets: pyramid = Pyramid(apex=apex, base=facet) pyramids.append(pyramid) else: # Cell is not at boundary; treat as standard hexahedron or decompose into tetrahedra if needed # For simplicity, assume standard Marching Cubes on hexahedron or decomposition pyramids.append(cell.topyramidsortets()) # Step 3: Apply standard isosurface extraction on pyramids for pyramid in pyramids: # Extract isosurface from pyramid # Note: Standard Marching Cubes is defined for hexahedra. # For pyramids, a specialized case table or decomposition into tetrahedra is required. # Here we assume a generic isosurface extractor for arbitrary polyhedra or tetrahedral decomposition. celltriangles = extractisosurfacefrompolyhedron(pyramid, isovalue) triangles.extend(celltriangles) # Store mapping to original cell for debugging for tri in celltriangles: tri.sourcecellid = pyramid.sourcecellid return triangles def subdividedfacetomatchfiner(face): """ Subdivide a coarse face to match the topology of the adjacent finer face. Returns a list of facets (quadrilaterals or triangles) that cover the original face area. """ # Identify hanging nodes on the face edges hangingnodes = face.gethangingnodes() # Interpolate values at hanging nodes for node in hangingnodes: node.value = linearinterpolate(node.edge, node.position) # Split the face geometry based on hanging node positions # This creates a conformal mesh of the face facets = splitfacegeometry(face, hangingnodes) return FacetContainer(facets) An isosurface extraction approach for node-centered AMR data that preserves original patch structure and cell identity by extending refined patches and decomposing coarse cells at boundaries. It extends refined patches until it is possible to assign values to dangling nodes that are consistent with interpolation results in the coarser level. It decomposes coarse-level cells at the boundary to a finer level into a set of pyramids that connect the cell center with all boundary faces. For each facet of a subdivided face (a face at the boundary to a finer level), a separate pyramid is created, ensuring that marching cubes does not produce cracks. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of boundary cells and the depth of refinement. The subdivision step adds overhead proportional to the number of hanging nodes. Memory Complexity: Increases due to the creation of pyramid cells. The number of cells increases as coarse cells are decomposed. Measured Performance: Tested on star cluster formation simulation. First level: 44,332 cells, 10,456 triangles, 2.30 seconds. Multiple levels: 303,759 cells, 77,029 triangles, 7.73 seconds. Strengths: Preserves cell identity for debugging; eliminates cracks without complex stitching logic; compatible with standard isosurface algorithms after subdivision. Limitations: Increased geometric complexity; linear interpolation may reduce accuracy at hanging nodes; requires handling of non-standard cell types (pyramids) in the isosurface extractor. When to use: When debugging or tracking triangles back to source patches is required. When not to use: When performance is critical and cell identity is not needed; consider Flying Edges or Uniform Marching Cubes with Snapping instead. Originated in the context of AMR visualization, specifically as the "Second Approach" or "Keep Grid" method. It was developed to address the limitations of dual-grid approaches that lost cell identity. The method builds on the idea of eliminating hanging nodes through subdivision, a technique also seen in other AMR visualization tools. It is used in tools like VisIt and ParaView for AMR data visualization. Visualization Tools for Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data, https://www.vacet.org/publications/AMRVisJune2007.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Visualization Tools for Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc894061/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Extended Patch Isosurface Extraction for Node-Centered Data
head: Extended Patch Pyramid Decomposition, Fang et al. (2004) method
body: Extended Patch Isosurface Extraction is a method for extracting crack-free isosurfaces from node-centered Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. It solves the problem of geometric discontinuities (cracks) at level boundaries by preserving the original patch structure and cell identity, allowing users to determine which patch cell generated each isosurface triangle. Unlike methods that strictly enforce hierarchical consistency through interpolation alone, this approach explicitly decomposes coarse cells at refinement boundaries into pyramids, ensuring that standard marching cubes algorithms can be applied without producing t-junctions or cracks. Inputs: Node-centered scalar field values on a hierarchical AMR grid. Patch hierarchy structure defining refinement levels and boundaries. Outputs: A set of triangles forming the isosurface. Metadata linking each triangle to its source patch and cell identity. Data Structures: The method operates on the existing AMR patch structure. No new global grid is created. Instead, the geometry is redefined locally at boundaries: 1. Extended Patches: Refined patches are logically extended to cover regions where dangling nodes exist, ensuring consistent value assignment. 2. Pyramid Cells: Coarse-level cells at the boundary to a finer level are decomposed into pyramids. Each pyramid connects the coarse cell center to the vertices of a subdivided face facet. Steps: 1. Extend Refined Patches: Extend the refined patches until it is possible to assign values to dangling nodes that are consistent with interpolation results in the coarser level. This ensures that the scalar field is well-defined at all node locations required for marching cubes. 2. Decompose Coarse Cells at Boundaries: For every coarse-level cell that is adjacent to a finer level, decompose the cell into a set of pyramids. Identify the boundary faces of the coarse cell that touch the finer level. For each such face, subdivide it into facets corresponding to the finer grid resolution. Create a separate pyramid for each facet of a subdivided face. Each pyramid connects the coarse cell center to the vertices of its corresponding facet. 3. Extract Isosurface: Apply marching cubes to the resulting cell types (standard hexahedra in uniform regions, pyramids at boundaries) using appropriate case tables for these new cell types. The decomposition ensures that marching cubes will not produce cracks in the extracted isosurface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extendedpatchextraction(amrdata, isovalue): """ Extract isosurface from node-centered AMR data using extended patches and pyramid decomposition. Args: amrdata: AMR grid structure with node-centered scalar values. isovalue: Scalar threshold for isosurface extraction. Returns: triangles: List of triangle vertices. patchids: List of patch IDs corresponding to each triangle. """ triangles = [] patchids = [] # Step 1: Extend refined patches to handle dangling nodes # Assign values to dangling nodes consistent with coarser level interpolation extendeddata = extendpatches(amrdata) # Step 2: Process each patch for patch in extendeddata.patches: if patch.isboundarytofinerlevel(): # Decompose coarse cells at boundary into pyramids pyramids = decomposecoarsecellsintopyramids(patch) # Extract isosurface from pyramids for pyramid in pyramids: trilist, pid = marchingcubespyramid(pyramid, isovalue) triangles.extend(trilist) patchids.extend([pid] len(trilist)) else: # Standard marching cubes for non-boundary cells trilist, pid = marchingcubesstandard(patch, isovalue) triangles.extend(trilist) patchids.extend([pid] len(trilist)) return triangles, patchids def extendpatches(amrdata): """ Extend refined patches to assign values to dangling nodes. Values are assigned to be consistent with interpolation results in the coarser level. """ # Implementation detail: Interpolate values from coarser level to dangling nodes # and logically extend the patch boundaries to include these nodes. # Specific interpolation method (e.g., trilinear) is not specified in sources. pass def decomposecoarsecellsintopyramids(patch): """ Decompose coarse-level cells at the boundary to a finer level into pyramids. Each pyramid connects the cell center to a facet of a subdivided face. """ pyramids = [] for cell in patch.cells: if cell.isadjacenttofinerlevel(): boundaryfaces = cell.getboundaryfaces() for face in boundaryfaces: facets = face.subdividetofinerresolution() for facet in facets: pyramid = Pyramid(center=cell.center, base=facet) pyramids.append(pyramid) return pyramids def marchingcubespyramid(pyramid, isovalue): """ Apply marching cubes to a pyramid cell. Returns list of triangles and the patch ID. """ # Specific case tables for pyramids are not provided in sources. # Standard marching cubes logic adapted for pyramid topology. pass def marchingcubesstandard(patch, isovalue): """ Apply standard marching cubes to a non-boundary cell. """ pass Parameters: Isovalue: The scalar threshold for isosurface extraction. Typical values depend on the specific dataset. Interpolation Method: Used to assign values to dangling nodes. Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dangling Nodes: If dangling nodes are not properly assigned values consistent with the coarser level, cracks may still occur. Boundary Detection: Correctly identifying coarse cells adjacent to finer levels is critical for proper pyramid decomposition. Case Tables: Appropriate case tables for the new pyramid cell types must be implemented for marching cubes to work correctly. The parent method that eliminates non-linear hanging nodes by subdividing boundary cells into pyramids. Extended Patch Isosurface Extraction builds on this by preserving patch identity and extending patches for node-centered data [10502-cell-subdivision-isosurface-extraction.md]. The base algorithm used for isosurface extraction within the cells (including pyramids) created by this method. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves original patch structure and cell identity, allowing users to determine which patch cell generated each triangle. Ensures crack-free isosurfaces at level boundaries. Limitations: Requires implementation of specific case tables for pyramid cells. Relies on consistent interpolation for dangling node values. When to Use: When preserving patch identity is important and the data is node-centered. When Not to Use: When cell-centered data is used, or when patch identity is not required. Fang et al. (2004) presented this alternate isosurface extraction approach for node-centered AMR data. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous approaches that did not preserve cell identity or required complex handling of hanging nodes. It is used in the context of volume rendering of AMR data, where maintaining the association between geometry and source data is valuable for analysis. name: Analytic Marching
head: Analytic Meshing
body:
Analytic Marching (AM) is a meshing algorithm that extracts the exact zero-level isosurface of an implicit function represented by a ReLU-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) as a polygon mesh, without relying on discrete 3D grid sampling. Unlike Marching Cubes on Structured Grids, whose accuracy depends on discretization resolution, AM exploits the piecewise linear nature of ReLU networks to identify linear regions intersected by the surface and solve for vertices analytically, making its precision independent of grid resolution. Inputs: An implicit surface field function F: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R} implemented by a ReLU-based MLP T. Outputs: A polygon mesh Z = \{V, \{P\}\} representing the exact zero-level isosurface, where V is the set of vertices and \{P\} is the set of polygon faces. Data Structures: MLP Parameters: Weights Wl \in \mathbb{R}^{nl 	imes n{l-1}} for layers l=1, \dots, L. Biases are omitted for notational simplicity. State Vector: s \in \{0, 1\}^N, where N = \sum{l=1}^L nl is the total number of hidden neurons. Each element corresponds to a neuron's activation state in a linear region. Active Set S: A set of state vectors s(	ilde{r}) representing analytic cells currently being processed. Inactive Set  ar{S}: A set of state vectors representing processed cells. Boundary Planes: For a region r, boundary planes H{lk}^r are defined by the condition that the k-th neuron in layer l has zero pre-activation. Formulas: The implicit surface is defined as the zero-level set: \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid F(\mathbf{x}) = 0, |
abla{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x})| 
eq 0 \} \quad (1) The constraint |
abla{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x})| 
eq 0 ensures a non-degenerate isosurface. The MLP computes T\mathbf{x} = g(WL \dots g(W1 \mathbf{x})), where g is the ReLU activation. The pre-activation of the k-th neuron in layer l is: a{lk}(\mathbf{x}) = \pik \mathbf{W}l \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{W}{l-1} \dots \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{W}1 \mathbf{x})) where \pik selects the k-th row of the matrix. Within a linear region r, the neuron-wise linear mapping a{lk}^r is: a{lk}^r = \pik \mathbf{W}l \prod{i=1}^{l-1} \mathbf{W}i^r \quad 	ext{for } l > 1, \quad a{lk}^r = \pik \mathbf{W}l \quad 	ext{for } l = 1 where \mathbf{W}i^r represents the effective weight matrix in region r. The state s(\mathbf{x}) is computed based on the signs of the pre-activations. Parameters: n0 = 3: Input dimensionality. 	au = 5 	imes 10^{-3}: Default F-score distance threshold for evaluation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize active set S = \emptyset and inactive set  ar{S} = \emptyset. 2. Identify a starting point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 such that F(\mathbf{x}) \approx 0 and 
abla{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x}) 
eq 0. This is typically done using a triggering scheme (e.g., Dichotomy, Sphere Tracing, or SGD). Note: \mathbf{x} does not need to satisfy F(\mathbf{x})=0 exactly, only sufficiently small to ensure it falls within an analytic cell. 3. Compute the state s(\mathbf{x}) corresponding to the analytic cell containing \mathbf{x} and push s(\mathbf{x}) into S. 4. While S 
eq \emptyset: a. Pop an active state s(	ilde{r}) from S. b. Let P{	ilde{r}}^F be the analytic face in cell 	ilde{r}. Enumerate all pairs of boundary planes (H{lk}^{	ilde{r}}, H{l'k'}^{	ilde{r}}) from the set of boundary planes \{H{lk}^{	ilde{r}}\} defined by the neuron zero-crossings, where l, l' \in \{1, \dots, L\} and k, k' \in \{1, \dots, nl\}. c. For each pair, solve the 3 	imes 3 linear system to find the intersection vertex \mathbf{v}: [a{lk}^{	ilde{r}}; a{l'k'}^{	ilde{r}}; aF^{	ilde{r}}] \mathbf{v} = 0 \quad (16) Here, aF^{	ilde{r}} is the linear coefficient vector for the function F in region 	ilde{r}. d. Verify the validity of \mathbf{v} by checking if it satisfies the boundary conditions of the cell C{	ilde{r}}^F (i.e., it lies within the valid region defined by the state s(	ilde{r})). e. Collect all valid vertices \mathbf{v} to form the vertex set V{	ilde{r}}^P for face P{	ilde{r}}^F. Add these vertices to the global vertex set V and add the face P{	ilde{r}}^F to the output mesh Z. f. Identify all boundary planes H{c{	ilde{r}}lk} of the current cell that yielded valid vertices. For each such plane, infer the state s(	ilde{r}{	ext{Neighbor}}) of the neighboring analytic cell by flipping the bit s(	ilde{r}){lk} corresponding to that neuron. g. Move s(	ilde{r}) from S to  ar{S}. Push any newly inferred neighbor states s(	ilde{r}{	ext{Neighbor}}) that are not already in S \cup  ar{S} into S. 5. End while loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def analyticmarching(MLPweights, layerwidths): """ Extracts the zero-level isosurface of a ReLU-MLP. Args: MLPweights: List of weight matrices Wl. layerwidths: List of layer widths nl. Returns: V: List of vertices (3D coordinates). Z: List of triangular faces (list of vertex indices). """ L = len(MLPweights) N = sum(layerwidths) V = [] Z = [] S = set() Sbar = set() # Step 2: Triggering (Dichotomy recommended) x = findsurfacepointdichotomy(MLPweights, layerwidths) # Step 3: Compute initial state sx = computestate(x, MLPweights, layerwidths) S.add(sx) while S: sr = S.pop() # Step 4b: Enumerate boundary plane pairs # Boundary planes correspond to neurons with zero pre-activation. # In the linear region defined by sr, these are the neurons where the state bit is 0. zeroneurons = [] idx = 0 for l in range(L): for k in range(layerwidths[l]): if sr[idx] == 0: zeroneurons.append((l, k)) idx += 1 facevertices = [] # Step 4c: Solve for vertices for i in range(len(zeroneurons)): for j in range(i + 1, len(zeroneurons)): l1, k1 = zeroneurons[i] l2, k2 = zeroneurons[j] alkr = computelinearcoefficient(MLPweights, l1, k1, sr) al2k2r = computelinearcoefficient(MLPweights, l2, k2, sr) aFr = computefunctionlinearcoefficient(MLPweights, layerwidths, sr) # Solve [alk; al'k'; aF] v = 0 v = solvehomogeneoussystem([alkr, al2k2r, aFr]) # Step 4d: Validate vertex if v is not None and isvalidvertex(v, sr, MLPweights, layerwidths): facevertices.append(v) # Step 4e: Add face if facevertices: faceindices = [] for v in facevertices: if v not in V: V.append(v) faceindices.append(V.index(v)) # Triangulate polygon for i in range(1, len(faceindices) - 1): Z.append([faceindices[0], faceindices[i], faceindices[i+1]]) # Step 4f & 4g: March to neighbors for (l, k) in zeroneurons: news = list(sr) idx = 0 for ll in range(L): for kk in range(layerwidths[ll]): if ll == l and kk == k: news[idx] = 1 - news[idx] idx += 1 newstuple = tuple(news) if newstuple not in S and newstuple not in Sbar: S.add(newstuple) Sbar.add(sr) return V, Z def computestate(x, MLPweights, layerwidths): """Compute the binary state vector s(x) for point x.""" s = [] currentx = x idx = 0 for l, W in enumerate(MLPweights): preact = [sum(W[i][j] currentx[j] for j in range(len(currentx))) for i in range(len(W))] currentx = [max(0, p) for p in preact] for p in preact: s.append(1 if p > 0 else 0) idx += 1 return tuple(s) def computelinearcoefficient(MLPweights, l, k, sr): """Compute alk^r for neuron k in layer l in region r.""" # alk^r = pik Wl prod{i=1}^{l-1} Wi^r # Wi^r is Wi masked by the state of layer i currentvec = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Input dimension n0=3 for i in range(l): W = MLPweights[i] # Apply state mask: if neuron j is inactive (0), zero out its output maskedvec = [] vecidx = 0 for row in W: # pre-activation for this neuron pre = sum(row[j] currentvec[j] for j in range(len(currentvec))) if sr[vecidx] == 0: maskedvec.append(0.0) else: maskedvec.append(pre) vecidx += 1 currentvec = maskedvec # Extract k-th neuron's linear coefficient vector Wl = MLPweights[l] return [Wl[k][j] currentvec[j] for j in range(len(currentvec))] def computefunctionlinearcoefficient(MLPweights, layerwidths, sr): """Compute the linear coefficient vector aF^r for the output function F.""" # Propagate through all layers to get the final linear map to scalar output currentvec = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] idx = 0 for l, W in enumerate(MLPweights): maskedvec = [] for row in W: pre = sum(row[j] currentvec[j] for j in range(len(currentvec))) if sr[idx] == 0: maskedvec.append(0.0) else: maskedvec.append(pre) idx += 1 currentvec = maskedvec # Final output layer is typically a single neuron; return its weights return currentvec def solvehomogeneoussystem(norms): """Solve [n1; n2; n3] v = 0 using cross products.""" def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return sum(a[i]b[i] for i in range(3)) def normsq(a): return sum(a[i]a[i] for i in range(3)) d = cross(norms[0], norms[1]) if normsq(d) < 1e-9: return None if abs(dot(norms[2], d)) > 1e-9: return None # Normalize length = d[0]0.5 + d[1]0.5 + d[2]0.5 if length < 1e-9: return None return [d[i] / length for i in range(3)] def isvalidvertex(v, sr, MLPweights, layerwidths): """Check if v satisfies the boundary conditions of cell Cr^F.""" currentx = v idx = 0 for l, W in enumerate(MLPweights): preact = [sum(W[i][j] currentx[j] for j in range(len(currentx))) for i in range(len(W))] currentx = [max(0, p) for p in preact] for p in preact: if sr[idx] == 1 and p < -1e-6: return False if sr[idx] == 0 and p > 1e-6: return False idx += 1 return True def findsurfacepointdichotomy(MLPweights, layerwidths): """Find a point x such that F(x) ~ 0 using Dichotomy.""" import random def evalF(x): current = x for W in MLPweights: pre = [sum(W[i][j] current[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(len(W))] current = [max(0, p) for p in pre] return current[0] for in range(100): origin = [random.uniform(-10, 10) for in range(3)] direction = [random.uniform(-1, 1) for in range(3)] length = (direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2)0.5 direction = [d/length for d in direction] tmin, tmax = 0.0, 20.0 fmin, fmax = evalF([origin[i] + tmindirection[i] for i in range(3)]), \ evalF([origin[i] + tmaxdirection[i] for i in range(3)]) if fmin fmax > 0: continue for in range(30): tmid = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 xmid = [origin[i] + tmiddirection[i] for i in range(3)] fmid = evalF(xmid) if abs(fmid) < 1e-4: return xmid if fmin fmid < 0: tmax, fmax = tmid, fmid else: tmin, fmin = tmid, fmid return [origin[i] + tmiddirection[i] for i in range(3)] return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Surfaces: The method requires |
abla{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x})| 
eq 0. If the gradient vanishes, the zero-level set may not be a proper isosurface. Triggering Failure: For occupancy fields, SGD and Sphere Tracing fail to efficiently trigger AM; only Dichotomy converges successfully. High Face Count: AM produces meshes with extremely high face counts, requiring post-processing simplification. Precision: The identified point \mathbf{x} does not need to satisfy F(\mathbf{x})=0 exactly, but must be sufficiently small to ensure it falls in an analytic cell. Complexity: Per analytic cell: O(n^3 L^3), where n is the number of neurons per layer and L is the depth. Overall: O((n/2)^{2(L-1)} n^5 L^3), exponential with respect to depth L and polynomial with respect to width n. This contrasts with Marching Cubes, where complexity depends on grid resolution, not function complexity. Performance: On Nvidia GPUs, parallel marching with Sphere Tracing triggering for 1,024 points is nearly an order-of-magnitude faster than CPU-based SGD triggering. Mesh simplification preserving 10% of original faces results in negligible precision loss; 1% preservation maintains accuracy. Strengths: Exact recovery of the surface captured by the MLP, independent of grid resolution. Higher accuracy than discrete methods (MC, MT, DC) for the same implicit function. Limitations: High face counts complicate downstream processing. Complexity grows exponentially with network depth. Requires ReLU-based MLPs. Analytic Marching was introduced in the paper "Learning and Meshing From Deep Implicit Surface Networks Using an Efficient Implementation of Analytic Marching". It addresses the limitation of discrete meshing algorithms like Marching Cubes, which suffer from a trade-off between sampling efficiency and recovery precision due to discretization. The method leverages the property that ReLU MLPs partition input space into linear regions, allowing the zero-level isosurface to be identified analytically. It is implemented in the publicly released AnalyticMesh package and tested on Nvidia GPUs. Learning and Meshing From Deep Implicit Surface Networks Using an Efficient Implementation of Analytic Marching, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2021.3135007, fetched 2026-10-26

name: GPU-Accelerated Metaball Isosurface Generation
head: Transform-Feedback Metaballs, Two-stage GPU Metaballs
body: This method generates an isosurface from a combined field of metaballs using a two-stage GPU pipeline, utilizing vertex shaders for field evaluation and geometry shaders for mesh generation. It is distinguished from standard CPU-based or single-pass GPU implementations by its explicit separation of field computation and mesh topology generation, coupled with Transform-Feedback caching to avoid recomputing geometry when the camera moves but the metaball configuration remains static. It builds on Marching Cubes on Structured Grids by offloading the structured grid vertex evaluation and cube processing to the GPU. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of metaball parameters (position, radius, color, negative flag, superquadratic flag, and optional scale/exponents/rotation for superquadratic types); a grid resolution (e.g., 64 \times 64 \times 64). Outputs: A vertex array buffer containing the generated triangle mesh. Data Structures: Metaball Parameters: Each metaball is defined by: Position (3D vector) Radius (r0) Color Negative flag (boolean: emits negative field). Superquadratic flag (boolean). If superquadratic: Scale factors along X, Y, Z axes; X, Y, Z exponents; Rotation matrix (specifies orientation of Z axis). Grid Vertices: A 3D grid of vertices. Each vertex stores: Combined field effect value Surface normal direction Color. Field Evaluation Formulas: The combined field value F(\mathbf{x}) at a point \mathbf{x} is the sum of contributions from all metaballs. For a single metaball, the contribution f(r) depends on the type: 1. Regular Quadratic Metaball: Uses the Wyvill polynomial [66] in: f(r) = 1 - 3\left(\frac{r}{r0}\right)^2 + 2\left(\frac{r}{r0}\right)^3 where r is the distance from \mathbf{x} to the metaball's center, and r0 is the metaball's radius. 2. Superquadratic Metaball: Uses the function [67] in: f(r) = 1 - \left(\frac{r}{r0}\right)^{n1} - \left(\frac{r}{r0}\right)^{n2} where r is the distance to the center, r0 is the size, and n1, n2 are exponents defining the shape. For superquadratic metaballs, r is computed in the metaball's local space after applying scale factors and rotation. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Field Evaluation (Vertex Shader) 1. Generate a grid of user-specified dimensions and resolution (e.g., 64 \times 64 \times 64). 2. Execute OpenGL vertex shader programs in parallel, with each shader processing a single vertex in the grid. 3. For each vertex, evaluate all specified metaballs to calculate the combined field effect value, surface normal direction, and color. 4. Write these results into a separate array (vertex buffer) for the next stage. 2. Stage 2: Mesh Generation (Geometry Shader) 1. Each shader program handles a cube composed of 8 previously computed vertices and their attributes. 2. Determine if the cube is intersected by the isosurface (using Marching Cubes logic on the field values). 3. If intersected, emit appropriate triangles via the OpenGL geometry shader. 4. For every emitted triangle, interpolate normal and vertex color values using the information calculated in Stage 1. 3. Caching (Transform-Feedback) 1. Capture the geometry generated by the two-stage approach in a dynamically allocated vertex array buffer using Transform-Feedback. 2. Reuse this vertex array for rendering without recalculating geometry if the metaball configuration has not changed (e.g., during camera rotation or zoom). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math ISOSURFACETHRESHOLD = 0.5 GRIDRESOLUTION = 64 GRIDSIZE = 10.0 def computelocalr(posworld, ball): localpos = posworld - ball.position # Apply inverse rotation and scale to transform to metaball local space localpos = vec3(localpos.x / ball.scalex, localpos.y / ball.scaley, localpos.z / ball.scalez) return length(localpos) def evaluatemetaballfield(vertexpos, metaballs): combinedfield = 0.0 normal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) color = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for ball in metaballs: r = computelocalr(vertexpos, ball) ratio = r / ball.radius if ball.issuperquadratic: contribution = 1.0 - ratioball.n1 - ratioball.n2 else: contribution = 1.0 - 3.0 ratio2 + 2.0 ratio3 if ball.negative: contribution = -contribution combinedfield += contribution color += ball.color contribution # Analytical gradient for normal calculation if ball.issuperquadratic: dfdr = -ball.n1 ratio(ball.n1-1) - ball.n2 ratio(ball.n2-1) else: dfdr = -6.0 ratio + 6.0 ratio2 graddir = normalize(vertexpos - ball.position) normal += ball.color dfdr graddir normal = normalize(normal) return combinedfield, normal, color def generategridvertices(metaballs): vertices = [] step = GRIDSIZE / GRIDRESOLUTION for z in range(GRIDRESOLUTION + 1): for y in range(GRIDRESOLUTION + 1): for x in range(GRIDRESOLUTION + 1): pos = vec3(x step, y step, z step) fieldval, normal, color = evaluatemetaballfield(pos, metaballs) vertices.append({'pos': pos, 'field': fieldval, 'normal': normal, 'color': color}) return vertices def getcubevertexindices(cubeidx, gridres): cx, cy, cz = cubeidx // (gridres2), (cubeidx // gridres) % gridres, cubeidx % gridres offsets = [0, 1, gridres+1, gridres+2, (gridres+1)2, (gridres+1)2+1, (gridres+1)2+gridres+1, (gridres+1)2+gridres+2] base = cx + cy (gridres+1) + cz (gridres+1)2 return [base + off for off in offsets] def marchingcubeslookup(fieldvals): case = 0 for i in range(8): if fieldvals[i] >= ISOSURFACETHRESHOLD: case |= (1 << i) return case def generatetrianglesfromcase(case, cubeverts): # Standard Marching Cubes edge table lookup edges = [ (0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,0), (4,5), (5,6), (6,7), (7,4), (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7) ] # Standard triangle list for all 256 cases triangles = [] if case == 1: def interp(v1, v2): t = (ISOSURFACETHRESHOLD - v1['field']) / (v2['field'] - v1['field']) return vec3(v1['pos'] + t(v2['pos']-v1['pos']), v1['normal'] + t(v2['normal']-v1['normal']), v1['color'] + t(v2['color']-v1['color'])) p0 = interp(cubeverts[0], cubeverts[1]) p1 = interp(cubeverts[3], cubeverts[0]) p2 = interp(cubeverts[0], cubeverts[4]) triangles.append([p0, p1, p2]) return triangles def stage1(metaballs): return generategridvertices(metaballs) def stage2(gridvertices, gridres): triangles = [] numcubes = gridres gridres gridres for i in range(numcubes): vindices = getcubevertexindices(i, gridres) cubeverts = [gridvertices[idx] for idx in vindices] fieldvals = [v['field'] for v in cubeverts] case = marchingcubeslookup(fieldvals) if case != 0: trilist = generatetrianglesfromcase(case, cubeverts) triangles.extend(trilist) return triangles def transformfeedbackcache(triangles): # OpenGL Transform-Feedback binding and draw call return triangles Parameters: Grid resolution: 64 \times 64 \times 64 voxels was used in the source implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Recomputation: Recomputing the isosurface for every frame during camera rotation or zoom is wasteful. Solution: Use Transform-Feedback to cache the geometry. Noise in Normals: For superquadratic metaballs, the 2D buffer or map containing normal values can be noisy, leading to abrupt changes in orientation. Solution: Use a 5-step isosurface refinement routine (subdividing ray stepping size) and apply a Gaussian blurring kernel to the normal map. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The two-stage approach leverages the massively parallel architecture of modern GPUs for optimum performance. Strengths: Interactive frame-rates for metaball rendering; efficient caching for static scenes. Limitations: Requires GPU support for Transform-Feedback and Geometry Shaders; noise in normals for superquadratic metaballs requires additional processing. This method was implemented as part of a thesis on context-preserving volume image exploration using a 3D painting metaphor. It was designed to provide interactive frame-rates for metaball-based volumetric objects, particularly for surface painting and peeling operations. The approach builds on the Marching Cubes algorithm and utilizes OpenGL's vertex and geometry shaders. Context-Preserving Volume Image Exploration Using A 3D Painting Metaphor, https://doi.org/10.32920/ryerson.14646888, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Dual Grid Isosurface Extraction
head: Dual Grid Marching Cubes
body: Dual Grid Isosurface Extraction is a method for extracting crack-free isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data by treating cell centers as vertices of a new grid. It solves the problem of dangling nodes and resulting surface discontinuities that occur when standard Marching Cubes is applied to vertex-centered resampled AMR data. It differs from its siblings by leveraging the natural gap between coarse and fine grid levels in the dual representation to prevent dangling nodes, rather than using post-processing fixes or polygon collapsing (14936-dual-grid-non-manifold-contouring.md). Inputs and Outputs: Input: AMR scalar field data defined on cell centers. Output: A manifold triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Data Structures: The method constructs a dual grid. Vertices: The vertices of the dual grid correspond to the cell centers of the original AMR grid. Topology: The dual grid is a structured grid that is "shrunk" by one cell in each axial direction relative to the original grid boundaries. This creates a geometric gap between coarse and fine grid levels. Steps: 1. Construct Dual Grid: Map each cell center of the AMR grid to a vertex in the dual grid. The scalar value associated with each dual vertex is the original cell-centered value. 2. Identify Gap: Recognize that the dual grid structure inherently creates a gap between the coarse and fine grid regions due to the one-cell shrinkage in each axial direction. 3. Extract Isosurface: Apply the standard Marching Cubes algorithm (as defined in Grid Structure and Topology) on the dual grid vertices. The gap ensures that no dangling nodes exist at the boundaries of refinement levels, preventing cracks. 4. Stitching (if required): If the gap between coarse and fine grids results in uncovered regions, a tessellation scheme (stitch cells) is used to merge the levels seamlessly. This is handled by the variant Dual Grid Isosurface Extraction with Stitch Cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructdualgrid(AMRcells): """ Maps AMR cell centers to dual grid vertices. AMRcells: List of cells, each with center coordinates (x, y, z) and value v. Returns: A structured grid representation where vertices are cell centers. """ # The dual grid is defined by the function values at the cell centers. # The grid shrinks by one cell in each axial direction relative to the original grid. # This creates a gap between coarse and fine grids. dualvertices = [] for cell in AMRcells: dualvertices.append({ 'pos': cell.center, 'value': cell.value }) return dualvertices def extractisosurfacedualgrid(dualvertices, isovalue): """ Applies Marching Cubes on the dual grid. """ # Since the dual grid handles the topology via the gap, # we can use the standard Marching Cubes logic on the dual vertices. # The key is that the dual grid structure prevents dangling nodes. # 1. Build the voxel structure from dual vertices # Note: The exact voxelization depends on the AMR hierarchy structure. # For a uniform dual grid representation: voxels = buildvoxelsfromdualvertices(dualvertices) triangles = [] for voxel in voxels: # Get values at the 8 corners of the voxel in the dual grid values = [vertex['value'] for vertex in voxel.corners] # Compute case index caseindex = 0 for i in range(8): if values[i] < isovalue: caseindex |= (1 << i) # Look up edge intersections and triangles # edgetable and triangletable are from Grid Structure and Topology edgemask = edgetable[caseindex] triindices = triangletable[caseindex] # Calculate intersection points edgeintersections = {} for edgeidx in range(12): if (edgemask >> edgeidx) & 1: # Interpolate on the edge of the dual grid voxel p1 = voxel.corners[edgestart[edgeidx]] p2 = voxel.corners[edgeend[edgeidx]] v1 = p1['value'] v2 = p2['value'] # Linear interpolation t = (isovalue - v1) / (v2 - v1) pos = lerp(p1['pos'], p2['pos'], t) edgeintersections[edgeidx] = pos # Generate triangles for i in range(0, len(triindices), 3): if triindices[i] == -1: break e1, e2, e3 = triindices[i], triindices[i+1], triindices[i+2] p1 = edgeintersections[e1] p2 = edgeintersections[e2] p3 = edgeintersections[e3] triangles.append((p1, p2, p3)) return triangles Extracts continuous, crack-free isosurfaces from AMR data by constructing a dual grid that connects cell centers, thereby eliminating dangling nodes inherent in standard Marching Cubes on vertex-centered resampled data. It differs from previous crack-fixing solutions that create polygons, collapse polylines, or use triangle fans by using a dual grid and tessellated "stitch cells" to maintain topological consistency without interpolation artifacts. Choose this when seamless merging of AMR levels is required without manual gap handling. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels in the dual grid, similar to standard Marching Cubes. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of cell centers in the AMR data. Strengths: Eliminates cracks caused by dangling nodes in AMR data without requiring complex post-processing or interpolation artifacts. Limitations: Requires a stitching mechanism (like stitch cells) to handle the geometric gaps between coarse and fine levels if a continuous mesh across levels is needed. When to use: When extracting isosurfaces from AMR data where standard vertex-centered resampling leads to topological errors. The method was introduced to address issues in extracting isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. Standard Marching Cubes on vertex-centered resampled AMR data suffers from dangling nodes, which cause cracks in the extracted surface. The dual grid approach, defined by cell-centered values, was proposed to solve these problems by leveraging the natural gap between grid levels. Extraction of Crack-free Isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/vissym01/025-034, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dual Grid Isosurface Extraction with Stitch Cells
head: Dual Grid Method, First Approach
body: This method extracts continuous, crack-free isosurfaces from cell-centered Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data by constructing a dual grid that connects cell centers, thereby eliminating dangling nodes inherent in standard Marching Cubes on vertex-centered resampled data. It differs from previous crack-fixing solutions that create polygons, collapse polylines, or use triangle fans by using a dual grid and tessellated "stitch cells" to maintain topological consistency without interpolation artifacts. Inputs: AMR hierarchy of cell-centered scalar data. Isosurface value v. Outputs: A manifold triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Data Structures: Dual Grid: A grid where vertices correspond to the centers of the original AMR cells. Edges connect centers of adjacent cells. Stitch Cells: Tessellated geometry filling gaps between hierarchy levels. In 3D, these must share only vertices, edges, and complete quadrilateral faces. Tetrahedra are not used because cells must share quadrilaterals as faces. Steps: 1. Construct Dual Grid: Connect the centers of adjacent cells in the AMR hierarchy to form the dual grid vertices and edges. 2. Apply Marching Cubes: Perform Marching Cubes on the dual grid using the original cell-centered values associated with the dual vertices. Linear interpolation along edges is permitted as it is inherent to Marching Cubes, but no other interpolation is performed. 3. Identify Gaps: Locate regions between hierarchy levels where fine and coarse patches meet. These gaps contain dual grid vertices/edges that are not part of the standard dual grid connectivity of the coarse or fine patches. 4. Tessellate Gaps with Stitch Cells: Fill the identified gap regions using stitch cells. The tessellation must satisfy: only the gap region is tessellated; the complete gap region is tessellated; stitch cells share only vertices, edges, and complete faces (quadrilaterals in 3D) with the surrounding geometry. 5. Handle Multiple Patches: If multiple fine patches are adjacent, merge them by "upgrading" edges to quadrilaterals and vertices to edges to handle the connectivity correctly. Specific configuration cases include: all coarse grid points unrefined; two neighboring coarse grid points refined; two diagonally opposed coarse grid points refined; and all coarse grid points refined. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Standard Marching Cubes on cell-centered data creates dangling nodes (vertices present only in fine levels), causing cracks. Resampling to vertex-centered data requires consistent values to avoid problems; linear interpolation avoids problems but introduces artifacts. In 3D, stitch cells cannot use tetrahedra because cells must share quadrilaterals as faces. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Tested on an AMR simulation of star cluster formation (Root level 32x32x32, Data set: Greg Bryan, Theoretical Astronomy Group, MIT). Strengths: Uses original data values for Marching Cubes; no dangling nodes; avoids interpolation artifacts. Limitations: Requires complex tessellation logic for gaps and multiple patch adjacency. This method is described in the context of "Current State of the Art in Adaptive Mesh Refinement Visualization". It is contrasted with previous crack-fixing solutions mostly in the context of Octree-based hierarchies, such as creating polygons to fit cracks [Shu et al., 1995], collapsing polylines to lines [Shekhar et al., 1996], and creating triangle fans [Westermann et al., 1999]. The dual grid approach is labeled the "First Approach" in this context. Visualization Tools for Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data, https://www.vacet.org/publications/AMRVisJune2007.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Dual-Grid Non-Manifold Contouring
head: Dual-grid approach, Voxel-based contouring
body: Dual-Grid Non-Manifold Contouring extracts non-manifold meshes from segmented volumes containing multiple materials by utilizing a dual grid structure where material attributes are associated with voxel centers rather than cell corners. Unlike generalized marching cubes, which requires large lookup tables for multi-material cases (e.g., 58 triangulations for three materials), this method avoids lookup tables entirely by generating quadrilateral faces at voxel boundaries and resolving topological ambiguities through a priority-based vertex splitting mechanism. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume grid where each voxel v is assigned a discrete material attribute m(v). The grid is treated as a dual grid, meaning material values reside at voxel centers. Output: A non-manifold mesh composed of quadrilateral faces. Each face is tagged with the material attributes of the two adjacent voxels. Data Structures Material Grid: A 3D array storing integer material IDs at voxel centers. Face List: A list of quadrilateral faces. Each face is defined by four vertices and stores two material tags (one for each adjacent voxel). Vertex Map: A mapping from geometric positions to topological vertices. Vertices may be split to handle non-manifold topology. Algorithm Steps 1. Grid Shift: Conceptually shift the hexahedral grid by half a cell width in each direction so that material attributes are associated with voxel centers. 2. Face Generation: Iterate over every pair of adjacent grid voxels in a 6-neighborhood (sharing a face). For each pair (vi, vj) with different material attributes m(vi) \neq m(vj), create a quadrilateral face representing their common boundary. 3. Tagging: Tag each generated face with the material attributes of the two adjacent voxels, m(vi) and m(vj). 4. Initial Vertex Creation: For every cell (corresponding to the primal grid cell used in standard Marching Cubes) intersected by a surface component, generate one initial vertex at the geometric center of the face intersection. 5. Ambiguity Resolution: Resolve topological ambiguities (e.g., separating two sheets of the same material) using a priority ordering of material attributes. Material components of greater priority are merged in ambiguous cases. 6. Virtual Movement: Implement priority merging by virtually moving mesh components toward the material of lower priority. Since every face is associated with two materials, the direction of this virtual movement is unique. 7. Vertex Splitting: Split vertices incident to faces moving in opposite directions into multiple topological vertices, each associated with an individual mesh component. 8. Constraint Check: Do not perform vertex splitting if at least one polygon contains both components of a split vertex. This ensures only quadrilaterals are generated, as splitting in such cases would produce non-quadrilateral faces. These cases occur in regions with three or more adjacent materials. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualgridcontouring(materialgrid, griddimensions): """ Extracts non-manifold mesh from segmented volume using dual grid approach. Args: materialgrid: 3D array of material IDs at voxel centers. griddimensions: Tuple (nx, ny, nz) defining the grid size. Returns: faces: List of quadrilateral faces, each represented as a tuple of 4 vertices. Each vertex is a tuple (x, y, z). Each face also stores material tags (m1, m2). """ faces = [] # Map from geometric vertex key to list of topological vertices # Key: (x, y, z) rounded to grid precision # Value: List of (vertexindex, materialpriority) vertexmap = {} # Step 1 & 2: Generate faces for adjacent voxels for x in range(griddimensions[0] - 1): for y in range(griddimensions[1] - 1): for z in range(griddimensions[2] - 1): # Get materials of adjacent voxels in 6-neighborhood # We process each face once by checking specific neighbors # e.g., +x, +y, +z directions # Face between (x,y,z) and (x+1,y,z) m1 = materialgrid[x, y, z] m2 = materialgrid[x+1, y, z] if m1 != m2: # Create quadrilateral face at the boundary # Vertices are at the corners of the shared face # Assuming unit grid spacing, face is at x + 0.5 v1 = (x + 0.5, y, z) v2 = (x + 0.5, y + 1, z) v3 = (x + 0.5, y + 1, z + 1) v4 = (x + 0.5, y, z + 1) # Tag face with materials face = { 'vertices': [v1, v2, v3, v4], 'materials': (m1, m2) } faces.append(face) # Register vertices in map for potential splitting for v in [v1, v2, v3, v4]: key = roundvertex(v) if key not in vertexmap: vertexmap[key] = [] vertexmap[key].append({'face': face, 'material': m1}) vertexmap[key].append({'face': face, 'material': m2}) # Face between (x,y,z) and (x,y+1,z) m1 = materialgrid[x, y, z] m2 = materialgrid[x, y+1, z] if m1 != m2: v1 = (x, y + 0.5, z) v2 = (x + 1, y + 0.5, z) v3 = (x + 1, y + 0.5, z + 1) v4 = (x, y + 0.5, z + 1) face = { 'vertices': [v1, v2, v3, v4], 'materials': (m1, m2) } faces.append(face) for v in [v1, v2, v3, v4]: key = roundvertex(v) if key not in vertexmap: vertexmap[key] = [] vertexmap[key].append({'face': face, 'material': m1}) vertexmap[key].append({'face': face, 'material': m2}) # Face between (x,y,z) and (x,y,z+1) m1 = materialgrid[x, y, z] m2 = materialgrid[x, y, z+1] if m1 != m2: v1 = (x, y, z + 0.5) v2 = (x + 1, y, z + 0.5) v3 = (x + 1, y + 1, z + 0.5) v4 = (x, y + 1, z + 0.5) face = { 'vertices': [v1, v2, v3, v4], 'materials': (m1, m2) } faces.append(face) for v in [v1, v2, v3, v4]: key = roundvertex(v) if key not in vertexmap: vertexmap[key] = [] vertexmap[key].append({'face': face, 'material': m1}) vertexmap[key].append({'face': face, 'material': m2}) # Step 5-8: Resolve ambiguities and split vertices # Note: The source describes a virtual movement based on priority. # Here we implement the core logic of splitting based on face directions. # Define a simple priority function (e.g., material ID) def getpriority(materialid): return materialid finalfaces = [] processedvertices = {} for key, vertexentries in vertexmap.items(): # Determine if splitting is needed # Split if faces incident to this vertex move in opposite directions # "Moving toward lower priority" implies direction is determined by material difference # Collect unique materials at this vertex materialsatvertex = set() for entry in vertexentries: materialsatvertex.add(entry['material']) # If only one material, no split needed (manifold) if len(materialsatvertex) == 1: finalfaces.extend(vertexentries) continue # Check for split condition: faces moving in opposite directions # This requires comparing priorities of adjacent materials for each face splitneeded = False for entry in vertexentries: m1, m2 = entry['face']['materials'] # Determine direction of virtual movement for this face # Move towards lower priority if getpriority(m1) > getpriority(m2): direction = m2 # Moving towards m2 else: direction = m1 # Moving towards m1 # Check if another face at this vertex moves in opposite direction # This is a simplified check; full implementation requires tracking all incident faces # For the purpose of this article, we note that splitting occurs here pass # Simplified implementation: If multiple materials, split vertex # Create separate topological vertices for each material component uniquematerials = list(materialsatvertex) for mat in uniquematerials: # Create a new topological vertex for this material processedvertices[(key, mat)] = [] # Re-assign faces to split vertices for entry in vertexentries: m1, m2 = entry['face']['materials'] # Assign face to vertices corresponding to its materials # This ensures non-manifold connectivity is preserved pass return faces def roundvertex(v): return (round(v[0], 6), round(v[1], 6), round(v[2], 6)) Parameters and Edge Cases Priority Ordering: A strict total ordering of material attributes is required to resolve ambiguities. The choice of priority affects the final topology. Three or More Materials: In regions where three or more materials meet, vertex splitting must be skipped if a polygon contains both components of a split vertex to maintain quadrilateral topology. Precision: Geometric coordinates are computed at face centers (half-integer offsets). Floating-point precision issues may arise when determining vertex equality; rounding is necessary. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels, as each voxel face is processed once. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of surface faces. The method avoids large lookup tables, reducing memory overhead compared to generalized marching cubes for high material counts. Strengths: Handles non-manifold topology naturally; no lookup table required for multi-material cases; generates quadrilateral meshes which are suitable for certain fairing and subdivision techniques. Limitations: Requires a priority ordering for ambiguity resolution, which may not always reflect the true physical topology; vertex splitting logic is complex to implement correctly for general cases; may produce gaps if material boundaries are not well-defined. When to Use: Segmented volumes with multiple distinct materials where non-manifold topology is expected or desired (e.g., medical imaging with overlapping tissues). When Not to Use: Single-material volumes (standard Marching Cubes is simpler); cases where manifold topology is strictly required without post-processing. The method was proposed as an alternative to generalized marching cubes for extracting non-manifold meshes from segmented volumes, particularly in the context of modeling a human heart from MRI data. Generalized marching cubes, as proposed by [HSSZ97], requires a lookup table with 58 topologically different triangulations for three materials, which becomes intractable for eight materials. The dual-grid approach, inspired by earlier work on dual grids [Gib98, Nie04], was adopted to avoid constructing such large lookup tables. The method was presented at EuroVis 2005. name: Analytical Error Approximation for Edge-Crossing
body: This method provides an analytical approximation of the geometric error introduced by the linear interpolation of edge-crossing vertices in Marching Cubes (MC) algorithms. It visualizes the reconstructed isosurface error directly from the volume data without requiring sampling, ensemble data, or high-resolution target meshes. It is computationally more efficient than isosurface comparison methods because it avoids the overhead of generating and comparing additional surfaces. The method estimates the uncertainty of the vertex position on an edge by analyzing the local gradients (slopes) of the scalar field along that edge. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric scalar field data V, isovalue I, and the standard MC lookup tables (edgeTable, triangleTable). Output: A scalar field or texture representing the estimated error magnitude at each edge intersection, or a visual overlay on the extracted mesh. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard MC structures defined in Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration: 1. Edge Intersection Table (edgeTable): 256-entry bitmask indicating which of the 12 edges intersect the isosurface [Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling]. 2. Triangle Connection Table (triangleTable): 256x16 array defining the triangulation for each case [Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling]. 3. Edge Intersections (edgeintersections): An array of 12 vectors (or nulls) storing the interpolated vertex positions for the current voxel [Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling]. Method Steps: 1. Compute Case Index: For each voxel, determine the 8-bit case index C based on the sign of V(vi) - I at the 8 vertices [Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling]. 2. Identify Intersecting Edges: Use edgeTable[C] to identify which edges ek (k \in 0..11) are intersected. 3. Calculate Edge Slopes: For each intersecting edge connecting vertices va and vb, compute the divided difference (slope) Sk: Sk = \frac{V(vb) - V(va)}{d{ab}} where d{ab} is the Euclidean distance between va and vb. 4. Approximate Error: The error approximation is derived from these slopes. While the source states the method "effectively approximates the edge-crossing error" using these slopes, it does not provide the explicit closed-form formula for the error magnitude in the provided text. The error is computed directly from the volume data using these local derivatives. 5. Visualize: Map the computed error values to a color scale or opacity to visualize the uncertainty. Parameters: Interpolation Method: The method is designed for linear interpolation. Isovalue: The threshold I used for case index calculation [Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hidden Features: The method helps detect features missed by standard MC with linear interpolation, particularly where high-order interpolation would reveal different topologies. Ambiguity: Standard MC ambiguity cases (46, 47, 98, 99, 210, 213, 214, 215) may still require specific handling (e.g., Lookup Table and Ambiguity Handling) as the error approximation relies on the base vertex positions and slopes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeedgecrossingerror(values, isovalue, edgetable, triangletable): """ Computes the analytical error approximation for edge-crossing vertices. values: list of 8 scalar values at voxel corners. isovalue: the threshold I. edgetable: 256-entry bitmask array. triangletable: 256x16 array. Returns: list of error magnitudes for intersecting edges. """ # 1. Compute Case Index caseindex = 0 for i in range(8): if values[i] < isovalue: caseindex |= (1 << i) # 2. Get Edge Mask edgemask = edgetable[caseindex] # 3. Identify Intersecting Edges and Compute Slopes # Note: The exact formula for error magnitude from slopes is not provided in. # This implementation assumes a placeholder calculation based on slope magnitude. # In a full implementation, the specific analytical function from would be applied here. edgeerrors = [] for k in range(12): if (edgemask >> k) & 1: # Get vertex indices for edge k (standard MC edge definition) # Edge definitions depend on the specific vertex ordering convention. # Assuming standard ordering: # e0=(0,1), e1=(1,2), e2=(2,3), e3=(3,0) # e4=(4,5), e5=(5,6), e6=(6,7), e7=(7,4) # e8=(0,4), e9=(1,5), e10=(2,6), e11=(3,7) vindices = getedgevertices(k) va = values[vindices[0]] vb = values[vindices[1]] # Calculate slope (divided difference) # Distance dab is assumed to be 1.0 for unit cubes or normalized dab = getedgelength(k) slope = (vb - va) / dab # Error approximation placeholder: # states error is approximated from slopes. # A common proxy for linear interpolation error is proportional to the square of the slope # or the magnitude of the second derivative, but does not specify the exact formula. # We store the slope magnitude as a proxy for the "uncertainty" contribution. errormagnitude = abs(slope) edgeerrors.append(errormagnitude) return edgeerrors def getedgevertices(edgeindex): """Returns the indices of the two vertices for a given edge index (0-11).""" edges = [ (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0), # Bottom (4, 5), (5, 6), (6, 7), (7, 4), # Top (0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7) # Vertical ] return edges[edgeindex] def getedgelength(edgeindex): """Returns the length of the edge. Assumes unit cube for simplicity.""" # In a real implementation, this would account for voxel dimensions dx, dy, dz return 1.0 A measure for spatial accuracy defined as the maximum distance between the location where the surface (or gradient) is calculated and a reference surface. It allows evaluation of error independent of observation angle. Formula: The spatial error bound for voxel space volume rendering is E{voxel} \approx (dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2) / 2, where dx, dy, dz are the voxel distances in the x, y, and z directions. Parameters: The re-sampling distance should be equal to or smaller than the voxel distances to ensure the error bound is not severely influenced by the re-sampling process. Pitfalls: In shear-warp algorithms, when data is rotated under the worst-case angle of 45 degrees, the re-sampling distance on the rays increases to \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2}. If voxel dimensions are equal, this distance is 1.73 voxels large, leading to clearly visible artifacts. Comparison: Unlike grey-value or frequency domain error criteria which compare re-sampling functions in isolation, the spatial error bound accounts for how re-sampling functions are embedded in volume visualization algorithms, specifically addressing errors caused by calculating gradients at wrong locations. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels, as it processes each voxel independently to compute edge slopes. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not require storing additional high-resolution meshes or ensemble data. Strengths: Computationally more efficient than isosurface comparison methods; applicable to any volumetric data; does not require sampling or additional information. Limitations: The exact analytical formula for the error magnitude is not explicitly detailed in the provided source text. It is specific to the linear interpolation method. The method was introduced to address limitations in visualizing uncertainties caused by interpolation methods in Marching Cubes. It was developed by researchers associated with UT-Battelle, LLC, under contract with the U.S. Department of Energy. The work aims to provide insights into uncertainties and detect hidden features missed by standard MC with linear interpolation. Estimation and Visualization of Isosurface Uncertainty from Linear and High-Order Interpolation Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00043v1, fetched 2026-10-26 Iso-Surface Volume Rendering: speed and accuracy for medical applications, https://doi.org/10.3990/1.9789036513982, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Surface Properties and Estimation
body: This family computes geometric attributes (normals, area) or improves visual quality (smoothing) of isosurfaces extracted from scalar fields. It addresses limitations of raw isosurface extraction, such as jagged artifacts in binary data. It differs from its siblings, which focus on mesh topology and connectivity [30-isosurface-extraction.md], by operating on the resulting geometry or the input field to refine surface representation. All methods in this family operate on the output of an isosurface extraction algorithm or the underlying scalar field. The core mechanism involves evaluating local geometric properties or applying transformations to the scalar data to influence the final mesh. 1. Geometric Evaluation: For normals and area, the method evaluates the local geometry of the generated mesh primitives (triangles) or the underlying scalar field gradients. 2. Field Transformation: For smoothing, the method transforms the input scalar field (e.g., binary to continuous signed distance) before extraction to ensure a smoother isosurface. 3. Post-Processing or Pre-Processing: Methods are categorized by whether they modify the mesh after extraction (normals, area) or the input data before extraction (smoothing). Computes surface normals for an isosurface mesh by approximating the gradient of the underlying scalar field at vertex positions using central differences, then normalizing the result. Differs from geometric normal estimation by relying on the analytic properties of the scalar field, providing smoother normals that reflect underlying data density rather than just discretized mesh topology. Choose when accurate lighting calculations are required and the scalar field is accessible. Estimates the surface area of a solid by summing the areas of the triangular polygons produced by the marching cubes algorithm. Differs from siblings by focusing on the aggregate geometric measure (area) rather than local vector properties or topological smoothing. Choose when quantitative analysis of surface extent is needed. Note that standard linear implementations lack multigrid convergence for certain orientations. Converts a binary volume embedding into a continuous signed scalar field to eliminate jagged, stair-stepped artifacts inherent in extracting isosurfaces directly from discrete masks. Differs from siblings by operating on the input scalar field prior to extraction rather than post-processing the resulting mesh geometry. Preserves topological information of the original binary embedding without eroding fine details. Choose when extracting surfaces from binary masks to avoid low-quality meshes. A post-processing technique to obtain a smooth surface from voxelized particle spheres by iteratively applying a smoothing kernel to the reciprocal of extracted depth values. Apply a 3×3 smoothing kernel to the reciprocal of the extracted depth values iteratively. Let the number of iterations depend on the distance of the processed surface point to the camera to keep the world-space radius of the filter approximately constant. Follow the stored surface links to identify the right connected surface points for each pixel's neighborhood during filtering. Differs from standard smoothing by using surface links to traverse the topology rather than spatial grid neighbors, ensuring correct smoothing along the surface geometry. Used in voxelization pipelines for particle data to refine surface quality and compute geometric metrics. Memory-Efficient On-The-Fly Voxelization of Particle Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/pgv.20151150, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SEVA (Surface Extraction with Volumetric Adaptivity)
head: two pass surface extraction algorithm
body: SEVA is a two-pass algorithm for incremental surface extraction from hexahedral finite element meshes that accommodates volumetric adaptivity, such as element removal or failure. It identifies paired internal surfaces by hashing local connectivity and nodal weights, then constructs a polygon list containing only external (unpaired) surfaces. It is distinguished from standard marching cubes by its explicit handling of element removal via a master surface list counter, ensuring that previously hidden interior surfaces are correctly exposed as external surfaces when adjacent elements fail. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of active hexahedral elements, each defined by 8 nodes. Each node has a global index j and spatial coordinates. An activity vector indicating element validity (for adaptivity). Output: A polygon vertex pointer list containing global node numbers and element material numbers, ready for vertex coordinate gathering and rendering. Data Structures: 1. Hash Table: An array of length 6 N{hex}, where N{hex} is the number of hexahedral elements. Each entry stores: hashkey: The computed hash value for the face. elementid: The index of the hex element. faceid: The index of the face within the element (0-5). Entries are added in sequential order as faces are processed. 2. Master Surface List: A dynamic list constructed during Pass 1. Each entry contains: hashvalue: The unique hash key. surfacecount: Integer counter (max 2). elementids: List of element indices associated with this hash. faceids: List of face indices associated with this hash. 3. Polygon Vertex Pointer List: The final output structure containing global node indices and material IDs for rendering. Parameters: Nodal Weight (wj): Defined as wj = 10^{(j-1)}, where j is the local node index within the element (j \in [1, 8]). This exponential weighting provides dispersion in hash keys to minimize collisions, though collisions are handled by the sorting step. Steps: 1. Pass 1: Hashing and Sorting 1. Initialize the Hash Table with 6 N{hex} empty slots. 2. For each active hexahedral element e: a. For each of the 6 faces f of element e: i. Identify the 4 nodes defining face f. Let their local indices be k1, k2, k3, k4. ii. Retrieve the global node indices G{km} for these local nodes. iii. Sort the global node indices in ascending order to form the sorted local surface connectivity vector S{ij} = [\min(G), \dots, \max(G)]. iv. Compute the hash key H using the formula: H = \text{hash}(S{ij}, wj) Where wj corresponds to the nodal weights of the nodes in S{ij}. Note: The source defines wj = 10^{(j-1)} based on local node index j. The hash function combines the sorted connectivity and weights. v. Store (H, e, f) in the next available slot in the Hash Table. 3. Perform an indexed heap sort on the Hash Table entries based on H in ascending order. This is an O(N \log N) operation. 2. Pass 1 (Continued): Master Surface List Construction 1. Initialize an empty Master Surface List. 2. Traverse the sorted Hash Table. 3. Identify groups of adjacent entries with identical hash keys H. 4. For each group: a. Create a new entry in the Master Surface List with hashvalue = H. b. Set surfacecount = number of entries in the group (typically 1 or 2). c. Populate elementids and faceids from the group entries. Note: A count of 2 indicates paired (internal) surfaces. A count of 1 indicates an unpaired (external) surface. 3. Pass 2: Polygon List Generation 1. Initialize an empty Polygon Vertex Pointer List. 2. Iterate through the Master Surface List. 3. For each entry where surfacecount == 1: a. This represents an external surface. b. Retrieve the elementid and faceid. c. Add the global node numbers for the 4 vertices of this face to the Polygon Vertex Pointer List, along with the element's material number. 4. Concatenate any active shell elements onto the Polygon Vertex Pointer list. 4. Volumetric Adaptivity Handling (Element Removal) When an element fails or is removed: a. Identify all faces of the failed element. b. For each face, locate its corresponding entry in the Master Surface List (using the pre-computed hash or element/face mapping). c. Decrement the surfacecount for that hash entry. d. If surfacecount becomes 1, the surface is now considered valid (exposed interior surface) and will be included in the Polygon Vertex Pointer List in the next Pass 2 execution. Note: The canonical local node numbering scheme for hex elements ensures that freshly exposed polygon normals face outwards, guaranteeing consistent lighting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesevahash(elementnodes, globalnodes): """ Computes the hash key for a single hexahedral face. elementnodes: list of 8 local node indices for the element. globalnodes: dict mapping local node index to global node index. Returns: hashkey, sortedglobalnodes """ # Define the 4 nodes for each of the 6 faces of a hexahedron # Using standard hexahedron face definitions (indices 0-7) facedefinitions = [ [0, 1, 2, 3], # Face 0 [4, 5, 6, 7], # Face 1 [0, 1, 5, 4], # Face 2 [2, 3, 7, 6], # Face 3 [0, 3, 7, 4], # Face 4 [1, 2, 6, 5] # Face 5 ] hashtable = [] for faceidx, facenodeslocal in enumerate(facedefinitions): # Get global node indices for this face globalindices = [] for localnode in facenodeslocal: globalindices.append(globalnodes[localnode]) # Sort global indices for canonical representation sortedglobalindices = sorted(globalindices) # Compute nodal weights wj = 10^(j-1) where j is local node index # Note: The source uses local node index j for weight calculation weights = [] for localnode in facenodeslocal: j = localnode + 1 # 1-based index weights.append(10 (j - 1)) # Hash function combines sorted connectivity and weights # The exact hash implementation is not specified, but it must be deterministic # and sensitive to the set of nodes and their weights. hashkey = hash((tuple(sortedglobalindices), tuple(weights))) hashtable.append({ 'hashkey': hashkey, 'elementid': elementid, 'faceid': faceidx, 'globalnodes': sortedglobalindices }) return hashtable def sevaextract(elements, globalnodesmap, elementactivity): """ Main SEVA algorithm. elements: list of elements, each with local node indices. globalnodesmap: dict mapping (elementid, localnodeidx) -> globalnodeidx elementactivity: list of booleans indicating if element is active. """ hashtable = [] # Pass 1: Build Hash Table for elemidx, element in enumerate(elements): if not elementactivity[elemidx]: continue # Map local nodes to global nodes currentglobalnodes = {} for localidx, globalidx in enumerate(element.localnodes): currentglobalnodes[localidx] = globalidx facehashes = computesevahash(element.localnodes, currentglobalnodes) for fh in facehashes: fh['elementid'] = elemidx hashtable.append(fh) # Sort hash table by hashkey hashtable.sort(key=lambda x: x['hashkey']) # Build Master Surface List masterlist = [] i = 0 while i < len(hashtable): currenthash = hashtable[i]['hashkey'] group = [] while i < len(hashtable) and hashtable[i]['hashkey'] == currenthash: group.append(hashtable[i]) i += 1 masterlist.append({ 'hashvalue': currenthash, 'surfacecount': len(group), 'entries': group }) # Handle Adaptivity: Decrement counts for failed elements # This step assumes we have a previous masterlist state or re-compute # based on current active elements. The source implies updating counts # when elements fail. For a fresh extraction, we just use the counts. # Pass 2: Generate Polygon List polygonlist = [] for entry in masterlist: if entry['surfacecount'] == 1: # External surface facedata = entry['entries'][0] elemid = facedata['elementid'] faceid = facedata['faceid'] # Get global nodes for this face # Note: We need to re-fetch global nodes or store them in hashtable # For simplicity, assume we can retrieve them from elements/globalnodesmap element = elements[elemid] facedef = [ [0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6, 7], [0, 1, 5, 4], [2, 3, 7, 6], [0, 3, 7, 4], [1, 2, 6, 5] ][faceid] globalfacenodes = [] for localnode in facedef: globalfacenodes.append(globalnodesmap[(elemid, localnode)]) polygonlist.append({ 'nodes': globalfacenodes, 'material': element.materialid }) return polygonlist Time Complexity: The dominant operation is the heap sort of the hash table, which is O(N \log N), where N is the number of faces (6 N{hex}). Memory Complexity: The hash table requires 6 N{hex} entries. The master surface list is at most 6 N{hex} entries but typically much smaller due to pairing. Strengths: Efficiently handles dynamic meshes where elements are added or removed (volumetric adaptivity). It correctly exposes internal surfaces when adjacent elements fail, which is critical for finite element simulations with failure criteria (e.g., DYNA3D). Limitations: Relies on a hash function that, while providing dispersion, does not guarantee uniqueness. Collisions are resolved by the sorting and grouping step, but this requires careful implementation to ensure adjacent identical hashes are correctly identified as paired surfaces. The algorithm is specific to hexahedral elements and their canonical numbering scheme. When to use: Finite element data visualization, particularly for temporal interpolation ("in-betweening") and simulations involving element failure/sliding interfaces (e.g., TWEENER, GRIZ). SEVA was developed for visualizing high-resolution, transient, 3-D finite element situations. It was initially implemented in a finite element data visualizer called TWEENER, used for interpolating between discrete states of simulation results for video animation ("in-betweening"). A modified version is used in GRIZ. The algorithm addresses the challenge of identifying paired internal surfaces in the presence of volumetric adaptivity, such as element removal based on maximum strain failure criteria in DYNA3D simulations.
