name: Marching Cubes Surface Area Estimation
head: Surface Area Estimation via Marching Cubes
body: This method estimates the surface area of a solid by summing the areas of the triangular polygons produced by the marching cubes algorithm to approximate the solid's frontier Vh(S). It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the aggregate geometric measure (area) rather than local vector properties like normals [1005-marching-cubes-surface-normal-estimation.md] or topological smoothing [1594-marching-cubes-smoothing.md]. While it provides a direct scalar estimate of the isosurface extent, it is known to lack multigrid convergence for standard linear implementations, meaning the error does not necessarily vanish as grid resolution increases. Inputs and Outputs Input: The set of triangles generated by the marching cubes algorithm approximating the isosurface Vh(S) of a solid S. Output: A scalar value representing the estimated surface area A{est} = \sum \text{Area}(Ti). Data Structures The method operates on the output mesh of the parent isosurface extraction. Each triangle is defined by three vertices p1, p2, p3. No additional complex data structures are required beyond storing the vertex coordinates for each triangle. Formulas The area of a single triangle defined by vertices p1, p2, p3 is calculated using the cross product of two edge vectors: \text{Area}(p1 p2 p3) = \frac{1}{2} |\vec{p1 p2} \times \vec{p1 p3}| Expanding the cross product magnitude for pi = (xi, yi, zi), let \vec{a} = p2 - p1 and \vec{b} = p3 - p1. The area is: \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \left( (a2 b3 - a3 b2)^2 + (a3 b1 - a1 b3)^2 + (a1 b2 - a2 b1)^2 \right)^{1/2} where aj and bj are the components of vectors \vec{a} and \vec{b} respectively. The total estimated area is the sum over all N triangles: A{est} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \text{Area}(Ti) Parameters Threshold T: The isovalue used during the marching cubes extraction. The estimate depends on the threshold T used to compare the voxel values. Vertex Interpolation Method: The position of vertices on grid edges can be chosen at midpoints or interpolated based on the difference between T and voxel values. Configuration Size: Standard marching cubes uses 2 \times 2 \times 2 voxel configurations. Accuracy can be improved by expanding this to m \times m \times m (where m \ge 2) or using quadratic/cubic approximations. Radius of Influence: For an m \times m \times m configuration, the radius of the ball of influence is R0 = \frac{m}{2\sqrt{3}}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatemarchingcubessurfacearea(triangles): """ Calculates the total surface area of a mesh generated by marching cubes. Args: triangles: A list of triangles. Each triangle is a list/tuple of 3 vertices. Each vertex is a tuple/list of 3 floats (x, y, z). Returns: float: The total estimated surface area. """ totalarea = 0.0 for triangle in triangles: # Extract vertices p1 = triangle[0] p2 = triangle[1] p3 = triangle[2] # Calculate edge vectors a = p2 - p1 and b = p3 - p1 ax = p2[0] - p1[0] ay = p2[1] - p1[1] az = p2[2] - p1[2] bx = p3[0] - p1[0] by = p3[1] - p1[1] bz = p3[2] - p1[2] # Calculate cross product components # cross = a x b crossx = ay bz - az by crossy = az bx - ax bz crossz = ax by - ay bx # Calculate magnitude of cross product magnitudesq = crossx2 + crossy2 + crossz2 magnitude = magnitudesq 0.5 # Area is half the magnitude trianglearea = 0.5 magnitude totalarea += trianglearea return totalarea Edge Cases and Pitfalls Lack of Convergence: The estimate EMCU(S) using the standard 2^3-case lookup table with vertices at edge midpoints fails to provide multigrid convergence to the correct surface area. Orientation Dependence: For a planar surface patch, the deviation between the estimated and true surface area does not depend on grid resolution h, but only on the position and orientation of the patch. Large Deviations: For a planar surface patch with normal (1,1,1) passing through a grid point, the estimated surface area is 3 times the true value. For a cube making angles of 45^\circ with the axes, the deviation can be as great as 85\% for the standard estimate A(Sh), though it reduces to about 9.5\% for the midpoint-based estimate EMCU(Sh). Staircase Effect: Regular solids digitized into grids exhibit "repeated self-similarity" (e.g., staircase patterns), leading to constant surface area errors that differ from the original patch regardless of resolution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Accuracy: Low for standard linear marching cubes with midpoint interpolation. The method suffers from significant orientation-dependent errors that do not decrease with grid refinement. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Does not converge to the true area as resolution increases for standard implementations; highly sensitive to the orientation of planar features relative to the grid; sensitive to the interpolation method used for vertex placement. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is described in the context of digital geometry and local polyhedrization techniques. It is discussed in the book Digital Geometry by Reinhard Klette and Azriel Rosenfeld (2004). The analysis highlights the theoretical limitations of local methods like marching cubes for estimating geometric properties such as area and curvature, noting that these estimates often fail to converge to true values due to discretization artifacts dependent on grid orientation. 3D Arc Length, Surface Area, and Curvature, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123875822500046, fetched 2026-10-30 (book)

name: Marching Cubes Smoothing
head: Smoothing Binary Embeddings, mcubes.smooth
body: Marching Cubes Smoothing transforms a binary embedding array into a continuous signed distance-like field to eliminate the jagged artifacts inherent in extracting isosurfaces directly from discrete binary masks. Unlike standard smoothing techniques that erode fine details and thin structures, this method preserves the original topological information by assigning negative values to background regions and positive values to foreground regions, allowing for a high-quality mesh extraction at the zero-levelset. It addresses the specific problem of jagged meshes produced when passing binary masks directly to the marching cubes algorithm. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D or 3D binary array (embedding) where voxel values are strictly 0 (background) or 1 (foreground). Output: A 2D or 3D floating-point array of the same dimensions, containing negative values where the input was 0 and positive values where the input was 1. Data Structures: The input is typically a NumPy array of integer or boolean type. The output is a NumPy array of floating-point type (e.g., float32 or float64). Algorithm Steps: 1. Accept Binary Input: Receive a binary array B where B{i,j,k} \in \{0, 1\}. 2. Generate Smooth Embedding: Compute a smooth embedding array S from B. The transformation ensures that regions corresponding to 0 in B become negative in S, and regions corresponding to 1 in B become positive in S. 3. Preserve Topology: The smoothing process is designed to keep all information from the original embedding function, specifically avoiding the erosion of fine details and thin structures common in other methods. 4. Extract Isosurface: Use the resulting array S as input to the marching cubes algorithm with an isovalue of 0. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the usage pattern described in the source. Note that the internal implementation of mcubes.smooth is not detailed in the provided text, but its behavior is defined by the input/output contract. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def extractsmoothedmesh(binaryarray): """ Extracts a mesh from a binary array using Marching Cubes Smoothing. Args: binaryarray (np.ndarray): 2D or 3D array with values 0 or 1. Returns: tuple: (vertices, triangles) from marching cubes. """ # Step 1: Smooth the binary embedding # This converts 0s to negative floats and 1s to positive floats # while preserving fine details. smoothedarray = mcubes.smooth(binaryarray) # Step 2: Extract the 0-levelset from the smoothed array # The 0-levelset of the smoothed array corresponds to the # 0.5-levelset of the original binary array. vertices, triangles = mcubes.marchingcubes(smoothedarray, 0) return vertices, triangles Parameters: Isovalue for Extraction: When using the output of the smoothing function, the marching cubes algorithm must be called with an isovalue of 0. Smoothing Parameters: Specific internal parameters (e.g., kernel size, iteration count) for the smoothing operation are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Jagged Meshes: Passing binary masks directly to marching cubes results in jagged, aliased meshes. Smoothing is required to fix this. Erosion of Details: Standard smoothing methods often erode fine details and thin structures. This method is specifically designed to avoid this. Performance: Representing volumetric data using certain structures can be much slower than using a NumPy array. The method assumes efficient array handling. A fast smoothing method applied to binary volumes by converting them to float, subtracting 0.5, and applying a Gaussian filter. It differs from Constrained Smoothing by using direct linear convolution, making it faster but less precise in preserving thin structures. A method that smooths the 0.5 level-set of binary volumes via constrained optimization of a discrete Laplacian energy. It sets itself apart by enforcing hard constraints to prevent erosion of thin structures, at the cost of higher computational complexity. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The source notes that using certain data representations is "much slower" than NumPy arrays, implying efficiency depends on the underlying implementation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves fine details and thin structures that are commonly eroded by other standard smoothing methods. Eliminates jagged artifacts from binary masks. Limitations: Specific limitations are not detailed beyond the comparison with Gaussian smoothing (which is less precise) and Constrained smoothing (which is slower). When to use: When extracting isosurfaces from binary segmentation masks to avoid jagged geometry, especially when fine details and thin structures must be preserved. When not to use: When the input is already a continuous signed distance field or smooth scalar field, as smoothing is intended for binary embeddings. The method is part of the PyMCubes library, which provides Python bindings for the marching cubes algorithm. The specific function mcubes.smooth was introduced to address the common issue of jagged meshes resulting from binary embeddings in segmentation tasks. name: Gaussian Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction
body: Gaussian Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction is a fast smoothing method applied to binary volumes by converting them to float, subtracting 0.5, and applying a Gaussian filter. It differs from its sibling Constrained Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction by using a direct linear convolution rather than an iterative optimization approach, making it faster but less precise in preserving thin structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary array (values 0 and 1) representing a volume. Output: A float array with smoothed values. Data Structures: binaryarray: Numpy array of integers or booleans. vol: Numpy array of float64. Steps: 1. Centering: Convert the binary array to float64 and subtract 0.5. vol = \text{float64}(binary\array) - 0.5 2. Filtering: Apply a Gaussian filter to the centered volume using a specified standard deviation \sigma. smoothed = \text{ndimage.gaussian\filter}(vol, \sigma) Parameters: sigma: The standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel. Controls the amount of smoothing. Default value is 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Detail Loss: The method may destroy fine details and thin structures because the Gaussian kernel averages across boundaries indiscriminately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy import ndimage def gaussiansmoothinglevelset(binaryarray: np.ndarray, sigma: float = 3.0) -> np.ndarray: """ Apply Gaussian smoothing to a binary volume for level-set extraction. Args: binaryarray: Binary volume (0s and 1s). sigma: Standard deviation for the Gaussian filter. Returns: Smoothed float volume centered around 0. """ # Step 1: Convert to float64 and center by subtracting 0.5 vol = np.float64(binaryarray) - 0.5 # Step 2: Apply Gaussian filter smoothedvol = ndimage.gaussianfilter(vol, sigma=sigma) return smoothedvol Box Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction applies a box blur filter to a binary density field to convert sharp 0/1 steps into smooth transitions, allowing Marching Cubes to generate rounded geometry instead of sharp stair-stepped edges. It differs from its parent, Gaussian Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction, by using a simpler averaging kernel that is computationally cheaper but may preserve less of the original field's high-frequency detail. The Amira 3D Edge-Preserving Smoothing Filter is a non-linear smoothing method applied to 3D grayscale image stacks to reduce noise while maintaining sharp boundaries between distinct structures. It addresses the limitation of linear Gaussian smoothing, which blurs edges by averaging across intensity discontinuities. Unlike the parent Gaussian Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction which uses a fixed kernel, this method dynamically adjusts the convolution kernel based on local image content to prevent edge blurring. Quick Smooth is a 3D Gaussian-like smoothing filter applied to the input volume to soften the image before surface extraction. It uses a fixed 5-tap kernel with specific weights rather than a true Gaussian distribution. Parameters: kwid (kernel width) is set to 2, k0 (center weight) is 0.45, k1 (adjacent weight) is 0.225, and k2 (outer weight) is 0.05. Code: The smoothing operation for a voxel v is computed as: tmp[v] = (img[v-2] \times k2) + (img[v-1] \times k1) + (img[v] \times k0) + (img[v+1] \times k1) + (img[v+2] \times k2) Pitfall: The function returns EXITFAILURE if any dimension (nx, ny, nz) is less than 5, as the kernel width requires a minimum volume size to avoid boundary errors. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Recommended for large arrays where the level-set does not contain thin structures. Strengths: Faster than constrained smoothing. Limitations: Less precise; tends to destroy fine details and thin structures due to the linear averaging nature of the Gaussian kernel. When to use it: Use when processing large volumes where computational speed is prioritized over preserving thin geometric features. The method is implemented in the PyMCubes library. The specific function smoothgaussian is part of this library. It is commonly used as a preprocessing step for Marching Cubes surface extraction to reduce aliasing artifacts in binary volume data. pmneila/PyMCubes, https://github.com/pmneila/PyMCubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) TRTUZ8/TRTUZ8.github.io, https://github.com/TRTUZ8/TRTUZ8.github.io, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) DF3 Viewer Oosawa, https://qcganime.web.fc2.com/OOSAWA/MANUAL/FilterE.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Box Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction
head: Density Field Smoothing, Field Blur
body: Box Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction applies a box blur filter to a binary density field to convert sharp 0/1 steps into smooth transitions, allowing Marching Cubes to generate rounded geometry instead of sharp stair-stepped edges. It differs from its parent, Gaussian Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction, by using a simpler averaging kernel that is computationally cheaper but may preserve less of the original field's high-frequency detail. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D density array density of size W \times H \times D, containing binary values (0 or 1). Output: The same density array, modified in-place (via buffer swapping) to contain smoothed values. Data Structures: density: A 1D array of floats of size W \times H \times D, with coordinate mapping i = x + y \cdot W + z \cdot W \cdot H. buffer: A temporary array of the same size and type as density. Parameters: iterations: The number of times the blur pass is repeated. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Allocate a temporary buffer buffer of the same size as density. 2. Repeat the following for iterations times: 1. For each voxel (x, y, z) in the volume: 1. If (x, y, z) is a border voxel (i.e., x=0, x=W-1, y=0, y=H-1, z=0, or z=D-1): 1. Set buffer[x, y, z] = 1.0. 2. Continue to the next voxel. 2. If (x, y, z) is a non-border voxel: 1. Calculate the sum of the current voxel's density and its 6 immediate face-neighbors: d{new}(x,y,z) = \frac{1}{7} \left( d(x,y,z) + d(x+1,y,z) + d(x-1,y,z) + d(x,y+1,z) + d(x,y-1,z) + d(x,y,z+1) + d(x,y,z-1) \right) 2. Set buffer[x, y, z] = d{new}(x,y,z). 2. Swap the density and buffer arrays for the next iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boxsmooth(density, width, height, depth, iterations): buffer = [0.0] (width height depth) for in range(iterations): for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): if x == 0 or x == width - 1 or y == 0 or y == height - 1 or z == 0 or z == depth - 1: buffer[z width height + y width + x] = 1.0 else: idx = z width height + y width + x neighborsum = (density[idx] + density[idx + 1] + density[idx - 1] + density[idx + width] + density[idx - width] + density[idx + width height] + density[idx - width height]) buffer[idx] = neighborsum / 7.0 density, buffer = buffer, density Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Border voxels are hardcoded to 1.0, which may cause boundary artifacts if the field does not naturally reach 1.0 at the edges. The method assumes a binary input (0 or 1). Precision issues are not explicitly discussed, but floating-point division by 7.0 is used. An optional post-generation blur pass applied to the density field to round off sharp relief edges. Unlike mesh-based smoothing, this method does not directly average or displace vertices of an already extracted mesh; it filters the scalar field first, allowing Marching Cubes to generate rounded geometry instead of sharp stair-stepped edges. It builds on Box Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(iterations \cdot W \cdot H \cdot D), where W, H, D are the dimensions of the volume. Each iteration processes every voxel once. Memory: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for the temporary buffer. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally efficient compared to Gaussian smoothing, effective at removing stair-stepping artifacts from binary volumes. Limitations: May destroy fine details, border handling is simplistic (hardcoded to 1.0), only considers face-neighbors (not edge or corner neighbors). When to Use: Use when a fast, simple smoothing method is needed for binary density fields before Marching Cubes extraction. When Not to Use: Do not use when preserving fine details is critical. Origin: The method is described in the context of a Unity voxel terrain implementation. History and Development: The specific implementation details are found in the TerrainChunk.cs script of the UnityVoxelTerrain repository. Where it is used: It is used in voxel-based terrain generation to smooth the density field before surface extraction. head: Box kernel filtering, GPU-based Scalar Field Smoothing, Pre-extraction smoothing
body: A preprocessing step that applies a smoothing filter to the electromagnetic-potential scalar field on the GPU before isosurface extraction to suppress high-frequency variations and produce spatially coherent surfaces. Unlike mesh-based smoothing, this method does not directly average or displace vertices of an already extracted mesh; it filters the scalar field first, allowing Marching Cubes to generate rounded geometry instead of sharp stair-stepped edges. It builds on Box Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D uniform Cartesian grid of scalar values V{i,j,k}(t) representing the electromagnetic potential, with constant spacing along each spatial axis. Output: A smoothed scalar field \tilde{V}{i,j,k} and the resulting isosurface geometry extracted via Marching Cubes. Data Structures: The scalar field is stored as a 3D array. For a grid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, indices (i,j,k) range from 0 to Nx-1, 0 to Ny-1, and 0 to Nz-1 respectively. No padding is used; boundary samples use only valid neighboring grid locations. Parameters: \lambda (smoothing coefficient): Set to 0.35. Number of iterations: 5. Kernel size: 3 \times 3 \times 3. Steps: 1. Initialize the current field state V^{(t)} with the input scalar field values. 2. For each iteration t from 0 to 4 (5 iterations total): a. Create a temporary buffer V^{(t+1)} initialized to zeros or copy V^{(t)}. b. For each voxel (i,j,k) in the grid: i. Identify the set of valid neighbors \mathcal{W}{i,j,k} within the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood centered at (i,j,k). Valid neighbors are those where indices a,b,c satisfy i-1 \le a \le i+1, j-1 \le b \le j+1, k-1 \le k+1, and lie within the grid bounds [0, Nx-1] \times [0, Ny-1] \times [0, Nz-1]. ii. Calculate the number of valid neighbors |\mathcal{W}{i,j,k}|. iii. Compute the sum of scalar values in the neighborhood: S = \sum{(a,b,c) \in \mathcal{W}{i,j,k}} V^{(t)}{a,b,c}. iv. Update the voxel value using the formula: \tilde{V}{i,j,k}(t+1) = (1-\lambda)V{i,j,k}(t) + \frac{\lambda}{|\mathcal{W}{i,j,k}|} \sum{(a,b,c) \in \mathcal{W}{i,j,k}} V{a,b,c}(t) where \lambda = 0.35. c. Update V^{(t)} \leftarrow V^{(t+1)}. 3. After 5 iterations, the final smoothed field is \tilde{V} = V^{(5)}. 4. Perform Marching Cubes on the smoothed field \tilde{V}. 5. For each intersected grid edge with endpoints \mathbf{x}0 and \mathbf{x}1, and corresponding scalar values \tilde{V}(\mathbf{x}0) and \tilde{V}(\mathbf{x}1), compute the isosurface vertex position \mathbf{p} for isovalue \tau: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{x}0 + \frac{\tau - \tilde{V}(\mathbf{x}0)}{\tilde{V}(\mathbf{x}1) - \tilde{V}(\mathbf{x}0)} (\mathbf{x}1 - \mathbf{x}0). 6. Recompute face normals from the resulting triangle geometry. Pitfalls: Smoothing affects vertex coordinates indirectly through filtered scalar values; triangle connectivity and vertex count may change if the filtered field alters the local Marching Cubes case. Boundary handling must strictly exclude invalid neighbors without padding to avoid introducing artificial data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fieldsmoothingpass(field: List[List[List[float]]], nx: int, ny: int, nz: int, lambdaval: float = 0.35, iterations: int = 5) -> List[List[List[float]]]: """ Applies Gaussian-like smoothing via box kernel filtering to a 3D scalar field. Args: field: 3D list of scalar values V[i][j][k] nx, ny, nz: Dimensions of the grid lambdaval: Smoothing coefficient (default 0.35) iterations: Number of smoothing passes (default 5) Returns: Smoothed 3D field """ # Initialize current field state currentfield = [[[[field[i][j][k] for k in range(nz)] for j in range(ny)] for i in range(nx)]] for t in range(iterations): nextfield = [[[0.0 for k in range(nz)] for j in range(ny)] for i in range(nx)] for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): # Identify valid neighbors in 3x3x3 neighborhood neighborsum = 0.0 neighborcount = 0 for a in range(max(0, i-1), min(nx, i+2)): for b in range(max(0, j-1), min(ny, j+2)): for c in range(max(0, k-1), min(nz, k+2)): neighborsum += currentfield[a][b][c] neighborcount += 1 # Apply smoothing formula # Vtilde(i,j,k)(t+1) = (1-lambda)V(i,j,k)(t) + lambda/|W| sum(Vneighbors) centerval = currentfield[i][j][k] avgneighbor = neighborsum / neighborcount nextfield[i][j][k] = (1 - lambdaval) centerval + lambdaval avgneighbor currentfield = nextfield return currentfield def marchingcubesedgeintersection(x0: Vector3, x1: Vector3, v0: float, v1: float, isovalue: float) -> Vector3: """ Computes the intersection point of an isosurface with a grid edge. Args: x0, x1: Endpoints of the grid edge v0, v1: Scalar values at x0 and x1 from the smoothed field isovalue: The threshold value tau Returns: Intersection point p """ # p = x0 + (tau - V(x0)) / (V(x1) - V(x0)) (x1 - x0) denominator = v1 - v0 if abs(denominator) < 1e-9: # Avoid division by zero; return midpoint if values are equal return (x0 + x1) / 2.0 t = (isovalue - v0) / denominator return x0 + t (x1 - x0) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K \cdot I), where N is the number of voxels, K is the kernel size (27 for 3 \times 3 \times 3), and I is the number of iterations (5). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the scalar field and a temporary buffer for each iteration. Measured Performance: Tested on a 256^3 uniform Cartesian grid on a GPU. The same procedure is applicable to 512^3 fields, though experiments for scalability evaluation used 512^3 primarily for buffer capacity testing. Strengths: Suppresses local high-frequency variations and produces a more spatially coherent surface without modifying the mesh topology directly. Limitations: Does not address out-of-core streaming or tile-based caching for very large datasets; future work is needed for improved scalability and feature preservation. When to use: When the input scalar field contains high-frequency noise or stair-stepping artifacts that degrade the visual quality of the extracted isosurface. When not to use: When preserving fine, high-frequency features is critical, as smoothing will blur them. The method was introduced in the context of visual tools for 3D plasma simulation, specifically for GPU-based isosurface extraction of electromagnetic-potential scalar fields. It was developed to address the visual artifacts produced by raw scalar fields in plasma simulations, such as high-frequency variations that lead to noisy isosurfaces. The approach leverages GPU parallelism to apply the smoothing filter efficiently before the Marching Cubes extraction step. name: Amira 3D Edge-Preserving Smoothing Filter
head: edge-preserving-smoothing filter
body: The Amira 3D Edge-Preserving Smoothing Filter is a smoothing method applied to 3D grayscale image stacks to reduce noise while preventing edge blurring. It addresses the limitation of linear Gaussian smoothing by varying the convolution kernel dynamically based on local image content to smooth regions while preserving boundaries. Unlike the parent Gaussian Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction which uses a fixed kernel, this method adapts to local intensity variations. Inputs: A 3D grayscale image stack. Outputs: A smoothed 3D image stack. Data Structures: The volume is processed as a 3D array of intensity values. Parameters: Contrast threshold C = 3.5. Smoothing sigma \sigma = 3. Step size S = 5. Stop threshold T = 25. Algorithm: 1. Apply the filter to the input image stack. 2. Iterate up to the stop threshold, varying the convolution kernel dynamically based on local image content to smooth regions while preventing edge blurring. 3. The sigma \sigma controls the base spread of the smoothing kernel. 4. The contrast threshold C determines the sensitivity to intensity differences for edge preservation. 5. The step size S and stop threshold T control the iteration progression and termination. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def amiraedgepreservingsmooth(volume, contrastthreshold=3.5, sigma=3.0, stepsize=5, stopthreshold=25): """ Applies the Amira 3D Edge-Preserving Smoothing Filter. """ import numpy as np from scipy.signal import fftconvolve currentvol = volume.copy() for k in range(stopthreshold): # The source states the filter varies the convolution kernel dynamically based on local image content. # The exact mathematical formulation for how the kernel varies is not provided in the sources. # Standard practice computes local intensity differences to modulate the kernel. localdiff = np.abs(np.gradient(currentvol, axis=0)) + \ np.abs(np.gradient(currentvol, axis=1)) + \ np.abs(np.gradient(currentvol, axis=2)) # Generate adaptive kernel: base spread controlled by sigma, edge preservation by contrastthreshold. # The exact kernel generation formula is not provided in the sources. kernel = np.exp(-(np.arange(-3, 4)2 + np.arange(-3, 4)[:, None]2 + np.arange(-3, 4)[:, None, None]2) / (2.0 sigma2)) kernel = kernel / kernel.sum() # Apply 3D convolution to smooth the volume. padsize = kernel.shape[0] // 2 paddedvol = np.pad(currentvol, padsize, mode='reflect') currentvol = fftconvolve(paddedvol, kernel, mode='valid') # The stepsize parameter is not given a specific algorithmic role in the sources. return currentvol Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary conditions: The source does not specify boundary handling; reflection padding is typical. Precision: Floating-point arithmetic is required to maintain intensity gradients accurately. Degenerate input: Uniform regions will be smoothed heavily; sharp edges will be preserved based on the contrast threshold. If the contrast threshold is too low, edges may be blurred. A linear smoothing method applied to 3D grayscale image stacks. It performs a three-dimensional convolution with a Gaussian kernel to smooth structures and interpolate borders in less-stretched sections based on neighboring gray values. It is used for general smoothing and balancing inhomogeneous stretching. Parameters: Kernel dimensions 3 \times 3 \times 3 (or 6 \times 6 \times 6 in some contexts) and standard deviation \sigma = (1, 1, 1) along the three spatial axes. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves sharp edges and boundaries while reducing noise in homogeneous regions. Limitations: Requires parameter tuning (contrast, sigma, step, stop) for optimal results. When to use: When edge preservation is critical for biological image stacks. When not to use: When uniform smoothing is sufficient and edge preservation is not required. The method is part of the Amira 3D software package (specifically Amira 4.1). It was applied to volume rendering from serial sections of biological specimens, such as Cristatella mucedo and Phoronis australis. It was used to smooth aligned image stacks before rendering, particularly for colored stacks based on paraffin wax sections where pre-rendering procedures were complex. name: Constrained Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction
head: Lempitsky CVPR10 smoothing
body: Constrained smoothing is a method to smooth the 0.5 level-set of binary volumes to improve mesh quality while preserving fine details, implemented via constrained optimization of a discrete Laplacian energy. It sets itself apart from Gaussian smoothing by enforcing hard constraints on the signed distance values to prevent the erosion of thin structures and fine details, at the cost of higher computational complexity and memory usage. Inputs: A binary volume array binaryarray (values 0 or 1). Outputs: A smoothed signed distance function (SDF) array distance of the same shape, where the 0.5 isosurface approximates the smoothed boundary. Data Structures: 1. Distance Array: A dense array of floats, same shape as input. 2. Band Indices: A list of 3D coordinates (i, j, k) where the optimization variables reside. 3. Filter Matrix (filterq): A sparse matrix representing the discrete Laplacian operator squared (L^T L), constructed only for band variables. 4. Optimization Vector (x): A 1D array of floats storing the SDF values for the band cells. Parameters: bandradius: Radius of the band around the level-set. Default: 4. maxiters: Maximum number of Jacobi iterations. Default: 500. reltol: Relative tolerance for stopping criterion. Default: 10^{-6}. weight: Jacobi relaxation weight. Default: 0.5. Steps: 1. Compute Signed Distance Function (SDF): Calculate the Euclidean distance transform for the binary array. Let distfunc(arr) be the distance transform of arr. \text{distance} = \begin{cases} \text{dist\func}(\text{binary\array}) - 0.5 & \text{if } \text{binary\array} == 1 \\ -\text{dist\func}(1 - \text{binary\array}) + 0.5 & \text{if } \text{binary\array} == 0 \end{cases} 2. Define Band and Border: Identify the optimization band as cells where |\text{distance}| \le \text{band\radius}. The border is implicitly handled by the constraints (cells where |\text{distance}| < 1 are clamped). 3. Build Filter Matrix (filterq): Construct a sparse matrix representing the discrete Laplacian energy on the band variables. For 3D, iterate over valid band indices. For each cell, the matrix row corresponds to the Laplacian operator. The diagonal is initialized to -2 for each axis, adding 1 for existing neighbors, and adding 1 to the diagonal for out-of-bounds neighbors (effectively treating out-of-bounds as fixed boundaries). The final matrix is Q = L^T L. 4. Initialize Variables: Set the optimization vector x to the SDF values of the band cells: x = \text{distance}[\text{band}]. 5. Set Hard Constraints: Define upper and lower bounds for each variable to preserve the sign and magnitude near the surface: upperbound: x where x < 0, else \infty. Clamped to 0 if |\text{upper\bound}| < 1. lowerbound: x where x > 0, else -\infty. Clamped to 0 if |\text{lower\bound}| < 1. 6. Iterative Optimization (Jacobi): Minimize energy E = \frac{1}{2} x^T Q x using Jacobi iteration with relaxation. Compute Jacobi preconditioner components: D^{-1} = \text{diag}(Q)^{-1} and R = D^{-1} - Q (off-diagonal part). Update: x{new} = \text{weight} \cdot (-D^{-1} R x) + (1 - \text{weight}) \cdot x. Apply constraints: x = \max(x, \text{lower\bound}) and x = \min(x, \text{upper\bound}). Check stopping criterion every 10 iterations: if relative energy improvement < 1 - (1 - \text{rel\tol})^{10}, stop. 7. Write Back: Update the distance array with the optimized x values at the band indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy import ndimage, sparse def constrainedsmoothing(binaryarray, bandradius=4, maxiters=500, reltol=1e-6, weight=0.5): """ Smooths the 0.5 level-set of a binary volume using constrained Laplacian optimization. """ # Step 1: Compute Signed Distance Function # distfunc computes Euclidean distance transform distpos = ndimage.distancetransformedt(binaryarray) distneg = ndimage.distancetransformedt(1 - binaryarray) distance = np.where(binaryarray, distpos - 0.5, -distneg + 0.5) # Step 2: Define Band bandmask = np.abs(distance) <= bandradius bandindices = np.argwhere(bandmask) numvars = len(bandindices) if numvars == 0: return distance # Step 3: Build Filter Matrix (L^T L) # Create a mapping from band index to variable index varmap = np.full(binaryarray.shape, -1, dtype=int) for idx, (i, j, k) in enumerate(bandindices): varmap[i, j, k] = idx # Pad for neighbor access paddedmap = np.pad(varmap, 1, mode='constant', constantvalues=-1) # Construct sparse matrix Q = L^T L # We build L first, then compute Q. # L is a sparse matrix where each row corresponds to a Laplacian stencil. # For 3D, each cell has 3 rows in L (one per axis). rows = [] cols = [] vals = [] # Iterate over band cells to build L # L[i, j] represents the contribution of variable j to the i-th Laplacian equation # There are 3 equations per cell (x, y, z derivatives) eqidx = 0 for i, j, k in bandindices: # X-axis neighbors # Diagonal: -2 (for 3D, -1 per axis? No, standard Laplacian is sum(neighbors) - degreecenter) # The source code sets diagonal to -2 for each axis check? # Source: filterq[3count, count] = -2. Then adds 1 for neighbors. # This implies the stencil is: -2 center + 1 left + 1 right. # This is a 1D Laplacian component. # X-axis rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(-2.0) # Left neighbor ni, nj, nk = i-1, j, k if paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] >= 0: # +1 because of padding neighborvar = paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(neighborvar) vals.append(1.0) else: # Out of bounds: adds to diagonal rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(1.0) # Right neighbor ni, nj, nk = i+1, j, k if paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] >= 0: neighborvar = paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(neighborvar) vals.append(1.0) else: rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(1.0) eqidx += 1 # Y-axis rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(-2.0) ni, nj, nk = i, j-1, k if paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] >= 0: neighborvar = paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(neighborvar) vals.append(1.0) else: rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(1.0) ni, nj, nk = i, j+1, k if paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] >= 0: neighborvar = paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(neighborvar) vals.append(1.0) else: rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(1.0) eqidx += 1 # Z-axis rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(-2.0) ni, nj, nk = i, j, k-1 if paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] >= 0: neighborvar = paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(neighborvar) vals.append(1.0) else: rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(1.0) ni, nj, nk = i, j, k+1 if paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] >= 0: neighborvar = paddedmap[ni+1, nj+1, nk+1] rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(neighborvar) vals.append(1.0) else: rows.append(eqidx) cols.append(varmap[i, j, k]) vals.append(1.0) eqidx += 1 L = sparse.csrmatrix((vals, (rows, cols)), shape=(3 numvars, numvars)) Q = L.T.dot(L) # Step 4: Initialize Variables x = distance[bandmask] # Step 5: Set Constraints upperbound = np.where(x < 0, x, np.inf) lowerbound = np.where(x > 0, x, -np.inf) # Clamp bounds if close to 0 upperbound = np.where(np.abs(upperbound) < 1, 0, upperbound) lowerbound = np.where(np.abs(lowerbound) < 1, 0, lowerbound) # Step 6: Jacobi Iteration # Precompute Jacobi components diag = Q.diagonal() jacobid = 1.0 / diag jacobir = Q.copy() jacobir.setdiag(0) jacobir = jacobir.tocsr() energynow = np.dot(x, Q.dot(x)) / 2.0 checkeach = 10 cumreltol = 1 - (1 - reltol)checkeach for i in range(maxiters): # Jacobi update: xnew = D^-1 (b - R x) where b=0 for homogeneous energy minimization? # Source: x1 = - jacobid jacobir.dot(x) # This corresponds to minimizing 0.5 x^T Q x. Gradient is Qx. # Jacobi step for Ax=b is x = D^-1 (b - (L+U)x). Here b=0. # So xnew = - D^-1 (Q - D) x = - D^-1 R x. x1 = - jacobid jacobir.dot(x) x = weight x1 + (1 - weight) x # Apply constraints x = np.maximum(x, lowerbound) x = np.minimum(x, upperbound) if (i + 1) % checkeach == 0: energybefore = energynow energynow = np.dot(x, Q.dot(x)) / 2.0 if energybefore == 0: break relimprovement = (energybefore - energynow) / energybefore if relimprovement < cumreltol: break # Step 7: Write Back distance[bandmask] = x return distance A mesh smoothing technique that reduces noise by moving vertices toward the average of neighbors. It is an isotropic filter that does not explicitly preserve sharp features and can oversmooth edges. Choose it for post-processing meshes where feature preservation is not critical. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of band cells and Jacobi iterations. Each iteration involves sparse matrix-vector multiplication. Convergence is linear with the relaxation weight. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of band cells and the sparsity of the Laplacian matrix. The matrix Q is sparse but larger than the original volume if the band is wide. Performance: Slower than Gaussian smoothing. Recommended for arrays smaller than (500, 500, 500). Strengths: Preserves fine details and thin structures that are often eroded by Gaussian smoothing. Limitations: Higher computational cost and memory usage. Sensitive to the bandradius parameter. When to use: When mesh quality is critical and fine details must be preserved, and the volume size is manageable. When not to use: For very large volumes or real-time applications where speed is paramount. The method is based on "Surface Extraction from Binary Volumes with Higher-Order Smoothness" by Victor Lempitsky, presented at CVPR 2010. It addresses the limitation of standard marching cubes which produces jagged surfaces from binary volumes, by providing a smooth signed distance field that respects the original topology. pmneila/PyMCubes, https://github.com/pmneila/PyMCubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Laplacian Smoothing
head: Isotropic spatial filter, Laplacian Relaxation, Laplacian Smooth
body: Laplacian Smoothing is a mesh smoothing technique that reduces geometric noise and jaggedness (such as the stairstepping artifact in isosurfaces) by moving each vertex toward the average position of its immediate neighbors. In gradient-based methods, it acts as an isotropic spatial filter applied to gradients. Unlike edge-aware filters, it does not explicitly preserve sharp features and may oversmooth edges if applied excessively. Inputs: A mesh defined by a list of vertices V and a list of triangles T. Outputs: A smoothed mesh with updated vertex positions V'. Data Structures: vertices: Array of 3D vectors [x, y, z]. triangles: Array of triplets of vertex indices [i, j, k]. neighbors: Adjacency list where neighbors[i] contains the unique indices of vertices connected to vertex i by an edge. Parameters: smoothIter (or postSmooth): Number of smoothing iterations. Default is 0 (no smoothing). alpha and beta: Smoothing parameters. Fixed at 0.1 and 0.5 respectively in some implementations. weight (blend factor): The fraction of the neighbor average to apply. In the conservative variant, this is 0.4 for the average and 0.6 for the original position. boundaryflag: Boolean flag controlling boundary handling or normalization during smoothing. Steps: 1. Build Adjacency List: Iterate through all triangles. For each triangle with vertex indices a, b, c, add bidirectional edges between (a,b), (b,c), and (c,a) to the adjacency list. Ensure no duplicate neighbors are added for each vertex. 2. Iterative Smoothing: For smoothIter iterations: a. Store current vertex positions in oldpos. b. For each vertex i: i. If neighbors[i] is empty, skip vertex i to prevent division by zero. ii. Compute the average position of neighbors: \text{avg}i = \frac{1}{|Ni|} \sum{j \in Ni} \text{old\pos}j where Ni is the set of neighbors of vertex i, and |Ni| is the count of neighbors. iii. Update the vertex position using a weighted blend: \text{new\pos}i = (1 - w) \cdot \text{old\pos}i + w \cdot \text{avg}i where w is the smoothing weight (e.g., 0.4). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def laplaciansmooth(vertices, triangles, smoothiter=1, weight=0.4, boundaryflag=True): # 1. Build adjacency list neighbors = [[] for in range(len(vertices))] for tri in triangles: a, b, c = tri for u, v in [(a, b), (b, a), (b, c), (c, b), (c, a), (a, c)]: if v not in neighbors[u]: neighbors[u].append(v) # 2. Iterative smoothing for in range(smoothiter): oldpos = [[v[0], v[1], v[2]] for v in vertices] for i in range(len(vertices)): if not neighbors[i]: continue # Skip isolated vertices # Calculate average of neighbors avg = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] count = len(neighbors[i]) for j in neighbors[i]: for k in range(3): avg[k] += oldpos[j][k] for k in range(3): avg[k] /= count # Update position with weighted blend for k in range(3): vertices[i][k] = (1.0 - weight) oldpos[i][k] + weight avg[k] return vertices A variant that uses a weighted blend (e.g., 60% original, 40% neighbor average) instead of fully replacing the vertex position with the average. This reduces the convergence rate and prevents excessive shrinkage or drift, making it suitable for preserving overall volume while reducing noise. A technique that balances internal Laplacian smoothing forces with external volume-adaptive forces to reconstruct piecewise linear material interfaces from volume fraction data. Unlike standard Laplacian Smoothing, which only reduces noise, this method adaptively pushes the interface to match known material volumes, preventing the shrinkage artifact inherent in pure Laplacian smoothing. It is chosen for multi-material junctions in VOF simulations where traditional methods fail due to manifold constraints. A mesh smoothing technique that strictly bounds positional error by constraining vertex movement to the dual-grid cell of origin. It differs from standard Laplacian smoothing by preventing the mesh from drifting arbitrarily far from the extracted topology. It serves as the primary smoothing step for the SurfaceNet extraction method, addressing jaggedness in non-manifold mesh extraction from multi-material volumes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective at removing high-frequency noise and jaggedness from isosurfaces; isotropic smoothing promotes smooth gradients. Limitations: Oversmooths sharp edges and features; converges slowly near edges for piecewise smooth targets; does not preserve volume or topology strictly without constraints. When to use: When the primary goal is noise reduction on smooth surfaces and edge preservation is not critical. When not to use: When sharp features must be preserved (use edge-aware filters). Laplacian smoothing has been applied to gradients in inverse rendering as a preconditioner of the form (I + \lambda L)^{-1}, where L is the Laplacian matrix. It is well-known that this operation acts as an isotropic spatial filter, related to the solution of the screened Poisson equation. In mesh processing, it is a standard technique for reducing jaggedness in extracted surfaces. Variants like the cotangent Laplacian have been explored for micro-mesh construction but offer limited benefits in standard inverse rendering. neurolabusc/nii2mesh, https://github.com/neurolabusc/nii2mesh, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3680528.3687606, fetched 2026-10-29 TRTUZ8/TRTUZ8.github.io, https://github.com/TRTUZ8/TRTUZ8.github.io, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) elyssov/prometheus-engine, https://github.com/elyssov/prometheus-engine, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Volume-Adaptive Active Interface Model
head: Active Contour Model for Volume Fractions, Adaptive Laplacian Smoothing with Volume Constraints
body: The Volume-Adaptive Active Interface Model is a mesh smoothing technique that reconstructs piecewise linear material interfaces from volume fraction data by iteratively balancing internal Laplacian smoothing forces with external volume-adaptive forces. It solves the problem of accurately representing multi-material junctions and complex topologies in volume-of-fluid (VOF) or embedded boundary simulations, where traditional methods like Piecewise Linear Interface Calculation (PLIC) fail due to manifold binary segmentation constraints. Unlike its parent Laplacian Smoothing, which only reduces noise, this method adaptively pushes the interface to match known material volumes, preventing the shrinkage artifact inherent in pure Laplacian smoothing. The method operates on a control point mesh defining the interface within a background grid of volume fraction data. It iteratively updates control point positions to minimize the discrepancy between reconstructed and known material volumes while maintaining surface smoothness. Inputs: A set of control points P = \{pi\} defining the piecewise linear interface (edges in 2D, triangles in 3D). Volume fraction data for M materials in a background grid. Parameters: \alpha (internal force weight), \beta (external force weight), \sigma (subdivision threshold). Outputs: Updated control point positions P' representing the reconstructed interface. Updated reconstruction error \epsilon for each material in each cell. Control Point: Stores 3D position pi. Neighbor List: For each pi, a list of indices of neighboring control points (1-ring). Face Material Marking: Each face f in the mesh is marked with the material ID A it bounds or separates. In multi-material junctions, faces surrounding pi may be associated with different materials. Volume Error: \epsilon(c, A), the signed difference between the known volume fraction of material A in cell c and the reconstructed volume. 1. Compute Internal Force: For each control point pi, calculate the average position d of its neighbors in the 1-ring. The internal force is: F{int} = d - pi This force acts to smooth the surface. 2. Compute External Force: For each material A present in the neighborhood of pi: Identify the set of faces RA surrounding pi that are marked with material A. Calculate the sum of normals \sum{f \in RA} \perpA(f), where \perpA(f) is the normal of face f oriented into material A. Compute the external force for material A: F{ext}(A) = \epsilon(c, A) \sum{f \in RA} \perpA(f) If \epsilon(c, A) > 0, material A has too much volume, and the force pushes the interface to reduce it. If \epsilon(c, A) < 0, the force pushes to increase it. 3. Select Material: To handle multi-material junctions stochastically, select a single material \xi randomly from the materials present in the neighborhood of pi. 4. Compute Total Force: Combine the internal and selected external forces: F = \alpha F{int} + \beta F{ext}(\xi) where \alpha and \beta are weighting parameters. 5. Update Position: Move the control point: p'i = pi + F 6. Update Volume Error: Incrementally update \epsilon by calculating the oriented volume swept by the 1-ring of pi as it moves to p'i. In 2D, line segments sweep to triangles. In 3D, triangles sweep to tetrahedra. Clip these swept volumes against the local mesh cells. Use the oriented volume of the clipped swept regions to update \epsilon for the relevant materials and cells. 7. Subdivision: If any face size exceeds the threshold \sigma (max line segment length in 2D, max triangle area in 3D), subdivide the face to maintain resolution. 8. Convergence: Decrease \alpha and \beta monotonically (e.g., proportional to the change in error) until convergence. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeadaptiveactiveinterfacemodel(controlpoints, volumefractions, alpha, beta, sigma, maxiterations): """ Reconstructs piecewise linear material interfaces from volume fraction data. Args: controlpoints: List of control point objects with position pi and neighbor indices. volumefractions: Grid of volume fractions for M materials. alpha: Weight for internal smoothing force. beta: Weight for external volume-adaptive force. sigma: Threshold for face subdivision (max length/area). maxiterations: Maximum number of iterations. Returns: Updated controlpoints. """ # Initialize reconstruction error epsilon for each cell and material epsilon = computeinitialvolumeerrors(controlpoints, volumefractions) for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Decrease weights monotonically based on error change alpha, beta = adjustweights(alpha, beta, epsilon) for pi in controlpoints: # 1. Compute Internal Force neighbors = getneighbors(pi) if not neighbors: continue d = averageposition(neighbors) Fint = d - pi.position # 2. Identify materials in neighborhood materialsinneighborhood = getmaterialsaround(pi, volumefractions) if not materialsinneighborhood: continue # 3. Select one material randomly xi = random.choice(materialsinneighborhood) # 4. Compute External Force for selected material Rxi = getfacesaround(pi, material=xi) sumnormals = sum(facenormal(f, material=xi) for f in Rxi) epsiloncxi = epsilon[pi.cellid][xi] Fext = epsiloncxi sumnormals # 5. Compute Total Force F = alpha Fint + beta Fext # 6. Update Position pi.position += F # 7. Update Volume Error Incrementally sweptvolumes = computesweptvolumes(pi, pi.position) # Old pos to new pos updateepsilon(epsilon, sweptvolumes, pi.cellid) # 8. Subdivision subdividefaces(controlpoints, sigma) if isconverged(epsilon, alpha, beta): break return controlpoints def computeinitialvolumeerrors(controlpoints, volumefractions): """ Computes the initial signed error between known and reconstructed volumes. Implementation detail: Iterate over all cells, compute volume of material regions defined by the initial mesh, and subtract from known volume fractions. """ epsilon = {} for cell in volumefractions.cells: epsilon[cell.id] = {} for material in volumefractions.materials: knownvol = volumefractions[cell.id][material] reconstructedvol = computereconstructedvolume(cell, controlpoints, material) epsilon[cell.id][material] = knownvol - reconstructedvol return epsilon def computesweptvolumes(pi, newpos): """ Computes the oriented volume swept by the 1-ring of pi moving to newpos. In 2D, sweep edges to triangles. In 3D, sweep triangles to tetrahedra. Return a map of (cellid, material) -> orientedvolume. """ swept = {} neighbors = getneighbors(pi) if is2d(): for edge in getedgesaround(pi, neighbors): triangle = sweepedgetotriangle(edge, pi.position, newpos) clipandaccumulate(swept, triangle) else: for face in getfacesaround(pi, neighbors): tet = sweepfacetotetrahedron(face, pi.position, newpos) clipandaccumulate(swept, tet) return swept def clipandaccumulate(swept, sweptgeom): """ Clips swept geometry against local mesh cells and accumulates oriented volume. For each cell intersecting sweptgeom, compute intersection volume. Add to swept[cellid][material] based on material orientation. """ for cell in intersectingcells(sweptgeom): vol = orientedvolumeofintersection(sweptgeom, cell) material = getmaterialforintersection(sweptgeom, cell) if material is not None: swept[cell.id][material] += vol \alpha: Weighting of the internal force. Typically set proportional to \beta and monotonically decreased relative to the change in error until convergence. \beta: Weighting of the external force. Decreased monotonically alongside \alpha. \sigma: Threshold parameter controlling maximum surface face size (max line segment length in 2D, max triangle area in 3D). Large values disable subdivision. Shrinkage: Laplacian smoothing tends to shrink curves. This is counter-balanced by the external force, which adaptively pushes the interface to match volume fractions rather than just increasing volume. Multi-material Junctions: The stochastic selection of a single material \xi per iteration handles complex junctions where multiple volumetric forces would otherwise conflict. Precision: Incremental volume updates are used for speed, but clipping swept volumes against local mesh cells is required for accuracy. Discrete Multi-Material Interface Reconstruction (MIR) is a method to reconstruct piecewise linear material interfaces from volume fraction data by discretizing cells into subcells, labeling them with material IDs, and optimizing the labeling to minimize interface energy while preserving volume fractions. It improves upon the Volume-Adaptive Active Interface Model by producing interfaces that are continuous across cell boundaries and suitable for visualization, whereas the parent model and alternatives like Piecewise Linear Interface Calculation (PLIC) are discontinuous across cell boundaries. Unlike PLIC, which is ambiguous for three or more materials due to the ordering of its binary segmentations, MIR explicitly handles n-material problems through a discrete labeling optimization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The incremental update of volume errors is noted as much faster than recomputing the entire volume each update. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the 2D 'A' letter dataset (202 cells, 17.5% mixed), the method achieved an average mixed cell error of 0.3924%. On the 2D 4-material junction dataset (7 cells, 42.86% mixed), the method achieved an average mixed cell error of 0.0043%. On the SF Bay bathymetry dataset (2582x10 grid, 6.13% mixed), the method achieved 0.7640% error per mixed cell, compared to 43.8410% for Meredith's method. On the Swirler dataset (128^3 grid, lower 64^3 octant), the rule-based marching method generated topology for 71% of mixed cells, while the discrete boundary method handled the swirler blades and central screen. Strengths: Handles multi-material junctions and complex topologies better than PLIC; captures volume accuracy and smoothness better than Meredith's method; captures fine details like swirler blades. Limitations: Stochastic selection may lead to non-deterministic results; requires careful tuning of \alpha and \beta; subdivision may be needed for large faces. When to use: When accurate volume preservation and smooth interfaces are required for multi-material VOF or embedded boundary simulations, especially in the presence of complex junctions. When not to use: When deterministic topology generation is strictly required without stochastic elements; when computational speed is critical and incremental volume updates are too slow for the specific hardware. The Volume-Adaptive Active Interface Model was developed as part of research into scientific visualization techniques for volume fraction data and function fields. It builds on the concept of active contour models (snakes) and Laplacian smoothing, adapting them to the specific constraints of volume fraction data in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and embedded boundary methods. The method was compared against PLIC, Meredith's method, and rule-based marching methods on various synthetic and real-world datasets, including VOF simulations of rising bubbles and low-swirl burners. name: Discrete Multi-Material Interface Reconstruction
head: Potts-model Interface Reconstruction, Subcell Labeling for Material Interfaces, Discrete Volume Fraction Labeling, MIR (Material Interface Reconstruction) labeling, Volume Fraction Labeling via Potts Model Optimization
body: Discrete Multi-Material Interface Reconstruction (MIR) is a method to reconstruct piecewise linear material interfaces from volume fraction data by discretizing cells into subcells, labeling them with material IDs, and optimizing the labeling to minimize interface energy while preserving volume fractions. It improves upon the Volume-Adaptive Active Interface Model by producing interfaces that are continuous across cell boundaries and suitable for visualization, whereas the parent model and alternatives like Piecewise Linear Interface Calculation (PLIC) are discontinuous across cell boundaries. Unlike PLIC, which is ambiguous for three or more materials due to the ordering of its binary segmentations, MIR explicitly handles n-material problems through a discrete labeling optimization. Inputs: A grid of cells C. For each cell c \in C, a tuple of volume fractions Vc = (v1, \dots, vn), where vi \ge 0 and \sum{i=1}^n vi = 1. Pure cells have one vi=1 and others 0; mixed cells have multiple non-zero vi. Number of materials n. Subdivision rate R (defining subcells per cell S = R^d for dimension d). Annealing temperature T. Outputs: A labeling f of the discretization D, where each subcell is assigned a material ID fx \in \{1, \dots, n\}. Optionally, a smoothed field or surface mesh extracted from f. Data Structures: Discretization D: A set of subcells. Only mixed cells are subdivided to save memory. Subcell Layout: Each subcell x stores its label fx. In 3D, with subdivision rate R, there are S = R^3 subcells per cell. Volume Fraction Storage: For each mixed cell, store Vc. Pure cells do not require subdivision or storage of subcell labels. Parameters: S: Number of subcells per cell. S = R^d. Typical R \in [5, 10]. T: Annealing temperature. Set to a low constant 0.25. N: Neighborhood. Directly incident subcells (8 neighbors in 2D, 26 in 3D). W{x,y}: Weighting function. Inverse magnitude of the offset between subcells x and y. Algorithm: 1. Discretize: For each mixed cell c \in C, divide it into S subcells of uniform fractional volume dA = 1/S. Form the discretization D. 2. Initialize Labeling: For each mixed cell c, assign initial labels to its subcells such that for each material i, there are approximately ki = \lfloor vi / dA \rfloor or \lceil vi / dA \rceil subcells with label i. The total number of subcells with label i must sum to the integer count closest to vi/dA while preserving the total volume constraint within the cell. Specifically, ensure \sum{x \in c} \delta(fx = i) \approx vi / dA. Randomly assign labels among subcells to satisfy these counts. 3. Optimize via Simulated Annealing: Repeat until convergence or time limit: Select a mixed cell c at random. Select two distinct subcells x, y within c at random. Calculate the energy change \Delta E resulting from swapping labels fx and fy. Accept the swap with probability P: P = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \Delta E < 0 \\ e^{-\Delta E / T} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} If accepted, update fx \leftrightarrow fy. 4. Post-Processing (Optional): Apply a narrow Gaussian kernel to the labeling field f to smooth interfaces for visualization. Extract surfaces using multi-material segmentation algorithms (e.g., multi-label Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring) on the smoothed field. Formulas: Subcell Volume: dA = 1/S. Local Potts-Model Energy: The energy at subcell x is: Ex(f) = \sum{y \in N} W{x,y} \cdot \delta(fx \neq fy) where \delta is the Kronecker delta (1 if true, 0 if false), N is the neighborhood of x, and W{x,y} is the weight. Total Energy: E(f) = \sum{x \in D} Ex(f) Energy Change for Swap: Let f' be the labeling after swapping labels of x and y. The energy change is: \Delta E = E{x,y}(f') - E{x,y}(f) where E{x,y}(f) = Ex(f) + Ey(f) is the initial energy of the pair. Note: Only neighbors of x and y contribute to the change in Ex and Ey. Volume Error Bound: The upper bound on per-cell error \epsilon(c) is: \epsilon(c) \le \begin{cases} (n-1)dA & \text{if } c \text{ is mixed} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def calculatepotentialenergy(subcell, labeling, neighborhood, weights): """ Calculates the local Potts-model energy for a single subcell. """ energy = 0.0 labelx = labeling[subcell] for neighbor in neighborhood[subcell]: labely = labeling[neighbor] if labelx != labely: energy += weights[(subcell, neighbor)] return energy def optimizemir(cells, volumefractions, R, T, maxtimeseconds): """ Optimizes the subcell labeling using simulated annealing. Args: cells: List of cell objects. Each has 'ismixed' flag and 'volumefractions' (list of n floats). R: Subdivision rate. S = R^d. T: Annealing temperature. maxtimeseconds: Time limit for optimization. Returns: labeling: Dictionary mapping subcellid -> materialid. """ # Determine dimension d from cell geometry (e.g., 2 or 3) d = cells[0].dimension S = R d dA = 1.0 / S # Data structures # subcellid is unique identifier for each subcell in mixed cells # labeling maps subcellid -> materialid (1..n) labeling = {} # Precompute neighborhoods and weights for mixed cells # This assumes a grid structure where neighbors are known neighborhood = {} weights = {} starttime = time.time() for cell in cells: if not cell.ismixed: continue # 1. Discretize and Initialize cellsubcells = generatesubcells(cell, S) # Returns list of subcellids nmaterials = len(cell.volumefractions) # Calculate target counts for each material # Counti = round(vi / dA) or floor/ceil to sum to S targetcounts = [] remainingvolume = 1.0 for i in range(nmaterials): vi = cell.volumefractions[i] # Approximate count count = int(round(vi / dA)) targetcounts.append(count) # Adjust counts to ensure sum is exactly S currentsum = sum(targetcounts) diff = S - currentsum # Distribute the difference to materials with largest fractional parts # (Simple greedy adjustment) if diff != 0: # Sort materials by fractional part of vi/dA fractionalparts = [(vi/dA - int(vi/dA), i) for i, vi in enumerate(cell.volumefractions)] fractionalparts.sort(reverse=(diff > 0)) for k in range(abs(diff)): idx = fractionalparts[k][1] if diff > 0: targetcounts[idx] += 1 else: targetcounts[idx] -= 1 # Assign labels randomly to subcells respecting targetcounts labelslist = [] for matid, count in enumerate(targetcounts, start=1): labelslist.extend([matid] count) random.shuffle(labelslist) for subcellid, matid in zip(cellsubcells, labelslist): labeling[subcellid] = matid # Precompute neighborhood and weights for these subcells for subcellid in cellsubcells: neighbors = getdirectlyincidentneighbors(subcellid, cellsubcells) neighborhood[subcellid] = neighbors for neighbor in neighbors: offset = getoffset(subcellid, neighbor) w = 1.0 / math.sqrt(sum(o2 for o in offset)) weights[(subcellid, neighbor)] = w weights[(neighbor, subcellid)] = w # 2. Optimization Loop while time.time() - starttime < maxtimeseconds: # Pick a random mixed cell mixedcells = [c for c in cells if c.ismixed] if not mixedcells: break cell = random.choice(mixedcells) cellsubcells = getsubcellsforcell(cell) if len(cellsubcells) < 2: continue # Pick two distinct subcells x, y = random.sample(cellsubcells, 2) # Calculate energy change # We need the current energy of x and y exold = calculatepotentialenergy(x, labeling, neighborhood, weights) eyold = calculatepotentialenergy(y, labeling, neighborhood, weights) Eold = exold + eyold # Swap labels labeling[x], labeling[y] = labeling[y], labeling[x] # Calculate new energy exnew = calculatepotentialenergy(x, labeling, neighborhood, weights) eynew = calculatepotentialenergy(y, labeling, neighborhood, weights) Enew = exnew + eynew deltaE = Enew - Eold # Accept or reject if deltaE < 0: pass # Accept else: if random.random() < math.exp(-deltaE / T): pass # Accept else: # Reject: swap back labeling[x], labeling[y] = labeling[y], labeling[x] return labeling def extractsurface(labeling, cells, R): """ Extracts surface mesh from labeling. Option 1: Extract co-incident faces between adjacent subcells with different labels. Option 2: Smooth labeling with Gaussian kernel, then use multi-label Marching Cubes. """ # Implementation depends on specific meshing library pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Boundaries: Extracting interfaces by identifying co-incident faces between adjacent subcells with different labels can result in unpleasant, sharp boundaries at the sub-cell scale. Smoothing the labeling field with a narrow Gaussian kernel before extraction is recommended. Volume Conservation: Graph cuts cannot be used because their optimization moves do not conserve volume. The swap-based simulated annealing ensures volume conservation. Pure Cells: Pure cells do not require subdivision or optimization, reducing memory usage significantly (by ~90% in sparse datasets). Convergence: Optimization for longer than 10 seconds per timestep often does not significantly improve results for complex cases, though brief optimization smooths interfaces. Time Complexity: Optimization is not cheap. Simulated annealing convergence time depends on the subdivision rate R and the complexity of the interface. Higher R lowers error but increases convergence time. In practice, 10 seconds per timestep is often sufficient. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of mixed cells and the subdivision rate S. By only subdividing mixed cells, memory can be reduced by approximately 90% in datasets where mixed cells constitute less than 6% of the total. Accuracy: The upper bound on per-cell volume error is \epsilon(c) \le (n-1)dA for mixed cells. For a 3D 2-material problem, the error is 0.8% with R=5 (S=125) and 0.1% with R=10 (S=1000). Strengths: Produces continuous interfaces across cell boundaries; suitable for visualization; handles n-materials; volume conservation with bounded error; easily parallelized. Limitations: Computationally expensive compared to PLIC; sharp artifacts if not smoothed; requires careful tuning of R and T (though T=0.25 is robust). When to Use: When visualizing material regions or extracting smooth, continuous surface meshes from volume fraction data is required, especially for n \ge 3 materials where PLIC is ambiguous. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and PLIC's discontinuity is acceptable; when volume conservation must be exact (not bounded error). Discrete Multi-Material Interface Reconstruction was introduced as a reinterpretation of MIR as a segmentation problem over a discretization of the problem’s original spatial domain. It builds on the Potts-model energy metric, widely used in interface problems from studying cellular structures to interpolating region boundaries between segmented images. The method was developed to address the limitations of PLIC, which is discontinuous across cell boundaries and ambiguous for three or more materials. It was tested on 2D and 3D fluid flow datasets, including bubble simulations and multi-fluid cylinder interactions. name: Constrained Laplacian Fairing
head: Constrained fairing, Dual-grid constrained smoothing
body: Constrained Laplacian Fairing is a mesh smoothing technique for isosurfaces extracted from segmented volumes, specifically designed to reduce geometric noise while strictly bounding positional error relative to the source grid. It differs from standard Laplacian smoothing by constraining vertex movement to the dual-grid cell of origin, preventing the mesh from drifting arbitrarily far from the extracted topology. It serves as the primary smoothing step for the SurfaceNet extraction method, addressing the jaggedness inherent in non-manifold mesh extraction from multi-material volumes. The method operates on a mesh composed of quadrilateral faces, where most vertices have valences between three and six. The algorithm proceeds in two main phases: an unconstrained centroid-based averaging pass, followed by a constrained relaxation pass. Input: A mesh M extracted from a volumetric grid. Each vertex v is associated with an initial dual-grid cell Cv (the voxel in which the vertex was created). The mesh topology is defined by face connectivity. Output: A smoothed mesh M' where vertex positions are updated. Mesh: Defined by a list of vertices and a list of faces. Each face is defined by an ordered list of vertex indices. Dual-Grid Mapping: A mapping from each vertex index to its initial grid cell coordinates (x, y, z). This is required to enforce the constraint. 1. Compute Face Centroids: For every face f in the mesh, compute its centroid cf. If a face has vertices v1, v2, \dots, vk, the centroid is: cf = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^{k} vi For quadrilateral faces (k=4), this is the arithmetic mean of the four vertex positions. 2. Compute Unconstrained Vertex Updates: For every vertex v, compute a new position v{new} as the centroid of the centroids of all incident faces. To avoid storing explicit vertex-to-face adjacency lists, traverse the faces: Initialize a sum vector S = \mathbf{0} and a counter N = 0. For each face f in the mesh: If v is a vertex of f: S \leftarrow S + cf N \leftarrow N + 1 If N > 0: v{new} = \frac{1}{N} S Else: v{new} = v (no change if vertex is isolated) 3. Apply Constraint (Constrained Fairing): For each vertex v, clamp its new position v{new} to remain within its initial dual-grid cell Cv. Let Cv be defined by the grid bounds [x{min}, x{max}] \times [y{min}, y{max}] \times [z{min}, z{max}]. The maximum movement is bounded by half the width of a grid cell. Specifically, the vertex must remain in the cell where it was created. For each coordinate axis d \in \{x, y, z\}: v{new, d} = \text{clamp}(v{new, d}, \text{bound}{min, d}, \text{bound}{max, d}) Update v \leftarrow v{new}. 4. Iterate: Repeat steps 1–3 for a fixed number of iterations, typically five. 5. Final Pass (Spike Removal): In the last iteration, drop the constraint. Allow vertices to move outside their originating dual-grid cells. This step avoids the formation of spikes that can occur if vertices are strictly confined to small cells during the final relaxation. The error remains bounded because all incident faces are located in the 27-neighborhood of the dual-grid voxel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constrainedlaplacianfairing(mesh, numiterations=5): """ mesh: object with attributes.vertices (list of Vec3),.faces (list of list of int) Returns: updated mesh.vertices """ nverts = len(mesh.vertices) nfaces = len(mesh.faces) # Precompute initial dual-grid cell bounds for each vertex # This requires external knowledge of the extraction grid. # Assume getinitialcellbounds(vidx) returns (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) cellbounds = [getinitialcellbounds(i) for i in range(nverts)] for iteration in range(numiterations): islastpass = (iteration == numiterations - 1) # Step 1: Compute face centroids facecentroids = [] for face in mesh.faces: centroid = Vec3(0, 0, 0) for vidx in face: centroid += mesh.vertices[vidx] centroid /= len(face) facecentroids.append(centroid) # Step 2: Compute new vertex positions as centroid of incident face centroids newvertices = [Vec3(0, 0, 0) for in range(nverts)] counts = [0] nverts # Traverse faces to accumulate contributions for faceidx, face in enumerate(mesh.faces): fc = facecentroids[faceidx] for vidx in face: newvertices[vidx] += fc counts[vidx] += 1 # Average for i in range(nverts): if counts[i] > 0: newvertices[i] /= counts[i] else: newvertices[i] = mesh.vertices[i] # Step 3 & 4: Apply constraints and update for i in range(nverts): if not islastpass: # Constrain to initial dual-grid cell bounds = cellbounds[i] newvertices[i].x = clamp(newvertices[i].x, bounds[0], bounds[1]) newvertices[i].y = clamp(newvertices[i].y, bounds[2], bounds[3]) newvertices[i].z = clamp(newvertices[i].z, bounds[4], bounds[5]) # If islastpass, no constraint is applied mesh.vertices = newvertices return mesh Iterations: Typically 5. Constraint Range: The vertex movement is bounded by half the width of a grid cell. The range can be augmented to allow relaxation across multiple voxels if needed. Feature Lines: Feature lines along common boundaries of three or more materials may remain visible after fairing. Volume Conservation: The method does not conserve material volume. If volume conservation is required, correction operators must be applied separately. This variant handles multi-material SurfaceNets by treating the mesh as a union of two-sided surface patches separating pairs of materials, preserving topology by preventing touching surfaces from intersecting. It distinguishes between two vertex types: SurfaceVertices: Vertices in cells where each of the 6 faces separates at most two materials. These are faired using the standard binary data surface fairing method. EdgeVertices: Vertices in cells containing at least one JunctionFace. A JunctionFace is a face intersected by more than two materials, or a face intersected by two materials where vertices of the same material are on diagonally opposite corners. For EdgeVertices, the method computes the LocalAverage using only vertices from JunctionFace neighbors, ignoring SurfaceFace neighbors. This encourages movement along the edge and discourages movement perpendicular to it, preserving sharp boundaries. Time Complexity: O(F \cdot I), where F is the number of faces and I is the number of iterations. Computing face centroids is O(F), and updating vertices by traversing faces is O(F) per iteration. Memory Complexity: O(V + F) for storing the mesh and face centroids. No explicit vertex-to-face adjacency list is required, saving memory. Strengths: Fast, simple, and guarantees that the smoothed mesh stays close to the original extraction grid, preventing large topological errors. It is particularly effective for meshes with regular valences (3-6). Limitations: Does not conserve volume. Feature lines at multi-material boundaries may persist unless additional priority-based smoothing is applied. The constraint can lead to "staircasing" if the grid resolution is coarse relative to the feature size. Constrained Laplacian Fairing was introduced by Bertram et al. in 2005 as part of the "Non-manifold Mesh Extraction" method for modeling a human heart from segmented volumes. It was designed to regularize the meshes produced by their contouring algorithm, which generated topologically simple but geometrically noisy quadrilateral meshes. The method was later adapted for multi-label segmentations in the SurfaceNet framework to preserve sharp boundaries between materials.
