name: Isosurface Characteristics Computation
head: Integral of Gradient, Mean Gradient, Total Area, Confined Volume, Curvature, Pekar et al. Isosurface Characteristics
body:
Isosurface Characteristics Computation is a method for quantifying the geometric and topological properties of an extracted isosurface, specifically calculating the integral of the gradient along the surface, mean gradient, total area, confined volume, and curvature. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Marching Cubes Surface Normal Estimation and Marching Cubes Surface Area Estimation by providing a unified framework for multiple scalar metrics derived from the underlying scalar field's gradient, rather than focusing on a single geometric primitive or post-processing step. The method operates on the scalar field V and the extracted isosurface S defined by V(\mathbf{x}) = c, where c is the isovalue. It computes five key characteristics: 1. Integral of the Gradient: The surface integral of the magnitude of the gradient vector field over the isosurface. 2. Mean Gradient: The average magnitude of the gradient over the volume or surface, often used to characterize edge strength. 3. Total Area: The total surface area of the isosurface. 4. Confined Volume: The volume enclosed by the isosurface. 5. Curvature: Local curvature measures (mean and Gaussian) at each point on the surface. Scalar Field V: A 3D grid of values V{i,j,k}. Isosurface Mesh S: A set of triangles \{Tk\} with vertices \mathbf{v}i. Gradient Field 
abla V: Computed from V using finite differences or analytical derivatives if V is defined by basis functions. 1. Compute Gradient Field: Calculate 
abla V(\mathbf{x}) for all points in the domain. For a grid, use central differences:  rac{\partial V}{\partial x} \approx  rac{V{i+1,j,k} - V{i-1,j,k}}{2\Delta x} Handle boundaries by using one-sided differences or clamping. 2. Extract Isosurface: Generate the mesh S using an extraction algorithm (e.g., Marching Cubes) for isovalue c. 3. Compute Total Area (A): Sum the areas of all triangles Tk in S. A = \sum{k} 	ext{Area}(Tk) For a triangle with vertices \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}: 	ext{Area}(Tk) =  rac{1}{2} \| (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) 	imes (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}) \| 4. Compute Confined Volume (Vol): Calculate the volume enclosed by S. Vol =  rac{1}{6} \sum{k} (\mathbf{a}k 	imes \mathbf{b}k) \cdot \mathbf{c}k Ensure consistent vertex winding order for signed volume. 5. Compute Integral of Gradient (I
abla): Integrate the magnitude of the gradient over the surface. I
abla = \intS \| 
abla V(\mathbf{x}) \| \, dA Approximate by summing over triangles: I
abla \approx \sum{k} 	ext{Area}(Tk) \cdot \| 
abla V(\mathbf{p}k) \| where \mathbf{p}k is the centroid of triangle Tk. Interpolate 
abla V at \mathbf{p}k from the grid. 6. Compute Mean Gradient ( ar{g}): Average gradient magnitude over the surface or volume.  ar{g} =  rac{1}{A} \intS \| 
abla V(\mathbf{x}) \| \, dA =  rac{I
abla}{A} Alternatively, compute over the volume Vol:  ar{g}{vol} =  rac{1}{Vol} \intV \| 
abla V(\mathbf{x}) \| \, dV 7. Compute Curvature: For each vertex or triangle, compute mean curvature H and Gaussian curvature K. Mean Curvature: H =  rac{1}{2}(\kappa1 + \kappa2) Gaussian Curvature: K = \kappa1 \kappa2 Use discrete differential geometry operators (e.g., cotangent weights) for mesh-based estimation. Isovalue c: The threshold for extraction. Grid Resolution: Affects gradient accuracy and mesh detail. Smoothing: Optional pre-processing of V to reduce noise in gradient/curvature. Noise: High-frequency noise in V leads to erratic gradients and curvature. Smoothing V is recommended. Boundary Effects: Gradient computation at domain boundaries requires careful handling. Degenerate Triangles: Zero-area triangles in the mesh can skew area and curvature calculations. Filter or merge them. Non-Manifold Geometry: Ensure the mesh is manifold for accurate volume and area integration. Unverified code. a, c - a)) # Step 4: Compute Confined Volume volume = 0.0 for tri in triangles: a, b, c = vertices[tri] volume += np.dot(np.cross(a, b), c) / 6.0 volume = abs(volume) # Ensure positive volume # Step 5: Compute Integral of Gradient integralgradient = 0.0 for tri in triangles: a, b, c = vertices[tri] centroid = (a + b + c) / 3.0 # Interpolate gradient at centroid gradatcentroid = interpolategradient(gradV, centroid, gridspacing) triarea = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(b - name: Volumetric Divergence Metric
head: VDC method, Volumetric Divergence, Volumetric Divergence Computation
body: The Volumetric Divergence Metric (VDC) estimates the accuracy of isosurfaces extracted by marching algorithms (such as Marching Cubes) by calculating the total volume between the produced mesh isosurface and the ideal trilinear interpolation isosurface. It sets itself apart from sibling metrics like the Tetrahedron Volumetric Divergence (TVD) Predictor by providing a highly accurate ground truth through recursive subdivision, whereas TVD uses a faster, closed-form geometric approximation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A voxel cube containing scalar field values at its 8 vertices; an isosurface extraction algorithm's output mesh intersecting the cube; a target subdivision depth d. Output: A scalar value representing the volumetric divergence for the cube, which is the sum of contributions from all leaf subcubes. Data Structures The method operates on a hierarchical structure of cubes. Cube: Defined by its 8 corner vertices and the scalar field values at those vertices. Subcube: A child cube formed by bisecting the parent cube along all three axes. Contribution: The volume of the symmetric difference between the region enclosed by the extracted mesh and the region enclosed by the trilinear isosurface within a specific subcube. Formulas The volumetric divergence RD between two closed surfaces A (extracted mesh) and B (trilinear isosurface) is defined as the volume of the region RD: RD = \text{Volume}((A{in} \cap B{out}) \cup (A{out} \cap B{in})) where A{in} and A{out} are the regions inside and outside surface A, and B{in} and B{out} are the regions inside and outside surface B. Parameters Subdivision Depth (d): The number of times the cube is recursively subdivided. Typical values: Depth 10 (VD10) is used for generating high-accuracy standard values. Depth 7 (VD7) is used for comparison. Higher depth increases accuracy but significantly increases execution time. Numbered Steps 1. Recursively and evenly subdivide a cube into 8 subcubes, repeating until a certain subdivision depth is reached. 2. Determine each subcube’s contribution to the volumetric divergence. 3. Sum the contributions of all subcubes to yield the volumetric divergence metric value. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevolumetricdivergence(cube, depth, maxdepth): if depth == maxdepth: # Determine the contribution of the current cube to the volumetric divergence # This involves calculating the volume between the extracted mesh triangles # and the trilinear isosurface within this subcube contribution = calculatesubcubecontribution(cube) return contribution else: # Subdivide the cube into 8 equal subcubes subcubes = subdividecube(cube) totalcontribution = 0 for subcube in subcubes: totalcontribution += computevolumetricdivergence(subcube, depth + 1, maxdepth) return totalcontribution divergencemetric = computevolumetricdivergence(rootcube, 0, d) Note: calculatesubcubecontribution computes the volume between the mesh and trilinear surface within a subcube. subdividecube bisects a cube along three axes to create 8 children. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Performance: The computational cost is very high. For a 256 \times 256 \times 44 dataset, computing VDC with depth 7 took approximately 10,000 times longer than extracting the isosurface via Marching Cubes (MC). Precision: The method relies on triangle-cube intersection tests and volume calculations. The sources do not specify numerical precision issues at high depths; instead, they note that higher subdivision depths increase accuracy. A fast approximation of VDC using closed-form geometric models of tetrahedra, suitable for real-time evaluation. Time Complexity: Exponential with respect to subdivision depth d, as the number of subcubes grows by a factor of 8 at each level (8^d). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of subcubes processed, though depth-first recursion allows for constant space relative to the total number of nodes if not storing all subcubes simultaneously. Measured Performance: On a frog dataset, VDC with depth 7 took 3961.2 seconds, while depth 3 took 27.8 seconds, depth 4 took 76.5 seconds, depth 5 took 272.6 seconds, and depth 6 took 1012.8 seconds. Strengths: Provides highly accurate estimation of isosurface error, serving as a ground truth for evaluating other metrics. Limitations: Extremely slow execution time, making it impractical for real-time applications or large datasets without significant optimization. When to use: When high-accuracy ground truth is required for validating isosurfacing algorithms or other error metrics. When not to use: When performance is critical or for real-time applications. The Volumetric Divergence Metric was introduced in [14] (cited in) to estimate the volumetric divergence between a produced mesh isosurface and the trilinear interpolation isosurface. It is related to the total volume between the 3D regions enclosed by these two surfaces. The method was used to generate standard volumetric divergence values (VD10) for evaluating the accuracy of marching isosurfacing algorithms. name: Tetrahedron Volumetric Divergence (TVD) Predictor
head: TVD predictor
body: The Tetrahedron Volumetric Divergence (TVD) Predictor is a metric that approximates the volumetric divergence between an extracted isosurface mesh (typically from Marching Cubes) and the ideal trilinear interpolation isosurface within a voxel cube. It models the volume between the planar mesh triangles and the curved ideal surface using tetrahedra, providing a computationally cheaper alternative to the recursive Volumetric Divergence Metric (VDC). While VDC relies on deep recursive subdivision to estimate error, TVD uses a closed-form geometric approximation based on triangle centroids and normals, making it suitable for real-time or high-performance evaluation of isosurface accuracy. The TVD predictor calculates a scalar value PT for each cube containing an extracted isosurface. The method assumes the extracted surface consists of planar triangles and the reference surface is defined by trilinear interpolation within the cube. Input: The vertices of the extracted mesh triangles within a single unit cube. For each triangle j, the three intersection points P{j,1}, P{j,2}, P{j,3} where the isosurface intersects the cube edges. The trilinear interpolation function f(x,y,z) defining the ideal isosurface (implicitly defined as f(x,y,z) = \text{iso}). Output: The TVD predictor value PT for the cube. No complex data structures are required beyond standard geometric primitives: Point: A 3D vector (x, y, z). Triangle: Defined by three Points P1, P2, P3. Vector: A 3D vector used for normals and directions. 1. Initialize Sum: Set PT = 0. 2. Iterate Triangles: For each triangle j in the extracted mesh within the cube (from j=0 to m-1): a. Calculate Normal: Compute the normal vector \mathbf{n}j of the triangle plane using the cross product of two edge vectors formed by the intersection points P{j,1}, P{j,2}, P{j,3}. \mathbf{n}j = (P{j,2} - P{j,1}) \times (P{j,3} - P{j,1}) b. Calculate Centroid: Compute the centroid Cj of the triangle. Cj = \frac{P{j,1} + P{j,2} + P{j,3}}{3} c. Define Line: Define a half-line starting at Cj with direction \mathbf{n}j. The parametric equation of the line is: L(t) = Cj + t \cdot \mathbf{n}j, \quad t \ge 0 d. Find Intersection Mj: Find the intersection point Mj of this half-line with the trilinear interpolation isosurface. Substitute L(t) into the trilinear interpolation equation f(x,y,z) = \text{iso}. This results in a cubic equation in t: a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d = 0. Solve for real roots t \ge 0. Fallback: If the half-line from the centroid has no intersection with the isosurface, iterate through the three vertices of the triangle. For each vertex Vk (k=1,2,3), define a median line from Vk through the centroid Cj. The source states: "we pick a new point along the median of the triangle from one of its vertices... Since the triangle and the trilinear interpolation isosurface meet at three vertices... we can always find an intersection point". Specifically, the algorithm considers the three triangle vertices one at a time until an intersection point is found. Let the found intersection point be Mj. e. Calculate Distance dj: Compute the distance dj between the centroid Cj and the intersection point Mj. dj = \| Cj - Mj \| This dj approximates the largest distance between the triangle plane and the trilinear isosurface. f. Calculate Area Sj: Compute the area Sj of the triangle. Sj = \frac{1}{2} \| (P{j,2} - P{j,1}) \times (P{j,3} - P{j,1}) \| g. Calculate Tetrahedron Volume Vj: Compute the volume of the tetrahedron formed by the triangle and the intersection point. Vj = \frac{1}{3} Sj dj h. Accumulate: Add Vj to the sum. 3. Finalize: Multiply the accumulated sum by 2 to obtain PT. PT = 2 \sum{j=0}^{m-1} Vj = 2 \sum{j=0}^{m-1} Sj dj The TVD predictor PT is defined as: PT = 2 \sum{j=0}^{m-1} Sj dj = 2 \sum{j=0}^{m-1} Vj Where: m is the number of triangles in the extracted mesh in the unit cube. Sj is the area of the j-th triangle. dj is the approximate largest distance between the j-th triangle plane and the trilinear interpolation isosurface. Vj is the volume of the tetrahedron generated from the j-th triangle. The constant multiplier 2 scales the TVD predictor values to match the values of the Volumetric Divergence Metric. Constant Multiplier: 2. This value is empirically determined to align the TVD predictor with the Volumetric Divergence Metric. No Intersection from Centroid: If the half-line from the triangle centroid perpendicular to the triangle plane does not intersect the trilinear isosurface, the algorithm must fallback. It iterates through the three triangle vertices, considering the median from each vertex, until an intersection is found. An intersection is guaranteed because the triangle vertices lie on the isosurface. Cubic Root Solving: Finding the intersection requires solving a cubic equation derived from the trilinear interpolation function. Comparison Fairness: When comparing TVD to VDC, note that VDC time includes subdivision computation that would also be required if TVD were used in an adaptive isosurfacing context. However, TVD is still significantly faster. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def crossproduct(v1, v2): return [ v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0] ] def dotproduct(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def subtract(v1, v2): return [v1[0]-v2[0], v1[1]-v2[1], v1[2]-v2[2]] def add(v1, v2): return [v1[0]+v2[0], v1[1]+v2[1], v1[2]+v2[2]] def scale(v, s): return [v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s] def magnitude(v): return math.sqrt(dotproduct(v, v)) def normalize(v): mag = magnitude(v) if mag == 0: return [0, 0, 0] return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] def solvecubic(a, b, c, d): """Solves at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d = 0 for real roots t >= 0.""" if abs(a) < 1e-12: # Quadratic fallback if abs(b) < 1e-12: if abs(c) < 1e-12: return [] return [-d/c] if c != 0 else [] disc = cc - 4bd if disc < 0: return [] sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) r1 = (-c + sqrtdisc) / (2b) r2 = (-c - sqrtdisc) / (2b) return [r for r in [r1, r2] if r >= 0] # Normalize b /= a; c /= a; d /= a # Cardano's method p = c - bb/3 q = 2bbb/27 - bc/3 + d disc = qq/4 + ppp/27 roots = [] if disc > 0: u = -q/2 + math.sqrt(disc) v = -q/2 - math.sqrt(disc) u = math.cbrt(u) if u >= 0 else -math.cbrt(-u) v = math.cbrt(v) if v >= 0 else -math.cbrt(-v) t1 = u + v - b/3 roots.append(t1) elif disc == 0: if q == 0: roots.append(-b/3) else: u = math.cbrt(-q/2) roots.append(2u - b/3) roots.append(-u - b/3) else: r = math.sqrt(-ppp/27) theta = math.acos(-q/(2r)) m1 = 2math.sqrt(-p/3) t1 = m1math.cos(theta/3) - b/3 t2 = m1math.cos((theta + 2math.pi)/3) - b/3 t3 = m1math.cos((theta + 4math.pi)/3) - b/3 roots.extend([t1, t2, t3]) return [t for t in roots if t >= 0] def trilinearinterpolationisosurfaceintersection(linepoint, linedir, isovalue, voxelcorners): """ Finds the intersection of a half-line with the trilinear isosurface. voxelcorners: List of 8 scalar values at the cube corners [0..7]. Returns the intersection point M or None if not found. """ # Compute cubic coefficients for f(P + tD) = iso # Trilinear interpolation along a line yields at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d = 0 # Coefficients derived from standard trilinear basis functions dx, dy, dz = linedir px, py, pz = linepoint # Precompute basis terms for trilinear interpolation along the line # f(t) = sum{i,j,k} c{ijk} (1-ti)^{1-i} ti^i... # Simplified coefficient calculation for trilinear interpolation: a = (voxelcorners[7] - voxelcorners[6] - voxelcorners[5] + voxelcorners[4] voxelcorners[3] + voxelcorners[2] + voxelcorners[1] - voxelcorners[0]) b = (voxelcorners[6] + voxelcorners[5] - 2voxelcorners[4] - voxelcorners[2] voxelcorners[1] + 2voxelcorners[0]) dx + \ (voxelcorners[7] - voxelcorners[5] - voxelcorners[3] + voxelcorners[1] voxelcorners[6] + voxelcorners[4] + voxelcorners[2] - voxelcorners[0]) dy + \ (voxelcorners[7] - voxelcorners[6] - voxelcorners[3] + voxelcorners[2] voxelcorners[5] + voxelcorners[4] + voxelcorners[1] - voxelcorners[0]) dz c = (voxelcorners[4] - 2voxelcorners[0]) dx2 + \ (voxelcorners[2] - 2voxelcorners[0]) dy2 + \ (voxelcorners[1] - 2voxelcorners[0]) dz2 + \ (voxelcorners[6] - voxelcorners[4] - voxelcorners[2] + voxelcorners[0]) dxdy + \ (voxelcorners[5] - voxelcorners[4] - voxelcorners[1] + voxelcorners[0]) dxdz + \ (voxelcorners[3] - voxelcorners[2] - voxelcorners[1] + voxelcorners[0]) dydz d = voxelcorners[0] - isovalue roots = solvecubic(a, b, c, d) if not roots: return None # Return closest intersection along the ray tmin = min(roots) return add(linepoint, scale(linedir, tmin)) def findintersectionfallback(trianglevertices, isovalue, voxelcorners): """Fallback if centroid line fails. Iterates through vertices using median direction.""" centroid = [(trianglevertices[0][0]+trianglevertices[1][0]+trianglevertices[2][0])/3, (trianglevertices[0][1]+trianglevertices[1][1]+trianglevertices[2][1])/3, (trianglevertices[0][2]+trianglevertices[1][2]+trianglevertices[2][2])/3] for vertex in trianglevertices: dirvec = subtract(centroid, vertex) if magnitude(dirvec) < 1e-12: continue dirvec = normalize(dirvec) M = trilinearinterpolationisosurfaceintersection(vertex, dirvec, isovalue, voxelcorners) if M is not None: return M # Vertices lie on the isosurface, so fallback to first vertex if all rays miss return trianglevertices[0] def computetvdpredictor(triangles, isovalue, voxelcorners): """ triangles: List of triangles, each triangle is a list of 3 points [P1, P2, P3]. isovalue: The isovalue. voxelcorners: Scalar field values at the 8 cube corners. Returns: TVD Predictor value PT. """ totalvolume = 0.0 for tri in triangles: P1, P2, P3 = tri # 1. Calculate Normal edge1 = subtract(P2, P1) edge2 = subtract(P3, P1) normal = crossproduct(edge1, edge2) # 2. Calculate Centroid centroid = [(P1[0]+P2[0]+P3[0])/3, (P1[1]+P2[1]+P3[1])/3, (P1[2]+P2[2]+P3[2])/3] # 3. Define Line and Find Intersection M dirvec = normalize(normal) M = trilinearinterpolationisosurfaceintersection(centroid, dirvec, isovalue, voxelcorners) # 4. Fallback if no intersection from centroid if M is None: M = findintersectionfallback(tri, isovalue, voxelcorners) # 5. Calculate Distance dj vecCM = subtract(M, centroid) dj = magnitude(vecCM) # 6. Calculate Area Sj Sj = 0.5 magnitude(crossproduct(edge1, edge2)) # 7. Calculate Volume Vj Vj = (1.0/3.0) Sj dj totalvolume += Vj # 8. Final Result PT = 2.0 totalvolume return PT Time Complexity: The TVD predictor is significantly faster than the Volumetric Divergence Metric (VDC). For a frog CT-scan dataset (256x256x44), VDC with subdivision depth 7 took 3961.2 seconds, while TVD took 0.35 seconds. It is also faster than the MC23 isosurfacing algorithm itself (0.47 seconds). Memory Complexity: Low. It requires storing only the triangle vertices and scalar field data for the current voxel. No recursive subdivision structures are needed. Accuracy: The TVD predictor correlates strongly with the Volumetric Divergence Metric (MD) for high-frequency base cases (e.g., base cases 1, 2, 5, 8, 17, 20, 21) with correlation coefficients close to +1. For complex shapes with internal ambiguity (base cases 6, 11, 14), the correlation is weaker but still positive. Error: On a synthetic 20x20x20 dataset, the TVD predictor error compared to VD10 (ground truth) was less than 13.5% for isovalues 40.5, 70.5, and 100.5. Strengths: Low computational cost, suitable for real-time evaluation, good approximation for common Marching Cubes base cases. Limitations: Approximation error can be higher for complex trilinear shapes or ambiguous cases. Relies on the assumption that the tetrahedron volume approximates the divergence well. When to use: When a fast estimate of isosurface accuracy is needed, or when integrating error estimation into adaptive isosurfacing pipelines where VDC is too slow. When not to use: When high-precision volumetric divergence is required and computational cost is not a constraint (use VDC instead). The Tetrahedron Volumetric Divergence (TVD) Predictor was introduced as a new metric to evaluate the accuracy of isosurfaces extracted by marching isosurfacing algorithms, specifically Marching Cubes. It was proposed to address the high computational cost of the existing Volumetric Divergence Computation (VDC) method, which recursively subdivides cubes. The method was tested on real datasets (frog CT-scan) and synthetic datasets to validate its correlation with VDC and its computational efficiency. name: Curvature-Based Anisotropy Estimation
head: Kindlmann et al
body: This method estimates anisotropy for surface shading by computing the principal curvatures of an isosurface. It serves as a baseline comparison against covariance-based methods, relying on differential geometry properties where principal curvature directions form an orthonormal basis in the tangent plane. Unlike covariance-based approaches that evaluate feature extent in both spatial and data domains, this method focuses strictly on the local geometry of the isosurface. Inputs: Scalar field volume, isovalue for surface extraction, precomputed gradient and Hessian fields. Outputs: Anisotropy parameters (principal curvature magnitudes and directions) for use in anisotropic BRDFs (e.g., Ward’s BRDF). Data Structures: Gradient Field: 3-component vector per voxel (\nabla f). Hessian Field: Symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix per voxel (H). Stored as 6 values due to symmetry (H{xx}, H{xy}, H{xz}, H{yy}, H{yz}, H{zz}). Steps: 1. Precomputation: Compute the Hessian matrix of the scalar field on a 3D grid. Filter the Hessian matrix to reduce noise. 2. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient vector \nabla f at each voxel. 3. Geometry Tensor Construction: At rendering time, for each shading point on the isosurface, construct the geometry tensor using the filtered gradient and Hessian. The geometry tensor relates to the shape operator or second fundamental form in differential geometry. 4. Eigen Decomposition: Compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the geometry tensor on-the-fly. The eigenvalues correspond to the principal curvature magnitudes (\kappa1, \kappa2). The eigenvectors correspond to the principal curvature directions. 5. Shading: Use the principal curvatures and their directions as input for an anisotropic BRDF, such as Ward’s BRDF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecurvatureanisotropy(shadingpoint, gradientfield, hessianfield): """ Computes anisotropy parameters from principal curvatures. Args: shadingpoint: 3D coordinate on the isosurface. gradientfield: Precomputed and filtered gradient field. hessianfield: Precomputed and filtered Hessian field. Returns: kappa1, kappa2: Principal curvature magnitudes. v1, v2: Principal curvature directions (eigenvectors). """ # 1. Retrieve precomputed data at the shading point grad = gradientfield.sample(shadingpoint) hess = hessianfield.sample(shadingpoint) # 2. Construct the geometry tensor (Shape Operator) # The shape operator S is typically defined as - (Jacobian of normal) projected to tangent plane. # In discrete grid terms, this involves the Hessian and Gradient. # Normal n = normalize(grad) # The geometry tensor G is derived from H and grad. # Note: Exact formulation of "geometry tensor" from H and grad is implied by differential geometry context. # Commonly, the Weingarten map or shape operator is computed. # Let's assume a standard projection-based construction for the shape operator S: # S = - (I - nn^T) H (I - nn^T) / |grad| # Or similar variant depending on specific implementation details not fully explicit in source. # However, source states: "geometry tensor is computed from the filtered gradient vector and Hessian matrix." # For implementation completeness, we define the standard differential geometry approach: n = normalize(grad) # Project Hessian onto tangent plane to get shape operator components # This step requires specific linear algebra operations not fully detailed in source text, # but is standard for extracting curvatures from Hessian. # We assume the source implies the standard extraction: # Eigenvalues of the shape operator are the principal curvatures. # Simplified representation of the tensor construction based on source description: # The source does not give the explicit formula for the "geometry tensor" from H and grad, # only that it is computed from them. We mark this as a gap. geometrytensor = constructgeometrytensor(grad, hess) # Placeholder for specific linear algebra construction # 3. Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors eigenvalues, eigenvectors = computeeigendecomposition(geometrytensor) # 4. Extract principal curvatures and directions # Eigenvalues correspond to principal curvature magnitudes kappa1 = eigenvalues[0] kappa2 = eigenvalues[1] # Eigenvectors correspond to principal curvature directions v1 = eigenvectors[0] v2 = eigenvectors[1] return kappa1, kappa2, v1, v2 Parameters: Filtering: The Hessian matrix is filtered during precomputation. Specific filter type and kernel size are not given in the sources. BRDF: Ward’s BRDF is used as the shading model. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts at Transitions: The method is susceptible to visual artifacts close to transitions of structures (e.g., boundaries of ellipsoids). Aliasing: Local estimation can lead to disturbing visual patterns (aliasing) when the dataset is noisy or features are small compared to image resolution. name: Covariance Matrix Estimation for Anisotropy
head: Ambient Sphere Covariance Estimation
body: This method estimates anisotropy by sampling a scalar field within an ambient sphere around each voxel to construct a 2D covariance matrix on the local tangent plane. It differs from curvature-based approaches by evaluating feature extent in both spatial and data domains, allowing it to capture anisotropy in volumetric structures rather than just sharp isosurfaces. Inputs: Scalar field volume, radius r, interval size \varepsilon, number of samples n, boolean filter flag f. Outputs: Symmetric 2x2 covariance matrix C stored at each voxel. Data Structures: Normal Vector: Stored per voxel. Covariance Matrix C: Symmetric 2x2 matrix. Stored as 3 values per voxel (quantized to 8 bits per channel). Steps: 1. Normal Estimation: For all voxels x, estimate a high-quality normal vector N(x) using the Sobel operator. Store N(x) at voxel x. 2. Covariance Initialization: For all voxels x, sample the scalar field value s at x. Initialize a symmetric 2x2 covariance matrix C to zero. 3. Ambient Sampling: Loop i from 1 to n: Draw a uniform sample point xi on a sphere of radius r centered at x. Sample the scalar field value si at xi. If s - \varepsilon \le si \le s + \varepsilon: Project xi onto the tangent plane at x using normal N(x) to get 3D point xp. Transform xp to a 2D point x2 in the tangent plane basis defined by N(x). Add x2 to the covariance matrix C. 4. Storage: Store the resulting symmetric 2x2 matrix C at voxel x. 5. Filtering (Optional): If flag f is true, for all voxels x, read C, apply a Gaussian filter, and store the filtered C back. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimateanisotropy(volume, r, epsilon, n, filterflag): # Step 1: Estimate normals normals = {} for x in volume.voxels: normals[x] = sobelnormal(volume, x) # Step 2-4: Estimate covariance matrices covariances = {} for x in volume.voxels: s = volume.sample(x) C = zeromatrix(2, 2) for i in range(n): # Draw uniform sample on sphere of radius r around x xi = uniformspheresample(center=x, radius=r) si = volume.sample(xi) # Check if sample lies within the isosurface interval if s - epsilon <= si <= s + epsilon: # Project to tangent plane xp = projecttotangentplane(xi, normals[x]) # Transform to 2D coordinates in tangent basis x2 = transformto2d(xp, normals[x]) # Update covariance matrix C = addpointtocovariance(C, x2) covariances[x] = C # Step 5: Optional Gaussian filtering if filterflag: for x in volume.voxels: C = covariances[x] C = gaussianfilter(C) covariances[x] = C return covariances Parameters: r: Radius of the ambient sphere. Controls feature size in the spatial domain. Small r provides local curvature info but requires filtering to avoid discrete artifacts. Large r accounts for large-scale structures but may make estimation overly isotropic and requires more samples n to maintain constant sample density. \varepsilon: Interval size in the data domain. Controls feature size in the scalar field. Small \varepsilon samples locally for sharp isosurfaces but causes noise artifacts. Large \varepsilon samples wide intervals, beneficial for volumetric structures, but may lose anisotropic details. n: Number of samples. Must be increased if r is large to maintain constant sample density. Pitfalls: Too few accepted samples (due to small \varepsilon or large r) can result in non-uniform clusters, falsifying anisotropy estimation because spatial position influences the covariance matrix. Memory: Requires 3 values per voxel for the gradient (normal) and 3 values per voxel for the symmetric 2x2 covariance matrix. This is more efficient than storing a symmetric 3x3 Hessian matrix (6 values). Performance: The method involves n samples per voxel. Performance scales linearly with n and the number of voxels. Strengths: Estimates anisotropy for structures with finite extent in both spatial and data domains. It can classify local isotropic areas as partially anisotropic if they are part of a larger anisotropic feature, making shading less susceptible to artifacts from strong variations or low signal-to-noise ratio. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of r and \varepsilon. Small parameters require extensive filtering or high n to avoid noise. Large parameters may lose anisotropic details. This method was introduced in "Anisotropic Ambient Volume Shading". It was developed to provide BRDF-independent anisotropy estimation that works for both sharp isosurfaces and volumetric structures, addressing limitations of derivative-based curvature computation. name: Precomputed Geometric Quantities for Contour Trees
head: B-spline contour quantification, Topology Change Graph coloring
body: This method precomputes the geometric properties (area and volume) of all possible contours for a 3D scalar field, enabling real-time evaluation for any selected isovalue without expensive surface extraction. It differs from post-extraction methods by using a contour tree to hierarchically aggregate B-spline functions, allowing immediate quantification of topological features. Inputs: A 3D scalar field f defined on a simplicial mesh; a contour tree CT of the field. Outputs: Precomputed B-spline functions for area and volume for every edge in the contour tree; a Topology Change Graph (TCG) with nodes colored by geometric quantities. Data Structures: 1. Simplicial Mesh: The domain of f. 2. Contour Tree (CT): A graph where nodes are critical points (minima, maxima, saddles) and edges represent continuous families of contours. 3. B-spline Functions: For each simplex s, univariate functions As(w) (area) and Vs(w) (volume) are precomputed. 4. Edge Data: For each edge e in CT, store: Se = \{s(e,1), \dots, s(e,n)\}: The set of simplices covering the region of the contour class. A(e, w): The merged area B-spline function. V(e, w): The merged volume B-spline function. V{e'}: Precomputed volume constants for upper/lower edges. Steps: 1. Compute Simplex Functions: For each simplex s in the mesh, compute the univariate B-spline functions As(w) and Vs(w) representing the area and volume of the isosurface within that simplex as a function of isovalue w. 2. Construct Contour Tree: Build the contour tree CT for the scalar field f. 3. Identify Covering Simplices: For each edge e = (v1, v2) in CT (where f(v1) \le f(v2)), identify the set of simplices Se that cover the region represented by the contour class of e. This is done by picking a seed cell in e and propagating to adjacent simplices. 4. Compute Edge Area Functions: For each edge e, compute the merged area function A(e, w) by summing the simplex functions: A(e, w) = \sum{k=1}^{n} A{s(e,k)}(w) where n = |Se|. 5. Identify Upper/Lower Edges: For each edge e, identify the set of upper edges E{upper}(e) and lower edges E{lower}(e) in the contour tree. These sets define the "inside" or "outside" regions relative to the contour class of e. 6. Compute Edge Volumes Incrementally: For each edge e' in the contour tree, compute the volume V{e'} of the region covered by its contour class. Compute V{e'} incrementally through the hierarchical structure of the contour tree. For each edge e, compute the merged volume function V(e, w): V(e, w) = \sum{k=1}^{n} V{s(e,k)}(w) + \sum{e' \in E(e)} V{e'} where E(e) is either E{upper}(e) or E{lower}(e), depending on the user's choice of which side (inside/outside) to quantify. 7. Runtime Evaluation: Given an isovalue w0 and an edge e, evaluate A(e, w0) and V(e, w0) to get the area and volume of the contour. 8. TCG Coloring: Construct a Topology Change Graph (TCG) where nodes represent contour segments. Color each node based on the geometric quantity (e.g., surface area) of the contour it represents, computed via the prefunctions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ # Step 1: Compute simplex-level B-splines simplexareasplines = {} simplexvolumesplines = {} for simplex in mesh.simplices: # Compute univariate B-splines for area and volume within this simplex # As(w) and Vs(w) are functions of isovalue w simplexareasplines[simplex] = computesimplexareabspline(simplex, scalarfield) simplexvolumesplines[simplex] = computesimplexvolumebspline(simplex, scalarfield) # Step 2: Build Contour Tree contourtree = buildcontourtree(scalarfield, mesh) # Step 3 & 4: Compute Edge Area Functions edgeareafunctions = {} for edge in contourtree.edges: # Identify simplices covering the region of this edge coveringsimplices = identifycoveringsimplices(edge, contourtree, scalarfield) # Sum the B-splines # A(e, w) = sum(As(w) for s in coveringsimplices) edgeareafunctions[edge] = mergebsplines( [simplexareasplines[s] for s in coveringsimplices]) # Step 5 & 6: Compute Edge Volumes Incrementally # First, compute Ve' for all edges (volume of the region covered by the contour class) # This requires hierarchical traversal edgeregionvolumes = {} for edge in contourtree.edges: # Ve' is the volume of the region covered by the contour class of edge e' # Computed incrementally via contour tree hierarchy edgeregionvolumes[edge] = computeedgeregionvolume(edge, contourtree) edgevolumefunctions = {} for edge in contourtree.edges: coveringsimplices = identifycoveringsimplices(edge, contourtree, scalarfield) # Determine upper and lower edges upperedges = getupperedges(edge, contourtree) loweredges = getloweredges(edge, contourtree) # Store both options for runtime selection # V(e, w) = sum(Vs(w)) + sum(Ve' for e' in E(e)) sumsimplexvolumes = mergebsplines( [simplexvolumesplines[s] for s in coveringsimplices]) sumupperregionvolumes = sum(edgeregionvolumes[eprime] for eprime in upperedges) sumlowerregionvolumes = sum(edgeregionvolumes[eprime] for eprime in loweredges) edgevolumefunctions[edge] = { 'simplexpart': sumsimplexvolumes, 'upperregionpart': sumupperregionvolumes, 'lowerregionpart': sumlowerregionvolumes } # Step 8: Color TCG nodes tcg = buildtopologychangegraph(contourtree) for node in tcg.nodes: # Get the corresponding edge in the contour tree edge = node.contouredge # Color based on area (or volume) # Area is evaluated at a representative isovalue or stored as a function node.color = evaluatebspline(edgeareafunctions[edge], node.representativeisovalue) return edgeareafunctions, edgevolumefunctions, tcg def evaluatecontourproperties(edgeareafunc, edgevolumefunc, isovalue, side='upper'): """ Evaluate area and volume for a specific isovalue and edge. """ area = evaluatebspline(edgeareafunc, isovalue) if side == 'upper': regionvol = edgevolumefunc['upperregionpart'] else: regionvol = edgevolumefunc['lowerregionpart'] simplexvol = evaluatebspline(edgevolumefunc['simplexpart'], isovalue) volume = simplexvol + regionvol return area, volume Parameters: B-spline Degree: Not given in the sources. Boundary Conditions: The definition of "inside" vs "outside" depends on the choice of upper or lower edges, which must be consistent with the user's intent. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a valid simplicial mesh and a well-defined contour tree. Computes divergence of vector fields to identify flow features. Use when analyzing fluid dynamics rather than scalar topology. Volumetric Divergence Metric Estimates anisotropy using curvature tensors. Use when directional properties of surfaces are more important than topological quantification. Runtime evaluation is O(1) per contour query. Memory Complexity: Requires storing B-spline coefficients for all simplices and edges. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables real-time interactive exploration of topological features without repeated surface extraction. Limitations: Requires precomputation for each timestep in time-varying data. Not given in the sources. When to use: Interactive visualization of time-varying scalar fields where users need to quickly assess geometric properties of contours. When not to use: When only a single isosurface extraction is needed, as the overhead of precomputation may not be justified. The method was introduced in 2006 by. It addresses the limitation of traditional approaches that extract features first and then compute geometric properties, which is too slow for interactive applications. name: Representative Isovalue Selection
head: Isosurface Similarity Map-based Isovalue Selection, SDV-based Isovalue Prioritization
body: This method automatically selects a subset of representative isovalues from a scalar dataset by identifying peaks in the isosurface similarity distribution, ensuring that selected values correspond to distinct geometric structures with low mutual similarity. Unlike methods that rely on frequency counts or magnitude thresholds, it uses a recursive partitioning strategy weighted by the Similarity Distribution Value (SDV) to order isovalues from most to least representative without requiring user-defined parameters. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sorted list of candidate isovalues V = \{h1, h2, \dots, hn\}, where n is the total number of candidates. Input: A similarity metric SMV(ha, hb) that computes the similarity between the isosurfaces generated at isovalue ha and hb. Input: A Similarity Distribution Value function SDV(hi) for each candidate hi, representing its average similarity to all other candidates in the current subset. Output: A priority queue Q containing all isovalues ordered by priority, such that extracting items from Q yields isovalues from most representative to least representative. Data Structures Priority Queue Q: A heap or sorted list storing tuples (hi, pi), where hi is the isovalue and pi is its calculated priority. Candidate Set V: A list of indices or isovalue objects, initially containing all candidates. Formulas 1. Selection of Maximum SDV: m \leftarrow \arg \max{hi \in V} SDV(i) Where m is the index of the isovalue with the highest SDV in the current subset V. 2. Priority Calculation: p \leftarrow |V| \cdot SDV(m) The priority p is the product of the size of the current subset |V| and the SDV of the selected isovalue m. 3. Penalty Update: pi \leftarrow \frac{pi}{1 + SMV(hm, hi)} After selecting hm, the priority pi of all remaining items i in the queue is reduced by a factor dependent on the similarity between hm and hi. Parameters SDV: The Similarity Distribution Value. The source does not provide the explicit formula for calculating SDV, only that it is used to rank isovalues initially based on their average similarity to others. SMV: The Similarity Measure Value. The specific implementation of SMV is not defined in the source text, only that it is used in the penalty formula. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize an empty priority queue Q and a set V containing all candidate isovalues. Call the recursive procedure prioritize(Q, V). 2. Recursive Partitioning (prioritize(Q, V)): a. Find the isovalue m in V with the maximum SDV: m \leftarrow \arg \max{hi \in V} SDV(i). b. Calculate the priority p for m: p \leftarrow |V| \cdot SDV(m). c. Enqueue m into Q with priority p. d. Split V into two subsets: V1 \leftarrow \{hi \in V: 1 \le i < m\} and V2 \leftarrow \{hi \in V: m < i \le |V|\}. e. Recursively call prioritize(Q, V1) and prioritize(Q, V2). 3. Extraction and Penalty: a. Extract the isovalue hm with the maximum priority from Q. b. For all remaining items i in Q, update their priority pi using the penalty formula: pi \leftarrow pi / (1 + SMV(hm, hi)). c. Repeat step 3 until Q is empty. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import heapq def representativeisovalueselection(isovaluelist, sdvfunc, smvfunc): """ Selects representative isovalues using SDV-based prioritization. Args: isovaluelist: List of isovalue objects, sorted by magnitude. sdvfunc: Function returning SDV for an isovalue index within a given subset. smvfunc: Function returning SMV between two isovalue objects. Returns: List of isovalue objects ordered by representativeness. """ n = len(isovaluelist) pq = [] # Min-heap storing (-priority, index) def prioritize(vindices): if not vindices: return bestidx = -1 maxsdv = -1.0 for idx in vindices: val = sdvfunc(vindices, idx) if val > maxsdv: maxsdv = val bestidx = idx priority = len(vindices) maxsdv heapq.heappush(pq, (-priority, bestidx)) v1 = [idx for idx in vindices if idx < bestidx] v2 = [idx for idx in vindices if idx > bestidx] prioritize(v1) prioritize(v2) prioritize(list(range(n))) result = [] while pq: negp, m = heapq.heappop(pq) result.append(isovaluelist[m]) for i in range(len(pq)): negpi, idx = pq[i] similarity = smvfunc(isovaluelist[m], isovaluelist[idx]) newp = -negpi / (1.0 + similarity) pq[i] = (-newp, idx) heapq.heapify(pq) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls Parameter Tuning: The algorithm requires no user-defined thresholds or parameters, avoiding issues related to parameter tuning. SDV Definition: The explicit formula for SDV is not provided in the source. Similarity Metric: The specific implementation of SMV is not defined in the source. Degenerate Input: If multiple isovalues have identical SDV values, the selection of m is arbitrary among them. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Automatically identifies representative isovalues without user-defined thresholds; ensures selected isovalues correspond to distinct structures by penalizing similarity to already selected values. Limitations: Requires a similarity metric SMV which can be computationally expensive to compute for many pairs; the definition of SDV is not standardized in the source. When to Use: Exploratory visualization tasks where the user intent is unknown and a diverse set of representative isosurfaces is needed. The method was introduced in the paper "Isosurface Similarity Maps" by the author(s) of, published in 2010 in the journal Computer Graphics Forum (Eurographics Association). It addresses the problem of selecting relevant isovalues for exploratory volume rendering, where the user's intent is not known a priori. The approach leverages the structured nature of the Isosurface Similarity Map (ISM) to automatically identify regions of high similarity and select representative isovalues from them. name: General-purpose Contour Extraction Routine Generator
head: ndarray-extract-contour
body: The General-purpose Contour Extraction Routine Generator is a code generator that produces a specialized JavaScript function for extracting surfaces from multi-dimensional ndarray data structures. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing grid cells and generating geometric primitives (vertices and faces) based on phase comparisons between adjacent cells. Unlike static isosurface algorithms that hardcode traversal logic, this method generates a custom loop structure at runtime, allowing for flexible iteration orders and multiple input arrays. It sets itself apart from siblings like Marching Cubes by decoupling the traversal engine from the surface definition, enabling the generation of arbitrary contouring routines rather than a single fixed algorithm. The method operates in two phases: generation (compilation) and execution. The generator creates a JavaScript function string that, when executed, performs the contour extraction. Generator Inputs: order: An array specifying the iteration order of the array dimensions (e.g., [1, 0] for 2D row-major). arrayArguments: The number of input ndarray objects to process (e.g., 2). scalarArguments: The number of extra scalar arguments passed to callbacks (e.g., 1). phase: A function phase(a, b, s) that computes the phase of a grid cell given array components and scalars. vertex: A callback vertex(x, y, a00,..., p00,..., s) invoked when a vertex is generated. cell: A callback cell(v0, v1, a0, b0, p0, p1, s) invoked when a face/cell is generated. getters: A boolean array indicating whether to use.get() or direct bracket access [] for array data. Generator Output: A JavaScript function extractContour that accepts the input arrays, scalars, and the callbacks defined above. Execution Inputs: The generated function receives the arrayArguments ndarray objects, scalarArguments scalars, and the vertex/cell/phase functions. The generated code manages memory for phase and vertex ID storage using a pool. Phase Pool (PHASES): A Uint32Array storing the phase value for each grid cell. Vertex ID Pool (VERTEXIDS): A Uint32Array mapping grid cell pointers to generated vertex indices. Pool Size: Calculated as 2 \times \prod{i=0}^{d-2} \text{shape}(\text{order}[i]), where d is the dimension. This size accounts for the current slice and the previous slice needed for boundary detection. Local Cell Data (cube(i, j)): Temporary variables storing the array values at the j-th corner of the current cell for the i-th input array. Local Phase Data (pcube(j)): Temporary variables storing the phase at the j-th corner of the current cell. Pointers (pointer(i)): Current memory offset for the i-th input array. Strides (stride(i, j)): Stride of the i-th array along dimension j. Deltas (delta(i, j)): Precomputed offset differences to access the j-th corner of the current cell relative to the base pointer. 1. Validation: The generator checks that dimension (length of order) is at least 2. If not, it throws an error. 2. Argument Assembly: The generated function signature includes variables for array data, offsets, strides, and pointers for each input array, plus scalar arguments. 3. Initialization: Initialize index(i) = 0 for all dimensions i. Initialize VERTEXCOUNT = 0. Allocate PHASES and VERTEXIDS pools of size 2 \times \prod{i=0}^{d-2} \text{shape}(\text{order}[i]). Initialize POINTER = 0. 4. Precomputation: Compute delta(i, j) for each array i and corner bitmask j (1 \le j < 2^d). delta(i, j) is the sum of strides for dimensions where the bit is set, subtracted from the base. Compute step(i, k) for each array i and dimension k. This defines the memory increment when moving to the next cell in dimension k, accounting for wrapping around smaller dimensions. Compute pdelta(j) and qcube(j) for efficient phase lookup and flipping during iteration. 5. Traversal Loop: The generator creates nested loops based on the order array. For each cell in the grid: 1. Read Current Cell Data: Load array values for the current cell (corner 0) into cube(i, 0) using pointer(i). 2. Compute Current Phase: Call phase(cube(i, 0),..., scalars) and store result in pcube(0) and PHASES[POINTER]. 3. Read Neighbor Phases: Load phases for other corners j (1 \le j < 2^d) from PHASES[POINTER + pdelta(j)] into pcube(j). 4. Boundary Check: If pcube(0) !== pcube(j) for any j, a boundary exists. Read Neighbor Data: Load array values for all corners j into cube(i, j) using pointer(i) + delta(i, j). Generate Vertex: Call vertex with coordinates, all cube(i, j) values, all pcube(j) values, and scalars. Store VERTEXCOUNT in VERTEXIDS[POINTER] and increment VERTEXCOUNT. Generate Faces: For each dimension k, check if the face perpendicular to k is crossed. If pcube(base) !== pcube(subset) (where base is all 1s and subset is base ^ (1<<k)), call cell with the vertices and data for the two adjacent cells. 5. Increment Pointer: POINTER += 1. 6. Iteration Management: After processing a slice (innermost loop), reset POINTER = 0 and call flip() to swap pdelta and qcube values, handling the transition to the next slice. Update pointer(i) by adding step(i, order[i]) when moving to the next cell in the outer loop. 7. Cleanup: Free the PHASES and VERTEXIDS pools. The following pseudocode represents the logic of the generated function, rewritten in Python-like syntax for clarity. It assumes the precomputed variables (delta, step, pdelta, qcube) are available. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractcontour(arrays, scalars, phasefunc, vertexfunc, cellfunc, order, typesig): dimension = len(order) if dimension < 2: raise ValueError("Dimension must be at least 2") arrayargs = len(arrays) scalarargs = len(scalars) shapes = [arrays[0].shape[j] for j in range(dimension)] strides = [[arr.stride[j] for j in range(dimension)] for arr in arrays] # Precompute deltas for each corner bitmask deltas = [] for i in range(arrayargs): row = [] for j in range(1, 1 << dimension): offset = 0 for k in range(dimension): if j & (1 << k): offset -= strides[i][k] row.append(offset) deltas.append(row) # Precompute steps for iteration steps = [] for i in range(arrayargs): row = [] for k in range(dimension): dimidx = order[k] s = strides[i][dimidx] if k > 0: prevdim = order[k-1] s -= strides[i][prevdim] shapes[prevdim] row.append(s) steps.append(row) # Allocate pools poolsize = 2 for i in range(dimension - 2, -1, -1): poolsize = shapes[order[i]] phases = [0] poolsize vertexids = [0] poolsize pointer = 0 vertexcount = 0 # Precompute pdelta and qcube (simplified logic based on source) # In the source, these handle phase lookup offsets and are swapped during iteration pdelta = [0] (1 << dimension) qcube = [0] (1 << dimension) for j in range(1, 1 << dimension): pdelta[j] = j # Simplified placeholder for actual offset calculation from source qcube[j] = j # Initialize indices and pointers indices = [0] dimension pointers = [arr.offset for arr in arrays] def getdata(arridx, ptr, usegetter): if usegetter: return arrays[arridx].get(ptr) else: return arrays[arridx].data[ptr] def processcell(): nonlocal pointer, vertexcount # 1. Read current cell data (corner 0) cubevals = [] for i in range(arrayargs): cubevals.append(getdata(i, pointers[i], typesig[i])) # 2. Compute current phase phaseargs = cubevals + scalars pcube0 = phasefunc(phaseargs) phases[pointer] = pcube0 # 3. Read neighbor phases pcube = [0] (1 << dimension) pcube[0] = pcube0 for j in range(1, 1 << dimension): pcube[j] = phases[pointer + pdelta[j]] # 4. Check for boundary crossing isboundary = any(pcube[0] != pcube[j] for j in range(1, 1 << dimension)) if isboundary: # Read neighbor data for j in range(1, 1 << dimension): for i in range(arrayargs): cubevals.append(getdata(i, pointers[i] + deltas[i][j], typesig[i])) # Generate vertex vertexargs = indices + cubevals + pcube + scalars vertexfunc(vertexargs) vertexids[pointer] = vertexcount vertexcount += 1 # Generate faces base = (1 << dimension) - 1 cornerphase = pcube[base] for k in range(dimension): subset = base ^ (1 << k) edgephase = pcube[subset] if cornerphase != edgephase: # Construct face arguments faceverts = [] temp = subset while temp > 0: bit = temp & -temp faceverts.append(vertexids[pointer + pdelta[bit]]) temp ^= bit faceverts.append(vertexids[pointer]) facedata = [] for i in range(arrayargs): if k & 1: facedata.append(cubevals[base]) facedata.append(cubevals[subset]) else: facedata.append(cubevals[subset]) facedata.append(cubevals[base]) facephases = [edgephase, cornerphase] if k & 1 else [cornerphase, edgephase] facescalars = scalars cellfunc(faceverts, facedata, facephases, facescalars) pointer += 1 # Iterative traversal matching the recursive structure # We simulate the nested loops over dimensions in order # To keep it clean and correct, we'll use a stack-based or explicit nested loop approach # But the source uses recursion. name: Surface Tessellation from Iso-Contours
head: Contour Reconstruction, Contour based reconstruction, Ribbon surface reconstruction, Triangulation of contours
body: Surface Tessellation from Iso-Contours is a surface extraction method that represents iso-surfaces by generating polygonal meshes from stacks of 2D contours extracted from consecutive slices of parallel planes within a data volume. It solves the problem of reconstructing a continuous 3D surface from discrete 2D cross-sections by triangulating the "ribbon" of surface area between adjacent contour sets. Unlike voxel-based methods like Marching Cubes which operate on cell interiors, this method operates directly on the boundary curves, differing primarily in how it establishes topological correspondence and triangulates the space between contours. Inputs: A sequence of 2D scalar slices (volumetric data) or pre-extracted 2D contour sets. Outputs: A triangular mesh representing the iso-surface. Data Structures: 1. Slice Data: A 2D array of scalar values per slice, indexed by (x, y, z) where z is the slice index. 2. Contour Set Cz: For each slice z, a list of closed polygonal chains (contours). Each contour is a list of vertices (x, y). 3. Classification Tree: A directed graph where nodes represent contours and edges represent topological relationships. Nodes: Each node N{z,i} corresponds to the i-th contour in slice z. Edges: A directed edge exists from a node in slice z to a node in slice z+1 if the corresponding contours have a geometric correspondence. 4. Geometric Correspondence Map: A mapping between vertices of contour S in slice z and vertices of contour(s) P in slice z+1. Steps: 1. Data Preparation: Read data slices into memory. Interpolate pixels to achieve structured slices to avoid pixilation artifacts. Extract 2D contours for each slice using thresholding or iso-contour following routines. Let S = \{S0, S1, \dots, Sm\} be the set of contours in slice z, and P = \{P0, P1, \dots, Pn\} be the set of contours in slice z+1. 2. Topological Reconstruction (Classification Tree): Build a classification tree where the number of layers equals the number of slices. Each node on layer z corresponds to a contour in slice z. Determine edges between nodes in adjacent layers by projecting the contours of adjacent slices into a 2D plane. If contours intersect in the projection, an edge exists between the corresponding nodes. Note: This process does not consider nested contours; if contour c is nested in b, the relation between a (previous slice) and c is ignored. 3. Geometric Correspondence Determination: Classify the relationship between adjacent contours into four basic types: pole, cylinder, independent branch, and connected branch. For each point S0 in contour set S, select its two nearest points P0 and P1 from the adjacent contour set P based on the determined geometric correspondence and the classification tree. 4. Triangulation (Ribbon Construction): Form a triangle S0 P0 P1 for each point S0 in set S. Repeat for all points in S to construct the triangular patches of the surface between the two slices. Alternative Triangulation Strategies: Minimum Cost Path (Keppel): Associate all possible triangular tiling arrangements with a directed graph. Search the graph to identify a minimum cost path corresponding to a surface that maximizes the enclosed volume. Minimum Area (Fuchs et al.): Minimize the surface area of the tessellated ribbon. Limited to simply branching structures. Shortest Diagonal (Christiansen & Sederburg): Map contours onto a unit square. Select triangulation based on the shortest diagonal. Ambiguous branching is resolved by user interaction. Maximally Smooth (Xu & Lu): Treat reconstruction as a functional minimization problem solved by a partial differential equation method, constraining the sum of curvatures to be minimum. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def surfacetessellationfromisocontours(slices, threshold): """ Reconstructs a triangular mesh from 2D slices using contour tessellation. Args: slices: List of 2D numpy arrays representing scalar fields for each z-slice. threshold: Scalar value to extract the iso-contour. Returns: vertices: Array of 3D vertices (x, y, z). triangles: Array of triangle indices. """ vertices = [] triangles = [] vertextoindex = {} # Step 1: Extract contours for each slice contours = [] for z, slicedata in enumerate(slices): contourlist = extract2dcontours(slicedata, threshold) contours.append(contourlist) # Step 2: Build Classification Tree and Determine Correspondences correspondences = [] for z in range(len(contours) - 1): currentcontours = contours[z] nextcontours = contours[z+1] adjacency = buildcontouradjacency(currentcontours, nextcontours) vertexmappings = [] for contouridx, currentcontour in enumerate(currentcontours): correspondingcontour = getcorrespondingcontour(currentcontour, nextcontours, adjacency) if correspondingcontour is None: vertexmappings.append([]) continue mappingsforcontour = [] for point in currentcontour: p0, p1 = findtwonearestpoints(point, correspondingcontour) if p0 is not None and p1 is not None: mappingsforcontour.append((point, p0, p1)) else: mappingsforcontour.append(None) vertexmappings.append(mappingsforcontour) correspondences.append(vertexmappings) # Step 3: Generate Vertices and Triangles for z, contourlist in enumerate(contours): for contour in contourlist: for point in contour: idx = len(vertices) vertices.append((point[0], point[1], z)) vertextoindex[(point[0], point[1], z)] = idx for z, vertexmappings in enumerate(correspondences): for contouridx, mappings in enumerate(vertexmappings): if not mappings: continue for mapping in mappings: if mapping is None: continue s0, p0, p1 = mapping idxs0 = vertextoindex.get((s0[0], s0[1], z)) idxp0 = vertextoindex.get((p0[0], p0[1], z+1)) idxp1 = vertextoindex.get((p1[0], p1[1], z+1)) if idxs0 is not None and idxp0 is not None and idxp1 is not None: triangles.append((idxs0, idxp0, idxp1)) return vertices, triangles def extract2dcontours(slicedata, threshold): """Extracts closed contours using Marching Squares.""" contours = [] rows, cols = slicedata.shape edgepoints = {} for y in range(rows - 1): for x in range(cols - 1): v00 = slicedata[y, x] v01 = slicedata[y, x+1] v10 = slicedata[y+1, x] v11 = slicedata[y+1, x+1] case = 0 if v00 >= threshold: case |= 1 if v01 >= threshold: case |= 2 if v11 >= threshold: case |= 4 if v10 >= threshold: case |= 8 if case == 0 or case == 15: continue def interp(v1, v2, p1, p2): t = (threshold - v1) / (v2 - v1) if v2 != v1 else 0.5 return (p1[0] + t(p2[0]-p1[0]), p1[1] + t(p2[1]-p1[1])) edges = [] if (case & 1) == 0: edges.append(interp(v00, v01, (x, y), (x+1, y))) if (case & 2) == 0: edges.append(interp(v01, v11, (x+1, y), (x+1, y+1))) if (case & 4) == 0: edges.append(interp(v11, v10, (x+1, y+1), (x, y+1))) if (case & 8) == 0: edges.append(interp(v10, v00, (x, y+1), (x, y))) # Standard Marching Squares edge pairing to form closed loops if case in [1, 14]: edges.append(edges[0]); edges.append(edges[3]) elif case in [2, 13]: edges.append(edges[0]); edges.append(edges[1]) elif case in [3, 12]: edges.append(edges[0]); edges.append(edges[1]); edges.append(edges[2]); edges.append(edges[3]) elif case in [4, 11]: edges.append(edges[1]); edges.append(edges[2]) elif case in [5, 10]: edges.append(edges[0]); edges.append(edges[2]) elif case in [6, 9]: edges.append(edges[1]); edges.append(edges[3]) elif case in [7, 8]: edges.append(edges[2]); edges.append(edges[3]) if len(edges) >= 2: contours.append(edges) return contours def buildcontouradjacency(currentcontours, nextcontours): """Determines which contours in currentcontours have geometric relations with contours in nextcontours.""" adjacency = {i: [] for i in range(len(currentcontours))} for i, c1 in enumerate(currentcontours): for j, c2 in enumerate(nextcontours): if contoursintersect(c1, c2): adjacency[i].append(j) return adjacency def contoursintersect(c1, c2): """Checks if two 2D contours intersect using polygon intersection.""" if not c1 or not c2: return False # Bounding box check first def bbox(poly): xs = [p[0] for p in poly]; ys = [p[1] for p in poly] return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys) b1, b2 = bbox(c1), bbox(c2) if b1[2] < b2[0] or b1[3] < b2[1] or b2[2] < b1[0] or b2[3] < b1[1]: return False # Segment intersection check def segintersect(p1, p2, p3, p4): def ccw(A,B,C): return (C[0]-A[0])(B[1]-A[1]) - (B[0]-A[0])(C[1]-A[1]) return ccw(p1,p3,p4)ccw(p2,p3,p4) <= 0 and ccw(p1,p2,p3)ccw(p1,p2,p4) <= 0 for i in range(len(c1)): for j in range(len(c2)): if segintersect(c1[i], c1[(i+1)%len(c1)], c2[j], c2[(j+1)%len(c2)]): return True return False def getcorrespondingcontour(currentcontour, nextcontours, adjacency): """Selects the specific contour from nextcontours that corresponds to currentcontour.""" # Find index of currentcontour in adjacency keys idx = -1 for k in adjacency: if adjacency[k] and currentcontour == nextcontours[adjacency[k][0]]: idx = k break if idx == -1: return None # If multiple correspondences exist, ambiguities arise # Here we pick the first valid correspondence return nextcontours[adjacency[idx][0]] def findtwonearestpoints(point, contour): """Finds the two nearest points on a contour to a given point.""" if len(contour) < 2: return None, None distances = [(p, math.hypot(point[0]-p[0], point[1]-p[1])) for p in contour] distances.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) return distances[0][0], distances[1][0] A data-driven technique for volume rendering that assists in the specification of transfer functions by identifying significant isosurfaces within a scalar field. It computes specific geometric and gradient-based measures for discretized scalar values to highlight structures of high importance, such as separation surfaces. Unlike histogram-based methods that rely on intensity distributions, Contour Spectrum focuses on the topological and geometric properties of the isosurfaces themselves, using a directed acyclic graph to track their evolution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient for data that is naturally organized in slices (e.g., medical CT/MRI). Can handle complex topologies if the correspondence rules are robust. Allows for manual intervention to resolve ambiguities. Limitations: Ambiguities arise when more than one contour exists on a slice, making it difficult to determine connections. The edge determination process does not consider nested contours, leading to topological errors in such cases. Requires interpolation to avoid pixilation, adding computational cost. Limited to simply branching structures for some minimum-area algorithms. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Surface Tessellation from Iso-Contours is one of the first methods used to represent iso-surfaces, dating back to the early days of volumetric rendering. Keppel was one of the first to devise a method to reconstruct the ribbon surface defined by two consecutive contours. Fuchs et al. presented a solution minimizing surface area. Christiansen and Sederburg achieved similar results by mapping contours to a unit square. Xu and Lu solved the problem using a partial differential equation method to maximize smoothness. The THREA04 system, developed by Mazziotta et al. in 1976, was capable of displaying 3D images from 20 sections using threshold segmentation and automatic boundary detection. The method is widely used in medical imaging for 3D reconstruction from CT or MRI slices. name: Contour Spectrum
head: Bajaj et al. Isosurface Measures, Bajaj et al. technique
body: Contour Spectrum is a data-driven technique for volume rendering that assists in transfer function specification by identifying significant isosurfaces within a scalar field. It computes geometric and gradient-based measures for discretized scalar values to highlight structures of high importance, such as separation surfaces. Unlike histogram-based methods that rely on intensity distributions, Contour Spectrum focuses on the topological and geometric properties of the isosurfaces themselves, using a directed acyclic graph to track their evolution. Inputs: A 3D scalar volume dataset and a set of discretized scalar values spanning the data range. Outputs: A set of scalar values mapped to optical attributes (typically opacity) via a transfer function, and a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representing the topological behavior of the isosurfaces. Data Structures: 1. Measure Vector: For each scalar value si, a vector containing the isosurface area A(si), the enclosed volume V{enc}(si), and the gradient integral G(si). 2. Topological DAG: A graph where nodes and edges register separations and junctions of connected isosurface segments as the defining scalar value varies monotonically. Steps: 1. Discretization: Define a set of scalar values si spanning the volume range. The discretization step size is Not given in the sources. 2. Surface Extraction: Extract the isosurface Iso(si) for each si using a standard mesh generation algorithm. 3. Measure Computation: For each Iso(si): a. Compute the surface area A(si) as the sum of the areas of the extracted mesh faces. b. Compute the enclosed volume V{enc}(si) as the volume bounded by the closed mesh. c. Compute the gradient integral G(si) = \int{Iso(si)} |\nabla V| \, dA as the integral of the gradient magnitude along the isosurface. 4. Topological Analysis: Construct the DAG by analyzing the connectivity of isosurface components across consecutive scalar values si and s{i+1}, registering separations (splitting) and junctions (merging). 5. Selection: Identify scalar values with high A(si), V{enc}(si), and G(si) as important separation surfaces. Identify noisy areas as regions with high topological activity (many junctions and separations) in the DAG. 6. Transfer Function Mapping: Associate the selected scalar values with opacity values in the transfer function to emphasize the corresponding structures. Parameters: Discretization step for scalar values: Not given in the sources. Thresholds for "high" measures: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise: Noisy regions exhibit high topological activity in the DAG, distinguishing them from true separation surfaces. Precision: Accurate computation of area, volume, and gradient integration requires robust mesh processing and accurate gradient estimation at the surface. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method requires surface extraction, geometric integration, and topological analysis for every discretized scalar value. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing computed measures and the topological DAG for all scalar values. Strengths: Provides geometric and topological insight into the data structure; effective at identifying significant separation surfaces; distinguishes noisy areas through topological activity analysis. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to per-scalar-value extraction and integration; sensitive to the discretization of scalar values. When to use: When the goal is to identify and emphasize significant internal structures in a volume based on their geometric and topological properties. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Contour Spectrum was proposed by Bajaj, Pascucci, and Schikore in 1997. It is a pioneering data-driven technique that assimilates surface fitting resources to discover isosurfaces after an initial specification. The method computes scalar field measures to help select values representing important structures, which are then associated with optical attributes via a transfer function. It was followed by automated detection methods using histograms, such as those by Kindlmann and Durkin (1998) and Sereda et al. (2006). Similar strategies were also proposed by Pekar et al.. name: THREAD System
head: Three dimensional Reconstruction And Display
body: The THREAD System reconstructs 3D surfaces from a sequence of 2D medical image slices by tessellating between detected outlines on consecutive planes. It sets itself apart from volumetric grid methods by operating directly on discrete slice contours rather than interpolating a full 3D scalar field. Inputs: A sequence of 2D image slices (e.g., 20 sections) containing scalar intensity data representing a sectioned object. Outputs: A set of surface polygons representing the reconstructed 3D surface, ready for rendering with hidden-line removal and shading. Data Structures: 1. Slice Outlines: For each slice i, a list of 2D coordinates (x, y) defining the boundary of the object of interest. 2. Surface Patches: A collection of polygonal faces connecting vertices from slice i to slice i+1. Steps: 1. Threshold Segmentation: Apply threshold segmentation with optional manual correction to each slice to separate the object of interest from the background. 2. Automatic Boundary Detection: Identify connected component outlines on the thresholded slices. 3. Inter-slice Tessellation: Define surfaces by tessellating the area between the outlines on consecutive slices. 4. Shading: Apply a simple surface-normal based shading algorithm to the resulting surface polygons. 5. Rendering: Display the sectioned object outlines and reconstructed surfaces at different angles, with or without hidden-line removal. Parameters: Threshold Value: Determines the segmentation boundary. Not given in the sources. Number of Slices: The method was demonstrated with 20 sections. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Changes: If the object's topology changes between slices (e.g., splitting or merging), the correspondence between outlines on slice i and i+1 becomes ambiguous. Missing Outlines: If a slice contains no object (background only), the tessellation step must handle the absence of vertices. Simulation Grid Cell Skipping: An optimization technique that accelerates surface extraction by skipping over empty and fully occupied simulation grid cells, processing only partially filled cells. It leverages coarse-grained cell status to bypass uniform data, building on the THREAD System's ray-marching framework. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The system was demonstrated processing 20 sections to display 30 images. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard polygonal tessellation and surface-normal based shading. Limitations: Resolution is constrained by the slice spacing and 2D image resolution. When to use: The sources do not specify operational guidelines for specific use cases. When not to use: The sources do not specify operational guidelines for specific use cases. The THREAD System was developed in 1976 by Mazziotta et al.. It was designed for stereotactic neurosurgery planning to visualize internal anatomical structures from sectioned object outlines. name: Simulation Grid Cell Skipping
head: Surface Extraction with Simulation Grid
body: Simulation Grid Cell Skipping is an optimization technique for surface extraction that accelerates iteration over voxel columns by skipping over empty and fully occupied simulation grid cells, processing only partially filled cells. It differs from standard voxel traversal by leveraging the coarse-grained status of simulation grid cells to bypass large volumes of uniform data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A simulation grid with cells classified as empty, full, or partially filled; a view ray for each voxel column. Output: A list of relevant voxels within partially filled cells for surface extraction. Data Structures: Simulation Grid: A regular 3D grid where each cell stores a status flag: EMPTY, FULL, or PARTIAL. Voxel Column: A sequence of voxels along a view ray. Packed Machine Words: Bits representing voxel occupancy, processed in chunks for efficiency. Numbered Steps: 1. For each voxel column, initialize a ray marcher along the view ray corresponding to that column. 2. Iterate over packed machine words rather than single bits, using bit counting intrinsics to quickly determine the next relevant bits to be considered. 3. March along the view ray through the simulation grid. 4. Keep marching through full or empty simulation grid cells until encountering a succession of partially filled cells. 5. Interrupt ray marching to iterate over the corresponding voxels when partially filled cells are encountered. 6. When the iteration reaches the end of the current set of connected partially filled cells, resume ray marching in the simulation grid. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Do not skip cells that have partially filled neighbors to avoid cutting off detailed boundary surfaces potentially formed by particles overlapping cell boundaries; only inner full and empty cells may be skipped. Ray marching precision may cause missed intersections if cell boundaries are not handled correctly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EMPTY, FULL, PARTIAL = 0, 1, 2 def simulategridcellskipping(grid, rays): """ Accelerates surface extraction by skipping empty/full cells. Args: grid: Object with.cellsize,.boundsmin,.boundsmax,.getcellat(),.getneighbor() rays: List of ray objects with.origin,.direction Returns: List of voxels to process for surface extraction """ processedvoxels = [] for ray in rays: t = 0.0 while True: pos = ray.origin + ray.direction t if not (grid.boundsmin[0] <= pos[0] < grid.boundsmax[0] and grid.boundsmin[1] <= pos[1] < grid.boundsmax[1] and grid.boundsmin[2] <= pos[2] < grid.boundsmax[2]): break cell = grid.getcellat(pos) # Pitfall: only skip inner full/empty cells haspartialneighbor = any( grid.getneighbor(pos, offset).status == PARTIAL for offset in get26offsets()) if cell.status in (EMPTY, FULL) and not haspartialneighbor: t += grid.cellsize continue # Interrupt ray marching to iterate over voxels in partially filled cells voxels = [] for word in cell.voxelbits: while word: # Use bit counting intrinsics to find next set bit bit = word & -word voxels.append({"bitmask": bit, "processed": True}) word ^= bit processedvoxels.extend(voxels) t += grid.cellsize return processedvoxels def get26offsets(): offsets = [] for dx in (-1, 0, 1): for dy in (-1, 0, 1): for dz in (-1, 0, 1): if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue offsets.append((dx, dy, dz)) return offsets A technique to exclude fully covered cells from isosurface extraction in simulations using Embedded Boundary (EB) methods, ensuring the surface geometry respects the boundary geometry defined by volume fractions. It differs from this method by specifically targeting EB-covered cells (volume fraction == 0) rather than just empty or fully occupied cells, and it requires specific ghost cell handling to avoid artifacts at AMR coarse/fine boundaries. Strengths: Significant speedup for simulations with large empty or full regions. Limitations: Overhead of checking neighbor status; less effective for highly fragmented partial regions. When to Use: SPH simulations with regular grids and distinct empty/full/partial regions. Not given in the sources.
