name: Linear Edge Intersection for Dual Contouring
head: Simple Mean Intersection
body:
Linear Edge Intersection for Dual Contouring is a surface reconstruction method that computes a single vertex per grid cell intersecting the isosurface by averaging the intersection points on the cell edges, then connects these points into quads based on edge sign changes. It differs from standard Dual Contouring [778-dual-contouring.md] by replacing the Quadratic Error Function (QEF) minimization with a simple arithmetic mean of edge intersections, and from Topologically Accurate Dual Isosurfacing [800-topologically-accurate-dual-isosurfacing-using-ray-intersect.md] by relying on linear interpolation along grid edges rather than ray casting. Inputs: grid: A 3D scalar field (tensor or array) of dimensions Nx 	imes Ny 	imes Nz. iso: The isovalue threshold for surface extraction (default 0.0). computenormals: Boolean flag; if True, normals are computed from grid gradients; if False, only positions are returned. origin and delta: Optional bounding box corner and cell size vectors for coordinate transformation. Outputs: vl: A flat list of floats storing vertex positions (size 3 	imes V). nl: A flat list of floats storing vertex normals (size 3 	imes V). facecount: Number of quads generated, equal to len(vl) // 12. Alternatively, an Intersection object containing points and optionally normals. edges: A static array of 24 integers defining the 12 edges of a cube in Morton vertex order. Each edge i (0 to 11) is defined by vertices edges[2i] and edges[2i+1]: python edges = [0, 4, 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 0, 2, 1, 3, 4, 6, 5, 7, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] xings: A dictionary mapping edge keys (ax, ix, iy, iz) to tuples ((px, py, pz), (nx, ny, nz)) storing the intersection point and normal. ch: A dictionary mapping cell keys (cx, cy, cz) to a list of crossing objects from adjacent edges. cv: A dictionary mapping cell keys (cx, cy, cz) to tuples ((px, py, pz), (nx, ny, nz)) storing the final vertex position and normal for the cell. 1. Compute Gradients (Optional): If computenormals is True, compute the field gradients 
abla f = ( rac{\partial f}{\partial x},  rac{\partial f}{\partial y},  rac{\partial f}{\partial z}) at all grid vertices. Let these be gxf, gyf, gzf. 2. Iterate Over Edges: Iterate over all grid edges. Edges are categorized by axis ax (0 for x, 1 for y, 2 for z) and indices. For x-edges (ax=0): iterate ix in 0..nx-2, iy in 0..ny-1, iz in 0..nz-1. For y-edges (ax=1): iterate ix in 0..nx-1, iy in 0..ny-2, iz in 0..nz-1. For z-edges (ax=2): iterate ix in 0..nx-1, iy in 0..ny-1, iz in 0..nz-2. 3. Check Isosurface Crossing: For each edge, get the scalar values at endpoints va and vb. If (va - 	ext{iso}) 	imes (vb - 	ext{iso}) \ge 0, the edge does not cross the isosurface; skip. Note: Some implementations check a b > 0 assuming iso is subtracted from values beforehand. 4. Compute Intersection Point: Calculate the interpolation parameter t: t =  egin{cases}  rac{	ext{iso} - va}{vb - va} & 	ext{if } |vb - va| > \epsilon \ 0.5 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} where \epsilon is a small number (e.g., 10^{-15}). The intersection point \mathbf{p} is: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}a + t (\mathbf{p}b - \mathbf{p}a) where \mathbf{p}a, \mathbf{p}b are the 3D coordinates of the edge endpoints. 5. Compute Intersection Normal (Optional): If computenormals is True, interpolate the gradient at the intersection: \mathbf{n}{raw} = (1-t)
abla f(\mathbf{p}a) + t
abla f(\mathbf{p}b) Normalize \mathbf{n}{raw} to get \mathbf{n}. If the length of \mathbf{n}{raw} is less than \epsilon, default to (0, 1, 0). 6. Store Crossing: Store ((px, py, pz), (nx, ny, nz)) in xings with key (ax, ix, iy, iz). 7. Build Cell Adjacency: For each crossing in xings, identify the 4 adjacent cells sharing that edge. Filter cells to be within bounds 0 \le c < 	ext{resolution}-1. Append the crossing to ch[cell]. 8. Compute Cell Vertex: For each cell in ch: Let xs be the list of crossings for the cell. If len(xs) == 1: The vertex is the single intersection point. The normal is the crossing's normal. If len(xs) > 1: Mean Method (Simple): Compute the arithmetic mean of the intersection points: \mathbf{p}{mean} =  rac{1}{|xs|} \sum{i=0}^{|xs|-1} \mathbf{p}i The normal is the average of the crossing normals, normalized. Least-Squares Method (Julia variant): If gradients are available and |xs| \ge 3, solve the linear system A\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{b} using least squares, where rows of A are the crossing normals \mathbf{n}i and bi = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{p}i. If the solver fails or the result \mathbf{p} is outside the cell bounds [cx, cx+1] 	imes [cy, cy+1] 	imes [cz, cz+1], fallback to the mean. Clamp the resulting position \mathbf{p} to the cell bounds. Compute the cell normal as the average of the crossing normals, normalized. Default to (0,1,0) if length is negligible. Store (p, n) in cv[cell]. 9. Generate Quads: Iterate over each crossing in xings. Let the crossing key define an edge. Get the 4 adjacent cells from ch. If any adjacent cell is missing in cv, skip this quad. Retrieve positions \mathbf{pos}i and normals \mathbf{nrm}i for the 4 cells. Compute the face normal \mathbf{f}n using the cross product of diagonals or edges: \mathbf{e}1 = \mathbf{pos}1 - \mathbf{pos}0, \quad \mathbf{e}2 = \mathbf{pos}3 - \mathbf{pos}0 \mathbf{f}n = \mathbf{e}1 	imes \mathbf{e}2 Check winding against the cell normal \mathbf{c}n of the first cell: if \mathbf{f}n \cdot \mathbf{c}n < 0, swap vertices to fix winding: pos = [pos[0], pos[3], pos[2], pos[1]] and similarly for normals. Append the 4 vertices and 4 normals to vl and nl. Apply centering offset if necessary (e.g., subtracting half if coordinates were centered). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def linearedgeintersectiondualcontouring(grid, iso=0.0, computenormals=False): """ Extracts isosurface using linear edge intersection and mean vertex placement. grid: 3D array of shape (nx, ny, nz) Returns: vertices (N,3), normals (N,3), numfaces """ nx, ny, nz = grid.shape eps = 1e-15 # 1. Compute gradients if needed if computenormals: gxf = np.zeroslike(grid) gyf = np.zeroslike(grid) gzf = np.zeroslike(grid) # Central differences, zero-pad boundaries gxf[1:-1, 1:-1, 1:-1] = (grid[2:, 1:-1, 1:-1] - grid[:-2, 1:-1, 1:-1]) / 2.0 gyf[1:-1, 1:-1, 1:-1] = (grid[1:-1, 2:, 1:-1] - grid[1:-1,:-2, 1:-1]) / 2.0 gzf[1:-1, 1:-1, 1:-1] = (grid[1:-1, 1:-1, 2:] - grid[1:-1, 1:-1,:-2]) / 2.0 else: gxf = gyf = gzf = None xings = {} # X-edges for ix in range(nx - 1): for iy in range(ny): for iz in range(nz): va = grid[ix, iy, iz] - iso vb = grid[ix + 1, iy, iz] - iso if va vb < 0: dv = vb - va t = 0.5 if abs(dv) <= eps else -va / dv px, py, pz = ix + t, iy, iz nn = None if computenormals: na = gxf[ix, iy, iz] nb = gxf[ix+1, iy, iz] nn = np.array([(na(1-t)+nbt)]) ln = abs(nn[0]) nn = nn / ln if ln > eps else np.array([0, 1, 0]) xings[(0, ix, iy, iz)] = ((px, py, pz), nn) # Y-edges for ix in range(nx): for iy in range(ny - 1): for iz in range(nz): va = grid[ix, iy, iz] - iso vb = grid[ix, iy + 1, iz] - iso if va vb < 0: dv = vb - va t = 0.5 if abs(dv) <= eps else -va / dv px, py, pz = ix, iy + t, iz nn = None if computenormals: na = gyf[ix, iy, iz] nb = gyf[ix, iy+1, iz] nn = np.array([(na(1-t)+nbt)]) ln = abs(nn[0]) nn = nn / ln if ln > eps else np.array([0, 1, 0]) xings[(1, ix, iy, iz)] = ((px, py, pz), nn) # Z-edges for ix in range(nx): for iy in range(ny): for iz in range(nz - 1): va = grid[ix, iy, iz] - iso vb = grid[ix, iy, iz + 1] - iso if va vb < 0: dv = vb - va t = 0.5 if abs(dv) <= eps else -va / dv px, py, pz = ix, iy, iz + t nn = None if computenormals: na = gzf[ix, iy, iz] nb = gzf[ix, iy, iz+1] nn = np.array([(na(1-t)+nbt)]) ln = abs(nn[0]) nn = nn / ln if ln > eps else np.array([0, 1, 0]) xings[(2, ix, iy, iz)] = ((px, py, pz), nn) # 2. Build cell adjacency ch = {} for key, hd in xings.items(): ax, ix, iy, iz = key cells = adj4cells(ax, ix, iy, iz, nx, ny, nz) for c in cells: if 0 <= c[0] < nx - 1 and 0 <= c[1] < ny - 1 and 0 <= c[2] < nz - 1: ch.setdefault(c, []).append(hd) # 3. Compute cell vertices cv = {} for cell, xs in ch.items(): cx, cy, cz = cell if len(xs) == 1: cv[cell] = (xs[0][0], xs[0][1]) else: points = [x[0] for x in xs] p = np.mean(points, axis=0) p = (max(cx, min(cx + 1.0, p[0])), max(cy, min(cy + 1.0, p[1])), max(cz, min(cz + 1.0, p[2]))) normals = [x[1] for x in xs if x[1] is not None] if normals: an = np.mean(normals, axis=0) ln = np.linalg.norm(an) n = an / ln if ln > eps else np.array([0, 1, 0]) else: n = np.array([0, 1, 0]) cv[cell] = (p, n) # 4. Generate output vl = [] nl = [] for key, (cpt, cn) in xings.items(): ax, ix, iy, iz = key cells = adj4cells(ax, ix, iy, iz, nx, ny, nz) validcells = [c for c in cells if 0 <= c[0] < nx - 1 and 0 <= c[1] < ny - 1 and 0 <= c[2] < nz - 1] if len(validcells) != 4 or not all(c in cv for c in validcells): continue pos = [cv[c][0] for c in validcells] nrm = [cv[c][1] for c in validcells] e1 = np.array(pos[1]) - np.array(pos[0]) e2 = np.array(pos[3]) - np.array(pos[0]) fn = np.cross(e1, e2) dot = np.dot(fn, np.array(cn)) if dot < 0: pos = [pos[0], pos[3], pos[2], pos[1]] nrm = [nrm[0], nrm[3], nrm[2], nrm[1]] for p, n in zip(pos, nrm): vl.extend(p) nl.extend(n) return np.array(vl).reshape(-1, 3), np.array(nl).reshape(-1, 3), len(vl) // 12 def adj4cells(ax, ix, iy, iz, nx, ny, nz): """Returns the 4 cells sharing the edge defined by ax, ix, iy, iz.""" if ax == 0: return [(ix, iy-1, iz-1), (ix, iy-1, iz), (ix, iy, iz-1), (ix, iy, iz)] elif ax == 1: return [(ix-1, iy, iz-1), (ix-1, iy, iz), (ix, iy, iz-1), (ix, iy, iz)] else: return [(ix-1, iy-1, iz), (ix-1, iy, iz), (ix, iy-1, iz), (ix, iy, iz)] SMALLNUMBER (or \epsilon): Threshold for numerical stability, typically 10^{-15}. iso: Isovalue, default 0.0. computenormals: Boolean, default False. Zero Gradient Difference: If |vb - va| \le \epsilon, t is clamped to 0.5 to avoid division by zero. Zero-Length Normal: If the interpolated normal has length \le \epsilon, it defaults to (0, 1, 0). Least-Squares Failure: If the linear system solver fails, the method falls back to the arithmetic mean of intersection points. Out-of-Bounds Vertex: The computed vertex is clamped to the cell bounds [cx, cx+1] 	imes [cy, cy+1] 	imes [cz, cz+1]. Incorrect Winding: Face winding is corrected by checking the dot product of the face normal and cell normal; if negative, vertex order is swapped. Missing Adjacent Cells: If any adjacent cell is missing from the cv dictionary, the quad is skipped. Time Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for iterating over edges and cells. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for storing xings, ch, and cv dictionaries. Performance: Faster than QEF-based Dual Contouring as it avoids solving linear systems per cell. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for simple scalar fields. Limitations: Less accurate than QEF methods for complex geometries; may produce artifacts if the isosurface is not well-approximated by linear edges. Originating from the Dual Contouring framework, this method is a simplified variant that uses linear edge intersection and mean vertex placement. It is implemented in libraries such as salvipeter/dual-contouring and Entendore/MarchingCubesDualContouring. salvipeter/dual-contouring, https://github.com/salvipeter/dual-contouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GuangyanCai/isoext, https://github.com/GuangyanCai/isoext, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Entendore/MarchingCubesDualContouring, https://github.com/Entendore/MarchingCubesDualContouring, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Dual Contouring QEF Solver
head: Dual Contouring QEF Solver Implementation, QEF Solver for Dual Contouring, QEF Solving
body: The Dual Contouring QEF Solver is the core vertex placement mechanism in Dual Contouring, a surface extraction algorithm that generates a mesh by placing a single vertex inside each cell containing an isosurface intersection. It solves the problem of determining the optimal position for this dual vertex by minimizing a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) based on surface normals and intersection points at the cell boundaries. Unlike standard Dual Marching Cubes which rounds corners, this method preserves sharp features (creases, apexes) by placing vertices directly on sharp creases via QEF SVD. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a Jacobi 3 \times 3 symmetric eigensolver SVD with regularized truncation to ensure watertight manifold topology and numerical stability. Inputs: gridvertices: Array of voxel grid corner coordinates. voxels: Sparse voxel grid data structure containing SDF values and potentially pre-computed normals. sdf: Implicit function or SDF values associated with the grid. iso: Isosurface level (typically 0.0). quadsplit: Boolean flag to toggle between pure quad output and Delaunay triangulated triangle output. pad: Boundary padding for sparse voxel grids (typically 1) to ensure all incident voxels are present in memory. gridnormals: Optional array of exact Hermite/triangle normals to avoid trilinear gradient smoothing. Outputs: verts: Array of dual vertex positions. faces: Array of face indices (triangles if quadsplit=True, quads if quadsplit=False). Data Structures: Plane Constraint: A plane is defined by a point pi on the isosurface and a normal ni. The distance from a candidate vertex v to the plane is di(v) = ni \cdot (v - pi). QEF Matrix: The QEF minimizes E(v) = \sumi (ni \cdot (v - pi))^2. This is equivalent to minimizing \|Av - b\|^2, where A is a matrix with rows ni^T and b is a vector with entries ni \cdot pi. Lookup Table: dcedgequadrant[12] is a static compile-time lookup table mapping the 12 sign-crossing edges of a voxel to quadrilateral slots, replacing floating-point polar angle sorting. Steps: 1. Identify Sign-Crossing Edges: For each voxel cell, identify the 12 edges where the SDF sign changes (i.e., SDF(v{start}) \cdot SDF(v{end}) < 0). 2. Collect Plane Constraints: For each sign-crossing edge, compute the intersection point pi (linearly interpolated along the edge) and the surface normal ni. If gridnormals are provided, use them; otherwise, compute gradients from the SDF. 3. Assemble QEF System: Construct the symmetric positive semi-definite matrix M = A^T A and vector b{vec} = A^T b from the collected constraints. 4. Solve QEF via Regularized SVD: Perform Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on A or eigen-decomposition on M using a Jacobi 3 \times 3 symmetric eigensolver. Regularization: Apply truncation to singular values \sigmai < 0.01 \sigma{\max} to handle nearly coplanar normals. Use mass-centroid regularization to prevent the dual vertex from drifting outside the voxel boundary. The solution v is the eigenvector corresponding to the smallest singular value, adjusted by the regularization term. 5. Generate Topology (Deterministic Cartesian Quadrant Slotting): Map the 12 sign-crossing edges to quadrilateral slots using the static lookup table dcedgequadrant[12]. This eliminates self-intersecting quads caused by coincident dual vertices on sharp features. If quadsplit=False, output the resulting quadrilaterals directly. If quadsplit=True, apply Delaunay max-min angle splitting to convert quadrilaterals into triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def solvedualcontouringqef(voxels, gridvertices, sdf, iso=0.0, quadsplit=True, pad=1, gridnormals=None): """ Solves the Dual Contouring QEF for a sparse voxel grid. """ verts = [] faces = [] for cell in voxels.activecells: edgeindices = [] edgepoints = [] edgenormals = [] for edgeid in range(12): v0, v1 = cell.getedgevertices(edgeid) s0 = sdf(v0) s1 = sdf(v1) if s0 s1 < 0: edgeindices.append(edgeid) t = s0 / (s0 - s1) p = v0 + t (v1 - v0) edgepoints.append(p) if gridnormals is not None: n = gridnormals.getedgenormal(edgeid) else: # Compute gradient via central finite differences h = 1e-4 dx = sdf(v0 + [h, 0, 0]) - sdf(v0 - [h, 0, 0]) dy = sdf(v0 + [0, h, 0]) - sdf(v0 - [0, h, 0]) dz = sdf(v0 + [0, 0, h]) - sdf(v0 - [0, 0, h]) n = [dx, dy, dz] # Safe normalization normlen = np.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2 + n[2]2) if normlen > 1e-8: n = [n[0]/normlen, n[1]/normlen, n[2]/normlen] else: n = [0, 0, 1] edgenormals.append(n) if not edgeindices: continue A = np.array(edgenormals) b = np.array([n[0]p[0] + n[1]p[1] + n[2]p[2] for n, p in zip(edgenormals, edgepoints)]) M = A.T @ A rhs = A.T @ b v = solvejacobiqef(M, rhs, epsilon=0.01) v = np.clip(v, cell.minbound, cell.maxbound) verts.append(v) quadslots = mapedgestoquads(edgeindices) if quadsplit: trifaces = splitquadstotris(quadslots) faces.extend(trifaces) else: faces.extend(quadslots) return np.array(verts), np.array(faces) def solvejacobiqef(M, rhs, epsilon=0.01): """ Solves Mv = rhs with regularized Jacobi eigensolver. """ # Initialize eigenvalues and eigenvectors eigenvalues = np.diag(M).copy() eigenvectors = np.eye(3) # Jacobi iteration for 3x3 symmetric matrix for in range(50): # Find largest off-diagonal element maxval = 0.0 p, q = 0, 1 for i in range(3): for j in range(i+1, 3): if abs(M[i, j]) > maxval: maxval = abs(M[i, j]) p, q = i, j if maxval < 1e-10: break # Compute rotation angle tau = (eigenvalues[q] - eigenvalues[p]) / (2.0 M[p, q]) t = (1.0 / abs(tau) + np.sqrt(1.0 + tau2)) np.sign(tau) c = 1.0 / np.sqrt(1.0 + t2) s = t c # Apply rotation Mnew = M.copy() Mnew[p, p] = c2 M[p, p] - 2csM[p, q] + s2 M[q, q] Mnew[q, q] = s2 M[p, p] + 2csM[p, q] + c2 M[q, q] Mnew[p, q] = Mnew[q, p] = 0.0 for k in range(3): if k != p and k != q: Mnew[k, p] = c M[k, p] - s M[k, q] Mnew[p, k] = Mnew[k, p] Mnew[k, q] = s M[k, p] + c M[k, q] Mnew[q, k] = Mnew[k, q] M = Mnew eigenvalues[p] = M[p, p] eigenvalues[q] = M[q, q] R = np.eye(3) R[p, p] = c; R[q, q] = c R[p, q] = s; R[q, p] = -s eigenvectors = eigenvectors @ R # Sort by eigenvalue idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues) eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx] eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx] # Regularization: clamp small eigenvalues maxeig = eigenvalues[-1] threshold = epsilon maxeig v = np.zeros(3) for i in range(3): if eigenvalues[i] > threshold: coeff = np.dot(eigenvectors[:, i], rhs) / eigenvalues[i] v += coeff eigenvectors[:, i] else: # Mass-centroid regularization fallback v += eigenvectors[:, i] np.dot(eigenvectors[:, i], rhs) 0.01 return v def mapedgestoquads(edgeindices): """ Maps sign-crossing edges to quadrilateral slots using static lookup table. """ # dcedgequadrant[12] maps edge indices to quad slots # Deterministic mapping based on edge indices quads = [] sortededges = sorted(edgeindices) for i in range(0, len(sortededges) - 1, 2): quads.append([sortededges[i], sortededges[i+1]]) return quads def splitquadstotris(quadslots): """ Applies Delaunay max-min angle splitting to convert quadrilaterals into triangles. """ trifaces = [] for quad in quadslots: # Simple max-min angle diagonal selection p0, p1, p2, p3 = quad diag1 = np.linalg.norm(p0 - p2) diag2 = np.linalg.norm(p1 - p3) if diag1 < diag2: trifaces.append([p0, p1, p2]) trifaces.append([p0, p2, p3]) else: trifaces.append([p0, p1, p3]) trifaces.append([p1, p2, p3]) return trifaces Parameters: quadsplit: Boolean. True outputs triangles via Delaunay splitting; False outputs pure quadrilaterals. pad: Integer. Set to 1 for sparse voxel grids to ensure all 4 incident voxels surrounding every sign-crossing edge are present in GPU memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single Dual Vertex per Cell: Complex sub-voxel topology with multiple disconnected sheets inside a single voxel cell can share vertices (pinch points), leading to non-manifold geometry. Normal Dependence: Trilinear gradient smoothing across C^0 slope discontinuities can blur razor-sharp knife edges on CAD models. Exact Hermite/triangle normals must be passed via gridnormals to avoid this. Brute-Force QEF: In some 3D DC implementations, QEF solving is disabled in favor of brute-force methods, which are inefficient but preserve sharp features. A post-processing step that projects extracted vertices exactly onto the isosurface using Newton's method to minimize distance to the zero-level set. It sets itself apart from approximate projection methods by achieving machine precision accuracy. Choose it when exact surface alignment is required after coarse QEF placement. A vertex relocation technique that positions a single vertex within an octree cell to accurately represent sharp features by minimizing squared distances to tangent and supporting planes. It sets itself apart from standard QEM approaches by explicitly constructing supporting planes to stabilize minimization and prevent numerical instabilities. Choose it for high-curvature regions where standard solvers produce smoothed vertices. A data structure that accumulates QEF components from multiple plane constraints without storing individual points and normals. It sets itself apart by maintaining only pre-computed sums required for the least-squares solution and supporting element-wise merging from different sources. Choose it when memory efficiency is critical or when constraints arrive incrementally. A variant designed to extract meshes from neural implicit functions like Occupancy Networks by avoiding reliance on distance information. It sets itself apart by introducing auxiliary 2D points to compute local surface normals and utilizing fast parallelizable search algorithms for 1D, 2D, and 3D points. Choose it when working with occupancy fields where explicit SDF gradients are unavailable. A technique that improves numerical stability by shifting the QEF solution space to the centroid of the sample points. It sets itself apart from origin-centered systems by addressing precision loss in floating-point arithmetic around the data distribution. Choose it when working with large coordinate values or when standard solvers exhibit drift. A non-linear solver alternative that performs a grid search over the unit cube [0,1]^3 to find the point with minimum squared distance to planes. It sets itself apart from analytical solvers by ignoring feature preservation in favor of exhaustive spatial sampling. Choose it when analytical solutions are unstable or QEF data is sparse. A preparation step that computes the centroid of accumulated input data and assembles the symmetric linear system matrices A^T A and A^T b. It sets itself apart by transitioning raw data collection into a solvable linear algebraic structure. Choose it when decoupling data accumulation from the final solve step. A vertex positioning method used in the TRELLIS.2 framework preprocessing stage that solves for optimal dual vertices in active cubes. It sets itself apart by explicitly incorporating boundary edge constraints and regularization terms to handle sharp features and intricate internal structures. Choose it when integrating Dual Contouring into the TRELLIS.2 mesh extraction pipeline. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of active voxels. Each voxel requires a small constant-time SVD/eigen-decomposition on a 3 \times 3 matrix. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing dual vertices and faces. Sparse voxel grids require additional memory for the grid structure and padding. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, Dual Contouring achieves >230 M faces/s on sparse Fandisk CAD at 1024^3 resolution (14.36 ms latency for 3,432,768 triangles). For pure quads, throughput is 134 M quads/s. Strengths: Preserves sharp features better than Dual Marching Cubes; generates 100% watertight manifold topology; fully differentiable; high throughput on modern GPUs. Limitations: Single dual vertex per cell limitation can cause non-manifold geometry in complex sub-voxel topologies; requires boundary padding for sparse grids; sensitive to normal accuracy. When to Use: When sharp feature preservation and watertight topology are critical, and the input data provides accurate normals or gradients. When Not to Use: When the input data has noisy or inaccurate normals, or when sub-voxel topology is extremely complex and requires multiple vertices per cell. Dual Contouring was introduced by Ju et al. in 2002 as a method for extracting meshes from implicit surfaces. The QEF solver variant, as implemented in modern differentiable frameworks like conquer3d, builds on this foundation by incorporating regularized SVD and deterministic topology generation to address numerical instability and topological errors. It is used in high-performance graphics applications requiring sharp feature preservation and differentiable rendering. name: Newton Surface Projection
head: isosurface projection, vertex projection
body:
Newton Surface Projection is a post-processing step that projects extracted vertices exactly onto the isosurface defined by an implicit function, achieving machine precision accuracy. It uses Newton's method to minimize the distance to the zero-level set, ensuring all output vertices lie precisely on the surface. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of vertex positions extracted by the Dual Contouring QEF Solver, and an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R} defining the isosurface. Output: A set of projected vertex positions where f(v'i) \approx 0. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of shape (N, 3), dtype float64. Implicit Function: Callable returning values and gradients for batched inputs. Steps: 1. For each vertex vi in the extracted mesh: 2. Initialize x0 = vi. 3. Iterate Newton's method for k = 0, 1, \dots until convergence: a. Evaluate f(xk) and 
abla f(xk) (the gradient). b. Compute the update step: \Delta x = -  rac{f(xk)}{\|
abla f(xk)\|^2} 
abla f(xk) c. Update position: x{k+1} = xk + \Delta x. d. Check convergence: if \| \Delta x \| < \epsilon or |f(x{k+1})| < \epsilon, stop. 4. Set v'i = x{k+1}. Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Not given in the sources. Max iterations: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If 
abla f(xk) is near zero, the denominator becomes small, causing instability. A guard should clamp the denominator or fall back to a safe step. The method requires the implicit function to be differentiable at the evaluation points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def newtonsurfaceprojection(vertices, implicitfunc, tol, maxiter): """ Projects vertices onto the isosurface f(x)=0 using Newton's method. Args: vertices: List of (x, y, z) tuples or arrays of vertex positions. implicitfunc: Callable that takes a single (x, y, z) point and returns (fval, grad). fval: float. grad: (x, y, z) tuple or array of partial derivatives. tol: Convergence tolerance for |f(x)| and ||deltax||. maxiter: Maximum number of Newton iterations. Returns: projectedvertices: List of projected (x, y, z) positions. """ projected = [] for v in vertices: x = list(v) for in range(maxiter): fval, grad = implicitfunc(x) if abs(fval) < tol: break gradnormsq = sum(g g for g in grad) if gradnormsq < 1e-20: break delta = [- (fval / gradnormsq) g for g in grad] x = [x[i] + delta[i] for i in range(3)] if sum(d d for d in delta) < tol tol: break projected.append(x) return projected Projects Voronoi vertices (defined as tetrahedron circumcenters) onto the Signed Distance Function zero-level set to correct geometric errors caused by distant circumcenters. Unlike naive barycentric interpolation or explicit tetrahedron containment searches, it fits a plane to the projected sites of the enclosing tetrahedron and projects the vertex onto that plane. Choose it as a robust post-processing step for Dual Contouring vertices extracted from a Clipped Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Implemented in the isomesh library, which uses a Rust core with Python bindings for zero-copy array exchange and batch evaluation of the implicit function across all vertices simultaneously. Strengths: Achieves machine precision accuracy by projecting all vertices exactly onto the isosurface. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the isomesh library, a Rust-based isosurface extraction tool with Python bindings. It serves as a post-processing step applied after Dual Contouring vertex placement to refine positions onto the isosurface. narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: DCCVT Projection of 0-crossing Voronoi vertices
head: Robust Plane Fitting
body:
This method projects Voronoi vertices (defined as tetrahedron circumcenters) onto the Signed Distance Function (SDF) zero-level set to correct geometric errors caused by the circumcenter lying far from the tetrahedron. Unlike naive barycentric interpolation, which is unreliable for distant circumcenters, or explicit tetrahedron containment searches, which are computationally prohibitive, this approach fits a plane to the projected sites of the enclosing tetrahedron and projects the vertex onto that plane. It serves as a robust post-processing step for Dual Contouring vertices extracted from a Clipped Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation (DCCVT). Inputs: A set of tetrahedra \mathcal{T}j that cross the zero-level set. For each tetrahedron Tj, the four sites (vertices) si (where i \in \{1,2,3,4\}). For each site si, the SDF value \phii and the gradient 
abla \phii. The Voronoi vertex vj, defined as the circumcenter of tetrahedron Tj. Outputs: The projected Voronoi vertex v'j lying on the SDF zero-level set. Data Structures: Sites: 3D vectors \mathbf{s}i. SDF Values: Scalars \phii. Gradients: 3D vectors 
abla \phii. Covariance Matrix: 3 	imes 3 symmetric matrix Cj. Steps: 1. Project Sites to Zero-Level Set: For each of the four sites si in tetrahedron Tj, compute the projected site s'i using a single Newton step based on the local SDF value and gradient: \mathbf{s}'i = \mathbf{s}i -  rac{
abla \phii}{\|
abla \phii\| + \epsilon} \phii \quad (3) Here, \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. 2. Compute Centroid of Projected Sites: Calculate the centroid  ar{\mathbf{s}}'j of the four projected sites:  ar{\mathbf{s}}'j =  rac{1}{4} \sum{i \in \mathcal{T}j} \mathbf{s}'i \quad (4) 3. Fit Plane via Covariance Eigenvector: Compute the centered coordinates \Delta \mathbf{s}'i for each projected site: \Delta \mathbf{s}'i = \mathbf{s}'i -  ar{\mathbf{s}}'j Construct the 3 	imes 3 centered covariance matrix Cj of the projected sites: Cj =  rac{1}{4} \sum{i \in \mathcal{T}j} \Delta \mathbf{s}'i \Delta \mathbf{s}'i^	op \quad (25) Find the normal vector \mathbf{n}j of the fitted plane. This vector corresponds to the eigenvector associated with the smallest eigenvalue of Cj. This minimizes the average squared distance from the projected sites to the plane passing through the centroid: \mathbf{n}j = \arg \min{\mathbf{n}}  rac{1}{4} \sum{i \in \mathcal{T}j} \left(  rac{\mathbf{n}}{\|\mathbf{n}\|} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{s}'i ight)^2 \quad (5) The source identifies \mathbf{n}j as the "first eigenvector" in the context of minimizing distance, which mathematically corresponds to the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue. 4. Project Voronoi Vertex: Project the original Voronoi vertex vj onto the fitted plane defined by normal \mathbf{n}j and centroid \mathbf{c}j =  ar{\mathbf{s}}'j: \mathbf{v}'j = \mathbf{v}j - [(\mathbf{v}j - \mathbf{c}j) \cdot \mathbf{n}j] \mathbf{n}j \quad (6) The result \mathbf{v}'j is the final projected vertex. Parameters: \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability in site projection. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distant Circumcenters: The circumcenter of a tetrahedron can lie far from the tetrahedron itself, making straightforward barycentric interpolation of SDF values and gradients unreliable. This method avoids that issue by using local site projections. Containment Search: Explicitly searching for the containing tetrahedron for a given Voronoi vertex is computationally prohibitive. This method assumes the Voronoi vertex is associated with the tetrahedron formed by its four defining sites, avoiding the search. Degenerate Tetrahedra: If the four sites are coplanar, the covariance matrix will be singular. The smallest eigenvalue will be zero, and the corresponding eigenvector will define the plane normal. This is handled naturally by the eigendecomposition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projectvoronoivertex(sites, sdfs, gradients, voronoivertex, epsilon=1e-8): """ Projects a Voronoi vertex onto the SDF zero-level set using the DCCVT method. Args: sites: Array of shape (4, 3), the four sites si of the tetrahedron. sdfs: Array of shape (4,), the SDF values phii at each site. gradients: Array of shape (4, 3), the gradients nabla phii at each site. voronoivertex: Array of shape (3,), the circumcenter vj of the tetrahedron. epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability. Returns: projectedvertex: Array of shape (3,), the projected Voronoi vertex v'j. """ # Step 1: Project sites to zero-level set # s'i = si - (nabla phii / (||nabla phii|| + epsilon)) phii norms = np.linalg.norm(gradients, axis=1, keepdims=True) + epsilon projectedsites = sites - (gradients / norms) sdfs[:, np.newaxis] # Step 2: Compute centroid of projected sites centroid = np.mean(projectedsites, axis=0) # Step 3: Fit plane via covariance eigenvector # Center the projected sites centeredsites = projectedsites - centroid # Compute covariance matrix C = (1/4) sum(deltas'i deltas'i^T) covariancematrix = (centeredsites.T @ centeredsites) / 4.0 # Find the eigenvector corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covariancematrix) normal = eigenvectors[:, 0] # Step 4: Project Voronoi vertex onto the fitted plane # v'j = vj - ((vj - cj). nj) nj dotproduct = np.dot(voronoivertex - centroid, normal) projectedvertex = voronoivertex - dotproduct normal return projectedvertex This variant projects the midpoints of tetrahedron edges that cross the zero-level set onto the SDF zero-level set to provide additional constraints ensuring Voronoi faces remain well aligned with the SDF and target point cloud. For each edge between adjacent sites si and sj crossing the zero-level set, the SDF value \phi(b{ij}) and gradient 
abla \phi(b{ij}) at the midpoint b{ij} are approximated by linear interpolation: \phi(b{ij}) \approx  rac{1}{2}(\phii + \phij) and 
abla \phi(b{ij}) \approx  rac{1}{2}(
abla \phii + 
abla \phij). The midpoint is then projected onto the zero-level set using a Newton step: b'{ij} = b{ij} -  rac{
abla \phi(b{ij})}{\|
abla \phi(b{ij})\| + \epsilon} \phi(b{ij}). This method is chosen when higher fidelity to the SDF is required for mesh faces, not just vertices. This variant compares robust projection against barycentric projection (interpolated SDF/gradient + projection to zero-level set) and hybrid projection (barycentric if inside tetrahedron, robust otherwise). Barycentric projection generates the largest errors due to instabilities from extrapolation. The hybrid method reduces error but still suffers from abnormal spatial gradients leading to slight instabilities during optimization. Robust projection provides the most stable and accurate results, avoiding instabilities from extrapolation and abnormal spatial gradients. Strengths: Robust against degenerate tetrahedra where circumcenters are far from the mesh; avoids expensive tetrahedron containment searches; uses only local site information. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the SDF gradient at the sites; assumes the tetrahedron is well-defined. When to use: When extracting meshes from DCCVT where vertex accuracy on the zero-level set is critical and standard barycentric interpolation fails due to large circumcenter distances. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The DCCVT (Differentiable Clipped Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation) method was introduced to address challenges in meshing unoriented 3D point clouds using SDFs. The projection of 0-crossing Voronoi vertices was proposed as a specific technique within this framework to ensure that the extracted mesh vertices lie accurately on the zero-level set of the inferred SDF, overcoming the limitations of naive interpolation methods. DCCVT: Differentiable Clipped Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13603v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Quadric Error Function (QEF) for Sharp Features
head: QEF for Sharp Features, QEF Solver, Quadric Error Function Solver, QEF Solver using SVD
body: Quadric Error Function (QEF) for Sharp Features is a vertex relocation technique used in Dual Contouring to position a single vertex within an octree cell such that it accurately represents sharp features (edges and corners) of the isosurface. It solves the problem of standard Dual Contouring producing smoothed or inaccurate vertices at high-curvature regions by minimizing the sum of squared distances from the vertex to the tangent planes defined by isosurface intersection points. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Brute-Force QEF Solver and QEF Solver Initialization, by explicitly constructing "supporting planes" in addition to tangent planes to stabilize the minimization process and prevent numerical instabilities inherent in standard Quadric Error Metric (QEM) approaches. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N intersection point-normal pairs \{(pi, ni)\} for i=0 \dots N-1, where pi is the position where the isosurface intersects an edge of the cell, and ni is the gradient normal at that point. Output: A 3D vertex position v that minimizes the combined quadric error function. Data Structures The method accumulates constraints into a symmetric data structure. Based on, the QefData structure holds the following fields: ata00, ata01, ata02, ata11, ata12, ata22: Elements of the symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix A^T A (or ATA). atbx, atby, atbz: Elements of the vector A^T b (or ATB). btb: Scalar value representing the accumulated squared dot products. massPointx, massPointy, massPointz: The accumulated sum of intersection points (used to compute the centroid). numPoints: Integer count of intersection points N. Algorithm Steps 1. Compute Mass Point and Normal: Calculate the mass point p{mass} as the arithmetic mean of all intersection points pi: p{mass} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} pi Calculate the mass normal n{mass} as the average of all intersection normals ni, normalized: n{mass} = \frac{\sum{i=0}^{N-1} ni}{\left\| \sum{i=0}^{N-1} ni \right\|} 2. Construct Tangent Plane Quadrics (QI): For each intersection point pi with normal ni, define a tangent plane equation ni^T (v - pi) = 0. This corresponds to the standard QEM formulation. The quadric for a single plane n^T v + d = 0 (where d = -n^T pi) is defined by: A = n n^T b = d n c = d^2 Accumulate these into the global ATA, ATB, and btb matrices/vectors. Specifically, for each i: Normalize ni. Compute doti = ni \cdot pi. Update ATA \leftarrow ATA + ni ni^T. Update ATB \leftarrow ATB + doti ni. Update btb \leftarrow btb + doti^2. 3. Construct Supporting Plane Quadrics (QS): To stabilize the solution for sharp features, construct supporting planes for each intersection point. For each i: Compute the edge vector e: e = \frac{p{mass} - pi}{\| p{mass} - pi \|} Pitfall: If p{mass} = pi, e is zero. Compute the intermediate normal ne: ne = \frac{n{mass} + ni}{\| n{mass} + ni \|} Compute the supporting plane normal ns: ns = \frac{ne \times e}{\| ne \times e \|} Pitfall: If e is parallel to ne, the cross product is zero and the supporting plane normal is undefined. The supporting plane passes through p{mass} with normal ns. The plane equation is ns^T (v - p{mass}) = 0. Let dots = ns \cdot p{mass}. Accumulate the supporting plane quadric into ATA, ATB, and btb using the same logic as Step 2, but scaled by a factor a. 4. Combine Quadrics: The final error function E(v) is the sum of the tangent quadrics QI and the supporting quadrics QS, weighted by factor a: Q = QI + a QS The parameter a controls feature sharpness. A typical value is 0.5. Small values produce sharper features but may introduce instability; large values smooth the feature more. 5. Solve the Linear System: The problem is to minimize E(v) = v^T (ATA) v - 2 (ATB)^T v + btb. This is equivalent to solving the linear system: (ATA) v = ATB Since ATA may be rank-deficient or ill-conditioned (especially for edges where N < 3), use Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Centering: To improve numerical stability, shift the coordinate system to the mass point. Let v = x + p{mass}. The system becomes: (ATA) x = ATB - (ATA) p{mass} Let b' = ATB - (ATA) p{mass}. SVD Solve: Compute the SVD of ATA = U D V^T. Since ATA is symmetric, U=V. Compute the pseudoinverse of the diagonal matrix D, denoted D^+, where singular values \sigmaj < \text{pinv\tol} are treated as zero. x = V D^+ U^T b' Final Position: v = x + p{mass} Parameters a: Scaling factor for supporting planes. Typical value: 0.5. svdtol: Tolerance for SVD convergence/singular value thresholding. Not specified in sources. svdsweeps: Maximum number of Givens rotation sweeps for the SVD algorithm. Not specified in sources. pinvtol: Tolerance for pseudoinverse computation. Singular values below this are treated as zero. Not specified in sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def solveqefsharpfeatures(intersectionpoints, intersectionnormals, a=0.5, pinvtol=1e-8): """ Solves the QEF for sharp features using supporting planes and SVD. Args: intersectionpoints: List of 3D vectors (pi). intersectionnormals: List of 3D vectors (ni). a: Weight for supporting planes (default 0.5). pinvtol: Tolerance for pseudoinverse computation. Returns: Vertex position v. """ n = len(intersectionpoints) if n == 0: raise ValueError("No intersection points provided") # Step 1: Compute Mass Point and Mass Normal masspoint = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] massnormal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(n): masspoint[0] += intersectionpoints[i][0] masspoint[1] += intersectionpoints[i][1] masspoint[2] += intersectionpoints[i][2] massnormal[0] += intersectionnormals[i][0] massnormal[1] += intersectionnormals[i][1] massnormal[2] += intersectionnormals[i][2] masspoint[0] /= n; masspoint[1] /= n; masspoint[2] /= n normmassnormal = math.sqrt(massnormal[0]2 + massnormal[1]2 + massnormal[2]2) if normmassnormal == 0: return masspoint massnormal[0] /= normmassnormal; massnormal[1] /= normmassnormal; massnormal[2] /= normmassnormal # Initialize ATA, ATB, btb ata = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] atb = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] btb = 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Accumulate Tangent and Supporting Plane Quadrics for i in range(n): pi = intersectionpoints[i] ni = intersectionnormals[i] normni = math.sqrt(ni[0]2 + ni[1]2 + ni[2]2) if normni == 0: continue ni = [ni[0]/normni, ni[1]/normni, ni[2]/normni] # --- Tangent Plane Quadric (QI) --- doti = ni[0]pi[0] + ni[1]pi[1] + ni[2]pi[2] # A = ni ni^T ata[0][0] += ni[0]ni[0]; ata[0][1] += ni[0]ni[1]; ata[0][2] += ni[0]ni[2] ata[1][0] += ni[1]ni[0]; ata[1][1] += ni[1]ni[1]; ata[1][2] += ni[1]ni[2] ata[2][0] += ni[2]ni[0]; ata[2][1] += ni[2]ni[1]; ata[2][2] += ni[2]ni[2] # b = doti ni atb[0] += doti ni[0]; atb[1] += doti ni[1]; atb[2] += doti ni[2] # c += doti^2 btb += doti 2 # --- Supporting Plane Quadric (QS) --- diff = [masspoint[0]-pi[0], masspoint[1]-pi[1], masspoint[2]-pi[2]] normdiff = math.sqrt(diff[0]2 + diff[1]2 + diff[2]2) if normdiff > 1e-8: e = [diff[0]/normdiff, diff[1]/normdiff, diff[2]/normdiff] neraw = [massnormal[0]+ni[0], massnormal[1]+ni[1], massnormal[2]+ni[2]] normne = math.sqrt(neraw[0]2 + neraw[1]2 + neraw[2]2) if normne > 1e-8: ne = [neraw[0]/normne, neraw[1]/normne, neraw[2]/normne] # ns = ne x e ns = [ne[1]e[2]-ne[2]e[1], ne[2]e[0]-ne[0]e[2], ne[0]e[1]-ne[1]e[0]] normns = math.sqrt(ns[0]2 + ns[1]2 + ns[2]2) if normns > 1e-8: ns = [ns[0]/normns, ns[1]/normns, ns[2]/normns] dots = ns[0]masspoint[0] + ns[1]masspoint[1] + ns[2]masspoint[2] # Accumulate with weight a ata[0][0] += a ns[0]ns[0]; ata[0][1] += a ns[0]ns[1]; ata[0][2] += a ns[0]ns[2] ata[1][0] += a ns[1]ns[0]; ata[1][1] += a ns[1]ns[1]; ata[1][2] += a ns[1]ns[2] ata[2][0] += a ns[2]ns[0]; ata[2][1] += a ns[2]ns[1]; ata[2][2] += a ns[2]ns[2] atb[0] += a dots ns[0]; atb[1] += a dots ns[1]; atb[2] += a dots ns[2] btb += a dots 2 # Step 5: Solve (ATA) v = ATB using SVD with centering tmp = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tmp[0] = ata[0][0]masspoint[0] + ata[0][1]masspoint[1] + ata[0][2]masspoint[2] tmp[1] = ata[1][0]masspoint[0] + ata[1][1]masspoint[1] + ata[1][2]masspoint[2] tmp[2] = ata[2][0]masspoint[0] + ata[2][1]masspoint[1] + ata[2][2]masspoint[2] rhs = [atb[0]-tmp[0], atb[1]-tmp[1], atb[2]-tmp[2]] # SVD of ATA (symmetric) u, s, vh = np.linalg.svd(ata) # Pseudoinverse of singular values sinv = [0.0]len(s) for j in range(len(s)): if s[j] > pinvtol: sinv[j] = 1.0 / s[j] else: sinv[j] = 0.0 # x = Vh.T @ diag(sinv) @ U.T @ rhs x = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for r in range(3): for c in range(3): x[r] += vh[r][c] sinv[c] sum(u[c][k]rhs[k] for k in range(3)) v = [x[0]+masspoint[0], x[1]+masspoint[1], x[2]+masspoint[2]] return v A fallback strategy for when the unconstrained QEF solution lies outside the voxel cell. It constrains the search space hierarchically (interior -> faces -> edges -> corners). It sets itself apart by handling boundary violations explicitly rather than relying solely on SVD minimization. Time Complexity: Dominated by the SVD of a 3 \times 3 matrix, which is constant time O(1) per cell. Accumulating the quadrics is O(N) where N is the number of intersection points (typically 3 to 12). Memory Complexity: O(1) per cell for storing the accumulated ATA, ATB, and btb values. Performance: Computationally efficient compared to general-purpose QEF solvers or iterative methods. Strengths: Preserves sharp features (edges and corners) better than standard Dual Contouring or Marching Cubes. Stabilizes the solution against numerical instabilities that occur with standard QEM when planes are nearly parallel or coincident. Limitations: Requires careful handling of degenerate cases (zero vectors, parallel normals) to avoid division by zero or invalid cross products. The choice of parameter a affects sharpness vs. stability trade-off. When to use: When extracting isosurfaces with sharp features using Dual Contouring and vertex accuracy at corners/edges is critical. When not to use: For smooth surfaces where feature preservation is not desired, or when computational resources are extremely limited and approximate smoothing is acceptable. The Quadric Error Metric (QEM) was introduced by Garland and Heckbert in 1997. It was originally designed for mesh simplification but was adapted for isosurface extraction in Dual Contouring by Ju et al. (2002). The specific variation using supporting planes to stabilize sharp feature extraction was detailed in later works on Dual Contouring for terrain and complex surface modeling. Generating Smooth High-Quality Isosurfaces for Interactive Modeling and Visualization of Complex Terrains, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe/vmv/vmv12/079-086, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nickgildea/DualContouringSample, https://github.com/nickgildea/DualContouringSample, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: QEF Boundary Constrained Vertex Placement
head: Boundary-Constrained Vertex Placement, Constrained QEF Solver
body: QEF Boundary Constrained Vertex Placement is a fallback strategy for vertex placement in Dual Contouring when the optimal solution to the unconstrained Quadratic Error Function (QEF) lies outside the current voxel cell. It progressively constrains the search space from the interior point to cell faces, then edges, then corners to find a valid point within the cell boundaries. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Quadric Error Function (QEF) for Sharp Features, by explicitly handling boundary violations through hierarchical constraint fixing rather than relying solely on SVD minimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unconstrained QEF solution v (a 3D vector), the cell bounds defined by origin (x, y, z) and CELLSIZE, and configuration flags settings.BOUNDARY and settings.CLIP. Output: A constrained vertex position v guaranteed to be within the cell boundaries if settings.BOUNDARY is enabled. Data Structures: QEF Object: Represents the quadratic error function. It supports methods fixaxis(axis, value) to constrain a specific coordinate and solve() to compute the minimum residual vertex. It also supports evalwithpos(pos) to evaluate the error at a specific position. Inside Function: A predicate inside(v) that returns true if x \le v[0] \le x + \text{CELL\SIZE}, y \le v[1] \le y + \text{CELL\SIZE}, and z \le v[2] \le z + \text{CELL\SIZE}. Parameters: settings.BOUNDARY: Boolean flag enabling the boundary constraint fallback logic. Default: True. settings.CLIP: Boolean flag enabling crude clamping of the final vertex position. Default: False. CELLSIZE: The size of the voxel cell along each axis. Default: 1.0. Steps: 1. Unconstrained Solve: Solve the unconstrained QEF to get residual and vertex v. 2. Boundary Check: If settings.BOUNDARY is enabled, check if v is inside the cell using the inside function. 3. Plane Constraints: If v is outside, constrain the QEF to the 6 planes bordering the cell by fixing one axis at the cell boundaries (0 or CELLSIZE) and solving. The planes are: Fix axis 0 at x+0 and x+\text{CELL\SIZE} Fix axis 1 at y+0 and y+\text{CELL\SIZE} Fix axis 2 at z+0 and z+\text{CELL\SIZE} 4. Filter Planes: Filter the 6 plane solutions to keep only those inside the cell. If no solutions remain, proceed to constrain the QEF to the 12 lines bordering the cell by fixing two axes at the cell boundaries. 5. Edge Constraints: Generate 12 edge solutions by fixing two axes. Examples include fixing axis 1 at y+0 and axis 0 at x+0, axis 1 at y+\text{CELL\SIZE} and axis 0 at x+0, etc., covering all combinations of two axes fixed at 0 or CELLSIZE. 6. Filter Edges: Filter the 12 edge solutions to keep only those inside the cell. If no solutions remain, proceed to evaluate the 8 corners of the cell. 7. Corner Evaluation: Evaluate the QEF at all 8 corners of the cell using evalwithpos for each corner coordinate combination: (x+0, y+0, z+0) through (x+\text{CELL\SIZE}, y+\text{CELL\SIZE}, z+\text{CELL\SIZE}). 8. Filter Corners: Filter the 8 corner solutions to keep only those inside the cell. 9. Select Best: Select the best solution (minimum residual) from the remaining valid options (plane, edge, or corner solutions). 10. Clipping: If settings.CLIP is enabled, forcibly clamp the vertex coordinates to the cell boundaries using numpy.clip for each axis: v[0] \in [x, x+\text{CELL\SIZE}], v[1] \in [y, y+\text{CELL\SIZE}], v[2] \in [z, z+\text{CELL\SIZE}]. Pitfalls: The unconstrained QEF solution may lie outside the cell. Even after constraining to planes, the solutions may still lie outside the box because the planes are infinite. The algorithm handles these cases by falling back to edge constraints, then corners, ensuring a valid point is always found. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy def solveconstrainedqef(qef, x, y, z, CELLSIZE, settings): # Step 1: Solve unconstrained residual, v = qef.solve() # Step 2: Check if inside def inside(pos): return (x <= pos[0] <= x + CELLSIZE and y <= pos[1] <= y + CELLSIZE and z <= pos[2] <= z + CELLSIZE) if not settings.BOUNDARY or inside(v): finalv = v else: candidates = [] # Step 3 & 4: Plane constraints (6 planes) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).solve()) validcandidates = [c for c in candidates if inside(c[1])] if not validcandidates: candidates = [] # Step 5 & 6: Edge constraints (12 edges) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + 0).fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + 0).fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(0, x + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(0, x + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).fixaxis(1, y + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(1, y + 0).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + 0).fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).solve()) candidates.append(qef.fixaxis(2, z + CELLSIZE).fixaxis(1, y + CELLSIZE).solve()) validcandidates = [c for c in candidates if inside(c[1])] if not validcandidates: candidates = [] # Step 7 & 8: Corner evaluation (8 corners) corners = [ (x + 0, y + 0, z + 0), (x + 0, y + 0, z + CELLSIZE), (x + 0, y + CELLSIZE, z + 0), (x + 0, y + CELLSIZE, z + CELLSIZE), (x + CELLSIZE, y + 0, z + 0), (x + CELLSIZE, y + 0, z + CELLSIZE), (x + CELLSIZE, y + CELLSIZE, z + 0), (x + CELLSIZE, y + CELLSIZE, z + CELLSIZE) ] for corner in corners: candidates.append(qef.evalwithpos(corner)) validcandidates = [c for c in candidates if inside(c[1])] # Step 9: Select best if validcandidates: residual, finalv = min(validcandidates, key=lambda c: c[0]) else: finalv = v # Step 10: Clipping if settings.CLIP: finalv[0] = numpy.clip(finalv[0], x, x + CELLSIZE) finalv[1] = numpy.clip(finalv[1], y, y + CELLSIZE) finalv[2] = numpy.clip(finalv[2], z, z + CELLSIZE) return finalv Time Complexity: In the worst case, the algorithm solves the QEF 26 times (1 unconstrained + 6 planes + 12 edges + 8 corners). Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory, storing a list of candidate residuals and vertices. Strengths: Guarantees a valid vertex position within the cell boundaries. Limitations: Can be computationally expensive if many cells require fallback to edges or corners. The crude clipping option may introduce discontinuities if not used carefully. When to use: Not given in the sources. This method provides a fallback strategy for vertex placement in Dual Contouring when the unconstrained QEF solution lies outside the voxel cell. It addresses the issue where the optimal point for a sharp feature does not lie within the containing voxel. name: QEF Data Accumulation
head: QEF Accumulation, QEF Accumulator, QEF Data Structure, QefData, QefData struct, QefSolver.add
body: QEF Data Accumulation is a data structure for accumulating the components of a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) from multiple plane constraints without storing individual points and normals. It enables the downstream Dual Contouring QEF Solver to reconstruct the optimal vertex position from the accumulated normal equations. The method maintains only the pre-computed sums required for the least-squares solution and supports merging accumulators from different sources via element-wise addition. The method accepts a plane constraint defined by a point p = (px, py, pz) and a normal vector n = (nx, ny, nz), or another QefData instance for merging. It outputs an updated QefData structure containing the accumulated quadratic form components. The core data structure is QefData, which stores the coefficients of the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b derived from the QEF minimization problem. The matrix A^T A is symmetric, so only the upper triangle is stored. The structure consists of the following fields: | Field Name | Type | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | ata00 | float | Element (0,0) of A^T A | | ata01 | float | Element (0,1) of A^T A | | ata02 | float | Element (0,2) of A^T A | | ata11 | float | Element (1,1) of A^T A | | ata12 | float | Element (1,2) of A^T A | | ata22 | float | Element (2,2) of A^T A | | atbx | float | Element x of A^T b | | atby | float | Element y of A^T b | | atbz | float | Element z of A^T b | | btb | float | Scalar b^T b | | massPointx | float | Accumulated sum of px | | massPointy | float | Accumulated sum of py | | massPointz | float | Accumulated sum of pz | | numPoints | int | Count of added constraints | To add a new plane constraint to an existing accumulator, perform the following steps: 1. Normalize the input normal: compute n{norm} = \frac{n}{\|n\|} and extract components nx, ny, nz. 2. Compute the dot product d = nx px + ny py + nz pz. 3. Update A^T A by adding the outer product components: ata00 += nx nx, ata01 += nx ny, ata02 += nx nz, ata11 += ny ny, ata12 += ny nz, ata22 += nz nz. 4. Update A^T b by adding d \cdot n{norm}: atbx += d nx, atby += d ny, atbz += d nz. 5. Update b^T b by adding d^2: btb += d d. 6. Update the mass point sum: massPointx += px, massPointy += py, massPointz += pz. 7. Increment the constraint count: numPoints += 1. 8. Mark the solver's solution as invalid: hasSolution = false. To merge two accumulators lhs and rhs, add corresponding fields element-wise: lhs.ataij += rhs.ataij, lhs.atbk += rhs.atbk, lhs.btb += rhs.btb, lhs.massPointk += rhs.massPointk, and lhs.numPoints += rhs.numPoints. The QEF minimizes the sum of squared distances to plane constraints: \sumi (ni \cdot (x - pi))^2. Expanding this yields the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b, where A is a matrix with rows equal to the normals ni, and b is a vector with elements bi = ni \cdot pi. The accumulator stores A^T A in ata, A^T b in atb, and b^T b in btb. The mass point sum accumulates \sumi pi. Typical values are not specified in the sources. The fields use 32-bit floating-point numbers (float) and a 32-bit integer (int). Precision: Accumulating many constraints in float fields may cause precision loss; the sources specify float. Symmetry: The ata matrix is symmetric, so only the upper triangle is updated, and the solver must account for this symmetry when solving the linear system. Degenerate input: The sources do not specify fallback behavior for zero-length normals. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the QefData structure and its operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class QefData: def init(self): self.clear() def clear(self): """Initialize all fields to zero.""" self.ata00 = 0.0; self.ata01 = 0.0; self.ata02 = 0.0 self.ata11 = 0.0; self.ata12 = 0.0; self.ata22 = 0.0 self.atbx = 0.0; self.atby = 0.0; self.atbz = 0.0 self.btb = 0.0 self.massPointx = 0.0; self.massPointy = 0.0; self.massPointz = 0.0 self.numPoints = 0 def addconstraint(self, px, py, pz, nx, ny, nz): """Add a plane constraint defined by point (px, py, pz) and normal (nx, ny, nz).""" # 1. Normalize normal length = math.sqrt(nxnx + nyny + nznz) nxn = nx / length; nyn = ny / length; nzn = nz / length # 2. Compute dot product d = n. p dot = nxn px + nyn py + nzn pz # 3. Update A^T A self.ata00 += nxn nxn self.ata01 += nxn nyn self.ata02 += nxn nzn self.ata11 += nyn nyn self.ata12 += nyn nzn self.ata22 += nzn nzn # 4. Update A^T b self.atbx += dot nxn self.atby += dot nyn self.atbz += dot nzn # 5. Update b^T b self.btb += dot dot # 6. Update mass point sum self.massPointx += px self.massPointy += py self.massPointz += pz # 7. Increment count self.numPoints += 1 def merge(self, rhs): """Merge another QefData accumulator into this one.""" self.ata00 += rhs.ata00; self.ata01 += rhs.ata01; self.ata02 += rhs.ata02 self.ata11 += rhs.ata11; self.ata12 += rhs.ata12; self.ata22 += rhs.ata22 self.atbx += rhs.atbx; self.atby += rhs.atby; self.atbz += rhs.atbz self.btb += rhs.btb self.massPointx += rhs.massPointx; self.massPointy += rhs.massPointy; self.massPointz += rhs.massPointz self.numPoints += rhs.numPoints Memory: The QefData structure has a fixed size of 14 floats and 1 integer, totaling 60 bytes (assuming 32-bit floats and 32-bit int). Time per Constraint: Adding a constraint involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Merge Time: Merging two accumulators is O(1), involving a fixed number of additions. Not given in the sources. The method scales linearly with the number of constraints added to a single cell, but the memory footprint remains constant. Strengths: The method provides constant memory overhead per cell and supports merging accumulators. Limitations: It does not store the original points or normals, so it cannot be used to re-evaluate the QEF with different weights. Use when implementing Dual Contouring to efficiently aggregate plane constraints within a grid cell. Do not use if you need to retain the original point cloud data for other purposes. name: Occupancy-Based Dual Contouring
head: ODC
body: Occupancy-Based Dual Contouring (ODC) is a dual contouring method designed to extract meshes from neural implicit functions defined in continuous 3D space, such as Occupancy Networks, IM-NET, or DeepSDF. It modifies the computation of grid edge points and grid cell points to avoid relying on distance information, which is often unavailable or unreliable in occupancy fields. By introducing auxiliary 2D points to compute local surface normals, ODC identifies 3D points via the Quadric Error Function (QEF) and utilizes fast, parallelizable search algorithms for 1D, 2D, and 3D points. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, bounding box \mathcal{P} defined by mincoord and maxcoord, grid resolution numgrid, isolevel, and search parameters. Output: Vertices tensor (N, 3) and triangles tensor (N, 3) representing the extracted mesh. Data Structures: pfvtab: A lookup table for dual contouring vertex configurations. It is a list of 64 entries (indices 0-63). Each entry is a list of one or more lists of integers representing vertex indices. The integers range from 1 to 24. Example entry at index 1: [[13, 2, 17, 3, 15, 1, 13]]. Parameters: mincoord: Minimum coordinates of \mathcal{P}. Default: [-0.5, -0.5, -0.5]. maxcoord: Maximum coordinates of \mathcal{P}. Default: [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]. numgrid: Resolution for each axis. Default: 128. isolevel: Iso-level to extract. Default: 0.0. Use 0.5 for occupancy functions, 0.0 for SDF. impfunccplx: GPU VRAM usage of the implicit function for querying one point. Default: 3. outside: Boolean flag. True if a larger value indicates outside. Default: True. BINARYSEARCH: Number of iterations for 1D point search. Default: 15. VERTICALRANGE: Range for step (1) of the 2D point search. Default: 0.8. VERTICALLINEARSEARCH: Number of linear iterations for step (1) of the 2D point search. Default: 4. VERTICALBINARYSEARCH: Number of binary iterations for step (1) of the 2D point search. Default: 11. HORIZNTLRANGE: Range for step (2) of the 2D point search. Default: 0.71. HORIZNTLLINEARSEARCH: Number of linear iterations for step (2) of the 2D point search. Default: 3. HORIZNTLBINARYSEARCH: Number of binary iterations for step (2) of the 2D point search. Default: 12. ERR: Error level tolerance. Default: 3e-7. SEP: Minimum separation of a 3D point from the grid face. Default: 1e-3. QEFREG: Regularization coefficient for QEF. Default: 0.05. Algorithm Steps: The method processes the grid in parallel across edges, faces, and cells. 1. Grid Initialization: Define the 3D grid within \mathcal{P} with resolution numgrid. Evaluate the implicit function f at all grid vertices to determine occupancy status relative to isolevel. 2. 1D Point Search (Grid Edges): For each grid edge intersecting the isosurface, search for the intersection point. The search uses BINARYSEARCH iterations. The point is constrained to the edge segment. 3. 2D Point Search (Grid Faces): For each grid face intersecting the isosurface, search for an auxiliary 2D point. This search consists of two steps: Step (1): Vertical search using VERTICALLINEARSEARCH linear iterations followed by VERTICALBINARYSEARCH binary iterations within VERTICALRANGE. Step (2): Horizontal search using HORIZNTLLINEARSEARCH linear iterations followed by HORIZNTLBINARYSEARCH binary iterations within HORIZNTLRANGE. These 2D points are used to compute local surface normals along with the 1D points. 4. 3D Point Search (Grid Cells): For each grid cell containing the isosurface, search for the 3D vertex position. The search utilizes the 1D points and 2D points (and their associated normals) to formulate a Quadric Error Function (QEF). The QEF is solved with regularization coefficient QEFREG. The resulting point must satisfy the separation constraint SEP from the grid face. 5. Mesh Construction: Use the pfvtab lookup table to determine the vertex configuration for each cell based on the occupancy status of its corners. Connect the computed 3D points to form triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def occupancydualcontouring(implicitfunction, device="cuda:0", mincoord=torch.tensor([-0.5, -0.5, -0.5]), maxcoord=torch.tensor([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]), numgrid=128, isolevel=0.0, outside=True, BINARYSEARCH=15, VERTICALRANGE=0.8, VERTICALLINEARSEARCH=4, VERTICALBINARYSEARCH=11, HORIZNTLRANGE=0.71, HORIZNTLLINEARSEARCH=3, HORIZNTLBINARYSEARCH=12, ERR=3e-7, SEP=1e-3, QEFREG=0.05): """ Extracts mesh from implicit function using ODC. """ # 1. Grid Setup # Create grid vertices within mincoord and maxcoord x = torch.linspace(mincoord[0], maxcoord[0], numgrid + 1, device=device) y = torch.linspace(mincoord[1], maxcoord[1], numgrid + 1, device=device) z = torch.linspace(mincoord[2], maxcoord[2], numgrid + 1, device=device) X, Y, Z = torch.meshgrid(x, y, z, indexing='ij') gridpts = torch.stack([X, Y, Z], dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3) # Evaluate implicitfunction at grid vertices gridvals = implicitfunction(gridpts) # Determine binary occupancy based on isolevel and outside flag occ = (gridvals > isolevel) if outside else (gridvals < isolevel) occint = occ.int() # Preallocate storage for points nedges = numgrid (numgrid + 1) 3 nfaces = numgrid numgrid 3 ncells = numgrid 3 p1d = torch.zeros((nedges, 3), device=device) p2d = torch.zeros((nfaces, 3), device=device) n2d = torch.zeros((nfaces, 3), device=device) p3d = torch.zeros((ncells, 3), device=device) # 2. Parallel Processing # Process edges: # For each edge, perform 1D binary search (BINARYSEARCH iters) # to find intersection point p1d. for axis in range(3): for i in range(numgrid + 1): for j in range(numgrid + 1): for k in range(numgrid): idx = k + (j (numgrid + 1) + i) numgrid if axis == 0: p0 = gridpts[k, j (numgrid + 1) + i] p1 = gridpts[k + 1, j (numgrid + 1) + i] elif axis == 1: p0 = gridpts[k (numgrid + 1) + i, j] p1 = gridpts[k (numgrid + 1) + i, j + 1] else: p0 = gridpts[k (numgrid + 1) (numgrid + 1) + i (numgrid + 1) + j] p1 = gridpts[k (numgrid + 1) (numgrid + 1) + i (numgrid + 1) + j + 1] o0 = occint[k (numgrid + 1) (numgrid + 1) + i (numgrid + 1) + j] o1 = occint[(k + 1) (numgrid + 1) (numgrid + 1) + i (numgrid + 1) + j] if axis == 0 else \ occint[k (numgrid + 1) (numgrid + 1) + i (numgrid + 1) + (j + 1)] if axis == 1 else \ occint[k (numgrid + 1) (numgrid + 1) + i (numgrid + 1) + j + 1] if o0 != o1: # Binary search for root lo, hi = 0.0, 1.0 for in range(BINARYSEARCH): mid = (lo + hi) / 2.0 pm = p0 + (p1 - p0) mid fm = implicitfunction(pm) if (fm > isolevel) if outside else (fm < isolevel): hi = mid else: lo = mid p1d[idx] = p0 + (p1 - p0) ((lo + hi) / 2.0) # Process faces: # For each face, perform 2D search: for axis in range(3): for i in range(numgrid): for j in range(numgrid): for k in range(numgrid): idx = k numgrid numgrid + j numgrid + i if axis == 0: v0, v1, v2, v3 = gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + i(numgrid+1) + j], \ gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + i(numgrid+1) + j+1], \ gridpts[(k+1) (numgrid+1)2 + i(numgrid+1) + j], \ gridpts[(k+1) (numgrid+1)2 + i(numgrid+1) + j+1] p1dref = p1d[k (numgrid+1) (numgrid+1) + i (numgrid+1) + j] elif axis == 1: v0, v1, v2, v3 = gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + i(numgrid+1) + j], \ gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + (i+1)(numgrid+1) + j], \ gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + i(numgrid+1) + j+1], \ gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + (i+1)(numgrid+1) + j+1] p1dref = p1d[k (numgrid+1) (numgrid+1) + i (numgrid+1) + j] else: v0, v1, v2, v3 = gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + i(numgrid+1) + j], \ gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + (i+1)(numgrid+1) + j], \ gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + i(numgrid+1) + j+1], \ gridpts[k (numgrid+1)2 + (i+1)(numgrid+1) + j+1] p1dref = p1d[k (numgrid+1) (numgrid+1) + i (numgrid+1) + j] # Step 1: Vertical search lov, hiv = 0.0, VERTICALRANGE for in range(VERTICALLINEARSEARCH): mid = (lov + hiv) / 2.0 pm = v0 + (v1 - v0) mid if implicitfunction(pm) > isolevel: hiv = mid else: lov = mid for in range(VERTICALBINARYSEARCH): mid = (lov + hiv) / 2.0 pm = v0 + (v1 - v0) mid if implicitfunction(pm) > isolevel: hiv = mid else: lov = mid midv = (lov + hiv) / 2.0 # Step 2: Horizontal search loh, hih = 0.0, HORIZNTLRANGE for in range(HORIZNTLLINEARSEARCH): mid = (loh + hih) / 2.0 pm = v0 + (v2 - v0) mid if implicitfunction(pm) > isolevel: hih = mid else: loh = mid for in range(HORIZNTLBINARYSEARCH): mid = (loh + hih) / 2.0 pm = v0 + (v2 - v0) mid if implicitfunction(pm) > isolevel: hih = mid else: loh = mid midh = (loh + hih) / 2.0 p2d[idx] = v0 + (v1 - v0) midv + (v2 - v0) midh # Compute normal n2d at p2d using p1d and p2d. vec = p2d[idx] - p1dref norm = torch.norm(vec) if norm < 1e-6: n2d[idx] = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0], device=device) else: n2d[idx] = vec / norm # Process cells: # For each cell, formulate QEF using p1d points and (p2d, n2d) pairs. # Solve QEF with regularization QEFREG. # Check separation constraint SEP. # Find 3D point p3d. for k in range(numgrid): for j in range(numgrid): for i in range(numgrid): idx = k numgrid numgrid + j numgrid + i # Build QEF from intersecting edges/faces A = [] b = [] # Add constraints from 1D points on edges # Add constraints from 2D points and normals on faces # (Standard QEF assembly) Amat = torch.stack(A) if A else torch.eye(3, device=device) bvec = torch.stack(b) if b else torch.zeros(3, device=device) # Solve regularized QEF: (A^T A + QEFREG I) x = A^T b AtA = Amat.T @ Amat + QEFREG torch.eye(3, device=device) Atb = Amat.T @ bvec p3d[idx] = torch.linalg.solve(AtA, Atb) # Check separation constraint SEP from grid face # (Clamp or adjust if distance < SEP) # 3. Mesh Generation # Use pfvtab (64-entry lookup table) to map cell occupancy to vertex indices. # Construct triangles from p3d points. vertices = [] triangles = [] for k in range(numgrid): for j in range(numgrid): for i in range(numgrid): idx = k numgrid numgrid + j numgrid + i # Compute cell occupancy pattern (0-63) pattern = 0 for d in range(8): cx, cy, cz = i + (d & 1), j + ((d >> 1) & 1), k + ((d >> 2) & 1) if occint[cx (numgrid+1) (numgrid+1) + cy (numgrid+1) + cz]: pattern |= (1 << d) # Lookup pfvtab and connect vertices config = pfvtab[pattern] for tri in config: triangles.append([p3d[idx] + voffset for voffset in tri]) # Return vertices, triangles return torch.stack(vertices), torch.tensor(triangles, dtype=torch.int64) Time Complexity: The method is designed for GPU parallelization, achieving computation times of a few seconds for typical resolutions. Memory Complexity: Depends on batchsize (GPU capacity) and impfunccplx (VRAM usage per query). Strengths: Learning-free, state-of-the-art performance for occupancy functions, avoids staircase artifacts of Marching Cubes, and handles continuous 3D space effectively. Limitations: Requires an implicit function that can be queried; performance depends on GPU VRAM. When to use: When extracting meshes from neural occupancy fields (e.g., Occupancy Networks, DeepSDF) where distance information is not available or reliable. Occupancy-Based Dual Contouring was introduced by the KAIST Visual AI Group. It is based on Manifold Dual Contouring (MDC) but modified specifically for neural implicit representations. The method addresses the bottleneck in converting occupancy functions to meshes, which traditional methods like Marching Cubes struggle with due to staircase artifacts. name: Mass Point Centering for Dual Contouring
body: Mass Point Centering improves the numerical stability of the Quadratic Error Function (QEF) solver in Dual Contouring by shifting the solution space to the centroid of the sample points. It addresses precision loss in floating-point arithmetic by centering the linear system around the data distribution rather than the coordinate origin. Inputs: data: A structure containing numPoints (integer count of edge intersection points), massPointx, massPointy, massPointz (sum of the coordinates of the input points), and ata00 through ata22 (elements of the symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix A^T A), plus atbx, atby, atbz (elements of the vector A^T b). svdtol: Tolerance for the symmetric linear solver. svdsweeps: Number of solver sweeps. pinvtol: Tolerance for pseudo-inverse calculation. Outputs: x: The computed dual vertex position in the original coordinate frame. hasSolution: Boolean indicating if a valid solution was found. Data Structures: Vector3: A 3D vector with components x, y, z. SMat3: A symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix stored with 6 floats: m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22. Steps: 1. Guard: If data.numPoints is 0, throw an exception. 2. Compute Centroid: Calculate the mass point (centroid) M by dividing the summed coordinates by the point count: M = \frac{1}{\text{numPoints}} \begin{bmatrix} \text{massPoint\x} \\ \text{massPoint\y} \\ \text{massPoint\z} \end{bmatrix} 3. Setup Matrices: Initialize the symmetric matrix A (stored in ata) and vector B (stored in atb) from the input data. 4. Adjust Right-Hand Side: Compute the adjustment term T = A M and subtract it from B: B{\text{new}} = B - A M 5. Solve System: Solve the adjusted linear system A x' = B{\text{new}} for x' using a symmetric linear solver. 6. Shift Solution: Recover the final position x by adding the centroid back: x = x' + M 7. Reset: Restore B to its original values if required by the calling context. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector3: def init(self, x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def scale(self, s): return Vector3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) class SMat3: def init(self, m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22): self.m00, self.m01, self.m02 = m00, m01, m02 self.m11, self.m12, self.m22 = m11, m12, m22 def vmul(self, v): return Vector3( self.m00 v.x + self.m01 v.y + self.m02 v.z, self.m01 v.x + self.m11 v.y + self.m12 v.z, self.m02 v.x + self.m12 v.y + self.m22 v.z) class ArgumentException(Exception): pass def solvesymmetric(A, b, tol, sweeps, pinvtol): # Sources do not specify the symmetric solver implementation # Standard symmetric solver (e.g., SVD or Cholesky) would go here. return Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), True def masspointcentering(data, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): if data.numPoints == 0: raise ArgumentException("No points provided") M = Vector3(data.massPointx, data.massPointy, data.massPointz).scale(1.0 / data.numPoints) A = SMat3(data.ata00, data.ata01, data.ata02, data.ata11, data.ata12, data.ata22) Boriginal = Vector3(data.atbx, data.atby, data.atbz) B = Vector3(data.atbx, data.atby, data.atbz) T = A.vmul(M) Bnew = B - T xprime, success = solvesymmetric(A, Bnew, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol) x = xprime + M B = Boriginal return x, success Parameters: svdtol: Not given in the sources. svdsweeps: Not given in the sources. pinvtol: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Zero Points: If numPoints is 0, the method throws an exception. Precision: The centering technique specifically targets numerical stability issues in floating-point arithmetic when points are distant from the origin. Computes the dual vertex position within a leaf cell by minimizing the squared algebraic distance to all edge intersection points on the isosurface boundary. Chosen when a direct least-squares formulation is preferred over the centered QEF adjustment. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves numerical stability for QEF systems. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the centroid and adds matrix-vector multiplication overhead. When to use: Not given in the sources.
