name: Screened Poisson Surface Reconstruction
head: Poisson Surface Reconstruction, SPSR, Surface Extraction via Screened Poisson Surface Reconstruction
body:
Screened Poisson Surface Reconstruction (SPSR) is an optimization-based method that fits a manifold surface directly to a single oriented point cloud without prior training. It solves a screened Poisson equation to interpolate a scalar field from oriented samples, extracting the zero-level set as a watertight mesh. Unlike marching cubes, which evaluates a volumetric grid and often produces non-watertight meshes or requires searching for an ideal level-set threshold, SPSR leverages the surface definition of the underlying differentiable renderer to create an oriented point set, which is then interpolated into a manifold surface. Inputs: An oriented point cloud consisting of positions \mathbf{c}i and unit normals \mathbf{n}i for i=1 \dots N. Outputs: A watertight triangle mesh. Data Structures: The input is a list of surfels. Each surfel i contains: \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Oriented unit normal. wi \in \mathbb{R}: Optional weight (default 1.0). Method: 1. Field Definition: Define a scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) such that its gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) approximates the vector field defined by the point cloud normals. The target vector field \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{x}) is constructed by weighting the normals of nearby points. 2. Poisson Equation: Solve for f by minimizing the energy functional: E(f) = \int{\Omega} |
abla f(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{x})|^2 d\mathbf{x} + \lambda \int{\Omega} |f(\mathbf{x})|^2 d\mathbf{x} The first term ensures 
abla f \approx \mathbf{V} (interpolation), and the second term (screening) with parameter \lambda prevents the solution from drifting to infinity, ensuring stability. 3. Discretization: Discretize the domain \Omega using a uniform grid or octree. The vector field \mathbf{V} is typically estimated using Shepard interpolation or similar kernel weighting of the input normals. 4. Linear System: The minimization leads to a sparse linear system A f = b, where A is the screened Laplacian matrix and b depends on the vector field samples. 5. Solve: Solve the linear system for f using a sparse linear solver (e.g., Conjugate Gradient). 6. Extraction: Extract the isosurface f(\mathbf{x}) = 0 using a marching cubes algorithm. Parameters: \lambda (screening parameter): Controls the trade-off between interpolation accuracy and smoothness. Not given in the sources. pointWeight: Interpolation weight. Reducing this parameter relaxes the interpolation constraint, which is recommended to mitigate under-sampling artifacts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Under-sampling: In regions where the partition-of-unity condition is not met (e.g., surface boundaries or rapid geometric variation), Shepard normalization acts as a kernel regression (Nadaraya–Watson estimator) rather than an interpolant. This causes surfel centers to deviate from the true surface. Artifacts: Using SPSR with high interpolation weight in under-sampled regions may produce artifacts because the method attempts to interpolate through smoothed approximations. Sparse Inputs: The method struggles with sparse or heavily corrupted inputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def screenedpoissonsurfacereconstruction(points, normals, lambdascreen=1.0, pointweight=1.0): """ Reconstructs a mesh from oriented points using Screened Poisson Surface Reconstruction. Args: points: List of 3D positions (N, 3). normals: List of unit normals (N, 3). lambdascreen: Screening parameter for the Poisson equation. pointweight: Interpolation weight to relax constraints in under-sampled regions. Returns: vertices: (M, 3) array of mesh vertices. faces: (K, 3) array of mesh face indices. """ # 1. Construct the vector field V(x) from the point cloud # V(x) is typically a weighted sum of normals using a kernel function K # V(x) = sumi (wi ni K(||x - ci||)) / sumi (wi K(||x - ci||)) # Note: The exact kernel and discretization scheme (grid vs octree) are implementation-specific. # 2. Discretize the domain and build the linear system # The system is A f = b # A = Laplacian + lambdascreen Identity # b is derived from the divergence of the vector field V or its projection onto the basis functions # 3. Solve the linear system # f = solve(A, b) # 4. Extract the zero-level set # Use Marching Cubes on the scalar field f to extract the mesh vertices, faces = marchingcubes(f, level=0) return vertices, faces A variant used to generate watertight, colored triangle meshes from implicit surface representations like 3D Gaussians. It differs by leveraging differentiable renderer outputs to create oriented point sets and transferring material attributes via interpolation. Time Complexity: Depends on the solver and grid resolution. Solving the sparse linear system is typically O(N) to O(N \log N) for well-conditioned systems, where N is the number of grid cells or points. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of grid cells and non-zeros in the Laplacian matrix. Strengths: Produces watertight, manifold meshes suitable for physics simulation and fabrication. Robust to noise compared to simple interpolation methods. Limitations: Struggles with sparse or heavily corrupted inputs. Requires careful tuning of the pointWeight parameter to handle under-sampled regions. When to use: When a watertight mesh is required from an oriented point cloud, especially in inverse rendering pipelines where material attributes need to be transferred to the mesh. When not to use: For sparse inputs or when the input point cloud is heavily corrupted, as the method may produce artifacts or fail to converge to a meaningful surface. Screened Poisson Surface Reconstruction was introduced by Kazhdan and Hoppe in 2013. It builds on the original Poisson Surface Reconstruction by Hoppe et al. (1992), adding a screening term to stabilize the solution. It is widely used in computer graphics for surface reconstruction from point clouds, particularly in the context of inverse rendering and 3D reconstruction from multi-view images or neural radiance fields. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Poisson Surface Reconstruction for Mesh Export
head: Oriented point cloud meshing, Poisson mesh extraction
body:
Poisson Surface Reconstruction for Mesh Export is a method to generate watertight, colored triangle meshes from implicit surface representations, such as 3D Gaussians or neural radiance fields, by solving a Poisson equation on an oriented point cloud. It differs from marching cubes, which evaluates a volumetric grid and often produces non-watertight meshes or requires searching for an ideal level-set threshold. This method builds on Screened Poisson Surface Reconstruction by leveraging the surface definition of the underlying differentiable renderer to create an oriented point set, which is then interpolated into a manifold surface. Inputs: An implicit surface representation (e.g., 3D Gaussians with means \mui, covariances \Sigmai, and colors). Training views (camera poses and intrinsics). Outputs: A watertight, colored triangle mesh. Data Structures: Oriented Point Cloud: A list of points P = \{pj\} where each pj = (x, y, z) has an associated normal vector  ar{n}j and color cj. Vector Field V: Estimated from the oriented point cloud, representing the gradient of the indicator function. Indicator Function \chi: A scalar field where \chi=1 inside the surface and \chi=0 outside. Steps: 1. Render Point Cloud: Render the object's point cloud from all training views to obtain point locations p = (x, y, z). 2. Compute Normals: Estimate the normal  ar{n} for each point. Two methods are described: Rasterization Locality: For a point p, identify its horizontal screen-space neighbor px and vertical neighbor py. Compute the normal as:  ar{n} =  rac{(p - px) 	imes (p - py)}{\|(p - px) 	imes (p - py)\|}. The sign of the normal must face the camera that created it. Gaussian Normal Blending (Alpha Compositing): For 3D Gaussians, blend local normal estimates ni from all contributing Gaussians using alpha compositing. The local normal estimate for Gaussian i is: ni =  rac{\Sigma^{-1}(v ti - \mui)}{\|\Sigma^{-1}(v ti - \mui)\|} where \Sigma is the covariance, v is the view direction, ti is the center of the Gaussian in view space, and \mui is the mean. This method is preferred for view consistency and requires no neighbors. 3. Quality Filtering (Optional): Reject intersections that fail a quality threshold. If wi is the weight of Gaussian i, reject if \maxi(wi) \le \epsilon, where \epsilon is typically 0.9. 4. Solve Poisson Equation: Solve the Poisson equation to produce the watertight mesh: 
abla \cdot 
abla \chi = 
abla \cdot V. This is solved via well-conditioned sparse linear systems with Dirichlet boundary constraints. The solution produces a surface that is a 2-manifold folded in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: Poisson Tree Depth: Controls the resolution of the reconstruction. Deeper trees produce more detail but amplify noise and artifacts. Typical values range from 6 to 10 for standard scenes, with 12 used in some implementations for high detail. Quality Threshold (\epsilon): Typically 0.9. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def poissonmeshexport(gaussians, trainingviews): """ Export a watertight mesh from 3D Gaussians using Poisson Surface Reconstruction. """ pointcloud = [] # Step 1 & 2: Render points and compute normals for view in trainingviews: # Render point cloud for this view points, depths, colors = renderpointcloud(gaussians, view) for i, p in enumerate(points): # Compute normal using Gaussian blending (preferred for view consistency) # Find contributing Gaussians for this pixel contributinggaussians = getcontributinggaussians(p, view, gaussians) if not contributinggaussians: continue # Blend normals using alpha compositing blendednormal = blendnormalsalphacompositing(contributinggaussians, view) # Add to point cloud pointcloud.append({ 'position': p, 'normal': blendednormal, 'color': colors[i] }) # Step 4: Solve Poisson Equation # The specific solver implementation depends on the library (e.g., Open3D, libigl) # We assume a function that takes an oriented point cloud and returns a mesh mesh = solvepoissonequation(pointcloud, depth=12) return mesh def blendnormalsalphacompositing(gaussians, view): """ Blend local normal estimates using alpha compositing. In experiments, MASt3R and Screened Poisson are used for mesh initialization, though the framework is agnostic to the specific reconstruction method. name: Surface Recovery via Alpha Thresholding and Poisson Reconstruction
head: Mesh-based Baseline, Poisson surface reconstruction, SfM and MVS pipeline
body: A method to generate high-quality, watertight triangle meshes from trained neural radiance field representations by identifying surface points through alpha thresholding and reconstructing geometry via Poisson surface reconstruction. It serves as a post-training surface extraction technique, contrasting with methods designed primarily for novel-view synthesis which often produce noisy artifacts. It is distinct from the conventional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) baseline, which relies on external stereo reconstruction pipelines rather than internal neural field gradients. Inputs: A trained neural radiance field model (e.g., NeRF, Instant-NGP, or the specific representation described in). Camera poses and intrinsic parameters associated with the training data. Outputs: A textured triangle mesh (vertices, faces, and texture maps). Data Structures: Point Cloud: A set of 3D points \mathbf{p}i and associated normal vectors \mathbf{n}i. Mesh: A triangle soup or manifold mesh defined by vertex indices and texture coordinates. Parameters: Alpha Threshold (\alpha{th}): 0.95. Used to identify surface points by sampling high-gradient regions. Grid Resolution: 512^3 for baseline comparisons using Marching Cubes. Octree Depth: 10 for the screened Poisson surface reconstruction in the SfM baseline. Texture Resolution: 4096 \times 4096 pixels for texture projection. Steps: 1. Surface Point Identification: Sample the neural field to identify points on the object surface. This is achieved by finding locations where the alpha (opacity) value exceeds the threshold \alpha{th} = 0.95. These locations correspond to high-gradient regions in the density field. 2. Normal Estimation: Predict or estimate the normal vector \mathbf{n}i for each identified surface point \mathbf{p}i. 3. Poisson Reconstruction: Perform Poisson surface reconstruction using the set of points \{\mathbf{p}i\} and normals \{\mathbf{n}i\} to generate a watertight mesh. Note: The specific implementation of the Poisson solver (e.g., screened vs. standard) is not detailed for the primary method in, but the SfM baseline uses screened Poisson reconstruction with an octree depth of 10. 4. Texture Projection (Baseline Only): For the SfM and MVS baseline comparison, project texture maps from registered input images onto the generated mesh at a resolution of 4096 \times 4096 pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def surfacerecovery(neuralfield, alphathreshold=0.95): """ Extracts a mesh from a neural field using alpha thresholding and Poisson reconstruction. """ # 1. Sample the field to find surface points # In practice, this involves ray marching or grid sampling to find iso-surfaces surfacepoints = [] surfacenormals = [] # Iterate through a grid or sample rays to find points where alpha > threshold for point in samplespace(): alpha = neuralfield.getalpha(point) if alpha > alphathreshold: surfacepoints.append(point) # Estimate normal from gradient of the field or predicted normal normal = neuralfield.getnormal(point) surfacenormals.append(normal) # 2. Perform Poisson Surface Reconstruction # This solves for a scalar function whose gradient best fits the vector field # defined by the normals, resulting in a watertight mesh. mesh = poissonreconstruction(surfacepoints, surfacenormals) return mesh Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating Artifacts: NeRF and Instant-NGP are designed for novel-view synthesis, not surface reconstruction, leading to noisy reconstructions with floating artifacts. Interior Visibility: Interior features (e.g., the inside of a shell) are poorly reconstructed by standard NeRF, Instant-NGP, and NeuS due to limited visibility from camera views. Methods using geometry-based sampling (like NeRFifyMesh) can capture these features better. Metric Sensitivity: Evaluation is typically done using Chamfer Distance. Accuracy: Outperforms NeRF and Instant-NGP on all tested objects and NeuS on 3 of 4 objects based on Chamfer Distance. Comparison to SfM/MVS: The conventional SfM and MVS pipeline (using COLMAP and PatchMatch) serves as a baseline. The neural field-based method avoids the need for explicit stereo matching and depth fusion. Limitations: Standard neural fields struggle with occluded or interior geometry. Origin: The method is described in the context of "NeRFifyMesh," a technique for optimizing neural radiance fields from textured meshes for robotics scene building. Development: It addresses the limitation of existing NeRF variants (NeRF, Instant-NGP, NeuS) which produce noisy surfaces or fail to capture interior details. Usage: Used in robotics simulation environments where accurate geometry for collision interactions is required. name: Dual Contouring Feature Point Iterative Projection
head: Feature Point Iterative Projection, Iterative Feature Point Projection
body: An iterative method to find a feature point (vertex) in dual contouring by projecting a point onto planes defined by edge midpoints and normals, minimizing the distance to these planes. It differs from standard dual contouring by using a fixed-iteration projection approach rather than solving a full quadratic error function (QEF) system, and from MLS Projection by relying on simple plane projections rather than moving least squares fitting. Inputs: A voxel cell (cube) with intersecting edges. For each intersecting edge: the midpoint of the edge intersection with the isosurface, and the surface normal at that midpoint. The center of the voxel cell. Outputs: A single 3D point (the feature point) inside the voxel cell. Data Structures: Plane: Defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} and a scalar distance d from the origin, such that the plane equation is \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. \mathbf{n}: Normalized 3D vector. d: Scalar, computed as -\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} where \mathbf{p} is a point on the plane (e.g., the edge midpoint). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the current point \mathbf{c} to the center of the voxel cell. 2. For each intersecting edge i, create a plane Pi using the edge's midpoint \mathbf{m}i and normal \mathbf{n}i: \mathbf{n}i = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{n}i). di = -\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{m}i. 3. Iterate k from 0 to iterations - 1: a. For each plane Pi, calculate the signed distance from \mathbf{c} to the plane: \text{dist}i = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{c} + di. b. Calculate the shortest distance vector (displacement) for each plane: \mathbf{v}i = \text{dist}i \cdot \mathbf{n}i. c. Average the displacement vectors: \mathbf{avg} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{v}i. where N is the number of intersecting edges. d. Update the current point: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{avg} \cdot \text{step\factor}. 4. Return \mathbf{c} as the feature point. Parameters: iterations: Number of projection steps. Typical value: 5. stepfactor: Multiplier for the averaged distance vector. Typical value: 0.7. Convergence occurs without scaling (factor 1.0), but 0.7 stabilizes convergence speed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-intersecting planes: The algorithm may fail if the planes do not intersect within the voxel, leading to divergence or unstable results. Direction of update: Subtracting the averaged vector moves the point towards the planes (convergence). Adding it moves the point away from the intersection (divergence). Precision: Normals must be normalized before computing plane distances. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefeaturepoint(intersectingedges, voxelcenter): # Step 1: Initialize point to voxel center c = voxelcenter # Precompute planes planes = [] for midpoint, normal in intersectingedges: # Normalize normal n = normalize(normal) # Compute plane distance d such that n.x + d = 0 for point x on plane d = -dot(n, midpoint) planes.append((n, d)) numiterations = 5 stepfactor = 0.7 # Step 3: Iterate for in range(numiterations): avgdisplacement = Vector3(0, 0, 0) for n, d in planes: # Calculate signed distance from c to plane dist = dot(n, c) + d # Calculate displacement vector v = n dist avgdisplacement += v # Average displacement vectors N = len(planes) if N > 0: avgdisplacement = avgdisplacement / N # Update point c = c - avgdisplacement stepfactor return c class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return Vector3(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def truediv(self, scalar): return Vector3(self.x / scalar, self.y / scalar, self.z / scalar) def dot(a, b): return a.x b.x + a.y b.y + a.z b.z def normalize(v): length = (dot(v, v)) 0.5 return Vector3(v.x / length, v.y / length, v.z / length) Alternative Formulation: Instead of subtracting the averaged distance vector, one can project the point onto each plane individually and then average the projected points. This is mathematically equivalent: 1. For each plane Pi, calculate the projected point: \mathbf{v}i = \mathbf{c} - \text{dist}i \cdot \mathbf{n}i. 2. Average the projected points: \mathbf{c} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{v}i. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, avoids solving linear systems. Limitations: Quality depends on normal accuracy; may fail with non-intersecting planes. When to use: Real-time applications or when QEF solving is too expensive. When not to use: High geometric accuracy required with noisy normals. This method was discussed in a community Q&A to fix a divergence bug caused by an inverted update direction in a dual contouring implementation. It was proposed as a correction to a common implementation error where the update direction was inverted, causing divergence. The approach is a simplified iterative solver for the feature point location problem in dual contouring. name: Dual Contouring of Signed Distance Data
head: DCSDD
body: Dual Contouring of Signed Distance Data (DCSDD) is an algorithm for reconstructing explicit polygonal meshes from discretely sampled Signed Distance Function (SDF) data, specifically designed to recover sharp features. It builds on Dual Contouring and Surface Nets by solving a quadratic optimization problem to determine optimal vertex placement within each grid cell, relying solely on discrete SDF samples without requiring gradient information or arbitrary function access. Unlike Dual Contouring which typically requires Hermite data (positions and normals), DCSDD derives the necessary constraints directly from the SDF values, setting a new state of the art for medium and high-resolution SDF reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A regular 3D grid of discretely sampled Signed Distance Function (SDF) values. Output: An explicit polygonal mesh (vertices and faces). Data Structures: SDF Grid: A 3D array storing scalar distance values. The resolution determines the grid cell size. Hermite Data: For each grid cell intersecting the isosurface, the algorithm maintains or computes Hermite data (position and normal) at the intersection points. In DCSDD, these are derived from the SDF samples rather than provided as input. Vertex Position: A 3D vector v representing the reconstructed vertex position within the grid cell. Energy Terms: The optimization minimizes a composite energy function involving Hermite consistency and regularization terms. Parameters: outeriters: Number of iterations in the outer loop. Default: 100. inneriters: Number of iterations in the inner loop (local energy minimization). Default: 100. hermiteupdate: Boolean flag indicating whether to refine Hermite positions from the mesh. Default: True. mu: Regularization weight. Default: 0.1. dcweight: Weight of the Dual Contouring (Hermite) energy term. Default: 0.02. newhermiteposweight: Blend weight for updating Hermite positions. Default: 0.2. newhermitenormalweight: Blend weight for updating Hermite normals. Default: 0.2. newfaceposweight: Blend weight for updating face positions. Default: 0.2. batchsize: Number of SDF grid points processed per batch. Default: 200000. verbose: Boolean flag to print per-iteration energy values. Default: False. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each grid cell, identify the edges intersecting the zero-level set of the SDF. Compute initial Hermite data (intersection position and normal) for these edges using linear interpolation and finite differences or gradient approximation from the SDF grid. 2. Outer Loop: Iterate outeriters times: a. Hermite Update (if hermiteupdate is True): Refine the Hermite positions and normals based on the current mesh state or SDF data, blending new estimates with existing ones using newhermiteposweight, newhermitenormalweight, and newfaceposweight. b. Inner Loop (Local Energy Minimization): For each grid cell containing a vertex to be placed: i. Define the local energy function E(v) for the vertex position v. The energy typically includes a term penalizing deviation from the Hermite constraints (position and normal consistency) and a regularization term weighted by mu. ii. Solve the quadratic optimization problem for v using inneriters iterations. The optimization minimizes E(v) subject to the constraints derived from the Hermite data. iii. Update the vertex position v in the cell. c. Mesh Generation: After placing vertices in all cells, generate the mesh topology by connecting vertices within each cell according to the dual contouring scheme (typically forming a convex polyhedron or triangle fan). 3. Output: Return the generated mesh. Formulas: The specific quadratic energy function E(v) is not explicitly detailed in the provided sources, but it is described as a combination of Hermite energy (weighted by dcweight) and regularization (weighted by mu). The optimization solves for v that minimizes this energy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: SDF values must be accurate; noise can lead to incorrect Hermite data and poor mesh quality. Boundaries: Cells at the grid boundary may have fewer intersecting edges, requiring special handling for Hermite data generation. Degenerate Input: If the SDF is flat or has no zero-crossings in a cell, no vertex is placed. Platform: The implementation was tested on macOS only; issues may arise on other platforms. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualcontouringsdf(sdfgrid, options): """ Reconstruct mesh from SDF grid using Dual Contouring of Signed Distance Data. Args: sdfgrid: 3D numpy array of SDF values. options: ContouringOptions object with parameters. Returns: vertices: Array of vertex positions. faces: Array of face indices. """ # Initialize Hermite data for each cell hermitedata = initializehermitedata(sdfgrid) # Outer loop for outeriter in range(options.outeriters): # Refine Hermite data if enabled if options.hermiteupdate: hermitedata = refinehermitedata(hermitedata, sdfgrid, options) # Inner loop: local energy minimization for each cell vertices = [] for cell in cellsintersectingisosurface(sdfgrid): # Get Hermite constraints for this cell constraints = hermitedata[cell] # Solve quadratic optimization for vertex position v # Minimize E(v) = dcweight HermiteEnergy(v, constraints) + mu Regularization(v) v = solvequadraticoptimization(constraints, options.dcweight, options.mu, options.inneriters) vertices.append(v) # Generate mesh topology from vertices faces = generatemeshtopology(vertices, sdfgrid) if options.verbose: print(f"Outer iteration {outeriter}, Energy: {computeenergy(vertices, hermitedata, options)}") return vertices, faces def initializehermitedata(sdfgrid): """ Compute initial Hermite data (position and normal) for edges intersecting the zero-level set. Uses linear interpolation for position and finite differences for normal. """ hermitedata = {} for cell in allcells(sdfgrid): intersectingedges = findintersectingedges(cell, sdfgrid) hermitedata[cell] = [] for edge in intersectingedges: # Linear interpolation for position pos = interpolateposition(edge, sdfgrid) # Finite difference for normal normal = computenormal(edge, sdfgrid) hermitedata[cell].append({'pos': pos, 'normal': normal}) return hermitedata def refinehermitedata(hermitedata, sdfgrid, options): """ Refine Hermite positions and normals using blend weights. """ newhermitedata = {} for cell, constraints in hermitedata.items(): newconstraints = [] for constraint in constraints: # Blend new estimates with existing ones newpos = blend(constraint['pos'], computenewpos(constraint, sdfgrid), options.newhermiteposweight) newnormal = blend(constraint['normal'], computenewnormal(constraint, sdfgrid), options.newhermitenormalweight) newconstraints.append({'pos': newpos, 'normal': newnormal}) newhermitedata[cell] = newconstraints return newhermitedata def solvequadraticoptimization(constraints, dcweight, mu, inneriters): """ Solve the quadratic optimization problem for vertex position v. Minimizes E(v) = dcweight sum((v - posi)^2) + mu sum((v - center)^2) using inneriters iterations. """ # Initial guess for v (e.g., cell center) v = cellcenter(constraints) for i in range(inneriters): # Compute gradient of E(v) grad = computegradient(v, constraints, dcweight, mu) # Update v using gradient descent or similar method v = v - learningrate grad return v def computegradient(v, constraints, dcweight, mu): """ Compute the gradient of the energy function E(v). """ grad = np.zeros(3) for constraint in constraints: pos = constraint['pos'] grad += 2 dcweight (v - pos) # Add regularization gradient center = cellcenter(constraints) grad += 2 mu (v - center) return grad def computenewpos(constraint, sdfgrid): """ Compute new position estimate for Hermite data refinement. Assume it involves projecting the current position # onto the zero-level set using SDF values. return constraint['pos'] # Placeholder def computenewnormal(constraint, sdfgrid): """ Compute new normal estimate for Hermite data refinement. Assume it is the average of the corner positions # of the grid cell. return np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) # Placeholder def computeenergy(vertices, hermitedata, options): """ Compute the total energy for verbose output. Assume it sums the Hermite and regularization energies # for all vertices. return 0.0 # Placeholder Traditional dual contouring using Hermite data (positions and normals) as input. The batch processing (batchsize) helps manage memory but does not change asymptotic complexity. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of grid cells and the size of Hermite data per cell. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of parameters (e.g., mu, dcweight); implementation tested only on macOS; performance may vary on other platforms. name: Neural and Learning-based Extraction
body: Neural and Learning-based Extraction methods generate explicit triangle meshes from implicit representations (such as Signed Distance Fields or occupancy fields) by integrating the extraction process into a differentiable computational graph. Unlike static algorithms like Marching Cubes, these methods allow the mesh geometry to be optimized via gradient descent to fit target scalar values or visual objectives. They set themselves apart from sibling methods by treating grid deformations and topological weights as learnable parameters, enabling the resolution of topological ambiguities and the production of high-fidelity surfaces directly from neural network outputs. This family inherits the discretized domain traversal and surface determination mechanisms from Isosurface extraction. MISE generates a 3D mesh from a trained Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) model by querying an implicit occupancy field using an adaptive resolution algorithm. It sets itself apart from uniform grid-based extraction methods by iteratively refining the sampling grid only where the occupancy field is ambiguous, thereby achieving high-fidelity meshes with significantly fewer model evaluations than static high-resolution marching cubes. It is chosen when the implicit function is expensive to evaluate and the surface geometry is sparse or complex. FlexiCubes is a differentiable isosurface extraction method that converts a Signed Distance Field (SDF) defined on a voxel grid into a triangle mesh, specifically designed for gradient-based optimization of geometric, visual, or physical objectives. Unlike static extraction methods, it introduces learnable per-cube weights (beta, alpha, gamma) and vertex deformations to resolve topological ambiguities and improve mesh quality during training. It builds on Neural and Learning-based Extraction by providing a fully differentiable pipeline where the mesh geometry itself becomes an optimization variable. It is chosen when optimizing a mesh to fit a target SDF or when training a neural network to output geometry directly. This method generates multi-resolution ground truth data for training Neural Marching Cubes (NMC) by computing per-grid-cell labels (case IDs, vertex positions, and plane parameters) from high-resolution voxel and surface intersection data. It solves the problem of creating accurate training targets for a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that predicts Marching Cubes configurations, enabling the network to learn the mapping from input fields to mesh primitives. It differs from gradient-based methods by explicitly using computed surface intersection points and their normals for least-squares fitting to determine plane parameters, rather than relying solely on voxel occupancy or field gradients. It is chosen when training a CNN to replace the extraction step for inference speed. This method extracts a triangle mesh from a trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by querying the learned density field \sigma on a 3D grid and applying the marching cubes algorithm at a specific threshold. It solves the problem of converting a volumetric, implicit representation into an explicit, watertight geometric mesh suitable for standard rendering pipelines or downstream geometry processing. It differs from its siblings, MISE and FlexiCubes, by relying on a fixed-resolution regular grid and a static isosurface threshold rather than adaptive refinement or learned cube templates. It is chosen for standard NeRF-to-mesh conversion where differentiability is not required. Differentiable Marching Cubes (DiffMC) is a mesh extraction method that generates explicit, watertight manifold meshes from scalar fields (typically Signed Distance Fields) by optimizing learnable grid deformations and per-cube weights. It builds on Neural and Learning-based Extraction by introducing a deformable grid and differentiable FlexiCubes operator, allowing the mesh geometry to be optimized via gradient descent to fit target scalar values. Unlike static extraction methods, DiffMC dynamically adjusts surface representation through gradient-based optimization, producing significantly smoother surfaces than tet-based alternatives like DMTet when extracting from density fields. It is chosen when high-quality SDF-to-mesh conversion is needed within a differentiable optimization loop. The family originates from the need to bridge the gap between implicit neural representations (like NeRFs and SDFs) and explicit polygonal meshes for downstream applications. Early work focused on static extraction from NeRF density fields. The introduction of differentiable extraction, such as MISE, allowed for adaptive sampling. Subsequent developments like FlexiCubes and Differentiable Marching Cubes enabled end-to-end training of geometry by making the extraction process differentiable with respect to grid parameters. Ground truth generation methods were developed to train CNNs for fast inference, replacing the differentiable optimization step with a learned approximation. name: MISE (Meshing Isosurfaces by Extracting)
head: DVR Mesh Generation via MISE, Meshing Isosurfaces by Extracting
body: MISE generates a 3D mesh from a trained Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) model by querying an implicit occupancy field using an adaptive resolution strategy. It avoids the computational cost of evaluating the field on a uniform high-resolution grid. Inputs: A trained DVR model f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}. A bounding box defining the spatial domain. Parameters: threshold, resolution0, upsamplingsteps, padding, pointsbatchsize. Outputs: A 3D mesh extracted via marching cubes on a dense grid. Data Structures: points: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates. values: A tensor of shape (N, 1) containing model outputs (logits). MISE hierarchy structure managing active points and grid levels. Steps: 1. Threshold Conversion: Convert the float occupancy threshold t to log-odds space for the model output: t{\text{logit}} = \ln(t) - \ln(1 - t) 2. Initialization: If upsamplingsteps is 0: generate a uniform grid of points using make3dgrid with resolution nx = \text{resolution0}, evaluate them, and reshape to a 3D grid. If upsamplingsteps > 0: initialize the MISE extractor with resolution0, upsamplingsteps, and t{\text{logit}}. 3. Adaptive Querying Loop: Query points from the MISE extractor: points = meshextractor.query(). While points.shape[0] != 0: normalize points to the bounding box coordinates, evaluate the model in batches of size pointsbatchsize, update the MISE structure with the evaluated values, and query the next set of points. 4. Densification: Convert the MISE structure to a dense 3D grid using meshextractor.todense(). Apply marching cubes on the dense grid using the original float threshold t. Parameters: threshold: Occupancy threshold for marching cubes. Default: 0.5. resolution0: Starting resolution for MISE. Default: 16. upsamplingsteps: Number of upsampling steps. Default: 3. padding: Padding added to the bounding box size. Default: 0.1. pointsbatchsize: Batch size for point evaluation. Default: 100000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Convert threshold to log-odds thresholdlogit = np.log(threshold) - np.log(1.0 - threshold) # 2. Initialization if upsamplingsteps == 0: points = make3dgrid(resolution0, bboxmin, bboxmax) values = evaluatemodel(model, points, pointsbatchsize) grid = reshapeto3dgrid(values, resolution0) else: # Initialize MISE extractor (simplified hierarchy management) finalres = resolution0 (2 upsamplingsteps) meshextractor = MISEExtractor(resolution0, upsamplingsteps, thresholdlogit, padding) # 3. Adaptive Querying Loop points = meshextractor.query() while points.shape[0] != 0: normalizedpoints = normalizetobbox(points, bboxmin, bboxmax) values = evaluatemodel(model, normalizedpoints, pointsbatchsize) meshextractor.update(values) points = meshextractor.query() # 4. Densification grid = meshextractor.todense() # Extract mesh using marching cubes on the dense grid vertices, faces,, = marchingcubes(grid, level=threshold) return vertices, faces class MISEExtractor: """Simplified MISE hierarchy manager based on source steps.""" def init(self, resolution0, upsamplingsteps, threshold, padding): self.resolution0 = resolution0 self.upsamplingsteps = upsamplingsteps self.threshold = threshold self.padding = padding self.activepoints = [] self.values = {} def query(self): """Return points to evaluate. Returns empty array when convergence is reached.""" if not self.activepoints: return np.array([]) points = np.array(self.activepoints) self.activepoints = [] return points def update(self, values): """Update hierarchy with evaluated values and generate next active points.""" # Standard MISE logic: mark cells near threshold as active for next level # Placeholder for exact hierarchical subdivision logic not detailed in sources pass def todense(self): """Convert hierarchy to a dense 3D grid.""" finalres = self.resolution0 (2 self.upsamplingsteps) grid = np.full((finalres, finalres, finalres), np.nan) # Fill grid with stored values at corresponding voxel indices return grid make3dgrid, normalizetobbox, evaluatemodel, reshapeto3dgrid, and marchingcubes are standard operations implemented here for self-containment. The MISEExtractor class implements the high-level query/update loop from the evidence; exact hierarchical subdivision logic is omitted as the sources do not provide it. Time Complexity: Sub-linear in the volume of the domain, as it only queries points near the isosurface. Complexity depends on the number of active points in the MISE hierarchy. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of points queried and the final dense grid size. The dense grid size is determined by the final resolution after upsampling steps. Strengths: Adaptive resolution, efficient memory usage for complex shapes. Limitations: Requires iterative querying, which may be slower for simple shapes compared to uniform grid methods. Sensitive to the choice of resolution0 and upsamplingsteps. When to use: When extracting high-fidelity meshes from neural implicit representations where uniform grid evaluation is too expensive. When not to use: For simple shapes where a low-resolution uniform grid suffices, or when real-time extraction is required and the overhead of adaptive querying is prohibitive. It provides a method to efficiently extract meshes from the learned occupancy fields without the computational cost of evaluating the field on a dense uniform grid. name: FlexiCubes
head: FlexiCubes Surface Extraction with Gradient-Based Optimization, Flexible Isosurface Extraction for Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization
body:
FlexiCubes is a differentiable isosurface extraction method that extracts a triangle mesh from a Signed Distance Field (SDF) defined on a voxel grid by optimizing learnable weight parameters within each voxel cube. It is designed specifically for gradient-based mesh optimization, allowing the surface to adapt to geometric, visual, or physical objectives. Unlike standard Marching Cubes which uses fixed lookup tables, FlexiCubes learns local deformation weights (beta, alpha, gamma) to minimize reconstruction error and improve mesh quality, such as reducing floaters and ensuring developability. It builds on Isosurface extraction by replacing the static topology determination with a differentiable, optimization-driven process. Inputs: Input mesh (OBJ format) or known SDF values. Voxel grid resolution R (integer, 4 \le R \le 512). Optimization parameters: learning rate, max iterations, convergence threshold, clamp value, and regularizer weights. Outputs: Extracted triangle mesh (vertices and faces). Optional: Optimized weight tensors and loss values. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: Constructed at resolution R. Contains: xnx3: Vertex positions of shape (Nv, 3), where Nv = (R+1)^3. cubefx8: Cube connectivity of shape (Nc, 8), where Nc = R^3, listing the 8 vertex indices for each cube. 2. Learnable Parameters: sdf: Tensor of shape (Nv,), representing SDF values at grid vertices. deform: Tensor of shape (Nv, 3), representing vertex displacement offsets. weight: Tensor of shape (Nc, 21), split into: beta: Indices 0–11, shape (Nc, 12). alpha: Indices 12–19, shape (Nc, 8). gamma: Index 20, shape (Nc,). 3. TriangleMeshDistance (TMD): A query structure built from the input mesh vertices and faces to compute SDF values. Steps: 1. Initialization: If starting from a mesh: Load OBJ, normalize to unit cube, and compute scale factor. Construct TMD structure from input mesh vertices and faces. Construct voxel grid at resolution R to get xnx3 and cubefx8. Initialize sdf: If not provided, sample from uniform distribution and subtract 0.1. If provided, use known SDF. Initialize deform to zeros. Initialize weight (beta, alpha, gamma) to zeros. 2. Deformation Calculation: Compute deformed grid vertices gridverts using: 	ext{grid\verts} = \mathbf{x} +  rac{2 - 10^{-8}}{2R} 	anh(	ext{deform}) where \mathbf{x} are the original grid vertex positions xnx3. The factor (2 - 10^{-8}) avoids numerical issues at boundaries. 3. Surface Extraction (Differentiable): Call the FlexiCubes extraction function with gridverts, sdf, cubefx8, resolution R, and weights beta, alpha, gamma. Set training=True to produce 4 triangles per quad for better mesh quality; otherwise, 2 triangles per quad. The function returns the extracted mesh, the Laplacian deviation loss L{dev}, and gradients with respect to the weights. 4. Loss Computation: SDF Regularization: Compute mean SDF regularization loss L{sdf} on grid edges, weighted by sdfweight (default 0.2). Laplacian Deviation: Add L{dev} weighted by optldevweight (default 0.5). Weight Regularization: Add L1 regularization on beta and alpha (indices 0–19), weighted by 0.1. Optional SDF Loss: If optimizing SDF values, sample points on the ground truth mesh, compute MSE between predicted and ground truth SDF, weighted by 2 	imes 10^3. Optional Developability: If enabled, add mesh developability regularization. Total Loss L = L{sdf} + L{dev} + L{weighteg} + \dots. 5. Optimization Loop: For each iteration: Compute gradients of L with respect to beta, alpha, gamma via backpropagation through the extraction step. Update weights using gradient descent (or Adam optimizer with default LR 0.01):  eta \leftarrow  eta - \eta 
abla eta L \alpha \leftarrow \alpha - \eta 
abla\alpha L \gamma \leftarrow \gamma - \eta 
abla\gamma L If optclamp > 0, clamp weights to [-	ext{opt\clamp}, 	ext{opt\clamp}]. Check convergence: If |	ext{prev\loss} - 	ext{current\loss}| < 	ext{opt\convergence} and iteration > 5, break. Update prevloss. 6. Final Extraction: If optimization is disabled, extract surface directly without gradients. Return final mesh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def loadobj(path): """Standard OBJ parser returning vertices (V, 3) and faces (F, 3).""" verts, faces = [], [] with open(path, 'r') as f: for line in f: parts = line.strip().split() if not parts: continue if parts[0] == 'v': verts.append([float(x) for x in parts[1:]]) elif parts[0] == 'f': faces.append([int(x) for x in parts[1:]]) return torch.tensor(verts, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(faces, dtype=torch.int64) def normalizetounitcube(verts): """Scales vertices to unit cube, returns scale factor and normalized vertices.""" minv, maxv = verts.min(dim=0)[0], verts.max(dim=0)[0] center = (minv + maxv) / 2.0 scale = 1.0 / (maxv - minv).max() return scale, (verts - center) scale def constructvoxelgrid(res): """Generates grid points and cube connectivity for resolution R.""" points = torch.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, res + 1) grid = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid(points, points, points, indexing='ij'), dim=-1) gridverts = grid.reshape(-1, 3) N = res + 1 cubefx8 = [] for i in range(res): for j in range(res): for k in range(res): idx = i N N + j N + k cubefx8.append([idx, idx+1, idx+N, idx+N+1, idx+NN, idx+NN+1, idx+NN+N, idx+NN+N+1]) return gridverts, torch.tensor(cubefx8, dtype=torch.int64) def computesdf(tmdverts, tmdfaces, gridverts): """Computes SDF at grid vertices by querying mesh triangles.""" sdf = torch.zeros(gridverts.shape[0], dtype=torch.float32) for i in range(gridverts.shape[0]): p = gridverts[i] mindist = float('inf') for f in range(tmdfaces.shape[0]): v0, v1, v2 = tmdverts[tmdfaces[f]] # Project p onto triangle plane, check barycentric coords # Simplified: distance to triangle edges/vertices # Standard TMD implementation handles this efficiently dist = torch.sqrt(((p - v0)2).sum()) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist sdf[i] = mindist return sdf def flexicubesextractkernel(gridverts, sdf, cubefx8, res, beta, alpha, gamma, training): """Standard FlexiCubes extraction kernel. Returns mesh, Ldev, grads.""" # Placeholder for the actual C++/CUDA kernel logic # Computes interpolated vertex positions, determines topology per cube, # assembles triangles, and computes Laplacian deviation loss. # Gradients are computed w.r.t. beta, alpha, gamma. mesh = torch.zeros((0, 3), dtype=torch.float32) Ldev = torch.tensor(0.0, requiresgrad=True) grads = type('Grads', (), {'dbeta': beta.grad.clone(), 'dalpha': alpha.grad.clone(), 'dgamma': gamma.grad.clone()})() return mesh, Ldev, grads def flexicubesextract(inputmeshpath, resolution, optiterations=100, learningrate=0.01, optconvergence=1e-4, optclamp=0.0, optldevweight=0.5, sdfweight=0.2, training=True): # Step 1: Load and normalize input mesh verts, faces = loadobj(inputmeshpath) scale, verts = normalizetounitcube(verts) # Step 2: Construct voxel grid gridvertsinit, cubefx8 = constructvoxelgrid(resolution) numvertices = gridvertsinit.shape[0] numcubes = cubefx8.shape[0] # Step 3: Initialize learnable parameters sdf = torch.randn(numvertices, requiresgrad=True) - 0.1 deform = torch.zeros(numvertices, 3, requiresgrad=True) weight = torch.zeros(numcubes, 21, requiresgrad=True) beta = weight[:,:12] alpha = weight[:, 12:20] gamma = weight[:, 20] prevloss = float('inf') for iter in range(optiterations): # Step 4: Compute deformed grid vertices gridverts = gridvertsinit + (2 - 1e-8) / (2 resolution) torch.tanh(deform) # Step 5: Extract surface with gradients mesh, Ldev, grads = flexicubesextractkernel( gridverts, sdf, cubefx8, resolution, beta, alpha, gamma, training) # Step 6: Compute losses Lsdf = sdf.abs().mean() sdfweight Ldevterm = Ldev.mean() optldevweight Lweightreg = weight[:,:20].abs().mean() 0.1 totalloss = Lsdf + Ldevterm + Lweightreg # Step 7: Backpropagation totalloss.backward() # Step 8: Update weights with torch.nograd(): beta -= learningrate grads.dbeta alpha -= learningrate grads.dalpha gamma -= learningrate grads.dgamma if optclamp > 0.0: beta = torch.clamp(beta, -optclamp, optclamp) alpha = torch.clamp(alpha, -optclamp, optclamp) gamma = torch.clamp(gamma, -optclamp, optclamp) # Step 9: Check convergence losschange = abs(prevloss - totalloss.item()) if losschange < optconvergence and iter > 5: break prevloss = totalloss.item() # Clear gradients for next iteration beta.grad.zero() alpha.grad.zero() gamma.grad.zero() # Final extraction without gradients for output finalgridverts = gridvertsinit + (2 - 1e-8) / (2 resolution) torch.tanh(deform.detach()) finalmesh,, = flexicubesextractkernel( finalgridverts, sdf.detach(), cubefx8, resolution, beta.detach(), alpha.detach(), gamma.detach(), training=False) return finalmesh Parameters: resolution: Voxel grid resolution. Range: [4, 512]. Default: 64. learningrate: Adam optimizer learning rate. Default: 0.01. optiterations: Max optimization iterations. optconvergence: Threshold for loss change to stop. optclamp: Max absolute value for weight clamping. If > 0, weights are clamped to [-	ext{opt\clamp}, 	ext{opt\clamp}]. optldevweight: Weight for Laplacian deviation loss. Default: 0.5. sdfweight: Weight for SDF regularization loss. Default: 0.2. training: Boolean. If True, produces 4 triangles per quad; if False, 2 triangles per quad. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Numerical Issues: The deformation scaling factor uses (2 - 10^{-8}) instead of 2 to avoid numerical instability at the grid boundaries. Resolution Scaling: FlexiCubes voxel grid with resolution R has (R+1)^3 vertices. Regularization Weights: Strong regularization can hinder convergence. A method that extracts meshes by optimizing a continuous implicit function to match a discrete isosurface, focusing on high-quality topology. Choose when you need a smooth, watertight mesh from a discrete volume without learning-based weights. A technique to generate high-quality training data for neural Marching Cubes variants. Choose when you need to train a neural network to predict Marching Cubes weights. Extracts meshes from NeRF density fields using differentiable rendering or volume rendering techniques. Choose when your input is a NeRF rather than a voxel grid SDF. Makes the standard Marching Cubes algorithm differentiable by relaxing the discrete topology decisions. Choose when you need a simpler differentiable surface extraction without learnable per-cube weights. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations. Each iteration involves a forward pass through the voxel grid (O(R^3)) and a backward pass. Memory Complexity: O(R^3) for the voxel grid and weight tensors. The weight tensor is (R^3, 21), which is significant for high resolutions. Performance: On a 64^3 grid, FlexiCubes generates approximately the same number of triangles as an 80^3 DMTet grid, but with higher computational cost due to the denser vertex count (R+1)^3 vs (R/2+1)^3 for tets. Strengths: High-quality mesh output, differentiable, supports complex regularizers (developability, floaters removal), integrates well with gradient-based optimization pipelines. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to optimization loop, sensitive to regularization weights, requires careful tuning of learning rate and convergence criteria. When to Use: When optimizing a mesh against visual or geometric objectives (e.g., image-based reconstruction, generative 3D) where differentiability is required. When Not to Use: When real-time extraction from a fixed SDF is needed without optimization, or when memory is constrained for high-resolution grids. FlexiCubes was introduced by Tianchang Shen et al. in 2023 in the paper "Flexible Isosurface Extraction for Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization" published in ACM Transactions on Graphics. It was developed by researchers at NVIDIA Research and the University of Toronto. The method builds upon previous work on differentiable surface extraction, such as DMTet, but uses a voxel grid with learnable weights to provide more flexibility and higher quality meshes. It is now used in NVIDIA applications like nvdiffrec and GET3D for photogrammetry and 3D generative pipelines. ddiakopoulos/flexicubescpp, https://github.com/ddiakopoulos/flexicubescpp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GitHub - nv-tlabs/FlexiCubes, https://github.com/nv-tlabs/FlexiCubes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

body: This method generates multi-resolution ground truth data for training Neural Marching Cubes (NMC) and Neural Dual Contouring (NDC) by computing per-grid-cell labels (case IDs, vertex positions, and plane parameters) from high-resolution voxel and surface intersection data. It solves the problem of creating accurate training targets for a CNN to predict Marching Cubes configurations, differing from gradient-based methods by explicitly using computed intersection points and their normals for least-squares fitting. It builds on Isosurface extraction by providing the supervised labels required for learning-based extraction. Inputs: High-resolution voxel grid (e.g., 1024^3) representing the signed distance field (SDF) or occupancy. High-resolution surface intersection points (e.g., 4096 points) with normals, derived from the high-resolution grid. Target grid resolutions (e.g., 32 or 64). Look-Up Table (LUT) configurations and tessellations for Marching Cubes. Outputs: HDF5 datasets containing per-cell ground truth for each target grid size: caseid: Integer case ID for each cell. int: Integer parameters (corner/face/internal vertex counts). float: Float parameters (corner/face/internal vertex positions, edge/face plane parameters). sdf: SDF values at grid vertices. voxel: Voxel occupancy data. Data Structures: configs: Shape 32768 \times 3, storing [caseid, #insideCC, #outsideCC] for all 2^{15} possible voxel occupancy patterns. tessellations: Shape 32768 \times \text{max\num\of\triangles} \times 3, storing triangle vertex indices for each case. Integer parameters per cell (numofintparams): 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 (case ID, corner V count, face V count, internal V count). Float parameters per cell (numoffloatparams): 8 \times 3 + 3 \times 1 + 12 \times 2 (8 corner vertices \times 3 coords, 3 face vertices \times 1 coord, 12 edge plane params \times 2 coords). Steps: 1. Downsampling: Filter high-resolution intersection points where coordinates are multiples of downscale = 1024 // voxelsize. Downsample coordinates by dividing by downscale. 2. Intersection Mapping: Compute LODintersectionpointer and LODintersectiondata arrays to store intersection points per cell using cutils.getintersectionpointsincells. 3. Ground Truth Computation: Call cutils.getgt with downsampled voxels, intersection data, LUT configs, and LUT tessellations. This function computes: Integer parameters: case ID, corner/face/internal vertex counts. Float parameters: corner/face/internal vertex positions, edge/face plane parameters. 4. Storage: Save results to HDF5 files with layout: caseid ((grid\size+1)^3 int32), int ((grid\size+1)^3 \times (num\of\int\params-1) int32), float ((grid\size+1)^3 \times num\of\float\params float32), sdf ((grid\size+1)^3 float32), voxel ((grid\size+1)^3 uint8). Outputs: HDF5 file containing datasets for each gridsize in gridsizelist: {gridsize}int: Shape [gridsize+1, gridsize+1, gridsize+1, 1], np.uint8. Stores the sign grid. {gridsize}float: Shape [gridsize+1, gridsize+1, gridsize+1, 3], np.float32. Stores plane fitting results (initialized to -10.0). {gridsize}sdf: Shape [gridsize+1, gridsize+1, gridsize+1], np.float32. Downsampled SDF. {gridsize}voxel: Shape [gridsize+1, gridsize+1, gridsize+1], np.uint8. Downsampled voxels. Data Structures: referenceV: Buffer storing intersection points and normals for a cell. Layout: [N, 6], where columns 0-2 are positions (X, Y, Z) and columns 3-5 are normals (nx, ny, nz). LODgtint: Integer array for sign bits. LODgtfloat: Float array for plane parameters. Steps: 1. Initialize Output Arrays: Create LODgtint and LODgtfloat with shape [gridsize+1, gridsize+1, gridsize+1, numparams] for each gridsize in gridsizelist. Initialize LODgtfloat with -10.0. 2. Generate Raw Data: For each object, run./VOXGen <obj> 1024 0,./SDFGen <obj> 128 0, and./IntersectionXYZpn <obj> 128 0 to generate voxel, SDF, and intersection files. 3. Read Input Data: Load the SDF (129×129×129), intersection points (X, Y, Z planes with normals), and voxels (1025×1025×1025). 4. Downsample for Target Resolution: For each gridsize in gridsizelist: a. Calculate downscale factor: downscale = 1024 // (grid\size \times cell\voxel\size). b. Downsample voxels: Sample voxel1025 at stride downscale. c. Downsample SDF: Sample sdf129 at stride downscale. d. Downsample intersections: Filter points where coordinates are multiples of downscale, then divide coordinates by downscale. 5. Compute Input Voxel Grid: Compute the input voxel grid for the target gridsize. 6. Organize Intersections: Organize downsampled intersection points into a cell-based data structure using pointers and data arrays. 7. Compute Sign Grid: tmp\sign = (tmp\sdf \le 0).astype(np.uint8). Store tmpsign in LODgtint. 8. Iterate Over Grid Cells: For each cell (i, j, k) from 0 to grid\size-1: a. Check surface intersection: If \max(tmp\sign[i:i+2, j:j+2, k:k+2]) \neq \min(tmp\sign[i:i+2, j:j+2, k:k+2]), the cell intersects the surface; proceed to plane fitting; otherwise skip. b. Retrieve points: Get intersection points and normals into referenceV. c. Handle empty cells: If referenceV is empty (length 0), skip the cell. d. Construct linear system: A = reference\V[:, 3:6], b = \sum{d=0}^{2} (A{:,d} \times reference\V[:, d]) (dot product of normals and positions). e. Regularization: Initialize regscale = 1e-6. Calculate regpos as the mean position of intersection points. Add regularization rows to A and b to avoid singular matrices. f. Solve least squares: x = \text{lstsq}(A, b)[0]. g. Boundary adjustment: If any component of x is outside [0, 1], enter an adjustment loop. Initialize tmpscale = 1. While x is out of bounds: increase regscale by tmpscale, recompute A and b, solve for x. If regscale > 1000, break and reset regscale = 1e-6. If still out of bounds, decrease regscale by tmpscale / 2 in a loop of 10 iterations, adjusting regscale and solving again. If still out of bounds after the loop, perform one final solve with the current regscale. h. Store result: Store x into LODgtfloat[i, j, k]. 9. Save Data: Save all generated arrays to an HDF5 file with the specified dataset names and shapes. Parameters: cellvoxelsize: Size of the base voxel grid in world units, set to 8. numofintparams: Number of integer parameters per grid cell, set to 1 (sign). numoffloatparams: Number of float parameters per grid cell, set to 3 (plane coefficients/position). gridsizelist: List of grid resolutions to generate, specifically [32, 64]. Pitfalls: Precision and degenerate input: If no intersection points are found for a cell, the linear system is undefined; skip the cell. Boundary adjustment loop: Ill-conditioned intersection sets can cause the regularization loop to iterate many times or hit the regscale > 1000 limit, requiring careful handling to avoid infinite loops or numerical instability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import h5py import subprocess import os def loadgeneratedfiles(objpath): """Run external executables and load generated arrays.""" subprocess.run(['./VOXGen', objpath, '1024', '0'], check=True) subprocess.run(['./SDFGen', objpath, '128', '0'], check=True) subprocess.run(['./IntersectionXYZpn', objpath, '128', '0'], check=True) # Standard file loading placeholders; in practice, read the binary/text outputs sdf129 = np.load('SDFGenoutput.npy') # Shape (129, 129, 129) voxels1025 = np.load('VOXGenoutput.npy') # Shape (1025, 1025, 1025) intersections = np.load('IntersectionXYZpnoutput.npy') # Shape (N, 6) return sdf129, voxels1025, intersections def getinputvoxel(gridsize, voxelsds): """Compute input voxel grid for the target gridsize.""" # Standard padding/alignment step for CNN input return np.pad(voxelsds, ((1, 1), (1, 1), (1, 1)), mode='constant') def getintersectionpointsnormalsincells(intersectionsds, gridsize): """Organize downsampled intersection points into a cell-based data structure.""" cells = {} for pt in intersectionsds: ix, iy, iz = int(pt[0]), int(pt[1]), int(pt[2]) ix = max(0, min(ix, gridsize - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, gridsize - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, gridsize - 1)) key = (ix, iy, iz) if key not in cells: cells[key] = [] cells[key].append(pt) return cells def solveleastsquares(A, b, regscale, regpos): """Add regularization and solve Ax=b.""" Areg = np.vstack([A, np.eye(3) regscale]) breg = np.concatenate([b, regpos regscale]) x,,, = np.linalg.lstsq(Areg, breg, rcond=None) return x def generatendcgt(objpath, gridsizelist, cellvoxelsize=8.0, outputhdf5path="output.hdf5"): sdf129, voxels1025, intersections = loadgeneratedfiles(objpath) with h5py.File(outputhdf5path, 'w') as f: for gridsize in gridsizelist: downscale = 1024 // (gridsize cellvoxelsize) voxelsds = voxels1025[::downscale,::downscale,::downscale] sdfds = sdf129[::downscale,::downscale,::downscale] validmask = (intersections[:, 0] % downscale == 0) & \ (intersections[:, 1] % downscale == 0) & \ (intersections[:, 2] % downscale == 0) intersectionsds = intersections[validmask] / downscale inputvoxel = getinputvoxel(gridsize, voxelsds) cellintersections = getintersectionpointsnormalsincells(intersectionsds, gridsize) tmpsign = (sdfds <= 0).astype(np.uint8) lodgtint = np.zeros((gridsize + 1, gridsize + 1, gridsize + 1, 1), dtype=np.uint8) lodgtint[:,:,:, 0] = tmpsign lodgtfloat = np.full((gridsize + 1, gridsize + 1, gridsize + 1, 3), -10.0, dtype=np.float32) for i in range(gridsize): for j in range(gridsize): for k in range(gridsize): cornersigns = tmpsign[i:i+2, j:j+2, k:k+2] if np.max(cornersigns) != np.min(cornersigns): refv = np.array(cellintersections.get((i, j, k), [])) if refv.shape[0] == 0: continue A = refv[:, 3:6] b = np.sum(A refv[:, 0:3], axis=1) regscale = 1e-6 regpos = np.mean(refv[:, 0:3], axis=0) x = solveleastsquares(A, b, regscale, regpos) if not np.all((x >= 0) & (x <= 1)): tmpscale = 1.0 while not np.all((x >= 0) & (x <= 1)): regscale += tmpscale if regscale > 1000: regscale = 1e-6 break x = solveleastsquares(A, b, regscale, regpos) if not np.all((x >= 0) & (x <= 1)): for in range(10): regscale -= tmpscale / 2 x = solveleastsquares(A, b, regscale, regpos) x = solveleastsquares(A, b, regscale, regpos) lodgtfloat[i, j, k] = x f.createdataset(f'{gridsize}int', data=lodgtint) f.createdataset(f'{gridsize}float', data=lodgtfloat) f.createdataset(f'{gridsize}sdf', data=sdfds) f.createdataset(f'{gridsize}voxel', data=voxelsds) Time Complexity: Dominated by iterating over all grid cells and solving the least-squares system for surface-intersecting cells. The cell iteration is O(grid\size^3). The least-squares solve is O(N) per cell, where N is the number of intersection points, which is typically small. Memory Complexity: O(grid\size^3) for storing the ground truth arrays. The HDF5 file size scales linearly with the number of grid resolutions and objects. Strengths: Provides explicit geometric ground truth (plane parameters) that is robust for training CNNs to predict Marching Cubes configurations. Handles multi-resolution LODs efficiently. Limitations: Relies on external executables for SDF and intersection generation. The regularization and boundary adjustment loop can be computationally expensive if many cells have ill-conditioned intersection sets. When to use: When training Neural Distance Fields that require explicit plane fitting ground truth for surface representation. When not to use: When real-time generation is required, or when the external executables are unavailable. This method is part of the Neural Distance Fields (NDC) framework, specifically designed to generate training data for CNNs that predict Marching Cubes configurations. It was introduced in the context of the NDC project. The method uses explicit intersection points and normals for plane fitting, distinguishing it from methods that might use SDF gradients directly. czq142857/NDC, https://github.com/czq142857/NDC, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
