name: Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees
head: Primal Isosurface Extraction on Octrees, Unconstrained Octree Isosurface Extraction
body: This method extracts a provably watertight isosurface directly from an arbitrary octree without requiring tree refinement or modification of vertex values. Unlike dual marching cubes, which can generate topological holes in flat regions, this primal approach guarantees that the isosurface separates samples on opposite sides of the isovalue by introducing an isovertex along every isovalue-crossing edge. It sets itself apart by using binary edge-trees to resolve inconsistencies at face boundaries between leaf nodes of different depths, ensuring watertightness even when the octree topology is unconstrained. Inputs: An arbitrary octree structure where nodes may have varying depths and no depth-disparity constraints are enforced. Scalar values associated with the vertices of the octree. A target isovalue (scalar threshold) for extraction. Outputs: A triangulated polygon mesh representing the watertight isosurface. Octree Node: children: Array of 8 child nodes (or null if leaf). vertices: Array of 8 scalar values associated with the node's corners. geometry: Spatial bounds (min/max coordinates) of the node. Edge-Tree Node: value: Binary integer (0 or 1). children: Array of 2 child nodes (since an octree edge is shared by two sibling nodes, the edge-tree is a binary tree). associatededge: Reference to the specific octree edge in the parent octree node. Isovertex: position: 3D coordinate along the octree edge. edgeref: Reference to the octree edge where the isovertex resides. 1. Construct Edge-Trees: For each edge in the octree, construct a binary edge-tree. The root of the edge-tree corresponds to the coarsest octree edge. If an octree edge is subdivided, its children in the octree define the children in the edge-tree. The topology of the edge-tree is inherited from the octree's subdivision history. 2. Compute Edge-Tree Values: For each edge-tree node, compute its binary value based on the scalar values at the endpoints of the associated octree edge and the isovalue. Let v{start} and v{end} be the scalar values at the two endpoints of the octree edge. Let I be the isovalue. The binary value v{node} is defined as: v{node} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } (v{start} < I \land v{end} \ge I) \lor (v{start} \ge I \land v{end} < I) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This indicates whether the edge crosses the isovalue. Note that multiple crossings along a single edge result in a value of 0 if both endpoints are on the same side. 3. Propagate Edge-Tree Values: For interior nodes in the edge-tree, the value is determined by the sum modulo 2 of its children's values. This ensures consistency across different levels of the octree. v{parent} = \left( \sum{i=1}^{2} v{childi} \right) \mod 2 This property guarantees that if an edge has value 1 (crossing), it has a unique child with value 1, allowing for a consistent definition of the isovertex position. 4. Define Isovertices: For each octree edge with value 1, traverse down the edge-tree to find the unique leaf node with value 1. The isovertex is defined at the position corresponding to this leaf edge. If the edge has value 0, no isovertex is defined for that edge. 5. Extract Isopolygons per Leaf Node: For each leaf node in the octree: Iterate over the 6 faces of the node. On each face, identify the iso-edges (edges of the face that have value 1). Use a marching-squares-like algorithm to link iso-edges sharing common isovertices to form closed loops (isopolygons) on the face. If a face has no iso-edges, no polygon is generated for that face. 6. Resolve Depth-Disparity Inconsistencies: When face-adjacent leaf nodes have different resolutions (depths), the iso-edges computed independently may not match. Identify coarser nodes that are adjacent to finer nodes. Copy the iso-edges from the finer neighbors to the coarser node. Flip the orientation of the copied iso-edges to maintain consistent winding order. This step ensures that the boundary between nodes of different resolutions is watertight. 7. Triangulate Isopolygons: The extracted isopolygons are 3D polygons that may be non-planar. Use a minimum area triangulation algorithm for 3D polygons to convert each isopolygon into a set of triangles. The algorithm minimizes the sum of the areas of the resulting triangles to ensure a smooth and accurate representation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurface(octree, isovalue): """ Extracts a watertight isosurface from an arbitrary octree. Args: octree: Root node of the octree. isovalue: Scalar threshold for extraction. Returns: List of triangles representing the isosurface. """ # Step 1 & 2: Construct Edge-Trees and Compute Leaf Values edgetrees = buildedgetrees(octree) computeedgetreeleafvalues(edgetrees, isovalue) # Step 3: Propagate Values (Mod 2 Sum) Bottom-Up propagateedgetreevalues(edgetrees) # Step 4: Define Isovertices isovertices = defineisovertices(edgetrees) # Step 5: Extract Isopolygons isopolygons = [] for leaf in octree.leaves(): facepolygons = extractfacepolygons(leaf, isovertices) isopolygons.extend(facepolygons) # Step 6: Resolve Depth-Disparity resolvedepthdisparity(isopolygons, octree) # Step 7: Triangulate triangles = [] for polygon in isopolygons: triangles.extend(minareatriangulate(polygon)) return triangles class EdgeTreeNode: def init(self, octreeedge): self.associatededge = octreeedge self.value = 0 self.children = [] self.parent = None def buildedgetrees(octree): """ Builds binary edge-trees for all edges in the octree. """ edgetrees = {} # Map each octree edge to its edge-tree root for node in octree.allnodes(): for edge in node.edges: if edge not in edgetrees: edgetrees[edge] = EdgeTreeNode(edge) # Link children based on octree subdivision for node in octree.allnodes(): if node.isleaf(): continue for i, child in enumerate(node.children): # Each octree edge is shared by two sibling nodes # The edge-tree children correspond to the subdivided edges for edge in child.edges: if edge in edgetrees: parentedge = edgetrees[edge].associatededge if parentedge in edgetrees: parenttree = edgetrees[parentedge] if len(parenttree.children) < 2: parenttree.children.append(edgetrees[edge]) edgetrees[edge].parent = parenttree return edgetrees def computeedgetreeleafvalues(edgetrees, isovalue): """ Computes initial binary values for edge-tree leaf nodes based on endpoint values. """ for edge, tree in edgetrees.items(): if tree.children: continue # Skip interior nodes; only compute leaves vstart = tree.associatededge.startvertex.value vend = tree.associatededge.endvertex.value if (vstart < isovalue and vend >= isovalue) or (vstart >= isovalue and vend < isovalue): tree.value = 1 else: tree.value = 0 def propagateedgetreevalues(edgetrees): """ Propagates values up the edge-tree using mod 2 sum. """ # Process from leaves to root to ensure children are computed first nodesbydepth = sorted(edgetrees.values(), key=lambda n: n.depth if hasattr(n, 'depth') else 0, reverse=True) for tree in nodesbydepth: if tree.children: tree.value = (tree.children[0].value + tree.children[1].value) % 2 def defineisovertices(edgetrees): """ Defines isovertices by traversing edge-trees. """ isovertices = {} for edge, tree in edgetrees.items(): if tree.value == 1: # Traverse down to find unique leaf with value 1 current = tree while current.children: # Find child with value 1 for child in current.children: if child.value == 1: current = child break # Define isovertex at the leaf edge position (linear interpolation) isovertices[edge] = current.associatededge.interpoint(isovalue) return isovertices def extractfacepolygons(leaf, isovertices): """ Extracts isopolygons from a leaf node's faces using marching squares logic. """ polygons = [] for face in leaf.faces: isoedges = [edge for edge in face.edges if edge in isovertices] if len(isoedges) == 2: # Connect the two crossing edges p1 = isovertices[isoedges[0]] p2 = isovertices[isoedges[1]] polygons.append([p1, p2]) elif len(isoedges) == 4: # Marching squares: connect opposite pairs p1 = isovertices[isoedges[0]] p2 = isovertices[isoedges[2]] p3 = isovertices[isoedges[1]] p4 = isovertices[isoedges[3]] polygons.append([p1, p2]) polygons.append([p3, p4]) return polygons def resolvedepthdisparity(isopolygons, octree): """ Resolves inconsistencies between nodes of different depths. """ coarsetofinemap = {} for coarse in octree.leaves(): for neighbor in coarse.faceadjacentleaves(): if neighbor.depth > coarse.depth: if coarse not in coarsetofinemap: coarsetofinemap[coarse] = [] coarsetofinemap[coarse].append(neighbor) for coarse, fineneighbors in coarsetofinemap.items(): coarsepolyindices = [i for i, p in enumerate(isopolygons) if coarse in p] finepolyindices = [i for i, p in enumerate(isopolygons) if any(n in p for n in fineneighbors)] # Copy iso-edges from finer neighbors to coarser node with flipped orientation for fine in fineneighbors: for idx in finepolyindices: poly = isopolygons[idx] if len(poly) == 2: # Flip orientation flipped = [poly[1], poly[0]] # Add to coarse node's polygon list isopolygons.append(flipped) def minareatriangulate(polygon): """ Triangulates a 3D polygon using minimum area algorithm. Uses dynamic programming to minimize sum of triangle areas. """ n = len(polygon) if n < 3: return [] # DP table for minimum weight triangulation dp = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] # Initialize with triangle areas for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 2, n): dp[i][j] = trianglearea(polygon[i], polygon[j], polygon[(i + 1) % n]) # Fill DP table for length in range(3, n + 1): for i in range(n - length + 1): j = i + length - 1 dp[i][j] = float('inf') for k in range(i + 1, j): cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + trianglearea(polygon[i], polygon[k], polygon[j]) if cost < dp[i][j]: dp[i][j] = cost # Reconstruct triangles (simplified for brevity) triangles = [] for i in range(1, n - 1): triangles.append([polygon[0], polygon[i], polygon[i + 1]]) return triangles def trianglearea(p1, p2, p3): """Computes area of a triangle given 3D points.""" v1 = [p2[j] - p1[j] for j in range(3)] v2 = [p3[j] - p1[j] for j in range(3)] cross = [v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]] return 0.5 (cross[0]2 + cross[1]2 + cross[2]2)0.5 Isovalue: The scalar threshold for extraction. Flatness Measure: Used in the context of generating the adaptive octree, defined as the ratio of the length of the mean curvature vector of the intersected surface to its area. This guides octree refinement and is not part of the extraction algorithm itself. Multiple Isovalue-Crossings: If an edge has multiple crossings, the edge-tree assigns a value of 0 if both endpoints are on the same side. This ensures a consistent binary representation and prevents ambiguity in isovertex definition. Depth-Disparity: Without resolving depth-disparity, the extracted mesh may not be watertight. The method handles this by copying iso-edges from finer neighbors to coarser nodes. Topological Holes: Dual marching cubes can generate topological holes if the adaptive octree is much coarser than the model thickness. This primal method avoids this by guaranteeing that the isosurface separates samples on opposite sides of the isovalue. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The algorithm involves traversing the octree and edge-trees, which is linear in the number of nodes and edges. The triangulation step is more complex but depends on the number of polygons. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method requires storing edge-trees, which adds memory overhead compared to methods that do not use them. Not given in the sources. The paper evaluates the method in the context of mesh simplification and compares it to dual marching cubes, but specific performance metrics (e.g., FPS, memory usage) are not provided. The method scales with the size of the octree. Since it does not require refinement, it can handle large, arbitrary octrees efficiently. Strengths: Guarantees watertightness for arbitrary octrees. Does not require tree refinement or modification of vertex values. Avoids topological holes common in dual marching cubes. Limitations: Requires additional memory for edge-trees. The triangulation step for non-planar polygons can be computationally expensive. Use this method when extracting isosurfaces from arbitrary, unconstrained octrees where watertightness is critical and tree refinement is not desirable. Do not use if the octree is already constrained (e.g., depth-disparity limited) and a simpler method like Marching Cubes with Octree is sufficient. Do not use if computational efficiency is the primary concern and watertightness can be approximated. The method was introduced by Michael Kazhdan, Allison Klein, Ketan Dalal, and Hugues Hoppe in their paper "Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees". The paper builds on previous work in isosurface extraction from octrees, such as the work by Wilhelms and Van Gelder [WG92] and Bloomenthal [Blo88]. The key innovation is the use of edge-trees to resolve inconsistencies in arbitrary octrees. The method is used in mesh simplification and surface reconstruction, particularly in scenarios where adaptive octrees are generated based on surface flatness or other criteria. It is also used in computer graphics for generating watertight meshes from volumetric data. name: Consistent Isovertex Definition via Edge-Trees
head: Edge-Tree Isovertex Definition, Edge-Tree Traversal for Isovertex
body: This method defines the position of an isovertex on an octree edge consistently by traversing an "edge-tree" to a unique leaf node with value 1, ensuring watertightness in isosurface extraction. It solves the problem of ambiguous isovertex positions when a coarse edge contains multiple sign changes, which causes standard polygonization methods like [Blo88] to fail. Unlike methods that refine the tree or modify vertex values, this approach uses the existing edge-tree structure to resolve ambiguity, contributing to closed isopolyline loops and shared polygon edges. It differs from the minimal edge definition in [JLSW02] only when there is more than one isovalue-crossing along an edge. Inputs: An octree representing the scalar field. An edge-tree structure associated with the octree edges. A scalar isovalue. Outputs: A set of isovertices, each associated with an octree edge. Data Structures: Edge-Tree Node: Represents an octree edge or a sub-segment of it. value: Binary integer (0 or 1). 1 indicates an isovalue crossing (sign change) exists in the segment represented by this node. 0 indicates no crossing. children: List of child nodes (for interior nodes). Leaf nodes have no children. geometry: Geometric representation of the edge segment (start point, end point) for interpolation. Algorithm: 1. Identify Crossing Edges: For every edge e in the octree, determine if it crosses the isovalue by checking if the scalar values at the endpoints have different signs relative to the isovalue. 2. Compute Edge-Tree Values: For every interior node in the edge-tree, compute its value based on its children. The binary value of an interior node is the sum modulo 2 of its children's values: \text{value}(\text{parent}) = (\text{value}(\text{child}1) + \text{value}(\text{child}2)) \pmod 2 This property guarantees that if an edge e has value = 1, it must have a unique child that also has value = 1. 3. Traverse to Leaf: For each edge e with value = 1: Start at the root node of the edge-tree corresponding to e. Recursively traverse down the unique child that has value = 1. Continue until a leaf node \tilde{e} is reached. The path e \supseteq \dots \supseteq \tilde{e} consists entirely of nodes with value = 1. 4. Define Isovertex Position: Assign the isovertex position p to be the position defined by the leaf node \tilde{e}. Denote this assignment as p \in e. The position p is interpolated within the segment represented by \tilde{e} based on the scalar values at the endpoints of \tilde{e}. Note: p \in e and e' \supseteq e does not imply p \in e'. The isovertex is tied to the specific leaf \tilde{e}, not the coarse edge e. 5. Handle Multiple Crossings: If an edge has multiple sign changes, standard polygonization fails. This method handles it by assigning the isovertex to the finest leaf node in the edge-tree that still indicates a crossing, effectively resolving ambiguity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeedgetreevalues(node): """Recursively computes the binary value of an edge-tree node based on its children.""" if node.isleaf(): return node.value childvalues = [computeedgetreevalues(child) for child in node.children] node.value = sum(childvalues) % 2 return node.value def findisovertex(edgeroot): """Traverses the edge-tree to find the leaf node defining the isovertex.""" if edgeroot.isleaf(): return edgeroot for child in edgeroot.children: if child.value == 1: return findisovertex(child) raise ValueError("No child with value 1 found") def interpolateposition(leafnode, isovalue): """Linear interpolation within the leaf segment based on endpoint scalar values.""" t = (isovalue - leafnode.scalarstart) / (leafnode.scalarend - leafnode.scalarstart) return leafnode.startpoint + t (leafnode.endpoint - leafnode.startpoint) def defineisovertices(octreeedges, isovalue): """Defines isovertices for all edges in the octree.""" isovertices = {} for edge in octreeedges: if edge.hassignchange(): edge.edgetreeroot.value = 1 computeedgetreevalues(edge.edgetreeroot) for edge in octreeedges: if edge.edgetreeroot.value == 1: leafnode = findisovertex(edge.edgetreeroot) p = interpolateposition(leafnode, isovalue) isovertices[edge] = p return isovertices Parameters: Isovalue: The scalar threshold for extraction. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Sign Changes: Standard polygonization fails if an edge has multiple sign changes. This method handles it by assigning the isovertex to the finest leaf node in the edge-tree that still indicates a crossing. Notation Ambiguity: The notation p \in e does not imply p \in e' for an ancestor edge e' \supseteq e. The isovertex is tied to the specific leaf \tilde{e} in the edge-tree, not the coarse edge e itself. Precision: Interpolation within the leaf segment may introduce precision errors if the leaf segment is very small or if the scalar field values are close to the isovalue. Twin Isovertex Pairing is a post-processing step in octree-based isosurface extraction that closes open isopolylines into closed isopolygons by identifying and connecting "twin" isovertices. It solves the problem of watertightness in meshes extracted from arbitrary octrees where a single edge may contain multiple sign changes, resulting in isovertices with valence one that cannot be paired within the local leaf node. Unlike methods that refine the tree or modify vertex values, this method uses the existing edge-tree structure to pair vertices, ensuring the resulting mesh is watertight without altering the underlying scalar field representation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use / When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in the paper "Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees". It addresses the challenges of isosurface extraction on arbitrary octrees, where traditional methods like Marching Cubes may produce cracks or non-watertight meshes due to inconsistent isovertex definitions. The method builds on the properties of edge-trees to ensure consistency. name: Twin Isovertex Pairing for Isopolyline Closure
head: Isopolyline Closure, Isovertex Pairing
body: Twin Isovertex Pairing is a post-processing step in octree-based isosurface extraction that closes open isopolylines into closed isopolygons by identifying and connecting "twin" isovertices. It solves the problem of watertightness in meshes extracted from arbitrary octrees where a single edge may contain multiple sign changes, resulting in isovertices with valence one that cannot be paired within the local leaf node. Unlike methods that refine the tree or modify vertex values, this method uses the existing edge-tree structure to pair vertices, ensuring the resulting mesh is watertight without altering the underlying scalar field representation. Input: An octree where each edge e has an associated binary value (0 or 1) derived from the sign changes of the scalar field along that edge. An isovertex p is defined on an edge e with valence one (an endpoint of an open isopolyline). Output: A twin isovertex p' and an iso-edge (p, p') added to the set of iso-edges for the leaf node N, reducing the count of valence-one isovertices. The method relies on the Edge-Tree structure established in Consistent Isovertex Definition via Edge-Trees. Edge Node: Represents an octree edge at a specific level of refinement. Fields: value: Binary integer (0 or 1). Indicates the parity of sign changes on the edge. 1 implies an odd number of sign changes (isovertex exists); 0 implies an even number (no net isovertex or paired isovertices at this scale). parent: Reference to the parent edge node. children: References to child edge nodes (if not a leaf). Isovertex: Defined by a leaf edge node e' in the edge-tree. The position is interpolated on the geometric edge corresponding to e'. The procedure finds the twin p' for an isovertex p located on edge e. 1. Check for Restricted Octree Special Case: If the octree is a restricted octree [WKE99], there can be at most two valence-one isovertices per edge. In this case, the twin p' is simply the other valence-one isovertex on the same edge e. Connect p and p' directly. Terminate. 2. Traverse Up to Find Ancestor with Value 0: Starting from edge e, traverse up the parent pointers until finding the first ancestor edge \tilde{e} such that \tilde{e}.value == 0. 3. Select the Sibling Branch: Identify the two children of \tilde{e}. Since \tilde{e} has value 0, both children must have value 1 due to the mod 2 sum property. One child is an ancestor of the original edge e; the other child is not an ancestor of e. Select the non-ancestor child as the starting point for the downward traversal. 4. Traverse Down to Leaf: Starting from the selected child, traverse down the edge-tree following only nodes with value == 1 until reaching a leaf node e'. 5. Define Twin and Close Edge: The isovertex p' is defined by the leaf node e'. Add the iso-edge (p, p') to the set of iso-edges for the leaf node N associated with the original isovertex p. This connects the open isopolyline endpoint p to p', reducing the number of valence-one isovertices along N. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findtwinisovertex(pedge, edgetreeroot, isrestricted): # Step 1: Restricted octree special case if isrestricted: # The sources do not specify the traversal mechanism for restricted octrees, # only that the twin is the other valence-one isovertex on the same edge. pass # Step 2: Traverse up to find the first ancestor with value 0 current = pedge while current.value != 0: if current.parent is None: raise ValueError("Root edge must have value 0. No twin found.") current = current.parent ancestorzero = current # Step 3: Identify the sibling branch sibling = None for child in ancestorzero.children: if not isancestorof(child, pedge): sibling = child break if sibling is None: raise ValueError("Could not find sibling branch. Structure invariant violated.") # Step 4: Traverse down through nodes with value 1 to a leaf current = sibling while current.children: foundchild = False for child in current.children: if child.value == 1: current = child foundchild = True break if not foundchild: raise ValueError("Path to twin broken: no child with value 1 found.") return current def isancestorof(ancestor, descendant): current = descendant while current is not None: if current is ancestor: return True current = current.parent return False Restricted Octrees: In restricted octrees [WKE99], the algorithm simplifies significantly. The twin is the other valence-one isovertex on the same edge. This is because the number of isovertices on an edge with valence one must always be even, and restricted octrees limit this to at most two. Precision: The position of the twin isovertex p' is determined by the leaf node e' in the edge-tree. The interpolation precision depends on the resolution of the leaf node. Valence: This method specifically handles isovertices with valence one. Isovertices with higher valence are handled by the standard local polygonization logic. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures watertightness without modifying the scalar field or refining the tree. Leverages the hierarchical structure of the octree for efficient pairing. Deterministic and robust for arbitrary octrees. Limitations: Requires the edge-tree structure to be fully built and consistent. Performance depends on the depth of the octree. When to Use: Use this method as the final step in isosurface extraction from arbitrary octrees to close isopolylines. It is particularly useful when the octree is not restricted and multiple sign changes can occur on a single edge. Twin Isovertex Pairing was introduced in the context of unconstrained isosurface extraction on arbitrary octrees. The method addresses the limitations of earlier polygonization methods (such as [Blo88]) which struggled with edges exhibiting multiple sign changes. By defining isovertices consistently via edge-trees and then pairing them using the tree's hierarchy, the method guarantees that the extracted isopolylines form closed loops, satisfying the requirements for a watertight polygonal mesh. The approach was detailed in the paper "Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees". name: Adaptive Octree Generation with Flatness Criterion
head: Adaptive Octree Generation
body: This method generates an adaptive octree discretization for isosurface extraction by recursively refining nodes based on the geometric flatness of the surface intersection within them. It differs from sibling methods that rely on uniform sampling thresholds or simple interval trees by explicitly measuring curvature-to-area ratios to determine refinement, ensuring that highly curved regions are resolved with higher density while flat regions remain coarse. It serves as the spatial subdivision stage for subsequent surface extraction algorithms like Dual Marching Cubes. Inputs: A scalar field function F(\mathbf{p}) defined over 3D space. A threshold value T for isosurface extraction. A root bounding box (the initial octree node). Parameters: SamplingSize, Threshold, Dropoff, HorizontalScale, VerticalScale. Outputs: An adaptive octree where leaf nodes represent voxels containing the isosurface or empty space, refined according to the flatness criterion. Vertex values assigned to the octree vertices via Euclidean distance transform sampling. Data Structures: The octree consists of nodes. Each node contains: Bounds: A bounding box (min/max coordinates) defining the spatial extent. Depth: Integer depth level (root is 0). Children: An array of 8 child nodes (if not a leaf), or null (if a leaf). Children are ordered in a fixed pattern based on coordinate offsets relative to the node's min corner: 0. (-X, -Y, -Z) 1. (+X, -Y, -Z) 2. (+X, -Y, +Z) 3. (-X, -Y, +Z) 4. (-X, +Y, -Z) 5. (+X, +Y, -Z) 6. (+X, +Y, +Z) 7. (-X, +Y, +Z) Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Start with the root node. 2. Iterate: Recursively refine nodes that intersect the surface. 3. Calculate Sampling Interval: For a node at Depth, compute the sampling interval: \text{samplingSize} = \text{SamplingSize} \times \ln(\text{Depth} + 2) 4. Determine Sample Count: Calculate the number of samples per axis (nx, ny, nz) required to cover the node's bounds with the calculated interval: n{axis} = 1 + \lceil \frac{\text{Bounds.size}{axis}}{\text{samplingSize}} \rceil 5. Minimum Sample Check: If any axis has fewer than 3 samples (nx < 3 or ny < 3 or nz < 3), do not split the node. 6. Sample Field: Iterate over the interior samples only. For z from 1 to nz-2, y from 1 to ny-2, and x from 1 to nx-2: a. Compute sample position using linear interpolation within the node bounds: xF = \text{Lerp}(\text{Bounds.min}x, \text{Bounds.max}x, \frac{x}{nx}) (Similarly for yF and zF) b. Evaluate the field F(xF, yF, zF). c. Determine if the sample is above or below the threshold T: aboveThreshold = SampleField(xF, yF, zF) > Threshold. d. Track flags: isBelow |= !aboveThreshold; isAbove |= aboveThreshold. e. If both isBelow and isAbove are true, the node intersects the surface. Break early from the sampling loop. 7. Split Decision: If the node intersects the surface, calculate the flatness of the intersection: \text{flatness} = \frac{\|\vec{H}\|}{\text{Area}} where \vec{H} is the mean curvature vector of the intersected surface and \text{Area} is its area. Recursively refine nodes that intersect the surface and whose intersection is not "too flat". 8. Child Creation: If splitting, create children in fixed order using min/max offsets. 9. Vertex Value Assignment: Assign values to the vertices of the octree by sampling the Euclidean distance transform. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) class Vector3Int: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class Bounds: def init(self, min, max): self.min = min self.max = max @property def size(self): return self.max - self.min class OctreeNode: def init(self, bounds, depth, children=None): self.bounds = bounds self.depth = depth self.children = children def generateadaptiveoctree(rootbounds, fieldfunc, threshold, samplingsizebase): """ Generates an adaptive octree based on flatness criterion and field sampling. """ root = OctreeNode(bounds=rootbounds, depth=0, children=None) queue = [root] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) # 1. Calculate sampling interval based on depth samplingsize = samplingsizebase math.log(node.depth + 2) # 2. Determine number of samples per axis nsamples = Vector3Int( 1 + math.ceil(node.bounds.size.x / samplingsize), 1 + math.ceil(node.bounds.size.y / samplingsize), 1 + math.ceil(node.bounds.size.z / samplingsize)) # 3. Check minimum sample requirement if nsamples.x < 3 or nsamples.y < 3 or nsamples.z < 3: continue # Cannot split, remains leaf # 4. Sample interior points isbelow = False isabove = False intersects = False for z in range(1, nsamples.z - 1): for y in range(1, nsamples.y - 1): for x in range(1, nsamples.x - 1): # Linear interpolation for position posx = node.bounds.min.x + (node.bounds.max.x - node.bounds.min.x) (x / nsamples.x) posy = node.bounds.min.y + (node.bounds.max.y - node.bounds.min.y) (y / nsamples.y) posz = node.bounds.min.z + (node.bounds.max.z - node.bounds.min.z) (z / nsamples.z) val = fieldfunc(Vector3(posx, posy, posz)) if val <= threshold: isbelow = True if val > threshold: isabove = True if isbelow and isabove: intersects = True break if intersects: break if intersects: break # 5. Split decision if intersects: # Flatness check: flatness = norm(meancurvaturevector) / area. # Sources do not provide implementation details for the "too flat" threshold. # Create 8 children newsize = node.bounds.size 0.5 # Fixed order: 0:-X-Y-Z, 1:+X-Y-Z, 2:+X-Y+Z, 3:-X-Y+Z, 4:-X+Y-Z, 5:+X+Y-Z, 6:+X+Y+Z, 7:-X+Y+Z offsets = [ Vector3(0, 0, 0), Vector3(1, 0, 0), Vector3(1, 0, 1), Vector3(0, 0, 1), Vector3(0, 1, 0), Vector3(1, 1, 0), Vector3(1, 1, 1), Vector3(0, 1, 1) ] children = [] for i, offset in enumerate(offsets): childmin = node.bounds.min + offset newsize childmax = childmin + newsize childbounds = Bounds(childmin, childmax) childnode = OctreeNode(bounds=childbounds, depth=node.depth + 1, children=None) children.append(childnode) queue.append(childnode) node.children = children else: node.children = None return root Parameters: SamplingSize: Base physical spacing between samples. Default: 1.0f. Threshold: Field value threshold for isosurface extraction. Default: 0.5f. Dropoff: Controls vertical falloff of the field. Default: 100.0f. HorizontalScale, VerticalScale: Scale factors for field sampling coordinates. Default: 0.01f, 0.05f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Disparity: To avoid cracks in subsequent marching cubes steps, the depth disparity between adjacent nodes should be restricted to at most one. This may require post-processing refinement of leaves. Flatness Calculation: The flatness formula requires computing the mean curvature vector and area of the intersected surface. Interior Sampling: Iterating only over interior samples (1 to n-2) ensures sampling inside the node but may miss surface intersections very close to the node boundaries if the grid is coarse. OcMesher is a method for extracting memory-efficient, highly detailed triangle meshes from unbounded scenes represented by signed distance functions (SDFs). It uses a view-dependent adaptive octree structure driven by a given set of camera views to refine geometry only where visible. Unlike parent methods that generate octrees based on surface flatness alone, OcMesher incorporates camera projection metrics to prioritize resolution based on projected pixel density. This method constructs an octree leaf node representing a voxel containing an isosurface by solving a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) to determine the precise surface position and normal from edge intersections. It builds on Adaptive Octree Generation with Flatness Criterion by refining surface location within the leaf using a least-squares geometric fit rather than Euclidean distance transform sampling. It differs from OcMesher by relying on a global QEF solver over all edge crossings rather than local marching cubes-style triangulation. This method converts an input triangle mesh into a watertight 2-manifold surface with roughly uniformly distributed vertices using an octree-based signed distance field (SDF) representation and isosurface extraction. It differs from uniform grid marching cubes by adaptively refining only the volume near the surface, reducing storage and computation linearly with the final mesh size. Unlike sibling methods that fit explicit surface primitives (e.g., QEF) or use complex occlusion handling, this pipeline guarantees topological correctness by defining "positive" space via boundary-connected BFS and resolving non-manifold ambiguities through vertex/edge splitting. Strengths: The flatness criterion provides a geometrically meaningful refinement metric. Limitations: The flatness calculation (mean curvature/area) is computationally expensive and difficult to implement accurately. Requires post-processing to ensure depth disparity constraints for crack-free rendering. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from research on unconstrained isosurface extraction on arbitrary octrees. Implementation details in demonstrate a practical application of adaptive octree generation for dual marching cubes, although it simplifies the flatness check. name: OcMesher
head: OcMesher Octree Construction and Mesh Extraction, View-Dependent Octree-based Mesh Extraction
body: OcMesher is a method for extracting memory-efficient, highly detailed triangle meshes from unbounded scenes represented by signed distance functions (SDFs). It uses a view-dependent adaptive octree structure driven by a given set of camera views to refine geometry only where visible. Unlike parent methods that generate octrees based on surface flatness alone, OcMesher incorporates camera projection metrics to prioritize resolution based on projected pixel density. Inputs: cameras: A tuple (camposes, Ks, Hs, Ws) where camposes are N \times 4 \times 4 world-to-camera matrices, Ks are N \times 3 \times 3 intrinsic matrices, and Hs, Ws are heights and widths. bounds: Axis-aligned bounding box limits [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz]. kernels: A list of callable functions Ki(\mathbf{p}) that return the SDF value at point \mathbf{p}. Parameters: pixelspercube (default 8), invscale (default 10), mindist (default 1), memorylimitmb (default 1000), bisectioniters (default 15), enclosed (default True), simplifyoccluded (default True), visiblerelaxiter (default 2), coarsecount (default 500000). Outputs: A list of triangle meshes containing vertices, faces, and visibility tags. Data Structures: struct node: Contains cube c and int nxts[8]. nxts[i] is the index of the i-th child in the nodes vector, or -1 if absent. Leaf nodes are marked by nxts[0] = -2. struct cube: Contains int coords[3] and int L. L is the level. Special values: L >= 0 (regular), L == -1 (boundary), L == -2 (exterior). struct computedvertex: Contains T c[3] (coordinates), l, r (SDF values). Camera data is flattened into a numpy array of shape (23 ncameras). Each camera entry stores: inverse pose (first 12 values, 3 \times 4), intrinsic matrix K (9 values), height H (1 value), width W (1 value). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute scene center \mathbf{c}{center} as the midpoint of bounds. Compute size S = 1.1 \times \max(\text{bounds dimensions}). Flatten camera data into the cameras array. 2. Coarse Visibility: Initialize root node at coords=[0,0,0], L=0. Push root to a priority queue ordered by projectedsize. While queue not empty and node count < coarsecount: pop node with highest projectedsize. If projectedsize < invscale, break. Expand node fully into 8 children. Push children to queue. Mark remaining nodes as grid nodes and return nblocks. 3. Coarse Refinement (SDF-aware): Loop while finegroup() returns inc > 0: finegroup() batches nodes into memory-limited chunks. Call fineiteration() with SDF pointer. While n > 0: get positions via fineiterationoutput(). Compute SDFs: \text{sdf} = \min{k} Kk(\text{positions}). Pass SDFs to fineiteration(). fineiteration identifies bipolar edges (SDF sign changes) and expands nodes containing them. 4. Visibility Filtering: Call visfilter(simplifyoccluded, visiblerelaxiter) to return nvisblock. This removes blocks occluded by the mesh geometry. 5. Fine Mesh Construction: Initialize nv array. Visible Blocks: While finaliteration() returns n > 0: get positions via finaliteration2(). Compute SDFs using kernelcaller. Call finaliteration3() with SDFs. Occluded Blocks: Call finaliterationoccluded(). If n != 0, get positions, compute SDFs, call finaliteration3occluded(). Remaining: Reset nv to zeros. Call finalremaining(). 6. Per-Element Mesh Extraction: For each element e: Get vertex centers via getvertscenter(e, centers). Compute center SDFs: centersdf = kernelcaller(kernels[e], centers). Initialize cubes array. Call updateverts(e, emptysdf, emptysdf, cubes). Bisection Refinement: Repeat bisectioniters times: compute SDFs for cubes: sdf = kernelcaller(kernels[e], cubes). Call updateverts(e, sdf, centersdf, cubes). Get left/right vertices via getlrverts(e, cubes, cubesr). Compute SDFs for left/right: sdfl, sdfr. Call finalizeverts(e, sdfl, sdfr, vertices). Construct faces via constructfaces(e, vertices, cnts) returning nve, nvf, nf. 7. Edge and Face Vertex Refinement: Get extra vertex centers: edgeverticesc, faceverticesc via getextravertscenter. Compute their SDFs: ecentersdf, fcentersdf. Initialize left/right extra vertices arrays. Call updateextraverts with empty SDFs. Bisection Refinement: Repeat bisectioniters times: compute SDFs for left/right edge/face vertices. Call updateextraverts with computed SDFs. Get refined left/right extra vertices via getlrextraverts. Compute SDFs for refined vertices. Call finalizeextraverts to produce final edgevertices and facevertices. 8. Final Assembly: Concatenate vertices, edgevertices, facevertices. Get visibility tags via getinviewtag. Create mesh objects. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import heapq def ocmesher(cameras, bounds, kernels, pixelspercube=8, invscale=10, mindist=1, memorylimitmb=1000, bisectioniters=15, enclosed=True, simplifyoccluded=True, visiblerelaxiter=2, coarsecount=500000): # 1. Initialization camposes, Ks, Hs, Ws = cameras ncameras = len(camposes) camerasflat = np.zeros(23 ncameras, dtype=np.float64) for i in range(ncameras): invpose = np.linalg.inv(camposes[i])[:3,:4].ravel() K = Ks[i].ravel() camerasflat[23i: 23(i+1)] = np.concatenate([invpose, K, [Hs[i]], [Ws[i]]]) center = (bounds[0::2] + bounds[1::2]) / 2.0 size = 1.1 np.max(bounds[1::2] - bounds[0::2]) # 2. Coarse Visibility nodes = [{'coords': np.array([0,0,0], dtype=np.int32), 'L': 0, 'nxts': [-1]8}] pq = [(-projectedsize(nodes[0]['coords'], nodes[0]['L'], camerasflat, pixelspercube, mindist), 0)] heapq.heapify(pq) while pq and len(nodes) < coarsecount: negsize, idx = heapq.heappop(pq) if -negsize < invscale: break expandoctree(nodes, idx) for i in range(8): if nodes[idx]['nxts'][i] != -1: childidx = nodes[idx]['nxts'][i] heapq.heappush(pq, (-projectedsize(nodes[childidx]['coords'], nodes[childidx]['L'], camerasflat, pixelspercube, mindist), childidx)) # 3. Coarse Refinement (SDF-aware) # Memory-batched processing loop endnode = 0 while endnode < len(nodes): startnode = endnode cubessize = 0 verticessize = 0 batchnodes = [] while endnode < len(nodes): node = nodes[endnode] s = node['L'] ss = 1 << s cubessize += (ss+1)3 verticessize += (ss+1)3 batchnodes.append(endnode) if (verticessize >> 20) 64 > memorylimitmb: break endnode += 1 # Evaluate SDFs for batch positions = getbatchpositions(batchnodes, nodes) sdfbatch = kernelcaller(kernels, positions, enclosed, bounds) sdfmin = np.min(sdfbatch, axis=-1) # Bipolar expansion for idx in batchnodes: node = nodes[idx] s = node['L'] ss = 1 << s for edge in getcubeedges(ss): v1, v2 = edge s1 = sdfmin[v1] s2 = sdfmin[v2] if (s1 >= 0) != (s2 >= 0): expandoctree(nodes, idx) break # 4. Visibility Filtering nvisblock = visfilter(simplifyoccluded, visiblerelaxiter, nodes) # 5. Fine Mesh Construction nv = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32) visiblenodes = nodes[:nvisblock] # 6. Per-Element Mesh Extraction meshes = [] inviewtags = [] for e in range(len(kernels)): ke = [kernels[e]] centers = np.zeros((nv[e], 3), dtype=np.float64) getvertscenter(e, centers, visiblenodes) centersdf = kernelcaller(ke, centers, enclosed, bounds) cubes = np.zeros((nv[e] 8, 3), dtype=np.float64) updateverts(e, np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), cubes, visiblenodes) for in range(bisectioniters): sdf = kernelcaller(ke, cubes, enclosed, bounds) updateverts(e, sdf.astype(np.float32), centersdf.astype(np.float32), cubes, visiblenodes) cubesr = np.zeroslike(cubes) getlrverts(e, cubes, cubesr, visiblenodes) sdfl = kernelcaller(ke, cubes, enclosed, bounds) sdfr = kernelcaller(ke, cubesr, enclosed, bounds) vertices = np.zeros((0, 3), dtype=np.float64) finalizeverts(e, sdfl.astype(np.float32), sdfr.astype(np.float32), vertices, visiblenodes) faces = np.zeros((0, 3), dtype=np.int32) nve, nvf, nf = constructfaces(e, vertices, faces, visiblenodes) # 7. Edge/Face Refinement edgeverticesc = np.zeros((nve, 3), dtype=np.float64) faceverticesc = np.zeros((nvf, 3), dtype=np.float64) getextravertscenter(edgeverticesc, faceverticesc, visiblenodes) ecentersdf = kernelcaller(ke, edgeverticesc, enclosed, bounds) fcentersdf = kernelcaller(ke, faceverticesc, enclosed, bounds) edgeverticeslr = np.zeros((nve 2, 3), dtype=np.float64) faceverticeslr = np.zeros((nvf 4, 3), dtype=np.float64) updateextraverts( np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), np.zeros(0, dtype=np.float32), edgeverticeslr, faceverticeslr, visiblenodes) for in range(bisectioniters): esdf = kernelcaller(ke, edgeverticeslr, enclosed, bounds) fsdf = kernelcaller(ke, faceverticeslr, enclosed, bounds) updateextraverts( esdf.astype(np.float32), fsdf.astype(np.float32), ecentersdf.astype(np.float32), fcentersdf.astype(np.float32), edgeverticeslr, faceverticeslr, visiblenodes) edgeverticesr = np.zeros((nve 2, 3), dtype=np.float64) faceverticesr = np.zeros((nvf 4, 3), dtype=np.float64) getlrextraverts(edgeverticeslr, edgeverticesr, faceverticeslr, faceverticesr, visiblenodes) esdfl = kernelcaller(ke, edgeverticeslr, enclosed, bounds) esdfr = kernelcaller(ke, edgeverticesr, enclosed, bounds) fsdfl = kernelcaller(ke, faceverticeslr, enclosed, bounds) fsdfr = kernelcaller(ke, faceverticesr, enclosed, bounds) finaledgevertices = np.zeros((nve, 3), dtype=np.float64) finalfacevertices = np.zeros((nvf, 3), dtype=np.float64) finalizeextraverts( esdfl.astype(np.float32), esdfr.astype(np.float32), finaledgevertices, fsdfl.astype(np.float32), fsdfr.astype(np.float32), finalfacevertices, visiblenodes) # 8. Assembly allvertices = np.concatenate([vertices, finaledgevertices, finalfacevertices]) inviewtag = np.zeros(allvertices.shape[0], dtype=bool) getinviewtag(e, inviewtag, visiblenodes) inviewtags.append(inviewtag) meshes.append({'vertices': allvertices, 'faces': faces, 'inviewtag': inviewtag}) return meshes, inviewtags def projectedsize(coords, L, camerasflat, pixelspercube, mindist): # Simplified projection metric based on evidence r = np.linalg.norm(coords) + mindist W = camerasflat[22] pixang = np.arctan(W / 2 / camerasflat[12]) 2 / W ang = pixang pixelspercube return 1.0 / (r ang) def expandoctree(nodes, idx): node = nodes[idx] if node['nxts'][0] == -2: return base = len(nodes) for i in range(8): childcoords = node['coords'].copy() for k in range(3): childcoords[k] += ((i >> k) & 1) << node['L'] nodes.append({'coords': childcoords, 'L': node['L'] + 1, 'nxts': [-1]8}) node['nxts'][i] = base + i def kernelcaller(kernels, XYZall, enclosed=True, bounds=None): if len(XYZall) == 0: return np.zeros((0, len(kernels)), dtype=np.float32) step = 10000000 sdfs = [] for i in range(0, len(XYZall), step): XYZ = XYZall[i:i+step] sdfsi = [] outbound = np.zeros(len(XYZ), dtype=bool) if enclosed: for c in range(3): outbound |= XYZ[:, c] <= bounds[c2] outbound |= XYZ[:, c] >= bounds[c2+1] for kernel in kernels: sdf = kernel(XYZ) if enclosed: sdf[outbound] = 1.0 sdfsi.append(sdf) sdfs.append(np.stack(sdfsi, axis=-1).astype(np.float32)) return np.concatenate(sdfs, axis=0) def updateverts(e, sdfl, sdfr, cubes, nodes): # Bisection refinement: move vertices towards zero-crossing for i in range(len(cubes)): if sdfl[i] >= 0 != sdfr[i] >= 0: t = sdfl[i] / (sdfl[i] - sdfr[i]) cubes[i] = cubes[i] + t (cubes[i] - cubes[i]) # Placeholder for actual bisection logic # In practice, this iteratively subdivides cube edges where signs differ def constructfaces(e, vertices, faces, nodes): # Standard isosurface face generation from signed vertices nve, nvf, nf = 0, 0, 0 # Iterate over cube faces, check vertex signs, generate triangles return nve, nvf, nf def visfilter(simplifyoccluded, visiblerelaxiter, nodes): # Occlusion check based on camera visibility return len(nodes) def getbatchpositions(batchnodes, nodes): return np.array([n['coords'] for n in nodes if n in batchnodes]) def getcubeedges(ss): edges = [] for i in range(ss): for j in range(ss+1): for k in range(ss+1): edges.append(((i,j,k), (i+1,j,k))) edges.append(((i,j,k), (i,j+1,k))) edges.append(((i,j,k), (i,j,k+1))) return edges def getvertscenter(e, centers, nodes): pass def getlrverts(e, cubes, cubesr, nodes): pass def finalizeverts(e, sdfl, sdfr, vertices, nodes): pass def getextravertscenter(edgeverticesc, faceverticesc, nodes): pass def updateextraverts(sdfe, sdff, sdfec, sdffc, edgelr, facelr, nodes): pass def getlrextraverts(edgelr, edger, facelr, facer, nodes): pass def finalizeextraverts(esdfl, esdfr, edgev, fsdfl, fsdfr, facev, nodes): pass def getinviewtag(e, tag, nodes): pass Subtopics: Octree Leaf Construction with QEF Surface Fitting: Uses Quadratic Error Functions to fit surfaces at octree leaves. Choose when higher geometric accuracy per vertex is needed at the cost of increased computation per leaf. Time Complexity: Dominated by SDF evaluations across the octree hierarchy. The coarse step prioritizes nodes by projected size, yielding O(N \log N) behavior relative to node count. The fine step scales linearly with visible blocks and bisection iterations. Memory Complexity: Bounded by memorylimitmb during memory-batched coarse refinement and coarsecount for the initial octree expansion. Performance: Used in Infinigen for procedural synthetic data generation. It is memory-efficient for unbounded scenes because it only generates geometry in view-dependent regions. Strengths: Handles unbounded scenes; view-dependent refinement reduces mesh size; handles multiple SDF kernels. Limitations: Requires camera poses and intrinsics; SDF evaluation can be slow for complex kernels; enclosed mode clamps out-of-bounds values which may affect boundary accuracy. OcMesher was developed by Zeyu Ma at Princeton University. It is used by default in the Infinigen project to speed up video generation and export terrain meshes. The method was presented in the paper "View-Dependent Octree-based Mesh Extraction in Unbounded Scenes for Procedural Synthetic Data" (arXiv:2312.08364). princeton-vl/OcMesher, https://github.com/princeton-vl/OcMesher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Octree Leaf Construction with QEF Surface Fitting
head: QEF-based Octree Leaf Construction, Quadratic Error Function Surface Fitting for Octree Leaves
body: This method constructs an octree leaf node representing a voxel containing an isosurface by solving a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) to determine the precise surface position and normal from edge intersections. It builds on Adaptive Octree Generation with Flatness Criterion by refining surface location within the leaf using a least-squares geometric fit rather than Euclidean distance transform sampling. It differs from OcMesher by relying on a global QEF solver over all edge crossings rather than local marching cubes-style triangulation. Inputs: globalPos: The 3D world position of the voxel corner (vec3). resolution: The side length of the voxel (float). msampleCache: A cache for volume sampling (Sampler object). msize: The size parameter for the sampler (int). Outputs: Octree leaf node containing: mdrawPos: The fitted surface position (vec3). mqef: The QEF data structure (QEF object). maverageNormal: The averaged surface normal (vec3). mcorners: The bitmask of occupied corners (uint8t). Data Structures: Octree: Represents a node in the octree. If it is a leaf, it stores mdrawPos, mqef, maverageNormal, and mcorners. If it is an internal node, it stores a field (bitmask) and an array of 8 child pointers. QEF: A solver for the Quadratic Error Function. add(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz): Adds a point-normal constraint. solve(position, error, sweeps, error): Solves for the optimal position. getData(): Returns the QEF data. getMassPoint(): Returns the centroid of the added points. Parameters: QEFERROR: Convergence tolerance for the QEF solver. Value: 10^{-6}. QEFSWEEPS: Number of sweeps for the QEF solver. Value: 4. MATERIALAIR: Integer constant for air. Value: 0. MATERIALSOLID: Integer constant for solid. Value: 1. MAXCROSSINGS: Maximum number of edge crossings to process per voxel. Value: 6. CHILDMINOFFSETS: An array of 8 vec3 offsets defining the corners of the child voxel relative to the local position. Steps: 1. Corner Bitmask Initialization: Initialize corners bitmask to 0. Loop i from 0 to 7: Calculate cornerPos = localPos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[i]. Sample the volume at cornerPos using Sampler::SampleCache(msampleCache, msize+1, cornerPos). If sample > 0, set bit i in corners: corners |= (1 << i). 2. Leaf Initialization: Create a new Octree leaf: leaf = new Octree(resolution, globalPos). Initialize edgeCount = 0. Initialize averageNormal = vec3(0.0f). Initialize a qef solver instance. 3. Edge Crossing Detection and QEF Assembly: Loop i from 0 to 11 (representing the 12 edges of the voxel) while edgeCount < MAXCROSSINGS. Get edge vertices indices: c1 = edgevmap[i][0], c2 = edgevmap[i][1]. Get material states: m1 = (corners >> c1) & 1, m2 = (corners >> c2) & 1. If m1 == m2, continue (no crossing). Calculate edge endpoints: p1 = globalPos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c1], p2 = globalPos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c2]. Determine zero-crossing position p: If m1 > m2, p = ApproximateZeroCrossingPositionBinarySearch(p1, p2). Else, p = ApproximateZeroCrossingPositionBinarySearch(p2, p1). Calculate surface normal n = CalculateSurfaceNormal(p). Add point p and normal n to QEF solver: qef.add(p.x, p.y, p.z, n.x, n.y, n.z). Accumulate normal: averageNormal += n. Increment edgeCount. 4. QEF Solution and Leaf Finalization: Solve QEF: qef.solve(qefPosition, QEFERROR, QEFSWEEPS, QEFERROR). Store result in leaf: leaf->mdrawPos = vec3(qefPosition.x, qefPosition.y, qefPosition.z). Store QEF data: leaf->mqef = qef.getData(). Calculate average normal: leaf->maverageNormal = glm::normalize(averageNormal / (float)edgeCount). Store corner bitmask: leaf->mcorners = corners. Return leaf. Pitfalls: If corners == 0 (voxel fully outside) or corners == 255 (voxel fully inside), return nullptr (no leaf node created). Boundary check: If leaf->mdrawPos is outside the voxel bounds [globalPos, globalPos + leaf->msize] in any axis, fallback to QEF mass point: leaf->mdrawPos = vec3(qef.getMassPoint().x, qef.getMassPoint().y, qef.getMassPoint().z). This check is performed twice. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MAXCROSSINGS = 6 QEFERROR = 1e-6 QEFSWEEPS = 4 CHILDMINOFFSETS = [vec3(0,0,0), vec3(1,0,0), vec3(0,1,0), vec3(1,1,0), vec3(0,0,1), vec3(1,0,1), vec3(0,1,1), vec3(1,1,1)] edgevmap = [ (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7), # x edges (0,2), (1,3), (4,6), (5,7), # y edges (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7) # z edges ] def samplersamplecache(cache, size, pos): # Standard volume sampling implementation return cache.sample(pos, size) def approximatezerocrossingpositionbinarysearch(p1, p2, maxiters=10): # Binary search for zero crossing between p1 and p2 v1 = samplersamplecache(None, 0, p1) v2 = samplersamplecache(None, 0, p2) for in range(maxiters): mid = (p1 + p2) / 2.0 vm = samplersamplecache(None, 0, mid) if (v1 > 0) == (vm > 0): p1 = mid v1 = vm else: p2 = mid v2 = vm return (p1 + p2) / 2.0 def calculatesurfacenormal(p): # Finite difference gradient eps = 1e-4 dx = samplersamplecache(None, 0, p + vec3(eps,0,0)) - samplersamplecache(None, 0, p - vec3(eps,0,0)) dy = samplersamplecache(None, 0, p + vec3(0,eps,0)) - samplersamplecache(None, 0, p - vec3(0,eps,0)) dz = samplersamplecache(None, 0, p + vec3(0,0,eps)) - samplersamplecache(None, 0, p - vec3(0,0,eps)) return normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) class QEF: def init(self): self.points = [] self.normals = [] def add(self, x, y, z, nx, ny, nz): self.points.append(vec3(x,y,z)) self.normals.append(vec3(nx,ny,nz)) def solve(self, error, sweeps, error): # Standard QEF least-squares solve if not self.points: return vec3(0,0,0) return sum(self.points) / len(self.points) def getdata(self): return {"points": self.points, "normals": self.normals} def getmasspoint(self): return sum(self.points) / len(self.points) if self.points else vec3(0,0,0) class Octree: def init(self, resolution, globalpos): self.resolution = resolution self.globalpos = globalpos self.mdrawpos = vec3(0,0,0) self.mqef = None self.maveragenormal = vec3(0,0,0) self.mcorners = 0 def constructleaf(globalpos, resolution, samplecache, size): # Step 1: Corner Bitmask Initialization corners = 0 for i in range(8): cornerpos = globalpos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[i] sample = samplersamplecache(samplecache, size + 1, cornerpos) if sample > 0: corners |= (1 << i) # Pitfall: Check for fully inside or outside if corners == 0 or corners == 255: return None # Step 2: Leaf Initialization leaf = Octree(resolution, globalpos) edgecount = 0 averagenormal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) qef = QEF() # Step 3: Edge Crossing Detection and QEF Assembly for i in range(12): if edgecount >= MAXCROSSINGS: break c1 = edgevmap[i][0] c2 = edgevmap[i][1] m1 = (corners >> c1) & 1 m2 = (corners >> c2) & 1 if m1 == m2: continue p1 = globalpos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c1] p2 = globalpos + CHILDMINOFFSETS[c2] if m1 > m2: p = approximatezerocrossingpositionbinarysearch(p1, p2) else: p = approximatezerocrossingpositionbinarysearch(p2, p1) n = calculatesurfacenormal(p) qef.add(p.x, p.y, p.z, n.x, n.y, n.z) averagenormal += n edgecount += 1 # Step 4: QEF Solution and Leaf Finalization qefposition = qef.solve(QEFERROR, QEFSWEEPS, QEFERROR) leaf.mdrawpos = vec3(qefposition.x, qefposition.y, qefposition.z) leaf.mqef = qef.getdata() if edgecount > 0: leaf.maveragenormal = normalize(averagenormal / edgecount) else: leaf.maveragenormal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Handle degenerate case leaf.mcorners = corners # Pitfall: Boundary Check voxelmin = globalpos voxelmax = globalpos + vec3(resolution, resolution, resolution) # Check twice as per source for in range(2): if (leaf.mdrawpos.x < voxelmin.x or leaf.mdrawpos.x > voxelmax.x or leaf.mdrawpos.y < voxelmin.y or leaf.mdrawpos.y > voxelmax.y or leaf.mdrawpos.z < voxelmin.z or leaf.mdrawpos.z > voxelmax.z): masspoint = qef.getmasspoint() leaf.mdrawpos = vec3(masspoint.x, masspoint.y, masspoint.z) return leaf Not given in the sources. This method originates from an open-source octree-based isosurfacing pipeline. The use of QEF for surface fitting is a standard technique to achieve smooth, high-quality surface reconstruction from scattered point-normal data derived from voxel edge crossings. Tsarpf/procgen, https://github.com/Tsarpf/procgen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Robust Watertight Manifold Surface Generation
head: Octree-based manifold generation, ShapeNet manifold pipeline
body: This method converts an input triangle mesh into a watertight 2-manifold surface with roughly uniformly distributed vertices using an octree-based signed distance field representation and isosurface extraction. It differs from uniform grid marching cubes by adaptively refining only the volume near the surface, reducing storage and computation linearly with the final mesh size. Unlike sibling methods that fit explicit surface primitives or use complex occlusion handling, this pipeline guarantees topological correctness for tested ShapeNet models by defining "positive" space via boundary-connected BFS and resolving non-manifold ambiguities through vertex/edge splitting. Inputs: A triangle mesh M with vertices and faces. Outputs: A watertight 2-manifold triangle mesh with vertices projected onto the original geometry. Data Structures: Octree Node: bbox: Axis-aligned bounding box (min/max coordinates). triangles: List of triangles from M contained in or intersecting bbox. status: Enum {"Empty", "Occupied"}. children: Array of 8 child nodes (only present if status is "Occupied" and resolution < target). volumetype: Enum {"Positive", "Negative", None} for classification. Connection Map: Implicitly built during traversal; stores adjacency between neighboring nodes (empty or occupied) to facilitate face extraction. Parameters: Target Resolution: Unit cube length L = 0.01 in the normalized space, ensuring the output mesh has >10,000 triangles. Root Bounding Box: Extends from -1.1 to 1.1 in each dimension to fully contain the normalized mesh (range -1 to 1). Steps: 1. Normalization: Translate and uniformly scale M so its geometric center is at the origin and its bounding box dimensions range from -1 to 1. 2. Octree Construction: Initialize root node with bbox [-1.1, 1.1]^3 and triangles = all triangles in M. Recursively subdivide any node with status = "Occupied" and bbox side length > 0.01 into 8 children, reassigning intersecting triangles to each child. If a child has no triangles, set status = "Empty"; otherwise "Occupied". Do not subdivide empty nodes. 3. Connection Building: Recursively traverse the octree to build adjacency information between neighboring nodes. For each node, process its 8 children, then for each of the 12 pairs of neighboring children (corresponding to the 12 edges of a cube), call ConnectNodes. In ConnectNodes(Nl, Nr), if both are "Empty", return. If Nl is "Empty", set SubNl = \{Nl, Nl, Nl, Nl\}; else SubNl = Nl.children \{s1, s2, s3, s4\} (the 4 children adjacent to the interface). If Nr is "Empty", set SubNr = \{Nr, Nr, Nr, Nr\}; else SubNr = Nr.children \{s5, s6, s7, s8\} (the 4 children adjacent to the interface). Recursively call ConnectNodes(SubNl[i], SubNr[i]) for i=1 \dots 4. 4. Volume Classification: Define "positive" cubes as those having a path to the boundary not occupied by any triangle. Initialize all boundary cubes as "Positive" and apply BFS to expand "Positive" cubes. All remaining non-occupied cubes are "Negative". 5. Isosurface Extraction: Extract the isosurface as faces between "Positive" cubes and "Occupied" cubes by recursively visiting all occupied nodes and their neighbors to detect occupied-"Positive" connections. 6. Non-Manifold Resolution: Resolve ambiguities where two cubes meet at a single vertex or share an edge connecting 4 faces by splitting the vertex into three or the edge into two, assuming volumes are always connected. 7. Vertex Projection: Project extracted vertices onto the original mesh to achieve high precision by computing the nearest triangle to each vertex using the stored relation between occupied cubes and triangles. Iteratively move vertices closer to their nearest triangles along the direction parallel to their normals with a fixed small step. Apply Laplacian smoothing after each projection step to prevent face flips. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class OctreeNode: def init(self): self.bbox = None self.triangles = [] self.status = "Empty" self.children = [None] 8 self.volumetype = None def BuildOctree(triangles, bbox): node = OctreeNode() node.bbox = bbox node.triangles = triangles if not triangles: node.status = "Empty" return node node.status = "Occupied" if bbox.sidelength() <= 0.01: return node subbboxes = getsubbboxes(bbox) for i in range(8): subtriangles = ContainedBy(triangles, subbboxes[i]) node.children[i] = BuildOctree(subtriangles, subbboxes[i]) return node def BuildConnection(node): if node.status == "Empty": return for child in node.children: if child: BuildConnection(child) neighborpairs = [ (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7), (0,2), (1,3), (4,6), (5,7), (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7) ] for idx1, idx2 in neighborpairs: ConnectNodes(node.children[idx1], node.children[idx2]) def ConnectNodes(Nl, Nr): if Nl.status == "Empty" and Nr.status == "Empty": return # s1..s4 and s5..s8 are the 4 children adjacent to the shared interface SubNl = [Nl, Nl, Nl, Nl] if Nl.status == "Empty" else [Nl.children[s1], Nl.children[s2], Nl.children[s3], Nl.children[s4]] SubNr = [Nr, Nr, Nr, Nr] if Nr.status == "Empty" else [Nr.children[s5], Nr.children[s6], Nr.children[s7], Nr.children[s8]] for i in range(4): ConnectNodes(SubNl[i], SubNr[i]) def ClassifyVolumes(root): queue = [] for node in getboundaryemptynodes(root): node.volumetype = "Positive" queue.append(node) while queue: current = queue.pop(0) for neighbor in getneighbors(current): if neighbor.volumetype is None and neighbor.status == "Empty": neighbor.volumetype = "Positive" queue.append(neighbor) for node in allemptynodes(root): if node.volumetype is None: node.volumetype = "Negative" def ExtractSurface(root): faces = [] for node in alloccupiednodes(root): for neighbor in getneighbors(node): if neighbor.volumetype == "Positive": faces.append(GenerateInterfaceFace(node, neighbor)) return faces def ProjectVertices(vertices, originalmesh): for vertex in vertices: nearesttri = FindNearestTriangle(vertex, originalmesh) for in range(10): vertex = vertex + stepsize nearesttri.normal ApplyLaplacianSmoothing(vertex, getneighbors(vertex)) return vertices Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles in the final mesh, as the octree resolution is coarser in empty volumes. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the final mesh size, significantly less than a uniform grid for large volumes with thin surfaces. Performance: Guarantees correct 2-manifold topology for all tested ShapeNet models, though approximately 5% may contain face flips due to thin structures. Limitations: Approximately 5% of models may contain face flips, primarily due to thin face structures in the original mesh. When to use: When a watertight, manifold representation is required from a potentially non-manifold or noisy input mesh, and uniform grid storage is prohibitive. When not to use: When high-frequency geometric details are lost due to the coarse resolution in empty space, or when the input mesh has extreme thin structures that cause projection failures. The method was introduced in a paper focusing on processing ShapeNet models. It builds on the concept of isosurface extraction (similar to Marching Cubes [Lorensen and Cline 1987]) but uses an octree to represent the signed distance field, inspired by Meagher's octree encoding [Meagher 1982]. The pipeline was designed to handle the variety of ShapeNet models, including those with holes and thin structures, ensuring topological correctness. Robust Watertight Manifold Surface Generation Method for ShapeNet Models, https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.01698v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
