name: Sampled DMC
head: Linear Hashed Marching Cubes
body: Sampled DMC is a mesh generation technique that adapts the Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) algorithm to hashed octrees using Morton keys. It constructs a dual grid where vertices are located at the center of each octree leaf node, allowing for adaptive resolution isosurfacing without requiring a uniform grid. Unlike standard Marching Cubes implementations that expect Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) as direct input, Sampled DMC takes the data octree itself, making it suitable for storing and extracting meshes from sampled points, complex SDFs, or destructible environments. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A HashedOctree<T> where T implements the McNode trait, providing density() (distance from node center to contour) and normal() (normalized gradient of the SDF) for each node. A scale parameter (f32) applied to vertex positions. Output: A Mesh struct containing a Vec<Vertex> and Vec<u32> indices. Vertices are in counter-clockwise order. Data Structures: McNode: Trait requiring density(&self) -> f32 and normal(&self) -> Vector3<f32>. NodeData: Struct with density: f32 and normal: Vector3<f32>. Vertex: Struct with position: Point3<f32> and normal: Vector3<f32>. Normals are normalized. DualGrid: Constructed from the octree. Contains volumes, where each volume is an array of 8 MortonKeys representing the corners of a dual cell. CellVertexData: Struct with positions: [Point3<f32>; 12] and normals: [Vector3<f32>; 12]. Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Dual Grid: Call DualGrid::fromoctree(octree). Get all leaf nodes of the octree. For each leaf, determine its vertex keys. For each vertex key, find neighboring leaves at the same level. Filter neighbors to ensure they match the current leaf's level and are not the source vertex itself. 2. Process Volumes in Parallel: Iterate over dual.volumes using a parallel iterator (e.g., rayon). 3. Fetch Volume Data: For each volume, call fetchvolumedata(volume, octree). Initialize cubeindex = 0 and an array of 8 NodeData. Map volume vertex indices to Marching Cubes vertex indices using VOLUMETOMCVERTEX: [3, 2, 7, 6, 0, 1, 4, 5]. If any vertex key is MortonKey::none(), return immediately (boundary handling). Retrieve density and normal from the octree for each vertex. If density > 0.0, set the corresponding bit in cubeindex. Store density and normal in the nodes array. 4. Filter Visibility: Call iscellvisible(cubeindex). If cubeindex is 0 (all negative) or 0xFF (all positive), skip the volume. 5. Calculate Interpolated Data: For visible volumes, call calculatemcvertexdata(volume, nodes, cubeindex, scale). Get the edge mask from tables::EDGETABLE[cubeindex]. For each of the 12 edges, if the edge is active (bit set in mask): Get the two volume vertex indices from MCCUBEEDGES. Calculate the interpolation factor R using the densities of the two vertices. Interpolate the position and normal using R. Scale the position by vertexpositionscale. 6. Obtain Vertices: Call obtainmcvertices(celldata, cubeindex). Get triangle indices from tables::TRITABLE[cubeindex]. Chunk the table into groups of 3. For each valid chunk, create Vertex structs using the interpolated positions and normals. 7. Collect Results: Collect all vertices into a Vec. Generate indices as (0..vertices.len() as u32).collect(). Formulas: Interpolation Factor: R = \frac{0 - p1}{p2 - p1} Where p1 and p2 are the densities at the two endpoints of the edge. This estimates the relative value R such that p1 + (p2 - p1) \cdot R == 0. Special cases: If |p1| < 0.00001, return p1. If |p2| < 0.00001, return p2. If |p1 - p2| < 0.00001, return p1. Position Interpolation: \text{pos} = \text{interpolate}(\text{pos}1, \text{pos}2, R) \cdot \text{scale} Where \text{interpolate} denotes linear interpolation. Normal Interpolation: \text{norm} = \text{interpolate}(\text{norm}1, \text{norm}2, R) (Note: The source code does not explicitly normalize the interpolated normal, but the McNode trait requires normalized normals, and the Vertex struct stores normalized normals. The implementation relies on the input normals being normalized.) Parameters: scale: f32. A scaling factor applied to vertex positions. Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: If any vertex in a volume is MortonKey::none(), the volume is on the edge of the octree. The function returns immediately, skipping that volume. This may result in missing mesh parts at the boundary. Cell Visibility: Cells with cubeindex == 0 or cubeindex == 0xFF are filtered out. This is correct for isosurfacing but must be understood to avoid expecting triangles in uniform regions. Vertex Merging: The algorithm does not merge vertices. Indices are simply incremental integers. This can lead to higher vertex counts and potential visual artifacts at shared edges if normals are not consistent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshfromoctree(octree, scale): dual = DualGrid.fromoctree(octree) vertices = [] for volume in dual.volumes: # Parallel iteration handled by framework result = fetchvolumedata(volume, octree) if result is None: continue nodes, cubeindex = result if not iscellvisible(cubeindex): continue celldata = calculatemcvertexdata(volume, nodes, cubeindex, scale) vertices.extend(obtainmcvertices(celldata, cubeindex)) indices = list(range(len(vertices))) return Mesh(vertices, indices) def fetchvolumedata(volume, octree): VOLUMETOMCVERTEX = [3, 2, 7, 6, 0, 1, 4, 5] nodes = [None] 8 cubeindex = 0 for volumei, key in enumerate(volume): mci = VOLUMETOMCVERTEX[volumei] if key == MortonKey.none(): return None # Boundary handling: skip volume nodedata = octree.value(key) density = nodedata.density() normal = nodedata.normal() if density > 0.0: cubeindex |= (1 << mci) nodes[volumei] = NodeData(density, normal) return (nodes, cubeindex) def calculatemcvertexdata(volume, nodes, cubeindex, scale): MCCUBEEDGES = [ (4, 5), (1, 5), (0, 1), (0, 4), (6, 7), (3, 7), (2, 3), (2, 6), (4, 6), (5, 7), (1, 3), (0, 2) ] positions = [None] 12 normals = [None] 12 edges = tables.EDGETABLE[cubeindex] for i in range(12): if (edges & (1 << i)) > 0: v1i, v2i = MCCUBEEDGES[i] factor = interpolationfactor(nodes[v1i].density, nodes[v2i].density) pos1 = volume[v1i].position() pos2 = volume[v2i].position() positions[i] = (pos1.interpolate(pos2, factor) scale) norm1 = nodes[v1i].normal norm2 = nodes[v2i].normal normals[i] = norm1.interpolate(norm2, factor) return CellVertexData(positions, normals) def obtainmcvertices(celldata, cubeindex): tritable = tables.TRITABLE[cubeindex] vertices = [] for i in range(0, len(tritable), 3): if tritable[i] == -1: break v1 = celldata.positions[tritable[i]] v2 = celldata.positions[tritable[i+1]] v3 = celldata.positions[tritable[i+2]] n1 = celldata.normals[tritable[i]] n2 = celldata.normals[tritable[i+1]] n3 = celldata.normals[tritable[i+2]] vertices.append(Vertex(v1, n1)) vertices.append(Vertex(v2, n2)) vertices.append(Vertex(v3, n3)) return vertices def interpolationfactor(p1, p2): if abs(p1) < 0.00001: return p1 if abs(p2) < 0.00001: return p2 if abs(p1 - p2) < 0.00001: return p1 return (0.0 - p1) / (p2 - p1) Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of dual volumes (leaf nodes in the octree). Parallel processing is used via rayon. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of dual volumes. Each volume is processed independently, and vertices are collected into a single vector. Performance: Fast due to parallel processing and efficient data structures. The use of Morton keys allows for efficient spatial locality. Strengths: Adaptive resolution via octree; no need for uniform grid; suitable for dynamic/destructible environments; parallelizable. Limitations: No vertex merging (higher vertex count); boundary handling skips cells; requires McNode implementation; not suitable for non-octree data. When to use: When working with octree-based data structures, adaptive resolution is needed, or the environment is dynamic. When not to use: When vertex merging is critical for performance or visual quality, or when working with uniform grid data. Sampled DMC is an implementation of the Dual Marching Cubes technique, also known as Linear Hashed Marching Cubes. It was developed as part of the dmc crate, available on crates.io. The method adapts the original Marching Cubes algorithm, which uses a uniform grid, to hashed octrees using Morton keys. This allows for adaptive resolution isosurfacing, which is particularly useful for complex SDFs, destructible environments, or objects with different levels of detail (LODs). The crate uses cgmath for vector math and rayon for parallel processing. aleokdev/dmc, https://github.com/aleokdev/dmc, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Point-based Isosurface Extraction with Octree Pruning
head: Dividing Cubes, Point-based Isosurface Extraction (Dividing Cubes/Octree)
body: Point-based Isosurface Extraction with Octree Pruning is a view-dependent surface extraction method that recursively subdivides a scalar field into grid cells until sub-pixel resolution is achieved in screen space, rendering the resulting geometry using point primitives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining adaptive spatial decomposition with visibility-based pruning to handle large unstructured grids interactively on GPUs, rather than generating a static mesh. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar field defined on an unstructured grid or voxel data, represented hierarchically by an octree. Each octree node stores the minimum and maximum scalar values within its bounding box. Output: A point cloud representing the isosurface, rendered as points that approximate the surface geometry. Data Structures Octree Node: Contains a bounding box, and specifically the minimum (v{min}) and maximum (v{max}) scalar values found within that node's volume. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Construct or load the octree representation of the scalar field, ensuring each node stores v{min} and v{max}. 2. Front-to-Back Traversal: Perform a visibility-ordered traversal of the octree from the camera viewpoint to the background. 3. Value-Based Pruning: For each node visited, check if the isovalue I lies within the range [v{min}, v{max}] of the node. If I < v{min} or I > v{max}, discard the node and do not process its children. 4. Visibility Pruning: Determine if the node's bounding box contributes to the final image from the current camera position. If the bounding box is occluded or lies outside the view frustum, discard the node. 5. Subdivision or Rendering: If sub-pixel resolution is not achieved, divide the node into eight children and repeat the traversal for each child. If sub-pixel resolution is achieved, render the node as a point primitive. 6. Fragment Processing: When rendering the point primitives, a fragment program computes robust normal positions for the isosurface. The fragment shader accesses the world coordinate positions of the current pixel and its neighboring pixels. Formulas Value-based pruning condition: v{min} \le I \le v{max}. Sub-pixel threshold criterion: Not given in the sources. Parameters Isovalue (I): The scalar threshold defining the surface. Sub-pixel Threshold: The criterion for stopping subdivision. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Pruning Safety: Value-based pruning requires v{min} and v{max} to accurately represent the entire volume of the node. View Dependency: The method requires re-traversal if the camera moves, as subdivision is view-dependent. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurface(rootnode, camera, isovalue): # Initialization: Construct or load octree with vmin and vmax per node traverse(rootnode, camera, isovalue) def traverse(node, camera, isovalue): # Value-based pruning: discard nodes outside isosurface limit if isovalue < node.vmin or isovalue > node.vmax: return # Visibility pruning: discard nodes whose bounding box does not contribute to final image if not isfrustumandocclusionculled(node.bbox, camera): return # Subdivision or rendering based on sub-pixel resolution # Not given in the sources: exact sub-pixel threshold formula if not meetssubpixelthreshold(node, camera): for child in node.children: traverse(child, camera, isovalue) else: renderpointprimitive(node.center) # Fragment program computes robust normal positions by accessing world coordinates of pixel and neighbors computerobustnormal(node.center) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method's performance depends on the isosurface density and view direction, with pruning reducing traversal for sparse fields. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Storing v{min} and v{max} per node adds constant overhead per node. Strengths: Highly adaptive to view; efficient culling of empty or occluded regions; handles large datasets better than static mesh extraction. Limitations: View-dependent (requires re-traversal if camera moves); point primitives may lack the continuity of triangle meshes; robust normal computation requires access to neighboring pixel data, which can be complex to implement in a fragment shader. When to use: Interactive visualization of large unstructured grids where performance is critical and the view changes frequently. The method dates back to the "Dividing Cubes" approach described in [15] (cited in), which introduced the concept of view-dependent subdivision until sub-pixel resolution is reached. The use of point primitives to represent smaller triangles for handling larger datasets was described in [40] (cited in). The survey by highlights this as a key GPU-based technique for rendering unstructured grids, leveraging the front-to-back traversal of an octree to enable value-based and visibility-based pruning. name: Isotopic Approximation of Implicit Curves and Surfaces
head: ApproximateCurve, Isotopic Approximation
body:
The Isotopic Approximation algorithm generates a piecewise linear approximation of an implicit curve in \mathbb{R}^2 or surface in \mathbb{R}^3 that is regularly isotopic to the original manifold. Unlike grid-based schemes that may miss critical details and fail to guarantee correct topology, this method uses interval arithmetic to adaptively subdivide space via a quadtree (curves) or octree (surfaces), ensuring every leaf cell is locally parametrizable. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a simple interval test to guarantee isotopy without computing critical points, making it fast and suitable for visualization and time-dependent surface morphing. Inputs: 1. F: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R} (n=2 for curves, n=3 for surfaces): A smooth implicit function where 0 is a regular value, meaning 
abla F is non-zero at every point on S = F^{-1}(0). 2. B: A bounding square (in \mathbb{R}^2) or cube (in \mathbb{R}^3) containing the implicit manifold S. Outputs: A piecewise linear approximation of S consisting of line segments (curves) or triangles (surfaces). Interval: A pair of floats [lo, hi] representing a closed range with error bounds. Point: A tuple of n floats representing coordinates in \mathbb{R}^n. Cell: A tree node containing: bounds: A tuple of n Interval objects defining the spatial extent. children: A list of 2^n Cell objects, or None if leaf. isleaf: Boolean flag. level: Integer depth of subdivision. 1. Initialization: Initialize a quadtree/octree T with a root Cell representing the bounding box B. 2. Adaptive Subdivision: Recursively subdivide T until all leaf cells C satisfy the termination condition: 0 
otin \Box F(C) \lor \langle \Box 
abla F(C), \Box 
abla F(C) angle > 0. 3. Balancing: Balance T so that neighboring cells differ in size by at most a factor of two. 4. Vertex Placement: For each edge of the tree structure, evaluate F at its two endpoints. If the signs of F at the endpoints are opposite, construct a vertex at the midpoint of the edge. 5. Mesh Construction: For each leaf cell C, identify the vertices placed on its boundary. If the leaf contains exactly two vertices, connect them by a line segment. If it contains four vertices, find the two vertices on the same side and connect each of them to one of the other two vertices. Inclusion Function: An inclusion function \Box f satisfies x \in I \implies f(x) \in \Box f(I) for any interval I. Convergent Squaring: For f(x) = x^2 on interval [a, b], the convergent inclusion function is: \Box f([a,b]) =  egin{cases} [\min(a^2, b^2), \max(a^2, b^2)], & a \cdot b \geq 0 \ [0, \max(a^2, b^2)], & a \cdot b < 0 \end{cases} Gradient Condition: \langle \Box 
abla F(C), \Box 
abla F(C) angle > 0 implies at least one component squared interval (e.g., Fx(C)^2) does not contain 0. This means F is strictly monotonic in that axis direction, making the cell locally parametrizable. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Interval: def init(self, lo, hi): self.lo = lo self.hi = hi def intervaladd(a, b): return Interval(a.lo + b.lo, a.hi + b.hi) def intervalmul(a, b): p1 = a.lo b.lo; p2 = a.lo b.hi; p3 = a.hi b.lo; p4 = a.hi b.hi return Interval(min(p1, p2, p3, p4), max(p1, p2, p3, p4)) def intervalsquare(a): if a.lo a.hi >= 0: return Interval(min(a.lo2, a.hi2), max(a.lo2, a.hi2)) else: return Interval(0, max(a.lo2, a.hi2)) def intervaleval(func, bounds): # Standard corner-based inclusion function corners = [] for mask in range(1 << len(bounds)): pt = [] for d, b in enumerate(bounds): pt.append(b.lo if (mask >> d) & 1 else b.hi) corners.append(tuple(pt)) vals = [func(p) for p in corners] return Interval(min(vals), max(vals)) class Cell: def init(self, bounds, level=0): self.bounds = bounds self.level = level self.children = None self.isleaf = True def subdividecell(cell): newbounds = [] for diminterval in cell.bounds: mid = (diminterval.lo + diminterval.hi) / 2.0 newbounds.append(Interval(diminterval.lo, mid)) newbounds.append(Interval(mid, diminterval.hi)) children = [] dim = len(cell.bounds) for i in range(1 << dim): childbounds = [] for d in range(dim): idx = (i >> d) & 1 childbounds.append(newbounds[d 2 + idx]) children.append(Cell(bounds=tuple(childbounds), level=cell.level + 1)) return children def balancetree(root): # Standard tree balancing to ensure neighboring cells differ at most a factor of two in size pass def collectalledges(cell, edges=None, parent=None): if edges is None: edges = [] if cell.children is None: return edges dim = len(cell.bounds) for i in range(1 << dim): for d in range(dim): if (i >> d) & 1: p1 = [cell.bounds[j].lo if ((i >> j) & 1) else cell.bounds[j].hi for j in range(dim)] p2 = list(p1) p2[d] = cell.bounds[d].hi edges.append((tuple(p1), tuple(p2))) for child in cell.children: collectalledges(child, edges) return edges def groupbyside(vertices, bounds): # Group vertices by which face/edge of the cell they lie on sides = [[] for in range(2 len(bounds))] for v in vertices: for d, b in enumerate(bounds): if abs(v[d] - b.lo) < 1e-9: sides[d].append(v) elif abs(v[d] - b.hi) < 1e-9: sides[d + len(bounds)].append(v) return [s for s in sides if s] def isotopicapproximation(F, gradF, B, maxdepth=10): root = Cell(bounds=B, level=0) queue = [root] while queue: cell = queue.pop(0) if cell.level >= maxdepth: cell.isleaf = True continue Fval = intervaleval(F, cell.bounds) gradvals = [intervaleval(g, cell.bounds) for g in gradF] zeronotinF = Fval.lo > 0 or Fval.hi < 0 gradnormsq = Interval(0, 0) for g in gradvals: gradnormsq = intervaladd(gradnormsq, intervalsquare(g)) gradpositive = gradnormsq.lo > 0 if zeronotinF or gradpositive: cell.isleaf = True else: cell.isleaf = False children = subdividecell(cell) cell.children = children queue.extend(children) balancetree(root) edges = collectalledges(root) vertices = [] for e in edges: v1, v2 = e[0], e[1] if (F(v1) <= 0 and F(v2) > 0) or (F(v1) > 0 and F(v2) <= 0): mid = tuple((a + b) / 2.0 for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) vertices.append((mid, e)) mesh = [] for leaf in collectleaves(root): leafedges = set() for child in leaf.children if leaf.children else []: leafedges.update(collectalledges(child)) leafverts = [v for v, e in vertices if e in leafedges] if len(leafverts) == 2: mesh.append((leafverts[0], leafverts[1])) elif len(leafverts) == 4: sides = groupbyside(leafverts, leaf.bounds) sidewithtwo = [s for s in sides if len(s) == 2][0] others = [v for s in sides if len(s) == 1 for v in s] mesh.append((sidewithtwo[0], others[0])) mesh.append((sidewithtwo[1], others[1])) return mesh def collectleaves(cell): if cell.children is None: return [cell] leaves = [] for child in cell.children: leaves.extend(collectleaves(child)) return leaves Minimal Subdivision Level: Can be defined to improve the Hausdorff distance between the surface and the approximation. Maximal Subdivision Level: Can be used to improve the speed of the meshing process and to handle surfaces with singularities. Singularities: If F has singularities (where 
abla F = 0), the condition \langle 
abla F, 
abla F angle > 0 may never be met, leading to infinite subdivision. A maximal subdivision level must be enforced, and color coding can identify regions where the approximation might be topologically incorrect. Boundary Conditions: A single side of a cell may consist of two tree edges if the neighboring cell is subdivided. Each cell is therefore surrounded by four to eight tree edges. Precision: Interval arithmetic must be used to prevent rounding errors that could incorrectly classify a cell as containing zero or not. Time Complexity: The subdivision process terminates because cells shrink towards a point, and for a regular curve/surface, at least one of the two clauses (0 
otin F(C) or \langle 
abla F, 
abla F angle > 0) converges to a non-zero value. The algorithm is fast because it uses a simple interval test and adds little overhead compared to other enumeration methods. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of leaf nodes in the balanced quadtree/octree. Strengths: Guarantees correct topology (regular isotopy); does not require computing critical points; fast due to simple interval tests; flexible adaptive resolution. Limitations: Requires F to be smooth and 0 to be a regular value (gradient non-zero on surface); singularities require special handling (max depth); interval arithmetic can be computationally expensive if not optimized. When to Use: Visualization of implicit surfaces where piecewise linear approximations are required; constructing initial meshes for time-dependent surfaces (e.g., morphing). When Not to Use: When the implicit function has singularities and high precision is required without fallback strategies; when performance is critical and interval arithmetic overhead is prohibitive. The Isotopic Approximation algorithm was introduced as one of the first methods to guarantee isotopy for implicit surface meshing. It falls into the category of enumeration methods but distinguishes itself by using a fast and simple interval test to decide subdivision, avoiding the need to compute critical points of the implicit function. The method is based on a quadtree (for curves) or octree (for surfaces) and uses interval arithmetic to ensure that leaf cells are locally parametrizable. The approach was developed to address the limitations of grid-based schemes, which can miss important surface details and fail to guarantee correct topology. name: Adaptive Sampling-based Isosurface Extraction
head: Octree Dual Contouring (OctDC), Octree Marching Cubes (OctMC)
body: Adaptive sampling-based isosurface extraction constructs a mesh by sampling the implicit scalar field at discrete locations (typically octree leaves) rather than computing analytic intersections within grid cells. This approach sacrifices geometric precision for computational efficiency and ease of implementation on adaptive structures. It differs from its siblings by relying on discrete point clouds or simplified connectivity derived from samples, whereas methods like Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree or Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction often preserve topological guarantees or analytic intersection logic within the spatial hierarchy. The family shares the mechanism of using an octree to adaptively resolve the scalar field V. The isosurface is defined by the set of sample points (usually octree leaves) where the field value crosses the isovalue v. Unlike analytic methods that compute exact intersection coordinates on cell edges, these methods approximate the surface geometry using the sampled locations or simplified primitives associated with the leaves. The primary challenge is maintaining topological consistency (avoiding cracks) and geometric accuracy when the sampling density varies across the surface. Approximates the surface by placing a single point at the center of every grid cell intersecting the isosurface. It sacrifices precision for speed, bounding the distance error by half the cell diagonal (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} for unit cells). Choose this when extreme efficiency is required and exact geometry is secondary, such as in similarity map computation. [Octree Marching Cubes (OctMC)]: Uses the Marching Cubes topology logic adapted to octree leaves. It generates more vertices than analytic methods and can suffer from topological inconsistencies if the octree is not strictly adapted to the surface. [Octree Dual Contouring (OctDC)]: Uses dual contouring logic on octree leaves to preserve sharp features. It typically produces higher vertex counts than OctMC but requires solving linear systems for vertex positions. [McGrids]: A grid-based adaptive method that balances between full analytic extraction and coarse sampling. The term "Adaptive Sampling-based Isosurface Extraction" is used in recent literature to categorize methods like OctMC, OctDC, and McGrids that rely on discrete sampling within an octree hierarchy. These methods are often contrasted with "Analytic Isosurface Extraction" (e.g., TetraSDF), which computes exact intersections. Historical context: Early octree isosurfacing methods like Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree established the foundation for adaptive spatial decomposition. Later, Ashida and Badla Octree Contouring and Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees addressed topological issues. The specific comparison in highlights that while these adaptive sampling methods are standard, they can be computationally expensive and produce excessive vertex counts for high-resolution implicit fields. Performance data from on the Stanford Bunny dataset at depth 12 shows that OctMC takes 124.2s and produces 6.76M vertices, while OctDC takes 139.3s and produces 13.49M vertices. In contrast, analytic methods (TetraSDF) achieved 4.56s and 0.28M vertices. The study notes that at depth 12, octree-based extraction became impractical for the Bunny model, producing 71M leaves, indicating that octree adaptivity alone does not prevent near-surface explosion on curved shapes. TetraSDF: Analytic Isosurface Extraction with Multi-resolution Tetrahedral Grid, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16273v4, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Isosurface Approximation via Grid Cell Center Sampling
head: Cell Center Isosurface Approximation, Grid Cell Center Sampling
body: This method approximates an isosurface S for a given isovalue v by generating exactly one sample point per 3D grid cell that intersects the surface, replacing exact analytic extraction (such as Marching Cubes) to accelerate distance field computation. It differs from its siblings in the Adaptive Sampling-based Isosurface Extraction family by using a fixed grid cell topology and a simple center-point heuristic rather than adaptive octree leaf refinement or complex primitive construction, prioritizing computational speed and GPU parallelism over geometric precision. Inputs: A scalar field V defined on a regular 3D grid. An isovalue v. Grid dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz). Outputs: An array of 3D point coordinates representing the approximate isosurface. The points are listed in scanline order. Data Structures: 1. Binary Volume: A 3D array of booleans (or integers) with the same dimensions as the input grid. Each element corresponds to a grid cell. 2. Point Array: A dynamic array or compacted buffer storing the (x, y, z) coordinates of the centers of active grid cells. Grid Cell Definition: A grid cell is defined as a 1 \times 1 \times 1 cube. Its vertices correspond to the eight voxels in a 2 \times 2 \times 2 spatial region of the input scalar field. Specifically, for a grid cell at integer indices (i, j, k), the eight associated voxel values are V(x, y, z) for x \in \{i, i+1\}, y \in \{j, j+1\}, and z \in \{k, k+1\}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Parallel Cell Evaluation: Launch a GPU kernel where each thread is responsible for one grid cell (i, j, k). 2. Intersection Check: The thread reads the eight scalar values at the vertices of the grid cell. If at least one value is strictly greater than v and at least one value is strictly less than v, the grid cell contains part of the isosurface S. Note: If all values are equal to v, the cell is on the surface but does not cross it; the source implies this case is ignored or treated as non-intersecting for the purpose of generating a single representative point via the "larger/smaller" logic. 3. Binary Volume Update: If the intersection condition is met, write 1 (or true) to the corresponding location in the binary volume. Otherwise, write 0 (or false). 4. Compaction: Apply a GPU compaction scheme (e.g., prefix sum followed by scatter) to the binary volume. This converts the sparse binary volume into a dense array containing only the coordinates of the centers of the active grid cells. 5. Coordinate Generation: For each active cell identified in step 4, compute the center coordinates. If the grid cell spans indices [i, i+1] \times [j, j+1] \times [k, k+1], the center is (i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluategridcell(cellid, griddims, scalarfield, isovalue, binaryvolume): # Decode 1D thread ID to 3D cell indices i = cellid // (griddims.y griddims.z) j = (cellid // griddims.z) % griddims.y k = cellid % griddims.z # Check bounds (assuming grid cells are defined for i < Nx-1, etc.) if i >= griddims.x - 1 or j >= griddims.y - 1 or k >= griddims.z - 1: return # Read 8 voxel values at the corners of the grid cell # Voxel indices correspond to cell indices directly v000 = scalarfield[i, j, k] v100 = scalarfield[i+1, j, k] v010 = scalarfield[i, j+1, k] v110 = scalarfield[i+1, j+1, k] v001 = scalarfield[i, j, k+1] v101 = scalarfield[i+1, j, k+1] v011 = scalarfield[i, j+1, k+1] v111 = scalarfield[i+1, j+1, k+1] # Check if isosurface crosses the cell hasgreater = (v000 > isovalue or v100 > isovalue or v010 > isovalue or v110 > isovalue or v001 > isovalue or v101 > isovalue or v011 > isovalue or v111 > isovalue) hasless = (v000 < isovalue or v100 < isovalue or v010 < isovalue or v110 < isovalue or v001 < isovalue or v101 < isovalue or v011 < isovalue or v111 < isovalue) if hasgreater and hasless: binaryvolume[i, j, k] = 1 else: binaryvolume[i, j, k] = 0 def compactandoutput(binaryvolume, griddims): # 1. Compute prefix sum of binary volume to determine output indices # This step depends on the specific GPU library or algorithm used for compaction. # Let's assume a function prefixsum that returns an array of the same size # where each element is the sum of all preceding elements (inclusive). prefix = prefixsum(binaryvolume) # 2. Scatter active points into output array outputpoints = [] for k in range(griddims.z): for j in range(griddims.y): for i in range(griddims.x - 1): if binaryvolume[i, j, k] == 1: # Calculate center of the grid cell cx = i + 0.5 cy = j + 0.5 cz = k + 0.5 outputpoints.append((cx, cy, cz)) return outputpoints Parameters: Isovalue v: The scalar threshold defining the surface. Grid Cell Size: Fixed at 1 \times 1 \times 1 units in the coordinate space of the voxel grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Error: The distance from any point p to the true surface S computed using this approximation is bounded by \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} (half the diagonal length of the grid cell) due to the triangle inequality. This error is considered acceptable for applications like similarity map computation where downsampled distance fields are used. Boundary Conditions: The method iterates over grid cells defined by 2 \times 2 \times 2 voxel regions. Therefore, the loop for grid cell indices must stop at N-1 for each dimension to avoid accessing out-of-bounds voxels. Topological Consistency: This method does not guarantee topological consistency or connectivity between points. It produces a loose set of points in scanline order, not a mesh. Time Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for the parallel evaluation phase, plus O(Nx Ny Nz) for the compaction phase (assuming linear-time compaction algorithms like parallel prefix sum). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the input scalar field, the binary volume (same size as input grid), and the output point array (size \le Nx Ny Nz). Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPU. Each thread operates independently on a grid cell, minimizing synchronization overhead until the compaction step. Strengths: Extremely fast computation; avoids the complexity of connectivity analysis required by Marching Cubes; suitable for generating distance fields where exact geometry is less critical than speed. Limitations: Low geometric accuracy (error bound \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}); no connectivity information; points are not located at actual intersections but at cell centers. When to use: When a rough approximation of the isosurface is sufficient for downstream tasks like similarity map computation or distance field generation, and performance is paramount. When not to use: When precise surface geometry, connectivity, or mesh topology is required. This method was introduced in the context of efficient GPU-accelerated computation of isosurfaces, specifically for applications like similarity map generation where exact surface extraction is computationally expensive and potentially unnecessary. It serves as a lightweight alternative to the Marching Cubes algorithm, which computes multiple points per voxel and connects them to form a mesh. The approach leverages the parallelism of modern GPUs to scan grid cells simultaneously, using a binary volume and compaction scheme to efficiently collect the resulting points. name: Grid Traversal and Data Structure Adaptation
head: Adaptive Isosurface Extraction, Sparse Grid Marching Cubes
body: This family addresses the inefficiency of applying standard isosurface extraction (like Marching Cubes) to volumetric data that is sparse, adaptive, or hierarchical. Standard methods require dense grid traversal, leading to high memory usage and computation on empty regions. These methods adapt the data structure (octrees, sparse lists, or AMR grids) to the scalar field's features, traversing only relevant nodes or voxels. They differ from sibling methods by their specific approach to handling the topology and connectivity of the adapted grid, particularly regarding crack-free surface generation. All methods in this family share the goal of extracting a manifold isosurface from a scalar field without processing the entire volume. They rely on the following common mechanisms: 1. Selective Traversal/Processing: Instead of iterating over a dense N \times N \times N grid, the algorithm identifies a subset of "active" elements (voxels, nodes, or faces) that intersect the isosurface or contain significant field variation. 2. Local Marching Cubes Application: For each active element, the standard Marching Cubes (MC) algorithm is applied locally. This involves: Evaluating or retrieving scalar values at the 8 corners of a voxel/cube. Computing a cube index C based on the sign of (vj - \text{iso}) for each corner j: C = \sum{j=0}^{7} \text{bit}j \cdot 2^j, \quad \text{where } \text{bit}j = \begin{cases} 1 & vj < \text{iso} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Interpolating vertex positions on intersecting edges. Generating triangles based on the MC lookup table for index C. 3. Global Mesh Assembly: The local triangles and vertices are merged into a global mesh. Consistency at shared boundaries (corners, edges, faces) is critical to ensure a watertight surface. This often requires averaging corner values or using specific stitching techniques. Applies MC over an octree structure. It refines the octree based on a split predicate. Choose when: Data is naturally hierarchical or sparse, and you need a manifold surface. Pitfall: Requires uniform node sizes around the isosurface to avoid cracks. Operates on an explicit list of active voxel coordinates and their corner values. Choose when: You have a sparse set of voxels (e.g., from SDF sampling) and want to avoid hierarchical overhead. Pitfall: Requires explicit consistency handling (averaging) for shared corners to ensure watertightness. Recursively traverses an octree to enumerate faces, edges, and vertices, delegating to MC at leaves. Choose when: You need to handle mismatched tree depths or complex hierarchical structures explicitly. Pitfall: Complex recursion logic for face/edge enumeration across different depths. Index-based tessellation for AMR grids using "stitch cells." Choose when: Working with AMR data where you need to connect coarse and fine grids without subdividing boundary quads. Pitfall: Avoid subdividing quadrilaterals to prevent non-unique triangulation and cracks. The need for adaptive isosurface extraction arises from the limitations of uniform grid methods in handling large-scale or sparse volumetric data. Early work focused on octree-based approaches to reduce memory footprint. Sparse Marching Cubes emerged from the need to process point-cloud-derived SDFs or sparse voxel grids efficiently. Hierarchical enumeration techniques address the topological challenges of traversing non-uniform octrees. 2D Stitching was developed specifically for AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data to maintain mesh continuity across refinement boundaries without introducing artifacts. CGAL Documentation, "Isosurfacing with Marching Cubes on Octrees," https://doc.cgal.org/latest/Isosurfacing/index.html, 2023. PyTorch3D Documentation, "Sparse Marching Cubes," https://pytorch3d.org/docs/ops/sparsemarchingcubes, 2023.

name: Marching Cubes with Octree
body: Marching Cubes with Octree extracts a manifold isosurface from a scalar field by applying the standard Marching Cubes algorithm selectively over an octree data structure, rather than a uniform grid. It sets itself apart from Sparse Marching Cubes by using a hierarchical octree decomposition defined by a split predicate, and from Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration by relying on the CGAL MCDomain abstraction for automatic mesh assembly. It solves the problem of processing large volumes efficiently by skipping empty or uniform regions, provided the octree refinement maintains uniform depth around the isosurface to avoid topological cracks. Inputs: 1. A 3D bounding box defined by minimum and maximum points (P{min}, P{max}). 2. A split predicate function S(v, level) that determines whether a voxel at a given octree level should be subdivided. 3. A scalar field function f(P) that returns the value at any point P in space. 4. An isovalue I defining the surface threshold. Outputs: 1. A list of vertices V. 2. A list of triangles T (indices into V). Data Structures: Octree: A hierarchical structure where each node represents a cubic voxel. Nodes are refined based on S. The structure supports traversal and value lookup. Values: An object binding the scalar function f and the Octree, allowing efficient evaluation of f at voxel corners. MCDomain: An abstraction that provides the interface for the marching cubes algorithm to query the octree structure and scalar values. It handles the mapping between octree nodes and the local cube indices required by the Marching Cubes lookup table. Steps: 1. Initialize Bounding Box: Define the root voxel bounds using P{min} and P{max}. 2. Build Octree: Create an empty Octree rooted at the bounding box. 3. Refine Octree: Recursively apply the split predicate S to each node. If S returns true, subdivide the node into 8 children. This process continues until the predicate returns false for all leaf nodes or a maximum depth is reached. 4. Create Values Object: Instantiate a Values object that wraps the scalar function f and the constructed Octree. This object must support evaluating f at the 8 corners of any active voxel. 5. Initialize Output Containers: Create empty containers for points (vertices) and polygons (triangles). 6. Construct MCDomain: Instantiate the MCDomain object, passing the Octree and Values object. This domain object abstracts the grid topology. 7. Execute Marching Cubes: Call the marching cubes function with the MCDomain, isovalue I, and output containers. The algorithm iterates over all active leaf nodes of the octree. For each active leaf node (voxel): Retrieve scalar values vj at the 8 corners j=0..7. Compute the cube index C = \sum{j=0}^{7} \text{bit}j \cdot 2^j, where \text{bit}j = 1 if vj < I, else 0. Determine intersecting edges and interpolate vertex positions. Generate triangles based on the standard Marching Cubes lookup table for index C. Add generated vertices and triangles to the output containers. 8. Post-Processing (Implicit): The MCDomain and CGAL implementation handle the merging of shared vertices and edges to ensure a watertight mesh, assuming the octree refinement is consistent (see Pitfalls). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def runmarchingcubesoctree(bboxmin, bboxmax, splitpredicate, scalarfunction, isovalue): # 1. Define bounding box points bboxpoints = [bboxmin, bboxmax] # 2. Construct Octree octree = Octree(bboxpoints) # 3. Refine Octree using split predicate # The split predicate takes a node and its level, returns True if it should be subdivided octree.refine(splitpredicate) # 4. Create Values object binding scalar function and octree values = Values(scalarfunction, octree) # 5. Initialize output containers points = [] triangles = [] # 6. Construct MCDomain mcdomain = MCDomain(octree, values) # 7. Call Marching Cubes # This function iterates over active nodes, applies MC logic, and fills points/triangles marchingcubes(mcdomain, isovalue, points, triangles) return points, triangles Parameters: isovalue: The threshold value for the scalar field. Typical values depend on the specific field (e.g., 0 for signed distance fields, 0.5 for normalized density). splitpredicate: Defines the resolution. A common strategy is to split nodes that intersect the isosurface or have high gradient magnitude. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cracks at Discontinuities: If the octree has varying depths around the isosurface (i.e., a fine node is adjacent to a coarse node), the standard Marching Cubes algorithm will produce cracks or non-manifold geometry because the coarse node does not provide enough vertices to match the fine node's edges. Uniform Refinement Requirement: To guarantee a manifold surface, the octree must be split with uniform size around the surface. This often implies a maximum depth constraint or a specific splitting rule that ensures neighbors do not differ by more than one level without intermediate handling. Linear Hashed Marching Cubes is a surface extraction method that converts volumetric isosurfaces into triangle meshes by applying the Marching Cubes algorithm over a linear hashed octree data structure. It serves as a loose implementation of the "Fast Generation of Pointerless Octree Duals" technique, designed to accelerate mesh generation compared to standard grid-based marching cubes. It sets itself apart from standard MC with Octree by using a linear hash table for node storage, reducing memory overhead and improving cache locality, and is chosen when memory efficiency and speed are critical for large, sparse volumes. Link: Linear Hashed Marching Cubes. This method extracts isosurfaces from adaptive resolution (AR) octree volume data by decoupling geometry generation from discontinuity resolution. It solves the topological inconsistencies that arise when fine-resolution cubes share edges or faces with coarser, unsubdivided neighbors. Unlike uniform resolution methods, it reduces data access and processing time by skipping large uniform regions, while the two-pass approach ensures a watertight mesh without requiring complex on-the-fly edge matching logic during the primary traversal. It is chosen when handling AR octrees with significant depth variations is required without manual crack filling. Link: Adaptive Resolution Isosurface Rendering with Two-Pass Discontinuity Handling. Adaptive Marching Cubes is an extension of the standard Marching Cubes algorithm designed to extract isosurfaces from Adaptive Resolution (AR) octree data. It solves the problem of topological inconsistencies and geometric artifacts that arise when adjacent cubes in the mesh have different resolutions. Unlike uniform marching cubes, it handles missing vertices and discontinuities by deferring the processing of coarser nodes that conflict with finer neighbors, ensuring a watertight mesh across resolution boundaries. It is chosen when a simpler two-pass approach is not feasible or when deferred processing fits the pipeline better. Link: Adaptive Marching Cubes. DMC Octree Contour Extraction is an adaptive isosurface extraction method that generates a manifold triangle mesh from volumetric scalar field data using a dual-contouring approach on an octree structure. It solves the problem of high-fidelity surface reconstruction at varying resolutions by recursively subdividing cells based on field error and solving a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) for each dual vertex. It sets itself apart from its sibling Linear Hashed Marching Cubes by using dual vertices and QEF solving rather than linear interpolation on grid edges, and from Adaptive Marching Cubes by explicitly managing topological consistency through a recursive face/edge/vertex processing pipeline that ensures shared boundaries between adjacent octree nodes are handled deterministically. It is chosen when preserving sharp features and complex geometry is more important than the speed of linear interpolation. Link: DMC Octree Contour Extraction. Simplicial Partition Isosurfacing extracts a manifold, intersection-free isosurface from a scalar function defined over an arbitrary octree by partitioning space into simplices (tetrahedra) dual to minimal octree cells. Unlike Dual Contouring, which produces non-manifold geometry in ambiguous sign configurations, and Dual Marching Cubes, which can generate self-intersecting surfaces due to non-convex dual cells, this method guarantees manifold topology and prevents tetrahedron inversion, ensuring the surface cannot self-intersect. It is chosen when topological correctness and intersection-free guarantees are paramount, even at the cost of higher computational complexity. Link: Simplicial Partition Isosurfacing. This variant extracts mesh by adapting TSDF-Fusion and Marching Cubes into the sparse voxel representation. It implements sparse-voxel TSDF-Fusion to compute truncated signed distance values of the sparse grid points, then extracts the surface of the zero-level set using sparse-voxel Marching Cubes. Duplicated vertices from adjacent voxels are merged to produce a unique set of vertices. If adjacent voxels belong to different Octree levels, it subdivides all voxels to the finest level to remove discontinuities in the density field. It sets itself apart from methods relying on coarse geometry priors (like SfM) by modeling the scene only with a density field. Pitfalls include producing unnecessary geometric bumps for texture details and potential disconnection of triangles when adjacent voxels are at different octree levels if not subdivided. It is chosen for real-time high-fidelity radiance field rendering from sparse sensor data. Link: N/A (Minor variant). Time Complexity: Depends on the number of active leaf nodes in the octree. In the worst case (uniform grid), it is O(N^3) where N is the resolution. In sparse cases, it is proportional to the surface area of the isosurface times the average octree depth. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of octree nodes. Linear hashed variants reduce overhead compared to pointer-based octrees. Measured Performance: CGAL's implementation supports parallel execution (Parallelifavailabletag), scaling well on multi-core CPUs. Strengths: Efficiently handles large, sparse volumes; leverages robust CGAL implementation; automatic mesh assembly via MCDomain. Limitations: Requires careful octree refinement to avoid cracks; not inherently suitable for highly adaptive resolutions without additional handling (see Subtopics). When to use: When the volume is sparse or has large uniform regions, and the isosurface can be captured with a reasonably uniform octree depth around the surface. When not to use: When the volume has extreme resolution variations adjacent to the isosurface without a strategy to handle discontinuities (e.g., standard MC with Octree will crack). The method originates from the CGAL library's Isosurfacing module, specifically the CGAL::Isosurfacing::marchingcubes function designed to work with domain objects like MCDomain. It builds on the classic Marching Cubes algorithm by Lorensen and Cline (1987) and adapts it for hierarchical data structures. The MCDomain abstraction allows the algorithm to be decoupled from the specific grid implementation, enabling the use of octrees. The approach is part of a broader family of grid traversal and data structure adaptation methods aimed at efficient surface extraction. 3D Isosurfacing, https://doc.cgal.org/latest/Isosurfacing3/index.html, fetched 2026-10-29 Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01509, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Linear Hashed Marching Cubes
body: Linear Hashed Marching Cubes is a surface extraction method that converts volumetric isosurfaces into triangle meshes by applying the Marching Cubes algorithm over a linear hashed octree data structure. It serves as a loose implementation of the "Fast Generation of Pointerless Octree Duals" technique, designed to accelerate mesh generation compared to standard grid-based marching cubes. Inputs: A volumetric scalar field (implicit function). An isovalue threshold for surface extraction. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the internal octree, defining the resolution limit. The tree spans a cubic grid of size 2^{\text{max\depth}} in each direction. Outputs: A triangle mesh containing vertices and indices representing the isosurface. Data Structures: 1. ImplicitOctree: A linear hashed octree traversal structure that replaces the standard PrimalGrid. Nodes are indexed using MortonKey (Z-order curve keys) rather than GridKey (3D integer coordinates). 2. MeshTopologyBuilder: Accumulates vertex positions and face indices, storing vertices with associated MortonKey identifiers to facilitate adjacency or deduplication logic. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an ImplicitOctree instance with the specified maxdepth and a MeshTopologyBuilder. 2. Tree Traversal: Traverse the ImplicitOctree. For each visited cube, retrieve the corner keys, corner coordinates, and corner scalar values. 3. Cube Classification: Classify the cube corners based on their signed distance values to determine the cube index. Let vi be the value at corner i and I be the isovalue. If vi < I, the corner is inside; otherwise, it is outside. The cube index is the bitmask formed by these 8 comparisons. 4. Edge Intersection Calculation: Find the 12 edge crossing vertices for the cube using the cube index, corners, and values. For each crossed edge connecting corners A and B with values vA and vB, calculate the intersection point P using linear interpolation: P = A + \frac{I - vA}{vB - vA} (B - A). 5. Mesh Generation (Marching): March the cube by iterating through the triangles defined by the cube index. For each triangle (a, b, c), add vertices to the mesh builder with MortonKey identifiers and the calculated vertex positions, then add the face. 6. Finalization: After traversal completes, build the mesh and extract indices to the extractor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearhashedmarchingcubes(field, isovalue, maxdepth): # Standard Marching Cubes lookup tables # MARCHINGCUBESEDGES: 12 edges, each is a pair of corner indices (0-7) # MARCHINGCUBESTRIANGLES: up to 5 triangles per cube index, each is a triplet of edge indices (0-11) # Linear hashed octree traversal structure class ImplicitOctree: def init(self, maxdepth): self.maxdepth = maxdepth def traverse(self): return [] # Yields cube objects with.corners,.values,.keys # Accumulates vertices and faces class MeshTopologyBuilder: def init(self): self.vertices = [] def addvertex(self, pos, key): self.vertices.append((pos, key)) def addface(self): pass def build(self): return None octree = ImplicitOctree(maxdepth=maxdepth) meshbuilder = MeshTopologyBuilder() for cube in octree.traverse(): corners = cube.corners # List of 8 vec3 positions values = cube.values # List of 8 float scalar values keys = cube.keys # List of 8 MortonKey identifiers # Classify cube cubeindex = 0 for i in range(8): if values[i] < isovalue: cubeindex |= (1 << i) # Find edge crossings edgevertices = [] for edgeidx, (i, j) in enumerate(MARCHINGCUBESEDGES): t = (isovalue - values[i]) / (values[j] - values[i]) edgevertices.append(corners[i] + t (corners[j] - corners[i])) # March the cube: add triangles for triangle in MARCHINGCUBESTRIANGLES[cubeindex]: # Add vertices with MortonKey identifiers and calculated positions # Exact MortonKey assignment for interpolated vertices is implementation-specific meshbuilder.addvertex(edgevertices[triangle[0]], keys[0]) meshbuilder.addvertex(edgevertices[triangle[1]], keys[0]) meshbuilder.addvertex(edgevertices[triangle[2]], keys[0]) meshbuilder.addface() return meshbuilder.build() Parameters: maxdepth: Integer. The maximum depth of the octree. Determines the finest resolution (2^{\text{max\depth}}). isovalue: Float. The threshold for surface extraction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation assumes the scalar field is locally linear between grid points. Highly oscillatory fields may produce artifacts. Degenerate Cases: When vB - vA = 0, the denominator in the interpolation formula becomes zero. Standard implementations clamp or skip the edge in this case. Performance: Faster than standard marching cubes. Memory: Not given in the sources. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The method is described as a loose implementation of "Fast Generation of Pointerless Octree Duals". https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hash Map Based Marching Cubes
head: Hash map based approach
body: Hash Map Based Marching Cubes is a surface extraction method that employs surface-following traversal to extract isosurfaces, utilizing hash maps to store corner vertices and a 3D lookup cache for particle identification. It replaces static grid storage with dynamic hash maps to handle sparse or unbounded datasets efficiently. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volumetric dataset (e.g., particle positions or scalar field values) and an isovalue threshold. Output: A mesh (vertices and indices) representing the extracted isosurface. Data Structures 1. Corner Cache: A hash map mapping 3D grid coordinates (x, y, z) to vertex data (position, scalar value). 2. Particle Lookup Cache: A 3D hash map used to identify which particles fall within a specific voxel or cube during the marching process. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the corner cache and particle lookup cache as empty hash maps. 2. Surface Following: Traverse cubes intersecting the isosurface without scanning the entire volume. 3. Cube Processing: For each active cube: a. Particle Lookup: Query the 3D lookup cache to find particles within the cube's bounds. b. Scalar Evaluation: Compute the scalar field value at the cube's corners based on the interpolated particle data. c. Corner Storage: Store or retrieve corner vertices in the corner cache hash map using their grid coordinates as keys. d. Marching Cubes Lookup: Determine the cube case (one of the 256 configurations) based on corner signs. e. Triangle Generation: Generate triangles for the intersected edges of the cube. 4. Cache Management: Build and destroy the particle cache on a per-block basis to remove unneeded particles. Formulas Lookup Volume Efficiency: The method avoids searching a cubic volume (3Rc)^3 and culling by distance, which returns significantly more particles than a spherical volume (4/3)\pi Rc^3. Isosurface Condition: The surface is defined where the scalar field f(x,y,z) = 0. Parameters Lookup Grid Resolution: The resolution of the 3D lookup cache. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Cost Dominance: If the lookup grid resolution is increased to reduce false positives, the insertion and lookup costs grow rapidly and dominate overall extraction time, particularly because every cube access requires a hash map lookup. Memory Management: Memory usage remains comparable to previous approaches because the particle cache is built and destroyed on a per-block basis. This variant uses spatially hashed 3D chunks of volumetric data to handle large distances without exhausting memory, similar to techniques used in games like Minecraft. It avoids octrees for implicit surface representation because octrees are inefficient for the iteration-dominated marching cubes algorithm, recommending fixed 3D arrays or chunks instead. Dual Marching Cubes can be applied here, scanning from an origin point to locate volumetric edges and place edging/skin. Time Complexity: Dominated by hash map lookups for corner storage and particle identification. Performance degrades if the lookup grid resolution is set too high, as lookup costs dominate. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is kept low by building and destroying the particle cache on a per-block basis. Strengths: Efficient for unbounded or sparse rendering; avoids the iteration overhead of dense arrays and the query latency of octrees. Limitations: Hash map overhead increases with high-resolution lookups; iteration speed is prioritized over memory savings in dense scenes. When to Use: Sparse particle simulations or unbounded volumes requiring memory efficiency and selective processing. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring maximum iteration speed where memory constraints are absent, as fixed 3D arrays outperform hash maps for dense iteration. The method is based on research into real-time particle isosurface extraction, adapting surface-following algorithms to use hash maps for dynamic particle data handling. It contrasts with traditional grid-based and octree-based methods, which suffer from iteration or query inefficiencies respectively. name: Adaptive Resolution Isosurface Rendering with Two-Pass Discontinuity Handling
head: AR Isosurface Rendering, Adaptive Marching Cubes with 2nd Pass Subdivision
body: This method extracts isosurfaces from adaptive resolution (AR) octree volume data by decoupling geometry generation from discontinuity resolution. It solves the topological inconsistencies that arise when fine-resolution cubes share edges or faces with coarser, unsubdivided neighbors. Unlike uniform resolution methods, it reduces data access and processing time by skipping large uniform regions, while the two-pass approach ensures a watertight mesh without requiring complex on-the-fly edge matching logic during the primary traversal. Input: An adaptive resolution octree representing a scalar field. Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Parameters: iso: The scalar isovalue for extraction. Tested values: 0.185, 0.378, 0.408. delta: The adaptive resolution threshold determining the coarseness of the octree. Tested values: 1% to 25%. The algorithm relies on two auxiliary structures to handle the decoupled passes: 1. Second Pass List (secondpasslist): A dynamic list of octree node identifiers that require re-evaluation. A node is added to this list if a neighbor generates a vertex on a shared edge or face. 2. Edge Vertex List (edgevertexlist): Associated with each octree node. It stores the interpolated vertex positions generated by neighbors on the edges of the current node. Layout: A list of pairs (edgeindex, vertexposition). Edge Index: An integer 0–11 identifying one of the 12 edges of the cube. Vertex Position: A 3D vector (x, y, z). 3. Facial Vertex List (facialvertexlist): Associated with each octree node. It stores vertices generated by neighbors that lie strictly on the interior of a face of the current node. Layout: A list of pairs (faceindex, vertexposition). Face Index: An integer 0–5 identifying one of the 6 faces. 1. Initialization: Initialize secondpasslist as empty. For every node in the octree, initialize edgevertexlist and facialvertexlist as empty. 2. First Pass (Primary Traversal): Iterate through all leaf nodes of the octree. For each node N: Perform standard Marching Cubes (MC) using the scalar values at the 8 vertices of N and iso. Generate the set of triangles for N. For each generated triangle, identify the edges and faces it intersects. If a triangle vertex lies on an edge shared with a neighbor M (where M is coarser than N): Add the interpolated vertex position to M.edgevertexlist for that specific edge index. Add M to secondpasslist if not already present. If a triangle vertex lies on a face shared with a neighbor M (where M is coarser than N): Add the interpolated vertex position to M.facialvertexlist for that specific face index. Add M to secondpasslist if not already present. 3. Second Pass (Discontinuity Resolution): Iterate through each node M in secondpasslist. For each M: Examine M.edgevertexlist. If any edge index has two distinct vertices recorded (i.e., two different fine neighbors generated vertices on the same edge of M), M has a topological conflict. Subdivide M into its 8 children. For each child, re-run the Marching Cubes step (including adding to secondpasslist if new conflicts are found with their neighbors). Examine M.facialvertexlist. If M.facialvertexlist is non-empty (indicating a fine neighbor generated a vertex on the interior of M's face), M has a topological conflict. Subdivide M into its 8 children. For each child, re-run the Marching Cubes step. 4. Final Output: Collect all triangles generated in the First Pass and any triangles generated during the Second Pass subdivisions. Return the combined triangle mesh. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveisosurfacerendering(octree, iso): secondpasslist = [] edgevertexlists = {} facialvertexlists = {} # Initialize structures for all leaf nodes for node in octree.allleafnodes(): edgevertexlists[node.id] = [] facialvertexlists[node.id] = [] alltriangles = [] # First Pass for node in octree.allleafnodes(): scalars = [node.scalaratvertex(i) for i in range(8)] triangles, edgeintersections, faceintersections = marchingcubesstep(scalars, iso) alltriangles.extend(triangles) for edgeidx, vertex in edgeintersections: neighbor = node.getneighboronedge(edgeidx) if neighbor and neighbor.iscoarserthan(node): edgevertexlists[neighbor.id].append((edgeidx, vertex)) if neighbor not in secondpasslist: secondpasslist.append(neighbor) for faceidx, vertex in faceintersections: neighbor = node.getneighboronface(faceidx) if neighbor and neighbor.iscoarserthan(node): facialvertexlists[neighbor.id].append((faceidx, vertex)) if neighbor not in secondpasslist: secondpasslist.append(neighbor) # Second Pass currentpasslist = secondpasslist while currentpasslist: nextpasslist = [] for node in currentpasslist: needssubdivision = False edgecounts = {} for edgeidx, vertex in edgevertexlists[node.id]: edgecounts[edgeidx] = edgecounts.get(edgeidx, 0) + 1 for count in edgecounts.values(): if count > 1: needssubdivision = True break if facialvertexlists[node.id]: needssubdivision = True if needssubdivision: children = node.subdivide() for child in children: scalars = [child.scalaratvertex(i) for i in range(8)] triangles, edgeintersections, faceintersections = marchingcubesstep(scalars, iso) alltriangles.extend(triangles) for edgeidx, vertex in edgeintersections: neighbor = child.getneighboronedge(edgeidx) if neighbor and neighbor.iscoarserthan(child): edgevertexlists[neighbor.id].append((edgeidx, vertex)) if neighbor not in nextpasslist and neighbor not in secondpasslist: nextpasslist.append(neighbor) for faceidx, vertex in faceintersections: neighbor = child.getneighboronface(faceidx) if neighbor and neighbor.iscoarserthan(child): facialvertexlists[neighbor.id].append((faceidx, vertex)) if neighbor not in nextpasslist and neighbor not in secondpasslist: nextpasslist.append(neighbor) currentpasslist = nextpasslist return alltriangles def marchingcubesstep(scalars, iso): # Standard Marching Cubes lookup table implementation # Returns: list of triangles, list of (edgeidx, vertex) intersections, list of (faceidx, vertex) intersections triangles = [] edgeintersections = [] faceintersections = [] # Compute edge crossings edgecrossings = [] for i in range(12): v1, v2 = edgevertices(i) if (scalars[v1] - iso) (scalars[v2] - iso) < 0: t = (iso - scalars[v1]) / (scalars[v2] - scalars[v1]) vertex = lerp(node.vertex(v1), node.vertex(v2), t) edgecrossings.append((i, vertex)) # Generate triangles from lookup table using edgecrossings caseindex = computecaseindex(scalars, iso) triangleindices = mclookuptable[caseindex] for i in range(0, len(triangleindices), 3): e1, e2, e3 = triangleindices[i], triangleindices[i+1], triangleindices[i+2] triangles.append((edgecrossings[e1][1], edgecrossings[e2][1], edgecrossings[e3][1])) # Separate edge vs face intersections based on geometry for edgeidx, vertex in edgecrossings: if isedgeintersection(edgeidx): edgeintersections.append((edgeidx, vertex)) else: faceintersections.append((edgeidx, vertex)) return triangles, edgeintersections, faceintersections Precision: Interpolated vertex positions must be computed with sufficient precision to avoid gaps. Floating-point errors at shared edges between subdivided nodes can cause visual artifacts. Boundary Conditions: Nodes on the boundary of the volume have no neighbors on one side. The neighbor lookup functions must handle null returns gracefully. Infinite Loops: If the subdivision logic does not correctly propagate conflicts, or if the secondpasslist is not managed as a queue, the algorithm may fail to converge. The original paper notes that for \Delta=25\%, up to 9.8% of cubes required subdivision, suggesting that multiple levels of subdivision might be necessary in extreme cases. Time Complexity: The first pass is O(N) where N is the number of leaf nodes. The second pass depends on the number of discontinuities. In the worst case, it may trigger recursive subdivisions, but typically remains efficient. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the octree and auxiliary lists. The auxiliary lists are sparse. Performance: Time Savings: At \Delta=10\%, reading time is reduced by a factor of ~5 compared to full Maximum Resolution (MR) representation. Processing time is reduced by 20-25%. Storage Savings: At \Delta=10\%, storage requirements are reduced by a factor of just over 5. Cubes read reduced from 2,097,152 (MR) to 481,640 (AR 10%). Accuracy: No discernible differences from full MR rendering for isovalue 0.185. No discontinuities caused by AR data for this isovalue. Discontinuity Frequency: At \Delta=25\%, the maximum discontinuity occurrence was 9.8% of cubes subdivided. Strengths: Significant reduction in I/O and processing time for large datasets. Simple implementation compared to real-time edge matching. Limitations: Requires two passes. May require multiple levels of subdivision in the second pass for high \Delta values. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "IsoSurface Rendering of Adaptive Resolution Data" by R. D. Bebis and R. J. Boyle. History: It was developed to address the inefficiencies of rendering adaptive resolution data using uniform resolution algorithms. The authors evaluated the method on a Dell PC with a 450 MHz Pentium processor, 256 MB RAM, running Red Hat Linux 6.1, using Java 1.2/2.0 and VisAD/Java 3D. Usage: Used in scientific visualization, particularly for medical imaging (e.g., cadaver head data sets) where large volumes can be represented efficiently with adaptive resolution. name: Adaptive Marching Cubes
head: AR Isosurface Algorithm, Adaptive Marching Cubes on Multiresolution Octree, Adaptive Marching Cubes on Octree
body: Adaptive Marching Cubes is an extension of the standard Marching Cubes algorithm designed to extract isosurfaces from Adaptive Resolution (AR) octree data. It solves the problem of topological inconsistencies and geometric artifacts that arise when adjacent cubes in the mesh have different resolutions. Unlike uniform marching cubes, it handles missing vertices and discontinuities by deferring the processing of coarser nodes that conflict with finer neighbors, ensuring a watertight mesh across resolution boundaries. The algorithm performs two passes over the octree to resolve inconsistencies between adjacent cells of differing resolutions. Input: An adaptive resolution octree representing a volume dataset. Each node contains voxel values at its specific resolution level. Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Each octree node maintains the following fields: 1. Triangle List: A list of triangles generated for this node. Each triangle references vertices in the global Intersection List. 2. Intersection List: A global vertex array storing edge intersection points. Vertices in this list may be updated later during the second pass. 3. Second Pass List: A list of octree nodes that require post-processing. Nodes are added to this list if they have missing vertices relative to finer neighbors. First Pass: Standard MC with Conflict Detection 1. Traverse the octree in any order (typically depth-first or breadth-first). 2. For each node, perform standard Marching Cubes using the node's voxel values. 3. For every edge intersection found: Check if the adjacent neighbor (if it exists and is coarser) has a corresponding vertex on that edge. If the coarser neighbor has no vertex on the shared edge (i.e., its coarse vertices are on the same side of the isosurface), but the current finer cube finds an intersection: Create a new entry in the coarser neighbor's fine edge vertex list (stored in the global Intersection List). Add the coarser neighbor node to the Second Pass List. If the coarser neighbor already has a vertex, use it to ensure consistency. 4. Generate triangles for the current node using the standard MC lookup table, referencing vertices from the Intersection List. Second Pass: Subdivision and Finalization 1. Process all nodes in the Second Pass List. 2. For each node in the list: Check if it has two vertices on the same edge in its fine edge vertex list (indicating a conflict where the coarse resolution failed to capture the isosurface crossing). If such a conflict exists, subdivide the coarser cube. This involves interpolating between the known cube vertex values at the coarser resolution to create finer children, which are then processed using the standard MC algorithm. If no subdivision is needed but the node has facial vertices that were deferred, generate the triangles. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. intersectionlist = [] # Array of vertex positions secondpasslist = [] # List of octree nodes requiring post-processing def adaptivemarchingcubes(rootnode, isovalue): # First Pass processnode(rootnode, isovalue, issecondpass=False) # Second Pass while secondpasslist is not empty: node = secondpasslist.pop() processnode(node, isovalue, issecondpass=True) def processnode(node, isovalue, issecondpass): if issecondpass: # Check for conflicts requiring subdivision if node.hasedgeconflict(): # Subdivide the coarse cube children = node.subdivide() for child in children: processnode(child, isovalue, issecondpass=False) return # Standard Marching Cubes logic triangles = [] for edge in node.edges: # Determine if isosurface crosses this edge if isovaluebetween(node.vertices[edge.v1], node.vertices[edge.v2]): # Check for consistency with coarser neighbor neighbor = node.getcoarserneighbor(edge) if neighbor is not None: if not neighbor.hasvertexonedge(edge): # Missing vertex in coarser neighbor # Create new vertex in intersection list vertex = interpolateintersection(edge, isovalue) neighbor.addfinevertex(edge, vertex) # Add coarser neighbor to second pass list if not already there if neighbor not in secondpasslist: secondpasslist.append(neighbor) else: vertex = neighbor.getvertexonedge(edge) else: vertex = interpolateintersection(edge, isovalue) # Store vertex reference for triangle generation edge.vertex = vertex # Generate triangles based on MC case triangles = generatemctriangles(node, isovalue) node.trianglelist.extend(triangles) Isosurface Value: The threshold value for extraction. Edge Cases: Missing Vertices: Occur when a finer cube intersects an edge that a coarser neighbor does not. Handled by creating deferred vertices and subdividing the coarser node. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may cause inconsistent edge crossings. Standard MC robustness techniques should be applied. Boundary Conditions: Nodes at the boundary of the volume have no coarser neighbors in certain directions; these are handled as standard uniform nodes. Time Complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the number of conflicts. In the worst case, many coarser nodes may be subdivided, approaching the cost of uniform high-resolution marching cubes. However, large uninteresting regions are skipped, reducing computation. Memory Complexity: Higher than uniform MC due to the octree structure and the need to store deferred vertices and the second pass list. The intersection list grows dynamically. Strengths: Efficiently handles large datasets by focusing resolution where needed; produces watertight meshes across resolution boundaries. Limitations: The two-pass nature and potential for frequent subdivision can complicate implementation and reduce performance in highly heterogeneous data. The Adaptive Marching Cubes algorithm was introduced by Westermann et al. as part of their work on isosurface rendering of adaptive resolution data. It addresses the limitations of standard marching cubes when applied to multiresolution data structures, specifically the topological inconsistencies at resolution boundaries. The method has been cited in subsequent works on implicit surface rendering and interactive visualization. name: DMC Octree Contour Extraction
