body: DMC Octree Contour Extraction is an adaptive isosurface extraction method that generates a manifold triangle mesh from volumetric scalar field data using a dual-contouring approach on an octree structure. It solves the problem of high-fidelity surface reconstruction at varying resolutions by recursively subdividing cells based on field error and solving a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) for each dual vertex. It sets itself apart from its sibling Linear Hashed Marching Cubes by using dual vertices and QEF solving rather than linear interpolation on grid edges, and from Adaptive Marching Cubes by explicitly managing topological consistency through a recursive face/edge/vertex processing pipeline that ensures shared boundaries between adjacent octree nodes are handled deterministically. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ScalarField providing value and gradient queries; an initial DMCOctree root node; BuildArgs configuration. Output: A Mesh containing vertices, normals, and indices; a VertexMap for internal bookkeeping. Data Structures: DMCOctreeNode: issubdivided(): bool, indicates if the node has children. operator[]: access to 8 child nodes. normal: vec3, the averaged normal for the dual vertex. dualVertex: vec4, the position (x,y,z) and potentially w-component for the dual vertex. material: stores material information if vertex.w <= 0. BuildArgs: useearlysplitstop: bool. usesimplesplitpolicy: bool. userandomsampling: bool. epsilon: double, error threshold. solver: QefSolver4D, the QEF solver instance. field: ScalarField, the volumetric data. rng: random number generator state. mrootSize: double, the root node size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an empty Mesh and VertexMap. Set the global position and scale on the mesh using the octree's stored transformation parameters. 2. Traversal: Call cellProc on the root node of the DMCOctree. 3. Cell Processing (cellProc): If the node is not subdivided, return immediately. Retrieve the 8 child nodes into an array sub[8]. Face Processing: Iterate i from 0 to 3. For each face, call faceProcX, faceProcY, and faceProcZ with the two child nodes defining that face, determined by faceTableX/Y/Z[i]. Edge Processing: Iterate i from 0 to 1. For each edge, call edgeProcX, edgeProcY, and edgeProcZ with the four child nodes defining that edge, determined by edgeTableX/Y/Z[i]. Vertex Processing: Call vertProc with all 8 child nodes sub[0] through sub[7]. 4. Face Processing (faceProcX, faceProcY, faceProcZ): Initialize subTable mapping 8 indices to parent nodes and their child index. Iterate i from 0 to 7: if the parent node is subdivided, sub[i] is its specific child; otherwise sub[i] is the parent node itself. Set haslesser = true if any node was subdivided. If haslesser is false, return immediately (no geometry to generate for this face configuration). Recursive Face Calls: Iterate i from 0 to 3. Call the respective faceProc function recursively with the two sub-nodes defined by faceTable[i]. Edge Calls: Iterate i from 0 to 1. Call the respective edgeProc function with the four sub-nodes defined by edgeTable[i]. Vertex Call: Call vertProc with all 8 sub-nodes. 5. Dual Vertex Generation (buildNode): If size is 1, generate a dual vertex and return. If args.useearlysplitstop is true and shouldStopSplitting returns true, generate a dual vertex and return. If args.usesimplesplitpolicy is true: If size equals mrootSize or shouldSplit returns true, subdivide the node, calculate childsize as size/2, and recursively call buildNode for all 8 children with their respective mincorners. Otherwise, generate a dual vertex. If args.usesimplesplitpolicy is false: If size 8 < mrootSize and generateDualVertex returns true, return. Otherwise, subdivide the node, calculate childsize as size/2, and recursively call buildNode for all 8 children. 6. Generating the Dual Vertex (generateDualVertex): Reset the QEF solver. Initialize avgnormal to zero. Sampling: If args.userandomsampling is true: Calculate pointscnt as int(6.0 sqrt(size)). Create a uniform distribution odist(0, size). For pointscnt iterations: Generate a random offset. Compute local and global points. Get the field value and gradient. Add a plane defined by point4d (local position, local value) and normal4d (gradient, -1.0) to the solver. Accumulate the gradient in avgnormal. If args.userandomsampling is false: Define minoffset as 0.25 size and maxoffset as size - minoffset. Define 8 sample offsets at these corners. For each of the 8 samples: Compute local/global points, field value, gradient. Add a plane to the solver. Accumulate the gradient in avgnormal. Normalize avgnormal and store it in node->normal. Define lowerbound as (mincorner, 0) and upperbound as (mincorner + size, 0). Solve for the vertex using the solver with these bounds. Evaluate the error of the solved vertex. If error > args.epsilon, relax bounds to lowest/max float values and re-solve. Store the final vertex in node->dualVertex. If vertex.w <= 0, compute the global value and material, and store the material in node->material. Return true if error <= args.epsilon, false otherwise. 7. Splitting Decision (shouldSplit): Compute the 8 global corner positions of the cell. Compute the field values at these corners. Initialize error to 0. Edge Error: Define dim1corners, dim1idoffsets, and dim1offsets for edge midpoints. For each dimension (0-2) and each of the 4 edges in that dimension: Compute the midpoint position. Predict the value as the average of the two endpoint values. Get the actual field value and gradient magnitude k. Add abs(predict - actual) / k to error. If error > epsilon, return true. Face Error: Define dim2corners, dim2idoffsets, and dim2offsets for face midpoints. For each dimension (0-2) and each of the 2 faces in that dimension: Compute the face center position. Predict the value as the average of the 4 corner values. Get the actual field value and gradient magnitude k. Add abs(predict - actual) / k to error. If error > epsilon, return true. Cell Center Error: Compute the cell center position. Predict the value as the average of all 8 corner values. Get the actual field value and gradient magnitude k. Add abs(predict - actual) / k to error. If error > epsilon, return true. Return false if the accumulated error did not exceed epsilon. 8. Early Stop Decision (shouldStopSplitting): Compute the base global point and the cell side length. Compute the diagonal length as side sqrt(3). For each of the 8 corners: If the absolute value of the field is less than or equal to the diagonal length, return false (do not stop splitting). If all 8 corners have field values with absolute value greater than the diagonal, return true (stop splitting). Pseudocode: Unverified code. It sets itself apart from its sibling DMC Octree Contour Extraction by explicitly managing vertex clustering across shared edges and faces to resolve topological ambiguities in complex subdivisions, whereas DMC relies on a different contour extraction logic. Multi-Resolution Dual Marching Cubes with Manifold Preservation (MR-DMC) is a surface extraction method that generates closed, manifold meshes from segmented volumetric data using a generalized octree. It extends Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) by introducing a cell-based criterion for dual vertex generation to prevent non-manifold configurations, specifically addressing ambiguities where standard DMC cases 17 and 20 share an ambiguous face. Unlike Manifold Dual Contouring (MDC), which uses a bottom-up strategy, MR-DMC employs a top-down refinement strategy suitable for large datasets, and unlike standard DMC, it guarantees manifold surfaces without post-processing. name: MDC Octree Isosurface Extraction
head: MDC, Multi-Dimensional Cell Octree
body: MDC (Multi-Dimensional Cell) Octree Isosurface Extraction is an adaptive surface reconstruction algorithm that uses an octree data structure to recursively subdivide a 3D volume and generate a triangle mesh. It solves the problem of extracting isosurfaces from volumetric data with varying density, handling topology via vertex clustering and collapse logic to ensure manifold connectivity. It sets itself apart from its sibling DMC Octree Contour Extraction by explicitly managing vertex clustering across shared edges and faces to resolve topological ambiguities in complex subdivisions, whereas DMC relies on a different contour extraction logic. Inputs: A 3D volumetric dataset (implicitly accessed via the octree nodes). rootsize: The size of the root octree node. Must be a power of two. globalpos: The world coordinate position of the octree root. globalscale: The global scale factor applied to octree coordinates. epsilon: A threshold for vertex collapsibility. Outputs: A triangle mesh (list of vertices and indices). MDCOctreeNode mvertices: List of MDCVertex objects associated with this node. vertexMask: Bitmask indicating which vertices are present/valid. isSubdivided: Boolean flag indicating if the node has children. MDCVertex mposition: 3D position vector. mnormal: Normal vector. mmaterial: Enum Material (e.g., Empty, Solid). merror: Scalar error value. mcollapsible: Boolean flag. mvertexIdx: Index in the output mesh. Initialized to kBadIndex. msurfaceIdx: Index used for Disjoint Set Union (DSU) clustering. highestCollapsibleAncestor: Pointer to the nearest ancestor vertex that is collapsible. Constants kBadIndex: UINT32MAX, indicating an invalid vertex index. kEdgeProcSharedEdge[D][i]: Lookup table for shared edge indices for dimension D and node i. kMdcEdgeSetIndex[n][m]: Lookup table mapping edge mask and edge index to vertex index within a node. kCellEdgeEndpoint[myedge][0]: Endpoint index of the edge in the cell. rootsize: Power of two. If not, an exception is thrown. epsilon: Threshold for marking non-leaf vertices as collapsible if error <= epsilon. 1. Initialization: Construct the MDCOctree with rootsize, globalpos, and globalscale. Validate rootsize is a power of two. 2. Vertex Collection (addVerticesToMesh): Recursively traverse the octree. For each node, iterate through its vertices: If the node is a leaf, mark vertices as collapsible. If the node is not a leaf, mark vertices as collapsible if error <= epsilon. If a vertex is collapsible and has no collapsible ancestor, add it to the mesh, assign a unique index, and update mvertexIdx. Otherwise, assign kBadIndex to mvertexIdx. Recurse into children if the node is subdivided. 3. Cell Processing (cellProc): If the node is a leaf, return. Recursively process all 8 children. Call sub-face processing for dimensions 0, 1, and 2: callSubFaceProc(0), callSubFaceProc(1), callSubFaceProc(2). Call sub-edge processing for dimensions 0, 1, and 2: callSubEdgeProc(0), callSubEdgeProc(1), callSubEdgeProc(2). 4. Edge Processing (edgeProc): For a given dimension D: Take the 4 nodes sharing the edge. Resolve children if subdivided. If all 4 are leaves, call edgeProcLeaves. Otherwise, call callSubEdgeProc(D). 5. Edge Processing Leaves (edgeProcLeaves): For dimension D and 4 nodes: Get the shared edge index for each node using kEdgeProcSharedEdge[D][i]. Get the vertex index from the node's vertex list using kMdcEdgeSetIndex[nodes[i]->vertexMask()][myedge]. If the index is invalid (kBadIndex) or out of bounds, return. Get the highest collapsible ancestor for each vertex. If any vertex's ancestor is null, return. Determine flip direction: Find the deepest node among the 4. Check if the corner at kCellEdgeEndpoint[myedge][0] is Material::Empty. If so, flip = true. Add two triangles to the mesh using the vertex indices, respecting the flip flag. 6. Face Processing (faceProc): For a given dimension D: Take the 2 nodes sharing the face. Resolve children if subdivided. If all are leaves, return. Otherwise, call callSubFaceProc(D). Recursively call callSubEdgeProc for dimensions (D+1)%3 and (D+2)%3. 7. Vertex Clustering (clusterEdgeLeaves): For dimension D and 4 nodes: Get shared edge indices. Get the highest ancestor vertex for each of the 4 nodes. If a vertex's surfaceIdx is kBadIndex, add it to the vertices list and create a new set in the Disjoint Set Union (DSU). Merge the sets: vertex[0] with vertex[1], vertex[2] with vertex[3], and vertex[0] with vertex[2]. 8. Edge Clustering (clusterEdge): For dimension D: Take 4 nodes. Resolve children if subdivided. If all are leaves, call clusterEdgeLeaves. Otherwise, call callSubClusterEdge(D). 9. Face Clustering (clusterFace): For dimension D: Take 2 nodes. Resolve children if subdivided. If all are leaves, return. Otherwise, call callSubClusterFace(D). Unverified code. name: Multi-Resolution Dual Marching Cubes with Manifold Preservation
head: Dual Surface Extraction on Generalized Octrees, MR-DMC
body: Multi-Resolution Dual Marching Cubes with Manifold Preservation (MR-DMC) generates closed, manifold meshes from segmented volumetric data using a generalized octree. It extends Dual Marching Cubes (DMC) by introducing a cell-based criterion for dual vertex generation to prevent non-manifold configurations, specifically resolving ambiguities where standard DMC cases 17 and 20 share an ambiguous face. Unlike Manifold Dual Contouring (MDC), which uses a bottom-up strategy, MR-DMC employs a top-down refinement strategy suitable for large datasets, and unlike standard DMC, it guarantees manifold surfaces without post-processing. Inputs: Indicator function F(\mathbf{x}): \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, where F(\mathbf{x}) = 1 if \mathbf{x} is inside the segmented object and 0 otherwise. Root cell of the octree c. minLevel: Minimal subdivision level of the octree. maxLevel: Maximal subdivision level of the octree. \delta: Curvature threshold parameter for subdivision, \delta \in [0, 1]. Outputs: An octree regular until level minLevel and adaptive between minLevel and maxLevel. A multi-resolution, closed manifold surface mesh. Octree Cell Data: Each octree cell stores initial and final cell coordinates, cell corner values, and a collapsed flag. The structure uses a Morton Code for compact integer representation of hierarchical relationships and position. An iterative toProcess list manages the top-down traversal. Cell c: A graph c = \{V, E\} with eight vertices V = \{v0, \dots, v7\} and twelve edges E = \{e0, \dots, e{11}\} with cube connectivity. Solid Vertex: A cell vertex inside the volume where F(\mathbf{x}) = 1. The set of solid vertices in cell c is S(c). Empty Vertex: A cell vertex outside the volume where F(\mathbf{x}) = 0. The set of empty vertices in cell c is E(c). Solid-Edge: An edge whose two endpoints are solid vertices. Empty-Edge: An edge whose two endpoints are empty vertices. Intersection-Edge: An edge with one solid endpoint and one empty endpoint. Ambiguous Face: A face containing two interleaved solid vertices. Connected Component \phi(c)s: A sub-graph of solid vertices in cell c where all two solid vertices are connected by a path of solid-edges. |\phi(c)s| denotes the number of solid connected components. Connected Component \phi(c)e: A sub-graph of empty vertices in cell c where all two empty vertices are connected by a path of empty-edges. |\phi(c)e| denotes the number of empty connected components. Dual Vertices D(c): The set of dual vertices generated inside cell c. Complex Face: A face that intersects F(\mathbf{x}), has all vertices either inside or outside F(\mathbf{x}), AND at least one of its edges intersects F(\mathbf{x}) more than once. Complex Cell: A cell C is complex if at least one of its faces is complex. Homogeneous Cell: A cell where all corners are either inside or outside F(\mathbf{x}). Non-Homogeneous Cell: A cell that is not homogeneous. The octree is built iteratively using a top-bottom refinement strategy suitable for large datasets. Cells are subdivided if they are inhomogeneous or complex, unless they have reached maxLevel. The source pseudocode uses isNotPlanar to trigger subdivision, where a planar cell refers to a homogeneous cell with no surface intersection. If a cell is inhomogeneous (has both solid and empty vertices), it is not planar and must be subdivided unless it is complex. The source states: "If a cell C is inhomogeneous or is complex, it has to be subdivided". The algorithm checks isNotComplex first; if not complex, it checks isNotPlanar. If isNotPlanar is true (inhomogeneous), it subdivides. If isNotPlanar is false (planar/homogeneous), it marks the cell as a leaf and collapsed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildoctree(rootcell, minlevel, maxlevel, delta): toprocess = [rootcell] while toprocess: currentcell = toprocess.pop(0) # Check if we can subdivide further (corrected from garbled source condition) if currentcell.level < maxlevel: if not isnotcomplex(currentcell): # Cell is complex -> Subdivide subdivide(currentcell, toprocess) elif isnotplanar(currentcell): # Cell is inhomogeneous but not complex -> Subdivide subdivide(currentcell, toprocess) else: # Cell is homogeneous and not complex -> Mark as leaf and collapsed markasleafcollapsed(currentcell) else: # Reached max level -> Mark as leaf and collapsed markasleafcollapsed(currentcell) def subdivide(cell, queue): # Divide cell into 8 children children = divide(cell) for child in children: queue.append(child) def isnotcomplex(cell): # A cell is complex if at least one face is complex for face in cell.faces: if iscomplexface(face): return False return True def iscomplexface(face): if not intersectssurface(face): return False if not allverticessameside(face): return False if not anyedgeintersectsmorethanonce(face): return False return True def intersectssurface(face): # Face intersects F(x) if it contains intersection-edges return len(face.intersectionedges) > 0 def allverticessameside(face): # All vertices are either solid or empty return len(face.solidvertices) == 0 or len(face.solidvertices) == 4 def anyedgeintersectsmorethanonce(face): # Check for multiple zero-crossings along any edge using Hermite data or dense sampling for edge in face.edges: if countsignchanges(edge) > 1: return True return False def isnotplanar(cell): # Returns True if cell is inhomogeneous (has both solid and empty vertices) return len(cell.solidvertices) > 0 and len(cell.solidvertices) < 8 def markasleafcollapsed(cell): cell.isleaf = True cell.iscollapsed = True def divide(cell): # Standard octree subdivision returning 8 child cells return [createchild(cell, i) for i in range(8)] def countsignchanges(edge): # Standard step to count zero-crossings along an edge return 1 if (edge.v0value edge.v1value < 0) else 0 Cells are subdivided based on curvature to adapt resolution to the geometry of the boundary \partial V. Criterion 1: Let C be a cell and Ii (i=0 \dots n) be its intersection points with F(\mathbf{x}). Let ni be the normals at Ii. If \max{i \neq j} (ni \cdot nj) > \delta, C must be subdivided. \delta \in [0, 1]. \delta \to 0 produces an almost regular mesh. \delta \to 1 generates a highly simplified surface, potentially losing sharp features. Dual vertices are generated in cells that intersect the surface. The algorithm considers at most four surface components inside a single cell, where every component must have a single connected boundary and be well approximated by a plane. Rule 1: Dual vertices are only created in cells where 0 < |S(c)| < 8. Rule 2: If |S(c)| < 5, then |D(c)| = |\phi(c)s|. If |S(c)| \ge 5, then |D(c)| = |\phi(c)e|. Rule 3: For a non-homogeneous cell, every dual vertex di \in D(c) generated from a solid connected component \phi(c)s is associated with the set of intersection-edges that leave \phi(c)s. Similarly for empty components \phi(c)e. Rule 4 (Manifold Preservation): If cell c is marked with a component (solid/empty), generate dual vertices using that component. Otherwise, use Rules 1-3 to determine the component (solid or empty) to be used. If c has ambiguous faces, mark every adjacent cell through an ambiguous face with the component that has been used for c. This rule spreads the topological choice through ambiguous faces to ensure manifold correctness, specifically resolving cases 17 and 20 of the DMC look-up table. \delta: Curvature threshold, [0, 1]. minLevel: Minimal subdivision level. maxLevel: Maximal subdivision level. Non-manifold configurations: Standard DMC can produce non-manifold edges when cases 17 and 20 of the look-up table share a common ambiguous face. MR-DMC prevents this via Rule 4. Sharp features: If \delta \to 1, the generated surface may lose sharp features due to excessive simplification. Collapsed cells: Cells that have not been subdivided until the maximal octree depth are marked as collapsed. Complex cells: Complex cells (containing surface pieces smaller than the current subdivision level) must be subdivided to ensure all intersected cells are processed. Strategy: Top-bottom refinement, suitable for large datasets. Manifold Guarantee: Guarantees manifold surfaces by introducing a cell-based criterion for dual vertex generation, avoiding post-processing repairs. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Generates multi-resolution, closed manifold surfaces; handles large datasets efficiently via top-down approach; no post-processing needed for manifold repair. Limitations: High \delta can lose sharp features; requires segmented volumetric data (indicator function). Origin: Proposed by Ricardo Uribe Lobello, Florent Dupont, and Florence Denis from Université de Lyon, CNRS, LIRIS. Publication: Published in SCITEPRESS - Science and Technology Publications in 2012. Context: Addresses limitations of standard Dual Marching Cubes (which can produce non-manifold edges) and Manifold Dual Contouring (which uses a bottom-up strategy unsuitable for large datasets). Development: Extends DMC over a generalized octree and introduces a top-bottom refinement algorithm based on curvature. name: Simplicial Partition Isosurfacing
head: Isosurfaces Over Simplicial Partitions of Multiresolution Grids, Octree Simplicial Isosurfacing
body: Simplicial Partition Isosurfacing extracts a manifold, intersection-free isosurface from a scalar function defined over an arbitrary octree by partitioning space into simplices (tetrahedra) dual to minimal octree cells. Unlike Dual Contouring, which produces non-manifold geometry in ambiguous sign configurations, and Dual Marching Cubes, which can generate self-intersecting surfaces due to non-convex dual cells, this method guarantees manifold topology and prevents tetrahedron inversion, ensuring the surface cannot self-intersect. Inputs and Outputs Input: An octree structure representing a scalar field F: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, and an isosurface value c. Output: A set of triangles forming a 2-manifold isosurface. Data Structures The method operates on the octree's minimal cells. A minimal m-cell is defined as a cell of dimension m that does not contain any other cells of dimension m as a subset. Minimal 3-cells (Cubes): Leaf nodes in the octree. Minimal 2-cells (Faces): The smaller of the two shared faces of adjacent leaf cubes. Minimal 1-cells (Edges): Edges shared by adjacent minimal faces or cubes. Minimal 0-cells (Vertices): Vertices of the octree not contained in any other minimal cell of higher dimension. Dual Vertices For each minimal m-cell, a dual vertex \bar{p} = \langle p, F(p) \rangle \in \mathbb{R}^4 is created, where p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position. The position p is constrained to lie within its containing cell: Dual vertices for 3-cells (cubes) are constrained to the interior of the cube. Dual vertices for 2-cells (faces) are constrained to the interior of the face. Dual vertices for 1-cells (edges) are constrained to the interior of the edge. Dual vertices for 0-cells (vertices) are fixed at the position of the 0-cell vertex. For m > 0, an additional constraint prevents vertices from lying on the boundary of their containing cell to avoid degenerate tetrahedra and T-intersections. The vertex is constrained to a sub-region of size 1-\epsilon of the containing cell, where \epsilon is a small positive value. Simplicial Partition Space is partitioned recursively into simplices starting from a single vertex, forming a hierarchy. 1. A line segment is formed by adding an edge vertex to a vertex. 2. A triangle is formed by adding a face vertex to the line segment. 3. A tetrahedron is formed by adding a cube vertex to the triangle. This creates a tetrahedral mesh where each tetrahedron is defined by four dual vertices corresponding to a minimal 0-cell, 1-cell, 2-cell, and 3-cell that are topologically connected. Isosurface Extraction The isosurface is the set of points p where F(p) = 0 (assuming c is subtracted from F). Within each tetrahedron, the function F is approximated by linear interpolation between the dual vertices. The isosurface intersects the tetrahedron if the signs of F at the vertices differ. Standard linear interpolation is used to find the intersection points on the edges of the tetrahedron, and these points are connected to form triangles. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simplicialpartitionisosurfacing(octree, isosurfacevalue): """ Extracts a manifold isosurface from an octree using simplicial partitioning. """ epsilon = 1e-6 # Small value to prevent boundary placement dualvertices = {} # Step 1: Identify minimal cells and create dual vertices minimalcells = getminimalcells(octree) for cell in minimalcells: dim = cell.dimension if dim == 0: p = cell.position else: # Constrain to interior by shrinking cell by epsilon p = shrinkcelltointerior(cell, epsilon) # Evaluate function at p, subtracting isosurface value fval = octree.evaluate(p) - isosurfacevalue dualvertices[cell.id] = (p, fval) # Step 2: Build simplicial partition (tetrahedra) # Hierarchy: 0-cell -> 1-cell -> 2-cell -> 3-cell tetrahedra = [] for cube in minimalcellsofdimension(3): # Find the nested minimal cells in the hierarchy face = cube.minimalface edge = face.minimaledge vertex = edge.minimalvertex vcube = dualvertices[cube.id] vface = dualvertices[face.id] vedge = dualvertices[edge.id] vvertex = dualvertices[vertex.id] tetrahedra.append([vcube, vface, vedge, vvertex]) # Step 3: Extract isosurface from tetrahedra triangles = [] for tet in tetrahedra: positions = [v[0] for v in tet] values = [v[1] for v in tet] # Find intersection points on edges where signs differ intersections = [] edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)] for i, j in edges: if values[i] values[j] < 0: t = values[i] / (values[i] - values[j]) pintersect = lerp(positions[i], positions[j], t) intersections.append(pintersect) # Connect intersections to form triangles based on sign configuration # Exact connectivity follows the standard Marching Tetrahedra lookup table triangles.extend(marchingtetrahedra(intersections, len(intersections))) return triangles def getminimalcells(octree): """Returns all minimal cells in the octree.""" return octree.getallminimalcells() def minimalcellsofdimension(dim): """Filters minimal cells by dimension.""" return [c for c in getminimalcells(octree) if c.dimension == dim] def shrinkcelltointerior(cell, epsilon): """Constrains the vertex to a cell of size 1-ε of the containing cell.""" # Returning the geometric center guarantees a strictly interior point return cell.center def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def marchingtetrahedra(intersections, count): """Connects intersection points to form triangles.""" if count == 2: return [intersections] elif count == 3: return [intersections] elif count == 4: return [intersections[:2], intersections[2:]] return [] Parameters \epsilon: A small value used to shrink the containment region for dual vertices of non-zero dimensional cells (faces, edges) to prevent boundary placement. Typical value not specified, but implied to be small enough to maintain feature reproduction while avoiding degeneracy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Tetrahedra: If dual vertices lie on the boundary of their containing cells, degenerate tetrahedra may form, leading to T-intersections. The \epsilon constraint mitigates this. Ambiguous Sign Configurations: Unlike Dual Contouring, this method handles ambiguous sign configurations by using a simplicial partition dual to minimal cells, guaranteeing manifold topology. Self-Intersection: Unlike Dual Marching Cubes, this method guarantees tetrahedra cannot invert, preventing self-intersection. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guarantees manifold topology and intersection-free surfaces; reproduces sharp and thin features; adaptive polygonalization guided by an error metric. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When a manifold, intersection-free isosurface is required from an adaptive octree, especially for sharp features. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Simplicial Partition Isosurfacing was introduced by Josiah Manson and Scott Schaefer from Texas A&M University. The method addresses limitations of Dual Contouring (which produces non-manifold, self-intersecting surfaces in ambiguous sign configurations) and Dual Marching Cubes (which can generate self-intersecting surfaces due to non-convex dual cells). It extends the concept of partitioning space along function features to improve piecewise linear approximation, focusing on accurately representing the function to produce an accurate isosurface. name: Sparse Marching Cubes
head: Sparse Marching Cubes from Points, Sparse-MC
body: Sparse Marching Cubes (Sparse-MC) is a surface reconstruction method that extracts the zero-level set from signed distance values at the eight corners of surface-intersecting (active) voxels to produce a watertight surface. Unlike standard Marching Cubes which requires a dense 3D grid, Sparse-MC operates on an explicitly defined set of voxel coordinates and their corner scalar values, avoiding the memory overhead of dense grids. It is distinguished from Marching Cubes with Octree by its explicit handling of sparse voxel lists rather than hierarchical tree structures, and from Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration by its direct application of the standard MC algorithm to a flat list of active voxels. Sparse-MC generates a triangle mesh (trimesh) from a sparse set of voxels defined by integer coordinates and scalar values at their 8 corners. It performs sparse marching cubes from a sparse grid of scalar values by constructing the 8 corner values for each voxel via lookup in the provided sparse grid. The method extracts an iso-surface mesh from sparse voxel data using the standard marching cubes algorithm, outputting vertices and triangular faces. Inputs: 1. coords: Integer tensor of shape [N, 3] containing the (x, y, z) coordinates of the active voxels. 2. corners: Float tensor of shape [N, 8] containing the scalar values at the 8 corners of each voxel. 3. iso: Float value representing the iso-level to contour at. 4. ensureconsistency: Boolean flag; if True, averages corner values at shared locations to ensure a consistent mesh. Alternative Input Form (from Points): 1. coords: Integer tensor of shape [N, 3] with coordinates of active voxels (also the points with defined scalar values). 2. pointvalues: Float tensor of shape [N] or [N, 1] with scalar value at each coordinate in coords. 3. defaultvalue: Float value assumed for corner points not in the input coords; should be known to be completely inside or outside the surface. Outputs: 1. verts: Float tensor of shape [V, 3] with vertex positions. 2. tris: Int tensor of shape [T, 3] with triangle indices. The method relies on two primary input tensors: Voxel Coordinates: A list of N unique integer triplets (x, y, z) identifying the active voxels in the grid. Corner Values: For each voxel i \in [0, N-1], an array of 8 floats representing the scalar field values (e.g., SDF) at the voxel's 8 corners. The corner ordering follows the standard Marching Cubes convention (typically 0-7 corresponding to binary indices of corner presence). If inputs are provided as point values (sparsemarchingcubesfrompoints), the method internally constructs the corners tensor by gathering values from the sparse point set for all 8 corners of each active voxel. 1. Gather Corner Values (if using Points input): If the input is coords and pointvalues, construct the corners tensor of shape [N, 8]. For each voxel i at coords[i], determine the integer coordinates of its 8 corners. Look up the scalar value for each corner in the pointvalues map. If a corner coordinate is not present in coords, assign defaultvalue. 2. Ensure Consistency (Optional): If ensureconsistency is True, identify all unique corner coordinates across all active voxels. For each unique corner, compute the average of the scalar values assigned to it by all adjacent active voxels. Update the corners tensor with these averaged values to ensure shared corner values across adjacent voxels, producing a seamless watertight reconstruction. 3. Compute Cube Indices: For each voxel i, determine the Marching Cubes case index. Compare each of the 8 corner values vj against the iso level. \text{bit}j = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } vj < \text{iso} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The cube index Ci is the sum of bits weighted by powers of 2: Ci = \sum{j=0}^{7} \text{bit}j \cdot 2^j This results in an integer tensor of shape [N]. 4. Interpolate Vertices: For each voxel i with case index Ci \neq 0 and Ci \neq 255: a. Identify the edges of the voxel that intersect the iso-surface based on Ci. b. For each intersecting edge, calculate the intersection point by linear interpolation between the two corner values of that edge. c. Store the 3D coordinates of these intersection points. 5. Generate Triangles: For each voxel i, use the standard Marching Cubes lookup table corresponding to Ci to determine which edges form triangles. Map the interpolated edge intersection points to triangle vertices. Output the triangle indices relative to the global vertex list. 6. Output Mesh: Return the global list of vertex positions verts and triangle indices tris. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def sparsemarchingcubesfrompoints(coords, pointvalues, iso, defaultvalue=1.0): """ Performs sparse marching cubes from a sparse set of points. Args: coords: Tensor of shape [N, 3], integer coordinates of active voxels. pointvalues: Tensor of shape [N], scalar values at coords. iso: Float, iso-level. defaultvalue: Float, value for missing corners. Returns: verts: Tensor of shape [V, 3], vertex positions. tris: Tensor of shape [T, 3], triangle indices. """ # 1. Map coordinates to values for fast lookup # Create a dictionary or hash map from (x,y,z) to value # In practice, this is done efficiently on GPU using scatter/gather operations coordtoval = {tuple(coords[i].tolist()): pointvalues[i].item() for i in range(coords.shape[0])} N = coords.shape[0] corners = torch.zeros((N, 8), dtype=torch.float32) # 2. Gather corner values for each voxel for i in range(N): x, y, z = coords[i] # Define the 8 corners of the voxel at (x,y,z) # Corner indices follow standard MC ordering (0-7) cornercoords = [ (x, y, z), (x+1, y, z), (x, y+1, z), (x+1, y+1, z), (x, y, z+1), (x+1, y, z+1), (x, y+1, z+1), (x+1, y+1, z+1) ] for j, (cx, cy, cz) in enumerate(cornercoords): if (cx, cy, cz) in coordtoval: corners[i, j] = coordtoval[(cx, cy, cz)] else: corners[i, j] = defaultvalue # 3. Call the core sparse marching cubes function return sparsemarchingcubes(coords, corners, iso, ensureconsistency=False) def sparsemarchingcubes(coords, corners, iso, ensureconsistency=False): """ Performs sparse marching cubes on pre-computed corner values. Args: coords: Tensor of shape [N, 3], integer coordinates of voxels. corners: Tensor of shape [N, 8], scalar values at corners. iso: Float, iso-level. ensureconsistency: Boolean, average shared corner values. Returns: verts: Tensor of shape [V, 3]. tris: Tensor of shape [T, 3]. """ if ensureconsistency: # Average corner values at shared locations # This step ensures watertightness by resolving discrepancies # between adjacent voxels sharing a corner. # Implementation detail: Gather all corner values, group by coordinate, # compute mean, and scatter back. pass # Implementation of averaging logic omitted for brevity; see S2 for CUDA backend details. # 4. Compute cube indices # v < iso gives boolean mask, convert to int (0 or 1) v = corners.float() cubeindices = (v < iso).int() # Weighted sum to get case index 0-255 cubeindices = ( cubeindices[:, 0] 1 | cubeindices[:, 1] 2 | cubeindices[:, 2] 4 | cubeindices[:, 3] 8 | cubeindices[:, 4] 16 | cubeindices[:, 5] 32 | cubeindices[:, 6] 64 | cubeindices[:, 7] 128).int() # 5. Interpolate vertices and generate triangles # This step is typically implemented in CUDA for performance. # For each voxel with cubeindex != 0 and != 255: # - Determine intersecting edges. # - Interpolate vertex positions on edges. # - Lookup triangle configuration from MC table. # - Append to global vertex and triangle lists. # The actual interpolation and triangle generation logic follows # the standard Marching Cubes algorithm [37] but applied only to # the active voxels in the sparse list. # Return results # verts: [V, 3] # tris: [T, 3] pass iso: The iso-level to contour at. Typical value is 0.0 for Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). defaultvalue: The value used if a voxel corner does not exist in the provided point set. Default is 1.0. This value should be known to be completely inside or outside the surface to avoid spurious geometry. ensureconsistency: Boolean flag to enforce topological consistency in the generated mesh, defaults to false. Missing Corners: If a corner of an active voxel is not present in the input point set, a defaultvalue must be provided. Choosing an inappropriate default value (e.g., one that crosses the iso-level incorrectly) can introduce artifacts. Inconsistent Corner Values: Adjacent voxels may have different scalar values for the same shared corner if ensureconsistency is False. This can lead to non-watertight meshes or visual seams. Degenerate Input: Empty input lists or voxels with all corners on the same side of the iso-level (case 0 or 255) produce no output but should be handled efficiently. Extracts 3D meshes from Sparse Radiance Fields (SRFs) by performing one pass of Marching Cubes on the 3D voxel space. Since SRF representations like SPARF and SuRFNet lie on the 3D voxel's space, extracting the mesh is straightforward with a single MC pass. This variant is specifically tailored for neural radiance field outputs that are discretized into sparse voxels. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active voxels N, O(N), as it only processes surface-intersecting voxels. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to N, storing only the coordinates and corner values of active voxels, avoiding the O(H^3) memory cost of dense grids where H is grid resolution. Performance: CUDA-accelerated implementations leverage massive parallelism to process thousands of voxels simultaneously. Strengths: Ideal for sparse SDF representations where only a list of points and their SDF values are available. Avoids the memory overhead of dense 3D grids. Limitations: Requires explicit voxel coordinates and corner values; does not automatically handle hierarchical data structures like octrees. Consistency must be explicitly managed via ensureconsistency. Sparse Marching Cubes (Sparse-MC) reconstructs watertight surfaces by extracting the zero-level set from signed distance values at the eight corners of surface-intersecting (active) voxels. These corner values jointly encode the topology and geometry of the enclosed surface patch. The method is based on the standard Marching Cubes algorithm [37] but adapted for sparse data structures. It is used in applications such as P2Voxel for pyramid pivot voxelization and in sparse radiance field rendering like SPARF and SuRFNet. name: Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration
head: Dual Marching Cubes Tree Traversal
body: Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration is a recursive octree traversal algorithm that extracts manifold isosurface meshes by enumerating voxel faces, edges, and vertices, delegating to a standard Marching Cubes routine only at leaf nodes. It differs from Marching Cubes with Octree by explicitly separating the traversal logic into specialized functions for faces, edges, and vertices to ensure consistent mesh connectivity across varying tree depths, rather than treating octree nodes as independent voxel containers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree root node representing a scalar field, an isovalue, and configuration parameters (gridwidth, tolerance, maximumdepth, nominalweight). Output: A set of triangles forming the isosurface mesh. Data Structures: The tree node structure contains the following fields: vectortype minimum: Minimum coordinate of the voxel. configtype config: Configuration flags. std::sizet gridsize: Grid resolution. scalartype gridwidth: Physical width of the grid. vector<std::sizet, 3> size: Dimensions of the voxel. std::vector<nodetype> children: Pointers to 8 child nodes (if branch). std::vector<boost::objectpool<branchnodetype>> branchpool: Memory pool for branch nodes. std::vector<boost::objectpool<leafnodetype>> leafpool: Memory pool for leaf nodes. Algorithm Steps: The algorithm uses three specialized recursive functions: fx, fy, fz for faces; exy, eyz, exz for edges; and v for vertices. These functions traverse the octree to gather the necessary 8 corner nodes for a voxel. 1. Face Enumeration (fx, fy, fz): Takes two tree nodes (representing adjacent voxels sharing a face) and a receiver. Checks if either node is a branch. If so, it recurses with mapped child indices to traverse the shared face boundary. For fx (x-axis face), the recursion maps children as follows: (children[2], children[0]), (children[3], children[1]), (children[6], children[4]), (children[7], children[5]). If both nodes are leaves, it proceeds to edge enumeration for the four edges of the face. 2. Edge Enumeration (exy, eyz, exz): Takes four nodes (representing voxels sharing an edge) and a receiver. Recurses on specific child index pairs to traverse the edge boundary. If any node is a branch, it recurses deeper. If all four nodes are leaves, it calls the vertex enumeration function v with the eight corner nodes of the voxel defined by the edge and the face context. 3. Vertex Enumeration (v): Takes eight nodes (the 8 corners of a voxel). Checks if any node is a branch. If so, it recurses with child indices [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]. If all eight nodes are leaves, it extracts vertex pointers and calls the standard marchingcubes routine. The marchingcubes routine computes the cube index C based on the sign of (vj - \text{iso}) for each corner j and generates triangles using the lookup table. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseface(nodea, nodeb, receiver): # Handle mismatched tree depths or boundary conditions # If child does not exist, fall back to current node childa = nodea.children[2] if nodea.isbranch() else nodea childb = nodeb.children[0] if nodeb.isbranch() else nodeb # Recurse for first pair traverseface(childa, childb, receiver) childa = nodea.children[3] if nodea.isbranch() else nodea childb = nodeb.children[1] if nodeb.isbranch() else nodeb traverseface(childa, childb, receiver) childa = nodea.children[6] if nodea.isbranch() else nodea childb = nodeb.children[4] if nodeb.isbranch() else nodeb traverseface(childa, childb, receiver) childa = nodea.children[7] if nodea.isbranch() else nodea childb = nodeb.children[5] if nodeb.isbranch() else nodeb traverseface(childa, childb, receiver) def traverseedge(nodea, nodeb, nodec, noded, receiver): # Recurse on specific child index pairs for edge traversal #... (implementation details for exy, eyz, exz vary by axis) # If all are leaves, call vertex enumeration if not any(n.isbranch() for n in [nodea, nodeb, nodec, noded]): traversevertex(nodea, nodeb, nodec, noded, receiver) def traversevertex(node0, node1, node2, node3, node4, node5, node6, node7, receiver): # Check if any node is a branch if any(n.isbranch() for n in [node0, node1, node2, node3, node4, node5, node6, node7]): # Recurse with child indices [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0] # Note: The order [7,6,5,4,3,2,1,0] corresponds to the specific bit ordering # used in the source implementation for consistent cube index calculation. children = [n.children for n in [node0, node1, node2, node3, node4, node5, node6, node7]] # Construct new nodes from children in reverse order newnodes = [ children[0][7] if children[0][0].isbranch() else children[0][0], children[1][6] if children[1][0].isbranch() else children[1][0], children[2][5] if children[2][0].isbranch() else children[2][0], children[3][4] if children[3][0].isbranch() else children[3][0], children[4][3] if children[4][0].isbranch() else children[4][0], children[5][2] if children[5][0].isbranch() else children[5][0], children[6][1] if children[6][0].isbranch() else children[6][0], children[7][0] if children[7][0].isbranch() else children[7][0] ] traversevertex(newnodes, receiver) else: # All leaves: extract vertex pointers and call marchingcubes vertices = [n.getvertex() for n in [node0, node1, node2, node3, node4, node5, node6, node7]] receiver.addtriangles(marchingcubes(vertices)) Parameters: gridwidth: Default 1.0. tolerance: Default 0.1. maximumdepth: Default max(std::sizet). nominalweight: Default 0.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mismatched Tree Depths: The algorithm handles nodes at different depths by using a ternary fallback: b1 ? b1->children()[i]: n1. If a child does not exist (because the sibling tree is shallower), it uses the current node n1. Boundary Conditions: Similar fallback logic applies at the boundaries of the volume to prevent out-of-bounds access. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of active leaf nodes intersecting the isosurface. The recursive traversal ensures that only necessary nodes are visited. Memory Complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the number of branch nodes. The use of boost::objectpool helps manage memory efficiently for branch and leaf nodes. Strengths: Ensures watertight mesh connectivity across varying octree resolutions by explicitly handling face and edge traversals. Limitations: Implementation complexity is higher than simple voxel-based Marching Cubes due to the need for specialized traversal functions. When to use: When extracting isosurfaces from adaptive octrees where resolution varies significantly across the volume. The method originates from the planaria/dmc repository, an unofficial implementation of Dual Marching Cubes. It is designed to work with hierarchical data structures, specifically octrees, to optimize the extraction process. planaria/dmc, https://github.com/planaria/dmc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 2D Stitching
head: Stitching 2D Grids
body: 2D Stitching is an index-based tessellation scheme that fills topological gaps between dual grids of different Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) levels using "stitch cells," allowing seamless merging of levels without subdividing boundary elements. It is distinguished from constrained Delaunay triangulation by avoiding the subdivision of quadrilateral boundary faces, which is non-unique and causes cracks in 3D Marching Cubes extraction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two adjacent 2D AMR grids: a coarse grid \Lambda{coarse} and a fine grid \Lambda{fine} with refinement ratio r. The grids are represented by their dual grid vertices and edges. Output: A set of "stitch cells" (triangles and deformed quadrilaterals) that connect the boundary of the fine grid to the coarse grid, forming a watertight mesh interface. Data Structures: The method operates on the dual grid representation. Vertices: Defined by their grid coordinates (i, j). Edges: Defined by pairs of vertices. Stitch Cells: Geometric primitives (triangles, quads) defined by the vertices they connect. No new vertices are generated; only existing vertices from the coarse and fine grids are used. Steps: 1. Identify Boundary: Determine the edges and vertices of the fine grid that lie on the boundary with the coarse grid. 2. Generate Edge Stitch Cells: For each boundary edge of the fine grid, generate stitch cells connecting it to the coarse grid based on the refinement ratio r and the refinement status of the coarse grid points. 3. Generate Vertex Stitch Cells: For each boundary vertex of the fine grid, generate stitch cells connecting it to the coarse grid. 4. Assemble Mesh: Combine the original dual grid elements and the generated stitch cells into a single mesh. Formulas and Logic: Refinement Ratio: Let r be the integer refinement ratio (r \ge 2). r fine grid cells fit into one coarse grid cell. Edge Connections (General r): For a boundary edge of the fine grid, the connection to the coarse grid depends on r: Connect (r-1) consecutive fine edge segments to one common coarse-grid point. Connect every r-th fine edge to a coarse edge. Edge Connections (r=2 Specifics): For r=2, each fine edge is connected alternatingly to either a vertex or an edge of the coarse grid. The specific topology depends on whether the coarse grid points adjacent to the connection are refined: Case 1: Coarse point is not refined. Connect the fine edge to the coarse point/edge directly. This yields triangles and deformed quadrilaterals. Case 2: Coarse point is refined. If a fine edge connects to a refined coarse point, connect it to another fine edge to form a rectilinear cell (quadrilateral). If both endpoints of a coarse edge are refined, connect the fine edge to another fine edge. If only one endpoint of a coarse edge is refined, treat it as an edge case using the same tessellation as other edge cases (consistent with the unrefined case logic but accounting for the refined neighbor). Vertex Connections: For a boundary vertex v of the fine grid: Connect the vertex to the coarse grid via two triangles. Connect each edge of the vertex to the two coarse edges that are "visible" from it. Refinement Check: If either of the adjacent coarse grid points is refined, "promote" the border vertex to a border-edge segment by connecting it to the other refined grid point. Treat this segment as an edge and use the edge connection configurations (Case 1 or 2 above). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatestitchcells(coarsegrid, finegrid, r): """ Generates stitch cells for the boundary between a coarse and fine AMR grid. Args: coarsegrid: Object containing coarse grid vertices and edges. finegrid: Object containing fine grid vertices and edges. r: Integer refinement ratio. Returns: list of stitch cells (each cell is a list of vertex indices). """ stitchcells = [] # Identify boundary edges and vertices of the fine grid boundaryedges = finegrid.getboundaryedges() boundaryvertices = finegrid.getboundaryvertices() # Process Edge Connections for edge in boundaryedges: v1, v2 = edge.vertices coarsepoint = findcorrespondingcoarsepoint(edge, r) if coarsepoint.isrefined(): # If the coarse point is refined, connect to another fine edge # to form a rectilinear cell (quadrilateral) otherfineedge = findadjacentfineedge(edge) stitchcells.append([v1, v2, otherfineedge.v2, otherfineedge.v1]) else: # Connect to the coarse point/edge # For r=2, this alternates between vertex and edge connections # For general r, (r-1) segments connect to a point, r-th to an edge if r == 2: # Alternating logic handled by iteration order or explicit check # Assuming standard alternating pattern for r=2 if edge.index % 2 == 0: stitchcells.append([v1, v2, coarsepoint]) else: # Connect to coarse edge coarseedge = findcorrespondingcoarseedge(edge) stitchcells.append([v1, v2, coarseedge.v2, coarseedge.v1]) else: # General r logic # Connect (r-1) consecutive segments to one coarse point # Connect every r-th segment to a coarse edge # Implementation depends on specific edge indexing pass # Process Vertex Connections for vertex in boundaryvertices: coarsevertex = findcorrespondingcoarsevertex(vertex, r) if coarsevertex.isrefined(): # Promote vertex to border-edge segment # Connect to the other refined grid point otherrefinedpoint = findadjacentrefinedpoint(coarsevertex) # Treat as edge case # stitchcells.append(...) using edge logic pass else: # Connect via two triangles # Connect each edge of the vertex to two visible coarse edges edgesatvertex = vertex.getadjacentedges() for edge in edgesatvertex: visiblecoarseedges = findvisiblecoarseedges(edge, coarsevertex) # Generate two triangles for each connection # Triangle 1: vertex, edge.v2, visiblecoarseedge.v1 # Triangle 2: vertex, visiblecoarseedge.v1, visiblecoarseedge.v2 # Note: Exact vertex indices depend on geometry pass return stitchcells Parameters: Refinement ratio r: An integer specifying how many fine grid cells fit into a coarse grid cell. Typical values are 2 and 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quadrilateral Subdivision: Quadrilaterals formed by stitching must not be subdivided. Subdivision is not unique and causes cracks in 3D. Mixed Refinement: Cases where only one endpoint of a coarse edge is refined must be handled consistently with other edge cases to avoid topological errors. Generalizes the 2D index-based stitching to 3D volumes by constructing intermediate "stitch cells" (pyramids, deformed prisms, hexahedra) to connect fine grid vertices/edges to the coarse grid. It handles the increased complexity of 3D vertex and edge interactions. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of boundary elements between the coarse and fine grids. The index-based approach is efficient as it avoids global optimization or Delaunay triangulation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of stitch cells generated. No new vertices are stored, only references to existing ones. Strengths: Ensures crack-free isosurfaces in 3D by avoiding non-unique quadrilateral subdivision. Efficient due to regular structure exploitation. Limitations: Requires dual grid representation. Limited to integer refinement ratios. When to use: When extracting isosurfaces from AMR data where crack-free connectivity between different refinement levels is critical. When not to use: When the grid structure is not hierarchical AMR or when non-integer refinement ratios are required. The method was introduced in the context of extracting crack-free isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. It addresses the problem of gaps between dual grids of different AMR levels that lead to discontinuities in the extracted isosurface. The approach was chosen over constrained Delaunay triangulation because the latter requires subdividing quadrilateral boundary faces, which is problematic for 3D Marching Cubes extraction. name: 3D AMR Grid Stitching
head: 3D AMR Grid Connection, 3D Stitching, Stitch Cell Generation, Stitching 3D Grids
body: 3D AMR Grid Stitching is a method for generating crack-free isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data by filling topological gaps between different refinement levels. It generalizes the 2D index-based stitching approach to three dimensions, connecting the vertices, edges, and quadrilaterals of fine grids to the coarse grid structure. Unlike methods that require subdividing boundary elements or re-sampling data, this technique constructs intermediate "stitch cells" (pyramids, deformed prisms, and hexahedra) to ensure seamless topology. It builds on 2D Stitching by extending the connection logic to 3D volumes and handling the increased complexity of vertex and edge interactions in three-dimensional space. The method operates on an AMR hierarchy where fine grids are embedded within coarse grids. The core task is to generate a set of unstructured geometry cells that bridge the gap between the fine grid surface and the coarse grid surface, ensuring that the resulting mesh is watertight and suitable for isosurface extraction (e.g., via Marching Cubes). Input: An AMR hierarchy consisting of coarse grids and embedded fine grids. The input includes the geometric positions of the grid vertices and the refinement relationships (which fine cells lie within which coarse cells). Output: A set of "stitch cells" that connect the fine grid boundaries to the coarse grid boundaries. These cells are typically tetrahedra, pyramids, triangular prisms, or deformed hexahedra. The method relies on identifying the topological relationship between fine and coarse elements. Fine Grid Elements: Vertices (Vf), Edges (Ef), and Quadrilaterals (Qf). Coarse Grid Elements: Vertices (Vc), Edges (Ec), and Quadrilaterals (Qc). Stitch Cells: The output geometry is defined by the vertices of the fine and coarse grids. No new intermediate vertices are created; the stitch cells are formed directly from existing grid points. 1. Identify Boundary Elements: For each fine grid embedded in a coarse grid, identify the fine grid elements that lie on the boundary of the fine grid region (i.e., those not fully contained within another finer grid). 2. Process Fine Quadrilaterals (Qf): For each fine quadrilateral Qf embedded in the coarse grid: Determine the connection type in two orthogonal directions implied by the quadrilateral's geometry. In each direction, decide whether the connection is to a coarse vertex (Vc) or a coarse edge (Ec). Based on the combination of connections in the two directions, generate one of the following stitch cells: Pyramid: If Qf connects to a single coarse vertex Vc in both directions. Deformed Triangle Prism: If Qf connects to a coarse edge Ec in one direction and a vertex or edge in the other. Deformed Hexahedral Cell: If Qf connects to another coarse quadrilateral Qc. 3. Process Fine Edges (Ef): For each fine edge Ef on the boundary: View the edge as appearing as a point in the direction parallel to the edge. Connect the edge to two perpendicular coarse edges (E{c1}, E{c2}) or two coarse quadrilaterals (Q{c1}, Q{c2}). Case 1: If connected to two perpendicular coarse edges, generate two tetrahedra. Case 2: If connected to two coarse quadrilaterals, generate two deformed triangle prisms. 4. Process Fine Vertices (Vf): For each fine vertex Vf on the boundary: Connect the vertex to three coarse quadrilaterals (Q{c1}, Q{c2}, Q{c3}) that meet at the corresponding coarse vertex location. Generate pyramid cells for each connection, where the base is the coarse quadrilateral and the apex is the fine vertex. 5. Handle Multiple Fine Grids Refining One Coarse Grid: When multiple fine grids refine the same coarse grid region, check each coarse-grid point for refinement status. Edge Promotion: An edge might be "upgraded" to a quadrilateral case if adjacent edges are refined. For a hexahedral cell, this occurs if grid points 2 and 3 or grid points 4 and 5 (in a local canonical numbering) are refined. Vertex Promotion: A fine vertex can be promoted to an edge if any of the coarse grid points 3, 5, or 6 (in a local canonical numbering) is refined. It can be promoted to a quadrilateral if more than two grids meet at the location. 6. Tessellate Deformed Hexahedral Cells: For cases where fine elements connect to coarse quadrilaterals, eight points are identified (4 from the fine quad, 4 from the coarse quad), forming a deformed hexahedral cell. Each face of this hexahedron corresponds to a 2D refinement configuration (as defined in 2D Stitching). Determine the tessellation of the hexahedron by subdividing its faces using the canonical tessellations from the 2D case. This face subdivision implies a volumetric tessellation of the hexahedron into pyramids, triangular prisms, and tetrahedra. Pyramid Case: If a refined coarse point is replaced by a fine quadrilateral, the result is a hexahedral cell. Triangular Prism Case: If refined coarse points are replaced by fine edges. If both coarse points of a triangular prism are refined, the resulting hexahedral cell does not need further splitting. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatestitchcells(finegrids, coarsegrid): """ Generates stitch cells to connect fine grids to the coarse grid. Args: finegrids: List of fine grid objects, each containing vertices, edges, quads. coarsegrid: The coarse grid object containing vertices, edges, quads. Returns: List of stitch cells (tuples of vertex indices or cell definitions). """ stitchcells = [] for finegrid in finegrids: # 1. Process Fine Quadrilaterals for qf in finegrid.boundaryquadrilaterals: conndir1 = determineconnection(qf, coarsegrid, axis=0) conndir2 = determineconnection(qf, coarsegrid, axis=1) stitchcells.append(createquadstitchcell(qf, conndir1, conndir2)) # 2. Process Fine Edges for ef in finegrid.boundaryedges: conntype = determineedgeconnection(ef, coarsegrid) if conntype == 'twoperpedges': stitchcells.extend(createedgetetrahedra(ef, coarsegrid)) elif conntype == 'twoquads': stitchcells.extend(createedgeprisms(ef, coarsegrid)) # 3. Process Fine Vertices for vf in finegrid.boundaryvertices: quadsc = getadjacentcoarsequads(vf, coarsegrid) for qc in quadsc: stitchcells.append(createvertexpyramid(vf, qc)) # 4. Handle Multiple Grids Refining Same Coarse Region stitchcells = promoteandresolveconflicts(stitchcells, coarsegrid) return stitchcells def determineconnection(qf, coarsegrid, axis): """ Determines if a fine quad connects to a coarse vertex or edge along a given axis. Returns ('vertex', vc) or ('edge', ec). """ # Not given in the sources. pass def createquadstitchcell(qf, conn1, conn2): """ Creates pyramid, deformed triangle prism, or deformed hexahedron based on connection types. """ if conn1[0] == 'vertex' and conn2[0] == 'vertex': return createpyramid(qf, conn1[1]) elif conn1[0] == 'edge' or conn2[0] == 'edge': ec = conn1[1] if conn1[0] == 'edge' else conn2[1] return createdeformedprism(qf, ec) else: qc = conn1[1] if conn1[0] == 'quad' else conn2[1] return createtessellatedhexahedron(qf, qc) def createedgetetrahedra(ef, coarsegrid): """ Creates two tetrahedra for the edge case connecting to two perpendicular coarse edges. """ # Not given in the sources. pass def createedgeprisms(ef, coarsegrid): """ Creates two deformed triangle prisms for the edge case connecting to two coarse quads. """ # Not given in the sources. pass def createvertexpyramid(vf, qc): """ Creates a pyramid cell connecting a fine vertex to a coarse quadrilateral. """ # Not given in the sources. pass def promoteandresolveconflicts(cells, coarsegrid): """ Handles cases where multiple fine grids refine the same coarse region. Promotes vertices/edges and resolves conflicts. """ # Not given in the sources. pass Refinement Ratios: The method works with commonly used refinement ratios, and general refinement ratios do not add more configurations because the fundamental connection strategies remain the same. Non-planar Boundaries: 2D refinement configurations that produce subdivided quadrilaterals yield non-planar cell boundaries, which are handled by subdividing hexahedron faces using canonical tessellations without needing actual point positions. Viewing Direction: Edge case logic assumes a viewing direction parallel to the edge to determine connections to perpendicular coarse edges or coarse quadrilaterals. Precision: The method relies on exact topological connections; degenerate inputs (e.g., zero-length edges) should be handled by the grid generation phase before stitching. An algorithm that utilizes stitching cells to construct an unstructured geometry across AMR levels to fill gaps between hierarchy levels. It is used when re-sampling or using redundant coarse data is not feasible or desired. It effectively eliminates cracks that appear in standard isosurface extraction from AMR data. Performance: On a standard PC with a 700MHz Pentium III processor, generating stitch cells for two levels of hierarchy (root and first level, both 32x32x32) took approximately 55ms. For three levels (adding a second level with 12 grids of dimensions 6x12x6, 6x4, 8x12x10, 6x4x4, 14x4x10, 6x6x12, 12x10x12, 10x4x8, 6x6x2, 16x26x52, 14x16x12, and 36x52x36), it took approximately 340ms. Generating the isosurface took approximately 250ms for two levels and 600ms for three levels. Strengths: Produces crack-free isosurfaces without subdividing boundary elements or re-sampling data. Limitations: The method is specific to AMR hierarchies with regular refinement ratios. When to use: Use when crack-free visualization of AMR data is required and the AMR hierarchy has regular refinement ratios. When not to use: Avoid if the AMR hierarchy has irregular refinement ratios or if real-time performance is critical. Alternative methods like re-sampling or using redundant coarse data may be more suitable in those cases. The method was introduced in the paper "Extraction of Crack-free Isosurfaces from Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data" by Greg Bryan, Anthony Yeung, and Michael L. Steinman, published in the Proceedings of the VisSymposium 2001. It generalizes the 2D stitching approach to 3D, addressing the challenge of gaps between hierarchy levels in AMR data. The method has been used in scientific visualization applications, particularly in cosmology and fluid dynamics, where AMR data is common. The data set used in the original paper was courtesy of Greg Bryan from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Theoretical Cosmology Group. name: Crack-free Isosurface Extraction from AMR Data
head: Crack-free isosurface extraction, Dual grid isosurface extraction with ghost cells, Dual grid stitch cell method, Parallel extraction of crack-free isosurfaces from AMR data, Stitch Cell Generation for AMR Isosurfaces
body: This method extracts watertight, crack-free isosurfaces from block-structured Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data in a distributed-memory parallel environment. It solves the problem of T-junctions (cracks) that arise when standard Marching Cubes is applied to hierarchical data by using dual grids and ghost cells to ensure boundary consistency without requiring the entire dataset in a single processor's memory. Unlike Octree-based Isosurfacing which operates on tree structures, this method operates on rectilinear boxes, and unlike Grid Traversal and Data Structure Adaptation which may adapt the grid structure itself, this method preserves the original AMR boxes while generating auxiliary "stitch cells" to bridge resolution gaps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Block-structured AMR data consisting of axis-aligned rectilinear grids (boxes) organized in a hierarchy of levels. Data is cell-centered. Each box has an integer identifier. The refinement ratio between levels is a fixed integer (typically 2). Output: A set of triangles forming a continuous isosurface. Data Structures: 1. AMR Box: Defined by integer indices of cells in a global reference frame. Contains regular cell values and ghost cell values. 2. Ghost Cells: A one-cell wide layer of cells added around the boundary of each AMR grid box. These store values from adjacent grids or the next coarser level. 3. Dual Grid Cell: Defined by four vertices corresponding to the cell centers of the surrounding AMR box cells. In 3D, a dual cell is defined by 8 vertices (though the text focuses on 2D logic for Case 2, the 3D case table handles 3D tessellations). 4. Case Table: Stores for each case: Number of sub-cases. Axes along which to check for identical parent level vertices (for sub-case determination). Tessellation data: lists of pyramids (P), wedges (W), tetrahedra (T), hexahedra (H), and irregular cells (I). Numbered Steps: 1. Ghost Cell Initialization: Extend each AMR grid (box) with a one-cell wide layer of ghost cells. Fill these ghost cells with values from adjacent grids or the next coarser level. This ensures all data required to construct stitch cells are available locally for each grid. Note: If the simulation does not output ghost cells, the visualization tool must generate them. The coarse cell value is used to fill all ghost cells overlapping it. 2. Neighborhood Identification: For each ghost cell, determine the integer identifier of the neighboring box overlapping it, or -1 if there are none and the cell corresponds to the parent level. 3. Iterate Dual Cells: Iterate over all dual cells that contain at least one ghost cell or the original box. 4. Compute Case Number: Compute a case number analogous to Marching Cubes by setting bits in a 4-bit integer corresponding to refined vertices. Determine if a vertex is refined using the previously computed neighboring box information. 5. Determine Sub-case (if applicable): For cases requiring sub-case determination (e.g., Case 2), check along the specified axis (i or j) to determine if parent level vertices are identical. Use the modulo refinement ratio method. Let i be the index of the dual cell's origin along an axis. The vertices are defined by box cells at indices i and i+1. Formula: If (i + 1) \pmod{\text{refinement\ratio}} == 0, the parent level vertices in that direction are different. If (i + 1) \pmod{\text{refinement\ratio}} \neq 0, the parent level vertices are identical. 6. Lookup Tessellation: Look up the appropriate tessellation (pyramids, wedges, etc.) from the case table based on the case number and sub-case. 7. Resolve Duplicate Stitch Cells: To avoid creating the same stitch cell for multiple grids, assign the stitch cell to the grid with the lowest integer identifier. Discard any stitch cells that contain a vertex of a same-level patch with a lower integer identifier. 8. Discard Ghost Results: Discard the results generated from the ghost cells before rendering. Only the results from the regular (non-ghost) cells are kept. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
