Args: amrboxes: List of Box objects. Each Box has: id: integer identifier extents: (mini, minj, mink, maxi, maxj, maxk) in global cell indices values: 3D array of cell-centered scalar values ghostvalues: 3D array of ghost cell values (initially empty) neighborids: map from ghost cell offset to neighbor box id isovalue: Scalar value for isosurface extraction refinementratio: Integer, e.g., 2 Returns: List of triangles (vertices) """ alltriangles = [] # Step 1: Initialize Ghost Cells # This step assumes a prior function initializeghostcells exists # which fills ghostvalues based on adjacent boxes and coarser levels. # Implementation detail: For a ghost cell at offset (di, dj, dk) # from a box boundary, find the overlapping box or parent cell. initializeghostcells(amrboxes) # Step 2 & 3: Iterate over all relevant dual cells # We process each box independently. for box in amrboxes: boxtriangles = [] # Determine the range of dual cells to process. # A dual cell is defined by 4 (2D) or 8 (3D) surrounding box cells. # We need to process dual cells that contain at least one ghost cell # or the original box. # In 2D, a dual cell at (i, j) is defined by box cells (i,j), (i+1,j), (i+1,j+1), (i,j+1). # The box cells range from mini to maxi. # Dual cells range from mini-1 to maxi (since dual cell i uses i and i+1). # We must include ghost cells, so the range extends by 1 in each direction. mini = box.extents.mini - 1 maxi = box.extents.maxi minj = box.extents.minj - 1 maxj = box.extents.maxj mink = box.extents.mink - 1 maxk = box.extents.maxk for i in range(mini, maxi + 1): for j in range(minj, maxj + 1): for k in range(mink, maxk + 1): # Get the 8 vertices of the dual cell # Vertices correspond to cell centers of surrounding box cells vertices = [] for di in [0, 1]: for dj in [0, 1]: for dk in [0, 1]: # Global index of the box cell gi = i + di gj = j + dj gk = k + dk # Determine if this vertex is refined # A vertex is refined if it belongs to a finer level box # or if it is a ghost cell that overlaps a finer level box. # The text says: "Whether a vertex is refined or not can be # determined using the previously computed neighboring box information." # Logic: Check if the global cell (gi, gj, gk) is covered # by a finer level box. If so, it is refined. isrefined = isvertexrefined(gi, gj, gk, amrboxes) vertices.append(isrefined) # Step 4: Compute Case Number # 4-bit integer, bit b set if vertex b is refined casenumber = 0 for b, isref in enumerate(vertices): if isref: casenumber |= (1 << b) # Step 5: Determine Sub-case if needed subcase = 0 caseinfo = CASETABLE[casenumber] if caseinfo.hassubcases: # Check axes specified in caseinfo.axestocheck for axis in caseinfo.axestocheck: # Use modulo refinement ratio method # If axis is i, check i+1 # If axis is j, check j+1 # If axis is k, check k+1 indexplusone = i + 1 if axis == 'i' else (j + 1 if axis == 'j' else k + 1) if (indexplusone % refinementratio) != 0: # Parent level vertices are identical # This affects the sub-case index subcase |= 1 # Bitwise logic depends on specific case table definition # Note: The text implies sub-case determination is more complex # involving multiple axes. The case table stores which axes to check. # For simplicity, we assume a single bit per axis check for now. # In reality, Case 5 has 4 sub-cases. # Step 6: Lookup Tessellation tessellation = caseinfo.gettessellation(subcase) # Step 7: Resolve Duplicate Stitch Cells # Check if this stitch cell belongs to this box or a neighbor with lower ID # A stitch cell belongs to the grid with the lowest integer identifier. # Discard if it contains a vertex of a same-level patch with a lower ID. # Implementation: For each vertex in the tessellation, find the # box ID that owns that vertex. If the minimum ID among same-level # patches is lower than box.id, discard. minneighborid = getminneighboridfordualcell(i, j, k, amrboxes) if minneighborid < box.id: continue # Discard this stitch cell # Add triangles to result for tri in tessellation: # Get actual coordinates for the vertices # Vertices are cell centers. # Need a function to convert global cell index to physical coordinates vcoords = [getcellcenter(gi, gj, gk) for gi, gj, gk in tri] boxtriangles.extend(vcoords) alltriangles.extend(boxtriangles) # Step 8: Discard Ghost Results # The pseudocode above processes dual cells including those in ghost zones. # However, the text says "Discard the results generated from the ghost cells". # This implies we should only keep triangles that are fully contained within # the regular cells of the box, or simply that the ghost cells are only used # to provide data for the boundary regular cells. # The text says: "Only the results from the regular (non-ghost) cells are kept". # In the dual grid approach, the "regular" dual cells are those fully inside # the box. Dual cells touching the ghost layer are used to generate stitch cells # at the boundary. The triangles generated from these boundary dual cells # are stitch cells. The triangles generated from internal dual cells are # standard MC triangles. # The text says "Discard the results generated from the ghost cells". # This likely means we do not render triangles that are solely within the # ghost zone, but stitch cells at the boundary are kept if they belong to this box. # The duplicate resolution step (Step 7) handles the ownership of stitch cells. # So, we keep all triangles generated by this box that passed the duplicate check. return alltriangles def isvertexrefined(gi, gj, gk, amrboxes): """ Determines if a global cell (gi, gj, gk) is refined (covered by a finer level box). """ for box in amrboxes: if box.level > 0: # Check finer levels if box.contains(gi, gj, gk): return True return False def getminneighboridfordualcell(i, j, k, amrboxes): """ Finds the minimum box ID among same-level patches that overlap the dual cell. """ # This requires checking the neighborids map for the ghost cells # surrounding the dual cell. minid = float('inf') # Check neighbors of the dual cell's vertices # If a vertex is a ghost cell, it has a neighborid. # If a vertex is a regular cell, its box ID is the box's ID. # We only care about same-level patches. # Simplified: Iterate over the 8 vertices. If the vertex is in a ghost cell, # get its neighborid. If it's in a regular cell, get the boxid. # Filter for same-level boxes. Return min. return minid # Placeholder for complex neighbor lookup logic Parameters: Refinement Ratio: An integer specifying how many child level cells a parent level cell contains along each axis. In the example data, the refinement ratio is 2 for all levels. Ghost Cell Layer Width: A one-cell wide layer of cells added around the boundary of each AMR grid box. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: T-junctions: Cracks in the isosurface caused by re-sampling cell-centered AMR data to a vertex-centered representation for standard Marching Cubes. Solved by using dual grids (cell centers) instead. Duplicate Stitch Cells: Multiple grids might try to create the same stitch cell. This is handled by assigning the stitch cell to the grid with the lowest integer identifier and discarding cells containing a vertex of a same-level patch with a lower identifier. Identical Parent Vertices: When two parent level vertices map to the same parent level grid cell, a stitch cell must be generated connecting to that single vertex. This occurs when the modulo check indicates identical vertices. Ghost Data Generation Bottleneck: Runtime increases with core count due to increased inter-node communication, not just data volume. Communication time increases linearly with data transferred between nodes. Uses hierarchical tree structures (octrees) to represent data. Sets apart by operating on tree nodes rather than rectilinear boxes. Choose when data is naturally hierarchical in a tree structure. Link Adapts the grid structure itself to facilitate traversal. Sets apart by modifying the underlying data representation. Choose when grid adaptation is required for other visualization tasks. Link Time Complexity: Stitch cell generation scales well and consistently up to the largest tested number of tasks, composing the smallest runtime among pipeline phases. Memory Complexity: The method allows processing AMR data on a per-grid basis, avoiding the memory bottleneck of previous dual-grid approaches that required the entire dataset in a single processor's memory. Measured Performance: Hydrogen Flame: 2,581 boxes, 3 levels, 48,531,968 grid cells, 8.1GB data. Isosurface ~2.2 million triangles. Methane Flame: 7,747 boxes, 3 levels, 1,525,420,032 grid cells, 592GB data. Isosurface ~29.7 million triangles. Hardware: Cray X6 "Hopper" at NERSC, 6,384 nodes, 153,216 cores, AMD Magny-Cours 2.1GHz, 24 cores/node, 32GB/64GB RAM/node. Peak 1.28 Petaflops/s. Scaling: Strong scaling of stitch cell generation. Ghost data generation runtime is approximately flat up to 312 cores for the hydrogen flame problem, but increases significantly with core count due to inter-node communication (linear with data transferred). Strengths: Produces continuous isosurfaces with no discontinuities. Parallelizable. Simplified implementation using case tables. Limitations: Ghost data generation can become a bottleneck due to inter-node communication at high core counts. Requires at least one layer of grid cells between child level and parent level boundary for some AMR codes (BoxLib, Chombo satisfy this; Enzo may not without generalization). The method was presented by H. Weber, H. Childs, and J. S. Meredith in 2012. It builds on prior work utilizing dual grids and filling resulting gaps with stitch cells. Previous dual-grid approaches defined stitch cell generation procedurally with many special cases and required serial processing of the entire dataset. This method simplifies stitch cell generation using a case table and enables parallelization using ghost cells. It is designed for block-structured AMR simulation codes such as BoxLib, Chombo, SAM-RAI, and Enzo. name: Unstructured and Arbitrary Grid Methods
body: This family extracts isosurfaces from scalar fields defined on non-Cartesian domains, including arbitrary polyhedral cells and hybrid unstructured grids [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md, 5321-gallagher-nagtegaal-bicubic-method.md]. It sets itself apart by operating directly on complex cell geometries without requiring decomposition into tetrahedra or reliance on predefined configuration tables for ambiguous faces [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. All methods in this family operate on a discretized domain where each cell contains scalar values at its vertices. The core mechanism involves traversing the grid cells, evaluating the scalar field against an isovalue to detect intersections, and generating geometric primitives (polygons or polynomial patches) at those intersections. Adjacent primitives are connected to form a coherent mesh. This method extracts isosurfaces from scalar fields defined on arbitrary polyhedral cells (convex, non-convex, planar, or non-planar) by approximating the surface locally at each cell as a polygonal surface (isopolygon) [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. It solves the topological inconsistencies and holes inherent in standard Marching Cubes on ambiguous faces by treating face boundaries systematically using general polygon tracing rules, rather than relying on predefined configuration tables [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. Unlike Marching Tetrahedra, it operates directly on arbitrary polyhedra without decomposing them into tetrahedra [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. Inputs: Scalar field values \phi{ip} at every vertex ip of the grid. Isovalue \tilde{\phi} defining the surface. Geometric coordinates \mathbf{x}{ip} of every vertex. Connectivity data: for each cell, the list of faces, and for each face, the list of vertices defining its boundary. Outputs: A set of isopolygons, where each polygon is defined by an ordered sequence of 3D points (vertices) lying on the cell edges. Data Structures: IA[ip]: Integer tag for vertex ip. IA(ip) = 1 if \phi{ip} > \tilde{\phi}, else 0. Strict inequality is used to prevent division by zero [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. IPVINT[j, i']: Index of the \tilde{\phi}-vertex inserted on the i'-th edge of face boundary j. visited(ip1, ip2): Boolean flag to track if an edge has been processed to avoid double-counting shared edges between faces [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. Steps: 1. Tagging: For every vertex ip in the grid, compute IA(ip) = 1 if \phi{ip} > \tilde{\phi}, else 0 [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. 2. Cell Selection: Identify cells where the scalar field crosses the isovalue. A cell is selected if \max(\phi) > \tilde{\phi} and \min(\phi) < \tilde{\phi} [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. 3. Vertex Insertion (Indexing): For each selected cell, iterate through all face boundaries j. For each edge i' in face j, defined by vertices ip1 = IPV(j, i) and ip2 = IPV(j, i+1) (with wrap-around): If IA(ip1) \neq IA(ip2), the edge is intersected. If the edge has not been visited, assign a new unique index to this intersection point and mark the edge as visited. If already visited, retrieve the existing index. Store this index in IPVINT[j, i']. If IA(ip2) == 1, mark the inserted vertex as a "key vertex" [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. 4. Vertex Arrangement (Tracing): Construct the isopolygons by linking the inserted vertices. Initialize the first vertex of the first isopolygon to the first inserted vertex index [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. Recursively find the next vertex: For the current vertex index, find the face boundary j where this vertex is a "key vertex". The next vertex in the polygon is the vertex preceding the current one in that face boundary's intersection list: prevφ = IPVINT(j, i'-1) (handling wrap-around) [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. If prevφ is not the first vertex of the current polygon, add it to the polygon. If the loop closes (next vertex equals the first vertex), start a new isopolygon if unassigned vertices remain [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. 5. Positioning: For each \tilde{\phi}-vertex on an edge defined by ip1 and ip2, compute its 3D position \tilde{\mathbf{x}}\phi using linear interpolation [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]: \tilde{\mathbf{x}}\phi = \mathbf{x}{ip2} - \frac{\phi{ip2} - \tilde{\phi}}{\phi{ip2} - \phi{ip1}} (\mathbf{x}{ip2} - \mathbf{x}{ip1}) Strict inequalities in step 1 ensure \phi{ip2} \neq \phi{ip1}, preventing division by zero [951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurface(vertices, scalarvalues, cellfaces, isovalue): """ vertices: List of 3D coordinates [x, y, z] scalarvalues: List of scalar values at each vertex cellfaces: List of cells, where each cell is a list of faces, and each face is a list of vertex indices isovalue: The threshold scalar value """ IA = [1 if s > isovalue else 0 for s in scalarvalues] globalphivertices = [] # Stores (ip1, ip2) tuples for each global phi index globaliskey = [] # True if ip2 > isovalue edgetophiidx = {} # Dict mapping sorted edge tuple to global index isopolygons = [] # List of lists of global phi indices for cell in cellfaces: cellscalars = [scalarvalues[v] for v in cell] if max(cellscalars) <= isovalue or min(cellscalars) >= isovalue: continue visitededges = set() cellphiindices = [] facephilists = [] # Step 3: Vertex Insertion for face in cell: nface = len(face) facephi = [] for i in range(nface): ip1 = face[i] ip2 = face[(i + 1) % nface] if IA[ip1] != IA[ip2]: edgekey = tuple(sorted((ip1, ip2))) if edgekey not in visitededges: visitededges.add(edgekey) phiidx = len(globalphivertices) globalphivertices.append((ip1, ip2)) globaliskey.append(IA[ip2] == 1) facephi.append(phiidx) else: facephi.append(edgetophiidx[edgekey]) facephilists.append(facephi) cellphiindices.extend(facephi) # Step 4: Vertex Arrangement if not cellphiindices: continue assigned = [False] len(cellphiindices) for start in range(len(cellphiindices)): if assigned[start]: continue polygon = [] curr = start while True: polygon.append(curr) assigned[curr] = True phiidx = cellphiindices[curr] if not globaliskey[phiidx]: break for j, fphi in enumerate(facephilists): if phiidx in fphi: pos = fphi.index(phiidx) prevpos = (pos - 1) % len(fphi) nextlocal = fphi[prevpos] if assigned[nextlocal]: if nextlocal == start: isopolygons.append([cellphiindices[k] for k in polygon]) break curr = nextlocal break # Step 5: Positioning resultpolygons = [] for polyglobalindices in isopolygons: polypoints = [] for phiidx in polyglobalindices: ip1, ip2 = globalphivertices[phiidx] x1, y1, z1 = vertices[ip1] x2, y2, z2 = vertices[ip2] s1, s2 = scalarvalues[ip1], scalarvalues[ip2] t = (s2 - isovalue) / (s2 - s1) px = x2 - t (x2 - x1) py = y2 - t (y2 - y1) pz = z2 - t (z2 - z1) polypoints.append((px, py, pz)) resultpolygons.append(polypoints) return resultpolygons The Gallagher-Nagtegaal Bicubic Method is an isosurface extraction technique that replaces the triangular facets of traditional marching cubes with visually continuous bicubic polynomial patches [5321-gallagher-nagtegaal-bicubic-method.md]. It solves the problem of geometric discontinuity and aliasing artifacts on unstructured or rectilinear grids by processing each volume element in isolation [5321-gallagher-nagtegaal-bicubic-method.md]. Unlike sibling methods that rely on linear interpolation or global mesh coherence, this method prioritizes local smoothness and independent element processing to facilitate efficient microcoding and parallelization [5321-gallagher-nagtegaal-bicubic-method.md]. Definition: A method for extracting isosurfaces of scalar fields defined on hybrid unstructured grids containing pentahedral elements (square pyramids and right triangular prisms) directly, avoiding the need to subdivide non-tetrahedral cells into tetrahedra or use indirect triangulation methods. Steps: Construct look-up tables for square pyramidal cells with accurate topological considerations, and construct look-up tables for triangular prismatic cells with accurate topological considerations. Comparison: Unlike indirect methods that subdivide non-tetrahedral cells into tetrahedra to use marching tetrahedra, or triangulate intersection points using standard algorithms, this method processes nearly all types of hybrid unstructured grids directly without subdivision. History: The method is based on the basic ideas underlying the well-established marching cubes and marching tetrahedra algorithms, which are applied to hexahedral and tetrahedral elements, respectively. Standard approaches often require converting unstructured data into tetrahedral or hexahedral elements, which can introduce topological errors or computational overhead. The Gallagher-Nagtegaal method addresses the visual quality issues of linear interpolation by fitting bicubic patches, while the polyhedral and pentahedral methods extend robustness to complex cell types [S1, 5321-gallagher-nagtegaal-bicubic-method.md]. name: Isosurface extraction on arbitrary polyhedral grids
head: General polygon tracing procedure, Generalized marching cubes for arbitrary grids, Isopolygon extraction, Isosurface extraction on arbitrary polyhedral cells, Method for isosurface extraction on arbitrary polyhedral cells
body: This method extracts isosurfaces from scalar fields defined on arbitrary polyhedral cells (convex, non-convex, planar, or non-planar faces) by approximating the local isosurface as a polygonal surface (isopolygon) using a general polygon tracing procedure. It solves the topological inconsistencies and non-2-manifold artifacts inherent in standard Marching Cubes when handling ambiguous face configurations by systematically treating face boundaries and avoiding reliance on predefined configuration lookup tables. Unlike Marching Tetrahedra, it operates directly on arbitrary polyhedra without decomposing cells into tetrahedra, offering geometric flexibility at the cost of higher computational complexity per cell. The method extracts an isosurface for a given isovalue \tilde{\phi} from a scalar field \phi defined on the vertices of an arbitrary polyhedral grid. The output is a set of non-planar polygons (isopolygons) representing the isosurface within each intersected cell. Input: Grid geometry: List of cells, where each cell is defined by a list of faces, and each face by a list of vertex indices. Scalar field: Values \phi{ip} at each vertex ip. Isovalue: \tilde{\phi} (scalar threshold). Output: List of isopolygons, where each polygon is defined by an ordered sequence of 3D position vectors \tilde{\mathbf{x}}{\tilde{\phi}}. For each cell, the algorithm uses the following structures: IA[ip]: Integer tag for vertex ip. 1 if \phi{ip} > \tilde{\phi}, else 0. IPV(j, i): Index of the i-th vertex of face boundary j. NIPV(j): Number of vertices in face boundary j. IPVINT(j, i): Stores the global index \tilde{\phi} of the intersection point on the i-th edge of face boundary j. NIPVINT(j): Count of intersected edges on face boundary j. visited(ip1, ip2): Boolean flag to track if the edge between vertices ip1 and ip2 has been processed to avoid double-counting shared edges. iskey[phiidx]: Boolean flag marking a \tilde{\phi}-vertex as a "key" vertex. A vertex is key if it lies on an edge (ip1, ip2) where IA(ip2) = 1. IPVISO(k, ik): 2D array storing the global index of the ik-th vertex of the k-th isopolygon. 1. Tagging: For every vertex ip in the grid, compute IA(ip) = 1 if \phi{ip} > \tilde{\phi}, else 0. 2. Cell Selection: Identify cells where the scalar field crosses the isovalue using an interval-based approach: cells with maximum scalar value > \tilde{\phi} and minimum scalar value < \tilde{\phi}. 3. Insertion of \tilde{\phi}-vertex indices: Iterate through all faces of all selected cells to identify intersected edges and assign global indices to intersection points. 4. Arrangement of \tilde{\phi}-vertices: Trace the boundaries of the isosurface within each cell to order the intersection points into closed polygons (isopolygons). 5. Positioning: Compute the 3D coordinates of each \tilde{\phi}-vertex using linear interpolation. For each selected cell, iterate through its face boundaries j = 1 \dots N{faces}. For each face, iterate through its edges i = 1 \dots NIPV(j). Let ip1 = IPV(j, i) and ip2 = IPV(j, i+1) (with wrap-around for the last edge). 1. Check if the edge is intersected: if IA(ip1) \neq IA(ip2). 2. If intersected: Check if the edge (ip1, ip2) has been visited. If not visited: Increment global counter \tilde{\phi}{count}. Mark edge (ip1, ip2) as visited. Assign new index \tilde{\phi} = \tilde{\phi}{count}. If already visited: Retrieve existing index \tilde{\phi} for edge (ip1, ip2). Store this index in IPVINT(j, i) = \tilde{\phi}. Mark this \tilde{\phi}-vertex as a "key" vertex if IA(ip2) = 1. Increment NIPVINT(j). This step orders the \tilde{\phi}-vertices into polygons. It assumes an anticlockwise order when viewed from the outside of the region with positive scalar field (IA=1). 1. Initialize polygon counter k=1 and vertex index within polygon ik=1. 2. Select the first unassigned \tilde{\phi}-vertex index as the start of the first polygon: IPVISO(k, 1) = 1 (assuming index 1 is unassigned, or finding the first unassigned). 3. Loop while there are unassigned \tilde{\phi}-vertices: Let current vertex index be curr = IPVISO(k, ik). Find the face boundary j and edge index i' such that IPVINT(j, i') == curr AND curr is marked as a key vertex. The next vertex in the polygon is the previous vertex on that face boundary: previdx = IPVINT(j, i'-1) (with wrap-around modulo NIPVINT(j)). If previdx is not the start vertex of the current polygon (IPVISO(k, 1)): Increment ik. Set IPVISO(k, ik) = previdx. Mark previdx as assigned. Else (loop closed): If there are still unassigned \tilde{\phi}-vertices: Increment k. Set ik = 1. Find the next unassigned \tilde{\phi}-vertex index. Set IPVISO(k, 1) = nextunassigned. Else: Terminate loop. For each \tilde{\phi}-vertex with global index \tilde{\phi}, located on the edge between vertices ip1 and ip2: \tilde{\mathbf{x}}{\tilde{\phi}} = \mathbf{x}{ip2} - \frac{\phi{ip2} - \tilde{\phi}}{\phi{ip2} - \phi{ip1}} (\mathbf{x}{ip2} - \mathbf{x}{ip1}) where \mathbf{x}{ip1}, \mathbf{x}{ip2} are the 3D positions and \phi{ip1}, \phi{ip2} are the scalar values. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractisosurfacearbitrarypolyhedra(cells, vertices, scalarfield, isovalue): """ cells: List of cells. Each cell is a list of faces. Each face is a list of vertex indices. vertices: List of 3D position vectors. scalarfield: List of scalar values corresponding to vertices. isovalue: The threshold value for the isosurface. Returns: List of polygons. Each polygon is a list of 3D position vectors. 1) % len(facephi) prevphi = facephi[previ] if prevphi == startphi: foundnext = False break else: nextphi = prevphi foundnext = True break if foundnext: break if not foundnext: break assignedphi.add(nextphi) polygonvertices.append(nextphi) currentphi = nextphi polygon3d = [] for phiidx in polygonvertices: targetedge = None for edge, idx in edgetophiindex.items(): if idx == phiidx: targetedge = edge break ip1, ip2 = targetedge xip1 = vertices[ip1] xip2 = vertices[ip2] phiip1 = scalarfield[ip1] phiip2 = scalarfield[ip2] t = (phiip2 - isovalue) / (phiip2 - phiip1) diff = [xip2[d] - xip1[d] for d in range(3)] scaleddiff = [t d for d in diff] pos = [xip2[d] - scaleddiff[d] for d in range(3)] polygon3d.append(pos) allpolygons.append(polygon3d) for phi in assignedphi: if phi in cellphiindices: cellphiindices.remove(phi) return allpolygons Isovalue (\tilde{\phi}): Typical value is 0 for signed distance fields or volume fractions. Double-Counting: Handled by checking if an edge was previously visited during the sequential traversal of face boundaries; if already visited, the existing index is reused. Ambiguities: Discrete data may introduce ambiguities (e.g., interpolation issues), but the method handles this via general tracing rules rather than configuration tables, ensuring consistent results even in ambiguous configurations that cause holes in Marching Cubes. Non-Planar Polygons: The resulting isopolygons may be non-planar, but most visualization applications can handle these, or they can be decomposed into triangles. Unlike structured grid methods (e.g., Marching Cubes), it handles arbitrary tetrahedral connectivity by processing each cell's vertices through a vertex program that classifies them relative to the isovalue and outputs intersection points directly. This method accelerates isosurface extraction on arbitrary polyhedral grids by replacing on-the-fly topological analysis with rapid table lookups. It solves the problem of high computational cost in general cell geometries by pre-computing vertex connectivity for all possible sign configurations. Unlike the standard Marching Cubes which relies on a fixed 256-entry table for cubes, this approach is geometry-agnostic, allowing the same optimization strategy to be applied to arbitrary cell types. Time Complexity: The method is generally slower than optimized Marching Cubes due to the lack of pre-computed lookup tables for arbitrary geometries. On an iMac Pro (2017) with 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon W, gcc -O3, the proposed method is on average 1.8 times slower than Marching Cubes with an extended lookup table (21 patterns). Parallelization: The algorithm can be parallelized using the OpenMP API to speed up operations over grids, achieving up to a 6x speedup with all available threads. Memory: Requires storage for cell geometry, scalar field, and intermediate structures for edge intersection tracking and polygon tracing. Strengths: Handles arbitrary polyhedral grids (convex/non-convex, planar/non-planar faces) without cell decomposition. Avoids topological inconsistencies (holes, non-2-manifold surfaces) common in Marching Cubes on ambiguous faces. Limitations: Slower than lookup-table-based methods on regular grids. Produces non-planar polygons which may require decomposition for some rendering pipelines. When to use: When working with unstructured or arbitrary polyhedral grids where topological consistency is critical and cell decomposition (e.g., Marching Tetrahedra) is undesirable or too costly. When not to use: When maximum performance on regular hexahedral grids is required and topological ambiguities are not a concern (use Marching Cubes). Marching Cubes suffers from topological inconsistencies in ambiguous configurations, while Marching Tetrahedra requires decomposing complex polyhedral cells into tetrahedra, adding computational cost. The method is implemented in the open-source library isoap (GPLv3 license) for interface reconstruction in Volume of Fluid (VOF) methods, CFD visualization, and medical imaging. It is used in advanced PLIC (Piecewise Linear Interface Calculation) schemes and for visualization with conventional graphics-rendering tools. name: Livnat et al. algorithm for unstructured tetrahedral grids
head: Livnat's algorithm
body: This method extracts isosurfaces from unstructured 3D scalar fields defined on tetrahedral meshes by streaming cells directly into graphics hardware, computing triangles during rendering time without storing them explicitly. It sets itself apart from CPU-based extraction by leveraging vertex shaders for immediate feedback on isovalue changes, and from brute-force GPU methods by optionally using a hybrid CPU/GPU interval tree to pre-select intersecting cells, achieving up to 7x speedup over brute-force GPU rendering. Unlike structured grid methods (e.g., Marching Cubes), it handles arbitrary tetrahedral connectivity by processing each cell's vertices through a vertex program that classifies them relative to the isovalue and outputs intersection points directly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of tetrahedra, where each tetrahedron is defined by 4 vertices. For each vertex, the input data includes a 3D position, a normal vector, a scalar value, and a unique identifier i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\} indicating the vertex's role in the current tetrahedron processing batch. The global isovalue (isoValue) is passed as a uniform parameter. Output: A stream of vertices forming triangle strips of length 4 that approximate the isosurface. The rasterizer discards degenerate triangles (zero area) generated for non-intersecting or single-triangle cases. Data Structures: 1. Vertex Input Structure: Contains the entire tetrahedron's data for every input vertex to satisfy GPU pipeline constraints. Fields: 4 corner positions (\mathbf{coord}{1..4}, vec3), 4 corner normals (\mathbf{nrml}{1..4}, vec3), 4 scalar values (isoV, float), 4 swizzled scalar values (for optimization), and the unique identifier i. Size: 144 bytes per vertex. Total per tetrahedron: 4 \times 144 = 576 bytes. 2. Lookup Tables (Alternative Implementations): Table 2 (Edge Lookup): Maps the 16 classification patterns and input vertex ID i to an edge index (12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34) or 0. Size: 16 \times 4 = 64 entries. Each entry specifies which edge to intersect for the i-th output vertex. Table 3 (Edge Traverse Order): An alternative to Table 2 to fit within older hardware limits (96 constants). Maps input vertex ID i to a sequence of 3 edge tests. i=1: Test edges 12, 13, 24. i=2: Test edges 14, 13, 24. i=3: Test edges 23, 24, 13. i=4: Test edges 34, 24, 13. Edge Table & Jump Table: Used in the Table 2 approach to determine edge masks and offsets based on the intersection bitmask. Algorithm Steps: The algorithm operates in two main modes: Brute Force (GPU only) and Hybrid (CPU + GPU). 1. Pre-processing (Hybrid Mode Only): Build an interval tree on the CPU to store the min/max scalar values of each tetrahedron. For a given isovalue, query the interval tree to identify tetrahedra where min \le isoValue \le max. These are the candidate cells. 2. Vertex Shader Processing (Per Tetrahedron): Four input vertices are sent to the vertex pipeline for each tetrahedron, each carrying the full tetrahedron data and a unique ID i. Step 1: Classification. Calculate the signed distance of each vertex to the isovalue: Fk = sk - isoValue \quad \text{for } k \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\} Classify each vertex as positive (+) if Fk > 0 or negative (-) if Fk \le 0. This results in a 4-bit classification pattern covering 16 cases. Step 2: Edge Intersection Determination. Method A (Table 2 / Bitmask): Determine intersecting edges by checking if the product of signed distances at edge endpoints is negative: E = (Fu \cdot Fv) < 0.0 for each edge. Create a 6-bit bitmask E for the 6 edges (12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34). Compute index: idx = \text{dot}(E, [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]). Lookup edge configuration from Jump Table and Edge Table to get edge weights/masks. Method B (Table 3 / Sequential Test): Based on input vertex ID i, sequentially test the three edges specified in Table 3. If an edge intersects (endpoints have different signs), compute the intersection point and output it. If no intersection is found after 3 tests, output a degenerate vertex (0,0,0,0). Step 3: Intersection Point Calculation. Identify the two active edges (or one, if only one triangle is formed) that intersect the isosurface. Calculate scalar values at the intersection points on these edges using linear interpolation. For an edge between vertices A and B with scalars sA, sB: frac = \frac{isoValue - sA}{sB - sA} The intersection point position \mathbf{p}{int} is: \mathbf{p}{int} = (1 - frac) \mathbf{p}A + frac \mathbf{p}B The normal \mathbf{n}{int} is interpolated similarly: \mathbf{n}{int} = (1 - frac) \mathbf{n}A + frac \mathbf{n}B Note: In the Table 2 approach, barycentric coordinates E are interpolated from edge weights, and position/normal are computed as weighted sums of all 4 vertices using these coordinates. Step 4: Output Generation. If the tetrahedron contains 0 triangles (no intersection), output 4 degenerate vertices (e.g., (0,0,0,0)). If 1 triangle, output 1 valid triangle and 2 degenerate vertices. If 2 triangles, output 2 valid triangles sharing an edge. The output vertices are rendered as a triangle strip of length 4. The indices are chosen such that the stream forms the correct triangulation or degenerate patches. Step 5: Transformation. Transform the computed 3D position to clip space: \mathbf{hpos} = M{wvp} \cdot \mathbf{p}{int} Output the homogeneous position and interpolated normal. Pseudocode (Table 3 Approach): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(IN, isoValue, worldViewProj): # IN contains coord1..4 (vec3), nrml1..4 (vec3), isoV1..4 (float), i (int) coords = [IN.coord1, IN.coord2, IN.coord3, IN.coord4] normals = [IN.nrml1, IN.nrml2, IN.nrml3, IN.nrml4] scalars = [IN.isoV1, IN.isoV2, IN.isoV3, IN.isoV4] i = IN.i - 1 # Convert 1-based source ID to 0-based index # Step 1: Classification F = [s - isoValue for s in scalars] # Helper to check if edge (u, v) intersects the isosurface def edgeintersects(u, v): return (F[u] > 0) != (F[v] > 0) # Helper to compute intersection point on edge (u, v) def computeintersection(u, v): denom = scalars[v] - scalars[u] if denom == 0.0: denom = 1e-9 # Guard against division by zero frac = (isoValue - scalars[u]) / denom pos = coords[u] + frac (coords[v] - coords[u]) normal = normals[u] + frac (normals[v] - normals[u]) return pos, normal # Step 2 & 3: Sequential Edge Tests based on i (Table 3) # Edges are 1-based in source, converted to 0-based here if i == 0: edges = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3)] elif i == 1: edges = [(0, 3), (0, 2), (1, 3)] elif i == 2: edges = [(1, 2), (1, 3), (0, 2)] elif i == 3: edges = [(2, 3), (1, 3), (0, 2)] else: edges = [] for u, v in edges: if edgeintersects(u, v): pos, normal = computeintersection(u, v) # Transform to clip space hpos = [ worldViewProj[0][0]pos[0] + worldViewProj[0][1]pos[1] + worldViewProj[0][2]pos[2] + worldViewProj[0][3], worldViewProj[1][0]pos[0] + worldViewProj[1][1]pos[1] + worldViewProj[1][2]pos[2] + worldViewProj[1][3], worldViewProj[2][0]pos[0] + worldViewProj[2][1]pos[1] + worldViewProj[2][2]pos[2] + worldViewProj[2][3], worldViewProj[3][0]pos[0] + worldViewProj[3][1]pos[1] + worldViewProj[3][2]pos[2] + worldViewProj[3][3] ] return {"HPOS": hpos, "COL0": normal} # Step 4: No intersection found for this vertex role # Output degenerate vertex as specified by sources return {"HPOS": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0], "COL0": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]} Parameters: isoValue: The scalar threshold. Typically a float. worldViewProj: The combined transformation matrix. Memory: 144 bytes per vertex input. 576 bytes per tetrahedron streamed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: GPU vertex programs cannot generate variable numbers of outputs. Cases with 0 or 1 triangle must output degenerate (zero-area) triangles, which are discarded by the rasterizer. Memory Limits: If the tetrahedral grid exceeds video memory, transferring data via AGP bus causes a 10-20x performance drop. Isovalue Changes: Changing the isovalue in Hybrid mode requires updating the interval tree nodes in video memory, causing a slight frame rate decrease. Precision: Linear interpolation assumes linear scalar variation within the tetrahedron. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of tetrahedra processed. In Brute Force mode, all tetrahedra are processed. In Hybrid mode, only intersecting tetrahedra are processed, reducing N by ~70% for typical datasets. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the tetrahedral data in video memory. 576 bytes per tetrahedron. Performance: On nVidia GeForce FX 5800 Ultra (128MB) with elec2 dataset (142,131 tetrahedra): 9.92 million tetrahedra/sec (diffuse lighting). On nVidia GeForce Quadro FX 3000 (256MB) with elec1 dataset (19,549 tetrahedra): 7.22 million tetrahedra/sec (diffuse lighting). Hybrid CPU/GPU version achieves ~7x speedup over GPU Brute Force. Pure CPU implementation achieves about half the performance of the hardware accelerated method. Strengths: Immediate feedback for isovalue changes. High throughput when data fits in VRAM. Handles unstructured grids natively. Limitations: High memory usage per tetrahedron (576 bytes). Performance degrades significantly if data does not fit in VRAM. Requires modern GPU with vertex shader support. The algorithm was introduced by Livnat et al. in 2001/2002 for realtime isosurface extraction using graphics hardware. It addresses the limitations of CPU-based extraction and the memory overhead of storing explicit triangle meshes. The method leverages the parallel processing power of GPUs to compute isosurfaces on the fly. The hybrid approach incorporates interval trees for spatial selection, a technique previously used in CPU-based volume rendering. Realtime Isosurface Extraction with Graphics Hardware, https://doi.org/10.2312/egs.20041007, fetched 2026-10-26 marching cubes algorithm, https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/marching-cube-algorithm, fetched 2026-10-30 (book)

name: Performance Optimization via Lookup Table
head: Pre-computed connectivity
body: This method accelerates isosurface extraction on arbitrary polyhedral grids by pre-computing vertex connectivity for all possible sign configurations and storing it in a lookup table for rapid access during extraction. Unlike standard methods constrained to specific cell geometries, it is geometry-agnostic, allowing the same optimization strategy to be applied to arbitrary cell types. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a scalar field defined on an arbitrary polyhedral grid and an isovalue \tilde{\phi} as input, and outputs a set of triangles representing the isosurface. The core data structure is a lookup table mapping each possible vertex sign configuration to a pre-computed list of vertex indices (connectivity) that form the isosurface segments within that cell. Pre-computation Phase: 1. Identify the cell geometry and determine the number of vertices N per cell. 2. Generate all 2^N possible sign patterns of vertex values relative to the isovalue. 3. For each pattern, compute the exact connectivity (which vertices are connected by the isosurface) using the specific geometric constraints of the cell. 4. Store these connectivity lists in a lookup table indexed by the sign pattern integer. Extraction Phase: 1. Iterate through each cell in the grid. 2. Evaluate the scalar field at each vertex of the cell. 3. Determine the sign of each vertex relative to the isovalue (+1 if > \tilde{\phi}, -1 if < \tilde{\phi}, 0 if = \tilde{\phi}). 4. Construct an integer index from these signs (e.g., treating signs as bits). 5. Retrieve the pre-computed connectivity list from the lookup table using this index. 6. Generate triangles using the vertex indices from the retrieved list. Formulas: The connectivity is determined by solving for the intersection of the isosurface with the cell edges. For a linear interpolation, the intersection point P on an edge between vertices Vi and Vj with values \phii and \phij is: P = Vi + \frac{\tilde{\phi} - \phii}{\phij - \phii} (Vj - Vi) where Vi and Vj are the spatial coordinates of the cell vertices, \phii and \phij are their scalar field values, and \tilde{\phi} is the target isovalue. The lookup table stores the indices of vertices involved in these intersections. Parameters: The cell geometry defines the size of the lookup table (2^N entries). For a cube, N=8, resulting in 256 entries. Parallel execution using OpenMP (-fopenmp) can significantly speed up the extraction phase. Edge Cases: Floating-point precision errors may cause sign flips. A small epsilon tolerance is often used when comparing vertex values to the isovalue. Degenerate cases where vertices lie exactly on the isosurface require explicit handling to avoid undefined connectivity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputeconnectivity(N): table = {} for pattern in range(1 << N): connectivity = computecellconnectivity(pattern, N) table[pattern] = connectivity return table def extractisosurface(grid, lookuptable, isovalue): triangles = [] for cell in grid.cells: signs = [] for vertex in cell.vertices: if vertex.value > isovalue: signs.append(1) elif vertex.value < isovalue: signs.append(-1) else: signs.append(0) index = 0 for i, s in enumerate(signs): if s > 0: index |= (1 << i) connectivity = lookuptable[index] for tri in connectivity: triangles.append(tri) return triangles Decomposes cubes into five tetrahedra to extract isosurfaces from regular voxel grids, covering all 81 sign patterns including degenerate cases. It is deterministic and topology-agnostic, solving V - L = 0 directly without ambiguity checks. Choose it when guaranteed manifold output is required without topology post-processing. A data structure that maps tetrahedra during extraction on unstructured or arbitrary polyhedral grids by providing anchor displacements and neighbor offsets for vertices around a cube corner. It eliminates exhaustive tetrahedron searches during decomposition. Choose it when processing highly irregular grids where neighbor traversal dominates runtime. Pre-computation is O(2^N \cdot C) where C is the cost of computing connectivity for one cell type. Extraction is O(1) per cell for table lookup, plus O(V) for triangle generation. Memory complexity is O(2^N \cdot K) where K is the average number of vertices per connectivity list, which remains small for standard cells like cubes. On an iMac Pro (2017, 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon W), using OpenMP with all available threads achieves a \times 6 speedup compared to single-threaded execution. Without pre-computation, the method is on average 1.8 times slower than optimized Marching Cubes on cubes. The method is geometry-agnostic and fast, but pre-computation cost and exponential memory growth with vertex count per cell are limitations. The method originated in the context of generalizing isosurface extraction to arbitrary grids to address the computational inefficiency of on-the-fly topological analysis for non-standard cell geometries. It builds on the principles of Marching Cubes but extends the lookup table concept to arbitrary polyhedral cells. name: Tetrahedral Marching Cubes (5-tetrahedra method)
head: 5-tetrahedra-per-cube extraction, SurfaceExtractorTetrahedra
body: This method extracts an isosurface from a scalar field defined on a regular voxel grid by decomposing each cube into five tetrahedra and performing linear interpolation within each tetrahedron. It covers all 81 possible sign patterns of the vertex values, including degenerate cases where vertices lie exactly on the isosurface. Unlike the standard Marching Cubes which relies on a 256-entry lookup table and resolves ambiguities via topology checks, this method is deterministic and topology-agnostic, solving the equation V - L = 0 directly. Inputs: A 3D scalar field V defined on a grid of voxels, and a scalar level L. Outputs: A set of vertices and triangles forming a manifold mesh. Data Structures: The implementation replaces standard associative containers with maps keyed by canonical strings to ensure deterministic ordering and exact arithmetic. Vertices: Stored in a map keyed by a canonical string representation of the rational coordinates (reduced to lowest terms). Vertex indices are assigned in insertion order. Edges/Triangles: Stored in maps keyed by canonical strings. Sorted at the end by a custom operator< to match std::set iteration order. Arithmetic: Uses int64t for internal calculations, mapping onto IEEE doubles. This remains exact as long as products stay within the safe-integer range (2^{63}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Decomposition: For each voxel cube, decompose it into 5 tetrahedra. The standard decomposition connects the cube center to the 6 faces, or more commonly, splits the cube into 6 tetrahedra; however, the 5-tetrahedra method specifically partitions the cube into 4 corner tetrahedra and 1 central tetrahedron (or equivalent partition covering the volume). Note: The source describes a partition into four corner tetrahedra plus a central one for gradient calculation, implying a specific geometric split. 2. Sign Pattern Evaluation: Determine the signs of the scalar field values at the 8 vertices of the cube relative to the level L. There are 2^8 = 256 combinations, but due to symmetry and the nature of the tetrahedral split, the logic handles 81 distinct sign patterns. 3. Intersection Calculation: For each tetrahedron in the cube: Identify edges where the scalar value crosses the level L (sign change). Compute the intersection point on these edges using linear interpolation. Form triangles from the intersection points. 4. Gradient and Orientation: Calculate the gradient at intersection points to determine triangle orientation. Pitfall (Odd-Parity Branch): In the original implementation, the GetGradient function for odd-parity cubes contained a bug. The condition dx + dy + dz >= 0 was used to select the central tetrahedron (index 6572). Since dx, dy, dz are fractional offsets in [0, 1], this sum is always \ge 0, making the branch for the central tetrahedron (index 0752) unreachable. Fix: The condition must be changed to dx + dy + dz >= 2. The cutting plane through vertices (1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,1) is defined by dx + dy + dz = 2. 5. Mesh Assembly: Collect all generated triangles. Sort edges and triangles by their canonical keys to ensure consistent ordering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extracttetrahedral(field, level, griddims): # Maps for deterministic ordering vertexmap = {} # Key: canonicalstring(coord), Value: index edgeset = {} # Key: canonicalstring(edge), Value: True triangleset = {} # Key: canonicalstring(triangle), Value: True vertices = [] triangles = [] # Iterate over all voxels for x in range(griddims.x - 1): for y in range(griddims.y - 1): for z in range(griddims.z - 1): # Get 8 corner values v = [field[x+i, y+j, z+k] for i in [0,1] for j in [0,1] for k in [0,1]] # Determine sign pattern signs = [1 if val > level else -1 if val < level else 0 for val in v] # Decompose cube into 5 tetrahedra # Tetrahedra indices refer to the 8 corners of the cube # Standard 5-tet decomposition: # T1: 0,1,3,7 # T2: 1,3,2,7 # T3: 1,2,6,7 # T4: 2,6,3,7 # T5: 3,6,7 (Central? Or specific partition) # The source mentions "four corner tetrahedra plus a central one" # for gradient logic. We assume a standard partition covering the cube. tetrahedra = [ [0, 1, 3, 7], [1, 3, 2, 7], [1, 2, 6, 7], [2, 6, 3, 7], [3, 6, 7, ?] # The 5th tetrahedron definition is implicit in the source's gradient logic ] for tet in tetrahedra: # Check if tetrahedron intersects the isosurface # A tetrahedron intersects if vertices have mixed signs tetsigns = [signs[i] for i in tet] if not (all(s >= 0 for s in tetsigns) or all(s <= 0 for s in tetsigns)): # Find intersecting edges edges = getintersectingedges(tet, tetsigns, v, level) # Compute intersection points points = [] for edge in edges: p = linearinterpolate(edge, v, level) points.append(p) # Form triangles # For a tetrahedron, the intersection is a polygon (triangle or quad) # Triangulate the polygon tris = triangulatepolygon(points) for tri in tris: # Add vertices to map triindices = [] for p in tri: key = canonicalstring(p) if key not in vertexmap: vertexmap[key] = len(vertices) vertices.append(p) triindices.append(vertexmap[key]) # Add triangle to set trikey = canonicalstring(sorted(triindices)) if trikey not in triangleset: triangleset[trikey] = True triangles.append(triindices) # Sort triangles and edges for consistency triangles.sort(key=lambda t: canonicalstring(sorted(t))) return vertices, triangles def getgradient(x, y, z, field, level): # dx, dy, dz are fractional offsets dx, dy, dz = x % 1, y % 1, z % 1 # Determine which tetrahedron the point lies in # Odd-parity branch fix: use >= 2 instead of >= 0 if dx - dy - dz >= 0: # Corner tetrahedron 1205 return computegradient1205(dx, dy, dz, field) elif dx - dy + dz <= 0: # Corner tetrahedron 3027 return computegradient3027(dx, dy, dz, field) elif dx + dy - dz <= 0: # Corner tetrahedron 4750 return computegradient4750(dx, dy, dz, field) elif dx + dy + dz >= 2: # Fixed condition # Central tetrahedron 0752 return computegradient0752(dx, dy, dz, field) else: # Corner tetrahedron 6572 return computegradient6572(dx, dy, dz, field) Cube-based surface extraction using a vertex-edge table (VETable) and ear-clipping. It resolves the four-cut face ambiguity by evaluating the sign of the determinant f{00}f{11} - f{01}f{10}, adding a branch point when \det == 0. Unlike the tetrahedra extractor which solves V - L = 0, the cubes extractor solves 2V - (2L+1) = 0. To extract the same surface, voxels must be doubled and the level set to 2L+1. Complexity: Linear in the number of voxels, O(N), where N is the number of voxels. Each voxel is processed independently. Memory: Proportional to the number of surface triangles and vertices. The use of maps for canonical strings adds overhead compared to direct array indexing but ensures deterministic ordering. Performance: The method is robust and handles degenerate cases (zero-valued vertices) explicitly. The int64t arithmetic ensures precision but may be slower than floating-point operations if not optimized. The bug fix in the odd-parity branch is critical for correct orientation. Strengths: Topology-agnostic, no lookup table size limitations, handles all sign patterns including degenerate ones. Limitations: Slower than lookup-table-based methods due to per-voxel computation and map overhead. Requires careful handling of the gradient calculation to avoid orientation errors. The method is part of the gtengine-js library, specifically ported in PR #131 (B46) by gradientspaceai. It derives from the SurfaceExtractor base class and is designed to be a deterministic alternative to the standard Marching Cubes algorithm. The implementation addresses specific bugs in the gradient calculation for odd-parity cubes, ensuring correct triangle orientation. name: Tetrahedral Marching Cubes Neighbor Lookup
head: Vertex Neighbor Lookup Table, Vertex neighbor lookup table around cube corner
body: The Tetrahedral Marching Cubes Neighbor Lookup is a lookup table providing anchor displacements (\Deltai) and neighbor tetrahedron offsets (ti) for vertices surrounding a specific cube corner, used to map tetrahedra for isosurface extraction. It is a performance optimization component of the Tetrahedral Marching Cubes method. Input: A cube corner c = (cx, cy, cz) \in \{0, 1\}^3. Output: A set of entries, each containing an index range i, an anchor displacement \Deltai = (\Delta{x,i}, \Delta{y,i}, \Delta{z,i}), and a neighbor tetrahedron offset ti. The core data structure is a lookup table (referred to as Table A8 in the source). The table columns are the index range i, \Deltax, \Deltay, \Deltaz, and ti. Rows group indices sharing the same configuration. For the canonical corner c=(0,0,0), the entries are: i=1–6 has \Delta=(-1,-1,-1) and ti=-5; i=7–8 has \Delta=(-1,-1,0) and ti=1,2; i=9–10 has \Delta=(-1,0,-1) and ti=0,5; i=11–12 has \Delta=(-1,0,0) and ti=0,1; i=13–14 has \Delta=(0,-1,-1) and ti=3,4; i=15–16 has \Delta=(0,-1,0) and ti=2,3; i=17–18 has \Delta=(0,0,-1) and ti=4,5; i=19–24 has \Delta=(0,0,0) and ti=0–5. 1. Select Cube Corner: Identify the cube corner c = (cx, cy, cz) \in \{0, 1\}^3 for the lookup. 2. Retrieve Base Entries: Look up the base entries in the lookup table corresponding to the canonical corner (e.g., (0,0,0)). 3. Adjust Displacements: For each entry, adjust the anchor displacement to account for the specific cube corner by adding the corner coordinates: \Deltai \leftarrow \Deltai + c. 4. Map Tetrahedra: Use the adjusted configurations (\Deltai, ti) to map tetrahedra for isosurface extraction. Cube Corner c: A 3D vector with components in \{0, 1\}. The table is defined per cube corner because vertices of each tetrahedron can be mapped to a cube corner. Self Configuration Coincidence: For a specific cube corner c and tetrahedron offset t, one row in the lookup table may coincide with the self configuration (\Delta0=(0, 0, 0), t0=t). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getneighborlookup(c): """ Retrieve and adjust the neighbor lookup table for a given cube corner c. Args: c (tuple): The cube corner coordinates (cx, cy, cz), each in {0, 1}. Returns: list: A list of tuples, each containing (starti, endi, deltax, deltay, deltaz, ti). """ # Base lookup table for corner (0, 0, 0) as defined in the source # Format: (startindex, endindex, deltax, deltay, deltaz, tivalues) basetable = [ (1, 6, -1, -1, -1, [-5]), (7, 8, -1, -1, 0, [1, 2]), (9, 10, -1, 0, -1, [0, 5]), (11, 12, -1, 0, 0, [0, 1]), (13, 14, 0, -1, -1, [3, 4]), (15, 16, 0, -1, 0, [2, 3]), (17, 18, 0, 0, -1, [4, 5]), (19, 24, 0, 0, 0, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) ] adjustedentries = [] for starti, endi, dx, dy, dz, tvals in basetable: # Adjust displacements by adding the cube corner coordinates adjdx = dx + c[0] adjdy = dy + c[1] adjdz = dz + c[2] # Yield each ti value for the current displacement for t in tvals: adjustedentries.append((starti, endi, adjdx, adjdy, adjdz, t)) return adjustedentries The parent method that decomposes a cube into five tetrahedra for isosurface extraction. It differs by performing the actual surface extraction rather than just neighbor lookup. Choose it when extracting surfaces on tetrahedral grids. Tetrahedral Marching Cubes (5-tetrahedra method) Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the TetraSDF framework for analytic isosurface extraction on multi-resolution tetrahedral grids. TetraSDF: Analytic Isosurface Extraction with Multi-resolution Tetrahedral Grid, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16273v4, fetched 2026-10-26
