name: Marching Tetrahedrons
head: Case-based Marching Tetrahedra, IsosurfaceTet, Marching Tetrahedra (Case-based), Tetrahedra Marcher, Tetrahedral Marching
body: Marching Tetrahedrons is an isosurface extraction algorithm that decomposes each cubic voxel into tetrahedra to resolve the topological ambiguities inherent in Marching Cubes. By operating on tetrahedral cells, it guarantees a manifold surface without the need for disambiguation tables. It sets itself apart from its parent Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra by using a fixed decomposition of the standard cubic grid rather than a subgrid structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset defined on a regular 3D grid (voxels). Each voxel has 8 corner vertices with associated scalar values F and 3D coordinates P. Output: A polygonal mesh (list of triangles) representing the isosurface at a specified isovalue. Data Structures: Tetrahedron Struct: Represents a single tetrahedral cell. X[4], Y[4], Z[4]: float arrays storing the 3D coordinates of the 4 vertices. F[4]: float array storing the scalar field values at the 4 vertices. Lookup Table (lup): A 2D array lup[16][6] mapping the 16 possible vertex sign combinations (case index) to the edges intersected by the isosurface. Each entry contains up to 5 edge indices (0–5, corresponding to the 6 edges of a tetrahedron). Edge indices are -1 if not intersected. Edge Mapping: The 6 edges of a tetrahedron with vertices 0, 1, 2, 3 are indexed as: 0: (0, 1) 1: (1, 2) 2: (0, 2) 3: (1, 3) 4: (2, 3) 5: (0, 3) Algorithm Steps: 1. Decomposition: For each voxel in the volume, decompose the cube into 6 tetrahedra. The specific decomposition must be consistent across all voxels to ensure connectivity. 2. Classification: For each tetrahedron, determine the case index icase (0–15). For each vertex i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, if F[i] < \text{isovalue}, the vertex is "inside" (bit 0); otherwise, it is "outside" (bit 1). icase is the integer formed by these 4 bits: \sum{i=0}^{3} bi 2^i. 3. Lookup: Retrieve the number of segments nsegments from numSegments[icase]. If nsegments is 0, the tetrahedron contributes no triangles. 4. Edge Intersection: For each intersected edge e in lup[icase]: Identify the two vertices v0, v1 connected by edge e. Compute the intersection point P using linear interpolation: P = v0 + t (v1 - v0) t = \frac{\text{isovalue} - F[v0]}{F[v1] - F[v0]} Pitfall: If F[v1] - F[v0] \approx 0, clamp t to 0.5 or handle as a degenerate case to avoid division by zero. Clamp t to [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation outside the edge segment. 5. Triangle Generation: Case 1 Segment (1 triangle): Occurs when icase has 1 or 3 inside vertices. If 1 inside vertex: The 3 edges connecting the inside vertex to the 3 outside vertices are intersected. Connect the 3 intersection points to form 1 triangle. If 3 inside vertices: The 3 edges connecting the single outside vertex to the 3 inside vertices are intersected. Connect the 3 intersection points to form 1 triangle. Case 2 Segments (2 triangles): Occurs when icase has 2 inside and 2 outside vertices. The 4 intersected edges form a quadrilateral. Triangulate the quadrilateral into 2 triangles. The diagonal choice depends on icase to maintain manifold consistency: For icase 3, 6, 9, or 12: Connect vertices 1-2-3. For icase 5 or 10: Connect vertices 0-2-3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marchingtetrahedrons(volume, isovalue, dimensions): """ volume: 3D array of scalar values [X, Y, Z] isovalue: float threshold dimensions: tuple (xdim, ydim, zdim) Returns: list of triangles, each triangle is a list of 3 points (x,y,z) """ triangles = [] xdim, ydim, zdim = dimensions # Edge mapping for a tetrahedron with vertices 0,1,2,3 edgevertices = [(0,1), (1,2), (0,2), (1,3), (2,3), (0,3)] # Lookup table from lup = [ [-1,-1,-1,-1,-1,-1], # 0 [0, 2, 5, -1, -1, -1], # 1 [0, 1, 4, -1, -1, -1], # 2 [0, 1, 2, 4, -1, -1], # 3 [1, 2, 5, -1, -1, -1], # 4 [0, 1, 2, 5, -1, -1], # 5 [0, 2, 3, 4, -1, -1], # 6 [3, 4, 5, -1, -1, -1], # 7 [3, 4, 5, -1, -1, -1], # 8 [0, 2, 3, 4, -1, -1], # 9 [0, 1, 4, 5, -1, -1], # 10 [1, 2, 4, -1, -1, -1], # 11 [1, 2, 3, 5, -1, -1], # 12 [0, 1, 3, -1, -1, -1], # 13 [0, 2, 5, -1, -1, -1], # 14 [-1,-1,-1,-1,-1,-1] # 15 ] numsegments = [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 0] # Tetrahedra definitions for a voxel (consistent decomposition) # Indices refer to voxel corners 0-7. tetradefs = [ [0, 1, 2, 4], [1, 5, 2, 6], [2, 6, 3, 7], [4, 5, 6, 7], [1, 4, 5, 7], [0, 1, 4, 7] ] for z in range(zdim - 1): for y in range(ydim - 1): for x in range(xdim - 1): # Gather 8 voxel corners corners = [] for i in range(8): cx = x + (i & 1) cy = y + ((i >> 1) & 1) cz = z + ((i >> 2) & 1) corners.append((cx, cy, cz, volume[cx, cy, cz])) for tetra in tetradefs: vpos = [corners[i][:3] for i in tetra] vval = [corners[i][3] for i in tetra] # Compute case index icase = 0 for i in range(4): if vval[i] >= isovalue: icase |= (1 << i) nseg = numsegments[icase] if nseg == 0: continue # Compute intersection points pts = [] for eidx in lup[icase]: if eidx == -1: break v0, v1 = edgevertices[eidx] p0, p1 = vpos[v0], vpos[v1] f0, f1 = vval[v0], vval[v1] denom = f1 - f0 if abs(denom) < 1e-6: t = 0.5 else: t = (isovalue - f0) / denom t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) pts.append(p0 + t (p1 - p0)) # Generate triangles if nseg == 1: triangles.append([pts[0], pts[1], pts[2]]) else: # nseg == 2 triangles.append([pts[0], pts[1], pts[2]]) if icase in [3, 6, 9, 12]: triangles.append([pts[1], pts[2], pts[3]]) else: # icase in [5, 10] triangles.append([pts[0], pts[2], pts[3]]) return triangles An isosurface extraction method that uses an adaptive octree to subdivide a 3D volume only where the scalar field contains the target isovalue. At the leaf nodes (1x1x1 cubes), the volume is decomposed into tetrahedra, and the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm is applied to generate the mesh. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform-grid processing by reducing memory usage and computational cost for sparse or complex datasets. Unlike Naive Isosurface Extraction which processes every voxel, this method explicitly constructs an octree data structure to manage resolution adaptivity before decomposing leaf nodes into tetrahedra for precise surface intersection. Naive Isosurface Extraction is a surface extraction algorithm that processes each tetrahedron independently to generate a collection of individual, unconnected polygons. It differs from standard Marching Tetrahedra by iterating through all tetrahedra and their edges to find intersections with an isosurface, rather than using the standard 14-case lookup table based on vertex signs. GPU Vertex Shader Isosurface Extraction is a hardware-accelerated method for tessellating large unstructured tetrahedral grids by storing grid data in textures and performing isosurface extraction in the vertex shading unit. It solves the problem of data redundancy and memory limitations inherent in previous register-based GPU methods, which could not handle grids larger than ~1 million tetrahedra due to register pressure and PCI-Express transfer bottlenecks. Unlike its siblings, it uses indirect indexing via vertex texture lookup (Shader Model 3.0) to avoid sending redundant geometry for shared vertices, enabling the processing of millions of tetrahedra. Tetrahedral Volume Integration is a method for computing the scalar volume enclosed by an isosurface generated via tetrahedral decomposition. It solves the problem of quantifying the material volume within a grid cell by summing the volumes of the tetrahedra parts that lie inside the isosurface. Unlike surface extraction methods that only output geometry, this method provides a volumetric metric, distinguishing it from siblings like Marching Tetrahedrons which focus on triangle generation. Barycentric Mapping for Material Interfaces is an algorithm for reconstructing piecewise two-manifold boundary surfaces between multiple materials in a grid where each cell contains fractional volumetric information for each material. It transforms the reconstruction problem to analyze a dual data set where vertices have associated barycentric coordinate tuples representing material fractions. It sets itself apart from standard isosurface extraction by operating directly on volume-fraction data in unstructured triangular meshes, using the geometric properties of Voronoi cells in barycentric space to define interfaces rather than scalar field thresholds. Unlike SLIC, Youngs, or Gueffier algorithms which produce generally discontinuous interfaces and are limited to 2D or specific normal estimates, this algorithm produces a crack-free piecewise two-manifold, handles any number of materials per element, works on any grid structure (via tetrahedral conversion), and does not rely on application-specific hydrodynamics knowledge. An algorithm to extract isosurfaces from tetrahedral meshes on GPU that avoids sparse output arrays by using a prefix sum to determine output offsets, allowing separate handling of cells generating 1 vs 2 triangles. It builds on Marching Tetrahedrons by optimizing the memory layout and execution divergence of the triangle generation phase. An iso-surface extraction method that decomposes a voxel cube using a center cubic lattice (involving more tetrahedra per cube than the first method), resulting in more triangles, higher execution time, but better visual quality for complex models. When averaging values of a tetrahedron with one vertex inside and one outside along a long edge, positions outside the cube have zero value and inside have threshold value, causing artifacts at edges for medium cubes. It generates more triangles than the First Algorithm because each cube participates in a double amount of tetrahedra, leading to higher memory and execution time. It produces higher radius error from vertices and worse area/volume approximation than the First Algorithm, but provides better visual impression for complex models due to human eye sensitivity to edges and gradient changes. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels. Each voxel is decomposed into a constant number of tetrahedra (typically 6), and each tetrahedron is processed in constant time. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output mesh, as the number of triangles is proportional to the number of voxels. Performance: It is significantly slower than Marching Cubes because it generates approximately 4x more geometry (triangles). The increased vertex count also leads to higher memory bandwidth usage. Strengths: Guarantees a manifold surface without topological ambiguities. Works on unstructured tetrahedral grids as well as structured cubic grids. Simpler case analysis than Marching Cubes (only 8 cases, reducible to 3 by symmetry). Limitations: Higher computational cost and memory usage due to increased triangle count. Potential for degenerate triangles if interpolation is not handled carefully. Visual artifacts can occur with the "Second Algorithm" variant due to edge averaging. Marching Tetrahedrons was introduced by Doi and Koide as an alternative to Marching Cubes to resolve the topological ambiguities present in the latter. It works by decomposing each cubic voxel into tetrahedra, which eliminates the ambiguous cases (such as cases 6 and 7 in Marching Cubes) because a tetrahedron can only be split in one topologically consistent way for any given vertex configuration. The method has been widely studied for GPU acceleration due to its simplicity and parallelizability. adrian-sierra/Marching-Tetrahedrons, https://github.com/adrian-sierra/Marching-Tetrahedrons, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Scrawk/Marching-Cubes, https://github.com/Scrawk/Marching-Cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric Render Engine - GitHub, https://github.com/mikejernil/volumetric-render-engine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Torbenhjl/Marching-Tetrahedra-on-CT-headscan, https://github.com/Torbenhjl/Marching-Tetrahedra-on-CT-headscan, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) aaron-eugene/PlaneVoxelLab, https://github.com/aaron-eugene/PlaneVoxelLab, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Smooth Voxel Terrain (Part 2) – 0 FPS, https://0fps.net/2012/07/12/smooth-voxel-terrain-part-2/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) DAV Center: Marching Tetrahedra, https://daac.hpc.mil/gettingStarted/MarchingTetrahedra.html, fetched 2026-10-29 Isosurface Extraction on GPU with CUDA - POLARIS, https://polaris.imag.fr/arnaud.legrand/teaching/2009/iso-cuda.html, fetched 2026-10-30 Two Methods for Iso-Surface Extraction from Volumetric Data and Their Comparison, https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03446v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Octree Marching Tetrahedra
body: Adaptive Octree Marching Tetrahedra is an isosurface extraction method that uses an adaptive octree to subdivide a 3D volume only where the scalar field contains the target isovalue. At the leaf nodes (1x1x1 cubes), the volume is decomposed into tetrahedra, and the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm is applied to generate the mesh. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform-grid processing by reducing memory usage and computational cost for sparse or complex datasets. Unlike Naive Isosurface Extraction which processes every voxel, this method explicitly constructs an octree data structure to manage resolution adaptivity before decomposing leaf nodes into tetrahedra for precise surface intersection. Inputs: A 3D scalar field stored in a 1D array (e.g., teapotColour) of size 256 \times 256 \times 256. A target isovalue iso. Outputs: A list of vertices (newvert) and implied connectivity representing the isosurface. Data Structures: Point: A structure containing integer coordinates x, y, z. Default constructor initializes to (-1, -1, -1). Octree Node: point: Pointer to a Point. If NULL, the node is internal. If (-1, -1, -1), the node is empty. topLeftFront: Point defining the minimum corner (x1, y1, z1). bottomRightBack: Point defining the maximum corner (x2, y2, z2). children: A vector of 8 pointers to child Octree nodes. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Construction (make): For a node defined by topLeftFront (x1, y1, z1) and bottomRightBack (x2, y2, z2), calculate midpoints midx, midy, midz. Iterate through all voxels in the node's bounds to find miniso and maxiso from the scalar field using index z 256 256 + y 256 + x. Recursive Subdivision: If the node dimensions are greater than 1 (checked by (midx - x1) > 1 || (midy - y1) > 1 || (z2 - midz) > 1), create 8 child octants. The children are defined by the bounds: Child 0: (x1, y1, z1) to (midx, midy, midz) Child 1: (midx, y1, z1) to (x2, midy, midz) Child 2: (x1, midy, z1) to (midx, y2, midz) Child 3: (midx, midy, z1) to (x2, y2, midz) Child 4: (x1, y1, midz) to (midx, midy, z2) Child 5: (midx, y1, midz) to (x2, midy, z2) Child 6: (x1, midy, midz) to (midx, y2, z2) Child 7: (midx, midy, midz) to (x2, y2, z2) Recursively call make() on children if their dimensions exceed 1. 2. Leaf Processing (explore): When a leaf node is reached (dimensions equal 1, i.e., x2 - x1 = 1, y2 - y1 = 1, z2 - z1 = 1), identify the 8 vertices of the cube. Calculate indices into the scalar field array. Let a be the index for topLeftFront: a = z1 \cdot 256^2 + y1 \cdot 256 + x1 The other vertex indices are derived relative to a and the fixed width 256: b = a + 1 c = a + 257 d = a + 256 e = a + 256^2 f = e + 1 g = e + 257 h = e + 256 Retrieve scalar values col for the vertices involved in the tetrahedral decomposition. The source code decomposes the cube into 5 tetrahedra: (h,g,c,f), (h,c,d,b), (d,a,e,b), (h,d,e,b), (h,c,f,b). 3. Marching Tetrahedra Logic (tetra): Determine the case index based on which vertices are inside the isosurface (val > iso). For each edge connecting a vertex inside the isosurface to one outside, compute the intersection point using linear interpolation: P{inter} = P1 + \frac{iso - val1}{val2 - val1} (P2 - P1) where P1, P2 are vertex coordinates and val1, val2 are their scalar values. Store resulting vertices in newvert and increment the pointer p. Specific cases (e.g., 0x0C, 0x0E) define which edges are intersected. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Point: def init(self, x=0, y=0, z=0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Point(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Point(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, s): return Point(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) class OctreeNode: def init(self, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2): self.topLeftFront = Point(x1, y1, z1) self.bottomRightBack = Point(x2, y2, z2) self.children = [] def interpolate(p1, p2, v1, v2, iso): if v2 == v1: return p1 t = (iso - v1) / (v2 - v1) return p1 + (p2 - p1) t def buildoctree(node, scalarfield, width=256): x1, y1, z1 = node.topLeftFront.x, node.topLeftFront.y, node.topLeftFront.z x2, y2, z2 = node.bottomRightBack.x, node.bottomRightBack.y, node.bottomRightBack.z midx, midy, midz = (x1 + x2) // 2, (y1 + y2) // 2, (z1 + z2) // 2 if (x2 - x1 == 1) and (y2 - y1 == 1) and (z2 - z1 == 1): processleaf(node, scalarfield, width) return if (midx - x1 > 1) or (midy - y1 > 1) or (z2 - midz > 1): bounds = [ ((x1,y1,z1), (midx,midy,midz)), ((midx,y1,z1), (x2,midy,midz)), ((x1,midy,z1), (midx,y2,midz)), ((midx,midy,z1), (x2,y2,midz)), ((x1,y1,midz), (midx,midy,z2)), ((midx,y1,midz), (x2,midy,z2)), ((x1,midy,midz), (midx,y2,z2)), ((midx,midy,midz), (x2,y2,z2)) ] for (bx1, by1, bz1), (bx2, by2, bz2) in bounds: child = OctreeNode(bx1, by1, bz1, bx2, by2, bz2) node.children.append(child) if (bx2 - bx1 > 1) or (by2 - by1 > 1) or (bz2 - bz1 > 1): buildoctree(child, scalarfield, width) else: processleaf(child, scalarfield, width) def processleaf(node, scalarfield, width=256): x1, y1, z1 = node.topLeftFront.x, node.topLeftFront.y, node.topLeftFront.z x2, y2, z2 = node.bottomRightBack.x, node.bottomRightBack.y, node.bottomRightBack.z a = z1 width width + y1 width + x1 b, c, d = a + 1, a + width + 1, a + width e, f, g, h = a + width width, e + 1, e + width + 1, e + width coords = [ Point(x1, y1, z2), Point(x2, y1, z2), Point(x1, y1, z1), Point(x2, y1, z1), Point(x1, y2, z2), Point(x2, y2, z2), Point(x1, y2, z1), Point(x2, y2, z1) ] vals = [scalarfield[h], scalarfield[g], scalarfield[c], scalarfield[f], scalarfield[d], scalarfield[b], scalarfield[a], scalarfield[e]] tets = [ (0,1,2,3), (0,2,4,5), (4,6,7,5), (0,4,7,5), (0,2,3,5) ] for t in tets: tetraextract([vals[i] for i in t], [coords[i] for i in t]) def tetraextract(vals, coords): case = 0 for i, v in enumerate(vals): if v > iso: case |= (1 << i) intersections = [] edges = [(0,1),(0,2),(0,3),(1,2),(1,3),(2,3)] for i, j in edges: if (vals[i] > iso) != (vals[j] > iso): intersections.append(interpolate(coords[i], coords[j], vals[i], vals[j], iso)) # Standard MT triangle assembly from intersected edges triverts = [] for k, p in enumerate(intersections): triverts.append(p) # Assemble triangles based on case bitmask if case in [0x3, 0xC, 0x5, 0xA, 0x9, 0x6, 0xF, 0x0]: pass # No triangles for empty/full cases else: # Connect intersections sequentially to form triangles for i in range(0, len(triverts) - 2, 2): newvert.append(triverts[i]) newvert.append(triverts[i+1]) newvert.append(triverts[i+2]) Parameters: iso: Target isovalue. width: Fixed grid width for indexing. Source hardcodes 256. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grid Indexing Assumption: The source code assumes a fixed grid width of 256 for index calculation (z 256 256 + y 256 + x). This will fail for volumes with different Y-axis dimensions or non-standard strides. Vertex Labeling Ambiguity: The variable names a through h in the source code do not consistently correspond to standard vertex positions. The mapping between col array indices and Vertices array indices in the tetra function is unclear and may lead to incorrect edge intersections if not carefully reverse-engineered. An extension that introduces "dual vertices" within octree cells to minimize distance to local tangent planes, improving sharp feature approximation and reducing sliver triangles. Choose this when high-fidelity geometry is required and the basic tetrahedralization produces artifacts. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of leaf nodes in the octree. In the worst case (uniform subdivision), N is proportional to the total number of voxels. In the best case (sparse data), N is significantly smaller. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the octree structure and the resulting mesh vertices. The octree nodes add overhead compared to a flat grid. Performance: Reduces computation time for sparse volumes by avoiding processing empty or uniform regions. Performance degrades if the isosurface is complex and requires deep subdivision across the entire volume. Strengths: Efficient for sparse data; adaptive resolution allows high detail where needed. Limitations: Hard-coded indexing in the reference implementation limits flexibility; vertex labeling ambiguity complicates implementation; standard MT can produce sliver triangles. When to use: When the volume is sparse or has varying feature density, and memory is a constraint. When not to use: When the volume is dense and uniform, or when strict topological correctness is required without additional post-processing (standard MT can have connectivity issues at boundaries). The method originates from an implementation by yashwanth850, described in a GitHub repository "Domain-search-isosurface-extraction". It builds upon the foundational Marching Tetrahedra algorithm by incorporating an adaptive octree structure to manage spatial subdivision. The specific implementation details, including the octree traversal and tetrahedral decomposition, are derived from this source code. yashwanth850/Domain-search-isosurface-extraction, https://github.com/yashwanth850/Domain-search-isosurface-extraction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Simplicial Partitioning with Dual Vertices
head: Adaptive simplicial partitioning, Dual vertex placement on simplicial partitions
body: Adaptive Simplicial Partitioning with Dual Vertices is an isosurface extraction method that constructs a simplicial complex from an adaptive octree to facilitate mesh generation. It differs from standard Marching Tetrahedra by introducing "dual vertices" within octree cells (cubes, faces, edges) rather than using only the grid vertices. These dual vertices are positioned to minimize distance to local tangent planes, allowing for better approximation of sharp features and reducing the sliver triangles common in naive tetrahedralizations. It builds on Adaptive Octree Marching Tetrahedra by refining the geometric representation within the leaf nodes and their shared boundaries. Inputs: An adaptive octree representing a scalar field F(\mathbf{p}), a target isovalue I, and a small epsilon \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}) to prevent boundary degeneracy. Outputs: A set of tetrahedra forming the isosurface mesh. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains spatial bounds, scalar values at vertices, and a flag indicating if it is a leaf (minimal 3-cell). Dual Vertex: A 4D point \bar{p} = \langle \mathbf{p}, F(\mathbf{p}) \rangle \in \mathbb{R}^4, where \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position and F(\mathbf{p}) is the function value. For 0-cells (vertices), \bar{p} coincides with the octree vertex. For m-cells (m > 0), \mathbf{p} is constrained to lie strictly inside the cell, scaled by 1-\epsilon. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify Minimal Cells: Traverse the octree to find all minimal m-cells. A minimal m-cell is a cell of dimension m that does not contain any other cells of dimension m as a subset. Minimal 3-cells are leaf cubes. Minimal 2-cells are faces shared by adjacent leaf cubes. Minimal 1-cells are edges shared by adjacent minimal faces. Minimal 0-cells are vertices. 2. Sample Field Data: For each minimal m-cell, sample the scalar field F(\mathbf{p}) and the normal vector \bar{n}i = \langle \nabla F(\mathbf{p}i), -1 \rangle at each octree vertex \mathbf{p}i on the boundary of the cell. If m < 3, restrict the gradient \nabla F(\mathbf{p}i) to the subspace defined by the cell by projecting it onto that subspace. 3. Compute Dual Vertices: For each minimal m-cell, compute the dual vertex \bar{x} = \langle \mathbf{x}, F(\mathbf{x}) \rangle by minimizing the squared distance to the tangent planes defined by the boundary samples. The tangent plane at vertex \mathbf{p}i is defined by normal \bar{n}i and point \bar{p}i. Solve the constrained optimization problem: \min{\bar{x}} \sumi (\bar{n}i \cdot \bar{x} - \bar{n}i \cdot \bar{p}i)^2 subject to the constraint that the spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} lie within the cell scaled by 1-\epsilon. This is a quadratic minimization with box constraints. A standard method for solving this is described by Lindstrom et al. [LS01]. Pitfall: In regions of high curvature, the function value F(\mathbf{x}) derived from this plane intersection may be a poor estimate (consistently high or low), potentially causing dimpling. 4. Recursive Tetrahedralization: Construct the simplicial complex recursively based on dimension m. Base Case (m=0): Each minimal 0-cell (vertex) is a 0-simplex (point) consisting of its dual vertex. Recursive Step: For each minimal (i+1)-cell with a dual vertex, connect this dual vertex to all i-simplices defined on the boundary of the (i+1)-cell. This forms a set of (i+1)-simplices. Example: Edges (1-simplices) are formed by connecting edge-dual vertices to the 0-simplices (vertices) at their endpoints. Example: Faces (2-simplices) are formed by connecting face-dual vertices to the 1-simplices (edges) on their boundary. Example: Cubes (3-simplices/tetrahedra) are formed by connecting cube-dual vertices to the 2-simplices (faces) on their boundary. 5. Isosurface Extraction: Apply the standard Marching Tetrahedra algorithm [DK91] to the resulting tetrahedra (3-simplices) to extract the isosurface. The scalar values at the dual vertices are used to determine which edges of the tetrahedra intersect the isovalue. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivesimplicialpartitioning(octree, isovalue, epsilon): """ Extracts isosurface using adaptive simplicial partitioning. Args: octree: Root node of the adaptive octree. isovalue: The target scalar value for the isosurface. epsilon: Small value to constrain dual vertices away from cell boundaries. Returns: List of tetrahedra (each defined by 4 indices into the dual vertex list). """ minimalcells = collectminimalcells(octree) dualvertices = {} # Step 2 & 3: Compute dual vertices for cell in minimalcells: boundarypts = getboundaryvertices(cell) samples = [] for pi in boundarypts: fval = evaluatefield(pi) grad = computegradient(pi) if cell.dim < 3: grad = projectgradientontosubspace(grad, cell) n4d = (grad[0], grad[1], grad[2], -1.0) p4d = (pi[0], pi[1], pi[2], fval) samples.append((p4d, n4d)) A = [s[1][:3] for s in samples] b = [dot4(s[1], s[0]) for s in samples] xspatial = solveboxconstrainedleastsquares(A, b, cell.bounds, epsilon) fx = evaluatefield(xspatial) dualvertices[cell.id] = (xspatial[0], xspatial[1], xspatial[2], fx) # Step 4: Recursive Tetrahedralization simplices = {0: [], 1: [], 2: []} tetrahedra = [] for cell in minimalcells: if cell.dim == 0: simplices[0].append([cell.id]) elif cell.dim == 1: verts = [cell.id] + [b.id for b in getboundarycells(cell, 0)] simplices[1].append(verts) elif cell.dim == 2: verts = [cell.id] for edge in getboundarycells(cell, 1): verts.extend(simplices[1][edge.idx]) simplices[2].append(verts) elif cell.dim == 3: verts = [cell.id] for face in getboundarycells(cell, 2): verts.extend(simplices[2][face.idx]) tetrahedra.append(verts) # Step 5: Isosurface Extraction mesh = [] for tet in tetrahedra: vals = [dualvertices[v][3] for v in tet] mesh.extend(marchingtetrahedrastep(tet, vals, isovalue)) return mesh def collectminimalcells(node): """Traverses octree to collect minimal cells of all dimensions.""" cells = [] if node.isleaf: cells.append(node) # Boundary cells (faces, edges, vertices) are derived from adjacent leaves for adj in node.adjacentleaves: if adj is not None: cells.extend(adj.boundarycells) else: for child in node.children: cells.extend(collectminimalcells(child)) return cells def getboundaryvertices(cell): return cell.vertices def computegradient(p): h = 1e-5 dx = (evaluatefield((p[0]+h, p[1], p[2])) - evaluatefield((p[0]-h, p[1], p[2]))) / (2h) dy = (evaluatefield((p[0], p[1]+h, p[2])) - evaluatefield((p[0], p[1]-h, p[2]))) / (2h) dz = (evaluatefield((p[0], p[1], p[2]+h)) - evaluatefield((p[0], p[1], p[2]-h))) / (2h) return (dx, dy, dz) def projectgradientontosubspace(grad, cell): """Projects gradient onto the subspace defined by the cell dimension.""" if cell.dim == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) elif cell.dim == 1: edgedir = normalize(cell.vertices[1][0]-cell.vertices[0][0], cell.vertices[1][1]-cell.vertices[0][1], cell.vertices[1][2]-cell.vertices[0][2]) dot = sum(gd for g, d in zip(grad, edgedir)) return (dotedgedir[0], dotedgedir[1], dotedgedir[2]) elif cell.dim == 2: # Project onto face plane by removing normal component facenormal = computefacenormal(cell) dot = sum(gn for g, n in zip(grad, facenormal)) return (grad[0]-dotfacenormal[0], grad[1]-dotfacenormal[1], grad[2]-dotfacenormal[2]) return grad def solveboxconstrainedleastsquares(A, b, bounds, epsilon): """Solves min ||Ax - b||^2 subject to bounds using projected gradient descent.""" lower = tuple(b (1 - epsilon) for b in bounds[0]) upper = tuple(b (1 - epsilon) for b in bounds[1]) x = [(lower[i] + upper[i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] lr = 0.01 for in range(100): Axb = [sum(a xi for a, xi in zip(row, x)) - bi for row, bi in zip(A, b)] grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): for row, diff in zip(A, Axb): grad[i] += 2.0 row[i] diff x = [x[i] - lr grad[i] for i in range(3)] x = [max(lower[i], min(upper[i], x[i])) for i in range(3)] return tuple(x) def getboundarycells(cell, dimension): return cell.boundarycells[dimension] def marchingtetrahedrastep(tet, vals, isovalue): """Standard Marching Tetrahedra lookup table implementation.""" intersections = [] # Standard MT logic: determine case from sign bits, interpolate edge intersections, return triangles return intersections A post-processing step to reduce sliver triangles by moving dual vertices onto the isosurface while keeping them within their respective cells. Time Complexity: Dominated by the octree traversal and the solution of the least-squares problem for each minimal cell. The least-squares problem is small (constant size per cell) but involves solving a constrained quadratic program. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of minimal cells in the octree, as each requires storing a dual vertex. Strengths: Better approximation of sharp features compared to standard grid-based methods; reduces T-intersections by constraining dual vertices within cells; adaptive resolution allows for efficient representation of complex geometries. Limitations: The function value estimation at dual vertices can be inaccurate in high-curvature regions, leading to visual artifacts like dimpling. The recursive tetrahedralization and subsequent Marching Tetrahedra step add complexity. When to use: When high-quality isosurfaces with sharp features are required from adaptive data, and standard Marching Cubes/Tetrahedra produce insufficiently smooth or accurate results. The method was introduced by Lindstrom et al. in the paper "Isosurfaces Over Simplicial Partitions of Multiresolution Grids". It extends the concept of simplicial partitions to multiresolution grids (octrees), allowing for adaptive refinement. The approach addresses the limitations of uniform grid methods and standard adaptive methods by providing a more flexible geometric representation within the cells. name: Triangulation Improvement via Isosurface Projection
head: Moving dual vertices to the isosurface, Surface triangulation improvement
body: A post-processing step for isosurface extraction that reduces sliver triangles by moving dual vertices onto the isosurface while keeping them within their respective cells. It differs from standard Marching Tetrahedra by explicitly correcting vertex positions to minimize geometric error, addressing the issue where vertices pass close to the isosurface and create numerous small, sliver triangles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A simplicial partition with dual vertices x located within cells, and a scalar field F(p). Output: An improved mesh where dual vertices lie on the isosurface F(p)=0, with degenerate triangles removed. Data Structures: Dual vertices: Stored with their associated cell dimension m (0 for vertex, 1 for edge, 2 for face, 3 for cube). Boundary graph: Adjacency list or Union-Find structure for topological testing. Parameters: \epsilon: Small constant used in the parent method to scale cells, which defines cell boundaries. Bisection tolerance: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Ordering: Process cells from highest dimension m to lowest dimension 0 (3 to 0). This ensures that when a vertex is processed, its position is independent of lower-dimensional vertices that might depend on it. 2. Topological Safety Test: Before moving a dual vertex x in an m-cell, verify that the portion of the isosurface intersecting the cell is a topological disk. Build a graph of edges on the cell boundary connecting dual vertices of dimension i < m. For m=1 (edge): Test that the two boundary vertices have opposite signs. For m=2 (face): Check that there are exactly two sign changes along the boundary ring. For m=3 (cube): Use the Union-Find algorithm to find connected components in the boundary graph. The test passes if the boundary forms a connected sheet with two disjoint inside/outside vertex sets. If the test fails, do not move the vertex. 3. Direction Selection: If the test passes, evaluate the error at each dual vertex on the boundary (dimension i < m) that has an opposite sign to x. Choose the boundary vertex v{bound} with the smallest error. The error metric is defined by Equation 1 in the source, which is not provided here. 4. Bisection: Perform a bisection algorithm between the current dual vertex x and the chosen boundary vertex v{bound} to find a new position x{new} such that F(x{new}) = 0 and x{new} lies on the isosurface. 5. Update: Replace x with x{new}. 6. Degeneracy Removal: After all vertices are processed, remove any triangles that become degenerate due to the vertex movement. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def improvetriangulation(dualvertices, scalarfield, boundarygraphs): # Process from m=3 down to m=0 for m in [3, 2, 1, 0]: for cell in dualvertices: if cell.dimension != m: continue x = cell.vertex boundaryvertices = getboundaryvertices(cell) # Not given in the sources. # Topological Safety Test if not istopologicallysafe(cell, boundaryvertices, scalarfield): continue # Find best direction oppositevertices = [v for v in boundaryvertices if scalarfield(v) scalarfield(x) < 0] if not oppositevertices: continue # Select vertex with smallest error (Equation 1 not provided in sources) vbound = min(oppositevertices, key=lambda v: computeerror(v, x)) # Not given in the sources. # Bisection to find isosurface intersection xnew = bisectionisosurface(x, vbound, scalarfield) # Update vertex position cell.vertex = xnew # Remove degenerate triangles removedegeneratetriangles(dualvertices) # Not given in the sources. def istopologicallysafe(cell, boundaryvertices, scalarfield): m = cell.dimension if m == 1: if len(boundaryvertices) != 2: return False return scalarfield(boundaryvertices[0]) scalarfield(boundaryvertices[1]) < 0 elif m == 2: signchanges = 0 for i in range(len(boundaryvertices)): v1 = boundaryvertices[i] v2 = boundaryvertices[(i + 1) % len(boundaryvertices)] if scalarfield(v1) scalarfield(v2) < 0: signchanges += 1 return signchanges == 2 elif m == 3: graph = buildboundarygraph(cell) # Not given in the sources. components = unionfindcomponents(graph) # Standard Union-Find. if len(components) != 1: return False signs = [scalarfield(v) for v in graph.nodes] haspos = any(s > 0 for s in signs) hasneg = any(s < 0 for s in signs) return haspos and hasneg return True def bisectionisosurface(x1, x2, scalarfield, tol=1e-6): while distance(x1, x2) > tol: # Standard Euclidean distance. mid = (x1 + x2) / 2.0 fmid = scalarfield(mid) if fmid == 0: return mid if scalarfield(x1) fmid < 0: x2 = mid else: x1 = mid return x1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Moving vertices can change topology, creating non-manifold geometry if the portion of the isosurface intersecting the cell is not a topological disk. The topological safety test is required to prevent this. The value at the dual vertices and the magnitude of the gradient cannot be used to indicate proximity to the isosurface because no restrictions are placed on F(p). Time Complexity: Depends on the bisection iterations and the Union-Find operations. The Union-Find algorithm takes nearly linear time to find connected components in a graph. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the boundary graph for topological testing. Strengths: Reduces sliver triangles; preserves sharp features; exact topological safety test. Limitations: Can create non-manifold geometry if the safety test is skipped; requires careful handling of degenerate triangles. Developed for isosurfaces over simplicial partitions of multiresolution grids. It adapts a technique similar to Hall et al. [HW90]. The method addresses the issue of sliver triangles in Marching Tetrahedra-like methods where vertices pass close to the isosurface. name: Naive Isosurface Extraction
body: Naive Isosurface Extraction is a surface extraction algorithm that processes each tetrahedron independently to generate a collection of individual, unconnected polygons. It differs from standard Marching Tetrahedra by iterating through all tetrahedra and their edges to find intersections with an isosurface, rather than using the standard 14-case lookup table based on vertex signs. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh containing N tetrahedra. A scalar field defined at the vertices of the mesh. A scalar isovalue f{iso} defining the level set. Outputs: A polygonal surface representation consisting of a list of vertices and a list of polygons. Data Structures: Input Tetrahedron: Defined by 4 vertex indices and associated scalar values. Output Points: A dynamic list of 3D coordinates. Output Cells: A dynamic list of polygons, where each polygon is defined by a list of vertex indices into the Output Points list. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Output: Create empty lists for output vertices and polygons. 2. Loop over Tetrahedra: For each tetrahedron Ti in the input mesh: a. Check Intersection: Call IsCellOnLevelSet(Ti, f{iso}). Retrieve scalar values for all vertices of Ti. Determine if the level set intersects Ti. If not intersected, continue to the next tetrahedron. b. Compute Intersection Polygon: Call ComputeSimpleIntersection(Ti, f{iso}). Initialize an empty list pointIds to store vertex indices of the resulting polygon. Loop over Edges: Iterate through all 6 edges of the tetrahedron. Check Edge Intersection: For each edge, call IsCellOnLevelSet(edge, f{iso}). Compute Intersection Point: If the edge is intersected, call ComputeEdgeIntersection(edge, f{iso}). Calculate the intersection point P using linear interpolation. Add P to the Output Points list and record its index. Append the index to pointIds. Order Vertices: Call ReOrderTetEdges(pointIds, Ti) to ensure consistent winding. This function re-orders the list of intersected edges such that the list describes a consistent winding around the tetrahedron. Insert Polygon: Call Output->InsertNextCell(VTKPOLYGON, pointIds). 3. Finalize: Return the constructed output surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def naiveisosurfaceextraction(tetmesh, vertexcoords, scalarfield, isovalue): """ Extracts isosurface from a tetrahedral mesh using the naive approach. Args: tetmesh: List of tetrahedra, each defined as [v0, v1, v2, v3] (vertex indices). vertexcoords: Array of 3D coordinates indexed by vertex index. scalarfield: Array of scalar values indexed by vertex index. isovalue: The scalar value defining the isosurface. Returns: outputpoints: List of 3D coordinates. outputpolys: List of polygons, each defined as a list of vertex indices. """ outputpoints = [] outputpolys = [] def iscellonlevelset(cellvertices, isovalue): scalars = [scalarfield[v] for v in cellvertices] return min(scalars) <= isovalue <= max(scalars) def computeedgeintersection(v0, v1, f0, f1, isovalue): if abs(f1 - f0) < 1e-10: return ((v0[0] + v1[0]) / 2.0, (v0[1] + v1[1]) / 2.0, (v0[2] + v1[2]) / 2.0) t = (isovalue - f0) / (f1 - f0) return (v0[0] + t (v1[0] - v0[0]), v0[1] + t (v1[1] - v0[1]), v0[2] + t (v1[2] - v0[2])) def reordertetedges(intersectededges): # Re-orders the list of intersected edges to form a consistent winding around the tetrahedron if len(intersectededges) < 2: return intersectededges adj = {i: [] for i in range(len(intersectededges))} for i, (e1, e2) in enumerate(intersectededges): for j, (e3, e4) in enumerate(intersectededges): if i != j and (e1 == e3 or e1 == e4 or e2 == e3 or e2 == e4): adj[i].append(j) visited = [False] len(intersectededges) cycle = [] curr = 0 while not visited[curr]: visited[curr] = True cycle.append(intersectededges[curr]) nxt = adj[curr][0] if adj[curr] else -1 if nxt == -1 or visited[nxt]: break curr = nxt return cycle for tet in tetmesh: v0, v1, v2, v3 = tet if not iscellonlevelset(tet, isovalue): continue pointids = [] intersectededges = [] edges = [(v0, v1), (v0, v2), (v0, v3), (v1, v2), (v1, v3), (v2, v3)] for va, vb in edges: fa = scalarfield[va] fb = scalarfield[vb] if (fa - isovalue) (fb - isovalue) < 0: pa = vertexcoords[va] pb = vertexcoords[vb] pintersect = computeedgeintersection(pa, pb, fa, fb, isovalue) idx = len(outputpoints) outputpoints.append(pintersect) pointids.append(idx) intersectededges.append((va, vb)) orderededges = reordertetedges(intersectededges) edgetoidx = {e: pointids[i] for i, e in enumerate(intersectededges)} finalids = [edgetoidx[e] for e in orderededges] outputpolys.append(finalids) return outputpoints, outputpolys Parameters: isovalue: The scalar threshold defining the level set. tolerance: Not explicitly defined in the naive source, but precision issues with floating-point comparisons in iscellonlevelset can cause cracks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Vertices: The naive approach creates a new vertex for every intersection on every tetrahedron, leading to duplicate vertices at shared edges and non-manifold surfaces with cracks. Inconsistent Winding: If the order of vertices in the generated polygon is inconsistent, visual artifacts like cracks appear. Performance: The approach is slow compared to optimized implementations because it does not reuse vertex data and may perform redundant calculations. Adaptive Octree Marching Tetrahedra is a variant that uses an adaptive octree structure to refine the mesh only where necessary, reducing the number of tetrahedra processed. It differs from Naive Isosurface Extraction by dynamically adjusting resolution based on scalar field gradients, rather than processing a uniform or pre-defined tetrahedral mesh. Choose this when high-resolution details are localized and computational resources are limited. Link to sibling article. Naive Tetrahedral Surfacing is an isosurface extraction method that processes each tetrahedron independently to generate a collection of individual, unconnected polygons. It differs from standard Marching Tetrahedra by iterating through all tetrahedra and their edges to find intersections with an isosurface, rather than using the standard 14-case lookup table based on vertex signs. This approach builds on Marching Tetrahedrons by operating on the tetrahedral subgrid structure. Link to child article. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot E), where N is the number of tetrahedra and E is the number of edges per tetrahedron (constant 6). However, due to the lack of vertex reuse and potential inefficiencies in polygon construction, it is significantly slower than optimized methods. Memory Complexity: O(V{out} + F{out}), where V{out} is the number of output vertices and F{out} is the number of output polygons. Since vertices are duplicated, V{out} can be up to 6 times larger than necessary for a manifold surface. Measured Performance: The naive implementation is notably slower than VTK's optimized implementation, as noted in the exercise comparison. Strengths: Simple to implement; no complex data structures for neighbor lookup or vertex merging required. Limitations: Produces non-manifold surfaces with cracks due to duplicate vertices and inconsistent winding. Not suitable for applications requiring manifold connectivity or efficient rendering. When to Use: Educational purposes or simple visualization where manifold connectivity is not critical. When Not to Use: Production rendering, simulation, or any application requiring manifold surfaces or high performance. The naive approach to isosurface extraction from tetrahedral meshes is described in visualization exercises by Julien Tierny. It serves as a baseline for understanding the challenges of surface extraction, such as vertex duplication and winding consistency, before introducing more sophisticated techniques like vertex reuse or lookup tables. name: Naive Tetrahedral Surfacing
head: Naive Tetrahedral Marching Tetrahedra, Pairwise Intersection Method, Tetrahedral Marching Tetrahedra (Naive/Brute-Force Variant)
body: Naive Tetrahedral Surfacing is an isosurface extraction method that processes each tetrahedron independently to generate a collection of individual, unconnected polygons. It differs from standard Marching Tetrahedra by iterating through all pairs of sample points to find intersections with an isosurface, rather than using the standard 14-case lookup table based on vertex signs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tetrahedron defined by four sample points (vertices) and their corresponding scalar field values. Input: isoval, the scalar threshold defining the isosurface. Output: A list of 3D vertices (vertices) representing the intersection points on the tetrahedron edges. Data Structures: samppts: A list of 4 Vector3 objects representing the tetrahedron vertices. surfvals: A list of 4 float values representing the scalar field evaluated at each vertex in samppts. lessthaniso: A list of Vector3 objects containing vertices where value < isoval. lessval: A list of float values corresponding to lessthaniso. morethaniso: A list of Vector3 objects containing vertices where value >= isoval. moreval: A list of float values corresponding to morethaniso. vertices: An output list of Vector3 objects storing the calculated intersection points. Steps: 1. Evaluate the scalar function at all sample points (vertices) of the tetrahedron to obtain surfvals. 2. Partition the sample points and their values into two lists: lessthaniso and lessval for points where value < isoval, and morethaniso and moreval for points where value >= isoval. 3. Iterate through every point v1 in lessthaniso and every point v2 in morethaniso to form candidate edges. 4. For each pair (v1, v2), calculate the intersection vertex newvertex using linear interpolation. 5. Add newvertex to the output vertices list. If the index i of the morethaniso point is even, push to front; otherwise, push to back. This ordering logic is specific to this implementation's output format and does not guarantee consistent triangle winding or connectivity without further processing. Formula: The intersection vertex is calculated as: \text{new\vertex} = \frac{v1 \cdot \text{diff}2 + v2 \cdot \text{diff}1}{\text{diff\tot}} Where: \text{diff\tot} = |val1 - val2| \text{diff}1 = |val1 - \text{iso\val}| \text{diff}2 = |val2 - \text{iso\val}| This is equivalent to standard linear interpolation: \text{new\vertex} = v1 + (v2 - v1) \cdot \frac{\text{iso\val} - val1}{val2 - val1} Parameters: isoval: The scalar threshold value defining the isosurface. Typical value depends on the field (e.g., 0 for signed distance fields). eps: A hardcoded epsilon value (0.1) used in lessthan for lexicographical comparison of points, though the code comments note this function was abandoned because duplicate vertices are considered acceptable. Pitfalls: The algorithm performs a pairwise comparison of all 'less' and 'more' points. For a tetrahedron with 4 vertices, if 2 are less and 2 are more, this results in 2 \times 2 = 4 intersection calculations, whereas standard MT only generates 2 edges. This is computationally inefficient and may generate redundant or incorrect geometry if the topology assumption (that every less point connects to every more point) is invalid for the specific scalar field distribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from typing import List def naivetetrahedralsurfacing(samppts: List[Vector3], surfvals: List[float], isoval: float) -> List[Vector3]: """ Extracts isosurface intersection vertices from a single tetrahedron using naive pairwise intersection. Args: samppts: List of 4 Vector3 vertices of the tetrahedron. surfvals: List of 4 floats, scalar values at each vertex. isoval: The isosurface threshold. Returns: List of Vector3 intersection points. """ lessthaniso: List[Vector3] = [] lessval: List[float] = [] morethaniso: List[Vector3] = [] moreval: List[float] = [] vertices: List[Vector3] = [] # Step 2: Partition points for i in range(4): if surfvals[i] < isoval: lessthaniso.append(samppts[i]) lessval.append(surfvals[i]) else: morethaniso.append(samppts[i]) moreval.append(surfvals[i]) # Step 3 & 4: Pairwise intersection for i, v1 in enumerate(lessthaniso): val1 = lessval[i] for j, v2 in enumerate(morethaniso): val2 = moreval[j] difftot = abs(val1 - val2) # Guard against division by zero if values are identical if difftot == 0: continue diff1 = abs(val1 - isoval) diff2 = abs(val2 - isoval) # Formula: newvertex = (v1 diff2 + v2 diff1) / difftot newvertex = (v1 diff2 + v2 diff1) / difftot # Step 5: Add to output with specific ordering # If the index of the morethaniso point is even, push to front; otherwise, push to back if j % 2 == 0: vertices.insert(0, newvertex) else: vertices.append(newvertex) return vertices Time Complexity: O(1) per tetrahedron, but with a higher constant factor than standard MT. In the worst case (2 less, 2 more vertices), it performs 4 intersection calculations instead of 2. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per tetrahedron for storing partitioned lists. Strengths: Simple to implement; does not require a complex case lookup table. Limitations: Generates redundant vertices; does not produce connected polygons directly; computationally inefficient for certain configurations; lacks topological consistency guarantees. When to use: When simplicity of implementation is prioritized over performance and connectivity, or for educational purposes. When not to use: When high performance, mesh connectivity, or topological correctness is required. Naive Tetrahedral Surfacing is an unofficial method described in a GitHub repository. It represents a brute-force variant of the Marching Tetrahedra algorithm, abandoning the standard case-based approach in favor of pairwise edge intersection. The specific implementation details, including the epsilon value and vertex ordering logic, are derived from this source. ajinkyajayawant/surfacing-tetrahedral, https://github.com/ajinkyajayawant/surfacing-tetrahedral, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Vertex Shader Isosurface Extraction
head: Vertex Shader Isosurface Extraction, Vertex shader tetrahedral marching, Pascucci's Programmable Isosurfacing
body: GPU Vertex Shader Isosurface Extraction is a hardware-accelerated method for tessellating large unstructured tetrahedral grids by storing grid data in textures and performing isosurface extraction in the vertex shading unit. It solves the problem of data redundancy and memory limitations inherent in previous register-based GPU methods, which could not handle grids larger than ~1 million tetrahedra due to register pressure and PCI-Express transfer bottlenecks. Unlike its siblings, it uses indirect indexing via vertex texture lookup (Shader Model 3.0) to avoid sending redundant geometry for shared vertices, enabling the processing of millions of tetrahedra. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unstructured tetrahedral grid defined by vertex positions, scalar values, and connectivity (tetrahedron-to-vertex indices). An isovalue scalar threshold. Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface. Data Structures: The method uses four 1D textures. Each texel stores four values (RGBA components) or packed geometry/scalars: 1. tetratexture: One texel per tetrahedron, storing the indices of its four vertices in the RGBA components. 2. verticestexture: One texel per vertex, packing 3D geometry in the XYZ components and the scalar value in the Alpha (A) component. An optional extra texel per vertex can store a precomputed gradient. 3. tableofcasestexture: A 1D lookup table mapping (caseindex, vertexnumber) pairs to the index of the intersected edge. The table is symmetric, so only the first half is stored. Some edge indexes are duplicated to handle all configurations, resulting in stacked vertices that are discarded during rendering. 4. tableofedgestexture: A 1D lookup table mapping edge indices to their two endpoint vertex indices. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Generate the tableofcasestexture and tableofedgestexture based on the Marching Tetrahedra topology. Iterate over each vertex of the grid to pack its 3D geometry and scalar value into a texel in verticestexture. Iterate over each tetrahedron to pack its four vertex indices into a texel in tetratexture. Load all textures into graphics memory and load the vertex shading program. 2. Rendering Loop (Per Tetrahedron): Set the isovalue parameter for the shader. Send the current tetrahedron index to the GPU. Issue a draw call for a single quadrilateral with 4 vertices (representing the 4 corners of the tetrahedron). The vertex shader is executed once for each vertex of the quadrilateral. 3. Vertex Shader Execution (for each vertex v of the quadrilateral, v \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}): Retrieve Tetrahedron Indices: Read the four vertex indices of the current tetrahedron from tetratexture using the cell index. Retrieve Vertex Data: Read the location and scalar value for each of the four vertices from verticestexture using the indices obtained above. Determine Configuration: Extract scalar values from the alpha channel and compare against the isovalue to determine the case index. Exploit Symmetry: Map the case index to the first half of the symmetric table. Lookup Intersected Edge: For the current vertex v being processed, look up the intersected edge index from tableofcasestexture using the key index 4 + v. Lookup Edge Endpoints: Retrieve the two endpoint vertex indices of the intersected edge from tableofedgestexture. Interpolate and Output: Linearly interpolate the intersection point on the edge with the isosurface using the scalar values of the endpoints and the isovalue. Output the vertex at this interpolated location. Note: In cases where no intersection occurs for a specific vertex configuration, the shader may output degenerate polygons or stacked vertices which are discarded by the rasterizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class float4: def init(self, r, g, b, a): self.r, self.g, self.b, self.a = r, g, b, a class float3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def tex1D(texture, index): """Standard 1D texture lookup returning a 4-component vector.""" return texture[index] def dot(v, w): return v.rw.r + v.gw.g + v.bw.b + v.aw.a def lerp(a, b, t): return a + (b - a) t def vertexshader(cellindex, isovalue, vertexnumber): # 1. Get tetrahedron vertex indices tetraindices = tex1D(tetratexture, cellindex) # 2. Get vertex data (pos, scalar) for all 4 vertices v0data = tex1D(verticestexture, tetraindices.r) v1data = tex1D(verticestexture, tetraindices.g) v2data = tex1D(verticestexture, tetraindices.b) v3data = tex1D(verticestexture, tetraindices.a) # 3. Extract scalars scalars = float4(v0data.a, v1data.a, v2data.a, v3data.a) # 4. Compute case index flags = float4( 1.0 if scalars.r >= isovalue else 0.0, 1.0 if scalars.g >= isovalue else 0.0, 1.0 if scalars.b >= isovalue else 0.0, 1.0 if scalars.a >= isovalue else 0.0) caseindex = dot(flags, float4(1, 2, 4, 8)) # 5. Symmetry reduction if caseindex >= 8: caseindex = 15 - caseindex # 6. Lookup intersected edge for this specific vertex of the quad edgeindex = tex1D(tableofcasestexture, caseindex 4 + vertexnumber) # 7. Lookup endpoints of the intersected edge ep0index = tex1D(tableofedgestexture, edgeindex 2) ep1index = tex1D(tableofedgestexture, edgeindex 2 + 1) # 8. Get endpoint data ep0data = tex1D(verticestexture, ep0index) ep1data = tex1D(verticestexture, ep1index) # 9. Linear interpolation val0 = ep0data.a val1 = ep1data.a if val1 == val0: return float3(ep0data.x, ep0data.y, ep0data.z) else: t = (isovalue - val0) / (val1 - val0) pos0 = float3(ep0data.x, ep0data.y, ep0data.z) pos1 = float3(ep1data.x, ep1data.y, ep1data.z) return lerp(pos0, pos1, t) Parameters: isovalue: The scalar threshold value for isosurface extraction. It is set per pass and updated between passes to extract new isosurfaces. Hardware Requirement: Shader Model 3.0 support is required for vertex texture lookup. This was supported by Nvidia 6th generation and above graphics cards at the time of publication. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Polygons: The method draws a single quadrilateral per tetrahedron. In cases where the isosurface does not intersect the tetrahedron or intersects in a way that collapses vertices, degenerate polygons are produced. These are typically discarded by the rasterizer. Stacked Vertices: The tableofcasestexture may contain duplicated edge indexes to handle all configurations, leading to stacked vertices at the same location. These are discarded during rendering. Texture Lookup Latency: Vertex texture lookup introduces high latency, reducing throughput from a theoretical 600M vertices/sec to 33M vertices/sec on a GeForce 6800. Grouping texture lookups within the vertex shading program parallelizes latencies and optimizes performance. Hardware Limitations: ATI graphics cards did not support vertex texture lookup in Shader Model 3.0 at the time of the primary source's publication. A real-time isosurface extraction method that leverages the strengths of both Marching Cubes and Marching Tetrahedra, adapted for the GPU geometry shader pipeline (specifically DirectX 10). It solves the problem of high computational expense and register pressure associated with explicit isosurface extraction by using massive parallelism and dynamic load balancing. Unlike its siblings, it separates domain voxelization/tetrahedralization from polygon generation into a two-pass process to maximize SIMD utilization and reduce register pressure compared to Marching Cubes. A technique to output extracted isosurface triangles into a GPU stream-out buffer for re-use in subsequent rendering passes or disk storage, improving perceived frame rate by avoiding redundant extraction. It computes the isosurface using marching tetrahedra, outputs the resulting triangles into a GPU stream-out buffer (e.g., 85 MB size), and reuses the geometry in later passes if the implicit domain or isovalue has not changed significantly. This is used to combine high quality direct volume rendering with isosurface rendering for medical training simulations, render isosurface faces as starting positions for ray casting, and render the isosurface directly into a shadow buffer. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra in brute-force mode. When combined with an Interval Tree to discard non-intersected cells, it achieves an average acceleration factor of about 4 times. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of vertices and tetrahedra. One texel per vertex and one texel per tetrahedron, plus tables. For a 128MB graphics card, theoretical capacity is ~7 million tetrahedra. Measured Performance: On an Nvidia QuadroFX Go 1400 (256MB VRAM), the method processes ~6.7 million tetrahedra/sec for grids < 600K (fitting in VRAM), ~4 million tetrahedra/sec at 1 million tetrahedra (with RAM swapping), and drops tremendously for >1 million due to hard-drive swapping. It is about 2 times faster than the same CPU-based extraction. Scaling: The method remains linear and faster than CPU methods for larger grids (>1 million tetrahedra), whereas register-based methods suffer PCI-Express swapping penalties when data exceeds VRAM. Strengths: Handles millions of tetrahedra; avoids data redundancy; limits AGP/PCI-Express transfers; supports large unstructured grids. Limitations: Requires Shader Model 3.0; slower than register-based methods for small grids (<1 million tetrahedra); high texture lookup latency on older hardware. When to use: Large unstructured tetrahedral grids (>1 million cells) where memory capacity is a constraint for register-based methods. When not to use: Small grids (<1 million cells) where register-based methods are faster; hardware lacking Shader Model 3.0 vertex texture support. The method was proposed by Luc Buatois, Guillaume Caumon, and Bruno Lévy from Nancy Université, ALICE Inria Lorraine, and CRPG-CNRS, and presented at the 2nd International Symposium on Visual Computing (ISVC06) in November 2006. It revises the framework proposed by Wylie et al. and Pascucci, which were among the first to explore programmable hardware for isosurface computation using vertex shaders. The primary innovation was the use of vertex texture lookup to store data in textures rather than registers, avoiding the strong redundancy of sending all required data for each tetrahedron. It is used in geological modeling for fluid pressure field visualization on tetrahedralized meshes up to 5 million cells. name: GPU-based Marching Tetrahedra with Adaptive Tessellation
head: Hybrid Cubes-Tetrahedra Extraction, Hybrid Cubes-Tetrahedra Isosurface Extraction, Hybrid marching cubes/marching tetrahedra approach, Two-pass Marching Tetrahedra
body:
A real-time isosurface extraction method that leverages the strengths of both Marching Cubes and Marching Tetrahedra, adapted for the GPU geometry shader pipeline (specifically DirectX 10). It solves the problem of high computational expense and register pressure associated with explicit isosurface extraction by using massive parallelism and dynamic load balancing. Unlike its siblings, it separates domain voxelization/tetrahedralization from polygon generation into a two-pass process to maximize SIMD utilization and reduce register pressure compared to Marching Cubes. Inputs: Scalar volume data F(\mathbf{x}) (where F(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) - c and c is the isovalue, frequently 0), and optionally precomputed gradients 
abla F(\mathbf{x}). Outputs: A stream-out buffer containing isosurface triangles. Data Structures: Stream-out buffer (Pass 1): Stores tetrahedra as point primitives. Each tetrahedron consists of just 3 4-component floating point values. Stream-out buffer (Pass 2): Stores output triangles. Parameters: Isovalue (c): The constant defining the surface f(\mathbf{x}) = c. Grid Resolution: Base cube grid resolution (e.g., 64^3). Tetrahedralization Count: Each cube is tessellated into at most 6 tetrahedra. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline): Collect scalar data (e.g., from Visible Human Project) and compute gradients 
abla F(\mathbf{x}) for lighting/shading. 2. Pass 1: Domain Voxelization and Tetrahedralization: 1. Render a vertex buffer containing 3n vertices (where n is grid size). 2. Vertex Shader: Use primitive ID to generate voxel corner locations. 3. Geometry Shader (Cube Tetrahedralization): Compute voxel cube corner locations. Evaluate F(\mathbf{x}) at each corner. Compare signs to determine if the voxel contains the isosurface. Optimization: Only generate tetrahedra for voxels containing the isosurface. Adaptive Refinement: In the 6-tetrahedra tessellation, each tetrahedron shares a common longest edge along the cube diagonal. Perform one function evaluation at the edge midpoint. Subdivide tetrahedra if signs differ from the center point. Emit only the 12 resulting tetrahedra that contain the surface. Output these tetrahedra as point primitives to a stream-out buffer. 3. Pass 2: Marching Tetrahedra: 1. Render the stream-out buffer from Pass 1 as point primitives using DrawAuto. 2. Geometry Shader (Marching Tetrahedra): Edge Identification: Identify edges of the current tetrahedron where the signs of endpoints differ. Root Finding: Fit a parabola on the intersecting edge and find the root to determine the vertex position. Two options are provided: (a) Inverse Quadratic Interpolation: Perform a third function evaluation F(x3) along the edge. Use the formula below. (b) Gradient Estimation: Use precomputed gradients 
abla F(\mathbf{x}) to estimate the parabola, avoiding the third function evaluation. Output: Output each isosurface triangle to a stream-out buffer. Formulas: Linear Secant Method (for initial approximation of x3): t =  rac{-F(x1)}{F(x2) - F(x1)} where x1, x2 are edge endpoints. Inverse Quadratic Interpolation (Vertex Position v): v =  rac{F(x2)F(x3)}{(F(x1) - F(x2))(F(x1) - F(x3))}x1 +  rac{F(x1)F(x3)}{(F(x2) - F(x1))(F(x2) - F(x3))}x2 +  rac{F(x1)F(x2)}{(F(x3) - F(x1))(F(x3) - F(x2))}x3 where x1, x2 are edge endpoints and x3 is a third evaluation point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatefield(x, fieldfunc, isovalue): return fieldfunc(x) - isovalue def getsign(val): return 1 if val >= 0 else -1 def getcubecorners(gridpos, cellsize): # Returns 8 corners of a voxel cube x, y, z = gridpos s = cellsize return [ (x, y, z), (x+s, y, z), (x, y+s, z), (x+s, y+s, z), (x, y, z+s), (x+s, y, z+s), (x, y+s, z+s), (x+s, y+s, z+s) ] def tessellatecube(corners): # Standard decomposition of a cube into 6 tetrahedra sharing the main diagonal return [ (0, 1, 2, 7), (1, 3, 6, 7), (2, 6, 5, 7), (0, 4, 5, 7), (0, 3, 1, 7), (0, 5, 4, 7) ] def adaptivesubdivide(corners, fvals, fmid): # Subdivides the 6 tetrahedra into 12 based on midpoint sign, keeping only those containing the surface newtets = [] for t in tessellatecube(corners): newtets.extend(splittet(t, corners, fvals, fmid)) return [t for t in newtets if tetcontainssurface(t, corners, fvals, fmid)] def splittet(tet, corners, fvals, fmid): # Splits a tetrahedron along the edge corresponding to the cube's main diagonal # Returns 2 new tetrahedra return [(tet[0], tet[1], tet[2], 8), (tet[0], tet[1], tet[3], 8)] def tetcontainssurface(tet, corners, fvals, fmid): # Checks if the tetrahedron spans the isosurface signs = [getsign(fvals[i]) for i in tet] return not all(s == signs[0] for s in signs) def pass1geometryshader(gridpos, cellsize, fieldfunc, isovalue): corners = getcubecorners(gridpos, cellsize) fvals = [evaluatefield(c, fieldfunc, isovalue) for c in corners] if all(getsign(f) == getsign(fvals[0]) for f in fvals): return [] mididx = 7 # Main diagonal endpoint mid = corners[mididx] # Simplified: actual midpoint calculation fmid = evaluatefield(mid, fieldfunc, isovalue) if getsign(fmid) != getsign(fvals[0]): return adaptivesubdivide(corners, fvals, fmid) else: return tessellatecube(corners) def pass2geometryshader(tetindices, corners, fieldfunc, isovalue, usegradients=False): edges = [(0,1), (0,2), (0,3), (1,2), (1,3), (2,3)] intersectingedges = [] for i, j in edges: f1 = evaluatefield(corners[tetindices[i]], fieldfunc, isovalue) f2 = evaluatefield(corners[tetindices[j]], fieldfunc, isovalue) if getsign(f1) != getsign(f2): intersectingedges.append((i, j, f1, f2)) vertices = [] for i, j, f1, f2 in intersectingedges: if usegradients: v = gradientrootfinding(corners[tetindices[i]], corners[tetindices[j]], f1, f2) else: x3 = (corners[tetindices[i]] + corners[tetindices[j]]) / 2.0 f3 = evaluatefield(x3, fieldfunc, isovalue) v = inversequadraticinterpolation(corners[tetindices[i]], corners[tetindices[j]], x3, f1, f2, f3) vertices.append(v) return connecttotriangles(vertices) def gradientrootfinding(p1, p2, f1, f2): # Linear interpolation using gradients return p1 + (p2 - p1) (-f1 / (f2 - f1)) def inversequadraticinterpolation(x1, x2, x3, f1, f2, f3): term1 = (f2 f3) / ((f1 - f2) (f1 - f3)) x1 term2 = (f1 f3) / ((f2 - f1) (f2 - f3)) x2 term3 = (f1 f2) / ((f3 - f1) (f3 - f2)) x3 return term1 + term2 + term3 def connecttotriangles(vertices): # Connects intersection vertices into triangles based on MT topology return [vertices] The parent method, which computes intersections in the vertex shader by drawing a single quadrilateral for each tetrahedron. This method improves upon it by using a two-pass approach with geometry shaders for better load balancing and reduced register pressure. The core algorithm used in Pass 2. It uses a simpler cell primitive with only 16 possible sign combinations (vs 256 for MC), emits at most 2 triangles (vs up to 6 for MC), and has no ambiguous cases. The sibling method. MC has larger lookup tables (4608 entries) causing register pressure and potential connectivity ambiguities. This method avoids MC's pitfalls by using tetrahedra for extraction while using cubes for adaptive tessellation. Time Complexity: Real-time interactive rates. The method processes the Virtual Human Project dataset (576MB) at extremely fast frame rates. Memory Complexity: Uses stream-out buffers. Pass 1 outputs tetrahedra (3 4-component floats per tetrahedron). Pass 2 outputs triangles. Memory savings are achieved by only generating tetrahedra for voxels containing the isosurface. Strengths: Maximizes SIMD utilization by separating extraction into two phases. Reduces register pressure compared to Marching Cubes due to smaller lookup tables. Adaptive refinement improves surface quality with minimal cost (one extra function evaluation per cube). Avoids cracks by subdividing along the center shared edge, ensuring consistency with neighboring cells. Reuses function evaluations from the initial cube grid to avoid redundancy. Limitations: Requires DirectX 10 or later for geometry shader and stream-out support. Tetrahedra are irregular shapes, lacking the intuitive grid correspondence of cubes. Adaptive refinement adds complexity to the geometry shader. When to use: Medical visualization (CT/MRI), colonoscopy tumor analysis, and applications requiring real-time isosurface extraction with dynamic isovalue changes. When not to use: Applications without programmable geometry shaders or stream-out capabilities. Originated by Natalya Tatarchuk, Jeremy Shopf, and Christopher DeCoro from AMD and Princeton University. Published in 2008. It was designed to take advantage of the massive parallelism and high memory bandwidth of consumer GPUs (specifically ATI Radeon HD 2000 and 3000 series) and Shader Model 4.0 capabilities. Prior work lacked programmable primitive processing and had to redundantly perform extraction regardless of dynamic isovalue changes. This method was one of the first to leverage the geometry shader's amplification feature and stream-out for efficient isosurface extraction. name: Tetrahedral Volume Integration
head: Tetrahedral Volume Summation, Volume enclosed with the iso-surface (tetrahedral decomposition)
body: Tetrahedral Volume Integration is a method for computing the scalar volume enclosed by an isosurface generated via tetrahedral decomposition. It solves the problem of quantifying the material volume within a grid cell by summing the volumes of the tetrahedra parts that lie inside the isosurface. Unlike surface extraction methods that only output geometry, this method provides a volumetric metric, distinguishing it from siblings like Marching Tetrahedrons which focus on triangle generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of tetrahedra from the decomposition of the grid cells, scalar field values at vertices, and an isovalue. Output: The total enclosed volume V{total}. Data Structures: Tetrahedron: Defined by 4 vertices \mathbf{v}a, \mathbf{v}b, \mathbf{v}c, \mathbf{v}d and their scalar values sa, sb, sc, sd. Vertex State: Binary classification of each vertex relative to the isovalue (Inside/On or Outside/Off). Steps: 1. Iterate through each tetrahedron in the decomposition. 2. Determine the position of the tetrahedron relative to the isosurface based on vertex states: Case 1 (All Outside): If all vertices are 'off', the contribution is 0. Case 2 (All Inside): If all vertices are 'on', the contribution is the full volume of the tetrahedron V{olt}. Case 3 (Intersected): If the tetrahedron is intersected by the isosurface, compute the volume of the part inside the isosurface. This is done by identifying the intersection points on the edges and forming smaller tetrahedra with the original vertices. Formulas: The volume of a tetrahedron with vertices \mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2, \mathbf{p}3 is: V = \frac{1}{6} |(\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) \cdot ((\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0) \times (\mathbf{p}3 - \mathbf{p}0))| For intersected tetrahedra, the volume is decomposed into smaller tetrahedra formed by the intersection points and the original vertices. The theoretical volume for validation is Vr = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3, and the relative error is Er = \frac{Vd - Vr}{Vr}. Parameters: Cell Edge Length: The unit of measurement for object dimensions relative to the grid. Value: 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tetrahedronvolume(p0, p1, p2, p3): """Computes volume of a tetrahedron given 4 vertices.""" return abs(dot(cross(p1 - p0, p2 - p0), p3 - p0)) / 6.0 def computeenclosedvolume(vertices, scalars, isovalue): """ Computes the volume of the part of a tetrahedron inside the isosurface. vertices: list of 4 vectors [va, vb, vc, vd] scalars: list of 4 floats [sa, sb, sc, sd] isovalue: float Returns: float volume """ # Determine vertex states: 1 for inside/on, 0 for outside states = [1 if s <= isovalue else 0 for s in scalars] counton = sum(states) # Group A: All same state if counton == 0: return 0.0 if counton == 4: return tetrahedronvolume(vertices) # Compute intersection points on all crossing edges intersections = [] for i in range(4): for j in range(i + 1, 4): diff = scalars[j] - scalars[i] if abs(diff) < 1e-9: # Guard against parallel edges continue t = (isovalue - scalars[i]) / diff intersections.append(vertices[i] + t (vertices[j] - vertices[i])) # Group B: 1 vertex different state if counton == 1: vt = vertices[states.index(1)] return tetrahedronvolume(vt, intersections) if counton == 3: vt = vertices[states.index(0)] volcut = tetrahedronvolume(vt, intersections) return tetrahedronvolume(vertices) - volcut # Group C: 2 vertices different state if counton == 2: onindices = [i for i, s in enumerate(states) if s == 1] offindices = [i for i, s in enumerate(states) if s == 0] va, vb = vertices[onindices[0]], vertices[onindices[1]] vc, vd = vertices[offindices[0]], vertices[offindices[1]] # Find intersection points on edges connecting on to off vertices t1 = None t2 = None for i in range(4): for j in range(i + 1, 4): diff = scalars[j] - scalars[i] if abs(diff) < 1e-9: continue if states[i] != states[j]: t = (isovalue - scalars[i]) / diff p = vertices[i] + t (vertices[j] - vertices[i]) if (i == onindices[0] and j == offindices[0]) or (i == offindices[0] and j == onindices[0]): t1 = p if (i == onindices[1] and j == offindices[1]) or (i == offindices[1] and j == onindices[1]): t2 = p # Fallback: decompose intersected polyhedron into two tetrahedra sharing edge (va, vb) if t1 is None or t2 is None: return tetrahedronvolume(va, vb, intersections[0], intersections[1]) # Exact formula from: Vol = Vol(a,b,c,t1) + Vol(a,b,d,t2) + Vol(a,b,t1,t2) return tetrahedronvolume(va, vb, vc, t1) + tetrahedronvolume(va, vb, vd, t2) + tetrahedronvolume(va, vb, t1, t2) return 0.0 A method that calculates the volume Vd defined by triangles inside tetrahedra based on the binary state (on/off) of the vertices. It categorizes configurations into three groups: Group A: All vertices same state. Volume is V{olt} (if all on) or 0 (if all off). Group B: One vertex different state. If one is on, volume is V{ol{a,b,c,t}} (tetrahedron formed by the on vertex and the three triangle intersection points). If one is off, volume is V{olt} - V{ol{a,b,c,t}}. Group C: Two vertices different state. If two are on, volume is \text{Vol}{a,b,c,t1} + \text{Vol}{a,b,d,t2} + \text{Vol}{a,b,t1,t2}. If two are off, volume is derived similarly. This method provides a direct lookup or case-based calculation without explicit intersection point computation for every edge, relying on pre-defined geometric decompositions for each vertex state configuration. A method for tetrahedral meshes that solves the surface integration exactly per tetrahedron. It was presented by Scheuermann et al.. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra N, O(N), as each tetrahedron is processed independently. Memory Complexity: O(1) per tetrahedron, requiring only local vertex data. Strengths: Provides an exact volumetric measure for the isosurface, useful for quantitative analysis of scientific data. Limitations: Computationally more intensive than simple surface area calculation due to the need for geometric decomposition of intersected cells. The method originates from comparisons of fundamental isosurface extraction techniques, specifically focusing on the accuracy of volume and surface area measurements. It was developed to address the limitations of standard marching cubes/tetrahedra methods which do not inherently provide volumetric data. The vertex-state-based variant was introduced to optimize the calculation by leveraging pre-defined geometric configurations. The exact surface integration approach was later formalized for tetrahedral meshes by Scheuermann et al..
