name: Multiresolution and Adaptive Extraction
body: This family covers methods that extract isosurfaces from hierarchical volume data by dynamically adjusting extraction resolution to balance computational cost and visual fidelity. It sets itself apart from fixed-resolution approaches by using frame-timing feedback to modulate detail [7457-adaptive-minimum-projected-size-adjustment.md], omitting geometric reconnection to maximize display rates [7512-non-reconnected-multiresolution-isosurfacing.md], or employing oracle-driven traversal with explicit crack patching to guarantee watertightness [11830-adaptive-multiresolution-extraction-with-oracle.md]. All methods in this family operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values or occupancy states at its vertices or centers. For detailed traversal, surface determination, and mesh coherence mechanisms, see Surface extraction. A dynamic level-of-detail control mechanism that adjusts the minimum projected size of surface elements frame-to-frame based on measured rendering times. It differs from distance-based LOD by using a cubic weighting of time deviations to prevent oscillation and maintain target framerates during interaction. Choose this when interactive performance stability is prioritized over absolute geometric consistency across frames. A surface extraction method that generates independent surface primitives per cell without enforcing geometric connectivity between adjacent cells of different resolutions. It solves the overhead of neighbor tracking by accepting visual cracks, relying on sufficient polygon density to make gaps negligible. Choose this for real-time applications where minor gaps are acceptable and maximum display rates are critical. A technique that adaptively extracts meshes from coarser-resolution octree nodes using an oracle structure to manage level of detail and patch cracks at resolution junctions. It differs from leaf-only traversal by exploiting multiresolution data to process higher-resolution volumes at real-time rates while guaranteeing continuity. Choose this when a watertight, crack-free mesh is required at high performance levels. Not given in the sources. Notes on Multiresolution and Adaptive Extraction, provided in prompt.

name: Adaptive Minimum Projected Size Adjustment
head: adaptive LOD control, framerate-driven projected size scaling
body: Adaptive Minimum Projected Size Adjustment is a dynamic level-of-detail (LOD) control mechanism for isosurface extraction that automatically adjusts the minimum projected size of surface elements frame-to-frame to maintain a target framerate during user interaction. Unlike fixed minimum projected size approaches, which cause surface complexity to scale directly with camera distance and can result in poorly or over-populated geometry, this method balances detail and performance based on actual frame timing. It ensures that the displayed surface remains refined during idle moments while preventing excessive geometry generation during active interaction. The method operates by modulating the minimum projected size threshold used during the surface extraction process. It does not recompute the geometry every frame but rather adjusts the criteria for which geometric primitives are generated or retained based on the rendering performance of the previous frame. Inputs and Outputs Input: The measured elapsed time of the previous frame (t{measured}), the desired display time (t{target}), and the current minimum projected size (s{current}). Output: The updated minimum projected size (s{next}) for the subsequent frame. Data Structures No specific complex data structures are required beyond the scalar variables for timing and size. The method assumes the underlying isosurface extraction algorithm accepts a minimum projected size parameter. Parameters t{target}: The desired frame duration used as the baseline for time-difference calculation. Typical value: Not given in the sources. \alpha: The exponent applied to the time difference to modulate adjustment sensitivity. Value: 3. Algorithm Steps 1. Measure Frame Time: At the end of each frame, measure the elapsed time since the previous frame end, denoted as t{measured}. 2. Calculate Time Difference: Compute the difference between the measured frame time and the desired display time: \Delta t = t{measured} - t{target} 3. Compute Weighted Factor: Raise the time difference to the third power to compute the weighted growing factor, preserving the sign of the difference: \Delta s = (\Delta t)^3 This cubic weighting minimizes the influence of the adjustment when the display time is near the goal and emphasizes it when it is far, preventing oscillation and ensuring smooth convergence. 4. Update Minimum Projected Size: Update the minimum projected size using the computed weighted growing factor. The exact update rule depends on whether the system is in interaction or idle mode: During Interaction: The size is adjusted based on \Delta s. If the frame took too long (\Delta t > 0), the minimum projected size increases (coarsening the mesh). If the frame was faster than desired (\Delta t < 0), the size decreases (refining the mesh). During Idle: When the user is idle, the limit projected size is progressively reduced toward zero to allow fully detailed geometry rendering over time. 5. Apply to Extraction: Use the updated s{next} as the minimum projected size threshold for the next frame's surface extraction pass. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateminimumprojectedsize(tmeasured, ttarget, scurrent, isidle): """ Updates the minimum projected size for the next frame based on frame timing. Args: tmeasured: Time taken to render the previous frame. ttarget: Desired frame duration. scurrent: Current minimum projected size. isidle: Boolean flag indicating if the user is idle. Returns: snext: The new minimum projected size. """ # Step 1 & 2: Calculate time difference deltat = tmeasured - ttarget # Step 3: Compute weighted factor using cubic exponent # Preserving sign: if deltat is negative, deltas is negative deltas = deltat 3 # Step 4: Update size if isidle: # During idle, progressively reduce size toward zero for full detail # Linear/multiplicative decay is standard; exact rate not specified in sources. snext = scurrent 0.9 if snext < 1e-6: snext = 0.0 else: # During interaction, adjust based on frame time deviation # The source states "update... using the computed weighted growing factor" # but does not specify the exact additive/multiplicative formula. # A common implementation for such adaptive controls is additive adjustment. snext = scurrent + deltas # Guard against negative size if snext < 0: snext = 0.0 return snext Edge Cases and Pitfalls Oscillation: If the exponent were linear, small fluctuations in frame time could cause jittering in mesh density. The cubic exponent (\alpha=3) mitigates this by dampening small differences and amplifying large ones. Idle Detection: The transition between interaction and idle modes must be robust. If the system incorrectly identifies interaction as idle, the mesh may become overly dense and cause performance drops. If it fails to detect idle, the mesh may remain coarsely sampled even when the user stops interacting. Boundary Conditions: The minimum projected size must be clamped to a non-negative value, as negative sizes are invalid. Time Complexity: The adjustment logic itself is O(1), involving basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead is required for the adjustment logic itself. Strengths: Maintains a consistent framerate during user interaction. Allows for high-fidelity rendering during idle periods. Adapts to varying camera distances without manual tuning. Limitations: Does not address cracks between adjacent cells of different sizes. The authors explicitly chose not to reconnect surface elements, accepting that field resolution differences may cause visual artifacts. Performance is dependent on the accuracy of frame time measurement and the responsiveness of the user interaction detection. When to Use: Ideal for interactive volume sculpting and visualization systems where user interaction speed and visual fidelity need to be balanced. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced by Eric Ferley, Marie-Paule Cani, and Jean-Dominique Gascuel in their 2001 paper "Resolution Adaptive Volume Sculpting". It was developed as part of a system for interactive volume sculpting, addressing the limitations of fixed minimum projected size controls which failed to provide sufficient refinement during idle moments and caused poor or over-populated geometry during zooming. The approach is integrated into their resolution adaptive volume sculpting system. Resolution Adaptive Volume Sculpting, https://doi.org/10.1006/gmod.2001.0558, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Non-reconnected Multiresolution Isosurfacing
head: Crack Suppression via Polygon Density, deliberate crack omission, non-reconnected multiresolution cells
body: Non-reconnected Multiresolution Isosurfacing is a surface extraction technique that intentionally omits geometric reconnection between adjacent cells of different resolutions to maintain interactive frame rates during dynamic Level of Detail (LOD) selection. It solves the problem of computational overhead in tracking neighbors and reconnecting surface elements in unconstrained hierarchies, relying on sufficient polygon density to keep resulting cracks visually negligible. Unlike sibling methods that enforce mesh coherence through explicit reconnection or oracle-based constraints, this method accepts visible gaps as a trade-off for speed, particularly in dynamic sculpting contexts where the surface is constantly changing. The method operates on a discretized domain (typically a regular grid or octree) where each cell contains scalar values. The core principle is the independent rendering of surface elements per cell without enforcing connectivity constraints between adjacent cells of different resolutions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical scalar field (e.g., octree or grid hierarchy) and a dynamic stopping level selection criterion per frame. Output: A set of independent surface polygons (triangles/quads) rendered per cell. No unified mesh connectivity is generated. Data Structures: Cell Hierarchy: A tree structure where nodes represent cells at various resolution levels. Surface Elements: For each active cell, a list of polygons intersecting the isosurface. The exact layout depends on the base isosurfacing algorithm (e.g., Marching Cubes) but is treated as an opaque list of vertices and indices for rendering. Steps: 1. Dynamic LOD Selection: At each frame, determine the stopping level in the cell hierarchy for display. This selection is dynamic and does not enforce connectivity constraints between adjacent cells. 2. Independent Surface Extraction: For each active cell at the selected level, extract the isosurface elements independently. Do not query or track neighboring cells for connectivity purposes. 3. Render Independent Elements: Render the surface elements found at each cell. No reconnection of surface elements between adjacent cells is performed. 4. Visual Verification: Rely on the density of polygons to ensure cracks remain "hardly visible". If the polygon count is low, cracks may be visible; drawing more triangles does not solve the fundamental issue of field resolution mismatches. Parameters: sufficientpolygonthreshold: An implicit threshold where polygon density makes cracks visually negligible. This justifies the omission of reconnection. The exact numerical value is not specified in the sources. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Cracks: Visible gaps may appear due to field resolution mismatches between adjacent cells. This is a fundamental issue of the method, not a bug. Distant Neighbors: In an unconstrained hierarchy, adjacent cells may be distant by more than one resolution level. This makes neighbor tracking computationally expensive and slows display rates. Dynamic Surface: The method is designed for scenarios where the surface is always changing (e.g., sculpting), making reconnection efforts potentially wasteful. Export Limitations: The output is not a standard mesh with connectivity. If a standard mesh is required for export, a global offline reconnection process must be performed separately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernonreconnectedisosurface(hierarchy, isovalue, frametime): """ Renders the isosurface by processing each cell independently. No connectivity is enforced between adjacent cells. """ # 1. Dynamic LOD Selection # Determine which cells to process based on dynamic criteria for this frame. # This is not a static hierarchy traversal but a frame-specific selection. activecells = selectactivecellsdynamic(hierarchy, frametime) # 2. Independent Surface Extraction allpolygons = [] for cell in activecells: # Extract surface elements for this cell independently. # No neighbor lookup or connectivity constraint is applied. polygons = extractisosurfaceindependent(cell, isovalue) allpolygons.extend(polygons) # 3. Render # Render the collected polygons. # Cracks may be visible if polygon density is insufficient. renderpolygons(allpolygons) # Note: If a standard mesh is needed for export, a global offline reconnection # must be performed on the final surface representation. A technique that modifies scalar values at boundary face centers to ensure continuity, contrasting with this method's deliberate omission of reconnection. Time Complexity: Lower than reconnection-based methods because it avoids neighbor tracking and surface reconnection overhead. The cost is dominated by independent surface extraction per cell. Memory Complexity: Lower memory overhead for mesh connectivity structures, as no global connectivity graph is maintained. Measured Performance: Applied in a resolution adaptive volume sculpting system to maintain interactive rates during dynamic LOD selection. Specific frame rates or hardware metrics are not provided in the sources. Strengths: High performance in dynamic environments; avoids the computational cost of neighbor tracking; suitable for unconstrained hierarchies where neighbors may be distant. Limitations: Visual cracks may appear, especially at low polygon densities; not suitable for applications requiring a watertight or connected mesh without post-processing; cracks are a fundamental issue of field resolution mismatches, not solvable by simply adding more triangles. When to Use: Interactive sculpting or visualization where frame rate is critical and the surface is constantly changing. When Not to Use: Applications requiring a standard, connected mesh output without offline reconnection; static scenes where visual perfection is prioritized over speed. The method was introduced in the context of "Resolution Adaptive Volume Sculpting" by Eric Ferley, Marie-Paule Cani, and Jean-François Dufour. It was developed to address the need for interactive performance in dynamic sculpting systems where users manipulate scalar fields in real-time. The approach contrasts with other multiresolution isosurface constructions that pay attention to cracks and enforce connectivity. The system was demonstrated with examples sculpted using a 2D-mouse with a "virtual trackball" metaphor, and additional material was available at the INRIA Imagis lab website. Resolution Adaptive Volume Sculpting, https://doi.org/10.1006/gmod.2001.0558, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Boundary Face Center Value Adjustment
head: Modifying the center value of a boundary face
body: Boundary Face Center Value Adjustment is a technique used in multiresolution isosurface extraction to ensure continuity of the isosurface at boundaries where resolution levels change. It solves the problem where an isosurface intersects opposite edges of a boundary face, which can cause visual cracks if the high-resolution isoline does not pass through specific intersection points. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by intentionally modifying the underlying scalar data values at boundary face centers rather than post-processing the mesh geometry or reconnecting polygons. Inputs: Scalar field data V. Isovalue threshold iso. A boundary face F at a multiresolution boundary where resolution differs by one level. Vertices of the face: v1, v2, v3, v4. Center vertex c of the face. Midpoint m of the edge connecting the two vertices on the low-resolution side (or derived from geometry). Scalar value at a specific intersection point p on the high-resolution edge. Outputs: Updated scalar value v(c) at the center vertex c. Data Structures: The scalar field is stored in a multiresolution hierarchy (e.g., wavelet tree). Boundary faces are identified as those shared between cells of different resolution levels. Each face has a center vertex c whose scalar value is stored separately or derived. Steps: 1. Identify boundary faces where the isosurface intersects. 2. For each such face, determine if the isoline intersects opposite edges. If it intersects adjacent edges, no adjustment is typically needed for continuity along the shared boundary. 3. If the isoline intersects opposite edges, calculate the scalar value at the center vertex c to force the high-resolution isoline to pass through a specific intersection point p on one of the high-resolution edges. 4. Apply the adjustment formula based on the scalar value e at point p. 5. (Optional/Reversible) To undo the modification before further processing (like forward wavelet transform), restore v(c) to the average of the four vertex values. Formulas: Let e be the scalar value at point p (normalized or relative to the isovalue context as per the source's garbled text, likely e = V(p) - iso or similar, but the source uses e directly in the conditional). The source text is garbled, but the logic implies: Let m' be the scalar value at the midpoint m (or a related reference value). Let v(m') be the scalar value at m. The update rule for v(c) is: If e > 0.5: e = 2e - 1 v(c) = iso - e \cdot (m' - v(m')) + v(m') Else: e = 2e v(c) = iso - e \cdot (m' - v(m')) + v(m') Note: The source text contains significant OCR errors in the formula. The variable m' and v(m') are not clearly defined in the provided text snippet, but the structure suggests a linear interpolation or correction based on the error e and a reference value m. The term iso - e \cdot (m' - v(m')) + v(m') resembles a correction to align the value at c such that the isoline passes through p. Without clearer source text, the exact definition of m' and v(m') is ambiguous, but the conditional structure is preserved. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adjustboundaryfacecenter(v, iso, p, m, mprime, vmprime): """ Adjusts the scalar value at the center of a boundary face to ensure isosurface continuity. Args: v: Dictionary or array of scalar values at vertices. iso: Isovalue threshold. p: Point on the high-resolution edge where the isoline must pass. m: Midpoint of the edge on the low-resolution side. mprime: Reference scalar value (definition ambiguous in source). vmprime: Scalar value at mprime. Returns: New scalar value for the center vertex c. """ # Calculate e, the scalar value at p. # Source text is garbled: "e = scalar value at p". # Assuming e is the value V(p) or a normalized error. # Given the condition e > 0.5, it likely refers to a normalized value # or the value relative to a range. We assume e is provided or calculated # as V(p) for the sake of structure, but the source implies e is derived. # Let's assume e is the scalar value at p for the conditional check. e = v[p] if e > 0.5: e = 2 e - 1 vc = iso - e (mprime - vmprime) + vmprime else: e = 2 e vc = iso - e (mprime - vmprime) + vmprime return vc def restoreboundaryfacecenter(v, facevertices): """ Reverses the adjustment by setting the center value to the average of the four vertices. """ v1, v2, v3, v4 = facevertices vcenter = (v[v1] + v[v2] + v[v3] + v[v4]) / 4.0 return vcenter Parameters: Isovalue iso: The threshold for surface extraction. Threshold for e: 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opposite Edges Intersection: If the isoline passes through opposite edges, it may be impossible to adjust v(c) so that the high-resolution isoline passes through both intersection points p and q. The implementation adjusts the value so the isoline passes through p, guaranteeing coincidence along at least half the face. This may cause hairline cracks on the other half. Reversibility: The modification is reversible. Before performing any iteration of the forward wavelet transform involving only the high-resolution region, restore the scalar values at the centers of all faces along multiresolution boundaries by setting the scalar value at the center of a face to the average of the scalar values of its four vertices. Time Complexity: The change at a particular vertex is a function of only its immediate neighbor and the current isovalue, making the operation efficient. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the scalar field and identification of boundary faces. No additional large data structures are mentioned. Measured Performance: Experimental results on multiresolution boundary faces intersecting the isosurface show that approximately 4.19% develop cracks. The maximum crack area is 2.84% of the low-resolution boundary face area, while the average crack area is 1.22%. Strengths: Efficient, local operation; ensures continuity along at least half the face; reversible. Limitations: May leave hairline cracks on the other half of the face in specific geometric configurations (opposite edge intersections). Origin: The technique is described in "Seamless Multiresolution Isosurfaces Using Wavelets". History: It is part of a broader approach to multiresolution isosurfacing that uses wavelets to manage data resolution and addresses the specific issue of cracks at resolution boundaries. Usage: Used in volume rendering and scientific visualization where seamless isosurfaces are required across multiresolution datasets. name: Adaptive Multiresolution Extraction with Oracle
head: Adaptive Surface Reconstruction with Oracle-based LOD, Crack-free adaptive marching cubes, Westermann et al. adaptive extraction
body: Adaptive Multiresolution Extraction with Oracle is a technique that adaptively extracts meshes from coarser-resolution nodes to gain speed, using an 'oracle' structure to manage level of detail and patch cracks at resolution junctions. It solves the problem of cracks appearing at junctions where finer-resolution octree cells are adjacent to coarser cells by patching resulting meshes to guarantee continuity. Unlike methods that process only the deepest leaves, this approach exploits the multiresolution nature of the octree to process higher-resolution volumes at real-time rates by adaptively deciding to extract the mesh from fewer, coarser-resolution nodes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree data structure representing a 3D scalar field. Output: A watertight, crack-free triangular mesh representing the isosurface. Data Structures: Octree: Hierarchical structure where each node represents a voxel or group of voxels. Leaf nodes contain the scalar data or occupancy information. Oracle Structure: A data structure built during a single pass of the octree. It stores the determined level of detail (LOD) or traversal depth for each region. Numbered Steps: 1. Oracle Construction: Perform a single pass of the octree to build the 'oracle' structure. This structure determines the level of detail (depth of the octree to be traversed) for each region based on view-dependent and geometric criteria. Curvature Oracle: Implement an oracle for predicting maximum surface curvature within each leaf node. Regions of low curvature use fewer polygons (shallower traversal), while high curvature regions traverse to the finest level. Focus Point Oracle: Determine octree traversal depth based on distance to the camera view position. Regions closer to the view point may be traversed to finer levels. 2. Adaptive Traversal: Traverse the octree using the depths determined by the oracle. Extract the mesh from the nodes at the specified depth. This allows coarser nodes to be used in low-detail areas and finer nodes in high-detail areas. 3. Crack Patching: Patch the resulting meshes to guarantee continuity at junctions between different resolution levels. This step is critical because cell corner values may vary at junctions in the octree, leading to cracks when surfaces are extracted from adjacent cells of different resolution. The method involves modifying the mesh geometry at these junctions to ensure vertices align and edges connect properly. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Curvature Threshold: Not given in the sources. Distance Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cracks: Cracks appear when surfaces are extracted from adjacent cells of different resolution because cell corner values vary at junctions. This is the primary challenge addressed by the patching step. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveextractionwithoracle(octreeroot, cameraposition, isovalue): """ Performs adaptive multiresolution surface extraction using an oracle. Args: octreeroot: The root node of the octree data structure. cameraposition: The 3D position of the camera. isovalue: The scalar threshold for surface extraction. Returns: A list of triangles forming the crack-free mesh. """ # Step 1: Build Oracle Structure # The oracle maps each node to its target traversal depth. oracle = {} def buildoracle(node, depth): if node is None: return # Curvature oracle: predict max surface curvature in leaf node maxcurvature = estimatemaxcurvature(node) # curvaturedepth = mapcurvaturetodepth(maxcurvature) # # Focus point oracle: determine depth based on distance to camera nodecenter = getnodecenter(node) # distance = euclideandistance(nodecenter, cameraposition) # distancedepth = mapdistancetodepth(distance) # # Combine criteria: use the finer (deeper) depth finaldepth = max(curvaturedepth, distancedepth) oracle[node] = finaldepth # Recurse to children if deeper traversal is needed if depth < finaldepth and node.haschildren(): for child in node.children: buildoracle(child, depth + 1) buildoracle(octreeroot, 0) # Step 2: Adaptive Traversal and Mesh Extraction meshtriangles = [] def extract(node, currentdepth): targetdepth = oracle.get(node, currentdepth) if currentdepth == targetdepth: # Extract mesh from this node at the specified resolution meshtriangles.extend(marchingcubes(node, isovalue)) # elif currentdepth < targetdepth and node.haschildren(): # Recurse to children until target depth is reached for child in node.children: extract(child, currentdepth + 1) # If currentdepth > targetdepth, stop recursion to prevent over-traversal extract(octreeroot, 0) # Step 3: Crack Patching # Patch the resulting meshes to guarantee continuity at junctions meshtriangles = patchcracks(meshtriangles, octreeroot, oracle) # return meshtriangles def estimatemaxcurvature(node): # Standard curvature estimation from scalar gradients at node vertices return 0.0 def mapcurvaturetodepth(curvature): # Maps curvature magnitude to octree depth level return 0 def getnodecenter(node): # Computes geometric center of the node's bounding box return (0, 0, 0) def euclideandistance(p1, p2): # Standard Euclidean distance calculation return ((p1[0]-p2[0])2 + (p1[1]-p2[1])2 + (p1[2]-p2[2])2)0.5 def mapdistancetodepth(distance): # Maps camera distance to octree depth level return 0 def marchingcubes(node, isovalue): # Standard Marching Cubes algorithm for isosurface extraction return [] def patchcracks(triangles, octree, oracle): # Aligns boundary vertices at resolution junctions to eliminate cracks return triangles Adjusts mesh resolution based on projected size on screen. Choose when screen-space error is the primary concern. Adaptive Minimum Projected Size Adjustment Extracts meshes at different resolutions without reconnecting them, potentially leading to cracks. Choose when performance is critical and cracks are acceptable or handled differently. Non-reconnected Multiresolution Isosurfacing Uses a particle system with gradient-weighted projection for adaptive extraction. Choose when particle-based methods better suit the data distribution. Extended Particle System with Gradient-Weighted Projection Time Complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the distribution of curvature/distance. Generally faster than full-resolution extraction due to adaptive coarsening. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the octree and the oracle structure. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the complexity of the scalar field and the camera position. Strengths: Real-time rates for high-resolution volumes; handles view-dependent and geometric criteria. Limitations: Requires complex patching logic to avoid cracks; oracle construction adds overhead. When to use: When real-time rendering of high-resolution volumetric data is required, and cracks must be avoided. When not to use: When simplicity of implementation is prioritized over performance, or when cracks are acceptable. The technique was proposed by Westermann et al. [WKE99] as an improvement over methods like Wilhlems and Van Gelder, which processed only the deepest leaves of the octree. It builds upon previous view-dependent extraction methods, such as Livnat et al. [LH98]. The main insight was recognizing that speedups could be gained by adaptively deciding to extract the mesh from fewer, coarser-resolution nodes. The primary challenge addressed is the appearance of cracks at junctions where finer-resolution octree cells are adjacent to coarser cells. name: Extended Particle System with Gradient-Weighted Projection
head: decoupled particle iteration
body:
A surface extraction method using a particle system where repulsive and attractive forces are decoupled in time, using gradient-weighted projection to settle particles on the isosurface and Voronoi diagrams for incremental insertion. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly separating the temporal dynamics of attraction (projection to the isosurface) and repulsion (distribution optimization), allowing for adaptive weighting between grayscale and second-order gradient terms during the projection phase. Inputs: A discretized scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) defined on a voxel pyramid (multiresolution grid). A target isosurface scalar value f0. Parameters: \alpha (dynamic weight for grayscale projection),  eta (dynamic weight for Laplacian projection). Outputs: A set of particle positions \{\mathbf{p}i\} representing the extracted isosurface. Data Structures: Particle: Contains position \mathbf{p}, velocity (implicit in displacement \Delta \mathbf{p}), and status. Voxel Pyramid: Hierarchical grid levels from coarse to fine. Gradient Field: First-order gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) interpolated from the scalar field. Laplacian Field: Second-order gradient (Laplacian) 
abla^2 f(\mathbf{p}) interpolated from the scalar field. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pyramid Construction: Construct a voxel pyramid from the input scalar field. 2. Initialization: Traverse the coarsest scale of the voxel pyramid. Identify "response units" (cells indicating surface presence). For each response unit, create one particle at the approximate position corresponding to the mesh center generated by the Marching Cubes (MC) algorithm lookup table for that cell. Apply small random perturbations to initial particle positions using the Mersenne Twister algorithm to avoid local extrema caused by symmetry. 3. Iteration Loop (until equilibrium or max levels): Gradient-Weighted Projection (Attraction): Define deviation: \phi(\mathbf{p}) = f(\mathbf{p}) - f0. Compute first-order Taylor expansion: \phi(\mathbf{p} + \Delta \mathbf{p}) \approx \phi(\mathbf{p}) + 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \Delta \mathbf{p}. Set approximation to zero and solve for displacement direction using gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{p}): \Delta \mathbf{p} = \lambda 
abla f(\mathbf{p}). Compute grayscale projection term \Delta \mathbf{p}{grayscale} and Laplacian projection term \Delta \mathbf{p}{lapdaction} (based on second-order gradient/zero-crossings). Combine with dynamic weights: \Delta \mathbf{p} = \alpha \cdot \Delta \mathbf{p}{grayscale} +  eta \cdot \Delta \mathbf{p}{lapdaction}. Update particle position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \Delta \mathbf{p}. Weight Scheduling: In early iterations, \alpha is high and  eta is low (grayscale dominates for fast convergence). In late iterations, \alpha decreases and  eta increases (Laplacian dominates for fine edge adjustment). Repulsion (Distribution Optimization): Treat repulsion as a local short-range force. Extract the tangential component of the repulsive force relative to the surface normal. Apply this tangential component to optimize particle distribution among neighbors. Equilibrium Check: Calculate average particle displacement across the system. If average displacement > threshold, continue iteration. 4. Incremental Insertion: When equilibrium is reached at a given scale, construct a Voronoi diagram of the current particle set. Identify regions with high curvature or large Voronoi cell areas. Insert new particles in these regions to refine the surface representation. 5. Refinement: Move to the next finer level of the voxel pyramid. Repeat steps 3-4 using the refined particle set as initialization for the finer scale. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extendedparticlesystemextraction(scalarfield, f0, pyramidlevels): # 1. Initialize particles at coarsest level particles = [] coarsestgrid = pyramidlevels[0] for cell in coarsestgrid.cells: if isresponseunit(cell): # Get approximate center from MC lookup table p = getmcmeshcenter(cell) # Add small random perturbation using Mersenne Twister p += mersennetwisterrandomsmallvector() particles.append(Particle(position=p)) # 2. Iterate through pyramid levels for level in pyramidlevels: while not isequilibrium(particles): for particle in particles: p = particle.position grad = interpolategradient(scalarfield, p) laplacian = interpolatelaplacian(scalarfield, p) # Gradient-Weighted Projection # Compute grayscale and laplacian displacement components # Note: Exact formulas for deltapgrayscale and deltaplapdaction # are derived from Newton iteration and zero-crossing logic deltapgrayscale = computegrayscaleprojection(p, grad, f0) deltaplapdaction = computelaplacianprojection(p, laplacian, f0) # Dynamic weights: alpha high early, beta high late alpha = getdynamicalpha(iterationcount) beta = getdynamicbeta(iterationcount) deltap = alpha deltapgrayscale + beta deltaplapdaction particle.position += deltap # Repulsion: Tangential component extraction for particle in particles: neighbors = getnearbyparticles(particle, shortrangeradius) for neighbor in neighbors: repulsiveforce = computerepulsion(particle.position, neighbor.position) # Extract tangential component relative to surface normal normal = interpolategradient(scalarfield, particle.position) tangentialforce = extracttangentialcomponent(repulsiveforce, normal) particle.position += tangentialforce repulsionweight # 3. Incremental Insertion via Voronoi voronoi = constructvoronoidiagram(particles) for cell in voronoi.cells: if ishighcurvature(cell) or cell.area > threshold: newp = getvoronoicellcenter(cell) newp += mersennetwisterrandomsmallvector() particles.append(Particle(position=newp)) return particles Parameters: \alpha: Dynamic weight coefficient for the grayscale projection term. High in early iteration, low in late iteration.  eta: Dynamic weight coefficient for the Laplacian projection term. Low in early iteration, high in late iteration. Threshold for equilibrium: Not given in the sources. Short-range radius for repulsion: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Symmetry: Initial particle distribution symmetry can cause local extrema traps. Mitigated by Mersenne Twister perturbations. Gradient Magnitude: In regions with small gradients, step size is enlarged to accelerate convergence; in large gradients, step size is reduced for accuracy. Equilibrium Definition: Average particle displacement is used as an approximation of the 'energy gradient'. Adjusts particle projection size adaptively. Adaptive Minimum Projected Size Adjustment Extracts isosurfaces without reconnection steps. Non-reconnected Multiresolution Isosurfacing Uses an oracle to guide multiresolution extraction. Adaptive Multiresolution Extraction with Oracle Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Decoupling forces allows for better distribution optimization and precise surface settling. Gradient-weighted projection provides adaptive convergence speed and accuracy. Voronoi-based insertion allows for local refinement in high-curvature areas. Limitations: Requires construction of voxel pyramid and gradient/Laplacian fields. Equilibrium checking may be computationally expensive if convergence is slow. When to use: Suitable for industrial CT data and other scalar fields where precise surface extraction and adaptive refinement are needed. Originated in the paper "Surface Extraction for Industrial CT Based On Adaptive Particle System". The method builds on traditional particle system-based surface extraction algorithms but introduces decoupled force mechanisms and gradient-weighted projection. It is designed for industrial CT data, leveraging multiresolution voxel pyramids for efficient processing. Surface Extraction for Industrial CT Based On Adaptive Particle System, https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9502773/v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Memory and Performance Optimization
body: This family covers methods that extract isosurfaces from volumetric datasets by partitioning the domain into manageable units to reduce memory usage and enable streaming or incremental updates. Extracts isosurfaces by processing two adjacent slices at a time, using a hash table to share vertices across cell boundaries. It differs from standard Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration by explicitly managing vertex identity via edge keys, and from Sparse Marching Cubes by focusing on memory constraints rather than spatial sparsity. Choose this when generating watertight meshes from massive data that cannot fit in memory. Processes the volume in slabs using a todo list and slice caches to manage connectivity. It differs from surface-following methods by not requiring all slices in memory, enabling lower working memory and improved cache locality. Choose this for large volumes where unidirectional processing is insufficient due to complex topology requiring back-tracking. Regenerates meshes for a 3x3x3 neighborhood of voxel chunks after local noise modifications, ensuring visual continuity across chunk boundaries. Validation: Check that target chunk coordinates (x, y, z) are strictly inside map bounds: x > 0, x < x{chunks}, y > 0, y < y{chunks}, z > 0, z < z{chunks}. Iteration: Iterate x from \x-1 to \x+1, y from \y-1 to \y+1, and z from \z-1 to \z+1. Reset: For each chunk, call ResetChunkMeshData to clear old mesh buffers. Polygonize: Call MarchThroughChunk to polygonize the chunk's noise data into a mesh. Render: Call DrawSingleMesh to render the newly generated chunk mesh. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for y in range(y - 1, y + 1): for z in range(z - 1, z + 1): for x in range(x - 1, x + 1): chunks[x, y, z] = ResetChunkMeshData(chunks[x, y, z]) MarchThroughChunk(chunks[x, y, z]) DrawSingleMesh(chunks[x, y, z]) Not given in the sources. millerc3/Marching-Cubes, https://github.com/millerc3/Marching-Cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Streaming Marching Cubes
head: Hash table vertex sharing, Polygon-Vertex Identification for Isosurface Polygons
body: Streaming Marching Cubes with Hash Table Vertex Sharing is a memory-optimized isosurface extraction method that processes volumetric data in a streaming fashion while ensuring topological consistency through explicit vertex sharing. It solves the dual problems of excessive memory consumption for large datasets and the generation of duplicate vertices at shared cell edges, which complicates downstream mesh processing. Unlike standard Marching Cubes, which may generate multiple vertices for the same geometric point, this method uses a hash table to link polygon vertices to cell edges, guaranteeing that adjacent polygons share identical vertex instances. It builds on Memory and Performance Optimization by combining streaming data access with explicit vertex identification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset V defined on a 3D grid, an isovalue C, and the grid dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz). Output: A triangle mesh representing the isosurface S(x,y,z) = C, where shared vertices are uniquely identified. Data Structures: 1. Hash Table (H): A dictionary mapping a unique key (representing a cell edge) to a vertex object. Key: A tuple or hashable representation of the two grid nodes defining the cell edge. For a grid-aligned edge, this is typically the pair of integer coordinates (i1, j1, k1) and (i2, j2, k2) of the nodes. Value: The 3D position (x, y, z) of the interpolated vertex on that edge. 2. Streaming Buffer: A memory buffer holding only two slices of the volume data (e.g., current and next z-slice, or current and next y-slice depending on traversal order) to minimize RAM usage. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Create an empty hash table H. Initialize the streaming buffer with the first two slices of the volume data. 2. Traverse Cells: Iterate through the volume data in a streaming manner, processing one cell at a time. For each cell, identify the 8 corner nodes. 3. Sign Determination: For each of the 8 nodes ni of the current cell, compute the sign of S(ni) - C, where S(ni) is the scalar value at node ni. 4. Skip Non-Isosurface Cells: If all 8 signs are equal (all positive or all negative), the cell does not intersect the isosurface. Skip further processing for this cell. 5. Identify Intersecting Edges: Determine which cell edges intersect the isosurface. A cell edge connects two nodes na and nb. The edge intersects the isosurface if the signs of S(na) - C and S(nb) - C are different. 6. Vertex Identification and Registration: For each intersecting edge defined by nodes na and nb: Construct the edge key K = \text{hash}(na, nb). Check if K exists in H. If K exists: Retrieve the existing vertex position V{pos} from H. This ensures vertex sharing. If K does not exist: Interpolate the vertex position V{pos} on the edge between na and nb using linear interpolation based on S(na), S(nb), and C. Register V{pos} in H with key K. 7. Generate Triangles: Use the standard Marching Cubes lookup table to determine the topology of the isosurface within the cell. Generate the triangles using the vertex positions retrieved or created in Step 6. 8. Stream Next Slice: Advance the streaming buffer to load the next slice of the volume data, discarding the oldest slice to maintain constant memory usage. 9. Repeat: Continue until all cells are processed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def streamingmarchingcubeswithhashsharing(volume, isovalue, dimensions): """ volume: 3D array of scalar values isovalue: float C dimensions: tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) """ H = {} # Hash table: key=(node1idx, node2idx), value=(x, y, z) triangles = [] # Helper to get or create vertex on edge def getvertexonedge(nodeidx1, nodeidx2, nodeval1, nodeval2): key = (nodeidx1, nodeidx2) if key in H: return H[key] # Linear interpolation # t = (isovalue - nodeval1) / (nodeval2 - nodeval1) # vertex = nodepos1 + t (nodepos2 - nodepos1) # Note: Exact interpolation formula depends on coordinate system # Assuming standard linear interpolation for isosurface t = (isovalue - nodeval1) / (nodeval2 - nodeval1) pos1 = getnodeposition(nodeidx1, dimensions) pos2 = getnodeposition(nodeidx2, dimensions) vertex = pos1 + t (pos2 - pos1) H[key] = vertex return vertex # Streaming loop: iterate over z-slices for z in range(dimensions[2] - 1): # Load current and next slice into memory slicecurrent = volume[:,:, z] slicenext = volume[:,:, z+1] # Iterate over x and y for the current slab of cells for y in range(dimensions[1] - 1): for x in range(dimensions[0] - 1): # Get 8 nodes of the current cell nodes = [ (x, y, z), (x+1, y, z), (x+1, y+1, z), (x, y+1, z), (x, y, z+1), (x+1, y, z+1), (x+1, y+1, z+1), (x, y+1, z+1) ] values = [ slicecurrent[y, x], slicecurrent[y, x+1], slicecurrent[y+1, x+1], slicecurrent[y+1, x], slicenext[y, x], slicenext[y, x+1], slicenext[y+1, x+1], slicenext[y+1, x] ] # Determine signs signs = [1 if v > isovalue else -1 for v in values] # Skip if no intersection if all(s == signs[0] for s in signs): continue # Identify intersecting edges and get vertices # Standard MC edge indices for a cube: # 0:(0,1), 1:(1,2), 2:(2,3), 3:(3,0), 4:(4,5), 5:(5,6), 6:(6,7), 7:(7,4) # 8:(0,4), 9:(1,5), 10:(2,6), 11:(3,7) edges = [ (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0), (4, 5), (5, 6), (6, 7), (7, 4), (0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7) ] edgevertices = [] for eidx1, eidx2 in edges: if signs[eidx1] != signs[eidx2]: v = getvertexonedge(nodes[eidx1], nodes[eidx2], values[eidx1], values[eidx2]) edgevertices.append(v) else: edgevertices.append(None) # Generate triangles based on MC case caseindex = sum(1 << i for i, s in enumerate(signs) if s == 1) # Standard MC triangle configuration table lookup # This part depends on the specific MC implementation variant # For brevity, assuming a function that returns triangle indices into edgevertices triindices = getmctriangles(caseindex) for tri in triindices: v1 = edgevertices[tri[0]] v2 = edgevertices[tri[1]] v3 = edgevertices[tri[2]] if v1 and v2 and v3: triangles.append((v1, v2, v3)) return triangles Parameters: Isovalue (C): The scalar threshold for surface extraction. Typical values depend on the data range. Hash Table Size: Not given in the sources. Should be sized to accommodate the number of unique cell edges intersecting the isosurface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limitations: Cell-edge data is not usually preserved in volume data structures due to limited memory space, necessitating this explicit identification process. Precision: Linear interpolation assumes the scalar field is well-behaved between nodes. Degenerate Input: If S(na) = S(nb) = C, the sign is zero. The sources define sign as equal or not equal. Standard practice is to treat zero as positive or negative consistently to avoid ambiguity. Processes data in slabs and caches vertex data to reduce hash table lookups. Choose when cache locality is more critical than minimal memory footprint. [9753-marching-slices-with-slab-based-caching.md] Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of cells, with a constant factor dependent on hash table operations. Memory Complexity: O(E) where E is the number of unique cell edges intersecting the isosurface, plus O(S) for the streaming buffer where S is the size of two slices. This is significantly lower than storing the entire volume or all cell-edge data. Measured Performance: Allows processing of extremely large datasets that would not fit in memory. Strengths: Minimal memory usage, guaranteed vertex sharing for clean mesh topology. Limitations: Hash table overhead; potential cache misses if the hash table is large. When to Use: Large volumetric datasets where memory is constrained and mesh quality (shared vertices) is important. When Not to Use: Small datasets where memory is not a constraint, or when real-time performance is critical and hash table overhead is prohibitive. The concept of vertex identification using a hash table was described in the context of patient-specific geometric modeling and isosurface propagation algorithms. The streaming aspect of Marching Cubes, allowing processing of extremely large datasets by keeping only two slices in memory, was originally developed and patented by GE Medical Systems for use in their CT and MRI equipment. The patent has expired, placing the algorithm in the public domain. marching cubes, https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/marching-cube, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Marching Cubes Marching Cubes, https://daac.hpc.mil/gettingStarted/MarchingCubes.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Marching Slices with Slab-based Caching
head: Marching Slices, Slab-based Marching Cubes
body: Marching Slices is an isosurface extraction algorithm that reduces memory usage by processing a volume one slice at a time, caching only the data necessary for the current processing unit. It solves the problem of high memory residency required by traditional marching cubes by partitioning the volume into slabs and using boundary consistency via slice caches to ensure geometric continuity. Unlike surface-following marching cubes which keeps all Nz + 1 slices in memory, this approach uses significantly less working memory and is faster due to increased locality of memory accesses. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field defined on a grid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Output: A stream of triangles (vertices and indices) representing the isosurface. Data Structures: The algorithm treats the volume as a vertical array of Nz slabs of size Nx \times Ny \times 1 cubes. The slabs are numbered 0 to Nz-1 (where z increases upwards). Each slab is bounded above and below by a two-dimensional slice, with adjacent slabs sharing slices. The slices are numbered 0 to Nz. 1. Todo List: For each of the Nz slabs, a linked list containing integer (x, y) tuples representing cubes in the slab that may need to be rendered. 2. Slice Cache: Allocated for the slice above and below a slab being polygonized. Each cache consists of: A 2D corner index array of size (Nx + 1) \times (Ny + 1). Each element stores an index to retrieve a computed corner from the corner cache (or 0 if not computed). A corner cache: A dynamically resizing vector storing the actual corner values (interpolated positions). Done Flags: Each element in the corner index array also includes two boolean flags: doneabove and donebelow. These indicate whether the cubes immediately above and below the slice at that corner location have been rendered. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create Nz empty todo lists, one for each slab. Identify seed cubes. Since field values are not known a-priori, the algorithm cannot simply march back-to-front. It must find seed cubes and add their (x, y) coordinates to the corresponding slab's todo list. Allocate a common memory pool for slice caches. 2. Processing Loop: While there are non-empty todo lists in any slab: 1. Select a slab s with a non-empty todo list. 2. Ensure slice caches are allocated for the slice below slab s (slice s) and the slice above slab s (slice s+1). If a cache is not allocated, allocate it and initialize its corner index array and done flags to zero/false. 3. While slab s's todo list is not empty: 1. Pop a cube (x, y) from slab s's todo list. 2. Polygonize: Perform the standard marching cubes lookup for the cube defined by corners at (x, y, z) and (x+1, y+1, z+1) within slab s. 3. Corner Retrieval: For each of the 8 corners of the cube: Check the corner index array of the relevant slice cache (above or below depending on the corner's z-coordinate). If the index is 0, compute the corner position (interpolate based on field values) and store it in the corner cache. Update the index array with the new cache index. 4. Mark Done: For each of the 8 corners, update the doneabove and donebelow flags in the respective slice caches to indicate that the cubes adjacent to these corners in the current slab have been processed. 5. Neighbor Propagation: For each of the 8 corners, check the adjacent cubes in neighboring slabs. If a neighbor cube has not been processed (checked via the done flags in the slice cache of the other slab), add its (x, y) coordinate to the todo list of that neighbor slab. Specifically, if a corner is shared with a cube in slab s-1 (below) or s+1 (above), and that cube's done flag is false, push the cube's (x, y) to the respective slab's todo list. 4. Cache Management: After slab s's todo list is empty, check if the slice cache below slab s (slice s) can be deallocated. This is safe if the todo list for slab s-1 is also empty. Similarly, check if the slice cache above slab s (slice s+1) can be deallocated if the todo list for slab s+1 is empty. When a slice cache is deallocated, reset its corner index arrays by clearing nonzero indices and done flags using the (x, y) entries in its corner caches, and return the memory to the common pool. 3. Completion: The algorithm completes when there are no more todo list items for any slab in the block. Flush the accumulated index and vertex buffers to the video card. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marchingslices(volume, isovalue, Nx, Ny, Nz): # Data structures todolists = [[] for in range(Nz)] slicecaches = [None] (Nz + 1) cornerpool = [] # 1. Initialization seeds = findseeds(volume, isovalue, Nx, Ny, Nz) for (x, y, z) in seeds: if 0 <= z < Nz: todolists[z].append((x, y)) # 2. Processing Loop while any(todolists): slab = next(i for i, tl in enumerate(todolists) if tl) # Ensure caches for slices below (slab) and above (slab+1) if slicecaches[slab] is None: slicecaches[slab] = allocatecache(Nx, Ny) if slicecaches[slab + 1] is None: slicecaches[slab + 1] = allocatecache(Nx, Ny) while todolists[slab]: x, y = todolists[slab].pop() # Polygonize cube at (x, y, slab) corners = getcubecorners(x, y, slab) triangles = marchcube(volume, isovalue, corners) outputtriangles(triangles) for cx, cy, cz in corners: cache = slicecaches[cz] if cache.index[cx][cy] == 0: pos = interpolatecorner(volume, (cx, cy, cz), isovalue) idx = len(cornerpool) cornerpool.append(pos) cache.index[cx][cy] = idx + 1 # Mark done flags if cz == slab: cache.doneabove[cx][cy] = True elif cz == slab + 1: cache.donebelow[cx][cy] = True # Propagate to neighbors if cz == slab + 1 and not slicecaches[slab + 1].doneabove[cx][cy]: if slab + 1 < Nz: todolists[slab + 1].append((cx, cy)) if cz == slab and not slicecaches[slab].donebelow[cx][cy]: if slab > 0: todolists[slab - 1].append((cx, cy)) # Cache management if slab > 0 and not todolists[slab - 1]: if slicecaches[slab] is not None: deallocatecache(slicecaches[slab]) slicecaches[slab] = None if slab + 1 < Nz and not todolists[slab + 1]: if slicecaches[slab + 1] is not None: deallocatecache(slicecaches[slab + 1]) slicecaches[slab + 1] = None flushbuffers() def allocatecache(Nx, Ny): return { 'index': [[0] (Ny + 1) for in range(Nx + 1)], 'doneabove': [[False] (Ny + 1) for in range(Nx + 1)], 'donebelow': [[False] (Ny + 1) for in range(Nx + 1)] } def deallocatecache(cache): for x in range(len(cache['index'])): for y in range(len(cache['index'][0])): cache['index'][x][y] = 0 cache['doneabove'][x][y] = False cache['donebelow'][x][y] = False def findseeds(volume, isovalue, Nx, Ny, Nz): seeds = [] for z in range(Nz): for y in range(Ny): for x in range(Nx): if volume[x, y, z] < isovalue and (x == 0 or volume[x-1, y, z] >= isovalue): seeds.append((x, y, z)) return seeds def getcubecorners(x, y, slab): return [ (x, y, slab), (x+1, y, slab), (x, y+1, slab), (x+1, y+1, slab), (x, y, slab+1), (x+1, y, slab+1), (x, y+1, slab+1), (x+1, y+1, slab+1) ] def interpolatecorner(volume, corner, isovalue): x, y, z = corner v0 = volume[x, y, z] v1 = volume[x+1, y, z] if x < Nx else volume[x, y, z] t = (isovalue - v0) / (v1 - v0) if v1 != v0 else 0.0 return (x + t, y, z) def marchcube(volume, isovalue, corners): return [] def outputtriangles(triangles): pass def flushbuffers(): pass Parameters: Number of slices in memory: Typically three slices are kept in memory at the same time. Grid Size: For a 110 \times 110 \times 110 grid, the cache memory used is below 1MB. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Seeding Failure: Seeding algorithms may fail to find all local minima, causing the algorithm to step downwards to render connected cubes in slabs below that were missed. This requires additional slices to store the abandoned frontier and breaks the unidirectional order of polygonization. Arbitrary Order: Because field values are not known a-priori, the algorithm must support arbitrary forward/reverse traversal order, which complicates the simple "march back-to-front" assumption. Redundant Visits: Care must be taken to avoid redundant visits to completed cubes. The done flags in the slice cache prevent this. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower than full-volume marching cubes. For a 110 \times 110 \times 110 grid, memory usage is below 1MB. It uses much less working memory than surface-following marching cubes which keeps all Nz + 1 slices in memory. Time Complexity: Faster than hash-map based approaches due to the avoidance of hash map lookup costs. The use of 2D arrays for corner indices provides O(1) access time. Strengths: Low memory footprint, high performance due to memory locality, straightforward parallelization of blocks. Limitations: Seeding failures can lead to complex traversal patterns and potential performance degradation if many slabs need to be revisited. When to Use: Suitable for real-time applications or environments with strict memory constraints where the volume is too large to fit in memory. The Marching Slices algorithm was introduced in the paper "Real-time particle isosurface extraction". It was developed to address the memory limitations of traditional marching cubes when dealing with large volumes or real-time applications. The method builds on the principles of isosurface extraction but optimizes for memory by processing the volume in slabs and caching only necessary boundary data.
