name: Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field
head: Guidance Field Advancing Front, Schreiner et al. method
body:
This method extracts isosurfaces from implicit functions using an advancing front algorithm guided by a scalar field g(\mathbf{x}) that constrains edge lengths based on surface curvature and user parameters. It solves the problems of front interference detection and poor triangle shaping inherent in standard adaptive advancing front algorithms by providing a theoretical foundation for edge size selection. Unlike its parent Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces, which relies on intrinsic geometry heuristics, this method uses a guidance field to bound the Hausdorff distance and aspect ratio of triangles, ensuring robust front intersection tests. Inputs: Implicit function f(\mathbf{x}), its gradient 
abla f, its Hessian H(f), isovalue k, accuracy parameter ho, and well-shapedness parameter \eta. Outputs: A triangulated mesh approximating the isosurface f(\mathbf{x}) = k. Data Structures: Sample Set S: A set of 3D points on the surface. Guidance Field g: A scalar field defined as the lower envelope of cone functions. Active Fronts: A collection of front objects, where each front represents a boundary edge or sequence of edges on the mesh. 4D KD-Tree: Used for culling samples, storing points as [sx, sy, sz, sr] where sr is the height of the cone function at the sample location. Parameters: ho: Controls reconstruction accuracy. Determines the angle subtended by edges on the minimum osculating circle. Typical values: 0.2, 0.3, 0.5. \eta: Controls the rate of triangle expansion (well-shapedness). Bounds the ratio of adjacent edge lengths |e1|/|e2| \le \eta if |e1| > |e2|. Typical values: 2, 3, 5. Steps: 1. Generate Initial Samples: Create a jittered random set of points inside cells neighboring the surface. Project these points onto the surface f(\mathbf{x})=k using gradient descent. 2. Compute Guidance Field: For each sample s \in S, compute the ideal edge length \iota(s) and the cone function 	ilde{g}s(\mathbf{x}). The guidance field is the lower envelope: \iota(s) =  rac{2 \sin(ho/2)}{\kappa{\max}(s)} 	ilde{g}s(\mathbf{x}) = (1 - \eta^{-1}) \cdot |\mathbf{x} - s| + \eta^{-1} \cdot \iota(s) g(\mathbf{x}) = \min{s \in S} 	ilde{g}s(\mathbf{x}) where \kappa{\max}(s) is the maximum absolute curvature at s. 3. Cull Guidance Field: Remove samples dominated by others to reduce memory and query time (see Minimal Guidance Field Culling). 4. Seed the Front: Compute seed points (e.g., using efficient algorithms like [6] in) and project them onto the surface using gradient descent. Initialize the Active front set with these seeds. 5. Advance Front: While Active is not empty: a. Get a front from Active. b. Check if it is OK to add a triangle using parameters ho and \eta. c. If OK, add the triangle to the front. d. If not OK, get the interfering front. e. If the interfering front is the same as the current front, split the front into two new fronts (f1, f2), remove the old front, and add the two new fronts to Active. f. If the interfering front is different, merge the current front and the interfering front into a new front, remove both from Active, and add the new front to Active. 6. Create New Triangles: Determine the correct edge size from the guidance field g. Project the new point onto the surface using the dihedral angle of the edge as a free parameter and searching for the isovalue. Curvature Calculation: The maximum curvature \kappa{\max} is derived from the geometry tensor G. Let \mathbf{n} = 
abla f / |
abla f| be the normalized gradient. The projection matrix onto the tangent plane is: P = I - \mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^T The bound for \kappa{\max} is given by: \kappa{\max} \le \|P\| \cdot \|H\| \cdot \|P\| \cdot \|I/|
abla f|\| where \|\cdot\| denotes the Frobenius norm \|M\|2 = \sqrt{\sum m{ij}^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TRIANGULATE(f, gradf, hessf, k, rho, eta): # 1. Generate Samples # Create jittered random points in cells neighboring the surface S = [] for cell in neighboringcells(f, k): points = jitteredrandompointsincell(cell) for p in points: # Project onto surface via gradient descent projected = gradientdescentprojection(f, k, p) if projected is not None: S.append(projected) # 2. Compute Guidance Field # For each sample, compute ideal edge length and cone function guidancefieldsamples = [] for s in S: n = normalize(gradf(s)) H = hessf(s) P = identitymatrix() - outerproduct(n, n) # Compute kappamax bound normP = frobeniusnorm(P) normH = frobeniusnorm(H) normgradinv = 1.0 / abs(dot(gradf(s), gradf(s))) 0.5 kappamaxbound = normP normH normP normgradinv # Ideal edge length iotas = (2 sin(rho / 2)) / kappamaxbound # Cone function parameters: slope (1 - eta^-1), intercept eta^-1 iotas guidancefieldsamples.append({ 'point': s, 'iota': iotas, 'slope': 1.0 - 1.0/eta, 'intercept': (1.0/eta) iotas }) # 3. Cull Guidance Field guidancefieldsamples = CULL(guidancefieldsamples, rho, eta) # 4. Seed Fronts Active = SEEDFRONTS(S) # Uses efficient seed point algorithm [6] # 5. Advance Front while len(Active) > 0: front = GETANYFRONT(Active) if OKTOADDTRIANGLE(front, rho, eta): ADDTRIANGLETOFRONT(front, rho, eta) else: other = GETINTERFERINGFRONT(front) if other == front: f1, f2 = SPLIT(front) REMOVEFRONTS(Active, {front}) ADDFRONTS(Active, {f1, f2}) else: newfront = MERGE(front, other) REMOVEFRONTS(Active, {front, other}) ADDFRONTS(Active, {newfront}) def OKTOADDTRIANGLE(front, rho, eta): # Check front interference using guidance field properties # Returns True if adding the triangle does not cause interference # and respects curvature bounds pass def GETINTERFERINGFRONT(front): # Find another front that interferes with the current front # based on the guidance field g(x) pass def ADDTRIANGLETOFRONT(front, rho, eta): # Determine correct edge size from guidance field g # Project new point onto surface using dihedral angle # Add triangle to mesh and update front pass A technique to reduce the number of samples in a guidance field by removing samples that are 'dominated' by others. A sample s1 dominates s2 if the edge length required for curvature at s1 is always smaller than that of s2, ensuring the guidance field remains sufficient and Lipschitz-continuous. Steps: 1. Insert all points in the guidance field into a 4-dimensional kd-tree. The coordinates for each sample s are [sx, sy, sz, sr], where [sx, sy, sz] is the sample's location in \mathbb{R}^3, and sr is the height of the function 	ilde{g}s at s. 2. Sort the samples by their maximum curvature (\kappa{max}) in descending order. 3. Iterate through the sorted samples. For each sample si, if it is not already marked as dominated, construct a cone c defined by si, user parameters ho and \eta, apex [sx, sy, sz, sr], axis [0, 0, 0, 1], and angle 	an^{-1}(\eta/(\eta-1)). 4. Perform a kd-tree query to find all points lying inside the cone c. Mark all such points as dominated. If all children of a kd-tree node are marked, mark the node itself to prune branches. 5. Discard all marked samples from the guidance field g(\mathbf{x}). Time Complexity: The guidance field evaluation is efficient using kd-tree queries, avoiding the need to splat values into a regular grid. Culling typically removes a large percentage of sample points, resulting in significantly faster guidance field queries and lower memory usage. Table 1 in shows that culling can reduce running time from ~27 minutes to ~7 minutes for a large dataset, despite the overhead of culling. Memory Complexity: Reduced significantly by culling unnecessary samples. In some cases, less than half of a percent of points remain in the guidance field after culling. Strengths: Robust front interference tests proven by guidance field properties; prevents sharp changes in triangle size; bounds Hausdorff distance and aspect ratio; no need for regular grid splatting. Limitations: Assumes the surface is smooth; requires sufficient sampling to guarantee feature reproduction; computing curvature bounds can be expensive for high-gradient regions. When to use: When high-quality, robust isosurface extraction is required without downstream processing, and the surface is smooth. When not to use: For surfaces with sharp features that violate the smoothness assumption, or when extremely high performance is needed and some mesh quality degradation is acceptable (consider parallel variants or marching cubes). The method is based on the advancing front algorithm of Schreiner et al. [45] in, which introduced a solid theoretical foundation for advancing front algorithms using a guidance field. It addresses limitations of previous methods that relied on heuristics for front interference and suffered from poorly shaped triangles due to sharp curvature changes. The guidance field construction ensures that g(\mathbf{x}) is bounded above by 2 \sin(ho)/\kappa{\max} and has a gradient magnitude never greater than 1-\eta^{-1}. name: Multi-threaded Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction
head: Parallel Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction
body:
This method parallelizes the Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field [947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md] to accelerate mesh generation by distributing computational work across multiple CPU cores. It solves the performance bottleneck of sequential front projection and guidance field evaluation. Unlike its parent method, which relies on intrinsic geometry for quality, this variant specifically optimizes throughput via thread-level parallelism while maintaining the bounded distance and normal error guarantees of the underlying algorithm. It sets itself apart from standard parallel marching cubes by producing meshes that require negligible downstream processing, albeit at a slower raw execution speed. The method extends the single-threaded advancing front algorithm by parallelizing the most computationally intensive phases: the computation of the guidance field, the culling of candidate points, and the projection of points onto the advancing fronts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An implicit function f(\mathbf{x}) defining the surface, a target isovalue k, and a guidance field g(\mathbf{x}) (computed by the parent method or provided externally). The function must admit well-defined gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) and Hessian Hf(\mathbf{x}). Output: A triangle mesh approximating the isosurface f(\mathbf{x}) = k. Data Structures: Worker Queue: A thread-safe queue containing tasks for worker threads. Tasks typically involve projecting a specific point or edge onto the current front. Front Data Structure: The advancing front, maintained as a set of edges or vertices. Access to shared state (the front) must be synchronized or partitioned to avoid race conditions during parallel updates. Guidance Field: A scalar field g(\mathbf{x}) used to constrain edge lengths based on curvature. Parameters: Thread Count (T): The number of worker threads. The source uses T=4 for experiments. ho, \eta: Guidance field parameters controlling sampling density and smoothing. Typical values are not explicitly defined in the source text, but the method is robust across different settings. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the advancing front with seed points or edges derived from the guidance field. 2. Parallel Guidance and Culling: Compute the guidance field g(\mathbf{x}) and perform point culling in parallel across all available threads. This step determines which regions require refinement based on local curvature. 3. Task Distribution: Distribute the work of projecting points onto the advancing fronts to a set of T worker threads. Each thread processes a subset of points or edges. 4. Parallel Projection: Worker threads independently project candidate points onto the front, evaluating f(\mathbf{x}) and using 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) to find the intersection with the isosurface. 5. Front Update: As projections complete, the front is updated. Synchronization mechanisms (e.g., locks or atomic operations) are required if multiple threads modify the same front segments simultaneously. 6. Mesh Generation: Triangles are formed from the projected points and added to the output mesh. Formulas: The method relies on the implicit function representation: f(\mathbf{x}) = k The surface normal is given by: \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}) =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{x})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{x})\|} The guidance field g(\mathbf{x}) constrains the maximum edge length L in the mesh: L \leq g(\mathbf{x}) where g(\mathbf{x}) is derived from the curvature (Hessian) of f. The source states the mesh has bounded distance error and bounded normal error. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multithreadedadvancingfrontextraction(f, k, guidancefield, numthreads): """ Extracts isosurface from implicit function f using parallel advancing front. Args: f: Implicit function callable f(x) returning scalar value. k: Isovalue threshold. guidancefield: Precomputed or callable scalar field g(x) for edge length constraints. numthreads: Number of worker threads. Returns: List of triangles (vertices). """ # Initialize the advancing front with seed points front = initializefront(f, k, guidancefield) # Initialize thread-safe queue for tasks taskqueue = ThreadSafeQueue() # Parallel Guidance Field Computation and Culling # Compute guidance values and cull invalid points in parallel parallelcomputeguidanceandcull(f, k, guidancefield, front, taskqueue) # Worker Thread Function def worker(): while True: try: task = taskqueue.get(timeout=1.0) except Empty: break # Project point onto the front projectedpoint = projectpointontofront(task.point, front, f, k) # Update front and generate triangles if valid if projectedpoint is not None: updatefront(front, projectedpoint, task) generatetriangles(front, projectedpoint) taskqueue.taskdone() # Launch worker threads threads = [] for in range(numthreads): t = Thread(target=worker) t.start() threads.append(t) # Wait for completion for t in threads: t.join() return front.gettriangles() def parallelcomputeguidanceandcull(f, k, guidancefield, front, taskqueue): """ Computes guidance field and culls points in parallel. """ # Determine candidate points based on initial sampling or grid candidates = getcandidatepoints(front) # Parallel loop over candidates for point in candidates: # Compute guidance value gval = guidancefield(point) # Cull logic: check if point is valid for front projection if isvalidforfront(point, front, gval): taskqueue.put(Task(point=point)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Corners: The method requires the implicit function to admit a well-defined gradient and Hessian. Sharp corners do not admit a regular isosurface representation where f(\mathbf{x}) = k and 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) 
eq 0. Concurrency: Race conditions may occur if multiple threads update the front simultaneously. Proper synchronization is required. Precision: The method assumes band-limited reconstruction of sampled volumes, ensuring smoothness. A coarse-to-fine surface extraction strategy that constructs a voxel pyramid from CT data, computes curvature fields, and iteratively refines high-curvature regions to guide adaptive particle sampling, reducing artifacts and topological errors compared to direct threshold-based methods. It generates high-quality triangle meshes using a curvature-based guidance field. It sets itself apart from its sibling Multi-threaded Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction by explicitly using a multi-scale pyramid and statistical curvature thresholds to drive the refinement process, rather than relying solely on the intrinsic geometry of the implicit function at a single resolution. Time Complexity: The algorithm is slower than Marching Cubes (MC) or Marching Tetrahedra (MT) implementations. Running times are typically several minutes for larger datasets. For example, on the specified hardware, times were 5:18 for Aneurism BS, 12:16 for Engine BS, and 5:50 for Skull CR. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments were conducted on a PC with two dual-core AMD Opteron processors at 2.25GHz, 4GB RAM, SuSE Linux 10.0. Four threads were used for all experiments. Scaling: The algorithm is mostly local, allowing decisions and actions to be taken independently of the reconstruction of distant surface parts, which facilitates parallelization. Strengths: Generates high-quality meshes with bounded distance and normal error. 99% of triangles have quality at least half of optimal, and the median quality is within 3% of optimal. Triangle counts are often less than MC. The resulting meshes require negligible or no downstream processing. Limitations: Slower than MC/MT. Requires well-defined gradient and Hessian. When to use: When high mesh quality and minimal downstream processing are prioritized over raw speed. Applicable to high-order meshes (typically degree ~10) where the technique is oblivious to the underlying mesh as long as gradient and Hessian are computable. When not: When real-time performance is critical and lower quality mesh is acceptable. The method originates from the work on high-quality extraction of isosurfaces from regular and irregular grids. It builds on the Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field [947-advancing-front-isosurface-extraction-with-guidance-field.md]. The implementation was tested on various models including Catmull-Rom splines and B-splines, demonstrating robustness across different surface definitions and parameter settings. name: Advancing Front Meshing with Curvature Guidance
head: Multi-scale Adaptive Refinement Strategy, curvature-adaptive nested refinement method
body: A coarse-to-fine surface extraction strategy that constructs a voxel pyramid from CT data, computes curvature fields, and iteratively refines high-curvature regions to guide adaptive particle sampling, reducing artifacts and topological errors compared to direct threshold-based methods. It generates high-quality triangle meshes using a curvature-based guidance field. It sets itself apart from its sibling Multi-threaded Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction by explicitly using a multi-scale pyramid and statistical curvature thresholds to drive the refinement process, rather than relying solely on the intrinsic geometry of the implicit function at a single resolution. Inputs: Original CT data (grayscale volume), threshold value for isosurface detection, adjustable parameter k for curvature thresholding, dilation width n (typically 1 or 2 voxels), and maximum scale level L. Outputs: A refined set of voxel units (particles) at the finest scale, ready for surface extraction via an advancing front or particle system method. Data Structures: Voxel Pyramid: A list of volume levels l = 0, \dots, L. Level 0 is the coarsest (downsampled), Level L is the finest (original or highest resolution). Each level contains a 3D grid of voxel values. Voxel Unit: A cube defined by integer coordinates (i, j, k) and its 8 vertices. Response Region: A set of voxel units at scale l where the isosurface passes through. High-Curvature Region: A subset of the response region where curvature exceeds a statistical threshold. Candidate Region: The high-curvature region after morphological dilation, mapped to the next finer scale. Steps: 1. Construct Voxel Pyramid: Apply 3D guided filtering (an extension of guided filtering [22] to 3D) to the original CT data to suppress artifacts while preserving edges. Downsample the filtered data to create the pyramid levels l=0 to L. 2. Compute Fields: For each scale level l in the pyramid, compute the gradient field \nabla F and the curvature field. The gradient at any point is defined as: \nabla F = \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial F}{\partial z} \right) where F is the voxel grayscale value. The gradient is computed using difference methods. The curvature field is derived from the gradient/voxel information to reflect local surface complexity. 3. Initialize Coarse Scale: Start at the coarsest scale l = 0. Identify all response units. A voxel unit at (i, j, k) is a response unit if the grayscale values of its 8 vertices contain a sign change relative to the isosurface threshold. This indicates the isosurface passes through the unit. Collect all such units into the response region for scale l. 4. Iterative Refinement (Coarse-to-Fine): While l < L: a. Calculate Curvature Statistics: For all voxel units in the current response region at scale l, compute the mean curvature \mu and standard deviation \sigma. \mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} Ci \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (Ci - \mu)^2} where Ci is the curvature of the i-th voxel unit and N is the number of units in the response region. b. Determine High-Curvature Region: Compute the statistical threshold \theta: \theta = \mu + k \cdot \sigma where k is an adjustable parameter. Mark all voxel units in the response region with curvature C > \theta as the high-curvature region. c. Morphological Dilation: Apply morphological dilation to the high-curvature region with a width of n voxels. This expands the region to prevent missing important geometric features and ensure consistent reconstruction across scales. The result is the candidate region. d. Map to Finer Scale: Map the candidate region from scale l to the corresponding spatial locations in scale l+1. Set l \leftarrow l + 1. Repeat steps 4a-4d for the new scale l. 5. Final Extraction: Once the finest scale L is reached, the final set of response units (particles) is used for surface extraction. The method decouples repulsive and attractive forces in the particle system to adjust the force mechanism during iteration, further improving mesh quality. Parameters: k: Adjustable parameter for curvature threshold sensitivity. Not given in the sources. n: Dilation width in voxels. Typically 1 or 2. L: Maximum number of levels in the voxel pyramid. Determined by the downsampling factor of the input data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Partial Volume Effect: Traditional filtering may exacerbate partial volume effects, introducing errors. The use of 3D guided filtering helps mitigate this. Aliasing Artifacts: If the high-curvature region is directly mapped without dilation, important features may be missed, leading to aliasing and inconsistent reconstruction across scales. Topological Errors: Direct threshold-based methods can produce topological errors. The curvature-guided approach reduces these by ensuring adequate sampling in complex regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The multi-scale approach adds overhead for pyramid construction and iterative refinement but reduces the total number of samples needed compared to uniform high-resolution sampling. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the voxel pyramid and curvature fields at each level. Strengths: Reduces artifacts and topological errors; adapts sampling density to surface complexity; handles high-curvature surfaces well. Limitations: Requires construction of a voxel pyramid; dependent on the choice of parameters k and n. When to use: When extracting surfaces from CT data with high curvature variations and where topological correctness and mesh quality are critical. When not to use: For simple, low-curvature surfaces where uniform sampling is sufficient and computational resources are limited. The method was proposed in the context of surface extraction for industrial CT data, aiming to address topological errors and artifacts common in traditional filtering and direct thresholding methods. It builds on the concept of using a curvature-based guidance field for advancing front meshing, originally proposed by Scheidegger et al. [109] and extended by Schreiner et al. [110] to minimize geometric error and sample count. The specific multi-scale adaptive refinement strategy is detailed in the paper "Surface Extraction for Industrial CT Based On Adaptive Particle System". name: Region-growing Iso-surface Extraction
head: Normal consistency constrained marching triangles, Novel region-growing algorithm, Region-growing based iso-surface extraction algorithm
body: Region-growing Iso-surface Extraction is a surface extraction method that generates high-quality, curvature-adaptive semi-regular meshes while preserving sharp features and extracting all disjoint components of an iso-surface. It improves upon the original Marching Triangles algorithm by introducing a novel normal consistency constraint, which ensures robustness for complex topologies by guaranteeing that the intersection of the Delaunay sphere of a new triangle and the iso-surface is a topological disk. Unlike standard marching cubes which processes cubes independently, this method builds on Region-growing and Advancing Front by explicitly tracking connectivity across cube boundaries to solve topological ambiguity and hole-generation problems. The algorithm operates on a volumetric dataset to extract an iso-surface defined by a threshold value. It produces a triangular mesh where triangle sizes adapt to local surface curvature. Inputs: Volumetric dataset V (scalar field). Iso-surface threshold value T. Outputs: Triangular mesh M representing the iso-surface. Data Structures: Boundary Particles: A set of points on the iso-surface. Each particle p stores its 3D position \mathbf{p}, its surface normal \mathbf{n}, and a status flag (e.g., unvisited, visited, boundary). Growth Queue: A priority queue storing candidate triangles or edges for expansion. Prioritization is based on curvature or feature importance. Visited Set: A hash map or grid-based structure tracking processed boundary particles to prevent re-processing. Algorithm Steps: 1. Boundary Particle Sampling and Classification: Sample points on the iso-surface from the volume. Classify them based on local geometric properties (e.g., curvature, gradient magnitude) to identify potential seed locations and feature points. 2. Feature Position Extraction: Identify sharp features and high-curvature regions. These positions are marked as high-priority seeds to ensure sharp features are preserved in the final mesh. 3. Prioritized Seed Initialization: Initialize the growth front by selecting seed triangles from the high-priority feature positions and other classified boundary particles. Seeds are added to the growth queue with priorities determined by their geometric significance. 4. Front Propagation: Loop until the queue is empty or all disjoint components are extracted: a. Dequeue the highest-priority candidate triangle t{new}. b. Normal Consistency Check: Verify that the normal vector of t{new} is consistent with the normals of its neighboring existing triangles on the front. Specifically, ensure that the intersection of the Delaunay sphere of t{new} and the iso-surface is a topological disk. This constraint is more robust than the original Marching Triangles' Delaunay face property check alone. c. If the check passes, add t{new} to the mesh M. d. Generate new candidate triangles from the boundary edges of t{new}. e. Classify and prioritize these new candidates based on local curvature and feature strength. f. Add valid candidates to the growth queue. 5. Visited Boundary Particle Identification: Mark particles associated with added triangles as visited. Ensure that particles belonging to disjoint components are identified and initialized as new seeds if they were not reached by the current front. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def regiongrowingisosurfaceextraction(volume, threshold): # Step 1: Boundary particle sampling and classification boundaryparticles = sampleboundaryparticles(volume, threshold) classifyparticles(boundaryparticles) # Step 2: Feature position extraction featurepositions = extractfeaturepositions(boundaryparticles) # Step 3: Prioritized seed initialization growthqueue = PriorityQueue() visited = set() mesh = Mesh() # Add feature positions as high-priority seeds for pos in featurepositions: seedtriangle = createseedtriangle(pos, boundaryparticles) growthqueue.push(seedtriangle, priority=HIGH) visited.add(pos.id) # Add other classified particles as lower-priority seeds for particle in boundaryparticles: if particle not in visited and particle.isseedcandidate: seedtriangle = createseedtriangle(particle, boundaryparticles) growthqueue.push(seedtriangle, priority=LOW) visited.add(particle.id) # Step 4 & 5: Front propagation and visited identification while not growthqueue.isempty(): candidate = growthqueue.pop() # Normal consistency constraint check if isnormalconsistent(candidate, mesh, boundaryparticles): # Ensure Delaunay sphere intersection is a topological disk if istopologicaldisk(candidate.delaunaysphere, volume, threshold): mesh.addtriangle(candidate) # Generate new candidates from boundary edges newcandidates = generateboundarycandidates(candidate, boundaryparticles) for newcand in newcandidates: if newcand not in visited: # Prioritize based on curvature/feature strength priority = calculatepriority(newcand) growthqueue.push(newcand, priority=priority) visited.add(newcand.id) else: # Discard inconsistent candidates pass return mesh def isnormalconsistent(triangle, mesh, particles): # Check if triangle normal is consistent with neighbors # Returns True if consistent, False otherwise pass def istopologicaldisk(sphere, volume, threshold): # Check if intersection of sphere and iso-surface is a topological disk # Returns True if topological disk, False otherwise pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disjoint Components: The algorithm must explicitly check for unvisited boundary particles after the main loop to ensure all disjoint components are extracted. Topological Ambiguity: The normal consistency constraint is critical for handling complex topologies where standard Delaunay checks might fail. Sharp Features: Failure to prioritize feature positions may result in loss of sharp features in the output mesh. A variant that reconstructs surfaces by propagating from seed triangles through a queue of "growth edges". It solves topological ambiguity and hole-generation by explicitly tracking connectivity across cube boundaries, using specific topological configurations for triangle and quadrangle edges. A semi-automatic technique that extracts connected regions of interest from a 3D volume by iteratively adding neighboring voxels to a user-selected seed point based on statistical similarity criteria. It distinguishes itself by relying on local homogeneity rather than global cut optimization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The algorithm generates high-quality curvature-adaptive semi-regular meshes and preserves sharp features. It is robust for large-scale volumetric datasets with complex topology and geometry. Strengths: Generates evenly-sized and quasi-equilateral meshes; adapts to local surface properties (curvature); preserves sharp features; extracts all disjoint components; robust against topological ambiguity via normal consistency constraints. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When high-quality, curvature-adaptive meshes are required, especially for complex topologies or when sharp features must be preserved. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The algorithm was proposed by Jian Xi and Ye Duan in 2008. It builds on the concept of the marching triangles algorithm, which generates higher quality evenly-sized and quasi-equilateral meshes by iteratively joining new triangles to the current region boundary. The original marching triangles algorithm did not adapt well to local surface properties, requiring many small triangles for surfaces with large curvature variations. This new algorithm improves upon it by using a prioritized seed initialization scheme and normal consistency constraints. A novel region-growing based iso-surface extraction algorithm, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cag.2008.09.007, fetched 2026-10-27

name: 3D reconstruction based on edge growth
body: 3D reconstruction based on edge growth is a region-growing iso-surface extraction technique that propagates from seed triangles through a queue of growth edges. It addresses topological ambiguity and hole generation in 3D models by explicitly tracking iso-surface connectivity across cube boundaries and extracting only triangles connected to the current growth front. Inputs: A 3D scalar field (volume data), an iso-surface threshold Y, and one or more seed triangles (manually selected or from a designated 3D area). Outputs: A set of iso-surface triangles forming the reconstructed mesh. Cube Grid: The volume is discretized into cubes. Each cube maintains two integer markers: Processing Marker (records how the cube was processed) and Growth Marker (records how the cube's growth information is put into the growth queue). Growth Queue: Stores pending growth edge information, including edge type, endpoints, and associated cube index. Growth Edge Types: Triangle edges (endpoints on adjacent edges, forming a triangle) and quadrangle edges (endpoints on opposite sides, dividing the cube into two quadrangles). The algorithm uses a three-segment interpolation method, which lies between linear interpolation and midpoint selection. For an edge with endpoints p1, p2 having gray values hu1, hu2, and iso-surface threshold Y, the intersection point coordinates are calculated such that the intersection lies strictly between the two endpoints on that side. To resolve topological configurations, vertices are named relative to the growth edge endpoints I and II, and the surface containing the growth edge (SS). The surface opposite to SS is named S\S. Triangle Edge Naming: The vertex on SS that forms a triangle with the growth edge is named SS. The vertices on SS adjacent to SS are named SS\I and SS\II. The vertex on SS diagonal to SS is named SS\I\II. Vertices on S\S share the same suffix as their adjacent counterparts on SS. Quadrangle Edge Naming: On SS, the vertex adjacent to I that meets the threshold requirement is named SS\I, while the adjacent vertex that does not meet the requirement is named SS\UP\I. The vertex adjacent to II that meets the requirement is named SS\II, while the adjacent vertex that does not meet the requirement is named SS\UP\II. Vertices on S\S share the same suffix as their adjacent counterparts on SS. The algorithm defines 17 specific topological configurations to handle the extraction of iso-surface triangles connected to the growth edge. Triangle Edge Configurations (11 types): Select a reference point SS. Compare its gray value hu{SS} with threshold Y. If hu{SS} > Y, vertices with hu > Y "meet requirements" (large dots); others do not (small dots). If hu{SS} \le Y, vertices with hu \le Y "meet requirements"; others do not. Based on the pattern of meeting/non-meeting vertices, one of 11 configurations is selected to extract the connected triangles. Quadrangle Edge Configurations (6 types): Compare all 8 cube vertices with threshold Y. Divide vertices into "meeting requirements" and "not meeting requirements". Select the smaller set (size 1 to 4) as the reference set. Apply the naming convention defined above. Based on the pattern, one of 6 configurations is selected to extract the iso-surface. Each cube has two markers with levels 0–4. Level 0 indicates the cube has not been processed. Level 4 indicates the cube has been processed and no further processing is required. Levels 1–3 indicate the cube has been processed but may still need processing. Marker Assignment Rules: 1. After extracting the seed triangle, set both markers of the corresponding cube to 4. 2. When growth edge information is added to the growth queue, increment the cube's Growth Marker by 1. 3. After processing a cube, set the Processing Marker based on the topological configuration used: Set to 4 if configuration is: 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 15, or 17. Set to 3 if configuration is: 2, 3, 6, 9, 12, 14, or 16. Increment by 1 if configuration is: 1. New Growth Edge Detection: After interpolation, determine if the intersection of the iso-surface and the cube surface forms a new growth edge. It is a new growth edge if the edge's processing label and the growth label of adjacent cubes sharing the side are both not 4. Processing Constraints: If Processing Marker is 4, skip further processing of the cube. If Growth Marker is 4, do not add growth information to the growth queue. If Processing Marker is >1 and <4, only extract iso-surface for topological configuration 1. 1. Initialize all cube markers to 0. 2. Initialize an empty growth queue. 3. Select a seed triangle (manually or from a designated area). 4. Extract the iso-surface for the seed triangle using the appropriate configuration. 5. Set the Processing Marker and Growth Marker of the seed cube to 4. 6. While the growth queue is not empty: a. Dequeue a growth edge (type, endpoints I, II, cube index). b. Check if the cube's Growth Marker is 4. If so, skip. c. Check if the cube's Processing Marker is 4. If so, skip. d. Determine the edge type (Triangle or Quadrangle). e. Apply the naming convention for the cube vertices. f. Determine the topological configuration based on vertex values relative to Y. g. Extract the iso-surface triangles for this configuration. h. Update the cube's Processing Marker according to the configuration rules. i. Check adjacent cube faces for new growth edges. j. If a new growth edge is found and adjacent cubes' growth labels are not 4: i. Enqueue the new growth edge. ii. Increment the cube's Growth Marker. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Solves topological ambiguity and hole generation common in 3D reconstruction by ensuring connected iso-surface extraction. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from a 2021 paper on a marching cube algorithm based on edge growth. It addresses the issue of ambiguous topology configurations that lead to holes in 3D models. A marching cube algorithm based on edge growth, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vrih.2021.08.006, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Region Growing Segmentation
head: Local region growing, Region Growing for Volume Segmentation, Semi-automatic Feature Finding, Volume Seedling, Volumetric region growing
body:
Region growing segmentation is a semi-automatic technique that extracts connected regions of interest from a 3D volume by iteratively adding neighboring voxels to a user-selected seed point based on statistical similarity criteria. It solves the problem of isolating specific features (e.g., cracks, vessels) in noisy data where global thresholding fails, distinguishing itself from Restricted Region Growing by allowing flexible cost functions and from Graph-based Isosurface Segmentation (Min-Cut) by relying on local homogeneity rather than global cut optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume V (density/intensity values), a user-selected seed voxel s, and parameters k (strictness) and p (weighting). Output: A binary mask volume M of identical resolution to V, where M[i,j,k]=1 if the voxel belongs to the segmented region, and 0 otherwise. Alternatively, a label volume storing structure identifiers. Data Structures: Volume V: 3D array of scalar values. Mask M: 3D boolean or integer array, initialized to false/0. Queue Q: FIFO queue for voxels to be processed. Visited Set Vis: Hash set or boolean array to track processed voxels to prevent cycles. Formulas: The membership of a candidate voxel c is determined by a cost function. Three variants are defined in: 1. Data Value Criterion (f{ca}): f{ca} =  rac{|v - vs|}{k \cdot \sigmav} Where v is the data value of c, vs is the data value of the seed s, k is a user constant (k>0, default 1), and \sigmav is the standard deviation of the data values of the 26 neighbors of s. 2. Gradient Magnitude Criterion (f{cb}): f{cb} =  rac{|g - gs|}{k \cdot \sigmag} Where g is the gradient magnitude of c, gs is the gradient magnitude of s, and \sigmag is the standard deviation of the gradient magnitudes of the 26 neighbors of s. 3. Combined Criterion (f{cc}): f{cc}(p) = f{ca} \cdot p + f{cb} \cdot (1 - p) Where p is a weight. By default, p =  rac{\sigmav}{\sigmav + \sigmag}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Mask M to all zeros. Initialize Queue Q as empty. Initialize Visited Vis as empty. User selects seed voxel s at coordinates (xs, ys, zs). Compute seed statistics: vs = V[s], gs = |
abla V[s]|. Compute neighbor statistics for s: Let N(s) be the 26 immediate neighbors of s. \sigmav = 	ext{std}(\{V[n] \mid n \in N(s)\}). \sigmag = 	ext{std}(\{|
abla V[n]| \mid n \in N(s)\}). Calculate default weight p =  rac{\sigmav}{\sigmav + \sigmag} if not specified. Push s to Q. Mark s as visited. Mark M[s] = 1. 2. Iteration: While Q is not empty: Pop current voxel c from Q. For each neighbor n of c (6-connected or 26-connected, typically 26 for robustness): If n is within volume bounds AND n is not in Vis: Calculate cost C = f{cc}(p) using V[n] and |
abla V[n]| against seed stats vs, gs, \sigmav, \sigmag. If C < 1: Mark M[n] = 1. Add n to Vis. Push n to Q. Else: Discard n (boundary or dissimilar region). 3. Termination: Loop ends when Q is empty. Result is the mask M. Pseudocode: Unverified code. If None, computed from seed neighbors. """ import numpy as np from collections import deque # 1. Initialization mask = np.zeroslike(volume, dtype=bool) visited = set() queue = deque() sx, sy, sz = seedcoords seedval = volume[sx, sy, sz] # Compute gradient magnitude at seed (using simple finite differences) # Note: Gradient computation should be consistent for all voxels gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(volume) seedgrad = gradmag[sx, sy, sz] # Get 26 neighbors of seed neighborsseed = get26neighbors(sx, sy, sz, volume.shape) if not neighborsseed: mask[sx, sy, sz] = True return mask # Compute standard deviations of seed's neighbors neighborvals = [volume[n] for n in neighborsseed] neighborgrads = [gradmag[n] for n in neighborsseed] sigmav = np.std(neighborvals) sigmag = np.std(neighborgrads) # Handle division by zero if sigma is 0 if sigmav == 0: sigmav = 1e-9 if sigmag == 0: sigmag = 1e-9 # Determine weight p if p is None: p = sigmav / (sigmav + sigmag) # Add seed to queue queue.append(seedcoords) visited.add(seedcoords) mask[sx, sy, sz] = True # 2. Iteration while queue: cx, cy, cz = queue.popleft() # Get 26 neighbors of current voxel currentneighbors = get26neighbors(cx, cy, cz, volume.shape) for nx, ny, nz in currentneighbors: if (nx, ny, nz) not in visited: # Calculate cost functions vn = volume[nx, ny, nz] gn = gradmag[nx, ny, nz] # fca fca = abs(vn - seedval) / (k sigmav) # fcb fcb = abs(gn - seedgrad) / (k sigmag) # fcc cost = fca p + fcb (1 - p) # Check threshold if cost < 1.0: mask[nx, ny, nz] = True visited.add((nx, ny, nz)) queue.append((nx, ny, nz)) return mask def computegradientmagnitude(volume): # Simple central difference gradient magnitude # This is a placeholder for a standard gradient calculation # In a real implementation, use scipy.ndimage or similar # For self-containedness, we assume a helper exists or implement basic diff gx = np.gradient(volume, axis=0) gy = np.gradient(volume, axis=1) gz = np.gradient(volume, axis=2) return np.sqrt(gx2 + gy2 + gz2) def get26neighbors(x, y, z, shape): neighbors = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz if 0 <= nx < shape[0] and 0 <= ny < shape[1] and 0 <= nz < shape[2]: neighbors.append((nx, ny, nz)) return neighbors Parameters: k: Controls strictness of homogeneity. Default: 1. Must be >0. p: Weight for data value vs gradient. Default:  rac{\sigmav}{\sigmav + \sigmag}. Connectivity: 26-connected is standard for robustness in this context. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise-induced leakage: Noisy data can cause regions to grow through thin (1-2 voxel wide) connections into adjacent features. This is mitigated by using f{cc} (which uses gradients) or post-processing filtering. Seed Selection: In noisy data, small or thin features are hard to select. Interactive slicing and scatterplot visualization of scalar/gradient values assist selection. Boundary Precision: The method relies on local statistics; if the seed's neighborhood is not representative of the region, the growth may fail or leak. Valley Cell Construction decomposes a feature space into non-overlapping regions called valley cells, where each cell contains exactly one isolated local maximum. It structures the feature space for clustering or segmentation by identifying the boundaries between basins of attraction for local maxima. It differs from Graph-based Isosurface Segmentation (Min-Cut) by using topological region growing from maxima rather than global cut optimization, and from Restricted Region Growing by explicitly handling topological degeneracies (multi-maximum saddles) via node duplication to ensure a valid cell decomposition. This method segments a 3D volume by treating voxels containing a specific isosurface as nodes in a graph, connected via neighborhood connectivity, and finding an optimal cut to separate user-defined foreground and background seed regions. Unlike traditional volume segmentation which operates on the entire voxel grid and suffers from label volume precision limits and computational expense, this approach restricts the graph to the sparse subset of voxels intersecting the iso-surface, integrating directly with isosurface rendering pipelines. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit formulation of the segmentation problem as a min-cut optimization on the isosurface domain, whereas Valley Cell Construction focuses on geometric valley detection and Restricted Region Growing relies on iterative classification of doubt voxels. Restricted Region Growing is a segmentation technique that defines rough locations for each material part in a volumetric model by growing regions from seed voxels, restricted by noise distribution to prevent leaking through weak boundaries. It serves as a fast pre-processing step to classify the main bodies of materials, thereby reducing the graph size for subsequent Graph-cut operations. Unlike general region growing, which is prone to leaking through weak spots in object boundaries, this method ensures that selected initial seeds have neighborhoods with similar CT values and low gradients, preventing selection in boundary areas. This method isolates a specific anatomical structure (e.g., the spine) from a 3D volume by combining global intensity thresholding with spatial connectivity analysis. It differs from its siblings by strictly selecting the single largest contiguous region after thresholding, rather than exploring graph cuts, valley cells, or restricted growth paths. It serves as a robust post-processing step to remove noise and small artifacts in binary segmentation masks. Watershed Segmentation is a region-growing technique used to extract connected regions from 3D volumes, specifically applied here for brain mask extraction and vessel mask extraction in MRI data. It isolates regions of interest by treating the volume as a topographic landscape, where intensity values define elevation. Unlike Restricted Region Growing which relies on pre-defined connectivity criteria, this method leverages the gradient structure of the image to define boundaries. It serves as a preprocessing step for volume rendering, enabling the blending of anatomical details with pathological tissue indicators. Adaptive Region Growing Cost Functions are a set of criteria used to determine voxel membership during region growing, leveraging data values, gradient magnitudes, and their statistical properties to extract features robustly. Unlike methods that rely solely on data intensity or require post-processing adjacency checks to discard thin connections, this approach integrates gradient information directly into the cost function to better capture boundaries and handle noise. It builds on Region Growing Segmentation by providing a flexible, adaptive mechanism for defining the "similarity" between a seed and candidate voxels. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels in the segmented region, O(N{region}), as each voxel is processed once. The total time depends on the size of the feature. For a plastic data set, calculations took under 3 seconds on a 1.8GHz Pentium 4. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the mask/label volume and visited set, where V is the total volume size. The queue size is bounded by the surface area of the growing region. Strengths: Semi-automatic nature allows user guidance for ambiguous features; handles complex topologies better than simple thresholding; flexible cost functions allow tuning for specific noise characteristics. Limitations: Prone to leakage through noise-induced thin connections if not using gradient-aware costs (f{cc}) or post-processing; requires careful seed placement; performance degrades if the region is very large relative to the volume. When to use: When global thresholding fails due to noise or intensity inhomogeneity, and the user can identify representative seed points. Ideal for extracting specific structures like cracks or vessels in CT/MRI data. When not to use: When fully automatic segmentation is required without user interaction; when the feature of interest has no distinct statistical difference from the background in the seed's neighborhood. Region growing is a fundamental segmentation technique in image processing, originally described by Ballard and Brown (1982) and Rosenfeld and Kak (1982). In the context of volume visualization, it was adapted for industrial CT data and nondestructive testing applications, where it is often coupled with interactive browsing. The specific cost functions f{ca}, f{cb}, and f{cc} were introduced to handle noisy data and gradient-based boundaries. It is also related to the "volume seedling" method by Cohen et al. (1992) for MRA data. name: Valley Cell Construction
head: Region growing from maxima, Valley cell decomposition
body: Valley Cell Construction decomposes a feature space into non-overlapping regions called valley cells, where each cell contains exactly one isolated local maximum. It structures the feature space for clustering or segmentation by identifying the boundaries between basins of attraction for local maxima. It differs from Graph-based Isosurface Segmentation (Min-Cut) by using topological region growing from maxima rather than global cut optimization, and from Restricted Region Growing by explicitly handling topological degeneracies (multi-maximum saddles) via node duplication to ensure a valid cell decomposition. Inputs: A discretized feature space represented as a 2D triangular mesh with scalar values at vertices. The mesh enforces a piecewise linear approximation of the density function. Outputs: A set of valley cells, each associated with a unique maximum, and a map of saddle correspondences including persistence values. Data Structures: Mesh: Triangular mesh T. Each triangle has 3 vertex indices. Vertices: Store scalar value v. Saddles: Identified critical points. Store a set of associated maxima \mathcal{M}S. Cells: Set of triangles belonging to a specific maximum. Steps: 1. Identify Critical Points: Identify local maxima, minima, and saddles on the mesh. A saddle is an extreme where two ridge lines and two valley lines meet. 2. Region Growing: Initialize a cell for each maximum m. For each maximum, recursively add neighboring triangles to its cell. Stopping Condition: Stop growing a cell when the boundary reaches a valley line or a triangle whose vertices are all minima. During growth, track the correspondence between the growing cell and the saddles encountered on its boundary. 3. Saddle Update and Persistence Calculation: After growing, each saddle S has a set of connected maxima \mathcal{M}S. Calculate the persistence of saddle S relative to a maximum m \in \mathcal{M}S as the difference in scalar values: p(S, m) = v(m) - v(S) The persistence of the saddle S is defined as the minimum difference between the saddle value and its associated maximum values: p(S) = \min{m \in \mathcal{M}S} (v(m) - v(S)) 4. Handle Degeneracies (Saddle Duplication): In degenerate cases (e.g., multiple valley lines meeting at a saddle, or paths ending at a junction), a single saddle may belong to more than two cells (associated with k > 2 maxima). To resolve this, duplicate the saddle node k-1 times. Replace the original saddle S with k distinct saddle instances S1, S2, \dots, Sk. Each instance Si is associated with exactly one maximum from \mathcal{M}S. Note: This is similar to unfolding a k-fold saddle but only duplicates the node, not the paths. 5. Boundary Persistence Calculation: Each boundary between two adjacent valley cells is associated with at least one saddle. Calculate the boundary persistence as the minimum persistence of all saddles associated with that boundary: p{\text{boundary}} = \min{S \in \text{Boundary}} p(S) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructvalleycells(vertices, triangles): # vertices: list of scalar values # triangles: list of tuples (v0, v1, v2) nverts = len(vertices) ntris = len(triangles) # Precompute triangle adjacency triadj = {i: set() for i in range(ntris)} for i in range(ntris): for j in range(i + 1, ntris): if len(set(triangles[i]) & set(triangles[j])) == 2: triadj[i].add(j) triadj[j].add(i) # 1. Identify critical points minima = [v for v in range(nverts) if all(vertices[v] <= vertices[n] for tri in triangles if v in tri for n in tri if n != v)] maxima = [v for v in range(nverts) if all(vertices[v] >= vertices[n] for tri in triangles if v in tri for n in tri if n != v)] saddles = [v for v in range(nverts) if v not in maxima and v not in minima] # 2. Region growing cells = {m: set() for m in maxima} saddlemaxmap = {s: set() for s in saddles} for m in maxima: stack = [i for i, tri in enumerate(triangles) if m in tri] visited = set() while stack: triidx = stack.pop() if triidx in visited: continue visited.add(triidx) cells[m].add(triidx) tri = triangles[triidx] if any(v in minima for v in tri): continue for nidx in triadj.get(triidx, []): if nidx not in visited: shared = set(tri) & set(triangles[nidx]) if len(shared) == 2: # Valley line check isvalley = all(vertices[e] <= vertices[o] for e in shared for o in triangles[nidx] if o not in shared) if isvalley: saddlev = [v for v in shared if v in saddles] if saddlev: saddlemaxmap[saddlev[0]].add(m) else: stack.append(nidx) # 3. Saddle Update and Persistence saddleinfo = {} for s in saddles: maxset = saddlemaxmap.get(s, set()) if not maxset: saddleinfo[s] = {'persistence': 0.0, 'maxima': []} continue pers = min(vertices[m] - vertices[s] for m in maxset) saddleinfo[s] = {'persistence': pers, 'maxima': list(maxset)} # 4. Saddle Duplication newsaddles = [] for s, info in saddleinfo.items(): k = len(info['maxima']) if k > 2: for i in range(k): newsaddles.append({'value': vertices[s], 'persistence': vertices[info['maxima'][i]] - vertices[s], 'maxima': [info['maxima'][i]]}) else: newsaddles.append({'value': vertices[s], 'persistence': info['persistence'], 'maxima': info['maxima']}) # 5. Boundary Persistence boundaries = [] for i in range(ntris): for j in triadj.get(i, []): if i < j: shared = set(triangles[i]) & set(triangles[j]) if len(shared) == 2: boundarysaddles = [s for s in newsaddles if s['value'] in shared] pers = min(s['persistence'] for s in boundarysaddles) if boundarysaddles else 0.0 boundaries.append({'edge': shared, 'persistence': pers}) return cells, newsaddles, boundaries A mesh-free method that grows a surface by seeding points on an adaptive ellipsoid around existing surface points and converging them to the valley surface (maximal convexity ridge) using polynomial approximation or Newton iteration. Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles in the mesh for the region growing phase, assuming efficient neighbor traversal. Saddle duplication is proportional to the number of degenerate saddles. Strengths: Provides a clear topological decomposition of the feature space. Explicitly handles noise and discretization artifacts through boundary persistence, allowing for cell simplification. Limitations: Degenerate cases (multi-fold saddles, junctions) require special handling (duplication). The method relies on the quality of the underlying mesh and critical point identification. Use Cases: Automating transfer function design by clustering 2D density plots; isolating semantic features in volume data. The method is inspired by the Morse complex construction scheme described in [EHZ03]. It was formalized for automating transfer function design in the context of 2D density plots for volume exploration. The approach uses region growing from maxima [HP74] to tessellate the feature space into valley cells, ensuring each cell contains an isolated maximum. name: Valley Surface Extraction via Point Seeding and Convergence
head: Valley surface extraction, Mesh-Free Valley Surface Extraction, Mesh-Free Valley Surfaces, Valley Surface Construction
body:
Valley Surface Extraction via Point Seeding and Convergence is a mesh-free algorithm that extracts adaptive, non-manifold valley and ridge surfaces from complex-valued 3D scalar fields by decoupling surface extraction from triangulation. It solves the problem of extracting maximal convexity ridges (valleys) in fields where traditional iso-surface methods fail due to the lack of sign changes across the structure and large variations in function values along the feature. Unlike Valley Cell Construction which decomposes the space into cells, this method grows a connected skeleton directly by seeding points on adaptive ellipsoids around existing surface points and converging them to the valley surface using local polynomial approximations or Newton iteration. Inputs: Scattered scalar field data f(x,y,z) (potentially complex-valued, e.g., acoustic pressure). Outputs: A set of points forming the valley surface, connected via a parent-child graph, along with normals and curvature estimates. Data Structures: Point: Contains position p \in \mathbb{R}^3, normal n \in \mathbb{R}^3, parent pointer, list of children, and convergence status. Local Field Approximation: A trivariate polynomial h(x,y,z) fitted via Moving Least Squares (MLS) to provide f, 
abla f, and Hf (Hessian) at any query point. Grid: Uniform grid for fast neighbor lookup, cell size s{grid} \approx 2.5 	imes 	ext{avg point distance}. Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence threshold, typically 10^{-10} to 10^{-4}. 	heta: Merging threshold, empirically \approx 0.8 	imes 	ext{distance to parent}. lod: Level of Detail, influencing mesh resolution and extraction time. r{seed}: Initial seed ellipsoid axes length, set to s{grid}/4 for the first seeding step. Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Construct a uniform grid with cell size s{grid} \approx 2.5 	imes 	ext{average point distance}. Set MLS kernel radius r{MLS} \approx s{grid}. Increase r{MLS} and adjacent cells if point density is low. 2. Initialization (Find First Point): Iterate over grid cell centroids x. Perform Newton iteration to find an initial surface point: x{i+1} = xi - e3  rac{
abla f(xi) \cdot e3}{\lambda3(xi)} where e3 is the eigenvector of maximum curvature and \lambda3 is the corresponding eigenvalue of Hf. Compute the ridge normal n using the approximation: ni = \sumj  rac{\partial e3}{\partial xj} e{3j} + \sumj  rac{\partial e{3j}}{\partial xj}  rac{\partial f}{\partial xi}  rac{\partial f}{\partial xj} This requires third derivatives of f (via cubic polynomial approximation or finite differences). If third derivatives are unavailable or unstable, use e3 as a rough normal approximation. The first converged point becomes the initial seed p{seed} and parent for subsequent growth. 3. Region Growing Loop: While there are surface points p that have not yet seeded neighbors: a. Seeding: For point p with normal np and parent p{parent}: Compute curvature estimates to determine ellipsoid axes r1, r2. Curvature Approximation: Let e = p - p{parent}. Compute p' by mirroring e through n{p{parent}}. Compute radius r of circle through p, p{parent}, p': r =  rac{e^T \cdot e}{2.0 \cdot (e^T \cdot n{p{parent}})} Compute orthogonal edge e\perp by projecting np 	imes e onto the neighborhood triangle-fan. Compute radius r\perp similarly for e\perp. Set ellipsoid axes r1, r2 proportional to r and r\perp. Constrain extremal lengths to s{grid}. Define ellipse E in plane orthogonal to np: E(t) = p + R  egin{bmatrix} r1 \cos(t) \ r2 \sin(t) \end{bmatrix} where R rotates the local frame such that one axis points toward p{parent}. Sample t \in [0, 2\pi] with step \Delta t = \pi/3. Create child points at these positions. b. Convergence: For each child point q: Check Boundaries: If q is on data boundary, \lambda3(q)=0, or \lambda2(q)=\lambda3(q) (partial umbilic), stop convergence for this point. Converge: Use either Analytical Minimum Finding or Constrained Newton Iteration. Analytical (Quadratic): Fit quadratic trivariate polynomial h(x,y,z) = c \cdot [1, x, y, z, x^2, xy, y^2, yz, z^2, xz]^T via MLS. Restrict to line g(t) = q + t \cdot e3. Find minimum of (h \circ g)(t) analytically. Newton: x{i+1} = xi -  rac{
abla fp}{\|
abla fp\|} ((Hf \cdot 
abla fp) \cdot 
abla fp) where 
abla fp is projected to the plane of convergence. Convergence Check: Point converged if:  rac{
abla f^T \cdot e3}{\|
abla f\|} < \epsilon Divergence Handling: If point diverges or leaves domain, reinitialize to midpoint between q and p{parent}. Restart iteration with finite-difference normal. Repeat until convergence or distance to parent < minimum. c. Merging: If distance from converged point q to closest existing point q{exist} is < 	heta: Merge q into q{exist}. Abandon q. Connect p{parent} to q{exist}'s parent if needed to maintain graph connectivity. d. Normal Update: After all children of p converge, update np based on child positions to reflect the mesh normal rather than just the curvature direction. 4. Restart: If disconnected structures exist, restart the algorithm from step 2 with a new initial point. 5. Non-Manifold Handling (Branching): At partial umbilic points (\lambda2 \approx \lambda3) or valley lines (e2 > 0, 
abla f \perp e2): Restrict Newton iteration to the plane orthogonal to minimal curvature direction e1. If \lambda2 \gg 0 near degenerate lines, extract connector structure by replacing \lambda3 in the initialization equation with \lambda2 to merge crease lines with degenerate lines. p1 return dot(e, e) / (2.0 dot(e, p3 - p2)) def sampleellipse(center, normal, r1, r2, step): # Constructs local frame where one axis points to parent, samples ellipse pass # Standard rotation and sampling def findclosestexisting(point, surfacepoints): # Brute-force or grid-based nearest neighbor search pass def mergepoints(new, existing, surfacepoints): # Updates parent pointers and graph connectivity pass def updatenormal(p, children, surfacepoints): # Averages child positions to update mesh normal pass def fitquadraticmls(center, radius, points, fieldfunc): # Standard MLS quadratic fitting pass def findanalyticalminimum(poly, center, direction): # Solves univariate polynomial minimum along direction pass def checkconvergence(point, epsilon, fieldfunc): grad = evaluategradient(point, fieldfunc) e3 = principaleigenvector(evaluatehessian(point, fieldfunc)) return dot(grad, e3) / norm(grad) < epsilon def evaluatelocalfield(point, radius, points, fieldfunc): # Returns gradient and Hessian via MLS pass def principalcurvature(hess): # Returns eigenvector/eigenvalue of max curvature pass def getneighbors(point): # Returns neighborhood triangle-fan basis pass def computeaveragedistance(points): # Standard statistical measure pass def generategridcentroids(points, cellsize): # Standard grid generation pass A method to extract valley surfaces in complex scalar fields by identifying branching locations (partial umbilics) and connecting them using constrained gradient-based surface integration, specifically handling non-manifold regions where standard surface growing fails. Time Complexity: Higher than grid-based methods due to repeated field evaluations during point convergence. Tracing accurate slope lines increases computation times by a factor of ~5. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of surface points. The method maintains a parent-child graph and local polynomial coefficients for each point. Measured Performance: On a 2.16 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo with 4 GB RAM, for an L-shape 137Hz high-res dataset: Analytical quadratic minimum finding: 19s for 2000 points, 25s for 2900 points. Constrained Newton iteration: 25s for 2000 points, 31s for 2900 points. Low resolution meshes extract faster but may incorrectly merge structures. Strengths: Mesh-free, curvature-adaptive, handles non-manifold structures and branching naturally, decouples extraction from triangulation, suitable for arbitrary neighborhood structures (scattered data). Limitations: Computation times are generally higher than grid-based methods due to repeated field evaluation; sensitive to noise (reduces surface quality due to inaccurate curvature/normal computations); low resolution can lead to incorrect merging of distinct structures. When to use: Complex-valued scalar fields (e.g., acoustic pressure), scattered data, when non-manifold branching is expected, when mesh-free representation is preferred. The method was introduced in the context of visualizing complex-valued scalar fields from low-frequency acoustics FEM simulations, specifically to visualize wave nodes and anti-nodes. It builds on the concept of maximal convexity ridges, which classify extrema, crease lines, and crease surfaces based on local curvature properties (\lambda{k+1} > 0 and 
abla f \cdot ei = 0 for i > k). Unlike traditional iso-surface methods (e.g., Marching Cubes) which fail due to lack of sign changes, this approach relies on local properties only, avoiding global extrema detection and streamline computation required by watershed or slope line segmentation. The specific implementation details, including the seeding and convergence steps, are detailed in.
