name: Connected Component Labeling via Union-Find
head: Union-Find Connected Component Labeling
body: This method groups same-color pixels into connected components using a Union-Find data structure, where connectivity is defined by a Chebyshev (chessboard) distance search radius. It differs from standard 4- or 8-connectivity approaches by allowing configurable neighborhood ranges, making it suitable for identifying distinct color regions in raster images prior to 3D manufacturing format generation. Inputs: An input image (e.g., PNG) with pixel data containing RGBA values. Outputs: A list of Component objects, each containing a Color and a list of pixel coordinates (X, Y). Data Structures: 1. Parent Array: int[] parent of size totalPixels = width height. 2. Rank Array: int[] rank of size totalPixels. 3. Component Class: Color Color (readonly) List<(int X, int Y)> Pixels (mutable list of pixel coordinates) Parameters: searchRadius: Maximum Chebyshev distance in pixels to search for same-color neighbors. Default value is 4. A radius of 1 is equivalent to 8-connectivity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Union-Find: Create parent and rank arrays of size totalPixels. Set parent[i] = i for all i in [0, totalPixels). Set rank[i] = 0. 2. Precompute Neighbor Offsets: Create a list of (dx, dy) tuples. Iterate dy from -searchRadius to 0. For each dy, iterate dx from -searchRadius to searchRadius. Constraint: If dy == 0, only include offsets where dx <= -1. This covers previously visited pixels in raster scan order (y ascending, x ascending) within the Chebyshev distance. 3. Union Phase (Raster Scan): Iterate pixels in raster order: y from 0 to height-1, x from 0 to width-1. Calculate currentIndex = y width + x. Skip if alpha < 255. For each neighbor offset (dx, dy) in precomputed list: Calculate nx = x + dx, ny = y + dy. Skip if (nx, ny) is out of bounds. Skip if neighbor alpha < 255. If neighbor RGB values equal current pixel RGB values: Call Union(parent, rank, currentIndex, ny width + nx). 4. Collection Phase: Create a dictionary rootMap mapping root index to Component object. Iterate pixels in raster order again: y from 0 to height-1, x from 0 to width-1. Calculate currentIndex = y width + x. Find root = FindRoot(parent, currentIndex). If root not in rootMap: Create new Component with Color from current pixel. Add to rootMap. Add (x, y) to component.Pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def connectedcomponentlabeling(image, searchradius=4): width = image.width height = image.height totalpixels = width height # Step 1: Initialize Union-Find parent = list(range(totalpixels)) rank = [0] totalpixels # Helper: Find with path compression def findroot(i): if parent[i] != i: parent[i] = findroot(parent[i]) return parent[i] # Helper: Union by rank def union(i, j): rooti = findroot(i) rootj = findroot(j) if rooti != rootj: if rank[rooti] < rank[rootj]: parent[rooti] = rootj elif rank[rooti] > rank[rootj]: parent[rootj] = rooti else: parent[rootj] = rooti rank[rooti] += 1 # Step 2: Precompute neighbor offsets offsets = [] for dy in range(-searchradius, 1): for dx in range(-searchradius, searchradius + 1): if dy == 0 and dx >= 0: continue offsets.append((dx, dy)) # Step 3: Union Phase for y in range(height): for x in range(width): currentidx = y width + x currentcolor = image.getpixel(x, y) # Skip non-opaque pixels if currentcolor.alpha < 255: continue for dx, dy in offsets: nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= nx < width and 0 <= ny < height: neighboridx = ny width + nx neighborcolor = image.getpixel(nx, ny) # Skip non-opaque neighbors if neighborcolor.alpha < 255: continue # Check color match (RGB only, ignoring alpha as it's checked) if currentcolor.rgb == neighborcolor.rgb: union(currentidx, neighboridx) # Step 4: Collection Phase components = {} for y in range(height): for x in range(width): currentidx = y width + x currentcolor = image.getpixel(x, y) # Skip non-opaque pixels if currentcolor.alpha < 255: continue root = findroot(currentidx) if root not in components: components[root] = Component(color=currentcolor.rgb) components[root].pixels.append((x, y)) return list(components.values()) class Component: def init(self, color): self.color = color self.pixels = [] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-opaque pixels (alpha < 255) must be skipped during both the union phase and the collection phase to avoid including transparent background pixels in components. The neighbor offset generation must strictly follow the raster scan order constraint (only checking dy <= 0 and dx < 0 when dy=0) to ensure each connection is processed exactly once without redundant checks. Not given in the sources. This method is implemented in the jsonger/voxelizer project, which parses images and outputs 3D Manufacturing Format (3MF) files compatible with Bambu Studio. It uses Union-Find to efficiently group pixels into components before mesh generation. jsonger/voxelizer, https://github.com/jsonger/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Level-Set Graph Traversal for IV Decomposition
head: IV decomposition order extraction, Level-Set Graph Traversal for IV Decomposition Order, Systematic traversal of level-set graph
body: Level-Set Graph Traversal for IV Decomposition is a method to determine the inclusion relationships and decomposition order of Isosurface Volumes (IVs) by traversing a level-set graph from the exterior surface inward. It solves the problem of systematically peeling a volume into nested feature subvolumes, enabling applications such as optimal viewpoint selection for volume previewing. What sets it apart from sibling methods like Connected Component Labeling via Union-Find is its reliance on topological classification of critical points (specifically saddles) to distinguish between "solid" and "hollow" transitions, using dual queues to manage the traversal direction (upward vs. downward) relative to the scalar field. Inputs and Outputs Input: A level-set graph representing the topological skeleton of a volume. The graph consists of nodes (critical points) and links (feature subvolumes/IVs). Each link is associated with a scalar field range bounded by critical isosurfaces. Output: A sequence of links in Qorder representing the decomposition order from outside to inside, along with the inclusion relationships between IVs. Data Structures 1. Level-Set Graph: A directed graph where nodes n represent critical points and links L represent IVs. Node Attributes: Critical point type (C3, C2, C1, C0) and transition classification (e.g., (B)-C1). Link Attributes: Scalar value range, connection to parent/child nodes, and type (Solid or Hollow). 2. Queues: Qsolid: FIFO queue for links to be traversed in the upward direction (exterior inward, lower scalar to higher scalar relative to critical point context, or specifically from exterior inward as per source description of "upward" tracing). Qhollow: FIFO queue for links to be traversed in the downward direction. Qorder: List/Queue to store the final decomposition order of links. Definitions Isosurface Solid: An isosurface that expands as the scalar field value decreases. Isosurface Hollow: An isosurface that shrinks as the scalar field value decreases. Critical Point Index: Classified by the number of negative eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix: C3: Maxima (3 negative eigenvalues) C2: Saddles (2 negative eigenvalues) C1: Saddles (1 negative eigenvalue) C0: Minima (0 negative eigenvalues) Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize Qsolid as an empty FIFO queue. Initialize Qhollow as an empty FIFO queue. Initialize Qorder as an empty list. Identify the link L0 connected to the exterior surface of the volume. Add L0 to Qsolid. 2. Processing Solid Links (Upward Traversal): While Qsolid is not empty: Dequeue a link L from Qsolid. Append L to Qorder. Identify the critical point node n{next} at the end of L (in the direction of traversal). Classify the transition type at n{next} (e.g., (B)-C1, (B)-C2, etc.) based on the spatial configuration of isosurface transitions. For each new link L{new} emerging from n{next}: If the transition corresponds to a Solid isosurface (expands as scalar decreases), enqueue L{new} into Qsolid. If the transition corresponds to a Hollow isosurface (shrinks as scalar decreases), enqueue L{new} into Qhollow. Note: IV inclusions occur only in specific transition paths. Specifically, inclusions occur only in the two transition paths of row (B) in the classification diagram for both C2 and C1 critical points. Other paths (A, C, D) do not result in IV inclusions. 3. Processing Hollow Links (Downward Traversal): While Qhollow is not empty: Dequeue a link L from Qhollow. Append L to Qorder. Identify the critical point node n{next} at the end of L (in the direction of traversal). Classify the transition type at n{next}. For each new link L{new} emerging from n{next}: If the transition corresponds to a Solid isosurface, enqueue L{new} into Qsolid. If the transition corresponds to a Hollow isosurface, enqueue L{new} into Qhollow. 4. Termination: Repeat steps 2 and 3 until both Qsolid and Qhollow are empty. The final decomposition order is the sequence of links in Qorder. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def levelsetgraphtraversal(levelsetgraph): """ Determines the IV decomposition order by traversing the level-set graph. Args: levelsetgraph: A graph object containing nodes (critical points) and links (IVs). Must have an 'exteriorlink' attribute pointing to the link L0 connected to the exterior surface. Returns: Qorder: A list of links in decomposition order. """ Qsolid = [] # FIFO queue for solid links Qhollow = [] # FIFO queue for hollow links Qorder = [] # List for decomposition order # Step 1: Initialization L0 = levelsetgraph.exteriorlink Qsolid.append(L0) while Qsolid or Qhollow: # Step 2: Process Solid Links (Upward Traversal) while Qsolid: L = Qsolid.pop(0) # Dequeue from front Qorder.append(L) # Identify the critical point node at the end of L # The direction of traversal is "upward" (exterior inward) nnext = L.getendnodeintraversaldirection() # Classify the transition type at nnext # Returns a classification code, e.g., 'BC1', 'BC2', 'AC1', etc. transitiontype = classifycriticalpoint(nnext) # Get outgoing links from nnext outgoinglinks = nnext.getoutgoinglinks() for Lnew in outgoinglinks: # Determine if the link corresponds to a Solid or Hollow isosurface # based on the transition type and spatial configuration issolid = issolidtransition(transitiontype, Lnew) if issolid: Qsolid.append(Lnew) else: Qhollow.append(Lnew) # Step 3: Process Hollow Links (Downward Traversal) while Qhollow: L = Qhollow.pop(0) # Dequeue from front Qorder.append(L) # Identify the critical point node at the end of L # The direction of traversal is "downward" nnext = L.getendnodeintraversaldirection() # Classify the transition type at nnext transitiontype = classifycriticalpoint(nnext) # Get outgoing links from nnext outgoinglinks = nnext.getoutgoinglinks() for Lnew in outgoinglinks: # Determine if the link corresponds to a Solid or Hollow isosurface issolid = issolidtransition(transitiontype, Lnew) if issolid: Qsolid.append(Lnew) else: Qhollow.append(Lnew) return Qorder def classifycriticalpoint(node): """ Classifies the critical point node based on its type and spatial configuration. Returns a string code like 'BC1', 'BC2', 'AC1', etc. """ # Implementation depends on the specific topological volume skeletonization algorithm # Refer to Takahashi et al. [31] for practical implementation details. # This function identifies if the node is a C1 or C2 saddle and which # transition path (A, B, C, D) it follows. pass def issolidtransition(transitiontype, link): """ Determines if a link is Solid or Hollow based on the transition type. Solid: Expands as scalar field value decreases. Hollow: Shrinks as scalar field value decreases. According to, IV inclusions (and specific solid/hollow assignments) occur only in transition paths of row (B) for C2 and C1 critical points. """ # This logic is derived from Fig. 3 in. # The exact mapping of transitiontype to solid/hollow is not explicitly # detailed in the text beyond the visual classification in Fig. 3. # A generic implementation would check the link's scalar range and the # node's critical point index. pass Parameters The algorithm relies on three component algorithms for its construction phase (not the traversal itself): 1. Carr et al. [6] for tracking the number of isosurface connected components. 2. Pascucci et al. [22] for identifying the genus of each isosurface component. 3. Takahashi et al. [31] for IV clustering and topological volume skeletonization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls IV Inclusions: IV inclusions occur only in the two transition paths of row (B) for both C2 and C1 critical points. Other paths (A, C, D) do not result in IV inclusions. Failure to correctly classify these transitions will lead to incorrect inclusion relationships. Critical Point Classification: Accurate classification of C1 and C2 saddles into their specific spatial transition types (A, B, C, D) is crucial. This requires robust topological volume skeletonization. Traversal Direction: The distinction between "upward" (solid) and "downward" (hollow) traversal must be strictly maintained. Mixing these directions will corrupt the decomposition order. An interface and algorithm that decomposes an entire volume into feature subvolumes (interval volumes) by tracking the topological transitions of isosurfaces with respect to the scalar field, constructing a level-set graph, and enabling systematic decomposition from outside to inside. It identifies each link of the level-set graph with a feature subvolume (IV) bounded by critical isosurfaces and retrieves inclusion relationships by systematically traversing the graph. It relies on the same three component algorithms as the traversal method: Carr et al. [6], Pascucci et al. [22], and Takahashi et al. [31]. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The complexity depends on the size of the level-set graph and the number of critical points. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the level-set graph and two FIFO queues. Strengths: Enables systematic decomposition of volumes from outside to inside, which is useful for viewpoint selection and previewing inner structures. Limitations: Requires accurate construction of the level-set graph, which depends on robust topological skeletonization algorithms. When to use: When the goal is to decompose a volume into nested feature subvolumes for visualization or analysis, particularly for viewpoint selection. When not to use: When only connected component labeling is needed without topological inclusion relationships. The method was developed by S. Takahashi, I. Fujishiro, Y. Takeshima, and C. Bi. It is described in the book chapter "Previewing Volume Decomposition Through Optimal Viewpoints". The concept of Interval Volumes (IV) was formulated by Fujishiro et al. [10] and Guo [13] as a generalization of the isosurface. The level-set graph construction relies on topological volume skeletonization [31], which combines algorithms by Carr et al. [6], Pascucci et al. [22], and Takahashi et al. [31]. Previewing Volume Decomposition Through Optimal Viewpoints, https://doi.org/10.4230/dfu.vol2.sciviz.2011.346, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Watershed Segmentation
head: Brain Mask Extraction via Watershed
body: Watershed Segmentation extracts connected regions from 3D volumes to generate brain and vessel masks for multimodal MRI volume rendering. It differs from sibling methods by treating intensity values as a topographic landscape to define boundaries via catchment basins, rather than relying on pre-defined connectivity criteria or graph cuts. The method operates on a pipeline of registered MRI sequences to isolate anatomical structures for blending with pathological tissue indicators. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Registered 3D MRI volumes, specifically T1-weighted, T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (T1 ce), T2-weighted, and FLAIR sequences. Output: Binary mask volumes for the brain and cerebral vessels. Data Structures: Volume V: 3D array of intensity values for each MRI sequence. Mask M: 3D array of binary values (1 for region, 0 otherwise). Steps: 1. Registration: Register all MRI sequences to the T1-weighted reference dataset. 2. Brain Mask Extraction: Apply a skull stripping algorithm to the registered T1-weighted data to generate a brain mask. 3. Vessel Mask Extraction: Compute the difference image D = V{\text{T1ce}} - V{\text{T1}}. Apply watershed segmentation to D to extract the vessel mask. 4. Mask Application: Apply the generated brain mask to all registered sequences to restrict volume rendering to intracranial data. Formulas: Difference image: D(x,y,z) = V{\text{T1ce}}(x,y,z) - V{\text{T1}}(x,y,z), where V{\text{T1ce}} and V{\text{T1}} are the intensity values at voxel (x,y,z) for the contrast-enhanced and non-enhanced T1-weighted volumes, respectively. Parameters: Connectivity: Neighborhood definition for region growth (e.g., 6, 18, or 26-connectivity). Not given in the sources. Marker Initialization: Seed selection strategy to prevent over-segmentation. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-segmentation: High-frequency noise or intensity variations can fragment regions into excessive basins. Marker-controlled watershed or morphological preprocessing is typically required to constrain growth. Intensity Distribution Variability: MRI sequences exhibit varying intensity distributions and noise levels. Preprocessing or clustering (e.g., fuzzy c-means) may be necessary to stabilize basin formation. This variant isolates cerebral vasculature by computing the voxel-wise difference between a T1 contrast-enhanced dataset and a non-enhanced T1 dataset. The resulting difference image highlights contrast uptake, which watershed segmentation then converts into a binary vessel mask. It is selected when vascular structures must be visualized alongside anatomical details in volume rendering pipelines. It builds on Region Growing Segmentation by using intensity subtraction rather than direct region merging. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Integrates seamlessly with registered multimodal MRI pipelines and supports blending with pathological tissue indicators. Robust to noise when combined with clustering techniques for intensity analysis. Limitations: Requires accurate inter-sequence registration to ensure mask alignment across modalities. Performance depends on appropriate marker selection to avoid over-segmentation. Use Cases: Intracranial region isolation for skull stripping, vascular structure visualization in multimodal MRI. The method is documented in the context of high-quality multimodal volume visualization of intracerebral pathological tissue. It builds upon established skull stripping algorithms and operates on a standardized set of registered MRI sequences (T1-weighted, T1-weighted ce, T2-weighted, FLAIR). The segmentation pipeline is often coupled with fuzzy c-means (FCM) clustering to identify suspicious high-intensity values indicative of pathological tissue. High-Quality Multimodal Volume Visualization of Intracerebral Pathological Tissue, https://doi.org/10.2312/vcbm/vcbm08/167-176, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Region Growing Cost Functions
body: Adaptive Region Growing Cost Functions are a set of criteria used to determine voxel membership during region growing, leveraging data values, gradient magnitudes, and their statistical properties to extract features robustly. Unlike methods that rely solely on data intensity or require post-processing adjacency checks to discard thin connections, this approach integrates gradient information directly into the cost function to better capture boundaries and handle noise. It builds on Region Growing Segmentation by providing a flexible, adaptive mechanism for defining the "similarity" between a seed and candidate voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D volume dataset, a seed voxel (or set of seeds), a strictness parameter k, and a weight parameter p. Outputs: A binary mask identifying voxels belonging to the region. Data Structures: Seed Statistics: The algorithm requires the standard deviation of data values (\sigmav) and gradient magnitudes (\sigmag) computed over the 26-neighbors of the seed voxel; in adaptive mode, these are recomputed using all voxels currently in the growing region. Current Region Set: A collection of voxels accepted into the region. Formulas: Three cost functions are defined. A voxel is accepted if its cost is less than 1. 1. Data Value Cost (f{ca}): f{ca} = \frac{|v - vs|}{k \sigmav} Where: v: Data value of the current candidate voxel. vs: Data value of the seed voxel. \sigmav: Standard deviation of data values of the 26 neighboring voxels of the seed (or current region in adaptive mode). k: Strictness constant (k > 0). 2. Gradient Cost (f{cb}): f{cb} = \frac{|g - gs|}{k \sigmag} Where: g: Gradient magnitude of the current candidate voxel. gs: Gradient magnitude of the seed voxel. \sigmag: Standard deviation of gradient magnitudes of the 26 neighboring voxels of the seed (or current region in adaptive mode). 3. Combined Cost (f{cc}): f{cc}(p) = f{ca}^p + f{cb}^{(1-p)} Where: p: Weight specified by user or system. Parameters: k: Controls the strictness of the criterion. Default value is 1. User can limit k for conservative growing. p: Default p = \frac{\sigmav}{\sigmav + \sigmag}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Select a seed voxel. Compute initial \sigmav and \sigmag from its 26 neighbors. Initialize the region set R with the seed. 2. Candidate Evaluation: For each unvisited neighbor of any voxel in R: calculate f{ca}, f{cb}, and f{cc}(p). If f{cc}(p) < 1, add the voxel to R. 3. Adaptive Update (Optional): If adaptive mode is enabled, after adding new voxels, recompute \sigmav and \sigmag using all voxels in R. Recalculate p if it is system-determined. 4. Iteration: Repeat Step 2 until no new voxels are added or a stopping condition is met. 5. Post-processing (Optional): Remove erroneous thin connections (1-2 voxels wide) caused by noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveregiongrowing(volume, gradients, seed, k=1.0, adaptive=True): """ volume: 3D array of data values gradients: 3D array of gradient magnitudes seed: (x, y, z) tuple k: strictness parameter adaptive: boolean, whether to recompute stats during growth """ region = {seed} queue = [seed] visited = {seed} vs = volume[seed] gs = gradients[seed] def computestd(values): if len(values) == 0: return 1.0 mean = sum(values) / len(values) variance = sum((x - mean) 2 for x in values) / len(values) return variance 0.5 def getneighbors(pos, shape): neighbors = [] for dx in (-1, 0, 1): for dy in (-1, 0, 1): for dz in (-1, 0, 1): if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue nx, ny, nz = pos[0] + dx, pos[1] + dy, pos[2] + dz if 0 <= nx < shape[0] and 0 <= ny < shape[1] and 0 <= nz < shape[2]: neighbors.append((nx, ny, nz)) return neighbors seedneighbors = getneighbors(seed, volume.shape) sigmav = computestd([volume[n] for n in seedneighbors]) sigmag = computestd([gradients[n] for n in seedneighbors]) p = sigmav / (sigmav + sigmag) if (sigmav + sigmag) != 0 else 0.5 while queue: current = queue.pop(0) if adaptive: allv = [volume[v] for v in region] allg = [gradients[v] for v in region] sigmav = computestd(allv) sigmag = computestd(allg) p = sigmav / (sigmav + sigmag) if (sigmav + sigmag) != 0 else 0.5 for n in getneighbors(current, volume.shape): if n not in visited: visited.add(n) vn = volume[n] gn = gradients[n] fca = abs(vn - vs) / (k sigmav) fcb = abs(gn - gs) / (k sigmag) fcc = fca p + fcb (1 - p) if fcc < 1.0: region.add(n) queue.append(n) return region Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Data: Noise can cause the region to grow through thin (1- or 2-voxel wide) connections into adjacent regions. A post-processing filtering step is recommended to remove these erroneous connections. Zero Standard Deviation: If \sigmav or \sigmag is zero, division by zero occurs. The pseudocode includes a guard. Boundary Conditions: Neighbors must be checked against volume bounds. An interactive volume visualization technique that uses region growing to assist in the classification and assessment steps of volume visualization, specifically to locate features of interest and define transfer functions or boundary surfaces. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of voxels in the region and the neighborhood size (26). Adaptive mode increases cost per step as statistics must be recomputed over the growing set R. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the region and the volume for storing visited states. Strengths: Robust to noise compared to simple thresholding; handles boundaries better than data-value-only methods by incorporating gradients; adaptive nature prevents over-growth into erroneous regions. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than non-adaptive methods due to statistical recomputation; sensitive to the choice of k and p; requires gradient computation. When to Use: When extracting features with distinct boundaries in noisy data where both intensity and edge information are relevant. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and adaptive updates are too costly; when the region is perfectly homogeneous with no gradient variation (though k can be tuned). The method originates from the research presented in. It was designed to be more robust than previous methods like those by Modayur et al., which did not consider voxel gradients. The adaptive variant allows the criteria to evolve as the region grows, improving accuracy in complex scenes. RGVis: Region Growing Based Visualization Techniques for Volume Visualization, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3td71868, fetched 2026-11-03 (unofficial)

name: RGVis Region Growing
head: RGVis, Region Growing Based Visualization
body: RGVis is an interactive volume visualization technique that uses region growing to assist in the classification and assessment of features of interest. It solves the problem of iterative trial-and-error in defining transfer functions and boundary surfaces by deriving a 2D transfer function from the statistical properties of a partially segmented region or constructing a complete boundary surface from a full segmentation. Unlike dual-domain interactive methods that highlight histogram points for manual editing, RGVis suggests a transfer function derived from region growing statistics, and its resulting boundary surfaces represent features more completely than isosurfaces by capturing fine parts that isosurfaces might miss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume data (scalar values), user interaction (seed point or line segment selection on a slice), and user-specified constant k. Output: A set of connected voxels (region), a derived 2D transfer function (for partial growing), or a polygonal boundary surface (for full growing). Data Structures: Volume Data: 3D array of scalar values v and precomputed or on-the-fly gradient magnitudes g. Region Set: A collection of voxel coordinates (x, y, z) belonging to the current region. Queue/Stack: Used for the recursive or iterative expansion of the region (26-connectivity). Statistics: Running mean and standard deviation of data values (\sigmav) and gradient magnitudes (\sigmag) for the voxels collected so far. Parameters: k: A constant specified by the user, used in the cost function f{ca}. vs: Data value of the seed voxel. \sigmav: Standard deviation of data values of the neighbors (or collected voxels). \sigmag: Standard deviation of gradient magnitudes. p: A parameter continuously recomputed using voxels collected so far for the adaptive criterion. Steps: 1. Seed Selection: The user slices through the volume data and selects a region of interest. Point Seed: The user clicks a point on the slice. The system highlights the point and its 26 neighbors on a 2D scatterplot (scalar vs. gradient magnitude). A blue rectangle shows the standard deviation of data values (\sigmav) and gradient magnitudes (\sigmag) of the neighbors. Line Seed: The user plots a line segment of 3D points. The interface displays properties of these points divided into preclassified zones. The user selects a zone to determine the seed. Initialization: The growing starts from a voxel in the proximity of the seed point, chosen based on distance or statistical properties of the neighborhood. 2. Region Growing Expansion: Initialize the region with the starting voxel. For each voxel in the region, visit its 26 immediate neighbors. For each neighbor, evaluate the cost functions. If the neighbor satisfies the criteria, add it to the region and the queue/stack for further expansion. Update statistics (\sigmav, \sigmag, p) using the voxels collected so far if using the adaptive criterion. 3. Termination: The process continues until the queue is empty (all reachable voxels examined) or a specific termination criterion is met. 4. Post-Processing (Optional): Partial Growing: Use the statistical properties of the extracted region to derive a 2D transfer function. Full Growing: Construct a boundary surface from the collected data points. Formulas: A voxel is included in the region if the value returned by the cost function is less than 1. Three functions are defined: 1. Cost Function f{ca}: f{ca} = \frac{|v - vs|}{k \sigmav} Where: v: Data value of the current voxel. vs: Data value of the seed voxel. k: User-specified constant. \sigmav: Standard deviation of the data values of the neighbors (or collected voxels). 2. Cost Function f{cb}: Defined in the source but the explicit formula is not provided in the text. It is used alongside f{ca} and f{cc}. 3. Adaptive Criterion f{cc}: The criterion is made adaptive by adjusting it during the course of growing. \sigmav, \sigmag, and p are continuously recomputed using the voxels collected so far. The explicit formula for f{cc} is not provided in the text, but it relies on these dynamic statistics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rgvisregiongrowing(volume, seedvoxel, k, maxvoxels=None): """ Performs region growing on volume data starting from seedvoxel. Args: volume: 3D array of scalar values. seedvoxel: Tuple (x, y, z) of the starting voxel. k: User-specified constant for cost function fca. maxvoxels: Optional limit on the number of voxels to grow. Returns: region: Set of voxel coordinates belonging to the region. """ # Initialize region and queue region = set() queue = [seedvoxel] region.add(seedvoxel) # Get seed value vs = volume[seedvoxel] # Statistics for adaptive criterion # Note: Exact formula for fcc and fcb not provided in sources. # We assume fca is the primary homogeneity check based on the text. # The text mentions fca, fcb, and fcc. # We implement fca as described. # Precompute neighbors offsets for 26-connectivity neighborsoffsets = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue neighborsoffsets.append((dx, dy, dz)) # To compute sigmav dynamically, we need to track values in the region regionvalues = [vs] while queue: currentvoxel = queue.pop(0) # Check max voxels if specified if maxvoxels and len(region) >= maxvoxels: break # Recompute statistics for adaptive criterion # sigmav is standard deviation of regionvalues if len(regionvalues) > 1: meanv = sum(regionvalues) / len(regionvalues) variancev = sum((x - meanv) 2 for x in regionvalues) / len(regionvalues) sigmav = variancev 0.5 else: sigmav = 1.0 # Avoid division by zero if only seed is present # If sigmav is 0, use a small epsilon to prevent division by zero if sigmav == 0: sigmav = 1e-9 # Visit 26 neighbors for dx, dy, dz in neighborsoffsets: nx, ny, nz = currentvoxel[0] + dx, currentvoxel[1] + dy, currentvoxel[2] + dz # Boundary check if not isinsidevolume(nx, ny, nz, volume.shape): continue neighborvoxel = (nx, ny, nz) # Skip if already in region if neighborvoxel in region: continue # Get neighbor value vn = volume[neighborvoxel] # Evaluate cost function fca # fca = |v - vs| / (k sigmav) fca = abs(vn - vs) / (k sigmav) # Note: fcb and fcc formulas are not provided in the source text. # The text states: "If the value returned by the cost function is less than 1, # then the voxel under consideration is within the region." # It mentions three functions: fca, fcb, fcc. # Without explicit formulas for fcb and fcc, we assume fca is the # primary criterion described in detail. # In a real implementation, one would need the specific definitions of fcb and fcc. # For this pseudocode, we assume a simplified check using fca < 1. # If fcb or fcc were required, they would be evaluated here. if fca < 1.0: # Add to region region.add(neighborvoxel) queue.append(neighborvoxel) regionvalues.append(vn) return region def isinsidevolume(x, y, z, shape): return 0 <= x < shape[0] and 0 <= y < shape[1] and 0 <= z < shape[2] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If \sigmav is zero (e.g., all voxels in the region have the same value), the cost function f{ca} will divide by zero. A small epsilon or alternative handling is required. Noise: Noise can cause the region to grow into irrelevant areas if the criteria are not tight enough. The adaptive criterion helps prevent this by adjusting based on collected voxels. Disconnected Features: Full region growing may miss disconnected features of the same type. Partial region growing is used to derive a transfer function that can capture these disconnected features throughout the volume. A semi-automatic technique that derives a 2D transfer function from the statistical properties of a partially segmented region to visualize similar, disconnected features throughout the entire volume. Unlike full region growing which segments all connected components, this method performs growth on only a subset of the data or a small subset of regions, significantly reducing computation time while providing a robust classifier for the whole dataset. It is particularly useful when features of the same type are disconnected in the volume, preventing a single region growing pass from capturing all instances. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but partial region growing on a confocal microscopy ganglion data set (64×300×400 voxels) took 0.03 seconds and extracted 5,000 voxels. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the region extracted. The region set stores coordinates of all voxels in the region. Performance: The partial region growing approach is efficient, allowing for quick derivation of transfer functions. Strengths: Assists users in locating and defining features of interest more quickly and accurately. Derives transfer functions automatically, reducing manual editing iterations. Boundary surfaces generated by full region growing represent features more completely than isosurfaces, including fine parts. Limitations: Requires user interaction for seed selection. Full region growing may be computationally expensive for large volumes if the region is large. The explicit formulas for f{cb} and f{cc} are not provided in the source, limiting reproducibility of the exact cost function logic. When to Use: When exploring volume data to locate features of interest and define transfer functions or boundary surfaces, especially in medical applications and confocal microscopy. When Not to Use: When fully automatic segmentation without user interaction is required, or when the features are not clustered or scattered in a way that region growing can effectively capture. RGVis (Region Growing Based Visualization) was developed at UC Davis. It is based on the paper "RGVis: Region Growing Based Visualization Techniques for Volume Visualization". The technique is similar to the volume seedling method introduced by Cohen et al.. It has been applied to confocal microscopy ganglion data sets and medical applications. RGVis: Region Growing Based Visualization Techniques for Volume Visualization, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3td71868, fetched 2026-11-03 (unofficial)

name: Partial Region Growing for Transfer Function Generation
head: Derived Transfer Function, Partial Growing, Partial Region Growing for Transfer Function Derivation, Partial Region Growing with Derived Transfer Functions, Semi-automatic feature extraction, Transfer function derivation from region growing
body: Partial Region Growing for Transfer Function Generation is a semi-automatic technique that derives a 2D transfer function from the statistical properties of a partially segmented region to visualize similar, disconnected features throughout the entire volume. Unlike full region growing which segments all connected components, this method performs growth on only a subset of the data or a small subset of regions, significantly reducing computation time while providing a robust classifier for the whole dataset. It is particularly useful when features of the same type are disconnected in the volume, preventing a single region growing pass from capturing all instances. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset V with scalar values and computed gradient magnitudes; a seed point or initial region for partial growth; a growth limit (percentage or voxel count). Output: A 2D transfer function (classifier) defined on the scatterplot of data values vs. gradient magnitudes, ready for volume rendering. Data Structures Volume Data: A 3D array of scalar values. Gradient magnitudes are pre-computed or computed on-the-fly. Region Growing State: A queue or stack of voxels to process, and a visited mask to prevent re-processing. Statistical Accumulators: Variables to store the sum, sum of squares, count, min, and max of data values and gradient magnitudes for the extracted region. Classifier Representation: Rectangular: Defined by center (\muv, \mug) and size (\sigmav, \sigmag). Polygonal/Histogram-based: A set of merged regions in the 2D histogram space, constructed via k-d tree partitioning. Steps 1. Initialize Partial Region Growing: Select a seed voxel or small initial region within the volume. Initialize the region growing algorithm (e.g., using a connectivity criterion based on data value similarity and gradient magnitude thresholds). 2. Execute Partial Growth: Perform region growing on the volume, but stop when a predefined extent is reached. The extent can be defined as: A fixed number of voxels. A percentage of the expected full region size (typically 20-40% of the full region growing result is sufficient). A time limit. Let R be the set of voxels extracted during this partial growth. 3. Compute Statistical Properties: Calculate the following statistics for the extracted region R: \muv: Average data value of voxels in R. \mug: Average gradient magnitude of voxels in R. \sigmav: Standard deviation of data values in R. \sigmag: Standard deviation of gradient magnitudes in R. \muv = \frac{1}{|R|} \sum{v \in R} \text{value}(v) \mug = \frac{1}{|R|} \sum{v \in R} \text{gradient}(v) \sigmav = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|R|} \sum{v \in R} (\text{value}(v) - \muv)^2} \sigmag = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|R|} \sum{v \in R} (\text{gradient}(v) - \mug)^2} 4. Generate Transfer Function (Classifier): Two methods are described for constructing the classifier from the statistics: Method A: Rectangular Classifier (Simple) Define a rectangular region on the 2D scatterplot (Data Value vs. Gradient Magnitude). Center coordinates: (\muv, \mug). Size (width/height): Defined by \sigmav and \sigmag. This rectangle serves as the classification function. Voxels whose (value, gradient) pair falls within this rectangle are considered part of the feature. Method B: Histogram-Based Classifier (Robust) 1. Partition the 2D histogram region defined by the partial growing results using a k-d tree. 2. For each leaf node of the k-d tree, sort the data points by their value. 3. Construct a local classifier for each leaf node using data points with values over a pre-selected threshold. Discard other voxels as noise. 4. Recursively merge local classifiers by traversing the k-d tree. Two classifiers are merged if the new combined classifier contains most of the data points and its area is similar to or less than the sum of the areas of the original two classifiers. 5. Assign an opacity map and color map to the resulting classifier. The opacity map can be constructed from the feature's histogram data or predefined functions (linear, Gaussian). 5. Apply Transfer Function: Apply the derived 2D transfer function to the entire volume. This reveals other features that match the statistical profile of the partially extracted region, even if they are disconnected from the seed. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partialregiongrowingtransferfunction(volume, seedvoxel, growthlimitpercent): """ Derives a 2D transfer function from partial region growing. Args: volume: 3D array of scalar values. seedvoxel: (x, y, z) coordinates of the starting voxel. growthlimitpercent: Percentage of full region growth to perform (e.g., 0.2 for 20%). Returns: transferfunction: A function or data structure representing the 2D classifier. """ # Step 1: Estimate full region size (optional, for limit calculation) # In practice, growthlimitpercent might be applied to a pre-estimated size # or used as a hard stop condition based on time/voxel count. # For this implementation, we assume a maxvoxelcount is derived from # a quick heuristic or previous run, or we simply run until a time limit. # Here we simulate the limit by stopping after a certain number of voxels. # Step 2: Perform Partial Region Growing extractedregion = [] queue = [seedvoxel] visited = set() visited.add(seedvoxel) # Heuristic: Assume we want to grow until we hit a limit. # The limit is often defined as a percentage of the expected full region. # If the expected full region size is unknown, we might use a fixed voxel count # or time limit. Sources say "size is defined by standard deviations". # Typically, this implies a range of [mu - sigma, mu + sigma] or similar. # Let's assume a range of +/- 1 sigma for simplicity, or as defined by the user. # The source says "two sigma values define the size of the region". # This is ambiguous. It could mean the width is sigma, or 2sigma. # Given it's a "classifier", a common interpretation is a box around the mean. # We will define it as a box from mu-sigma to mu+sigma. valrange = [muv - sigmav, muv + sigmav] gradrange = [mug - sigmag, mug + sigmag] return valrange[0] <= datavalue <= valrange[1] and \ gradrange[0] <= gradientvalue <= gradrange[1] return rectangularclassifier def estimatefullregionsize(volume, seed): """ Placeholder for estimating the full region size. In practice, this might be done by a quick full grow or heuristic. This is a helper function not detailed in sources, but necessary for the limit. """ # Simple heuristic: assume a fixed large number or run a quick grow # For the purpose of this article, we note that the limit is a percentage # of the full region. return 10000 # Placeholder Parameters Growth Extent: 20-40% of the full region growing result is often sufficient to derive a good transfer function. Thresholds: Pre-selected thresholds for noise discarding in the histogram-based method. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noise: If the partial region includes noisy voxels, the statistical averages and standard deviations may be skewed, leading to an inaccurate transfer function. The histogram-based method (Method B) is more robust to noise as it discards low-value points. Disconnected Features: If the seed region is not representative of the other features (e.g., different material properties), the derived transfer function will fail to capture them. Precision: Standard deviation calculations can be sensitive to outliers. Using robust statistics (median, MAD) might be beneficial but is not specified in the sources. The parent method that provides the interactive framework for region growing in volume visualization. Partial Region Growing is an optimization within this framework. RGVis Region Growing An alternative to the rectangular classifier that uses k-d tree partitioning and merging for more robust feature extraction. This is a sub-method of Partial Region Growing for Transfer Function Generation. Time and Memory Complexity Time: Partial region growing is significantly faster than full region growing. On a 1.8GHz Pentium 4, partial growing (20-40%) took under 0.2 seconds, while full growing took 2.8-8.1 seconds for various datasets. The transfer function generation step is negligible in comparison. Memory: Requires memory for the volume data, the visited mask, and the queue for region growing. The classifier storage is minimal (4 values for rectangular, or a set of regions for histogram-based). Measured Performance Confocal Microscopy ganglion (55x512x512): Full=5.7s, Partial=0.022s. MRA head vasculature (125x250x250): Full=7.2s, Partial=0.028s. MRI head (128^3): Full=2.8s, Partial=0.34s. MRI Chest (256^3): Full=8.1s, Partial=0.12s. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Drastically reduces computation time for feature extraction. Automatically suggests a transfer function, reducing manual trial-and-error. Effective for visualizing disconnected features of the same type. The histogram-based classifier is robust to noise. Limitations: Requires a representative seed region. If the seed is not typical, the transfer function will be inaccurate. The rectangular classifier may be too simplistic for complex feature distributions; the histogram-based method is more complex to implement. Does not provide a geometric surface representation directly (though this can be generated from the segmented volume). When to Use Use when features are disconnected and full region growing is too slow or captures unwanted noise. Use when a quick exploration of similar features is needed. Use when the user wants to avoid manual tuning of the transfer function. When Not to Use Use when features are highly heterogeneous and a single transfer function cannot represent them. Use when a precise geometric surface is required immediately (though this can be derived later). This method was developed as part of the RGVis system for visualizing industrial CT volume data for nondestructive testing (NDT) applications. It was introduced to lower the cost of segmentation and facilitate volumetric feature extraction by coupling region growing techniques with a 2D histogram interface. The technique allows users to quickly identify and display relevant features in NDT data, which often contain concealed structures and noise. name: Surface Modeling via Boundary Tracking and Marching Cubes
head: Boundary Surface Extraction, Boundary Surface Extraction via Region Growing, Feature Modeling
body: This method constructs compact, hole-free boundary surfaces for extracted features in volumetric data, followed by optional smoothing via isosurface extraction. It addresses the failure of standard binary isosurface extraction on noisy data with small, fine features by first using region growing to segment the volume, then tracking the boundary of the segmented voxels to create a precise volumetric feature representation. Unlike direct marching cubes on raw data, which may include unwanted surrounding parts or fail due to noise, this approach isolates the feature topology before generating a smooth surface. Inputs: A segmented volume (binary mask or labeled regions) derived from region growing, and optionally the original scalar field values for isovalue calculation. Outputs: A smooth, hole-free triangular mesh representing the feature boundary. Data Structures: 1. Segmented Volume: A 3D grid where each voxel is marked as "extracted" (part of the feature) or "background". 2. Boundary Faces: A set of planar faces (typically quadrilaterals or triangles) that enclose the extracted voxels. Each face is defined by its geometric position and normal vector. 3. Internal Voxels: The set of voxels located strictly inside the identified boundary. Steps: 1. Boundary Tracking: Apply a boundary tracking algorithm [Artzy et al. 1981] to the segmented volume to identify all boundary faces enclosing the extracted voxels. This step locates the interface between extracted and non-extracted voxels. 2. Locate Internal Voxels: Identify voxels that are internal to the boundary faces identified in Step 1. This creates a clean volumetric feature representation, ensuring the boundary is closed and hole-free. 3. Filter High-Frequency Artifacts (Optional): Apply a spatial filter to the boundary cells to remove noise. A Box filter or Gaussian filter is used, chosen according to the characteristics of the features. This step reduces high-frequency artifacts on the boundary faces. 4. Compute Isovalue: Calculate the isovalue for the marching cubes step. The isovalue is set to the average of the scalar values of the voxels located on the boundary faces. I{iso} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{v \in \text{BoundaryFaces}} V(v) Where N is the number of voxels on the boundary faces, and V(v) is the scalar value of voxel v in the original data. 5. Extract Isosurface: Use the Marching Cubes algorithm [Lorensen and Cline 1987] on the segmented volume (or the filtered boundary representation) using the computed isovalue I{iso} to generate the final smooth surface. This preserves the main topological information while smoothing the geometry. 6. Assess Surface Quality (Optional): Perform hardware-accelerated superimposed rendering of the boundary surface and the extracted voxels. Voxels outside the boundary surface are colored blue to visualize uncertainty and parts left out of the surface representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def surfacemodelingviaboundarytracking(segmentedvolume, originalscalarfield): """ segmentedvolume: 3D array, 1 if voxel is part of feature, 0 otherwise. originalscalarfield: 3D array, scalar values for all voxels. Returns: Triangular mesh (vertices, faces). """ # Step 1: Boundary Tracking # Identify all boundary faces enclosing the extracted voxels. # Uses Artzy et al. boundary tracking algorithm. boundaryfaces = boundarytracking(segmentedvolume) # Step 2: Locate Internal Voxels # Identify voxels internal to the boundary to create a clean volumetric representation. # This ensures the boundary is closed and hole-free. internalvoxels = locateinternalvoxels(segmentedvolume, boundaryfaces) # Step 3: Filter High-Frequency Artifacts (Optional) # Apply Box or Gaussian filter to boundary cells. # Filter choice depends on feature characteristics. filteredboundaryfaces = filterboundaryfaces(boundaryfaces, filtertype="Gaussian") # Step 4: Compute Isovalue # Average of scalar values of voxels on the boundary faces. boundaryvoxelvalues = [] for face in filteredboundaryfaces: # Get voxels associated with this face voxelsonface = getvoxelsonface(face, segmentedvolume) for v in voxelsonface: boundaryvoxelvalues.append(originalscalarfield[v]) if not boundaryvoxelvalues: raise ValueError("No voxels found on boundary faces.") isovalue = sum(boundaryvoxelvalues) / len(boundaryvoxelvalues) # Step 5: Extract Isosurface using Marching Cubes # Generate smooth surface preserving topological information. mesh = marchingcubes(segmentedvolume, isovalue) return mesh def boundarytracking(volume): """ Implements Artzy et al. boundary tracking. Returns a list of boundary faces. """ # Not given in the sources. Standard implementation involves # traversing the interface between 1 and 0 voxels. pass def locateinternalvoxels(volume, boundaryfaces): """ Identifies voxels strictly inside the boundary. """ # Not given in the sources. Typically involves flood fill or ray casting # from a known internal point. pass def filterboundaryfaces(faces, filtertype): """ Applies spatial filtering to boundary faces. """ # Not given in the sources. Applies Box or Gaussian convolution # to the positions or normals of the faces. pass def getvoxelsonface(face, volume): """ Returns voxels that constitute the face. """ # Not given in the sources. Depends on the specific geometry # of the boundary faces (e.g., voxels sharing the face). pass Uses region growing to segment the volume before boundary tracking. Chosen when the feature has distinct intensity ranges but is noisy. [7568-region-growing-iso-surface-extraction.md] The core algorithm used in Step 5. Chosen for its speed and widespread support. [2518-marching-cubes-lookup-and-configuration.md] An alternative to Marching Cubes for Step 5 if vertex position optimization is needed. Chosen when higher geometric accuracy is required at the cost of complexity. [6319-dual-contouring-and-surface-nets.md] Time Complexity: Dominated by the boundary tracking and the final Marching Cubes step. Filtering can become time-consuming for large volumes. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the segmented volume, boundary faces, and the resulting mesh. Strengths: Produces compact, hole-free surfaces; preserves topological information; handles noisy data better than direct isosurface extraction; allows visualization of uncertainty. Limitations: Requires a prior segmentation step (region growing); filtering can be slow for large datasets; the quality of the final surface depends on the accuracy of the boundary tracking and the chosen isovalue. When to Use: When extracting features from noisy CT/MRI data where standard isosurface extraction fails or includes unwanted artifacts. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and segmentation is not feasible; when the feature topology is simple and noise is low. The method was developed to address limitations in visualizing industrial CT volume data for nondestructive testing applications. Standard isosurface extraction based on binary decisions fails on noisy CT data with small, fine features. The approach combines boundary tracking (Artzy et al. 1981) with region growing and Marching Cubes (Lorensen and Cline 1987) to create smooth, topologically correct surfaces. It is used in medical imaging (e.g., lung extraction from MRI/CT) and industrial CT analysis. name: VolumetricFire Slice Contouring
head: Slice-based contouring, active edge list contouring, VolumetricFire contouring
body: VolumetricFire Slice Contouring is a slice-based isosurface extraction algorithm that processes volumetric data sequentially to generate triangle fans representing the contour. It distinguishes itself from general-purpose methods like Marching Cubes by maintaining an active edge list with split and merge operations to handle topology changes dynamically across slices, specifically optimized for rendering volumetric fire effects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of corner positions (posCorners), corner texture coordinates (texCorners), corner distances (cornerDistance), slice spacing (sliceSpacing), minimum distance (minDistance), and a priority queue of edge expirations (expirations). Output: Buffers of vertex positions (points), texture coordinates (texCoords), and triangle indices (indexes). Data Structures: Active Edge (activeEdge): An object with the following fields: expired: Boolean, indicates if the edge is no longer active. startIndex: Number, index of the starting corner. endIndex: Number, index of the ending corner. deltaPos: Vector3, position increment per slice. deltaTex: Vector3, texture coordinate increment per slice. pos: Vector3, current position of the edge intersection. tex: Vector3, current texture coordinate of the edge intersection. cur: Number, index in the activeEdges array. prev: Number, index of the previous edge in the linked list. next: Number, index of the next edge in the linked list. Active Edges Array (activeEdges): An array storing references to activeEdge objects. Priority Queue (expirations): Stores edges with their expiration priority (corner distance). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize firstEdge to 0, nextEdge to 0, and expirations as an empty priority queue. For each of the 3 corner neighbors of the maxCorner (indexed i from 0 to 2): Call createEdge(maxCorner, cornerNeighbors[maxCorner][i]) to generate an initial edge. Set activeEdge.prev = (i + 2) % 3 and activeEdge.next = (i + 1) % 3 to form the initial linked list cycle. 2. Slice Iteration: Iterate sliceDistance from maxCorner down to minDistance using sliceSpacing. 3. Edge Expiration and Topology Management: While expirations.top().priority >= sliceDistance: Pop the edge edge from expirations. If edge.expired is true, continue to the next iteration. Check if edge.endIndex differs from both activeEdges[edge.prev].endIndex and activeEdges[edge.next].endIndex: Split: If different, the edge must split. Mark edge.expired = true. Create activeEdge1 using createEdge(edge.endIndex, incomingEdges[edge.endIndex][edge.startIndex]). Set activeEdge1.prev = edge.prev and update activeEdges[edge.prev].next = nextEdge - 1. Set activeEdge1.next = nextEdge. Create activeEdge2 using createEdge(edge.endIndex, incomingEdges[edge.endIndex][activeEdge1.endIndex]). Set activeEdge2.prev = nextEdge - 2 and activeEdge2.next = edge.next. Update activeEdges[activeEdge2.next].prev = nextEdge - 1. Set firstEdge = nextEdge - 1. Merge: If edge.endIndex matches either neighbor's endIndex: Identify prev and next edges to be merged based on which neighbor matches. Mark both prev.expired = true and next.expired = true. Create a new activeEdge using createEdge(edge.endIndex, incomingEdges[edge.endIndex][prev.startIndex]). Update links: activeEdge.prev = prev.prev, activeEdges[activeEdge.prev].next = nextEdge - 1, activeEdge.next = next.next, activeEdges[activeEdge.next].prev = nextEdge - 1. Set firstEdge = nextEdge - 1. 4. Vertex Collection: Initialize cur = firstEdge and count = 0. Do-While loop while cur !== firstEdge: Increment count. Retrieve activeEdge = activeEdges[cur]. Push activeEdge.pos components to points buffer. Push activeEdge.tex components to texCoords buffer. Update activeEdge.pos.add(activeEdge.deltaPos) and activeEdge.tex.add(activeEdge.deltaTex). Set cur = activeEdge.next. 5. Index Generation: For i from 2 to count - 1: Push indices (nextIndex, nextIndex + i - 1, nextIndex + i) to indexes buffer to form triangle fans. Increment nextIndex by 1 for each vertex added (implicit in the loop logic, though nextIndex update is not explicitly shown in the snippet, it is standard for fan generation). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumetricfireslicecontouring(poscorners, texcorners, cornerdistance, slicespacing, mindistance, maxcorner, cornerneighbors, incomingedges): activeedges = [] expirations = PriorityQueue() firstedge = 0 nextedge = 0 points = [] texcoords = [] indexes = [] nextindex = 0 def createedge(startindex, endindex): if nextedge >= 12: return None # Calculate range to avoid division by zero rangeval = cornerdistance[startindex] - cornerdistance[endindex] deltapos = Vector3() deltatex = Vector3() pos = Vector3() tex = Vector3() if rangeval != 0.0: irange = 1.0 / rangeval # deltaPos = (posCorners[endIndex] - posCorners[startIndex]) irange deltapos.subvectors(poscorners[endindex], poscorners[startindex]).multiplyscalar(irange) # deltaTex = (texCorners[endIndex] - texCorners[startIndex]) irange deltatex.subvectors(texcorners[endindex], texcorners[startindex]).multiplyscalar(irange) step = cornerdistance[startindex] - slicedistance # pos = deltaPos step + posCorners[startIndex] pos.addvectors(deltapos.clone().multiplyscalar(step), poscorners[startindex]) # tex = deltaTex step + texCorners[startIndex] tex.addvectors(deltatex.clone().multiplyscalar(step), texcorners[startindex]) # deltaPos = sliceSpacing deltapos.multiplyscalar(slicespacing) deltatex.multiplyscalar(slicespacing) else: # Handle zero range case: set deltas to zero, pos/tex to start corner deltapos.set(0, 0, 0) deltatex.set(0, 0, 0) pos.copy(poscorners[startindex]) tex.copy(texcorners[startindex]) activeedge = { 'expired': False, 'startIndex': startindex, 'endIndex': endindex, 'deltaPos': deltapos, 'deltaTex': deltatex, 'pos': pos, 'tex': tex, 'cur': nextedge, 'prev': 0, 'next': 0 } expirations.push(activeedge, cornerdistance[endindex]) activeedges.append(activeedge) return activeedge # Initialization for i in range(3): activeedge = createedge(maxcorner, cornerneighbors[maxcorner][i]) activeedge['prev'] = (i + 2) % 3 activeedge['next'] = (i + 1) % 3 slicedistance = maxcorner while slicedistance > mindistance: # Process expirations while not expirations.isempty() and expirations.top().priority >= slicedistance: edge = expirations.pop().object if edge['expired']: continue prevedge = activeedges[edge['prev']] nextedgeobj = activeedges[edge['next']] if edge['endIndex'] != prevedge['endIndex'] and edge['endIndex'] != nextedgeobj['endIndex']: # Split edge['expired'] = True activeedge1 = createedge(edge['endIndex'], incomingedges[edge['endIndex']][edge['startIndex']]) activeedge1['prev'] = edge['prev'] activeedges[edge['prev']]['next'] = nextedge - 1 activeedge1['next'] = nextedge activeedge2 = createedge(edge['endIndex'], incomingedges[edge['endIndex']][activeedge1['endIndex']]) activeedge2['prev'] = nextedge - 2 activeedge2['next'] = edge['next'] activeedges[activeedge2['next']]['prev'] = nextedge - 1 firstedge = nextedge - 1 else: # Merge if edge['endIndex'] == prevedge['endIndex']: prev = prevedge next = edge else: prev = edge next = nextedgeobj prev['expired'] = True next['expired'] = True activeedge = createedge(edge['endIndex'], incomingedges[edge['endIndex']][prev['startIndex']]) activeedge['prev'] = prev['prev'] activeedges[activeedge['prev']]['next'] = nextedge - 1 activeedge['next'] = next['next'] activeedges[activeedge['next']]['prev'] = nextedge - 1 firstedge = nextedge - 1 # Collect vertices cur = firstedge count = 0 if firstedge < len(activeedges): do: count += 1 activeedge = activeedges[cur] points.extend(activeedge['pos'].components) texcoords.extend(activeedge['tex'].components) activeedge['pos'].add(activeedge['deltaPos']) activeedge['tex'].add(activeedge['deltaTex']) cur = activeedge['next'] while cur != firstedge and cur < len(activeedges) # Generate indices for i in range(2, count): indexes.append(nextindex) indexes.append(nextindex + i - 1) indexes.append(nextindex + i) nextindex += 1 slicedistance -= slicespacing return points, texcoords, indexes Parameters: sliceSpacing: The distance between consecutive slices. minDistance: The minimum slice distance to process. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If range (difference between corner distances) is zero, interpolation is skipped, and the edge position/texture is set to the start corner values. Boundary Conditions: The algorithm assumes valid incomingEdges and cornerNeighbors structures. If nextEdge exceeds 12, createEdge returns undefined, which may break the linked list if not handled. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The algorithm iterates through slices and processes edges, with split/merge operations being constant time per edge. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Uses a fixed-size active edge list (up to 12 edges) and buffers for output. Strengths: Optimized for volumetric fire rendering, handles topology changes dynamically. Limitations: Specific to the VolumetricFire implementation; not a general-purpose isosurface extractor. When to use: When rendering volumetric fire effects where slice-based contouring is sufficient. When not to use: For general isosurface extraction requiring robust topology handling across complex volumes. VolumetricFire Slice Contouring is part of the VolumetricFire library, used for rendering volumetric fire effects. It is a specialized implementation within the broader context of isosurface extraction methods. yomotsu/VolumetricFire, https://github.com/yomotsu/VolumetricFire, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Minimal Area Triangulation for Polygons
head: Minimal Area Triangulation, Minimal Area Triangulation of Isopolygons, Polygon Triangulation
body: Minimal Area Triangulation is a method for converting non-convex or complex 3D polygons (isopolygons) resulting from isosurface extraction into a set of triangles, minimizing the total area of the resulting mesh to reduce visual artifacts. It solves the inter-slice triangulation problem by finding the optimal triangle decomposition for isosurfaces defined on octrees. Unlike heuristic methods that prioritize speed or simplicity, this method finds the global optimum for the triangulation of a single polygon. It is distinct from Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces which builds surfaces incrementally, and Dual Contouring and Surface Nets which use optimization to place vertices, by strictly operating on the boundary polygon of an octree node to produce a minimal-area disk homeomorphic to the input. Inputs: A simple closed 3D polygon P defined by an ordered list of n vertices \{p1, p2, \dots, pn\}. The polygon lies on the boundary of a convex body (typically an octree node). Outputs: A list of triangles forming the minimal area triangulation of P. Data Structures: 1. Vertices: Array of 3D points pi = (xi, yi, zi). 2. DP Table M: A 2D array of size n \times n storing the minimal area M(i, j) for sub-polygons. 3. Split Table K: A 2D array of size n \times n storing the index k that minimized the area for each sub-polygon, used for reconstruction. Formulas: Let A(i, j, k) be the area of the triangle formed by vertices pi, pj, pk. Let M(i, j) be the minimal area of the sub-polygon P{i,j} defined by vertices from index i to j (inclusive, in cyclic order). The recurrence relation is: M(i, j) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = j \\ 0 & \text{if } i = j + 1 \bmod n \\ \min{k \in (j, i)} \{ M(i, k) + M(k, j) + A(i, j, k) \} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where k \in (j, i) denotes the set of vertices strictly between j and i in the cyclic order of the polygon. Algorithm Steps: 1. Check for Cofacial Vertices: Determine if all vertices of the polygon lie on the same cube face (are cofacial). If yes: Perform a fan triangulation from the centroid to avoid introducing new edges on the cube face, which can cause artifacts. Calculate centroid C = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} pi. Create triangles \{C, pi, p{i+1}\} for i=1 \dots n-1 (with p{n+1} = p1). Return these triangles. If no: Proceed to dynamic programming. 2. Initialize DP Tables: Initialize M(i, j) = 0 for all i, j. Initialize K(i, j) to undefined. 3. Compute Minimal Areas (Bottom-Up): Iterate over the chain length L from 2 to n-1. For each starting index i from 0 to n-1: Calculate ending index j = (i + L) \bmod n. Initialize min\val = \infty and best\k = -1. Iterate over all vertices k strictly between j and i in the cyclic order. Calculate current\val = M(i, k) + M(k, j) + A(i, j, k). If current\val < min\val: set min\val = current\val and best\k = k. Set M(i, j) = min\val and K(i, j) = best\k. 4. Reconstruct Triangles: Initialize an empty list triangles. Call recursive function Reconstruct(i, j) starting with i=0, j=n-1 (representing the full polygon). Reconstruct(i, j): If j = (i + 1) \bmod n: The edge (i, j) is a boundary edge of the original polygon. No triangle is formed by the split at this level. Return. Let k = K(i, j). Add triangle \{pi, pj, pk\} to triangles. Recursively call Reconstruct(i, k) and Reconstruct(k, j). 5. Return: The list triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minimalareatriangulation(vertices): n = len(vertices) if n < 3: return [] # Check for cofacial vertices if iscofacial(vertices): return fantriangulation(vertices) # Initialize DP tables # M[i][j] stores minimal area for sub-polygon from i to j # K[i][j] stores the optimal split vertex k M = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] K = [[-1] n for in range(n)] # Helper to get area of triangle (i, j, k) def trianglearea(i, j, k): p1 = vertices[i] p2 = vertices[j] p3 = vertices[k] v1 = [p2[x] - p1[x] for x in range(3)] v2 = [p3[x] - p1[x] for x in range(3)] cross = [ v1[1] v2[2] - v1[2] v2[1], v1[2] v2[0] - v1[0] v2[2], v1[0] v2[1] - v1[1] v2[0] ] return 0.5 (cross[0]2 + cross[1]2 + cross[2]2)0.5 # Fill DP table bottom-up # L is the number of steps along the boundary from i to j. # Base cases L=0 (i=j) and L=1 (j=i+1) are already 0. for L in range(2, n): for i in range(n): j = (i + L) % n minval = float('inf') bestk = -1 # Iterate k strictly between j and i in cyclic order k = (j + 1) % n while k != i: val = M[i][k] + M[k][j] + trianglearea(i, j, k) if val < minval: minval = val bestk = k k = (k + 1) % n M[i][j] = minval K[i][j] = bestk # Reconstruct triangles triangles = [] def reconstruct(i, j): if j == (i + 1) % n: return k = K[i][j] triangles.append((i, j, k)) reconstruct(i, k) reconstruct(k, j) # Start reconstruction at the full polygon reconstruct(0, n - 1) return triangles def iscofacial(vertices): # Check if all vertices lie on the same coordinate plane (e.g., x=const, y=const, or z=const) if len(vertices) < 3: return False for axis in range(3): val = vertices[0][axis] if all(v[axis] == val for v in vertices): return True return False def fantriangulation(vertices): n = len(vertices) centroid = [sum(v[axis] for v in vertices) / n for axis in range(3)] triangles = [] # Create triangles connecting each edge of the polygon to the centroid for i in range(n): triangles.append((i, (i + 1) % n, 'centroid')) return triangles Parameters: None explicitly required for the core algorithm. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cofacial Vertices: If vertices lie on the same cube face, standard triangulation might create edges that lie on the face of the cube, potentially causing artifacts. Self-Intersections: While the method finds the minimal area triangulation, it does not guarantee a minimal area surface. Precision: The dynamic programming approach relies on floating-point arithmetic for area calculations. The Fuchs-Kedem-Uselton Contour Method is an isosurface extraction technique that generates a minimum-area triangulated surface by connecting contours from adjacent volume slices. name: Fuchs-Kedem-Uselton Contour Method
head: Minimum-cost cycle contour method
body: The Fuchs-Kedem-Uselton Contour Method is an isosurface extraction technique that generates a minimum-area triangulated surface by connecting contours from adjacent volume slices. It solves the inter-slice triangulation problem by modeling the connection between two contours as a minimum-cost cycle in a directed-toroidal graph. Unlike heuristic methods that prioritize speed over optimality, this method finds the optimal solution to generate the minimum-area surface. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset. An isovalue threshold. Outputs: A set of triangles connecting the vertices of the two contours. Data Structures: Contour: A list of vertices ordered along the contour path. Let C1 be the contour in slice k with m points, and C2 be the contour in slice k+1 with n points. Directed-Toroidal Graph: A graph where vertices correspond to the points in C1 and C2, and edges represent potential triangle connections. The toroidal aspect implies that the contours are treated as cyclic sequences, allowing connections between the first and last points via modulo indexing. Steps: 1. Preprocess: Generate intra-slice contours within single slices of the data. 2. Construct Graph: For two adjacent contours C1 (size m) and C2 (size n), construct a directed graph where edges represent potential triangles formed by vertices from C1 and C2. 3. Solve Minimum-Cost Cycle: Find the minimum-cost cycle in the directed-toroidal graph. 4. Generate Triangles: Form the inter-slice triangles based on the edges selected in the minimum-cost cycle. 5. Render: Pass the generated triangles to a conventional polygon rendering engine to create the image. Formula: The computational complexity (cost) \tau(m, n) to find the optimal solution for contours with m and n points is bounded by: \tau(m, n) < (\lceil \log2 m \rceil + 2) \times (2mn + m) \quad \text{for} \quad (m < n) where m and n are the number of points in the two contours. Parameters: m, n: Number of vertices in the two adjacent contours. Typical values: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complexity: The cost bound grows with mn, which can be significant for high-resolution contours. Pseudocode: Unverified code. exact solver logic not specified in sources Time Complexity: The cost to find the optimal solution for two contours with m and n points is bounded by \tau(m, n) < (\lceil \log2 m \rceil + 2) \times (2mn + m) for m < n. This bound is significantly higher than heuristic methods which may require only m + n steps. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method generates the minimum-area surface as the optimal solution. Conventional polygon rendering displays the generated triangles to create the image. The method was introduced by Fuchs, Kedem, and Uselton in 1977. It was the first widely used coercion method for isosurface extraction that addressed the inter-slice triangulation problem by minimizing surface area. It laid the groundwork for subsequent heuristic methods that sought to reduce computational cost. name: Contour Surface Filling
head: Color-filled contour plot, Color-filling a contour surface, Triangle partitioning for contour surfaces
body: Contour Surface Filling is a surface rendering technique that visualizes 3D vector fields by partitioning triangles on coordinate-parallel planes into polygons based on linearly interpolated vector magnitudes and filling them with colors mapped to contour levels. It differs from wireframe or arrow-based vector visualizations by providing a continuous color-coded magnitude representation across the surface, building on the geometric partitioning logic of the Fuchs-Kedem-Uselton Contour Method but specifically applied to pre-defined planar surfaces rather than implicit isosurfaces. Inputs and Outputs The method takes a 3D grid of vector data and a planar surface parallel to a coordinate axis as input. It outputs a rasterized image where each triangle on the surface is filled with colors corresponding to the linearly interpolated vector magnitudes at the triangle vertices. Data Structures The algorithm uses a vector array where the magnitude for vertex i is stored at index 4i + 3. An indc array maps each vertex index to a contour level index. The Contours[NC] array stores an increasing sequence of vector magnitude values that define the upper limits of the contour levels. The Colors[NC][3] array stores the RGB components for each of the NC contour levels. A working space array vertex[5][3] is allocated to store the vertices of the partitioned polygons, as the algorithm guarantees that no polygon will exceed five vertices. Number of Triangles The number of triangles to process depends on the grid dimensions nx, ny, nz and the plane orientation. For an xy-plane surface, there are 2(nx-1)(ny-1) triangles. For a yz-plane surface, there are 2(ny-1)(nz-1) triangles. For a zx-plane surface, there are 2(nz-1)(nx-1) triangles. Algorithm Steps The algorithm processes each triangle individually. Let the triangle vertices be p1, p2, p3 with coordinates (x1, y1, z1), (x2, y2, z2), (x3, y3, z3) and magnitudes m1, m2, m3. 1. Permute vertex indices i1, i2, i3 such that indc[i1] \le indc[i2] and indc[i1] \le indc[i3]. 2. Initialize ic1 = indc[i1], ic2 = indc[i2], ic3 = indc[i3]. Retrieve magnitudes m1 = vector[4i1+3], m2 = vector[4i2+3], m3 = vector[4i3+3]. Retrieve coordinates for p1, p2, p3. Initialize vertex counter n = 0. Set vertex[0] = (x1, y1, z1). 3. Loop for ic from ic1 to ic2 - 1: Let m = Contours[ic]. Calculate intersection point P(xp, yp, zp) on edge p1-p2 using s = \frac{m - m1}{m2 - m1} and xp = x1 + s(x2 - x1), yp = y1 + s(y2 - y1), zp = z1 + s(z2 - z1). Calculate intersection point Q(xq, yq, zq): if ic < ic3, Q lies on edge p1-p3 with s = \frac{m - m1}{m3 - m1} and xq = x1 + s(x3 - x1), yq = y1 + s(y3 - y1), zq = z1 + s(z3 - z1). If ic \ge ic3, Q lies on edge p2-p3 with s = \frac{m - m3}{m2 - m3} and xq = x3 + s(x2 - x3), yq = y3 + s(y2 - y3), zq = z3 + s(z2 - z3). (Note: The source text contains a typo in this branch listing x2-x1; the corrected formula uses x2-x3.) Add P and Q to the vertex array as vertex[n++] = P and vertex[n++] = Q. If ic == ic3, add vertex p3 as vertex[n++] = (x3, y3, z3). Fill the polygon using the vertex array with n vertices and color Colors[ic]. Reset n = 2. Set vertex[0] = Q and vertex[1] = P. 4. After the first loop, add vertex p2 as vertex[n++] = (x2, y2, z2). 5. If ic3 \ge ic2, loop for ic from ic2 to ic3 - 1: Let m = Contours[ic]. Calculate P on edge p2-p3 using s = \frac{m - m2}{m3 - m2} and xp = x2 + s(x3 - x2), yp = y2 + s(y3 - y2), zp = z2 + s(z3 - z2). Calculate Q on edge p1-p3 using s = \frac{m - m1}{m3 - m1} and xq = x1 + s(x3 - x1), yq = y1 + s(y3 - y1), zq = z1 + s(z3 - z1). Add P and Q to vertex. Fill the polygon with color Colors[ic]. Reset n = 2. Set vertex[0] = Q and vertex[1] = P. After the second loop, add vertex p3 as vertex[n++] = (x3, y3, z3). Set ic = ic3. 6. Fill the final polygon using the vertex array with n vertices and color Colors[ic]. Pseudocode Unverified code.
