name: Task Shader Block-wise Stream Compaction
head: Task Shader Cell Classification and Task Generation
body: Task Shader Block-wise Stream Compaction is a GPU-driven visibility determination technique that identifies volume blocks containing isosurface geometry and generates a compact list of those blocks to drive subsequent mesh shader workgroups. It solves the problem of high draw times in scenes with high depth complexity by avoiding the extraction and rendering of geometry for blocks that are occluded by closer volume data. Unlike its siblings, it operates on a flat list of fixed-size blocks rather than a hierarchical structure, using a custom task and mesh shader pipeline to detect occupancy before generating proxy geometry. It outperforms methods that process depth textures of previously established occluder representations, such as hierarchical occlusion maps [ZMHH97] and iterative depth warping [LKE18]. The method functions as a lightweight raster occlusion culling pass that is a hybrid between basic raster occlusion culling [KT14] and hierarchical raster occlusion culling [LL20]. It resolves potential visibility only for fixed-size blocks, using a custom task and mesh shader pipeline to efficiently detect occupied blocks before creating proxy geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset organized into fixed-size blocks; a min-max texture storing the scalar value range for each block; the isovalue for extraction. Output: A dense list of indices for occupied blocks; mesh shader workgroups dispatched to process these blocks. Data Structures: Min-Max Texture: Stores the minimum and maximum scalar values for each volume block. Accessed via texture sampling. Block Occupancy Index Array: A dense array storing the indices of blocks determined to contain isosurface geometry. Num Occupied Blocks: A scalar value indicating the total count of occupied blocks found in the current task shader workgroup. Parameters: Task Shader Workgroup Size: Processes a localized group of 256 blocks. Mesh Shader Workgroup Size: Each mesh shader workgroup processes sets of 32 occupied blocks. The final workgroup may process between 1 and 32 blocks. Proxy Geometry: A single quad per block, rather than three cube faces. Steps: 1. Task Shader Analysis: The task shader analyzes a localized group of 256 blocks. For each block, it samples the min-max texture at the corresponding location. 2. Occupancy Determination: The occupancy of each block is determined by checking if the isovalue lies between the sampled minimum and maximum values. 3. Stream Compaction: A dense list of occupied blocks is generated in the same manner as a dense list of occupied cells is created in the isosurface extraction stage. This involves a local prefix sum algorithm for stream compaction, avoiding atomic variables to improve performance. No list offset or length buffers are required because workgroups operate on fixed-length lists. 4. Mesh Shader Dispatch: The task shader emits mesh shader workgroups. Each workgroup processes 32 occupied blocks, except the final workgroup which may process 1–32 blocks. 5. Proxy Geometry Creation: In the mesh shader, each thread computes an offset into the blockoccupancyindex array based on thread and workgroup indices, ensuring the index is less than numoccupiedblocks. Each active thread creates proxy geometry for one occupied block. 6. Proxy Geometry Definition: The proxy geometry for each block consists of a single quad containing the bounding box of the block projected into screen space with the minimal z-coordinate of the block's corners. This reduces triangles from 6 to 2 per block, primitives per workgroup from 224 to 64, and vertices from 224 to 128. 7. Rasterization: The proxy geometry is passed to the rasterizer. Fragments that pass the early depth test and representative fragment test write to a buffer to determine the final potentially visible set (PVS). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def taskshaderworkgroup(blockindices256, minmaxtexture, isovalue): occupiedindices = [] # Step 1 & 2: Identify occupied blocks for i in range(256): blockidx = blockindices256[i] minval, maxval = minmaxtexture[blockidx] if minval <= isovalue <= maxval: occupiedindices.append(blockidx) # Step 3: Stream Compaction numoccupied = len(occupiedindices) # Write compacted list and count to output buffers outputoccupiedlist = occupiedindices outputoccupiedcount = numoccupied # Step 4: Dispatch Mesh Shader Workgroups nummeshworkgroups = math.ceil(numoccupied / 32) for w in range(nummeshworkgroups): # Dispatch mesh shader workgroup w meshshaderworkgroup(w, numoccupied) def meshshaderworkgroup(workgroupid, numoccupied): # Step 5: Compute offset # Standard shader intrinsic for local thread ID threadid = getthreadid() if threadid < numoccupied: offset = workgroupid 32 + threadid blockidx = outputoccupiedlist[offset] # Step 6: Create Proxy Geometry # Generate single quad bounding box with minimal z vertices = generatequadproxy(blockidx) # Write to vertex/index buffers writegeometry(vertices) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Depth Testing: Rasterizing fewer primitives increases the likelihood of early termination of rasterization via the representative fragment test [KTB18] extension. This extension terminates early-depth testing if at least one fragment shader instance is invoked, but cannot terminate for multiple associated primitives. Multi-View Rendering: Using multi-view rendering features to rasterize proxy geometry per-eye in a joint pass is facilitated by generating one quad per eye. Rendering more than 3 sides of a cube would require accounting for blocks located between the viewer's eyes on cardinal axes. Conservative Visibility: The method ensures visibility determination is conservative rather than probabilistic. Raster Occlusion Culling is a GPU-driven visibility determination technique that identifies a potentially visible set (PVS) of voxel blocks by rasterizing lightweight proxy geometry, replacing expensive individual hardware occlusion queries with a single efficient rasterization pass followed by GPU-driven stream compaction. It solves the problem of high draw times in scenes with high depth complexity by avoiding the extraction and rendering of geometry for blocks that are occluded by closer volume data. Unlike its siblings, it operates on a flat list of fixed-size blocks rather than a hierarchical structure, using a custom task and mesh shader pipeline to detect occupancy before generating proxy geometry. It outperforms methods that process depth textures of previously established occluder representations, such as hierarchical occlusion maps [ZMHH97] and iterative depth warping [LKE18]. This compute shader pass compactifies the raw visibility indices generated by the preceding raster occlusion culling stage and constructs two distinct Potentially Visible Set (PVS) datasets: PVS{curr} and PVS{curr-prev}. It solves the problem of efficiently preparing visibility data for temporal coherence by identifying blocks visible in the current frame and those newly visible since the last frame, enabling the selection of optimal occluders for subsequent rendering passes. GPU-driven visibility culling is a technique that uses per-subchunk metadata (AABB, terrain/water draw ranges) to test visibility on the GPU and emit indirect draw commands only for visible subchunks. It differs from CPU-side culling by offloading the visibility test and command buffer population to the GPU, allowing the CPU to remain free for scene management and chunk loading. It builds on Task Shader Block-wise Stream Compaction by utilizing the metadata prepared there to drive the compute dispatch and indirect execution. Time Complexity: The task shader processes blocks in fixed groups of 256, and mesh shaders process occupied blocks in groups of 32. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of blocks processed, but significantly reduced by culling occluded blocks. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the min-max texture and the block occupancy index array. No list offset or length buffers are required due to fixed-length workgroup operations. Performance: Rasterizing fewer primitives (2 triangles per block vs. 6) reduces buffer writes in the fragment shader stage and increases the likelihood of early depth testing termination. Strengths: Reduces the number of task shader workgroups launched for blocks that will not contribute to the displayed isosurface. Avoids atomic variables in stream compaction, improving extraction performance. Limitations: Operates on a single level of occlusion culling, unlike hierarchical methods. Visibility determination is conservative, potentially including some occluded blocks. When to Use: Scenes with high depth complexity where ray-marching performance is limited by resolution. When view-dependent visibility information can be exploited to reduce rendering overhead. When Not to Use: Scenes with low depth complexity where the overhead of the culling pass may outweigh the benefits. The technique was introduced in "Efficient Direct Isosurface Rasterization of Scalar Volumes" by Kubisch and Tavenrath. It builds on prior work in raster occlusion culling [KT14, LL20] and probabilistic culling for particle rendering [IRR22]. The method addresses the linear dependence of ray-marching performance on display resolution by leveraging the optimization of modern GPU rasterization units. It is used in real-time volume graphics for direct isosurface visualization. name: Raster Occlusion Culling
head: Depth Buffer Occlusion Culling, GPU-driven occlusion culling, Hybrid Raster Occlusion Culling, Lightweight Raster Occlusion Culling, Raster Occlusion Culling for Dense Volume Data
body: Raster Occlusion Culling is a GPU-driven technique that determines the visibility of voxel blocks by rasterizing lightweight proxy geometry (typically quads) and using the resulting depth buffer to identify a Potentially Visible Set (PVS). It replaces expensive individual hardware occlusion queries with a single efficient proxy rasterization pass followed by GPU-driven stream compaction. This method sets the PVS for subsequent isosurface extraction stages, avoiding the generation of geometry for blocks that are fully occluded by closer volumes. It differs from its sibling Task Shader Block-wise Stream Compaction by performing the actual depth-based visibility test via rasterization rather than purely via compute-based occupancy checks, and from GPU-driven Visibility Culling by relying on standard rasterization hardware for occlusion testing rather than ray tracing or other visibility acceleration structures. The method operates in a pipeline involving task shaders, mesh shaders, rasterization, and compute shaders to filter voxel blocks. Input: A volume dataset with a precomputed min-max texture (2-channel volume texture storing min/max values per block). The resolution of this texture is X/U \times Y/V \times Z/W, where X, Y, Z are volume dimensions and U, V, W are block dimensions. Output: A dense list of indices representing the PVS of occupied blocks (PVS{curr}) and optionally a list of blocks visible since the last frame (PVS{curr-prev}). 1. Min-Max Texture: A 2-channel volume texture (e.g., RG32UI or similar format depending on data type) storing the minimum and maximum scalar values for each voxel block. 2. Visibility Buffer: A buffer (often an image or structured buffer) where fragments write the implicit ID of the block they belong to if they pass depth tests. 3. Task Shader Interface: python struct Task { uint32t baseID; uint32t numoccupiedblocks; uint8t blockoccupancyindex[256]; }; This structure is passed to the mesh shader. It does not require list offset or length buffers because mesh shader workgroups operate on lists of fixed lengths (32 blocks). 4. PVS Lists: Arrays of indices storing the compacted list of visible block IDs. 1. Task Shader: Block-wise Stream Compaction The task shader analyzes a localized group of 256 blocks. For each block, sample the min-max texture at the block's location. Determine occupancy by checking if the target isovalue lies between the sampled minimum and maximum values: min\val \leq isovalue \leq max\val If occupied, add the block's index to a local occupancy list. Generate a dense list of occupied blocks. Emit mesh shader workgroups, each processing a fixed set of 32 occupied blocks (the final workgroup may process 1–32 blocks). 2. Mesh Shader: Proxy Geometry Creation Each active thread in the mesh shader computes an offset into the blockoccupancyindex array based on thread and workgroup indices, ensuring the index is less than numoccupiedblocks. Each active thread creates proxy geometry for one occupied block. Proxy Geometry: A single quad representing the bounding box of the block projected into screen space, using the minimal z-coordinate of the block's corners. This reduces triangles from 6 to 2 per block (compared to Kubisch's 3 visible cube faces). Vertices per workgroup: 128 (vs 224 for 32 blocks in Kubisch). Primitives per workgroup: 64. Write vertex and index buffers for the quad proxies. 3. Rasterization Rasterize the proxy geometry. Perform standard depth testing with glDepthFunc(GLLEQUAL) (or equivalent). Utilize the Representative Fragment Test extension [KTB18] if available. This allows the rasterizer to terminate early-depth testing for a primitive if at least one fragment shader instance was invoked (i.e., one fragment is visible). Fewer primitives increase the likelihood of this early termination. Multi-view Rendering: When rendering per-eye, generate one quad per eye. This is simpler than rendering 3+ sides if a block is located between viewer eyes on cardinal axes. 4. Fragment Shader: Visibility Buffer Update For each fragment passing the early depth test and representative fragment test, write the implicit ID of the block into a preallocated slot of the visibility buffer. 5. Compute Shader: PVS Generation and Compactification Run a bit compactification kernel on the visibility buffer to create indices for PVS{curr}. Build two PVS sets in a final compute shader pass: PVS{curr}: Used in the next frame for best occluders based on temporal coherence. PVS{curr-prev}: Determines blocks that became visible since the last frame. Compute shaders are used here to allow larger block sizes and better utilization of streaming multiprocessors compared to mesh shaders. Block Analysis Size: 256 blocks per task shader workgroup. Mesh Shader Workgroup Size: 32 blocks. Isovalue: The scalar threshold for isosurface extraction. Representative Fragment Test: Enabled via graphics API extension to optimize early depth termination. Conservatism: The method is conservative, not probabilistic, ensuring no occupied blocks are incorrectly culled. This contrasts with probabilistic methods like [IRR22]. Multi-view Rendering: If using 3 visible cube faces instead of a single quad, one must account for rendering more than 3 sides if a block is located between the viewer's eyes on any cardinal axis. Using a single quad per eye simplifies this. Temporal Coherence: Effective use of occlusion culling historically required careful exploitation of spatial and temporal coherence. The method maintains PVS{curr-prev} to handle blocks becoming visible. Precision: The min-max texture lookup must be precise enough to avoid false positives (blocks marked occupied when they are not) or false negatives (occupied blocks culled). Defines the spatial resolution at which visibility is determined, balancing accuracy against computational overhead. It sets the size of culling regions (typically aligned with leaf-level octree nodes) and influences aliasing artifacts. Determines block visibility by rasterizing bounding boxes and checking depth test passes, incorporating accumulated opacity into the depth test to ensure blocks behind fully opaque foreground volumes are correctly culled. A fully GPU-driven technique that reduces rasterization overhead by performing rasterization on a coarser level for group nodes and refining visibility results through ray traversal down to the leaf level. It builds on Raster Occlusion Culling by exploiting spatial coherence through hierarchical grouping. A visibility culling technique where triangles are marked as visible and forwarded to graphics hardware rather than being rendered by the CPU. It projects polygons onto a hierarchical structure (meta-tiles) and recursively checks subtiles for potential visibility, leading to a logarithmic search. If a meta-cell size is approximately the size of a single pixel, recursion stops, and a single point with an associated normal (estimated by the field gradient) is forwarded to the graphics hardware. This differs from Greene's implementation by not rendering the visible portion on the CPU but relying on the graphics accelerator. A culling technique using a visibility buffer to prune non-visible clusters, performing back-face and occlusion culling without requiring a hierarchical Z-buffer or storing cluster bounds/normal cones. It uses the last metacell of each cluster to store a cluster bound (AABB). Visibility is updated via a compute shader pass after cell rasterization, and a second visibility buffer records new clusters becoming visible to trigger full cell rasterization in a second pass. Pitfalls include flickering artifacts during fast camera movements when non-visible clusters become visible. Time Complexity: The culling pass is dominated by the rasterization of proxy geometry. The number of primitives is proportional to the number of potentially occupied blocks. Stream compaction is O(N) where N is the number of blocks. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the min-max texture (O(V) where V is volume size), visibility buffer (O(W \times H)), and PVS lists (O(B) where B is number of blocks). Performance: Outperforms methods that process depth textures of previously established occluder representations, such as hierarchical occlusion maps [ZMHH97] and iterative depth warping [LKE18]. It is effective for scenes with high depth complexity. Scalability: Not scalable for extremely high polygon counts in general scenes if the fragment shader is heavy, but effective for volume rendering where the fragment shader cost is amortized or avoided by culling. Strengths: Conservative visibility determination (no false culls); efficient use of GPU rasterization hardware; reduced primitive count (2 triangles per block) improves early depth termination. Limitations: Requires precomputed min-max textures; relies on rasterization hardware which may have overhead for very small proxy geometries if not batched effectively. Raster Occlusion Culling was introduced by Kubisch and Tavenrath [KT14] as the state-of-the-art approach for efficient visibility determination in general scenes. It replaced earlier GPU-driven occlusion culling methods that relied on hardware occlusion query objects [CCG07], which required careful exploitation of spatial and temporal coherence. Follow-up works include Lee and Lee [LL20] (iterative hierarchical version) and Lee et al. [LJSL21] (fully GPU-driven hierarchical algorithm with ray traversal). The method is widely used in direct isosurface rasterization pipelines for scalar volumes. name: Occlusion Culling Granularity
head: Block-Based Occlusion Culling Granularity, Occlusion Buffer Sampling Resolution
body: Occlusion Culling Granularity defines the spatial resolution at which the visibility of voxel blocks is determined during the raster occlusion culling phase. It serves as a critical configuration parameter that balances the accuracy of the occlusion test against the computational overhead of the proxy geometry rasterization. This method sets the size of the culling regions (typically aligned with the leaf-level of a reference octree) and determines how the resulting occlusion buffer is sampled, directly influencing aliasing artifacts and shading quality. The method configures the granularity of the occlusion test by defining the dimensions of the culling blocks and the resolution of the sampling grid used to interpret the depth buffer. Inputs and Outputs Input: The spatial extent of the potentially visible region (PVR) defined by the parent culling stage; the cone aperture angle \theta for shading calculations. Output: A binary visibility mask for each culling block, determining whether the block is passed to the extraction stage. Data Structures Culling Block: A 3D region of cells. The standard configuration uses a block size of 8 \times 8 \times 8 cells. Occlusion Buffer: A 2D depth buffer generated by rasterizing proxy geometry (e.g., bounding boxes) of the potentially visible blocks. Sampling Grid: A 2D grid overlaid on the occlusion buffer to determine visibility. Tested resolutions include 2 \times 2 and 13 \times 13 samples per block. Parameters Culling Block Size: 8 \times 8 \times 8 cells. This aligns with the leaf-level granularity of the ray-marching reference implementation to ensure fair performance comparison. Extraction Block Size: 8 \times 8 \times 4 cells. Task Shader Workgroups: 2 workgroups are launched per potentially visible region to cover the 8 \times 8 \times 8 culling block, accounting for the mismatch between culling granularity (8 \times 8 \times 8) and extraction granularity (8 \times 8 \times 4). Sampling Resolution: The number of samples taken from the occlusion buffer per culling block. Values of 2 \times 2 and 13 \times 13 are used. Steps 1. Define Culling Regions: Partition the volume into regions of size 8 \times 8 \times 8 cells. 2. Launch Task Shaders: For each potentially visible region, launch two task shader workgroups. Each workgroup processes a subset of the extraction blocks (8 \times 8 \times 4) that fit within the 8 \times 8 \times 8 culling region. 3. Rasterize Proxy Geometry: Rasterize the bounding volumes of the blocks in the region to generate the occlusion buffer. 4. Sample Occlusion Buffer: Determine the visibility of the block by sampling the occlusion buffer. The resolution of this sampling grid is chosen based on the desired anti-aliasing quality. For low cone aperture angles (\theta), the occlusion extent is small, and lower resolutions (e.g., 2 \times 2) suffice. For high cone aperture angles (e.g., \theta = 85^\circ), the occlusion extent is large, and higher resolutions (e.g., 13 \times 13) are required to reduce aliasing. 5. Filter Blocks: Discard blocks determined to be fully occluded by the sampling result. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Aliasing: Using a low sampling resolution for high \theta values results in significant aliasing artifacts because the cone base covers many texels in the occlusion buffer. Granularity Mismatch: The extraction stage operates on 8 \times 8 \times 4 blocks, while culling is performed on 8 \times 8 \times 8 regions. This requires launching multiple workgroups per region to ensure all extraction blocks are processed. A configuration that aligns the culling granularity with the leaf-level of the ray-marching reference octree (8 \times 8 \times 8 cells) to ensure a fair performance comparison between the rasterization-based approach and the reference. It requires launching two task shader workgroups per region to accommodate the 8 \times 8 \times 4 extraction block size. Choose this when benchmarking against ray-marching baselines. Defines the density of samples taken from the occlusion buffer to determine block visibility. Higher resolutions (e.g., 13 \times 13 vs 2 \times 2) reduce aliasing, particularly for large cone aperture angles (\theta) where the occlusion extent covers many texels. Choose higher resolutions when visual quality is prioritized over the minimal overhead of additional samples. Time Complexity: The cost is dominated by the rasterization of proxy geometry and the sampling of the occlusion buffer. The number of task shader workgroups is fixed at 2 per region regardless of the actual number of blocks, due to the granularity mismatch. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the occlusion buffer. The sampling grid resolution affects cache efficiency but not the primary buffer size. Strengths: Aligning with the reference octree leaf level allows for direct, fair comparison with ray-marching methods. Limitations: The fixed granularity (8 \times 8 \times 8) may not be optimal for all scene densities. High sampling resolutions are necessary for high \theta values to avoid aliasing, increasing computational cost. When to use: When comparing against ray-marching baselines or when the scene structure matches the 8 \times 8 \times 8 leaf level. When not to use: When the scene has significant variation in density that does not align with the fixed block size, or when high \theta shading is required but performance is critical (low sampling resolution may be insufficient). The concept of occlusion culling granularity in this context originates from research on efficient direct isosurface rasterization of scalar volumes. The specific configuration of 8 \times 8 \times 8 culling blocks and 8 \times 8 \times 4 extraction blocks was introduced to facilitate a fair comparison with a ray-marching reference implementation. The impact of sampling resolution on aliasing in directional occlusion shading models was further detailed in subsequent work on interactive direct volume rendering. name: Volumetric Occlusion Culling via Occlusion Queries
head: Ray-based occlusion culling, Visibility detection using occlusion queries
body: A visibility detection method that determines if a voxel block is visible (not fully occluded by closer voxels) by rasterizing its bounding box and checking for fragment depth test passes. It differs from standard binary occlusion culling by incorporating accumulated opacity into the depth test, ensuring that blocks behind fully opaque foreground volumes are correctly culled. Inputs and Outputs Input: A voxel block to test, defined by its axis-aligned bounding box; the current ray-marched depth buffer containing the depth at which maximum opacity was reached for each pixel; camera projection and view matrices. Output: A boolean visibility flag for the block, or a fragment count used for priority-based loading. Data Structures Depth Buffer: A 2D render target storing floating-point depth values. Each pixel (u, v) stores D{opacity}, the depth along the view ray where accumulated opacity reached a threshold (typically 1.0), or 1.0 (maximum depth) if the ray did not reach full opacity. Bounding Box Geometry: A triangulated mesh representing the axis-aligned bounding box of the voxel block. Steps 1. Prepare Depth Buffer: During the ray marching pass, for each ray, write the depth D{opacity} at which the ray reaches total opacity to the framebuffer. If the ray does not reach total opacity within the volume, write the maximum depth value (e.g., 1.0 in normalized device coordinates or the far plane distance). 2. Initialize Occlusion Query: Begin an asynchronous GPU occlusion query. 3. Rasterize Bounding Box: Rasterize the triangulated bounding box of the voxel block without performing actual ray tracing. 4. Depth Test: For each fragment generated by the bounding box, compare its depth against the prepared depth buffer. 5. Interrogate Result: Check if the occlusion query is complete. If the test has not finished, the CPU thread synchronizes and waits for the GPU to finish the rasterization and query execution. 6. Determine Visibility: Retrieve the number of fragments that passed the depth test. If the count meets or exceeds the configured fragment threshold, the block is considered visible and scheduled for loading. Formulas Let D{opacity} be the depth value stored in the framebuffer for a given pixel, representing the depth at which the ray reached total opacity. Let D{voxel} be the depth of the fragment generated by the voxel block's bounding box at that pixel. The visibility condition for a specific ray/pixel is: D{voxel} > D{opacity} If D{voxel} \le D{opacity}, the voxel is occluded by foreground matter that has already reached full opacity. If D{voxel} > D{opacity}, the voxel is visible. For the entire block, the block is visible if: \text{fragment\count} \ge \text{FragmentThreshold} Parameters Fragment Threshold: The minimum number of fragments required to trigger block loading. This value can be adjusted based on system load to prioritize the most visible blocks. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Projection Alignment: Requires perfect alignment between the OpenGL projection/viewpoint and the ray tracing projection/viewpoint to ensure correct visibility detection. Asynchronicity and Scheduling: Occlusion queries are executed asynchronously by the GPU, allowing the CPU to continue immediately after initialization. The visibility test must be anticipated before tracing, but too much anticipation ignores unrendered foreground matter that might occlude the block. Scheduling must overlap query times with loading times of already detected visible blocks to hide latency. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently culls blocks behind fully opaque volumes using standard GPU hardware occlusion queries. Limitations: Sensitive to projection mismatches. Requires careful scheduling to handle asynchronous query results and avoid stalling the CPU. This method is described in the context of interactive exploration of extended and detailed procedural volumes. It adapts standard hardware occlusion queries to the specific requirements of volumetric rendering, where visibility depends on accumulated opacity rather than simple geometric occlusion. name: Potentially Visible Hidden Volume (PVHV)
head: Linear Novel View PVHV Definition
body: Potentially Visible Hidden Volumes (PVHVs) are 3D volumes that are occluded at a known source view but potentially visible at novel views. They solve the problem of redundant fragment capture in multi-view image warping by allowing batch-testing of source fragment visibilities without iterating individual novel views. Unlike classical occlusion culling or Potential Visible Sets (PVS) which rely on the shapes or bounding volumes of occluders, PVHVs utilize edge-based geometric analysis of foreground fragments, making the visibility determination simpler and more efficient. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Source view s, a set of novel views N bounded by a distance E from s, the farthest view n \in N, depth texture Z from previous rendering layers, and a fragment p to test. Outputs: Boolean indicating if fragment p is inside the PVHV Hs(N), requiring capture for warping. Data Structures: Fragment: A 3D point p = (px, py, pz) in world or view space, with depth pz. Blocker: A foreground fragment f with depth fz. Outer Blocker: An adjacent farther fragment g with depth gz. Formulas and Definitions: The scene volume W is decomposed into visible volume Vs and hidden occlusion volume Os for source view s. The PVHV for a specific novel view n is defined as: Hs(n):= Os \cap Vn Objects in Hs(n) are unavailable in the foreground rendered for s but require capture for n. Redundancy (fragments invisible from both s and n) is found at Os - Hs(n). For a set of novel views N spanning distance E from s, let n be the farthest view in N. The PVHV Hs(N) encompassing all views in N is defined by the following conditions for a point p \in W: 1. Depth: pz > fz (the fragment is behind the inner blocker f). 2. Radial Bound: |p - p'| < R(p, f), where R(p, f) is the radius of the Local COC (LCOC) determined by the distance to the blocker. 3. Side Bound: (p - p') \cdot (n - s) < 0, ensuring p is on the correct side of the edge ray e(s, f) to exclude fragments on the left, ensuring f is the inner occluder. Here, p' is the projection of p onto the line segment connecting s and n, or specifically the point on the edge ray e(s, f) closest to p in the context of the 2D triangle definition for linear views. The edge rays are e(s, f) emanating from s through f, and e(n, f) emanating from n through f. Parameters: E: The distance spanned by the set of novel views N from the source view s. It acts as the scaling factor for the LCOC radius. n: The farthest view in the set of novel views N. Used to define the direction vector n-s and the edge ray e(n, f). Algorithm Steps (Effective Depth Peeling with PVHV): 1. Render the scene to obtain depth texture Z for the current layer. 2. For each fragment p in the current layer: a. Identify the inner blocker fragment f such that fz < pz and f occludes p from s. b. Check if p is inside the PVHV Hs(N) using the conditions above. c. If p \in Hs(N), mark p for capture in multi-fragment rendering. d. If p \notin Hs(N), it is completely hidden from all novel views in N and can be culled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isinpvhp(p, f, n, s, E): """ Check if fragment p is in the Potentially Visible Hidden Volume defined by inner blocker f, source view s, and farthest novel view n. """ # Condition 1: Depth must be behind the blocker if p.z <= f.z: return False # Condition 2: Radial bound (LCOC radius) # R(p, f) is derived from the distance and E. # The source defines |p - p'| < R(p, f). # Assuming p' is the projection on the edge ray e(s,f) or similar geometric construct. # For implementation, this is often approximated or computed via the specific LCOC radius formula. # Here we assume a function computelcocradius exists which uses E and geometry. radius = computelcocradius(p, f, E) distancetoedge = computedistancetoedgeray(p, s, f) if distancetoedge >= radius: return False # Condition 3: Side bound (dot product) # (p - p'). (n - s) < 0 # p' is the point on the edge ray e(s,f) corresponding to p's depth or projection. # In the 2D linear case, this ensures p is to the right of e(s,f) relative to n-s. # We assume a helper to get the vector from the edge ray to p at the same depth. vectortoedge = computevectortoedgeray(p, s, f) viewdisplacement = n - s if dot(vectortoedge, viewdisplacement) >= 0: return False return True def effectivedepthpeeling(Z, s, n, E): """ Process fragments to determine which need capture for novel views N. """ capturedfragments = [] for p in fragmentsfromdepthtexture(Z): f = findinnerblocker(p, Z) if f is not None: if isinpvhp(p, f, n, s, E): capturedfragments.append(p) else: # Cull p as it is hidden from all novel views in N pass else: # p is visible from source, always capture capturedfragments.append(p) return capturedfragments Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The condition (p - p') \cdot (n - s) < 0 is critical to ensure f is the inner occluder; failing this may include fragments on the left side of the edge ray e(s, f) which are not potentially visible. For linear views, the PVHV is a 2D triangle. For areal views, it is a 3D volume. The method assumes fragments have a square shape for the edge ray definition. For circular areal views (e.g., Depth of Field rendering), the PVHV is modeled as a revolution of the 2D linear PVHV triangle, forming a cone. The implementation uses the same 2D equation but defines n as the farthest view along the projection of f-s onto the novel view plane. To handle the full circular view efficiently, the algorithm throws circular samples around the blocker q, which is equivalent to revolving the line search bound, forming a fully circular cone that concatenates two half-cone PVHVs. This avoids test redundancy for all rotational variations. For point novel views, the exact PVHV is a truncated variant of the linear PVHV, cut by an additional edge e(n, g) where g is the outer blocker. However, computing the exact shape requires finding both f and g, adding complexity. The method approximates this by using the larger linear PVHV volume to conservatively include the point view PVHV. This merging scheme is similar to occluder fusion or virtual occluders in PVS. Time Complexity: The method allows batch-testing visibilities without iterating individual novel views, reducing the complexity from O(N \times F) to O(F) where N is the number of novel views and F is the number of fragments. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth textures and fragment data. No additional large geometric structures are needed compared to bounding volume approaches. Strengths: Simpler and more efficient than classical occlusion culling as it requires less occluder information (only fragment edges). Reduces warping cost by culling redundant fragments prior to warping. Limitations: Requires a coarse yet conservative bound of potential view displacements rather than individual novel views. Clipping by view frusta is not strictly necessary as fragments outside can be ignored during warping, but the PVHV definition itself does not inherently clip to frusta. When to use: Multi-view image warping where a bound of novel views is known. When not to use: When precise visibility for individual, widely dispersed novel views is required without a bounding envelope, or when occluder shapes are complex and fragment edges are insufficient. PVHVs were introduced by Janghun Kim and Sungkil Lee in the paper "Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume Rendering for Multi-View Warping" (2023). The approach is similar to shadow volumes in terms of using 3D volumes to determine visibilities. It was realized in Depth Peeling (DP) as Effective Depth Peeling (EDP) to reduce the number of completely hidden fragments and capture important fragments early. name: Hierarchical Raster Occlusion Culling
head: Lee et al. hierarchical raster occlusion culling
body: Hierarchical Raster Occlusion Culling is a fully GPU-driven technique that reduces rasterization overhead by performing rasterization on a coarser level for group nodes, and refining visibility results through ray traversal down to the leaf level. It builds on Raster Occlusion Culling by applying spatial coherence exploitation through hierarchical grouping of objects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Hierarchical spatial structure of voxel blocks and camera parameters. Output: Dense list of visible leaf-level blocks for rendering. Data Structures: Hierarchy Tree: Nodes are organized in levels, with group nodes representing aggregated bounding volumes of their children and leaf nodes representing individual voxel blocks. Proxy Geometry: Each node has an associated proxy geometry (typically an axis-aligned bounding box) used for rasterization. Steps: 1. Coarse Rasterization: Rasterize the proxy geometry of group nodes at a higher level of the hierarchy to determine which coarse regions potentially contain visible geometry. 2. Ray Traversal Refinement: For regions identified as potentially visible in the coarse pass, perform ray traversal down the hierarchy tree by casting rays from the camera through the coarse visible regions to intersect child nodes. 3. Leaf Visibility Determination: Continue traversal until leaf nodes are reached, marking a leaf block visible if the ray traversal confirms it is not occluded. 4. Stream Compaction: Collect the indices of all visible leaf blocks into a dense list for rendering. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Hierarchy Depth: The number of levels to rasterize coarsely. Not given in the sources. Ray Count: Number of rays per coarse region. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ray-triangle intersection precision at leaf levels may cause flickering if not handled with epsilon offsets. Degenerate Input: Empty regions in the hierarchy should be skipped during traversal to avoid unnecessary ray casting. An iterative version of raster occlusion culling that works on a select number of hierarchy levels, applying spatial coherence exploitation through hierarchical grouping of objects. Time Complexity: Reduced compared to full leaf rasterization, as only coarse nodes are rasterized initially. Exact complexity depends on hierarchy depth and ray traversal cost. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the hierarchy tree and proxy geometries. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significantly reduces rasterization overhead by avoiding per-leaf rasterization and exploits spatial coherence. Limitations: Ray traversal adds computational overhead. Not given in the sources. When to use: Large-scale volume rendering with high block counts where rasterization is the bottleneck. Not given in the sources. When not to use: Scenes with very few blocks or where ray traversal overhead exceeds rasterization savings. Not given in the sources. The concept of hierarchical grouping for occlusion culling was introduced by Martin et al. [MBW08]. Lee and Lee [LL20] proposed an iterative version of raster occlusion culling. Lee et al. [LJSL21] introduced the fully GPU-driven hierarchical raster occlusion culling algorithm, aiming to reduce overall rasterization overhead by combining coarse rasterization with ray traversal refinement. name: Cluster Visibility Buffer Culling
head: Cluster Culling, Cluster Visibility Buffer, Visibility Buffer Culling, Visibility Culling via Visibility Buffer
body: Cluster Visibility Buffer Culling is a technique to prune non-visible voxel clusters by storing visibility bits per cluster, avoiding full cell rasterization for occluded or back-facing groups. It differs from hierarchical Z-buffer approaches by using a visibility buffer texture updated via compute shaders and splatting, eliminating the need for pre-computed cluster bounds or normal cones. Inputs: Active grid cells extracted from voxel data, grouped into clusters. Cluster bounding boxes stored in the last metacell of each cluster. Previous frame's visibility buffer state. Outputs: A list of visible clusters for full cell rasterization. Updated visibility buffer indicating current frame's visible clusters. Data Structures: Cluster Bound: Stored in the last metacell of each cluster. It is an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Visibility Buffer: An RG32UI texture (two 32-bit unsigned integer channels). One channel typically stores the visibility bit or cluster ID, and the other may store auxiliary data or be unused depending on implementation specifics. ID Texture: Generated during cell rasterization to capture cluster IDs of visible cells. Steps: 1. Preparation: During CPU-side isosurface extraction, divide volume data into blocks (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16) and extract active grid cells in Morton order. Pad the last cluster of each block with empty metacells to ensure its size becomes 16, preventing spillover into different volume blocks. Store the cluster bound (AABB) in the last metacell of each cluster instead of cell metadata. Upload extracted metacells and grid cells to GPU buffer textures. 2. Initial Rasterization: Perform cell rasterization for all clusters. During this pass, render cells as billboards/splats. For each fragment, perform a ray-box intersection test with the cell. 3. Capture Visibility: Use an RG32UI texture as a visibility buffer to capture cluster IDs of visible cells during the cell rasterization pass. 4. Clear and Update: After cell rasterization, clear the current visibility buffer bits. Update the visibility buffer from the ID texture in a separate compute shader pass. 5. Splatting for Non-Visible Clusters: Render cells of non-visible clusters as single pixel splats to update the visibility buffer, similar to disk-based deferred splatting. This step identifies clusters that have become visible since the last frame. 6. Second Pass for New Visibility: Introduce a second visibility buffer to record new clusters becoming visible. Perform full cell rasterization for these newly visible clusters in a second pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clustervisibilityculling(clusters, previousvisibilitybuffer, camera): """ clusters: List of cluster objects, each containing: cells: List of active grid cells bound: AABB stored in last metacell id: Unique cluster identifier previousvisibilitybuffer: RG32UI texture from previous frame camera: Current camera state """ # Step 1: Initial Rasterization Pass # Render all cells. Capture cluster IDs of visible cells into an ID texture. idtexture = rendercells(clusters, camera) # Step 2: Clear Visibility Buffer cleartexture(previousvisibilitybuffer) # Step 3: Update Visibility Buffer from ID Texture # Use a compute shader to aggregate cluster IDs from the ID texture # into the visibility buffer. updatevisibilitybuffercompute(idtexture, previousvisibilitybuffer) # Step 4: Identify Non-Visible Clusters # Clusters not present in the updated visibility buffer are considered non-visible # for the current frame, except for those that might have just become visible. nonvisibleclusters = getclustersnotinbuffer(clusters, previousvisibilitybuffer) # Step 5: Splatting for Non-Visible Clusters # Render cells of non-visible clusters as single pixel splats # to detect if they have become visible. newvisibilitybuffer = rendersplats(nonvisibleclusters, camera) # Step 6: Merge Visibility States # Combine previous and new visibility states finalvisibilitybuffer = mergevisibilitybuffers(previousvisibilitybuffer, newvisibilitybuffer) # Step 7: Second Pass for Newly Visible Clusters # Identify clusters that are newly visible newlyvisibleclusters = getnewlyvisibleclusters(finalvisibilitybuffer, previousvisibilitybuffer) # Perform full cell rasterization for newly visible clusters rendercells(newlyvisibleclusters, camera) return finalvisibilitybuffer def updatevisibilitybuffercompute(idtexture, visibilitybuffer): """ Compute shader to update visibility buffer based on ID texture. """ # For each pixel in idtexture: # clusterid = idtexture.read(pixelcoord).r # if clusterid != 0: # visibilitybuffer.atomicor(clusterid, 1) pass def rendersplats(clusters, camera): """ Render clusters as single pixel splats. """ # For each cluster in clusters: # if isbackfacing(cluster, camera): # continue # if isoccluded(cluster, camera): # continue # rendersinglepixelsplat(cluster, camera) pass Parameters: Cluster Size: Up to 120 active grid cells per cluster. Block Size: 16 \times 16 \times 16 voxels per block. Metacells per Cluster: 16 metacells per cluster segment. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flickering Artifacts: During fast camera movements, non-visible clusters becoming visible may cause flickering artifacts. This is mitigated by using a second visibility buffer to record new clusters becoming visible and performing full cell rasterization for them in a second pass. However, some flickering may still occur. Back-Face Culling: Back-face culling is performed using normals computed in the tessellation shader from corner values. Conservative Culling: The visibility culling is not conservative but avoids generating a hierarchical Z-buffer or storing cluster bounds/normal cones. A technique to generate a depth and visibility buffer for voxel clusters by rasterizing cluster bounding boxes and ray tracing the internal 8^3 grid to determine voxel occupancy, storing results in a 64-bit integer format. It rasterizes the bounding box (rotated, translated cube) of each cluster using instancing and a simple vertex/fragment shader setup. In the vertex shader, each cluster is transformed using its relative index inside the respective object and the object's world transform. In the fragment shader, the 8^3 grid of the cluster is ray-traced using the Amanatides et al. (1987) voxel traversal algorithm. If a hit is detected, a 64-bit unsigned integer is composed containing: 24 bits for depth, 31 bits for the cluster index, and 9 bits for the voxel index. The 64-bit unsigned integer stored in the visibility buffer has the following bit layout: bits 0-23 (24 bits) for depth, bits 24-54 (31 bits) for cluster index, bits 55-63 (9 bits) for voxel index. Cluster grid size is 8^3 voxels per cluster. Voxel index bit width is 9 bits, allowing indexing of up to 512 voxels (8^3). Cluster index bit width is 31 bits, allowing indexing of over 2 billion clusters. Depth bit width is 24 bits. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of clusters and cells. Initial rasterization is O(N{cells}), visibility buffer update is O(N{visible\cells}), and splatting is O(N{non\visible\clusters}). Memory Complexity: O(N{clusters}) for visibility buffer storage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of clusters and cells. Performance may degrade with fast camera movements due to flickering artifacts. Strengths: Avoids hierarchical Z-buffer generation and storage of cluster bounds/normal cones. Efficiently prunes non-visible clusters. Limitations: Not conservative culling. Potential flickering artifacts during fast camera movements. When to Use: Suitable for real-time isosurface rendering where performance is critical and conservative culling is not required. When Not to Use: Not suitable when conservative culling is necessary or when flickering artifacts are unacceptable. Originated from the paper "Clustered Grid Cell Data Structure for Isosurface Rendering". The method builds on deferred splatting techniques. It is used in real-time isosurface rendering and hybrid ray tracing applications. name: PVS Compactification and Temporal Coherence Pass
head: PVS Compactification, PVS Compactification and Output Pass, PVS Data Construction, Temporal PVS Generation
body: This compute shader pass compactifies the raw visibility indices generated by the preceding raster occlusion culling stage and constructs two distinct Potentially Visible Set (PVS) datasets: PVS{curr} and PVS{curr-prev}. It solves the problem of efficiently preparing visibility data for temporal coherence by identifying blocks visible in the current frame and those newly visible since the last frame, enabling the selection of optimal occluders for subsequent rendering passes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A visibility buffer containing raw block indices written by the fragment shader stage of the raster occlusion culling pass. Each fragment passing the early depth test and representative fragment test writes its block's implicit ID into a preallocated slot. Outputs: PVS{curr}: A compacted list of block indices visible in the current frame, used in the next frame for temporal coherence-based occluder selection. PVS{curr-prev}: A list of blocks that became visible since the last frame, used to determine new visibility events. Data Structures: The sources do not specify the exact memory layout (e.g., struct of arrays vs. array of structs) or bit-packing details for the PVS datasets. The visibility buffer is described as having "preallocated slots". Steps: 1. Bit Compactification: Execute a bit compactification kernel on the raw indices in the visibility buffer to produce the current frame's potentially visible set, denoted as PVS{curr}. 2. Temporal Data Construction: Execute a single compute shader pass to generate both PVS{curr} and PVS{curr-prev}. This pass compares the current visibility state with the previous frame's data to identify newly visible blocks. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pvscompactificationandtemporalcoherencepass(visibilitybuffer, prevpvs): # Step 1: Bit Compactification # Compact the sparse visibility buffer into a dense list of current visible blocks # The exact bit-packing and compactification algorithm is not given in the sources. pvscurr = [blockid for blockid in visibilitybuffer if blockid is not None] # Step 2: Temporal Coherence Data Construction # Identify blocks in pvscurr that were not in prevpvs pvscurrprev = [blockid for blockid in pvscurr if blockid not in set(prevpvs)] return pvscurr, pvscurrprev Parameters: Shader Type: Compute shaders are used instead of mesh shaders. Block Size: Larger block sizes can be launched for this pass compared to mesh shaders, allowing better utilization of streaming multiprocessors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-view Rendering: When using multi-view rendering features to rasterize proxy geometry per-eye in a joint pass, one quad must be generated per eye. Occlusion Geometry: If a block lies between the viewer's eyes along any of the three cardinal axes, more than 3 sides of the block may need to be rendered to ensure correct occlusion culling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The use of compute shaders allows for larger block sizes and better utilization of streaming multiprocessors compared to mesh shaders. Strengths: Combines compactification and temporal data construction into a single pass, reducing kernel launch overhead. Limitations: Requires careful handling in stereo/multi-view rendering scenarios due to potential multi-sided visibility requirements. This method is part of the "Lightweight Raster Occlusion Culling" technique for efficient direct isosurface rasterization of scalar volumes. It builds on the reference implementation of Kubisch [Kub14] but improves upon it by generating both PVS{curr} and PVS{curr-prev} in a single compute shader pass, whereas the reference implementation likely used separate passes. The technique is implemented in both mono and stereo modes. name: GPU-driven Visibility Culling
head: Indirect draw culling, Per-subchunk culling
body: GPU-driven visibility culling is a culling technique that uses per-subchunk metadata (AABBs, terrain/water draw ranges) to test visibility on the GPU and emit indirect draw commands only for visible subchunks. It reduces the number of task shader workgroups launched by avoiding geometry extraction for blocks not visible in the display. It builds on Task Shader Block-wise Stream Compaction by utilizing the metadata prepared there to drive the compute dispatch and indirect execution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A buffer containing per-subchunk metadata, specifically Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) and draw ranges for terrain and water elements. Output: A buffer of indirect draw commands corresponding only to subchunks that pass the visibility test. Data Structures: Subchunk Metadata Buffer: Contains AABBs (typically 6 floats: min/max x, y, z) and draw range information. Indirect Draw Command Buffer: Stores the arguments for indirect draw calls. Each entry typically contains: vertexcount (uint32), instancecount (uint32), firstvertex (uint32), firstinstance (uint32). Steps: 1. Visibility Test: Test the AABB of each subchunk against the view frustum or camera position. 2. Emit Commands: Emit indirect draw commands only for subchunks that pass the visibility test. 3. Dispatch: Execute the draw calls using the indirect command buffer. Parameters: MULTIDRAWINDIRECTCOUNT: A GPU feature that allows the GPU to control how many indirect draw commands are executed, enabling dynamic draw counts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cullsubchunks(subchunkdata, frustumplanes, camerapos, outputcommands, commandcount): """ Compute shader equivalent: filters subchunks based on frustum/camera visibility and writes indirect draw commands to the output buffer. commandcount is a mutable list acting as a shared counter across threads. """ for i in range(len(subchunkdata)): aabbmin = subchunkdata[i].aabbmin aabbmax = subchunkdata[i].aabbmax drawoffset = subchunkdata[i].drawoffset drawcount = subchunkdata[i].drawcount if isaabbvisible(aabbmin, aabbmax, frustumplanes, camerapos): cmdidx = commandcount[0] commandcount[0] += 1 outputcommands[cmdidx] = { 'vertexcount': drawcount, 'instancecount': 1, 'firstvertex': drawoffset, 'firstinstance': 0 } def isaabbvisible(aabbmin, aabbmax, frustumplanes, camerapos): """ Checks if an AABB is inside the view frustum or in front of the camera. Uses standard half-space tests for frustum planes and a simple depth check. """ # Check against each frustum plane (left, right, bottom, top, far) for plane in frustumplanes: # Plane equation: Ax + By + Cz + D <= 0 for inside # Quick rejection: if both min and max corners are outside (positive), AABB is outside valmin = plane.a aabbmin[0] + plane.b aabbmin[1] + plane.c aabbmin[2] + plane.d valmax = plane.a aabbmax[0] + plane.b aabbmax[1] + plane.c aabbmax[2] + plane.d if valmin > 0 and valmax > 0: return False # Check if AABB is behind the camera (near plane or camera position check) if aabbmax[2] < camerapos[2]: return False return True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure AABB coordinates are in the same coordinate space as the view frustum. Boundary Conditions: Handle subchunks exactly on the frustum boundary correctly to avoid flickering or missing geometry. Degenerate Input: Handle subchunks with zero volume or invalid AABBs gracefully. A rendering optimization that uses a compute shader to filter visible chunks and generates indirect draw arguments on the GPU, reducing CPU-GPU synchronization overhead. It differs from CPU-side culling by offloading the visibility test and command buffer population to the GPU, allowing the CPU to remain free for scene management and chunk loading. It builds on GPU-driven Visibility Culling by utilizing the metadata prepared there to drive the compute dispatch and indirect execution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces CPU-GPU synchronization overhead, allows CPU to remain free for other tasks, dynamic draw counts. Limitations: Requires GPU support for indirect drawing and MULTIDRAWINDIRECTCOUNT. name: GPU-Based Chunk Culling via Indirect Commands
head: Compute Shader Culling, Compute Shader Frustum Culling with Indirect Draw, Frustum culling in compute shader, GPU frustum culling, GPU-side Frustum Culling, Indirect Draw Culling, Indirect Rendering Culling
body: A rendering optimization that uses a compute shader to filter visible chunks and generates indirect draw arguments on the GPU, reducing CPU-GPU synchronization overhead. It differs from CPU-side culling by moving the visibility test and command buffer population entirely to the GPU, and from general GPU-driven visibility culling by specifically targeting chunk-based mesh data and using atomic counters to compact the output command list. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of chunk mesh data (bounding boxes, geometry references) and camera frustum parameters (position, plane normals/distances). Output: An indirect draw command buffer containing draw calls only for visible chunks. Data Structures: 1. IndirectCommand (CPU-side preparation, D3D12 style): renderresources: Struct containing sceneconstantbufferindex and chunkconstantbufferindex. indexbufferview: D3D12INDEXBUFFERVIEW. drawarguments: D3D12DRAWINDEXEDARGUMENTS struct with fields: IndexCountPerInstance (uint) InstanceCount (uint) StartIndexLocation (uint) BaseVertexLocation (int) StartInstanceLocation (uint) 2. MeshData (GPU-side input, GLSL std430): center: vec3 (mesh center position). data1: uint (packed: bits 0-2 are normalID, bits 3-31 are squaresCount). size: vec3 (bounding box half-extents or size). data2: uint (packed: startSquare offset). 3. GPUCullRenderResources (CPU-side constants, D3D12 style): numberofchunks: u32. indirectcommandsrvindex: u32. outputcommanduavindex: u32. sceneconstantbufferindex: u32. 4. IndirectDrawArgs (GPU-side output, GLSL std430): count: uint. instanceCount: uint. first: uint. baseInstance: uint. 5. Uniforms (Camera data): position: vec3. farPlane, leftPlane, rightPlane, upPlane, downPlane: vec4 (xyz = plane normal, w = distance). Numbered Steps: 1. CPU Preparation: Iterate through loaded chunks and populate a vector of IndirectCommand structs. Set root constants (D3D12) or uniforms (OpenGL) with GPUCullRenderResources and camera frustum planes. Copy CPU data to the indirect command buffer's upload resource. 2. GPU Culling Dispatch: Reset the UAV counter buffer to zero. Transition the indirect command buffer state: COPYDEST -> UNORDEREDACCESS. Dispatch the compute shader. Workgroup count is ceil(meshData.size() / threadGroupSize). One workgroup per mesh is typical. 3. Compute Shader Execution: Read MeshData from the readonly buffer. Reconstruct the normal vector from data1: normalID = data1 & 7u (mask 3 bits). Axis index: normalID >> 1. Sign: normalID & 1u. Normal vector: axis (-2 float(normalID & 1u) + 1). Test visibility against the camera frustum: Check if the mesh is behind the camera relative to its normal: dot(center - normal size - position, normal) > 0. If true, discard. Check if the bounding box is outside any frustum plane (far, left, right, up, down) using outsidePlane. If visible: Atomically increment the command counter. Write the IndirectDrawArgs (or equivalent draw arguments) to the output buffer at the returned index. 4. Execution: Transition the indirect command buffer state: UNORDEREDACCESS -> INDIRECTARGUMENT. Issue a memory barrier for indirect commands. Execute indirect draw using the counter offset to determine the number of commands. Pseudocode (Compute Shader Logic): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. kernel void cullmeshes(uint3 meshid) { uint index = meshid.x; MeshData mesh = meshDataBuffer[index]; // Reconstruct normal uint normalID = mesh.data1 & 7u; uint axisIdx = normalID >> 1; int sign = -2 int(normalID & 1u) + 1; vec3 normal = vec3(0.0); if (axisIdx == 0) normal.x = float(sign); else if (axisIdx == 1) normal.y = float(sign); else normal.z = float(sign); // Check if facing away from camera vec3 centerToPos = mesh.center - frustumPosition; if (dot(centerToPos, normal) > dot(mesh.size, normal)) { // Simplified backface check based on source return; } // Frustum culling if (outsidePlane(mesh.center, mesh.size, farPlane)) return; if (outsidePlane(mesh.center, mesh.size, leftPlane)) return; if (outsidePlane(mesh.center, mesh.size, rightPlane)) return; if (outsidePlane(mesh.center, mesh.size, upPlane)) return; if (outsidePlane(mesh.center, mesh.size, downPlane)) return; // Write command uint cmdIndex = atomicAdd(commandsCount, 1u); commandsBuffer[cmdIndex] = IndirectDrawArgs( mesh.data1 & 0x1FFFFFFFu, // squaresCount as count 1u, mesh.data2, // startSquare as first 0u); } bool outsidePlane(vec3 center, vec3 size, vec4 plane) { vec3 normalSign = sign(plane.xyz); vec3 closestPoint = center + size normalSign; return dot(closestPoint, plane.xyz) + plane.w < 0.0; } Parameters: MAXCHUNKSTOBEDRAWN: Maximum number of indirect draw calls per frame. Used as the second argument to ExecuteIndirect. threadGroupSize: Typically 32 or 64, depending on hardware and implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resource State Transitions: Must strictly follow API rules (e.g., D3D12: INDIRECTARGUMENT -> COPYDEST -> UNORDEREDACCESS -> INDIRECTARGUMENT). Missing transitions cause validation errors or undefined behavior. Normal Reconstruction: Assumes normalID >> 1 maps to axis index (0=x, 1=y, 2=z) and normalID & 1 maps to sign. Backface Culling: The logic dot(center - normal size - position, normal) > 0 ignores meshes whose normal points away from the camera position relative to the mesh center. Time Complexity: O(N) for culling, where N is the number of chunks. The compute shader dispatch is parallelized. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the indirect command buffer and mesh data. Performance: Reduces CPU-GPU synchronization overhead by eliminating CPU-side frustum culling and command buffer population. Strengths: Efficient for large scenes with many chunks; minimal CPU intervention. Limitations: Requires GPU support for indirect drawing and compute shaders; overhead of buffer management and state transitions. When to use: Large voxel terrains or chunk-based scenes where culling is a bottleneck. When not to use: Small scenes where CPU culling is sufficient; hardware without indirect draw support. Originating from implementations in voxel engines and terrain renderers, this technique leverages modern GPU capabilities (compute shaders, indirect drawing) to optimize rendering. name: Mesh Shader: Transient Isosurface Extraction
head: Direct Isosurface Rendering, Direct Isosurface Visualization, Efficient Direct Isosurface Rasterization, Mesh Shader Isosurface Extraction, Task and Mesh Shader Isosurface Extraction, Transient Isosurface Extraction, Transient Isosurface Extraction and Rendering, Transient Isosurface Extraction and Rendering of PVS
body: Transient isosurface extraction is a rasterization-based method that extracts isosurface geometry "on the fly" using task and mesh shader pipelines, passing primitives directly to the rasterizer without intermediate explicit mesh storage. It solves the high memory bandwidth and storage costs of indirect methods (like standard Marching Cubes) and the resolution-dependent performance penalties of ray marching. Unlike its parent method, Task Shader Cell Classification, which only classifies cells and emits workgroups, this method performs the actual geometry extraction and projection within the mesh shader stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dense scalar volume, a min-max grid (2-channel volume texture storing min/max values per block), and a Potentially Visible Set (PVS) of block indices. Output: Triangle primitives passed directly to the rasterizer. Data Structures: The method processes volume blocks of size U \times V \times W cells. The standard setting is U=8, V=8, W=4, totaling 256 cells per block, allowing 8-bit indexing. The memory interface block between the task shader and mesh shader is defined as: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Task { uint32t baseID; uint8t denseoccupancyindex[256]; uint8t occupiedcelllistoffset[32]; uint8t occupiedlistlength[32]; } INTERFACETASKMESHEXTRACTANDDRAW; baseID: 32-bit index of the block. denseoccupancyindex: Compact list of occupied cell indices within the block. occupiedcelllistoffset: Start offset for each mesh shader workgroup's cell list. occupiedlistlength: Length of each mesh shader workgroup's cell list. Parameters: Workgroup Size: 32 threads for both task and mesh shaders. Vertex Limit: Maximum 96 vertices per mesh shader workgroup. Min Cells per Workgroup: 8 cells (ensures 8 \times 12 vertices \le 96, assuming max 12 vertices per cell). Max Lists per Block: 32 (calculated as 256 / 8). Steps: 1. Task Shader: Cell Classification and Vertex Count Generation. The task shader workgroup (32 threads) processes a block of 256 cells. Each thread handles multiple cells. Threads sample voxels to determine the state of their assigned cells using the Marching Cubes (MC) algorithm. Threads store occupancy flags and write the vertex count (not the geometry) for each cell into a shared memory buffer. The MC algorithm stops after determining the per-cell vertex count to minimize interface block memory usage. 2. Task Shader: Stream Compaction and Task Generation. Reduction: An intra-warp reduction determines the offset of each occupied cell in the denseoccupancyindex buffer. Expensive atomic operations are omitted; offsets are shared via subgroupBroadcast operations. List Division: A single thread traverses the denseoccupancyindex buffer. It accumulates vertex counts to build lists for mesh shader workgroups. A list ends when it contains 32 cells OR the accumulated vertex count would exceed 96. Buffer Update: The start offset and length for each list are stored in occupiedcelllistoffset and occupiedlistlength. Task Count: One thread writes the total number of mesh shader workgroups to glTaskCountNV. 3. Mesh Shader: Lookup. Each mesh shader workgroup (32 threads) uses glWorkGroupID to look up the start offset and length of its specific cell list from the interface buffers. 4. Mesh Shader: Extraction and Projection. Each active thread determines its cell ID and location. The thread performs the full MC algorithm to extract vertices and indices representing the isosurface. Intra-warp Reduction: An efficient intra-warp reduction determines the write offsets for each thread to write indices and projected vertices into output arrays. Projection: Generated vertices are evenly distributed across the warp and projected cooperatively by all threads. Primitive Count: One designated thread writes the total primitive count produced by the workgroup. The primitives are passed directly to the rasterizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def taskshaderworkgroup(blockid, volume, minmaxgrid): denseoccupancyindex = [255] 256 sharedvertexcounts = [0] 256 # 1. Cell Classification and Vertex Count Generation # Each thread handles 8 cells (256 / 32) for locali in range(8): cellidx = threadid + locali 32 # Standard MC lookup to determine occupancy and vertex count # Task shader stops after vertex count state = getmcstate(cellidx, volume) if state != EMPTY: denseoccupancyindex[cellidx] = cellidx sharedvertexcounts[cellidx] = getmcvertexcount(state) # 2. Stream Compaction (Intra-warp Reduction) # Compute prefix sum of occupied cells to get offsets occupiedoffsets = [0] 256 count = 0 for i in range(256): if denseoccupancyindex[i] != 255: occupiedoffsets[i] = count count += 1 # 3. List Division (Thread 0) if threadid == 0: occupiedcelllistoffset = [0] 32 occupiedlistlength = [0] 32 listcount = 0 currentoffset = 0 currentvertexsum = 0 currentcellcount = 0 for i in range(256): if denseoccupancyindex[i] != 255: v = sharedvertexcounts[i] if currentcellcount == 32 or currentvertexsum + v > 96: occupiedcelllistoffset[listcount] = currentoffset occupiedlistlength[listcount] = currentcellcount listcount += 1 currentoffset = i currentvertexsum = 0 currentcellcount = 0 currentvertexsum += v currentcellcount += 1 if currentcellcount > 0: occupiedcelllistoffset[listcount] = currentoffset occupiedlistlength[listcount] = currentcellcount listcount += 1 glTaskCountNV = listcount def meshshaderworkgroup(workgroupid, interfaceblock): # 1. Lookup offset = interfaceblock.occupiedcelllistoffset[workgroupid] length = interfaceblock.occupiedlistlength[workgroupid] # 2. Extraction and Projection # Each thread processes one cell cellidx = interfaceblock.denseoccupancyindex[offset + threadid] # Standard MC extraction for vertices and indices vertices, indices = extractmcgeometry(cellidx) projectedvertices = projectvertices(vertices) # Intra-warp reduction for write offsets writeoffsets = [0] 32 count = 0 for i in range(32): if i < length: writeoffsets[i] = count count += 1 # Write output writeoutput(writeoffsets[threadid], projectedvertices, indices) # 3. Primitive Count if threadid == 0: writeprimitivecount(totalprimitivesgenerated) A variant that partitions volumes into larger blocks and extracts persistent meshlets, using hierarchical subblocks to respect meshlet size constraints. Choose when persistent geometry buffers are preferred over transient extraction. A rasterization-based approach that avoids intermediate explicit mesh storage by extracting primitives on the fly. Choose when minimizing memory bandwidth and storage is critical compared to ray-marching. Time Complexity: The method's cost is less dependent on rendering resolution compared to ray marching, as rasterization hardware is highly optimized. Measured Performance: At 3840 × 2160 pixels, direct isosurface rasterization outperformed min-max octree ray marching in all tested scenes: CT Head (0.19ms vs 1.54ms), Vertebra (0.26ms vs 1.95ms), Chameleon (1.26ms vs 2.59ms), and Timeseries Supernova (0.29ms vs 1.41ms). Memory: Requires negligible additional memory and little preprocessing, avoiding the significant memory bandwidth overhead of storing explicit isosurface representations. Strengths: Suitable for interactive analysis with frequent isovalue adjustments; integrates easily into existing rasterization pipelines; supports multi-view stereo. Limitations: Vertex duplication occurs because cells are processed independently; unique vertex extraction is omitted to avoid branch divergence in sparse cells. Task and mesh shaders have limited output sizes compared to compute shaders. The method was proposed in "Efficient Direct Isosurface Rasterization of Scalar Volumes" (2023). It leverages the NVIDIA task and mesh shader pipelines (OpenGL API terminology) to extract and rasterize geometry on the fly. The approach builds on raster occlusion culling techniques [KT14, LJSL21] to identify potentially visible blocks (PVS). It uses the Marching Cubes cell classification [LC87] for geometry extraction.
