name: Greedy face merging
body: Greedy face merging is a family of surface extraction algorithms that generate a minimal triangle mesh from voxel data by merging adjacent coplanar faces of identical material into larger axis-aligned quads. It solves the problem of excessive vertex and draw call counts in naive voxel rendering (one quad per exposed face) by reducing geometry significantly compared to per-face meshing. Unlike Binary Greedy Meshing with Packed Quads which operates on binary occupancy using bitwise operations, standard variants process explicit material IDs and support multiple voxel types and attributes. It differs from Greedy Meshing / Face Culling by actively merging adjacent faces into maximal rectangles rather than just culling internal faces. The core mechanism sweeps the voxel volume along each of the three principal axes (n \in \{0, 1, 2\} corresponding to X, Y, Z). For each normal n, the algorithm defines the tangent t = (n + 1) \pmod 3 and bitangent b = (n + 2) \pmod 3. 1. Sweep Slices: The volume is iterated along the normal axis n. For each slice index s, a 2D mask M of size Dt \times Db is constructed. 2. Visibility Check: For each cell (t, b) in the slice, the algorithm determines if the face is exposed. A face is exposed if the voxel V(s, t, b) differs from its neighbor in the normal direction V(s \pm 1, t, b), or if the neighbor is out of bounds and the boundary policy dictates an exposed surface. If exposed, the mask entry is set to the mergeKey of the voxel material; otherwise, it is set to 0. Boundary handling treats out-of-bounds neighbors as air or solid based on a boundaryPolicy. 3. Greedy Expansion: The 2D mask is scanned in lexicographic order (row b from 0 to Db-1, column t from 0 to Dt-1) to find maximal rectangles. The algorithm finds the first unprocessed non-zero cell (t0, b0), expands width w while cells match the material ID, and expands height h while all cells in the resulting rectangle [t0, t0 + w) \times [b0, b0 + h) match the material ID and are unprocessed. A quad is emitted with origin (t0, b0, s), normal n, and dimensions (w, h). All cells in the rectangle are marked as processed (e.g., mask set to 0) to prevent double-counting. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def greedyfacemerge(volume, dims, boundarypolicy="air", mergekey=None): """ volume: function (x, y, z) -> materialid dims: tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) boundarypolicy: "air" (default) or "solid" mergekey: function (materialid, x, y, z) -> int. Default: identity. """ if mergekey is None: mergekey = lambda m, x, y, z: m quads = [] # Iterate over the 3 normal axes: 0=X, 1=Y, 2=Z for n in range(3): t = (n + 1) % 3 # Tangent axis b = (n + 2) % 3 # Bitangent axis dimt, dimb, dimn = dims[t], dims[b], dims[n] # Mask stores the merge key if visible and unprocessed, else 0 mask = [0] (dimt dimb) # Iterate through each slice along the normal axis for s in range(dimn): # 1. Build Visibility Mask for slice s for y in range(dimb): for x in range(dimt): coords = [0, 0, 0] coords[n] = s coords[t] = x coords[b] = y voxelval = volume(coords) exposed = False # Check both neighbors along the normal axis for dir in [-1, 1]: nbs = s + dir if 0 <= nbs < dimn: nbcoords = coords.copy() nbcoords[n] = nbs nbval = volume(nbcoords) if voxelval != nbval: exposed = True break else: # Out of bounds neighbor if boundarypolicy == "air": exposed = True # Air neighbor implies exposed face break else: # solid exposed = False # Solid neighbor implies internal break if exposed: mask[y dimt + x] = mergekey(voxelval, coords) else: mask[y dimt + x] = 0 # 2. Greedy Expansion on the 2D Mask for y in range(dimb): for x in range(dimt): idx = y dimt + x key = mask[idx] if key == 0: continue # Start of a new quad w = 1 # Expand width while x + w < dimt and mask[y dimt + (x + w)] == key: w += 1 h = 1 # Expand height while y + h < dimb: rowmatch = True for k in range(w): if mask[(y + h) dimt + (x + k)] != key: rowmatch = False break if not rowmatch: break h += 1 # Emit Quad origin = [0, 0, 0] origin[n] = s origin[t] = x origin[b] = y quads.append({ 'origin': origin, 'normal': n, 'width': w, 'height': h }) # Mark cells as processed (set to 0) for dy in range(h): for dx in range(w): mask[(y + dy) dimt + (x + dx)] = 0 return quads Standard greedy meshing processes material IDs and visibility masks sequentially across three principal axes to maximize quad size. It handles opaque blocks and uses a mergeKey function to allow merging based on attributes beyond material ID, such as ambient occlusion or UV offset. Choose this for general voxel rendering where material consistency is key. Extends standard greedy face merging to handle voxel volumes containing both opaque and undefined (transparent/empty) blocks, ensuring that only exposed faces of opaque materials are meshed while correctly handling visibility against undefined neighbors. It differs from standard Greedy Meshing by explicitly defining visibility logic for "undefined" block types, preventing the emission of internal faces between opaque blocks and undefined space, and ensuring no geometry is generated for undefined blocks themselves. Choose this for games or simulations with transparent/empty space logic. Algorithm to merge exposed triangular faces into large rectangular quads to minimize triangle count, operating on 2D slices of the voxel data. Extract faces that lie in the same geometric plane and share the same color. Represent the extracted faces as a 2D binary grid where 1 indicates an occupied face and 0 indicates empty space. Use a dynamic programming algorithm to find the largest rectangle of 1s in the grid. Render the identified rectangle as two triangles, remove those faces from the grid, and repeat until all faces are accounted for. Applied to 577 color-planes, the model uses 2,966 triangles (1,483 rectangular faces), a 1,000-fold improvement over naive and 2% of the exposed-faces approach. Greedy meshing originated as a method to reduce the vertex count of voxel-based terrains, which are naturally represented as grids of cubes. The naive approach of rendering every exposed face results in O(N) faces for N voxels, which is computationally expensive. The greedy approach reduces this to a minimal set of quads. The algorithm is widely used in voxel engines, Minecraft-like games, and procedural terrain generation systems. The specific variant handling opaque/undefined blocks is common in games that support transparency or void space. name: Voxel Mesh Generation (Run-based Greedy Meshing)
head: Greedy Mesh Generation, Optimised voxel mesh generation, Sector's Edge meshing
body: Voxel Mesh Generation (Run-based Greedy Meshing) is a CPU-based algorithm that converts voxel data into a manifold triangle mesh by merging adjacent faces into rectangular quads to reduce draw calls and vertex count. It builds on Greedy Meshing by extending the 2D greedy approach to 3D chunks, specifically optimizing for generation speed over minimal triangle count. Unlike standard greedy meshing which produces fewer triangles but requires complex data structures, this method uses a linear scan with a done mask to achieve significantly faster generation times, making it suitable for real-time chunk regeneration in multiplayer environments. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A chunk of voxel data (typically 32 \times 32 \times 32 blocks). Each block has a type (texture/health) and visibility flags. Output: A vertex buffer containing packed 32-bit integers representing vertex attributes, and an index buffer (or implicit indices via AppendQuad logic). Data Structures: 1. Chunk Data: A 1D array of size CHUNK\SIZE^3 (32,768) storing block types. 2. Visit Masks: Six boolean arrays of size CHUNK\SIZE^3 (visitXN, visitXP, visitZN, visitZP, visitYN, visitYP) to track which faces have already been generated for each block, preventing duplicates. 3. Vertex Buffer: A dynamic integer array (int[]) storing packed vertex data. Each vertex is a single 32-bit integer. 4. Packed Vertex Layout (32-bit int): Bits 0–5 (6 bits): X position (0–31). Bits 6–11 (6 bits): Y position (0–31). Bits 12–17 (6 bits): Z position (0–31). Bits 18–22 (5 bits): Texture ID (0–31). Bits 23–26 (4 bits): Health/Brightness (0–15). Bits 27–29 (3 bits): Normal (0–7, corresponding to face direction). Bits 30–31: Unused/Reserved. Algorithm Steps: The algorithm iterates through each chunk. For each chunk, it initializes the vertex buffer and visit masks. It then scans the chunk along the Z-axis (depth), then X-axis (width), and finally Y-axis (height) to find runs of visible blocks. 1. Initialization: Set vertexBuffer.used = 0. Initialize visitXN, visitXP, visitZN, visitZP, visitYN, visitYP to false. Load neighbor chunk references for X-, X+, Y-, Y+, Z-, Z+ directions. Handle boundary conditions where neighbor is null if the chunk is at the map edge. 2. Scan Loop: Iterate k from 0 to CHUNK\SIZE-1 (Z-axis). Calculate kCS2 = k CHUNKSIZESQUARED. Determine minZEdge (k==0) and maxZEdge (k==CHUNK\SIZE-1). Iterate i from 0 to CHUNK\SIZE-1 (X-axis). Calculate heightMapAccess = k CHUNKSIZE + i. Get j = MinY[heightMapAccess] and topJ = MaxY[heightMapAccess]. These define the vertical range of non-empty blocks for this (i, k) column. Determine minXEdge (i==0) and maxXEdge (i==CHUNK\SIZE-1). Iterate j from MinY to MaxY-1 (Y-axis). Calculate access = kCS2 + i CHUNKSIZE + j. If block[access] is not EMPTY, call CreateRun(block, i, j, k,...). 3. CreateRun (Face Generation): For a block at (i, j, k) with type B: Calculate textureHealth16 = indexToTextureShifted[B.index] | ((B.health / 16) << 23). Calculate jS = j << 6 and jS1 = (j + 1) << 6. These are used for run-length encoding in the vertex buffer. Check X- Face: If !visitXN[access] and DrawFaceXN returns true (block is visible on this side): Set visitXN[access] = true. Initialize length = jS1. Loop while length < Constants.ChunkSizeShifted: Calculate chunkAccess for the next block in the Y-direction. If DifferentBlock(chunkAccess, B) break. Set visitXN[chunkAccess] = true. Append quad using BlockVertex.AppendQuadX. Increment length by (1 \ll 6). Check X+ Face: Similar to X-, using visitXP and AppendQuadX. Check Z- Face: Similar to X-, using visitZN and AppendQuadZ. Check Z+ Face: Similar to X-, using visitZP and AppendQuadZ. Check Y- and Y+ Faces: Similar logic using visitYN/visitYP and corresponding AppendQuad functions. 4. Vertex Buffer Extension: If vertexBuffer.used > vertexBuffer.data.Length - 2048, extend the buffer by 2048 integers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatechunkmesh(chunk): CHUNKSIZE = 32 CHUNKSIZESQUARED = 1024 CHUNKSIZECUBED = 32768 CHUNKSIZESHIFTED = 32 << 6 # Initialize buffers vertexbuffer = [] visitmasks = { 'XN': [False] CHUNKSIZECUBED, 'XP': [False] CHUNKSIZECUBED, 'ZN': [False] CHUNKSIZECUBED, 'ZP': [False] CHUNKSIZECUBED, 'YN': [False] CHUNKSIZECUBED, 'YP': [False] CHUNKSIZECUBED } # Pre-calculate neighbor chunks neighbors = getneighborchunks(chunk) for k in range(CHUNKSIZE): kCS2 = k CHUNKSIZESQUARED minZEdge = (k == 0) maxZEdge = (k == CHUNKSIZE - 1) for i in range(CHUNKSIZE): heightMapAccess = k CHUNKSIZE + i jmin = chunk.MinY[heightMapAccess] jmax = chunk.MaxY[heightMapAccess] minXEdge = (i == 0) maxXEdge = (i == CHUNKSIZE - 1) iCS = i CHUNKSIZE access = kCS2 + iCS + jmin for j in range(jmin, jmax): block = chunk.data[access] if block.kind != EMPTY: createrun( block=block, i=i, j=j, k=k, i1=i+1, k1=k+1, y=j + chunk.chunkPosY CHUNKSIZE, access=access, minX=minXEdge, maxX=maxXEdge, minY=(j==0), maxY=(j==CHUNKSIZE-1), minZ=minZEdge, maxZ=maxZEdge, iCS=iCS, kCS2=kCS2, vertexbuffer=vertexbuffer, visitmasks=visitmasks, neighbors=neighbors) access += 1 if len(vertexbuffer) > len(vertexbuffer) - 2048: # Placeholder for length check extendvertexbuffer(vertexbuffer, 2048) def createrun(block, i, j, k, i1, k1, y, access, minX, maxX, minY, maxY, minZ, maxZ, iCS, kCS2, vertexbuffer, visitmasks, neighbors): texturehealth = (block.indextotextureshifted | ((block.health // 16) << 23)) jS = j << 6 jS1 = (j + 1) << 6 # X- Face if not visitmasks['XN'][access] and drawfacexn(j, access, minX, kCS2, neighbors): visitmasks['XN'][access] = True chunkaccess = access + 1 length = jS1 while length < CHUNKSIZESHIFTED: if differentblock(chunkaccess, block): break visitmasks['XN'][chunkaccess] = True appendquadx(vertexbuffer, x=i, yL=j, yR=length, kL=0, kR=0, normal=3, texturehealth=texturehealth) # Normal 3 = XN chunkaccess += 1 length += (1 << 6) # X+ Face if not visitmasks['XP'][access] and drawfacexp(j, access, maxX, kCS2, neighbors): visitmasks['XP'][access] = True chunkaccess = access + 1 length = jS1 while length < CHUNKSIZESHIFTED: if differentblock(chunkaccess, block): break visitmasks['XP'][chunkaccess] = True appendquadx(vertexbuffer, x=i+1, yL=j, yR=length, kL=0, kR=0, normal=2, texturehealth=texturehealth) # Normal 2 = XP chunkaccess += 1 length += (1 << 6) # Z- Face if not visitmasks['ZN'][access] and drawfacezn(j, access, minZ, iCS, neighbors): visitmasks['ZN'][access] = True chunkaccess = access + 1 length = jS1 while length < CHUNKSIZESHIFTED: if differentblock(chunkaccess, block): break visitmasks['ZN'][chunkaccess] = True appendquadz(vertexbuffer, xL=i, xR=0, yL=j, yR=length, z=0, normal=5, texturehealth=texturehealth) # Normal 5 = ZN chunkaccess += 1 length += (1 << 6) # Z+ Face if not visitmasks['ZP'][access] and drawfacezp(j, access, maxZ, iCS, neighbors): visitmasks['ZP'][access] = True chunkaccess = access + 1 length = jS1 while length < CHUNKSIZESHIFTED: if differentblock(chunkaccess, block): break visitmasks['ZP'][chunkaccess] = True appendquadz(vertexbuffer, xL=i, xR=0, yL=j, yR=length, z=1, normal=4, texturehealth=texturehealth) # Normal 4 = ZP chunkaccess += 1 length += (1 << 6) def appendquadx(buffer, x, yL, yR, kL, kR, normal, texturehealth): shared = x | texturehealth | normal # Packed vertices: yR|kL|shared, yL|kL|shared, yR|kR|shared, yL|kR|shared buffer.append(yR | kL | shared) buffer.append(yL | kL | shared) buffer.append(yR | kR | shared) buffer.append(yL | kR | shared) # Indices for two triangles: 0,1,2 and 1,3,2 # Note: The source uses a specific index generation logic, but for packed vertices, # the geometry is defined by the packed values themselves. # The source code shows AppendQuadX writes 6 integers (4 vertices + 2 indices? No, 6 vertices for 2 triangles?) # Actually, looking at source: AppendQuadX writes 6 integers. # buffer.data[used] = yR | kL | shared # buffer.data[used+1] = buffer.data[used+4] = yL | kL | shared # buffer.data[used+2] = buffer.data[used+3] = yR | kR | shared # buffer.data[used+5] = yL | kR | shared # This implies a specific vertex layout for the GPU shader. pass def appendquadz(buffer, xL, xR, yL, yR, z, normal, texturehealth): shared = z | texturehealth | normal buffer.append(xR | yR | shared) buffer.append(xR | yL | shared) buffer.append(xL | yR | shared) buffer.append(xL | yL | shared) pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Array Index Out of Bounds: The original width-finding loop in some implementations checks mask[sum + w] before ensuring w < 15 - x, causing out-of-bounds access. The fix is to check bounds first: w < 15 - x && mask[sum + 1 + w] == type. Buffer Overflow: The vertex buffer must be dynamically extended if it nears capacity (e.g., when used > data.Length - 2048). Boundary Conditions: Neighbor chunks must be checked for null references at map edges to avoid crashes when accessing adjacent chunks. Monotone Mesh Generation is a CPU-based algorithm that converts voxel data into a manifold triangle mesh by decomposing the surface into monotone polygons along scan lines and triangulating them. It builds on Voxel Mesh Generation (Run-based Greedy Meshing) by replacing per-voxel face extraction with a sweep-line approach that merges adjacent faces into larger polygons, ensuring manifold geometry without per-voxel vertex duplication. Unlike the basic greedy approach which optimizes for speed over minimal triangle count, this method produces cleaner, lower-poly geometry by creating larger planar patches. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The algorithm runs in O(N) time relative to the number of blocks in the chunk, with a very small constant factor due to the linear scan and simple bitwise operations. Memory: Requires O(N) memory for the chunk data, visit masks (6 \times N booleans), and the vertex buffer. The vertex buffer size is proportional to the number of visible faces. Measured Performance: Benchmarks on a Ryzen 5 1600 CPU show the following average Chunk Mesh Generation Times (CMGT) per chunk: Crashed Freighter (799 chunks): 0.527 ms. Soltrium Temple (648 chunks): 0.432 ms. Aegis Desert (441 chunks): 0.456 ms. Magma Chamber (293 chunks): 0.535 ms. Arena (108 chunks): 0.278 ms. Scaling: The algorithm is designed for single-threaded chunk generation but can be parallelized by processing multiple chunks on different threads, as mesh generation and VBO buffering are kept separate. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Extremely fast generation speed (~390% faster than standard greedy meshing). Simple data structures and bitwise packing make it efficient for CPU execution and GPU buffering. Limitations: Produces ~20% more triangles than standard greedy meshing due to less aggressive merging. Not suitable for scenes requiring minimal polygon counts. When to Use: Use this method when real-time chunk regeneration is critical, such as in multiplayer voxel games with frequent world modifications. When Not to Use: Avoid if minimal triangle count is the primary optimization goal, or if the scene is static and can be pre-processed with slower, more optimal algorithms. This algorithm was developed for the game Sector's Edge (and its successor Vercidium) to handle real-time mesh regeneration for multiple players on older hardware. It was published as part of the Vercidium project's technical blog and source code repository. The approach is a variation of greedy meshing adapted for 3D chunks with a focus on speed and simplicity over optimal triangle reduction. body: Monotone Mesh Generation is a CPU-based algorithm that converts voxel data into a manifold triangle mesh by decomposing the surface into monotone polygons along scan lines and triangulating them. It builds on Voxel Mesh Generation (Run-based Greedy Meshing) by replacing per-voxel face extraction with a sweep-line approach that merges adjacent faces into larger polygons, ensuring manifold geometry without per-voxel vertex duplication. Inputs: Voxel: Sparse map of FIntVector (x, y, z) to uint8 (color index). Size: FIntVector representing the bounding box dimensions. Palette: Array of FColor corresponding to color indices. ImportOption: Configuration struct containing bImportXYCenter (boolean). Outputs: OutRawMesh: Mesh structure containing: VertexPositions: TArray<FVector3f> of unique vertex coordinates. WedgeIndices: TArray<uint32> of vertex indices forming triangles (triplets). WedgeTexCoords[0]: TArray<FVector2f> texture coordinates for each wedge. WedgeColors: TArray<FColor> color for each wedge. FaceMaterialIndices: TArray<uint32> material index for each face. FaceSmoothingMasks: TArray<uint32> smoothing mask for each face. Data Structures: FFace: Represents a 1D segment on a scan line. Color: int32 (positive for outward-facing, negative for inward-facing/normal flip). Left: float x-coordinate of the start of the segment. Right: float x-coordinate of the end of the segment. FPolygon: Represents a monotone polygon being built. Color: int32. Left: TArray[FVector2f] vertices forming the left chain (sorted by Y). Right: TArray[FVector2f] vertices forming the right chain (sorted by Y). Algorithm Steps: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def CreateRawMesh(Voxel, Size, ImportOption): OutRawMesh = FRawMesh() for Dimension in range(3): Axis = [Dimension, (Dimension + 1) % 3, (Dimension + 2) % 3] Plane = [0, 0, 0] for Plane[Axis[2]] in range(Size[Axis[2]]): Polygons = CreatePolygons(Voxel, Size, Axis, Plane) for Polygon in Polygons: WritePolygon(OutRawMesh, Axis, Polygon, Plane) if ImportOption.bImportXYCenter: Offset = [Size.X 0.5, Size.Y 0.5, 0.0] for i in range(len(OutRawMesh.VertexPositions)): OutRawMesh.VertexPositions[i] = [OutRawMesh.VertexPositions[i][j] - Offset[j] for j in range(3)] OutRawMesh.CompactMaterialIndices() return OutRawMesh def CreatePolygons(Voxel, Size, Axis, Plane): OutPolygons = [] for Py in range(Size[Axis[1]]): Faces = CreateFaces(Voxel, Size, Axis, Plane, Py) Frontier = [] NextFrontier = [] FrontierIndex = 0 FaceIndex = 0 while FrontierIndex < len(Frontier) and FaceIndex < len(Faces): polyidx = Frontier[FrontierIndex] poly = OutPolygons[polyidx] face = Faces[FaceIndex] leftx = poly.Left[-1][0] rightx = poly.Right[-1][0] if leftx < face.Right and face.Left < rightx and face.Color == poly.Color: poly.Left.append((face.Left, Py)) poly.Right.append((face.Right, Py)) NextFrontier.append(polyidx) FrontierIndex += 1 FaceIndex += 1 else: if rightx <= face.Right: poly.CloseOff(Py, Plane[Axis[2]]) FrontierIndex += 1 if face.Right <= rightx: idx = len(OutPolygons) OutPolygons.append(FPolygon(face.Color, [(face.Left, Py)], [(face.Right, Py)])) NextFrontier.append(idx) FaceIndex += 1 Frontier = NextFrontier for idx in Frontier: OutPolygons[idx].CloseOff(Py, Plane[Axis[2]]) return OutPolygons def CreateFaces(Voxel, Size, Axis, Plane, Py): OutFaces = [] D = [0, 0, 0] D[Axis[2]] = -1 prevcolor = 0 for Px in range(Size[Axis[0]]): P = [0, 0, 0] P[Axis[0]] = Px P[Axis[1]] = Py P[Axis[2]] = Plane[Axis[2]] Back = Voxel.get(tuple(P + D), 0) Front = Voxel.get(tuple(P), 0) if (Back == 0) == (Front == 0): color = 0 elif Back: color = -Back else: color = Front if prevcolor != color: if prevcolor != 0: OutFaces[-1].Right = Px if color != 0: OutFaces.append(FFace(color, Px, Px)) prevcolor = color if prevcolor != 0: OutFaces[-1].Right = Px return OutFaces def WritePolygon(OutRawMesh, Axis, Polygon, Plane): LeftIndex = [] RightIndex = [] WriteVertex(OutRawMesh, Axis, Polygon.Left, LeftIndex, Plane) WriteVertex(OutRawMesh, Axis, Polygon.Right, RightIndex, Plane) ColorIndex = Polygon.Color - 1 if Polygon.Color > 0 else -Polygon.Color - 1 Flipped = Polygon.Color < 0 Left = 1 Right = 1 LastSide = True def CrossProduct(a, b): return a[0] b[1] - b[0] a[1] List = [(LeftIndex[0], Polygon.Left[0]), (RightIndex[0], Polygon.Right[0])] while Left < len(Polygon.Left) or Right < len(Polygon.Right): if Left == len(Polygon.Left): Side = True elif Right < len(Polygon.Right): Side = Polygon.Left[Left][1] > Polygon.Right[Right][1] else: Side = False if Side: Index = RightIndex[Right] Vertex = Polygon.Right[Right] else: Index = LeftIndex[Left] Vertex = Polygon.Left[Left] if Side != LastSide: while len(List) > 1: WriteWedge(OutRawMesh, List[0][0], List[1][0], Index, ColorIndex, Flipped == Side) List.pop(0) else: while len(List) > 1: Normal = CrossProduct([List[-1][1][0]-Vertex[0], List[-1][1][1]-Vertex[1]], [List[-2][1][0]-Vertex[0], List[-2][1][1]-Vertex[1]]) if Side == (Normal > 0): break if Normal != 0: WriteWedge(OutRawMesh, List[-1][0], List[-2][0], Index, ColorIndex, Flipped == Side) List.pop() List.append((Index, Vertex)) if Side: Right += 1 else: Left += 1 LastSide = Side def WriteVertex(OutRawMesh, Axis, Chain, IndexArray, Plane): for pt in Chain: Vertex = list(Plane) Vertex[Axis[1]] += pt[0] Vertex[Axis[2]] += pt[1] idx = OutRawMesh.VertexPositions.AddUnique(Vertex) IndexArray.append(idx) def WriteWedge(OutRawMesh, Index1, Index2, Index3, ColorIndex, Flipped): OutRawMesh.WedgeIndices.Add(Index1 if not Flipped else Index2) OutRawMesh.WedgeIndices.Add(Index2 if not Flipped else Index1) OutRawMesh.WedgeIndices.Add(Index3) TexCoord = (((ColorIndex + 0.5) / 256.0), 0.5) OutRawMesh.WedgeTexCoords[0].Add(TexCoord) OutRawMesh.WedgeTexCoords[0].Add(TexCoord) OutRawMesh.WedgeTexCoords[0].Add(TexCoord) OutRawMesh.FaceMaterialIndices.Add(0) OutRawMesh.FaceSmoothingMasks.Add(0) Parameters: ImportOption->bImportXYCenter: Boolean. If true, centers the mesh in XY by subtracting (Size.X/2, Size.Y/2, 0) from all vertices. ColorIndex: Used in WriteWedge to generate texture coordinates. Formula: ((double)ColorIndex + 0.5) / 256.0. name: Binary Greedy Meshing with Packed Quads
head: BGM, Binary Greedy Mesher, Binary Greedy Meshing, Binary Greedy Plane, Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing, Greedy Cubic
body: Binary Greedy Meshing (BGM) is a surface extraction algorithm that generates maximal axis-aligned quads from a binary voxel volume (solid/empty) by treating voxel slices as bitmasks and greedily expanding rectangles using bitwise operations. It solves the problem of excessive triangle counts in blocky voxel terrain by merging adjacent visible faces into the largest possible quads, reducing geometry by 1.88×–2.60× in triangle count and up to 54.5× in memory compared to Marching Cubes, while maintaining a blocky aesthetic. Unlike Greedy Meshing, which typically processes individual faces or runs sequentially, BGM operates on packed binary planes (1 bit per voxel), allowing the entire greedy expansion to be performed with CPU-native bitwise instructions (trailing zeros, shifts, masks) rather than branching logic, significantly reducing clock cycles. The algorithm processes a voxel chunk by first generating face masks for all six directions, then grouping voxels by block type and ambient occlusion (AO) pattern into binary planes, and finally applying a bitwise greedy merge to each plane to emit quads. Input: A voxel chunk of size N \times N \times N (typically N=16 or N=32) with block types and a Signed Distance Field (SDF) or height field determining solidity. Output: A list of quads, each defined by position (x, y, z), dimensions (w, h), face direction, block type, and AO value. These are typically encoded into a packed 8-byte record for instanced rendering. 1. Axis Columns Buffer (axisCols) Stores the voxel presence for the chunk. Size: NP^2 \times 4 \times 3 bytes, where NP = N + 2 (padding for neighbors). Layout: Three NP \times NP grids (one per axis: X, Y, Z). Each grid stores voxel presence as 1 bit per block position, packed into 32-bit integers. Indexing: For axis A \in \{0, 1, 2\}, row r, column c: \text{index} = ((r \cdot NP) + c) \cdot 4 + (A \cdot NP^2 \cdot 4) The bit at position b within the 32-bit word is set using bitwise operations. 2. Face Masks Buffer (colFaceMasks) Stores the exposed faces for culling. Size: NP^2 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 bytes. Layout: For each axis, two masks per row: one for "outward" faces (Up/Right/Back) and one for "inward" faces (Down/Left/Forward). Computation: Derived from axisCols by detecting transitions from air to solid or solid to air along the axis direction. 3. Binary Plane Hash Map (xdata) Groups binary planes by block type and AO pattern. Key: A 32-bit integer combining a 9-bit AO index and block type bits. \text{key} = \text{ao\index} \mid (\text{block\type} \ll 9) Value: An array of 32 32-bit integers, where each integer represents a column of voxel solid statuses for a specific Y-slice. 4. Packed Quad Record (VoxelQuadEncoding) Size: 8 bytes (64 bits). Layout: Geometry Word (32 bits): x (5 bits), y (5 bits), z (5 bits), w-1 (5 bits), h-1 (5 bits), face direction (3 bits), reserved (4 bits). Extents are stored biased-by-one (i.e., w-1) to support full 32³ chunks. Material Word (32 bits): A separate 32-bit word containing 8 bits of material data. 1. Build Voxel Grid: Iterate over the chunk volume. For each solid voxel at (x, y, z), set the corresponding bit in axisCols for the X, Y, and Z axes. The grid includes padding (NP = N+2) to handle neighbor chunks. 2. Cull Faces: For each axis and each row in the axis columns, compute the face masks: Outward Mask (e.g., Up): M{out} = C \ \& \ \sim(C \ll 1) Inward Mask (e.g., Down): M{in} = C \ \& \ \sim(C \gg 1) Where C is the 32-bit column value. This identifies the first solid voxel in each vertical run. 3. Generate Axis Planes: For each of the 6 face directions, iterate over the face masks. For each set bit (face), determine its 2D position (u, v) on the plane. Compute the 3x3 Ambient Occlusion (AO) neighborhood index for the voxel. Create a key from the AO index and block type. Set the corresponding bit in the column mask for that key and Y-slice. 4. Greedy Mesh Each Plane: For each binary plane (defined by key and Y-slice), apply the greedy meshing loop: Iterate over each row r of the plane. Skip leading air (zero bits) using trailingzeros. Find the height h of the current solid run using trailingzeros on the inverted bits. Create a mask for the height: Mh = (1 \ll h) - 1. Expand horizontally (w) by checking if subsequent rows match the current height mask. Remove the used bits from subsequent rows to prevent reuse. Emit a quad with position, width, height, and attributes. 5. Emit Quads: Convert the generated quads into the packed 8-byte format and append to the output list. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trailingzeros(n: int) -> int: """Returns the number of zero bits following the lowest-order one-bit.""" if n == 0: return 32 return (n & -n).bitlength() - 1 def trailingones(n: int) -> int: """Returns the number of one bits following the lowest-order zero-bit.""" return trailingzeros(~n & 0xFFFFFFFF) def greedymeshbinaryplane(data: list[int], lodsize: int) -> list[dict]: """ Greedy mesh a single binary plane represented as a list of 32-bit integers (columns). data: List of 32-bit integers, where each integer represents a column of voxels. lodsize: The width/height of the plane (number of rows/columns). Returns: List of quads {x, y, w, h}. """ quads = [] for row in range(lodsize): y = 0 while y < lodsize: # Skip leading air (zeros) shiftedrow = data[row] >> y airheight = trailingzeros(shiftedrow) y += airheight if y >= lodsize: break # Find height of solid run using trailingzeros on inverted bits invertedrow = ~shiftedrow h = trailingones(invertedrow) # Create mask for height h: 0b11...1 (h times) if h == 32: hasmask = 0xFFFFFFFF else: hasmask = (1 << h) - 1 # Shift mask to align with current y mask = hasmask << y # Expand horizontally w = 1 while row + w < lodsize: nextrowcheck = (data[row + w] >> y) & hasmask if nextrowcheck != hasmask: break # Remove the used bits from the next row to prevent reuse data[row + w] &= ~mask w += 1 # Emit quad quads.append({'x': row, 'y': y, 'w': w, 'h': h}) # Move y past the current run y += h return quads def buildfacemasks(axiscols: list[int], sizep: int) -> list[int]: """ Build face masks from axis columns. axiscols: List of 32-bit integers representing voxel presence. sizep: Padded size of the grid. Returns: List of face masks (outward and inward for each axis). """ facemasks = [] for axis in range(3): for i in range(sizep sizep): col = axiscols[i] # Outward mask: solid where air meets solid (ascending) outward = col & ~(col << 1) # Inward mask: solid where solid meets air (descending) inward = col & ~(col >> 1) facemasks.append(outward) facemasks.append(inward) return facemasks CHUNKSIZE: The dimension of the voxel chunk. Common values are 16 or 32. CHUNKSIZEP: Padded dimension, CHUNK\SIZE + 2 (e.g., 18 for 16x16). BLOCKTYPES: Number of distinct block types. Typically small (e.g., 3). Padding: The voxel grid must be padded by 1 on all sides (size+2) to correctly sample the 3x3 AO neighborhood for edge voxels. Uniform padding on all three axes is required for identical code paths for all six directions. Extents: Width and height in the packed quad record must be stored biased-by-one (w-1, h-1) to support full 32³ chunks. Using unbiased extents causes the 2-byte encoding to fail for large quads. AO Collisions: The AO index uses 9 bits. If block types or AO patterns exceed bit limits, collisions may occur. Contract Mismatch: The C++ voxel quad header and GLSL unpacking shader must match exactly. A mismatch causes silent transposition or offset errors. Face Basis: The kWidthIsInnerExtent table varies by face direction due to U/V ordering. Incorrect mapping transposes quads (1x8 becomes 8x1) but does not lose geometry. A performance-oriented variant that combines face visibility generation and greedy merging into a single streaming traversal, retaining only two rolling face data slices to improve cache locality. A traditional run-based approach that processes faces sequentially without bitwise packing. A chunked approach with explicit face culling and quad expansion logic. A general greedy meshing method for voxel faces. A 3D greedy meshing variant that merges cubes instead of quads. Time Complexity: O(N^2) per face direction, where N is the chunk size. The bitwise operations make the constant factor very small. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for the face masks and binary planes. The packed quad output is O(Q), where Q is the number of quads. Performance: For a 16x16 chunk, BGM takes approximately 0.116ms, a 2.49ms improvement over traditional part-based methods. Geometry Reduction: Reduces triangle count by 1.88×–2.60× compared to Marching Cubes for rugged/terraced terrain, and reduces geometry bytes by 39.5×–54.5×. Strengths: Extremely fast due to bitwise operations; low memory footprint; minimal draw calls via instancing. Limitations: Only suitable for blocky, axis-aligned geometry; requires uniform padding; sensitive to AO and block type grouping. Binary Greedy Meshing was developed as an optimization for voxel graphics, leveraging bitwise operations to accelerate the greedy meshing process. It was popularized in the context of Lua-based voxel engines (e.g., Roblox) and C++ voxel engines (e.g., OloEngine). The method treats the voxel volume as a binary field and uses bitwise tricks to find maximal rectangles, significantly outperforming traditional run-based greedy meshing in terms of clock cycles. name: Streaming Binary Greedy Meshing
head: SBUG streaming step, Streaming Binary Greedy Meshing (SBUG) Core Loop
body: Streaming Binary Greedy Meshing (SBGM) is a performance-oriented variant of Binary Greedy Meshing that combines face visibility generation and greedy merging into a single streaming traversal. It retains only two rolling face data slices instead of six full chunk face arrays, significantly improving cache locality by ensuring data is consumed immediately after generation. SBGM processes a voxel chunk one x-slice at a time. It maintains two FaceSlice buffers (current and next) and emits quads for all six face directions as compatible runs terminate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: voxels (uint8t), opaque (uint64t), MeshData& md. Output: md.vertices (array of 6 uint64t buffers), md.facevertexcounts (array of 6 sizet), md.vertexcount (sizet). Data Structures: Chunk Dimensions: Chunk Size CS = 62, Padded Size CSP = 64, Padded Area CSP2 = 4096. Mask: PMASK = ~(1ull << 63 | 1ull) excludes top and bottom bits of a 64-bit integer. FaceSlice: cpp struct FaceSlice { uint64t xneg[CSP]; uint64t xpos[CSP]; uint64t zneg[CSP]; uint64t zpos[CSP]; uint64t yneg[CSP]; uint64t ypos[CSP]; uint8t ynegspan[CSP2]; uint8t yposspan[CSP2]; }; MeshData: Contains merge state arrays (forwardmerged, posforwardmerged, yrightmerged, cachepad0, yposrightmerged, cachepad1, zforwardmerged, cachepad2, zposforwardmerged) and vertex buffers (vertices, facevertexcounts, vertexcount). Offsets are defined by staticassert constants (e.g., MERGEDPOSFORWARD). Outputs: Array of 6 pointers to uint64t, one for each face direction (0: X+, 1: X-, 2: Z+, 3: Z-, 4: Y+, 5: Y-). Core Loop: 1. Initialize two FaceSlice buffers. Build slices for x=1 and x=2. 2. Iterate x from 1 to CS. 3. For each x, determine the right neighbor slice: if x < CS, right = next; otherwise right = &zeroslice. 4. For each z from 1 to CS: Calculate slicevoxels = voxels + x CSP2 and col = slicevoxels + z CSP. Calculate spanbase = z CSP. If current->xneg[z] is non-zero, call meshxbits with col, -1, x, z, current->xneg[z], current->xneg[z+1], merged + MERGEDFORWARD, and outputs[1]. If current->xpos[z] is non-zero, call meshxbits with col, +1, x, z, current->xpos[z], current->xpos[z+1], merged + MERGEDPOSFORWARD, and outputs[0]. If current->yneg[z] is non-zero, call meshyendbitsxmajor with col, -1, x, z, current->yneg[z], right->yneg[z], current->ynegspan + spanbase, right->ynegspan + spanbase, merged + MERGEDYRIGHT + spanbase, and outputs[5]. If current->ypos[z] is non-zero, call meshyendbitsxmajor with col, +1, x, z, current->ypos[z], right->ypos[z], current->yposspan + spanbase, right->yposspan + spanbase, merged + MERGEDYPOSRIGHT + spanbase, and outputs[4]. If current->zneg[z] is non-zero, call meshzbits with col, -1, z, x, current->zneg[z], right->zneg[z], merged + MERGEDZFORWARD + spanbase, and outputs[3]. If current->zpos[z] is non-zero, call meshzbits with col, +1, z, x, current->zpos[z], right->zpos[z], merged + MERGEDZPOSFORWARD + spanbase, and outputs[2]. 5. Swap current and next pointers. 6. If x + 2 <= CS, call buildfaceslice(voxels, opaque, x + 2, next) to prepare the next slice's data. Helper Functions: buildfaceslice: Loads column occupancy bits for left, mid, and right slices, computes xneg and xpos by masking with PMASK and neighbor occupancy, stores results in slice.xneg/z and slice.xpos/z, and sets slice.xneg[CS+1] and slice.xpos[CS+1] to 0 as sentinels. Calls buildyfaceslice. buildyfaceslice: Iterates z from 1 to CS, computing negcurrent and poscurrent bits from column occupancy and neighbors, calls buildyfacecolumn for each z, updates prevocc/currentocc/nextocc, and handles z=CS sentinel by setting negnext/posnext to 0. buildyfacecolumn: Processes negbits and posbits separately: for each bit y, checks if neighbor has same material; if so, increments forward span and removes bit; else stores forward span to spanend, resets forward span to 0, and updates terminal bits. meshxbits: Iterates bitshere: finds lowest set bit y, checks if bitsnext has same bit and same material; if so, increments forwardspan and continues; else computes height by comparing bitshere and bitsnext, merges forward spans, creates quad via getquad, and removes processed bits. meshzbits: Iterates bitshere: finds lowest set bit y, checks if bitsnext has same bit and same material; if so, increments forwardspan and continues; else computes height by comparing bitshere and bitsnext, merges forward spans, creates quad via getquad, and removes processed bits. meshyendbitsxmajor: Iterates bitshere: finds bit y, checks if bitsright has same bit, forwardspan equals spanright[y], and same material; if so, increments rightspan; else computes startz/startx/lengthz/widthx from spans, creates quad via getquad, resets rightspan, and removes processed bits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. CS = 62 CSP = 64 CSP2 = 4096 PMASK = ~(1 << 63 | 1) class FaceSlice: def init(self): self.xneg = [0] CSP self.xpos = [0] CSP self.zneg = [0] CSP self.zpos = [0] CSP self.yneg = [0] CSP self.ypos = [0] CSP self.ynegspan = [0] CSP2 self.yposspan = [0] CSP2 def mesh(voxels, opaque, md): slices = [FaceSlice(), FaceSlice()] zeroslice = FaceSlice() current = slices[0] nextslice = slices[1] buildfaceslice(voxels, opaque, 1, current) buildfaceslice(voxels, opaque, 2, nextslice) outputs = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] begins = outputs[:] for x in range(1, CS + 1): right = nextslice if x < CS else zeroslice for z in range(1, CS + 1): col = voxels[x CSP2 + z CSP] spanbase = z CSP if current.xneg[z]: outputs[1] = meshxbits(col, -1, x, z, current.xneg[z], current.xneg[z+1], md.forwardmerged, MERGEDFORWARD, outputs[1]) if current.xpos[z]: outputs[0] = meshxbits(col, 1, x, z, current.xpos[z], current.xpos[z+1], md.posforwardmerged, MERGEDPOSFORWARD, outputs[0]) if current.yneg[z]: outputs[5] = meshyendbitsxmajor(col, -1, x, z, current.yneg[z], right.yneg[z], current.ynegspan, spanbase, right.ynegspan, spanbase, md.yrightmerged, MERGEDYRIGHT, spanbase, outputs[5]) if current.ypos[z]: outputs[4] = meshyendbitsxmajor(col, 1, x, z, current.ypos[z], right.ypos[z], current.yposspan, spanbase, right.yposspan, spanbase, md.yposrightmerged, MERGEDYPOSRIGHT, spanbase, outputs[4]) if current.zneg[z]: outputs[3] = meshzbits(col, -1, z, x, current.zneg[z], right.zneg[z], md.zforwardmerged, MERGEDZFORWARD, spanbase, outputs[3]) if current.zpos[z]: outputs[2] = meshzbits(col, 1, z, x, current.zpos[z], right.zpos[z], md.zposforwardmerged, MERGEDZPOSFORWARD, spanbase, outputs[2]) current, nextslice = nextslice, current if x + 2 <= CS: buildfaceslice(voxels, opaque, x + 2, nextslice) for face in range(6): md.facevertexcounts[face] = outputs[face] - begins[face] md.vertexcount += md.facevertexcounts[face] return md.vertexcount def buildfaceslice(voxels, opaque, x, slice): for z in range(CSP): mid = opaque[x CSP + z] left = opaque[(x - 1) CSP + z] right = opaque[(x + 1) CSP + z] slice.xneg[z] = mid & PMASK & ~left slice.xpos[z] = mid & PMASK & ~right slice.xneg[CS + 1] = 0 slice.xpos[CS + 1] = 0 buildyfaceslice(voxels, opaque, x, slice.yneg, slice.ypos, slice.ynegspan, slice.yposspan, slice.zneg, slice.zpos) def buildyfaceslice(voxels, opaque, x, negend, posend, negspanend, posspanend, zneg, zpos): negforward = [0] CSP posforward = [0] CSP prevocc = opaque[x CSP + 0] currentocc = opaque[x CSP + 1] columnbits = currentocc & PMASK negcurrent = columnbits & ~(currentocc << 1) poscurrent = columnbits & ~(currentocc >> 1) for z in range(1, CS): col = voxels[x CSP2 + z CSP] nextocc = opaque[x CSP + z + 1] nextbits = nextocc & PMASK negnext = nextbits & ~(nextocc << 1) posnext = nextbits & ~(nextocc >> 1) buildyfacecolumn(col, z CSP, negcurrent, poscurrent, negnext, posnext, negforward, posforward, negend, posend, negspanend, posspanend, z) prevocc = currentocc currentocc = nextocc columnbits = nextbits negcurrent = negnext poscurrent = posnext zneg[CS] = columnbits & ~prevocc zpos[CS] = columnbits & ~opaque[x CSP + CS + 1] buildyfacecolumn(voxels[x CSP2 + CS CSP], CS CSP, negcurrent, poscurrent, 0, 0, negforward, posforward, negend, posend, negspanend, posspanend, CS) def buildyfacecolumn(col, spanbase, negcurrent, poscurrent, negnext, posnext, negforward, posforward, negend, posend, negspanend, posspanend, zidx): negbits = negcurrent negterminal = negcurrent while negbits: y = (negbits & -negbits).bitlength() - 1 ymask = 1 << y negbits &= negbits - 1 material = col[y] if (negnext & ymask) != 0 and material == col[y + CSP]: negforward[y] += 1 negterminal &= ~ymask else: negspanend[spanbase + y] = negforward[y] negforward[y] = 0 posbits = poscurrent posterminal = poscurrent while posbits: y = (posbits & -posbits).bitlength() - 1 ymask = 1 << y posbits &= posbits - 1 material = col[y] if (posnext & ymask) != 0 and material == col[y + CSP]: posforward[y] += 1 posterminal &= ~ymask else: posspanend[spanbase + y] = posforward[y] posforward[y] = 0 negend[zidx] = negterminal posend[zidx] = posterminal def meshxbits(col, sign, x, z, bitshere, bitsnext, forwardmerged, mergedoffset, outptr): while bitshere: y = (bitshere & -bitshere).bitlength() - 1 ymask = 1 << y material = col[y] forwardspan = forwardmerged[mergedoffset + y] if (bitsnext & ymask) != 0 and material == col[y + CSP]: forwardspan += 1 bitshere &= ~ymask continue heightbits = (bitshere & ~bitsnext) >> y maxheight = (~heightbits & -~heightbits).bitlength() - 1 if ~heightbits else 64 height = 1 while height < maxheight: nexty = y + height if forwardspan != forwardmerged[mergedoffset + nexty]: break if material != col[nexty]: break forwardmerged[mergedoffset + nexty] = 0 height += 1 quadmask = ((1 << height) - 1) << y bitshere &= ~quadmask width = forwardspan + 1 startz = z - forwardspan forwardspan = 0 if sign > 0: outptr += 1 else: outptr += 1 return outptr def meshzbits(col, sign, z, x, bitshere, bitsnext, forwardmerged, mergedoffset, outptr): while bitshere: y = (bitshere & -bitshere).bitlength() - 1 ymask = 1 << y material = col[y] forwardspan = forwardmerged[mergedoffset + y] if (bitsnext & ymask) != 0 and material == col[y + CSP2]: forwardspan += 1 bitshere &= ~ymask continue heightbits = (bitshere & ~bitsnext) >> y maxheight = (~heightbits & -~heightbits).bitlength() - 1 if ~heightbits else 64 height = 1 while height < maxheight: nexty = y + height if forwardspan != forwardmerged[mergedoffset + nexty]: break if material != col[nexty]: break forwardmerged[mergedoffset + nexty] = 0 height += 1 quadmask = ((1 << height) - 1) << y bitshere &= ~quadmask width = forwardspan + 1 startx = x - forwardspan forwardspan = 0 if sign > 0: outptr += 1 else: outptr += 1 return outptr def meshyendbitsxmajor(col, sign, x, z, bitshere, bitsright, spanhere, spanbasehere, spanright, spanbaseright, rightmerged, mergedoffset, spanbasemerged, outptr): while bitshere: y = (bitshere & -bitshere).bitlength() - 1 ymask = 1 << y bitshere &= bitshere - 1 material = col[y] forwardspan = spanhere[spanbasehere + y] rightspan = rightmerged[mergedoffset + spanbasemerged + y] if (bitsright & ymask) != 0 and forwardspan == spanright[spanbaseright + y] and material == col[y + CSP2]: rightspan += 1 continue startz = z - forwardspan startx = x - rightspan lengthz = forwardspan + 1 widthx = rightspan + 1 rightspan = 0 if sign > 0: outptr += 1 else: outptr += 1 return outptr def getquad(x, y, z, w, h, type): return (type << 32) | (h << 24) | (w << 18) | (z << 12) | (y << 6) | x def columnmask(opaque, x, z): return opaque[z + x CSP] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sentinels: z=CS is padding, so y spans must terminate here by setting negnext/posnext to 0 in buildyfacecolumn. z=CS+1 sentinel: slice.xneg[CS+1] and slice.xpos[CS+1] are set to 0 to stop forward merges at the last interior column. Quad Counts: Quad counts may differ between SBGM and BGM because SBGM merges adjacent faces in a different order, though the benchmark validator confirms functionally equivalent coverage. Extends SBGM by integrating a 4-state vertex model that bakes occlusion intensity directly into vertex attributes, distinguishing it from sibling methods that output uniform ao=0 for all opaque blocks. Performance: On a Ryzen 5 5600x with Windows 10, MSVC 19.44.35221.0, on a 64x64 grid at 8 iterations, SBGM achieves 37.52 us/chunk median throughput (26,650 chunks/s) compared to BGM's 100.27 us/chunk, a 2.67x speedup. Strengths: Improved cache locality by reducing exposed face data to two 11 KiB slices that are immediately consumed, avoiding L1 cache evictions. Limitations: Requires AVX2/BMI/BMI2 support. Quad counts may differ from BGM due to merge order. SBGM is a performance-oriented variant of Binary Greedy Meshing (BGM). Traditional BGM builds six full-chunk face masks (180 KiB total) which do not fit in L1 data cache (32/48 KiB) and get evicted before meshing. SBGM traverses a chunk one x-slice at a time, reducing exposed face data to two 11 KiB slices that are immediately consumed for meshing, improving cache locality. dmadevice/streaming-binary-greedy-meshing, https://github.com/dmadevice/streaming-binary-greedy-meshing, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing with Ambient Occlusion
head: AO Meshing, Ambient Occlusion Vertex Calculation, Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing
body: Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing with Ambient Occlusion is a surface extraction method that generates a blocky mesh from voxel data while calculating per-vertex ambient occlusion (AO) values based on the solidity of surrounding voxels. Unlike sibling methods that treat all non-air blocks as opaque and output uniform ao=0, this method preserves per-vertex AO values derived from the surrounding voxel neighborhood. Inputs: A voxel chunk with solid/air classification and access to neighboring chunks for boundary sampling. Outputs: A list of vertices, each containing position, AO value (0–3), face normal, and block type. Data Structures: ambientcorners: An array of 8 booleans representing the solidity of the 8 voxels surrounding a face corner in 3D space. Quad: A geometric primitive defined by direction, position, color, and four corner coordinates. Vertex: Packed into a u32 containing position (IVec3), AO (u32), normal (u32), and block type (u32). Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate through all voxels in the chunk. For a 32^3 chunk, indices range from 0 to 32 \times 32 \times 32 - 1. 2. For each voxel at position (x, y, z), determine if it is solid. 3. Check adjacent neighbors to identify exposed faces. If the current voxel is solid and an adjacent neighbor in a specific direction is not solid (air), a face is exposed. 4. Call pushfaceao for the exposed face, passing the chunk references, mesh buffer, face direction, voxel position, color, and block type. 5. Inside pushfaceao: a. Retrieve the 8 surrounding corner voxels for the face direction using ambientcornervoxels. b. Initialize a Quad from the direction, position, and color. c. Iterate over the four corners of the quad. For each corner index i (0 to 3): i. Calculate the index into the ambientcorners array: index = i 2. ii. Identify three relevant neighbor states: side1 at ambientcorners[index], side2 at ambientcorners[(index + 2) % 8], and sidecorner at ambientcorners[(index + 1) % 8]. iii. Calculate the raw AO count: aocount = side1 + side2 + sidecorner. iv. Apply clamping logic: If both side1 and side2 are solid (value 1), the corner is fully occluded regardless of sidecorner. Set aocount = 3. v. Push a vertex to the mesh with the calculated aocount as an attribute. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class IVec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z @staticmethod def fromarray(arr): return IVec3(arr[0], arr[1], arr[2]) class Direction: def getnormal(self): return 0 # Returns normal index for the face direction class Quad: def init(self, corners): self.corners = corners @staticmethod def fromdirection(dir, vpos, color): # Generates 4 corner positions for the exposed face based on direction return [IVec3(0,0,0), IVec3(1,0,0), IVec3(1,1,0), IVec3(0,1,0)] def ambientcornervoxels(chunksrefs, dir, vpos): # Returns 8 integers (0 or 1) for the solidity of surrounding voxels. # The sources do not give the exact neighbor sampling logic for chunk boundaries. return [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0] def makevertexu32(position, ao, normal, blocktype): # Packs vertex attributes into a 32-bit integer return (position.x << 24) | (ao << 20) | (normal << 16) | blocktype def pushfaceao(chunksrefs, mesh, dir, vpos, color, blocktype): ambientcorners = ambientcornervoxels(chunksrefs, dir, vpos) quad = Quad.fromdirection(dir, vpos, color) for i, corner in enumerate(quad.corners): index = i 2 side1 = ambientcorners[index] side2 = ambientcorners[(index + 2) % 8] sidecorner = ambientcorners[(index + 1) % 8] aocount = side1 + side2 + sidecorner if side1 == 1 and side2 == 1: aocount = 3 mesh.vertices.append(makevertexu32(corner, aocount, dir.getnormal(), blocktype)) Parameters: aocount: Ambient occlusion value for the vertex, ranging from 0 (fully open) to 3 (fully occluded). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Sampling: When processing voxels at the edge of a chunk, ambientcornervoxels must sample from neighboring chunks to avoid incorrect AO values. Anisotropy: The diagonal split of the quad affects AO interpolation. If diagonal vertex pairs have different AO sums, the shading gradient may appear inconsistent. Anisotropy correction (flipping the diagonal) is required if (AO{00} + AO{11}) \neq (AO{10} + AO{01}). Precision: AO values are discrete integers (0–3). The evidence maps these tiers to brightness factors (1.0, 0.7, 0.5, and 0.2) and bakes them directly into vertex data. It builds on Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing with Ambient Occlusion. Unlike its sibling Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing without Ambient Occlusion, which treats all non-air blocks as opaque and outputs vertices with ao=0, this method preserves per-vertex AO values derived from surrounding voxel solidity. Converts a greedy mesh quad into four vertex indices while applying ambient occlusion (AO) blending and correcting for interpolation anisotropy. It solves the problem where vertex-based AO values create visible seams or inconsistent shading gradients across a quad face due to the arbitrary direction of the splitting diagonal. It differs from its parent Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing with Ambient Occlusion by actively rotating the vertex order to ensure the diagonal connects vertices with higher combined occlusion, thereby smoothing the gradient. A runtime technique that evaluates the solid state of neighboring voxels directly surrounding each vertex of an exposed face to calculate ambient occlusion (AO) values for baking into vertex data. When generating a quad for a voxel face, each of the four vertices touches three neighboring voxel positions in the plane perpendicular to the face: two edge-adjacent neighbors (sharing an edge with the face) and one corner-diagonal neighbor (sharing only a corner with the face). The AO value is calculated using a lookup table or simple summation: if both edge-adjacent blocks are solid, the corner block is fully occluded regardless of its state, yielding maximum occlusion (value of 3). If neither edge block is solid, the corner block determines whether the value is 0 (open air) or 1 (corner blocked). If only one edge block is solid, the value scales proportionally (value of 1 or 2 depending on the corner). This yields four discrete shading tiers (0 to 3), which are mapped to brightness factors (such as 1.0, 0.7, 0.5, and 0.2) and baked directly into vertex data. name: Multi-Block Binary Meshing with AO
body: Multi-Block Binary Meshing with AO generates mesh vertices for a specific face direction by iterating over all defined block types and axes, handling ambient occlusion (AO) by packing it into the pindex. It differs from its sibling Greedy Quad Vertex Generation with AO and Anisotropy by explicitly managing the iteration over block types and axes to support multiple material types within the same meshing pass. Inputs: lod: The voxel data structure containing the binary slices. facedir: The direction of the face being generated (e.g., +X, -Y). MESHABLEBLOCKTYPES: A list of block types that require meshing. Outputs: A vector of vertices, where each vertex contains position, AO value, and block type information. Data Structures: xdata: A HashMap or array mapping pindex to [u32; 32]. The pindex encodes both the ao value and the blocktype. ao: Stored in the lower 9 bits (pindex & 0b111111111). blocktype: Stored in the upper bits (pindex >> 9). GreedyQuad: Represents a merged quad geometry. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty vertices vector. 2. Iterate over each axis from 0 to size (the dimension of the voxel grid). 3. For each axis, iterate over each blocktype in MESHABLEBLOCKTYPES. 4. Initialize xdata as a HashMap or array mapping pindex to [u32; 32]. If a pindex is not present, insert [0u32; 32]. 5. For each pindex and data in xdata: a. Extract ao from pindex using pindex & 0b111111111. b. Extract blocktype from pindex using pindex >> 9. c. Call greedymeshbinaryplane(data, lod.size()) to get a list of GreedyQuad objects. 6. For each quad returned: a. Call appendvertices with vertices, facedir, axis, lod, ao, and blocktype. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiblockbinarymeshingwithao(lod, facedir, meshableblocktypes): vertices = [] lodsize = lod.size() for axis in range(lodsize): for blocktype in meshableblocktypes: xdata = {} # Populate xdata by iterating over lod slices, packing pindex = (blocktype << 9) | ao for pindex, data in xdata.items(): ao = pindex & 0b111111111 extractedblocktype = pindex >> 9 quads = greedymeshbinaryplane(data, lodsize) for quad in quads: appendvertices(vertices, facedir, axis, lod, ao, extractedblocktype, quad) return vertices def greedymeshbinaryplane(data, lodsize): greedyquads = [] for row in range(len(data)): y = 0 while y < lodsize: shifted = data[row] >> y if shifted == 0: y += 32 continue # trailing zeros tz = (shifted & -shifted).bitlength() - 1 y += tz if y >= lodsize: continue # trailing ones onesshifted = shifted >> y h = 0 while h < 32 - y and (onesshifted & 1): h += 1 onesshifted >>= 1 greedyquads.append((row, y, h)) y += h return greedyquads def appendvertices(vertices, facedir, axis, lod, ao, blocktype, quad): # Standard vertex generation from quad bounds and axis v1, v2, v3, v4 = createquadvertices(quad, facedir, axis, lod, ao, blocktype) newvertices = [v1, v2, v3, v4] if facedir.reverseorder(): newvertices = [newvertices[0]] + newvertices[1:][::-1] if (v1.ao > 0) ^ (v3.ao > 0): newvertices.append(newvertices.pop(0)) vertices.extend(newvertices) def createquadvertices(quad, facedir, axis, lod, ao, blocktype): # Computes 4 vertex positions from quad bounds, axis, and lod dimensions return [ Vertex(quad.minpos, ao, blocktype), Vertex(quad.maxpos, ao, blocktype), Vertex(quad.minpos, ao, blocktype), Vertex(quad.maxpos, ao, blocktype) ] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure that the pindex packing does not overflow the integer type used. Boundaries: Handle cases where lod.size() is 0 or negative. Degenerate Input: If data is all zeros, greedymeshbinaryplane should return an empty list of quads. body: This method generates mesh vertices for a face direction without ambient occlusion, iterating over block types and axes, using a fixed array for xdata. It outputs vertices with ao=0 and blocktype=0. Inputs: lod: The voxel chunk data structure, providing access to block types and dimensions. facedir: The normal direction of the face being generated. axis: The axis along which the iteration proceeds. Outputs: A vector of mesh vertices. Data Structures: xdata: A fixed array of 32 unsigned 32-bit integers ([u32; 32]). GreedyQuad: A struct containing x, y, w (width), and h (height) of the generated quad. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize an empty vertices vector. 2. Iterate over each axis from 0 to size. 3. Iterate over each blocktype in MESHABLEBLOCKTYPES. 4. Initialize xdata as [0u32; 32]. 5. Call greedymeshbinaryplane(xdata, lod.size()) to get quads. 6. For each quad, call appendvertices with vertices, facedir, axis, lod, ao=0, blocktype=0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binarygreedyvoxelmeshingnoao(lod, facedir): vertices = [] for axis in range(3): for blocktype in MESHABLEBLOCKTYPES: xdata = [0] 32 # The source notes do not specify the population logic for xdata. quads = greedymeshbinaryplane(xdata, lod.size()) for quad in quads: appendvertices(vertices, facedir, axis, lod, ao=0, blocktype=0) return vertices def greedymeshbinaryplane(data, lodsize): greedyquads = [] for row in range(len(data)): y = 0 while y < lodsize: shifted = data[row] >> y tz = (shifted & -shifted).bitlength() - 1 if shifted else 32 y += tz if y >= lodsize: continue shifted = data[row] >> y h = (shifted ^ (shifted + 1)).bitlength() - 1 hasmask = (1 << h) - 1 if h < 32 else 0xFFFFFFFF mask = hasmask << y w = 1 while row + w < lodsize: nextrowh = (data[row + w] >> y) & hasmask if nextrowh != hasmask: break data[row + w] &= ~mask w += 1 greedyquads.append({'x': row, 'y': y, 'w': w, 'h': h}) return greedyquads Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The xdata array is fixed at 32 bits. name: Binary Greedy Meshing with Transparency Support
head: Binary Greedy Mesher with Transparency Support, NE/NETC Face Culling, Transparent Voxel Greedy Mesher
body: Binary greedy meshing with transparency support extends standard binary greedy meshing to correctly render voxel chunks containing partially transparent blocks (e.g., glass) and opaque blocks with internal gaps (e.g., doors). It solves the problem of over-culling faces that are visible through transparent voxels by generating face masks that include transparent voxels adjacent to solid ones, ensuring correct visibility while maintaining minimal face count. Unlike its sibling Binary Greedy Voxel Meshing without Ambient Occlusion, which treats all non-air blocks as opaque for culling purposes, this method distinguishes between solid and transparent states to preserve necessary geometry for rendering pipelines that respect depth testing. Inputs: A chunk of voxel data, where each voxel has a BlockData structure containing: issolid(): Boolean indicating if the block occupies space. istransparent(): Boolean indicating if the block allows visibility through it. opaquefacesbitset: A u8 bitmask where bits 0–5 indicate if the corresponding face (up, down, left, right, front, back) is opaque. CHUNKSIZE: The logical dimension of the chunk. CHUNKSIZEP: The padded dimension used for array layouts, typically CHUNKSIZE + 2 to handle boundary padding. Outputs: A set of face masks (colfacemasks or facecols) that determine which voxel positions contribute to mesh vertices for each of the 6 face directions. Mesh vertices generated from these masks, mapped to world coordinates. The algorithm relies on 64-bit integer bitmasks to represent voxel occupancy along each axis. The layout assumes a chunk size of 64 or less per axis to fit within a u64. 1. axiscols: [[[u64; CHUNKSIZEP]; CHUNKSIZEP]; 3] Stores bitmasks for all solid voxels. Index [axis][coord1][coord2] contains a u64 where the bit at position coord3 is set if the voxel at (coord1, coord2, coord3) is solid. Axis mapping: Axis 0 (X): axiscols[0][z][x] has bit y set. Axis 1 (Y): axiscols[1][y][z] has bit x set. Axis 2 (Z): axiscols[2][y][x] has bit z set. 2. axiscolsopaque: [[[u64; CHUNKSIZEP]; CHUNKSIZEP]; 3] Stores bitmasks for solid AND non-transparent voxels. Layout identical to axiscols, but bits are only set if the voxel is solid and istransparent() is false. 3. colfacemasks: [[[u64; CHUNKSIZEP]; CHUNKSIZEP]; 6] Stores the final culling masks for mesh generation. Index 2 axis + 0 corresponds to the descending face mask (e.g., bottom face for Y-axis). Index 2 axis + 1 corresponds to the ascending face mask (e.g., top face for Y-axis). 4. facecols (Optional, for per-face transparency): [[[u64; CHUNKSIZEP]; CHUNKSIZEP]; 6] Stores bitmasks for solid voxels, indexed by specific face direction (0–5) rather than axis. 5. facecolsopaque (Optional, for per-face transparency): [[[u64; CHUNKSIZEP]; CHUNKSIZEP]; 6] Stores bitmasks for solid and opaque voxels, indexed by specific face direction. 1. Initialize Arrays: Initialize axiscols, axiscolsopaque, colfacemasks, facecols, and facecolsopaque to zero. 2. Populate Column Masks: Iterate over every voxel (x, y, z) in the chunk. For each voxel with BlockData b: If b.issolid() is true: Set the corresponding bit in axiscols for all three axes: python axiscols[0][z][x] |= 1 << y axiscols[1][y][z] |= 1 << x axiscols[2][y][x] |= 1 << z If using per-face transparency, set bits in facecols for all 6 faces: python facecols[0][z][x] |= 1 << y # Up facecols[1][z][x] |= 1 << y # Down facecols[2][y][z] |= 1 << x # Left facecols[3][y][z] |= 1 << x # Right facecols[4][y][x] |= 1 << z # Front facecols[5][y][x] |= 1 << z # Back If b.issolid() and not b.istransparent() (or specific face is opaque): Set the corresponding bit in axiscolsopaque: python axiscolsopaque[0][z][x] |= 1 << y axiscolsopaque[1][y][z] |= 1 << x axiscolsopaque[2][y][x] |= 1 << z If using per-face transparency, use opaquefacesbitset to set bits in facecolsopaque: python def bitsetat(bitset, i): return (bitset >> i) & 1 facecolsopaque[0][z][x] |= bitsetat(b.opaquefacesbitset, 0) << y facecolsopaque[1][z][x] |= bitsetat(b.opaquefacesbitset, 1) << y facecolsopaque[2][y][z] |= bitsetat(b.opaquefacesbitset, 2) << x facecolsopaque[3][y][z] |= bitsetat(b.opaquefacesbitset, 3) << x facecolsopaque[4][y][x] |= bitsetat(b.opaquefacesbitset, 4) << z facecolsopaque[5][y][x] |= bitsetat(b.opaquefacesbitset, 5) << z 3. Compute Face Masks: Iterate over each axis axis in 0..3, and coordinates z, x in 0..CHUNKSIZEP. Retrieve the solid column mask: col = axiscols[axis][z][x]. Compute the opaque column mask: colopaque = col & axiscolsopaque[axis][z][x]. Compute solid face masks using bitwise shifts to detect transitions from solid to air: Descending (e.g., bottom face): soliddescending = col & ~(col << 1). Ascending (e.g., top face): solidascending = col & ~(col >> 1). Compute opaque face masks: Descending: opaquedescending = colopaque & ~(colopaque << 1). Ascending: opaqueascending = colopaque & ~(colopaque >> 1). Combine masks to allow faces where either a solid-to-air transition occurs OR an opaque-to-air transition occurs (preserving visibility through transparent voxels): python colfacemasks[2 axis + 0][z][x] = soliddescending | opaquedescending colfacemasks[2 axis + 1][z][x] = solidascending | opaqueascending Note: If using per-face transparency (facecols), replace axiscols with facecols and axiscolsopaque with facecolsopaque in the above calculations, iterating over face indices 0..5 instead of axes. 4. Generate Mesh: Iterate over the face masks to generate vertices. For each axis in 0..3, and coordinates z, x in 0..CHUNKSIZEP: Retrieve the mask: col = colfacemasks[axis][z + 1][x + 1]. Remove padding bits: Shift right by 1 to remove right padding: col >>= 1. AND with inverse of 1 << CHUNKSIZE to remove left padding: col &= ~(1 << CHUNKSIZE). While col != 0: Get the axial coordinate: y = (col & -col).bitlength() - 1. Clear the least significant bit: col &= col - 1. Map to voxel position: python if axis in (0, 1): voxelpos = (x, y, z) elif axis in (2, 3): voxelpos = (y, z, x) else: voxelpos = (x, z, y) Generate mesh geometry for the face at voxelpos. CHUNKSIZE: Logical chunk dimension. Must be \le 64 for u64 bitmasks. CHUNKSIZEP: Padded dimension, typically CHUNKSIZE + 2. opaquefacesbitset: Block-specific u8 bitmask for per-face opacity. Padding Removal: Failure to remove padding bits from the column mask before processing leads to invalid voxel positions. Right padding is removed by shifting right by 1, and left padding by ANDing with the inverse of 1 << CHUNKSIZE. Transparency Ordering: The rendering pipeline must respect transparency ordering (e.g., via depth testing and sorting transparent faces back-to-front) to correctly render the generated transparent faces. Block Type Consistency: Greedy meshing typically requires adjacent faces to have the same block type and ambient occlusion settings to be merged. This method only handles the visibility culling; merging logic remains separate. Time Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of voxels in the chunk, for the population phase. The mask generation is O(C^2) where C is the chunk dimension, due to the 2D iteration over axes. Mesh generation is proportional to the number of exposed faces. Memory Complexity: O(C^2) for the bitmasks. Specifically, 3 \times CP^2 \times 8 bytes for axiscols and axiscolsopaque, and 6 \times CP^2 \times 8 bytes for colfacemasks. Strengths: Significantly reduces over-culling in scenes with transparent blocks compared to standard binary greedy meshing. Maintains the performance benefits of bit-parallel operations. Limitations: Requires a rendering pipeline that supports transparency sorting. Per-face transparency adds complexity and memory overhead. When to use: When rendering voxel worlds with glass, water, or other transparent materials where standard greedy meshing would incorrectly hide visible faces behind transparent blocks. This method was developed as an extension to binary greedy meshing to address the limitations of treating all non-air blocks as opaque for culling purposes. It was discussed in the context of the binarygreedymesherdemo repository, aiming to support transparent voxel textures like glass and opaque blocks with gaps like doors. The technique leverages bitwise operations to efficiently compute face masks that account for transparency, ensuring minimal face count while preserving visual correctness. name: Minecraft-style Voxel Meshing with AO and Flip
head: Greedy Mesh Generation, Minecraft-style Voxel Meshing, Voxel Face Mesh Generation with AO and Flip
body: This method generates a mesh for a voxel segment by merging adjacent blocks of the same type into larger rectangular faces, reducing draw calls and vertex count. It extends binary greedy meshing by incorporating ambient occlusion (AO) values into the vertex data and using a "flip" bit to optimize triangle winding order based on AO distribution. It builds on Multi-Block Binary Meshing with AO by adding the specific logic for AO-based flip determination and vertex packing for the final geometry generation. Inputs: A voxel segment (typically 16×16×16 blocks), a visibility mask, and block type data. Outputs: A list of vertices (position, color, packed data) and an index buffer for each face direction. Data Structures: 1. mask: Array of 4096 integers. mask[i] stores the block type ID. If the block is null or not visible, it stores BlockType.AIR. 2. done: Array of 4096 booleans. done[i] is true if the block at index i has already been included in a merged face. 3. v0, v1, v2, v3: Vertex structures containing position, color, and packed data. 4. packeddata: A packed integer or struct containing world coordinates, voxelid, faceid, ao value, and flipid. Parameters: segmentsize: 16 (standard Minecraft chunk segment size). faceid: Integer distinguishing the face direction (e.g., 4 for TOP, 5 for FRONT). AIR: Constant representing empty space. Steps: 1. Initialize Mask: Iterate i from 0 to 4095. If segment.getBlock(i) is null or !segment.getBlock(i).isVisible(), set mask[i] = AIR. Else, set mask[i] = segment.getBlock(i).getType(). Initialize done[i] = false for all i. 2. Iterate Face Directions: Loop through the 6 face directions i (0=TOP, 1=BOT, 2=LEFT, 3=RIGHT, 4=FRONT, 5=BACK). Skip if the face is not visible to the camera (culling). 3. Pre-check: If all blocks in the segment have mask[j] == AIR or the face is not visible for any block, skip this face direction. 4. Scan for Merged Faces: Iterate y from 0 to 15, z from 0 to 15, x from 0 to 15. Calculate linear index: sum = x + (z << 4) + (y << 8). If done[sum] is true, continue. Let type = mask[sum]. If type == AIR, set done[sum] = true and continue. If the block at sum does not have the current face i visible, set done[sum] = true and continue. 5. Determine Dimensions (Greedy Expansion): Find the width w and height h of the largest rectangle of blocks with type that are not done. For TOP/BOT faces (x-z plane): Find w: Iterate w from 0 while w < 15 - x AND mask[sum + 1 + w] == type AND !done[sum + 1 + w]. Find h: Iterate h from 0 while h < 15 - z. For each h, check if all blocks in the row sum + (h << 4) + k for k from 0 to w match type and are not done. If any block fails, break. Mark all cells in the rectangle (x, z) to (x+w, z+h) as done. For LEFT/RIGHT faces (z-y plane): Find w (along z-axis): Iterate w from 0 while w < 15 - z AND mask[sum + (w << 4) + 1] == type AND !done[sum + (w << 4) + 1]. Find h (along y-axis): Iterate h from 0 while h < 15 - y. For each h, check if all blocks in the column sum + (h << 8) + (k << 4) for k from 0 to w match type and are not done. If any block fails, break. Mark all cells in the rectangle as done. For FRONT/BACK faces: The reference snippet skips these with a temporary placeholder, but the general greedy logic applies to the x-y plane. 6. Calculate Ambient Occlusion and Flip ID: For the four corners of the generated rectangle, calculate AO values using getao. Let the corners be indexed 0, 1, 2, 3. Determine flipid: flipid = (ao[1] + ao[3]) > (ao[0] + ao[2]). This boolean determines the winding order of the triangles to optimize for AO shading continuity. 7. Pack Vertex Data: For each of the 4 corners of the rectangle, create a vertex v using packdata. Arguments: World coordinates (e.g., bX, bY, bZ), voxelid, faceid, ao value, and flipid. Store these in v0, v1, v2, v3. 8. Generate Geometry: Call addVertices(type.getColor(), i, bX, bY, bZ, w, h). Add vertex positions based on face type. Add indices for two triangles using the last 4 vertices added: indices are (size-4, size-3, size-2) and (size-2, size-1, size-4). If flipid is true, add indices in the order v3, v1, v0, v3, v2, v1. If false, add in the order v0, v2, v1, v0, v3, v2. Pseudocode: def generatemesh(segment, segmentabspos): segX, segY, segZ = segmentabspos.x 16, segmentabspos.y 16, segmentabspos.z 16 mask = [0] 4096 done = [False] 4096 vertices = [] indices = [] # 1. Initialize mask for i in range(4096): block = segment.getblock(i) if block is None or not block.isvisible(): mask[i] = BlockType.AIR else: mask[i] = block.gettype() # 2. Iterate face directions (0=TOP, 1=BOT, 2=LEFT, 3=RIGHT, 4=FRONT, 5=BACK) for face in range(6): if not shouldrendersegside(face, segX, segY, segZ): continue # 3. Pre-check: skip if all blocks are AIR or face not visible continueface = True for j in range(4096): if mask[j] == BlockType.AIR: done[j] = True continue block = segment.getblock(j) if not block.issidevisible(face): done[j] = True else: done[j] = False continueface = False if continueface: continue # 4. Scan for merged faces for y in range(16): y = y << 8 bY = y + segY for z in range(16): z = z << 4 bZ = z + segZ for x in range(16): sumidx = x + z + y if done[sumidx]: continue bX = x + segX typeid = mask[sumidx] # 5. Find width w and height h w, h = 0, 0 if face in (0, 1): # TOP/BOT # Fixed boundary check: check limit first, then next block while w < 15 - x and mask[sumidx + 1 + w] == typeid and not done[sumidx + 1 + w]: w += 1 h = 0 while h < 15 - z: rowok = True for k in range(w + 1): if mask[sumidx + (h << 4) + k] != typeid or done[sumidx + (h << 4) + k]: rowok = False break if not rowok: break h += 1 for j in range(h + 1): for k in range(w + 1): done[sumidx + (j << 4) + k] = True elif face in (2, 3): # LEFT/RIGHT while w < 15 - z and mask[sumidx + (w << 4) + 1] == typeid and not done[sumidx + (w << 4) + 1]: w += 1 h = 0 while h < 15 - y: colok = True for k in range(w + 1): if mask[sumidx + (h << 8) + (k << 4)] != typeid or done[sumidx + (h << 8) + (k << 4)]: colok = False break if not colok: break h += 1 for j in range(h + 1): for k in range(w + 1): done[sumidx + (j << 8) + (k << 4)] = True else: # FRONT/BACK continue # TEMP in source # 6. Calculate AO and flipid # AO calculation logic not specified in sources ao = getaocorners(bX, bY, bZ, w, h, face) flipid = (ao[1] + ao[3]) > (ao[0] + ao[2]) # 7. Pack vertex data # Packing logic not specified in sources v0 = packdata(bX, bY, bZ, 0, face, ao[0], flipid) v1 = packdata(bX, bY, bZ, 1, face, ao[1], flipid) v2 = packdata(bX, bY, bZ, 2, face, ao[2], flipid) v3 = packdata(bX, bY, bZ, 3, face, ao[3], flipid) # 8. Generate geometry addvertices(typeid.getcolor(), face, bX, bY, bZ, w, h, v0, v1, v2, v3) def addvertices(color, face, x, y, z, w, h, v0, v1, v2, v3): # Vertex positions if face == 0: # TOP v0.pos = (x - 0.5, y + 0.5, z - 0.5) v1.pos = (x - 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5 + h) v2.pos = (x + 0.5 + w, y + 0.5, z + 0.5 + h) v3.pos = (x + 0.5 + w, y + 0.5, z - 0.5) elif face == 1: # BOT v0.pos = (x - 0.5, y - 0.5, z - 0.5) v1.pos = (x + 0.5 + w, y - 0.5, z - 0.5) v2.pos = (x + 0.5 + w, y - 0.5, z + 0.5 + h) v3.pos = (x - 0.5, y - 0.5, z + 0.5 + h) elif face == 2: # LEFT v0.pos = (x - 0.5, y + 0.5 + h, z + 0.5 + w) v1.pos = (x - 0.5, y + 0.5 + h, z - 0.5) v2.pos = (x - 0.5, y - 0.5, z - 0.5) v3.pos = (x - 0.5, y - 0.5, z + 0.5 + w) # RIGHT/FRONT/BACK follow similar logic relative to face normal and dimensions # Indices size = len(vertices) vertices.extend([v0, v1, v2, v3]) if flipid: indices.extend([size, size+1, size+2, size+2, size+3, size+1]) else: indices.extend([size, size+2, size+1, size, size+3, size+2]) Pitfalls: Boundary Check: When finding width w, the condition mask[sum + w] == type checks the block at w=0 which is already known to be type. The loop should check mask[sum + 1 + w] to find the next block, and must check w < 15 - x before accessing the array to prevent ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. AO Calculation: getao must correctly sample neighboring blocks to determine the darkness of each corner. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of blocks in the segment (4096 for a 16×16×16 chunk). Each block is visited a constant number of times during the greedy expansion. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the mask and done arrays. Performance: Significantly reduces vertex count and draw calls compared to per-block meshing. The greedy merging is efficient for large uniform areas. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for voxel games with blocky geometry, integrates AO for shading. Limitations: Only merges axis-aligned rectangles, so diagonal or complex shapes are not optimized. The "flip" optimization is specific to the AO winding order and may not apply to all shading models. When to use: Voxel-based games with static or infrequently changing chunks. When not to use: Dynamic meshes with frequent updates, or non-voxel geometry. The method originates from community implementations for voxel-based games like Minecraft, where reducing draw calls is critical for performance. The greedy meshing approach itself is a well-known optimization in voxel rendering, first popularized by the need to render large Minecraft worlds efficiently. The specific "flip" logic based on AO sums is documented in community codebases.
