name: Greedy Meshing UV Recomputation & Gradient Stabilization
head: Greedy UV tiling, Stable gradient sampling for greedy faces
body: This method is a shader injection technique that recomputes UV coordinates and texture derivatives for faces generated by greedy meshing to ensure correct texture tiling and stable mipmapping across block boundaries. It solves the problem of visual artifacts caused by discontinuous UV coordinates at the edges of merged quads, which lead to unstable mip level selection and visible seams in distant patterned textures. It sets itself apart from vanilla rendering by explicitly computing smooth gradients per face orientation and routing greedy faces to specialized sampling functions, rather than relying on interpolated texture coordinates. The method operates as a fragment shader injection that intercepts rendering for greedy-meshed faces. It identifies these faces, reconstructs local UVs based on the block position and face orientation, clamps them to avoid border artifacts, and computes stable derivatives for mipmapping. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: vGreedyFaceId: Varying integer identifying the face type. vTexCoord: Original interpolated texture coordinates (smooth). vBlockPos: Varying block position (smooth). sampler: The texture sampler object. uTexelSize: Uniform texture texel size (optional, for sampling). Outputs: gmTexCoord: Corrected UV coordinates for sampling. gmdu, gmdv: Stable screen-space derivatives. Data Structures: The method relies on specific ID ranges to identify greedy faces and map them to sprite sizes: IDs 234–239: 64px sprites, face indices 0–5. IDs 240–245: 32px sprites, face indices 0–5. All other greedy IDs: 16px sprites, face indices 0–5. Numbered Steps: 1. Identify Greedy Face: Check if the current fragment belongs to a greedy-meshed face by verifying if vGreedyFaceId falls within the range [234, 251]. 2. Determine Sprite Parameters: Map the face ID to a sprite pixel size (spritePixels) and local face index (0–5) based on the ranges defined above. 3. Compute Sprite Space: Calculate the sprite's texture space size and origin: \text{spriteSize} = \frac{\text{spritePixels}}{\text{textureSize}(sampler, 0)} \text{spriteOrigin} = v\TexCoord - \text{spriteSize} \times 0.5 where textureSize(sampler, 0) returns the dimensions of the texture. 4. Calculate Local UVs: Compute local UV coordinates based on the face index (0–5) using the fractional block position vBlockPos: Face 0: (fx, 1.0 - fz) Face 1: (fx, fz) Face 2: (1.0 - fx, 1.0 - fy) Face 3: (fx, 1.0 - fy) Face 4: (fz, 1.0 - fy) Face 5: (1.0 - fz, 1.0 - fy) where fx = \text{fract}(v\BlockPos.x), fy = \text{fract}(v\BlockPos.y), fz = \text{fract}(v\BlockPos.z). Let this result be gmlocal. 5. Compute Final UV: Calculate the UV coordinate using the formula: \text{uv} = \text{spriteOrigin} + \text{local} \times \text{spriteSize} 6. Clamp UV: Clamp the computed UV to the inner sprite region to avoid border sampling artifacts: \text{uv} = \text{clamp}(\text{uv}, \text{spriteOrigin} + \text{halfTexel}, \text{spriteOrigin} + \text{spriteSize} - \text{halfTexel}) where \text{halfTexel} = 0.5 / \text{textureSize}(sampler, 0). 7. Compute Stable Derivatives: Compute stable texture derivatives by taking screen-space gradients of the original smooth vTexCoord components, scaled by the sprite size, instead of using the discontinuous fractured UVs. 8. Sample: Route sampling using the corrected UV and derivatives. The evidence specifies that sampleNearest is used in both cases: sampleNearest(sampler, gmTexCoord, uTexelSize, gmdu, gmdv, gmtexelScreenSize) for greedy faces, and sampleNearest(sampler, gmTexCoord, uTexelSize) for non-greedy faces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gmfaceId = int(round(vGreedyFaceId)) gmisGreedy = 234 <= gmfaceId <= 251 gmTexCoord = vTexCoord if gmisGreedy: # Map ID to sprite size and face index (0-5) if 234 <= gmfaceId <= 239: spritePixels = 64 faceIndex = gmfaceId - 234 elif 240 <= gmfaceId <= 245: spritePixels = 32 faceIndex = gmfaceId - 240 else: spritePixels = 16 faceIndex = gmfaceId - 246 # Base ID for other sprites not specified in sources # Get texture dimensions texSize = texturesize(sampler, 0) # Compute sprite size in texture space spriteSize = vec2(float(spritePixels) / texSize.x, float(spritePixels) / texSize.y) # Compute sprite origin spriteOrigin = vTexCoord - spriteSize 0.5 # Compute fractional block position fx = fract(vBlockPos.x) fy = fract(vBlockPos.y) fz = fract(vBlockPos.z) # Compute local UV based on face index if faceIndex == 0: local = vec2(fx, 1.0 - fz) elif faceIndex == 1: local = vec2(fx, fz) elif faceIndex == 2: local = vec2(1.0 - fx, 1.0 - fy) elif faceIndex == 3: local = vec2(fx, 1.0 - fy) elif faceIndex == 4: local = vec2(fz, 1.0 - fy) elif faceIndex == 5: local = vec2(1.0 - fz, 1.0 - fy) else: local = vec2(0.0, 0.0) # Compute final UV uv = spriteOrigin + local spriteSize # Clamp to avoid border artifacts halfTexel = 0.5 / texSize gmTexCoord = clamp(uv, spriteOrigin + halfTexel, spriteOrigin + spriteSize - halfTexel) gmdu = dFdx(vTexCoord) gmdv = dFdy(vTexCoord) gmtexelScreenSize = sqrt(gmdu gmdu + gmdv gmdv) Parameters: Face ID ranges: 234–251. Sprite sizes: 64px, 32px, 16px. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuous UVs: Fractured UVs (fract(vBlockPos.)) cause discontinuities at block boundaries, leading to unstable mip level selection for distant patterned textures. This is solved by computing derivatives from smooth vTexCoord or vBlockPos directly. Vertex Color Alpha: Vertex color alpha is repurposed as a face marker in some shader paths. This is solved by routing main's uses through a corrected copy (gmVertexColor) with alpha forced to 1.0 for greedy faces, preserving cutout discard behavior. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Implemented in the GreedyMeshing mod for Minecraft, targeting Sodium renderer compatibility and VulkanMod debug rendering. Strengths: Eliminates visible seams and mipmapping instability on greedy-meshed faces. Limitations: Requires specific varying variables (vGreedyFaceId, vBlockPos) to be passed to the shader. Relies on specific ID ranges for face identification. This method is part of the GreedyMeshing mod (package hi.sierra.greedymeshing) for Minecraft. It addresses issues arising from the vanilla and Sodium stock samplers, which compute derivatives from interpolated texture coordinates, causing instability. The technique is specifically designed for compatibility with the Sodium renderer and VulkanMod debug rendering. name: Chunked Voxel Mesh Generation with Face Culling and Quad Expansion
head: Chunk-based Greedy Meshing, FrontGreedyMesh, Greedy Meshing with Chunked Processing, TopGreedyMesh
body: Chunked Voxel Mesh Generation with Face Culling and Quad Expansion is a CPU-based algorithm that converts discrete 3D voxel data into optimized triangle meshes by merging adjacent coplanar faces of identical voxel types into larger quads. It solves the problem of excessive vertex and draw call counts in voxel worlds by reducing primitive density while preserving sharp, axis-aligned surfaces suitable for architectural geometry. It differs from standard face culling (which only removes hidden faces) by actively merging contiguous blocks into maximal axis-aligned rectangles, and it differs from Marching Cubes by maintaining discrete voxel boundaries rather than smoothing surfaces. This method builds on Greedy Meshing by processing data in fixed-size chunks and handling inter-chunk visibility. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 1D array of voxel data representing a chunk (e.g., blockArray1D), neighbor chunk data for boundary checks, and metadata (chunk size, block size, world offset). Output: A mesh structure containing vertices, indices, and optionally UVs/normals. Data Structures: Voxel Array: A 1D array where each element represents a voxel. The index is calculated as index = j + (i \times ChunkSize) + (k \times ChunkSize^2), where i is X, j is Y, and k is Z. Visit Arrays: Boolean arrays (e.g., visitXN, visitXP, visitYN, visitYP, visitZN, visitZP) of size ChunkSize^3 to track which faces have already been merged into a quad, preventing double-counting. Vertex Packing (Optional): Vertices can be packed into a single 32-bit integer to save memory. Layout: x (6 bits), y (6 bits), z (6 bits), voxelid (8 bits), faceid (3 bits), aoid (2 bits), flipid (1 bit). Alternatively, explicit structs with position, normal, color, and material are used. Face Type Encoding: Face normals can be encoded in the upper bits of vertex attributes (e.g., yp=0<<27, yn=1<<27, etc.). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize empty vertex and index lists. Initialize visit arrays to false. If using heightmaps, initialize min/max altitude arrays to optimize Y-range iteration. 2. Voxel Iteration: Iterate through all voxels in the chunk. The order varies by implementation: Z (k), X (i), Y (j). Z, Y, X. X, Y, Z. For each voxel at (i, j, k), check if it is solid (index > 0). 3. Face Visibility Check: For each of the 6 face directions (±X, ±Y, ±Z), determine if the face is visible. A face is visible if: The adjacent voxel is empty (index == 0). Boundary Handling: If the voxel is at a chunk boundary, check the neighbor chunk. If the neighbor chunk is null or outside the world bounds, the face is visible. If the neighbor chunk exists, check the corresponding voxel in the neighbor chunk. For example, for the X- face at chunk boundary X=0, check neighborChunk.data[31 ChunkSize + j + k ChunkSize^2]. Exception: For the Top (Y+) face, do not cull based on the maximum Y chunk boundary, as players may move above the map. 4. Face Culling and Merging (Quad Expansion): If a face is visible and not yet visited (check visit array): Mark the current voxel's face as visited. Expand along the secondary axis: For X-faces (±X), expand along the Z-axis (and then Y-axis). For Y-faces (±Y), expand along the X-axis (and then Z-axis). For Z-faces (±Z), expand along the X-axis (and then Y-axis). Note: Some implementations only expand along one axis (e.g., Z for top faces). Expansion Logic: Iterate in the secondary direction (e.g., for X- face, iterate Z from k to ChunkSize). Check if the neighbor voxel has the same type (and health/texture). Check if the neighbor's face in the same direction is also visible and not visited. If both conditions are met, mark the neighbor's face as visited and continue. If not, stop expansion. The length of the merge is the number of consecutive matching voxels. Generate Quad: Create a quad spanning the merged area. Calculate vertices based on the start position, the merged width/length, and the face normal. Calculate UVs and normals. Add vertices and indices to the mesh. Indices are typically two triangles forming a quad: [0, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3] or [2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 0] depending on winding order. 5. Finalization: Convert lists to arrays. Recalculate normals and tangents if necessary. Optimize the mesh (e.g., vertex cache optimization). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatechunkmesh(chunkvoxels, chunksize, neighborchunks): vertices = [] indices = [] # Initialize visit arrays for all 6 faces visit = { 'xn': [False] (chunksize 3), 'xp': [False] (chunksize 3), 'yn': [False] (chunksize 3), 'yp': [False] (chunksize 3), 'zn': [False] (chunksize 3), 'zp': [False] (chunksize 3) } # Iterate through all voxels for k in range(chunksize): # Z for i in range(chunksize): # X for j in range(chunksize): # Y voxel = chunkvoxels[i + j chunksize + k chunksize 2] if voxel.index == 0: continue # Check X- face if isfacevisible(i, j, k, 'xn', chunkvoxels, chunksize, neighborchunks): if not visit['xn'][i + j chunksize + k chunksize 2]: lengthz, lengthy = expandface(i, j, k, 'xn', chunkvoxels, chunksize, visit['xn']) addquadtomesh(vertices, indices, i, j, k, 'xn', lengthz, lengthy, voxel) markvisited(i, j, k, 'xn', chunkvoxels, chunksize, visit['xn'], lengthz, lengthy) # Check other 5 faces similarly... # (Code omitted for brevity, follows same pattern) return vertices, indices def isfacevisible(i, j, k, face, voxels, size, neighbors): # Determine neighbor coordinates if face == 'xn': if i == 0: if neighbors['xn'] is None: return True # Check neighbor chunk voxel return neighbors['xn'].getvoxel(31, j, k).index == 0 else: return voxels[i - 1 + j size + k size 2].index == 0 #... handle other faces similarly return False def expandface(i, j, k, face, voxels, size, visitarray): # Example for X- face, expanding along Z then Y lengthz = 1 while k + lengthz < size: neighboridx = i + j size + (k + lengthz) size 2 if voxels[neighboridx].index != voxels[i + j size + k size 2].index: break if visitarray[neighboridx]: break lengthz += 1 lengthy = 1 while j + lengthy < size: # Check if the entire column in Z matches for dz in range(lengthz): neighboridx = i + (j + lengthy) size + (k + dz) size 2 if voxels[neighboridx].index != voxels[i + j size + k size 2].index: return lengthz, lengthy if visitarray[neighboridx]: return lengthz, lengthy lengthy += 1 return lengthz, lengthy def addquadtomesh(vertices, indices, i, j, k, face, lengthz, lengthy, voxel): # Calculate world positions #... # Add 4 vertices # Add 6 indices pass def markvisited(i, j, k, face, voxels, size, visitarray, lengthz, lengthy): # Mark all visited voxels in the merged area for dy in range(lengthy): for dz in range(lengthz): idx = i + (j + dy) size + (k + dz) size 2 visitarray[idx] = True Processes chunks to generate triangle meshes and combines adjacent coplanar faces into quads. Chosen when smooth surfaces are needed but draw calls must be reduced. Generates quads specifically for the front-facing (positive Z) surfaces of a voxel chunk. Chosen when only front-facing optimization is required or for specific rendering passes. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the chunk, as each voxel is visited a constant number of times. The merging step adds overhead but reduces the final mesh size. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the voxel data and O(F) for the output mesh, where F is the number of faces. The visit arrays add O(N) memory. Performance: On a CPU, a 64³ chunk (~50-100K triangles) can be generated in ~2ms. Strengths: Significantly reduces vertex and triangle count for large solid volumes compared to naive face culling. Produces sharp, axis-aligned surfaces ideal for architectural voxel art. Limitations: Does not smooth surfaces, making it less suitable for organic shapes. Requires careful handling of chunk boundaries and neighbor data. The greedy approach may not produce the globally optimal mesh (e.g., it might miss merges that require a different iteration order). When to Use: Static voxel worlds, architectural designs, terrain generation where performance is critical and sharp edges are desired. When Not to Use: Organic terrain requiring smooth surfaces (use Marching Cubes), dynamic scenes with frequent voxel changes where re-meshing overhead is prohibitive. The algorithm originates from the need to optimize voxel rendering in games like Minecraft. It extends 2D greedy meshing techniques to 3D by processing voxel chunks. Key implementations include the Vercidium Engine, Unity-based voxel engines, and Python-based renderers. name: Chunk-based Marching Cubes with Face Combination
head: Chunk Meshing
body: Chunk-based Marching Cubes with Face Combination is a voxel meshing algorithm that processes 3D voxel data in fixed-size cubic chunks to generate triangle meshes for visible surfaces. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by operating on discrete voxel indices rather than scalar fields, and it explicitly combines adjacent coplanar faces into quads to reduce vertex count and draw calls. Inputs: A 3D array of voxels, where each voxel contains at least an index field (byte) representing material or occupancy. A chunk size constant, Constants.ChunkSize, defining the cubic dimensions of the processing unit. A boolean flag m.ShouldMeshBetweenChunks controlling boundary behavior. Neighbor chunk references for boundary visibility checks. Outputs: A list of vertex records forming quads for visible, combined faces. Data Structures: Voxel: A struct containing at least index (byte). Memory is contiguous within a chunk. Visit Pointer Array: A 1D integer array aligned with voxel faces, used to mark processed faces. Each entry stores a comparison token unique to the current chunk processing pass. Mesh Data Buffer: A dynamic list of vertex records. Each vertex stores position (x, y, z), normal (nx, ny, nz), texture coordinates (u, v), and textureID. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set a unique comparison token for the current chunk pass. Initialize the visit pointer array with values not equal to comparison. 2. Iterate Voxels: Loop through each voxel (i, j, k) in the chunk. 3. Check Faces: For each of the 6 face directions, check if the face has been meshed by comparing the visit pointer against comparison. 4. Visibility Check: If not meshed, call DrawFace to determine visibility. Common Logic: DrawFace checks if the adjacent voxel's index is 0 (empty). If so, the face is visible. Boundary Logic: If the face is at a chunk boundary, check m.ShouldMeshBetweenChunks. If true, render. If false, check if the neighbor chunk is allocated. If not allocated, assume empty and render. If allocated, sample the neighbor voxel. 5. Mark Meshed: If visible, mark the face as meshed by setting the visit pointer to comparison. 6. Combine Faces: Iterate along the two axes parallel to the face plane. Check if adjacent voxels have the same index, are visible, and are not yet meshed. If valid, mark them meshed and increment the span counters lengtha and lengthb. 7. Generate Triangles: For each combined face of size lengtha by lengthb, generate four vertices forming a quad. Set the normal based on face direction and map texture coordinates to (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1). 8. Repeat: Continue until all voxels and faces are processed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processchunk(voxels, chunksize, shouldmeshbetweenchunks, neighborchunks): comparison = 1 visitarray = [0] (chunksize 3 6) meshdata = [] stridey = chunksize stridez = chunksize chunksize facestride = chunksize 3 # Face indices: 0=Z+, 1=Z-, 2=X+, 3=X-, 4=Y+, 5=Y- facedirs = Edge Cases: Unallocated Neighbor Chunks: If a neighbor chunk is not allocated, the face is rendered, assuming the neighbor is empty (index 0). Precision: Integer arithmetic is used for indices and lengths, avoiding floating-point errors. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the chunk, as each voxel is visited once and face combination is linear. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the voxel data and visit array, plus O(M) for the mesh output, where M is the number of visible faces. Performance: Reduces vertex count by combining coplanar faces, leading to fewer draw calls and better performance for large, uniform regions. Strengths: Efficient for voxel-based scenes, reduces overdraw, simple implementation. Limitations: Only works with discrete voxel data, may produce blocky meshes compared to smooth surface extraction methods. name: Greedy Meshing for Voxel Faces
head: Greedy Meshing for Voxels, Greedy Meshing with Face Attributes, Greedy meshing for complex voxel data, Quad merging, Voxel face greedy meshing, Voxel face merging
body: Greedy Meshing for Voxel Faces is a mesh simplification technique that reduces the number of triangles and draw calls in voxel rendering by merging adjacent coplanar voxel faces into larger rectangular quads. Unlike standard greedy meshing, which merges voxels based solely on existence or a single block type, this method compares voxel faces based on multiple attributes (such as material type, transparency, and lighting) to determine mergeability. It builds on Greedy Meshing by extending the 2D slice processing to handle face-level attributes, ensuring that only faces with identical attributes are merged. The algorithm processes a voxel chunk by iterating through six face directions (Top, Bottom, Left, Right, Front, Back). For each direction, it extracts a 2D cross-section of visible faces, generates a mask of mergeable regions, and creates quads for maximal rectangles of identical faces. Input: A 3D voxel grid voxels[CHUNKWIDTH][CHUNKHEIGHT][CHUNKDEPTH] where each voxel is a VoxelFace object. A VOXELSIZE scalar for world coordinate scaling. Output: A list of quads, each defined by four vertices (position, color/UV), and a list of triangle indices. VoxelFace: Encapsulates face attributes. transparent (boolean): If true, the face is culled and not rendered. type (int): The material or block type identifier. side (int): The face normal direction (0=SOUTH, 1=NORTH, 2=EAST, 3=WEST, 4=TOP, 5=BOTTOM). equals(VoxelFace other): Returns true if this.transparent == other.transparent and this.type == other.type. Note: Some implementations also require corner lighting to be identical to preserve ambient occlusion. Mask: A 1D array mask[CHUNKWIDTH CHUNKHEIGHT] (or 2D equivalent) storing VoxelFace references or null. It tracks which faces have been merged into existing quads. Working Arrays: x[3]: Current position in the chunk (x, y, z). q[3]: Direction vector for neighbor checks (one component is 1, others 0). du[3], dv[3]: Delta vectors for quad width and height. 1. Initialization: Initialize x = [0, 0, 0], q = [0, 0, 0], du = [0, 0, 0], dv = [0, 0, 0]. Create mask array of size CHUNKWIDTH CHUNKHEIGHT (for the 2D slice) initialized to null. Initialize empty vertex and triangle lists for the chunk. 2. Direction Loop: Iterate through six face directions. This is often implemented using a boolean toggle loop to handle back-face and front-face culling or orientation: python backFace = True b = False while b != backFace: # Process current direction #... backFace = backFace and b b = not b This loop runs twice, covering all six axes (3 dimensions × 2 directions). 3. Axis Processing: For each direction, iterate d from 0 to 2 (representing X, Y, Z axes). Calculate perpendicular axes: u = (d + 1) % 3, v = (d + 2) % 3. Set q[d] = 1 (direction of sweep) and q[u] = q[v] = 0. Determine the side constant based on d and backFace (e.g., if d=0 and backFace is true, side = WEST). Reset x[0] = x[1] = x[2] = 0. 4. Sweep and Mask Generation: Sweep along dimension d from x[d] = -1 to x[d] < CHUNKSIZE[d]. For each slice x[d]: Reset n = 0 (index into mask). Iterate x[v] from 0 to CHUNKSIZE[v]-1 and x[u] from 0 to CHUNKSIZE[u]-1. Get voxelFace at x (if x[d] >= 0) and voxelFace1 at neighbor x + q (if x[d] < CHUNKSIZE[d] - 1). If both faces exist and voxelFace.equals(voxelFace1) is true, set mask[n] = null (indicating these faces are merged/hidden). Otherwise, set mask[n] = voxelFace1 if backFace is true, else mask[n] = voxelFace. Increment n. Increment x[d]. 5. Quad Generation: Reset n = 0. Iterate j (corresponding to v) from 0 to CHUNKSIZE[v]-1 and i (corresponding to u) from 0 to CHUNKSIZE[u]-1. If mask[n] is not null: Calculate Width w: Start w = 1. While i + w < CHUNKSIZE[u] and mask[n + w] is not null and mask[n + w].equals(mask[n]), increment w. Calculate Height h: Start h = 1. Loop while j + h < CHUNKSIZE[v]: Loop k from 0 to w-1. Check if mask[n + k + h CHUNKSIZE[u]] is null or does not equal mask[n]. If so, set done = true and break inner loop. If done is true, break height loop. Create Quad: Set x[u] = i, x[v] = j. Set du[u] = w, du[v] = du[d] = 0. Set dv[v] = h, dv[u] = dv[d] = 0. If mask[n].transparent is false, generate vertices for the quad using x, du, dv, and VOXELSIZE. Vertices are typically: 1. x 2. x + du 3. x + du + dv 4. x + dv Add triangle indices (e.g., 0,1,2 and 0,2,3) to the triangle list, adding an offset if combining results from multiple directions. Zero Out Mask: Loop l from 0 to h-1 and k from 0 to w-1, set mask[n + k + l CHUNKSIZE[u]] = null to mark as processed. Increment i by w and n by w h (or appropriate stride) to skip processed region. 6. Combine Results: After processing all six directions, combine the vertex and triangle lists. Ensure triangle indices are offset by the cumulative vertex count from previous directions. VOXELSIZE: Size of a single voxel in world units. Default is 1. Used to scale vertex coordinates. CHUNKWIDTH, CHUNKHEIGHT, CHUNKDEPTH: Dimensions of the voxel chunk. Typically 16x16x16 or similar powers of two. Transparency: Transparent faces must be skipped during meshing to avoid rendering culled geometry. The algorithm checks mask[n].transparent before adding a quad. Lighting/AO: A face whose four corners have different lighting values must not be merged with neighbors to preserve correct ambient occlusion shading. This requires the equals method to compare corner lighting attributes. Boundary Conditions: If no adjacent chunk exists in a direction (e.g., UP, DOWN), the corresponding block array is created with size 0 to prevent null access. If no chunk exists above the top layer, the top face generation is skipped entirely. Index Offsets: Each directional job starts with an empty vertex list, so triangle indices within each job are relative to 0. When combining, an additional offset must be added to triangle indices to account for the accumulated vertex count from previous directions. Performance: This method requires more calculations per chunk on initial world build or when blocks are added/removed, making it expensive for dynamic updates. Extends this method by ensuring that adjacent voxel faces are merged into a single quad only if they share the same block type (e.g., material, texture) and orientation. Unlike standard greedy meshing, which merges all coplanar faces regardless of material, this method preserves visual distinctions between different block types (e.g., keeping grass and dirt transitions separate) while still maximizing quad size within homogeneous regions. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the chunk, as each voxel face is visited a constant number of times during the sweep and mask generation. However, the constant factor is higher than simple face culling due to the mask generation and quad expansion logic. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the mask array and vertex/triangle buffers. The mask array size is proportional to the surface area of the chunk in each direction. Measured Performance: On a flat chunk of ground, the number of quads is reduced from 2,048 to 2. This drastically reduces draw calls for large flat surfaces. Strengths: Significantly reduces vertex and triangle count for large flat surfaces, improving rendering performance by reducing draw calls. Allows for attribute-based merging (type, transparency, lighting). Limitations: More expensive calculation per chunk on initial world build or when the player removes/adds a block. Performance may not improve or may even slow down due to texture tiling in the shader and the cost of re-generating chunks for lightmap changes. When to Use: Ideal for static or semi-static voxel worlds with large flat areas. Not recommended for highly dynamic scenes with frequent block changes unless combined with incremental meshing techniques. Greedy Meshing for Voxel Faces was developed by Robert O'Leary, based on the work of Mikola Lysenko. It was implemented in the JMonkeyEngine and later adapted for other engines like 'mira' (in Rust) and Unity. The technique is a variation of the original greedy meshing algorithm described by Lysenko in 2012, extended to handle complex voxel data with multiple face attributes. It is widely used in voxel engines to optimize rendering performance by reducing the number of draw calls. roboleary/GreedyMesh, https://github.com/roboleary/GreedyMesh, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Voxel faces that lie side by side are joined into large quads, https://github.com/mcdearman/mira/pull/82, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) BloodyFish/UnityVoxelEngine, https://github.com/BloodyFish/UnityVoxelEngine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) How can I improve rendering speeds of a Voxel/Minecraft type game?, https://gamedev.stackexchange.com/questions/22664/how-can-i-improve-rendering-speeds-of-a-voxel-minecraft-type-game, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Greedy meshing for complex voxel data, https://hub.jmonkeyengine.org/t/greedy-meshing-for-complex-voxel-data/28017, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Greedy Meshing with Block Type Masking
head: Greedy meshing with multiple block types, Greedy meshing with orientation bits
body: Greedy Meshing with Block Type Masking extends Greedy Meshing for Voxel Faces by ensuring that adjacent voxel faces are merged into a single quad only if they share the same block type (e.g., material, texture) and orientation. Unlike standard greedy meshing, which merges all coplanar faces regardless of material, this method preserves visual distinctions between different block types (e.g., keeping grass and dirt transitions separate) while still maximizing quad size within homogeneous regions. Inputs: A voxel grid where each voxel has an associated block type identifier and orientation. Outputs: A set of quads, each associated with a specific block type and orientation. Data Structures: The core modification is to the mask array used in the greedy meshing algorithm. Instead of a boolean or simple integer indicating presence, the mask stores an integer encoding both block type and orientation. Mask Layout: An integer array where each element corresponds to a voxel position. Bit Packing: At least 1 bit is reserved for orientation. The remaining bits store the block type (color, material ID, etc.). Note: The exact number of bits for type depends on the maximum number of block types supported. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Mask: Create a mask array of the same dimensions as the voxel grid. For each voxel, compute an integer value by combining its orientation bit and block type bits. 2. Scan for Quads: Iterate through the voxel grid to find exposed faces. 3. Group by Type: When scanning for a greedy quad, compare the mask values of adjacent voxels. Only group voxels into a single quad if their mask values are identical (i.e., same type and orientation). 4. Mesh Generation: Perform the greedy meshing process separately for each unique block type/orientation combination. This effectively partitions the voxel surface into homogeneous regions and merges faces within each region. 5. Output: Generate quads for each merged region. Each quad retains the block type information for rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def greedymeshwithblocktypes(voxelgrid, blocktypes, orientations): """ voxelgrid: 3D array of booleans indicating voxel presence blocktypes: 3D array of integers representing block type IDs orientations: 3D array of integers representing orientation bits Returns: List of quads, each with position, size, type, and orientation """ # Step 1: Initialize mask with combined type and orientation # Mask value = (orientation << typebits) | blocktypeid # Assuming 1 bit for orientation and remaining bits for type typebits = 31 # Example: 31 bits for type, 1 bit for orientation mask = zeroslike(voxelgrid, dtype=int) for x, y, z in voxelgrid.nonzero(): mask[x, y, z] = (orientations[x, y, z] << typebits) | blocktypes[x, y, z] quads = [] visited = zeroslike(voxelgrid, dtype=bool) # Step 2 & 3: Scan and group by type for x, y, z in voxelgrid.nonzero(): if visited[x, y, z]: continue currentmask = mask[x, y, z] currenttype = currentmask & ((1 << typebits) - 1) currentorient = (currentmask >> typebits) & 1 # Find maximal quad of same type and orientation # This involves scanning in 2D plane perpendicular to face normal # For simplicity, assume we are processing a specific face direction # In practice, this loop iterates over all 6 face directions # Example: Processing top face (normal +Y) if isexposedtop(x, y, z, voxelgrid): # Find width and height of contiguous region with same mask width = 1 while x + width < gridwidth and not visited[x + width, y, z] and \ mask[x + width, y, z] == currentmask: width += 1 height = 1 while y + height < gridheight and not visited[x, y + height, z] and \ mask[x, y + height, z] == currentmask: height += 1 # Create quad quad = { 'position': (x, y, z), 'size': (width, height), 'type': currenttype, 'orientation': currentorient, 'normal': (0, 1, 0) # Example for top face } quads.append(quad) # Mark as visited for i in range(width): for j in range(height): visited[x + i, y + j, z] = True return quads Parameters: typebits: Number of bits allocated for block type. Must be sufficient to represent all unique block types. orientationbits: Number of bits for orientation. Minimum 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertex Splitting: If using a single draw call with a texture atlas, vertices shared by multiple block types must be split. Each copy of the vertex must have distinct texture coordinates pointing to the correct region in the atlas. Texture Wrapping: If using a flat 2D atlas, hardware sampling does not support wrapping for arbitrary atlas regions. The shader must manually handle texture wrapping using shader math. Degenerate Input: Ensure that block type IDs are consistent and that orientation bits are correctly aligned with the face normal being processed. A variant where each group of merged faces of the same block type is rendered as a separate sub-mesh. Each sub-mesh is assigned a distinct material corresponding to its block type and rendered in its own draw call. This approach simplifies texture coordinate management but increases draw call overhead. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels. The algorithm scans each voxel a constant number of times (once per face direction). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the mask and visited arrays. Performance: Reduces the number of triangles compared to raw voxel rendering by merging coplanar faces of the same type. However, it may result in more draw calls if using separate sub-meshes per type. Strengths: Preserves visual distinctions between block types while optimizing mesh size. Simple to implement by modifying the mask array. Limitations: Increased complexity in texture coordinate management if using a single draw call. Potential for more draw calls if using sub-meshes. When to Use: When rendering voxel worlds with multiple distinct block types (e.g., grass, dirt, stone) and visual fidelity between types is important. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and block types are not visually distinct, or when the overhead of multiple draw calls is unacceptable. This method was discussed in the context of optimizing voxel mesh rendering in Unity, specifically addressing how to handle different block types on an optimized voxel mesh. It builds on the principles of greedy meshing introduced in earlier works on voxel surface extraction. name: Integrating AO with Greedy Meshing
head: AO-aware Greedy Meshing, Greedy Meshing with AO-Aware Merge Rule, Greedy Meshing with Ambient Occlusion, Greedy Meshing with Baked Ambient Occlusion
body: Integrating Ambient Occlusion (AO) with Greedy Meshing resolves the conflict between merging coplanar voxel faces into large quads and the natural variation of occlusion values across individual block boundaries. Unlike standard greedy meshing which prioritizes minimal polygon count, this method enforces strict visual continuity of lighting by ensuring that the interpolated shading on a merged quad accurately represents the occlusion of every unit face it replaces. It achieves this through specific merge rules, compact data packing, or shader-based reconstruction strategies. Inputs: A 3D voxel grid with exposed faces. Per-vertex AO values for each unit face. Material type and facing direction for each face. Outputs: A mesh of merged quads where vertex attributes (AO, material, normal) are consistent across the entire quad surface. To minimize memory bandwidth during procedural mesh generation, AO data is packed efficiently: AO Storage: Since AO values are discrete (4 levels), each vertex AO requires only 2 bits. Quad Packing: All four vertices of a quad are stored in 8 bits (1 byte) total. Vertex Structure: This 1-byte AO value is packed alongside face normal indicators and texture IDs into a single 32-bit unsigned integer per vertex. 1. Define AO-Aware Merge Rule: Before baking vertex AO, define the rule that ensures the bilinear interpolation of AO across a merged quad equals the AO values of every unit face it replaces. 2. Evaluate Merge Criteria: For adjacent coplanar faces, check if they can be merged. A face is eligible for merging if it shares the same material type, has the same facing direction, and has an identical four-corner AO tuple. 3. Execute Merge (Restricted Strategy): If the criteria are met, merge the faces into a single quad. This "Restricted Merging" strategy preserves accurate vertex-based shading at the cost of a slightly higher polygon count compared to unrestricted merging. 4. Alternative: Texture Atlas Baking: If vertex-based merging is too restrictive, generate a low-resolution texture atlas containing pre-computed AO gradients. Apply UVs from the merged quad across the continuous surface to sample these gradients. 5. Alternative: Fragment-Shader Reconstruction: Pass unmerged face bounds as custom vertex attributes or instanced data. The fragment shader calculates edge proximity and distance-to-corner shading analytically, allowing geometry to remain unmerged while shading remains correct. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def canmergefaces(facea, faceb): """ Check if two adjacent faces can be merged based on AO consistency. Returns True if materials, directions, and AO tuples match. """ if facea.material != faceb.material: return False if facea.direction != faceb.direction: return False # Compare the 4-corner AO tuple (each value is 0-3) return facea.aotuple == faceb.aotuple def packvertex(normal: int, materialid: int, aovalues: tuple) -> int: """ Pack vertex data into a 32-bit unsigned integer. aovalues: tuple of 4 integers (0-3) representing per-vertex AO levels. """ # Pack 4 x 2-bit AO values into a single byte (8 bits) aobyte = (aovalues[0] << 6) | (aovalues[1] << 4) | (aovalues[2] << 2) | aovalues[3] # Pack into 32-bit integer: [normal(8)] [material(8)] [ao(8)] [padding(8)] packed = (normal << 24) | (materialid << 16) | aobyte return packed AO Levels: The source specifies four discrete levels per vertex. Precision: Using 2-bit storage for AO prevents precision issues associated with floating-point colors but limits shading granularity. Halo Bricks: When building volume meshes, a one-cell halo is used across brick seams for culling and AO calculation. A halo brick arrival makes the mesh stale, triggering a re-mesh to drop now-occluded seams. Visual Continuity: The primary pitfall is incorrect interpolation. If the merge rule is not defined before baking, the bilinear interpolation across the merged quad may not match the original unit face AO values, causing visual artifacts. Merges coplanar faces of the same block, face, state, and per-vertex AO into larger quads to reduce vertex count while preserving shading. A quad only grows along an axis where its per-vertex AO doesn't change, so the AO shading (and the AO-aware diagonal flip) looks exactly as it did with one quad per face. Damaged or burning blocks are excluded from merging. On real terrain this cuts solid vertices by about 35% around the castle, 30% on wooded plains, and 16% in mountains. Unlike standard greedy meshing that averages or discards AO, this method preserves exact per-vertex AO shading by restricting growth to constant-AO axes. Polygon Count: Restricted merging results in a slightly higher polygon count than standard greedy meshing because it prevents merging faces with different AO values. Memory Bandwidth: Packing AO into 2-bit fields within a 32-bit integer minimizes memory bandwidth during procedural mesh generation. Performance: The method is CPU-based for surface generation in the cited implementation, with no GPU involvement in the meshing step. Visual Quality: Ensures visual continuity of lighting across merged geometry, which is the primary advantage over standard greedy meshing. This method is part of the broader effort to optimize voxel rendering by reducing draw calls while maintaining visual fidelity. The specific implementation details regarding AO-aware merging and data packing are found in the spallmesh module and related discussions on baking dynamic ambient occlusion in procedural voxels. name: Greedy Meshing (Back Face)
head: BackGreedyMesh
body: Greedy Meshing (Back Face) is a specialized surface extraction method that generates quads for the back-facing surfaces (negative Z direction) of a voxel chunk. It extends the 2D greedy meshing algorithm to three dimensions by extracting 2D slices from the 3D voxel grid along the Z-axis and processing them to merge adjacent blocks of the same type into larger rectangles. It is distinct from general greedy meshing [3519-greedy-meshing.md] because it operates exclusively on the back-facing boundary, requiring specific handling of neighbor chunks to determine visibility at the chunk's rear edge. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: blockArray1D: A 1D NativeArray<byte> representing the voxel data of the current chunk. blockArray1Dback: A 1D NativeArray<byte> representing the voxel data of the neighbor chunk located behind the current chunk (in the negative Z direction). colors: A NativeArray<Color32> mapping block IDs to vertex colors. chunkWidth, chunkLength, chunkHeight: Integer dimensions of the chunk. blockSize: Float size of a single voxel. chunkToBack: Boolean flag indicating if the chunk has a back neighbor. Outputs: vertices: A NativeList<GreedyVertex> containing the generated quad vertices. triangles: A NativeList<int> containing the triangle indices. Data Structures The algorithm uses a temporary 1D array blocks of size chunkWidth chunkHeight to store the processed visibility state for the current Z-slice. The layout is row-major: blocks[x + (chunkWidth y)]. Algorithm Steps 1. Iterate Z-Slices: Loop z from 0 to chunkLength. If z == 0 and chunkToBack is false, skip this iteration (no back face to generate). 2. Initialize Slice Visibility: Create the temporary blocks array for the current z-slice. For each x in 0..chunkWidth-1 and y in 0..chunkHeight-1: Calculate the 1D index in the neighbor chunk: neighboridx = x + (chunkWidth (z - 1)) + (chunkWidth chunkLength y). If z > 0: Check if the neighbor voxel exists: if blockArray1Dback[neighboridx] > 0, set blocks[x + (chunkWidth y)] = 0 (occluded). Otherwise, copy the current chunk's block ID: blocks[x + (chunkWidth y)] = blockArray1D[x + (chunkWidth z) + (chunkWidth chunkLength y)]. If z == 0: Check the back neighbor at the end of the chunk: neighboridx = x + (chunkWidth (chunkLength - 1)) + (chunkWidth chunkLength y). If blockArray1Dback[neighboridx] > 0, set blocks[x + (chunkWidth y)] = 0. Otherwise, copy the current block ID. 3. Greedy Merge (2D): Iterate x from 0 to chunkWidth-1 and y from 0 to chunkHeight-1. Let blockID = blocks[x + (chunkWidth y)]. If blockID == 0, continue (already consumed or empty). Calculate Height: Initialize height = 0. While y + height < chunkHeight and blocks[x + (chunkWidth (y + height))] == blockID: Increment height. Calculate Width: Initialize width = 1. Initialize canExtend = true. While canExtend and x + width < chunkWidth: Check if the entire vertical strip at x + width matches blockID for all h in 0..height-1. Condition: blocks[(x + width) + (chunkWidth (y + h))] == blockID for all h. If mismatch, set canExtend = false. If match, increment width. Mark Consumed: For i in 0..width-1 and j in 0..height-1: Set blocks[(x + i) + (chunkWidth (y + j))] = 0. Generate Quad: Calculate center coordinates: xCenter = (x + width / 2.0f) blockSize yCenter = (y + height / 2.0f) blockSize zPos = z blockSize Calculate half-dimensions: halfWidth = (width blockSize) / 2.0f halfHeight = (height blockSize) / 2.0f Define vertices (back face, Z = zPos): v0 = (xCenter + halfWidth, yCenter - halfHeight, zPos) v1 = (xCenter + halfWidth, yCenter + halfHeight, zPos) v2 = (xCenter - halfWidth, yCenter + halfHeight, zPos) v3 = (xCenter - halfWidth, yCenter - halfHeight, zPos) Add vertices to vertices list. Let index be the current vertex count before adding these four. Add triangles to triangles list: (index + 0, index + 1, index + 2) (index + 2, index + 3, index + 0) Pseudocode Unverified code. 1)) + (chunkWidth chunkLength y) if blockArray1Dback[neighboridx] > 0: blocks[idx] = 0 else: currentidx = x + (chunkWidth z) + (chunkWidth chunkLength y) blocks[idx] = blockArray1D[currentidx] # 2D Greedy Meshing on the slice for y in range(chunkHeight): for x in range(chunkWidth): blockID = blocks[x + (chunkWidth y)] if blockID == 0: continue # Calculate Height height = 0 while y + height < chunkHeight and blocks[x + (chunkWidth (y + height))] == blockID: height += 1 # Calculate Width width = 1 canExtend = True while canExtend and x + width < chunkWidth: # Check if the entire column at x+width matches blockID for height match = True for h in range(height): if blocks[(x + width) + (chunkWidth (y + h))] != blockID: match = False break if match: width += 1 else: canExtend = False # Mark as consumed for i in range(width): for j in range(height): blocks[(x + i) + (chunkWidth (y + j))] = 0 # Generate Quad xCenter = (x + width / 2.0) blockSize yCenter = (y + height / 2.0) blockSize zPos = z blockSize halfWidth = (width blockSize) / 2.0 halfHeight = (height blockSize) / 2.0 v0 = (xCenter + halfWidth, yCenter - halfHeight, zPos) v1 = (xCenter + halfWidth, yCenter + halfHeight, zPos) v2 = (xCenter - halfWidth, yCenter + halfHeight, zPos) v3 = (xCenter - halfWidth, yCenter - halfHeight, zPos) vertices.append(v0) vertices.append(v1) vertices.append(v2) vertices.append(v3) index = len(vertices) - 4 triangles.append((index + 0, index + 1, index + 2)) triangles.append((index + 2, index + 3, index + 0)) return vertices, triangles Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Conditions: The algorithm relies on blockArray1Dback to determine visibility at the chunk's rear. If chunkToBack is false, the front-most slice (z=0) is skipped, but subsequent slices are processed normally. If blockArray1Dback is not provided or empty, visibility checks may fail or return incorrect occlusion states. Precision: Floating-point calculations for vertex centers and half-dimensions use standard float precision. For very large chunks, potential floating-point drift may occur, though blockSize is typically small. Degenerate Input: If blockArray1D contains only 0s, no vertices or triangles are generated. If chunkWidth or chunkHeight is 0, the loops do not execute. Generates quads for the back-facing surfaces. Chosen when only the rear boundary of a chunk needs to be meshed, often as part of a multi-pass system. Link: Greedy Meshing (Back Face). Generates quads for the front-facing surfaces. Complements the back face method. Link: Greedy Meshing (Front Face). Generates quads for the left, right, top, and bottom faces. Link: Greedy Meshing (Side Faces). Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot L), where W, H, L are chunk dimensions. Each voxel is visited a constant number of times during the slice initialization and greedy merge steps. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the temporary blocks array per slice. The output size depends on the number of merged quads. Performance: Measured performance depends on the density of visible blocks. High occlusion (many 0s) reduces the number of quads generated. The algorithm is efficient for sparse voxel grids. Strengths: Reduces triangle count by merging adjacent quads. Simple to implement. Limitations: Only handles back-facing surfaces. Requires neighbor chunk data for accurate boundary culling. Not suitable for generating the entire mesh in a single pass. Greedy Meshing (Back Face) is part of a broader family of greedy meshing algorithms used in voxel engines. It was implemented in the UnityVoxelEngine project by BloodyFish. The method extends the 2D greedy meshing concept to 3D by processing slices along the Z-axis, specifically targeting the back-facing boundary. It is often used in conjunction with other face-specific greedy meshing methods to generate the complete mesh for a voxel chunk. name: Block Subdivision
body: Block subdivision partitions a volumetric particle set into disjoint spatial blocks to enable sequential, memory-bounded surface extraction while maintaining a seamless global result. It differs from global hashing approaches by limiting the active memory footprint to a single block's cache, reducing overhead to approximately 12% for typical configurations, and enabling independent multi-threaded rendering of each block. Inputs: List of particles, each with position and radius of influence Rc. Block dimensions in cubes: W \times H \times D. Cube size: S. Isosurface threshold: T. Margin width in cubes: M (determined by Rc and S). Outputs: Vertex and index buffers for the isosurface mesh. Data Structures: Block List: A collection of disjoint blocks covering the volume. Particle Cache: For each block, a list of particles within distance Rc of the block boundary, plus all particles inside the block. This cache accelerates field value calculations. Parameters: Rc: Radius of influence of a particle. Determines the margin size and particle inclusion range. S: Size of a cube (voxel edge length). T: Threshold value for surface generation. M: Margin width in cubes. Calculated such that the physical margin covers distance Rc. Steps: 1. Partition Volume: Divide the global volume containing particles into a grid of disjoint blocks. 2. Build Particle Lists: For each block, identify all particles located within the block. Additionally, identify all particles located outside the block but within a distance Rc from the block's boundary. Insert these external particles into the block's particle list to ensure field consistency at the boundaries. 3. Expand Geometry: Conceptually expand the block's processing volume by a margin of M cubes in all directions. This expanded volume encloses the region where particles from the margin might influence the interior field values. 4. Process Blocks Sequentially: Iterate through each block in the list: a. Initialize Cache: Load the block's particle list into a lookup cache. b. Marching Slices: Execute the marching slices algorithm over the expanded volume (original block + margin). c. Field Calculation: For each cube in the expanded volume, calculate the field value f(r) based on nearby particles in the cache. The field function is defined as: f(r) = \begin{cases} (r/\sqrt{2}Rc)^4 - (r/\sqrt{2}Rc)^2 + 0.25 & \text{if } r < Rc \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where r is the distance from the sample point to the particle. d. Boundary Instrumentation: To guarantee the marching slices algorithm can traverse the closed isosurface, force field values to zero at sample points on the outer boundary of the margin. This is achieved by instrumenting the lookup cache to exclude particles when sampling points lie exactly on the margin boundary. e. Mesh Generation: Generate vertices and indices for cubes where the isosurface intersects. Do not output mesh triangles for cubes located in the margin region. f. Buffer Output: Write the generated vertices and indices to the user-specified buffers. 5. Repeat: Continue until all blocks are processed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def blocksubdivision(particles, blockdims, cubesize, threshold, radiusinfluence): """ particles: List of dicts with 'pos' (x,y,z). blockdims: Tuple (W, H, D) in number of cubes. cubesize: Float S. threshold: Float T. radiusinfluence: Float Rc. """ # Margin width in cubes to enclose Rc margincubes = math.ceil(radiusinfluence / cubesize) # Step 1: Partition volume into disjoint blocks # Generate grid coordinates for blocks blocks = [] for bx in range(blockdims[0]): for by in range(blockdims[1]): for bz in range(blockdims[2]): blocks.append({'min': [bxcubesize, bycubesize, bzcubesize], 'max': [(bx+1)cubesize, (by+1)cubesize, (bz+1)cubesize]}) allvertices = [] allindices = [] for block in blocks: # Step 2: Build particle list for this block blockparticles = [] for p in particles: # Check if inside block or within Rc of boundary dx = max(block['min'][0] - p['pos'][0], 0, p['pos'][0] - block['max'][0]) dy = max(block['min'][1] - p['pos'][1], 0, p['pos'][1] - block['max'][1]) dz = max(block['min'][2] - p['pos'][2], 0, p['pos'][2] - block['max'][2]) dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if dist <= radiusinfluence: blockparticles.append(p) # Step 3: Expand geometry by margin margindist = margincubes cubesize expandedmin = [block['min'][i] - margindist for i in range(3)] expandedmax = [block['max'][i] + margindist for i in range(3)] # Step 4: Process block sequentially # Iterate over cubes in expanded volume for cx in range(math.floor(expandedmin[0]/cubesize), math.ceil(expandedmax[0]/cubesize)): for cy in range(math.floor(expandedmin[1]/cubesize), math.ceil(expandedmax[1]/cubesize)): for cz in range(math.floor(expandedmin[2]/cubesize), math.ceil(expandedmax[2]/cubesize)): cubemin = [cxcubesize, cycubesize, czcubesize] cubemax = [(cx+1)cubesize, (cy+1)cubesize, (cz+1)cubesize] # Determine if cube is in the margin region ismargin = (cx < 0 or cx >= blockdims[0] or cy < 0 or cy >= blockdims[1] or cz < 0 or cz >= blockdims[2]) # Step 4c: Field Calculation fieldvalues = [] for corneridx in range(8): corner = [cubemin[i] + ((corneridx >> i) & 1) cubesize for i in range(3)] # Step 4d: Boundary Instrumentation if (abs(corner[0] - expandedmin[0]) < 1e-6 or abs(corner[0] - expandedmax[0]) < 1e-6 or abs(corner[1] - expandedmin[1]) < 1e-6 or abs(corner[1] - expandedmax[1]) < 1e-6 or abs(corner[2] - expandedmin[2]) < 1e-6 or abs(corner[2] - expandedmax[2]) < 1e-6): fieldval = 0.0 else: fieldval = 0.0 for p in blockparticles: r = math.sqrt((corner[0]-p['pos'][0])2 + (corner[1]-p['pos'][1])2 + (corner[2]-p['pos'][2])2) if r < radiusinfluence: normr = r / (math.sqrt(2) radiusinfluence) fieldval += (normr4 - normr2 + 0.25) fieldvalues.append(fieldval) # Step 4e: Mesh Generation if not ismargin: # Step 4b: Marching Slices logic # Marching slices traversal and polygonization per # mesh = marchingslicescube(fieldvalues, threshold, cubemin, cubesize) # allvertices.extend(mesh.vertices) # allindices.extend(mesh.indices) pass # Margin cubes: only sign check needed for traversal, no output # Step 4f: Buffer Output # In practice, buffers are written per block or accumulated pass return allvertices, allindices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Closed Isosurface Assumption: The marching slices algorithm assumes a closed surface. If particles in the margin are not handled correctly, traversal may fail. Forcing field values to zero at the outer margin boundary resolves this. Seams: Varying cube size S between blocks for Level of Detail (LOD) control can cause visible seams. Care must be taken to ensure compatibility at block boundaries. An algorithm that uses a stack to iteratively subdivide a cuboid volume based on the number of divisible sides (D) to identify empty space and polygonize surfaces, avoiding recursion. It pushes the entire volume as a cuboid onto a stack, then iteratively pops cuboids. If a cuboid and its neighbours are empty, it is discarded. If D equals 0, the cuboid is polygonized. If (D | (1 << s)) >> (s - 1) is true, side s of the cuboid is divided. If the new length of side s equals 1, D is updated: D ← D | (7 - (1 << s)). The side index s cycles through 0, 1, 2 via s ← (s + 1) % 3. Both new cuboids are pushed onto the stack. If the condition is false, s is updated and the original cuboid is pushed back. D represents the divisible sides of a cuboid, calculated based on X, Y, Z dimensions. Time Complexity: The overhead of blocking is approximately 12% of total work for randomly distributed particles in a typical 100x100x100 block with a 5-cube margin. This is significantly lower than hashing approaches, which require hashing for both corner retrieval and particle lookups. Memory Complexity: Memory footprint is limited to a single block's particle cache and corner values, making it suitable for large volumes that do not fit in memory. Performance: For a 100x100x100 block with a 5-cube margin, 25% of the cubes in the expanded 110x110x110 volume are margin cubes. Traversing margin cubes costs approximately half that of normal cubes since only the sign of the field is needed and no vertices are generated. Strengths: Low memory usage. Enables multi-threaded rendering (one thread per block). Efficient for static scenes: blocks with no moving particles can be redrawn by re-outputting old buffers without polygonization. Supports visibility culling and LOD control. Limitations: Requires sequential processing of blocks if memory is strictly limited, though parallelization is possible across blocks. Margin overhead increases with larger Rc relative to block size. When to use: Surface modeling with moving particles, large unbounded volumes, hardware with limited memory per thread/buffer, or when visibility culling is beneficial. When not to use: When global hashing is more efficient for the specific particle distribution, or when strict real-time constraints prevent the overhead of block management (though the overhead is small). Block subdivision was introduced in the context of real-time particle isosurface extraction. It addresses the challenge of rendering large volumes of particles without exceeding memory limits, by partitioning the problem into manageable, independent chunks. The method builds upon the marching slices algorithm, which processes the volume slice by slice to further reduce memory usage. name: VoxelMesherBlocky
head: Blocky mesher, Minecraft-like mesher
body: VoxelMesherBlocky is a surface extraction method for blocky, voxel-based terrains that generates meshes by combining small geometric primitives corresponding to specific model IDs into larger chunks. It solves the problem of rendering large voxel worlds efficiently by culling faces that occlude each other, thereby reducing draw calls and vertex count without performing greedy meshing. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on a predefined library of block models and its chunk-based assembly approach, similar to the technique used in Minecraft. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Voxel data stored in VoxelBuffer.CHANNELTYPE. Input: A VoxelBlockyLibraryBase resource containing a list of models (e.g., grass, dirt, wood) where the list index corresponds to the model ID. Output: A chunked mesh where faces occluding each other are culled. Data Structures: VoxelBlockyLibraryBase: A resource holding a list of models. The index in this list serves as the unique ID for the model. VoxelBuffer: Stores the voxel data, specifically using the CHANNELTYPE channel. Steps: 1. Library Initialization: Create or load a VoxelBlockyLibraryBase resource. This library contains the geometric definitions for all block types (e.g., grass, dirt, wood, leaves, water, shrubs, stairs, door parts). 2. Voxel Data Access: Read the voxel data from the VoxelBuffer using the CHANNELTYPE channel. 3. Model Identification: For each voxel or group of voxels, identify the corresponding model ID based on the data in the buffer. The index in the library list corresponds to this ID. 4. Mesh Combination: Combine small meshes corresponding to these model IDs into chunks. This involves assembling the geometric primitives defined in the library for the active models. 5. Face Culling: Cull faces that occlude each other within the chunks. This reduces the number of visible faces but does not merge adjacent faces into larger quads (greedy meshing). Parameters: Library: VoxelBlockyLibraryBase instance. Data Channel: VoxelBuffer.CHANNELTYPE. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method does not perform greedy meshing, so adjacent identical faces are not merged into larger polygons, potentially leading to higher vertex counts compared to greedy methods. The library must be properly initialized with all required models before meshing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. library = VoxelBlockyLibraryBase() library.addmodel(grass) library.addmodel(dirt) library.addmodel(wood) voxelbuffer = getvoxelbuffer() voxeldata = voxelbuffer.getchannel(VoxelBuffer.CHANNELTYPE) chunks = [] for chunk in voxelchunks: chunkmesh = Mesh() for voxel in chunk.voxels: modelid = voxeldata.getid(voxel.position) if modelid is not None: model = library.getmodel(modelid) # Add model geometry to chunk mesh chunkmesh.addgeometry(model.geometry) # Cull occluding faces within the chunk chunkmesh.cullfaces() chunks.append(chunkmesh) return chunks This variant involves a baking process for the voxel mesher. It likely pre-processes or optimizes the mesh generation for static or semi-static voxel data. Specific details on the baking algorithm or optimizations are not provided in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficiently reduces draw calls by culling occluding faces; simple to implement with a predefined library of models. Limitations: Does not perform greedy meshing, which may result in higher vertex counts compared to methods that merge adjacent faces. When to Use: Suitable for blocky, Minecraft-like terrains where a library of predefined block models is available and greedy meshing is not required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for terrains requiring greedy meshing or where memory efficiency is critical due to higher vertex counts. VoxelMesherBlocky is part of the Voxel Tools documentation, focusing on blocky terrains similar to those found in Minecraft. It is designed to work with VoxelBuffer.CHANNELTYPE for voxel data storage and utilizes a VoxelBlockyLibraryBase for model definitions. name: Rendering and Post-Processing
body: Rendering and Post-Processing handles the visual presentation of blocky voxel meshes generated by Blocky meshing, addressing transparency artifacts and geometric jaggedness. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Greedy face merging by operating on pre-generated geometry to optimize rendering order or refine surface topology, rather than modifying the initial mesh extraction topology. Sorts transparent chunk meshes back-to-front relative to the camera's dominant viewing axis to enable correct alpha blending without global depth sorting. Choose this for transparent voxel environments where performance is critical and full depth sorting is too expensive. Refines blocky meshes using surface diffuse flow smoothing and Catmull-Clark tessellation to approximate smooth surfaces. Choose this when visual fidelity is prioritized over the raw voxel aesthetic. Extends grid content to a flat area fitting the camera's view, typically used with displacement textures like Phoenix FD Ocean Texture. The ocean surface generates only when liquid touches the sides and bottom of the grid, which act as a container. Mesh detail depends on camera resolution: one or several polygons per pixel are generated based on the Ocean Subdivisions option. The techniques originate from fluid simulation post-processing in 3ds Max plugins (Phoenix FD). Other methods in this family, such as chunk sorting and subdivision surface adaptation, originate from real-time rendering engines for voxel-based games. Not given in the sources. FireSmoke Rendering - Phoenix for 3ds Max, https://documentation.chaos.com/space/PHX4MAX/124396558, fetched 2026-10-27 def generateblockmeshalphaindices(blockspos, camerapos, viewvector, reverseddirection): """ Generates draw indices for transparent block meshes. blockspos: dict or nested list structure indexed by axis direction (0,1,2). camerapos: tuple (cx, cy, cz) viewvector: tuple (vx, vy, vz) reverseddirection: bool, True if traversal should start from back """ absvx = abs(viewvector[0]) absvy = abs(viewvector[1]) absvz = abs(viewvector[2]) if absvx >= absvy and absvx >= absvz: greatestdir = 0 greatestmag = viewvector[0] elif absvy >= absvx and absvy >= absvz: greatestdir = 1 greatestmag = viewvector[1] else: greatestdir = 2 greatestmag = viewvector[2] shouldreverselist = greatestmag < 0 indices = [] axismap = ['X', 'Y', 'Z'] currentblocks = blockspos[axismap[greatestdir]] axes = [0, 1, 2] secondaryaxis = (greatestdir + 1) % 3 tertiaryaxis = (greatestdir + 2) % 3 otherpos = [camerapos[secondaryaxis], camerapos[tertiaryaxis]] for i in range(len(currentblocks)): blocki = currentblocks[i] for j in range(len(blocki)): blockij = blocki[j] for k in range(len(blockij)): blockijk = blockij[k] if blockijk[0] >= otherpos[1]: break indices.extend(blockijk[1]) for k in range(len(blockij) - 1, -1, -1): blockijk = blockij[k] if blockijk[0] < otherpos[1]: break indices.extend(blockijk[1]) for j in range(len(blocki) - 1, -1, -1): blockij = blocki[j] for k in range(len(blockij)): blockijk = blockij[k] if blockijk[0] >= otherpos[1]: break indices.extend(blockijk[1]) for k in range(len(blockij) - 1, -1, -1): blockijk = blockij[k] if blockijk[0] < otherpos[1]: break indices.extend(blockijk[1]) if shouldreverselist: # Sources do not specify internal list reversal mechanics. pass return indices def renderblockmeshalpha(gl, chunkmeshes, camerapos, viewvector, fogfar): """ Renders the scene using Block Mesh Alpha Rendering. """ chunkdistances = {} for chunkid, chunk in chunkmeshes.items(): cx = chunk.pos[0] 32 + 16 cy = chunk.pos[1] 32 + 16 cz = chunk.pos[2] 32 + 16 dist = abs(cx - camerapos[0] + 16) + abs(cy - camerapos[1] + 16) + abs(cz - camerapos[2] + 16) chunkdistances[chunkid] = dist sortedchunks = sorted(chunkmeshes.items(), key=lambda item: chunkdistances[item[0]], reverse=True) gl.blendFuncSeparate(gl.SRCALPHA, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA, gl.ONE, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) for chunkid, chunk in sortedchunks: indices = generateblockmeshalphaindices(chunk.blockspos, camerapos, viewvector, False) gl.bindVertexArray(chunk.vao) gl.bindBuffer(gl.ELEMENTARRAYBUFFER, chunk.indexbuffer) gl.drawElements(gl.TRIANGLES, len(indices), gl.UNSIGNEDINT, 0) def fragmentshadershading(vertex1): """ Calculates shading value from packed vertex data. vertex1: 32-bit unsigned integer """ shadedata = (vertex1 >> 20) 0.2 + 0.4 return shadedata def fragmentshaderfog(distance, fogfar): """ Calculates fog amount. distance: float, length of camera-space position vector fogfar: float, 256.0 """ edge0 = fogfar - 64.0 edge1 = fogfar t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (distance - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) fogamount = t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) return fogamount def qualityenhance(mesh, mode='general'): """ Applies smoothing and tessellation to a mesh. mode: 'general' for standard meshes, 'cloud' for cloud layers. """ if mode == 'general': mesh = applysmoothing(mesh) mesh = tessellatewithdisplacement(mesh) elif mode == 'cloud': tessellatedquad = dividequadinto9segments(mesh.quad) for vertex in tessellatedquad.outervertices: vertex.alpha = 0.0 for vertex in tessellatedquad.innervertices: vertex.alpha = 1.0 rendercloud(tessellatedquad) return mesh def applysmoothing(mesh): """ Applies discrete Laplace smoothing using surface diffuse flow. Pi^{new} = Pi^{old} + lambda sum{j in N(i)} (Pj - Pi) """ lambdafactor = 0.5 # Mesh Smooth parameter newvertices = [] for vertex in mesh.vertices: neighbors = mesh.getneighbors(vertex) displacement = sum((mesh.vertices[n].pos - vertex.pos) for n in neighbors) newpos = vertex.pos + lambdafactor displacement newvertices.append(Vertex(newpos, vertex.tangent)) mesh.vertices = newvertices return mesh def tessellatewithdisplacement(mesh): # Sources do not provide explicit tessellation shader code; uses bicubic patches and displacement maps. pass def dividequadinto9segments(quad): # Standard 3x3 grid subdivision logic. pass def rendercloud(quad): # Rasterization with SRCALPHA and ONEMINUSSRCALPHA blending. pass

name: Block Mesh Alpha Rendering
head: ChunkMesh Alpha Rendering, Transparent Face Sorting & Rendering
body: Block Mesh Alpha Rendering is a rendering technique for voxel-based environments that uses a custom index ordering algorithm to sort visible faces back-to-front relative to the camera's primary viewing axis, enabling correct alpha blending without full scene depth sorting. It sorts transparent chunk meshes by distance to the camera and renders them with blending enabled to handle transparency correctly. Unlike general-purpose transparent rendering which requires global depth sorting, this method exploits the grid structure of voxel chunks to determine a valid draw order efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of voxel chunks (typically 32 \times 32 \times 32), camera position (Cx, Cy, Cz), camera view vector (vx, vy, vz), and a collection of transparent chunk meshes. Output: A rasterized image with correctly blended transparent surfaces. Data Structures: Vertex Packing: Each vertex is stored as two 32-bit unsigned integers (vertex0, vertex1). vertex0: Bits 0-9: x position (10 bits) Bits 10-19: y position (10 bits) Bits 20-31: z position (12 bits) vertex1: Bits 0-9: Texture layer (10 bits) Bits 10-14: Texture coordinate x (5 bits) Bits 15-19: Texture coordinate y (5 bits) Bits 20-31: Shade data (12 bits) Block Position Index (blocksPos): A nested array structure used to track visible transparent blocks for index generation. The structure follows blocksPos[greatestDir][secondary][tertiary], where each leaf node contains [coordinate, [indices]] and blocksPos[greatestDir][secondary][tertiary][1] holds the list of vertex indices for that block. Parameters: Chunk Size: 32 units. Fog Far Distance: 256 units (32 \times 8). Camera Matrix Scale: 0.0625 (1/16) to convert world units to chunk units. Alpha Discard Threshold: 0.4. Fragments with alpha < 0.4 are discarded to prevent artifacts from effectively invisible surfaces. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Primary Axis: Calculate the absolute values of the camera's view vector components (vx, vy, vz). Identify greatestDir as the axis (X, Y, or Z) with the largest absolute component. 2. Determine Traversal Direction: Calculate greatestMag as the signed magnitude of the view vector component along greatestDir. If greatestMag is negative, reverse the list of blocks along the greatestDir axis to ensure traversal starts from the back relative to the camera view. 3. Calculate Chunk Distances: For all chunks, compute the Manhattan distance from the camera to the chunk center. The distance is calculated as chunkDist = |chunk.x 32 - Cx + 16| + |chunk.y 32 - Cy + 16| + |chunk.z 32 - Cz + 16|. Sort the chunks in descending order of chunkDist (far to near). 4. Generate Indices for Transparent Meshes: For each shader's transparent chunk meshes, perform the following nested iteration to build the index buffer: Let blocksPos be the index structure for the current shader. Iterate through the blocksPos array along the greatestDir axis. For each block at index i along greatestDir: Iterate through the secondary axis blocks (index j) using a rectilinear distance check against the camera's position on the other two axes (otherPos). Forward Tertiary Iteration: Iterate through tertiary axis blocks (index k) from start to end. If the block's coordinate is \ge the camera's coordinate on the tertiary axis, break the loop. Add all indices from blocksPos[i][j][k][1] to the output index list. Reverse Tertiary Iteration: Iterate through tertiary axis blocks (index k) from end to start. If the block's coordinate is < the camera's coordinate on the tertiary axis, break the loop. Add all indices from blocksPos[i][j][k][1] to the output index list. Secondary Axis Reverse: After processing all tertiary blocks for the forward secondary iteration, iterate through secondary axis blocks (index j) in reverse order. Forward Tertiary (Reverse Secondary): For each secondary block in reverse, iterate through tertiary axis blocks (index k) from start to end. Apply the same coordinate comparison logic against otherPos. Add indices if valid. Reverse Tertiary (Reverse Secondary): Iterate through tertiary axis blocks (index k) from end to start. Apply the same coordinate comparison logic. Add indices if valid. If the traversal direction was reversed in Step 2, reverse the blocksPos list back to its original order. 5. Render: Bind the generated index buffer. Set blend function: gl.blendFuncSeparate(gl.SRCALPHA, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA, gl.ONE, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA). Draw the triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. 1, -1, -1): blockijk = blockij[k] if blockijk[0] < otherpos[1]: break indices.extend(blockijk[1]) # Reverse Secondary Axis Iteration for j in range(len(blocki) - 1, -1, -1): blockij = blocki[j] # Rectilinear check against camera position on secondary axis if blockij[0] >= otherpos[0]: break # Forward Tertiary (for reverse secondary) for k in range(len(blockij)): blockijk = blockij[k] if blockijk[0] >= otherpos[1]: break indices.extend(blockijk[1]) # Reverse Tertiary (for reverse secondary) for k in range(len(blockij) - Sort Chunks Far to Near sortedchunks = sorted(chunkmeshes.items(), key=lambda item: chunkdistances[item[0]], reverse=True) # 3. Set Blend Function # gl.blendFuncSeparate(gl.SRCALPHA, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA, gl.ONE, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) # 4. This prevents rendering artifacts from semi-transparent surfaces that are effectively invisible. Index Structure Assumption: The index generation algorithm assumes a specific nested array structure for blocksPos: blocksPos[greatestDir][secondary][tertiary][1] contains the list of indices for each block. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: This method is optimized for voxel-based environments with frequent updates (block placing/destroying). It avoids the high cost of global depth sorting by leveraging the grid structure. Strengths: Efficient handling of transparency in voxel worlds; supports dynamic updates; reduces overdraw by sorting chunks. Limitations: Limited to voxel/chunk-based geometry; sorting is approximate (based on chunk distance and axis-aligned traversal), which may cause minor blending artifacts at chunk boundaries if not handled carefully.
